name: Use of disciplinary record in future proceedings
description: The record of this disciplinary proceeding, including the Final Order, shall be considered (1) when addressing any further complaint or evidence of the same or similar misconduct brought to the Office's attention, and/or (2) in any future disciplinary proceeding (a) as an aggravating factor in determining discipline and/or (b) to rebut any statement or representation by or on Respondent's behalf.
guidance: The Final Order is to be treated as precedent/consideration material in future matters involving the same practitioner and may aggravate or rebut claims in later proceedings.

name: Written description requirement (separate from enablement)
description: 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and the first paragraph of pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112 require that the “specification shall contain a written description of the invention ....” This requirement is separate and distinct from the enablement requirement.
guidance: Purpose: to convey that the inventor possessed the claimed subject matter and to inform the public what is claimed. Citations: Ariad (en banc), Vas‑Cath, Univ. of Rochester v. G.D. Searle, Capon v. Eshhar. Rejections must be based on substantive law even though Guidelines assist examiners.

name: Sufficiency of detail to show possession
description: The specification must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail that one skilled in the art can reasonably conclude that the inventor had possession of the claimed invention.
guidance: Possession alone does not cure lack of written description. This is a fact‑based inquiry varying with the nature of the invention (Enzo Biochem, Moba, Vas‑Cath).

name: Means of showing possession (words/structures/figures/formulas)
description: An applicant shows that the inventor was in possession by describing the claimed invention with all of its limitations using such descriptive means as words, structures, figures, diagrams, and formulas that fully set forth the claimed invention.
guidance: Examples: structural chemical formulas, drawings, descriptive words. Lockwood; possession may be shown by actual reduction to practice or by showing the invention was 'ready for patenting'.

name: Original specification and originally‑filed claims as potential description
description: A satisfactory description may be found in originally‑filed claims or any other portion of the originally‑filed specification; however, not all originally‑filed claims necessarily have adequate written support in the specification.
guidance: Examiner must examine the specification and drawings to assess support for claims (In re Koller, In re Gardner, In re Wertheim).

name: Fact‑based, case‑by‑case inquiry
description: Compliance with the written description requirement is essentially a fact‑based inquiry that will 'necessarily vary depending on the nature of the invention claimed.'
guidance: Considerations include nature of the invention, amount of knowledge imparted to skilled artisans, and whether the specification reasonably conveys possession (Enzo Biochem, Vas‑Cath).

name: Presumption of adequacy for original claims but examiner's initial burden
description: There is a presumption that an adequate written description of the claimed invention is present when the application is filed; however, the PTO (examiner) has the initial burden of presenting evidence or reasons why persons skilled in the art would not recognize in the disclosure a description of the invention defined by the claims.
guidance: To make a prima facie case, the examiner must identify claim limitations not adequately supported and explain why (In re Wertheim).

name: Claim as a whole analysis
description: For each claim, determine what the claim as a whole covers; claim construction is essential and each claim must be separately analyzed and given its broadest reasonable interpretation in light of and consistent with the written description.
guidance: Include preamble language and the transitional phrase; consider the import of preamble and transitional terms such as 'comprising', 'consisting essentially of', 'consisting of' (In re Katz; Genentech v. Chiron; PPG).

name: Evaluate sufficiency of structures, acts, or functions recited
description: The examiner should evaluate each claim to determine if sufficient structures, acts, or functions are recited to make clear the scope and meaning of the claim, including the weight to be given the preamble.
guidance: Absence of definitions or details for well‑established terms should not be the basis for a written description rejection; determine whether limitations are structural or functional in context (Bell Communications Research; Corning Glass).

name: Combination claims require description of the combination (not just elements)
description: A claim drawn to a particular combination of elements may be unsupported even if the specification lists each element separately, where there is inadequate description of the particular combination.
guidance: Examiner must clearly and specifically explain why the specification does not support the claimed combination (Hyatt v. Dudas; Stored Value Solutions example). Burden then shifts to applicant to point out support or amend.

name: Genus/species disclosure limits — laundry list problem
description: A 'laundry list' disclosure of every possible moiety does not necessarily constitute a written description of every species in a genus because it would not 'reasonably lead' those skilled in the art to any particular species.
guidance: Genus disclosure may not support claims to a subgenus or specific species without adequate particularity (Fujikawa; In re Ruschig; In re Lukach; Purdue Pharma v. Faulding).

name: Claims that encompass unstated structures/elements may lack support
description: A claim may read on additional structures (e.g., promoters, coding regions) beyond a disclosed sequence; although a sequence may be disclosed, there may be insufficient description of other structures embraced by the claim.
guidance: Example given: 'A gene comprising SEQ ID NO:1.' Consider whether other structures are adequately described; see MPEP § 2106 for subject matter eligibility guidance.

name: New or amended claims must be supported by original disclosure (no new matter)
description: New or amended claims which introduce elements or limitations that are not supported by the as‑filed disclosure violate the written description requirement and the proscription against new matter (35 U.S.C. 132 and 251).
guidance: Support may be express, implicit, or inherent. Applicant may amend spec to include originally claimed material. See In re Rasmussen, In re Benno, In re Smith. Examiner should require applicant to point to support; a simple statement may suffice in some cases (MPEP refs).

name: Omission of an essential limitation raises written description issue
description: Omission of a limitation can raise an issue whether the inventor had possession of a broader, more generic invention; a claim that omits matter disclosed to be essential may not comply with the written description requirement.
guidance: Examples: PIN/NIP v. Platte Chem., Gentry Gallery v. Berkline, Johnson Worldwide v. Zebco, Tronzo v. Biomet. If spec states a feature is 'the only possible location' or 'essential', omitting it in claim can be fatal.

name: Written description sufficiency may overlap with enablement/indefiniteness issues
description: A claim which omits matter disclosed to be essential may also be subject to rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) as not enabling or under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) as indefinite; written description, enablement, and definiteness can be related.
guidance: Cited cases: In re Mayhew; In re Venezia; In re Collier. See MPEP § 2172.01 for related guidance.

name: Examiner prima facie methodology
description: To make a prima facie case of lack of written description, the examiner must identify the claim limitations that are not adequately supported, and explain why the claim is not fully supported by the disclosure.
guidance: Provide clear and specific explanation (Hyatt v. Dudas example). For amended/new claims, indicate that applicant should point to where support exists or the examiner will explain why disclosure does not convey possession. Burden shifts to applicant after prima facie showing.

name: Applicant response burden for new/amended claims
description: With respect to newly added or amended claims, applicant should show support in the original disclosure for the new or amended claims; if applicant points out where support exists and the examiner still finds lack of possession, the examiner has the initial burden of presenting reasoning as to why persons skilled in the art would not recognize the support.
guidance: MPEP references (2163.04, 2163.06, 714.02). A 'simple statement' may suffice in some contexts; otherwise examiner should explain deficiencies.

name: Broadest reasonable interpretation of claims in view of specification
description: Each claim must be given its broadest reasonable interpretation in light of and consistent with the written description.
guidance: Claim construction affects written description analysis; consider transitional phrases and claim language import. Cases: In re Katz; In re Morris; Corning; Genentech; PPG.

name: Importance of level of skill and predictability in the art
description: Written description issues depend on the knowledge and level of skill in the art and whether those skilled in the art would have been permitted to immediately envisage the claimed product arising from the disclosure.
guidance: Where the art is unpredictable, broader or genus claims may require more detailed disclosure. See Fujikawa, Purdue Pharma examples.

name: Commitments and Contingencies Disclosure
description: USPTO is party to routine administrative proceedings and legal actions; management discloses reasonably possible or probable amounts for claims and litigation.
guidance: Disclose amounts that are reasonably possible or probable and provide context (e.g., expected payments for labor relations claims, suits where adverse outcome probable). Note whether any payments were made from the Judgment Fund and whether there are major long-term commitments.

name: Patentability requirements for design (industrial design) patents
description: A design patent is granted for artistic and design solutions determining the appearance of an article; the claimed design must be novel and original.
guidance: Significant features determining aesthetic and/or ergonomic characteristics (form, configuration, decoration, colour pattern) must be new worldwide before the priority date (absolute novelty). Originality = significant features caused by the creative nature of the article's characteristics. Designs must not be solely dictated by technical function, nor include certain excluded subject-matter (e.g., architecture, unstable forms).

name: Terms of protection
description: Effective exclusive-right terms: 20 years from filing for an invention; 10 years from filing for a utility model (may be extended up to 3 years); 15 years from filing for an industrial design (may be extended up to 10 years).
guidance: Term extension available for invention patents relating to medicines, pesticides or agrochemical substances that require market authorization: extension equals elapsed period from filing to first market authorization minus five years. Effective term extensions may apply to independent claims relating to compounds/compositions.

name: Claims structure restrictions and claim-fee consequences
description: A claim set should not comprise a multiple-dependent claim forming the basis for a further multiple-dependent claim. If it does, applicants may substitute multiple references by single references; excess claims may incur claim fees.
guidance: Amendment strategies (e.g., preserving feature combinations by adding dependent claims each with single reference) may increase costs. In nullity actions patent owner can amend independent claims by incorporating features from dependent claims or description; in infringement proceedings only independent claims are relevant.

name: Statute of limitations for infringement claims
description: The statute of limitations for patent infringement is three years starting from the date the patent holder knew or should have known of the infringement.
guidance: Claims outside this window are time-barred.

name: Preparing a patent infringement statement of claim (evidence needs)
description: Crucial preparation issues: obtain sample of infringing product; for chemical products get independent laboratory analysis; collect evidence that product was introduced into civil-law transactions; translate and certify all foreign-language documents.
guidance: Sending a warning letter is not a prerequisite and may provoke counter-actions (e.g., infringer filing a patent). Suit generally filed where infringer is located.

name: Effects of claim wording and equivalents in infringement analysis
description: An invention or utility model is deemed to be used if a product contains each feature of an independent claim or a feature equivalent thereto (a feature that had become known in the given field before the infringing act).
guidance: Patent owners should draft claims carefully; equivalence doctrine can broaden scope in infringement analyses; independent claims determine infringement in proceedings.

name: Standards of review on appeal from PTAB
description: Legal conclusions by the PTAB are reviewed de novo; factual findings are reviewed for substantial evidence; claim construction in IPRs was held to be under the broadest reasonable interpretation at the PTAB (per Cuozzo Speed) but the Federal Circuit reviews factual aspects of claim construction (e.g., extrinsic evidence) for substantial evidence and ultimate claim construction de novo.
guidance: Cuozzo Speed held that 35 U.S.C. § 314(d) 'prohibits review of the decision to institute IPR' and that the PTAB may apply the broadest reasonable interpretation standard to claim construction for unexpired patents in IPRs. The court cited Teva for the framework: review of underlying factual determinations concerning extrinsic evidence for substantial evidence and ultimate construction de novo. 'Substantial evidence means “such relevant evidence as a reasonable mind might accept as adequate to support a conclusion.”'

name: Inspection checklist for amended applications
description: All amended applications put on the examiner’s desk should be inspected at once to determine the following: (D) If the changes made by the amendment warrant transfer (MPEP § 903.08(d)). (E) If the case is special (MPEP § 708.01). (F) If claims suggested to applicant for interference purposes have been copied. (G) If there is a traverse of a requirement for restriction (MPEP § 818.03(a)). (H) If “easily erasable” paper or other nonpermanent method of preparation or reproduction has been used (MPEP § 714.07). (J) If a terminal disclaimer has been filed (MPEP § 508.01, § 804.02, § 804.03, and § 1490). (K) If any matter involving security has been added (MPEP § 115).
guidance: Examiners must promptly check these items when an amendment reaches the examining group; related MPEP sections cited for further detail.

name: Status of amendments filed before first Office action
description: An amendment filed before the first Office action, but not filed along with the original application, does not enjoy the status of part of the original disclosure (see MPEP § 608.04(b)).
guidance: An application will be accorded a filing date based upon submission of a complete specification including claims and any required drawings; oath/declaration and/or filing fee may be submitted later. If application under 37 CFR 1.53(b) is filed without a signed oath but accompanied by an amendment, that amendment is considered part of the original disclosure. Amendments canceling claims to reduce filing fee should be filed with the application because only claim-canceling amendments are entered before filing fee calculation.

name: Recommendation on claim breadth at filing/first reply
description: Applicants are encouraged to include, at filing or no later than the first reply, claims varying from the broadest believed allowable to the most detailed they are willing to accept.
guidance: Providing a range of claim scope at the outset may alleviate difficulties in prosecution after final rejection.

name: Reasons for refusal mapped to form paragraphs (e.g., 7.72–7.80)
description: Specific refusal reasons map to standard form paragraphs: 7.72 (no convincing showing under 1.116(b)), 7.73 (raises new issues), 7.75 (form for appeal not improved), 7.76 (additional claims presented), 7.78 (proposed new claims would be allowable if submitted separately), 7.79 (affidavit/exhibit considered but insufficient), 7.80 (affidavit/exhibit not considered because no good reasons shown).
guidance: Follow required precedences (e.g., 7.71 must precede these paragraphs) and provide explanations or examples when new issues are extensive.

name: Claims available to right owner in case of infringement (Article 149)
description: Right owner whose industrial property right is infringed can claim from the court: (a) to determine the existence of infringement; (b) to prevent possible infringement; (c) to stop the infringing actions; (ç) to remedy infringement and compensate material and moral damages; (d) to seize the products causing infringement or requiring penalty, as well as instruments, such as devices and machines exclusively used in their production, without preventing the production of products other than infringing products; (e) to be granted property right on products, devices and machines seized in accordance with subparagraph (d); (f) to take measures to prevent the continuity of infringement, in particular at the expense of the infringer to change the shapes of products and instruments such as device and machine seized according to subparagraph (d), to erase the trademarks on them or to destroy them if it is inevitable for preventing the infringement; (g) announcement of the final judgment at the expense of the opposite party fully or in summary through daily newspapers or other means or notification to relevant parties if there is any justified reason or interest.
guidance: If claim (e) accepted, value of devices/machines deducted from compensation; any excess paid to opposite party by right owner. Announcement remedy (g) form and scope determined in ruling; right for announcement void unless demanded within three months after final ruling. Compensation of moral damage may not be claimed for geographical signs and traditional product names.

name: Compensation obligation for infringers (Article 150)
description: Those who commit acts deemed as infringement on industrial property right shall be obliged to compensate the damage of the right owner.
guidance: Additional compensation may be claimed if the reputation of the industrial property right suffers damage because products/services are used or produced in an inferior or improper manner. Prior to instituting compensation proceedings, the right owner may ask the court to order the person responsible for compensation to submit documentation related to the use of the industrial property right to determine evidence or amount of damages.

name: Number of claims
description: Count of claims in the patent document (claims variable).
guidance: Claims reflect the scope of legal protection and the technology/product 'space' covered. More claims have been associated with higher value and greater litigation likelihood; comparisons should account for office differences in claiming practices.

name: Claims-to-backward-citations ratio (Claims_Bwd)
description: The ratio of number of claims over number of backward patent citations for a patent.
guidance: Combines legal breadth (claims) with technological antecedents (backward citations) as a proxy for the size of the protected technology/product space; interpret carefully where backward citation counts are low or zero.

name: Use of EPO PATSTAT and office-specific data considerations
description: Indicators in the paper are compiled using EPO patent applications in the PATSTAT (EPO, April 2012) database; EPO-specific procedures (e.g., European patent being validated nationally) affect indicator values.
guidance: Office-specific practices (citation propensity, claim length, class assignment) influence indicators. For cross-office comparisons, use harmonised methods and be aware that using multiple offices without adjustment may bias results. The provided SQL codes ease replication on other office data but office differences remain.

name: Preliminary amendment may be disapproved if it unduly interferes with first Office action preparation
description: A preliminary amendment may be disapproved if the preliminary amendment unduly interferes with the preparation of a first Office action. Factors considered include the state of preparation of a first Office action as of the date of receipt (37 CFR 1.6) and the nature of any changes to the specification or claims that would result from entry of the preliminary amendment.
guidance: Applicants are encouraged to file preliminary amendments as soon as possible. If the examiner has already begun significant preparation (search/draft) before receipt, and entry would require significant additional time, entry may be denied (SPE approval required).

name: Two-condition test for denying entry after safe harbor
description: If a preliminary amendment is filed after the safe-harbor time periods, entry may be denied only if two conditions are met: (A) the examiner has devoted a significant amount of time preparing a first Office action before the amendment's receipt date; and (B) entry of the amendment would require significant additional time in preparing the Office action.
guidance: Examples of changes that would satisfy condition (B) include: amends the claims; adds numerous new claims; amends the specification to change the scope of the claims; amends the specification raising a new matter issue; includes arguments; includes an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 or 1.132; includes evidence traversing rejections from a prior Office action. This list is not exhaustive. If the two conditions are met, the examiner should obtain SPE approval before denying entry.

name: Form paragraph 7.46 use and content
description: Form paragraph 7.46 should be used to notify applicant that the entry of a preliminary amendment is denied because the amendment unduly interferes with preparation of an Office action.
guidance: The paragraph must state the date of receipt (37 CFR 1.6), describe state of preparation (e.g., claim analysis/search/draft status), and explain specifically how entry would require significant additional time (e.g., conduct prior art search in another classification, revise Office action extensively). Include warning about timely filing a responsive reply to avoid abandonment and suggest resubmitting the amendment with a responsive reply if not final.

name: Requirement for fully responsive reply (37 CFR 1.111(b))
description: To be entitled to reconsideration or further examination, the applicant must reply to the Office action. The reply must be reduced to writing which distinctly and specifically points out the supposed errors in the examiner’s action and must reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the prior Office action.
guidance: The reply must present arguments pointing out the specific distinctions believed to render the claims patentable over applied references. A general allegation that the claims define a patentable invention without specifics does not comply. The reply must appear to be a bona fide attempt to advance the application or reexamination proceeding.

name: Supplemental replies: limits and entry conditions (37 CFR 1.111(a)(2))
description: A supplemental reply that is supplemental to a reply in compliance with 37 CFR 1.111(b) will not be entered as a matter of right except as provided. The Office may enter a supplemental reply if it is clearly limited to cancellation of a claim(s); adoption of the examiner suggestion(s); placement of the application in condition for allowance; reply to an Office requirement made after the first reply was filed; correction of informalities (e.g., typographical errors); or simplification of issues for appeal.
guidance: A supplemental reply will be entered if filed within a period during which action by the Office is suspended under 37 CFR 1.103(a) or (c). If a supplemental reply is not approved for entry, the examiner should notify applicant in the subsequent Office action and applicant should include desired changes in the reply to the next Office action. Submission of a supplemental reply may reduce accumulated patent term adjustment under 37 CFR 1.704(c)(8). Use form paragraph 7.147 to notify applicant when supplemental reply is not entered.

name: Claims presented without pointing out patentable novelty
description: Claims presented in an amendment with no attempt to point out the patentable novelty should not be allowed; such an amendment may be held not fully responsive.
guidance: If the claims as amended are clearly open to rejection on the record, a final rejection should generally be made. If statutory reply period has expired or nearly expired, set time to furnish proper reply per MPEP § 714.03.

name: Immediate inspection checklist for amendments
description: Actions by applicant, especially filed near end of reply period, should be inspected immediately upon filing to determine whether they are completely responsive to the preceding Office action to prevent abandonment.
guidance: Examiner should inspect whether: amendment is properly signed (MPEP § 714.01(a)); filed within statutory/shortened time limits; fully responsive and complies with 37 CFR 1.121; changes warrant transfer; application is special; claims for interference have been copied; traversal of a restriction requirement exists; amendment prepared on non-permanent paper; applicant has cited references; terminal disclaimer filed; any security-related matter added. Prompt supplemental action may be needed if amendment crosses with the mailed action.

name: Scope of a claim attempting to patent a principle (Morse)
description: A claim that purports to cover the essence of an invention (e.g., 'the use of the motive-power of the electric or galvanic current ... however developed, for marking or printing intelligible characters') without limitation as to means may be invalid for being unlimited in respect to the means by which the principle could be effected.
guidance: In O'Reilly v. Morse a majority held such a broad claim invalid; the question is whether the inventor can monopolize the application of a natural force by any and all machinery or only his specific machinery and equivalents.

name: Specification must enable a mechanic to construct the invention
description: The specification must describe the invention sufficiently to enable mechanics acquainted with the art to build and put it in operation according to the inventor's plan.
guidance: In Watt's case a special verdict found the specification sufficient to enable a mechanic to build an engine operating on the plan; enablement affects whether the patent is for a manufacture and the permissible scope of claims.

name: Failure to undertake a full Graham analysis
description: A proper obviousness determination must analyze all four Graham factors: scope and content of the prior art; differences between the prior art and the claims; level of ordinary skill in the art; and relevant secondary considerations.
guidance: Challenge any faulty or incomplete Graham analysis. Under KSR the four factors are not alternatives — all must be analyzed. Use cases (Kinetic Concepts, Vicor) and MPEP § 2141.1; ensure examiner applies analogous-art tests and considers prior art in its entirety (In re Bigio, In re Wesslau, Abbott Labs. v. Sandoz).

name: Examiner ignored a claim limitation
description: If the prior art or combination does not disclose one or more claim limitations, a rejection is improper — all claim limitations must be considered.
guidance: Point out omitted limitations and argue the examiner improperly overlooked them. Cite MPEP § 2143.03 and supporting case law (Medrad, Kinetic Concepts). Show that absent disclosure of a limitation, rejection cannot stand.

name: Prior art did not recognize the unsolved problem or suggest the solution
description: An examiner cannot infer motivation to combine references if the prior art did not recognize the problem the inventor solved or did not suggest the claimed solution.
guidance: Argue that recognition of a need does not render the particular solution obvious (Cardiac Pacemakers v. St. Jude); show the references address different problems and that combining them is not suggested. Cite Broadcom v. Emulex, Insite Vision v. Sandoz, and Monarch Knitting precedent.

name: Consequences of failing to timely file appeal brief
description: Failure to file the brief and/or the appeal brief fee within the permissible time will result in dismissal of the appeal.
guidance: Form PTOL-468 is used to notify the patent owner that the appeal is dismissed. Reexamination prosecution is terminated and a Notice of Intent to Issue Ex Parte Reexamination Certificate (NIRC) will be issued indicating status of claims at time of final rejection.

name: Appeal brief content requirements (37 CFR 41.37)
description: The appellant shall file a brief of the authorities and arguments on which he or she will rely to maintain the appeal, including a summary of claimed subject matter which must refer to the specification by page and line number, and to the drawing by reference characters, and a copy of the claims involved.
guidance: Only one copy of the appeal brief is required; where a third-party requester exists, a copy must be served on that requester. For reexamination, the copy of claims should be double-spaced, start on a new page, and include all underlining and bracketing per 37 CFR 1.530(f); new claims added in reexamination should be completely underlined (departure from MPEP § 1205.02 for applications). The brief and every paper relating to an appeal should indicate the art unit number and reexamination control number. Briefs must be responsive to every ground of rejection stated by the examiner; a reply brief, if filed, shall be entered, but amendments/affidavits/evidence are subject to 37 CFR 1.116 and 41.33.

name: Treatment of claims when appellant identifies fewer than all rejected claims
description: If the notice of appeal or appeal brief identifies fewer than all of the rejected claims as being appealed, the examiner will treat all pending, rejected claims as being on appeal.
guidance: The examiner must maintain all of the rejections set forth in the Office action from which the appeal is taken unless appellant has overcome the rejection (e.g., by persuasive arguments, acceptable terminal disclaimer, or evidence). In situations where appellant requests holding a rejection in abeyance or presents no argument on a rejection, the examiner should maintain the rejection in the examiner’s answer.

name: Definition of information 'material to patentability' (37 CFR 1.555(b))
description: Information is material when it is not cumulative to information of record and (1) it is a patent or printed publication that establishes, by itself or in combination with other patents/printed publications, a prima facie case of unpatentability of a claim; or (2) it refutes or is inconsistent with a position the patent owner takes in opposing an argument of unpatentability relied on by the Office or asserting an argument of patentability.
guidance: A prima facie case of unpatentability is established when the information compels a conclusion that a claim is unpatentable under the preponderance-of-evidence standard, giving each claim term its broadest reasonable construction consistent with the specification, before considering any contrary evidence.

name: Information Disclosure Statement (IDS) content, timing, and format
description: Individuals are strongly encouraged to file IDSs in accordance with 37 CFR 1.98 within two months of the order to reexamine, or as soon thereafter as possible. An IDS filed under 37 CFR 1.555 by the patent owner after the order and before the first action on the merits may be submitted as part of a statement under 37 CFR 1.530 or as a separate paper.
guidance: If filed as part of a 1.530 statement the submission may include discussion of patentability issues; if filed separately it must be limited to a listing of the information and an explanation of its relevance (discussion of patentability issues in a separate IDS paper is improper). Copies of cited documents must be supplied per 37 CFR 1.98(a): legible copy of each foreign patent; each publication or the relevant portion (other than U.S. patents and published U.S. patent applications unless required); for each cited pending unpublished U.S. application, the specification including claims and any drawings or the portion which caused it to be listed; and all other information or portions causing it to be listed. The exception in 1.98(d) does not apply to reexamination proceedings.

name: Interviews in ex parte reexamination proceedings (37 CFR 1.560)
description: Interviews between examiners and patent owners (or their attorneys/agents) must be conducted in the Office during Office hours at times designated by the examiner; interviews will not be permitted at other times or places without Director authority. Interviews for discussion of patentability of claims will not be conducted prior to the first official action (except limited passive-role amendment situations initiated by the examiner).
guidance: Interviews should be arranged in advance. Requests by third-party requesters to participate or attend interviews will not be granted. In every interview, a complete written statement of the reasons presented at the interview must be filed by the patent owner as a separate part of a response to an outstanding Office action or as a separate paper within one month from the interview date (whichever is later). Telephone interviews by support staff to discuss filing defects may be permitted. Where a panel review was conducted, panel members will be included in interviews where possible. The patent owner's role should be passive if the examiner initiates an interview solely to provide an amendment which will make the claims patentable.

name: Reissue broadening timing under 35 U.S.C. 251
description: When the reissue is applied for within 2 years (or properly claims the benefit of a broadening reissue application filed within 2 years of the patent grant), the examiner does not go into the question of undue delay.
guidance: If a reissue broadening is timely (within 2 years or claims benefit of such), undue delay is not examined; otherwise, potential statutory bars may apply. (Context: 35 U.S.C. 251)

name: Assignee limitation on filing reissue
description: The assignee of the entire interest may file a reissue application only in cases where it does not 'enlarge the scope of the claims of the original patent.'
guidance: Claims that enlarge scope may be rejected as barred by the statute; however, courts (e.g., In re Bennett) have permitted correction of erroneous filings by assignees in some cases.

name: Rejection of previously allowed claims requires primary examiner approval
description: A claim noted as allowable shall thereafter be rejected only after the proposed rejection has been submitted to the primary examiner for consideration of all the facts and approval of the proposed action.
guidance: Great care should be exercised before authorizing such rejection. Full faith and credit should generally be given to a previous examiner's search and action unless a clear error or knowledge of other prior art exists. Examiners should not take an entirely new approach or make a new search merely hoping to find something. Use Form Paragraph 7.50 to note previously allowed claims now rejected.

name: Final rejection may be made on second or subsequent examination (37 CFR 1.113)
description: On the second or any subsequent examination or consideration by the examiner the rejection or other action may be made final.
guidance: When made final, applicant's reply is limited (appeal or restricted amendment routes). The examiner must repeat or state all grounds of rejection then considered applicable and clearly state reasons in support thereof. Reply to a final rejection must include cancellation of, or appeal from, each rejected claim. If any claim stands allowed, reply must comply with requirements or objections as to form.

name: Do not make final where new rejection is on prior art not of record for amended claims that should reasonably have been expected
description: A second or subsequent action should not be made final if it includes a rejection, on prior art not of record, of any claim amended to include limitations which should reasonably have been expected to be claimed.
guidance: Example: a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112 for incompleteness that could be answered by amendment — examiner should anticipate amendment and avoid making final. See MPEP § 904 et seq.

name: Summary judgment — genuine dispute of material fact
description: Summary judgment is improper where genuine disputes of material fact exist; issues such as whether prior art discloses claim elements, embodiment equivalence, or functionality are fact questions that must go to the trier of fact.
guidance: On summary judgment courts must draw all reasonable inferences in favor of the non-moving party. 'Common sense' or similar extrapolations used to support obviousness at summary judgment must be articulated with sufficient clarity for review (Perfect Web; Plantronics).

name: Obviousness — motivation to combine and factual nature
description: Whether a person of ordinary skill would have been motivated to combine prior art disclosures is a question of fact (University of Strathclyde v. Clear-Vu).
guidance: District courts must not resolve genuinely disputed factual issues (e.g., whether prior art teaches essential claim elements or whether a marketed product embodies prior art) on summary judgment; motivation to combine requires articulated reasoning if relying on 'common sense.'

name: Nexus requirement for secondary considerations
description: To rely on evidence like commercial success or copying as objective indicia, a nexus is required between those indicia and the patented features.
guidance: The record must support a reasonable factfinder's conclusion that the success or copying is attributable to the claimed features, not to extraneous factors; disputed nexus issues require factfinding.

name: Claim construction and prosecution history relevance
description: Prosecution history of related applications and examiner statements (e.g., indefiniteness re planar vs cambered) can materially bear on claim construction and litigation strategy.
guidance: Withholding related prosecution history can undermine an adversary's ability to frame claim construction and defenses; failure to disclose such materials may support unclean hands or inequitable conduct findings if relevant and withheld.

name: Prevailing party determination under § 285
description: A prevailing party is one that effects a material alteration in the legal relationship between the parties (Shum; B.E. Tech.).
guidance: Dismissal with prejudice of an opponent's counterclaims (resulting in inability to enforce patents against accused products) constitutes a material alteration qualifying the movant as the prevailing party; a party need not prevail on all claims to be 'prevailing.'

name: Future validation and improvement via multi-source embeddings and expert-curated STS datasets
description: Point towards leveraging multi-source patent embeddings and improving/validating patent embeddings by creating domain-expert curated Semantic Textual Similarity (STS) benchmark datasets.
guidance: Recognize limitations of current benchmarks and plan for creating or using expert-labeled STS datasets; consider combining multiple patent text sources (claims, abstracts, descriptions, metadata) to produce richer embeddings.

name: Alice two-step test for §101
description: The Supreme Court’s two-step test: at Alice step one, review whether a claim is directed to a patent-ineligible concept (e.g., an abstract idea); at Alice step two, review whether the claim recites elements sufficient to transform the abstract idea into a patent-eligible application.
guidance: Apply Alice step one to identify whether the claimed concept is an abstract idea; if so, apply step two to determine whether the claim adds an inventive concept or elements that transform the idea into patent-eligible subject matter. (Cites: Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank, 573 U.S. 208.)

name: §101 conventionality inquiry (jury question)
description: At step two, the jury was asked whether the elements of the asserted claim, individually and as an ordered combination, involved activities or technology that were 'well-understood, routine, or conventional' to a skilled artisan at the time of the invention.
guidance: The party asserting ineligibility must prove by clear and convincing evidence that claim elements were well-understood, routine, or conventional; factual record (testimony, evidence) can resolve this for the jury.

name: Types of evidence supporting infringement findings
description: Expert testimony, documentary evidence (e.g., website guides), and source code can constitute substantial evidence that an accused device meets a claim limitation (e.g., 'receives temperature measurements from inside the structure').
guidance: Corroborating documentary evidence and conceded testimony from opposing experts strengthen an infringement finding; focus on whether evidence supports the claimed functional reading (not just the device’s internal measurements).

name: Use of patent-owner written statements in reexamination
description: Expands documents that may be cited in a reexamination proceeding to include written statements of the patent owner that have been filed in a proceeding before a Federal court or the USPTO regarding the scope of claims.
guidance: These written statements (documents, pleadings, evidence) shall be considered only to determine the proper meaning of the claims that are the subject of the request in a proceeding and are not intended to be a basis for institution of a reexamination proceeding; intended to prevent patent owners from offering differing interpretations of prior art in different proceedings.

name: Tax-strategy patents treated as prior art
description: Mandates that tax strategies are 'insufficient to differentiate a claimed invention from the prior art' (i.e., future tax strategies will be considered indistinguishable from publicly available information relevant to claims).
guidance: An exclusion is made for software that enables filing returns or assists with finances, but the exclusion does not apply to the tax-strategy-related parts of such software; aims to keep tax-law interpretation and strategy in public domain.

name: Accelerated Examination (Article 61) — eligibility for preferential examination
description: According to Article 61 of the Korean Patent Act, the Minister of the Ministry of Intellectual Property may direct an examiner to examine one application in preference over another if it falls under any one of the listed types or circumstances.
guidance: Eligibility circumstances include: 1) Where a person, other than the applicant, is commercially and industrially working the invention claimed in a patent application after the laying-open of the application; 2) Where the Minister deems it necessary to urgently process a patent application prescribed by Presidential Decree; 3) Where a patent application prescribed by Presidential Decree is deemed necessary for disaster prevention, response, recovery, etc. The term 'patent application prescribed by Presidential Decree' (subparagraph 2) covers a.–o.: a) applications in the defense industry; b) applications directly related to green technology under the Framework Act on Carbon Neutrality and Green Growth; c) applications directly related to export promotion; d) applications concerning official duties of the State or local governments (including certain national/public school technology transfer filings); e) applications filed by certain defined enterprises (venture businesses, technology-innovative SMEs, exemplary companies re: employee invention compensation, SMEs with IP management certification) provided claimed invention relates to their business and at least one applicant belongs to the enterprise at original filing; f) applications concerning results of national R&D programs; g) applications serving as basis of a priority claim under treaties (limited to cases where a patent is being processed by a foreign patent office based on that priority claim); h) applications under which an invention is being practiced or is being prepared to be practiced by the applicant; i) applications directly related to businesses in regulatory sandbox; j) applications related to medical R&D within high-tech medical complexes under the regulatory sandbox; k) applications mainly for prevention or elimination of pollution (environmental pollution prevention facilities/measures); l) applications filed by a person aged 65 or older or by a person whose health is likely to incapacitate them from following prosecution procedures unless expedited; m) applications utilizing AI, IoT, 3D printing, autonomous vehicles, Big Data, cloud computing, intelligent robots, smart city, VR/AR, innovative medicine, new renewable energy, customized healthcare, drones, next-generation telecommunications, intelligent semiconductors, high‑tech materials, blockchain (assigned with 4IR-related new patent classification); n) international patent applications for which the Ministry conducts international search as an ISA under the PCT; o) applications related to high technologies (e.g., semiconductor) essential to national economy/competitiveness when publicly notified by the Minister. Additional accelerated routes: ② preferential examination where the Minister has agreed with a foreign patent office counterpart; ③ where a petitioner requested a designated specialized agency to conduct a prior-art search and asked that agency to notify the Minister of the results. For subparagraph 3 (new Jun. 22, 2021), 'patent application prescribed by Presidential Decree' may include items such as: (1) applications directly related to medical treatment/disease control products under Infectious Disease Control and Prevention Act; (2) applications related to disaster safety products certified under relevant law; (3) applications subject to public notice for accelerated examination in response to a disaster emergency. Applicants desiring accelerated examination must submit a written request with a detailed statement explaining necessity and any supporting evidence. (Flow chart referenced.)

name: Domestic Priority Claim — timing and basis
description: An applicant may make a domestic priority claim based on an invention described in the specification or drawings initially attached to an earlier application of a patent or utility model registration.
guidance: The domestic priority claim must be made within 1 year of the filing date of the earlier application for which the applicant has the right to obtain a patent. (Flow chart referenced.)

name: Unexpected results — commensurate in scope with claimed invention
description: The objective evidence of nonobviousness must be commensurate in scope with the claims which the evidence is offered to support.
guidance: Whether unexpected results are unexpectedly improved results or a property not taught by the prior art, the showing must be reviewed to see if the results occur over the entire claimed range. If the evidence is limited to a narrow species or narrow conditions, it may be insufficient to rebut a prima facie case for broader claims (citing In re Clemens; In re Grasselli).

name: Use of species or narrower-range data to support a genus or broader claimed range
description: Nonobviousness of a genus or claimed range may be supported by data showing unexpected results of a species or narrower range under certain circumstances.
guidance: A broader claimed range can be supported if one of ordinary skill can determine a trend in the exemplified data allowing reasonable extension of probative value. Limited species testing may be inadequate if it does not provide basis to conclude similar results across the generic scope (citing In re Kollman; In re Lindner).

name: Demonstrating criticality of a claimed range
description: To establish unexpected results over a claimed range, applicants should compare a sufficient number of tests both inside and outside the claimed range to show the criticality of the claimed range.
guidance: Comparative testing should be sufficient in amount and scope to demonstrate criticality; courts have reversed or affirmed based on whether tests were commensurate with claim scope (citing In re Hill).

name: Comparison with the closest prior art (affidavit/declaration requirements)
description: An affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 must compare the claimed subject matter with the closest prior art to be effective to rebut a prima facie case of obviousness.
guidance: Compare claimed invention with disclosure of each cited reference to determine number and importance of common limitations. Deviations from reference disclosures should be explained and evaluated; applicants may compare against prior art closer than the examiner relied upon. Where there are two equally close references, unexpected results over only one will not rebut obviousness unless teachings are sufficiently similar so testing one informs about the other (citing In re Burckel; In re Merchant; In re Holladay; Ex parte Humber; In re Johnson; In re Payne). Applicant is not required to compare to non‑existent prior art suggested by combinations of references.

name: Nexus between claimed invention and commercial success (burden of proof)
description: An applicant asserting commercial success to support nonobviousness bears the burden of proof of establishing a nexus between the claimed invention and the evidence of commercial success.
guidance: The term 'nexus' designates a factually and legally sufficient connection so the evidence is probative. The PTO must rely on the applicant to provide hard evidence of commercial success; showing commercial success of articles not covered by the claims is not probative (citing In re Huang; In re GPAC; In re Paulsen; Ex parte Remark). Commercial success abroad is relevant as well.

name: Commercial success must be commensurate in scope with the claims
description: Objective evidence of commercial success must be commensurate in scope with the claims; commercial success must be due to claimed features, not unclaimed features.
guidance: Evidence of success of a product broader or narrower than the claims may be insufficient. An affidavit stating sales of a product 'constructed according to the disclosure and claims' is not enough because it lacks proof the sold product corresponds to the claimed invention. If the commercial product is not coextensive with the claimed invention, applicants must show a legally sufficient relationship between the claimed feature and the commercial product/process (citing In re Tiffin; Joy Technologies; In re Hollingsworth; Demaco).

name: Commercial success must be derived from the claimed invention (not extraneous business factors)
description: Commercial success must flow from the functions and advantages disclosed or inherent in the specification and not from promotion, advertising, brand recognition, or other business events extraneous to the merits of the claimed invention.
guidance: Examiners must determine success is directly derived from claimed features in a marketplace where consumers choose on objective principles. Conclusory inventor opinions are insufficient to show nexus. Licensing evidence must be carefully appraised because licensing can succeed for reasons unrelated to invention merits. In design patents, establishing nexus is especially difficult because sales may be due to brand or performance rather than design (citing In re Mageli; In re Noznick; Demaco; Pentec; Hybritech; Litton Systems).

name: Sufficiency of disclosure (enablement) — applicant burden after prima facie showing
description: Once the examiner establishes a prima facie case of lack of enablement under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, the burden falls on the applicant to present persuasive arguments supported by suitable proofs where necessary that one skilled in the art could make and use the claimed invention using the disclosure as a guide.
guidance: Affidavits or declarations cannot be used to establish facts the specification should recite. Evidence supplementing a deficient specification must show the information to be read into the specification was known to those skilled in the art. Opinion testimony merely asserting disclosure exists is given little weight; testimony that explains underlying factual basis may be admitted and weighed on a case-by-case basis (citing In re Brandstadter; In re Howarth; In re Buchner; In re Smyth; In re Oppenauer; Glaser v. Strickland).

name: Claim-by-claim validity principle (35 U.S.C. § 253(a), § 282(a), § 288)
description: Section 253(a) states that '[w]henever a claim of a patent is invalid the remaining claims shall not thereby be rendered invalid.' This requirement also appears in 35 U.S.C. §§ 282(a) and 288.
guidance: Any practice or rule must preserve the statutory principle that validity and enforceability are determined on a claim-by-claim basis; a rule that eliminates claim-by-claim analysis and renders all claims unenforceable because a single claim is invalid contradicts these statutes.

name: Prohibition on rendering unrelated claims unenforceable
description: The proposed rule would render all claims of a patent unenforceable as a result of the invalidity of any claim in another patent encompassed by a terminal disclaimer.
guidance: Rulemaking should not allow an invalidity determination for one claim to preclude enforceability of another claim that is not patentably indistinct; doing so is inconsistent with statutes and relevant Federal Circuit decisions (e.g., Ortho Pharm. Corp. v. Smith).

name: Avoid creating incentives for gamesmanship and shifting adjudication to examiners
description: Linking enforceability of multiple patents via terminal disclaimers creates an incentive for challengers to target a single claim to potentially render an entire family unenforceable.
guidance: Policy should avoid shifting validity/enforceability adjudication from Article III courts (and PTAB processes) to examiners without evidentiary hearings, which risks inconsistent and less robust evaluations.

name: Preserve continuation practice under 35 U.S.C. § 120
description: Continuation practice allows applicants to pursue claims of different wording, scope, and variation and is essential to define claim scope; continuations are entitled to the parent's priority date subject to § 120 limits.
guidance: Regulations should not undermine the statutory continuation mechanism, should respect written description/enabling requirements (35 U.S.C. § 112, M.P.E.P. § 201.07), nor improperly restrict applicants’ ability to file continuations.

name: Avoid rulemaking premised on unsupported litigation-cost claims
description: There is no demonstrated correlation that a greater number of continuations (or patents) necessarily increases litigation costs for generics or biosimilars; only asserted claims need be addressed in litigation.
guidance: Regulatory action should not be justified by unfounded assumptions about litigation volume or cost increases; consider actual assertion patterns (e.g., small fraction of claims typically asserted).

name: Avoid filing preliminary amendments
description: Applicants should not file any preliminary amendment with the application.
guidance: Submitting applications without accompanying preliminary amendments reduces Office processing and helps ensure correct printing of patent application publications. If a preliminary amendment is present on the filing date, it becomes part of the original disclosure under 37 CFR 1.115(a)(1) and will be included in the patent application publication. Generally a substitute specification (excluding claims) is required for preliminary amendments to the specification (other than claims). Applicants are advised to incorporate desired amendments into the text of the specification (including a new set of claims) rather than filing preliminary amendments, even in continuation or divisional applications (subject to rules on new matter).

name: Preliminary amendment formatting and substitute specification requirement
description: If a preliminary amendment present on the filing date is not in a format usable for publication, the Office will issue a notice requiring the applicant to submit the amendment in a format usable for publication.
guidance: Generally, a substitute specification (excluding claims) is required for any preliminary amendments to the specification (other than the claims) that are present on the filing date. Although a substitute specification is a usable format for publication, applicants should avoid filing a substitute specification with the application because the application size fee will be calculated based on the application papers including the clean version and marked-up version of the substitute specification.

name: Incorporating amendments in continuations/divisionals (no new matter)
description: In a continuation or divisional application, a new specification reflecting amendments made in the parent application may be submitted together with a copy of the oath or declaration from the previously filed application so long as no new matter is included in the specification.
guidance: Specific references to prior applications required by 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or 120 and 37 CFR 1.78(a) for applications filed on or after September 16, 2012 may be submitted in an application data sheet (ADS) rather than in a preliminary amendment. If the specific reference is submitted in a preliminary amendment, a substitute specification will not be required if the preliminary amendment only adds or amends a benefit claim.

name: Appendices printing rules
description: Appendices, other than those containing 'Sequence Listings' (for apps filed before July 1, 2022), 'Sequence Listing XMLs' (for apps filed on/after July 1, 2022), or 'Large Tables', are not printed if they are contained on pages located after the claims.
guidance: If the application includes multiple claim sets in the specification, the Office may treat pages located after the first set of claims as appendices. Computer program listings may be printed if included in the specification before the claims, but 'Computer Program Listing Appendices' submitted via the USPTO patent electronic filing system or on a read-only optical disc in accordance with 37 CFR 1.96(c) and 37 CFR 1.52(e) are not printed as part of the patent or patent application publication.

name: Redacted publication option when foreign-filed applications are less extensive
description: If an applicant has filed applications in one or more foreign countries and such foreign-filed applications corresponding to the U.S. application are less extensive than the U.S. application, the applicant may submit a redacted copy of the U.S. application eliminating any part or description not also contained in the corresponding foreign applications.
guidance: The Director may only publish the redacted copy unless the redacted copy is not received within 16 months after the earliest effective filing date for which a benefit is sought. The provisions of section 154(d) will not apply to a claim if the description published in the redacted application does not enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the subject matter of the claim.

name: Good statement of the rejection (structure)
description: Claim X is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Reference A in view of Reference B. Identify which reference teaches each claimed element, state what elements are not taught, and explain why it would have been obvious to combine or modify the references to obtain the claimed invention.
guidance: Provide an explicit mapping of claimed elements to teachings of the applied reference(s). State the missing element(s) and supply a reasoned rationale why a person of ordinary skill would have made the modification or combination (e.g., to obtain an expected advantage, to prevent error, to streamline a business process). Use concrete citations to the references when possible and show the logical link; avoid mere conclusory statements.

name: Rationale implicitly contained in a reference
description: Where a reference implicitly suggests the claimed modification, the examiner may rely on that implicit teaching as the rationale supporting an obviousness rejection.
guidance: Explain how the reference's disclosure implies the added steps or modification (e.g., security/authorization is implied when matching account holder ID/password). Show why the implicit teaching would lead the ordinary artisan to the claimed feature rather than merely asserting it.

name: Rationale reasoned from official notice
description: An examiner may take Official Notice of facts that are well known and not subject to reasonable dispute to support an obviousness rationale.
guidance: When taking Official Notice, provide illustrative examples or commonplace analogies (the manual pizza-order verification example) to show the fact is well known and explain why it makes the claimed modification obvious. Do not merely state Official Notice without supplying supporting factual context.

name: Design choice / lacks advantage is insufficient
description: A simple statement that a claimed difference is a 'design choice' or 'lacks an advantage or unexpected result' is not an adequate factual rationale for an obviousness rejection.
guidance: Avoid conclusory language. Instead, supply objective reasoning or evidence showing why the modification would have been made by one of ordinary skill (e.g., expected advantages, industry routine, technical motivation).

name: Known system/machine with computer program — mere implementation without functional improvement is not inventive
description: Putting a known system on a programmed computer (or adding software that merely performs the same manual steps) is often unpatentable absent an inventive improvement in functionality, performance, or technical effect.
guidance: Demonstrate whether the claimed program provides more than expected automation (e.g., a new algorithmic technique producing an unexpected technical result). If it does not, explain why a skilled artisan would simply have automated the manual process and thus it is obvious.

name: Common General Knowledge (CGK)
description: Common general knowledge consists of what is generally known and accepted by the POSITA in the relevant field at the relevant date.
guidance: Examples: board games, a particular 3-dimensional board, pieces, mechanized arm and claw, and hydraulic pistons per se can be CGK depending on the field. The examiner may identify CGK in the report to support claim construction and patentability analysis.

name: Problem–solution analysis and identification of essential elements
description: Examiners should identify the problem outlined in the description, the solution contemplated by the inventor, and the essential elements that lead to that solution.
guidance: Example language used in reports: state the problem (e.g., 'finding an improved method of playing the game'), set out the solution (e.g., 'inclusion of hydraulic pistons at each corner'), and distinguish contextual features from essential elements (e.g., the board, pieces, arm and claw provide context but the hydraulic pistons are the essential elements). This analysis supports determinations such as statutory subject-matter and claim scope.

name: Statutory character of the claim (is the claim statutory?)
description: Determine whether the essential elements provide a new practical application and thereby constitute statutory subject-matter under the Patent Act.
guidance: In examples the manual concludes 'Yes' where the essential elements (e.g., hydraulic pistons allowing board tilting) provide a new practical application to a context (e.g., a game board). Examiners should explain the essential elements and why they render the claim statutory or not.

name: Search of the prior art
description: Prior art includes all information made available to the public anywhere before the claim date (subject to limited exceptions). Search scope should identify relevant prior art for patentability assessment.
guidance: In practice, prior art relied on includes published patent documents, journal articles, textbooks, manuals, etc. The scope of a Canadian examiner's search depends partly on earlier searches; examiners are not required to search claimed matter having defects (unity, divisional, new matter). Even where an International Searching Authority performed a comprehensive search, a Canadian examiner will at minimum search Canadian patent documents (e.g., for double-patenting or anticipation). Examiners should consider available foreign search results and, if relying on them in a report, indicate which documents were identified. Further searches may be undertaken when appropriate and need not be limited to Canadian documents; searches are generally limited by dates, keywords, and IPC codes. Examiners should aim to identify all relevant prior art in the first report but acknowledge documents may be missed; if relevant prior art is identified later, the examiner must cite it against the claimed invention.

name: Content and form of an examiner's report
description: An examiner's report is a notice identifying defects in the application and containing a requisition under subsection 86(2) or 86(5) of the Patent Rules; it communicates defects and related requisitions to the applicant.
guidance: A requisition typically begins with language like 'The examiner has identified the following defects in the application' and ends with language requiring amendment or argument. Reports may include additional informative content: date and origin of recent amendments, number of claims on file, statement regarding the search performed, identification and discussion of prior art, general prosecution comments, and the examiner's view of POSITA, CGK, problem, solution, and essential elements. Reports should be as comprehensive as possible to enable informed prosecution decisions. A Final Action is a specific report issued when prosecution appears to have reached an impasse. Examiners do not issue reports when the application is compliant or contains only minor defects; in such cases the examiner will approve the application for allowance or issue a conditional notice of allowance. Separate requisitions under sections 85 and 94 may be included; requirements to request continued examination under section 85.1 may be included as informative statements. Each separate requisition and any separate requirement must be responded to within the time period indicated or the application will be abandoned.

name: Withdrawal of an examiner's report — grounds and procedure
description: An examiner's report may be withdrawn in exceptional circumstances where facts demonstrate a need to withdraw the report.
guidance: Situations include: report sent in error; wrong address due to CIPO error; report so uninformative it prevents applicant from recognizing defects; mailing/processing errors (missing pages, incorrect due date); report based on incorrect pages of claims/description/drawings affecting relevancy; delays greater than one month between report date and applicant's receipt where the report contains a requisition or requirement under sections 85, 85.1 or 94. Requests to withdraw must be in writing (phone requests not considered). For certain grounds a time limit applies (earlier of four months after report date and the day the applicant responds). If withdrawn, obligation to respond to requisitions is removed and the withdrawn report does not count toward the report count for continued examination; often a new report will be issued with a new response time based on the new report's date. If request concerns an allegedly improper requisition under sections 85 or 94.1, or an improperly-identified requirement under 85.1, generally the report will not be wholly withdrawn; instead the specific improperly-identified requisition or requirement may be withdrawn, removing the obligation to respond to that requisition but leaving other requisitions intact.

name: Abstract requirements (section 55)
description: An application must contain an abstract (in English or French, same language as the application) that provides a concise summary of the disclosure in the description, claims and drawings and meets specific content and form requirements.
guidance: Section 55 requires the abstract to: contain a concise summary of the disclosure and where applicable include the chemical formula that best characterizes the invention; specify the technical field; be drafted to allow clear understanding of the technical problem, the gist of the solution, and the principal use(s); be suitable as a scanning/searching tool; and be no more than 150 words. The abstract must start on a new page with a separate heading and avoid patent jargon so technicians, scientists and others can understand it. The abstract must not refer to merits or speculative applications or compare the invention with the prior art. Abstracts may contain chemical or mathematical formulae but must not contain drawings.

name: Description and disclosure general requirements (subsection 27(3))
description: The description, together with the claims, form the specification; the description must provide a clear and complete disclosure so the POSITA can identify what has been invented and be enabled to practice it.
guidance: Cited authorities emphasize disclosure is the quid pro quo for patent exclusivity. The description must answer 'What is your invention?' and 'How does it work?' so that, at the expiry of the monopoly, the public (POSITA) can make the same successful use of the invention using only the specification.

name: Avoid claims directed to an 'abstract idea'
description: Claims that are directed to fundamental economic practices or abstract ideas (e.g., 'intermediated settlement' or 'risk hedging') are not patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. §101.
guidance: Abstract ideas are excluded because they would provide a monopoly over an idea and preempt the basic tools of science and technology. Determine whether claimed subject matter is a fundamental economic practice or otherwise an abstract idea before drafting or during prosecution.

name: Claim specific hardware producing a particular outcome
description: Claims that tie functionality to particular hardware producing a particular outcome are more likely to be patent-eligible.
guidance: Favor claims covering functionality linked with a specific structure rather than business procedures performed by a general-purpose computer. Recite hardware elements that provide meaningful limitations rather than generic labels.

name: Avoid 'token' or generic computer components
description: Using generic terms like 'data processing system,' 'communications controller,' or 'data storage unit' as mere placeholders does not make a claim patentable.
guidance: These are considered 'token' components and do not provide patentability. Instead, describe particular hardware or how components are structured and interact in a non-generic way.

name: Recite particular hardware components where appropriate
description: Claim particular hardware components (e.g., a particular GPU, specialized device, or memory configured in a new way) to tie the invention to a machine.
guidance: For example, for graphics technologies recite a particular GPU or memory configured to improve performance; for streaming video characterize operations as performed by specialized devices in an apparatus that interact to process and manage the data.

name: Emphasize hardware structure or distinctive interactions among elements
description: Elements should indicate a particular structure or be claimed to interact in a distinctive way to show the claimed invention is not merely functional.
guidance: Either claim the elements themselves to indicate a particular structure, or claim that they are structured to interact in a distinctive way that provides technical advantages.

name: Draft method claims that tie operations to configured hardware
description: Claiming an inventive concept as a method claim that emphasizes operations performed by specific types of hardware configured to perform those operations can help address infringers and meet Alice requirements.
guidance: Method claims should describe that steps are performed by hardware that is configured to perform operations constituting an overall technological approach to achieving a useful result with a computer.

name: Ensure system and computer-readable medium claims recite specific hardware
description: System and computer-readable medium claims that fail to recite specific hardware are vulnerable to §101 rejection (as happened in Alice).
guidance: System/medium claims should recite non-generic hardware or structural limitations rather than abstract functionality stored on or executed by unspecified machines.

name: Include comprehensive drawings, hardware implementations, architectures, and flowcharts
description: Prepare specification drawings and flowcharts that show examples of hardware implementations and architectures and specify how hardware is involved in performing method operations.
guidance: Comprehensive drawings and flowcharts provide material to support claims and arguments during prosecution and can show how the claimed invention involves specific hardware or improvements.

name: Draft the disclosure to emphasize specific hardware structures and alternatives
description: The written description should emphasize specific hardware structures that implement claimed functionality and discuss multiple alternative examples.
guidance: Discuss multiple alternatives and implementation examples to create prosecution avenues and supply fallback claim language tying functionality to particular machines or structures.

name: Claim software via specialized device/apparatus language when helpful
description: For software inventions, characterizing steps as operations by specialized components or devices in an apparatus may tie the invention to particular machines.
guidance: E.g., for a user interface on a mobile device, claim specialized components that interact to receive input, process it, and provide output, rather than only reciting steps performed by 'a processor.'

name: Inventions directed to computer architectures should claim elements and interactions that provide advantages
description: Claims to processor, memory, or network designs that specifically claim hardware elements and their interaction to obtain advantages are less likely to be affected by Alice.
guidance: Focus on specific hardware elements and how their interaction yields technical advantages, not merely reciting abstract functions.

name: Be cautious claiming automation of non-computer procedures
description: Automating procedures that could be carried out without a computer (even if laborious) may be difficult to patent under Alice.
guidance: Show that the claimed automation provides a technical improvement or specific hardware implementation rather than merely automating a human-performed or conventional business process.

name: Anticipate increased §101 rejections for pending patents and prepare strategies
description: Alice may lead to an increase in non-statutory subject matter rejections for pending patent applications.
guidance: Strategies include amending claims to recite particular hardware components, emphasizing hardware-performed functionality in the specification, and preparing alternative claim sets and disclosure to support prosecution responses.

name: Alice/Mayo two-step framework
description: Apply the two-step framework set forth by the Supreme Court in Mayo and Alice: (1) determine whether the claim is 'directed to' a patent-ineligible concept (e.g., an abstract idea); (2) consider the elements of each claim individually and 'as an ordered combination' to determine whether the additional elements 'transform the nature of the claim' into a patent-eligible application (a search for an 'inventive concept').
guidance: Use Mayo Collaborative Servs. v. Prometheus and Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank as the governing test. At step one ask what the claim is directed to; at step two examine whether claim elements (alone or combined) add significantly more than the ineligible concept.

name: Accurate claim characterization at step one
description: Characterize the claim based on its language and the functions it recites (do not overgeneralize or misstate the claim).
guidance: The district court’s characterization should reflect the claim terms (e.g., 'A computer-implemented method for decoding a transmission signal' comprising steps of receiving, deinterleaving, combining, and decoding). A party's rephrasing that is not meaningfully different from the claim language does not show error. Do not import unclaimed limitations to alter the directed-to inquiry.

name: Generic computer implementation is insufficient
description: Claims that merely invoke generic processes and machinery (e.g., 'using a computer processor' or otherwise do not require specialized hardware) are more likely to be abstract.
guidance: If the claim fails to disclose specific means or methods and instead recites generic computer implementation, that supports a finding of abstraction (Two-Way Media). A requirement for a 'specialized computer' can distinguish eligible claims.

name: Improvement-in-functionality requirement for computer-technology claims
description: To qualify as a patent-eligible improvement, claims must be directed to an improvement in the functionality of the computer or network platform itself, not merely to applying an abstract idea in a technological field.
guidance: Use Customedia: show that the claim improves computer or network functionality itself (e.g., a new way the computer operates), rather than just an abstract idea implemented on a computer.

name: Inventive-concept analysis of ordered combinations at step two
description: At step two, consider whether the elements individually or in combination provide an 'inventive concept' that transforms the abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter.
guidance: Merely reciting the ineligible concept plus conventional steps is insufficient. If the asserted benefits are not tied to the particular ordered combination claimed (or the specification shows the same benefits for different orders), the order does not supply an inventive concept.
