name: Do not rely on unclaimed specification details to supply inventive concept
description: Technological details disclosed in the specification but not captured in the claim language cannot be used to supply the inventive concept necessary for eligibility.
guidance: Follow Intell. Ventures, Am. Axle, and ChargePoint: the specification cannot be used to import additional details or performance benefits into the claims when those details are not claimed. Evaluate inventive concept based on the claim as written.

name: Elements known in the prior art or routine/mental operations do not supply inventive concept
description: If claim elements (other than the alleged inventive step) were used in the prior art, or if the alleged inventive step is basic arithmetic/mental operations, those cannot supply the inventive concept.
guidance: Identify prior art usage of claimed steps. Basic combining/averaging or arithmetic that can be performed mentally or by hand is not enough (see discussion that combining may be 'add[ing] and averag[ing]'). Also note BSG Tech: use of the ineligible concept cannot supply the inventive concept.

name: Partial revocation and limitation of claims
description: If the grounds for revocation affect the patent only in part, the patent shall be limited by a corresponding amendment of the claims and revoked in part.
guidance: Allows limiting patent via claim amendment where revocation grounds are partial.

name: Limits of what the Court may award
description: The Court shall decide in accordance with the requests submitted by the parties and shall not award more than is requested.
guidance: Parties shape the scope of relief; court cannot exceed claimed relief.

name: Sanctions for non-compliance with orders
description: If a party does not comply with the terms of an order of the Court, that party may be sanctioned with a recurring penalty payment payable to the Court. The individual penalty shall be proportionate to the importance of the order to be enforced and shall be without prejudice to the party's right to claim damages or security.
guidance: Sanctions are proportionate and do not preclude separate damage claims.

name: Field selection for searches
description: The Lens allows you to select fields to be searched. They include: Lens Id, Pub Key, Kind, Pub Num, Pub Year, Title, Abstract, Inventor, Owner, Full Text, Claims, Classification Ipcr, Classification Nat, Classification Cpc, Cites Patent Pub Key, Cites Patent Count.
guidance: Choose appropriate searchable fields to focus results (e.g., Title, Abstract, Claims, Full Text). Note that an assignee field is not present; use the “Applicants” field selection for similar results. The “Owners” field is specifically US assignment data used to supplement EPO‑derived Applicant as published data. The Lens provides links to global patent status information using OPS of the EPO as default.

name: Patent document view and metadata export
description: Document view tabs include summary & full text, family and legal information, notes, collection options, make a note, and document preview. Download citation options include RIS, BibTeX, CSV or JSON. You can download PDF and open scanned document previews; key search terms are highlighted.
guidance: When reviewing a record, examine summary, full text, claims, and family/legal information. Use notes and collection annotations to record findings; export bibliographic metadata in the format your workflow requires.

name: Scope of settlement: full resolution of disciplinary action arising from stipulated facts
description: The Proposed Settlement Agreement 'resolves all disciplinary action by the United States Patent and Trademark Office ("USPTO" or "Office") arising from the stipulated facts set forth below.'
guidance: A settlement may be structured to fully resolve specified disciplinary claims arising from the agreed-upon facts; parties should be explicit about the scope of release or resolution in the Agreement.

name: Most recent international work product must be submitted and show patentability indication
description: Applicants must submit a copy of the most recent international work product (WO/ISA, WO/IPEA, or IPER) unless it is already of record in the U.S. application, and that work product must indicate that the claim(s) has novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability.
guidance: If the work product is not in English, an English translation is required. If the submitted work product includes any Box VIII observations (clarity/support issues), the applicant must identify and explain why the claim(s) is not subject to the observation; failure to do so makes the U.S. application ineligible. If the international work product is already of record, simply state when it was filed in the U.S. application.

name: All U.S. application claims must sufficiently correspond to PCT claims
description: All claims in the U.S. application must 'sufficiently correspond' to, or be amended to 'sufficiently correspond' to, one or more of the corresponding PCT application claims indicated as having novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability.
guidance: The USPTO considers claims to 'sufficiently correspond' where, accounting for translation and claim format differences, the claims are of the same or similar scope, or are narrower in scope. A narrower claim is one that is further limited by an additional feature. Applicants must submit a 'claims correspondence table' indicating how each U.S. claim corresponds to the indicated PCT claim(s). In practice, identical or nearly identical claims are most likely to be accepted; claims that increasingly vary from the patentable claim risk rejection.

name: Submit claims correspondence table
description: Applicants must submit a claims correspondence table that indicates how all claims in the U.S. application sufficiently correspond to the PCT claim(s) indicated as patentable in the international work product.
guidance: The table should map each U.S. claim to one or more indicated PCT claims and explain any differences (e.g., narrowing limitations, translation or format-induced changes). Properly documenting correspondence is essential for eligibility.

name: Strategic recommendations to maximize PCT-PPH effectiveness
description: Practical strategies include seeking a favorable WO/ISA (routinely available ~18 months from priority) as the basis for PCT-PPH; filing a Chapter II Demand to obtain a WO/IPEA or IPER if WO/ISA is unfavorable; designating a Trilateral Office as ISA/IPEA when possible; filing a continuation (rather than a U.S. national stage entry) to reduce administrative delay when entering the U.S. national phase; and including a set of narrower claims in the PCT to increase the chance of a favorable work product.
guidance: These are recommended practices (not formal requirements) intended to increase the likelihood and timeliness of successful PCT-PPH participation. Applicants should weigh these options (e.g., choosing ISA/IPEA, Chapter II demand, continuation vs national stage) based on timing and prosecution strategy.

name: Classification of general chemical formulae (Markush-type)
description: Procedure for classifying general chemical formulae that cover large sets of related compounds and may map to many classification places.
guidance: Step 1: Classify all 'fully identified' compounds that are novel and unobvious if they are (i) specifically claimed as such or in a composition, (ii) products of a claimed process, or (iii) derivatives. A 'fully identified' compound has exact structure by name/formula or deducible from preparation with not more than one alternative and is characterised by a physical property or worked example. Step 2: If no fully identified compounds are disclosed, classify the general formula in the most specific group(s) that cover most potential embodiments, limited to a single or very small number of groups. Step 3: Optional (non-obligatory) classification of other compounds within scope may be made. If classifying all fully identified compounds would lead to many symbols (e.g., >20) and many subgroups under one higher group, the classifier may reduce symbols by classifying at the higher group only; otherwise classify in all more specific subgroups.

name: Classification of unsearched patent documents
description: For unsearched publications, classify all claimed subject matter that is potentially novel and unobvious according to the opinion of a classifier expert; also classify potentially novel/unobvious unclaimed disclosure.
guidance: If the classifier is not an expert in the art, use all claims to determine subject matter to be classified. As with other levels, it's desirable to classify/index additional information useful for search.

name: Notification of abandonment (PTOL-1432) and applicant responsibility
description: The Patent Examining Corps mails a Notice of Abandonment form PTOL-1432 to the correspondence address of record in all applications which become abandoned for failure to prosecute; mere failure to receive the notice does not affect the status of abandonment.
guidance: This mailing enables applicants to take action to reinstate inadvertently abandoned applications (often by petition to revive under 37 CFR 1.137). If neither Office action nor notice was received and lack of diligent action is claimed, suspect a problem with correspondence address of record and promptly file a paper notifying the Office of the change of address (see MPEP §§ 402 and 601.03).

name: Treatment of abstracts/abbreviatures/defensive publications as prior art
description: Abstracts, abbreviatures, and defensive publications must be referred to as publications and are cited as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a) or 102(b) effective from the date of publication in the Official Gazette.
guidance: They may be used alone or in combination with other prior art in rejecting claims under 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103. Defensive publications are listed with 'U.S. Patent Documents'; abstracts and abbreviatures are listed under 'Other References' with specific citation formats provided.

name: Interview Summary form PTOL‑413 and PTOL‑413B procedures and required contents
description: Examiners must complete an Interview Summary form PTOL‑413 for each interview where a matter of substance was discussed; if examiner initiated, PTOL‑413B may be used. PTOL‑413 shall be given a paper number, placed in the file, and listed on the contents list; a duplicate is given to applicant at conclusion or mailed for telephonic/email/video interviews.
guidance: PTOL‑413 records: (A) application number; (B) name of applicant; (C) name of examiner; (D) date; (E) type of interview; (F) participants; (G) whether an exhibit/demonstration shown; (H) identification of claims discussed; (I) identification of specific prior art discussed; (J) indication whether agreement reached and description; (K) signature of examiner; (L) names of other USPTO personnel present. The complete recordation should also include: (A) brief description of exhibits/demonstrations; (B) claims discussed; (C) prior art discussed; (D) principal proposed substantive amendments (unless already described); (E) general thrust of principal arguments of applicant and examiner (not verbatim); (F) other pertinent matters; (G) general results/outcome; (H) for e-mail interviews, a paper copy must be placed in the file. If applicant’s interview record is incomplete/inaccurate and bears on patentability, examiner may give applicant one month to correct the record (extensions under 37 CFR 1.136(a) may be granted).

name: Panel composition requirements
description: The panel will consist of three, or more, members, one of whom will be a manager. The second member will be the examiner in charge of the proceeding. The manager may select the third member. The examiner-conferees will be primary examiners, or examiners who are knowledgeable in the technology of the invention claimed in the patent being reexamined and/or who are experienced in reexamination practice.
guidance: Majority of those present should be examiners who were not involved in the examination or issuance of the patent. An 'original' examiner should be chosen only if that examiner is the most knowledgeable in the art or there is some other specific and justifiable reason.

name: Old elements plus new matter can form patentable combination
description: The old matter may not, in itself, be patentable, but joined to the new matter, a combination may be formed which may be patented.
guidance: An inventor need not take separate patents for each new patentable matter; he may claim the limited use of the new matters in combination rather than exclusive use for every purpose.

name: Interference decided on patentable matter, not non-patentable elements
description: Where several elemental features are old and not now patentable, an interference must concern the matter that is now patentable (e.g., a new combination).
guidance: Claims that cover only old unpatentable elements do not create interference; only overlapping claims to patentable matter are relevant.

name: Novelty and prior art: elements not patentable if previously known
description: If elements such as a single telegraphic circuit, chemically prepared paper, or the signs themselves have been long known or previously patented, claims to them individually are not patentable.
guidance: Patentable claims must rest on new matter or new combinations producing new effects; prior patents/printed publications or secret archives may defeat novelty.

name: Construction (interpretation) of patents by courts
description: The construction of a patent is the province of the court (questions of law), although juries may decide factual matters; courts should be liberal in construction and guided by principles in specifications.
guidance: Courts decide extent of claim, sufficiency of invention, whether patent void as against public policy, and how to receive evidence of invention; principles guide how far courts may receive evidence to explain specifications.

name: Description and drawings as part of specification
description: Descriptions of machines may be partly in writing and partly by drawings; drawings form part of the specifications and should accompany them.
guidance: Whether drawings need to be to scale, duplicates required, and how drawings are used in claim construction are covered; drawings and models may be required and classified by the Commissioner.

name: Disclaimer effects on pending suits and costs
description: A statutory disclaimer may be recorded and taken as part of specifications; it affects pending litigation and may influence award of costs.
guidance: Disclaimers are a mechanism to limit claims and cure defects, but have procedural and substantive consequences.

name: Brooks two-part test (objective baselessness + subjective bad faith)
description: Under the Federal Circuit's Brooks-derived rule, an accused infringer may recover attorney fees under § 285 only if the patent-holder's claim was (1) objectively baseless and (2) brought in subjective bad faith.
guidance: District courts applying Brooks require the accused infringer to prove both elements (objective baselessness and subjective bad faith), typically by clear and convincing evidence. The Federal Circuit has applied this as a restrictive standard that limits fee awards absent a showing of bad faith. Icon defends this two-prong test as consistent with precedent and congressional intent; Octane argues it is too narrow and not party-neutral.

name: Totality-of-the-circumstances discretionary standard
description: A district court may exercise equitable discretion and consider the totality of the circumstances to determine whether a case is "exceptional" and therefore merits an award of attorney fees under § 285.
guidance: Proponents (including Octane and the United States) urge a totality approach that considers multiple non-exhaustive factors—such as reasonableness of the claim, choice of venue, and predatory patent litigation (including PAE activity)—similar to fee standards in other IP areas (copyright, trademark). The Court could therefore vacate Brooks and endorse broad district-court discretion rather than a rigid two-part test.

name: Textual and statutory-construction cues ('may' and 'exceptional' imply discretion)
description: The statutory text of § 285—specifically the use of the permissive 'may' and the modifier 'exceptional'—suggests district courts possess broad discretion to award fees.
guidance: Octane argues that the ordinary meaning of the statute supports equitable discretion and a totality-of-the-circumstances approach; interpreting § 285 so narrowly as to duplicate inherent authority would render the statute superfluous, which statutory-construction principles disfavour. Icon argues congressional intent and historical practice counsel restraint to avoid chilling meritorious claims.

name: Timing and opportunity to submit evidence before the Final Order matters
description: Whether a document was available to the respondent before the Director issued the Final Order (and whether the respondent had opportunity to submit it) is decisive in determining if evidence is 'new.'
guidance: Even if a document was produced after the respondent's earlier submission, if it existed and could have been submitted prior to the Final Order, it will not qualify as newly discovered evidence. The presence of a window of opportunity undermines a 'new evidence' claim.

name: Requisites of the Application
description: When a new application is assigned in the Technology Center, the examiner should review contents to determine if the application meets the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 111(a). Matters affecting filing date or abandonment (lack of oath/declaration, filing fee, or claims) should be checked before storage.
guidance: Examiner must ensure formal matters and completeness/clarity of disclosure per MPEP Chapter 600. If requisites are not met, applicant may be called upon for amendments — but such amendments must not include new matter. Check filing date determinants and whether claims, fees, and oath are present before placing application into storage.

name: Treatment of Obviously Informal Cases
description: When disclosure is informal or insufficient so a complete action on the merits is impractical, follow procedure: make a reasonable search to the extent possible; note informalities and drawing deficiencies; require specification revision to idiomatic English/US practice; reject claims under 35 U.S.C. 112 if informal.
guidance: Specifics: (A) reasonable search insofar as invention can be understood (if incomprehensible, state no search made), (B) point out informalities via attachments (MPEP § 707.07(a)), (C) require spec revision to idiomatic English and US practice, (D) reject informal claims for failing to define the invention per 35 U.S.C. 112 (a blanket rejection usually sufficient). Treat multiple obviously informal claims as a single claim for fee and examination. Encourage preliminary amendment within ~3 months to correct obvious informalities but do not permit new matter. Burden is on applicant to revise.

name: Search Duties and Treatment of Previous Examiner's Search
description: After reading the specification and claims, the examiner searches the prior art; the invention should be thoroughly understood before search. When assigned after actions by another examiner, give full faith and credit to the previous examiner's search and action unless there is a clear error or knowledge of other prior art.
guidance: Examiners should not take an entirely new approach or perform a new search merely in hope of finding something; see MPEP § 904–904.03 for searching. Informal cases still receive a search to avoid piecemeal prosecution. If a clear error or new pertinent art exists, examiner may revisit prior conclusions.

name: Authority to Require Information under 37 CFR 1.105
description: In course of examining or treating a matter in a pending or abandoned application, patent, or reexamination, the examiner or other Office employee may require submission from individuals identified under § 1.56(c) or any assignee of such information as may be reasonably necessary to properly examine or treat the matter.
guidance: Examples enumerated by 37 CFR 1.105(a)(1) include: (i) particularly relevant commercial databases known to inventors; (ii) whether a prior art search was made and what was searched; (iii)-(v) copies of non-patent literature/published applications/patents related to the claimed invention or used in drafting or invention process; (vi) identification of what is being improved; (vii) identification of any use of the claimed invention known to inventors at filing. Assignee-held information may also be required when assignee asserted right to prosecute.

name: Scope and Standard for Making a Requirement for Information (Reasonable Necessity)
description: There must be a reasonable basis for the information required that would aid in the examination or treatment of the matter. The scope should be narrowly defined and a requirement may be made only when the examiner has a reasonable basis for requiring information.
guidance: A requirement places substantial burden on applicant and should focus the reason and scope of expected response. It is not a substitute for the examiner performing a search (examiner must search per MPEP § 704.01 and §§ 904–904.03). Criteria generally met where (A) claimed subject matter cannot be adequately searched by class or keyword among patents and typical non-patent sources (e.g., new tech area), or (B) the application file or lack of relevant prior art found justifies asking applicant if he/she has information relevant to patentability. When the applicant is likely to be most knowledgeable (scarcity of art) requiring areas of search is justified.

name: Examples of Information Reasonably Required (non-exhaustive list)
description: Other examples (not exhaustive) of information that may be reasonably required include: name/citation of relevant indexed journal or treatise; trade name of goods/services embodying claimed subject matter; citations and copies of advertising/promotional literature for such goods/services; journal articles describing such goods/services; trade names/providers of competitors; written descriptions/analyses prepared by inventors/assignees about competing goods/services; identification of pending or abandoned applications by the inventors/assignee disclosing similar subject matter; reply to a protest under 37 CFR 1.291; explanation of technical material in a publication (e.g., inventor’s publication); identification of changes in reformatted continuing applications; mark-up for CIPs showing added subject matter; comments on new Federal Circuit decisions; publication dates of undated documents.
guidance: This list (704.11(a) A–M and others) provides concrete examples of the types of supporting background, commercial, or documentary material that an examiner may reasonably request to properly determine prior art context and patentability. These items are illustrative and not exhaustive.

name: Timing and Appropriateness for Making a Requirement for Information
description: A requirement under 37 CFR 1.105 is discretionary and may be made at any time once necessity is recognized; optimum time is prior to or with a first action on the merits because the examiner can most readily consider and apply the response. Ordinarily a request should not be made with or after a final rejection.
guidance: Prior to first action: appropriate where search/preliminary analysis shows claimed matter cannot be adequately searched, e.g., new tech area; factors to consider include whether IDS submitted, adequacy of background, related documents written by inventor/assignee not submitted, references to non-patent literature without copies supplied, admissions in specification unfamiliar to examiner, etc. With the first action: may be combined with a first-action rejection if file or lack of prior art justifies asking applicant. Not appropriate with first-action allowance or Ex parte Quayle. After first action: may be appropriate when file justifies asking applicant, but rarely based on lack of relevant prior art; requirements should generally be in non-final actions because reply must be considered. Under limited circumstances, requirements may be made in issued or abandoned applications (e.g., revival, change of inventorship, reexamination).

name: Expungement of Information: Petition Standards under 37 CFR 1.59
description: Information in an application will not be expunged and returned except as provided in 37 CFR 1.59(b). Information forming part of the original disclosure (specification including claims, drawings, and any preliminary amendment incorporated into the oath/declaration) will not be expunged. An applicant may request expungement of other information by petition under 37 CFR 1.59(b) with required fee and must establish to the Commissioner's satisfaction that return is appropriate.
guidance: Return of information originally submitted pursuant to MPEP § 724.02 is appropriate where the petitioner satisfies factors (e.g., trade secret/proprietary/unintentional submission causing irreparable harm/not otherwise public/commitment to retain/establishment that info is not material under 1.56/fee). For inadvertently submitted information, petitioner must satisfy criteria including showing unintentional submission and irreparable harm, and include petition fee. Information that is part of the original disclosure is ordinarily not expungable; petitions to expunge original disclosure require an additional waiver under 37 CFR 1.183 and are ordinarily denied.

name: Written-description requirement (35 U.S.C. § 112)
description: The [patent] specification shall contain a written description of the invention, and of the manner and process of making and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to which it pertains, or with which it is most nearly connected, to make and use the same, and shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor or joint inventor of carrying out the invention.
guidance: Statutory mandate; purpose is to put the public in possession of what the party claims as his own invention. The AIA amendments do not alter the written-description analysis here. The written-description requirement is a prerequisite for patenting and the 'hallmark' of the requirement is demonstration of possession in the specification.

name: Demonstrating possession by disclosure of all limitations
description: An applicant may show possession of the claimed invention by describing it with all of its limitations using 'such descriptive means as words, structures, figures, diagrams, formulas, etc.'
guidance: The specification must disclose the claimed subject matter with sufficient particularity and clarity so that a POSA would understand that the inventor invented what is claimed. Mere aspirational, exploratory, or theoretical research without disclosure of the claimed limitations is insufficient.

name: State-of-the-art / priority-date focus
description: Written description is judged based on the state of the art as of the priority date; evidence illuminating the state of the art subsequent to the priority date is not relevant to written description.
guidance: Claims added later or clinical results obtained after the filing/priority date cannot be used to supply written-description support for an earlier filing date. The inquiry asks what the POSA could deduce from the specification as of the filing date.

name: Burden and standard of proof; appellate review
description: Whether a claim meets the written-description requirement is a question of fact reviewed for clear error on appeal. Patent invalidity under the written-description doctrine must be established by clear and convincing evidence.
guidance: District-court fact findings (including witness credibility) receive deference on appeal; appellate courts should not reweigh credibility absent a definite and firm conviction that a mistake was made.

name: When claiming results: express-result claims require adequate support
description: An inventor need not prove that a claimed pharmaceutical compound actually achieves a certain result, but when the inventor expressly claims that result, the result must be supported by adequate disclosure in the specification.
guidance: If the claim expressly recites a therapeutic result (e.g., a therapeutically effective amount for treating a disease), the specification must contain disclosure that supports that asserted result as of the filing date; mere later demonstration of efficacy does not retroactively supply written-description support.

name: Blaze-marks doctrine for genus-to-species claims
description: When a specification discloses a broad genus and the claims recite a particular species within that genus, the specification must provide sufficient 'blaze marks' to guide a reader through the disclosed possibilities toward the claimed species.
guidance: Laundry-list or broad genus disclosures without guidance are insufficient to support species claims. Blaze marks are required when the disclosure is a large number of unmarked possibilities; if the specification specifically points out the claimed species (or otherwise provides guidance), blaze marks may be satisfied.

name: Avoid conflating written description with obviousness/POSA expectations
description: The written-description inquiry is distinct from obviousness; what a POSA would expect regarding success from the prior art (obviousness context) should not be overlaid onto the written-description inquiry.
guidance: Written description asks whether the specification demonstrates possession as of the filing date, not whether a POSA would have expected the claimed invention to be successful based on prior-art analysis. Caution: statements about POSA expectations may be relevant only insofar as they reflect what the specification itself would have taught a POSA.

name: Specific claim limitations (e.g., dosages, indications) require linking disclosure
description: Claims that recite a specific parameter (such as a particular dosage for a therapeutic indication) must be supported by the specification such that a POSA would understand that the inventor possessed that specific parameter for the claimed use as of the filing date.
guidance: A single, passing mention of a specific dose buried in a broad range and not linked to the claimed indication may be insufficient. Anti-patterns: (1) listing broad ranges labeled 'effective' without tying particular values to the claimed therapeutic effect; (2) 'anchoring' a particular dose among broad ranges that also include known-ineffective or implausible doses.

name: Objective inquiry into the specification as a whole
description: The specification must reasonably convey to those skilled in the art that the inventor had possession of the claimed subject matter; the inquiry considers the specification as a whole.
guidance: Isolated passages must be read in context. The court will assess the overall disclosure (methods, examples, definitions, figures) to determine whether the claimed invention is supported. However, selecting only selectively plucked disclosures to assemble claim support is disfavored.

name: Specification definitions affect scope of claimed terms
description: If the specification defines a claim term (e.g., 'therapeutically effective amount'), that definition informs the written-description inquiry and what a POSA would understand the claim to mean.
guidance: Definitions in the specification that tie claimed terms to certain outcomes (clinical or biological) will shape whether the disclosure supports the claimed result; parties cannot later recharacterize the meaning inconsistent with the specification to cure a written-description defect.

name: Statutory enablement requirement (35 U.S.C. §112(a))
description: The specification must contain a written description of the invention and of the manner and process of making and using it 'in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art ... to make and use the same.'
guidance: The disclosure must enable a person having ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA) to make and use the full scope of what is claimed. The article repeatedly cites the statutory text and explains that enablement is not satisfied unless the full claimed scope is taught.

name: Claim particularity and definiteness (35 U.S.C. §112(b))
description: Claims must 'particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the inventor ... regards as the invention.'
guidance: Claims define the metes-and-bounds of the monopoly; drafters seek breadth but must remain within what the specification supports. Overbroad or vague claiming risks invalidation under the disclosure requirements and other doctrines (e.g., indefiniteness).

name: Structural claims (what to disclose for structure-based claiming)
description: Claims that describe the elements of an invention in relation to each other and their arrangement (example: bicycle pulley components).
guidance: Structural claims disclose elements and interactions so a PHOSITA can construct the invention; when structure is disclosed, enablement is generally straightforward for those embodiments described.

name: Functional claims / means-plus-function (§112(f))
description: An element may be expressed as a means or step for performing a specified function without reciting structure, but the claim is construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents.
guidance: Functional claiming allows describing results rather than structure, but patent scope is limited to the structures (and equivalents) actually disclosed in the specification. The statutory text governs; courts construe such claims to the corresponding disclosed structure and equivalents.

name: Genus claims and the 'quality common' requirement
description: Genus claims cover species sharing a common attribute or property; to validly claim a genus an inventor must identify a 'quality common' to all members that distinguishes them and is adapted to the claimed use (Incandescent Lamp).
guidance: Courts (e.g., Incandescent Lamp) will invalidate genus claims if the specification only discloses a few species without showing the common characteristic across the claimed genus; broad genus claims must teach how to select/identify members of the genus.

name: O’Reilly v. Morse principle (no claiming all manifestations without disclosure)
description: An inventor cannot claim an entire technology or 'every mode' of accomplishing a result unless the specification enables all such manifestations.
guidance: Morse's eighth claim (claiming all uses of galvanic current) was invalidated because it claimed far more than Morse had described/enabled. Anti-pattern: claiming a broad result without teaching how to achieve all implementations.

name: Full-scope enablement test
description: A patent's specification must enable the full scope of the invention as defined by its claims; enablement must cover the full range claimed without undue experimentation (endorsed by Amgen and earlier Federal Circuit cases).
guidance: Courts evaluate whether the disclosure teaches how to make and use the full claimed range; claiming a broad parameter or range without enabling embodiments across that range risks invalidation (illustrated by MagSil, Idenix, and Amgen).

name: In re Wands undue experimentation factors (eight-factor test)
description: Factors used to evaluate whether practicing the invention over the full scope would require undue experimentation: (1) quantity of experimentation necessary, (2) amount of direction/guidance presented, (3) presence/absence of working examples, (4) nature of the invention, (5) state of the prior art, (6) relative skill of those in the art, (7) predictability/unpredictability of the art, and (8) breadth of the claims.
guidance: These eight Wands factors are weighed holistically; presence of working examples, clear guidance, predictable art, and narrower claim breadth favor enablement. Cases apply these factors to determine whether experimentation is 'undue.'

name: Predictability of the art and PHOSITA skill are central considerations
description: Enablement analysis depends critically on how predictable the field is and what a PHOSITA can do given the specification and prior art.
guidance: Fields that are unpredictable (e.g., novel biotech) make broad claims harder to enable; courts consider the PHOSITA's skill level and available prior art in assessing whether undue experimentation would be required.

name: Written description: proof of possession (showing actual invention)
description: The specification must show that the inventor 'actually invented' the claimed invention—mere statement of desired result or function without description of the invention is insufficient.
guidance: Courts look for descriptions (e.g., sequences, structures, working examples) that demonstrate possession of the claimed invention. Anti-pattern: claiming a genus based on functional description alone without species or structural detail.

name: Antibody-specific enablement issues (the 'antibody exception' and its decline)
description: Historically, courts applied a lower enablement/written-description standard to antibody patents (the antibody exception / newly characterized antigen test), treating antibodies functionally; Amgen rejects tech-exceptionalism and applies the full-scope enablement test to antibodies.
guidance: Because antibodies are often conceived functionally (many antibodies can bind the same antigen), courts previously allowed broader claims based on functional teaching; Amgen realigns antibody enablement with statutory text—patents must enable the full claimed genus or provide sufficient species/structural disclosure (e.g., sequences).

name: Case-law examples applying full-scope enablement (MagSil, Idenix, Amgen)
description: MagSil invalidated claims that claimed resistive change ranges not enabled by the specification; Idenix invalidated claims requiring screening of many candidate compounds; Amgen held antibody genus claims invalid for lack of enablement of full scope.
guidance: These decisions illustrate how courts apply the full-scope/undue-experimentation principles: claims encompassing large unexplained ranges or requiring massive screening are vulnerable. Examples provide practical indicators (e.g., claimed ranges vs. disclosed achievements).

name: Practical disclosure strategies to meet enablement for broad coverage
description: To enable broader scopes, applicants can (a) disclose species/working examples (e.g., sequences), (b) provide clear methods and guidance for making/using embodiments, (c) disclose predictive correlations/common quality for the genus, or (d) enumerate many species (e.g., listing many sequences).
guidance: The article discusses hypotheticals where AI could allow listing large numbers of sequences (10,000) or providing AI model inputs/training data as a way to enable broad genus claims. Tradeoffs include USPTO/examiner workload and potential written-description/utility questions.

name: Policy principle: quid pro quo — monopoly in exchange for teaching
description: The fundamental patent rationale requires balancing claim scope with the disclosure given; patents grant limited monopolies so long as the public receives sufficient teaching to practice the invention.
guidance: This normative principle underlies enablement/written-description doctrine and motivates courts to invalidate claims that claim more than the disclosure justifies (preventing 'taking more benefit than given').

name: Arrangement of application elements (37 CFR 1.154)
description: The elements of the design application, if applicable, should appear in the following order: (1) Design application transmittal form; (2) Fee transmittal form; (3) Application data sheet (§ 1.76); (4) Specification; (5) Drawings or photographs; (6) The inventor's oath or declaration (§ 1.153(b)).
guidance: The specification should include sections in order: (1) Preamble (name of applicant, title of design, brief description of nature and intended use); (2) Cross-reference to related applications (unless in ADS); (3) Statement regarding federally sponsored research or development; (4) Description of the figure(s) of the drawing; (5) Feature description; (6) A single claim. Section headings should be uppercase without underlining or bold.

name: Title must designate particular article (37 CFR 1.153)
description: The title of the design must designate the particular article in which the design is embodied; no description other than reference to the drawing is ordinarily required.
guidance: The title identifies the article and may contribute to defining the scope of the claim. The title may be directed to the entire article or only a portion but may not be directed to less than the claimed design shown in full lines. A descriptive, accurate title aids classification and public notice. Amendments to title must have antecedent basis and not introduce new matter. Title and claim must correspond; examiners should object to inconsistencies under 37 CFR 1.153.

name: Title/claim correspondence and examiner latitude
description: Because the claim defines the subject matter, examiners should afford substantial latitude in title/claim language but require amendment if language is clearly misdescriptive, inaccurate, or unclear (would result in a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b)).
guidance: Use of vague terms like 'or the like' directed to the environment is allowed for environment wording in many cases, but indefiniteness can arise when such language refers to the area of articles defining the subject matter. Amendments to the title must be made throughout the application (except oath/declaration).

name: Permissible specification statements
description: Permissible statements include: (1) description of appearance of portions not illustrated; (2) description disclaiming portions not shown as forming no part of claimed design; (3) statement indicating purpose of broken lines (environmental structure/boundaries); (4) statement denoting nature and intended use; (5) 'characteristic features' statement describing a feature of novelty or nonobviousness.
guidance: Permissible statements must be present in the original filing if they later serve as antecedent basis. A 'characteristic features' statement may be included but may not serve as the basis for determining patentability—the overall appearance controls. Examiners will not suggest the inclusion of a characteristic feature statement; it is at applicant’s option.

name: Impermissible specification statements
description: Not permissible: (1) disclaimer statements directed to any portion of the claimed design shown in solid lines in the drawings (not permitted in specification of an issued design patent, though may be included in original application for antecedent basis); (2) statements describing or suggesting other embodiments not illustrated (except mirror images or shapes evident from shown view); (3) statements describing matters directed to function or unrelated to design.
guidance: Such statements, if included improperly, should be canceled; they may constitute new matter or improperly broaden scope. See MPEP § 2909.02 for international application disclaimers.

name: Design patents concern ornamental appearance only
description: Design patent applications are concerned solely with the ornamental appearance of an article of manufacture; functional and/or structural features are of no concern in design cases.
guidance: Function and structure are handled in utility patents. Avoid functional language in design specifications and claims.

name: Single claim requirement (37 CFR 1.153)
description: A design patent application may only include a single claim. The claim shall be in formal terms to the ornamental design for the article (specifying name) as shown, or as shown and described. More than one claim is neither required nor permitted.
guidance: The standard claim wording is 'The ornamental design for [article] as shown.' If the specification includes descriptive matter or modified forms, add 'and described' after 'shown.' The article description in the claim should be consistent with the title.

name: Full lines vs. broken lines in drawings
description: Full (solid) lines in the drawing show the claimed design; broken lines may be used for some purposes (e.g., environmental structure) but are not permitted to indicate unimportant or immaterial portions of the claimed design.
guidance: Broken lines may not be used to show hidden planes/surfaces or alternate positions of design components with full and broken lines in same view. Use broken lines to indicate environment or boundaries that form no part of design and explain their purpose in the specification.

name: Sufficiency and clarity of drawings/photographs (37 CFR 1.152)
description: The design must be represented by a drawing that complies with § 1.84 and must contain a sufficient number of views to constitute a complete disclosure of the appearance of the design. Drawings/photographs must be clear and complete so that nothing of the design is left to conjecture.
guidance: Use appropriate surface shading to show character/contour (solid black shading only to represent the color black). Photographs submitted in lieu of drawings must be limited to the design claimed and must not show environmental structure. If inconsistencies among views render overall appearance unclear, the claim should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a)/(b).

name: Views required and when a single planar view suffices
description: Drawings should contain a sufficient number of views (front, rear, top, bottom, sides) to disclose the complete appearance. Where three-dimensional aspects are not claimed, a single plan- or planar-view may be sufficient.
guidance: Perspective views are suggested for 3D designs. If a perspective view clearly discloses surfaces, other views may not be required. Duplicate or flat views without ornamentation may be omitted if the specification explains omission (e.g., 'other side identical' or 'bottom flat and devoid of surface ornamentation').

name: Color and lining-for-color guidance
description: Where drawings are lined for color, include the statement 'The drawing is lined for color.' Lining entire surfaces for color may interfere with clear showing of design because shading cannot be used simultaneously to define contours.
guidance: If color drawings/photographs filed, color is considered integral to disclosure and claim; omission of color later is permitted only if it is clear applicant had possession of underlying configuration without color at filing. Some designs disclosed in color cannot be accurately depicted in black-and-white lined drawings (e.g., multiple shades).

name: Use and description of broken lines (environment and boundaries)
description: Broken lines may illustrate environmental structure if clearly designated as environment in the specification; a descriptive statement explaining broken lines should be inserted (e.g., 'The broken line showing of [structure] is for the purpose of illustrating [portions of the article/environmental structure] and forms no part of the claimed design.').
guidance: Where superimposed broken lines showing environmental structure obscure full-line claimed disclosure, include a separate figure showing broken lines in addition to figures showing only claimed subject matter. When broken lines define a boundary of the design, use the statement: 'The [type] broken line(s) define the bounds of the claimed design and form no part thereof.'

name: Consistency among views and consequences of inconsistency
description: When inconsistencies are found among the views, the examiner should object and request that the views be made consistent; if inconsistencies are so significant that overall appearance is unclear, reject the claim under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b) as nonenabling and indefinite.
guidance: Corrected drawing sheets must be submitted to resolve inconsistencies. In appeals, drawings must be corrected prior to appeal if required.

name: Limits on combining photographs and ink drawings
description: Photographs and ink drawings are not permitted to be combined as formal drawings in one application.
guidance: If photographs are used in lieu of ink drawings, they must be limited to the design claimed and not disclose environmental structure. Combining the two leads to high probability of inconsistencies between elements.

name: Problem–solution / essential elements analysis
description: Essential elements of a claim are those elements that provide the solution to the identified problem (e.g., data acquisition vs data analysis).
guidance: Identify the problem the inventors set out to address in light of the specification and the common general knowledge (CGK) of the POSITA. Elements that provide means to acquire or implement the solution to that identified problem are essential elements of the claim. Elements that solve a different identified problem (e.g., data analysis) may be non-essential for a particular claim.

name: Statutory subject-matter (section 2)
description: Claims must define subject-matter that falls within a category of invention as defined in section 2 of the Patent Act.
guidance: When construing claims, ensure the essential elements put the claim within an allowable category of invention under section 2.

name: Novelty (subsection 28.2(1))
description: A claim is novel if no single prior art document discloses the essential elements of the construed claim.
guidance: Compare the construed essential elements to a single prior art reference. A commercially known plurality-measuring device that does not specifically acquire only the claimed subset of data does not anticipate. Note that change of claim wording (e.g., 'comprising' vs 'consisting') can affect novelty (e.g., 'consisting solely of' may be novel where 'comprising' is not).

name: Sufficiency of the description (subsection 27(3))
description: The description must 'correctly and fully describe the invention and its operation or use as contemplated by the inventor' and must be enabling.
guidance: Description must be clear, accurate, free from avoidable obscurity, and sufficiently full so nothing not described may be validly claimed. It must enable a POSITA to practise the full scope of the claimed invention without inventive effort. If practicing the full scope requires inventive ingenuity, the description is insufficient and claims are unsupported. The description should enable answers to 'What is your invention?: How does it work?'. An objection under subsection 27(3) may be raised where a broad claim is supported only by its own verbatim language or where the description fails to support prediction of utility.

name: Defect for unsupported claim breadth (relation to section 60 / subsection 27(3))
description: Claims that define more than the description supports may be defective under section 60 of the Patent Rules and/or subsection 27(3) of the Patent Act.
guidance: If claims are broader than the specific examples or embodiments in the description (e.g., a single polypeptide described but claims covering many variants), examiners may identify defects; claim scope must be supported by the description.

name: Defect for lack of clarity/distinctness (subsection 27(4))
description: Claims must be defined in distinct and explicit terms; use of variable symbols or vague terms can render a claim non-compliant with subsection 27(4).
guidance: When structure is needed to realize full scope, claims must include sufficient structural definition. Functional-only definitions may be unacceptable if they lack structural support or lead to unclear scope.

name: Defining biomolecules by structure (sequence identification)
description: For biomolecules, the clearest way to define a molecule is by its structure (e.g., nucleotide or amino acid sequence) and claim should explicitly refer to a SEQ ID NO that points to the sequence listing.
guidance: Claims to 'SEQ ID NO:x' alone may be interpreted as claims to mere information and be non-compliant with section 2; prefer claims like 'DNA encoding the protein comprising amino acids 1-260 of SEQ ID NO:2'. Beware of variable symbols (X, n) in sequences: they may make the claimed subject-matter indistinct.

name: Functional claim limitations for biomolecules
description: Functional language can be used to define biomolecules where it provides useful distinction, but the entire scope must be clear and fully supported by the description.
guidance: Functional language is acceptable if POSITA would not need inventive ingenuity to practise the full scope and representative embodiments are disclosed. If functional language requires inventive effort to realise the scope or makes the claim overly broad, the claim may be defective under section 60 of the Rules and/or subsection 27(4). When structure is needed to realise scope, the claim should include structural limitations in addition to function (e.g., percent identity plus statement of same biological activity). Example: where only one polypeptide sequence with xylanase activity is disclosed, broad functional claims or broad percent-identity claims without functional limitation may be defective or anticipated by prior art.

name: Avoid vague similarity/homology terms
description: Terms like 'substantially identical', 'homology', or 'similarity' are inadequate without clear definition and can render a claim indefinite.
guidance: Prefer explicit percent identity thresholds (e.g., 'at least 95% identical to SEQ ID NO:7') and use 'identity' rather than 'homology'. If terms like 'similarity' are used, provide a clear definition of what is meant.

name: Claims defined by hybridization
description: Claims that define nucleic acids by hybridization to a target must sufficiently define the hybridization conditions and parameters.
guidance: Because hybridization/wash conditions affect which nucleic acids are captured, claims relying on hybridization should specify parameters to avoid indefiniteness. If the target is a large family (degenerate sequences), scope can become unclear. If claim implies that a hybridizing nucleic acid encodes a functional polypeptide, the claim may be defective under subsection 27(4) unless the relationship is clear; indicate whether hybridization is to the complement where appropriate.

name: Obviousness considerations for sequence-based claims
description: Given an amino acid sequence in the prior art, nucleic acids encoding it are often obvious because they can be deduced by back-translation; conversely a known nucleic acid makes the amino acid sequence obvious.
guidance: Broad claims to 'a nucleic acid encoding protein X' may be obvious where the protein sequence is known. However, selection of a particular nucleic acid species with unexpected/advantageous properties can be inventive and should be analyzed as selection-type claims. Analyze claims against the four-step approach for obviousness, considering whether particular sequence selection would have been obvious to POSITA.

name: Identification of sequences used outside the sequence listing (SEQ ID NO references)
description: If a sequence included in the sequence listing is referred to in the claims, drawings or other parts of the description, the reference must include the sequence identification number preceded by 'SEQ ID NO:'.
guidance: Failure to identify sequences by their SEQ ID NO when referenced can be a defect under subsection 58(4). Example: specify both the sequence and '(SEQ ID NO:x)' when listing primers or oligonucleotides in the specification.

name: Case management across litigation phases to support recoverability
description: From document production to legal filings to depositions to expert opinion to trial – all phases of a case can be managed to support the recoverability (or lack thereof) of lost profit damages.
guidance: Proactively developing evidence (documents, witness statements, financial records), coordinating expert work, and framing issues in pleadings and discovery increases the likelihood that lost-profit claims will be provable; attorneys should plan evidentiary development with experts in mind.

name: Anticipation — Reeves Brothers eight-pronged formulations
description: Reeves Brothers (Justice Gibson) enumerated eight formulations used to determine whether prior art is anticipatory (e.g., give an exact prior description; give directions which will inevitably result in something within the claims; give clear and unmistakable directions; convey information so a person grappling with the same problem can say 'that gives me what I wish', etc.).
guidance: The eight formulations were not intended to be cumulative; they are various ways courts have expressed the test for anticipation. A single prior document can be anticipatory if it meets the relevant formulation(s).

name: Anticipation by publication — Beloit standard
description: From Beloit Canada Ltd. v. Valmet Oy: a prior single publication must contain all information, which for practical purposes is needed to produce the claimed invention without exercise of any inventive skill; the publication must contain clear directions such that a skilled person following it would in every case and without possibility of error be led to the claimed invention.
guidance: Anticipation requires a single prior disclosure that is enabling and sufficiently specific; aggregation of multiple documents to reach the invention does not establish anticipation.

name: Apotex two-part test for anticipation: disclosure and enablement
description: The Supreme Court in Apotex adopted a two-branch test: (1) prior disclosure — the prior art must indicate to a person skilled in the art that it discloses the special advantages of the later invention; and (2) enablement — the prior art must enable the skilled person to make or perform the later invention without undue burden.
guidance: Disclosure and enablement are distinct: disclosure establishes that the prior art points to the invention; enablement assesses whether a skilled person could actually make it without undue burden. Routine trials are acceptable; prolonged or arduous trial-and-error is not. The skilled person's common general knowledge may be used to supplement the prior patent. The prior patent must be considered as a whole (specification and claims).

name: Enablement — non-exhaustive factors (from Apotex)
description: The Court listed four non-exhaustive factors for enablement: consider the prior patent as a whole incl. specification and claims; allow the skilled person to use common general knowledge; require enough information to perform/make the later invention without undue burden (taking the field's nature into account); and obvious errors/omissions that a skilled person could readily correct do not defeat enablement.
guidance: Assessment of undue burden depends on the field: where experimentation is common, the threshold for undue burden is higher. If inventive steps would be required to implement the disclosure, the prior art is not enabling.

name: Non-obviousness requirement (s.28.3)
description: Section 28.3 of the Patent Act: the subject-matter of a claim must not have been obvious on the claim date to a person skilled in the art, having regard to information disclosed more than one year before the filing date by the applicant (or someone who obtained knowledge from the applicant) and information disclosed before the claim date by others.
guidance: This codifies the requirement that an invention include some element of inventiveness beyond the prior art. Like s.28.2, s.28.3 includes a one-year grace period for applicant disclosures.

name: Requirement to state claims (definite statement of invention to be protected)
description: The specification must conclude with a definite statement of what the applicant considers to be his invention and wishes to protect (i.e., express claims).
guidance: Express requirement in Norway and Russia; used by examiners/commissions to determine scope and for publication/advertising prior to opposition.

name: Patenting cost scenarios and assumptions
description: Cost scenarios (2, 7, 15 countries) assume an applicant that is a large company based in the USA, filing electronically when possible; priority year 2006; last maintenance year 2016; patent application has 30 pages (2 drawings), 15 claims, 2 convention priorities.
guidance: Methodology excludes in-house and pre-filing costs. No legal costs counted for USPTO procedure (assumed applicant can proceed without external support). ISA selection depends on scenario (USPTO or EPO). No Chapter II demand in the scenarios. List of countries for each scenario provided in Annex D.

name: Validity Confidence is High
description: The patent would likely survive a serious validity challenge.
guidance: Signals include: prior art was thoroughly searched and addressed during prosecution; independent claims are clearly differentiated from cited art; specification clearly enables and describes the full claim scope; subject-matter eligibility is unambiguous. High validity confidence reduces the patent's probabilistic invalidity risk.

name: Scope Confidence is High
description: A reader can predict claim construction and the patent's scope.
guidance: Look for: claim terms explicitly defined or having settled meaning in the art; prosecution history showing consistent claim interpretation; absence of ambiguous functional language without 35 U.S.C. §112(f) treatment; means-plus-function elements with clear corresponding structure in the specification. High scope confidence makes enforcement and licensing outcomes more predictable.

name: Continuation Pyramids (quality defect)
description: Long chains of continuations used to capture competitor products and expand claim scope.
guidance: Continuation pyramids signal post-hoc claim drafting and are often vulnerable to written-description challenges. Presence of extensive continuation practice lowers probabilistic quality even if individual claims were granted.

name: Functional Claiming Without Structural Support (quality defect)
description: Claims expressed in result-oriented or 'means for' language lacking corresponding structure in the specification.
guidance: Such functional claiming (e.g., issues highlighted by Williamson v. Citrix) creates vulnerability under §112 and reduces scope confidence because the claim may lack adequate structural support for enforcement.

name: Litigation Anomalies (quality signal)
description: Patent owner behavior in litigation that indicates weak underlying claims.
guidance: Examples include shifting claim construction positions across cases. Such tactical litigation behavior signals weaknesses in scope or validity and reduces confidence in the patent's probabilistic quality.

name: Probability asserted claim construction holds at Markman
description: Operative question: What is the realistic probability the asserted claim construction holds at Markman?
guidance: Assess clarity of claim terms, presence of explicit definitions, prosecution arguments, and intrinsic evidence that would constrain construction. Predictability of Markman outcomes relates directly to scope confidence.

name: Prosecution history supports non-trivial scope versus perfunctory prosecution
description: Operative question: Does the prosecution history support a non-trivial scope, or was prosecution perfunctory?
guidance: Evaluate whether claims were substantively negotiated and justified in view of art, or if grants appear routine/uncalled-for. Perfunctory prosecution reduces confidence in both scope and validity.

name: Elements of negligence claim for construction-defect (jury instruction standard)
description: To recover on negligence the plaintiffs must prove by a preponderance of the evidence (a) that the defendant was negligent, (b) that the defendant's negligence was a legal cause (proximate cause) of the plaintiffs' harm, and (c) that the plaintiffs suffered damages.
guidance: Superior court instructed the jury defining negligence and proximate cause; the jury's special verdicts finding negligence and causation support judgment. Appellate review may affirm on the independent negligence basis even if other theories (agency, partnership) are contested.

name: Standards for finding agency, joint venture, or partnership (fact-intensive inquiry)
description: Findings that defendants were agent, joint venturers, or partners may be based on conduct and relationships over time (e.g., shared activities, representations, business dealings) and may support joint and several liability when the jury so finds.
guidance: The jury found Riem to be Chisum's agent and that a partnership/joint venture existed; appellants argued insufficient evidence. The opinion reviews the factual record (brochures, mill ownership, representations) and sustains the jury verdicts. Although the court did not list formal elements in one place, it applied standard sufficiency-of-evidence review to these factual claims.

name: Constitutional claims regarding statute application — equal protection and due process contentions
description: A claim that a state court's failure to apply a statute of limitations to a nonresident amounts to denial of equal protection or deprivation of property without due process requires showing discriminatory application or procedural unfairness violating the Fourteenth Amendment.
guidance: Appellant urged that denying enforcement of the statutory limitation against a nonresident denied equal protection and due process. The brief frames such constitutional arguments as grounds for Supreme Court review (certiorari) when state action treats residents and nonresidents differently or ignores statute-based protections.

name: Pre-claim questions (understand the invention)
description: Prior to writing claim(s) answer these questions: What is the invention? What are the elements that make up the invention? How do the elements relate to one another? Do you have more than one invention? Tangible: Apparatus, machine, composition. Method: Making or Using. Are there multiple embodiments of the same invention?
guidance: Use these questions to identify components, relationships, statutory class (product vs method), and multiple embodiments before drafting claims.

name: Legal requirement: at least one claim particularly pointing out and distinctly defining the invention
description: A nonprovisional patent application must have at least one claim particularly pointing out and distinctly defining the invention.
guidance: Ensure claims meet this statutory requirement; claims are the legal definition of what is enforced. Claims must conform to the rest of the specification.

name: Independent vs dependent claim forms
description: A claim may be written in independent or dependent form. An independent claim is a standalone claim that contains all the limitations necessary to define an invention. A dependent claim must refer to a claim previously set forth and must further limit that claim.
guidance: Dependent claims incorporate by reference all limitations of the claim to which they refer; dependent claims must add a further limitation (do not remove or replace elements of the parent claim).

name: Support and enablement (written description/enablement)
description: Claims must be fully supported and enabled by the disclosure.
guidance: Use consistent terminology between specification and claims; ensure claim terms find clear support or antecedent basis in the description so terms are clearly understood by reference to the description (refer to 35 U.S.C. §112 requirements).

name: Claims must be a single sentence and ordered by scope
description: Claims must be drafted as a single sentence. Claims should be arranged in order of scope so the first claim presented is the broadest.
guidance: Format each claim as one sentence (capital letter to start, period at end); place broadest independent claims first to reflect scope ordering.

name: Types of claims by statutory category
description: Product - A claim that is directed to elements that can be: Active (a Device/Apparatus), Non-active (Composition or Article of Manufacture), Combination thereof. Method (Process) - A claim that describes/defines a series of acts or steps for performing a desired function or accomplishing an intended result.
guidance: Choose appropriate claim category for the invention; do not mix multiple statutory classes in a single claim (e.g., 'A widget and method for using same...').

name: Patent claim structure: preamble, transition, claim body
description: A claim has three parts: 1. Preamble: provides context for the claimed invention (may or may not limit). 2. Transitional phrase: establishes whether the claim is 'open', 'closed' or 'partially open'. 3. Claim body: recites the limitations (structure and/or acts in clear, full, concise terms) necessary to define the invention.
guidance: Draft each part carefully: use the preamble for context (avoid unnecessary functional language), choose the transition to control scope, and recite clear limitations in the body.

name: Preamble guidance (Three Basic Rules #1)
description: Every claim needs a preamble, which is the introductory phrase in a claim. The general rule is that the preamble of a claim does not limit the scope of the claim, but try and stay away from functional language.
guidance: Prefer simple nouns ('A shovel...') rather than functional preambles ('A shovel for digging...') unless the preamble is intended to limit claim scope.

name: Transitional phrases and meanings (Three Basic Rules #2)
description: Common transitions: 'comprising', 'consisting essentially of', and 'consisting of.' 'Comprising' means the invention includes but is not limited to the elements identified in the claim. 'Consisting essentially of' limits scope to the specified materials or steps 'and those that do not materially affect the basic and novel characteristic(s)'. 'Consisting of' is closed and limits to the elements identified in the claim.
guidance: Use 'comprising' most commonly for open scope; avoid non-standard transitional phrases (MPEP 2111.03) which may raise interpretation issues.

name: Antecedent basis rule (Three Basic Rules #3)
description: The first time you introduce a limitation you MUST introduce it with either 'a' or 'an' (primary antecedent basis). Subsequently refer to it by 'said' or 'the' (secondary antecedent basis).
guidance: Ensure every term referenced later in the claims has an earlier antecedent; failure causes ambiguity (e.g., referring to 'said lever' without earlier recitation).

name: Antecedent basis clarity issues (examples)
description: A lack of clarity arises where a claim refers to 'said lever' or 'the lever' when the claim contains no earlier recitation of a lever, or when two different levers are recited earlier and it's unclear which is intended.
guidance: Avoid ambiguous cross-references; disambiguate by naming or numbering elements or by clear antecedent language.

name: How to build claim sets (wrapping it all together)
description: Introduce components and characterizations necessary for the invention to work and for it to be different than the prior art. Example pattern: 1. A - insert title - comprising: A, B and C. Then dependent claims adding D, E, and specific characterizations using 'further comprising' and 'wherein.'
guidance: When adding a component use 'further comprising' and explain the connection; when further characterizing something already introduced use 'wherein'. Ensure dependent claims further limit the parent claim (35 U.S.C. 112(d), MPEP 608.01(n)).

name: Drafting approach: focus on the inventive concept
description: Focus on the inventive concept: What features set the invention apart from prior inventions? Identify fundamental elements. Omit unnecessary elements unless they are needed to distinguish over prior inventions. Select broad terms and identify their relationship carefully. Claim review and revision: Remove unnecessary claim elements.
guidance: Aim for claims that capture the core inventive features broadly while excluding unnecessary detail; balance breadth with patentability over prior art.

name: Patentability summary: novelty, non-obviousness, utility
description: A claimed invention must be novel, non-obvious and have a utility.
guidance: Claims alone do not make an invention patentable — ensure invention meets statutory requirements and the specification supports claims; don't treat the patent as a marketing brochure; analyze advantages and multiple inventive features.

name: Identify fundamental elements and prior art awareness
description: Understand the disclosure of the prior inventions. What have competitors previously done? Conduct a patentability search. Define the potential claim elements. Consider alternative embodiments; prior disclosures may help develop alternatives.
guidance: Use prior art search results to shape claim scope and identify novel elements; draft claims to cover key embodiments and reasonable alternatives.

name: Costs versus coverage tradeoff
description: How much can you afford to spend on claims? Independent in excess of 3 = $105 per (micro entity). Total claims in excess of 20 = $20 per (micro entity). Claim fees for small entity are double micro entity. Not just at time of filing, but during prosecution. Consider desired patent scope end state: broadest possible valid claim (longer prosecution) vs claims with a range of claim scopes (higher claim costs).
guidance: Plan claim quantity and scope according to budget and enforcement goals; factor in future prosecution costs.

name: Claim review: avoid too broad or too specific claims
description: Claims that are too broad may encompass prior art and be unpatentable. Claims that are too specific may unduly narrow protection and miss variations of the invention.
guidance: Use examples (slides showing 'too broad' and 'overly specific') to find the balance; iterative review and revision is necessary.

name: Claim drafting DOs (practical checklist)
description: Do: Consider drafting your specification first and then your claims based on terms used in the specification. Think about what legal protection you want and tailor claims accordingly. Look at the claims in patents issued in your field. Particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter regarded as the invention. Review and reconcile both the specification and claims, making necessary additions and corrections so that the claim terms find support (antecedence). Check for antecedent basis issues within the claims. Ensure that dependent claims further limit the claim from which they depend. (35 USC 112(d), MPEP 608.01(n))
guidance: Follow this checklist during drafting and pre-filing review; cross-check spec and claims for support and consistency.

name: Claim drafting CAUTIONS (do nots and pitfalls)
description: Do not use claims covering multiple statutory classes of invention ('A widget and method for using same...'). Do not use non-standard transitional phrases, which may raise questions of interpretation. (MPEP 2111.03). Do not use terms inconsistently between the claims and/or specification (e.g., visor, visor member, visor section...). Do not refer back to only a portion of another claim in a dependent claim (e.g., 'The widget of the apparatus of claim 1...'). Do not use a dependent claim to remove/replace an element from a previously presented claim from which it depends. Do not use functional language that is unconnected to the structure or steps that perform the function. Do not use terms in the claim that are unsupported by the specification. Do not use trademarks or tradenames in the claims; instead use generic terms (e.g., 'hook and loop fastener' instead of Velcro®). Do not use language that merely suggests, makes optional and, thus, does not limit the claim. Avoid using negative limitations unless clearly supported by the written disclosure (specification and drawings).
guidance: Treat this list as drafting red flags to avoid rejections, indefiniteness, inconsistent claim interpretation, or loss of claim scope during prosecution.

name: Board statement on how a claim may be amended (37 CFR 41.50(c))
description: The Board’s opinion may include an explicit statement of how a claim on appeal may be amended to overcome a specific rejection; when such a statement is included appellant has the right to amend in conformity with it, and such amendment will overcome the specific rejection.
guidance: An amendment in conformity with the Board’s explicit statement will overcome the specific rejection. The examiner must ensure the amendment actually conforms. The Board’s making of such a statement is discretionary; an offhand remark that a feature does not appear in a claim is not to be taken as authorization to amend unless the Board expressly states so (ex parte Norlund). The right to amend under 41.50(c) may be exercised only within the period allowed for seeking court review under 37 CFR 1.304.

name: New grounds of rejection by the Board (37 CFR 41.50(b))
description: If the Board has knowledge of grounds not involved in the appeal for rejecting any pending claim, it may include a statement to that effect with reasons, which constitutes a new ground of rejection; such a new ground is not final for judicial review.
guidance: When Board makes a new ground the appellant, within two months from date of decision, must either (1) reopen prosecution by submitting appropriate amendment and/or new evidence so the matter is remanded to the examiner, or (2) request rehearing addressing the new ground and stating with particularity points misapprehended or overlooked. If appellant does not act, appeal as to those claims terminates.

name: Examiner actions when reversed in whole (general guidance)
description: A complete reversal of the examiner’s rejection brings the case up for immediate action by the examiner; the examiner should not regard such reversal as a challenge to make a new search to uncover other references.
guidance: Second examiner should give full faith and credit to the prior examiner’s search. If the examiner has specific knowledge of reference(s) indicating nonpatentability of reversed claims, submit matter to Technology Center Director for authorization to reopen prosecution under 37 CFR 1.198; TC Director approval is placed on action reopening prosecution.

name: Procedure when no claims stand allowed (abandonment)
description: If no claims stand allowed after Board decision and the time for seeking court review has passed without review, proceedings are terminated and the application is to be stamped abandoned and sent to abandoned files; in ex parte reexamination a reexamination certificate should be issued under 37 CFR 1.570.
guidance: Examples illustrate conversion or abandonment when dependent claims were allowable only because of dependency on rejected independent claims. Examiners must follow specified approaches (convert dependent to independent by examiner’s amendment and issue, or set a 1-month time to rewrite dependent claims in independent form with no extensions under 37 CFR 1.136(a); failure results in abandonment).
