name: Shortened statutory period to correct formal matters when period for seeking court review has lapsed
description: When the period under 37 CFR 1.304 for seeking court review has expired and no further action taken by appellant, the proceedings as to rejected claims are terminated and the application will be passed to issue on allowed claims provided formal matters are promptly corrected.
guidance: Applicant required to correct outstanding formal matters within a shortened statutory period set to expire ONE MONTH or THIRTY DAYS, whichever is longer, from mailing date to avoid abandonment. Extensions of time may be granted under 37 CFR 1.136 for these formal corrections.

name: Novelty of the invention
description: A novel invention is one, which has not been disclosed, in the prior art where prior art means everything that has been published, presented or otherwise disclosed to the public on the date of patent... For an invention to be judged as novel, the disclosed information should not be available in the 'prior art'.
guidance: Detailed non-novelty examples/conditions: (a) anticipated by publication in any specification filed in India on or after 1 Jan 1912; (b) anticipated by publication in any document in any country before filing; (c) anticipated if claimed in any other complete specification filed earlier in India (even if published after); (d) anticipated by knowledge, oral or otherwise, in any local or indigenous community. Prior art includes disclosures in any language and any format.

name: Inventive step (non-obviousness)
description: Inventive step is a feature of an invention that involves technical advance as compared to existing knowledge or having economic significance or both, making the invention non obvious to a person skilled in the art. An invention shall not be considered as involving an inventive step, if, having regard to the state of the art, it is obvious to a person skilled in the art.
guidance: Key points: inventive step may include economic significance; judge by asking whether a non-inventive mind would have thought of the alleged invention; consider prior art in relevant field; combining teachings of documents is permissible if obvious to skilled person; assess invention as a whole (not merely parts); mere juxtaposition of known parts is likely obvious unless leading to synergistic effect; selection inventions should show surprising or unexpected technical solution; verifying previous predictions without advancement lacks inventive step. Examiner considerations listed: (a) scope and content of prior art; (b) assessing technical result/economic value; (c) differences between prior art and claimed invention; (d) defining technical problem; (e) final determination whether skilled person could bridge differences.

name: Unity of invention
description: The claim or claims of a complete specification shall relate to a single invention, or to a group of inventions linked so as to form a single inventive concept (S.10(5)). All claims must refer to the same inventive idea.
guidance: Acceptable groupings include: product, process for its manufacture and use of the product; process and apparatus for carrying out the process; product, process for its manufacture and apparatus. Examples provided (spray bottle product, mechanism, process; gene sequence + uses/antibody/kit) illustrate linked claims. If claims define distinct inventions the application should be divided.

name: Sufficiency of disclosure (complete specification)
description: Every complete specification shall (a) fully and particularly describe the invention and its operation or use and method by which it is to be performed; (b) disclose the best method of performing the invention which is known to the applicant and for which he is entitled to claim protection (S.10(4)).
guidance: Complete specification must disclose enough for a person skilled in the art to perform the invention; include deposition details and source/geographical origin of biological material when mentioned. Non-disclosure of source/geographical origin is a formal and substantive defect flagged in examination.

name: Clarity and succinctness of claims
description: The claim or claims of a complete specification shall be clear and succinct and shall be fairly based on the matter disclosed in the specification (S.10(5)).
guidance: Investigate whether claims are clearly and properly worded; whether they are succinct (no unnecessary repetition, verbosity, excessive number, redundancy); whether claims sufficiently define the invention; whether claims are fairly based on and supported by the description and consistent with it.

name: Software/computer program per se exclusion and technical contribution requirement
description: Computer programme per se is not patentable; inventions relating to application of computer program/software may be patentable when claimed in combination with hardware providing a 'technical advancement' over prior art.
guidance: Applicants must describe the technical contribution and how hardware is controlled by software to overcome prior problems; technical character must be clearly shown in claims. Case law examples and reasoning (EPO/UK/US cases) are cited.

name: Drawings: clarity and sufficiency
description: DRAWINGS - clear: figures not numbered; sectional lines not marked; reference letters/numerals not marked; same reference letters used for different parts; part denoted in figure not same as in page; drawings do/do not clearly illustrate features. DRAWINGS - sufficient: arrangement described or claimed should be illustrated.
guidance: Examiners check reproducibility, completeness (number of sheets, figures), that drawings support the description and claims; may require reproducible, correctly marked, and consistent drawings.

name: Claims: clarity, succinctness, definitiveness, consistency
description: CLAIMS - clear: claims not clear in expression or wording. CLAAMS - succinct: unnecessary repetition; verbose; large number; redundant. CLAIMS - definitive: claims do not sufficiently define the invention or are not sufficiently definitive. CLAIMS - consistent: claims not consistent with description, not supported by description, not fairly based on the matter disclosed.
guidance: Examiners must identify and object to unclear, verbose, over-broad, unsupported or inconsistent claims; indicate suggested amendments and grounds for objections.

name: Title: appropriateness and precision
description: TITLE - appropriate: inconsistent with description and claims. TITLE - precise: not precise, not clear in respect of word(s), vernacular words, does not sufficiently indicate the subject.
guidance: Examiner to request replacement or amendment to title to accurately and precisely reflect the invention.

name: Novelty / anticipation checks in examination
description: Novelty: (a) Invention anticipated by (i) prior publication (ii) prior claiming; (b) Claim(s) conflict with claim(s) of [other applications]; (c) Invention claimed in claim(s) prima facie lacking in novelty; (d) Specification not clearly worded; (e) Consideration deferred.
guidance: Examiners must search and identify prior art that anticipates the claimed subject matter and raise objections or defer consideration where necessary.

name: Examination sheet: checklist structure and categories
description: The Examination Sheet enumerates items (numbered) covering bibliographic details, PCT/national phase matters, statement & undertaking, specification components, inventorship, drawings, claims, title, abstract, patentability grounds, novelty, unity, identity, and other formal and substantive checks.
guidance: This structured checklist is to be filled by examiners and used to ensure that all required checks (formal and substantive) are performed uniformly; entries include yes/no flags and spaces for dates/signatures and miscellaneous notes.

name: Assessment of technical contribution for software-related inventions
description: When the invention involves software, the technical problem which needs to be solved by the invention should be sufficiently described as to how the hardware is controlled by the software to overcome the previously described problem. The 'technical character' of the invention should be brought out clearly in the claims.
guidance: Examiner should determine whether the claimed combination of hardware and software yields a technical advancement over prior art; mere automation or business/mental acts performed by software are insufficient; case law examples underscore requirement for 'technical contribution'.

name: Objective relationship test between misconduct and asserted claims
description: Require an objective threshold showing regarding the significance of the withheld or misrepresented information and its relationship to the patent claims before severe remedies are authorized.
guidance: This links remedial severity (e.g., unenforceability) to the factual and legal nexus between the misconduct and the specific claims at issue, to avoid blanket invalidation of entire patents for relatively immaterial misconduct.

name: 'Specific contribution over the prior art' is an improper damages standard
description: The phrase 'specific contribution over the prior art' is unclear, risks relitigation of validity during damages, and effectively imports novelty/nonobviousness-type issues into the damages phase.
guidance: If validity standards need modification, amend sections 102, 103, and 112 rather than section 284. Avoid enabling a second round of claim-construction/validity litigation at the damages phase.

name: Statutory enablement requirement (§112(a))
description: Specification must include "a written description of the invention, and of the manner and process of making and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art . . . to make and use the [invention]."
guidance: This is the baseline statutory command. Evaluation asks whether the disclosure enables a person skilled in the art to make and use the invention as claimed. The Court enforces the statutory language as written and reviews lower-court judgments accordingly.

name: Scope-of-claims vs specification (claims measure the invention)
description: If a patent claims an entire class of processes, machines, manufactures, or compositions of matter, the specification must enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the entire class; the claims measure the invention.
guidance: The broader the claim, the more the specification must enable. Courts compare the full scope of the asserted claims to the enabling disclosure. Precedents: Morse, Incandescent Lamp, Holland Furniture, Continental Paper Bag Co.

name: Enablement proportional to claim breadth
description: The more one claims, the more one must enable — a party seeking a broader monopoly must provide broader enabling disclosure.
guidance: Enablement is not a fixed quantity; it scales with claim breadth. A patentee cannot claim 'sovereignty over [an] entire kingdom' without enabling that kingdom. This principle applies irrespective of technology.

name: Examples plus disclosure of a common quality can suffice
description: A specification need not describe every embodiment if it gives one or a few examples and also discloses 'some general quality . . . running through' the claimed class that imparts a 'peculiar fitness' for the purpose.
guidance: Where the inventor identifies a general, enabling characteristic common to the claimed class, examples together with that disclosed quality can enable the full genus (illustrated by Incandescent Lamp). The specification should reveal how to select or recognize embodiments based on that common quality.

name: Functional claiming requires disclosure of enabling attributes (avoid pure functional drafting)
description: Claims that define a genus by function (what the thing does) still must be supported by disclosure showing how to make and use the full range of embodiments; mere functional description of inputs or components is insufficient.
guidance: Describing a key input or element only by its 'use or function' rather than its physical or chemical properties can render a claim non-enabled if it forces others to engage in 'elaborate experimentation' to find workable embodiments (see Holland Furniture).

name: Mere roadmaps or directions to perform research are insufficient
description: Instruction that amounts to a 'roadmap' (describe the inventor's trial-and-error process) or 'conservative substitution' (make substitutions and test) does not enable a claimed genus when it leaves practitioners to engage in random or extensive trial-and-error.
guidance: If the disclosed methods amount to research assignments or invite 'painstaking experimentation' or a 'hunting license,' they fail enablement. The Court treated Amgen's 'roadmap' and 'conservative substitution' as illustrative anti-patterns.

name: Teaching away / weight of prior-art statements
description: Whether statements in a prior art reference that limit the function or capability of a prior art device constitute teaching away from combining that reference with others.
guidance: Give fair consideration to statements that limit function/capability, but note that simplicity of the prior art is rarely a characteristic that weighs against obviousness of a more complicated device with added function. Case examples: In re Dance (claimed catheter obvious despite primary reference stressing simplicity), Allied Erecting v. Genesis Attachments (advantages/disadvantages do not necessarily obviate motivation to combine). If the prior art teaches that a proposed modification would render a process inoperable or produce undesirable properties, that may support teaching away (see cited cases).

name: Reasonable expectation of success required for obviousness
description: Where there is reason to modify or combine prior art to achieve the claimed invention, a prima facie obviousness rejection also requires a reasonable expectation (likelihood) of success in making the modification or combination to meet the claim limitations.
guidance: Expectation of success refers to the likelihood that combining/modifying prior art would achieve the claimed invention. It may be shown implicitly via the prior art teachings or explicitly; depending on circumstances implicit showing may be insufficient. Examiners should include, explicitly or implicitly, an indication of reasonable expectation of success in an obviousness rejection. Case examples: Elekta Ltd. v. ZAP Surgical Sys., Intelligent Bio‑Sys. v. Illumina, In re Merck & Co., Ex parte Blanc. Note: conclusive proof of efficacy is not required and absolute predictability is not required (OSI Pharm. v. Apotex; Acorda v. Roxane; PharmaStem; Pfizer v. Apotex). Preamble or other claim limitations relevant to intended purpose may be relevant to the reasonable expectation analysis (Eli Lilly v. Teva).

name: All claim limitations must be considered in obviousness analysis
description: Examiners must consider every limiting term in a claim when determining patentability over the prior art; 'All words in a claim must be considered in judging the patentability of that claim against the prior art.'
guidance: The subject matter of the properly construed claim (broadest reasonable interpretation) must be examined. Grammar and ordinary meaning as understood by one of ordinary skill often dictate whether language is limiting. If an independent claim is nonobvious under 35 U.S.C. 103, generally dependent claims are nonobvious, unless dependency is improper or dependent claim has a later effective filing date. See In re Wilson, In re Gulack, Axonics v. Medtronic, In re Fine. Examiners should avoid improperly narrowing claim scope to preferred embodiments (Axonics example).

name: Indefinite claim limitations must be considered (cannot be disregarded)
description: A claim limitation considered indefinite cannot be disregarded; if a claim has more than one reasonable interpretation and at least one renders the claim unpatentable over the prior art, reject the claim as indefinite and, when appropriate, reject over the prior art based on the interpretation that renders the prior art applicable.
guidance: Rejecting on both indefiniteness (35 U.S.C. 112(b)) and prior art grounds when appropriate avoids piecemeal review. However, examiners must not base prior art rejections on speculative or unreasonable claim interpretations; substantial speculation is improper (see In re Steele, In re Wilson, Ex parte Ionescu). See MPEP § 2175 and § 2111 for proper claim interpretation guidance.

name: Limitations lacking support in the original specification must still be considered
description: When evaluating obviousness, all claim limitations must be considered, including limitations that do not find support in the specification as originally filed (i.e., new matter or negative limitations).
guidance: Do not ignore negative limitations or terms absent from the specification when assessing patentability over the prior art. Example: Ex parte Grasselli (negative exclusions not in original specification were still properly considered). 'All words in a claim must be considered' (In re Miller, quoting In re Wilson).

name: Claim language types that may raise questions about limiting effect
description: Certain kinds of claim language may raise questions about whether they limit claim scope (this list is not exhaustive): preambles, clauses like 'adapted to', 'adapted for', 'wherein', 'whereby', contingent limitations, printed matter, and functional language associated with a claim term.
guidance: Examiners should analyze whether such language functions as a claim limitation in the specific factual context. See MPEP §§2111.01–2111.05 for discussion of preambles, transitional phrases, contingent limitations, printed matter, and functional language. Proper claim interpretation determines whether the prior art teaches the limitation.

name: OA Retrieval-Simulated Generation (OA-RS)
description: Provide a noisy candidate pool R_noise (top-k BM25 retrieved references combined with sampled ground-truth). The model must distinguish pertinent prior art from irrelevant noise to generate the Office Action.
guidance: Simulates realistic retrieval environments. The model must first evaluate candidate pool, select relevant references, and then map claim elements to chosen references. Performance measures should capture the model's robustness to noisy retrieval.

name: Applicant Rebuttal Generation (task)
description: Given an Office Action O_t and associated prior art R (and current claims C_t), generate a rebuttal B_t that contests specific rejection grounds and provides persuasive legal and technical arguments to overcome cited prior art.
guidance: The rebuttal task requires tripartite alignment: (i) grounding arguments in the OA's specific rejection grounds, (ii) contrasting technical features of claims vs. prior art, and (iii) maintaining logical consistency with intended claim scope. Focus on substantive argumentation rather than procedural filing formality.

name: LLM-as-a-Judge — Clarity
description: 1–10 scale focusing on legal readability, logical coherence, and document structure.
guidance: Assesses whether arguments are presented clearly in USPTO-style structure. High clarity requires clear headings, claim-rejection linkage, and unambiguous language.

name: LLM-as-a-Judge — Completeness
description: 1–10 scale focusing on coverage/utility of the feedback and whether all relevant issues are addressed.
guidance: Evaluates whether OA/rebuttal covers all applicable rejection groups, citations, and claim elements. Use in conjunction with Point-wise Coverage for rebuttals.

name: OA Decision Logic & Active Statute Gating
description: Before drafting, determine which statutes will be substantively applied (e.g., 101, 102, 103, 112, double patenting) and apply them strictly; decide allowance vs rejection based on claim language and technical reasoning; do not label Final unless criteria are met.
guidance: Active Statute Gating ensures the model only invokes statutes it substantively applies. Scope Lock requires grounding technical content in provided inputs. Decision Logic requires impartial determination, not assuming rejections by default.

name: Rebuttal prompt structure and constraints
description: Rebuttals must follow PTO-style structure: RESPONSE TO OFFICE ACTION; AMENDMENT AND REMARKS; I. Status of the Claims; II–VI (only if raised) sections for objections/rejections; Conclusion; REFINED CLAIMS. Strict statute gating: include only statutes raised in OA. Point-by-point responses tied to claim numbers and cited references. No new matter; amendments must be supported by original disclosure and marked (underlining/strikethrough).
guidance: Date handling: use OA date if provided. For limited OAs (e.g., Notice of Allowance or only double patenting) keep responses brief. Avoid boilerplate; each argument must be claim-specific. Ensure amendment compliance with standard PTO markings and no-new-matter rule.

name: No-New-Matter & Amendment Compliance
description: Any claim amendments in rebuttal must be fully supported by the original specification; use standard markings (underlining for additions, strikethrough for deletions) and status identifiers (Original/Currently Amended/Withdrawn/Canceled).
guidance: Evaluation penalizes introductions of new matter. Rebuttal evaluation specifically checks amendment_compliance; score reductions for unsupported amendments or hallucinated specification support.

name: Data collection & quality-control protocol
description: Multi-stage pipeline for dataset construction: automated filtering of noisy or metadata-broken records, manual audit by trained annotators verifying structural integrity of prosecution timelines and logical consistency between cited references and rejection grounds, and redaction of personally identifiable information.
guidance: Ensures high-fidelity full-stage benchmark: collect verbatim OAs, rebuttals, iterative claim versions, and full reference lists. Manual audits confirm claim-to-reference mappings and remove documents with excessive noise; redact PII for ethical compliance.

name: Reference selection & explanation requirement (OA-RO & OA-RS)
description: When references are provided (oracle or retrieved), the model must not blindly use all of them; it must select the most pertinent references and briefly explain the selection rationale (e.g., primary reference for §102 or combination for §103).
guidance: Require element-by-element mapping from claim limitations to chosen references. In OA-RS, first evaluate candidate pool and then select relevant refs; in OA-RO, select from oracle set. Penalize using irrelevant refs or failing to justify selection.

name: Significance of Transitional Phrases
description: Transitional phrases in patent claims define the scope of a claim with respect to additional components or steps and determine whether a claim is open-ended or closed to additional elements.
guidance: These phrases significantly impact the breadth of patent protection and how the claim is interpreted during patent examination or litigation. Choice of transitional phrase should be made with awareness of prosecution and enforcement consequences (MPEP 2111.03).

name: Comprising — open-ended / inclusive
description: The transitional phrase 'comprising' is open-ended and is inclusive of additional, unrecited elements.
guidance: Use 'comprising' when an open-ended claim is desired that allows the presence of additional components or steps beyond those recited. MPEP notes that 'comprising' is open-ended and inclusive of additional elements (MPEP 2111.03).

name: Consisting of — closed to unrecited elements
description: Claims using 'consisting of' are closed to unrecited elements and exclude additional components or steps not explicitly recited.
guidance: Use 'consisting of' when a closed claim scope is intended that expressly excludes any elements not recited. This limits claim breadth and can affect infringement and validity analyses (MPEP 2111.03).

name: Consisting essentially of — limits to basic and novel characteristics
description: The transitional phrase 'consisting essentially of' limits claim scope to the basic and novel characteristics of the claimed invention.
guidance: 'Consisting essentially of' excludes additional elements that materially affect the basic and novel properties of the invention but permits those that do not. This phrase narrows scope relative to 'comprising' but is broader than 'consisting of' (MPEP 2111.03).

name: Expanded vicarious liability: conditioning participation/benefit and establishing manner/timing
description: Liability under §271(a) can be found when an alleged infringer 'conditions participation in an activity or receipt of a benefit upon performance of a step or steps of a patented method and establishes the manner or timing of that performance.'
guidance: This is the Federal Circuit's en banc addition (Akamai 2015) to the attribution doctrines; it parallels copyright vicarious liability. Facts supporting this include contractual terms or business practices that make use of a service contingent on customers performing claim steps and that dictate how/when they do so (e.g., Limelight's form contract requiring customer tagging and establishing timing/manner).

name: Patentable subject can be a thing produced or a mode of producing it
description: The subject-matter may be either a thing produced (a tangible article) or the mode/process of producing a thing; but it must be one or the other and not merely an effect or abstract principle.
guidance: Courts treat 'manufacture' both literally (a new tangible article) and figuratively (a new method/process producing an effect). Patents for new compositions or new processes producing known substances can be proper; but the patent must accurately represent what is claimed (must not claim one thing in the patent and show another in the specification).

name: Doctrine of Equivalents — equivalency test
description: A claim requirement is satisfied under the doctrine of equivalents if the accused [part/step of the product/method] performs substantially the same function, in substantially the same way, to achieve substantially the same result as the claim requirement.
guidance: You may consider whether, at the time of the alleged infringement, persons of ordinary skill in the field would have known of the interchangeability of the [part/step] with the claimed requirement. Interchangeability at the present time is not sufficient. Known interchangeability is not necessary to find infringement under the doctrine of equivalents but may support a conclusion that the difference is not substantial. The patent holder must prove equivalency by a preponderance of the evidence. You may not apply the doctrine of equivalents to claim elements that were in the prior art or would have been obvious, or to subject matter that was described in the patent specification but not claimed if it was specific enough that one of ordinary skill would understand it was present in the patent.

name: Means-plus-function claims — literal infringement (35 U.S.C. §112(6))
description: A means-plus-function requirement covers only the specific structure disclosed in the patent specification for performing the claimed function and the equivalents of those specific structures; it does not cover all possible structures that could perform the function.
guidance: Judge will identify the structure in the specification that corresponds to the means-plus-function requirement. Jurors must first decide whether the accused product has any structure that performs the specific function; if not, the claim is not infringed. If it does, determine whether that structure is the same as or equivalent to the structure identified in the specification. To prove equivalence, the patent holder must show that a person of ordinary skill would have considered the differences insubstantial at the time the patent issued or that the structures/actions performed the function in substantially the same way to accomplish substantially the same result. In assessing interchangeability, the interchangeability must have been known at the time the patent issued and the structure must have been available then. If a method claim uses step-plus-function, substitute 'acts' for 'structure' accordingly.

name: Limitations on the doctrine of equivalents due to prosecution disclaimer/amendments
description: If the patent holder made certain claim changes or statements during prosecution, the doctrine of equivalents analysis cannot be applied to those claim requirements that were disclaimed or limited during prosecution.
guidance: Provide a list of the specific requirements (on a claim-by-claim basis) that the doctrine of equivalents cannot be applied to. Unless each of these requirements is literally present in the accused product/method, there can be no infringement of the claim as to those requirements.

name: Contributory infringement — elements (35 U.S.C. §271(c))
description: Contributory infringement can arise when someone supplies something that is used to infringe one or more patent claims. Someone other than the supplier must directly infringe a claim; if there is no direct infringement by anyone, there can be no contributory infringement.
guidance: Patent holder must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that: (1) the alleged infringer sells, offers to sell, or imports within the U.S. a component of a product or apparatus for use in a process during the patent term; (2) the component or apparatus has no substantial, noninfringing use; (3) the component or apparatus constitutes a material part of the invention; (4) at the time of supplying the component, the alleged infringer is aware of the patent or believed there was a high probability a patent existed and deliberately avoided learning of it; (5) at the time of supplying, the alleged infringer knows the component was especially made or adapted for use in infringing the patent or believed there was a high probability and deliberately avoided learning the infringing nature; and (6) the component has been used to directly infringe the claim. Define “non-infringing use” as a use other than as a component of the patented product or in the patented method that is not occasional, farfetched, impractical, experimental, or hypothetical.

name: Inducing infringement — elements (35 U.S.C. §271(b))
description: Inducement requires that someone else actually directly infringe a claim; there can be no inducement without direct infringement. The alleged inducer is liable only if the patent holder proves specific elements by a preponderance of the evidence.
guidance: Patent holder must prove: (1) the allegedly infringing acts are actually carried out by the alleged direct infringer and directly infringe the claim; (2) the alleged infringer took action during the patent term intending to cause the infringing acts by the direct infringer; and (3) the alleged infringer was aware of the patent and knew that the acts, if taken, would constitute infringement. For willful blindness issues, alternatives permit findings where the alleged infringer believed there was a high probability of infringement and deliberately avoided learning of it. In deciding inducement, you may consider whether the accused infringer actually believed the acts did not infringe and whether it relied on advice of counsel.

name: Willful infringement — subjective prong (standard and factors)
description: Willfulness requires that the patent holder show it is highly probable that, prior to the filing date of the complaint, the alleged infringer acted with reckless disregard of the patent claims. Willfulness is judged by clear and convincing evidence. The jury is limited to the subjective prong; the objective prong (whether a reasonable person would have considered there to be a high likelihood of infringement) is a matter of law for the judge.
guidance: To demonstrate ‘reckless disregard,’ the patent holder must persuade the jury that the alleged infringer actually knew, or it was so obvious that it should have known, that its actions constituted infringement. Consider all facts including: factors that suggest non-willfulness (acting consistent with industry standards, making a good-faith effort to avoid infringing such as designing around the patent; reliance on a well-supported opinion of counsel if invoked) and factors suggesting willfulness (intentional copying of a patented product; attempts to cover up infringement). The Committee does not recommend seeking an advisory opinion on the objective prong from the jury.

name: Invalidity — burden of proof
description: To prove invalidity of any patent claim, the alleged infringer must persuade the jury that it is highly probable that the claim is invalid.
guidance: This is the heightened standard associated with challenges to validity (clear and convincing/highly probable). Follow case authorities cited (e.g., Microsoft v. i4i).

name: Written description requirement (35 U.S.C. §112)
description: A claim is invalid if the specification does not contain an adequate written description demonstrating that the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention at the time the application was filed.
guidance: Alleged infringer must show by clear and convincing evidence that the specification fails to meet the written description requirement. The requirement is satisfied if a person of ordinary skill reading the original application would have recognized that the application described the invention as claimed; exact wording is unnecessary and missing claim limitations can be valid if necessarily implied to one of ordinary skill.

name: Enablement requirement (35 U.S.C. §112(1))
description: The specification must contain a sufficiently full and clear description to allow a person of ordinary skill in the art to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention at the time of the original filing without undue experimentation.
guidance: Alleged infringer must prove by clear and convincing evidence that the patent is not enabling. In assessing undue experimentation, consider: (1) scope of the claimed invention; (2) amount of guidance in the patent; (3) amount of experimentation necessary; (4) time and cost of necessary experimentation; (5) how routine the experimentation is in the field; (6) whether the patent discloses specific working examples; (7) nature and predictability of the field; and (8) level of ordinary skill in the art. No single factor is dispositive — weigh them in context of the invention and state of the art.

name: Prior art — definitions and effect of examiner consideration (pre- and post-AIA)
description: Prior art may include publicly known or available knowledge, uses, offers for sale, publications, or patents that disclose the claimed invention or elements thereof. Definitions differ depending on priority date relative to March 16, 2013 (AIA).
guidance: For claims with priority before March 16, 2013: prior art must have been made/known/used/published/patented before the invention or more than one year before filing; inventor's own publication less than one year before invention is not prior art. For claims with priority on/after March 16, 2013: prior art is material made/known/used/published/patented before the effective filing date or described in an earlier-filed published patent/application naming another inventor. Exceptions include disclosures by the inventor (within one year) or subject matter obtained from the inventor, and certain common-ownership exceptions. When a challenger relies on prior art considered by the Examiner during prosecution, the challenger bears a greater burden to overcome deference to the agency; prior art not considered by the Examiner may be given more weight. If invention date or date of prior art is disputed, jury must determine conception vs reduction to practice and diligence; definitions of conception and reduction to practice are provided.

name: Anticipation — not new / single-reference requirement
description: A claim is invalid as anticipated if all of its requirements existed in a single device, method, publication, or patent that predates the claimed invention (or the effective filing date post-AIA).
guidance: Alleged infringer must prove anticipation by clear and convincing evidence. The single reference need not use the same words as the claim, but all claim requirements must be present, stated or necessarily implied, so that a person of ordinary skill could make and use the claimed invention from that one reference. Illustrative ways to show lack of novelty include prior public knowledge/use in the U.S., prior patents or printed publications anywhere in the world, prior making by another in the U.S. (if not abandoned/secret), certain prior U.S. patents or published applications, or evidence that the named inventor learned the invention from another.

name: Statutory bars — timeliness of filing
description: A claim is invalid if the patent application was not filed within the time required by law (a statutory bar): all claim requirements must have been present in one prior art reference dated more than one year before the application filing date.
guidance: Alleged infringer must prove by clear and convincing evidence that the claim is invalid due to a statutory bar. Prior art for this purpose can include the inventor’s own work, use, or commercialization efforts. The instruction provides a list of ways to show the application was not timely filed (select applicable items for the case).

name: Statutory deadline for decision on request (3-month rule)
description: The Director (and under delegation the examiner) must determine whether a substantial new question of patentability is raised not later than three months after the filing of the request for inter partes reexamination (35 U.S.C. 312; 37 CFR 1.923).
guidance: The examiner's determination is based on the claims in effect at the time of the determination, becomes part of the official file, and is mailed to the patent owner and third-party requester. If the 3-month period ends on a weekend or federal holiday in D.C., mailing must be by the preceding business day.

name: Claims to be considered in determination (claims-in-effect rule)
description: The examiner's determination is based on the patent claims in effect at the time of the determination and will not consider amendments filed in a copending reexamination or reissue where a reexamination certificate or reissue patent has not yet issued.
guidance: The decision on the request should discuss all patent claims requested for reexamination, but should limit discussion to whether a substantial new question of patentability has been raised. The examiner SHOULD NOT reject claims in the order for reexamination; any rejection is made in the first Office action that normally accompanies the order for reexamination (see MPEP § 2660). Only one claim needs a substantial new question of patentability to order reexamination. If a request fails to apply the art to certain claims as required, those claims generally will not be reexamined; the Office may at its discretion reexamine non-requested claims or initiate reexamination on its own.

name: Second or subsequent request standard (different SNQ requirement)
description: When a second or subsequent request is filed while a first reexamination is pending, the presence of an SNQ depends on the art cited by the subsequent request and whether that art raises a substantial new question different from that in the pending reexamination.
guidance: If the subsequent request includes the same art that raised the SNQ in the earlier pending reexamination, the subsequent request should be denied. If it raises a different SNQ as to some claims but not others, the request may be granted in part. The subsequent requester must independently provide an SNQ different from that raised in the pending reexamination for the claims in effect at the time of determination. Once a different SNQ is established, the subsequent request may also provide information directed to proposed new or amended claims in the pending reexamination to permit examination of the entire patent package. If the patent owner can show the later request was filed for harassment, the owner may petition under 37 CFR 1.182 to suspend the second proceeding; if granted, prosecution of the later request may be suspended until conclusion of the first reexamination.

name: Requests filed after reissue or where reissue issues after request
description: If a reexamination request is filed on a patent after a reissue patent for that patent has already issued, the reexamination will be denied because the original patent has been surrendered.
guidance: To reexamine a reissued patent, a new request must be filed based on the specification and claims of the reissue patent. If the reissue patent issues after filing of a request, special handling and merger rules apply (see MPEP § 2686.03).

name: Prosecution history estoppel prevents reclaiming surrendered subject matter
description: Prosecution history estoppel is a legal limitation upon the doctrine of equivalents that operates to prevent a patentee from reclaiming subject matter surrendered during prosecution.
guidance: Estoppel ties the doctrine of equivalents to its underlying purpose: holding the inventor to representations made during prosecution. If patentee narrowed claims to obtain a patent, the patentee cannot later claim that the surrendered territory comprises unforeseen subject matter that should be deemed equivalent.

name: Rebuttable presumption that limiting amendment surrenders intervening subject matter
description: There is a rebuttable presumption that a limiting amendment surrenders "all subject matter between the broader and the narrower language" unless the patentee establishes an explanation.
guidance: Warner-Jenkinson placed the burden on the patentee to show an amendment was not for purposes of patentability; Festo preserves the presumption but allows rebuttal. If no explanation is established, a bar arises with regard to the intervening subject matter between original and amended claim language.

name: Policy balance: clarity of property boundaries vs coverage of equivalents
description: Courts must balance the patent policy promoting clarity and certainty of patent boundaries (to encourage investment) against equity allowing patents to reach "all equivalents to the claims described."
guidance: The opinion emphasizes that clarity and certainty are essential for investment, but that the doctrine of equivalents remains "firmly entrenched." Estoppel should be applied to serve the doctrine's purpose without creating undue uncertainty.

name: Implication for unchanged claim language (open question)
description: Festo raises but does not resolve whether the unforeseeability requirement (and related analysis) should apply to claim language that was not changed during prosecution.
guidance: Practitioners should note the Court's query about if/when unforeseeability will be required for unchanged claim language; this is a potential future litigation issue and may affect arguments about equivalence for unamended claims.

name: Ramifications for doctrine of equivalents and prosecution strategy
description: Festo may have narrowed the doctrine of equivalents and expanded prosecution history estoppel relative to the post-Warner-Jenkinson landscape by (a) clarifying that any narrowing amendment tied to Patent Act requirements may invoke estoppel and (b) imposing an unforeseeability-focused rebuttal standard.
guidance: Patent drafters/prosecutors should weigh the risk that narrowing amendments will create estoppel and consider claim drafting/prosecution strategies to preserve equivalents (e.g., careful claim language, record explanations). Litigators should frame or rebut estoppel arguments using the Court's listed rebuttal factors.

name: Use of fewer elements than claimed (when patent claims only the combination)
description: Where a patent claims only a combination of known elements, the use of some but not all of those elements (i.e., fewer than all) is generally not an infringement.
guidance: This rule is subject to the exception that substituting equivalents or omitting immaterial parts will not always avoid infringement; the central question remains whether the machines are substantially the same.

name: Statements and evidence required in restoration applications
description: The application must include a statement fully setting out the circumstances that led to the failure to pay the renewal fee. This statement may be supported by evidence and copies of any documents referred to.
guidance: Evidence must be of a recent date to show absence of undue delay. Evidence may cover several patents. Evidence must support claim that failure to pay was unintentional and that there has been no undue delay. Controller may call for further evidence (letters, deeds etc.).

name: Examination guidelines – scope and aim (Annexure I introduction)
description: Guidelines aim to help Examiners examine patent applications in pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, chemicals and biotechnology (isomers, polymorphs, pro-drugs, active metabolites, hydrates etc.) given public health, techno-economic and industrial significance.
guidance: Claims in applications may include new drug molecules, pharmaceutical preparations, synergistic combinations, combination of new chemical entity with known component, agrochemicals, new chemical products, new products via biotechnological/microbiological/biochemical processes, microorganisms, products from natural resources.

name: Key aspects to assess for product patents in chemicals/pharma/biotech
description: Significant aspects for grant of product patents: deciding appropriate prior art; assessment of novelty of claimed product/process; determination of inventive step; criteria for industrial applicability; unity of invention; sufficiency of disclosure and scope of the claim.
guidance: To qualify for a patent, inventor must show novelty, inventive step (non-obviousness), industrial applicability and that invention does not fall under non-patentable categories.

name: Patentability of isomers
description: Isomers (structural/positional and stereoisomers) are different compounds with same molecular formula. Structural isomers may be novel over prior art even if similar; stereoisomers are prima facie obvious—once racemate is known its enantiomers are obvious.
guidance: Structural isomers showing close structural and functional similarity may still be novel but may be obvious if enabling methods are available. Stereo isomers: product patent may not be granted for enantiomers of a known racemate; however, when a new compound is claimed for first time in optically active pure form, a product patent may be granted (examples and case law indicated).

name: Patentability of homologues
description: Homologues normally display add-on property and are structurally similar and may lack inventive step; examination must be case-by-case.
guidance: Prior art need not be true homologs to render claimed compounds prima facie obvious if structural and property similarity is close (case examples given).

name: Classify the invention: improving AI vs using AI
description: Identify whether the invention (1) improves AI/ML itself (models, training processes, hardware) or (2) uses AI/ML to improve another field, because each type requires different drafting and prosecution approaches.
guidance: Inventions improving AI often involve math/technical detail and are easier to prosecute and less likely to face §101 trouble; inventions using AI commonly land in non-AI art units, face more §101 and §103 scrutiny, and require different claim/context strategies.

name: Avoid over-explaining well-known AI concepts (be concise)
description: While you must explain implementation-specific details, avoid lengthy re-explanations of basic AI/ML concepts that are unnecessary and likely ignored by examiners.
guidance: Provide a brief background but focus disclosure on what is novel about your implementation and the concrete technical details relevant to the claims.

name: Do not describe AI as human-like thinking
description: Avoid language suggesting the AI 'decides', 'weighs', or 'thinks' in human terms; such language invites §101 rejections by analogizing steps to mental processes.
guidance: Replace human-like phrasing with precise technical descriptions (e.g., 'outputs a Boolean value' and then 'based on that Boolean the system proceeds'). Review and edit specification and claims to remove anthropomorphic phrasing.

name: Avoid black-box claim language
description: Claims that merely state 'determining, via a machine learning model, whether to trigger an alarm' or similar black-box formulations are vulnerable to obviousness and eligibility rejections.
guidance: Provide claim detail that shows how the ML is applied and linked to technology so examiners cannot treat the ML as a conventional algorithm substitution. Include intermediate steps and technical context rather than only high-level outcomes.

name: Avoid attributing impossible actions to ML (no 'AI magic')
description: Claims should not recite actions the ML model itself cannot perform (e.g., 'triggering, by a machine learning model, an alarm') when in practice the model outputs data used by other components to act.
guidance: Structure claims so that the ML outputs are received and then cause downstream system actions (e.g., ML outputs a Boolean → system triggers alarm).

name: Include multiple AI-specific active claim steps
description: Claims should explicitly recite multiple active steps specific to ML to highlight technical distinctions from conventional algorithms.
guidance: Helpful steps include: (1) training an ML model (describe training method and data), (2) providing formatted input to the trained model (describe input format), (3) receiving particular output from the model (describe output type), (4) utilizing the output (cause a physical or technological change), and (5) retraining the model (feedback loop). Explicitly reciting these steps helps resist §102/§103 and §101 rejections.

name: Emphasize retraining / feedback loops when possible
description: Including retraining of the ML model based on subsequent activity (e.g., user feedback) is viewed by examiners as a strong claim element and 'gold standard' for ML claims.
guidance: Draft claims and specification to show how retraining occurs (what data used, how weights change, what triggers retraining) to argue the invention improves the algorithm over time and is more than a static mental process or conventional computing.

name: Use clear claim structure and, where appropriate, emulate USPTO Example 39
description: Review and, where applicable, emulate the structure/approach of Example 39 of the USPTO's Subject Matter Eligibility Examples: Abstract Ideas to defend against §101 rejections.
guidance: Example 39's iterative training algorithm and multi-stage neural network training can be persuasive; similarity in structure can help persuade examiners but has limits (examiner may require similar multistep improvements).

name: Distinguish multiple ML models in claims
description: If the invention uses multiple task-specific ML models, explicitly distinguish them in claims (do not imply a single model performs disparate tasks).
guidance: Use ordinal identifiers like 'first training data'/'second training data' or 'first output'/'second output' to avoid ambiguity and to make it harder to design around claims; multiple models can strengthen arguments against §101 and §103 rejections.

name: Place AI steps in a technological context
description: Claims and specification should situate AI usage within preceding and following technological steps so the invention cannot be analogized to human mental processes or mere conventional hardware.
guidance: Describe what generated the input data, how input is preprocessed for the AI, how output is subsequently used (e.g., trigger a physical change, modify speed), and overall system context. Contextualizing inputs/outputs helps resist §101 rejections.

name: For inventions improving AI, claim specific technical aspects
description: When the invention improves AI itself, focus claims on specific model aspects (nodes, weights), mathematical functions, training approaches, and how they improve performance (accuracy, speed, efficiency).
guidance: Amend claims to explicitly indicate how particular steps improve the functioning of the ML model rather than claiming general decision-making improvements; this often overcomes §101 rejections for AI-improvement inventions.

name: Do not accept 'do this, but with AI' as sufficient
description: Claims that boil down to performing a known task 'but with AI' are unlikely to survive art or eligibility rejections.
guidance: Ensure the claim elements demonstrate technical innovation — e.g., novel training approaches, specific data formats, feedback loops, or concrete technological effects — rather than merely substituting ML for conventional algorithms.

name: Mechanical (technology area)
description: "An invention in which the claims cover the use of mechanical parts, either solely or predominantly, sometimes combined with heat, hydraulics, pneumatics, or other power sources or power transfer techniques."
guidance: Primary technology areas are mutually exclusive. Use claim language to determine classification. Mechanical patents in the dataset include inventions whose claims predominantly rely on mechanical parts and related power-transfer techniques.

name: Electronics (technology area)
description: "An invention in which the claims cover the use of traditional electronic circuitry or the storage or transmission of electric energy."
guidance: Classify based on claim language indicating traditional electronic circuitry or electric-energy storage/transmission. Electronics may overlap with data-processing elements, which the authors often combine with computer-related patents.

name: Chemistry (technology area)
description: "An invention in which the claims cover chemical reactions, chemical compounds with specific elements and proportions, and chemical processes specifying specific elements and amounts or proportions... includes 'small-molecule' chemistry; DNA, antibodies, and other large molecules are included in the biotechnology category instead."
guidance: Include inventions claiming specific chemical components/proportions and related processes. Note that chemistry patents may also be assigned to pharmaceutical industry category; use claim content to classify technology.

name: Software business method (software subset)
description: Narrow definition limited to patents "the claims of which obviously covered only such things as automated generation of customer proposals, advertising, financial techniques, the use of online catalogs."
guidance: Business-method patents are a subset of software. Do not include computer-controlled manufacturing methods. Because business-method is subset of software, it cannot be included simultaneously with the broader software category in regression models; authors ran alternative regressions where business-method and non-business-method software were mutually exclusive categories.

name: Industry category assignment procedure
description: "Unlike technology areas, the industry categories focused more attention on the business use of the patent than on the nature of the technology itself... we paid attention to the claim language in assigning a patent to one of eleven mutually exclusive industry categories, [and] we found it necessary to focus more attention to the written description and to extrinsic evidence, especially the Internet."
guidance: Assign industry based on claims, written description, and extrinsic evidence about business use (web searches, marketing materials). Industry categories are mutually exclusive in the study.

name: Computer & Other Electronics (industry)
description: "This industry encompasses inventions of all kinds that purport to advance the state of the art in computing or computer device manufacturing, or to enhance users’ experiences in employing computing technology... includes software and computer hardware inventions..."
guidance: Authors combined computer and traditional electronics because many patents include data processing elements; classify based on claims and evidence of end-use in computing or user-experience enhancement.

name: Construction (industry)
description: "The construction industry category includes inventions of all kinds related to the erection or maintenance of structures, or to excavation."
guidance: Classify patents whose claims pertain to structural erection/maintenance or excavation equipment/techniques.

name: Limitations on documents considered for determining obviousness
description: If the mistake is in the description, claims or drawings (or a correction/amendment thereof), the competent authority is limited to take into account only the contents of the description, claims and drawings and any correction/amendment concerned; if the mistake is in the request or certain other documents, the authority should also consider any documents submitted by the applicant (including priority documents) and any documents in the authority's international application file at the relevant date.
guidance: The scope of what may be considered depends on the document in which the mistake appears; paragraph references specify the applicable document lists.

name: Mistakes that cannot be rectified under Rule 91
description: Mistakes not rectifiable include: omissions of entire elements or sheets; mistakes in the abstract; mistakes in an Article 19 amendment (unless IPEA is competent); mistakes in a priority claim or notice correcting/adding priority if rectification would change the priority date.
guidance: Applicants must rely on other correction means (e.g., Rule 26bis) for such mistakes; examples include lost sheets or priority-date altering corrections.

name: Graham factual inquiries
description: The objective analysis for determining obviousness is based on the Graham v. John Deere Co. factual inquiries: (A) determining the scope and content of the prior art; (B) ascertaining the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art; and (C) resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art. Objective (secondary) evidence such as commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, and unexpected results must also be evaluated.
guidance: Evaluate these factors case-by-case; secondary considerations may be included in specification, on filing, or timely during prosecution; weight given is case-specific and not dispositive by mere submission.

name: Determining the scope and content of the prior art
description: Obtain a thorough understanding of the invention by reading the specification and claims; determine claim scope by giving the claims the 'broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.' Then determine what to search for and where to search.
guidance: See MPEP §904 for detailed search procedures. The search should cover claimed subject matter and disclosed features reasonably expected to be claimed.

name: Ascertaining differences between the claimed invention and the prior art
description: Interpret claim language and consider both the invention and the prior art as a whole to ascertain differences.
guidance: Use MPEP §2111 claim interpretation principles and consider entire disclosures (MPEP §2141.02).

name: Listing and articulating rationales to support obviousness rejections
description: After resolving Graham factual inquiries, determine whether the claimed invention would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill and articulate the rationale(s) supporting that conclusion; offer reasoned explanation avoiding conclusory generalizations.
guidance: KSR requires explicit analysis. Rejections on obviousness cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements; there must be articulated reasoning with rational underpinning (cf. In re Kahn).

name: Requirement to consider all claim limitations
description: All claim limitations must be considered in the obviousness analysis; the prior art reference(s) need not teach every limitation, but the examiner must explain why differences would have been obvious.
guidance: Ensure each limitation is addressed in the factual findings and rationale; the mere existence of differences does not establish nonobviousness (Dann v. Johnston).

name: Applicant's reply obligations under 37 CFR 1.111(b)
description: Applicants must distinctly and specifically point out supposed errors in the Office action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection; replies must present arguments pointing out specific distinctions believed to render the claims patentable over applied references.
guidance: A mere statement that the Office has not made a prima facie case or that reliance on common knowledge is unsupported is insufficient. If applicant disagrees with factual findings, an effective traverse must include a reasoned statement explaining the alleged error; otherwise the examiner may repeat the rejection and make the next action final (MPEP §706.07(a)).

name: Examples of applicant rebuttal arguments — inability to combine
description: Applicant may submit evidence demonstrating that one of ordinary skill in the art could not have combined the claimed elements by known methods (e.g., due to technological difficulties).
guidance: If credible, examiners should reassess the prior obviousness finding and evaluate whether the asserted difficulties negate the asserted rationale.

name: Broad but Bounded Scope
description: The claims should reach all natural extensions and improvements of the prospect that a rational developer would coordinate, but no further. Scope should match the technological field that the inventor's disclosure reasonably enables further investigation of.
guidance: Good claim scope captures the practical prospect (including foreseeable variants) while avoiding overreaching beyond what the disclosure and contribution justify. Evaluate whether claim breadth maps to realistic coordination needs rather than speculative monopolization.

name: Definite Boundaries (Notice Function)
description: Claim boundaries must be sufficiently clear that subsequent investors can identify the prospect and either (a) negotiate a license, (b) design around, or (c) develop within the prospect under the patentee's coordination.
guidance: Definiteness serves the notice function—claims should enable competent third parties to determine whether planned activity falls within the prospect. Ambiguous boundaries undermine negotiation, design-around, and coordinated development.

name: Claims map to the identified technological problem
description: The claims map directly onto the technological problem the inventor identified, not onto incidental embodiments.
guidance: Preferred drafting aligns claim scope with the problem addressed by the inventor, avoiding fixation on particular embodiments that do not reflect the real prospect. This supports coherent coordination of subsequent development.

name: Use of functional or generic claim language when appropriate
description: Claim language uses functional or generic terms where the prospect properly extends to functionally equivalent embodiments.
guidance: Where the prospect legitimately covers functional equivalents, drafting in functional/generic terms helps capture the coordinated field without artificial embodiment limits; but this must be supported by disclosure.

name: Dependent claims trace concrete embodiments without artificially narrowing the prospect
description: Dependent claims trace concrete embodiments without artificially narrowing the prospect.
guidance: Dependent claims should document specific embodiments while preserving the inventor's broader prospect; they should not be used to constrict the practical coordination space.

name: Claims that exceed disclosure without explanation ('paper claims')
description: The claims dramatically exceed the disclosed embodiments without explaining why the prospect is broader (signal: 'paper claims' without working examples).
guidance: This is an anti-pattern: broad claims unsupported by disclosure fail the prospect function by asserting rights to a non-staked prospect. Such claims should be scrutinized for enablement and written-description shortcomings.

name: Excessively narrow claims (wasteful duplication risk)
description: Claims are excessively narrow, leaving the surrounding prospect open to wasteful duplicative investment.
guidance: Overly narrow claims may fail to coordinate development, allowing multiple parties to duplicate efforts inefficiently. Evaluate whether claim narrowness undermines the system's coordination purpose.

name: Reject claims that exceed the inventor's actual prospect (enablement/written description)
description: Reject claims so broad that they exceed the inventor's actual prospect (enablement, written description).
guidance: Examiner rejections grounded in enablement and written-description doctrine serve the prospect aim by preventing overbroad, non-enabled monopolies.

name: Reject claims so narrow they fail to define a coordinated prospect
description: Reject claims so narrow that they fail to define a coordinated prospect (utility of the patent system itself).
guidance: Examiners should avoid allowing claims that are functionally useless for coordination; the patent must be useful for organizing follow-on development.

name: Demand definite claim boundaries enforceable under 35 U.S.C. 112(b)
description: Demand definite boundaries that subsequent investors can rely upon (35 U.S.C. 112(b)).
guidance: Definiteness requirements operationalize the notice function; examiners should ensure claims give third parties adequate notice of scope.

name: Notice clarity
description: Could a competent third-party investor read the claims and know whether their planned activity falls within the prospect?
guidance: This is the operational test of definiteness from the investor/developer perspective: clarity enables licensing, design-around, or coordinated development decisions.

name: Scope-disclosure match
description: Does the breadth of the claims correspond to the breadth of the inventor's actual technological contribution?
guidance: A good patent's claim breadth should be justified by the disclosure and the inventor's contribution—neither overreaching nor artificially narrow relative to the enabled prospect.

name: Legal topics coverage (112(a), 112(b), 101)
description: Workshops and training modules covering statutory/legal areas including 112(a), 112(b), and 35 U.S.C. 101 (multiple workshop levels referenced as 101 II, 101 III).
guidance: Training includes workshops and presentations on written description/claim definiteness (112(a), 112(b)) and subject-matter eligibility (101), presented at refresher and master levels with examples to improve examiner understanding and application in Office actions.

name: Search planning and mapping prior art (35 U.S.C. 102 and 103)
description: Plan and conduct a search, and map prior art to claims using 35 USC 102 (novelty) and 103 (obviousness).
guidance: STEPP Day 2 uses the information gathered during Day 1 to plan a search, conduct a search, and map prior art to claims. Training should teach practical search techniques and how to relate prior art to claim limitations.

name: Reasons for Allowance
description: Training on properly documenting and explaining Reasons for Allowance when claims are allowed.
guidance: Presented as a refresher/master level topic; aims to improve quality and clarity of the record regarding why claims are allowed.

name: Philosophical ethics should avoid vacuous slogans and provide substantive grounding
description: Phrases such as 'human dignity' may serve as comforting slogans but are inadequate unless given clear, substantive grounding and explanation.
guidance: Require that central moral claims be backed by coherent arguments, not merely rhetorical elevation. Test by asking what the slogan adds conceptually and whether it resolves real ethical disputes.

name: Identify judicial exception as recited in the claim (products of nature)
description: When a claim is alleged to recite a product of nature, the rejection should identify the exception as it is recited (i.e., set forth or described) in the claim, and explain using a reasoned rationale why the product does not have markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state.
guidance: Compare the claimed subject matter to its closest naturally occurring counterpart and explain whether isolation produced a marked difference in structure, function, or other properties. See MPEP § 2106.04(b) for products of nature and § 2106.04(c) for the markedly different characteristics analysis. Sample explanation: recite X isolated from naturally occurring Y, compare X to X in its natural state; if no indication isolation resulted in marked difference, treat X as a product of nature exception.

name: Explain why additional claim elements do not amount to significantly more (Step 2B)
description: After identifying the judicial exception, identify any additional elements recited in the claim beyond the exception and explain why they do not add significantly more to the exception. The explanation should address the additional elements both individually and as a combination when determining whether the claim as a whole recites eligible subject matter.
guidance: A rejection should be made only if it is readily apparent to an examiner relying on the examiner's expertise that the additional elements do not amount to significantly more. The examiner must provide a reasoned rationale so the applicant can respond. Conversely, when appropriate the examiner should explain why additional elements provide an inventive concept by adding a meaningful limitation. See MPEP § 2106.05 for considerations courts have found to qualify or not qualify as significantly more.

name: Explain why limitations are well-understood, routine, conventional
description: When concluding particular claim limitations are well-understood, routine, conventional activities (or elements) to those in the relevant field, the rejection should explain why the courts have recognized, or those in the relevant field would recognize, those claim limitations as being well-understood, routine, conventional activities.
guidance: Provide a reasoned explanation supporting that conclusion rather than just asserting conventionality. See MPEP § 2106.05(d) for more information and examples of elements that courts have found to be well-understood, routine, conventional activity.

name: Generic computer components/functions may not meaningfully limit the claim
description: For claim limitations that recite a generic computer component performing generic computer functions at a high level of generality, examiners can explain why these generic computing functions do not meaningfully limit the claim.
guidance: MPEP § 2106.05(f) lists computer functions courts have recognized as well-understood, routine, conventional when claimed in a merely generic manner. However, this is not universal: courts have found combinations of generic components can perform non-generic functions and thus amount to significantly more (e.g., DDR Holdings). Examiners should not assume all computer-implemented claims are ineligible and should analyze whether generic components in combination perform functions that are not merely generic.

name: Insignificant extra-solution activity and field-of-use limitations do not add meaningful limitation
description: Claim limitations that add insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., mere data gathering, storing data) or that generally link use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use do not meaningfully limit the claim.
guidance: Examples: adding a final step of storing data to a process that only recites computing a mathematical relationship does not add a meaningful limitation. Limiting use of an abstract idea to a particular industry (as in Flook) can be insufficient. See MPEP § 2106.05(g) for insignificant extra-solution activity and § 2106.05(h) for field-of-use/technological environment considerations.

name: Best practice: consult the specification and suggest claim amendments
description: In the event a rejection is made, it is a best practice for the examiner to consult the specification to determine if there are elements that could be added to the claim to make it eligible.
guidance: If such elements exist, the examiner should identify them in the Office action and suggest them as ways to overcome the rejection. This can assist the applicant in amending claims to recite significantly more than the judicial exception.

name: Evidentiary requirements for §101 rejections (no evidence required but may be used)
description: The courts consider the determination of whether a claim is eligible to be a question of law, so the court does not require evidence that a claimed concept is a judicial exception and generally decides eligibility without resolving factual issues. Similarly, at Step 2B there is no requirement for evidence to support a finding that the claim does not recite significantly more (e.g., that additional limitations are well-understood, routine, conventional activities).
guidance: If available, evidence may be provided to support an assertion or to rebut applicant arguments (e.g., specification statements, manuals, patents, court decisions). Care should be taken to ensure that facts of any cited case law comport with the facts of the application. Examples of cases demonstrating no evidence requirement are cited (e.g., FairWarning, OIP Techs., Content Extraction).

name: Use prior precedent to identify judicial exceptions
description: When determining whether claimed subject matter is judicially-excepted, the Federal Circuit typically compares the claimed subject matter to subject matter identified as an exception in its prior precedent.
guidance: Examiners should examine earlier cases in which a similar or parallel descriptive nature can be seen and consider what prior cases were about and how they were decided. See Amdocs and other cited cases for examples of using precedent to identify abstract ideas.

name: Evaluate applicant's response and reanalyze amended claims (2106.07(b))
description: After examiners identify and explain the reasons why a claim is directed to a judicial exception without significantly more, the burden shifts to the applicant to amend or present persuasive arguments/evidence. Examiners must carefully consider all applicant's arguments and evidence rebutting the eligibility rejection.
guidance: If applicant amends, determine the amended claim's broadest reasonable interpretation and perform the eligibility analysis again. If applicant's amendments/arguments persuasively establish eligibility, the rejection should be withdrawn. Applicant may argue that additional elements amount to significantly more individually or in combination (e.g., by improving technology, improving computer functioning, adding specific limitations other than conventional activity, or adding unconventional steps that confine the claim).

name: Appropriate examiner responses when maintaining a rejection
description: If an applicant properly challenges the examiner's findings but the examiner deems it appropriate to maintain the rejection, the examiner must provide a rebuttal in the next Office action. Examples of appropriate rebuttals include explaining why the abstract idea is similar to that in the cited case, reevaluating conventionality claims and providing evidence where appropriate, assessing 'specially programmed' or 'particular machine' assertions, and reconsidering Steps 2A/2B with respect to improvements and preemption concerns.
guidance: Specific examples: (1) explain why the abstract idea recited corresponds to an abstract idea in a cited Supreme Court or Federal Circuit decision; (2) if applicant disputes conventionality with argument/evidence, reevaluate and consider providing evidence to support the rejection; (3) mere addition of a generic computer/specially programmed computer does not automatically overcome eligibility rejections (Alice); (4) if applicant argues specificity or lack of preemption, reconsider whether claim improves computer functioning or technology and whether additional elements in combination amount to an inventive concept. See MPEP § 706.07(a) regarding new grounds of rejection.

name: Clarify the record when claims are found eligible or to explain rejections
description: When claims are deemed patent eligible, the examiner may make clarifying remarks on the record (e.g., reference the portion of the specification that describes the claimed improvement and note the claim elements that produce that improvement). Clarifying remarks may also be useful in explaining the rationale for a rejection.
guidance: Clarifying remarks may be made at any point during prosecution and with a notice of allowance. Explaining the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of a claim (for example, that a computer readable medium claim's BRI covers a carrier wave) will assist applicant in understanding and responding to a rejection and may include suggestions to overcome the rejection by submitting narrowing amendments.

name: § 271(f)(2) infringement elements (supply abroad)
description: [To show infringement under Section 271(f)(2), the Plaintiff must prove each of the following by a preponderance of the evidence:] (1) [the Defendant] actually supplied the components from the United States into a foreign country or caused them to be supplied from the United States to a foreign country; (2) [the Defendant] knew or should have known that the components were especially made or adapted for use in a product that infringes a claim of the patent; (3) those components have no substantial non-infringing use; and (4) [the Defendant] intended for the components to be combined into that product.
guidance: It is not necessary that the components actually were combined into an infringing product — it suffices that the defendant intended for them to be combined into a product that would have infringed if combined in the United States. In this context, a 'substantial use' is one that is not occasional, farfetched, impractical, experimental, or hypothetical.

name: § 271(g) infringement elements (product made by patented process)
description: [To show infringement under Section 271(g), the Plaintiff must prove that:] (1) the Defendant imported into the United States or, within the United States, sold/offered for sale/used a product that was made by a process that includes all steps of at least one claim of the patent; (2) the product was made between [issue date of patent] and [expiration date of patent/date of trial]; and (3) the Defendant imported/sold/offered for sale/used the product between [issue date] and [expiration date/date of trial].
guidance: You must decide whether the evidence establishes the product was 'made by' the claimed process.
