If the product was materially changed by later processes or is a trivial/non-essential part of another product, you must find it was not 'made by' the claimed process. Infringement under §271(g) does not require a single entity to perform the patented process.

name: Summary rule: Defendant's burden to prove invalidity
description: [The Defendant] must prove by clear and convincing evidence that each asserted claim is invalid.
guidance: The burden of proof for invalidity is clear and convincing evidence for each claim alleged invalid.

name: Invalidity of independent and dependent claims (claim-by-claim evaluation)
description: An independent claim does not refer to any other claim. A dependent claim refers to at least one other claim and includes all elements of the claim to which it refers plus additional elements. You must evaluate the invalidity of each asserted claim separately.
guidance: Even if an independent claim is invalid, dependent claims are not automatically invalid — decide validity claim-by-claim. (Text also states: if you find a dependent claim is invalid, you must find the independent claim from which it depends is also invalid.)

name: Person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA) perspective
description: The question of invalidity of a patent claim is determined from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art in the field of the claimed invention as of the time of the invention/effective filing date.
guidance: Use POSITA's knowledge and understanding at the relevant time when assessing prior art, enablement, and obviousness-related factual inquiries.

name: Anticipation (newness) standard
description: To prove anticipation, the Defendant must prove by clear and convincing evidence that the claimed invention is not new. To anticipate a claim, each element in the claim must be present in a single item of prior art and arranged or combined in the same way as recited in the claim.
guidance: You may not combine two or more items of prior art to find anticipation. Consider what a POSITA would have understood from review of the particular prior art reference. If inherency is alleged, instruct on inherency requirements.

name: Inherency in anticipation
description: Prior art inherently anticipates if the missing element(s) or feature(s) would necessarily result from what the single item of prior art teaches to a POSITA. A party claiming inherent anticipation must prove that the allegedly inherent element(s) necessarily are present by clear and convincing evidence.
guidance: Evidence outside the prior art reference (including experimental testing) may be used to show inherent elements. It is not required that a POSITA recognized the inherent disclosure at the time; likelihood is insufficient — the element must necessarily have existed or resulted.

name: Prior public knowledge (pre-AIA) as invalidating
description: A claim is invalid if the invention defined was publicly known by others in the United States before it was invented by the patentee (pre-AIA §102(a) standard).
guidance: If there is a factual dispute about date of invention or priority, instruct jury how to determine the Cutoff Date.

name: Prior public use (pre-AIA) definition and factors
description: A claim is invalid if the invention was publicly used by others in the United States before the invention date or was publicly used in the U.S. more than one year before the U.S. filing date. An invention was publicly used in the U.S. if an embodiment was both (1) accessible to the public or commercially exploited in the United States, and (2) ready for patenting.
guidance: Factors relevant: nature of the activity, public access to the use, confidentiality obligations, commercial exploitation (even if specifics kept secret), circumstances of testing/experimentation. Absence of affirmative steps to conceal is evidence of public use; secret third-party use is not public unless members of public or employees had access.

name: Prior public use (AIA) worldwide standard
description: Under AIA, a claim is invalid if the claimed invention was in public use anywhere in the world before the effective filing date. An invention was in public use if accessible to the public or commercially exploited anywhere in the world.
guidance: Commercial exploitation includes selling or promoting a product made using the invention even if the specifics were kept secret. To be public use, the invention also must have been ready for patenting at the time (reduced to practice or described sufficiently).

name: On-sale bar
description: A patent claim is invalid if before the cutoff an embodiment of the claimed invention was both (1) the subject of a commercial sale or offer for sale (pre-AIA: in the United States), and (2) ready for patenting.
guidance: A commercial offer for sale exists if another party could make a binding contract by accepting the offer. An offer for sale even if confidential can trigger the bar. It is not required that a sale was made or that the sale terms disclosed invention details. Ready for patenting requires reduction to practice or sufficiently specific descriptions enabling a POSITA.

name: Experimental use exception to public use/on-sale
description: Certain activities are experimental if they are a legitimate effort to test claimed features of the invention or to determine if the invention will work for its intended purpose. So long as the primary purpose is experimentation, it does not matter that the public used the invention or that the inventor incidentally derived profit from it.
guidance: Only experimentation by or under the control of the inventor (or assignee) qualifies; experimentation by a third party for its own purposes does not. The experimentation must relate to claimed features and be for technological improvement, not primarily for commercial exploitation. If plaintiff produces strong experimental-use evidence, the jury may find no prior public use or sale despite defendant's proof.

name: Prior invention (pre-AIA) defense
description: A claim is invalid if the invention was invented by another person in the United States before the patentee (pre-AIA). The Defendant must show by clear and convincing evidence that (1) before the patentee the third party reduced to practice a product/method that included all the claim features, or (2) the third party was first to conceive and exercised reasonable diligence in reducing to practice.
guidance: Additionally, the third party's product/method must have been sufficiently developed that one skilled in the art would have recognized it would work for its intended purpose. This defense may be negated if the invention was abandoned, suppressed, or concealed.

name: Determine what the claim as a whole covers
description: A determination as to what the claim as a whole covers.
guidance: In making this determination, the examiner should consider and discuss the full scope of the claim.

name: Compare claim scope with disclosure in the specification
description: A full review of the application to understand how the applicant provides support for the claimed invention including each element and/or step.
guidance: This review includes comparing the claim scope with the scope of the description; for amended claims compare scope to original claims and the specification (see decision trees in Appendices B and C).

name: Possession by one skilled in the art
description: A determination as to whether one skilled in the art would recognize that the applicant was in possession of the claimed invention as a whole at the time of filing.
guidance: This determination should include consideration of: actual reduction to practice; disclosure of drawings or structural chemical formulas; sufficient relevant identifying characteristics (complete structure, partial structure, physical and/or chemical properties, functional characteristics when coupled with a known or disclosed correlation between function and structure); method of making the claimed invention; level of skill and knowledge in the art; predictability in the art.

name: Consideration for single-embodiment/species claims
description: For each claim drawn to a single embodiment or species, consider whether one of ordinary skill in the art would recognize that the applicant was in possession of that embodiment or species at the time of filing.
guidance: Apply the same factors listed under 'Possession by one skilled in the art' specifically to the disclosed embodiment/species.

name: Consideration for genus claims (representative species requirement)
description: For each claim drawn to a genus, determine whether there is disclosure of a representative number of species which would lead one skilled in the art to conclude that the applicant was in possession of the claimed genus.
guidance: The number of species required to represent a genus will vary depending on the level of skill and knowledge in the art and the variability among the claimed genus: fewer species are required where skill and knowledge are high; more where the genus is highly variable.

name: Effect of transitional/open vs closed claim language
description: Understand how transitional phrases affect claim scope (e.g., 'comprising' vs 'consisting of').
guidance: Open transitional language ('comprising') may claim a genus that includes additional sequences or elements (broader scope); closed transitional language ('consisting of') limits the claim to the single species expressly recited. This affects whether the specification's disclosure of a single species supports the full claim scope.

name: Assess whether missing/omitted element makes amended claim broader than original
description: When claims are amended to remove a limitation, determine whether the amendment results in a claim broader than the original claim and whether the specification supports the broader scope.
guidance: Follow the decision tree where no benefit claimed (Appendix B) or where benefit claimed (Appendix C). If the missing element was a critical feature described in the specification, omission likely renders the amended claim unsupported by the specification (written description failure).

name: Critical feature analysis
description: Consider whether a feature omitted from a claim (or absent from the parent) is described in the specification as critical to proper functioning of the invention.
guidance: If the specification describes a feature as critical (e.g., shape is critical to function) then disclosure of only that species will not show possession of a broader genus; the broader claim is not entitled to the earlier filing date and fails written description for that scope.

name: Sufficiency of functional/flow-chart/software disclosure when supported by conventional hardware
description: Determine whether a specification that provides detailed functional flow diagrams or steps (but not source code) sufficiently describes the claimed computer-implemented invention.
guidance: Disclosing conventional hardware (e.g., a microprocessor capable of performing the functions) plus a detailed functional description/drawings can be sufficient for written description where one skilled in the art would understand what's being described and recognize the inventor was in possession of the invention.

name: Representative species via shared structural feature (e.g., SEQ ID)
description: A disclosed species that provides a structural feature common to members of a claimed genus may be representative of the genus if the complete structure of that common feature is provided.
guidance: If the claimed genus is defined by the presence of a particular structural element (e.g., a specific EST sequence) and the specification discloses the complete sequence, that species may be representative and support the genus when one skilled in the art can add flanking sequences by routine experimentation.

name: Sufficiency of identifying characteristics for proteins
description: Evaluate whether identifying characteristics provided in the specification (partial amino acid sequence, functional activity, molecular weight, purification data, method of isolation) are sufficient to show possession of the claimed protein.
guidance: Partial sequence plus functional data and an isolation/production method can be sufficient for written description of a protein claim if a person skilled in the art would recognize possession of the claimed protein from those identifying characteristics.

name: Sufficiency of identifying characteristics for DNAs encoding proteins
description: Assess whether disclosure supports claims to DNAs encoding a protein when the specification gives only partial protein sequence or other protein characteristics.
guidance: Partial protein sequence and protein characteristics may not provide sufficient identifying information about the DNA (e.g., size alone is insufficient). Disclosure of a method to obtain the DNA or cloning/isolation of the DNA (or deposited DNA) strengthens written description support; percentage of structure disclosed (e.g., % of amino-acid sequence) is relevant.

name: Consider presence or absence of art-recognized structure–function correlation
description: Determine whether an art-recognized correlation between structure and function exists and is disclosed in the specification.
guidance: When a known structure–function correlation is disclosed (or exists in the art), functional claims or claims based on partial structure may be better supported; absent such correlation, functional language is less likely to show possession of broad genus/species.

name: Use USPTO decision trees for amended/priority-benefit claim analysis
description: Follow the procedural decision trees provided in Appendix B (no benefit claimed) and Appendix C (benefit claimed) to determine entitlement to earlier filing dates and written-description outcomes.
guidance: These decision trees direct examiners to compare amended/amending claims to original claims and specification, evaluate missing elements and criticality, and then decide written description and entitlement issues.

name: Evidence of reduction to practice and methods of making
description: Assess whether the specification provides an actual reduction to practice or a method for making the claimed invention, as evidence of possession.
guidance: Actual working examples, procedures for isolation or synthesis, and concrete production steps strengthen written description support; their absence weighs against possession, especially for broad claims.

name: Scope of first search and expectation for subsequent searches
description: The first search should cover the invention as described and claimed, including the inventive concepts toward which the claims appear directed, and should not be extended merely to add immaterial variants.
guidance: Following the first Office action, the examiner normally need not make a second search unless claim amendments or newly available substantially more pertinent references justify it.

name: Analysis of claims: note claim breadth
description: The breadth of the claims should always be carefully noted; the examiner should be fully aware of what the claims do not call for, as well as what they do require. During examination claims are given the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.
guidance: See cited case law (In re Morris; In re NTP) and MPEP sections for claim analysis details; sketching or diagramming claims may assist in delineating limitations and breadth.

name: Recognize variant embodiments within claim scope
description: Claims may include within their breadth one or more variant embodiments not disclosed in the application that could anticipate or render obvious the claimed invention if found in a reference; such variants must be recognized during the search.
guidance: For apparatus claims, sketch two or more divergent embodiments as permitted by the claim to determine actual breadth; applicants are not required to submit such sketches.

name: Consider equivalents
description: All subject matter that is the equivalent of the subject matter as defined in the claim, even though different from the claim definition, must be considered unless expressly excluded by the claimed subject matter.
guidance: See MPEP sections on equivalents for discussion when claims use means or step-plus-function terminology.

name: Search analogous arts regardless of classification
description: Not only must the art be searched within which the invention is classifiable, but also all analogous arts must be searched regardless of where the claimed invention is classified.
guidance: Determination of analogous arts depends on necessary essential function/utility of the claimed subject matter, not the applicant's label; e.g., mixing-related inventions across different end-uses may be analogous for search purposes.

name: Examiners' Step 2A Prong One procedure for identifying abstract ideas
description: Examiners should (1) identify the specific limitation(s) in the claim that the examiner believes recites an abstract idea, and (2) determine whether the identified limitation(s) fall within at least one of the enumerated groupings of abstract ideas.
guidance: If the limitation(s) fall within at least one grouping, conclude the claim recites an abstract idea in Step 2A Prong One and proceed to Step 2A Prong Two to determine whether additional elements integrate the abstract idea into a practical application (see MPEP § 2106.04(d)). If the limitation(s) do not fall within any grouping, conclude the claim does not recite an abstract idea and is eligible at Step 2A Prong One (Pathway B), unless the claim recites another judicial exception (e.g., law of nature or natural phenomenon). See MPEP § 2106.04(a)(3) for rare exceptions.

name: Enumerated groupings of abstract ideas
description: The Office distills relevant case law into three enumerated groupings of abstract ideas: (1) mathematical concepts; (2) certain methods of organizing human activity; and (3) mental processes.
guidance: These groupings are rooted in Supreme Court and Federal Circuit precedent and are intended to shift examiners from a case-by-case comparison approach to generally applying the body of case law across technologies and claim types. Groupings are not mutually exclusive; a claim limitation may fall within more than one grouping.

name: Mathematical concepts (grouping)
description: Defined as mathematical relationships, mathematical formulas or equations, and mathematical calculations.
guidance: Case law identifies many concepts as falling within this grouping (e.g., methods for converting binary-coded decimal to pure binary (Benson); formulas for alarm limits (Flook); Arrhenius equation (Diehr); mathematical formula for hedging (Bilski)). When determining whether a claim recites a mathematical concept, consider whether the claim actually recites the mathematical concept or merely is based on or involves one. A limitation merely based on or involving a mathematical concept may not fall into this grouping if the mathematical concept itself is not recited in the claim. Mathematical concepts need not be expressed in symbols; words operating on data can serve the same purpose.

name: Mathematical relationships
description: A mathematical relationship is a relationship between variables or numbers and may be expressed in words or symbols (e.g., pressure = F/A, relationship between reaction rate and temperature (Arrhenius)).
guidance: Examples of relationships recited in claims include Arrhenius-style relationships, conversions between number systems, geometrical relations (antenna conductor lengths/angles), and organization/manipulation of information through mathematical correlations (Digitech). If the relationship itself is recited, that supports treating the limitation as a mathematical concept.

name: Mathematical formulas or equations
description: Claims that recite a numerical formula or equation (or textual equivalents like 'determining a ratio of A to B' or 'calculating F = ma') are within the mathematical concepts grouping.
guidance: Examples: specific electromagnetic standing wave formulas, Arrhenius equation, alarm-limit formulas, hedging formulas. Textual descriptions that are effectively a formula should be considered as reciting a mathematical equation.

name: Mathematical calculations
description: A mathematical calculation is a mathematical operation or act of calculating using mathematical methods (e.g., arithmetic operations, exponentiation, statistical analyses).
guidance: Claims reciting operations such as performing resampled statistical analysis, computing alarm-limit values, converting coordinates using formulae, performing calculations to manage insurance policies, or other algorithmic computations should be considered as reciting mathematical calculations when the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim in light of the specification encompasses such calculations.

name: Commercial or legal interactions
description: Includes agreements in the form of contracts, legal obligations, advertising, marketing or sales activities or behaviors, and business relations.
guidance: Claims reciting contractual relationships or transaction performance guarantees (e.g., buySAFE) and other business-related interactions are examples. If the claimed interaction is essentially a commercial/legal practice, the limitation may be treated as an abstract idea under this sub-grouping.

name: Managing personal behavior or relationships or interactions between people
description: Covers concepts such as social activities, teaching, following rules or instructions, and other ways of managing behavior or relationships between people.
guidance: This sub-grouping can encompass single-person activities (e.g., a person following instructions) or multi-person activities. Determine whether the claimed activity itself fits within managing behavior/relationships; if so, classify under this sub-grouping.

name: Mental processes (grouping)
description: Includes concepts performed in the human mind, such as observation, evaluation, judgment, and opinion.
guidance: If a claim limitation recites concepts that can be performed solely in the human mind (even if aided by conventional computer components), it may fall within the mental-processes grouping. If a limitation also fits other groupings (e.g., mathematical concepts), identify those groupings as appropriate.

name: Claims that do not recite an abstract idea — non-limiting examples
description: Non-limiting hypothetical examples of claims that do not recite (set forth or describe) an abstract idea include: i) a printer with belt/roller/printhead/ink cartridge; ii) a washing machine with tub/drive motor/controller/housing; iii) an earring sensor for blood glucose with memory; iv) a BRCA1 sequencing method with PCR amplification and sequencing; v) a method for loading BIOS into a local computer system from remote memory; vi) a GUI icon-rearrangement method based on usage metrics involving automatic movement; vii) a two-stage neural-network training regimen using transformed images and a second-stage negative set.
guidance: These examples illustrate claims that, although they may be based on or involve abstract ideas at some level, do not themselves set forth an abstract idea and thus are eligible at Step 2A Prong One (Pathway B). Use these as non-limiting guidance when determining whether a claim 'recites' an abstract idea.

name: Claims may fall into multiple groupings; identify at least one (preferably all)
description: The groupings are not mutually exclusive; some claim limitations may fall within more than one grouping or sub-grouping (e.g., a calculation that could be performed mentally is both a mathematical concept and a mental process).
guidance: Examiners should identify at least one applicable grouping, but preferably identify all groupings that apply to the limitation(s) before proceeding to Step 2A Prong Two.

name: If claim recites a different judicial exception, follow the corresponding analysis
description: If the claim recites another judicial exception (e.g., law of nature or natural phenomenon), examiners should follow the guidance specific to that exception (see MPEP §§ 2106.04(b) and 2106.04(c)).
guidance: Do not conclude eligibility solely because the claim does not fall into the abstract-idea groupings; check for other exceptions that may render the claim ineligible and apply their respective Step 2A analyses.

name: Non-English application filing and translation requirements
description: A nonprovisional application filed in a language other than English requires an English translation, a statement that the translation is accurate, and the processing fee set forth in § 1.17(i); provisional applications filed in a non-English language do not require an English translation at filing but will require one if benefit is claimed later.
guidance: If translation/statement/fees are not filed, applicant will be notified and given time to file or risk abandonment. A subsequently filed English translation must contain complete identifying data to permit association. The translation must be literal, accompanied by an accuracy statement, and a signed request that the English translation be used for examination. If idiomatic English/US practice issues exist, include a preliminary amendment to make necessary changes without introducing new matter (35 U.S.C. 132). Failure to timely file will result in abandonment. Applicants are advised this procedure is for emergency situations and should not be routine due to potential errors and administrative burden. Recommended that original filing include a cover letter and self-addressed return postcard containing identifying data in English.

name: Illustrations and graphics limitations in the written description
description: Graphical illustrations, diagrammatic views, flow-charts, and diagrams in the descriptive portion of the specification do not come within 37 CFR 1.58(a) (which permits tables, chemical and mathematical formulas in the specification in lieu of formal drawings). The written description portion of the specification must not contain drawings or flow diagrams.
guidance: Examiners should object and request formal drawings under 37 CFR 1.81 when an application contains graphs, drawings, or flow charts in the specification. A claim may incorporate by reference to a specific figure or table where there is no practical way to define the invention in words (see MPEP § 2173.05(s)). The description may contain tables but the same tables must not be included both in the drawings as a figure and in the description (applications under 35 U.S.C. 371 are excluded). Claims may contain tables if necessary to conform to 35 U.S.C. 112 or otherwise desirable; when printed the table will not be part of the claim but will be referenced.

name: Arrangement/order of application elements
description: 37 CFR 1.77: The elements of the application, if applicable, should appear in the following order: (1) Utility application transmittal form; (2) Fee transmittal form; (3) Application data sheet; (4) Specification; (5) Drawings; (6) Executed oath or declaration.
guidance: Specification should include the sections in order: Title; Cross-reference to related applications; Statement regarding federally sponsored research or development; Names of parties to joint research agreement; Reference to sequence listing/computer program listing appendix on compact disc; Background; Brief summary; Brief description of views of drawings; Detailed description; Claim(s); Abstract; Sequence listing if on paper. Section headings should be uppercase without underlining or bold. If no text follows a heading, use “Not Applicable.” Provisional applications are recommended to follow same format; ADS can be used to supply some data; if discrepancy between ADS and other parts, ADS controls except for naming and citizenship (see 37 CFR 1.76(d)).

name: Section heading formatting
description: The text of the specification sections (Title through Sequence Listing) should be preceded by a section heading in uppercase and without underlining or bold type.
guidance: If no text follows the section heading, state “Not Applicable.” Recommended that provisional applications follow the same general format although claims are not required.

name: Claims formal requirements
description: The claim or claims must commence on a separate sheet or electronic page (37 CFR 1.52(b)(3)). Where a claim sets forth a plurality of elements or steps, each element or step of the claim should be separated by a line indentation. There may be plural indentations to further segregate subcombinations or related steps.
guidance: See 37 CFR 1.75 and MPEP 608.01(i)-(p) for additional guidance. Claims should be formatted to clearly separate elements/steps and begin on a separate sheet.

name: Abstract of the disclosure requirements
description: A brief abstract of the technical disclosure must commence on a separate sheet under the heading “Abstract” or “Abstract of the Disclosure.” The abstract may not exceed 150 words and its purpose is to enable quick determination of the nature and gist of the technical disclosure.
guidance: Abstract should be a concise narrative limited generally to 50–150 words and not exceed 15 lines of text; should not include other parts of the application; avoid patent claim legal phrasing (e.g., “means,” “said”); should not state purported merits or speculative applications or compare with the prior art. Content should include what is new in the art; for machines give organization and operation, for articles give method of making, for chemicals give identity and use, for mixtures list ingredients, for processes list steps. For compounds/processes, include process for making and/or a use if not obvious. If modifications/alternatives exist, mention preferred modification/alternative by example. The abstract is prepared by the applicant; OPAP will review and examiner will require or edit as necessary; examiner should check abstract compliance early in prosecution and may require revisions via office action or formal amendment on allowance (see MPEP § 1302.04). Sample abstracts are provided for guidance.

name: Definition of 'condition for examination' (37 CFR 1.704(f))
description: An application filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a) is in condition for examination when it includes: a specification with at least one claim and an abstract (37 CFR 1.72(b)); papers in compliance with 37 CFR 1.52; drawings (if any) in compliance with 37 CFR 1.84; any required English translation; Sequence Listing/Sequence Listing XML compliance (if applicable); an inventor's oath/declaration or ADS per 1.63(b); basic filing, search, and examination fees; any certified copy required by 1.57(a); and any application size fee under 1.16(s).
guidance: For international applications entering the national stage, analogous documents and fees under 1.491/1.492 apply. Papers/drawings/sequence listings that are corrected by the latest reply prior to the mailing of an action under 35 U.S.C. 132 or a notice of allowance will be considered in compliance as of the filing date for PTA purposes.

name: Formal requirements for description and other IA elements
description: The description, claims, abstract and other elements of the IA must comply with specified form and content standards (including Annex C standards for sequence listings).
guidance: Description must contain required elements and numbering (5.094,5.012). Description must comply with standards in Annex C and related rules for electronic form (5.099-5.104,7.005-7.012,10.063,11.088). Free text and numbering guidance (5.013,5.099,7.012).

name: Time limits (filing/transmittal/translation/fees/entry into national phase)
description: Various fixed and recalculable time limits for transmittals, furnishing translations, paying fees, requesting SIS, entering national phase, and recalculation where priority claims change.
guidance: Time limits fixed from date of mailing (5.173,9.004). Specific time limits referenced for national phase entry (5.005, Nat. Phase), translations (4.014-4.016,6.015), IPE fee payments (10.042,10.047), requesting SIS (8.005), recalculation due to priority claim correction (6.040).

name: Technical terminology and words in drawings
description: Requirements on the use of technical terminology in the IA and words appearing in drawings; limitations on disparaging comments and value claims.
guidance: Technical terminology requirements (5.176). Words in drawings guidance (5.131). IA may not contain disparaging signs or comments (5.175). Abstracts not to claim alleged value of invention (5.169).

name: Presumption that all rejected claims are on appeal
description: The Board will presume that all of the rejected claims are on appeal except for any claims subsequently canceled by an amendment filed by appellant. Therefore, the examiner will treat all pending, rejected claims as being on appeal, and maintain all of the rejections set forth in the Office action from which the appeal is taken, unless appellant has overcome the rejection (e.g., by submitting persuasive arguments, an acceptable terminal disclaimer, or evidence).
guidance: In situations where the appellant requests to hold a rejection in abeyance or did not present any argument on a rejection in the appeal brief, the examiner should maintain the rejection in the examiner’s answer and should identify that the appellant has not argued the rejection in the appeal brief.

name: Examples of situations that constitute a new ground
description: Factual examples that will constitute a new ground include: changing statutory basis from 35 U.S.C. 102 to 103 (or vice versa) where issues differ; citing new calculations for overlapping ranges first identified in the answer; relying on a different structure in support of structural obviousness; pointing to different portion of the claim to maintain a 'new matter' 35 U.S.C. 112 rejection.
guidance: Examples from case law are provided (In re Hughes; In re Echerd; In re Kumar; In re Wiechert; In re Waymouth), illustrating that new statutory bases, new factual underpinnings, new calculations, or reliance on portions of references not previously relied upon may require designation as new ground because appellants must have a fair opportunity to respond.

name: Patent Term Extensions
description: A patent term extension adds up to 5 years to a pharmaceutical patent to compensate for time lost during FDA review.
guidance: 50% of the IND (clinical testing) phase + 100% of the NDA (FDA review) phase; capped at 5 years total; capped at 14 years from FDA approval; Only ONE patent per approved drug eligible for extension. Use extension calculations and claim selection strategically to maximize protected post-approval term.

name: Composition of matter patents
description: Patents directed to the drug substance/molecule (composition of matter).
guidance: Primary form of protection for novel small molecules and biologics; aim for both genus (Markush) coverage for breadth and specific compound claims for definiteness and enforceability.

name: Method of treatment patents
description: Patents claiming specific therapeutic uses, dosing regimens, routes, or patient populations.
guidance: Claim specific patient populations, specific dosing regimens, specific routes of administration, and precise indications (e.g., 'treating breast cancer in HER2+ patients') to maximize enforceability and avoid overbroad/use-speculative issues.

name: Method of manufacturing patents
description: Patents covering synthesis routes, intermediates, and manufacturing processes.
guidance: Disclose enabling synthesis routes and intermediates; may provide protection even if composition claims are narrow or invalidated; useful to block generic manufacturing methods.

name: Polymorph patents
description: Patents directed to specific crystalline forms (polymorphs) of a compound.
guidance: Claim distinct crystalline forms and provide characterization data; can extend effective exclusivity by covering solid-state forms used in products.

name: Combination therapy patents
description: Patents claiming combinations of active agents or combined regimens.
guidance: Draft claims to recite synergistic or unexpected combination effects and provide supporting data; combinations can create new exclusivity opportunities distinct from single-agent patents.

name: Selection patents
description: Patents claiming a selected subgenus or subpopulation drawn from a broader genus.
guidance: Use selection patents to capture unexpectedly superior members of a genus; ensure adequate written description and evidence that the selected subset was not obvious.

name: Composition claims drafting considerations
description: How to draft composition (chemical) claims to balance breadth and definiteness.
guidance: Consider a genus (Markush) for broad protection and specific compound claims for definiteness; include pharmaceutically acceptable salts, stereoisomers, prodrugs, and metabolites in the disclosure and claim set. Avoid overly broad Markush groups without adequate support.

name: Method of Treatment claims drafting considerations
description: How to draft method-of-treatment claims to improve enforceability and avoid invalidity.
guidance: Claim specific patient populations, dosing regimens, routes of administration, and specific indications (e.g., 'treating breast cancer in HER2+ patients'). Precise, concrete therapeutic claims help satisfy utility and written description expectations.

name: Written description requirement for genus claims
description: §112 written description obligation for genus/Markush claims in pharma.
guidance: Must show possession across the full claimed scope; for broad genus claims, include representative examples and disclosure sufficient to demonstrate possession of the claimed subgroups.

name: Enablement (Wands factors) in unpredictable arts
description: Enablement analysis under §112 using the Wands factors, especially demanding for unpredictable arts like pharmaceuticals.
guidance: Disclosure must enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the full scope without undue experimentation. Consider the Wands factors (nature of the invention, state of the art, amount of direction provided, presence of working examples, breadth of the claims, predictability of the art, level of ordinary skill). Provide detailed synthesis routes and working examples to satisfy enablement.

name: Functional/Amgen v. Sanofi standard for functional genus claims
description: Post-Amgen v. Sanofi standard for functional genus claims in biotech/pharma.
guidance: Functional genus claims require representative examples and a shared structural 'quality' across the examples; include representative exemplars and show shared properties to support broad functional claiming.

name: Utility requirement for pharmaceutical patents
description: Utility must be specific, substantial, and credible for claimed therapeutic uses.
guidance: Avoid laundry lists of speculative uses; provide data (pharmacology, clinical, or other convincing evidence) to demonstrate specific, substantial, and credible utility for claimed indications.

name: Inherency for functional limitations in apparatus claims
description: If a functional limitation in an apparatus claim is an inherent characteristic of the prior art structure, the examiner should explain that the prior art structure inherently possesses the claimed limitation.
guidance: When inherency is asserted, the burden shifts to the applicant to prove the prior art lacks the relied‑on characteristic. Cite case law (e.g., In re Schreiber, In re Swinehart). Examiners must make a prima facie showing and explain why the prior art structure inherently possesses the functional limitation.

name: Manner of operation/recited intended use does not distinguish an apparatus claim
description: A claim recitation regarding the manner in which an apparatus is intended to be employed (intended use) does not differentiate the claimed apparatus from a prior art apparatus if the prior art teaches all structural limitations of the claim.
guidance: Intended use or the way a device is employed is immaterial to structure; structural teachings in the prior art controlling. Example: Ex parte Masham — the Board affirmed rejection even though prior art used the device with different submersion because structure was the same. Examiner should focus on structural elements, not recited uses.

name: Structural differences control anticipation despite functional equivalence
description: Even if a prior art device performs all functions recited in a claim, it does not anticipate the claim if there is any structural difference between the claimed apparatus and the prior art device.
guidance: Means‑plus‑function limitations are met by structures equivalent to those in the specification (e.g., In re Donaldson). Courts may construe claims to require discrete structural elements (e.g., In re Robertson — three fastening elements required despite reference performing same function with two). Examiners must compare structural limitations, and consider means‑plus‑function linkage to disclosed structures.

name: Patentability analysis for computer‑implemented functional claim limitations (35 U.S.C. 102/103)
description: Functional language not limited to a specific structure covers all devices capable of performing the recited function; prior art that inherently performs the function may support a 102/103 rejection. Conversely, computer‑implemented functional limitations may narrow claims where hardware cannot meet limitations without enabling software.
guidance: Key considerations: (1) Functional claim language covering all capable devices — if prior art device can inherently perform the function, rejection may be appropriate (In re Translogic, Intel Corp. v. ITC, In re Schreiber, In re Best, In re Ludtke, In re Swinehart). (2) Claims may be construed to require a combination of hardware and enabling software where hardware alone cannot meet the limitation (Nazomi Communications v. Nokia). (3) The term 'computer' is commonly broad and should not be limited to specific characteristics absent definitional claim or specification language (In re Paulsen). (4) Broadly claiming automation of a manual function or implementing known functions on a general‑purpose computer can be obvious (Leapfrog, KSR, Muniauction); examiners should apply obviousness rationales (see MPEP §§2141, 2143 and exemplary rationales).

name: Material or article worked upon does not impart patentability to apparatus claims
description: Inclusion of the material or article worked upon by a claimed structure does not, without more, impart patentability to the claimed device; the device must be patentable based on its structural elements, not its intended article of use.
guidance: Claims directed to machinery that work upon an article are limited to the machine's structure — the process or the article handled (e.g., hair being wound around a core) is irrelevant to machine patentability (In re Otto, In re Young, In re Casey). This line of cases is limited to claims directed to machinery that works upon an article in its intended use.

name: Novel/nonobvious starting material or end product in process claims
description: When evaluating obviousness of a process or method claim that recites making or using a novel/nonobvious product, the entire claim must be considered; there are no per se rules that a process is patentable merely because it yields a novel product or vice versa.
guidance: Obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103 requires fact‑specific analysis considering all claim limitations (In re Ochiai, In re Brouwer, TorPharm v. Ranbaxy). A process yielding a novel and nonobvious product may nonetheless be obvious; conversely, a process yielding a known product may be nonobvious. Treat product recitations as material limitations in claim construction. Review illustrative cases (In re Durden, Albertson, Kanter, Pleuddemann, Kuehl, Mancy) for precedent.

name: Markush claim definition and general treatment
description: A Markush claim recites a list of alternatively usable members (Markush grouping). Any claim that recites alternatively usable members, regardless of format, should be treated as a Markush claim.
guidance: Markush style is common in chemistry, pharmacology, biology, and other fields but may also apply to mechanical features or process steps. A Markush grouping requires selection from a closed group (consisting of). See MPEP §2111.03 and §803.02 for election/search guidance.

name: Improper Markush grouping — rejection and prosecution procedures
description: A Markush claim is improper if members do not share a single structural similarity or a common use; such claims should be rejected on the merits under 'improper Markush grouping' principles (use Form Paragraph 8.40).
guidance: Examiner actions/guidance: (1) Use form paragraph 8.40 and explain why alternatives fail to meet both requirements. (2) Make improper Markush grouping rejection in the first action on the merits after presentation of the claim (compact prosecution). (3) Require election of species for search/examination if appropriate (see MPEP §803.02). (4) Suggest ways to overcome rejection (present each alternative in separate claims, propose a proper grouping supported by the spec, or present convincing arguments of commonality). (5) Also consider rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) if skilled artisans cannot determine metes and bounds (indefiniteness). (6) Maintain rejection until claim is amended or convincing arguments presented; reconsider if record later shows members share structural similarity and common use. (7) No Markush claim can be allowed until improper grouping rejection is overcome or withdrawn.

name: Examiner guidance for drafting and explaining improper Markush rejections (Form Paragraph 8.40 content)
description: Form Paragraph 8.40 provides the template text and examiner notes for rejecting a claim on the basis of an improper Markush grouping and specifies the information to be filled in and reasons to provide.
guidance: Use the form paragraph to state which claim(s) are rejected, identify the improper grouping, and explain why the alternatives do not meet the requirements (e.g., not same recognized class, not functionally equivalent, or do not share substantial structural feature leading to common use). Include suggestions to applicant for overcoming rejection. If election of species is appropriate, only issue form paragraph after applicant election where required. Follow compact prosecution timing rules and include examiner notes for bracketed insertions (claim numbers, description of group, reasons).

name: Directed to an abstract idea
description: Determine whether the representative claim is 'directed to an abstract idea' (e.g., organizing data, time stamping, using keywords to search hierarchical data, fundamental economic practice).
guidance: Courts examine whether the claim as a whole is aimed at an abstract idea (examples in the cases include data organization, time stamping, recommending products based on location). If a claim is found 'directed to an abstract idea,' the inquiry proceeds to whether there is an inventive concept. The record (pleadings, specification, prosecution history) can inform whether the claim is a particular technological improvement or merely an abstract idea.

name: Inventive concept / whether claim elements supply something 'more'
description: Assess whether the challenged claim elements, 'individually and as an ordered combination, lack an inventive concept' and thus fail to transform an abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter.
guidance: Courts look for an 'inventive concept' beyond the abstract idea — e.g., unconventional technological solutions, novel combinations or specific improvements to technology. Whether an inventive concept exists is often factbound; parties should present evidence (specification, prior art, expert testimony) because courts frequently find genuine disputes of material fact on this point.

name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activities
description: Evaluate whether the claimed computer functions are 'well-understood, routine, conventional activities' previously known to the industry.
guidance: Defendants bear responsibility to provide evidence that elements are conventional; lacking such evidence, courts often deny eligibility motions. Determinations of conventionality are frequently questions of fact for which discovery and expert input may be necessary.

name: Need for claim construction before §101 determination
description: Consider whether claim construction (Markman) is necessary before resolving a §101 question because disputed claim term meanings may affect whether a claim is abstract or contains an inventive concept.
guidance: Many courts defer ruling on eligibility until after claim construction if key terms are in dispute or if the proper scope of preemption or inventive-concept analysis depends on a 'settled interpretation of the claim language.' If claim construction will materially affect the eligibility analysis, dismissal is often denied as premature.

name: Whether parties dispute key terms
description: Identify whether the parties 'dispute the meaning of various terms among various claims' — such disputes can preclude resolving §101 early.
guidance: If the parties disagree on claim meanings that bear on the Alice test (e.g., scope of 'data', 'transformative concept'), courts usually find claim construction necessary and defer eligibility rulings until the terms are construed.

name: Presence of physical structures / hardware limitations
description: Assess whether the claims recite physical structures (e.g., 'discount vehicle with information', specialized sensors, multiple hardware components) or are 'limited to the field' of a technology in a way that makes them non-abstract.
guidance: Claims that include concrete physical structures, particular hardware configurations, or limitations tied to a technological field or problem are less likely to be deemed abstract. Courts have relied on such hardware recitations and field-specific limits to find claims directed to technological improvements rather than abstract ideas.

name: Specification/prosecution history showing technological improvement
description: Consider whether the specification or prosecution history 'articulates a solution to problems' in a technological realm or states novelty of a particular organization/approach, supporting an inventive concept.
guidance: Courts may rely on statements in the specification and prosecution history to infer that claims embody a particular technological improvement (e.g., hierarchical organization, specialized databases, sensor techniques). Such support can create factual issues precluding dismissal and bolster a finding of inventive concept.

name: Preemption / scope-of-preemption considerations
description: Assess whether the claim preempts a fundamental principle or would monopolize an abstract idea, and whether claim construction is needed to determine the scope of preemption.
guidance: Preemption concerns factor into the §101 inquiry. Courts have stated that claim construction aids in determining the scope of preemption, and if preemption cannot be assessed without construing terms, the eligibility decision is deferred.

name: Failure to identify a representative claim defeats early motion
description: Determine whether the movant has 'identified a representative claim' when asking the court to resolve eligibility across multiple asserted claims; failure to do so can be a basis to deny the motion.
guidance: Some courts have denied eligibility motions where neither party identified a representative claim or where the movant focused almost exclusively on one independent claim while moving against several dependent claims. Properly articulated representation or per-claim analysis is required.

name: Existence of a possible set of facts making claims eligible
description: Consider whether there 'are any set of facts that could be proven that would result in a determination that one or more of the claims are eligible.'
guidance: If the complaint or record plausibly alleges facts that, if proven, would show eligibility (e.g., novel technical details, unconventional combination), courts often deny dismissal without prejudice, allowing factual development.

name: When courts grant dismissal vs. deny: examples
description: Recognize patterns where courts have granted dismissal (e.g., claims purely time-stamping with no inventive concept) versus where courts deny or defer (e.g., disputes over conventionality, need for claim construction, presence of hardware/technical improvements).
guidance: Use case examples to predict outcomes: courts granted dismissal where claims plainly recited an abstract idea with no added inventive concept; courts denied or deferred where specification suggested technological improvements, physical structures were recited, or factual disputes over conventionality/inventive concept existed.

name: Determine whether a claim limitation invokes § 112(f) (3‑prong analysis)
description: Apply the 3‑prong analysis in MPEP § 2181(I): (A) the claim limitation uses the term “means” or “step” or a term used as a substitute for “means” that is a generic placeholder; (B) that term is modified by functional language (typically linked by “for”, or phrases like “configured to” or “so that”); and (C) the term is not modified by sufficient structure, material, or acts for performing the claimed function.
guidance: A limitation meeting all three prongs is to be interpreted under § 112(f). Use the claims, specification, and the understanding of persons of ordinary skill in the art to perform the analysis. If ambiguous, state the examiner's interpretation on the record. See MPEP § 2181(I).

name: Presumptions about use or absence of the words “means” or “step”
description: A claim limitation is presumed to invoke § 112(f) when it explicitly uses the term “means” or “step” and includes functional language. By contrast, a limitation that does not use the term “means” or “step” triggers the presumption that § 112(f) does not apply.
guidance: Always consider whether the presumptions are overcome by claim language (e.g., use of “means” plus sufficient structure overcomes the presumption; use of a generic placeholder with functional language and lacking structure invokes §112(f)). Document any overcoming of presumptions in the record.

name: Interpretation standard for ‘sufficient structure’
description: The standard is whether the words of the claim are understood by persons of ordinary skill in the art to have a sufficiently definite meaning as the name for structure.
guidance: Apply the Williamson v. Citrix standard (quoted in MPEP § 2181). There are no absolute lists; the examiner must evaluate the term in light of the specification and the commonly accepted meaning in the technological art because claim interpretation turns on the facts of each application.

name: Applicability rules for step-plus-function in process claims
description: Means-plus-function limitations are common; step-plus-function limitations are rare. In process claims, use of the phrase “step for” is presumed to invoke §112(f), but the term “step” alone and the phrase “steps of” tend to show that §112(f) does not apply. A step limitation must not recite an act to be treated under §112(f).
guidance: Most process claims include steps with acts described by verbs ending in “-ing” (e.g., passing, heating, reacting, transferring, determining), which will avoid §112(f). Structural elements may appear in both product and process claims—review all claim types for means/step plus-function issues. See MPEP § 2181(I).

name: Statutory construction and claim scope when § 112(f) applies
description: When § 112(f) applies, the claim limitation shall be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.
guidance: Recognize that invoking §112(f) can narrow claim scope relative to a non‑means formulation; that affects searching and prior-art application. Make the construction explicit in the record so applicants and the public understand how prior art was applied.

name: Make the prosecution record clear about § 112(f) interpretations
description: Establishing the interpretation of §112(f) limitations in writing during prosecution is critical to supporting a clear prosecution record.
guidance: Use available form paragraphs to create a claim interpretation section in an Office action, set forth presumptions and clarifying remarks, notify the applicant/public/courts how the claim was construed, and allow early clarification by the applicant so the examiner can revisit prior art if needed. See MPEP § 2181(VI).

name: Definiteness under § 112(b) for § 112(f) limitations
description: The corresponding structure must be disclosed in the specification itself in a way that one skilled in the art will understand what structure will perform the entire recited function; otherwise the claim fails §112(b) and is indefinite. The disclosed structure must be clearly linked or associated with the claimed function.
guidance: Definiteness is distinct from enablement; if no disclosure of structure for performing the entire recited function exists, find the claim indefinite. Indefiniteness based solely on an inconclusive 3‑prong analysis should be rare because examiners should be able to determine whether claim words recite structure using the claims, specification, and knowledge of POSITA. When ambiguous, state interpretation on the record. See MPEP § 2181(II) and following.

name: Special considerations for computer-implemented § 112(f) limitations (algorithm requirement)
description: For computer-implemented §112(f) claim limitations, the specification must disclose an algorithm for performing the claimed specific computer function, or the claim should be found indefinite.
guidance: The algorithm may be expressed in any understandable terms (mathematical formula, prose, flow chart, etc.). A disclosure that only identifies a general-purpose computer as the structure for performing a specific function is inadequate to satisfy §112(b). Assess sufficiency in light of the level of ordinary skill in the art. See MPEP § 2181(II)(B).

name: Adequate written description and enablement under § 112(a)
description: A §112(f) limitation that is indefinite under §112(b) for lack of disclosed corresponding structure will also lack adequate written description and may not be sufficiently enabled to support the full scope of the claim under §112(a).
guidance: Determine whether the specification describes the claimed invention in sufficient detail to show possession as of the filing date and whether the disclosure contains sufficient information for a person skilled in the art to make and use the invention. See MPEP § 2181(IV) and § 2185.

name: Use MPEP §§ 2181–2187 and available USPTO training resources
description: Examiners should refer to MPEP sections 2181–2187 for guidance on determining invocation of §112(f), making the record clear, and evaluating supporting disclosure under §§112(a) and (b). Refresher training (computer-based and instructor-led) is available through the Office of Patent Training.
guidance: Specific training modules include: “Examining Computer‑Implemented Functional Claim Limitations for Compliance with 35 U.S.C. § 112,” “Application of New Form Paragraphs for Addressing Issues Related to §112(f) or ‘Means‑plus‑Function’ Limitations,” and “Addressing 35 U.S.C. §112(f) or ‘Means‑plus‑Function’ Limitations in an Office Action using New Form Paragraphs.” Technology Center points of contact and intranet resources are available.

name: Secondary considerations / objective indicia of non-obviousness (nexus requirement)
description: How evidence like commercial success, long-felt need, industry praise, and copying are evaluated as objective indicia of non-obviousness.
guidance: The Board evaluates whether the secondary considerations are tied to the claimed invention (nexus). A coextensive commercial product can carry a presumption of nexus. Evidence of copying must show reproduction of the 'entire combination of features' that were assembled. Industry praise must be shown to be the direct result of claimed limitations; marketing or advertising explanations of success require a factual showing (timing and effect) to rebut nexus or persuasiveness.

name: Diligence in antedating / reduction to practice
description: Standards for showing conception and reasonably continuous diligence to antedate a reference.
guidance: Conception can be supported by inventor testimony and contemporaneous documents (e.g., invention disclosure forms) showing each claim element. Diligence is evaluated under a rule-of-reason standard: it need not be perfectly continuous but must be reasonably continuous. Corroborating documentary evidence and testimony reinforcing periods of activity (e.g., work on figures, attorney involvement) can satisfy diligence over the relevant period.

name: Mayo–Alice two-step test and 'significantly more' inquiry
description: Use of the Mayo and Alice framework, including the second element inquiry of whether the claimed invention is 'significantly more' than an abstract idea.
guidance: Commenters identified difficulties with applying the second element; several noted challenges determining whether a claim supplies 'significantly more' and how that should be evaluated in different technologies.

name: Whether the claim provides a technical solution to a technical problem
description: Assessment of whether a claimed invention provides a technical solution to a technical problem can support a finding of eligibility.
guidance: Commenters provided examples where the eligibility test showed a claimed invention provides a technical solution; this is cited as a way to distinguish patentable computer-implemented inventions from abstract ideas.

name: Whether computer-implemented elements (calculations, simulations, models, instruction sets) are patentable
description: Recognition that computer-implemented inventions often comprise calculations, simulations, models, instruction sets, etc., which commenters noted are not patentable by themselves.
guidance: Stakeholders debated how to treat such elements in claims and whether their inclusion can render a claim patent-eligible; impacts heavily discussed for AI and software-related patents.

name: Impacts on particular innovation sectors (life sciences and computer-related)
description: Assess how eligibility jurisprudence alters the landscape differently across sectors, with particular impacts on life sciences and computer-related industries.
guidance: Presentation emphasizes distinct sectoral impacts: life sciences claim heavy reliance on patents to recoup R&D costs; computer-related industries emphasize tools to curb overly broad patents.

name: Adequacy of patent protection to recoup life sciences R&D investment
description: Whether patent protection is sufficient to allow life sciences companies to recoup substantial R&D investments (e.g., ~$2.6 billion and ~12 years to bring a medicine to market).
guidance: Life sciences commenters stressed reliance on patents; examples given of diagnostic claims granted abroad but rejected in the U.S. on eligibility grounds, arguing this divergence harms companies.

name: Use of the eligibility standard to address overly broad patents and PAEs (patent assertion entities)
description: Whether the current eligibility framework serves as a useful tool to address overly broad patents and defend against abusive lawsuits by patent assertion entities.
guidance: Supporters (primarily from computer-related industries) asserted that the new eligibility standard helps curb overly broad claims and abusive enforcement; this is cited as a pro-eligibility-restriction rationale.

name: Specifics/structural parts classification
description: If structural or functional specifics/parts in the claimed invention are used only for a certain apparatus, classify into the place for that apparatus. If such specifics/parts can be used for more than two apparatuses, classify into the place for those specifics/parts. If no place exists for them, classify in place for the relevant apparatus.
guidance: Decision depends on breadth of applicability: single-apparatus use → apparatus place; multi-apparatus (>2) use → parts place.

name: Classification of Markush-type chemical compounds
description: For Markush-type chemical compounds generally defined in a formula, the general chemical formula shall be classified individually if the formula has a few relevant places (for example, less than 5). Specified compounds (designated by structure or identified by properties or described in an example) that are per se in the claimed invention, outputs of a claimed process, or their derivatives, shall be classified in each relevant place.
guidance: Defines 'specified' as (i) designated by structure/title/formula or inferred from a specific reactant, or (ii) identified with physical properties or described in a detailed example. Use multiple classifications when specific compounds are singled out.

name: Request for examination — general admissibility and requirements
description: A request for examination shall be made only for an application pending in KIPO; it is allowed only once per application and, once admitted, cannot be withdrawn. A valid request survives legal incapacity (e.g., death). An applicant may request examination only if a specification including claims is attached, or in foreign-language cases, only if a Korean translation pursuant to Article 42-3(2) is provided.
guidance: Ensures applications are complete (claims/translation) before requesting examination; one-time, irrevocable request rule emphasized.

name: Effects of a request for examination on proceedings
description: An application whose examination is requested shall be examined by an examiner; pendency can be terminated only by patent registration or rejection unless invalidated/withdrawn/abandoned. If the request is made before laying-open, the purpose of the request shall be published in the patent gazette upon publication (or immediately if request made after laying-open). Applicants lacking claims must amend to include claims by prescribed date in response to notification. If a third party filed the request, the Commissioner shall notify the applicant; the examiner shall notify the third party of the final decision (including withdrawal/abandonment).
guidance: Notification duties between KIPO, applicant, and third-party requester; amendment obligations to include claims.

name: Determine what applicant has invented and is seeking to patent
description: Review the complete specification, including the detailed description of the invention, any specific embodiments that have been disclosed, and the claims. Determine what, precisely, the applicant has invented and how the claims relate to and define that invention.
guidance: Review the full specification and claims to identify the invention; examine disclosed embodiments and how claim language maps to the disclosed invention. This is the foundational factual determination to guide subsequent claim construction and §112 analyses.

name: Interpret the claims
description: Give the claim its broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification as it would be interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art. Ascertain the boundaries of the subject matter encompassed by each claim.
guidance: Follow MPEP 2111. Determine whether any claim limitation invokes §112, ¶6; if so, construe that limitation to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents that perform the stated function. Also determine the effective filing date of each claim (see MPEP 201.11 & 706.02). See PART 1, section II and III.C of the 2011 Supplementary 112 Guidelines for additional guidance.

name: Conduct a thorough search of the prior art
description: Determine the state of the art and identify prior art references that are material to the patentability of the claimed invention.
guidance: Perform a comprehensive prior-art search to establish the relevant technological background and references material to novelty, non-obviousness, and other patentability issues that may interact with §112 analyses (e.g., to define ordinary skill in the art or what was known at filing).

name: Written description requirement (35 U.S.C. §112, ¶1)
description: Based on the written description, determine whether one of ordinary skill in the art would recognize that the applicant was in possession of the claimed invention as a whole at the time of filing the application.
guidance: Use PART 2, section I of the 2011 Supplementary 112 Guidelines and MPEP 2163. If the description lacks sufficient detail to support the claim, reject the claim as containing subject matter not described in the specification in such a way as to reasonably convey to one skilled in the relevant art that the inventor(s) had possession at filing. See FP 7.31.01 for procedural guidance on such rejections.

name: Enablement requirement (35 U.S.C. §112, ¶1)
description: Based on the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim, determine if the disclosure enables one skilled in the art to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation at the time of filing.
guidance: Follow MPEP 2164. If the disclosure is not enabling, reject the claims as containing subject matter not described in the specification in such a way as to enable one skilled in the art to make and/or use the invention (see FP 7.31.02). If lack of enablement is due to the scope of the claims, use FP 7.31.03. Consider scope versus teaching and whether undue experimentation would be required across the claim scope.

name: Best mode requirement (35 U.S.C. §112, ¶1)
description: Confirm whether the best mode of practicing the claimed invention is disclosed in the application.
guidance: Assume that the best mode is disclosed in the specification unless there is evidence showing the inventor possessed a best mode at filing and did not disclose it (see MPEP 2165). For cases with evidence of concealment of the best mode, follow FP 7.31.04. Evaluate whether an inventor's undisclosed preference rises to a best-mode concealment.

name: Definiteness requirement (35 U.S.C. §112, ¶2)
description: Under the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim, determine whether the metes and bounds of the claimed invention are clear and whether there is more than one reasonable interpretation of what is covered by the claim.
guidance: See PART 1, sections II-III of the 2011 Supplementary 112 Guidelines and MPEP 2173 et seq. Check for problematic term types: functional terms that merely recite a problem/result rather than structure/material/steps; terms of degree/subjective terms (and whether the specification provides a standard for measuring them); unclear Markush groups (whether a skilled artisan can envision all members); inconsistencies between claim and specification that prevent determining scope. For each §112, ¶6 limitation, determine whether the written description discloses the corresponding structure/material/acts linking to the claimed function—if not, reject under §112, ¶2. If metes and bounds are unclear, reject as indefinite (FP 7.34.01).

name: Proper dependent claim requirements (35 U.S.C. §112, ¶4)
description: Determine whether dependent claims comply with ¶4 by properly specifying further limitations and including all limitations of the claim upon which they depend.
guidance: If a dependent claim fails to specify a further limitation of the subject matter or fails to include all the limitations of the claim upon which it depends, reject the dependent claim under §112, ¶4 as unpatentable. Ensure claim dependency format and incorporation of limitations are correct.

name: Clearly communicate findings, conclusions, and their bases in an Office action; practice compact prosecution
description: When making a rejection under 35 U.S.C. §112, identify the particular claim language giving rise to the rejection and state the specific reason that the identified language does not comply with the relevant paragraph. Evaluate claims for patentability under all applicable statutes and attempt resolution through interview.
guidance: In Office actions include findings under §101, §102, §103, and non-statutory double patenting as applicable; raise any formal objections; and attempt to resolve issues via examiner-applicant interview to promote compact prosecution. For §112 rejections, explicitly cite the claim terms, the deficiency, and the statutory paragraph relied upon.

name: Statutory double patenting (same invention) — use of provisional rejection (¶ 8.32)
description: Claim [1] provisionally rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 as claiming the same invention as that of claim [2] of copending Application No. [3] (reference application). This is a provisional statutory double patenting rejection since the claims directed to the same invention have not in fact been patented.
guidance: Must be preceded by form paragraph 8.30 and is used only for double patenting rejections of the same invention claimed in another copending application (scope of claimed inventions identical). Do not use this paragraph where the claims directed to the same invention are in an issued patent (use form paragraph 8.31 instead). May be used where the patent and application under examination: (a) name the same inventive entity, (b) name different inventive entities but are commonly assigned, (c) are not commonly assigned but name at least one common inventor, (d) are filed by a common applicant, (e) claim patentably indistinct inventions made under a joint research agreement (pre-AIA 103(c)), or (f) claim patentably indistinct inventions with common ownership timing requirements under AIA. For pre-AIA and AIA prosecutions, additional specific form paragraphs (e.g., 8.27.fti, 8.27.aia, 7.15.02.fti) may be required as noted.

name: Nonstatutory double patenting (NSDP) — definition and appropriateness
description: A rejection based on nonstatutory double patenting is a judicially created doctrine grounded in public policy to prevent unjustified or improper timewise extension of the right to exclude granted by a patent. NSDP is appropriate where conflicting claims are not identical but at least one examined application claim is not patentably distinct from the reference claim(s) because the examined claim is anticipated by, or would have been obvious over, the reference claim(s).
guidance: When deciding whether NSDP is appropriate, first ask whether any invention claimed in the application is anticipated by or is an obvious variation of an invention claimed in the patent. The examiner should construe the claims in the application and the reference to determine differences and then determine patentable distinctness using anticipation and/or obviousness analyses (see Pfizer v. Teva and cited cases). A timely filed terminal disclaimer may overcome an NSDP rejection if requirements are met (see separate rubric).

name: Proper use of reference patent/application disclosure in NSDP analysis
description: No part of the reference patent or application may be used as if it were prior art when considering whether an application claim would have been anticipated by or is an obvious variation of the invention in a reference. This does not preclude all use of the reference disclosure to understand the meaning of the reference claims.
guidance: The specification may be used as a dictionary to learn the meaning of a term (Toro Co.; Renishaw; Phillips). Portions of the specification that provide support for the reference claims may be examined and considered when addressing whether a claim in the application defines an obvious variation of an invention claimed in the reference (In re Vogel). However, subject matter disclosed in the reference that does not fall within the scope of a reference claim cannot be used to support an NSDP rejection (that would treat the reference as prior art). When construing reference claims, determine which portions of the disclosure fall within the claim scope and limit consideration to those portions.

name: Anticipation analysis for NSDP
description: NSDP is appropriate where a claim in an application claims subject matter that is different but not patentably distinct from subject matter claimed in a prior patent or copending application because the claim under examination is anticipated by the reference claim(s).
guidance: This arises when, for example, the examined claim is generic to a species or sub-genus claimed in the conflicting patent/application (entire scope of the reference claim falls within scope of examined claim). In such cases an obviousness analysis is not required; the NSDP rejection should explain that the species or sub-genus in the conflicting patent or application anticipates the claimed genus and that issuing the genus would improperly extend the right to exclude. In genus-species or overlapping-scope situations where anticipation cannot be established, an obviousness analysis is typically required and the examiner should explain why it would have been obvious to select the claimed species given the genus (see MPEP § 2131.02 and § 2144.08).

name: Obviousness analysis for NSDP (Graham factors and content of rejection)
description: Where NSDP is not based on anticipation or an unjustified timewise extension rationale, it is analogous to the nonobviousness inquiry of 35 U.S.C. 103 except the patent disclosure is not prior art. The factual inquiries set forth in Graham v. John Deere should be considered.
guidance: Consider: (A) scope and content of the patent claim relative to the application claim; (B) differences between the claims; (C) level of ordinary skill in the art; (D) objective indicia of nonobviousness. Any NSDP rejection under an obviousness analysis should clearly state (A) the differences between the inventions defined by the conflicting claims and (B) the reasons why a person of ordinary skill would conclude the claimed invention is an obvious variation. Any secondary references used to support the obviousness analysis must be prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 (see MPEP §§ 2120, 2141).

name: One-way test for distinctness (when only one directional determination is needed)
description: If the patent term filing date of the application under examination is the same or later than that of a reference application or patent, only a one-way determination of distinctness is needed — i.e., whether the invention claimed in the application would have been anticipated by or an obvious variation of the invention claimed in the reference.
guidance: Apply a one-way test in these circumstances (see In re Berg). Even if the application under examination has the earlier patent term filing date, a one-way determination suffices absent a finding that (A) the PTO is solely responsible for any delays in prosecution (In re Hubbell) and (B) the applicant could not have filed the conflicting claims in a single earlier-filed application (In re Kaplan). If one-way test supports that the application claim would have been obvious over the patent claim, NSDP rejection is proper to prevent unjustified timewise extension.
