name: Terminal disclaimer as remedy to overcome NSDP
description: A timely filed terminal disclaimer in compliance with 37 CFR 1.321(c) or 1.321(d) may be used to overcome an actual or provisional rejection based on NSDP provided the reference application or patent is commonly owned with the examined application or claims an invention made as a result of activities under a joint research agreement.
guidance: Terminal disclaimer must be signed in compliance with 37 CFR 1.321(b). Filing a terminal disclaimer alone is not a complete reply; it must be accompanied by a reply requesting reconsideration of the prior Office action. For replies to non-final Office actions follow 37 CFR 1.111(a); for replies to final Office actions follow 37 CFR 1.113(c). See MPEP § 1490 for guidance regarding terminal disclaimers and withdrawal of NSDP rejections when these are the only rejections remaining. USPTO provides terminal disclaimer forms and eTerminal Disclaimer processing information on the website (forms PTO/SB/25, PTO/SB/26, PTO/AIA/25, PTO/AIA/26 depending on filing date).

name: Form paragraph and procedural use requirements for NSDP rejections (¶ 8.33 - 8.39)
description: Form paragraph 8.33 ('Basis for Nonstatutory Double Patenting, Heading Only') must precede any of form paragraphs 8.34 to 8.39 and be used only once in an Office action. Specific form paragraphs (8.34–8.39) are used to make particular NSDP rejections depending on whether the reference is a patent or a copending application and whether secondary references are used.
guidance: Use 8.34 for NSDP rejections based on a patent (no secondary reference), 8.35 for provisional NSDP rejections based on a copending application (no secondary reference), and other form paragraphs (8.36–8.39) where secondary references or equitable principles apply. Use appropriate additional form paragraphs for pre-AIA (fti) or AIA (aia) circumstances (e.g., 8.27.fti, 8.28.fti, 7.21.fti, 7.15.02.fti) as noted in examiner notes. Provide required bracketed insertions (claim numbers, patent/application numbers, explanation for anticipation or obviousness rationale).

name: Equitable/principles-based NSDP (unjustified timewise extension) and special approvals (Schneller/Schneller-type)
description: NSDP may also be based on equitable principles to prevent unjustified timewise extension of the patent term when issuance of a second patent would provide such an unjustified extension (e.g., claims to methods of use versus claims to compounds).
guidance: Cases like Geneva Pharmaceuticals and Schneller illustrate situations where disclosure outside the claim scope might nevertheless justify an equitable NSDP rejection. Schneller-type rejections will be rare and require consultation with the supervisory patent examiner (SPE) and approval of the Technology Center (TC) Director before making such a rejection. Each equitable NSDP situation must be decided on its own facts and the examiner should refer to subsection II.B.6 for detailed discussion.

name: Interim extension application contents
description: The application shall contain— (i) the identity of the product subject to regulatory review and the Federal statute under which such review is occurring; (ii) the identity of the patent for which interim extension is being sought and the identity of each claim of such patent which claims the product under regulatory review or a method of using or manufacturing the product; (iii) information to enable the Director to determine under subsection (a)(1), (2), and (3) the eligibility of a patent for extension; (iv) a brief description of the activities undertaken by the applicant during the applicable regulatory review period to date with respect to the product under review and the significant dates applicable to such activities; and (v) such patent or other information as the Director may require.
guidance: These five enumerated items are the mandatory contents for an interim-extension application; they form the factual and documentary basis the Director may rely on to determine eligibility under the statute.

name: Scope of rights during interim extension
description: The rights derived from any patent the term of which is extended under this paragraph shall, during the period of interim extension— (i) in the case of a patent which claims a product, be limited to any use then under regulatory review; (ii) in the case of a patent which claims a method of using a product, be limited to any use claimed by the patent then under regulatory review; and (iii) in the case of a patent which claims a method of manufacturing a product, be limited to the method of manufacturing as used to make the product then under regulatory review.
guidance: Interim-extension rights are strictly limited to the subject matter and uses that are under regulatory review—they do not broadly expand patent scope.

name: Plant-patent description and claim requirements
description: No plant patent shall be declared invalid for noncompliance with section 112 if the description is as complete as is reasonably possible. The claim in the specification shall be in formal terms to the plant shown and described.
guidance: Relaxed strictness compared to general sec.112 requirements: completeness 'as reasonably possible' suffices; claims must formally refer to the plant as shown and described.

name: Multiple dependent claim alternative-only reference
description: Any dependent claim which refers to more than one other claim (“multiple dependent claim”) shall refer to such other claims in the alternative only.
guidance: A multiple dependent claim shall not serve as a basis for any other multiple dependent claim. 35 U.S.C. 112(e) authorizes multiple dependent claims only in alternative form (e.g., “A machine according to claims 3 or 4, further comprising ---”). Cumulative claiming (e.g., “A machine according to claims 3 and 4, further comprising ---”) is not permitted. These limitations avoid undue confusion in determining how many prior claims are referred to in a multiple dependent claim.

name: Construction of dependent and multiple dependent claims
description: Claims in dependent form shall be construed to include all the limitations of the claim incorporated by reference into the dependent claim.
guidance: A multiple dependent claim shall be construed to incorporate by reference all the limitations of each of the particular claims in relation to which it is being considered. 35 U.S.C. 112 indicates that limitations of each claim incorporated into a multiple dependent claim must be considered separately—i.e., a multiple dependent claim does not contain all limitations of all alternative claims in any one embodiment.

name: Fee calculation for multiple dependent claims
description: For fee calculation purposes under § 1.16, a multiple dependent claim will be considered to be that number of claims to which direct reference is made therein.
guidance: Any claim depending from a multiple dependent claim will be considered to be that number of claims to which direct reference is made in that multiple dependent claim. An original application filed with or amended to include multiple dependent claims must have paid the fee set forth in § 1.16(j). Use form PTO/SB/07 together with PTO/SB/06 for fee computation; OPAP and TC technical support staff verify fees. If a multiple dependent claim is improper, OPAP may mark it; improper multiple dependent claim fee treatment and examples are provided (encircled numerals, counting rules, and example calculations).

name: Claims must conform to specification and have antecedent basis
description: The claim or claims must conform to the invention as set forth in the remainder of the specification and the terms and phrases used in the claims must find clear support or antecedent basis in the description so that the meaning of the terms in the claims may be ascertainable by reference to the description.
guidance: See § 1.58(a). Claims present on the filing date may be relied upon to establish disclosure if their content justifies it. If subject matter is claimed that is not shown in drawings or description but the claim itself is a clear disclosure, the claim should be treated on its merits and the drawing/description should be amended rather than objecting to the claim. However, if the claim does not provide its own description, it should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) for failing to provide an adequate written description.

name: Improvement-type independent claim structure
description: Where the nature of the case admits, as in the case of an improvement, any independent claim should contain in the following order: (1) A preamble comprising a general description of all the elements or steps of the claimed combination which are conventional or known; (2) A phrase such as 'wherein the improvement comprises,' and (3) Those elements, steps, and/or relationships which constitute that portion of the claimed combination which the applicant considers as the new or improved portion.
guidance: The form of claim required in 37 CFR 1.75(e) is intended for improvement-type inventions and is to be considered a combination claim. The preamble of this form is considered to positively and clearly include all elements recited therein as part of the claimed combination.

name: Order and grouping of claims by scope
description: The least restrictive claim should be presented as claim number 1, and all dependent claims should be grouped together with the claim or claims to which they refer to the extent practicable.
guidance: Claims should preferably be arranged in order of scope from broadest to most detailed. Where separate species are claimed, claims of like species should be grouped together where possible. Product and process claims should be separately grouped to facilitate classification and examination.

name: Line indentation / separation of claim elements
description: Where a claim sets forth a plurality of elements or steps, each element or step of the claim should be separated by a line indentation.
guidance: There may be plural indentations to further segregate subcombinations or related steps. In general, printed patent copies will follow the format used but printing difficulties may prevent duplication of unduly complex claim formats. See 37 CFR 1.75(i).

name: Use and formatting of reference characters in claims
description: Reference characters corresponding to elements recited in the detailed description and the drawings may be used in conjunction with the recitation of the same element or group of elements in the claims.
guidance: Reference characters should be enclosed within parentheses so as to avoid confusion with other numbers or characters which may appear in the claims. Generally, the presence or absence of such reference characters does not affect the scope of a claim. If reference characters are not enclosed within parentheses and that omission renders the claim indefinite, reject under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (use form paragraph 7.34.01).

name: Required claim wording and punctuation
description: While there is no set statutory form for claims, the present Office practice is to insist that each claim must be the object of a sentence starting with 'I (or we) claim,' 'The invention claimed is' (or the equivalent). Each claim begins with a capital letter and ends with a period. Periods may not be used elsewhere in the claims except for abbreviations.
guidance: If, at allowance, the quoted terminology is not present, it is inserted by the Office of Data Management. See Fressola v. Manbeck, 36 USPQ2d 1211 (D.D.C. 1995).

name: Handling duplicate or substantially duplicate claims
description: When two claims in an application comply with the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(d) but are duplicates, or are so close in content that they both cover the same thing despite slight wording differences, it is proper after allowing one claim to object to the other claim under 37 CFR 1.75 as being a substantial duplicate of the allowed claim.
guidance: Form paragraphs 7.05.05 (warning) and 7.05.06 (duplicate claim objection) may be used. If duplicate claims are present but not allowable, use 7.05.05 to give applicant opportunity to correct. If duplicate claims are allowable, use 7.05.06. Examiner notes emphasize applicant's right to restate the invention in a reasonable number of ways and that mere difference in scope can be enough to justify restatement.

name: Proper dependent claim test (35 U.S.C. 112(d))
description: In accordance with 35 U.S.C. 112(d), a claim in dependent form shall contain: (i) a reference to a claim previously set forth, and (ii) then specify a further limitation of the subject matter claimed.
guidance: A dependent claim shall be construed to incorporate by reference all the limitations of the claim to which it refers. The test is that the dependent claim must include every limitation of the claim from which it depends and specify a further limitation. Example: if claim 1 recites A, B, C, D, a claim reciting claim 1 with D omitted or replaced by E would not be a proper dependent claim even if it places further limitations on the remaining elements. Dependent claims that fail these requirements should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(d) (use form paragraphs 7.36 and 7.36.01).

name: Initial fee-purpose treatment of dependent claims
description: The initial determination, for fee purposes, as to whether a claim is dependent must be made by persons other than examiners; it is necessary, at that time, to accept as dependent virtually every claim which refers to another claim, without determining whether a true dependent relationship exists.
guidance: The initial acceptance of a claim as a dependent claim does not preclude a subsequent holding by the examiner that a claim is not a proper dependent claim. TC technical support staff and OPAP handle initial fee calculations and marking.

name: Unacceptable multiple dependent claim forms and common anti-patterns
description: Examples of unacceptable multiple dependent claim wording include: references that do not refer back in the alternative only (e.g., 'according to claim 3 and 4'), references to two sets of claims to different features (e.g., 'as in claim 1 or 4 made by the process of claims 5,6,7, or 8'), references to numerically following claims which are not understandable, and reference back to another multiple dependent claim.
guidance: Specific unacceptable examples are provided (e.g., 'A gadget according to claim 3 and 4, further comprising ---' or 'A gadget as in claims 1 or 2 and 7 or 8, which ---'). A multiple dependent claim may refer in the alternative to only one set of claims. A claim such as 'A device as in claims 1, 2, 3, or 4, made by a process of claims 5, 6, 7, or 8' is improper because 35 U.S.C. 112 allows reference to only a particular claim.

name: Handling added/amended multiple dependent claims and fees
description: When multiple dependent claims are added by amendment without the proper fee, the amendment should not be entered until the fee has been received.
guidance: TC technical support staff verifies compliance with statute/rules and calculates additional fees using PTO/SB/07. If improper reference is noted in an added/ amended multiple dependent claim, a notation should be made in the left margin next to the claim and the numeral in the Dep. Claim column on PTO/SB/07 circled to call the matter to the examiner's attention. If multiple dependent claims are added and fees are insufficient, applicant/agent should be contacted to pay the additional fee; include a copy of the fee calculation form for information.

name: Examiner procedures for claims referring to numerically following claims
description: If any series of dependent claims contains a claim with an improper reference to a numerically following claim which cannot be understood, the claim referring to a following claim should normally be objected to and not treated on the merits.
guidance: However, where a claim refers to a numerically following claim and the dependency is clear both as presented and as it will be renumbered at issue, all claims should be examined on the merits and no form objection need be made; in such cases an examiner's amendment should be prepared if the order of the claims is changed. Any unusual problems should be brought to the supervisor's attention. Examples A and B illustrate both treatments.

name: Office action clarity requirement for multiple dependent claim embodiments
description: The provisions of 35 U.S.C. 132 require that each Office action make it explicitly clear what rejection, objection and/or requirement is applied to each claim embodiment.
guidance: When identifying singular dependent claims which do not include a reference to a multiple dependent claim, reference should be made only to the number of the dependent claim. When identifying embodiments included within a multiple dependent claim, each embodiment should be identified by using the number of the claims involved, starting with the highest, as necessary. If all embodiments are subject to a common rejection/objection/requirement, reference may be made only to the number of the individual dependent claim.

name: Use of form paragraphs for claim informalities and objections
description: Specific form paragraphs are provided for common claim informalities and objections (e.g., ¶ 7.29.01 Claims Objected to, Minor Informalities; ¶ 7.29.02 Reference Characters Not Enclosed Within Parentheses; ¶ 7.29.03 Spacing of Lines; ¶ 7.45 Improper Multiple Dependent Claims).
guidance: Use form paragraph 7.29.01 to point out minor informalities (spelling, inconsistent terminology) which should be corrected; if informalities render claims indefinite use form paragraph 7.34.01 to reject under 35 U.S.C. 112(b). Use 7.45 for improper multiple dependent claims (insert suggested bracketed language). Use 7.05.05/7.05.06 for duplicate claim warnings or objections.

name: Eligibility for transitional practice under 37 CFR 1.129(a)
description: This application is subject to the provisions of Public Law 103-465, effective June 8, 1995. The application must have been filed on or before June 8, 1995 and have been pending for at least two years as of June 8, 1995 (taking into account any reference under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121 or 365(c)); for applications entering national stage under 35 U.S.C. 371 or filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a) claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 of a PCT application designating the U.S., the PCT international filing date will be used to determine pendency.
guidance: Form paragraph 7.41.01.fti may be used to notify applicant that the application qualifies under 37 CFR 1.129(a). Do not use the form paragraph in design or reissue applications, or in reexamination proceedings.

name: Permissible content of a 37 CFR 1.129(a) submission
description: The submission under 37 CFR 1.129(a) may comprise, but is not limited to, an information disclosure statement (IDS), an amendment to the written description, claims or drawings, a new substantive argument and/or new evidence.
guidance: No amendment considered as a result of payment of the fee under 1.17(r) may introduce new matter into the disclosure (35 U.S.C. 132). If applicant files multiple proposed amendments that conflict, applicant should provide specific instructions for entry or non-entry upon payment.

name: What counts as a 'submission' for RCE purposes
description: A 'submission' includes, but is not limited to, an information disclosure statement, an amendment to the written description, claims, or drawings, new arguments, or new evidence in support of patentability. If a reply to an Office action under 35 U.S.C. 132 is outstanding, the submission must meet the reply requirements of 37 CFR 1.111.
guidance: A request for suspension of action, an appeal brief or a reply brief (or related papers) will not be considered a submission under 1.114, though arguments in a previously filed appeal or reply brief may be incorporated by reference to satisfy submission requirement.

name: Alloy composition claims: total composition sum requirement
description: A claim directed to alloy should set forth the invention so that composition range of each component in alloy should be added up to be 100%. Regardless of whether the claim is stated as a close claim (“consisting of”) or an open claim (“comprising”), the total sum of composition range should not be over or under 100%.
guidance: If the minimum ratio of one component plus the maximum ratios of the others do not reach 100% (or exceed 100%), the claim is unclear and not accepted. Example: Claim listing Cu 40-80%, Zn 10-45%, Sn 1-5%, Be 0.6-3%, Si 0.8-4% — with Cu minimum 40% and other components' maxima summing only 57% → sum under 100% → deemed unclear. When claiming an alloy, list components and recite composition ranges exactly. See Part IX Chapter 7 for more.

name: Claims must recite matters necessary to specify the invention (Article 42(6))
description: The claims shall recite such matters regarded necessary to specify what is sought for patent protection as structures, methods, functions and materials or combination thereof.
guidance: Where an invention can be clearly specified by its effect or operation method rather than physical structure, the applicant may set forth the invention accordingly. Note: this provision does not by itself provide a ground for rejection or invalidation; an examiner shall not notify a ground for rejection based solely on this provision.

name: Role and legal prescription of claim drafting
description: Claims are prescribed in the law to ensure they determine the scope of protection; Korean law adopts a multiple-claims system allowing one or more claims directed to subject matters for which protection is sought.
guidance: Article 5 of the Enforcement Decree prescribes claim drafting requirements under the multiple-claims system; claims should be drafted with the legal role of defining scope in mind.

name: Definition and discrimination of independent vs dependent claims
description: Dependent claims narrow or add further limitations to specify an independent claim by adding technical elements or narrowing a generic concept to a species. Dependent claims are claims whose inventions are dependent on other claims and change accordingly when the referred claims change.
guidance: A claim that narrows or adds limitations but does not refer formally to the other claim(s) is not a dependent claim. Conversely, a claim that formally refers to an independent claim but does not narrow or add limitations (e.g., substituting A with B without narrowing) is not a dependent claim. Article 5(1) allows claims that substantiate the independent claim by narrowing or adding to be presented as dependent, but they may also be presented as independent claims.

name: Independent claims presentation (Article 5(1))
description: Independent claims shall be presented without referring to other claims in the form of standing alone; however, independent claims can refer to other claims within the scope in which the invention can be clearly understood to avoid redundant description.
guidance: Permitted examples include 'A product of … manufactured by the method of claim 1', 'A method of manufacturing a product of claim 1 by …', 'A method of … by using a product manufactured by the method of claim 1', 'A product manufactured with the device of claim 1'. Dependent claims must include the limitations of the claims they refer to.

name: Claims that must be treated as independent despite referring
description: Claims shall be treated as independent (not dependent) where they are presented in the form of decreasing the elements of the claims referred to or substituting the subject matter set forth in the claims referred to with other matter.
guidance: Example: Claim 1 recites a power transfer unit with a gear electric motor; Claim 2 recites the power transfer unit of claim 1 equipped with a belt conveyor instead of a gear electric motor — Claim 2 is treated as independent.

name: Proper number of claims (Article 5(2))
description: The claim shall be presented in a proper number according to the nature of the invention. Improper numbers include where two or more inventions of different categories are recited in one claim, where two or more subject matters are included, redundant identical claims, or where multiple claims are technically referred to many times within a single claim.
guidance: Examples: claiming two subject matters in one claim (e.g., a polymer and a contact lens using it) is improper. Referring to multiple claims repeatedly within a single claim (creating confusing nested references) is improper and may be exempted if it causes confusion similar to dependent claims referring to more than two claims.

name: Precedence in claim numbering (Article 5(7))
description: A claim referred to by another claim should precede the other claim in numbering to facilitate interpretation.
guidance: If a claim refers to itself or to a later-numbered claim, an examiner shall notify a ground for rejection citing violation of Article 42(8) and Article 5(7), or a ground for rejection citing indefiniteness under Article 42(4)(ii).

name: Claim presentation format: new line and sequential numbering (Article 5(8))
description: Each claim shall be presented in a new line and the claims shall be numbered in sequence. To clearly define configuration even within a single claim, a claim can be presented in several lines.
guidance: Example: a method claim can be structured with (A), (B), (C), (D) steps each on its own line to clarify procedural steps (e.g., heating, forging, re-heating, quenching).

name: System for deferral of submission of claims (filing spec without claims)
description: An applicant may attach a specification without claims at filing (deferral system) to allow speedy filing and time to prepare claims, but claims must be submitted within a time limit (three months after notification of intention of request for examination or 1 year and 2 months from priority date; transitional periods for pre-2014 filings).
guidance: Failure to submit claims by the deadline results in the application being deemed withdrawn the day after the deadline. If an applicant files a request for examination before submitting claims, the examiner shall return the written request and give opportunity for explanation. Applications filed without claims are not laid open for publication since they're deemed withdrawn once the deadline expires. Divisional/converted applications may have special extensions (claims may be submitted until 30 days from divisional/converted filing in certain cases). Whether deferral is used is determined by whether the 'Patent Claims' identification symbols are deleted in the specification form; presence of the heading means deferral is not employed (even if claims area contains blanks or punctuation).

name: Unity of invention: statutory requirements (Article 45 & Enforcement Decree Article 6)
description: A single patent application may cover a group of inventions linked so as to form a single general inventive concept. Requirements: (1) the claimed inventions shall be technologically correlated; (2) the claimed inventions shall have the same or corresponding technological features, where such technological features are improvements over the prior art.
guidance: The 'special technical features' refer to improvements compared with prior art; they need not be identical (e.g., providing elasticity via a spring vs a rubber block can be corresponding). Determination of unity generally requires consideration of prior art; unity may be determined a priori in some cases but often a posteriori after prior art search.

name: Procedure to determine unity of invention
description: Unity is determined by selecting a first invention, specifying its special technical features as improvements over prior art, selecting a second invention and its special technical features, then checking whether these special features are the same or corresponding; if so, the inventions form a single general inventive concept.
guidance: Steps: (1) choose first invention and identify special technical features vs prior art (may include multiple features); (2) choose second invention and identify its special features; (3) check technical correlation by comparing special features; (4) iterate for all claims; (5) select first invention as subject to examination (and include inventions in the first technical group). Examiner must notify lack of unity on all claims and specify that concerned inventions do not share the same or corresponding special technical features. Lack of unity is a ground for rejection, not invalidation; examiners need not require divisional filings if examination can be completed without additional prior art search.

name: Examples and rules illustrating unity (generic/species, corresponding features, non-corresponding features)
description: Unity is met when dependent claims include all special technical features of the independent claim (generic/species), when claims disclose corresponding special technical features (e.g., expander vs compressor as corresponding sub-combinations), and where combinations/sub-combinations exist. Unity is not met where claims recite distinct, non-corresponding special technical features (e.g., control circuit A vs control circuit B as separate special features).
guidance: Examples provided: (a) independent claim A+B with dependent claims adding C or D → unity; (b) claim 1 filament A, claim 2 lamp B comprising filament A, claim 3 searchlight comprising B → unity; (c) claims with corresponding sub-combinations (expander/compressor) → unity among claims; (d) claims with distinct special features → unity only where common features exist (e.g., claim1 with A and claim3 using A → unity; claim1 vs claim2 with different control circuits → not unity).

name: Unity determination for product vs manufacturing method
description: Unity between a product invention and a manufacturing method invention of that product is determined based on whether the manufacturing method is 'suitable' for manufacture of the product.
guidance: 'Suitable' means that when the manufacturing method is practiced, the product is manufactured. 'Suitable' does not mean the product cannot be manufactured by other methods or that the method cannot be used for other products. Examples: (1) chemical material X (product) and method for manufacturing X → common special technical feature is chemical material X → unity. (2) corrugated cardboard with cavity filled by intumescent resin and method of charging and heating → the product created by the method is the claimed product → unity.

name: Claims requiring a computer may still recite a mental process
description: Claims can recite a mental process even if they are claimed as being performed on a computer (e.g., Benson; Mortgage Grader).
guidance: In evaluating whether a claim that requires a computer recites a mental process, examiners should carefully consider the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim in light of the specification. Review the specification to determine if the claimed invention is described as a concept that is performed in the human mind and applicant is merely claiming that concept performed (1) on a generic computer, (2) in a computer environment, or (3) merely using a computer as a tool. In those situations the claim is considered to recite a mental process. Case citations: Benson (algorithm could be performed mentally), Mortgage Grader (anonymous loan shopping could be performed by humans).

name: Performing a mental process on a generic computer
description: A claimed mental process performed on a generic computer may be an abstract idea (example: Voter Verified; Versata).
guidance: If the specification describes steps as human cognitive actions historically performed by people, the fact that the steps are performed on generic computer hardware does not necessarily make the claim non-abstract. Examples: Voter Verified (voting/verification steps are "human cognitive actions"); Versata (determining a price implemented using general purpose computer hardware was still directed to abstract idea). Use specification and case law to determine whether the computer adds anything other than generic implementation.

name: Performing a mental process in a computer environment
description: A mental process performed in a computer environment (i.e., describing how systems receive, screen, distribute data analogous to human action) can be directed to an abstract idea (example: Symantec; FairWarning).
guidance: Examiners should evaluate whether the claimed computer-environment steps merely mirror human decision-making (e.g., screening mail or detecting misuse) and lack claim limitations that foreclose performance by a human. If the claims, aside from generic computer-implemented steps, can be performed mentally or with pen and paper, treat as an abstract idea. Use specification support and relevant Federal Circuit decisions to support the analysis.

name: Using a computer as a tool to perform a mental process
description: Claims that merely use a computer as a tool to perform processes humans can do mentally are directed to mental-process abstract ideas (examples: Mortgage Grader; Berkheimer).
guidance: Where claimed steps are recited at a high level of generality and the computer is just a tool for performing parsing, comparing, grading, or other cognitive activities, the claim is likely directed to a mental process. Cite cases where the concept itself (e.g., anonymous loan shopping; parsing/comparing data) is identified as the abstract idea despite computer implementation.

name: Both product and process claims may recite a mental process
description: Product claims (e.g., systems, computer-readable media) and process claims alike may recite mental processes and thus be directed to an abstract idea.
guidance: Do not assume only method claims recite mental processes. Examples of product claims reciting mental processes include content extraction APIs, anonymous loan shopping systems, computer-readable media with fraud-detection instructions, electronic post offices, self-verifying voting systems, monitoring systems, and storage media implementing pricing methods (cases cited: Content Extraction; Mortgage Grader; CyberSource; Symantec; Voter Verified; Electric Power Group; Versata). For such claims, analyze whether the claimed product merely embodies a mental-process concept implemented generically by hardware or code. Treat the phrase "mental processes" as referring to the type of abstract idea, not the statutory claim category.

name: Tentative abstract idea procedure
description: If an examiner believes a claim limitation should be treated as an abstract idea but it does not fall within the enumerated groupings, treat it as a "tentative abstract idea" and follow the prescribed procedure.
guidance: Apply the subject matter eligibility framework: (a) If the claim as a whole integrates the tentative abstract idea into a practical application → Step 2A: NO (eligible at Pathway B). (b) If not integrated → Step 2A: YES (directed to a judicial exception) → proceed to Step 2B: if the claim as a whole provides an inventive concept → eligible at Pathway C; if not → examiner should bring the application to the attention of the Technology Center (TC) director. A rejection of a claim reciting a tentative abstract idea must be approved by the TC director (approval indicated in the file) and justified in the record. The TC Director's approval triggers use of form paragraph 7.05.017 and the TC Director's signature; Patents Management will notify the public (e.g., USPTO website). Examiners may conduct interviews in response to Step 2B rejections; TC Director interview is not necessary for the examiner to withdraw/maintain the rejection. Examiners are not required to obtain TC Director approval to withdraw or maintain such a §101 rejection.

name: Laws of nature and natural phenomena exceptions (general)
description: Laws of nature and natural phenomena include naturally occurring principles/relations and nature-based products that are naturally occurring or do not have markedly different characteristics compared to what occurs in nature; these are judicial exceptions to patent eligibility.
guidance: The basic tools of science and technology are not patentable (cases: Funk Bros.; Diamond v. Chakrabarty). Examples courts have identified as laws/natural phenomena include isolated DNA (Myriad), cloned animals (Roslin), correlations involving DNA, metabolic correlations (Mayo), correlations between biomarkers and disease risk (Cleveland Clinic v. True Health), electromagnetism (O’Reilly v. Morse), bacterial qualities (Funk), primers (Ambry), chemical principles (Tilghman), cell-free fetal DNA (Ariosa), genotype–drug response correlations (Vanda). However, not every claim that describes a natural ability or product is an exception; claims that apply or transform natural phenomena (e.g., treatment methods, manufacturing processes) may be eligible (examples: Rapid Litigation Mgmt. v. CellzDirect; Tilghman). If a claim recites a law/natural phenomenon, further analysis in Step 2A Prong Two is needed to determine whether the claim integrates the exception into a practical application.

name: Products of nature (definition and scope)
description: When a law of nature or natural phenomenon is claimed as a physical product it may be treated as a "product of nature"; this includes naturally occurring products and non‑naturally occurring products that lack markedly different characteristics from their natural counterparts.
guidance: Examples: isolated DNA (Myriad), cloned animals (Roslin), bacterial mixtures (Funk). The Office treats "law of nature," "natural phenomenon," and "product of nature" inclusively for Step 2A analysis. Non-naturally occurring products that are structurally identical to natural counterparts remain products of nature (Ambry). The key inquiry for non-naturally occurring products is whether they possess "markedly different characteristics" from natural counterparts. If a claim recites a nature-based product limitation, apply the markedly different characteristics analysis (MPEP §2106.04(c)) to determine whether the limitation is a product-of-nature exception. If the claim clearly does not tie up a judicial exception, consider the streamlined analysis in §2106.06.

name: Markedly different characteristics analysis — when to perform
description: Apply the markedly different characteristics analysis only to the nature-based product limitations in a claim to determine whether those products are "product of nature" exceptions.
guidance: Be careful not to overextend the analysis to claim elements that are not nature-based when the claim as a whole is not nature-based. If the nature-based product limitation is naturally occurring, no need to perform the analysis because it is by definition directed to a naturally occurring product and falls under the product of nature exception. For claims that include nature-based products as only part of a larger claimed invention, analyze whether the claim also recites another exception that would require further eligibility analysis.

name: Markedly different characteristics analysis — how to perform and consequences
description: Compare the claimed nature-based product to its naturally occurring counterpart to determine whether it possesses markedly different characteristics; this analysis informs Step 2A Prong One.
guidance: If the claimed nature-based product has markedly different characteristics, the claim does not recite a product-of-nature exception and is eligible at Step 2A: NO (Pathway B), unless another exception applies. For claims where the entire claim is a single nature-based product, showing a markedly different characteristic in that product obviates further analysis (no Step 2B needed). If the nature-based product does not exhibit markedly different characteristics from a naturally occurring counterpart, the claim recites a product-of-nature exception and requires further analysis in Step 2A Prong Two (and possibly Step 2B). Use Chakrabarty and Roslin comparisons as precedents (compare claimed bacterium/sheep to naturally occurring counterparts).

name: BRI and claim-drafting recommendations for nature-based products
description: Under the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of claims, a nature-based product limitation may encompass both eligible and ineligible embodiments; examiners should address this in prosecution.
guidance: If a claim's BRI encompasses both markedly different and not markedly different embodiments (e.g., "cloned giraffe" might cover both types), then the claim may recite a product of nature and requires further analysis. If a claim is ultimately rejected for failing to encompass an inventive concept (Step 2B: NO), it is best practice for the examiner to point out the BRI in the Office action and recommend an amendment to narrow the claim to embodiments that are not directed to products of nature or otherwise eligible. For claims that recite a nature-based product limitation but clearly do not tie up any judicial exception, consider the streamlined eligibility analysis in MPEP §2106.06.

name: Lilly written description doctrine (Regents of UC v. Eli Lilly)
description: The Lilly written description requirement (from Regents of UC v. Eli Lilly, 1997) has been relied on by the Federal Circuit to invalidate originally filed claims (e.g., claims directed to the insulin gene) and has been expanded in reach.
guidance: The blog traces the doctrine's origin and notes its expansion in both the courts and the PTO. Treat as a distinct doctrine the court has used to police claim scope and sufficiency of disclosure, beyond classical enablement.

name: Specific structural disclosure required for broad functional claims (University of Rochester)
description: In University of Rochester v. G.D. Searle the Federal Circuit found claims invalid because 'the specification did not specifically describe any non-steroidal compound that would perform the claimed function.'
guidance: When a claim recites a broad function (e.g., 'a method for selectively inhibiting PGHS-2 ... comprising administering a non-steroidal compound'), the specification may be required to identify specific compounds or structural examples that perform that function; absent such specifics, written description may be found lacking.

name: Requirement to 'describe some way of performing the claimed methods' (Ariad)
description: The Federal Circuit in Ariad stated that '[R]egardless of whether the asserted claims recite a compound, Ariad still must describe some way of performing the claimed methods.'
guidance: Functional method claims that broadly claim any method achieving a result require the specification to describe at least some manner of performing the claimed method; mere recitation of the result without disclosure of a way to achieve it can fail written description.

name: 'Descriptive link' requirement between disclosed structures and claimed function
description: The Ariad majority concluded there was 'no descriptive link between the table of decoy molecules and reducing NF-kB activity.'
guidance: The court used lack of an explicit link between structural examples and the claimed functional outcome as a basis for invalidity. The blog criticizes this as a novel/conclusory requirement created by the majority (i.e., the court coined a 'descriptive link' requirement rather than relying on established doctrine).

name: Commensurateness / breadth constraint: disclosure must bear the weight of claim scope
description: Claims can be invalidated when 'the disclosure is insufficient to bear the weight of the vast scope of these generic claims.'
guidance: A key evaluative standard is whether the specification's disclosure is commensurate with the breadth of the claims; overly broad claims that claim more than the specification justifies are susceptible to invalidation under the written description doctrine (as applied by Lilly cases).

name: Enablement requirement (Section 112): enable full scope without undue experimentation
description: To survive the enablement requirement the specification 'must describe the manner and process of making and using the invention so as to enable a person of skill in the art to making use the full scope of the invention without undue experimentation.'
guidance: Judge Linn (concurrence) and the blog emphasize that enablement is the traditional, established doctrine for policing claim scope — i.e., disclosure must enable the full scope of claimed subject matter. The post argues enablement, not written description, is the appropriate tool for policing overbroad functional claims, though courts have struggled to articulate a workable standard for policing claim scope via enablement.

name: Prophetic examples may satisfy written description in chemical arts
description: The court acknowledged that 'prophetic examples are routinely used to satisfy the written description requirement in the chemical arts.'
guidance: Although prophetic (i.e., hypothetical/future-directed) examples can often satisfy written description for chemical or biotech inventions, the court in Ariad still found the particular prophetic disclosure insufficient — illustrating that the adequacy of prophetic examples is fact-specific and may be judged against the claimed scope.

name: Patent eligibility constraint: cannot claim a natural phenomenon
description: Claims that 'wholly encompassing a natural phenomenon' may be patent ineligible; Lilly argued Ariad's claims were patent ineligible for wholly encompassing a natural phenomenon, but the Federal Circuit avoided that issue by deciding written description instead.
guidance: Patent eligibility (e.g., exclusion of natural phenomena) remains a separate ground to evaluate claims; courts may choose to decide a case on written description or enablement grounds without reaching eligibility, but eligibility is a distinct doctrinal filter for claim validity.

name: PTO practice: aggressive application of Lilly written description separate from enablement
description: The Patent Office has become much more aggressive in applying Lilly written description as a requirement of patentability separate and distinct from the enablement requirement.
guidance: Examiner practice and PTO policy increasingly invoke Lilly-style written description scrutiny; practitioners should be aware that the PTO may apply written description as an independent hurdle beyond enablement when examining biotech claims.

name: Domain-specific expansion: Lilly applied originally to biomolecules and then to method claims
description: Lilly written description had previously been applied primarily to biomolecule claims (nucleic acids and antibodies); University of Rochester marked the first instance applying the doctrine to method claims, and Ariad continued that trend.
guidance: The scope of the written description doctrine has expanded from structural biomolecule claims to functional and method claims in the biotech context, meaning practitioners drafting biotech claims must consider both structural disclosure and method/function linkages.

name: Applicant’s Reply Requirements (37 CFR 1.111(b))
description: 37 CFR 1.111(b) requires applicant to distinctly and specifically point out the supposed errors in the Office’s action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the Office action.
guidance: The reply must present arguments pointing out the specific distinction believed to render the claims patentable over any applied references. If an applicant disagrees with any factual findings by the Office, an effective traverse must include a reasoned statement explaining why the applicant believes the Office has erred. A mere statement that the Office has not established a prima facie case or unsupported assertions about common knowledge will not be considered substantively adequate; Office personnel may repeat the rejection and make the next Office action final. (See MPEP §706.07(a).)

name: Secondary Considerations as Evidence of Nonobviousness
description: Certain objective indicia (secondary considerations) can rebut an obviousness determination.
guidance: Examples of secondary considerations include commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, and unexpected results (citing Graham v. John Deere). These types of evidence may be submitted to demonstrate that the claimed combination produced unexpected or nonroutine results, or that ordinary skill could not have combined elements by known methods.

name: Examples of Rebuttal Evidence to Show Nonobviousness
description: Applicants may submit evidence or argument showing why the claimed subject matter would have been nonobvious.
guidance: Illustrative showings include: (A) one of ordinary skill could not have combined the claimed elements by known methods (e.g., technological difficulties); (B) the elements in combination do not merely perform the functions that each element performs separately; (C) the results of the claimed combination were unexpected. Office personnel should reconsider any initial obviousness determination in view of such evidence (see In re Piasecki; In re Eli Lilly & Co.).

name: Pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) — Burden to Establish Applicability
description: An applicant subject to pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 who wants to invoke pre‑AIA 103(c) bears the burden of establishing conditions that disqualify certain prior art.
guidance: To avail the benefits of pre‑AIA 103(c) the applicant must establish that subject matter used in the rejection and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment. For joint research agreements (post‑Dec 10, 2004), the applicant must show (A) the invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the date of invention; (B) the invention was made as a result of activities within the scope of the agreement; and (C) the application discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties. See MPEP §706.02(l)(1)–(2) and relevant case law.

name: Analogous Art Requirement for References in 103 Rejections
description: To be proper in an obviousness rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103, a reference must be analogous prior art to the claimed invention.
guidance: A reference is analogous if: (1) it is from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention (even if addressing a different problem), or (2) it is reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor (even if not in the same field). 'Reasonably pertinent' means the reference would have logically commended itself to an inventor's attention in considering the problem. See In re Bigio; KSR v. Teleflex; In re ICON Health and Fitness; In re Klein. Examiner may state their understanding of the problem to support pertinence.

name: Analogy Considerations in Specific Arts (chemical, mechanical, electrical, design)
description: Analogous art determinations may vary by technological area; cross‑field references can be analogous when they address the same problem or are within the scope of the inventor's field of endeavor.
guidance: Examples: chemical arts — references on absorbing biologically active materials can be pertinent across food/preservative contexts (Ex parte Bland); mechanical — toothbrush art applied to hair brushes due to structural similarity (In re Bigio); electrical — circuits solving rate‑limiting problems can be pertinent to pacemaker design (Medtronic v. Cardiac Pacemakers); design — prior designs are analogous if they have the same general use as the claimed design (In re Rosen; Ex parte Pappas). Examiners should apply these principles contextually.

name: Claimed Invention Must Be Considered As A Whole
description: When ascertaining differences between prior art and claims, interpret claim language and consider both the invention and prior art references as a whole.
guidance: The question under 35 U.S.C. 103 is whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious, not whether individual differences themselves would have been obvious. See case law (Stratoflex v. Aeroquip; Schenck v. Nortron; In re Hirao). Examiners must avoid focusing solely on an isolated structural difference or limiting the analysis to a subset of claim limitations.

name: Do Not Reduce the Invention to a 'Gist' or 'Thrust'
description: Distilling an invention down to a 'gist' or 'thrust' disregards the requirement to analyze the subject matter 'as a whole.'
guidance: Restricting consideration to a single perceived advantage or conceptual thrust may improperly ignore express claim limitations (see W.L. Gore; Bausch & Lomb; Jones v. Hardy; Panduit Corp.). Examiners should analyze all claim limitations rather than treating the invention as an abstract advantage or single‑word solution.

name: Clear, predictable, and consistently applied eligibility standard
description: “The standard for determining whether an invention is eligible for patenting should be clear, predictable, and consistently applied.”
guidance: Stakeholders repeatedly request clarity and consistent application across courts and the USPTO to reduce uncertainty. Lack of clarity forces applicants and examiners to guess which claims will survive, increasing prosecution and litigation costs and reducing reliable expectations for investors and innovators.

name: Claims should provide meaningful exclusion of competitors (sufficient scope)
description: Patents that do issue should provide meaningful exclusion of competitors in the market rather than being of narrow scope and uncertain value.
guidance: Stakeholders report that issued patents are sometimes narrow and may not exclude competitors effectively. Evaluations should consider whether claim scope is sufficient to incentivize investment and commercialization.

name: Patent eligibility should not force extraneous limitations into claims
description: Applicants report needing to “add otherwise extraneous limitations to claims for the sole purpose of satisfying an undefined standard.”
guidance: Undefined or vague eligibility standards encourage claim-drafting anti-patterns—tacking on irrelevant technical details solely to survive eligibility scrutiny. Reform or guidance should reduce incentive for such workarounds.

name: Eligibility rules should balance preventing overly broad/abusive patents and enabling innovation
description: Supporters of current jurisprudence argued the new standard is a useful tool for addressing overly broad patents and defending against abusive suits by patent assertion entities (PAEs).
guidance: A policy rubric should weigh the benefit of curbing abusive/overbroad claims (reducing litigation and PAE harm) against the risk of deterring valid, technically inventive claims. Consider both deterrence of abusive assertions and downstream investment effects.

name: Avoid treating routine software/AI steps as patent-eligible without technical contribution
description: Some argued AI software inventions are more likely to be directed toward abstract ideas under Alice and subsequent case law than other software inventions, suggesting careful scrutiny of purported technical contribution.
guidance: Eligibility analysis should focus on whether claimed software/AI steps add a technical solution or are routine/abstract data manipulation. Anti-patterns include granting patents for high-level functional descriptions lacking technical implementation detail.

name: Priority_of_inventive_act
description: Priority consists in prior conception of the idea and prior embodiment of the idea in a practically operative art or reasonable diligence in perfecting such embodiment; successful claimant must establish priority by a clear preponderance of evidence (not necessarily beyond reasonable doubt).
guidance: Must overcome presumptions against claimant arising from earlier applications/patents and affirmatively establish right to priority as against other parties (sufficient to defeat their patents in courts).

name: Weight_of_self-serving_oath_of_invention
description: The assertion by a party that he 'invented' at a certain date is of little weight against contrary facts.
guidance: Oaths claiming invention dates must be supported by corroborating evidence; uncorroborated assertions are weak (see Slade v. Blair).

name: Effect_of_no_priority_proved
description: Where neither party proves priority, judgment is rendered against both so that both may be enabled to appeal.
guidance: A defeated claimant still has remedy in equity; a judgment in interference is not final except within the Patent Office—defeated parties may sue by bill in equity under statutory provisions.

name: 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 analysis (novelty and obviousness)
description: Review begins with a comparison of the claimed subject matter to what is known in the prior art; if no differences are found the claim lacks novelty under 35 U.S.C. 102; if differences exist they must be assessed in light of a person of ordinary skill to determine obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103.
guidance: See MPEP §§ 2131-2146 and §§ 2150-2159 for specific guidance on patentability determinations. Differences identified must be assessed against knowledge possessed by a person of ordinary skill in the art.

name: 35 U.S.C. 101 statutory scope (four categories)
description: A claimed invention must come within one of the four statutory categories set forth by 35 U.S.C. 101: process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter (or a useful improvement thereof).
guidance: See MPEP § 2106.03 for a discussion of the four categories. Establishing that the claim falls within a statutory category is the first criterion of subject matter eligibility.

name: Naming and correctness of inventor(s)
description: Inventor(s) must be properly identified in the application (rules differ for applications filed before and after September 16, 2012); incorrect inventorship should be addressed and corrected when possible.
guidance: See MPEP § 2109 for inventorship discussion and MPEP § 602.01(c) et seq. for correction of inventorship. In rare clear situations where correct inventorship is not named and no request to correct has been filed, the examiner should reject claims under appropriate statutory provisions (e.g., 35 U.S.C. 101 and 115 for AIA, or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f)).

name: Subject matter eligibility two-criteria framework
description: Two criteria govern subject matter eligibility: (a) the claim must fall within one of the four statutory categories; and (b) the claim must not be directed to a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon/product of nature) unless the claim as a whole includes additional limitations amounting to significantly more than the exception.
guidance: See MPEP § 2106.03 and § 2106.04 for detailed information. Judicial exceptions are limited to abstract ideas, laws of nature, and natural phenomena (including products of nature).

name: Utility requirement (35 U.S.C. 101 utility)
description: A claimed invention must be useful and have a utility that is specific, substantial and credible.
guidance: Rejection for lack of utility is appropriate when (1) it is not apparent why the invention is useful because the applicant failed to identify any specific and substantial utility and there is no well established utility, or (2) an asserted specific and substantial utility is not credible. Rejections for lack of utility should not be based on frivolousness, fraudulence, or public policy. See MPEP § 2107 and subsections for form paragraphs and precedent.

name: Human organisms excluded from patentability (AIA sec. 33(a))
description: Claims directed to or encompassing a human organism are excluded from patentability; the broadest reasonable interpretation of a claim that encompasses a human organism must be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 and AIA sec. 33(a).
guidance: Use form paragraph 7.04.03 to reject a claim under 35 U.S.C. 101 and section 33(a). Precede this paragraph with form paragraph 7.04.01 which quotes 35 U.S.C. 101, and in the Office action explain why the claim is interpreted to read on a human organism.

name: Use Alice/Mayo two-part framework for judicial exceptions
description: The Alice/Mayo two-part test is the required framework: (Step 2A) determine whether claims are directed to an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon; (Step 2B) if so, determine whether the claim recites additional elements amounting to significantly more than the judicial exception (the 'inventive concept').
guidance: The Alice/Mayo test is the only test that should be used to evaluate eligibility of claims under examination. Other tests (e.g., machine-or-transformation, 'useful, concrete, and tangible' result, In re Alappat 'special purpose computer' test) are not standalone tests and should be considered only as part of the integration or 'significantly more' analysis. See MPEP § 2106.04 and § 2106.05 for detailed guidance.

name: Claim construction: establish broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI)
description: Establish the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim as a whole prior to examining for eligibility; claim interpretation sets coverage boundaries and influences whether claims fall within statutory categories or encompass exceptions.
guidance: Determining BRI is essential and claim interpretation affects both criteria for eligibility and the Alice/Mayo analysis. See MPEP § 2111 for more information. Examples (Mentor Graphics, Synopsys, Enfish, Amdocs) illustrate how construction can change eligibility outcomes.

name: Follow the eligibility flowchart and Pathways A/B/C
description: Use the provided flowchart to determine eligibility: Step 1 (statutory category), Step 2A (directed to judicial exception?), Step 2B (significantly more?). Claims eligible via Pathway A (streamlined/self-evident), Pathway B (not directed to a judicial exception), or Pathway C (directed to exception but recite significantly more).
guidance: If uncertain whether streamlined analysis (Pathway A) applies, conduct the full eligibility analysis. If a claim is not eligible via any pathway, reject under 35 U.S.C. 101. The flowchart promotes examination efficiency and consistency.

name: Mayo/Alice two-step framework
description: A two-step test for patent eligibility: (1) determine whether claims are directed to a judicial exception (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea); (2) if so, determine whether claim elements, individually and as an ordered combination, contain an 'inventive concept' sufficient to transform the claimed exception into a patent-eligible application.
guidance: If a claim is not directed to an exception under step 1, it is patent-eligible. If step 1 is met (claim directed to an exception), courts proceed to step 2 to search for an inventive concept. The article repeatedly applies this framework to diagnostic method claims and ties each case outcome to the two-step analysis.

name: Inventive concept requirement (Step 2)
description: After step 1 finds a claim directed to an exception, step 2 requires looking for an 'inventive concept'—additional elements that transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application.
guidance: An inventive concept must do more than simply state the ineligible concept plus conventional steps. The courts evaluate whether the additional elements meaningfully limit or transform the claim beyond the natural law or phenomenon itself. Examples throughout the article show claims failing step 2 when only routine techniques or generic steps were appended.

name: Claims that merely recite a discovery of a correlation + routine steps will likely be ineligible
description: Claims that consist essentially of (a) identifying a natural correlation or phenomenon and (b) appending conventional laboratory or detection steps to observe that correlation typically fail the Mayo/Alice test.
guidance: Multiple Federal Circuit decisions invalidated diagnostic method claims on this basis: Mayo (metabolite correlations), Ariosa (cffDNA detection steps appended to natural phenomenon), Genetic Techs. (linkage correlation plus amplification/analysis), Cleveland Clinic (MPO correlation + normal detection). The article emphasizes that such claims 'merely tell those interested in the subject about the correlations that the researchers discovered.'

name: Claim breadth matters — narrowly tailored claims may fare better than broad claims
description: Broadly drafted diagnostic claims that encompass the natural correlation plus generic steps have fared poorly; it remains possible that narrow, specifically tailored diagnostic claims could survive the Mayo/Alice test.
guidance: The article notes that most claims invalidated post-Mayo were broad and that whether a narrowly-tailored claim could pass step 2 is an open question. This indicates claim scope is an important factor in eligibility analysis.

name: Preamble/claim language and added diagnosis steps can change eligibility
description: Small differences in claim wording (e.g., reciting 'detecting JUL-1' vs. 'diagnosing julitis') can alter whether a claim is considered directed to a natural law and thus whether it survives step 1.
guidance: USPTO Example 29 is highlighted: Claim 1 (detecting JUL-1) was treated as patent-eligible under Step 1, whereas Claim 2, which added an explicit 'diagnosing' limitation, was treated as directed to the natural law (correlation between JUL-1 and disease) and held ineligible. The example drew public criticism for seeming arbitrary; claim drafter should be mindful how preamble and added outcome/diagnosis language can affect the analysis.

name: Composition claims may be treated differently when they involve human-made alterations
description: Claims to compositions that are not naturally occurring (e.g., cDNA lacking introns) can be patent-eligible because they are not naturally occurring, whereas mere isolation of natural products may not be.
guidance: Myriad held that isolated genomic DNA was not patent-eligible because the nucleotide sequence existed in nature, but cDNA (exon-only sequence) was eligible because it does not occur in nature. Thus composition claims that involve human-made structural changes can avoid the natural-product exception.

name: Claim assessment can be done limitation-by-limitation or considering the claim as a whole
description: Courts may analyze claims element-by-element and/or consider the claim as a whole when determining whether additional elements provide an inventive concept under step 2.
guidance: Cleveland Clinic is cited for the court's approach in which it examined claims both limitation-by-limitation and as an entirety and concluded the claims did not 'sufficiently transform' the natural correlation. Drafters should consider both perspectives when evaluating claim language.

name: Factual inquiry into whether techniques were standard may be required (possible discovery)
description: Whether claimed steps were 'standard' or 'conventional' at the time of filing can be a factual question requiring discovery and further factual development in litigation.
guidance: In Athena the district court initially indicated discovery was needed to determine whether techniques were standard; after discovery the court found the techniques to be standard and invalidated the claims. This shows that the eligibility outcome can depend on factual record about what was routine in the art at filing.

name: Administrative guidance and case law can yield inconsistent or unpredictable outcomes
description: USPTO guidance (e.g., Example 29) and court decisions have sometimes reached different or seemingly inconsistent conclusions for similar claim language, producing uncertainty in the field.
guidance: The article notes public criticism of USPTO Example 29 for treating two nearly identical claims differently and observes that courts and the USPTO have struggled to apply the Mayo/Alice framework consistently. Practitioners should be aware of this unpredictability and the potential for differing outcomes across tribunals and claim drafts.

name: Exceptions to plaintiff's recovery of costs
description: Plaintiff cannot recover costs where it appears at trial that one or more patent claims are void for lack of being the subject of a patent, for want of invention, or for want of novelty, and no proper disclaimer was filed before suit; where only a small part of alleged infringement is found; where defendant offered before suit to submit to patent and pay a definite sum as damages equal to plaintiff’s recovery; and where parts of the patents or claims sued upon are not recovered.
guidance: In partial-success situations, whether plaintiff recovers costs on successful patents/claims is case-specific and may vary.

name: Witness fees taxable rules and limits
description: Witness fees are generally taxable against the defeated party whether testimony was oral or by deposition, but are not taxable when deposition is not offered or, if offered, not admitted; fees for more than three witnesses to one fact are not taxable unless necessity shown by affidavit.
guidance: Whether a defeated party is taxable with fees for witnesses who testified without a subpoena is unsettled; service by a private person suffices. Parties should support claims for additional witness fees with affidavit showing necessity.

name: Mere Instructions To Apply An Exception
description: When determining whether a claim integrates a judicial exception into a practical application (Step 2A Prong Two) or recites significantly more than the exception (Step 2B), examiners should ask whether the additional elements amount to more than a recitation of the words 'apply it' (or an equivalent) or are more than mere instructions to implement an abstract idea or other exception on a computer.
guidance: The additional element(s) must do 'more than simply stat[e] the [judicial exception] while adding the words 'apply it'' (Alice; Mayo). Claims that are nothing more than an instruction to apply the abstract idea using a generic computer do not render the abstract idea eligible (Alice). Examiners may, when appropriate, explain on the record why additional elements meaningfully limit the judicial exception. Consider overlap with other considerations (improvement, particular machine/transformation, well-understood routine/conventional) to assist analysis, but do not evaluate well-understood/routine/conventional in Step 2A Prong Two (that is for Step 2B). For formulating eligibility rejections see MPEP §2106.07(a). Key authorities: Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank; Mayo Collaborative Services v. Prometheus; Gottschalk v. Benson; BASCOM; McRO; Thales Visionix; Ultramercial; Electric Power Group.

name: Claim recites only the idea of a solution or outcome (result-oriented claiming)
description: Whether the claim recites only the idea of a solution or outcome — i.e., the claim fails to recite details of how a solution to a problem is accomplished and instead attempts to cover any solution with no mechanism or steps described.
guidance: Result- or outcome-focused claims that attempt to cover any solution to an identified problem with no restriction on how the result is accomplished are equivalent to 'apply it' and do not integrate the judicial exception into a practical application. In contrast, claiming a particular solution or a particular way to achieve the outcome may integrate the exception or provide significantly more. Examples/cases: Electric Power Group v. Alstom (caution against claims 'so result focused... as to effectively cover any solution'); Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One (claims modifying an XML document lacked specifics and were ineligible). Other relevant cases: Internet Patents Corp. v. Active Network; Intellectual Ventures v. Symantec; Intellectual Ventures v. Erie Indem. Use this consideration to determine whether claimed steps provide specific mechanisms or are merely functional results.

name: Particularity or generality of the application of the judicial exception
description: Whether the claim's application of the judicial exception is particular (confined to a practical application) or general (broad applicability across many fields), which affects whether the claim provides meaningful limitations beyond the exception.
guidance: Claims with broad applicability that generically recite an effect or claim every mode of accomplishing an effect may merely add the words 'apply it' and lack meaningful limitation (Internet Patents Corp. v. Active Network). Historical examples include O'Reilly v. Morse and The Telephone Cases. Conversely, limitations that confine the judicial exception to a particular, practical application may provide significantly more or integrate the exception into a practical application — e.g., BASCOM (installation of a filtering tool at a specific location with customizable features confined abstract idea of filtering to a particular application) and DDR Holdings (technological solution to an Internet problem). Examiners should evaluate whether the limitation restricts the exception to a specific technological implementation or environment.

name: Insignificant Extra-Solution Activity
description: Whether additional elements add only insignificant extra-solution activity to the judicial exception — activities incidental to the primary process or product that are nominal or tangential (pre-solution or post-solution activities).
guidance: Extra-solution activity includes pre-solution activities (e.g., gathering data) and post-solution activities (e.g., printing a report). The addition of insignificant extra-solution activity does not amount to an inventive concept, particularly when the activity is well-understood or conventional (Parker v. Flook; Mayo). Examiners should assess each claim on its merits and may consider other considerations (particular machine/transformation, field of use, well-understood/routine/conventional) to determine whether an element is insignificant extra-solution activity, but should not evaluate well-understood/routine/conventional in Step 2A Prong Two. Courts have identified categories of insignificant activity (enumerated below) and examiners should explain in rejections why such activities do not meaningfully limit the claim. See MPEP §2106.07(a) for rejection formulation.

name: Insignificant extra-solution activity: whether the limitation is significant
description: Consideration (2) under 2106.05(g): whether the limitation imposes meaningful limits on the claim such that it is not merely nominal or tangential to the invention.
guidance: Limitations that are merely tangential or restrict access in ways that do not meaningfully limit the claimed invention have been found insignificant (Ultramercial v. Hulu; Apple v. Ameranth). This consideration is evaluated in both Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B. Examiners should assess whether the limitation meaningfully confines the claimed invention beyond the judicial exception.

name: Substantial New Question of Patentability (SNQ)
description: The presence or absence of “a substantial new question of patentability” determines whether or not reexamination is ordered; the term is not defined in the statute and must be developed case-by-case using case law.
guidance: A prior art patent or printed publication raises an SNQ where there is a substantial likelihood that a reasonable examiner would consider the prior art important in deciding patentability. It is sufficient that an SNQ exists as to at least one claim. The same question of patentability is not an SNQ if it has been (A) decided in a final holding of invalidity by a federal court (after all appeals), (B) decided in an earlier concluded examination or review by the Office, or (C) raised to or by the Office in a pending reexamination or supplemental examination. It is not necessary that a prima facie case of unpatentability exist; an SNQ can exist even if the examiner would not necessarily reject the claim as fully anticipated or obvious. See In re Etter and related citations.

name: Old Art (previously cited/considered) May Serve as Sole Basis
description: For reexamination ordered on or after November 2, 2002, reliance on previously cited/considered art ("old art") does not necessarily preclude the existence of an SNQ based solely on that old art.
guidance: Determinations where old art is used as the sole basis require a fact-specific inquiry; old art may constitute an SNQ if it is presented/viewed in a new light or in a different way (e.g., in view of a material new argument or claim scope interpretation). When using old art solely, include form paragraph 22.01.01 in the order and explain how the old art is being presented in a new light. The form paragraph explains bracket insertions and must be used only the first time the already-cited art is applied in the proceeding.

name: Claims Considered in Decision
description: The claims of the patent in effect at the time of the determination are the basis for deciding whether an SNQ is present (37 CFR 1.515(a)).
guidance: The Office’s determination will generally be limited to the claims for which reexamination was requested, but the examiner is not strictly limited and can base an SNQ on other claims of the patent. If the requester wanted all claims reexamined, they should have included them. The Office may also initiate reexamination on non-requested claims under 35 U.S.C. 303(a). Amendments/new claims in copending reexamination or reissue proceedings will not be considered when deciding the request.

name: Second or Subsequent Request Must Present a Different SNQ
description: If a second or subsequent request is filed while a first ex parte reexamination is pending, the second/subsequent request is evaluated based on whether it raises a substantial new question of patentability different from that raised in the pending reexamination.
guidance: If the second request includes prior art that raised the SNQ in the pending reexamination, it should be denied. If it raises a different SNQ as to some claims but not others, it may be granted in part. The decision is based on the claims in effect at the time of determination (37 CFR 1.515(a)). A second/subsequent request may also provide information directed to proposed new or amended claims in the pending reexamination, but to be granted it must independently provide a different SNQ for the existing claims in effect at the time.

name: Partial Grant Possibility for Subsequent Requests
description: Where a subsequent request raises a different SNQ as to some patent claims but not others, the request may be granted in part.
guidance: Examples cited include orders in specific reexamination control numbers. Examiner should grant reexamination only for claims where a different SNQ is presented.

name: Effect of Prior Favorable Office Decisions on Same Art
description: An SNQ is not raised by prior art presented in a request if the Office has previously considered the same question of patentability as to the claim and reached a favorable decision for the patent owner based on the same art.
guidance: Refer to In re Recreative Technologies. Examiner should check file history to determine whether the art presented was previously cited/considered ("old art").

name: Patent Owner Statements Not Considered at Ordering Stage
