description: A patent owner claim scope statement and accompanying information submitted pursuant to 37 CFR 1.501(a)(2) will not be considered by the examiner when making the determination to order reexamination under 35 U.S.C. 304.
guidance: 35 U.S.C. 301(d) provides that such statements and additional information submitted pursuant to 35 U.S.C. 301(c) are not to be considered by the Office for any purpose other than to determine the proper meaning of a patent claim in an ordered proceeding. These materials will be considered during the examination stage if reexamination is ordered.

name: Claim Construction Standard for Ordering
description: In determining whether to order reexamination, the Office will determine the proper meaning of the patent claims by giving the claims their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification (In re Yamamoto), except for expired patents where Phillips claim construction applies.
guidance: For expired patents in reexamination, claim construction follows Phillips v. AWH Corp. (ordinary and customary meaning) as applied by the courts. If reexamination is ordered, owner statements and accompanying information will be considered during the examination stage to the fullest extent possible when determining claim scope.

name: Reexamination After Reissue of Patent
description: Where a request for reexamination is filed on a patent after a reissue patent for that patent has already issued, reexamination will be denied because the patent on which the request is based has been surrendered.
guidance: If reexamination of the reissued patent is desired, a new request for reexamination that includes and is based on the specification and claims of the reissue patent must be filed. See MPEP § 2285 for related timing issues.

name: SNQ Can Be Presented for Claims Not Requested
description: Although the examiner ordinarily concentrates on claims for which reexamination was requested, the finding of an SNQ can be based upon a claim of the patent other than the ones requested.
guidance: The request may seek reexamination of particular claims, but the examiner can determine an SNQ is present as to other claims without finding an SNQ for the requested claims. The decision on the request should discuss all patent claims requested for reexamination.

name: Factors for determining sanctions
description: Before sanctioning a practitioner, the Court must consider: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty owed to a client, the public, the legal system, or the profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of the actual or potential injury caused by the practitioner's misconduct; and (4) the existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors. (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b)).
guidance: The decision applies these four factors: finds violation of duties to client and profession; finds knowing/intentional conduct (based on accepting fees, misrepresentations, ignoring courts and RFIs); documents actual/potential injury (lost fees, jeopardized IP, dismissal of civil claim, bench warrant); and finds aggravating factors (multiple offenses, ignoring investigation and communications). The court uses ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions as guidance in assessing aggravation/mitigation.

name: AI-assisted inventions not categorically unpatentable
description: AI assisted inventions are not categorically unpatentable for improper inventorship; use of an AI system (or other advanced tools) by a natural person(s) does not preclude that natural person(s) from qualifying as the inventor (or joint inventors) if the natural person(s) significantly contributed to the claimed invention.
guidance: Focus of inventorship analysis is on the human contributions, specifically whether they meet the Pannu factors. Applications and patents must not list any entity that is not a natural person as the inventor or joint inventor, even if an AI system may have been instrumental in the creation.

name: Claim-by-claim and case-by-case analysis
description: Application of the Pannu factors to determine whether a natural person significantly contributed to an AI-assisted invention is made on a claim-by-claim and case-by-case basis.
guidance: No requirement that each named joint inventor contribute to every claim — a contribution to a single claim is sufficient — but each claim must have at least one natural person inventor. Each inventor must make a significant contribution to conception, and at least one inventor must have recognition and appreciation.

name: Guiding Principle Gp4 — essential building block developers may be inventors
description: A natural person who develops an essential building block from which the claimed invention is derived may be considered to have provided a significant contribution to the conception of the claimed invention even though not present for each activity that led to conception.
guidance: In some situations, the person who designs, builds, or trains an AI system in view of a specific problem to elicit a particular solution could be an inventor, where that designing/building/training is a significant contribution to the invention created with the AI system.

name: After-final amendment entry limitations
description: Entry of a proposed after-final amendment cannot be made as a matter of right unless it merely cancels claims or complies with a formal requirement made in a previous Office action. Amendments touching the merits may be admitted only upon a showing of good and sufficient reasons why they are necessary and why they were not presented earlier.
guidance: Explain the narrow circumstances in which after-final amendments will be entered and the burden on the applicant to show good and sufficient reasons for merit-affecting amendments.

name: Determining the identity of claimed inventions (novelty assessment procedure)
description: Novelty is assessed by determining whether each claimed invention falls under inventions excluded by Article 29(1)(1)–(2). If it does, it's not novel; if not, it's novel. Each claim must be considered separately.
guidance: The examiner shall judge novelty per claim. Claims must describe the subject matter for which protection is sought (Article 42(4)), so identity of invention is determined by the matters described in the claims.

name: General principles for defining inventions disclosed in claims
description: When claim language is clear, the claimed invention is defined as stated in the claim. Terminology in claims is given its general meaning in the technical field unless a specific meaning is explicitly defined in the description. Interpretation should be objective and reasonable considering common general knowledge at filing.
guidance: Examiners should avoid narrowing interpretation by referencing detailed description/embodiments. If subject matter appears only in description/drawings and not in claims, the examiner should not treat it as claimed. Detailed description/drawings may be used to understand claims but not to add matter not in claims. Examples: 'cream' in claims should not be limited to a particular embodiment; drawings' rotation directions should not limit claims if not in claim language.

name: Applicant-defined terms / specific definitions
description: If an applicant specifically defines a term in the detailed description so that it clearly differs from the general meaning, that specific definition will be used to interpret the term in the claims.
guidance: Merely describing the specific concept of a term in the description does not automatically constitute a binding specific definition unless clearly intended. A term should be interpreted consistently across the specification; specific definitions in the description override general technical meaning when clearly stated (Supreme Court cited).

name: Handling obscure or unclear claim terms
description: If a claim term is obscure/unclear, the examiner should examine whether the claimed invention can be grasped in view of the detailed description, drawings and common general knowledge at filing; if it can, the examiner may notify refusal reasons on both lack of description and novelty together.
guidance: If a claim remains unclear even after consulting description/drawings/general knowledge, novelty examination is not conducted and a refusal for deficiency in specification is notified.

name: Interpreting claims that specify products by function/characteristic/property
description: When a claim specifies a product by its function, property or characteristic, it should generally be construed to cover every product that has that function/characteristic, unless the expression is specifically defined otherwise in the description.
guidance: Take common general technical knowledge into account; however, in some cases a function/characteristic expression should not be construed broadly if context dictates. Example: 'means to selectively join plastic materials' would not apply to materials (e.g., magnetics) that are difficult to join with plastic.

name: Interpreting use-limited claims (product-by-use)
description: Where a claim limits a product by its use, the claim should be interpreted as covering a product specially suitable for the disclosed use, considering specification, drawings and common general knowledge at filing.
guidance: A product that meets all technical characteristics but is not appropriate for the claimed use (or requires conversion) should not be regarded as the claimed product. If the product is not suitable for the use, the use-limitation may have no effect on defining the claimed invention and thus may not help preserve novelty. Example: a 'crane hook' is distinct from 'fishing hooks' even if both are hooks, because size/strength suit specific uses.

name: Product-by-process claims (product defined by manufacturing process)
description: A product claim that defines the product by its manufacturing process should, in principle, be construed as claiming the product per se; novelty/inventive step are determined by comparing the claimed product itself with prior art unless there is a special reason in the claim description.
guidance: Special reasons to accept process-limited product claims are extremely exceptional (e.g., when it's greatly difficult to define the product otherwise). If an identical product can be obtained by a different process, the claimed product is not novel.

name: Ambiguity via Paronymous or Similar Words
description: Arguments exploit words of similar form or root (paronymous terms) that have distinct meanings, producing misleading inferences.
guidance: Watch for shifts in connotation or morphological relatives (example: Cicero's use of cupiditas/cupidus) that covertly change the claim's force.

name: Knowingly giving false or misleading information to a client (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(2)(i))
description: Proscribed conduct includes 'Knowingly giving false or misleading information or knowingly participating in a material way in giving false or misleading information to, a client in connection with any immediate, prospective, or pending business before the Office.'
guidance: Applied to attorney-client communications about patentability, scope of claims, and representations about what a patent covers; knowingly misleading a client about matter before the USPTO violates the Code.

name: Examples of misconduct fact patterns that meet the standards
description: Examples applied here: making material amendments to a final draft application without client consent or disclosure; knowingly assuring a client of patentability despite prior art that precludes the claimed scope; negotiating/attempting to pay a client not to file disciplinary complaints.
guidance: These concrete fact patterns illustrate how regulatory prohibitions and sanctioning factors are applied to real practitioner conduct.

name: Claim must definitely state what inventor intends to protect
description: That what the inventor intends to protect must be definitely described.
guidance: Every claim must definitely state the invention the inventor intends to secure; modifications of the invention the inventor intends to protect must be definitely described (cases cited: Saigent v. Carter, etc.).

name: Consistency of adjunctive devices across claims
description: That the adjunctive devices referred to in all the Claims for an invention must be the same in themselves and in their relation to the invention.
guidance: When adjuncts are referenced across multiple claims, they should be consistent in identity and relationship; inconsistent or varying adjunct descriptions risk ambiguity or invalid claims (Ex parte Stanbridge cited).

name: Enumeration of elements as operative invention is proper
description: That the enumeration of such elements as constitute the operative invention is a proper mode of claiming it.
guidance: Listing the constituent elements of a combination as the claimed invention is an acceptable way to define a combination claim (see Ex parte Farrow and related cases).

name: Do not state elements not essential to the invention
description: That elements not essential to the invention should not be stated in the Claim.
guidance: Non-essential or merely auxiliary elements should generally be omitted from claims; including them can obscure the real invention and create defects (see discussion on auxiliary elements).

name: Do not claim auxiliary or merely auxiliary elements
description: That what is described as merely auxiliary must not be claimed.
guidance: Matter characterized in the specification as auxiliary, not essential, should not be elevated into the claim; doing so risks overreaching (Ex parte Wheat example).

name: If invention is new only for certain purposes, claim must be limited to those purposes
description: When the invention is new and patentable only when considered with reference to certain purposes or objects, it must be claimed only in connection with such purposes or objects.
guidance: A claim to an instrument or art that is old in itself but new in a particular use must specifically claim the new use or mode of operation; a claim to the old instrument without that limitation would be void (illustrated by new use doctrine).

name: Claim should be neither broader nor narrower than necessary
description: The Claim should express no more and no less than is necessary to convey an accurate understanding of the actual invention which had been made.
guidance: Overbroad claims (claiming more than the inventor made) and underbroad claims (failing to capture the actual invention) are both problematic. If an additional independent feature is the essence of the invention, the claim should focus on that feature and stop there rather than enumerating unrelated old elements.

name: Claims must avoid including matter previously patented or in public possession
description: A Claim including any matter before patented, or in possession of the public, is fatally defective; such matter should not be mentioned unless expressly disclaimed.
guidance: Claims should not incorporate previously patented/public matter; if necessary, the applicant must disclaim the old subject-matter clearly. A disclaimer in a pending application must explain and not contradict the claim (cases and notes cited).

name: Claim must correspond with the description (no claim broader than described matter)
description: The Claim is the request for protection and must entirely correspond with the Description and be based upon the matter therein contained; no invention can be claimed unless previously described so a skilled person could practice it without further inventive skill.
guidance: Claims cannot broaden beyond the disclosed description; features not delineated in the specification cannot be inserted into the claim even if a mechanic would discover them. A claim based on an insufficient description is void (numerous cases cited under §515).

name: Description may illustrate the claim but may not enlarge it; claim controls when conflict exists
description: The Claim may be illustrated but not enlarged by the Description; when the Description and Claim disagree, the Claim controls.
guidance: Description cannot be used to expand the legal scope of a claim; where conflict makes the whole ambiguous, the invention must be found in one or the other and contradictions can render the whole void (McKesson v. Camdick; Railroad Co. v. Mellon examples).

name: Matter described as auxiliary not essential cannot be claimed
description: Features of the invention described as auxiliary, but not essential to the invention, cannot be stated in the Claim.
guidance: Auxiliary matter that is not part of the inventive essence should not be claimed; claims should focus on essential elements (repeated principle across sections).

name: Cannot claim all modes of effecting an end if only one mode described
description: A Claim for all modes of effecting a result when the invention has been previously described as a single mode of effecting it is invalid.
guidance: You cannot claim the entire genus of ways to achieve a result if the specification only describes a single specific mode; that would improperly broaden the claim (Lawther v. Hamilton; Ex parte Demming cited).

name: Claims may be narrower than described; claim single operative element if sufficient
description: The invention claimed may be narrower than that described; if a single new element in the described invention is a complete operative means it may be claimed alone.
guidance: A restricted claim to a single new operative element is permissible and can indirectly protect the whole invention if that element is essential to operation (Ex parte Sturges, etc.).

name: No particular form of words required, but clarity and precision needed
description: No particular form of words is required for the statement of the Claim; language must be sufficiently clear and accurate to define the invention to the mind of the reader.
guidance: While formalistic phrasing is unnecessary, claims must convey the essential character of the invention precisely; general/ambiguous claims are void, though inartificial phrasing that does not create uncertainty is tolerated (§516 and case law).

name: Avoid useless words, multiplicity of synonyms, and equivocal terms
description: Useless words should not be inserted nor synonymous words be multiplied; equivocal words are never permitted.
guidance: Superfluous or repetitive wording tends to create ambiguity; equivocal phrasing renders claims doubtful and can lead to invalidity (examples and case citations provided).

name: Every claimed element must be clearly stated, not merely inferred
description: Every element claimed must be clearly stated, not merely inferred; a Claim must assert, not rest in doubtful implications.
guidance: Claims that merely refer the reader to the description without asserting the invention are insufficient; vague or inferred elements are grounds for rejection (Ex parte Holt; Fricke v. Hum examples).

name: Do not use indefinite expressions like 'means' or 'mechanism' without clarity
description: A Claim cannot use such indefinite expressions as 'means,' 'mechanism,' etc., in a way that leaves essential elements undefined.
guidance: Words like 'means' or 'mechanism' may be used to denote non-essential appliances but cannot be used to obscure or omit essential elements of the invention; indefinite terminology that fails to disclose the invention is impermissible (Ex parte Holt, Ex parte Demming).

name: Equivalents are covered but should not be expressly claimed; use with caution
description: Equivalents are legally covered by a Claim though not mentioned, but the term 'equivalent' or expressly claiming equivalents is equivocal and should be inhibited; 'or equivalent devices' must not be used unless equivalents are described or other special conditions apply.
guidance: The doctrine of equivalents operates to cover unanticipated equivalents, so expressly adding 'equivalents' may create undefined scope. Expressly claiming equivalents is generally improper unless the specification describes them or unless claiming one would completely bar claiming the other (cases: Burden v. Coming; Ex parte Reid; Ex parte Bogart; Ex parte Dolph).

name: The petition defines the scope of review; petitioners must raise all arguments in the petition
description: The petition, not the Board, defines the scope of instituted review; petitioners must raise all potential arguments and claim construction positions in the petition or risk forfeiture.
guidance: Cites SAS II and 35 U.S.C. §312(a)(3): failure to include arguments/claim constructions in the petition can forfeit the right to rely on them later (e.g., in reply). Practitioners should ensure petitions comprehensively present arguments they may later need.

name: Consistency required in claim construction between institution and final written decision
description: The PTAB may not inconsistently construe claim terms between its institution decision and its final written decision without giving the parties an opportunity to be heard, because that would be a change of theories midstream.
guidance: Patent owners should consider raising claim construction positions in preliminary responses since winning a preliminary construction can be significant; if the Board alters a construction without notice, that can be grounds for APA reversal (SAS I, WesternGeco). When a party puts a construction at issue, the Board may alter it but must give opportunity to respond.

name: Prima facie obviousness framework and burden allocation
description: During examination and reexamination, the examiner must first set forth a prima facie case, supported by evidence, showing why the claims would have been obvious in light of the prior art. Once the examiner sets out this prima facie case, the burden shifts to the patentee to provide evidence or argument sufficient to rebut the examiner's evidence.
guidance: If examiner fails to establish a prima facie case, applicant has no obligation to rebut. If prima facie case is established, applicant may submit evidence (e.g., comparative test data) or arguments; examiner must then weigh all evidence in making the final determination.

name: Avoiding hindsight and correct temporal perspective
description: To reach a proper determination under 35 U.S.C. 103, the examiner must step backward in time and into the shoes worn by the hypothetical person of ordinary skill in the art — that time is "before the effective filing date of the claimed invention" (or at time of invention for pre-AIA).
guidance: Knowledge of the applicant's disclosure must be put aside to avoid hindsight, though it can inform differences and searches; explicit factual basis from prior art must support the legal conclusion.

name: Office action requirements for a 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection
description: After indicating that the rejection is under 35 U.S.C. 103, the examiner should set forth in the Office action: (A) the relevant teachings of the prior art relied upon; (B) the difference(s) in the claim over the applied reference(s); (C) the proposed modification of the applied reference(s) necessary to arrive at the claimed subject matter; and (D) an explanation as to why the claimed invention would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the relevant time.
guidance: Preferably cite relevant column/page/line numbers for references. Include every reference relied on, even if minor, so the record clearly communicates basis for rejection (see In re Hoch).

name: Use of known technique to improve similar devices (rationale)
description: Use of known technique to improve similar devices (methods, or products) in the same way is a rationale supporting obviousness.
guidance: Demonstrate that the technique was known in the art and that its application to the claimed device would have been an ordinary design choice.

name: Required factual findings for combination-by-known-methods rationale
description: When using the 'combining prior art elements according to known methods' rationale, Office personnel must articulate: (1) a finding that the prior art included each element claimed (not necessarily in a single reference); (2) a finding that one of ordinary skill could have combined the elements as claimed by known methods and that each element performs same function as it does separately; (3) a finding that one of ordinary skill would have recognized that the results of the combination were predictable; and (4) whatever additional Graham factual findings are necessary to explain a conclusion of obviousness.
guidance: If any of these findings cannot be made, this rationale cannot support an obviousness rejection. Use factual record to justify each finding; see Anderson's-Black Rock and KSR.

name: Teaching away reduces likelihood of obviousness
description: When the prior art criticizes, discredits, or otherwise discourages the solution claimed (teaches away), that prior art weighs against a finding of obviousness; mere disclosure of alternatives alone does not constitute teaching away.
guidance: If prior art suggests the combination would be impractical or undesirable, demonstrate why a skilled artisan would nonetheless have adopted it; cases like Adams and Crocs illustrate how teaching away supports nonobviousness.

name: Factor a) — Markedly different product
description: Whether the natural products recited in the claim are 'markedly different' from what exists in nature.
guidance: If the recited natural product is structurally or functionally altered in a way that is significant relative to its natural counterpart, factor a) may be satisfied. Examples and counterexamples: isolated nucleic acids may have minor structural changes (broken bonds) but lack significant functional differences and thus may not be 'markedly different' (see Myriad discussion); bacteria unchanged from nature are not markedly different. Use specification/record to assess whether the product has been meaningfully altered.

name: Factor b) — Additional elements meaningfully limit claim scope (not foreclose others)
description: Whether elements in addition to the judicial exception narrow the scope of the claim so that others are not substantially foreclosed from using the natural products in other ways.
guidance: Satisfied when claimed additional elements impose specific limitations (e.g., defined temperatures, times, steps, particular physical integration) that leave substantial alternative uses of the natural products open to others. Example: thermal cycling steps that limit amplification to a particular protocol meaningfully limit scope.

name: Factor c) — Elements relate to the natural products in a significant way
description: Whether the claimed elements relate to the natural products in a significant (more than insignificant or tangential) way.
guidance: Satisfied when elements directly manipulate or integrate natural products (e.g., forming a structure that physically integrates natural products, or steps that directly manipulate the products). Use the nature of the relationship (physical integration, direct manipulation) to judge significance.

name: Factor d) — Claimed elements do more than describe with general instructions
description: Whether the claimed elements do more than merely describe the natural products with general instructions to use or apply them.
guidance: Satisfied when the claim recites a specific practical application (e.g., a firework assembly including particular components; use of a particular antibody and detection method) rather than abstract/general instructions. If only a general instruction to apply the principle is recited, factor d) is not satisfied.

name: Factor e) — Machine-or-transformation
description: Whether a machine is recited or a transformation is performed.
guidance: Factor e) is satisfied if the claim includes a recited machine or a transformation; if neither is recited, factor e) is not satisfied. Use this factor where applicable to identify tangible machines/transformations in the claim.

name: Factor f) — Additional elements are more than well-understood, purely conventional, or routine
description: Whether the additional claimed elements add anything more than what is well-understood, purely conventional, or routine in the relevant art.
guidance: Satisfied when the specification/record shows that an additional element is not routine or conventional (e.g., a newly created antibody). If the added elements are routine/conventional in the art (e.g., standard heating and cooling steps in PCR), factor f) is not satisfied.

name: Factor h) — Claim recited at high level of generality covering substantially all practical applications
description: Whether the claimed elements are recited at such a high level of generality that the claim covers substantially all practical applications of the judicial exception.
guidance: Satisfied when claim language is broad enough to preempt substantially all uses (e.g., broad instruction to expose to sunlight) and thus weighs against eligibility. If specific limitations prevent coverage of substantially all practical applications, factor h) is not satisfied.

name: Factor i) — Claimed elements are required for use of the judicial exception
description: Whether the claimed elements are required to apply or use the natural products/principle (i.e., whether everyone who uses the judicial exception would be required to use the claimed elements).
guidance: If the claim forces everyone using the natural product/principle to employ the claimed additional elements, factor i) is satisfied (weighs against eligibility). If alternative means exist (e.g., different antibodies or detection methods), factor i) is not satisfied.

name: Factor l) — Mere field-of-use or attempt to limit to a particular technological environment
description: Whether the claimed elements are merely a field-of-use limitation or an attempt to limit application of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment.
guidance: Satisfied when the claim simply restricts use to a particular field or environment without adding a meaningful inventive application (e.g., limiting white light principle to treatment of mood disorder using sunlight alone). Such limitations count against eligibility.

name: Apply factors per claim type (process vs product)
description: Apply the factors according to whether the claim is to a product (manufacture/composition) or a process; some factors (e.g., a and g) are not relevant to process claims.
guidance: When analyzing process claims, factors a and g (about product being 'markedly different') are not relevant. Other factors (b–f, h–l) remain applicable but must be interpreted in context (e.g., whether steps meaningfully limit scope, integrate the principle, are conventional). Use examples in guidance: process claims with thermal cycling satisfied b, c, d but not e/f in example.

name: Overall balancing test — 'significantly different' determination
description: After evaluating factors toward and against eligibility, balance them to determine whether the claim as a whole recites something 'significantly different' than the judicial exception.
guidance: If the factors weigh toward 'significantly different', the claim qualifies as eligible subject matter; if they weigh against, the claim does not qualify. Apply all relevant factors and consider specification/record evidence when balancing. Examples: manufacture/composition claims with integrated, specific elements may weigh toward eligibility; pure compositions of natural products often weigh against.

name: When claim recites an abstract idea and a natural product — follow MPEP §2106(II)
description: If a claim recites both an abstract idea and a natural product, analyze Question 3 using only the guidance in MPEP §2106(II), which controls the practical-application analysis for abstract ideas.
guidance: Do not conflate analyses — the handling of abstract ideas is controlled by §2106(II). Use that section's guidance about applying/practical-application of judicial exceptions when the claim includes an abstract idea (see H example regarding BRCA2 sequence comparison).

name: Use of form paragraph ¶7.05.13 for 35 U.S.C. 101 rejections
description: Revised form paragraph 7.05.13 is to be used when rejecting claims (machine, composition, manufacture, or process claims) that recite or involve a law of nature/natural principle, natural phenomenon, or natural product for lack of subject matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 101.
guidance: ¶7.05.13 language: 'the claimed invention is not directed to patent eligible subject matter. Based upon an analysis with respect to the claim as a whole, claim(s) [1] do not recite something significantly different than a judicial exception. The rationale for this determination is explained below: [2]'. Examiner Note: this form paragraph should be used when rejecting claim(s) that have a law of nature/natural principle or a natural phenomenon, e.g., a natural product, as a claim limitation. Must be preceded by form paragraphs 7.04 and 7.05.

name: Categories of IPTAB trials
description: Main trial categories include: appeal against decision to reject an application; trial for correction (narrowing claims, clerical error correction, clarifying ambiguous description); trial for invalidation; trial to confirm the scope of rights; and patent opposition.
guidance: Each category has its own statutory basis (e.g., Article 132-17 for appeal vs rejection; Article 136 for correction; Article 133 for invalidation; Article 135 for scope confirmation; Article 132-2 for opposition).

name: Preparatory hearing agenda items
description: Preparatory hearings (often by conference call) commonly address: trial dates and number of trials; deadlines for arguments and evidence (including expert affidavits); whether to request time-consuming evidentiary methods (verification, appraisal, expert witness); designation of a technical advisor; whether to hold a technical explanatory session; whether to hold claim construction hearing first; coordination with pending correction petitions; parallel hearings with related cases; and confirmation/summary of disputed issues.
guidance: Use preparatory hearings to fix procedural timelines and narrow issues; be prepared with proposed schedules and evidentiary plans.

name: Infirmity of proof (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(ii))
description: Whether there was such an infirmity of proof establishing the conduct as to give rise to the clear conviction that the Office could not, consistently with its duty, accept the state's final conclusion on that subject.
guidance: This is a difficult showing. Consent to the state findings undermines an infirmity claim. Private civil settlements (including provisions requiring withdrawal of a grievance) do not bind bar counsel and do not by themselves create an infirmity of proof. Relevant state case law (cited in the decision) indicates settlements or withdrawal by a complainant will not necessarily preclude disciplinary action.

name: Publicity/finality argument (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(iv))
description: Any argument that the practitioner was not publicly censured, publicly reprimanded, placed on probation, disbarred, suspended, or disciplinarily disqualified (i.e., challenges based on the nature/publication or finality of the state discipline).
guidance: The practitioner may attempt to argue that the state action was not a public sanction or was otherwise not final; to prevent reciprocal discipline the practitioner must show by clear and convincing evidence a genuine issue of material fact on this ground. The Decision treats such procedural/finality claims narrowly and requires substantial proof.

name: Consent to state discipline and effect on defenses
description: A practitioner's consent to a state stipulated resolution or consent judgment (including admissions or specific findings) weakens or precludes claims that the state proceeding suffered infirmity of proof or was unjust.
guidance: If the respondent expressly consented to findings of fact and discipline, those admissions are highly probative and make it difficult to satisfy the Selling defenses by clear and convincing evidence. Lack of an appeal from the state discipline further undermines respondent's challenges.

name: Citations in the ISR (Rule 43.5)
description: The ISR shall contain citations of the documents considered to be relevant.
guidance: The method for identifying cited documents is governed by the Administrative Instructions. Citations of particular relevance should be specially indicated; citations not relevant to all claims shall be cited in relation to the specific claim(s). Relevant passages should be identified (page/column/line) where practicable.

name: Start, basis and scope of supplementary international search (Rule 45 bis.5)
description: The Authority specified for supplementary search shall start promptly upon receipt of required documents (or may delay until additional documents or until 22 months from priority date). The search is based on the international application as filed or an accepted translation and shall take due account of the ISR and written opinion where available; Authority may exclude claims not subject of the international search or decide not to establish a supplementary ISR if Article 17(2)(a) declaration exists.
guidance: Supplementary search shall cover at least the documentation indicated in the applicable agreement; Authority may restrict search to certain claims consistent with limitations/conditions; if a limitation wholly excludes search, request is considered not submitted.

name: Competence of International Searching Authorities for supplementary searches (Rule 45 bis.9)
description: An ISA is competent to carry out supplementary international searches if its preparedness to do so is stated in the applicable agreement under Article 16(3)(b), subject to limitations and conditions in that agreement. The ISA that carried out the international search under Article 16(1) may not carry out the supplementary search for that application.
guidance: Limitations may include subject-matter restrictions, caps on number of supplementary searches in a period, and limits on number of claims covered; applicants must select Authorities competent under the agreements.

name: Statement under Article 19(1) length and content limits (Rule 46.4)
description: The statement under Article 19(1) shall be in the publication language and shall not exceed 500 words if in English (or translated into English); it shall be identified by a heading (e.g., 'Statement under Article 19(1)'). The statement shall contain no disparaging comments on the ISR or relevance of its citations; reference to citations may only be made in connection with an amendment of that claim.
guidance: Keep the statement concise, respectful, and focused on amendments rather than criticizing the ISR.

name: Form of amendments — replacement sheets and accompanying letter (Rule 46.5)
description: Amendments under Article 19 require submission of replacement sheet(s) containing a complete set of claims in replacement of all claims originally filed, accompanied by a letter identifying claims that differ, claims cancelled, and indicating the basis for amendments in the application as filed.
guidance: Provide a clear mapping between original and amended claims and cite the support in the originally filed application.

name: Claim construction — determine what each claim as a whole covers
description: Each claim must be separately analyzed and given its broadest reasonable interpretation in light of and consistent with the written description; consider entire claim including preamble language, transitional phrase, and body.
guidance: Include preamble and transitional phrase weight when construing claims. 'Comprising' is open-ended (covers recited elements alone or combined with unrecited elements). 'Consisting essentially of' occupies a middle ground but for 35 U.S.C. 102/103 searching it will be treated as equivalent to 'comprising' unless the specification clearly defines what materially changes the invention. Applicant bears the burden of showing that additional steps/components are excluded by 'consisting essentially of.' Do not import limitations from the specification into the claims. Absence of definitions for well-established terms/procedures is not a basis for a 35 U.S.C. 112 rejection.

name: Review the entire application for support of each element/step
description: Before deciding whether the written description requirement is satisfied, review claims and the entire specification (including embodiments, figures, and sequence listings) to understand how applicant provides support for each claimed feature.
guidance: Evaluate the specification from the standpoint of one of ordinary skill in the art at the filing date; determine the field of the invention and the level of skill. There is generally an inverse correlation between level of skill in the art and the specificity of disclosure necessary. Use teachings in the specification to assess whether each claim limitation is supported.

name: Written description shows possession by disclosure of an actual reduction to practice
description: Possession may be shown by describing an actual reduction to practice: the inventor constructed an embodiment or performed a process that met all claim limitations and determined the invention would work for its intended purpose.
guidance: Reduction to practice provides strong evidence of possession. For biological materials, a deposit in accordance with 37 CFR 1.801 et seq. may evidence reduction to practice. Case law examples: Cooper v. Goldfarb; UMC Elecs.; Estee Lauder; Mahurkar.

name: Written description shows possession by drawings or structural/chemical formulas
description: A clear depiction of the invention in detailed drawings or structural chemical formulas that permit one skilled in the art to recognize that applicant had possession can satisfy the written description requirement.
guidance: Drawings alone may suffice in some instances. Generic formulas in chemical claims often indicate what the genus encompasses and can be adequate. Cases: Vas-Cath; In re Wolfensperger; Autogiro; Eli Lilly.

name: Written description shows possession by identifying characteristics
description: Disclosure of sufficiently detailed, relevant identifying characteristics (e.g., sequence, structure, binding affinity, binding specificity, molecular weight, length) can demonstrate possession of a claimed biological or chemical entity.
guidance: Identifying characteristics may include partial structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics coupled with known correlations between function and structure, restriction enzyme maps, unique cleavage patterns, isoelectric points, antibody cross-reactivity, or expression of mRNA producing the protein. The characteristics must distinguish the claimed invention from other materials and lead one skilled in the art to conclude applicant had possession.

name: Functional claiming alone is generally insufficient for certain claims (e.g., coding sequences)
description: A functional definition by itself does not suffice to describe a coding sequence or other molecular structures because it indicates what the gene does rather than what it is.
guidance: For chemical inventions, precise definition by structure, formula, chemical name, or physical properties is required; simply providing assays or a plan for identifying active compounds is not enough. Case examples: Eli Lilly; Univ. of Rochester v. G.D. Searle.

name: Means-plus-function (35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph) support requirement
description: If a claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112, para. 6 (means- or step-plus-function), it must be interpreted to cover the corresponding structure, materials, or acts described in the specification and equivalents.
guidance: A means-plus-function limitation is adequately described under 35 U.S.C. 112, para. 1 if: (1) the written description links/associates adequately described particular structure/material/acts to the recited function; or (2) it is clear that one skilled in the art would know what structure/material/acts perform the recited function. Consider the disclosure in the summary, detailed description, original claims, abstract, and drawings. Note: a 35 U.S.C. 112, para. 2 rejection cannot stand where there is adequate para.1 description for means-plus-function recitations.

name: Analysis for claims drawn to a single embodiment or species
description: When a claim is limited to a single disclosed embodiment/species, analyze whether the application describes possession of that species by (A) actual reduction to practice, (B) reduction to detailed drawings or structural chemical formulas, or (C) sufficiently detailed identifying characteristics.
guidance: Specifically: (1) Determine whether the application describes the complete structure (or acts of a process) of the claimed invention as a whole; a complete structure typically satisfies 35 U.S.C. 112, para.1. (2) If the complete structure is not disclosed, determine whether other relevant identifying characteristics suffice to show possession (e.g., when there is a well-established correlation between structure and function, function plus minimal structure may suffice). Functional disclosure alone is insufficient where no correlation exists.

name: Factors to consider when determining whether possession is shown
description: Determination that applicant was in possession is a factual inquiry considering multiple factors.
guidance: Consider the level of skill and knowledge in the art, partial structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics (especially if coupled with a known correlation between function and structure), and the method of making the claimed invention. Disclosure of any combination of such identifying characteristics that distinguish the claimed invention from other materials and would lead one of skill in the art to conclude possession is sufficient.

name: Adjust disclosure expectations to the nature and predictability of the art
description: The amount and type of description necessary under 35 U.S.C. 112 varies with the nature and scope of the invention and with the existing scientific and technological knowledge in the field.
guidance: In mature, predictable arts (e.g., well-known microprocessor programming), disclosure of function and a capable device may suffice. In emerging or unpredictable technologies, or where traits are not reasonably predictable, more detailed disclosure (e.g., structure, examples, testing) is required. Disclosure of only a method of making and function may not support a product claim in unpredictable arts.

name: Product-by-process claim support
description: A product-by-process claim's written description requirement is satisfied if the process has actually been used to produce the product; otherwise, the requirement may not be met.
guidance: If it is unclear that the acts in the specification can be performed or that the product is produced by the claimed process, written description support for a product-by-process claim may be insufficient.

name: Conventional/art-known subject matter need not be disclosed in detail
description: Information that is conventional or well known to one of ordinary skill in the art need not be described in detail in the specification to satisfy the written description requirement.
guidance: Rely on patents and printed publications in the art to determine maturity and the level of knowledge/skill in the art. In mature technologies, a written description question generally should not be raised for claims present in the application when originally filed even if the specification discloses only method and function.

name: Claim as a whole must be supported including preamble and transitional phrase
description: The claim as a whole — preamble, transitional phrase, and body — must be sufficiently supported by the specification to satisfy the written description requirement; applicant shows possession by describing the claimed invention with all its limitations.
guidance: Evaluate whether sufficient structures, acts, or functions are recited to make clear the scope and meaning of the claim, including the weight to be given the preamble. Determination whether preamble recitations are structural limitations requires review of the entire application to understand what the inventors actually invented and intended to encompass.

name: Perspective and timing for written description assessment
description: Assess whether a skilled artisan would have understood the inventor to be in possession of the claimed invention at the time the application was filed; the description need not use the exact words of the claim.
guidance: The inquiry is factual and case-by-case. If a skilled artisan would understand possession despite lack of every nuance in the specification, the requirement is met. Support can be shown even if actual reduction to practice is absent if the disclosure provides sufficient identifying characteristics.

name: Secondary Considerations / Objective Indicia of Nonobviousness
description: Certain factors may help determine whether the invention would have been obvious; no factor alone is dispositive and the obviousness of the invention must be considered as a whole.
guidance: Provide only instructions relevant and supported by admitted evidence. Consider whether: (1) products covered by the claim were commercially successful due to the merits of the claimed invention rather than advertising or other features; (2) there was a long-felt need satisfied by the claimed invention; (3) others tried but failed to solve the problem; (4) others copied the claimed invention; (5) the claimed invention achieved unexpectedly superior results over the closest prior art; (6) others in the field or the defendant praised the invention or expressed surprise; (7) others accepted licenses because of the merits. These factors are relevant only if there is a nexus between the consideration and the invention; the patentee bears the burden of proving nexus and admissibility. (Citing Graham, U.S. v. Adams, Apple v. Samsung, WBIP v. Kohler.)

name: Enablement Requirement (35 U.S.C. §112)
description: [The Defendant] contends that claim(s) ___ are invalid for lack of enablement. The Defendant bears the burden of establishing by clear and convincing evidence that the specification fails to satisfy the enablement requirement.
guidance: A patent must disclose sufficient information to enable persons of ordinary skill in the field of the invention as of the effective filing date to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation. Patents are written for persons of ordinary skill, so the specification need not state information such persons would likely know. The fact that some experimentation may be required does not mean the patent is not enabled. Factors to consider for undue experimentation include: the quantity of experimentation necessary and whether that experimentation involves only known or commonly used techniques; the amount of direction or guidance disclosed in the patent; the presence or absence of working examples; the nature of the invention; the state of the prior art; the relative skill of those in the art; the predictability of the art; and the breadth of the claims. Enablement is a question of law for the Court; the jury should be instructed on subsidiary fact issues only if there are specific factual issues for the jury to decide. (Citing 35 U.S.C. §112; Amgen v. Sanofi; In re Wands.)

name: Written-Description Requirement
description: [The Defendant] contends that claim(s) ___ are invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description requirement. The Defendant bears the burden of establishing by clear and convincing evidence that the specification fails to satisfy the written-description requirement.
guidance: A patent must contain a written description of the product or method claimed to ensure the applicant actually invented the claimed subject matter. To satisfy the requirement, the specification must describe each and every limitation of a patent claim in sufficient detail (the exact words need not be used). The written-description requirement is satisfied if persons of ordinary skill would recognize from the specification that the inventor possessed the subject matter claimed as of the effective filing date, even if claims changed later. It is unnecessary to spell out every detail or provide specific examples, but enough must be included to convince POSA that the inventor possessed the full scope of the invention. Factors to consider include: the nature and scope of the patent claims; the complexity, predictability, and maturity of the technology; the existing knowledge in the field; and the scope and content of the prior art. Written-description sufficiency is decided claim-by-claim and is a question of fact (instruct jurors only if specific claims are challenged and there is sufficient evidentiary support). (Citing 35 U.S.C. §112; Ariad; Boston Sci.; Vas‑Cath.)

name: Damages—General Principles (35 U.S.C. §284)
description: If you find that the accused device or method infringes any asserted claims and those claims are not invalid, you must determine the amount of damages to be awarded the plaintiff for the infringement. The Plaintiff must prove each element of its damages, including amount, by a preponderance of the evidence.
guidance: Damages must compensate the plaintiff for the infringement (putting the plaintiff in about the same financial position it would have been in but for the infringement). The damages award cannot be less than a reasonable royalty. Do not add anything to punish, to set an example, or for interest. The jury should address damages only if it finds one or more asserted claims both not invalid and infringed. (Citing 35 U.S.C. §284; WesternGeco; ResQNet; Aro; etc.)

name: Applications related to companies certified as venture businesses — eligibility & documentary/timing requirements
description: Rules governing expedited examination requests when an applicant is a company certified as a venture business under the relevant Act.
guidance: Key criteria and examiner guidance: (i) Joint filing with at least one certified venture business => accept. (ii) If the certified venture company's name and the applicant's name are identical => accept. (iii) At least one of: filing date, date of request for expedited examination, or date of determination on expedited examination must fall within the certificate's valid period. (iv) Documentary proof: the original confirmation of being a venture business should be used; a copy may be used if recognized identical; an evaluation notice cannot replace the confirmation. (v) Relevance: if there is no correlation between the venture business type and the claimed invention, the request is not accepted; examiner must order correction and may accept if correlation is well-explained. (vi) How to examine correlation: based on requester’s written explanation and evidential documents (business registration certificate, etc.); examiners may compare company overview/main products and claimed invention on the official venture-business confirmation/announcement website; if correlation cannot be found/accepted, order correction. Additional procedural guidance where the company named on the confirmation is not the applicant: if applicant cannot file in company name because company is not a legal entity, the examiner may treat the application as filed by the venture business only when the applicant and the head of the venture business are the same; business registration certificate may be ordered to determine legal entity status (note: registration-number digits 81–87 indicate legal entity).

name: Applications by Inno-Biz (innovation business) — eligibility, timing, proof, and relevance
description: Guidelines for expedited-examination requests filed by companies designated as Inno-Biz under the relevant Act.
guidance: Principal rules: (i) Joint application where at least one applicant is an Inno-Biz => recognize request. (ii) If Inno-Biz company name and applicant name are identical => recognize request. If names differ, only those applications that qualify under the venture-business rules (4.6) are eligible. (iii) Timing: the applicant must constitute an Inno-Biz at at least one of the filing date, request date, or determination date. (iv) Documentary proof: original Inno-Biz Confirmation issued by the Small & Medium Business Administration is required; copies acceptable if identical. (v) Relevance: where no relevance exists between business type and claimed invention, the application is not eligible; examiner shall order correction and may accept if relevance is well-explained. (vi) Relevance determination: based on the requester’s written explanation and evidential documents (business registration certificate, etc.); examiners may consult the Inno-Biz certified company information system website to compare business type and invention content; if relevance cannot be confirmed, order correction.

name: Companies with outstanding employee invention compensation systems — eligibility and proof
description: Rules for applications filed by companies designated as having outstanding employee invention compensation systems (Invention Promotion Act).
guidance: Key guidance: (i) Joint filing with at least one applicant so designated => accept. (ii) Where the designated company's title and applicant name are identical => accept; if different, handle under the venture-business rules (4.6). (iii) Timing: the company must hold the designation at least at one of filing date, request date, or determination date. (iv) Documentary proof: original Certificate of Company with Outstanding Employee Invention Compensation System issued by KIPO is required; copy acceptable if identical. (v) Relevance: if the company’s business type is not relevant to the claimed invention, the request is not eligible; examiner will issue a notice to complement the request; if relevancy is explained, accept. (vi) Relevance determination: based on evidential documents attached to the written explanation (business registration certificate, etc.); if relevance cannot be identified, examiner issues a correction order.

name: Applications related to outcomes of national quality authentication projects (NeP/NeT/industrial convergence) — eligibility and recognition
description: Eligibility for expedited examination when the claimed invention is a direct outcome of national quality authentication/certification projects (new product, new technology, industrial convergence product, or certain agricultural/maritime tech certifications).
guidance: Subjects listed: (i) products authenticated as new products (NeP), (ii) technologies certified as new technology (NeT), (iii) products certified as industrial convergence products, (iv) patents re: tech accredited as new technology in maritime/fisheries field. Examination guidance: NeP authenticates products with significant economic/technological impact and high performance among commercialized products based on first local tech or substitutes; certification issued by Minister through evaluation per KATS standards. NeT authenticates technologies that enhance performance or improve productivity, typically completed tech with prototype testing and commercializable within two years; certification issued by Minister via Korea Industrial Technology Association. Industrial Convergence Product authentication covers products from creative combination across industries/tech and is certified by the relevant central administrative institution. If it is unclear whether the claimed invention is the direct outcome, the examiner may order verification; however, if it is likely related and there are no special grounds to doubt, the examiner may recognize eligibility without further investigation.

name: Applications forming basis of priority claim under treaty & related PCT/self-designation rules
description: Guidance for expedited-examination requests for applications that form the basis of a priority claim under international treaties and for related PCT/self-designation situations.
guidance: Examiners should check whether a foreign-filed application claims priority under the Paris Convention based on the Korean application. For PCT-based filings filed claiming priority, a request for expedited examination shall be recognized except for PCT self-designation applications; priority claim can be determined using PCT Form PCT/RO/105. Converted applications, divisional applications, or applications with domestic priority filed based on the treaty-priority-forming application are NOT eligible for expedited examination as they are not the application forming the basis of the treaty priority claim (example provided). For PCT self-designation where a PCT application designates the Republic of Korea, the prior-filed Korean application may be deemed withdrawn after 1 year and 3 months; therefore a request for expedited examination on the prior-filed application will not be recognized. If a prior-filed request was filed, the examiner shall order correction indicating the ground for rejection; if self-designation is not withdrawn within the designated period, the examiner shall dismiss the request.

name: Claimed invention being practiced or to be practiced by applicant — subject and evidentiary standards
description: Criteria and evidential requirements for expedited-examination requests where the claimed invention is being practiced or prepared to be practiced by the applicant (including special statutory categories: parts/materials-specialized companies, government-supported competition awardees, component/material technology development businesses, start-ups, etc.).
guidance: Subjects: includes statutory categories (e.g., parts·materials-specialized companies where the claimed invention relates to that business; inventions awarded in government-hosted open contests/competitions if financially supported by government for commercialization or patent filing). Definitions & standards: 'practicing' is identical to practicing by a person other than the applicant; 'practicing as a business' means running a business — personal/domestic/educational/one-time experimental practice generally do not constitute business practice, unless a one-time non-profit practice is carried out as business for public interest. Determination procedures: requester must explain that the invention is being practiced or prepared to be practiced as a business in the written expedited-examination explanation and submit evidential documents. Examiner recognizes practicing/preparation where the explanation and evidential documents confirm the practice. Types of admissible evidence for practicing (or preparing) include written explanation, photos of prototypes, catalogs, product manuals, samples. For practicing-as-business recognition, admissible evidential documents include examples such as business license, transaction sheets indicating the product matches claimed invention, delivery confirmation, purchase contracts, product supply agreements, plant registration certificates, investment records, loan issuance, agreements related to practicing (subject, period, place, condition), lease-rental agreements, evidential documents on component/material technology development business, and other evidence. Special case for construction-field new-technology accreditation: record document management number and concerned art in request form; field-applicability or test data and relevant KAIA webpage references may suffice to deem practiced. Identicalness requirement: the invention being practiced (or prepared to be practiced) must be identical to the claimed invention; requester must prove identicalness via articles, photographs, or other evidential documents plus written explanation; if identity cannot be confirmed, examiner shall order correction.

name: Recognition of applications filed by companies confirmed as component & material technology development businesses
description: Special recognition rules for companies confirmed as component & material technology development businesses.
guidance: A request for expedited examination by a company so confirmed is accepted as being practiced or prepared to be practiced as a business without submission of the general evidential documents listed above. Relevancy between parts·materials-specialized business and the claimed invention is determined based on proving documents (business license, etc.) enclosed in the expedited request form and, if necessary, by referring to the Korea Institute for Advancement of Technology network. If relevancy cannot be checked/confirmed, examiner shall propose supplement. Joint-filing rules apply (if one applicant is such a company, accept) but acceptance when company name and applicant name differ follows the venture-company rules (4.6) mutatis mutandis. Timing requirement: at least one of filing date/request date/determination date the company must hold the confirmation. Documentary proof: original confirmation required, copy acceptable if identical.

name: Slander/libel by denying title (first inventor) actionable if malicious
description: Statements derogatory to the title of the patentee as the first and true inventor are slanders/libels for which a remedy may be obtained when made by persons having no claim to the invention and when malicious and causing special damage.
guidance: Rival inventors who claim the invention must act in good faith (e.g., promptly apply for a patent) or lose the excuse for public attack; moderation in language is required.

name: Infringement only of the invention claimed and described
description: The invention whose manufacture, use, or sale constitutes infringement is the invention covered and protected by the patent; the patent protects only the patentable subject-matter which it specifically claims.
guidance: A device not covered by the patent does not infringe even if it effects the same purpose; elements not described or only partially disclosed in the patent (though indispensable) are not susceptible of infringement.

name: Identity determined by same tests as novelty
description: The identity of the invention made, used, or sold by the alleged infringer with that described and claimed in the patent is determined by the same tests applied in ascertaining novelty when comparing with prior art.
guidance: Novelty and infringement are distinct but related; expert evidence and precedents guide the comparison.

name: Claims must be considered 'as a whole'
description: The § 101 inquiry must focus on the claims as a whole rather than abstracting to a high-level concept not reflected in the claim language.
guidance: Do not frame the 'abstract idea' at an overbroad level of generality untethered from the actual claim limitations; follow Diehr and Parker v. Flook in examining the claim language and its specific limitations.

name: Inventive concept requirement: 'significantly more' than the abstract idea
description: To survive § 101 step two, claims must recite an 'inventive concept' — something more than the abstract idea that ensures the claimed invention in practice amounts to significantly more.
guidance: An inventive concept cannot be merely the application of the abstract idea using 'well-understood, routine, conventional' activity. Courts should look for technical improvements, specific arrangements, or other limitations that convert an abstract idea into a patent-eligible application.

name: 'Well-understood, routine, conventional' determinations are factual
description: Whether elements of a claim are 'well-understood, routine, or conventional' is often a question of fact that can turn on the record.
guidance: Per Cellspin, Berkheimer, and related authority, factual disputes about conventionality should normally be resolved on the merits (not on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion). If a plaintiff pleads plausible factual allegations that particular implementations were not conventional, the court must accept those allegations at the pleading stage.

name: Specifications are not admissions that claim elements are conventional
description: Patent specifications are drafted for § 112 written-description/enablement purposes and should not be treated as admissions that claimed components were 'conventional' or 'well-understood.'
guidance: Courts should not use boilerplate or explanatory language in the specification as conclusive evidence that claimed components are conventional; such reliance risks conflating § 112/§101/§102 analyses.

name: Machine-or-transformation test as a 'useful and important clue'
description: The machine-or-transformation test is a relevant indicator for determining patent eligibility.
guidance: While not dispositive, presence of a claimed machine or transformation (e.g., Diehr/Bilski guidance) supports eligibility analysis and helps distinguish patentable inventions from abstract ideas.

name: Avoid high-level abstract-idea characterizations untethered to claims
description: Courts should not invalidate claims by characterizing them at an overly high level of abstraction (e.g., 'collecting, analyzing, manipulating, and displaying data') when the claims recite specific apparatus features and operations.
guidance: The 'abstract idea' formulation must be tied to the claim language; inventors may claim concrete interfaces or operations (like icons tied to specific operations) that are not equivalent to mere data-display abstractions.

name: Pleadings standard on §101 motions — specific, plausible factual allegations required
description: On a Rule 12(b)(6) motion, plaintiffs must allege specific, plausible factual allegations about inventive concepts or non-conventional implementations to survive dismissal.
guidance: Courts must accept well-pled factual allegations and not dismiss as merely conclusory statements that claim elements are inventive; quoting claims/spec may be insufficient without context showing non-conventional implementation (Cellspin, Aatrix, Am. Bankers).

name: Limit invalidity rulings to asserted claims rather than entire patents
description: When adjudicating eligibility, courts should confine invalidity determinations to the specific asserted claims rather than invalidating entire patents wholesale.
guidance: The petition criticizes the Claims Court for applying its § 101 ruling to the entirety of the patents rather than to particular asserted independent claims; best practice is to cabin rulings to the claims at issue.

name: Recite Elements with Reference Numbers (in the spec)
description: In the specification, every element of every claim should appear with a reference number that links to a figure.
guidance: This makes claim construction easier and reduces 112 indefiniteness risk.

name: Use Dependent Claims Strategically
description: Draft dependent claims to meaningfully narrow by independently useful dimensions.
guidance: Dependent claims should narrow on dimensions that are independently meaningful: a different material, a different range, a different mode of operation. Do not waste dependent claims on trivial restatements.

name: Do not use Negative Limitations Without Spec Support
description: Negative claim limitations (e.g., "free of X") require explicit specification disclosure of absence of X.
guidance: "Wherein the device is free of X" requires explicit spec disclosure that X is absent. Otherwise, 112(a) written description failure.

name: Do not use "Whereby" Clauses to Distinguish Prior Art
description: Avoid relying on whereby/result clauses to provide limiting features for patentability/distinction.
guidance: Whereby clauses are usually held non-limiting (they describe results). If you need a feature to distinguish prior art, recite it positively in the body of the claim.

name: Do not use the Word "Means" Without Intent
description: Using "means for X" invokes means-plus-function treatment under 35 U.S.C. §112(f) (formerly 112 ¶6).
guidance: If you write "means for X," you have invoked 112(f) and the claim is limited to the corresponding structure in the spec, plus equivalents. Use intentionally or not at all.

name: Do not use Trademarks as Claim Terms
description: Avoid trademarks or brand names as claim language because their meaning/scope can change over time.
guidance: Trademarks change scope as products change. "An iPhone" today does not mean an iPhone in 2030. Use the generic technical term.

name: Statute of limitations for disciplinary enforcement (28 U.S.C. § 2462)
description: A five-year federal statute of limitations applies to actions enforcing civil fines or penalties; an action must be commenced within five years from when the claim first accrued.
guidance: A claim accrues when factual and legal prerequisites for filing suit are in place. The decision finds one alleged dishonored check from July 2002 time-barred while later checks were within the five-year period.

name: Claim construction standard: broadest reasonable interpretation
description: A claim in an unexpired patent shall be given its broadest reasonable construction in light of the specification in which it appears.
guidance: Section 42.300(b) and related: consistent with 35 U.S.C. 326 and longstanding USPTO practice (e.g., Yamamoto). Justifications include ability to amend claims, preponderance standard, absence of presumption of validity, and consistency across merged proceedings.

name: Required contents of a petition (precise relief and specificity)
description: The petition must identify each claim being challenged, the specific grounds on which each claim is challenged, how the claims are to be construed, why the claims as construed are unpatentable, and the exhibit numbers and portions of evidence relied upon.
guidance: Section 42.304(b) and 35 U.S.C. 322(a)(3)-(4). Purpose is to provide an efficient means to identify legal and factual bases supporting a prima facie case and to give the patent owner notice.

name: Timing and authorization for motions to amend
description: Patent owners must seek authorization to file a motion to amend claims after a patent owner response; late motions may be denied to preserve ability to complete the proceeding within the one-year period.
guidance: Sections 42.121 and 42.221 require authorization so Board can determine proper scheduling and possibly deny late motions that would impede timely completion.

name: Grouping of claims in petitions
description: Petitioners may group claims where the basis for alleged unpatentability of grouped claims is the same, but must provide sufficient notice as to the merits of the challenge for each claim so challenged.
guidance: Grouping is permitted, but the petition still must provide specific reasoning and evidence tying the ground to each claim in the group.

name: Specificity and evidentiary sufficiency in petitions
description: Petition must set forth a full statement of the reasons for the relief requested, including a detailed explanation of the significance of the evidence, specify where each claim element is found in prior art, and provide specific citations to the evidence; corroborating evidence must be included if necessary.
guidance: Sections 41.22(a)(3), 41.104, and 41.204 require detail sufficient to meet statutory grounds for unpatentability and to establish a prima facie case; where corroboration is necessary (e.g., on-sale/public use), include it with the petition.

name: Claim construction uniformity across merged proceedings
description: A single claim construction standard (broadest reasonable interpretation) must be used throughout a proceeding reviewing patentability, including any new or amended claims and claims from merged proceedings (reexamination, reissue, derivation).
guidance: Avoids inconsistencies and inefficiencies; historical USPTO and Federal Circuit practice supports broadest reasonable interpretation in Office patentability proceedings.

name: Apportionment required when a gross license covers multiple patents/claims
description: If a gross license fee covers more than one invention or many patents, and the defendant infringes only some claims or one claim, the license fee is not a proper measure of damages unless it can be fairly apportioned to the infringed claim(s).
guidance: Where the license cannot be shown to have been paid for the specific claim in question, the royalty may be irrelevant and nominal damages only may be recoverable. Examples: cases where rescinded contracts or whole-machine licenses were not usable without proof of proportionate value.

name: Necessity of proving causal link for price reduction or lost sales
description: Loss by reduction of prices or reduction of sales must be proved to be due solely or to a definite extent to the defendant's infringement; conjecture is insufficient.
guidance: If the plaintiff had begun reducing prices before the infringement, or multiple causes could explain the decline, the claimed loss must be specifically attributed to the defendant's acts (see Comely v. Marckwald).

name: Claim of foreign priority entitlement
description: Clarify when the examiner considers the subject matter of a foreign priority document for determining whether an applicant is entitled to a claim of priority.
guidance: Updated to clarify the circumstances under which subject matter in a foreign priority document may be considered for entitlement to a priority claim (see Chapter 200 changes).

name: Treatment of multiple dependent claims
description: Clarified treatment of multiple dependent claims and instruction to treat each version separately in Office actions.
guidance: Added guidance and cross references (MPEP § 608.01(n)); cites Nested Bean decision; clarifies that each version of a multiple dependent claim is treated separately for Office actions and fee determinations.

name: Substantive patentability doctrines (inventorship, claim interpretation, 35 U.S.C. 102/103/112)
description: Updated case law and guidance on inventorship, claim interpretation, anticipation under 35 U.S.C. 102, obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103, written description, enablement, and definiteness requirements under 35 U.S.C. 112.
guidance: Chapter 2100 updated to include recent case law and to clarify prior art exceptions under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) and updated enablement guidance consistent with Amgen v. Sanofi.

name: Examination of written arguments (with or without amendment)
description: Where a written argument is submitted along with an amendment, an examiner shall review both the argument and the amendment in depth and determine as to whether the notified grounds for rejection can be overcome or not. Also, where only a written argument is submitted without an amendment, an examiner shall consider sufficiently an argument to determine as to the notified grounds for rejection can be overcome or not.
guidance: A written argument or other documents including experiment results in response to the notification of the grounds for rejection shall not be a part of the specification. However, as these documents are submitted to clarify or verify matters in the detailed description, an examiner may refer to them to decide patentability.
