If an applicant insists matters to be amended in a written argument but fails to submit an amendment, the examination shall be made on the detailed description and claims as notified; where insisted amendments and actual amendments differ, examination is based on the actual amendments.

name: Final specification determination after multiple amendments
description: The final specification to be examined shall be determined automatically through the Patent Net after reflecting amendment to the detailed description, claims and drawings. An amendment to the full text of the specification shall be replaced as the final specification to be examined.
guidance: When multiple written amendments are submitted, the final specification is determined as a combination of the most recent (final) amended elements per part (detailed description, each claim, drawings). Example provided showing how 1st and 2nd amendments combine per-element to form the 2nd amended specification.

name: Request and use of documents/samples for examination
description: If considered necessary to expedite examination, an examiner may ask an applicant to submit documents and other reference materials required for examination.
guidance: Requested documents include: related documents and translations for international applications and other offices' outcomes; a claim-to-description mapping by paragraph; a statement explaining relations among claims for voluminous applications; a written summary/gist when subject matter is too complex; samples or experimental results where effects cannot be verified otherwise (to confirm sufficiency); statements explaining derivation of formulas, definitions and meanings of technical terms; clarification of applicants' claims in arguments when hard to understand. Requests must be specific, made under examiner's name, and fall within the period for submission of written arguments. Documents are only reference material and cannot substitute or supplement the specification. Examiners must keep lists, store and return documents with care; if applicant fails to respond, examiner shall not invalidate the application procedure. Evidential documents that are periodicals or published copies may be used as prior art without further evidence; other documents may be used as prior art only if the examiner is confident of the facts without further evidence.

name: Admitting or dismissing amendments in response to final notification of grounds for rejection
description: Unlike non-final notifications, when receiving an amendment in response to the final grounds for rejection, an examiner shall determine whether to dismiss the amendment before assessing patentability. If issuance of the final notification is inappropriate, the examiner shall admit the amendment. Where the final grounds are appropriate and amendment fails to meet amendment scope under Article 47(2) and (3) or generates new grounds for rejection (except certain deletions), the amendment shall be dismissed.
guidance: If no amendment is made or amendment limited to response to final notification (e.g., just reducing claim) and final notification was inappropriate (should have been non-final), the examiner shall notify grounds again instead of rejecting. If applicant treats a final as non-final and submits amendments as non-final, examiner may decide to reject. When multiple amendments are submitted within the written-argument period, examiner determines admission in reverse order of submission. Examples (Ex1–Ex5) illustrate what constitutes a 'new ground for rejection' generated by amendment and cases where deletions are admitted despite causing downstream deficiencies.

name: Status of claims (37 CFR 41.37(c)(1)(iii))
description: A statement of the status of all the claims in the application or patent under reexamination; for each claim appellant must state whether it is canceled, allowed or confirmed, rejected, withdrawn, objected to, etc.; each claim on appeal must be identified.
guidance: This avoids confusion as to which claims are on appeal and the precise wording of those claims, particularly where claims were amended after final rejection.

name: Summary of claimed subject matter (37 CFR 41.37(c)(1)(v))
description: A concise explanation of the subject matter defined in each of the independent claims involved in the appeal, which must refer to the specification by page and line number, and to the drawing, if any, by reference characters.
guidance: For each independent claim and each dependent claim argued separately, every means-plus-function and step-plus-function element (35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph) must be identified and the corresponding structure, material, or acts in the specification set forth with page/line and drawing references. Failure to provide this summary will result in Office notice to amend the brief.

name: Grounds of rejection to be reviewed on appeal (37 CFR 41.37(c)(1)(vi))
description: A concise statement of each ground of rejection presented for review; the statement must be specific (e.g., 'unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. 103 over Smith in view of Jones'), and must not include argument.
guidance: A statement such as 'Whether claims 1 and 2 are unpatentable' is insufficient. Do not include arguments here; arguments belong in the Argument section. Each ground must be separately stated under its own heading.

name: Argument (37 CFR 41.37(c)(1)(vii))
description: The appellant's contentions with respect to each ground of rejection presented and the basis for those contentions, including citations of authorities, statutes, and parts of the record relied on.
guidance: Simply pointing out what a claim recites is not an argument for patentability. 'Any arguments or authorities not included in the brief or reply brief filed pursuant to § 41.41 will be refused consideration by the Board, unless good cause is shown.' Arguments made first at oral hearing are not normally entitled to consideration. A supplemental paper is allowed only if new, relevant authority becomes available after filing. Each ground of rejection must be treated under a separate heading; claims may be argued separately or grouped, but grouping can waive argument for individual claims. Best practice: include a subheading for each claim you want separately considered.

name: Timely filed brief referred to examiner and possible examiner actions
description: A timely filed brief will be referred to the examiner for consideration and preparation of an examiner's answer if the brief is proper and the application is not allowable.
guidance: The examiner's answer may withdraw the rejection of claims, and may determine that it is necessary to reopen prosecution to enter a new ground of rejection (see MPEP § 1207.04).

name: When 35 U.S.C. 112(f) applies (invocation trigger)
description: Examiners will apply 35 U.S.C. 112(f) to a claim limitation that uses the term 'means' or generic placeholder associated with functional language, unless that term is (1) preceded by a structural modifier, defined in the specification as a particular structure or known by one skilled in the art, that denotes the type of structural device (e.g., 'filters'), or (2) otherwise modified by sufficient structure or material for achieving the claimed function. Similarly, examiners will apply 35 U.S.C. 112(f) to a claim limitation that uses the term 'step for' unless that term is modified by sufficient acts for performing the claimed function.
guidance: Examples and case law: generic placeholders like 'mechanism,' 'element,' 'member' coupled with a function typically invoke 112(f) absent structural meaning (Massachusetts Inst. of Tech., Williamson). A generic placeholder preceded by a structural modifier (e.g., 'detent mechanism') may avoid 112(f) where the modifier denotes a type of structural device understood in the art (Greenberg).

name: How to determine whether a modifier denotes structure
description: To determine whether a word, term, or phrase coupled with a function denotes structure, examiners may check whether: (1) the specification provides a description sufficient to inform one of ordinary skill in the art that the term denotes structure; (2) general and subject matter specific dictionaries provide evidence that the term has achieved recognition as a noun denoting structure; and/or (3) the prior art provides evidence that the term is an art-recognized structure to perform the claimed function.
guidance: This is an evidentiary, fact-based inquiry (Ex parte Rodriguez, precedential). Use specification disclosure, dictionaries, and prior art to assess whether the modifier imparts structural significance.

name: Applicant can rebut presumption of invocation
description: During examination, applicants have the opportunity and the obligation to define their inventions precisely, including whether a claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f). If the term 'means' or 'step' or a generic placeholder is modified by sufficient structure, material or acts for achieving the specified function, the USPTO will consider that presumption has been rebutted and will not apply 35 U.S.C. 112(f) until such modifying language is deleted from the claim limitation.
guidance: Applicants should include structure/material/acts in the claim language or clarify in specification/arguments to rebut the means-plus-function presumption.

name: Element-by-element analysis required
description: It is necessary to decide on an element by element basis whether 35 U.S.C. 112(f) applies. Each claim must be independently reviewed to determine the applicability of 35 U.S.C. 112(f) even where the application contains substantially similar process and apparatus claims.
guidance: Do not infer that a limitation in a claim is governed by 112(f) merely because similar language appears in another claim that invokes 112(f) (O.I. Corp., IMS Technology). Interpret each limitation based on its own language and the specification.

name: Corresponding-structure disclosure requirement
description: The corresponding structure (or material or acts) of a means- (or step-) plus-function limitation must be disclosed in the specification itself in a way that one skilled in the art will understand what structure (or material or acts) will perform the recited function.
guidance: If there is no disclosure of structure, material or acts for performing the recited function, the claim fails to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112(b). Disclosure may be explicit, implicit/inherent, or in drawings if it would have been clear to those skilled in the art (Atmel; Dossel; Vas-Cath). A bare statement that known techniques can be used does not disclose structure (Biomedino).

name: Invocation of 112(f) does not relieve 112(a)/(b) requirements
description: The invocation of 35 U.S.C. 112(f) does not exempt an applicant from compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre-AIA first and second paragraphs). Means-plus-function language can be used in the claims, but the claims must still accurately define the invention and the specification must meet written description and enablement.
guidance: Assess written description and enablement separately; structure disclosure for 112(f) is closely related to written description/enablement issues (Donaldson, In re Knowlton, Aristocrat).

name: Computer-implemented means-plus-function: algorithm disclosure required
description: For a computer-implemented 35 U.S.C. 112(f) claim limitation, the specification must disclose an algorithm for performing the claimed specific computer function, or else the claim is indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b).
guidance: When the disclosed structure is a computer programmed to carry out an algorithm, the disclosed structure is that special-purpose computer programmed to perform the disclosed algorithm, not merely a general purpose computer (Net MoneyIN, In re Aoyama, WMS Gaming, Aristocrat).

name: General purpose computer alone is insufficient (except for basic coextensive functions)
description: The corresponding structure is not simply a general purpose computer by itself but the special purpose computer as programmed to perform the disclosed algorithm. A microprocessor or general purpose computer lends sufficient structure only to basic functions coextensive with a microprocessor (e.g., 'receiving,' 'storing,' 'processing' data). All other computer-implemented functions require disclosure of an algorithm.
guidance: EON Corp. and Katz: a microprocessor suffices only where the claimed function is coextensive with the microprocessor itself. 'Special programming' includes any functionality not coextensive with a general-purpose computer (EON Corp.).

name: Form and sufficiency of an algorithm disclosure
description: An algorithm may be expressed in any understandable terms including as a mathematical formula, in prose, in a flow chart, or in any other manner that provides sufficient structure.
guidance: The sufficiency of the algorithm is determined in view of what one of ordinary skill in the art would understand as sufficient to define the structure and make the boundaries of the claim understandable. The examiner should determine whether one skilled in the art would know how to program the computer to perform the necessary steps (Aristocrat, Finisar, Intel).

name: Multiple functions require disclosure for all functions
description: Where a means-plus-function limitation performs multiple identifiable functions, the specification must disclose adequate corresponding structure (or algorithm) to perform all of the claimed functions.
guidance: If the specification discloses an algorithm that only accomplishes one of multiple functions, the limitation is treated as if no algorithm were disclosed (Noah, Williamson, Media Rights Technologies). Case examples found claims indefinite where structure/algorithm for certain functions (e.g., 'coordinating' or 'diverting a data pathway') were not disclosed.

name: Consequences of failing to disclose corresponding structure/algorithm
description: If the specification explicitly discloses no corresponding algorithm (for computer-implemented limitations) or otherwise fails to disclose corresponding structure/material/acts for the claimed function, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre-AIA second paragraph) is appropriate and the claim may be indefinite.
guidance: Federal Circuit precedent upholds invalidity where no operative algorithm or corresponding structure is disclosed (Advanced Ground Information Systems v. Life360; Blackboard; Media Rights; Noah). The examiner should reject as indefinite when disclosure is lacking.

name: First and further medical use / purpose-limited product claims (Articles 54(4) and (5))
description: Allow purpose-limited product claims for known substances or compositions when used for new medical applications (first and further medical use claims).
guidance: Articles 54(4) and (5) enable claiming new therapeutic uses of known compounds via purpose-limited product claims (e.g., Swiss-type or EPC 2000 second medical use formulations), preserving novelty for new medical indications.

name: Classification of fully identified compounds from general chemical formulae (Step 1)
description: Classification should be given to all 'fully identified' compounds that are novel and unobvious if they are (i) specifically claimed as such or in a composition, (ii) products of a claimed process, or (iii) derivatives of either of these. A compound is considered 'fully identified' where the structure is given by exact chemical name or formula, or can be deduced from its preparation from specified reactants (not more than one of which is selected from a list of alternatives), and the compound is characterised by a physical property or its preparation is described in a worked example giving practical details.
guidance: Do not treat empirically-identified-only compounds as 'fully identified'. Classify all qualifying fully-identified, novel, unobvious compounds into the most specific groups.

name: Classification of searched but unexamined patent documents
description: All claimed subject matter that appears to be novel and unobvious in view of the search results must be classified as invention information along with any novel and unobvious constituents or components of the claimed subject matter. Any unclaimed subject matter that appears novel and unobvious by the search results must also be classified.
guidance: Rely on search results to determine which claim-elements and unclaimed disclosures are treated as invention information.

name: Content of the publication
description: The publication must contain the description, the claims and any drawings as filed, and specify, where possible, the person(s) designated as the inventor(s). It also indicates the designated Contracting States. The publication also contains any new or amended claims filed by the applicant, together with the ARIPO search report and the abstract determined by the Search Division if available before termination of the technical preparations for publication; otherwise the abstract filed by the applicant is published.
guidance: When the time limit for paying designation fees is still running the publication shows as designated all States party to the Harare Protocol on the date the application was filed; definitive designations (paid) are announced later in the Register and Journal. If a request for correction of errors is allowed it must be incorporated in the publication; if a correction decision is pending on items third parties might take at face value (e.g. priority claims), this must be mentioned on the front page, as must requests for correction and any communication received from the applicant. Further data may be included at the Director General's discretion. The publication may not contain any designation of States finally deemed withdrawn or withdrawn by the applicant before technical preparations for publication end. Originals are used where they meet physical requirements; otherwise amended/replacement documents that meet physical requirements are used. Prohibited material is omitted and the place/number of words or drawings omitted is indicated. Sequence listings filed on date of filing are published as part of the description; those filed later are published as an annex.

name: Scope and completeness of the search
description: The ARIPO search is essentially a thorough, high‑quality, all‑embracing search but 100% completeness cannot always be obtained. The search should be carried out to reduce to a minimum the possibility of failing to discover complete anticipations for any claims or other highly relevant prior art.
guidance: Accept lower recall for less relevant prior art; use examiner judgement and available facilities to approximate the scope of an International search. Consult PCT‑specified documentation and use available resources efficiently while aiming to find highly relevant anticipations.

name: Basis for the search (claims as starting point)
description: The search should be made on the basis of the claims, with due regard to the description and drawings. The claims determine the extent of the protection which will be conferred if a patent is granted.
guidance: Analyse claims to identify the subject‑matter to be searched but consult description/drawings for essential features and examples; include features indicated in the description as essential even if not literally in the claims.

name: Interpretation of claims for the search
description: The search should not be restricted to the literal wording of the claims, nor broadened to include everything derivable by a person skilled in the art from the description. It should be directed to essential features and take into account changes in the objective technical problem occurring during the search; consider well‑known equivalents to claim features.
guidance: Searchers should balance literal and purposive interpretation: include equivalents and commonly known variants that may undermine inventive step, but avoid undue enlargement beyond what is supported. Claims referencing description parts (allowed only where 'absolutely necessary') should still be searched if technical features are unambiguously defined there.

name: Exclusion of abandoned claims from the search
description: For ARIPO applications, claims that are deemed to have been abandoned for non‑payment of fees must be excluded from the search. This applies to directly‑filed ARIPO applications and supplementary ARIPO searches for ARIPO‑PCT applications entering the ARIPO phase.
guidance: Verify fee payment status and exclude abandoned claims from search scope. If a claim has been abandoned but later restored, confirm timelines and whether a supplementary search is required.

name: Anticipation of possible amendments to claims during search
description: Insofar as possible and reasonable, the search should cover the entire subject‑matter to which the claims are directed or to which they might reasonably be expected to be directed after amendment (e.g., include detailed embodiments shown in description even if claims are functional only).
guidance: When claims are functional or broad but the description contains detailed non‑trivial examples, include those examples in the search. Aim to anticipate reasonable claim amendments that applicants may make and search accordingly, within reason and resource limits.

name: Handling of unduly broad or speculative claims (Rule 7(1))
description: No special search effort need be made for searching unduly wide or speculative claims beyond the extent to which they relate to matter sufficiently disclosed in the application and supported by the description.
guidance: Do not extend the search to unrelated fields merely because of broad wording unless it's probable such an extended search could produce documents enabling a reasonable objection for lack of novelty/inventive step. If the disclosure is too deficient to enable a meaningful search over the whole claimed scope consider an incomplete search or declaration taking place of a search report.

name: Search for combinations and sub‑combinations of elements
description: For claims characterized by a combination of elements the search should be directed towards the combination; when searching the sections for this purpose, sub‑combinations and individual elements should be searched in those sections at the same time. Additional sections for sub‑combinations/individual elements should be searched only if necessary to establish novelty for assessing inventive step of the combination.
guidance: Search both the full combination and relevant sub‑combinations in the initial sections consulted; only expand to other units if needed to determine novelty/inventive step. Ensure documentation of which sub‑combinations were considered and why further search was or was not necessary.

name: Inclusion of different claim categories in the search
description: When the application contains claims of different categories, all these must be included in the search. However, if a product claim clearly seems both new and non‑obvious, the examiner should make no special effort to search claims for a process which inevitably results in manufacture of that product or for use of the product. When an application contains only one category it may be desirable to include others in the search.
guidance: Include product/process/use claims as appropriate but use pragmatic judgment: e.g., starting products in chemical process claims may be assumed part of the prior art and need not be searched unless indicated otherwise. Document scope decisions in the search report.

name: Procedure prior to searching — analysis of the application
description: When taking up an application to be searched the examiner should first consider the application to determine the subject of the claimed invention: make a critical analysis of the claims in light of the description and drawings to identify the problem, the inventive concept, essential features to the solution, and results and effects obtained.
guidance: Include technical features not in claims if description indicates they are essential; identify search keywords, classification units and strategy based on this analysis. Use this analysis to prioritize sections and resources for the search.

name: Re-issue available only to correct inadvertence, accident, or mistake (not to add new invention)
description: The statutes authorize the Commissioner to amend a defective patent by re-issuing it in corrected form, but prohibit exercising that power to introduce any new invention or to cure defects that were originally intentional or fraudulent; re-issue is permitted only where the defect arose from inadvertence, accident, or mistake and without fraudulent or deceptive intent.
guidance: Practical test: (1) original patent must be inoperative or invalid due to defective/insufficient specification or because patentee claimed more than entitled to; (2) the error must have arisen by inadvertence/accident/mistake; (3) correction must not introduce new matter or a new invention; (4) no fraudulent/deceptive intent. Cases: Giant Powder Co. v. California Vigorit Powder Co.; Flower v. Rayner; Whitely v. Swayne.

name: Fraud (actual or constructive) in procurement invalidates re-issue
description: If a re-issue was procured by actual fraud, corrupt collusion between applicant and Commissioner, or by constructive fraud (e.g., extending claims deceptively beyond the original invention to take advantage of others), the re-issued patent will be held invalid.
guidance: Distinguish actual fraud (collusion, corrupt procurement) from constructive fraud (deceptive extension beyond original scope). Where fraud is alleged, courts may require a direct proceeding (often an equity bill) to impeach the re-issue. Cases and commentary: Swift v. Whisen; Ball v. Langles; Jordan v. Dobson; authorities showing courts invalidate patents procured by fraud.

name: Distinction between utility (35 U.S.C. 101) and enablement (35 U.S.C. 112(a))
description: The requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) as to how to use the invention is different from the utility requirement of 35 U.S.C. 101: 101 requires some specific, substantial, and credible use; 112(a) requires an indication of how the use can be carried out.
guidance: Rejections based on lack of utility (101) should be imposed separately from enablement (112(a)) rejections when grounds differ. If a claim is nonuseful or inoperative (101), it necessarily fails the how-to-use aspect of enablement and both rejections should be made. Examiners should not maintain a 112(a) rejection grounded on lack of utility unless a proper 101 rejection exists.

name: Enablement must be commensurate in scope with the claims (use Wands factors)
description: All questions of enablement are evaluated against the claimed subject matter; examiners will use the Wands factors to ascertain whether the amount of experimentation required to enable the full scope of the claimed invention is reasonable.
guidance: First determine exactly what subject matter is encompassed by each claim (claims construed as a whole, dependent claims incorporate limitations). Examiner should identify any claimed subject matter not enabled and explain why, applying the Wands factors and citing unresolved questions that raise doubt. Enabling disclosure may be by specific example or broad terminology; the specification must teach how to make and use the full scope without undue experimentation (Amgen v. Sanofi, McRO, Wyeth & Cordis, Enzo Life Sciences, Idenix, In re Wright, In re Buchner).

name: Ranges and genus claims require reasonable enablement across claimed scope
description: When a range is claimed, there must be reasonable enablement of the scope of the range; a specification that warns against higher values within a claimed range suggests those values may not work.
guidance: Evaluate whether the disclosure reasonably enables the claimed range or genus. Case examples: AK Steel, Sanofi-Aventisub, In re Fisher, Amgen v. Chugai (EPO analogs), In re Goodman, In re Vaeck, Pac. Biosciences v. Oxford Nanopore. Broad claims that lack adequate disclosure for many embodiments may be rejected for lack of enablement.

name: Single means claim vulnerability to enablement rejection
description: A single means claim (means-plus-function recitation not in combination with another recited element) is subject to an enablement rejection if it covers every conceivable means for achieving the stated purpose while the specification discloses at most only those means known to the inventor.
guidance: Apply In re Hyatt: if the claim covers all conceivable means but specification discloses few, rejection is appropriate. Similarly, claims reciting only a property/result that cover every structure accomplishing it may be nonenabling.

name: Handling inoperative embodiments within claim scope
description: The presence of inoperative embodiments within the scope of a claim does not necessarily render the claim nonenabled; the standard is whether a skilled person could determine which embodiments would be inoperative or operative with no more effort than is normally required in the art.
guidance: Prophetic examples do not per se make disclosure nonenabling (Atlas Powder). However, where claims encompass significant numbers of inoperative embodiments and the specification fails to identify operable embodiments, requiring undue experimentation to find operable ones, a 112(a) enablement rejection is appropriate (Atlas Powder, In re Cook, In re Angstadt).

name: Unclaimed feature taught as critical -> enablement rejection
description: A feature which is taught as critical in a specification and is not recited in the claims should result in a rejection under the enablement provision of 35 U.S.C. 112.
guidance: Determine criticality by considering the entire disclosure; merely 'preferred' features are not 'critical' (In re Goffe). Only make such a rejection when the specification's language makes clear the limitation is critical for the invention to function. Broad language in the disclosure tends to rebut criticality.

name: Best mode requirement — two-prong test
description: The specification shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor of carrying out the invention; compliance requires (1) a subjective inquiry whether the inventor possessed a best mode at filing, and (2) an objective inquiry whether the written description disclosed the best mode so a person skilled in the art could practice it.
guidance: All applicants must disclose the best mode contemplated for the claimed subject matter even if the inventor is not the discoverer. Failure to disclose the best mode need not be active concealment. Case references: In re Nelson, Eli Lilly v. Barr, Benger Labs. Note: AIA (post-September 16, 2011) amended 35 U.S.C. 282 so failure to disclose best mode is not a defense to invalidate a patent, but the USPTO still examines best mode during prosecution.

name: Best mode and enablement are separate requirements
description: The best mode provision of 35 U.S.C. 112 is a separate and distinct requirement from the enablement requirement (35 U.S.C. 112(a)).
guidance: Failure to set forth any mode at all is effectively a nonenablement issue, but best mode focuses on concealing a preferred way to practice the claimed invention. See In re Newton and related authorities.

name: Substantive Requirement for Domestic Priority (basis of claim)
description: A domestic priority claim can be made based on the invention disclosed in the specification or drawing(s) originally attached to the prior-filed application; inventions disclosed other than in the claims can be the basis of the claim.
guidance: The prior-filed application shall be neither a divisional application nor a converted application. The prior-filed application must not have been invalidated, withdrawn or abandoned, nor a decision to grant a patent or utility model registration become final and binding at the time of filing the later application. If the prior-filed application was withdrawn/abandoned on the filing date of the later application, the priority claim is deemed valid if clearly made earlier than the invalidation time.

name: Effect of Domestic Priority Claim (retroactive filing date for identical inventions)
description: For inventions identical with those disclosed in the specification or drawings of the prior-filed application, the later-filed application is deemed to have been filed at the time of filing the prior-filed application when applying certain statutory provisions.
guidance: Specifically affects application of: Article 29(1),(2) Novelty and Inventive Step; Article 29(3) main sentence (enlarged concept of novelty); Article 30(1) (exception to public disclosure); Article 36(1)-(3) (first-to-file rules); Article 96(1)(3); Article 98; Article 103 (prior use non-exclusive license); Article 105(1),(2); Article 129 (presumption of process); Article 136(5) (trial for correction).

name: Prior-filed application deemed withdrawn after 1 year 3 months
description: The prior-filed application to which priority is claimed is deemed withdrawn when one year and three months have elapsed from its filing date, subject to exceptions.
guidance: Exceptions include where the prior-filed application has been abandoned, invalidated, or withdrawn, or where a decision to grant or a trial decision to reject has become final and conclusive, or where the priority claim based on the prior-filed application has been withdrawn. For multiple prior-filed applications, withdrawn status is determined per application from each filing date, not simultaneously.

name: Amendment/Additions to Domestic Priority Claim (timing and eligible persons)
description: An applicant may amend or add the domestic priority claim within one year and four months from the filing date of the prior-filed application (earliest filing date if multiple prior-filed applications exist).
guidance: Only the applicant who fulfilled Article 55(1) and made the priority claim at filing can amend/add. Applications that may be added must meet Article 55(1) requirements: (①) prior filed within one year before later filing; ② prior not divisional/converted; ③ prior not invalidated/withdrawn/abandoned and no final grant decision; ④ applicants identical; ⑤ priority-related items clearly written. The time to determine requirement ① is at filing of later application; requirements ③ and ④ are judged at time of amendment. Priority claims based on theoretical or unspecified third-party applications are inherently invalid and cannot be added.

name: Scope of amendment to priority claim and limits after deadlines
description: Within one year and four months from the prior-filed filing date, amendment can include whole or partial withdrawal of priority claims in multiple claims, correction of clerical errors, and adding priority claims.
guidance: Priority claim cannot be withdrawn once one year and three months have elapsed (Article 56(2)). After one year and four months only clerical-error corrections are permitted, similar to Treaty-based priority amendments. When adding a domestic application to multiple priority claims, the relevant earliest filing date rule applies.

name: Formality Examination of Domestic Priority Claim
description: Upon submission of an application claiming domestic priority or a written amendment, the examiner shall examine the formalities of the priority claim based on the specification and written amendment.
guidance: If errors in formality are found, the examiner requests amendment; if irregularities persist the examiner invalidates the procedure for the domestic priority claim. The formality examination covers all requirements of the domestic priority claim except unity of invention. The scope allowed for amendment may change depending on whether one year and four months has elapsed from the prior-filed filing date.

name: Formalities when international application enters national phase claiming domestic priority
description: When an international application claiming priority based on a domestic application enters the national phase (or designating only Korea), the examiner shall determine if the prior-filed application was pending at the time of the formality examination, since such a priority is deemed domestic.
guidance: If the prior-filed application was invalidated, withdrawn, abandoned, or a decision to grant became final at the filing date of the international application, the examiner shall request amendment; if not remedied the priority claim shall be invalidated.

name: Clear articulation of reasons supporting obviousness
description: A key to supporting any rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 is the clear articulation of the reasons why the claimed invention would have been obvious.
guidance: Provide facts and reasoning in accordance with Examination Guidelines for Determining Obviousness; merely including conclusory statements in an Office action is insufficient to establish a prima facie case and to shift the burden to Applicant.

name: Combining prior art elements using known methods to yield predictable results
description: All claimed elements were known in the prior art and one skilled in the art could have combined the elements as claimed by known methods with no change in their respective functions and the combination would have yielded predictable results.
guidance: Findings required: 1) Prior art included each claimed element (not necessarily in a single reference); 2) One of ordinary skill could have combined the elements by known methods and each element would perform the same function as separate; 3) One of ordinary skill would have recognized the results of the combination were predictable.

name: Simple substitution of one known element for another
description: The claim would have been obvious because the substitution of one known element for another would have yielded predictable results to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention.
guidance: Findings: 1) Prior art contained a device/method differing from the claimed invention by substitution of components; 2) The substituted components and their functions were known in the art; 3) One of ordinary skill could have substituted one known element for another and the results would have been predictable. Note: no motivation as to why to swap is needed. Caution: combining elements is not sufficient if results would not have been predictable.

name: Known work in one field prompting predictable variations in same or different field (market/design incentives)
description: The claim would have been obvious because design incentives or market forces provided a reason to make an adaptation and the invention resulted from applying prior knowledge in a predictable manner.
guidance: Findings: 1) Prior art scope included a similar or analogous device (same or different field); 2) Design incentives or market forces would have prompted adaptation; 3) Differences between the claimed invention and prior art were encompassed in known variations or known principles; 4) One of ordinary skill, in view of incentives/forces, could have implemented the variation and it would have been predictable. Evidence of market forces should be made of record; if notoriously well-known, Official Notice may be taken.

name: Map claim limitations to pertinent sections of prior art
description: Examiner is to map all the claim limitations to the pertinent sections of the prior art references.
guidance: When drafting a rejection, explicitly indicate which portions of each reference disclose each claim limitation; slides illustrate mapping but do not provide a full exposition of the rejection.

name: Proofread rejections for internal consistency and completeness
description: Proof read your rejections after writing them to verify that the claims recited in the statement of rejection matches the claims discussed in the body of the rejection, that the references cited to reject dependent claims include all of the references applied to reject any claims from which they depend, and that your overall action is clear and concise.
guidance: Check for matching claim numbers, complete application of references to dependent claims, and clarity in the overall action. Ensure factual support and mapping are present.

name: Corporate-officer authorization under 37 C.F.R. § 11.14(e)(3) is fact-specific
description: A claim that a practitioner acted as a designated corporate officer (and thus was authorized to file) requires evidence that the practitioner in fact acted in that corporate capacity; mere designation or later claim does not automatically legitimize filings.
guidance: TMEP guidance (e.g., §§ 611.02, 611.06(d)) may interpret § 11.14(e)(3), but a party alleging corporate-officer practice must demonstrate through record evidence that filings were made in the officer role; an asserted automatic cloak of authority without supporting legal authority is rejected.

name: Waiver and suspension of rules — correct statutory/regulatory provision
description: Petitions to waive regulations must invoke the correct provision: § 1.183 applies only to Part 1 regulations (patent practice); Part 11 regulations (practitioners) are not waivable under § 1.183; petitions to waive Part 11 rules must identify the regulation and show extraordinary circumstances under § 11.3 if applicable.
guidance: Citing a nonexistent or inapplicable waiver provision is fatal. For disciplinary/regulatory waivers in Part 11, the petitioner must identify the specific regulations to be waived and demonstrate the extraordinary situation required by § 11.3; unsupported claims of innocence or political motivation are insufficient.

name: Sufficiency of pleading patent infringement
description: A plaintiff is 'not required to plead infringement on an element-by-element basis'—a complaint need only place the accused infringer on notice of what activity is being accused of infringement.
guidance: Detailed infringement theory and claim charts that provide fair notice will survive a motion to dismiss, particularly for simpler technologies. Courts should not resolve contested factual disputes about operational roles on a motion to dismiss.

name: Claim construction at the Rule 12(b)(6) stage
description: A district court may construe claims when deciding a motion to dismiss if the construction is based solely on intrinsic evidence; this is 'proper and routine' and is not procedurally erroneous even if done without a separate Markman proceeding.
guidance: Courts have wide latitude in how they conduct claim construction; relying on intrinsic evidence alone to interpret claim scope at 12(b)(6) is permissible and reviewed de novo.

name: Interpreting plural terms and 'group' language
description: Plural terms (like 'group' or plural nouns) are presumptive indicators but not dispositive that multiple items are required; the meaning may be 'one or more' depending on context and specification.
guidance: Claim interpretation must go beyond ordinary/commonsense meaning where appropriate—consider specification, prosecution history, and extrinsic evidence; do not assume 'group' requires 'two or more' without deeper analysis.

name: When specification/'present invention' language limits claims
description: If a specification consistently describes an aspect (e.g., 'pre-fetching' advertisements) as part of the 'present invention,' that language can support a limiting claim construction tying the claim term to that aspect.
guidance: Examine whether the written description uniformly associates the claimed term with a particular feature and consult prosecution history (e.g., applicant statements) that may confirm a limiting meaning.

name: Do not read exemplary embodiments into claims ('for example' is non-limiting)
description: Language in the specification that presents an embodiment 'for example' indicates that the embodiment is exemplary and should not be read as a required limitation into the claims.
guidance: Avoid importing specific location, structure, or other embodiment details (e.g., requiring colocation at a cable-TV head-end) unless the claim language or clear intrinsic evidence mandates such a limitation.

name: Printed matter doctrine two-step test
description: First determine whether the limitation is directed to printed matter (i.e., claims the content/information being communicated). Second, if it is printed matter, determine whether the informational content has a functional or structural relationship to the substrate such that it should be given patentable weight.
guidance: The act of communication or the fact that information exists is not itself 'content'—claims to 'encrypted communications' or 'program code' without claiming particular content may not be 'printed matter.' Apply the two-step test before denying patentable weight.

name: Avoid importing narrow technical limitations absent supporting claim language
description: Do not narrow a claim term to a particular technical implementation (e.g., 'back channel' limited to 'fixed band of frequencies or time slots') when nothing in the claim language requires that limitation and the specification shows broader embodiments.
guidance: If the specification describes both fixed and dynamic embodiments, the exemplified (fixed) embodiment is not a constraint unless the claim unambiguously requires it; avoid construing each subphrase in isolation if dependent on a rejected construction.

name: PTAB implicit claim construction principle
description: If the outcome of the Board's analysis effectively establishes the scope and boundaries of a claim term, the Board has construed the claim—even if it says it did not 'engage in claim construction.'
guidance: Appellate review will treat such determinations as claim construction and assess whether the Board's implicit construction is legally correct based on claim language and intrinsic evidence.

name: Capability-to-infringe / 'reasonably capable' standard
description: An accused device may be found to infringe if it is 'reasonably capable' of satisfying the claim limitations; a product that is 'readily configurable to infringe' can meet the capability standard.
guidance: But the patentee must prove the capability with evidence that alleged infringing functionality is accessible to customers (not only to manufacturer technicians or experts), and show actual configurability—not mere testimony that someone 'could have' configured it without proof that customers can or did.

name: Induced infringement pleading standard (knowledge + affirmative inducement)
description: To state a claim for induced infringement, a patent owner must plausibly allege (1) direct infringement by a third party and (2) that the alleged infringer affirmatively induced that infringement with knowledge that the induced acts constituted patent infringement.
guidance: Market communications (press releases, websites, labeling) combined with contextual facts (e.g., describing the product as 'generic' to a brand whose majority sales are for the patented use) can support a plausible claim of inducement even where a skinny-label/carve-out exists; clarity and consistency in a generic manufacturer's communications are important to avoid inducement liability.

name: Doctrine of equivalents (DOE) evidentiary sufficiency
description: A jury verdict finding infringement under the doctrine of equivalents can be set aside if the evidentiary record is inadequate to support equivalence for the point of novelty.
guidance: Court must assess whether evidence supports that the accused product performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result for the claimed point of novelty; insufficient evidence permits judgment as a matter of law of noninfringement.

name: Interpreting claim modifiers such as 'single'
description: Modifiers like 'single' in a claim (e.g., 'identifying a single biomolecule') should be given their ordinary meaning in context and can require capability to perform the claimed function on one item alone (i.e., examine one molecule by itself rather than an ensemble).
guidance: The specification's emphasis on the modifier can confirm that inclusion of a word like 'single' was intended to require that specific capability; look to specification and ordinary meaning to resolve disputes.

name: Joint research agreement exception under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(c)
description: To treat subject matter disclosed by another as commonly owned (and thus not available as prior art under 102(a)(2)), three conditions must be met: (1) the subject matter disclosed was developed and the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of one or more parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the effective filing date; (2) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (3) the application for patent discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement.
guidance: A 'joint research agreement' is defined as a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement between two or more persons or entities for experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention (35 U.S.C. 100(h)). To invoke the exception, applicant must provide a signed statement asserting the facts (on or beginning on a separate sheet and signed per 37 CFR 1.33(b)), amend the application to include the parties' names (37 CFR 1.71(g)), and pay any required processing fee (37 CFR 1.17(i)) unless the amendment is timely per 1.17(g)(2). The Office will not request corroborating evidence absent independent evidence raising doubt about the agreement's existence or nature.

name: Presumption of common ownership for joint inventors and applicant duties
description: When an application names joint inventors, the examiner presumes that the subject matter of claims was commonly owned at the time inventions were effectively filed absent evidence to the contrary.
guidance: Applicant is advised (and obligated under 37 CFR 1.56) to point out the inventor and effective filing dates of any claim that was not commonly owned at the time a later invention was effectively filed so the examiner can consider 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C). Use this paragraph in all applications with joint inventors unless claims clearly limit to a single invention.

name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 103 — timing and application of obviousness
description: Under AIA 35 U.S.C. 103, obviousness is determined as of the effective filing date of the claimed invention (rather than as of the date the claimed invention was made). AIA 103 requires consideration of 'the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art.'
guidance: Practically, pre-AIA obviousness practice largely continues to apply, but examiners must use the effective filing date as the relevant date. Non-enabling disclosures are still prior art 'for all they teach' for purposes of obviousness under 103. Examiners should follow MPEP § 2141 et seq. and USPTO patent examination guidance when formulating obviousness rationales. Use specified form paragraphs (e.g., 7.20.aia and related paragraphs) where required (first actions on the merits and final rejections).

name: Definiteness / Indefiniteness (35 U.S.C §112(b))
description: Patent claims define the scope of protection for an invention. If there are ambiguities in a claim, it is rejected by the patent office. In the US, this is referred to as indefiniteness (35 U.S.C § 112(b)) and is among the most frequent reasons for patent application rejection.
guidance: Claims must avoid ambiguity; meeting the definiteness requirement under 35 U.S.C. §112(b) is essential to prevent rejection. Use examiner reasons for indefiniteness as the operative legal/administrative standard.

name: Dataset design: domain restriction and scale
description: PEDANTIC is a novel dataset of 14k US patent claims from patent applications relating to Natural Language Processing (NLP), annotated with reasons for indefiniteness.
guidance: Curate datasets with clear scope (e.g., domain-limited to NLP-related claims) and sufficient scale (thousands of examples) to support model training and evaluation; document selection criteria and domain focus.

name: Identifying functional language
description: A claim limitation is functional when it recites a feature by what it does rather than by what it is.
guidance: Functional language can appear in limitations that invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f) and in limitations that do not invoke §112(f). Limitations that do not invoke §112(f) are typically recited with some structure, material or action to define a capability or purpose. Consider whether the phrase describes a feature by its operation/result instead of structural identity. See MPEP 2111 and 2181 and related training modules.

name: Three-prong §112(f) analysis (invoke §112(f)?)
description: Use the three-prong analysis in MPEP 2181 to determine whether the claim limitation invokes §112(f).
guidance: Prong A: does the limitation recite “means” or a generic placeholder for means? (e.g., 'module' may be a generic placeholder). Prong B: is the generic placeholder modified by functional language? Prong C: is the limitation lacking sufficient structure, material, or acts for performing the claimed function? If Prongs A–C are met, §112(f) applies. Examples: 'color translation module' can be a generic placeholder invoking §112(f) when coupled with functional language; 'aesthetic correction circuitry' may not be a generic placeholder if the specification defines it as a specific circuit.

name: BRI when §112(f) is invoked
description: When §112(f) is invoked, the BRI of the 'means-plus-function' limitation is restricted to the corresponding structure in the supporting disclosure, and its equivalents.
guidance: The corresponding specification disclosure that identifies and links the structure, material or act to the claimed function is considered part of the claim limitation for construction. A reference must disclose the corresponding structure or its equivalent to anticipate the claim. See MPEP and training modules on BRI and §112(f).

name: BRI when §112(f) is not invoked
description: When §112(f) is not invoked and an element is recited along with a function, that element is construed as being capable of performing the function; i.e., the BRI of that element is limited by the function.
guidance: Distinguish between a recited function that limits claim scope and an intended use/result that does not impose structural limits. If the recited structure already performs the function, the functional phrase may simply reflect an intended result and not further limit scope (see examples where boundaries are clear). Record the BRI as necessary.

name: Distinguish function versus intended use/result
description: There is a distinction between reciting a function compared to reciting an intended use or result.
guidance: A functional limitation can provide a patentable distinction by imposing limits on the function of a structure/material/action. Typically no patentable distinction is made by an intended use or result unless the use/result imposes some structural or manipulative difference on the recited structure or action. Use this distinction when construing claim scope and when deciding whether the functional phrase limits the claim.

name: Does functional language limit claim scope (anticipation requirement)?
description: Determine whether the functional language limits the claim scope — i.e., must a prior art reference disclose this functional limitation to anticipate the claim?
guidance: If the limitation imposes a functional requirement not satisfied by simply meeting recited structure, then a prior art reference must disclose that function (or an inherent function) to anticipate. If the structure recited in the claim necessarily performs the function, the functional language may not impose an additional limit (and structural prior art may anticipate regardless of explicit disclosure of the function). Examples discussed in the worksheet illustrate both outcomes.

name: Definiteness of functional language under 35 U.S.C. 112(b)
description: The boundaries imposed by a functional limitation must be clearly defined to be definite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b); language that merely states a result without providing boundaries is indefinite.
guidance: Consider whether one of ordinary skill in the art can determine what structure/material/act in the claim performs the function; whether the limitation has well defined boundaries or only expresses a problem/result; and what an anticipatory reference would need to disclose to satisfy the limitation. If boundaries are not reasonably clear, reject under §112(b), identify the specific indefinite language, explain why, and, when possible, suggest resolution. See MPEP 2173.02, 2173.05(g), 2181, 2182.

name: Adequacy of corresponding structure for 'means'-type §112(f) limitations
description: For 'means'-type claims, the specification must adequately disclose a corresponding structure/material/act that performs the recited function.
guidance: Adequate disclosure requires that (a) the corresponding structure/material is disclosed so OOSK will understand what specific structure is identified to perform the recited function; (b) it is sufficient to perform the entire recited function; and (c) it is clearly linked to the function in the written description. If any element is missing, §112(f) limitation may be indefinite or improperly supported.

name: Examiner action when functional language is indefinite
description: When the examiner determines that the boundaries of a claim are not reasonably clear, a rejection under §112(b) should be made.
guidance: The rejection must identify the specific indefinite claim language and explain why it renders the claim unclear. The examiner should, when possible, suggest how the indefiniteness may be resolved (e.g., amend to specify structure). Under compact prosecution principles, also consider other applicable rejections (§101, §102, §103, §112(a)). Sample rejection language is provided in the worksheet.

name: Relationship between §112(b) indefiniteness and §112(a) written description
description: Functional claim language found indefinite typically lacks an adequate written description under §112(a).
guidance: An indefinite, unbounded functional limitation would cover all ways of performing a function and indicate insufficient disclosure to show possession of the invention. Thus, a §112(b) rejection based on functional indefiniteness should often be accompanied by a §112(a) written description rejection.

name: Prior art (102/103) implications of functional language
description: Functional claim language that is not limited to a specific structure covers all devices capable of performing the recited function; prior art may anticipate or render obvious depending on disclosure or inherent capabilities.
guidance: If the prior art explicitly discloses the function or a structure that performs the function (same means, equivalent means, or different means that accomplishes the function inherently), anticipation may be appropriate. For §112(f) limitations, the prior art must disclose the corresponding structure or an equivalent to anticipate; non-equivalent structures may render the claim obvious. Examiners must state how they are interpreting the functional term with respect to the applied prior art.

name: Record-keeping and making the BRI clear
description: It is best practice to make the record clear during prosecution by explaining the BRI of claim terms, including any functional language.
guidance: When functional language is interpreted (either as means-plus-function or as structural element capable of performing a function), explain the interpretation on the record and how it affects rejections. This includes stating the BRI when applying prior art and documenting assumptions used for compact prosecution.

name: Suggested claim amendments to resolve indefiniteness
description: When functional language is indefinite, applicant can resolve issues by amending the claim to specify how the function is performed, provided support exists in the specification.
guidance: Examples: specify a particular structure such as 'aesthetic correction circuitry' that performs the function; specify circuitry that modifies signals based on user input; or add disclosed algorithms or structural details from the specification. Amendments should be supported by the specification so that BRI and definiteness are clarified.

name: Procedural guidance: examine each claim individually and early
description: Every claim must be examined individually based on the particular elements recited therein; separate worksheet for each claim; use of worksheet is optional.
guidance: Under compact prosecution, each claim should be examined for compliance with every statutory requirement for patentability in the initial review. When functional claim language is found indefinite, make appropriate rejections and consider accompanying rejections (e.g., §112(a)), and address how the functional term is interpreted relative to the applied prior art.

name: Statutory basis: 35 U.S.C. 101
description: Patent eligibility in the United States is statutorily defined by 35 U.S.C. 101; this section of the law outlines the basic criteria for patentable subject matter.
guidance: Use 35 U.S.C. 101 as the foundational statute when assessing whether claimed subject matter falls within the scope of patent-eligible inventions.

name: Statutory categories of patentable subject matter
description: Congress deemed four categories of invention to be the appropriate subject matter of a patent—process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter.
guidance: Claims should be analyzed to determine whether they fall within one of these four statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter).

name: Statutory category check (Step 1)
description: Determine whether the claim recites a statutory category of invention (process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter).
guidance: Step 1: YES if the claim is directed to a statutory category (examples: method/process claims, systems/machines, non-transitory computer-readable media as a manufacture). The examples treat method, system, and non-transitory medium claims as satisfying Step 1 when properly characterized (e.g., a non-transitory computer-readable medium is a manufacture).

name: Judicial exception identification (Step 2A)
description: Decide whether the claim is 'directed to' a judicial exception such as an abstract idea, mathematical relationship, or method of organizing human activity.
guidance: Identify whether the claimed subject matter recites concepts similar to those courts have found abstract (e.g., fundamental economic practices, methods of organizing human activity, mathematical relationships, an idea itself). If the claim is directed to such a judicial exception, proceed to Step 2B. If the examiner does not identify an abstract idea recited in the claim, the claim should be deemed not directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: NO).

name: Significantly more / inventive concept (Step 2B)
description: If the claim is directed to a judicial exception, determine whether additional claim elements, individually or as an ordered combination, amount to significantly more than the exception (i.e., provide an inventive concept).
guidance: Evaluate whether limitations add meaningful practical application beyond the abstract idea. Generic computer implementation typically does not supply 'significantly more.' However, limitations that improve computer functionality or another technological field (e.g., improved memory use, faster computation, improved signal acquisition) can supply significantly more. Consider both individual elements and their ordered combination (examples: RCT blue-noise mask, SiRF GPS).

name: Generic computer components are insufficient
description: Recitations of generic computer components (CPU, memory, display, network, program) performing conventional functions do not by themselves transform an abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter.
guidance: When computer components are recited at a high level of generality and only perform basic functions (storing, retrieving, transmitting, displaying), treat them as insufficient to supply an inventive concept. Examples: claims that merely say 'perform on a computer' or claim CPU/memory/network to do conventional tasks (Planet Bingo, buySAFE, Ultramercial) are ineligible under Step 2B: NO.

name: Improvement to computer/other technology counts as 'significantly more'
description: Limitations that show an improvement in the functioning of the computer itself or an improvement in another technology/technical field can amount to significantly more than the abstract idea.
guidance: Findings of eligibility can rest on showing that the claimed elements yield technological improvements (e.g., reduced memory use, faster computation, improved image quality, enhanced GPS signal-acquisition sensitivity). Use technical fact patterns (blue noise mask halftoning, GPS pseudo-range/server model) to show how the claim improves computer/technical functioning and thus satisfies Step 2B: YES.

name: Rooted in computer technology / internet-centric problem
description: A claimed solution that is necessarily rooted in computer technology to solve a problem specifically arising in the realm of computer networks may not be an abstract idea.
guidance: Distinguish claims that merely apply a business practice on the Internet from those that solve an Internet-specific technical problem (DDR Holdings example). If the claim's limitations are necessarily rooted in computer/internet technology rather than merely implementing a known human/business practice electronically, that favors eligibility (Step 2A: NO or Step 2B: YES depending on context).

name: Ordered-combination analysis
description: Assess claim elements both individually and as an ordered combination to determine whether they together confer significantly more than the judicial exception.
guidance: Even if individual additional elements are generic or insignificant, their particular arrangement or interplay may provide an inventive concept. Examples (RCT, SiRF) analyze the combination of steps/elements and conclude the ordered combination yields improvements that qualify as 'significantly more.'

name: Claims analyzed under broadest reasonable interpretation
description: Claims should be analyzed for eligibility in accordance with their broadest reasonable interpretation during examination.
guidance: Apply the broadest reasonable interpretation to claim language when identifying whether a claim is directed to a judicial exception and when evaluating additional limitations. This affects whether features are considered generic or specific enough to supply 'significantly more.'

name: Limiting an abstract idea to a particular technological environment is insufficient
description: Merely stating 'apply the abstract idea on the Internet' or otherwise limiting the idea to a technological environment does not by itself make the claim patent eligible.
guidance: Court cautions: 'not all claims purporting to address Internet-centric challenges are eligible'—merely implementing an abstract idea in a particular environment is insufficient; additional meaningful limitations showing technical improvement are required (see DDR cautionary language and Ultramercial reasoning).

name: Perform mass-balance/stoichiometric accounting in chemical processes
description: Account for masses in reactions (examples: 100 grains of phosphore absorb 154 grains of air base to form 254 grains of acid; water composition experiments balancing O and H).
guidance: Track and report how much of each substance is consumed and produced; use these balances to deduce composition (e.g., composition of water, formation of acids) and to support nomenclature and theoretical claims.

name: Treat 'elements' as the terminal results of analysis, not speculative simples
description: Regard what are called elements as the last results of analysis ('les derniers résultats que nous en obtenons') rather than hypothesized indivisible molecules; avoid asserting speculative atomic claims.
guidance: Define elements operationally—substances obtained as ultimate products of analysis—and avoid extending beyond experimentally established composition when discussing elemental theory.

name: Two-step Alice/Mayo framework
description: The Court uses a two-step framework: first determine whether the claims are directed to a patent-ineligible concept (e.g., an abstract idea); second, determine whether the claim elements contain an "inventive concept" sufficient to transform the abstract idea into a patent-eligible invention.
guidance: Apply step 1 to identify whether the claim is 'directed to' an abstract idea; if so, apply step 2 to examine whether elements add something significantly more than the abstract idea itself. Both steps are required to resolve § 101 eligibility under Alice.

name: Step 1 — determine if claims are directed to an abstract idea
description: The first step of the eligibility inquiry is to determine whether the claims at issue are directed to a patent-ineligible concept (e.g., an abstract idea).
guidance: Do not restrict 'abstract ideas' only to 'preexisting, fundamental truth[s] that exist in principle apart from any human action'—economic practices like risk hedging or intermediated settlement can be 'abstract ideas.' Use precedent (e.g., Bilski) and analyze whether the claimed concept is a longstanding building block of commerce or technology.

name: Step 2 — look for an 'inventive concept' that transforms the abstract idea
description: If the claims are directed to an abstract idea, assess whether the claim elements, individually or as an ordered combination, contain an 'inventive concept' sufficient to transform the claimed abstract idea into a patent-eligible application.
guidance: Merely stating an abstract idea and adding the words 'apply it' is not enough. Limiting the use of an abstract idea to a particular technical environment is also insufficient absent additional inventive concept. The inquiry focuses on whether the additional elements do more than well-understood, routine, conventional activity.

name: Generic computer implementation does not render an abstract idea patent eligible
description: Implementing an abstract idea on a generic computer does not transform that abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter under § 101.
guidance: A claim that requires a 'substantial and meaningful role for the computer' is not necessarily patent eligible; the Court focuses on the type of use of the computer. If the computer is performing 'well-understood, routine, conventional activit[ies]' previously known to the industry, those computer limitations do not 'transform the abstract idea into a patent-eligible invention.'

name: Recitation of specific or conventional hardware cannot save an otherwise ineligible claim
description: Reciting particular hardware or a system with specific hardware cannot save a claim that is otherwise ineligible where the hardware does not offer a meaningful limitation beyond generally linking the use of the method to a particular technological environment.
guidance: Evaluate whether hardware elements add anything 'meaningful' beyond conventional implementation; mere linking to a technological environment is insufficient under Alice (slip op., at 16).

name: Vulnerability of claim types and software/algorithm novelty
description: Computer-implemented inventions—especially those whose novelty lies in an algorithm implemented through software—remain vulnerable to § 101 attack; method and computer-readable medium claims were found ineligible in Alice, and system claims are not necessarily immune.
guidance: Anticipate that litigation will focus on whether the claimed invention is based on an 'abstract idea' and whether claims contain inventive concept beyond conventional computation. There is a judicial preference for dedicated physical elements over purely software implementations; non-practicing entities' business-model-style patents are particularly at risk.

name: Transfer/appeal practice with P.R.
description: When an appeal is taken from rejection of claims all examinable in the reporting TC and the application is otherwise allowable, formal transfer to that TC should be made for appeal purposes; the receiving TC takes jurisdiction and prepares the examiner’s answer.
guidance: At allowance, the application may issue from that TC with classification determined by the controlling claims.

name: Limitations on use of Patentability Reports
description: P.R. practice is not obligatory and should be used only where it will save total examiner time or improve quality due to specialized knowledge.
guidance: Where claims are directed to the same character of invention but differ in scope only, prosecution by P.R. is never proper. Exemplary situations ordinarily not proper for P.R. include: (A) claims related as manufacturing process and product defined by the process; (B) claims related as product and a process that merely makes the product; (C) claims related as a combination distinguished only by characteristics of a subcombination and that subcombination per se.

name: Nature and goal of examination
description: After reading the application and understanding the claimed invention, a prior art search is made and the application is reviewed with the prior art to determine whether the claims define a useful, novel, nonobvious, and enabled invention clearly described in the specification.
guidance: The goal of examination is to clearly articulate any rejection early in prosecution so the applicant can provide evidence of patentability and reply completely at the earliest opportunity. Examiner then reviews all evidence before issuing next Office action. If information reasonably necessary should be required from the applicant under 37 CFR 1.105, that requirement should generally be made prior to or with the first Office action on the merits.

name: Rejection language and citation of references
description: If the invention is not considered patentable, the claims or those considered unpatentable will be rejected. In rejecting claims for want of novelty or obviousness, the examiner must cite the best references at his or her command.
guidance: When a reference is complex or shows inventions other than that claimed, the particular part relied on must be designated as nearly as practicable. The pertinence of each reference, if not apparent, must be clearly explained and each rejected claim specified.

name: Reliance on admissions and facts known to examiner
description: In rejecting claims the examiner may rely upon admissions by the applicant (or patent owner in reexamination) as to any matter affecting patentability and may rely upon facts within his or her knowledge.
guidance: Admissions in the specification or made during prosecution may be used for anticipation or obviousness determinations regardless of statutory category.

name: Use of subject matter developed by another under 35 U.S.C. 103
description: Subject matter developed by another which qualifies as prior art only under 35 U.S.C. 102(e), (f) or (g) may be used as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 103 unless the entire rights to the subject matter and the claimed invention were commonly owned or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person at the time the claimed invention was made.
guidance: To overcome a 103 rejection based on such subject matter via 35 U.S.C. 103(c)(2), the applicant must provide a statement that the prior art and the claimed invention were made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the date of invention, that the claimed invention was made as a result of activities within the scope of that agreement, and that the application discloses the names of the parties to the joint research agreement. Definitions of 'joint research agreement' are provided.

name: Uniform application of patentability standards
description: Standards of patentability (novelty, usefulness, unobviousness, enablement) must be the same throughout the Office in every art, regardless of whether the art is complex, newly developed, crowded, or competitive.
guidance: An application should not be allowed unless issues pertinent to patentability have been raised and resolved in examination and prosecution. Apply the 'preponderance of the evidence' test: reject a claim if, in view of prior art and evidence of record, it is more likely than not unpatentable. Recitation of detailed features ('picture' claim) is not itself justification for allowance.

name: Handling defects in form or omission of a limitation
description: When patentable subject matter is disclosed but claims cannot be allowed because of defects in form or omission of a limitation, the examiner should not stop with a bare objection/rejection.
guidance: The examiner’s action should be constructive and when possible should offer a definite suggestion for correction.

name: Distinction between rejections and objections
description: A 'rejection' is refusal to grant claims because subject matter is unpatentable (merits); an 'objection' addresses form (e.g., dependency on a rejected claim if dependent claim otherwise allowable).
guidance: Use the term 'rejected' for claims denied on merits. A rejection is subject to review by the Board; objections and formal matters are not decided by the Board and should not be combined in appeals.

name: Prior art rejections should use the best available art
description: Prior art rejections ordinarily should be confined strictly to the best available art; the language used should be unequivocal.
guidance: Exceptions allowed where propriety turns on claim interpretation, a claim is met only in terms by a reference not disclosing inventive concept, or a pertinent reference may be antedated by affidavit/declaration. Such rejections should be backed up by the best other art available and avoid merely cumulative rejections.

name: Reliance on admitted prior art
description: A statement by an applicant in the specification or made during prosecution identifying the work of another as 'prior art' is an admission which can be relied upon for anticipation and obviousness determinations regardless of statutory categories.
guidance: Where the admitted prior art anticipates the claim but does not qualify as prior art under any paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 102, the claim may be rejected as anticipated by the admitted prior art without citing to 35 U.S.C. 102.

name: Distinction between 35 U.S.C. 102 (anticipation) and 103 (obviousness)
description: For anticipation under 35 U.S.C. 102, the reference must teach every aspect of the claimed invention explicitly or implicitly; any feature not directly taught must be inherently present. For 35 U.S.C. 103, the reference teachings must be modified to meet the claims and the modification must have been obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: Keep the distinction in mind when framing rejections; see MPEP §§ 2131–2146 for further guidance on patentability determinations under 102 and 103.

name: Invocation of 35 U.S.C. 112(f) does not exempt other 112 requirements
