description: The invocation of 35 U.S.C. 112(f) does not exempt an applicant from compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (or pre‑AIA first and second paragraphs). Means‑plus‑function language can be used in the claims, but the claims must still accurately define the invention.
guidance: Cases: Donaldson; In re Knowlton. Examiners must ensure written description and definiteness requirements are met even when 112(f) is invoked; a means‑plus‑function limitation cannot avoid those statutory duties.

name: Clearly link/associate disclosed structure to the claimed function
description: The structure disclosed in the written description is corresponding structure only if the specification or prosecution history clearly links or associates that structure to the function recited in the means‑plus‑function limitation.
guidance: Cite: B. Braun; Telcordia. The link is the quid pro quo for employing 112(f). If one skilled in the art cannot identify what structure/material/acts perform the claimed function, a 112(b) rejection is appropriate.

name: Computer‑implemented 112(f) limitations require disclosure of an algorithm
description: For a computer‑implemented 35 U.S.C. 112(f) claim limitation, the specification must disclose an algorithm for performing the claimed specific computer function, or else the claim is indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b).
guidance: Cite: NetMoneyIN; In re Aoyama; WMS Gaming. The disclosed structure for a computer‑implemented function is the special‑purpose computer programmed to perform the disclosed algorithm, not merely a general‑purpose computer alone.

name: General‑purpose computer alone is insufficient except in rare coextensive cases
description: A microprocessor or general purpose computer serves as structure only where the claimed function is coextensive with the microprocessor itself; most computer‑implemented functions require disclosure of an algorithm (special programming).
guidance: Cite: EON Corp.; In re Katz; Ergo Licensing. Examples of functions that may be coextensive: 'receiving', 'storing', 'processing' data. All other computer‑implemented functions require an algorithm disclosure.

name: Algorithm may be expressed in any understandable form
description: An algorithm may be expressed as a mathematical formula, in prose, in a flow chart, or in any other manner that provides sufficient structure.
guidance: Cite: Finisar; Microsoft Computer Dictionary. Source code listing is not required; the algorithm must be a finite sequence of steps that sufficiently describe how to perform the claimed function so a person of ordinary skill can implement it.

name: Sufficiency of algorithm judged by one skilled in the art
description: If the specification explicitly discloses an algorithm, the sufficiency of that disclosure is determined in light of the level of ordinary skill in the art; the examiner should determine whether one skilled in the art would know how to program the computer to perform the necessary steps (enablement and written description).
guidance: Cite: Aristocrat; AllVoice; Intel. If the algorithm disclosure is adequate, it can convert a general purpose microprocessor into a special purpose computer for claim support.

name: Algorithm must cover all claimed functions of a multi‑function limitation
description: When a means‑plus‑function limitation performs multiple identifiable functions, the specification must disclose adequate corresponding structure/algorithm for all of the claimed functions; disclosure for only some functions is treated as if no algorithm were disclosed for the others.
guidance: Cite: Williamson; Noah. Example: 'distributed learning control module' required structure for 'receiving', 'relaying', and 'coordinating' — failure to disclose algorithm for 'coordinating' rendered the limitation indefinite.

name: No reliance on incorporated‑by‑reference or prior art for corresponding structure
description: The corresponding structure/material/acts cannot include any structure disclosed only in material incorporated by reference or in a prior art reference; the specification itself must disclose the structure.
guidance: Cite: Pressure Prods.; Atmel; Default Proof. Office personnel must review the specification without reliance on incorporated documents; merely mentioning prior art references does not give patentable claim to structures in those references.

name: Examiner procedure: determine function then review written description for corresponding structure
description: Once the examiner determines that a claim limitation is a means‑plus‑function limitation invoking 112(f), the examiner should determine the claimed function and then review the written description of the specification (including drawings) to determine whether corresponding structure/material/acts that perform the claimed function are disclosed.
guidance: Drawings, figures, tables, sequence listings may provide the disclosure (Vas‑Cath). If the examiner cannot identify corresponding structure, make a 112(b) rejection and consider a requirement for information under 37 CFR 1.105.

name: Three primary situations warranting 112(b) rejection when 112(f) is invoked
description: A rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (or pre‑AIA 112 second paragraph) may be appropriate when: (1) it is unclear whether a limitation invokes 112(f); (2) 112(f) is invoked and there is no or insufficient disclosure of structure/material/acts; and/or (3) 112(f) is invoked and the supporting disclosure fails to clearly link or associate disclosed structure/material/acts to the claimed function.
guidance: Examiners should document which of the three situations applies. If invocation is ambiguous, consider claim language, specification, and how a skilled artisan would understand the claim in light of the disclosure.

name: Ambiguous claim language requires holistic assessment and opportunity to amend
description: If the 3‑prong analysis for determining whether 112(f) applies is inconclusive because of ambiguous words in the claim, the examiner, after considering the claims, specification, and skilled artisan understanding, should determine whether the claim recites sufficiently definite structure; applicants have opportunity to present arguments or amend claims to clarify applicability of 112(f).
guidance: If applicant disagrees, they may amend or argue during prosecution to clarify whether 112(f) applies; examiners should make a reasoned determination based on the whole record.

name: Means‑plus‑function limitation limits claim to disclosed structure and equivalents (no importing nonrecited functions)
description: If the written description sets forth corresponding structure/material/acts in compliance with 112(b), the claim limitation must be construed to cover that disclosed structure/material/acts and equivalents. Functional limitations not recited in the claim, or structural limitations in the specification unnecessary to perform the claimed function, cannot be imported into the claim.
guidance: Cite: Welker; Wenger. Examiner and courts construe the claim to the disclosed corresponding structure and its equivalents; applicants cannot expand claim scope by importing extra elements from the spec.

name: When 112(b) indefiniteness for lack of corresponding structure exists, written description and enablement concerns follow
description: A means‑plus‑function limitation found indefinite under 112(b) for failure to disclose sufficient corresponding structure will also lack adequate written description under 112(a) and may not be enabled to support the full scope of the claim.
guidance: Examiners should consider whether disclosure contains sufficient information to enable one skilled in the art to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention (see MPEP §§2161.01, 2163.03, 2164.08). Cite: Ariad (genus/species functional claiming concerns).

name: Special guidance on mode of implementation (hardware vs software) for 112(f) limitations
description: By choosing to use a means‑plus‑function limitation and invoke 112(f), the applicant limits that claim limitation to the disclosed structure (implementation by hardware or combination of hardware and software) and equivalents; the examiner should not construe the limitation as covering pure software implementation when the disclosure indicates hardware or hardware/software combination.
guidance: If no corresponding structure is disclosed (i.e., only software per se without an algorithm and corresponding programmed computer), the limitation should be deemed indefinite and rejected under 112(b). However, a claim including such an indefinite limitation is not necessarily directed as a whole to software per se unless it lacks other structural limitations.

name: Claims (Art. 84 and formal requirements)
description: Formal and clarity requirements for claims, and assessment under Article 84 EPC.

name: Examples concerning essential features
description: Illustrative examples to determine which features are essential to the claimed invention.

name: Statutory grounds for reissue (35 U.S.C. 251)
description: Reissue is available 'whenever any patent is, through error without any deceptive intention, deemed wholly or partly inoperative or invalid, by reason of a defective specification or drawing, or by reason of the patentee claiming more or less than he had a right to claim in the patent.'
guidance: Reissue requires surrender of the patent and payment of the fee; no new matter may be introduced; Commissioner may issue multiple reissues for distinct parts; application provisions apply except that assignee may make/swear application if it does not seek to enlarge claims. Reissue enlarging claims must be applied for within two years of grant.

name: What constitutes an 'error' supporting reissue
description: An error arises from conduct during preparation/prosecution of the application that caused the patent to be deemed wholly or partly inoperative or invalid under 35 U.S.C. 251; mere spelling/grammar/typographical/editorial/clerical corrections that do not cause such inoperativeness do not justify reissue.
guidance: Common bases: (A) claims too narrow or too broad; (B) disclosure inaccuracies; (C) failure to or incorrect claiming of foreign priority; (D) failure to reference or incorrect reference to copending applications. Case law examples (e.g., In re Wilder, Ex parte Scudder) illustrate when reissue applies (e.g., attorney's failure to appreciate scope, misjoinder corrections). Some failures (e.g., failure to timely file divisional) are not correctable by reissue.

name: Diligence/timing rule for broadening reissue claims (two-year rule)
description: No reissued patent shall be granted enlarging the scope of the claims of the original patent unless applied for within two years from the grant of the original patent.
guidance: If a broadening reissue is filed within two years, diligence is presumed and the examiner should not normally reject for delay. A filing on the two-year anniversary is considered within two years. See MPEP § 1412.03 for practice on broadening reissue claims.

name: Content required in a reissue application
description: A reissue application must contain the same parts required for an original patent application, complying with all applicable rules, and additionally must satisfy reissue-specific requirements.
guidance: The reissue specification (including claims and drawings) should be the copy of the patent submitted; a reissue oath/declaration complying with 37 CFR 1.63 and 1.175 is required; where patent is assigned, written consent of all assignees and evidence of ownership are required; an offer to surrender the original patent is recommended (required before allowance); priority claims (35 U.S.C. 119/120) and IDS may be filed. Missing parts (oath/fee/assignee consent) may be supplied later under 37 CFR 1.53(f) with surcharge if applicable. Use Box REISSUE for expedited initial filings only.

name: Form of specification in a reissue application (formatting rules)
description: The entire specification and claims of the patent must be included, with matter to be omitted enclosed in square brackets and additions underlined; claims should not be renumbered and numbering of new claims should follow the highest numbered patent claim. No new matter may be introduced.
guidance: Cut-up soft copies of the original patent (single column mounted separately) are recommended for preparing the reissue specification; however, amendments after filing must follow 37 CFR 1.121(b). For twice reissued patents, use double underlining and double bracketing; printed patents may use bold face and double bracketing. Entire words or chemical formulas must be shown as changed — partial-word changes are not permitted. Charts/tables/formulas spanning columns should not be split but provided in entirety and may extend beyond the column width.

name: Reissue claims must be for the same general invention as the original patent
description: Reissue claims must be for the same invention disclosed as being the invention in the original patent; the entire disclosure (not just claims) is considered to determine the patentee's objective intent.
guidance: The proper test is an objective inquiry confined to the intent manifested by the original patent (In re Amos). Reissue claims will satisfy 35 U.S.C. 251 where (A) they are described and enabled by the original specification such that 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph is satisfied, and (B) nothing in the original specification indicates an intent not to claim the subject matter. Explicit statements in the original spec that an embodiment is unsuitable can bar reissue claims to it; mere failure to claim a disclosed embodiment is usually not fatal.

name: Recapture rule (prohibition on recapturing surrendered subject matter)
description: A reissue will not be granted to 'recapture' claimed subject matter that was surrendered in the original prosecution to obtain allowance of the patent.
guidance: Apply the two-step Clement/Mentor test: (1) determine in what aspects the reissue claims are broader than the patent claims (e.g., omission of a limitation), and (2) determine whether those broader aspects relate to subject matter formerly surrendered (look to prosecution history for arguments/changes made to overcome prior art or objections). If limitations omitted were presented/argued/stated to obtain allowance, recapture exists and is impermissible. Examiners must review prosecution history of the original file to determine surrender.

name: Examination standard for reissue applications
description: A reissue application is examined in the same manner as an original application, including review of reissue oath/declaration, claims for broadening or new matter, and issues of fraud/inequitable conduct or duty of disclosure.
guidance: Initial examiner review should inspect for required submissions (oath, assignee consent, proof of ownership). Rejections and actions (including protests, interference considerations, and stays in litigation-related cases) should follow existing examination practice; various form paragraphs (e.g., 14.15–14.22) exist for common deficiencies.

name: Legal definition of novelty
description: An invention is novel if there is no older document or disclosure that alone includes and/or describes all essential features of the invention. Novelty can also hold if aggregation of prior disclosures does not reveal all essential features or experts would not find it obvious to integrate missing features.
guidance: Novelty assessment critically relies on the concept of features (those elements outlined in the patent claims).

name: Features as basis for novelty
description: Features are the elements the invention needs to comprise to be the invention and are outlined in the patent claims (independent claims list essential features). Features can be physical elements, properties, or processing steps; in many jurisdictions features cannot be negative.
guidance: Feature identification must handle synonymy and homonyms; features cannot generally be introduced as negative limitations after filing; later exclusions are limited by the description.

name: Supervised learning for novelty
description: Train classifiers (SVM, Naive Bayes, neural networks, LSTM, GRU, BERT-based) using target claims and relevant prior art to predict novelty; inputs often include target claims and cited prior-art paragraphs.
guidance: Concerns: deep models can be black-box and may not detect novelty via explicit feature comparison. Explainable approaches (e.g., BERT models that output relevant claim sets) can provide supporting evidence and improve trustworthiness.

name: Patentability via feature-combination comparison
description: Decompose patent claims into features and formulate feature combinations; compare the target patent feature combination with prior art to evaluate novelty and non-obviousness following legal definitions.
guidance: Proof-of-concept methods exist but may not scale; limitations include inability to detect homonyms/synonyms; recent LLMs may help improve feature extraction and matching.

name: Litigation prediction inputs and importance
description: Predict whether a patent will cause litigation using multiple inputs: metadata (number of claims, patent type), claim texts, citation-graph features summarizing patent citations, and lawsuit records of companies.
guidance: Empirical findings show metadata has the highest impact on litigation prediction; including lawsuit records and improved representations of patent-company relations can increase precision significantly.

name: Patent valuation task definition
description: Estimate the monetary or strategic value of a single patent, application, or portfolio; the value depends on portfolio context, functionality, scope of claims, dependencies on other patents, and potential for licensing or blocking competitors.
guidance: Valuation can be formulated as regression (predict numeric value) or classification (high-quality vs not, multi-level quality grading).

name: Guidelines 2021 deletion requirement for embodiments not covered by independent claims
description: The 2021 update of the Guidelines for Examination required that embodiments “in the description which are no longer covered by the independent claims must be deleted … unless these embodiments can reasonably be considered to be useful for highlighting specific aspects of the amended claims”, and further that in such case “the fact that an embodiment is not covered by the claims must be prominently stated”.
guidance: This represents an extremely strict approach introduced in 2021 that made minimal amendments insufficient in many cases; the text should be treated as a formal standard applicants and examiners relied on during prosecution. The guidance implies deletion of embodiments not covered by the claims unless they clearly serve to highlight aspects of the amended claims, and if retained they must be prominently labelled as not covered.

name: Board of Appeal T 1989/18 — no legal basis for general requirement to streamline description
description: BoA 3.3.04 found there is no legal basis for the requirement that the description should be streamlined with the claims, and set aside a refusal based solely on the description identifying embodiments as part of the invention that were not part of the invention as defined by the claims.
guidance: The Board examined possible legal bases (Art. 84, Art. 69 EPC, R.42(1)(c), R.48(1)(c)) and rejected them as justifying a general obligation to remove unclaimed subject-matter from the description. Practical takeaway: where claims are clear and supported by the description, the mere presence of additional embodiments in the description does not automatically justify refusal under Art.84 EPC.

name: Article 84 EPC — scope and limitations regarding description amendments
description: Art. 84 EPC requires claims to be clear and to be supported by the description; however, subject-matter in the description that does not appear in the claims is not prohibited and does not necessarily affect clarity of the claims.
guidance: BoA reasoning: clarity of claims is the central requirement; additional unclaimed material in the description does not per se render claims unclear. When assessing whether amendments to the description are required, focus on whether the extra description impairs understanding of the technical problem/solution or clarity/support of the claims.

name: Article 69 EPC and Rules 42(1)(c), 48(1)(c) EPC are not a general justification for deleting description matter
description: BoA held Art.69 EPC is irrelevant to amendments to the description because it concerns claim construction rather than defining the subject-matter for protection. R.42(1)(c) EPC was found satisfied if passages do not impair understanding of the technical problem and solution. R.48(1)(c) EPC aims to prevent publication of matter contrary to morality/public order and cannot be used to require removal of 'unnecessary information'.
guidance: When arguing against examiner objections to description content, practitioners can rely on these limitations in using Art.69, R.42(1)(c) and R.48(1)(c) as legal bases for compulsory deletion; stress whether the contested passages actually impair understanding or offend public order/morality.

name: Claim-like clauses in the description need not be deleted if they do not affect claim clarity (T 1444/20)
description: BoA 3.3.01 in T 1444/20 held there is no reason why the presence of the section 'Specific embodiments of the invention' or 'claim-like clauses' should affect the clarity of the claims; numbered embodiments cannot be mistaken for claims since they are evidently part of the description and not denoted as 'claims'.
guidance: The Board criticized the Guidelines for requiring mandatory removal of claim-like clauses while simultaneously acknowledging they may or may not cause a lack of clarity. Practical implication: do not delete claim-like fallback language from the description automatically — deletion is only justified if the clauses actually result in lack of clarity of the claims.

name: Avoid labelling an embodiment as 'not covered by the claims' — deletion preferred to prevent carving a 'hole' in protection
description: Labelling an embodiment as “not covered by the claims” might carve a “hole” into the scope of protection, the extent of which is difficult to foresee. It may provide a basis to argue that the claimed invention is a selection from described alternatives, with consequences under national law (e.g., German doctrine of equivalents / decision X ZR 76/14).
guidance: Anti-pattern: prominently stating an embodiment is not covered by the claims. Better practice: fully delete such an embodiment from the description if the embodiment is not to fall within the scope. If retained, be aware of possible limiting consequences in infringement proceedings, especially in jurisdictions applying selection-from-alternatives reasoning that may exclude unclaimed alternatives as equivalents.

name: Prior minimal amendment practice (pre-2021) and limited wording options
description: Before 2021, it was often sufficient to supplement the description with statements such as “the invention is defined by the claims” to avoid extensive edits; the 2021 Guidelines made this approach less likely to be sufficient.
guidance: When considering how much to change the description before grant, note historical practices but do not assume they still carry weight. Use minimal clarifying statements cautiously and consider recent case law and examiners' likely expectations.

name: Voluntary cessation doctrine / burden to show conduct will not recur
description: A defendant claiming that its voluntary compliance moots a case 'bears the formidable burden of showing that it is absolutely clear the allegedly wrongful behavior could not reasonably be expected to recur.' (citing Already v. Nike and Friends of the Earth).
guidance: Initial burden on the defendant to demonstrate that the allegedly wrongful conduct cannot reasonably be expected to recur; if defendant meets that burden, the plaintiff must then show it 'engages in or has sufficiently concrete plans to engage in activities not covered by' the defendant’s covenant/disavowal. Example: Nike’s broad covenant satisfied the defendant’s burden because it 'allow[ed] Already to produce all of its existing footwear designs . . . and any ‘colorable imitation’ of those designs.' (Already).

name: Covenant/disavowal must be coextensive with asserted injury
description: A covenant not to sue or a disavowal of appeal only moots a case when it is 'coextensive with the asserted injury' such that it 'encompasse[s] all of its allegedly unlawful conduct' tied to the plaintiff’s asserted injury.
guidance: Evaluate whether the covenant/disavowal covers the full scope of the plaintiff’s claimed injury (e.g., existing products and foreseeable variants). If it is broad enough, the court may find the voluntary cessation test satisfied; if narrow, plaintiff may still show ongoing injury. See Already (covent broad enough) and this case (Cytonome disavowal treated as coextensive with ABS’s asserted injury).

name: Kessler doctrine / preclusion effect of final noninfringement judgment
description: A final district-court judgment of noninfringement gives the accused devices 'a status as noninfringing devices,' barring the patentee from asserting that they infringe the same patent claims a second time (Kessler doctrine as applied in Brain Life, SpeedTrack, MGA).
guidance: Where final judgment in district court determined noninfringement (and claims could have been or were asserted), the patentee is estopped from relitigating infringement against essentially the same products; this reduces the plaintiff’s (patentee’s) ability to threaten renewed suit and thus bears on mootness/standing in related proceedings.

name: Photographs — black and white and color
description: Photographs, including photocopies of photographs, are not ordinarily permitted in utility and design patent applications but will be accepted if photographs are the only practicable medium for illustrating the claimed invention (e.g., electrophoresis gels, blots, autoradiographs, cell cultures, histological tissue cross sections, animals, plants, in vivo imaging, TLC plates, crystalline structures, and ornamental effects in design applications).
guidance: Photographs must be of sufficient quality so that all details are reproducible in the printed patent. If the subject admits illustration by a drawing, the examiner may require a drawing instead. Color photographs will be accepted if the conditions for color drawings and black and white photographs are satisfied (see paragraphs (a)(2) and (b)(1)). Photographs must be developed on paper meeting the sheet-size and margin requirements of the rule (see paragraphs (f) and (g)).

name: Views — general requirements
description: The drawing must contain as many views as necessary to show the invention. The views may be plan, elevation, section, or perspective views. Detail views of portions of elements, on a larger scale if necessary, may also be used.
guidance: All views of the drawing must be grouped together and arranged on the sheet(s) without wasting space, preferably in an upright position, clearly separated from one another, and must not be included in the sheets containing the specifications, claims, or abstract. Views must not be connected by projection lines and must not contain center lines. Waveforms of electrical signals may be connected by dashed lines to show relative timing.

name: Infirmity of proof (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(ii))
description: There was such infirmity of proof establishing the conduct as to give rise to the clear conviction that the Office could not, consistently with its duty, accept as final the conclusion on that subject.
guidance: Practitioner must demonstrate substantial defects in the evidence supporting the state finding. Participation in the state hearing, stipulation to facts, or admissions at the state proceeding strongly undermine a claim of infirmity of proof.

name: Effect of stipulation/admissions and failure to appeal
description: A practitioner's stipulation to the facts, admission of rule violations, and agreement that a public reprimand was appropriate make it particularly difficult to demonstrate a genuine issue of material fact to avoid reciprocal discipline.
guidance: The Final Order emphasizes that admitting facts and agreeing to sanction, and not appealing the state determination, undercuts claims of due process defects, infirmity of proof, or grave injustice.

name: Exceptions where owner does not disclaim (situations preserving later extended term)
description: In making the above disclaimer, the owner does not disclaim the terminal part of the term of any patent granted on the instant application that would extend to the expiration date of the full statutory term of the prior patent ... in the event that said prior patent later: (a) expires for failure to pay a maintenance fee; (b) is held unenforceable; (c) is found invalid by a court of competent jurisdiction; (d) is statutorily disclaimed in whole or terminally disclaimed under 37 CFR 1.321; (e) has all claims canceled by a reexamination certificate; (f) is reissued; or (g) is in any manner terminated prior to the expiration of its full statutory term as presently shortened by any terminal disclaimer.
guidance: List of concrete events that, if they occur to the prior patent, permit the owner NOT to have disclaimed the terminal portion that would correspond to the prior patent's full statutory term. The form requires these exceptions to be explicitly stated.

name: Amendments to the drawing held by the examiner to contain new matter are not entered
description: Amendments to the drawing held by the examiner to contain new matter are not entered until the question of new matter is settled.
guidance: This practice of nonentry because of alleged new matter does not apply to amendments to the specification and claims. See MPEP § 714.16.

name: Amendment not complying with 37 CFR 1.121 is not entered
description: An amendment including changes to the specification/claims which is not in compliance with 37 CFR 1.121 (e.g., one which does not include replacement paragraphs or claim listings) should not be entered.
guidance: See MPEP § 714 for compliance details and required formatting (replacement paragraphs, claim listings).

name: Exception: substitute specification with amendments may be entered in part (deny entry of substitute spec)
description: An 'amendment' presenting an unacceptable substitute specification along with amendatory matter (e.g., amendments to claims or new claims) should be entered in part: the substitute specification should be denied entry and so marked, while the rest of the paper should be entered.
guidance: Applicant should be advised that the substitute specification has not been entered. See 37 CFR 1.125 and MPEP § 608.01(q). Under current practice, proper substitute specifications may be voluntarily filed and will normally be accepted; however, entry after a notice of allowance (37 CFR 1.312) is not a matter of right.

name: Permitted use of 37 CFR 1.131 — antedating references under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)
description: Affidavits/declarations may be used to antedate a reference or activity that qualifies as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a) and not under 35 U.S.C. 102(b), e.g., where the prior art date is less than 1 year prior to applicant's effective filing date (subject to 'same patentable invention' limitations).
guidance: If the prior art reference under 102(a) is a U.S. patent or application publication, the reference may not be antedated if it claims the same patentable invention. See MPEP § 715.05 for 'same patentable invention.'

name: Inappropriate use of 37 CFR 1.131 if reference claims the same patentable invention
description: An affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 is not appropriate where the reference U.S. patent or U.S. patent application publication claims the same patentable invention.
guidance: See MPEP § 715.05 and MPEP Chapter 2300. If reference and application are commonly owned and not patentably distinct, consider terminal disclaimer or 37 CFR 1.130 affidavit to overcome 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection (MPEP § 718).

name: Inappropriate use of 37 CFR 1.131 where double patenting applies
description: An affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 is not appropriate where the reference is a prior U.S. patent to the same entity claiming the same invention (double patenting issue).
guidance: Consider double patenting doctrine and appropriate remedies (terminal disclaimer, etc.).

name: Form paragraph 7.57 — Affidavit/Declaration Under 37 CFR 1.131: Ineffective - Heading
description: Form paragraph to state: 'The [1] filed on [2] under 37 CFR 1.131 has been considered but is ineffective to overcome the [3] reference.'
guidance: Must be followed by one or more of form paragraphs 7.58–7.63 or a paragraph setting forth the proper basis for insufficiency (e.g., failure to establish acts performed in this country, scope not commensurate with claim). Examiner notes indicate bracket insertions and sequencing requirements.

name: Activities applied against the claims can be antedated by 1.131 (if not statutory bar)
description: Unless it is a statutory bar, a rejection based on an activity showing the claimed invention was used or known prior to filing may be overcome by an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 establishing a date of invention prior to the activity; alternatively, a 1.132 affidavit may show the activity was performed by the applicant.
guidance: See MPEP § 715.02 and 715.01(d) for specifics; proper evidentiary showing required.

name: How much of the claimed invention must be shown in a 1.131 affidavit — general rule
description: A 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit or declaration must establish possession of either the whole invention claimed or something falling within the claim (such as a species of a claimed genus), so the claim as a whole reads on it.
guidance: See In re Tanczyn: showing part of a multi-element claim that omits an element may be insufficient. However, if examiner has treated a claim limitation as obvious (in a 103 rejection) and has not cited a reference teaching that limitation, a 1.131 affidavit may be sufficient even if it does not show that particular feature or modification (In re Stryker). Also, an affidavit need not show identical disclosure of the reference if it shows completion commensurate with the extent of the invention claimed (In re Wakefield).

name: Grace Period Inventor Disclosure Exception (AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1)(A))
description: A disclosure that would otherwise qualify as prior art under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) will not be treated as prior art if: (1) the disclosure was made one year or less before the effective filing date of the claimed invention; and (2) the disclosure is by the inventor or a joint inventor.
guidance: Office personnel determine necessary evidence case-by-case depending on whether it is apparent from the disclosure itself or the patent application specification that the disclosure is by the inventor or a joint inventor. If the disclosure (e.g., publication) names the inventor/joint inventor as author/inventor and does not name additional authors/joint inventors and is within one year, it will be treated as a grace period inventor disclosure and not prior art. If the publication names additional persons not named in the application, it may be treated as prior art. Applicants may include a statement designating grace period inventor disclosures in the specification (see 37 CFR 1.77(b)(6) and MPEP § 608.01(a)) and may provide a copy of the disclosure to expedite examination.

name: Intervening Disclosure Exception Focusing on Subject Matter (AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1)(B))
description: A disclosure that would otherwise be prior art under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) may be excepted if the subject matter disclosed in the intervening disclosure had, before such disclosure, been publicly disclosed by the inventor, a joint inventor, or another who obtained the subject matter directly or indirectly from them.
guidance: The exception focuses on the subject matter, not the mode of disclosure; the prior disclosure need not be in the same form or verbatim. The exception may apply only to portions of the intervening disclosure that were previously publicly disclosed (e.g., if prior disclosure included elements A,B,C and intervening shows A,B,C,D, then only D is prior art). Examples: species/genus rules (a prior-disclosed species can render a later-disclosed genus excepted for the genus; converse yields prior art for the species). Determination under 102(b)(1)(B) does not compare subject matter to the claimed invention — that is handled under anticipation/obviousness.

name: Determining 'Effectively Filed' Date Under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(d)
description: For 102(a)(2) purposes, a U.S. patent document is prior art as of either its actual filing date or the filing date of a prior application to which it claims priority/benefit (per 35 U.S.C. 102(d)).
guidance: A U.S. patent document is 'entitled to claim' priority/benefit if it contains the priority/benefit claim, was filed within applicable filing period, and has a common inventor or same applicant. The 102(d) 'effectively filed' concept differs from entitlement to priority under other statutes; examiners need not evaluate whether any claim is actually entitled to priority under §§119/120/121/365/386 when applying a document as prior art under 102(d). See MPEP §2152.01 and MPEP §2136.03 for related discussion.

name: AIA Eliminates Hilmer Doctrine for 102(d)
description: Under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(d), a U.S. patent document that claims priority to prior-filed foreign or international applications is effectively filed as of the earliest such application that describes the subject matter, eliminating the pre-AIA Hilmer doctrine limitation.
guidance: Thus foreign priority dates may be used for a U.S. patent document's effective prior art date under AIA 102(d) if the earlier application describes the subject matter; for applications where AIA changes do not apply, Hilmer may still control. See MPEP §2136 for nuances.

name: Provisional Rejections Under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) for Copending U.S. Applications
description: If an earlier filed, copending, unpublished U.S. patent application discloses subject matter that would anticipate claims in a later-filed application with a different inventive entity, the examiner should determine whether a provisional rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) can be made.
guidance: Provisional rejection is appropriate when an earlier-filed copending application, if published or patented, would be prior art under 102. Such provisional rejections can be overcome in the same manner as 102(a)(2) rejections (see MPEP §2152.06) or by abandoning and refiling a new application containing subject matter of both. Use form paragraph 7.15.01.aia for provisional 102(a)(2) rejections. If copending applications have at least one common inventor/applicant or are commonly assigned and effective filing dates differ, provisional rejection should be made. If there is no common inventor/applicant/assignee and the earlier application is unpublished under 35 U.S.C. 122(a), confidentiality must be maintained and no rejection relying on the unpublished application can be made.

name: Prior Art Exception Under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(B) (Inventor or Inventor-Originated Prior Public Disclosure) for 102(a)(2)
description: A disclosure that would otherwise be prior art under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) may be excepted if the subject matter disclosed had been previously publicly disclosed by the inventor, a joint inventor, or another who obtained the subject matter directly or indirectly from them (102(b)(2)(B)).
guidance: As with 102(b)(1)(B), the exception focuses on subject matter and not mode or verbatim identity of disclosure. The exception may apply only to previously disclosed subject matter (partial exception); genus/species examples apply similarly. Affidavits/declarations may be used to show prior public disclosure by the inventor or originator (see MPEP §§2155.02, 2155.03). Determination under 102(b)(2)(B) does not involve comparison to the claimed invention (anticipation/obviousness is separate).

name: 1952 Act standard: common general knowledge only
description: Under the 1952 Act standard (as applied in Minnesota Mining & Manufacturing Co v Beiersdorf (Australia) Ltd), inventive step may be assessed only against the common general knowledge of the person skilled in the art in Australia; prior publications or products cannot be used unless they are shown to be part of that common general knowledge.
guidance: The claimed invention cannot be invalidated by prior publications unless the publication is proven to be notoriously well-known in Australia. This standard is described as 'very low' in terms of required inventiveness and applies to patents originally filed under the 1952 Act (subject to transitional protections).

name: Mark type selection
description: Click the appropriate circle to indicate the Mark type: Standard Characters, Special Form (Stylized and/or Design), Sound Mark.
guidance: Use 'Standard Characters' for word(s)/letter(s)/punctuation/numbers with no design element and no claim to font style, size or color. If you object to the USPTO-generated image for standard characters, use 'Special Form', attach your own image file and check the box to claim standard characters; the appropriateness of that claim will be determined during examination.

name: Novelty — eight‑pronged anticipation test
description: There is an eight-pronged test to determine whether anticipation occurs in Canada: prior art must (1) give an exact prior description; (2) give directions which will inevitably result in something within the claims; (3) give clear and unmistakable directions; (4) give information equal to that given by the subject patent for practical utility; (5) convey information so a person grappling with the same problem would say 'that gives me what I wish'; (6) give information to a person of ordinary knowledge so he must at once perceive the invention; (7) in absence of explicit directions, teach an 'inevitable result' provable only by experiments; and (8) satisfy all these tests in a single document without making a mosaic.
guidance: Anticipation requires that a single prior disclosure provide all information necessary to produce the claimed invention without inventive skill. The 'no mosaic' principle — you cannot combine multiple prior documents to find anticipation — is emphasized.

name: Excluded subject‑matter (what cannot be patented)
description: Some matters cannot be patented, including 'disembodied ideas, concepts or discoveries', scientific principles and abstract theorems, methods of medical treatment or surgery, higher life forms, forms of energy, features of solely intellectual or aesthetic significance, and printed matter.
guidance: The list of prohibited matters differs from other jurisdictions. The page also notes certain plant matters and medical treatments within the body are excluded; diagnoses based on tests may be patentable. The exclusions must be considered when drafting claims to avoid abstract or non‑statutory subject matter.

name: Requesting priority / earlier filing date (Paris Convention/WTO)
description: A subsequently filed Canadian patent application can request priority back to an earlier-filed foreign or domestic patent application (within applicable time-limits) to obtain an earlier 'effective filing date' for overlapping subject matter.
guidance: The page notes the common 12‑month priority window under the Paris Convention/WTO members; priority can affect novelty and obviousness assessments if properly claimed and supported.

name: Patent infringement — exclusive rights and infringing acts
description: Once patented, exclusive rights are granted to the patent holder (s.42 of the Patent Act). Any interference with the patent holder's 'full enjoyment of the monopoly' can be infringement. Making, constructing, using, or selling a patented invention without permission can constitute infringement. Possession, use in a process, and inducement/procurement may also count as infringement.
guidance: Assess infringement by comparing alleged acts to the patent claims and considering statutory rights. The page emphasizes the broad scope of possible infringing acts (including indirect forms like inducement). Remedies and defences are handled in courts (Federal Court, provincial/territorial courts).

name: Explain office-action response and counsel client choices
description: The patent drafter should explain their draft response to the office action to the client and give the client the opportunity to make choices about claim amendments.
guidance: Clients may better assess business implications of narrowing claims (e.g., whether narrowed protection is still useful or can be designed around). Patent drafters should present amendment options and trade-offs so the client can decide strategy.

name: No new matter principle for amendments
description: When amending the application, a universal rule in most jurisdictions is that no new matter (new subject matter) beyond that originally disclosed as of the filing date may be added (except to remedy obvious mistakes).
guidance: This rule applies to claims, description, and drawings. The purpose is to balance applicants' right to amend with third parties' reliance on the original disclosure and the first-to-file principle. Drafting a complete disclosure pre-filing is therefore paramount.

name: Draft comprehensive original disclosure
description: Prepare an application with sufficiently detailed disclosure of the invention and with a proper set of claims that are a solid foundation for possible amendments later.
guidance: Because examiners may cite prior art unknown at filing, a broad and detailed original disclosure enables permissible narrowing and amendment without introducing new matter.

name: EPO standard: 'directly and unambiguously derivable' test
description: In Europe, matters not directly and unambiguously derivable by those skilled in the art from the original disclosure are considered new matter and cannot be introduced after filing.
guidance: Patent drafters often file extensive multiple dependent claims and explain all possible combinations in the description to satisfy this strict standard at the EPO.

name: Key questions when substantially amending claims
description: When amending the claims substantially and limiting their scope, examiners may pay attention to: (i) unity of invention, (ii) whether amended claims are seriously inconsistent with the description (i.e., requiring description amendment), (iii) whether all amended claims are supported by the description as filed.
guidance: Before submitting substantial claim amendments, evaluate these three issues and prepare corresponding description amendments or justifications to avoid new-matter and consistency objections.

name: Broadening claims and deleting features—jurisdictional constraints
description: Broadening a claim by removing features is permissible in many jurisdictions if no new matter is introduced, but some jurisdictions (e.g., Japan, EPO, China) prohibit deleting features consistently presented as 'essential' because deletion may introduce new technical matter.
guidance: Avoid wording in the description that describes embodiment features as 'essential' or 'indispensable' unless necessary; evaluate local rules before attempting to broaden.

name: Adding new claims during prosecution—rules differ by country
description: Adding a new claim during prosecution is generally allowed if no new matter is introduced, but some jurisdictions have special rules restricting additions (e.g., Japan prohibits claim changes that change the special technical feature after first office action; US limits substantial claim amendments after final office action).
guidance: Check country-specific prohibitions and timing constraints (e.g., US allows only claim deletion, examiner-requested amendments, or amendments that raise no new issue after final action).

name: Getting claims allowed—prepare persuasive, clear responses
description: Respond to the office action with clear, concise, and persuasive arguments why claims are patentable over the cited prior art; provide proposed claim amendments where appropriate.
guidance: Examiners may perform supplemental searches, reinterpret prior art, or issue further office actions if unconvinced. Responses should address the examiner's reasoning and consider the 'broadest reasonable interpretation' of claims in view of prior art.

name: Patent portfolio strategy: offensive and defensive uses
description: Patents can be used offensively (to block, license, or litigate against competitors) or defensively (to protect against infringement suits); owning multiple patents increases bargaining power, enables cross-licensing, and makes design-arounds harder.
guidance: Consider portfolio breadth, claim quality, and complementary patents rather than relying on a single patent. Licensing strategies can start with smaller targets to build momentum rather than immediately targeting large players.

name: Antecedent basis requirement
description: All terms in a claim must be properly introduced before being modified or referenced; claim terms must find clear support or antecedent basis in the specification so that the meaning of the terms may be ascertainable by reference to the specification.
guidance: Ensure every claim term can be traced to an earlier recitation in the claims or to the specification so its meaning is ascertainable. Lack of antecedent basis can create clarity/indefiniteness problems, though absence of identical wording in the specification does not automatically render a term indefinite.

name: Article usage when introducing and referring to elements
description: Use indefinite article 'a' or 'an' when introducing an element for the first time; use definite article 'the' or 'said' when referring back to the introduced element.
guidance: Introduce elements with 'a' or 'an' (e.g., 'a lever') on first recitation; thereafter refer back with 'the', 'said', or 'such'. Consistently follow this convention throughout the claim to show antecedent relationship.

name: Restriction on definite/demonstrative articles prior to introduction
description: The definite articles 'the,' 'said,' and 'such' cannot be used unless the noun has already been introduced in the claim.
guidance: Do not use 'the', 'said', or 'such' to introduce a noun; they are only appropriate when the noun has a prior antecedent recitation in the claim (or in an incorporated claim).

name: Antecedent basis in dependent claims
description: In a dependent claim, the antecedent basis should be present in that dependent claim or any claim upon which that claim is dependent (since a dependent claim incorporates all of the claims from which it depends, by reference).
guidance: When drafting dependent claims, ensure any terms introduced are either present in the dependent claim itself or in the claim(s) it depends from; check the claim dependency chain for proper antecedent support.

name: Antecedent basis vs. identical wording in the specification
description: The mere fact that a term has no antecedent basis in the specification disclosure does not necessarily mean the term is indefinite; there is no requirement that the words in the claim must match those used in the specification disclosure.
guidance: Claims may use different wording than the specification so long as the meaning is ascertainable by reference to the specification; do not assume lack of identical terms in the spec automatically causes indefiniteness—assess whether the claim term has clear support or is reasonably understandable in context.

name: Drafting best practices to avoid antecedent problems
description: Review and reconcile both the specification and claims; first introduction uses 'a'/'an' and later references use 'the'/'said'; avoid implicit antecedence where ambiguous; antecedent problems are typically drafting oversights easily corrected.
guidance: Perform a claims/spec reconciliation pass to locate and fix missing antecedents, eliminate implicit antecedence, add explicit identifiers for repeated elements, and correct article/number usage. Treat antecedent issues as correctable drafting errors before filing or during prosecution.

name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.101 — Competent representation
description: Practitioner shall provide competent representation (37 C.F.R. § 11.101).
guidance: Examples of failing competent representation cited: not informing client of a Notice to File Missing Parts and not responding (leading to abandonment of the application); failing to file claims in an international application and failing to respond to an Invitation to Correct (resulting in no international filing date). The Order ties these failures to lack of competence in performing patent prosecution services (drafting, filing, prosecuting).

name: Continuation filings and claim-drafting risk
description: Continuation applications that reuse the same description and drawings but assert different claims can produce separate patents whose claims may be the same as or obvious variants of claims in the parent or sibling patents.
guidance: Applicants should draft claims across continuations carefully to avoid obtaining multiple patents that claim the same subject matter or obvious variations. Different wording or rearranged claim features can mask similarities and lead to missed double patenting rejections.

name: Ownership, assignment, and common-ownership constraints
description: Terminal disclaimer and some avoidance strategies require common ownership of the later and reference patents; if ownership differs (e.g., patents assigned to different entities or sold), terminal disclaimers may not be effective.
guidance: Situations such as an inventor changing employers or patents being sold can prevent filing an effective terminal disclaimer and allow an earlier patent owned by another to be used to invalidate a later claim for double patenting.

name: Inter-examiner inconsistency and differing terminology can hide double patenting
description: Different examiners (or different claim terminology) across family members can lead to missed obviousness-type double patenting rejections.
guidance: Large application families examined by different examiners may use dissimilar claim language; applicants should be mindful that different wording can obscure substantially similar claim scope and cause problems later in litigation or enforcement.

name: Consideration of equivalents and functional similarity in claim comparisons
description: When comparing claims for double patenting, courts and examiners will consider whether different words describe equivalent or functionally similar features (e.g., 'spring' vs 'rubber band', 'gear' vs 'cog', 'housing' vs 'cabinet').
guidance: Even if one claim recites more detailed elements and another uses broader or different terminology, functional equivalence can lead to a finding of obviousness-type double patenting.

name: Filing date and expiration timing effects
description: Earlier-filed patents may expire earlier and can still be used to invalidate later patents via double patenting; timing of filing and issuance affects availability of remedies like terminal disclaimers.
guidance: In the example, patent C was filed earlier and expired before patents A/B; patent C's existence and expiration timing meant Tempus could not rely on a terminal disclaimer against C (since Tempus did not own C), and C could be used to invalidate the later claim B1.

name: Always consider double patenting during prosecution and enforcement
description: Double patenting raises numerous issues in various factual scenarios and should always be a consideration for a patent applicant, patent owner, or an accused infringer.
guidance: Because double patenting can be subtle and arise from terminology, continuations, ownership changes, or earlier-filed patents, proactive assessment and claim strategy are recommended throughout prosecution and when asserting patents.

name: Rationales supporting obviousness (exemplary list A–G)
description: Exemplary rationales that may support a conclusion of obviousness include several articulated bases.
guidance: List (A) Combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results; (B) Simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results; (C) Use of known technique to improve similar devices (methods, or products) in the same way; (D) Applying a known technique to a known device (method, or product) ready for improvement to yield predictable results; (E) “Obvious to try” – choosing from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions, with a reasonable expectation of success; (F) Known work in one field may prompt predictable variations in same or different field based on design incentives/market forces; (G) Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art that would have led one of ordinary skill to modify or combine teachings to arrive at the claimed invention. See MPEP §2143 and §2144–§2144.09 for examples and additional guidance.

name: Requirement to clearly articulate reasons for a 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection
description: The key to supporting any rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 is the clear articulation of the reason(s) why the claimed invention would have been obvious.
guidance: Obviousness rejections cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements; there must be some articulated reasoning with rational underpinning (KSR citing In re Kahn). The analysis supporting a 103 rejection should be made explicit and the Office action should clearly communicate findings and how conclusions are supported by facts. Office personnel should consider multiple rationales and explicitly state the rationale relied upon.

name: Consideration of applicant's rebuttal evidence (secondary considerations and unexpected results)
description: Office personnel should consider all timely rebuttal evidence when reevaluating any obviousness determination.
guidance: Rebuttal evidence may include 'secondary considerations' such as commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, and evidence of unexpected results (citing Graham). After rebuttal is presented, examiners must reconsider the obviousness determination in view of the entire record and articulate how conclusions change or remain. Examples of applicant evidence for combination claims include: (A) inability to combine by known methods due to technological difficulties; (B) combination elements do not merely perform their separate functions; (C) claimed combination produced unexpected results. See MPEP §2145 and §716–§716.10 regarding affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132.

name: Content of the prior art must be evaluated as of the time the invention was made (avoid hindsight)
description: Content of the prior art is determined at the time the invention was made to avoid impermissible hindsight.
guidance: Decisionmakers must 'cast the mind back' to the time of invention and not use knowledge of the claimed invention to interpret prior art. See MPEP §2145 paragraph X.A. and the cited case law (W.L. Gore v. Garlock). Examiners should avoid hindsight reasoning when articulating rationale for combining references.

name: 35 U.S.C. 103(c) — burden and evidence to show disqualification of certain prior art
description: Applicant seeking benefits of 35 U.S.C. 103(c) must establish that subject matter qualifying as prior art only under 102(e),(f),(g) was owned by or subject to assignment to the same person at the time the invention was made, or that joint research agreement conditions are met.
guidance: Applicant bears the burden to show: (A) claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the invention date; (B) invention resulted from activities within scope of the joint research agreement; (C) application discloses or is amended to disclose names of parties to the agreement. For common ownership evidence and JRAs see MPEP §706.02(l)(2) and related case law (e.g., Ex parte Yoshino, In re Bartfeld).

name: Analogous art requirement for use of a reference in a 103 rejection
description: To rely on a reference under 35 U.S.C. 103, the reference must be analogous prior art to the claimed invention.
guidance: A reference is analogous if (1) it is from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention (even if addressing a different problem), or (2) it is reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor (even if not in the same field). 'Reasonably pertinent' means the reference would have logically commended itself to an inventor's attention in considering his problem. Examiner should consider the problem as reflected in the specification and may include a statement of the examiner's understanding of the problem to support analogy. See Bigio, KSR, In re Icon Health, In re Clay, and In re Klein decisions; see MPEP guidance.

name: Analogous art considerations across different arts (chemical, mechanical, electrical, design examples)
description: Specific considerations and precedent exist for analogy in chemical, mechanical, electrical, and design arts.
guidance: Chemical arts: teachings across carrier/absorbent/dye arts may be pertinent if problem is chemical in nature (Ex parte Bland, Stratoflex, In re Mlot-Fijalkowski). Mechanical arts: broad prior art exploration is often reasonable where similar problems exist (Stevenson; In re Bigio; In re Deminski). Electrical arts: designers look to solutions for analogous problems like rate-limiting (Medtronic). Design arts: a prior design is of the type claimed if it has the same general use; examples and MPEP §1504.03 provide further guidance (In re Rosen, Ex parte Pappas, In re Butera). These precedents illustrate how art-specific facts inform analogy analysis.

name: Differences between prior art and claimed invention — consider the claimed invention as a whole
description: In determining differences between the prior art and the claims, the question under 35 U.S.C. 103 is whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious, not whether the differences themselves would have been obvious.
guidance: Interpret claim language and consider both invention and prior art references as a whole. Case law (Stratoflex, Schenck, In re Hirao) shows that admitted unobvious aspects of a multi-part claim can render the subject matter as a whole nonobvious. Examiners should avoid isolating individual differences and must weigh the combined contribution of claim limitations.

name: Do not distill an invention to a 'gist' or 'thrust' that disregards the 'as a whole' requirement
description: Reducing an invention to a single gist or thrust and ignoring express claim limitations violates the 'as a whole' analysis required under 35 U.S.C. 103.
guidance: Decisions (W.L. Gore; Bausch & Lomb v. Barnes-Hind) demonstrate that focusing on a single conceptual insight while ignoring express limitations can lead to improper obviousness findings. Examiners must analyze all claimed limitations and not treat claims as though they read differently than written.

name: Step 1: statutory category
description: Evaluate Step 1: Does this claim fall within a statutory category?
guidance: If the claim recites a series of steps it is a process (Step 1 = Yes). Example: "The claim recites a series of steps and, therefore, is a process."

name: Step 2A Prong One: identify abstract idea and grouping
description: (a) Identify the specific limitation(s) in the claim that you believe recites an abstract idea; (b) Determine whether the identified limitation(s) falls within at least one of the groupings of abstract ideas enumerated in the 2019 PEG.
guidance: Follow the 2019 PEG groupings (mathematical concepts; mental processes; certain methods of organizing human activity) to categorize the identified limitation. Example: the "encoding" step was identified as reciting mathematical concepts because it explicitly states formulas/calculations.

name: 2019 PEG grouping — Mathematical concepts
description: Mathematical concepts include mathematical relationships, mathematical formulas or equations, and mathematical calculations.
guidance: If a claim step explicitly uses formulas/calculations (e.g., CA = MA^e (mod n)), treat it as a mathematical concept under Step 2A Prong One. The example finds the encoding step recites mathematical concepts because the claim explicitly states the mathematical relation.

name: 2019 PEG grouping — Mental processes
description: Mental processes are concepts performed in the human mind (including an observation, evaluation, judgment, opinion).
guidance: A claim element that, under its broadest reasonable interpretation, can be practically performed in the human mind is a mental process. Mere recitation of generic computer components (e.g., "by the network appliance") does not remove the limitation from the mental processes grouping. Example: a "comparing" step was found to be a mental process because it could be performed mentally absent more specific technological limitations.

name: 2019 PEG grouping — Certain methods of organizing human activity
description: Includes fundamental economic principles or practices (e.g., hedging, insurance, mitigating risk), commercial or legal interactions (contracts, legal obligations, advertising/marketing/sales activities), and managing personal behavior/relationships or interactions between people.
guidance: Use this grouping when the claimed concept is essentially an organizational/human-activity method. The guidance lists these categories for mapping claim limitations under Step 2A Prong One.

name: Step 2A Prong Two: meaningful limit / practical application
description: Evaluate whether additional element(s) or a combination of elements in the claim apply, rely on, or use the judicial exception in a manner that imposes a meaningful limit on the judicial exception, such that it is more than a drafting effort designed to monopolize the exception.
guidance: Look for additional elements or specific combinations that integrate the judicial exception into a practical application or provide a specific technological improvement (e.g., collecting NetFlow data only when abnormal to avoid excess traffic and improve network monitoring). If the claim as a whole integrates the mental process into a practical application, Step 2A = No (not directed to abstract idea).

name: Step 2B: inventive concept / "significantly more"
description: Evaluate Step 2B: Does the claim provide an inventive concept, i.e., does the claim recite additional element(s) or a combination of elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception in the claim?
guidance: Mere instructions to apply an exception on a generic computer cannot provide an inventive concept. Determine whether additional elements are more than well-understood, routine, conventional activity in the field. If not, the claim remains ineligible (Step 2B = No).

name: Recitation of generic computer components is insufficient
description: The mere nominal recitation of a generic computer or network appliance does not take a claim limitation out of a judicial exception (e.g., mental processes) nor does it supply an inventive concept.
guidance: Anti-pattern: adding "by the network appliance" without more specific technical detail still allows the limitation to be performed in the mind or be considered generic automation; does not meaningfully limit or provide 'significantly more.'

name: When a combination of additional elements can make the claim eligible
description: If the combination of additional elements uses the judicial exception in a meaningful way beyond generally linking it to a technological environment, and sufficiently limits the use of the judicial exception to a practical application, the claim may be more than a drafting effort to monopolize the exception.
guidance: Example: the cryptography example — the combination of receiving, transforming, encoding (with explicit mathematical formulas) and transmitting the ciphertext to a computer terminal over a communication channel was found to use mathematical concepts in a specific manner that limits the use of the mathematical concepts to the practical application, supporting eligibility under Step 2A Prong Two.

name: Drafting a rejection for an ineligible claim
description: If a claim is ineligible, the rejection should identify the abstract idea, identify the additional elements and explain why they do not integrate the abstract idea into a practical application, and explain why the additional elements do not provide an inventive concept.
guidance: Include a reference to the appropriate enumerated grouping of abstract ideas. Use the new form paragraphs created for use with the 2019 PEG; a sample rejection is posted on the microsite.

name: Mapping claim limitations to example analyses (exemplar guidance)
description: Use the provided examples to guide mapping of specific claim language to PEG groupings and Prong Two/Step 2B conclusions.
guidance: Examples illustrate subtleties: explicitly recited mathematical relations (encoding) -> mathematical concept; a transformation recited without explicit formulas may not be an abstract idea and may not be performable in the mind; collecting data 'when abnormal' that reduces network load -> specific technical improvement. Use these patterns when analyzing real claims.

name: No amendments after patent expiration (except cancellations)
description: Pursuant to 37 CFR 1.530(j), no amendment may be proposed for entry in an expired patent; if the patent expires during reexamination, all amendments to the claims and all claims added during the proceeding are withdrawn and canceled.
guidance: Carry out withdrawal by placing a diagonal line across all amended/new claims and text added to the specification in the amendment papers; notify patent owner in next Office action that amendments are improper and subsequent reexamination is on unamended patent claims. Examiner should ensure all rejected/objected claims are canceled and may issue examiner's amendment canceling such claims. Only cancellation of original patent claims is permitted in an expired patent; no amendments other than cancellation will be incorporated into the patent by a certificate after expiration.

name: Cancellation of entire claim(s)
description: To cancel an original patent claim, provide an in-writing, direct cancellation of the entire claim.
guidance: Example wording: 'Claim 4. [canceled]' or 'Cancel claim 6.' Ensure cancellation is explicit in amendment papers.

name: Amendment of new claims (must present entire amended text & support)
description: An amendment of a new claim (a claim presented in the reexamination proceeding) must present the entire text of the new claim containing the amendatory material, and it must be underlined throughout the claim; the presentation cannot contain bracketing or other indication of what was in the previous version of the claim.
guidance: Although the amended claim does not indicate what changed from the previous version, the patent owner must point out what is changed in the 'Remarks' portion of the amendment. Per 37 CFR 1.530(e), each change in the claim must be accompanied by an explanation of the support in the disclosure of the patent (the reexamination specification) for the change.

name: Excess claims fees apply for claims added during reexamination
description: Excess claims fees under 35 U.S.C. 41(a)(2) and 37 CFR 1.20(c) apply to excess claims proposed to be added to a patent during reexamination. The independent claims fee applies for each independent claim in excess of three and in excess of the number of independent claims in the patent being reexamined; the total claims fee applies for each claim in excess of twenty and in excess of the number of claims in the patent being reexamined.
guidance: No excess claims fee is due if the amendment only revises existing claims without adding new claims. Examples illustrate combinations of canceled and added claims and when fees apply. Claims disclaimed under 35 U.S.C. 253 or canceled via prior Reexamination Certificate, reissue patent, or Certificate of Correction are not counted in the patent for fee calculations. If fees are not paid when presenting excess claims, a Notice of Defective Paper (PTOL-475) will set a one-month time period to correct the fee deficiency; failure to pay can result in termination of prosecution per 37 CFR 1.550(e).

name: Petition fees for filing petitions in ex parte reexamination
description: A petition in an ex parte reexamination proceeding must be accompanied by the fee set forth in 37 CFR 1.20(c)(6), except for enumerated exceptions (e.g., petitions to extend period for response under 1.530(c), petitions to accept delayed response under 1.550(e), petitions under 1.78 for unintentionally delayed benefit claim, and petitions for correction of inventorship under 1.530(l)).
guidance: Fee amounts (as of cited revision): $1,940 for a large entity, $970 for a small entity, $485 for a micro entity (available for patent owners only). See 37 CFR 1.550(i) for scope of exceptions.

name: Conduct of ex parte reexamination (general procedural rules)
description: After the times for filing the statement and reply expire, reexamination is conducted according to procedures established for initial examination under sections 132 and 133 and will result in issuance of an ex parte reexamination certificate. Reexamination proceedings are to be conducted with special dispatch within the Office. The patent owner may propose any amendment or new claim to distinguish the invention from cited prior art, but no amendment or new claim enlarging the scope of a claim will be permitted.
guidance: A full search will not routinely be made by the examiner. After a third party requester files a request for ex parte reexamination, any document filed by either the patent owner or the requester must be served on the other party per § 1.248; lack of service may result in refusal of consideration. Reexamination proceeds even if notice to patent owner is returned undelivered (notice under 37 CFR 1.11(c) is constructive). Active participation by third party ends with the reply under § 1.535; no further submissions by requester will be acknowledged unless in accordance with §§ 1.510 or 1.535 or were entered prior to the order for reexamination under § 1.525.

name: Written description as a threshold issue
description: Written description may be treated as a threshold issue under § 41.201, narrowed to provoked interferences where applicants copy claims to provoke an interference.
guidance: Written description addresses the problem complementary to repose under 35 U.S.C. 135(b): the claim was timely, but lacks an adequate written description. The provision is narrowed to provoked interferences because of concern applicants would copy claims merely to provoke inter partes administrative challenges. The Office will not examine an applicant’s intent to provoke an interference where the opportunity to have done so is clear; otherwise practice would be open to abuse and misconduct. (Cites Snitzer v. Etzel and policy discussion.)

name: Examiner requirement to add an interfering claim (§41.202(c))
description: An examiner may require an applicant to add an interfering claim; the applicant must either comply by adding the proposed claim (or a better claim) or contest the requirement, with possible consequences for refusal.
guidance: Applicant’s remedy is to comply or to add a better claim or contest. Refusal to copy a supported claim can result in disclaimer (In re Ogiue). §41.202(c) modified to require showings like §41.202(a)(2)–(a)(6) when the interference would be with a patent. Disputes as to satisfaction of procedural requirements may be petitioned.

name: Patentability showing when adding or amending claims/counts (§41.208(c))
description: Whenever a claim or count is added or amended, the movant must show that the claim or count does not run afoul of any known patentability problem; §41.208(c) is limited to this patentability showing requirement.
guidance: Requirement often obliges proving a negative; acceptable alternatives include showing unawareness of a basis for unpatentability. Where prior prosecution or an opponent’s motion raised a patentability question, the movant must address that specific issue. For claims, movant must show where written description can be found (§41.110(c)(2)). For counts, a broadened count must be patentable over prior art so embodiments unpatentable over prior art cannot be used to prove priority.

name: Consolidation and procedural scope of new part 41
description: Major rule changes consolidate ex parte appeals, inter partes reexamination appeals, and patent interference rules into a new part 41, with Subparts for general Board provisions, ex parte appeals, inter partes reexamination appeals, contested cases, and interference-specific practice.
guidance: Notable changes: delegation to Chief Administrative Patent Judge for certain petitions, limited amendments filed after filing a brief, changed format/content of appeal brief, clarified when interference-in-fact exists, clarified claim correspondence and benefit of earlier applications, requirements when adding a claim to provoke an interference, and use of a two-way unpatentability test. These are interpretative/rules of practice and procedure under 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(A).

name: Analysis of claims and orientation of the search
description: Examiners must first determine the subject of the claimed invention by critically analysing the claims in light of the description and drawings; the search is directed to the invention defined by the claims interpreted with due regard to the description and drawings, with emphasis on the inventive concept.
guidance: Follow Chapter 5 guidance on relationship between disclosure and claims; search directed to claims as filed (subject to allowed rectifications).

name: Full coverage principle
description: In principle, and insofar as possible and reasonable, the international search should cover the entire subject matter to which the claims are directed or to which they might reasonably be expected to be directed after amendment.
guidance: Example: functional claims that have detailed examples in the description require the search to include the detailed example; economic reasons may justify some restrictions where claims are broad and many examples exist.

name: Treatment of speculative or unduly wide claims
description: No special search effort need be made for unduly wide or speculative claims beyond the extent they are supported by the description; extension only justified if probable that extended search could produce a document enabling a reasonable objection of lack of novelty or inventive step.
guidance: If a meaningful search for unsupported scope can be carried out without much extra effort, extend search; examples provided (telephone exchange vs telegraph exchanges).

name: Interpretation of claim wording by skilled person
