description: Words of a claim must be read as understood by a person skilled in the relevant art according to their normal meaning and scope in that art.
guidance: See paragraphs 15.20–15.28 for guidance on interpreting particular claim types and features.

name: Two-part (Jepson) claims and technological background
description: In two-part claims the preamble is a limitation and, in certain circumstances, it may be desirable to extend the search to include the 'technological background' including the preamble, state of prior art in the description, and general technological background.
guidance: Treat the preamble portion (before 'characterized by' or 'the improvement comprising') as limiting; include background where useful to locate best prior art.

name: Search strategy for combination claims and sub-combinations
description: For combination claims (e.g., A+B+C) search should be directed to the combination and concurrently to sub-combinations and individual elements (AB, AC, BC, A, B, C) in relevant classification units; searching additional units for sub-combinations or individual elements only if necessary to establish novelty for assessing inventive step.
guidance: Ensure classification units searched cover both combination and relevant sub-combinations where needed.

name: Different categories of claims (product/process/etc.)
description: When application contains claims of different categories that satisfy unity, all must be included in the search; when claims are only of one category it may be desirable to include other categories in the search (e.g., process claims may require searching for the product).
guidance: In chemical process claims, starting products generally form part of the state of the art and need not be searched; intermediate products searched only when claimed; final products highly recommended to be searched except when evidently known.

name: Indefiniteness standard ('insolubly ambiguous')
description: Under current Federal Circuit law, a claim is indefinite only if it is 'insolubly ambiguous.' Indefiniteness is treated as a pure question of law normally decided in connection with claim construction.
guidance: Indefiniteness is often decided during claim construction; some indefiniteness rulings may be embedded inside claim-construction orders and not styled as summary judgment. The Federal Circuit has been hostile to expansive indefiniteness findings, but the Supreme Court (e.g., Nautilus) may broaden the doctrine. Practitioners should accordingly watch claim-draft clarity and expect courts to address definiteness at the claim-construction stage.

name: Means-plus-function / software claims: algorithm disclosure requirement
description: For means-plus-function limitations in software patents, courts require disclosure of the corresponding structure — typically an algorithm — in the specification; absent adequate algorithm disclosure, the claim may be indefinite.
guidance: Cases cited (Function Media, ePlus, Noah, Ergo, Typhoon Touch, In re Aoyama, Aristocrat, WMS Gaming) explain that the specification must disclose the algorithm or corresponding structure performing the claimed function. The disclosed structure need not be software code verbatim (Typhoon), but must show a 'step-by-step process' for reaching the result. Failure to disclose sufficient algorithmic structure can render a means-plus-function claim indefinite.

name: Claim construction as prerequisite to substantive summary judgment
description: Claim construction (Markman) is usually a prerequisite to most substantive rulings in a patent case (validity and infringement), because the construed scope of the claim determines many summary-judgment issues.
guidance: Markman requires courts to decide claim construction as a matter of law, typically during a pretrial 'Markman hearing.' Because claim construction precedes many summary-judgment motions, courts often resolve claim terms first; claims that cannot be construed may give rise to indefiniteness rulings as part of that process.

name: Asymmetric burdens for summary judgment (patentee vs accused infringer)
description: To obtain summary judgment of infringement, a patentee must show a lack of disputed issues of material fact for all elements of the claimed invention; an accused infringer seeking summary judgment of noninfringement need only show a lack of disputed issues of material fact for any single element.
guidance: This asymmetry makes SJ more available and advantageous to accused infringers: defendants can move on one or more discrete bases and need only negate one element. Plaintiffs (patentees) face a higher burden at the SJ stage and must clear every element to obtain SJ of infringement.

name: Rise of indefiniteness challenges linked to software patents and claim construction
description: Indefiniteness challenges have grown in prevalence—now a large category of adjudicated challenges—partly because many decisions in the dataset involve software patents and because the Federal Circuit applied indefiniteness more vigorously to software means-plus-function claims; claim construction itself has become common and invites indefiniteness rulings.
guidance: Practitioners litigating software patents should anticipate more indefiniteness attacks, particularly on means-plus-function claim language, and should ensure the specification discloses sufficient structure/algorithmic detail. Empirical counts of indefiniteness may understate true prevalence because some indefiniteness rulings occur as part of claim-construction orders.

name: GAO study requirements (Section 34)
description: Section 34 requires GAO to conduct a study compiling information on: (1) the annual volume of litigation brought by non-practicing entities (NPEs), (2) the number of such cases found to be without merit, (3) the impact of such litigation on the time to resolve patent claims, (4) the related costs, (5) the economic impact, and (6) the benefit to commerce.
guidance: GAO should compile reasonably available information on these six topics; where underlying data do not exist or are not reasonably available, GAO is not obligated to include them. GAO may use a smaller sample size when necessary and should note any limitations on data or methodology in its report.

name: Scope/definition of 'commercially used the subject matter' for prior user rights
description: The phrase 'commercially used the subject matter' is intended broadly to apply to a person's commercial use of any form of subject matter, whether embodied in a process or embodied in a machine, manufacture, or composition of matter used in a manufacturing or other commercial process.
guidance: This broad construction is meant to protect businesses that invested in and used proprietary technologies. Note: if a technology is embedded in a product and made publicly available, that public availability may itself constitute prior art against later patent claims.

name: Restriction to applications filed before event dates (Alice, Berkheimer, 2019 PEG)
description: Datasets are restricted to applications filed before the relevant event (Alice decision, Berkheimer memorandum, or 2019 PEG) to mitigate endogeneity from applicant behavior (e.g., redrafting after events).
guidance: This mitigates applicant-driven changes in claim language/prosecution that could confound examiner behavior. Robustness checks relax these restrictions (e.g., extend start date to 2011) to test sensitivity.

name: Use of claim scope covariates (ICC and ICL)
description: Claim scope is proxied using independent claim count (ICC) and shortest independent claim length (ICL) from the Patent Claims Research Dataset; these are added to application-level datasets as covariates.
guidance: Used to control for differences in claim breadth that might confound §101 rejection likelihood. For proprietary datasets (Berkheimer/2019 PEG analysis), these application-level text covariates may be unavailable.

name: Text-based measure of abstractness of application language
description: A text-based measure of abstract language in patent claims (application abstractness) was developed from PGPub or granted patent claims text (USPTO bulk XML).
guidance: Used as an application-level covariate and in interaction terms (double/triple interactions) to explore heterogeneous treatment effects; not available for proprietary datasets covering non-public apps.

name: Additional covariates for non-random assignment
description: Include various application- or technology-level covariates (claim scope, abstractness, average abstractness, number of examiners, applications per examiner, within-examiner variance) to reduce omitted variable bias arising from non-random assignment to Alice-affected group.
guidance: These covariates help ensure comparability of treatment/control and isolate the causal effect of the event. Proprietary data limitations may prevent inclusion of some covariates for certain event analyses.

name: Petition for retroactive license — evidentiary showing and supporting documents
description: The explanation ... must include a showing of facts rather than a mere allegation of action through error. The showing of facts ... should include statements by those persons having personal knowledge of the acts regarding filing in a foreign country and should be accompanied by copies of any necessary supporting documents such as letters of transmittal or instructions for filing.
guidance: Substantiate claims of error with affidavits/declarations from witnesses with personal knowledge and supporting documentary evidence; describe acts covering the period up to and including each proscribed foreign filing.

name: Markush group propriety
description: The materials set forth in the Markush group ordinarily must belong to a recognized physical or chemical class or to an art-recognized class. When the Markush group occurs in a claim reciting a process or a combination (not a single compound), it is sufficient if the members of the group are disclosed in the specification to possess at least one property in common which is mainly responsible for their function in the claimed relationship, and it is clear from their very nature or from the prior art that all of them possess this property.
guidance: Double inclusion of an element by members of a Markush group is not, in itself, sufficient basis for objection or rejection — facts of each case must be evaluated to determine indefiniteness. The mere fact that a compound may be embraced by more than one member of a Markush group does not necessarily render claim scope unclear (example: 'selected from the group consisting of amino, halogen, nitro, chloro and alkyl' acceptable even though 'halogen' is generic to 'chloro'). Where a Markush expression is applied only to a portion of a chemical compound, propriety is determined by considering the compound as a whole. Alternative phrasings ('selected from the group consisting of A, B, C and D' vs 'R is A, B, C or D') are acceptable if the grouping is proper. See MPEP § 803 and § 715.03 for more.

name: Subgenus / Genus claim acceptability
description: Genus, subgenus, and Markush-type claims, if properly supported by the disclosure, are all acceptable ways for applicants to claim their inventions.
guidance: Examiners should not reject Markush-type claims merely because there are genus claims that encompass them. See MPEP § 608.01(p) and § 715.03. See also restriction practice in MPEP § 803.02.

name: Use of 'optionally' in claims
description: The term 'optionally' can be acceptable in claim language where there is no ambiguity as to which alternatives are covered by the claim.
guidance: If the list of potential alternatives can vary and ambiguity arises, rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph is proper; exam decisions include Ex parte Cordova and Ex parte Wu. Examiner must analyze whether 'optionally' creates confusion about alternatives covered.

name: Negative limitations
description: Negative limitations are not inherently ambiguous or uncertain so long as the boundaries of the patent protection sought are set forth definitely (even if negatively).
guidance: Older courts criticized negative limitations, but more recent cases find them definite when boundaries are clear (e.g., In re Wakefield, In re Barr). Any negative limitation or exclusionary proviso must have basis in the original disclosure; if alternative elements are positively recited in the specification they may be explicitly excluded in the claims (In re Johnson). A negative limitation without basis in the original disclosure should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph (written description). Lack of literal basis in the specification for a negative limitation may not by itself be sufficient to establish a prima facie lack of descriptive support (Ex parte Parks). See MPEP § 2163–§ 2163.07(b).

name: Aggregation is non-statutory
description: A claim should not be rejected on the ground of 'aggregation.'
guidance: Rejection for 'aggregation' is non‑statutory (In re Gustafson, In re Collier). If a claim omits essential matter or fails to interrelate essential elements, other statutes or MPEP § 2172.01 may apply.

name: Prolix claims
description: Claims should be rejected as prolix only when they contain such long recitations or unimportant details that the scope of the claimed invention is rendered indefinite.
guidance: Reject when long recitations prevent determination of the metes and bounds of claimed subject matter (i.e., render claim indefinite). Use rejection sparingly and only where indefiniteness results from prolixity.

name: Double inclusion
description: There is no per se rule that 'double inclusion' is improper in a claim; the governing consideration is the reasonable construction of claim language.
guidance: Facts of each case must be evaluated to determine whether multiple inclusion of one or more elements gives rise to indefiniteness. A compound embraced by more than one member of a Markush group does not automatically create uncertainty; however, device claims that can be read to include the same element twice may be indefinite (Ex parte Kristensen). Older cases should be applied with care (Ex parte White, Ex parte Clark, In re Kelly).

name: Product-by-process claims
description: A product-by-process claim (a product claim that defines the claimed product in terms of the process by which it is made) is proper.
guidance: A device, apparatus, manufacture, or composition claim may reference the process in which it is intended to be used without being objectionable under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, provided it is clear the claim is directed to the product and not the process. Applicants may present claims of varying scope even when necessary to describe the claimed product in product-by-process terms (cases: In re Luck, In re Pilkington, In re Steppan, Ex parte Pantzer).

name: Product and process in same claim (improper)
description: A single claim which claims both an apparatus and the method steps of using the apparatus is indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph.
guidance: System claims that recite actions of users or method steps can create confusion as to when infringement occurs and have been held indefinite (In re Katz Interactive Call Processing Patent Litigation; IPXL v. Amazon; Ex parte Lyell). Examiners should reject such claims as indefinite.

name: "Use" claims (process without steps) are problematic
description: Attempts to claim a process without setting forth any steps involved in the process raise an issue of indefiniteness under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph.
guidance: Claims reciting mere use (e.g., 'A process for using monoclonal antibodies...') have been held indefinite (Ex parte Erlich). Some authorities suggest 35 U.S.C. 101 may be more appropriate in certain cases. Recommended practice: reject 'use' claims under alternative grounds based on 35 U.S.C. 101 and 112. However, claims that clearly recite a step of 'utilizing' have been held not indefinite in some cases (Ex parte Porter).

name: Omnibus claims should be rejected
description: Omnibus claims (e.g., 'A device substantially as shown and described') are indefinite and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph.
guidance: Such claims fail to point out what is included or excluded by the claim language (Ex parte Fressola). Use Form Paragraph 7.35 for rejection; see MPEP § 706.03(d) and § 1302.04(b) for examiner amendment/cancellation procedures.

name: Reference to figures or tables in claims
description: Where possible, claims are to be complete in themselves; incorporation by reference to a specific figure or table is permitted only in exceptional circumstances.
guidance: Incorporation by reference is a 'necessity doctrine', not for applicant convenience. Use only where no practical way to define invention in words and where incorporation is more concise than duplicating drawing or table. Reference characters corresponding to elements in detailed description/drawings may be used with recitation of same element(s) in claims. See Ex parte Fressola and MPEP § 608.01(m).

name: Chemical formula claims not indefinite absent error
description: Claims to chemical compounds and compositions often use formulas; these structures should not be considered indefinite or speculative in the absence of evidence that the assigned formula is in error.
guidance: Absence of corroborating spectroscopic or other data cannot be the basis for finding the structure indefinite (Ex parte Morton, Ex parte Sobin). A claim is not indefinite merely because a structure is not fully presented (In re Fisher). Compounds may be claimed by an adequate name, a combination of physical/chemical characteristics, or by the process by which made (Ex parte Brian).

name: Trademarks/trade names in claims
description: The presence of a trademark or trade name in a claim is not per se improper under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, but must be carefully analyzed to determine how the mark/name is used.
guidance: A trademark identifies a source of goods, not the goods themselves; using a trademark/trade name to identify or describe a particular material/product renders the claim indefinite and is improper (Ex parte Simpson). If a trademark appears but is not intended as a limitation, examiner should ask whether its presence causes confusion about claim scope; if so, reject under 112, second paragraph. See MPEP § 608.01(v) and Appendix I for examples.

name: Mere function of a machine (process claims)
description: Process or method claims should not be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, solely because they define the inherent function of a disclosed machine or apparatus.
guidance: If the process claim is otherwise patentable, it should not be rejected merely because disclosed apparatus will inherently carry out the recited steps (In re Tarczy-Hornoch).

name: Practice Compact Prosecution — interpret claim and apply art with explanation
description: Under compact prosecution, the examiner should review each claim for compliance with every statutory requirement for patentability in the initial review and identify all applicable grounds of rejection in the first Office action to avoid unnecessary delays.
guidance: When a claim term or phrase renders the claim indefinite, the examiner should make a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, and also make rejection(s) under 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103 as they apply based on the examiner's interpretation of the claim. The examiner must state on the record how the claim term is being interpreted relative to prior art to avoid piecemeal examination (see 37 CFR 1.104(a)(1); MPEP § 706; § 707.07(g)).

name: Prior art rejection strategy for indefinite claims
description: Two approaches for handling prior art rejections when claims are considered indefinite: (1) where uncertainty is not great and at least one interpretation renders claim unpatentable, enter both an indefiniteness rejection and a prior-art rejection based on the interpretation; (2) where great confusion exists, do not base a rejection on prior art.
guidance: First approach is generally recommended to avoid piecemeal examination and to give applicant appreciation for relevant prior art; when making prior-art rejections based on an interpretation, the examiner must state how the claim is being interpreted. If the claim is highly ambiguous such that meaningful prior-art comparison would require speculation, prior-art rejection should be avoided (In re Steele). See Ex parte Ionescu for example.

name: Relationship between 35 U.S.C.112 first and second paragraphs
description: Requirements of the first and second paragraphs of 35 U.S.C. 112 are separate and distinct: lack of commensurate enabling disclosure is a 112 first-paragraph issue (written description/enablement), whereas indefiniteness is a 112 second-paragraph issue.
guidance: If specification disclosure/enabling disclosure is not commensurate in scope with the claim, the claim should be rejected under 112, first paragraph (e.g., In re Borkowski). If the specification discloses a feature as essential, failure to recite it in the claim may be a 112 first-paragraph problem (In re Mayhew). Amending a claim to include matter not described in the application as filed may warrant a 112 first-paragraph rejection (In re Simon, In re Panagrossi). Examiners should distinguish between lack of descriptive support/enablement and indefiniteness.

name: Identifying 35 U.S.C.112 sixth paragraph (means/step-plus-function) limitations
description: Guidelines for examination of 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph 'means or step plus function' limitations: such limitations must be interpreted consistent with the written description of the invention and Donaldson requires giving effect to corresponding structure disclosed in the specification when construing means-plus-function language.
guidance: Under Donaldson, the PTO may not disregard structure disclosed in the specification when construing means-plus-function language; examiners must apply 112, sixth paragraph where appropriate while giving claims their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification. See In re Donaldson, TriMed v. Stryker, Altiris v. Symantec, and related Federal Circuit precedent.

name: Three‑prong test for invoking 112 sixth paragraph
description: Examiners will apply 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph to a claim limitation if it meets the following 3-prong analysis: (A) the claim limitation uses the phrase 'means for' or 'step for' or a non-structural term (a term simply substituting for 'means for'); (B) the phrase is modified by functional language; and (C) the phrase is not modified by sufficient structure, material, or acts for achieving the specified function.
guidance: The limitation is presumed to invoke 112 sixth paragraph when it explicitly uses 'means for' or 'step for' and includes functional language; that presumption is overcome when the limitation further includes the structure necessary to perform the recited function (TriMed). Conversely, absence of the phrase 'means for' triggers a rebuttable presumption that 112 sixth paragraph does not apply (Phillips, CCS Fitness, Personalized Media). The presumption is strong and not readily overcome (Lighting World, Inventio). Non-structural 'nonce' words may be treated as equivalents of 'means for' if they are not recognized names of structure (Lighting World). Examiners should analyze whether the claim recites sufficient structure to avoid means-plus-function treatment.

name: Alice/Mayo two-step framework for patent-eligibility
description: Step 1: Are the claims directed to a patent-ineligible concept (abstract idea, law of nature, product of nature)? Step 2: If so, do the claim elements contain an 'inventive concept' sufficient to transform the ineligible concept into a patent-eligible application?
guidance: Transformation requires more than reciting the ineligible concept plus conventional steps or 'apply it' language. Alice applied this test to software; courts apply the same logic to natural-products claims to ask whether isolation/purification supplies the required inventive concept.

name: Framing the §101 inquiry: focus on similarities vs differences
description: How one frames comparison between claimed product and natural counterpart (emphasizing similarities or differences) can determine eligibility: Myriad focused on similarities (information content), leading to ineligibility.
guidance: Courts may look either to whether the claimed product is materially different from the natural product (differences approach) or to whether claim effectively appropriates what is the same (similarities/information approach). The article argues that focusing on information (similarities) drove Myriad's result.

name: Method of claiming is not determinative but revealing
description: Whether a claim is worded as a composition of matter, a method, or otherwise is not dispositive of §101 eligibility; the form of claiming may instead reveal what the patentee actually seeks to appropriate (idea/information vs transformed matter).
guidance: The USPTO and courts have recognized that claim form can point to a deeper problem—claims that in substance claim information/ideas (even if drafted as compositions) are suspect—so claim drafting should emphasize transformative features and concrete, inventive aspects.

name: Preemption and the risk of monopolizing research tools
description: A central policy concern in §101 is whether a claim would 'preempt' use of fundamental tools or knowledge and thereby impede future innovation; patents should not grant monopolies over basic scientific building blocks.
guidance: Mayo and Funk Bros. highlight this concern. Evaluate whether granting the claimed monopoly would 'tend to impede innovation more than it would tend to promote it.' Narrow claims that avoid broad preemption are preferred.

name: Value of composition-of-matter patents to incentivize drug R&D
description: Composition of matter patents (versus process/use patents) are the most prized form of protection in pharmaceuticals because they provide long-term certainty necessary to justify multi-year, multi-billion-dollar investments.
guidance: Process claims are harder to enforce and FDA exclusivity is limited; therefore denying composition protection to isolated natural products biases R&D away from such drugs. Policy assessments of §101 should weigh this incentivization role.

name: Distinguish claims directed to information versus composition of matter
description: Claims primarily directed to the information encoded in a molecule (e.g., a gene sequence) are qualitatively different from claims directed to the physical composition that has been transformed by human effort.
guidance: When evaluating claims, determine whether their core is information/idea monopolization (which Myriad invalidated) or a new composition with changed properties/utility (potentially eligible). Draft claims to emphasize concrete structural/functional changes when possible.

name: USPTO post-Myriad guidance and its expansive reading
description: The USPTO has read Myriad as eliminating the isolated and purified exception for many natural products, prompting revised examination guidance (2014 PTO Guidance and later updates).
guidance: Practitioners should be aware of PTO guidance, scholarly debate, and divergent practitioner views; argue claim drafting and evidence focused on transformative inventive concepts and the non-information-encoding character of the claimed molecule to counter PTO rejections.

name: Material/factual questions determine patentability in some borderline cases
description: Whether a claimed application of a process to a different substance is patentable may depend on factual questions (e.g., whether 'spent madder' is chemically or practically a different substance from 'fresh madder').
guidance: Courts should direct juries to find facts such as chemical differences or prior knowledge in the art; the patentable character should not be drawn as a narrow legal inference when material factual disputes exist. Treat such distinctions as questions of fact material to validity.

name: When a process produces a materially different product ('new metal' etc.)
description: If a claimed process produces a product that is materially different in properties (e.g., a 'new metal') — by reason of superior properties or cheapness — that fact strongly supports treating the process as patentable.
guidance: Crane and Sturz cases: courts sometimes justified patentability on the ground that the product resulting from the new process was effectively new (different in quality or cost). Evaluate product-level differences as a significant indicium of inventive novelty.

name: Correction of preprinted prior application data
description: If there is an error in the preprinted prior application data, correction or entry of the data in the Patent Data Portal database can be made by technical support staff of the Technology Center, if appropriate. If the error was an applicant error, the examiner should require correction via a corrected or supplemental application data sheet or an amendment, as appropriate.
guidance: Upon entry of corrected data, print a new bib-data sheet and scan into the file. A petition for an unintentionally delayed benefit claim may also be required. See MPEP § 601.05 et seq., § 211.02(a), and § 211.04.

name: Statutory requirements for benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 and 119(e)
description: Under 35 U.S.C. 120 and 119(e), an application may have the same effect as the earlier application as to an invention disclosed in the manner provided by 35 U.S.C. 112(a) if filed before patenting/abandonment and if it contains or is amended to contain a specific reference to the earlier filed application; failure to submit such an amendment within the required pendency time may be considered waiver.
guidance: The Director may establish procedures, including fee (41(a)(7)), to accept an unintentionally delayed submission of an amendment. For provisional claims under 119(e)(1), the later-filed nonprovisional must be filed not later than 12 months after the provisional; the Director may extend by up to 2 months for unintentional delay under regulations. See statutory text quoted (35 U.S.C. 120, 35 U.S.C. 119(e)) and MPEP § 211.

name: Scope of discovery (relevance and admissibility)
description: Parties may obtain discovery regarding any nonprivileged matter that is relevant to any party's claim or defense — including the existence, description, nature, custody, condition, and location of documents or other tangible things and the identity and location of persons who know of any discoverable matter. Relevant information need not be admissible at trial if the discovery appears reasonably calculated to lead to the discovery of admissible evidence. All discovery is subject to limits imposed by Rule 26(b)(2)(C).
guidance: Discovery may extend beyond matters specifically raised in the pleadings to any matter that might serve as the basis for additional claims or defenses, but fishing expeditions are prohibited. In TTAB proceedings the scope is often narrower than in district court, and proportionality principles apply (including with respect to ESI).

name: Federal and state court jurisdiction over patent matters
description: Allocation of jurisdiction between federal and state courts for patent-related claims; scope of federal equity powers.
guidance: Federal courts have jurisdiction over many patent questions and possess ordinary equity powers (citations: 853-866; 1256; 1094). They generally lack jurisdiction over certain license issues in some contexts. See cross-references to circuit/supreme courts and state courts.

name: Function versus means in claim construction
description: Distinction between claiming a function and claiming means; how courts construe functional claims.
guidance: Function is distinct from means, end, effect; a claim for function may be void in some contexts, but claims for function are often construed to cover corresponding means if possible. The function is the measure of the means; claims for a machine's function are scrutinized (citations: 144; 145; 232; 234; 518; 539 n.1; 530).

name: Infringement — actors and vicarious liability
description: Who may commit infringement: individuals, corporate officers, employees, licensees, co-owners, public bodies and limitations on governmental liability.
guidance: The United States generally is immune (claims against US must be in Court of Claims). Officers, employees, corporations, municipal bodies, contractors, agents, and licensees can incur liability depending on control and benefit. Licensees acting within license scope do not infringe; departures from license may create infringement and contractual remedies. Co-owners and vendees have particular rules (citations: 910-921; 910 n.6; 911-912; 915-917; 913-916; 905; 979; 1044).

name: Claims (Art.84 and formal requirements)
description: Requirements for claims clarity, support by the description, and formal requirements under Article 84 EPC and related rules.
guidance: Covers claim structure, dependency, clarity objections, and examples of compliant/ non‑compliant claim wording.

name: Annex — Examples concerning essential features
description: Illustrative examples to determine essential features of claims and their identification.
guidance: Provides worked examples to assist examiners and applicants in identifying essential features.

name: Peripheral claiming doctrine
description: Most countries follow a 'peripheral claiming' doctrine in which the claims establish the outer limits of patent protection.
guidance: Draft claims to set the limits of the scope of protection sought. Do not assume a 'central claiming' approach unless filing in a rare jurisdiction that uses it. Claims should be written with examiners, courts and potential licensees in mind so the intended boundaries are clear.

name: Use of plain language (the vs said)
description: While the words 'the' and 'said' are interchangeable in claims drafting (e.g., 'the pencil' or 'said pencil'), the latter is increasingly old-fashioned and jurisdictions trend toward plain language.
guidance: Prefer plain language over legalese (avoid 'said' where unnecessary), especially if litigation in jurisdictions (e.g., U.S.) may involve lay juries. Use wording that aids comprehension.

name: Punctuation and formatting of claims
description: For clarity, claims are frequently more extensively punctuated than grammatically required: a comma typically separates the preamble from the transitional phrase; a colon typically separates the transition from the body; the body is often broken into small paragraphs with elements separated by semi-colons and the penultimate element followed by '; and,' the last ending with a full stop.
guidance: Follow the model: Preamble, transitional phrase: – Element (#1); – Element (#2); and – Element (#3). In some countries (e.g., U.S.) each element or combination should be indented on its own line; in others indentation is optional. Use punctuation to ensure the claim will be interpreted as intended.

name: Proper antecedent basis
description: Elements in a patent claim must demonstrate correct antecedent basis: introduce an element with 'a' or 'an' on first use and refer back to it with 'the' thereafter; each new claim set must re-establish antecedent basis.
guidance: Failure to provide correct antecedent basis may cause ambiguity (e.g., whether 'the pencil' refers to the same pencil). To refer to multiple instances, use 'first' and 'second' or 'an' and 'another'. Draft each claim independently and re-introduce elements in each new claim set.

name: Reference numerals and parenthetical expressions
description: Some jurisdictions (PCT) prefer reference numerals in parentheses after claim elements to link claims to drawings; many countries state numerals shall not be interpreted as limiting the claims; some jurisdictions avoid or prohibit numerals.
guidance: Use reference numerals where encouraged to support comprehension, but be aware that (i) adding substantive text inside parentheses may create 'special features' and be interpreted as limiting, (ii) some offices may reject parenthetical expressions without numerals (e.g., '(concrete) molded brick'), and (iii) inclusion of numerals does not incorporate the drawings into the claim. If filing in jurisdictions (e.g., U.S.) that discourage numerals, avoid them.

name: Meaning and use of claim phrases ('wherein', 'whereby', etc.)
description: Certain words have special meanings in claims: words such as 'wherein', 'whereby', 'such that', 'so as to', and 'configured to' are used to further define structure or provide a function associated with a structure; a 'wherein clause' is generally used to describe a function, operation or result that flows from the previously recited structure or function.
guidance: Know how courts/examiners in relevant jurisdictions interpret these phrases and use them appropriately. Use 'wherein' when the result necessarily follows from the recited structure or function; consider effects on claim scope and dependency when choosing phrasing.

name: Requirement for multiple elements (avoid single-element claims)
description: Many patent offices require claims to recite at least two elements; a single-element claim can be impossibly broad.
guidance: Avoid drafting trivially broad single-element claims (e.g., 'A computer, comprising: a processor.') which may read on prior art or trivial items. Include enough limitations to meaningfully define the invention's scope relative to the prior art.

name: Two-part (improvement / Jepson) claims
description: A two-part claim (also called an improvement or Jepson claim) sets out the most relevant known prior art in the preamble, uses a transitional phrase (e.g., 'characterized by'/'characterized in that' or 'wherein the improvement comprises'), and the body characterizes the improvement (the novel elements).
guidance: Be aware that the two-part format constitutes an implicit admission that the first part is prior art. The EPO prefers two-part claims where appropriate and advises that the first part should indicate the technical class and prior-art features necessary for definition. Consider whether the two-part form is appropriate—it's often unsuitable for inventions that are combinations of known integers of equal status, certain process modifications, complex interrelated systems, or new chemical compounds. You may initially draft standard format claims and switch if required by an examiner.

name: Alternative elements and Markush claims
description: Many jurisdictions allow alternative elements in a single claim; expressions such as 'metal or plastic' can be ambiguous in claims. Markush claim format ('wherein element A is selected from the group consisting of X, Y and Z') is commonly used (especially in chemistry) to claim alternatives.
guidance: Use 'and/or' or explicit phrasing ('selected from the group consisting of...') where inclusive alternatives are meant; use 'either ... or ...' for exclusive alternatives. If combinations of members are possible, explicitly say so (e.g., 'and combinations thereof'). Markush groups must not be ambiguous; if one alternative is anticipated by prior art, the entire Markush claim may lack novelty—consider separate dependent claims for group members and ensure unity of invention requirements are met.

name: Functional elements and means-plus-function claims
description: Functional language can define a claim element by what it accomplishes rather than by what it is. Means-plus-function claims use the word 'means' followed by a function and are interpreted variably across jurisdictions—often limited to the structures disclosed in the specification and their equivalents.
guidance: A functional element is acceptable so long as a person skilled in the art can perform the function without inventive skill. Means-plus-function claims typically must be supported by adequate disclosure of structures in the specification; explicitly describe structures that perform recited functions (e.g., 'tapes, adhesives, rivets') to avoid overly narrow constructions. Avoid reciting unnecessary structures or failing to identify which structures perform the function. Beware that wholly functional claim sets risk rejection as mere desiderata (desired result without how to achieve it). Mixing means-plus-function and structural claim elements is possible and often desirable.

name: Claim sets: independent and dependent claims (scope, fees, balance)
description: A patent specification normally contains one or more independent claims and several dependent claims. All applications must contain at least one independent claim directed to the essential features necessary to satisfy legal patentability requirements (e.g., novelty, inventive step).
guidance: Draft a balanced set of claims (broad and narrow) to protect different aspects and levels of detail. Consider costs: many offices levy filing/examination/grant fees based on claim counts (and extra fees for multiple dependent claims in some offices like the USPTO). Avoid both overly broad and overly narrow claims; ensure claims are clear and reasonable in number relative to the invention's complexity. Dependent claims inherit all features of their parent claim and are always narrower.

name: Independent claims characteristics and unity of invention
description: Independent claims represent the broadest claims and stand alone; multiple independent claims may be needed to cover different aspects. Unity of invention requires that multiple independent claims in one application relate to one invention or a group of inventions linked as a single general inventive concept.
guidance: Prepare several independent claims when the invention encompasses different aspects or when strategically varying breadth is useful to hedge against unknown prior art. Be mindful of jurisdictional limits on the number/kind of independent claims (e.g., EPO limits independent claims per category). Ensure independent claims include essential features for the technical effect and comply with unity requirements to avoid objections or divisionals.

name: Dependent claims formatting and effects
description: A dependent claim refers back to a preceding claim and includes all features of that claim even if not repeated; dependent claims make the text more concise and are inherently narrower than the claim they depend on.
guidance: Signal dependencies clearly (e.g., 'The apparatus of Claim 1, further comprising...'). Use dependent claims to capture fallback positions and specific embodiments. Remember that some offices charge additional fees for multiple dependent claim forms and that dependent claims should be reasonable in number and clear in scope.

name: Laws of Nature and Natural Phenomena, Generally
description: Laws of nature and natural phenomena include naturally occurring principles/relations and nature-based products that are naturally occurring or that do not have markedly different characteristics compared to what occurs in nature. The courts have often described these exceptions using other terms, including 'physical phenomena,' 'scientific principles', 'natural laws,' and 'products of nature.' The basic tools of scientific and technological work are not patentable because they are part of the storehouse of knowledge.
guidance: Cites Supreme Court and precedent: Funk Bros.; Diamond v. Chakrabarty; Parker v. Flook; O’Reilly v. Morse; Funk. Explains consequence: such subject matter is not patentable under §101 absent further analysis. Use this concept in Step 2A Prong One to identify whether a claim recites one of these judicial exceptions.

name: Claims Describing Natural Abilities/Responses May Still Be Eligible
description: Not every claim describing a natural ability, quality of a product, or natural process necessarily recites a law of nature or natural phenomenon; claims that are directed to active process steps or applications (rather than mere observation/detection of a natural ability) can be eligible at Prong One.
guidance: Examples: process steps for fractionating/recovering/cryopreserving hepatocytes (CellzDirect) found eligible because not focused merely on observing ability to survive freeze-thaw cycles. A method of treating cancer where cancer cells' inability to survive chemotherapy is not considered a law of nature. Method of treating headaches with aspirin — the body's natural response is not a law of nature when claimed as treatment. If such claims recite another exception they require further Prong Two (and Step 2B) analysis.

name: Products of Nature Exception
description: When a law of nature or natural phenomenon is claimed as a physical product, courts often refer to the exception as a 'product of nature.' Products of nature include naturally occurring products and non-naturally occurring products that lack markedly different characteristics from natural counterparts.
guidance: A synthetic product that is structurally identical to a natural counterpart is not patent eligible (Ambry Genetics). The key inquiry is whether the claimed product possesses 'markedly different characteristics' from any naturally occurring counterpart. If not, it's a product of nature and requires further Step 2A Prong Two analysis. Examples: Myriad (isolated DNA) and Ambry (primers) described as products of nature; Chakrabarty bacterium not a product of nature because it had markedly different characteristics.

name: Markedly Different Characteristics Analysis (Step 2A Prong One)
description: The markedly different characteristics analysis is used to identify product-of-nature exceptions by comparing the claimed nature-based product limitation to its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state. It is part of Step 2A Prong One of the Office's eligibility framework.
guidance: Markedly different characteristics can be expressed as structure, function, and/or other properties and are evaluated case-by-case based on what is recited in the claim. If the claimed nature-based product exhibits markedly different characteristics, it does not recite a product-of-nature exception and is eligible at Step 2A (Pathway B: NO), unless the claim recites another exception.

name: When to Perform the Markedly Different Characteristics Analysis
description: Apply the markedly different characteristics analysis only to nature-based product limitations in a claim, and avoid over-applying it to claim elements that, when viewed as a whole, are not nature-based.
guidance: If the nature-based product limitation is naturally occurring, no need to perform the analysis (it is by definition a product-of-nature exception). If the limitation is non-naturally occurring (e.g., due to human intervention), perform the analysis. Consider claim type (product, product-by-process, process) when deciding whether to apply the analysis.

name: Application to Product Claims and Combinations
description: For product claims, apply the analysis to the entire claimed product. For a nature-based product produced by combining components, analyze the resultant nature-based combination rather than components separately. For claims that combine nature-based products with non-nature elements, apply the analysis only to the nature-based product limitation.
guidance: Examples: for a claimed 'probiotic composition comprising Lactobacillus and milk' analyze the mixture. For a 'yogurt starter kit comprising Lactobacillus in a container with instructions,' analyze Lactobacillus only; container and instructions are evaluated separately in Prong Two (and Step 2B if needed). Funk Bros. shows only the bacterial mixture was analyzed even though other elements were claimed.

name: Selecting the Appropriate Naturally Occurring Counterpart(s)
description: The first step is selecting the appropriate naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state to which the claimed nature-based product is compared.
guidance: If the claimed product is derived from a naturally occurring thing, that natural thing is the counterpart (e.g., deoxyacid A compared to acid A). Do not confuse the counterpart with other naturally co-occurring material (e.g., compare an isolated gene to the gene, not the whole chromosome). If multiple counterparts exist, compare to the closest natural counterpart; examiner should use expertise to select one and, as a best practice, identify the selected counterpart in the Office action if not already clear. For combinations with no natural counterpart, compare to the individual component counterparts (Funk Bros.).

name: Identifying Appropriate Characteristics for Analysis
description: Identify characteristics to compare that are actually possessed by the claimed product as recited in the claim or encompassed within its broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI). Characteristics may be structure, function, and/or other properties.
guidance: Appropriate characteristics must be possessed by the claimed product. Examiners determine these from claim language and BRI. Non-limiting types of characteristics include: biological or pharmacological functions/activities (e.g., protein-encoding information, binding ability), chemical and physical properties (e.g., alkalinity, ductility), phenotype (shape, size, color, behavior), and structure/form (physical plasmids, chemical/crystalline form, nucleotide sequence, genotype). Use case law examples (Myriad, Ambry, Chakrabarty, Parke-Davis, Roslin) to identify relevant characteristics.

name: Evaluating Whether Characteristics Are 'Markedly Different'
description: To be 'markedly different,' a characteristic must be changed compared to the naturally occurring counterpart and not merely inherent, incidental, or resulting from isolation; the change should generally be caused by applicant's efforts or influences.
guidance: If there is no change in any characteristic, the claimed product lacks markedly different characteristics and is a product-of-nature exception. If at least one characteristic changed due to applicant's efforts, it will generally be considered markedly different. Examples: Chakrabarty bacterium (structural—additional plasmids—and functional—degrade multiple hydrocarbons—markedly different → eligible); cDNA (Myriad) structural change (exons only) distinguished from genomic DNA → eligible; isolated genomic BRCA sequences (Myriad): incidental structural changes from isolation were not enough → ineligible. Courts emphasize the difference cannot be merely incidental to isolation or inherent in the natural counterpart.

name: Effect of Markedly Different Characteristics on Eligibility and Further Analysis
description: If a claimed nature-based product has markedly different characteristics from its natural counterpart, the claim does not recite a product-of-nature exception and is eligible at Step 2A (Pathway B: NO), unless the claim recites another judicial exception.
guidance: If the nature-based product lacks markedly different characteristics, the limitation is a product-of-nature exception and requires further analysis in Step 2A Prong Two (and Step 2B if needed) to determine whether the claim integrates the exception into a practical application or otherwise presents an 'inventive concept.' Examiners should consider recommending claim amendments to narrow the BRI where appropriate.

name: Examiner Best Practices Regarding Product-of-Nature Analysis
description: Procedural and record-keeping practices examiners should follow when performing and documenting markedly different characteristics/product-of-nature analyses.
guidance: Best practices include: identify the selected naturally occurring counterpart in the Office action if not already clear to assist applicant response; point out the broadest reasonable interpretation and recommend possible amendments to narrow claims if a claim is rejected as failing to encompass an inventive concept (Step 2B: NO); consider whether streamlined eligibility analysis (MPEP §2106.06) is appropriate for claims that clearly do not seek to tie up judicial exceptions.

name: Alice two-step framework
description: Patent eligibility is evaluated under Alice: (1) determine whether the claims are directed to a patent-ineligible concept (an 'abstract idea'); and (2) if so, determine whether the claim elements, individually and as an ordered combination, provide an 'inventive concept' sufficient to transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application.
guidance: Apply step 1 to identify the focus of the claims; if the claims are 'directed to' an abstract idea, proceed to step 2 to ask whether the claim contains something 'more' than the abstract idea—an inventive concept.

name: Directed-to-abstract-idea criterion
description: Claims are 'directed to' an abstract idea if they focus on collecting, analyzing, and/or displaying information or otherwise recite only the result or desired outcome without describing how to achieve it technologically.
guidance: The court will characterize the claims' focus; overly broad characterizations (e.g., merely 'collecting geographic information and displaying nearby stores') support finding an abstract idea when the claims lack technological detail.

name: Need for technological details or improvement
description: To avoid abstraction, claims must recite a particular assertedly inventive technology or improvement in computer functionality rather than generic functional language describing desired results.
guidance: Claims that 'merely use functional language to describe the desired result, without any technological details about how that result is implemented or that improves on existing computer technology' are susceptible to §101 invalidation.

name: Collecting/analyzing/displaying information is ordinarily abstract
description: Claims that are limited to gathering, analyzing, and displaying information—even if directed to a particular field—are generally treated as abstract ideas.
guidance: See Electric Power Group: tracking real-time changes and displaying results without claiming a particular way of collecting/analyzing/displaying is abstract. Limitations that only organize existing information into a new form do not overcome abstraction.

name: Concrete, specific rule-based implementations can be eligible (McRO example)
description: Claims that recite detailed, specific computerized rules or relationships that materially change how a task is performed can be patent eligible.
guidance: McRO upheld claims because they required rules rendered in a specific way (relationships between sub-sequences of phonemes, timing, and morph weight sets) and thus went beyond merely organizing information or automating conventional activity.

name: Inventive concept requirement at Alice step 2
description: At step 2, claims must include an inventive concept beyond well-understood, routine, conventional computer components or techniques; generic implementation on a computer is insufficient.
guidance: The inquiry asks whether limitations are described in highly generic functional terms and whether the patent 'invoke[s] any assertedly inventive programming,' 'new technique[s] for analyzing' data, or 'an arguably inventive set of components or methods' that generate new data.

name: Limiting to a field of endeavor does not confer eligibility
description: Restricting an abstract idea to a particular field (e.g., mapping or locating businesses) generally does not make the claim patent eligible.
guidance: Electric Power Group and similar precedents hold that field-specific limits do not transform a claim directed to information processing into patent-eligible subject matter absent a technological improvement.

name: Speed/efficiency improvements via conventional computers are insufficient
description: Claiming that added computer functionality increases the speed or efficiency of a process does not render an otherwise abstract idea patent-eligible.
guidance: Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One: 'merely adding computer functionality to increase the speed or efficiency of the process does not confer patent eligibility on an otherwise abstract idea.'

name: Specification admissions on conventionality
description: Statements in the patent specification admitting that components or techniques are conventional (e.g., that devices have GPS, display maps, search for businesses) can establish that claim limitations are well-known and routine.
guidance: A specification that acknowledges that generic and pre-existing computer functionality can perform all claimed steps limits plausible allegations that components were unconventional and thus can support §101 dismissal.

name: Denial of leave to amend for futility
description: A district court's denial of leave to amend is reviewed for abuse of discretion, but if denial is based on futility the court applies the legal sufficiency standard of Rule 12(b)(6) (i.e., de novo review of whether an amended complaint would state a claim).
guidance: Leave may be denied when any amendment would be futile—e.g., where the patent specification and intrinsic record demonstrate as a matter of law that the claims are directed to ineligible subject matter and cannot be cured by additional allegations or evidence.

name: Limit claims/description to materials/modes actually known to work
description: If the specification implies applicability to substances or methods not then known to be usable for the specified purpose, the patentee cannot be required to foresee later successful uses; the words should be understood as referring to materials then known to be available.
guidance: Lord Tenterden's approach: interpret 'other substances' as those known at the time to be available for the purpose, not everything which will burn in some sense.

name: Plainest and easiest mode must be disclosed (enablement in most practical form)
description: The patentee must point out the plainest and most easy way of producing what he claims and make the public acquainted with the mode he adopts.
guidance: Seidlitz powder case: if recipes produce ingredients that are available commercially, making the specification look like an elaborate essential process misleads and is bad.

name: If different claimed things include one that fails to produce the claimed effect, careful judgment required
description: If one claimed thing is later found not useful, courts have been reluctant to void the patent altogether unless the specification misled the public or presented the item as essential.
guidance: Lewis v. Marling and related cases: if a part was claimed but not described as essential and was initially thought necessary, later disuse may not void the patent; context and presentation matter.

name: The description must not give effects that cannot accurately be produced
description: Patentee should inform the inquirer of the exact nature of the manufacture; claiming results that cannot be produced is fatal to the grant.
guidance: Courts have invalidated patents where the product or results described in the specification did not in fact have the qualities or effects asserted.

name: Synchronization of application components
description: Connects and synchronizes every element of a patent application — specification, claims, figures, chemical structures and biological sequences — so that changes are reflected across the whole application.
guidance: Ensure part references, terminology and numbering are automatically synchronized across specification, claims and drawings to maintain consistency and reduce errors. Rowan positions this as fundamental to improving quality and compliance with drafting requirements.

name: Terminology and terms management
description: Import, define and manage key concepts and terminology consistently throughout the application leveraging a Terms Manager feature.
guidance: Maintain consistent usage of defined terms across claims, specification, and figures to avoid inconsistency-related examination problems and improve readability and legal robustness.

name: Antecedent basis and claim support checking
description: Analyze drafts to check for antecedent basis errors and whether claims are supported by the specification.
guidance: Automatically flag antecedent basis problems and missing claim support so drafters can correct specification language or claim wording before filing or amendment, reducing §112/112 rejections.

name: Predictive NLP for prosecution risk and classification
description: Use Natural Language Processing optimized for patent language to predict art units, potential 112 issues, drawing parts lists, claim trees and other prosecution-related analytics.
guidance: Leverage predictive analytics to anticipate examination risks and to prioritize drafting or amendment work; use predictions to inform prosecution strategy and reduce office actions.

name: Automated part numbering and integrated drawing tool
description: Built-in drawing tool designed for patent application drawings with numbering synchronized with other parts of the application and automatic part numbering.
guidance: Create figures and part references that automatically synchronize with claims and specification to avoid mismatches between drawings and text and to streamline figure creation.

name: Claim amendment synchronization and validation
description: Automate amendments with USPTO markup styling, claim status rollover, claim status inserts and automatic synchronization of amendments to parallel claim elements, and validate that amendments are supported in the specification.
guidance: When amending claims, ensure the system synchronizes changes across dependent claims, maintains formatting consistent with office expectations, and verifies that amended claim language has basis in the specification to reduce examination risk.

name: Maintain practitioner control over AI outputs
description: Task-based, AI-assisted tools enable control over inputs while managing generated outputs so practitioners retain full control of the drafting process.
guidance: Target sections appropriate for AI generation (e.g., summary, abstract, flowcharts, claim transformations), review and edit generated content, and tailor AI capabilities to organizational and practitioner preferences for responsible use.

name: Technology-specific support (chemistry & biotechnology)
description: Unique support for chemistry and biotechnology drafting needs, including compound and sequence management and an integrated chemical structure tool.
guidance: Use specialized tools for compound and sequence handling to ensure correct representation and linkage across specification, claims and figures in life-science/chemistry applications.

name: Consistency analysis across drafts, publications, and amendments
description: Review analyzes consistency of terms in draft applications, published applications, and amended claims for error checking and predictive analysis to improve prosecution outcomes.
guidance: Compare multiple document states (drafts, published apps, amended claims) to find inconsistencies that could harm prosecution or enforcement; use findings to correct the corpus before filing or submission.

name: Efficiency and measurable prosecution outcomes
description: Use of the tool should deliver productivity gains and reduced office actions (claims cited: 36% average productivity gain, 18% reduction in number of Office Actions, 44% fewer 112 rejections, 5x faster to prepare Office Action response shells).
guidance: Track quantitative KPIs (productivity, office action rates, time-to-response) to evaluate ROI of adopting the drafting/prosecution platform; use metrics to validate quality and process improvements.

name: Draft generation and claim transformation capabilities
description: Embedded, task-based GenAI assistants and AI chat with intelligent prompt assistance to generate and manage sections of draft applications such as summary, abstract, flowchart generation and claim transformations.
guidance: Employ AI to draft routine or structured sections and to perform claim transformations, but review generated outputs for legal sufficiency and alignment with strategy; use prompt assistance to guide AI toward jurisdictional and client-specific norms.

name: Mandatory contents of a patent application
description: A patent application should contain: Form-1 (application), proof of right (endorsement or assignment), provisional/complete specification (Form-2), Form-3 (Section 8) if applicable, Form-5 (declaration as to inventorship) where required, power of authority if filed through agent, priority documents if applicable, signatures and dates, drawings signed, and where biological material from India is used — permission from National Biodiversity Authority and source of geographical origin.
guidance: Section 7, Rule 8 and related provisions. Provisional specification cannot be filed for Convention applications. Fees vary based on pages/claims (First Schedule).

name: Provisional and complete specification requirements
description: Complete specification must include title, field of invention, prior art and problem to be solved, objects, summary, detailed description, drawings, abstract, best method, and claims; provisional specification and content rules apply where provisional is filed.
guidance: Chapter 5 (05.01–05.03). Filing complete specification within twelve months from provisional filing is mandatory; claims must be clear and unity respected.

name: Claims: structure, clarity, unity, scope and significance
description: Claims must be clear in structure and scope, show unity of invention and their significance and scope must be indicated in the specification; clarity and unity are examined and may be objected to.
guidance: 05.03.12–05.03.16. Examiner will raise objections on lack of clarity, lack of unity, or improper scope; applicants should draft claims to meet statutory/office expectations.

name: Offences and penalties under the Act
description: Various offences (contravening secrecy directions, falsification of register entries, unauthorized claim of patent rights, misuse of 'Patent Office' words, refusal/failure to supply information, practice by non-registered persons, offences by companies) attract penalties.
guidance: Chapter 16 lists specific contraventions and related consequences; enforcement provisions must be followed.

name: Refusal to search unclear or defective international applications
description: If the ISA considers the description, claims or drawings fail to comply with prescribed requirements to such an extent that a meaningful search cannot be carried out (e.g., unclear description or claims), it may declare it will not establish a search report, in whole or in part. Where only some claims are unsearchable, it will establish a partial search report for the searched claims.
guidance: Partial search report contains declaration under Article 17(2)(b) that certain claims were unsearchable. Multiple dependent claims not complying with Rule 6.4(a) second/third sentences may be unsearchable (see paragraph 5.113).

name: Required contents of the international search report
description: The ISR must contain citation of documents considered relevant, classification of the subject matter (IPC), an indication of fields searched (identified by classification) and any electronic database searched (including, where practicable, the search terms used). Citations of particular relevance must be specially indicated; citations not relevant to all claims must be related to the specific claim(s); relevant passages must be identified (page/column/lines). An ISR must not contain any expression of opinion, reasoning, argument or explanation of any kind.
guidance: Full details in Rule 43. Emphasis that ISR is purely a citation/classification document, not an opinion piece.

name: Applicant response opportunities to ISR and written opinion
description: Regulations do not specifically provide an opportunity to respond to the ISR, except that under Article 19 the applicant has one opportunity to amend the claims. For the written opinion, applicants may submit informal comments to the International Bureau to rebut the written opinion if international preliminary examination is not requested; there is no maximum word count for informal comments and they should be clearly identified as such.
guidance: Informal comments will be made publicly available on PATENTSCOPE; recommended to submit before 28 months from priority to ensure availability to designated Offices upon national phase entry. Comments after 30 months will be kept in IB file but not transmitted. Formal responses must be filed with an IPEA under Article 34 as part of Chapter II; if a demand for Chapter II is filed, informal comments under Chapter I will not be forwarded to designated Offices but remain public.

name: Nature and timing of the written opinion of the ISA
description: The ISA establishes, at the same time as the ISR or accompanying declaration, a preliminary and non‑binding written opinion on whether the claimed invention appears to be novel, to involve an inventive step and to be industrially applicable (similar in scope to the written opinion by IPEA). The written opinion is established within the same time limits as the ISR (3 months from receipt of the search copy or 9 months from priority date) and is in the language in which the ISR is established.
guidance: Ref: Rule 43bis.1(a), Article 18(1), Rule 42. The relevant prior‑art date for the written opinion is the international filing date or the priority date where priority claimed (different from the date used in establishing the ISR).

name: Identification of the international application in Box I of the supplementary search request
description: The applicant should clearly identify the international application by its international application number, international filing date (use specified date format) and title, as provided for in Box No. I. If a new title has been established by the ISA, that title should be indicated. Where several priorities claimed, the earliest filing date should be indicated as the priority date; a file reference not exceeding 25 characters may be added.
guidance: Ref: Rule 45bis.1(b)(i), Section 109, Section 110. Accurate identification avoids misrouting.

name: Date of commencement of damages — products: marking and notice rules
description: Damages commence on the date the alleged infringer has both infringed and been notified of the alleged infringement. If patentee sells a product that includes the claimed invention, determine whether the patentee has 'marked' the product with the patent number (placing 'patent' or 'pat.' with the number on substantially all products). Patentee bears burden of proving substantial compliance with marking.
guidance: If patentee substantially complied with marking (including reasonable efforts by licensees), constructive notice applies and damages begin without actual notice. If not marked, damages begin on date alleged infringer received actual notice (filing of the complaint qualifies). If patent granted after infringing activity began, damages calculated from patent issue date; if patent granted before infringing activity began, from date infringement began. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. § 287; Crystal Semiconductor; Maxwell; Nike; Am. Med. Sys.; Devices for Med.

name: Amendment (glossary definition)
description: Amendment: A patent applicant’s change to one or more claims or to the specification either in response to an office action taken by an Examiner or independently by the patent applicant during the patent application examination process.

name: Claim (glossary definition)
description: Claim: Each claim of a patent is a concise, formal definition of an invention and appears at the end of the specification in a separately numbered paragraph. A claim marks the boundaries of the patent; claims may be independent or dependent (dependent claims refer to and incorporate other claims).
guidance: A device or method infringes only if it contains each and every requirement (limitation) of a claim.

name: Elements / Limitations / Requirement (glossary definitions)
description: Elements / Limitation / Requirement: The required parts of a device or the required steps of a method. A limitation/requirement is a required part of an invention set forth in a patent claim and is often used interchangeably with the word 'requirement.'
guidance: A device or method infringes a patent if it contains each and every requirement (limitation) of a patent claim.

name: Examination (glossary definition)
description: Examination: Procedure before the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office whereby an Examiner reviews the filed patent application to determine if the claimed invention is patentable.

name: Patent (glossary definition)
description: Patent: An exclusive right granted by the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office to an inventor to prevent others from making, using, or selling an invention for a term of 20 years from the date the patent application was filed (or 17 years from issuance). The patent has three parts: specification, drawings, and claims; it is granted after examination (prosecution history).

name: Specification (glossary definition)
description: Specification: A required part of a patent application and an issued patent. It is a written description of the invention and of the manner and process of making and using the claimed invention.

name: Effective filing date for continuation/divisional (35 U.S.C. 120/365(c))
description: If the application is a continuation or divisional of one or more earlier U.S. applications or international applications and the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 120 or 365(c) are satisfied, the effective filing date of the claimed invention is the same as the earliest filing date in the line of continuation or divisional applications.
guidance: Requires satisfaction of the statutory benefit/priority requirements (35 U.S.C. 120/365(c)). See related MPEP sections for determination in PCT national-stage continuations (e.g., §§211.01(c), 1895).

name: Effective filing date for continuation-in-part (CIP)
description: If the application is a continuation-in-part of an earlier U.S. application or international application, any claims in the new application not supported by the specification and claims of the parent application have an effective filing date equal to the actual filing date of the new application; any claims fully supported under 35 U.S.C. 112 by the earlier parent application have the effective filing date of that earlier parent application.
guidance: Distinguish per-claim support: unsupported/new matter -> new filing date; fully supported claims -> benefit of earlier parent's date under 35 U.S.C.112. Verify written-description support in parent and any intermediate applications.

name: Effective filing date when claiming provisional benefit (35 U.S.C. 119(e))
description: If the application properly claims benefit under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) to a provisional application, the effective filing date of the claimed invention is the filing date of the provisional application for any claims which are fully supported under the first paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112 by the provisional application.
guidance: At least one claim in the reference seeking provisional benefit must be supported by the provisional's written description in compliance with pre-AIA 35 U.S.C.112 first paragraph (see Dynamic Drinkware; Amgen v. Sanofi).

name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) prior-art date rules
description: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) allows the use of certain international application publications, U.S. patent application publications, and certain U.S. patents as prior art as of their respective U.S. filing dates, and may use an international filing date as the prior-art date if the international filing date was on or after November 29, 2000, the international application designated the United States, and it was published by WIPO under PCT Article 21(2) in English.
guidance: References based on international applications filed prior to Nov. 29, 2000 are subject to the pre-AIPA version of 102(e). See MPEP §2136 for detailed examination guidelines. Determine whether the reference’s prior-art date is the international filing date or an earlier U.S. filing date for which priority/benefit is properly claimed.

name: Form paragraph 7.12.fti — Pre-AIA 102(e) (AIPA/2002 amendments) guidance
description: Form paragraph for pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejections, including the statute text and extensive Examiner Notes specifying when the paragraph should be used (types of references, PCT conditions, benefit/priority claim considerations, provisional support requirements, and non-application of foreign priority claims).
guidance: Examiner Notes include: (1) use only for U.S. patents/pubs filed under 111(a), or PCT-derived refs with international filing date on/after Nov.29,2000, or designating US design patents; (2) consider benefit claims under 119(e), 120, 121, 365(c), 386(c) only if subject matter is appropriately supported in earlier-filed disclosures; (3) provisional benefit requires at least one claim in the reference be supported by the provisional in compliance with pre-AIA 112 first paragraph; (4) if PCT publication not in English or did not designate US, may not be applied under 102(e) but may under 102(a)/(b); (5) various additional cautions and precedence rules. Must be preceded by 7.07.fti and may be preceded by 7.08–7.11.fti as appropriate.

name: Form paragraph 7.12.01.fti — Pre-AIPA 102(e) for refs from PCT filed prior to Nov.29,2000
description: Form paragraph for references that are U.S. patents issued directly or indirectly from international applications with international filing dates prior to November 29, 2000; uses pre-AIPA 102(e) rules to determine prior-art date.
guidance: Examiner Notes: (1) use only for U.S. patents issued from national stage/continuations of PCT filings pre-Nov.29,2000; (2) prior-art date may be date of compliance with 371(c)(1),(2),(4) if national stage; (3) if issued from continuing application claiming benefit under 120/121/365(c), prior-art date may be actual U.S. filing date of continuing app; (4) consider benefit claims to earlier-filed U.S. provisionals/nonprovisionals only if subject matter is supported; (5) provisional benefit requires 112 support. Must be preceded by 7.07.fti.

name: Form paragraph 7.15.fti — Rejection format for pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a),(b),(g)
description: Template rejection: 'Claim(s) [1] is/are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 [2] as being [3] by [4].' with instructions for inserting appropriate paragraph letters, characterization (clearly anticipated/anticipated), and identification of prior art relied upon.
guidance: Must be preceded by 7.07.fti (and possibly 7.08–7.14.fti or 7.103); if 102(e) also applied use accompanying specific 7.15.01–7.15.03 paragraphs; for certain applications (filed on/after Mar.16,2013 with earlier priority) precede with 7.06. Follow bracket guidance for correct insertion and explanations.

name: Form paragraph 7.15.01.fti — Provisional rejection under 102(e) for copending application with common assignee/applicant/joint inventor
description: Provisional rejection when a copending application with an earlier filing date (and common assignee/applicant/at least one common joint inventor) discloses the claimed invention; based upon presumption of future publication/patenting of the copending application.
