guidance: Used for copending apps not yet published under 122. May be overcome by showing under 37 C.F.R. 1.132 that invention disclosed in the copending app was derived from applicant (not 'by another') or by 37 C.F.R. 1.131(a) if not same invention. Cannot be overcome by terminal disclaimer. Consider nonstatutory double patenting and require claim amendment/cancellation as appropriate; use relevant double-patenting paragraphs (8.30–8.39) where needed. For apps with filing dates on/after Mar.16,2013 claiming priority to pre-Mar.16,2013, precede with 7.06.

name: Form paragraph 7.15.02.fti — Rejection under 102(e) where reference has common assignee/applicant/joint inventor
description: Rejection that claims are anticipated under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) by a reference that has a common assignee, applicant, or at least one common joint inventor; based on earlier effective U.S. filing date of the reference.
guidance: Examiner Notes: (1) use only when reference is a U.S. patent or publication with earlier effective filing date and has common assignee/applicant/joint inventor; (2) apply AIPA/2002 amended 102(e) if appropriate (or pre-AIPA rules for PCT refs filed before Nov.29,2000); (3) consider benefit claims to earlier-filed provisionals/nonprovisionals only if subject matter is properly supported; (4) a provisional reference must have at least one claim supported by the provisional under pre-AIA 112 first paragraph; (5) PCT pubs not in English/did not designate US do not qualify for 102(e) and should be applied under 102(a)/(b); (6) use appropriate additional form paragraphs for double patenting, priority, and obviousness (e.g., 8.33–8.39, 7.13.fti, 7.14.fti, 7.21.01.fti). Must be preceded by 7.12.fti or 7.12.01.fti.

name: Form paragraph 7.15.03.fti — Rejection under 102(e) where no common assignee or inventor
description: Rejection that claims are anticipated under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) by a patent or patent application publication with an earlier filing date, where the reference is not required to have a common assignee or common inventor.
guidance: Apply amended 102(e) as appropriate (AIPA/2002), consider whether the reference qualifies under 7.12.fti (PCT conditions, provisional support, benefit claims). If the reference is a PCT publication filed prior to Nov.29,2000 or not in English/did not designate US, do not use 7.15.03.fti — instead consider 102(a)/(b). Precede with 7.12.fti or other required paragraphs.

name: Placement of claims in document
description: APPEARS TOWARDS THE END OF THE ISSUED PATENT OR PATENT APPLICATION.
guidance: Claims are normally located near the end of the patent document or application specification.

name: Parts of a claim — overall structure
description: A claim comprises: a. THE PREAMBLE; b. TRANSITIONAL PHRASE; c. THE BODY.
guidance: All claims should be drafted with these three parts in mind; each part has distinct functions and wording conventions.

name: Transitional phrase — open-ended 'comprising'
description: OPEN-ENDED PHRASE (comprising) — 'including', 'containing', 'characterized by' — do not exclude any additional unrecited elements — expand the scope of the claim by allowing for other elements or limitations.
guidance: Use 'comprising' or similar open terms when you intend to allow additional, unrecited components; example format: 'An apparatus, comprising: element1; element2; and element3.'

name: Transitional phrase — closed 'consisting of'
description: CLOSED PHRASE (consisting of) — limits the scope of the claim to nothing more than the specifically recited elements — claim covers only elements named and nothing more.
guidance: Use 'consisting of' to exclude any additional elements. For compositions, percentages should add up to 100% when using 'consisting of' (example chemical compound consisting of 50% A; 25% B; 25% C).

name: Body of the claim — elements and relationships
description: Must recite elements and limitation of the Claim. Explains how the different elements exist in relationship to one another.
guidance: Do not merely catalog parts; show how elements are connected or interact. Example contrasting weak vs proper body: 'four legs; 16 screws; and a top.' (mere list) versus 'a head portion connected to the handle; and a protrusion being secured to the handle.' (shows relationships).

name: Improvement (Jepson) type claims
description: Preamble – statement of the most relevant prior art. Transitional Phrase – 'wherein the improvement comprises'. The body – provides the novel feature/s of the invention.
guidance: Use this format to highlight improvements over cited prior art. Example: 'A game device having [prior art elements], wherein the improvement comprises a protrusion being secured to the handle.'

name: Means‑plus‑function claims
description: Recite function performed by structures disclosed in the specification instead of specifically defined structures. Interpretation varies from jurisdiction to jurisdiction. The means‑plus‑function clauses recited in the claim must be adequately described by the structure carrying the recited function.
guidance: When using 'means for ...' ensure the specification discloses corresponding structure to avoid indefiniteness; jurisdictional interpretation differs, so check local law. Example: 'a means for holding rice; and a heater configured to heat the rice-holding means.'

name: Claim punctuation conventions
description: A comma separates the preamble from the transitional phrase. A colon separates the transitional phrase from the body. The small paragraphs that define and describe the logical elements are separated with semi colons.
guidance: Follow punctuation rules to improve clarity and conform to practice: Preamble, transitional phrase: Element (#1); Element (#2); and Element (#3). Use colon after 'comprising:' and semicolons between elements; use commas appropriately before transitional/characterizing clauses.

name: Reference numerals and bracket expressions
description: Claims may include reference numerals and bracket expressions (e.g., An apparatus (10), comprising: a plurality of printed pages (11); a binding (12)... ).
guidance: Reference numerals may be used to link claim elements to drawings but are not substitute limitations. Bracketed numerals can clarify correspondence to figures.

name: Special claim phrases to define structure or function
description: Use of special words such as 'wherein', 'whereby', 'such that' to further define a structure or provide a function associated with a given structure.
guidance: Use these clauses to add functional or relational limitations (e.g., 'a cover attached to the binding, wherein the cover is detachable from the binding'). Place such clauses appropriately (often after a comma or characterizing phrase).

name: Multiple elements requirement (minimum elements)
description: Many patent offices including the IPPHL require claims to recite at least two elements.
guidance: Avoid single-element claims in jurisdictions that require multiple elements; provide at least two elements (e.g., processor and memory) unless a single-element claim is permissible.

name: Independent claim characteristics
description: INDEPENDENT CLAIM — BROADEST CLAIM. STAND ALONE AND DOES NOT NEED A LIMITATION FROM ANOTHER CLAIM IN ORDER TO BE COMPLETE. PATENT APPLICATION MAY HAVE MORE THAN ONE (1) INDEPENDENT CLAIM.
guidance: Draft independent claims to capture the broadest inventive concept while remaining supportable in the specification. It's acceptable to have multiple independent claims directed to different aspects (apparatus, method, composition).

name: Dependent claim characteristics and limits
description: DEPENDENT CLAIM — DEPENDS ON ANOTHER (EITHER AN INDEPENDENT CLAIM OR DEPENDENT CLAIM). MUST NOT EXTEND THE SCOPE OF THE PROTECTION OF THE INVENTION DEFINED IN THE INDEPENDENT CLAIM/S. 'FALL BACK' DURING EXAMINATION.
guidance: Dependent claims should add limitations narrowing an independent claim and provide fallback positions during prosecution. Ensure dependency language correctly references the claim(s) relied upon.

name: Apparatus claim specifics
description: Apparatus Claims — Protect an apparatus or device. Recite in the preamble what the apparatus 'is' and/or 'what it does'. Recite in the claim's body the essential inventive elements.
guidance: Structure apparatus claims with a clear preamble and body reciting the inventive elements and their relationships (example: camera support with pivotal mounting and legs).

name: Method claim specifics
description: Method Claims — Recite a sequence of steps that complete a task or accomplish a result. Active Steps may be recited in order of performance, but are usually interpreted as being performed in any order unless otherwise specified.
guidance: If step order is critical, state it explicitly; otherwise courts/offices may treat steps as order-independent. Example method claim enumerates boiling water; adding sugar; adding tea leaves; filtering; adding milk.

name: Composition claim specifics
description: Composition claim — Used where claimed invention pertains to the chemical nature of the materials or components used. Claims a 'thing' like a device claim.
guidance: Recite components and, where needed, their relative amounts or ranges. Example electroplating solution listing components and amounts (grams per liter, pH-modifying substrate quantities). Consider using 'comprising' vs 'consisting of' depending on scope intent.

name: Product‑by‑process claims
description: Product-by-Process Claims — Claims a product defined in terms of a process of manufacture. Some jurisdictions treat as product claims; other jurisdictions treat as method claims.
guidance: Verify that claiming a product-by-process is the best approach for protection; consequences for patentability/enforceability vary by jurisdiction. Example: 'A metallic salt obtained by a process comprising the steps of ...'.

name: Deposited material and the Budapest Treaty
description: Where an invention involves a biological material, and the material has been deposited, then the patent agent may often claim the material deposited. The Budapest Treaty requires signatory countries to recognize a deposit with any depository approved by WIPO.
guidance: Include deposit accession numbers in claims/specification and confirm the depository is WIPO-approved to ensure cross-jurisdictional recognition under the Budapest Treaty.

name: Software claim formats
description: Software Claims — Used where the claimed invention pertains to computer software and/or hardware. Can use device and method claims to cover software inventions. Can also use specialized claim formats to provide an additional scope of protection.
guidance: Consider multiple claim formats (apparatus, method, computer-readable medium, data structure) to maximize protection. Draft claims to avoid purely abstract formulations where local law requires technical character.

name: Computer‑readable medium claim format
description: Software claim type — 'computer readable media' format: 'A computer-readable storage medium storing instructions that when executed by a computer cause the computer to perform a method for using a computer system to [a specified function], the method comprising: [list the inventive method steps].'
guidance: Use this format to claim software implemented inventions in a tangible medium. Ensure the claimed instructions map to inventive technical steps disclosed in the specification.

name: Data structure claim format
description: Software claim type — 'data structure' format: 'A memory for storing data for access by an application program being executed on a data processing system, comprising: a data structure stored in the memory, the data structure including information resident in a database used by the application program and including: a first data object configured to … a second data object configured to …; and a third data object configured to ….','
guidance: Use data-structure style claims to claim particular data arrangements or schemas that embody inventive aspects; recite relationships and configurations of data objects.

name: Omnibus claims
description: Omnibus Claims — Refer to the description or the drawings without providing any specific limitations. Examples: 'An apparatus for harvesting corn as described in the description.' 'A juice machine as shown in Figure 4.' Not all patent offices allow omnibus claims.
guidance: Omnibus claims are simple but their acceptability varies by office; include an omnibus claim where possible but base prosecution strategy primarily on other claim types that define clear technical limitations.

name: Design claims — limitation on number
description: Design claim — Only one claim is typically permitted.
guidance: For design patents/registrations, draft a single claim to the ornamental design (e.g., 'The ornamental design for an umbrella substantially as shown.'). Include appropriate figures.

name: Legible copy requirements (37 CFR 1.98(a)(2))
description: FR 1.98(a)(2) requires a legible copy of: (A) each foreign patent; (B) each publication or that portion which caused it to be listed, other than U.S. patents and U.S. patent application publications unless required by the Office; (C) for each cited pending unpublished U.S. application, the application specification including the claims, and any drawing of the application, or that portion of the application which caused it to be listed including any claims directed to that portion; and (D) all other information or that portion which caused it to be listed.
guidance: Submit legible copies of the exact portions that caused the reference to be listed; follow 37 CFR 1.98(a)(2) when preparing an IDS or otherwise submitting references.

name: Contents: entire specification, claims, drawings; no new matter; two-year limit for broadened claims (37 CFR 1.173)
description: An application for reissue must contain the entire specification, including the claims, and the drawings of the patent. No new matter shall be introduced into the application. No reissue patent shall be granted enlarging the scope of the claims of the original patent unless applied for within two years from the grant of the original patent, pursuant to 35 U.S.C. 251.
guidance: Ensure the reissue includes a full copy of the printed patent specification and drawings; do not add new matter; note the two-year bar for claim broadening.

name: Specification copy format and required accompanying documents
description: The entire specification, including the claims, of the patent for which reissue is requested must be furnished as a copy of the printed patent, in double column format, each page on only one side of a single sheet of paper. A re-typed specification is not acceptable. A copy of any disclaimer (37 CFR 1.321), certificate of correction (37 CFR 1.322–1.324), or reexamination certificate (37 CFR 1.570) issued in the patent must be included.
guidance: Preserve columnar structure and formatting rules (37 CFR 1.52); include prior certificates/disclaimers so the reissue is relative to the patent as last changed.

name: Amendment presentation and formatting rules (37 CFR 1.173(b)-(e),(g) and 1.52)
description: An amendment may be submitted at the time of filing of a reissue application either by (A) physically incorporating the changes within the specification by cutting the column of the printed patent and inserting the added material and rejoining the remainder of the column (markings pursuant to 37 CFR 1.173(d) must be used) with the columnar structure preserved and the physically modified page complying with 37 CFR 1.52(a)(1), or (B) providing a separate amendment paper with the reissue application.
guidance: A caret and line from text to a newly added phrase typed legibly in the margin is deemed to satisfy the 'written by typewriter or machine printer in permanent dark ink' requirement under 1.52(a)(1)(iv). Presentation of insertions/deletions as part of original reissue specification is an amendment under 37 CFR 1.173(b); follow MPEP §1453 for amendment practice. A preliminary amendment cancelling all original claims without presenting any new claims is inappropriate under 37 CFR 1.115(b)(1).

name: Claims requirement at filing (reissue vs 37 CFR 1.53(b))
description: The provision allowing an application to be accorded a filing date 'with or without' claims (37 CFR 1.53(b)) does not apply in reissue applications because 37 CFR 1.173(a)(1) requires the entire specification, including the claims, of the original patent.
guidance: Do not file a reissue application without claims; a preliminary amendment that cancels all claims without new claims is improper.

name: Inventor's oath or declaration rules for reissue (37 CFR 1.175)
description: The inventor, or each individual who is a joint inventor of a claimed invention in a reissue application must execute an oath or declaration for the reissue application, except as provided in 37 CFR 1.64. The inventor's oath or declaration may be signed by the assignee of the entire interest if: (1) the application does not seek to enlarge the scope of the claims of the original patent; or (2) the application for the original patent was filed under 37 CFR 1.46 by the assignee of the entire interest.
guidance: A reissue applicant may file a substitute statement in lieu of the inventor’s oath or declaration as provided in 37 CFR 1.64. For continuation/divisional reissue applications, a copy of an earlier reissue oath/declaration may be used provided certain conditions (no claim broadening or earlier original filing-by-assignee conditions) are met. See MPEP §1414 for forms PTO/AIA/05 and PTO/AIA/06 and additional content requirements.

name: Test of Enablement (undue experimentation)
description: Whether the disclosure, when filed, contained sufficient information regarding the subject matter of the claims as to enable one skilled in the pertinent art to make and use the claimed invention; cast as whether the experimentation needed to practice the invention is undue or unreasonable.
guidance: Apply the Minerals Separation/Hyde formulation and related precedent (e.g., In re Wands; United States v. Telectronics): the proper test is whether a person reasonably skilled in the art could make or use the invention from the patent disclosures plus knowledge in the art without undue experimentation. The specification need not teach what is well known in the art.

name: Scope of claim vs enablement (broader claims require broader enablement)
description: If a patent claims an entire class (genus) of processes, machines, manufactures, or compositions of matter, the specification must enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the entire class; 'the more one claims, the more one must enable.'
guidance: Amgen (2023) applied this principle to invalidated genus antibody claims that were defined functionally; broader functional/genus claims will require disclosure enabling the full scope. The specification does not always need to describe every embodiment, but broader claim scope increases the disclosure burden.

name: Functional claiming and risk of non-enablement
description: Functionally defined genus claims (claims defined by result or function rather than structure) are at risk of failing enablement if the specification does not adequately enable the full scope of the claimed functionally-defined class.
guidance: Example: Amgen's claims to a genus of antibodies defined by binding function were found not to enable the full scope. Functional claiming without structural or enabling guidance across the genus can render claims invalid for lack of enablement.

name: Examples plus general quality disclosure may suffice for genus enablement
description: A few examples can suffice to enable a claimed class if the specification also discloses some general quality running through the class that gives it a peculiar fitness for the particular purpose, thereby reliably enabling the full class.
guidance: The specification need not describe with particularity every embodiment if it discloses general qualities or principles that reliably enable the class. However, courts will evaluate whether those examples and generalizations truly enable the full claimed scope (Amgen discussion).

name: Swiss three-prong test (Switzerland)
description: Federal Patent Court of Switzerland adopted an approach similar to the German three-prong test, asking three questions:
guidance:
The three questions (as used by the Swiss court):
1) Do the replaced features have the same objective function (same effect)?
2) Are the replaced features and their same objective function obvious to a person skilled in the art on the basis of the teaching of the patent (accessibility)?
3) After reading the wording of the claim in light of the description, would a person skilled in the art consider the replaced features as a solution of equal value (equal value)?
Guidance/examples: Swiss decisions applied these questions to deny or find equivalence (e.g., denial where patent teaching explicitly allowed replacement of toxic chromium by metallic catalysts and the alternative TEMPO was not a solution of equal value; finding of equivalence where replacement was basic undergraduate knowledge). The Federal Supreme Court has affirmed the approach in later cases but may analyze embodiments and 'key teachings' of the patent.

name: Purposive construction (UK/Catnic)
description: UK courts moved from literal/textual infringement to a 'purposive construction' of patent claims: the question is whether a skilled person reading the patent would understand that strict compliance with a word or phrase within the claim was intended by the patentee to be an essential requirement.
guidance: Purposive construction balances literal claim wording against patent description and drawings to avoid purely literalism and to identify which claim terms are essential. It underpins later UK approaches (Improver/Protocol questions and the Actavis formulation).

name: Improver/Protocol questions (UK historical three-step test)
description: A three-step test (the 'Improver' or 'Protocol' questions) became widely used in the UK to determine non-literal infringement prior to the Actavis reform.
guidance: The Improver questions provided a structured means of assessing whether a variant was equivalent to a claimed element. (The Wikipedia entry notes these questions became stable with Improver v Remington and Kirin-Amgen decisions, but does not reproduce their exact wording here.)

name: 35 U.S.C. § 112 ¶ 6 statutory equivalents (means-plus-function) (United States)
description: The United States has a statutory equivalents doctrine codified in 35 U.S.C. § 112 ¶ 6, which extends to equivalents available at the patent's issuance and applies to means-plus-function claims.
guidance: Means-plus-function claims under §112¶6 are construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents. The statutory regime limits how equivalents are assessed for such claim language.

name: Judicial doctrine of equivalents (United States — Warner-Jenkinson / triple-identity)
description: The US judicial doctrine of equivalents (non-statutory) extends to technological equivalents developed after the patent is granted and is applied to individual claim limitations. The legal test (Warner-Jenkinson Co. v. Hilton Davis Chem. Co.) asks whether the difference is 'insubstantial.'
guidance:
One way to assess 'insubstantial' difference is the 'triple identity' test: the accused feature
- performs substantially the same function,
- in substantially the same way,
- to obtain the same result
as the limitation literally recited in the claim. The doctrine also applies when two elements are interchangeable and a person of ordinary skill in the art would have known they were interchangeable at the time of infringement. The doctrine operates limitation-by-limitation (not to the invention as a whole).

name: Prosecution history estoppel (United States — limit on equivalents)
description: Prosecution history estoppel prevents a patentee from recapturing through equivalents subject-matter that was surrendered during patent prosecution by amendment or argument narrowing claim scope.
guidance: If the patentee abandoned certain literal claim coverage by amending claims during prosecution (e.g., narrowing), the patentee is estopped from later arguing that the surrendered coverage is insubstantially different from the literally claimed limitation. This limits the reach of the doctrine of equivalents.

name: Public dedication / disclosure dedication rule (United States)
description: A patentee may not invoke the doctrine of equivalents to recapture subject matter that was disclosed in the patent specification but not claimed (public dedication principle).
guidance: Material that was described in the specification but expressly or implicitly left unclaimed is treated as dedicated to the public and cannot later be reclaimed by equivalents arguments.

name: WIPO Basic Proposal Article 21(2) equivalents test (harmonization attempt)
description: WIPO's 1991 'Basic Proposal' for a Treaty Supplementing the Paris Convention proposed that a claim shall cover equivalents and set out two alternative conditions under which an element is generally considered equivalent:
guidance:
The two conditions (as quoted):
(b)(i) 'the equivalent element performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way and produces substantially the same result as the element as expressed in the claim,' or
(b)(ii) 'it is obvious to a person skilled in the art that the same result as that achieved by means of the element as expressed in the claim can be achieved by means of the equivalent element.'
This proposal illustrates harmonization attempts but is not binding international law.

name: EPC 2000 Protocol on the Interpretation of Article 69 (European approach to equivalents)
description: EPC 2000 amended the Protocol on the Interpretation of Article 69 to require courts of contracting states to take due account when considering infringement 'of any element which is an equivalent to an element specified in the claims.'
guidance: The Protocol amendment instructs courts to consider equivalents when determining extent of protection but did not define 'equivalent', so national courts retain interpretive freedom; the amendment aimed to foster uniformity but its lack of a binding definition limits harmonization.

name: Prohibited content and phrasing (no merits/speculation/title repetition/stock phrases/claim-style language)
description: Do NOT contain statements on the alleged merits or value of the claimed invention; NOT contain statements on speculative application; NOT repeat information given in the title; NOT use phrases that can be implied ('The disclosure concerns,' 'This invention relates to'); NOT use claim-style phraseology like 'means' and 'said'.
guidance: Avoid promotional language, speculation about applications, redundant title text, boilerplate lead-ins, and claim terminology. Using claim terms like 'means' or 'said' risks turning the abstract into claim recitation; instead use plain technical terms.

name: Required content elements (what to include)
description: A good abstract should include: a statement of what the invention is (technical area); the technical features of the invention; the principal use of the invention; a short summary of the technical disclosure.
guidance: Ensure the abstract states the field/technical area in opening words, summarizes the principal technical features and principal use, and provides a brief summary of the technical disclosure sufficient for search/classification purposes without claim formalities.

name: Best-practice drafting techniques
description: Write the abstract last, after claims are finalized; mirror the broadest independent claim language (without claim formality); use clear technical terms searchable by examiners and the public; include the field of technology in opening words; avoid trademark designations and trade names.
guidance: Draft the abstract after claims to ensure it reflects claim scope; echo the broadest independent claim's concepts but in narrative form (not in claim syntax). Prefer generic technical terminology (avoid trade names/trademarks) to improve searchability and classification.

name: Specific factual conduct factors evidencing unreasonable/unexplained delay or abuse
description: Enumerated prosecution behaviors that indicate unreasonable or unexplained delay or constitute abuse of the patent system: (i) presenting claims many years or decades after their priority dates; (ii) bulk-filing many photocopied applications; (iii) failing to demarcate/divide applications as instructed; (iv) dramatically increasing/unduly multiplying claims (contrary to 37 C.F.R. 1.75(b)); (v) rewriting/shifting claims in large part or entirety (contrary to 37 C.F.R. §1.145); (vi) presenting numerous duplicate or patentably indistinct claims across applications without informing the PTO (contrary to MPEP §§2001.06(b), 2004(9)); (vii) failing to identify written-description support for claims (contrary to MPEP §§714.02, 2163.06); (viii) re‑filing claims previously lost in interference proceedings; (ix) failing to take allowed claims but refiling them years later; (x) failing to prosecute §145 actions.
guidance: The opinion repeatedly cites these specific practices (and cites the CFR and MPEP provisions) as evidence of abusive or unexplainable delay in Hyatt’s prosecution. The court treats these factors cumulatively under the totality-of-the-circumstances test.

name: Standard of review on appeal and Rule 52(c) context
description: Appellate standards: district court factual findings reviewed for clear error; legal conclusions reviewed de novo; the district court’s determination of prosecution laches is reviewed for abuse of discretion. Rule 52(c) may be used for judgment on partial findings in nonjury trials when a party has been fully heard on an issue.
guidance: From opinion: “We review the district court’s factual findings for clear error and its legal conclusions de novo... We review a district court’s determination of prosecution laches for abuse of discretion... Rule 52(c) provides that, in a nonjury trial, if a party has been fully heard on an issue and the court finds against the party on that issue, ‘the court may enter judgment against the party on a claim or defense that... can be maintained or defeated only with a favorable finding on that issue.’” The court vacated a Rule 52(c) judgment and remanded for further proceedings.

name: Two-way distinctness and reasons for insisting on restriction
description: Where claims to a combination and claims to subcombinations are presented together and the combination requires the particulars of at least one subcombination, both two-way distinctness and reasons for insisting on restriction are necessary.
guidance: Two-way distinctness must be shown (see subsequent relationship-specific tests). Restriction is only proper when there would be a serious burden if restriction were not required, as evidenced by separate classification, status, or field of search (see MPEP § 806.05(c)). Use form paragraphs such as 8.16 for subcombinations. If inability to show two-way distinctness or reasons for burden, restriction should not be required.

name: Subcombination distinctness
description: Each subcombination is distinct from the combination as claimed if: (A) the combination does not require the particulars of the subcombination as claimed for patentability (e.g., to show novelty and unobviousness), and (B) the subcombination can be shown to have utility either by itself or in another materially different combination.
guidance: See MPEP § 806.05(c) and form paragraph 8.16. Examiner must show by example that one of the subcombinations has utility other than in the disclosed combination. If applicant elects a subcombination and claims thereto are found allowable, withdrawn claims that depend from or require all limitations of the allowable subcombination will be examined for patentability per 37 CFR 1.104 (MPEP § 821.04). If applicant rebuts examiner's suggested alternate use as impossible/unreasonable, burden shifts to examiner to document a viable alternative use or withdraw the requirement.

name: Process and apparatus distinctness
description: A process and apparatus for its practice are distinct if either: (A) the process as claimed can be practiced by another materially different apparatus or by hand; or (B) the apparatus as claimed can be used to practice another materially different process (MPEP § 806.05(e)).
guidance: Form paragraph 8.17 may be used. The examiner bears the burden to provide reasonable examples that recite material differences (the example need not be documented). If applicant proves there is no material difference or that a process cannot be performed by hand (if so argued by examiner), the burden shifts to the examiner to document another materially different process or apparatus or withdraw the requirement. A process can be practiced by hand if it can be performed without using any apparatus.

name: Product and process of using distinctness
description: A product and a process of using the product are distinct if either: (A) the process of using as claimed can be practiced with another materially different product; or (B) the product as claimed can be used in a materially different process (MPEP § 806.05(h)).
guidance: Form paragraphs 8.20 and 8.21.04 should be used for restriction requirements between product and method of using. The examiner must provide an example (not necessarily documented). If applicant proves the alternative use cannot be accomplished, the burden shifts to the examiner to support a viable alternative use or withdraw the requirement. All restriction requirements between product and process of using should be followed by form paragraph 8.21.04 to notify applicants about potential rejoinder.

name: Related products or related processes distinctness criteria
description: To support restriction between two or more related product inventions or related process inventions, both two-way distinctness and reasons for insisting on restriction are necessary. For related inventions (not combination/subcombination), inventions are distinct if: (A) the inventions as claimed do not overlap in scope (mutually exclusive); (B) the inventions as claimed are not obvious variants; and (C) the inventions as claimed are either not capable of use together or can have a materially different design, mode of operation, function, or effect (MPEP § 806.05(j)).
guidance: The burden is on the examiner to provide an example to support the determination (example need not be documented). Intermediate vs final product example: distinctness if intermediate useful to make other than the final product and species are patentably distinct. See form paragraphs 8.14.01, 8.14 (intermediate-final), and 8.16 (subcombinations) as appropriate. If generic or linking claims are present, see MPEP § 809.

name: Linking claims and effect on restriction
description: Linking claims are claims which, if allowable, would require rejoinder of otherwise divisible inventions (e.g., genus claims linking species, subcombination claims linking plural combinations).
guidance: Linking claims and the inventions they link are usually all products or all processes. Where an application includes distinct inventions and linking claims, restriction can still be required; linking claims must be examined with and considered part of the invention elected. When all claims directed to the elected invention are allowable, any allowable linking claim requires withdrawal of the restriction and rejoining of previously withdrawn claims that depend from or require all limitations of the allowable linking claim. If withdrawn claims were cancelled by applicant, examiner must notify applicant that canceled nonelected claims depending from an allowable linking claim may be reinstated by amendment and then fully examined for patentability (see MPEP § 821.04).

name: Election of species — when required and grouping unpatentable species
description: Election of species may be required even prior to a search (A) in applications with a plurality of species and no generic claims, and (B) in applications with both species claims and generic or Markush claims. Election should not be required between claimed species considered clearly unpatentable (obvious) over each other; the examiner should group species considered clearly unpatentable over each other (MPEP § 808.01).
guidance: In applications with only generic claims, restriction cannot be required unless the generic claims encompass such multiplicity of species that an unduly extensive and burdensome search would be necessary. If applicant presents species claims to more than one patentably distinct species after an Office action on only generic claims with no restriction, the Office may require election of a single species for examination. If a generic claim is found allowable, treat the application as indicated in MPEP § 809 and § 821.04(a).

name: Rejoinder practice (withdrawal of restriction and rejoinder of claims)
description: If claims to elected combination inventions are allowable or if a linking claim becomes allowable, the examiner must reconsider and withdraw the restriction requirement; any subcombinations or non-elected claims that were searched and determined allowable must be rejoined and examined for patentability. In Ochiai/Brouwer situations, notice of potential rejoinder of process claims must be given (form paragraph 8.21.04).
guidance: Upon allowance of the elected product, withdrawn process claims that depend from or require all limitations of the allowable product claim will be considered for rejoinder; rejoined claims must meet all patentability criteria (35 U.S.C. 101, 102, 103, 112). Withdrawn process claims not commensurate in scope with an allowable product will not be rejoined. To retain right to rejoinder, applicant should amend process claims to require the limitations of the product claims during prosecution; failure to do so may result in loss of right to rejoinder. The prohibition against double patenting rejections of 35 U.S.C. 121 does not apply where restriction is withdrawn before issue (MPEP § 804.01).

name: Proposed USPTO rule: unenforceability if tied (directly or indirectly) to a patent with invalidated claims
description: The USPTO's May 10, 2024 proposed rule would require applicants, upon filing a terminal disclaimer to obviate ODP, to agree that the underlying patent is enforceable only if the patent 'is not, and has never been, tied directly or indirectly to a patent by one or more terminal disclaimers filed to obviate nonstatutory double patenting where any claim has been invalidated under anticipation or obviousness by the USPTO or federal court or statutorily disclaimed.'
guidance: Under the proposed rule, if a reference patent (directly tied) has a claim invalidated over prior art, patents tied via terminal disclaimers could become unenforceable. This expands risk and ties enforceability to the validity of other patents in the chain.

name: Chain‑reaction risk from indirect links via series of terminal disclaimers
description: Patents and co‑pending applications within a patent family may be indirectly linked together based on a series of terminal disclaimers identifying other family members as reference applications or patents; in this scenario, a patent family that is tied directly and indirectly together by a series of terminal disclaimers risks being unenforceable in its entirety if one claim in any one patent is invalidated over prior art.
guidance: Practitioners and stakeholders should evaluate not only direct terminal disclaimers but also the network of terminal disclaimers that may indirectly link family members. The proposed rule could cause a chain reaction wiping out entire patent families, even when disputed subject matter is distinguishable.

name: Scope when principle is not new: confined to the particular method described
description: Where the principle is not new, the patentee is confined to the particular method described in the specification, and the patent will not be allowed to cover other methods; the doctrine of mechanical equivalents will not be applicable.
guidance: Courts are 'more jealous' in such cases and will hold patentee to his described means. Examples: Curtis v. Platt; Bovill v. Pimm; Boyd v. Horrocks. If prior art shows the objective was known, the patentee cannot claim broadly to exclude all other means of achieving it.

name: When restriction is proper (core two-part test)
description: A restriction requirement between patentably distinct inventions is proper only if: (A) the inventions are independent or distinct as claimed; and (B) there would be a serious burden on the examiner if restriction is not required.
guidance: If the search and examination of all claims can be made without serious burden, the examiner must examine them on the merits even if they include independent or distinct inventions. Examiners must provide reasons and/or examples to support conclusions, though citation of documents is not generally required.

name: Requirement to provide reasons/examples for restriction
description: Examiners must provide reasons and/or examples to support conclusions for restriction requirements, but need not cite documents to support the restriction requirement in most cases.
guidance: Where plural inventions are capable of being viewed as related in two ways, both applicable criteria for distinctness must be demonstrated to support a restriction requirement. If applicant has expressly admitted obviousness between claimed inventions, restriction should not be required.

name: Markush-type claim unity and treatment
description: Members of a Markush group ordinarily must belong to a recognized physical/chemical class or art-recognized class. For Markush groups in process or combination claims, members must be disclosed to possess at least one property in common that is mainly responsible for their function in the claimed relationship.
guidance: Unity exists where Markush members (1) share a common utility, and (2) share a substantial structural feature essential to that utility. If members are few or closely related so that full search/examination can be made without serious burden, examine all members. If a Markush encompasses independent/distinct inventions, the examiner may require provisional election of a single species (use form paragraphs 8.01 or 8.02 as applicable). After election, examine the Markush claim with respect to the elected species and as necessary to determine patentability; do not extend the prior art search unnecessarily to cover all nonelected species.

name: Rejoinder of process claims requiring an allowable product claim
description: When claims to a product and to a process of making and/or using that product are presented, and applicant elects the product, withdrawn process claims which depend from or otherwise require all the limitations of an allowable product claim will be considered for rejoinder. Upon rejoinder, the restriction requirement between the elected product and rejoined process(es) will be withdrawn.
guidance: All rejoined process claims must depend from or otherwise require all limitations of the allowable product claim. If applicant cancels all nonelected process claims before rejoinder, preserve restriction to protect 35 U.S.C. 121 rights. Amendments after final rejection or allowance are governed by applicable CFR sections (e.g., 1.116, 1.312) and rejoinder timing affects entry of amendments.

name: Provisional double patenting practice and interaction with restriction
description: When restriction requirements are made and withdrawals/rejoinders occur, claims presented in continuations or divisionals that are anticipated by or include all limitations of a claim allowable in the present application may be subject to provisional statutory and/or nonstatutory double patenting rejections over the instant application's claims.
guidance: If restriction requirement is withdrawn (e.g., due to rejoinder or allowance of linking/generic claim), 35 U.S.C. 121 protections no longer apply; examiners should consider provisional double patenting rejections and related MPEP sections (e.g., § 804.01). Applicants should be advised of potential double patenting consequences when rejoin/withdrawal occurs.

name: Form paragraph and procedural requirements when making restriction/election and notifications
description: Use specified form paragraphs (e.g., 8.01, 8.02, 8.21.04, 8.29, 8.41, 8.42, 8.43, 8.46–8.50, etc.) to set forth restriction or election requirements, notices for transitional applications, rejoin notifications, and condition-for-allowance letters involving withdrawn claims with traverse.
guidance: Form paragraphs prescribe exact wording and are to be used in the appropriate circumstances (e.g., provisional election of species in Markush claims, notification of transitional restriction status, rejoinder after allowable product claim). Follow examiner notes in MPEP for when to use each paragraph and for bracket insertions.

name: Board decision scope — affirm, reverse, remand
description: The Board, in its decision, may affirm or reverse each decision of the examiner on all issues raised on each appealed claim, or remand the reexamination proceeding to the examiner for further consideration.
guidance: Affirmance of a rejection constitutes general affirmance of the examiner's decision on that claim except as to any ground specifically reversed. Remand may be used where further consideration or procedure is needed.

name: Reversal of examiner’s refusal to adopt third-party proposed rejection
description: The reversal of the examiner’s determination not to make a rejection proposed by the third party requester constitutes a decision adverse to the patentability of the claims which are subject to that proposed rejection and will be set forth in the Board’s decision as a new ground of rejection under paragraph (b).
guidance: Such a reversal is treated as a new ground of rejection and triggers the special post-decision options for the patent owner; it also means the decision is not final for judicial review (when a new ground is included).

name: Board may include new grounds of rejection (37 CFR 41.77(b))
description: If the Board reverses the examiner’s determination or has knowledge of any grounds not raised in the appeal for rejecting any pending claim, it may include in its opinion a statement to that effect with its reasons, which statement shall constitute a new ground of rejection of the claim.
guidance: Any decision including a new ground of rejection is not final for judicial review. When the Board makes a new ground, the owner, within one month from the date of the decision, must exercise one of two options to avoid termination: (1) reopen prosecution by filing an amendment/new evidence, or (2) request rehearing under § 41.79 addressing the new ground and stating with particularity the points misapprehended or overlooked.

name: CRU processing and timing after Board decision; NIRC issuance
description: After an appeal has been decided, a copy of the decision is mailed to all parties, the original is placed in the file, and the clerk forwards the file to the Central Reexamination Unit (CRU) immediately if the examiner is reversed, and after about six weeks if the examiner is affirmed or after a rehearing decision is rendered. The CRU processes the decision and forwards the file to the examiner via the CRU Director so that a Notice of Intent to Issue Inter Partes Reexamination Certificate (NIRC) can be issued to terminate the prosecution.
guidance: Form paragraph 26.67.01 is used when NIRC is issued. The CRU staff uses the Board decision to prepare appropriate amendments and cancellations in the NIRC and to instruct the examiner on claim status.

name: Pre‑AIA first‑to‑invent rule (pre‑AIA patentability)
description: Under pre‑AIA law the first person to invent a claimed invention had priority and was entitled to a patent, even if another inventor first filed a patent application; pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(g) and interference proceedings determined priority of invention.
guidance: Interference proceedings were lengthy, costly, and required corroborating evidence of invention date; were a central reason Congress moved to first‑inventor‑to‑file. See pre‑AIA §§ 102(g), 135; H.R. Rep. No. 112‑98.

name: Replacement of interferences by derivation proceedings
description: The AIA repealed interference provisions and replaced them with derivation proceedings to address situations where an earlier filer may have derived the claimed invention from a later filer.
guidance: AIA §§ 3(h)–(i) (amending 35 U.S.C. §§ 135, 291); interferences determined first inventor; derivation determines whether earlier filer derived the invention.

name: Three AIA § 3(n) patent categories and consequences
description: AIA § 3(n) creates: (1) Pure pre‑AIA patents/applications (only pre‑AIA effective filing dates) subject to pre‑AIA patentability and interferences; (2) Pure AIA patents/applications (only post‑March 16, 2013 effective filing dates) subject to AIA patentability and derivations; (3) Mixed patents/applications (contain both pre‑ and post‑effective filing date claims) subject to AIA patentability but also to pre‑AIA interference provisions.
guidance: Identifying which category a patent/application falls into determines whether interferences or derivations and which statutory standards apply.

name: Claim term defined by implication (usage in specification)
description: The meaning of a particular claim term may be defined by implication, that is, according to the usage of the term in the context of the specification.
guidance: See Phillips v. AWH Corp., Vitronics. But where the specification is ambiguous as to whether the inventor used claim terms inconsistent with their ordinary meaning, the ordinary meaning will apply (example: Merck v. Teva — 'about' should be given its plain and ordinary meaning 'approximately' rather than 'exactly' when the specification passage is too ambiguous to redefine it).

name: Do not interpret claims to omit a disclosed embodiment absent evidence
description: Claims should not be interpreted in a way that would omit a disclosed embodiment, absent evidence to the contrary.
guidance: When intrinsic evidence (specification/prosecution history) shows embodiments, claim construction should avoid reading claims so narrowly that those embodiments are excluded unless there is clear contrary evidence. Example: court found specification defined two different types of 'Wide' point of view while claim language was broader; claim required one or the other but not both.

name: Disavowal (disclaimer) requires clear and unmistakable evidence
description: Applicant may rebut the presumption of plain meaning by clearly disavowing the full scope of the claim term in the specification; disavowal is only considered when it is clear and unmistakable.
guidance: See SciMed Life Sys. v. Advanced Cardiovascular Sys.; disavowal can, in some cases, be made by implication (e.g., specification contains only disparaging remarks about a feature and every embodiment excludes that feature — In re Abbott Diabetes Care). Examiner should make any implicit disavowal-based interpretation clear on the record. See also MPEP § 2173.05(a). Note: prosecution history estoppel is inapplicable during prosecution to limit claims of pending applications (see In re Clarke for distinction).

name: Flowchart for determining meaning of a claim term (non-112(f))
description: A decision sequence examiners should follow to ascertain proper claim interpretation based on plain meaning/BRI when 35 U.S.C. 112(f) is not invoked.
guidance: Steps: (1) Determine whether claim term has an ordinary and customary meaning to a person of ordinary skill in the art. If yes, check specification for a special definition. If spec provides a special definition, use it and acknowledge/identify it in the Office action; if not, apply the ordinary meaning. (2) If the term does not have an ordinary meaning, check the specification for a meaning. If no reasonably clear meaning can be ascribed after considering spec and prior art, apply the broadest reasonable interpretation and reject under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) and object to the specification under 37 CFR 1.75(d). If the specification provides a meaning, the examiner should use the meaning provided and may acknowledge it in the Office action.

name: Effect of preamble must be determined case-by-case
description: The determination of whether a preamble limits a claim is made on a case-by-case basis in light of the facts in each case; there is no litmus test defining when a preamble limits the scope of a claim.
guidance: General principle: '[A] claim preamble has the import that the claim as a whole suggests for it.' Evaluate the preamble in context of entire claim and record; see Catalina Mktg., Bell Communications Research, Pitney Bowes for guideposts and examples.

name: Preamble statements limiting structure are claim limitations
description: Any terminology in the preamble that limits the structure of the claimed invention must be treated as a claim limitation.
guidance: Assess the entirety of the application to understand what the inventors actually invented and intended to encompass without importing extraneous limitations from the specification. Cases: Corning Glass Works, Pac-Tec, In re Stencel (example where collar structure in preamble limited the driver claim).

name: Preamble reciting purpose or intended use may be non-limiting unless it imparts structural difference
description: If the body of a claim fully and intrinsically sets forth all limitations of the claimed invention, and the preamble merely states the purpose or intended use, the preamble is not considered a limitation; however, if the preamble's stated purpose results in a structural (or manipulative for process claims) difference from the prior art, it may limit the claim.
guidance: Evaluate whether the preamble gives 'life, meaning, and vitality' to the claim (Pitney Bowes). During examination, determine whether the recited purpose/intent produces a structural difference over prior art; a prior art structure capable of performing the intended use meets the limiting intended-use preamble. Reliance on the preamble during prosecution to distinguish prior art can transform the preamble into a claim limitation (Metabolite Labs., Catalina Marketing). Examples and contrasting cases provided (Rowe v. Dror, Jansen, Poly‑America, Intirtool). See MPEP § 2112-2112.02 for related guidance.

name: Transitional phrase 'comprising' is open-ended/inclusive
description: 'Comprising' (synonymous with 'including,' 'containing,' or 'characterized by') is inclusive or open-ended and does not exclude additional, unrecited elements or method steps.
guidance: Determination is case-by-case, but 'comprising' signals that named elements are essential while permitting additional elements (Mars Inc., Invitrogen, Genentech, Gillette). Example: a claim 'comprising' a group of blades can encompass devices with additional blades. See MPEP § 2111.03 I.

name: Transitional phrase 'consisting of' is closed/exclusive
description: 'Consisting of' excludes any element, step, or ingredient not specified in the claim.
guidance: Historically construed as closing the claim to inclusion of materials other than recited ones except ordinary impurities (In re Gray, Ex parte Davis). Nuances: courts have found exceptions where additional items are unrelated to claimed invention (Norian). For Markush/group selections, 'consisting of' signals a closed group; when 'consisting of' appears in a clause of the body it strongly presumes closure of that clause's element, but it limits only that clause (see Multilayer Stretch Cling Film, In re Crish, Mannesmann Demag, and the discussion on interaction with an overall 'comprising' transition).

name: Transitional phrase 'consisting essentially of' occupies a middle ground
description: 'Consisting essentially of' limits the scope of a claim to the specified materials or steps 'and those that do not materially affect the basic and novel characteristic(s)' of the claimed invention.
guidance: This phrase is between 'consisting of' (closed) and 'comprising' (open). For 102/103 prior art application, absent clear indication in the specification of what the basic/novel characteristics are, 'consisting essentially of' may be construed as equivalent to 'comprising' (PPG). Applicant bears the burden of showing additional components/steps would materially change the invention. Can be used to modify method steps; interpret in light of the specification (In re Herz, PPG, AK Steel, In re Janakirama-Rao, Ex parte Hoffman).

name: Written description requirement applies to Jepson claim preamble
description: The preamble of a Jepson claim must be supported by the same sufficient written description required under 35 U.S.C. § 112 for the invention itself.
guidance: In re Xencor holds that the entirety of a Jepson claim, including the preamble recitation of known subject matter, constitutes the claimed invention for written description purposes. Applicants cannot treat the preamble as exempt from § 112 scrutiny merely because it admits prior art.

name: Preamble can be substantively limiting
description: A Jepson claim preamble may be substantively limiting such that it contributes to the claimed invention.
guidance: The PTAB's Appeals Review Panel and the Federal Circuit found that the Jepson preamble at issue was limiting; when a preamble is limiting, its content must be supported in the specification for written description purposes.

name: Specification must show possession of the entire claimed scope (including preamble) as of filing date
description: The specification must demonstrate the applicant's possession of the entire scope of the claimed invention, including any features recited in the preamble.
guidance: The court emphasized that applicants must show they possessed the full scope claimed (not just the 'improvement') at the filing date; otherwise claims may be invalid for lack of written description.

name: Representative species disclosure required when claiming a genus
description: When a claim covers a genus of embodiments (e.g., a genus of antibodies), the specification must list or describe a representative number of species to support that genus.
guidance: The Federal Circuit noted the specification did not list or describe a representative number of species for the claimed anti-C5 antibodies, resulting in an insufficient showing to support the entire genus.

name: Cannot rely on general statements that preamble subject matter is 'well known'
description: An applicant cannot avoid written description support by merely stating in the specification that the preamble subject matter is already well known.
guidance: If the claim covers the prior art as applied to the improvement, the specification itself must demonstrate possession of that scope; a conclusory 'well known' statement will not substitute for disclosure.

name: Jepson format increases risk of invalidity; use cautiously
description: Because Jepson claims concede the preamble as prior art and now require written description support for the preamble, their use increases the risk of claim invalidity and is generally unattractive.
guidance: Most U.S. practitioners will likely refrain from Jepson claims except in very narrow circumstances; consider drafting conventional claims instead and resist examiner requests for Jepson format where possible.

name: If using Jepson claims, thoroughly describe the admitted prior art portion including representative embodiments
description: When choosing Jepson format, the specification must thoroughly describe the admitted prior art portion—providing representative embodiments—so that the preamble subject matter is supported under § 112.
guidance: Alternatively, during prosecution the applicant may present robust evidence that the preamble subject matter is widely known in the field, but absent that the specification must disclose the admitted prior art features to avoid written description rejection.

name: Jepson claims historically used for mechanical and method improvements to streamline prosecution
description: Practitioners have traditionally reserved Jepson claims for mechanical improvements and occasionally method improvements to accelerate prosecution or to satisfy an examiner's preference.
guidance: Given the Federal Circuit's decision, even in mechanical or method contexts the safer approach is to use conventional claim drafting unless there is a compelling, narrow reason to use Jepson format.

name: Risk of patently claiming fictional or overly broad subject matter without written description support
description: Requiring written description for every aspect of the Jepson claim (including preamble) guards against granting patents on subject matter the inventor did not possess (e.g., a hypothetical 'time travel machine' recited in the preamble).
guidance: The court used a time-travel-machine hypothetical to illustrate why written description support for preamble content is necessary to prevent applicants from claiming things they do not actually invent or possess.

name: Privilege doctrine and crime-fraud exception in unenforceability claims
description: Privilege issues commonly arise in unenforceability claims because they often involve prosecution communications and litigation counsel work product.
guidance: Attorney–client privilege applies as it does generally; absent a showing under the crime-fraud exception, the privilege may be asserted even if it appears to obstruct fact gathering critical to the unenforceability claim (In re Rhone-Poulenc Rorer). Courts must analyze scope of waiver and application of crime-fraud carefully.

name: Mandatory stay and use of Commission record under §1659(a)-(b)
description: 28 U.S.C. §1659(a) provides a mandatory stay of district court proceedings for claims involving the same issues as an ITC §337 proceeding if timely requested; §1659(b) governs use of the ITC record after dissolution of the stay.
guidance: A party that is also a respondent in an ITC proceeding can obtain a stay as of right if request is made within 30 days after being named as a respondent or within 30 days after the district court action is filed, whichever is later. The stay remains until the Commission’s determination becomes final. After dissolution, the ITC record may be transmitted to the district court and admissible subject to protective orders and the Rules of Evidence/Procedure.

name: Factors for district court's discretion to stay proceedings related to ITC
description: Even with §1659’s mandatory stay language, courts assess whether to stay additional patents/claims or the entire proceeding when only some patents overlap with ITC matters.
guidance: Courts balance factors such as (1) possible damage from granting a stay; (2) hardship or inequity to a party required to go forward; and (3) orderly course of justice measured by simplification/complication of issues, proof, and legal questions. Courts consider timing, progress of ITC vs district case, amount of discovery, and whether staying conserves judicial resources (FormFactor; ILJIN factors; Micron; Alloc). A respondent still may need to make a clear case of hardship or inequity before a stay will be entered.

name: Preclusive effect (or lack) of ITC determinations on district court proceedings
description: Whether ITC adjudications (claim construction, validity, infringement, defenses) have preclusive/res judicata effect in subsequent district-court litigation.
guidance: Generally, ITC patent determinations do not have preclusive effect in district court litigation (Tex. Instruments v. Cypress Semiconductor), though some circuits/cases have afforded preclusive effect in particular circumstances (e.g., Balt. Luggage; Union Mfg.). District courts may nonetheless consider ITC rulings when assessing related cases.

name: Document indexing and correct document description selection
description: Users must select from the list of document descriptions to specify the files being submitted (e.g., specification, claims, abstract, drawing; amendment after allowance vs preliminary amendment vs amendment after final).
guidance: The selected document description assigns a document code used by USPTO systems (IFW, PAIR, SCORE) and routes the submission appropriately. Incorrect indexing may delay processing, route a submission to publication instead of the examiner, or cause other misprocessing.

name: Interim copies of foreign priority documents and text-file requirements
description: Interim copies of foreign priority documents under 37 CFR 1.55(j) may be submitted via EFS‑Web for specified application types, but a certified copy must be provided before patent grant to perfect the priority claim.
guidance: Main parts of the interim copy (Abstract, Drawings, Specification, Claims, Sequence Listing/Computer Program Listings) may be filed as a single PDF and must be indexed using 'Interim copy of Foreign Priority Application'. TXT-only parts (sequence listings, large tables, program listings) may be uploaded as TXT files (or on compact disc) with specific file-naming conventions (start with country code and foreign application number, indicate part order if split), and sequence listings over 25 MB must be split into multiple files under the 25 MB upload limit.

name: Submission qualifies for entry under 37 CFR 1.501
description: A submission under 37 CFR 1.501 must be limited to patents, printed publications, and/or patent owner written claim scope statements and additional information and include the requisite citation description and information and proof of service on the patent owner.
guidance: May be submitted via mail, hand-delivery, or the USPTO patent electronic filing system if properly filed as a 1.501 prior art submission (not as a follow-on paper). Submissions under 1.501 cannot be filed for design or plant patents. Both registered and unregistered users may make an electronic submission. Submitting papers directly into the patent by someone other than the patent owner’s representative may violate the Office's electronic filing agreement.

name: Basic characteristics of ex parte reexamination
description: Ex parte reexamination characteristics include: (A) anyone can request reexamination at any time during enforceability; (B) under 35 U.S.C. 304, prior art is limited to patents or printed publications applied under 102/103 (but 257 is not limited); (C) a substantial new question of patentability must be present; (D) the proceeding is ex parte in nature; (E) decision on the request must be made no later than 3 months from filing; (F) a reexamination proceeding will normally be conducted to conclusion and issuance of a reexamination certificate; (G) the scope of a claim cannot be enlarged by amendment; (H) files are open to the public (subject to noted exceptions).
guidance: These are procedural constraints and expectations for conducting ex parte reexamination, e.g., timeframes ('special dispatch') and limitations on allowable rejections and amendments.

name: 37 CFR 1.510(b)(2) — identification of every claim and detailed explanation
description: The request must include an identification of every claim for which reexamination is requested, and a detailed explanation of the pertinency and manner of applying the cited prior art to every claim.
guidance: For each patent owner statement relied upon under § 1.501(a)(2), the request must explain how that statement is used to determine claim meaning and how each relevant claim is interpreted. The requester may, if appropriate, point out how claims distinguish over cited prior art.

name: 37 CFR 1.510(b)(4) — copy of the entire patent and format requirements
description: A request must include a copy of the entire patent (front face, drawings, specification/claims in double column format) for which reexamination is requested, and a copy of any disclaimer, certificate of correction, or reexamination certificate issued in the patent.
guidance: All copies must have each page plainly written on only one side of a sheet of paper.

name: Restrictions on examiner communications and third-party inquiries
description: Examiners should not discuss or answer inquiries from third parties (non-patent owners) about specific reexamination proceedings; such parties should be referred to Technology Center Quality Assurance or Central Reexamination Unit supervisory specialists. Only strictly procedural matters (not directed to any specific reexamination proceeding) may be discussed.
guidance: Employees who conducted a concluded reexamination should not discuss whether a certain reference was considered or whether a claim would have been allowed. Patent practitioners must not make improper inquiries of examiners (see 37 CFR 11.804).

name: Evidentiary hierarchy for claim construction
description: The most important source in the evidentiary hierarchy of claim construction is the ordinary meaning of the language of the claims themselves and other intrinsic sources like the prosecution history. Extrinsic evidence (dictionaries, expert testimony, scholarly articles) is of secondary importance.
guidance: Give primary weight to intrinsic evidence (claims, specification, prosecution history) when determining claim meaning; consult extrinsic evidence only secondarily. The Phillips decision clarified that intrinsic evidence controls the interpretation of claim terms and that extrinsic evidence should not supplant intrinsic sources.

name: Ordinary meaning of claim language in context
description: Words of the claims should be given their ordinary meaning in the context of the patent documents, as interpreted by a person of ordinary skill in the art to which the patent pertains.
guidance: Interpret claim terms by how a POSITA (person of ordinary skill in the art) would understand them within the full context of the patent (claims + specification + figures). Do not isolate claim words from the patent context when determining their ordinary meaning.

name: Intrinsic evidence: specification and other claims as interpretive clues
description: The other claims and the specification can provide important clues to the intended meaning of the claim language.
guidance: Use the specification and the prosecution history to illuminate ambiguous claim terms; read claims in light of the specification and related claim language to ensure consistent meaning across the patent.

name: Patentee may act as lexicographer
description: The patentee can act as his own lexicographer by defining terms in the specification, and such patentee-defined meanings can control claim construction.
guidance: If the specification clearly defines a term contrary to its ordinary meaning, the patentee's definition governs. Look for explicit definitions or clear intent in the specification indicating the inventor's chosen meaning.

name: Prosecution history is informative but less authoritative
description: The prosecution history is an important intrinsic source, but it should be viewed with more skepticism than the plain language of the claims themselves because it represents a back-and-forth between the Patent Office and the inventor and lacks the clarity of the final claim language.
guidance: Consider statements and amendments made during prosecution to interpret claim scope, but treat them with caution; prosecution statements may be less precise and can be ambiguous compared to the claims and specification.

name: Dictionaries should not be accorded weight tantamount to claim language
description: Dictionaries may be used, but the Federal Circuit repudiated prior authority suggesting dictionaries could be accorded weight tantamount to the claim language itself (see repudiation of Texas Digital).
guidance: Do not treat dictionary definitions as dispositive if they conflict with the claim language or specification; dictionaries are only one form of extrinsic evidence and must yield to intrinsic evidence and any express patentee definitions.

name: Appellate standard of review for claim construction (law vs factual findings)
description: Phillips endorsed that claim construction is a matter of law reviewed de novo on appeal; however, subsequent Supreme Court precedent (Teva v. Sandoz) held that factual findings underlying claim construction are reviewed for clear error.
guidance: When construing claims, recognize that legal determinations remain subject to de novo review but subsidiary factual determinations (e.g., those relying on extrinsic evidence or factual findings about how a POSITA would understand a term) are reviewed under the clear-error standard post-Teva. Consider both the legal/factual components when assessing appellate review posture.

name: Written Opinion content (PCT Rule 43 bis.1)
description: The International Searching Authority shall establish a written opinion as to whether the claimed invention appears to be novel, to involve an inventive step (to be non-obvious), and to be industrially applicable; and whether the international application complies with the requirements of the Treaty and these Regulations in so far as checked by the ISA.
guidance: The written opinion is established at the same time as the international search report or declaration under Article 17(2)(a). It should also be accompanied by other observations provided for in the Regulations (e.g., clarity of claims, description and drawings, support of claims). Applicable provisions (Articles 33(2)-(6), 35(2)-(3), Rules 43.4, 43.6bis, 64, 65, 66.1(e), etc.) apply mutatis mutandis. If the ISA cannot form a meaningful opinion for certain claims (see Rules 43 bis.1(b), 66.1(e)), it must indicate that in Box No. III of Form PCT/ISA/237.

name: Fields to be covered by the international search (PCT Rule 33.2)
description: The international search shall cover all technical fields and search files which may contain material pertinent to the invention, including not only the art where the invention is classifiable but also analogous arts regardless of where classified.
guidance: Determine analogous arts in light of the necessary essential function or use of the invention, not only expressly indicated functions. The search should embrace subject matter generally recognized as equivalent to the claimed invention for all or certain features, even if described differently.

name: Orientation of the international search (PCT Rule 33.3)
description: The international search shall be made on the basis of the claims, with due regard to the description and drawings, and with particular emphasis on the inventive concept towards which the claims are directed.
guidance: As far as possible and reasonable, the search shall cover the entire subject matter to which the claims are directed or which they might reasonably be expected to be directed after amendment. Focus on claim scope and inventive concept when selecting search fields and terms.

name: Relevant date for prior art in international preliminary examination (PCT Rule 64.1(b))
description: For purposes of Article 33(2) and (3) the relevant date is generally the international filing date, except where a valid priority is claimed; then the filing date of the earlier application is the relevant date (with specific rules for late international filings within two months of priority expiry).
guidance: If the International Preliminary Examining Authority considers the priority claim invalid, the relevant date may be the international filing date. Carefully verify and record the effective relevant date when assessing prior art for the written opinion and preliminary examination.

name: Examiners encouraged to cite supportive prior art beyond novelty/inventive step
description: Examiners are encouraged to cite prior art that might assist in determining other requirements (e.g., sufficient support of claims by description, industrial applicability) and documents important for background or showing level of ordinary skill, but should not spend time searching for these unless there is a special reason.
guidance: Cite documents putting doubt upon validity of priority claims, documents that improve understanding of the invention, or documents illustrating background. Do not expand the search beyond standard parameters solely to find such documents, but cite relevant post-dating documents to show universal facts when appropriate. Be mindful that different designated Offices may have different effective-date definitions and select citations accordingly when reasonable.

name: No search when claims/description/drawings are unclear or inadequately supported
description: If the ISA considers that the description, claims, or drawings fail to comply with prescribed requirements to such an extent that a meaningful search cannot be carried out, it may declare that it will not establish a search report; similarly, if the claims are so unclear or inadequately supported no meaningful opinion can be formed.
guidance: Examples include missing or non-compliant nucleotide/amino acid sequence listings, improper multiple dependent claims (PCT Rule 6.4(a)), or other deficiencies preventing meaningful assessment of novelty, inventive step, or industrial applicability. In such cases the ISA may not address those issues in its written opinion per Rules 43 bis.1(b) and 66.1(e).

name: Procedure for claims not searched and for unclear claims (reporting and forms)
description: Where some claims are unsearchable or relate to subject matter the ISA will not search, the ISA searches the remaining claims and indicates any unsearched claims and reasons in Box No. II of Form PCT/ISA/210; if none are searched, the ISA declares no search report established using Form PCT/ISA/203.
guidance: If the application cites an inaccessible document essential to understanding the invention, the ISA may postpone the search and request a copy; if not received, attempt the search then indicate inability or restriction. For written opinion, indicate in Box No. III of Form PCT/ISA/237 that no opinion will be established regarding novelty, inventive step, or industrial applicability for those claims and refer to the search report or declaration for details.

name: Time limits and publication timing for search report and written opinion (PCT Rule 42.1 / 43 bis.1(a))
description: Publication of the international application occurs at 18 months from earliest priority date (or 18 months from filing if no priority). The Office's goal is to have the search report and written opinion mailed so they reach the International Bureau by the end of 16 months from the priority date (or 9 months from filing date if no priority claim).
guidance: For applications filed on or after July 1, 2014, the written opinion of the ISA and any informal applicant comments will be made publicly available in their original language at publication. The timing ensures sufficient time for technical publication preparations (by 17.5 months). See PCT Rule 42.1 and 43 bis.1(a) for details.

name: Contents and limitations of the international search report (PCT Article 18 / Rule 43)
