description: The international search report contains citations of documents considered relevant, the classification of the subject matter, and an indication of the fields searched. The search report records the results (Form PCT/ISA/210) and is transmitted to the applicant and International Bureau.
guidance: Citations of particular relevance must be specially indicated; citations relevant only to certain claims must be cited in relation to those claims; if only certain passages are relevant, identify page/column/line. The search report should identify prior art only and must not include opinion, reasoning, argument or explanation as to cited prior art — those belong in the written opinion (Form PCT/ISA/237).

name: Preparing and filling Form PCT/ISA/210 (first sheet boxes and general form rules)
description: The first sheet indicates the total number of sheets in the report (count only filled-in sheets from Form PCT/ISA/210). Box 1a indicates language of search basis (language filed or English translation), Box 1b indicates rectification of an obvious mistake under PCT Rule 91.
guidance: Enter the correct number of sheets (exclude blank sheets). Use the first sheet and available continuation sheets as directed (continuations for nucleotide listings, unsearched claims/unity lack, abstract text, and extra/second-sheet continuation for citations). Follow the July 2022 PCT/ISA/210 variant guidance where applicable.

name: Which parts of the international search report are published and continuation-sheet usage
description: Only the 'second sheet', the 'continuation of second sheet', the 'continuation of first sheet (2)' (if any), the 'extra sheet' (if any), and any separate sheet with patent family information are published by the International Bureau; the 'first sheet' and some continuation first sheets contain information already on the front page of the published international application.
guidance: Use the specific continuation sheets for their intended purposes: continuation of first sheet (1) for sequence listings and search basis, continuation of first sheet (2) when claims were found unsearchable or unity lacking, continuation of first sheet (3) for the abstract text, and continuation of second sheet for additional citations when space is insufficient. The patent family annex is not currently used by the U.S. ISA.

name: Voluntary amendment of specification (Form No.1) — authority and specification
description: For voluntary amendment of the specification (description, claims, drawing, etc.) the request must specify the amendment and reference Section 3(10)(g) of the Harare Protocol and Administrative Instructions 27(1) & (2).
guidance: Specify the exact amendment(s) and include any required annexes showing red-ink changes; ensure signatures and dates are provided.

name: Invitation by ARIPO to correct application (Form No.11) — formal requirements and filing date consequence
description: After examination pursuant to Rules 14/15 and related Instructions, ARIPO may find the application on the face of it does not fulfil Rule 5(1)(a),(b),(c) requirements or prescribed formal requirements and request corrections within 2 months together with payment of prescribed fee. The application shall not be accorded a filing date until said requirements are fulfilled.
guidance: Identify which element fails (request, description, claims, abstract) and provide correction instructions; for missing abstract, applicant may file abstract within 2 months or pay ARIPO to prepare it.

name: Request for substantive examination form specifics (Form No.13A) — fee prerequisite
description: A Request for Substantive Examination must be made on Form No.13A in accordance with Section 3(3) and Rule 18(1)(a); the request is not deemed filed until the substantive examination fee (including any additional fee and claims fee) has been paid.
guidance: Provide application number, filing date, applicant details and list fee items; include signature and date.

name: Require proof and corroboration in opening petitions for 'on sale' and 'public use' evidence
description: Petitions invoking 'on sale' and 'public use' prior art should require proof in the opening Petition, including evidence of corroboration.
guidance: Oral testimony or affidavits regarding public use or on-sale evidence must be corroborated; the petition must specify where each element of the construed claim is found in the prior art. Documents used to corroborate testimony must be sufficiently complete, clear, and detailed to show that each and every element of a claim is present. Proposed amendment to § 42.204(b)(4)-(5): (4) specify how the construed claim is unpatentable and require corroboration for no-document evidence; (5) provide the exhibit number of supporting/corroborating evidence and state relevance and specific portions relied upon. The Board may exclude or give no weight to evidence where relevance or supporting portions are not identified.

name: Claim construction standard should reflect adjudicative nature (use Phillips/Markman)
description: IPR and PGR trials are not examinations, and the claim construction rules should reflect that—they should use claim construction 'in light of the specification and prosecution history' (district court standard), not the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) used for examination.
guidance: BRI is an examination tool appropriate where iterative amendment is available; IPR/PGR provide only limited amendment opportunities and are adjudicative in nature. Applying BRI would unfairly broaden claim scope for validity determinations and create conflicts with concurrent district court infringement proceedings. Amend proposed §§ 42.100(b) and 42.200(b) to adopt the federal district court (Phillips/Markman) standard.

name: Do not require claim construction submissions in derivation petitions
description: The proposed rules to require submission of claim construction in derivation proceedings are unnecessary and inappropriate.
guidance: Submission of claim construction by one party often invites burdensome rebuttals; the identity of language of a count (in derivation contexts) typically provides sufficient basis for a derivation petition without requiring formal claim construction submissions.

name: Fulfill disclosure obligations under IQA, PRA, e-Government Act, and EO 12,866
description: The NPRMs neglect to disclose significant material information required by the Information Quality Act, Paperwork Reduction Act, e-Government Act, and Executive Order 12,866; USPTO must correct these omissions.
guidance: Agencies must provide data, analyses, and objective support for claims in the NPRM; for example, failure to disclose assumptions and analyses underlying burden estimates and economic effects must be remedied and made available for public comment.

name: Type‑volume and page limits — petitions and motions
description: Specified word counts/page limits apply and include any statement of material facts to be admitted or denied; the word count/page limit excludes table of contents, table of authorities, mandatory notices under § 42.8, certificate of service or word count, and appendix exhibits or claim listing.
guidance: Specific limits: IPR petition 14,000 words; PGR petition 18,700 words; CBM petition 18,700 words; derivation petition 14,000 words; motions (excluding motions to amend) 15 pages; motions to amend 25 pages. Petitions to institute must comply but may be accompanied by a motion to waive word counts showing interests of justice and appending proposed overlength petition.

name: Judgment scope, adverse judgment requests, recommendations, and estoppel
description: A judgment disposes of all issues that were, or by motion reasonably could have been, raised and decided. A party may request adverse judgment against itself at any time (examples: disclaimer, cancellation of all claims, concession of unpatentability or derivation, abandonment). A judgment may include recommendations for further action by an examiner or Director.
guidance: Estoppel: Petitioners (except in derivation) or their privies are estopped in the Office from requesting or maintaining proceedings on a claim for which they obtained a final written decision on patentability in IPR, PGR, or CBM on any ground raised or that reasonably could have been raised, subject to exceptions (e.g., settlements under 35 U.S.C. 317 or 327). Patent applicants/owners are precluded from actions inconsistent with an adverse judgment (e.g., obtaining claims not patentably distinct from finally refused/canceled claims or amendments denied during trial), except where a different written description exists.

name: Clerical handling and entry of amendments
description: The reexamination clerk handles initial clerical processing; amendments complying with 37 CFR 1.530(d)-(j) will be entered for reexamination in the reexamination file.
guidance: Amendments entered for reexamination even if they do not have legal effect until certificate issued. “New matter” amendments to disclosure must be canceled and claims containing new matter rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112. New matter to drawings ordinarily not entered. Amendments that enlarge claim scope will be entered but appropriate claims will be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 305. For merged reissue-reexamination, see MPEP §§ 2283, 2285.

name: Final action — development of clear issue before final
description: Before issuing a final action, a clear issue should be developed between the examiner and patent owner, with the examiner providing information and references twice to define the Office’s position.
guidance: Initial decision ordering reexamination will identify new questions of patentability raised by prior art. First Office action should reflect consideration of arguments/amendments in request and owner's statement and replies, and should fully apply all relevant grounds of rejection to the claims. The second Office action following decision ordering reexamination is intended to be final in accordance with MPEP § 706.07(a).

name: Timing and scope of account of profits
description: An account of profits cannot be had where none arose before the action was begun, but such an account is not confined to those which accrued before the interlocutory decree was entered, but may be made to include all profits realized by the defendant from infringing the complainant's right, at any time prior to the closing of the account. And such an account will be taken in conformity with the statutes relevant thereto, as they existed at the respective dates when the infringement occurred.
guidance: Claims for an account should cover all defendant profits from infringement up to the closing of the account, applying the law and statutes in effect at the time of each infringement.

name: When to apply markedly different characteristics analysis
description: Apply the markedly different characteristics analysis only to nature-based product limitations in a claim; do not overextend the analysis to claim elements that are not nature-based. If the nature-based product limitation is naturally occurring, there is no need to perform the analysis; if it is not naturally occurring (e.g., due to human intervention), then perform the analysis to determine whether it is a product of nature exception.
guidance: The analysis compares the claimed nature-based product to its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state. Example distinctions: a claim to 'a Lactobacillus bacterium' should be analyzed as a nature-based product; a claim to a kit containing Lactobacillus plus non-nature elements should have only the nature-based limitation analyzed here (the other elements are evaluated later in Prong Two or Step 2B).

name: Product claims: analyze the entire claimed nature-based product
description: When the claim is to a nature-based product by itself, apply the markedly different characteristics analysis to the entire claimed product.
guidance: If the claim recites a nature-based combination produced by combining components (e.g., 'a probiotic composition comprising a mixture of Lactobacillus and milk'), analyze the resultant combination rather than each component separately. If the claim is solely a nature-based product and a marked difference is shown, no further Step 2A/2B analysis is necessary for the product-of-nature question (the claim would be NO at Step 2A Pathway B unless another exception is present). Case example: Chakrabarty applied analysis to the entire genetically modified bacterium.

name: Claims combining nature-based and non-nature elements: limit analysis to the nature-based limitation
description: When a claim includes a nature-based product in combination with non-nature elements, perform the markedly different characteristics analysis only on the nature-based product limitation.
guidance: Non-nature elements (e.g., containers, instructions) are not subject to this analysis but will be considered later in Prong Two (and Step 2B if needed) if the nature-based product is found to lack marked differences. Example: in a 'yogurt starter kit comprising Lactobacillus in a container with instructions', analyze the Lactobacillus for marked differences; the container and instructions are evaluated separately.

name: Product-by-process claims: focus on whether the claimed product has markedly different characteristics
description: For product-by-process claims, the markedly different characteristics analysis turns on whether the nature-based product recited in the claim has markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart.
guidance: See MPEP § 2113 for additional product-by-process claim guidance. The analysis centers on the product itself (what it is) rather than the recited process steps when determining marked difference.

name: Identifying appropriate characteristics to compare
description: Identify characteristics possessed by the claimed product (as defined by the claim language and its broadest reasonable interpretation) to use in the comparison to the natural counterpart; characteristics may be structural, functional, or other properties.
guidance: Appropriate characteristics must be possessed by the claimed product — unclaimed characteristics cannot be relied on. Characteristics can be explicit in the claim (e.g., chemical name indicating structure) or inferred from the broadest reasonable interpretation (e.g., 'isolated gene B' implies nucleotide sequence and encoded protein). Courts consider structure, function, and other properties. Non-limiting example categories: biological/pharmacological functions (e.g., protein-encoding information; binding ability), chemical/physical properties (alkalinity, ductility), phenotype (shape, size, color, behavior), and structure/form (plasmids presence, chemical/crystalline form, nucleotide sequence, genotype).

name: Outcome rule based on analysis result
description: If the nature-based product limitation exhibits markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart, the limitation is not a product of nature exception and the claim is eligible at Step 2A (Pathway B) unless another exception is recited; if the claimed product lacks markedly different characteristics, it is a product of nature exception and requires further analysis in Step 2A Prong Two (and possibly Step 2B).
guidance: For claims where the entire claim is a single nature-based product, showing a marked difference ends the product-of-nature inquiry (Step 2B not necessary). For claims including additional limitations, examiners must consider whether other exceptions are recited that would require additional eligibility analysis. Examples: Chakrabarty and Myriad illustrate opposite outcomes: Chakrabarty’s genetically modified bacterium had markedly different structural and functional characteristics and was eligible; Myriad’s isolated genes lacked marked differences (isolation alone insufficient) and were product-of-nature exceptions.

name: Illustrative examples and anti-patterns
description: Court decisions provide examples of products that either possess or lack markedly different characteristics to guide application of the standard.
guidance: Examples of marked differences: Chakrabarty’s bacterium (additional plasmids and ability to degrade multiple hydrocarbons); Myriad’s cDNA (structurally different exon-only nucleotide sequence). Examples lacking marked differences: Myriad’s isolated genomic BRCA genes (isolation alone is incidental change), Ambry primers (single-stranded primers had the same nucleotide sequence and innate binding function), Roslin clones (cloned animals were genetic copies lacking claimed marked differences; unclaimed phenotypic variances cannot establish marked difference), In re Marden (ductility an inherent characteristic). These examples illustrate anti-patterns (changes that are incidental, innate, or unclaimed will not establish marked difference) and support application of the evaluation guidance above.

name: Universities must diligently pursue ownership claims; statutes of limitations can bar relief
description: Delay or failure to pursue assignment or ownership claims can result in losing the ability to enforce such obligations due to statutes of limitations or similar defenses.
guidance: Case: University Patents Inc. v. Kligman — the court ruled the university's suit was barred by the statute of limitations despite an implied obligation. Prompt action is important.

name: Written description and enablement requirement: full, clear, concise, exact terms
description: A patent must contain 'a written description of the invention, and of the manner and process of making and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art' to make and use the invention (the written description/enablement requirement).
guidance: This requirement is especially significant for securing and enforcing broad claims in unpredictable technologies. Satisfying both possession (written description) and enablement is necessary; courts may apply a stringent standard for unpredictable arts.

name: Unpredictable technologies demand more disclosure and limit broad functional claims
description: Technologies considered 'unpredictable' (e.g., catalysis, pharmaceuticals, biotechnology) are subject to a more stringent written description/enablement standard, making it harder to obtain broad functionalized claims based solely on mechanism or function.
guidance: Patents claiming genes/proteins functionally rather than structurally have fared poorly; courts often require more specific exemplification or working examples. Litigation often reveals that having only one or few working examples is risky in these fields.

name: Specific sequence knowledge/possession is often required for DNA/protein claims
description: Courts have required adequate descriptive possession of nucleotide or amino acid sequences; mere reference to DNA encoding a protein may be insufficient without adequate structural description or sequence information.
guidance: In re Wallach: knowledge of the complete amino acid sequence may establish possession of the DNA, but knowledge of only short fragments (e.g., 11 amino acids of a 185–192 amino acid protein) was insufficient. University of Rochester v. G.D. Searle: broad method claims lacking identification of specific drugs invalidated for failing written description/enabling disclosure.

name: Exemplify extensively in patent disclosure for unpredictable arts
description: Patent disclosures should exemplify as much as possible the scope of the claimed technology, including how to make and use it, and should define each term, component, and step in sufficient detail.
guidance: Do not rely exclusively on illustrative or prophetic examples without testing representative examples. Identify as many specific compounds as possible in pharmaceutical contexts; articulate operative limits and include tested working examples where feasible.

name: Pursue broad method claims including methods for making/using genes or proteins
description: Where appropriate, claim methods for making genes or proteins or using them (e.g., as probes, screening assays, DNA microchips) since method claims may sometimes survive written description/enablement scrutiny better than broad functional genus claims.
guidance: Method claims for manufacture or use can offer alternative protection and may help prevent importation or use of products made by proprietary methods.

name: Re-issue of manufacture limited to same concrete instrument or dependent inventions
description: An original patent for a manufacture can be re-issued only for the same concrete instrument, or for inventions upon which the production of such manufacture may depend; essential characteristics attributed in original must be found in re-issue.
guidance: Text (§676): "Whatever essential characteristics have been attributed to the manufacture in the original specification must be found in it as described and claimed in the re-issue; and ... the identity of the invention must be distinctly traceable."

name: Elements/sub-combinations of design may be claimed if they answer requirements
description: The elements and sub-combinations of the original design, if answering the stated requirements, may be claimed in the re-issue.
guidance: Text: "The elements and sub-combinations of the original design, if answering the requirements already mentioned, may be claimed in the re-issue;" see §§477, 588 notes.

name: Re-issue cannot embrace matter previously or impliedly excluded
description: A re-issued patent cannot embrace matter that was expressly disclaimed in the original, or impliedly excluded by the original descriptions and limitations; the inventor is bound by statements and limitations in the original patent.
guidance: Text (§680): "The nature of the subject-matter which the inventor intended and attempted to describe and claim in his original specifications may be further indicated by the limitations which he has imposed ... in consequence of these his re-issue may be confined within narrower boundaries than the character of his invention would otherwise require." Cases cited: Beecher Mfg. Co. v. Atwater Mfg. Co., Avery v. etc.

name: Statements and limitations in original are binding; omissions may void re-issue
description: Statements in the original patent (including professed dispensations or limitations) are binding upon the patentee and omission of limitations in the re-issue that enlarge the invention are invalid; re-issue cannot enlarge invention by omitting words in original claim.
guidance: Text: "The statements of an inventor in his original Claim and specifications are binding upon him ... That a re-issue enlarging the invention by omitting words found in the original Claim is invalid," with cases Matthews v. Iron Clad Mfg. Co., James v. Campbell, etc.

name: Re-issue cannot convert erroneous causal statements into new claimed causes
description: Where the original attributes effects to erroneous causes, the patentee's subsequent discovery of the true causes cannot be made available by re-issue to claim the newly discovered causes.
guidance: Text: "Where he mistakes the nature of his invention, and in the original specification attributes the effects which it produces to erroneous causes, his subsequent discovery of the true causes cannot be made available to him by a re-issue..." Cases: Eames v. Andrews, Andrews v. Hovey.

name: Identity of invention determined by comparing specifications (and drawings/models)
description: The identity of the invention claimed in the re-issue with that attempted to be covered in the original is ascertained, in most cases, by a simple comparison of their respective specifications; where drawings/models are involved they are the proper objects of comparison.
guidance: Text (§681): "The identity ... is ascertained ... by a simple comparison of their respective specifications ... Where the invention is of a nature admitting of illustration by drawings or models, this is the only investigation which can be made." Cases: Ex parte Seibert, Ex parte Baldwin.

name: If identity not apparent on face, re-issue may be sustained; if apparent difference, re-issue void
description: If on the face of the two specifications it is apparent that the re-issue claims a substantially distinct invention, the re-issue is void; if diversity is not apparent, the re-issue will be sustained as to this requirement.
guidance: Text: "If on the face of the two specifications ... it is apparent that the invention claimed in the re-issue is substantially distinct ... the re-issue is void. If the diversity is not apparent, the re-issue ... will be sustained."

name: Drawings and model may be inspected; model presumptions and lost-model rules
description: Original drawings and model may be inspected to determine identity; if a feature claimed in re-issue is absent from specification/drawings, the model will be presumed to contain it unless produced; where model lost, changes in drawings only on most conclusive evidence.
guidance: Text: "Drawings and model originally filed may be examined ... a dilapidated model may be aided by evidence ... when a feature claimed in the re-issue is absent ... the model will be presumed to contain it unless the model is produced. Where the model is lost ... no change can be permitted ... except upon the most conclusive evidence." Cases: Johnsen v. Beard; Hendy v. Golden State & Miners' Iron Works; Flower v. Detroit.

name: Possession of the claimed invention
description: The specification must show that applicant was in possession of the claimed invention; the disclosure must be 'full, clear, concise, and exact' so that a skilled artisan recognizes applicant had the invention as claimed.
guidance: If a complete structure is disclosed, the written description requirement is satisfied for that species or embodiment. The inquiry is factual and considers whether the disclosure conveys with reasonable clarity to those skilled in the art that applicant was in possession of the invention as of the filing date (Vas-Cath, Ralston Purina, Lockwood citations).

name: Complete structure disclosure satisfies species support
description: When the application as filed discloses the complete structure (or acts of a process) of the claimed invention as a whole, the written description requirement is satisfied for that species.
guidance: No rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (pre-AIA 112, first paragraph) for lack of written description should be made for that species if complete structure is disclosed.

name: Factors to consider in determining possession
description: Possession is assessed by considering multiple factors rather than a single test.
guidance: Factors include level of skill and knowledge in the art, partial structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics (esp. if coupled with known/disclosed structure-function correlation), and the method of making the claimed invention. Any combination of such identifying characteristics that distinguishes the claimed invention from other materials and leads one of skill to conclude possession may suffice.

name: Greater disclosure required in unpredictable/emerging arts
description: For inventions in unpredictable or emerging technologies, more evidence in the specification is required to show possession than in mature, predictable arts.
guidance: Disclosure of only a method of making plus function may not support claims (e.g., product-by-process) in unpredictable arts; reduction to practice or more detailed structure may be needed (Fiers, Amgen, Burroughs Wellcome).

name: Product-by-process claims: need clarity that process produces product
description: A product-by-process claim is supported when the specification shows the process actually produces the product or otherwise evidences possession of the product; mere process description or product characterization may be insufficient.
guidance: If the acts set forth cannot be shown to be performable or to produce the product, the written description may fail. When the process has actually been used to produce the product, written description for the product-by-process claim is clearly satisfied.

name: Characterization alone may be insufficient to show possession
description: Describing only properties or characterization of a product without enabling or structural disclosure may fail to evidence possession of the claimed invention.
guidance: Court precedent (Amgen) explains that conception of complex chemical compounds requires ability to define and distinguish the compound structurally or by method of preparation, not solely by a principal biological property.

name: Genus claims require representative number of species
description: Claims to a genus may be supported by disclosure of a 'representative number of species' that are adequately described and are representative of the entire genus.
guidance: When substantial variation exists within the genus, a sufficient variety of species must be described to reflect that variation; failure to disclose representative species requires rejection for lack of written description (AbbVie example).

name: Single species may support genus in some circumstances
description: Disclosure of only one species can support a claim to a genus only if the disclosure indicates the patentee has invented species sufficient to constitute the genus or when a skilled artisan would understand the genus is contemplated.
guidance: Examples include situations where the specification makes clear the invention is not limited to the particular species disclosed (Rasmussen, In re Herschler, In re Smythe). Courts caution, however, that unpredictability in the art may prevent a single-species disclosure from being representative.

name: Disclosure must reasonably convey the inventor had possession of the later-claimed subject matter
description: The dispositive test is whether the disclosure 'reasonably conveys to the artisan that the inventor had possession at that time of the later claimed subject matter.'
guidance: Objective standard per Gosteli/Vas-Cath; possession may be shown by words, structures, figures, diagrams, formulas, reduction to practice, or 'ready for patenting' disclosures such as drawings or structural chemical formulas.

name: Specification need not use claim terms verbatim
description: The subject matter need not be described in the exact terminology of the claim to satisfy the written description requirement.
guidance: However, if a claim amendment introduces limitations not present in the original disclosure (departure/addition/deletion), the examiner should conclude the subject matter is not described and reject under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or deny benefit of the earlier filing date.

name: Each claim limitation must be supported in the original disclosure
description: To comply with written description (or to be entitled to an earlier filing/priority date), each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure.
guidance: If an explicit limitation is not present, it must be shown that a person of ordinary skill would have understood at filing that the description requires that limitation (Hyatt v. Boone). Inherency requires that missing matter is necessarily present and recognized by persons of ordinary skill; probabilities or possibilities are insufficient (In re Robertson).

name: Elements described as essential must be claimed
description: If the originally filed disclosure identifies elements as essential or critical, those elements must be included in any claim directed to the invention.
guidance: Failure to claim elements described as essential can result in rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or denial of priority/benefit (Johnson Worldwide, Gentry Gallery, Tronzo citations).

name: Examiner burden to rebut presumption of adequate written description
description: A description as filed is presumed adequate; the examiner has the initial burden to present evidence/reasoning by a preponderance to explain why persons skilled in the art would not recognize the claimed invention in the original disclosure.
guidance: The examiner must have a reasonable basis for challenge and, when rejecting, must set forth express factual findings supporting the lack of written description (Wertheim, In re Marzocchi). A general allegation of 'unpredictability' is insufficient.

name: Rejection content requirements: identify limitations and establish prima facie case
description: When rejecting a claim for lack of written description, the examiner should (A) identify the claim limitation(s) at issue and (B) establish a prima facie case with reasons why a person skilled in the art would not have recognized possession in view of the application as filed.
guidance: A simple statement pointing out where support is not apparent may suffice when applicable; examiners should suggest claim amendments that can be supported by the original disclosure, being mindful not to introduce new matter.

name: Means-(or step-)plus-function limitations require corresponding structure/materials/acts disclosure
description: A limitation expressed in means- or step-plus-function language must be supported by disclosure of corresponding structure, material, or acts in the specification; absent such disclosure the limitation is indefinite and also lacks adequate written description.
guidance: Under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre-AIA sixth paragraph), the claim covers the corresponding structure and equivalents. If the specification fails to disclose sufficient corresponding structure that performs the entire function, the limitation is indefinite (In re Donaldson).

name: Amendments and new claims must be supported by original disclosure for priority/benefit
description: New or amended claims (or claims asserting entitlement to an earlier filing/priority date under 35 U.S.C. 119/120/365/386) must be supported by the original disclosure as required by 35 U.S.C. 112(a).
guidance: Applicant should specifically point out the support for amendments; examiner's initial burden applies. Lack of support requires rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or denial of benefit of the earlier filing date.

name: Typical circumstances giving rise to written description issues
description: Written description issues commonly arise on claim amendments, reliance on parent filing date (35 U.S.C. 120), reliance on foreign/provisional priority (35 U.S.C. 119), interference counts, original claims that are functionally defined or broad genera, and indefiniteness of means-plus-function limitations.
guidance: Be alert to these contexts and apply the same description analysis. For interference/priority contexts, the earlier application must meet the written description requirement for the subject matter of the count or claimed priority.

name: Amendments after grant — scope and limits
description: After grant, the patentee may apply in Form-13 for amendment of application, complete specification or any related document; request shall state nature of proposed amendment and reasons.
guidance: Amendments are allowable only by way of disclaimer, correction or explanation and only to incorporate actual fact; no amendment shall claim or describe matter not in substance disclosed before amendment; amended pages filed in duplicate with cancelled originals; substantive amendments are published and open to opposition within three months.

name: Definition of 'reasonable requirements of the public' (Section 84(7))
description: Reasonable requirements deemed not satisfied if: I. refusal to grant licence prejudices existing/developing trade or industry or demand not met to adequate extent or export market not supplied/developed or establishment/development of commercial activities in India prejudiced; II. conditions imposed by patentee on grant of licences or purchase/use of patented article/process prejudice manufacture/use/sale of non-protected materials or establishment/development of trade/industry; III. patentee imposes exclusive grant-back, prevention to challenges or coercive package licensing; IV. invention not being worked in India on commercial scale to adequate extent or fullest extent reasonably practicable; V. working in India on commercial scale is prevented or hindered by importation from abroad by patentee or persons claiming under him or persons buying from him or others against whom patentee is not taking proceedings.

name: The Claims
description: Formal and substantive requirements for the claims included in the international application.
guidance: Claims must be clear and supported by the description; see paragraphs 5.128–5.163 for number/format/definiteness and for amendments under Article 19 and Chapter II.

name: Mayo two-step framework
description: First determine whether the claims are directed to a patent-ineligible concept (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea). If so, then ask whether the claim's elements, considered individually and 'as an ordered combination,' transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application.
guidance: Step two is described as a search for an 'inventive concept'—an element or combination of elements sufficient to ensure the patent amounts to significantly more than the ineligible concept itself. (Cites Mayo Collaborative Services v. Prometheus.)

name: Identify whether claim is directed to an abstract idea
description: Claims drawn to fundamental economic practices or methods of organizing human activity—such as hedging or intermediated settlement—are 'abstract ideas' and fall within the §101 exception.
guidance: The Court treats longstanding commercial practices (e.g., hedging in Bilski; intermediated settlement in Alice) as abstract ideas. Presence of mathematical formulas is not required for a finding of abstraction; methods organizing human activity can qualify.

name: Consider claim elements individually and as an ordered combination
description: When applying step two, consider each element of the claim separately and then consider the elements together as an 'ordered combination' to determine whether they add enough to transform the abstract idea into an inventive application.
guidance: This approach is consistent with treating patent claims as a whole while still searching for any 'inventive concept.' The Court explicitly commands this twofold consideration (individual + ordered combination).

name: Search for an 'inventive concept' at Mayo step two
description: A claim that recites an abstract idea must include additional features—an 'inventive concept'—sufficient to ensure the claim is more than a drafting effort designed to monopolize the abstract idea.
guidance: Examples: Mayo held mere instructions to apply a law of nature were insufficient; Diehr was patent-eligible because the claim included steps that improved a technological process. The inventive concept must be more than conventional or routine activity.

name: Functional, generic hardware recitations do not confer patent eligibility
description: Reciting generic computer components (e.g., 'data processing system,' 'communications controller,' 'data storage unit') in functional terms that merely perform conventional calculations, storage, and transmission does not provide a meaningful limitation beyond implementing the idea on a computer.
guidance: System claims that add only generic hardware configured to perform the same abstract idea are substantively no different from method claims and fail §101 for the same reasons; the Court warns against letting 'draftsman's art' determine eligibility.

name: System and media claims rise or fall with method claims when they add nothing substantive
description: If system and computer-readable medium claims add no substantive limitation beyond the abstract idea as implemented on a generic computer, they are patent ineligible along with the method claims.
guidance: The Court notes petitioner conceded media claims rise or fall with method claims; system claims that merely recite a handful of generic components configured to implement the idea add nothing 'of substance.'

name: Claims must be considered 'as a whole' while searching for inventive concept
description: Although Mayo directs courts to consider claim elements both individually and in combination, the general rule remains that patent claims must be considered as a whole.
guidance: The Court cites Diamond v. Diehr to emphasize consistency: one should examine claims as a whole but still perform the step-two inquiry to identify whether the combination supplies an inventive concept.

name: Avoid letting claim drafting decide eligibility ('draftsman’s art')
description: Patent eligibility under §101 should not depend simply on how the claim is drafted—reciting an abstract idea in different words or attaching generic technological labels should not render it eligible.
guidance: The Court warns that interpreting §101 to permit claims that merely rephrase abstract ideas or tack on conventional computer language would 'make patent eligibility depend simply on the draftsman’s art' and eviscerate the exclusion for abstract ideas.

name: Business-method claims may be ineligible as non-§101 'processes'
description: Claims that 'merely describe a method of doing business' may not qualify as a 'process' under §101 and thus can be patent-ineligible.
guidance: Justice Sotomayor's concurrence (citing Bilski) reiterates that organizing human activity/business methods are typically not processes under §101. This guidance supports treating business-method patents skeptically under the abstract-idea framework.

name: Method-of-use patent listing limitation
description: A patent that is identified as claiming a method of using such drug shall be filed pursuant to section §355(c)(2) for listing in the Orange Book only if the patent claims a method of use approved in the application.
guidance: Method-of-use patents are listable only when they claim a use that is approved in the NDA (i.e., the specific approved indication/use). Patents claiming unapproved or peripheral uses should not be listed.

name: Improper listing may support monopolization or use of 'improper means'
description: Improperly listing patents in the Orange Book may constitute an 'improper means' of competition and may be actionable as monopolization where there is willful acquisition or maintenance of monopoly power by improper conduct.
guidance: To pursue monopolization claims requires proof of willful acquisition/maintenance of monopoly power via improper conduct. Courts have recognized that Orange Book mislisting can be evidence of 'improper means.' Such conduct may also be relevant in merger review and private antitrust suits.

name: Handling when an expedited-requested application becomes a prior-filed application claiming domestic priority
description: If an application requested for expedited examination becomes a prior-filed application of an application claiming domestic priority, it is treated differently depending on timing and status: eligibility may be lost, the examiner may order supplementation, dismiss the request, or withhold examination until the prior-filed application is deemed withdrawn.
guidance: Key subrules: a prior-filed application is deemed withdrawn when 1 year and 3 months have passed from filing the prior-filed application; if prior-filed status is confirmed before determination the application is not eligible and the examiner orders correction within a designated period and then dismisses if not remedied; if the priority claim is withdrawn before dismissal, the request may be deemed valid; if the application becomes a prior-filed application after determination of expedited eligibility, the examiner shall withhold examination until the application is deemed withdrawn. Also, if a patent is granted on the prior-filed application before withdrawal, a later-filed application cannot be granted.

name: Determination of identicalness between third-party practiced invention and claimed invention
description: A requester must clarify and prove that the invention practiced by a third party is identical with the claimed invention; the requester may submit evidential documents (photos, purchase details, certified mail copies, product samples, etc.) and explanatory descriptions.
guidance: An examiner compares submitted evidential materials to determine identicalness and may order supplementation if insufficient. If it's difficult for requester to obtain cooperation but identicalness appears highly likely, examiner may accept the request without additional documents except in obvious non-identical cases. If the two inventions are different, the examiner shall dismiss the request.

name: Handling requests based on applicant's warning to third party
description: A person who received a warning letter about practicing the published invention may request expedited examination by submitting the warning or a copy plus detailed conditions (date, means, contents). The examiner shall recognize the request unless there is a special ground to reject the fact the applicant delivered a warning or the practicing party's product is clearly different from the claimed invention.

name: Definition and scope of 'green technology' for expedited eligibility
description: Green technology is technology that minimizes greenhouse gas and pollutant emissions and saves/uses energy effectively across socioeconomic activities—examples include greenhouse gas reduction, energy efficiency, cleaner production/energy, resource circulation, eco-friendly technologies, and convergence technologies; it is defined under the Framework Act on Low Carbon Green Growth and Patent Act enforcement decree.
guidance: Requester must explain why the claimed invention constitutes green technology in the written explanation; the examiner decides based on the applicant's argument. If there is no ground for denial that the invention saves/uses energy efficiently and minimizes emissions, it shall be recognized as green technology. A non-exhaustive list of major green tech initiatives and '17 new growth engine' technologies is provided as illustrative examples. If no explanation is given or invention appears irrelevant, the examiner shall order correction of the request.

name: Applications directly related to promotion of export: evidential documents and identicalness
description: Applications directly related to the promotion of export may be eligible if supported by evidential documents such as statement of export result, arrival of letter of credit, buyer's request for patent/utility/design rights, export contracts, evidence of adoption as international standards, or other export-related documents.
guidance: The invention to be exported and the claimed invention must be identical; the requester must prove identicalness. Normally identicalness cannot be determined from request documents alone; however, the examiner can accept the request without requiring additional evidential documents if there is a high possibility they are the same and no particular grounds to doubt it.

name: Vaikuttavan aineen esiintyminen peruspatentin vaatimuksissa
description: Voitteen määritteleminen: vaikuttava(t) aine(et) on oltava esitetty peruspatentin patenttivaatimuksissa, jotta peruspatentin voitaisiin katsoa suojaavan tuotetta (C-322/10 ja C-493/12).
guidance: SPC voidaan myöntää vain, jos peruspatentin vaatimuksista ilmenee, että kyseinen vaikuttava aine tai sen yhdistelmä kuuluu patentin kattamaan keksintöön; tarkista claim wording ja tulkinta.

name: Selection of representative claim(s) for Official Gazette and certificate printing
description: The examiner must indicate a representative claim and an appropriate drawing figure for printing on the certificate cover sheet and in the Official Gazette.
guidance: Instructions: (A) select the broadest claim; (B) ordinarily designate one claim per invention (in reexamination select only one claim); (C) do not select a dependent claim unless the independent claim is also printed; for multiple dependent claims list the entire chain for one embodiment; in reexamination a dependent claim may be selected where the independent original has been canceled; in reissue select the broadest claim with changes or the broadest additional reissue claim.

name: Recording claim selection and numbering on forms
description: When recording representative claim(s) or claim numbers, enter claim numbers clearly; separate multiple claims by commas; refer to renumbered patent claim numbers rather than original claim numbers if different.
guidance: Ensure clarity and use renumbered claim numbers when applicable.

name: Telephone contact before canceling all claims
description: Prior to canceling claims and issuing a NIRC because claims are to be canceled, the examiner should telephone the patent owner to inquire if a timely response or appeal was filed to ensure a timely response has not been misdirected within the Office.
guidance: If patent owner indicates no timely filing or cannot be reached, examiner proceeds to issue a NIRC terminating prosecution. If owner was reached, the telephone interview will be made of record and attached to the NIRC.

name: Drafting examiner's amendment to cancel all claims
description: When all live claims are canceled, the examiner will issue a NIRC and attach an examiner's amendment canceling all live claims; the amendment should point out why the claims have been canceled.
guidance: Examples of appropriate statements are provided, e.g., failure to timely respond referencing 37 CFR 1.550(d) and MPEP § 2266, or affirmation by Board decision with no timely appeal.

name: Reasons for patentability/confirmation required
description: Reasons for patentability and/or confirmation are required for each claim found patentable, unless all claims are canceled in the proceeding.
guidance: Box 2 of form PTOL-469 is checked and reasons provided as an attachment. The examiner should indicate why the claims are clearly patentable over the cited patents/printed publications, similar to reasons for allowance in an application (see MPEP § 1302.14). The reasons may be set forth on PTOL-476 or by using form paragraph 22.16. Examiner may refer to portions of the record which clearly establish patentability. Patent owner comments must be labeled and submitted promptly to avoid delays.

name: Amended or new claim may not enlarge scope
description: An amended or new claim may not enlarge the scope of the patent claims.
guidance: See MPEP § 2250 for limits on amendments that would enlarge claim scope.

name: Designation language and categorization of claims (confirmed vs patentable)
description: Original patent claims found patentable are generally designated 'confirmed' while new and amended patent claims are generally designated 'patentable'; examiner may use 'patentable' to refer to any claim that defines over the cited patents/printed publications.
guidance: There is no need to separate 'confirmed' and 'patentable' categories when setting forth reasons for patentability/confirmation. Where all claims are canceled, no reasons are provided.

name: Contents required in ex parte reexamination certificate
description: The reexamination certificate must set forth the results of the proceeding and the content of the patent following reexamination and will: cancel any patent claims determined unpatentable; confirm any patent claims determined patentable; incorporate amended or new claims determined patentable; make any changes in the description approved; include statutory or terminal disclaimers filed by owner; identify unamended claims held invalid on final holding by another forum; identify any patent claims not reexamined; be mailed on its date to patent owner and a copy to requester; identify patent claims dependent on amended claims determined patentable.
guidance: See 35 U.S.C. 307 and 37 CFR 1.570 for statutory/regulatory bases. If a certificate cancels all claims, no further Office proceedings will be conducted regarding that patent. If reexamination concluded by grant of reissued patent, the reissued patent constitutes the certificate. Notice of issuance will be published in Official Gazette on date of issuance.

name: Special petition procedures when reexamination certificate cancels all claims but reissue copending
description: If a reexamination certificate cancels all claims but a reissue application is copending, the patent owner may file a petition under 37 CFR 1.183 requesting waiver of 37 CFR 1.570(d) provisions to address claims pending in the reissue application.
guidance: Petition must be accompanied by a paper cancelling any claim within scope of canceled claims and explaining why remaining reissue claims can be patentable despite cancellation by certificate. Such paper will be available to the examiner if petition granted. See 37 CFR 1.570(d).

name: Markedly different characteristics (Chakrabarty test)
description: A product of nature must possess 'markedly different characteristics' from a naturally occurring counterpart to qualify as patent-eligible composition of matter.
guidance: Originates from Diamond v. Chakrabarty and was applied/quoted by lower courts in Myriad. The district court required that, considered as a whole, the claimed invention be sufficiently distinct in its fundamental characteristics from natural phenomena to possess a 'distinctive name, character, [and] use.' The Federal Circuit and later PTO guidance interpret this to require a demonstrable change in chemical identity/structure.

name: Focus on differences vs similarities framing
description: Whether analysis should focus on differences between the claimed material and the natural material (Myriad/Fed. Cir. approach) or on their similarities (AMP/district court approach) can determine eligibility.
guidance: The Supreme Court's framing emphasized the overwhelming similarities between isolated DNA and native DNA (particularly informational content), making structural differences ancillary; the choice of framing resembles a § 103‑style inquiry and materially affects outcomes.

name: Claim language: composition-of-matter vs information-focused claims
description: Claims expressed in terms of chemical composition (a unique molecule) can support eligibility based on chemical changes; claims that focus on genetic/informational content rather than chemical composition are more likely to be treated as claiming natural phenomena and thus ineligible.
guidance: The Supreme Court noted Myriad's claims were 'not expressed in terms of chemical composition' and focused on the genetic information encoded, which weighed against eligibility; drafting that emphasizes chemical/structural features rather than mere sequence/information may preserve eligibility.

name: Claim breadth and avoidable workarounds
description: Broad claims that are concerned primarily with information (e.g., sequence) can be avoided by minor chemical variations, revealing that such claims do not depend on creation of a unique molecule and therefore are more vulnerable to § 101 exclusion.
guidance: The Supreme Court observed that if a claim truly depended on a unique molecule, infringers could avoid by adding or changing nucleotides; because Myriad's claims were concerned with information, this suggested ineligibility. Drafters should therefore consider whether claim scope anchors on chemical/structural novelty.

name: Alice/Mayo two-step §101 framework
description: Apply the two-step Alice/Mayo analysis: (1) determine whether the claims are directed to an abstract idea (or other ineligible concept); (2) if so, determine whether the claims recite an ‘inventive concept’ that transforms the abstract idea into patent-eligible application.
guidance: Courts look to whether claims recite a specific technological solution or merely result-oriented, functional language. Generic computer components performing conventional tasks typically do not supply an inventive concept. Claims that improve computer functionality or recite specific means or methods that solve a technical problem may be eligible. Case examples: Chewy (targeted advertising found abstract), AI Visualize (data retrieval/manipulation/display at high level of generality found abstract), Contour (claims found eligible where they recited a specific dual-recording wireless camera solution).

name: Functional/result-oriented claim language signals abstraction
description: Claims drafted using largely result-focused, functional language are strong indicators of an abstract idea and are frequently found ineligible under §101.
guidance: Courts cite result-oriented phrasing and omission of how steps are performed as reasons to find abstractness; claiming goals such as 'achieving X' without specific technical means often fails Alice step two. (Beteiro, AI Visualize, Mobile Acuity).

name: Conventional components and conventional steps do not supply inventive concept
description: Use of generic databases, servers, conventional offline/batch processing, GPS in phones, templates, or automation of human tasks ordinarily will not provide the 'inventive concept' required at Alice step two.
guidance: Claims that merely automate abstract ideas using well-understood, routine, conventional computer components or that claim improved speed/efficiency without novel technical means are typically ineligible. (Chewy, Broadband, Beteiro, Contour contrast).

name: Requirement that claims show how a technical problem is solved
description: To be eligible, claims that involve computer/technical subject matter should recite how the claimed elements effect the solution to the technological problem, not merely state the result.
guidance: Courts examine whether the specification and claim limitations disclose details of the purported technical solution; mere specification descriptions without claim limitations specifying the details often fail to show an inventive concept. (AI Visualize, Mobile Acuity, Contour).

name: PTAB motion-to-amend requirements and Motion-to-Amend Pilot Program
description: Motions to amend should contain written-description support for substitute claims (37 C.F.R. § 42.121(b)), but the Motion-to-Amend Pilot permits the patent owner to file replies that may supply missing written-description evidence.
guidance: The PTAB may accept evidence submitted with a reply under the Pilot Program to correct or supplement an initial motion to amend; appellate courts will consider whether any procedural error was harmless (i.e., no prejudice). (ZyXEL v. UNMRI).

name: Interference §135(b)(1) time-bar and 'same or substantially the same subject matter' analysis
description: 35 U.S.C. § 135(b)(1) bars later-filed application claims that are the same as or for the same (or substantially the same) subject matter as a claim of an issued patent if not made prior to one year from the patent grant; this is a statute of repose with limited exceptions.
guidance: Courts apply a comparison (two-way test) to determine whether pre-critical-date claims provide support for later claims; material differences (e.g., presence/absence of a limitation like 'free of containment material') can render a claim time-barred. There is an exception where the applicant was 'already claiming substantially the same invention' during the critical period. (Speck v. Bates).

name: Indefiniteness standard
description: Claims must be sufficiently definite so that a person of ordinary skill can determine the scope of the claims with reasonable certainty.
guidance: The Year-in-Review includes a dedicated section on indefiniteness (IV.A) addressing the standard and cases; patentees should ensure claim terms are defined or used in a way that avoids uncertainty (heading present; cases not shown in excerpt).

name: Doctrine of equivalents and inducement standards
description: Proving infringement under the doctrine of equivalents remains subject to a high evidentiary bar; inducement analyses consider labels and other contextual factors to determine whether inducement occurred.
guidance: The Federal Circuit reaffirmed a high bar for doctrine-of-equivalents claims and continued to explore what external indicia (e.g., skinny labels) can be considered in inducement assessments. Practitioners should craft infringement theories with clear nexus to claim elements and evidence of intent where inducement is alleged.

name: Claim construction guidance: specification limits vs non-limiting embodiments; printed-matter doctrine
description: When construing claims, courts assess whether the specification limits claim scope to the 'present invention' or whether preferred embodiments are non-limiting; printed-matter doctrine issues also arise in claim interpretation.
guidance: The document contains a section (VIII) addressing specification-limiting issues and the printed-matter doctrine; patentees should avoid language that unintentionally limits claims and ensure claim scope is supported by specification disclosure.

name: Seventh defence—construction of claims not proper in plea
description: The seventh defence involves construction of the claims of the letters patent and therefore is not proper matter for a plea.
guidance: Letters patent are not void merely because they describe something not shown in the original application; only when they claim something not indicated or described in the specification or drawings of the original application are they obnoxious to this defence. The question what letters patent claim is a question of law for the court and cannot properly be raised by plea, demurrer, or motion to dismiss because the court must construe the claims and compare them with the original application, which must be introduced as evidence. This defence therefore should be set up in the answer (except where the complainant takes the initiative).

name: Fourteenth defence—depends on necessity for disclaimer; set up in answer
description: The fourteenth defence was generally required to be set up in an answer because it primarily depends upon the necessity for a disclaimer and that necessity depends upon the claim being obnoxious to one or more of the first three defences.
guidance: Because the interplay among defences (especially those not suitable for pleas) determines need for disclaimer, the answer is the proper vehicle.

name: Fifteenth defence—not proper subject for plea; depends on original patent validity/operativeness
description: The fifteenth defence is not proper subject-matter of a plea because it depends upon the original patent being inoperative or invalid due to defective/insufficient specification, or upon lack of novelty in part of the original patent.
guidance: It may depend on construction of the original patent or proof that persons skilled in the art could make/use the invention from the original specification; statements of legal construction or universal factual claims are not suitable in a plea. It cannot be raised by motion to dismiss unless the original letters patent are incorporated in the bill and the question is solely one of construction.

name: Eighteenth defence—double patent identity; motion if identity plain
description: The eighteenth defence (alleging that the later patent is a double of a prior patent) may be made by motion to dismiss where the bill is based on the prior patent as well as on its alleged double.
guidance: A plea is unsuitable unless the disputed claim(s) in the subsequent patent can be plainly seen to be identical with claim(s) in the prior patent; if construction is required to determine identity the matter is one of law and improper for plea.

name: Twenty-fifth defence—non-infringement: motion to dismiss only if obvious from bill
description: The twenty-fifth defence (non-infringement) may be interposed by a motion to dismiss where the bill sets forth the claims alleged to be infringed and the particular character of the defendant's doings.
guidance: Such motions will be dismissed except where non-infringement is obvious from the bill without reference to prior art. If motion denied, defendant may plead non-infringement in answer and support with evidence within five days after denial. U.S. precedents generally do not permit pleas of non-infringement though English equity practice might. Economical drafting can sometimes make non-infringement apparent on the face of the bill but that is usually difficult.

name: After Final Consideration Pilot 2.0 (AFCP 2.0) request requirements
description: To use AFCP 2.0, the applicant should submit a request for consideration under AFCP along with a response that includes an amendment to at least one independent claim; the amendment must not broaden the scope of the independent claim.
guidance: Only one AFCP 2.0 request may be filed in response to an outstanding final rejection. If the amendment necessitates additional search/consideration that cannot be completed within allotted time, the examiner may issue an advisory action. If no additional search is required or it can be completed within time, the examiner will determine if the amendment places the application in condition for allowance; if not, the examiner will contact the applicant and request an interview. AFCP 2.0 has been found effective in advancing prosecution and reducing likelihood of filing an RCE.

name: Filing a continuation application
description: A continuation application has the same disclosure as the pending application but may claim different scope; it undergoes new examination and does not get abandoned when the pending application is abandoned.
guidance: Continuation applications allow pursuing claims of varying scope or re-drafting rejected claims. However, if rejected claims from the parent are presented unchanged in the continuation, the first office action on the continuation may itself be a final rejection. Use continuation to preserve prosecution options while pursuing different claim scopes.

name: Patentable subject matter
description: The subject matter claimed must be the type of invention that is patentable under applicable law (e.g., technical inventions; exclusions such as mathematical algorithms or certain methods of medical treatment may apply in some jurisdictions).
guidance: Check national/regional rules for excluded subject matter (e.g., laws on biological material, software, medical methods); when borderline, draft claims and description to emphasize technical/functional features; note that countries differ on software, genetic materials, methods of treatment.

name: Disclosure requirement (sufficiency / enablement / written description)
description: The application must disclose the invention sufficiently clearly and completely so that a person skilled in the art can carry it out (including written description requirements where applicable).
guidance: Ensure the description supports the full scope of the claims; include embodiments, working examples, reference to drawings; beware of introducing new matter when amending; keep clear linkage between claims and description.

name: Patentable subject matter specifics for computer programs
description: Software as such may be excluded in some jurisdictions, but software-implemented inventions (systems/methods delivering a technical effect) can be patentable.
guidance: Draft to highlight a technical effect, system or method, and efficiency or new data-processing approach rather than a pure algorithm; avoid claiming pure mathematical algorithms.

name: Understanding the invention (core inventive concept)
description: Determine the core inventive concept that provides the novel technical contribution to be protected by claims.
guidance: Focus drafting (claims and description) on the core inventive idea; identify embodiments and variations to support broad and fallback claim scope.

name: Inventorship
description: Identify and record correct inventors — persons who contributed to the claimed inventive features.
guidance: Accurate inventorship is legally important; document contributions and resolve multi-inventor situations; consider jurisdiction-specific representation rules.

name: Typical parts of a patent application (Request, Description, Claims, Drawings, Abstract, Application format)
description: A patent application should contain a request/formality section, a description, claims, drawings (if applicable), an abstract, and conform to required format.
guidance: Follow national/regional application format rules; prepare clear request, well-structured description and an informative abstract; include drawings with reference indicators; ensure formalities to avoid procedural rejections.

name: Prepare the claims first
description: Drafting claims before the description helps set clear protection goals and ensures the description supports claimed scope.
guidance: Use claims to define invention boundaries and then craft description and embodiments to support them; avoids unintended gaps between claims and description.

name: Broad and narrow claims
description: Include both broad (to maximize scope) and narrow (to ensure allowability) claims in a claim set.
guidance: Balance breadth with support in the description; include fallback narrower claims to survive examination; consider claim-dependent structures to cascade fallbacks.

name: Patent protection and infringement: all-elements rule
description: Infringement analysis requires that an accused product/process includes all elements of a claim (the all-elements rule).
guidance: Draft claims with clear elements and consider variants/alternatives to capture likely infringers; avoid ambiguous claim language that could limit enforcement.

name: Parts of a claim (claim format)
description: Claims typically have parts (preamble, transition, body) and must be structured to set out elements/limitations precisely.
guidance: Use appropriate claim grammar and transitional terms; ensure the preamble and body support the intended scope; consider two-part (Jepson-style) claim formats where applicable.

name: Grammar of a claim and other detail
description: Claims must use careful grammar and word choice to avoid ambiguity and unintended limitations.
guidance: Avoid vague terms, undefined relative terms, inconsistent terminology; include definitions in the description; use consistent reference numerals and indefinite/definite articles judiciously.

name: Two-part claims or improvement claims
description: Two-part claims (preamble/characterizing portion) are used to define known features and distinguish the invention (often used at EPO).
guidance: When using two-part claims, clearly state known features and the characterizing elements; ensure support in description and alignment with prior art arguments.

name: Independent claims
description: Independent claims stand on their own and set out the essential elements of an invention without relying on other claims.
guidance: Draft multiple independent claims of different types (product, method, use) to provide layered protection; ensure each independent claim is adequately supported by the description.

name: Dependent claims
description: Dependent claims add specific limitations to independent claims and provide narrower fallback positions.
guidance: Order dependent claims logically; ensure each dependent claim refers properly to the claim it depends on; include useful optional features and preferred embodiments as dependents.

name: Claims referring to features of another claim
description: Claims may refer to features in other claims to build hierarchical claim sets and combinations.
guidance: Ensure cross-reference clarity and support in the description; follow formal drafting rules for referencing other claims.

name: Claim sets based on set theory
description: Design claim sets deliberately to cover the universe of embodiments using set-theoretic relationships (unions, intersections) among claim elements.
guidance: Use claim drafting strategies to cover combinations and alternatives systematically; analyze coverage and gaps using set-theory thinking.

name: Schematic example of drafting a set of claims
description: Practical examples illustrating how to draft complementary independent and dependent claims to cover an invention.
guidance: Use schematic examples as templates; ensure real applications include specific technical details and support.

name: Product claims (basic type)
description: Claims directed to physical products or apparatus.
guidance: Define structural features and essential components; include materials, configurations and optional features in dependents.

name: Process / method claims (basic type)
description: Claims directed to methods or processes for producing an effect or using a product.
guidance: List steps in clear sequence; consider claim preambles and possible statutory exclusions (e.g., medical methods in some jurisdictions); include apparatus/product claims as complements.

name: Parameter claims
description: Claims that define invention by specified parameters or ranges (e.g., concentration, temperature).
guidance: Support ranges and parameters with experimental data and description; specify preferred ranges and provide justification to avoid undue breadth.

name: General use claims
description: Claims that assert broad intended uses (general purpose claims) for compositions or devices.
guidance: Provide adequate support and examples of uses in the description; watch legal standards for claims to uses (especially second medical use claims).

name: Medical indication (second medical use) claims
description: Claims directed to the use of a substance for a particular medical indication, including therapeutic uses.
guidance: Follow jurisdictional claim formats (e.g., Swiss-type or EPC 2000 formats); include clinical/experimental support for the indication; heed exclusions for medical treatment methods where present.

name: Composition claims
description: Claims for compositions of matter (chemical formulations, mixtures, compounds).
guidance: List components, concentrations, preparation methods where relevant; include preferred embodiments and examples; consider Markush language for alternatives.

name: Biotechnology claims
description: Claims covering biological materials, organisms, sequences, proteins, and related biotechnological inventions.
guidance: Provide functional descriptions, depositional information where required, and clear experimental support; be attentive to ethical and legal limitations in some jurisdictions.

name: Patent claim design (strategic design of claim scope)
description: Formulate an overall claim strategy to balance broad protection, enforceability, and support; include different claim types and fallback positions.
guidance: Consider competitors' products, prior art, prosecution history, and enforcement strategy; include dependent claims, multiple claim types, and alternatives to maximize enforceable coverage.

name: Clarity, claim word choice and inconsistencies
description: Claims and description must be clear and consistent; define terms and avoid relative/ambiguous expressions that create uncertainty.
guidance: Define key terms in the description; avoid conflicting terminology between claims and description; watch for undefined relative terms (e.g., 'substantially', 'about').

name: Defining terms
description: Provide explicit definitions of technical terms and alternative meanings used in the application.
guidance: Include definitions in the description to control claim interpretation and avoid ambiguity; use examples to illustrate terms.

name: Distinguishing elements
description: Identify and describe the features that distinguish the invention from the prior art and that should appear in claims.
guidance: Emphasize inventive features in claims and description; prepare arguments for examination distinguishing claims from cited prior art.

name: Uncertainty (avoidance)
description: Draft to minimize legal and technical uncertainty in claim scope and description disclosure.
guidance: Prefer precise language, concrete examples, numerical ranges, and clear functional descriptions to reduce interpretive disputes.

name: Use of the word 'in' and other prepositions
description: Small words like 'in', 'on', 'for' can materially affect claim scope and should be used deliberately.
guidance: Consider jurisdictional interpretations; define intended usage in description; be consistent.

name: Inconsistency (avoid)
description: Avoid inconsistencies between claims, description and drawings that could undermine support or clarity.
guidance: Cross-check all parts of the application; update descriptions if claims are amended; maintain consistent numbering and terminology.

name: Putting this into practice (practical drafting tips)
description: Concrete examples and practice-oriented tips on implementing drafting principles in real applications.
guidance: Use provided diagrams and sample claim sets as drafting templates; perform iterative review with technical inventors.

name: Claim variations and modifications of the invention
description: Draft description and claims to cover foreseeable variations and modifications of the inventive concept.
guidance: List alternative materials, configurations, parameter ranges, and process steps in the description to support broader claim language.

name: Avoiding unnecessary limitations
description: Do not include unnecessary limitations in claims or description that would unduly narrow protection.
guidance: Be cautious when incorporating examples into claim language; keep illustrative embodiments clearly labelled as examples.

name: Negative limitations and disclaimers
description: Negative claim limitations (exclusions) and disclaimers may be used but have legal and support implications.
guidance: Ensure negative limitations have basis in the disclosure or are allowable disclaimers under applicable law; avoid ad hoc disclaimers without support.

name: Claims and competing products
description: Draft claim scope with an eye to competing products and likely design-arounds.
guidance: Perform freedom-to-operate and competitor product analysis; include alternatives and broader functional language where support permits to cover likely infringers.

name: Using multiple claim types for the same invention
description: Seek protection through different claim categories (product, process, use, system, computer-readable medium) to maximize enforceability.
guidance: Ensure each claim type is supported by the description; consider strategic use based on jurisdiction (e.g., method vs product).

name: Ensuring that the description supports the claims
description: The description must provide adequate support for the full scope of the claims to avoid added-matter and enablement rejections.
guidance: Include specific embodiments, examples, and explicit disclosure for claim alternatives; avoid attempting to later broaden claims beyond original disclosure.

name: Claim point of view (claim drafting perspective)
description: Draft claims from the perspective of defining what is to be excluded from others (scope) while ensuring support and clarity.
guidance: Adopt claim drafting viewpoint that balances enforcement objectives with prosecution practicality and description support.

name: Narrowing a patent claim during prosecution
description: Amendments made during prosecution often narrow claims — know how to do so without introducing new matter.
guidance: Ensure amendments are supported by the original disclosure; understand jurisdictional rules for allowable amendments and timing (e.g., broadening limitations).
