name: 'Reading on' a patent claim
description: Understand and draft to control whether claims 'read on' (cover) particular products/processes — important for infringement and validity analyses.
guidance: Use precise element definitions; consider claim construction principles and likely interpretations by courts/examiners.

name: Claim construction in the courts
description: Be aware that courts interpret claims according to established doctrines (e.g., prosecution history, specification) which affect enforcement.
guidance: Draft specification to shape favorable claim construction; avoid inconsistent statements that could narrow claim interpretation later.

name: Key audiences of patent applications
description: Patent documents are read by multiple audiences — examiners, competitors, licensees, courts, investors — and should be drafted accordingly.
guidance: Tailor clarity, technical depth and legal framing to these audiences: clear claims for enforcement, sufficient technical disclosure for enablement, and accessible summaries for business stakeholders.

name: Order in which to draft a patent application
description: Recommended sequence: prepare claims first, then description, drawings, abstract and formal parts.
guidance: Following the recommended order aids coherence and ensures description supports claimed scope; use checklists and templates.

name: Drafting parts of a description: Title of invention
description: Provide a succinct, descriptive title that reflects the technical field and invention.
guidance: Keep title informative but not limiting; align with claims and field of invention statements.

name: Drafting parts of a description: Background art
description: Describe relevant prior art and the technical problem the invention addresses.
guidance: Frame background to highlight shortcomings of prior art and motivate claimed features; avoid admissions that could be used to construe claim scope inadvertently.

name: Drafting parts of a description: Summary of invention
description: Provide a clear summary of the invention and its advantages over prior art.
guidance: Use summary to introduce key features that will appear in claims; do not limit to only preferred embodiments.

name: Drafting parts of a description: Brief description of drawings
description: List and briefly describe each drawing figure and its content.
guidance: Coordinate figure references with description and claims; use consistent numbering and reference indicators.

name: Drafting parts of a description: Description of embodiments
description: Provide detailed embodiments showing how to make and use the invention, including working examples where appropriate.
guidance: Include multiple embodiments, preferred options, experimental data, and variations to support broad claim scope and enablement.

name: Drafting drawings: Types of drawing
description: Use appropriate drawings (schematics, flowcharts, chemical structures, graphs) to illustrate embodiments.
guidance: Follow office rules for drawing standards; include necessary detail to support claims; label reference indicators clearly.

name: Drafting drawings: Reference indicators
description: Use reference numerals/indicators in drawings and description consistently to identify elements.
guidance: Define reference numerals in the description; avoid over-reliance on numerals for claim scope — claims should stand alone.

name: Drafting drawings: Drawings provided by the inventor
description: Incorporate inventor-provided drawings while ensuring they meet formal requirements and adequately support claims.
guidance: Review and, if necessary, redraw or annotate to meet office standards and to improve clarity for prosecution and enforcement.

name: Drafting an abstract
description: Prepare a concise abstract summarizing the technical disclosure of the application (used for searching and indexing).
guidance: Keep abstract informative and within office length limits; avoid claims-like language that could be limiting; follow office formatting rules.

name: Application filing procedures in specific jurisdictions (USPTO, EPO, PCT)
description: Follow jurisdiction-specific procedures and formal requirements for filing and prosecution (examples: USPTO, EPO, PCT guidance).
guidance: Consult office guides and rules (e.g., EPO Guidelines, PCT Applicant’s Guide); adapt claim formats (two-part claims at EPO), fee structures and timing to each office.

name: Drafting responses to office actions
description: Craft persuasive responses combining legal arguments, claim amendments and technical evidence where appropriate.
guidance: Use clear claim amendments with support; provide prior art distinctions and technical explanations; consider examiner interviews to resolve issues.

name: Broadening claims and adding claims
description: Understand rules and risks when broadening claims or adding new claims after filing (often restricted after certain stages).
guidance: Observe jurisdictional limits on broadening amendments; use divisional/continuation strategies when additional claim scope is desired.

name: Divisional applications, continuation applications and continuation-in-part applications
description: Use procedural vehicles to pursue additional claims or new matter (subject to rules on added matter and priority).
guidance: File divisionals to pursue separate inventions; use continuations to pursue different claim scope; CIPs may add new material but affect priority — verify jurisdictional rules.

name: Patent strategy: Offensive blocking patenting
description: Use patenting offensively to block competitors and mount attacks on competitors' freedom-to-operate.
guidance: Develop claims targeting competitor products/processes; consider timing and scope to maximize blocking effect; prepare for enforcement costs.

name: Patent strategy: Design-around techniques
description: Anticipate and plan for design-arounds by competitors; use claim drafting to reduce ease of design-arounds.
guidance: Include functional and alternative claim language, parameter ranges and broad claim types to impede straightforward design-arounds; plan enforcement and licensing responses.

name: Filing date and basic filing contents
description: The filing date is assigned where the application contains: (a) an express or implicit indication that the grant of a patent is requested; (b) a part which, at first sight, appears to be the description of an invention and one or more claims; and (c) proof of payment of the prescribed fees. For any international application, the filing date is that assigned by the receiving office.
guidance: These three elements are required at the time of filing to secure a filing date; international applications follow receiving office assignment.

name: Publication content and timing for applications
description: The Organization shall publish for each application the filing number, filing date, applicant and inventor details (unless inventor requests omission), agent, validly claimed priorities, priority date/countries/numbers, title, abstract, international application info if applicable, and international patent classification symbols. The Organization shall also publish the specifications, the claim(s) and any drawings. Publication shall occur within 18 months of filing date or priority date (save for international applications).
guidance: Comprehensive bibliographic and substantive material is published; implementing regs determine exact procedure.

name: Amendments prior to grant limited by original disclosure
description: Prior to the grant, the applicant may modify the claims, the specification, the drawings and the abstract. Such modifications may not exceed the disclosure of the invention appearing in the application as filed.
guidance: No added matter beyond the original disclosure is permitted in pre-grant amendments.

name: Invalidity grounds for patents
description: Patents shall be declared invalid if: (a) invention is not new, lacks inventive step or not industrially applicable; (b) invention not patentable under Article 2; (c) specification does not comply with Article 13(d)(i) or does not completely and honestly state true methods. Certificates of addition not linked to principal patent likewise invalid. Invalidity may relate to all or some claims.
guidance: Substantive grounds allow full or partial invalidation; also applies to certificates of addition.

name: Specification must support the title of the patent (no incongruity)
description: The specification must support the title of the patent; the latter should not indicate one thing and the former describe another as the subject of the grant.
guidance: If the petitioner represented himself as inventor of matter not truly claimed in the specification, the grant may be void. Example: a patent for a tapering brush was not supported by a specification describing bristles of unequal length (not actually tapering).

name: Do not claim more than the actual invention (no over‑claiming)
description: The specification must not attempt to cover more than that which is the proper subject for protection; if a patentee seeks by his specification any more than he is strictly entitled to, his patent is rendered ineffectual.
guidance: Claims exceeding the inventor's true discovery may invalidate the entire grant. Example: a patent for a machine plus an improvement where the machine part could not be sustained made the whole grant invalid for attempting to cover too much.

name: If one of several asserted effects is not produced, specification is bad
description: When several effects are specified and one of them is not produced, the specification is defective and the patent may be void.
guidance: The patentee should not claim results that are not actually achieved by the described invention.

name: Determining if a claim 'recites' an abstract idea
description: The update provides additional information on how the USPTO determines if a claim 'recites' an abstract idea.
guidance: Use the explanations and examples in the update to assess whether claim language recites subject matter that falls within an abstract idea; follow the USPTO's procedures and illustrative examples to inform the factual and legal analysis.

name: How groupings within the abstract idea exception are determined
description: The update provides additional information on how groupings within the abstract idea exception are determined.
guidance: Apply the USPTO's approach to categorize abstract ideas into appropriate groupings when analyzing claims, using the update's explanations to choose consistent groupings for examination and reasoning.

name: Procedures to identify 'tentative abstract ideas'
description: The update explains the procedures examiners can use to identify 'tentative abstract ideas'.
guidance: Examiners should follow the described procedures to form and document tentative determinations about abstract-idea character, refining those determinations with claim context and examples before issuing a final rejection.

name: Evaluating integration of a judicial exception into a practical application
description: The update provides more information on how examiners evaluate whether a judicial exception is integrated into a practical application.
guidance: Use the update's tests and examples to determine whether claim limitations integrate a judicial exception into a practical application (i.e., whether the claim as a whole applies, uses, or improves a technology or technical field).

name: Examiner responsibility to provide adequate notice for subject matter eligibility rejections
description: The update addresses the examiner’s responsibility to provide adequate notice to applicants in making a subject matter eligibility rejection.
guidance: When issuing an eligibility rejection, examiners must give clear, adequate notice explaining the basis for the rejection (including how the claim is characterized and which judicial exception is implicated) so applicants can respond meaningfully.

name: Use of additional examples in life sciences and data processing
description: The update includes additional helpful examples in the life sciences and data processing areas.
guidance: Refer to these sector-specific examples to see how the 2019 PEG applies in life sciences and data processing contexts; use them as illustrative precedent for claim analysis and examiner training.

name: Language(s) in which the patent application must be filed (Question 1)
description: Applicants must file the patent application, including the specification, in the official language of the country of filing (some AMSs allow English or choice between English and local language). The language of filing is used as the language of proceedings and for amendments.
guidance: If filed in a non-official language, a translation (title, abstract, claims, description and drawings) must be filed within a specified period or upon request of the patent office. Myanmar: proceedings in official language even if English selected.

name: Documents and information required for filing a patent application (Question 2)
description: The set of documents and data that must accompany a filing (e.g., specification, claims, abstract, drawings, applicant particulars, power of attorney where required).
guidance: Requirements vary by AMS; guidelines summarize common/core documents relevant to substantive examination and cross-reference national formal requirements in the Comparative Study Report (CSR).

name: Calculation of filing fees per application, per claim, or per excess claims over a certain number (Question 7)
description: How filing and claim-related fees are computed (flat fee, per claim, excess-claim surcharges).
guidance: Fee structures differ across AMSs; ACG-PE lists common approaches that affect claim drafting strategies.

name: Assessment of unity of invention (Question 28 / 2.6)
description: Criteria used to determine whether claims relate to a single general inventive concept (unity) or require division.
guidance: ACG-PE defines 'unity of invention' and provides evaluation methodology, including assessment relative to prior art; aligns with international practice where common among AMSs.

name: Amendment of claims of published patent application (Question 37 / 3.4)
description: Whether and how applicants can amend claims after publication and procedural limits.
guidance: Post-publication amendments are allowed in many systems subject to national rules; ACG-PE summarises timing and scope.

name: Publication of granted patent specification (Question 37A / 3.5)
description: When and how the granted patent specification is published and what it contains.
guidance: Includes bibliographic data, claims as granted and possibly amendment statements; practice varies by AMS.

name: Pharmaceutical product, drug & foodstuff (Question 5.2.10)
description: Specific considerations for patentability of pharmaceutical products, drugs and foodstuffs (e.g., second medical use, safety exclusions).
guidance: Includes treatment of second medical use claims and interplay with public health considerations; national approaches summarised.

name: Conditions for clarity of invention (Questions 49 and 50 / 7.1)
description: Requirements for claims to be clear, concise and supported by the description; claims must define the matter for which protection is sought.
guidance: ACG-PE provides examples of clarity defects and guidance on claim drafting to meet clarity standards.

name: Terms not allowed in the claims and descriptions for reasons of lack of clarity (Question 51 / 7.2)
description: List of vague, ambiguous or non-permissible terms (e.g., 'substantial', 'suitable', 'etc.') and practices to avoid imprecision.
guidance: Offers examples and explanation why such terms are unacceptable; provides allowed alternatives and remedial amendment practices.

name: Rules for drawings and figures in relation to the clarity requirement (Question 52 / 7.3)
description: Standards for drawings/figures (legibility, reference signs, completeness) and how they support clarity of description and claims.
guidance: Specifies how drawings should be referenced, when they must be amended to support claims and common formal defects.

name: Multiple dependencies of claims (Question 53 / 7.4)
description: Guidance on whether multiple dependent claims are permitted and how they should be formulated for clarity.
guidance: ACG-PE summarises AMS positions on multiple dependent claims and provides drafting examples to avoid ambiguity.

name: Use claims (Question 56 / 7.7)
description: Rules for claims to the 'use' of a product or compound and the required support in the description.
guidance: Covers first vs second medical use claims and drafting requirements to meet clarity and sufficiency.

name: Product-by-process claims (Question 57 / 7.8)
description: Treatment of product-by-process claim types and when process-based limitations are acceptable as product-defining features.
guidance: ACG-PE explains examination approach: product-by-process claims may be allowable where product cannot be otherwise defined, but novelty/inventive step assessed on product per se.

name: Use of ranges (e.g., dosage) in claims (Question 60 / 7.9)
description: How numerical ranges should be claimed and interpreted and the requirements for support/enablement of claimed ranges.
guidance: Includes guidance on endpoints, selection inventiveness, and drafting to avoid undue breadth.

name: Use of limitations and disclaimers in claims (Question 61 / 7.10)
description: Permissible use of disclaimers (positive/negative limitations), their admissibility and effect on clarity and support.
guidance: ACG-PE distinguishes allowable disclaimers (e.g., to restore novelty over accidental disclosures) from impermissible ones; gives examples and form requirements.

name: Use of imprecise terms (Question 62 / 7.11)
description: How examiners treat imprecise/qualitative terms and when such terms render claims unclear or unsupported.
guidance: Suggests remedies: define terms in description, provide measurable parameters or examples.

name: Requirement of amendment of a claim to also amend the description in order to meet the requirement of clarity (Question 65 / 7.14)
description: When amending claims requires corresponding amendments to the description/drawings to preserve clarity and support.
guidance: ACG-PE explains interdependence of claims and description and how examiners handle inconsistencies arising from claim amendments.

name: Patent search for priority and non-priority-based applications (Question 71 / 9.2)
description: Search strategies tailored to priority-claim families versus direct national filings without priority.
guidance: ACG-PE outlines typical search scopes for each filing route and how to identify relevant family members and prior art.

name: Determining the scope of the claimed invention (Question 10.2 / Chapter 10.2)
description: Methods for interpreting claim scope for novelty assessment (literal interpretation, equivalents, claim construction principles).
guidance: Includes treatment of claim language, dependent claims and how the description supports claim interpretation.

name: Alternatives (Question 10.3.5)
description: How alternative embodiments disclosed in prior art affect novelty and claim breadth.
guidance: ACG-PE addresses combination/disclosure of multiple alternatives and their effect in anticipation.

name: Definition of inventive step (Question 11.2 / Chapter 11.2)
description: Legal standard used to determine whether the claimed invention involves an inventive step (non-obviousness).
guidance: ACG-PE describes standard tests (problem-solution approach, obviousness tests) as used across AMSs.

name: Claims dependency and inventive step (Question 11.7)
description: How claim dependency affects inventive step analysis (assessment of dependent claim limitations and multiple independent claims).
guidance: Guidance on how to evaluate inventive step for narrower dependent claims and relationship to main claim inventive merits.

name: Obligation to provide available work results from the priority application(s) (Question 129 / 14.2)
description: Applicant obligations to submit work products (search & examination reports, written opinions) from the first filing office when requesting ASPEC work sharing.
guidance: Lists minimum documents (written opinion/WO/ISA/IPEA/IPER, claims included) and notes English as the working language for ASPEC submissions.

name: ASPEC/PCT-ASPEC request procedural requirements
description: How to make ASPEC and PCT-ASPEC requests, what to indicate on forms (e.g., PCT-ASPEC remark), and additional communication steps (email monitoring authority/focal point).
guidance: Minimum documents include copy of ISA/IPEA report and at least one claim found allowable by first office; requests may be made up to final decision and e-ASPEC may replace separate forms where supported.

name: Mandatory requirements for filing an ASPEC application (table summary)
description: Country-by-country practical requirements for ASPEC (need for local agent, necessity to enclose written opinion, claim correspondence table, hardcopy form requirements, e-ASPEC availability).
guidance: ACG-PE provides a summary table per AMS showing specific local filing practices and mandatory procedural steps; applicants must consult national rules.

name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(ii) — Infirmity of proof
description: [T]here was such infirmity of proof establishing the conduct as to give rise to the clear conviction that the Office could not, consistently with its duty, accept as final the conclusion on that subject.
guidance: Respondent must show more than disagreement with factfinding; he must demonstrate a 'such an infirmity of proof' that accepting the state conclusion would be inconsistent with the Office's duty. This is a difficult, narrow showing. Deference is given to the trier-of-fact's credibility determinations; relitigation of credibility does not ordinarily demonstrate infirmity (citing In re Zdravkovich and case law). Core undisputed facts supporting state findings strongly undercut an infirmity claim.

name: Reasonable likelihood that requester will prevail (RLP)
description: For reexaminations filed on or after September 16, 2011 and prior to September 16, 2012, the determination is whether the request and prior art establish a reasonable likelihood that the requester will prevail with respect to at least one challenged claim.
guidance: The RLP standard is an elevated threshold compared to the SNQ standard (House Report describes it as requiring information showing a reasonable likelihood of success). If a proceeding was terminated/vacated without resolving the RLP question, the issue can be re-presented in a new request. The Office must state in the granting decision that there is an RLP (for requests in this date range).

name: Claims considered in deciding request
description: The claims of the patent in effect at the time of the determination (37 CFR 1.923) are the basis for deciding whether an SNQ or RLP is present.
guidance: The Office's determination is generally limited to the claim(s) for which reexamination was requested. A requester must set forth the pertinency and manner of applying cited prior art to every claim for which reexamination is requested (35 U.S.C. 311(b)(2); 37 CFR 1.915(b)). Failure to apply the art to certain claims means the requester is not statutorily entitled to reexamination of those claims; failure to comply with 1.915(b) may result in no filing date being awarded. The examiner may nevertheless base an SNQ/RLP on claims other than those requested (e.g., claims in effect at determination time). The decision should discuss all requested claims, but the examiner should not reject claims in the order for reexamination (rejections belong in the first Office action).

name: Requirement to set forth pertinency and manner of applying cited prior art
description: A requester must 'set forth the pertinency and manner of applying cited prior art to every claim for which reexamination is requested' (35 U.S.C. 311(b)(2); 37 CFR 1.915(b)).
guidance: If the requester fails to apply the art to certain claims, those claims generally will not be reexamined. A request failing to set forth the pertinency and manner of applying cited art may not be given a filing date. Thus each cited reference must be applied to each claimed element/claim that requester seeks to challenge.

name: Prior adverse decisions by the Office on same or substantially identical prior art
description: A prior Office decision adverse to the patentability of a claim based upon prior art patents or printed publications would usually mean that a substantial new question of patentability is present.
guidance: Such adverse decisions could arise from a reissue application abandoned after rejection without disclaimer, or other Office proceedings. Examiner should consider prior Office adverse decisions when determining SNQ.

name: Effect of federal court decisions on SNQ/RLP determination
description: Federal court decisions affect the SNQ/RLP inquiry differently depending on finality: (A) a final holding that a claim is not invalid does not necessarily preclude SNQ/RLP; (B) a non-final holding of invalidity/unenforceability is not controlling; (C) a final holding of invalidity/unenforceability after all appeals binds the Office.
guidance: The Office makes an independent determination because courts and the Office may apply different standards of proof and claim construction. Where a claim was finally held invalid or unenforceable, the requester will not have SNQ/RLP as to those claims. Where court factual findings exist, the Office may accord deference to factual findings but is not bound except in the final-invalidity-after-appeals case. See Ethicon v. Quigg and In re Swanson for illustrations.

name: Second or subsequent reexamination requests when reexamination is pending
description: When a reexamination is pending and a second/subsequent request is filed, the presence of an SNQ depends on the art cited in the subsequent request. The subsequent request must independently provide a 'different' substantial new question of patentability with respect to the claims in effect at the time of determination.
guidance: If the subsequent request includes the art that raised the SNQ in the earlier pending reexamination, reexamination should be ordered only if the new art raises a 'different' SNQ. If it raises the same SNQ, it is not new and should be denied. If different as to some claims but not others, grant in part. Once a different SNQ is provided for existing claims, the second request may also include info directed to proposed new/amended claims in the pending reexamination so the entire patent package can be examined without wasteful subsequent filings.

name: Content required in decision ordering reexamination
description: If a request for reexamination is granted, the examiner’s decision granting the request will state that an SNQ has been raised (for pre-9/16/2011 requests) or that there is an RLP (for requests between 9/16/2011 and 9/15/2012), and will include an order for inter partes reexamination where applicable.
guidance: The decision will (A) identify all claims and issues, (B) identify the patents/printed publications relied upon, and (C) provide a brief statement of the rationale supporting each SNQ/RLP. The order may be accompanied by the initial Office action on the merits, and if the order resulted from a petition, the subsequent inter partes reexam will ordinarily be conducted by a different examiner.

name: Reexamination requests filed after reissue
description: Where a request for reexamination is filed on a patent after a reissue patent for that patent has already issued, reexamination will be denied because the patent on which the request is based has been surrendered.
guidance: If reexamination of the reissued patent is desired, a new request based on the reissue patent's specification and claims must be filed. If the reissue issues after the filing of a request, see MPEP § 2686.03 for handling.

name: Required contents of application (Article 90(1) list)
description: An application shall state: 1) name and domicile of applicant (or corporation name/place of business), 2) agent name/place of business (and designated patent attorney if a firm), 3) patent number and indication of claims for which the term is to be extended, 4) length of extension applied, 5) details of approval under Article 89(1), and 6) the ground for extension as prescribed by Ordinance (with substantiating materials).
guidance: The application must be filed to the Commissioner of the Korean Intellectual Property Office and contain all listed items; omissions can be grounds for rejection or return.

name: Documents to attach and form-filling requirements
description: Applicant must attach 'a copy of the evidential document of the ground for extension' and 'a copy of the evidential document of representation' (when represented) using Annexed Form No. 30, and fill specified boxes: applicant name(s); patent number and application number; name of the invention; all claims including active pharmaceutical ingredients for which extension is sought; ground for extension details and evidential documents; number of days for the period (capped at five years); date of approval; content of approval (with evidential documents showing licensee status).
guidance: For drugs, evidential documents include clinical investigation plans, items license, evidential documents for Phase III trials conducted overseas, and agency review periods. For agrochemicals, include test application copies and registration certificates; for raw materials include test/analysis applications and registration. The claims must clearly state how they include the approved items (examples provided).

name: Determination of identicalness of composition between claimed and approved substance
description: The approved substance must have the same composition as the substance recited in claims (for substance inventions) or as the matter manufactured by the claimed method (for method inventions).
guidance: For substance inventions compare the claimed substance and approved substance directly. For manufacturing-method inventions compare the substance produced by the disclosed method with the approved substance; manufacturing methods need not be compared. If compositions are not identical, examiner shall notify a ground for rejection under Article 91(1).

name: Determination of identicalness of use for use-inventions
description: If the patented subject matter is a use invention, the use of the approved substance must be the same as the use of the substance disclosed in the patent; if not, the patent term shall not be extended even if compositions are identical. If the claimed use includes the approved use, the uses are deemed the same.
guidance: This requires comparison of claimed therapeutic/functional uses versus those in the approval. If approved use is narrower than claimed use but included within claimed use, extension may be allowed; if disparate, reject.

name: Determine whether a claim element is a functional claim element
description: First, examiners should determine whether any given claim element is a functional claim element. Often the answer will be obvious because the element is structural.
guidance: If the element does not contain obvious structure, whether or not it uses the words “means for,” examiners should ask the applicant to clarify on the record whether the claim element is intended to invoke section 112(f). This determination is the starting point for further action (clarification, amendment, or rejection).

name: Document invocation of §112(f) in written record and interview summaries
description: When the issue arises during prosecution, examiners should ensure the record reflects whether claim elements invoke §112(f).
guidance: While that will normally happen during the written record of rejection and amendment, if the issue arises during an interview the examiner should specify in the interview summary whether or not the claim elements discussed invoke section 112(f). Explicit documentation avoids ambiguity about claim scope later in litigation or prosecution.

name: Require applicant to point out corresponding structure when invoking §112(f)
description: If an applicant does intend to invoke section 112(f), the applicant should be required to point out the corresponding structure in the specification that supports that means-plus-function claim element.
guidance: If there is no such structure in the specification, the claim should be rejected as indefinite. In some circumstances it may be appropriate to clarify on the record what the applicant regards as equivalent to that structure (e.g., when distinguishing prior art). Case law cited: Function Media v. Google; ePlus v. Lawson; In re Aoyama; Typhoon Touch; Aristocrat; WMS Gaming (examples of requiring disclosure of corresponding structure or algorithms).

name: If applicant does not intend to invoke §112(f), require identification or addition of structure
description: If an applicant does not intend to invoke section 112(f), and the structural component of the claim element is not obvious, the applicant should be required to identify the structure in the claim element that performs the claimed function.
guidance: If the applicant cannot satisfactorily point to structure in the claim itself that performs the claimed function, the examiner should (or should) require the applicant to amend the claim to add such structure. This prevents purely functional claim language from escaping §112(f) limits by avoiding the phrase 'means for.'

name: Reject or treat as means-plus-function when appropriate and make scope-limiting basis explicit
description: If an applicant does not provide appropriate structure for a claim element, the examiner can reject the claim for failure to comply with section 112(f).
guidance: Alternatively, the examiner can point out the absence of structure and proceed to examine the claim as a means-plus-function claim. If an examiner takes the latter course, he should make explicit on the record that the claim is being allowed only because the broadest reasonable interpretation of that claim is nonetheless limited to the structure disclosed in the specification and equivalents thereof.

name: Clarify on the record what applicant regards as equivalents to disclosed structure
description: In some circumstances it may be appropriate to clarify on the record what the applicant regards as equivalent to that structure.
guidance: Example: if an applicant seeks to distinguish prior art on the ground that the structure she discloses is different than that in the prior art, it would be helpful to establish on the record whether the applicant regards those two structures as equivalent. Doing so helps resolve later disputes about claim scope and equivalents.

name: Use on-the-record determinations to identify and limit functional claiming
description: By establishing on the record whether a claim element invokes section 112(f) and what structure it covers, examiners can help identify functional claims and limit them to their proper scope.
guidance: Proactive on-the-record clarification (invocation, corresponding structure, and equivalence) enables examiners to reject applications that improperly seek to control all ways of performing a function and reduces overbroad functional claiming that fuels invalid claims and troll litigation.

name: Determine what invention is sought to be patented
description: Prior to focusing on statutory requirements, examiners must determine precisely what the inventor has invented and is seeking to patent by reviewing the complete specification, detailed description, embodiments, the claims, and any asserted utilities.
guidance: Under the principles of compact prosecution, each claim should be reviewed for compliance with every statutory requirement in the initial review. Examiners should state all reasons and bases for rejecting claims in the first Office action, explain deficiencies clearly, indicate how rejections may be overcome when practicable, and fully develop reasons for non-prior-art rejections (e.g., written description, enablement, utility) rather than mere conclusions.

name: Identify and understand any utility for the invention
description: Determine whether the claimed invention as a whole is useful and identify any asserted utility or practical application disclosed by the applicant.
guidance: A complete disclosure should indicate why the applicant believes the invention is useful (the purpose or how it may be used). The statement of utility must enable one of ordinary skill in the art to understand why the invention is useful. Applicant may assert more than one utility but only one is necessary; alternatively, a well-established utility in the contemporaneous art may suffice. Note difference between 'practical application' for utility and 'practical application' in subject matter eligibility analysis.

name: Review the detailed disclosure and specific embodiments
description: Use the written description and specific embodiments to understand what the applicant regards as the invention, its function, and the features necessary to accomplish an asserted practical application.
guidance: Determine (A) the function of the invention (what it does when used as disclosed) and (B) the features necessary to accomplish at least one asserted practical application. Correlate disclosed embodiments to claim limitations to ensure proper interpretation and to support claim scope.

name: Review the claims (identify and evaluate each claim limitation)
description: Claims define the property rights and must be carefully scrutinized by identifying each claim limitation and correlating each limitation to the disclosure.
guidance: For process claims, identify steps/acts; for products, identify physical structures/materials. Correlate each claim limitation to portions of the specification that describe the limitation, including means-/step-plus-function language. Give claims their broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the disclosure. Consider plain meaning, grammar, and how a person skilled in the art would understand terms. Be aware of language that may or may not be limiting (e.g., preamble statements of intended use, 'adapted to' clauses, 'wherein'/'whereby' clauses, contingent limitations, printed matter, functional terms). Consider all claim limitations as a whole.

name: Give claims their broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) in light of the disclosure
description: When interpreting claims during prosecution, apply the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.
guidance: Do not read positive limitations from the specification into claims that do not themselves impose that limitation. Means-/step-plus-function limitations should be interpreted consistently with corresponding structures/materials/acts described in the specification and equivalents. Consider MPEP §§ 2111 and 2181–2186 for further guidance.

name: Correlate claim limitations to supporting disclosure (including means-plus-function)
description: Ensure each claim limitation has a corresponding disclosure in the specification; for means-/step-plus-function limitations, identify corresponding structure/materials/acts.
guidance: Search must consider any structure or material described in the specification and equivalents corresponding to claimed means-/step-plus-function limitations per 35 U.S.C. 112(f) and MPEP §§ 2181–2186. If a limitation invokes 112(f), interpret to cover corresponding structure/materials/acts described and their equivalents; if disclosure lacks corresponding structure, consider indefiniteness or written description rejections and advise applicant how to respond.

name: Determine compliance with 35 U.S.C. 101 (subject matter eligibility)
description: Evaluate whether the claimed invention falls within one of the four statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter) and whether it is directed to patent-eligible subject matter and not a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon/product of nature) unless the claim as a whole includes additional limitations amounting to significantly more.
guidance: Consider the four interpreted requirements of §101 and related caselaw (e.g., Alice, Myriad, Chakrabarty, Bilski). Use the analytical framework and stepwise eligibility guidance in MPEP § 2106 (Eligibility Step 1: statutory categories; Eligibility Step 2A: whether directed to judicial exception; Eligibility Step 2B: whether amounts to significantly more). Avoid focusing solely on §101 to the detriment of §§102/103/112 analyses except in extreme cases.

name: Eligibility Step 2A — Determine whether claim is directed to a judicial exception
description: Assess whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon/product of nature.
guidance: If the claim is directed to a judicial exception, evaluate whether the exception is integrated into a practical application (integration/prong one) and consider analyses such as markedly different characteristics, integration into practical application, particular machine/transformation, improvements to computer/technology, and particular treatment or prophylaxis as relevant indicators of integration.

name: Eligibility Step 2B — Determine whether claim amounts to 'significantly more' than the judicial exception
description: If a claim is directed to a judicial exception, decide whether additional claim limitations in combination amount to significantly more than the exception itself.
guidance: Consider improvements to computer functionality or other technology, particular machine or transformation, well-understood routine conventional activity, mere instructions to apply an exception, insignificant extra-solution activity, field of use and technological environment, and other meaningful limitations. Use MPEP § 2106.05 and related subsections for examples and analyses.

name: Evaluate compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (definiteness / claims must particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention)
description: Determine whether the claims set forth the subject matter the inventor regards as the invention and whether the claims particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention with reasonable precision and particularity in light of the disclosure.
guidance: Analyze claim language definiteness in light of the disclosure as interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art. Consider issues such as new terminology, relative terminology, numerical ranges, lack of antecedent basis, functional limitations, negative limitations, omnibus claims, multiple alternatives, and other specific topics identified in MPEP § 2173 et seq.

name: Evaluate compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(a) — written description, enablement, best mode
description: Assess the three separate requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(a): (A) adequate written description, (B) enablement, and (C) best mode.
guidance: Written description: specification must reasonably convey that the applicant was in possession of the claimed invention as of the filing date. Enablement: specification must enable one skilled in the art to make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation; consider undue experimentation factors, predictability of the art, quantity of experimentation, working examples, and special issues for biological/chemical/computer programming. Best mode: two-prong inquiry — did inventor possess a best mode at filing, and if so, is it disclosed so a skilled person could practice it.

name: Enablement — specification must be enabling as of the filing date
description: Determine whether the specification enables a person skilled in the art to make and use the claimed invention as of the filing date without undue experimentation.
guidance: Consider art predictability, quantity of experimentation required, whether working examples are provided, whether critical information is missing, and whether enablement is commensurate in scope with the claims. For issues of operability and enablement in prior art rejections, follow MPEP §§ 2164 et seq.

name: Supporting a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 (obviousness) — prima facie case
description: When asserting an obviousness rejection, establish a prima facie case by comparing claimed invention to prior art, identifying differences, determining level of ordinary skill, and showing motivation/suggestion to combine with reasonable expectation of success as appropriate.
guidance: Consider analogous vs nonanalogous art, differences between prior art and claimed invention, level of ordinary skill, legal concept of prima facie obviousness, suggestion or motivation to modify references, reasonable expectation of success, consideration of applicant's rebuttal, and secondary considerations. All claim limitations must be considered; do not dissect claims into isolated elements.

name: 35 U.S.C. 112(f) invocation and three-prong test for means-plus-function
description: Determine whether a claim limitation should be interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (or pre-AIA sixth paragraph) using a three-prong analysis: whether the claim uses 'means' or a generic placeholder, whether it recites functional language, and whether it recites sufficient structure/material/acts to perform the function.
guidance: If 112(f) applies, interpret the limitation to cover corresponding structure/materials/acts described in the specification and equivalents. Use form paragraphs (e.g., 7.30.05–7.30.07, 7.34.23–7.34.24) to explain invocation or non-invocation and to instruct applicant on possible responses (amend claims, show sufficient structure, or clarify record). If result of three-prong test is inconclusive, require applicant to clarify whether limitation is to be interpreted under 112(f).

name: Consider all claim limitations together; do not dissect claims into isolated elements
description: Evaluate claims as a whole when conducting eligibility, novelty, or obviousness analyses rather than examining isolated claim elements separately.
guidance: A new combination of steps or elements may be patentable even if constituents were well known. In subject matter eligibility and other analyses, avoid ignoring presence of old elements within a claim when assessing the claim as a whole (citing Diamond v. Diehr).

name: Naming of inventor and inventorship requirements
description: Confirm correct identification of inventor(s) per filing date (rules differ before and after September 16, 2012) and ensure inventor(s) are properly named as applicants where required.
guidance: If application clearly does not name correct inventorship and applicant has not filed a request to correct inventorship under 37 CFR 1.48, reject claims under 35 U.S.C. 101 and 115 (for AIA applications) or under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f) as appropriate. See MPEP § 2109 and § 602.01(c) et seq. for correction procedures.

name: Types of evidence establishing lack of ornamentality
description: Examples of proper evidentiary basis for a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 171 that a claim is lacking in ornamentality would be common knowledge in the art, the appearance of the design itself, the specification of a related utility patent, information provided in the specification, or the fact that an article would be hidden during its ultimate end use.
guidance: If evidence is based on common knowledge or 'well-known' facts, take official notice and state it; insert source of evidence (utility patent, brochure, response to letter of inquiry, etc.) in examiner notes.

name: Acceptable evidence to establish ornamentality (affidavits/declarations)
description: An affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 may be submitted over applicant’s signature explaining, specifically and in depth, which features or areas of the claimed design were created with 'thought of ornament.'
guidance: Affidavit must be specific and in-depth. Declarations from representatives of the company which commissioned the design are also acceptable if they explain which features were created with ornament in mind.

name: Examiner evaluation of ornamentality evidence — design as a whole
description: The examiner must evaluate evidence in light of the design as a whole to decide if the claim is primarily ornamental; determination is not based on the size or amount of features identified as ornamental but rather on their influence on the overall appearance of the design.
guidance: Assess influence on overall appearance rather than counting features or measuring size.

name: Functional/hidden features not counted for novelty
description: When a claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102, features of the design which are functional and/or hidden during end use may not be relied upon to support patentability.
guidance: Differences solely in functional considerations do not negate anticipation; if applicant wants to rely on such features, they must first establish ornamentality under 35 U.S.C. 171 (see MPEP § 1504.01(c)).

name: Foreign filing/priority and 102(d)/172 practice
description: Registration of a design abroad is considered equivalent to patenting under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) and 35 U.S.C. 102(d). The U.S. design application must be made within 6 months of the foreign filing to claim priority for designs.
guidance: Rejections under 102(d)/172 should only be made when the examiner knows the foreign registration/patent actually issued before the U.S. filing date based on an application filed more than six months prior; include form paragraph ¶ 15.03.01 when appropriate.

name: Nonobviousness evaluation (Graham factors adapted for design)
description: The basic factual inquiries for obviousness (Graham) apply to designs: (A) determining scope and content of the prior art; (B) ascertaining differences between the claimed design and the prior art; (C) resolving the level of ordinary skill in the art; and (D) evaluating secondary considerations.
guidance: Apply these factors in the design context; collect facts to support prima facie obviousness determination.

name: Differences between prior art and claimed design — overall appearance
description: In determining 35 U.S.C. 103(a) patentability, it is the overall appearance of the design that must be considered. Mere differences are not alone sufficient for patentability; identify all differences and state if any are de minimis.
guidance: Cite In re Leslie and In re Lamb; when differences are de minimis from a design viewpoint, the rejection should so state.

name: Prima facie obviousness standard for designs
description: To establish prima facie obviousness, all the claim limitations must be taught or suggested by the prior art; the proper standard is whether the design would have been obvious to a designer of ordinary skill with the claimed type of article.
guidance: Use Graham inquiries adapted for design; ensure references together teach/suggest all claim limitations to support a prima facie obviousness finding (In re Nalbandian).

name: "comprising" (open-ended/inclusive)
description: "The transitional term 'comprising', which is synonymous with 'including,' 'containing,' or 'characterized by,' is inclusive or open-ended and does not exclude additional, unrecited elements or method steps."
guidance: Use of 'comprising' signals that the named elements are essential but other elements may be added and still fall within the claim scope. Case law: Mars Inc. v. H.J. Heinz Co.; Invitrogen Corp. v. Biocrest Mfg.; Genentech, Inc. v. Chiron Corp.; Moleculon Research Corp. v. CBS, Inc.; In re Baxter; Ex parte Davis. Example: In Gillette Co. v. Energizer Holdings, the use of 'comprising' in the preamble and 'group of' made the claim presumptively open-ended, covering razors with more than three blades. Interpret 'comprising' as leaving the claim open for inclusion of unspecified ingredients or steps even in major amounts.

name: "consisting of" (closed/exclusive)
description: "The transitional phrase 'consisting of' excludes any element, step, or ingredient not specified in the claim."
guidance: Treat 'consisting of' as closed language that generally prevents inclusion of unrecited elements. Case law: In re Gray; Ex parte Davis (defines 'consisting of' as closing the claim to inclusion of other materials except ordinary impurities). Note exceptions/facts matter: Norian Corp. v. Stryker Corp. — a kit 'consisting of' claimed chemicals was found to be infringed even though it included an unrelated spatula because the spatula was unrelated to the claimed invention. Also, a claim depending from a 'consists of' claim generally cannot add an element or step. When 'consists of' appears in a clause of the body (not immediately after the preamble), it limits only that clause's element set; it does not necessarily close the claim as a whole (Mannesmann Demag Corp. v. Engineered Metal Products Co.; In re Crish example). 'Group consisting of' is often used to signal a closed Markush-type group.

name: "consisting essentially of" (middle ground / material-effect test)
description: "The transitional phrase 'consisting essentially of' limits the scope of a claim to the specified materials or steps 'and those that do not materially affect the basic and novel characteristic(s)' of the claimed invention."
guidance: 'Consisting essentially of' is intermediate between fully open 'comprising' and fully closed 'consisting of.' Key points: (1) Determine what the basic and novel characteristics are (read the specification); absent a clear indication of those characteristics, courts may construe 'consisting essentially of' as equivalent to 'comprising' for prior art purposes (PPG Industries v. Guardian Industries). (2) Applicant bears the burden of showing that introduction of additional steps/components would materially change the invention (In re De Lajarte; Ex parte Hoffman). (3) Specification can define quantitative or qualitative limits that establish what would be a material change (AK Steel Corp. v. Sollac — silicon >0.5% materially altered properties). (4) Although typically used for compositions, it can be applied to method steps if read in light of the specification (Ex parte Hoffman). Case law: In re Herz; PPG Industries; Atlas Powder; In re Janakirama-Rao; Water Technologies Corp. v. Calco; AK Steel; In re De Lajarte; Ex parte Hoffman.

name: Clause-level vs preamble-level use of transitional terms
description: When transitional language such as 'consists of' appears in a clause of the body of a claim rather than immediately following the preamble, it limits only the element set forth in that clause; other elements are not necessarily excluded from the claim as a whole.
guidance: Read transitional language in context. Example: Mannesmann Demag Corp. v. Engineered Metal Products Co. and In re Crish — use of 'consists' in a clause did not limit the entire claim due to the presence of 'comprising' elsewhere; 'comprising' can preserve openness for other portions of the claim. In claim construction, determine which portion of the claim the transitional phrase attaches to and apply limits accordingly.

name: Interpretation of other transitional phrases ('having', 'composed of', etc.)
description: Transitional phrases such as 'having' and 'composed of' must be interpreted in light of the specification to determine whether open or closed claim language is intended; 'composed of' has been interpreted as either 'consisting of' or 'consisting essentially of' depending on facts.
guidance: Do not assume a single default for terms like 'having' or 'composed of.' Case law: Lampi Corp. v. American Power Products (term 'having' interpreted as open); Crystal Semiconductor Corp. v. TriTech Microelectronics (no presumption that 'having' opens the claim); Regents of the Univ. of Cal. v. Eli Lilly (term 'having' permitted inclusion of other moieties). 'Composed of' may be treated like 'consisting of' or 'consisting essentially of' depending on specification and evidence (AFG Industries v. Cardinal IG; In re Bertsch). Always interpret such transitional language in light of the specification and relevant facts.

name: Texas Disciplinary Rule 1.02(a)(2) — Scope of representation
description: Investigatory Panel 8-2 concluded Respondent violated Texas Disciplinary Rule 1.02(a)(2) (scope of representation).
guidance: The panel's findings include actions outside a client's consent (e.g., settling a client's claim without consent), illustrating scope-of-representation violations.

name: Inherency and functional limitations in apparatus claims
description: Features of an apparatus may be recited structurally or functionally. If a functional limitation is an inherent characteristic of the prior art structure, the examiner should explain that the prior art structure inherently possesses the recited limitation; the burden then shifts to applicant to establish that the prior art does not possess the characteristic relied on.
guidance: Treat functional limitations as inherency issues when prior art structure would inherently possess the claimed function. Provide an explanation in the rejection showing the prior-art structure inherently has the characteristic. Applicant must rebut with evidence that the prior art lacks that characteristic. (Cases: In re Schreiber; Bettcher Industries v. Bunzl USA; In re Swinehart.)

name: Manner of operating device does not differentiate apparatus claim from prior art
description: A claim reciting the manner in which an apparatus is intended to be employed does not necessarily differentiate the apparatus from a prior art apparatus if the prior art teaches all structural limitations of the claim.
guidance: Do not treat recitations of intended use or manner of operation as patentably distinguishing where the prior art discloses the claimed structure. Example: Ex parte Masham — differences in amount of submersion were immaterial because structure was the same.

name: Functional claim language breadth for computer-implemented limitations
description: Functional claim language not limited to a specific structure covers all devices capable of performing the recited function; if prior art discloses a device inherently capable of performing the claimed function, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102 and/or 103 may be appropriate.
guidance: If the claim language imposes no structural limitation, give it a broad scope covering devices 'capable of' the function. Explain how the prior art device is capable of performing the recited function. (Cases: In re Translogic Technology; Intel Corp. v. U.S. ITC; In re Schreiber; In re Best; In re Ludtke; In re Swinehart.) See MPEP § 2112 for more on functional limitations.

name: Claim construction for computer-implemented limitations (hardware vs software)
description: Computer-implemented functional claim limitations may be construed to require specific structure (e.g., a combination of hardware and software) when hardware alone cannot meet the limitations; conversely, terms like 'computer' are given their broad ordinary meaning unless limited by other claim terms or the specification.
guidance: Determine whether the limitation requires enabling software or specific algorithmic structure; if hardware cannot perform the limitation absent software, construe the claim as an apparatus comprising hardware and software capable of practicing the limitation. Do not limit 'computer' to a narrow class unless the specification clearly does so. (Cases: Nazomi Communications v. Nokia; Intel Corp.; In re Paulsen.)

name: Obviousness of automating known functions on general-purpose computers
description: Broadly claiming an automated means to replace a manual function to accomplish the same result generally does not distinguish over the prior art; implementing a known function on a general-purpose computer may be obvious if it is the predictable use of prior art elements.
guidance: When assessing obviousness of computer implementations, consider whether automation is merely the predictable application of known techniques (KSR). Applying modern electronics or Internet/browser technologies to older mechanical or information processes may be routine and therefore obvious. (Cases: KSR Int’l Co. v. Teleflex; Leapfrog Enters. v. Fisher-Price; Muniauction v. Thomson; In re Venner.) See MPEP § 2141 et seq. for further guidance and exemplary rationales.

name: All claim limitations considered when assessing obviousness of processes (no per se product/process rules)
description: Obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103 requires a highly fact-dependent analysis considering the claimed subject matter as a whole; there are no per se rules that a conventional process becomes patentable just because it produces a nonobvious product, or vice versa.
guidance: Treat language reciting making or using of a nonobvious product as a material limitation of a process claim. Evaluate obviousness case-by-case; prior cases illustrate that a process yielding a novel product may be obvious and a process yielding a well-known product may be nonobvious. (Cases: In re Ochiai; In re Brouwer; TorPharm v. Ranbaxy; In re Durden; In re Albertson; In re Kanter; In re Pleuddemann; In re Kuehl; In re Mancy.)

name: Markush claim principles
description: A 'Markush' claim recites a list of alternatively usable members (a Markush grouping). Such claims require selection from a closed group 'consisting of' the alternative members, and are proper when the group members share a single structural similarity and a common use.
guidance: Treat any claim that recites alternatively usable members as a Markush claim regardless of wording. Ensure the grouping is closed and that members share required structural similarity and common use. See MPEP § 2111.03 and case law (In re Harnisch; Ex parte Markush; Abbott Labs v. Baxter).

name: Markush grouping format neutrality
description: The treatment of claims reciting alternatives is not governed by the particular format used; alternatives may be set forth in various phrasings but should be treated as Markush groupings when they recite alternatively usable members.
guidance: Do not alter analysis based on phrasing (e.g., 'selected from the group consisting of' vs 'wherein the material is A, B, or C'). Markush-style claiming appears often in chemistry, pharmacology, biology, metallurgy, ceramics, and can apply to mechanical features or process steps as well.

name: Markush grouping indefiniteness under 35 U.S.C. 112(b)
description: A Markush grouping may be indefinite if the list of alternatives is not a closed grouping or if the group is so expansive that persons skilled in the art cannot determine the metes and bounds of the claimed invention.
guidance: Evaluate Markush claims for closure and reasonable scope. If the grouping is open-ended or too broad to permit skilled artisans to determine boundaries, raise 35 U.S.C. 112(b) issues. See MPEP § 2173.05(h) and § 2111.03 for details.

name: Prior art presumed operable/enabling when it discloses all claimed elements
description: When a reference expressly anticipates or makes obvious all elements of a claimed invention, that reference is presumed to be operable/enabling; the burden is on applicant to rebut that presumption with evidence.
guidance: An examiner making a proper prima facie case of anticipation need not independently investigate enablement; provide adequate notice under § 132. Applicant can submit rebuttal evidence of nonenablement. (Cases: In re Sasse; In re Antor Media Corp.) See MPEP § 716.07.

name: Efficacy not required for prior art enablement
description: A prior art reference can be enabling for anticipation even if it does not disclose a utility or proof of efficacy for the claimed invention.
guidance: For anticipation, it is sufficient that the claimed compound or article and a process of making it are taught by the reference; proof of efficacy is not required. (Cases: In re Schoenwald; Impax Labs v. Aventis Pharm.) See MPEP § 2122.

name: Enabling disclosure requires sufficient detail to avoid undue experimentation
description: A reference must disclose the subject matter in sufficient detail to enable a person of ordinary skill in the art to carry out the claimed invention; mere naming or description is insufficient if production would require undue experimentation.
guidance: If a reference merely names a compound or plant but would require undue experimentation to practice it, it is not an enabling disclosure for anticipation. Consider whether the public was in possession of the invention (In re Donohue) and whether supplementary evidence shows operability. (Cases: In re Hoeksema; Elan Pharm. v. Mayo Foundation; In re Donohue.)

name: Use of secondary evidence to show operability for 35 U.S.C. 102 rejections
description: Even if the primary reference does not itself teach how to practice the invention, secondary evidence (other patents or publications) can be cited to show public possession of the method of making or using, enabling a 35 U.S.C. 102 rejection.
guidance: Combine references when the primary reference teaches every claimed element but lacks a teaching of how to make/use; secondary references can demonstrate that the public could practice the invention. (Case: In re Donohue.) See MPEP § 2131.01 for details.

name: Inoperative prior art may be relied upon for obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103
description: A non-enabling or inoperative prior art reference may nonetheless qualify as prior art for the purpose of determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103.
guidance: Do not automatically discard inoperative references when assessing obviousness; analyze whether the reference would have rendered the claimed invention obvious in view of the prior art. (Cases: Beckman Instruments v. LKB Produkter AB; Symbol Techs. Inc. v. Opticon Inc.)

name: Evidence of unsuccessful attempts can show non-enablement for compounds
description: Attempts to prepare a compound that were unsuccessful before the date of invention can be adequate to show inoperability of a prior art reference disclosing only the structure.
guidance: Affidavits or experimental evidence demonstrating that known methods failed to make the claimed compound before the critical date can overcome a rejection based on a reference that merely discloses structure. However, mere assertion that an author did not attempt synthesis is insufficient if other evidence shows synthesis methods were known. (Cases: In re Wiggins; In re Donohue; In re Hoeksema.)

name: Plant genetics enabling: ability to reproduce the plant is required
description: For claims to plants, the prior art reference, combined with prior-art knowledge, must enable one of ordinary skill to reproduce (grow/cultivate) the plant; pictures alone are often insufficient unless the plant was accessible (e.g., commercially available seeds) and reproducible without undue experimentation.
guidance: Consider whether the publication plus availability (e.g., seeds, sales, or possession) put the skilled artisan in possession such that asexual reproduction is possible without undue experimentation. (Cases: In re LeGrice; Ex parte Thomson; In re Elsner.)

name: Pictures/drawings may constitute enabling disclosure for apparatus/articles
description: Pictures and drawings may be sufficiently enabling to put the public in possession of the article pictured, and thus may be used to reject claims to the article, provided the picture shows all claimed structural features and how they are put together.
guidance: Evaluate whether the illustration discloses all structural elements and assembly details necessary to practice the claimed article. If so, the picture can be an enabling prior art disclosure. (Case: Jockmus v. Leviton.) See MPEP § 2125 for drawings as prior art.

name: Pre‑AIA (pre‑Sep 16, 2012) missing parts and oath/declaration rules
description: For applications accorded a filing date that do not include the appropriate filing fee, search fee, examination fee, or oath/declaration, the applicant will be notified under pre‑AIA 37 CFR 1.53(f) and given a period to file the missing parts and pay the surcharge under 37 CFR 1.16(f) to prevent abandonment.
guidance: The oath/declaration filed in reply must be executed by the inventors and must identify the specification and any amendment filed with the specification which includes subject matter not otherwise included in the specification (including claims) or drawings. Amendments filed with the oath may not include new matter; if an oath improperly refers to an amendment containing new matter, a supplemental oath deleting the reference will be required under pre‑AIA 37 CFR 1.67. Alterations made prior to execution of the oath and filing are considered part of the original disclosure.

name: 35 U.S.C. 111(a) — Required contents of a patent application
description: An application for patent shall be made in writing and shall include: (A) a specification as prescribed by section 112; (B) a drawing as prescribed by section 113; and (C) an oath or declaration as prescribed by section 115.
guidance: The application shall be accompanied by the fee required by law. The fee, oath or declaration, and one or more claims may be submitted after the filing date within such period and under such conditions (including payment of a surcharge) as prescribed by the Director; failure to submit within the prescribed period will result in abandonment. The filing date is the date on which a specification, with or without claims, is received in the USPTO.

name: 37 CFR 1.57(a)(1) — Notification and required submissions when ADS reference and correspondence address provided
description: If the applicant has provided a correspondence address, the applicant will be notified and given a period within which to file a copy of the specification and drawings from the previously filed application, an English translation if necessary (and pay the §1.17(i) fee), and pay the surcharge required by §1.16(f) to avoid abandonment.
guidance: Such a notice may be combined with a notice under 37 CFR 1.53(f) (e.g., requiring at least one claim and payment of filing fees).

name: Submission of actual copy of previously filed application — no modifications allowed
description: In response to a notice requiring a copy of the specification and drawings from the previously filed application, applicants must submit an actual copy of the specification (including any claims) and drawings without any modifications.
guidance: If the specification and drawings submitted in response are modified (updated, corrected, or reformatted), they will not satisfy the copy requirement of 35 U.S.C. 111(c) and 37 CFR 1.57(a). Any desired changes must be made by amendment under 37 CFR 1.121 without adding new matter.

name: Consequences and revival for reference filing abandonment
description: An application abandoned under 37 CFR 1.57(a)(1) or (a)(2) is treated as having never been filed; it may be revived under 37 CFR 1.137 and a copy of the specification and drawings of the previously filed application submitted to the Office to cure the defect.
guidance: An applicant may claim priority or benefit only if the application is revived under 37 CFR 1.137 and the required copy is submitted.

name: Provisional application filing date and amendment limits (post‑Dec 18, 2013)
description: A provisional application filed on or after December 18, 2013 will be given a filing date as of the date a specification, with or without claims, is received in the Office. Amendments, other than those required to make the provisional comply with applicable regulations, are not permitted after the filing date of the provisional application.
guidance: For provisional applications filed prior to December 18, 2013, filing date rules follow pre‑PLT 37 CFR 1.53(c). See MPEP §601.01(f)/(g) for treatment of omitted drawings or missing figures.

name: Applicability of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(b)
description: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(b) is applicable to biotechnological processes only; only applications subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 are subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(b).
guidance: See MPEP § 2159 to determine whether an application is subject to pre-AIA examination. Pre-AIA 103(b) precludes rejection of process claims that involve the use or making of certain nonobvious biotechnological compositions of matter under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a).

name: Effect on process patent term and composition claims under 103(b)
description: A patent issued on a process under pre-AIA 103(b)(1) shall also contain the claims to the composition of matter used in or made by that process, or shall, if such composition is claimed in another patent, be set to expire on the same date as such other patent.
guidance: This statutory requirement ensures the process patent's term aligns with the composition patent when composition claims are in a different patent.

name: Presumption of common ownership for joint inventors (¶7.20.02.fti)
description: When an application names joint inventors, the examiner presumes the subject matter of various claims was commonly owned at the time inventions were made absent evidence to the contrary.
guidance: Applicant is advised of the duty under 37 CFR 1.56 to identify inventor and invention dates for any claim not commonly owned so the examiner can consider applicability of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) and potential 102(e), (f) or (g) prior art. This paragraph must be used in all applications with joint inventors unless claims are clearly restricted to a single claimed invention.

name: Form paragraph ¶7.21.fti — Rejection under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a)
description: Use ¶7.21.fti to state that specific claims are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over identified prior art.
guidance: This paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.20.fti or 7.103. An explanation of the rejection must follow (see MPEP § 2144). If the rejection relies on prior art under pre-AIA 102(e), apply the amended pre-AIA 102(e) rules per AIPA to determine the reference's prior art date (with listed exceptions). Insert claim numbers and prior art in the designated brackets.

name: Provisional obviousness rejection based on copending application (¶7.21.01.fti)
description: Use ¶7.21.01.fti to provisionally reject claims as obvious over a copending application that would be prior art under pre-AIA 102(e) if published or patented and that has a common assignee, common applicant, or at least one common (joint) inventor.
guidance: This provisional rejection is based on a presumption of future publication or patenting of the copending application. It may be overcome by: (1) a showing under 37 CFR 1.132 that the invention disclosed was derived from the inventive entity of this application; (2) a showing of an earlier date of invention under 37 CFR 1.131(a); or (3) showing the copending application is disqualified under pre-AIA 103(c). Use appropriate procedures to determine the copending application’s 102(e) date (AIPA rules) as noted.

name: Rejection using reference that has common assignee/applicant/joint inventor (¶7.21.02.fti)
description: When a reference qualifies as prior art under pre-AIA 102(e) and has a common assignee, common applicant, or at least one common inventor, the claim(s) may be rejected under pre-AIA 103(a) over that reference.
guidance: This rejection may be overcome by: (1) showing under 37 CFR 1.132 derivation of the reference from the applicant; (2) showing an earlier invention date under 37 CFR 1.131(a); or (3) an oath/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(c) and a terminal disclaimer per 37 CFR 1.321(c) where applicable. Use pre-AIPA 102(e) rules to determine the reference's date when appropriate. Insert claim numbers, reference, and identification (assignee/applicant/inventor) as directed.

name: Test for Obviousness (Graham factors) (¶7.23.fti)
description: The factual inquiries for determining obviousness under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) are: (1) determining the scope and contents of the prior art; (2) ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue; (3) resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; (4) considering objective evidence (secondary considerations) indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
guidance: This summary of the Graham factors may be used, if appropriate, in response to arguments regarding the applicability of factors for determining obviousness. An explanation must follow when using form paragraphs that cite obviousness.

name: Use of ¶7.27.fti — Combined rejection under pre-AIA 102 or pre-AIA 103(a)
description: ¶7.27.fti states a claim is rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 (specific paragraph) as anticipated or, in the alternative, under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as obvious over identified art.
guidance: This paragraph is NOT intended to be commonly used as a substitute for proper separate rejections. Use separate rejections under 102 or 103 when possible. Examples where ¶7.27.fti may be appropriate include: disputed claim interpretation that could lead to either a 102 or 103 rejection; references that disclose all claim limitations except a property/function where inherency is uncertain; small genus/species issues; product-by-process variations; means-plus-function uncertainties; overlapping ranges without a specific example in the reference. A full explanation must follow and other form paragraphs must precede ¶7.27.fti as appropriate.

name: Continued applicability of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 and transitional rules
description: The AIA revisions to 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 do not apply to any application filed before March 16, 2013; such applications remain governed by pre-AIA 102 and 103. Applications filed on or after March 16, 2013 may still be subject to pre-AIA 102 in certain situations (e.g., if they have never contained a claim with an effective filing date on or after March 16, 2013).
guidance: Filing an RCE or entering national stage does not change an application's pre-AIA status. MPEP §§ 2131-2138 provide guidance on prior art available for pre-AIA applications. Use the application’s actual/ effective filing date and claim history to determine which regime applies.

name: AIA changes to prior art scope (AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) and (a)(2))
description: Under the AIA, AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) bars patents when the claimed invention was patented, described in a printed publication, or in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public before the effective filing date. AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) bars patents when the claimed invention was described in a patent or application published/issued naming another inventor and effectively filed before the claimed invention's effective filing date.
guidance: AIA 102(a) revises what qualifies as prior art; see MPEP for applying these provisions in examination.

name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1) — one-year grace period and measurement
description: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1) provides that disclosures made one year or less before the effective filing date shall not be prior art if: (1) the disclosure was made by the inventor/joint inventor or by another who obtained the subject matter directly/indirectly from the inventor; or (2) the subject matter had been publicly disclosed earlier by the inventor or someone who obtained it from the inventor.
