guidance: The one-year grace period is measured from the filing date of the earliest U.S. or foreign patent application to which a proper benefit/priority claim has been asserted and that supports the claimed invention per 35 U.S.C. 112(a). The grace period is extended to the next business day if it would otherwise end on a weekend or federal holiday. Under the AIA the date of invention is not relevant for antedating prior art.

name: AIA definitions relevant to 102/103 (claimed invention, effective filing date, inventor)
description: AIA 35 U.S.C. 100 defines 'claimed invention' as the subject matter defined by a claim; 'effective filing date' as the earlier of the actual filing date or the filing date of the earliest application to which benefit/priority is properly claimed (provided that earlier application supports the claimed invention per 35 U.S.C. 112(a)); 'inventor' and 'joint inventor' are defined as the individual(s) who invented or discovered the subject matter.
guidance: These definitions affect how prior art and grace-period rules are applied under the AIA; ensure claimed subject matter is supported in the earlier application per 112(a) when claiming benefit/priority.

name: Support Requirement (Patent Act Article 36(6)(i))
description: Part II, Chapter 2, Section 2: Support Requirement (Patent Act Article 36(6)(i))
guidance: Requirement that claims be supported by the description; guidance and examples illustrating adequate vs inadequate support are in the linked document.

name: Clarity Requirement (Patent Act Article 36(6)(ii))
description: Part II, Chapter 2, Section 3: Clarity Requirement (Patent Act Article 36(6)(ii))
guidance: Standards for clarity of claim language and claim scope; examples of unclear claim drafting and corrective measures provided in the linked PDF.

name: Conciseness Requirement (Patent Act Article 36(6)(iii))
description: Part II, Chapter 2, Section 4: Conciseness Requirement (Patent Act Article 36(6)(iii))
guidance: Expectations that claims be concise (avoid unnecessary limitations or repetition); see linked guidance for interpretation.

name: Claims Including Specific Expressions
description: Part III, Chapter 2, Section 4: Claims Including Specific Expressions
guidance: Guidance on how to treat claims that include particular phrasing or specific expressions that may affect novelty/inventive-step assessments; see examples in linked material.

name: Requirements for Amendments (Patent Act Article 17bis)
description: Part IV, Chapter 1: Requirements for Amendments (Patent Act Article 17bis)
guidance: Standards for allowable amendments to description, claims, or drawings during prosecution; see linked chapter for scope and restrictions.

name: OPLA screening under 37 CFR 1.292 and referral to examiner
description: Once the Office of Patent Legal Administration (OPLA) staff member has determined that the petition meets the formal requirements of 37 CFR 1.292, and the application’s status warrants consideration of the petition, he or she will prepare a letter for the Patent Legal Administrator, forwarding the petition and the application file to the examiner for determination of whether a prima facie case of public use or sale in this country of the claimed subject matter is established by the petition.
guidance: OPLA determines formal sufficiency and whether application status warrants evaluation; then forwards petition, any party papers, and the file to the examiner for prima facie determination; acceptance of additional papers is discretionary but protracted filings discouraged.

name: Prima facie showing standard for public use/on-sale bar
description: A prima facie case is established by the petition if the examiner finds that the facts asserted in the affidavit(s) or declaration(s), as supported by the exhibits, if later proved true by testimony taken in the public use proceeding, would result in a statutory bar to the claims under 35 U.S.C. 102(b) alone or in combination with 35 U.S.C. 103.
guidance: Examiner must identify exactly what was in public use or on sale, whether it was in use/on sale in this country more than 1 year before the effective filing date, and whether the pending claims read on or are obvious over the alleged public use/on-sale matter; compare all pending claims with the alleged matter, not just claims identified by petitioner.

name: Complaint content when petition alleges obviousness over public use/on-sale matter
description: In situations where the petition alleges only that the claims are obvious over subject matter asserted to be in public use or on sale, the petition should include prior art or other information on which it relies and explain how the prior art or other information in combination with the subject matter asserted to be in public use or on sale renders the claims obvious.
guidance: Petitioner should supply the supporting prior art or rationale and explain combinations; examiner is not expected to perform a prior art search in evaluating the petition, but may rely on known prior art to find a prima facie case of obviousness even if petition alleged only anticipation.

name: Examiner memorandum to Patent Legal Administrator
description: After having made his/her determination, the examiner will forward a memorandum to the Patent Legal Administrator, stating his or her findings and his or her decision as to whether a prima facie case has been established. The findings should include a summary of the alleged facts, a comparison of at least one claim with the device alleged to be in public use or on sale, and any other pertinent facts.
guidance: Prepare memorandum in triplicate, addressed to Patent Legal Administrator, and include sufficient factual summary and claim-to-device comparison to aid the preliminary hearing.

name: Limitations on testimony topics in public use proceedings
description: In all public use proceedings, whether the ultimate issue is anticipation under 35 U.S.C. 102(b) or obviousness over 35 U.S.C. 103, testimony will be limited to the issues of public use or on sale. No testimony will be received on whether the claimed subject matter would have been obvious over subject matter asserted to be in public use or on sale.
guidance: Testimony focuses on factual issues of public use/on-sale; questions of legal obviousness over prior art are not to be explored by testimony in these proceedings.

name: Scope of review of examiner’s final decision
description: There is no review from the final decision of the examiner in the public use proceedings. A petition under 37 CFR 1.181 requesting the Commissioner exercise supervisory authority to vacate the examiner’s decision will not be entertained except where there is a showing of clear error. Once the application returns to its ex parte status, appellate review under 35 U.S.C. 134 and 141-145 may be had of any adverse decision rejecting claim(s) as a result of the examiner’s decisions as to public use or sale.
guidance: Petition under 1.181 is limited to clear error; standard appellate avenues apply after return to ex parte status.

name: Duty to disclose trade secret/proprietary/protective-order materials (37 CFR 1.56/1.555)
description: Inventors and others covered by 37 CFR 1.56(c) and 1.555 have a duty to disclose to the Office information they are aware of which is material to patentability. 37 CFR 1.56(b) states that information is material to patentability when it is not cumulative and (1) it establishes, by itself or in combination, a prima facie case of unpatentability of a claim; or (2) it refutes, or is inconsistent with, a position the applicant takes in opposing an argument of unpatentability relied on by the Office, or asserting an argument of patentability.
guidance: Trade secret or proprietary classification does not relieve the duty to disclose material information; applicants/patent owners must disclose material information even if subject to protective order; a prima facie case uses preponderance standard and broadest reasonable claim construction.

name: Narrow specification and scope of requirements
description: A requirement for information under 37 CFR 1.105 should be narrowly specified and limited in scope because it burdens applicant and examiner.
guidance: Only warrant a requirement where the benefit from the information exceeds the burden of obtaining it; specify particular art area and claimed subject matter to avoid overly burdening applicant and avoid irrelevant volumes of information.

name: Form paragraphs: Art relied upon for various purposes (¶¶ 7.115–7.117)
description: Separate requirements may ask for: (¶7.115) publications used as sources for the description of prior art (title, citation, copy, and concise explanation of contribution); (¶7.116) publications relied upon for development of the invention (title, citation, copy, concise explanation of reliance); (¶7.117) publications relied upon for drafting claimed subject matter (title, citation, copy, concise explanation of reliance in distinguishing claims).
guidance: Each is limited to documents actually relied on (not merely believed relevant); include concise explanations of each publication's role.

name: Form paragraph: Results of Applicant’s Prior Art Search (¶ 7.118)
description: Require state whether any prior art search was performed; if so, list citations for each prior art collection searched and provide copies/citations of art considered material to demonstrating the knowledge of a person of ordinary skill.
guidance: Specify attributes of prior art that most closely approximate claimed subject matter to narrow focus of reply.

name: Form paragraph: Details of Improvement Over the Prior Art (¶ 7.121)
description: Require statement of specific improvements of the subject matter in claims over the disclosed prior art and indicate specific elements providing improvements; for means/steps-plus-function claims, provide specific page and line numbers in the disclosure describing structure/acts.
guidance: Used to substantiate distinctions over prior art and identify supporting portions of the disclosure.

name: When Patentability Reports are not proper (exemplary situations)
description: P.R. is ordinarily not proper where claims are related as a manufacturing process and a product defined by the process; where claims are related as product and process that merely makes the product; or where claims are related as a combination and a subcombination (per se) — the examiner having jurisdiction can usually give a complete examination.
guidance: Do not use P.R. where claims differ only in scope or where one examiner can efficiently examine both aspects; P.R. only when it will save total examiner time or improve quality.

name: Handling disagreements and appeals involving P.R.
description: If the primary examiner in the receiving TC does not agree with the P.R., they may consult; if agreement cannot be reached, the jurisdictional examiner need not rely on the P.R. and may make their own action, removing the P.R. If an appeal is taken where claims are examinable in the reporting TC and application otherwise allowable, formal transfer for appeal only may be made to the reporting TC.
guidance: On allowance the application may be sent to issue by the appropriate TC with classification determined by controlling claims; notify reporting TCs upon allowance or abandonment.

name: Unity: common special technical feature among claims
description: Where a claim (e.g. Claim 1) recites a special technical feature that is common among other claims (e.g. Claims 2 and 3), unity of inventions is met among all claims that share that common special technical feature.
guidance: Example: Claim 1 = Filament A; Claim 2 = Lamp B comprising Filament A; Claim 3 = Searchlight comprising Lamp B comprising Filament A and Spinning rim C. Filament A is the common special technical feature among all claims; unity is met.

name: Lack of unity when claims recite non-identical/non-corresponding special technical features
description: Where claimed special technical features are not identical or do not correspond, unity is not met between claims that recite different special technical features (even if they share a common context of use).
guidance: Example: Claims for control circuit A and control circuit B are different special technical features; unity is met between a control-circuit claim and an apparatus claim using that specific circuit (e.g. Claim1 and Claim3), but not between Claim1 and Claim2 (different circuits) or between apparatus claims that use different circuits.

name: Unity when some claims recite multiple features (combinations) vs single features
description: When some claims recite individual features (Feature A or Feature B) and another claim recites their combination (A and B), unity is met between each single-feature claim and the combination claim, but not between the two single-feature claims themselves.
guidance: Example: Claim1 = conveyor belt with Feature A; Claim2 = conveyor belt with Feature B; Claim3 = conveyor belt with Features A and B. Unity is met between Claim1 & Claim3 and between Claim2 & Claim3, but not between Claim1 & Claim2.

name: Product vs manufacturing method: 'suitable' test for unity
description: Unity between a product claim and a manufacturing-method claim of the product is determined based on whether the manufacturing method is 'suitable' for manufacturing the claimed product.
guidance: 'Suitable' means that when the manufacturing method is practiced the product is manufactured. 'Suitable' does not require exclusivity (the product may be manufacturable by other methods and the method may be usable for other products). Examples show that a method expressly described as a method of manufacturing Product X is suitable and thus shares a common special technical feature (the product).

name: Product vs method of treating the product: definition of 'treating'
description: 'Treating the product' means applying external effects to maintain or exert the product's functions without changing its nature; methods of transfer or storage are examples and correspond to the product claim for unity purposes.
guidance: Example: Claim1 = prefabricated home with special structure; Claim2 = method of storing such prefabricated home — Claim2 corresponds to treating the subject matter of Claim1 and unity is met.

name: Method vs machinery/equipment directly used to practice the method
description: When machinery, equipment or other products are directly used for practicing a claimed method (i.e., directly used for manifestation of the method's special technical features), unity is met between the method claim and the equipment claim.
guidance: 'Suitable' for being directly used is determined by whether the equipment is directly used for manifestation of the special technical features of the method. Microorganisms used in production may be treated as manufacturing devices if their role is direct.

name: Markush-type claims: alternatives with corresponding qualities/functions
description: Where alternative elements are recited in Markush style within a single claim, if the alternative elements have corresponding qualities or functions, unity of inventions is met.
guidance: If a Markush group includes alternative chemicals that meet the stated criteria (see other chapters), consider the group to have corresponding qualities/functions. If at least one alternative is found to lack novelty, the examiner should review unity of inventions.

name: Limits on grouping multiple intermediates/end products
description: One application can claim more than one different intermediate material used in different processes to produce a single end material if major structural elements are identical, but more than two different intermediate materials used in other structures of end products cannot be filed as one application.
guidance: If intermediate and end products are separated by an intermediate material that is not novel, they cannot be filed as one application. For groups of compounds, each intermediate compound should correspond to one compound in the end-product group; correspondence is required but not always possible.

name: Examination order: determine unity on independent claims first
description: Unity of invention shall be first determined on independent claims; if independent claims meet the unity requirement, dependent claims referring to them are deemed to satisfy unity.
guidance: If independent claim is later deleted or amended into different content, unity may no longer be satisfied and re-evaluation is required.

name: When dependent claims must be re-evaluated for unity due to prior art
description: If a cited (independent) claim lacks novelty or inventive step over prior art and thus lacks 'special technical features', unity among claims depending on that cited claim cannot be assumed and dependent claims need additional review to determine whether identical or corresponding special technical features exist among them.
guidance: Example grouping shows dependent claims split into separate invention groups when independent claim offers no improvement over prior art.

name: Application procedure: evidential documents and statements
description: Applicants intending to file inventions related to micro-organisms shall deposit the micro-organism and attach evidential deposit document to the patent application; if the microorganism is easily obtainable by a skilled person, deposit may be omitted but the application must state how to obtain it and include deposit number in original specification if deposited.
guidance: For divisional, converted, or priority-claim applications, the intention to rely on a deposit must be stated and proving documents attached or referenced to previously submitted documents to avoid duplication.

name: Deposit timing and priority considerations for national/international filings
description: For national-phase entries of international applications, microorganism should be deposited to the international depositary authority before the filing date of the patent application and the intention and proving documents enclosed; for domestic priority claims, deposits in prior applications can be relied upon if deposit number disclosed in prior specification.
guidance: Deposits made before the priority date and disclosed properly can convey priority effect; timely deposit is required for priority benefit.

name: Required contents of a PCT application
description: In general, a PCT application requires most of the same data as a national patent application. A PCT application must include: a request (including bibliographic data about the applicant(s)); a description (written disclosure of the invention); one or more claims (defining the scope of protection sought from the application); one or more drawings (where required); and an abstract (summary of the invention).

name: Ex parte Quayle - claimed design patentable but formal matters remain
description: This application is in condition for allowance except for the following formal matters: [1]. Prosecution on the merits is closed in accordance with practice under Ex parte Quayle.
guidance: Use when examiner determines the claim is patentable under all statutory requirements but formal matters need to be addressed prior to allowance. Set a shortened two-month statutory period for reply (extensions under 37 CFR 1.136 possible but reply cannot exceed six months). If, after a reply, a rejection should be given, withdraw indication of allowability and reopen prosecution using the specified form paragraph.

name: Computer-generated electronic images must meet article-of-manufacture requirement
description: Design applications for computer-generated electronic images must comply with the article of manufacture requirement of 35 U.S.C. 171.
guidance: Apply the complete-disclosure review and follow the specific procedures in subsection I (review title/claim, specification, drawings) to determine whether the design is embodied in an article of manufacture (e.g., a display panel).

name: Title and claim must adequately designate an article of manufacture
description: Review title and claim language to determine whether they describe a design for an article of manufacture under 35 U.S.C. 171; titles/claims should not be for an icon or GUI alone but for an article (e.g., 'computer screen with an icon').
guidance: Object under 37 CFR 1.153(a) or 1.1067(a) when title/claim fail to designate a particular article. Examples of inadequate titles/claims: 'display screen with virtual image', 'virtual image for display on computer screen', 'computer icon'. Examples of adequate titles/claims: 'computer screen with an icon', 'display panel with GUI', 'portion of a computer screen with an icon'.

name: Specification must contain characteristic feature statement when appropriate
description: Review the specification to determine whether a characteristic feature statement is present and whether it describes the claimed subject matter as a computer icon or GUI embodied in a display panel or portion thereof.
guidance: A descriptive (characteristic feature) statement can narrow claim scope (see McGrady v. Aspenglas). Use it to determine proper claim scope and support for amendments.

name: Drawings must show the article (display panel) in sufficient views
description: Review the drawing to determine whether a display panel, or a portion thereof, is shown in sufficient views to fully disclose the design as embodied in the article.
guidance: If drawing does not depict the icon/GUI embodied in a display panel (solid or broken lines), reject under 35 U.S.C. 171. If disclosure as a whole suggests embodiment, indicate drawing may be amended to overcome rejection; warn that adding new matter will not be allowed and may render claim subject to 35 U.S.C. 112(a) rejection.

name: Examples illustrating acceptable and unacceptable presentations
description: Provided examples (e.g., 'Computer display screen with icon' — acceptable; 'Virtual paper stack' — not acceptable) show when claims/titles/drawings comply with 35 U.S.C. 171 or should be objected/rejected.
guidance: Use examples to guide objections and rejections; where possible suggest replacement figures or amendments supported by original disclosure. Note examples of acceptable and unacceptable claim language and titles.

name: Changeable (animated) computer-generated images — descriptive statement required
description: Animated or changeable images may be the subject of a design claim shown in two or more views. A descriptive statement must be included describing the transitional nature and making clear that the process/period of transition forms no part of the claimed design.
guidance: Provide sample descriptive statements (e.g., 'The appearance of the image sequentially transitions between the images shown in Figs. 1-8. The process or period in which one image transitions to another image forms no part of the claimed design.'). Object to title/claim if they fail to designate a particular article (37 CFR 1.153/1.1067) and suggest amending to 'computer display screen with an animated icon.'

name: Design comprising multiple articles or multiple parts
description: A claimed design may encompass multiple articles or multiple parts within a single article, but the title must identify a single entity of manufacture made up by the parts (e.g., set, pair, combination, unit, assembly).
guidance: Include a descriptive statement in the specification clarifying that the claim is directed to the collective appearance. If separate parts are shown in a single view, embrace parts by a bracket '}'. For multiple parts of a single article, show article in broken lines and parts in solid lines (no bracket needed). See MPEP §1503.01.

name: Ornamentality vs. functionality — primary ornamentality requirement
description: To be patentable, a design must be 'primarily ornamental.' In determining whether a design is primarily functional or ornamental, view the claimed design in its entirety; the ultimate question is the overall appearance, not the function or decoration of separate features.
guidance: Consider that ornamentality must be created for the purpose of ornamenting (In re Carletti). The determination is qualitative based on ornamental contribution to the design as a whole, not quantitative based on feature size. Distinguish functionality of the article from functionality of the particular design of such article.

name: Prima facie evidentiary basis required for rejection under 35 U.S.C. 171 (lack of ornamentality)
description: An examiner must make a prima facie showing that the claimed design lacks ornamentality and provide sufficient evidentiary basis for factual assumptions relied upon in such showing.
guidance: Proper evidentiary bases include the appearance of the design itself, examiner's knowledge of the art, replies to inquiries, brochures emphasizing functional/mechanical features, specification of an analogous utility patent, or information in the application. Rejections must be supported by evidence; do not make rejections absent such evidence (see In re Jung, In re Oetiker).

name: The Three Audiences for a Patent Application
description: A patent specification is read by (1) the examiner, who decides whether to allow it; (2) a future district court judge or jury, who decides claim construction and infringement; and (3) a future PTAB panel, who decides validity.
guidance: Drafting choices that satisfy one audience may hurt another. The first draft should be examiner-friendly; later drafts must be litigation-friendly. Balance language and structure to serve initial prosecution while preserving litigation strength.

name: Three Independent Claims, Twenty Total
description: The USPTO filing fee includes three independent claims and twenty total claims. Use them all.
guidance: Draft three independent claims of varying scope plus seventeen dependent claims that systematically narrow. This gives negotiating leverage with the examiner and creates a more robust claim portfolio.

name: Claim Differentiation as a Drafting Tool
description: Use dependent claims deliberately to affect the interpretation of independent claims via claim differentiation.
guidance: When claim 2 adds 'wherein the widget is metal,' that creates a presumption that claim 1 covers non-metal widgets too. Use dependent claims to broaden or shape the construction of independent claims by negative implication.

name: Drafting in Layers
description: Structure the specification in multiple layers to serve different needs.
guidance: Layer 1: paragraphs that read like a textbook for a POSITA. Layer 2: paragraphs that recite the elements of each claim, almost word-for-word, so every claim term has clear antecedent support. Layer 3: paragraphs that describe alternatives, ranges, and equivalents. All three layers belong in the spec to support prosecution and later litigation/analysis.

name: Novelty vs inventive step — scope of prior art
description: Novelty is destroyed if a claimed invention is identical to the prior disclosure; inventive step is lacking if the claimed invention could have been made easily by a person skilled in the art based on prior art.
guidance: Prior art for novelty is usually confined to the same technical field, whereas prior art for inventive step may come from different fields; recombination of known elements normally affects inventive step but not necessarily novelty; strict equivalents in prior art may destroy novelty while broad equivalents generally do not.

name: Direct notice to defendant
description: A second way [the Plaintiff] can give notice of its patent[s] is to directly notify [the Defendant] with a specific claim that the [allegedly infringing product] infringed the [abbreviated patent number] patent. This type of notice starts from the date [the Defendant] received the notice.
guidance: Direct notice establishes the start date for liability from the date received.

name: Entire Market Value Rule (EMVR) and smallest salable unit
description: Royalties for multi-component products should be based not on the entire product but on the 'smallest salable unit' that practices the patented invention and has close relation to the claimed invention. If that unit contains non-infringing features unrelated to the patented feature(s), damages must be based only on the portion of that unit's value attributable to the patented technology. The EMVR is a narrow exception allowing use of entire product revenues only if the patented feature is the sole driver of customer demand or substantially creates product value.
guidance: EMVR is narrow and requires plaintiff to show patented feature drives demand for the entire product. May involve estimating feature value that was never separately sold. (Cites cases.)

name: Willful infringement—general standard
description: If jurors find defendant infringed a valid claim, they must determine whether the infringement was willful. To show willfulness, plaintiff must prove it is more likely than not that defendant knew of plaintiff's patent and intentionally infringed at least one asserted claim. Jurors may consider whether defendant's behavior was deliberate or intentional, but knowledge alone is not sufficient.
guidance: Assess totality of circumstances and defendant's knowledge at the time of the challenged conduct. A finding of willfulness does not affect the amount of damages the jury awards, but willfulness may be considered later. (Cites Halo and other cases.)

name: Process patent: all claimed acts required or equivalents
description: No process patent is infringed where any one of the series of acts which constitute the process is omitted by the supposed infringer, unless some equivalent act is substituted for the one omitted.
guidance: Precisely what constitutes equivalency between acts is not rigidly defined by the Supreme Court; reasoning indicates an act is equivalent when it works in substantially the same way to accomplish the same result. Example: tamping oil wells with benzine held equivalent to tamping with water (Roberts torpedo patent).

name: Only what is claimed is covered by patent; unclaimed described matter not infringement
description: It is not an infringement of a patent to make, use, or sell any specimen of any invention described but not claimed therein, because a patent covers only what it claims.
guidance: Distinguish between descriptive disclosure and the scope defined by the claims; infringement analysis focuses on claims.

name: Infringement of any one claim infringes the patent
description: Whoever infringes any one claim of a patent infringes the patent, whether or not the patent contains other claims which he does not infringe.
guidance: Each claim is independently enforceable; a finding of infringement as to one claim supports a patent infringement verdict.

name: Results alone are not determinative; means/mode of operation matter
description: The respective results of a patented thing and an alleged infringing thing do not furnish a criterion for infringement; identical results can be produced by substantially different means and not infringe, and different results may still be infringement if the thing is within the claim.
guidance: Courts focus on whether the accused device uses substantially the same means/mode of operation as the claimed invention, not merely whether the outcome is the same.

name: Addition to a patented machine/manufacture does not avoid infringement
description: Addition to a patented machine or manufacture (including duplicating parts) does not enable the maker/user/seller of the patented thing with the addition to avoid a charge of infringement.
guidance: This holds even where the added device facilitates operation or improves performance. However, restoring an omitted part of an older structure (when the patent claims a combination that omits that part) may not infringe the later combination if the result is a substantially different combination.

name: Omission of an element of a combination averts infringement
description: Omission of one element or ingredient of a combination covered by any claim averts any charge of infringement based on that claim, whether or not the omitted ingredient was essential to the combination or necessary to operativeness.
guidance: A combination is an entirety; if one element is omitted the claimed thing disappears. Every part of a claimed combination is conclusively presumed material; evidence to the contrary is generally inadmissible. Examples and many cases are cited.

name: Combination claims to results: infringement by sufficient described devices
description: A patentee may claim so much of the described mechanism as produces a particular described result; such a claim is infringed by anyone who makes, uses, or sells an apparatus made up of enough of the described devices to produce the specified result by the specified mode of operation.
guidance: This is distinct from broad combination claims; focus on the claimed result and specified mode of operation when assessing infringement of such claims.

name: Status of defeated applicant claims (§97.221)
description: After final notice of priority and expiration of appeal time, the claims constituting the priority issue stand finally disposed of without further action by the Commissioner.
guidance: Finality rule for priority determinations — precludes further administrative re-litigation of same priority claims.

name: Chapter 0600 - Parts, Form, and Content of Application
description: MPEP chapter describing the required parts of a patent application, form requirements, and content standards for specification, claims, drawings, and abstracts.

name: Chapter 2100 - Patentability
description: MPEP chapter covering substantive patentability requirements (novelty, non‑obviousness, statutory subject matter, utility, written description, enablement, and claim issues).

name: Primary object of examination: patentability over the prior art
description: The primary object of examination is to determine whether the claims are patentable over the prior art.
guidance: Examiners should concentrate effort on essential matters (prior art) and minimize undue emphasis on non-prior-art or 'technical' rejections. When a major technical rejection is proper (e.g., lack of proper disclosure, undue breadth, utility), the rejection should include a full development of reasons rather than mere conclusions or stereotyped expressions. Using form paragraphs to state rejections reduces misunderstanding as to grounds of rejection.

name: Use of form paragraphs to state non-prior-art rejections
description: When incorporating standard language in office actions, use the prescribed form paragraphs.
guidance: If language in form paragraphs is incorporated into the office action to state the rejection, there will be less chance of misunderstanding as to grounds of rejection. Refer to the specific MPEP sections for nonstatutory subject matter, Atomic Energy Act issues, duplicate claims, double patenting, new matter, foreign filing without a license, disclaimers, res judicata, reissue, and 35 U.S.C. 112 issues.

name: Form paragraph 7.31.01 — Rejection: Written description (35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph)
description: Claim rejected for containing subject matter not described in the specification such that it would not reasonably convey possession to one skilled in the art at the time of filing.
guidance: This rejection must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.01. In bracket identify by page/line/drawings the subject matter not properly described and explain the position, including any examiner questions not satisfactorily resolved that raise doubt as to possession.

name: Form paragraph 7.31.02 — Rejection: Enablement (35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph)
description: Claim rejected as containing subject matter not enabled to allow one skilled in the art to make and/or use the invention.
guidance: Precede with 7.30.01. In bracket identify claimed subject matter lacking enablement and explain why specification is not enabling, including examiner questions not resolved. If problem is scope, use 7.31.03. Also make a separate enablement analysis per In re Wands and undue experimentation factors (MPEP §§2164–2164.08(c)). If an essential component/step is not recited, use 7.33.01.

name: Form paragraph 7.31.03 — Rejection: Scope of enablement (35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph)
description: Use when specification is enabling for some subject matter but does not reasonably provide enablement for the full scope of the claims.
guidance: Precede with 7.30.01. In bracket 2 identify subject matter for which specification is enabling (by reference to portions of the specification). In bracket 3 identify the subject matter for which specification is not enabling and explain why (make clear whether the deficiency is make/use/make and use). Include examiner questions not resolved. Use when claim scope is not commensurate with enabling disclosure.

name: Form paragraph 7.33.01 — Essential subject matter missing from claims (enablement)
description: Claim rejected because subject matter considered critical or essential by applicant to practice the invention is missing from the claim and thus not enabled.
guidance: Precede with 7.30.01. In bracket recite the subject matter omitted from the claims. Examiner must cite statement/argument/date/drawing or other evidence demonstrating that applicant considered the feature essential and give rationale for omission rendering claim not enabled (see In re Mayhew).

name: 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph — claims must particularly point out and distinctly claim
description: The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the applicant regards as his invention.
guidance: Use form paragraph 7.30.02 as the statutory quotation in first actions and final rejections; otherwise use 7.103. Follow with appropriate 7.34–7.35 form paragraphs for specific defects in claim definiteness or correspondence to applicant's stated invention.

name: Form paragraph 7.34 — Failure to claim applicant's invention (35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph)
description: Claim rejected for failing to set forth the subject matter which applicant(s) regard as their invention, based on applicant statements outside the application as filed.
guidance: Precede with 7.30.02. Identify the paper/submission (Paper No. and date) where applicant stated something inconsistent with claim scope; set forth what applicant stated and explain how that indicates the invention is different from what's claimed.

name: Form paragraph 7.34.01 — Indefinite: failure to particularly point out (35 U.S.C.112, second paragraph)
description: Claim rejected as indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter regarded as the invention.
guidance: Precede with 7.30.02. Follow with one or more of form paragraphs 7.34.02–7.34.06 as applicable. Where possible, identify the particular term(s)/limitation(s) rendering the claim indefinite and why; if the scope can be determined by one skilled in the art, this rejection is not appropriate.

name: Form paragraph 7.34.02 — Terminology inconsistent with accepted meaning
description: Term in a claim used in a manner repugnant to the usual meaning renders the claim indefinite.
guidance: Applicant may be his own lexicographer but cannot give a term a meaning repugnant to usual meaning. Identify the term used by applicant and the meaning assigned versus the accepted meaning. Support examiner's accepted meaning with authoritative references (textbook/dictionary). Precede with 7.34.01.

name: Form paragraph 7.34.03 — Relative term (term of degree) rendering claim indefinite
description: A relative term of degree is indefinite where claim/specification does not provide a standard for ascertaining the requisite degree and one of ordinary skill would not be reasonably apprised of scope.
guidance: In bracket explain which parameter/quantity/limitation has been rendered indefinite by the term. Precede with 7.34.01.

name: Form paragraph 7.34.04 — Broad range and narrow range/limitation in same claim
description: A claim that recites a broad range or limitation together with a narrow range or limitation within that broad range in the same claim is indefinite.
guidance: This creates ambiguity whether narrow language is exemplary or required. Insert the broader and narrower ranges and explain why ambiguity arises. Precede with 7.34.01.

name: Form paragraph 7.34.05 — Lack of antecedent basis in the claims
description: Claim limitation lacks proper antecedent basis making scope indeterminate.
guidance: Use only in aggravated situations where lack of antecedent basis makes claim scope indeterminate. Insert the limitation lacking antecedent basis and indicate where in the claim it appears. Precede with 7.34.01.

name: Form paragraph 7.34.06 — Use claims (method of using a product without steps) indefinite and possibly nonstatutory
description: A claim directed to the use of something without setting forth the steps of the method/process is indefinite and may be an improper process claim under 35 U.S.C. 101.
guidance: Insert what is being used and explain lack of steps. Example: 'a method for using monoclonal antibodies of claim 4 to purify interferon' — without steps, unclear what method is encompassed. See MPEP § 2173.05(q). Precede with 7.34.01.

name: Form paragraph 7.34.07 — Claims are a literal translation
description: Claims that appear to be literal translations into English from foreign documents and are replete with grammatical and idiomatic errors are narrative and indefinite.
guidance: Such claims fail to conform with U.S. practice. Precede with 7.34.01.

name: Form paragraph 7.34.08 — Indefinite language: 'for example'
description: Use of the phrase 'for example' in a claim renders it indefinite because it is unclear whether following limitations are part of the claimed invention.
guidance: Precede with 7.34.01. See MPEP § 2173.05(d).

name: Form paragraph 7.34.09 — Indefinite language: 'or the like'
description: Use of 'or the like' renders the claim indefinite because it includes elements not actually disclosed, making scope unascertainable.
guidance: Precede with 7.34.01. See MPEP § 2173.05(d).

name: Form paragraph 7.34.10 — Indefinite language: 'such as'
description: Use of 'such as' renders a claim indefinite because it is unclear whether the limitations following the phrase are part of the claimed invention.
guidance: Precede with 7.34.01. See MPEP § 2173.05(d).

name: Form paragraph 7.34.12 — Essential steps omitted (35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph)
description: Claim rejected for omitting essential steps, amounting to a gap between steps.
guidance: Precede with 7.30.02. Recite omitted steps and give rationale why they are critical or essential (see MPEP § 2172.01).

name: Form paragraph 7.34.13 — Essential elements omitted (35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph)
description: Claim rejected for omitting essential elements, amounting to a gap between elements.
guidance: Precede with 7.30.02. Recite omitted elements and rationale for considering them critical or essential.

name: Form paragraph 7.34.14 — Essential cooperative relationships omitted
description: Claim rejected for omitting essential structural cooperative relationships of elements, amounting to a gap in necessary structural connections.
guidance: Precede with 7.30.02. Recite omitted structural cooperative relationships and give rationale why they are critical/essential (see MPEP § 2172.01).

name: Form paragraph 7.34.15 — Rejection guidance for pro se applicants
description: Claims by pro se applicants may be narrative, replete with indefinite and functional language and fail to present complete operative devices.
guidance: Claim must be in one-sentence form, specify structure clearly, organized and correlated to present a complete operative device. Use when applicable. Precede with 7.30.02 or 7.103.

name: Form paragraph 7.35 — Omnibus type claim rejection (35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph)
description: Claim rejected as indefinite where it fails to point out what is included or excluded (omnibus claim).
guidance: Precede with 7.30.02. Use to reject 'omnibus' claims (no further explanation necessary). Example: 'A device substantially as shown and described.' See MPEP § 1302.04(b) for cancellation upon allowance.

name: Form paragraph 7.35.01 — Trademark or trade name used as claim limitation
description: Claim containing a trademark/trade name as a limitation fails 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, because trademarks identify source, not goods, making claim scope uncertain.
guidance: Insert trademark/trade name and where used; specify the material/product identified or described by the trademark. Explain indefinite identification/description; cite Ex parte Simpson. Precede with 7.30.02 or 7.103.

name: Duplicate claims (706.03(k))
description: When two claims are duplicates or so close that they cover the same thing despite slight wording differences, the examiner may object to the duplicate under 37 CFR 1.75.
guidance: After allowing one claim, object to the other claim as a substantial duplicate of the allowed claim. Form paragraphs 7.05.05 and 7.05.06 may be used where duplicate claims are present.

name: Nonelected inventions and plural claiming guidance (706.03(m))
description: A patent is supposed to be limited to one invention or several closely related indivisible inventions, but applicants may restate the invention in a reasonable number of ways by plural claiming.
guidance: Courts have confirmed applicant's right to plural claiming; mere difference in scope between claims can be sufficient. However, when duplicate claims are present, examiners should object as described above. Limitations on multiple inventions are handled through election/requirement practice (see broader MPEP text for procedure).

name: English translation requirement for non-English provisional (37 CFR 1.78)
description: If the application claims benefit to a provisional application filed in a language other than English, an English translation of the non-English provisional application and a statement that the translation is accurate must be filed in the provisional application. If these items are missing, the applicant must supply (1) the missing items in the provisional application and (2) a confirmation in the present application that the translation and statement were filed in the provisional; failure to do so before the Office action deadline may result in abandonment.
guidance: Do not use this paragraph if a translation and statement were filed in the nonprovisional application before Nov 25, 2005. Insert the provisional application numbers and filing dates into the form paragraph as instructed.

name: Prior-filed application must be entitled to a filing date and basic filing fee paid to claim benefit (37 CFR 1.78)
description: An application claiming the benefit of a prior-filed application is not entitled to the benefit if the prior-filed application was not entitled to a filing date and/or did not include the basic filing fee as required by the applicable rules for international, design, nonprovisional, or provisional applications.
guidance: Applicant is required to delete the benefit claim from the Application Data Sheet (ADS) or, for applications filed before Sept 16, 2012, from the ADS or the first sentence(s) of the specification as appropriate. Insert the prior application number and relevant filing date(s) into the form paragraph.

name: Timeliness requirements for benefit claims (35 U.S.C. 119(e), 120, 121, 365(c), 386(c); 37 CFR 1.78)
description: Benefit claims must be submitted during the pendency of the application and within the later of: (a) four months from the actual filing date of the application, or (b) sixteen months from the filing date of the prior application (with special rules for national stage filings under 35 U.S.C. 371). For applications filed before Sept 16, 2012, the reference must be included in the first sentence(s) of the specification; for applications filed on or after that date, the specific reference must be included in an ADS. For benefit claims under 35 U.S.C. 120/121/365(c)/386(c), the reference must include the relationship (continuation, divisional, or continuation-in-part) of the applications.
guidance: If untimely, the applicant may file a petition for an unintentionally delayed benefit claim under 37 CFR 1.78(c) (for 119(e)) or 1.78(e) (for 120/121/365(c)/386(c)) accompanied by the required reference, the petition fee (37 CFR 1.17(m)), and a statement that the entire delay was unintentional. The Director may require additional information. Use this paragraph only for original applications under 35 U.S.C. 111(a) on or after Nov 29, 2000 and for national stage applications under 35 U.S.C. 371; DO NOT use for design applications.

name: Arrangement and section order of the specification in a utility application (37 CFR 1.77(b))
description: The specification of a utility application should include the following sections in order (each in uppercase without underlining/bold): (a) TITLE OF THE INVENTION; (b) CROSS-REFERENCE TO RELATED APPLICATIONS; (c) STATEMENT REGARDING FEDERALLY SPONSORED RESEARCH OR DEVELOPMENT; (d) THE NAMES OF THE PARTIES TO A JOINT RESEARCH AGREEMENT; (e) INCORPORATION-BY-REFERENCE OF MATERIAL SUBMITTED ON A COMPACT DISC OR AS A TEXT FILE VIA EFS-WEB; (f) STATEMENT REGARDING PRIOR DISCLOSURES BY THE INVENTOR OR A JOINT INVENTOR; (g) BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION (Field and Description of Related Art); (h) BRIEF SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION; (i) BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE SEVERAL VIEWS OF THE DRAWING(S); (j) DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION; (k) CLAIM OR CLAIMS (commencing on a separate sheet); (l) ABSTRACT OF THE DISCLOSURE (separate sheet); (m) SEQUENCE LISTING (if applicable). If no text follows a heading, the phrase 'Not Applicable' should follow it.
guidance: These are preferred layout guidelines and are suggested for applicant use. For design and plant applications, see other MPEP sections. Headings should appear in upper case.

name: Claims formatting — separate sheet, indentation of elements/steps (37 CFR 1.75, 1.52(b)(3))
description: Claims must commence on a separate sheet or electronic page. When a claim sets forth a plurality of elements or steps, each element/step should be separated by a line indentation; plural indentations may be used to segregate subcombinations or related steps.
guidance: See MPEP § 608.01(i)-(p) for more on claim drafting and indentation conventions.

name: Antedating when reference is commonly owned (37 CFR 1.130 requirements)
description: When the rejection to be overcome is under 35 U.S.C. 103 in view of a U.S. patent or U.S. patent application publication that is commonly owned, 37 CFR 1.130(a) requires: (1) a terminal disclaimer in accordance with 37 CFR 1.321(c); and (2) an oath or declaration stating inter alia that the inventor named in the application or patent under reexamination is the prior inventor under 35 U.S.C. 104.
guidance: The inventor in the application/patent under reexamination must have invented the claimed subject matter before the actual date of invention of the reference claims. The affidavit/declaration may be signed by inventor(s), attorney/agent of record, or assignee(s) of the entire interest. 37 CFR 1.130 also interacts with interference rules (37 CFR 41.206) and antedating restrictions in 37 CFR 1.131 (anticommon-claiming requirements). See MPEP § 804.03 and § 706.02(l)(3).

name: Procedure for correcting data on the file wrapper or PALM bib-data sheet
description: If an error is noticed in data on the file wrapper or PALM bib-data sheet, the examiner should correct it in red ink and forward the application to the TC technical support staff for database correction and printing of a new bib-data sheet or adhesive label, following series-specific procedures.
guidance: Correction methods vary by application series: for 08/ or earlier series, make correction in red ink on file wrapper and forward for PALM correction; for 09/series correct on PALM bib-data sheet and forward; for 10/ and above series correct on file wrapper and forward for printing an adhesive label. Examples of instances requiring correction include changes in inventorship (37 CFR 1.48), filing date corrections, prior U.S. application number errors, and corrections to benefit claims under 35 U.S.C. 120/121/365(c). See MPEP §§ 605.04(g), 202.02, 201.11, and 1302.09.

name: Public use proceedings — petition requirements and filing conditions (37 CFR 1.292)
description: A petition to institute public use proceedings (ex parte or inter partes) under 37 CFR 1.292 must make a prima facie showing (supported by affidavits/declarations) that the claimed invention was in public use or on sale more than one year before filing, and must meet filing, service, fee, and timing requirements.
guidance: Requirements to have the petition entered in the application file: (1) accompanied by fee per 37 CFR 1.17(j); (2) served on the applicant per 37 CFR 1.248 or filed in duplicate if service not possible; (3) submitted prior to publication of the application or mailing of notice of allowance under 37 CFR 1.311, whichever occurs first. Duplicate copies should only be submitted after diligent effort to serve applicant. Notice of petition may be entered in lieu of bulky papers; any public use papers not physically entered will be publicly available when the file wrapper is available. The Director has discretion to institute proceedings and may designate officials, set hearing times, and use part 41, subpart D procedures. Petitioner eligibility: any member of the public (including representatives filing on behalf of unnamed principals). Distinguish ex parte (petitioner not entitled to inspect pending application) vs inter partes (petitioner may be privy to contents in reissue-inter partes situations). Petitions by parties to an interference involving the application are generally disallowed post-February 11, 1985, except narrow historical exceptions; public use issues in interferences should be raised by motion under 37 CFR 41.121(a)(1).

name: Pre-classification review and correction by examiner
description: Pre-classification of ordinary applications is conducted by a specialized classification organization; an examiner shall review whether the technical subject-matter of the claimed invention is classified appropriately pursuant to CPC/IPC and whether application is within scope of his/her classification before examination to confirm classification.
guidance: If inappropriate, the examiner should apply for correction, request reallocation, or ask Policy Division to correct classification and reallocate application.

name: Principle for determining technical subject-matter for classification
description: On the basis of technical contents of an application, classification place among section, class, sub-class, main group, and sub-group shall be determined. The technical subject-matter is determined based on matters in claims in light of description and drawings. If claim unclear or delayed, the description or drawings determine technical subject-matter.
guidance: Classification is based on essential contents of claimed invention as a whole rather than formality like category of invention (example: electronic radio circuit classified as whole circuit unless core concerns specific part). If claims differ from description, description/drawings are additional information.

name: Classification of specific/structural parts
description: If structural or functional specifics or parts in the claimed invention are used only for a certain apparatus, the claimed invention shall be classified into the place for the apparatus. However, if such specifics or parts can be used for more than 2 apparatus, it is advisable to classify into the place for those specifics or parts. Where there is no place for them, classify in place for the relevant apparatus.
guidance: Choose classification reflecting reusability and generality of the part.

name: Factors indicative of experimental purpose (13-factor list)
description: Courts consider multiple factors to determine whether an on-sale/public-use was for experimentation rather than commercial exploitation: (1) necessity for public testing, (2) amount of control retained by inventor, (3) nature of the invention, (4) length of test period, (5) whether payment was made, (6) secrecy obligation, (7) whether records were kept, (8) who conducted experiment, (9) degree of commercial exploitation during testing, (10) whether invention reasonably requires evaluation under actual conditions, (11) whether testing was systematically performed, (12) whether inventor continually monitored the invention during testing, (13) nature of contacts with potential customers.
guidance: Customer’s awareness of purported testing is a critical attribute. No single factor or particular combination is necessarily determinative; examiner must assess scope and length of activity as reasonable for claimed experimental purpose. Cases: Allen Eng’g; EZ Dock; Electromotive Div. of GM.

name: Continuation-in-part (CIP) breaks chain of priority for foreign and U.S. parents
description: Filing a CIP that includes new subject matter not entitled to the parent filing date breaks the chain of priority; the CIP's effective filing date governs and applicant may lose benefit of foreign or U.S. parent filing dates for claims not supported by the parent.
guidance: If a foreign application issues into a patent before the CIP filing date, the foreign patent may be used in a 102(d)/103 rejection against CIP claims that are not entitled to parent filing dates. Case: In re Van Langenhoven; Ex parte Appeal No. 242-47.

name: 102(d) — 'same invention' requirement
description: 'Same invention' means the subject matter claimed in the U.S. application could have been presented in the foreign patent; claims need not be identical and may be of different statutory classes if the foreign specification supports the U.S. claims.
guidance: If the foreign patent fully discloses the invention and provides options supporting U.S. claims, 102(d) applies even if the foreign claims differ. Case: In re Kathawala (Spanish patent disclosing compounds/methods supported composition claims in U.S.). Examiner should assess whether foreign specification supports claimed U.S. subject matter.

name: Claims must distinctly specify the subject matter
description: Every patent application must include one or more claims that distinctly specify the subject matter being patented.
guidance: Claims are the heart of the application and define the boundaries of your invention and exclusive rights; poorly drafted or missing claims can render an invention vulnerable to copying. Use precise, legally-oriented technical language to define what is protected.

name: Include both independent and dependent claims
description: Independent claims outline essential elements and must be capable of asserting novelty on their own; dependent claims add details/constraints and narrow scope.
guidance: Craft a meticulous array of both independent and dependent claims to capture various dimensions of the invention; dependent claims reinforce and give fallback positions if broader claims are rejected.

name: Claim structure: preamble, transitional phrase, body
description: A patent claim typically contains a preamble (identifies category), a transitional phrase, and a body (lists elements/steps).
guidance: Ensure each part is carefully written: the preamble should identify the invention category without unnecessarily restricting scope; the transitional phrase determines open vs closed scope; the body must list all elements/limitations clearly and precisely.

name: Avoid functional language in the preamble
description: The preamble should introduce the invention's category and avoid functional language that could unintentionally narrow scope.
guidance: Craft the preamble so it frames context but does not limit claim breadth by describing functions rather than structural/definitional elements.

name: Choose transitional phrases deliberately ('comprising' vs 'consisting of')
description: Transitional phrases affect claim breadth: 'comprising' is open/inclusionary; 'consisting of' is closed/exclusionary.
guidance: 'Comprising' allows additional, unrecited elements; 'consisting of' limits the claim to the specified elements only. Select based on desired claim breadth and enforcement strategy.

name: Use clear, precise, and definite language
description: Claims must be clear, concise, and definite so that the scope is ascertainable and enforceable.
guidance: Avoid ambiguity or vagueness; examiners may object or reject claims that are unclear or indefinite. Use consistent terms and appropriate article usage (see next criterion).

name: Consistent article and reference usage ('a'/'an' then 'said'/'the')
description: Use 'a' or 'an' when an element is first introduced and 'said' or 'the' on subsequent references for clarity and exactitude.
guidance: This conventional wording strategy helps define singular/plural and dependencies across claim elements and supports enforceability.

name: Draft from broadest to narrowest (claim hierarchy strategy)
description: Begin with the broadest claim(s) and then draft progressively narrower dependent claims.
guidance: This 'broad-to-narrow' approach eases examination and provides fallback positions. A strategic claim set balances broad independent claims with focused dependent claims.

name: Balance broad vs narrow claims strategically
description: Broad claims cover more variations but are harder to enforce and may face prior-art obstacles; narrow claims are easier to enforce but allow close design-arounds.
guidance: Often the recommended hybrid approach is to have broad independent claims plus narrower dependent claims to combine coverage and enforceability; consider prior art when choosing breadth.

name: Use multiple claim sets and recommended claim counts
description: A well-crafted application typically includes multiple claims — the article recommends around 20 total claims with at least 3 independent claims.
guidance: Multiple claim sets increase durability and options during prosecution. Ensure each claim is meaningfully different and supported by the specification.

name: Claims must be supported by the specification and drawings
description: Every individual claim must be solidly backed by information in the original filing documentation (specification and drawings).
guidance: Lack of support can lead to rejections or invalidity; ensure embodiments, terminology, and examples in the description enable the full scope of the claimed subject matter.

name: Anticipate and address examiner scrutiny (novelty, non-obviousness, support, clarity)
description: During examination the patent office reviews claims for clarity, definiteness, novelty, non-obviousness, and support in the specification.
guidance: Draft claims and claim sets with prior art and examiner objections in mind; prepare fallback claim language and arguments to overcome rejections for anticipation or obviousness.

name: Iteratively refine claims during prosecution
description: Claims should be revisited and refined throughout prosecution to respond to examiner concerns and to improve scope and enforceability.
guidance: Be prepared to amend claims, consolidate aspects, or add dependent claims as prosecution proceeds to address objections and strengthen the application.

name: Labeling, numbering, and placement of claims
description: Claims are typically located at the end of the written specification, labeled 'Claims', and numbered consecutively; the first claim is generally independent.
guidance: Follow standard formatting: label dependent claims as such and ensure each dependent claim properly references an earlier claim for clarity and formal compliance.

name: Avoid claims that are too expansive beyond the invention or prior art
description: Claims perceived as overly broad risk rejection when they encompass beyond the original invention or fail to account for existing prior art.
guidance: Maintain precision; do not attempt to claim unrelated subject matter. Ensure claim scope tracks what is disclosed and novel over prior art to reduce rejection risk.

name: Consider claim construction and downstream litigation implications
description: Claims should be drafted with an eye toward how courts will construe them (e.g., Markman hearings), focusing on accessibility to non-specialists and reflecting inventor intent.
guidance: Draft term definitions and consistent terminology to shape likely claim construction; remember that claim language influences both infringement and validity analyses.

name: Use examples and real-world claim models for guidance
description: Study exemplar claims (e.g., CRISPR systems, powered exoskeleton, Apple iPhone design patent) to learn how complex technologies and designs are protected.
guidance: Analyze well-drafted claims to see how features and embodiments are claimed; adapt useful phrasing and structural approaches appropriate to your technology while ensuring support.

name: Seek experienced patent counsel
description: Patent claim drafting benefits from experienced patent attorneys who align legal requirements with business objectives.
guidance: Consult qualified counsel early to craft robust claims, perform prior art searches, and manage prosecution strategy rather than relying solely on self-drafting.

name: Draft claims to be enforceable and commercially useful
description: Claims should not only meet legal requirements but also align with commercial goals to provide meaningful protection against competitors.
guidance: Consider likely infringing variations, enforcement practicality, and market strategy when choosing what to claim and how broadly to claim it.

name: Applicability of 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1)(A)/102(b)(2)(A) exceptions (1.130(a))
description: Whether the disclosure addressed in the affidavit/declaration is subject to the exceptions of 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1)(A) or 102(b)(2)(A).
guidance: 37 CFR 1.130(a) is not available if: (1) the disclosure was made more than one year before the effective filing date of the claimed invention (see MPEP § 2152.01 to determine effective filing date); or (2) the disclosure applied in the rejection is a U.S. patent or U.S. patent application publication that claims the same or substantially the same invention and the affidavit contends that an inventor named in that patent/publication derived the claimed invention from the inventor(s) named in the application. See MPEP § 717.01, subsection II for more on when declarations under 37 CFR 1.130(a) are not available.

name: When 37 CFR 1.131(a) affidavits are inappropriate
description: An affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(a) is not appropriate in specified situations.
guidance: Specific inapplicable situations include: (A) application subject to current 35 U.S.C. 102 and affidavit not directed to pre‑AIA 102(g) evidence; (B) reference publication date is more than 1 year prior to effective filing date (statutory bar under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)); (C) reference U.S. patent or application publication claims interfering subject matter (see 37 CFR 41.203(a)); (D) foreign patent for same invention issued before domestic filing where foreign application was filed >12 months earlier (pre‑AIA 102(d)); (E) applicant's effective filing date is prior to the reference's effective date (affidavit unnecessary); (F) reference claims same invention and claimed invention under examination is subject to statutory double patenting; (G) applicant has clearly admitted on the record that the subject matter is prior art; (H) subject matter relied upon is prior art under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f); (I) subject matter corresponding to a lost count in an interference may be unavailable or barred by interference estoppel (see cited cases and MPEP guidance).

name: How much of the claimed invention must be shown (possession requirement)
description: The 37 CFR 1.131(a) affidavit or declaration must establish possession of either the whole invention claimed or something falling within the claim (such as a species of a claimed genus), in the sense that the claim as a whole reads on it.
guidance: An affidavit that shows only part of the claimed invention (e.g., missing an element) is generally insufficient (In re Tanczyn). However, if differences are so small as to render the claims obvious over the reference(s), the affidavit need only show no more than the reference shows (In re Stryker). The affidavit must still establish possession of the basic inventive concept and not merely what a reference shows (In re Spiller).

name: General rule as to generic claims (species antedating genus)
description: A reference or activity applied against generic claims may (in most cases) be antedated as to such claims by a 37 CFR 1.131(a) affidavit showing completion of the invention of only a single species within the genus before the prior art date of the reference or activity.
guidance: Precedents (Ex parte Biesecker; In re Fong; In re Dafano) support this, but practice differs for cases in unpredictable arts — see MPEP § 715.03 for guidance relative to predictability.

name: Functional claim limitations
description: Functional language in a claim can be permissible but may render a claim indefinite if it fails to provide a clear-cut indication of scope or merely states a problem to be solved or a result obtained.
guidance: Consider context (specification disclosure and knowledge of a person of ordinary skill). Functional limitations that do not recite the particular structure, materials, or steps accomplishing the function may encompass all means or methods of resolving the problem and thus may not be supported by the written description or commensurate with the enabling disclosure (35 U.S.C. 112(a) / pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112 first paragraph). Examples: claims reciting only intended results like 'aesthetically pleasing' were indefinite (Datamize); 'fragile gel' held indefinite where defined functionally (Halliburton); but 'transparent to infrared rays' was definite where specification showed consistent transmission (Swinehart). Examiners should consider whether the limitation gives clear scope, sets defined boundaries versus stating only a problem/result, and whether one skilled in the art would know what structures/steps are encompassed. During prosecution ambiguity may be resolved by: (1) using a quantitative metric (numeric limitation); (2) showing the specification provides a formula plus examples that meet/do not meet the limitation; (3) showing the specification gives general guidelines and examples sufficient for a skilled artisan; or (4) amending to recite particular structure that accomplishes the function. See 35 U.S.C. 112(b) vs 112(a) distinctions, relevant case law (Ariad, Hyatt, Halliburton, Marosi, Oakley) and MPEP §§2161-2164.08(c).

name: Markush groups / alternative limitations
description: A claim reciting a list of alternatives (a Markush group) is an acceptable claim form and should not automatically be rejected as confusing under 35 U.S.C. 112(b); treatment depends on whether the group is closed or open and whether the metes and bounds are ascertainable.
guidance: Markush grouping = closed list (e.g., 'selected from the group consisting of A, B, and C'). If the group is open-ended (uses 'comprising' or 'consisting essentially of') and is intended to be a selection from a list, it can be indefinite because other alternatives are unclear (In re Kiely). If combinations/mixtures of members are intended, include qualifying language (e.g., 'at least one member', 'or mixtures thereof'). A large number of alternatives does not by itself make a Markush claim indefinite (breadth is not indefiniteness), but if the group is so expansive that a skilled artisan cannot determine the metes and bounds (e.g., massive number of distinct chemical compounds), reject under 35 U.S.C. 112(b). Double inclusion within a Markush group (redundant or overlapping members) is not per se improper — evaluate facts (Eli Lilly v. Teva example). See MPEP §2117, §803.02 and cited cases (Abbott Labs, Gardner).

name: Use of the term 'optionally' in alternatives
description: The use of 'optionally' to indicate an alternative member in a list can be acceptable provided there is no ambiguity as to which alternatives are covered by the claim.
guidance: If 'containing A, B, and optionally C' leaves no ambiguity, it is acceptable (Ex parte Cordova, Ex parte Wu). If the list of alternatives can vary and ambiguity arises about coverage, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) is proper and should explain the confusion.

name: Old combination (do not reject on this ground)
description: A claim should not be rejected on the non-statutory ground of 'old combination'; claims should instead be judged by statutory provisions such as 35 U.S.C. 112(b).
guidance: The historical doctrine (Lincoln Engineering) is no longer a proper basis for rejection following the 1952 Patent Act. A rejection for old combination required a single reference disclosing a combination functioning substantially the same, but current practice is to evaluate claims under the statutory language (pointing out and distinctly claiming). See In re Bernhart, Ex parte Barber, Radio Steel and Mfg. Co., and related cases.

name: Aggregation (do not reject on this ground)
description: Claims should not be rejected on the non-statutory ground of 'aggregation.'
guidance: Aggregation rejections are non-statutory (In re Gustafson, In re Collier). If a claim omits essential matter or fails to interrelate essential elements as defined in the specification, examine under appropriate statutory grounds and MPEP §2172.01.

name: Claims combining product and process (product and process in same claim)
description: A single claim that combines an apparatus/product and method steps (product and process) is indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b).
guidance: Claims that mix statutory classes (e.g., a system claim that includes actions by users) create confusion about when direct infringement occurs and are therefore indefinite (Katz Interactive Call Processing Litigation, IPXL Holdings v. Amazon). Example: a system claim requiring a user action can be unclear whether infringement occurs upon making the system or upon user action. Ex parte Lyell and related decisions address such indefiniteness.

name: Argue Claims Separately
description: The PTAB will not evaluate the patentability of any claims not individually addressed.
guidance: Separately argue as many dependent claims as possible; place such arguments under separate sub-headings for ease of readability; identify which claims rise/fall together; group claims thoughtfully to make it clear which claims are being challenged and why.

name: Address Examiner Errors
description: Dispute factual errors and legal errors made by the examiner.
guidance: Identify and explain errors such as: claim and reference misinterpretations; citations of non-analogous art; improper combinations under §103; failure to provide reasoned rationale (KSR); failure to address all claim limitations. Show why the examiner's findings are incorrect and support with evidence/precedent.

name: Summary of claimed subject matter (Required Section under 37 CFR 41.37)
description: Required Section: Summary of claimed subject matter
guidance: Provide a concise summary of the claimed subject matter so the Board can quickly understand the invention and claim scope, as required by 37 CFR 41.37.

name: Keep arguments concise and focused
description: Keep arguments concise and focused
guidance: Avoid unnecessary verbosity; present focused, tightly reasoned arguments that directly address the rejection and relevant claim limitations.

name: Use claim charts to compare prior art with claim language
description: Use claim charts to compare prior art with claim language
guidance: Employ claim charts to show element-by-element comparisons between prior art references and claim limitations to clarify distinctions or show lack of teaching/ motivation.

name: Permissible grounds for revocation (admissible grounds of opposition)
description: A European patent may only be opposed on the grounds that: (1) the subject-matter of one or more claims is not patentable (in particular not novel or not inventive); (2) the patent does not disclose the invention sufficiently clearly and completely for it to be carried out by a person skilled in the art; (3) the subject-matter of the patent extends beyond the content of the application as filed.
guidance: Other grounds (e.g., lack of clarity of claims or 'theft' of the invention) are not admissible as opposition grounds.

name: Scope of examination limited to opposed subject-matter
description: The Opposition Division is bound to the extent to which the patent has been opposed; it will not examine subject-matter (e.g., independent claims) that have not been attacked.
guidance: Opponents should ensure they attack all claims they want examined; proprietor defenses on unopposed claims may not be examined.

name: Amendments must be occasioned by a ground of opposition and not extend protection
description: Amendments may be chosen from the whole content of the original patent application’s disclosure as long as the scope of protection is not extended beyond the granted patent’s scope; amendments need to be occasioned by a ground of opposition (not mere cosmetic or clarity edits).
guidance: Opposition proceedings must not be used to reformulate claims/descriptions for mere clarity or to adapt to competitors; amended claims must be directly and unambiguously derivable from the original disclosure.

name: Limitations on late/new requests and late submissions at oral proceedings
description: Requests submitted in oral proceedings are, as a rule, not admitted unless readily discussable or reacting to a new objection; primarily only small editorial amendments are permitted during oral proceedings.
guidance: Parties should present prepared claim sets and defenses in earlier rounds; reliance on the oral proceedings to introduce major new claim sets is risky.

name: Eligibility Step 1: The Four Categories of Statutory Subject Matter
description: Determining whether a claim falls within one of the four statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter).

name: Eligibility Step 2A: Whether a Claim is Directed to a Judicial Exception
description: Analysis step to determine if a claim is directed to a judicial exception (e.g., abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon).

name: Examples of Claims That Do Not Recite Abstract Ideas
description: Illustrative examples of claim types that should not be considered abstract ideas for eligibility purposes.

name: The Markedly Different Characteristics Analysis
description: Analysis to determine whether a claim recites markedly different characteristics from a natural product or phenomenon.

name: Evaluating Improvements in the Functioning of a Computer, or an Improvement to Any Other Technology or Technical Field in Step 2A Prong Two
description: Assessment of claimed improvements to computer functionality or other technological fields when evaluating practical application.

name: Eligibility Step 2B: Whether a Claim Amounts to Significantly More
