description: Analysis of whether claim limitations add 'significantly more' beyond a judicial exception (the Alice/Mayo framework's step 2B).

name: Well-Understood, Routine, Conventional Activity
description: Analysis of whether claimed additional elements are merely well-understood, routine, or conventional activity (weighing against eligibility).

name: Other Meaningful Limitations
description: Consideration of other meaningful claim limitations that may support eligibility under step 2B.

name: Eligibility is Self Evident
description: When eligibility is self-evident from the claim language or record, obviating extended analysis.

name: Clear Improvement to a Technology or to Computer Functionality
description: When the claim clearly improves technology or computer functionality, supporting eligibility under streamlined analysis.

name: Claim Interpretation; Broadest Reasonable Interpretation
description: Guidance on claim construction under the broadest reasonable interpretation standard (for examination).

name: Plain Meaning
description: Consideration of a claim term's plain meaning during claim interpretation.

name: Effect of Preamble
description: Guidance on when the preamble of a claim limits or does not limit claim scope.

name: Transitional Phrases
description: Treatment of transitional phrases (e.g., 'comprising', 'consisting of') in claim scope analysis.

name: Functional and Nonfunctional Descriptive Material
description: Guidance distinguishing functional versus nonfunctional descriptive material in claims and specs.

name: Composition, Product, and Apparatus Claims
description: Inherency and other considerations specific to composition/product/apparatus claim types.

name: Process Claims
description: Inherency and other considerations specific to process claim types.

name: Apparatus and Article Claims — Functional Language
description: Treatment of functional language in apparatus and article claims.

name: Material or Article Worked Upon by Apparatus
description: Considerations where claims recite a material or article worked upon by an apparatus.

name: Rejection Over Prior Art’s Broad Disclosure Instead of Preferred Embodiments
description: Guidance on rejecting claims over a reference's broad disclosure rather than only disclosed preferred embodiments.

name: Scope of Reference’s Disclosure Which Can Be Used to Reject Claims When the Reference Is a "Patent" but Not a "Publication"
description: Limits on using the disclosure of a patent (versus a publication) for claim rejections.

name: Admissions as Prior Art
description: When admissions (e.g., in the specification or elsewhere) can be used as prior art against claims.

name: All Claim Limitations Must Be Considered
description: An obviousness analysis must account for all claim limitations, not just a subset.

name: Support for the Claimed Subject Matter in Disclosure
description: Requirements that the specification support the claimed subject matter (adequate written description).

name: Changes to the Scope of Claims
description: How claim amendments affect written description considerations.

name: Test of Enablement
description: Specific tests and factors used to evaluate whether a specification enables the full scope of the claims.

name: How to Make the Claimed Invention
description: Enablement requirement that the specification teach how to make the claimed invention as of the filing date.

name: How to Use the Claimed Invention
description: Enablement requirement that the specification teach how to use the claimed invention.

name: Enablement Commensurate in Scope With the Claims
description: Enablement must be commensurate with the scope of the claims; broader claims require broader enabling disclosure.

name: Single Means Claim
description: Enablement and written description considerations for single means or functional claiming.

name: Inoperative Subject Matter
description: Treatment of claim elements or embodiments that are inoperative and their effect on enablement.

name: Two Separate Requirements for Claims Under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, Second Paragraph
description: Overview of the two distinct requirements under 112(b) (definiteness/particularity).

name: Subject Matter Which the Inventor or a Joint Inventor Regards as The Invention
description: Guidance on identifying what the inventor regards as the invention for claim/scope purposes.

name: Claims Must Particularly Point Out and Distinctly Claim the Invention
description: Definiteness standards and how claims must particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention.

name: Interpreting the Claims
description: Procedures and principles for claim interpretation in the context of definiteness and scope.

name: Determining Whether Claim Language is Definite
description: Standards and tests for assessing claim definiteness under 112(b).

name: Correspondence Between Specification and Claims
description: How correspondence between the spec and claims affects definiteness and claim interpretation.

name: Breadth Is Not Indefiniteness
description: Principle distinguishing permissible breadth of claims from indefiniteness.

name: Specific Topics Related to Issues Under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, Second Paragraph (new terminology, relative terminology, numerical ranges, antecedent basis, functional limitations, alternative limitations, negative limitations, etc.)
description: Detailed subtopics addressing common 112(b) issues (new terminology, relative terms, ranges, lack of antecedent basis, functional claiming, negatives, multiplicity, prolox, double inclusion, product-by-process, use claims, omnibus claims, references to figures/tables, chemical formula, trademarks in claims, mere function of machine, etc.).

name: Identifying and Interpreting a (section truncated in index)
description: Index entry for a section on identifying and interpreting certain claim elements or claim formats (heading truncated in listing).

name: Relationship to the Doctrine of Equivalents
description: Guidance on how claim drafting and interpretation relate to the doctrine of equivalents.

name: Pending (unpublished) applications confidentiality and limited use
description: Pending U.S. applications that have not been published are generally preserved in confidence (37 CFR 1.14(a)) and are not available as references, except as provided by specific regulations.
guidance: Claims in one nonprovisional application may be rejected on claimed subject matter of a copending nonprovisional application of the same inventive entity. AIPA (1999) rules require publication of most applications 18 months after earliest filing date, with enumerated exceptions (no longer pending, secrecy order, provisional application, design patent application, reissue). Applicants may request nonpublication (MPEP § 1122). See MPEP §§ 804, 2127.

name: U.S. patents as prior art (effective date rules)
description: The face patent date (date of patenting) is usually cited, but the filing date is ordinarily the effective date as a reference (35 U.S.C. 102(e)); earlier effective U.S. filing dates (e.g., benefit of provisional or prior U.S. filings) may control.
guidance: Examiners must determine the proper effective date of a U.S. patent (including claims to earlier priority) when using it as prior art. See MPEP §§ 706.02(f)(1), 2127. Examples: reissue patents use effective date of original application; patents issuing from applications claiming a provisional may have 102(e) date as provisional filing date.

name: Corresponding specifications and patent family analysis
description: A family of patents (same invention in multiple countries) may include documents with identical, translated, or varied disclosures; priority claims may affect earliest effective dates.
guidance: Examiners should check corresponding family members for earlier publications/issues and verify whether earlier family members disclose the subject matter needed for a rejection. Use DWPI, INPADOC, Chemical Abstracts, WPI, and STIC for family tracing.

name: Analysis of claims for search planning
description: Search planning requires careful analysis of claims, consideration of variant embodiments within the scope of the claim, equivalents, and analogous arts.
guidance: Search should cover claimed subject matter and disclosed features that might reasonably be expected to be claimed in amendments. Consider variant embodiments and equivalents when selecting search terms and classes.

name: Classified search expectations
description: A proper field of search normally includes the subclass where the claimed subject matter would be classified and all related subclasses, digests, and cross-reference art collections.
guidance: Search from the largest combinations down to elementary parts; prioritize areas likely to contain the best references; consult other examiners or supervisory examiners for unfamiliar subject matter.

name: Conducting a comprehensive search for first action
description: A careful and comprehensive search, commensurate with the limitations appearing in the most detailed claims, should be made when preparing the first action on the merits so that subsequent actions may be final or allowance requires only updates.
guidance: Search should cover claims and disclosed features that might be claimed later; applicants help by filing claims ranging from broad to more detailed. Use best references to forestall future broader claims; consult STIC/ITRP as needed.

name: Alice / two-part eligibility (general)
description: Claims that are merely abstract ideas (e.g., mathematical concepts and certain methods of organizing human activity) are patent-ineligible unless they include 'significantly more.'
guidance: Apply the two-part Alice test: (1) determine whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea (mathematical concept, mental process, or method of organizing human activity); (2) if so, determine whether additional elements transform the claim into a patent-eligible application (i.e., provide an 'inventive concept' or 'significantly more'). The specification should describe how the claimed invention provides an improvement to the technical field to support eligibility (e.g., the Specification describes that using DeepSpeech learning ... achieves higher performance than traditional methods).

name: Claims must recite technical implementation (not just formulas)
description: Mathematical formulas in the specification are not sufficient if the mathematical formulas are 'not recited in the claims.' Claims should be directed to a specific implementation comprising technical elements (e.g., AI and computer speech recognition) rather than abstract formulas.
guidance: If the claims merely recite computations or formulas without tying them to a particular technical implementation, the Examiner/PTAB may find them to be abstract. Draft claims to include technical elements or steps that show how the computation is performed in a concrete system.

name: Avoid language that makes claims 'methods of organizing human activity'
description: Terminology such as 'contract document' or other labels tied to legal/administrative interactions can make claims vulnerable to subject-matter-ineligibility as 'methods of organizing human activity.'
guidance: Be cautious when claiming operations framed as legal or business interactions; consider recasting claims to emphasize technical mechanisms or improvements rather than the human/social/legal activity itself (Ex parte Coquard).

name: Improvements in computing must be to the computers/technology, not just to tasks
description: Arguments that a claim 'improves computing' are unpersuasive if the specification describes only using generic computing devices to perform the task; the claim must represent an improvement in the computers themselves or computer functionality.
guidance: Show that claimed features change how the computer operates (unconventional architecture, specialized hardware, concrete routines) rather than merely using a generic computer as a tool to perform a mental or organizational task (PTAB reasoning in Coquard and related cases).

name: Mental processes judicial exception (claims performable by human mind)
description: Claim steps that can be performed in the human mind are a judicial exception (mental processes) and can render claims ineligible.
guidance: If claim elements can be performed mentally (even if also recited as performed electronically), the claim may be directed to a mental process. Showing a concrete computer-rooted implementation and explaining why performance cannot practically be done in the mind helps. Merely reciting storage or a processor is insufficient to overcome this if other claim elements can be done mentally (Ex parte Vasey, Kerr).

name: Broad claim scope that covers mental performance remains ineligible unless impractical to perform mentally
description: If, under its broadest reasonable interpretation, a claim covers performance in the mind except for generic computer recitations, it remains in the mental processes category unless the claim cannot practically be performed in the mind.
guidance: Avoid claim language that, when broadly read, permits purely mental performance; instead, narrow or add concrete, computer-specific limitations showing practical impossibility of mental performance (Ex parte Kerr).

name: Provide detailed implementation of computer/ML elements (enablement and eligibility support)
description: A patent specification should provide sufficient detail of how computer/ML elements are implemented (hardware, functional requirements, flowcharts, unconventional routines) to avoid being characterized as 'well-understood, routine, and conventional.'
guidance: Include detailed disclosures (e.g., flow charts, specific hardware or software architecture, concrete routines) that explain how each claimed element operates; lack of such detail supports a finding that additional elements are conventional and do not supply 'significantly more.'

name: Avoid reciting mere calculations without describing supporting circuitry
description: Claims that 'merely recite performing certain calculations without detailing any particular hardware circuitry' can be viewed as mathematical steps performable with pen and paper and therefore as abstract ideas or mental processes.
guidance: Tie computational steps to specific hardware or constrained computing contexts that transform the mathematical operation into a practical application (Ex parte Rupp).

name: Generic 'device' recitations without detail are conventional
description: If the specification illustrates a device only as a generic box and does not describe details, a claimed device (e.g., 'chromatography analysis device') may be considered well-understood, routine, or conventional.
guidance: Describe the device components, their interconnection, and how they operate in detail to show the device is not merely a generic conventional element (Ex parte Harada).

name: Enablement: specification must enable the full scope claimed (Amgen principle)
description: If a patent claims an entire class of processes, machines, or structures, the specification must enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the entire class; 'the more one claims, the more one must enable.'
guidance: Provide disclosure sufficient to avoid undue experimentation across the full scope of the claims. Broad 'genus' claims require commensurately broad enabling disclosure; conclusory assertions of enablement are insufficient (In re Starrett, Amgen citation).

name: Describe 'how' claimed functional results are achieved (claims must identify how)
description: Claims cannot simply state a functional result; they should identify 'how' the functional result is achieved by limiting claim scope to concrete structures or concrete actions.
guidance: Limit claims to particular techniques, rules, structures, or concrete actions and include supporting description in the specification explaining the mechanisms by which the results are obtained (Realtime Data v. Array Networks; Am. Axle & Mfg. citation).

name: Avoid result-oriented claim drafting lacking inner functionality
description: Result-oriented claims that could be performed with pen and paper and fail to recite inner functionality are likely directed to abstract ideas and vulnerable under Section 101.
guidance: Draft claims that recite internal steps, data structures, or mechanisms rather than high-level results; include specificity in claim and specification about how mapping/annotation/ordering functions are implemented (IBM v. Zillow).

name: Detectability as a value/claim-drafting consideration
description: A patent is more valuable if infringement is easily detectable. Detectable features are observable from the use, appearance, or construction of a product or process embodying an AI invention.
guidance: Identify and claim features observable at inference (during operation), publicly disclosed materials (papers, specs, advertising), or aspects amenable to reverse-engineering. Consider claiming inputs/outputs, prompting behavior, or observable interactions that reveal the presence of the claimed AI feature.

name: Use of public disclosures and reverse-engineering for detectability
description: AI features may be detectable via public documents (academic publications, user guides, advertising) or reverse-engineering; SaaS products complicate reverse-engineering but publicly available data or structures may expose inputs/outputs.
guidance: Draft specification/claims to tie inventive aspects to publicly observable behaviors or published details where possible, and consider strategies to preserve evidence of use for enforcement.

name: Avoid definitive safety/effectiveness claims in patent applications
description: Do not make definitive statements that the underlying invention 'is safe', 'error free', or similarly absolute claims, as these can create product liability exposure or public scrutiny.
guidance: Use cautious factual language about datasets, testing, and performance. Use terms like 'inhibits safety issues' or 'enhances the likelihood of an accurate prediction' and avoid categorical guarantees (Practice Tip under Safe and Effective).

name: Algorithmic discrimination protections and disclosure
description: Systems should be designed to include 'proactive equity assessments' and 'use of representative data' to protect against bias; patent practitioners should counsel inventors on measures to avoid discriminatory algorithms and disclose such measures.
guidance: Ask inventors whether the system assesses people and how it addresses bias; disclose proactive measures and datasets used to train models in the specification to both reduce third-party discrimination claims and provide potential claimable elements (Practice Tip under Algorithmic Discrimination Protections).

name: Data privacy cautiousness in drafting
description: Ensure data collection conforms to reasonable expectations; avoid broadening claims to encompass sensitive personal data and be cautious when describing types of data used in AI applications (HIPAA and other restrictions may apply).
guidance: Limit and define data-related claim language for sensitive domains, describe consent/usage boundaries where relevant, and avoid wording that implies abusive data practices. Consider legal/regulatory constraints and the Blueprint's guidance when drafting.

name: Four-step approach to computer program 'as such' exclusion
description: One approach consists in applying the following four steps: (1) Properly construe the claim; (2) Identify the actual contribution made by the invention; (3) Determine whether the actual contribution falls solely within the excluded subject matter or not 'as such'; (4) Determine whether the actual or alleged contribution is actually technical in nature ('Technical contribution').
guidance: Examiners must construe the invention from the claims and specification, objectively assess the contribution (not be bound by applicant's statement), and only proceed to other substantive aspects (novelty, inventive step) if the invention passes the technical character test.

name: Definition of 'computer-implemented invention'
description: 'Computer-implemented invention' is a term intended to cover claims involving computers, computer networks or other programmable apparatus wherein at least one feature is implemented by means of a computer program.
guidance: Distinguish between a computer program (sequence of executable instructions) and a computer-implemented method (method performed on a computer).

name: Unity of invention requirement (definition)
description: A patent application can claim only one invention or a group of closely related inventions. Unity of invention requires that the claims relate to a single invention, or at most a group of inventions linked by a single general inventive concept; inventions share a 'single general inventive concept' if the claims as interpreted in light of the description/drawings have the same or corresponding special technical features that achieve the same technical effect or solve the same technical problem over the prior art.
guidance: Unity is relevant in pre-grant proceedings only; lack of unity is not a ground for revocation after grant. A finding of lack of clarity is not by itself sufficient to find lack of unity. Divisional applications are generally allowed irrespective of unity objections (except Thailand).

name: Evaluation of unity of invention / determining 'special technical features'
description: The examiner assesses unity by determining whether two or more inventions detailed in the claims have the same or corresponding special technical features. An examiner determines 'special technical features' from the claims in light of the description, drawings and common general knowledge as of the filing date. 'Same' and 'corresponding' means the features achieve the same technical effect or solve the same technical problem (e.g., alternative solutions or interrelated features).
guidance: Examples: a metal spring and a block of rubber may correspond because both achieve resilience. If special technical feature of one invention is the same as or corresponds to that of another, unity is fulfilled. If not, only the inventions belonging to the unified group are designated for examination.

name: Minimum reasoning methodology for lack of unity findings
description: To assess non-unitary subject-matter, the patent office may apply 'minimum reasoning' methodology: identify common or corresponding subject-matter, explain why this subject-matter cannot provide a single general inventive concept due to lack of same/corresponding special technical features, and explain why there is no technical relationship among the groups of inventions if not apparent.
guidance: The analysis may include identification of non-common technical features and why claims may be grouped together, statement of why these features/demonstrated technical properties are different, and explanation of why their technical properties are different. Provide sufficient (minimum) reasoning rather than narrow literal approaches. Examples and PCT paragraphs cited for illustration.

name: Assessment of unity with regard to prior art
description: An examiner determines 'special technical features' based on claims, description and common general knowledge. Lack of unity may become apparent after a document found in search shows that a linking feature lacks novelty or is obvious, so claims joined thereby no longer share a common inventive concept. If groups of inventions have the same corresponding special technical feature, unity is present.
guidance: Example provided: Claim 1 polymeric compound A and Claim 2 packaging composed of A both share polymeric compound A as special technical feature that contributes over prior art — unity present. If an independent claim does not avoid prior art, carefully consider whether dependent claims still have inventive link.

name: Clarity requirement for the invention (claims, description, abstract, drawings)
description: All AMS require the abstract, claims, description, and drawings, if any, to be clear and concise. If the description, claims or drawings are so unclear that no meaningful opinion can be formed on novelty, inventive step or industrial applicability, examination may be restricted to claims or parts that are sufficiently clear.
guidance: Issues of clarity should be raised separately from novelty/inventive step. If examiner cannot establish an opinion on a claim, they may object for lack of clarity. Clarity of claims is vital to assessing novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability.

name: PCT claim requirements: define protection, be clear/concise, supported by description
description: The PCT Guidelines require that claims must (i) define the matter for which protection is sought; (ii) be clear and concise; and (iii) be fully supported by the description. Claims must be drafted in terms of the 'technical features of the invention'. The two-part form should be used 'whenever appropriate'.
guidance: Apply these requirements to individual claims and claims as a whole. Use two-part form where helpful; ensure support in description for claimed features.

name: Claims should not rely on references to description/drawings except when absolutely necessary
description: The claims must not, in respect of the technical features of the invention, rely on references to the description or drawings 'except where absolutely necessary.'
guidance: Avoid cross-references from claims to descriptive portions or figures; if unavoidable, justify necessity. Reliance on references can be grounds for clarity objections.

name: Kinds of claims and product vs activity distinction
description: Two basic kinds of claim: claims to a physical entity (product, apparatus) and claims to an activity (process, use). Product-by-process, means-plus-function, and product/apparatus limitations in process claims are recognised and subject to specific PCT guidance.
guidance: Choose appropriate claim category; be mindful of special rules (e.g., product-by-process treatment, means-plus-function interpretation). See PCT ISPE GL cross-references for details.

name: Independent and dependent claims requirements
description: All applications will contain one or more independent main claims directed to the essential features of the invention. Dependent claims concerning specific forms must include all the features of at least one independent claim.
guidance: Ensure dependent claims fall within scope of an independent claim and include the essential features of the invention. Dependent claims cannot omit essential features required to define the invention.

name: Interpretation of claims by a Person Skilled in the Art (PSIA)
description: Claims should be interpreted the same way for search and examination. Each claim should be read giving the words the ordinary meaning/scope that would be attributed by a PSIA at the relevant time, unless the description gives words a special meaning by explicit definition.
guidance: Draft claims with PSIA ordinary meaning in mind; where special definitions are needed, define terms clearly in the description.

name: Open and closed claims / transition phrases affect search and scope
description: In evaluating novelty or inventive step, the examiner should consider the transition phrase used (e.g., 'consisting of', 'comprising', 'characterized by', 'consisting essentially of'), as the subject matter to be searched depends on the transition phrase.
guidance: Select transition phrases deliberately to achieve intended claim scope. Understand how search/examination will treat 'open' vs 'closed' language.

name: Conditions for clarity of claim language (PSIA boundary certainty)
description: The meaning of the terms of a claim must be clear for a Person Skilled in the Art from the wording of the claim alone. If a PSIA can determine the boundaries of the claimed invention with a reasonable degree of certainty, the claim complies with clarity. Breadth is not necessarily lack of clarity. An independent claim should clearly specify all essential features needed to define the invention (except those implied by generic terms).
guidance: Assess clarity in light of application disclosure, prior art, and PSIA interpretation at time of invention. For process claims, ensure process as claimed necessarily results in the claimed product when carried out reasonably; otherwise internal inconsistency leads to lack of clarity.

name: List of terms and expressions that may cause lack of clarity
description: In the AMS, the following terms when used in claims and descriptions may be regarded as ambiguous, inadequate, unclear or too broad and thus lead to lack of clarity: indefinite/relative words (e.g., 'thin', 'wide', 'strong'); terms of approximation (e.g., 'about', 'approximately', 'somewhat'); ambiguous adverbs (e.g., 'preferably', 'more preferably', 'in particular', 'substantially', 'mostly', 'similarly', 'for example', 'such as'); references (e.g., 'as described in part...', 'as illustrated in figure...'); trademarks/trade names/proper names; and multiple outcomes e.g., 'and/or'.
guidance: Avoid or carefully justify use of such terms. Where approximate terms are necessary, provide measurable ranges or definitions in the description. Avoid vague references and ensure terms are defined or used where their meaning is clear to PSIA.

name: Presence of multiple subcombination claims as evidence
description: Where claims to two or more subcombinations are presented along with a claim to a combination that includes the particulars of at least two subcombinations, the presence of a claim to the second subcombination is evidence that the details of the first subcombination are not required for patentability (and vice versa).
guidance: Use concrete claim-set examples (e.g., ABC/B/C) to show that particulars of a subcombination are not required for patentability of the combination. This supports restricting subcombinations from each other and from the combination.

name: Reconsideration and rejoinder when elected claims become allowable
description: Upon determining that all claims directed to an elected combination invention are allowable, the examiner must reconsider the propriety of the restriction requirement; if the combination is allowable in view of patentability of at least one subcombination, the restriction between the elected combination and patentable subcombination(s) will be withdrawn and allowable subcombinations that were searched must be rejoined. If a subcombination is elected and determined allowable, nonelected claims requiring all the limitations of the allowable claim will be rejoined (see MPEP § 821.04).
guidance: When allowable linking/ elected claims appear, withdraw restriction and rejoin dependent/non-elected claims that require all limitations. Follow rejoinder practice in MPEP § 821.04 and use the appropriate form paragraphs (e.g., 8.21.xx).

name: Generic claims and species interplay in restriction
description: Where subcombinations (or species) are species under a claimed genus and related, restriction must be determined by both election-of-species practice and related-inventions practice; if restriction is improper under either practice, it should not be required (MPEP § 806.04(b)).
guidance: Carefully assess generic claims: restriction generally cannot be required when only generic claims are presented unless the generic claim encompasses so many species that an unduly extensive search would be necessary. If species claims and generic claims co-exist, election of species may be required prior to search on merits in some situations.

name: Notice of potential rejoinder in Ochiai/Brouwer situations
description: When restriction is required between product and process claims, if applicant elects product claims and product claims are later found allowable, withdrawn process claims that depend from or otherwise require all the limitations of the allowable product claim will be considered for rejoinder; rejoined process claims must meet all requirements of 35 U.S.C. 101, 102, 103 and 112 (MPEP § 821.04(b)).
guidance: Examiner must include form paragraph 8.21.04 in such restriction requirements. Applicant is advised to amend process claims during prosecution to require the limitations of the product claims to retain the right to rejoinder; failure may result in loss of rejoinder. Note: the prohibition against double patenting rejections under 35 U.S.C. 121 does not apply where restriction is withdrawn by examiner before patent issues.

name: Product vs process of using distinctness
description: A product and a process of using the product are distinct if (A) the process of using as claimed can be practiced with another materially different product; or (B) the product as claimed can be used in a materially different process (MPEP § 806.05(h)).
guidance: Examiner must provide an example (not necessarily documented); if applicant shows the suggested alternative use cannot be accomplished, examiner must support another viable alternative or withdraw requirement. Use form paragraphs 8.20 and 8.21.04 where appropriate.

name: Related products/processes distinctness (three-part test)
description: For related product inventions or related process inventions, inventions are distinct if (A) the inventions as claimed do not overlap in scope (mutually exclusive); (B) the inventions are not obvious variants; and (C) the inventions are either not capable of use together or can have a materially different design, mode of operation, function, or effect (MPEP § 806.05(j)). Two-way distinctness and reasons for insisting on restriction are necessary.
guidance: Burden on examiner to provide an example; if applicant shows examiner's example not workable examiner must suggest another or withdraw restriction. Use form paragraphs 8.14.01 and 8.16 depending on relationship. See MPEP § 802.01 for relatedness guidance.

name: Intermediate-final product distinctness
description: An intermediate product and a final product are distinct inventions if the intermediate and final products are mutually exclusive (not overlapping in scope), are not obvious variants, and the intermediate product as claimed is useful to make other than the final product (MPEP § 806.05(j)).
guidance: Use form paragraph 8.14 for intermediate-final product restriction requirements; conclude restriction basis with one of form paragraphs 8.21.01–8.21.03.

name: Examination reasons required for insisting on restriction
description: Every requirement to restrict must include: (A) the reasons (not mere conclusion) why each invention as claimed is independent or distinct from the other(s); and (B) the reasons why there would be a serious burden on the examiner if restriction is not required (MPEP § 808).
guidance: Reasons must be concise and specific. For combination/subcombination relationships point out why subcombination has separate utility and why combination does not require particulars. Where a disclosed relationship between species exists, discuss it and explain why it does not prevent restriction. Mere conclusory statements are inadequate. Use appropriate form paragraphs (8.01, 8.02, 8.14–8.20.02).

name: Election of species — when required and how handled
description: When restriction between species is appropriate, the examiner should send a restriction requirement or place a telephone requirement to restrict. Identify generic claims or indicate none are present (MPEP § 809.02(a)). Election of species may be required prior to a search in applications with multiple species and no generic claims or with species plus generic claims.
guidance: Election of species should not be required between species clearly unpatentable over each other; group together species considered clearly unpatentable over each other. If only generic claims are presented, restriction cannot be required unless the generic recites/encompasses a multiplicity of species making search unduly extensive. If applicant later presents species claims after an office action on generic claims, the Office may require election.

name: Linking claims and their effect on restriction/rejoinder
description: Linking claims (e.g., genus claims linking species or subcombination claims linking combinations) may prevent restriction if allowable; linking claims and the inventions they link are examined with the elected invention. When all claims directed to the elected invention are allowable, if any linking claim is allowable the restriction must be withdrawn and non-elected claims depending from or requiring all limitations of the linking claim must be rejoined and examined (MPEP § 809).
guidance: If restriction was predicated on nonallowability of linking claims, applicant may retain non-elected claims in the application. If canceled nonelected claims exist, upon allowance of linking claims the examiner must notify applicant that canceled claims depending on the allowable linking claim may be reinstated and will be examined. See MPEP § 821.04 for rejoinder practice.

name: Evidence considered for mistakes in description/claims/drawings
description: For mistakes in the description, claims or drawings (or corrections/amendments thereof), the competent authority shall, for the purposes of the obviousness test, only take into account the contents of the description, claims and drawings and, where applicable, the correction or amendment concerned.
guidance: External documents or file contents beyond the description/claims/drawings and the specific correction/amendment are excluded when assessing whether the rectification is obvious.

name: Non-rectifiable mistakes (general exclusions)
description: A mistake shall not be rectifiable under Rule 91.1 if: (i) the mistake lies in omission of one or more entire elements of the international application (Article 3(2)) or entire sheets; (ii) the mistake is in the abstract; (iii) the mistake is in an amendment under Article 19, unless IPEA is competent; or (iv) the mistake is in a priority claim or notice correcting/adding a priority claim under Rule 26 bis.1(a) where rectification would change the priority date.
guidance: Paragraph notes that this does not affect operation of other specific Rules (20.4, 20.5, 26 bis and 38.3). These are hard exclusions where rectification is not available.

name: Identification of a judicial exception triggers further analysis
description: Identification of a judicial exception in a claim merely indicates further analysis for eligibility should be conducted.
guidance: If a claim recites a concept that falls within a judicial exception, examiners must perform the eligibility analysis (e.g., the Alice/Mayo two-step). Identifying an exception is not itself a final determination of ineligibility; it signals the need for additional inquiry into whether the claim as a whole is directed to, or amounts to, practical application or significantly more.

name: Examples of laws of nature and natural phenomena
description: Examples of laws of nature and natural phenomena: An isolated DNA; A correlation that is the consequence of how a certain compound is metabolized by the body; Electromagnetism to transmit signals; The chemical principle underlying the union between fatty elements and water; The Arrhenius equation for calculating the cure time of rubber; (and similar natural laws/phenomena).
guidance: These concrete examples (drawn from court decisions) illustrate the types of concepts courts have treated as laws of nature or natural phenomena. Use them to inform, but not constrain, claim analysis. Where claims recite such concepts, determine whether the claim integrates the concept into a practical application or is merely directed to the concept itself.

name: Examples of abstract ideas
description: Examples of abstract ideas: Mitigating settlement risk; Hedging; Creating a contractual relationship; Using advertising as an exchange or currency; Processing information through a clearinghouse; Generating insurance-policy-related tasks based on rules to be completed upon the occurrence of an event; Managing a stable-value protected life insurance policy; Comparing new and stored information and using rules to identify options; Comparing a patient’s gene with the wild-type gene, and identifying any differences that arise; Collecting data, recognizing certain data within the collected data set, and storing that recognized data in a memory; Using categories to organize, store, and transmit information; Organizing information through mathematical correlations; Managing a game of Bingo; A formula for updating alarm limits; A mathematical formula relating to standing wave phenomena; A mathematical procedure for converting one form of numerical representation to another.
guidance: These are illustrative abstract-idea concepts identified in case law. When claims involve processes such as mental steps, fundamental economic practices, certain methods of organizing human activity, or mathematical relationships, examiners should evaluate whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea and, if so, whether additional claim elements transform it into a patent-eligible application (i.e., provide 'significantly more').

name: Case chart content and structure
description: For each case (arranged in chronological order), the chart provides: (1) a link to the entire court opinion, (2) the patent number(s) or application number(s) at issue, (3) the subject matter of the patent/application, (4) whether the claims were eligible or ineligible, and (5) the USPC/CPC classification.
guidance: The chart is a factual reference tool for examiners. Each entry gives the citation and factual context needed to compare a pending application to precedent. The chart will be updated with future decisions; use the links to read full opinions for detailed reasoning rather than relying solely on the chart summary.

name: Use the case chart to identify applications needing detailed eligibility analysis
description: Examiners may find this information useful in identifying those applications that may require a detailed eligibility analysis during examination.
guidance: Use similarities in subject matter, claim scope, and classification as prompts to examine eligibility more carefully, but do not treat chart similarity as dispositive. Follow the prescribed eligibility analysis and consult the cited opinions for reasoning and context.

name: Each case turns on its own facts — similarity is not determinative
description: It is important to remember that each case turns on its own facts. Therefore, the mere fact that a pending application may be similarly classified to a patent or an application in this chart, or have similar subject matter, does not necessarily indicate an eligibility issue.
guidance: When comparing a pending application to cases in the chart, focus on the actual claim language, asserted inventive concept, and factual detail in the court's analysis. Do not infer eligibility outcomes solely from classification or high-level topic similarity; perform the full legal and factual analysis.

name: Fields retained for pretraining
description: Retain abstracts, the first independent claim, and DWPI (where available) from patent records as the primary fields for pretraining.
guidance: Non-essential text (figure references, non-English characters) should be removed. Only the first independent claim per patent was retained to control input scope.

name: Experimental repetition and seeds
description: Run experiments multiple times with different random seeds and average results to quantify variance.
guidance: This work ran four seeds per (dataset, model) and reported mean ± std; use multiple seeds to support statistical claims and compute confidence intervals.

name: Independent Claim Length (Word Count)
description: The number of words in the first independent claim. Shorter claims are systematically broader; longer claims are narrower.
guidance: Compute using claim-parsing (e.g., USPTO's Python parser against the Patent Claims Research Dataset). Use the first independent claim as the canonical measure of claim breadth; interpret shorter word counts as broader scope (fewer limiting elements).

name: Independent Claim Count
description: The number of independent claims in the patent. Higher counts often signal a scope-laddering strategy (multiple breadth tiers asserted in parallel).
guidance: Count independent claims to detect strategic layering of breadth. Extremely high independent-claim counts (e.g., 20+) can signal fee-bypass or other non-quality-driven strategies; typical ranges vary by technology (see industry calibration).

name: Allowance Probability (validation outcome)
description: Whether broader (shorter) claims are more likely to be rejected and narrower claims more likely allowed without amendment.
guidance: Use allowance probability as a downstream validation check: unexpectedly high allowance probability for very short claims may indicate examiner permissiveness or other anomalies.

name: Forward Citations (validation outcome)
description: Broader-scope patents (shorter independent claims) tend to receive more forward citations.
guidance: Forward-citation counts can be used to corroborate that measured breadth captures pioneering or blocking value; treat as supportive evidence rather than sole proof of quality.

name: Litigation Incidence (validation outcome)
description: Patents with broader independent claims are more likely to be litigated.
guidance: Higher litigation incidence for broad claims supports the measure's relevance to economic stakes; use litigation frequency to contextualize risk associated with breadth.

name: Claim Amendment Patterns (validation/outcome indicator)
description: Word-count typically grows during prosecution as examiners force narrowing amendments; patterns of amendment are informative about examination engagement.
guidance: Track change in claim length from as-filed to as-issued; substantive lengthening during prosecution is a positive signal of examination and applicant concession.

name: Anomalously Short Claims at Issuance (quality red flag)
description: An independent claim that issued without lengthening through prosecution—and is significantly shorter than peers in the same art unit—is a quality red flag.
guidance: Possible explanations: genuinely groundbreaking claim (rare) or inadequate examination (common). Flag such patents for deeper substantive review rather than accepting breadth at face value.

name: Claim-Lengthening as a Quality Signal
description: A patent whose independent claim grew substantially during prosecution shows examiner engagement and applicant concession; the final claim is more likely to survive validity challenge than the as-filed version.
guidance: Interpret growth in independent-claim word count during prosecution as evidence that the claim was meaningfully narrowed to meet examination objections; combine with other markers for quality assessment.

name: Claim-Count Strategy / Claim Ladder
description: Use of multiple independent claims at varying lengths (a 'claim ladder') provides litigation flexibility: broad independent claim, mid-tier independent claims, and narrow independent claims.
guidance: Quality-conscious drafting often includes one broad claim (litigation reach), mid-tier fallbacks (validity fallback), and narrow claims targeted to commercial products. Evaluate whether independent claims form a coherent ladder rather than trivial or duplicative variants.

name: Final Independent Claim Length at or Above Art-Unit Median (at-issuance marker)
description: A final independent claim whose length is at or above the art-unit median suggests substantive narrowing during prosecution and is a positive scope-quality marker.
guidance: Always compare to the appropriate art-unit baseline rather than raw counts. Being at/above the median suggests the claim is not unusually broad for that examiner/technology.

name: Number of Independent Claims Appropriate to the Technology (at-issuance marker)
description: The count of independent claims should be appropriate to the technology (e.g., typically 1–3 for chemistry, 1–5 for software).
guidance: Assess whether independent-claim count falls within industry norms for the art unit; deviations may be strategic or indicative of abnormal drafting/examination practices.

name: Claim Word Count Grew Between Filing and Issuance (at-issuance marker)
description: An increase in independent-claim word count from filing to issuance is an indicator of examiner engagement and claim narrowing.
guidance: Treat growth as a positive quality signal — the final issued claim is more likely to withstand validity challenges than the original broad filing.

name: Final Claim Length Significantly Below Art-Unit Median (red flag)
description: A final independent claim that is much shorter than the art-unit median at issuance is a red flag for poor examination or an unusually broad grant.
guidance: Investigate whether the shortness was justified by disclosure or novelty; absent strong justification, consider the patent suspect for overbroad scope.

name: Single Short Independent Claim with Minimal Amendment History (red flag)
description: A patent with only one short independent claim and little-to-no amendment during prosecution is suspicious.
guidance: Such patents may reflect inadequate examination or an unusually successful attempt to claim broad subject matter; require deeper substantive evaluation.

name: All Independent Claims Clustered at Extreme Breadth without Intermediate Fallback (red flag)
description: If all independent claims are similarly extremely broad with no mid-tier or narrow fallbacks, the claim set lacks robustness.
guidance: A healthy claim set should include intermediate fallbacks to preserve enforceable scope; absence suggests tactical or drafting deficiencies.

name: Industry/Art-Unit Calibration Requirement
description: Quality assessment must account for systematic differences in claim length across art units (e.g., pharmaceuticals short, software longer, mechanical medium).
guidance: Do not rely on raw word counts. Always calibrate measures against art-unit baselines and known disciplinary drafting conventions; consider structural support requirements (e.g., biotech) when interpreting length.

name: Operative Test Step 1: First Independent Claim Word Count
description: Measure the first independent claim word count for the patent under review.
guidance: This is the primary numeric input to the scope assessment; compute consistently (tokenization method should match validation dataset if comparing to benchmarks).

name: Operative Test Step 2: Compare to Art-Unit Median
description: Compare the first independent claim word count to the median for the relevant art unit.
guidance: Use the art-unit median to determine whether a claim is unusually short or long for that technology/examiner context; this comparison is central to flagging anomalies.

name: Operative Test Step 4: Independent-Claim Count and Breadth Distribution
description: Count independent claims and assess their breadth distribution across tiers (broad, mid-tier, narrow).
guidance: Determine whether the claim set forms a coherent ladder with meaningful intermediate fallbacks rather than trivial dependents or duplicated breadth.

name: Operative Test Step 5: Dependent Claims Narrowness (real scope ladder vs. trivial dependents)
description: Assess whether dependent claims are meaningfully narrower and provide real fallbacks rather than trivial, cosmetic additions.
guidance: Evaluate dependent claims for substantive narrowing; trivial dependents do not constitute a useful scope ladder and weaken the patent's resilience.

name: Estoppel (estoppel in pais and related doctrines)
description: Estoppel as a defence alleges that plaintiff's conduct (acts, omissions, or relations) has reasonably misled the defendant so that plaintiff should be barred from pursuing the remedy. Both equitable and legal forms are recognized, with equitable estoppel sometimes broader.
guidance: Core principles: estoppel arises when plaintiff intentionally or negligently misleads defendant, or when plaintiff omitted duties whose performance would have prevented defendant's actions. Equity focuses on effect of conduct, not motive; courts of law have increasingly adopted wider equitable views. Specific applications and limits: (1) Silence works as estoppel only where there was a duty to speak. (2) Failure to mark patented articles ('patented' stamping) estops patentee from claiming substantial damages for infringements occurring before the defendant received notice. (3) Delay in suing may create estoppel in equity (laches) but is less certain at law unless it evidences abandonment. (4) A suit against one infringer gives notice to others; subsequent delay cannot create estoppel as to them. (5) Actions creating an implied license (e.g., extensive tolerated use) may be treated as estoppel. (6) Relations such as transferor/transferee or prior ownership can create estoppel — e.g., a former owner in a suit by his assignee cannot deny validity. (7) Limitations: mere fact defendant was misled is not always sufficient; the conduct must be such that plaintiff should reasonably have expected the defendant to be influenced. Examples and authorities are given (Pickard v. Sears; Bassett v. Bradley; Greenwood v. Bracher; Gear v. Grosvenor; others). Also noted: estoppel may bar recovery of damages but may not always bar injunctive relief depending on circumstances.

name: Defendant may plead any defence unless estopped (limitations on availability of defences)
description: Defendant is entitled to set up any of the recognized defences in an infringement suit unless he is estopped from doing so by his own prior conduct or agreements; prior conduct binds defendants as it does plaintiffs.
guidance: General rule: all defenses enumerated may be pleaded unless defendant's prior acts, admissions, licenses, or transactions estop him. Illustrative constraints: (1) A licensee cannot attack the validity of the patent while the license is in force (except to show the license was exceeded); to challenge validity the licensee must repudiate the license. (2) A former owner or assignor through whom plaintiff's title derives generally cannot deny validity. (3) A defendant who has used and advertised an invention may be estopped from claiming it lacks utility. (4) Fraudulent patentees who knowingly procured invalid patents may be estopped from asserting certain defences; conversely bona fide patentees defeated in interference may sometimes later challenge patentability. (5) Prior positions (e.g., letting another take out a patent, accepting license fees, etc.) can preclude inconsistent defenses. Parties must examine whether prior litigation positions, transfers, covenants (e.g., covenants not to contest validity), or conduct create estoppel before pleading certain defences. (Authorities and many case examples cited throughout.)

name: Prioritized Examination — General (37 CFR 1.102(e))
description: A request for prioritized examination must comply with 37 CFR 1.102(e) and be accompanied by the prioritized examination fee (37 CFR 1.17(c)), the processing fee (1.17(i)), and, if not already paid, the publication fee (1.18(d)). An application for which prioritized examination is requested may not contain or be amended to contain more than four independent claims, more than thirty total claims, or any multiple dependent claim.
guidance: Prioritized examination will not be accorded to international applications not in the national stage under 35 U.S.C. 371, design applications, reissue applications, provisional applications, or reexamination proceedings. No more than 15,000 requests will be accepted per fiscal year. A request must also meet specific requirements for either newly filed applications (Track One) or RCEs (PE-RCE).

name: Prioritized Examination — Claims Limitations
description: The application must contain, or be amended to contain, no more than four independent claims and no more than thirty total claims, and must not contain any multiple dependent claims.
guidance: After prioritized examination is granted, an amendment resulting in more than four independent claims, more than thirty total claims, or a multiple dependent claim will terminate prioritized examination. If the application does not meet the claim limit when the request is considered, the decision will provide one month to amend claims consistent with the requirements; that one-month period is not extendable.

name: Track One (New Application) — Additional Filing Requirements
description: To obtain Track One prioritized examination for a newly filed 35 U.S.C. 111(a) application, the application must include a specification as prescribed by 35 U.S.C. 112 with at least one claim, a drawing when necessary, and an inventor's oath or declaration or an application data sheet meeting 1.53(f)(3)(i). Utility applications must be filed via the USPTO patent electronic filing system; plant applications must be filed in paper.
guidance: Applications must be filed on or after Sep 26, 2011 to be eligible as Track One. Filing must include required filing/search/examination fees; any excess claims/size fees due must be paid before Track One status is granted. A nonpublication request may be submitted but the publication fee still must be paid when requesting prioritized examination (refund may be requested later if not published). Color drawings permitted but petition required for entry of color. If required items omitted, follow-on submissions are allowed only if submitted the same day as filing of the application and prioritized request; only registered Patent Center users can submit such follow-on documents electronically on the same day.

name: Maximizing Benefit of Prioritized Examination (Applicant Recommendations)
description: To maximize the benefit of prioritized examination, applicants should: (A) acquire a good knowledge of the state of the prior art to file a clear specification with a complete schedule of claims from broadest to narrowest; (B) submit an application in condition for examination; (C) file replies that are completely responsive to Office actions and within the shortened statutory period; and (D) be prepared to conduct interviews with the examiner.
guidance: The phrase 'in condition for examination' is the same as used for accelerated examination (see MPEP §708.02(a) subsection VIII.C). These practices help the Office meet its goal of final disposition within 12 months on average.

name: Prosecution Under Prioritized Examination — Time Periods and Termination
description: Time periods set for reply in Office actions for prioritized applications are the same as set forth in MPEP §710.02(b). Filing a petition for an extension of time or a request for suspension of action will terminate prioritized examination. An amendment resulting in >4 independent claims, >30 total claims, or a multiple dependent claim will terminate prioritized examination.
guidance: Upon termination, the application is removed from the examiner's special docket and placed on the examiner's regular docket. The Office's goal is final disposition within twelve months, on average, of the date prioritized status was granted; 'final disposition' means mailing of notice of allowance, mailing of a final Office action, filing of a notice of appeal, completion of examination per 37 CFR 41.102, filing of an RCE, or abandonment.

name: Refund of Fees for Prioritized Examination Requests
description: If a request for prioritized examination is dismissed, the prioritized examination fee (37 CFR 1.17(c)) will be refunded automatically (if paid). The processing fee (1.17(i)) will be retained to cover processing costs. Application fees (basic filing, search, examination, and any required application size or excess claim fees) cannot be refunded under 37 CFR 1.26.
guidance: Applicant may request a refund of the search fee and any excess claims fees by filing a petition for express abandonment under 37 CFR 1.138(d). Applicant may request refund of the publication fee per MPEP §1126 if the application is not published under 35 U.S.C. 122(b). Termination of prioritized examination does not entitle applicant to a refund of the prioritized examination fee on the grounds that prioritized examination was terminated.

name: Availability of copies of the priority document (Rule 17.2)
description: If the applicant complies with Rule 17.1, the International Bureau shall, at the specific request of a designated Office, promptly but not prior to international publication furnish a copy of the priority document to that Office; no such Office shall ask the applicant to furnish it; translations are not required before the expiration of the applicable time limit under Article 22.
guidance: The IB shall not make copies public prior to international publication. After publication, IB shall furnish a copy to any person upon request and subject to reimbursement of cost unless the international application was withdrawn or the priority claim was withdrawn.

name: Determination of compliance with Article 11(1) and international filing date (Rule 20.1–20.2)
description: Promptly after receipt, the receiving Office shall determine whether the papers fulfill Article 11(1). If positive, the receiving Office shall accord the international filing date as the date of receipt, stamp the request as prescribed, make that copy the record copy, notify the applicant of the international application number and filing date, and send a copy of the notification to the IB.
guidance: For Article 11(1)(iii)(c) it is sufficient to indicate the applicant's name in a way that allows identity to be established even if misspelled or abbreviated. For Article 11(1)(ii) it is sufficient that the parts appearing to be description and claims be in a language accepted by the receiving Office under Rule 12.1(a).

name: Missing parts — completion, incorporation by reference, and filing date effects (Rule 20.5)
description: If a part of the description, claims or drawings is missing (but not an entire element of Article 11(1)(iii)(d) or (e)), the receiving Office shall invite the applicant to either furnish the missing part or confirm incorporation by reference, and to make observations within the time limit. If the missing part is furnished on or before the date on which all Article 11(1) requirements are fulfilled and within the applicable time limit, it shall be included and the receiving Office shall accord as international filing date the date on which all requirements are fulfilled.
guidance: If furnished after the date on which the requirements were fulfilled but within the time limit, the receiving Office shall include the part and correct the international filing date to the date it received that part and notify the applicant. The applicant may, within one month of notification of correction, request that the missing part be disregarded (i.e., treated as not furnished) and the correction not made.

name: Erroneously filed elements and parts — correction and filing date effects (Rule 20.5 bis)
description: If an entire element of Article 11(1)(iii)(d) or (e) or a part of description/claims/drawings is or appears to be erroneously filed (including all drawings erroneously filed), the receiving Office shall invite the applicant to either furnish the correct element/part or confirm incorporation by reference, and to make observations within the time limit. If the correct element/part is furnished before all Article 11(1) requirements are fulfilled but within the time limit, the correct element/part is included, the erroneously filed element/part removed, and the receiving Office shall accord as the international filing date the date on which all requirements are fulfilled.
guidance: If the correct element/part is furnished after the date on which requirements were fulfilled but within the time limit, the receiving Office shall include the correct element/part, remove the erroneously filed one, correct the international filing date to the date on which it received the correct element/part and notify the applicant. If a correct element/part is considered to have been contained in the application on the earlier date under Rule 20.6(b), the erroneously filed element/part remains and the filing date is the date on which Article 11(1) requirements were fulfilled.

name: Burden of proof — preponderance of the evidence
description: To prevail in this inter partes review of the challenged claims, Petitioner must prove unpatentability by a preponderance of the evidence. 35 U.S.C. § 316(e); 37 C.F.R. § 42.1(d).
guidance: All factual findings and ultimate conclusions as to unpatentability are measured against the preponderance standard; cite supporting declarations/exhibits accordingly.

name: Obviousness standard under 35 U.S.C. § 103 and KSR
description: A patent claim is unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. § 103(a) if the differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art are such that the subject matter, as a whole, would have been obvious at the time of the invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art. KSR Int’l Co. v. Teleflex Inc., 550 U.S. 398 (2007).
guidance: Apply KSR principles (need for a reason to combine elements, not simply showing elements existed separately) and consider the whole-claim context.

name: Graham factors for obviousness
description: The question of obviousness is resolved on the basis of underlying factual determinations, including: (1) the scope and content of the prior art; (2) any differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art; (3) the level of skill in the art; and (4) objective evidence of nonobviousness. Graham v. John Deere Co., 383 U.S. 1 (1966).
guidance: Weigh the strength of each Graham factor in every case; secondary considerations (objective indicia) must be considered and weighed (Stratoflex).

name: Motivation to combine and reasonable expectation of success
description: It is important to identify a reason that would have prompted a person of ordinary skill in the relevant field to combine elements in the way the claimed invention does. A person of ordinary skill must have had a reasonable expectation of success. (KSR; PAR Pharm., Inc. v. TWi Pharms., Inc., 773 F.3d 1186 (Fed. Cir. 2014)).
guidance: Show documentary/technical reasons in the prior art or POSA knowledge that would motivate combining references and make success reasonably expected, not merely possible after-the-fact.

name: Claim construction standard in IPR — broadest reasonable construction
description: In an inter partes review, the Board interprets a claim term in an unexpired patent according to its broadest reasonable construction in light of the specification of the patent in which it appears. 37 C.F.R. § 42.100(b); Cuozzo Speed Techs., LLC v. Lee, 136 S. Ct. 2131 (2016).
guidance: Assign claim terms their ordinary and customary meaning to one of ordinary skill in the art in context of the entire patent disclosure; special definitions must be clear, deliberate, and precise (Paulsen).

name: Use of prosecution history in claim construction
description: An invention is construed with reference to the prosecution history to exclude interpretations disclaimed during prosecution; statements during prosecution can be relevant to reinforce the meaning of claim language. (Graham; Chimie v. PPG; D’Agostino; Microsoft).
guidance: If applicant expressly defined a term during prosecution (e.g., specified a comparator), the Board will give effect to that choice; prosecution statements can bind claim scope or at least reinforce interpretation.

name: Claim terms need only be construed as necessary
description: Claim terms need only be construed to the extent necessary to resolve the controversy. Wellman, Inc. v. Eastman Chem. Co., 642 F.3d 1355 (Fed. Cir. 2011).
guidance: Don't over-interpret terms; construe only those needed to decide patentability issues before the Board.

name: Indefiniteness and applicant as lexicographer (35 U.S.C. § 112 issues)
description: An examiner may reject claims as indefinite under 35 U.S.C. § 112; an applicant may overcome such a rejection by providing a specific definition for a claim term in prosecution (applicant may be his own lexicographer). Paulsen, 30 F.3d 1475.
guidance: Prosecution admissions and responses can define claim scope for later IPR construction; the Board will respect such special definitions even if they lead to odd results.

name: Prohibition on new matter in motions to amend
description: A motion to amend is subject to the statutory and regulatory prohibition on introducing new matter: 35 U.S.C. § 316(d)(3) and 37 C.F.R. § 42.121(a)(2)(ii) (no new matter).
guidance: Proposed substitute claims must have adequate written-description support in the original disclosure (specification/provisional); if substitute claim introduces new matter, motion to amend must be denied.

name: Adverse judgment by party (requesting judgment against itself)
description: A party may request judgment against itself at any time during a proceeding. 37 C.F.R. § 42.73(b). Section 42.73(a) requires that a 'judgment' disposes of all issues that were, or reasonably could have been raised or decided.
guidance: A petitioner can request partial adverse judgment (e.g., withdraw a ground) and SAS/Office guidance confirms a petitioner can request adverse judgment on claims/grounds; Board will consider scope implications and final decision must dispose of issues as required by rule.

name: Effect of SAS/Institution scope on final decision
description: The petitioner's contentions define the scope of the litigation from institution through conclusion; after SAS Inst., Inc. v. Iancu, only claims still challenged by the petitioner at the end must be addressed in the Board’s final written decision.
guidance: Petitioners can limit scope post-institution by withdrawing grounds or requesting adverse judgment; Board follows USPTO SAS Q&As in applying procedures.

name: Standard for sealing materials in IPRs — good cause and confidential information
description: There is a strong public policy for making IPR materials public (35 U.S.C. § 316(a)(1); 37 C.F.R. § 42.14). A party may move to seal certain information, but only 'confidential information' (trade secret or other confidential research, development, or commercial information) is protected. 37 C.F.R. § 42.2. The standard for granting a motion to seal is 'for good cause.' 37 C.F.R. § 42.54(a). The movant bears the burden to explain why the information is confidential. 37 C.F.R. § 42.20(c).
guidance: Provide specific, narrowly tailored justification showing material constitutes confidential business information and why public disclosure would harm competitive interests; generic claims are insufficient.

name: Reissue — prohibition on new matter
description: Reissue cannot add new matter; new claims must be based on the same disclosure as the original patent (no new matter allowed).
guidance: Reissue cannot be used to introduce subject matter not originally disclosed (so no CIP-type additions). Conforming drawings to the specification is allowed; adding entirely new drawings is not.

name: Reissue — broadening claims (time limit and conditions)
description: Broadening reissue (new claims broader than original) may be filed but only within two years of the original patent issue date; new claims must be based on the same disclosure (no new matter).
guidance: All inventors and relevant parties must agree; cannot broaden to reclaim subject matter given up during original prosecution (recapture doctrine). If any aspect of a claim is broadened, the claim is considered broadened. Oath by inventors required if broadening.

name: Reissue — narrowing and same-scope reissue types
description: Narrowing reissue is used to overcome newly-discovered prior art and has no time limit; same-scope reissue adds claims of the same scope (often to avoid indefiniteness errors).
guidance: Narrowing reissue functions similarly to a statutory disclaimer with no two-year limit. Same-scope claims are often used to fix claim clarity issues.

name: Reissue — things reissue can correct (inventorship, priority, disclosure flaws)
description: Reissue can correct: errors curable by amendment during prosecution or by filing a continuation; errors not correctible through CoC or Disclaimer; inaccurate disclosure (can conform drawings/specification but not add new drawings); inventorship errors when consent is lacking; priority errors not curable by CoC (e.g., failure to perfect priority).
guidance: Some priority failures (e.g., failing to claim 119(e) provisional or missing a divisional deadline) may not be curable by reissue—check specific exceptions.

name: Reissue — things reissue cannot do (recapture, terminal disclaimer, best mode)
description: Cannot add new matter; cannot recapture subject matter intentionally given up during original prosecution (recapture doctrine); cannot undo a terminal disclaimer; cannot fix best mode errors.
guidance: If a reissue introduces claims the examiner deems to claim a distinct invention, a restriction requirement may be imposed on those new claims.

name: Reissue — required application contents, format, and amendments rules
description: Reissue filing must include a copy of the specification, claims, and drawings (new copies of all drawings required), double-column format on single-sided sheets, copies of any disclaimers/CoC/reexamination certificates if available, and disclosure of related proceedings; amendments in reissue must be non-cumulative and show all changes from the original every time.
guidance: Do not use strikethrough or double square brackets to show deletions; explain new claims; show status of all claims (pending/cancelled); amended/new drawings must be on a separate sheet in red ink labeled 'amended', 'new', or 'cancelled'; new claims receive next available claim numbers and old numbers must not be reassigned.

name: Reissue vs Reexamination — key distinctions
description: Reissue: only patent owner may file; any prior art may be cited; reissue can broaden within 2 years; reissue requires a mistake to initiate; no automatic extensions. Reexamination: anyone can file; limited to patents and printed publications as prior art; cannot broaden claims; no mistake required; automatic extensions may apply.
guidance: Select reissue if fixing owner-identified substantive errors or inventorship/priority problems; use reexamination for art-based challenges to patentability where broadening is not sought.

name: Amendments and claim numbering in reissue
description: Amendments in reissue are non-cumulative and must show all changes from the original each time; when adding new claims, assign the next claim number available — do not reassign original claim numbers.
guidance: Follow reissue-formatting rules for clarity and examiner processing; preserve an audit trail of all changes.

name: Disclaimer — nature, who may disclaim, and formalities
description: A disclaimer is a way for the patent owner to give back to the public a portion of the patent's protection by disclaiming one or more claims (statutory disclaimer) or giving up patent term (terminal disclaimer). Only the owner (or part-owner) may disclaim; it must be in writing, recorded at the PTO, and a fee must be paid; must be done without deceptive intent.
guidance: Use statutory disclaimers when a claim is invalid or defective; use terminal disclaimers to overcome certain rejections (but they give up term). Terminal disclaimers in applications are revocable before patent issue (or before reexamination certificate issues), but disclaimers are otherwise irrevocable and binding on successors-in-interest.

name: Required contents of an ARIPO patent application
description: An ARIPO patent application consists of: a completed ARIPO Form 3 (Request Form); a description of the invention; one or more claims; one or more drawings (if any); an abstract; prescribed application fees or a written undertaking to lodge the fees; and designation of at least one state.
guidance: All listed elements must be present for a correctly constituted application; missing elements can prevent according a filing date or lead to formality rejections.

name: Formality examination scope
description: Formality examination covers certain formal aspects of the application.
guidance: Specifically checked items include the form and content of the application for registration, drawings and abstract, designation of the inventor, power of attorney, necessary translations, fees due, and technical and physical requirements of the description and claims. Noncompliance may lead to refusal but the applicant is afforded an opportunity to rectify deficiencies within prescribed time limits.

name: Safekeeping property — separation and record preservation
description: A practitioner shall hold property of clients or third persons that is in the practitioner's possession in connection with a representation separate from the practitioner's own property. Funds shall be kept in a separate account maintained in the state where the practitioner’s office is situated (or elsewhere with client consent). Other property shall be identified and appropriately safeguarded. Complete records of such account funds and other property shall be kept and preserved for a period of five years after termination of the representation.
guidance: On receiving funds/property in which a client/third person has an interest, the practitioner shall promptly notify that person, promptly deliver any funds/property they are entitled to receive, and, upon request, render a full accounting. When property is claimed by two or more persons, keep property separate until dispute resolved and promptly distribute undisputed portions.

name: Functional claiming definition
description: “A claim term is functional when it recites a feature ‘by what it does rather than by what it is’ (e.g., as evidenced by its specific structure or specific ingredients). …There is nothing inherently wrong with defining some part of an invention in functional terms. Functional language does not, in and of itself, render a claim improper.”
guidance: Functional language is permitted, but whether it invokes 35 U.S.C. §112(f) or renders a claim indefinite depends on context, the specification disclosure, and the knowledge of a person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA).

name: Statutory standard — 35 U.S.C. §112(f) (means-plus-function)
description: An element in a claim for a combination may be expressed as a means or step for performing a specified function without the recital of structure, material, or acts in support thereof, and such claim shall be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.
guidance: When §112(f) applies, claim scope is limited to the corresponding structure/material/acts disclosed in the specification and their equivalents. The slide deck also emphasizes the practical effect that §112(f) interpretation often narrows claim scope and ties claim coverage to spec disclosure.

name: USPTO 3-prong test for invoking §112(f)
