description: Per MPEP 2181(I), interpret a limitation under §112(f) if: (1) the claim limitation uses the phrase “means” or a substitute generic placeholder; (2) that phrase is modified by functional language (typically linked by “for”); and (3) the phrase is not modified by sufficient structure or material for performing the claimed function.
guidance: Apply all three prongs—generic placeholder, functional modification, and lack of sufficient structure—to determine whether §112(f) should apply. The USPTO uses this test in examination and documents examples of non-means claims that should be interpreted as invoking §112(f).

name: Presumption from use of “means for” and how to overcome it
description: If a claim uses the literal “means for” plus functional language there is a presumption that §112(f) is invoked.
guidance: The presumption can be overcome if the claim term (or surrounding claim language/specification) recites sufficient structure to perform the claimed function. Examining record should document how the presumption was overcome and identify the corresponding structure in the specification.

name: Invocation of §112(f) where “means” is not used (nonce/generic placeholders)
description: A claim that does not explicitly recite “means for” may still be interpreted under §112(f) when it (1) uses a generic placeholder for structure, (2) includes functional language, and (3) lacks sufficient structure to perform the claimed function.
guidance: Williamson v. Citrix weakened the strong presumption that a claim without “means” does not invoke §112(f), so courts and examiners will analyze nonce terms (e.g., “module,” “component,” “unit”) under the 3-prong test to decide. Document the analysis on the record during prosecution.

name: Sufficient structure requirement for software/computer-implemented MPF claims
description: For software-related means-plus-function elements, the corresponding structure required in the specification often must include the algorithm(s) that transform a general-purpose computer into a special-purpose machine (see Aristocrat; Alappat). Conversely, basic functions that any general-purpose computer can perform without special programming may not require a disclosed algorithm (see Katz).
guidance: If the claimed function is specialized (requires special programming), include step‑by‑step description of the algorithm, flowcharts, or textual/pseudo-code tying the structure to the function. Cases: Aristocrat (algorithm required), EON (indefiniteness for lack of algorithm), Katz (standard microprocessor may suffice for non-specialized operations).

name: Risks and benefits of a §112(f) interpretation
description: Invoking §112(f) may lead to a narrower claim interpretation limited to structures disclosed in the specification and equivalents, but it can also make invalidity attacks easier if the specification lacks corresponding structure.
guidance: Benefits: prior art must disclose corresponding structure/equivalents and §112(f) can help with §101 arguments in some contexts. Risks: exposure to §112(a) enablement/written-description and §112(b) indefiniteness rejections/invalidity; narrower scope can enable design-arounds and non-infringement defenses.

name: Determining indefiniteness under §112(b) when §112(f) is implicated
description: Two central inquiries: (1) Does the specification disclose adequate structure for performing the claimed function (e.g., algorithm for software)? (2) Is the disclosed structure linked to the claimed function, or is it mere generic hardware/black box?
guidance: If structure is missing (Aristocrat/Aristocrat-related, EON) or not linked to the function (B. Braun Medical), the limitation may be indefinite. See MPEP 2173.02 for examiner guidance. Flowcharts or algorithmic descriptions can be sufficient if they concretely tie structure to function.

name: USPTO guidance on specialized vs non-specialized computer-implemented functions
description: Specialized computer functions require “special programming” for a general-purpose computer; non-specialized functions are commonly performed by general-purpose computers by a POSITA (e.g., receiving, sending, storing data).
guidance: For non-specialized functions, claim formats such as “processor configured to [function]” may avoid §112(f) (see Katz). For specialized functions, the specification should disclose algorithms and structural details. USPTO training materials and examples discuss when non-means claim language should nonetheless be treated as invoking §112(f).

name: Claim drafting practices to avoid unintended invocation of §112(f)
description: No bright-line language guarantees avoiding §112(f); still, practical practices include: avoid explicit use of “means” or “step” for plus a function; avoid coined/nonce terms that do not connote structure; in some cases include explicit MPF claims elsewhere in the application/continuation to vary scope.
guidance: Consider varying claim scope across independent/dependent claims and across continuations. Where the functional element is at the point of novelty, recite sub-steps or known operations to show sufficient structure and reduce §112(f) risk. There is no foolproof template—context matters.

name: Specification drafting practices to support functional claims
description: Draft the specification to include technical descriptions, algorithms (when not off-the-shelf), flow diagrams, and explanations linking disclosed structure to claimed functions; describe how functional components interact and list alternative algorithms and examples.
guidance: Provide enough detail to support §112(a)/(b) if §112(f) is applied: specific algorithms, flowcharts, pseudo-code, interaction descriptions, and examples of alternatives/equivalents. Also consider including explicit means/step-for claims in the original filing or continuations to preserve options.

name: Invention disclosure meeting checklist for functional elements
description: For each function/component, verify whether it is off-the-shelf (OTS) or requires custom/special programming; for OTS components, obtain specific examples; for custom components, obtain algorithmic details and alternatives (flow diagrams, pseudo-code) and how components interact.
guidance: Drill down with inventors to capture sufficient structural detail for the specification. Collect examples of OTS implementations and document alternatives/equivalents to support later §112(f) analyses and possible MPF claim drafting.

name: USPTO Clarity of the Record expectations regarding §112(f)
description: When §112(f) issues are at play, examiners should document all §112(f) presumptions, explain how presumptions were overcome (if they were), identify on the record the structure in the specification that performs the function, and address specific claim limitations when relying on prior art.
guidance: Prosecutors should expect clearer Office Actions and should likewise record arguments and identify corresponding structure during interviews and amendments. The PTO’s pilot aimed to improve clarity around §112(f) analyses and reasons for allowance/rejection.

name: Litigation and IPR strategies concerning §112(f)
description: As petitioner: argue claim indefiniteness for lack of disclosed structure and/or pursue prior-art invalidity; if a panel finds insufficient structure they may not institute on the MPF claim but state lack of corresponding structure in decision. As patent owner: argue that the broadest reasonable interpretation of an MPF claim is the disclosed structures and equivalents.
guidance: Combine §112(f) arguments with §101 or §112(a)/(b) strategies as appropriate. For non-infringement, exploit narrower §112(f) constructions to design around. In IPRs, prepare to argue both indefiniteness and prior-art anticipation/obviousness depending on the panel’s findings.

name: Impact of Williamson v. Citrix on §112(f) presumption and claim interpretation
description: Williamson (Fed. Cir. en banc 2015) eliminated the strong presumption that §112(f) is not invoked if a claim does not explicitly recite “means for” or “step for,” making it easier to find §112(f) invoked by nonce terms.
guidance: Although the presumption remains that claims not reciting means/step-for do not invoke §112(f), Williamson requires a more searching inquiry into whether a term is a generic placeholder lacking structural meaning to a POSITA. Practitioners should anticipate more frequent §112(f) analyses for non-means language.

name: Examiner focus on software-related functional limitations
description: USPTO examination guidance emphasizes evaluating §112(f) limitations particularly in software/computer claims to provide a clear prosecution record and ensure functional claim boundaries are explained and justified.
guidance: Examiners will apply training materials and examples to identify limitations that invoke §112(f) and will seek to document corresponding structures, especially for specialized computer functions requiring disclosed algorithms. Applicants should be prepared to cite spec paragraphs/figures and explain structure-function links.

name: Combination patent identity and infringement test
description: A patented combination's identity depends on the presence in the combination of each of the claimed elements (or their equivalents) and upon their co-operation in the specific manner to produce the ultimate result; infringement requires making, using, or selling a combination in which precisely the same elements or their equivalents are united under the same co-operative law.
guidance: Omission of an element, a different number/character/mode of cooperation, or a differently combined set of elements generally creates a different invention and is not infringement unless equivalents supply omitted features (see §922 and authorities).

name: Equivalents in combination patents may produce infringement
description: A combination is infringed if equivalents of claimed elements are used in the same plan of cooperation; courts ask whether an omitted part is supplied by an equivalent.
guidance: When an omitted element is replaced by an equivalent performing substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve the same result, infringement may be found (see Water Meter Co. v. Desper; Dederick v. Whitman Agricultural Co.).

name: Using less than all elements of a combination usually not infringement
description: The use of less than all the elements of a patented combination does not infringe the combination patent alone, unless the omitted element is supplied by an equivalent or some other legal theory applies.
guidance: Courts examine whether the defendant's device supplies the function of the omitted element by an equivalent; merely performing the same overall result by a different combination typically falls outside the combination claim (cases: Byerly v. Cleveland Linseed Oil Works; Newark Mach. Co. decisions).

name: Directed to — two-prong inquiry (Step 2A)
description: "Directed to" in Step 2A is a two-prong inquiry: Prong One — evaluate whether the claim recites a judicial exception; Prong Two — evaluate whether the claim recites additional elements that integrate the exception into a practical application of the exception.
guidance: Prong One asks whether the claim recites an abstract idea, law of nature/natural principle, or natural phenomenon/product of nature. Prong Two asks whether additional elements integrate that exception into a practical application, using considerations from case law (e.g., insignificant extra-solution activity, particular treatment or prophylaxis).

name: Step 2A Prong One — Judicial exceptions (identification)
description: Determine whether the claim recites a judicial exception: abstract ideas; laws of nature/natural principles; or natural phenomena/products of nature (MPEP 2106.04).
guidance: Examiners determine if claim limitations fall into one or more of these exception categories (see separate guidance for each grouping). Examples in the MPEP illustrate claims that do and do not recite these exceptions.

name: Abstract ideas — three groupings
description: Abstract ideas are evaluated by whether claim limitations fall within at least one of three groupings: mathematical concepts; mental processes; and certain methods of organizing human activity (MPEP 2106.04(a)).
guidance: Examples identify claims that do not recite abstract ideas; examiners should map claim limitations to these groupings (e.g., arithmetic operations as 'mathematical concepts'; steps performable in the human mind as 'mental processes').

name: Products of nature — Markedly Different Characteristics (MDC) analysis
description: For nature-based products, use the Markedly Different Characteristics (MDC) analysis to determine whether a claim limitation is a 'product of nature' exception (MPEP 2106.04(c)).
guidance: MDC can be shown by structural changes (Examples 16, 28, 30) or changes in function resulting from combinations (Examples 17, 28, 30, 44) — e.g., changes in rate of cell growth, immunogenic effect, taste, glycemic control. If the claimed product is not markedly different from the natural product, it is a product-of-nature exception.

name: Step 2A Prong Two — Integration into a practical application
description: Evaluate whether the additional elements in the claim integrate the judicial exception into a practical application (MPEP 2106.04(d)).
guidance: Integration requires the additional element(s) to apply, rely on, or use the judicial exception in a manner that imposes a meaningful limit on the exception so that the claim is more than a drafting effort designed to monopolize the exception. Prong Two uses court considerations such as 'insignificant extra-solution activity' and 'particular treatment or prophylaxis' to evaluate integration.

name: Insignificant extra-solution activity and mere instructions to apply the exception
description: Claim limitations that are mere data-gathering steps, insignificant extra-solution activity, or high-level instructions to apply the exception do not integrate the exception into a practical application.
guidance: Examples: 'obtaining' or 'detecting' steps that are routine data-gathering; administering a treatment recited at high generality (mere instruction). Such additional elements are treated as insignificant or as mere instructions and do not confer eligibility under Step 2A Prong Two or Step 2B.

name: Step 2B: Significantly more / Inventive concept
description: Examine whether the additional elements in the claim amount to 'significantly more' — i.e., whether they provide an inventive concept beyond the judicial exception (MPEP 2106.05).
guidance: Step 2B uses considerations from case law including 'improvements to the functioning of a computer/other technology' and whether elements are 'well-understood, routine, conventional activity' (further explained in MPEP 2106.05(a)-(h)). Eligibility requires that additional elements amount to an inventive concept, individually or in combination.

name: Well‑understood, routine, conventional activity (negative indicator)
description: If additional elements are well-understood, routine, or conventional activities, they do not supply the inventive concept needed to make the claim eligible under Step 2B.
guidance: Examples: use of conventional immunoassays, conventional autoradiography, or routine reagent use — when the claimed additional steps are routine in the field, they are treated as not providing 'significantly more.'

name: Improvements to technology or functioning (positive indicator)
description: Claim elements that improve the functioning of a computer or other technology can indicate 'significantly more' and support eligibility under Step 2B.
guidance: Courts and the MPEP recognize technological improvements as a basis for finding an inventive concept; examiners should evaluate whether additional elements improve how a technology operates or solve a technological problem.

name: Unconventional or non-routine steps/reagents/techniques can add an inventive concept
description: Use of unconventional reagents, non-routine techniques, or steps not shown to be routine in the art can be treated as more than mere instructions and can provide an inventive concept (examples: porcine antibodies; scanning near-field optical microscopy (SNOM)).
guidance: If there is no evidence that a reagent or technique was routinely or conventionally used for the claimed purpose, that element may be an unconventional step that is more than mere instructions to apply the exception and can render the claim eligible (as shown in Example 29 claim 3 and Example 31 claim 70).

name: Compact prosecution – initial comprehensive review
description: Under the principles of compact prosecution, each claim should be reviewed for compliance with every statutory requirement for patentability in the initial review of the application, even if one or more claims are found to be deficient with respect to some statutory requirement.
guidance: Deficiencies should be explained clearly, particularly when they serve as a basis for a rejection. Whenever practicable, USPTO personnel should indicate how rejections may be overcome and how problems may be resolved.

name: Repeat and clearly state all grounds in a final rejection
description: In making such final rejection, the examiner shall repeat or state all grounds of rejection then considered applicable to the claims in the application, clearly stating the reasons in support thereof.
guidance: Before final rejection a clear issue should be developed between the examiner and applicant. All outstanding grounds of rejection of record should be carefully reviewed and reiterated in the final rejection.

name: Do not make final when prior art is not of record for amended claims
description: A second or subsequent action should not be made final if it includes a rejection on prior art not of record of any claim amended to include limitations which should reasonably have been expected to be claimed.
guidance: An examiner cannot be expected to foresee every applicant amendment, but should avoid finalizing when prior art not previously of record is applied to claims that could reasonably have been expected as filed. See MPEP § 904 et seq.

name: Do not allow claims amended without showing patentable novelty
description: If an applicant amends the claims without attempting to show patentable novelty, the examiner should not allow the claims.
guidance: Claims may be finally rejected if, in the opinion of the examiner, they are clearly open to rejection on grounds of record. See MPEP § 714.04.

name: Requirements for Section 2(f) acquired distinctiveness claims/declarations
description: To amend an application under Section 2(f) and claim acquired distinctiveness, the evidence/declaration must support that the mark has 'become distinctive' through substantially exclusive and continuous use and, where required, specifically attest that distinctiveness existed prior to the date of the declaration.
guidance: The Examining Attorney deemed an earlier declaration insufficient because it did not specifically attest that the mark had acquired distinctiveness prior to the date of the declaration. Practitioners must ensure the declaration meets the Office's evidentiary and attestation requirements.

name: Prohibition on procuring registration by fraud / material misrepresentation with intent to deceive
description: A trademark registration procured by a false and material misrepresentation made with intent to deceive the USPTO may be cancelled and gives rise to potential discipline; the factfinder may require proof by clear and convincing evidence.
guidance: Example: jury found by clear and convincing evidence that the registration was obtained by fraud based on a false claim of acquired distinctiveness. Practitioners must avoid knowingly or recklessly making material misrepresentations to the Office.

name: Indefiniteness — intrinsic evidence must provide guidelines/examples
description: Because the intrinsic evidence provides a general guideline and examples sufficient to enable a person of ordinary skill in the art to determine the scope of the claims, the claims are not indefinite even though the construction defines the term without reference to a precise numerical measurement. (Enzo Biochem, Inc. v. Applera Corp., 599 F.3d 1325, 1335 (Fed. Cir. 2010)).
guidance: Evaluate whether the specification and figures supply enough conceptual guidance (examples, functions, or context) so a POSITA can ascertain claim bounds. Anti-pattern: relying only on extrinsic evidence or numerical thresholds when the intrinsic record lacks any guideline.

name: Indefiniteness — proper focus of the test
description: The test for indefiniteness does not depend on a potential infringer's ability to ascertain the nature of its own accused product to determine infringement, but instead on whether the claim delineates to a skilled artisan the bounds of the invention. (SmithKline Beecham Corp. v. Apotex Corp., 403 F.3d 1331, 1340–41 (Fed. Cir. 2005)).
guidance: Assess claim clarity from the viewpoint of a POSITA at the time of invention using intrinsic evidence (and permissible extrinsic evidence), not from the accused infringer's perspective. Anti-pattern: measuring definiteness by whether an accused product can be easily tested against the claim.

name: Graham factual inquiries for obviousness
description: The four Graham factual inquiries: (1) determining the scope and content of the prior art; (2) ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue; (3) resolving the level of ordinary skill in the art; and (4) considering objective evidence indicating obviousness or non-obviousness. (Graham v. John Deere, cited; summarized in KSR).
guidance: Structure obviousness analysis around these four factors. Collect and analyze prior-art disclosures, map claim limitations to references, articulate POSITA qualifications, and assemble/assess secondary considerations (objective indicia) if present. Scoring note: omission of any Graham factor undermines a complete legal analysis.

name: KSR principle — predictable combination is likely obvious
description: "The combination of familiar elements according to known methods is likely to be obvious when it does no more than yield predictable results." (KSR Int’l Co. v. Teleflex Inc., 550 U.S. 398 (2007)).
guidance: If a claimed combination merely uses prior-art elements in their established functions to achieve predictable results, that combination tends toward obviousness. Emphasize whether the claimed improvement is more than the predictable use of prior-art elements. Anti-pattern: treating mere novelty of combination as sufficient without showing non‑predictability or synergistic effect.

name: Motivation-to-combine — flexible, context-dependent analysis
description: The motivation-to-combine analysis is a flexible one: '[a]ny need or problem known in the field of endeavor at the time of invention and addressed by the patent can provide a reason for combining the elements in the manner claimed,' and the analysis 'need not seek out precise teachings directed to the specific subject matter of the challenged claim, for a court can take account of the inferences and creative steps that a person of ordinary skill in the art would employ.' (quoting KSR; Intel Corp. v. PACT XXP Schweiz AG, 61 F.4th 1373, 1379–80 (Fed. Cir. 2023)).
guidance: Look for general field problems, known techniques, or commonly-used design choices that would lead a POSITA to combine references. Evidence of generalizability, analogies, or common design tradeoffs supports motivation. Anti-pattern: treating 'motivation' as requiring an explicit sentence in a reference saying "combine this with that."

name: Use of prosecution history and figures as intrinsic interpretive evidence
description: Intrinsic evidence such as patent figures and prosecution statements can exemplify and clarify claim scope (e.g., figures exemplifying cylindrical pockets; prosecution arguments distinguishing references).
guidance: Consider drawings, specification passages, and arguments made during prosecution to construe claim terms and to understand what a POSITA would have understood. Use prosecution history to interpret why applicants distinguished prior art, but treat attorney statements in prosecution cautiously if unsworn. Anti-pattern: ignoring intrinsic evidence in favor of post hoc interpretations.

name: Functional sufficiency for claim limitations (example: 'substantially cylindrical')
description: A functional/operational test can define a 'degree' term: e.g., the pocket 'needs to be sufficiently cylindrical to enable the massaging head to be attached while the massage device’s piston is reciprocating. If the massaging head can be attached while the massage device’s piston is reciprocating, the pocket is substantially cylindrical.' (Patent Owner's asserted functional standard).
guidance: Functional tests tied to the invention's operation can supply sufficient guidance to a POSITA to make a degree term definite. Evaluate whether the functionality described in the specification or prior art provides an operative standard. Anti-pattern: defining degree terms in purely subjective or aspirational language with no operational anchor.

name: Functional configuration sufficiency for claim elements (example: 'quick release connector configured to secure while reciprocating')
description: Prior-art language such as 'changing of the patter assembly ... can be easily accomplished ... automatically disconnected merely by turning each other' can be reasonably understood to satisfy a claim recitation of a 'quick release connector' that secures a massaging head while the piston reciprocates.
guidance: When evaluating whether a prior-art disclosure meets a functional claim limitation, consider whether the prior art's description and figures show that the structure is configured to perform the claimed function (e.g., secure during reciprocation and permit quick removal). Anti-pattern: requiring an explicit label 'quick release' in the reference when the functional behavior is disclosed.

name: Common priority date and support by priority document
description: The Israeli application and the corresponding patent must share a common priority date.
guidance: The common priority may come from the Israeli application, the corresponding patent, or a third application that both claim. In cases of multiple priority claims, Modified Examination is possible only if the claim set is supported by the common priority document.

name: Claims dependency preservation when reducing claim count
description: Modified Examination may be requested with a reduced number of claims, but claim dependency relationships must remain unchanged.
guidance: Applicants can streamline the claim set for Modified Examination, provided that dependencies among retained claims are preserved; avoid altering dependency structure in ways that would change claim scope relationships.

name: Presumption of meeting patentability provisions
description: A patent granted via Modified Examination is presumed to meet various patentability provisions.
guidance: The memorandum lists presumptions including novelty, inventive step, unity of the invention, sufficiency of disclosure, and support of the claims by the description. Applicants should be aware this is a presumption tied to the corresponding patent and may have strategic implications.

name: Strategic downside: alignment with corresponding patent limitations
description: Using Modified Examination may cause the Israeli patent to align with restrictions or limitations found in the corresponding patent, potentially narrowing scope.
guidance: Applicants should consider whether acceptance of corresponding-patent claim scope is appropriate, especially if broader claim scope in Israel is desired. Modified Examination expedites prosecution but can limit claim breadth.

name: § 112(b) indefiniteness success rates
description: Indefiniteness arguments under § 112(b) show strong technology differences—never successful in mechanical or biotech in this sample, succeeded nearly one-quarter of the time in software patent cases and about one-third in electronics.
guidance: Report success rates by technology. Discuss doctrinal reasons (e.g., lack of standard language in software claims, means-plus-function issues) and cite relevant Federal Circuit cases (Aristocrat line).

name: § 112 enablement/written description (inadequate disclosure) success rates
description: Arguments based on enablement and written description (whether claim scope is supported by disclosure) show very different patterns: one-third of mechanical patent decisions and three-quarters of biotechnology patent decisions on these grounds resulted in invalidity, far more than in software and electronics.
guidance: Report frequency and percentage by technology. Note small sample caveats for technologies like biotechnology and potential loss of significance when adding full controls.

name: Record reviews of documents cited in PTAB trials
description: A review of documents cited in a related trial before the Patent Trial and Appeal Board should be recorded (whether the claims have similar scope or not).
guidance: Record the trial number, document reviewed, U.S. Patent on trial and date reviewed; examples include IPR, PGR, CBM entries.

name: Interference search when application in condition for allowance
description: When an application is in condition for allowance, an interference search must be made by using the most efficient and effective manner based on the claimed subject matter in the broadest claim.
guidance: Examples: text search, classified search, or combination searches of US-PGPUB database in PE2E-SEARCH. Consider each effective filing date for CIPs. If claim directed to a nucleotide or peptide sequence, examiner must submit a request to STIC to perform an interference search of the sequence.

name: Understand the goals/benefits of conducting a prior art search
description: Use the search to inform patent decisions and reduce downstream problems.
guidance: Key benefits listed: avoid submitting patent applications with claims that are not patentable and will be easily rejected; determine whether your invention is novel; develop a strong patent claim strategy before filing (reduce chance of extensive amendments); account for close prior art in drafting by describing advantages or improvements to support non-obviousness; understand how your idea fits into the technological field; be better prepared to discuss your invention with a patent attorney and explain what aspects might be patentable.

name: If you find prior art, assess its effect and adjust patent strategy
description: Discovering prior art does not necessarily invalidate a patent claim; analyze how the reference affects claim scope and what steps can overcome it.
guidance: The page advises that finding prior art can be discouraging but may not invalidate the entire patent. Consider how prior art affects different types of claims and consult resources or a patent attorney for strategies to overcome obstacles (e.g., drafting differences, claiming distinguishing features, or focusing on inventive improvements). The firm offers an eBook covering these strategies.

name: Prohibition on Parent and Divisional Claiming Same Subject-Matter
description: Parent and divisional applications shall not claim the same subject-matter; claims should not be substantially identical in scope or claim subject-matter claimed in the other, even in different words.
guidance: Difference between claimed subject-matter of the two applications must be clearly distinguishable.

name: Contest Between Examiner and Applicant
description: Examiner safeguards public interest by allowing exclusivity only based on valid patent claims covered by the disclosure; applicant or attorney may present arguments to obtain broader protection.

name: Refusal of Claims — Principles
description: If invention not patentable in any manner all claims will be refused. If some claims are patentable and others not, only the latter will be refused and patent may still be granted for allowable claims.
guidance: In refusals for want of novelty or inventive step, Examiner must cite the most relevant references, designate the particular part relied on where necessary and clearly explain pertinence. Claims may be refused for non‑compliance with Sections 35.1 and 36.1 of the IP Code.

name: Final Refusal or Action — Limitations and Reiteration
description: On the second or any subsequent examination the refusal or objection may be declared final. Applicant's recourse is limited to filing an appeal or petition. In making final refusal, Examiner shall reiterate all grounds of refusal previously considered and may not cite additional grounds not previously raised.
guidance: Petition for final objections not involving claim refusal; Appeal for final refusal involving claims not allowed.

name: Amendments by the Applicant — No New Matter
description: Applicant may amend during examination provided such amendment does not include new matter outside scope of the disclosure contained in the application as filed.
guidance: Amendments after final action may be introduced during appeal for deleting claims, complying with form, or presenting refused claims in better form. Amendments after final refusal may be admitted upon showing good cause and sufficient justification why not earlier presented.

name: No Broadening of Disclosure After Filing
description: No deletion or addition shall broaden the disclosure of an application to include new matter after the filing date. All post‑filing amendments must conform to at least one version as of the filing date; matter not found in the original disclosure cannot be added even with supplemental oath and can only be claimed in a separate application.

name: Amendment of Claims — Basis and Avoidance of References
description: Claims may be amended by canceling claims, presenting new claims, or amending language. When presenting new or amended claims applicant must point out how they avoid any reference or ground of refusal and indicate which part of the original disclosure constitutes the basis for the amendments.

name: Strict caps on continuation applications
description: Impose strict limits on patentees' ability to delay prosecution through continuation filings.
guidance: Limiting continuations (for example the PTO's proposed three-continuation-as-of-right rule) would reduce uncertainty caused by applicants changing claims long after initial filing and issuance. The paper cites proposals and PTO regulations attempting to cap continuations as a way to prevent indefinite claim-drafting and surprise rights.

name: Limitations that are not 'significantly more' — appending well-understood, routine, conventional activities
description: Simply appending well-understood, routine, conventional activities previously known to the industry, specified at a high level of generality, does not amount to significantly more.
guidance: Example: a claim to an abstract idea requiring no more than a generic computer to perform generic functions; courts describe such computer functions as 'well-understood, routine, conventional activit[ies]'. (Alice Corp.; see MPEP § 2106.05(d)).

name: Limitations that are not 'significantly more' — insignificant extra-solution activity
description: Adding insignificant extra-solution activity (activity that does not meaningfully contribute an inventive concept) does not make a claim significantly more than the judicial exception.
guidance: Example: mere data gathering in conjunction with a law of nature or abstract idea (e.g., obtaining information about credit card transactions solely so an abstract mental process can analyze it). (CyberSource v. Retail Decisions; MPEP § 2106.05(g)).

name: Tangibility/physicality is not dispositive
description: The mere physicality or tangibility of an additional element(s) is not a relevant consideration in Step 2B and does not automatically provide an inventive concept.
guidance: Courts: a computer is a tangible machine, but mere recitation of physical components (e.g., computer hardware) does not guarantee eligibility; physical steps (e.g., DNA amplification) do not necessarily provide sufficient inventive concept. Conversely, lack of physicality does not doom claims if there is a genuine improvement to technology (see Enfish, McRO, Genetic Technologies).

name: Step 2B evaluation method — identify and evaluate additional elements individually and in combination
description: Examiner should identify additional claim elements beyond the judicial exception(s), then evaluate those additional elements individually and as an ordered combination to determine whether they contribute an inventive concept (i.e., amount to significantly more).
guidance: Evaluation should reference Supreme Court considerations and MPEP §2106.05(a)-(h). The inquiry is not a weighing test — it's whether the additional elements, considered individually and in combination, contribute an inventive concept. See Alice and Mayo analyses and examples (Alice, BASCOM).

name: Claims evaluated on a claim-by-claim basis
description: Examiners should examine each claim for eligibility separately; similar claims should not be assumed to stand or fall together.
guidance: A dependent claim may be eligible if it recites additional elements that amount to significantly more even if the independent claim is ineligible. Consider each claim's particular elements and scope.

name: Handling multiple judicial exceptions in a claim
description: Unless it is clear that the claim recites discrete exceptions, examiners should avoid parsing a claim into multiple exceptions; if multiple discrete exceptions are present, examiners may select one exception and conduct the analysis for efficiency.
guidance: If analysis for the selected exception finds an additional element or combination that amounts to significantly more, the claim should be considered patent eligible. If not, consider rejection. (Cited: University of Utah Research Foundation v. Ambry Genetics).

name: Improvement-to-technology consideration (improvement to computer/functioning or other technical field)
description: Examiners should consider whether the claim purports to improve the functioning of the computer itself or any other technology or technical field — i.e., whether it presents a technological solution to a technological problem.
guidance: This consideration can be evaluated at Step 2A or Step 2B and supports streamlined analyses when self-evident. Key cases: DDR Holdings, Enfish, Amdocs, McRO, Visual Memory. See MPEP § 2106.05(a).

name: Claim must reflect the disclosed improvement and be evaluated under the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI)
description: Even if the specification discloses an improvement, the claim itself must reflect that improvement when considered under BRI; examiners must consider the claim as a whole (ordered combination) and avoid oversimplification.
guidance: If the claim's full scope does not capture the improvement described in the specification, eligibility may not be shown (e.g., Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec). Evaluate specific claim requirements, not just general statements.

name: Improvement must be to a particular solution/way of achieving an outcome rather than merely claiming an idea/outcome
description: A claim that covers a particular solution or particular way to achieve a desired outcome is more likely to show an improvement to technology than one that merely claims the idea of a solution or an outcome.
guidance: Courts have relied on specificity of claimed solution (e.g., McRO: particular rules for animation) to find claims directed to technological improvements rather than abstract ideas. Overlap exists with particular_machine and mere_instructions considerations.

name: Indicators that a claim improves computer functionality (positive examples)
description: Certain specific kinds of changes indicate an improvement to computer functionality (not exhaustive): modifications to protocols, inventive distribution of functionality, methods of rendering images, unconventional distributed architectures to reduce congestion, configurable memory systems, technical details for image transmission, particular server structures, specific programming/design methods.
guidance: Court-cited examples: (i) DDR Holdings: modified hyperlink protocol; (ii) BASCOM: inventive distribution for filtering; (iii) Research Corp.: halftone rendering; (iv) Amdocs/Openet: unconventional distributed network architecture; (v) Visual Memory: configurable memory system; (vi) TLI Communications: technical transmission/classification details (lack of details can make claims ineligible); (vii) TLI Communications: particular server structure; (viii) Apple v. Ameranth: particular way of programming menus. Use these as guidance but assess each claim's specifics.

name: Requirement that computer-implemented method claims must be limited to computer implementation to show computer-functionality improvement
description: For a method claim to be considered an improvement to computer functionality, its BRI must limit the claim to computer implementation; if the claim's entire scope can be performed mentally or verbally, it cannot be said to improve computer technology.
guidance: Examples: Synopsys (method could be performed without a computer), RecogniCorp (encoding/decoding process did not require a computer). If embodiments exist that can be practiced without a computer, the improvement consideration may fail.

name: Examples that may not be sufficient to show improvement (negative examples)
description: Certain claimed benefits or uses are unlikely to show an improvement to computer functionality if they rely only on general-purpose computer capabilities or automation of manual processes.
guidance: Court-cited non-sufficient examples: (i) generating restaurant menus with functionally claimed features (Ameranth); (ii) speeding data analysis solely from general-purpose computer capabilities (FairWarning); (iii) merely using a computer to perform an abstract idea (Return Mail); (iv) mere automation of manual processes like generic loan-application processing (Credit Acceptance, LendingTree); (v) recording/transmitting/archiving images using conventional/generic tech without showing inventive solution (TLI Communications).

name: Improvements to other technology/technical fields can show eligibility
description: Improvements outside of computer functionality — i.e., to other technologies or technical fields — can also demonstrate patent eligibility when the claim recites a particular technical advance.
guidance: Court examples include: (i) computerized method operating a rubber molding press with thermocouple monitoring (Diehr); (ii) new telephone/server combinations (TLI Communications); (iii) advances in downloading for streaming (Affinity Labs); (iv) specific digital data compression methods (DDR Holdings, Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec); (v) integrating virus screening into the Internet (Symantec); (vi) components/methods that generate new data (Electric Power Group v. Alstom); (vii) particular configuration and methods for inertial sensors (Thales Visionix). Use these examples to recognize technological improvements beyond general computing.

name: Findings of misrepresentation as basis for discipline
description: Specific misrepresentations (telling employer she had taken/passed/been sworn in and providing a false Illinois Bar registration number) are useable factual bases for a disciplinary finding under the cited rule.
guidance: The order details timeline and admissions (hiring interview statements, false sworn-in claim, false registration number, employer confrontation and admission) as supporting the violation.

name: Substantial New Question (SNQ) determination for reexamination
description: Examiner determines whether a 'substantial new question of patentability' (SNQ) affecting any claim exists; an SNQ can be raised by patents/printed publications presented in a new light (PTA 2002). Decision on a request must be made no later than 3 months from its filing date.
guidance: If an SNQ is found an order for ex parte reexamination is issued. The 3-month decision clock is statutory; SNQ analysis may consider previously examined references if re-presented with new reasoning.

name: Amendment limitation in ex parte reexamination
description: The scope of a claim cannot be enlarged by amendment in a reexamination.
guidance: Only narrowing or confirmation amendments are permitted; broadening amendments are prohibited in reexamination.

name: Reexamination conclusion: NIRC and reexamination certificate
description: Examination concludes with issuance of a Notice of Intent to Issue a Reexamination Certificate (NIRC); the reexamination certificate is part of the issued patent and will list cancellations, confirmations, patentable amended/new claims, statutory/terminal disclaimers, and any claims not reexamined.
guidance: The reexamination certificate formally records the outcome of the proceeding and modifies the patent accordingly.

name: Supplemental examination procedural limits
description: Determination whether an SNQ is raised generally occurs within 3 months; determination limited to items identified in the request as applied to identified claims and based on claims in effect at the time; no amendments accepted and no interviews conducted during supplemental examination; the proceeding concludes with issuance of a supplemental examination certificate.
guidance: Patent owner must promptly notify the USPTO of any federal court decision involving the patent while supplemental examination is pending or after filing.

name: Reissue purpose and basic constraints
description: Reissue permits errors in the original patent to be corrected, permits claims to be broadened if a broadening reissue is filed within two years of issuance of the original patent, may correct inventorship, but not all errors are correctable (see 35 U.S.C. §§ 251 & 252; MPEP §1401-1470).
guidance: Reissue is an owner-initiated corrective vehicle subject to strict statutory timing and substantive limits.

name: Oath/declaration signature rules (general and for broadening reissue)
description: Oath/declaration must include 37 CFR 1.63 requirements and generally must be signed by the inventors. For broadening reissue (37 CFR 1.175): the oath/declaration must identify at least one claim sought to be broadened and all inventors are required to sign except in limited exceptions (e.g., original application filed under 1.46 by the assignee on/after 9/16/2012 or use of substitute statement under 1.64). If there are no broadened claims, the assignee of entire interest may sign.
guidance: Signature/authority rules vary depending on whether scope is being broadened; missing inventor signatures for broadening reissue are typically fatal.

name: Use of prior oath/declaration for continuing reissue
description: For a continuing reissue application, a copy of the inventor’s oath/declaration from the earlier-filed post-AIA reissue parent application may be used provided the inventor executed the earlier oath, the continuing reissue does not seek to enlarge the scope of the original patent claims, or the original application was filed under 37 CFR 1.46 by the assignee of the entire interest.
guidance: This avoids re-signing in limited continuing-application situations; be careful about scope-expansion restrictions.

name: Reissue specification and drawings requirements
description: Reissue specification (including claims) is filed in double-column format (copy of printed patent). Original drawings: clean copies of printed patent drawing sheets are filed as the formal drawings; new drawing sheets are required for any new or amended figures (see 37 CFR 1.84 and 1.173).
guidance: Submitting proper formatted specification and correct drawing changes is necessary for a compliant reissue application.

name: General limitations on reissue eligibility
description: Reissue may correct errors such as error in scope of claims, inventorship, priority to foreign application, benefit claim to domestic application, error in drawing or specification, and error in filing terminal disclaimer. Expired patents are not eligible for reissue; term cannot be extended by eliminating 35 U.S.C. §120 benefits; subject matter surrendered to obtain the original patent cannot be recaptured.
guidance: Reissue is limited in subject matter and term effects; review MPEP §1402 for detailed examples.

name: Two-year limit on broadening reissue
description: No broadening of claim coverage is permitted unless a broadening reissue application was filed within two years from the grant of the original patent (35 U.S.C. §251(d)). Intent to broaden must be established in the reissue application within two years; a reissue filed within two years for other reasons may not be broadened later after the two-year date.
guidance: Strict statutory two-year bar; courts and MPEP require timely assertion of intent to broaden.

name: Test for 'Broadened Reissue Claim' (broadening meaning)
description: An amended/new claim in the reissue that contains within its scope any conceivable invention that would not have infringed any of the claims of the original patent (i.e., causes previously non-infringing subject matter to now infringe) constitutes a broadened reissue claim.
guidance: Use factual inquiry (Would previously non-infringing inventions now infringe?) and consult case law (Tillotson, In re Self) and MPEP §1412.03(I).

name: Recapture prohibition in reissue
description: Patentee cannot recover via broadening in reissue subject matter surrendered in an effort to obtain allowance of the original patent claims (recapture rule). Deliberate withdrawal/amendment to obtain allowance is not considered an 'error' correctable by reissue.
guidance: Recapture is a substantive bar even within the two-year window; see 3-step recapture test in MPEP §1412.02 and relevant case law.

name: 3-step test for impermissible recapture
description: 1) Determine whether and in what respect the reissue claims are broader than the original claims; 2) Determine whether the broader aspects relate to subject matter surrendered in original prosecution; 3) Determine whether reissue claims were materially narrowed in other respects related to surrendered subject matter.
guidance: Use this test (MPEP §1412.02) to analyze recapture issues; materially narrowing limitations must be related to surrendered subject matter to avoid recapture (see In re Mostafazadeh).

name: Original-patent requirement for reissue (same invention)
description: Reissue claims must be for the same invention as disclosed as being the invention in the original patent per 35 U.S.C. 251. To seek a 'new' invention by reissue, the specification must clearly and unequivocally disclose the newly claimed invention as a separate invention.
guidance: Reissue cannot be used to claim an invention not clearly disclosed in the original patent; satisfy 'original patent requirement' or risk rejection.

name: Narrowing reissue claims permitted
description: A reissue application may add one or more claims that are narrower than one or more broader existing patent claims; adding narrower claims without amending or canceling the broader patent claims may be correctable by reissue (e.g., In re Tanaka). The declaration may be signed by the assignee instead of inventor(s) in some situations.
guidance: Narrowing reissue is an accepted use of reissue to correct overbroad claims or add fall-back positions, subject to signature/ownership rules.

name: CRU monitoring and interplay with PTAB/AIA proceedings
description: The CRU closely monitors pending and concluded PTAB post-grant proceedings and reviews all PTAB determinations before taking action in an ex parte reexamination proceeding or pending reissue application involving the same patent. Considerations include 35 U.S.C. 315(e)(1) estoppel, 35 U.S.C. 325(d) discretionary denial, 37 CFR 42.73(d)(3) patent owner estoppel, and conflicting positions on claim construction or prior art.
guidance: AIA allows multiple types of challenges; CRU must account for estoppel and possible duplicative arguments when deciding whether to proceed with reexamination or reissue activity.

name: Federal Register notice re: amendments during pending AIA trial
description: Notice (Apr 22, 2019) summarizes existing Office practice regarding claim amendments by patent owner through reissue or reexamination during a pending AIA trial, and summarizes factors the PTAB considers in determining whether to stay or suspend reissue/reexamination proceedings and when to lift such stays.
guidance: Public notice outlines coordination and factors considered when Office proceedings overlap with PTAB trials; consult notice for policy on amendments during AIA trials.

name: Claims measure the invention
description: The claims measure the invention. They may be explained and illustrated by the description. They cannot be enlarged by it.
guidance: Claims define the scope; the specification can clarify but not broaden claim scope beyond the plain import of the claim language (citing Continental Paper Bag Co. v. Eastern Paper Bag Co. and related authorities).

name: Limit claim construction to plain import of claim terms
description: It is unjust to construe a claim in a manner different from the plain import of its terms; the claim is a statutory requirement to define precisely what is claimed.
guidance: Courts should avoid reading into claims elements not present and should not alter the claim to include something more or different than its words express.

name: Do not import dispensable elements to avoid infringement
description: A claim will not be narrowed by importing into it, by construction, any dispensable element, in order to enable an infringer to escape the consequences of his infringement.
guidance: Claims should not be artificially narrowed by reading in nonessential/speculative elements from the specification just to avoid finding infringement.

name: Effect of failure to put invention to practical use
description: When no practical use has been made of the patent the claims will be narrowly construed, the reason being that the patent lacks support from public acquiescence.
guidance: Conversely, a practical success constituting a distinct advance in the art warrants a liberal construction of claims.

name: Proceedings in the Patent Office can prevent narrowing
description: Claims will not be narrowed where the proceedings in the Patent Office clearly show that the inventor intended to claim and the Patent Office intended to grant the broader monopoly.
guidance: Contemporaneous prosecution history showing intent to obtain broader claims militates against judicial narrowing.

name: Specification may illustrate but not enlarge claims
description: The description may explain and illustrate the claim but cannot be used to enlarge the claim beyond its terms.
guidance: Descriptions of particular devices or arrangements cannot be treated as limiting absent clear intent; illustrations serve to explain but not to broaden the statutory claim.

name: Explicit description of alternatives can affect construction
description: If the patentee explicitly states that there might be alternatives for the device described, courts have given broader construction than if no alternatives were mentioned.
guidance: A declaration in the specification that alternatives are possible may support a broader claim interpretation than a specification that appears to fix a single arrangement.

name: Best mode disclosure does not necessarily limit claim scope
description: While statutory provision requires disclosure of the best mode, it is not clear that this requirement affects the scope of the claims; inventor may state the best mode but not be confined to it.
guidance: Patentee must disclose best mode but may not be confined to only that disclosed mode; patents would be of little worth if so confined.

name: Claims cannot be construed to cover incidental or recommended processes
description: A claim for a process, substantially as described, cannot be construed to cover an incidental process set forth in the description but merely recommended there, instead of being required or essential to the principal process.
guidance: Recommended or preferable steps in the specification do not expand the scope of a process claim unless the claim itself includes them.

name: Preferable language in specification does not restrict claims
description: A patentee of a manufacture is not restricted to a construction which he describes in the specification merely as 'preferable,' unless specifically limited by the claims.
guidance: Statements of preference in the spec are insufficient to limit claim scope absent express claim language.

name: Claims cannot be altered by construction to cover more or fewer elements
description: When a claim clearly covers a combination of certain elements, it cannot, by construction, be altered to cover more elements so as to be valid, or to cover fewer elements and thus be rendered more likely to be infringed.
guidance: Courts should not rewrite claims to change the elements covered; claimed combinations stand as written.

name: Cannot read in elements that are not equivalents
description: A claim cannot be construed to cover other elements in place of some that may be omitted, unless those omitted elements are equivalents.
guidance: Replacement of claim elements by non-equivalents through construction is impermissible.

name: Patentee's acts and conduct may limit claim (estoppel/laches)
description: The acts and conduct of the owner of a patent (e.g., long-standing constructions placed on a claim with knowledge of noninfringing sales) may give a construction to a claim which will avoid infringement; this may be placed on laches or estoppel grounds.
guidance: Long acquiescence or conduct that indicates a narrow construction can preclude later assertion of a broader scope.

name: Broadening changes in prosecution cannot be construed away to save validity
description: Where the change made in the Patent Office was a broadening one, it cannot be construed away in order to ascribe validity to the patent.
guidance: If the applicant broadened claims during prosecution and obtained allowance, courts will not later construe them as if the broadening did not occur to avoid invalidity.

name: Limitations and amendments made to obtain allowance generally bind patentee
description: An applicant who, on rejection, inserted limitations and restrictions into his specification for the purpose of obtaining his patent cannot later claim it shall be construed as if such limitations were not contained in it.
guidance: Material modifications made in obedience to PTO requirements are ordinarily treated as limiting; however courts recognize undue narrowing and may lean toward liberality where PTO requirements were unwarranted.

name: Incidental amendments for phraseology do not limit claims
description: Merely incidental amendments, not made in pursuance of references or real reasons given by the Patent Office, but in deference to PTO preferences for particular phraseology, will not be construed to limit claims so as to make them narrower than the inventions they were designed to cover.
guidance: Courts avoid giving effect to trivial or stylistic amendments as disclaimers of scope.

name: Concessions in argument not carried into claims do not limit claims
description: Concessions addressed to the Examiner in arguments which are not carried into the claims do not limit the claims as finally allowed.
guidance: Only what's embodied in claim language and formal amendments ordinarily binds; pure prosecutorial argument lacks the same binding effect.

name: Withdrawn proposed amendments do not limit claims
description: An amendment proposed but subsequently withdrawn cannot be construed to impose a limitation on the claim as issued.
guidance: Only successful/entered amendments are relevant to restricting claim scope.

name: Construction is a question of law; experts limited to terms of art
description: Questions of construction are questions of law for the judge, not of fact for the jury. Judges may avail themselves of experts for the meaning of terms of art or science used in the patent, but expert testimony on construction of the patent as a whole is inadmissible.
guidance: Experts can explain technical meaning, but ultimate claim interpretation is judicial.

name: Disclaimer cannot confine claim to ground not appearing in the patent
description: A disclaimer cannot confine a claim to ground which does not appear in the patent to constitute an invention; even if that ground is narrower than what was originally claimed.
guidance: You cannot use a disclaimer to retroactively convert a claim into something that the patent never disclosed as inventive.

name: Disbursing officer's authority to pursue legal remedies
description: It is accordance with military usage and general practice that an officer of the Army charged with disbursement of public funds may pursue in his own name and representative capacity the proper legal remedies when such funds are illegally appropriated or withheld by third parties.
guidance: This duty should not be imposed on the head of the department; the disbursing officer should file and prove claims (e.g., in bankruptcy) and prosecute collection with due and reasonable diligence to support future applications to be discharged from liability for losses resulting from depository failure (R.35,365, May 7, 1874).

name: Obvious To Try — Four Required Findings
description: To reject a claim based on an 'obvious to try' rationale, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries and then articulate: (1) a finding that at the time of the invention there had been a recognized problem or need in the art; (2) a finding that there had been a finite number of identified, predictable potential solutions to the recognized need or problem; (3) a finding that one of ordinary skill in the art could have pursued the known potential solutions with a reasonable expectation of success; and (4) whatever additional findings based on the Graham factual inquiries may be necessary to explain a conclusion of obviousness.
guidance: If any of these findings cannot be made, the 'obvious to try' rationale cannot be used to support a conclusion of obviousness. Examiners must explicitly state these findings in the record and tie them to the Graham factors.

name: Obvious To Try Not Appropriate When Prior Art Offers Only Vague Guidance or Numerous Undirected Options
description: An obvious-to-try rationale is erroneous when (1) it would have been 'obvious to try' merely to vary all parameters or try many possible choices where the prior art gives no indication which parameters are critical or which choices are likely to succeed, or (2) it would have been to explore a new technology or general approach where the prior art gives only general guidance as to the particular form of the claimed invention or how to achieve it.
guidance: Apply this limitation when prior art leaves too many undirected options or only general exploratory guidance; cite Kubin and O'Farrell reasoning. If prior art does not indicate which parameters or choices are promising, do not rely on 'obvious to try.'

name: Post-filing submission of Sequence Listing XML - required statements
description: Submission of a “Sequence Listing XML” after the filing date requires that the applicant provide: (1) a request to amend the specification to include an updated incorporation by reference statement of the material in the “Sequence Listing XML” (37 CFR 1.835(a)(2)); (2) a statement that identifies the basis for the amendment with specific references to particular parts of the application as originally filed (specification, claims, drawings) for all sequence data in the “Sequence Listing XML” in the application as originally filed (37 CFR 1.835(a)(3)); and (3) a statement of no new matter (37 CFR 1.835(a)(4)).
guidance: Must explicitly request amendment to include incorporation-by-reference paragraph, cite exact basis in originally filed materials for all sequence data, and affirm no new matter. These three elements are required for any Sequence Listing XML submitted after the filing date.

name: Computer Program Listing Appendix — thresholds and placement
description: Per 37 CFR 1.96: a computer program listing of 300 lines or fewer (each line ≤72 characters) may be submitted either as drawings or as part of the specification. Any listing having more than 60 lines submitted as part of the specification must be positioned at the end of the description but before the claims; listings of 301 lines or more must be submitted as an electronic ASCII plain text file (Computer Program Listing Appendix) via EFS or on a read-only optical disc.
guidance: If listing ≤300 lines you may include in spec or as drawings; if >300 lines must be electronic appendix. If included in the spec and >60 lines, place at end before claims. Follow substitution-sheet rules for amendments to in-spec listings.

name: Specification must teach how to practice claimed method
description: The specification must be adequate to teach how to practice the claimed method. If such practice requires a particular apparatus, then the application must provide a sufficient disclosure of that apparatus if such is not already available.
guidance: When analyzing method claims (including computer-implemented methods), examiners should ensure the specification enables practice of the method without undue experimentation; disclosure of required apparatus is necessary if not already known in the art. (Cited: In re Ghiron; In re Gunn.)

name: Applicant burden to show enablement after reasonable basis advanced
description: Once USPTO personnel have advanced a reasonable basis or presented evidence to question the adequacy of a disclosure, the applicant must show that the specification would enable one of ordinary skill in the art to make and use the claimed invention without resorting to undue experimentation.
guidance: Typical applicant responses include submitting affidavits, referencing prior art patents or technical publications, presenting arguments of counsel, or combinations of these approaches.

name: Commercial availability and clarity of prior art use for enablement
description: The commercial availability of an identified prior art computer system is pertinent to enablement, but merely citing publications may not be sufficient to meet the applicant’s burden.
guidance: Citing excerpts from technical publications is insufficient unless it is clear which parts of the cited material could be used and how they would be interconnected to construct the claimed device. This is less critical when the cited components are standard parts of an identified prior-art system and a standard device attached thereto. (Cited: In re Forman.)

name: Integration of prior-art components required to show enablement by old components
description: Merely showing that components enumerated in a block diagram were old does not demonstrate how each would be interconnected to function in a complex combination; the specification must set forth the integration of the prior art.
guidance: If the specification does not set forth how prior-art components interconnect to produce the claimed results, undue experimentation may be required. Patents used to show components are "old" must be analyzed for germane relevance and whether they provide better detail than the applicant’s disclosure. Also, known programming techniques do not establish enablement unless they are of similar complexity to the disclosed techniques. (Cited: In re Scarbrough; In re Knowlton.)

name: Examiner burden to provide reasonable basis for nonutility/nonenablement
description: When the examiner concludes that an application claims an invention that is nonuseful, inoperative, or contradicts known scientific principles, the burden is on the examiner to provide a reasonable basis to support this conclusion.
guidance: The examiner has the initial burden of challenging an asserted utility; only after the examiner provides evidence showing a PHOSITA would reasonably doubt the asserted utility does the burden shift to the applicant to rebut. (Cited: In re Fisher; In re Swartz; In re Brana; In re Bundy.)

name: Applicant rebuttal standard for asserted utility
description: If a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 has been properly imposed, the burden shifts to the applicant to rebut the prima facie showing.
guidance: There is no predetermined amount or character of evidence required; the character and amount of evidence needed vary depending on the claim and whether the asserted utility appears to contravene established scientific principles. The applicant's evidence need only make it more likely than not that the asserted utility is true—not "beyond a reasonable doubt." (Cited: In re Oetiker; In re Gazave; In re Chilowsky; In re Irons; MPEP § 2107.02.)

name: Utility satisfied but enablement still required
description: In some instances, the utility of the claimed invention will be provided, but the skilled artisan will not know how to effect that use; in such a case no rejection will be made under 35 U.S.C. 101, but a rejection will be made under 35 U.S.C. 112(a).
guidance: An invention may be highly useful yet not enabled if the specification fails to teach one skilled in the art how to use it. (Cited: Mowry v. Whitney.)

name: Specification must teach how to make/use full scope without undue experimentation
description: The specification must teach those skilled in the art how to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention without 'undue experimentation' or that any experimentation must be 'reasonable.'
guidance: Not everything necessary need be disclosed—what is well-known may be omitted. The scope of enablement must bear a 'reasonable correlation' to the scope of the claims. The more one claims, the more one must enable. (Cited: Amgen v. Sanofi; In re Wright; In re Buchner; In re Fisher.)

name: Range and genus claims require reasonable enablement across claimed scope
description: When a range is claimed, there must be reasonable enablement of the scope of the range; for genus claims, although not every variant must be described, the scope claimed must be reasonably enabled.
guidance: If the specification indicates certain values won't work or warns against portions of a range, yet claims encompass them, enablement may fail (e.g., AK Steel). Genus claims that claim overly broad embodiments when only a few examples are taught may be inadequately enabled (e.g., Amgen). Conversely, some claims (e.g., DNA encoding a specifically identified protein sequence) may be enabled if a skilled artisan could readily determine embodiments.

name: Scope-of-enablement rejection must identify non-enabled claim subject matter and explain why
description: A scope-of-enablement rejection must identify the claimed subject matter for which the specification is not enabling and explain why the specification is not enabling, applying the Wands factors.
guidance: The examiner's explanation should include any unresolved questions the examiner posed that raise doubt as to enablement and show why those questions were not satisfactorily resolved. This is an enablement (112(a)) rejection, not a definiteness (112(b)) rejection.

name: Form of disclosure not dispositive: examples or broad terminology acceptable
description: An enabling disclosure may be set forth by specific example or broad terminology; the exact form of disclosure is not dispositive.
guidance: Claims are not rejected as broader than the enabling disclosure for noninclusion of limitations that are presumed to be within ordinary skill; one does not look to the claims but to the specification to find out how to practice the claimed invention. (Cited: In re Marzocchi; In re Skrivan.)

name: Claims interpreted in light of the specification; broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with spec
description: When analyzing enabled scope, teachings of the specification must not be ignored; claims are to be given their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.
guidance: Interpreting claims in view of the specification does not mean everything in the specification must be read into the claims. The record must be clear so the public has notice of the patentee's scope of protection when the patent issues. (Cited: Raytheon Co. v. Roper; W.L. Gore & Assoc.; In re Johnson.)

name: Use case examples (Amgen/EPO analogs) as guidance for genus claim adequacy
description: Broad claim scope (e.g., claiming all analogs or broad classes) requires commensurate enabling disclosure; disclosing only a few exemplars may not enable claiming all possible variants.
guidance: Amgen illustrates that extensive but generic statements about many analogs are not sufficient if details for preparing only a few analogs are disclosed. The applicant must provide enabling disclosure commensurate with claim breadth, otherwise claims may be rejected as broader than the enabling disclosure.

name: Required 'submission' content under 37 CFR 1.114
description: A submission under 37 CFR 1.114 may include an information disclosure statement (IDS), an amendment to the written description, claims, or drawings, new arguments, or new evidence in support of patentability.
guidance: Previously filed arguments may be considered submissions if they are responsive within the meaning of 37 CFR 1.111. If the submission is absent or not entered, different form paragraphs apply (e.g., ¶¶ 7.42.10–7.42.14). Use bracketed items to identify date(s) and nature of submission.

name: RCE on appeal lacking submission but claims allowed — pass to issue on allowed claims
description: If an RCE filed after appeal includes the fee but lacks the required submission, and there are allowed claims, the appeal is withdrawn and the application will be passed to issue on the allowed claims; rejected claims are considered terminated.
guidance: Use form paragraph 7.42.11; cancel dependent/rejected claims as appropriate (insert canceled claim numbers). Use with Notice of Allowability.

name: Dependent claim objected as depending on rejected base claim but allowable if rewritten independently
description: Claim [1] objected to as being dependent upon a rejected base claim, but would be allowable if rewritten in independent form including all of the limitations of the base claim and any intervening claims.
guidance: Use form paragraph 7.43 to inform applicant that claim would be allowable if rewritten; include specific claim numbers in brackets.

name: Allowable subject matter for claims rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (indefiniteness) — rewrite/amend to overcome rejection
description: A noted independent or dependent claim rejected solely on the basis of 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre-AIA second paragraph) would be allowable if rewritten or amended to overcome the rejection.
guidance: Use form paragraphs 7.43.01 and 7.43.02; used when rejection under 112(b) is sole basis and rewriting/amending would cure the rejection. For dependent claims, include limitations of base and intervening claims.

name: Specification fails to provide proper antecedent basis — correction required
description: The specification is objected to as failing to provide proper antecedent basis for the claimed subject matter; specific corrections are required.
guidance: Use form paragraph 7.44; cite 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1) and MPEP §608.01(o); identify the corrections in bracket 1.

name: Failure to present claims for interference may constitute disclaimer (AIA-specific caution)
description: Failure to present claims and/or take necessary steps for interference after notification that interfering subject matter is claimed constitutes a disclaimer of the subject matter, amounting to a concession that the patentee is the first inventor (In re Oguie).
guidance: Use form paragraph 7.48.aia only in applications examined under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102/103 where there is an earlier effective filing date claim (or specific references) per bracketed conditions. Use only after applicant has been notified and has refused to copy claims.

name: Suspension of action due to possible interference — limited period
description: When all claims are allowable but a potential interference exists, ex parte prosecution is suspended for a period of [1] months (maximum six months) pending interference determination.
guidance: Use form paragraph 7.53; TC Director must approve second/subsequent suspensions (MPEP §1003) and their signature must appear on the letter.

name: Special situations that may result in abandonment
description: Certain specific procedural situations often give rise to questions of abandonment, including: (A) copying claims from a patent when not suggested by the Office does not constitute a reply; (B) abandonment through withdrawal of or failure to prosecute an appeal to the Board; (C) abandonment through dismissal of appeals to the Federal Circuit or civil action absent a timely responsive amendment; (D) claims suggested for interference near end of period for reply; (E) FWC application under former 1.62; (F) continued prosecution application (CPA) filings; (G) improper RCE filed prior to Board decision that can be treated as withdrawal of appeal; (H) RCE filed without timely submission meeting reply requirements when reply to final action outstanding; (I) allowed application prior to issue fee payment may become abandoned if an RCE is improperly filed without appropriate fee/submission.
guidance: Each listed situation references the relevant MPEP section for further instruction (e.g., §1215.x for appeals, §706.07(h) for RCE treatment). Examiners and applicants should be aware that improper filings (e.g., RCE without required submission/fee) will not toll existing time periods and can cause abandonment.

name: Termination of proceedings under 35 U.S.C. 120
description: Termination of proceedings (for purposes of copendency) occurs when the earlier application is patented, abandoned, or proceedings on it are terminated; 'before' is interpreted as 'not later than.'
guidance: Examples: (A) failure to pay issue fee results in termination as of the date fee was due; (B) losing an interference as to all claims terminates proceedings as of the date appeal/review was due if no appeal filed; (C) termination after Board decision; (D) termination after court decision. See MPEP § 711.02(c) for details.

name: Divisional generally retains parent's filing date, with exceptions
description: A divisional application shall retain the same filing date as the parent application unless particular conditions make retroactive filing-date benefit unfair.
guidance: Examples of when divisional shall be deemed filed on its actual filing date: (①) divisional corresponds to 'another application' under Article 29(3) of the Patent Act or to a 'patent application' under Article 4(3) of the Utility Model Act; (②) where applicant requests application of proviso of Article 30(1)(1) and certain evidential filings; (③) where priority under Treaty is claimed but purport/country/date requirements not met; (④) where domestic priority is claimed but prior-filed application not properly indicated.
