New subject matter added to divisional specification/drawings should not get parent's filing date.

name: Examination of divisional scope depends on filing-date regime (pre-/post-2006)
description: The substantive examination standard for a divisional depends on whether the parent was filed before Sept 30, 2006 or on/after Oct 1, 2006, especially when the divisional claims inventions not described in the parent.
guidance: If parent pre-2006 and divisional claims inventions not described in parent, examiner issues preliminary notice for inadmissible division and, if division not accepted, examines on divisional's actual filing date; the published parent gazette can be used as prior art. If parent on/after Oct 1, 2006, examiner shall notify grounds for rejection and decide to reject if not cured by argument/amendment. If inventions not described are deleted by amendment, examiner may examine based on the parent's filing date.

name: Divisional may claim Treaty or Domestic priority; reference dates determined by earliest relevant filings
description: A divisional application may claim priority under the Treaty or Domestic Priority; reference date(s) for patentability of each invention are determined by the filing date of the prior-filed application that first disclosed the given invention.
guidance: When chains of filings exist, the divisional retains the filing date of its immediate parent for subject matter covered by that parent's filing, but the reference date for a specific invention may be an earlier prior-filed application depending on which application first disclosed that invention. See provided example (Inventions B, C, D). Article 36(2) applies when same invention described in both.

name: Special treatment when parent received decision to grant on/after 29 July 2015
description: When examining a divisional from a parent that received a certified copy of decision to grant on or after July 29, 2015, examiners must take account of conflicts and pending correction trials.
guidance: If applicant does not request trial for correction when filing a divisional for an invention disclosed only in parent description or recited in the parent's claims, examiners should check whether claimed inventions are identical and inform applicant of conflicting application in the rejection notice. If applicant divides a portion of an invention described in the granted parent with a trial for correction requested, examination of the divisional should be deferred until the trial concludes.

name: Procedure for filing a converted application (Form and statements required)
description: When filing a converted application the applicant must file a new patent application attaching the specification or relevant documents (Form XIV) and state the purport of the converted application and identify the original application forming the basis of conversion.
guidance: Failure to properly state the original application or incorrect indication will render conversion not legitimate. Reliance on evidential documents of the original can be stated instead of resubmission where identical. Specific additional procedural rules apply for foreign-language filings (translations), claim insertion when original lacked claims, and fees/translations for international applications.

name: Interviews preceding amendments after allowance (37 CFR 1.312)
description: After an application is sent to issue, it is technically no longer under the jurisdiction of the primary examiner; detailed consideration of claims prior to filing an amendment under 37 CFR 1.312 should not be given by interview.
guidance: Requests for interviews on cases where notice of allowance has been mailed should be granted only with specific approval of the Technology Center Director upon a written showing of extraordinary circumstances.

name: Specification amendments format
description: Amendments to the specification (other than claims, computer listings, and sequence listings) must be made by adding, deleting or replacing a paragraph, by replacing a section, or by a substitute specification.
guidance: Amendments must unambiguously identify the paragraph/section to be modified (paragraph number, page and line, or other unambiguous method) and be accompanied by replacement or new paragraph(s); replacement paragraphs must include markings showing all changes; new paragraphs must be presented in clean form without underlining.

name: Amendment sections must begin on separate sheets
description: Each section of an amendment document (e.g., specification amendments, claim amendments, drawing amendments, and remarks) must begin on a separate sheet.
guidance: Recommended amendment paper order: (A) cover sheet/table of contents with application info; (B) 'Amendments to the Specification'; (C) 'Amendments to the Claims' with complete claim listing; (D) 'Amendments to the Drawings' discussing changes; (E) remarks section; (F) any drawings attachments ('Replacement Sheet', 'New Sheet', 'Annotated Sheet').

name: Disclosure consistency requirement
description: The disclosure must be amended, when required by the Office, to correct inaccuracies of description and definition and to secure substantial correspondence between the claims, the remainder of the specification, and the drawings.

name: Claim status identifiers and listing
description: The status of every claim must be indicated after its claim number by using one of the following identifiers in parentheses: (Original), (Currently amended), (Previously presented), (Canceled), (Withdrawn), (New), and (Not entered).
guidance: Alternative identifiers (e.g., 'Original Claim', 'Presently amended', 'Canceled without prejudice', 'Previously added', 'New claim', 'Not entered claim') may be accepted if clear. In U.S. national stage applications, specific PCT-origin statuses must be used as directed.

name: Acceptable alternative status identifiers
description: The Office will waive certain provisions and accept alternative status identifiers that are not specifically set forth in 37 CFR 1.121(c) if the amendment otherwise complies and the status is accurate and clear.
guidance: List of acceptable alternatives provided (e.g., 'Original Claim', 'Presently amended', 'Canceled without prejudice', 'Previously added', 'New claim', 'Not entered claim'). When accepted the examiner need not correct them and applicant will not be required to submit corrective amendment.

name: Examiner's amendments (37 CFR 1.121(g))
description: The Office may make amendments to the specification, including the claims, by examiner's amendment without paragraph/section/claim replacement to expedite prosecution and reduce cycle time; such examiner's amendments need not comply with paragraphs (b)(1), (b)(2), or (c).
guidance: Examiner's amendment should include the reason why the amendment is non-compliant and indicate how it was corrected. Authorization from applicant or attorney/agent is not required for non-substantive corrections (format/typographical). Authorization and appropriate extensions are required if changes are substantive (e.g., cancellation of a claim or change the scope of the claims), and must be given within the time period for reply set in the last Office action.

name: Patents: What They Provide (scope of rights)
description: A patent gives the holder the right to exclude others from making, using, selling, offering to sell, and importing any patented invention; patent claims legally define the protectable invention.
guidance: A patent does not necessarily provide an affirmative right to practice a technology (others' broader patents may block practice). Claims determine the scope of protection; inventors must work with counsel during drafting and prosecution.

name: Inventorship Definition and Determination
description: Under U.S. law, an inventor is a person who takes part in the conception of the ideas in the patent claims; inventorship may change as claims change during prosecution.
guidance: Determination can be intricate and may require counsel. Employers or funders are not inventors. Inventors are asked to sign Inventor's Declarations and Assignments at filing.

name: Abbreviatures
description: Abbreviatures (per Notice of October 13, 1964) contain a specific portion of the disclosure, preferably a detailed representative claim and, if drawings exist, a figure; the publication of such abbreviatures was discontinued in 1965.
guidance: Abbreviatures are publications and should be cited accordingly as prior art; include citation format examples when listing in references.

name: Items required on Interview Summary (PTOL-413)
description: The PTOL-413 form provides for recordation of: (A) application number; (B) name of applicant; (C) name of examiner; (D) date of interview; (E) type of interview; (F) name of participants; (G) indication whether an exhibit was shown; (H) identification of claims discussed; (I) identification of specific prior art discussed; (J) indication whether an agreement was reached and description; (K) signature of examiner; (L) names of other USPTO personnel present.
guidance: The form reminds the applicant of responsibility to record substance of interview. When the substance is adequately recorded on PTOL-413 or attachment, examiner may check box indicating applicant need not supplement form. An examiner’s amendment that incorporates the complete recordation may substitute for completing PTOL-413.

name: Required substantive content when recording interviews
description: The complete and proper recordation of the substance of any interview should include at least applicable items: (A) brief description of any exhibit shown or demonstration; (B) identification of claims discussed; (C) identification of specific prior art discussed; (D) identification of principal proposed substantive amendments discussed; (E) general thrust of principal arguments of applicant and examiner; (G) general results or outcome of the interview; (H) for electronic mail interviews, a paper copy of the Internet e-mail contents must be placed in the file.
guidance: Identification of arguments need not be verbatim or highly detailed; general nature sufficient so principal arguments are understood in context. Examiner expected to carefully review applicant’s record of interview; may give applicant one month under 37 CFR 1.135(c) to supply omissions or corrections for replies to nonfinal Office actions.

name: Interviews after notice of allowance / during issue process
description: After an application is sent to issue (technical jurisdiction change under 37 CFR 1.312), an interview involving detailed consideration of claims or prior art to determine allowability should not be given; requests for interviews on cases where a notice of allowance has been mailed should be granted only with specific approval of the Technology Center Director upon a showing in writing of extraordinary circumstances.
guidance: An applicant is not entitled to a greater degree of consideration informally than is provided by formal amendments; consideration of an amendment presented informally after issue may not be demanded as a matter of right.

name: Manner of making amendments in application (37 CFR 1.121) — specification other than claims
description: Amendments to the specification (other than claims and certain listings) are made by submitting: (i) an instruction unambiguously identifying the location to delete, replace, or add a paragraph; (ii) any replacement or added paragraph(s) in clean form (without markings); and (iii) another version of any replacement paragraph(s) on pages separate from the amendment, marked up to show all changes relative to the previous version (brackets for deletions, underlining for additions, or equivalent).
guidance: A marked-up version is not required for purely added or deleted paragraphs beyond stating that a paragraph has been added or deleted. Amendments must comply with § 1.52 and filing requirements. This provides for clear identification of changes and facilitates examiner processing.

name: Claim term construction / breadth of claim terms
description: Claim terms are construed from the specification and context; e.g., 'The term "information processing apparatus" is broad and can be met by any number of information processing components.'
guidance: Broad claim-language can be met by multiple types of devices (personal computer, remote server, etc.); parties must explain why terms require narrower constructions, supported by specification or prosecution history.

name: Evidence must show how a POSITA would locate the document on the website with reasonable diligence
description: Petitioner must present evidence that a skilled person could reasonably find the website and then the document thereon using ordinary diligence (Samsung Elecs. Co. v. Infobridge Pte. Ltd.).
guidance: Demonstrations or testimony identifying the navigation path, site search functionality, or contemporaneous indexing help; claiming 'found in three clicks' requires showing those clicks reflect natural POSITA behavior and reasonable diligence rather than guided or artificial navigation.

name: Evidence of distribution or sales to show publication
description: If asserting that a manual or document was published via distribution with product sales, petitioner must present evidence of actual distribution/sales and that the document accompanied those sales before the critical date.
guidance: An untimely or unsupported claim of distribution (e.g., first presented in reply without sales figures or contemporaneous records) will not satisfy the printed-publication burden.

name: Special authorities not implied by general power of attorney
description: A representative (except a patent administrator of an overseas resident) cannot perform certain acts unless he/she obtains special authority: converting, abandonment or withdrawal of an application (including patent term extension withdrawal), abandonment of a patent right, withdrawal of patent application, withdrawal of request, withdrawal of Domestic Priority under Article 55(1), petition for trial or designation of subagent under Article 132(3).
guidance: Phrases like 'all matters regarding to the application' in a power of attorney do not include these special authorities unless expressly stated. Special authority must be explicitly described when relating to priority claims or other named special acts; sample power-of-attorney wording is provided in guidance.

name: Reissue application scope limitation (35 U.S.C. 251)
description: 35 U.S.C. 251 forbids the granting of a reissue 'enlarging the scope of the claims of the original patent' unless the reissue is applied for within 2 years from the grant of the original patent.
guidance: This prohibition is absolute and applies to any claim broader in any respect than the claims of the original patent; such claims may be rejected as being barred by 35 U.S.C. 251. However, when the reissue is applied for within 2 years (or properly claims the benefit of a broadening reissue application filed within 2 years of the patent grant), the examiner does not go into the question of undue delay. The same section permits filing of a reissue by the assignee of the entire interest only where it does not enlarge scope. A defective reissue oath is a ground for rejecting all claims in the reissue application (see MPEP § 1444). Note that a reissue application is 'special' and remains so even if applicant does not make a prompt reply.

name: Rejection of previously allowed claims — supervisory approval and deference
description: A claim noted as allowable shall thereafter be rejected only after the proposed rejection has been submitted to the primary examiner for consideration of all the facts and approval of the proposed action.
guidance: Great care should be exercised in authorizing such a rejection. Full faith and credit should be given to the search and action of a previous examiner unless there is a clear error in the previous action or knowledge of other prior art. In general, an examiner should not take an entirely new approach or make a new search in the mere hope of finding something. When rejecting a previously allowed claim due to newly discovered art, use Form Paragraph 7.50 and the action requires the signature of a Primary Examiner (MPEP § 1004).

name: Final rejection general rule (37 CFR 1.113) — when permitted and reply limits
description: On the second or any subsequent examination or consideration by the examiner the rejection or other action may be made final, whereupon applicant's reply is limited to appeal, or to amendment as specified in § 1.114 or § 1.116; petitions may be taken for objections/requirements not involved in the rejection.
guidance: In making such final rejection, the examiner shall repeat or state all grounds of rejection then considered applicable to the claims, clearly stating the reasons in support thereof. Reply to a final rejection must include cancellation of, or appeal from, the rejection of each rejected claim. Before final rejection is in order a clear issue should be developed between examiner and applicant: thoroughly search and apply references in the first action, and the applicant should amend with a view to avoiding all grounds of rejection and objection. Avoid switching subject matter or shifting to different sets of references in successive actions as this defeats early termination. The examiner should not issue hasty and ill-considered final rejections; the applicant is entitled to a full and fair hearing.

name: Form paragraph 7.39 and 7.39.01 — final action wording and applicant options
description: ¶7.39: 'THIS ACTION IS MADE FINAL.' Applicant is reminded of the extension of time policy as set forth in 37 CFR 1.136(a). ¶7.39.01: explains options after final rejection (appeal or limited amendment) and filing requirements for Notice of Appeal and appeal fee.
guidance: A shortened statutory period for reply to this final action is set to expire THREE MONTHS from the mailing date; if a first reply is filed within TWO MONTHS and advisory action mailed after the three-month period, the shortened period expires on the date the advisory action is mailed; in no event will the statutory period expire later than SIX MONTHS from mailing date. Form paragraph 7.39 should not be used in reissue litigation cases or reexamination proceedings (examiner notes). 7.39.01 clarifies that an amendment after final cannot be made as a matter of right unless it merely cancels claims or complies with earlier formal requirements; amendments touching merits may be admitted only upon showing good and sufficient reasons why necessary and why not presented earlier. Failure to file Notice of Appeal properly within the period for reply (or obtain extension) will result in abandonment. The Office Action Summary Form PTOL-326 should be used in all Office actions up to and including final rejections. See MPEP §§ 714.12 and 714.13 for amendments after final rejection and §2271 for final rejection practice in reexamination.

name: When final rejection is proper on second or subsequent action
description: Under present practice, second or any subsequent actions on the merits shall be final, except where the examiner introduces a new ground of rejection that is neither necessitated by applicant’s amendment of the claims, nor based on information submitted in an IDS under 37 CFR 1.97(c) with the fee.
guidance: Where information is submitted in an IDS during the period set forth in 37 CFR 1.97(c) with the fee, the examiner may use the information and make the next Office action final whether or not the claims have been amended, provided no other new ground of rejection not necessitated by amendment is introduced. If information is submitted in reply to a requirement under 37 CFR 1.105, the examiner may NOT make the next Office action final unless all instances of application of such art are necessitated by amendment. A second/subsequent action should not be made final if it includes a rejection, on prior art not of record, of any claim amended to include limitations which should reasonably have been expected to be claimed. An examiner cannot be expected to anticipate applicant amendments except in limited circumstances (e.g., where examiner suggests how applicant can overcome a 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph rejection).

name: Guard against allowing amended claims where patentable novelty not pointed out
description: In the consideration of claims in an amended case where no attempt is made to point out the patentable novelty, the examiner should be on guard not to allow such claims.
guidance: The claims may be finally rejected if, in the opinion of the examiner, they are clearly open to rejection on grounds of record. See MPEP § 714.04 for further guidance.

name: Whether its involvement is extra-solution activity or a field-of-use
description: Determine the extent to which the machine or apparatus imposes meaningful limits on the claim versus contributing only nominally or insignificantly (e.g., data gathering or field-of-use limitation).
guidance: If the machine's contribution is nominal or merely identifies a source of data (e.g., the Internet), it will not provide 'significantly more'. See Bilski, CyberSource and MPEP § 2106.05(g) & (h) for more on insignificant extra-solution activity and field of use.

name: Particular Transformation (M-or-T) consideration
description: Whether the claim effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing — a clue to patentability of a process claim that does not include particular machines.
guidance: Transformation of an article is an important clue but not a stand-alone test. All claims must be evaluated under Alice/Mayo; satisfying M-or-T alone is not sufficient (Bilski; Diamond v. Diehr examples). See the five factors below for evaluating a recited transformation and consider other Step 2B factors (MPEP § 2106.05(a)-(h)).

name: Factor 3: Nature of the transformation (type/extent of change)
description: Assess the type or extent of change in state or thing resulting from the claimed transformation (e.g., new function/use versus mere change of location).
guidance: Transformations that yield a new function or use are more likely to provide significantly more; mere relocation is unlikely to. Example: process transforming raw synthetic rubber into precision-molded products (Diamond v. Diehr) provides significantly more.

name: Factor 5: Whether the transformation is extra-solution activity or a field-of-use
description: Whether the claimed transformation merely imposes field-of-use limits or otherwise contributes only nominally to execution of the claimed method.
guidance: If the transformation is only a field-of-use limitation or nominal activity (e.g., administering a drug where administration was treated as only a field-of-use in Mayo), it likely does not provide significantly more. See MPEP § 2106.05(g) & (h).

name: Computer function: Web browser navigation functions (back/forward)
description: Browser back and forward button functionality is an example of a generic computer function that courts have treated as well-understood/routine when claimed generically.
guidance: Cited case: Internet Patent Corp. v. Active Network.

name: Life-science technique: Determining level of a biomarker in blood by any means
description: Measuring biomarker levels in blood is a recognized well-understood, routine, conventional activity when claimed generically.
guidance: Cited cases: Mayo; Cleveland Clinic Foundation v. True Health Diagnostics.

name: Life-science technique: Amplifying and sequencing nucleic acid sequences
description: Amplifying and sequencing nucleic acids is recognized as conventional when recited generically in claims.
guidance: Cited case: University of Utah Research Foundation v. Ambry Genetics.

name: Other conventional activity: Arranging hierarchy, sorting information, eliminating less restrictive pricing information and determining price
description: Arranging hierarchical groups, sorting information and determining pricing based on that sorting can be conventional when claimed generically.
guidance: Cited case: Versata Dev. Group v. SAP America.

name: Fee calculation for amendments and claims
description: The additional fees, if any, due with an amendment are calculated on the basis of the claims (total and independent) which would be present, if the amendment were entered.
guidance: An amendment of a claim (unless it changes a dependent claim to an independent claim or adds to the number of claims referred to in a multiple dependent claim) and replacement of a claim by a claim of the same type do not require additional fees. For fee purposes a claim is treated as dependent if it contains reference to one or more other claims. Any claim in dependent form that is not a proper dependent claim (e.g., does not include every limitation of the claim on which it depends) will be required to be canceled, and further claims depending on it will likewise be required to be canceled. Applicant may amend to place claims in proper dependent form or redraft as independent claims upon payment of any necessary additional fee. Unentered claims will not be counted when calculating the fee due in subsequent amendments. The additional fees due with an amendment are required prior to any consideration of the amendment by the examiner. Money paid for a proposed amendment is not refunded by reason of nonentry of the amendment.

name: Application of insufficient/unspecified payments (nonprovisional)
description: If a payment submitted for the fees due on filing in a nonprovisional application under 35 U.S.C. 111(a) is insufficient and the applicant has not specified the fees to which the payment is to be applied, the Office will apply the payment in the following order until the payment is expended:
guidance: Ordered application: (1) the basic filing fee (37 CFR 1.16(a),(b),(c), or (e)); (2) the non-electronic filing fee (37 CFR 1.16(t)); (3) the non-DOCX fee (37 CFR 1.16(u)); (4) the application size fee (37 CFR 1.16(s)); (5) the late filing surcharge (37 CFR 1.16(f)); (6) the processing fee for an application filed in a language other than English (37 CFR 1.17(i)); (7) the search fee (37 CFR 1.16(k)-(n)); (8) the examination fee (37 CFR 1.16(o)-(r)); and (9) the excess claims fee (37 CFR 1.16(h)-(j)). The Office will treat a deposit account authorization to charge “the basic filing fee” as authorization to charge basic filing, search, and examination fees unless specifically limited.

name: Specification disclosure requirement (35 U.S.C. 112(a) / 37 CFR 1.71)
description: To obtain a valid patent, the application as filed must contain a full and clear disclosure of the invention as prescribed by 35 U.S.C. 112(a). The specification must include a written description of the invention and of the manner and process of making and using the same, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to make and use the invention (37 CFR 1.71(a)).
guidance: The specification must set forth the precise invention and distinguish it from the prior art, describe a specific embodiment, and explain the mode of operation when applicable. The best mode contemplated by the inventor must be set forth. If a newly filed application obviously fails to disclose the invention with the clarity required, revision should be required. All amendments and claims must find descriptive basis in the original disclosure; no new matter may be introduced after filing. The written description must not include information unrelated to the invention.

name: Specification and related sections must begin on separate sheets/pages
description: The specification must commence on a separate sheet. The claim(s), abstract, and "Sequence Listing" (if required) should not be included on a sheet including any other part of the application (37 CFR 1.71(f)).
guidance: Claims, abstract, and sequence listing should each begin on a new page because each is separately indexed in the Image File Wrapper. There should be no overlap on a single page of more than one section of the disclosure.

name: Spacing, page numbering, and paragraph numbering rules
description: The specification lines should be 1 1/2 or double spaced; pages of the specification including claims and abstract must be numbered consecutively starting with 1; paragraphs (other than claims/abstract) may be numbered at filing and should use Arabic numerals with at least four numerals enclosed in square brackets (e.g., [0001]) and highlighted in bold.
guidance: Paragraph numbers should appear to the right of the left margin as the first item in each paragraph, followed by a gap. Nontext elements (tables, formulae, sequence data) are considered part of the numbered paragraph around or above them and should not be independently numbered. Paragraph or section headers are not considered paragraphs and should not be numbered.

name: Language and translation requirements for non-English filings
description: Applications may be filed in a language other than English, but different requirements apply depending on type of application.
guidance: For nonprovisional applications under 35 U.S.C. 111(a) filed in a language other than English, an English translation, a statement that the translation is accurate, and the processing fee (37 CFR 1.17(i)) are required; if not filed the applicant will be notified and given time to file or face abandonment. For provisional applications (35 U.S.C. 111(b)) filed in a language other than English, an English translation is not required in the provisional application. See § 1.78(a) for claiming benefit of a provisional in a nonprovisional.

name: U.S. not liable for private counsel in court-martial defense
description: A claim by an attorney for services rendered as counsel for an accused officer in a court-martial trial is without merit as against the United States; the Government has nothing to do with its payment.
guidance: Defense counsel fees in court-martial matters are not payable by the United States absent specific statutory authority.

name: No statutory provision for certain travel/collection expenses
description: Claims for time, cost, and expenses incurred in going to collect fees due a civilian witness before a court-martial have no statutory basis for payment.
guidance: Absent a law specifically authorizing payment, such claims should be denied.

name: No claim for detention awaiting trial absent statute
description: A soldier (or civilian wrongly detained on suspicion of desertion) has no legal claim for damages against the United States for a period during which he was detained awaiting trial or clearance, even if innocent in fact.
guidance: Relief for detention-related damages requires express statutory authorization.

name: Erroneous payment recovery: bank vs United States
description: When a pay certificate erroneously given to a soldier was indorsed and presented by banks and paid by a paymaster, the second bank that refunded the paymaster has no legal claim against the United States; its recourse is against the first bank.
guidance: When an erroneous payment is discovered, the remedy of intermediaries is a private action, not a claim against the United States.

name: Paymaster recourse after being 'held responsible' (Court of Claims under sec. 1059 R.S.)
description: When a paymaster seeks relief from liability for public funds stolen while in his charge, he should credit himself in his accounts; if disallowed at the Treasury, his recourse is an application for relief to the Court of Claims under section 1059 R.S. The right to recourse accrues only after the disbursing officer has been 'held responsible' by the accounting officers.
guidance: Administrative accounting determinations must first be made; judicial recourse follows only after being formally held responsible by accounting officers.

name: The role of the claims of a patent
description: Explains that the claims of a patent define the invention and establish the scope of the patentee's rights; they are what the patent owner must prove the defendant infringed.
guidance: Jury should be instructed that the claims, not the specification or prosecution history alone, define what is covered by the patent; claims must be construed to determine their meaning and scope before applying infringement standards.

name: How a claim defines what it covers
description: A claim must be interpreted to determine which devices, methods, or products it covers. The claim language gives notice of what is claimed.
guidance: Provide jurors guidance on reading claim terms in context of the patent as a whole and applying court's claim construction; emphasize plain meaning unless special definitions provided in the specification or by the court.

name: Independent and dependent claims
description: Distinguishes independent claims (stand-alone recitations of the invention) from dependent claims (which refer back to and further limit another claim).
guidance: Jury should understand that dependent claims incorporate the limitations of the claims they depend from and may be narrower in scope.

name: Claim interpretation / claim construction
description: Provides the standard approach and rules for interpreting claim language, including reliance on intrinsic evidence (claims, specification, prosecution history) and, when appropriate, extrinsic evidence (dictionaries, expert testimony).
guidance: Court's construction of disputed claim terms is binding on the jury; instruct jury to apply those constructions when determining infringement or validity.

name: Section 112, paragraph 6 (means-plus-function) claim requirements
description: Explains the rules for claims that invoke 35 U.S.C. §112, para.6 (means-plus-function), i.e., when a claim recites a function to be performed rather than structure, the claim is construed to cover the corresponding structure disclosed in the specification and equivalents.
guidance: If a claim limitation is governed by §112 ¶6, the jury must compare the accused device to the claimed function and the corresponding structure (and equivalents) disclosed in the patent's specification.

name: Infringement — Generally
description: Sets the overarching requirement that the patent owner must prove infringement of at least one claim of the patent by a preponderance of the evidence.
guidance: Instruct jurors that infringement analysis requires comparing accused product/method to the properly construed claim limitations; all claim limitations must be met (either literally or under doctrine of equivalents) for infringement.

name: Direct infringement — Literal infringement
description: Direct (literal) infringement occurs when the accused product or action meets every limitation of a claim exactly as construed.
guidance: Jury must find that each claim limitation is present in the accused product or method as previously defined by the court; if any claim limitation is missing, there is no literal infringement.

name: Direct infringement — Literal infringement of §112, para.6 claim requirements
description: When a claim limitation is governed by §112 ¶6, literal infringement requires that the accused product include the structure corresponding to the claimed function as disclosed in the specification.
guidance: Jury must compare accused device to the specification's disclosed structure for the claimed function; mere performance of the function is insufficient absent the corresponding structure.

name: Direct infringement — Doctrine of equivalents
description: A party may infringe under the doctrine of equivalents if the accused product or process does not literally meet the claim limitations but performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result.
guidance: Provide jurors with the function-way-result test and caution them about limitations on the doctrine (e.g., prosecution history estoppel, prior art) and that it cannot be used to vitiate a claim limitation.

name: Limitations on direct infringement under the doctrine of equivalents
description: Explains restrictions on applying the doctrine of equivalents, including that it cannot be applied so broadly as to cover what the patentee gave up during prosecution or to read out claim limitations.
guidance: Jury should consider prosecution history, claim amendments, and prior art when deciding whether equivalents are barred or limited; the doctrine is fact-specific and cannot erase claim language.

name: Direct infringement: one or more system components located outside the United States
description: Explains when a system claim may or may not be infringed if some components are located outside the U.S.
guidance: Jury must consider whether the acts in the U.S. satisfy all claim limitations under controlling precedent (e.g., whether control/benefit theory or joint enterprise applies).

name: Direct infringement: acts of multiple parties must be combined to meet all claim limitations
description: Addresses situations where no single party performs all claim steps, but collective acts of multiple parties might meet claim limitations.
guidance: Jury should be instructed on standards for attributing others' actions to the defendant (e.g., contractual arrangements, directions, control) and the limitations on proving infringement by divided performance.

name: Validity — Written description requirement
description: Patent specification must contain a written description that shows the inventor had possession of the claimed invention at the time of filing.
guidance: Jury evaluates whether the specification reasonably conveys to a skilled artisan that the inventor had possession of the claimed subject matter; look for adequate disclosure of claimed features.

name: Validity — Enablement requirement
description: Patent must enable a person of ordinary skill in the art to make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
guidance: Jury should consider the scope of the claims, the level of ordinary skill, the breadth of the disclosure, and whether undue experimentation would be needed.

name: Validity — Anticipation (prior art) for pre-AIA patents
description: A claim is anticipated if a single prior art reference discloses each and every limitation of the claimed invention.
guidance: Jury must compare the claim limitations to the prior art reference as a whole; anticipation requires that the prior art enable the claimed invention and be enabling to a person of ordinary skill.

name: Validity — Prior art and obviousness (post-AIA and pre-AIA distinctions)
description: Addresses the applicable prior art framework for patents with effective filing dates before vs on/after March 16, 2013, and the standard for obviousness as a separate ground of invalidity.
guidance: Jury should be instructed which statutory regime applies and, for obviousness, consider the Graham factors and relevant case law (e.g., KSR): (1) scope and content of prior art, (2) differences between prior art and claim, (3) level of ordinary skill, and (4) secondary considerations.

name: Obviousness — Scope and content of the prior art
description: Part of the obviousness inquiry requires evaluating what the prior art discloses relative to the claimed invention.
guidance: Jury should compare claim elements to the prior art, identify differences, and decide whether a person of ordinary skill would be motivated to combine references to reach the claimed invention.

name: Written description requirement standard
description: The objective standard: does the description clearly allow persons of ordinary skill in the art to recognize that he or she invented what is claimed (i.e., that the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention as of the filing date sought).
guidance: Possession may be shown by words, structures, figures, diagrams, formulas, disclosure of a reduction to practice, or showing the invention was 'ready for patenting.' The subject matter need not be described literally (in haec verba), but the disclosure must reasonably convey possession of the later‑claimed subject matter.

name: Each claim limitation must be supported in the disclosure
description: Each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure; if not, the claim must be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre‑AIA 112 first paragraph) or benefit/priority denied.
guidance: If an element described as essential or critical by the applicant is omitted from a claim, the claim fails the written description requirement; ensure that every limitation of the claim is described/supported.

name: Statement of rejection requirements (prima facie showing)
description: When rejecting for lack of written description the examiner should: (A) identify the claim limitation(s) at issue; and (B) establish a prima facie case with reasons why a person skilled in the art would not recognize that the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention from the application as filed.
guidance: A clear statement identifying the limitation and specific reasons (not mere conclusory statements) is required; a simple pinpoint statement may suffice if the support is not apparent and applicant hasn't identified support. See Hyatt v. Dudas.

name: Suggest claim/specification amendments when appropriate (avoid new matter)
description: When appropriate, the Office action should suggest amendments that can be supported by the application's written description, while being mindful of the prohibition against adding new matter.
guidance: Recommend claim narrowing or specific amendments that map to disclosed support; avoid proposing changes that would introduce content beyond the originally filed disclosure (Rasmussen).

name: Genus/subgenus/species support: representative number of species
description: A claimed genus may require disclosure of a representative number of species to be adequately described; a single species supports a genus only in limited circumstances where the disclosure indicates the patentee invented species sufficient to constitute the genus.
guidance: When substantial variation exists within the genus, describe sufficient species reflecting that variation. One species suffices only if it would lead one skilled in the art to the full scope of the genus (Enzo, Rasmussen, AbbVie/Janssen examples). 'Laundry list' disclosures of every possible moiety are often insufficient.

name: Original claim sufficiency (functional language vs how performed)
description: An original claim may lack written description support when it defines the invention in purely functional language specifying a desired result but the disclosure fails to sufficiently identify how the function is performed or the result is achieved.
guidance: Functional claiming without descriptive identifying characteristics (structure, steps, examples) may fail. Also, mere appearance of claim language in the specification does not necessarily satisfy the requirement if the specification does not reasonably convey possession.

name: Omission of a limitation described as essential undermines written description
description: If a claim omits matter that the specification describes as essential or critical to the invention, the claim does not comply with the written description requirement.
guidance: Case examples (Gentry Gallery, Johnson Worldwide) show claims broadening by omitting an 'essential' element can be invalid; examine whether the specification characterizes features as 'only possible' or 'outside the stated purpose' indicating essentiality.

name: Addition of generic claim elements or broadening must be supported
description: Introduction of new claim elements that broaden the claim (e.g., adding generic or broader language, altering numerical ranges) must be supported by the original disclosure or will violate the written description requirement.
guidance: Analyze whether added generic language was reasonably contemplated by the disclosure; consider whether the disclosure teaches against other species or indicates that the inventor possessed the broader subject matter.

name: Range limitations must be supported by original disclosure
description: When claims recite numerical ranges or change numerical limits after filing, determine whether the original disclosure reasonably conveys support for the claimed ranges (including endpoints and open‑ended 'at least' language).
guidance: Open‑ended limits (e.g., 'at least 35%') may read on embodiments outside disclosed ranges and fail written description; use cases (In re Wertheim, Purdue, General Hosp.) to evaluate overlap, explicit maxima/minima, and whether disclosed values convert to ranges.

name: Inherent disclosure/inherency standard
description: To rely on inherent disclosure, extrinsic evidence must make clear that the missing descriptive matter is necessarily present in the thing described and that it would be recognized by persons of ordinary skill; inherency cannot be established by probabilities or possibilities.
guidance: Evaluate whether the specification necessarily includes the property or element claimed, not merely that it might or probably does. Cite In re Robertson and Yeda Research decisions.

name: Interference/count correspondence requires written description support
description: A claim corresponding to a count in an interference proceeding must be supported by the specification as provided by 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre‑AIA 112 first paragraph; an earlier application relied upon for benefit must also meet these requirements for the count subject matter.
guidance: Assess whether the earlier application supplies the disclosure needed for the count; broad generic disclosure to a class of compounds is not sufficient for a specific compound lacking description (Fields v. Conover).

name: Combination elements need not act simultaneously — successive cooperative action can support patentability
description: The rule does not require all parts of a patentable combination to act at the same time; successive action of elementary parts that contributes to a single practical result can form a valid combination.
guidance: Justice Curtis: if arranged so successive action of each contributes to produce one practical result that is the product of the whole, a valid claim may be made. It is enough that, in normal progressive use, the parts co-operate some of the time.

name: Truthfulness and candor: absence of false statements
description: False statements or misrepresentations about one's recognition or status before the USPTO weigh against a finding of good moral character and reputation.
guidance: Specific falsehoods (e.g., a statement claiming that reciprocity had been granted when it had not) are cited as evidence of lack of truthfulness. The Office expects the highest degree of candor and good faith from practitioners (Kingsland v. Dorsey).

name: Ignorance of USPTO rules is not an adequate excuse
description: An applicant's claim that noncompliance resulted from ignorance of USPTO rules or confusion over website guidance does not excuse unauthorized practice or false statements.
guidance: TMEP provisions and CFR language are construed to make the limitations clear (e.g., TMEP §602.06(c) when read in full). The applicant is ultimately responsible for complying with rules; the Director's discretionary authority and clear regulatory text mean ignorance is not a defense.

name: Apply Fintiv factors to parallel ITC proceedings
description: The Board will apply the Fintiv factors when there is a parallel proceeding at the International Trade Commission (ITC).
guidance: Although an ITC final invalidity determination does not have preclusive effect, it is difficult as a practical matter to assert patent claims that the ITC has determined are invalid. Instituting an IPR/PGR where the ITC has set a target date for completing its investigation earlier than the Board's deadline to issue a final written decision may increase duplication and expenses, making denial more likely. Conversely, the Board is less likely to deny institution under Fintiv where the ITC projected final determination date is after the Board's deadline to issue a final written decision. (See Fintiv, Paper 11 at 8-9.)

name: Common violations detected in audits (procedural non-compliance list)
description: Detected violations include: failure to check applications for state secrets; ambiguity in designation of rightholders in state contracts; improper registration activities that misstate ownership (e.g., claiming joint ownership without basis); failure to carry out state inventory of results; failure by contractors to notify state customer of creation of protectable results; failure of state customer to send decisions on form of legal protection to contractor; failure to send patent-research reports; and failure to conduct required patent research.
guidance: 567 violations of compulsory legislative requirements were detected among considered contracts; audits resulted in orders to eliminate violations. Specific example: Roscosmos had created protectable results but had not registered rights or sent required decisions to contractors.

name: Structural property features (baseline)
description: Statistical counts and document-structure derived features computed from specification documents (baseline feature set). Examples listed include: number of characters in title; number of characters in specification; number of sheets of drawings; number of claims; number of independent claims; depth of claims tree; whether IPC includes 'A'; number of combinations of IPC; number of inventors; number of cited references; number of positive expressions.
guidance: Use structural properties as a baseline feature set. Most are simple counts and are easy to compute at large scale. Omit features that require expensive manual work (e.g., number of applications an examiner has examined) when automating for large corpora. Structural features capture surface-level document characteristics but are limited in semantic content.

name: Treatment of international applications and translations
description: Where a prior-filed application serving as a domestic priority claim is an international application, inventions commonly stated in both the domestic-priority-claiming application and the prior-filed international application (limited to specification, claims, or drawings submitted at the international filing date) are considered filed at the international filing date. Korean translation of PCT Articles 19/34 written amendments submitted within the reference date are treated as voluntary amendments under Article 47 of the Patent Act. An examiner may request copies of documents cited in the ISR/IPER where necessary.
guidance: Scope of inventions of an international application relied upon as 'another application' is limited to the inventions described in the specification, claims or drawings of the international application as of the international filing date and its translation; rules differ depending on filing date (before/after Jan 1, 2015). An international application deemed withdrawn for failure to file Korean translation within the specified period cannot be treated as 'another application' for enlarged-concept-of-novelty purposes. For amendments of foreign-language international applns, amended matters are limited to those described in the original document or its Korean translation as of filing; care must be taken when determining added matter under Article 208(3).

name: Statutory categories of grounds for rejection
description: The grounds for rejection include: ① the claimed invention is not patentable pursuant to Articles 25, 29, 32, 36(1),(3) or 44; ② application filed by person not entitled under Article 33(1) or claimed invention not patentable under the proviso of that Article; ③ violation of Treaty provisions; ④ failure to satisfy requirements in Article 42(3)(i), (4), (8) or Article 45; ⑤ an amendment is out of scope prescribed in Article 47(2); ⑥ a divisional filed out of scope (Article 52(1)); ⑦ a converted application filed out of scope (Article 53(1)).
guidance: When issuing a notice, the examiner should reference the relevant statutory provisions (see 5.1(2)). These categories frame reasons for non-final or final rejection and for refusing to enter amendments.

name: Exception — incomprehensible claims due to lack of clarity
description: Where contents of a claimed invention cannot be comprehended due to lack of clarity in the description, the examiner shall notify only the ground(s) for rejection under Article 42(3) or (4) without conducting prior art search or assessing novelty/inventive step.
guidance: However, if the lack of clarity is insignificant such that understanding is possible, the examiner shall conduct prior art search and review patentability to the extent of comprehension, and notify those grounds together with Article 42(3),(4) violations.

name: Exception — certain grounds to be notified without patentability assessment
description: Where it is certain that a claim has newly added matter, or where uncertainty exists under Article 32 (e.g., contravention of public order), or where it is clear the claim is not a statutory subject matter or not industrially applicable, the examiner shall notify those grounds for rejection without judging novelty or inventive step.
guidance: These are grounds that can be addressed independently of patentability assessments and should be raised immediately in the notice.

name: Form and specificity of notices — stipulate provisions and claim-level basis
description: When notifying a ground for rejection, the examiner shall stipulate the relevant provisions of the Act or laws. For multiple claims, grounds for rejection should be indicated on a claim-by-claim basis.
guidance: Details on claim-level examination are referenced in Section 5.4; notices should make it clear which claim each ground pertains to to enable focused applicant response.

name: Inventive-step rejection must explain differences to closest prior art
description: When notifying rejection for lack of inventive step, the examiner shall clearly describe the difference between the invention recited in the claims and the closest prior art reference.
guidance: Exception: if both lack of novelty and lack of inventive step are notified together, the examiner may follow the novelty assessment method for the novelty ground and may notify inventive-step rejection on the logic that a skilled person could easily make the invention from the prior art (i.e., where the claimed invention is identical to the prior art). See Part 3, Chapter 3, 5.1 for inventive step assessment procedure.

name: Decision to reject based on same claim when prior opportunity provided
description: A decision to reject an application may be made when the claimed invention still lacks novelty or inventive step over the same reference(s) relied upon in the original notice and the applicant has had an opportunity to submit written arguments.
guidance: In principle, rejection is permissible when (①) the concerned claim is rejected under the same statutory provision and (②) the claim lacks novelty/inventive step over the same reference or same combination of references. Example: claim amended by adding an element described in the description but still lacks inventive step over the same reference — rejection can be made.

name: Decision to reject based on other claims (identity/substantial identity)
description: If a claim under examination is amended to be identical (including 'substantially identical') to another claim which was rejected, a decision to reject the amended claim can be made on the basis of the grounds previously notified to the other claim.
guidance: Examples show amended claim becoming identical to previously-rejected claim or adding limitations of another rejected claim; in such cases a rejection decision based on prior notice is allowed.

name: When amendment necessitates a new ground (new combination of references)
description: If an amendment causes the need to rely on a new combination of references to reject the amended claim, a new ground of rejection is considered necessary and, depending on the stage of examination, the examiner shall issue a second office action (non-final) or refuse to enter the amendment and continue examination with the original claim.
guidance: Examples illustrate cases where amendments introduce elements requiring new reference combinations. If the new combination arose from simple errors in a prior notice, the examiner should refuse entry of the amendment rather than issue a decision to reject based on the new combination.

name: Determination whether applicant was given opportunity re: description deficiencies
description: Where a term or phrase found to be indefinite in a claim is changed by amendment, the applicant may not be considered to have had a realistic opportunity to respond (they could amend without recognizing the deficiency), and thus a decision to reject cannot be made without special circumstances.
guidance: Only where the amended claim still fails to overcome the previously-notified ground and the claim language substantially coincides with the previously-notified language may rejection proceed without a new opportunity. Examples clarify when non-final vs final rejection should be issued depending on whether claim language changed and whether prior-notified deficient language persists.

name: Broadest reasonable interpretation for claim analysis
description: Claims are analyzed for eligibility in accordance with their broadest reasonable interpretation.
guidance: Apply the broadest reasonable interpretation when determining whether claims fall into statutory categories and when assessing whether they are directed to a judicial exception or include additional elements that add significantly more. Examples throughout the guidance use this interpretive standard.

name: Step 1 — Statutory category check
description: Determine whether the claim is directed to a statutory category (e.g., composition of matter, process, machine, or manufacture).
guidance: If a claim is not directed to any statutory category, it fails Step 1. If it is directed to a statutory category, proceed to the judicial-exception analysis (Step 2A). Examples: the guidance treats compositions of matter (bacteria, nucleic acids, antibodies, cells, food compositions) as statutory categories (Step 1: YES).

name: Step 2A — Judicial exception: product of nature analysis
description: Determine whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception such as a 'product of nature' (i.e., whether it claims something that exists in nature). For nature-based products, use the 'markedly different characteristics' analysis to decide if the claimed product is an exception.
guidance: If the claimed nature-based product is not markedly different from its natural counterpart, the claim is directed to a product-of-nature exception (Step 2A: YES) and proceeds to Step 2B. If it is markedly different, it is not directed to the exception (Step 2A: NO) and qualifies as eligible subject matter. Examples: bacterial mixtures, nucleic acids, antibodies, cells, foods are analyzed under this test.

name: Markedly different characteristics (core criterion)
description: A claimed nature-based product must have 'markedly different characteristics' (structural, functional, or other) compared to its naturally occurring counterpart to avoid being a product-of-nature exception.
guidance: Characteristics may be structural (sequence, chemical bonds, single-molecule vs. separate molecules), functional (new biological activities, infectivity, expression patterns, growth rates), or other observable differences. Examples: (i) a bacterial combination that causes one species to infect a new plant species; (ii) nucleic acid sequence substitutions or labels that change function or structure; (iii) vectors combining heterologous sequences; (iv) chimeric/humanized/variant antibodies; (v) cells with induced phenotypic changes (marker expression, increased oxygen utilization); (vi) mixed cell populations with interacting cells producing new biological properties.

name: Claims that encompass natural and non-natural embodiments — effect on eligibility
description: If a claim covers both embodiments that are identical to what exists in nature and embodiments that are changed, the claim can be directed to a product-of-nature exception because it encompasses natural embodiments.
guidance: Example: a claim to 'an antibody to Protein S' that covers naturally occurring murine or coyote antibodies as well as engineered antibodies fails the marked-difference test because at least some embodiments are identical to nature. Narrowing the claim (e.g., to human antibodies, specific CDR sequences, chimeric/humanized antibodies, or variant Fc domains) can render it eligible.

name: Antibody-specific markers of marked difference
description: Limiting antibody claims to non-naturally occurring antibodies or engineered changes can establish marked differences.
guidance: Claims limited to human antibodies (where no human antibodies to the antigen occur naturally), to antibodies defined by specific CDR sequences (e.g., SEQ ID NOs), to chimeric or humanized antibodies (fusion proteins combining parts of different species), or to antibodies comprising engineered variant Fc domains (amino acid modifications) are treated as having different structural and/or functional characteristics and thus can be eligible. A broad claim to 'an antibody' that includes naturally occurring antibodies fails the marked-difference test.

name: Step 2B — 'Significantly more' analysis
description: If a claim is directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: YES), determine whether the claim as a whole includes additional elements or combinations that amount to 'significantly more' than the exception such that the claim is eligible.
guidance: Elements that are well-understood, routine, and conventional (e.g., generic containers) do not add significantly more. Recitations at a high level of generality that merely instruct practitioners to use known techniques typically fail Step 2B. Conversely, combinations or specific limitations that confine the claim to a particular useful application and demonstrably improve the relevant technology (e.g., scaffold+cells that facilitate faster tissue regeneration) can amount to 'significantly more' and render the claim eligible. The analysis asks whether any element or combination ensures the claim amounts to more than the judicial exception itself.

name: Generic laboratory steps or well-understood elements do not confer eligibility
description: Routine, conventional laboratory practices (e.g., isolating cells, placing cells in generic containers) do not supply the 'significantly more' needed to transform a claim directed to a product-of-nature into eligible subject matter.
guidance: Example: a claim reciting a population of cells 'in a container' is insufficient when the container is recited at a high level of generality and is normally used in the art. Such recitations merely tell a scientist to use existing, routine equipment and therefore add nothing significant.

name: Specific combination elements can add 'significantly more' if they improve technology or confine application
description: A claim element or combination that is not routine and that confines the claim to a particular useful application or improves a technological field may supply 'significantly more.'
guidance: Example: pacemaker cells combined with a biocompatible three-dimensional scaffold (not general container) that facilitates faster tissue regeneration and is not merely routine can render the claim 'significantly more' and eligible. The scaffold plus cells provided a specific improvement in regenerative medicine rather than a generic linking of elements.

name: Funk Brothers principle — discovery of natural quality is not patentable
description: Discovering that natural strains or species have certain qualities (e.g., non-inhibition) and packaging them together without altering their properties is not patentable subject matter.
guidance: An applicant's discovery of natural properties and the mere application/aggregation of those properties (e.g., selecting non-inhibitive strains and packaging them as an inoculant) is considered an application of nature's handiwork and may fail the marked-difference test. The aggregation produces no new organisms, no structural change, and no enlargement of utility; such claims were held ineligible in Funk Brothers.

name: Mixture existence in nature — burden on examiner
description: If an examiner asserts a claimed mixture exists in nature and uses that to deny marked difference, the examiner must show that the particular mixture exists in nature.
guidance: Even if the components could theoretically occur together in nature, eligibility is not negated unless the examiner can demonstrate that the claimed particular mixture actually exists in nature. Reference: Myriad footnote and examples where absence of proof of natural occurrence supports eligibility.

name: The European patent application — Content (other than claims)
description: Requirements for the content of a European patent application outside of the claims (description, abstract, drawings etc.).
guidance: See Part F, Chapter II and Annexes (checklist for abstract, units) for specifics and examples.

name: Address utility and specification sufficiency
description: Respond to rejections concerning the invention's utility or insufficiency of the specification by proving usefulness and adequate disclosure.
guidance: Provide evidence or explanation of utility and ensure the specification enables a person skilled in the art to practice the invention; amend specification or claims only in compliance with written description and enablement rules.

name: Address procedural and formal rejections
description: Correct errors in formal aspects (improper claim drafting, inadequate drawings, non-compliance with format rules) that lead to procedural rejections.
guidance: Ensure compliance with office formatting, drawing, and formal filing requirements. Small formal errors can lead to wasted cycles; maintain meticulous attention to procedural rules.

name: Amendments must comply with strict claim-scope rules
description: Amendments made in response to rejections must follow strict rules, particularly concerning claim scope and not impermissibly broadening claims.
guidance: Ensure amendments address examiner concerns without introducing new matter or improperly broadening claim scope. Balance narrowing to overcome rejections with preserving claim value.

name: Provide persuasive factual and legal arguments and claim amendment suggestions
description: Responses should include persuasive factual and legal argumentation and, where appropriate, well-considered claim amendments.
guidance: Use tailored legal reasoning and factual support targeted to the examiner's grounds (novelty, obviousness, utility, etc.). Suggested amendments should strategically overcome rejections while maintaining protection.

name: Time of deposit — general rule (no later than filing date / priority date)
description: The deposit must be made not later than the filing date of the patent application (or, where priority is claimed, by the priority date).
guidance: Explicitly stated for Spain, Sweden, EPO, Ukraine, MK (Macedonia) and others. Some jurisdictions allow narrow additional time for filing evidence in limited circumstances (e.g., Macedonia: evidence may be filed additionally for valid reasons within 90 days).

name: Patent Scope (IPC classes)
description: Number of distinct IPC sub-classes assigned to the patent.
guidance: Greater number of IPC subclasses suggests broader claimed scope. Use with claim-count metrics and normalization by technology area to infer breadth of technical coverage.

name: Claim Count and Independent Claim Count
description: Total number of claims and number of independent claims in the patent.
guidance: Higher claim counts and more independent claims can signal a broader scope strategy. Combine with IPC-based scope metrics and examination outcomes to assess asserted breadth.

name: Claim of ownership before domestic courts (layout designs)
description: If the layout design has already been registered, claim of ownership shall be filed before the competent domestic court; the action shall lapse within three years from publication of the registration certificate. Action brought against a defendant who acts in bad faith is not subject to statutory limitations.
guidance: Final decision transferring registration shall be communicated to the Organization for recording and publication (Article 38).

name: Priority claiming procedure and effects
description: To claim priority under the International Convention, applicant must submit application to the Organization within 12 months of earlier filing. Applicant must attach or submit within six months a written statement specifying date/number/country of earlier filing and a certified copy of the earlier application. Where multiple earlier applications exist, priority may be based only on the earliest. Priority deems application as filed on date of first application for protection conditions; applicant may request deferment of examination for not more than two years from expiry of priority term or three years from filing date of first application.
guidance: Failure to submit required items in time results in loss of priority; items received more than six months after filing are inadmissible (Article 14).

name: Compact prosecution / initial comprehensive review
description: Under the principles of compact prosecution, each claim should be reviewed for compliance with every statutory requirement for patentability in the initial review of the application. Examiners should state all reasons and bases for rejecting claims in the first Office action.
guidance: Deficiencies should be explained clearly, particularly when they serve as a basis for a rejection. Whenever practicable, examiners and patent reexamination specialists should indicate how rejections may be overcome and how problems may be resolved. A failure to follow this approach can lead to unnecessary delays in prosecution.

name: Identify and understand any asserted utility
description: The claimed invention as a whole must be useful. Examiners should review the application to identify any asserted utility.
guidance: A complete disclosure should contain some indication of the practical application for the claimed invention (why the applicant asserts the invention is useful). The utility statement must enable one of ordinary skill in the art to understand why the applicant asserts the invention is useful. The application may describe more than one utility, but only one is necessary; alternatively, the examiner may rely on contemporaneous art establishing a well‑established utility. See MPEP §2107 for utility examination guidelines.

name: Claims define property rights — perform thorough claim analysis
description: Claims define the property rights provided by a patent and require careful scrutiny to identify the boundaries of protection sought and how claims relate to the inventor's indicated invention.
guidance: Examiners must determine scope by thoroughly analyzing the claim language before checking statutory compliance. Begin by identifying and evaluating each claim limitation (steps for processes; structures/materials for products). Correlate each claim limitation to all portions of the disclosure that describe it, in all cases — including means-/step-plus-function language. Consider grammar and plain meaning as understood by one of ordinary skill; some language may raise questions as to limiting effect (see list A–F in MPEP: preamble/field of use, 'adapted to/for', 'wherein/whereby', contingent limitations, printed matter, terms with functional language). Do not dissect a claim into elements and evaluate in isolation; consider the claim as a whole.

name: Conduct a thorough prior art search
description: Prior to evaluating patentability, examiners are expected to conduct a thorough search of the prior art.
guidance: Search both claimed and unclaimed aspects of the invention if there is reasonable expectation the unclaimed aspects may be later claimed. Account for structure/materials described in the specification and their equivalents corresponding to claimed means-/step-plus-function limitations, in accordance with 35 U.S.C. 112(f) and MPEP §§2181–2186. See MPEP §§904–904.03 for how to conduct a search.

name: Determine compliance with 35 U.S.C. 101 (subject matter eligibility and utility)
description: Section 101 has been interpreted as imposing four requirements: (i) only one patent may be obtained for an invention; (ii) inventor(s) identification requirements; (iii) the claimed invention must be eligible for patenting; and (iv) the claimed invention must be useful (have utility).
guidance: Patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 101 is a threshold inquiry, but even if eligible the claim must also satisfy 102, 103, and 112. Examiners should avoid focusing solely on 101 to the detriment of other statutory requirements. See MPEP §§2104, 2106, 2107 for details.

name: Evaluate compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(b) — definiteness and claiming what inventor regards as invention
description: 35 U.S.C. 112(b) contains two distinct requirements: (A) that the claims set forth the subject matter the inventor regards as the invention, and (B) that the claims particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention.
guidance: An application is deficient under the first requirement when evidence outside the application shows the inventor regards the invention as different from what is claimed. An application fails the second requirement when claims do not set out and define the invention with reasonable precision and particularity; definiteness must be analyzed in light of the disclosure as interpreted by one of ordinary skill. See MPEP §§2171–2173 and related subsections for particulars, including 112(f) scope and related issues.

name: Written description requirement
description: An applicant's specification must reasonably convey to those skilled in the art that the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention as of the date of invention.
guidance: See MPEP §2163 for standards, typical circumstances where issues arise, burden on the examiner, changes to claim scope, and relationship to new matter and amendments.

name: Enablement requirement
description: An applicant's specification must enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
guidance: Complex experimentation is not undue if persons of skill routinely engage in it. Consider tests of enablement, undue experimentation factors, working and prophetic examples, predictability of the art, and quantity of experimentation. See MPEP §2164 and subsections (2164.01–2164.08) for evaluation details including examples in chemical, biological, and computer programming cases.

name: Determine compliance with 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 (novelty and nonobviousness)
description: Reviewing for 102 and 103 begins with comparing claimed subject matter to what is known in the prior art. If no differences are found, the claim lacks novelty (35 U.S.C. 102). If differences are found, assess whether those differences render the claim nonobvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art (35 U.S.C. 103).
guidance: If differences exist, assess them in light of knowledge of a person of ordinary skill to determine obviousness. Use MPEP §§2131–2146 (anticipation/102) and §§2141–2146 (obviousness/103) for guidance including scope/content of prior art, level of ordinary skill, prima facie obviousness, reasonable expectation of success, and consideration of applicant rebuttal arguments and evidence.

name: Step 1 — statutory category
description: Evaluate Step 1: Does this claim fall within at least one statutory category?
guidance: Determine whether the claim recites a statutory category (e.g., process, machine, manufacture, composition). Example: A non-transitory computer-readable storage medium is a "manufacture" and thus Step 1 = Yes because the BRI covers only statutory embodiments (not a transitory signal). If claim recites a series of steps, it may be a "process."

name: Step 2A Prong One — identify abstract idea / judicial exception
description: Evaluate Step 2A Prong One: (a) identify the specific limitation(s) in the claim that you believe recite an abstract idea; and (b) determine whether the identified limitation(s) falls within at least one of the groupings of abstract ideas enumerated in MPEP 2106.04(a)(2).
guidance: Map claimed limitations to abstract-idea groupings (e.g., mathematical concepts, mental processes, laws of nature). Examples from the guidance: converting time-frequency representation into embeddings is a mathematical equation in prose; clustering with k-means is a mathematical calculation; applying binary masks is a mathematical calculation; comparing a PRS against top-quartile reference values is a mental process; describing genotype-phenotype relationships can implicate a law of nature.

name: Step 2A Prong Two — additional elements and practical application
description: Evaluate Step 2A Prong Two: (a) identify whether there are any additional elements recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception; and (b) evaluate those additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether the claim as a whole integrates the exception into a practical application.
guidance: Consider whether additional elements meaningfully limit the abstract idea or show an improvement to technology/technical field. Elements that merely gather data or perform generic steps may be "insignificant extra-solution activity." By contrast, reciting specific technical steps or improvements (e.g., DNN-aided cluster assignments that are synthesized into time-domain waveforms and produce a technical improvement) can integrate the exception into a practical application.

name: Step 2B — inventive concept (significantly more than the judicial exception)
description: Evaluate Step 2B: Does the claim provide an inventive concept, i.e., does the claim recite additional element(s) or a combination of elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception in the claim?
guidance: Determine whether additional elements (or their combination) add significantly more than the abstract idea. Mere instructions to apply the exception or insignificant extra-solution activity cannot provide an inventive concept. Example: a generic directive to administer an "appropriate treatment" does not supply an inventive concept; routine laboratory techniques (e.g., analyzing DNA to provide sequence information) are insufficient.

name: Integration into practical application — indicators of meaningful limitation
description: Factors that indicate a claim integrates the judicial exception into a practical application (i.e., meaningfully limits the abstract idea).
