guidance: Indicators include reciting technical improvements to computer technology or another technical field, reciting details of how a machine (e.g., a DNN) performs the claimed steps that produce a technical result, and using the exception to identify a specific population and implement a particular treatment tailored to that population (e.g., administering Compound X eye drops to glaucoma patients identified as high risk by PRS).

name: Broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) for claim construction
description: Use the broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the specification to determine the scope of claim terms and embodiments.
guidance: Interpret claim limitations in view of the specification; do not disregard limitations simply because they appear in a "wherein" clause — a wherein clause can have patentable weight. The BRI may distinguish between statutory and non-statutory embodiments (e.g., excluding transitory signals when the claim recites a non-transitory medium).

name: Mapping limitations to abstract-idea groupings (examples)
description: Specific examples of mapping claim limitations to abstract-idea groupings (mathematical concepts, mental processes, laws of nature).
guidance: Concrete mappings provided: converting a time-frequency representation into embeddings = mathematical concept; clustering embeddings with k-means = mathematical calculation; applying binary masks = mathematical calculation; extracting spectral features and generating words = processing leading to transcription (may involve abstract ideas); calculating a weighted polygenic risk score by multiplication and addition = mathematical calculation; comparing PRS to known thresholds = mental process; describing genotype-phenotype relationships = law of nature.

name: Particularity/specific treatment can provide meaningful limits
description: A dependent claim that adds particularity (specific treatment, drug, or technical step) can meaningfully limit the abstract idea and integrate it into a practical application.
guidance: Example: Claim 2 specifying that the "appropriate treatment is Compound X eye drops" was found to give the claim patentable weight where the particular treatment is tied to the identified patient population, and thus the abstract idea is used to deliver a particular treatment to a defined group.

name: No fixed list; case-by-case analysis
description: There is no fixed list of terms that automatically render a claim eligible or ineligible; SME analysis is fact- and claim-specific.
guidance: The 2024 AI SME Update reiterates that USPTO guidance in MPEP Sections 2103–2106.07(c) applies across technologies and that the examples provided are illustrative; examiners and practitioners must evaluate every claim on a case-by-case basis.

name: Formal training topics provided to attorneys (Q44)
description: Whether the firm provides formal training (other than one-on-one mentorship/review) to attorneys on topics such as Business development; Personal growth or development; Leadership; Practice skills (e.g., claim drafting, case law review); Team dynamics or team building.
guidance: Yes percentages shown overall and by firm-size/segment with Number of Firms Reporting; table notes 'Percentages based on total of all respondents.'

name: Respondent brief limited scope
description: The respondent brief shall be limited to issues raised in the appellant brief to which the respondent brief is directed (37 CFR 41.68(a)(3)).
guidance: Respondent may include arguments previously made of record or supporting the examiner’s findings with respect to claims addressed in the opposing party’s appellant brief, but may not propose new grounds of rejection (especially requester respondents).

name: Respondent brief — Status of claims statement
description: A statement accepting or disputing appellant’s statement of the status of claims; if disputed, specify errors with particularity (37 CFR 41.68(b)(1)(iii)).
guidance: If respondent disputes appellant’s status statement, the respondent must identify the precise errors rather than merely asserting disagreement.

name: Respondent brief — Summary of claimed subject matter
description: A statement accepting or disputing appellant’s summary of the subject matter defined in each independent claim involved; if disputed, specify the errors (37 CFR 41.68(b)(1)(v)).
guidance: If disputing, explain precisely why appellant’s summary is incorrect.

name: Examiner’s answer — scope and obligation to respond to briefs
description: Primary examiner may furnish a written answer to appellant and/or respondent briefs explaining the invention, references relied on, grounds of rejection, and reasons for patentability; the answer should provide a written statement in answer to each appellant and each respondent brief (37 CFR 41.69 and MPEP guidance).
guidance: The examiner’s answer should call attention to errors in appellant’s copy of claims, report conclusions on affidavits/declarations/exhibits admitted to the record, and include rebuttal of all arguments in the briefs. If a ground or reason is not addressed, the proceeding will be remanded by the Board to the examiner.

name: Examiner’s answer — required items (A–N)
description: The examiner’s answer must include, in the order indicated, items such as: Real Party in Interest; Related Appeals and Interferences; Status of Claims; Status of Amendments; Summary of Claimed Subject Matter; Grounds of Rejection to be Reviewed on Appeal (with subheadings); Findings of Patentability to be Reviewed (with subheadings); Claims Appendix; Evidence Relied Upon; Grounds of Rejection explanations; Determinations of Patentability explanations; explicit no-new-ground statement; Response to Argument; Related Proceedings Appendix; and Period for Providing a Rebuttal Brief (MPEP § 2677 I.(A)-(N)).
guidance: The answer must follow the order and include subheadings and 'None' where appropriate; failure to include required items can lead to remand or other corrective action.

name: Grounds of rejection explanations — 35 U.S.C. 112 first paragraph (written description/enablement)
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, the examiner’s answer must explain how the first paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112 is not complied with, including how the specification and drawings do not describe the subject matter and/or would not enable a person skilled in the art without undue experimentation (MPEP § 2677 I.(I)(1)).
guidance: Include consideration of undue experimentation factors (see MPEP § 2164.01(a)). Explain specifically how spec/drawings fail to describe/enable each rejected claim.

name: Grounds of rejection explanations — 35 U.S.C. 112 second paragraph (definiteness)
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, the examiner’s answer must explain how the claims do not particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter (MPEP § 2677 I.(I)(2)).
guidance: Provide concrete explanations identifying claim language that fails to meet the definiteness standard.

name: Grounds of rejection explanations — 35 U.S.C. 102 (anticipation)
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102, the examiner’s answer must explain why the rejected claims are anticipated, pointing out where all specific limitations recited in the rejected claims are found in the prior art relied upon (MPEP § 2677 I.(I)(3)).
guidance: Cite specific locations (page/col/line/drawing) in the reference where each claim limitation appears.

name: Grounds of rejection explanations — 35 U.S.C. 103 (obviousness)
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103, the examiner’s answer must state the ground of rejection, point out where each specific limitation is found in the prior art, identify differences between the rejected claims and the prior art (primary reference), and explain why it would have been obvious to modify the primary reference to arrive at the claimed subject matter (MPEP § 2677 I.(I)(4)).
guidance: Explain the rationale for combining references and why the combination would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill at the time of the invention.

name: Feature-by-feature comparison when correspondence unclear
description: Where questions remain as to how limitations in the claims correspond to features in the art, the examiner must compare at least one rejected claim feature-by-feature with the art relied upon, aligning claim language side-by-side with references to specific page/column/line/drawing reference and quotations as appropriate (MPEP § 2677 I.(I)(5)).
guidance: This comparison should be explicit and precise to show where each limitation is found or why it is not met.

name: Determinations of patentability — required explanations
description: For each determination of patentability (inapplicability of a proposed rejection), the examiner’s answer must provide a clear explanation why the proposed-for-rejection claims are not subject to the proposed rejection, with parallel, specific requirements for 112(1), 112(2), 102, 103 (MPEP § 2677 I.(J)(1)-(5)).
guidance: Explain which claim limitations are not found in the proposed-rejection art, identify differences, and explain why the claimed subject matter is patentable; if the requester’s rejection is a combination, explain rationale for not making that combination.

name: Response to argument requirement in examiner’s answer
description: The examiner’s answer must state whether the examiner disagrees with each contention of appellants and respondents and explain the reasons for disagreement; if any ground of rejection or inapplicability is not argued/responded to by the appropriate party, examiner must point out each claim affected (MPEP § 2677 I.(L)).
guidance: Provide reasoned explanations and cite the parts of the record supporting the examiner’s position.

name: Alice/Mayo two-part test (Step 2A/2B) – baseline eligibility evaluation
description: All claims must be evaluated for eligibility using the two-part test from Alice/Mayo: (1) determine whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A); and if so, (2) determine whether the claim elements individually or as an ordered combination add significantly more such that the claim amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception (Step 2B).
guidance: If a claim is not directed to an exception at Step 2A, or amounts to significantly more than any recited exception in Step 2B, the claim is eligible even if it fails the machine-or-transformation test. Conversely, a claim is ineligible under Alice/Mayo even if it would pass the machine-or-transformation test. Use the Alice/Mayo framework as the controlling test and treat other tests (e.g., machine-or-transformation) only as helpful clues, not as stand-alone determinative tests.

name: Improvement to existing technology (improvement consideration)
description: Whether the claim provides an improvement in technology or in a technical field — i.e., an improvement in an existing technological process, device, or system — is relevant to the eligibility analysis.
guidance: Claims that describe how the claimed elements enable automation or otherwise improve a technological process (e.g., specific rules that enabled automation of animation tasks, modifications to machinery or processes, new methods of downloading/streaming, particular data-compression methods, novel sensor configurations, etc.) can weigh in favor of eligibility. Improvement must be to technology itself (not merely an improvement in an abstract idea or business practice). Examples of sufficient improvements: particular computerized operation of a rubber molding press (Diamond v. Diehr), new telephone/server combinations (TLI Communications), improved downloading for streaming (Affinity Labs), improved data compression (DDR Holdings / Intellectual Ventures), specific GUIs that improve trader transaction accuracy, improved process for preserving hepatocytes (Rapid Litigation Mgmt.). Examples of insufficient improvements: applying a commonplace business method on a general purpose computer (Alice), merely improving information available to a trader without improving computers or technology (Trading Technologies v. IBG). To show a computer assists in improving technology, claims should recite details about how a computer aids the method, the extent of aid, or the significance of the computer — mere generic computer components or instructions to apply an exception are insufficient (see MPEP §2106.05(f)).

name: Particular transformation (machine-or-transformation / article transformation clue)
description: Determine whether the claim effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing; such a transformation is a clue to patentability for process claims that do not include particular machines.
guidance: An 'article' includes a physical object or substance that must be particular (specifically identifiable). 'Transformation' means the article changes to a different state or thing, usually more than mere relocation. A transformation resulting in a new or different function/use is stronger evidence of significantly more. Mental processes or mere manipulation of abstract data do not qualify as eligible transformations. Relevant factors: (1) particularity vs generality of the transformation (more particular favors eligibility); (2) degree to which the recited article is particular (generic recitation disfavors eligibility); (3) nature/extent of the change in state or thing (change of function/use favors eligibility; mere location change does not); (4) nature of the article transformed (physical/tangible transformations weigh more than transformations of intangible concepts); (5) whether the transformation is merely extra-solution activity or a field-of-use limitation (nominal contribution disfavors eligibility). Examples: transformative chemical/physical processes (Tilghman; Diamond v. Diehr) contrast with data-only manipulations or field-of-use steps (Mayo). The M-or-T test is a clue only; always apply Alice/Mayo as controlling.

name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity (Step 2B consideration)
description: In Step 2B, determine whether additional claim elements (beyond the judicial exception) are well-understood, routine, and conventional activities known in the art; if so, they do not amount to 'significantly more.'
guidance: If additional elements are specific limitations that are unconventional or confine the claim to a particular useful application, this favors eligibility (example: DDR Holdings where claims modified conventional hyperlink behavior to produce a hybrid webpage). If additional elements are merely well-known or routine (example: Mayo, where measuring metabolites by any known process was routine), then they do not supply an inventive concept. Evaluation of this consideration overlaps with the improvement consideration, the 'mere instructions to apply an exception' consideration (MPEP §2106.05(f)), and the insignificant extra-solution activity consideration (MPEP §2106.05(g)). Note: whether an element is known in the art (novelty/obviousness) is a different question from whether it is routine/conventional for Step 2B purposes; a feature known in the art can still be unconventional in how it is used and thus favor eligibility (e.g., Enfish features were non-conventional despite prior art). Examiners should analyze whether additional elements, alone or in combination, meaningfully transform the exception into a patent-eligible application rather than simply reciting routine activity at a high level of generality.

name: Transitional phrases define claim scope (case-by-case)
description: The transitional phrases 'comprising', 'consisting essentially of' and 'consisting of' define the scope of a claim with respect to what unrecited additional components or steps, if any, are excluded from the scope of the claim. The determination of what is or is not excluded by a transitional phrase must be made on a case-by-case basis in light of the facts of each case.
guidance: Interpretation depends on particular facts and the specification; no automatic rule applies beyond the general meanings of the common transitional phrases. Always read transitional language in light of the remainder of the claim and the specification.

name: Comprising — open-ended / inclusive transition
description: The transitional term 'comprising' (synonymous with 'including,' 'containing,' or 'characterized by') is inclusive or open-ended and does not exclude additional, unrecited elements or method steps.
guidance: Use 'comprising' when an open-ended claim is intended. Case law examples: courts have held 'comprising' permits additional steps (Invitrogen) and additional components (Gillette: a claim 'comprising' guard, cap and group of blades encompassed razors with more than three blades). Even when a Markush group is used to list alternatives, a 'comprising' transition can allow additional components functionally similar to listed members (Amgen v. Amneal). The term signals that named elements are essential but that other elements may be added and still be within claim scope.

name: Consisting of — closed / exclusive transition
description: The transitional phrase 'consisting of' excludes any element, step, or ingredient not specified in the claim (except for ordinary impurities).
guidance: Use 'consisting of' to close the claim to unrecited elements. A claim depending from a claim that 'consists of' the recited elements cannot add another element or step. However, closure under 'consisting of' applies to the clause in which it appears (a body-clause 'consisting of' creates an exceptionally strong presumption that that claim term is closed to unrecited elements), and does not necessarily exclude other separate elements of the claim as a whole. There are factual exceptions (e.g., Norian v. Stryker: an added spatula unrelated to the claimed invention did not avoid infringement). For Markush group selections, 'consisting of' indicates a closed group for selection unless the claim includes qualifying language indicating combinations/mixtures are intended.

name: Consisting essentially of — middle-ground transition (material-effect test)
description: The transitional phrase 'consisting essentially of' limits the scope of a claim to the specified materials or steps 'and those that do not materially affect the basic and novel characteristic(s)' of the claimed invention.
guidance: 'Consisting essentially of' occupies a middle ground between 'consisting of' (closed) and 'comprising' (open). To exclude additional steps or components under this phrase, the applicant must show that the additional matter would materially change the basic and novel characteristics of the invention. If the specification does not identify what the basic and novel characteristics are, courts may construe 'consisting essentially of' as equivalent to 'comprising' for purposes of 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103. Specification statements (e.g., numerical limits or discussion of deleterious effects) can establish what materially alters the invention (see AK Steel example). The applicant bears the burden to establish exclusion by 'consisting essentially of.' This language can be used for compositions or method steps (Ex parte Hoffman).

name: Markush groups and mixtures — presumption of closed group; drafting to include mixtures
description: A claim element defined by selection from a group of alternatives (a Markush grouping) is presumed closed to alternatives outside the list unless qualifying language indicates otherwise.
guidance: If the drafter intends to encompass combinations or mixtures of the alternatives in a Markush group, include qualifying language such as 'at least one member selected from the group' or 'or mixtures thereof.' In the absence of such language, there is a presumption that the Markush group is closed to combinations or mixtures. Intrinsic evidence in dependent claims or specification statements can overcome this presumption (see Multilayer Stretch Cling Film). For open claims using 'comprising', additional functionally similar components outside the Markush group may still be within scope (see Amgen v. Amneal). See MPEP § 2117 for further discussion.

name: Location of transition (preamble vs clause) matters
description: When 'consisting of' (or other transitional language) appears in a clause of the body of a claim rather than immediately following the preamble, there is an exceptionally strong presumption that the term set off with 'consisting of' is closed to unrecited elements of that clause.
guidance: A body-clause 'consisting of' limits only the element set forth in that clause; it does not necessarily close the claim as a whole. Conversely, a transition immediately following the preamble (e.g., 'the apparatus consisting of:') can signal closure of the claimed combination. Always analyze the syntactic location of the transitional phrase when construing scope.

name: Other transitional phrases ('having', 'composed of') — fact-specific interpretation
description: Transitional phrases such as 'having' and 'composed of' must be interpreted in light of the specification to determine whether open or closed claim language is intended; 'composed of' may be interpreted like either 'consisting of' or 'consisting essentially of' depending on the facts.
guidance: Do not assume a uniform meaning for less-common transitions. 'Having' has been interpreted as open in some contexts but does not create a universal presumption of openness. 'Composed of' may be treated as 'consisting of' or 'consisting essentially of' depending on specification and evidence (see AFG Industries and Bertsch). Evaluate specification language and intrinsic/extrinsic evidence to determine intended scope.

name: Specification requirements for architectural-design inventions
description: Architectural-design inventions combine space(s) with function(s); functions of spaces must be stated in claim(s) and the description, and interactions among unit-space functions should be described when the functional effect is not recognizable from placement alone.
guidance: When shape and structure of things are directly stated in claims, also state the function of the space and interactions among functions in the specification to adequately define the invention.

name: Clarity of invention category for architectural-design claims
description: Because architectural-design expressions (apartment design, floor plan, structure system, plan system) may blur whether the claim is for a product or a method, the category of claimed subject matter must be clear.
guidance: Clearly specify whether the invention is a product (e.g., apartment), a method for constructing a product, or a method for designing. Example: a claim described as a 'method of designing' but actually claiming a product combination should be recast as a product claim.

name: Novelty and inventive-step assessment for architectural-design inventions
description: Objectives and effects of architectural-design inventions are associated with function of unit spaces and interactions among functions; when assessing novelty/inventive step, function and effect must be considered.
guidance: Do not construe claims by excluding the function; excluding function may make the claim too broad and render it non-novel in view of prior art with identical components but different objectives/effects (example: housing unit vs hospital). Consider function and effect based on differences in space functions.

name: Categories for computer-related invention claims
description: Computer-related inventions may be claimed as (1) method inventions (series of steps), (2) product inventions (specify multiple functions performed), (3) computer-readable-medium claims with program code recorded to install/execute/distribute, and (4) computer-readable-medium claims with data recorded when the data structure determines operations.
guidance: Claims that recite 'computer program recorded in a medium' (or compatible terms) are allowed; claims to a computer program per se (not recorded in a medium) are not allowed. Example claim formats are provided for each category.

name: Indefiniteness from ambiguous actor in 'using a computer' claims
description: Claims phrased as 'using a computer, comprising the steps of ...' can be indefinite regarding who (human or computer) performs each step.
guidance: If a claim can be construed both as a human operating a computer as a mere tool and as an information-processing method by computer software, it is indefinite. Draft claims to clarify whether steps are performed by human operators or by computer-implemented means.

name: Program-as-means definiteness requirement for medium claims
description: A program recorded on a medium makes the computer operate as functional means, but the program per se does not function as a 'means'.
guidance: To be definite, phrase claims to reflect that the program makes the computer operate as specific functional means (e.g., 'the program makes the computer operate as an order-receiving means...') rather than implying the program itself is a functional means.

name: Undefined-terms lead to indefiniteness
description: If a claim uses uncommon technical terms, abbreviations, or symbols that are not defined in the specification and are not common general knowledge, the claimed invention is unclear.
guidance: Ensure terms used in claims are defined in the description or are part of common general knowledge at the filing date; otherwise provide definitions to avoid indefiniteness.

name: Requirement to specify technical relationships among elements
description: A claim is unclear when it fails to specify the technical relationships between elements that define the invention (e.g., mere statement that a program is being transmitted does not define a product invention).
guidance: Claims must specify technical relationships (how elements interact or are structured) so that the invention can be recognized as a technical product or process.

name: Category clarity for program signals/products/outputs
description: Ambiguity about which category subjects like program signals, program signal sequences, program products, and program outputs fall into makes claims unclear.
guidance: Clarify the category (product, method, medium) for such subject matter in claims and descriptions so examiners can properly assess them.

name: Avoid vague qualitative expressions (e.g., 'high speed') in claims
description: Using comparative or qualitative adjectives without objective criteria (e.g., 'high speed') obscures claim scope.
guidance: Either remove such vague terms or provide objective criteria (thresholds, measurements) to make the scope clear; otherwise recast claim to avoid the vague qualifier.

name: Claims reciting only results without means are indefinite
description: Claims that recite solely the results to be accomplished (functions) without specifying concrete means, products, or processes are not recognizably claimed.
guidance: Use the following determinative points for function-defined claims: (i) if a person skilled in the art can introduce specific matter(s) realizing the function from the claim plus common general knowledge, the claim scope is clear; (ii) if not, scope is generally unclear; (iii) exceptions exist where the specification/drawings properly define the matter only with function; (iv) if the connection between function and technology level is hard to understand, the scope can be considered unclear because novelty/inventive-step/violation assessments are impractical.

name: Enablement requirement for computer-related inventions
description: The description must enable a person skilled in the art, using ordinary technical means and ordinary creative activity, to carry out the claimed invention on the basis of the specification, drawings, and common general knowledge as of the filing.
guidance: Assess whether the description provides sufficient detail for implementation; if not, notify rejection under Patent Act 42(3)(i).

name: Examples of enablement violations (computer-related)
description: Typical enablement violations include: (1) use of uncommon terms/abbreviations/symbols without definition; (2) abstract statements of steps/functions without disclosure of implementation on hardware/software; (3) GUI-only explanations without implementation details; (4) functional block diagrams/flowcharts insufficient to show hardware/software structure; (5) mismatch between function-defined claims and flowchart-only embodiments.
guidance: When these issues are found, determine that the invention cannot be carried out by a skilled person and issue the appropriate exam findings. Provide concrete implementation details or program listings with sufficient explanation where needed.

name: Procedure to assess subject-matter eligibility (computer-related)
description: Assessment proceeds by: (1) understanding the claimed invention from the claim language; (2) determining whether information processing by software is concretely implemented by using hardware resources; (3) if not concretely implemented, concluding the claimed invention does not constitute a creation of technical ideas utilizing a law of nature.
guidance: Apply this three-step check. Example: a computer that contains input/processing/output means that 'prepares a summary' does not necessarily show cooperative concrete implementation; if the processing means cannot be said to cooperatively work to concretely implement the information processing, the claim may not be statutory.

name: Disclaimer not a method to amend defective description
description: A disclaimer cannot be employed to alter or reform the Description; it only eliminates superfluous matter from the Claims.
guidance: If the Description requires amendment to give effect to a Claim, or a Claim demands restatement to avoid obscurity, or new Claims are necessary, these must be sought by re-issue, not by disclaimer. Although descriptive matter incidental to a disclaimed excess may be withdrawn, a disclaimer cannot change the character of the invention or create a new patentable scope (Haileas v. Albany Stove Co., Union Metallic Cartridge Co. v. United States Cartridge Co.).

name: Disclaimer's effect limited to removed excess
description: The effect of a disclaimer is confined to the excess which it removes from the apparent protection of the patent; otherwise the patent remains operative as before.
guidance: A disclaimer does not add to the patent nor broaden protection. It does not affect other valid claims standing by themselves. Disclaiming a species does not necessarily affect a genus claim; disclaimed matter is treated as if never part of the patent for construction purposes.

name: Patent read as amended; interpretation without disclaimed matter
description: After disclaimer the patent stands read as if the disclaimer were incorporated into the original specification; both Claims and Descriptions are interpreted without reference to withdrawn matter.
guidance: The disclaimer is considered part of the specification upon recording. Objectionable phrases may be removed provided no new construction is given to remaining text. A disclaimer cannot be used to make remaining parts retroactively valid if they were unsupported (cases: Dunbar v. Myers; Schillinger v. Cranford).

name: Disclaimers cannot be used to obtain rights to un-described matter or create new patents
description: A disclaimer cannot be used to make a patent cover what is not described or claimed as part of the invention or to convert a Claim into one for something else; it cannot produce new patentable scope.
guidance: If a patentee seeks to change the character of the invention or to obtain coverage for matter not described, the proper remedy is surrender and re-issue (or obtaining a new patent), not a disclaimer. Disclaimers are solely to eliminate separable excess; any attempt to use them to expand rights is rejected by courts (White v. Gleason Mfg. Co.; Foxwell v. Bostock).

name: Sectional/territorial disclaimers and their local effect
description: A disclaimer filed by a sectional or territorial owner limits the patent only as to the interest owned by that disclaimant; the same patent may be operative to different extents in different territories or as to different owners.
guidance: After such disclaimer, the patent in effect makes distinct claims of right in different sections of the country, potentially resulting in 'two specifications' for the same invention: one operative for the disclaimant's section and another for others. The patent as amended will limit and define the disclaimant's rights while other parties hold under the patent in its original form.

name: When disclaimer withdraws re-issue/new matter, remaining new matter may be discarded
description: Where a disclaimer withdraws a new re-issue claim and leaves only what was covered by the original, any new matter remaining in the Description must be discarded.
guidance: A disclaimer that effectively nullifies the new re-issue Claim cannot leave stray new matter in the specification; courts have required that such new matter be discarded if not properly supported by the original (Schillinger v. Cranford and related authority).

name: Avoid speculation when making 103 rejections
description: A rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 should not be based on considerable speculation about the meaning of terms employed in a claim or assumptions that must be made as to the scope of the claims.
guidance: Cites In re Steele. Examiners should not base obviousness rejections on speculative interpretations of claim language; clarify claim meaning before relying on prior art.

name: Distinguish 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (insufficient disclosure) from 112(b) (indefiniteness)
description: If a specification's disclosure is not commensurate in scope with the subject matter encompassed by a claim, that fact alone does not render the claim indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b); rather, the claim may be based on an insufficient disclosure under 35 U.S.C. 112(a).
guidance: Examples: In re Borkowski, In re Mayhew—if the specification shows a feature is essential to practice of the invention but claims omit it, examiner may reject under 112(a) (lack of enablement/support). If claim is amended to include matter not described in the application as filed, rejection under 112(a) (pre-AIA first paragraph) may be appropriate (In re Simon).

name: General interpretation rule for 112(f)/pre-AIA sixth-paragraph limitations
description: The broadest reasonable interpretation of a claim limitation that invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (or pre-AIA sixth paragraph) is 'the structure, material or act described in the specification as performing the entire claimed function and equivalents to the disclosed structure, material or act.'
guidance: Cites In re Donaldson Co. The PTO must not disregard structure disclosed in the specification when rendering patentability determinations; means-plus-function limitations are often construed more narrowly than non-means limitations.

name: Three-prong analysis to determine whether a claim limitation invokes 112(f)
description: Examiners will apply 35 U.S.C. 112(f) to a claim limitation only if it meets a 3-prong analysis: (A) the claim limitation uses the term 'means' or 'step' or a generic placeholder; (B) that term is modified by functional language; and (C) the term is not modified by sufficient structure, material, or acts for performing the claimed function.
guidance: If all three prongs are met, treat the limitation under 112(f); if not, do not. If unclear, a 112(b) rejection may be appropriate. When treating under 112(f), the Office action must state that treatment and explain reasons if a 'means' term is not treated under 112(f).

name: Prong A — presence of 'means'/'step' or a generic placeholder
description: The claim limitation is presumed to invoke 112(f) when it explicitly uses the term 'means' or 'step' and includes functional language. The presumption is overcome when the limitation further includes the structure necessary to perform the recited function.
guidance: Cites TriMed v. Stryker and Altiris v. Symantec. Generic placeholders that may invoke 112(f) include 'mechanism for,' 'module for,' 'device for,' 'unit for,' 'component for,' 'element for,' 'member for,' 'apparatus for,' 'machine for,' and 'system for.' The list is not exhaustive; other generic placeholders may invoke 112(f).

name: Prong B — functional modification requirement
description: The term 'means' or the generic placeholder must be modified by functional language (typically linked by 'for' or similar linking phrase) such that the element is set forth at least in part by the function it performs rather than specific structure, material, or acts.
guidance: Functional linkage can be via words like 'for', 'so that', 'configured to'. Mere use of 'means' without an associated function rebuts invocation of 112(f). For method claims, step-plus-function is implicated only when steps are described by function without acts (avoid converting ordinary 'ing' steps into step-plus-function).

name: Prong C — absence of sufficient structure/material/acts
description: The term 'means' or generic placeholder must not be modified by sufficiently definite structure, material, or acts for achieving the specified function; if the claim itself recites sufficient acts or structure, 112(f) does not apply.
guidance: Examples where 112(f) did not apply because structure was recited: 'second baffle means' where 'baffle' imparts structure; lists of structures underlying the element; 'perforation means' where perforation describes supporting structure. Conversely, 'spring means' has been held to invoke 112(f). Examiner must consider structural modifiers and sufficiency of structure.

name: Rebuttable presumption when term does not use 'means'
description: A claim limitation that does not use the term 'means' or 'step' triggers a rebuttable presumption that 35 U.S.C. 112(f) does not apply; the presumption is overcome if the claim term fails to 'recite sufficiently definite structure' or recites 'function without reciting sufficient structure.'
guidance: Cites Phillips en banc and Williamson. Substitute/generic placeholder terms can act as a generic placeholder and may nonetheless invoke 112(f) if they lack sufficient structural meaning to one of ordinary skill.

name: Applicant options when examiner does not treat limitation as invoking 112(f)
description: If the examiner has not interpreted a claim limitation as invoking 112(f) but an applicant wishes it to be treated under 112(f), applicant must either amend the claim to include the phrase 'means' or 'step', or rebut the presumption that 112(f) does not apply by showing the claim limitation is written as a function without sufficient structure.
guidance: Cites Watts and Masco; for method claims lacking 'step for' language, there must be a showing that the limitation contains no act to construe it as step-plus-function.

name: Office action procedures when applying or not applying 112(f)
description: Where a claim limitation meets the 3-prong analysis and is being treated under 112(f), the examiner will include a statement in the Office action that the claim limitation is being treated under 112(f). If a claim uses 'means' or 'step' but the examiner determines a prong is not met, the Office action must explain why the limitation is not being treated under 112(f).
guidance: If treatment is unclear, a rejection under 112(b) may be appropriate. Ensure Office actions clearly state rationale to allow applicant to respond and to preserve proper prosecution record.

name: Element-by-element and independent claim review requirement
description: It is necessary to decide on an element-by-element basis whether 35 U.S.C. 112(f) applies; not all terms in a means-plus-function clause are limited to what is disclosed in the written description because 112(f) applies only to the means/step that performs the recited function.
guidance: Each claim must be independently reviewed even when similar language appears in apparatus and process claims; do not infer 112(f) applicability across claims without separate analysis (O.I. Corp., IMS Technology examples).

name: Requirement to disclose corresponding structure in the specification
description: The corresponding structure (or material or acts) of a means- (or step-) plus-function limitation must be disclosed in the specification itself in a way that one skilled in the art will understand what structure will perform the recited function.
guidance: Cites Atmel and In re Donaldson Co. Disclosure may be explicit or implicit/inherent if clear to skilled artisans. Incorporation by reference to technical documents may, in some cases, be sufficient to indicate precise structure (Atmel example). If no structure is disclosed, the claim fails 112(b)/second paragraph (e.g., Biomedino, Cardiac Pacemakers).

name: Failure to disclose corresponding structure leads to indefiniteness under 112(b)
description: If an applicant employs means-plus-function language but fails to set forth an adequate disclosure of corresponding structure, the claim may fail to 'particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention' as required by 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (or pre-AIA second paragraph).
guidance: Cites In re Donaldson Co.; practical consequence is a 112(b) rejection for indefiniteness where no corresponding structure is contained in the specification.

name: Tests/resources to determine whether a modifier denotes structure
description: To determine whether a word, term, or phrase coupled with a function denotes structure, examiners should check: (1) whether the specification provides a description sufficient to inform one of ordinary skill that the term denotes structure; (2) whether general and subject-matter specific dictionaries provide evidence that the term is recognized as a noun denoting structure; and (3) whether the prior art provides evidence the term has an art-recognized structure to perform the claimed function.
guidance: Cites Ex parte Rodriguez and Williamson. Use specification, dictionaries, and prior art as objective indicia of whether a claim term is structural.

name: Effect of modifying language — presumption rebutted by sufficient structure
description: If the term 'means' or a generic placeholder is modified by sufficient structure, material, or acts for achieving the specified function, the presumption that 112(f) applies is rebutted and 112(f) will not be applied (until such modifying language is deleted).
guidance: Examiner should recognize when claim language itself provides enough structure; examples where detailed recitation of structure removes element from 112(f) purview include Rodime v. Seagate and Cole v. Kimberly-Clark.

name: Regulations must not require preemptive filing of claims to anticipate all contingencies
description: § 42.73(3)(ii) would require a patent owner to contemplate all possible resolutions and preemptively file claims to meet every conceivable contingency, imposing burdens beyond those allowed under the Paperwork Reduction Act.
guidance: Avoid rules that force speculative, burdensome paperwork or claim filings; comply with PRA limitations on paperwork burden.

name: Derivation proceedings require a single textual description ('count') to define scope
description: The NPRM proposes no 'count' but requires showing petitioner's claim is 'the same or substantially the same' and 'not patentably distinct' from the invention disclosed to the respondent; without a single textual description ('count') it is unclear how scope will be determined.
guidance: Adopt a 'count' or single textual description of the derived subject matter broad enough to encompass common subject matter of claims in both applications, as in interference practice.

name: Use a two-phase process (scope/count then derivation) in derivation proceedings
description: IEEE-USA is skeptical that derivation can be adequately addressed by mere claim comparisons in a single phase; the Board should clarify whether a two-way test will be applied and how scope determinations will be made without a count.
guidance: Implement a first phase to examine scope/define derived subject matter and a second phase to determine whether it was derived from the petitioner.

name: Clarify treatment of non-patentably distinct claims and remaining patentably distinct claims in derivations
description: NPRM is silent on how non-patentably distinct claims to joint inventions or remaining patentably distinct claims will be treated; this affects the Board's ability to correct inventor naming and define claim status.
guidance: Provide mechanisms to determine status of claims of differing scope and the treatment of claims that recite subject matter not conceived or communicated to the deriving party.

name: Unity of invention - definition and assessment
description: A patent application must relate to one invention only or to a group of inventions so linked as to form a single general inventive concept.
guidance: Assessment is conducted using a priori and a posteriori approaches. The link must be a technical relationship expressed in the claims as the same or corresponding special technical features. Lack of unity must be determined solely from the language of the claims as properly construed and, where appropriate, by regard to relevant prior art.

name: Information to be published in the patent gazette/bulletin
description: Publication must contain the title, description, claims, and representative drawings as filed, including sequence listings filed on the filing date and late-filed missing parts (if not withdrawn).
guidance: Publication also includes applicant’s name and address, inventor(s), patent agent (if any), and priority application number and date. Publication must not include amendments that introduce new matter beyond the disclosure as filed. Specific contents per AMS are detailed in CSR.

name: Amendment of claims of published patent applications
description: Amending claims of a published application before grant (voluntarily or at examiner request) is a normal prosecution step and is allowed subject to conditions.
guidance: Amendments must not introduce subject-matter extending beyond the initial application. An amendment is unallowable if the overall change presents information not directly and unambiguously derivable from the application as filed, even accounting for implicit matter. If an applicant convincingly shows the introduced subject-matter is an obvious clarification to a PSIA, the amendment may be permitted. Limiting an allowable claim or improving clarity in a clearly desirable manner is normally allowed. Considerations after substantial limitation include unity of invention and alignment between description and claims. Re-publication after amendment is generally not required (exception: Viet Nam); in Singapore amendments are made available on the dossier.

name: Publication of granted patent specifications
description: Most AMS publish the granted patent specification (approved claims, description, drawings) enabling assessment of granted rights.
guidance: Exceptions: Cambodia does not publish granted patents; Singapore publishes only a reference to grant. Final publication helps licensing, enforcement, and freedom-to-operate assessments.

name: Substantive examination - general scope
description: Substantive examination involves a prior art search and assessment of patentability: novelty, inventive step, industrial applicability, and exclusions from patentable subject-matter.
guidance: Other requirements considered include enablement (PSIA can carry out invention), clarity of claims, unity of invention, and whether amendments exceed the original disclosure. Examiners raise objections when requirements are not met and invite amendments or explanations; if objections are overcome a patent is granted, otherwise refused.

name: Clarity of invention (scope of substantive examination item 3)
description: Claims and terms must be clear so that the PSIA can understand the meaning of the terms from the claim wording alone.
guidance: Clarity is crucial for assessing novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability; see Chapter 7 for details.

name: Novelty (scope of substantive examination item 5)
description: The claimed invention must be new — not in public use or known by others prior to the effective filing date.
guidance: Novelty considerations are detailed in Chapter 10.

name: Options for expediting substantive examination
description: Mechanisms exist to accelerate substantive examination including bilateral PPH, regional PPH (ASPEC programmes), and national fast-track programmes.
guidance: PPH allows an applicant to request accelerated examination at an office of later examination when claims are found patentable by an office of first filing/examination. ASEAN regional programmes include ASPEC Prosecution Highway, PCT-ASPEC programme, and ASPEC for Industry 4.0. National fast-track schemes exist in Malaysia, Thailand (pilot), and Singapore (with caps and conditions such as applicant residency, limits per entity, requirement to indicate reasons). Specific caps, fees and expected grant timelines vary by program and country.

name: Recordation is not determinative of title or validity
description: The recordation of a document is not a determination by the Office of the effect of the document on the chain of title or its validity; the Office will determine effect on title only when necessary (MPEP §§ 324, 325; 37 CFR 3.54).
guidance: Recording preserves history of claimed interests but does not resolve competing claims or legal effect; parties seeking to rely on title should ensure proper documentation and may need later adjudication.

name: Subservient (blocking) patent / dominant patent relationship
description: A broad patent can 'dominate' a narrower one, producing a subservient (narrower) patent that cannot be practiced without a license from the holder of the dominant patent; conversely the dominant patentee cannot practice the particular improved feature claimed in the narrower patent without a license.
guidance: Although courts may characterize an inventor's patent as subservient (often in litigation), the holder of a subservient patent still gains advantages: (1) she can exclude the holder of the broad patent from practicing her improvement (bargaining leverage), and (2) she may reduce the 'lost profits' component of the dominant patentee's damages because the dominant patentee would not have fully replaced infringer's sales that were based on the improvement.

name: Reverse doctrine of equivalents
description: Where a defendant's device literally falls within the claims but has 'so far changed the principle of the device that the claims of the patent, literally construed, have ceased to represent his actual invention,' the defendant may be excused from infringement (the 'reverse' doctrine of equivalents).
guidance: Applied rarely; courts ask whether the accused product is 'so far changed in principle' or performs in a 'substantially different way' (Westinghouse/Boyden example; SRI v. Matsushita discussed). Trial courts must often make factual determinations about whether the device is sufficiently changed in principle to warrant the defense.

name: Enablement concern with very broad claims
description: Broad claims that encompass embodiments which can be made only after significant additional research raise special concerns: such breadth may cover later, substantial improvements not contemplated at filing.
guidance: Cases like Westinghouse/Boyden illustrate that even if literal claim language could read on later inventions, courts may refuse to find infringement if the later invention is a 'manifest departure from the principle of the ... patent.' Enablement/claim breadth issues thus inform infringement analysis and reverse equivalents.

name: Kitch's prospect theory and its limits
description: Kitch analogized patents to mining claims: patents grant a prospect allowing a single right-holder to coordinate development, mitigate duplication, and potentially be more efficient than rivalry.
guidance: Critique: centralized control often underdevelops parts of the prospect, suffers from cognitive and organizational limits, and licensing tailored coordination is costly. Empirical evidence suggests rivalry often produces broader exploration than centralized control; transaction costs and licensing frictions make Kitch's idealized coordination unlikely in practice.

name: Assessment questions for patent-scope effects in cumulative technologies
description: When analyzing cumulative technologies, ask: (1) What are the consequences of 'pioneer' patents? (2) How do broad patents on components affect subsequent development?
guidance: The paper focuses on impact on subsequent innovation rather than whether a patent should have been granted at all, and accepts that claiming the general inventive principle may be justified but asks how breadth alters the environment for follow-on development (historical examples: Selden patent, Edison).

name: Analogy to property/mining law as a rationale for limiting scope
description: Just as mining and mineral claim systems limit claim boundaries and require active work to prevent hoarding/speculation, patent doctrines should limit breadth to prevent overly broad exclusion that preempts valuable follow-on work.
guidance: The legal analogy suggests practical mechanisms (requirements to work claims, limits on breadth) that constrain speculative or hoarding behavior; policy should aim for a regime protecting improvers' bargaining position relative to pioneers.

name: Statement of infringement content
description: The statement of infringement should allege that the defendant, without any license, did make, or did use, or did sell, the subject of whatever claim or claims the plaintiff intends to prosecute at the trial; and that the infringement occurred within the territory covered by the plaintiff's title and within the time the plaintiff held title.
guidance: While alleging any one of making, using, or selling is sufficient to show a cause of action, evidence of one will not support proof of another; therefore plead as many types (make/use/sell) as the plaintiff expects to be able to prove.

name: Defense 7: claims differ from original application (lack of original support)
description: That the invention claimed in the original patent is substantially different from any indicated, suggested, or described in the original application therefor.
guidance: Foundational on the spirit of patent laws; evidence must be drawn from outside the patent and introduced regularly; normally made by special plea.

name: Defense 16: reissue claims broader than original and delayed application
description: That the claims of the reissue patent in suit are broader than those of the original, and that the reissue was not applied for until a long time had elapsed after the original was granted.
guidance: First element requires comparative construction of original and reissue; second element (delay) is a variable fact depending on circumstances—both elements are factual and should be pleaded by special plea.

name: Language To Be Used in Rejecting Claims
description: Language To Be Used in Rejecting Claims (MPEP 707.07(d)).

name: Abstract must not claim advantages
description: Tiivistelmä ei saa sisältää keksinnön etuja tai arvoa koskevia väitteitä (PatA 18 §, PatM 26 §).
guidance: Abstract should be factual and descriptive only; avoid promotional or evaluative language about benefits or value.

name: Filing date entitlement and priority request timing for biological deposit
description: Tullakseen osalliseksi patenttilain 6 §:ssä mainitusta etuoikeudesta hakijan on kirjallisesti pyydettävä etuoikeutta 16 kuukauden kuluessa ensimmäisen etuoikeuden perustaksi ilmoitetun hakemuksen tekemispäivästä (ks. C.2.2). (PatA 10 §).
guidance: To claim priority rights, the priority must be requested in writing within statutory periods; for biological material deposit issues see specific deposit timing (deposit at latest on filing date or priority date to secure priority in respect of the biological material).

name: 37 CFR 1.111(b) requirements for replies and traverses
description: 37 CFR 1.111(b) requires applicant to distinctly and specifically point out the supposed errors in the Office’s action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the Office action.
guidance: The reply must present arguments pointing out the specific distinction believed to render the claims patentable over any applied references. If an applicant disagrees with any factual findings by the Office, an effective traverse of a rejection based wholly or partially on such findings must include a reasoned statement explaining why the applicant believes the Office has erred substantively as to the factual findings. A mere statement or argument that the Office has not established a prima facie case of obviousness or that the Office’s reliance on common knowledge is unsupported by documentary evidence will not be considered substantively adequate. Office personnel may repeat the rejection made in the prior Office action and make the next Office action final. See MPEP § 706.07(a).

name: Consideration of applicant's rebuttal evidence
description: Office personnel should consider all rebuttal evidence that is timely presented by the applicants when reevaluating any obviousness determination.
guidance: Rebuttal evidence may include secondary considerations (e.g., commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others) and evidence of unexpected results. Applicants may submit evidence or argument showing: (A) one of ordinary skill could not have combined the claimed elements by known methods (e.g., technological difficulties); (B) the elements in combination do not merely perform the function that each element performs separately; or (C) the results of the claimed combination were unexpected. Once rebuttal evidence is presented, office personnel should reconsider initial determinations in view of the entire record, review all rejections and proposed rejections for continued viability, and clearly communicate findings and conclusions. Follow MPEP § 706.07(a), MPEP § 2145, and MPEP § 716–§ 716.10 regarding affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132 and related procedures.

name: Determine prior art content as of the time the invention was made to avoid hindsight
description: The content of the prior art is determined at the time the invention was made to avoid impermissible hindsight.
guidance: Decisionmakers must attempt to 'forget' what they have been taught about the claimed invention and cast the mind back to the time the invention was made, considering the perspective of one skilled in the art at that time. See MPEP § 2145 for discussion of rebutting applicant arguments that a rejection is based on hindsight.

name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) — burden to establish applicability
description: An applicant subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 who wants to avail of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) bears the burden of establishing the conditions under which 103(c) applies.
guidance: To establish disqualification of certain prior art under 103(c), the applicant must show that the subject matter used in the rejection and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person. For joint research provisions (applications pending on or after December 10, 2004) the applicant must establish: (A) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; (B) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (C) the application discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement. Note date limitations for pre-AIA provisions and see MPEP § 706.02(l)(1) and § 706.02(l)(2) for requirements to establish common ownership or joint research agreements.

name: Analogous art requirement for reliance under 35 U.S.C. 103
description: To rely on a reference in an obviousness rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103, the reference must be analogous prior art to the claimed invention.
guidance: A reference is analogous art if: (1) it is from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention (even if it addresses a different problem); or (2) it is reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor (even if not in the same field). 'Reasonably pertinent' means the reference would have logically commended itself to an inventor's attention in considering the problem. The examiner should consider the problem faced by the inventor as reflected in the specification and may include a statement of the examiner's understanding of the problem to support pertinence. Applicant arguments that the examiner misconstrued the problem and relied on nonanalogous art should be fully considered in light of the specification. See KSR, In re Bigio, In re Icon Health and Fitness, In re Klein, and related cases.

name: Analogy considerations in the design arts
description: Design art analogy depends on whether prior designs are of the same general use as the claimed design or would reasonably fall within the knowledge of a designer of ordinary skill.
guidance: Examples and case law (MPEP § 1504.03, In re Rosen, Ex parte Pappas, In re Butera) illustrate that contemporary designs in related furniture or structural contexts may be analogous, while designs for unrelated uses (e.g., metal ball anode) may be nonanalogous if a designer would not have reason to look to them.

name: Consider differences between prior art and claimed invention 'as a whole'
description: Ascertaining differences requires interpreting claim language and considering both the invention and the prior art references as a whole; the question under 35 U.S.C. 103 is whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious.
guidance: Do not isolate or overweight individual differences; consider admitted unobvious aspects of components or steps in light of the entire claimed combination. Case examples (Stratoflex, In re Hirao) demonstrate that combinations of steps or integrated structures may render the invention nonobvious even if individual parts were known.

name: Do not distill the invention to a 'gist' or 'thrust' that disregards 'as a whole' analysis
description: Distilling an invention down to the 'gist' or 'thrust' disregards the requirement to analyze the subject matter 'as a whole.'
guidance: Focusing only on a perceived advantage or single feature (e.g., a one-word solution or isolated limitation) can ignore express limitations and other claim elements and lead to improper obviousness conclusions. See W.L. Gore, Bausch & Lomb, Jones v. Hardy, Panduit for examples where such distillation was rejected.

name: Format for changes to patent claims (showing amendments)
description: For changes to the patent claims, one must submit a copy of the entire patent claim with the amendments shown by underlining and single bracketing.
guidance: Example: Amend claim 6 as follows: Claim 6. (amended), The apparatus of claim [5] 1 wherein the [first] second piezoelectric element is parallel to the [second] third piezoelectric element.

name: Re-presentation of original patent claims (no markup)
description: When re-presenting an original patent claim (i.e., presenting it unchanged), present it with no underlining or bracketing.
guidance: Example: Amend claim 4 to read as original patent claim 4: Claim 4. The apparatus of claim 1 wherein the first piezoelectric element is perpendicular to the second piezoelectric element.

name: Presentation of new claims (formatting)
description: Each proposed new claim (a claim not found in the patent that is newly presented in the reexamination proceeding) should be presented with underlining throughout the claim, including the claim number and status indicator.
guidance: Example: Insert new claim 7 as follows: Claim 7 (New). The apparatus of claim 5 further comprising electrodes attaching to said opposite faces of the second and third piezoelectric elements.

name: Amendment of new claims (presentation and support)
description: An amendment of a new claim must present the entire text of the new claim containing the amendatory material, and it must be underlined throughout the claim, including the claim number and status indicator. The presentation cannot contain any bracketing or other indication of what was in the previous version of the claim.
guidance: Patent owner must point out what is changed in the “Remarks” portion of the amendment. As per 37 CFR 1.530(e), each change made in the claim must be accompanied by an explanation of the support in the disclosure of the patent (the reexamination specification) for the change.

name: Procedure for fee deficiency in excess claims fees
description: If excess claims fees required by 37 CFR 1.20(c)(3) and (c)(4) are not paid with presentation of the excess claims, a Notice of Defective Paper in Ex Parte Reexamination will be issued to correct the defect (fee deficiency).
guidance: For third-party requested reexaminations, a one-month time period (PTOL-475) will be set for correction. For patent-owner requested reexaminations or Director ordered reexaminations, a two-month time period (PTO-2311) will be set. Extension of time may be requested under 37 CFR 1.550(c). If unpaid within the time set, prosecution will be terminated under 37 CFR 1.550(e) effecting abandonment. In responses to a final Office action, the examiner should notify the owner of the fee deficiency in the advisory action.

name: Conduct of ex parte reexamination proceedings (general rules)
description: After times for filing the statement and reply have expired, reexamination will be conducted according to procedures for initial examination (sections 132 and 133). The patent owner is permitted to propose any amendment and new claims to distinguish the invention from cited prior art, but no proposed amendment or new claim enlarging the scope of a claim will be permitted.
guidance: All proceedings, including appeals, will be conducted with special dispatch. Ex parte reexamination will result in issuance of an ex parte reexamination certificate under 37 CFR 1.570. The patent owner will be given at least thirty days to respond to any Office action and may include statements and/or proposed amendments or new claims in response to rejections.

name: Formal requirements and manner of making amendments
description: Proposed amendments in ex parte or inter partes reexamination must be made by filing a paper directing specified changes to the patent specification (including claims) or drawings, and must comply with 37 CFR 1.530 and 1.52 formal requirements.
guidance: Specification changes require submission of the entire text of an added or rewritten paragraph, including markings; claims require the entire text of each claim being changed and each new claim; each changed claim should be followed by a parenthetical like '(amended)'; drawings changes require a red-ink sketch and, upon approval, new sheets complying with 37 CFR 1.84 (identify amended figures as 'Amended', new ones as 'New', canceled figures bracketed).

name: Marking conventions for amendments
description: Any changes to the specification, including claims, must show matter to be omitted by enclosing it in brackets and matter to be added by underlining (37 CFR 1.530(f)).
guidance: For paper files use red ink to draw lines through amended claim/paragraphs and bracket canceled claim(s) or paragraph(s) which are part of the patent; substituted copies are indicated by reference letter/number (e.g., A1, A2). IFW entries are made per specified scanning and marking procedures.

name: Status of claims and support for claim changes
description: When there is an amendment to the claims, pages separate from the pages containing the changes must be supplied showing the status (pending or canceled) as of the date of amendment of all patent claims and all added claims, and an explanation of the support in the disclosure for the changes.
guidance: This ensures that claim status and basis in the specification are clear to the examiner and will be part of the reexamination record.

name: No enlargement of claim scope and no new matter
description: No amendment may enlarge the scope of the claims of the patent or introduce new matter. No amendment may be proposed for entry in an expired patent (other than cancellation of claims), and no amendment other than cancellation will be incorporated into the patent by a certificate issued after expiration.
guidance: Although Office actions will treat proposed amendments as though entered, proposed amendments are not effective until the reexamination certificate is issued. Amendments that introduce new matter or enlarge scope will be disallowed.

name: Limited value of the Method of Agreement under plurality of causes
description: Finding multiple instances that agree only in one antecedent raises only a trifling presumption of causation when many causes can produce the effect.
guidance: Even if a set of prosperous nations only share a restrictive policy, that coincidence by itself gives almost no weighty presumption that the restrictive system caused prosperity. Be skeptical of claims of causation based solely on agreement across complex social cases.

name: Purpose of claim charts
description: Claim charts are essential tools in patent law, particularly in cases of patent enforcement. Claim charts are a visual tool that can effectively present complex technical information clearly and concisely and significantly help to decide authorities/courts in the matters of Patent Litigation and help them understand the extent of infringement or non-infringement while studying every detail of the claim.
guidance: A strong claim chart is supported by expert comments from an industry expert testifying the infringement of claimed features by the infringing product. It plays a key role in the swift movement of the case and helps both the plaintiff and defendants assess their position in a Patent Litigation.

name: Tabular representation aligning claim elements to product evidence
description: A claim chart is a tabular representation of claimed features of a patent on one side and relevant excerpts from the product description/product features on the other side to highlight how the infringing product is infringing every claimed feature of their patent.
guidance: A well-structured claim chart requires a thorough understanding of patented technology and features of the accused potentially infringing product. Along with technical knowledge of the field of invention, a detailed understanding of marketing-related keywords is essential.

name: Understand the patented technology and define scope of claim
description: Thoroughly understand the patented technology and interpret scope of the claims using detailed description, prosecution history, and other extrinsic sources to ensure the broadest possible interpretation of claimed elements such that it covers a wide range of products.
guidance: Identify the independent claims with the broadest scope of protection and interpret the claim in a way that maximizes its coverage while staying within reasonable bounds based on the detailed description of the subject patent and the knowledge of a person skilled in the art.

name: Indirect references and inferential evidence
description: If direct disclosure of any claim element is not found, but the final or intermediate output or product feature suggests the presence of the concerned claim feature in the product, then evaluate backend logic to see if disclosed frontend features imply the use of the claimed feature.
guidance: Support inferential claims with expert comments citing appropriate logic/arguments. Example: product documents tout a 'secure transaction' feature that—based on technical reasoning—would only be possible using the claimed encryption algorithm; highlight and substantiate this inference with expert testimony.

name: Teardown reports for mechanical or apparatus claims
description: For mechanical inventions or apparatus claims, teardown reports (disassembling the device) are an effective way to determine whether a product is infringing on the patented claim.
guidance: Dismantle the device to expose independently identifiable parts for detailed analysis; teardown reveals construction and operation allowing comparison with patent claims (example: inspect hinge mechanism in a foldable smartphone to compare to a claimed hinge).

name: Reverse engineering for semiconductor and fabrication-related technologies
description: In technologies related to fabrication of semiconductor devices and processes, reverse engineering reports are effective to ascertain infringement by analyzing layered structures of a semiconductor device.
guidance: Reverse engineering semiconductor chips requires sophisticated machinery and highly skilled analytical expertise; involves deconstructing logic gates, data paths, and conducting layerwise analysis to map to claimed structures/processes.

name: Doctrine of equivalents analysis when literal infringement not found
description: If the accused product/process does not literally infringe, consider whether it infringes under the doctrine of equivalents: does the accused product/process contain elements identical or equivalent to each claimed element of the patented invention?
guidance: Determine equivalence by analyzing the role played by each element in the context of the specific claim and assess whether a substitute element matches the function, way, and result of the claimed element or plays a substantially different role.

name: Support claim chart findings with expert testimony/comments
description: A strong claim chart is supported by expert comments from an industry expert testifying the infringement of claimed features by the infringing product.
guidance: Use experts to validate inferential evidence, explain technical mappings (e.g., backend logic, equivalence reasoning), and provide authoritative linkage between claimed elements and product evidence; explicitly cite expert logic in the chart where direct disclosures are absent.

name: Use of marketing and domain keywords in identifying evidence
description: Along with technical knowledge, a detailed understanding of marketing-related keywords is essential for preparing an effective claim chart.
guidance: Search and analyze marketing materials, product descriptions and related keywords that may reveal or imply claimed features; use these terms to locate indirect or contextual evidence and to validate product versions or features.

name: SAS Institute (IPR institution scope)
description: When the USPTO institutes an IPR, it must decide the patentability of all the claims the petitioner challenged.
guidance: USPTO and PTAB practice must reflect SAS: institute decisions should address every challenged claim, which impacts institution decisions and case management.

name: Cuozzo (BRI standard and appealability of institution)
description: The Supreme Court upheld the USPTO regulation requiring the PTAB to apply the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) standard in IPR proceedings and held that the decision to institute an IPR is not appealable to federal courts.
guidance: This establishes interpretation standards for claim construction in AIA proceedings and limits interlocutory judicial review of institution decisions.

name: Amgen v. Sanofi — enablement standard for functional claims
description: Amgen held that patent claims that claim antibodies by what they bind to were invalid under 35 U.S.C. § 112 for lack of enablement because it would take undue experimentation to identify which of millions of candidates bind to a specific protein.
guidance: This sets a high bar for enablement of broad functional claiming (e.g., antibodies) and affects examination and post-issuance review standards on enablement and undue experimentation.

name: Alice Step One — focus on specific asserted improvement vs abstract idea
description: At step one, courts consider whether the focus of the claims is on 'the specific asserted improvement in computer capabilities . . . or, instead, on a process that qualifies as an 'abstract idea' for which computers are invoked merely as a tool.' Claims that focus on a result/effect and merely invoke generic processes are likely directed to an abstract idea.
guidance: Cites Enfish, Finjan, McRO. Courts should assess the claim's 'character as a whole' and determine whether the claimed invention improves computer technology itself or instead implements a longstanding practice using a computer.

name: Alice Step Two — inventive concept must be more than routine or conventional
description: At step two, additional claim elements must provide an inventive concept beyond the abstract idea; they are insufficient if they are 'well-understood, routine, conventional activities' or merely generic computer components. A claim that simply states the abstract idea and adds 'apply it' fails.
guidance: Quotes Alice and Mayo. Uses examples where generic computer implementations failed (Ultramercial, buySAFE, OIP Techs.). Reminds that the inquiry examines elements individually and as an ordered combination to see if they 'transform the nature of the claim.'

name: When claims should be treated as representative (patentee's failure to distinguish)
description: Courts may treat a claim as representative 'if the patentee does not present any meaningful argument for the distinctive significance of any claim limitations not found in the representative claim or if the parties agree to treat a claim as representative.'
guidance: Practical rule: if patentee fails to articulate a meaningful differentiation of dependent or other independent claims from the representative claim in the record/pleadings, the court can treat the representative claim as dispositive for the group.

name: Role of claim construction in § 101 analysis
description: Although claim construction is not a prerequisite to a § 101 determination, eligibility analysis 'requires a full understanding of the basic character of the claimed subject matter' and it is often desirable—and often necessary—to resolve claim construction disputes prior to a § 101 analysis.
guidance: Cites Content Extraction, Bancorp Services. Courts may proceed without formal construction when claim meaning is obvious from the patent and record, but should avoid ruling on § 101 when disputed constructions could alter the outcome.

name: Use of precedent to identify 'abstract ideas' (targeted advertising example)
description: The Federal Circuit has repeatedly held that targeted advertising and information tailoring (e.g., collecting/using viewing history to recommend content, tailoring ads by time of day) are abstract concepts not patentable under § 101.
guidance: Cites Broadband iTV, Free Stream Media, Intellectual Ventures I. This provides a precedent-based rubric: if claims are materially similar to those ruled abstract in precedent, that weighs toward ineligibility.

name: Generic computer components do not make an abstract idea patent-eligible
