description: Claims that merely apply an abstract idea using generic computer components (e.g., 'a computer', 'a manager', 'a delivery module') or that add routine data storage/selection/measurement steps are not transformed into an inventive concept.
guidance: Examples and citations include OIP Techs., Ultramercial, Customedia. The Court should scrutinize whether claimed components are 'non-generic' and how they change computer functionality.

name: Dependent-claim specificity: minor structural or functional additions may be insufficient
description: Dependent claims that add only minor structural or functional features—storing user profiles, using different types of data, sending a delivery plan or product catalog, specifying client device types—may still be 'substantially similar' to an abstract representative claim and fail to transform the claim into patent-eligible subject matter if they lack specificity or inventive technical detail.
guidance: Practical analysis: group dependent claims by added features and evaluate whether any added limitation meaningfully improves computer functionality or is merely generic.

name: Factual disputes about conventionality or novelty preclude judgment on pleadings
description: If there are underlying factual questions (e.g., whether an asserted component is 'well-understood, routine, or conventional' or whether an architecture is novel/non-generic), those factual disputes can preclude resolving § 101 at the pleading stage and make judgment on the pleadings improper.
guidance: Cites Revell, BSG Tech, Turbe. The court should deny a Rule 12(c) motion where factual development (discovery, claim construction) is needed to resolve whether elements supply an inventive concept.

name: Court should avoid § 101 dismissal when claim meaning is contested and could be dispositive
description: When a plaintiff articulates a specific claim construction issue (e.g., meaning of 'social connections') that could affect whether claims are directed to an abstract idea or whether they improve computer functionality, the court should defer § 101 ruling until after claim construction and factual development.
guidance: Cites the court's practice and cases (e.g., Execware v. BJ’s) declining to decide § 101 where claim construction could change the outcome; admonishes against adopting a construction at pleading stage that may be unfavorable and later prove incorrect.

name: Physical/tangible form requirement for non-process claims
description: "For all categories except process claims, the eligible subject matter must exist in some physical or tangible form." (Digitech cited)
guidance: If a claimed invention is not a 'concrete thing,' 'tangible article,' or combination of substances, it may fail §101. Use physical or tangible implementation language where appropriate; be cautious when claims only define abstract systems (e.g., symbol systems).

name: Data recitations require actionable effect
description: Elements of a claim that recite data is not given weight unless that data can act upon something.
guidance: Avoid mere recitation of data; claim data that 'result or causes something to happen or be controlled.' Be cautious claiming monetary data. If you must claim data, tie it to operations, control, or physical effects.

name: Printed-matter/storage recitation caution
description: Query whether claiming it as stored on a storage device would make it eligible. Might be rejected as mere printed matter.
guidance: Merely reciting storage of data on a medium may not overcome §101 rejections; tie storage to functional interaction or processing that alters behavior or causes action.

name: Abstract idea when result-oriented without technical detail
description: An abstract idea was found because the claims were result oriented, without technical detail. (Interval Licensing)
guidance: Claims that are phrased as desired outcomes or high-level results, without specific technical means, risk being characterized as abstract ideas. Include technical detail and mechanisms in claim language.

name: Focus on technical solutions/improvements for UI inventions
description: Practitioners should focus on technical solutions, technical improvements or improved functionality for user-interface based inventions.
guidance: For UI inventions, draft claims and spec to show how the UI change improves system functionality or technical operation (not merely aesthetics or presentation).

name: Avoid overly broad claim interpretation
description: Be careful seeking an overly broad interpretation of your claims; broad interpretations can import prior art and make the claim appear abstract or preemptive.
guidance: Argue for claim constructions that highlight the claimed technical features; use specification support to constrain claim meaning where helpful.

name: Argue non-preemption when possible
description: Assert that the claims do not preempt all use of the claimed abstract idea; distinguish prior cases by showing narrower scope or specific technical means.
guidance: Emphasize claim limitations that leave other approaches open; use arguments about non-preemption as part of Alice Step 1/Step 2 analyses.

name: Leverage the specification to show the technical problem and solution
description: The opinion leans heavily on the specification for identifying the problem and ensuring the solution is in the claims. (KPN, SRI, Packet Intelligence)
guidance: Draft the specification to describe the technical problem, explain why it is technical, and detail the specific technical means used to solve it. Use intrinsic evidence to support claim construction and eligibility arguments.

name: Claims directed to a non-abstract technological improvement
description: Claims may be patent-eligible under Alice Step 1 if they are directed to a non-abstract improvement in an existing technological process (e.g., improved error checking in data transmission).
guidance: Frame the claims as improvements to technology (specific methods/devices) and show how the claimed limitations provide a technical benefit or improvement over prior art.

name: Draft dependent claims to delineate specific solution when independent claim is broad
description: If the client wants a broader independent claim, ensure there are dependent claims that clearly delineate the specific solution.
guidance: Include dependent claims that recite specific implementations, parameters, and mechanisms so that a court can point to concrete claim language if a broad independent claim is challenged.

name: Genus claims: non-preemption vs enablement/written-description risk
description: Genus claims may avoid preemption and thus pass §101, but may implicate enablement and written description issues under 35 U.S.C. § 112.
guidance: If drafting broad 'genus' claims, ensure the specification supports and enables the full breadth claimed to mitigate §112 risk even if §101 is satisfied.

name: Do not oversimplify claim language in eligibility analysis
description: Courts must be careful to avoid oversimplifying the claims by looking at them generally and failing to account for the specific requirements of the claims.
guidance: When arguing eligibility, focus on the precise claim limitations and how they constrain the invention; avoid reducing claims to an overly abstract characterization.

name: Express technical problem/solution in both spec and claims
description: Presenting a 'technological solution to a technological problem' in the specification is valuable; the specification bolsters conclusions that claims are directed to a technological solution.
guidance: Describe the technical shortcomings of prior art, articulate the concrete technical improvements provided by the invention, and mirror those aspects in claim language.

name: Claim specific means of achieving the asserted technical result
description: Be sure that the specific aspects of how to achieve the technical solution are claimed — relying solely on the specification may be insufficient.
guidance: Include concrete components, data structures, algorithms, or processing steps in claims, not just a description in the spec, so the claims themselves recite the 'how.'

name: Caution about heavy reliance on the specification
description: The specification is being more heavily relied on for determining patent eligibility under §101; however, courts differ on whether reliance on the spec vs claim language is appropriate.
guidance: Use the specification to support and construe claim terms, but ensure claims stand on their own by reciting tangible technical features and steps.

name: Physical aspect alone insufficient to avoid abstract-idea finding
description: The physicality of items involved (e.g., paper checks being processed and transported) is not by itself enough to exempt claims from being directed to an abstract idea.
guidance: Show that claimed physical steps change how computers operate or materially improve data capture/processing; avoid merely adding conventional physical actions as token 'physical' elements.

name: Emphasize interruption of preemption through claim limitations and alternatives
description: Claims that avoid preempting all approaches to an abstract idea (e.g., by specifying limitations or alternatives) are less likely to be invalid under §101.
guidance: Draft claims to include concrete, limiting features (e.g., specific data manipulations, timing/permutation techniques, tables) and identify alternative approaches left open by the claims.

name: Priority right: conditions for effectivity
description: Priority right of an application comes into effect provided all administrative and substantive requirements are fulfilled; for substantive requirements, the claimed element in the application must be disclosed in the priority document.
guidance: Priority claims require that the priority document actually disclose the claimed elements; applies to first applications filed in member states/under PCT (Article 5 section (2), Article 7 section (2), Article 30).

name: Application components and requirement that claims be supported by description
description: Claims must describe the subject matter of the invention sought for protection and must be clearly elaborated and supported by the description. The application also requires abstract, drawings (technical drawing), and other standard components.
guidance: Emphasizes the support requirement between claims and description; defines 'abstract' and 'drawing' (Article 25 points c–e).

name: Genetic resources and traditional knowledge disclosure
description: The origin of genetic resources and/or traditional knowledge related to the invention must be mentioned clearly and truthfully in the description to ensure resources/knowledge are not claimed by other countries and to encourage Access Benefit Sharing (ABS).
guidance: Mandatory disclosure aimed at ABS and preventing misappropriation of genetic resources/traditional knowledge (Article 26).

name: Prohibition on extending scope of invention via amendments
description: To 'extend the scope of invention' means adding essence/subject, new information or removing technical features in description/drawings/claims that causes extension of claim scope — this is not permitted.
guidance: Amendments are restricted to prevent introducing new matter or broadening the claimed subject (Article 39 section 2).

name: Invention information and inventive thing (definitions for classification purpose)
description: ‘Invention information’ is all novel and unobvious subject matter in a patent document (description, drawings, claims) that represents an addition to the state of the art; an 'inventive thing' is any part of the invention information which is novel and unobvious in itself.
guidance: Invention information should usually be determined using the claims of the patent document for guidance; these definitions inform what must be represented by classification (see also 'obligatory classification').

name: Amendments filed after appeal but before brief (37 CFR 41.33(a))
description: Amendments filed after the date of filing an appeal and prior to the date a brief is filed may be admitted as provided in 37 CFR 1.116.
guidance: A new amendment must be submitted in a separate paper. Entry of a new amendment in an application on appeal is not a matter of right. Admitted amendments may be to cancel claims, comply with form requirements, present rejected claims in better form for consideration on appeal, or amend the specification or claims upon a showing of good and sufficient reasons why necessary and not earlier presented (see 37 CFR 41.33(a)). If denied, examiner should use PTOL-303 to notify applicant of non-entry and reasons.

name: Amendments filed on or after filing a brief (37 CFR 41.33(b))
description: Amendments filed on or after the date of filing a brief may be admitted only to: (1) cancel claims where cancellation does not affect scope of any other pending claim, or (2) rewrite dependent claims into independent form.
guidance: 37 CFR 41.37(c)(2) provides that a brief shall not include any non-admitted amendment. Amendments filed with a brief must be in a separate paper. Rewriting dependent claims into independent form includes (A) adding parent claim limitations to a dependent claim to make it independent, and (B) rewriting an independent claim to incorporate a dependent claim's subject matter and canceling the dependent claim; examiners use PTOL-304 to notify applicant of non-entry after filing a brief.

name: Examiner response and entry of amendments
description: Examiners must respond to all amendments filed after an appeal has been taken and prior to transfer of jurisdiction to the Board under 37 CFR 41.35(a).
guidance: If examiner indicates in an advisory action that an amendment would be entered, the examiner must state how individual rejections set forth in the final Office action will be impacted (except where amendment merely cancels claims). If the examiner determines an amendment clearly places the application in condition for allowance, the examiner may enter the amendment and allow the application. Except for amendments meeting conditions noted, all other amendments submitted after the filing of a notice of appeal will not be entered except as permitted by specified regulations (e.g., 37 CFR 41.39(b)(1), 41.50...).

name: New grounds of rejection in examiner's answer
description: An examiner's answer may include a new ground of rejection, but any rejection that relies upon evidence not relied upon in the Office action shall be designated as a new ground.
guidance: New grounds of rejection must be prominently identified and must be approved by the Director (delegated to TC Directors or designee). For each new ground, a complete explanation supporting the rejection must be provided with proper reference to the applicable statute, prior art references relied upon, and the claim numbers affected. If an answer contains a new ground, the applicant has TWO MONTHS to either reopen prosecution (request reopening under 37 CFR 1.111 with or without amendment/evidence) or maintain the appeal by filing a reply brief addressing each new ground per 37 CFR 41.37(c)(1)(iv); reply briefs may not be accompanied by amendments/evidence.

name: Examiners' obligation to identify how final rejections apply to amended/added claims
description: Where an amendment under 37 CFR 1.116 or 41.33 would be entered for appeal purposes, the examiner must identify (in an advisory action) how one or more individual rejections set forth in the final rejection would be used to reject the added or amended claim(s).
guidance: This identification is required to make clear how the final rejection would be applied to the newly added or amended claims.

name: Increase clarity of issued claims (procedural/format reforms)
description: Implement reforms (e.g., claim templates, default dictionaries) to improve claim clarity and reduce downstream disputes over claim scope.
guidance: Clearer claims reduce uncertainty and potentially litigation; authors note this is complementary to time-allocation reforms but requires separate cost–benefit analysis.

name: Particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention (35 U.S.C. 112(b))
description: Core statutory requirement that claims must "particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention" to provide clear public notice of what constitutes patent infringement.
guidance: Claims must define the metes and bounds of the invention so that the public can determine what is and is not covered. This is the foundational criterion against which all claim language is judged.

name: Test for definiteness: understanding by a person of ordinary skill
description: Would a person of ordinary skill in the art understand the claim scope when read in light of the specification?
guidance: The ultimate question is whether POSITA, reading the claim with the specification, would understand the scope. Examiners should assess claim scope in view of the specification and relevant background knowledge.

name: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation during prosecution
description: Claims are given their broadest reasonable construction consistent with the specification while under examination.
guidance: During prosecution the claim language is interpreted broadly, but the interpretation must still be reasonable and consistent with the specification. This affects whether terms appear indefinite under the broader construction.

name: Clarity Standard: reasonable certainty
description: Claims must inform those skilled in the art with "reasonable certainty" about the boundaries of the claimed invention.
guidance: The standard is not absolute precision but that the claim scope be reasonably certain to a POSITA. Ambiguity that leaves uncertainty as to claim scope may render a claim indefinite.

name: Contextual evaluation of claim terms
description: Claim terms are evaluated based on the specification, the prior art, and the level of ordinary skill in the field.
guidance: Terms cannot be read in isolation—context from the specification and the technical field helps define meaning. Prior art and the understanding of a POSITA inform whether language is sufficiently definite.

name: Terms of degree (category of potential indefiniteness)
description: Use of degree terms such as "substantially," "approximately," "comparable" that express gradations rather than precise measures.
guidance: These terms are fact-specific and are not automatic grounds for rejection; examiners must explain why a given degree term leaves claim boundaries unclear rather than relying on a blanket rule.

name: Relative terms (category of potential indefiniteness)
description: Use of comparative or relative descriptors like "lightweight," "high-speed," "similar."
guidance: Relative terms may be indefinite if no objective standard for comparison exists in the claim or specification. Whether indefinite depends on context and whether a POSITA would understand the relative measure.

name: Subjective language (category of potential indefiniteness)
description: Phrases expressing subjective judgment such as "aesthetically pleasing," "superior" when unaccompanied by objective standards.
guidance: Subjective descriptors can render claims indefinite absent objective criteria or structure in the specification that anchors the subjective term.

name: Vague approximations (category of potential indefiniteness)
description: Terms like "about," "essentially," "roughly" that indicate approximation.
guidance: Approximation language may be permissible depending on context (e.g., where slight variations are intended), but examiners must show how such terms create an unclear boundary for the claimed scope in the specific case.

name: Unclear references / lack of antecedent basis
description: References such as "said lever" without an antecedent basis or other unclear referential language.
guidance: Claims must provide proper antecedent basis and clear referents; failure to do so can make the claim indefinite because the referent cannot be located or understood by a POSITA.

name: Functional claims (results-only language)
description: Claims that describe only a desired result or problem solved without reciting structure, material, or acts that accomplish it.
guidance: Purely functional claiming (results without corresponding structure) may be indefinite because it fails to disclose the metes and bounds of the invention; evaluation is fact-specific.

name: Examiners must establish a clear record identifying indefinite terms
description: Examiners are required to identify the specific indefinite term and explain in detail why claim boundaries are unclear.
guidance: The Office action must do more than assert indefiniteness; it should pinpoint the exact language and articulate why that language would not permit a POSITA to discern claim scope.

name: Adequate explanation requirement (avoidance of conclusory statements)
description: Examiners should avoid mere conclusory statements and must demonstrate how the scope becomes unclear.
guidance: Rejections that only state a conclusion without explaining why claim language is indefinite are inadequate. The record should show the factual and legal basis for the examiner's determination.

name: Applicant response options to indefiniteness rejections
description: Applicants may respond by amending claims, providing persuasive explanations showing how a POSITA would understand the term, or submitting supporting evidence such as declarations or technical dictionary references.
guidance: Common responses include claim amendment to add clarity, arguments showing that the specification or common usage provides sufficient guidance, and extrinsic evidence (declarations, dictionaries) if appropriate to demonstrate how POSITA would understand the term.

name: Follow MPEP 2106 flowchart for SME analysis
description: Use the flowchart in MPEP 2106, subsection III, to determine whether a claim satisfies the criteria for subject matter eligibility and to organize the eligibility analysis.
guidance: The slides indicate examiners should follow the flowchart when analyzing claims (Step 1, Step 2A Prong One, Step 2A Prong Two, Step 2B). The examples are analyzed using that flowchart. Following the flowchart will help organize thoughts when analyzing a claim for subject matter eligibility.

name: Step 1 — Statutory category test
description: Determine whether the claim falls within at least one statutory category (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter).
guidance: If the claim recites an integrated circuit it is a machine/manufacture; if it recites a series of steps it is a process. Step 1 must be answered Yes to proceed to further analysis.

name: Step 2A Prong One — identify judicial exception
description: Identify specific claim limitation(s) that you believe recite a judicial exception and determine whether those limitation(s) fall within the abstract idea groupings enumerated in MPEP 2106.04(a)(2).
guidance: Two-part evaluation: (a) identify the limitation(s) alleged to be an abstract idea; (b) determine if the limitation falls within mathematical concepts, mental processes, or certain methods of organizing human activity. Claims that merely involve an exception but do not recite one may be eligible and not require further analysis.

name: Abstract idea grouping — Certain Methods of Organizing Human Activity
description: Includes fundamental economic principles or practices (hedging, insurance, mitigating risk), commercial or legal interactions (agreements, contracts, advertising, marketing, sales), and managing personal behavior or relationships (social activities, teaching, following rules).
guidance: Use this grouping when claim limitations relate to business practices, legal/commercial interactions, or interpersonal management activities as enumerated in MPEP 2106.04(a)(2).

name: Step 2A Prong Two — limitations indicative of integration into a practical application
description: Identify additional elements beyond a judicial exception and evaluate whether they integrate the exception into a practical application (making the claim more than an abstract idea).
guidance: Limitations indicative of integration include: improvements to the functioning of a computer or other technology/technical field (MPEP 2106.05(a)); applying/using an exception to effect a particular treatment/prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition (MPEP 2106.04(d)(2)); applying the judicial exception with/by use of a particular machine (MPEP 2106.05(b)); effecting a transformation or reduction of an article to a different state or thing (MPEP 2106.05(c)); applying/using the judicial exception in some other meaningful way beyond generally linking it to a technological environment such that the claim as a whole is more than a drafting effort designed to monopolize the exception (MPEP 2106.04(d)(2) and 2106.05(e)).

name: Step 2A Prong Two — limitations not indicative of integration (insignificant extra-solution activity)
description: Certain claim recitations do not show integration into a practical application and are not sufficient to render an abstract idea patent eligible at Step 2A Prong Two.
guidance: Examples include: adding the words 'apply it' (or equivalent) or mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer; merely using a computer as a tool; adding insignificant extra-solution activity; generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use. Note: Step 2A Prong Two does NOT include the 'well understood, routine, conventional' (WURC) consideration—WURC is considered only in Step 2B.

name: Step 2B — inventive concept and WURC consideration
description: Determine whether the claim provides an inventive concept (i.e., additional element(s) or combination that amount to 'significantly more' than the judicial exception), adding consideration of whether additional elements are well-understood, routine, conventional (WURC).
guidance: Step 2B includes the considerations from Step 2A plus WURC (MPEP 2106.05(d)). Limitations indicative of an inventive concept include improvements to computer functioning or other technology (MPEP 2106.05(a)), applying the exception with/by particular machine (MPEP 2106.05(b)), effecting a transformation (MPEP 2106.05(c)), applying the exception in some other meaningful way beyond mere linking (MPEP 2106.04(d)(2) & 2106.05(e)), and adding a specific limitation that is not well-understood, routine, or conventional (MPEP 2106.05(d)). Limitations not indicative include appending WURC activities, adding 'apply it' or insignificant extra-solution activity, or mere linking to a technological environment (MPEP 2106.05(f),(g),(h)).

name: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) in claim construction
description: Interpret claim terms under the broadest reasonable interpretation standard when establishing the claim scope for SME analysis.
guidance: BRI examples given: 'continuous data' = any data measured with many possible values; 'discretizing' includes binning, clustering, rounding; backpropagation/gradient descent treated as optimization/mathematical calculations. Do not disregard limitations (a 'wherein' clause has weight); consider the plain meaning and specification when evaluating whether claim language limits the scope (e.g., specifying 'Compound X eye drops' imparts patentable weight).

name: Distinguish claims that 'recite' an exception versus those that merely 'involve' it
description: Be careful to distinguish claims that actually recite a judicial exception (which require further eligibility analysis) from claims that merely involve an exception but do not recite it (which may be eligible without further analysis).
guidance: Quoting Supreme Court guidance: '[a]t some level, all inventions embody, use, reflect, rest upon, or apply laws of nature, natural phenomena, or abstract ideas.' Examiners should carefully determine whether a claim recites an exception or merely involves it.

name: Use examples cautiously; case-by-case analysis; no fixed keyword list
description: Examples (including examples 47–49) are illustrative only and should be interpreted based on their fact patterns; there is no fixed list of terms that render a claim eligible or ineligible.
guidance: It is not necessary for a claim to mirror an example claim to be eligible. Older examples may be inconsistent with current guidance and should be used with caution. Every claim must be evaluated on a case-by-case basis using MPEP SME guidance.

name: Technical-improvement requirement for considering 'using' an ANN or computer as more than generic
description: To conclude a claim improves computer functioning or technology (and thus integrates the exception), the specification and claim must present a technical explanation of the asserted improvement and the claim must reflect that improvement.
guidance: Merely 'using' an ANN or computer at a high level of generality amounts to instructions to implement the exception on a generic computer and will not, by itself, establish eligibility. The claim/specification must show how the claimed elements effect a technological improvement (e.g., real-time remediation as an actual technical improvement rather than a stated outcome).

name: Top-up searches (finding documents published/available after the ISR)
description: The IPEA shall conduct a search ('top‑up search') to discover documents referred to in Rule 64 which have been published or have become available subsequent to the date on which the international search report was established, unless it considers such a search would serve no useful purpose. If situations in Article 34(3) or (4) or Rule 66.1(e) exist, the top‑up search shall cover only those parts of the international application that are the subject of international preliminary examination.
guidance: Top‑up searches differ from additional searches (top‑up finds recently available prior art; additional searches respond to claim amendments). Perform top‑up searches in all Chapter II examinations except rare cases (e.g., subject matter not to be examined, claims so unclear/inadequately supported that no meaningful opinion can be formed, or no ISR for certain claims). If relevant documents discovered that lead to a new objection not necessitated by an amendment, issue a second written opinion.

name: Basis of opinion (Box I) — language, amendments, sequences, and new matter
description: When completing Box No. I, item 1 of Form PCT/IPEA/408, the examiner must indicate whether the opinion has been established on the basis of the international application in the language in which it was filed or on a furnished translation. The opinion is established on the basis of any amendments, rectifications, priority and/or unity holdings and shall answer questions concerning novelty, inventive step, and industrial applicability for each claim under examination.
guidance: List substitute/rectified/incorporated sheets as originally filed/furnished pages; indicate amended claims filed under Article 19 as amended; if opinion based on nucleotide/amino acid sequence, indicate purpose/time/format as described; itemize whether amendments cancelled any pages/claims/drawings/sequence listings; if amendments appear to go beyond original disclosure point this out in Box I item 4 and explain in Supplemental Box; new matter on a replacement sheet is disregarded for establishing the opinion but non-new-matter portions are considered; mark Box I item 5 if opinion takes into account rectification under Rule 91 and item 6 if it takes into account supplementary international search reports.

name: Priority (Box II) — treatment of priority documents and translations
description: Where the priority document is provided by the applicant after the preparation of the search report and the ISA written opinion, any written opinion of the IPEA and/or the IPER should reconsider the validity of the priority claim. The IPEA may request a copy of the priority document from the IB and, if necessary, a translation from the applicant. If outcome requires issuing an opinion without waiting for translation, issue opinion in the meantime and note under 'Additional observations' in Box No. II.
guidance: If the priority document is in a foreign language, invite applicant to furnish a translation within two months. Failure to furnish the copy or translation may result in establishing the written opinion and/or IPER as if the priority had not been claimed. Indicate boxes in item 1 of Box No. II appropriately.

name: Non-establishment of opinion (Box III) — when novelty/IS/IA cannot be considered
description: Box No. III is intended to cover situations where some or all claims are so unclear or inadequately supported by the description that the question of novelty, inventive step (nonobviousness), and industrial applicability cannot be considered, or where the international application or claims relate to subject matter which does not require international preliminary examination, or where no international search report has been established for the claims.
guidance: Fill Box No. III in accordance with instructions for Box No. III of Form PCT/ISA/237 (MPEP § 1845.01).

name: Box VIII — observations on clarity and support
description: In Box No. VIII, the examiner notifies the applicant of observations made as to the clarity of the claims, the description, the drawings, or on the question whether the claims are fully supported by the description.
guidance: Fill Box No. VIII in accordance with the instructions for Box No. VIII of Form PCT/ISA/237 (MPEP § 1845.01).

name: Reciting only the idea of a solution or outcome
description: Whether the claim recites only the idea of a solution or outcome (i.e., the claim fails to recite details of how a solution to a problem is accomplished). Recitations that attempt to cover any solution to an identified problem with no restriction on how the result is accomplished and no description of the mechanism are equivalent to the words "apply it."
guidance: Result-oriented or purely functional claims that lack specific steps or mechanisms are likely mere instructions to apply the judicial exception. Examples include claims that only describe creating or modifying documents (e.g., dynamic XML modifications) without describing how the computer performs the modifications (Intellectual Ventures v. Capital One; Electric Power Group). Claiming a particular solution or way to achieve the outcome may integrate the exception into a practical application; mere result-focused language cautioned against.

name: Particularity versus generality of the application
description: The particularity or generality of the application of the judicial exception: broadly applicable claims across many fields may not provide meaningful limitations that integrate the exception into a practical application; a claim that generically recites an effect or every mode of accomplishing an effect amounts to merely adding 'apply it.'
guidance: Claims that confine the judicial exception to a particular, practical application may amount to significantly more (e.g., BASCOM: installation of a filtering tool at a specific location with customizable features). Historical cases (O'Reilly v. Morse; The Telephone Cases) show claims that attempt to monopolize a law or effect across all means are ineligible. Evaluate whether the limitation confines the abstract idea to a specific technological implementation or environment.

name: Whether the limitation imposes meaningful limits (significance)
description: Determine whether the limitation is significant — i.e., it imposes meaningful limits on the claim so that it is not merely nominal or tangentially related to the invention.
guidance: Limitations that meaningfully restrict the scope of the claim may be treated as adding significantly more and are considered in both Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B. Examples where limitations were found insignificant include restricting public access to media (Ultramercial) and certain electronic menu ordering features (Ameranth). Provide explanation in eligibility rejections about why a limitation is not significant when applicable.

name: Whether the limitation amounts to necessary data gathering and outputting
description: Consider whether the limitation is merely necessary data gathering or outputting that all uses of the recited judicial exception would require (e.g., measuring metabolites, presenting offers and gathering statistics).
guidance: Such necessary data-gathering/output steps have been treated as insignificant extra-solution activity (Mayo; OIP Technologies). This consideration is relevant in both Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B analyses. Examiners should explain why such data-gathering/output steps do or do not meaningfully limit the claim.

name: Examples of Insignificant Extra-Solution Activities
description: Concrete categories and examples the courts have found to be insignificant extra-solution activity: (a) Mere data gathering (performing clinical tests, testing systems for responses, presenting offers and gathering statistics, obtaining transaction info, consulting/updating logs, determining biomarker levels); (b) Selecting a particular data source or type (limiting a database index to XML tags, taking certain types of food orders, selecting info in power-grid environment, requiring user request to view advertisement); (c) Insignificant application (cutting hair after determining style; printing/downloading menus); (d) Insignificant computer implementation (using conventional computers/implementation).
guidance: These illustrative examples (with cited cases: In re Grams; In re Meyers; OIP Technologies; CyberSource; Ultramercial; Mayo; Intellectual Ventures v. Erie Indem.; Ameranth; Electric Power Group; In re Brown; Fort Properties; Bancorp; etc.) help identify extra-solution activities that are nominal and do not add an inventive concept. Examiners should explain why such activities do not meaningfully limit the claim when making an eligibility rejection.

name: Continued obligation to determine micro entity qualification (37 CFR 1.29(g)-(h))
description: A certification of entitlement to micro entity status need only be filed once in an application or patent and remains in effect until changed pursuant to paragraph (i). However, a fee may be paid in the micro entity amount only if status as a micro entity is appropriate on the date the fee is being paid. Prior to submitting a certification, a determination of entitlement should be made that each applicant qualifies for micro entity status under 1.29(a) or (d) and that any other party holding rights qualifies for small entity status under §1.27. For gross income basis claims, a new determination must be made each year because gross income may change; determine that no inventor's gross income exceeds the maximum qualifying gross income and that no assignments to entities exceeding the maximum qualifying gross income exist. For 35 U.S.C. 123(d) claims, determine that applicants still obtain the majority of income from an institution of higher education as defined.
guidance: Micro entity status is evaluated at each fee payment date. Check the USPTO website for 'maximum qualifying gross income' annually. The Office generally will not question certifications made in accordance with requirements, but applicants must re-evaluate eligibility before each micro-fee payment.

name: Scope of examination in ex parte reexamination (37 CFR 1.552(a))
description: Claims in an ex parte reexamination proceeding will be examined on the basis of patents or printed publications and, with respect to subject matter added or deleted in the reexamination proceeding, on the basis of the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112.
guidance: When new or amended subject matter is presented, enablement and written description under 35 U.S.C. 112 are applied to that amendatory matter; original claim matter is generally not reexamined under 112 except as specified elsewhere.

name: No enlargement of claim scope permitted (37 CFR 1.552(b) / 35 U.S.C. 305)
description: Claims in ex parte reexamination will not be permitted to enlarge the scope of the claims of the patent; proposed amended or new claims enlarging scope are not allowed.
guidance: 35 U.S.C. 305 states no proposed amended or new claim enlarging scope will be permitted. Examiner must reject any claim that enlarges scope under 35 U.S.C. 305 (use form paragraph 22.11). A claim 'enlarges the scope' if it is broader than each and every claim of the patent (see MPEP §1412.03).

name: Use of patent owner statements to construe claims (37 CFR 1.552(d))
description: Any statement of the patent owner and accompanying information submitted pursuant to 37 CFR 1.501(a)(2) that is of record may be used after reexamination has been ordered to determine the proper meaning of a patent claim when applying patents or printed publications.
guidance: Such statements are considered at the examination stage (after order) for claim interpretation in connection with prior art applied to the claim.

name: Reexamination under 35 U.S.C. 304: basis and limits
description: Reexamination ordered under 35 U.S.C. 304 provides a reexamination of patent claims on the basis of prior art patents and printed publications; 35 U.S.C. 112 is addressed only with respect to new claims or amendatory subject matter.
guidance: Any new or amended claims are examined to ensure they do not enlarge the scope of the original patent claims (see 35 U.S.C. 305). Double patenting issues may also be considered during such reexamination.

name: Applicable prior art regime and effective filing dates
description: The prior art regime under which the application for the patent was examined (first-inventor-to-file or first-to-invent) generally governs reexamination; exceptions arise when amended/new claims have effective filing dates on/after March 16, 2013 or when benefit claims to earlier applications are involved.
guidance: If a new/amended claim has an effective filing date on/after March 16, 2013, reexamination is conducted under first-inventor-to-file rules. If a benefit claim to an earlier application with filing date before March 16, 2013 is made, reexamination may be under first-to-invent rules only if the prior application's written description provides adequate 35 U.S.C. 112 support for all relevant claims and claim presentations. See MPEP Chapter 700 for details and statutory text (35 U.S.C. 102) as applied to each regime.

name: Intervening patents/printed publications as prior art
description: Rejections may be based on intervening patents or printed publications where the patent claims under reexamination are entitled only to the filing date of the patent and are not supported by an earlier foreign or U.S. application whose filing date is claimed.
guidance: Intervening patents/prints are prior art under cases like In re Ruscetta and In re van Langenhoven; the Office may perform 35 U.S.C. 112 written description priority analysis during reexamination (In re NTP). See MPEP §211.

name: Admissions by patent owner and their use
description: Admissions by the patent owner of record or in a court record may be utilized in combination with a patent or printed publication in reexamination, but an admission alone may not establish an initial SNQ under 35 U.S.C. 303.
guidance: A submission under 35 U.S.C. 301 may include patent owner statements from court or Office proceedings; if relied upon in the request, the requester must explain how the statement is used to determine claim meaning per 37 CFR 1.510(b)(2). Admissions in the record are part of the scope/content of the prior art (Graham) and require no independent proof; third parties cannot submit admissions made outside the record or court. Under 35 U.S.C. 257, admissions need not be combined with patents or printed publications.

name: Claim interpretation standards in reexamination
description: Original patent claims in reexamination ordered under 35 U.S.C. 304 are examined only on the basis of prior art patents/printed publications applied under 35 U.S.C. 102/103; claim terms should be construed consistently with judicial interpretations and the broadest reasonable interpretation standard.
guidance: If related litigation has a judicial claim construction, examiner should acknowledge and assess consistency with the broadest reasonable construction and provide reasoning when adopting a different construction. During reexamination (including 257), claims are given the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification; limitations in the specification are not to be read into claims. For expired patents, Phillips standard (ordinary and customary meaning) applies. The statutory presumption of validity (35 U.S.C. 282) does not apply in reexamination.

name: Limited scope for 35 U.S.C. 112 compliance in 304
description: In reexaminations ordered under 35 U.S.C. 304, 35 U.S.C. 112 compliance (enablement and written description) should be considered only as to amendatory and new text presented in the reexamination proceeding.
guidance: A term in an original patent claim cannot be examined as too broad under 112 unless the amendatory matter creates the issue. Rewriting a dependent claim as independent cannot be examined under 112 unless the rewriting raises a new question (e.g., lack of antecedent). The Office may determine entitlement to a priority/benefit date and perform a 112 written description priority analysis (see In re NTP).

name: 35 U.S.C. 112 issues in reexamination ordered under 257
description: Reexaminations ordered under 35 U.S.C. 257 may involve any issues under 35 U.S.C. 112, not limited to matter added or deleted during reexamination, and may include original subject matter in the specification, claims, and drawings.
guidance: Examiner should consider enablement, written description, and other 112 grounds across original and amended materials as necessary in 257 proceedings.

name: New matter prohibition and written-description rejections
description: 35 U.S.C. 305 provides for examination under 35 U.S.C. 132, which prohibits introduction of new matter into the disclosure; new matter added to claims should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, for failing written-description.
guidance: Examiners should consider relationship between written description and new matter prohibition (see MPEP §2163.06); when new matter affects claim limitations, apply 112 rejection accordingly.

name: Amendment of the specification must meet 35 U.S.C. 112
description: When the specification is amended in a reexamination proceeding, the examiner must ensure the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112 are met since amendments can redefine claim term scope and cause claims to be unclear or unsupported.
guidance: Amendments to the specification can cause failure of claims to comply with 112 even where claim language is unchanged; examiner should assess and, if appropriate, reject claims under relevant 112 grounds.

name: Criteria for determining claim enlargement (35 U.S.C. 305 / MPEP §1412.03)
description: A claim presented in reexamination 'enlarges the scope' of the patent where it is broader than each and every claim of the patent; a claim is broadened if it contains any conceivable product/process that would not have infringed the original patent, even if narrower in other respects.
guidance: Use MPEP §1412.03 guidance to determine broadening; employ form paragraph 22.11 for rejections under 35 U.S.C. 305. Examiner should identify and explain the claim limitations that broaden the scope (see bracket 2 in form paragraph).

name: Scope limited to 'live' claims and requester requirements
description: The Office's determination in both the order for reexamination and the examination stage will generally be limited to review of the 'live' claims for which reexamination has been requested; the requester must set forth pertinency and manner of applying cited prior art to every claim requested.
guidance: If requester fails to apply the art to certain claims per 37 CFR 1.510(b), those claims generally will not be reexamined. The Office has discretion to reexamine claims not requested on individual facts and may add claims during examination if intervening prior art raises an SNQ as to those claims.

name: Phillips v. AWH Corp. (claim construction framework)
description: Claim terms carry their ordinary and customary meaning as understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of invention, with that meaning informed primarily by the intrinsic record: i.e., the claims, the specification, and the prosecution history.
guidance: Phillips (en banc) is described as the undisputed foundation of claim construction doctrine and leads citation counts in 2025. The decision resolved tension about the relative weight of intrinsic versus extrinsic evidence, subordinating dictionaries and expert testimony to the patent document itself. (Data based on parsing CAFC's 2025 precedential patent decisions through December 15, 2025.)

name: Identification of an initial submission as a 35 U.S.C. 371 national-stage filing
description: Applicant’s initial submission under 35 U.S.C. 371 must be identified as a submission to enter the national stage under 35 U.S.C. 371; otherwise it will be treated as a filing under 35 U.S.C. 111(a) (unless clearly a 35 U.S.C. 154(d)(4) provisional-rights submission).
guidance: Acceptable ways to identify the submission include selecting “371 National Stage” in the USPTO electronic filing system, using transmittal Form PTO-1390, or including an inventor’s oath/declaration that identifies the international application by international application number as the application to which the oath/declaration is directed. Notably, merely claiming priority of an international application in an oath/declaration does not indicate a submission under 35 U.S.C. 371. Examiners should check for Form PCT/DO/EO/903 (Notice of Acceptance of Application under 35 U.S.C. 371) and bib-data indications; if neither is present and no evidence indicates national-stage processing was desired, treat as a 111(a) filing. If both indications are present, treat as 371. For questions, consult International Patent Legal Administration.

name: Benefit claims to prior U.S. provisional, nonprovisional, or international applications
description: A national stage application may include a benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) (provisional), or 120 and 365(c) (prior U.S. national or international applications). Conditions mirror those in MPEP §§ 201.07, 201.08, 211 et seq. and require compliance with 37 CFR 1.78 (and 1.78(d) for 120/365(c)).
guidance: To obtain benefit under 119(e), the national stage application must comply with 37 CFR 1.78(a): the prior provisional must be entitled to a filing date (37 CFR 1.53(c)), basic filing fee paid on provisional within required period (37 CFR 1.16(d)), the provisional must name at least one inventor named in the later international application, and the provisional must disclose the inventor’s invention claimed in at least one claim of the national stage app in the manner of 35 U.S.C. 112 first paragraph. The national stage application must reference the provisional by number (series code and serial) within the time in 1.78(a)(4). If the international filing date is prior to Sept.16,2012 the reference may be in ADS or first sentence(s) of specification; on/after Sept.16,2012 the reference must be in ADS (37 CFR 1.78(a)(3), pre-AIA 1.78(a)(5)(iii)). Translational requirements apply if provisional was non-English. Restoration of benefit or priority may be possible via petitions under 37 CFR 1.78(b) or 1.78(c) (and analogous 1.55 petitions where applicable). Failure to timely submit required references under 1.78(d)(3) for 120/365(c) is considered a waiver of benefit unless a petition for unintentional delay is granted.

name: Standard of proof — preponderance of the evidence
description: Petitioner has demonstrated, by a preponderance of the evidence, that claims 1–9 are unpatentable. (Final Written Decision pursuant to 35 U.S.C. § 318(a))
guidance: An IPR petitioner must prove unpatentability by a preponderance of the evidence. The Board's final determination is based on whether the petitioner has met that burden for the challenged claims.

name: Claim construction standard
description: We construe claims 'using the same claim construction standard that would be used to construe the claim in a civil action under 35 U.S.C. 282(b), including construing the claim in accordance with the ordinary and customary meaning of such claim as understood by one of ordinary skill in the art and the prosecution history pertaining to the patent.' (37 C.F.R. § 42.100(b); Phillips v. AWH Corp.)
guidance: Only terms 'in controversy' need express construction and only to the extent necessary to resolve the controversy (citing Nidec and Vivid). Use intrinsic evidence (claims, specification, prosecution history) to construe terms; do not adopt limiting constructions absent highly persuasive evidence.

name: Obviousness legal framework — Graham factors
description: A claim is unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. § 103 if differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious to a POSITA. Determine (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between claimed subject matter and prior art; (3) level of skill in the art; and (4) objective evidence of nonobviousness (secondary considerations).
guidance: Resolve obviousness on the basis of underlying factual determinations and apply legal reasoning (Graham v. John Deere). Address motivation to combine and reasonable expectation of success when combining references.

name: Scope and content of the prior art
description: Evaluate the teachings, disclosures, and specific embodiments of the asserted prior-art references (e.g., what Hays, van Datta, Levkovitz disclose regarding advertisement delivery, client requests, ad insertion, tagging of assets, bots/electronic agents, etc.).
guidance: Analyze prior-art references in detail (figures, passages, examples) to determine whether they anticipate or render obvious specific claim limitations; cite specific paragraphs/figures as the record supports.

name: Differences between claims and prior art; reasons to modify or combine
description: Identify any differences between the claimed limitations and the prior art and articulate why a skilled artisan would modify or combine references, with a rational underpinning, to arrive at the claimed invention.
guidance: A valid obviousness combination requires articulated reasons to combine references and, where relevant, a reasonable expectation of success; evidence of specific advantages or teachable motivations (e.g., user customization benefits) supports a motivation to combine.

name: Use of specification and prosecution history in claim interpretation
description: The specification and prosecution history are used to interpret claim terms, and examples in the specification may rebut overly narrow constructions (e.g., a preferred embodiment showing skins/ad updates that would be excluded by narrowing).
guidance: Do not adopt a claim construction that excludes a preferred embodiment absent highly persuasive evidentiary support (Vitronics). Prosecution history may inform but does not automatically limit claim scope.

name: Preamble and limitation analysis
description: Determine whether preamble language is limiting based on claim language, specification, and prosecution history; the Board need not decide whether a preamble is limiting if not necessary to resolve the controversy.
guidance: Assess whether preamble provides essential structure/meaning to the claim or merely states intended use; litigation positions and record evidence guide whether to treat the preamble as a limitation.

name: 37 CFR 1.111 — form and content of reply to non-final Office action
description: Reply must be reduced to writing which distinctly and specifically points out the supposed errors in the examiner's action and must reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the prior Office action.
guidance: The reply must present arguments pointing out the specific distinctions believed to render the claims patentable over applied references. A general allegation that the claims define a patentable invention without specifically pointing out how the claim language distinguishes over the references does not comply. See 37 CFR 1.111(b).

name: Supplemental replies — limits and entry conditions
description: A reply supplemental to a reply in compliance with § 1.111(b) will not be entered as a matter of right except where clearly limited to specific categories (cancellation of claims; adoption of examiner suggestions; placement in condition for allowance; reply to a requirement made after the first reply; correction of informalities; simplification of issues for appeal).
guidance: A supplemental reply will be entered if filed within the period during which action by the Office is suspended under § 1.103(a) or (c). See 37 CFR 1.111(a)(2)(i)-(ii).

name: Amendments in reply must point out patentable novelty and avoidance of references
description: When amending in reply to a rejection, the applicant or patent owner must clearly point out the patentable novelty believed to be present in the claims in view of the art and must show how the amendments avoid such references or objections.
guidance: This applies to amendments in both applications and reexaminations (see MPEP § 2666.01; 37 CFR 1.111(c)).

name: Reexamination responses follow application examination rules (substance)
description: Inter partes reexamination proceedings are conducted in accordance with §§ 1.104 through 1.116; accordingly, 37 CFR 1.111 applies to the patent owner's response in reexamination.
guidance: Requests for reconsideration must be in writing and distinctly point out each supposed error; reasons must state how claims define over references and why any 35 U.S.C. 112 rejections are incorrect or inapplicable. Affidavits under 37 CFR 1.131 and 1.132 may be used subject to limitations (see below).

name: Affidavit limitations — 1.131 cannot 'swear back' when reference claims same invention
description: An affidavit under 37 CFR 1.131 may not be used to 'swear back' of a reference patent if the reference patent is claiming the same invention as the patent undergoing reexamination.
guidance: In that situation consider affidavit under 37 CFR 1.130 (see MPEP § 718), or raising the issue via interference/reissue if appropriate.

name: Manner of making specification amendments
description: Changes to the specification other than claims must be made by submission of the entire text of an added or rewritten paragraph including markings, except an entire paragraph may be deleted by a statement deleting the paragraph without presenting its text.
guidance: The precise insertion point must be identified. This applies whether amendment is submitted on paper or compact disc (see §§ 1.96 and 1.825).

name: Markings for added and omitted matter
description: Matter to be omitted must be enclosed in brackets; matter to be added must be underlined.
guidance: These markings apply to all changes relative to the patent being reexamined made to the specification and claims.

name: Amendments must not introduce new matter or enlarge claim scope
description: No amendment may enlarge the scope of the claims or introduce new matter. No amendment may be proposed for entry in an expired patent (other than cancellation).
guidance: Amended or new claims which broaden or enlarge scope should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 314(a). The test for enlargement under 35 U.S.C. 314(a) is the same as under 35 U.S.C. 251 (see In re Freeman). If the patent expires during reexamination, amendments are improper and reexamination continues on unamended claims. See handling of new matter at MPEP § 2670 and enlargement discussion at § 2658.

name: Statutory contents of the complete specification
description: 'The complete specification ... must particularly describe and ascertain the nature of the invention, and in what manner it is to be performed, and must be accompanied by drawings if required. It must commence with the title, and must end with a distinct statement of the invention claimed.'
guidance: Form of instrument is Form C (Second Schedule, Patents Rules, 1890). Examiner will ascertain whether the nature of the invention has been fairly described and whether application, specification and drawings have been prepared in the prescribed manner and the title sufficiently indicates the subject-matter. If inadequate, the Comptroller may require amendments or refuse acceptance (subject to appeal).

name: Relationship between provisional and complete specifications (same invention requirement)
description: The complete specification must describe substantially the same invention as the provisional; the nature of the invention must be the same though improvements and developments within the scope allowed by the provisional may be added.
guidance: It is permissible to narrow the provisional (e.g. provisional sets out a principle, complete claims a special mechanism) and to introduce improvements, mechanical equivalents, and developments 'within the ambit' of the provisional. But introducing a material addition or claiming something larger or different than disclosed in the provisional invalidates the patent (cases: Bailey v. Roberton, Edison phonograph case, etc.). The patentee cannot rely on the provisional to cure defects in the complete specification.

name: Clear definition of the invention and distinct claims
description: The specification must accurately define the invention so the reader may clearly understand of what it consists and must end with a distinct statement of the invention claimed; vague formulations are insufficient.
guidance: The patentee should state 'My improvement consists in this...' or describe by reference to figures. A claim stating only 'I claim the improved machine substantially as described' is inadequate and may be colourable compliance only. Courts have invalidated patents where the specification did not indicate with reasonable clearness what novelty was claimed (Philpott v. Hanbury; Fairburn v. Household). Where a second patent for improvements is obtained, distinguish clearly the later improvements from earlier invention.

name: Title must correspond to the invention described
description: If any part of the invention, as described in the complete specification, does not fall within the title, the patent may be invalid.
guidance: However, a specification that expressly indicates applicability beyond the title (e.g. railway carriage doors applicable to doors of any carriage) may extend claims beyond narrow title wording. Care should be taken to ensure title and specification align.

name: Cannot rely on provisional to cure complete specification defects
description: A patentee will not be allowed to read the provisional specification with the view of aiding or supplying defects in the complete specification.
guidance: The complete specification must stand on its own as a fair and sufficient disclosure of the invention claimed; provisional may not be used to patch insufficiencies in the complete instrument (Macfarlane v. Price, etc.).

name: Claim Construction for the Case (judge-provided constructions)
description: The judge provides the meaning of any claim language that must be interpreted and the jury must accept those meanings when deciding infringement and invalidity.
guidance: [READ STIPULATIONS AND COURT’S CLAIM CONSTRUCTIONS]. Judge's constructions control. (Cites Teva Pharm. v. Sandoz; Phillips; Markman.)

name: Construction of Means-Plus-Function (§112(f)/¶6) Claims
description: When a claim uses a 'means' or 'step' for performing a function, that clause may be a means-plus-function element requiring special interpretation; it does not cover all means/steps that perform the recited function. The court identifies the recited function and the structure (or step) in the specification/drawings that performs it, or equivalents.
guidance: Jury must use the court's interpretation of the means-plus-function element for infringement and validity. Consider whether Instruction 2.2 is necessary where the phrase 'means for' is not used but §112(f) may apply. (Cites 35 U.S.C. § 112; Mettler-Toledo; JVW; Utah Med.; Valmont.)

name: Infringement—Generally
description: Patent owner has the right to exclude others from importing, making, using, offering to sell, or selling the claimed invention in the U.S. during the term of the patent. Any person or entity engaging in those acts without permission infringes the patent. A claim may be infringed directly or indirectly.
guidance: When deciding infringement, compare the accused product/method to the patent claims (not to the plaintiff’s commercial product). Distinguish direct vs indirect infringement, literal infringement vs doctrine of equivalents, and induced vs contributory infringement. (Cites 35 U.S.C. § 271; Limelight; WordTech.)

name: Direct Infringement—Literal Infringement (all-elements rule)
description: A patent claim is literally infringed only if the accused product/method includes each and every element or method step recited in that patent claim. If the accused product/method lacks one or more elements, it does not literally infringe that claim.
guidance: Determine literal infringement with respect to each claim individually. The same accused element may satisfy more than one claim element. Use the court's claim constructions when comparing. (Cites Limelight; Hutchins; Amstar.)

name: Direct Infringement—Joint Infringement (attribution rules)
description: If multiple parties perform steps of a claimed method, the defendant is liable only if the defendant personally performed all acts necessary to infringe or if the acts of others are attributable to the defendant via direction or control or formation of a joint enterprise.
guidance: A joint enterprise requires proof of four elements: (1) agreement among group members; (2) common purpose to be carried out by group; (3) community of pecuniary interest in that purpose; and (4) equal right to a voice in the direction of the enterprise. If neither direction/control nor joint enterprise is found, no direct infringement. (Cites Limelight; Akamai; Eli Lilly; Nalco.) Practice note: Explain joint infringement and inducement side-by-side to avoid jury confusion.

name: Literal Infringement of Means-Plus-Function or Step-Plus-Function Claims
description: To establish infringement of a means-plus-function/step-plus-function claim, the plaintiff must prove (1) the accused product/method performs the recited function and (2) the accused structure/step is identical or equivalent to the structure/step described in the patent specification and drawings for performing that function.
guidance: First decide whether the accused product has any structure/step that performs the specific function. If so, decide whether that structure/step is the same as, or equivalent to, the structure recited in the specification. Equivalence is judged from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art—differences are insubstantial if they perform the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result. (Cites §112; Williamson; Brilliant Instruments; Cybor; others.)

name: Infringement of Dependent Claims
description: Independent claims do not refer to other claims. A dependent claim refers to at least one other claim and includes all elements recited in the dependent claim as well as all elements of the independent claim to which it refers.
guidance: To establish literal infringement of a dependent claim, the plaintiff must show the accused product/method includes each and every element of the independent claim and the dependent claim. If the independent claim is not literally infringed, the dependent claim cannot be literally infringed. (Cites Wahpeton Canvas; Shatterproof Glass.)

name: Meaning of 'Comprising', 'Consisting of', and 'Consisting Essentially of'
description: 'Comprising' means including the following but not excluding others. 'Consisting of' means including the following and excluding others. 'Consisting essentially of' means including the following and possibly including unlisted components/steps that do not materially affect the invention.
guidance: If a claim uses 'comprising', the presence of additional components/steps does not defeat literal infringement. If 'consisting of' is used, additional components/steps defeat literal infringement. If 'consisting essentially of' is used, additional components/steps are permitted only if they do not negate an element or materially affect the basic and novel properties of the invention. Practice note: If claim is literally infringed, no need to resort to the doctrine of equivalents. (Cites cases including Shire Dev.; Multilayer; PPG.)

name: Doctrine of Equivalents—When Literal Infringement Fails
description: If the accused product/method does not literally infringe, it may still infringe under the doctrine of equivalents if it contains components/steps that are equivalents of the claim elements that are not literally present. The accused product must have an equivalent for each individual claim element that is not literally present.
guidance: Equivalence may be shown by demonstrating the accused component performs substantially the same function, in substantially the same way, to achieve substantially the same result, or by showing it is insubstantially different. Consider whether persons of ordinary skill would have known of interchangeability at the time, though known interchangeability is not necessary. The same accused component may satisfy multiple claim elements; multiple accused components may satisfy a single claim element. (Cites Warner-Jenkinson; Graver Tank.)

name: Doctrine of Equivalents Limitation—Prosecution History Estoppel
description: If the patentee made a representation or argument, or an amendment to the claim for reasons related to patentability, there is a presumption that the equivalent subject matter has been surrendered and the doctrine of equivalents cannot be applied to those elements unless the presumption is rebutted.
guidance: This is determined by the court as a matter of law. If applied, the judge will list elements on a claim-by-claim basis to which DOE cannot be applied; those elements must be literally present for infringement. (Cites Festo; Federal Circuit authority.)

name: Doctrine of Equivalents Limitation—Subject Matter Dedicated to the Public
description: If the court determines certain subject matter from the patent has been dedicated to the public, the doctrine of equivalents cannot be applied to those elements; they must be literally present for infringement.
guidance: Court will list affected elements on a claim-by-claim basis. (Cites SanDisk; Pfizer v. Teva; Johnson & Johnston.)

name: Actively Inducing Patent Infringement (Inducement) — Elements
description: To find that the defendant actively induced infringement, the plaintiff must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that (1) a single actor is responsible for direct infringement (all components/steps) and (2) the defendant actively induced these acts.
guidance: To prove inducement the plaintiff must establish that (1) the defendant aided, instructed, or otherwise acted with intent to cause acts constituting direct infringement; (2) the defendant knew of the patent, or showed willful blindness to its existence; (3) the defendant knew, or showed willful blindness, that the actions of the alleged direct infringer would infringe at least one claim; and (4) the alleged direct infringer infringed at least one claim. Willful blindness requires subjective belief of a high probability a patent existed plus deliberate actions to avoid learning of it. (Cites §271(b); Commil; Limelight; Global-Tech.) Practice note: Distinguish inducement from joint infringement in jury instructions.

name: Infringement by Supplying All or a Substantial Portion of Components Abroad (§271(f)(1))
description: To show infringement under §271(f)(1), the plaintiff must prove: (1) the product as intended to be assembled outside the U.S. included all elements of at least one claim; (2) the defendant supplied (or caused to be supplied) components from the U.S. that made up all or a substantial portion of the invention; and (3) the defendant specifically intended to induce the combination of those components into a product that would infringe if assembled in the U.S.
guidance: A substantial portion of components requires a quantitative, not qualitative, assessment; exporting a single component of a multi-component invention cannot create liability under §271(f)(1). (Cites §271(f)(1); Life Techs. v. Promega; Microsoft v. AT&T.)

name: Contributory Infringement—Elements
description: To find contributory infringement, the plaintiff must prove someone other than the defendant directly infringed a claim and that the defendant (1) sold, offered for sale, or imported within the U.S. a component of the infringing product or an apparatus for use in the infringing method; (2) the component/apparatus is not a staple article or commodity of commerce capable of substantial non-infringing use; (3) the component/apparatus constitutes a material part of the claimed invention; and (4) the defendant knew the component was especially made or adapted for use in an infringing product/method.
guidance: A 'staple article or commodity of commerce capable of substantial non-infringing use' has other non-infringing uses that are not occasional, farfetched, impractical, experimental, or hypothetical. Defendant's knowledge may be shown by willful blindness (subjective high probability plus deliberate avoidance). (Cites §271(c); Commil; Global-Tech; Aro; Toshiba.)

name: Infringement by Supplying Components Especially Made/Adapted for Use Abroad (§271(f)(2))
description: To show infringement under §271(f)(2), the plaintiff must prove: (1) the defendant supplied components from the U.S. into a foreign country or caused them to be supplied; (2) the defendant knew or should have known the components were especially made or adapted for use in a product that infringes a claim; (3) those components have no substantial non-infringing use; and (4) the defendant intended the components to be combined into that product.
guidance: It is not necessary that the components actually were combined into an infringing product—intended combination suffices. (Cites §271(f)(2); WesternGeco; Microsoft; Cardiac Pacemakers.)

name: Summary of Invalidity Defense—Burden and Standard
description: Defendant contends asserted claims are invalid and must prove by clear and convincing evidence that each asserted claim is invalid.
guidance: Court will instruct jury in more detail about defendant's specific invalidity contentions. (Standard: clear and convincing evidence.)

name: Elements of the International Application
description: Required components and formal elements that must be present in an international application (request, description, claims, drawings, abstract, etc.).

name: No Search Required if Claims Are Unclear
description: Policy and procedure when claims are so unclear that no meaningful search can be made.

name: Procedure for Claims Not Required To Be Searched and for Claims That Are Unclear
description: Procedural steps the ISA follows for claims excluded from search or found unclear, including notice to applicant.

name: Jepson-format claims imply admission of preamble as prior art
description: Drafting a claim in Jepson format is taken as an implied admission that the preamble subject matter is prior art of another, unless applicant provides a credible reason to the contrary or the preamble describes applicant's own work.
guidance: In re Fout held Jepson preamble to be admitted prior art; In re Ehrreich and Reading & Bates show the implication may be overcome with explanation (e.g., Jepson used to avoid double patenting) or if preamble describes applicant's own work.

name: Anticipation requires every element in single reference
description: A claim is anticipated only if each and every element of the claim is found, either expressly or inherently, in a single prior art reference.
guidance: Verdegaal Bros. v. Union Oil and Richardson v. Suzuki: elements must be arranged as required by the claim (not an ipsissimis verbis test — identical terminology not required). Multiple references may be permissible in some 102 contexts (see MPEP § 2131.01), but pure anticipation is single-reference.

name: Proving an 'enabled disclosure' via extra references
description: Extra references and extrinsic evidence can be used to show the primary reference enables the claimed invention when the primary reference otherwise discloses the claimed composition/structure.
guidance: In re Samour and In re Donohue: publication taught claimed compound structure while patents taught methods of making such compounds; showing enablement of primary reference via secondary references is permissible and motivation to combine is not required for anticipation.

name: Species anticipates genus
description: A species disclosed in the prior art that falls within a claimed genus will anticipate the genus claim.
guidance: In re Slayter and In re Gosteli support that a specific species disclosed anticipates a broader genus claim (subject to priority issues).

name: Naming a claimed species anticipates regardless of listing size
description: If a reference clearly names the claimed species, that species anticipates the claim no matter how many other species are named in the reference.
guidance: Ex parte A and In re Sivaramakrishnan: even a comprehensive listing (e.g., Merck Index) that specifically names the compound or additive anticipates the species claim; being listed as representative or among many does not defeat anticipation.

name: Generic disclosure anticipates species if 'at once envisaged'
description: A generic disclosure will anticipate a claimed species when the species can be 'at once envisaged' from the disclosure — i.e., a person of ordinary skill would immediately recognize the specific species from the generic teaching.
guidance: Sanofi-Synthelabo, Osram Sylvania, Kennametal, In re Petering, In re Schauman: factors include size and limitation of the genus, preferred embodiments, ability to draw the structural formula or name the compound from the disclosure, and whether express contemplation of combinations exists. When arriving at a specific compound requires selecting and combining multiple lists of alternatives, anticipation requires that the classes be sufficiently limited or well delineated.

name: Anticipation of ranges — specific example within claimed range
description: A specific example in the prior art that falls within a claimed range anticipates the range claim.
guidance: Titanium Metals v. Banner and In re Petering: an actual data point within the claimed range (e.g., graph point) is sufficient to anticipate a claimed compositional range.

name: Anticipation of overlapping ranges requires 'sufficient specificity'
description: When prior art teaches a range overlapping or touching the claimed range but provides no specific examples within the claimed range, anticipation depends on whether the prior art discloses the claimed range with 'sufficient specificity' (case-by-case).
