guidance: ClearValue v. Pearl River (narrow claimed range anticipated by broader prior range where no evidence of criticality across range) vs Atofina (broader prior range did not sufficiently describe a narrower claimed range where claimed range was shown to be critical). If insufficient specificity, the examiner should consider nonobviousness (evidence of unexpected results) and may issue a combined 102/103 rejection with reasoned statements on both anticipation and obviousness (Ex parte Lee). See MPEP § 2144.05 for obviousness of ranges.

name: Order of substantive examination steps
description: The examination of the application proceeds in the following order: 1) Understanding of the invention; 2) Assessment of Patentability of the subject matter; 3) Assessment of sufficiency of disclosure; 4) Check for unity of invention; 5) Appraisal of Industrial applicability; 6) Classification of the invention; 7) Determination of priority of each claim; 8) Novelty search; 9) Determination of the inventive step; 10) Judgment of the validity of claims.
guidance: Follow this sequential procedure when examining or preparing an application to anticipate examiner scrutiny and objections.

name: Indian standard: Relative novelty (not absolute) and documents to consider
description: Indian Patents Act requires Relative Novelty (not Absolute Novelty). The examiner should search whether the invention claimed has been anticipated by: a) Indian patent specifications published before the date of filing but on or after 01.01.1912 (S.13(1)(a)); b) Indian patent specifications filed before the date of filing or claiming earlier priority but published on or after the filing date (S.13(1)(b)); c) Any publication in India or elsewhere effected before the filing date (S.13(2)); d) Indian patent specifications published before the date of filing but on or after the priority date of the application (S.13(1)(a)).
guidance: Search scope is defined by Indian statute — consider relevant Indian and foreign publications as specified; be mindful of priority dates and publication dates.

name: Actions the Controller may take in cases of anticipation
description: If the invention is anticipated by prior publication as per S.13 the Controller may refuse the complete specification unless the applicant shows that the priority date of his claim is not later than that of the cited document or amends the complete specification to the Controller's satisfaction. If anticipated by prior claiming (S.13(1)(b)) the Controller may direct that a reference to that other specification be inserted in the applicant's specification unless the applicant shows an earlier priority date or amends. The Controller may also direct insertion of a reference to another patent which could be infringed and may delete such reference later on request when conditions change.
guidance: When anticipation is found, remedies include refusal, mandated insertion of references, or allowing amendments; applicants should consider priority evidence or claim amendments to overcome objections.

name: Change/substitution of applicant (S.20) — procedure and proof
description: A claim for substituting an applicant/applicants has to be made in Form 6 with the prescribed fee along with the original assignment/agreement or an official/notarized copy thereof. The Controller may call for other proof of title or written consent of the assignor/s if required. By virtue of a written assignment or agreement from the applicant or by operation of law the claimant(s) may claim the patent or specific interest; the Controller, if satisfied, may direct that the application proceed in the name of the claimant(s).
guidance: File Form 6 and attach assignment documents and fee; be prepared to supply further evidence of title if Controller requests.

name: Specification and claims as components of the patent
description: The patent application includes a 'specification' containing a written description of the claimed invention telling what the invention is, how it works, how to make it, and how to use it. The specification concludes with one or more numbered sentences called the patent 'claims.' When the patent is granted, the claims define the boundaries of its protection and give notice to the public of those boundaries.
guidance: The figures and text provide context and examples, but it is the claims that define the breadth of coverage.

name: Prior art and its use in examination
description: The PTO searches for and reviews information that is publicly available or submitted by the applicant called 'prior art.' The Examiner reviews prior art to determine whether the invention is truly an advance over the state of the art at the time the application was filed. A patent lists the prior art the Examiner considered (the 'cited references').
guidance: Prior art generally includes information demonstrating the state of technology that existed before the claimed invention was made or before the application was filed.

name: Claim-by-claim analysis
description: In deciding infringement and invalidity, issues are assessed on a claim-by-claim basis; each claim is effectively treated as if it were a separate patent and may cover more or less than another claim.
guidance: Jury must determine what each claim covers and then apply infringement/invalidity analyses to each asserted claim.

name: Judge’s role in claim construction
description: It is the judge's role to define the terms of the claims, and it is the jury's role to apply those definitions to the issues in the case. The jury must accept the court's definitions of claim terms provided to them.
guidance: If the court has provided claim constructions or a glossary, the jury is to apply those definitions throughout the case; the judge's constructions are not an indication of views on infringement or validity.

name: How a claim defines what it covers (claim elements/limitations)
description: A claim sets forth, in words, a set of requirements (claim elements or limitations) in a single sentence. If a device or method satisfies each of these requirements, then it is covered by the claim.
guidance: When a thing meets all the claim elements, the claim 'covers' that thing. Understanding claim language is necessary to decide infringement and validity.

name: Transitional claim language: 'comprising', 'consisting of', 'consisting essentially of'
description: The instructions explain how transitional phrases affect claim scope: e.g., 'comprising' is open-ended and allows additional undisclosed elements; 'consisting of' is closed and means 'I claim what follows and nothing else'; 'consisting essentially of' is intermediate in scope.
guidance: The page cites authorities (cases) illustrating these meanings and their practical effect on claim breadth.

name: Anticipation (novelty) standard
description: A claim is not new (is anticipated) if all of the elements of the claim are present in a single previous device or method, or sufficiently described in a single previous printed publication or patent.
guidance: Anticipation must be proven by clear and convincing evidence (see burden of proof entry).

name: Obviousness standard
description: A claim may be invalid as obvious even if every element is not shown in a single piece of prior art; it is invalid if it would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the field at the relevant time.
guidance: Jury will consider a number of questions (to be instructed later) in deciding whether claimed inventions are obvious; invalidity by obviousness must be proven by clear and convincing evidence.

name: Invalidity/unenforceability proof allocation
description: The accused infringer must persuade the jury by clear and convincing evidence that a claim is invalid (and/or unenforceable).
guidance: The accused infringer will present evidence of invalidity and may rebut the patent holder's proofs; the sequence of presentation (opening, evidence, rebuttal, closings) is described in the trial outline.

name: Anticipation evidence types
description: Anticipation can be shown by a single previous device or method, or a single previous printed publication or patent that sufficiently describes all claim elements.
guidance: This clarifies what qualifies as prior art for anticipation purposes; the Examiner's cited references are examples of prior art considered during prosecution.

name: Determine prior related proceeding art status before making rejections
description: Prior to making any rejection in the ongoing reexamination, determine for any prior related Office proceeding what prior art was (i) relied upon to reject any claim, or (ii) cited and discussed.
guidance: This determination is required to decide whether reexamination reuses art already considered and thereby whether Portola Packaging requires termination or withdrawal of rejections.

name: Terminate prosecution when only rejections rest on previously considered art
description: Terminate the prosecution of any reexamination in which the only remaining rejections are entirely based on prior art that was, in any prior related Office proceeding, previously (i) relied upon to reject any claim, and/or (ii) cited and its relevance to patentability of a claim discussed.
guidance: Before terminating, the Director may search for new art to determine whether a substantial new question of patentability exists (see 35 U.S.C. 303 and 305).

name: Foreign language prior art translation may create SNQ
description: If a foreign language prior art reference was cited and discussed in any prior Office proceeding but never completely and accurately translated into English during the original prosecution, a complete and accurate translation submitted in a reexamination request may be appropriate to order and/or conduct reexamination.
guidance: A reexamination request should explain why the more complete/accurate translation actually teaches what is required by the claims.

name: Required wording when terminating prosecution under Portola Packaging
description: If prosecution of an ongoing reexamination is terminated under Portola Packaging, the Notice of Intent to Issue Ex Parte Reexamination Certificate should state: 'The prosecution of this reexamination is terminated based on In re Portola Packaging, Inc., 110 F.3d 786, 42 USPQ2d 1295 (Fed. Cir. 1997). No patentability determination has been made in this reexamination proceeding.'
guidance: If a rejection is withdrawn to comply with Portola, the Office action withdrawing such rejection should explicitly state that the rejection(s) based upon _______ is/are withdrawn in view of In re Portola Packaging and that no patentability determination of the claims in view of such prior art has been made.

name: Standards for rejecting claims for novelty/obviousness
description: If the invention is not patentable, the claims will be rejected. When rejecting for want of novelty or for obviousness, the examiner must cite the best references at his or her command, designate the particular part relied on when a reference is complex, clearly explain the pertinency of each reference if not apparent, and specify each rejected claim.
guidance: Designate specific portions of complex references 'as nearly as practicable' and explain how the references apply to each rejected claim.

name: Reliance on admissions and facts within examiner knowledge
description: In rejecting claims the examiner may rely upon admissions by the applicant, or the patent owner in reexamination, as to any matter affecting patentability and may rely upon facts within his or her knowledge (subject to applicable rules).
guidance: When relying on facts within personal knowledge of an Office employee, the data shall be as specific as possible and, if called for by the applicant, supported by that employee's affidavit (subject to contradiction/explanation).

name: Reasons for allowance documentation
description: If the examiner believes the record does not make clear his or her reasons for allowing a claim, the examiner may set forth such reasoning. The reasons shall be incorporated into an Office action rejecting other claims or be the subject of a separate communication.
guidance: The applicant or patent owner may file a statement commenting on reasons for allowance within specified time; examiner's failure to respond to such a statement does not imply anything.

name: Treatment of dependent claims in reexamination
description: If an unamended base patent claim (a claim appearing in the reexamination as it appears in the patent) has been rejected or canceled, any claim which is directly or indirectly dependent thereon should be confirmed or allowed if the dependent claim is otherwise allowable. The dependent claim should not be objected to or rejected merely because it depends on a rejected or canceled patent claim, and no rewriting into independent form is required.
guidance: If a new base claim (not appearing in the patent) has been canceled, a claim depending thereon should be rejected as indefinite. If a new base claim or an amended patent claim is rejected, a dependent claim should be objected to if otherwise patentable and require rewriting in independent form.

name: Form and content requirements for Office Actions (first action)
description: The examiner's first Office action must be a statement of the examiner's position, typed, and sufficiently detailed that the second Office action can properly be made a final action. The first action must clearly set forth the pertinency and manner of applying cited prior art to the claims.
guidance: The examiner may cut-and-paste claim charts included in the request but must carefully review them; later actions must address all patent owner responses. If claims are patentable, indicate why in a manner similar to reasons for allowance. Treat inappropriate arguments per 37 CFR 1.552(c). Given finality of reexamination, actions must be thorough and complete.

name: Content examples in sample Office action (include statutory quotation and clear explanations)
description: A sample first Office action may include quotations of statutory provisions (e.g., 35 U.S.C. 103) forming basis for obviousness rejections, explicit explanations of how references combine to make claims obvious, and statements regarding issues outside the scope of reexamination.
guidance: Include clear explanation why claims are rejected or allowed, identification of cited references and their roles, and advice to patentees about related options (e.g., reissue) for issues not within reexamination scope.

name: Suspension and merger requirement when divisional timely filed (37 CFR 1.177(c))
description: If a divisional reissue application is timely filed, the divisional will be examined and action in the first reissue application containing the original patent claims will be suspended once those claims are determined allowable.
guidance: Further suspensions (usually six-month periods) may be granted to await completion of examination in the divisional. Once a divisional containing added claims is determined allowable, the examiner will issue a requirement under 37 CFR 1.177(c) for applicant to merge the claims of the suspended first reissue application with the allowable claims of the divisional into a single application (place all claims in one application and expressly abandon the other). The requirement will set a two-month period for compliance. Failure to timely respond or refusal to comply may result in the divisional passing to issue alone while prosecution reopens in the suspended first reissue application and a rejection based on lack of error under 35 U.S.C. 251 is made (which may be made final). Abandonment of the first reissue can result in surrender of the original patent claims.

name: Restriction among newly added claims allowed
description: Restriction between multiple inventions recited in the newly added claims will be permitted provided the added claims are drawn to several separate and distinct inventions.
guidance: In such a case the original patent claims would be examined in the first reissue application and applicant may file divisional reissue applications for each separate and distinct invention identified in the examiner’s restriction requirement.

name: Election of species and rejoin requirement
description: Where an election of species requirement is made between species claimed in the original patent claims and a claimed species added in the reissue application, if (1) the non-elected claims to the added species depend from (or otherwise include all limitations of) a generic claim which embraces all species claims, and (2) the generic claim is found allowable, then the non-elected claims directed to the added species that was not subject to restriction in the original prosecution must be rejoined with the elected claims of the original patent.
guidance: See MPEP § 821.04(a) for rejoin practice and details.

name: Consequences when the same claim presented in multiple reissue applications
description: If the same claim of the patent is presented for examination in more than one of the reissue applications, in different amended versions, certain rejections are required.
guidance: Examiner should make: (A) a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 251 that the reissue application is not correcting an error in the original patent because original claim would be superseded by reissuance in the other application; and (B) a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112 that the claim is indefinite because the invention is not particularly pointed out and distinctly claimed due to inconsistent coverage between applications. Applicant should be advised to revise one application and cancel/present appropriately in the other (example procedure provided).

name: Double patenting considerations in multiple reissue practice
description: If the same or similar claims are presented in more than one of the multiple reissue applications, the possibility of statutory or nonstatutory double patenting should be considered.
guidance: Appropriate double patenting rejections should be made. A terminal disclaimer may be filed to overcome a nonstatutory double patenting rejection. The terminal disclaimer is necessary to ensure common ownership in accordance with 37 CFR 1.321(c)(3) or common enforcement in accordance with 37 CFR 1.321(d)(3) of the reissue patents during enforcement in the remainder of the original patent term.

name: Reissue oath/declaration copy acceptance conditions (37 CFR 1.175(f)(1))
description: The requirement for the inventor’s oath or declaration for a continuing reissue application that claims the benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, 365(c), or 386(c) in compliance with § 1.78 may be satisfied by a copy of the inventor’s oath or declaration from the earlier-filed reissue application, provided that: (i) the inventor executed an oath for the earlier-filed reissue application, (ii) the continuing reissue application does not seek to enlarge the scope of the claims of the original patent, or (iii) the application for the original patent was filed under § 1.46 by the assignee of the entire interest.
guidance: In the remarks accompanying a continuing reissue application, applicant should explain why the copy is sufficient. If the copy does not comply with 37 CFR 1.175(f)(1), the examiner should reject the claims under 35 U.S.C. 251 as being based on a defective oath/declaration and require a new oath/declaration (see MPEP § 1414).

name: Identification on filing to avoid Bauman-type (non-reissue) treatment
description: If filing a continuation reissue application as opposed to a Bauman type continuation application, there must be an identification, on filing, that the application is a continuation reissue application; likewise for a divisional reissue application.
guidance: If the application data sheet or specification states the application is a 'continuation' or 'divisional' of its parent reissue application without indicia, it may be treated as a Bauman type continuation (which is not a reissue and cannot claim the original patent filing date). The application data sheet should separately identify the application as (1) a continuation or divisional of the parent reissue application, and (2) a reissue of the original patent. Examples of acceptable first-sentence continuity language are provided in the MPEP (Examples 1–9).

name: Indicia that a continuing reissue application is being filed (recommended list)
description: Indicia that a continuing reissue application is being filed include: (1) a 37 CFR 1.175 reissue oath/declaration (not merely a copy of the parent's), (2) a specification and/or claims in proper double-column reissue format per 37 CFR 1.173, (3) amendments in proper format per 37 CFR 1.173, (4) a 37 CFR 3.73 statement of assignee ownership and consent by assignee, (5) a correct transmittal letter identifying the application as a reissue filing under 35 U.S.C. 251 (Form PTO/AIA/50 recommended), and (6) an identification phrase in the specification such as 'a reissue continuation of application number [parent]'.
guidance: It is recommended that the first line of the specification contain the continuity language to help ensure Office recognizes the application as a continuation reissue or divisional reissue application even if the application data sheet contains the benefit claim(s).

name: Abstract — content and drafting
description: Abstract as element of IA: content of abstract; drafting of abstract; abstract must consist of summary of disclosure in description, claims and drawings.
guidance: References: 5.010-5.012, 5.164-5.173, 5.165-5.169; abstract drafting guidance (5.165-5.169), figure to be published with abstract (5.087, 5.170, 5.171), length of abstract (5.169A), defective or missing abstract provisions (5.173, 7.022), correction following ISA approval (5.174), physical requirements and placement in IA (5.172, 5.011).

name: Claims — form, categories and amendments
description: Standards for drafting claims (including dependent and multiple dependent claims), physical/formal requirements of claims, and amendment procedures applying to claims.
guidance: General claim guidance 5.112-5.127; dependent and multiple dependent claims 5.127, 5.113; amendment issues 9.004-9.011, 11.045-11.047; physical requirements 5.124; categories of claims in IA 5.116; SISA/SISA-related filing rules 8.003, Annex SISA.

name: Defects — influence on international filing date and correction mechanisms
description: Types of defects in the IA, Request, Demand or priority claim that may or may not influence the international filing date, plus mechanisms and time limits for correction.
guidance: Defects influencing international filing date 6.012, 6.025-6.026; defects not influencing date 6.032; incorporation by reference of missing elements 6.012, 6.024-6.031; defects in abstract 5.173, 7.022; correction of defects generally 6.024-6.056.

name: Claim-as-a-whole analysis vs. isolating limitations
description: One view (articulated by the Federal Circuit) is that patent eligibility should be assessed by considering the claim as a whole rather than isolating individual limitations.
guidance: The Federal Circuit stated: 'it is inappropriate to determine the patent eligibility of a claim as a whole based on whether selected limitations constitute patent-eligible subject matter.' This supports evaluating the combination of steps/limitations together when assessing §101.

name: Physical transformation / concrete-step support for eligibility
description: Physical transformations or concrete, technical steps (e.g., administering a drug to a patient, performing measurements) can weigh in favor of patent eligibility under tests like machine-or-transformation.
guidance: The Federal Circuit found the steps of administering the drug (transforming the patient) and measuring metabolites (concrete laboratory steps) to be transformative, supporting patentability. Mayo discusses this view even though the Supreme Court ultimately rejected Prometheus's claims.

name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity does not make a claim patent-eligible
description: If the steps that apply a law of nature merely instruct practitioners to engage in well-understood, routine, conventional activity, those steps generally do not make the claim patent-eligible.
guidance: The Supreme Court: 'Because methods for making such determinations were well known in the art, this step simply tells doctors to engage in well-understood, routine, conventional activity previously engaged in by scientists in the field. Such activity is normally not sufficient to transform an unpatentable law of nature into a patent-eligible application of such a law.'

name: Precedent harmonization and reliance on historic cases
description: Determination of §101 eligibility relies on harmonizing and applying prior precedents (e.g., O'Reilly v. Morse, Neilson v. Harford, Bilski, LabCorp, Alice), which frame limits on claiming natural laws or abstract ideas.
guidance: The Mayo opinion and article reference earlier cases and note that the Court sought to align its treatment of patent-eligibility with historical precedents. The Court also expressed deference to Congress for crafting policy changes if needed.

name: USPTO examination guidance post-Mayo / administrative standards
description: After Mayo, the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office issued preliminary and interim guidelines (later incorporated into the MPEP) for examiners on process claims that include a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or correlation as a limiting element or step.
guidance: The Wikipedia article notes USPTO preliminary guidelines (March 21, 2012), interim guidelines (July 3, 2012), and later guidance implementing Mayo/Alice incorporated into the MPEP (notably Sections 2103 through 2106.07(c)). Examiners are directed to apply the Mayo/Alice framework when assessing claims.

name: Prohibition on constructing a 'mosaic' for novelty
description: One may not make a 'mosaic' out of prior art information (selecting and combining isolated items across documents to create an anticipation).
guidance: Anticipation requires a single prior disclosure that clearly and unmistakably teaches the claimed invention; piecing together from multiple unrelated sources to create an 'anticipation' is prohibited. (Australia — 3M case referenced)

name: Burden and shifting of proof for internet/new media disclosures
description: Burden of proof that a particular piece of information was disclosed on the internet rests on the Patent Office during prosecution, or on the party who claims nullity; if applicant/plaintiff has the information easily available, burden may shift to them.
guidance: Proving precise publication dates and access on the internet can be difficult; evidence standards and who must produce evidence are important considerations. (Argentina; Australia)

name: Scope of evidence and argument limitations on appeal
description: On RCE, new evidence, new arguments, and certain new claim amendments can be presented. On appeal, new evidence and claim amendments are limited after filing; new arguments generally allowed only in the appeal brief (not in reply brief), unless Examiner's answer introduces a new ground of rejection.
guidance: If you need to introduce new evidence or amendments, an RCE may be appropriate; preserve and present all arguments you want considered before appealing.

name: Suggested argument format
description: Address each ground of rejection under a separate heading and identify the ground by claim number, statutory basis, and references. Example headings: 'Whether claims 1-3 are unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. §103 over Reference A in view of Reference B.'
guidance: Use clear headings that map to issues; include precise claim numbers, statutory provisions, and references to aid reviewer navigation.

name: Arguing claims separately when necessary
description: Use a separate heading or subheading for any claim you want the PTAB to consider separately (example shows separate subheadings A/B for different claims).
guidance: If a claim has distinct issues or you want discrete treatment, make separate headings and explain differences clearly.

name: Common successful arguments to show examiner error
description: Show that the examiner: misunderstood/mischaracterized the claimed invention or pending claims; misunderstood the cited prior art; or misunderstood or misapplied the law or legal basis for the rejection.
guidance: Frame arguments to fit one or more of these categories and support them with record evidence, specification citations, or legal analysis.

name: Demonstrate examiner misinterpretation of the invention
description: Show that the examiner’s characterization of the claimed invention or interpretation of claim language is inconsistent with the specification (identify specific portions of the specification).
guidance: Cite specific specification paragraphs and explain why the examiner’s interpretation of a claim limitation is improper.

name: Show prior art was misunderstood or does not disclose elements
description: Explain why the examiner’s understanding of a prior art reference is incorrect — e.g., why the reference does not disclose or suggest a particular claim element.
guidance: Provide specific comparisons between the claim limitation and the reference, showing gaps or differences in disclosure or motivation to combine.

name: Reasonable likelihood to institute (35 U.S.C. § 314(a))
description: Under 35 U.S.C. § 314(a), the Board “may not authorize an inter partes review to be instituted unless . . . the information presented in the petition . . . and any response . . . shows that there is a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail with respect to at least 1 of the claims challenged in the petition.”
guidance: This is the threshold for institution — the Board evaluates the petition, any preliminary response, and the evidence of record to determine whether petitioner has demonstrated a reasonable likelihood of prevailing on at least one challenged claim. Findings made for institution are preliminary and not final; final determinations depend on the full trial record. By rule and SAS/ Iancu, when instituting review the Board must authorize review on all challenged claims and on all grounds asserted for each claim (see 37 C.F.R. § 42.108(a)).

name: Petition particularity requirement (35 U.S.C. § 312(a)(3); 37 C.F.R. § 42.104(b)(4))
description: “The petitioner has the burden from the onset to show with particularity why the patent it challenges is unpatentable.” (Harmonic Inc.). 35 U.S.C. § 312(a)(3) and 37 C.F.R. § 42.104(b)(4) require the petition to identify with particularity the evidence that supports the grounds and to specify where each element of the claim is found in the prior art relied upon.
guidance: Petitions must map claim elements to specific disclosures in cited references and explain how the references render the claims unpatentable. This burden never shifts to Patent Owner. Lack of particularity is a basis to deny institution.

name: Legal standard for obviousness (35 U.S.C. § 103; Graham factors)
description: A claim is unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. § 103(a) if the differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: Obviousness is resolved based on Graham factors: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art; (3) level of ordinary skill in the art; and (4) secondary considerations (objective indicia). The Board applies these factual determinations when assessing whether a petitioner has shown a reasonable likelihood of prevailing on obviousness grounds.

name: Definition and use of the person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA)
description: The Board preliminarily defines the level of skill in the art (POSITA) relevant to the challenged claims using evidence in the record (e.g., education, degrees, and practical experience).
guidance: The POSITA definition should be grounded in the patent and cited prior art and the parties’ evidence. The Board may adopt a preliminary definition (here: bachelor’s degree in electrical or mechanical engineering and two years' experience in designing/implementing hardware components) and notes that more experience can compensate for lack of a degree. Parties may suggest clarifications; the POSITA determination informs claim meaning and obviousness analysis.

name: Claim construction standard (Phillips/37 C.F.R. § 42.100(b))
description: Claim terms are construed according to Phillips v. AWH Corp.: terms receive their ordinary and customary meaning to a person of ordinary skill in the art, read in the context of the claim and the entire patent, including the specification.
guidance: The Board construes terms as in a civil action under 35 U.S.C. § 282(b) per 37 C.F.R. § 42.100(b). Only those claim terms that are in controversy need be expressly construed and only to the extent necessary to resolve the dispute (Nidec/Vivid). Parties should point to specific portions of the specification, prosecution history, and relevant extrinsic evidence when arguing constructions.

name: What counts as 'previously presented' art/arguments and when denial is appropriate
description: Art/arguments must have been presented during proceedings pertaining to the challenged patent for § 325(d) to apply; merely being in an early-stage third-party filing is not always sufficient to deny institution.
guidance: The Board compares the stage and substance of the parallel proceeding: if the parallel proceeding is more advanced, has resulted in claim amendments or a completed reexamination considering the same art, denial under § 325(d) is more likely. If the parallel proceeding is in an early stage, or claims have not been amended and the Office has not made a final determination, the Board may decline to exercise discretion to deny. Prejudice (e.g., statutory bars to filing an IPR) also weighs against denial.

name: Presumption regarding separately listed claim limitations and when they may be satisfied by the same prior-art structure (Becton Dickinson / Google clarification)
description: There is a presumption that separately listed claim limitations may indicate separate and distinct physical structure, but that presumption can be rebutted by the intrinsic record of the patent.
guidance: Becton, Dickinson is not a per se rule; Google LLC v. EcoFactor clarified that the presumption is rebuttable. The Board examines the intrinsic record (specification, claim language) to determine whether a single structure in a prior reference can satisfy multiple claim limitations. Expert testimony and reference disclosures may support such a mapping where the patent does not demand separate physical structures.

name: SAS rule on institution scope (37 C.F.R. § 42.108(a))
description: When instituting review, the Board will authorize the review to proceed on all of the challenged claims and on all grounds of unpatentability asserted for each claim.
guidance: The Board's institution decision is necessarily on all challenged claims and all grounds asserted in the petition; the Board will not partially institute on a subset of claims/grounds (SAS Inst., Inc. v. Iancu).

name: How claim element mappings and obviousness combinations are evaluated at institution
description: The Board examines whether the cited references teach the claim elements (including structural placements and functional interconnections) and whether a person of ordinary skill would have been motivated to combine references with a reasonable expectation of success.
guidance: The Board reviews the references, expert declarations, annotated figures, and arguments from parties. Disputes about whether a reference discloses a limitation (e.g., location of a socket or whether separate structures are required) are resolved preliminarily with attention to intrinsic record, prior-art disclosure, and expert testimony. Where reasonable factual disputes remain, the Board may still institute if petitioner shows a reasonable likelihood of prevailing on at least one claim.

name: Contents of an RCE submission
description: As set forth in 37 CFR 1.114, a submission may include an information disclosure statement, an amendment to the written description, claims, or drawings, new arguments, or new evidence in support of patentability.
guidance: If submission does not comply with 1.111, use form paragraph 7.42.08 (not 7.42.04). Previously submitted arguments may count as a submission if they are responsive within meaning of 1.111.

name: New matter prohibition for RCE amendments
description: 35 U.S.C. 132(a) provides that '[n]o amendment shall introduce new matter into the disclosure of the invention.' Any amendment entered pursuant to 37 CFR 1.114 that is determined to contain new matter should be treated in the same manner that a reply under 37 CFR 1.111 determined to contain new matter is currently treated.
guidance: If applicant seeks to add new matter, the procedure in 37 CFR 1.114 is not available; applicant must file a continuation-in-part under 37 CFR 1.53(b). Also, because 35 U.S.C. 132(b) and 37 CFR 1.114 provide continued examination of an application (not a continuing application), an applicant cannot file an RCE to obtain continued examination on the basis of claims that are independent and distinct from those previously claimed and examined as a matter of right (i.e., cannot 'switch inventions') (see 37 CFR 1.145). See MPEP § 706.03(o) for handling new matter.

name: Handling RCE on appeal lacking fee/submission — no claims allowed
description: A request for continued examination under 37 CFR 1.114 filed after appeal that lacks the fee and/or the submission and where no claim is allowed: the appeal is withdrawn and the application is abandoned (proceedings as to rejected claims terminated).
guidance: Use form paragraph 7.42.10 when appropriate; see MPEP § 1215.01.

name: Handling RCE on appeal lacking fee but including submission; claim allowed
description: If an RCE including a submission was filed after appeal but lacks the fee required by 37 CFR 1.17(e), the submission has not been entered and the appeal is withdrawn; since proceedings as to rejected claims are terminated and at least one claim is allowed, the application will be passed to issue on allowed claim(s).
guidance: Use form paragraph 7.42.13. Note the submission is not entered per 37 CFR 1.116(c).

name: Prepare for §101 rejections while drafting the application
description: During initial drafting, identify technical problems and technical solutions, and draft the application with substantial technical details sourced from the inventors.
guidance: Explicitly capture: (i) the technical problem; (ii) the technical solution; and (iii) substantial technical details that support the solution. Ensure these items come from the inventors so the specification supports later claim amendments and arguments about technical contribution.

name: Draft the specification with substantial technical detail
description: The technical problem, technical solution, and technical details should be described with substantial technical detail in the application.
guidance: Substantial technical detail in the specification both supports claim amendments (adding technical limitations) and underpins arguments that the invention is rooted in technology rather than a mental or business method. Capture implementation details, data flows, algorithms, interfaces, hardware interactions, etc., as appropriate.

name: Amend claims during prosecution to add technical details
description: During prosecution, amend the claims to add more technical details to avoid §101 rejections, while trying to preserve valuable scope.
guidance: Adding details is not trivial: balance the goal of overcoming §101 with client-value scope. Identify technical details that a plausible infringer would need; including such details is 'okay' when necessary for enforcement. Use claim drafting skill to maximize scope while inserting meaningful technical limitations.

name: Use the appeal process at the right time
description: If fighting §101 rejections through multiple office actions without success, consider appeal to the PTAB.
guidance: Typical triggers: third or fourth office action; earlier appeal may be warranted if Examiner has a particularly low allowance rate. Before appealing, ensure 'Are the claims in good shape?' and 'Are your arguments in good shape?'—i.e., fix claim language and prepare robust legal/technical arguments before appeal.

name: Require the Examiner to specify an alleged abstract idea
description: Make sure the Examiner has actually identified an alleged abstract idea; challenge sloppy or vague characterizations.
guidance: Examiners sometimes say things like 'these claims are similar to others that courts have determined are directed to abstract ideas' or treat each claim feature as a separate abstract idea. Force the Examiner to define the alleged abstract idea precisely so you can show how the claims are not directed to that abstract idea or how they meaningfully limit it.

name: Argue claims incorporate the alleged 'abstract idea' into a practical application (impose a meaningful limit)
description: Claims are patent eligible if they 'use the judicial exception in a manner that imposes a meaningful limit on the judicial exception, such that the claim is more than a drafting effort designed to monopolize the judicial exception.'
guidance: Show that the claimed invention integrates the alleged abstract idea into a practical application (e.g., produces a technical effect, requires particular technical steps or apparatus) and therefore imposes a meaningful limit. Use real examples where the claimed subject matter could not be rejected under §102/103 to bolster the meaningful-limit argument.

name: Demonstrate that the claims cover only a tiny portion of the alleged abstract-idea universe
description: Once the Examiner specifies an alleged abstract idea, show that your claims cover a tiny portion (or effectively zero) of that universe, indicating the claims do not pre-empt the idea.
guidance: This directly captures the Supreme Court's pre-emption policy: if the claims occupy only a narrow slice of the abstract concept, they impose a meaningful limit. Note that not all Examiners accept this type of argument—be prepared with concrete technical distinctions and examples.

name: Be pragmatic: prune or avoid filings unlikely to succeed under §101
description: By learning what works, practitioners can identify and prune cases that are less likely to succeed (or choose not to file them in the first place).
guidance: Recognize subject-matter areas (e.g., certain software inventions) where allowance is more difficult and allocate resources accordingly: either bolster the specification and claims to address §101 up front or decide not to file if the chances of overcoming §101 are too low relative to cost and client value.

name: Factors showing possession of claimed species
description: Determination of possession is a factual determination reached by considering a number of factors. Factors to be considered include the level of skill and knowledge in the art, partial structure, physical and/or chemical properties, functional characteristics alone or coupled with a known or disclosed correlation between structure and function, and the method of making the claimed invention.
guidance: Disclosure of any combination of such identifying characteristics that distinguish the claimed invention from other materials and would lead one of skill in the art to conclude that the applicant was in possession of the claimed species is sufficient. (See Eli Lilly.)

name: Description requirement varies with nature and scope of invention
description: The description needed to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112 varies with the nature and scope of the invention at issue, and with the scientific and technologic knowledge already in existence.
guidance: Patents and printed publications in the art should be relied upon to determine whether an art is mature and what the level of knowledge and skill is in the art. In mature technologies where skill/knowledge are high, a written description question should not be raised for claims present in the application when originally filed, even if the specification discloses only a method of making the invention and the function of the invention. (See In re Hayes example: disclosing a capable microprocessor may suffice.)

name: Greater disclosure required in emerging or unpredictable arts
description: For inventions in emerging and unpredictable technologies, or for inventions characterized by factors not reasonably predictable, more evidence is required to show possession.
guidance: Disclosure of only a method of making the invention and the function may not support a product claim (other than product-by-process). Where process has actually been used to produce the product, written description for a product-by-process claim is satisfied; but if it is not clear the acts can be performed or product produced, requirement may not be satisfied. Partial structure without additional characterization may not be sufficient (see Amgen). Reduction to practice can be the only evidence corroborating conception/possession in such contexts.

name: Species claims must meet applicable tests
description: Any claim to a species that does not meet the test described under at least one of (a), (b), or (c) must be rejected as lacking adequate written description under 35 U.S.C. 112, para. 1.
guidance: The text references specific tests (i)(A), (i)(B), (i)(C) (e.g., reduction to practice, reduction to drawings, or identifying characteristics). If a species claim fails those tests, reject for lack of written description.

name: Genus claims: representative number of species or identifying characteristics
description: A claimed genus may be satisfied through sufficient description of a representative number of species by actual reduction to practice, reduction to drawings, or by disclosure of relevant, identifying characteristics (structure, physical/chemical properties), or by functional characteristics coupled with a known/disclosed correlation between function and structure, or by combination of such characteristics sufficient to show possession of the claimed genus.
guidance: A 'representative number of species' means the species adequately described are representative of the entire genus; when there is substantial variation within the genus, one must describe a sufficient variety of species to reflect that variation. If representative species are not disclosed, the genus claim must be rejected. (Cites: Eli Lilly, Enzo, Noelle, etc.)

name: One species may sometimes support a genus
description: Disclosure of only one species within a genus adequately describes a claim to that genus only if the disclosure 'indicates that the patentee has invented species sufficient to constitute the gen[us].'
guidance: There are situations where one species adequately supports a genus (examples: Rasmussen, In re Herschler, In re Smythe) — e.g., when the skilled person would understand that variation among species is unimportant for the claimed invention's operation.

name: Specification cannot support overly expansive claim language by describing only one embodiment
description: A specification cannot always support expansive claim language and satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112 'merely by clearly describing one embodiment of the thing claimed.'
guidance: The key issue is whether a person skilled in the art would understand that the applicant had invented, and was in possession of, the invention as broadly claimed. (Cites: LizardTech v. Earth Resource Mapping.)

name: Required findings when rejecting for lack of written description
description: When rejecting a claim for lack of written description, the examiner must set forth express findings of fact to support the conclusion.
guidance: Findings should: (A) identify the claim limitation at issue; and (B) establish a prima facie case by providing reasons why a person skilled in the art at the time of filing would not have recognized that the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention in view of the disclosure. A general allegation of 'unpredictability in the art' is not sufficient. When appropriate, suggest claim amendments supportable by the application, mindful of the prohibition against adding new matter.

name: Support for new or amended claims / entitlement to earlier priority date
description: To comply with the written description requirement or to be entitled to an earlier priority/filing date under 35 U.S.C. 119, 120, or 365(c), each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure.
guidance: If an explicit limitation is not present in the original written description, it must be shown that a person of ordinary skill would have understood at filing that the description requires that limitation. If the original disclosure does not provide support for each claim limitation, or if an element described as essential is not claimed, a new or amended claim must be rejected or the priority denied. (Cites: Hyatt v. Boone, In re Wright, In re Robins, In re Smith, In re Robertson.)

name: Ways to show possession (acceptable forms of disclosure)
description: Possession may be shown by describing the claimed invention with all limitations using words, structures, figures, diagrams, and formulas that fully set forth the claimed invention.
guidance: Possession may be shown by actual reduction to practice, by showing invention was 'ready for patenting' (e.g., disclosure of drawings or structural chemical formulas), or by describing distinguishing identifying characteristics sufficient to show possession. (Cites: Pfaff, Regents of Univ. of California v. Eli Lilly, Amgen.)

name: Subject matter need not be described literally; inherency and implicit description
description: The subject matter of a claim need not be described literally (i.e., using the exact words) for the disclosure to satisfy the description requirement; implicit or inherent support may sometimes be sufficient.
guidance: To establish inherency, extrinsic evidence must make clear that the missing descriptive matter is necessarily present in the thing described and would be recognized by persons of ordinary skill. Inherency cannot be established by probabilities or possibilities. If a claim is amended to include subject matter not present in the application as filed, examiner should conclude the claim is not described and reject under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph or deny benefit of filing date as appropriate. (Cites: In re Robertson.)

name: Common procedural circumstances raising written description issues
description: Written description issues most typically arise in certain circumstances: amendments affecting a claim, reliance on the filing date of a parent application under 35 U.S.C. 120, reliance on priority under 35 U.S.C. 119, and support for a claim corresponding to a count in an interference.
guidance: In these contexts, ensure that claims are supported in the earlier or original disclosure in the manner required by 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph. (Cites: Wright, Tronzo, Scheiber, Ziegler, Kawai, Gosteli, Hyatt.)

name: Remarks accompanying 37 CFR 1.312 amendments must state reasons
description: As to amendments affecting the disclosure, the scope of any claim, or that add a claim, the remarks accompanying the amendment must fully and clearly state the reasons on which reliance is placed to show: (A) why the amendment is needed; (B) why the proposed amended or new claims require no additional search or examination; (C) why the claims are patentable; and (D) why they were not presented earlier.
guidance: This is required for amendments under 37 CFR 1.312 that affect disclosure/claim scope or add claims. See MPEP § 713.04 and § 713.10 regarding interviews.

name: Sufficient reasons for recommending non-entry of a 1.312 amendment
description: Where appropriate, any one of the following reasons is considered sufficient to recommend non-entry: (A) an additional search is required; (B) more than a cursory review of the record is necessary; or (C) the amendment would involve materially added work on the part of the Office (e.g., checking excessive editorial changes in the specification or claims).
guidance: These are typical justifications for recommending non-entry under 37 CFR 1.312; where claims added are dependent claims usual reasons may be less likely though new matter, sufficiency, or undue multiplicity could arise.

name: Use of form paragraphs for entry/not entry/entered-in-part
description: Form paragraph 7.85: 'Amendment Under 37 CFR 1.312 Entered' (useable for amendments not affecting claim scope by primary examiner or those affecting scope which require SPE signature). Form paragraph 7.87: 'Amendment Under 37 CFR 1.312 Not Entered' (specify reasons). Form paragraph 7.86: 'Amendment Under 37 CFR 1.312 Entered in Part'.
guidance: When recommendation is completely adverse, type reasons for nonentry on PTO-271 signed by primary examiner. If entered-in-part, indicate which changes entered and which not, with explanation.

name: Amendments embodying merely formal matters may be entered without SPE signature
description: Amendments which embody merely the correction of formal matters in the specification, formal changes in a claim without changing the scope thereof, or the cancellation of claims may be indicated 'Enter Formal Matters Only' and do not require submission to the supervisory patent examiner prior to entry.
guidance: If disapproved in whole or in part, they require the signature of the supervisory patent examiner. See MPEP § 714.16.

name: Amendments to drawings held to contain new matter are not entered until new-matter issue resolved
description: Amendments to the drawing held by the examiner to contain new matter are not entered until the question of new matter is settled. This practice does not apply to amendments to the specification and claims.
guidance: See MPEP §§ 608.04 and 706.03(o) for new matter procedures.

name: Amendments not in compliance with 37 CFR 1.121 (no replacement paragraphs/claims) are denied entry
description: An amendment including changes to the specification/claims which is not in compliance with 37 CFR 1.121 (i.e., one which does not include replacement paragraphs/claims) will be denied entry.
guidance: See MPEP § 714.22 for the manner of making amendments and formatting requirements under 37 CFR 1.121.

name: Amendments that include unacceptable substitute specification should be entered in part
description: An amendment presenting an unacceptable substitute specification along with other amendatory matter (e.g., claim changes) should be entered in part: deny entry of the substitute specification and enter the rest of the paper.
guidance: Advise applicant that substitute specification has not been entered. See 37 CFR 1.125 and MPEP § 608.01(q) for substitute specification submission requirements.

name: Post-March 1, 2001: amendments that rewrite specification but fail 1.121 should be entered in part
description: An amendment filed after March 1, 2001 that amends the specification not in compliance with 37 CFR 1.121 and that presents rewritten or new claims should be entered in part: deny the proposal to amend the specification and enter the remainder that complies with 1.121.
guidance: Advise applicant that the specification amendments have not been entered; act on the application when reached in turn. See 37 CFR 1.121 and MPEP § 714.

name: Amendment by instruction to delete/replace/add paragraphs (37 CFR 1.121(b)(1))
description: Amendments to the specification (other than claims/listings) may be made by submitting: (i) an instruction unambiguously identifying the location to delete/replace/add paragraphs; (ii) any replacement/added paragraph(s) in clean form (no markings); and (iii) another version of replacement paragraph(s) on separate pages marked up to show all changes relative to the previous version.
guidance: Marked-up changes may be shown by brackets (deleted) or underlining (added) or equivalent; no marked-up version required for an added or deleted paragraph as long as the instruction states it has been added or deleted.

name: Amendment by substitute specification (37 CFR 1.121(b)(3))
description: The specification (other than claims) may be amended by submitting an instruction to replace the specification, a substitute specification in compliance with § 1.125(b), and another version of the substitute specification marked up to show all changes relative to the previous version.
guidance: Follow §1.125(b) requirements for substitute specifications; include marked-up comparison.

name: Disclosure consistency: Office may require amendments to secure correspondence among claims/specification/drawings (37 CFR 1.121(e))
description: The disclosure must be amended, when required by the Office, to correct inaccuracies of description and definition, and to secure substantial correspondence between the claims, the remainder of the specification, and the drawings.
guidance: Examiner may require applicant to amend to maintain consistency across disclosure elements.

name: Exception for examiner's amendments (37 CFR 1.121(g))
description: Changes to the specification, including the claims, made by the Office in an examiner's amendment may be made by specific instructions to insert or delete subject matter set forth in the examiner's amendment; compliance with certain paragraphs of 1.121 is not required for examiner's amendments.
guidance: Follow instructions identifying precise insertion/deletion points; paragraph (b)(1),(b)(2),(c)(1) compliance not required for examiner's amendments.

name: Amendment of amendments: replacement paragraphs must be wholly rewritten and canceled matter reinstated only by subsequent amendment
description: When a replacement paragraph/section to the specification is to be amended, it should be wholly rewritten and the original insertion canceled so no interlineations or deletions appear in the clause as finally presented. Matter canceled by amendment can be reinstated only by a subsequent amendment presenting the canceled matter as a new insertion. A claim canceled by amendment may be reinstated only by a subsequent amendment presenting the claim as a new claim with a new claim number.
guidance: Maintain clean final text; follow rules for reinstatement (new insertion/new claim number).

name: Swearing back of reference under 37 CFR 1.131: substantive showing and limits
description: When any claim is rejected, the inventor (or qualified party) may submit an oath/declaration to establish invention prior to the effective date of the reference. Prior invention may not be established under this section in countries other than the U.S., NAFTA members, or WTO members (with date limitations). Prior invention may not be established if rejection is based on a U.S. patent/application publication of another claiming the same patentable invention or if based on a statutory bar. The showing must be of such character and weight to establish reduction to practice prior to the effective date, or conception prior to the effective date coupled with due diligence to reduction to practice or filing. Original exhibits or photocopies must accompany the affidavit/declaration or their absence satisfactorily explained.
guidance: Observe the geographic and date limitations (no establishment outside designated countries or before specified dates in NAFTA/WTO members). See 37 CFR 1.131 for full requirements.

name: Relative weight of linguistic meaning versus purpose of the invention
description: Whether claim terms should be interpreted primarily by their ordinary linguistic meaning (as the Phillips majority favored) or by reference to the purpose/invention (as the dissent favored).
guidance: The majority gives great weight to linguistic considerations and little weight to the purpose of the invention, while the dissent does the opposite; courts sometimes treat purpose as 'lip service' rather than a controlling factor (Phillips, 415 F.3d at 1324-27; Lourie, J., concurring/dissenting).

name: Specification as 'always highly relevant' to claim construction
description: The specification contains a written description of the invention and is always highly relevant to the claim construction analysis.
guidance: Quoting Vitronics: 'The specification contains a written description of the invention . . . . Thus, the specification is always highly relevant to the claim construction analysis.' Courts repeatedly rely on the specification in construing claims (Vitronics, 90 F.3d at 1582).

name: Ordinary and customary meaning must be discerned from intrinsic record context
description: The 'ordinary and customary meaning' of a claim term is to be discerned by reference to the context of the intrinsic record (not solely by extrinsic sources like dictionaries).
guidance: Nystrom holding: the ordinary meaning must be discerned by reference to the context of the intrinsic record and not by reference to a dictionary, treatise, or other extrinsic source.

name: Person of ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA) perspective
description: Claims are construed through the eyes of a person having ordinary skill in the relevant field, who reads the patent documents with an understanding of their meaning in the field.
guidance: Multiform Desiccants: courts start by reviewing the same resources as PHOSITA—specification and prosecution history; the PHOSITA standard is the central lens for claim construction.

name: Prosecution history may provide relevant linguistic context
description: Although not physically attached to the claims like the specification, prosecution history can in some circumstances provide relevant linguistic context for claim meaning.
guidance: Examples: Liebel-Flarsheim (patentee deleted words during prosecution suggesting claims do not include that subject matter). Use prosecution history when it contains clear statements bearing on meaning.

name: PTO standard during examination: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI)
description: PTO examiners are instructed to adopt a 'broadest reasonable interpretation' when approaching claim language during prosecution to guard against patentee tricks.
guidance: In re Yamamoto, 740 F.2d 1569, 1571 (Fed. Cir. 1984). The PTO historically construes claims more broadly during prosecution than courts do in litigation.

name: Statutory conditions for obtaining a patent (101-103, 112)
description: Patentability and claim drafting must satisfy statutory requirements under 35 U.S.C. §§ 101-103, 112.
guidance: Sections outline subject matter eligibility, novelty/non-obviousness, and written description/enablement/definiteness requirements that bear on claim scope and interpretation.

name: Efficiency standard as a normative paradigm for determining scope
description: Determining patent scope is guided by an 'efficiency standard' balancing incentives for innovation against avoidance of monopolies.
guidance: Cited authorities (Bonito Boats; Merges & Nelson) frame claim scope as an economic-policy tradeoff; some scholars urge policy-informed construction when textual methods are inconclusive.

name: Distinction between ambiguity and vagueness and their interpretability
description: Differentiate linguistic ambiguity (multiple discrete meanings) from vagueness (indeterminate boundaries); legal uncertainty is not identical to linguistic uncertainty.
guidance: Vagueness cannot be solved by better interpretative tools; literature conflates vagueness and generality but they are distinct. Example: a claim to 'everything' is not vague even if broad.

name: Patentee use of ambiguous language as a strategic tactic
description: Patentees may intentionally use ambiguous claim language to pursue 'two-faced' arguments (e.g., broad in court, narrow in prosecution).
guidance: Distinguish deliberate ambiguity (strategic drafting) from invoking ambiguous case law; the problem's severity depends on PTO competency and incentives (Bessen & Meurer; Burk & Lemley).

name: When textual methods yield indeterminate results, policy considerations may inform construction
description: If the Phillips methodology does not yield a clear interpretation, courts may consider policy aimed at promoting technological progress to inform claim construction.
guidance: Scholars (Lee; Burk & Lemley) suggest using policy arguments to resolve interpretive indeterminacy rather than relying solely on textualist tools.

name: Reverse doctrine of equivalents is rarely used to find non-infringement
description: The Federal Circuit has been reluctant to affirm findings of non-infringement under the reverse doctrine of equivalents.
guidance: Roche Palo Alto v. Apotex notes the court 'has never affirmed a finding of non-infringement under the reverse doctrine of equivalents.' This limits use of that doctrine in narrowing claim scope.

name: Use of technical advisors or special masters for complex claim construction
description: Courts may appoint technical advisors or special masters to assist with technological determinations in claim construction.
guidance: TechSearch v. Intel and studies (Kesan & Ball) support the use of special masters or technical assistance in complex patent cases.

name: Interpretation should rely on ordinary English usage conventions as linguistic context (not invention-centered reasoning)
description: The specification and general subject matter of the patent can provide ordinary-language context (e.g., 'inventory' likely means physical objects) but this is distinct from defining claims by the patentee's inventive contribution.
guidance: Authors argue for inferring meaning from ordinary usage/context rather than restricting meaning to the patentee's conception of the invention (discussion of 'inventory' examples; Winans v. Denmead).

name: Claims as the best evidence of what ideas the patentee intends to convey
description: The claim language is the best evidence of the patentee's communicated ideas; one should not require knowledge of the inventor's idea before interpreting the language.
guidance: Critique of invention-centered approaches: to say one must know the idea before understanding language is conceptually backward; language should be interpreted on its terms.

name: Field-specific searching
description: Search by discrete bibliographic and content fields: inventor name; assignee name; application number / publication number; classification (CPC, IPC, USPC); claim text; specification text; date ranges; priority dates.
guidance: Use fielded searches to target documents precisely (e.g., search claim text vs. specification). Combine field searches to narrow results to specific applicants, classifications, or time windows.

name: Drafting informed by search patterns
description: When drafting applications, use technical terminology examiners are likely to find, include synonyms in claim language, consider classification placement when drafting, and anticipate which references examiners will likely cite.
guidance: Use insights from prior-art searches to shape claim language and specification wording (include synonyms and classification-relevant terms) to improve discoverability and reduce avoidable citations.

name: Dependent Claim
description: A claim that refers back to and further limits another claim (see: Claim, Dependent).
guidance: Used to add narrower features; must properly depend from an earlier claim and is a drafting device to create claim hierarchies.

name: Design Patent Subject Matter
description: Design patents protect only the ornamental appearance or shape characteristics of an article of manufacture.
guidance: Design patents are numbered separately (preceded by D); drafting and claims must be limited to appearance/ornamentality (see MPEP 901.04, 1502).

name: Disclosure (Description & Enablement Requirements)
description: Disclosure refers to an invention disclosure or portions of a patent application; it must be sufficient so one skilled in the art (1) understands what is being claimed (description requirement) and (2) can make and use the invention (enablement). In the U.S., the best mode must be disclosed.
guidance: Ensure disclosures teach how to make/use the invention and particularly point out the claimed subject matter; reference MPEP 608, 2161, 2162 for detailed requirements.

name: Enablement
description: Support within a disclosure for a claimed invention such that a person skilled in the art is taught how to make and use the invention (MPEP 2164, 2164.01).
guidance: Draft the specification to enable without undue experimentation; include detailed examples/embodiments where necessary.

name: Enabling Disclosure (U.S.)
description: A description sufficient to enable a person skilled in the art to carry out the invention.
guidance: Covers both 'how to make' and 'how to use' aspects; tie descriptions to claims to avoid insufficiency/invalidity.

name: Indefiniteness of Claim (35 U.S.C. §112)
description: Claims must be sufficiently definite to provide a standard by which a third party can determine with some degree of certainty whether a practice would infringe; an indefinite claim fails to particularly point out the claimed invention (MPEP 706.03(d), 2171, 2173).
guidance: Draft clear claim language; avoid ambiguous terms and ensure claim scope can be reasonably ascertained.

name: Elements of a Claim
description: Portions of the claim body that describe features of the invention and how those features interrelate (MPEP 608.01(m)).
guidance: Claims should be structured so each essential element is identified and tied to the specification; missing essential elements can be grounds for rejection or invalidity.

name: Means-Plus-Function (Means for Claim)
description: A claim technique reciting an element as a 'means for' accomplishing a function (means-plus-function language), governed by MPEP 2181.
guidance: When using means-plus-function language, the claim is interpreted to cover the corresponding structure described in the specification and equivalents; ensure specification discloses adequate structure to support such claims (avoid indefinite means-plus-function without disclosure).

name: Level of Ordinary Skill / Hypothetical Person Skilled in the Art
description: A hypothetical person of ordinary skill in the art is the baseline for judging enablement and obviousness; the relevant level depends on the nature of the technology and may include engineers, practitioners, or academics (MPEP 2141.03).
guidance: When evaluating enablement or obviousness, identify the appropriate skill level and ensure the disclosure and claims are drafted accordingly.

name: Novelty / Effective Date / Prior Art Availability
description: A reference's effective date determines whether it is prior art against a claimed invention; novelty requires the claimed invention not be fully anticipated by a prior art reference (Effective Date discussion and Local Novelty).
guidance: Establish correct priority/filing dates (foreign, in-convention) and be mindful of prior publications and their effective dates when assessing novelty.

name: Information in the File History / File Wrapper Estoppel
description: The file history (file wrapper) contains all prosecution papers; narrowing amendments or representations made during prosecution can create prosecution history estoppel (file wrapper estoppel), limiting post-issue claim scope and application of the doctrine of equivalents.
guidance: Be cautious in amendments and arguments during prosecution; avoid statements that later undermine claim scope or support an estoppel defense.

name: Double Patenting and Terminal Disclaimer
description: Double patenting is the attempt to obtain more than one patent on the same invention or obvious variants; leads to double patenting rejections for improper multiple patents (see MPEP 804 series).
guidance: Address double patenting by distinguishing claims, filing terminal disclaimers when appropriate, or ensuring claims are patentably distinct.

name: Doctrine of Claim Differentiation
description: A judicial rule of claim construction that where two claims have apparently similar meaning, an effort should be made to interpret them so they have distinct meanings.
guidance: Draft claim sets with conscious differentiation between independent and dependent claims to reduce ambiguity and support broader/smaller scopes as intended.

name: Doctrine of Equivalents
description: An equitable doctrine that can find infringement even when accused product/process does not literally infringe, to prevent insubstantial changes that avoid literal infringement.
guidance: Be aware that prosecution history estoppel and claim amendments can limit application; consider both literal and equivalent scope when drafting and enforcing claims.

name: Insufficiency / Insufficient Disclosure
description: A ground of invalidity where the description does not enable one skilled in the art to practice the invention (insufficient disclosure / failure to teach).
guidance: Avoid omitting essential elements, steps, or cooperative relationships in the specification and claims; include adequate detail and examples to support claimed subject matter (MPEP 608.01p).

name: Interference (Priority Determination)
description: A priority contest in the U.S. PTO to determine which of multiple parties was first to invent commonly claimed subject matter (MPEP 2300.01).
guidance: Prepare documentary evidence of invention dates and diligence; note that interference practice is specific to U.S. pre-AIA rules and priority contexts.

name: Claims: Limitation and Linking Claims
description: Limitations are claim language that constrains breadth; linking claims join separate species or link product/process/apparatus claims (MPEP 809 series).
guidance: Structure claim sets to include proper limitations and linking claims where strategic; watch for restriction/election issues and clarity.

name: Statutory Subject Matter Classes (Machine, Manufacture, Method, Composition)
description: Patentable subject matter under U.S. law includes machines, manufactures, methods (processes), and compositions of matter (MPEP 2105 series).
guidance: Draft claims to clearly fall within a statutory class and describe embodiments corresponding to the claimed class.

name: Intervening Rights (Reissue / Reexamination Effects)
description: A defense arising when a patent is later reissued with broader claims due to error; persons who practiced the broadened claims prior to reissue may have intervening rights to continue practice without infringement (MPEP 1460).
guidance: Consider intervening rights implications when amending or reissuing patents; drafting and prosecution strategies can affect third-party rights.

name: Infringement Standards: Literal and By Equivalents
description: Literal infringement occurs when an accused product/process contains every recital of a claim; infringement by equivalents applies when differences perform identical functions in substantially the same way to achieve the same result.
guidance: When drafting and evaluating patents, consider both literal claim scope and potential doctrine of equivalents coverage; prosecution history estoppel can limit equivalents.

name: Damages: Lost Profits vs Reasonable Royalty
description: Lost profits measure damages tied to profits the patentee would have earned but for infringement; when lost profits are not provable, damages are measured by a reasonable royalty.
guidance: Preserve records and economic evidence to support lost profits claims where possible; licensing and market data are relevant.

name: Prescription for Claims Drafting to Avoid File-Wrapper Estoppel
description: Narrowing amendments and representations during prosecution can preclude asserting broader interpretations after issuance (file wrapper/prosecution history estoppel).
guidance: Draft claims and make prosecution remarks judiciously; consider alternatives such as continuations to preserve broader claim possibilities.

name: Terminal disclaimer must be for the terminal portion of entire patent term
description: A terminal disclaimer directed to particular claim(s) will not be accepted; the disclaimer must be of a terminal portion of the term of the entire patent to be granted.
guidance: The statute does not provide for conditional disclaimers; a proposed disclaimer contingent on allowance of certain claims cannot be accepted.

name: Effect on continuing applications and CPAs
description: A terminal disclaimer filed to obviate a double patenting rejection is effective only with respect to the application identified in the disclaimer unless by its terms it extends to continuing applications.
guidance: A terminal disclaimer filed in a parent application normally has no effect on a continuing application claiming benefits under 35 U.S.C. 120, except it carries over to a Continued Prosecution Application (CPA) filed under 37 CFR 1.53(d) because the CPA retains the parent's application number. To prevent carryover to a CPA, file a petition under 37 CFR 1.182 with the required fee requesting the terminal disclaimer not be carried over.

name: Disclaimer cannot be directed to particular claim(s) (14.26.02)
description: A terminal disclaimer directed to a particular claim or claims is not acceptable.
guidance: Must be preceded by form paragraphs 14.24/14.25 and 14.26. Refer to MPEP §1490 for discussion.

name: Utility of dependent claims follows independent claim (same statutory class)
description: A dependent claim is treated as defining an invention that has utility if the independent claim from which the dependent claim depends is drawn to the same statutory class of invention as the dependent claim and the independent claim defines an invention having utility. An exception exists where the utility specified for the invention defined in a dependent claim differs from that indicated for the invention defined in the independent claim.
guidance: If an applicant has established utility for a species within a claimed genus and presents a generic claim covering the genus, as a general matter that claim should be treated as sufficient under 35 U.S.C. 101 unless it can be established that other species clearly encompassed by the claim do not have utility. In such cases encourage amendment to exclude non-usable species.

name: One credible assertion of specific utility suffices
description: An applicant need only make one credible assertion of specific utility for the claimed invention to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 101 and 35 U.S.C. 112; additional statements of utility, even if not 'credible', do not render the claimed invention lacking in utility.
guidance: Cited cases: Raytheon v. Roper; In re Gottlieb; In re Malachowski. If applicant makes one credible assertion, utility for the claimed invention as a whole is established.

name: Applicant statements alone cannot, standing alone, support lack-of-utility rejection
description: Statements made by the applicant in the specification or incident to prosecution cannot, standing alone, be the basis for a lack of utility rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 or 35 U.S.C. 112.
