guidance: Office should not require removal of nonessential statements relating to utility from a disclosure regardless of technical accuracy. Be careful not to read unclaimed results, limitations, or embodiments into a claim.

name: Detect asserted or well-established utility on initial examination
description: Upon initial examination, the examiner should review the specification to determine if there are any statements asserting that the claimed invention is useful for any particular purpose. A complete disclosure should include a statement identifying a specific and substantial utility for the invention unless the invention has a well-established utility.
guidance: If no statements found, determine if the claimed invention has a 'well-established utility' (see separate criterion). If not, proceed with rejection procedure and inform applicant to indicate why invention is useful and where support exists in the specification.

name: Asserted utility must be specific and substantial
description: A statement of specific and substantial utility should fully and clearly explain why the applicant believes the invention is useful and must enable one ordinarily skilled in the art to understand why the claimed invention is useful. Vague assertions (e.g., 'biological activity', 'pharmacological effects') are insufficient.
guidance: Examples of insufficient statements: unspecified 'biological activity' (Brenner v. Manson), disclosure that something is 'plastic-like' or can form 'films' (In re Ziegler), or mere 'biologically active'. A proper statement usually explains the purpose or how the invention may be used (e.g., useful in treating a particular disorder).

name: Initial burden on the Office to make a prima facie case with evidentiary support
description: To properly reject under 35 U.S.C. 101, the Office must (A) make a prima facie showing that the claimed invention lacks utility, and (B) provide a sufficient evidentiary basis for factual assumptions relied upon in establishing the prima facie showing.
guidance: The examiner must do more than merely question operability; set forth factual reasons that would lead one skilled in the art to question the statement of operability. If the Office cannot develop a proper prima facie case, rejection should not be imposed.

name: Specificity required in rejection wording and use of form paragraphs
description: Rejections under 35 U.S.C. 101 based on lack of utility must include a detailed explanation why the claimed invention has no specific and substantial credible utility. The MPEP provides form paragraphs (e.g., 7.05.02–7.05.04) and formats A/B/C for different scenarios (no asserted utility; not specific and substantial; not credible; multiple utilities).
guidance: Use Format A/B/C as appropriate: insert claim numbers and words like 'specific and substantial' or 'credible' per guidance; for multiple utilities address each utility. Where enablement issues also exist, make separate 35 U.S.C. 112 rejections using Wands factors.

name: How applicant may rebut a prima facie rejection for lack of utility
description: If a proper prima facie rejection is imposed, the burden shifts to the applicant to rebut. Rebuttal may be by claim amendments, arguments/reasoning, or new evidence submitted in an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 or by a printed publication. New evidence must be relevant to issues raised.
guidance: Declarations that merely express conclusions without establishing a nexus to supporting evidence have limited probative value (In re Grunwell; In re Buchner). Examiners must fully consider and respond to each substantive element of applicant's response and only maintain rejection if totality shows utility not specific, substantial, and credible.

name: Scope of a patent for an improvement
description: If a mere addition is made to an existing machine to produce the same effects in a better manner, the patent covers the improvement only and not the whole machine.
guidance: A patent cannot be for an effect only but for an effect produced in a given manner or by a peculiar operation. Examples: the inventor of a patent lever improved a watch but could not patent the whole watch; no patent can be obtained for abstract operations (e.g., admeasurement of time) but only for a new mode or application of machinery. If new effects are produced by an old unaltered machine, a patent for that is not legally supported. Conversely, if the principles of the machine are new, the inventor may claim the whole machine. Where an improvement overlaps a still-running earlier patent, a new patent that claims only the improvement may be valid; it comes into force after the old patent's expiration or may be used via license or purchase under the former patent.

name: Effect of claiming parts and combination (coverage of parts vs combination)
description: If a patentee describes several distinct and independent parts intended to be used in combination and is the first inventor of each, the patent covers all the parts and the combination; use of any one part by another is infringement. But if the inventor is not the original inventor of the several things and the combination itself is the subject-matter, use of parts not amounting to the same combination is not infringement.
guidance: Thus whether a patentee may enforce against use of individual parts depends on whether he was the original inventor of those parts or whether his invention is limited to the combination only. The specification's accuracy and distinctness in stating particulars of the invention materially affect the scope.

name: Requirement of accurate and distinct specification; claiming beyond invention voids patent
description: A patentee is confined to the particulars and summary of the invention stated in the specification; if the patent covers particulars that are not new, the patent is void even if those particulars are slight or of little importance.
guidance: Obscure language in a specification makes it difficult to ascertain the nature and extent of the invention claimed. Courts cannot reject a claim that appears in the specification; if included and found not to be new the whole patent may be invalid. The patentee cannot later expand beyond the scope he summed up as his invention.

name: References must be enabling to support an obviousness conclusion
description: A conclusion of obviousness requires that the reference(s) relied upon be enabling in that it put the public in possession of the claimed invention.
guidance: If the prior art fails to disclose or render obvious a method for making a claimed compound at the time the invention was made, the compound may not be legally concluded obvious. (In re Hoeksema, 399 F.2d 269, 274, 158 USPQ 596, 601 (CCPA 1968)).

name: Absence of a method for making a claimed compound can overcome obviousness presumption
description: The absence of a known or obvious process for making the claimed compounds overcomes a presumption that the compounds are obvious based on close structural relationships to prior art compounds.
guidance: Failure of the prior art to disclose or render obvious a method for making any composition of matter (compound or mixture) precludes a conclusion that the composition would have been obvious. (In re Hoeksema; In re Grose).

name: Once PTO makes a prima facie case, applicant bears burden to present contrary enabling evidence
description: Once a prima facie case of obviousness is made by the PTO through citation of references, the burden is on the applicant to produce contrary evidence establishing that the relied-on reference would not enable a skilled artisan to produce the claimed compounds.
guidance: Applicants must submit evidence (declarations, data) showing the reference is not enabling for the claimed invention. (In re Hoeksema; Ashland Oil v. Delta Resins & Refractories).

name: Rebuttal evidence must be reasonably commensurate in scope with the claimed invention
description: The proffered evidence must be reasonably commensurate in scope with the claimed invention; evidence that is not commensurate may be insufficient to rebut a prima facie case.
guidance: Evidence need not show unexpected results over the entire range of properties; a showing for a single member or a narrow portion can suffice if a skilled artisan could ascertain a trend allowing reasonable extrapolation. Cases: In re Kulling; In re Grasselli; In re Chupp; In re Clemens; In re Lindner; In re Albrecht; In re Soni (procedural limits).

name: Unexpected results can rebut prima facie obviousness but are evaluated case-by-case
description: A showing of unexpected superior properties may be sufficient to overcome a prima facie case of obviousness, but whether it suffices depends on the scope of claims, whether the showing is representative, and other motivations in the prior art.
guidance: Single exemplary showing may suffice when it establishes reasonable correlation to the claim scope (Chupp, Clemens); but unexpected properties for one species may be insufficient for a broad subgenus in some contexts (Grasselli, Greenfield, Lindner, Dillon, Albrecht). Each case evaluated on totality of circumstances.

name: Number of references combined is not dispositive against obviousness
description: Reliance on a large number of references in an obviousness rejection does not, without more, weigh against a finding of obviousness.
guidance: Even a detailed claim has been affirmed as obvious based on many references (e.g., thirteen references in In re Gorman). The quantity alone is not determinative.

name: Claim interpretation: limitations from specification are not to be read into the claims
description: Although claims are interpreted in light of the specification, limitations appearing only in the specification should not be imported into the claims unless clearly required.
guidance: Claims are not limited by the specification's examples or uses if such limitations are not recited in the claim language. (In re Van Geuns; Constant v. AMD; Ex parte McCullough). See MPEP §§2111-2116.01 for claim interpretation law.

name: Proceeding contrary to accepted wisdom is evidence of nonobviousness
description: Where the claimed invention proceeds contrary to the accepted wisdom or conventional practice in the art, this can be evidence supporting nonobviousness.
guidance: Known disadvantages that would discourage pursuit of a solution may be taken into account (In re Hedges; United States v. Adams). The totality of prior art should be considered.

name: Apply preponderance of the evidence standard in patentability determinations
description: The standard to be applied in all cases is the 'preponderance of the evidence' test: an examiner should reject a claim if, in view of the prior art and evidence of record, it is more likely than not that the claim is unpatentable.
guidance: See MPEP §706(I) for the preponderance standard.

name: Copies required per 37 CFR 1.98(a)(2)
description: (2) A legible copy of: (i) Each foreign patent; (ii) Each publication or that portion which caused it to be listed, other than U.S. patents and U.S. patent application publications unless required by the Office; (iii) For each cited pending unpublished U.S. application, the application specification including the claims, and any drawing of the application, or that portion ...; and (iv) All other information or that portion which caused it to be listed.
guidance: Applicants must supply legible copies of the cited documents or relevant portions, except for certain U.S. patents/app pubs unless requested. (1.98(a)(2))

name: Examiner checklist: requirement of copies for specific types of references
description: Examiners must ensure copies are provided for: (a) each cited foreign patent document; (b) each cited NPL publication, or portion causing listing; (c) each cited U.S. pending application not stored in IFW; (d) all information cited (e.g., affidavit or Office action) other than the specification, including claims and drawings, of a pending U.S. application; and (e) all other cited information or the portion which caused it to be listed.
guidance: If copies are missing, examiner may line-through and inform applicant of reasons; see MPEP 609.01.

name: Use of IDS information in new ground of rejection — timing and fee consequences
description: If information submitted during the period set forth in 37 CFR 1.97(c) with a statement under 1.97(e) is used in a new ground of rejection on unamended claims, the next Office action will not be made final. However, information submitted with a fee under 1.17(p) during this period may be used to support a new ground of rejection and the next Office action may be made final when necessitated by amendment; similarly, new grounds necessitated by amendment may make next action final.
guidance: Whether a new ground of rejection can be final depends on timing, presence of 1.97(e) statement vs fee, and whether rejection was necessitated by applicant amendment. See MPEP §609.04(b) and form paragraph 7.40.01 example.

name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a) — proscription of disreputable or gross misconduct
description: Section 10.23(a) proscribes engaging in disreputable or gross misconduct.
guidance: The Director concluded a plain reading of § 10.23(a) shows there is no element of intent required by that provision; claims that all provisions of the Rules of Professional Conduct require intent are unsupported. False certification under disciplinary rules is not the same as inequitable conduct in patent litigation (Therasense inapposite).

name: Changes shown by markings
description: Any changes relative to the patent being reexamined which are made to the specification, including the claims, must include the following markings: the matter to be omitted must be enclosed in brackets; the matter to be added must be underlined.
guidance: Applies to all specification and claim changes made during reexamination proceedings; ensures clarity of deletions and additions.

name: Amendment of disclosure when required
description: The disclosure must be amended, when required by the Office, to correct inaccuracies of description and definition, and to secure substantial correspondence between the claims, the remainder of the specification, and the drawings.
guidance: Office may require specification/drawing amendments to ensure consistency with claims; such amendments are directed to correcting inaccuracies and securing substantial correspondence.

name: Amendments must be relative to the patent as filed
description: All amendments must be made relative to the patent specification, including the claims, and drawings, which are in effect as of the date of filing the request for reexamination.
guidance: Amendments are judged against the patent document in effect on the request filing date—not against any later drafts.

name: No enlargement of claim scope
description: No amendment may enlarge the scope of the claims of the patent or introduce new matter. No amendment may be proposed for entry in an expired patent. Moreover, no amendment, other than the cancellation of claims, will be incorporated into the patent by a certificate issued after the expiration of the patent.
guidance: Amendments cannot broaden claim scope or add subject matter; time-limited restriction for expired patents—only cancellations permitted after expiration.

name: Petition fee requirement in ex parte proceedings
description: A petition in an ex parte reexamination proceeding must be accompanied by the fee set forth in § 1.20(c)(6), except for specific petitions (e.g., certain extension petitions, acceptance of delayed responses, unintentionally delayed benefit claims, and correction of inventorship petitions).
guidance: Most petitions require payment; listed exceptions do not require the § 1.20(c)(6) fee.

name: Scope of reexamination (evidence and statutory bases)
description: Claims in an ex parte reexamination will be examined on the basis of patents or printed publications and, with respect to subject matter added or deleted in the reexamination proceeding, on the basis of the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112.
guidance: Reexamination uses patents/printed publications as primary art sources; added/deleted subject matter is judged for compliance with 35 U.S.C.112 (written description/enablement/definiteness).

name: No enlargement of claims in reexamination
description: Claims in an ex parte reexamination proceeding will not be permitted to enlarge the scope of the claims of the patent.
guidance: Reexamination cannot be used to broaden claim scope; a substantive limitation on allowable amendments.

name: Use of patent owner statements of record
description: Any statement of the patent owner and any accompanying information submitted pursuant to § 1.501(a)(2) which is of record in the patent being reexamined may be used after a reexamination proceeding has been ordered to determine the proper meaning of a patent claim when applying patents or printed publications.
guidance: Prior statements of the patent owner (e.g., in file history) can be used as claim construction evidence in reexamination.

name: Definition of material information in reexamination
description: Information is material when it is not cumulative and (1) it is a patent or printed publication that establishes, by itself or in combination, a prima facie case of unpatentability of a claim; or (2) it refutes or is inconsistent with a position the patent owner takes in opposing unpatentability relied on by the Office or asserting patentability.
guidance: Prima facie of unpatentability means information compels a conclusion of unpatentability under the preponderance standard, giving each term its broadest reasonable construction consistent with the specification, before considering contrary evidence.

name: Director discretion on suspension/merger when litigation or concurrent files
description: If a patent in ex parte reexamination is or becomes involved in litigation, the Director shall determine whether to suspend the reexamination. If ex parte reexamination is ordered while a prior ex parte reexamination is pending and prosecution in the prior one has not been terminated, proceedings will usually be merged resulting in issuance of a single certificate. Similar merger/suspension rules apply for reissue applications and interferences under specified conditions.
guidance: Director has authority to suspend or merge based on overlap or pendency in other proceedings; procedures for merger include maintaining same claims during merged prosecution.

name: Required components and organizational attachments for request
description: The request should include a cover sheet itemizing each component submitted, a table of contents, an explanation of how the claims patentably distinguish over the items of information, and an explanation of why each item does or does not raise a substantial new question of patentability.
guidance: These organizational elements facilitate Office review and are expected per § 1.615.

name: Office determination on substantial new question (SNQ)
description: Within three months after the filing date of a request, the Office will determine whether a substantial new question of patentability affecting any claim is raised by any of the items presented. The determination will generally be limited to a review of the item(s) identified in the request as applied to the identified claim(s) and will be based on the claims in effect at the time of the determination.
guidance: SNQ review is targeted and time-limited; determination becomes part of the official patent record.

name: Patent grant conditions and issuance of letters patent
description: A patent is granted after the application is approved and the payment of the corresponding fee is proven, with the issuance of the respective letters patent (Article 38 of the LPI).
guidance: Payment of the fee and evidence must be made within 60 days of the granting date (Article 38(1)). A patent is deemed granted on the date of publication of the respective act (Article 38(3)). The letters patent must contain the number, title and nature of the patent; the name of the inventor; the holder’s identification and address; the term of validity; the specifications; the claims; the drawings; and the data relating to priority (Article 39).

name: Mandatory contents of a patent application (formal filing requirements)
description: A patent application must contain: I – request; II – specifications; III – claims; IV – drawings, if applicable; V – abstract; and VI – proof of payment of the filing fee (Article 19 of the LPI).
guidance: Articles 22–26 and INPI Normative Rulings No. 30 and 31 regulate filing conditions. Forms are available on the INPI website. Minimum conditions for accepting an application include technical content, application, and proof of payment; if insufficient but containing key data, the applicant may be given 30 days to meet requirements (Article 21).

name: Priority date rules and evidence
description: The priority date is the date of filing. Priority claims may be supplemented within 60 days by other priorities prior to the filing date (Article 16).
guidance: Priority claims must be supported by appropriate documents (number, date, title, specifications, and, if applicable, claims and drawings) with translations as required. If proof is not presented at filing, it must be provided within 180 days (or 60 days in some national-processing cases). Failure to provide evidence within time limits results in loss of priority (Article 16(7)). For international (PCT) filings, translations may be due when national processing starts.

name: Publication timing and content of publication
description: A patent application is kept secret for 18 months from the filing date or earliest priority date, after which it is published, except as provided in Article 75 (Article 30).
guidance: Publication may be brought forward at applicant’s request; publication must contain identifying data and make available specifications, claims, abstract and drawings. In specified cases, biological material becomes available upon publication (Article 30(1)–(3)).

name: Scope and conduct of substantive examination
description: During technical examination a search report and opinion are prepared concerning: I – patentability of the application; II – suitability of the application given the nature claimed; III – reformulation of the application or division; and IV – technical requirements (Article 35).
guidance: Searches are conducted by engineers and technicians specialized in patent system and technological fields; they check wording against legal standards and the state of the art worldwide. Any interested party can submit comments and documents during this stage.

name: Documents and evidence to be submitted during examination
description: Once examination is requested, within 60 days, whenever requested, the applicant must submit: I – objections, search for prior art and examination results for corresponding applications abroad when priority is claimed; II – documents required for regularization and examination; and III – simple translation of priority documents replaced by a declaration, when applicable (Article 34).
guidance: Failure to provide requested items within 60 days can lead to dismissal.

name: Declaration and effects of patent nullity (grounds and consequences)
description: Patent nullity is declared administratively when: I – any legal requirement has not been met; II – specifications and claims do not comply with Articles 24 and 25; III – the subject matter extends beyond the content of the application originally filed; or IV – any essential formalities to granting were not met during processing (Article 50).
guidance: Partial nullity is possible if remaining claims are patentable by themselves (Article 47). Nullity takes effect from the filing date (ex tunc) (Article 48). An action for nullity may be filed by the INPI or any person with legitimate interest within six months from grant; nullity proceedings continue even if patent term has expired (Articles 51 and 51(1)). Due process applies, holder has 60 days to respond; INPI president issues decision and publishes it when final and unappealable (Articles 50–57).

name: M2: 0-valent and monovalent carbon chain coding and retrieval guidance
description: Set M2 codes describe isolated carbon chains or carbon chains bonded to one terminating atom (M210 general and M211–M216 specific 1–6 C codes; M220 general and M221–M226 specific 7–19+ C codes).
guidance: One of the general codes M210 or M220 is always added to the code record when a specific code from M21/M22 is assigned (e.g., propyl chain not multiply bonded receives M210 and M213). Prior to 1981, specific codes in M21/M22 were only assigned if no polyvalent chains present; from 1981 forward, specific codes assigned only if chain length specifically claimed or exemplified. Therefore comprehensive retrieval is best achieved by searching M210 or M220 rather than the more specific chain-length codes. If structure contains both 0/1-valent and polyvalent chains and a user includes a specific chain-length code, place that code in the search statement with codes from 1981/week 27 onward (green codes), while the applicable general code is placed with codes from 1972–1981/week 26 (blue codes). Sets M2 are applicable to multiple subheadings per table; check exceptions (M232/M233/M240 applicability years).

name: Scope/volume of legal protection
description: The legal protection for inventions/useful models is specified by their formulas (claims); for industrial designs by aggregate substantial properties reflected in product/model/figure photographs.
guidance: Claims/formula define scope; for designs the list of essential features and images determine protection.

name: Temporary legal protection from publication
description: A filed invention is given temporary legal protection within the scope of the published claims from date of publication of application information until the date of publication of grant information.
guidance: If refusal ruling is final, temporary protection does not apply. Persons who used claimed invention during this period shall pay compensation to patent holder after patent grant; amount by agreement.

name: Grounds for disputing and invalidating patents
description: A patent may be disputed/invalidated in whole or partly if: (a) the patented object fails to correspond to patentability terms; (b) the claims of an invention/useful model contain aggregate essential features of an industrial design absent in initial materials; (c) authors or patent holders are incorrectly indicated.
guidance: Objections on such grounds are examined by Appeal Chamber within six months of arrival; further appeals available to Supreme Patent Chamber.

name: Disseize (challenge to ownership) — remedies and time bars
description: A person claiming to be the legal right owner may demand the court to transfer the design owner right or be recognized as owner; partial rights follow joint-ownership rules.
guidance: Claims must be made within three years after publication (registered) or presentation (unregistered), except where the defendant acted in bad faith (no limitation). Final decisions are registrable and published; if application is registered during proceedings, the proceeding converts into one about the registered design.

name: Protective order content — exclusions to confidentiality
description: Orders typically provide that designated confidential/trade secret information may not include information which (a) at or prior to disclosure is known to or independently developed by the discovering party; (b) is public knowledge or becomes available to the public without violation; (c) is revealed to the public by a person having the unrestricted right to do so; or (d) is acquired by the discovering party from a third party lawfully possessing the information.
guidance: These exclusions narrow the scope of protectable material and prevent misuse of confidentiality claims to cover public or previously-known information.

name: First Inventor to File / First to Invent
description: Comparison of pre-AIA first-to-invent rules (§102(g) interference proceedings to determine earlier inventor) with AIA's first-inventor-to-file regime. AIA replaces first-to-invent concepts with a system where effective filing date governs rights.
guidance: Under AIA §102(a)(2) precludes a patent if the claimed invention was described in a patent or patent application naming another inventor and "effectively filed before the effective filing date of the claimed invention." Effective: March 16, 2013; applies to claims with effective filing date on or after that date.

name: Prior Art Definitions (§102 / §103 changes)
description: Pre-AIA §§102/103 defined prior art by knowledge/use in U.S., printed publications, public use/on sale (and 12-month grace). AIA revises §102 to preclude patents for inventions patented, described in a printed publication, or "in public use, on sale or otherwise available to the public" anywhere before the inventor's effective filing date; §103's timing language likewise shifts to before the effective filing of the claimed invention.
guidance: AIA §102(a)(1) and §102(a)(2) incorporate patents/published applications as prior art with effective filing date doctrines (foreign filing dates can be prior art); In re Hilmer overruled. "On sale" interpreted as publicly on sale. Applicable to claims with effective filing dates on/after March 16, 2013.

name: Grace Period (AIA §102(b)(1))
description: AIA replaces the pre-AIA 12-month grace language with narrower exceptions: a disclosure is not prior art if made by the inventor (or someone who obtained the subject matter from the inventor) within one year before the effective filing date, or if the subject matter was previously publicly disclosed by the inventor (or someone who obtained it from the inventor) before the disclosure.
guidance: Effective March 16, 2013. Applies to patent applications and patents containing claims with effective filing dates on/after March 16, 2013. The chart reproduces statutory phrasing: §102(b)(1) conditions (A) and (B).

name: Post-Grant Review (PGR) (§321-329)
description: AIA creates PGR procedures permitting third parties to petition to cancel one or more patent claims within nine months of issue/reissue on broad grounds of unpatentability (except best mode).
guidance: §324 allows institution where it is more likely than not at least one challenged claim is unpatentable OR the petition raises a novel/unsettled legal question. Petitioner may assert any invalidity grounds (except best mode) and rely on patents, printed publications, affidavits/declarations. Patent owner may file one motion to amend. Estoppel attaches after final decision; PGR is unavailable if petitioner first filed a civil action. Final decision within one year (six-month extension for good cause). Effective on/after Sept 16, 2012 for patents issued/reissued less than nine months (limited to first-inventor-to-file).

name: Prosecute claims of appropriate scope
description: Prosecute claims of sufficient scope to read on the competition, yet just narrow enough to avoid the prior art.
guidance: Balance claim breadth against prior art; aim to capture competitors' implementations while remaining patentable. Craft multiple claim scopes (broad independent, narrower fallbacks) so that at least some claims survive prior-art attacks.

name: Provide full written description support
description: Fully describe the inventor’s conception to provide support for the broadest claim construction possible and to comply with the requirements of various written description laws.
guidance: Include general descriptions as well as specific embodiments so the specification supports broad functional claim language; avoid limiting the disclosure to narrow examples only; ensure the specification permits the claimed scope under §112/written description.

name: Obtain strong, enforceable claims
description: Obtain strong, enforceable claims that will withstand validity challenges and be difficult to design around to achieve non-infringement.
guidance: Draft claims to be defensible in validity fights and to reduce easy design-arounds (e.g., functional claim drafting, multiple claim formats, careful fallback claim sets). Consider enforceability risks from prosecution history and specification statements.

name: Patent’s own words can restrict claim scope
description: Statements in the specification and prosecution history that would have no impact in other jurisdictions may narrow claim scope in the U.S.; the specification is the single best guide to the meaning of a disputed term (Phillips v. AWH).
guidance: Avoid language in the specification or arguments that will be used to limit claim terms during claim construction. Be mindful that how terms are described or exemplified in the spec can be used to construe claims narrowly in litigation.

name: Avoid troublesome specification drafting practices
description: Several drafting habits can inadvertently narrow claims or create problems: vague claim terms with corresponding narrow disclosure; inconsistent use of terms; highlighting non-claimed features of embodiments; narrow examples without a more general description; describing unclaimed benefits; attributing the word 'invention' to unclaimed features; ordinary words may be limiting.
guidance: Ensure consistent terminology throughout the application; accompany examples with broader descriptions; avoid emphasizing only narrow aspects or non-claimed features; do not call unclaimed features 'the invention.' Use generic language to support broader constructions.

name: Be precise and consistent in wording and definitions
description: Word choice (e.g., 'at' vs. 'to', 'is' vs. 'may be', 'the invention is' vs. 'the invention may include') can determine claim scope.
guidance: Define claim terms broadly and consistently; where appropriate use functional language, ranges, and examples rather than absolute definitive statements. Carefully review specification wording to avoid inadvertent limitations (illustrated by Chef America v. Lamb-Weston where 'to' vs 'at' affected claim construction).

name: Avoid 'patent profanity' in specification and prosecution
description: Avoid using suggestive limiting adjectives or labels (e.g., 'peculiar', 'significant', 'critical', 'special', 'essential', 'key', 'necessary', 'preferable (?)') that may be interpreted as limitations on the invention.
guidance: Do not label features as 'essential' or 'critical' unless you intend to limit the claim to those features; prefer neutral descriptions and functional embodiments that preserve flexibility in claim interpretation.

name: Avoid unnecessary amendments and arguments
description: Unnecessary amendments and/or arguments may create potential estoppels and narrow claim scope; amendments for patentability can surrender claim scope and equivalents.
guidance: Make the Examiner bear the burden of rejection. In the first response, attack the basis of the rejection rather than immediately amending. If amendment is necessary, be surgical and preserve the most valuable embodiments; keep arguments concise and focused to avoid creating estoppels in prosecution history.

name: Consider industry-specific predictability differences
description: The level of predictability differs by art: chem/bio are often characterized as unpredictable, while mechanical/electrical arts are more predictable.
guidance: Tailor obviousness/enablement arguments to the field; in unpredictable arts emphasize lack of reasonable expectation of success; in predictable arts recognize that obviousness may be easier to show and plan claim strategies accordingly.

name: Surrendering equivalents / doctrine of equivalents risk
description: Narrowing amendments made for patentability create a presumption that equivalents for the narrowed element were surrendered (prosecution-history estoppel), which can limit ability to rely on the doctrine of equivalents.
guidance: Avoid or minimize narrowing amendments when possible; if necessary, preserve equivalents by careful claim drafting, dependent claims, and by framing arguments to avoid broad concessions. Be aware that literal claim scope, specification, prosecution history, amendments, arguments, and §112 issues all interplay with DOE analysis.

name: Ensure examples and experimental statements are accurate and supported
description: Examples written in the past tense suggest the work was done; using examples relied on for patentability increases scrutiny.
guidance: Verify with inventors whether experiments were actually performed before filing. Check that examples correctly reflect what was done, confirm any comparative data are statistically significant, and search for inventor publications or other statements inconsistent with the examples. Use Rule 132 declarations where appropriate to support factual claims.

name: Claim-drafting tactics: use multiple tiers, dependent claims, and alternative independent claims
description: Craft multiple tiers of claim strategies so that if one falls you have backups; use dependent claims effectively and consider additional independent claims to recite subject matter alternatively to avoid the prior art.
guidance: Design claim sets with layered fallback positions (broad → intermediate → narrow). If amending, preserve alternative claim paths (e.g., different independent claim formats) to reduce the risk that a single amendment or rejection will destroy all enforceable scope.

name: Prosecution argument style: concise, focused, and prior-art-focused
description: When arguing, concentrate on the Examiner’s prior-art rationale and be concise and focused to avoid making unnecessary concessions that narrow claim scope.
guidance: Avoid extended narrative about the invention itself when responding to rejections; instead, dissect the Examiner's cited references and explain why they do not teach/modify/combine to yield the claimed invention. Keep arguments technical and prior-art-centric.

name: Avoid overreaching obviousness rebuttals that create enablement problems
description: When rebutting obviousness, do not overemphasize how difficult it would be to make the modification suggested by the Examiner in a way that later undermines enablement.
guidance: Strike a balance: present enough evidence of unpredictability or lack of reasonable expectation of success to defeat obviousness without asserting claims about enablement that could be used against you later. Establish an appropriate level of ordinary skill in the art consistent with both obviousness and enablement positions.

name: No patent for an art or principle in the abstract
description: A claim that undertakes to cover an art or principle in the abstract (e.g., 'the cutting of ice of a uniform size by means of an apparatus worked by any other power than human') renders the patent void, unless a timely disclaimer saves it.
guidance: If a claim attempts to appropriate an abstract principle or art rather than a concrete application or apparatus, courts will treat it as non-patentable. Example: a broad first clause claiming an art generally was likely 'mere surplusage' and not the invention; the patent properly covered only the apparatus.

name: Distinguish apparatus claims from abstract statements; surplusage may be disregarded
description: Where a claim includes both a general (possibly abstract) clause and a specific clause, the invention may reside in the specific clause and the general clause be treated as surplusage.
guidance: Courts will look to the face of the claim to find where the invention resides; non-misleading surplus language need not invalidate the patent but may be rejected as inessential. Draft claims to focus on the concrete machine/method that embodies the invention.

name: Discovery + practical application of a new property of matter is patentable if sufficiently enabled
description: The practical application of a newly discovered property of matter (e.g., a property of lead) is a patentable invention if the specification describes a process sufficiently to enable an ordinary mechanic to construct and apply it.
guidance: Le Roy v. Tatham and related authorities show that novelty may rest in the new property and its application rather than novel machinery. But if the specification does not sufficiently describe the process (or the claim is drafted to claim something else), the patent may fail.

name: Specification and claim construction should be liberal and substance-focused
description: The specification and claim should be construed 'benignly' — looking through inartificial phrases to the substance of what was really invented, to protect the patentee's true discovery when ascertainable from the specification as a whole.
guidance: Courts will take the specification and patent together, avoid hyper-technical invalidation on forms of expression, and try to identify the 'thing really invented' if the language fairly supports it. Drafting should still be clear, but courts may interpret imperfect language liberally to effect the invention.

name: Functional/purposive claim limitations tie scope to use and may preserve validity
description: A claim that limits a combination to its use for a specified purpose or 'in any other manner substantially the same' (e.g., 'when used to form pipes of metal, under heat and pressure, in the manner set forth, or in any other manner substantially the same') ties the claim to the employment of the new property and may avoid a claim to the machinery per se.
guidance: Use purposive functional limitations to show that the claimed combination is claimed only in the context of the novel application; this can prevent construction that the patentee claimed the apparatus in the abstract.

name: Claim Construction (purpose and effect)
description: Claim construction is the legal process of determining the exact meaning and scope of the words used in a patent's claims; the judge issues a binding definition that governs the rest of the case.
guidance: The claim construction result—often issued in a 'Claim Construction Order'—establishes the scope of the patent's protection and can dramatically strengthen or weaken a case, frequently leading to settlement or dispositive motions. Example: disputes over terms like 'durable' determine whether accused products fall within the claim scope.

name: Hierarchy of Evidence — intrinsic evidence paramount (Phillips)
description: Judges must give greatest weight to intrinsic evidence (the patent claims, the specification, and the prosecution history) when construing claim terms.
guidance: Start—and, if possible, end—your analysis with intrinsic evidence. The specification is described as the 'single best guide' to claim meaning. Do not rely on extrinsic evidence to contradict intrinsic evidence.

name: Intrinsic Evidence — Claims
description: The claims are the starting point for construction; words in the claims are generally given their ordinary and customary meaning as understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA).
guidance: Interpret claim language in context of the whole patent. Emphasize plain/ordinary meaning unless the specification or prosecution history demonstrates a special definition or limitation.

name: Intrinsic Evidence — Specification
description: The specification is the detailed written description (including drawings) and serves as the patent's internal dictionary for interpreting claim terms.
guidance: A specification can define or limit claim terms (e.g., describing 'fastening mechanism' as 'a screw and nut combination' may narrow the claim). Use specification language to support or oppose broader constructions; avoid relying on examples in the specification to assert unlimited scope if specification indicates otherwise.

name: Inventor Testimony (limited weight)
description: An inventor's testimony about what they intended a term to mean is generally given little weight in claim construction.
guidance: Courts focus on the public patent document rather than a patentee's subjective, after-the-fact intent. Avoid relying on inventor testimony to create or expand claim scope; use documentation in the specification/prosecution history instead.

name: PHOSITA Standard (person having ordinary skill in the art)
description: Claims are construed from the perspective of a hypothetical Person Having Ordinary Skill In The Art (PHOSITA) at the time of filing.
guidance: Determine the relevant field and the level of ordinary skill appropriate to that field and filing date. Use PHOSITA perspective to interpret ordinary meaning and to assess whether extrinsic sources reflect contemporaneous understanding.

name: Appellate Standard of Review (Teva)
description: On appeal, claim constructions based only on intrinsic evidence are reviewed de novo, but factual findings based on extrinsic evidence are reviewed for clear error.
guidance: Implication: winning factual disputes (e.g., via convincing expert evidence) at the district court can make the factual findings harder to overturn on appeal. Tailor trial-level presentation accordingly—present clear, well-documented factual support if you need deference on appeal.

name: Ordinary and Customary Meaning default
description: Absent clear contrary evidence in the intrinsic record, claim terms receive their ordinary and customary meaning as understood by a PHOSITA.
guidance: Only deviate from ordinary meaning when the specification or prosecution history clearly defines or limits a term. Parties should avoid inventing special definitions unsupported by the patent record.

name: Prosecution Disclaimer / Avoiding Recapture
description: Statements or amendments during prosecution that limit claim scope can prevent patentees from later asserting broader interpretations in litigation.
guidance: Search the file wrapper for explicit disclaimers or arguments of narrowness. Use such history to estop broader interpretations; patentees should avoid making statements during prosecution that will be used to limit claims later.

name: Local Patent Rules and Jurisdictional Procedures
description: Procedures, timing, and mechanics of Markman hearings vary by district (e.g., D. Del., E.D. Tex., N.D. Cal., W.D. Tex.), which materially affects strategy and scheduling.
guidance: Know the local rules: some courts have early hearings (rocket dockets), others emphasize written briefing and tutorials. Prepare for jurisdiction-specific requirements like joint claim construction statements, tutorials, or compressed schedules.

name: Joint Claim Construction Chart / Prehearing Statement (procedural requirement)
description: Parties commonly must meet and confer to create a joint chart listing disputed terms, each party's proposed constructions, and the evidence relied upon.
guidance: This document crystallizes disputes for the judge and is often required by local patent rules. Make the chart precise, cite intrinsic passages, and explain why each disputed term should be construed a certain way.

name: Claim Construction Briefing (opening, responsive, reply)
description: Parties submit detailed briefs arguing for their proposed constructions, grounding arguments in intrinsic evidence and supporting extrinsic materials as needed.
guidance: Opening briefs present initial arguments; responsive briefs rebut opponent points; reply briefs address new issues. Fill briefs with citations to claims, specification, and prosecution history; include expert declarations only where necessary to resolve technical factual matters.

name: Claim Construction Order (finality and downstream effects)
description: After the hearing, the judge issues a written Claim Construction Order listing each disputed term and the court's official definition; this order governs the remainder of the case.
guidance: A favorable order can prompt settlement or support summary judgment; an unfavorable order may be devastating. Plan follow-on litigation strategy (e.g., summary judgment motions, settlement negotiations, or appeal) based on the court's constructions.

name: Strategic Goals of Parties (broad vs. narrow constructions)
description: Plaintiffs (patent holders) generally seek broad claim constructions to maximize infringement exposure; defendants seek narrow constructions to avoid infringement.
guidance: Frame arguments accordingly: patentees should tie broad readings to specification disclosures and absence of disclaimers; defendants should identify limiting language and prosecution statements that support narrower readings.

name: Scienter requirement for inducement (knowledge and affirmative intent)
description: Inducement contains a knowledge/intent element: the alleged inducer must have known (or should have known) that its actions would induce actual infringement and must have had an affirmative intent to cause direct infringement.
guidance: Federal Circuit in DSU Medical: intent requires that the alleged inducer knew or should have known its actions would induce infringement. The article notes uncertainty about how far an alleged inducer must assess patent validity or study whether induced acts infringe specific claims.

name: Use of circumstantial evidence to satisfy scienter
description: Circumstantial evidence and inference may be used to establish the requisite knowledge and specific intent for inducement; this creates a relatively low threshold for satisfying scienter.
guidance: Because scienter can often be established through inference, inducement claims frequently present fact questions for juries; summary judgment for defendants may fail where material facts and reasonable inferences favor the non-moving party.

name: Direct infringement definition and strict liability (35 U.S.C. § 271(a))
description: Direct infringement under 35 U.S.C. § 271(a) occurs when someone without authority makes, uses, offers to sell, sells, or imports a patented invention in the U.S. For method claims, the direct infringer must perform every claim step (literally or via equivalents).
guidance: Direct infringement is a strict liability tort: motive, mistake, or lack of knowledge of the patent are irrelevant. Determination requires proper claim construction and comparing claim limitations to the accused device/process.

name: Divided (multiple-actor) infringement standards
description: When multiple independent entities perform steps of a claimed method, liability for direct infringement may attach only if one entity directs or controls the other's performance or the entities form a joint enterprise.
guidance: Federal Circuit en banc decisions require either (1) direction/control over performance or (2) joint enterprise for finding single-entity direct infringement when steps are divided among actors. Facts showing the defendant set up the manner/timing so others must perform steps can support liability (e.g., Limelight).

name: Claim construction importance and standards (Markman, Phillips, Teva)
description: Claim construction is central to infringement and validity; claims are given their customary and ordinary meaning to a person of ordinary skill in the art. Judges (not juries) construe claims (Markman), and Teva holds that clear-error review applies to district court factual findings in claim construction.
guidance: Proper claim construction precedes infringement comparison. Teva establishes that factual findings in construction are reviewed for clear error while ultimate legal issues remain de novo on appeal; Phillips guides reliance on intrinsic evidence for claim meaning.

name: USPTO Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidelines (two-step Alice/Mayo process)
description: The USPTO's January 7, 2019 Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidelines provide a two-step process for determining whether a claim is drawn to patent-eligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 101 (Alice/Mayo framework).
guidance: The Guidelines aim to provide more consistent rulings; they supersede prior guidance but note that claims previously considered eligible should remain eligible. The article emphasizes ongoing lack of clarity and shifting case law on § 101.

name: Definition of 'final decision' for 37 CFR 1.703(a)(5)
description: 'Final decision' means: (1) the decision is the last decision in the review by the Board (or by a federal court); and (2) the decision does not require further action by the applicant to avoid termination of proceedings as to the rejected claims.
guidance: A Board decision containing a new ground of rejection under 37 CFR 41.50(b) requires applicant action and is not a 'final decision' for 1.703(a)(5). 'Final decision' for 1.703(a)(5) does not require finality for judicial review (e.g., reversal of all rejections can be 'final' for PTA even if not appeal-final).

name: 37 CFR 1.704(f) 'in condition for examination' definition
description: An application filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a) is 'in condition for examination' when it includes: a specification including at least one claim and an abstract (§ 1.72(b)); papers in compliance with § 1.52; drawings if any in compliance with § 1.84; any required English translations (§ 1.52(d)/1.57(a)); a sequence listing where applicable (§§ 1.821–1.825); the inventor's oath/declaration or an ADS (§ 1.63(b)); basic filing fee, search fee, examination fee; any certified copy required by § 1.57(a); and any application size fee required under § 1.16(s). International national-stage applications have analogous requirements (§ 1.492 fees etc.).
guidance: An application is considered to have papers/drawings/sequence listing in compliance for purposes of this paragraph on the filing date of the latest prior reply correcting those items if that reply is prior to mailing of an action under 35 U.S.C. 132 or a notice of allowance, whichever occurs first.

name: Handling of amendments filed with notice of appeal (after-final amendments)
description: If appellant files an amendment, a notice of appeal and an appeal brief on the same date after a final action, 37 CFR 1.116 applies; such an amendment is not entered as a matter of right but may be admitted if it cancels claims or complies with form requirements or, for specification/claims amendments, upon showing good and sufficient reasons why not earlier presented.
guidance: Amendments filed after final action may be considered but are not guaranteed entry; if an amendment is filed with a reply under 37 CFR 1.111 and then a notice of appeal is filed prematurely, the Office will consider the reply first.

name: Office procedure following a Federal Circuit decision (mandate and consequences)
description: After the Federal Circuit decides the appeal, the Clerk forwards a certified copy of the court's decision (the 'mandate') which is entered in the application file; the mandate date marks conclusion of the appeal. The Office acts according to whether all claims were rejected, some claims allowed, remand is required, or prosecution should be reopened.
guidance: If all claims remain rejected, proceedings terminate on the mandate date and the application is ordinarily not open to subsequent amendment (applicant must have filed any continuation prior to mandate). If some claims allowed, the examiner should either convert dependent claims to independent form and issue, or set a 2-month time limit for appellant to rewrite dependent claims in independent form. Any Office action proposing to reopen prosecution after a court decision must be forwarded to the Deputy Commissioner for Patent Examination Policy for approval.

name: Prima facie case of unpatentability (definition)
description: A prima facie case of unpatentability is established when the information compels a conclusion that a claim is unpatentable under the preponderance of evidence burden-of-proof standard, giving each term its broadest reasonable construction consistent with the specification, and before consideration of evidence attempting to establish patentability.
guidance: Apply broadest reasonable construction consistent with the specification and evaluate whether the evidence, standing alone or combined, compels unpatentability under the preponderance standard.

name: Inadvertent omission incorporation rules
description: If all or a portion of the specification or drawings is inadvertently omitted but completely contained in a prior-filed application for which a priority/benefit claim under § 1.55 or § 1.78 is present, the claim shall be considered an incorporation by reference of the prior-filed application as to the omitted portion.
guidance: The application must be amended to include the omitted portion within any Office-set time but no later than the close of prosecution (§ 1.114(b)) or abandonment. Applicant must supply a copy of the prior-filed application (except where not required), an English translation where applicable, and identify where the omitted portion is found in the prior-filed application. International-effect rules: such amendments are effective only as to the U.S.; PCT rules may apply for wider effect.

name: Restriction on incorporation of essential material
description: "Essential material" may be incorporated by reference only by way of incorporation to a U.S. patent or U.S. patent application publication that does not itself incorporate such essential material by reference. 'Essential material' is material necessary to: (1) provide a written description and enablement (35 U.S.C. 112(a)); (2) describe the claimed invention to particularly point out and distinctly claim (35 U.S.C. 112(b)); or (3) describe structure/material/acts corresponding to a claimed means or step under 35 U.S.C. 112(f).
guidance: Do not attempt to incorporate essential material from non-U.S. patent sources or from documents that themselves incorporate the essential material by reference. Essential material omission can render claim support defective.

name: Permitted content and placement of chemical and mathematical formulas/tables
description: The specification, including the claims, may contain chemical and mathematical formulae but shall not contain drawings or flow diagrams. The description may contain tables (but the same tables should not be included in both the drawings and description). Claims may contain tables if necessary to conform to 35 U.S.C. 112 or otherwise desirable.
guidance: Follow § 1.52 formatting rules; avoid duplicative placement of tables in drawings and description; use tables in claims only when required/appropriate.

name: Expungement of information from application file
description: Information in an application will not be expunged except as provided in paragraph (b) of § 1.59 or §§ 41.7(a) or 42.7(a). Information forming part of the original disclosure (written specification including claims, drawings, and any preliminary amendment present on the filing date) will not be expunged.
guidance: An applicant may petition to expunge information (excluding original-disclosure material) by filing a petition with the fee in § 1.17(g) and establishing to the Director's satisfaction that expungement is appropriate; upon grant the Office provides notice. The Office will furnish copies of an application upon request and payment of the fee in § 1.19(b) unless the application has been disposed of.

name: Pre-AIA specific oath/declaration additional requirements
description: Under pre-AIA § 1.63, an oath/declaration must: be executed as required by § 1.66 or § 1.68; identify each inventor by full name (family name plus at least one given name); identify country of citizenship of each inventor; identify the application to which it is directed; state the signer has reviewed and understands the contents of the application (including claims as amended); and acknowledge the duty to disclose information material to patentability as defined in § 1.56.
guidance: Pre-AIA oath/declarations also required mailing/residence addresses (if not supplied on an ADS) and identification of relevant foreign applications for priority claims. These additional requirements apply to applications filed before the AIA applicability dates indicated in the MPEP.

name: Reference naming a claimed species anticipates regardless of listing size
description: A reference that clearly names the claimed species anticipates the claim no matter how many other species are additionally named (e.g., a species listed among thousands is 'described' for §102(a) purposes).
guidance: If the prior art explicitly names the claimed compound/species, the comprehensiveness of the listing does not negate anticipation. Case examples: Ex parte A (17 USPQ2d 1716) and In re Sivaramakrishnan. Compare to genus-species analyses when the species is not explicitly named.

name: Generic formula anticipates species when species can be 'at once envisaged'
description: A generic chemical formula will anticipate a claimed species covered by the formula when one of ordinary skill in the art is able to 'at once envisage' the specific compound from the generic teaching (i.e., can draw the structural formula or write the name of the compound).
guidance: Anticipation from a generic teaching requires sufficiently limited/well-delineated substituent classes. Examiners may look to preferred embodiments to determine which compounds can be anticipated. In re Petering and In re Schauman illustrate that a limited set of permutations (e.g., ~20 compounds) or limited variable sites/substituents can make a generic disclosure anticipatory; broad/enumerative generic formulas covering vast/infinite species do not anticipate.

name: Specific prior-art example within a claimed range anticipates the range
description: If a prior art reference discloses a specific example that falls within a claimed numerical or compositional range, that example anticipates the claimed range.
guidance: Example: Titanium Metals Corp. v. Banner — a data point inside claimed alloy composition range anticipated the claim. This is a straightforward anticipation where the exact claimed composition is disclosed as an example.

name: Overlapping or touching prior-art range anticipates only with 'sufficient specificity'
description: When a prior art reference teaches a range that overlaps or touches the claimed range but provides no specific example within the claimed range, anticipation requires that the reference disclose the claimed range with 'sufficient specificity' (fact-dependent).
guidance: Determination is case-by-case: narrow claimed ranges vs broad prior ranges may not be disclosed with sufficient specificity (see Atofina v. Great Lakes Chem.). Examiners must articulate reasons for anticipation and may combine 35 U.S.C. 102/103 rejections if ambiguous. The concept parallels 'clearly envisaging' a species from a generic teaching.

name: Nonanalogous art or 'teaches away' arguments are inapplicable to anticipation
description: Arguments that a prior reference is nonanalogous art or teaches away from the invention are not germane to a §102 anticipation analysis; a reference that explicitly or inherently discloses every claimed limitation is anticipatory regardless of field or disparaging language.
guidance: Teaching away and analogous-art analysis are relevant to obviousness inquiries, not to whether a reference discloses every claim limitation for novelty. Cases: Twin Disc, Inc.; Celeritas Technologies Ltd. v. Rockwell Int'l; Atlas Powder Co. See also cases addressing optional ingredients and exclusions (Upsher-Smith Labs v. Pamlab).

name: 35 U.S.C. 102(b) — CIP and effective filing date implications
description: For continuation-in-part (CIP) applications, claims not supported by the parent get the CIP filing date; any prior art with a critical date more than one year before the CIP filing date can bar the CIP claims under §102(b).
guidance: Claims relying on matter added in the CIP lack the parent's earlier priority date; see Paperless Accounting v. BART (Fed. Cir.). Examiners should determine effective dates when assessing §102(b) bars.

name: Sufficiency of disclosure (Article 5)
description: The international application must 'disclose the invention in a manner sufficiently clear and complete for the invention to be carried out by a person skilled in the art.'
guidance: The description together with drawings must supply all technical information required to enable a skilled person to put the invention into practice and enable the reader to understand the contribution to the art. See paragraphs 5.43 to 5.53 for application to all claims.

name: Brief description of drawings requirements
description: If drawings are included they should first be briefly described (e.g., 'Figure 1 is a plan view...').
guidance: When referring in the description to drawing elements, use the name of the element as well as its number (e.g., 'resistor 3 is connected to capacitor 5 via switch 4'). Description and drawings should be consistent, especially reference numbers. Examiner need not rigorously require deletion of superfluous references after amendment deletions, but all reference numbers used in description or claims should appear on drawings. (Paragraphs 4.08–4.09)

name: Sufficiency and irreparable insufficiency
description: Applicant is responsible for supplying sufficient disclosure at filing to meet Article 5 for all claims; serious insufficiency cannot be cured subsequently without offending Article 34(2)(b).
guidance: Insufficiency can render claims too broad and fail support requirements. Two special irreparable cases: (a) dependence on chance (irreproducible results, e.g., certain microbiological processes), and (b) inherently impossible inventions contrary to physical laws (e.g., perpetual motion). (Paragraphs 4.12–4.13)

name: PGR — patent owner amendments
description: Patent Owner has two months to file preliminary response; allowed 1 motion to amend by cancellation of any challenged claim and, for each challenged claim, can propose substitute claims; subsequent motions may be entered upon joint request of the parties or for good cause; substitute claims cannot expand scope or introduce new matter.
guidance: Amendment opportunities are limited: initial motion is essentially the primary chance to amend; substitute claims must be commensurate with original disclosure. Entry of later motions is narrowly circumscribed.

name: Markush claims and biological deposits (Mexico)
description: Markush claims are patentable if duly supported in the specification and meet patentability requirements. Mexico accepts deposits of a wide range of microorganisms/materials under recognized IDAs (Budapest Treaty).

name: Claim clarity and drafting recommendations (Mexico)
description: Claims should be clear, concise and not extend beyond contents of the specification. Claims should be drafted according to the technical features of the invention. The first claim must be independent and relate to the essential feature; independent claims should, if possible, include a preamble (features already in prior art) and a characterizing part (novel subject matter). Further technical features should be pursued via dependent claims, ensuring consistent dependence.

name: Method and process claim scope and exclusions (Mexico)
description: Methods and process claims are patentable if they meet patentability requirements except for: (i) essentially biological processes for plants/animals; (ii) methods that are mental processes, playing games, doing business, mathematical methods; (iii) methods of presenting information; (iv) methods of surgical, therapeutic or diagnostic treatment applicable to humans/animals (subject to claim formulation).
guidance: Therapeutic methods may be claimed as Swiss-type or purpose-limited product claims; IMPI practice varies.

name: PCT application formalities (Mexico)
description: Requirements when entering national phase/PCT: copy of International application as published (specification, claims, abstract, PCT publication sheet); formal drawings (translate legends to Spanish); copy of amendments during international phase; assignment of rights not required; power of attorney on behalf of applicant.

name: Paris Convention regular application formalities (Mexico)
description: Required: copy of specification, claims and abstract; formal drawings (if any); certified copy of priority right document; data sheet with inventors' and applicants' details and priority info; assignment of rights; power of attorney.

name: PPH program participation requirements (Mexico)
description: To request PPH participation, provide: copies of all relevant Office actions from foreign office showing allowable/patentable claims (with Spanish translations); copies of patentable claims determined by USPTO (with Spanish translation); an IDS listing documents cited by USPTO and copies of cited documents (including non-patent literature) unless available to IMPI; ensure MX examination has not begun and MX publication has occurred.
guidance: Divisional applications are not published in Mexico — watch timing; IMPI may retrieve some foreign documents from public PAIR, but applicants should submit missing copies.

name: Claim amendments after grant (Mexico)
description: Text or drawings of a granted patent may only be amended by the patent owner to (i) correct obvious/form errors; and (ii) limit the scope of the claims. Authorized changes shall be published in the Official Gazette. An amendment after allowance is requested in writing with brief reasons.

name: Definition of patent infringement (Mexico)
description: Infringement generally occurs when a third unauthorized party makes, uses or sells a patented product or process. The test of infringement is whether the patent claims would cover the accused product or process via claim construction (legal) and claim coverage (factual).
guidance: Infringement can only be literal under IP Law; doctrine of equivalents not recognized. For process claims where the patent is for a process obtaining a product, the defendant bears burden to show product was made by another process if product is new or there is substantial likelihood the accused product was made by the patented process and patentee cannot determine the process.

name: IMPI administrative infringement procedure (Mexico)
description: IMPI handles infringement in first instance via administrative proceedings: plaintiff files a formal written claim; IMPI admits the claim and serves notice to defendant who has 10 days to answer; both parties must produce supporting evidence at filing/answer; IMPI decides on the merits.
guidance: IMPI is an administrative agency, not a court of law. Criminal sanctions may apply for recidivism through PGR (Federal District Attorney Office).

name: Statute of limitations and damages timing (Mexico)
description: There is no general statute of limitations stated, however there is a two-year limitation period to pursue a civil action for damages; thus timing affects damages claims. Monetary relief available in civil actions typically consists of actual losses and lost profits.

name: Filing requirements (documents and parties)
description: Full name and address of the applicant(s); Full name and address of inventor(s); Invention specification including claims, description, abstract and drawings; Certified copy of priority document if convention priority is claimed (can be claimed and filed within three months from the application filing date); International publication, international search report, international preliminary examination report for entry of PCT application into national phase; Simply signed Power of Attorney (POA).
guidance: These are the mandatory elements to file a Eurasian Patent application at the Eurasian Patent Organization (EAPO). Note the certified copy of priority document may be submitted within three months of filing when priority is claimed. For PCT national/regional phase entry, include the international documents (publication, ISR, IPRP) as applicable.

name: Publication timing and options
description: The patent application is published after expiration of 18 months from the application filing date or priority date (if any). It may, however, be published earlier at the applicant's request upon payment of an additional fee.
guidance: Publication ordinarily occurs at 18 months but can be accelerated upon request and fee. Publication affords provisional protection between publication and grant within the scope of the published claims on the territory of all Contracting States.

name: Provisional protection after publication
description: The Publication of the Eurasian Patent Application affords provisional legal protection within the scope of the published claims on the territory of all the Contracting States.
guidance: From publication until grant, the applicant has provisional protection limited to the published claims. Consider timing of enforcement or licensing decisions in that provisional window.

name: Objects not patentable (excluded subject matter)
description: The following objects are not patentable as inventions in Eurasia: Discoveries; Scientific theories and mathematical methods; Presentation of information; Business organization and management methods; Symbols, schedules and rules; Methods of performing mental acts; Computer programs and algorithms; Topographies of integrated circuits; Projects and plans for structures and buildings and for land development; Solutions concerning solely the outward appearance of manufactured goods and aimed at satisfying aesthetic requirements.
guidance: These categories are explicitly excluded from patentability under the Eurasian system. If an invention touches excluded subject matter, draft claims and disclosures to emphasize technical character and technical contribution to avoid exclusion where possible.

name: Disclosure requirement (general)
description: In return for exclusive rights, patent holders must sufficiently disclose information about the invention so the public can learn about the invention and avoid reinventing it; disclosure also ensures patent scope is clearly communicated so others can avoid infringement or challenge the patent.
guidance: Disclosure objectives: dissemination of technological information, preventing unjustified extension of rights to undisclosed subject matter, and clarity of claim scope. Failure to properly disclose at filing can make it impossible to add new subject matter later.

name: Support requirement (or written description requirement)
description: Claims must be supported by the description (written description in the United States): there must be a basis in the description for the subject matter of every claim and claims must not be broader than justified by the description and drawings.
guidance: A claim is supported unless there are well‑founded reasons to believe a person skilled in the art could not extend the teaching of the description to the whole field claimed. U.S. written description requires describing the claimed invention in sufficient detail that a skilled person would reasonably conclude the inventor had possession of the claimed invention at filing. See Modules IV–VII for practical drafting guidance.

name: Clarity requirement (definiteness requirement)
description: Claims must be clear and concise and distinctly define the subject matter of the invention, using neither vague nor indefinite terms.
guidance: Terms in a claim are given their normal meaning in the relevant art; where needed, the drafter can include explicit definitions in the description to give special meaning. Description and drawings may be taken into account when interpreting claims. Draft claims with clarity so third parties can analyze what is and is not covered.

name: Priority claims (Paris Convention and PCT)
description: Applicants from Paris Convention or WTO member states can claim priority when filing subsequent applications in those territories within 12 months of the first application; PCT also allows priority claims.
guidance: Valid priority means subsequent applications are not invalidated by actions between the priority date and the subsequent filing date. Docket the first application's filing date and check with the applicant before its first anniversary about foreign filing intentions. Determine special rules for countries not party to the Paris Convention.

name: Identifying patentable inventions (focus on concept)
description: From disclosures/interviews, focus on the patentable inventions (the inventive concept) rather than prototypes or nonpatentable details; the drafter often articulates what constitutes the invention to be claimed.
guidance: Explore with the inventor the problem they solved in light of prior art to craft essential claim elements. Do not assume inventors know what is patentable; ask probing questions to identify novel and inventive aspects.

name: Claims drafting requirements
description: Claims define the scope of exclusive protection in terms of technical features; they are the legally operative part and must be clear, concise, and fully supported by the description.
guidance: Draft claims in the proper formal claim format. Consider drafting claims first to guide the rest of the specification. Ensure claim words are given appropriate meanings and that claim scope is justified by the description and drawings.

name: Drawings purpose and content
description: Drawings provide visual support to describe the invention and facilitate understanding; they may include figures, tables, flow charts and diagrams, and a representative drawing is often placed on the front page of a published patent document.
guidance: Include drawings where necessary to understand the invention; ensure consistency with the description and claims.

name: Abstract requirements
description: The abstract is a short summary (digest) of the invention, limited to a certain number of words, typically including key features recited in the claims.
guidance: The abstract aids patent searches and gives an overview of the invention. Keep within jurisdictional word-limits and ensure it reflects claim features.

name: Overlapping, approaching, and similar ranges, amounts, and proportions
description: In the case where the claimed ranges “overlap or lie inside ranges disclosed by the prior art” a prima facie case of obviousness exists.
guidance: Case law examples: In re Wertheim; In re Woodruff (prior art "about 1-5%" allowed concentrations slightly above 5%); In re Geisler (thickness ranges). If ranges overlap, prima facie obviousness is established. But consider if the prior art range is so broad as to encompass many distinct compositions (analogous to genus issues). See MPEP § 2131.03 and § 2144.08.

name: Routine optimization does not support patentability absent criticality
description: Generally, differences in concentration or temperature will not support the patentability of subject matter encompassed by the prior art unless there is evidence indicating such concentration or temperature is critical.
guidance: Discovering optimum or workable ranges by routine experimentation is not inventive (In re Aller, Peterson, In re Hoeschele). See KSR v. Teleflex for caution about granting patents based on combinations found in prior art. If claimed ranges fall within broad prior art scope, examiner should look for evidence of criticality or unexpected results.

name: Examiner must articulate a rationale supporting a routine-optimization rejection
