description: In order to properly support a rejection on the basis that an invention is the result of 'routine optimization', the examiner must make findings of relevant facts and present the underpinning reasoning in sufficient detail.
guidance: The articulated rationale must explain why it would have been routine optimization to arrive at the claimed invention and why a person of ordinary skill would have had a reasonable expectation of success to formulate the claimed range. See In re Stepan; Arendi v. Apple; In re Van Os. Mere statements of 'common sense' without reasoned analysis are insufficient.

name: Rebuttal by showing the claimed parameter was not recognized as 'result-effective'
description: Applicants may rebut a prima facie case by showing that the claimed variable was not recognized in the prior art to be a result-effective variable (i.e., the prior art did not indicate that changing that variable affects the result).
guidance: Antonie described the 'result-effective variable' exception; it's narrow. E.I. DuPont de Nemours v. Synvina and Applied Materials discuss that lack of any prior-art disclosure of a relationship between the variable and result supports this rebuttal. Applicants must articulate why the variable would not have been recognized as result-effective in the prior art.

name: When a single prior-art reference discloses a genus, seek additional prior art and analyze specific factors
description: When a single prior art reference discloses a genus encompassing the claimed species/subgenus but does not expressly disclose the claimed species, Office personnel should attempt to find additional prior art; absent additional art, consider specific factors to determine if a single-reference 103 rejection is appropriate.
guidance: If no additional art is found, evaluate the structure of the genus and species, physical/chemical properties and utilities, predictability of the technology, and the number of species encompassed by the genus (MPEP § 2144.08 II).

name: Ascertain the differences between the prior art and the claims (Graham factor B)
description: Compare the claimed species/subgenus to the closest disclosed prior-art species/subgenus to determine similarities and differences in structure, properties, and utilities.
guidance: Identify the closest disclosed species and make explicit findings on similarities/differences. The issue under §103 is whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious (Stratoflex).

name: Determine the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art (Graham factor C)
description: Evaluate the relevant prior art from the standpoint of a hypothetical person having ordinary skill in the art at the time the claimed invention was made.
guidance: Use the prior art to infer level of skill; consider any applicant-submitted evidence. Authorities: Ryko Mfg. Co. v. Nu-Star; Uniroyal v. Rudkin-Wiley. See MPEP §§ 2141 and 2141.03 for guidance.

name: Determine whether one of ordinary skill would have been motivated to select the claimed species
description: After analyzing Graham factors, determine if it would have been obvious for a person of ordinary skill to select the claimed species/subgenus from the prior-art genus, considering all relevant prior-art teachings.
guidance: Focus on the size of the genus (but do not apply per se rules), predictability, prior-art teachings, and totality of circumstances. A very small genus may render members envisagable (Petering). Make explicit findings about motivation.

name: Make explicit factual findings when relying on a genus-to-species obviousness rationale
description: Office personnel should make findings as to (A) structure of prior-art genus and species, (B) physical/chemical properties and utilities disclosed for the genus, (C) predictability of the technology, and (D) number of species encompassed by the genus.
guidance: These findings inform whether the selection of the claimed species from a genus would have been obvious. Use these findings before concluding a prima facie genus-to-species obviousness rejection.

name: Requirement to include at least one claim / role of claims
description: A nonprovisional patent application must have at least one patent claim particularly pointing out and distinctly defining the invention; claims define the rights granted and are the most important part of the patent application.
guidance: The specification must fully define the invention, but only aspects covered by claims will result in awarded rights. Claims are reviewed by the examiner and ultimately define the scope of exclusive rights.

name: Independent versus dependent claim form
description: A claim may be written in either independent or dependent form. An independent claim stands alone and does not refer to any other claim. A dependent claim refers to a previous claim and further limits the invention.
guidance: A claim in dependent form incorporates by reference all the limitations of the claim to which it refers. Use independent claims to define broad scope; use dependent claims to add narrower limitations and fallback positions.

name: Dependent-claim specifics: preamble matching, transitions, and chaining
description: For dependent claims the preamble must match the preamble from the broadest independent claim in the chain. The transition for a dependent claim will either be 'wherein' (used to further narrow something already introduced) or 'further comprising' (used when introducing something new).
guidance: Dependent claims can depend from other dependent claims (chaining). Maintain proper claim ordering (all claims depending on claim 1 should appear before claims depending on claim 2, etc.) to avoid formal objections (e.g., Rule 1.75(g) objection).

name: Preamble requirement and content
description: Every patent claim needs a preamble (the introductory phrase in a claim). The general rule is that the preamble of a claim does not limit the scope of the claim.
guidance: Avoid functional language in the preamble when possible (e.g., prefer 'A shovel…' to 'A shovel for digging…'), because functional wording may be unnecessary and could introduce complications. Functional language is not always wrong and may be used in limited circumstances if it obtains allowance, but avoid it as best practice.

name: Transition wording: 'comprising' vs 'consisting of'
description: Every patent claim needs a transition. The most common transitions are 'comprising' and 'consisting of.' 'Comprising' means the invention includes but is not limited to the elements identified in the claim (open). 'Consisting of' is closed and means the invention is only what is described.
guidance: 'Comprising' is normally used for mechanical, electrical, software, and method inventions to obtain broader protection. 'Consisting of' is more common in chemical, biotech, and highly unpredictable arts where you want to limit the claim to what you know works; using 'consisting of' narrows the universe of possible prior art but may be appropriate in unpredictable fields.

name: Antecedent (primary/secondary) basis rules
description: The first time you introduce a limitation (element, characteristic, internal reference, etc.) in a patent claim you must introduce it with either 'a' or 'an' (primary antecedent basis). Subsequently refer to the already-introduced limitation by either 'said' or 'the' (secondary antecedent basis).
guidance: This grammar is a term of art in claim drafting and is critical; misuse of 'a/an' vs 'said/the' can create ambiguity or lack proper antecedent basis. Beginners often find this difficult because 'a', 'an', and 'the' are common English words but have precise legal effect in claims.

name: Dependent-claim transitions vs independent transitions
description: Within dependent claims, use 'wherein' when narrowing something already introduced; use 'further comprising' when introducing a new element in the dependent claim.
guidance: Be careful to distinguish whether the dependent claim is adding a new limitation (use language that introduces it) versus further limiting an existing limitation. This affects claim scope and proper incorporation of limitations by reference.

name: Exception for preamble/transition in certain chemical/element claims
description: A preamble and transition should be thought of as absolutely required unless you are claiming a new compound or synthetically created element — extraordinary situations where claims may not have a preamble and/or a transition.
guidance: See cited example patents (e.g., U.S. Patent No. 2,699,054 and 3,161,462) and MPEP 2173(t) for situations where preamble/transition may be omitted; these are exceptional and generally not applicable to ordinary mechanical/electrical/software claims.

name: Scope of discovery (Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(1))
description: Parties may obtain discovery regarding any nonprivileged matter that is relevant to any party's claim or defense, including documents, tangible things, and identity/location of persons having knowledge of discoverable matter.
guidance: Relevant information need not be admissible at trial if discovery appears reasonably calculated to lead to the discovery of admissible evidence. Discovery may be taken as to matters not specifically raised in pleadings and to matters that might serve as the basis for additional claims or defenses, but parties must avoid 'fishing expeditions.'

name: Permissible contents of submissions under 1.114
description: As set forth in 37 CFR 1.114, a submission may include an information disclosure statement, an amendment to the written description, claims, or drawings, new arguments, or new evidence in support of patentability.
guidance: Previously submitted entered arguments after final that were not persuasive may nevertheless be considered a submission under 1.114 if they are responsive within the meaning of 1.111 to the outstanding Office action. If the submission does not comply with 1.111 use form paragraph 7.42.08; if no compliance use 7.42.04 or 7.42.05 depending on context.

name: Proof when inventor refuses to join
description: If refusal to sign is the reason for filing under 37 CFR 1.47, the circumstances of presentation of the application papers and the refusal must be specified in a statement of facts by the person who presented the papers and/or to whom the refusal was made.
guidance: Send a copy of the application papers to the last known address or the inventor’s counsel. Refusal must be shown: for oral refusals, provide who was present, the time and place; statements by someone not present at the refusal will not be accepted. For written refusals, include a copy (redacted if necessary to remove unrelated material). Proof that a bona fide attempt to present the entire application (specification, claims, drawings, oath/declaration) was made may be sufficient. If the applicant concludes refusal occurred, all supporting facts and documentary evidence should be stated and submitted, and any reason given by the inventor should be included.

name: Substantive certifications required by 37 CFR 10.18(b)
description: By presenting any paper to the USPTO the party certifies: (1) all statements of the party’s own knowledge are true and statements on information and belief are believed to be true; and (2) to the best of the party’s knowledge, information and belief formed after a reasonable inquiry that (i) the paper is not presented for an improper purpose, (ii) the claims/legal contentions are warranted by existing law or by a nonfrivolous argument, (iii) allegations/factual contentions have evidentiary support or likely will after reasonable opportunity, and (iv) denials of factual contentions are warranted or reasonably based on a lack of information or belief.
guidance: These certifications mirror Rule 11(b) standards. Parties must conduct an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances before filing. Tolerance exists for allegations made on information and belief but the party has a continuing duty not to persist in unsupported contentions after reasonable opportunity for investigation/discovery.

name: Distinctive character / minimum degree of distinctiveness
description: Assessment whether the sign 'lacks the minimum degree of distinctiveness' for the goods and services concerned and 'is not capable of being perceived as an indication of commercial origin.'
guidance: Consider the sign as a whole; determine whether the relevant public can perceive it as denoting trade origin rather than merely describing kind, contents, purpose or promotional claims. Visual elements (colours, font, background) must be capable of diverting attention from any non-distinctive message to salvage distinctiveness; if they do not, refusal under Article 7(1)(b) follows.

name: Dominant element in complex marks
description: In a complex sign, establish whether any element is dominant for the overall impression; weak or descriptive elements cannot be the dominant element.
guidance: If all elements are descriptive/non-distinctive they share equal value; a proprietor cannot claim dominance for a weak element to establish confusion. Evaluate figurative/word elements for dominance and distinctiveness.

name: Evidence required to prove saturation of prior art for designs
description: To prove saturation of the prior art/state of the market, parties must present clear, precise and coherent evidence (market surveys, trade fair reviews, statements from trade associations, etc.).
guidance: Saturation is a high evidentiary threshold: absence of sufficiently specific evidence undermines claims based on saturation when assessing individual character or novelty of designs.

name: Use of well-known facts and evidence of reputation
description: Well-known facts (e.g., widely known geographic regions, publicised events) and evidence of reputation (sales figures, press articles) are relevant in assessing perception, reputation and likelihood of confusion.
guidance: Require substantiation: claims relying on reputation or well-known facts must be supported by concrete evidence showing the extent and territorial scope of recognition on the filing date.

name: § 104.32 Procedure for requesting indemnification (Employee indemnification)
description: Sets procedures employees must follow when seeking indemnification for civil actions brought against them for actions within scope of employment: upon being served with process, the employee must deliver process and a detailed report to the General Counsel within five calendar days; requests for indemnification must be submitted through supervisory chain and include documentation.
guidance: Required documentation includes copies of verdict/judgment/settlement proposals, explanation of how employee was acting within scope of employment, and statement of other indemnification sources (insurance). Failure to timely satisfy initial requirements may preclude consideration; the procedure references FTCA and DOJ regulations for filing administrative claims.

name: Obviousness-type nonstatutory double patenting (ODP) trigger
description: An obviousness-type nonstatutory double patenting rejection is appropriate where the conflicting claims are not identical, but at least one examined application claim is not patentably distinct from the reference claim(s) because the examined application claim is either anticipated by, or would have been obvious over, the reference claim(s).
guidance: The analysis parallels 35 U.S.C. 103 obviousness determinations (Graham factors). The patent underlying the double patenting rejection is not considered prior art for 103, but the same factual inquiries apply. Form paragraphs (e.g., 8.36, 8.34, 8.35) are available for use depending on whether the reference is a patent or a copending application and whether secondary references are cited.

name: Graham factual inquiries for obviousness-type double patenting
description: Apply the Graham v. John Deere factual inquiries when determining obviousness-type double patenting: (A) determine the scope and content of the patent claim relative to the application claim; (B) determine the differences between the scope and content of the patent claim and the application claim; (C) determine the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; (D) evaluate any objective indicia of nonobviousness.
guidance: The conclusion of obviousness-type double patenting is made in light of these factual determinations. Examiner should articulate these issues when making an ODP rejection.

name: Required explanation in an obviousness-type double patenting rejection
description: Any obviousness-type double patenting rejection should make clear: (A) the differences between the inventions defined by the conflicting claims — a claim in the patent compared to a claim in the application; and (B) the reasons why a person of ordinary skill in the art would conclude that the invention defined in the claim at issue is anticipated by, or would have been an obvious variation of, the invention defined in a claim in the patent.
guidance: Provide explicit rationale tying claim differences to why the application claim is anticipated or an obvious variation. If relying on an obviousness rationale, insert an explanation of the obviousness analysis (bracketed text guidance appears in form paragraphs).

name: Use of the patent disclosure in ODP analysis
description: The disclosure of the patent may not be used as prior art for obviousness; however, the specification can be used as a dictionary to learn the meaning of a claim term and those portions of the specification which provide support for the patent claims may be examined and considered when addressing whether a claim in the application defines an obvious variation of an invention claimed in the patent.
guidance: Only the portion of the patent disclosure that pertains to the invention claimed in the patent supports the patent claims and may be considered. Courts recognize it is difficult to define 'obvious variation' categorically; focus on whether the application claim is an obvious variation of an embodiment disclosed in the patent that supports the patent claim.

name: One-way vs two-way obviousness test
description: If the application at issue is the later filed application or both are filed on the same day, only a one-way determination of obviousness is needed. A two-way test is applied only when the patent is the later filed application and the applicant could not have filed the claims in a single application and there is administrative delay.
guidance: One-way test: consider whether the application claim would have been anticipated by or an obvious variation of the patent claim. Two-way test: apply the Graham analysis twice (application vs patent and patent vs application); an ODP rejection is appropriate only where each analysis compels a conclusion of obviousness. Absent clear administrative delay and inability to have filed claims together, examiners may use the one-way test and shift burden to applicant to show two-way required.

name: Administrative delay and burden to justify two-way test
description: A two-way determination is only appropriate where (A) there was administrative delay on the part of the Office causing delay in prosecution of the earlier-filed application; and (B) applicant could not have filed the conflicting claims in a single (earlier-filed) application.
guidance: If the record does not clearly show administrative delay and inability to have filed claims together, apply one-way test. Courts examine the reasons for delay (applicant-requested extensions, abandonments, appeals, interferences) to decide responsibility for delay. Examples: Berg, Emert, Pierce, General Foods.

name: Conditions for using terminal disclaimers to overcome ODP
description: A timely filed terminal disclaimer in compliance with 37 CFR 1.321(c) or 1.321(d) (and signed per 1.321(b)) may be used to overcome an actual or provisional rejection based on a nonstatutory double patenting ground provided the reference application or patent either is shown to be commonly owned with this application, or claims an invention made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of a joint research agreement.
guidance: USPTO provides terminal disclaimer forms (including eTerminal Disclaimer). The filing date determines which form to use. See MPEP §1490 for guidance regarding terminal disclaimers and withdrawal of ODP rejections when terminal disclaimer is the only remaining rejection. Note limitations (priority/benefit claims under 35 U.S.C. 119 not considered for earlier-filed determination).

name: Common ownership / inventive entity / joint research agreement considerations
description: Nonstatutory double patenting form paragraphs may be used where the patentably indistinct invention is claimed in a patent or copending application that is: (a) by the same inventive entity; or (b) by a different inventive entity and is commonly assigned even though there is no common inventor; or (c) not commonly assigned but has at least one inventor in common; or (d) made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of a joint research agreement (pre-AIA 103 context) ; or (e) under AIA, commonly owned or deemed commonly owned under specified AIA provisions.
guidance: Ensure the proper factual predicate for common ownership or joint research agreement. If file does not establish common ownership at the relevant time, use additional form paragraphs (e.g., 8.28.fti) to resolve priority or benefit issues.

name: Two-way ODP application procedure and consequence
description: When a two-way obviousness determination is required, apply the Graham analysis twice, once with the application claims as the claims in issue, and once with the patent claims as the claims in issue; an obvious-type double patenting rejection is appropriate only where each analysis compels a conclusion that the invention defined in the claims in issue is an obvious variation of the invention defined in a claim in the other application/patent.
guidance: If either analysis does not compel obviousness, no obviousness-type double patenting rejection is made (though other nonstatutory double patenting bases may apply). Use form paragraphs 8.33 and appropriate follow-on paragraphs; document analyses carefully.

name: Priority/benefit claims and determination of earlier-filed application for double patenting
description: Priority or benefit claims under 35 U.S.C. 119(a) and (e) are not taken into account in determining which is the earlier-filed application for double patenting purposes (both for pre-AIA and AIA contexts, as noted).
guidance: Consult MPEP §1490 and the specific AIA/pre-AIA paragraphs for guidance when terminal disclaimers or withdrawal of ODP rejections are at issue; be mindful that benefit claims do not alter the earlier-filed determination used for ODP analysis.

name: Invalidity of independent and dependent claims — separate evaluation
description: There are two types of claims: independent and dependent. An independent claim does not refer to any other claim. A dependent claim refers to at least one other claim and includes all elements of the claim to which it refers.
guidance: You must evaluate the invalidity of each asserted claim separately. Even if an independent claim is invalid, dependent claims that depend from it are not automatically invalid — each claim must be considered separately. However, if you find a dependent claim invalid, then you must find the independent claim from which it depends invalid as well because the dependent claim includes all elements of the independent claim. (Citations: Comaper v. Antec; Callaway v. Acushnet; Ormco v. Align Tech.)

name: Person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA)
description: Invalidity of a patent claim is determined from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art in the field of the claimed invention as of the [time of the invention/effective filing date].
guidance: Prior art must be evaluated from the perspective of that person of ordinary skill as of the relevant date. (Citations: 35 U.S.C. §103; KSR v. Teleflex; Continental Can v. Monsanto.)

name: Anticipation (novelty) — single-reference requirement
description: To anticipate a claim, each element in the claim must be present in a single item of prior art and arranged or combined in the same way as recited in the claim. You may not combine two or more items of prior art to find anticipation.
guidance: In determining whether every element is found in the prior publication/patent/etc., consider what a person of ordinary skill would have understood from review of that reference. If inherency is alleged, instruct the jury on inherency. (Citations: NetMoneyIN v. Verisign; Toro v. Deere; Schering v. Geneva.)

name: Prior public knowledge (pre-AIA) — criterion
description: [The Defendant] contends that claim ___ is invalid because the invention was publicly known by others in the United States before [§102(a) (pre-AIA) Cutoff Date].
guidance: That claim is invalid if the invention was publicly known by others in the U.S. before it was invented by the patentee. If date of invention or priority date is disputed, instruct jury how to determine Cutoff Date. (Citations: 35 U.S.C. §102(a) (pre-AIA); Minnesota Mining v. Chemque; Ecolochem v. S. Cal. Edison.)

name: Ready for patenting / Reduction to practice
description: An invention is ready for patenting when there is reason to believe it would work for its intended purpose. It is ready when (1) reduced to practice, or (2) inventor has prepared drawings/descriptions sufficient to allow a person of ordinary skill to make or use the invention. An invention is reduced to practice when (1) constructed or performed within scope of the patent claims, and (2) determined that it works for its intended purpose.
guidance: This 'ready for patenting' standard applies to public use and on-sale bar analyses. (Citations: Cooper v. Goldfarb; Grain Processing; Moleculon Research.)

name: Experimental use exception
description: [The Plaintiff] contends that __ should not be considered a prior public use or placing the invention on sale because that use/sale was experimental.
guidance: Activities are experimental if a legitimate effort to test claimed features or determine if invention works for intended purpose; primary purpose must be experimentation. Only experimentation by or under control of the inventor (or assignee) qualifies; experimentation by a third party for its own purposes does not. Experimentation must relate to claimed features and technological improvement, not commercial exploitation; incidental profit is permissible. A test done primarily for marketing is not experimental. If defendant shows it is highly probable there was a prior public use/sale, burden shifts to plaintiff to show experimental purpose and, if convincing, the jury may find no prior public use/sale. (Citations: City of Elizabeth v. Nicholson Pavement; Clock Spring; Lisle; Allen Eng'g; LaBounty.)

name: Printed publication — accessibility and enablement
description: [The Defendant] contends that claim ___ is invalid because the invention was described in a printed publication before the relevant cutoff date.
guidance: A printed publication must have been maintained in tangible form (printed pages, electronic file, microfilm, photos, Internet publication, photocopies) and sufficiently accessible to persons interested and ordinarily skilled. Disclosure must be complete enough to enable one of ordinary skill to use the invention without undue experimentation. Information is publicly accessible if distributed or otherwise made available such that persons interested and of ordinary skill exercising reasonable diligence can locate it. Issued patents and published patent applications are printed publications. If accessibility is disputed, give additional instruction on accessibility. (Citations: 35 U.S.C. §102(a),(b) pre-AIA; §102(a)(1),(a)(2) AIA; In re NTP; In re Lister; Kyocera Wireless.)

name: Diagnostic methods practised on the human or animal body are excluded (Article 52(4)/53(c))
description: Article 52(4) EPC (now Article 53(c)) excludes from patentability methods for treatment by surgery or therapy and diagnostic methods practised on the human or animal body.
guidance: The Enlarged Board previously clarified the exclusion of diagnostic methods in G-1/04; applicants and examiners should treat diagnostic methods practised on the body as potentially excluded subject-matter unless claims are specifically drafted to avoid that.

name: Claims can be construed/drafted to avoid excluded subject-matter if essential features are explicitly specified
description: It is possible for a patent claim to be construed in a manner that avoids subject-matter excluded from patent protection provided that the claims 'explicitly specify all of the essential features needed to define the invention.'
guidance: Applicants may present/amend claims to omit or avoid the surgical/therapeutic/diagnostic step, but disclosure rules (requirement to disclose all essential features) will limit how far applicants can strip out excluded steps without losing support/validity. See EBoA confirmation of this principle (G-1/04).

name: Phase 2 - Prior Art Search (Days 3-10)
description: Conduct a professional search of patents and non-patent literature in the relevant field.
guidance: Search report should identify the 5-10 closest references with detailed analysis of which claim elements each one discloses. (Timing: Days 3-10.)

name: Phase 3 - Claim Strategy (Days 10-12)
description: Decide overall claim strategy based on the search results.
guidance: Decisions should address: what is the broadest claim scope that distinguishes over the closest art; the key narrowing dimensions for dependent claims; what claim types (method, system, apparatus, CRM) make sense; and the overall portfolio architecture (single filing vs. a family of filings). (Timing: Days 10-12.)

name: Phase 4 - Independent Claim Drafting (Days 12-15)
description: Draft multiple independent claims of varying scope.
guidance: Draft 3-4 independent claims. The broadest is the 'moonshot'; the narrowest is the 'picture claim'. Cross-check each independent claim against the closest art to confirm distinguishing elements. (Timing: Days 12-15.)

name: Phase 5 - Dependent Claims (Days 15-18)
description: Create a ladder of dependent claims that narrow the independent claims across different dimensions.
guidance: Build a claim ladder that systematically narrows on different dimensions. Each rung should be independently meaningful and not a trivial restatement. (Timing: Days 15-18.)

name: Phase 6 - Specification Drafting (Days 18-30)
description: Draft the specification by describing figures, interactions, alternatives, and ensuring support for claim terms.
guidance: Walk through the figures one at a time; describe what each shows, how the components interact, and what alternatives exist. Ensure every claim term has antecedent support in the spec. Include 'in some embodiments' framings throughout. (Timing: Days 18-30.)

name: Phase 8 - Senior attorney review for legal sufficiency (Days 30-35)
description: Have a senior attorney review the draft for legal sufficiency and prosecution robustness.
guidance: Senior attorney should check claim scope, support in the spec, prosecution strategy, and litigation considerations. (Timing: Days 30-35.)

name: Review checklist — antecedent basis
description: Verify antecedent basis for claim terms.
guidance: Run through checklist to ensure every claim term has proper antecedent support in the specification and consistent introduction/definition.

name: Review checklist — consistent terminology
description: Ensure consistent terminology across claims and specification.
guidance: Confirm the same term is used consistently and synonyms are avoided where they would create ambiguity.

name: Review checklist — claim ladder
description: Confirm the claim ladder is systematic and meaningful.
guidance: Check dependent claims form a logical ladder that narrows across different dimensions rather than repeating the same limitation.

name: Review checklist — embodiment count
description: Assess number and variety of embodiments disclosed.
guidance: Ensure multiple embodiments and variations are described to support broad claim scope and alternatives.

name: Review checklist — no patent profanity
description: Remove or avoid 'patent profanity' in the specification or claims.
guidance: Ensure language that could unduly limit claim scope or introduce admissions (so-called 'patent profanity') is identified and corrected.

name: Phase 9 - Filing (Day 35)
description: File the application electronically and submit required documents.
guidance: File electronically through Patent Center. Submit specification, claims, abstract, drawings, oath/declaration, application data sheet, and IDS. Pay filing fees. (Timing: Day 35.)

name: Quality Checks Throughout
description: Ongoing evaluative questions to apply at every phase of the workflow.
guidance: At each phase, ask: does this still distinguish over the closest art? does the spec still support the claims? would I be comfortable with this in litigation? does this leave room for design-around?

name: Weight to accord rebuttal evidence
description: Evidence presented in a timely manner should not be ignored but need not be accorded the same weight; examiners must determine the relative weight of rebuttal evidence (e.g., nexus, commensurateness with the claimed invention). An obviousness rejection should be made or maintained only if evidence of obviousness outweighs evidence of nonobviousness.
guidance: Consider whether a nexus exists between the claimed invention and the proffered evidence and whether the evidence is commensurate in scope with the claimed invention. The standard is the 'preponderance of the evidence' (see MPEP §706). The mere presence of some credible rebuttal evidence does not automatically require withdrawal of an obviousness rejection. See MPEP §716.01(d).

name: Presumption of nexus and nexus requirement
description: A presumption of nexus may arise where marketed products are coextensive with the claims, but coextensiveness alone does not decide the overall nexus question; objective evidence lacks nexus if it exclusively relates to a feature 'known in the prior art.'
guidance: Evaluate nexus using MPEP §716.01(b) guidance. When secondary considerations are tied only to an element that the prior art disclosed, nexus may be lacking. Case example: Yita LLC v. MacNeil IP LLC (Fed. Cir. 2023) — Board's presumption and nexus findings reversed when nexus rested on legal errors. Ensure secondary consideration evidence is linked to the claimed invention as a whole, not solely to a feature known in the prior art. See Rambus v. Rea and WBIP v. Kohler guidance.

name: Physical combinability not required to combine references
description: A determination of obviousness based on multiple references does not require actual physical substitution of elements; the test is whether the combined teachings would have suggested the claimed invention to a PHOSITA.
guidance: Cite In re Mouttet, In re Etter, In re Keller, In re Sneed, In re Nievelt. However, the claimed combination cannot change the principle of operation of the primary reference or render it inoperable for its intended purpose (see MPEP §2143.01 VI).

name: Do not import unclaimed limitations from the specification into claims
description: Although claims are interpreted in light of the specification, limitations from the specification are not read into the claims unless compelled by the intrinsic record.
guidance: Do not construe claims to include specification-only limitations absent clear evidence that the patentee intended those limitations to define the claim scope. Case examples: In re Van Geuns; Constant v. AMD; Ex parte McCullough. See MPEP §§2111–2116.01 for claim interpretation law.

name: Teaching away doctrine — nature and weight matter
description: A prior art reference that 'teaches away' from the claimed invention is significant evidence in determining obviousness, but the substance and degree of the teaching away must be weighed; mere preference does not equal teaching away.
guidance: Assess whether the prior art criticizes, discredits, or discourages the claimed solution. References that merely disclose multiple alternatives or express general preference do not necessarily teach away. Case examples: In re Gurley; In re Fulton; UCB v. Actavis; Schwendimann v. Neenah. If references expressly teach away from combination, combining them may be improper (see In re Grasselli).

name: Proceeding contrary to accepted wisdom can indicate nonobviousness
description: When the claimed approach proceeds contrary to accepted wisdom in the art, that fact is evidence supporting nonobviousness.
guidance: Consider totality of prior art; known disadvantages that would discourage searching for new inventions may be relevant. Case example: In re Hedges; United States v. Adams.

name: Burden of disclosure and duties for applications with related foreign filings or joint inventors
description: Applicants who combine subject matter from related applications or name joint inventors must disclose invention dates and common ownership information under 37 CFR 1.56; absent contrary evidence, examiners assume compliance with duty of disclosure.
guidance: Foreign applicants combining related applications should provide invention dates and ownership information to enable examiner consideration of potential 103(a) rejections based on 102(f)/(g). For inventions not commonly owned at the time of invention, claims in a single application are not shielded from 103(a) rejections based on that prior art. See MPEP §2146.01.

name: Complete applications (nonprovisional and provisional)
description: Complete applications (nonprovisional and provisional)
guidance: Defines what constitutes a complete provisional or nonprovisional application (e.g., required parts such as specification, claims where applicable, drawings, fees, oath/declaration or application data). See chapter for filing completeness consequences and processing.

name: Handling missing pages, claims, drawings, specifications
description: Missing pages, claims, drawings specifications
guidance: Policies for addressing missing or incomplete parts of an application (e.g., how missing pages or omitted claims/drawings are treated, correction procedures, time limits).

name: Claims: format, numbering, and statutory requirements
description: Claims format, numbering, and statutory requirements
guidance: Standards for claim drafting including proper format, sequential numbering, statutory subject matter, definite language, antecedent basis, and formal requirements.

name: Dependent claim structures
description: Dependent claim structures
guidance: Rules governing dependent claims (proper dependency, incorporation of limitations, multiple dependent claim restrictions, and proper referencing).

name: Drawings: completeness and consistency standards
description: Completeness and consistency standards
guidance: Requirements that drawings be complete and consistent with the specification and claims (all elements shown when necessary, consistency of reference numerals and figures).

name: New matter restrictions
description: New matter restrictions
guidance: Prohibition against introducing new matter into the specification/claims after filing and procedures for determining whether an amendment adds new matter.

name: Obviousness-type double patenting (nonstatutory double patenting)
description: Under U.S. law, an inventor, patent owner or joint researchers may obtain more than one patent with claims that vary in only minor (patentably indistinct) ways from each other. The USPTO will reject such claims under “obviousness-type double patenting” (also known as “nonstatutory double patenting”).
guidance: The Office will allow claims to issue only as long as the practice of obtaining similar claims across patents isn’t used to extend the patent exclusivity term or allow multiple parties to harass an alleged infringer. This standard is intended to balance incentivizing innovation while providing certainty to competitors and the public.

name: Proposed third condition for terminal disclaimers (enforceability requirement)
description: To overcome double patenting the patentee would need to agree that the patent with the terminal disclaimer will be enforceable only if the patent is not tied and has never been tied through one or more terminal disclaimers to a patent in which any claim has been finally held unpatentable or invalid over prior art.
guidance: This new enforceability condition is intended to reduce the cost of separately challenging each patent in a group of multiple patents directed to indistinct variations of a single invention, streamline and expedite patent disputes, narrow validity issues, and provide greater certainty to competitors and the public. The precise scope and application would be defined in the final rulemaking.

name: Burden and standard of proof for internet and other disclosures
description: Who must prove a disclosure and what standards apply: (Egypt) In court cases one must provide a written document as evidence of prior art disclosure and there are no specific rules for internet evidence. (Finland) A party claiming a disclosure has occurred should carry the burden of proof; evidence principles should remain technology-neutral.
guidance: When alleging an internet disclosure, be prepared to show contemporaneous, reliable evidence (archived pages, timestamps, logs). Courts may be skeptical of unaudited digital evidence because of ease of manipulation.

name: Utility patent components
description: A utility patent consists of a cover page listing administrative information, a written description (specification and drawings), and one or more claims that define the metes and bounds of the exclusive rights.
guidance: Cover page includes abstract and representative drawing; claims set the owner's exclusive rights; the specification must enable public practice after expiration.

name: Claims must 'particularly and distinctly' define invention (35 U.S.C. §112)
description: Claims must particularly and distinctly define the subject matter regarded as the invention; they set the metes and bounds of the patent owner's exclusive rights.
guidance: Claims can be independent, dependent, or multiple dependent; drafting skill is critical; punctuation rule: one period only at end of the claim sentence.

name: Applicant as lexicographer / claim term definition
description: An inventor and drafter may act as their own lexicographer and give words uncommon meanings, but the application must define words used in an uncommon manner.
guidance: Certain words retain fixed legal effect (e.g., 'comprising' = open, 'consisting of' = closed).

name: Claim scope (broad vs narrow) and organization
description: Claims vary in scope: broad claims include fewer limitations and cover broader subject matter; claims are often arranged from broadest to narrowest.
guidance: Use independent claims for self-contained scope and dependent claims to add limitations and fallback positions; multiple dependent claims refer back to two or more claims.

name: Filing requirements and filing date rules (35 U.S.C. §111)
description: A nonprovisional application that can mature into a patent consists of a specification, drawings if necessary, an oath/declaration, and required filing fees; the filing date is when the specification and drawings (if necessary) and at least one claim are received (or deposited by Express Mail under certain conditions).
guidance: Certain formal defects can be corrected later (possibly with fees); provisional applications have different (lesser) requirements and are not examined or maturing.

name: Oath or declaration contents
description: The oath/declaration must be signed by the actual inventor(s) and state that the signer has reviewed the specification, believes they are the original and first inventor of the claimed subject matter, and acknowledges the duty to disclose material information.
guidance: If inventor dead/incapacitated or refuses to sign, limited alternatives exist under rules (37 C.F.R.).

name: Restriction/election requirements
description: If an application claims more than one invention, the examiner can require restriction (inventions clearly different) or election of species (related inventions with generic claim); applicant must elect one invention for prosecution.
guidance: For non-elected inventions, applicant may file divisional applications; election requirement can affect prosecution strategy.

name: Continuation, continuation-in-part, and divisional practice
description: Applicants may file continuation, continuation-in-part, or divisional applications to pursue non-elected claims or to continue prosecution with altered claim scope or added subject matter.
guidance: Continuations keep the benefit of earlier filing dates for common subject matter; CIPs add new matter with different priority consequences.

name: Prosecution history and prosecution history estoppel
description: Statements and amendments made during prosecution form the prosecution history and can estop the patentee from later asserting claim scope under doctrines like prosecution history estoppel.
guidance: Amendments narrowing claims for patentability reasons can limit doctrine of equivalents scope.

name: Literal infringement and doctrine of equivalents
description: Infringement can be literal (accused product/practice meets all claim limitations) or under the doctrine of equivalents (accused product/function is equivalent despite not literally meeting limitations).
guidance: Tests include function-way-result and hypothetical claim analyses; range/reverse doctrine of equivalents and limits exist; prosecution history estoppel can restrict equivalents.

name: Priority, foreign priority, and international procedures
description: Priority rules govern filing dates, including foreign priority claims and use of Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) and provisional applications for priority benefit.
guidance: Provisional applications provide a priority date but do not mature into patents; GATT/NAFTA/other treaty implementations affect terms and filing practice.

name: Claim drafting formalities and drafting advice
description: Claims should be drafted with attention to form (one period at end), choice of open vs closed claim language ('comprising' vs 'consisting of'), and a hierarchy of claims from broad to narrow; skilled claim-drafting resources and treatises exist.
guidance: Claims drafting is a specialized skill; many reference texts and training exist; changes in number/form of claims can trigger fees and prosecution consequences.

name: Basis for imposing restriction
description: The claims of an application may properly be required to be restricted to one of two or more claimed inventions only if they are able to support separate patents and they are either independent or distinct.
guidance: References MPEP §§ 802.01, 806.06, 808.01 for 'independent' and MPEP § 806.05–§ 806.05(j) for 'distinct'. The examiner must consider whether separate patents could be supported for the claimed inventions before requiring restriction.

name: Prima facie showing of serious examination burden (how to show)
description: A serious examination burden may be prima facie shown by appropriate explanation of non-prior-art issues under 35 U.S.C. 101, pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, and/or 35 U.S.C. 112(a) relevant to one invention that are not relevant to the other invention.
guidance: Identify substantive statutory issues unique to one claimed invention (e.g., 101 eligibility, written description, enablement) to demonstrate examination burden.

name: Markush claims: provisional election permissible
description: When examining a Markush claim, the examiner may generally require a provisional election of species from among patentably indistinct species or patentably indistinct groups of species. The applicant’s election serves as a starting point for the search and examination of the claim.
guidance: See MPEP § 2117 for determination of proper Markush grouping and for improper grouping rejections; both an election requirement and an improper grouping rejection may apply.

name: When to require provisional election for Markush claims
description: If a claim that includes a Markush grouping reads on two or more patentably distinct inventions, a provisional election of species requirement may be made at the examiner’s discretion, except if members are few or so closely related that search/exam can be made without serious burden.
guidance: Do not require election between species that are not patentably distinct or when the Markush group is proper and causes no serious burden. Avoid inviting applicant to elect a group that would be clearly rejectable as improper or under 35 U.S.C. 112(a).

name: Prohibition on requiring limitation of proper Markush group absent patentability rejection
description: An examiner may not seek to require an applicant to limit the scope of a claim directed to a proper Markush group to a subset of species that falls within the scope of the claim in the absence of a rejection of the claim for not complying with patentability requirements.
guidance: Do not use Ex parte Quayle actions or Notices of Non-Responsive Amendment to force such limitations without a patentability rejection.

name: Transitional application refunds when linking/generic claim allowable
description: Whenever divided inventions in a transitional application are rejoined because a linking claim or a generic claim is allowable and applicant paid the fee for the additional invention/species, applicant should be notified that he or she may request a refund of the fee paid.
guidance: Use MPEP §§ 806.04(d), 821.04, and § 821.04(a) to determine when nonelected species are no longer withdrawn from consideration.

name: Tie reasonable royalty to claimed invention's marketplace footprint
description: Reasonable royalty determination must be tied to the claimed invention's footprint in the marketplace and is typically determined by a hypothetical negotiation between a willing licensor and willing licensee.
guidance: Hypothetical negotiation is determined at the time just before infringement began and is based on the assumption that the patent is valid and infringed (ResQNet.com; Lucent Technologies). The royalty typically equals a specified royalty rate applied to a royalty base; counsel must ensure the rate and base correspond.

name: Smallest Saleable Patent‑Practicing Unit (SSU)
description: General rule: royalties should be based on the SSU to limit compensation for non‑infringing components; counsel must understand claimed invention because it may broadly relate to different potential SSUs.
guidance: If EMVR does not apply, identify SSU, then determine whether patented feature has value beyond SSU and apportion accordingly. In negotiation, licensor may propose a larger base if factual support exists that patented feature impacts multiple components (Fractus v. Samsung).

name: Negotiation‑specific risk discounts (invalidity/non‑infringement/business)
description: In negotiations, the reasonable royalty should be discounted by the risk that the patents are invalid or not infringed and other business considerations.
guidance: Risk expressed between 0% (clear invalidity or missing claim element) and 100% (no possibility of invalidity and all claim elements practiced). Assign risk ranges by understanding potential litigation challenges, file history, and case law. Formula: Reasonable Royalty(Negotiated) = ((Royalty Base) × (Reasonable Royalty Rate)) × Risk of Invalidity × Risk of Non‑infringement × Business Considerations Factor.

name: Decision to reject when amended claim identical to previously-notified rejected claim
description: Where the amended claim is identical to the other claim to which a ground of rejection was notified, a decision to reject shall be made.
guidance: If an amended claim duplicates a claim already notified as containing a ground of rejection, the examiner must make a decision to reject that amended claim (examples in the manual illustrate identical/newly added claims identical to previously-notified indefinite claims).

name: Non-final rejection — scope and triggers
description: A 'non-final rejection' may be issued regardless of voluntary amendments if it is the first notice since the start of examination, where an unamended portion of the specification includes a ground for rejection, or where the ground arises from the description/claims before amendment rather than from the amendment itself.
guidance: Examples: (1) issuing novelty/inventive-step rejection based on pre-amendment claim content even after the claim was amended; (2) notifying additional inventions within a single claim in stages — subsequent notifications are non-final; (3) ex-officio re-examination and remanded applications have special rules resulting in non-final notices in certain circumstances. Examiner should issue non-final when grounds are not necessitated by amendments.

name: Final rejection necessitated by amendment — definition and prerequisites
description: A final rejection necessitated by amendment is issued where the ground for rejection arises from amendments made in response to a previously issued notice of rejection; prerequisites include that written amendments were submitted and a new ground of rejection was incurred because of the amendment.
guidance: Specific examples: (1) amendments adding new matter or exceeding scope (divisional/converted); (2) amendments that introduce elements causing lack of novelty or inventive step (requiring new prior art search); (3) newly added claims or claims changed equivalent to new additions that contain novelty/inventive-step problems. If an amended claim equals another claim never notified for rejection, issue non-final instead.

name: Purpose of claim-by-claim examination
description: An examiner examines an application on a claim-by-claim basis to ensure that when notifying grounds of rejection for multi-claim applications, specific claims and reasons are identified so applicants can identify which claims are remediable.
guidance: The aim is to avoid vague, application-level rejections that make it hard for applicants to know what to amend or delete to preserve patentable subject matter.

name: Written notice component: 'Relevant Provisions regarding Grounds for Rejection'
description: 'Relevant Provisions regarding Grounds for Rejection' specifies claims containing the grounds for rejection and the relevant statutory provisions; if the ground is not directly related to claims, state the matters containing the ground.
guidance: If an amendment adds new matter or exceeds scope in a divisional/converted application, those newly added or excluded matters must be stated as grounds for rejection here.

name: Written notice component: 'Specific Grounds for Rejection' — specificity requirements
description: 'Specific Grounds for Rejection' must set out more specific reasons for the matters notified as grounds for rejection so applicants can respond effectively.
guidance: Requirements include: (①) state grounds per claim (can group to avoid redundancy); ② indicate which parts of prior art are used in comparison and select closest prior art; ③ specify prior art references and describe differences and inventive-step assessment in an understandable way; ④ separate grounds for independent and dependent claims and include dependent-claim grounds; ⑤ prepare (when helpful) a component comparison table mapping claimed features to prior-art features and supply examiner assessment and common general knowledge reasoning.

name: Preparation of written decision to reject — structure
description: A written decision to reject is prepared similarly to a written notice of grounds for rejection, except entries reflect 'matters where the ground for rejection is not overcome' and relevant statutory provisions for those matters; sections include Claims to be Examined, Relevant Provisions for Matters Where Grounds Not Overcome, Patentable Claims, Grounds for Decision to Reject, and Considerations in Amendment Submission.
guidance: If no written argument or amendment was submitted in response to prior notice, an examiner may omit separate 'Examination Results' and 'Rationale for Decision to Reject' sections. Newly added claims identical to previously-notified rejected claims are considered an opportunity to have argued and are listed as matters where rejection grounds are not overcome.

name: Grounds for Decision to Reject — level of explanation
description: 'Grounds for Decision to Reject' must state specific rationale for grounds not overcome and explain why applicant's amendments or arguments do not overcome the rejection.
guidance: When both written arguments and amendments are submitted, the examiner must explain why the amendment fails and why arguments are denied. For claims without practical amendments or dependent claims without direct amendment, a short statement that the previously-notified ground is not overcome may suffice.

name: Disclosure of evidence standard
description: If a party presents reasonable evidence sufficient to support its claims that necessary documents or information (relating to liability, quantum of damages or validity) are under the control of the opposing party or a third party, the court may order disclosure of the relevant material, with protective measures for confidential information.
guidance: Use disclosure orders when documentary evidence is in the control of the opponent or third parties; anticipate confidentiality protocols and protective measures.

name: Claim interpretation principles
description: Principles governing how claims are to be interpreted in examination and litigation.
guidance: Covers jurisdictional claim construction practices (e.g., USPTO broadest reasonable interpretation, EPO problem-solution approach implications, written description considerations). Emphasis on understanding how different offices construe claim scope to draft appropriately.

name: Independent and dependent claim structures
description: Correct form and structure for independent and dependent claims.
guidance: Fundamentals of drafting claim sets, how to structure dependencies, appropriate scope allocation between independent and dependent claims, and exercises to practice drafting proper claim chains.

name: Specification writing for enablement and written description
description: Drafting the specification to meet enablement and written description requirements.
guidance: Emphasizes providing sufficient disclosure to enable the invention and to support claimed subject-matter; ties to common pitfalls such as insufficient enablement and lack of written description support.

name: Drawing requirements
description: Requirements and best practices for patent drawings.
guidance: Covers formal drawing requirements and how drawings should support claims and specification; practice exercises to produce drawings complying with various offices' rules.

name: PCT international filing strategy
description: Strategic considerations for filing under the PCT and managing international prosecution.
guidance: Covers timing, claim drafting choices for international protection, and how PCT practice affects later national phase prosecution.

name: Ambiguous claim language
description: Avoidance of ambiguous or unclear wording in claims.
guidance: Identify examples of ambiguous language, practical exercises to rewrite ambiguous claims into precise language, and explanation of how ambiguity leads to rejections or narrow interpretation.

name: Missing antecedent basis
description: Ensuring terms in claims have proper antecedent basis.
guidance: Teach detection and correction of missing antecedent references to prevent indefiniteness and support issues.

name: Improper transitional phrases
description: Use of correct transitional phrasing (e.g., 'comprising', 'consisting of').
guidance: Explain the legal effect of transitional phrases and common mistakes that unintentionally broaden or limit claim scope.

name: Insufficient enablement
description: Avoiding failure to provide enough disclosure to enable the claimed invention.
guidance: Practical exercises demonstrating adequate experimental detail, ranges, and examples to meet enablement across jurisdictions.

name: Lack of written description support
description: Ensuring claims are supported by the specification's written description.
guidance: Training to match claim scope to what is described and to avoid added-matter and written-description rejections.

name: Improper means-plus-function language
description: Avoiding or correctly drafting means-plus-function claim language.
guidance: Explain when means-plus-function is interpreted narrowly to the disclosed structure/acts and how to draft alternatives to prevent unintended limitation.

name: Patent profanity (limiting language)
description: Avoiding inadvertent limiting language that constrains claim scope.
guidance: Identify 'patent profanity' examples and demonstrate rewriting to preserve appropriate scope; emphasize common wording that introduces unintended limitations.

name: Inconsistent terminology between specification and claims
description: Maintain consistent terms and definitions across specification and claims.
guidance: Exercises to standardize terminology, prevent mismatch that can cause interpretation problems or lack of support.

name: AI/software invention drafting
description: Approaches to drafting inventions in AI and software domains.
guidance: Covers particular challenges for software/AI (e.g., technical character, functional claiming, examples, and support) and best practices to improve patentability.

name: Practice-oriented outcome: draft all-important claims
description: Skill in drafting claims that effectively define and protect inventions.
guidance: Focus on drafting claims that balance breadth and support, include dependent claim strategies, and align with prosecution strategy.

name: Practice-oriented outcome: adapt drafting style across jurisdictions
description: Skill in tailoring applications to the expectations of different patent offices.
guidance: Training to adapt language, claim formats, and disclosures to anticipate and avoid office-specific objections and rejections.

name: Practice-oriented outcome: anticipate common rejection patterns
description: Ability to foresee likely examination rejections and draft to reduce them.
guidance: Includes learning common rejection patterns per jurisdiction and drafting tactics to mitigate such risks (e.g., claim amendments, support, and argument strategies).

name: Certification and signature obligations (37 CFR 10.18 / 1.4)
description: By presenting any paper to the USPTO (signing, filing, submitting, or later advocating), the party certifies: (1) statements of own knowledge are true, statements on information and belief are believed to be true, and false statements are punishable under 18 U.S.C. 1001; and (2) to the best of the party’s knowledge, information and belief, formed after reasonable inquiry, the paper is not for an improper purpose; claims/legal contentions are warranted by existing law or by nonfrivolous argument for change; factual contentions have evidentiary support or likely will after reasonable investigation; denials are warranted on the evidence or reasonably based on lack of information or belief.
guidance: 37 CFR 10.18(a)-(c) and related discussion. Violations may jeopardize validity/enforceability of application/patent and may lead to sanctions including holding facts established, returning papers, precluding filing/presentation, monetary sanctions, terminal disclaimers, or terminating proceedings. Practitioners may also face disciplinary action. The 'reasonable inquiry' standard tracks Fed. R. Civ. P. 11: reasonableness depends on time available and probability more investigation will uncover important evidence; does not create duty to perform a prior art search before filing an application. OED handles determinations of violations and possible practitioner discipline.

name: Prima facie case of equivalence
description: If the examiner finds that a prior art element (A) performs the function specified in the claim, (B) is not excluded by any explicit definition provided in the specification for an equivalent, and (C) is an equivalent of the means- (or step-) plus-function limitation, the examiner should provide an explanation and rationale in the Office action as to why the prior art element is an equivalent.
guidance: Include explanation and rationale in the Office action (see In re Bond). If the examiner shows at least one of the supporting factors for equivalence (see MPEP § 2183), conclude the claimed limitation is met by the prior art element. The examiner should also demonstrate, where appropriate, why it would have been obvious to substitute applicant’s described structure, material, or acts for that described in the prior art reference (see In re Brown).

name: Even if nonequivalence shown, examiner must consider obviousness (35 U.S.C. 103)
description: If applicant shows that the prior art element is not an equivalent, the examiner must still make a 35 U.S.C. 103 analysis to determine if the claimed means- (or step-) plus-function would have been obvious from the prior art to one of ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: A finding of nonequivalence prevents anticipation but does not prevent a determination of obviousness. Apply 102/103 rejections where appropriate (including when balance of claim limitations are anticipated by the prior art).

name: Applicant may bear burden when specification is silent about equivalents
description: Where the specification is silent as to what constitutes equivalents and the examiner has made out a prima facie case of equivalence, the burden is placed upon the applicant to show that a prior art element which performs the claimed function is not an equivalent of the structure, material, or acts disclosed in the specification.
guidance: Applicant reasons may include: (A) teachings in the applicant’s specification that particular prior art is not equivalent; (B) teachings in the prior art reference that tend to show nonequivalence; (C) 37 CFR 1.132 affidavit evidence of facts tending to show nonequivalence (see In re Noll, Hybritech).

name: Interpretation of limitations must be consistent with the specification
description: When the applicant relies on teachings in the applicant’s own specification, the examiner must ensure the applicant is interpreting the means- (or step-) plus-function limitation consistent with the disclosure in the specification; if the specification defines what is meant by the limitation for the purposes of the claimed invention, the examiner should interpret the limitation as having that meaning.
guidance: If no definition is provided use judgment to determine scope. The scope of equivalents depends on how the element is described; a claim may be limited to particular structure/material/acts or may embrace equivalents, depending on the disclosure (see NOMOS, Ishida). Avoid reading limitations broader or narrower than the specification supports.

name: Equivalence requires performance of the identical function
description: Unless an element performs the identical function specified in the claim, it cannot be an equivalent for the purposes of 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA 112 sixth paragraph.
guidance: Use Pennwalt and related authority. First establish identity of function, then examine 'way' and 'result' indicia; there is no single litmus test for equivalence—use multiple indicia from MPEP § 2183.

name: Mere allegations of nonequivalence are insufficient
description: A bare statement or opinion by applicant that the element shown in the prior art is not an equivalent is not persuasive; the examiner should consider and weigh indicia and evidence presented and determine whether, on balance, the applicant has met the burden of proof.
guidance: If applicant argues limitation is limited to specific characteristics not described in the specification, the claim should not be allowed until amended to recite those specific structural or additional functional characteristics. Examiner should require factual or documentary support (see MPEP § 2184, In re Fitzgerald, Swinehart).

name: Applicant may amend claims to avoid equivalence
description: Applicant may amend claims during prosecution to (1) further limit the function so there is no longer identity of function with the prior art element, or (2) replace the means- (or step-) plus-function limitation with specific structure, material or acts that are not described in the prior art.
guidance: Advise applicant of these options when appropriate; amendments may resolve 112(f) or prior art issues.

name: Relationship to the doctrine of equivalents (DOE)
description: DOE arises in infringement litigation; in determining equivalence under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) during examination, decisions involving the DOE should be considered but should not unduly influence the 112(f) determination.
guidance: The essential inquiry is whether a substitute matches the function, way, and result of the claimed element (Warner-Jenkinson). But 112(f) applies a restrictive role—limit broad functional language to corresponding structure described in the specification and equivalents thereof; treat DOE precedent as informative but not controlling for ex parte examination (see MPEP § 2186).

name: Three-prong test for invoking 35 U.S.C. 112(f) and rebuttable presumptions
description: A claim limitation meets the three-prong test and will be interpreted under 112(f) when: (A) the limitation uses the term 'means' or 'step' or a generic placeholder substitute; (B) the placeholder is modified by functional language (typically linked by 'for' or similar); and (C) the placeholder is not modified by sufficient structure, material, or acts for performing the claimed function.
guidance: Use this test in form paragraph 7.30.05. The use of 'means' creates a rebuttable presumption that 112(f) applies; absence of 'means' creates a rebuttable presumption that 112(f) does not apply. The presumptions are rebutted when claim language establishes sufficient structure/material/acts or conversely recites only function without sufficient structure.

name: Invoking 112(f) despite absence of the word 'means' (form ¶7.30.06)
description: Claims that do not use 'means' may nonetheless be interpreted under 112(f) when they use a generic placeholder coupled with functional language without reciting sufficient structure to perform the recited function and the generic placeholder is not preceded by a structural modifier.
guidance: Identify such claim limitations and inform applicant. If applicant does not intend such an interpretation, they may amend the limitation to recite sufficient structure or show that sufficient structure is present. Use form paragraph 7.30.06 once in an Office action where applicable and identify the claim/limitations involved.

name: Not invoking 112(f) despite presence of 'means' (form ¶7.30.07)
description: A claim limitation that uses 'means' or 'step' may nonetheless not be interpreted under 112(f) when the limitation recites sufficient structure, materials, or acts to entirely perform the recited function.
guidance: Identify such limitations and inform applicant. If applicant intends 112(f) treatment, they may amend to remove the structure/materials/acts or show lack of sufficient structure. Use form paragraph 7.30.07 once in an Office action where applicable and identify the claim/limitations involved.

name: Remedies when disclosure of corresponding structure is lacking or not clearly linked (form ¶7.34.23)
description: When disclosure of the structure, material, or acts for performing the function recited in a claim is lacking, insufficient, or not clearly linked, the examiner should suggest remedies such as: (a) amending the written description to expressly recite corresponding structure/material/acts and clearly link them to the claimed function without new matter; or (b) stating on the record what corresponding structure/material/acts, implicitly or inherently set forth in the specification, perform the claimed function.
guidance: In the Office action, specify the limitation invoking 112(f) and explain why disclosure is insufficient (e.g., no structure that performs the function, structure does not perform the entire function, or no association between structure and function). Refer applicant to 37 CFR 1.75(d), MPEP §§ 608.01(o), 2181 for additional guidance.

name: Interpretation of claims (general)
description: Claims should be interpreted for search purposes following the EPO Guidelines.
guidance: Apply Section B-III, 3.2 of the Guidelines for Examination mutatis mutandis. Interpret claims to determine the subject-matter to be searched.

name: Claims with explicit references to description or drawings
description: If claims contain explicit references to features elucidated in the description or drawings, the examiner should search those features as long as they are unambiguously defined by specific parts of the description.
guidance: Explicit references are permissible only where 'absolutely necessary' (cf. GL/PCT-EPO F-IV, 4.17). If reference does not clearly identify which subject-matter is included, the examiner may contact the applicant informally before the search (see GL/PCT-EPO B-VIII, 3.3). For 'omnibus claims' (e.g. 'substantially as herein described') do not request informal clarification and designate the search report as complete. If the reference appears unjustified, raise an objection in the written opinion.

name: Amended claims / incorporated missing parts — general rule
description: There is no right to amend the application until after the international search has been established; the search must be carried out on the transmitted search copy except for permitted corrections.
guidance: Obvious mistakes or formal matters contrary to the PCT called to the applicant's attention by the RO may be corrected (GL/PCT-EPO H-IV). Substantive amendments (reformulation of claims, deletion/limitation of claims, taking subject-matter from description into claims) must be refused at this stage even if called 'corrections'.

name: Anticipation of amendments to claims
description: Anticipate possible amendments to claims when planning/searching.
guidance: Apply Section B-III, 3.5 of the Guidelines for Examination in the EPO mutatis mutandis (GL/ISPE 15.25). Consider how likely amendments could affect search scope.

name: Broad claims
description: Special considerations apply when claims are broad.
guidance: Apply Section B-III, 3.6 of the EPO Guidelines mutatis mutandis (GL/ISPE 15.26). Take care to search the breadth that is meaningfully defined.

name: Combination of elements in a claim
description: Examine and search for combinations of claim elements appropriately.
guidance: Apply Section B-III, 3.9 of the Guidelines mutatis mutandis (GL/ISPE 15.31). Consider likely combinations when selecting prior art.

name: Subject-matter excluded from search
description: The examiner may exclude certain subject-matter from the search where the EPO as ISA is not required to deal with it or where lack of clarity/support prevents meaningful search.
guidance: Exclude subject-matter under Art.17(2)(a) and Rule 39 when appropriate (GL/ISPE 15.33). If clarity/support of description/claims/drawings is so deficient that no meaningful search can be carried out, indicate exclusion and reasons.

name: PCT Direct processing and informal comments
description: Under PCT Direct, applicants claiming priority from an earlier application searched by the EPO may file a PCT Direct letter with informal comments aimed at overcoming earlier search objections; examiner may take these into account.
guidance: Requirements: (a) informal comments filed with RO in specified form, (b) international application claims priority of an earlier application searched by EPO. PCT Direct letters must be self-contained and submitted as a separate PDF document titled 'PCT Direct/informal comments', include marked-up differences if claims/description differ, and be filed in the ways specified. Examiner will acknowledge and address PCT Direct content in the written opinion provided the requirements are met; explicit reference to earlier search opinion only if annexed. PCT Direct letters become public on PATENTSCOPE.

name: Verification of claimed priority date(s) and dates for cited documents
description: Verify claimed priority dates and use correct date references for documents cited in the search report; handle intermediate documents and doubts per Guidelines.
guidance: Apply Section B-VI,5.1–5.3 mutatis mutandis (GL/ISPE 11.02–11.06). Consider documents published after the filing date and Rule 51bis.1(a)(v), Art.55 EPC. Extend search if doubts as to priority validity require redating.

name: Notice of prior use must extend to the entire claimed invention
description: The allegations of the notice must not be limited to one or more of the elements of which the patented art or article consists, but must extend to the entire invention claimed.
guidance: Notice that only points to individual elements is insufficient; notice must cover the whole invention as claimed (see cited authorities such as Evans v. Eaton).

name: Evidence of the state of the art admissible without notice
description: No notice is required in order to admit evidence concerning the state of the art at the date when the inventive act of the patentee is claimed to have been performed.
guidance: State-of-the-art evidence serves to define the exact scope of the alleged invention by comparing prior art to the invention; such evidence may disclose want of novelty but is not excluded for that reason (see Stevenson v. Magowan, Eachus v. Broomall).

name: Superiority of a property shared with prior art can rebut prima facie obviousness
description: Evidence that the claimed compound or invention is unexpectedly superior in a property it shares with the prior art can rebut a prima facie case of obviousness even if superiority is shown only for some uses or species.
guidance: No set number of examples required (In re Chupp). Examples: improved herbicidal control for specific crops was sufficient even when average on others. See Ex parte A and related decisions.

name: Burden on applicant to establish unexpectedness and explain data
description: Applicants bear the burden to establish that differences in results are unexpected and of both statistical and practical significance, and to explain proffered data in any declaration offered as evidence of nonobviousness.
guidance: Mere conclusions are not entitled to weight (Ex parte Gelles; Ex parte C). '[A]ppellants have the burden of explaining the data in any declaration they proffer' (Ex parte Ishizaka). Direct and indirect comparative tests commensurate in scope with claims are probative (In re Boesch; In re Blondel; In re Fouche).

name: Comparisons must be made with the closest prior art (and deviations explained)
