guidance: A presumption of regularity supports prosecutorial decisions; mere evidence of selectivity without proof of improper purpose is insufficient. Case citations: United States v. Armstrong; United States v. Hendrickson.

name: Show every feature specified in the claims
description: The drawing in a nonprovisional application must show every feature of the invention specified in the claims. (37 C.F.R. 1.83(a))
guidance: Any feature recited in the claims should be depicted in the drawings. If a claimed feature is not shown, the examiner will object and require corrected drawing sheets in reply to the Office action to avoid abandonment. If a drawing figure is to be canceled, remove it from the replacement sheet and renumber remaining figures with consistent changes to the brief description of the several views.

name: Conventional features may be represented by symbols or labeled boxes
description: Conventional features disclosed in the description and claims, where their detailed illustration is not essential for a proper understanding of the invention, should be illustrated in the drawing in the form of a graphical drawing symbol or a labeled representation (e.g., a labeled rectangular box). (37 C.F.R. 1.83(a))
guidance: Do not omit conventional elements entirely if they are necessary to understand the claimed invention; instead use simplified graphical symbols or labeled representations when detailed illustration is not essential.

name: If claimed subject matter not shown, show it or cancel the claim (no new matter)
description: The drawings must show every feature of the invention specified in the claims. Therefore, the [feature] must be shown or the feature(s) canceled from the claim(s). No new matter should be entered. (¶ 6.36, under 37 C.F.R. 1.83(a))
guidance: If a claimed element is missing from the drawings, the applicant must either add the missing illustration or amend the claims to remove the element; you may not add new matter in the process of correcting drawings.

name: Step 2B: Additional elements amount to 'significantly more'
description: Step 2B asks: Does the claim recite additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception? Examiners should identify additional elements beyond the judicial exception(s) and evaluate whether they contribute an inventive concept (i.e., amount to significantly more).
guidance: Answer by identifying additional elements and evaluating those additional elements individually and in combination with respect to the considerations the Supreme Court and Federal Circuit have identified (see MPEP §§ 2106.05(a)-(h)). This evaluation determines whether the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more (YES → eligible at Pathway C) or does not (NO → reject under 35 U.S.C. 101).

name: Identify additional elements beyond the judicial exception
description: Examiners should first identify whether there are any additional elements (features/limitations/steps) recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception(s).
guidance: Carry over the identification of additional element(s) from Step 2A Prong Two. Use the full claim language and the specification to determine what additional elements are present.

name: Analyze claim 'as a whole' and avoid oversimplifying
description: Evaluate the claim as an ordered combination, 'as a whole,' and avoid oversimplifying by looking too generally or ignoring specific claim requirements.
guidance: Do not determine eligibility by treating elements in isolation if their combination provides the inventive concept. Be careful to account for the specific requirements of the claims (citing McRO and Diamond v. Diehr guidance).

name: Examine each claim separately
description: Each claim should be examined for eligibility separately; claims should not be judged to automatically stand or fall with similar claims in an application.
guidance: A dependent claim may be eligible if it recites additional elements that amount to significantly more even if the independent claim is ineligible.

name: Improvements to computer functionality or other technology (MPEP §2106.05(a))
description: Consider whether the claim 'purport(s) to improve the functioning of the computer itself' or 'any other technology or technical field.' Improvement in computer functionality or technology is a key indicator of an inventive concept.
guidance: Evaluate improvement both in Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B. Relevant Federal Circuit cases include Enfish, McRO, DDR Holdings, Amdocs, Visual Memory, etc. Look for a technical solution to a technological problem and specification disclosure showing how the improvement is achieved.

name: Specification must provide technical explanation of asserted improvement
description: If it is asserted that the invention improves conventional functioning of a computer or technology, the specification should provide a technical explanation sufficient for one of ordinary skill in the art to recognize the claimed improvement.
guidance: The disclosure must include sufficient detail; conclusory assertions of improvement are insufficient. The specification need not use explicit 'improvement' language, but the improvement must be apparent to one of ordinary skill in the art from the disclosure. Evidence submitted under 37 CFR 1.132 cannot be used to supplement the specification.

name: Method claims must be limited to computer implementation to show computer-functionality improvement
description: For a method claim to improve computer functionality, the broadest reasonable interpretation must be limited to a computer implementation; if the scope can be performed mentally or verbally, it cannot be said to improve computer technology.
guidance: Cite Synopsys v. Mentor Graphics and RecogniCorp v. Nintendo: claims that can be performed mentally or without a computer are not improvements in computer technology. Ensure claim scope excludes purely mental/analog embodiments if relying on computer-functionality improvement.

name: Examples of features/circumstances courts have found may show an improvement
description: The MPEP lists example features that courts have indicated may show an improvement in computer functionality or technology (e.g., modifications to hyperlink protocol, inventive distribution of network functionality, specific data structures, unconventional network architectures, memory systems with programmable characteristics, technical details for image transmission, particular server structures, particular programming or UI implementations, security-profile methods, improved user interfaces, 3D spreadsheet navigation, license-restricted software operation).
guidance: Use these case-based examples (Enfish; DDR; BASCOM; Research Corp.; Amdocs; Visual Memory; TLI; Apple/Ameranth; Finjan; Core Wireless; Data Engine; Ancora) to identify analogous facts where claims include concrete technical improvements rather than abstract ideas implemented on generic computers.

name: Examples of features/circumstances courts have found insufficient
description: The MPEP also lists examples the courts have indicated may not be sufficient to show an improvement (e.g., functionally claimed menus, speed-up solely from general-purpose computer, mere automation of manual processes, recording/transmitting/archiving images with conventional tech, barcode affixation without technical detail, high-level instructions to display information, database usage improvements not improving functionality, arranging GUI info without technical means).
guidance: Use these non-examples (Ameranth; FairWarning; Credit Acceptance; TLI; Secured Mail; Interval Licensing; BSG Tech; Trading Technologies) to recognize when claimed features merely use conventional technology or are high-level business/organizational solutions rather than technical improvements.

name: Procedural outcome: Pathway C eligibility vs 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection
description: If the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the exception itself (inventive concept found), the claim is eligible at Pathway C and the eligibility analysis is complete; if not, the claim is not patent-eligible and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101.
guidance: For claims found ineligible, examiners should follow MPEP § 2106.07 for forming an ineligibility rejection. Document the analysis of additional elements and the considerations relied upon.

name: Patent applications — objects and required oath
description: An applicant must file in the Patent Office an application describing and claiming a patentable invention resulting from his own creative act and must support his application by an oath that he believes himself the first and true inventor of the art or instrument therein described.
guidance: If examination finds allegations correct, petition is formally allowed and letters-patent issued. Primary objects: (1) secure exclusive privilege; (2) prevent a similar grant to a rival. References to later discussion of description, claims, drawings, fees, etc.

name: Caveat purpose — priority protection (general nature)
description: A caveat is intended to secure to an inventor the opportunity to have the question of priority between himself and a rival determined before the issue of letters-patent to either; it is a written notice that the caveator claims to be the first and true inventor of the art or instrument described.
guidance: Its effect is to entitle the caveator to notice of subsequent applications for the same subject matter; it does not protect against public use, does not substitute for due diligence in perfecting/reducing invention to practice, and gives no substantive advantage over rivals other than the notice right.

name: Notice and procedure upon subsequent applications (suspension and interference)
description: When a rival files an application during the life of a caveat and the Office finds the described invention patentable and apparently corresponding to that in the caveat, proceedings on the application are suspended, the rival application is deposited in secret archives, and the caveator is notified to file his application so claims can be determined; if both applications claim the same invention an interference will be declared.
guidance: The caveator must present his application within three months from the expiration of ordinary mail transmission time for the notice from Washington. If the Office or mail fails to give notice and a patent issues, the patentee cannot take advantage of that patent in later interference between him and the caveator.

name: Required specification sections: Latin name and varietal denomination
description: Include the Latin name of the genus and species of the plant claimed as well as the varietal denomination.
guidance: Provide accurate botanical identification using accepted Latin genus/species names and a clear varietal denomination for the claimed cultivar.

name: Required specification sections: Background
description: Background includes the field of invention and a description of the relevant prior art.
guidance: Explain the technical field and summarize prior related plants/techniques to contextualize the novelty and advantages of the claimed plant.

name: Required specification sections: Brief Description of the Drawings/Photographs
description: Natural language explanation of what is shown in drawings or photos, including perspective, angle, partial or complete views.
guidance: Describe photos/drawings clearly and link illustrations to claimed distinguishing features; note whether views are partial or complete.

name: Required specification sections: Detailed Botanical Description (content elements)
description: A complete botanical description of the claimed plant is required, covering numerous plant parts and characteristics.
guidance: Detail items that should be included: genus and species; habit of growth; cultivar name; precocity; botanical characteristics of plant structures (buds, bark, foliage, flowers, fruit, etc.); fertility/fecundity; other distinguishing features such as disease resistance, drought/cold tolerance, fragrance, color, timing of flowering, productivity, rooting ability, extract quality, etc. Describe characteristics in botanical terms and provide substantive detail even for features shown in photographs.

name: Claim drafting constraints for plant patents (ONE claim only)
description: Plant patents get only one claim; 'You only get ONE claim!'
guidance: The single claim must be a single sentence in formal language covering the plant 'as shown and described' and the language should be drawn to the plant as a whole. Clauses should point out and distinctly claim the unusual characteristics. Do not claim parts or products of the plant. Claim drafting is specialized — consider a patent attorney.

name: Drawings and photographs requirements
description: Drawings/photographs must showcase the most distinctive and novel features; photographs are required in many cases.
guidance: Illustrations must show whatever is stated in the claim language and be no smaller than 50% to scale of the actual plant. Photographs are required for plant patents; color photographs are required if one of the claimed features deals with color.

name: Consider hiring a patent attorney
description: Recommendation: you really shouldn't file a plant (or any) patent application on your own — hire a professional patent attorney.
guidance: Confirm the person is a registered patent attorney (look them up in USPTO registry). The attorney can assist with inventorship, claim drafting, ensuring the specification meets 37 CFR 1.163(a), handling related applications, and overall prosecution strategy.

name: Types of claims considered 'concerning' patent and listed IP rights (scope of exclusive jurisdiction)
description: Claims that typically require expert technical knowledge and thus fall under exclusive jurisdiction include injunctions against infringement, disposal/destruction, recovery of reputation, damages, transfer or extinguishment of patent registration, claims to establish/extinguish exclusive/nonexclusive licenses, remuneration for employee invention, royalty claims, and confirmation of attribution of IP rights.
guidance: Courts concentrate such cases to specialized courts to leverage judges' technical expertise; parties asserting or defending such claims should frame issues to show they involve technical matters requiring specialized adjudication.

name: Subject-matter jurisdiction allocation (single judge vs panel)
description: Judicial power of a district court is exercised by a single judge in principle, but certain cases (Article 32(1)) are heard by a three-judge panel. Claims for monetary awards exceeding KRW 500 million go to a three-judge panel; multiple claims are summed to determine value; cases seeking injunctions or registration/transfer/extinguishment (where value cannot be calculated) go to district court panels.
guidance: A case originally assigned to a single judge may be taken by a panel court upon its decision. Parties should evaluate the monetary and non-monetary relief sought to anticipate bench composition.

name: Brief content for damages contentions
description: A claimant seeking compensatory damages should specify the legal provisions forming the basis for calculating damages and identify the exhibit number associated with each legal element; to dispute alleged facts, the other party should provide a detailed answer rather than a simple denial.
guidance: Tie factual allegations to statutory/legal elements and exhibits; bare denials are insufficient—provide documentary or factual rebuttal.

name: Confidentiality protective orders for trade secrets
description: A party may refuse to produce a document claiming it contains confidential information; the court may order an in camera review (parties and counsel excluded). Under Article 14-4 of the Unfair Competition Prevention and Trade Secret Protection Act, a party may petition for a confidentiality protective order to prevent unauthorized disclosure of trade secrets in litigation alleging unfair competition/trade-secret violation.
guidance: Seek confidentiality protective orders and in camera review to limit disclosure scope; expect procedures that restrict access and permit limited dissemination consistent with protecting trade secrets.

name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b) — Prohibition on false/misleading information and requirement of reasonable inquiry
description: Submitting documents that include false, misleading, fictitious, or fraudulent information violates §11.18(b)(1); submitting without a reasonable inquiry into the factual basis violates §11.18(b)(2).
guidance: Examples: false or misleading domicile, attorney information, signatory information (e.g., named signatory did not personally sign), applicant information, or claims of use. Submitting such information to circumvent USPTO rules, or without evidentiary support, is improper and may constitute an intent to mislead or circumvent rules.

name: Experimental use ends upon actual reduction to practice ('completeness')
description: Experimental use 'means perfecting or completing an invention to the point of determining that it will work for its intended purpose.' Therefore, experimental use 'ends with an actual reduction to practice.'
guidance: If evidence shows the inventor considered the invention 'complete,' awaiting approvals (e.g., UL) will not usually overcome that conclusion; see RCA Corp., Interroyal Corp., and Skil Corp. citations. Modifications resulting from experimentation must be features of the claimed invention to be probative.

name: Reasonableness of scope and length of experimental activity
description: Once experimental activity is advanced by an applicant, the examiner must determine whether the scope and length of the activity were reasonable in terms of the experimental purpose intended and the nature of the subject matter.
guidance: No single factor or combination is necessarily determinative; examiner evaluates overall reasonableness against the claimed purpose and technological context.

name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(d) — the same invention must be involved
description: The 'same invention' means that the application claims could have been presented in the foreign patent; the foreign specification supporting the U.S. claims can trigger the bar even if claims differ.
guidance: Foreign patent need not have identical claims; if the foreign patent fully discloses the invention and supports U.S. claim subject matter, 102(d) applies (In re Kathawala example). Examiner should assess whether foreign patent supports the claimed subject matter.

name: Alice/Mayo two-step framework (Step 2A and Step 2B)
description: Apply the Office’s two-step inquiry: determine whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A) and, if so, determine whether additional elements individually or in combination provide an inventive concept that amounts to 'significantly more' (Step 2B).
guidance: Use Step 2A to assess whether a claim is 'directed to' an abstract idea (judicial exception). If a judicial exception is present, use Step 2B to evaluate whether the claim's additional elements provide an inventive concept — considering elements both individually and in combination.

name: Clarified Step 2A — improvements in computer-related technology
description: Improvements in computer-related technology are not limited to the operation of a computer or network per se, but may also include allowing computer performance of a function not previously performable by a computer.
guidance: An indication of an improvement in computer-related technology may include: (1) a teaching in the specification about how the claimed invention improves a computer or other technology; and (2) claiming a particular solution to a problem as opposed to merely claiming the idea of a solution.

name: Clarified Step 2B — consider elements in combination
description: Examiners should consider additional elements in combination, as well as individually, when determining whether a claim amounts to 'significantly more' (i.e., whether there is an inventive concept).
guidance: Do not evaluate additional claim elements only in isolation; assess whether an ordered combination of elements provides something more than the judicial exception itself. BASCOM reiterated this combined-elements approach.

name: Teaching in the specification as evidence of technological improvement
description: A specification teaching about how the claimed invention improves a computer or other technology is an indication that the claim may be directed to a specific technological improvement rather than an abstract idea.
guidance: Look for explicit disclosure explaining how the invention enhances computer performance, solves a technological problem, or enables a computer to perform functions it could not previously perform; such teachings support eligibility under Step 2A.

name: Claiming a particular solution vs. claiming an idea
description: Claims that recite a particular solution to a problem (concrete steps/implementation) are more likely to be seen as directed to a patent-eligible invention than claims that only recite the abstract idea of a solution.
guidance: Draft and examine claims to describe concrete, specific implementations and technical solutions rather than high-level concepts or goals.

name: Unconventional combination/arrangement of generic components
description: Eligibility may be found from generic computer components working together in an unconventional manner to solve a technological problem.
guidance: Amdocs: the court found the claimed invention 'entails an unconventional technical solution (enhancing data in a distributed fashion) to a technological problem (massive record flows...)'. Use evidence of unconventional arrangements that produce a technical improvement to support eligibility.

name: Claims that improve graphical user interfaces (GUIs) may not be abstract
description: Claims reciting systems and methods for improving the display and interaction of information via a GUI, where the improvement has no 'pre-electronic trading analog', can be found not directed to an abstract idea.
guidance: Trading Tech: claims that recite more than merely 'setting, displaying, and selecting' data — i.e., that produce an improvement in GUI functionality — can be eligible. Emphasize the specific GUI improvement and its technical effect.

name: Software and computer-related improvements appropriately claimed are not abstract
description: Software and other improvements in computer-related technology are not abstract when they are appropriately claimed as providing a technical improvement or solution.
guidance: When claims recite concrete improvements to computer-related technology (e.g., performance, new capabilities, technical problem solutions), frame and analyze them as technological improvements rather than as abstract ideas.

name: Whether features disclosed but not claimed may affect eligibility
description: A question before the Federal Circuit (Amdocs en banc petition) asks whether features disclosed in the specification but not claimed may confer patentability.
guidance: Ensure claim drafting captures the inventive technical features; when relying on specification disclosures to show a technical solution, be mindful of the limits of relying on unclaimed features to establish claim eligibility.

name: Non-precedential/precedential decisions as guidance (use facts/details)
description: Federal Circuit decisions — both precedential and non-precedential — provide examples of how claims were evaluated for eligibility and the factual bases relied upon (e.g., Enfish, Bascom, Amdocs, Trading Tech).
guidance: Use the reasoning and factual findings in these decisions as guidance: identify factual parallels (e.g., technological problem solved, unconventional arrangement, specific improvements) rather than relying on broad labels like 'abstract idea' alone.

name: Refund of search fee and excess claims fee via express abandonment (37 CFR 1.138(d))
description: An applicant seeking a refund of search and excess claims fees by express abandonment must submit a declaration of express abandonment by petition under 37 CFR 1.138(d) before an examination has been made of the application.
guidance: The date on any certificate of mailing/transmission under 37 CFR 1.8 is not considered for determining whether the petition was filed before an examination. If a refund request is not filed with the declaration or within two months after filing the declaration, the Office may retain the entire fees; the two-month period is not extendable. ‘‘Examination has been made’’ is defined by actions shown in the One Patent Service Gateway as having been counted (e.g., first Office action on the merits, restriction/election, notice of allowance, etc.). If PDP status is higher than 031 before/on the day the petition was filed, the petition will be denied. Technical preparations for publication generally begin four months prior to projected publication; timely electronic filing is recommended. Use of form PTO/AIA/24B (or PTO/SB/24B) is recommended.

name: Termination of proceedings (effect on copendency and dates)
description: Proceedings are terminated (for purposes such as copendency under 35 U.S.C. 120) in specified situations, with 'before' interpreted as 'not later than' (i.e., 'before' = 'not later than').
guidance: Situations causing termination include: (A) issue fee not paid and application abandoned for failure to pay the issue fee (proceedings terminated as of the date issue fee was due); (B) application in an interference loses interference to all claims — proceedings terminated as of date appeal was due if no appeal filed; (C) termination after decision by the Board (see MPEP § 1214.06); (D) termination after decision by the court (see MPEP § 1216.01).

name: Reconsideration of a holding of abandonment (insufficiency vs no reply)
description: When advised of abandonment, applicant may ask for reconsideration if they disagree (claiming there was no abandonment in fact); examiner may reverse a holding if an amendment received during the period was in fact responsive.
guidance: Reversal that the application was never abandoned is not a 'revival' but a determination there was no abandonment. If amendment reached the Office after expiration and there is no dispute as to dates, no reconsideration is possible; where dates or responsiveness are disputed, applicant may take issue and seek correction or petition. See MPEP § 711.03(a)-(b).

name: Forms for express abandonment and related petitions
description: Specific forms are recommended/available for filing letters of express abandonment and petitions under subsections of 37 CFR 1.138: PTO/AIA/24 (or PTO/SB/24), PTO/AIA/24A (or PTO/SB/24A), and PTO/AIA/24B (or PTO/SB/24B).
guidance: Form PTO/AIA/24 may be used for filing a letter of express abandonment or abandonment in favor of a continuing application. PTO/AIA/24A may be used for a petition for express abandonment under 1.138(c) to avoid publication. PTO/AIA/24B may be used for a petition under 1.138(d) to obtain a refund of search and excess claims fees. Use of recommended forms and electronic filing is encouraged to ensure timely processing.

name: Purpose of re-issue
description: The purpose of surrender and re-issue is not to introduce new features, ingredients, or devices into the patent, but to render effectual the actual invention for which the original patent should have been granted.
guidance: Re-issue is to correct or perfect a defective or insufficient description (including the Claim) to give effect to the invention the patentee intended to secure; it is not to broaden the patent by adding new features beyond what was described, suggested, or substantially indicated in the original specification, drawings, or model.

name: No claiming matters inconsistent with original specification/drawings/model
description: A re-issue cannot claim matters inconsistent with the specification, drawings, and model of the original, even if such matters were claimed in the original patent.
guidance: Claims in the re-issue that are inconsistent with the original disclosure are invalid; re-issue cannot be used to assert rights to elements not supported by the original patent documents (see Ex parte Warren and related cases).

name: Original disclosure may appear in specification, drawings, or model
description: The inventor's attempt to describe and claim the invention may appear in the original specification, the drawings, or the Patent Office model.
guidance: If the attempt to cover the alleged subject-matter is shown in any one of these (and can be reasonably interpreted in light of the actual invention), re-issue may be permissible; the model may be used as evidence even if later lost, provided other records are consistent.

name: No parol (oral) proof to add matter not indicated
description: No parol proof is admissible to show that the inventor intended to describe or claim matter not indicated to some extent in his original patent.
guidance: Matters must appear in the written specification, drawings, or model; oral testimony cannot be used to justify inclusion of new matter in a re-issue.

name: Substantial-indication test for original disclosure
description: The original specification, drawings, or model must afford some substantial indication or suggestion of the actual invention intended to be monopolized.
guidance: If an inventor cannot express the idea with sufficient particularity (words, pictures, materials), the matter may lie outside the industrial domain or requires a new application; re-issue requires that the original at least substantially indicate the claimed subject-matter.

name: Test: would original have matched re-issue absent substantive defects
description: A re-issue is sufficiently indicated in the original whenever the Patent Office or courts, examining the original in light of the actual invention or the perfect re-issue specification, can perceive that if the original claims and descriptions had been free from substantive defects the inventions claimed originally and in the re-issue would have been identical.
guidance: This is the practical test used by the Office and courts: re-issue is allowed to correct substantive defects that masked identity, provided the original documents point toward the same invention.

name: Office model alone insufficient to support new claim unless inventor's intent shown
description: The Office model alone is not sufficient basis for a new claim in a re-issue unless it also appears that the inventor originally intended to claim the feature in question.
guidance: A model that contradicts the drawings and specification cannot by itself justify an expanded re-issue; model evidence must be corroborated by the written disclosure or other contemporaneous records (see Flower v. Detroit, Ex parte Hunt).

name: Language variance allowed if identity of subject-matter preserved
description: Variances between the descriptions and claims of the original and the re-issue are permissible so long as the identity of the subject-matter is preserved.
guidance: Differences in wording, titles, or descriptions do not defeat re-issue provided the same invention is intended; re-issue may use different language to clarify or narrow/expand claims within the original scope.

name: Non-machine patents: specification may be made more certain but not broader
description: In re-issue of patents other than machine patents, the specification may be made more certain or the claim made to correspond with the specification, but not made broader than the original invention.
guidance: For non-machine cases, re-issue can clarify or tighten description/claims but cannot add new substantive matter beyond what the original indicated (contrast with machine-patent limits).

name: Re-issue may make definite what was previously only inferable
description: A re-issue may make definite what was before reached only by inference in the original patent.
guidance: Re-issue can cure vagueness or uncertainty by explicitly describing and claiming what the original implied, so long as the implied matter truly belonged to the original invention.

name: Claims may be enlarged or restricted; description covering more than claims is immaterial
description: In a re-issue that enlarges the claims the claims alone are involved, and if the Description covers more than the claims it is of no consequence.
guidance: Re-issue can restrict or enlarge claims consistent with the original invention; the mere fact that the description mentions more does not control the claim scope if not properly claimed originally.

name: Re-issue may restate invention and claim essential but unclearly stated features
description: A re-issue may restate the invention and claim such essential features as are not clearly stated in the original.
guidance: If the original failed to clearly express essential features, re-issue can be used to put them into proper form, provided support exists in the original disclosure (Woven Wire Mattress Co. v. Wire Web Bed Co.).

name: Re-issue may claim matters found in original description though not in original claims
description: A re-issue may claim matters that are found in the original Description even though the inventor made no attempt to insert them in his original Claims.
guidance: Claims originally omitted but supported by the description may be embraced in a re-issue, subject to the usual support/indication limits (Eickemeyer Blocking Mach. Co. v. Pearce).

name: Office model cannot alone justify new claim in re-issue
description: The Patent Office model alone is not a sufficient basis for a new claim in a re-issue unless corroborated and showing original intent to claim the feature.
guidance: Model evidence must not contradict drawings/specification and must be interpreted with caution; office model alone cannot create entitlement to new matter (reiterating multiple citations).

name: Mere instructions to apply a judicial exception
description: Claims that amount to nothing more than an instruction to apply the [judicial exception] while adding the words 'apply it' (or an equivalent) are not patent-eligible. For example, claims that amount to nothing more than an instruction to apply the abstract idea using a generic computer do not render the abstract idea eligible.
guidance: Supreme Court cases (Alice, Mayo, Gottschalk v. Benson) show that reciting a judicial exception plus generic application (e.g., 'apply it' on a generic computer) is insufficient. Examiners should explain why recited elements do not meaningfully limit the claim when claiming implementation on a generic computer. Consider overlap with other considerations (improvement to computer or technology, particular machine/transformation, well-understood/routine/conventional) to determine whether elements are more than mere instructions to apply an exception. See MPEP §2106.07(a) for formulating rejections.

name: Recites only the idea of a solution or outcome
description: Whether the claim recites only the idea of a solution or outcome (i.e., fails to recite details of how a solution to a problem is accomplished). Recitation of claim limitations that attempt to cover any solution with no restriction on how the result is accomplished and no description of the mechanism does not integrate a judicial exception into a practical application or provide significantly more.
guidance: Result-oriented or functional claiming that covers any solution to an identified problem is equivalent to the words 'apply it' and has been found ineligible (Electric Power Group; Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec; Internet Patents v. Active Network). In contrast, claiming a particular solution or way to achieve an outcome may integrate the judicial exception into a practical application. Use case examples (e.g., Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One; Electric Power) to explain why additional limitations are merely result-oriented or instead supply meaningful technical detail.

name: Invokes computers or other machinery merely as a tool
description: Whether the claim invokes computers or other machinery merely as a tool to perform an existing process. Use of a computer or other machinery in its ordinary capacity (to receive, store, transmit data, etc.) or simply adding a general-purpose computer to an abstract idea does not integrate the judicial exception into a practical application or provide significantly more.
guidance: Cases (Affinity Labs v. DirecTV; TLI Communications v. AV Auto; Alice; Gottschalk v. Benson; Versata; FairWarning) show invoking generic devices in their ordinary capacity is insufficient. Conversely, claims that improve computer capabilities or an existing technology (e.g., McRO, Enfish) may integrate the exception. Examiners should identify whether the claimed machine elements merely perform conventional tasks or instead provide technical improvements to the machine/technology (see MPEP §§2106.04(d)(1), 2106.05(a)).

name: Whether the limitation is significant (imposes meaningful limits)
description: Whether the additional limitation imposes meaningful limits on the claim so that it is not nominally or tangentially related to the invention. If the limitation is insignificant or merely restricts public access, it may be token extra-solution activity.
guidance: Examples where courts found limitations insignificant: Ultramercial (restricting public access to media), Apple v. Ameranth (menu ordering features), Ultramercial/In re Brown examples. This consideration applies in Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B. Examiners should explain why a limitation is or is not meaningful in the context of claim as a whole.

name: Examiners must explain why additional elements do not meaningfully limit the claim
description: For claim limitations that do not amount to more than a recitation of 'apply it' (or equivalent), examiners should explain why they do not meaningfully limit the claim in an eligibility rejection.
guidance: Provide specific reasoning in the rejection (e.g., implementing an abstract idea on a generic computer does not integrate it into a practical application in Step 2A Prong Two or add significantly more in Step 2B). Cite relevant case law (Alice, Mayo) and MPEP §2106.07(a) for guidance on drafting subject matter eligibility rejections.

name: Damages argument form and defendant's rebuttal
description: Plaintiff's argument regarding amount of damages shall indicate the applicable legal provision and cite an evidence number for each essential element; defendant's response must include detailed rebuttal and specify actual transferred volumes or profits where relevant.
guidance: Any fact not specifically denied by the defendant may be deemed undisputed. If plaintiff claims damages under Article 128(1) defendant must state actual transferred volume; under Article 128(3) defendant must state actual profit amount and grounds for calculation (sales revenues, expenses, profit margins).

name: Technical solution (Article 2.2 Chinese Patent Law)
description: The solution is the technical solution as provided for in Article 2.2 Chinese Patent Law, and constitutes the subject matter of patent protection.
guidance: The solution must utilize technical means in conformity with the laws of nature and obtain a technical effect. Examples: measuring sugar content of preharvest apples by a portable near-infrared spectroscopic sensor (claims 1-2) and a prediction method that uses physical measurements and meteorological data plus machine learning to predict future sugar content (claim 3) are judged to be technical solutions because they (i) solve a technical problem, (ii) use technical means, and (iii) obtain technical effects. If these three elements are present, CNIPA concludes the subject matter constitutes patent protection.

name: 'Processed by a computer' as a determinative claim feature
description: If a claim states it is 'processed by a computer', examiners assess whether specific computing or processing of information depending on the intended use has been implemented by concrete means or procedures on which software and hardware resources cooperate.
guidance: JPO: When 'processed by a computer' appears in the claim, list concrete computational steps to show cooperation of software and hardware; if present, the claim is likely an 'invention'. If the wording 'processed by a computer' is absent, the examiner must refer to the description and common general technical knowledge to assess whether the method is nevertheless processed by a computer. (See JPO analysis for the mathematical-model and CNN training examples.)

name: Concrete hardware-software implementation
description: A method is regarded as an invention when information processing by software has been concretely implemented by using hardware resources (cooperation of software and hardware resources).
guidance: JPO repeatedly stresses that concrete implementation by concrete means or procedures (e.g., specific steps carried out by a computer: training models, performing convolutions, pooling operations, data acquisition steps) supports characterization as an 'invention' because it establishes a specific operating method of an information processing device. The guideline expects examiners to identify such concrete steps in claim text or description.

name: Does the invention improve internal performance or cause technical change to the computer?
description: Assess whether the claimed computer-implemented process improves the internal performance of the computer or causes any technical change to its composition or function.
guidance: CNIPA: If the computer is 'just a device to carry out the solution' and the establishing process neither improves the computer's internal performance nor causes any technical change to the computer's composition or function, the claimed method may be treated as non-technical (abstract mathematical method) and thus not a patentable technical solution. Contrast: where the method has specific technical associations with the internal structure or improves execution effect of hardware (e.g., selecting optimal training scheme to improve hardware execution), CNIPA finds technical effect.

name: Technical nature of data and processing steps
description: Whether the data processed in each step are technical (physical/image/meteorological/text/semantic data) and whether each step is closely related to achieving an accurate technical result.
guidance: CNIPA and JPO accept claims where processed data have 'exact technical implications' (e.g., physical measurements, image data, meteorological condition data, semantic text data) and the steps are closely related to the technical objective (e.g., predicting sugar content, image recognition across sizes, enriching semantic information). If the data and processing are merely abstract (general feature values, tag values) without a specific application field, the claim may be treated as abstract.

name: Claim clarity / title must indicate product vs process (Article 26.4 Chinese Patent Law)
description: Claims (and their titles) must clearly define the extent of the patent protection sought; the title should indicate whether the claim is for a product or a process.
guidance: Example: Claims titled 'Sugar content data' did not clearly indicate whether they were product or process claims; CNIPA found they 'do not define the extent of the patent protection sought in a clear manner' and thus do not comply with Article 26.4. Applicants were advised to modify the title to e.g., 'A collection method of sugar content data'. Examiners should check titles and claim wording for clarity of claim category and scope.

name: Use of description and common general technical knowledge when claim wording is silent
description: If a claim is silent about being processed by a computer, examiners must refer to the description and common general technical knowledge to assess whether the claimed method is nonetheless implemented by a computer.
guidance: JPO guidance: When 'processed by a computer' is not explicitly found in the claim, the examiner assesses from the specification and common general technical knowledge whether the method is processed by a computer; if so, the same 'software-implemented technical solution' approach applies. This requires examiners to analyze the specification for indications of hardware cooperation or intended implementation.

name: Demonstrating technical association with hardware/internal structure supports patentability
description: For inventive-step/technicality assessment, showing specific technical associations with the internal structure of the computer system or that the method improves hardware execution supports finding of a technical solution
guidance: CNIPA example (training-method case): the method 'has specific technical associations with the internal structure of the computer system, and improves the execution effect of hardware in the training process', yielding a technical effect that improves internal performance — thereby constituting a technical solution. Examiners should look for whether claimed measures change or optimize hardware execution, resource use, or internal arrangements.

name: Treatment of unbaptized infants and the universality of God’s salvific will
description: Thesis: the fate of unbaptized infants, though difficult, does not refute the universality of God’s saving will; the Church has not dogmatically defined their ultimate fate and theologians hold divergent opinions.
guidance: Surveys positions: Bellarmine’s claim that unbaptized infants are excluded (restricted and to be qualified); possibilities include baptism of blood, baptism of desire, God’s mercy cleansing original sin enabling a natural beatitude (Gutberlet), and the need for caution (no certain solution). Emphasizes responsibility of human agents (parents/priests) for administering Baptism and that exceptions (invincible ignorance, natural order) complicate culpability. Scriptural and magisterial affirmations of God’s universal mercy are cited as supporting that infants participate in divine mercy.

name: God gives sufficient grace to all adult human beings
description: Article assertion: in relation to adults, God manifests His saving will by bestowing sufficient grace upon all (sufficient graces are given to just, sinners, and heathen). God is not obliged to bestow efficacious grace to all, but sufficient grace (including gratia prima vocans) is granted.
guidance: Thesis I (de fide): God gives just men sufficient grace to keep His commandments; sufficiency is evidenced by scripture (e.g., 'the commandments are not heavy') and patristic teaching. Church teaches sufficient grace is at their disposal when called (urgente praecepto); proximate vs remote sufficient grace distinction is noted (gratia proxime sufficiens vs gratia remote sufficiens). The theological argument: the state of grace implies claim to necessary graces; divine promises and 'ad impossibile nemo tenetur' support the claim.

name: Clerical handling and entry of amendments; treatment of new matter and claim scope changes
description: Amendments submitted with a request under 35 U.S.C. 302, or after reexamination is ordered under 35 U.S.C. 304 or 257, which comply with 37 CFR 1.530(d)-(j), will generally be entered in the reexamination file if submitted prior to a final action. Any 'new matter' amendment to the disclosure (35 U.S.C. 132) will be required to be canceled, and claims containing new matter will be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112. A 'new matter' amendment to the drawing is ordinarily not entered. Where an amendment enlarges the scope of the claims of the patent, the amendment will be entered; however the appropriate claims will be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 305.
guidance: See MPEP §§ 2234, 2250, 608.04(a,c) for detailed entry procedures; entry for purposes of reexamination does not give legal effect until certificate issuance.

name: Claim construction — do method-of-treatment claims require clinical efficacy?
description: Whether the claim term 'method of treating' should be construed to require clinical efficacy in a human patient, or whether such a requirement improperly imports limitations from the specification.
guidance: Claims should not be read to require efficacy absent express disavowal or lexicography; reading an efficacy threshold into a 'method of treating' claim can be legally erroneous and materially affect patentability. See Phillips v. AWH Corp., 415 F.3d 1303, 1323 (Fed. Cir. 2005). If patent owner convinced Examiner to require evidence of clinical efficacy, that may have lowered the bar to allowance improperly.

name: Unexpected results must be substantial and supported to rebut obviousness
description: When asserting unexpected results (efficacy or tolerability) to rebut prima facie obviousness, the improvement must be substantial and supported by appropriate evidence from the viewpoint of a POSA.
guidance: Post-filing references may be considered, but claimed improvements must be more than marginal; routine medical practices (e.g., dose reduction correlating with lower toxicity) weigh against finding unexpected results. Case law: Regeneron v. Mylan and Genentech precedent cited for routine medical practices being obvious in dosing contexts. Wainberg (post-filing) here is argued not to show substantial unexpected improvements; other post-filing refs (Nichetti, Nevala-Plegamm) further undercut unexpected-result claims.

name: Content of the bill vs affidavits for preliminary injunctions (Equity Rules effect)
description: Previously bills were required to state prior adjudication or acquiescence supporting presumptions of validity; under the present Equity Rules a bill is merely a statement of ultimate facts and allegations of prior adjudication/acquiescence are better presented in affidavits accompanying the motion. The bill must contain a specific prayer for an injunction pendente lite and conform to requisites of bills in equity (Equity Rule 25).
guidance: Do not plead evidentiary allegations as ultimate facts in the bill; reserve evidentiary claims (prior adjudication or public acquiescence) for the affidavits on the motion where they show probable eventual success.

name: Product-of-nature / markedly different characteristics
description: If the claimed subject matter's characteristics are innate to a naturally occurring material and are not markedly different from its natural counterpart, the claim is a product of nature exception and is ineligible.
guidance: Examples: primers that maintain the exact same nucleotide sequence as natural DNA (In re BRCA1/2; Ambry Genetics) were held products of nature because their ability to serve as starting materials was innate to DNA; ductile vanadium (In re Marden) was ineligible because ductility is an inherent characteristic; cloned animals that are exact genetic replicas (Roslin/Dolly) lacked markedly different characteristics. Alleged phenotypic differences (e.g., height, weight) do not make the clone markedly different if those differences are not claimed. Structural differences not claimed are generally irrelevant (see Roche v. Cepheid).

name: Integration into a practical application (Step 2A Prong Two)
description: A claim as a whole integrates a recited judicial exception into a practical application when the claim applies, relies on, or uses the judicial exception in a manner that imposes a meaningful limit on the exception so the claim is more than a drafting effort to monopolize the exception.
guidance: If integration is present, the claim is not directed to the judicial exception (Step 2A: NO) and is eligible at Pathway B. If not, the claim is directed to the exception (Step 2A: YES) and requires further Step 2B analysis. Examiners should use the listed considerations to evaluate integration (see subsequent rubric entries) and follow the procedure described (identify additional elements; evaluate individually and in combination).

name: Consideration: improvement in functioning of a computer or other technology
description: An additional element (or combination) that demonstrates an improvement in the functioning of a computer, or an improvement to another technology or technical field, indicates the claim integrates the judicial exception into a practical application.
guidance: Evaluate the specification to determine if disclosure provides sufficient detail such that one of ordinary skill would recognize the claimed invention as providing the improvement; the specification need not explicitly state the improvement but must make it apparent to one skilled in the art. The claim must reflect the components or steps that provide the improvement (it need not literally recite 'thereby increasing the bandwidth'). At Step 2A, do not consider whether the improvement is over well-understood, routine, conventional activity. Examples of eligible improvements: Enfish (self-referential table), McRO (automatic lip synchronization), Visual Memory (enhanced memory), Finjan (virus scanning improvement), SRI v. Cisco (network monitoring). See MPEP § 2106.05(a) for further detail.

name: Consideration: applying/using the judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis
description: An additional element that applies or uses the judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition may integrate the exception into a practical application and render the claim not directed to the exception.
guidance: This consideration is particularly relevant to diagnostic/therapeutic claims. Example: Vanda — claims reciting genotyping and administering a drug in a genotype-dependent dose were held eligible because the steps used the natural-law relationship to safely treat patients rather than merely gather data. Treatment/prophylaxis examples include acupuncture, administration of medication, dialysis, transplants, phototherapy, physiotherapy, radiation therapy, surgery, etc. Distinguish from Mayo where administering a drug was ancillary/diagnostic rather than therapeutic in effect.

name: Consideration: implementing the exception with or using it in conjunction with a particular machine or manufacture integral to the claim
description: If the claim implements the judicial exception with a particular machine or manufacture that is integral to the claim, that may show the exception is integrated into a practical application.
guidance: Evaluate whether the particular machine/manufacture is integral (not merely incidental). Specific embodiments and how the machine is used should be considered in light of the specification and claim language. Specificity of how the machine is invoked can be relevant (see specificity rubric). See MPEP § 2106.05(b).

name: Consideration: effecting a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing
description: An additional element that effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing is a meaningful limitation that can integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.
guidance: Assess whether the claimed steps produce a physical transformation or meaningful change in the article. See MPEP § 2106.05(c) for application and examples. Physical steps alone are not automatically sufficient; evaluate how the transformation is tied to the claimed exception and whether it meaningfully limits the exception.

name: Consideration: applying or using the judicial exception in some other meaningful way beyond mere linkage to a technical environment
description: If the claim applies or uses the judicial exception in a meaningful way beyond generally linking it to a particular technological environment or field of use, that may indicate integration into a practical application.
guidance: This is a catch-all category for meaningful uses that do more than attach the exception to a technical field. The claim must be more than a drafting effort to monopolize the exception. See MPEP § 2106.05(e) for examples and further discussion.

name: Anti-pattern: merely reciting 'apply it' or implementing on a computer
description: Merely reciting the words 'apply it' (or equivalent), merely including instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer, or merely using a computer as a tool to perform an abstract idea does not integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.
guidance: Such recitations are insufficient to impose a meaningful limit on the exception (see MPEP § 2106.05(f)). Examiners should look for more substantive interactions between the exception and claim elements.

name: Anti-pattern: adding insignificant extra-solution activity
description: Adding insignificant or conventional extra-solution activity to the judicial exception does not integrate the exception into a practical application.
guidance: Insignificant post-solution activity that merely appends routine steps to an abstract idea or law of nature will not render the claim eligible (see MPEP § 2106.05(g)). However, note that at Step 2A examiners should not exclude consideration merely because an element is conventional (see separate rubric on conventionality exclusion).

name: Anti-pattern: generally linking the exception to a technological environment or field-of-use
description: Generally linking the use of a judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use, without more, does not integrate the exception into a practical application.
guidance: Claims that only identify a field or environment but do not meaningfully apply the exception within that environment are insufficient (see MPEP § 2106.05(h)). The analysis should focus on whether the linkage is meaningful and imposes a limit beyond mere field-of-use language.

name: Tangibility/physicality is not determinative
description: Mere physicality or tangibility of an additional element or elements is not a relevant consideration in Step 2A Prong Two; physical implementation does not guarantee eligibility.
guidance: The Supreme Court and Federal Circuit have made clear that physical implementation alone (e.g., running an abstract idea on a computer, performing DNA amplification steps) is not sufficient to render a claim eligible. Conversely, non-physical or intangible improvements may still integrate the exception if they meaningfully improve technology or the claimed process (see Alice, Genetic Technologies, Enfish, McRO).

name: Specificity of claim limitations matters
description: The specificity of claim limitations is relevant to the evaluation of whether additional elements integrate the exception into a practical application, including whether the claim uses a particular machine, effects a transformation, or merely instructs to apply an exception.
guidance: A mere recitation of a broad result is less persuasive than limitations that explain how to achieve the result. Lack of disclosure about how to implement claimed steps (e.g., Parker v. Flook — failure to explain selection of variables or monitoring means) can indicate that additional elements are insignificant post-solution activity. See MPEP §§ 2106.05(b), (c), (f).

name: Evaluation procedure: identify additional elements and evaluate individually and in combination
description: To determine if additional elements integrate a judicial exception into a practical application, (1) identify any additional elements recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception(s), and (2) evaluate those elements individually and in combination using the listed considerations.
guidance: Not all considerations will apply to every claim; more than one consideration may be relevant to an element. The analysis is not a weighing test — number or type of considerations is less important than whether the additional elements meaningfully limit the exception. Evaluate the significance of the additional elements relative to the invention and whether the claim as a whole integrates the exception into a practical application. See MPEP §§ 2106.04(d) and 2106.05(a)-(h).

name: Claim-specific examination (each claim evaluated separately)
description: Examiners should examine each claim for eligibility separately based on the particular elements recited therein; claims should not be judged to automatically stand or fall with similar claims in an application.
guidance: One claim may be ineligible as directed to a judicial exception while a dependent claim reciting additional meaningful elements may be eligible. Consider each claim's full limitation set and how those limitations interact when evaluating integration into a practical application.

name: Improvement-evaluation detail: sufficiency of specification and claim reflection
description: When evaluating whether a claim shows an improvement in technology, the specification must provide sufficient detail so that one of ordinary skill would recognize the improvement (not merely conclusory), and the claim itself must reflect the disclosed improvement.
guidance: The specification need not use the word 'improvement' but must disclose enough detail for the improvement to be apparent. A conclusory assertion of improvement without detail should not lead the examiner to find that the claim improves technology. The claim should include the components or steps providing the improvement, though it need not explicitly state the improvement in result-oriented language. See MPEP § 2106.05(a).

name: Use of judicial decisions and examples to inform analysis
description: Examiners should consider judicial precedent and examples (e.g., Solutran, Finjan, Vanda, Enfish, McRO) to inform whether additional elements integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.
guidance: Examples illustrate how courts have applied considerations: e.g., Solutran (claims to crediting merchant before scanning were long-standing practice and not an improvement), Finjan (security profile provided technical improvement and was eligible), Vanda (genotype-based dosing used law of nature to treat patients and was eligible). Use these as analogies when relevant but focus on claim-specific facts and the MPEP considerations.

name: When to compare claimed and accused designs with prior art
description: In some instances the designs will be sufficiently distinct that it is clear the patentee has not met its burden; in other instances, when not plainly dissimilar, comparison with the prior art will aid resolution.
guidance: Use prior-art comparisons especially where similarities are not obvious or where many prior art examples exist; determine whether differences that are subtle in isolation become significant in view of the prior art.

name: 35 U.S.C. 101 (subject matter eligibility and related topics)
description: Become more knowledgeable about 35 U.S.C. 101 and the following topics derived therefrom: statutory categories of invention, the utility requirement, eligible subject matter, and double patenting.
guidance: Covers the statutory categories of invention and the utility/eligible-subject-matter analysis examiners must apply when determining whether a claimed invention is directed to patent-eligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. 101.

name: 35 U.S.C. 112(a) — written description and enablement
description: Explore 35 U.S.C. 112 section (a) and the corresponding concepts including written description and enablement.
guidance: Module 'Introduction to 35 U.S.C. 112(a)' explains examiner expectations for the specification: sufficient written description to show possession of the claimed invention and enablement to teach making and using the invention without undue experimentation.

name: 35 U.S.C. 112(b) and (d) — claim clarity and dependent claims
description: Explore 35 U.S.C. 112 sections (b) and (d), focusing on claim clarity and proper dependent claim form.
guidance: Module 'Introduction to 35 U.S.C. 112(b) and (d)' covers requirements for clear, definite claim language and correct structure/format for dependent claims and multi-part claims.

name: 35 U.S.C. 112(f) — means-plus-function claiming
description: Introduction to 35 U.S.C. 112(f) and analysis for means-plus-function claim language.
guidance: Module '35 U.S.C. 112(f) Introduction' teaches how to identify means-plus-function claim elements and the corresponding requirement to find adequate structure in the specification to support the claim under 112(f).

name: Claim interpretation — broadest reasonable interpretation
description: Learn how to give claims their broadest reasonable interpretation, including such topics as the effect of the preamble, functional language, intended use, and product-by-process claims.
guidance: Modules ('Claim interpretation Introduction' and Parts 1–2) provide guidance on applying the broadest reasonable interpretation standard, and on how specific claim features (preamble, functional language, product-by-process) affect claim scope and interpretation.

name: Written description requirement (35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph)
description: The specification must show that the applicant was in possession of the claimed invention at the time of filing.
guidance: Examiner analysis asks whether the disclosure (taken with the pre-existing knowledge in the art) would have led one of ordinary skill to conclude the applicant possessed the full scope of the claimed invention; examples conclude either 'satisfies' or 'fails' the written description requirement based on facts such as structural disclosure, functional limitations, and predictability.

name: Possession via disclosure of a representative species
description: Disclosure of a specific species (e.g., an amino acid sequence shown as SEQ ID NO: 3) can demonstrate possession of a broader claimed genus if that species is representative of the genus and shares structural features common to the genus.
guidance: If the disclosed species embodies structural features shared by each member of the claimed genus, and those in the art would recognize that representativeness, a single species may suffice to show possession of the genus (Example 10). Predictability that other species will retain the function increases representativeness.

name: Claims defined by percent identity represent partial structure
description: Claims reciting a protein or nucleic acid defined as 'at least X% identical' to a disclosed sequence represent only a partial structure (e.g., 95% or 85% identity).
guidance: Because percent-identity claims leave unspecified which residues may vary, the specification must teach or otherwise enable recognition of which positions can change and still fall within the claimed genus or retain claimed function. Lack of teaching on which residues can vary may cause written description failure (Examples 10, 11).

name: Need to teach which residues/positions can vary while retaining function
description: For genus claims that allow variation (percent identity or variant lists), the specification should indicate which amino acids/positions may vary without losing the claimed activity.
guidance: If there is no disclosure or art-recognized correlation identifying allowable substitutions (or functional domains), one of ordinary skill cannot determine which variants within the percent-identity genus retain the claimed function, leading to a written description failure (Example 10, Claim 3; Example 11A).

name: Structure–function correlation increases sufficiency
description: A disclosed correlation between structural features (e.g., domains, active site residues) and function provides information on which variants will retain activity and supports claiming a genus.
guidance: Examples showing deletion studies or domain identification (binding/catalytic domains) and statements predicting effects of conservative vs non-conservative substitutions are persuasive evidence that a single species supports a genus (Example 11B). The degree of correlation required varies with the type of activity (structural proteins vs enzymatic/ligand activities).

name: Reduction to practice / actual exemplars strengthen written description
description: Disclosure of an actual reduction to practice (experimental data, sequences, deposited materials) for species within the claimed genus supports that the inventor possessed the genus.
guidance: When the specification discloses only a single species experimentally reduced to practice, claims to broader genera that include functionally defined variants may fail unless other correlating disclosure exists (Example 11, Example 13). Practice notes advise separate enablement analysis where appropriate.

name: Function-only claiming requires structural support
description: Claims framed principally by function (e.g., 'proteins that catalyze A→B') must be supported by disclosure linking structure to that function; merely claiming function across a broad set without structural correlation is insufficient.
guidance: If the specification discloses only one species that performs the function but does not teach which structural variations preserve the function, the written description fails for function-defined genus claims (Example 10, Claim 3).

name: Antisense oligonucleotide genus sufficiency based on target sequence and art-recognized correlations
description: For antisense oligonucleotide claims complementary to an mRNA, disclosure of the mRNA sequence (full-length complement) and art-recognized correlations (accessible regions, Shine-Dalgarno targeting, GC-content considerations) can support possession of representative antisense species.
guidance: Because algorithms and empirical rules exist to predict antisense activity and the full-length complement is a predictable effective species, the specification may be sufficient even absent actual antisense sequences; routine screening methods disclosed in the specification further support sufficiency (Example 12).

name: Antibody claims — adequacy of antigen disclosure and routine methods
description: An adequately characterized antigen (e.g., purified antigen, amino acid sequence, physical/chemical properties) together with routine methods for producing antibodies may support claims to antibodies against that antigen even without disclosing antibody sequences or a deposit.
guidance: Those of ordinary skill in immunology consider antigen description plus established antibody production techniques sufficient to conclude possession of antibodies to that antigen (Example 13). Evidence of general antibody class/structure knowledge also supports this conclusion.

name: Claims to antibodies across species require cross-species structural correlation
description: When a claim encompasses antibodies binding a protein from multiple species, the specification must disclose shared structural features or correlations between species (e.g., murine vs human Protein X) to show possession of the broader genus.
guidance: Functional-only statements predicting human Protein X behavior, without sequence or structural evidence or correlation to murine Protein X, are insufficient to support antibodies to non-disclosed species; an antibody claim to a genus including other species can fail absent such cross-species data (Example 14).

name: Partial structural disclosure (e.g., '95% identical') vs complete structure
description: Recitation of a partial structure (percent identity) provides partial information about the claimed molecules, but not which parts vary; the sufficiency of such recitation depends on whether the specification teaches how variation relates to structure and function.
guidance: Examiner analysis treats percent-identity recitations as partial structure requiring additional disclosure or art-knowledge to link variation to function; if the specification does not identify allowable variation or correlate structure to activity, written description may fail (Examples 10–11).

name: Art-recognized substitution/exchange groups and empirical knowledge inform analysis
description: Empirical knowledge—such as amino acid exchange groups, expected effects of substitutions on tertiary structure, and known limits of substitution tolerance—can inform whether the specification would have put one in possession of the claimed genus.
guidance: Technical notes reference literature (e.g., exchange group concepts, Chothia & Lesk) to guide the examiner; such background may allow broader claims to be supported if the art would expect structure or function conservation under certain substitutions (Example 11).

name: Teaching methods of making/identifying claimed species matters
description: Disclosure of methods for making or identifying variants (e.g., protocols for producing antibodies, gene-walking, computational screening) supports the conclusion that the inventor had possession of representative species of the claimed genus.
guidance: When the specification discloses preferred screening methods or routine production protocols, and such methods are sufficient for a skilled artisan to make/test members of the genus, written description is more likely satisfied (Examples 12, 13, 14).

name: Functional disclaimers or absence of functional limitation affect scope
description: Whether claims include or omit functional limitations (e.g., requiring catalytic activity or not) affects written description analysis; claims lacking functional limitations may encompass inert variants and require broader structural disclosure.
guidance: Example 10's Claim 2 lacked a functional limitation and thus encompassed variants irrespective of function—analysis focused on structural disclosure and whether the specification described a sufficient portion (95%) of the structure to show possession.

name: Board discretion to manage multiple proceedings
description: The Board has broad discretion to stay, transfer, consolidate, or terminate multiple proceedings (e.g., multiple AIA trials, reexaminations, reissue) involving the same patent claims and will tailor solutions to the unique circumstances of each case to optimize efficiencies and fairness.
guidance: The Board considers interests of justice and fairness, case-specific facts, and its ability to meet statutory deadlines when managing multiple proceedings; the Office will continue to develop its approach via case law and add discussion to its Practice Guide.

name: When to stay a copending reexamination or reissue in favor of an AIA trial
description: Whether to stay a copending reexamination or reissue in favor of an AIA trial is determined on a case-by-case basis with factors including overlap of issues, stage of copending proceeding, potential duplication of work, timing relative to the trial, and whether claim amendments are possible.
guidance: The Office has granted and denied stays depending on circumstances (e.g., degree of overlap, stage of reexamination, differences in evidence). The Office will continue case-by-case decisions and will not adopt blanket rule changes at this time.

name: Applying Board claim construction to copending reexamination
description: Where a reexamination is not stayed, questions arise whether the Board’s claim construction should be applied in the reexamination or whether briefing should be allowed; the Office will consider such matters case-by-case.
guidance: No general rule is provided; parties have proposed applying Board constructions to avoid inconsistent decisions, but the Office leaves these determinations to case-specific resolution.

name: Consolidation of copending reexamination/reissue with an AIA trial
description: Consolidation of an AIA trial with a copending reexamination or reissue is evaluated case-by-case; some commenters find consolidation impractical or prejudicial, while others propose a set of factors to weigh.
guidance: Factors to consider include: type of additional proceeding; time between filings; stage and duration of proceedings; scope and overlap of claims; identity and relations of third-party filers; number of proceedings; whether ex parte reexamination would lose procedures if transferred; relation to district court litigation; appeals; parties' expressed interests; potential cost/resource savings; and ability of the Board to reach timely conclusions. The Office will weigh these and other facts in deciding consolidation.

name: Markedly different characteristics (product-of-nature analysis, Step 2A)
description: For a nature-based product recited in a claim, determine whether the product has 'markedly different characteristics' from its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state. If it does, the claim does not recite a 'product of nature' exception (Step 2A: NO) and is eligible unless the claim recites another exception; if it does not, the claim is directed to an exception (Step 2A: YES) and the analysis proceeds to Step 2B.
guidance: Non-limiting examples of characteristics considered when determining whether there is a marked difference include: biological or pharmacological functions or activities; chemical and physical properties; phenotype (including functional and structural characteristics); and structure and form (chemical, genetic or physical). For single nature-based product claims, a showing of a markedly different characteristic is sufficient for eligibility (no Step 2B needed). If a 101 rejection is made, identify the exception as recited in the claim and explain why the product does not have markedly different characteristics (provide reasons referencing the naturally occurring counterpart). Examples: Chakrabarty (genetically modified bacterium with new degradative ability found markedly different); Myriad (isolated DNA identical to natural gene not markedly different; cDNA/exons-only sequence may be markedly different).

name: Step 2B - 'Significantly more' (inventive concept) analysis
description: For a claim determined to be directed to a judicial exception, determine whether any element or combination of elements in the claim is sufficient to ensure that the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception itself (the search for an 'inventive concept').
guidance: Consider the claim as a whole: individual elements viewed alone may not add significantly more, but their combination might. A claim directed to an exception must include additional features that apply the exception in a meaningful way and are not merely drafting to monopolize the exception. Every claim must be examined individually based on its particular elements and ordered combination.

name: Examples of limitations that may qualify as 'significantly more' (positive indicators)
description: Limitations that may be enough to qualify as 'significantly more' when recited with a judicial exception.
guidance: Non-exhaustive examples include: improvements to another technology or technical field; improvements to the functioning of the computer itself; applying the judicial exception with, or by use of, a particular machine; effecting a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing; adding a specific limitation other than what is well-understood, routine and conventional in the field, or adding unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application; and other meaningful limitations beyond generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment. (Citations: Diehr, Alice, Bilski, Mayo as discussed.)

name: Limitations that are not enough to qualify as 'significantly more' (negative indicators / anti-patterns)
