description: Examples of claim limitations or additions that courts have found insufficient to transform a judicial exception into patent-eligible subject matter.
guidance: Limitations found not enough include: adding the words 'apply it' (or an equivalent) with the judicial exception, or mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer; simply appending well-understood, routine and conventional activities previously known to the industry (specified at a high level of generality); adding insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., mere data gathering in conjunction with a law of nature or abstract idea); and generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use (field-of-use limitation). (Citations: Alice, Mayo, Flook, Benson, etc.)

name: Consider claim elements individually and as ordered combination
description: Evaluate whether individual claim elements, or their ordered combination, supply the necessary 'something more' to transform an exception into an eligible application.
guidance: Individual elements that seem insignificant on their own may, when considered as an ordered combination, amount to significantly more than the judicial exception. Conversely, an ordered combination that merely joins routine computer functions or conventional steps may still fail. Always analyze the claim as a whole and avoid automatically treating similar claims in an application as standing or falling together.

name: Claims reciting multiple judicial exceptions
description: Procedure when a claim is directed to a plurality of judicial exceptions (e.g., a law of nature plus an abstract idea).
guidance: Conduct the eligibility analysis for one of the exceptions. If the claim recites an element or combination that amounts to significantly more than that exception, consider whether those additional elements also amount to significantly more for the other claimed exception(s) to ensure no preemption. Additional elements that satisfy Step 2B for one exception will likely satisfy Step 2B for all exceptions in the claim. If the claim fails under Step 2B for one exception, the claim is ineligible and no further eligibility analysis is needed.

name: Streamlined eligibility analysis (efficiency for clearly eligible claims)
description: For efficiency, use a streamlined eligibility analysis for claims that may or may not recite a judicial exception but clearly do not seek to tie up any judicial exception; full analysis not required where eligibility is self-evident.
guidance: Examples: complex manufactured industrial products or processes that recite meaningful limitations along with a judicial exception (e.g., a robotic arm assembly with a control system), an artificial hip prosthesis coated with a naturally occurring mineral, or products that merely include ancillary nature-based components (e.g., cellphone with a gold electrical contact or plastic chair with wood trim). If there is doubt whether the applicant is effectively seeking coverage for the judicial exception itself, perform the full analysis.

name: Rejection drafting and identification of the exception
description: When issuing a 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection, examiners must identify how the exception is recited in the claim and explain why the claim is considered to recite an exception or lacks markedly different characteristics.
guidance: The rejection should: identify the exception as it is recited (set forth or described) in the claim; explain why it is an exception; explain why the product does not have markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart when applicable; if the claim includes additional elements, identify those elements and explain why they do not add significantly more to the exception. See MPEP 2103(VI) and 2106(III) for guidance on making the rejection.

name: Complete examination under all patentability requirements
description: Regardless of whether a 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection is made, examiners must perform a complete examination of every claim under the other patentability requirements.
guidance: Examine claims under 35 U.S.C. 102 (novelty), 103 (non-obviousness), 112 (specification/claims requirements including utility, inventorship and double patenting), and consider non-statutory double patenting as applicable. See MPEP 2103 et seq. and 2106(III).

name: Plant patent Latin name and variety denomination
description: Plant patent applicants should state the Latin name and the variety denomination for the plant claimed (Pre-AIA 37 CFR 1.76(b)(3)).
guidance: The Latin name and variety denomination are usually in the specification and will be included in any plant patent or plant patent application publication if included in an ADS or patent application. UPOV database compilation requires Latin name and variety denomination; including this information in an ADS makes compilation more efficient.

name: Graham factor — scope and content of the prior art
description: One of the Graham factors: determine the scope and content of the prior art relevant to the claimed invention.
guidance: Accurate identification of relevant prior art is the first analytical step in the U.S. obviousness inquiry; it informs subsequent comparison to the claims.

name: EPO Problem–Solution Approach — determine distinguishing aspects
description: Stage 2: determine the features that distinguish the claimed invention from the closest prior art.
guidance: This step isolates the technical contribution over the prior art that will be analyzed for inventive step.

name: EPO Problem–Solution Approach — identify the technical effect
description: Stage 3: identify the technical effect resulting from the distinguishing features.
guidance: Establishing a technical effect links claim features to concrete improvements and supports formulation of the objective technical problem.

name: Parameter (definition)
description: A 'parameter' refers to a property that needs to be measured, typically anything associated with a number (e.g. particle size, molecular weight, viscosity).
guidance: Identify which claim features are parameters early in drafting; consider whether they can be measured in multiple ways or are 'usual' vs 'unusual' in the field.

name: Unclear parameter — measurement method requirement (F‑IV, 4.11)
description: The EPO requires that the method for measuring a parameter (or at least a reference thereto) 'must appear completely in the claim itself' unless a narrow exception applies.
guidance: Per current Guidelines (post‑2019 F‑IV,4.11), include a measurement method in the claim or ensure the description provides sufficient detail to allow incorporation; be aware that the Guidelines' wording ('must') is interpreted strictly by examiners.

name: Missing measurement method in the application
description: If the application contains a parameter in a claim but no measurement method in the description, the claim may be refused for lack of clarity (Article 84 EPC) and the application can be caught in the trap.
guidance: Avoid omitting measurement methods at drafting stage; if already omitted, be prepared for difficult prosecution, provide documentary evidence, experimental data or expert declarations to support an exception, or amend claims (watch added-matter constraints).

name: Measurement method referencing trademarks
description: A detailed measurement method that refers to equipment or reagents by trademark can provoke further clarity objections (Guidelines F‑IV, 4.8) and may also lead to insufficiency objections (F‑III, 7).
guidance: Draft measurement methods to avoid reliance on proprietary names where possible; if proprietary components are essential, describe their functional properties or provide non‑proprietary alternatives to facilitate incorporation into claims.

name: Essential parameter — cannot be removed without added matter problems
description: The trap requires the parameter be 'essential' to the invention so that it cannot be removed from claims without introducing added matter (Article 123(2) EPC); if essential and unclear, the application may be refused.
guidance: Draft independent claims carefully: consider fallback claim sets that remove or reframe parameters; ensure support in the description for alternative claim formulations to avoid being unable to amend without contravening Article 123(2).

name: Policy justification: clarity for third parties (Article 84 EPC)
description: The EPO's strict approach is grounded in policy: Article 84 EPC requires claims to be clear so third parties can assess infringement — ambiguous parameters measured differently could lead to inconsistent infringement assessments.
guidance: Balance the need for clear, unambiguous claim scope with drafting strategies that protect applicant interests (detailed measurement methods where necessary, or accepting broader interpretations with known risks).

name: Alternative approach: broadest reasonable interpretation (applicant‑friendly option)
description: An alternative is to interpret an un‑defined parameter as encompassing any reasonable measurement method (broadest reasonable interpretation), which would be considered clear but broad; this is used for identity/similarity terms and in some Boards' insufficiency decisions (e.g. T 2001/10).
guidance: Be aware of pros/cons: broader claims may survive clarity objections but risk losing novelty/inventive step or triggering insufficiency across the broader scope. Applicants could choose to omit measurement methods knowingly, accepting potential adverse consequences.

name: Proving exceptions requires documentary/experimental evidence or expert declarations
description: To rely on exceptions (common general knowledge or uniformity across methods), applicants may need to submit experimental data and/or expert declarations to convince the Examining Division.
guidance: Collect and reference supporting experimental results, inter‑laboratory comparisons, standard practice references, or expert statements at filing or during prosecution to substantiate claims that a parameter is clear without a specific measurement method.

name: Practice points (practical drafting checklist)
description: Practical recommendations: (1) any parameter used to define the invention should be accompanied by a measurement method; (2) the measurement method should have sufficient detail to unambiguously define the parameter; (3) the measurement method should be drafted so it can be readily incorporated into a claim without causing further European objections.
guidance: Apply these points especially to independent claims and to any parameter that might conceivably be used in claims; if an application was not drafted this way, be prepared for difficult prosecution and consider strategic claim amendments early.

name: Intervening rights for new or amended claims (§§318(c), 328(c))
description: Intervening rights apply to new or amended claims incorporated into a patent in inter partes or post-grant review, affecting damages and the date from which they may accrue.
guidance: Amendments that substantively alter claim scope can limit damages to the date of conclusion of review (section 252 first paragraph). Intervening-rights protection helps a challenger who, upon discovering patent-defeating prior art, narrows claims and wants to practice the invention without retrospective liability; the Federal Circuit has applied intervening rights to narrowing amendments.

name: Elevated institution threshold and front-loading requirement
description: The AIA raised the threshold for instituting inter partes and post-grant review and required petitioners to front-load their case, tying challenges to specific validity arguments against particular claims.
guidance: The elevated threshold was intended to prevent challenges from 'mushrooming' into additional arguments or claims after institution and to make proceedings more efficient and timely. This front-loading, combined with the elevated threshold, was a key reform to enable meeting one-year resolution deadlines and to reduce burdens on patent owners.

name: Return of illegitimate application documents (Enforcement Rules Article 11) — list of grounds
description: KIPO or the President of the Trial and Appeal Board shall not deem application documents legitimate (and shall return them) where they fall under enumerated grounds, such as: violation of Enforcement Rules Article 2 (improper form), unclear application/document type, missing name/applicant code/address, not written in Korean, specification missing (including description), specification attached but missing claims when amendment period elapsed, applicant lacks domicile/place of business in Korea (except registered patent administrator), documents not submitted within designated period, extension requests for non-extendable periods, extension requests submitted after applicable expiration, documents submitted after termination of proceeding, documents submitted by person not entitled, unclear required ancillary forms, electronic submissions not using KIPO software or in unprocessable electronic format, and other listed subparagraphs.
guidance: Each enumerated ground includes procedural consequences (return/invalidity). For electronic submissions, KIPO-provided software/format must be used; otherwise the electronic document may be unprocessable and thus illegitimate. Fees or other formal requirements must be met; some specific subparagraphs (e.g., 5-2 re: missing claims) reference elapsed amendment periods.

name: Comity and res judicata limits in disciplinary context
description: Res judicata bars relitigation of a claim only where a court has rendered a final judgment on the merits of the same claim or cause of action; comity involves reciprocal recognition of sister-jurisdiction disciplinary acts.
guidance: Absent a state proceeding or final judgment, OED may still discipline a practitioner. The absence of state bar action means there is no judicial act to trigger comity in favor of declining sanction. Kroll supports Director's broad authority to discipline even when states have not acted.

name: Novelty (legal definition)
description: Patent novelty: the invention has not been known or used in the prior art; novelty focuses on the invention’s features compared to the prior art in a legal context.
guidance: Differentiate this legal concept from technological novelty/originality; assessment should compare specific features (claims) against prior art disclosures rather than relying on generic texts like titles/abstracts.

name: Definition of 'practice before the Office' for trademark matters (37 C.F.R. § 11.5(b)(2) and TMEP guidance)
description: Practice before the Office in trademark matters includes consulting or giving advice in contemplation of filing, preparing and prosecuting applications, preparing amendments requiring written argument, conducting opposition/cancellation or concurrent use proceedings, and appeals to the TTAB.
guidance: Activities such as drafting substantive Responses to Office Actions or remaining attorney-of-record while suspended qualify as practice. Claiming corporate-officer status to file is insufficient without supporting evidence and does not excuse unauthorized practice.

name: Contents of a patent application (Article 19)
description: A patent application must contain: I – request; II – specifications; III – claims; IV – drawings, if applicable; V – abstract; and VI – proof of payment of the filing fee.
guidance: Forms required to file are available from INPI’s website. Minimum conditions for accepting a filing include technical content, the application, and proof of payment of the filing fee (Article 21). If insufficient but containing data on object, applicant and inventor, the INPI may issue requirements to be met within 30 days.

name: Priority claim and evidence deadlines (Article 16)
description: A priority claim is made upon filing and may be supplemented within 60 days by other priorities prior to the Brazilian filing date; it must be supported by a document of origin and translation as required. If proof is not presented at filing, it must be provided within 180 days; translations for internationals must be provided within 60 days of national processing starting.
guidance: Where the Brazilian filing is faithfully contained in the document of origin, a statement by the applicant may replace the translation. Failure to provide evidence within the time limits results in loss of priority.

name: Publication timing and content (Articles 30, 226)
description: Applications are kept secret for 18 months from the filing date or earliest priority date and are published thereafter in the RPI, unless early publication is requested. Publication must contain data identifying the application and make available specifications, claims, abstract and drawings.
guidance: Applicants may request early publication; biological material referenced under Article 24(1) becomes available to the public upon publication.

name: Scope and results of technical/substantive examination (Article 35–36)
description: During technical examination, a search report and opinion are prepared concerning: I – patentability; II – suitability of the application given the nature claimed; III – reformulation of the application or division; IV – technical requirements. If the opinion finds non-patentability or issues requirements, the applicant is notified to provide comments within 90 days.
guidance: Searches are conducted by engineers and technicians across technological fields and may include worldwide prior art. Any interested party may submit comments and documents during this stage. If requirements are not met, the application will be definitively dismissed; if answered, the examination proceeds.

name: Administrative nullity grounds (Article 50) and effects
description: A patent’s nullity is declared administratively when: I – any one of the legal requirements has not been met; II – the specifications and the claims do not comply with Articles 24 and 25 respectively; III – the subject matter extends beyond the content of the application originally filed; IV – any formalities essential to the granting have not been met during processing. Nullity may be partial if remaining claims are patentable; nullity takes effect from the filing date.
guidance: Nullity proceedings may be filed by the INPI on its own initiative or by any person with legitimate interest within six months from grant (Article 51). Proceedings continue even if the patent has terminated (ex tunc effects).

name: Nullity administrative procedure / due process (Articles 51–57)
description: Once nullity proceedings are filed, due process is followed: patent holders may make a statement within 60 days; INPI issues an opinion and notifies holder and claimant within the same period; the INPI’s president decides and decision is published once final and unappealable to notify third parties.
guidance: Nullity proceedings continue regardless of patent term expiry; partial nullity possible if remaining claims are independently patentable.

name: Documentary explanation requirement for correction of mistranslation
description: Where documentary materials accompanied by a statement of correction of a mistranslation do not explain reasons for correction or where reasons for correction are not sufficiently described so that appropriateness of correction is hard to evaluate, amendment shall be ordered on the ground of insufficient reasons for correction, and the appropriateness of correction shall be evaluated after translation errors are resolved through amendment.
guidance: If amendment cannot relieve insufficient reasons for correction, correction of the mistranslation itself shall be invalidated. Examples: (1) no objective explanation why pre-amendment translation is unreasonable and post-amendment translation is reasonable; (2) vague claims that error arose from interpretation/context without sufficient description.

name: Examiner's response when applicant disputes disclosure in foreign-language specification
description: Where a notice of grounds for rejection is issued based on a foreign-language patent application and the applicant can argue that the invention under examination is not disclosed in the foreign-language specification, the reasons for rejection shall be overcome.
guidance: If applicant shows that the foreign-language spec does not disclose the claimed subject matter, the examiner must withdraw the rejection. Separately, if new matter is found in the pending foreign-language application, a notice shall be issued on ground of introduction of new matter.

name: Treatment of first-to-file rule when prior-filed application contains new matter
description: Where an invention claimed in the prior-filed application includes new matter beyond the foreign-language specification, the claimed invention cannot be relied on in issuing a rejection based on Article 36(1)-(3) of the Patent Act; new matter introduced in a prior-filed application claim cannot be a bar to a later application.
guidance: Same principle applies to foreign-language patent applications to conform to the first-to-file rule.

name: Basic approach: treat foreign-language applications as regular domestic applications
description: A foreign-language application is considered as a regular domestic application; divisional, converted, or domestic priority-claim applications shall be permitted accordingly.
guidance: For divisional/converted applications and domestic priority claims, requirements are evaluated on the basis of the foreign-language specification. However, because foreign-language specs commonly coincide with Korean translations, examiners may depend on Korean translations when determining retroactive filing dates or similar issues.

name: Application with domestic priority claim — evaluation method
description: Effects of an application claiming domestic priority to a foreign-language application shall be evaluated by comparing the Korean translations of the prior-filed application and the specification and drawings of the application claiming domestic priority.
guidance: If Korean translations of the prior-filed application have not yet been filed when the domestic-priority application is filed, the examiner shall compare the prior-filed application's specification and drawings with those of the claiming application. Otherwise examination proceeds similarly to other foreign-language application cases.

name: Specification and claim — must cover patentable matter shown
description: The claim covers only the matter claimed, but the specification covers all patentable matter shown in the specification, drawings, or model; claims must not contradict disclaimers and must be supported by description.
guidance: Description and claims treated separately though construed together; disclaimers must explain claim and not contradict it; ambiguity in description or claims can be fatal; excessive or ambiguous claims scrutinized.

name: Defenses to infringement — novelty, utility, prior use, public use, abandonment, fraud
description: Defenses include lack of inventive act, want of novelty, prior patent/publication/use, abandonment to the public, lack of utility, fraudulent specification, ambiguity, excessive or ambiguous claims, surrender or repeal of patent, and denial of plaintiff's title.
guidance: Each defense has particular requisites of pleading and proof; many require notice in pleadings; courts treat each defense with established evidentiary rules.

name: Explanation of rejection over the prior art
description: The Examiner’s Answer shall explain how the claimed subject matter is rendered unpatentable over the prior art. If the rejection is based upon a combination of references, the Examiner’s Answer ... shall explain the rationale for making the combination.
guidance: Examiner must set forth reasoning tying claim limitations to prior art and state why the combination makes the claim unpatentable; use clear rationale when combining references.

name: Feature-by-feature comparison for 35 U.S.C. 102/103 rejections
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103 where there may be questions as to how limitations in the claims correspond to features in the prior art, the examiner ... should compare at least one of the rejected claims feature by feature with the prior art relied on in the rejection.
guidance: The comparison shall align the language of the claim side by side with a reference to the specific page, line number, drawing reference number and quotation from the prior art, as appropriate.

name: Rejections related to amendments under 37 CFR 1.116 (individual rejections)
description: If an amendment under 37 CFR 1.116 proposes to add or amend claims and appellant was advised by advisory action which individual rejections would be used to reject the added/amended claims, then (1) the appeal brief must address the rejection(s) of the added/amended claim(s) and (2) the examiner’s answer may include the rejection(s) of the added/amended claims.
guidance: The rule authorizes only those individual rejections previously indicated; it does not authorize rejections based on combinations of previously-unidentified individual rejections (e.g., combining A in view of B and C when not advised). Amendments combining limitations that create new issues may be refused entry.

name: Abuse-of-rights defense (lack of inventive step)
description: A patentee’s claim for damages or injunction may constitute an abuse of rights and be impermissible when it is clear the patented invention lacks an inventive step and will be invalidated by an administrative invalidation proceeding; the court handling the infringement suit may review and determine inventive step to decide the defense.
guidance: In practice the clarity requirement is met when the judge finds the invention lacks an inventive step in the infringement suit. The defense is treated similarly where the patent lacks novelty or sufficient description. The plaintiff may reply by filing a correction to narrow claims or correct errors, provided the correction does not substantially alter what is claimed (can be done in IPTAB or separate correction petition). (Cited: Daebeobwon (Sup. Ct), Jan. 19, 2012, 2010Da95390.)

name: Required contents and timing for briefs (statements of case)
description: Parties must submit written briefs in advance. New offensive/defensive methods must be filed in time to be served at least seven days before trial; briefs should be timely to allow opponent’s response.
guidance: Specific cautions: inventive-step contentions need element-by-element charts identifying prior-art elements and mapping to patented elements; for combined prior art, specify primary prior art and explain how others combine and why combination is obvious to a person of ordinary skill. Infringement contentions must list product name/type numbers, attach drawings/photos, and include element-by-element charts comparing accused product/process with the patent, described both individually and graphically. Damages claims must specify legal provisions used for calculation and identify exhibit numbers tied to each legal element. When disputing allegations, respond with detailed answers rather than simple denials. (Civil Procedure Act articles and court rules cited.)

name: Computer-generated electronic images may be claimed without depicting a physical device
description: Applicants may present the design as a computer-generated electronic image (e.g., an icon or interface) shown alone, without any surrounding physical device in the drawings.
guidance: The specification must make clear that this image is embodied in an article of manufacture. Showing the image alone allows applicants to capture the true ornamental essence without being boxed in by hardware, but lines and shapes must precisely define scope since there is no physical frame for context.

name: Broken lines (dashed lines) indicate environmental structure not claimed
description: Broken lines may be used to show environmental structure that is not part of the claimed design (e.g., room walls, floor, ceiling, device outlines).
guidance: The new guidance clarifies flexible use of broken lines for computer-generated designs. Show the claimed design in solid lines and environmental or supporting structures in broken lines. Mastery of what to render in solid versus broken lines is critical to defining scope and complying with USPTO conventions.

name: Examination focuses on whether the design is directed to a statutory article of manufacture
description: The Office will assess whether the design is embodied in an article of manufacture rather than treating presentation rules as determinative or allowing abstract claims.
guidance: Presentational flexibility does not change statutory eligibility. Ensure claims and specification demonstrate that the design is not an abstract concept but is tied to a tangible article of manufacture.

name: Choose presentation: standalone image versus environmental context
description: Applicants must choose whether to show the design as a standalone image or with environmental context (e.g., device, room).
guidance: Use broken lines to disclaim structures you do not wish to claim. Consider which presentation best captures the ornamental essence and strategic breadth you want. Removing unnecessary physical structures can broaden scope, but choose views carefully to fully define the design.

name: Show all perspectives necessary to fully define the design
description: Drawings must show enough views to completely disclose the ornamental appearance of the claimed design.
guidance: Standalone images may require fewer views than device-attached drawings, but applicants must still show all perspectives needed to define the design. A skilled draftsman can determine the optimal number and type of views.

name: Precision and clarity of lines and shapes are paramount
description: When drawings show the claimed subject alone (no physical frame), the clarity and precision of lines and shapes must precisely define the scope of protection.
guidance: Without a device frame to constrain meaning, every line matters—imprecise rendering can unintentionally narrow or fail to capture intended features. High-quality, precise drawings improve enforceability and examination outcomes.

name: Revisit pending applications to take advantage of new guidance
description: Pending design patent applications for computer-generated interfaces, icons, or related subject matter should be reviewed in light of the guidance.
guidance: In some instances, it may be possible to file a continuation or request to amend drawings to remove unnecessary physical structures and thereby broaden protection. Evaluate existing portfolios for opportunities to update drawings or claims.

name: Use broken lines to show environmental context for holograms/projections
description: For holographic or projected designs, show environment elements (windshield, room, vehicle HUD) in broken lines to indicate they are not part of the claimed design.
guidance: This illustrates how the design appears in situ while preserving claim focus on the holographic/projection element. Broken-line environmental depiction helps clarify what is claimed vs. not claimed.

name: Do not rely on device outlines in prior art-limiting ways
description: Past practice of showing a device even when not claimed often unintentionally constrained protection; new guidance permits avoiding that limitation.
guidance: Removing unnecessary device outlines can broaden scope, but ensure the specification still ties the design to an article of manufacture and that drawings remain sufficiently descriptive.

name: Make restriction requirement final after traversal if still proper
description: If, upon reconsideration, the examiner is still of the opinion that restriction is proper, the examiner should maintain the restriction requirement and make it final in the next Office action. See MPEP § 803.01.
guidance: The examiner should reply to the reasons or arguments advanced by applicant in the traverse. Form paragraph 8.25 should be used to make a restriction requirement final. If the requirement is made final, the claims to the nonelected invention should be clearly indicated as being withdrawn from consideration (use form paragraph 8.05).

name: If requirement made final indicate withdrawn nonelected claims using form paragraph 8.05
description: When a restriction requirement is made final, nonelected claims must be shown as withdrawn from further consideration pursuant to 37 CFR 1.142(b).
guidance: Form paragraph 8.05 wording identifies withdrawn claim and whether it is an --invention-- or --species-- and shows applicant retained right to petition under 37 CFR 1.144. Use this to preserve the petition record.

name: When reconsideration shows restriction improper, withdraw and act on merits
description: If the examiner, upon reconsideration, is of the opinion that the requirement for restriction is improper in whole or in part, he or she should clearly state in the next Office action that the requirement for restriction is withdrawn in whole or in part, specify which groups have been reinstated, and give an action on the merits of all the claims directed to the elected invention and any invention reinstated with the elected invention.
guidance: Provide explicit reinstatement information and proceed to substantive examination of reinstated claims.

name: Election without traverse treated as final election
description: Where the initial requirement is not traversed (either expressly or by virtue of an incomplete reply), the examiner should take appropriate action on the elected claims including determining whether the restriction requirement should be withdrawn in whole or in part. Form paragraphs 8.25.01 or 8.25.02 should be used to acknowledge the election without traverse.
guidance: If the reply is incomplete (not distinctly and specifically pointing out supposed errors), treat as election without traverse (MPEP § 818.01(a)); use 8.25.02 for incomplete reply.

name: Treatment of claims added after an Office action (original presentation) — 37 CFR 1.145
description: Claims added by amendment following action by examiner and drawn to an invention other than the one previously claimed should be treated under 37 CFR 1.145; applicant will be required to restrict to the invention previously claimed if the amendment is entered, subject to reconsideration and review under §§ 1.143 and 1.144.
guidance: Use form paragraph 8.04 (Election by Original Presentation) to explain why newly submitted claim is directed to independent/distinct invention. Applicant must distinctly and specifically point out supposed errors in restriction to preserve right to petition. Traversal must be timely; failure to timely traverse results in loss of right to petition.

name: Rejoinder eligibility — claim must require all limitations of an allowable claim
description: In order to be eligible for rejoinder, a claim to a nonelected invention must depend from or otherwise require all the limitations of an allowable claim. A withdrawn claim that does not require all the limitations of an allowable claim will not be rejoined.
guidance: Where restriction was between product and process and product is elected and allowable, all claims to nonelected process invention must depend from or otherwise require all limitations of an allowable claim to be eligible for rejoinder. Applicant is advised to amend nonelected claims during prosecution to require limitations of elected invention to retain right to rejoinder.

name: Withdrawal of restriction removes 35 U.S.C. 121 protection and can create double patenting issues
description: Once the restriction requirement is withdrawn, the provisions of 35 U.S.C. 121 are no longer applicable. Claims in a divisional that are anticipated by or include all limitations of an allowable claim in the parent may be subject to double patenting rejections.
guidance: Cite In re Ziegler and MPEP §804.01. Advise applicants that divisional claims may be subject to provisional statutory and/or nonstatutory double patenting rejections over claims of the instant application.

name: Rejoinder between product inventions or between process inventions — withdraw restriction when claims require all limitations
description: Where restriction was required between independent or distinct products, or between independent or distinct processes, and all claims directed to an elected invention are allowable, the examiner should withdraw any restriction requirement between the elected invention and any nonelected invention that depends from or otherwise requires all the limitations of an allowable claim.
guidance: Claims that require all limitations of an allowable claim will be rejoined and fully examined. Claims that do not will remain withdrawn from consideration. Once restriction withdrawn, 35 U.S.C.121 no longer applies; double patenting considerations apply.

name: Amendments presenting additional dependent claims entered as matter of right if earlier
description: An amendment presenting additional claims that depend from or otherwise require all the limitations of an allowable claim will be entered as a matter of right if the amendment is presented prior to final rejection or allowance, whichever is earlier.
guidance: Amendments submitted after final rejection are governed by 37 CFR 1.116; after allowance by 37 CFR 1.312.

name: Form paragraph 8.45 — Elected invention allowable; rejoin all previously withdrawn claims
description: Where all claims to nonelected inventions depend from or require all limitations of an allowable claim, notify applicant that restriction requirement is withdrawn and previously withdrawn claims are rejoined and will be fully examined under 37 CFR 1.104.
guidance: Insert identification of rejoined claims and advise applicant divisional claims anticipated by or including limitations of an allowable claim may be subject to provisional double patenting rejections. Use 8.43 instead where elected invention is product and previously nonelected process claims are rejoined.

name: Form paragraph 8.49 — Elected invention allowable; claims stand withdrawn (restriction maintained)
description: When elected invention is allowable but nonelected claims do not require all limitations of an allowable claim, the restriction requirement is maintained and the nonelected claims remain withdrawn from further consideration.
guidance: Use this paragraph to explain why nonelected claims are still withdrawn. Use alternative paragraphs if nonelected claims have been canceled or if restriction is withdrawn in whole/part.

name: Form paragraph 8.50 — Elected invention allowable; partial withdrawal/partial rejoin
description: If some nonelected claims require all limitations of an allowable claim and others do not, withdraw restriction as to claims that require all limitations and maintain it for others; notify applicant which claims are rejoined and which remain withdrawn.
guidance: Specify which groups/species are affected, whether withdrawal is full or partial, and the dates. Advise about double patenting consequences for divisional applications.

name: Cancellation of nonelected claims by applicant — reinstatement by timely amendment
description: If nonelected claims which depended from or required all limitations of an allowable claim were canceled by applicant, the canceled claim(s) may be reinstated by applicant if submitted in a timely filed amendment in reply to the action. Upon entry, such amended claim(s) will be examined for patentability under 37 CFR 1.104.
guidance: Use form paragraphs 8.46, 8.47 or 8.47.01 as appropriate depending on timing (before final rejection, after final rejection, other outstanding issues). Time windows (e.g., two months) apply; if no timely amendment, application may be passed to issue.

name: Claim construction requirement in Petitions
description: Petitioners are required by the rules to construe the full breadth of each claim term in each challenged claim, even if not necessary to establish unpatentability.
guidance: USPTO commentary applies the "broadest reasonable construction in light of the specification" standard: claim terms receive their plain meaning unless inconsistent with the specification. Detailed constructions only needed for terms that take on a special meaning in view of the specification. Alternative proposed constructions are permissible. For §112(f) (means/step‑plus‑function) limitations, the construction must identify specific portions of the specification that disclose the corresponding structure, material, or acts.

name: Use of patent owner prior statements
description: A petitioner may submit statements of the patent owner filed in other proceedings before a federal court or the USPTO (but not the ITC) in which the owner took a position on claim scope.
guidance: Such statements may be submitted with the Petition or separately, but the Board will consider them only after the trial has been instituted.

name: Threshold for instituting post‑grant review
description: The Board will institute post‑grant review if the Petition, unrebutted, demonstrates that it is "more likely than not that at least one of the claims challenged in the Petition is unpatentable."
guidance: USPTO views this standard as harder to meet than the "reasonable likelihood" standard for IPR. The Board will take into account any Patent Owner Preliminary Response in determining whether the standard is met. The standard is applied claim‑by‑claim and ground‑by‑ground.

name: Filing fees for post‑grant review petitions
description: Post‑grant review petition fees depend on the number of claims challenged: fee for up to 20 claims is $35,800; $800 for each claim over 20; no small/micro entity discount.
guidance: Dependent and multiple dependent claims are counted as in IPR. Fees may make PGR much more expensive than IPR or inter partes reexamination. USPTO indicated adopting a staged fee structure with limited subsidization in separate rulemaking.

name: Statutory estoppel for petitioners, real parties, and privies
description: Estoppel applies on a claim‑by‑claim basis after a final Board decision under the same standard as IPR: arguments "raised or reasonably could have been raised" during the proceeding are precluded.
guidance: Because PGR permits broader grounds, estoppel likewise covers a broader range of arguments — after PGR final decision, petitioner, real parties, and privies are estopped from raising arguments based on §§101, 102, 103, 112 (except best mode), and/or 251 that were raised or reasonably could have been raised.

name: Determination of "technological invention" for BPM eligibility
description: When determining whether a patent is for a technological invention, the USPTO will consider whether the claimed subject as a whole recites a technological feature that is novel and unobvious over the prior art and solves a technical problem using a technical solution.
guidance: Claims reciting a novel and nonobvious device or machine that performs a financial service will be considered technological; claims that merely recite known prior art technology or a predictable combination used in a normal way to perform a financial service will not be considered technological. Parties must sometimes address novelty and nonobviousness as threshold eligibility issues.

name: General trial format and timing before the Board
description: IPR, PGR, and transitional PGR are conducted entirely before the Board in a trial format; time from institution to final decision will generally be 12 months or less (six‑month extensions available but rarely used).
guidance: During trial, petitioner must prove unpatentability by a preponderance of the evidence (lower than clear and convincing in federal court); no presumption of patentability; claim construction uses the USPTO broadest reasonable construction standard (which may be broader than federal court claim construction). Federal Rules of Evidence generally govern.

name: Petition content and strategy
description: The Petition is the petitioner's principal brief and must establish the threshold standard for institution; it should, as much as possible, contain all fully developed arguments and all evidence available to support those arguments so the petition alone establishes unpatentability of challenged claims.
guidance: Petitioners should take great care before withholding arguments or evidence for supplemental information because discovery will mainly be used to rebut patent owner arguments, not to develop petitioner's own case.

name: Preliminary Patent Owner Response (optional) — timing and scope
description: The patent owner may file an optional Preliminary Patent Owner Response no later than three months after the USPTO notice that the proceeding has been granted a filing date. The response must be limited to reasons why no trial should be instituted under 35 U.S.C. §314 (IPR) or §324 (PGR).
guidance: Page limits: 60 pages for IPR, 80 pages for PGR. The Preliminary Response may include evidence but new testimonial evidence only if in the "interests of justice." Examples of permissible arguments: statutory bar to review, asserted references not being prior art, prior art lacking a material limitation in all independent claims, prior art teaching away from proposed combination, petitioner's claim interpretation is unreasonable, brief §101 explanation, proceeding too complex to be completed within statutory time frames.

name: Institution notice limitations and rehearing
description: If the Board institutes trial for at least one challenged claim, it will mail a Notice identifying the claims and issues upon which the trial is based; claims/grounds not included in the Notice will not be part of the trial (subject to supplemental information or amendments).
guidance: A party dissatisfied with inclusion/exclusion of a claim or ground may request rehearing. Institution is claim‑by‑claim and ground‑by‑ground.

name: Patent Owner Response (full) — timing, content, evidence
description: The Patent Owner Response must be filed within three months after the Notice of trial (unless the Board sets a different time), is treated as an opposition, and is subject to the same page limits as the Petition.
guidance: It should identify all involved claims believed to be patentable, explain the basis, and be filed with all supporting evidence (affidavits/declarations) and certified translations of non‑English documents. Unlike the Preliminary Response, the Patent Owner Response may include new testimonial evidence and other new evidence without Board authorization, and can expand arguments and evidence on issues that institution did not prevent the owner from addressing. The patent owner need only establish patentability by a preponderance of the evidence.

name: Motion to amend the patent — requirements and limits
description: Patent owner has a right to file one motion to amend after conferring with the Board; additional motions require Board authorization. Each motion must show: (1) support in the original disclosure for each amended/added claim; and (2) support in earlier disclosure for any benefit of earlier filing date sought.
guidance: Motions to amend will not be authorized where the amendment does not respond to a ground involved in the trial, broadens claim scope, or introduces new matter. Motion and corresponding opposition each have 15‑page limits; proposed amendments are attachments that don't count toward page limits. Motions must be filed no later than the Patent Owner Response unless the Board sets a different deadline; late motions require good cause or Board authorization. Rules establish a rebuttable presumption that only one substitute claim is needed to replace each challenged claim and that the number of replacement claims must be "reasonable." Claim fees may be required if claim counts increase. The Board may deny a motion to amend without prejudice if original claims remain patentable.

name: Opposition to motions to amend and evidentiary scope
description: Petitioners may oppose motions to amend without authorization and may submit evidence (e.g., expert declarations) directed to proposed substitute claims.
guidance: Unless otherwise agreed, petitioner's opposition to a motion to amend is limited to 15 pages and cannot be addressed in the Reply to the Patent Owner Response; parties should address briefing limits in the preliminary conference call.

name: Petitioner's Reply limitations
description: The petitioner may file a Reply to the Patent Owner Response at a time set in the Scheduling Order, but the Reply may only respond to arguments raised in the Patent Owner Response.
guidance: If the Reply raises a new issue or belatedly presents evidence, the entire Reply will not be considered and may be returned. Examples of new issues include new evidence necessary to make out a prima facie case for unpatentability of an original claim or evidence that could have been presented earlier. Reply page limit is 15 pages. Because of this constraint, petitioners should fully present and develop their arguments in the Petition and/or supplemental information; the Reply generally cannot cure defective Petition arguments.

name: Construction and scope of license measured by claims and patent
description: The scope of a license is measured by and construed with reference to the patent and the Claim to which it is limited.
guidance: Scope may also be ascertained by the instrument itself, the conduct of the parties, and by construing several instruments together; moral conditions outside the instrument do not determine scope.

name: Licensor's duties regarding enforcement against infringers
description: If the licensor covenants to prosecute infringers, he fulfills the agreement if he stops them in any way; licensor is not necessarily bound to protect licensee against claims under adverse patents.
guidance: Licensor's covenant to sue does not prevent licensee from suing in the licensor's name; licensor not estopped to deny validity when sued by licensee for failing to prosecute; details depend on covenant wording.

name: License to multiple rights and limitations as to specific article numbers or parts
description: A license covering a certain number of articles carries the right to keep that number complete; licenses limited to particular articles do not authorize other articles unless necessary for enjoyment of the license.
guidance: Where an article is covered by several patents, a license may avail as to all; license under one patent or claim gives no protection against another patent unless encompassed.

name: Identify and explain the judicial exception recited in the claim (Step 2A Prong One)
description: A subject matter eligibility rejection should point to the specific claim limitation(s) that recites (i.e., sets forth or describes) the judicial exception and explain why those claim limitations set forth or describe a judicial exception.
guidance: Point to specific claim limitations and explain why they are considered an exception (e.g., abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon, product of nature). When the claim describes but does not expressly set forth the exception, explain what subject matter the limitations describe and why that described subject matter is a judicial exception. See MPEP § 2106.04 for more information.

name: Identification of abstract idea must mirror claim recitation and map to abstract idea groupings
description: When the examiner determines the claim recites an abstract idea, the rejection should identify the abstract idea as it is recited (i.e., set forth or described) in the claim and explain why it falls within one of the groupings of abstract ideas (mathematical concepts, mental processes, or certain methods of organizing human activity).
guidance: Alternatively, if not within those groupings, use the "tentative abstract idea" procedure and provide justification for treating a specific limitation as an abstract idea. While not required, the explanation may cite an appropriate court decision; avoid relying on non-precedential decisions unless facts uniquely match and ensure the cited decision is reasonably tied to the facts. Sample explanation: 'The claim recites the step of comparing collected information to a predefined threshold, which is an act of evaluating information that can be practically performed in the human mind. Thus, this step is an abstract idea in the "mental process" grouping.'

name: Identify and explain laws of nature and natural phenomena as recited in the claim
description: When the examiner determines the claim recites a law of nature or a natural phenomenon, the rejection should identify the law/natural phenomenon as it is recited in the claim and explain using a reasoned rationale why it is considered a law of nature or natural phenomenon.
guidance: Provide a reasoned rationale (see MPEP § 2106.04(b)). Sample explanations: 'The claim recites the correlation of X, and X is a law of nature because it describes a consequence of natural processes in the human body...' or 'The claim recites X, which is a natural phenomenon because it occurs in nature and exists in principle apart from any human action.'

name: Identify and explain product-of-nature exceptions (markedly different characteristics analysis)
description: When the examiner finds a product of nature, the rejection should identify the exception as recited in the claim and explain using a reasoned rationale why the product does not have markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state.
guidance: Compare the claimed product to its closest naturally occurring counterpart and explain why there is no indication of marked differences in structure, function, or other properties. See MPEP §§ 2106.04(b)-(c). Sample: 'The claim recites X, which was isolated from naturally occurring Y. Because there is no indication that isolation resulted in a marked difference, X is a product of nature exception.'

name: Identify additional claim elements and evaluate integration into a practical application (Step 2A Prong Two)
description: After identifying the judicial exception, identify any additional elements (features/limitations/steps) recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception and evaluate whether they integrate the exception into a practical application.
guidance: Explain the integration inquiry by addressing the additional elements both individually and in combination, using the considerations set forth in MPEP §§ 2106.04(d), 2106.05(a)-(c) and (e)-(h). Give weight to all claimed additional elements even if they are well-understood, routine, conventional activity. Remember that a new combination of known steps may be eligible (Diamond v. Diehr).

name: Explain why additional elements do or do not add 'significantly more' (Step 2B)
description: For Step 2B, the rejection should explain why the additional elements, taken individually and in combination, do not result in the claim, as a whole, amounting to significantly more than the identified judicial exception.
guidance: If certain claim elements are concluded to be well-understood, routine, conventional activities, the examiner must expressly support that conclusion in writing with one of the options specified in Subsection III. Address whether additional elements add meaningful limitations or merely implement the exception on generic computer components, add insignificant extra-solution activity, or merely impose a field-of-use limitation.

name: Rejections only when conclusion is readily apparent to examiner based on expertise
description: A rejection should be made only if it is readily apparent to an examiner relying on the examiner's expertise in the art in the Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B inquiries that the additional elements do not integrate the exception into a practical application and do not amount to significantly more than the recited judicial exception.
guidance: When making a rejection, explain the rationale underlying the conclusion so that applicant can effectively respond. Conversely, when appropriate, explain why the additional elements do integrate an exception into a practical application or provide an inventive concept by adding a meaningful limitation. See MPEP §§ 2106.04(d) and 2106.05 and MPEP § 2106.07(c) for clarifying the record when a claim is found eligible.

name: Support required when asserting elements are 'well-understood, routine, conventional' (evidentiary requirement)
description: Examiners should not assert that an additional element (or combination of elements) is well-understood, routine, or conventional unless the examiner finds, and expressly supports the rejection in writing with one or more of the specified supports.
guidance: Permitted supports (Subsection III): (A) citation to an express statement in the specification or an applicant statement demonstrating the element is well-understood/routine/conventional (e.g., described as commercially available or not described in detail because well-known); (B) citation to one or more relevant court decisions (ensure the claim limitations match in manner and generality); (C) citation to a publication (book, manual, review article) demonstrating wide prevalence or common use in the relevant field (single patent/publication usually insufficient); (D) an examiner taking official notice based on personal knowledge that an element is widely prevalent or in common use (use only when certain; see MPEP § 2144.03 for procedures). Do not base a finding solely on the specification being silent regarding the element.

name: Treatment of generic computer components and generic computing functions
description: For claim limitations that recite a generic computer component performing generic computer functions at a high level of generality, examiners can explain why these generic computing functions do not meaningfully limit the claim.
guidance: Keep in mind courts have found some computer-implemented processes to be significantly more than an abstract idea when generic components in combination perform functions that are not merely generic (see DDR Holdings). See MPEP § 2106.05(f) for examples of generic computing functions found to be mere instructions to implement an exception on a computer. Explain why generic recitations amount to no meaningful limitation where appropriate.

name: Insignificant extra-solution activity and field-of-use limitations do not make claims eligible
description: Claim limitations that add insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., mere data gathering) or that generally link the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use generally do not meaningfully limit the claim.
guidance: Provide an explanation why such limitations fail to integrate the exception into a practical application. Examples: adding a final step of storing data to a process of computing area (mathematical relationship) does not add a meaningful limitation; limiting use to a particular industry (Parker v. Flook) is insufficient. See MPEP §§ 2106.05(g) and (h).

name: Consideration of claim element combinations — new combinations may be eligible
description: When evaluating additional elements, examiners must consider elements both individually and in combination, because a new combination of steps in a process may be patent eligible even though all the steps individually were well known.
guidance: Cite Diamond v. Diehr as authority. It is particularly critical to address the combination of additional elements because while individually-viewed elements may not integrate an exception, their combination may amount to significantly more by meaningfully limiting the judicial exception. See MPEP § 2106.05 for Step 2B considerations.

name: Best practice — suggest claim elements from the specification that could make claim eligible
description: In the event a rejection is made, it is a best practice for the examiner to consult the specification to determine if there are elements that could be added to the claim to make it eligible and, if so, identify those elements in the Office action and suggest them as a way to overcome the rejection.
guidance: Identify specific specification disclosure that could be used to amend claims to add meaningful limitations that integrate the exception into a practical application.

name: Use of prescribed form paragraphs for §101 rejections
description: Use specific form paragraphs for rejections involving statutory categories and judicial exceptions: 7.04.01, 7.05, 7.05.01, 7.05.016, and when applicable 7.05.017 (tentative abstract idea requiring TC Director signature).
guidance: Form paragraph rules: 7.04.01 (Statement of Statutory Basis) must precede first use of 35 U.S.C. 101 in first actions and final rejections. 7.05 should precede 7.05.01 and be followed by a detailed explanation using one or more of the specific form paragraphs. For claims directed to a judicial exception without providing significantly more, use 7.05.016 (and 7.05.017 for tentative abstract ideas). See examiner notes for bracketed instructions on filling each form paragraph.

name: Required content for form paragraph 7.05.016 (bracketed instructions)
description: Form paragraph 7.05.016 must state that the claimed invention is directed to [law of nature/natural phenomenon/abstract idea/product of nature] without significantly more and include bracketed material that identifies the exception, how it is recited, why it is not integrated into a practical application, and why additional elements do not amount to significantly more.
guidance: Follow the examiner notes: bracket 1 — identify type of exception; bracket 2 — identify the exception by reference to how recited in the claim and explain why it is an exception (e.g., map to abstract idea grouping or explain product-of-nature comparison); bracket 3 — explain why combination of additional elements fails to integrate into a practical application (examples: generic computer elements merely implement abstract idea, data gathering is insignificant); bracket 4 — explain why additional elements do not amount to significantly more. For tentative abstract ideas, include 7.05.017 and TC Director signature.

name: Requisites of the Application (35 U.S.C. 111(a))
description: When a new application is assigned in the examining group, the examiner should review contents to determine if the application meets the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 111(a). Matters affecting filing date or abandonment (lack of oath/declaration, filing fee, or claims) should be checked before placing the application in storage.
guidance: Examiners must ensure the application meets MPEP Chapter 600 requisites (formal matters and completeness/clarity of disclosure). If requisites are not met, applicant may be called for necessary amendments, which must not include new matter.

name: Search: Understand Invention Before Searching
description: After reading the specification and claims, the examiner searches the prior art. The invention should be thoroughly understood before a search is undertaken; nevertheless, informal or imperfectly understood cases are also given a search to avoid piecemeal prosecution.
guidance: See MPEP Chapter 900 for detailed search guidance. When assigned after another examiner, give full faith and credit to prior examiner's search and action unless there's clear error or knowledge of other prior art. Generally avoid entirely new approach or new search just to hope of finding something.

name: Sequence of Examination in P.R. Cases
description: If supervisory patent examiners cannot agree as to order of examination by groups, the supervisory examiner having jurisdiction will direct a complete search be made prior to referring the application for report; reporting group will be advised of results.
guidance: If a different sequence of search is expedient, modify order accordingly. Where claims are directed to same character of invention but differ only in scope, P.R. is never proper.

name: Rejection of Claims — General Standard and Practice (37 CFR 1.104)
description: If the invention is not considered patentable, or not patentable as claimed, the claims (or those considered unpatentable) will be rejected. In rejecting claims for want of novelty or for obviousness, the examiner must cite the best references and designate the particular part relied on when reference is complex. The pertinence of each reference must be clearly explained and each rejected claim specified.
guidance: The goal is to articulate any rejection early so applicant can reply and provide evidence. Examiner should review all evidence, arguments, and responsive evidence before issuing next Office action. Examiner may rely on admissions by applicant or facts within knowledge (including 102(f)/(g) prior art as permitted under 103). When multiple features present in reference, designate parts relied upon as nearly as practicable.

name: Distinction Between Rejection and Objection
description: A 'rejection' refuses to grant claims because subject matter is unpatentable (merits), while an 'objection' addresses improper claim form. Rejections are subject to Board of Patent Appeals and Interferences review; objections (formal matters) generally are reviewable only by petition to the Commissioner.
guidance: Do not combine formal objections with rejections in appeals improperly. Use the terms accurately in examiner's action. Examples: dependency on a rejected claim is a form matter and treated as an objection if dependent claim otherwise allowable.

name: 35 U.S.C. 103 — Nonobviousness Rejections (Contents and Practice)
description: A patent may not be obtained though the invention is not identically disclosed as in 102 if differences between claimed invention and prior art are such that claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art. Rejections under 103 must set forth the basis for combining references and explain pertinence.
guidance: Include contents of 103 rejection (706.02(m) form paragraphs). Provisional rejections combining 102(e) and 103 may be used. Ensure proper factual findings, rationale for combining references, and apply the Graham factual inquiries (scope, differences, level of ordinary skill, objective indicia). See MPEP §706.02 for details and form paragraphs.

name: Non-Precedential/Non-Prior-Art Rejections (35 U.S.C. 101, 112, etc.)
description: Rejections not based on prior art include 35 U.S.C. 101 (patentable subject matter / utility), 35 U.S.C. 112 first paragraph (written description, enablement, best mode), 35 U.S.C. 112 second paragraph (definiteness), barred by Atomic Energy Act, new matter, duplicate claims, disclaimer, reissue, res judicata, and other non-art bases for rejection.
guidance: Follow section-specific MPEP guidance: 706.03(a) provides guidelines for utility requirement (101) and interplay with 112; 706.03(c)/(d) cover 112 first and second paragraphs. For new matter and duplicative claims, apply the procedural rules and form paragraphs identified. Ensure the applicant is given constructive guidance for correction when possible.

name: Defects in Form or Omission of a Limitation — Constructive Examiner Action
description: When claims are intended to be directed to patentable subject matter but cannot be allowed because of defects in form or omission of a limitation, the examiner should not stop with a bare objection or rejection but should offer a definite suggestion for correction.
guidance: Be constructive and identify how claims can be amended to be allowable. Where patentable subject matter disclosed but not claimed, note aspects/features unclaimed and indicate that if properly claimed they may receive favorable consideration.

name: Completeness and Clarity of Examiner's Action
description: Examiner's action must be complete on formal matters, require new oath when necessary, satisfy draftsperson requirements, use correct language in rejecting claims, note all outstanding requirements, answer all material traversed, avoid piecemeal examination, and notify applicants of inaccuracies in amendments. Each claim should be mentioned in each letter, and when claims are allowable that should be stated.
guidance: Follow MPEP §707.07 and subparts for detailed procedures including numbering paragraphs, comment on examples, reviewing/initialing, signing by authorized examiner, entry date, and mailing returned Office actions. Ensure the office action is clear and addresses all presentable issues.

name: Affidavits and Declarations Traversing Rejections; Swearing Back (37 CFR 1.131/1.132)
description: Affidavits or declarations under 37 CFR 1.131 (swearing back of reference) and 1.132 (other traversing affidavits) have different requirements. Who may make the affidavit, formal requirements, factual and documentary evidence needed, and practice relative to showing how much of the claimed invention must be shown, genus-species issues, and predictability questions are covered.
guidance: Distinguish between 1.131 (antenuptial or swearing back against a reference with specific statutory situations) vs 1.132 affidavits. Examiners should review affidavits for evidence of prior public use/sale or failure to disclose best mode and for sufficiency. See MPEP §715 and §716 for guidance on diligence, who may make affidavits, and forms.

name: Evidence and Weighing of Nonobviousness (Objective Indicia) (MPEP §716)
description: Guidance on generally applicable criteria for nonobviousness: objective evidence categories include unexpected results, commercial success (commensurate in scope with claimed invention), long-felt need and failure of others, skepticism of experts, copying, inoperability of references, and other probative evidence. Evidence must be weighed and compared with closest prior art; burden is on applicant for some assertions.
guidance: See MPEP §716.01–716.03 for details: (a) objective evidence of nonobviousness, (b) nexus requirement and evidence of claims, (c) weighing objective evidence, (d) evidence must show unexpected results commensurate in scope, (e) comparison with closest prior art, (f) declared advantages disclosed or inherent. Declarations/affidavits should follow prescribed forms. Commercial success and other indicia must be tied (nexus) to claimed invention and commensurate in scope.

name: File Wrappers and Record Keeping (Arrangement, Papers, Indexing)
description: Papers in file wrapper must be arranged and indexed: name/residence of inventor, title, prints, data entered on file wrapper, changed classification during examination, index of claims, field of search, foreign filing dates, related applications, public use proceeding testimony, and preliminary handling.
guidance: Follow MPEP §719 for organization of the file wrapper. Maintain completeness and clarity of the patent file wrapper. Ensure required data are entered and accessible for subsequent prosecution, appeals, or public inspection where applicable.

name: §101 is a threshold test; satisfy other statutory requirements
description: The §101 patent-eligibility inquiry is only a threshold test. Even if an invention qualifies under §101, it must also satisfy the conditions and requirements of this title, including novelty (§102), nonobviousness (§103), and full and particular description (§112).
guidance: Applicants should not assume §101 eligibility guarantees a patent; novelty, nonobviousness, and adequate disclosure remain essential safeguards and may limit overbroad claims.

name: Business methods are not categorically excluded
description: Section 101 does not categorically exclude business methods from being 'processes'; the term 'method' may include some methods of doing business. Federal statute (§273) contemplates the existence of at least some business method patents.
guidance: Although business methods are not per se unpatentable, courts should be wary: business-method claims raise issues of vagueness and potential overbreadth, and other statutory requirements (§102/§103/§112) and precedent (e.g., abstract-idea doctrine) will constrain patentability.

name: Diehr principle — application of mathematical formulas/laws to a process may be patentable
description: An application of a law of nature or mathematical formula to a known structure or process may be deserving of patent protection; the invention must be considered as a whole rather than dissecting old and new elements and ignoring the presence of old elements.
guidance: Claims that integrate an algorithm or law into a concrete industrial process (e.g., molding rubber with computer calculations) can be patentable; evaluate the claim holistically and whether it is an attempt to patent the formula itself.

name: Policy concern: set an appropriately high bar for business-method-like claims
description: If a low bar is set for patenting business-method-like inventions, examiners and courts could be flooded with claims that chill creative endeavor and dynamic change; vagueness and suspect validity are particular problems.
guidance: Use precedent (Benson, Flook, Diehr) and the requirements of novelty, nonobviousness, and particularity of description (§102/§103/§112) to limit grants and prevent undue preemption; consider statutory features like §273 and policy goals when assessing business-method claims.

name: Filing date requirements for nonprovisional applications (37 CFR 1.53(b))
description: Under 37 CFR 1.53(b), a filing date is assigned to a nonprovisional application as of the date a specification containing a description and claim and any necessary drawings are filed in the USPTO. Failure to meet any of the requirements in 37 CFR 1.53(b) will result in the application being denied a filing date. The filing date to be accorded such an application is the date on which all of the requirements of 37 CFR 1.53(b) are met.
guidance: The filing fee, search fee and examination fee for an application filed under 1.53(b) and the oath or declaration can be submitted after the filing date, but no amendment may introduce new matter into the disclosure after the filing date. If an application accorded a filing date lacks parts, applicant will be notified and given time to file missing parts (generally 2 months). Applicants should submit copies of notices and include application number on correspondence to aid processing. See related provisions 37 CFR 1.53(e),(f) and MPEP guidance on handling missing parts.

name: Conversion from provisional to nonprovisional (37 CFR 1.53(c)(3))
description: A provisional application may be converted to a nonprovisional application and accorded the original filing date of the provisional. The conversion must be accompanied by the fee set forth in § 1.17(i) and an amendment including at least one claim as prescribed by the second paragraph of 35 U.S.C.112 unless the provisional already contains such a claim. The resulting nonprovisional must include the filing fee, search fee, examination fee, an oath or declaration pursuant to §§ 1.63, 1.162, or 1.175, and the surcharge required by § 1.16(f) if applicable. The request must be filed prior to abandonment of the provisional or expiration of twelve months.
guidance: Conversion affects patent term: the term of any patent issuing from the application will be measured from at least the filing date of the provisional; applicants should consider claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C.119(e) instead, which is less expensive and results in a longer patent term. No refund of provisional fees; time limits are strict. See MPEP for practical considerations.

name: Applications filed under 37 CFR 1.53(d) (continuation/divisional of design applications)
description: 37 CFR 1.53(d) may be used to file either a continuation or a divisional application (but not a continuation-in-part) of a design application. The prior nonprovisional application must be a design application complete as defined by 37 CFR 1.51(b). Any application filed under 1.53(d) must disclose and claim only subject matter disclosed in the prior nonprovisional application and must name as inventors the same or less than all inventors named in the prior application. Under 1.53(d) the filing date assigned is the date on which a request, on a separate paper, for an application under 1.53(d) is filed; the application must be filed before payment of the issue fee on the prior application, abandonment, or termination of proceedings.
guidance: Filing fee, search fee and examination fee and the oath/declaration for an application filed under 1.53(b) or 1.53(d) can be submitted after the filing date. No amendment may introduce new matter after the filing date. See MPEP §201.06(d) for CPA limitations and related practice changes (e.g., CPAs limited to design applications effective July 14, 2003).

name: Oath or declaration requirements and limitations
description: An oath or declaration filed in reply to a notice under 37 CFR 1.53(f) must be executed by the inventors and must identify the specification and any amendment filed with the specification which includes subject matter not otherwise included in the specification (including claims) or drawings of the application. No new matter may be included after the filing date of the application.
guidance: If an amendment is filed with the oath/declaration after the filing date, it may be identified but may not include new matter. If the oath/declaration improperly refers to an amendment filed after the filing date which contains new matter, a supplemental oath/declaration will be required pursuant to 37 CFR 1.67(b) deleting the reference. If an amendment is filed the same day the application is filed, it is part of the original papers and new matter is not considered. Alterations prior to execution of the oath and the filing are considered part of the original disclosure.

name: Treatment of applications filed without all pages of specification — notices and applicant options
description: OPAP reviews application papers to determine whether all pages of specification are present. If filed without all pages but containing something that can be construed as a written description, at least one drawing figure if necessary, and (for nonprovisional) at least one claim, OPAP will mail a “Notice of Omitted Items” indicating a filing date was accorded but pages are lacking. If the application contains nothing that can be construed as a written description, OPAP will mail a “Notice of Incomplete Application” indicating lack of the specification required by 35 U.S.C.112 and no filing date is granted.
guidance: If mailed a Notice of Omitted Item(s), within 2 months applicant may: (A) file a petition under 37 CFR 1.53(e) with fee and evidence that the pages were received (petition fee refunded if successful); (B) submit omitted pages in a nonprovisional application with an oath/declaration and a petition under 37 CFR 1.182 requesting the later filing date (2-month non-extendable); or (C) accept the application as deposited by not filing a petition (constructive acceptance), in which case amendment to renumber pages and cancel incomplete sentences should be made by preliminary amendment prior to first Office action to avoid delay. If the omitted portion is wholly contained in a prior-filed application and priority is claimed, applicant may submit an amendment under 37 CFR 1.57(a) within 2 months. The 2-month period is not extendable under 37 CFR 1.136.
