For provisional applications the USPTO will generally not grant petitions under 1.182 to accept omitted pages; applicant should file a new provisional application.

name: Criteria for an application to be entitled to a filing date despite omissions and examiner actions
description: An application is entitled to a filing date if the application contains something that can be construed as a written description, at least one drawing figure if necessary under 35 U.S.C.113 (first sentence), and at least one claim. If a Technology Center discovers an application filed without pages and a Notice of Omitted Items was not mailed by OPAP, the examiner should determine whether the application is entitled to a filing date.
guidance: If entitled to a filing date, the examiner should notify applicant of the omission in the next Office action and require applicant to: (A) accept the application as filed without all pages; (B) file omitted pages with an oath/declaration and a petition under 37 CFR 1.182 requesting the date of submission as the filing date; or (C) file a petition under 37 CFR 1.53(e) with supporting evidence that the pages were deposited with the original filing. The original application papers that are present in the USPTO on the date of deposit form the original disclosure for filing date purposes.

name: Alice/Mayo step one — directed to natural phenomenon or abstract idea
description: Determine whether the claims are directed to a patent-ineligible concept such as a natural phenomenon or abstract idea.
guidance: Court evaluates the 'focus' of the claims to see if they recite subject matter like a product of nature or an abstract idea; example here: claims reciting combinations of nutrients that exist in almonds were found directed to a product of nature. (Cites: Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank Int’l, Mayo Collaborative Servs. v. Prometheus.)

name: Alice/Mayo step two — additional limitations must supply an inventive concept
description: If claims are directed to a natural phenomenon or abstract idea, determine whether additional claim limitations transform the ineligible concept into patent-eligible subject matter.
guidance: Additional limitations that are 'well-known and conventional' do not supply the requisite inventive concept; merely adding conventional packaging, crushing, administering, selecting, determining, or routine computer components is insufficient. (Cites: Alice; Genetic Techs.; PersonalWeb.)

name: Product of nature analysis
description: Claims that effectively claim a composition or combination that exists in nature are patent-ineligible as a product of nature.
guidance: Court compares claimed compositions to naturally occurring substances (example: dosages and components recited are found in almonds); limiting the form (e.g., mixtures or non-specific varieties) does not necessarily avoid a product-of-nature finding if the claimed combination exists in nature.

name: Abstract idea — conventional computer implementation does not rescue claims
description: Claims to an abstract idea are not rendered patent-eligible merely by implementing the idea with routine or conventional computer components.
guidance: Claim elements that add only conventional computer components or automate an abstract idea (e.g., meal planning) do not transform the claim under Alice step two. (Example: claim 112 found directed to meal planning; adding computer system components was conventional.)

name: Obviousness under 35 U.S.C. §103
description: A claim is unpatentable if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention would have been obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention.
guidance: Overlapping dosage ranges in prior art create a presumption of obviousness; challenger must produce evidence of teaching away or unexpected results to overcome the presumption. Court may rely on expert testimony that benefits were well-known in the art to support obviousness. Prior art from the same field of endeavor is particularly persuasive.

name: Rebutting obviousness — teaching away and unexpected results
description: To rebut a presumption of obviousness, a patentee may show that prior art taught away from the claimed invention or that the claimed invention produces unexpected results.
guidance: Conclusive assertions are insufficient; the patentee must produce evidence. Failure to show teaching away or unexpected results supports summary judgment of obviousness.

name: Written description / §112 considerations
description: Claims must satisfy the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. §112 by showing the inventor possessed the claimed invention as described in the specification.
guidance: Examiner may reject claims for lack of written description; Board and courts review such rejections on the merits. Procedural default (failure to brief an issue) can lead to summary affirmance on §112 grounds.

name: Indefiniteness and improper dependency consequences
description: Claims can be rejected as indefinite or improperly dependent if claim language fails to provide clear scope or correct dependency structure.
guidance: Failure to present substantive arguments on these grounds on appeal can result in summary affirmance of the rejections; the Board may summarily affirm rejections where appellant does not meaningfully contest them.

name: Sovereign immunity waiver and jurisdiction for money damages
description: Waivers of sovereign immunity for money damages must be expressed unequivocally by Congress; the Tucker Act grants the Court of Federal Claims exclusive jurisdiction over non-tort money damages claims exceeding $10,000.
guidance: Statutes like 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331, 1338, and 35 U.S.C. §145 do not, absent clear statutory language, waive sovereign immunity for money damages; plaintiffs seeking >$10,000 must generally proceed in the Court of Federal Claims under the Tucker Act.

name: Judicial recusal standard
description: Recusal requires showing that a judge has a substantial interest or bias that would tempt an average judge to be biased; adverse rulings alone generally do not establish bias.
guidance: Judicial rulings, critical remarks, or hostile statements ordinarily do not support a successful recusal claim; the movant must show facts establishing a substantial interest or personal bias beyond judicial rulings.

name: Situations where reward is not payable
description: Rewards are not to be paid for partial performance, for merely giving notice of location without delivery, without delivery, for apprehension of a man discharged without honor (except by mistake), when a deserter is arrested abroad without authority, when extradited on other charges, when delivered to civil custody without request, or where there is evidence of collusion or no evidence of desertion; no reimbursement for damages/expenses if wrong man arrested.
guidance: Claimants for reward must have effected proper delivery under authorized circumstances; exclude cases of partial performance, mere information, wrong person, or improper custody/authority. (Detailed list items V.F and subitems.)

name: Description supports the claims (support requirement)
description: There must be a basis in the description for the subject matter of every claim; the support requirement does not mean description and claims must be drafted in identical terms but typically the scope of the claims will not be interpreted more broadly than the description and drawings.
guidance: Only reasonable restrictions on claim breadth relate to the prior art and whether the disclosure is supported. Always provide adequate support in the description for client’s claims; you cannot add wholly new material in response to an examiner’s objections. Try to anticipate narrower elements you may later need to add to claims and embed support for these in the description at the outset. The support requirement protects the public from claims broader than justified and protects the applicant from attempting to claim unsupported subject matter.

name: Degree of generalization in claims
description: Claims are typically generalizations from one or more particular examples, and the admissible degree of generalization varies with the field of technology and relevant prior art.
guidance: Claims for inventions that open new fields may be more extensively generalized than improvements in well-known fields. A fair claim is neither so broad that it goes beyond the invention nor so narrow as to deprive the applicant of a just reward. The applicant may cover obvious modifications, equivalents and uses where reasonable to do so (i.e., when variants will have the properties or uses ascribed in the description). If claiming broad categories (e.g., all plant seedlings) but disclosure or evidence supports only a subset, restrict claims accordingly unless convincing evidence of broader applicability is provided.

name: Extent of disclosure relative to desired claim breadth
description: The amount of disclosure required depends on the scope of protection sought: broader protection generally requires more extensive disclosure; narrow protection may require less.
guidance: Unnecessarily extensive disclosure is not prohibited but increases cost and shares more of the invention with the public. For broader patent protection, provide a more extensive disclosure; for narrow protection, a single embodiment may suffice. Counsel clients about the likely impact of breadth and possible need for alternative amendments before widening claim breadth.

name: Consistent claim point of view
description: All limitations or elements in a single claim should have a consistent point of view (for example, all steps in a method claim should be performed by the same party).
guidance: A consistent point of view matters for naming parties who could directly infringe a claim. Where inventive components are spread across different parties (e.g., battery vs flashlight manufacturers, client vs server), a claim mixing actors may make direct infringement harder to prove and reduce licensing/enforcement leverage. Draft separate claims shifting the point of view (e.g., client-only, server-only, combination, or component-only claims) while retaining the original claim as appropriate. Consider evidence and detection issues for direct versus indirect infringement when setting point of view.

name: Draft claims to facilitate enforcement and licensing (direct vs indirect infringement)
description: Claims should be drafted so that direct infringement is provable and so they support licensing and enforcement strategies.
guidance: Direct infringement is generally easier to prove and often a prerequisite for alleging contributory or induced infringement. Product claims are typically easier to detect and prove than method/process claims. If no single party practices an entire claim, it may be difficult to enforce; draft claims (and claim families) to enable at least one claim to read on entities you expect to license or sue. Anticipate need to detect and evidence indirect infringement when direct infringement is unlikely.

name: All-elements rule — ensure claims read on client’s embodiments
description: A claim reads on an accused product or process only if every element of the claim is present (all-elements rule).
guidance: Make sure at least one claim in the application reads on the embodiments made, used or sold by the client. If claims do not read on the client’s embodiment, the drafter may have misunderstood the invention or the client’s practice may have changed. After grant, incorrect claim coverage may prevent valid marking and make it hard to collect lost profits (though reasonable royalties may still be available). Regularly verify claim scope against client embodiments.

name: Narrowing claims during prosecution (amendment strategies and limits)
description: Claims may need to be narrowed during prosecution to render them patentable; narrowing can be achieved by (i) adding new elements, (ii) adding a limitation to a previously recited element, and/or (iii) further defining how previously recited elements interoperate.
guidance: Often the prior art can be overcome not by adding wholly new limitations but by further defining existing elements or their interrelations (e.g., amending to add that ‘A receives the output of B’). When adding new elements, ensure the element further defines an existing structural/functional element or is a relational element; the new element must be present in the description as of the filing date (no new matter). Most patent offices require clear showings of changes: indicate amendments (e.g., labels such as [Amended], strike-through for deletions, underlining for additions) according to local rules. Avoid adding elements that would significantly and unnecessarily reduce the client’s protection without counseling the client on impacts.

name: Formal requirements for showing amendments
description: Patent offices commonly require clear identification of changes when amending claims during prosecution.
guidance: Submit amendments in the format required by local patent rules (e.g., indicate amended claims, use strike-through for deletions and underlining for newly added words) so examiners can easily see what has changed. Follow local procedural rules for amendment presentation to avoid form rejections or confusion.

name: Subject-matter eligibility and exclusions from patentability
description: Many jurisdictions exclude certain subject matter from patent protection; the scope and specifics of exclusions vary significantly between jurisdictions and over time (e.g., judicial exceptions in the United States, broader statutory exclusions elsewhere).
guidance: Patent drafters may sometimes overcome exclusions by redrafting claims—wording changes can avoid an exclusion even where the description is substantively the same. Exercise particular care with biotechnology inventions (e.g., discoveries, embryos, uses contrary to public order/morality) and methods of treatment, which may be excluded in some jurisdictions. Consider reformatting claims (e.g., claim manufacturing or testing methods or new products for use in treatment) to seek allowable protection. Stay up to date with national/regional laws and case law in jurisdictions important to clients.

name: Requirement for industrial applicability (including sequences)
description: Inventions must be capable of industrial application; in some fields this has specific manifestations—for example, gene sequences or partial sequences must have a disclosed industrial application or function.
guidance: A mere nucleic acid sequence without an indication of function is generally not patentable; where a sequence is used to produce a protein, specify which protein/part is produced and its function, or indicate other applicable functions (e.g., promoter activity). Recast claims where necessary to demonstrate industrial applicability (for example, reframing a subjective ‘fashion advice’ device as an inventory-management device if appropriate). Follow regional rules such as the EPO’s requirement to indicate how the invention is capable of exploitation when not self-evident.

name: Claim construction in courts and defining claim terms
description: Courts interpret claims by reading the claims and the description, giving terms their ordinary meaning to a person skilled in the art, and using additional intrinsic or extrinsic evidence as needed.
guidance: If the claims and description do not clearly communicate a specific meaning, courts refer to the general meaning to a person skilled in the art; in the U.S. dictionaries and extrinsic materials may be used but courts typically begin with ordinary meaning and then consult the description and prosecution history. When creating new terms, where multiple meanings exist, or where ambiguity may arise, define terms explicitly in the description (the description can act as a glossary). Aim for a self-contained application that can be understood without external context. Be cautious about relying on the doctrine of equivalents — it is unpredictable; draft claims to give terms ordinary and customary meanings to the person skilled in the art to maximize certainty.

name: Specification shows improvement to technology
description: The specification need not explicitly set forth the improvement, but it must describe the invention such that the improvement would be apparent to one of ordinary skill in the art; a conclusory, bare assertion of an improvement without necessary detail is insufficient.
guidance: An indication that the claimed invention provides an improvement can include a discussion in the specification that identifies a technical problem and explains the details of an unconventional technical solution expressed in the claim, or identifies technical improvements realized by the claim over the prior art. Examples: McRO (specification explained how rules automated animation tasks); contrast Affinity Labs (failure to provide details was dispositive).

name: Claim reflects the disclosed improvement (claim-as-a-whole)
description: After finding the specification discloses an improvement, the claim must be evaluated to ensure the claim itself reflects the disclosed improvement in technology; the claim must include the components or steps of the invention that provide the improvement.
guidance: The claim itself does not need to explicitly recite the improvement (e.g., 'thereby increasing the bandwidth of the channel'), but the full scope of the claim under the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) should be considered. Evaluate the claim 'as a whole,' i.e., 'as an ordered combination, without the requirements of individual steps.' Be careful to avoid oversimplifying claims by looking at them generally and failing to account for specific claim requirements (citing Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec and McRO).

name: Particularity of claimed solution vs claiming an idea/outcome
description: Determine whether the claim covers a particular solution to a problem or a particular way to achieve an outcome, as opposed to merely claiming the idea of a solution or the outcome itself.
guidance: This consideration overlaps with 'particular machine' and 'mere instructions to apply an exception' analyses; evaluation of those considerations may assist in determining whether a claim satisfies the improvement consideration (citing McRO and DDR Holdings).

name: Improvement to computer functionality (vs computer as tool)
description: For computer-related technologies, determine whether the claim purports to improve computer capabilities (an improvement to computer functionality) or merely invokes a computer as a tool to perform an existing process.
guidance: Court examples: Enfish (improved way computer stores/retrieves data demonstrated eligibility) contrasted with cases where a computer was merely added post-hoc. The claim should show a specific implementation of a solution to a software problem rather than a generic addition of a computer.

name: Claim scope must be limited to computer implementation to show computer improvement
description: A method claim's broadest reasonable interpretation must be limited to computer implementation to be considered an improvement to computer technology; if the entire scope can be performed mentally or verbally, it cannot be said to improve computer technology.
guidance: Cases: Synopsys (method could be performed mentally — ineligible), RecogniCorp (process practicable verbally/telephone — ineligible). If a claimed process covers both computer and non-computer embodiments, it may fail to improve computer technology.

name: Negative examples: insufficient to show computer-functionality improvement
description: Illustrative examples where courts found claimed subject matter did not amount to an improvement in computer functionality or technology.
guidance: Includes (i) generating restaurant menus with functionally claimed features (Ameranth), (ii) speeding up analysis solely by virtue of general-purpose computer (FairWarning), (iii) mere automation of manual processes on generic computers (Credit Acceptance; LendingTree), (iv) recording/transmitting/archiving images using conventional tech without technical details (TLI Communications), (v) affixing barcode without technical limitations (Secured Mail Solutions), (vi) instructions to display two sets of information without how to achieve it (Interval Licensing), (vii) improving information stored by a database is not necessarily improving database functionality (BSG Tech), (viii) arranging GUI info to assist traders (Trading Technologies).

name: Require details how computer aids method; mere generic computer additions insufficient
description: To show that computer involvement assists in improving technology, claims must recite details regarding how a computer aids the method, the extent to which it aids the method, or the significance of a computer to the performance of the method; merely adding generic computer components is not sufficient.
guidance: The claim must include more than mere instructions to perform the method on generic components or machinery. See MPEP § 2106.05(f) for 'mere instructions to apply an exception' guidance.

name: Machine-or-transformation is a useful clue but not a standalone test
description: The machine-or-transformation (M-or-T) test is a useful and important clue and investigative tool when determining patent eligibility, but it is not a stand-alone test and does not supersede the Alice/Mayo framework.
guidance: All claims must be evaluated under the two-part Alice/Mayo test: if a claim passes Alice/Mayo it is eligible even if it 'fails' the M-or-T test; if a claim fails Alice/Mayo it is ineligible even if it passes the M-or-T test (citing Bilski, McRO, DDR Holdings).

name: Particularity or generality of machine/apparatus elements
description: When assessing whether a recited machine provides 'significantly more,' consider how specifically the machine or its elements are identified in the claim (not 'any and all machines').
guidance: Examples: Mackay Radio (claim recited particular antenna shape/angles) and Eibel Process (particular Fourdrinier machine structure). A general-purpose computer performing conventional functions does not qualify as a particular machine (Ultramercial; TLI Communications; Eon v. AT&T). If applicant adds generic computer elements and asserts 'programmed' or 'particular machine,' examiner should determine whether the added elements integrate the exception into a practical application or provide significantly more.

name: Machine involvement as extra-solution activity or field-of-use
description: Consider the extent to which the recited machine or apparatus imposes meaningful limits on the claim (i.e., whether its involvement is extra-solution activity or merely a field-of-use).
guidance: Use of a machine that contributes only nominally or insignificantly to execution (e.g., only a data gathering step or field-of-use limitation) will not integrate the judicial exception or provide significantly more (Bilski; CyberSource). See MPEP §§ 2106.05(g) & (h) for more.

name: Description of misconduct warranting reciprocal discipline (state findings)
description: The Arizona ruling found violations of Arizona Rules of Supreme Court 41(b)(7) and Rules of Professional Conduct ER 3.5(d), ER 8.2(a), and ER 8.4(d) by writing motions and other procedural documents containing inflammatory statements regarding the presiding judge and by filing frivolous counterclaims and motions.
guidance: The Order identifies specific types of conduct (inflammatory statements about a judge, conduct likely to disrupt a tribunal, making false statements about a judge's qualifications or integrity, conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice, filing frivolous claims/motions) as grounds that supported the state suspension and the reciprocal discipline.

name: No patent for an abstract principle; must claim a practical mode
description: It is essential that the specification should describe some practical mode of carrying the principle into effect; the patentable subject-matter is the mode of carrying the principle into effect, not the principle itself.
guidance: Example: a claim merely stating cutting ice by any non-human power was void. The specification must describe a practical mode so that the claim is for the mode, not the abstract principle. If only a principle is appropriated, the claim is void.

name: When claiming a combination, every claimed component must be considered
description: If the specification describes several things, and one or more of them is not new, the court must decide whether the patent can be sustained as a patent for the combination; a patent for a combination of three things cannot at the same time be a patent for any two of them.
guidance: General principle: combination claims are for the whole combination as claimed; you cannot simultaneously claim all subcombinations as the same invention. Courts examine novelty of each component when construing combination claims.

name: Enablement: full, clear, and exact description to enable skilled persons
description: The statute requires the patentee to describe the manner and process of making, constructing, using, and compounding his invention in such full, clear, and exact terms, avoiding unnecessary prolixity, as to enable any person skilled in the art to which it appertains to make, construct, compound, and use the same.
guidance: This is the core enablement requirement; failure to meet it is a factual question for the jury. The specification must enable without undue experimentation and must particularly point out the part or combination claimed.

name: For machines: explain the principle and several contemplated modes; particularly specify claimed part/improvement
description: In case of any machine, the patentee shall fully explain the principle and the several modes in which he has contemplated the application of that principle and shall particularly specify and point out the part, improvement, or combination which he claims as his own invention.
guidance: The specification should both teach the inventive principle and illustrate multiple modes/applications where relevant, and must clearly identify what is claimed so the public understands the monopoly's scope.

name: Fees, fee discounts and excess claim fees
description: Different search/examination options carry different fees (listed on the page) and a fee discount and excess claim fees may apply for the different options.
guidance: Check the specific fee schedule and eligibility for discounts; account for excess claim fees (additional claims beyond a threshold) when budgeting for search/examination.

name: Applicant traverse requirements (37 CFR 1.111(b))
description: 37 CFR 1.111(b) requires applicant to distinctly and specifically point out the supposed errors in the Office’s action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the Office action.
guidance: The reply must present arguments pointing out the specific distinction believed to render the claims patentable over any applied references. An effective traverse must not be merely a conclusory assertion; it must 'distinctly and specifically' identify errors. If insufficient, Office personnel may repeat the rejection and make the next action final (see MPEP §706.07(a)).

name: Types of rebuttal evidence for combination claims
description: Examples of evidence or argument applicants may submit to rebut a combination-based obviousness rejection.
guidance: Applicants may demonstrate that (A) one of ordinary skill could not have combined the claimed elements by known methods (e.g., technological difficulties); (B) the elements in combination do not merely perform the function that each performs separately; or (C) the results of the claimed combination were unexpected. Such evidence should be timely presented and considered in conjunction with the entire record.

name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) — burden to show applicability
description: An applicant subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 who wants to invoke pre-AIA 103(c) has the burden of establishing that subject matter used in a rejection and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.
guidance: For joint research agreement benefits the applicant must establish: (A) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; (B) the claimed invention resulted from activities within the scope of the agreement; and (C) the application discloses or is amended to disclose the parties' names. See MPEP §2146.01 and §2146.02 and related case law for limits and date-related restrictions.

name: Analogous art requirement for use in an obviousness rejection
description: To rely on a reference under 35 U.S.C. 103, the reference must be analogous prior art to the claimed invention.
guidance: A reference is analogous if (1) it is from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention (even if it addresses a different problem), or (2) it is reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor (even if not in the same field). Examiners must determine analogous art for obviousness analysis and cite supporting reasons and case law (In re Bigio; KSR).

name: Interpret claim language and consider invention and references as a whole
description: Ascertaining differences between prior art and the claims requires interpreting the claim language and considering both the invention and the prior art references as a whole.
guidance: See MPEP §§2111-2116.01 for claim interpretation law. Consider whether claim language limits the scope and how limitations weight in the overall obviousness analysis (MPEP §2143.03 for claim-limiting examples).

name: Consider the claimed invention 'as a whole' in obviousness inquiry
description: The question under 35 U.S.C. 103 is whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious, not whether the differences themselves would have been obvious.
guidance: Do not focus solely on a single difference or element; evaluate the combination and overall invention (Stratoflex; Schenck; In re Hirao). Admissions of unobviousness for some elements can render the combination nonobvious when considered as a whole.

name: Avoid distilling the invention to a 'gist' or 'thrust'
description: Distilling an invention down to the 'gist' or 'thrust' disregards the requirement of analyzing the subject matter 'as a whole.'
guidance: Examples show that focusing on a single advantage or treating claims as though they read differently than allowed is improper. Examiners should not ignore express claim limitations or reduce the claimed invention to a one-word solution or a single concept (W.L. Gore; Bausch & Lomb; Panduit).

name: Applicants alleging discovery of a problem source must substantiate
description: Applicants who allege the inventor discovered the source of a problem must provide evidence substantiating the allegation.
guidance: Evidence can be affidavits/declarations or a clear and persuasive assertion in the specification. Unsubstantiated counsel statements are insufficient (In re Wiseman; In re Kaslow). Examiners should require substantive support when such claims are presented.

name: Notice and opportunity to respond under the APA
description: The APA requires the PTAB to timely inform the patent owner of the matters of fact and law asserted and to give interested parties an opportunity to submit and consider facts and arguments, including rebuttal evidence.
guidance: Failure to provide adequate notice or an opportunity to respond (e.g., relying heavily on material first cited in a petitioner’s reply) can violate the APA and lead to vacatur/remand (NuVasive, EmeraChem). Specificity in petitions and institution decisions matters: detailed claim charts and identified passages constrain what the patent owner can be fairly expected to address.

name: PTAB decisions must provide sufficient explanation and support
description: The PTAB must disclose clear, adequately sustained grounds and reasoning underlying its determinations so that courts can perform meaningful review under Chenery and related precedents.
guidance: PersonalWeb and Shinn Fu emphasize that the amount of explanation required depends on context: more complex or obscure technologies or nonobvious prior‑art combinations demand more detailed analysis. Failure to explain why references disclose claim elements or why a skilled artisan would be motivated to combine them can lead to vacatur/remand.

name: Claim construction standard — broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI)
description: Under Cuozzo the USPTO may use the broadest reasonable interpretation for claim construction in PTAB proceedings.
guidance: BRI remains permissible at the PTAB, but the PTAB must still reach reasonable constructions in light of the specification; simple reliance on dictionary definitions without context may not result in the broadest reasonable interpretation (PPC Broadband).

name: Means‑plus‑function claim construction requirements
description: When construing means‑plus‑function limitations, the PTAB must identify the claimed function and the corresponding structure, material, or acts in the specification that perform that function.
guidance: IPcom required the PTAB to identify the corresponding algorithm or structure even when applying BRI; failure to do so requires vacatur and remand for proper construction.

name: Statements made during IPR can create prosecution disclaimer
description: Patent owner statements during IPR proceedings (pre‑ or post‑institution) can be used to support claim constructions under the doctrine of prosecution disclaimer.
guidance: Aylus: a patent owner’s preliminary response asserting a limiting interpretation was deemed a “clear and unmistakable” disavowal relied upon during later claim construction in district court.

name: Presentation of chemical or mathematical formulae
description: Formulae may be written by hand or drawn if necessary but recommended to use drafting aids. Formulae may be grouped together on sheets and paginated with description; designate each formula by a reference sign and refer to them in the description. Formulae may also be placed after claims as drawings if complying with drawing requirements.
guidance: Grouping formulae can be practical; ensure each formula is referenced in the description. When filed as drawings, comply with drawing requirements (paragraph 5.157 and Rules 11.10–11.13).

name: Claims must define protection sought, be clear, concise and supported
description: The claim(s) must 'define the matter for which protection is sought.' Claims must be clear and concise and fully supported by the description. Claims should, whenever appropriate, be in two distinct parts: statement of prior art and statement of features for which protection is sought (characterizing portion).
guidance: Follow Rule 6 for number/numbering, manner of claiming, dependent claims and two-part claim format when applicable.

name: Multiple dependent claims rules and national differences
description: Under the PCT, a multiple dependent claim referring to more than one other claim must do so in the alternative only, and cannot serve as basis for another multiple dependent claim. However, many national laws permit different manner of claiming; use of different national style is permitted under PCT but may require amendments during national phase for States that do not permit it.
guidance: Applicants must decide drafting style with awareness that some International Searching Authorities may find meaningful search impossible and that national Offices may require claim adaptation.

name: Criteria for satisfying unity of invention (special technical features)
description: Unity is present only when there is a technical relationship among claimed inventions involving one or more of the same or corresponding special technical features. 'Special technical features' are those that define a contribution each claimed invention makes over the prior art.
guidance: Determination is made without regard to how claims are phrased. Initial unity assessment (assuming claims avoid prior art) is made before search and may be reconsidered based on search results. Annex B contains detailed criteria and illustrations.

name: Permitted combinations of different claim categories
description: Rule 13 permits inclusion of combinations such as (i) an independent claim for a product plus an independent claim for a process specially adapted to manufacture the product and a use claim; (ii) an independent claim for a process plus an independent claim for an apparatus specifically designed for carrying out the process; (iii) product + process + apparatus combinations where contributions correspond.
guidance: A process is 'specially adapted' if it inherently results in the product; an apparatus is 'specifically designed' if its contribution over prior art corresponds to the process's contribution. Mere capability to be used in the process is insufficient.

name: Apparatus considered specifically designed test
description: An apparatus or means is considered specifically designed for carrying out a claimed process if the contribution over the prior art of the apparatus corresponds to the contribution the process makes over the prior art; mere capability to be used is insufficient.
guidance: Draft apparatus claims so their inventive contribution mirrors the process contribution when relying on combined-category unity.

name: Mayo two-step framework for evaluating §101
description: First, determine whether the claims at issue are directed to a patent-ineligible concept (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea). If so, then consider the elements of each claim both individually and 'as an ordered combination' to determine whether the additional elements transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application.
guidance: The second step is a search for an 'inventive concept'—an element or combination sufficient to ensure the patent amounts to significantly more than a patent upon the ineligible concept itself.

name: Mere recitation of generic computer implementation is insufficient
description: Simply appending conventional steps, specified at a high level of generality, to a method already well known in the art is not enough to supply the 'inventive concept' needed to make the transformation. Stating an abstract idea while adding the words 'apply it with a computer' simply combines those two steps, with the same deficient result.
guidance: If a claim only instructs implementation of an abstract idea on an unspecified, generic computer, that does not provide 'practical assurance' that the claim is more than a drafting effort to monopolize the idea. Compare with Benson and Flook.

name: Search for an 'inventive concept' beyond conventional activity
description: A claim that recites an abstract idea must include 'additional features' that supply an inventive concept sufficient to transform the claimed abstract idea into a patent-eligible application; simply applying well-understood, routine, conventional activities is not enough.
guidance: Evaluate whether claimed elements are well-known and routine (e.g., electronic recordkeeping, obtaining data, adjusting balances, issuing instructions). If they are conventional, they do not constitute an inventive concept.

name: Consider claim elements both individually and as an ordered combination
description: To determine if additional elements transform the claim, courts must consider the elements of each claim both individually and 'as an ordered combination' to see if the combination adds something not present when steps are considered separately.
guidance: Even if individual elements are ordinary, an innovative ordered combination that changes the nature or improves technology may supply the inventive concept (contrast Diehr where combination improved a technological process).

name: Eligibility when claim improves computer functioning or other technology
description: Claims are patent eligible when they use an abstract idea in a manner that improves an existing technological process or the functioning of the computer itself (Diehr: use of a mathematical equation within a process that solved a technological problem transformed the claim).
guidance: Look for concrete technical improvements (new ways of measuring, controlling, or interfacing with hardware; novel algorithms tied to specific computer architecture) rather than mere use of a computer to perform abstract steps.

name: System and media claims must recite meaningful hardware limitations beyond generic components
description: System claims that merely recite a handful of generic computer components (e.g., data processing system, communications controller, data storage unit) configured to implement the abstract idea add nothing of substance and are not patent eligible.
guidance: Functional language describing generic hardware that performs routine calculation, storage, and transmission functions does not avoid §101 ineligibility; avoid allowing patent eligibility to 'depend simply on the draftsman's art.'

name: Use precedent examples as touchstones for ineligible/eligible claims
description: Prior cases identify illustrative examples: Benson (algorithm converting BCD to binary — abstract), Flook (mathematical formula for alarm limits — abstract), Bilski (hedging — abstract), Diehr (computer-implemented rubber-curing process — eligible because it improved a technological process).
guidance: Compare the claimed invention to these precedents to determine whether it more closely resembles an abstract idea merely implemented on a computer or a technological improvement that transforms the claim into eligible subject matter.

name: Obviousness legal standard
description: A patent claim is invalid if the claimed invention would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the field [at the time the application was filed] [as of the effective filing date of the claimed invention] [as of (insert date)].
guidance: The court makes the ultimate legal determination of obviousness based on factual findings. The jury (if asked) should be presented with the underlying factual issues as specifically as possible. For post-AIA claims use the effective filing date option.

name: Level of ordinary skill in the field
description: Determine the level of ordinary skill that someone would have had [at the time the claimed invention was made] [as of the effective filing date of the claimed invention].
guidance: Consider all evidence introduced at trial, including (1) levels of education and experience of persons working in the field; (2) types of problems encountered in the field; and (3) sophistication of the technology. Parties may present differing contentions about the level of skill.

name: Difference between the claimed invention and the prior art
description: Decide what difference, if any, existed between the claimed invention and the prior art.
guidance: If dispute is limited to a specific claim limitation, present only that issue as the 'difference' factor. Consider whether a prior art reference discloses particular claim limitations.

name: Combining known elements (reason to combine / motivation to combine)
description: A claim composed of several elements is not proved obvious merely by showing each element was independently known in the prior art; consider whether there was a reason for a person of ordinary skill to combine elements as in the claimed invention.
guidance: Consider whether there is teaching, suggestion, or motivation in prior art to make the claimed modification or combination, whether the change was predictable use of prior art elements, whether a known technique was applied as before, and whether the claimed invention would have been 'obvious to try' with a reasonable expectation of success. Be careful to avoid hindsight bias.

name: Time reference for obviousness determination
description: Decide whether obviousness is judged as of the time the claimed invention was made or as of the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
guidance: Use the effective filing date option for post-AIA claims (effective filing dates on or after March 16, 2013). Put yourself in the position of a person of ordinary skill at that time and do not consider later knowledge or the patent's teaching.

name: Anticipation (novelty) — glossary definition
description: Anticipation exists when a claimed invention describes an earlier invention and therefore is not new and is not entitled to be patented.
guidance: Anticipation is a distinct ground of invalidity (novelty) from obviousness and requires that a single prior art reference disclose every claim limitation.

name: Claim / Elements — infringement test
description: Each claim is a concise formal definition of an invention; a device or method infringes a patent if it contains each and every required part (element) or step of the claim.
guidance: Claims may be independent or dependent. A dependent claim incorporates the limitations of the referenced claim(s). For infringement, all claim limitations must be present in the accused device or method.

name: Prioritized examination fee and program limits
description: A fee of $4,800 shall be established for filing a request ... for prioritized examination of a nonprovisional application for an original utility or plant patent. In addition to the prioritized examination fee, the filing, search, and examination fees (including excess claims and application size fees), processing fee, and publication fee remain due.
guidance: Director may prescribe conditions for acceptance and limit the number of accepted prioritized examination filings. Until regulations are prescribed: (i) no application requesting prioritized examination may contain or be amended to contain more than 4 independent claims or more than 30 total claims; (ii) Director may not accept more than 10,000 requests per fiscal year for prioritization until regulations set another limit. Small entities receive 50% reduction for prioritized examination fee. All prioritized examination fees are credited to the USPTO Appropriation Account and may be used only for specified purposes. Fee terminates when Director first sets/adjusts that fee under statutory fee-setting authority.

name: Tax strategies deemed within the prior art
description: For purposes of evaluating an invention under section 102 or 103, any strategy for reducing, avoiding, or deferring tax liability, whether known or unknown at the time of the invention or application, shall be deemed insufficient to differentiate a claimed invention from the prior art.
guidance: Defines 'tax liability' broadly to include Federal, State, local, and foreign laws. Exclusions: does not apply to inventions used solely for preparing a tax return/filing (including data recording/transmission/organization for such filing) or to methods/apparatus/technology/software used solely for financial management to the extent severable from any tax strategy or not limiting use of any tax strategy. Rule of construction: nothing implies other business methods are patentable or that business-method patents are valid.

name: Definition of covered business method patent
description: 'Covered business method patent' means a patent that claims a method or corresponding apparatus for performing data processing or other operations used in the practice, administration, or management of a financial product or service, except that the term does not include patents for technological inventions.
guidance: Director shall issue regulations to assist in determining whether a patent is for a technological invention; rule of construction: nothing in this section amends/interprets subject-matter categories under section 101.

name: Removal of patent/copyright/plant variety protection cases to federal court
description: New 28 U.S.C. §1454: A civil action in which any party asserts a claim arising under Acts of Congress relating to patents, plant variety protection, or copyrights may be removed to the federal district court where the action is pending.
guidance: Special rules: if removal is based solely on this section, any party may remove and time limitations in section 1446(b) may be extended for cause shown. The removing court is not precluded from hearing claims that the state court lacked jurisdiction over. Remand rules specify remand of claims not basis for removal or outside original/supplemental jurisdiction.

name: rejection_112
description: Equals 1 if 35 USC 112 rejection(s) raised, 0 otherwise
guidance: Indicator whether the action includes a written-description/enablement/claim-definiteness (112) rejection.

name: Core Standard — specification must convey possession
description: "The fundamental test asks whether 'the specification conveys with reasonable clarity to those skilled in the art that, as of the filing date sought, the inventor was in possession of the invention as now claimed.'"
guidance: An applicant demonstrates possession by describing the claimed invention with all its limitations using words, structures, figures, diagrams, and formulas that fully set forth the claimed invention. Evaluation is from the perspective of a person skilled in the art as of the filing date.

name: Written description separate from enablement
description: The written description requirement is 'separate and distinct from the enablement requirement' and serves to demonstrate the inventor actually possessed the claimed subject matter.
guidance: Do not conflate enablement (whether one can make and use the invention) with written description (whether the inventor was in possession of the claimed subject matter). Both requirements may be analyzed independently.

name: Presumption of adequacy and examiner burden
description: There is a presumption that adequate written description exists when the application is filed.
guidance: The examiner bears the initial burden of presenting evidence explaining why a skilled artisan would not recognize that the description supports the claims. Examiners must establish a prima facie case rather than rely on conclusory statements.

name: Non-literal support allowed (not in haec verba)
description: The specification need not use identical language (in haec verba) to be sufficient.
guidance: A description is adequate if a skilled artisan would understand the inventor possessed the invention even if the exact claim phrasing is not present. Examiners should evaluate whether support is express, implicit, or inherent, not require verbatim terms.

name: Possession may be shown through concrete evidence
description: Possession may be shown by actual reduction to practice; drawings or chemical formulas; or identifying characteristics such as structure, physical/chemical properties, or functional characteristics with established structure-function correlation.
guidance: Examples: constructing an embodiment that meets all claim limitations (reduction to practice); detailed structural depictions in drawings or formulas; identifying characteristics that, given an established structure-function correlation, make clear the inventor had the claimed subject matter.

name: Single species/embodiment claims require complete support
description: Single species or single embodiment claims must show complete structure, reduction to drawings, or sufficient identifying characteristics distinguishing the species/embodiment from other materials.
guidance: For claims to a single species, the specification should provide enough detail (structure, drawings, or identifying characteristics) so that a skilled artisan recognizes the claimed species as the inventor's possession and can distinguish it from others.

name: Genus claims require representative species or equivalent proof
description: Genus claims require disclosure of a 'representative number of species' reflecting the genus variation, unless one species alone demonstrates the inventor possessed the broader genus (a fact-dependent inquiry).
guidance: Broad genus claims cannot ordinarily be supported by disclosure of only a single species in unpredictable arts unless substantial evidence shows the inventor possessed the entire genus. Examiner should consider predictability of the art and the number/nature of disclosed species.

name: Means-plus-function claims require corresponding structure
description: Means-plus-function claims must disclose adequate corresponding structure, materials, or acts that perform the claimed function; indefinite means-plus-function claims also lack written description.
guidance: A purely functional recitation without disclosure of structure (or materials/acts) corresponding to that function will typically fail the written description requirement. Examiner should identify missing corresponding structure when evaluating such claims.

name: Support requirement for new or amended claims
description: For new or amended claims, each limitation must be 'expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure.'
guidance: When claims are amended or added, examiners must verify that every claim limitation finds support in the original filing. Lack of such support can justify a written description rejection or a refusal to accord priority to an earlier filing.

name: Priority/benefit claim support requirement
description: Subject matter must be disclosed in the manner required by 35 U.S.C. 112(a) in the earlier-filed application to receive that earlier filing date for priority/benefit purposes.
guidance: When an applicant asserts priority to an earlier application, the earlier disclosure must meet written description standards for the specific subject matter asserted. Examiner should assess whether the earlier application itself provided adequate written description of the claimed subject matter.

name: Critical limitations and common written description failures
description: Claims omitting elements described as essential to the invention lack adequate description; broad genus claims may be unsupported by a single species in unpredictable arts; functional description alone typically fails absent established structure-function correlation; generic disclosure of a broad class does not necessarily support specific compounds or species.
guidance: Look for omitted 'critical' elements that the specification treats as essential. Be wary where only functional language is provided without structural correlation, or where a generic disclosure attempts to cover specific chemical/biological species without adequate species-level support.

name: Examiner methodology for making a written description rejection
description: When making a written description rejection, the examiner must: (1) identify specific claim limitations lacking support; (2) establish a prima facie case explaining why skilled artisans would not recognize possession; (3) base findings on substantive law, not procedural guidelines; (4) respond thoroughly to applicant arguments and evidence upon reply; and (5) consider the nature of the invention and state of the art.
guidance: Examiners must provide reasoned, evidence-based findings rather than conclusory assertions (a general assertion of 'unpredictability in the art' alone is insufficient). After applicant reply, examiners should address arguments and any evidence submitted and reassess the prima facie case in view of the record.

name: Specific identification in application (37 CFR 1.804(a))
description: The biological material deposited must be specifically identified in the application for patent as filed to meet the description requirement of 35 U.S.C.112 and provide antecedent basis for the deposited material.
guidance: Specification should clearly show the invention was capable of reduction to practice; adding depository, accession number, and deposit date after filing may be permissible (see Lundak example) but the application as filed must make clear the material is described/claimed.

name: Examination procedures—when deposit is needed and acceptability (37 CFR 1.809(a)-(b))
description: The examiner shall determine in each application/reexamination/reissue if a deposit is needed and, if needed, whether a deposit made is acceptable for patent purposes. If a needed deposit has not been made or is unacceptable, the examiner shall reject affected claims under appropriate provision(s) of 35 U.S.C.112 explaining why a deposit is needed and/or why the deposit cannot be accepted.
guidance: Applicant/patent owner must reply by making an acceptable original/replacement/supplemental deposit or assuring the Office in writing that an acceptable deposit will be made, or arguing why a deposit is not needed or should be accepted. Other replies are nonresponsive and the rejection will be repeated until satisfied.

name: Adopt first-inventor-to-file standard
description: The bill adopts a 'first-inventor-to-file' standard (as opposed to current 'first-to-invent'), aligning the U.S. with the rest of the world and providing a more transparent and cost-effective process.
guidance: Supporters claim it levels the playing field internationally and reduces expensive priority disputes; critics worry about impacts on small/independent inventors. Data cited: over seven years nearly 3 million applications filed and only a vanishingly small number would have different outcomes under the change.

name: Need not list every possible substitutable substance
description: All the substances which will answer the purpose of the invention need not be stated, only the public must not be misled.
guidance: Rationale: permissible breadth, but avoid claiming a class when not all members are suitable.

name: Common defects summary (eight defects)
description: A specification is bad when: 1) terms are ambiguous; 2) necessary descriptions omitted; 3) parts claimed are not original; 4) things are put in to mislead; 5) the drawings are incorrect; 6) one of different ways/ingredients named fails; 7) one of several effects specified is not produced; 8) the things described are not the best known to the patentee.
guidance: This is a concise checklist of recurring defects in English law (note from Godson's work). Use as screening rubric for adequacy.

name: Written description support for negative limitations
description: A negative limitation need not be recited in the specification verbatim, but 'there generally must be something in the specification that conveys to a skilled artisan that the inventor intended the exclusion, such as a discussion of disadvantages or alternatives.' (Novartis Pharms. Corp. v. Accord Healthcare, Inc.)
guidance: To support importing a negative limitation into a claim, the specification must convey to a POSITA that the exclusion was intended. Look for express statements, discussions of disadvantages/alternatives, or other disclosure indicating intent to exclude. Mere silence is insufficient.

name: Do not import limitations from preferred embodiments (Liebel‑Flarsheim)
description: It is generally improper to read limitations from a preferred embodiment into a claim (the Liebel‑Flarsheim principle).
guidance: Even when the specification discloses an embodiment that includes a particular feature, you should not automatically limit claim scope to that embodiment. Written‑description support for a feature (including a negative limitation) is necessary to import it, but is not sufficient if doing so would improperly read a preferred embodiment limitation into the claim.

name: Limit claim construction to terms in controversy and only as necessary
description: Courts/Boards 'need only construe terms that are in controversy, and only to the extent necessary to resolve the controversy.' (Nidec Motor Corp. v. Zhongshan Broad Ocean Motor Co., quoting Vivid Techs.)
guidance: Only construe claim terms when necessary for resolving the institution question or the specific dispute; avoid broader or unnecessary constructions. Parties may later brief constructions at trial if needed.

name: Institution standard — reasonable likelihood of prevailing on unpatentability under §103(a)
description: For purposes of instituting IPR, the Petition must demonstrate a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner will prevail in establishing that the challenged claims are unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. §103(a) over the cited prior art (e.g., a asserted combination of references).
guidance: The preliminary record must show that the combination of references and arguments sufficiently addresses each claim limitation and provides a reasonable likelihood of proving obviousness. The Board evaluates the petition's factual and claim‑by‑claim showings at the institution stage.

name: Obviousness combination test — motivation to combine and predictable results
description: A claimed invention is obvious if a person of ordinary skill would have been motivated to combine prior art teachings and would have expected to obtain predictable results (e.g., applying a known technique to a known device to yield predictable results).
guidance: When asserting obviousness over a combination (here, Wu + Doherty), show (a) how each limitation is taught or suggested, (b) a reason a POSITA would combine the references (benefits, commonplace approach), and (c) that the combination yields predictable results. Isolated teachings should not be considered without a rationale to combine.

name: Written description support is necessary but not sufficient to import limitations
description: Written‑description support for a limitation (including negative limitations) is a necessary condition to import that limitation into a claim, but is not sufficient by itself to justify importing a limitation from the specification into a claim.
guidance: Even if the specification contains language that could support a limitation, courts/boards must still avoid importing limitations improperly (see Liebel‑Flarsheim). The party seeking to import a limitation must show both support and that importing is proper in light of claim language and the specification as a whole.

name: Do not limit claims to a single example or embodiment
description: It is generally improper to limit claim scope based on a single example; claims should not be confined to one disclosed embodiment absent clear disavowal or lexicographic intent.
guidance: Be cautious about relying on one embodiment to define claim scope. The Board will not construe claims to the scope of a single example unless the specification clearly requires it; parties should present broader claim meaning only when necessary and supported.

name: Preliminary claim interpretation may incorporate disclosed examples for institution
description: For institution purposes, certain claim interpretations may reasonably include disclosed examples when the specification and record support that reading (e.g., 'changing a predetermined advertisement insertion point ...' includes skipping over an insertion point to arrive at a different insertion point in response to user activity).
guidance: At institution, the Board may adopt a preliminary interpretation informed by the specification's examples and operation. Parties will have opportunity to brief construction and factual issues later at trial; the institution interpretation is limited to what is necessary for the institution decision.

name: Dependent claims follow independent claim showing at institution
description: When dependent claims depend directly or indirectly from an independent claim that the petitioner shows is unpatentable for institution purposes, the dependent claims that are materially similar will also be treated as sufficiently supported for institution.
guidance: A successful preliminary showing on an independent claim often supports institution on dependent claims; petitioners should briefly explain how each dependent limitation is taught or suggested by the cited art or the combination.

name: Amendment must not enlarge or materially vary original invention
description: No amendment shall be allowed that would make the specification as amended claim an invention substantially larger than or substantially different from the invention claimed by the specification as it stood before the amendment.
guidance: It is the duty of the Comptroller and law officers, when hearing applications for leave to amend, to see that the proposed amendment does not extend the scope of the patent, or alter the claims such that the invention would become substantially larger or different; if doubtful, amendment ought to be allowed 'at the patentee's peril.' (References: s.18(8) of Patents Act 1883; Iffath and Frost's Patent; Lake's Patent.)

name: Disclaimer may sever subordinate part claims but cannot create new claims
description: Where a specification claims both a general combination and some subordinate parts, a disclaimer may sever and reject the claim to any of the parts; but a specification cannot be altered so as to be made to claim a combination or parts if they were not previously claimed.
guidance: A patentee cannot strike out a whole claim and insert another claim to a subordinate part where the original contained a distinct and specific claim to the operation believed to be new. (Illustration: Surry's Patent, 6 R.P.C. 108; Gaulard & Gibbs; United Horseshoe Co. v. Swedish Horsenail Co.)

name: Method claims can be limited by disclaimer to the particular method described
description: If there is a claim to all methods of effecting a certain result, it may be cut down by disclaimer to the particular method described in the specification.
guidance: Example: Ashworth's Patent, 2 Griff. P.C. 6 — general method claim narrowed to the specific method disclosed.

name: Cross‑appeal timing and limitations (37 CFR 41.61(b),(e),(f))
description: Within fourteen days of service of an opposing party’s notice of appeal, a patent owner or third party requester who has not filed a notice of appeal may file a notice of cross appeal. The time for filing the notice of cross appeal may not be extended. Where the notice of cross appeal is timely filed but defective (e.g., missing fee, missing proof of service, unsigned, failure to identify appealed claims), 37 CFR 41.61(f) provides one opportunity to file, within a non‑extendable period of one month, an amended cross appeal correcting the defects.
guidance: Cross appeals are only permitted from a "notice of appeal," not from a "notice of cross appeal." If multiple requesters are present, cross appeal timing runs from the earlier applicable appeal as specified. If a cross appeal is untimely or the original appeal period expired, the later requester may be unable to appeal.

name: Appellant’s brief: required content and order (37 CFR 41.67(c)(1)(i)–(xi))
description: The appellant’s brief shall contain the following items under appropriate headings and in the order indicated: (i) Real party in interest; (ii) Related appeals and interferences; (iii) Status of claims; (iv) Status of amendments; (v) Summary of claimed subject matter (including identification of every means‑plus‑function and step‑plus‑function and corresponding specification/drawing references); (vi) Issues to be reviewed on appeal; (vii) Argument (contentions with citations, separate heading per issue, grouping/waiver rules); (viii) Claims appendix; (ix) Evidence appendix; (x) Related proceedings appendix; (xi) Certificate of service.
guidance: Each issue must be treated under a separate heading. For patent owner appellants, identify rejected claims being appealed; for requester appellants, identify claims with favorable determinations being appealed. Copies of decisions in related proceedings must be included in the appendix. A statement that merely points out what a claim recites will not be considered an argument for separate patentability.

name: Amendments, affidavits, declarations, exhibits after appeal filing (37 CFR 41.63)
description: (A) Amendments filed after filing an appeal cancelling claims may be admitted where such cancellation does not affect scope of any other pending claim; (B) All other amendments filed after filing an appeal will not be admitted except where patent owner reopens prosecution under 37 CFR 41.77(b)(1); (C) Affidavits or other evidence filed after filing an appeal will not be admitted except where prosecution is reopened under 37 CFR 41.77(b)(1).
guidance: If the examiner wants the patent owner to provide an amendment or evidence during appeal stage, the examiner must reopen prosecution, accept the amendment/evidence for entry, permit timely comment by third party requester, and then issue a new Action Closing Prosecution (ACP). See MPEP § 2673.01.

name: Respondent’s brief: required content and specificity (37 CFR 41.68(b)(1)(i)–(x))
description: The respondent brief shall contain, under appropriate headings and in order: (i) Real party in interest; (ii) Related appeals and interferences; (iii) Status of claims (accept or dispute appellant’s statement, specifying errors with particularity if disputed); (iv) Status of amendments (accept/dispute with particularity if disputed); (v) Summary of claimed subject matter (accept/dispute with particularity if disputed); (vi) Issues to be reviewed on appeal (accept/dispute; may provide counter statement); (vii) Argument (accept/dispute appellant’s contentions, specify errors and bases with citations; each issue under separate heading); (viii) Evidence appendix; (ix) Related proceedings appendix; (x) Certificate of service.
guidance: If respondent disputes appellant’s statements, the respondent must specify errors with particularity. The respondent may make counter‑stated issues and must treat each under separate headings.

name: Continuation‑in‑part (C‑I‑P) application definition and requirements
description: A continuation-in-part is an application filed during the lifetime of an earlier nonprovisional application, repeating some substantial portion or all of the earlier application and adding matter not disclosed in the earlier application. The continuation-in-part may only be filed under 37 CFR 1.53(b). The C‑I‑P must claim the benefit of the prior nonprovisional application under 35 U.S.C. 120 or 365(c.
guidance: A continuation-in-part CANNOT be filed as a continued prosecution application (CPA) under 37 CFR 1.53(d). An application claiming the benefit of a provisional under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) should not be called a 'continuation-in-part' of the provisional. The mere filing of a C‑I‑P does not itself create a presumption that the applicant acquiesces in any rejections outstanding in the copending national nonprovisional application. For the alleged C‑I‑P to derive the benefit of the earlier filing date, it must meet other requirements of 35 U.S.C. 120 and 37 CFR 1.78, such as: (A) common inventor(s); (B) filed before patenting/abandonment/termination of proceedings on the first application; and (C) contains or is amended to contain a specific reference to the earlier filed application (submitted in the first sentence(s) of the specification or in an application data sheet per 37 CFR 1.76(b)(5)). See MPEP § 201.11 and form paragraph 2.06.

name: Claiming the benefit of an earlier filing date under 35 U.S.C. 120 and 119(e) and 37 CFR 1.78
description: A later-filed application may be entitled to the benefit of the filing date of a prior nonprovisional or provisional application if certain statutory and regulatory conditions are met. Under 35 U.S.C. 120, the invention must be disclosed in the manner provided by the first paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112 in the earlier application, be filed before patenting/abandonment/termination of proceedings on the first application, and contain or be amended to contain a specific reference to the earlier filed application. Under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), a nonprovisional application claiming benefit of a provisional must be filed not later than 12 months after the provisional filing date and must contain or be amended to contain a specific reference to the provisional.
guidance: The Director may consider failure to timely submit the specific reference as waiver of benefit, and may establish procedures (including surcharge) to accept unintentionally delayed submissions. 37 CFR 1.78 requires that, to claim benefit of prior-filed copending nonprovisional or international applications: (a)(1) each prior-filed application must name at least one inventor named in the later application and disclose the named inventor’s invention in the manner of 35 U.S.C. 112 ¶1; and (2)(i) each prior-filed application must be either an international application entitled to a filing date under PCT Article 11 and designating the U.S., or entitled to a filing date under § 1.53(b) or (d) and have paid the basic filing fee under § 1.16 within the pendency of the application. Except for CPAs under § 1.53(d), any nonprovisional or international application claiming benefit must contain or be amended to contain a reference to each prior application identifying it by application number or international application number and filing date and indicating relationship of the applications. See MPEP § 201.11 for more details.

name: Final court holding of invalidity/unenforceability is binding
description: Upon the issuance of a final holding of invalidity or unenforceability by a Federal Court, the holding is binding on the Office.
guidance: Claims held invalid/unenforceable will be withdrawn from consideration in the reexamination; reexamination continues as to remaining claims. If all claims are finally held invalid/unenforceable, the CRU Director will vacate the reexamination (no substantial new question of patentability) and terminate prosecution. Where claims held invalid are referenced in an Office action, use form paragraph 26.80 at the beginning of the action.

name: Effect of final court holding of validity when requester was a party
description: If a final court decision upholding validity occurs during inter partes reexamination and the person who filed the request was a party to the litigation, the Office will discontinue examination of all claims affected by the holding of validity (for issues raised or that could have been raised by that patent owner/requester).
guidance: If 37 CFR 1.907(b) applies such that all claims cannot be maintained, the order to reexamine is vacated by the CRU Director and reexamination is terminated. If 1.907(b) applies to only some claims, those claims will not be treated and the examiner’s action must point out which claims are not treated and why. Note that 1.907(b) cannot be waived since it tracks statute (35 U.S.C. 317). Consult OPLA as needed.

name: Effect of final court holding of validity when requester was not a party
description: A final Court decision upholding validity during inter partes reexamination where the requester was not a party to the litigation will have no binding effect on the reexamination.
guidance: Ethicon v. Quigg establishes the Office is not bound by a court’s holding of patent validity because courts and the Office use different standards of proof (clear and convincing in court vs preponderance in the Office). Deference may ordinarily be given to the court’s factual findings where the evidence before the Office and the court is the same, but claims held valid by the court may still be rejected in reexamination if sufficient reasons are present.

name: Director authority and special dispatch (35 U.S.C. 314(c))
description: All inter partes reexamination proceedings shall be conducted with special dispatch unless otherwise provided by the Director for good cause.
guidance: The Director has statutory authority and discretion to suspend inter partes reexamination proceedings for "good cause." A District Court decision pending appeal on the validity of the same claims may provide good cause for suspension because of the potential for 35 U.S.C. 317(b) estoppel to attach. Decisions about suspension are fact-specific and should involve consultation with OPLA where appropriate.

name: Preparation of NIRC when no claims are allowed
description: Where all claims are rejected or objected to in the prior Office action, the examiner will issue an NIRC indicating all claims have been canceled and terminating prosecution.
guidance: Attach a formal examiner’s amendment canceling all live claims to PTOL-2068. In the remarks of the examiner’s amendment, point out why claims have been canceled. Since all claims are canceled, no reasons for patentability are attached. No panel review conference is needed; issuance is ministerial.

name: Reasons for patentability and/or confirmation requirement
description: Reasons for patentability must be provided for each claim identified as patentable in the NIRC unless all claims are canceled in the proceeding.
guidance: In the attachment to the NIRC, indicate why the claims found patentable are clearly patentable over the cited patents/printed publications. This is similar to reasons for allowance in an application (see MPEP §1302.14). Where the record is clear, examiner may refer to particular portions of the record. Use Form PTOL-476 or form paragraph 26.70 (¶ 26.70 Reasons for Patentability and/or Confirmation) as preferred formats. Patent owner must be notified it may submit comments on the reasons for patentability.

name: Patentable vs confirmed claim terminology
description: Original patent claims found patentable in reexamination are generally designated as 'confirmed'; new or amended claims are generally 'patentable.'
guidance: For purposes of setting forth reasons for patentability/confirmation, the examiner may use 'patentable' to refer to any claim that defines over the cited patents/printed publications. There is no need to separate 'confirmed' and 'patentable' categories when preparing reasons.

name: Reexamination procedural reminders (checklist A–M)
description: A list of items requiring special attention before forwarding the case for CRU SPE/TC QAS review: (A) examine all claims with a substantial new question (SNQ) of patentability; (B) no renumbering of patent claims permitted (new claims may require renumbering); (C) amendments must conform to 37 CFR 1.530(d)-(k); (D) prior art must be listed on proper forms (PTO-892, PTO-1449, PTO/SB/08A/08B/42); (E) examiner and clerk checklists must be fully completed and in agreement; (F) multiple copending reexaminations often merged; (G) copending reissue application forwarding to OPLA for potential merger; (H) reasons for patentability/confirmation are required for each patentable claim; (I) no issue fee in reexamination; (J) claims may not be amended or new claims added after patent expiration; (K) original drawings cannot be physically changed (use new sheets); (L) amended/new claims may not enlarge scope; (M) if patent expired, all amendments/added claims must be withdrawn and rejected/ objected claims canceled by examiner’s amendment.
guidance: Each item cites relevant MPEP sections (e.g., §2643, §2666.01, §2250, §2657, §2666.02, §2658) and emphasizes administrative compliance (forms, checklists, merging procedures, drafting of examiner’s amendments) before forwarding the case.

name: Procedure when all claims are canceled in the reexamination proceeding
