description: When all claims in the reexamination proceeding are to be canceled (e.g., patent owner fails to timely respond or Board affirms examiner and appeal times expire), the examiner will issue an NIRC indicating all claims canceled and terminating prosecution.
guidance: Attach an examiner’s amendment cancelling all live claims and state the reason for cancellation in the amendment (example wording provided: cite last Office action date and statute/regulation such as 37 CFR 1.957(b) and MPEP §2666.10). Use the NIRC (Form PTOL-2068) and follow ministerial steps for termination.

name: Defenses based on specification concealment, over‑claiming, prior use, or prior description
description: The defendant may prove that the specification filed does not contain the whole truth, contains more than is necessary, that concealment or addition was intended to mislead, that the invention was in use, or described in a prior public work, or that the patentee surreptitiously obtained the patent; in such cases judgment shall be for the defendant and the patent declared void.
guidance: Statute enumerates multiple substantive invalidity defenses tied to lack of candor, insufficiency, overclaiming, and lack of novelty (prior use/prior publication).

name: Offers to supply generic products not evidence of intent to infringe
description: An offer to execute orders for a class of articles (when no particular form is mentioned) is not evidence of an intention to infringe a patent for that class where the specification does not claim every kind of that class of article.
guidance: Where specification does not claim every kind, it is presumed that offers refer to non-infringing forms (Grainne v. Drysdale). Be specific in offers/advertising to avoid inference of intent to infringe.

name: Effect of allowed amendment (disclaimer/compromise/explanation) on damages (Patents Act 1888 s.20)
description: When an amendment by way of disclaimer, correction, or explanation has been allowed under the Patents Act of 1888 (sect. 20), no damages are obtainable in any action in respect of the use of the invention before the amendment unless the patentee establishes to the satisfaction of the Court that his original claim was framed in good faith and with reasonable skill and knowledge.
guidance: Amendments narrowing claims can limit retrospective damages unless good-faith drafting is proved.

name: Timing and procedures for claim construction and dispositive motions
description: Set timing and procedures for claim construction and dispositive motions: determine timing of summary judgment relative to claim construction; if not addressed by local rule, set a schedule for exchanges of claim terms, proposed constructions, and supporting evidence
guidance: Coordinate Markman schedule with summary judgment practice; set explicit deadlines for term exchanges and evidence to avoid late surprises.

name: Winnowing patents/claims and claim-term limits
description: Discuss the number of patents and patent claims that would be tried and possible ways of winnowing; discuss limits on the number of claim terms submitted for construction
guidance: Require explanation of the significance of each disputed term (e.g., effect on infringement/validity) and ask parties to rank disputed terms by significance.

name: Claim construction hearing logistics
description: Discuss claim construction hearing logistics: identify disputed subsidiary factual issues; discuss whether live witnesses should be called
guidance: Encourage use of graphics, animations, and other visual displays to aid in understanding the technology and disputed claim terms; schedule a pre-claim-construction conference to finalize logistics after positions have crystallized.

name: Summary judgment dependence on claim construction
description: Discuss whether any summary judgment issues depend on claim construction or can otherwise be resolved with little or no discovery, including: dispute about structure/function of accused products; any claim term that, once decided, will compel infringement or noninfringement; territorial issues; any claims or defenses purely legal in nature
guidance: If purely legal issues exist, consider first-track and second-track schedules for summary judgment to speed resolution (see Chapter 6).

name: Super-early limited claim construction
description: What are the 1 or 2 most important claim terms requiring construction? Should the Court consider a “super-early” limited claim construction hearing on those most important terms?
guidance: Consider a narrow early Markman on dispositive terms to streamline the case.

name: Narrowing the case
description: At what point(s) in the case will it be appropriate to limit/reduce the number of accused devices/functionalities, asserted patents, asserted claims, invalidity defenses (including obviousness combinations), and prior art references? Are there products not colorably different that may be added? Should damages or any other portion of the case be bifurcated?
guidance: Court is highly receptive to reasonable proposals to reduce scope at appropriate stages to improve efficiency.

name: Amendments and deadlines for pleadings and accused products
description: What will be the deadline for proposed amendments to the pleadings, including adding allegations of indirect and/or willful infringement as well as inequitable conduct? What will be the deadline for adding or altering the accused devices/functionalities, asserted claims, and prior art?
guidance: Set firm amendment deadlines to avoid late-expanding claims or accused products that disrupt case schedule.

name: Time to Trial and Final Relief
description: Typical speed of proceedings to key milestones (claim construction, trial, initial determination) and time to obtain final relief in the jurisdiction.
guidance: Time-to-trial varies widely across forums and even judges; e.g., certain U.S. districts (Western/Eastern Districts of Texas) had faster average times to claim construction/trial in 2021; USITC is comparatively fast (median ~9 months to claim construction, ~14 months to initial determination, ~18 months to final determination). Faster forums may be strategically preferred to obtain early leverage or influence other jurisdictions.

name: Patent Office Oppositions and Post-Grant Proceedings
description: Availability and strategic use of administrative procedures to challenge patent validity (EPO oppositions within 9 months of grant; U.S. PTAB inter partes review (IPR) and other AIA proceedings).
guidance: EPO oppositions, if successful, can invalidate all national designations but can be slow and may bar certain national nullity proceedings (e.g., blocking German Federal Patent Court nullity actions while an opposition is pending). IPRs can lead to invalidation, narrowing of claims, stays of district court litigation, or have no effect depending on timing and outcome.

name: Include a specific reference to the prior international (PCT) application
description: To obtain benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 and 365(c), the continuing U.S. application must include a specific reference to the prior international application.
guidance: If filed prior to Sept. 16, 2012 the specific reference must either be in the first sentence(s) of the specification following the title or included in an application data sheet (ADS) (see 37 CFR 1.78(d)(2) and 1.78(h)). If filed on or after Sept. 16, 2012, the specific reference must be contained in an ADS (37 CFR 1.78(d)(2)). The reference must identify the parent international application by international application number and international filing date and indicate the relationship of the applications (continuation, continuation-in-part, or division). The required reference must be submitted within the time period provided by 37 CFR 1.78(d)(3); that time period is not extendable. A certified copy (and English translation if necessary) of the international application may be required to perfect the benefit claim when the international application did not originate in the U.S. or when necessary (e.g., an intervening reference is found). If the international application was published under PCT Article 21, a certified copy is not normally necessary.

name: Copendency requirement (continuing application must be copending with the international application)
description: A U.S. national application is copending with a prior international application if the international application was pending on the filing date of the U.S. national application.
guidance: Generally an international application becomes abandoned as to the U.S. upon expiration of 30 months from the priority date (unless a proper submission under 35 U.S.C. 371 to enter the U.S. national phase is filed before that 30-month expiration). Thus a national application filed before the 30-month expiration will be copending unless the international application was withdrawn (either generally or as to the U.S.) prior to the filing of the national application. For older cases where the 20-month rule applied (20-month expiration before Apr. 1, 2002), additional rules (e.g., timely demand electing the U.S.) may apply. To determine withdrawal, the examiner may inspect the Home Copy of the international application file (if USPTO was receiving Office) or require applicant to certify non-withdrawal. Applicant should certify at filing that the international application has not been withdrawn to expedite examination. If the national application claiming benefit was filed after the 30-month period, there will be no copendency absent a timely and proper submission to enter the national phase under 35 U.S.C. 371. The existence of a national stage application may be checked via the Patent Data Portal and national stage records.

name: Intermediate international application benefit claims must include specific reference to earlier application
description: If benefit under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) and/or under 35 U.S.C. 120 and 365(c) is being claimed to an earlier filed national application via an intermediate international application, the intermediate international application must contain a specific reference to the earlier application as required by 37 CFR 1.78.
guidance: The specific reference will usually appear on the cover page of the published international application and/or in the first sentence(s) of the description of the published application. Lack of a proper reference in the published international application does not necessarily mean the reference was not contained in the intermediate international application (it may have been filed in a separate paper after publication or a petition to accept a late benefit claim may be present). Examiners may need to inspect the international application file (if USPTO was receiving Office) to determine whether 37 CFR 1.78 requirements were satisfied after publication. Examiner may contact International Patent Legal Administration for assistance. See MPEP § 211.04.

name: Timing rules and non-extendability of required submissions
description: Various required submissions and deadlines (e.g., the specific reference under 37 CFR 1.78(d)(3) and foreign priority claim under 37 CFR 1.55(d)(1)) are subject to strict time periods that are not extendable.
guidance: Applicants must ensure required references and priority claims are timely submitted in the correct form (ADS, specification placement, certified copies) because the statutory/regulatory time periods for these requirements are non-extendable. Examiners should verify whether filings meet these deadline requirements and may require supporting proof when appropriate.

name: Filing date for nonprovisional applications (37 CFR 1.53(b))
description: The filing date is the date on which a specification, with or without claims, is received in the Office for nonprovisional applications (except design/provisional special rules).
guidance: No new matter may be introduced into an application after its filing date. A continuing application may be filed under conditions specified in 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, 365(c) or 386(c) and § 1.78.

name: Filing date for design applications
description: For design patents (except continued prosecution design applications under paragraph (d)), the filing date is the date on which the specification as prescribed by 35 U.S.C. 112 (including at least one claim) and any required drawings are received in the Office.
guidance: Design application filing dates are subject to the same 'no new matter after filing' rule and to continued-prosecution-specific provisions where applicable.

name: Provisional application filing requirements (37 CFR 1.53(c))
description: The filing date of a provisional application is the date on which a specification, with or without claims, is received in the Office; a provisional must include the cover sheet required by § 1.51(c)(1) (which may be an ADS or cover letter identifying it as provisional).
guidance: No amendment other than to make the provisional comply with the statute/regulations may be made after the provisional filing date. If a provisional lacks the cover sheet, it will be treated as a nonprovisional application under § 1.53(b). Provisional applications are not examined and become abandoned no later than 12 months after filing (35 U.S.C. 111(b)(1)).

name: Conversion between provisional and nonprovisional applications
description: Conversion of a nonprovisional to provisional or provisional to nonprovisional is permitted under specified conditions and must be accompanied by the required processing/filing fees and, when converting to nonprovisional, an amendment including at least one claim as prescribed by 35 U.S.C. 112(b) unless already present.
guidance: Conversion to provisional does not entitle refund of fees paid. Conversion of a provisional to nonprovisional will cause the patent term to be measured from at least the provisional filing date; applicants are advised to consider claiming benefit of the provisional under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) instead of conversion to avoid adverse patent term impact. Requests to convert must be filed prior to the earliest of: abandonment, payment of the issue fee, or expiration of 12 months after the provisional filing date; accompany required fees (§ 1.17(i)) and any required filing/search/examination fees and surcharges.

name: Priority and benefit limitations for provisional applications
description: A provisional application is not entitled to the right of priority under 35 U.S.C. 119, 365(a), or 386(a) or § 1.55, nor to the benefit of an earlier filing date under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, 365(c), or 386(c) or § 1.78 of any other application.
guidance: No claim for priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or § 1.78(a) may be made in a design application based on a provisional application. Sequence data submissions in provisionals filed on or after July 1, 2022 must be by 'Sequence Listing XML' in compliance with §§ 1.831–1.834.

name: Continued prosecution (nonprovisional) / Continued prosecution application rules (37 CFR 1.53(d))
description: A continuation or divisional (but not continuation-in-part) of a prior nonprovisional may be filed as a continued prosecution application under paragraph (d) if certain conditions are met (e.g., design applications; prior application complete as defined; filed before payment of issue fee, abandonment, or termination).
guidance: The filing date of a continued prosecution application is the date a request on a separate paper is filed. The application must identify the prior application, disclose and claim only subject matter disclosed in the prior application, name the same inventors (with limited exceptions), include the request and use the prior application's file jacket and contents, be assigned the prior application's application number, and expressly abandon the prior application as of the filing date of the request. Filing fees for continued prosecution applications are the basic filing, search, and examination fees as specified.

name: Filing date and review of claimed subject matter
description: A filing date is normally granted before review of the subject matter claimed in a nonprovisional application; if the application appears sufficient, it is forwarded to the examiner for consideration in the regular course of examination.
guidance: If documents purporting to be a specification are so incoherent that they do not constitute a specification per 35 U.S.C. 112 and 37 CFR 1.71, the application will not be accorded a filing date until corrections are made (filing date becomes date corrections are made).

name: Inequitable conduct defense standard (clear and convincing; intent required)
description: "One or more claims of a patent may be held to be unenforceable, or other remedy imposed under paragraph (4), for inequitable conduct only if it is established, by clear and convincing evidence, that a person with a duty of disclosure to the Office, with the intent to mislead or deceive the patent examiner, misrepresented or failed to disclose material information to the examiner during examination of the patent."
guidance: Inequitable conduct requires clear-and-convincing proof that a person with a duty to disclose, acting with intent to mislead/deceive the examiner, misrepresented or withheld material information during prosecution.

name: Inequitable conduct: materiality standard
description: "(A) In general.—Information is material under this section if— (i) a reasonable examiner would have made a prima facie finding of unpatentability, or maintained a finding of unpatentability, of one or more of the patent claims based on the information, and the information is not cumulative to information already of record or previously considered by the Office; or (ii) information that is otherwise material refutes or is inconsistent with a position the applicant takes in opposing a rejection of the claim or in asserting an argument of patentability."
guidance: Materiality is defined either by whether a reasonable examiner would make/maintain a prima facie finding of unpatentability based on the information (non-cumulative), or whether the information refutes/inconsistently supports an applicant's asserted position on patentability.

name: Inequitable conduct: prima facie finding test and claim construction
description: "(B) Prima facie finding.—A prima facie finding of unpatentability under this section is shown if a reasonable examiner, based on a preponderance of the evidence, would conclude that the claim is unpatentable based on the information misrepresented or not disclosed, when that information is considered alone or in conjunction with other information or record. In determining whether there is a prima facie finding of unpatentability, each term in the claim shall be given its broadest reasonable construction consistent with the specification, and rebuttal evidence shall not be considered."
guidance: For prima facie unpatentability, use preponderance standard, give claim terms their broadest reasonable construction consistent with the specification, and do not consider rebuttal evidence in that determination.

name: Inequitable conduct: remedies (equitable balancing and listed options)
description: "Upon a finding of inequitable conduct, the court shall balance the equities to determine which of the following remedies to impose: (A) Denying equitable relief to the patent holder and limiting the remedy for infringement to reasonable royalties. (B) Holding the claims-in-suit, or the claims in which inequitable conduct occurred, unenforceable. (C) Holding the patent unenforceable. (D) Holding the claims of a related patent unenforceable."
guidance: Court must balance equities and may impose a range of remedies from denying equitable relief (limiting to reasonable royalties) up to rendering claims, the patent, or related patent claims unenforceable.

name: Disclaimer for overbroad original claims
description: Specifications may be amended by filing a disclaimer whenever, through inadvertence, accident, or mistake, the original claim was too broad, provided some material and substantial part of the thing patented is truly the patentee's own.
guidance: A disclaimer may be filed in the patent office by the patentee, his administrator, executors, and assigns, whether of the whole or of a sectional interest in the patent; thereafter it is taken and considered part of the original specification to the extent of the disclaimant's interest, and by those claiming by or under him subsequent to the record thereof. See also requirements under sections of Act of 1837 for when a disclaimer is to be filed and who should join.

name: Effect of renewal/extension on assignees and grantees
description: There is a statutory clause declaring 'the benefit of such renewal shall extend to assignees and grantees of the right to use the thing patented to the extent of their respective interests therein.'
guidance: However, it has been held that assignees under the original patent may not automatically acquire rights under an extended patent obtained pursuant to certain extension provisions unless such right is expressly conveyed to them by the patentee. Practical effect depends on the nature of the conveyance and statutory language; usage and prior recoveries under original patent may strengthen a claimant's right to an injunction after reissue.

name: Knowledge competencies (Part A)
description: Candidates must exhibit understanding of general patent prosecution issues governed by the Patent Act, Patent Rules, MOPOP, and case law.
guidance: Examples include designation of trademarks, incorporation by reference statements, proper reference to external documents, proper claim dependency structure, and other general practice issues.

name: Basic claim structure (example issue)
description: Knowledge of proper basic claim drafting and structure.
guidance: Includes correct dependency, wording, and structural principles for claims.

name: Claim types (example issue)
description: Recognition and treatment of different claim types (e.g., apparatus, method, composition).
guidance: Understand implications for drafting, support and examination.

name: Preambles (example issue)
description: Understanding the role and effect of claim preambles.
guidance: Know when preamble language affects claim scope and how examiners treat preambles.

name: Elements within claims (example issue)
description: Analysis of individual claim elements and their role in claim scope and support.
guidance: Evaluate element language for clarity, support, and patentability concerns.

name: Steps (method/process) (example issue)
description: Issues specific to method/process claims and their steps.
guidance: Includes ordering, dependencies, and support for step-based claims.

name: Product-by-process (example issue)
description: Issues arising for product-by-process claims.
guidance: Recognize limitations and support requirements for product-by-process claim forms.

name: Use of workpiece or Environmental element (example issue)
description: Claims involving the use of a workpiece or environmental element and attendant issues.
guidance: Understand how such elements affect claim scope and patentability analysis.

name: Negative limitations (example issue)
description: Use and support of negative claim limitations.
guidance: Know when negative limitations are allowable and how to support them in the specification.

name: Claim support (example issue)
description: Ensuring claims are supported by the disclosure.
guidance: Assess sufficiency of description to support claimed subject matter (written description/support requirement).

name: Antecedent (example issue)
description: Proper antecedent basis in claims (use of definite articles/phrases to introduce claim terms).
guidance: Avoid antecedent errors that create ambiguity or indefiniteness in claims.

name: Indefiniteness/ambiguity (example issue)
description: Identifying and addressing indefiniteness or ambiguity in claims or specification.
guidance: Candidates should be able to amend or argue to resolve indefiniteness objections.

name: Dependent claim errors (example issue)
description: Errors in dependent claim form or structure.
guidance: Recognize and correct dependency or referencing errors in dependent claims.

name: Appeal claims presumption
description: An appeal, when taken, is presumed to be taken from the rejection of all claims under rejection unless canceled by an amendment filed by the applicant and entered by the Office. (37 C.F.R. 41.31(c))
guidance: If appellant wishes to narrow which claims are on appeal, ensure any amendments to cancel claims are filed and entered by the Office; otherwise the appeal covers all rejected claims.

name: Board decision types and immediate consequences
description: Board decisions may be Affirmed, Affirmed‑in‑part, or Reversed. Affirmed: jurisdiction over an application or patent under ex parte reexamination passes to the examiner for any further action. Affirmed‑in‑part: the decision reverses all rejections pertaining to at least one, but not all, claims. Reversed: complete reversal of the examiner’s rejection(s).
guidance: If affirmed, proceedings are terminated unless an appeal to a court or civil action is timely filed, except where claims stand allowed or the decision requires further examiner action (37 C.F.R. 41.54; 1.197(a)). To continue prosecution after the Board’s decision, an amendment presenting new or amended claims together with an RCE under 37 C.F.R. 1.114 and fee (1.17(e)) may be filed. On reversal, the case is brought up for immediate examiner action; the examiner should not undertake a new search to find new references but, if the examiner knows of particular references indicating nonpatentability, the examiner should seek authorization (TC Director/CRU) under 37 C.F.R. 1.198 to reopen prosecution to enter a new rejection. See MPEP 1214.04 and MPEP § 706.07(h)(XI).

name: Anticipation (35 U.S.C. § 102) standard
description: To be anticipated, each and every element of the claim must be found, either expressly or inherently described, in a single prior art reference.
guidance: When claim elements are inherently taught, the result must be a necessary consequence of what was deliberately intended, but the prior art need not demonstrate that the authors appreciated the results (citing Atofina, Mehl/Biophile, Schering).

name: Obviousness (35 U.S.C. § 103) standard
description: Obviousness is determined by looking to the scope and content of the prior art, differences between the prior art and the claims at issue, and the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art (Graham factors).
guidance: Board may take account of inferences and creative steps a person of ordinary skill would employ (KSR). A claimed invention is unpatentable if differences render it obvious to a POSITA as of the effective filing date.

name: Level of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA)
description: Define the person of ordinary skill in the art based on the nature of the claimed invention and the prior art.
guidance: For method claims directed to treating patients, relevant POSITA may include clinicians (medical doctors) with experience treating cancer or with access to clinical-study expertise, as well as persons with research experience in immunology/genetics/clinical trials; determine scope from record and claim focus. Expert witnesses' qualifications must be supported; Board will accept testimony absent specific contrary argument.

name: 'In response to' claim-term interpretation
description: The phrase 'in response to' requires a causal relationship wherein the patient must be tested and, if determined to be MSI-H or dMMR, then the patient is treated with pembrolizumab.
guidance: This causal relationship differs from 'after'; however, the Board declined to import negative limitations excluding treatment of other patients not recited in the claim. The claim's scope is limited to what is recited; do not read unclaimed negative limitations into claim terms.

name: Open-ended transitional phrase 'comprising'
description: 'Comprising' in a method claim indicates the claim is open-ended and allows for additional steps.
guidance: Because 'comprising' is open-ended, additional steps taken in conjunction with the recited method steps are not excluded from claim scope.

name: Inherency principle and effect on efficacy
description: When a prior-art reference discloses steps that necessarily produce a claimed result, the result can be inherent even if the prior authors did not appreciate it.
guidance: If efficacy is a necessary consequence of the prior-art steps (e.g., dosage and treatment regimen disclosed), efficacy can be inherent and support anticipation; Mehl/Biophile cited.

name: Treatment of dependent-claim limitations in obviousness
description: When independent claims are shown to be anticipated, dependent claims may still be analyzed for obviousness over additional references for discrete limitations.
guidance: Patent Owner must specifically rebut obviousness for dependent-claim limitations; failure to address discrete limitations may permit Board to find them obvious if prior art supplies them with motivation and expectation of success.

name: What a design patent protects (ornamental design)
description: A design patent is directed to the ornamental design for an article of manufacture. 'Ornamental design' means the shape of the design, and/or the surface decoration on the design. A valid U.S. design patent gives the patent owner the right for 14 years from the date the patent is granted to prevent others from making, using, offering to sell, or selling the patented design within the United States or importing it into the United States without the patent holder’s permission.
guidance: Explains prosecution basics: application includes a specification with drawings/photographs and a single claim that refers to the drawings; examiner reviews prior art to determine if claimed design is patentable. Cited authority: 35 U.S.C. § 171.

name: Prior art (scope and content)
description: Prior art generally includes things that existed before the claimed design and might typically be a patent or a printed publication, public use, public display, or offers for sale.
guidance: Further detailed in anticipation and obviousness sections (e.g., public use, prior patents, printed publications, commercial use, foreign patents, one-year bars).

name: Claim scope defined by the drawings (overall visual impression)
description: The scope of the claim is defined by the drawing(s) in the design patent, not just by one feature. The scope encompasses its visual appearance as a whole and in particular the overall visual impression it creates.
guidance: Consider all features of the design as a whole, not isolated portions. The specification supplements drawings. The prosecution history may affect the claimed design. Cited authorities include Egyptian Goddess (Fed. Cir. en banc) and Elmer v. ICC Fabricating.

name: Burden of proof — clear and convincing evidence
description: When a party has the burden by clear and convincing evidence, it means the evidence has persuaded you that the claim or defense is highly probable; this is a higher standard than preponderance but less than beyond a reasonable doubt.
guidance: Used for certain issues such as proving invalidity or willful infringement. Cited authorities given (Pfizer v. Apotex; Intel v. ITC).

name: Claim construction — judge's role and acceptance by jury
description: It is the judge's job to provide the meaning of the claim(s) of the asserted design patent(s). The jury must accept the judge's meaning and use it when deciding infringement and validity.
guidance: Scope encompasses visual appearance as a whole; judge will instruct that claim covers what is shown and described. Cited authorities: Markman, Phillips, Egyptian Goddess.

name: Claim construction — functional features included if shown in solid lines
description: Functional features illustrated in solid lines are part of the claimed design if they contribute to the overall visual appearance.
guidance: Even if portions perform a function, if depicted in solid lines they contribute to the claimed visual appearance.

name: Infringement — compare accused product to the patent
description: In deciding infringement, jurors must compare the defendant’s accused product to the patent (the claim/drawings), not to the plaintiff’s commercial product, unless instructed otherwise.
guidance: Patent law gives the owner the right to exclude making/using/offering/selling/importing the patented design during the patent term.

name: Direct (literal) infringement
description: Literal infringement requires that the accused product falls within the scope of the claimed design as shown in the patent drawings; jury asked whether patent holder has proven infringement more probable than not.
guidance: Model verdict forms ask direct (literal) infringement questions; jury compares accused article to the claimed design as a whole.

name: Indirect infringement — inducing infringement (elements)
description: To prove inducing infringement, the patent holder must show (a) the defendant actively encouraged or instructed another person to use a product in a way that infringes the claim, (b) the defendant knew of the design patent at that time, (c) the defendant knew or should have known the encouragement/instructions would result in infringement, and (d) another person actually infringed the claim.
guidance: Model verdict form B frames these as separate elements to be proven by a preponderance of the evidence.

name: Indirect infringement — contributory infringement (elements)
description: To prove contributory infringement, the patent holder must show (i) the defendant supplied a part or component to another for use in a product that infringes the claim; (ii) the component was a material part of the infringing product; (iii) the defendant supplied the component with knowledge of the design patent and that the component was especially made or adapted for infringing use; and (iv) the component did not have a substantial non-infringing use.
guidance: Model verdict form B lists these elements; jury decides each by preponderance.

name: Invalidity — obviousness (ordinary-observer analysis and factors)
description: Invalidity can be based on obviousness: whether the claimed design would have been obvious to the ordinary observer at the time the patent application was filed. Consider level of ordinary skill, scope and content of prior art, differences between claimed design and prior art, and secondary considerations indicating nonobviousness.
guidance: Secondary considerations include commercial success due to the merits of the claimed design, copying by others, acceptance/praise/licensing. Factors indicating obviousness include independent design by others.

name: Invalidity — written description, enablement, and indefiniteness
description: Invalidity grounds include lack of adequate written description, lack of enablement (i.e., failure to enable a designer of ordinary skill to understand what the claimed design looks like), and indefiniteness.
guidance: Model verdict includes specific questions on whether the patent does not enable a designer of ordinary skill to understand the claimed design (clear-and-convincing standard).

name: Invalidity — improper inventorship and double patenting
description: Invalidity can be based on improper inventorship (patent does not list the actual inventors) and on double patenting (features producing the novel aesthetic effect are the same as novel structure claimed in a utility patent/application).
guidance: Model verdict includes separate questions for these defenses; standard is high probability (clear and convincing).

name: Board not obliged to consider new/amended claims while it has jurisdiction
description: The Board has no obligation to consider new or amended claims submitted while it has jurisdiction of the appeal.
guidance: Exceptions: proposed amendments that cancel claims without affecting scope of others, or rewrite dependent claims into independent form, may be remanded for examiner consideration (see MPEP § 1206). If a proposed amendment is effectively an abandonment of the appeal, the appeal will normally be dismissed.

name: Board decision may affirm, reverse, remand, or designate new ground
description: In its decision the Board may affirm or reverse the examiner in whole or in part, remand an application to the examiner, or include a statement designating a new ground of rejection.
guidance: Affirmance on any ground specified by the examiner constitutes a general affirmance for that claim except as to grounds specifically reversed. A new ground of rejection pursuant to 37 CFR 41.50(b) is non-final for judicial review. When the Board enters a new ground, appellant has two months to (1) reopen prosecution (submit amendment/new evidence) or (2) request rehearing (37 CFR 41.50(b)(1)-(2)). If the Board’s decision includes a remand, it is not final for judicial review (37 CFR 41.50(e)).

name: When examiner re-rejects after remand
description: If the examiner determines the amendment/new evidence does not overcome the rejection, the examiner will reject the claims again and make the rejection final if appropriate.
guidance: If applicant desires further review after such a subsequent rejection, they must file a new appeal limited to the new ground and follow normal appeal procedures (new notice of appeal, brief, fees).

name: Sufficiency of disclosure / enablement (general)
description: A patent application must disclose a claimed invention in sufficient detail so that the person skilled in the art could carry out that claimed invention.
guidance: This requirement is fundamental to patent law: a monopoly is granted in exchange for a disclosure of how to make or practice the invention. If a patent fails to contain such information, the patent is unenforceable or can be revoked. Inventors who do not want to teach the world may use trade secrets instead, but without an enabling patent they cannot stop competitors who independently develop the invention.

name: US statutory requirement: 35 U.S.C. §112 — written description and enablement
description: The US patent specification must contain a written description of the invention and of the manner and process of making and using it, 'in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art... to make and use the same.'
guidance: US law has been interpreted to contain two related but distinct requirements: written description and enablement. Written description justifies and supports the scope/terminology of the claims; enablement teaches how to make and use the invention. The two serve different purposes and are applied separately in practice.

name: Enablement: ability to practice without undue experimentation
description: A disclosure 'enables' the invention if it allows a person of ordinary skill in the art to practice the invention without undue experimentation.
guidance: Patents fail this test if they claim more than they teach (e.g., claiming all light bulbs but explaining only how to make one kind). A non-enabling claim may be rejected during examination or invalidated later. Enablement is evaluated as of the filing date, and patent owners cannot rely on experiments conducted post-application to establish enablement.

name: Undue experimentation and the Wands factors
description: Undue experimentation is the standard for failing enablement; it concerns unpredictability of outcome rather than merely quantity of work.
guidance: Federal Circuit (In re Wands) identified eight factors to consider: (1) the quantity of experimentation necessary; (2) the amount of direction or guidance presented; (3) the presence or absence of working examples; (4) the nature of the invention; (5) the state of the prior art; (6) the relative skill of those in the art; (7) the predictability or unpredictability of the art; and (8) the breadth of the claims. Predictable arts (mechanical, software) typically require little description (e.g., flow charts may suffice); unpredictable arts (chemistry, pharmaceuticals) require very detailed disclosure. Case examples: patents invalidated where specification did not enable PHOSITA without undue experimentation (e.g., some Lemelson patents). The Supreme Court (Amgen v. Sanofi) said the specification may call for a reasonable amount of experimentation to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention.

name: Written description / possession requirement
description: The written description requirement demands that the applicant's disclosure demonstrate possession of the invention and sufficiently support the claims, preventing speculative filings for inventions not yet actually invented.
guidance: Purpose: to prevent applicants from obtaining priority for inventions they have not yet invented. A written description deficiency can render claims invalid (example: University of Rochester v. G.D. Searle — claims to identifying inhibitors were invalid because no specific compounds were disclosed). Written description determines claim scope and prevents later asserting invention not described in the text.

name: Deposit of biological material as a means to meet disclosure
description: For biological materials that cannot be precisely described (e.g., cell lines, plasmids), making a deposit of the claimed material (e.g., under the Budapest Treaty) can be used to satisfy written description/enablement requirements.
guidance: In the US biological deposits may be made any time before patent issuance (and sometimes during reexamination), while many other countries require deposits before filing. Deposits are typically kept for around 30 years. The deposit option addresses difficulties in describing self-replicating biological materials where molecular structure is not available.

name: Procedural and evidentiary timing: enablement evaluated at filing date; written description treated differently
description: Enablement is determined as of the filing date of the patent application; written description is a factual inquiry tied to the disclosure and claims.
guidance: Because enablement is fixed at filing date, post-filing experiments generally cannot cure an enabling deficiency. US courts treat enablement as a question of law based on underlying factual findings, whereas the written description requirement is often treated as a question of fact (sometimes decided by a jury). These procedural distinctions affect litigation and invalidity defenses.

name: SG IP FAST (patent acceleration) eligibility criteria
description: To qualify for patent acceleration under SG IP FAST, the following criteria have to be met: a. Application must be first filed in Singapore i.e., no priority claim; b. Patents Form 1, prescribed fee and complete patent specification is filed; c. Patents Form 11 and prescribed fee is filed on the same day as Patents Form 1; d. Request for acceleration under SG IP FAST indicated on Patents Form 11; e. Application must contain 20 or fewer claims; f. Applicant needs to respond within 2 weeks from the date of receipt of Formalities Examination Adverse report (if issued); f. Applicant needs to respond within 2 months from date of receipt of written opinion (if issued); g. Reason(s) for requesting acceleration and the technology field to which the invention relates has to be furnished on Patents Form 11; and h. The request is within the cap on the number of requests that is imposed for the programme.
guidance: Note duplicate lettering in source (two 'f' entries). The respondent must meet each timing and filing requirement; indicate reasons and technology field on Form 11; the programme is capped—ensure quota availability.

name: Formalities officer pre-issuance checklist for Certificate of Grant
description: Once the request is received, the Formalities officer will review the following requirements – a. Fee has been paid; b. Date of filing has been accorded; c. Preliminary examination has been cleared; d. National security clearance has been issued, if applicable; e. The application is not treated as abandoned, withdrawn, refused or granted; f. Representation details and/or address for service on this form correspond with that on record; g. Examination report has been established from request for Search and/or Examination Report (Patents Form 11/12), Supplementary Examination Report (Patents Form 12A), or Examination Review Report (Patents Form 12B/13); h. The Examination report does not contain unresolved objections on lack of unity; i. Notice of Eligibility has been issued; j. The form is filed within 2 months from the date of issuance of Notice of Eligibility or extension approved; k. A set of consolidated specification is filed if required and within time; l. Consolidated specification aligns with all amendments/corrections/missing parts on record; m. Title of invention on record is the same as the consolidated specification; n. Number of claims indicated on the form corresponds to the number of claims in consolidated specifications.
guidance: If any requirements are not met, the Formalities officer will invite the applicant to clarify or rectify within 2 months, with a reminder if necessary. Rectifications typically use Form CM4 (correction types), CM1/CM2 for representation changes, and eCommunications for clarification letters.

name: Rectification procedure for errors before grant
description: To rectify errors, the applicant may file Form CM4 and indicate the relevant rule in which the correction is sought (Rules 58 and/or 91). Options include: 'Correction of Form lodged' for errors on the form; 'Correction of Specification of a Patent or of an Application for a Patent' for errors on the consolidated specification; 'Correction of any other document relating to a Patent or an Application for a Patent' for errors on other documents. Overpayments due to additional number of claims indicated on the form will be refunded after filing Form CM4; underpayments will be calculated and paid with Form CM4.
guidance: Follow the specified CM4 correction types. For title discrepancies due to translations or examiner changes, the officer will clarify with the applicant; voluntary amendments to the title are restricted and have prescribed routes.

name: Written description (possession of the invention)
description: Demonstrates the inventor was in possession of the invention as claimed (written description).
guidance: Describe the invention and its aspects clearly and specifically so the disclosure supports the full scope of the claimed subject matter; include support for claim limitations and variations.

name: Appropriate claim scope
description: Defines the invention in claims of appropriate scope, neither too broad (invalid over prior art) nor too narrow (easily designed around).
guidance: Balance breadth and patentability: draft claims wide enough to be meaningful but with support and distinctions over prior art; include fallback narrower claim sets.

name: Avoid estoppels
description: Avoids estoppels that would limit later claim construction or assertion.
guidance: Be cautious in specification and prosecution statements that could later be used to narrow claim interpretation; avoid admissions of intent or limitation unless necessary.

name: Prior art search
description: Identify the closest known references (prior art search).
guidance: Search relevant literature and patents to locate closest references, inform claim scope, and guide distinguishing language and fallback positions.

name: Claim drafting
description: Draft independent and dependent claims of varying scope (claim drafting).
guidance: Include multiple independent claims (different statutory categories where appropriate) and dependent claims that narrow on legally meaningful dimensions to provide layered protection and prosecution flexibility.

name: Specification drafting (support claim terms)
description: Write specification supporting all claim terms (specification drafting).
guidance: Ensure every claim term has support in the specification (definitions, embodiments, examples) and that the spec provides enablement and written description for claimed ranges and alternatives.

name: Drawings preparation
description: Prepare formal patent drawings (drawings preparation).
guidance: Provide clear, labeled figures with reference numbers matching the specification; drawings should illustrate embodiments and elements referred to in claims and description.

name: Review and revision
description: Multiple drafts; cross-check claims against spec for support (review and revision).
guidance: Iteratively revise claims and specification, checking antecedent basis, terminology consistency, and that claim scope is supported; use internal reviews to catch gaps or limiting language.

name: Single sentence claims
description: Each claim is a single sentence, however long (single sentence claims).
guidance: Compose claims as one sentence with correct punctuation and structure; avoid splitting claim elements into multiple sentences which may cause drafting or interpretation issues.

name: Antecedent basis
description: First mention of an element uses 'a' or 'an'; subsequent mentions use 'the' or 'said' (antecedent basis).
guidance: Maintain clear antecedent basis to avoid ambiguity in claim elements; ensure each term is introduced before being referred to with definite articles.

name: Consistent terminology
description: One term per concept throughout the application (consistent terminology).
guidance: Use the same term to refer to the same concept across claims and specification to avoid confusion or unintended narrowing; avoid introducing multiple synonyms for the same element unless defined.

name: Active voice for method steps
description: Method steps use active verbs (active voice).
guidance: Draft method claims and descriptions in active voice where appropriate to clearly attribute actions to the actor or apparatus and to improve clarity.

name: Reference numbers tied to figures
description: Each element in the spec is given a number that ties to the figures (reference numbers).
guidance: Assign consistent reference numerals in the specification and drawings to make element references unambiguous and to support claim interpretation.

name: No marketing language
description: Avoid superlatives and promotional terms (no marketing language).
guidance: Exclude marketing phrases or unsupported claims of superiority (e.g., 'best', 'superior') since they may introduce unintended limitations or provide no technical disclosure value.

name: Comprising (open transitional phrase)
description: 'Comprising': Open transitional phrase.
guidance: Use 'comprising' to indicate the claimed device/process includes the recited elements but may include additional elements; choose transitions deliberately to control claim scope.

name: Consisting of (closed transitional phrase)
description: 'Consisting of': Closed transitional phrase.
guidance: Use 'consisting of' to limit the claim to the listed elements only; recognize it excludes unrecited elements and therefore narrows scope sharply.

name: Means for (invoke 35 U.S.C. §112(f) in US)
description: 'Means for': Invokes 35 USC 112(f) in US.
guidance: Avoid or use 'means for' clauses with care: they can trigger means-plus-function claim treatment, which constrains the claim to the structures disclosed in the specification that perform the function.

name: Plurality defined
description: 'Plurality' means 'two or more' (plurality).
guidance: If using terms like 'plurality', ensure the specification and claims make clear what numerical range is intended (e.g., two or more) to prevent ambiguity.

name: Embodiment disclosure (multiple embodiments and alternatives)
description: Disclose multiple embodiments of the invention, including alternative materials, geometries, processes, and ranges (embodiment disclosure).
guidance: Provide alternative implementations, materials, parameter ranges, and fallback features to support broader claim construction and to provide prosecution fallback positions.

name: Claim hierarchy (independent and dependent claims)
description: A typical strong patent has several independent claims (covering method, system, apparatus, etc.) with dependent claims that narrow on legally meaningful dimensions (claim hierarchy).
guidance: Draft independent claims to cover different statutory categories and include dependent claims that add specific limitations, preferred ranges, or optional features to preserve enforceable fallbacks.

name: Continuation practice (planning for continuations)
description: Plan for continuation applications, which allow the applicant to pursue different claim scopes in subsequent applications based on the same disclosure (continuation practice).
guidance: Structure the disclosure and claim sets to enable future continuations: disclose alternatives and claim-supporting details now so later filings can pursue broader or different scopes without new matter issues.

name: Physicality/tangibility is not determinative
description: Mere physicality or tangibility of an additional element or elements is not a relevant consideration in Step 2B; a computer's physical existence alone is not an inventive concept.
guidance: Quoting Alice: a computer being a tangible system is 'beside the point' — physical implementation alone cannot render a judicial exception patent eligible; conversely, absence of physicality does not automatically doom claims (see Alice, Myriad, Enfish, Genetic Technologies, McRO).

name: Step 2B process: identify and evaluate additional elements individually and in combination
description: Step 2B asks whether the claim recites additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception. Examiners should first identify any additional elements and then evaluate those additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether they contribute an inventive concept.
guidance: Use the considerations the Supreme Court identified and those in MPEP §2106.05(a)-(h). The evaluation is not a weighing test; examine significance relative to applicant's invention and treat each claim separately. If claim contains multiple discrete exceptions, examiners may select one exception for efficiency, but should avoid parsing a single exception into multiple exceptions.

name: Examine each claim separately; dependent claims can differ in eligibility
description: Examiners should examine each claim for eligibility separately, based on the particular elements recited; claims should not be judged to automatically stand or fall with similar claims in an application.
guidance: One claim may be ineligible while a dependent claim that recites additional elements might be eligible because it amounts to significantly more.

name: Do not parse a single abstract-idea claim into multiple exceptions unless distinct
description: Unless it is clear that the claim recites distinct exceptions (e.g., a law of nature and an abstract idea), care should be taken not to parse the claim into multiple exceptions, particularly in claims involving abstract ideas.
guidance: If multiple discrete exceptions are clearly present, select one exception and conduct the analysis for that exception; if additional elements amount to significantly more than the selected exception, the claim should be considered eligible.

name: Consideration: improvements to computer functioning or other technology (MPEP §2106.05(a))
description: Determine whether the claim 'purport(s) to improve the functioning of the computer itself' or 'any other technology or technical field' — i.e., whether the claim searches for a technological solution to a technological problem.
guidance: This consideration may be relevant to Step 2A or Step 2B (or streamlined analyses). Consult precedent (Enfish, McRO, DDR, Amdocs, Visual Memory). To show an improvement, the specification should explain the technical problem and the unconventional technical solution; courts have relied on specification disclosure plus specific claim limitations to find improvements.

name: Specification must provide a technical explanation of the improvement
description: If it is asserted that the invention improves upon conventional computer functioning or conventional technology, a technical explanation as to how to implement the invention should be present in the specification.
guidance: Disclosure must provide sufficient detail such that one of ordinary skill would recognize the claimed invention as providing an improvement. Examples: McRO (specification explained how rules enabled automation) vs. Affinity Labs (spec failed to provide implementation details). See MPEP §2106.05(a).

name: Claim must reflect the improvement under broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI)
description: After determining that the specification discloses an improvement, the claim itself must be evaluated to ensure the claim reflects the improvement in technology under its full scope (BRI).
guidance: Consider the claim 'as a whole' and as an 'ordered combination' without ignoring individual step requirements. Avoid oversimplifying claims. Examples: Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec (claims didn't reflect alleged improvement even if specification argued so); McRO discussion of evaluating claim scope.

name: Improvement must be a particular solution (not merely an idea or outcome)
description: An important consideration is the extent to which the claim covers a particular solution to a problem or a particular way to achieve a desired outcome, as opposed to merely claiming the idea of a solution or outcome.
guidance: This consideration overlaps with 'particular machine' and 'mere instructions to apply' considerations (see DDR, McRO). Claims that specify particular ways or structures to achieve results are more likely to be eligible.

name: Method claims must be limited to computer implementation to show computer improvement
description: For a method claim to improve computer functionality, the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim must be limited to computer implementation; if the entire scope can be performed mentally or verbally, it cannot be said to improve computer technology.
guidance: Cases: Synopsys (entire steps could be performed mentally — ineligible), RecogniCorp (process could be practiced verbally or without a computer — ineligible). Ensure claim scope requires computer implementation.

name: Examples that may show an improvement in computer functionality or technology
description: Illustrative examples courts have indicated may show improvements: modification of hyperlink protocol to produce hybrid webpage (DDR); inventive distribution of network functionality for filtering (BASCOM); methods of rendering halftone images; distributed network architectures reducing congestion; configurable memory systems; technical details for transmitting images over cellular networks; particular server structures for organized digital images; specific software programming/design creating menus.
guidance: These examples are precedential illustrations where courts found improvements — examiners should compare claim and specification facts to these types of features when evaluating Step 2A/2B.

name: Examples that courts have indicated may not be sufficient to show improvement
description: Illustrative examples courts found insufficient: generating restaurant menus with functional features (Ameranth); accelerating analysis only by virtue of general-purpose computer speed (FairWarning); merely using a computer to perform an abstract idea (Return Mail); mere automation of manual processes (Credit Acceptance, LendingTree); recording/transmitting/archiving digital images using conventional technology without inventive solution (TLI Communications).
guidance: These are counter-examples: claiming conventional computer use, automation, or relying solely on general-purpose computer capacity typically fails to provide 'significantly more.' Examiners should be wary of such fact patterns.

name: Design claim covers whole design (not parts) — combination/subcombination rule
description: A design claim covers the entire design as a whole and does not extend to any individual part or portion thereof; patent protection does not extend to patentably distinct segregable parts.
guidance: Combination/subcombination subject matter that is patentably distinct must be supported by separate claims; because only a single claim is permissible in a design patent application, patentably distinct combinations/subcombinations require separate applications/claims. See KeyStone Retaining Wall Systems Inc. v. Westrock Inc., Ex parte Sanford, Blumcraft of Pittsburgh v. Ladd.

name: Traversal based on burden-to-search inapplicable for design patents
description: A traversal arguing 'no serious burden' to search the entire application (as in MPEP § 803) is not applicable to design patent applications.
guidance: The fact that embodiments may be searched together cannot preclude restriction if their appearances are patentably distinct, since patentably distinct embodiments cannot be supported by a single formal design claim.

name: Double patenting determinations and rejections
description: Two types of double patenting rejections: (1) 'same invention' statutory double patenting under 35 U.S.C. 171 (same design claimed twice), and (2) nonstatutory double patenting (judicial doctrine) to prevent prolongation of patent term where claims in a second patent are not patentably distinct from claims in a first patent.
guidance: Determination involves: Is the same design being claimed twice? If yes, apply 35 U.S.C. 171 rejection. If not, are the designs patentably indistinct variations of the same inventive concept? If yes, apply nonstatutory double patenting (obviousness-based) rejection. Double patenting rejections are based on comparison of claims; in design-versus-utility comparisons examiners must be able to recreate the design claimed from the utility claims without reliance on drawings. See MPEP § 804 for procedure charts and case law references.

name: Definition of a Markush grouping
description: A 'Markush grouping' is a style of claim drafting by which the applicant recites alternate species of a genus, often used in chemical patent claim drafting. A Markush structure is a representation of a group of chemical compounds that share a common core but differ in one or more variable groups (e.g., R1, R2).
guidance: Use a Markush grouping to represent a family of compounds that share a core structure but vary at defined positions. This is the conceptual baseline for determining whether a claim is a true Markush group rather than a mere list of disparate species.

name: Claim format and structure (example format)
description: Example format: 'A compound of the formula [Core Structure] wherein R1 is selected from the group consisting of [List of Substituents].'
guidance: This format provides a flexible framework by allowing the inventor to claim not just one specific compound, but a family of compounds. Use clear claim language that indicates selection from a group (e.g., 'selected from the group consisting of') when appropriate to express alternatives.

name: Members must share at least one property in common responsible for function
description: A Markush grouping is ordinarily proper if all the members are disclosed in the specification to possess at least one property in common which is mainly responsible for their function in the claimed invention.
guidance: The specification should disclose and link a common property (e.g., physicochemical property or biological activity) that explains why the grouped species operate interchangeably in the invention. Absent such a shared property, the grouping risks rejection.

name: Definiteness requirement (35 U.S.C. §112)
description: Markush claims must meet the definiteness requirement of 35 U.S.C. §112.
guidance: Claim language must be sufficiently clear and definite to inform those skilled in the art of the scope of the claim. Vague or ambiguous group descriptions can render a Markush claim indefinite.

name: Choice of transitional/open vs closed claim language
description: The term 'consisting of' is closed language that limits the claim to only the listed elements; 'comprising' is open-ended and allows for additional, unlisted elements.
guidance: Select transitional language deliberately: use 'consisting of' to expressly limit the claim to listed members; use 'comprising' to permit additional unrecited elements. Understand the legal effect of the chosen transition on claim scope and potential prior art/anticipation issues.

name: Clearly define substituents and provide examples in the specification
description: Each substituent in the Markush group should be well-defined, ideally with examples or definitions in the specification.
guidance: Provide explicit definitions, examples, or representative species in the disclosure for each substituent (R-group) to support written description and enablement across the claimed genus. Concrete examples reduce ambiguity and strengthen the claim against challenges.

name: Improper Markush rejection reasons (examiner triggers)
description: Examiners may reject a Markush claim as improper if: the members do not share a common structural feature; the members do not share a common use; or the grouping appears to be merely a list of disparate species.
guidance: When drafting, anticipate examiner scrutiny by ensuring structural and functional unity and by avoiding mere listing of unrelated species. If facing a rejection, respond by showing the recognized class, common property/use, or by amending to narrower, supported groupings.

name: Strategic advantage: conserve claims and claim families
description: Markush structures allow inventors to claim a wide range of structurally related compounds under a single patent claim and conserve writing additional claims, important because standard filing fees include only twenty total claims.
guidance: Use Markush groupings strategically to cover families of compounds and manage claim count/fees, but balance breadth with the need to satisfy §112 requirements and avoid improper grouping rejections.

name: Presence of an unexpected property is evidence of nonobviousness
description: If a claimed invention possesses a property not possessed by the prior art, that presence of an unexpected property supports nonobviousness.
guidance: Unexpected presence need not automatically establish nonobviousness; context and weight of other evidence matter. (Cites: In re Papesch; Ex parte Thumm; In re Payne.) See MPEP §2145 for latent properties.

name: Direct and indirect comparative tests are probative of nonobviousness
description: Direct or indirect comparisons of the claimed invention with the closest prior art, commensurate in scope with the claims, are valid probative evidence.
guidance: Comparative testing (direct or indirect) can rebut prima facie obviousness; must be commensurate in scope. (Cites: In re Boesch; In re Blondel; In re Fouche.)

name: Expected beneficial results are evidence of obviousness
description: Beneficial results that would have been expected from the prior art are evidence supporting obviousness.
guidance: If the claimed beneficial effect is taught or would have been expected, it weighs toward obviousness. (Cites: In re Gershon; Ex parte Blanc.)

name: Unexpected results must be commensurate in scope with the claims
description: Objective evidence of nonobviousness (including unexpected results) must be commensurate in scope with the claims they are offered to support (i.e., occur over the claimed range).
guidance: Showing unexpected results for only a narrow or different scope than claimed may be insufficient to rebut an obviousness rejection. Provide testing across the claimed range or explain why narrower data are predictive. (Cites: In re Clemens; In re Peterson; In re Grasselli.)

name: Commercial success evidence must be commensurate in scope with the claims
description: Commercial success must be due to the claimed features and be commensurate in scope with the claims being supported.
guidance: Affidavits claiming product was 'constructed according to the disclosure and claims' without evidence that sold product corresponds to claimed invention do not establish nexus. Evidence of success due to unclaimed features is insufficient. (Cites: In re Tiffin; Joy Technologies v. Manbeck; Ex parte Standish.)

name: Commercial success must flow from functions/advantages disclosed or inherent in the specification
description: Success of devices within the claims must flow from functions or advantages disclosed or inherent in the specification; success attributable to third-party modifications is not probative.
guidance: Evidence must show claimed features produced the commercial success; improvements by others cannot be credited to the applicant. (Cites: In re Vamco Machine & Tool.)

name: Definition of novelty destroying
description: Prior art is deemed 'novelty destroying' if it anticipates or references every element of at least one of a proposed invention’s claims.
guidance: Treat anticipation of all claim elements by a single prior-art document as the criterion for novelty destruction; this is the core labeling semantics used throughout the pipeline.

name: Prefer claim sets (entire claims) over short excerpts
description: Include broader claim sets rather than short claim excerpts when constructing examples.
guidance: Short excerpts (as used in PatentMatch) often lack context and hurt transformer models' ability to capture semantic relationships; claim sets better encapsulate essential elements defining novelty while providing context.

name: Dataset structure: row-wise to pairwise conversion
description: Convert dataset rows that contain a base patent and k related patents into a pairwise format where each example is a (base patent claims, related patent claims) pair with a binary label.
guidance: This pairwise format allows training sequence classification models. Label 1 for novelty-destroying pairs and 0 otherwise. Ensure nulls are used for missing claimed-related fields when fewer positives exist to keep k consistent per base patent if desired.

name: Use Google Patents web-scraping for up-to-date claim retrieval
description: Query Google Patents (web-scraping) for claims of cited patents because Google Patents can redirect to current patent numbers if numbers are outdated.
guidance: APIs may return outdated publication numbers; web redirects from Google Patents help obtain the most recent documents. Implement robust scraping and respect terms of service.

name: Statutory requirement to specify and point out the claim
description: The Act of Congress requires, that he 'shall, particularly, specify and point the part, improvement, or combination, which he claims as his own invention.'
guidance: This statutory duty underpins the need for reasonable certainty in the description so the public can know whether they violate the patent and can practice the invention when the term expires.

name: Liberal construction in favour of inventors (but within sound principles)
description: A liberal construction is to be given to a patent, and inventors sustained, if practicable, without a departure from sound principles.
guidance: Specifications should be sustained if they can fairly be read to cover the invention; courts should not be astute to avoid inventions. This encourages ingenuity but must not depart from legal principles or allow vague or insufficient claims.

name: Plaintiff may assert specification requires explanation of facts to determine extent of claim
description: The plaintiff is always entitled to say, that his specification requires the explanation of facts, to determine the extent of his claim and the character of his invention.
guidance: The court should receive evidence to ascertain whether such explanation is needed, but watch that evidence does not supply essential omissions. The construction (meaning) may be affected by evidence where the court has no judicial knowledge of technical terms or circumstances.

name: Use of drawings, language, and declared objects to construe claim scope
description: Looking to the whole specification and drawing, both the figure and language, [the court asks] could any one doubt that [a particular embodiment] was intended to be used in the new combination which was patented?
guidance: Courts may rely on drawings, explicit descriptions, and the inventor's stated objectives (e.g., increased velocity) to resolve ambiguities and determine which embodiments the patentee intended to claim.

name: Clarity and formal requirements of claims
description: Clarity of claims and other formal requirements are governed by Art.6 and related formal requirements, addressed in Part F, Chapter IV (Claims (Art. 6 and formal requirements)).
guidance: Contains examples concerning essential features and guidance on claim drafting/interpretation; where ISPE is silent EPO/EP practice on interpretation (including options chosen in Annex II) is applied. Multiple dependent claims, interpretation and conciseness follow the EPO‑selected ISPE options (see Appendix to Chapter 5).

name: Right to priority and priority document handling
description: Right to priority is governed by Art.8 and related Rules; the Guidelines set out requirements for priority claims and handling of priority documents (including fee for certified copy).
guidance: If missing parts/elements are later furnished, the 'completely contained' test (Rule 20.6) determines whether the original filing date is preserved. The test for 'completely contained' is stricter than the added‑subject‑matter test and requires identity (or translation) with the priority document; examiner checks and reporting obligations (WO‑ISA/IPER) are specified. The fee and time limits for restoration of priority rights are set out (fee to be paid within two months from expiry of the priority period).

name: Allowability of amendments / added subject‑matter
description: Allowability of amendments is governed by Art.19(2), Art.34(2)(b) and, for substantive assessment, the EPO applies Art.123(2) EPC guidelines mutatis mutandis.
guidance: Examiners must examine all amended pages (description, claims, drawings) to see whether they introduce subject‑matter not originally disclosed; amendments taken into consideration are not automatically allowable. Detailed cross‑references to the Guidelines for Examination in the EPO (sections H‑IV etc.) apply; many examples and rules (intermediate generalisations, disclaimers, broadening, deletion, etc.) are given and should be applied case‑by‑case.

name: EPO choices of ISPE policy options (Annex II)
description: Where the ISPE Guidelines leave ISAs/IPEAs a choice between alternative guidelines, the EPO has selected specific options for use as ISA/IPEA.
guidance: Annex II lists chosen options, e.g.: Appendix to Chapter 4 Point A4.05 References to prior art Option [1]; Appendix to Chapter 5 multiple dependent claims Option [2]; interpretation of claims Option [2]; 'use' claims first sentence applied; product‑by‑process Option [1]; conciseness Option [2]; Appendix to Chapter 9 excluded subject matter Option [2]; programs for computers Option [2]; Appendix to Chapter 12 novelty effective date Option [1]; Appendix to Chapter 13 EPO applies problem‑solution approach; Appendix to Chapter 14 industrial applicability criterion applied; Appendix to Chapter 20 disclaimer Option [2]. Examiners must apply these EPO choices when acting as ISA/IPEA.

name: Twenty-year term for utility and plant patents
description: For applications filed on or after June 8, 1995 (other than design patents), patent term begins on issue date and ends 20 years from the filing date of the application in the United States or, if claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, 365(c), or 386(c), from the earliest such application's filing date.
guidance: Design patents have different terms (see separate criterion). Continuations, divisionals, and continuation-in-part filings ending date rules follow the earliest benefit claim. Changes introduced by Patent Law Treaties Implementation Act added reference to 386(c).

name: Continuing application and international application term rules
description: A patent granted on a continuation, divisional, or continuation-in-part filed on or after June 8, 1995 ends twenty years from the filing date of the earliest application for which benefit is claimed under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, 365(c), or 386(c). Patents from international applications that enter the U.S. national stage have terms ending twenty years from the international filing date.
guidance: Continuation-in-part claiming benefit under 365(c) of an international application ends twenty years from the parent international filing date when applicable.

name: Trade secret, confidential, and protective-order material handling
description: Materials submitted in connection with a PTE application are generally part of the record and public unless properly identified and expunged; proprietary/trade secret info should be submitted in accordance with MPEP § 724.02 and identified by page/line/word as necessary. The Office will not initially determine which material is proprietary—applicant must identify it.
guidance: Information will not be made public as part of the patent file before a certificate of extension is issued. If the Office receives a FOIA request, applicant will be notified and given opportunity to substantiate proprietary claims before disclosure. If not expunged before certificate issuance, the information will be open to public inspection.

name: Duty to identify proprietary/material and petition to expunge
description: When submitting proprietary or trade secret material in a PTE application, applicant should identify specific proprietary portions; if necessary, a petition to expunge must be filed before issuance of the certificate to prevent disclosure. If petition to expunge is not filed prior to certificate issuance, the material becomes public.
guidance: The Office will notify applicant if a FOIA request is received for such material and provide an opportunity to substantiate claims before disclosure. See MPEP § 724.02 and PTE-specific handling.

name: Determine the closest prior art
description: The closest prior art is the most realistic starting point for reaching the invention. The overriding criterion is that it pertains to the same technical field and aims to solve the same or a similar technical problem as the invention. This generally means a prior art document which has a similar objective and requires the smallest number of modifications to reach the claimed invention.
guidance: Use the opinion accompanying the Search Report as a starting point. Do not choose a document merely because it shares many technical features if it does not belong to the same field or aim to solve the same problem (examples: battery cooling vs unrelated fields; yogurts vs cheeses).

name: Avoid ex post facto considerations when selecting closest prior art
description: Ex post facto considerations should be avoided in the determination of the closest prior art.
guidance: A document which does not mention the problem to be solved would not normally qualify as the closest prior art, regardless of the number of technical features it may have in common with the claimed invention. Do not rely on hindsight to identify a document as the closest prior art.
