name: Establish the objective technical problem
description: Compare the closest prior art and the claimed invention to identify differences between the two, then identify the technical effect of those differences. The technical effect is the technical advantage provided specifically by the differences. This technical effect is used to determine the objective technical problem solved by the invention, starting from the closest prior art.
guidance: Illustrative example: if the difference is a valve in a cooling circuit, the technical effect might be improved control over coolant flow, leading to better battery temperature control; the objective technical problem would be framed as 'how to improve temperature control of a battery?'.

name: Identify and associate technical effects to claim features in the description
description: When drafting the description, be careful to associate a technical effect to each of the features found in the claims.
guidance: Explicitly linking features to technical effects in the description will help defend any feature in the problem–solution approach during examination.

name: Evaluate inventive step by considering whether the skilled person would be prompted to modify the closest prior art
description: Determine whether there is any teaching in the rest of the prior art or in the closest prior art itself that would have prompted the skilled person, whose goal is to solve the objective technical problem, to modify or adapt the closest prior art to reach the claimed solution.
guidance: Positions of strength: (a) if none of the prior art documents provide solutions for solving the objective technical problem (e.g., none discuss a valve for coolant flow), you are in a strong position to defend inventive step; (b) if cited prior art discusses the objective technical problem but solves it with a different solution, you can also defend inventive step; (c) if prior art describes the same solution but not for solving the same technical problem, you should still be able to contest lack of inventive step.

name: Respond to an Article 56 EPC objection by explicitly following the problem–solution approach
description: When replying to an objection under Article 56 EPC, you should respond by clearly following the problem–solution approach and clearly stating each step of the approach.
guidance: A strong response includes explicit phrasing such as: 'The difference between document D1 and the claim is [...]', 'the technical effect of this difference is [...]', 'the objective technical problem is [...]', 'none of the cited prior art discloses the claimed solution for solving the objective technical problem' or 'Document D2 discloses a solution which is different to the claimed solution'. Such explicit wording is more likely to convince an examiner that the claimed invention is inventive.

name: Definition and basic function of a terminal disclaimer
description: A terminal disclaimer is a binding stipulation by a patent applicant that the patent’s term will not extend beyond the term of another patent.
guidance: Used by applicants to overcome USPTO rejections for nonstatutory (obviousness-type) double patenting; while it prevents term extension beyond the original patent, it can still expedite issuance of patents with duplicative claims that entrants must overcome.

name: Proposed enforceability condition for terminal disclaimers
description: Under the proposed rule, terminal disclaimers made to overcome a nonstatutory double patenting rejection would have to include a provision that the patent would be enforceable only if it has not been tied by a terminal disclaimer (to obviate nonstatutory double patenting) to another patent containing any claim that has been finally held unpatentable or invalid by a federal court or the USPTO, and for which all appeal rights have been exhausted.
guidance: This condition would mean that patents tied together by terminal disclaimers 'stand or fall together,' so invalidating the original claim would render later-filed patents with terminal disclaimers unenforceable.

name: Assessment criterion: whether terminal disclaimers facilitate patent thickets
description: Terminal disclaimers can expedite issuance of patents with duplicative claims and facilitate the growth of patent thickets by allowing applicants to quickly add more patents that fence off existing technologies.
guidance: Evaluate portfolios for duplicative claims linked by terminal disclaimers (e.g., Humira portfolio where many patents were duplicative and linked). Such linkage increases costs for entrants who must challenge multiple patents.

name: Policy balance criterion: reform should reduce gamesmanship while preserving alternatives
description: The proposed rule should reduce incentives for incumbents to file numerous duplicative patents tied by terminal disclaimers without foreclosing legitimate alternatives for applicants to address nonstatutory double patenting rejections.
guidance: Design reforms (like enforceability-conditioning disclaimers) to lower strategic filing while leaving in place reasonable options for patent owners to address legitimate claim-differentiation issues.

name: (R) Clarification/support for means/steps-plus-function claim limitations
description: Clarification of the correlation and identification of what structure, material, or acts set forth in the specification would be capable of carrying out a function recited in a means or steps plus function claim limitation.
guidance: If support for a means-plus-function limitation is not apparent and applicant cannot identify it, examiner may conclude no such support exists and make rejections under 35 U.S.C. 112 (written description) or 112 second paragraph (indefiniteness).

name: Interrogatories — support for means/steps-plus-function (35 U.S.C. 112, para. 6)
description: Interrogatory about the support found in the disclosure for means or steps plus function claims (35 U.S.C. 112, paragraph 6).
guidance: Seeks precise pointer to disclosure support for means-plus-function limitations.

name: Interrogatories — written description/enablement support for claim elements
description: Interrogatory of precisely which portion(s) of the disclosure provide the written description and enablement support for specific claim element(s).
guidance: Requires applicant to identify exact pages/lines/figures supporting claim elements.

name: Interrogatories — meaning of claim limitations/terms
description: Interrogatory of the meaning of claim limitations or terms used in the claims, including what teachings in the prior art would be covered by particular limitations or dictionary definitions that would define a particular claim term.
guidance: Particularly used where terms are not used per se in the specification; clarifies claim scope for examination.

name: Interrogatories — portions corresponding to admitted prior art
description: Interrogatory of which portions of each claim correspond to any admitted prior art in the specification.
guidance: Helps identify what in claims is already disclosed/admitted to be prior art by applicant.

name: Interrogatories — specific utility by claim
description: Interrogatory of the specific utility provided by the claimed subject matter on a claim-by-claim basis.
guidance: Clarifies enablement/utility issues claim-by-claim.

name: Interrogatories — whether dependent claim element is known in prior art
description: Interrogatory as to whether a dependent claim element is known in the prior art based on the examiner having a reasonable basis for believing so.
guidance: Seeks applicant admission or denial regarding prior art knowledge of dependent elements.

name: Interrogatories — support for added limitations in amended claim
description: Interrogatory of support for added limitations in an amended claim.
guidance: Used after amendments to identify disclosure basis for newly added limitations.

name: Factors for appropriateness of making requirement prior to first action
description: Factors to consider for making a separate requirement prior to the first action: (A) claimed subject matter in newly established art area without well-developed prior art; (B) whether applicant submitted an IDS; (C) whether specification's background adequately describes background; (D) whether related documents by inventor/assignee not submitted are found during search; (E) whether non-patent literature is referred to but a copy not supplied; (F) whether specification’s background describes information as known/conventional but it is unfamiliar to examiner and further details are relevant.
guidance: Use these factors to decide narrow pre-first-action requirements (e.g., restriction requirements, expanded search domains). Emphasizes narrowly specifying requirement to avoid undue burden.

name: Making a requirement — narrow specification and limited scope
description: A requirement under 37 CFR 1.105 should be narrowly specified and limited in scope because it burdens both applicant and the Office; only warranted where benefit exceeds burden in obtaining information.
guidance: Specify particular art area and particular claimed subject matter to avoid inviting large irrelevant volumes of information; indicate form expected (citations, copies, identification of collections, answers to questions, etc.). Prefer preparing requirement as a separate document attached or mailed so recipients can route appropriately.

name: Format content of a requirement (¶ 7.105 and heading)
description: The requirement must clearly indicate that a 37 CFR 1.105 requirement is being made, the basis for the requirement, and what information is being required. Requirements should specify art area and particular claimed subject matter and state why the requirement has been made and how the information is necessary to examination.
guidance: Form paragraph 7.105 Heading should begin any requirement and be followed by explanation and additional form paragraphs (7.106–7.121) as appropriate; conclude with form paragraphs 7.122–7.126 as appropriate.

name: Form paragraph 7.106 — Domain of search
description: The information is required to extend the domain of search for prior art; state classes/subclasses and describe the broader range of art to search necessary to establish level of knowledge in the art.
guidance: Insert description of art claimed but not found in classification system. Must be preceded by ¶ 7.105 and followed by concluding paragraphs.

name: Form paragraph 7.117 — Art relied upon for drafting claimed subject matter
description: Provide title, citation and copy of each publication that was relied upon to draft the claimed subject matter, with concise explanation of reliance in distinguishing claimed subject matter from prior art.
guidance: Helps assess whether drafting was influenced by prior publications; must be preceded by ¶ 7.105.

name: Form paragraph 7.120 — Names of products/services incorporating disclosed prior art
description: Provide the names of any products or services that have incorporated the disclosed prior art [1].
guidance: Specify attributes of prior art that most closely approximate claimed subject matter to narrow response scope.

name: Form paragraph 7.121 — Details of improvement over the prior art
description: State the specific improvements of the subject matter in claims [1] over the disclosed prior art and indicate the specific elements in the claimed subject matter that provide those improvements. For means/steps-plus-function claims, provide specific page and line numbers within the disclosure describing claimed structure and acts.
guidance: Limited to documents actually relied on; useful for assessing novelty and inventive step; must be preceded by ¶ 7.105.

name: Act of 1870 signature and drawings attachment rule
description: The act of 1870 provides that the 'specification and claim shall be signed by the inventor, and attested by two witnesses'; and a copy of the drawings 'shall be attached to the patent, as part of the specification.'
guidance: Under the 1870 statute the specification and claim must be signed/attested and drawings are to be attached to the patent as part of the specification — affecting formal sufficiency and the record on the patent itself.

name: Disclaimer to correct overbroad specification
description: Whenever any patentee shall have, through inadvertence, accident, or mistake, made his specification of claim too broad, claiming more than that of which he was the original or first inventor ... any such patentee ... may make disclaimer of such parts of the thing patented as the disclaimant shall not claim to hold by virtue of the patent or assignment, ... which disclaimer shall be in writing, attested by one or more witnesses, and recorded in the Patent Office, on payment ... of the sum of ten dollars. And such disclaimer shall thereafter be taken and considered as part of the original specification.
guidance: A disclaimer allows a patentee to limit an overbroad claim; it must be written, witnessed, recorded, and (historically) a fee paid. It becomes part of the original specification to the extent stated, but cannot affect pending actions except as to unreasonable neglect or delay in filing.

name: Effect of 1870 disclaimer provision (patent valid for bona fide part)
description: Whenever, through inadvertence, accident, or mistake, and without any fraudulent or deceptive intention, a patentee has claimed more than that of which he was the original or first inventor or discoverer, his patent shall be valid for all that part which is truly and justly his own, provided the same is a material or substantial part of the thing patented; and any such patentee ... may, on payment of the duty required by law, make disclaimer ... and it shall thereafter be considered as part of the original specification ...
guidance: The statute preserves validity for the material/substantial part actually invented and permits recorded disclaimers to limit the patent. A disclaimer does not affect actions pending at filing time except regarding unreasonable neglect or delay.

name: Limitations on disclaimers: cannot be used to convert impracticable generality into valid specific claim
description: A disclaimer that attempts to turn a specification for an impracticable generality into a claim for a specific process which cannot be discovered from the specification without conducting the same experiments as led to the discovery is void.
guidance: If the desired specific process is not disclosed in the original specification and would require the same experimental work to discover, a later disclaimer cannot validly create that specific claim (illustrated by Ralston v. Smith).

name: Specification must set forth materials, proportions, and processes (sufficiency of disclosure)
description: If the patentee has set forth fully the materials, their various proportions, and the processes necessary to the production of this composition of matter, he has done all that the law requires ... It should show what the patentee claims to have discovered or invented, wherein it differs from what was heretofore known, and by what combinations or processes the new material may be compounded.
guidance: For compositions or new products, disclose ingredients, proportions, and necessary processes. The description should show nature and design, separate new from old where feasible, and enable production without undue experimentation. Courts will not penalize imperfect language so long as the discovery and process are set forth.

name: Requirement to show what is old vs what is new (separation of new from old)
description: It is essentially proper, in patents for complicated machines, that the specification should clearly set forth what the patentee admits to be old and what he claims to be of his invention.
guidance: Careful separation of new from old and limitation of claims to particular parts or combinations is recommended, though not always required as a substantial part of the specification; clarifies boundaries of monopoly and aids construction.

name: Claims must be construed as machine, process, product, or result depending on description
description: The patentee's claim must be construed according to its words, and in view of the specification and the nature of the thing described; claims for a machine must be read as one for a machine, and not for a process or result, and vice versa (illustrated in Kay v. Marshall and other cases).
guidance: Courts examine both the language of the claim and the specification context to determine whether the claim is for a machine, a process, a composition, or merely a result. Mislabeling or ambiguous wording will be interpreted against overly broad readings; examples include Kay (machine vs result), McCormick, and Goodyear.

name: Result-oriented claim may be construed as claim to means/mechanism
description: A claim in words for the result was in reality for the means or mechanism by which that result was to be attained.
guidance: Even if a claim is worded as a claim to a result, if the specification describes particular means or mechanisms, courts will construe the claim as limited to those means or their equivalents (example: Howe's sewing-machine claim).

name: Reissue cannot broaden to an abstract principle; overly elastic claims invalid
description: An attempt to convert an improved machine into an abstraction, a principle, or mode of operation by use of general and abstract terms, making the specification so elastic that it might be construed to claim all means for the same purpose, is invalid.
guidance: Reissues or amended claims that broaden the patent to cover abstract principles beyond the inventor's disclosed contribution are subject to invalidation (illustrated by Burr v. Duryee). Care must be taken not to draft claims unbounded by the disclosed mechanisms.

name: Separate claims are to be read independently unless text indicates otherwise
description: Claims (e.g., No. 2 and No. 3 in McCormick's patent) were not to be read in connection with each other, but separately.
guidance: Each claim stands on its own for construction: do not assume dependent linkage among distinct claims unless the specification explicitly makes them dependent.

name: Substantial New Question of Patentability (SNQ) standard
description: A substantial new question of patentability is present where there is a substantial likelihood that a reasonable examiner would consider the prior art patent or printed publication important in deciding whether or not the claim is patentable.
guidance: It is only necessary that the prior art raise a substantial question as to at least one claim. A 'prima facie' case of unpatentability is not required. SNQ is absent where the same question of patentability has already been decided by a final holding of invalidity after all appeals or by the Office in a previous examination of the patent. Determinations are fact-specific and may be reconsidered by petition or during examination as described in MPEP §2246 and §2248.

name: Claims considered at time of determination
description: The examiner’s determination is based on the claims in effect at the time of the determination.
guidance: Amendments presented with the request by the patent owner in a pending reexamination, amendments in a reissue application on which no reissue patent has been issued, or certain other later-filed claim changes are not to be considered when deciding whether to order reexamination (see 37 CFR 1.515(a)).

name: Patent owner statements not considered for ordering decision
description: A patent owner claim scope statement and any accompanying information submitted pursuant to 37 CFR 1.501(a)(2) will not be considered by the examiner when making the determination of whether to order ex parte reexamination.
guidance: 35 U.S.C. 301(d) provides that written statements submitted pursuant to 35 U.S.C. 301(a)(2) and additional information under 35 U.S.C. 301(c) are not to be considered by the Office for any purpose other than determining the proper interpretation of a claim in a proceeding ordered under 35 U.S.C. 304.

name: Scope limited generally to claims requested
description: The Office’s determination in both the order for reexamination and the examination stage will generally be limited solely to a review of the claim(s) for which reexamination was requested.
guidance: It is only necessary to establish that a SNQ exists as to one claim to grant reexamination. If the requester did not request reexamination for certain claims, those claims will generally not be reexamined. The Office, however, has discretion to reexamine claims not requested (35 U.S.C. 303(a)) and may do so based on individual facts. Examples (Sony) and MPEP §§2242, 2283 discussed.

name: Second or subsequent request standard
description: If a second or subsequent request for ex parte reexamination is filed while a first ex parte reexamination is pending, the grant depends on the prior art cited by the later requester and whether it raises a substantial new question of patentability different from that raised in the pending reexamination.
guidance: If the later request cites the same SNQ as the pending proceeding, the second/subsequent request should be denied. A later request may provide a SNQ as to new or amended claims proposed in the pending reexamination only if it independently provides a different SNQ for the existing claims in effect at the time of determination (37 CFR 1.515(a)). If granted and it appears the request was filed for harassment, a petition under 37 CFR 1.182 may lead to suspension of prosecution on the second/subsequent reexamination.

name: Old art may be sole basis post-2002 statutory change
description: Public Law 107-273 (effective November 2, 2002) added that 'The existence of a substantial new question of patentability is not precluded by the fact that a patent or printed publication was previously cited by or to the Office or considered by the Office.'
guidance: Reliance on 'old art' that was previously cited/considered does not necessarily preclude a SNQ; determinations are fact-specific. Old art may form a SNQ where it is presented/viewed in a new light or with material new argument/interpretation (e.g., claim scope). Use form paragraph 22.01.01 when SNQ is based solely on old art; provide specifics explaining how the old art applies in a new way. See MPEP §2258.01 for use of old art during examination.

name: Effect of federal court decisions
description: A final holding of invalidity or unenforceability by the courts (after all appeals) is controlling on the Office and would preclude the presence of a SNQ as to the claims finally held invalid or unenforceable. Nonfinal (not-yet-final) court holdings are not controlling.
guidance: While the Office may accord deference to district court factual findings, the Office makes an independent determination on SNQ because different standards of proof apply. See cited cases (In re Swanson; In re Baxter; Ethicon v. Quigg).

name: Claim construction standard for reexamination ordering
description: In making the determination of whether to order reexamination, the Office will determine the proper meaning of the patent claims by giving the claims their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification, except in the case of an expired patent.
guidance: For expired patents, claim construction is pursuant to the Phillips standard: words are generally given their ordinary and customary meaning as understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention (Phillips v. AWH Corp.). See In re Yamamoto and Ex parte Papst-Motoren citations.

name: Duty of preservation / preservation obligation
description: A necessary precondition for effective discovery is that the information has been preserved, giving rise to a duty of preservation. The preservation obligation makes it unlawful for any party to destroy, hide, or render unusable information that is relevant to a claim or defense. The preservation obligation arises when a party first learns of the litigation or should have reasonably anticipated it—not merely when litigation is 'possible.'
guidance: Purpose is to compel a party to maintain and safeguard information likely to be requested through discovery even if harmful to the party. Failing to preserve documents and ESI may be remedied or punished by the court (e.g., additional discovery, monetary sanctions, or dispositive judgment). The duty does not require preservation of every possible piece of data; reasonable steps to preserve suffice (Fed. R. Civ. P. 37(e) intent to curtail excessive preservation). See cases such as Rimkus, Zubulake, Victor Stanley, and Apple v. Samsung for scope examples.

name: Principle 3 — limit preservation/discovery to what is relevant and necessary
description: Preservation, disclosure, and discovery of Protected Data should be limited in scope to that which is relevant and necessary to support any party’s claim or defense in order to minimize conflicts of law and impact on the Data Subject.
guidance: This Principle emphasizes heightened scrutiny for Protected Data: parties, Data Controllers, and courts should focus on information 'relevant and necessary' to claims/defenses and apply proportionality. If equivalent information is available from non-protected sources, seek to use those sources. Where disclosure is required (e.g., Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a)(1)(A)(ii)), take measures to comply with Data Protection Laws (confidentiality orders, stipulations). Do not produce Protected Data outside the scope of required disclosure merely for strategic advantage.

name: Preemption / abstract idea focus
description: Determine whether the claims excessively preempt the idea — courts ask whether a claim is directed to an abstract idea because it would 'tie up' basic tools of science and technology.
guidance: Preemption analysis is central: even a technologically meritorious advance may be ineligible if it 'totally preempt[s]' an idea (mathematical formulas are a canonical example). Courts examine whether claims focus on a specific means/method that improves the relevant technology or instead on a result/effect that itself is the abstract idea.

name: Look for a 'specific means or method that improves the relevant technology' (Bandai)
description: Claims should be evaluated to see whether they focus on a specific means or method that improves the relevant technology rather than being directed to a result or effect.
guidance: A 'specific asserted improvement' weighs against finding an abstract idea. The specificity of the improvement reduces preemptive effect; mere broad result-based claims are suspect. Courts treat specificity as evidence that the claim is technological rather than abstract.

name: MPEP intermediate prong: integration into a practical application
description: After finding a judicial exception, consider whether 'the claim recite[s] additional elements that integrate the [abstract idea] into a practical application.'
guidance: Integration exists when an improvement to computers or other technology is 'apparent' from the specification and the claims also disclose the improvement. If integration into a practical application is present, the claim is eligible and need not proceed to Alice step two. Examiners should look beyond the abstract idea to other claim elements.

name: Location of technological-improvement inquiry (step one vs step two)
description: Courts and the Office may search for technological improvements at either Alice step one, step two, or both; the inquiry's purpose is to identify claim limitations that alleviate preemption concerns.
guidance: Whether framed as 'technological improvements' (step one) or 'technological solution[s] to technical problem[s]' (step two), the same underlying search for features that prevent preemption is required. Dividing step one into an abstract-idea search and a specific-improvement search is one permissible approach, but attention to specificity and preemption should remain central.

name: Specificity of the asserted improvement
description: Courts usually discuss a 'specific asserted improvement,' not just an improvement; specificity matters because it reduces preemption concerns.
guidance: The degree of specificity and degree of improvement pull in opposite directions. Conclusory assertions of improvement do not suffice. Examiners and courts should require non-conclusory, concrete disclosure of how the claimed elements effect a specific technical improvement.

name: Identify recited mathematical relationships or mental processes
description: At Alice step one, determine whether the claim recites mathematical relationships/formulas or a mental process (which would indicate a judicial exception).
guidance: Examiners must look to both claim language and the specification—for example, 'transformations' described as 'mathematical transformation functions' or 'training' described as gradient-based optimization are mathematical and can indicate an abstract idea even if a formula is not explicitly recited.

name: Avoid being 'deceived by the draftsman's art'
description: Claims that disguise mathematical computation or abstract ideas with different terminology cannot avoid the abstract-idea inquiry.
guidance: Look to the substance: if the specification or claims disclose mathematical operations, data manipulation, or mentally performable steps, the abstract-idea exception can apply despite non-technical wording. Do not require explicit formulas to find a mathematical concept.

name: Data collection alone is not usually a technological improvement
description: Data collection steps, by themselves, are unlikely to constitute a technological improvement sufficient to render an otherwise abstract claim eligible.
guidance: If data collection is the only thing beyond the abstract idea, allowing eligibility would permit evasion of Alice via trivial data-collection steps. Courts have warned that minimal narrowing by adding trivial data steps does not satisfy Alice.

name: Inventive-concept analysis (Alice step two): elements other than the abstract idea
description: At step two, determine whether the claim includes elements 'other than the judicial exception' that transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application (i.e., supply an inventive concept).
guidance: Consider whether non-exception elements constitute a technical solution to a technical problem and whether those elements meaningfully limit preemption. An inventive concept that merely appends conventional or routine steps will fail. Courts balance whether the claimed additional elements prevent monopolization of the abstract idea.

name: Weigh technological solution against preemption risk at step two
description: Even if a claim discloses a technical solution (e.g., iterative training reducing false positives), evaluate whether allowing the claim would totally preempt the underlying idea (e.g., iterative training for facial recognition).
guidance: If the claim's non-abstract elements themselves would preempt basic tools or broadly claim the idea, the inventive-concept inquiry should weigh against eligibility. Look to whether remaining claim elements are substantive and limiting rather than generic or result-oriented.

name: Result-based claims and principles are not patentable
description: Claims directed to results, effects, or principles (even innovative ones) are not patentable; a principle is not patentable.
guidance: Claims that claim a desired outcome rather than a specific technical means to achieve it are vulnerable. Courts have repeatedly held that claiming a result (even an innovative result) without more is an ineligible abstraction.

name: Whether the invention gives computers new capabilities (Bandai/Enfish)
description: Claims that 'give computers new capabilities' or disclose a technological solution to a technological problem weigh against finding an abstract idea.
guidance: Where software or AI provides an improvement in computer functioning (e.g., enabling a computer to perform previously human-only tasks), courts have been more likely to find eligibility. The claimed improvement should be specific and concrete.

name: Datasets should generally be patent ineligible
description: Datasets (collections of data for training) are poor candidates for patent protection because they are redundantly protectable (trade secret, copyright), are unlikely to need patent incentives, and risk preempting broad scientific and economic activity.
guidance: Dataset patents could chill routine data-collection and analysis; datasets are often not processes or compositions of matter under §101 and may be obvious. Courts should be skeptical of dataset claims on eligibility and obviousness grounds.

name: Methods and trained models should usually be patent eligible
description: Machine-learning methods (how to train) and trained models (the programs that perform learned tasks) have stronger justifications for patenting because patents can incentivize their development without unduly chilling other innovation.
guidance: When methods or models provide specific technical improvements to computers or technical processes, they are likely to satisfy the eligibility inquiry. Evaluation should still test for preemption, specificity, and whether claimed elements are more than conventional steps.

name: Conclusive assertions of improvement are insufficient
description: An applicant's bare assertion that a claim provides an improvement is not enough; the improvement must be supported and apparent from the specification and claims.
guidance: Examiners and courts should require concrete disclosure of how claimed elements effect the asserted technical improvement. Mere conclusory language should be treated skeptically in both step-one and step-two inquiries.

name: Defense based on alleged fraudulent inducement — required elements to void contract
description: If an attorney claims the attorney-client relationship was voided by the client's fraudulent inducement, the attorney must show elements of fraudulent inducement: (1) a misrepresentation; (2) that the client knew the representation was false and intended to induce entry into the contract; (3) actual reliance by the attorney on the misrepresentation; and (4) that reliance caused injury to the attorney.
guidance: The decision cites Restatement §164 and case law; such a claim makes the contract voidable (not automatically nonexistent) and requires the party seeking to avoid duties to have expressed an election to do so. Anti-patterns: asserting fraud in conclusory fashion without particulars (courts disallow fraud claims that lack necessary detail).

name: Substantive standards for evaluating claims in post-grant review
description: In post-grant proceedings, claims should typically be evaluated to determine whether they meet the enablement and written description requirements of the act, and contain patentable subject matter under the standards defined in the statutes, case law, and as explained in relevant USPTO guidance.
guidance: Evaluation follows existing statutory and case-law standards, and USPTO guidance; includes consideration of patentable subject matter doctrines.

name: Deadline to seek IPR after being sued — one-year period
description: The final bill extends the deadline for allowing an accused infringer to seek inter partes review after he has been sued for infringement from 6 months to 1 year.
guidance: Extension recognizes difficulty in early litigation to identify relevant claims and accommodates defendants facing multiple vague claims; important given enhanced estoppel effects of IPR.

name: Intervening rights in IPR/PGR and claim amendment limits
description: The bill extends intervening rights to inter partes and post-grant review; the bill does not allow new matter to be introduced to support claims in IPR and PGR and does not allow broadening of claims in those proceedings.
guidance: Relevant to section 252: damages accrue only from the date of the conclusion of review if claim scope has been substantively altered (including narrowing). Intervening rights protect parties who acted on a challenger’s reasonable judgment that narrowing would be required.

name: Role of Patent Claims / Scope Definition
description: Patent claims are precise legal statements that define the scope of protection granted by a patent. They outline the boundaries of your invention, specifying what is new and non-obvious about it.
guidance: Claims are the part of the patent that is enforceable in a court of law, making them the most critical section of your patent application. Ensure claim elements reflect the inventive concept you wish to protect.

name: Types of Claims: Independent vs Dependent
description: There are two main types of claims: independent claims and dependent claims. Independent claims stand alone and cover the broadest aspects; dependent claims refer back to independents and add details/limitations.
guidance: Use independent claims to capture the core inventive concept and dependent claims to add fallback positions, embodiments, and specifics. Both types are essential for building a strong patent.

name: Independent Claims — Broad Scope of Protection
description: Independent claims should cover the broadest aspects of your invention, defining its essential elements in a way that maximizes the scope of protection.
guidance: Draft independent claims to encapsulate the core innovation without unnecessary limitations so competitors cannot easily design around the patent. Example: a wearable fitness tracker claim listing only essential components.

name: Balance Broadness with Defensibility
description: While broad claims are valuable, they must also be defensible. Overly broad claims can be easily challenged and invalidated if they do not sufficiently distinguish the invention from prior art.
guidance: Strike a balance: include distinctive features that differentiate from prior art to make claims both broad and defensible. Example: add a unique accuracy spec for a sensor to strengthen a broad tracker claim.

name: Focus on the Core Innovation / Identify Key Elements
description: Identify the core elements of your invention that make it novel and non-obvious. These key elements should be the focus of your independent claims.
guidance: Outline primary components or steps that define the invention; ensure each element contributes to overall functionality and novelty (e.g., charging station, power management, user interface for EV charging).

name: Avoid Overly Detailed Descriptions in Independent Claims
description: Independent claims should avoid getting bogged down in specific details or preferred embodiments; detailed descriptions belong in dependent claims and the specification.
guidance: Keep independent claims to broad inventive concept and move implementation specifics to dependent claims or the description to avoid unnecessarily narrowing the claim scope.

name: Use Simple and Direct Language
description: Effective independent claims use simple and direct language to ensure clarity and precision. Avoid technical jargon or complex sentence structures that might confuse the reader.
guidance: Write claim elements so they are easily understood (example: use 'multiple sensors connected to a computer' instead of 'a plurality of sensors operatively connected to a computational module').

name: Define Technical Terms
description: If your invention involves specialized terminology, define these terms clearly within the claim or in the detailed description to avoid ambiguity.
guidance: Provide explicit definitions in the specification or claim language (example: define 'biometric sensor array' as comprising heart rate, body temperature, and blood oxygen sensors).

name: Address Potential Prior Art
description: When drafting independent claims, anticipate potential prior art that might be cited by the examiner and ensure your claims clearly differentiate your invention from existing technologies.
guidance: Conduct thorough prior art searches and incorporate distinctive features into claims (example: emphasize dynamic load balancing in an EV charging station to distinguish from generic chargers).

name: Cover Various Implementations / Alternative Embodiments
description: Consider different ways your invention can be implemented and ensure independent and dependent claims cover these variations to broaden protection.
guidance: Include alternative elements or 'at least one of' language to encompass multiple embodiments (example: sensor array may include heart rate sensor, temperature sensor, or accelerometer).

name: Layered Claim Structure (Primary and Secondary Claims)
description: Use a layered claim structure where the primary independent claim covers the broadest aspect and secondary independent/dependent claims cover key variations or additional features.
guidance: This provides multiple levels of protection so if a broad claim is invalidated, narrower claims may remain enforceable. Draft secondary claims to capture important variations and combinations.

name: Filing Multiple Applications for Distinct Innovations
description: If your invention includes several distinct innovative aspects, consider filing multiple patent applications to cover each aspect comprehensively.
guidance: Separate hardware and software innovations (or distinct inventive concepts) into different applications to maximize protection and reduce risk of invalidation of broad claims.

name: Dependent Claims — Add Specific Features and Embodiments
description: Dependent claims should add specific features, details, or embodiments to broad independent claims and provide additional layers of protection.
guidance: Use dependent claims to state preferred materials, configurations, or parameter values that may be enforceable if broader claims fail (example: 'The smartphone of claim 1, wherein the touch-sensitive display is an OLED display').

name: Dependent Claims — Clarify and Refine the Invention
description: Use dependent claims to clarify and refine the scope of the invention by narrowing focus and providing more detail about specific aspects.
guidance: Dependent claims serve as fallbacks and make the invention's boundaries clearer for prosecution and litigation (example: adding a fingerprint sensor integrated into the display).

name: Avoid Ambiguity
description: Clarity is paramount in patent claims. Ambiguous language can render a claim unenforceable or open to broad interpretation that weakens your patent.
guidance: Define terms, use consistent wording, and avoid vague descriptors. Replace subjective phrases with objective metrics or structure when possible (example: specify exact energy consumption rather than 'energy-efficient').

name: Be Specific and Detailed where Appropriate
description: While independence benefits from breadth, dependent claims and specification should provide technical specifics and operational details to strengthen enforceability.
guidance: Include technical specifications, materials, configurations, and performance metrics in dependent claims and the description (example: motor rotor material and magnet arrangement).

name: Seek Peer and Legal Review
description: Have your claims reviewed by peers and patent professionals to catch inconsistencies, ambiguities, and potential weaknesses you might have missed.
guidance: Use external review as part of iterative drafting: legal review ensures compliance with legal requirements and improves enforceability.

name: Iterate and Refine Claims
description: Drafting strong patent claims is an iterative process; be prepared to revise and refine claims multiple times to clarify, strengthen, and broaden protection.
guidance: Rework claims after prior art searches, internal review, and feedback from counsel; each revision should aim to improve clarity and defensibility.

name: Cross-Reference Claims with the Specification
description: Ensure that your claims are fully supported by the detailed description in your patent application; each claim element should be described in the specification and drawings if applicable.
guidance: Cross-referencing is crucial for validity and enforceability—unsupported claim elements risk rejection under written-description/enablement requirements.

name: Avoid Overly Broad Claims (Common Pitfall)
description: Overly broad claims that do not adequately distinguish from prior art can be easily challenged and invalidated.
guidance: Ground broad claims in unique features disclosed in the specification; narrow where necessary to overcome prior art while preserving useful scope.

name: Ensure Novelty and Non-Obviousness
description: Claims must highlight the novelty and non-obviousness of the invention; failing to do so can lead to rejections based on prior art.
guidance: Emphasize unique features and advancements over existing devices/processes in claims and the specification to satisfy statutory requirements.

name: Maintain Consistent Terminology
description: Consistency in terminology across claims and the specification is crucial for clarity and enforceability; using different terms for the same element creates confusion.
guidance: Define terms and use them consistently (avoid 'heating element' in one claim and 'heat generator' in another). Consistency helps courts and examiners interpret claim scope.

name: Leverage Multiple Dependent Claims to Cover Embodiments
description: Multiple dependent claims can help cover various embodiments without drafting numerous individual claims, detailing different configurations, materials, or uses.
guidance: Use multiple dependents to provide combinations of features and cover alternate implementations efficiently (example: different heating elements for a process).

name: Enhance Claim Flexibility via Multiple Dependents
description: Multiple dependent claims offer flexibility in interpretation and enforcement, allowing combinations of features from different claims.
guidance: This structure makes it harder for others to avoid infringement by altering minor details because various combinations remain covered.

name: Build a Hierarchical Claim Set Strategically
description: Start with broad independent claims and progressively narrow through dependent claims to create a strategic hierarchy that preserves enforceable fallbacks.
guidance: A hierarchical set ensures that if broad claims are invalidated, narrower dependent claims may survive. Include claims covering core concept, key features, and alternatives.

name: Ensure Comprehensive Coverage in the Claim Hierarchy
description: Make sure the claim hierarchy collectively covers the invention’s core concept, specific features, and alternative embodiments for robust protection.
guidance: Map likely competitor design-arounds and ensure at least some claims address those paths; include fallbacks that remain valid under different prior-art scenarios.

name: Focus on the Invention’s Advantages
description: When drafting claims, emphasize the unique advantages and benefits of your invention to help demonstrate novelty and non-obviousness.
guidance: Claims and specification should highlight performance metrics or improvements (example: battery retains 80% capacity after 500 cycles) that support inventive step arguments.

name: Be Ready to Amend Claims During Prosecution
description: During examination you may need to amend claims in response to office actions or rejections; be prepared to adjust claims while maintaining meaningful protection.
guidance: Plan fallback claim language and narrowing strategies in advance so amendments preserve key inventive features when overcoming examiner objections.

name: Use Clear and Defensible Language
description: Ensure claims use clear, defensible language; ambiguities or vague terms can be exploited in litigation or patent challenges.
guidance: Prefer objective metrics and unambiguous structural descriptions; define necessary properties in the specification and avoid open-ended, indefinite phrasing.

name: Legal Quality
description: How likely the patent is to survive a validity challenge (litigation outcomes capture this).
guidance: For litigation strategy or enforcement decisions, prioritize indicators tied to validity and enforceability (examination depth, claim clarity, IPR/opposition history), and correct for selection effects in litigation data.

name: Drafting Quality
description: How well-drafted the patent document is (separate from validity or value).
guidance: Assess specification depth, claim structure, clarity and number of independent claims; drafting quality can affect enforceability and interpretation even if economic returns are small.

name: Pre-grant indicators (general)
description: Indicators available at issuance that can be used for early quality assessment.
guidance: Include number of claims, specification length, number of inventors, examination duration and rejection count, backward citations, family size at filing, and drafting characteristics. The authors find pre-grant indicators predict subsequent post-grant outcomes and are useful for real-time or early-stage assessment.

name: Operative pre-grant quality markers (detailed)
description: Concrete pre-grant features associated with higher quality.
guidance: Consider specification depth and number of working examples; number of independent claims; examination duration (longer often indicates more substantive examination); number of office actions before allowance; number of substantive (102/103/112) rejections in prosecution; and examiner-cited prior art beyond applicant IDS. These markers support early assessment and monitoring of examination quality.

name: Indicator-specific use-case matching
description: Select different indicators depending on the decision context (licensing, litigation, valuation, R&D, policy).
guidance: Examples: For licensing valuation use family size + renewals + technology field; for litigation strategy use examination depth + claim clarity + scope; for policy evaluation use composite multi-indicator scores; for early-stage assessment rely on pre-grant indicators (claim count, specification depth, examination signals).

name: Examiner's duty to perform a thorough examination (37 CFR 1.104(a)(1))
description: On taking up an application, the examiner shall make a thorough study of the application and a thorough investigation of available prior art relating to the claimed subject matter. The examination shall be complete as to compliance with statutes/rules and the patentability of the invention, and as to matters of form, unless otherwise indicated.
guidance: Thoroughness extends to applicable statutes/rules, patentability, and form. Search and investigation must be adequate to support any rejection or allowance.

name: Completeness of examiner's action and permissible limitations
description: The examiner's action will be complete as to all matters, except that in appropriate circumstances (e.g., misjoinder of invention, fundamental defects), the action may be limited to such matters before further action is made. Matters of form need not be raised until a claim is found allowable.
guidance: Limitations are permitted where further action would be premature; do not raise form issues prematurely if claim unallowable.

name: Cite best references and designate parts relied upon for 102/103 rejections
description: In rejecting claims for want of novelty or for obviousness, the examiner must cite the best references at his or her command. When a reference is complex or shows inventions other than that claimed, the particular part relied on must be designated as nearly as practicable; pertinence must be clearly explained and each rejected claim specified.
guidance: For 103 rejections explain how a reference is modified or plural references are combined. Provide figure/page citations and brief comments when necessary.

name: Reliance on applicant admissions and examiner knowledge
description: In rejecting claims the examiner may rely upon admissions by the applicant (or patent owner in reexamination) as to any matter affecting patentability and may also rely upon facts within his or her knowledge.
guidance: When a rejection is based on facts within the personal knowledge of an Office employee, the data shall be as specific as possible and may be supported by an affidavit of such employee when called for; such affidavit is subject to contradiction/explanation.

name: Reasons for allowance should be stated when record unclear
description: If the examiner believes the record of prosecution does not make clear the reasons for allowing a claim, the examiner may set forth such reasoning; the reasons shall be incorporated into an Office action rejecting other claims or be subject of separate communication.
guidance: Applicant or patent owner may file a statement commenting on reasons for allowance within specified time; failure to do so does not imply agreement.

name: Order of listing references and recommendation to point out pertinent features
description: When citing references for the first time, identifying data should be placed on PTO-892 attached to the Office action. No distinction is to be made between references on which a claim is rejected and those formerly referred to as 'pertinent'. It is recommended that the pertinent features of references which are not used as a basis for rejection be briefly pointed out.
guidance: Follow recommended listing order and briefly state pertinent features for clarity and for printing in the patent when appropriate.

name: Patent invalid if patentee claims more than he had right to claim; Commissioner may reissue corrected patent (13th-section)
description: If a patent is invalid because the patentee claimed more than he had a right to claim as new, the Commissioner may cause a new patent to be issued to the inventor for the same invention with proper scope.
guidance: Judge references the 13th section allowing correction (reissue) where an overbroad claim was made; the statute contemplates limiting claims to what is truly new.

name: Avoid the RCE loop (examiner incentives)
description: Examiners receive “counts” when an RCE is filed; counts measure Examiner productivity and can motivate Examiners to encourage RCE filings. After an RCE with claim amendments some Examiners routinely issue a new rejection and add a reference to teach the newly added feature, sometimes without justification.
guidance: Recognize the risk of repeated cycles where new references are added to defeat amendments. To minimize repeated RCE filings, consider other strategies (appeal, interviews, earlier claim drafting) and be cautious about amendments that invite superficial new rejections.

name: Strategic use of dependent claims to avoid final rejection
description: Include a range of dependent claims (including narrow, detailed claims) when filing the application or responding to a first nonfinal rejection. Examiners frequently overlook dependent claims and may improperly reject a narrow claim for the same reason as the independent claim.
guidance: When responding to the First Office Action, consider putting a narrow dependent claim into independent form without changing scope. If the Examiner later rejects the claim again but under different grounds, he/she cannot make the rejection final per MPEP §706.07(a). Use dependent claims proactively to preserve patentable fallback positions and to frustrate premature finality.

name: Interview the Examiner after the First Office Action
description: Interviewing the Examiner after the First Office Action is a cost-effective way to avoid a final Office Action; many times parties reach an agreement on how to put the application in condition for allowance.
guidance: If agreement cannot be reached during the interview, file a response that (1) includes claims applicant believes distinguish over the applied art and (2) includes scope the applicant is willing to accept. Interviews early in prosecution can prevent unnecessary escalation to finality or RCEs.

name: Use of a Notice of Appeal and Pre-Appeal Brief Review (PABR)
description: A Notice of Appeal may be filed in response to a final Office Action, either alone or with a Pre-Appeal Brief Review Request (PABR). If a PABR is used it must be filed with the Notice of Appeal.
guidance: PABR is appropriate only for clear factual or legal error in the rejection (objective criteria), such as failure to identify a claimed element or failure to explain how a reference meets claim recitations. PABR is not appropriate to argue interpretation of reference/claims or to argue obviousness (subjective issues). If PABR is unsuccessful, the applicant can file an RCE or file an Appeal Brief and continue the appeal.

name: Industrial application (Section 4)
description: The invention must be capable of industrial application.
guidance: Section 4 requires that the claimed subject-matter can be made or used in any kind of industry; MoPP explains how to determine practicality and real-world applicability during examination.

name: Aerotel/Macrossan four-step test (software/business methods)
description: UK courts apply a four-step test: 1. Properly construe the claim; 2. Identify the actual contribution; 3. Ask whether it falls solely within the excluded subject matter; 4. Check whether the actual contribution is technical in nature.
guidance: This test is the UK-specific approach used by courts (and reflected in examination practice) to determine whether computer-implemented or business-method claims are excluded. MoPP uses the test to frame claim construction and contribution analysis for such inventions.

name: Sufficiency / description (Section 14(3))
description: The specification must disclose the invention clearly enough and completely enough for it to be performed by a person skilled in the art and must cover the entire scope of the claim.
guidance: Section 14(3) insufficiency is a ground for refusal; MoPP explains requirements for enabling disclosure, scope coverage (no gaps between claim breadth and supporting description), and what constitutes adequate guidance for a skilled person.

name: Form and content of the application (Section 14)
description: Requirements as to the form and content of the patent application as set out in Section 14.
guidance: MoPP comments on formal requirements, necessary parts of the specification, claims and drawings, and procedural expectations; Section 14 has been subject to recent substantive updates (noted Jan 2026).

name: Applicant responsibility to present clear claims early
description: Applicants have a shared responsibility to reduce unnecessary continuations by presenting clear claims that capture the invention early in the process.
guidance: Incentives (e.g., fees increasing with number of continuing applications) could encourage clearer early claim drafting without eliminating the right to continue.

name: Reasons for allowance — comprehensive and clear
description: Examiner’s statement of reasons for allowance should be comprehensive and clear.
guidance: Reasons for allowance should not introduce unsupported claim limitations or broadening language not of record; should make the basis for allowance transparent to patentee and public (MPEP 1302.14).

name: Reasons for allowance — identify distinguishing claim elements
description: Examiner should identify claim elements or how combination thereof distinguish claimed invention over prior art.
guidance: Explain specifically what elements or combinations provide novelty/obviousness distinction so scope and basis are explicit.

name: Identify priority date for claim elements
description: Identify priority date for each claim element in continuing and continuation-in-part applications: which supported by original application, which have later effective date.
guidance: Explicitly state which claim elements derive benefit of earlier filings to avoid later ambiguity.

name: State interpretation of claim preamble and functional terms
description: Examiner should state the interpretation given in prosecution to claim preamble and any field of use or functional terminology.
guidance: If preamble not relied upon by examiner, that should be stated so patentee and public know how to interpret claim scope.

name: Identify file history estoppel and basis for allowance
description: Identification of file history estoppel: examiner should indicate claim amendments and arguments presented by applicant (e.g. disclaimers, admissions) which formed the basis for allowance.
guidance: Purpose is to eliminate subsequent uncertainty about claim scope and provide a clear record of concessions or limiting arguments.

name: Continue to review allowance decisions
description: Continue internal review of allowance to ensure reasons for allowance are sound and aligned with goal of valid, clear claims.
guidance: Post-allowance review should check record, reasons, and conformity with quality objectives (internal Quality Review suggested).

name: Means-plus-function in software — link function to structure
description: For software and other patents relying on 112(6) 'means plus function' claiming, attempt to link the function recited in the claim with structure recited in the specification.
guidance: Merely identifying such linkage could assist the examiner; failure may indicate need for stronger linking language or missing structure in specification.

name: Characteristics of high-quality applications
description: High quality applications examples: applications with defined terms, 30 pages or less of specification, examples that support claim limitations, 10 or fewer claims and IDS, and request for first office action interview.
guidance: This is a proposed template for what qualifies for accelerated processing or considered high quality by the Office.

name: Provide sample claim templates per art unit
description: Provide examples of high-quality patent applications and sample claim formats for each art group unit.
guidance: Publishing claim templates helps practitioners craft claims using techniques specific to an art unit and helps align expectations.

name: Use standard dictionaries or agreed third-party dictionary when undefined
description: In the absence of definitions, use standard dictionaries or adopt a mutual third-party dictionary selection process (IBM proposal).
guidance: A mutually agreed independent dictionary would aid claim interpretation and 112 determinations concerning disclosure adequacy and clarity.

name: Examiner should specify claim term definitions and sources
description: Claim construction: examiner should specify the definition of terms relied upon in prior art and applicant's claim and source of that claim construction.
guidance: Explicitly recording sources for claim term definitions improves transparency and reduces ambiguity.

name: Standard algorithm descriptive language for software filings
description: Applicants should be required to utilize standard algorithm descriptive language when source code is not disclosed.
guidance: Standardized descriptive language would aid search, examination and claim construction in computer science/software fields; propose compiling algorithms into a searchable database for reference.

name: Collect specified application-level data elements
description: Collect data regarding the application as filed: number of dependent and independent claims, whether an IDS was initially filed, how many references cited broken down by type (US patents, non-US patents, non-patent prior art).
guidance: Gather raw elements that enable derivation of various quality metrics and correlation analyses.

name: Track office actions, rejections by basis and correlated outcomes
description: Track number of office actions per application, number of rejections therein broken down by basis (obviousness, written description, etc.) and correlate to outcome (amendment/cancellation of claims, abandonment, RCE filing, etc.).
guidance: Enables identification of problematic rejection types and their downstream effects on pendency and allowances.

name: Correlate key claim terms to specification definitions
description: Correlation of key claim terms to definition or description in the specification for applications as filed, issued patents, and terms added by claim amendment.
guidance: Assess how closely claims map to specification disclosure; claims 'closer' to the specification are statistically more likely to be valid.

name: Result metrics — track claim outcomes at trial
description: Ultimate result metrics: outcome of claims at trial — validity upheld/reversed along with rationale (anticipation, obviousness, indefiniteness, inadequate description, non-enablement, claim construction issues, lack of antecedent basis, problems with means-plus-function support).
guidance: Linking prosecution/examination quality to trial outcomes provides the strongest measure of long-term patent quality and validity.

name: Patent Quality Index (PQI) — composite metrics
description: Develop composite metrics (Patent Quality Index) evaluating characteristics tied to validity: strength/accuracy of applicant and examiner search, sufficiency of support in specification for claims, effectiveness of office actions, closeness of claims to specification.
guidance: Use statistical analysis to identify characteristics associated with validity and optimize procurement processes; claims 'closer' to the specification tend to be more likely valid.

name: Scope limitation of testimony in public-use proceedings
description: In public use proceedings (whether issue is anticipation under 35 U.S.C. 102(b) or obviousness over 35 U.S.C. 103), testimony will be limited to the issues of public use or on sale.
guidance: No testimony will be received on whether the claimed subject matter would have been obvious over subject matter asserted to be in public use or on sale.

name: Definition of a prima facie case of unpatentability
description: A prima facie case of unpatentability is established when the information compels a conclusion that a claim is unpatentable under the preponderance of the evidence burden-of-proof standard, giving each term in the claim its broadest reasonable construction consistent with the specification, and before any consideration is given to evidence submitted in an attempt to establish a contrary conclusion of patentability.

name: Treatment of materials submitted in reexamination files (37 CFR 1.11(d))
description: Materials submitted under MPEP § 724.02 in a reexamination file open to the public under 37 CFR 1.11(d) will be maintained separate and not publicly available until a determination is made whether the information is important to a reasonable examiner in deciding whether a claim is patentable.
guidance: If any portion is found important, petition to expunge denied and information becomes permanent part of reexamination file and open to public; if not important, petition granted and information expunged. If no petition filed prior to mailing of a Notice of Intent to Issue Reexamination Certificate (NIRC), materials become permanent part of reexamination file and open to public.

name: Determination standard for expungement (importance to a reasonable examiner)
description: The examiner or appropriate Office official will determine whether any portion or all of submitted information is important to a reasonable examiner in deciding whether to allow the application to issue as a patent (or whether a claim is patentable in reexamination).
guidance: If information is found important, the petition to expunge will be denied and the materials will become part of the application/reexamination file and available to the public upon issuance; if found not important, the petition will be granted and the information expunged.

name: Expungement of information forming part of the original disclosure
description: A petition to expunge part of the original disclosure must be filed under 37 CFR 1.183 (directed to Office of Petitions) because it requires waiver of 37 CFR 1.59(a)(2).
guidance: The petition must explain why justice requires waiver; such petitions will ordinarily not be favorably entertained. Original disclosures (specification, claims, drawings, preliminary amendment incorporated into oath/declaration) are scanned and changing the USPTO record may not be possible.

name: When different effect is claimed, judge by character and importance of effect
description: Where the effect produced by the alleged invention is different, the test of a sufficient 'improvement' to sustain a patent will be the character and importance of the effect itself.
guidance: If the new effect is materially important or valuable (e.g., better quality, new functionality), that supports patentability even if the change is small in structure.

name: Improvement-on-existing-patent claimability
description: A patent including the subject-matter of a patent still in force is valid if the improvement only is claimed in the specification; the new patent will come into force after the expiration of the old one, or may be applied by using a license under the former patent or by purchasing the specific machine covered by the former patent.
guidance: Practical options include waiting for expiration, obtaining a license, or purchasing the patented apparatus; courts require the former patent specification to be read in infringement suits alleging improvements (cites Crane v. Price and related authority).

name: Machine-invention test: improvement judged by result
description: When a machine or combination of machinery is claimed, the gist of the objection often is whether the alleged new machinery serves the purpose better than the machinery formerly used; utility and improved performance are decisive.
guidance: Evaluate actual improvement in functioning or durability (example Brunton's chain-link and anchor cases — one part supported because substitution was materially beneficial; the other part failed because it was simple application of known mode and produced no superiority).

name: Subject-matter must be a thing made or an art/process
description: There can be no valid patent except it be for a thing made, or for the art or process of making or doing something.
guidance: Abstract ideas or things not made nor usable in a process fall outside patentability; ensure claim scope describes a concrete thing or a process of making/doing.

name: Standard of review for IPR appeals
description: We review legal issues de novo, but fact findings for substantial evidence; claim construction is reviewed de novo, while subsidiary fact findings are reviewed for substantial evidence; the Board’s ultimate conclusion of obviousness is reviewed de novo but underlying facts for substantial evidence.
guidance: Quoted standards: “We review the Board’s legal determinations de novo, but its fact findings for substantial evidence. ... We thus review claim construction de novo, but review subsidiary fact findings for substantial evidence. Similarly, we review the Board’s ultimate conclusion of obviousness de novo, but review its underlying findings of fact for substantial evidence.” (citing Acceleration Bay; Best Med.)

name: Narrow exceptions to § 314(d) (shenanigans/other reviewable questions)
description: Only narrow exceptions may permit review of institution decisions: colorable constitutional claims, challenges depending on other less closely related statutes, or questions of interpretation that reach well beyond § 314’s scope; actions clearly beyond statutory authority (e.g., canceling a claim under § 112) can be reviewable.
guidance: Cites Cuozzo and later cases: “The Supreme Court ... identified only possible narrow exceptions to § 314(d): 'appeals that implicate constitutional questions, that depend on other less closely related statutes, or [] present other questions of interpretation that reach, in terms of scope and impact, well beyond' § 314. ... For example, if the agency were to cancel a patent claim for indefiniteness under § 112—an action beyond its statutory authority—that would constitute a 'shenanigan' that may be properly reviewable.” The opinion rejects EBS’s ultra vires/stay argument as not meeting that threshold.

name: Board need not adopt prior district-court claim construction automatically
description: A prior judicial claim construction (especially a non‑appealed portion) does not automatically bind the PTAB in an IPR absent the parties timely making it of record and presenting argument; the Board may apply plain and ordinary meaning if parties do not press a prior construction.
guidance: 37 C.F.R. § 42.100 requires that a prior claim construction timely made of record will be considered, but the Board is not required in all cases to assess a previous judicial interpretation—particularly if neither party asks the Board to construe the term or explain why the prior construction is correct. The court cites Power Integrations: it 'did not impose a blanket rule requiring the Board to always evaluate the merits of any prior claim constructions' and limited that case to its circumstances.

name: Claim terms should not be construed to exclude disclosed embodiments absent clear disclaimer
description: Courts normally do not interpret claim terms to exclude embodiments disclosed in the specification; a limitation excluding a disclosed embodiment requires clear disclaimer/deliberate disavowal.
guidance: Quoted principle: 'We normally do not interpret claim terms in a way that excludes embodiments disclosed in the specification—we only do so amidst clear disclaimer or disavowal.' (citing Oatey Co.). The opinion applies this to reject reading gasoline out of scope where the specification expressly disclosed a gasoline‑only embodiment.

name: Limits on invoking prior-court constructions under 37 C.F.R. § 42.100
description: 37 C.F.R. § 42.100 provides that any prior claim construction determination that is timely made of record in the IPR proceeding will be considered, but it does not automatically compel the Board to adopt or analyze prior constructions absent party presentation.
guidance: The court held EBS did not preserve an argument that § 42.100 required the Board to adopt or substantively analyze the district court construction where EBS did not ask the Board to undertake that analysis or identify regulatory language supporting that obligation.

name: Use stats to decide whether to amend claims
description: Don't amend your claims unless you need to. Make better decisions about when and how to amend claims.
guidance: If an examiner historically allows broader claims or benefits from interviews/arguments, avoid unnecessary narrowing amendments. Use rejection patterns and allowance likelihood to decide whether to amend and how narrowly.

name: Use statistics to obtain broader patents / minimize unnecessary amendments
description: Obtain broader patents — Don't amend your claims unless you need to.
guidance: When examiner statistics indicate an allowance trend or receptivity to arguments, favor arguing rather than narrowing claims to preserve claim breadth. Use historical rejection types and allowance pathways to craft arguments that preserve scope.

name: Preparation
description: Use an Agenda (preferably PTOL-413A); review record in advance; consult with SPE or Primary if needed; consider any suggested claim language.
guidance: Prepare an agenda (PTOL-413A) and review the file history before the interview; have proposed claim language ready if applicable; consult supervisory personnel when needed to ensure productive discussion.

name: Cooperation
description: Keep an open mind; maintain a positive attitude; seek common ground; work on claim language.
guidance: Approach interviews collaboratively rather than adversarially; emphasize finding mutual agreement and constructive amendment of claim language where possible.

name: Benefits of Interviews
description: Leads to better understanding of the invention, applicant’s position, examiner’s position, and claim interpretation; advances/promotes compact prosecution; increases chance of disposal in next Office action.
guidance: Interviews statistically increase the likelihood of a disposal in the next Office action (presentation shows higher disposal percentages when interviews occur); use interviews to streamline prosecution and narrow disputes.

name: Suggested Sequence for an Effective Interview
description: Applicant/Representative explains invention; discuss how inventive concepts are (or are not) set forth in the claim language; discuss prior art and rejections; discuss any proposed language (from either party); establish common ground (each topic — agree or not).
guidance: Follow this sequence to structure the conversation: start with the invention overview, move to claim-language alignment with inventive concepts, address prior art/rejections, propose and discuss amendments, and record areas of agreement/disagreement.

name: Typical Interview Topics
description: Overview of the invention; state of the art; claim interpretation; prior art used in rejections; language in proposed amendment; 35 U.S.C. 101; 35 U.S.C. 112(1), 112(2), 112(6).
guidance: Use the interview to address substantive prosecution issues, including statutory grounds for rejection and specific claim language changes.

name: Documenting Interviews — Interview Summary (PTOL-413)
description: Interview Summary (PTOL-413) should include details enough to clarify the record, claim limitations discussed, claim interpretation issues, details of proposed amendment, agenda items, topics resolved (agreed to), and topics unresolved (not agreed to).
guidance: Complete a PTOL-413 summary after substantive discussions to ensure the file reflects what was discussed and any agreements or unresolved issues.

name: Definition of an 'Interview' and Off-the-Record Guidance
description: A discussion is an 'interview' if it touches on the merits of the case (claim language, prior art analysis, clarification of a rejection, etc.). Do not prosecute 'off the record.'
guidance: Substantive merit discussions must be documented; follow MPEP 713.04 and procedures for transmission/recording (see MPEP 502.01 for fax, 502.02 for e-sig, and 502.03 for email). Avoid informal, undocumented prosecution activities.

name: Evidence to the contrary — what can rebut the presumption
description: Evidence that a claim does not correspond in scope with that which an inventor regards as the invention may be found in statements outside the application.
guidance: Examples of such evidence include contentions or admissions contained in briefs or remarks filed by applicant (e.g., Solomon v. Kimberly-Clark Corp., 216 F.3d 1372, 55 USPQ2d 1279 (Fed. Cir. 2000); In re Prater, 415 F.2d 1393, 162 USPQ 541 (CCPA 1969)), or affidavits filed under 37 CFR 1.132 (e.g., In re Cormany, 476 F.2d 998, 177 USPQ 450 (CCPA 1973)). The content of the specification is not used as evidence that the scope of the claims is inconsistent with the subject matter which an inventor regards as his or her invention. Agreement or lack thereof between the claims and the specification is properly considered only with respect to 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (written description/enablement) or pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.

name: Shift in what inventor regards as the invention is permitted during pendency
description: 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (or the second paragraph of pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112) does not prohibit the inventor or a joint inventor from changing what the inventor regards as the invention during prosecution.
