guidance: Claims and submission of comparative evidence with respect to claimed subject matter which originally was only the preferred embodiment within broader claims have been permitted (In re Saunders, 444 F.2d 599, 170 USPQ 213 (CCPA 1971)). Continuation applications directed to originally disclosed subject matter that was not regarded as part of the invention when the parent was filed may still receive the parent's filing date under 35 U.S.C. 120 (In re Brower, 433 F.2d 813, 167 USPQ 684 (CCPA 1970)).

name: Unclaimed essential subject matter may trigger multiple types of rejections
description: If a claim omits subject matter disclosed to be essential to the invention, different statutory rejections may be appropriate depending on the facts.
guidance: Omitted essential matter may be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (first paragraph) as not enabling (see In re Mayhew, 527 F.2d 1229, 188 USPQ 356 (CCPA 1976)) or as lacking an adequate written description (see Gentry Gallery, Inc. v. Berkline Corp., 134 F.3d 1473, 45 USPQ2d 1498 (Fed. Cir. 1998)); under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (second paragraph) as indefinite (see In re Venezia, 530 F.2d 956, 189 USPQ 149 (CCPA 1976)); or under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) as failing to claim the subject matter the inventor regards as the invention (see In re Collier, 397 F.2d 1003, 158 USPQ 266 (CCPA 1968)). Essential matter may include missing elements, steps, or necessary structural cooperative relationships described by the applicant as necessary to practice the invention.

name: When a claim omits matter necessary to practice the invention — follow written description/enablement guidance
description: If a claim omits matter that appears necessary to describe the invention or to make and use the invention, examiners should consider rejections under the written description and enablement requirements.
guidance: Follow MPEP §2163 et seq. (especially §2163, subsection I, and §2163.05) for written description issues and MPEP §2164 et seq. (especially §2164.08(c)) for enablement issues to determine whether a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (first paragraph) should be made.

name: Interrelation of elements and indefiniteness analysis
description: A claim that fails to interrelate essential elements of the invention as defined in the specification may be indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b), but lack of interdependence does not automatically render a claim indefinite.
guidance: See In re Venezia, 530 F.2d 956 (CCPA 1976) for rejection where interrelation lacking. However, Ex parte Nolden, 149 USPQ 378, 380 (Bd. Pat. App. & Inter. 1965) and Ex parte Huber, 148 USPQ 447 (Bd. Pat. App. & Inter. 1965) show that a claim need not show interdependency, concurrency, or direct intercooperation among elements to satisfy 112(b). Use MPEP §2172 and related sections for guidance in determining whether an indefiniteness rejection is appropriate.

name: Requirement to explain basis for rejecting as omitting inventor-regarded essential matter
description: Rejections under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) for failing to claim the subject matter the inventor regards as the invention based on omission of essential matter must explain the basis for that conclusion.
guidance: The examiner must identify why the omitted matter is regarded by the inventor as essential and, where appropriate, identify where in the specification the unclaimed elements are described as essential. Failure to do so can lead to reversal (e.g., Ex parte Robertson, Appeal 2016-001938, op. at 4 (PTAB 2017)). Features labeled in the specification as preferred or illustrative are generally not critical or essential (In re Goffe, 542 F.2d 564, 191 USPQ 429 (CCPA 1976)). Broad disclosure language tends to rebut an assertion of criticality.

name: USPTO must decide SNQ within three months and issue certificate
description: In response to a supplemental examination request, the USPTO must determine, within three months, whether a substantial new question of patentability (SNQ) affecting any claim is raised by the information and then issue a supplemental examination certificate stating the result.
guidance: The supplemental examination commences with receipt of the request and concludes with issuance of the certificate; timing is therefore critical to obtain statutory protections before unenforceability is asserted in litigation.

name: Claim-limited SNQ review (generally)
description: By rule the USPTO will generally limit the determination of whether information raises an SNQ to only those claims identified by the patent owner in the request.
guidance: Although the USPTO generally will not review non-identified claims, it is not precluded from doing so. This claim-identification approach may have litigation implications and may be contrary to the plain language of §257(a); courts may ultimately decide scope of unenforceability protection when not all claims are identified.

name: No amendments or examiner interviews during supplemental examination
description: The USPTO will not permit amendments (including narrowing claims, cancelling claims, or correcting inventorship) during the supplemental examination stage, even if submitted with the request; examiner interviews are not permitted during supplemental examination.
guidance: Amendments to narrow claims, cancel claims, and to correct inventorship can be made during ex parte reexamination if ordered. Broadening claim amendments are not permitted during supplemental examination or ex parte reexamination. The only opportunity for an examiner interview will be during ex parte reexamination if ordered.

name: Claim cancellation and disclaimer strategies and limits
description: A patent owner will not be permitted to cancel claims in the request for supplemental examination to avoid reexamination being ordered; however, the owner may choose not to identify such claims in the request or may file a disclaimer of such a claim before requesting supplemental examination.
guidance: A disclaimer is immediately effective upon recordation and can reduce risk of unnecessary reexamination; the USPTO's SNQ determination is limited to claims in effect at the time of determination. The effect of omitting claims from the request on eventual unenforceability protection is uncertain and may be subject to judicial interpretation.

name: Ex parte reexamination procedural standards and risks
description: Ex parte reexamination is conducted without the presumption of validity and without the clear-and-convincing evidentiary standard applicable in court; patentability is determined under the preponderance-of-the-evidence standard and claims receive their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.
guidance: Reexamination immediately limits enforceability and could result in narrowing or cancellation of claims and creation of estoppels and intervening rights. Reexamination provides limited opportunities for presenting amendments, arguments, and evidence: shortened statutory reply periods (as short as 30 days, up to two months), only one guaranteed opportunity to freely amend rejected claims in response to a first non-final Office Action, extensions not granted as a matter of right, and no RCE or continuing application allowed during ex parte reexamination. A patent owner cannot withdraw from an ex parte reexamination once begun; failure to respond to an Office Action may result in a reexamination certificate adopting positions set forth in the last Office Action.

name: Re-issue limited to matters original attempted to claim
description: Re-issue cannot cover what the original might have claimed but only what the original attempted to claim; improper to embrace matters described but not attempted to be claimed in the original.
guidance: Compare the original specification/claims/drawings/models to determine what the original attempted to claim; do not add subject-matter that was merely suggested or described without any attempt to claim it.

name: Cannot claim matter merely claimed but not described
description: Re-issue cannot cover what is merely claimed but not described in the original.
guidance: Claims in the original that lack supporting description cannot be used as a basis to expand a re-issue; supporting description (specification, drawings, model) is required.

name: May cover matter outside judicial interpretation of original claims
description: Re-issue may cover matter not within the judicial interpretation of the original claims.
guidance: If the original text supports broader subject-matter than prior judicial construction recognized, a re-issue may claim that subject-matter (still subject to other constraints).

name: Identity primarily a question of interpretation
description: Identity with the original is primarily a question of interpretation, not of evidence.
guidance: Courts interpret specifications/claims (with reference to the state of the art at the time) to determine identity; extrinsic evidence is limited.

name: Method to determine what original attempted to describe and claim
description: What the original attempted to describe and claim is ascertained from the original specification itself compared with the actual invention and the re-issue specification.
guidance: Compare original document(s) to the actual invention and the proposed re-issue; the mode of determining attempt may appear in specification, drawings, or model.

name: Attempt to describe/claim may appear in specification, drawings, or model
description: The attempt of the original to describe and claim may appear either in the specification, drawings, or model.
guidance: Inspect all parts of the original record to locate any indication the inventor sought to claim particular subject-matter.

name: Presumption original intended to claim all properly claimable under its description
description: There is a presumption that the original intended to claim all that could properly have been claimed under its description.
guidance: This presumption supports some latitude in re-issue, but it is rebuttable by evidence of intentional exclusion or other limits.

name: Re-issue may amend patent to any extent necessary to secure the invention attempted in original
description: Re-issue may amend the patent to any extent necessary to secure the invention attempted to be described and claimed in the original.
guidance: Permitted amendments include clarifying language, correcting errors, and making definite what was previously inferential — but not adding new subject-matter beyond what was attempted originally.

name: Re-issue may vary in language, description, mode of making/use, claims count/scope
description: Re-issue may vary from the original in language, in general description, in statements of mode of making and use, in number and scope of claims, etc.
guidance: Variations in form and drafting are allowed so long as identity of subject-matter with the original is preserved.

name: May make definite what was previously matter of inference
description: Re-issue may make definite what was before matter of inference.
guidance: Permissible to convert implied disclosures into explicit claim language where original disclosure supports the inference.

name: May enlarge or narrow claims but enlargement is limited
description: Re-issue may enlarge or narrow claims, but cannot enlarge the patent or claims beyond permitted bounds; re-issue expressly enlarging claims is void as against the public and intervening rights.
guidance: Enlargements that affect third parties' rights or go beyond what was attempted in the original are defective; narrowings are generally acceptable but must not be used to improperly manipulate rights.

name: May enlarge claims when original inoperative due to narrowness
description: May enlarge claims when the original is inoperative from narrowness of claims.
guidance: If the original claim language rendered the patent inoperative as to the real invention, re-issue to enlarge claims may be allowed to secure the invention, subject to diligence and other constraints.

name: Generic vs specific: scope limits
description: A generic patent may cover all included species; cannot claim different species from the one claimed in the original; a specific patent cannot cover the genus.
guidance: Do not broaden a specific claim to a genus in re-issue; conversely, generic-to-specific coverage is permissible if supported by the original.

name: Combination-patent re-issue limitations
description: A combination-patent cannot re-issue to cover a combination of less than all the elements, or of different elements, or of the same elements differently combined; may claim as a combination what the original claimed as an article.
guidance: Re-issue cannot create claims to subcombinations inconsistent with original disclosure unless conditions for subcombinations are satisfied and not barred by delay/intervening rights.

name: May omit non-essentials or substitute equivalents
description: Re-issue may omit non-essentials or substitute equivalents; may cover elements when the original described them or equivalents.
guidance: Permitted to streamline claims by removing non-essential elements or by claiming equivalents, provided the original supports such treatment.

name: Presumption of intentional exclusion from failure to claim is prima facie only
description: Presumption of intentional exclusion from failure to claim clearly described matter is prima facie only and may be rebutted, especially if amendment is made without unreasonable delay.
guidance: Context, timing, and subsequent conduct determine whether omission was intentional.

name: Patent Office examination powers over re-issue
description: The Patent Office has the same power over re-issue as over the original: examination as to patentability, identity with original, and fact of inadvertence, etc.; patentability is determined by the state of the art at date of the original.
guidance: Expect substantive examination, not a rubber stamp; original grant does not guarantee allowance of re-issue claims.

name: Disclaimers in re-issue bind patentee but do not estop future re-issue unless excluded from original
description: Disclaimers in a re-issue bind the patentee in suits on that re-issue, but do not estop him from claiming the same matter in a new re-issue unless it was excluded from the original.
guidance: A re-issue disclaimer has immediate effect for that grant, but may not be an absolute bar against future action unless tied to the original patent's scope.

name: No new matter in amendments (37 CFR 1.121)
description: No amendment may introduce new matter into the disclosure of an application.
guidance: If new matter is introduced into the specification, the amendment should be objected to under 35 U.S.C. 132 (35 U.S.C. 251 for reissue) and the new matter required to be cancelled. If new matter has been entered into or affects claims, the claims should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, because the new matter is not described in the application as originally filed. The examiner must clearly identify the subject matter considered to be new matter. New matter in drawings is ordinarily not entered; substitute sheets containing new matter are likewise ordinarily not entered. An examiner’s holding of new matter may be petitionable or appealable (see MPEP §608.04(c)).

name: Reviewability of examiner’s new-matter holding
description: Where alleged new matter is confined to amendments to the specification, review of the examiner’s requirement for cancellation is by way of petition; where the alleged new matter is introduced into or affects the claims (necessitating rejection), the issue is appealable and should not be considered on petition.
guidance: See 37 CFR 1.181 and 1.191 for procedures; practice differs depending on whether claims are involved.

name: Arrangement and required sections of the specification (37 CFR 1.77)
description: The elements of the application should appear in a specified order (utility application transmittal form; fee transmittal; application data sheet; specification; drawings; executed oath/declaration). The specification should include sections in order: title of the invention; cross-reference to related applications; statement of federally sponsored research; names of parties to joint research agreement; reference to Sequence Listing/table/computer program listing on compact disc and incorporation-by-reference; background; brief summary; brief description of drawing views; detailed description; claim(s); abstract; Sequence Listing if on paper (37 CFR 1.77(b)(1)-(12)).
guidance: Text of these sections should be preceded by uppercase section headings without underlining or bold type. The specification must identify compact disc(s) and list files and total number of discs (see §1.52(e)(5)).

name: Computer program listing submission rules (37 CFR 1.96)
description: Descriptions of operation and general content of computer program listings should appear in the description portion of the specification. A computer program listing is a printout listing instructions, routines, and contents of a program; it may be in machine or machine-independent (object or source) language.
guidance: If the listing is ≤300 lines (each line ≤72 characters) it may be submitted as drawings or as part of the specification. If submitted as drawings, must comply with §1.84 and have at least one figure numeral on each sheet. If submitted in the specification and having more than 60 lines, it must be positioned at the end of the description but before the claims; any amendment must be by substitute sheet. Any listing >300 lines (up to 72 chars/line) must be submitted on compact disc as a 'computer program listing appendix' (will not be printed) and the specification must reference it at the location indicated in §1.77(b)(5). Multiple listings may be on one disc; separate compact disc is required for each application containing such an appendix. The appendix disc must meet strict specifications (computer compatibility: IBM PC/XT/AT or compatibles or Apple Macintosh; OS compatibility: MS-DOS, MS-Windows, Unix, or Macintosh; line terminator: ASCII CR+LF; control codes: only ASCII-defined characters; compression: uncompressed). No other formats allowed.

name: Claim construction awareness
description: Courts interpret claims and the description; claim interpretation is typically the most critical factor in determining infringement or validity.
guidance: Draft claims and description so their meaning is clear to a person skilled in the art; anticipate that only a few terms may determine scope. Prepare to support claim term meanings in the specification and prosecution history.

name: Favor ordinary meaning for claim terms
description: Courts (particularly in the U.S.) begin by giving terms in the claims their ordinary meaning to a person skilled in the art; only then do they consult the description, prosecution history, dictionaries, treatises or expert testimony if needed.
guidance: Avoid inventing unusual meanings for common terms unless you explicitly define them in the description. Be cautious when relying on external dictionaries; instead, aim for a self-contained application.

name: Define new or ambiguous terms in the description
description: Where a patent application creates a new term, where several meanings are possible and only one is meant, or where a term may be ambiguous, define it in the description section so the application is self-contained.
guidance: Use the description as a glossary of special claim terminology. Tie definitions to embodiments and avoid leaving meaning to external sources.

name: Draft claims as though no doctrine of equivalents exists
description: Because the doctrine of equivalents is unpredictable and varies by jurisdiction, draft claims to give terms their ordinary and customary meaning to a person skilled in the art rather than relying on equivalents for protection.
guidance: Seek literal coverage of key variants (e.g., use broader terms like 'metal fastener' rather than relying on a court to equate 'nail' with 'screw'). Know the doctrine's reach in each jurisdiction.

name: Avoid prosecution history estoppel
description: Communications during prosecution can foreclose application of the doctrine of equivalents in some jurisdictions (prosecution history estoppel).
guidance: Be careful in office-action responses not to make admissions that restrict claim scope (e.g., asserting 'only' nails are used) if you may later need to argue equivalents.

name: Draft the broadest main claim(s) early
description: Drafting first the broadest main claim(s) reciting the inventive features is an efficient way of formulating the essential inventive concept.
guidance: Use broad independent claims to capture the inventive concept, then draft dependent claims and the description to support and enable them.

name: Draft description to support claims (order and iteration)
description: After drafting claims, draft the title, technical field, background art and summary (or later as appropriate), then draft brief description of figures, detailed description of embodiments and drawings as a group; revisit and revise claims after drafting the description and drawings.
guidance: Iteratively check that claim terms are disclosed and supported in the description and drawings; remove extraneous claim elements that could limit scope; ensure consistency of terms and meaning.

name: Summary of invention: outline full scope and tie to claims
description: The summary should outline what has been invented in its full scope and explain how the inventor has overcome the background problem; it should, effectively, summarize the claims.
guidance: Consider turning each independent claim into a paragraph in the summary to ensure claim language appears in the description. Include advantageous effects only where they correspond to features of the broadest claims and avoid a broad 'meta' summary that goes beyond the claims and creates risks of implied but undeclared subject matter.

name: Brief description of drawings: state figures, type and perspective
description: The brief description of drawings should state what each drawing figure represents, the drawing type (photograph, line drawing, flowchart, etc.), and any visual perspective, and explain how drawings relate to embodiments.
guidance: Begin with a statement that drawings are illustrative of embodiments (where jurisdictional practice suggests) to avoid narrowing claims to only illustrated examples. Provide a short caption per figure (e.g., 'Figure 1 is a diagrammatic representation...').

name: Description of embodiments must enable and support claim amendment
description: The description of embodiments must (i) reflect inventor-provided disclosure, (ii) provide sufficient information to enable a person skilled in the art to reproduce the invention, and (iii) provide sufficient depth so claims can be narrowed later to avoid prior art cited by an examiner.
guidance: Include enough detail and alternatives at filing because substantive amendments adding new technical disclosure are generally not permitted after filing. Ensure embodiments are tied to drawings and use reference numerals appropriately.

name: Tie abstract claim terms to concrete embodiments
description: If claims use highly abstract terms, use the description of embodiments to tie those terms to specific examples so the meaning is clear and the term can be construed broadly.
guidance: E.g., state 'One example of warning device 102 is an automobile horn; other warning devices may be used' and list alternatives (siren, buzzer) to support broader interpretation.

name: Balance disclosure: err on inclusion to avoid insufficient support
description: Patent drafters should balance the risks of too-bare disclosure versus disclosing too much unclaimed subject matter; generally err on the side of inclusion to preserve options for narrowing claims.
guidance: Insufficient description at filing prevents later narrowing to overcome novelty or inventive-step objections. However, be aware excessive unclaimed disclosure may lead to dedication to the public of those aspects.

name: Avoid dedicating unclaimed subject matter
description: Unclaimed subject matter disclosed in the specification is considered dedicated to the public and cannot later be conferred patent rights unless claimed in an appropriate subsequent filing.
guidance: Draft claims before the description or ensure the description is tailored to support intended claims. Use divisional or continuation filings if unity issues reveal unclaimed inventions.

name: Avoid phrasing that artificially narrows scope ('the invention is ...')
description: Avoid saying 'the invention is X'; instead say 'an embodiment of the invention is X' or 'an exemplification of the apparatus/method', to preserve broader interpretation of claims.
guidance: Using 'the invention is' risks limiting the claims to the stated characterization and can hinder broad claim interpretation.

name: Avoid making context or examples inadvertently limiting
description: When describing components and operation or illustrative drawings, condition discussions to prevent the context or examples from becoming limiting parts of the invention.
guidance: Explicitly state that drawings/embodiments are illustrative and include multiple alternatives to support broader claim scope.

name: Consolidation of pending claims into a single clean set
description: Applicants may submit a clean version of all pending claims in one amendment paper, consolidating previous versions for patent printing and file clarity.
guidance: Providing a consolidated clean set is beneficial. In the consolidated clean set, parenthetical expressions from prior versions should not appear except when a claim is being amended. Submission of a clean set of all pending claims is construed as directing cancellation of all previous versions.

name: Examiner amendments authority (1.121(g))
description: The Office is permitted to make amendments to the specification, including the claims, by examiner’s amendments without paragraph/section/claim replacement to expedite prosecution and reduce cycle time.
guidance: Additions or deletions may be made by instructions to make the change at a precise location in the specification or the claims. See MPEP § 1302.04 for examiner amendment practice.

name: Start each amendment section on separate sheets
description: Each section of an amendment (Introductory Comments, Amendments to the Specification, Amendments to the Claims, Remarks) must begin on a separate sheet.
guidance: This facilitates separate indexing and electronic scanning for placement in an electronic file wrapper.

name: Waiver of two-version requirement under revised format
description: The requirement to provide two versions (a clean version and a marked-up version) of each replacement paragraph/section/substitute specification or claim is waived where an amendment is submitted in the revised format.
guidance: Under the revised amendment format (effective Jan 31, 2003), applicants need not provide both versions when following the specified format. Exceptions apply for reissue applications and reexaminations per 37 CFR 1.173 and 1.530(d)-(k).

name: Claim cancellation and new claim notation rules
description: A claim may be canceled by merely providing an instruction to cancel; any claims added by amendment must be indicated as (new) and must not be underlined; all claims in each amendment paper must be presented in ascending numerical order; consecutive canceled or withdrawn claims may be aggregated in a single statement.
guidance: E.g., 'Claims 1–5 (canceled)'. Follow numeric order for clarity and to conform to processing requirements.

name: Amendments must be fully responsive (37 CFR 1.111)
description: To be entitled to reconsideration or further examination, the applicant must reply and the reply must: be reduced to writing; distinctly and specifically point out the supposed errors in the examiner’s action; reply to every ground of objection and rejection; present arguments pointing out specific distinctions believed to render the claims patentable over applied references; and appear to be a bona fide attempt to advance the application.
guidance: A general allegation that the claims define a patentable invention without pointing out how the claims distinguish from the references does not comply. When amending in reply, clearly point out the patentable novelty and how amendments avoid references or objections. Formal defects and whether they touch merits may require insistence on compliance prior to indicating allowable subject matter.

name: Fee informality and form paragraphs for non-responsive replies
description: Informalities as to fees for additional claims are handled by technical support staff via form PTOL-319; use form paragraphs 7.95 and optionally 7.95.01 where a bona fide reply is not fully responsive.
guidance: Form paragraph 7.95 gives applicant a one‑month period (or 30 days) to supply omissions in a bona fide but non-responsive reply; 7.95.01 reminds applicant to submit substantive arguments under 'Remarks' addressing applied references and distinctions.

name: Misconduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation
description: Violations of the USPTO Code of Professional Responsibility and Rules of Professional Conduct prohibiting misconduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (cited: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(4) and 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c)).
guidance: Example factual predicate: intentionally inflating the time claimed on client matters so clients were billed for time not actually spent. Such intentional overbilling constitutes dishonesty/fraud/deceit and supports disciplinary action.

name: Prefer transparency over surreptitious narrowing
description: If a court believes that a particular claim's linguistic meaning is overbroad (compared to some conception of the real invention), it would be better and more transparent for that court to either invalidate the claim outright or at least explicitly invoke the construction-to-save-validity doctrine or the reverse doctrine of equivalents, rather than surreptitiously achieving the narrowing result by saying that the claim 'meant' the narrower scope all along.
guidance: Avoid covertly reassigning a narrower meaning to a claim term to reach the desired outcome; instead, use explicit doctrines (construction-to-save-validity or reverse DOE) or invalidate. Recognize judicial incentives against transparency and that naming the doctrinal route is preferable for clarity and accountability.

name: Distinguish interpretation from construction
description: Make a clear conceptual distinction between linguistic interpretation (what the claim text means) and construction (policy-driven choices about how to apply or limit claims relative to the invention); many disputes are actually about construction, not interpretation.
guidance: Before applying linguistic tools, ask whether the dispute is over semantic meaning or over whether the invention or policy should trump the linguistic meaning. Treat these as different analytical tasks; conflating them obscures judicial policy choices.

name: Vagueness requires construction, not interpretation
description: When a claim term is vague (has fuzzy boundaries, e.g., 'near'), no amount of linguistic knowledge will draw a precise line; such disputes cannot be resolved by interpretation and instead require courts to construct a precise boundary.
guidance: Do not attempt to resolve vagueness by synonym substitution (e.g., 'near' -> 'close to') which leaves the same indeterminacy. If the real issue is 'how close is close enough?', use constructional tools, fact-finding (experts/jury), or policy-based line-drawing rather than claiming interpretation resolves it. Example: Power-One (term 'near').

name: Only construct when dispute falls within the construction zone
description: Not every vague or broad claim causes litigation; a court should construct lines only when the dispute truly falls within the zone where language underspecifies—otherwise the disagreement may really be about whether to follow the language at all.
guidance: Assess whether proposed constructions go outside reasonable debate (e.g., construing 'biocompatible' to require zero reactivity when specification permits some reactivity). If a proposed construction is unreasonable given the document context, the dispute may be about following language vs invention, not mere vagueness.

name: Treat deliberate patentee ambiguity as a policy problem, not solvable linguistically
description: Patentees have incentives to craft ambiguous claims to persuade the PTO narrowly while deterring competitors broadly; while deliberate ambiguity exists, it cannot be solved by better linguistic tools but requires policy responses and examiner diligence.
guidance: Recognize the motive and possibility of deliberate ambiguity (illustrated by Plant Genetics) but focus remedies on procedural and policy measures (e.g., examiner scrutiny, claiming practices, estoppel doctrines) rather than new interpretative theories.

name: Do not conflate linguistic meaning with the invention
description: The claim's linguistic meaning is a distinct analytic object from what the patentee's invention is; treating text as ambiguous until the invention is known (Autogiro-style) collapses interpretation into anti-textualist construction.
guidance: Keep separate inquiries: first determine linguistic meaning using ordinary tools (specification, prosecution history, dictionaries, experts); only then, if necessary, decide whether policy or doctrine should alter the claim's effect relative to the inventor's disclosed invention.

name: Do not infer linguistic ambiguity from reversal rates
description: High appellate reversal rates in claim cases indicate legal or policy disagreement among judges—not necessarily linguistic ambiguity of claim text.
guidance: Avoid using reversal statistics as proof of linguistic indeterminacy. Consider selection effects (uncertain cases more likely to be litigated) and account for judges differing in textualist vs anti-textualist approaches as an explanation for reversals.

name: Skepticism toward the scientific jargon explanation
description: Although patent claims use technical language, disputes also arise over simple terms ('a', 'or', 'to'), and courts have resources (experts, technical advisors, dictionaries) to resolve technical understandings; thus jargon alone is an insufficient explanation for claim uncertainty.
guidance: Do not over-attribute claim disputes to scientific jargon. Use available resources (appointed technical advisors, special masters, expert witnesses) but recognize that these tools have not eliminated the core uncertainty, which often stems from policy disagreement.

name: Technological evolution does not equal linguistic change
description: Changes in the set of real-world objects that fit a description (e.g., analog to digital signals) do not constitute changes in linguistic meaning; the purported 'evolving language' theory conflates the two.
guidance: When assessing claims over time, distinguish whether semantic meaning changed (rare over patent lifespans) or whether covered technologies evolved. Policy choices determine whether claims should cover later-developed technology, not semantic drift.

name: Reject radical indeterminacy as a blanket explanation
description: The claim that 'all text is inherently unclear' and that one must first know 'the idea' to know what the claim says (Autogiro) is doctrinally dangerous and confuses linguistic indeterminacy with constructional choices.
guidance: Acknowledge that linguistic meaning often requires contextual evidence, but resist the posture that text is always ambiguous until the inventor's idea is known; maintain analytic separation and use linguistic tools before moving to invention-based constructions.

name: Field-of-use / technological-environment limitations do not make an abstract idea eligible
description: Limitations that merely limit an abstract idea to a particular technological environment or field of use (e.g., use on the Internet, in a telephone network, in a power-grid context, in a telephone network or Internet, in petrochemical industries, or on a generic computer) generally do not provide meaningful limits on the claim and therefore do not render the claim patent eligible.
guidance: Provides multiple examples and cited cases (FairWarning v. Iatric Sys.; Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec; Electric Power Group v. Alstom; Genetic Techs. v. Merial; Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One; Ultramercial v. Hulu; buySAFE v. Google; Parker v. Flook). Examiners should consider the terms “technological environment” and “field of use” interchangeably and recognize overlap with insignificant extra-solution activity (see MPEP §2106.05(g)). If a limitation generally links use of a judicial exception to a technological environment, the examiner should explain why that limitation does not meaningfully limit the claim.

name: Streamlined eligibility analysis (Pathway A) when eligibility is self-evident
description: Examiners may use a streamlined eligibility analysis (Pathway A) for efficiency when the eligibility of the claim is self-evident (e.g., the claim clearly improves a technology or computer functionality), concluding eligibility without a full Alice/Mayo analysis.
guidance: The result of the streamlined analysis will always be the same as the full analysis; it is not a way to avoid a finding of ineligibility. If doubt exists about whether the applicant is seeking coverage for a judicial exception, the full analysis should be used. The record may simply reflect eligibility by the absence of a §101 rejection or include clarifying remarks. Examples include claims to clear technological improvements (robotic arm control system, artificial hip prosthesis with a naturally occurring mineral coating). See MPEP §2106.05(a) and cited cases (Enfish; McRO). Use Pathway A only when eligibility is self-evident.

name: Eligibility is self-evident — when to avoid full analysis
description: A claim that may recite a judicial exception but, when viewed as a whole, clearly does not attempt to tie up the exception (and clearly does not prevent others from practicing the exception) may be eligible without the full analysis.
guidance: Examples: complex manufactured industrial products or processes with meaningful limitations; claims that merely include ancillary nature-based components (e.g., cellphone with a gold electrical contact). If a claim is a 'close call' on whether it improves technology or computer functionality, perform the full analysis (BASCOM example). Streamlined analysis appropriate only when self-evident.

name: Clear improvement to technology or computer functionality avoids abstract-idea characterization
description: Claims directed to clear improvements in computer-related technology or computer functionality are not necessarily abstract and therefore may avoid the full eligibility analysis.
guidance: Cites cases such as Enfish (self-referential table) and McRO (automatic lip synchronization) where claims were found eligible at Step 1. An examiner could reasonably find such claims eligible at Pathway A or B. See MPEP §2106.05(a) for details on what constitutes an improvement.

name: Rejections must be based on substantive law and supported to establish a prima facie case
description: Eligibility rejections must be grounded in substantive law under 35 U.S.C. §101 as interpreted by judicial precedent; examination guidance/examples do not themselves form a legal basis for rejection. Examiners must review the entire record and make claim-by-claim determinations. When a claim is likely ineligible, the examiner must formulate an Office action that sets forth a prima facie case of ineligibility that is clear and specific enough to give applicant sufficient notice to respond.
guidance: Examiners should review specification, claims, prosecution history, relevant case law, and prior art. Dependent claims must be considered separately (they can be eligible even if an independent claim is not, and vice versa). If rejection is maintained after applicant response, examiner must provide rebuttal. See MPEP §2106.03–.07 for procedural details.

name: Identify and evaluate additional claim elements for integration into a practical application (Step 2A Prong Two)
description: After identifying the judicial exception, the rejection should identify any additional claim elements beyond the exception and evaluate whether those elements, individually and in combination, integrate the exception into a practical application.
guidance: Use the considerations in MPEP §§2106.04(d), 2106.05(a)-(c) and (e)-(h). Give weight to all claimed additional elements, even if they are well-understood, routine, conventional. Explain why the additional elements do not integrate the exception into a practical application (or explain why they do). Address combinations of elements because a new combination of known steps may be patent eligible (Diamond v. Diehr). Provide clear rationale so applicant can respond effectively.

name: Explain why additional elements do not amount to 'significantly more' (Step 2B)
description: When concluding that claim is directed to a judicial exception and does not provide an inventive concept, the rejection must explain why the additional elements, taken individually and as a combination, do not result in the claim as a whole amounting to significantly more than the judicial exception.
guidance: If particular claim limitations are found to be well-understood, routine, conventional activities, the rejection must explicitly support that factual conclusion in writing (see evidentiary requirements below). For generic computer elements performing generic functions (e.g., using the Internet to gather data), explain why such generic computing functions do not meaningfully limit the claim; consider DDR Holdings and MPEP §2106.05(f) for examples where combinations of generic components were nevertheless not merely generic. See MPEP §2106.05 for additional considerations (insignificant extra-solution activity, field-of-use limitations, etc.).

name: Evidentiary support required when asserting elements are well-understood, routine, conventional (Step 2B)
description: An examiner should not assert that additional claim elements (or combinations) are well-understood, routine, or conventional unless the examiner expressly supports the rejection in writing with one or more specified forms of evidence or authority.
guidance: Three permissible supports: (A) citation to an express statement in the specification or to a statement by applicant during prosecution demonstrating that the element is well-understood/routine/conventional (e.g., described as commercially available or so well-known that particulars are not described); (B) citation to one or more court decisions discussed in MPEP §2106.05(d) that note the well-understood/routine/conventional nature of the element(s) (ensure the claim limitations match the court-found elements at the same level of generality); (C) citation to a publication demonstrating the element is well-understood/routine/conventional (book, manual, review article, etc.). A finding cannot be based solely on specification silence. See examples and cautions in MPEP §2106.05(d) and related subsections.

name: No general requirement for evidence when identifying the judicial exception (Step 2A Prong One)
description: Because courts treat identification of judicial exceptions largely as a question of law, examiners are not required to rely on extrinsic evidence (publications, affidavits) to find that a claim recites a judicial exception at Step 2A Prong One.
guidance: Cites cases (FairWarning; OIP Techs.; Content Extraction). However, the issue of whether additional elements are well-understood, routine, conventional may be a factual issue, and in those instances factual support is required (see Berkheimer, Interval Licensing, Rapid Litig.). Thus: no evidence required to identify an exception, but evidence/support required if asserting well-understood/routine/conventional in Step 2B (see above).

name: Generic computer components/functions at high level of generality do not necessarily confer eligibility
description: Claim limitations that recite generic computer components performing generic computer functions at a high level of generality (e.g., using the Internet to gather data) typically do not meaningfully limit an abstract idea and thus often do not render a claim patent eligible.
guidance: Examiners should explain why such generic computing functions fail to add meaningful limitations. Keep in mind DDR Holdings where courts found that certain computer-implemented combinations were significantly more than abstract ideas; consider whether claimed generic components, in combination, perform functions that are not merely generic. See MPEP §2106.05(f) for court-found examples of mere instructions to implement an exception on a computer.

name: Insignificant extra-solution activity and overlap with field-of-use limitations
description: Data-gathering steps limited to particular data sources or types (e.g., Internet, power grid data, XML tags) may be both insignificant extra-solution activity and field-of-use limitations; such limitations often do not meaningfully limit the claim.
guidance: Examples and case citations (Ultramercial; Electric Power; Intellectual Ventures v. Erie Indem.). Examiners should carefully consider each claim on its merits and evaluate overlapping considerations; explain in the rejection why such extra-solution or field-of-use limitations are insignificant or fail to provide meaningful limitation. See MPEP §2106.05(g) and (h).

name: Best practice: consult specification for amendable elements to overcome a §101 rejection
description: When making a rejection, it is a best practice for the examiner to consult the specification to determine whether there are elements that could be added to the claim to make it eligible, and if so, identify and suggest them in the Office action as ways to overcome the rejection.
guidance: Provides constructive guidance to applicants and helps clarify the record. Suggesting claim amendments that would result in eligibility is encouraged when appropriate.

name: Reissue oath/declaration: statement of belief re defect and at least one error
description: The reissue oath or declaration must state that the applicant believes the original patent to be wholly or partly inoperative or invalid by reason of a defective specification or drawing, or by reason of the patentee claiming more or less than the patentee had the right to claim in the patent, stating at least one error being relied upon as the basis for reissue.
guidance: Acceptable sample language is provided (e.g., 'Applicant believes the original patent to be partly inoperative or invalid by reason of a defective specification or drawing.'). If both grounds apply, include both statements. The oath/declaration must identify at least one specific error (a single word, phrase, or expression in the specification or an original claim is sufficient). It is not sufficient to make only a generic statement that the application is filed to correct errors or to merely reproduce claims with brackets/underlining without identifying a specific error.

name: Reissue oath/declaration: examiner must review sufficiency and compliance with 37 CFR 1.63
description: The question of the sufficiency of the reissue oath/declaration must in each case be reviewed and decided personally by the primary examiner; the oath/declaration must also comply with the requirements of 37 CFR 1.63.
guidance: 37 CFR 1.63(b) requires statements that applicant has reviewed and understands the specification and claims (as amended by any amendment specifically referred to), believes the named inventors to be the original and first inventors of the claimed subject matter, and acknowledges the duty to disclose information material to patentability as defined in 37 CFR 1.56. Use form paragraphs (e.g., 14.01.05 with appropriate form paragraphs 6.03–6.09) to indicate defects in compliance with 1.63.

name: Identification and sufficiency of the 'at least one error' relied upon
description: The oath/declaration must identify at least one error relied upon to support the reissue application; identification of a single word, phrase, or expression in the specification or an original claim suffices.
guidance: It is not necessary to explain how or when the error arose or was discovered; such statements will not be reviewed by the examiner. If the identified 'error' is not an appropriate error under 35 U.S.C. 251, the oath/declaration is defective and the examiner should indicate this. If multiple errors are identified and at least one is an appropriate reissue error, that one suffices to support reissue.

name: What counts as a reasonable pre-suit investigation
description: A reasonable pre-suit investigation includes obtaining opinions of counsel, developing designs or processes to avoid infringement (design-arounds), and conducting competent technical and claim analyses by qualified individuals.
guidance: The article gives examples: AVX obtained pre-suit opinions of counsel and developed design-arounds and thus avoided enhancement; Blue Ridge's engineer-conducted pre-suit investigation supported absence of enhancement; Zoll's reasoned claim construction and reliance on the specification/prosecution history was 'reasonable.' By contrast, reliance on 'people without expertise in reading patent claims' or not reading patents until depositions (Cisco) was viewed negatively.

name: Literal infringement of means-plus-function (35 U.S.C. §112) — general rule
description: For claims containing means-plus-function or step-plus-function clauses, [the Plaintiff] must prove that it is more likely than not that the part/step of the Defendant's product/method that performs the claimed function is identical to, or equivalent to, the structure/step described in the specification for performing the identical function.
guidance: First determine whether the accused product/method has any structure/step that performs the claimed function; if none exists, the means-plus-function limitation is not infringed. If it does, identify the accused structure/act and compare it to the structure/acts disclosed in the specification for identity or equivalence (person of ordinary skill perspective). Cites 35 U.S.C. §112 and Federal Circuit precedent.

name: Means-plus-function infringement — Alternative identification and comparison procedures
description: Alternative I: If the accused product/method performs the claimed function, identify the structure/step in the accused product that performs it and determine whether that structure/step is identical to, or equivalent to, any structure/step identified in the patent specification as performing the function. Alternative II: Identify the structure/act in the accused product that performs the function and determine whether that structure/act is identical to, or equivalent to, the specific corresponding structure/acts the court identified during claim construction.
guidance: Use the court-identified corresponding structure (if court has done claim construction) in comparing for equivalence. Equivalence is judged from perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art; insubstantial differences indicate equivalence. If all claim requirements are met by structures found in the accused product, the accused product infringes.

name: Infringement of dependent claims (literal)
description: A dependent claim refers to at least one other claim and incorporates all elements of the claim to which it refers plus additional elements. To establish literal infringement of a dependent claim, [the Plaintiff] must show that it is more likely than not that the Defendant's product/method includes each and every element of the dependent claim. If the independent claim from which the dependent claim depends is not literally infringed, then the dependent claim cannot be literally infringed.
guidance: Identify differences between the independent and dependent claims; dependent claim requires all elements of the independent claim plus its own additional elements. Citations to Federal Circuit cases provided.

name: Infringement of 'comprising' (open-ended) claims
description: The word 'comprising' means 'including the following but not excluding others.' If the Defendant's product/method includes all elements in the claim, the fact that it includes additional components or steps does not avoid literal infringement of a claim that uses 'comprising' language so long as the additional components/steps do not negate an element of the claim.
guidance: Assess whether extra components negate an element; if not, comprising claims remain infringed despite additional features. Cases cited (Invitrogen, AFG, Moleculon, AB Dick).

name: 35 U.S.C. §271(f)(1) — supplying substantial portion of components abroad (elements)
description: To show infringement under Section 271(f)(1), Plaintiff must prove it is more likely than not that (1) the product as intended to be assembled outside the U.S. included all limitations of at least one asserted claim, (2) Defendant supplied or caused to be supplied components from the U.S. that made up all or a substantial portion of the invention of any one asserted claim, and (3) Defendant specifically intended to induce the combination of the components into a product that would infringe the patent if assembled in the U.S.
guidance: Requires intent to induce combination and that components supplied from the U.S. made up all or a substantial portion; cites Cardiac Pacemakers, Microsoft v. AT&T, and other authority.

name: 35 U.S.C. §271(g) — infringement by import/sale/use of product made by patented process (elements)
description: To show infringement under Section 271(g), Plaintiff must prove it is more likely than not that (1) Defendant imported/sold/offered for sale/used a product that was made by a process including all steps of at least one asserted claim, (2) the product was made between the patent issue date and expiration (or date of trial), and (3) Defendant imported/sold/offered/used the product between the patent issue date and expiration (or date of trial).
guidance: You must decide whether evidence establishes the product was 'made by' the patented process. Exclude if the product was materially changed by later processes or the product is only a trivial/non-essential part of another product. Note on Section 295 presumption where patentee cannot determine the process (may require accused infringer to rebut presumption).

name: Doctrine of equivalents — element-by-element equivalence analysis
description: If the Defendant's product/method does not literally infringe an asserted claim, the jury must decide whether it infringes under the doctrine of equivalents. Under this doctrine, the product/method can infringe if it includes parts/steps that are equivalent to claim requirements that are not literally present. If the product/method is missing an equivalent part/step to even one claim part/step, it cannot infringe under the doctrine of equivalents; the analysis must be done for each individual requirement.
guidance: Equivalence is determined such that a part/step is equivalent if a person of ordinary skill would think the differences are not substantial as of the time of alleged infringement. One way is the function-way-result (FWR) test: performed substantially the same function, in substantially the same way, to achieve substantially the same result. Known interchangeability may be considered but is not necessary. The same accused element may satisfy more than one claim element.

name: Limitation on doctrine of equivalents — prior art (ensnarement)
description: You may not find that the Defendant's product/method infringes under the doctrine of equivalents if by doing so the patent claim would cover products/methods that were already in the prior art. Defendant has the burden of coming forward with evidence to show that it was in the prior art.
guidance: Ensnarement is ultimately a question of law for the court, but the jury may be asked for an advisory verdict in some cases. Cases cited (DePuy Spine, Fiskars, Conroy, Wilson Sporting Goods).

name: Limitation on doctrine of equivalents — prosecution history estoppel
description: If the court has determined that prosecution history estoppel applies to certain claim elements (i.e., an amendment was made for reasons related to patentability and presumption of surrender of equivalents has not been rebutted), the doctrine of equivalents analysis cannot be applied to those claim elements. Those elements must be literally present in the Defendant's product/method for there to be infringement.
guidance: The instruction assumes the court has made an estoppel determination as a matter of law; list of estopped elements should be provided claim-by-claim. Cites Festo and Warner-Jenkinson.

name: Limitation on doctrine of equivalents — subject matter dedicated to the public
description: When a patent discloses subject matter but does not include it within its claims, the patentee has dedicated that unclaimed subject matter to the public. If the patent discloses but does not claim subject matter alleged to be equivalent to an element, then that component/step alleged to be equivalent in Defendant's product/method cannot be an equivalent for purposes of the doctrine of equivalents, even if the failure to claim was unintentional.
guidance: The court should list elements that were disclosed but unclaimed; unless each such element is literally present there can be no infringement under the doctrine of equivalents for those elements. Cases cited include Pfizer and Toro.

name: Summary of invalidity defense (burden and scope)
description: [The Defendant] contends that the asserted claim(s) of the patents-in-suit are invalid. [The Defendant] must prove that it is highly probable that each asserted claim is invalid.
guidance: The jury must determine whether each asserted claim is invalid. The instruction introduces more detailed invalidity contentions to follow.

name: Invalidity of independent and dependent claims (evaluation rules)
description: You must evaluate the invalidity of each asserted claim separately. If you find that a dependent claim is invalid, then you cannot find that the independent claim to which that dependent claim refers is not invalid. Conversely, an independent claim can be found invalid, even though a dependent claim to which it refers is valid.
guidance: Dependent claims incorporate all elements of the claims they refer to plus additional elements; apply case law (Comparer, Callaway, Ormco) when assessing interdependencies.

name: Person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA) — perspective
description: The question of invalidity of a patent claim is determined from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art in the field of the asserted invention as of [date].
guidance: POSITA perspective is used throughout validity analyses (anticipation, obviousness, inherency, understandings of disclosures). Court should set the appropriate date.

name: Anticipation (novelty) — single-reference rule and burden
description: To prove anticipation, Defendant must prove it is highly probable that the claimed invention is not new. To anticipate a claim, each and every element in the claim must be present in a single item of prior art, and arranged or combined in the same way as recited in the claim. You may not combine two or more items of prior art to find anticipation.
guidance: Consider what a person of ordinary skill would have understood from review of the reference. Optional inherency instruction: consider not only what is expressly disclosed but also what is inherently present or results from practicing the prior art; inherency requires high probability and may be shown with evidence outside the reference (including testing). Cite Net MoneyIN, Toro, Schering, In re Robertson, etc.

name: Prior public knowledge (anticipation by public knowledge)
description: A patent claim is invalid if the invention defined in that claim was publicly known by others in the United States before it was invented by the patentee.
guidance: If there is a factual issue about date of invention, the jury should be instructed how to determine invention date; otherwise the court may instruct the date of invention as appropriate. Cite 35 U.S.C. §102(a) and cases.

name: Experimental use exception to public use / on-sale
description: Certain activities are experimental if they are a legitimate effort to test claimed features or to determine if the invention will work for its intended purpose. So long as the primary purpose is experimentation, it does not matter that the public used the invention or that the inventor incidentally derived profit from it.
guidance: Only experimentation by or under control of the inventor or assignee qualifies for the exception; experimentation by a third party for its own purposes generally does not qualify. The court must evaluate the primary purpose and control of testing to determine if an asserted public use/sale was experimental.

name: Ready for patenting — two alternative proofs
description: "'Ready for patenting' ... may be satisfied in at least two ways: by proof of reduction to practice before the critical date; or by proof that prior to the critical date the inventor had prepared drawings or other descriptions of the invention that were sufficiently specific to enable a person skilled in the art to practice the invention."
guidance: If detailed drawings/specifications available pre-critical date enable a skilled person to make the claimed invention, the invention can be 'ready for patenting' even absent reduction to practice. Cases: Pfaff (computer chip socket), Weatherchem (plastic dispensing caps).

name: Product embodying all claim limitations triggers on-sale bar
description: "If a product that is offered for sale inherently possesses each of the limitations of the claims, then the invention is on sale, whether or not the parties to the transaction recognize that the product possesses the claimed characteristics."
guidance: Subjective ignorance of particular properties by parties does not avoid the on-sale bar (Abbott Laboratories; STX v. Brine). Even subjective qualities inherent in a product cannot be an escape hatch.

name: Anticipation (pre-March 16, 2013 novelty standard)
description: For patents having an effective filing date before March 16, 2013: to be entitled to a patent, the invention must be 'new' and inventor must not have lost rights by delaying filing. Anticipation must be determined claim-by-claim. [Alleged infringer] must prove by clear and convincing evidence that the claim(s) is/are invalid.
guidance: Provides a list of ways a claim can be shown not new or the patentee lost rights (choose applicable): (1) known to or used by others in the U.S. before [date of invention] (publicly accessible); (2) already patented or described in a printed publication anywhere in the world before [date of invention]; (3) patented or described in a printed publication by patentee or anyone else more than a year before the effective filing date (on-sale/publication bars); (4) publicly used, sold, or offered for sale in the U.S. more than one year before effective filing date; (5) abandonment of the invention; (6) foreign patenting or foreign filing more than one year before U.S. filing; (7) described in a published patent application by another in the U.S. (or PCT designated and published in English) before [date of invention]; (8) described in a patent granted on an application by another filed before [relevant date]; (9) not invented by the named inventor; (10) made by someone else in the U.S. before patentee and not abandoned/suppressed/concealed. If an interference proceeding exists, additional instructions apply.

name: Prior Art (post-March 16, 2013 / AIA)
description: For patents having an effective filing date on or after March 16, 2013, prior art may include: (1) items publicly known or used, on sale, or otherwise made available to the public before the filing date; (2) publications made available to the public before the filing date; (3) patents and published patent applications naming another inventor that were filed before the filing date.
guidance: Exceptions: prior art does not include an item/publication that is the inventor’s own work, describes the inventor’s own work, or was obtained from the inventor (unless made public more than one year before filing). Also excludes patents/applications that disclose the inventor’s own work or were obtained from/owned by the same person (with similar one-year exception). For anticipation analysis, the alleged infringer must show by clear and convincing evidence that all claim requirements were present in a single prior reference (expressly or implicitly) so a person of ordinary skill could make and use the claimed invention from that one reference.

name: Obviousness (35 U.S.C. § 103)
description: A claimed invention must not have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the field at the time the invention was made or before the filing date to be patentable. [Alleged infringer] may establish invalidity by clear and convincing evidence that the claimed invention would have been obvious.
guidance: Consider level of ordinary skill, scope and content of the prior art, and differences between prior art and claimed invention. Existence of each element of claim in prior art does not necessarily prove obviousness—many inventions build on prior art. Factors to consider whether a person would have been prompted to combine known elements include: (1) predictable result of using prior art elements per known functions; (2) obvious solution to a known problem; (3) prior art teaches/suggests combining elements; (4) prior art teaches away from combining elements; (5) 'obvious to try' when finite predictable solutions exist and design/market pressure exists (but 'obvious to try' not sufficient in unpredictable technologies); (6) whether change resulted more from design incentives or market forces. To find obviousness, prior art must provide a reasonable expectation of success. Do not use hindsight; evaluate claim-by-claim. Consider objective (secondary) evidence such as commercial success, long-felt need, failed attempts by others, contemporaneous invention by others, copying, unexpected results, praise, expressions of surprise, licensing, and departure from accepted wisdom.

name: Scope and Content of the Prior Art (for obviousness)
description: Determine the scope and content of the prior art when assessing obviousness.
guidance: Scope includes prior art in the same field and prior art from different fields that a person of ordinary skill might combine using common sense. If attacking party relies on prior art considered by the Examiner during prosecution, that party bears the burden of overcoming deference to the agency. In combination-based invalidity defenses, use a flexible analysis considering whether the prior art teaches, suggests, or motivates the claimed combination.

name: Inequitable Conduct
description: Inequitable conduct occurs when a person involved in prosecution fails to supply material information or supplies false information or statements to the PTO with intent to deceive, rendering any patent issued unenforceable as a matter of fairness.
guidance: Burden: alleged infringer must prove by clear and convincing evidence both (1) that a person meaningfully involved in prosecution withheld material information or submitted materially false information/statements, and (2) that the person did so with intent to deceive the Examiner. Material: information is material if PTO would not have allowed the claim had it been aware; false/misleading statement is material if it convinces PTO to allow a claim it would not have. Affirmative egregious misconduct (e.g., filing an unmistakably false affidavit) may be material. Intent to deceive: negligence, oversight, carelessness, or even gross negligence does not establish intent. Intent can be direct (documents/testimony) or inferred, but may be inferred only where it is the single most reasonable inference from the evidence. Materiality and intent are separate; both must be proven by clear and convincing evidence to find inequitable conduct and unenforceability.

name: Equitable Estoppel
description: Patent holder may be estopped from relief where: (1) the patent holder communicated misleadingly to the infringer about lack of infringement or lack of litigation; (2) the infringer relied on that misleading communication; (3) the infringer will be materially harmed if patent holder is allowed to assert a claim inconsistent with its prior misleading communication.
guidance: Alleged infringer must prove each element by a preponderance of the evidence, but equitable estoppel need not be found even if elements are proven if finding it would be unfair. Communication can be written, spoken, conduct, silence, or a combination. Harm can be evidentiary (inability to present a full defense due to lost records/witnesses) or economic (changed economic position such that losses could have been avoided). Consider facts and circumstances as they existed at the time of the communication.

name: Prosecution Laches
description: Defense that owner is barred from enforcing claims due to unreasonably long delay in filing the claims of the patent and resulting prejudice to infringer, another private party, or the public.
guidance: Delay measured from the original application filing to the filing of the asserted patent. Determine whether delay was unreasonably long by considering facts/circumstances during the delay. Consider whether others invested in developing/manufacturing/selling products covered by the asserted patent during the delay, whether public practice of the invention was unfairly postponed, whether delay was intentional, and whether infringer/public were aware of pending applications. Authorities note prosecution laches may bar enforcement even if statutes/rules were followed when delay was unreasonable and unexplained.

name: Damages—Measure and Burden
description: If infringement of any valid claim is found, damages must adequately compensate the patent holder for the infringement and are not punitive. Patent holder has burden to establish amount of damages by a preponderance of the evidence.
guidance: Damages should put patent holder in approximately the same financial position as if infringement had not occurred. Types of damages include lost profits (actual reduction in business profits due to infringement) and reasonable royalty (amount the parties would have agreed upon as a fee for the use of the invention at a time before infringement began). Patent holder is entitled to recover no less than a reasonable royalty for each infringing act. More detailed instructions may be provided for specific damage theories (e.g., price erosion, convoyed sales) as appropriate.

name: Provisional specification — nature, content and timeline (4.1)
description: A provisional specification is a disclosure describing the nature of the invention; it must contain title and description, start with preamble 'The following specification describes the nature of the invention.' Claims need not be included. It is not a mere rough draft; provisional and complete specifications are permanent and independent documents.
guidance: Provisional spec should set forth object of invention, statement of principle/discovery and general statement of actual invention; include as much information as the applicant has. Filing a provisional gives a filing date and up to twelve months to file complete specification (though complete spec can be filed earlier). Provisional specification cannot be used for divisional, convention or PCT-designating-India applications (these must be accompanied by complete specification). Failure to file complete specification within time leads to abandonment unless request for postdating is filed on or before expiry of 12 months. Where multiple cognate provisional specs exist, applicant may request to file a single complete specification if they constitute a single invention; complete spec timing is computed from earliest filing.

name: Types of patent applications (ordinary, convention, PCT, national phase, patent of addition, divisional)
description: Different application types have specific definitions, requirements and effects: ordinary application, convention application (priority within 12 months), PCT international application, PCT national phase entry (within 31 months), application for patent of addition, and divisional application.
guidance: Convention application must be filed in India within 12 months of first filing in convention country and be accompanied by a complete specification and priority documents (with translation if necessary); multiple priorities require multiple fees. PCT international application gives international filing date and late national entry rights; Indian Patent Office is receiving office for nationals/residents. PCT national phase: can enter within 31 months; Form 1A preferred; documents filed with application treated as complete specification. Patent of addition: for slight modifications to an existing invention; no separate renewal fee during main patent term; expires with main patent unless made independent per S.54; must reference main patent/application number and state it is an improvement/modification. Divisional application: when parent claims more than one invention, applicant may divide; priority date same as parent; complete specification of divisional must not add matter beyond parent.

name: Specification and drawings requirements (Form 2)
description: The provisional/complete specification is submitted in Form 2; first page should contain the title of the invention, name/address/nationality of applicants, and a preamble to the description. Complete description should start from second page and include claims; abstract should follow signature; drawings (if any) may be attached thereafter.
guidance: Complete and provisional specifications are distinct documents; the complete specification must include claims for which protection is required and an abstract. The provisional specification has more limited content (see provisional spec rubric).

name: Statement re: claims with effective filing date on/after March 16, 2013
description: An applicant is not required to provide a statement if either (i) The application claims the benefit of a nonprovisional application in which a statement under § 1.55(k), paragraph (a)(6) of this section, or this paragraph that the application contains, or contained at any time, a claim to a claimed invention that has an effective filing date on or after March 16, 2013 has been filed; or (ii) the applicant reasonably believes on the basis of information already known to the individuals designated in § 1.56(c) that the later filed application does not, and did not at any time, contain a claim to a claimed invention that has an effective filing date on or after March 16, 2013.
guidance: Original wording provides the two alternative bases for omission of the statement; implementers should verify which condition applies before omitting the statement.

name: Certified copy and translation for certain international benefit claims
description: Where benefit is claimed under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, 365(c), or 386(c) to an international application or international design application which designates but did not originate in the United States, the Office may require a certified copy of such application together with an English translation if filed in another language.
guidance: Applicants claiming such benefit should be prepared to provide certified copies and translations when the parent did not originate in the U.S.

name: Patentably indistinct claims in reexamination/patents naming different inventors
description: If a patent or application under reexamination and at least one other application naming different inventors are owned by the same person and contain patentably indistinct claims, and there is no record statement indicating common ownership or assignment obligation on the effective filing date (or date of invention), the Office may require a statement whether the claimed inventions were commonly owned or subject to assignment to the same person on such date, and if not, indicate which named inventor is the prior inventor. Even if commonly owned, patentably indistinct claims may be rejected under the doctrine of double patenting.
guidance: When inventorship differs, provide clear record evidence of common ownership/assignment or identify prior inventor to avoid double patenting issues.

name: Effect of 35 U.S.C. 119(e)(1) change on certificates of correction
description: 35 U.S.C. 119(e)(1) is effective for all patents whenever granted and no longer requires that the amendment containing the specific reference be submitted during pendency. Thus, the prior prohibition on granting certificates of correction to add or correct a claim for the benefit of a prior provisional application no longer applies; a certificate of correction may now be available under certain conditions.
guidance: Under current law, correcting/adding provisional benefit by certificate of correction is possible but still subject to the other conditions and limitations described.

name: Categories of errors correctable by certificate of correction for benefit claims
description: Under certain conditions a certificate of correction can be used, with respect to a benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, 365(c), or 386(c), to correct: (A) the failure to make reference to a prior copending nonprovisional/international application designating the U.S. or international design application designating the U.S. pursuant to 37 CFR 1.78(d)(2); (B) an incorrect reference to such prior applications pursuant to 37 CFR 1.78(d)(2); (C) the failure to make reference to a prior provisional application pursuant to 37 CFR 1.78(a)(3); or (D) an incorrect reference to a prior provisional application pursuant to 37 CFR 1.78(a)(3).
guidance: Certificates may correct specific types of missing/incorrect references to prior applications (both provisional and nonprovisional/international) when conditions are met.

name: Conditions for certificate of correction for 35 U.S.C. 120 to a national application
description: Where a benefit claim based upon 35 U.S.C. 120 to a national application is to be asserted or corrected in a patent via a certificate of correction, the following conditions must be satisfied: (A) all requirements set forth in 37 CFR 1.78(d)(1) must have been met in the application which became the patent; (B) it must be clear from the record of the patent and parent application(s) that priority is appropriate; and (C) a grantable petition to accept an unintentionally delayed claim under 37 CFR 1.78(e) must be filed, including the petition fee as set forth in 37 CFR 1.17(m).
guidance: Satisfy regulatory prerequisites and ensure the record shows entitlement to priority; prepare and file the grantable 1.78(e) petition with fee.

name: Conditions for certificate of correction for international applications (35 U.S.C. 120 & 365(c)/386(c))
