description: Where a benefit claim based upon 35 U.S.C. 120 and 365(c) to an international application, or 35 U.S.C. 120 and 386(c) to an international design application, is to be asserted or corrected in a patent via a certificate of correction, the following conditions must be satisfied: (A) all requirements set forth in 37 CFR 1.78(d)(1) must have been met in the application which became the patent; (B) it must be clear from the record that priority is appropriate; (C) the patentee must submit with the request copies of documentation showing designation of states and any other information needed to make clear from the record that 35 U.S.C. 120 priority is appropriate; and (D) a grantable petition under 37 CFR 1.78(e) must be filed including the petition fee.
guidance: International priority corrections require additional documentation showing state designations and a grantable 1.78(e) petition with fee.

name: Conditions for certificate of correction for 35 U.S.C. 119(e) provisional benefit claims
description: Where a benefit claim based upon 35 U.S.C. 119(e) to a prior provisional application is to be asserted or corrected in a patent via a certificate of correction, the following conditions must be satisfied: (A) all requirements set forth in 37 CFR 1.78(a)(1) and (a)(2) must have been met in the application which became the patent; (B) it must be clear from the record that priority is appropriate; and (C) a grantable petition to accept an unintentionally delayed claim under 37 CFR 1.78(c) must be filed, including the petition fee as set forth in 37 CFR 1.17(m).
guidance: Provisional-benefit corrections require compliance with the a(1)/a(2) regulatory prerequisites, proof of entitlement, and a grantable 1.78(c) petition with fee.

name: Certificate-of-correction should not be granted if it would appear to extend patent term
description: If the grant of the petition under 37 CFR 1.78 with a request for a certificate of correction under 35 U.S.C. 255 would have the appearance of extending the patent term, the petition should not be granted. Example: changing to a later filing date for the earliest application for which domestic benefit is claimed could appear to extend the patent term even if effective filing date doesn't change.
guidance: Avoid certificate grants that create the impression of patent-term extension; examine term consequences carefully.

name: Examples where certificate under 35 U.S.C. 255 may not be appropriate
description: Exemplary non-appropriate situations include: (A) Adding/correcting a claim to a prior application before March 16, 2013 in a patent examined under AIA FITF when the 37 CFR 1.55/1.78 statement is not present; (B) Correcting a claim from a prior application before March 16, 2013 to one on/after March 16, 2013 in a patent examined under pre-AIA law; (C) Correcting a claim to a prior application that would result in a later effective filing date for the claimed invention; (D) Correcting a claim that would have the appearance of extending the patent term.
guidance: If examples align with a case at hand, certificates likely inappropriate; consider reissue or other remedies.

name: Use of form PTO/SB/44 (PTO-1050) and signature requirement
description: Applicants/attorneys are urged to submit the text of the correction on Certificate of Correction form PTO/SB/44 which can serve as camera copy. In addition to the form, the request must include a signed request identifying support in the application for any Office errors in the patent. If the request is not signed, it will not be accepted.
guidance: Always submit PTO/SB/44 and a signed request showing support for claimed Office errors; unsigned or non-form submissions risk delay or rejection.

name: Form content and formatting instructions
description: On PTO/SB/44: (A) identify exact point of error by reference to column and line number of printed patent for specification or claim changes; (B) conserve space by typing single space beginning two lines down from printed message; (C) start correction to each separate column as a sentence and use semicolons to separate corrections within same column where possible; (D) leave a two-inch space blank at bottom of last sheet for signature of attesting officer; (E) use quotation marks to enclose exact subject matter to be deleted or corrected and double hyphens (--) to enclose subject matter to be added, except formulas; (F) for formulas, set out only portion to be corrected or paste photocopy onto form.
guidance: Strict adherence to the form formatting instructions avoids processing delays; special handling for formulas.

name: Statutory disclaimers and terminal disclaimers general requirements (37 CFR 1.321)
description: A patentee owning whole or sectional interest may disclaim any complete claim or claims or dedicate to the public the entire term or any terminal part. To be recorded, the disclaimer must: (1) be signed by the patentee or attorney/agent of record; (2) identify the patent and complete claim(s) or term being disclaimed; (3) state the present extent of patentee’s ownership interest in the patent; and (4) be accompanied by the fee set forth in § 1.20(d).
guidance: Ensure disclaimers are signed, identify claims/term precisely, state ownership interest, and include the correct fee to be recordable.

name: Distinction between statutory disclaimer and terminal disclaimer
description: A statutory disclaimer denotes a disclaimer of one or more claims of an issued patent (35 U.S.C. 253); a terminal disclaimer denotes a disclaimer of the entire term or any terminal part of the term of a patent or a patent to be granted. Although both provided by statute, historically the phrases distinguish disclaimers of claims (statutory) vs disclaimers of term (terminal).
guidance: Choose the correct type of disclaimer based on whether relinquishing claims (statutory) or patent term (terminal).

name: Definition — Markman (Claim Construction) Hearing
description: A Markman hearing is a pre-trial hearing in a U.S. District Court during which a judge examines evidence from all parties on the appropriate meanings of relevant keywords used in a patent claim when patent infringement is alleged by a plaintiff. It is also known as a 'Claim Construction Hearing'.
guidance: Purpose: determine meanings of claim terms so the court can establish the scope of asserted patent claims prior to infringement analysis.

name: Importance of Markman ruling
description: The court determines patent infringement cases by interpreting the claims. A Markman hearing may encourage settlement since the judge’s claim construction finding can indicate a likely outcome of the patent infringement case as a whole.
guidance: Practical effect: judge’s construction influences jury instructions and overall case strategy; early construction can narrow or resolve issues and prompt settlement.

name: Intrinsic evidence is primary
description: Materials provided as a part of the patent application are referred to as intrinsic evidence. This comprises the claims, executive summary, and written description contained in the patent application itself, written or verbal correspondence between the patent applicant and the patent examiner that includes the prosecution history, prior art cited in the patent application, and previous comparable patents and their prosecution histories.
guidance: Courts generally look at intrinsic evidence to aid in claim construction; it is the starting point and often the decisive evidence for interpreting claim scope.

name: Extrinsic evidence is secondary/background
description: Any evidence that originates from outside sources is considered extrinsic. Extrinsic evidence in Markman hearings may include: definitions from dictionaries for common terms, for technical words, consult encyclopedias or engineering dictionaries, journals, or other scholarly works that cover the technology, the patent applicant’s testimony, or expert opinion.
guidance: Extrinsic evidence is helpful for education and background knowledge on the contested invention, even though courts generally look at intrinsic evidence to aid in claim construction.

name: Phillips v. AWH Corp framework for claim construction
description: In Phillips v. AWH Corp, the Federal Circuit (2004) established the current method for construing patent claims. This case established a foundation for claim formation, as did later judgments that cited Phillips.
guidance: The correct claim construction cannot be determined using a predetermined process; rather, a set of criteria are applied to choose the right construction. Courts apply Phillips' principles (focus on intrinsic evidence, appropriate role of extrinsic evidence, etc.).

name: District court discretion to hold a Markman hearing
description: The district court has the discretion to determine whether a Markman hearing is required. A Markman hearing is not necessary as a result of the Markman v. Westview Instruments ruling; rather, patent claims are decided by a judge rather than a jury.
guidance: Many district judges rule that a Markman hearing is not required; if paper records provide all relevant details, courts may resolve construction without a live hearing.

name: Court must establish claim scope before analyzing the accused product
description: Any patent litigation begins with the formulation of the patent claim. The court must establish the scope and significance of the asserted patent claims before looking at the allegedly infringing item.
guidance: Claim construction defines what constitutes protected intellectual property and frames infringement and validity analyses.

name: Use of technical tutorials and visual aids to explain claimed subject matter
description: IIPRD provides experienced professionals to build and support claim construction theories and technical tutorials to help prepare charts that can assist in describing the claimed subject matter to the judges and present the facts in easy-to-understand ways.
guidance: Well-prepared tutorials and charts can clarify complex technical concepts for judges and support claim construction positions.

name: Substantiate claim construction via critical review of specification, prosecution history, and expert evidence
description: Substantiate claim construction through critical review of specification, prosecution history, and expert evidence.
guidance: Practical step: systematically analyze intrinsic records and reconcile with expert testimony to support proposed constructions.

name: Prepare written opinions, notes, and documentation to support scope/interpretation
description: Draft opinions, notes, and documentation required to substantiate the scope/interpretation of claims and/or claim terms/elements and limitations.
guidance: Preparation of clear written positions (claim construction briefs, rebuttals, exhibits) is essential to persuade the court.

name: Develop validity defenses with comprehensive claim charts mapped to prior art
description: Set up a validity defence through comprehensive claim charts demonstrating scope of each claim term/element/limitation and mapping with prior art reference(s).
guidance: Use detailed claim charts to show how prior art reads on claim elements and to support invalidity arguments or to refine claim meaning.

name: Prepare claim construction contentions in compliance with USPTO/claim construction guidelines
description: IIPRD supports clients with preparation of patent claim construction contentions in compliance with claim construction guidelines established by the USPTO.
guidance: Ensure petitions and contentions (in court or at the PTO) conform to applicable guidance (e.g., Phillips principles, 37 CFR 42.100) and procedural rules to avoid waiver or rejection.

name: Panel review requirement and scope
description: A panel review will be conducted at each stage of the examiner’s examination in an ex parte reexamination proceeding, other than for notices of informality or incomplete response.
guidance: Panel reviews the examiner’s preliminary decision to reject and/or allow the claims prior to issuance of each Office action. Matters outside examiner jurisdiction (petitions, extensions of time, CRU support staff notices) are not reviewed by the panel.

name: After-final practice limits in reexamination
description: Once a proper final rejection is entered in reexamination, the patent owner no longer has a right to unrestricted further prosecution; amendments after final are governed by 37 CFR 1.116 (and after appeal by 37 CFR 41.33).
guidance: Patent owner cannot as a matter of right amend finally rejected claims, add new claims, or reinstate canceled claims. An amendment submitted after final but prior to appeal brief requires a showing under 37 CFR 1.116(b) except for amendments that merely cancel claims, adopt examiner’s suggestions, remove issues for appeal, or require cursory review. The first proposed amendment after final will be given sufficient consideration to determine whether it places claims in patentable condition; if not entered in entirety, examiner will briefly explain reasons. Second or subsequent amendments after final considered only to the extent they remove issues for appeal or put a claim in obvious patentable condition.

name: Appeal brief requirements and formatting for reexamination
description: The appeal brief must set forth the authorities and arguments relied on, include a summary of claimed subject matter referring to specification pages/lines and drawings by reference characters, and include a copy of the claims involved. The copy of claims on appeal must include all underlining and bracketing as required by 37 CFR 1.530(f); new claims should be completely underlined.
guidance: A fee per 37 CFR 41.20(b)(2) is required when filing the brief for the first time in a particular reexamination proceeding. Only one copy of the appeal brief is required; where third party requester exists, serve a copy on them. In merged proceedings, provide one original copy per reexamination proceeding/reissue application and serve third party requesters. Claims copy should be double spaced and start on a new page. Briefs must be responsive to every ground of rejection and should fully state appellant's position so no search of the record is required.

name: Defective notice of appeal cure procedure
description: Where a notice of appeal is defective, the patent owner will be notified using form PTOL-475 and given a 1-month or 30-day (whichever is longer) period to cure the defects.
guidance: If patent owner does not timely file a notice of appeal and/or appropriate fee, patent owner will be notified that the appeal is dismissed (use PTOL-468) and reexamination prosecution is terminated; a Notice of Intent to Issue Ex Parte Reexamination Certificate (NIRC) will be issued indicating claims' status at time of final rejection (or after second rejection where appeal was taken earlier).

name: Explanation presumption and burden reversal
description: When a claim covers a derivative (e.g., polymorph, salt), the IPO treats it as the same substance and places the burden on the applicant to rebut that presumption by showing significant property differences with regard to efficacy.
guidance: This reverses the usual examiner burden model used in the US/EU. Applicants should anticipate having to produce comparative efficacy evidence or persuasive scientific reasoning in prosecution and consider procedural challenges if the examiner fails to identify a specific comparator.

name: Definition and identification of the ‘known substance’ (threshold question)
description: Before efficacy comparison begins, the examiner must identify the specific prior-art compound that constitutes the baseline 'known substance' against which the new form is compared.
guidance: Per DS Biopharma (Delhi HC), the examiner must name the prior art compound, cite the prior art document, and establish a structural or functional relationship between that compound and the claimed invention. Absent this, a 3(d) objection can be challenged procedurally at the FER stage.

name: Delhi HC three-part procedural test for valid 3(d) objection
description: An examiner must (1) identify the specific prior art compound constituting the 'known substance'; (2) explain the structural or functional relationship between the claimed compound and that prior art; and (3) frame the objection with sufficient specificity to allow a meaningful comparison of therapeutic efficacy.
guidance: Failure on any element is grounds for remand. Applicants should use this procedural test as a first-line defense in prosecution to overturn inadequately reasoned 3(d) rejections before litigating substantive efficacy questions.

name: Valuation/NPV discount framework for India market exclusivity
description: Adjust the India-market exclusivity contribution of secondary patents probabilistically based on four factors: (1) whether the claim type is listed in the Explanation; (2) existence of published comparative therapeutic efficacy data; (3) likelihood of attracting pre-grant opposition; (4) originator's track record defending 3(d).
guidance: Practical guidance: polymorph/salt patents without comparative clinical data should be discounted 70–90% for India NPV; formulation/route patents with supporting clinical comparator data might be discounted 20–40%. Model compulsory license risk separately. Use portfolio-level analysis for companies with many secondary patents.

name: Types of persuasive evidence and submission formats
description: Most persuasive: peer‑reviewed published clinical trial data comparing the claimed form to the baseline compound. Also accepted: methodologically sound unpublished comparative studies and affidavits from qualified clinicians or pharmacologists.
guidance: Design prosecution/specification to include or signal an evidentiary roadmap. Where clinical evidence will only exist post‑filing, document trials/plans and be prepared to submit post‑filing clinical data; submit comparative pharmacodynamic endpoints where clinical endpoints are unavailable.

name: Safety improvements as potential 'therapeutic efficacy'
description: The Novartis judgment left open that improved safety profiles (significant reductions in adverse effects) can constitute enhanced therapeutic efficacy if supported by comparative clinical or pharmacological data.
guidance: If claiming safety as the basis for enhanced efficacy, submit comparative clinical data demonstrating clinically meaningful reductions in toxicity (e.g., dose‑limiting toxicity halved) rather than marketing statements or tolerability claims without comparative evidence.

name: Rationales that may support a conclusion of obviousness
description: Examples of rationales that may support a conclusion of obviousness include: (A) Combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results; (B) Simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results; (C) Use of known technique to improve similar devices (methods, or products) in the same way; (D) Applying a known technique to a known device (method, or product) ready for improvement to yield predictable results; (E) 'Obvious to try' – choosing from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions, with a reasonable expectation of success; (F) Known work in one field of endeavor may prompt variations of it for use in either the same field or a different one based on design incentives or other market forces if the variations are predictable to one of ordinary skill in the art; (G) Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art that would have led one of ordinary skill to modify the prior art reference or to combine prior art reference teachings to arrive at the claimed invention.
guidance: See KSR and MPEP § 2143 for discussion and examples illustrating how the cited rationales may be used to support a finding of obviousness; see MPEP §§ 2144–2144.09 for additional guidance regarding support for obviousness determinations.

name: Applicant's reply requirements under 37 CFR 1.111(b)
description: Once Office personnel have issued a rejection that establishes the Graham factual findings and concludes that the claimed invention would have been obvious, the burden shifts to the applicant to (A) show that the Office erred in these findings or (B) provide other evidence to show that the claimed subject matter would have been nonobvious. 37 CFR 1.111(b) requires applicant to distinctly and specifically point out the supposed errors in the Office’s action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the Office action.
guidance: The reply must present arguments pointing out the specific distinction believed to render the claims patentable over any applied references. An effective traverse of a rejection based wholly or partially on Office factual findings must include a reasoned statement explaining why the applicant believes the Office has erred substantively as to the factual findings. A mere statement that the Office has not established a prima facie case or that reliance on common knowledge is unsupported by documentary evidence is not substantively adequate under 37 CFR 1.111(b). Office personnel may repeat the rejection and make the next Office action final if traverse is inadequate (see MPEP § 706.07(a)).

name: Availability of prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 for use in 35 U.S.C. 103 rejections
description: Subject matter that is prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 can be used to support a rejection under section 103. Admitted prior art can be relied upon for both anticipation and obviousness determinations, regardless of whether the admitted prior art would otherwise qualify under statutory categories of 35 U.S.C. 102.
guidance: If it is established that a disclosure does not qualify as prior art under the appropriate section of 35 U.S.C. 102, then that disclosure is not prior art that can be used in an obviousness rejection. For instance, a 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) reference overcome by a declaration under 37 CFR 1.130(a) cannot be used in an obviousness rejection for a claimed invention subject to 35 U.S.C. 102; similarly for pre-AIA cases and 37 CFR 1.131. See MPEP §§ 901–901.06(d), §§ 2121–2129, and §§ 2151–2155 for overviews of what constitutes prior art.

name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) common ownership/joint research agreement requirements
description: An applicant subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 who wants to rely on pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) to overcome an obviousness rejection has the burden of establishing that prior-art subject matter used in the rejection and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person. For joint research provisions, the applicant must establish: (A) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the date the invention was made; (B) the invention was made as a result of activities within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (C) the application discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement.
guidance: These disqualifications apply only for subject matter which only qualifies as prior art under subsections (e), (f), or (g) of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and is used in a rejection under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a). Note limitations for certain filing/grant dates (e.g., applications filed prior to Nov. 29, 1999). See MPEP § 2146.02 for requirements to establish common ownership or a joint research agreement and MPEP § 2146.01 for related limitations.

name: Analogous art requirement for use under 35 U.S.C. 103
description: To rely on a reference under 35 U.S.C. 103, the reference must be analogous art to the claimed invention. A reference is analogous art if: (1) it is from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention (even if it addresses a different problem); or (2) it is reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor (even if not in the same field). It is not necessary for a reference to fulfill both tests.
guidance: The examiner must determine whether a reference is analogous art when analyzing obviousness. There is no analogous-art requirement for a reference being applied in an anticipation rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102. See In re Bigio and related case law; when more than one prior art reference is used, the references need not be analogous to each other (see Sanofi-Aventis; Corephotonics). Consider the disclosure of each reference 'in view of the reality of the circumstances' and from the vantage of common sense likely to be exerted by one of ordinary skill in the art.

name: Consider similarities and differences in structure and function
description: When evaluating whether a reference is analogous art or pertinent, similarities and differences in structure and function of the inventions disclosed in the references carry far greater weight than Patent Office classifications or cross-references.
guidance: Examiners should focus on structural similarities and functional overlap between references and the claimed invention when weighing analogy. See In re Ellis and examples provided where structural/functional overlap made references pertinent despite classification differences.

name: Differences between prior art and the claimed invention — consider the claim as a whole
description: Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims requires interpreting the claim language and considering both the invention and the prior art references as a whole. The question under 35 U.S.C. 103 is not whether the differences themselves would have been obvious, but whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious.
guidance: See MPEP §§ 2111–2116.01 for case law pertaining to claim interpretation and MPEP § 2143.03 for examples of claim language that may raise questions as to limiting effect. Case law (e.g., Stratoflex, Schenck) supports treating the claimed invention holistically in obviousness analysis.

name: Identify Rejection of Record Applied to New/Amended Claims
description: If a rejection of record is to be applied to a new or amended claim, specific identification of that ground of rejection should be given.
guidance: Cite the paragraph in the former Office letter in which the rejection was originally stated so applicant can trace the basis for the rejection being reapplied.

name: Unpersuasive Argument: Arguing Limitations Not Claimed
description: Features relied upon by applicant that are not recited in the rejected claim(s) are not given patentable weight; limitations from the specification are not read into the claims.
guidance: Use ¶7.37.08 (preceded by ¶7.37). Recite the features applicant relies upon and explain they are not claimed. Cite In re Van Geuns.

name: Unpersuasive Argument: Intended Use
description: A recitation of intended use must result in a structural difference between the claimed invention and the prior art to distinguish patentably; for process claims, intended use must result in a manipulative difference.
guidance: Use ¶7.37.09 (preceded by ¶7.37). Explain why intended use does or does not impart patentable weight. Cite In re Casey and In re Otto.

name: Unpersuasive Argument: Preamble Limitations
description: A preamble is generally not accorded patentable weight where it merely recites purpose or intended use and the body of the claim stands alone.
guidance: Use ¶7.37.10 (preceded by ¶7.37). Restate the preamble recitation and explain lack of patentable weight. Cite In re Hirao and Kropa v. Robie.

name: Unpersuasive Argument: General Allegation of Patentability
description: Applicant’s general allegation that the claims define a patentable invention fails to comply with 37 CFR 1.111(b) unless it specifically points out how the claim language patentably distinguishes over the references.
guidance: Use ¶7.37.11 (preceded by ¶7.37). Require specificity per the regulation.

name: Avoid Piecemeal Examination
description: Piecemeal examination should be avoided as much as possible; the examiner ordinarily should reject each claim on all valid grounds available, avoiding undue multiplication of references.
guidance: Apply major technical rejections (e.g., lack of disclosure, enablement, serious indefiniteness, res judicata) with full development of reasons rather than mere conclusions. Do not make secondary rejections on minor grounds where prior art discloses the 'heart' of the invention. Recognize language limitations and avoid premature negative limitations or indefiniteness rejections when an improved mode of definition is not known.

name: Drafting Claims for Pro Se Applicants
description: Where the examiner believes an applicant is unfamiliar with proper preparation, the examiner may draft one or more claims and indicate such claims would be allowed if incorporated by amendment.
guidance: This practice expedites prosecution and offers service to unrepresented inventors; it is desirable and permissible where appropriate. If the suggested claim is not embraced by the original oath/declaration, require supplemental oath or declaration under 37 CFR 1.67. Use form paragraph 7.43.04 and indicate complete text of suggested claim(s).

name: Allowable Except As To Form — Offer Definite Suggestions
description: When application discloses patentable subject matter but claims cannot be allowed because of defects in form or omission, the examiner should not stop with a bare objection; offer a definite suggestion for correction.
guidance: Examiner’s action should be constructive and may suggest an interview to accelerate agreement on allowable claims. If certain aspects are not claimed, note that and indicate that if properly claimed such claims may be favorably considered. If a claim is allowable but dependent on canceled/rejected claim, state it would be allowable if rewritten in independent form.

name: Indicate Allowable Subject Matter / Early Allowance of Claims
description: When the prior art has been fully developed and some claims are clearly allowable, the allowance of such claims should not be delayed.
guidance: Form paragraphs 7.43, 7.43.01, 7.43.02 may be used to indicate allowable subject matter. Use ¶7.97 to indicate claim allowed.

name: Comment on Examples and Test Results Carefully
description: Results of tests and examples should not normally be questioned unless there is a reasonable basis; if questioned, appropriate claims should be rejected as being based on insufficient disclosure under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
guidance: Applicant must reply with actual test results or relevant arguments showing strong reason to believe the predicted result; avoid introduction of new matter. If operability or utility is in doubt, consider rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 (see MPEP § 706.03(a) and § 2107 et seq.). See MPEP §§ 2161–2164.08(c) for written description and enablement guidance.

name: Documents required to file an application (ARIPO Form 3 and supporting documents)
description: To file the Applicant has to submit the following: a completed ARIPO Form 3 (Request form), a description of the invention, one or more claims, one or more drawings (if any), an abstract, prescribed application fees or a written undertaking to lodge the fees, designation of at least one state.
guidance: Applications may be filed by the applicant (inventor or assignee) or by an authorized representative (attorney, agent, or legal practitioner). Ensure all elements (description, claims, drawings, abstract) comply with ARIPO requirements before filing.

name: Presumption: 'means' invokes §112(f)
description: If the word 'means' appears in a claim element in combination with a function, it is presumed to be a means-plus-function element to which §112(f) applies.
guidance: The presumption that §112(f) is invoked is overcome and §112(f) will not be applied when the limitation further includes sufficient structure for performing the recited function.

name: Presumption: absence of 'means' ordinarily does not invoke §112(f)
description: When a claim limitation does not use 'means,' the claim limitation is presumed not to invoke §112(f).
guidance: This presumption can be overcome when the limitation uses a word that is a substitute for 'means' (a generic placeholder or nonce word) that is not recognized as the name of known structure that performs the specific function.

name: Three-prong MPEP 2181(I) test for invoking §112(f)
description: Apply the three-prong analysis to determine whether §112(f) applies: (A) the claim limitation uses 'means' or a substitute generic placeholder; (B) the phrase is modified by functional language (typically linked by 'for' or another linking word); and (C) the phrase is not modified by sufficient structure or material for performing the claimed function.
guidance: Evaluate all three prongs. Prong B does not require the transition 'for' specifically; other linking words such as 'so that' or 'configured to' may suffice if it is clear the element is reciting a function. In some circumstances no explicit linking word is necessary if surrounding words convey the function (but those words cannot convey specific structure).

name: Identify functional language (what vs. what it is)
description: A claim limitation is functional when it recites a feature by what it does rather than by what it is.
guidance: Functional language can appear in limitations that invoke §112(f) and in limitations that do not. Limitations that do not invoke §112(f) are typically recited with some structure, material or action that defines a capability or purpose served by the recited structure, material or action.

name: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) of functional language
description: Claims are given their broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the specification as would be interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: If §112(f) is invoked, the BRI of the means-plus-function limitation is restricted to the corresponding structure in the supporting disclosure and its equivalents (the corresponding specification is considered part of the claim limitation). When §112(f) is not invoked and an element is recited along with a function, that element is construed as being capable of performing the function — the BRI of that element is limited by the function. Distinguish reciting a function from reciting only intended use/result: an intended use/result typically does not limit claim scope unless it imposes a structural or manipulative difference.

name: Definiteness under 35 U.S.C. §112(b): claim boundaries must be clear
description: Functional limitations must impose clear boundaries to be definite under §112(b); claim language that merely states a result without specifying ways to achieve it is unclear.
guidance: Consider whether one of ordinary skill in the art can determine what structure, material, or act in the claim performs the function; whether the limitation has well-defined boundaries or only expresses a problem solved or intended result; and what an anticipatory reference would need to disclose to satisfy the limitation. These considerations are illustrative, not exhaustive.

name: Corresponding-structure disclosure requirements for means-type claims
description: When §112(f) is invoked, the specification must adequately disclose a corresponding structure, material or act that performs the function.
guidance: For 'means'-type claims, adequacy requires that the corresponding structure/material be: (a) disclosed so that one of ordinary skill will understand what specific structure or material the inventor identified to perform the recited function; (b) sufficient to perform the entire function recited in the claim limitation; and (c) clearly linked to the function in the written description.

name: When to make a §112(b) indefiniteness rejection and record requirements
description: If the examiner determines that the boundaries of a claim are not reasonably clear, a rejection under §112(b) should be made.
guidance: The rejection must identify the specific claim language that is indefinite and explain why that language renders the boundaries unclear. When possible, the examiner should suggest how the indefiniteness issues may be resolved to put the applicant on notice of their duty under §112(b).

name: Connection between indefiniteness and written-description (§112(a))
description: Functional claim language found indefinite typically lacks an adequate written description under §112(a) because an indefinite, unbounded functional limitation may cover all ways of performing the function and indicate the inventor has not provided sufficient disclosure.
guidance: In most cases, a §112(b) rejection based on unclear functional boundaries should be accompanied by a §112(a) rejection for failure to provide a written description supporting the claim.

name: Prior-art (§102/§103) considerations for functional limitations
description: Functional claim language not limited to a specific structure may cover all devices/materials capable of performing the recited function, which can make §102 or §103 rejections appropriate if prior art discloses a device/material that inherently performs the function.
guidance: When applying §102/§103 rejections based on functional language, the examiner must state on the record how the functional term is being interpreted relative to the applied prior art. Consider scenarios where the prior art explicitly discloses the function, where the structure in the prior art performs the function with the same means, an equivalent means, or a different means.

name: Compact-prosecution expectation
description: Under principles of compact prosecution, each claim should be examined for compliance with every statutory requirement for patentability in the initial review of the application.
guidance: Thus, when a claim term/phrase renders the claim indefinite, the examiner should make a §112(b) rejection as well as any other applicable rejections (e.g., §101, §102, §103, and/or §112) in the initial action.

name: Worksheet-driven examination steps (practical checklist)
description: Use a separate worksheet for each claim to identify functional language, apply the three-prong §112(f) test, determine BRI (depending on whether §112(f) is invoked), evaluate whether the functional language limits claim scope, assess definiteness and corresponding-structure sufficiency, and decide whether a §112(b) rejection is appropriate.
guidance: Specific worksheet items include: (Part I) identify functional language and whether §112(f) is invoked; (Part II) state BRI if §112(f) invoked or not and identify corresponding structure if invoked; (Part III) for §112(f) limitations, answer whether specification discloses structure performing the claimed function, whether it is sufficient to perform the entire function, and whether it is clearly linked to the function; for non-§112(f) functional language, determine whether boundaries are clear to one of skill in the art; (Part IV) determine applicability of prior-art rejections and whether to issue §112(b)/§112(a) rejections and suggest how applicant could resolve unclear boundaries. The worksheet is optional but recommended for each claim.

name: Nature of proceeding
description: Post grant review is a trial proceeding conducted at the Board to review the patentability of one or more claims in a patent on any ground that could be raised under § 282(b)(2) or (3).
guidance: This defines PGR as an adversarial trial before the PTAB specifically focused on claim patentability (distinct from other trials like inter partes review or derivation).

name: Use when a subgroup lacks a proper nomenclature
description: A Markush claim is appropriate when the sub-group of alternatives has no proper nomenclature to identify it, so the claim must create a generic name for that subgroup.
guidance: Example: listing a subset of alkali metals (lithium, sodium, potassium) as 'an alkali metal selected from the group consisting of...' creates a usable subgroup name when no established term exists for that subset.

name: Applicability across 35 U.S.C. §101 statutory classes
description: Markush claiming may be used with any of the recognized statutory classes — processes, machines, articles of manufacture, and compositions of matter.
guidance: However, for many mechanical and method inventions, a 'means for' or 'step for' claim (where a generic functional term exists) may be an alternative to Markush claiming; such 'means/step for' claims are governed by 35 U.S.C. §112(f). Choose Markush where no suitable generic term exists.

name: Accepted Markush claim forms (closed-group wording)
description: One accepted form: use 'selected from the group consisting of ...' together with the conjunctive 'and' to denote a closed group.
guidance:
The 'consisting of' + 'and' form indicates a closed list and helps avoid indefiniteness rejections. Example layout shown in the article:
'an alkali metal selected from the group consisting of lithium, sodium, and potassium'.

name: Accepted Markush claim forms (open alternative wording)
description: An alternate accepted form uses plain alternatives with 'is ... or ...' (using 'or' and omitting 'consisting of').
guidance: Do not mix elements of the two forms (e.g., do not combine 'consisting of'/'and' with the 'or' style). The second form should not use 'and.'

name: Do not mix the two Markush forms
description: Do not combine the closed 'selected from the group consisting of ... and' form with the 'is ... or ...' form; mixing forms undermines proper Markush syntax.
guidance: The article explicitly warns: 'Do not mix and match the first form with the second form' — follow one form consistently in the same claim clause to avoid ambiguity or rejections.

name: Members must share a characteristic / belong to a recognized class
description: Elements listed in a Markush group must share a characteristic or property — they should 'belong to a recognized physical or chemical class or an art-recognized class' (MPEP 2173.05(h)).
guidance: It is sufficient if the members are disclosed in the specification to possess at least one property in common which is mainly responsible for their function in the claimed relationship; the shared property should be clear from their nature or the prior art. Failure to show a common characteristic can lead to rejection.

name: Specify the shared property in the specification (best practice)
description: Best practice: explicitly state what shared property or characteristic unites the listed group members in the patent specification.
guidance: Stating the common property in the specification reduces risk of examiner rejection for indefiniteness or lack of proper grouping; if the claimed shared characteristic is too abstract or broad, an examiner may reject and require amendment into multiple dependent claims.

name: Example usage to illustrate proper drafting
description: Practical example: 'an alkali metal selected from the group consisting of lithium, sodium, and potassium' demonstrates both the purpose and form of a Markush claim.
guidance: Use concrete examples like the alkali metal listing to model claim language; examples help show closed-group syntax and when a Markush claim replaces multiple dependent claims.

name: Claiming priority to earlier domestic application
description: An application claiming priority under the Act from any prior application to the patent office shall contain a copy, in duplicate, on Form P2 of such prior application as well as the specification lodged in support of such prior application.

name: Microbiological inventions: deposit and disclosure requirements (28bis & 28A)
description: A complete specification claiming a microbiological process or product where no samples of the micro-organism are available to the public shall only be deemed fully to describe the invention if before acceptance: (a) a culture has been deposited in a culture collection recognised by the EPO for rule 28 of the EPC implementing regulations; (b) the complete specification gives relevant information available to the applicant on the characteristics of the micro-organism; (c) the complete specification gives the date when the culture was deposited, the culture collection and the file number of the deposit. For certain claims, deposit with an international depositary authority under the Budapest Treaty is required at lodging, with name/accession number stated (or added before publication).
guidance: Before acceptance applicant must furnish proof that samples are available to public in RSA. If accession number not in lodged specification it may be added before publication under section 50(1)(b). Communication of deposit information constitutes irrevocable consent to make culture available from the relevant date. Procedures exist for furnishing samples via Form P23 and Form P24 and undertakings to prevent third-party distribution until expiry/lapse of patent.

name: Title requirements
description: The title of an invention shall be as short and specific as possible and shall be descriptive of the nature of the invention claimed. Words such as 'improved', 'relating to' and the like shall not appear in the title.

name: Claims ordering
description: Each category of claims (product, process, apparatus, use and the like) shall as far as practicable, be arranged in order of decreasing scope.

name: Abstract content and length
description: The abstract on Form P8 shall be that of the technical disclosure contained in the complete specification, but shall not be used to interpret the scope of the claims. It shall be in narrative form and generally limited to a single paragraph of not more than 150 words. The form and phraseology of patent claims shall be avoided. Features mentioned in the abstract and illustrated in the drawing may be followed by the reference sign used in that drawing.

name: Reasonable Royalty—Entire Market Value Rule (EMVR)
description: Normally royalties should be based on the smallest salable unit that practices the patent and is closely related to the claimed invention; the entire market value rule is a narrow exception allowing damages based on entire product revenue only if the patented feature is the sole driver of customer demand or substantially creates the value of the product.
guidance: If the smallest salable unit is a multi-component product with non-infringing features, damages must be limited to value attributable to patented technology; EMVR applies only when patented feature solely drives demand. (Citations: Ericsson v. D-Link; VirnetX; LaserDynamics; Uniloc; Lucent; Rite-Hite.)

name: Willful Infringement—Generally
description: If plaintiff proves infringement of a valid claim by a preponderance, jury must determine whether infringement was willful. To show willfulness plaintiff must prove by a preponderance that defendant knew of plaintiff’s patent and intentionally infringed at least one asserted claim.
guidance: May consider malicious, wanton, deliberate, consciously wrongful, flagrant, or bad-faith behavior, but knowledge of the patent alone is insufficient. Assess all circumstances and defendant’s knowledge at the time of challenged conduct. If infringement found willful, it should not affect the amount of damages awarded by the jury. (Citations: Halo.)

name: 211.05-Sufficiency of Disclosure in Prior-Filed Application
description: Sufficiency of Disclosure in Prior-Filed Application (when prior disclosure supports benefit claim).

name: Alice/Mayo two-step test
description: A two-step process from the Supreme Court (Alice/Mayo) used to assess patent subject-matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101. Step 1: determine whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception (e.g., an abstract idea). Step 2: if so, determine whether the claim elements, individually and as an ordered combination, add an 'inventive concept' sufficient to transform the claim into patent-eligible subject matter.
guidance: Patent attorneys must analyze inventions thoroughly using this two-step framework. The test is central to determining whether software/AI inventions are too abstract to be patented; examiners and courts may apply it differently, and district courts often conduct independent eligibility analyses.

name: Categories of abstract ideas (USPTO AI guidance)
description: USPTO identifies three main categories of abstract ideas that commonly appear in AI claims: (1) Mathematical concepts (relationships, formulas, equations, calculations); (2) Methods of organizing human activity (business methods, workflows); (3) Mental processes (observations, evaluations, judgments that could in theory be done in the human mind).
guidance: Claims 'don’t include mental processes' when they contain limitations that can't practically be performed in the human mind; AI claims that simply rely on mathematical principles but don't recite formulas in claim language can sometimes be argued not to 'recite' a mathematical concept. Use this categorization to identify the exception implicated and to craft claims that avoid explicit recitation of abstract ideas.

name: Distinction: reciting vs. involving an abstract idea
description: USPTO distinguishes claims that explicitly 'recite' an abstract idea (triggering further eligibility analysis) from claims that merely involve or base themselves on an abstract idea without reciting it in the claim language.
guidance: Draft claims to avoid explicit recitation of abstract ideas where possible; emphasize concrete claim language showing technological implementation or limitations. This distinction affects whether a claim is treated as containing a judicial exception for Alice/Mayo analysis.

name: Inventive concept requirement (Alice Step Two)
description: In Step Two, the claim must contain an 'inventive concept' — additional elements that transform an abstract idea into a patent-eligible application by providing something significantly more than the judicial exception itself.
guidance: Show specific technical progress (improvements to computer operation or other technology), and avoid relying on elements that are common, ordinary, or conventional. The patent specification should clearly state a distinct technical challenge and its solution to support the inventive concept. For AI inventions, emphasize technological advances rather than broad applications.

name: Practical application integration ('technological solution to a technological problem')
description: An otherwise abstract idea can be patent-eligible if the claim integrates the abstract idea into a practical application that meaningfully limits it and shows a concrete technological improvement.
guidance: Demonstrate that the claim as a whole applies the abstract idea within a technical environment (e.g., network monitoring with remedial blocking actions, improved speech-transcription pipeline, or specific treatment protocols following AI diagnosis). Use claim elements that show how computing/technology is improved or how the abstract idea is functionally integrated.

name: USPTO AI Example 1 — Anomaly detection in network security (Examples 47-49 synthesis)
description: USPTO Example: An ANN that detects anomalies in network security produced three analyzed claims: Claim 1 (eligible) — apparatus claim for an application-specific integrated circuit implementing the ANN; Claim 2 (ineligible) — method merely leveraging ANN to identify anomalies; Claim 3 (eligible) — method integrating anomaly detection within network monitoring plus remedial blocking actions.
guidance: Lessons: prefer concrete machine/device claims or include practical, domain-specific follow-up actions that materially change system behavior. Merely claiming use of an ANN to analyze data without field-of-use or actionability risks ineligibility.

name: USPTO AI Example 2 — Speech separation with DNNs
description: USPTO Example: Broad method of applying DNNs to separate voices (Claim 1) is ineligible as it recites abstract mathematical analysis. Claims that specify application context (improving transcription accuracy, generating enhanced audio outputs) are eligible.
guidance: Tie signal-processing/AI methods to downstream technological benefits (e.g., clearer audio, better transcription) and concrete improvements in performance or functionality rather than claiming bare mathematical transformations.

name: USPTO AI Example 3 — AI in medical diagnosis and treatment
description: USPTO Example: An AI algorithm identifying disease from data (diagnosis) can be ineligible if treated as abstract data analysis or natural law; claims become eligible when linked to specific treatment steps (administering therapy) that transform insight into practical therapeutic action.
guidance: In medical AI, include intervention or concrete treatment steps or otherwise tie discoveries to applied protocols to avoid Mayo-style natural-law exclusions. Pure diagnostic correlations are vulnerable to rejection.

name: Machine-or-transformation test as a helpful (but not sole) tool
description: The machine-or-transformation test checks whether a process is tied to a particular machine or transforms an article into a different state; while useful, it is not the exclusive test for process patent eligibility.
guidance: Use machine-or-transformation factors to support eligibility arguments where appropriate (e.g., claim a specific machine implementation or a substantive transformation), but don't treat passing this test as automatically dispositive under Alice/Mayo.

name: Technical improvement examples that indicate inventive concept
description: Concrete technical improvements that can support eligibility include: better computer vision solving previously unsolvable problems; more efficient data processing reducing computational overhead; increased speed or accuracy in ML operations; novel neural network architectures addressing technical limitations; reduced resource requirements; improved handling of noisy/incomplete/corrupted data sets.
guidance: Where possible, quantify or specifically describe the technical benefit (reduction in computational load, accuracy gains, resource savings) in the specification and claims to demonstrate an inventive concept beyond abstract computation.

name: Avoid overly broad claim drafting and emphasize specificity
description: Claims that are overly broad or mirror categories frequently rejected by USPTO are at high risk under Alice/Mayo. Drafting should emphasize specific technical features and concrete effects.
guidance: Draft multiple independent claims covering different practical applications and specific technical elements; document incremental improvements in the specification; avoid generic language and broad functional claiming that merely recites high-level goals.

name: Engage with examiners and use prosecution strategy (continuations, appeals)
description: Proactive engagement with USPTO examiners, considered use of continuation applications, and strategic appeals can improve outcomes when facing Alice rejections.
guidance: Explain technical specifics to examiners, correct other rejection categories before appealing when helpful, and consider continuation practice to adapt claim scope to evolving case law and guidance. Thompson Patent Law reports these strategies can materially shorten prosecution time and increase allowance rates.

name: Federal Circuit and case-law constraints (e.g., Recentive Analytics v. Fox)
description: Recent Federal Circuit decisions reinforce that simply applying conventional machine learning algorithms to new data environments is not a patent-eligible inventive concept; courts demand demonstration of technological improvement.
guidance: When arguing eligibility, address relevant Federal Circuit precedent head-on and show how claim elements provide a technological improvement beyond applying standard ML techniques to a dataset. Use case law to craft contrasts between conventional application and claimed innovation.

name: Claims not performable in the human mind can avoid 'mental processes' exception
description: The USPTO notes that claims including limitations that cannot practically be performed mentally (e.g., massive dataset calculations, complex computations) are less likely to be treated as reciting a mental process.
guidance: Emphasize computational scale, data volumes, or operations infeasible for humans in claim and specification language to help distinguish claims from mental-process judicial exceptions.

name: Manner-of-invention (use of AI) doesn't change eligibility analysis
description: The USPTO states that how an invention was made (including via AI) does not affect subject-matter eligibility — examiners evaluate claims based on claim content and the improvements they recite.
guidance: Do not rely on the fact that AI assisted invention; instead, focus on drafting claim language that recites specific technical improvements. Also be mindful of prior-art issues from AI-generated outputs as potential novelty/non-obviousness challenges.

name: Handling of 37 CFR 41.50(b) new grounds of rejection
description: When the Board makes a new ground of rejection under 37 CFR 41.50(b), subsequent procedure depends on the appellant’s action; if appellant elects to proceed before the examiner by amending claims or submitting new evidence, prosecution is reopened; if appellant presents only arguments without amendment or evidence, jurisdiction should remain with the Board.
guidance: If appellant takes no action within two months after the Board’s new ground of rejection, the examiner should proceed as indicated in relevant paragraphs (I–III). Reopening prosecution before the examiner may incidentally overcome the originally affirmed rejection even though it is not open to further prosecution. If prosecution before the examiner is terminated without allowance, the file must be returned to the Board so that the original affirmance can be made final. A subsequent appeal may be filed limited to the 37 CFR 41.50(b) rejection and may not include the affirmed rejection.

name: Period for seeking court review lapsed — formal corrections and abandonment
description: If the period under 37 CFR 90.3 for seeking court review of a PTAB decision has expired and no court action was taken, proceedings as to the rejected claims are considered terminated; the application will be passed to issue on allowed claim(s) provided outstanding formal matters are promptly corrected.
guidance: Applicant must correct identified formal matters within a shortened statutory period set to expire TWO MONTHS from the mailing date of the notice to avoid ABANDONMENT. Extensions may be granted under 37 CFR 1.136. Use form paragraph (e.g., ¶ 12.297) to notify applicant and identify which claims/formal matters are at issue; prosecution is otherwise closed.

name: Dismissal of appeal for failure to file brief (37 CFR 41.37) — consequences for claims
description: If no brief is filed within the time prescribed by 37 CFR 41.37, the appeal stands dismissed by operation of the rule; unless appellant specifically withdraws the appeal as to rejected claims, dismissal should not be entered until the extended period (up to 5 months under 37 CFR 1.136(a)) to file the brief has expired.
guidance: If the application has no allowed claims, it will be abandoned; claims allowable only by dependency on rejected claims are treated as rejected. If allowed claims remain, the examiner should cancel rejected claims and issue the application with allowed claims only (examples provided: A–D). If formal matters remain, handle via examiner’s amendment (MPEP § 1302.04) or use form paragraph ¶ 12.209 to set a shortened period (TWO MONTHS) for correction; prosecution otherwise closed.

name: Institution threshold — reasonable likelihood
description: The petition must demonstrate there is a reasonable likelihood that at least one of the claims is unpatentable.
guidance: The PTAB will review the petition to determine whether the reasonable-likelihood standard is met as a predicate to instituting a PGR. This is analogous to institution standards used in other PTAB proceedings.

name: Patent owner response opportunity
description: The patent owner in a PGR has an opportunity to respond to the petitioner’s arguments and present counterarguments and evidence to support the patent’s validity.
guidance: After a petition is filed, the patent owner can submit a response to contest the petition’s merits and introduce evidence and arguments aimed at preserving claim validity during PTAB review.

name: Claim Construction Issue Identification and Joint Chart
description: Parties shall exchange a list of claim term(s)/phrase(s) they believe need construction and their proposed constructions. Parties will meet and confer to prepare a Joint Claim Construction Chart identifying disputed claim terms and each party’s proposed construction with citation(s) only to intrinsic evidence. A copy of the patent(s) and portions of the intrinsic record relied upon shall be submitted. This document will not be filed and shall not provide argument.
guidance: The Joint Chart is intended to present intrinsic-evidence-only positions without argument; timelines for exchange and submission are set in the scheduling order.

name: Claim Construction Briefing Sequence and Page Limits
description: Parties shall contemporaneously submit initial briefs on claim construction issues and contemporaneously submit answering/responsive briefs. No reply briefs or supplemental papers on claim construction shall be submitted without leave of the Court. Local Rule 7.1.3(4) controls page limitations for initial and responsive briefs.
guidance: Filing dates for briefs are set in the scheduling order; adhere to local rule page limits.

name: Designating Protected Material — Exercise of Restraint and Care
description: Each Party or Non-Party that designates information or items for protection must take care to limit any such designation to specific material that qualifies under appropriate standards. Mass, indiscriminate, or routinized designations are prohibited. Designations shown to be clearly unjustified or made for improper purpose expose the Designating Party to sanctions. If a designation is mistaken, the Designating Party must promptly notify others that it is withdrawing the mistaken designation.
guidance: Parties should limit designations to specific qualifying portions and avoid over-broad claims of confidentiality.

name: Translation of the international application (language & content requirements)
description: If the international application was not published in an EPO official language, the applicant must furnish the EPO with a translation of that application within 31 months of the filing date or, where applicable, the (earliest) priority date.
guidance: The translation must include the description, the claims as originally filed, any text in the drawings, and the abstract. It must also include indications under Rule 13bis.3 and 13bis.4 PCT for inventions relating to biological material and any published request for rectification (Rule 91.3(d) PCT). Proceedings in the European phase will be conducted in the language of the translation.

name: Grave-injustice analysis for resisting reciprocal discipline
description: A respondent may attempt to show that imposition of identical discipline by the Office would result in a 'grave injustice'; the analysis focuses on whether the severity of the original sanction 'fits' the misconduct (i.e., whether the original penalty was so ill-fitted to the misconduct that reciprocal discipline would be unjust).
guidance: Courts look at whether the state punishment was within the appropriate range of sanctions. Public reprimand is a lesser penalty and is generally appropriate where misconduct violates ethical standards but is not serious enough for suspension/disbarment. Grave-injustice claims require clear and convincing evidence that the sanction was outside acceptable bounds.

name: Definition and effect of licenses and types that disqualify
description: The term “license” includes nonexclusive as well as exclusive licenses and royalty-free as well as royalty-generating licenses. A grant of a non-exclusive license to a non-small entity will disqualify an applicant from claiming small entity status. Implied licenses to use and resell patented articles purchased from a small entity will not preclude claiming small entity status. An order to a firm to build a prototype for the applicant’s own use is not considered a license for purposes of the definitions.
guidance: Example: Ulead Systems, Inc. v. Lex Computer & Management Corp., 351 F.3d 1139 (Fed. Cir. 2003) cited for a non-exclusive license to a non-small entity disqualifying status. Be careful: presence of implied licenses from sale typically does not disqualify; explicit nonexclusive licenses to non-small entities do.

name: Fraud and penalties for improperly claiming small entity status
description: Any attempt to fraudulently establish status as a small entity, or pay fees as a small entity, shall be considered a fraud practiced or attempted on the Office. Improperly and with intent to deceive establishing status or paying small entity fees shall be considered fraud on the Office.
guidance: Consequences: fraud on the Office may lead to penalties and affect the application/patent. Applicants should make a determination of entitlement prior to asserting status (37 CFR 1.27(f)) and be aware that assertions carry certifications (see certification entries).

name: Government licenses, CRADA, and Federal agency exceptions
description: A license to a Federal agency resulting from a funding agreement under 35 U.S.C. 202(c)(4) will not preclude claiming small entity status provided: (A) the subject invention was made solely by employees of the small business concern or nonprofit organization; or (B) in the case of a Federal employee co-inventor, the Federal agency took action under 35 U.S.C. 202(e)(1) to exclusively license or assign whatever rights it currently holds or may acquire to the small business/nonprofit, subject to the license under 202(c)(4). For CRADA-related government use licenses under 15 U.S.C. 3710a(b), claiming small entity status is not prohibited in certain circumstances (e.g., retaining title to invention made solely by the small business/nonprofit, or government laboratory waived ownership or exclusively licensed ownership rights to the small entity). Additionally, specific situations described in 37 CFR 1.27(a)(4)(i) (e.g., use license to Government under rights determination Executive Order 10096, action under 15 U.S.C. 3710d(a), or retention under 35 U.S.C. 202(d) with conditions) do not constitute a license that prohibits small entity status.
guidance: Government organizations themselves cannot qualify as nonprofit organizations (501(c)(3) limitation). Universities and institutions of higher education qualify even with some government affiliation. Wholly owned subsidiaries of a nonprofit/university are considered part of the nonprofit/university for small entity qualification.

name: Entry of amendments during reexamination
description: Amendments submitted with a request filed under 35 U.S.C. 302, or after reexamination is ordered and which comply with 37 CFR 1.530(d)-(j), will generally be entered for purposes of reexamination if submitted prior to a final action.
guidance: A 'new matter' amendment to the disclosure (35 U.S.C. 132) will be canceled and claims containing new matter will be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112. New matter to drawings is ordinarily not entered. Where an amendment enlarges claim scope, the amendment will be entered but the appropriate claims will be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 305. See MPEP §§ 2234, 2250, 608.04.

name: Art cited by patent owner in prosecution can support a final action
description: Where art is submitted in a prior art citation (e.g., IDS) and not accompanied by a statement similar to 37 CFR 1.97(e), the examiner may use the submitted art and make the next Office action final whether or not claims were amended, provided no other new ground of rejection is introduced based on the new art.
guidance: See MPEP § 706.07(a) and § 2206; absence of required statement may permit immediate reliance on owner‑submitted art to make an Office action final.

name: Obviousness — combined teachings (In re Mouttet)
description: The test for obviousness is what the combined teachings of the references would have suggested to those having ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: Evaluate references both individually and collectively to determine whether a person of ordinary skill would have found the claimed limitation obvious. See In re Mouttet, 686 F.3d 1322, 1333 (Fed. Cir. 2012).

name: Reasonable expectation of success
description: There must be a reasonable expectation that combining or applying prior art teachings would succeed in achieving the claimed invention.
guidance: Assess whether a POSA would have reasonably expected the modifications or combinations to work in the claimed context (e.g., applying exclusion criteria to a different anti-VEGF agent). Evidence such as expert testimony that the expected outcome is predictable supports this factor.

name: Avoidance of hindsight reasoning
description: An obviousness determination must not rely on knowledge gleaned only from the applicant's disclosure; reconstruction must use only knowledge within the level of ordinary skill at the time.
guidance: Ensure that the analysis does not impermissibly use the claimed invention as a template to piece together prior art. In re McLaughlin (443 F.2d 1392) summarizes that reconstructions are proper only when they do not include applicant-only knowledge.

name: Sufficiency of prior art to teach or suggest each claim limitation
description: Prior art references must teach or suggest the specific claim limitation (either individually or in combination) to support an obviousness conclusion.
guidance: Examine whether the references, taken together, encompass the claimed subject matter (e.g., whether MACTEL and CATT’s exclusion criteria would include 'any ocular or periocular infection within the last 2 weeks prior to treatment'). If the combined teachings reasonably include the claimed limitation, that supports obviousness.

name: Whether substitution of one reference's disclosure would alter claimed population or result
description: Assess whether substituting a prior art disclosure for a claimed limitation would result in treating a materially different group or producing different results.
guidance: If substitution causes a different patient population or outcome (e.g., MACTEL’s 30-day chronic history versus claimed 2-week prior infection), explain why that difference is or is not material to obviousness.

name: General Plastic factor 6 — finite resources of the Board
description: Consideration of the Board’s finite resources when evaluating multiple petitions against the same patent claims.
guidance: If allowing successive petitions would unduly strain Board resources or permit petitioners to 'have multiple bites,' this factor supports discretionary denial.

name: Ornamental (non-functional) requirement
description: A design must be primarily decorative and not dictated by functional necessity; a design is ornamental if it is applied to an article of manufacture and is visible during normal use.
guidance: Quoted guidance from MPEP: ornamental means 'the appearance presented by the article which creates an impression through the eye upon the mind of the observer.' Courts use the functionality doctrine to deny design patents where claimed design is primarily dictated by function. Test whether alternative designs could achieve the same function — if no alternatives exist, the design is likely functional and not patentable as ornamental. Examples: a unique embossed pattern on a baby wipe qualifies; an ergonomically necessary curved wrench handle does not, whereas a wrench with intricate carvings purely for visual appeal may qualify.

name: Prohibition on functional elements within claims
description: Including design elements that serve a function (e.g., hinges, fasteners, ergonomically required contours) can compromise eligibility for a design patent.
guidance: If you are trying to protect how something works, consider a utility patent instead. Courts and the USPTO will analyze whether claimed features are dictated by function rather than ornament.

name: Common pitfalls causing delay or rejection
description: Common mistakes: inadequate or incorrect drawings, overlooking prior art, including functional claims, and waiting too long to file after public disclosure.
guidance: An experienced IP attorney can help avoid these avoidable errors and improve chances of approval.

name: When not to use a design patent
description: Do not pursue a design patent if the design is too similar to existing designs or if the claimed features are primarily functional.
guidance: If the design is not novel or is dictated by function, a design patent will likely be refused and pursuing it can expose you to infringement claims from existing patent holders. Evaluate alternatives (utility patent, trademark, copyright) and consult counsel.

name: Competence and limitations of International Searching Authorities for SIS
description: An International Searching Authority shall be competent to carry out supplementary international searches if its preparedness to do so is stated in the applicable agreement under Article 16(3)(b), subject to any limitations and conditions set out in that agreement. The ISA that carried out the main international search shall not be competent to carry out a supplementary international search for that same application.
guidance: Limitations may include subject-matter restrictions (beyond Article 17(2)), limits on the total number of SIS in a period, and limits that SIS will not extend beyond a certain number of claims. Check the SISA agreements (Annex SISA) for specified limitations and conditions.

name: Purpose, scope and procedural requirements for requesting SIS
description: The supplementary international search (SIS) is an optional service to allow additional searches by a SISA during the international phase, expanding linguistic and technical scope and reducing risk of new prior art in national phases. SIS will be carried out on the application as filed and will only cover one invention or group of inventions having unity of invention; there is no option for paying additional fees to search multiple inventions.
guidance: Requests for SIS must be filed prior to the expiration of 22 months from the priority date, submitted directly to the IB (not to individual SISAs), accompanied by a supplementary search handling fee (IB) and a supplementary search fee set by each SISA, payable in Swiss francs within one month. Applicants from certain States may be eligible for a 90% reduction in the handling fee. If the main ISA identified lack of unity before SIS is requested, SIS can be requested to concentrate on a non-first claimed invention (PCT Rule 45 bis.1(d)). SIS results not in English will be translated into English by the IB.

name: Scope of the international preliminary examination (IPEA examiner duties)
description: After the demand is checked for compliance, the examiner shall study the description, drawings, claims, documents describing prior art cited in the international search report, and the written opinion established by the ISA. Furthermore, the examiner shall search at least to the point of bringing the previous search up to date and any new prior art discovered and applied must be made of record (see Rule 66.1ter).
guidance: IPEA's task includes evaluating prior art and updating searches; new art must be entered into the record so it will be available to applicant and Offices.

name: Required content of the further written opinion (PCT Rule 66.2 items)
description: Any further written opinion should set forth, as applicable: (A) defects concerning subject matter not required to be examined or unclear/inadequately supported (Article 34(4)); (B) negative findings on claims for lack of novelty, inventive step or industrial applicability; (C) defects in form or contents; (D) findings that an amendment goes beyond the original disclosure; (E) observations on clarity of claims/description/drawings or support of claims (Rule 66.2); (F) decisions not to carry out IPE on a claim for which no ISR was issued; (G) if no acceptable sequence listing is available to allow meaningful IPE.
guidance: The further written opinion must fully state reasons for the opinion and identify defects so applicant can reply and amend.

name: Right and formalities for amendments during international preliminary examination (PCT Article 34, Rule 66.8)
description: The applicant shall have a right to amend the claims, description, and drawings in the prescribed manner and within the prescribed time limit before the international preliminary examination report is established. The amendment shall not go beyond the disclosure in the international application as filed. Rule 66.8 requires, subject to paragraph (b), a replacement sheet for every sheet that differs, accompanied by a letter drawing attention to differences, indicating the basis for the amendment in the application as filed and preferably explaining the reasons.
guidance: Where amendment is deletion or minor alteration, a copy of the relevant sheet containing alterations may be used if clarity is maintained. Cancellation of an entire sheet should be communicated in a letter explaining reasons. When amending claims, Rule 46.5 applies mutatis mutandis and the set of claims submitted replaces all previously filed claims. Under 37 CFR 1.485, amendments may be made at the time of filing the Demand or within the time limit set by the IPEA, but must comply with Rule 66.8.

name: Paperless procedures to enable efficiency and outsourcing (JPO)
description: JPO established a paperless system for all procedures, from filing to examiner’s decision, enabling outsourcing of prior-art searches to the private sector and significantly enhancing efficiency.
guidance: The report claims this enabled the world’s first outsourcing of prior-art searches and led to JPO processing rates two to four times those of the EPO and USPTO. The paperless system is therefore a procedural standard to improve timeliness and scalability.

name: Specification / enablement requirement
description: Before any inventor shall receive a patent he shall deliver a written description of his invention or discovery, and of the manner and process of making, constructing, using, and compounding the same, in such full, clear, and exact terms, avoiding unnecessary prolixity, as to enable any person skilled in the art or science ... to make, construct, compound and use the same; and shall particularly specify and point out the part, improvement, or combination, which he claims as his own invention or discovery.
guidance: In case of a machine, fully explain the principle and several modes of application and how it differs from other inventions; specifications and claims guide scope of grant; defective or insufficient descriptions are a ground for objection by the Commissioner and may require amendment.

name: Patent form, recording, and term
