description: All patents shall be issued in the name of the Secretary of the United States, under the seal of the Patent Office, and signed by the Secretary of State, and countersigned by the Commissioner; and shall be recorded, together with the descriptions, specifications, and drawings, in books to be kept for that purpose. Every such patent shall contain a short description or title of the invention ... and in its terms grant ... for a term not exceeding fourteen years, the full and exclusive right and liberty of making, using, and vending the said invention, referring to the specifications for particulars, and specifying what the patentee claims.
guidance: Patent is a formal recorded instrument; the title/short description must correctly indicate nature and design; specifications annexed define the particulars of the grant.

name: Practice before the Office in patent matters (examples)
description: Includes preparing or prosecuting any patent application; consulting or giving advice to a client in contemplation of filing; drafting the specification or claims; drafting an amendment or reply to an Office communication that may require written argument to establish patentability; drafting replies to communications; drafting communications for interference, derivation, reexamination proceedings, petitions, appeals to PTAB, or other patent proceedings.
guidance: Registration authorizes performance of services reasonably necessary and incident to preparation and prosecution of patent applications or other proceedings involving a patent application or patent.

name: Practice in design patent matters
description: Includes preparing or prosecuting a design patent application; consulting or giving advice in contemplation of filing a design patent application; drafting the specification or claim of a design patent application; drafting amendments or replies that may require written argument to establish patentability; drafting communications for interference, derivation, reexamination, petitions, appeals to PTAB, or other design patent proceedings.
guidance: Design patent registration authorizes performance of services reasonably necessary and incident to preparation and prosecution of design patent applications or other proceedings involving a design patent application or design patent in which the practitioner is authorized to participate.

name: Claim charts and word count treatment
description: A petitioner may file a claim chart to explain what the petitioner believes a claim means in comparison to another claim, a reference, or a specification.
guidance: Claim charts can streamline identification of key claim features and their comparison to evidence. Claim charts submitted as part of petitions, motions, responses, oppositions, or replies count toward applicable word limits but are not required to be double-spaced. A claim chart from another proceeding submitted as an exhibit will not count toward word limits.

name: Petition filing date – minimum procedural compliance
description: To obtain a filing date, the petition must meet certain minimum standards (see 37 C.F.R. § 42.106 and applicable statute).
guidance: Generally the petition must comply with statutory standards for the requested proceeding (e.g., IPR requires complete petition with required fee and certificate of service). A complete IPR petition must certify that the patent is eligible for IPR and that the petitioner is not barred/estopped, identify the claims challenged and the specific basis for the challenge (37 C.F.R. §§ 42.104, 42.106). Similar requirements apply for PGR and derivation.

name: Specific petition content requirements
description: A petitioner must certify availability of the patent/application for review, that it is not barred/estopped, identify each challenged claim and statutory grounds, provide claim construction(s), and state the relevance of the evidence to the issues raised.
guidance: For IPR and PGR, a petitioner must also identify how the construed claim is unpatentable over the relevant evidence (37 C.F.R. §§ 42.104(b), 42.204(b), 42.304(b)).

name: Claim construction standard used by the Board
description: The Board applies the same claim construction standard that would be used in a civil action under 35 U.S.C. § 282(b) — i.e., the Phillips framework — for petitions filed on or after Nov. 13, 2018.
guidance: The Board will construe claims based on the record of the proceeding, taking into account claim language, specification, prosecution history, and relevant extrinsic evidence as in Article III courts. Parties should point out specific portions of the specification, prosecution history, and extrinsic evidence they want considered and explain relevancy. Each party bears the burden of providing sufficient support for any construction advanced.

name: Claim construction under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f)
description: Where claim language may be construed under § 112(f), a petitioner must provide a construction that includes both the claimed function and the specific portions of the specification that describe the structure, material, or acts corresponding to each claimed function.
guidance: A party may elaborate on why § 112(f) should or should not apply. A petitioner who chooses not to address § 112(f) risks failing to satisfy 37 C.F.R. § 42.104(b)(3). See Williamson v. Citrix Online.

name: Prior claim construction determinations — consideration and weight
description: Any prior claim construction determination by a federal court or the ITC that is timely made of record in the proceeding will be considered by the Board and given appropriate weight.
guidance: Non-exclusive factors for weight include similarities between the records, whether the prior construction is final or interlocutory, and whether the terms are necessary to deciding issues. Submission of such determinations is mandatory under 37 C.F.R. § 42.51(b) if they are relevant information inconsistent with a party's position and should be submitted concurrent with the filing that contains the inconsistency.

name: Patent owner preliminary response — filing period and permitted content
description: For IPR and PGR, a patent owner may file a preliminary response within three months after the Notice of Filing Date Accorded to Petition to demonstrate that no review should be instituted.
guidance: A preliminary response may present arguments and supporting evidence (including testimonial evidence) such as: (1) statutory bar to petitioner, (2) asserted references not printed publications, (3) prior art lacks a material limitation, (4) prior art does not teach/suggest petitioner's combination, (5) petitioner's claim interpretation unreasonable, (6) for PGR §101 explanation of patent eligibility, (7) reasons to exercise Director's discretion to deny under §314 and/or §325(d).

name: Waiver of preliminary response and statutory disclaimer
description: A patent owner may elect to waive the preliminary response to expedite proceedings; no adverse inference will be drawn. A patent owner may also file a statutory disclaimer of one or more challenged claims to streamline proceedings.
guidance: If no challenged claims remain after disclaimer, the Board will terminate the proceeding. If some claims remain, institution decision is based solely on remaining claims.

name: Content and scope of Board's institution decision
description: In instituting a trial, the Board will either institute as to all claims challenged and on all grounds in the petition, or institute on no claims and deny institution; the Board will not institute on fewer than all claims or all challenges in a petition.
guidance: If a trial is instituted, the Board generally will provide analysis of the strengths and weaknesses of all challenges in the petition to guide the parties. The Board retains discretion to deny the petition as a whole under §§ 314(a) and 325(d) even when some claims meet threshold standards. If deficiencies affect only part of a petition, the panel will evaluate whether denying the entire petition better serves efficient administration and integrity of the patent system (35 U.S.C. §§ 316(b), 326(b); 37 C.F.R. §§ 42.108; 42.208).

name: Submission and use of statements from other proceedings
description: The Board may consider statements regarding claim construction or scope made by parties in other proceedings if timely made of record and the submitting party explains how they support or contradict proposed constructions.
guidance: Examples include prior claim constructions in district court/ITC and patent owner statements made in preliminary responses in prior AIA proceedings. Parties should point out specific statements, explain relevance, and provide supporting evidence. Each party bears the burden of providing sufficient support for constructions advanced. Submission rules (e.g., 37 C.F.R. §§ 42.51(b), 42.123, 42.223) and timing requirements apply.

name: Election of species required (general procedure)
description: Where restriction between species is appropriate the examiner should send a letter including only a restriction requirement or place a telephone requirement to restrict. Applicant should be required to elect a single disclosed species under 35 U.S.C. 121, and advised as to the requisites of a complete reply and his or her rights under 37 CFR 1.141.
guidance: Action steps: (A) Identify generic claims or indicate none present. (B) Clearly identify each disclosed species (preferably by figures/examples or by mechanical means/material/distinguishing characteristic). Provide reasons why the species are independent or distinct. (C) Require election of a single disclosed species and advise regarding complete reply and rights under 37 CFR 1.141.

name: Contents of a complete reply to an election of species requirement
description: A reply to a requirement made according to this section should include a proper election along with a listing of all claims readable thereon, including any claims subsequently added.
guidance: An argument that a claim is allowable or that all claims are generic is considered nonresponsive unless accompanied by an election. Election may be made with or without traverse; to preserve petition rights, election must be made with traverse and traversal must distinctly and specifically point out supposed errors.

name: Effect of allowance of a generic claim
description: Upon the allowance of a generic claim, applicant will be entitled to consideration of claims to additional species which depend from or otherwise require all the limitations of an allowable generic claim as provided by 37 CFR 1.141.
guidance: Allowing a generic claim can entitle applicant to rejoin additional species claims that depend from or require the generic claim limitations.

name: Requirement to restrict between linked inventions
description: Where an application includes two or more otherwise properly divisible inventions that are linked by a claim which, if allowable, would require rejoinder, the examiner should require restriction, either by a written Office action that includes only a restriction requirement or by a telephoned requirement to restrict (the latter being encouraged).
guidance: If linking claim later indicated allowable, withdraw restriction and rejoin claims requiring all limitations of allowable linking claim; advise applicant about provisional double patenting concerns for continuation/divisional claims.

name: Telephone restriction practice (procedure)
description: If an examiner determines that a requirement for restriction should be made, the examiner should formulate a draft and telephone the attorney or agent of record and request an oral election, with or without traverse, after the attorney or agent has had time to consider the restriction requirement. Arrange a second telephone call generally within 3 working days. If representative objects or fails to respond, mail a restriction letter referencing the unsuccessful call.
guidance: When an oral election is made, incorporate into the Office action a formal restriction requirement including date of election, attorney/agent name, a complete record of the telephone interview, followed by a complete action on the elected invention as claimed. Use form paragraphs 8.23 or 8.23.01 as appropriate.

name: Provide clear and detailed record of restriction requirement
description: The examiner must provide a clear and detailed record of the restriction requirement to provide a clear demarcation between restricted inventions so that it can be determined whether inventions claimed in a continuing application are consonant with the restriction requirement and therefore subject to the prohibition against double patenting rejections under 35 U.S.C. 121.
guidance: Mention particular claim limitations and reasons why such limitations support restriction; identify groups, give short descriptions, classification, and indicate disposition of every claim.

name: Outline of required elements in a restriction requirement
description: The outline to set forth a requirement to restrict includes: (A) Statement of the requirement and identification of each group; (2) List claims in each group; (3) Short description of extent of subject matter claimed in each group; (4) Classify each group.
guidance: Also take into account claims not grouped (linking claims—identify and state possible group assignments; other ungrouped claims—indicate disposition); provide factual points showing independence/distinctness; provide reasons for insisting upon restriction and a summary statement advising as to reply required and effects of allowance/cancellation.

name: Election fixed by action on claims
description: Election becomes fixed when the claims in an application have received an action on their merits by the Office.
guidance: Claims originally presented and acted upon determine the invention elected by an applicant; in an RCE, claims presented and acted upon should be treated as provided in MPEP § 821.03.

name: Election other than express (by originally presented claims, generic claims only, or cancellation)
description: Election may be made in other ways than expressly in reply to a requirement: (a) by originally presented claims treated as original claims for restriction purposes; (b) where only generic claims are first presented and prosecuted and later species claims are presented, the examiner may require election of a single species; (c) by optional cancellation of claims leaving claims to one invention which are then acted upon.
guidance: Use these principles when determining which invention is considered elected in the absence of an explicit election.

name: Scope of SPC vs basic patent (product definition)
description: The scope of the certificate may be more limited than the basic patent, as it is intended only to cover the product (understood as the active pharmaceutical ingredient in the strict sense) as approved for use, whereas the scope of a pharmaceutical patent can be broader.
guidance: Assessments of whether the basic patent 'protects' the product for SPC purposes require claim-to-product mapping; SPC protection cannot legitimately extend beyond the invention covered by the claims. Courts (and patent offices) may narrow SPC scope compared to patent scope; this supports the sui generis character of SPCs.

name: Grounds for SPC invalidation or cancellation
description: Article 15 provides that 'The certificate shall be invalid if: (a) it was granted contrary to the provisions of Article 3; (b) the basic patent has lapsed before its lawful term expires; (c) the basic patent is revoked or has been limited to the extent that the product would no longer be protected by the claims of the basic patent; or (d) after the basic patent has expired, grounds for revocation exist which would have justified such revocation or limitation.' Additionally, if the patent or the marketing authorisation are invalidated, the SPC is cancelled.
guidance: Practically, SPC validity depends on ongoing validity and scope of the underlying patent and on the legitimacy of the link to the MA; challenges to patents or MAs can invalidate SPCs. Example: French and Spanish courts revoked Truvada SPCs after challenges.

name: Examiner tone and affirmative identification of allowable subject matter
description: Avoid personal opinions about lack of patentable merit; identify claims judged allowable and suggest ways to amend rejected claims to make them allowable.
guidance: Do not express that an application 'appears to be' devoid of patentable subject matter. As part of first merit action, identify any claims judged allowable, and suggest amendments to rejected claims. If patentable subject matter is apparent but not properly claimed (especially for pro se applicants), consider drafting claims or suggesting allowance and mentioning possible desirability of an interview to accelerate agreement.

name: Language and specificity to be used in rejecting claims
description: Required phrasing and clarity when rejecting claims on substantive grounds.
guidance: Use the word 'rejected' for substantive refusals and fully and clearly state the ground of rejection. The opening sentence of each ground should expressly reference the statutory basis (e.g., 35 U.S.C. section). If a claim is rejected as broader than the enabling disclosure, explain why; if rejected as indefinite, point out where indefiniteness resides; if incomplete, specify missing elements. Avoid personal remarks. Avoid omnibus rejections like 'on the references and for the reasons of record' and avoid grouping claims together in a common rejection unless equally applicable to all claims in the group. See MPEP § 706.02(i),(j),(m) for language to be used.

name: When applicant's arguments are persuasive and prior rejection/objection withdrawn
description: If arguments are persuasive, withdraw the prior rejection/objection and state the basis for withdrawal.
guidance: Use ¶ 7.38.01 to notify that applicant's arguments were persuasive, identify page(s)/line(s) of applicant's remarks forming basis for withdrawal, and indicate what rejection/objection was withdrawn and to which claims/figures/specification parts it pertains.

name: Unpersuasive argument: Arguing limitations which are not claimed
description: Limitations from the specification are not read into the claims; arguments relying on features not recited in the rejected claim are unpersuasive.
guidance: Cite In re Van Geuns. Use ¶ 7.37.08 and note that claimed language controls; briefly recite the features applicant relies on as bracketed text.

name: Unpersuasive argument: Limitations in a preamble
description: A preamble generally is not accorded patentable weight where it merely recites purpose or intended use and the body of the claim stands alone.
guidance: Cite In re Hirao and Kropa v. Robie. Use ¶ 7.37.10 and restate the preamble recitation briefly; explain when preamble language is not given weight.

name: Avoidance of piecemeal examination
description: Examiners should avoid piecemeal examination; ordinarily reject each claim on all valid grounds while avoiding undue multiplication of references.
guidance: Apply major technical rejections (lack of disclosure, enablement, serious indefiniteness, res judicata) with full development of reasons rather than stereotyped conclusions. Do not make secondary minor rejections where prior art discloses the 'heart' of the invention. Situations allowing limited action include: application too informal, undue multiplicity of claims without election, misjoinder of inventions, or disclosure directed to perpetual motion. Where res judicata or other major grounds apply, accompany with other available grounds.

name: Each claim must be mentioned in each Office action
description: Every pending claim should be mentioned by number and its treatment or status given in each Office action.
guidance: Include a summary of status of all claims presented for examination; use Form PTO-326 'Office Action Summary'. Maintain Index of Claims per MPEP § 719.04. Claims retained under specific CFR provisions should be treated per MPEP § 821–821.04(b).

name: State when claims are allowable and offer constructive assistance
description: When patentable subject matter is found or claims would be allowable if corrected, the examiner should state this and offer constructive suggestions (including drafting claims for pro se applicants).
guidance: For pro se applicants, examiner may draft claim(s) and indicate they would be allowed if incorporated (¶ 7.43.04). If claims are allowable except as to form, provide definite suggestions for correction and consider recommending an interview. Where claims are otherwise allowable but dependent on cancelled/rejected claims, state they would be allowable if rewritten in independent form. Do not delay allowance of clearly allowable claims once prior art fully developed.

name: Dependent claim allowable if rewritten to overcome 35 U.S.C. 112 second paragraph rejection
description: If a dependent claim is rejected solely under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, it may be allowable if rewritten to include all limitations of the base claim and intervening claims.
guidance: Use ¶ 7.43.02 to indicate that claim [1] would be allowable if rewritten to overcome the 112 rejection; use only when dependent claim would be allowable after amendment as indicated.

name: Suggestion of allowable drafted claim(s) for pro se applicants
description: Examiners may draft and present suggested claim language to pro se applicants when such claims distinguish patentably over the art of record.
guidance: Use ¶ 7.43.04 to present suggested claim(s), insert complete text of suggested claim(s), and require supplemental oath/declaration under 37 CFR 1.67 if appropriate. Use form paragraph 7.97 to indicate allowance of claims when appropriate.

name: Two criteria for subject matter eligibility
description: First, the claimed invention must be to one of the four statutory categories. Second, the claim must not be directed to a judicial exception unless the claim as a whole includes additional limitations amounting to significantly more than the exception.
guidance: Explains the four statutory categories (processes, machines, manufactures, compositions of matter) and identifies judicial exceptions (abstract ideas, laws of nature, natural phenomena). Cites Alice/Mayo framework as the controlling two-part test and instructs that the Alice/Mayo test is the only test that should be used. Advises examiners to consult MPEP §§ 2106.03–2106.05 for details.

name: Statutory category requirement (Step 1)
description: A claim must fall within one or more of the four statutory categories enumerated in 35 U.S.C. 101: process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter.
guidance: Defines 'process' as a series of acts; explains machines/manufactures/compositions as physical/tangible things. For non-process categories, the claimed subject matter must exist in some physical or tangible form. If a claim's Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) covers non-statutory embodiments, the claim fails Step 1.

name: Broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of claim as a whole
description: Establish the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim prior to examining for eligibility, because BRI sets the boundaries of coverage and affects whether claims are statutory or encompass exceptions.
guidance: Claim construction affects both Step 1 and the Alice/Mayo analysis (Step 2A and 2B). If BRI embraces both statutory and non-statutory embodiments, the claim as a whole is non-statutory. Best practice: point out BRI and recommend applicant amendment when appropriate. See MPEP § 2111 for more on BRI.

name: Alice/Mayo two-part test (Step 2: Determine judicial exception and 'significantly more')
description: Step 2A: Determine whether the claims are directed to a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon). Step 2B: If so, determine whether additional elements individually or in combination provide 'significantly more' than the judicial exception (the 'inventive concept').
guidance: Described as the controlling framework; courts call the second part the search for an 'inventive concept.' Machine-or-transformation and other clues should be considered as part of the integration/'significantly more' determination, not as separate tests. See MPEP §§ 2106.04 and 2106.05 for detailed guidance.

name: Pathways A/B/C for streamlined eligibility evaluation
description: Three pathways to eligibility: Pathway A (self-evident eligibility/streamlined), Pathway B (claim falls within statutory category and is not directed to a judicial exception), Pathway C (claim is directed to a judicial exception but recites additional elements that amount to significantly more).
guidance: If examiner is uncertain whether streamlined analysis applies, conduct full eligibility analysis. Claims not eligible under any pathway should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101. See MPEP § 2106.06 for streamlined analysis rules.

name: Examples of non-statutory product claims
description: Non-limiting examples include products that do not have a physical or tangible form (e.g., 'data per se' or 'software per se'), transitory forms of signal transmission (e.g., propagating carrier waves), and subject matter expressly prohibited (e.g., humans per se).
guidance: Explains software expressed as code or instructions detached from any medium is intangible; transitory signals lack concrete structure; product claims must have physical/tangible form to satisfy Step 1.

name: If BRI covers statutory and non-statutory embodiments → reject under Step 1
description: A claim whose BRI covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments embraces non-statutory subject matter and therefore fails Step 1 and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101.
guidance: Best practice: point out BRI and recommend claim narrowing amendment. Use specified form paragraphs when making Step 1 rejections (see MPEP § 2106.07(a)(1)). Example: 'machine-readable medium' claims that encompass carrier waves can be non-statutory.

name: Step 2A: Determine whether claim is directed to an abstract idea (groupings and examples)
description: Identify whether the claim recites an abstract idea by reference to example categories and groupings of abstract ideas (including mathematical concepts, certain methods of organizing human activity, mental processes, etc.).
guidance: MPEP contains example lists and 'tentative abstract ideas' — examiners should use these groupings to analyze whether a claim is directed to an abstract idea and consult subsection 2106.04(a) for examples and guidance.

name: Markedly different characteristics analysis
description: Evaluate whether a product has 'markedly different characteristics' from a naturally occurring product such that it is not merely a natural product or phenomenon.
guidance: This is used when assessing laws of nature, natural phenomena, and products of nature — to determine whether claimed subject matter is significantly different from what occurs in nature (see MPEP § 2106.04(b)/(c)).

name: Integration of a judicial exception into a practical application (Step 2A prong two)
description: Assess whether the judicial exception is integrated into a practical application — i.e., whether the claim applies the exception in a way that imposes a meaningful limitation, ties it to a particular machine, transforms an article, or achieves a technical improvement.
guidance: If the exception is integrated into a practical application, the claim may be eligible at Step 2A (no need to go to Step 2B). See MPEP § 2106.04(d) and subsections for guidance on evaluating 'integration' (including improvements to computer functionality, particular treatment/prophylaxis, etc.).

name: Step 2B: Whether claim recites additional elements amounting to 'significantly more'
description: When claims are directed to a judicial exception, evaluate whether additional elements, individually or in ordered combination, provide 'significantly more' than the exception (i.e., an 'inventive concept').
guidance: MPEP § 2106.05 lists categories and examples of what can constitute significantly more (improvements to computer/technology, particular machine, particular transformation, meaningful limitations, etc.) and what typically does not (well-understood, routine, conventional activity; mere instructions to apply the exception; insignificant extra-solution activity).

name: Improvements to the functioning of a computer or to any other technology (Step 2A prong two and Step 2B)
description: Claims that improve computer functionality or other technology/technical fields can show integration into a practical application (Step 2A) or can supply 'significantly more' at Step 2B.
guidance: Evaluate whether the claim provides an unconventional technical solution to a technological problem or improves computer operation (see Enfish, McRO examples). Use this as a strong indicator of eligibility when adequately claimed/constructed.

name: Particular machine (Step 2B(b))
description: A claim that is tied to a particular machine can provide 'significantly more' than an abstract idea or other judicial exception.
guidance: Assess whether the machine limitation is more than a generic computer or conventional hardware; mere recitation of a computer is often insufficient unless it is a particular machine that imposes meaningful limits on the claim.

name: Particular transformation (Step 2B(c))
description: A transformation of an article to a different state or thing (the 'particular transformation' test) can supply 'significantly more' and support eligibility.
guidance: Consider whether the claimed process effects a transformation of a specific article and whether that transformation is central to the claim's eligibility analysis.

name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity (negative factor in Step 2B)
description: Limitations that merely recite well-understood, routine, conventional activity previously known in the field do not supply 'significantly more'.
guidance: Examiners should identify whether additional claim elements are well-known and conventional at the time of the claim. If so, such elements are unlikely to convert a judicial exception into patent-eligible subject matter (see MPEP § 2106.05(d)).

name: Other meaningful limitations and field-of-use considerations
description: Other claimed limitations — including particular techniques, data structures, or particular fields of use/technological environments — may be evaluated for whether they meaningfully limit the exception.
guidance: An abstract idea does not become nonabstract by limiting to a particular field of use or technological environment alone; however, meaningful limitations that impose technical improvements may support eligibility (see MPEP §§ 2106.05(e) and 2106.05(h)).

name: Streamlined analysis: eligibility is self-evident or clear technology improvement
description: When eligibility of a claim is self-evident (Pathway A) or there is a clear improvement to technology or computer functionality (2106.06(b)), a streamlined analysis may be used to find the claim eligible without full two-part analysis.
guidance: Examiners should use streamlined analysis only when appropriate for examination efficiency and consistency; if uncertain, perform the full Alice/Mayo two-part analysis. If a claim could be eligible under Pathway A but is analyzed further, it will be found eligible under Pathway B or C.

name: Formulating and supporting rejections for lack of subject matter eligibility
description: When rejecting for lack of subject matter eligibility, examiners must use appropriate form paragraphs and support the rejection with explanation tying claim limitations to the basis for ineligibility; see MPEP § 2106.07.
guidance: 2106.07(a)(1) identifies form paragraphs for § 101 rejections. 2106.07(b) instructs how to evaluate applicant responses; 2106.07(c) discusses clarifying the record. Rejections should explain BRI, the judicial exception identified, why the claim is directed to the exception, and why any additional elements are insufficient.

name: Examiners must still consider other patentability requirements (35 U.S.C. 102, 103, 112, utility, inventorship, double patenting)
description: 35 U.S.C. 101 is only a threshold inquiry. Even if an invention is eligible under § 101, the claim must satisfy novelty (102), nonobviousness (103), written description/enablement/definiteness (112), utility, inventorship, and double patenting requirements.
guidance: MPEP reminds examiners to continue complete examination under all applicable statutes and not to conflate § 101 eligibility with other requirements. Use MPEP § 2103 and relevant subsequent chapters for these analyses.

name: Evaluating applicant's responses and clarifying the record
description: When applicant responds to a § 101 rejection, examiners should evaluate arguments and evidence in view of the Alice/Mayo framework and update the record, requesting clarification or additional claim amendments if appropriate.
guidance: 2106.07(b) and (c) provide procedural considerations for evaluating responses and maintaining clear prosecution history. Examiner should articulate reasons for sustaining or withdrawing rejections and advise on amendment strategies.

name: Different claims, description and drawings for different States (Rule 87)
description: If the European Patent Office notes that, in respect of one or some of the designated Contracting States, the content of an earlier European patent application forms part of the state of the art pursuant to Article 54, paragraphs 3 and 4, the European patent application or European patent may contain for such State or States claims and, if the European Patent Office considers it necessary, a description and drawings which are different from those for the other designated Contracting States.
guidance: Allows state-specific claim sets (and, if necessary, description/drawings) where earlier applications affect novelty/priority in certain designated States.

name: Correction of errors in documents filed with the EPO (Rule 88)
description: Linguistic errors, errors of transcription and mistakes in any document filed with the European Patent Office may be corrected on request. However, if the request for such correction concerns a description, claims or drawings, the correction must be obvious in the sense that it is immediately evident that nothing else would have been intended than what is offered as the correction.
guidance: Correction requests are permitted for clear linguistic/transcription mistakes; corrections to core patent documents (description/claims/drawings) are restricted to obvious corrections only.

name: Jurisdiction for claims to the right to the grant of a European patent (Protocol on Recognition: Articles 1–8)
description: Article 1: Courts of the Contracting States shall, in accordance with Articles 2 to 6, have jurisdiction to decide claims against the applicant to the right to the grant of a European patent in respect of designated Contracting States. Article 2: Subject to Articles 4 and 5, if an applicant has residence or principal place of business within one of the Contracting States, proceedings shall be brought against him in the courts of that State. Article 3: If applicant has residence or principal place of business outside the Contracting States and the claimant is within a Contracting State, courts of the claimant's State have exclusive jurisdiction. Article 4: If the subject matter is the invention of an employee, the courts of the State whose law determines the right under Article 60(1) second sentence shall have exclusive jurisdiction. Article 5: Parties may agree to confer exclusive jurisdiction on a particular Contracting State's courts (subject to limits for employment contracts). Article 6: Where none of Articles 2–5 apply, the courts of the Federal Republic of Germany shall have exclusive jurisdiction. Article 7: Courts shall of their own motion decide jurisdiction pursuant to Articles 2–6. Article 8: In case of same claim proceedings in different Contracting States, the later court shall decline jurisdiction in favour of the earlier court; if earlier court's jurisdiction is challenged, the later court shall stay proceedings until final decision.
guidance: Allocates which national courts hear disputes about entitlement to grant of EP patents, includes forum selection by parties, special rules for employee inventions, and rules on lis pendens and jurisdictional conflicts.

name: Recognition of final decisions on entitlement (Protocol on Recognition: Articles 9–11)
description: Article 9: Subject to Article 11(2), final decisions given in any Contracting State on the right to the grant of a European patent shall be recognised without requiring a special procedure in the other Contracting States. The jurisdiction of the court whose decision is to be recognised and the validity of such decision may not be reviewed. Article 10: Exceptions where recognition does not apply: (a) where an applicant who has not contested a claim proves the initiating document was not notified regularly and sufficiently early to defend himself; or (b) where the applicant proves the decision is incompatible with another decision in proceedings between the same parties started earlier. Article 11: The Protocol prevails over conflicting provisions of other agreements on jurisdiction/recognition; it does not affect agreements between a Contracting State and a non‑party State.
guidance: Final entitlement decisions are broadly mutually recognised across Contracting States with narrow exceptions (notification defects or conflicting earlier decisions); protocol takes precedence over conflicting rules.

name: Role of transitional phrases in claims
description: Transitional phrases in patent applications specify whether the claim is limited to only the elements listed, or whether the claim may cover items or processes that have additional elements.
guidance: Transitional wording is important because it determines claim scope (whether additional, unnamed elements are allowed). Choose transitional language deliberately to control breadth of coverage and potential infringement consequences.

name: Open-Ended ("comprising")
description: Use of open-ended terms such as 'comprising' or 'which comprises' means that the claim encompasses all the elements listed, but may also include additional, unnamed elements.
guidance: Example: If a claim recites elements 'A' and 'B', practicing the invention using 'A' and 'B' infringes, and using 'A', 'B', and an additional element 'C' also infringes. Example claim: 'A therapeutic composition comprising a polynucleotide having the sequence of SEQ ID NO:1.' These claims may be fairly broad, since any composition that has SEQ ID NO:1 within it would infringe.

name: Closed-Ended ("consisting of")
description: Closed-ended claim language such as 'consisting of' means that the composition (or device, or method) has the recited elements (or steps) and no more.
guidance: Example: 'A therapeutic composition consisting of a protein having the sequence of SEQ ID NO:2 and a suitable buffer.' This covers only the composition of SEQ ID NO:2 and the specified buffer; if any additional elements are added (not defined in the specification as part of the 'suitable buffer'), the composition would not be covered by that claim. Use 'consisting of' when a deliberately narrow, exclusive claim scope is desired.

name: Combination of open-ended and closed-ended language (Markush groups)
description: Claims may combine open-ended and closed-ended language; e.g., an open-ended claim that incorporates a closed 'group consisting of' list (a Markush group) to specify alternatives while remaining open to additional elements.
guidance: Example: 'A recombinant DNA construct comprising a polynucleotide selected from the group consisting of SEQ ID NO:1, SEQ ID NO:2, SEQ ID NO:3, SEQ ID NO:4, and SEQ ID NO:5.' Interpretation: the composition must contain at least one of the specified sequences but may also contain any number of additional, unnamed elements. This is an example of a Markush Group, common in the chemical arts.

name: Subject matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 101
description: Determine subject matter eligibility under patent law (35 U.S.C. 101) of AI inventions.
guidance: The guidance update builds on previous guidance to provide further clarity and consistency to how the USPTO and applicants should evaluate subject matter eligibility of claims in patent applications and patents involving inventions related to AI technology. It is intended to assist USPTO personnel and stakeholders in determining subject matter eligibility during patent examination, appeal, and post-grant proceedings.

name: Whether a claim recites an abstract idea
description: Analyze whether a claimed invention 'recites an abstract idea' as part of the subject matter eligibility inquiry.
guidance: The guidance includes discussion and examples addressing particular inquiries such as whether a claim recites an abstract idea. The new examples provide additional analyses under 35 U.S.C. 101 of hypothetical claims to help determine whether a claim is properly characterized as an abstract idea.

name: Unity of invention — one invention only (Section 36)
description: A patent shall be granted for one invention only. Where an application describes more than one invention, the applicant may limit the claims to one invention only and any other invention disclosed may be made the subject of a divisional application (subsection 36(2)).
guidance: Unity is largely procedural—identifying lack of unity does not itself determine patentability; it requires the applicant to elect one invention for prosecution or to file divisionals for others.

name: Meaning of 'one invention only' — single general inventive concept
description: For the purposes of section 36, 'one invention' includes a group of inventions linked in such a manner that they form a single general inventive concept (section 88 of the Patent Rules).
guidance: The term 'invention' in the unity context is broader than the statutory definition in section 2 and can include 'aspects of a single invention'—claims that are so linked form one invention.

name: General inventive concept — criteria for linkage
description: Assess whether a 'single general inventive concept' exists linking the claims by considering the purpose of the invention: the claimed invention should provide a solution to a practical problem; claims defining that solution or refinements may relate to a single inventive concept. Generally, a set of claims will share a general inventive concept if a set of new and unobvious elements is common to each claim, provided they are required for proper operation in the invention's broadest aspects.
guidance: Inventive concept concerns how a result is obtained (the inventive aspects of a practical solution), not unity of result alone. The PCT expression 'special technical features' refers to novel and unobvious claim elements that define the contribution over the prior art.

name: A priori and a posteriori unity evaluations
description: Unity can be evaluated a priori (presence of a common set of elements among claims, without regard to prior art) and a posteriori (whether the common elements are new and unobvious over the prior art). A lack of unity may be identified by either analysis.
guidance: A typical a priori approach: identify the claim with the fewest elements and check if those elements (or corresponding equivalents) appear in all other independent claims. 'Corresponding' elements (equivalents whose roles correspond) can suffice. Prior art relevant to novelty/obviousness may be considered for a posteriori assessment.

name: Content and explanation required in a unity report
description: A report identifying lack of unity should explain the basis to enable the applicant to decide how to limit or divide claims: it should identify what the examiner considers the distinct inventions to be and provide sufficient detail why they do not share a single general inventive concept. For a posteriori defects, prior art supporting the conclusion should be cited and explained.
guidance: Where possible, the examiner should relate each identified invention to the specific claims that define it and set out groups of claims deemed to be 'one invention only', indicating which group each independent claim belongs to. Dependent claims are presumed to belong to the group of the claim they refer to unless explicitly indicated otherwise. If a lack of unity exists among alternatives in a single claim, the examiner should, where practical, separate the alternatives into groups.

name: Timing for identifying a lack of unity defect
description: Generally, a lack of unity should be identified in the first report written in respect of the claims that lack unity. However, if other defects (e.g. obviousness, ambiguity, lack of utility/support) bear on unity, the unity defect may be formally identified in a later report after advising the applicant that those defects impact unity.
guidance: A lack of unity introduced by applicant amendment may be identified regardless of prior examination duration. Where prior art raises the possibility of a posteriori lack of unity but some claims are anticipated/obvious, it may be preferable to resolve prior art defects first before formally identifying unity issues.

name: Exceptions and limited situations where 1.136(a) is inapplicable
description: Extensions with payment of a fee under 37 CFR 1.136(a) are not available in certain circumstances.
guidance: Examples of exceptions: (A) all extensions in a reexamination proceeding (see 37 CFR 1.550(c) and MPEP § 2265 for ex parte reexamination and 37 CFR 1.956/MPEP § 2665 for inter partes); (B) all extensions during an interference proceeding (but not preparatory proceedings where a claim is suggested for interference); (C) specific Office actions stating 37 CFR 1.136(a) is not applicable (e.g., reply to notice of allowability, reissue applications associated with litigation, applications in allowable condition with nonelected claims where time is set to cancel such claims); (D) limited instances where applicant is given a specified time limit to take certain actions.

name: References that 'teach away' from the invention
description: A prior art reference that "teaches away" from the claimed invention is a significant factor to consider in determining obviousness; the nature of the teaching must be weighed in substance.
guidance: Teaching away can be evidence of nonobviousness, but mere disclosure of multiple alternatives does not, by itself, teach away (In re Fulton). A reference criticizing, discrediting, or discouraging the claimed solution may teach away (In re Gurley). Where references teach away from a combination, it is improper to combine them (In re Grasselli). Examiners must assess how strongly a reference discourages the claimed approach and weigh that in the obviousness analysis.

name: Proceeding contrary to accepted wisdom evidences nonobviousness
description: Proceeding contrary to the accepted wisdom or conventional practice in the art can be evidence supporting nonobviousness.
guidance: If the prior art as a whole suggests a different approach (e.g., lower temperatures, different materials) and the claimed invention goes against that accepted wisdom yet achieves claimed results, that may support nonobviousness (In re Hedges). Known disadvantages in old devices that would discourage pursuit of the new invention are also relevant (United States v. Adams). Examiners should consider the totality of prior art and whether the claimed invention runs counter to accepted practice.

name: Statutory standard for disqualifying prior art under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c)
description: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) provides that subject matter developed by another person which qualifies as prior art only under subsections (e), (f), or (g) of section 102 shall not preclude patentability under §103 where the subject matter and the claimed invention were, at the time the claimed invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.
guidance: This statutory disqualification applies only to obviousness determinations under 35 U.S.C. 103; it does not disqualify prior art for purposes of 35 U.S.C. 102 rejections or double-patenting rejections. If subject matter qualifies as prior art under other subsections of 102 (e.g., 102(a) or (b)), it is not disqualified under pre-AIA 103(c). Applicants who assert disqualification must establish it (see MPEP §2146 and §2146.01).

name: Joint research agreement conditions for disqualification
description: For purposes of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c), subject matter developed by another and a claimed invention shall be deemed owned by the same person if (A) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; (B) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (C) the patent application discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement.
guidance: The term 'joint research agreement' means a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement for performance of experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention. All three conditions must be satisfied to treat the other's subject matter as commonly owned for §103 purposes. See MPEP §2146.02 and §2156 for related AIA provisions.

name: Effective dates and applicability of AIPA and CREATE Act amendments
description: Amendments (AIPA 1999 and CREATE Act 2004) changed the scope and effective dates of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c); applicability depends on filing dates and patent grant dates.
guidance: The 1999 AIPA amendment adding prior art under former 102(e) applied to applications filed on or after November 29, 1999. The CREATE Act (Dec. 10, 2004) made further amendments effective for patents (including reissue patents) granted on or after December 10, 2004, except those subject to the current 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103. For reexamination proceedings and reissue applications, examiners must check the patent/application dates to determine which version of §103(c) applies and whether recapture or other doctrines affect claim presentation. See MPEP §§2146, 2146.01, and §2159.

name: Definition of 'commonly owned' (100% ownership) and related constraints
description: For pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) purposes, 'commonly owned' is intended to mean the subject matter and the claimed invention are entirely or wholly owned by the same person(s) or organization(s) (i.e., 100% ownership) at the time the claimed invention was made.
guidance: If either the subject matter or claimed invention was owned less than 100% by the same entity(ies) at the relevant time, common ownership does not exist. For jointly-owned inventions, the reference must have been owned by (or subject to an obligation of assignment to) the same entities that owned the application at the time of the later invention. Licenses that retain basic ownership rights do not defeat ownership. The question is fact-specific and requires evidence of legal ownership or enforceable obligation to assign — moral or unenforceable obligations are insufficient.

name: Reissue, reexamination, and recapture considerations
description: Reissue and reexamination proceedings have special considerations: recapture doctrine and effective-date rules may limit use of amended §103(c) changes to avoid prior rejections or to present claims in reissue applications.
guidance: Where a patent was granted prior to Dec. 10, 2004 or applications were filed before Nov. 29, 1999, the specific applicable amendments vary; in some reissue scenarios, recapture may prevent presentation of claims amended/cancelled to overcome a previous §103 rejection even if subject matter might now be disqualified. Examiners should consult the Office of Patent Legal Administration via Technology Center Quality Assurance Specialist when such situations arise. See MPEP §§2146.01–2146.03 and §§804, 1490 for related practice.

name: Medical indication claims and formats
description: For new medical uses of known products, multiple claim formats exist (Swiss-type claims, purpose-limited product claims, use claims, substance-when-used claims, and method of treatment claims) and national laws and practice vary significantly as to permissibility and the protection conferred.
guidance: Identify the appropriate format(s) for each jurisdiction. Examples given: Swiss-type ('use of X in the manufacture of a medicament for treatment of Y'), purpose-limited product claims ('X for use in the treatment of Y' — EPO compulsory since 2011), use claims (accepted in countries like Germany, Canada, Australia), 'substance when used' claims, and method-of-treatment claims (accepted in US and Australia). The patentability and enforcement (e.g., who is a direct infringer, exemptions for medical practitioners) differ among countries. Professional tip: ensure the priority application's description supports selection of the most appropriate claim formats for later filings; include multiple formats where strategic.

name: Include multiple claim types for comprehensive protection
description: Draft a set of claims containing various claim types (product, use/medical-indication, process/preparation, method) so that if one claim type is invalidated another may still provide protection.
guidance: If a product claim is novel and nonobvious, related use and process claims will generally be considered novel; nonetheless, include product, use and process claims where appropriate to comprehensively protect the invention and mitigate risk. Example: include product claim for Product X, general/first medical use claim, specific medical-use claim, and a preparation process claim. Be mindful of differing national rules that may affect which claim types are necessary or effective.

name: Composition claims — element-level breadth choices
description: Composition claims describe the chemical nature or components of an invention; drafters may claim elements as narrowly or broadly as necessary in view of prior art and business objectives.
guidance: Decide element-by-element whether to specify exact compounds or use generic, functional wording (e.g., 'a pH-modifying substrate in an amount sufficient to adjust pH to 3.5–5.0') depending on novelty, scope desired, and prior art. A generically-stated element can encompass many alternatives (risk of overbreadth vs enforceability). Draft depending on whether you wish to capture any compound that performs the stated function or a specific identified chemical.

name: Biotechnology claims — sequence listings and deposit rules
description: Biotechnology inventions (cDNA, recombinant DNA, proteins, monoclonal antibodies, microorganisms, cultivars, etc.) may require special claim formats, sequence listings and deposit of biological material where words alone cannot adequately describe how to make and use the invention.
guidance: Where access to biological material is necessary for enablement, use the deposit system (Budapest Treaty) and include deposit references (e.g., ATCC accession numbers) in the application. Ensure compliance with national sequence-listing rules and deposit requirements; include adequate disclosure in the specification and follow deposit formalities to ensure the material is available for patent procedures across jurisdictions.

name: Computer-implemented invention claims and exclusions
description: Abstract ideas, software or computer programs 'as such', pure mental acts and business methods as such are excluded from patentable subject matter in many jurisdictions; acceptable claim formats include apparatus/product, method/process, use claims, computer-readable medium (Beauregard), data-structure (Lowry) and other jurisdiction-specific forms.
guidance: Draft a mix of claim types: method claims often capture dynamic algorithmic behavior (common as Claim 1), and product/apparatus claims should also be included. In jurisdictions that permit referring a product claim to method claims, a product claim can refer back to method claims; where such referencing is not allowed, rephrase method steps into apparatus 'means for …' language or specific functional language. Beware that 'means for' claim language has different interpretations by jurisdiction (e.g., US means-plus-function claim rules). Consider specialized formats (computer-readable medium claims, data-structure claims, propagated signal claims) appropriate to target jurisdictions. Professional tip: keep up to date with evolving national practice for software/CIIs and choose claim formats strategically.

name: Claim drafting order — prepare the claims first
description: Begin drafting a patent application by preparing the claims first because doing so helps refine the inventive concept and guides the description and other parts of the application.
guidance: Use the physical embodiment as a starting point but iteratively abstract and broaden the claim language to capture the inventive concept. Drafting claims first aids in identifying essential versus non-essential features and helps structure dependent claims and fallback positions.

name: Broad and narrow claims — build a claim set from broadest to narrowest
description: Draft a combination of broad and narrow claims to capture the full scope of an invention's novelty; an ideal claim set ranges from the broadest feasible claim to the narrowest dependent claims.
guidance: A practical approach is to start with a narrow claim and incrementally remove or generalize elements to arrive at the broadest allowable claim, then draft dependent claims from it. Use dependent claims to reintroduce omitted elements as fallback positions. Ensure each claim legitimately captures novel and nonobvious subject matter and avoid introducing non-novel elements that do not contribute to inventive step in the broadest claims.

name: Multiple independent claim sets and alternative focuses
description: Include multiple independent claim sets (e.g., apparatus/product, element-specific device, method/process, full-process) focusing on different aspects or alternative points of novelty of the invention.
guidance: Draft independent claim sets when each truly represents independent novelty or when the prior art is unclear. Use dependent claims within each set to recover features removed during broadening. Avoid creating alternative sets solely for the sake of alternatives unless they represent commercially significant distinct novelties; excessive trivial alternatives can draw examiner objections.

name: Align claim scope with inventor's objectives and commercial strategy
description: Before finalizing breadth, ensure the claims reflect the inventor's or applicant's commercial intentions and the likely scope of use/enforcement; do not automatically maximize breadth contrary to client wishes.
guidance: Ask: What are the goals of this invention? Who/what is likely to infringe? To whom could the patent be licensed? Is broad protection commercially desirable or risky? If the inventor envisions a very narrow, specific application, draft narrower claims; if broader adaptation is anticipated, draft broader claims but ensure each broader claim is supportable and defensible.

name: Conciseness, claim count and claim drafting practicalities
description: Some jurisdictions require that claims be 'concise' and may object to undue repetition, many trivial claims, or multiple alternatives within a single claim that obscure scope.
guidance: Avoid undue repetition between claims by using dependent claim form. Be mindful of what constitutes a reasonable number of claims in the target jurisdiction and avoid submitting many trivial variations that invite examiner objection. Do not present multiple alternatives within one claim in a way that obscures the claim's scope; where necessary, create separate dependent or independent claims for meaningful alternatives.

name: ISA entitlements when unity lacking (consequences)
description: If unity is not met, the International Searching Authority (ISA) is entitled to request the applicant to pay an additional search fee for each invention beyond the first or to limit the international search to the invention first mentioned in the claims if no additional fee is paid.
guidance: Applicants faced with a lack-of-unity finding can either pay additional search fees to obtain searches on further inventions or accept a limited international search. The ISA's actions are procedural consequences that affect the scope of the international search report.

name: Common categories of claims presumed to satisfy unity (PCT heuristics)
description: Under PCT certain combinations are commonly presumed to satisfy unity: product + process for making it + apparatus for making + use of product; multiple products that share a 'special technical feature'; combinations where there are corresponding contributions.
guidance: When drafting claims, coupling product, its making process, apparatus, and uses, or ensuring multiple products share a defined special technical feature, helps avoid unity objections. These are practical drafting heuristics rather than strict rules.

name: Strategic considerations for claim drafting and prosecution
description: Plan claim structure to minimize unity objections (especially for US-bound PCT applications), consider whether to prosecute multiple inventions abroad in the same case, and remember that US national stage applications use the PCT unity standard, not US restriction standard.
guidance: Practical strategies include drafting claims to emphasize a shared special technical feature, deciding whether to pursue separate filings in key jurisdictions, and anticipating additional search fees or protests. Use the 'common categories' heuristics and be mindful of differences in national practices.

name: Result-effective variable (not recognized in the prior art)
description: Applicants may rebut an obviousness rejection based on optimization by showing the claimed variable was not recognized in the prior art to be a result-effective variable.
guidance: Antonie provides the archetype where the prior art was silent regarding a variable in a critical ratio; E.I. Dupont v. Synvina discusses the concept and its narrowness. The examiner should require applicants to articulate why the variable would not have been recognized in the prior art. Note: after KSR, a known result-effective variable is one motivation among others for experimentation, but not the only one.

name: Obviousness of species when prior art teaches a genus — single-reference approach
description: When a single prior art reference discloses a genus encompassing the claimed species or subgenus but does not expressly disclose the particular claimed species, Office personnel should attempt to find additional prior art; absent that, consider specific factors to determine whether a single-reference 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection is appropriate.
guidance: Editor note: This MPEP section applies under AIA and pre-AIA regimes (timing differences noted). If additional art is not found, consider the list of detailed factors set out below (structure of genus, properties/utilities, predictability, number of species). See MPEP § 2144.08 and related subsections for full treatment.

name: Establishing a prima facie case of obviousness — Graham factors
description: To make out a case of obviousness, Office personnel must (A) determine the scope and contents of the prior art; (B) ascertain the differences between the prior art and the claims in issue; (C) determine the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; and (D) evaluate any evidence of secondary considerations.
guidance: Authority: Graham v. John Deere; burden: PTO must establish prima facie case, then burden shifts to applicant to rebut. See related cases (In re Bell, Rijckaert, Oetiker) and MPEP §§ 714.12, 714.13, 715.09 for guidance on dealing with rebuttal evidence and when such evidence may be disregarded.

name: Determine the scope and content of the prior art
description: After construing the claims, Office personnel should determine the scope and content of the relevant prior art; each reference used must qualify as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 and be analogous art.
guidance: For a prior art genus, make findings as to: (A) structure of disclosed genus and any expressly described species/subgenus; (B) physical/chemical properties and utilities disclosed and any suggested limitations; (C) predictability of the technology; and (D) the number of species encompassed, considering all variables. See Panduit Corp. v. Dennison and MPEP § 2141.01(a).

name: Ascertain differences between the closest disclosed prior art species and the claimed species
description: Identify the closest disclosed prior art species or subgenus and compare it to the claimed species to determine similarities and differences in structure, properties, and utilities; evaluate whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious.
guidance: Make explicit findings on similarities/differences; the inquiry is whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious (Stratoflex). Compare the claimed species to the closest prior art species of record and document structure, property, and utility differences.

name: Determine whether one of ordinary skill would have had a reason to select the claimed species
description: Based on the Graham findings and prior art teachings, determine whether it would have been obvious to select the claimed species/subgenus from the disclosed genus; consider specific indicia below.
guidance: To address this issue, focus on all relevant prior art teachings and consider factors such as size of genus, express teachings recommending selection, and structural similarity to preferred species; account for number of variables to be selected/modified and the significance of differences between prior art and claimed invention.

name: Consider express teachings in the prior art
description: If the prior art expressly teaches a particular reason to select the claimed species or subgenus, point out that disclosure and explain why it would have made selection obvious to one of ordinary skill.
guidance: Examples: Merck & Co. v. Biocraft Labs (express teaching to coadminister a named example), In re Kemps (one reference referring expressly to another). An express teaching may be an art-recognized equivalence or a specific disclosure that ties the references together.

name: Consider teachings of structural similarity
description: Consider whether a "typical," "preferred," or "optimum" species in the prior art is structurally similar to the claimed species, because structural similarity may provide a reason to select the claimed species based on expected similar properties.
guidance: Authorities: Dillon, In re Deuel. Structural relationships (e.g., homologs, conservative amino acid substitutions) may motivate modification. But consider number of variables and significance of differences (In re Jones, In re Susi); in biotechnology conservative substitutions may be expected to have little effect, but context matters.

name: Adequate disclosure (35 U.S.C. 112(a))
description: A patent application as filed must contain a full and clear disclosure of the invention in the manner prescribed by 35 U.S.C. 112(a). All amendments and claims must find descriptive basis in the original disclosure; no new matter may be introduced after the filing date.
guidance: The adequate disclosure requirement ensures the public receives something in return for patent rights. Applicant may rely on the specification with original claims and drawings as filed. See also 37 CFR 1.121(f) and MPEP § 608.04. If the application obviously fails to disclose with the clarity required by 35 U.S.C. 112, require revision (see MPEP § 702.01).

name: Specification must commence on separate sheet; section separation (37 CFR 1.71(f))
description: The specification must commence on a separate sheet, and each sheet including part of the specification may not include other parts of the application (claims, abstract, Sequence Listing). Claims, abstract, and Sequence Listing should each begin on a new page.
guidance: These sections are separately indexed in the Image File Wrapper (IFW); avoid overlap of sections on a single page.

name: Formatting of specification text (line spacing, font, single-column) (37 CFR 1.52(b)(2))
description: Specification (other than reissue/reexam) must have 1 1/2 or double spacing, text in a nonscript type font (e.g., Arial, Times Roman, Courier, preferably font size 12; captial letters at least 0.3175 cm high; may be no smaller than 0.21 cm), and only a single column of text.
guidance: Claims, abstract, and Sequence Listing have separate page rules. Paragraph numbering recommended in the [0001] format and placement; nontext elements are part of the surrounding paragraph.

name: Page and paragraph numbering rules (37 CFR 1.52(b)(5)-(6))
description: Pages of the specification (including claims and abstract) must be consecutively numbered starting with 1, with numbers centrally located above or preferably below the text. Paragraphs (other than claims/abstract) may be individually numbered using Arabic numerals with at least four numerals enclosed in square brackets (e.g., [0001]) and highlighted in bold.
guidance: Paragraph numbers should appear to the right of the left margin as the first item in each paragraph and be followed by a gap. Nontext elements and lists are considered part of the surrounding paragraph.

name: Requirements and warnings in Form PTO/SB/37
description: Form PTO/SB/37 (Request for Deferral of Examination) contains statements that deferral is suspension of action (may reduce patent term adjustment), requires the fees (processing and publication) when filed, provides for rescission of nonpublication under 37 CFR 1.213(b) if applicable, and includes signature, fee payment, and privacy/FOIA notices.
guidance: Form includes a warning that information may become public and that credit card information should not be included on the form (use PTO-2038). It states that the publication fee and processing fee are required when the request is filed and that applications will be scheduled for publication at 18 months from earliest claimed filing date if nonpublication is rescinded.

name: Parent application filing date can be 102(e) date only if it supports the relied-upon subject matter
description: A U.S. parent application's filing date is accorded as the 102(e) prior art date for a patent/application publication that claims benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 only if the earlier-filed parent properly supports the subject matter relied upon in the rejection in compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
guidance: Subject matter used in the rejection must be disclosed in the earlier application in compliance with 112(1) to be entitled to the earlier filing date under 102(e). See MPEP §706.02(f)(1) examples.

name: Overcoming a 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection by antedating or showing applicant's work
description: A 102(e) rejection can be overcome by antedating the filing date of the reference (e.g., affidavits/declarations under 37 C.F.R. 1.131) or by showing the relevant disclosure is applicant's own work (affidavit/declaration under 37 C.F.R. 1.132).
guidance: Antedating may also be achieved by an earlier foreign priority or provisional application if it supports the claims under 35 U.S.C. 119; a terminal disclaimer does not overcome a 102(e) rejection. See MPEP §706.02(b) for a list of methods and MPEP §§715–716 for requirements of 1.131/1.132 affidavits/declarations.

name: Combination claims in a reference do not establish patentee invented individual elements
description: The mere presence of combination claims in a reference is not evidence that the patentee invented the individual elements or subcombinations unless those elements/subcombinations are separately claimed.
guidance: Cite In re DeBaun and In re Facius: when elements are not separately claimed, inventorship of combination claims does not presumptively show inventorship of the individual elements. This matters when assessing whether a reference was derived from applicant or whether elements were contributed by applicant.

name: Inventor must contribute to conception; reduction to practice generally irrelevant
description: To be an inventor a person must contribute to the conception of the invention; merely suggesting a desired result without the means to accomplish it is not inventorship. Reduction to practice is generally irrelevant to inventorship except in limited circumstances.
guidance: Conception is the key inquiry. For chemistry, general knowledge of groups of compounds is insufficient — inventor must have conception of the specific claimed compounds. See In re Hardee, Board of Education v. American Bioscience, and other cited authorities. See MPEP §§2138.04–.05 for evidence required to establish conception or reduction to practice.

name: Search when description/claims fail Articles 5 and 6
description: Where the description or claims fail to meet the requirements of Articles 5 and 6 to such an extent that it is impossible to examine claimed subject matter as to novelty, inventive step or industrial applicability, the examiner examines the claimed subject matter to the extent possible and establishes a written opinion reflecting the inadequate support or other deficiencies (see paragraph 17.35).
guidance: Even after informal clarification by the applicant, objections on non-prior-art grounds remain in the written opinion because the claimed subject matter was and remains unclear absent such clarification. The written opinion should reflect inadequate support or other deficiencies for all or part of the claimed subject matter.

name: Need for clarification — defects in claim language
description: A need for clarification may arise where defects in the claims cause difficulty in determining scope, for example, obscure, inconsistent, vague or ambiguous expressions.
guidance: These defects include cases where claim language is not clear even after taking the description and drawings into account.

name: Search strategy for claims containing alternatives with unclear realizations
description: When claimed subject matter includes alternatives some of which are clear realizations and others unclear, the search examiner searches the clear realization; for unclear realizations the examiner determines the subject of search based on what might reasonably be expected to be claimed by amendment, taking into account the description, drawings and common general knowledge.
guidance: The written opinion and international preliminary examination report should establish opinions on novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability to the extent possible and explain why remainder could not be properly assessed. Examples: if claim is A+B+C+D and B is unclear, search to the extent possible; if an alternative is totally unclear so no reasonable subject can be determined, no search for that alternative is required.

name: Extent of search when part of claim is totally unclear
description: If an element of a claim is totally unclear such that it is impossible to determine subject matter that may reasonably be expected to be claimed, no search is performed for that portion; search may proceed for the rest.
guidance: Example: for (A1 or A2)+(B1 or B2), if A2 is totally unclear such that its reasonable scope cannot be determined, examiner need not search combinations involving A2 but should search combinations not involving the unclear alternative (e.g., A1+B1, A1+B2).

name: Independent claim containing references to multiple claims
description: An independent claim may also contain a reference to another claim and, where it contains a reference to more than one other claim and serves as a basis for a multiple dependent claim, the ISA may indicate under Article 17(2)(b) if national law does not allow that manner of drafting.
guidance: Such an indication should only be made if and to the extent a meaningful search is not possible and is noted in the written opinion.

name: Supplementary international search considerations
description: The considerations in the chapter (e.g., on unclear claims, exclusions, unity) apply in general to supplementary international searches under Rule 45bis, with additional limitations possible by authorities.
guidance: See specified paragraphs (15.76–15.97) for supplementary search specifics; authorities may apply additional limitations (paragraphs 15.87 and 15.88).

name: Unity of invention — single general inventive concept requirement
description: An international application should relate to only one invention or, if more than one, inclusion is permitted only if all inventions are so linked as to form a single general inventive concept (Rule 13.1). Unity exists when there is a technical relationship among claimed inventions involving one or more of the same or corresponding special technical features.
guidance: Special technical features are those technical features that define a contribution which each of the inventions, considered as a whole, makes over the prior art. Determination is made on the contents of the claims as interpreted in light of the description and drawings.

name: A priori vs a posteriori lack of unity
description: Lack of unity may be evident 'a priori' (before considering prior art) or 'a posteriori' (after considering prior art).
guidance: Example: independent claims A+X, A+Y, X+Y lack unity a priori; independent claims A+X and A+Y have unity a priori because A is common, but if A is known or obvious in the prior art, unity may be lacking a posteriori. Each case considered on merits; benefit of doubt to applicant; avoid narrow, literal or academic approaches.

name: Minimum reasoning methodology for assessing non-unitary subject-matter
description: Authority may apply the 'minimum reasoning' methodology: ascertain common/corresponding matter, explain why this matter cannot provide a single general inventive concept due to lack of same/corresponding special technical features, and explain why there is no technical relationship among the inventions, if not apparent.
guidance: Analysis may indicate non-common technical features and why claims are grouped, identify technical properties for each group demonstrated through features and explain differences; where appropriate (e.g., chemistry), explain structural or functional reasons claims are not similarly related. Examples provided in paragraphs 10.59E–10.59J.

name: Lack of unity a posteriori when independent claim does not avoid prior art
description: If an independent claim does not avoid the prior art, the examiner must consider whether there remains an inventive link among the claims dependent on that claim; absence of such link may justify an objection of lack of unity a posteriori.
guidance: This method is intended to be applied even before commencement of international search; initial unity determination based on assumption that claims avoid prior art may be reconsidered after search results.

name: Alternatives within single claim and Rule 13.3 implications
