description: Alternative forms of an invention may be claimed either in multiple independent claims or in a single claim; the same unity criteria apply and lack of unity may exist within a single claim if it contains distinct embodiments not linked by a single general inventive concept.
guidance: Rule 13.3 does not prevent an Authority from objecting to alternatives within a single claim on grounds such as clarity, conciseness of claims, or local claims fee systems.

name: Combination claims vs distinct embodiments (no unity objection normally)
description: Objection of lack of unity does not normally arise if a number of individual elements are claimed in a single claim (a combination) even if elements seem unrelated when considered individually.
guidance: Distinguish combination of elements from distinct embodiments presented as alternatives; unity objections target the latter where no single general inventive concept links alternatives.

name: Permissible combinations of different categories of claims (Rule 13.2 interpretation)
description: Permitted combinations include (i) product + process specially adapted for manufacture + use of product; (ii) process + apparatus specifically designed for carrying out the process; (iii) product + process specially adapted for its manufacture + apparatus specifically designed for the process.
guidance: A process is 'specially adapted' for manufacture if it inherently results in the product; an apparatus is 'specifically designed' if its contribution over prior art corresponds to the process's contribution. A single general inventive concept must link claims in various categories. Authorities should beware of proliferation of independent claims from combining provisions; accept such proliferation only exceptionally.

name: Meaning of 'specially adapted' and 'specifically designed'
description: 'Specially adapted' means the claimed process inherently results in the claimed product and implies a technical relationship between product and process (but does not mean alternate processes are impossible). 'Specifically designed' means the apparatus/means' contribution over prior art corresponds to the process's contribution (but does not imply apparatus cannot be used for other processes).
guidance: These definitions narrow when combinations qualify for unity under paragraph 10.12; they emphasize where the inventive emphasis resides (product vs process).

name: Markush practice — unity for alternatives (chemical/non-chemical)
description: A single claim defining alternatives ('Markush grouping') meets the unity requirement when the alternatives are of a similar nature.
guidance: For chemical compounds, 'similar nature' means: (A) all alternatives have a common property or activity, and (B) either (1) a common structure is present shared by all alternatives (a significant structural element or structurally distinctive portion essential to property/activity) or (2) all alternatives belong to a recognized class of chemical compounds in the art such that members are expected to behave similarly. Classification differences alone do not justify lack of unity. If at least one Markush alternative is not novel, unity should be reconsidered (though reconsideration does not necessarily mean an objection will be raised).

name: Unity of intermediate and final products
description: Unity is considered present between intermediate and final products where (A) the intermediate and final products have the same essential structural element (basic chemical structures the same or technically closely interrelated), and (B) they are technically interrelated meaning the final product is manufactured directly from the intermediate or via a small number of intermediates all containing the same essential structural element.
guidance: Unity may be recognized even when structures are unknown if sufficient evidence shows technical interrelation (e.g., intermediate incorporates essential element into final product). It is possible to accept different intermediates used in different processes for the final product provided they share the same essential structural element. Intermediates and final products must not be separated by an intermediate that is not new. For families of compounds, each intermediate compound must correspond to a compound claimed in the family of final products, though perfect congruence is not required.

name: Use of examples to illustrate unity assessment
description: The Guidelines provide numerous examples (Examples 1–39 and additional examples on lack of unity a posteriori) to illustrate applying unity principles in particular cases, including different claim categories, overlapping features, complementary forms, alternative forms, and dependent claims diverging from inventive concept.
guidance: Examine the provided examples (paragraphs 10.21–10.59A etc.) for practical application of principles such as combinations, Markush practice, intermediate/final products, and minimum reasoning methodology.

name: Patent Prosecution — definition and scope
description: Patent prosecution is the back-and-forth communication between you (the applicant) and the USPTO after filing. It includes: Responding to Office Actions; Amending claims; Explaining or arguing why your invention should be patentable; Continuing examination or appealing decisions if needed.
guidance: Understand prosecution as managing and negotiating your application with the examiner (note: 'prosecution' here is not criminal). Plan for iterative responses and possible appeals or continuations as part of strategy.

name: Non‑Final Office Action — characteristics and response deadline
description: The first formal response from the examiner: lists rejections (based on prior art or legal requirements) and may include technical objections (e.g., unclear language, improper claim structure). You have 3 months to respond (extendable to 6 months with fees).
guidance: Respond within the deadline or pay extension fees. Address both substantive rejections (e.g., prior art) and technical objections (e.g., claim clarity/format) in your response.

name: Final Office Action — limitations and subsequent options
description: If your first response doesn’t resolve all issues, the examiner will issue a final rejection. You still have options, but you can’t introduce new material or make unrestricted claim changes.
guidance: After a final action consider limited claim amendments, filing a continuing application, or appealing; avoid attempting to add new subject matter in response to a final rejection.

name: Permitted response methods and strategies
description: You can submit a written response that may include: Amending claims (e.g., to narrow them or add details); Arguments explaining how your invention differs from cited prior art; Declarations or technical evidence; Interviews with the examiner (optional but helpful).
guidance: Use claim amendments, clear legal and technical arguments, and evidentiary declarations where appropriate to overcome rejections. Examiner interviews can clarify issues and aid negotiation toward allowance.

name: Certified copy and translation for foreign-language international applications
description: Where benefit is claimed under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, 365(c), or 386(c) to an international application or international design application that designates but did not originate in the U.S., the Office may require a certified copy and an English translation if filed in another language.
guidance: Office discretion to request certified copy and translation when necessary.

name: Benefit under 35 U.S.C. 386(c) effective date limitation
description: Benefit under 35 U.S.C. 386(c) with respect to an international design application is applicable only to nonprovisional applications, international applications, and international design applications filed on or after May 13, 2015, and patents issuing thereon.
guidance: Do not claim 386(c) benefit for earlier filings.

name: Drawings cannot cure insufficiency of specification
description: Drawings submitted after the filing date may not be used to overcome any insufficiency of the specification due to lack of an enabling disclosure or otherwise inadequate disclosure, or to supplement the original disclosure for interpretation of the scope of any claim.
guidance: Do not rely on post-filing drawings to add new disclosure or amend the original enabling description.

name: Drawings must show every claimed feature
description: The drawing in a nonprovisional application must show every feature of the invention specified in the claims.
guidance: Conventional features whose detailed illustration is not essential may be illustrated by graphical symbols or labeled representations (e.g., labeled rectangular box). Tables and sequences included in the specification should not be duplicated in the drawings.

name: Photographs permitted only when practicable medium
description: Photographs (including photocopies) are not ordinarily permitted in utility and design applications but will be accepted if photographs are the only practicable medium for illustrating the claimed invention (e.g., gels, blots, micrographs, animals, plants, in vivo imaging, crystalline structures, or ornamental effects in design patents).
guidance: If the subject admits of illustration by a drawing, the examiner may require a drawing instead. Photographs must be of sufficient quality that all details are reproducible in the printed patent. Color photographs allowed only if color drawing/photo conditions are satisfied.

name: Views: types, grouping, separation, and prohibition of projection/center lines
description: Drawings must contain as many views as necessary (plan, elevation, section, perspective, detail views). All views must be grouped together, arranged without wasting space, clearly separated from one another, and must not be included on sheets containing specification, claims, or abstract. Views must not be connected by projection lines and must not contain center lines.
guidance: Waveforms of electrical signals may be connected by dashed lines to show relative timing. Views should be upright and readable when possible.

name: Required contents of an international application
description: An international application shall contain, as specified in the Treaty and the Regulations, a Request, a description, one or more claims, an abstract, and one or more drawings (where required). (PCT Art. 3(2) and Section 207 of the Administrative Instructions.)
guidance: All parts must conform to PCT requirements; drawings only when required for understanding. See related sections for form/content specifics (Request, description, claims, abstract, drawings).

name: Minimum elements required on filing
description: The international application must contain at least: (i) an indication that it is intended as an international application (PCT Rule 4.2); (ii) the designation of at least one Contracting State of the International Patent Cooperation Union (§ 1.432); (iii) the name of the applicant, as prescribed; (iv) a part which on the face of it appears to be a description; and (v) a part which on the face of it appears to be a claim. (PCT Art. 11(1)(iii))
guidance: These minimal elements suffice to obtain an international filing date; include clear parts so they visibly resemble a description and a claim.

name: Description content and best mode requirement (US designation)
description: The application must meet the requirements as to the content and form of the description set forth in PCT Rules 5, 9, 10, and 11 and Administrative Instructions sections 204 and 208. In international applications designating the United States the description must contain upon filing an indication of the best mode contemplated by the inventor for carrying out the claimed invention.
guidance: Comply with PCT content/form rules. For US designation, disclose the best mode on filing to meet the US-specific requirement.

name: Refund conditions and time limits
description: Any request for refund must be filed within two years from the date the fee was paid. If the Office charges a deposit account by an amount other than specifically indicated, refund requests based on such charge must be filed within two years from the deposit account statement date and include a copy of that statement. Time periods are not extendable.
guidance: Preserve payment records and act within two years for refund claims; include necessary documentation.

name: Restoration of right of priority (unintentional delay)
description: If the international filing date is later than the expiration of the priority period but within two months from that expiration, the right of priority may be restored upon request if the delay in filing was unintentional. The request must be filed not later than two months from the expiration of the priority period and must include a notice adding the priority claim if not contained, the petition fee (§1.17(m)), and a statement that the delay was unintentional. The Director may require additional information.
guidance: Restoration is available only for unintentional delays within the two-month window and requires fee and supporting statements; early publication requests can affect timing considerations.

name: Corrections and amendments during international processing
description: All corrections submitted to the US RO or US ISA must be in English, in the form of replacement sheets in compliance with PCT Rules 10 and 11, and accompanied by a letter drawing attention to differences between replaced and replacement sheets. Replacement sheets are not required for deletion of lines, correction of simple typographical errors, and one addition/change of not more than five words per sheet; such minor changes may be stated in a letter and, if appropriate, the US RO will make the deletion or transfer the correction provided such corrections do not adversely affect clarity and direct reproducibility. Amendments not complying with PCT Rules 10 and 11.1–11.13 may not be entered. Amendments of claims submitted to the IB shall be as prescribed by PCT Rule 46. Corrections/additions to the Request or declarations under PCT Rule 4.17 should be submitted to the IB as prescribed by PCT Rule 26ter.
guidance: Use replacement sheets for substantive corrections; minor typographical adjustments can be handled by letter subject to clarity constraints; nonconforming amendments will be refused.

name: Unity of invention requirement
description: An international and a national stage application shall relate to one invention only or to a group of inventions so linked as to form a single general inventive concept. Unity is fulfilled only when there is a technical relationship among the inventions involving one or more of the same or corresponding special technical features. 'Special technical features' are those that define a contribution which each claimed invention makes over the prior art. Combinations of categories that are accepted as having unity are limited to specific enumerated groupings (e.g., product + process specially adapted to manufacture that product; process + apparatus designed to carry out the process; product + process of use of product; etc.).
guidance: Draft claims and claim sets to demonstrate a single general inventive concept or to fall within the permitted category combinations; otherwise lack of unity objections and additional fees may follow.

name: Determination of unity by the International Searching Authority and consequences
description: Before establishing the international search report, the ISA will determine whether the application complies with the unity requirement. If ISA considers application lacks unity it shall inform the applicant and invite payment of additional fees (PCT Art.17 and Rule 40). The applicant is given a time period per PCT Rule 40.3 to pay additional fees. If no additional fees are paid, the international search will be performed only on the invention first mentioned ('main invention') in the claims. Lack of unity may be evident before considering the claims in relation to prior art or after taking prior art into account; ISA may raise the objection when prior art shows lack of common inventive concept.
guidance: Anticipate possible unity objections; consider structuring claims or being prepared to pay additional search fees or protest the objection.

name: Liability for damages caused by interlocutory relief (Article 302 CPC)
description: A party is liable for damage caused by the effectiveness of interlocutory relief if: I) the judgment is unfavorable to them; II) the party fails to provide means for service within five days after obtaining advance interlocutory relief; III) the effectiveness of the measure is ceased; or IV) the judge accepts preemption or limitation of plaintiff’s claim.
guidance: Liability applies regardless of redress for procedural damage; security or guarantee requirements exist to mitigate this risk.

name: Limits of judge’s cognizance and preclusion (pleading phase)
description: The judge’s cognizance on matters of fact and law is defined during the pleading phase; parties have the burden to discharge procedural burden by clearly indicating theories and evidence under penalty of procedural preclusion. If plaintiff fails to make claim adequately, judge’s cognizance limited to what was requested (Article 141 CPC).
guidance: Pre-trial order defines disputed points and binds the judgment. Failure to present facts/arguments in pleading phase may preclude later raising of those matters.

name: Amendment restrictions: correspondence-to-OEE-allowed-claims requirement
description: The PPH program only permits amendments that sufficiently correspond in scope to the allowable claims of an earlier-examined (OEE) application.
guidance: USPTO guidance (Official Gazette, 2014) explains that a U.S. claim that is narrower than OEE-allowable claims can 'sufficiently correspond' if presented as a dependent claim upon a claim of same/similar scope, and narrowing occurs when an OEE claim is amended to be further limited by an additional feature supported by the U.S. specification. Examiners may refuse narrowing amendments in certain situations (e.g., newly cited prior art requiring claim changes), and some examiners may impose amendment guidelines not present in non-PPH cases. Expect significantly reduced flexibility to amend claims during prosecution.

name: Certification requirement for claim correspondence
description: Applicants must provide a certification that any amended or newly added claims sufficiently correspond to allowable claims of the OEE application or narrow those claims.
guidance: Failure to provide the required certification may result in a notice of noncompliant amendment; if not remedied, this could lead to abandonment of the U.S. application. Ensure procedural compliance when submitting amendments in PPH cases; include the explicit statement/certification as required.

name: Potential for additional downstream cost (continuation practice) if amendments don't correspond
description: If desired amendments do not result in a narrower claim or do not sufficiently correspond to the allowed claims in the corresponding foreign application, a continuation application may be the only option, which can increase overall prosecution cost and may outweigh PPH cost savings.
guidance: When planning prosecution strategy, model scenarios where later claim changes are needed; the need to file continuations to regain flexibility can negate the immediate cost savings from PPH. Consider filing strategy, portfolio needs, and budget for potential follow-on filings.

name: Tradeoff assessment: flexibility versus efficiency
description: Although the PPH program offers efficiency and slightly higher allowance rates, applicants must consider whether flexibility (ability to amend claims broadly during prosecution) is more important than efficiency for a particular application.
guidance: This is the central decision criterion: weigh speed/cost/allowance benefits against amendment limits, certification burdens, inability to withdraw, and potential for later continuation costs. Use case-specific factors (portfolio strategy, likelihood of required claim changes, commercialization timelines) to decide.

name: Eligibility and procedural prerequisites for participating in PPH
description: PPH participation requires that the U.S. application correspond to an application in a participating patent office (OEE) and meet the program’s specific requirements for expedited examination.
guidance: Consult USPTO PPH program guidance and the listed FAQ/statistics documents to confirm eligibility, documentary requirements, and any region-specific rules before filing a PPH petition. Ensure claim correspondence, file necessary certifications, and confirm participating offices.

name: All claim limitations must be considered when judging patentability
description: "All words in a claim must be considered in judging the patentability of that claim against the prior art." If an independent claim is nonobvious under 35 U.S.C. 103, then claims depending therefrom are nonobvious.
guidance: Cite In re Wilson; also In re Fine re: dependence. Do not ignore claim language or selectively compare only some claim limitations to the prior art.

name: Indefinite claim limitations must be considered and cannot simply be disregarded
description: A claim limitation which is considered indefinite cannot be disregarded. If a claim admits more than one interpretation, and at least one interpretation renders the claim unpatentable over the prior art, the examiner should reject the claim as indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, and should also reject over the prior art based on the interpretation that renders the prior art applicable.
guidance: See Ex parte Ionescu (claims reversed as indefinite only); compare In re Wilson and In re Steele. Do not rely on speculative assumptions about claim meaning when making a 103 rejection.

name: Rationale different from applicant's stated purpose is permissible
description: It is not necessary that the prior art suggest the combination to achieve the same advantage or result discovered by applicant; motivation to combine can be based on a general problem rather than the specific problem solved by the inventor.
guidance: The prior art need not address the identical problem to motivate combination (In re Kahn; Cross Med. Prods. v. Medtronic; In re Linter; In re Dillon). Show that the art provided motivation to make the claimed compositions or combinations in expectation of similar properties or benefits.

name: Aesthetic design changes: ornamentation without mechanical function generally not patentable distinction
description: Matters relating to ornamentation alone, which have no mechanical function, generally cannot be relied upon to patentably distinguish the claimed invention from the prior art.
guidance: However, courts have found exceptions where shape/ornamentation produces a product distinct from the reference (Ex parte Hilton). Evaluate whether ornamentation yields a functional or patentably significant difference.

name: Omission of an element and its function is obvious if the element's function is not desired
description: Deletion of an element (and thereby its function) from a prior art reference is an obvious expedient where the function attributed to such element is not desired or required in the claimed context.
guidance: Examples: Ex parte Wu (omitting polybasic acid salts where their function not needed in certain environments); In re Larson; In re Kuhle. Show that omission would have been an expected design choice where the function was unnecessary.

name: Omission of an element with retention of the element's function is an indicia of unobviousness
description: If an element is omitted from a claimed invention but the function of that element is nonetheless retained (by other features), that omission can indicate unobviousness.
guidance: Example: In re Edge (elimination of intermediate layer while retaining its protective function by alternative structure supported unobviousness). Consider whether eliminating an element while preserving function shows insight contrary to the art's expectations.

name: Required subjects for discovery conference
description: The discovery conference shall discuss the subjects set forth in Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f) and any subjects set forth in the Board's institution order, including nature/basis of claims and defenses, settlement possibilities, preservation of discoverable information, and arrangements relating to disclosures, discovery, and introduction of evidence at trial.
guidance: Also discuss ACR, mediation/arbitration options, whether to alter disclosure or discovery procedures (including the Standard Protective Order), limitations on discovery, and stipulations to facilitate introduction of discovery materials at trial.

name: Contents of initial disclosures — witnesses
description: A party must provide the name and, if known, the address and telephone number of each individual likely to have discoverable information — along with the subjects of that information — that the disclosing party may use to support its claims or defenses (Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a)(1)(A)(i)).
guidance: Not every possible witness must be listed — only those likely to have discoverable information the party may use to support claims/defenses. If a trial witness is identified, provide subject matter and known contact information.

name: Contents of initial disclosures — documents and ESI
description: A party must provide a copy — or a description by category and location — of all documents, electronically stored information, and tangible things that the disclosing party has in its possession, custody, or control and may use to support its claims or defenses (Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a)(1)(A)(ii)).
guidance: Parties may either identify location or produce copies; the Board encourages actual exchange of copies rather than merely identifying location. ESI must be identified in initial disclosures where pertinent.

name: Initial disclosures are not exhaustive; standard for disclosure
description: Initial disclosures are intended to prompt routine disclosure of names of potential witnesses and basic information about documents and things that a party may use to support a claim or defense, not to substitute for all discovery.
guidance: A party need not identify every witness/document that may have discoverable information, only those it may use to support claims/defenses. Nevertheless, parties may stipulate (with Board approval) to rely on reciprocal disclosures in lieu of formal discovery.

name: Iterative prompting and demonstrable human effort as evidence
description: Repeatedly revising prompts and iterating many times (including hundreds of iterations) can demonstrate greater human control and significant human effort, potentially supporting an authorship claim.
guidance: Consider amount of iteration, demonstrable human decision-making in refining outputs, and whether iteration produced control over expressive elements. But iterative prompting may still be compared to roulette/spinning where unpredictability undermines authorship claims.

name: Black-box unpredictability undermines claim of control
description: Because many generative AI systems are 'black boxes' whose internal workings and decision processes are not transparent or predictable, it is difficult to show that a prompt deterministically produced specific expressive elements.
guidance: Consider lack of predictability and explainability when assessing whether a user's prompts meaningfully controlled the expressive outcome; inability to explain why certain elements appeared is evidence against authorial control.

name: Specific petition contents for 37 CFR 1.55(c)
description: A petition under 37 CFR 1.55(c) requires: (A) the priority claim in an application data sheet identifying the foreign application by application number, country (or intellectual property authority), day, month, and year of its filing (unless previously submitted); (B) the petition fee set forth in 37 CFR 1.17(m); and (C) a statement that the delay in filing the subsequent application within the twelve-month period (or six-month period for a design application) was unintentional.
guidance: The Director may require additional information where there is a question whether the delay was unintentional.

name: Circumstances where Office may require earlier filing or translation (37 CFR 1.55(g)(2)–(3))
description: The Office may require that the claim for priority and the certified copy be filed earlier than otherwise provided when: (i) the application is involved in an interference or derivation proceeding; (ii) when necessary to overcome the date of a reference relied upon by the examiner; or (iii) when deemed necessary by the examiner. An English language translation of a non-English foreign application is not required except in those same circumstances or when specifically required by the examiner.
guidance: If translation is required, it must be a translation of the certified copy and must be filed together with a statement that the translation of the certified copy is accurate.

name: Treatment of late or unintentionally delayed priority claims (37 CFR 1.55(d) & (e))
description: Claims for foreign priority not presented within the time period specified in 37 CFR 1.55 are considered waived. A claim presented after the time period may be accepted if it includes the required identification information and is accompanied by a grantable petition to accept the unintentionally delayed claim for priority.
guidance: See MPEP § 214.02 for procedural treatment of unintentionally delayed priority claims and the specific petition content and fee requirements.

name: Multiple priority claims rule
description: If more than one priority right is claimed for an application, priority commences from the date of the first valid priority right.
guidance: Procedural details are determined by regulation.

name: Other causes and effects of termination (surrender, expiry, withdrawal)
description: Trademark rights terminate by expiry of the protection term without renewal, or by surrender by the proprietor. Termination takes effect when the cause occurs. Proprietors may surrender all or part of the registered goods/services in writing; surrender takes effect on entry in the register and is published.
guidance: Marks cannot be surrendered without consent of recorded licensees or registered right owners, and cannot be surrendered if a third party claims rights and an interlocutory injunction is recorded. Applications may be withdrawn before registration, and surrender-withdrawal provisions apply similarly.

name: Step 1: Statutory Category Determination
description: Is the claim to a process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter? Evaluation of this step should be made after determining what applicant has invented by reviewing the entire application disclosure and construing the claims in accordance with their broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI).
guidance: Outcomes: If the claim as a whole does not fall within any statutory category (Step 1: NO) the claim is non-statutory and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 (use form paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01). If the claim as a whole falls within one or more statutory categories (Step 1: YES), proceed to analyze eligibility at Pathway A or Step 2A. Examiner should review the entire disclosure and apply BRI (see MPEP §2106, §2111) before concluding.

name: BRI covering both statutory and non-statutory embodiments
description: A claim whose BRI covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments embraces subject matter that is not eligible for patent protection and therefore is directed to non-statutory subject matter.
guidance: If BRI encompasses both statutory and non-statutory embodiments (e.g., machine-readable media covering both compact disc and transitory carrier waves), the claim fails Step 1 (Step 1: NO) and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101. Best practice: examiner should point out the BRI and recommend an amendment to narrow the claim to statutory embodiments if possible.

name: Step 2A: Whether a claim is directed to a judicial exception (recite vs involve)
description: Step 2A asks: Is the claim directed to a law of nature, a natural phenomenon (product of nature) or an abstract idea? A claim is directed to a judicial exception when a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea is recited (set forth or described) in the claim.
guidance: Recite means the exception is set forth or described in claim language (examples: Diehr's explicit equation; Mayo's wherein clause). If the claim as a whole is not directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: NO) it is eligible at Pathway B; if it is directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: YES) it requires further analysis at Step 2B to determine whether the claim amounts to significantly more than the exception itself. Consider the claim as a whole when performing Step 2A.

name: Do not parse a recited exception into multiple exceptions
description: Unless it is clear that the claim recites distinct exceptions, care should be taken not to parse a recited exception into multiple exceptions, particularly in claims involving abstract ideas.
guidance: For example, multiple mental-step manipulations of information should be considered a single abstract idea rather than multiple separate abstract ideas. However, if a claim recites multiple exceptions it is directed to at least one judicial exception and must be analyzed in Step 2B.

name: Identify the claimed concept and compare to court-identified abstract ideas
description: Examiners should determine whether a claim recites an abstract idea by (1) identifying the claimed concept (the specific claim limitation(s) the examiner believes may be an abstract idea), and (2) comparing the claimed concept to concepts previously identified as abstract ideas by the courts.
guidance: If the claimed concept is similar to one or more concepts previously identified as abstract ideas by the courts, conclude it is an abstract idea (Step 2A: YES) and proceed to Step 2B. If not similar and no basis to conclude it is an abstract idea, find Step 2A: NO and the claim is eligible at Pathway B unless it recites another exception. Use comparisons to precedent (e.g., Alice, Bilski, Flook) rather than judicial descriptors alone.

name: Claims that are improvements in computer functionality or other technology are not abstract
description: Some inventions pertaining to improvements in computer functionality or to improvements in other technologies are not abstract when appropriately claimed, and thus may be eligible at Step 2A.
guidance: Critical considerations: the specification should disclose sufficient details so a skilled artisan recognizes the claimed invention as providing an improvement; the claim itself must reflect the improvement (covers a particular solution or particular way to achieve an outcome rather than merely claiming the idea). Examiners must give the claim its BRI and evaluate both claim and specification. Examples of eligible claims include Enfish (self-referential table), McRO (automatic lip synchronization rules), Visual Memory (enhanced memory system).

name: Limitations on 'improvement' arguments (caveats)
description: Not every addition of a computer renders a claim an improvement in computer functionality.
guidance: If a claimed process can be performed without a computer, it cannot be characterized as an improvement in a computer. Mere automation of manual processes or increasing speed solely from a general-purpose computer's capabilities is insufficient to show an improvement. Mere implementation on conventional or generic components does not qualify. Examiners should consult MPEP §2106.05(a) for cases where claims did not reflect an improvement.

name: Resolve improvement questions early when possible
description: Although the question of whether a claim improves computer-functionality or other technology may be considered in either Step 2A or Step 2B, examiners are encouraged to resolve this question as early as possible in the eligibility analysis.
guidance: If a claim is clearly an improvement in technology (e.g., Enfish), it may be eligible at Pathway A under streamlined analysis or at Pathway B as not directed to an abstract idea. If unclear at Step 2A, the improvement may still contribute to eligibility under Step 2B.

name: Recitation requirement: involving vs reciting an abstract idea
description: If a claim is based on or involves an abstract idea, but does not recite it, then the claim is not directed to an abstract idea.
guidance: Examples: claims that are based on organizing information using a tabular format or that modify internet hyperlink protocol to produce a hybrid webpage may involve abstract ideas but not recite them, and thus are not directed to abstract ideas (see Enfish, DDR Holdings). Non-limiting hypotheticals (printer, washing machine, earring sensor, BRCA1 sequencing method, BIOS loading method) illustrate claims that do not set forth or describe an abstract idea.

name: Claims that recite an abstract idea but as a whole are directed to an improvement or do not tie up the abstract idea
description: If a claim recites an abstract idea, but the claim as a whole is directed to an improvement or otherwise clearly does not seek to tie up the abstract idea, then the claim is not directed to an abstract idea.
guidance: Even when a recitation of an abstract idea occurs, the overall claim may be eligible if it amounts to significantly more than the abstract idea (Step 2B analysis). The specification and claim must show a specific improvement or inventive concept that prevents preemption of the abstract idea.

name: Photographs: when acceptable and quality requirements
description: Photographs (including photocopies) are not ordinarily permitted but will be accepted when photographs are the only practicable medium to illustrate the claimed invention.
guidance: Examples where photographs are acceptable: electrophoresis gels, blots, autoradiographs, cell cultures, histological sections, animals, plants, in vivo imaging, TLC plates, crystalline structures, and ornamental effects in design applications. If the subject admits of illustration by a drawing, the examiner may require a drawing instead. Photographs must be of sufficient quality so all details are reproducible in the printed patent. Color photographs are accepted only if the conditions for color drawings (see 37 CFR 1.84(a)(2)) and black & white photograph criteria are satisfied.

name: Detailed description requirement (enablement and written description)
description: The detailed description required by 37 CFR 1.71 must be in such particularity as to enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the invention without extensive experimentation and must clearly convey enough information to show the applicant invented the claimed subject matter.
guidance: Applicant may use their own terminology if understandable; examiner may require necessary grammatical corrections but not perfect grammar. Reference characters must be applied properly (no single reference used for two different parts or for a part and its modification; see 37 CFR 1.84(p)). Every feature in the claims should be illustrated, and there should be no superfluous illustrations. The description functions as a 'dictionary' for the claims and must provide clear support/antecedent basis for all terms used in the claims. Cross-references: 37 CFR 1.71, MPEP §§ 608.01, 2161, 2162, 608.01(i),(o), § 1302.01, § 2111.01.

name: Statutory requirement of claims (35 U.S.C. 112)
description: The specification must conclude with a claim particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the applicant regards as the invention.
guidance: Claims are the definition of the protection granted; this statutory requirement underlies claim examination and rejections/objections.

name: Dependent claims: form and limitations (including multiple dependent claims)
description: One or more claims may be presented in dependent form, referring back to and further limiting another claim; a multiple dependent claim that refers to more than one other claim must refer to such claims in the alternative only and shall not serve as a basis for any other multiple dependent claim.
guidance: For fee calculation purposes, a multiple dependent claim is considered to be the number of claims to which direct reference is made. Any claim depending from a multiple dependent claim is considered likewise. Multiple dependent claims must be alternative (e.g., 'according to claims 3 or 4'); cumulative claiming ('claims 3 and 4') is improper. A multiple dependent claim may not refer to claims of different sets (e.g., cannot mix apparatus and process claim sets). If a multiple dependent claim depends from another multiple dependent claim, it should be objected to. See 35 U.S.C. 112(e) and 37 CFR 1.75(c).

name: Claims must conform to the specification and have antecedent basis
description: Claims must conform to the invention as set forth in the remainder of the specification and the terms and phrases used in the claims must find clear support or antecedent basis in the description so that their meaning may be ascertained by reference to the description (see § 1.58(a)).
guidance: Where subject matter not shown in drawing or description is claimed, but the original claim itself constitutes a clear disclosure, the claim should not be objected to merely because drawing/description lack that subject matter; rather the drawing/description should be amended to show it. However, if the claim does not provide its own descriptive disclosure and the subject matter is not shown/described, reject under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) for inadequate written description.

name: Recommended claim structure for improvement-type inventions
description: Where the nature of the case admits (e.g., an improvement), any independent claim should contain, in order: (1) a preamble listing conventional/known elements or steps; (2) a phrase such as 'wherein the improvement comprises,' and (3) the elements/steps/relationships constituting the new or improved portion.
guidance: This ordering helps clarify what is conventional versus claimed improvement; follow as appropriate for improvement claims.

name: Claim formatting and punctuation conventions
description: Each claim should be the object of a sentence starting with 'I (or we) claim,' 'The invention claimed is' (or equivalent), begin with a capital letter and end with a period; periods may not be used elsewhere except for abbreviations. Where a claim sets forth plurality of elements/steps, each element/step should be separated by a line indentation (37 CFR 1.75(i)).
guidance: Reference characters corresponding to elements may be used in claims but should be enclosed in parentheses to avoid confusion. There may be plural indentations to segregate subcombinations. Printing limitations may alter complex formats. Examiners may object to claims with crowded lines (use form paragraph 7.29.03) or missing parentheses around reference characters (7.29.02).

name: Arrangement of claims to facilitate examination
description: Claims should preferably be arranged in order of scope with the least restrictive claim presented first; dependent claims should be grouped with the claim(s) to which they refer; separate species, product and process claims should be grouped where possible.
guidance: Such arrangements facilitate classification and examination. Presenting claims by scope and grouping like claims reduces prosecution difficulties post-final rejection.

name: Duplicate claims practice
description: When two claims comply with 35 U.S.C. 112(d) but are duplicates or so close that they cover the same thing, it is proper after allowing one claim to object to the other as being a substantial duplicate.
guidance: Use form paragraph 7.05.05 to warn of duplicate claims (if not allowable) and 7.05.06 to object when duplicate. Examiner notes: give applicant opportunity to correct; if claims are allowable, use different paragraph. Dependent claims that do not specify a further limitation should be rejected with form paragraphs 7.36 and 7.36.01 rather than merely warned as duplicates.

name: Examiner handling of claims referring to numerically following claims
description: If dependent claims refer to numerically succeeding claims, examiners should object and not treat such claims on the merits if the reference cannot be understood; however, if dependency is clear (as presented and as it will be renumbered for issue), all claims should be examined on the merits and an examiner's amendment prepared if order changes.
guidance: Bring unusual problems to supervisor. Examples provided showing when to object (Example A) and when to examine and renumber (Example B). Ensure each Office action explicitly states what rejection/objection/requirement applies to each claim embodiment as required by 35 U.S.C. 132.

name: Identification practice for embodiments in multiple dependent claims
description: When referring to embodiments included in multiple dependent claims, identify each embodiment by claim numbers involved (starting with highest) as needed; when all embodiments are subject to a common rejection/objection, reference may be made only to the dependent claim number.
guidance: Table illustrates approved practice for identifying claims and embodiments. Follow guidance (A),(B),(C) in examiner practice for clarity in Office actions.

name: Handling and processing responsibilities for multiple dependent claims (OPAP, TC, Examiner)
description: OPAP verifies whether multiple dependent claims filed with the application are in proper alternative form and calculates filing fee implications; Technology Center (TC) technical support verifies compliance with statute/rules for multiple dependent claims added by amendment and calculates additional fees; examiners follow statutory rules in treating multiple dependent claims and object to improper forms.
guidance: OPAP uses form PTO/SB/07 in conjunction with PTO/SB/06 for fee calculation; TC staff will place PTO/SB/07 in file when multiple dependent claims are added later. If multiple dependent claim added without proper fee, amendment should not be entered until fee received; applicant should be contacted to pay additional fee; include copy of fee calculation form when notifying applicant of insufficient fee. If TC notes improper reference in added/amended multiple dependent claim, indicate by encircling numeral '1' in 'Dep. Claim' column on PTO/SB/07 to call examiner attention. Examiner must treat each claim embodiment individually (all claims should be examined).

name: Reference characters usage
description: Reference characters must be properly applied; no single reference character should be used for two different parts or for a given part and its modification.
guidance: See 37 CFR 1.84(p). Reference characters used in claims should be enclosed within parentheses to avoid confusion (object if not enclosed — form paragraph 7.29.02). Improper use may render claim indefinite; if so, use form paragraph 7.34.01 to reject under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) rather than just pointing out minor informalities.

name: Excess claims fees must fund examination time
description: Support increases in excess-claims fees only if the public receives assurance that increased fees will be spent on examination and/or giving examiners additional time to evaluate such cases.
guidance: Fee justification should be clear: applicants paying more for larger claim sets should result in direct additional examination resources.

name: Waiver of patent rights upon SIR publication and its impact
description: Waiver of patent rights to subject matter claimed in a SIR takes effect on publication and may affect patentability of claims in related applications; waiver applies to any inventions claimed in the SIR and may preclude patenting by the same inventor in related applications.
guidance: Examiners should apply standards similar to 'same invention' double patenting determinations to decide if waiver precludes patenting. Rejection due to waiver cannot be overcome by a terminal disclaimer. The holder of a SIR cannot file a reissue to recapture waived rights.

name: Basis of the patent application publication (what is published)
description: The publication will be based upon the specification and drawings deposited on the filing date of the application, the application data sheet and/or the inventor's oath/declaration; it may also include timely amendments to the specification (other than abstract/claims), amendments to abstract, complete claim listings, and amended drawings if submitted in time for technical preparation.
guidance: Applicants may provide an electronic copy (EFS) of the amended application within one month of the first Office communication including a confirmation number or within fourteen months of earliest filing date, whichever is later, to have the publication based on the amended copy. The Office will attempt to use applicant-submitted amendments but cannot guarantee inclusion.

name: Guidance to avoid preliminary amendments at filing
description: Applicants should not file preliminary amendments with the application; submitting no preliminary amendment reduces Office processing and helps ensure publications are printed correctly. A preliminary amendment present on filing is part of the original disclosure and may require substitute specification if not in a publishable format.
guidance: Where desired amendments exist, applicants should incorporate them into the text of the specification (including a new claim set) rather than submitting preliminary amendments. For continuation/divisional applications, new specification plus reference to prior oath/declaration may be used if no new matter is introduced.

name: Applicant and examiner treatment of entered third‑party submissions
description: After a compliant third‑party submission is entered, the applicant (where participating in e-Office Action) will be notified and the contents will be made available via private PAIR; the examiner should consider the listed publications and concise descriptions generally before issuing the next Office action, treating them similarly to an IDS.
guidance: The examiner should sign PTO/SB/429 to indicate consideration, clear the IDS flag in PALM, and provide a signed copy with the next Office action. The examiner’s signature indicates consideration only, not agreement with the third party's view. There is no need for the examiner to comment on concise descriptions in the Office action, but may apply the information as needed (e.g., rejecting claims).

name: Compact prosecution — review all statutory requirements in initial review
description: Each claim should be reviewed for compliance with every statutory requirement for patentability in the initial review of the application, even if one or more claims are found to be deficient with respect to some statutory requirement.
guidance: USPTO personnel should state all reasons and bases for rejecting claims in the first Office action. Deficiencies should be explained clearly, indicate how rejections may be overcome when practicable, and show how problems may be resolved to avoid unnecessary delays.

name: Determine what applicant has invented and seeks to patent
description: Prior to focusing on statutory requirements, examiners must determine precisely what the applicant has invented and is seeking to patent, and how the claims relate to and define that invention.
guidance: Review the complete specification (including detailed description and embodiments), the claims, and any asserted specific, substantial, and credible utilities. Correlate claim limitations to disclosure to ensure correct interpretation.

name: Review the claims and analyze claim scope thoroughly
description: Claims define the property rights provided by a patent and require careful scrutiny to identify boundaries of protection and how they relate to what applicant indicates is the invention.
guidance: Identify and evaluate each claim limitation; for processes identify steps, for products identify structures/materials. Correlate each claim limitation to all portions of the disclosure that describe it, including means/step-plus-function language. Consider the claim as a whole, not dissecting into isolated elements.

name: Give claims the broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the disclosure
description: USPTO personnel are to give claims their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the supporting disclosure (including express, implicit, or inherent disclosure).
guidance: Interpret means-plus-function limitations broadly but consistent with corresponding structures/materials and their equivalents in the specification. Use broad interpretation to reduce later overbroad claim construction; applicants may amend claims to reflect intended scope.

name: Do not import positive limitations from the specification into claims
description: While the specification can determine intended meaning of terms, a positive limitation from the specification cannot be read into a claim that does not itself impose that limitation.
guidance: A claim should be interpreted according to its grammar and intended meaning; only claim language limits scope unless claim is amended. See cited cases for examples.

name: Examples of language that may not be limiting in a claim
description: Certain phrases often raise questions about whether they limit claim scope, such as statements of intended use or field of use, 'adapted to'/'adapted for' clauses, 'wherein' clauses, and 'whereby' clauses.
guidance: Determination of whether particular language is limiting depends on specific facts; these examples are not exhaustive. See MPEP §§ 2111.02 and 2111.04 and case law (e.g., Griffin v. Bertina).

name: Consider the claim as a whole; avoid dissecting claimed invention into elements in isolation
description: Every limitation in the claim must be considered together; do not evaluate elements in isolation because a new combination of known steps may be patentable even if constituents were known.
guidance: See Diamond v. Diehr: appropriate to treat claims as whole when assessing patentability.

name: Conduct a thorough prior art search prior to 35 U.S.C. 101 analysis
description: Before evaluating claims under 35 U.S.C. 101, examiners are expected to conduct a thorough search of prior art (both U.S. and foreign patents and nonpatent literature) to aid understanding of the invention and to inform eligibility analysis.
guidance: Search both claimed and unclaimed aspects if there is reasonable expectation those aspects may be later claimed. Include structures/materials and equivalents corresponding to means-plus-function limitations (35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph).

name: Utility requirement — specific, substantial, and credible utility
description: A claimed invention must be useful or have utility that is specific, substantial and credible.
guidance: See MPEP § 2107 for detailed utility exam guidance. Utility must be such that a person of ordinary skill understands why the applicant believes the claimed invention is useful.

name: Adequate written description requirement (35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph)
description: The specification must reasonably convey to those skilled in the art that the applicant was in possession of the claimed invention as of the date of invention.
guidance: See MPEP § 2163 for standards, typical circumstances that raise issues, and burden on examiner. Written description ties claim scope to disclosure.

name: Enablement requirement (35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph)
description: The specification must enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
guidance: Consider working examples, predictability of the art, quantity of experimentation, and evidence as a whole. Enablement must be commensurate in scope with the claims. See MPEP § 2164 et seq.

name: 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph — definiteness and identification of invention
description: Second paragraph requires that claims set forth the subject matter applicants regard as their invention and particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention (definiteness).
guidance: Definiteness is analyzed in light of the specification as interpreted by one of ordinary skill. If admissions indicate applicant regards the invention differently from claims, reject under § 112 second paragraph. See MPEP § 2171-§ 2172.01 and § 2173 et seq.

name: Means/step-plus-function limitations — scope under 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph
description: Means or step-plus-function claim limitations are interpreted to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and their equivalents.
guidance: Give such limitations their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with corresponding structures in the specification and equivalents. If the disclosure is so broad that equivalents would encompass any means for performing the function, applicant may be required to demonstrate that claims are truly drawn to specific apparatus distinct from other apparatus capable of performing identical functions. See MPEP § 2181–§ 2186.

name: If nonequivalence is shown, examiner must still consider obviousness
description: Even when applicant shows that a prior art element is not equivalent to a claimed means/step, the examiner must determine whether the claim limitation is obvious under 35 U.S.C. 103.
guidance: A finding of nonequivalence prevents anticipation but does not prevent a 103 rejection. The examiner may rely on multiple references or alternative grounds where prior art elements differ yet perform the claimed function.

name: 35 U.S.C. 102 novelty analysis — compare claimed subject matter to prior art
description: Review begins with comparison of claimed subject matter to what is known in the prior art; if no differences are found, the claimed invention lacks novelty and is to be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102.
guidance: See MPEP § 2131 - § 2146 for specific guidance on anticipation and prior art categories (patents, publications, public use, on sale, applications as prior art, critical reference dates, etc.).

name: 35 U.S.C. 103 obviousness analysis — factors and prima facie case
description: To determine obviousness, assess scope/content of prior art, differences between prior art and claimed invention, and level of ordinary skill in the art to determine whether a prima facie case of obviousness exists.
guidance: Consider suggestion/motivation to modify references, reasonable expectation of success, that all claim limitations must be considered, and support rejections with rationale including implicit disclosure, scientific theory, common knowledge, or legal precedent. Consider applicant rebuttal arguments. See MPEP § 2131-§ 2146.

name: Search scope should include unclaimed aspects reasonably likely to be claimed later
description: A search must take into account any structure or material described in the specification and its equivalents which correspond to claimed means-plus-function limitations, and both claimed and unclaimed aspects should be searched if reasonably expected to be later claimed.
guidance: This ensures later claims are not allowed that the examiner could have identified earlier; search both patents and nonpatent literature.

name: Avoid overreliance on § 101 eligibility to the detriment of §§ 102, 103, 112
description: 35 U.S.C. 101 is a threshold test but not the sole tool for determining patentability; where a claim encompasses an abstract idea, 35 U.S.C. 112, 102, and 103 provide additional tools to ensure compliance.
guidance: Examiners should consider all statutory requirements and not treat an application solely on § 101 grounds except in the most extreme cases.

name: Exception for examiner's amendments
description: Changes to the specification, including the claims, of an application made by the Office in an examiner’s amendment may be made by specific instructions to insert or delete subject matter set forth in the examiner’s amendment by identifying the precise point in the specification or the claim(s) where the insertion or deletion is to be made.
guidance: Compliance with the normal claimant-amendment form requirements (e.g., paragraphs (b)(1), (b)(2), (c)(1)) is not required for examiner's amendments; the examiner can direct precise insertions/deletions as part of an examiner's amendment.

name: Amendment of amendments (replacement paragraphs/sections)
description: When a replacement paragraph or section to the specification is to be amended, it should be wholly rewritten and the original insertion canceled, so that no interlineations or deletions shall appear in the clause as finally presented.
guidance: Matter canceled by amendment can be reinstated only by a subsequent amendment presenting the canceled matter as a new insertion. A claim canceled by amendment can be reinstated only by a subsequent amendment presenting the claim as a new claim with a new claim number.

name: Situations where 37 CFR 1.131 is inappropriate (A–J)
description: An affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 is not appropriate in these situations: (A) reference publication date is more than 1 year prior to applicant's effective filing date (statutory bar under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)); (B) reference U.S. patent or U.S. patent application publication claims the same patentable invention; (C) reference is a foreign patent for the same invention to applicant issued prior to the filing date of the domestic application on an application filed more than 12 months prior (35 U.S.C.102(d)); (D) effective filing date of applicant's parent or Convention priority predates the reference (making affidavit unnecessary); (E) reference is a prior U.S. patent to same entity claiming same invention (double patenting); (F) reference is disclosure of a prior U.S. patent to the same party, not copending (dedication); (G) applicant has clearly admitted on the record that subject matter relied on in the reference is prior art; (H) subject matter relied upon is prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(f); (I) subject matter is prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(g); (J) subject matter corresponding to a lost count in an interference is prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(g) or barred by interference estoppel.
guidance: 37 CFR 1.131 is designed to permit overcoming rejections based on references/activities which are not statutory bars but have dates prior to the effective filing date; when subject matter is available under 102(g) by definition it cannot be overcome by 1.131 because it must have been made before applicant's invention. See cited case law for nuances and exceptions (e.g., Zletz, Deckler, McKellin).

name: Form paragraphs 7.57–7.64 — examiner response templates for 1.131 affidavits
description: Form paragraphs are provided for examiner use when responding to 37 CFR 1.131 affidavits/declarations: 7.57 (Ineffective — Heading), 7.58 (Ineffective — Claiming Same Invention), 7.59 (Ineffective — Insufficient Evidence of Reduction to Practice), 7.60 (Ineffective — Reference Is a Statutory Bar), 7.61 (Ineffective — Insufficient Evidence of Conception), 7.62 (Ineffective — Diligence Lacking), 7.63 (Ineffective — Insufficient Evidence of Actual Reduction to Practice), 7.64 (Effective To Overcome Reference).
guidance: Each form paragraph must be used with specified preceding/following paragraphs and examiner notes. Insert bracketed information and provide specific explanations in the indicated brackets (e.g., reasons for insufficiency, dates). Use appropriate sequencing when multiple deficiencies exist (e.g., follow 7.57 with 7.61 if conception insufficient).

name: Joint patent/application and co-authorship situations
description: When subject matter is disclosed but not claimed in a patent or application publication filed jointly by applicant and another, the joint patent/application publication is a valid reference unless overcome by affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 or an unequivocal declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 by applicant that he/she conceived or invented the subject matter relied on in the rejection.
guidance: Disclaimer by the other patentee/applicant should not be required but may be accepted. Where applicant is a co-author of a cited publication, applicant may overcome the rejection by filing an affidavit/declaration under 1.131 or a specific 1.132 establishing the article describes applicant's own work. Derivation must be shown by evidence that the patentee/applicant derived knowledge from applicant and that applicant made the invention on which the disclosure is based.

name: Pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/103(a) rejection — design claimed in design patent with earlier effective filing date and common assignee (¶15.19.06.fti)
description: Reject under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as obvious over the claim in an earlier design patent with an earlier effective filing date; based on different inventive entity it constitutes prior art under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e).
guidance: May be overcome by submitting an oath/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(c) stating current common ownership and that the inventor named is the prior inventor under 35 U.S.C. 104 (as in effect Mar 15, 2013). A terminal disclaimer under 37 CFR 1.321(c) is also required. An obviousness‑type double patenting rejection must be included. Provide patent numbers and an explicit obviousness explanation (follow with form paragraphs 15.70.fti and 15.67 or 15.68). For certain priority situations precede with 15.10.15.

name: Suggestion to overcome 35 U.S.C. 112(a)/(b) rejections in design applications — convert indefinites to broken lines (¶15.20.02)
description: Applicant may overcome 35 U.S.C. 112(a)/(b) rejections (indefiniteness/nonenabling) by disclaiming indefinite/nonenabling areas of the design by converting them to broken lines and amending the specification to state the broken‑line portions form no part of the claimed design.
guidance: Use a different form paragraph for international design applications (form paragraph 29.27). Insert the article title in bracket. This form paragraph must be preceded by 15.19.02.fti where applicable.

name: Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b) — claim not enabled/indefinite (¶15.21)
description: Reject when the claimed invention is not described in full, clear, concise, and exact terms to enable a person skilled in the art to make and use it (35 U.S.C. 112(a)) and/or fails to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter (35 U.S.C. 112(b)).
guidance: State that the claim is indefinite/nonenabling and provide full explanation of basis for rejection in the bracketed text. For apps with filing dates on/after Mar 16, 2013 that claim priority to pre‑Mar‑16‑2013 filings, precede with 15.10.15.

name: Combined 35 U.S.C. 112(a)/(b) and pre‑AIA 103 rejection when earlier design patent exists with no common assignee (¶15.19.07.fti)
description: Use when the claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a)/(b) as not enabled or indefinite and also rejected under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) over a design patent having an earlier effective filing date and no common assignee.
guidance: Provide a complete explanation of the basis for the 112 rejection in the bracketed area. Do not use this paragraph when separate rejections under 112(a) or (b) are appropriate. Insert patent number and explain differences for obviousness (follow with form paragraphs 15.70.fti and 15.67 or 15.68). Precede with 15.10.15 where applicable.

name: 35 U.S.C. 112(b) second paragraph — additional information requested when title ambiguous (¶15.21.01)
description: Use when the claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) second paragraph because the title of the article in which the design is embodied is too ambiguous to permit proper examination.
guidance: Request applicant to provide sufficient explanation of the nature and intended use of the article, and any helpful additional information (analogous fields of search, pertinent prior art, advertising brochures, filing of copending utility applications and utility application number if any). Warn that clarifying the title by specifying the article may introduce new matter (35 U.S.C. 132; 37 CFR 1.121).

name: 35 U.S.C. 171 double patenting rejection (design-design) — statutory double patenting (¶15.23)
description: Reject under 35 U.S.C. 171 when a claim is claiming the same design as that claimed in an earlier United States Design Patent (statutory double patenting).
guidance: Advise that information addressing the rejection should be submitted as a separate paper and not inserted into the specification (37 CFR 1.56). Form paragraph 15.23.02 (summary for 'same invention' type double patenting rejections) should follow.

name: 35 U.S.C. 112(b) second paragraph — scope cannot be determined (¶15.22)
description: Use this form paragraph when the scope of the claimed design cannot be determined and the claim is indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b)/pre‑AIA 112 second paragraph.
guidance: Provide a full explanation of the basis for the rejection in the bracketed text. This is used where the examiner cannot determine the scope from the claim/drawings.

name: 'Or the like' / 'or similar article' indefinite claim rejection (¶15.22.02)
description: Reject under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) second paragraph when the use of phrases like '--or the like--' or '--or similar article--' following the title creates indefiniteness.
guidance: Cancellation of the phrase in the claim and each occurrence throughout the papers (except the oath/declaration) will overcome the rejection (see Ex parte Pappas). Do not use this where the phrase is directed to the environment of the article embodying the design. Insert the exact phrase in the bracket.

name: Title fails to specify a known article of manufacture — 35 U.S.C. 112(b) rejection (¶15.22.03)
description: Reject when the claim title fails to identify an article of manufacture and the drawing disclosure does not inherently identify the article in which the design is embodied, rendering the claim indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b).
guidance: Cite Ex parte Strijland. Request clarification from applicant; warn about introduction of new matter if title is changed in the specification.

name: Provisional nonstatutory double patenting rejection (multiple references) (¶15.24.04)
description: Provisionally reject on nonstatutory double patenting of a copending application in view of one or more secondary references; assert that it would have been obvious to a designer to modify the copending claim as demonstrated by secondary references.
guidance: Explain how the copending claim is modified and identify secondary references that teach the modifications. Explain the judicial policy basis for the doctrine and note that a timely filed terminal disclaimer under 37 CFR 1.321(c) may overcome an actual or provisional nonstatutory rejection if common ownership is shown (37 CFR 1.131(c)). Provide information about eTerminal Disclaimers (USPTO forms and web‑based eTD). Precede with 15.24.06 and follow with 15.68.

name: Identical claim with common assignee — priority issues and abandonment risk (¶15.24.05.fti)
description: When the claim is directed to the same invention as a commonly assigned copending application, resolve priority under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f)/(g); terminal disclaimer has no effect because the basis for refusal is priority (not extension of monopoly).
guidance: Assignee must state which entity is the prior inventor; failure to comply may result in abandonment. This paragraph should precede all nonstatutory double patenting rejections as a heading (except 'same invention' type).

name: Identification of prior application(s) in nonprovisional applications — claiming benefit requirements (¶15.26)
description: To claim the benefit of a prior‑filed application, a continuation or divisional must include a specific reference to the prior application in compliance with 37 CFR 1.78; placement depends on filing date.
guidance: If filed before Sep 16, 2012 include the specific reference in the first sentence(s) of the specification following the title or in an application data sheet; if filed on/after Sep 16, 2012 include the specific reference in an application data sheet. For benefit claims under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, 365(c), or 386(c), the reference must include the relationship (continuation, divisional, continuation‑in‑part).

name: Proceeding for reduction/exemption: submission and reuse of evidential documents
description: Evidential documents supporting a claim for fee reduction/exemption must be submitted to the Commissioner of the Korean Intellectual Property Office; previously submitted evidential documents may be referenced in subsequent proceedings.
guidance: If evidential documents for persons with national merit, registered handicapped persons, or recipients of National Basic Livelihood Security have already been submitted to the Commissioner, re-submission may be unnecessary. To skip re-submission, state the intention to skip and provide index information of the submitted documents. Referencing rules (see separate referencing criterion) explain how to indicate references in forms.

name: Referencing already-submitted evidential documents (document reuse)
description: Where a person conducts more than two patent-related proceedings simultaneously or consecutively with the same evidential documents, the person may submit the original evidential documents for one proceeding and reference them in other proceedings by submitting copies or stating the intention to reference the original.
guidance: Referencing can be made in many specific cases including: power of attorney for representative proceedings; evidential documents showing an invention has not been disclosed; priority-claim documents; evidential documents of a representative of more than two parties; evidential documents of a successor in title; documents where permission/approval/consent of a third party is needed; nationality/certificate documents for foreigners; documents relating to changes/corrections of name/domicile/seal. When copies are submitted instead of originals, the intention to reference must be stated in the attached-documents box in the form; an example format for the statement is provided in the manual.

name: Identification and pinpointing of electronic documents
description: Citations to electronic documents should include sufficient locating information such as claim numbers, figure numbers, chemical formula numbers, mathematical formula numbers, table heading numbers, gene sequence numbers, and computer program listing numbers if available; specific headings within the document structure (e.g., Best Mode of Performing the Invention or Industrial Applicability) can be indicated if page, paragraph, and line numbers are not available; specific passages can be indicated if the document format includes pagination or an equivalent internal referencing system, or by the first and last words of the passage cited.
guidance: Office copies of an electronic document must be retained if the same document may not be available for retrieval in the future (important for Internet/online databases). If an electronic document is also available in paper form it need not be identified as electronic unless desirable. Examples (1-16) illustrate citation formats for various online/CD-ROM/Internet sources; include paragraph numbers (e.g., [0068]) or example numbers when available.

name: Completeness of examiner’s action
description: The examiner’s action must be complete as to all matters, except in appropriate circumstances (misjoinder, fundamental defects, etc.) where action may be limited; matters of form need not be raised until a claim is found allowable.
guidance: Follow 37 CFR 1.104. Limitations to full action are allowed in specified circumstances; ensure completeness except where justified by listed exceptions.

name: Improperly expressed rejections to avoid
description: An omnibus rejection 'on the references and for the reasons of record' is stereotyped and usually not informative and should be avoided; do not group a plurality of claims together in a common rejection unless equally applicable to all claims in the group.
guidance: Provide specific grounds for each rejection, tailored to the claims affected, to be informative to applicant and to the record.

name: Unpersuasive Argument: Bodily Incorporation (¶7.37.02)
description: The test for obviousness is not whether features of a secondary reference may be bodily incorporated into the structure of the primary reference; nor that the claimed invention must be expressly suggested in any one or all references; rather, the test is what the combined teachings of the references would have suggested to those of ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: Briefly restate applicant’s arguments and then explain why bodily incorporation is not required. Precede with ¶7.37. See In re Keller.

name: Unpersuasive Argument: Arguing Limitations Which Are Not Claimed (¶7.37.08)
description: Features upon which applicant relies that are not recited in the rejected claim(s) cannot be used to patentably distinguish the claims from the references; limitations from the specification are not to be read into the claims.
guidance: Recite the non-claimed features and specifically point out how the language of the claims patentably distinguishes them from the references. Precede with ¶7.37. See In re Van Geuns.

name: Unpersuasive Argument: Intended Use (¶7.37.09)
description: A recitation of intended use must result in a structural difference between the claimed invention and the prior art in order to patentably distinguish the claimed invention; if prior art structure can perform the intended use, it meets the claim.
guidance: Briefly restate applicant’s intended-use argument and explain why it does or does not patentably distinguish the claim. Precede with ¶7.37.

name: Unpersuasive Argument: Limitation(s) in Preamble (¶7.37.10)
description: A preamble is generally not accorded patentable weight where it merely recites the purpose of a process or the intended use of a structure and where the body of the claim can stand alone without the preamble.
guidance: Restate preamble recitation in question and explain why it is not given patentable weight. Precede with ¶7.37. See In re Hirao and Kropa v. Robie.

name: Unpersuasive Argument: General Allegation of Patentability (¶7.37.11)
description: Applicant’s general allegations that the claims define a patentable invention fail to comply with 37 CFR 1.111(b)/(c) because they do not clearly point out the patentable novelty in view of references or objections nor show how amendments avoid such references or objections.
guidance: Indicate that general allegations are insufficient and point to regulatory requirements for specificity. Precede with ¶7.37.

name: Piecemeal examination should be avoided
description: Piecemeal examination should be avoided as much as possible. The examiner ordinarily should reject each claim on all valid grounds available while avoiding undue multiplication of references; major technical rejections (lack of disclosure, lack of enablement, serious indefiniteness, res judicata) should be applied where appropriate.
