guidance: If a major technical rejection is proper, state it with full development of reasons rather than a mere conclusion. Situations where limited action on claims may be appropriate include: (A) application too informal for complete merits action; (B) undue multiplicity of claims with no successful election request; (C) misjoinder of inventions with no successful election request; (D) perpetual motion disclosures—cite best prior art and explain pertinency. Where a sound prior-art rejection discloses the 'heart' of the invention, minor secondary rejections ordinarily should not be made.

name: State when claims are allowable; constructive assistance to pro se applicants
description: When it becomes apparent that patentable subject matter exists in a pro se application, the examiner should draft one or more claims for the applicant and indicate such claims would be allowed if incorporated; in general, when claims disclose patentable subject matter but cannot be allowed due to defects in form, the examiner should not merely object or reject but offer definite suggestions for correction and may suggest interviews.
guidance: Apply this especially to inventor-filed applications to expedite prosecution. For 'allowable except as to form' situations, the examiner may note unclaimed aspects that if properly claimed may receive favorable consideration. If a claim is otherwise allowable but dependent on a canceled or rejected claim, state it would be allowable if rewritten in independent form.

name: Early allowance of claims (examiner-drafted claims)
description: If the examiner is satisfied after the search that patentable subject matter is disclosed and applicant intends to claim it, the examiner may draft claims considered to distinguish patentably over the art of record and present them to applicant for consideration.
guidance: Present drafted claims with explanation; this may encourage interviews and early agreement on allowable claims. Follow relevant form paragraph structure for presenting drafted claims.

name: Use of form paragraphs for corrections and replies
description: Specific form paragraphs (e.g., 7.81–7.83, 7.82.01, 7.37–7.38.02, 7.37.01–7.37.13, 7.43.03) exist to standardize corrections, supply copies, and state the examiner’s position regarding applicant arguments.
guidance: Use appropriate form paragraphs per the situation: correcting citations, supplying copies of references, indicating arguments not persuasive, withdrawing previous rejections, or making new grounds of rejection. Ensure the applicable bracketed content is filled with specific references (pages/lines/claim numbers/statutory bases).

name: Contents of specification (heading: section 32)
description: The Act prescribes contents required in provisional and complete specifications.
guidance: Specifications must include prescribed disclosures (description, claims, drawings where necessary); see section 32 and regulations for exact content and formalities.

name: Full description in prior patent/publication negates novelty
description: A full description in the specification of a prior public patent (or a printed publication) of the subject covered by a later patent negates novelty even though the earlier patent did not claim that subject.
guidance: Drawings in prior patents/publications that unmistakably disclose the invention can likewise anticipate; nothing can be used to contradict the face of a patent except what's on its face.

name: No amendment that enlarges or substantially changes the invention
description: No amendment shall be allowed that would make the specification, as amended, claim an invention substantially larger than or substantially different from the invention claimed by the specification as it stood before amendment.
guidance: (Statutory safeguard limiting scope of allowable amendments.)

name: Purpose and effect of a disclaimer
description: The object of a disclaimer is to enable a patentee to omit those parts of a specification which, if retained, would make the patent void. The disclaimer operates to strike out the parts of the specification disclaimed and does not serve to explain what is left; the disclaimer will be deemed part of the specification.
guidance: A disclaimer is not retrospective so as to make a person liable for infringement prior to the disclaimer unless the patentee establishes to the satisfaction of the Court that his original claim was framed in good faith and with reasonable skill and knowledge.

name: Prospect function of the patent system
description: The patent system performs a 'prospect' function: by awarding exclusive and publicly recorded ownership of a prospect shortly after its discovery, it tends to assure efficient allocation of resources among prospects, place management of each prospect in the entity best equipped to manage it, and cause information found by one entity to be communicated to others at an efficient rate.
guidance: This conception treats technological innovation as searches over prospects with varying costs and returns and views patents as analogous to mineral claims that organize investment and development of opportunities. Use this criterion to evaluate whether patent rules (scope, timing, recording, transferability) promote efficient allocation and management of innovation resources.

name: Scope of patent claims often exceeds the inventor's concrete contribution
description: Patent claims are 'an abstraction and generalization of an indefinitely large number of concrete, physical objects' and thus reach beyond what the reward theory would require; broad claims can cover later-developed superior embodiments or unforeseen uses (examples: fat separation, Selden automobile combination, diode patent covering triode, new therapeutic uses for a chemical).
guidance: Evaluate claim scope not only by the inventor's actual reduced embodiment but by the abstract claim language; anticipate that broad claims may preempt later improvements or alternative practical implementations and consider how such scope supports the prospect function (early reservation of an opportunity) while raising antipatent concerns.

name: Priority and early-filing rules force early patent applications
description: Rules awarding priority to the first to file (or first inventor in U.S. practice) create strong incentives to file as soon as a working version is found; senior/junior status and demanding standards of proof for prior inventorship make early filing practically decisive.
guidance: Assess how priority rules influence timing of applications and whether they cause claim-staking early in development (supporting prospect reservation) even when commercial value is uncertain. Note the 'near miss' risk where second discoverers lose rights regardless of relative investment.

name: Claims must be delimited to the inventor's invention; overbroad claims are invalid
description: The applicant must limit his claims to his invention in the claims portion of the patent document; if claims exceed the invention they are invalid (analogous to the mineral-claim boundary rules).
guidance: Assess claim drafting and scope carefully: the patent system requires specific delimitation in claims and boundary description, and these legal limits are a central evaluative criterion for validity.

name: Analogous institutional features between patents and mineral claims
description: The patent system parallels the American mineral-claim system in many respects: (1) neither requires demonstration of commercial significance to stake a claim; (2) priority is awarded to the first to discover/stake/file; (3) claims/boundaries must be specified; (4) there are obligations/mechanisms to return unpromising claims to the public (mining work vs. patent term/maintenance); (5) interests can be transferred before/after rights are established.
guidance: Use this analogy to evaluate institutional design choices (staking/filing requirements, claim scope, transferability, maintenance obligations) and how they affect incentives to search and develop technology.

name: Limited patent term and maintenance requirements serve to weed out unpromising claims
description: The mineral system's annual work requirement is paralleled in the patent system by a limited patent term (and in some systems by maintenance payments), which returns unpromising prospects to the public domain when the owner chooses not to continue investment.
guidance: Consider patent term and maintenance regimes as instruments to ensure that holders continue to invest in valuable prospects; evaluate whether these mechanisms effectively cause abandonment of low-value claims.

name: Effect of prior foreign patent on U.S. patent duration
description: The statute applies where a United States patent corresponds with any invention described in a prior foreign patent; in such cases the U.S. patent may be limited by the foreign patent's term.
guidance: Does not apply where the invention was only described (not claimed) in the foreign patent, or where the foreign patent never became operative due to non-compliance with foreign law. If the foreign patent was terminated before the U.S. application was filed the U.S. patent is void ab initio; if the foreign patent terminated while the U.S. application was pending, the U.S. patent is limited by the foreign patent as it would have been if issued on the day applied for. Extensions of a foreign patent (including potential extensions conferred by statute in force when the U.S. application was filed and issued) can affect whether and how the U.S. patent is limited; continuous extensions may extend the limiting effect. Differences in detail do not necessarily avoid the limitation—the true test is whether practicing what is described in the foreign patent would infringe the U.S. patent. A foreign patent for an apparatus does not necessarily limit a U.S. patent for the method, and related/dependent inventions may be affected differently (claims covering inventions patented abroad may expire with the foreign patent while remaining claims remain until U.S. patent expiration). Repeal ab initio of the foreign patent restores the U.S. patent to its full term.

name: Meaning of 'specification' and its component parts
description: When the statute uses 'specification' without the word 'claim' it covers both the claim and the description; when used with 'claim' it covers the description only.
guidance: The specification is composed of the description and the claim(s); proper characteristics of specifications are explained via the description and the claims (their required contents and form).

name: Claims: particularity, function/result limitation, and scope
description: Claims must "particularly point out and distinctly claim" the part, improvement, or combination claimed as the invention; a distinct and formal claim is necessary to ascertain scope and the patent grants no exclusive right except to what is thus claimed.
guidance: Claims "measure the invention." A claim covers a process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, or a design, and never merely the function or result. A specification may contain a claim for the whole invention and other claims for separate parts or sub-processes; the subject of a claim need not be operative alone. Each claim must satisfy tests of invention (inventive step), novelty, and utility. Matters disclosed but not covered by claim are not within the exclusive grant.

name: Undisclosed or unclaimed disclosures
description: Inventions, devices, and improvements disclosed by the specification but not covered by a claim are not secured by the patent.
guidance: The specification may describe more than is claimed; anything disclosed yet not claimed is effectively dedicated outside the patentee's exclusive grant and is not part of the monopoly. (Context: the book states this principle and proceeds to emphasize the measuring function of claims.)

name: Concepts relating to organizing human activity
description: Claims directed to schemes for organizing human activity or business practices (e.g., generating menus, taking restaurant orders, structuring a sales force, using advertising as currency, algorithms for scheduling visits).
guidance: The Federal Circuit treats such concepts as abstract ideas; merely implementing them using conventional computer components or describing them as performed on a device does not remove them from being abstract. Examples/case law: claims characterized as 'generating menus … or taking orders from restaurant customers' (Enfish/related discussion and 842 F.3d citations), In re Ferguson (structuring a sales force), Ultramercial v. Hulu (advertising as exchange), In re Maucorps (algorithm for number of visits).

name: Concepts relating to organizing/analyzing information analogous to mental work
description: Claims that organize or analyze information by steps analogous to human thought processes (e.g., translating functional descriptions, extracting and recognizing data from documents, detecting misuse via rule-based analysis).
guidance: Claims that can be performed mentally or are analogous to human reasoning are abstract unless they add significantly more (a technical improvement). Examples/case law: Synopsys v. Mentor Graphics (converting descriptions for logic circuits read on mental steps), Content Extraction (scanner + recognition + storage was viewed as data collection/recognition humans have long done), FairWarning (collect/analyze/notify to detect misuse). Additional examples: Intellectual Ventures v. Capital One Fin. (collect/display/manipulate data), Erie Indem. Co. indexing example, Versata pricing determination, RecogniCorp encoding/decoding, Digitech organizing via mathematical correlations, Return Mail, Internet Patents retention in navigation of forms.

name: Concepts having no particular concrete or tangible form
description: Claims directed to ideas that are conceptual frameworks or building blocks without a concrete instantiation (e.g., using advertising as currency, organizational/product group hierarchies to determine price, assigning hair designs to head-shape zones).
guidance: Courts characterize such claims as abstract because they are basic conceptual frameworks that lack a particular concrete application; these building-block ideas are patent-ineligible absent additional inventive concept. Examples/case law: Ultramercial (advertising as exchange), Versata (pricing via organizational/product hierarchies), In re Brown (haircutting method described as abstract).

name: Concepts relating to a mathematical relationship or formula (specific)
description: Claims that recite or depend on a specific mathematical relationship or formula (e.g., Arrhenius equation used to compute cure time) are directed to a mathematical concept and thus to an abstract idea/judicial exception.
guidance: A mathematical formula as claimed subject matter is an exception absent inventive concept in application. Example/case law: Diamond v. Diehr (Arrhenius equation in rubber-molding press: the equation itself is non-statutory), plus Benson, Flook, Mackay Radio & Tel. Co., Bilski.

name: Adding conventional computer components or automation is insufficient
description: Simply reciting generic computer components or automating a well-known human/business practice on a generic computer does not transform an abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter.
guidance: The Federal Circuit has repeatedly held that claims that add conventional computer implementation to an abstract idea remain directed to the abstract idea absent an inventive concept that provides a technological improvement. Example language: claims described as 'adding conventional computer components to well-known business practices' remain abstract (cases cited throughout the discussion, e.g., restaurant-order device example, Alice, and related Federal Circuit decisions).

name: 112(d) Rejection(s) compliance determination
description: Were all the 35 USC 112(d) Rejection(s) in compliance? (Yes or No)
guidance: The determination of compliance is based on the rejection properly identifying the claim(s), the statute and being supported by sufficient evidence to support the rejection. If a 112(d) rejection was made, the reviewer must answer Yes or No and, if No, continue through the question set to identify the noncompliance basis.

name: 112(d) Identify claim(s) and type of claim causing noncompliance
description: Identify the claim(s) with non-compliant 35 USC 112(d) rejection(s). The noncompliance is directed to limitations introduced in (check only one): Only the independent claim(s) / Only the dependent claim(s) / Both the independent claim(s) and dependent claim(s).
guidance: List each claim discussed individually as basis for the noncompliance and those dependent claims that inherit it. Choose the box based on where the limitation that is the basis for noncompliance first appears in the claim tree. Examples illustrate how to pick (independent vs dependent vs both).

name: 112(d) Failure due to lack of sufficient evidence
description: The rejection(s) does not provide sufficient evidence to support the rejection (must check at least one of 4(b)(i)-4(b)(ii)).
guidance: If checked, identify whether (i) the rejection does not provide sufficient evidence that the claim(s) does not specify a further limitation of the subject matter of the claim from which it depends, or (ii) the rejection does not provide sufficient evidence that the claim(s) does not include all of the limitations of the claim from which it depends. Explanation comments should be limited to the basis for lack of sufficient evidence and consistent with boxes checked.

name: 112(d) Additional Information/Feedback (root-cause boxes)
description: Reviewer should check all of the boxes 5a-d that apply to the noncompliance issue(s).
guidance: Boxes include: (a) The rejection(s) should have been made under 35 USC 112(b); (b) The noncompliance is the result of an unreasonable claim interpretation; (c) The rejection(s) was improperly based on the patentable significance of the further limitation; (d) None of the above. Do not guess the root cause; explanation comments must support each box checked.

name: 112(d) Characteristics of 112(d) Rejection(s)
description: Check all boxes that apply to characteristics exemplified in the rejections made under 35 USC 112(d).
guidance: Characteristics listed include: addresses substantially all claims individually / only groups claims of substantially similar scope (limited claim lumping); sets forth a claim interpretation that points out how the examiner is interpreting the claim/term/phrase; included detailed legal analysis of applicable legal issues and case law; Office action included appropriate suggestions to overcome rejections (not general FP language); None of the above. Guidance: use 'substantially' and 'reasonably' judgment; checking indicates presence of characteristic, not accolade-worthy quality.

name: 101 Subject Matter Eligibility prima facie standard
description: A claimed invention may be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 if it is not directed to one of the four statutory categories (process, machine, manufactures, composition of matter) or if the claim is directed to a judicial exception and the claim as a whole does not include additional limitations amounting to significantly more than the exception.
guidance: This defines the baseline for evaluating 101 subject-matter rejections and informs the compliance checks below.

name: 101 Subject Matter Eligibility compliance determination
description: Were all the 35 USC 101 Subject Matter Eligibility rejection(s) in compliance? (Yes or No)
guidance: Determination based on whether the rejection properly identifies the claim(s), the statute and is supported by sufficient evidence. Statutory compliance standards and scenarios should be consulted. If No, proceed to subsequent identification and explanation questions.

name: 101 Identify claim(s) and type of claim causing noncompliance
description: Identify the claim(s) with non-compliant 35 USC 101 Subject Matter Eligibility rejection(s) and indicate whether the noncompliance is directed to limitations introduced in only independent claims, only dependent claims, or both.
guidance: Each claim discussed individually as basis for noncompliance must be listed. Selection is based on where the limitation that is the root of noncompliance first appears in the claim tree. Examples illustrate selection.

name: 101 Reasons for noncompliance — 4a: failure to identify claims/statute
description: The rejection(s) does not properly identify the rejected claim(s) and/or identify the correct statute.
guidance: Check 4(a) when either claim(s) or statute is the basis of noncompliance. Do NOT check 4(a) when the issue is insufficient evidence to support an otherwise-identified rejection (use 4(b)-(e) instead). Do not use 4(a) to raise omitted rejections. Explanation box should be limited to the basis for noncompliance related to identification of claim(s) and/or statute; avoid rhetorical questioning and personalization.

name: 101 Reasons for noncompliance — 4c: Step 2A Prong One (judicial exception)
description: Step 2A, Prong One: The rejection(s) does not set forth sufficient evidence as to why the claimed invention is directed to a judicial exception.
guidance: If 4(c) checked, indicate whether (i) the rejection fails to set forth any judicial exception recited in the claim, or (ii) fails to correctly characterize the judicial exception. If (ii) is checked, at least one of: Product of Nature (fail to assess Markedly Different Characteristics), Law of Nature, Natural Phenomenon (other than products of nature), Abstract Idea — and for Abstract Idea choose categories from 2019 Revised Guidance: (a) Mathematical concept; (b) Certain methods of organizing human activity; (c) Mental process; (d) Tentative Abstract Idea — or indicate improper treatment under Section III(C) of 2019 Guidance.

name: 101 Reasons for noncompliance — 4d: Step 2A Prong Two (practical application)
description: Step 2A, Prong Two: The rejection(s) fails to set forth sufficient evidence as to why the claimed invention, as a whole, does not integrate the recited judicial exception into a practical application.
guidance: If checked, indicate (i) the rejection does not address Step 2A, Prong Two at all, or (ii) it addresses Step 2A, Prong Two but the discussion regarding lack of practical application is insufficient. Explanation comments should support boxes checked.

name: 101 Reasons for noncompliance — 4e: Step 2B (inventive concept)
description: Step 2B: The rejection(s) fails to set forth sufficient evidence as to why the claimed invention does not provide an inventive concept (i.e., additional elements do not amount to significantly more than the judicial exception itself).
guidance: If 4(e) checked, at least one of: (i) The rejection does not identify the additional element(s) in the claim; (ii) The rejection does not address each of the additional elements in the claim; (iii) The rejection relies on the rationale that the claim simply appends well-understood, routine, conventional activities specified at a high level of generality to the judicial exception but does not support it with an appropriate factual determination in accordance with the Berkheimer Memorandum.

name: 101 Additional Information/Feedback (root-cause boxes)
description: Reviewer should check all boxes 5a-c that apply to the noncompliance issue(s).
guidance: Boxes include: (a) The non-compliance is the result of an unreasonable claim interpretation; (b) The rejection is not based on the most current patent examination guidance; (c) None of the above. Comments should support reasoning for each box checked and reviewers should not guess root cause.

name: 101 Subject Matter Eligibility Characteristics checklist
description: Characteristics of 101 Subject Matter Eligibility Rejection(s) — check all that apply.
guidance: Characteristics include: addresses substantially all claims individually and limited claim lumping; provides a thorough explanation identifying each step/prong of 35 USC 101 guidelines with accompanying analysis; sets forth a claim interpretation used for rejection (BRI/special definitions); includes detailed legal analysis and applicable case law/policy; Office action included appropriate suggestions to overcome rejections (not general FP language); None of the above. Use 'substantially' and 'reasonably' to exercise judgment. Checking indicates presence, not accolade-worthiness.

name: 101 Utility prima facie standard
description: A claimed invention may be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 Utility when there is no assertion of a specific and substantial credible utility by the applicant, and the claimed invention does not have readily apparent well-established utility.
guidance: This sets the standard for evaluating utility rejections in the office action being reviewed.

name: 101 Utility compliance determination
description: Were all the 35 USC 101 Utility rejection(s) in compliance? (Yes or No)
guidance: Determination based on whether the rejection properly identifies the claim(s), the statute/subparagraph, and is supported by sufficient evidence. If No, proceed to identify claims and explain noncompliance.

name: 101 Utility identify claim(s) and root-of-noncompliance
description: Identify claim(s) with non-compliant 101 Utility rejection(s) and indicate whether noncompliance is directed to limitations introduced in only independent claims, only dependent claims, or both.
guidance: Same selection logic and illustrative examples as for other statute sections: choose based on where the limiting feature originates in claim tree; dependent claims that inherit noncompliance must be listed.

name: 101 Utility Reasons for noncompliance — 4b: insufficient evidence of lack of utility
description: The rejection(s) does not provide sufficient evidence to support that the claimed invention has no specific and substantial credible utility which has either been asserted by the applicant or would have been readily apparent to one of ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: Explanation comments should be consistent with boxes checked under 4(b). Avoid rhetorical questions and personalization.

name: 101 Utility Additional Information/Feedback (boxes 5a-d)
description: Reviewer should check all boxes 5a-d that apply to the noncompliance issue(s).
guidance: Boxes include: (a) The rejection(s) was based on an unreasonable claim interpretation; (b) The rejection(s) was based on applicant asserted utility failing to be credible; (c) The rejection(s) was based on lack of applicant asserted utility and failed to consider what would be readily apparent to one of ordinary skill in the art; (d) None of the above. Comments must support the boxes checked.

name: 101 Utility Characteristics checklist
description: Characteristics of 101 Utility Rejection(s) — check all that apply.
guidance: Characteristics include: addresses substantially all claims individually and limited claim lumping; sets forth a claim interpretation used for rejection; included detailed legal analysis of applicable legal issues and case law/policy; Office action included appropriate suggestions to overcome rejections (not general FP language); None of the above.

name: 101 Statutory Double Patenting compliance determination
description: Were all the 35 USC 101 Statutory Double Patenting rejection(s) in compliance? (Yes or No)
guidance: Determination based on whether the rejection properly identifies the claim(s), the statute and is supported by sufficient evidence. If No, continue to identify claims and the basis for noncompliance.

name: 101 Statutory Double Patenting identify claim(s) and root-of-noncompliance
description: Identify the claim(s) with non-compliant 35 USC 101 Statutory Double Patenting rejection(s) and whether the noncompliance is directed to limitations introduced in only independent claims, only dependent claims, or both.
guidance: Same claim-tree selection logic and examples as other sections; list each claim individually and include dependent claims that inherit noncompliance.

name: 101 Statutory Double Patenting whether another compliant double-patenting rejection applied
description: For all claims identified as having a noncompliant 101 Statutory Double Patenting rejection, was another compliant 101 statutory double patenting rejection applied? (Yes or No)
guidance: If every claim listed as noncompliant also has another compliant basis, answer Yes. Otherwise answer No. Consult MRF In-part Instruction for specifics.

name: Completeness of examiner's action
description: The examiner’s action will be complete as to all matters, except that in appropriate circumstances the action may be limited to such matters before further action is made. However, matters of form need not be raised by the examiner until a claim is found allowable.
guidance: Limitations on completeness are appropriate in cases such as misjoinder, fundamental defects, or where informalities exist; otherwise address all relevant matters.

name: Identify allowable claims and suggest amendments
description: The examiner should, as part of the first Office action on the merits, identify any claims which he or she judges, as presently recited, to be allowable and/or should suggest any way in which rejected claims may be amended to make them allowable.
guidance: Failure to do so implies to applicant that there appear to be no allowable claims. Where appropriate, suggest amendments to make claims allowable to expedite prosecution.

name: Avoid improperly expressed rejections (omnibus/grouping)
description: An omnibus rejection of the claim 'on the references and for the reasons of record' is stereotyped and usually not informative and should therefore be avoided. A plurality of claims should never be grouped together in a common rejection, unless that rejection is equally applicable to all claims in the group.
guidance: Provide specific grounds and explanations for each rejection and avoid blanket statements; separate grounds if different claims are rejected for different reasons.

name: Answer all material traversed and applicant arguments
description: Where the requirements are traversed, or suspension thereof requested, the examiner should make proper reference thereto in his or her action on the amendment. Where the applicant traverses any rejection, the examiner should, if he or she repeats the rejection, take note of the applicant’s argument and answer the substance of it.
guidance: If a rejection is applied to a new or amended claim, specifically identify that ground of rejection by citation of the paragraph in the former Office letter in which the rejection was originally stated.

name: Use form paragraphs for unpersuasive or moot arguments (7.37–7.38)
description: Form paragraphs 7.37 through 7.38 may be used where applicant's arguments are not persuasive or are moot because of new grounds of rejection.
guidance: Form paragraphs include specific scripted responses and must be preceded by paragraph 7.37 where indicated. Examples cover common argument types (age of references, bodily incorporation, hindsight reasoning, no suggestion to combine, nonanalogous art, number of references, results not contemplated by prior art, limitations not claimed, preamble weight, general allegation of patentability, intended use, etc.). When used, tailor bracketed insertions to the case and precede with required base paragraph(s).

name: Respond to specific common unpersuasive arguments (categories)
description: Specific response principles provided for common applicant arguments: age of references, bodily incorporation, hindsight reasoning, no suggestion to combine, nonanalogous art, excessive number of references, obtaining result not contemplated by prior art, arguing limitations not claimed, preamble issues, general allegation of patentability, intended use, arguing references individually.
guidance: Each form paragraph (e.g., 7.37.01 through 7.37.13) must be preceded by 7.37 and contains examiner notes on how to fill bracketed items. Apply the cited case law (e.g., In re Keller, In re McLaughlin, In re Fine, In re Oetiker, etc.) where relevant and explain why the argument is unpersuasive per the provided templates.

name: Situations permitting limited action on claims
description: Some situations exist where examination appears best accomplished by limiting action on the claims to a particular issue, such as when an application is too informal for complete action, undue multiplicity of claims with no election, misjoinder of inventions with no election, or disclosure directed to perpetual motion.
guidance: In such cases address the specific issue (e.g., request election, address informality) and cite appropriate MPEP sections (e.g., §702.01, §2173.05(n), §803, §806.02, §812.01). For perpetual motion cases, still cite best prior art available but do not necessarily apply it to the claims; conversely, certain rejections (res judicata, new matter, no prima facie showing for reissue, inoperativeness) should be accompanied by rejection on all other available grounds.

name: Common-ownership / relatedness conditions for double patenting
description: Use a double patenting rejection when the reference patent/application and the application under examination satisfy one or more relationship conditions: (a) name the same inventive entity, (b) name different inventive entities but are commonly assigned, (c) are not commonly assigned but name at least one joint inventor in common, (d) are filed by a common applicant (35 U.S.C. 118), (e) claim patentably indistinct inventions made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of a joint research agreement (pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c)) for pre‑AIA cases, or (f) claim patentably indistinct inventions and were commonly owned or deemed commonly owned as of the effective filing date under applicable AIA/FITF provisions.
guidance: This a–f list appears repeatedly and is the baseline test for whether various double patenting form paragraphs may be used. When applicable, additional form paragraphs (e.g., 8.27.fti/8.27.aia or 8.28.fti/8.28.aia) may also be required to resolve priority/common‑ownership evidence. Always consider whether the time of common ownership (effective filing date) matters (especially under AIA/FITF).

name: Provisional statutory double patenting rejection (¶ 8.32)
description: Use a provisional statutory double patenting rejection where claim [1] is provisionally rejected as claiming the same invention as claim [2] of a copending Application No. [3] (reference application) — i.e., the scope of the claimed inventions is identical and the identical claims have not been patented.
guidance: Requirements and notes: form paragraph 8.30 must precede this paragraph; do not use if the identical claims are in an issued patent (use 8.31 instead); do not use for nonstatutory double patenting; applicable relationship conditions (a–f) must be checked; use 8.28.fti/8.28.aia as appropriate to require assignee to name first inventor or to resolve ownership; if record evidence shows pre‑AIA 102(f)/(g) prior art, also make rejections using 7.15.fti/7.19.fti; under FITF/AIA, use 8.27.aia as appropriate and consider a 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) rejection if needed.

name: Basis for nonstatutory double patenting (¶ 8.33)
description: Nonstatutory double patenting is a judicially created doctrine to prevent unjustified timewise extension of the patent 'right to exclude' and harassment by multiple assignees. It is appropriate where conflicting claims are not identical but at least one claim is not patentably distinct from the reference claim(s) because it is anticipated by or would have been obvious over the reference claim(s).
guidance: When asserting nonstatutory (obviousness‑type) double patenting, an obviousness analysis is required only if the examined claim(s) are not anticipated by the reference claim(s). A timely filed terminal disclaimer in compliance with 37 C.F.R. 1.321(c)/(d) (and signed per 1.321(b)) may overcome the rejection if the reference is commonly owned or the invention arose under a joint research agreement. Examiner should cite MPEP §§ 717.02 and 706.02(l)(1)-(3) (AIA vs non‑AIA distinctions). USPTO eTerminal Disclaimer procedures/forms may be used (auto‑processing if all requirements met).

name: Provisional nonstatutory double patenting rejection — copending application primary reference, no secondary references (¶ 8.35)
description: Claim [1] provisionally rejected as unpatentable over claim [2] of copending Application No. [3] because, though not identical, the claims are not patentably distinct because [4]. This is provisional since the indistinct claims have not been patented.
guidance: Use this when the indistinct claims are in another copending application (not a patent). Form paragraph 8.33 must precede this paragraph. Insert reference application number in bracket 3 and explain anticipation/obviousness in bracket 4. If the reference application is commonly assigned now but does not show common ownership at the time of invention, also use 8.28.fti to resolve priority/ownership issues. Consider additional pre‑AIA 102(e)/103(a) rejections (form paragraphs 7.21.01.fti/7.21.02.fti) where earlier‑filed disclosures support a statutory rejection. Under FITF/AIA, also make 102(a)(2) or 103 rejections as appropriate. See MPEP §1490 for terminal disclaimer guidance and note that 35 U.S.C. 119(a)/(e) benefit/priority claims are not considered in double‑patenting earlier‑filed determination.

name: Allowable product — rejoinder of at least one process claim, less than all claims (¶ 8.42)
description: When a claim directed to an allowable product is present, a process claim (claim [2]) previously withdrawn due to a restriction requirement may be rejoined and examined if the process claim requires all the limitations of the allowable product claim; other claims not rejoined must not include all limitations of the allowable product claim.
guidance: Follow MPEP §821.04(b) and 37 C.F.R. 1.104. Insert the allowable product claim number(s) and rejoined process claim numbers in the indicated brackets; specify which claims are not rejoined and the subject matter of those claims. Withdrawal of the restriction requirement is effected as to the rejoined inventions; once withdrawn, 35 U.S.C. 121 no longer applies (see In re Ziegler). Warn applicant that continuation/divisional claims that are anticipated by or include all limitations of an allowable claim may be subject to provisional double patenting rejections over the instant application's claims. If ALL previously withdrawn process claims are being rejoined, use form paragraph 8.43 instead.

name: Elected invention allowable — rejoinder of all previously withdrawn claims (¶ 8.45)
description: When an elected invention (claim [1]) is allowable and other claims ([2]) previously withdrawn for restriction require all the limitations of an allowable claim, the restriction requirement is withdrawn and the previously withdrawn claims are rejoined and fully examined under 37 C.F.R. 1.104.
guidance: Use MPEP §821.04(a) procedures. If the elected invention is a product and previously nonelected process claims are rejoined, use 8.43 instead. Insert bracketed information as directed. Warn applicants that, as with other rejoinders, continuation/divisional claims could be subject to provisional double patenting rejections over allowable claims of the present application. Once the restriction is withdrawn, 35 U.S.C. 121 is no longer applicable.

name: Claim terms plain meaning in the art
description: Claim terms are given their plain meaning in the art being examined unless it is inconsistent with the specification.
guidance: Interpretation should follow ordinary meaning in the relevant technical field unless the specification clearly indicates a different meaning (See: MPEP 2111.01). Early explanation in Office actions helps applicants clarify meaning, amend claims, or respond effectively.

name: Interpret claims in light of the specification (without importing limitations)
description: Claims must be interpreted in light of the specification without reading limitations from the specification into the claims.
guidance: Use the specification to inform claim meaning but avoid importing limitations or narrowing the claim merely because a preferred embodiment is disclosed (See: MPEP 2111.01).

name: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) during examination
description: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) is always used to interpret claims under examination.
guidance: BRI does not mean the broadest possible interpretation; the interpretation must be consistent with the specification and how the term is commonly used in the art (MPEP 2111).

name: Consider every word in a claim
description: Also, every word in a claim must be considered in judging the patentability of that claim against the prior art: No limitation, functional or otherwise, can be ignored.
guidance: Every claimed term may have significance for patentability; do not disregard limitations simply because they are functional or appear non-structural (See: MPEP 2143.03).

name: Recognize claim parts and transitional phrases
description: A claim has three main parts: a preamble or introduction; a transitional phrase (comprising; consisting of; consisting essentially of); and a body reciting the elements of the invention.
guidance: Understand the meaning of transitional phrases: 'comprising' is open, 'consisting of' is closed, and 'consisting essentially of' is open but excludes materials or steps that materially affect the basic and novel characteristics of the invention (See: MPEP 608.01(m) & 2111.03).

name: Case-by-case determination whether a preamble limits a claim
description: The determination of whether a preamble limits a claim is made on a case-by-case basis in light of the facts in each case and should be based on: (1) The overall form of the claim; (2) The invention as disclosed in the specification; (3) The invention as illuminated in prosecution history.
guidance: There is no litmus test; evaluate the specific circumstances and record (See: MPEP 2111.02).

name: Indicators that a preamble will likely limit a claim
description: The preamble is necessary to give 'life, meaning and vitality' to the claim; the preamble provides antecedent basis for a limitation in the body; the preamble recites, and thereby limits, the structure of the claimed invention; the preamble recitation is relied upon during prosecution to distinguish the claimed invention from the prior art.
guidance: If any of these apply, treat the preamble language as a claim limitation (See: MPEP 2111.02 & 2111.02(II)). Examples: 'clock' imparting structure/necessity in an EL lamp claim; 'synthetic sheet material' requiring the prior art be synthetic and a sheet.

name: Indicators that a preamble will likely NOT limit a claim
description: The body of the claim following the preamble is a self-contained description and does not depend on the preamble for completeness; a preamble that describes the purpose or intended use generally does not limit the claims; the preamble merely extols benefits or features with no clear reliance on those benefits as patentably significant.
guidance: If the claim body stands alone and the preamble is only an intended use or example, the preamble ordinarily will not be treated as limiting (See: MPEP 2111.02 & 2111.02(II)). Examples: intended-use recitations where the reference need only be capable of the use (poncho as grill cover).

name: Key questions to determine whether a preamble limits
description: Ask: Does the preamble language provide antecedent basis for terms in the body? Does the language in the body set out the complete invention? Does the preamble merely provide a statement of purpose or intended use? Is the preamble essential to understanding limitations or terms in the body?
guidance: If the preamble provides antecedent basis or is essential to understanding the claim limitations, it will likely be limiting. Note: a new use for an old product does not render the old product patentable.

name: Structural limitations must be disclosed by prior art (capability vs. actual use)
description: If the preamble or body recites structural limitations (e.g., an electrode), an anticipating reference must disclose that structure or show the structure is capable of performing the claimed function.
guidance: A reference need not show actual practice so long as the reference structure could be so used and there is nothing disclosed that would prevent such use. However, positively claimed structural elements must be present (Example: electrode must be disclosed; electrode need only be capable of being placed on a patient's body).

name: Inherent properties can anticipate claimed characteristics
description: Where a claim recites material properties (e.g., hydrostatic head pressure, Gurley Hill Porosity, moisture vapor transmission rate), an anticipatory prior art composition need not expressly teach those values if the composition inherently possesses them.
guidance: Examiner may show that the prior art composition inherently possesses the claimed properties for anticipation to apply.

name: Functional 'whereby' clauses can impose structural limitations
description: Functional recitations (e.g., in a 'whereby' clause) may impose structural limitations if elements in the claim are designed to perform the recited function.
guidance: If the claimed structure is designed to perform the function, an anticipatory reference must be capable of being used to achieve that function (Example: servo-controlled yarn guide designed to underfeed/overfeed).

name: Examiner practice: explain claim interpretations early and in detail in Office actions
description: Clarity of claim terms in granted patents is improved when the interpretation of claim terms is explained in Office actions.
guidance: Early, detailed and correct claim interpretation benefits both examiners and applicants: reduces guesswork, enables persuasive responses or claim amendments, leads to more efficient prosecution, provides public notice of claim boundaries, and informs PTAB and courts of how claims were understood. Proper first Office Action analysis can reduce rework and make subsequent Office actions more likely to be final or allowance.

name: Examiner review of written arguments and amendments
description: Where a written argument is submitted along with an amendment, an examiner shall review both the argument and the amendment in depth and determine whether the notified grounds for rejection can be overcome based on such argument and amendment. Where only a written argument is submitted without an amendment, an examiner shall consider sufficiently the argument to determine whether the grounds for rejection can be overcome.
guidance: If a written argument insists matters to be amended but no amendment is submitted, examination shall be made on the description and claims; where there is discrepancy between argued amendments and actual amendments, examination is based on actual amendments; if matters are only disclosed in the written argument (not in amendment) indicating requirements are met, examiner may re-notify the same ground at his/her discretion.

name: Requests for documents and types of documents examiners may ask for
description: If considered necessary to expedite examination, an examiner may ask an applicant to submit documents and other references required for examination.
guidance: Typical requested documents include: related documents and translations for international applications; examination outcomes in other patent offices; a written statement mapping each claim's technical subject matter to description paragraph numbers; a statement explaining relations among claims when many; a written gist summary of claimed invention; samples or experiment results where needed to verify effects (only if they'd confirm sufficiency upon filing); statements explaining formula induction or definitions of technical terms; statements clarifying claims in written arguments; documents relevant to examination results of priority-claim applications and their Korean translation. Requests should specify which document and are made under the examiner's name; submission period falls within period for written argument.

name: Circumstances requiring additional search
description: During the examination stage, an examiner shall conduct additional searches where: (1) incomplete understanding of claimed invention found via written argument, personal interview, or information; (2) amended claims include subject matters not covered by original search; (3) claimed invention excluded from original search due to lack of unity of invention; (4) an international patent application enters domestic stage and its translation is expected; (5) other cases considered necessary for additional research.
guidance: Additional searches are required to ensure proper examination when scope or understanding changes.

name: Examination deferral or extension of processing period — grounds and limits
description: An examiner may defer an examination or extend the processing period within 2 months when an application falls under specified cases, noting deferral/extension is not allowed when Commissioner or examiner designates the processing period.
guidance: Grounds include: (i) prior-filed or conflicting applications not laid open or examination requests not made; (ii) period for domestic priority claim not elapsed; (iii) a patent trial or proceeding related to the application is pending (including administrative trial/litigation); (iv) required time due to outsourcing prior-art search, expert opinions, or consultation examination; (v) period for submission of evidential documents for priority right not elapsed; (vi) other necessary occasions. Deferral/extension must be reported to head and notified to applicant. Examiner must review >1/month whether reasons have been resolved and must conduct examination once reasons cleared by termination date. Further deferrals/extensions require reporting and are limited to two months except certain external-cause cases where extension allowed only for causes not imputable to the examiner.

name: Handling later-filed applications vs prior-filed applications
description: Where more than two patent applications are filed on the identical invention, the examiner shall defer examination for later-filed applications until the prior-filed application has been processed or laid-open or registered. However, where the later-filed application can be rejected based on the same ground as the prior-filed application, the examiner can start examination.
guidance: If prior-filed application is processed/laid-open/registered after deferral, examiner may conduct examination on later-filed application but final decision must apply Article 36(1) once claim scope of prior-filed application is determined. Table in guideline explains procedures depending on disclosure and identity of applicants.

name: Refund of search fee and excess claims fee under 37 CFR 1.138(d)
description: An applicant seeking refund of the search fee and excess claims fee by abandoning an application filed on or after Dec 8, 2004 must submit a declaration of express abandonment by way of petition under 1.138(d) before an examination has been made; certificate of mailing/transmission date under § 1.8 is not taken into account for determining timeliness.
guidance: If not filed before examination, Office may retain entire fees. A petition must be filed before an examination is 'made' and a two-month non-extendable period applies for requesting refund after declaration.

name: Termination of proceedings (copendency) definition under 35 U.S.C. 120
description: A second application is considered copending with an earlier application if it is filed before (A) the patenting, (B) the abandonment of, or (C) termination of proceedings on the earlier application. 'Before' has consistently been interpreted to mean 'not later than.'
guidance: This definition affects whether later applications can claim benefit/copedency to earlier filings.

name: Secondary considerations (objective indicia) as rebuttal evidence
description: Rebuttal evidence may include secondary considerations such as commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, and failure of others.
guidance: Secondary considerations (Graham) are relevant and must be considered but do not necessarily control the obviousness conclusion. Applicants must provide hard evidence (PTO lacks means to gather it). Evidence must be commensurate in scope with the claimed invention and attributable to the claimed invention (nexus requirement). See cases: Graham, Piasecki, GPAC, Huang, Paulsen, Kulling, Grasselli.

name: Unexpected results or properties
description: Evidence that the claimed invention yields unexpectedly improved properties or properties not present in the prior art may rebut a prima facie case of obviousness.
guidance: A showing of unexpected results must be based on evidentiary data, not argument or speculation (In re Mayne). Unexpected results for a single species or narrow portion can be sufficient if a skilled artisan could ascertain a trend and reasonably extend probative value (Clemens, Chupp). However, scope/commensurateness and existence of other motivations in prior art can limit the sufficiency of a new-use showing (Dillon, Grasselli, Greenfield, Lindner, Albrecht). See MPEP §716.02 - §716.02(g).

name: Enablement/absence of a method for making a claimed compound in prior art
description: If the prior art fails to disclose or render obvious a method for making the claimed compound, that absence may preclude a conclusion that the compound was in the public's possession and can rebut obviousness.
guidance: Applicant bears the burden to show that the relied-upon reference would not enable a skilled artisan to produce the claimed compounds (Hoeksema, Grose, Ashland Oil). Prior-art enablement is a key factor in structural-relationship obviousness rejections.

name: Nexus and commensurate-in-scope requirements
description: To obtain substantial weight for rebuttal evidence (e.g., commercial success, unexpected properties), applicant must establish a nexus between the evidence and the claimed invention, and the evidence must be reasonably commensurate in scope with the claimed invention.
guidance: The PTO relies on applicants to provide hard evidence of nexus (Ex parte Remark discussion). Evidence of commercial success for products not covered by the claims is not probative (Huang, GPAC, Paulsen). When assessing commensurateness, examiners should not require unexpected results across the entire scope of a chemical range; a superior property in one part of a spectrum can suffice if probative value can be reasonably extended (Chupp, Clemens), but examples exist where one-species results were insufficient (Grasselli, Greenfield, Lindner). See cases and MPEP guidance.

name: Arguments based on limitations not claimed are improper
description: Limitations disclosed in the specification but not recited in the claims should not be read into the claims to create patentability.
guidance: Claims are interpreted in light of the specification, but limitations from the specification are not to be imported into the claims absent claim language (Van Geuns, Constant).

name: Teaching away from the invention
description: A prior art reference that teaches away from the claimed invention is a significant factor in determining obviousness; the nature and substance of the teaching-away must be weighed.
guidance: Teaching away may preclude combining references where the references criticize, discredit, or discourage the claimed solution (In re Gurley, In re Grasselli). However, mere disclosure of alternatives without criticism does not constitute teaching away (In re Fulton). See MPEP §2141.02 and §2143.01.

name: Drawings must be acceptable (readable/reproducible) for publication
description: Drawings are accepted by OPAP if the drawings are readable and reproducible for publication purposes; drawings are either acceptable or unacceptable (no formal/informal distinction).
guidance: Examiners should review drawings for disclosure of the claimed invention and proper use of reference numerals. Objections to drawings in utility or plant applications will not be held in abeyance unless applicant is otherwise notified in an Office action (37 CFR 1.85(a)). Correct drawing corrections should be made promptly before allowance to avoid delays or reductions to term adjustment (37 CFR 1.704(c)(10)).

name: Drawings must show every feature of the invention specified in the claims
description: 37 CFR 1.83(a): The drawing in a nonprovisional application must show every feature of the invention specified in the claims; conventional features not essential to understanding may be illustrated with graphical symbols or labeled representations.
guidance: Tables and sequence listings included in the specification should not be duplicated in the drawings. Any structural detail essential for a proper understanding should be shown. If the invention is an improvement on an old machine, show the improved portion disconnected from the old structure and also another view showing connection (37 CFR 1.83(b)).

name: Requirement to employ competent draftsperson (form paragraph 6.21)
description: New corrected drawings in compliance with 37 CFR 1.121(d) are required; applicant is advised to employ a competent patent draftsperson outside the Office as the USPTO does not prepare new drawings.
guidance: Corrected drawings required in reply to Office action to avoid abandonment; requirement will not be held in abeyance. Examiner may insert specific reason for objection in bracket 1 of the form paragraph (e.g., drawings do not show every feature of the claims).

name: Complete illustration obligation — show structural details of importance
description: Any structural detail that is of sufficient importance to be described should be shown in the drawing. (Ex parte Good, 1911.)
guidance: Use form paragraphs (6.22.01, 6.22.04, 6.36) to require illustration when essential structural details are missing. If a feature is claimed but not shown, the feature must be shown or cancelled from the claim(s); no new matter should be entered.

name: Definiteness under 35 U.S.C. § 112 / Nautilus standard
description: Claims, viewed in light of the specification and prosecution history, must 'inform those skilled in the art about the scope of the invention with reasonable certainty.' (Nautilus, 134 S. Ct. at 2129).
guidance: Assess claim terms in context of specification and prosecution history to determine whether they provide objective boundaries for those of skill in the art. A lack of definiteness renders claims invalid. Terms of degree can be definite if they 'provide enough certainty to one of skill in the art when read in the context of the invention.' (Interval Licensing).

name: Use of intrinsic and extrinsic evidence for indefiniteness
description: If intrinsic evidence (claim language, specification, prosecution history) fails to supply an objective boundary, courts may consider extrinsic evidence (e.g., expert testimony) to determine definiteness.
guidance: District courts may rely on expert declarations to resolve indefiniteness where intrinsic record is silent or ambiguous; subsidiary factual findings based on extrinsic evidence are reviewed for clear error on appeal.

name: Objective boundary requirement for terms of degree
description: Terms of degree (e.g., 'minimal', 'substantial') are not per se indefinite, but the claims/specification/prosecution history must supply a point of comparison or objective baseline to interpret the degree term.
guidance: If the specification only shows extreme examples (e.g., no redundancy) but the claim contemplates some redundancy, and prosecution history does not explain 'how much' is permitted, the term may be indefinite (Sonix and Interval Licensing distinctions discussed).

name: Representative-claim treatment and waiver
description: Courts may treat a claim as representative when the patentee does not present meaningful argument for distinctive significance of limitations in other claims or parties agree to treat a claim as representative.
guidance: A patentee who advances meaningful, distinct arguments regarding dependent-claim limitations (e.g., arguing that dependent claims add inventive concepts) preserves those arguments; a court should not treat an independent claim as representative where the patentee has preserved separate arguments for dependents.

name: Alice two-step patent-eligibility framework
description: Step 1: determine whether the claims are directed to a patent-ineligible concept (laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract idea). Step 2: if so, consider the claim elements individually and as an ordered combination to determine whether additional elements transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application (i.e., whether an 'inventive concept' exists). (Alice, Mayo).
guidance: Apply Step 1 to identify the abstract idea (e.g., collecting/recognizing/storing data, classifying and storing digital images). At Step 2, examine whether claim limitations amount to 'well-understood, routine, conventional' activity or instead add an inventive concept that improves computer functionality.

name: Abstract-idea determination must focus on claimed improvements
description: To avoid being 'abstract', claim limitations must be directed to a specific asserted improvement in computer capabilities rather than using computers as mere tools.
guidance: Limiting an invention to a technological environment (e.g., parsing from source to object code) does not defeat abstractness absent evidence that the claimed steps improve computer functionality in some way (see Enfish, Visual Memory distinctions).

name: Factual nature of 'well-understood, routine, conventional' inquiry
description: Whether a claim element or combination is well-understood, routine, and conventional to a skilled artisan at the time of the patent is a question of fact.
guidance: Because this is a factual determination, it may preclude resolution on summary judgment if there is a genuine dispute of material fact. Such facts relevant to invalidity must be proven by clear and convincing evidence.

name: What can constitute an inventive concept under Alice step two
description: Claim limitations that capture purported unconventional activities that improve computer functionality—e.g., 'storing a reconciled object structure in the archive without substantial redundancy' and 'selectively editing an object structure linked to other structures to thereby effect a one-to-many change'—may supply an inventive concept.
guidance: If the specification and claims capture such improvements (and there is factual support), they can create a genuine issue of material fact about eligibility; summary judgment may be improper where these issues are disputed.

name: Joint research agreement (JRA) conditions under 35 U.S.C. 102(c)
description: Three statutory conditions that must be satisfied for a JRA to establish that disclosed subject matter and claimed invention are deemed owned by the same person.
guidance: A. Subject matter must have been developed and the claimed invention made by, or on behalf of, one or more parties to a joint research agreement that was in effect on or before the effective filing date (35 U.S.C. 102(c)(1)). B. The claimed invention must have been made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the JRA (35 U.S.C. 102(c)(2)). C. The application must disclose, or be amended to disclose, the names of the parties to the JRA (35 U.S.C. 102(c)(3)). The AIA defines JRA as a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement between two or more persons/entities for experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention.

name: Continuation applications (definition and requirements)
description: A continuation application is a re-filing of an existing patent application that uses the same specification and claims priority to the parent's filing date.
guidance: Receives a new serial number; must have the same specification as the parent (no new matter); claims the same subject matter as the earlier parent but may be used to pursue new claims targeting different aspects. Continuations are useful to capture new claim scope or respond to competitor activities.

name: Continuation-in-part (CIP) applications (definition and priority rules)
description: A CIP includes new matter in addition to the parent's disclosure and mixes original and new disclosure.
guidance: New matter does not receive the parent's earlier filing date; original matter retains priority date. Each claim's priority date depends on which disclosure (original or new matter) supports that claim. CIPs are useful for incremental improvements added after the original filing.

name: Strategic use: when to file each application type
description: Guidance mapping which continuing application type to use depending on prosecution circumstances.
guidance: Divisional: after a restriction requirement to pursue non-elected inventions. Continuation: to capture new claim scope, respond to competitor activities, or pursue broader/different claims. CIP: to incorporate post-filing improvements (new matter).

name: Priority-date determination for claims (general rule)
description: A claim's effective priority date depends on the disclosure in the parent or application that supports the claim.
guidance: For continuations and divisionals supported by the same specification, claims generally get the parent's filing date. For CIPs, only original matter gets the earlier date; new matter gets the CIP filing date. Each claim must be analyzed for whether it is supported by the earlier disclosure to determine its priority date.

name: Portfolio management when drafting the parent
description: Design the patent family tree at drafting to enable effective continuation/divisional practice and to cover commercial embodiments and design-arounds.
guidance: Ensure the specification supports divisional and continuation claims; cover competitor design-arounds; coordinate claim scope across family members; avoid over-breadth that invites invalidity challenges and avoid under-breadth that leaves commercial embodiments unprotected. Plan family strategy early.

name: Strategic continuation pendency (best practice)
description: Maintain continuation pendency strategically to preserve prosecution flexibility.
guidance: Best practice: maintain at least one continuation in every family pending until the patent term expires to allow adapting claims to new infringers, capturing claim scope discovered during litigation, and responding to design-arounds.

name: Restrictions, limits, and double-patenting considerations
description: Practical and legal limits on continuing application practice and interactions with patent term and double-patenting rules.
guidance: USPTO may try to limit continuation practice. Continuations cannot extend the patent term beyond the parent plus any RCE and applicable adjustments. Patent term adjustment (PTA) may differ between parent and continuation. If claims are not patentably distinct between applications, double-patenting issues arise and a terminal disclaimer may be required.

name: Prosecution best practices specific to continuations/divisionals/CIPs
description: Operational actions applicants should take when using continuing applications.
guidance: File continuations before the parent issue fee is paid; disclose all known prior art in continuations (duty of candor continues); consider request for continued examination (RCE) versus filing a continuation strategically; and carefully track the relationship between parent and continuations (family tree, claim dependencies, priority chains).

name: Design patents subject to § 103 nonobviousness
description: Design patents must meet the nonobviousness requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 103; the provisions relating to utility patents apply to design patents unless otherwise provided.
guidance: Apply the statutory language of § 103 to design claims, recognizing differences between utility and design patents (e.g., focus on overall appearance, visual impressions, artistry, and style rather than function or utility).

name: Apply Graham factors to design patents
description: Obviousness of a design patent claim should be determined based on factual criteria similar to those used for utility patents under Graham v. John Deere Co.
guidance: Use the Graham framework as adapted to designs: (1) scope and content of the prior art (with analogous art limitation), (2) differences between the prior art and the claimed design, (3) the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art (ordinary designer), and (4) consideration of secondary considerations/indicia of (non)obviousness when presented.

name: Scope and content of the prior art / analogous art requirement
description: References qualify for an obviousness determination only when they are analogous to the claimed design; analogous art defines the knowledge base of the person of ordinary skill and guards against hindsight.
guidance: Treat analogous art as a gateway: a reference must be in an art reasonably pertinent to the claimed design (typically same field of endeavor) or otherwise analogous. The analogous art test limits what may be considered in the obviousness inquiry and helps prevent reconstruction of the invention with hindsight.

name: Evaluate differences between the prior art and the claimed design (overall visual impression)
description: Assess the differences between the claimed design and the prior art in terms of the overall visual impression created by the design as a whole.
guidance: Consider the claimed design and prior art holistically (overall visual impression) and identify the specific differences (e.g., shapes, lines, creases, terminus). Do not conflate this inquiry with anticipation; for design patents, the visual impression as a whole is central.

name: Reject rigid 'basically the same' and 'so related' requirements (overrule Rosen-Durling)
description: The Rosen requirement that a primary reference be 'basically the same' and Durling's requirement that secondary references be 'so related' are improperly rigid and inconsistent with § 103 and KSR.
guidance: Adopt a flexible, common-sense approach to motivation to combine; do not terminate the obviousness inquiry merely because no single prior-art design is 'basically the same' as the claimed design.

name: Guard against hindsight and improper combinations
description: Combinations assembled only with the benefit of hindsight or from non-analogous arts that reconstruct the claimed design are insufficient to prove obviousness.
guidance: Ensure that combining references is supported by analogous-art analysis and record evidence demonstrating that an ordinary designer would have reasonably made the combination without impermissible hindsight.

name: Factor One — Incremental value contributed by the invention
description: Damages must be based only on the incremental value that the claimed invention contributes to the accused product, determined by comparing the allegedly infringing technology to the accused infringer's best ex ante alternative.
guidance: Juries should consider commercially acceptable non-infringing alternatives available at the negotiation date. The best alternative is determined by both cost to and value for the infringer; the maximum the infringer would pay equals the cost of the best alternative plus the incremental value of the invention over that alternative. Disregard 'switching costs' (e.g., redesign, retooling, inventory) when determining incremental value.

name: Examiner acceptance considerations for amendments
description: Examiners should accept amendments that restrict scope, improve clarity of the description, or amend claims in a manner clearly desirable without changing their subject-matter or scope.
guidance: An amended application must satisfy all other filing requirements. Examiners must ensure amendments do not add content beyond the application as filed.

name: Special considerations when claims are amended
description: When claims have been amended, examiners should consider unity of invention, whether the description needs corresponding amendment to remove serious inconsistency, and whether all amended claims are supported by the description.
guidance: If categories of claims are altered, the examiner may draw attention to potential inappropriateness of the title and/or abstract. (References: PCT ISPE GL, Chapter 20, Paragraphs 5.29–5.30; Chapter 20, Paragraph 20.09.)

name: Use of later-filed examples or statements as evidence
description: Later-filed examples or statements of advantage, even if not allowable into the application, may be taken into account by the examiner as evidence in support of allowability of claims.
guidance: If such evidence is used to support a positive conclusion (e.g., on inventive step), the examiner should mention this evidence in the examination report.

name: Admission of data or evidence submitted after filing
description: Applicants may submit data or evidence after filing to address examiner objections; admission depends on field and case.
guidance: As long as support can be found in the original disclosure (no new teaching), the examiner may consider the submitted data. If the post-filing data provides a new teaching (e.g., a selection invention without support in the application as filed), it would not be admissible. Example: claiming a specific compound merely by providing its advantages later is not allowable.

name: Broadening claims: pre-grant vs post-grant
description: There is no pre-grant restriction on broadening the scope of claims provided the amendment does not include matter extending beyond the disclosure as filed; post-grant amendments generally cannot broaden the scope of the claims.
guidance: If the disclosure in the application as filed is broader than the claims as filed, the applicant may amend before grant to align claims with the specification. Post-grant restrictions on broadening apply in most AMS.

name: Lack of support: support requirement for claim amendments
description: An amendment to include subject-matter from a claim into the description is permissible, but consideration must be given whether the amended description provides required support for the claims. Each claim limitation must be explicitly or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure.
guidance: Contradictions between claims and description must be resolved by amendment. Amendments introducing a negative limitation, exclusion or disclaimer should be examined for potential new-matter issues.

name: Post-grant amendments: effect and restrictions
description: Post-grant amendments, once allowed, have effect and are deemed always to have had effect from the date of grant; the test and considerations for added subject-matter are the same as for pre-grant amendments, but post-grant amendments cannot broaden claims.
guidance: Practices are similar across AMS; examine whether a post-grant amendment would extend protection or add subject-matter.

name: ASPEC work-sharing filing conditions for second IP Office
description: A patent application filed in a participating AMS as a 'second IP Office' must be a corresponding application of the application considered by the 'first IP Office' and must be supported by S&E documents from that first IP Office.
guidance: All claims filed in subsequent patent offices must correspond to a sufficient extent to the allowable/patentable claims referred to in the S&E documents from the first IP Office. The ASEAN Comparative Study Report (CSR) is a tool to assess compatibility of practices across ASEAN POs.

name: Statutory category determination (Step 1)
description: Determine whether the claim falls within a statutory category (e.g., process, composition of matter, machine, manufacture).
guidance: If the claim recites a process or a composition of matter, Step 1 is satisfied (e.g., a claim reciting steps of detecting JUL-1 in plasma is a process). This is the opening statutory-category inquiry before any exception analysis.

name: Apply Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) to identify closest naturally occurring counterpart
description: Use the claim's broadest reasonable interpretation (in view of the specification) to determine the claim scope and thereby identify the closest naturally occurring counterpart for comparison.
guidance: The BRI determines whether the claim as written encompasses naturally occurring material (e.g., whether a texiol/water mixture as claimed reads on the plant sap). Use the specification's definitions where provided to limit or define BRI.

name: Markedly different characteristics analysis (for nature-based products)
description: Compare the claimed nature-based product to its closest naturally occurring counterpart(s) to determine whether the claimed product has markedly different characteristics (structure, function, or other properties).
guidance: Marked differences can be structural, functional, organoleptic, time-release, physical form, dissolution behavior, etc. Examples include changed organoleptic properties (neutralized bitterness), altered physical form (solid gel), specific particle size distributions that change dissolution, or controlled‑release formulations. Cite Roslin and analyze whether the altered property is relevant to the nature of the invention.

name: Specificity of amounts/ratios alone insufficient for eligibility
description: Reciting particular concentrations, percentages, or ratios in a claim does not automatically render a nature-based claim eligible.
guidance: Merely claiming specific amounts (e.g., 1–5% texiol, 90% water) does not show a marked change in structure or function unless the applicant explains which characteristics are markedly different; best practice is to explain what characteristics differ and why those differences are relevant.

name: Assess whether additional elements amount to 'significantly more' (Step 2B)
description: Analyze whether any element or combination of elements beyond the judicial exception ensures that the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the exception.
guidance: Look for additional limitations that, alone or in combination, are unconventional, integrate the exception into a practical application, add meaningful limits on use, or otherwise transform the claim. Physical or tangible elements (obtaining, detecting, administering) do not automatically make a claim eligible; the totality and how those elements constrain use matter (see Alice, Mayo).

name: Integration of the exception into a practical application
description: Evaluate whether the additional elements integrate the judicial exception into a diagnostic, treatment, or other practical process so that the claim is not merely instructing practitioners to apply the exception.
guidance: Examples: claiming a particular treatment step tied to diagnostic detection can integrate the exception into a treatment process (ensuring accurate diagnosis and proper treatment) and thus may supply 'significantly more.' The combination should meaningfully limit the claim's scope and use.

name: Rejection/allowance record guidance
