description: Office actions and reasons for allowance should explain the basis for concluding that a claim is directed to an exception or is eligible, and should identify the exception(s) and closest natural counterpart(s).
guidance: A rejection should point to the nature‑based product or other exception in the claim and explain why it lacks markedly different characteristics or why additional elements do not amount to significantly more. If helpful, cite analogous court decisions (e.g., Roslin, Funk Brothers, Myriad, Diehr, Mayo). If the claim is eligible, the record may note that the exception exists but the claim recites additional limitations that are unconventional or integrate the exception into a practical application.

name: When Step 2B need not be performed
description: If analysis under Step 2A concludes the claim is not directed to any judicial exception (i.e., the claim has no exception or has markedly different characteristics), Step 2B is unnecessary.
guidance: If Step 2A resolves eligibility in favor of the claim, examiners need not perform the Step 2B 'significantly more' analysis. The record may nevertheless include explanatory remarks for clarity.

name: Use of analogous case law for explanatory support
description: When issuing a rejection or allowance, examiners may cite analogous court decisions to illustrate why a claimed invention is or is not like a judicially excluded category.
guidance: Examples: Roslin (cloned mammals), Funk Brothers (bacterial mixtures), Myriad (products of nature), Diehr (combinations), Mayo/Alice (laws of nature/abstract ideas). Use analogies to explain lack of marked changes or to support why combination/limitations supply significantly more.

name: Acts constituting practice in patent matters
description: Practice before the Office in patent matters includes, but is not limited to: preparing and prosecuting any patent application; consulting with or giving advice in contemplation of filing a patent application or other document with the Office; drafting the specification or claims of a patent application; drafting an amendment or reply to a communication from the Office that may require written argument to establish patentability; and drafting a reply to a communication from the Office regarding a patent application (37 C.F.R. § 11.5(b)(1)).
guidance: Case law and the decision interpret these activities as practicing law (In re Amalgamated Dev. Co.; In re Herren; Kennedy v. Bar Ass'n). Mere transcription of a client's words may not be practice, but translating/rephrasing client statements into legal/technical language, drafting claims, and drafting responses with legal argument do constitute practice.

name: Privilege assertions in investigations must be supported
description: When a respondent claims attorney-client privilege in response to OED RFIs, the claim must be accompanied by a privilege log or other supporting documentation.
guidance: Failure to provide a privilege log or adequate support for privilege assertions undermines the claim and supports OED's position that the respondent did not fully comply with the investigation.

name: Content requirements (37 CFR 1.98) — required elements
description: Any IDS filed under 1.97 must include: (a)(1) a list of all patents, publications, applications, or other information submitted (U.S. patents and U.S. patent application publications listed separately); (a)(2) a legible copy of each foreign patent, publication (or causing portion), each cited pending unpublished U.S. application spec/claims/drawings (or portion), and all other information or portion which caused listing; and (a)(3) for non-English items, a concise explanation of relevance and/or a copy of translation if available. Additionally, each page of the list must include application number; there must be a column next to each document for examiner initials; and a clear heading indicating the list is an Information Disclosure Statement.
guidance: Follow 37 CFR 1.98(a)(1)-(3) and 1.98(b) identifying details: U.S. patents by inventor/patent number/issue date; U.S. patent application publications by applicant/publication number/publication date; U.S. applications by inventor/application number/filing date; foreign patents with country/document number/publication or issue date; publications by publisher/author/title/relevant pages/date/place. Use PTO/SB/08 to ensure consistent format.

name: Copies and portions required to be submitted
description: A legible copy must be submitted for: each foreign patent; each publication or the portion which caused listing (except U.S. patents and U.S. patent application publications unless required); for each cited pending unpublished U.S. application, the application specification including claims and drawings or the portion causing listing; and all other information or the portion which caused it to be listed (37 CFR 1.98(a)(2)).
guidance: If documents are cumulative, one copy may suffice provided it is stated that the other citations are cumulative (see 1.98(c)). Copies need not be resubmitted if prior application is properly identified and relied on for earlier effective filing date under 35 U.S.C. 120 and earlier IDS complied with 1.98(a)-(c).

name: Primacy of the claims
description: The claims of a patent define the invention and the patentee’s right to exclude; they are of primary importance in ascertaining precisely what is patented.
guidance: Do not construe the patent in a manner different from the plain import of the claim terms; the claims are the sole measure of the grant. Historical authorities (Merrill, White, Aro, etc.) support treating claim language as the starting point for scope.

name: Ordinary and customary meaning to a POSITA
description: Claim terms are generally given their ordinary and customary meaning — i.e., the meaning the term would have to a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention (effective filing date).
guidance: Use this objective baseline to begin interpretation; the meaning must be ascertained in the technological and temporal context of the invention (citations: Vitronics, Innova, Home Diagnostics).

name: Contextual construction using intrinsic evidence
description: A claim term must be read in the context of the entire patent, including the specification and the prosecution history; the court should start with the intrinsic record.
guidance: Intrinsic evidence (claims, specification, prosecution history) usually provides the most reliable guide to meaning. The person of ordinary skill is deemed to read the claim in that full context; the intrinsic record often provides the technological and temporal context necessary to ascertain meaning.

name: Specification is the single best guide
description: The specification is highly relevant and usually dispositive for claim construction; it is the single best guide to the meaning of a disputed term.
guidance: Read claims in view of the specification. The specification may act as the patentee’s lexicography (explicit definition), may define terms by implication, or may show disavowal of claim scope. Because the specification was created to describe the invention, it can inform or control the proper construction even absent an express definition.

name: Claims themselves and other claims as interpretive tools
description: The words of the claims themselves, the context within the same claim, and the usage of terms in other claims (including dependent claims) inform claim meaning.
guidance: Consider how a term is used in the same claim and across claims; for example, modifiers in a claim ('steel baffles') can show that a term ('baffles') is not inherently limited to that modifier. Presence of a dependent claim that adds a limitation gives rise to a presumption that the independent claim lacks that limitation.

name: Prosecution history is part of intrinsic evidence
description: The prosecution history (file wrapper) should be consulted as part of intrinsic evidence; it can show how the patentee and PTO understood the invention and whether the patentee narrowed claim scope during prosecution.
guidance: Prosecution history can inform whether the inventor disclaimed or limited claim scope, but it is often ambiguous and less clear than the specification, so it may be less useful. Use it to exclude interpretations disclaimed during prosecution but be cautious about ambiguities.

name: Extrinsic evidence is secondary and less significant
description: Evidence external to the patent and prosecution history (dictionaries, treatises, expert testimony) may be admitted but is less significant than the intrinsic record in determining legally operative claim meaning.
guidance: Extrinsic evidence can shed light on background technology and how a POSITA would understand terms, but courts should weigh it cautiously and not let it override intrinsic evidence. It is permissible but unlikely to yield a reliable interpretation absent support from intrinsic materials.

name: Specification can define terms expressly or by implication (inventor’s lexicography)
description: A patentee may act as his own lexicographer; the specification may expressly define a claim term or define it by implication such that the patent controls the term’s meaning.
guidance: If the specification provides a clear alternative definition or shows an intentional disclaimer, that definition/disavowal governs claim construction. Such a definition need not be in an explicit definitional format — the specification’s usage can redefine terms by implication.

name: Avoid importing limitations from the specification into claims
description: Courts must not read limitations from the written description into the claims where the claims’ language does not so limit them.
guidance: Be wary of the 'cardinal sin' of importing limitations from the specification; however, closely relatedly, do not ignore the specification’s guidance — balance is required: do not import unintended limitations, but let the specification inform meaning and disclose any express or implied disavowal.

name: Construction as of effective filing date / temporal context
description: The meaning of claim terms is assessed as of the time of the invention or the patent’s effective filing date — the temporal context matters.
guidance: Interpretations should reflect the understanding of a POSITA at the relevant date (citations: Innova, PC Connector, Schering). Extrinsic sources and dictionaries should reflect the state of the art as of that time where possible.

name: When ordinary meaning is readily apparent, use common-sense/dictionaries
description: If the ordinary meaning of claim language is readily apparent even to lay judges, claim construction may be straightforward and general-purpose dictionaries may be helpful.
guidance: In such cases, little more than applying the widely accepted meaning of commonly understood words is necessary; reserve technical sources for when terms have special field-specific meanings.

name: PTO’s broadest reasonable construction during prosecution
description: The PTO applies the 'broadest reasonable interpretation' to claims during examination in light of the specification, and PTO rules require claim terms to find clear support in the description.
guidance: Although the PTO’s prosecutorial practice differs from judicial claim construction, courts may appropriately rely heavily on the written description (which the PTO also interprets) when construing claims. Recognize the differing standards but treat the specification as authoritative.

name: Required components of a submission under 37 CFR 1.114
description: As set forth in 37 CFR 1.114, a submission may include an information disclosure statement, an amendment to the written description, claims, or drawings, new arguments, or new evidence in support of patentability.
guidance: If a reply to the Office action is outstanding the submission must meet the reply requirements of 37 CFR 1.111. The submission may also consist of arguments in a previously filed appeal brief or reply brief, or an incorporation of such arguments in the transmittal letter or other paper accompanying the RCE.

name: After appeal to Federal Circuit or civil action — RCE generally unavailable
description: The procedure set forth in 37 CFR 1.114 is not available in an application after the filing of a Notice of Appeal to the Federal Circuit or commencement of a civil action in federal district court, unless the appeal or civil action is terminated and the application is still pending.
guidance: If an RCE is filed after court review, bring the application to the attention of the supervisory patent examiner or a quality assurance specialist to determine whether the RCE is proper. Unless the application contains allowed claims (or the court's mandate indicates further Office action), termination of an unsuccessful appeal or civil action results in abandonment. See MPEP § 1216.01.

name: Error rate (identification of legal error even when affirming)
description: Whether an appeals court identifies a legal error in a lower tribunal's analysis even while affirming the result; in the study, three coders reviewed 153 affirming opinions (excluding Rule 36) and found errors in only seven opinions (<5%).
guidance: Error rates indicate whether courts are reaching correct results for the right reasons; a low error rate supports the claim that the law can be predictably applied, and can serve as a benchmark for future empirical comparisons.

name: Patent owner statement timing and content (37 CFR 1.530)
description: Except as provided in §1.510(e), no statement or other response by the patent owner shall be filed prior to the determinations made in accordance with §1.515 or §1.520. If reexamination is ordered, the order will set a period of not less than two months from the date of the order within which the patent owner may file a statement on the new question of patentability, including any proposed amendments.
guidance: Any statement must clearly point out why the subject matter as claimed is not anticipated or rendered obvious by the prior art patents or printed publications, alone or in reasonable combinations. Where the request was filed by a third party requester, any statement must be served upon the requester in accordance with §1.248. First extensions may be granted up to one month for good and sufficient reasons; further extensions only in extraordinary situations.

name: Amendments in reexamination — general manner (37 CFR 1.530(d))
description: A proposed amendment in an ex parte or inter partes reexamination proceeding is made by filing a paper directing the specific changes to the patent specification, including claims, or drawings. Amendments may be submitted with a patent owner request, as part of a patent owner statement, or where permitted during prosecution under §1.550(a) or §1.937.
guidance: Specification changes (other than claims) must be made by submission of the entire text of an added or rewritten paragraph including markings per 1.530(f). An entire paragraph may be deleted by a statement deleting the paragraph without presenting its text. Precise insertion point must be identified. Markings compare to the original patent, not prior amendment.

name: Language and spacing/format requirements (37 CFR 1.52(b))
description: The application or proceeding and any amendments must comply with 1.52(a) and be in the English language or accompanied by an English translation. The specification and amendments must be 1.5 or double spaced, in a nonscript type font (e.g., Arial, Times Roman, or Courier, preferably font size 12; may be no smaller than 0.21 cm (0.08 inch) high), and only a single column of text.
guidance: The claim(s) must commence on a separate physical sheet or electronic page. The abstract must commence on a separate sheet or be submitted as the first page in reissue or reexamination proceedings. Noncompliant submissions will trigger a notice and opportunity to correct.

name: Status of claims and explanation of support for claim changes (37 CFR 1.530(e))
description: Whenever there is an amendment to the claims, the filer must supply, on pages separate from the changes, the status (pending or canceled) as of the amendment date of all patent claims and all added claims, and an explanation of the support in the disclosure of the patent for the changes to the claims made by the amendment paper.

name: Markings for changes (37 CFR 1.530(f))
description: Any changes relative to the patent being reexamined which are made to the specification, including the claims, must include the following markings: (1) matter to be omitted must be enclosed in brackets; and (2) matter to be added must be underlined.
guidance: All bracketing and underlining are made in comparison to the original patent; newly added paragraphs must be submitted completely underlined.

name: No enlargement of claim scope and new matter prohibition (37 CFR 1.530(j))
description: No amendment may enlarge the scope of the claims of the patent or introduce new matter. No amendment may be proposed for entry in an expired patent, and no amendment other than cancellation of claims will be incorporated into the patent by a certificate issued after the expiration of the patent.
guidance: Amendments are treated as entered for prosecution purposes if timely and compliant, but proposed amendments are not effective until the reexamination certificate is issued. See MPEP §2258 for enlargement-of-scope discussion and MPEP §2270 for new matter handling.

name: Amendment entry and fees
description: Amendments that comply with 37 CFR 1.530(d)-(j) and are formally presented pursuant to 37 CFR 1.52(a) and (b), and contain all fees required by 37 CFR 1.20(c), will be entered in the reexamination file pursuant to MPEP § 2234.
guidance: If adding claims, excess claim fees under 37 CFR 1.20(c)(3) and (4) may apply. Amended or new claims which broaden the scope of a claim should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 305; the test for enlargement is the same as that under the 2-year limitation for reissue applications adding enlarging claims (In re Freeman).

name: Bills in Equity — when must specify the claims alleged to be infringed
description: Bills in equity must specify the claims alleged to be infringed in certain circumstances — referenced section 579.
guidance: Standards for claim specificity in equitable pleadings; see section 579 for when specificity is required.

name: Claims — dedication to public for unclaimed subject-matter
description: All inventions not covered by claims are dedicated to the public — referenced section 176.
guidance: Failure to claim subject matter in patent specification results in dedication; strategic importance in drafting claims.

name: Claims — compound in respect of disclaimers
description: Compound claims in the context of disclaimers — referenced section 199.
guidance: How compound claims interact with disclaimers and what limitations follow.

name: Claims — construed broadly where invention successful
description: Claims are construed broadly where the invention has been successful — referenced section 185.
guidance: Courts may interpret claims liberally when the patented invention has proven commercially/methodologically successful.

name: Claims — construed in light of Patent Office limitations
description: Claims construed in light of Patent Office limitations — referenced sections 187, 187a.
guidance: Administrative prosecution history (limitations, rejections) affects claim construction.

name: Claims — construed in light of the specification
description: Claims construed in light of the specification — referenced section 182.
guidance: Claims should be read in view of the specification; specification can limit or explain claim scope.

name: Claims — construed in light of the state of the art
description: Claims construed in the light of the state of the art — referenced section 184.
guidance: Prior art context informs claim interpretation and scope.

name: Claims — construed liberally if Patent Office limitations unwarranted
description: Claims construed liberally if Patent Office limitations are unwarranted — referenced 187a.
guidance: If PTO-imposed limitations are deemed improper, courts may adopt a more liberal construction.

name: Claims — construed narrowly where patent not used
description: Claims construed narrowly where the patent is not used — referenced section 185.
guidance: Lack of commercial success or underuse may counsel narrower claim interpretation.

name: Claims — construed to cover real invention if possible
description: Claims construed to cover the real invention, if possible — referenced section 182.
guidance: Courts aim to effectuate the inventor's real invention within claim language where feasible.

name: Claims — containing statements of functions
description: Claims may contain statements of functions — referenced section 183.
guidance: Functional language in claims is permissible but has interpretive consequences; see section 183.

name: Claims — cover all uses of the device
description: Claims may cover all uses of the device — referenced section 180.
guidance: Claims can be drafted broadly to encompass all uses, subject to novelty and enablement constraints.

name: Claims — defective
description: Claims may be defective — referenced section 218.
guidance: Standards for when claims are considered defective (indefiniteness, lack of support, etc.).

name: Claims — differentiation between the several claims
description: Differentiation between the several claims of a patent — referenced section 177.
guidance: Each claim should be distinct and differences among claims evaluated for scope and validity.

name: Claims — each element must be described in specification
description: Each element of a claim must be described in the specification — referenced section 181.
guidance: Requirement ties to written description enablement: claimed elements should be supported in the specification.

name: Claims — elements not mentioned cannot be read into
description: Elements not mentioned in claims cannot be read into them (i.e., limitation by implication) — referenced section 181.
guidance: Cannot import unclaimed elements into claim scope via construction.

name: Claims — excessive
description: Excessive claims (too many) — referenced section 216.
guidance: Practical/fee/limitation issues when number of claims exceeds statutory or PTO allowance.

name: Claims — for single devices in reissues
description: Claims for single devices in reissues — referenced section 246.
guidance: Scope and limits on adding single-device claims in reissue proceedings.

name: Claims — function of
description: The function of claims — referenced section 176.
guidance: Claims define the monopoly and identify what is protected; drafting must align with this function.

name: Claims — functional in form
description: Claims may be functional in form — referenced sections 117a, 183, 220.
guidance: Use of means-plus-function or functional language and its interpretation under case law.

name: Claims — generic
description: Generic claims and their usage — referenced sections 116, 117a.
guidance: Generic claiming strategies and limits; interaction with enablement and written description.

name: Claims — how tested for co-extensiveness
description: How co-extensiveness of claims is tested — referenced section 180a.
guidance: Methods to determine when two claims are co-extensive (relevant for double patenting).

name: Claims — how written
description: How claims are written — referenced section 116.
guidance: Guidance on proper claim drafting/formalities (phrasing, antecedent basis, structure).

name: Claims — in combinations impliedly include connecting parts
description: In combination claims, connecting parts are impliedly included — referenced section 117.
guidance: Interpreting combination claims to include necessary connecting elements even if not explicitly recited.

name: Claims — indistinctness affects letters patent
description: How indistinctness of claims affects letters patent — referenced section 178.
guidance: Indefinite/indistinct claims can impair the enforceability or scope of a patent.

name: Claims — in specifications of compositions of matter
description: Claims in specifications of compositions of matter — referenced section 119.
guidance: How to claim chemical compositions, requirements for specificity, examples, and specimens.

name: Claims — in specifications of designs
description: Claims in specifications of designs — referenced section 120a.
guidance: Special rules for drafting claims in design patents (ornamentality, drawing reliance).

name: Claims — in specifications of machines
description: Claims in specifications of machines — referenced sections 117, 117a.
guidance: Drafting considerations for machine claims, including reference numerals and functional language.

name: Claims — in specifications of manufactures
description: Claims in specifications of manufactures — referenced sections 118, 170, 183.
guidance: How to claim manufactured articles and related enablement/textual requirements.

name: Claims — in specifications of processes
description: Claims in specifications of processes — referenced section 120.
guidance: Process claim drafting and issues (steps, result-oriented language, method vs product distinction).

name: Claims — insufficient
description: Insufficient claims — referenced section 218.
guidance: When claims fail for lack of support, enablement, or definiteness.

name: Claims — limitation by action in Patent Office
description: Claims may be limited by actions in the Patent Office — referenced sections 186, 187a.
guidance: Prosecution history estoppel and how amendments/remarks before the PTO affect claim scope.

name: Claims — process and product in same application
description: Process and product may be claimed in the same application — referenced section 176.
guidance: Drafting and examination implications of mixed statutory-class claims.

name: Claims — reference letters or numerals in
description: Use of reference letters or numerals in claims — referenced sections 117a, 182a.
guidance: Effect and permissibility of employing reference symbols from drawings in claim language.

name: Claims — specific
description: Specific claims and their treatment — referenced sections 116, 177a.
guidance: Role of particular/specific claims versus broader claims in patent scope and enforcement.

name: Claims — use of "means" or "mechanism"
description: Use of the word 'means' or 'mechanism' in claims — referenced section 117a.
guidance: Means-plus-function claim implications and statutory 35 U.S.C. §112(f) style consequences; how courts treat such language.

name: Combination — claim for combination not to be broadened by construction
description: A claim for a combination should not be broadened by construction — referenced section 186.
guidance: Avoid expanding combination claim scope by interpretive devices beyond the claimed combination.

name: Combination — co-operation of parts
description: Co-operation of parts in a combination — referenced sections 32, 33.
guidance: Elements of a combination patent must co-operate to produce the claimed result.

name: Combination — dissolved by omission of any element
description: A combination is dissolved by omission of any one element — referenced section 349.
guidance: All claimed elements of a combination are material; omission can avoid infringement.

name: Compositions of matter — claiming and prerequisites
description: Claims for compositions of matter; how reduced to practice; how infringed; prerequisites of patentability; specimens; subjects of patents — referenced sections 119, 141a, 369-373, 18, 128, 1.
guidance: Special rules for chemical compositions: enablement, reduction to practice, specimens (deposit), and infringement tests.

name: Construction of letters patent in light of PTO restrictions and actions
description: Letters patent construed in light of Patent Office restrictions and other actions — referenced sections 187, 187a.
guidance: Prosecution history impacts claim scope (estoppel, disclaimers).

name: Construction of letters patent with proper strictness
description: Claims should be construed with proper strictness where warranted — referenced section 186.
guidance: Narrow construction may be necessary to avoid overreaching or to save validity.

name: Dedication to the Public — unclaimed disclosures
description: Inventions described in the specification but not claimed are dedicated to the public — referenced sections 176, 186.
guidance: Importance of claiming all intended subject matter to avoid dedication.

name: Drawings — constitute part of letters patent; what must show; when required
description: Drawings constitute part of letters patent; description in specification; may aid construction of claims; may constitute birth of invention; unpublished ones never negative novelty; what must be shown; when required — referenced sections 126, 70, 141a, 172, 182, 56, 61.
guidance: Requirements for patent drawings and their role in claim construction and novelty determinations.

name: Equivalents — definition and tests
description: Equivalents among elements of machines/manufactures/processes/ingredients; defined; dependent on functions and ways of performing functions; may be disclaimed; element of age; range broader in meritorious invention; range commensurate with scope; substitution of equivalents not availing to avoid infringement; tests of equivalents; where claimable in reissues — referenced sections 350-370, 352-362, 247, 338, 369.
guidance: Doctrine of equivalents: how it is defined, tested, and limited in infringement analysis and reissue practice.

name: Evidence — comprehensive rules and topics
description: Evidence rules in patent cases: before masters; complainant's and defendant's in chief; documentary evidence; ex parte experiments; bills of exceptions; evidence in interferences; newly discovered evidence grounds for new trial/rehearing/bill of review; objections; evidence of abandonment, date of invention, damages, marking, prior art, validity, non-infringement, estoppel, claims indistinctness, specification insufficiency; proofs to rebut laches, etc. — referenced sections 490-541, 498-541, 507-533, 551-552, 539, 647, 652, 519-521, 491.
guidance: Exhaustive listing of evidentiary topics and specific evidentiary standards relevant to patent litigation.

name: Expert witnesses — proper use and effect on construction
description: Role of expert witnesses: cross-examination, hypothetical questions, testimony affecting construction of letters patent, testimony on motions for preliminary injunctions, testimony regarding state of the art and infringement/non-infringement; when proper/improper — referenced sections 499-501, 189, 676, 500, 498, 532.
guidance: Expert testimony standards and limitations for technical explanation and claim construction.

name: Form — effect on infringement and invention questions
description: Form as affecting questions of infringement (363-368) and invention (41).
guidance: Whether claim or product is merely a form change can determine infringement or inventive step outcomes.

name: Functions — considered in respect of equivalents and patentable subject matter
description: Functions considered when addressing equivalents; functions are not patentable subject matter; functions may be stated in claims; tests for 'substantially the same way' — referenced sections 352-353, 117a, 176, 183, 220, 3.
guidance: Functional claiming and the doctrine of equivalents interplay; not all functions per se are patentable.

name: Implied: "For the Purpose Set Forth" — nature of the phrase in a claim
description: Nature of the phrase 'for the purpose set forth' in a claim — referenced section 182.
guidance: Interpretive guidance on purposive claim language.

name: USPTO formal requirements for abstracts
description: The USPTO's requirements for patent abstracts are specific: Maximum 150 words for design patents; 250 words for utility patents; must be written as a single paragraph; must appear on a separate page; should not include legal conclusions or claim language; should not include 'I claim' or 'we claim' language; should be written in the third person ('the invention' not 'my invention').
guidance: Violating these requirements won’t necessarily invalidate the patent but will generate a USPTO objection that must be addressed during prosecution. Follow these formal constraints exactly (word count, paragraphing, page placement, voice, and exclusion of claim/legal-conclusion phrasing).

name: Summarize key structural or functional elements
description: Identify the most important components or steps of the invention.
guidance: You don’t need every embodiment or claim element—include the core components/steps that enable the invention so readers understand how it works. Prefer concrete mechanisms (e.g., 'compressed recurrent neural network trained on failure signature data') over abstract labels.

name: Be concise, accurate, and reflective of claim scope
description: The goal is a concise, accurate summary that reflects the invention's scope—not an exhaustive description.
guidance: Edit ruthlessly to stay within the word limit while ensuring the abstract aligns with finalized claims. Write the abstract after claims are finalized so it accurately reflects what is being claimed; large inconsistencies signal drafting problems.

name: Do not copy claim language verbatim; use plain accessible language
description: Many applicants paste the independent claim into the abstract, producing a text that is dense and legally oriented.
guidance: Rewrite claim content into plain third-person prose understandable to a technically literate reader who is not expert in claim syntax; avoid dense claim structure while preserving the invention's substance.

name: Describe invention mechanics, not only advantages
description: Don't lead with benefits without describing the structural or functional elements that produce those benefits.
guidance: If you claim improvements (e.g., reduced cost, improved throughput), briefly indicate how the invention accomplishes those improvements (components, steps, or mechanisms) rather than only stating the result.

name: Ensure consistency between abstract and claims
description: Although the abstract does not legally define claim scope, dramatic inconsistency between abstract and claims signals drafting problems.
guidance: Write the abstract after claims are finalized to avoid mismatches. If the abstract misrepresents the invention relative to the claims, it may cause confusion during prosecution or post-grant proceedings.

name: Amend surgically, not broadly
description: When responding to a rejection, amend only the claim element that is necessary to overcome the cited art.
guidance: Each amendment creates prosecution history estoppel that may foreclose later doctrine of equivalents arguments under Festo Corp. v. Shoketsu Kinzoku Kogyo Kabushiki Co. (Fed. Cir. en banc 2003). Do not broaden amendments beyond what is needed to get allowance; be precise and limited in scope.

name: Avoid 'cosmetic' amendments
description: Do not make amendments that change wording without affecting scope (e.g., changing 'device' to 'apparatus').
guidance: Such cosmetic amendments are wasteful: they may still create estoppel and signal lack of prosecution strategy. Avoid changes that do not meaningfully alter claim scope.

name: Watch the new matter bar
description: Any amendment that adds subject matter not supported by the originally filed disclosure is rejected as new matter (35 U.S.C. 132).
guidance: Before amending, confirm the new language is fully supported in the as-filed specification, not just present in the prior art you are distinguishing. Do not rely on prior-art references to supply support for added claim language.

name: Claim differentiation effects
description: Be aware that adding a limitation to one claim affects the claim hierarchy and may disrupt claim differentiation.
guidance: If you amend claim 1 by adding limitation X, claim 1 now requires X; a dependent claim that already recited X may be affected. Audit the claim set after each amendment to identify unintended interactions between independent and dependent claims.

name: Add new claims rather than only amending existing ones
description: If you have specification support for an additional inventive embodiment, add new claims instead of amending existing claims.
guidance: New claims do not carry the same prosecution history estoppel as amended claims and can be argued more cleanly. Use new claims to capture alternative embodiments or fallback positions supported by the spec.

name: Group-wide amendments for multiple claims
description: When multiple claims are rejected on the same ground, amend them in parallel with consistent language.
guidance: Inconsistent amendments across claims invite further rejections and examiner objections. Use consistent phrasing when the same limitation is being addressed in multiple claims to reduce confusion and additional prosecution rounds.

name: Present amended claims in markup and provide clean versions
description: Submit amended claims with markup (additions underlined, deletions bracketed) per 37 CFR 1.121 and also provide a clean full claim set after substantial amendments.
guidance: Follow 37 CFR 1.121 formatting rules for amendments. Markup shows exactly what changed; a clean version of the full claim set improves clarity for the examiner after substantial amendments.

name: Mere Instructions To Apply An Exception [2106.05(f)]
description: When determining whether a claim integrates a judicial exception into a practical application (Step 2A Prong Two) or recites significantly more than a judicial exception (Step 2B), consider whether the additional elements amount to more than a recitation of the words 'apply it' (or an equivalent) or are more than mere instructions to implement an abstract idea or other exception on a computer.
guidance: Supreme Court authority (Alice, Mayo, Benson) teaches that additional elements must do 'more than simply stat[e] the [judicial exception] while adding the words ‘apply it’.' Claims that are nothing more than instructions to apply an abstract idea using a generic computer do not render the idea eligible. Examiners may explain why additional elements meaningfully limit the judicial exception. This consideration often overlaps with other §2106 considerations (improvement, particular machine/transformation, well-understood routine/conventional); those analyses may assist but the well-understood, routine, conventional consideration is evaluated only in Step 2B, not in Step 2A Prong Two. Examiners should explain on the record why limitations do not meaningfully limit the claim and refer to MPEP §2106.07(a) for formulating eligibility rejections.

name: Whether the claim recites only the idea of a solution or outcome (2106.05(f)(1))
description: Determine whether the claim recites only the idea of a solution or outcome (i.e., fails to recite details of how a solution to a problem is accomplished). Recitation of claim limitations that attempt to cover any solution to an identified problem with no restriction on how the result is accomplished and no description of the mechanism is equivalent to the words 'apply it.'
guidance: Claims that are result-oriented and functional—covering any solution to an identified problem without specific steps—do not integrate the judicial exception into a practical application. By contrast, claiming a particular solution or a particular way to achieve an outcome may integrate the exception or provide significantly more. Case examples: Electric Power Group v. Alstom (result-focused claims), Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One (dynamic document/XML claims held ineligible for lacking specific steps). Examiners should analyze whether claimed steps disclose specific mechanisms rather than mere results.

name: Whether the claim invokes computers or other machinery merely as a tool (2106.05(f)(2))
description: Consider whether the claim invokes a computer or other machinery merely as a tool to perform an existing process (i.e., use in ordinary capacity to receive, store, or transmit data, or merely adding a general purpose computer).
guidance: Using a computer or machinery in its ordinary capacity or adding a generic computer to an abstract idea typically does not integrate the judicial exception into a practical application or provide significantly more. Examples of such tool-like use include Affinity Labs v. DirecTV (cellular telephone), TLI Communications v. AV Auto (telephone and server), and Alice (intermediated settlement on a generic computer). Conversely, claims that improve computer capabilities or an existing technology may integrate the exception (see McRO, Enfish). Examiners should compare whether the claim purports to improve technology/functionality or merely uses generic components as tools. See MPEP §§2106.04(d)(1) and 2106.05(a) for improvements discussion.

name: The particularity or generality of the application of the judicial exception (2106.05(f)(3))
description: Evaluate the particularity or generality of how the judicial exception is applied. A claim with broad applicability across many fields that generically recites an effect or claims every mode of accomplishing that effect may amount to merely adding 'apply it.'
guidance: Claims that generically state a desired result or effect without limiting how it is achieved do not provide a meaningful limitation (Internet Patents Corp. v. Active Network). Historical examples include O’Reilly v. Morse and The Telephone Cases where overly broad claims were held ineligible. By contrast, limitations that confine the exception to a particular practical application may amount to significantly more (BASCOM example: installation of a filtering tool at a specific ISP location with customizable features). Examiners must analyze whether claim language confines the exception to a particular technological application.

name: Insignificant Extra-Solution Activity [2106.05(g)]
description: Consider whether additional elements add more than insignificant extra-solution activity to the judicial exception. 'Extra-solution activity' includes activities incidental to the primary process or product, including pre-solution and post-solution activities (e.g., data gathering as pre-solution; printing a report as post-solution).
guidance: The addition of insignificant extra-solution activity—particularly if well-understood or conventional—does not amount to an inventive concept (Parker v. Flook; Mayo). Examiners should carefully consider each claim and may use related §2106 considerations (particular machine/transformation, well-understood routine/conventional, field of use) to assist in the determination; however, the well-understood, routine, conventional analysis belongs in Step 2B, not Step 2A. If limitations are merely data gathering, selecting data sources, or trivial post-solution steps, explain why they do not meaningfully limit the claim and cite MPEP §2106.07(a) for rejection formulation.

name: Whether the limitation is significant (2106.05(g)(2))
description: Determine whether the limitation imposes meaningful limits on the claim such that it is not nominally or tangentially related to the invention.
guidance: Limitations that merely restrict a claim in a token way (e.g., restricting public access to media, menu ordering types) have been found insignificant (Ultramercial; Ameranth). This significance inquiry is considered in both Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B. Examiners should analyze whether claimed limitations meaningfully confine the judicial exception or are nominal additions.

name: Whether the limitation amounts to necessary data gathering and outputting (2106.05(g)(3))
description: Consider whether the limitation is merely necessary data gathering and outputting—i.e., activities that all uses of the recited judicial exception require (mere inputs/outputs).
guidance: Measures such as gathering input data, presenting offers and collecting response statistics, or verifying transactions over the Internet have been treated as mere data gathering (Mayo; OIP Technologies). This consideration is relevant in Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B. Examiners should identify whether the claimed data gathering/output is intrinsic to practicing the exception and thus insignificant.

name: Field of Use and Technological Environment [2106.05(h)]
description: Determine whether additional elements merely link the use of a judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use. Merely indicating a field of use or technological environment does not make a claim eligible.
guidance: Supreme Court precedent (Diamond v. Diehr; Parker v. Flook) and Federal Circuit decisions (Bilski) show that limiting an abstract idea to a particular field or adding token post-solution components does not render the concept patentable. Examiners should not permit subject matter eligibility solely because an applicant limits the claim to a particular technological environment; analyze whether the limitation meaningfully integrates the exception into a practical application rather than merely narrowing its field of use.

name: Specific description of arrangement and component positioning
description: When drafting specifications, consider being specific in description of the arrangement and relative positioning of components of the system.
guidance: A specifically described arrangement provides a position supporting a technical improvement. In addition, more specific arrangement precludes allegations of pre-emption. (Representative claim context: content filtering system/BASCOM)

name: Provide problem/solution and repeatedly state advantages
description: When drafting your patent application, consider providing 'problem/solution' in the specification to highlight the various inventive concepts of your software related invention as an improvement over known prior art.
guidance: Consider explicitly and repeatedly stating advantages of your inventive concept that support the inventive concept captured in your claims as not routine or conventional. (Berkheimer practice tip #1)

name: Capture inventive concept in dependent claims; do not rely solely on representative independent claim
description: When filing an appeal to a 101 rejection, do not always rely on your independent claim as representative of all the pending claims at issue.
guidance: Consider identifying each dependent claim that has an additional limitation that is supported in the specification as an inventive concept improvement over known prior art. The Federal Circuit found that dependent claims 4–7 could present factual questions about inventive concept even when the independent claim was found abstract. (Berkheimer practice tip #2)

name: Alice Step 1 — show claims focus on specific means/method that improve technology
description: Assess whether the claim 'is directed to' an abstract idea (step 1) or instead to a specific means or method that improves a technological process or device.
guidance: Court decisions (e.g., Cardionet) emphasize that claims which 'focus on a specific means or method that improves' a technology are less likely to be characterized as abstract. Provide technical detail in the specification to demonstrate the claimed improvement. Rely on the intrinsic record to understand what the claims are directed to.

name: Alice Step 2 — conventionality is a question of fact; supply evidence
description: Under Alice step 2, whether a claim element or combination is 'well-understood, routine and conventional' to a skilled artisan is a question of fact.
guidance: Factual disputes about whether an aspect of the claims is inventive may preclude dismissal at pleadings or summary judgment (Berkheimer, Aatrix). When there is no genuine issue of material fact the question can be decided as a matter of law, but to avoid adverse rulings supply evidence (intrinsic or extrinsic) showing the inventive concept is not routine or conventional.

name: Emphasize unconventional aspects in specification (do not bury them in abstract-idea context)
description: When the application and claims relate to abstract ideas, any unconventional aspects of the technology should be emphasized and detailed in the specification.
guidance: Avoid describing the unconventional feature only in the context of the abstract idea; instead describe it as a technical improvement and document how it differs from known systems (BSG Tech practice tip).

name: Describe technical details and technical advantages in the specification
description: Provide technical details in the specification that explain how the invention improves functionality, efficiency, or other technological aspects of devices/systems.
guidance: Courts find the specification persuasive in determining what claims are directed to (Cardionet). For example, describing how storing objects without redundancy 'improves system operating efficiency and reduces storage costs' supported factual disputes about inventive concept (Berkheimer).

name: Avoid broad 'need' statements or background framing that characterize the invention as the abstract idea
description: Be careful regarding 'need' statements in the background that could be used to characterize the invention as a broad abstract idea (e.g., 'need for a communication network' leading to 'network-controlled charging stations').
guidance: If the specification frames the invention too broadly, courts may treat the claimed invention as an abstract idea. Instead, frame the problem narrowly as a technical problem and tie claimed features to technical solutions (ChargePoint practice tip).

name: New elements that are generic (e.g., wireless transmission) may be treated as abstract
description: Do not assume that adding a generic technology (like wireless transmission) will supply an inventive concept; courts may view such additions as part of the abstract idea if other claim elements are well-known.
guidance: Be mindful whether the claimed 'new' element is itself abstract or merely a generic implementation of the abstract idea; argue and document how it provides a technical improvement beyond generic use (Chamberlain practice tip).

name: Claims that merely collect and compare known information risk ineligibility unless a step acts on the comparison
description: Claims that perform only 'collecting and comparing known information' have been held ineligible, but claims that perform a step based on the comparison (or include a technical processing/immunization step) can be eligible.
guidance: If your claim performs any step based on a comparison of collected data or includes a technical action (e.g., immunization step in Classen analog), include and emphasize that in the claim and specification so the claim is not a bare information-collection/comparison abstraction.

name: Identify what applicant invented and establish BRI (Section I)
description: Review the disclosure to identify what applicant considers as the invention. (MPEP 2103(I)). Establish the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim.
guidance: Use a separate worksheet for each claim. Identify what applicant invented (summary sentence(s) of the invention) and then state the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim limitations (e.g., recited components and their functions). Suggested to use the 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance Quick Reference Sheet and flowchart when performing this step.

name: Directed to an abstract idea (Step 2A)
description: Courts have found certain concepts to be 'abstract ideas', for example fundamental economic practices, certain methods of organizing human activity, ideas themselves (standing alone), or mathematical relationships/formulae. A claim is 'directed' to an abstract idea when the abstract idea is recited (i.e., set forth or described) in the claim.
guidance: Choose A, B, or C: A) No — claim does not recite a concept similar to those found abstract (conclude SME analysis). B) Yes, but streamlined analysis appropriate (eligibility is self-evident; full analysis not needed). C) Yes — identify the claim limitation(s) that correspond to the abstract idea and explain why the recited subject matter is an abstract idea. When identifying similarity, refer to examples previously held abstract by courts (e.g., intermediate settlement in Alice, risk hedging in Bilski, tax-free investing in Fort Properties). If claiming 'directed to an abstract idea', continue to Step 2B unless streamlined analysis applies.

name: Use streamlined analysis when eligibility is self-evident
description: Yes, but the streamlined analysis is appropriate as the eligibility is self-evident, and a full eligibility analysis is not needed.
guidance: Apply streamlined analysis (refer to February 2015 Training Slides) when the claimed invention is not focused on the abstract idea and the claim clearly does not attempt to tie up the abstract idea such that others cannot practice it. If applicable, conclude SME analysis and continue with other patentability requirements.

name: Identify additional claim elements beyond the abstract idea (Step 2B presence check)
description: Are there any additional elements (features/limitations/steps) recited in the claim beyond the abstract idea identified above? Choose 1 or 2:
guidance: 1) No — if there are no additional elements beyond the abstract idea, conclude SME analysis by making a §101 rejection and continue with other patentability requirements (use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015). Also consider whether disclosure contains elements that could be added to make the claim eligible and identify them for applicant. 2) Yes — list the specific additional elements (e.g., memory, processor programmed to perform steps, network interface, controller, electronic funds transfer, kiosk with interactive display, smart card dispenser) and continue to evaluate their significance under Step 2B.

name: Evaluate the significance of additional elements (search for an inventive concept)
description: Identifying additional elements and evaluating their significance involves the search for an 'inventive concept' in the claim.
guidance: Consider all identified additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the abstract idea. Reasons supporting significance may include one or more of the following: improves another technology or technical field; improves the functioning of a computer itself; applies the abstract idea with, or by use of, a particular machine (not a generic computer performing generic functions; not merely adding 'apply it'); effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing; adds a specific limitation other than what is well-understood, routine and conventional in the field (not appending well-understood, routine, and conventional activities specified at a high level of generality); adds unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application (not adding insignificant extrasolution activity such as mere data gathering); adds meaningful limitations that amount to more than generally linking the use of the abstract idea to a particular technological environment.

name: Generic computer components / conventional implementation are insufficient (anti-pattern)
description: Generic computer components recited as performing generic computer functions that are well-understood, routine and conventional amount to no more than implementing the abstract idea with a computerized system.
guidance: If additional elements are recited at a high level of generality (e.g., 'memory,' 'processor,' 'network interface,' 'electronic funds transfer') and amount to conventional computer implementation or merely transmitting information through unspecified interfaces, they do not impose meaningful limits and therefore do not make the claim 'significantly more' than the abstract idea. Similarly, adding instructions to 'apply' an abstract idea or appending routine data-gathering do not provide the inventive concept.

name: Conclude SME analysis and procedural actions (Step 2B conclusion)
description: If any elements, individually or in combination, amount to 'significantly more' than the abstract idea, conclude SME analysis and continue examination under other patentability requirements. If not, conclude SME analysis by making a §101 rejection.
guidance: When concluding, explain in the record why the claim does or does not amount to significantly more (provide reasoning: which element(s) provide significantly more and how). Use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015 when making rejections. If the claim could be amended to add eligible elements, identify those elements and consider suggesting them to applicant. Clarify the record with remarks in the Office action where helpful (for example: 'the claim recites the abstract idea of X, but amounts to significantly more because Y').

name: United States not subject to adverse possession
description: While the United States is entitled to avail itself of statutes of limitation, it is not bound thereby; occupancy by private parties, however long continued, gives them no title thereto as against the United States.
guidance: Do not treat long user or possession as creating title against the sovereign; claims of prescriptive title or adverse possession against the United States are generally without legal foundation.

name: Referral to courts when title claims conflict
description: Where conflicting claims to title within a reservation are not clearly groundless, the Secretary should not attempt to pass upon the questions but should refer the parties to the courts for legal remedies.
guidance: Avoid departmental adjudication of complex title disputes; preserve defenses and refer to judicial process.

name: Designation of the invention (title)
description: A short and technically precise designation of the invention shall be given which corresponds to the title of the description; trademarks or fancy designations are not admitted.
guidance: Use common terms rather than generic placeholders (avoid 'appliance', 'means', 'device'). Innovations should not be anticipated in the designation; innovations belong in the claims.

name: Priority (domestic, foreign, exhibition)
description: Priority is generally determined by date of receipt at DPMA. Applicants may claim domestic, foreign (Paris Convention/TRIPS), or exhibition priority within prescribed time limits and must supply required information and copies of earlier applications within deadlines.
guidance: Domestic priority: within 12 months of earlier filing; claim must be made within two months of later filing for certain particulars; priority documents may need to be filed within 16 months for foreign priority. Exhibition priority: claim within six months from first display; evidence required before 16th month after first display. Failure to timely submit documents forfeits priority claim.

name: Sufficient disclosure requirement (description and carrying out invention)
description: The invention must be disclosed in the application in a manner sufficiently clear and complete for it to be carried out without difficulty by a person skilled in the art; claims, a technical description, and drawings if any, must be furnished.
guidance: This is a basic requirement at the date of filing; failure to satisfy it cannot be cured later and will prevent registration (application rejected unless a new application is filed).

name: Claims — scope and drafting principles
description: The scope of protection is determined by the terms of the claims (section 12a); claims may be in one part or two parts (preamble and characterising part) and may be arranged feature-wise.
guidance: If two-part claims used, state-of-the-art features go in the preamble using the technical designation from box (6); characterising part introduced by 'characterised in that' or equivalent. Essential features must be in the first (principal) claim; several independent claims allowed if unity respected. Dependent claims must refer to preceding claims and grouped suitably. Claims should not, except where absolutely necessary, rely on references to the description or drawings. Use reference signs to facilitate understanding when drawings present. Number claims consecutively in Arabic numerals. Claims may not contain descriptions of functions, applications and advantages — these belong in the description. Each claim must be introduced by the title.

name: Drawings — when required and format
description: Drawings are not mandatory but must be filed if the claims or description contain references to them. Photographs are not equivalent to drawings and cannot replace drawings if required.
guidance: If drawings are submitted later and the application contained a reference to them, the date drawings are received by DPMA will be deemed the filing date of the entire application (which may be advantageous). Drawings shall clearly show interaction of features, emphasise essential points, neglect unimportant details, use Arabic numerals as reference signs, have minimum margins per section 7, be in black with clean clear contours, and must not contain explanations (use reference signs instead). Claims, description and drawings must be on separate sheets.

name: Example-based guidance for novice applicants
description: The leaflet provides an example application (description, list of reference signs, claims and drawings) showing structure: state of the art, problem, solution, advantages, figures and explanatory reference signs.
guidance: Drafting aids: answer questions such as which parts does the device comprise? Where are particular parts located? In what manner are parts connected? Use the example as a model for assembling description and claims; remember scope of protection determined by claims.

name: Citation of Prior Art (35 U.S.C. 301; 37 CFR 1.501)
description: Any person at any time during the period of enforceability of a patent may cite patents or printed publications believed to have a bearing on patentability; an explanation of the pertinency and manner of applying such prior art to at least one claim is required and the citation and explanation will become part of the patent file. At the written request of the citer, identity may be excluded from the file.
guidance: The explanation must show pertinency/applicability to at least one claim (a broad statement of pertinency is minimum); patent-owner citations may explain how claims differ from the art. Citations entered in the patent file except as set forth in rules (see §§ 1.502, 1.902).

name: Content Requirements for Prior Art Citation
description: Submissions under 35 U.S.C. 301 are limited to written prior art consisting of patents or printed publications and must include an explanation of how the cited art is pertinent and applicable to at least one claim.
guidance: Preferred to include copies of cited patents/printed publications and necessary English translations; at minimum indicate how each cited item shows or teaches at least one limitation of at least one claim. Identify target patent by patent number, issue date, and patentee; use a cover sheet with identification and attach all documents. Affidavits/declarations (e.g., commercial success) may accompany citations. No fee required for submission under 37 CFR 1.501. Do NOT include issues not directed to patents/printed publications (e.g., 35 U.S.C. 112, public use, conduct of patent owner); such submissions should be returned.

name: Substantial New Question (SNQ) of Patentability — Criterion to Order Reexamination (37 CFR 1.515)
description: A request for ex parte reexamination will be granted (reexamination ordered) only if a substantial new question of patentability affecting at least one claim is found under the statutory/rule standard.
guidance: If SNQ found (1.515(a)), reexamination ordered (1.525) and new examiner assigned; if not found, reexamination is denied/terminated. Requester may petition Director under 1.515(c) to review denial. The SNQ determination must be supported by prior art and explanations provided in the request (see guidance for request content).

name: Request for Ex Parte Reexamination — Required Content and Supporting Papers (37 CFR 1.510)
description: A requester must submit a request containing identification of the patent, the fee, the prior art relied upon (patents/printed publications), and a statement applying the cited art to at least one claim showing why a substantial new question of patentability exists.
guidance: Include copies of the cited prior art, a copy of the printed patent, a certificate of service (or show service/duplicate), and any affidavits/declarations necessary to explain dates or content. Use of transmittal form PTO/SB/57 is available but not mandatory. Incomplete requests are processed per MPEP and may be returned or given time to correct.

name: Office Actions — Form, Content, Time for Response in Reexamination
description: During ex parte reexamination, the examiner issues office actions in accordance with the rules (e.g., 1.104) addressing patentability of claims; office actions may be final or non-final, and set time periods for patent owner response or amendment.
guidance: Panel review is conducted at each examination stage (except non-merits informality notices). The flowchart shows procedures for non-final action, final rejection, reopening prosecution, patent owner responses under 1.111/1.113/1.116, and notices of intent to issue reexamination certificate. Examine whether an office action is final; allow response periods and extensions per rules; use specific PTOL forms (e.g., PTOL-466 Office Action).

name: Intervening Rights Resulting from Reexamination
description: Proposed amended or new claims determined to be patentable in reexamination have intervening-rights consequences analogous to reissue (section 252 analogies); 35 U.S.C. 307 addresses certification of patentability/unpatentability and claim cancellation.
guidance: The MPEP references case law and explains that rights for prior users/makers/importers/substantial preparers prior to certificate issuance are governed similarly to reissue intervening rights. Examiners and practitioners should consider intervening-rights implications when claims are amended/confirmed.

name: Community service and achievements as relevant but not dispositive
description: Community service and personal achievements are relevant factors in evaluating rehabilitation.
guidance: Such activities may support a claim of rehabilitation but minimal compliance with sentencing terms or only doing the minimum required does not suffice to establish the trustworthiness necessary for practice before the USPTO.

name: Examiner's initial burden to establish a prima facie case
description: The USPTO bears the initial burden of factually supporting any prima facie conclusion of obviousness; the examiner must step back in time and into the shoes of the person of ordinary skill in the art when the invention was unknown and just before it was made. See MPEP §2142.
guidance: If the examiner does not establish a prima facie case, the applicant need not submit rebuttal evidence. Attack the sufficiency of the examiner’s factual support (lack of references, lack of reasoning) to avoid having to rebut and to avoid claim amendments that could create estoppel. Cite MPEP §2142 and pertinent case law.

name: Obviousness rationales — A: combining prior art elements to yield predictable results
description: Combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results is one common rationale for obviousness (MPEP §2143 grouping).
guidance: Show unpredictability, absence of teaching/suggestion/motivation to combine, or that combination would not yield the claimed result; cite relevant Federal Circuit authority discussed in the Guidelines.

name: Obviousness rationales — G: teaching, suggestion, or motivation to combine
description: Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation (TSM) in the prior art that would have led one of ordinary skill to modify or combine references to arrive at the claimed invention is a common rationale (MPEP §2143(I)).
guidance: Attack the asserted TSM: show no suggestion in the prior art, reliance on applicant’s disclosure (hindsight), or that the asserted motivation is unsupported by record evidence.

name: Complete Graham analysis required (four Graham factors)
description: Obviousness legal conclusion depends on: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between the prior art and the claims; (3) the level of ordinary skill in the art; and (4) relevant secondary considerations. All four must be analyzed (Graham; KSR; MPEP §2141).
guidance: Challenge any faulty or incomplete Graham analysis. Under the first factor, ensure references are analogous art and that issues like enablement, priority date, and the prior art’s entirety are considered. Treat the four factors as non‑alternatives that must be addressed.

name: Examiner ignored one or more claim limitations
description: All claim limitations must be considered when assessing patentability; if a reference does not disclose one or more limitations, a rejection is improper (MPEP §2143.03; Medrad; In re Grasselli).
guidance: Demonstrate overlooked limitations, interpret claim language (including function-based interpretations), and show the examiner failed to account for limitations even when §112 or new matter issues were raised.

name: IPRP (Ch. II) contents and public availability
description: The Chapter II international preliminary report on patentability (IPRP (Ch. II)) provides an opinion on novelty, inventive step, and industrial applicability and points out objections to claim form or clarity.
guidance: The IPRP (Ch. II) is made available to each elected patent office and becomes publicly available via the IB after 30 months from the earliest priority date; prosecution history may become public earlier through elected offices (e.g., EPO permits public file inspection). If confidentiality of prosecution is critical, consider implications of elected-office disclosure rules and selecting an IPEA (e.g., USPTO) accordingly.

name: Electronic republication rights and contract drafting (Tasini principle)
description: Republishing freelance works electronically (e.g., on databases, CD-ROMs, websites) may not be authorized by prior publication rights; electronic republication can create a new collective work rather than a permissible revision.
guidance: Contracts/licensing of third-party content should include explicit provisions addressing electronic republication rights. Authors and publishers should renegotiate to clarify electronic rights; licensors should expressly secure the intended electronic rights to avoid infringement claims.

name: Application to universities and scholarly-works practice
description: Universities must generally obtain a written signed agreement to rebut the presumption that materials created in the course of employment are works for hire; traditionally, universities have not claimed copyrights in scholarly works (faculty articles) and courts have recognized academic tradition of faculty ownership.
guidance: University policies should be explicit and signed to affect ownership. In practice, universities often avoid claiming scholarly works, though disputes have arisen; analyze policy language and statutory rules to determine ownership.

name: Particularity or generality of the transformation
description: The particularity or generality of the transformation recited in a claim is relevant: more particular transformations (e.g., tanning, dyeing, vulcanizing) are more likely to confine a patent monopoly within definite bounds and thus provide significantly more than a judicial exception.
guidance: Supreme Court examples (Gottschalk v. Benson, Corning) show that transformations that are sufficiently definite are favorable. A more particular transformation is likely to provide significantly more. See Tilghman v. Proctor and Diamond v. Diehr for examples of transformative processes that were meaningful.

name: Whether the transformation is extra-solution activity or merely a field-of-use limitation
description: Determine the extent to which the transformation imposes meaningful limits on execution of claimed method steps; transformations that contribute only nominally (e.g., data gathering, field-of-use) typically do not provide significantly more.
guidance: Mayo: administering a drug was treated as only a field-of-use limitation and did not provide significantly more. See MPEP §2106.05(g) & (h) for more on insignificant extra-solution activity and field of use.

name: Combination of conventional elements may amount to inventive concept
description: Even if individual additional elements are well-understood and routine, their combination may amount to an inventive concept (i.e., significantly more).
guidance: Diamond v. Diehr, Rapid Litigation Management (repeating freeze/thaw steps), and BASCOM (non-conventional arrangement of generic components) show combinations can render claims eligible. Examiners should consider combinations, not just individual elements.

name: Court-recognized routine computer function: performing repetitive calculations
description: Performing repetitive calculations by a computer has been treated as a generic, conventional use of computers and does not impose meaningful limits when recited at a high level.
guidance: Cases: Flook; Bancorp Services (computer used only for repetitive calculations did not meaningfully limit claims).

name: Court-recognized routine life-science technique: determining biomarker level
description: Determining the level of a biomarker in blood by any means has been recognized as a well-understood, routine, conventional laboratory technique when claimed generically.
guidance: Cases: Mayo; Cleveland Clinic Foundation. Such generic measurement steps may not provide significantly more than a judicial exception.

name: Court-recognized routine life-science technique: immunization
description: Immunizing a patient against a disease has been recognized as a routine/conventional activity in some contexts when recited generically.
guidance: Case: Classen Immunotherapies. Note immunization steps in claims can interact with other considerations (e.g., if integrated meaningfully they may favor eligibility).

name: Court-recognized routine life-science technique: freezing and thawing cells
description: Freezing and thawing cells have been recognized by courts as well-understood, routine laboratory activity when recited generically.
guidance: Case: Rapid Litigation Management (but repetition contrary to the art rendered claims inventive in that case).

name: Court-recognized routine activities (other fields): shuffling/dealing a deck of cards
description: Shuffling and dealing a standard deck of cards can be a routine conventional activity when recited in claims at a high level.
guidance: Case: In re Smith.

name: Court-recognized routine activities (other fields): determining an estimated outcome and setting a price
description: Determining an estimated outcome and setting a price are examples of routine activities recognized by courts when claimed generically.
guidance: Case: OIP Technologies.

name: Other meaningful limitations (overall consideration)
description: The claim should add meaningful limitations beyond generally linking the judicial exception to a particular technological environment; such meaningful limitations can transform the judicial exception into patent-eligible subject matter (relevant in Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B).
guidance: Considerations in MPEP §2106.05(a)-(d) are meaningful limitations when they amount to significantly more or integrate the exception into a practical application. Diehr and Classen are examples of meaningful limitations; Alice is an example where recited elements did not meaningfully limit the abstract idea.

name: Evaluate additional elements both individually and in combination
description: When determining whether additional elements meaningfully limit the judicial exception, examiners must evaluate elements both individually and as a combination; combinations may render the claim eligible even if individual elements do not.
guidance: Diamond v. Diehr and BASCOM illustrate that combinations of steps or generic components arranged non-conventionally may be patent-eligible. Examiners should explain on the record why elements meaningfully limit the claim when appropriate.

name: Mere instructions to apply an exception (the 'apply it' test)
description: Determine whether additional elements are no more than a recitation of the words 'apply it' (or equivalent) — i.e., mere instructions to implement an abstract idea or other exception (often on a generic computer); such recitations do not render an abstract idea eligible.
guidance: Supreme Court examples: Mayo (measuring metabolites was just an instruction to apply), Alice (recitation of computer amounted to mere instructions), Benson (conversion algorithm had no meaningful practical application absent a particular computer implementation). Examiners should avoid treating this as requiring narrow claims; broad claims can be eligible. Overlaps with other considerations (improvement, particular machine/transformation, well-understood conventional activity) should be evaluated to assist the analysis. Examiners should explain why limitations do not meaningfully limit when making a rejection.

name: Examination of documents cited in the application
description: Documents cited in the application should be examined if they are cited as the starting point of the invention, or as showing the state of the art, as alternative solutions to the problem concerned, or when they are necessary for a correct understanding of the application; however, when such citations clearly relate only to details not directly relevant to the claimed invention, they may be disregarded.
guidance: If a cited document is unpublished or not accessible but appears essential, the searching authority may request the applicant to provide a copy if possible within time limits. If no copy is received, the searching authority should attempt the search and, where necessary, indicate that a meaningful search was not possible or had to be restricted.

name: Search statement defining subject matter
description: The examiner may prepare a written search statement, defining the subject of their search as precisely as possible; claims may serve but may need to be generalized to cover all aspects and embodiments.
guidance: When preparing the search statement, bear in mind exclusion-from-search issues and lack of unity. If unity is lacking, examiner may search only the first invention or inventive concept. Avoid restricting searches unless unavoidable.

name: Restriction and handling of lack of unity
description: If the examiner determines that unity of invention is not satisfied, the examiner may choose to conduct a search on the basis of the first invention or inventive concept only. The examiner may also have to restrict the search in exceptional situations because no search at all is possible, but they should not do this if it can be avoided.
