guidance: Restricting or performing partial/no search should be an exception. If description/claims/drawings are unclear to the extent that no meaningful search can be made, indicate 'no meaningful search' limited to exceptional situations.

name: Consideration of claim types and forms
description: The claims should be construed and searched having particular regard to the various types and forms of claims used, such as two-part claims and product-by-process claims.
guidance: Adapt claim construction and search strategy to specific claim formats (e.g., product-by-process special guidance referenced).

name: Search focus: novelty, inventive step, sufficiency/support, industrial applicability
description: The examiner carries out the search, directing attention to any prior art likely to have bearing on novelty or inventive step. The examiner is encouraged to cite any prior art likely to be of assistance in determining sufficiency of description throughout the whole of the field claimed and the requirement that the claimed invention be fully supported by the description.
guidance: Identify documents highly relevant to novelty, inventive step, adequacy of support, and industrial applicability; note documents important for priority validity or background but do not spend time searching for them unless special reason.

name: Use of post-dating documents for factual background
description: Documents which do not qualify as prior art because they post-date the claimed invention may nevertheless be cited to show a universal fact, such as characteristics or properties of a material, or a specific scientific fact, or to show the level of ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: Post-dating documents can be used to establish general facts or skill level but not as novelty-destroying prior art.

name: Examiner determination of novelty and inventive step
description: The examiner determines whether the claimed invention meets the standards for novelty and inventive step.
guidance: Use identified prior art, enablement analysis, PSIA framework and other criteria in subsequent novelty and inventive step assessment.

name: Contents required in the search report
description: The contents of the search report provided by the patent office should include at least: list and details of prior arts identified during the search, date of first publication/availability to the public, weblink when available; scope of the patent search; databases used; classification (IPC); summary of the search; relevance of prior art(s) to the claim(s); comments or written opinion from the examiner on patentability.
guidance: Ensure search report documents prior-art specifics, scope, methods and examiner's assessment/opinion to support subsequent examination.

name: Partial search and 'no search' options and standards
description: Options for a partial search and/or a 'no search' are available in AMS. The aim is to issue search reports as complete as possible but certain situations lead to no report or only a partial report (e.g., authority not required to handle subject-matter, or description/claims/drawings fail to meet requirements such that no meaningful search can be made).
guidance: Interpret 'meaningful search' to mean complete enough to determine compliance with substantive requirements (novelty, inventive step, industrial applicability, sufficiency, support, clarity). Limit 'no meaningful search' to exceptional cases (totally unclear). If parts can be understood, perform search and recognize non-compliance may affect search extent.

name: Definition of novelty (general)
description: A claim in a patent application is said to be novel if it is not anticipated by prior art. PCT: 'The invention, as defined by a claim, lacks novelty if every element or step is explicitly or inherently disclosed within the prior art including any features implicit to a person skilled in the art.'
guidance: Apply the standard that every element/step must be present in the prior art (explicitly or inherently) to destroy novelty.

name: Methodology for determining scope via the Person Skilled In the Art (PSIA)
description: To determine whether an invention is new, the examiner shall compare the claimed invention to the identified prior art through the lens of a hypothetical 'Person Skilled In the Art' (PSIA) by (i) evaluating elements of the claim, (ii) determining if the prior art is part of the state of the art, and (iii) assessing whether each and every element or step was explicitly or inherently disclosed in combination.
guidance: Also consider the purpose/intended use of the invention in claim interpretation; disregard non-distinctive characteristics of intended use; consider implied characteristics arising from particular use (examples: catalyst vs dye; 'mould for molten steel' implies limitations).

name: Enablement requirement for prior art to destroy novelty
description: The prior art disclosure must enable a PSIA to carry out the claimed invention. A prior art document that is not enabling for the claimed invention does not destroy novelty.
guidance: Examine whether the prior art, together with knowledge generally available on the effective date, enables preparation/separation or practice of the claimed subject-matter. When considering NPL raising enablement questions, take appropriate outside knowledge into account. Note: non-enabling prior art may still be relied upon for inventive step analysis.

name: Generic vs specific disclosures
description: A generic disclosure does not usually take away the novelty of any specific example falling within that disclosure; conversely, a specific disclosure takes away the novelty of any generic claim embracing that disclosure.
guidance: Assess whether the prior art's generic teaching specifically or implicitly discloses the claimed specific example; many AMS adopt this principle.

name: Assessment of ranges for anticipation
description: Guiding principles when examining whether ranges are anticipated: (1) a specific example in the prior art within a claimed range anticipates the range; (2) prior art teaching a range overlapping/touching the claimed range may anticipate if it discloses the claimed range with 'sufficient specificity'; (3) a prior art broader range may not anticipate a narrow claimed range if the narrow range is a selection invention supported by evidence (e.g., unexpected results); (4) prior art ranges or values very close to but not overlapping the claimed range do not anticipate the claimed range.
guidance: Interpretation of 'sufficient specificity' is case-specific. Consider examples and jurisdictional nuances (e.g., Singapore, Viet Nam, Indonesia guidance). For selection inventions, unexpected results and narrowness/specificity support novelty; very close but non-overlapping values leave novelty intact but require inventive step analysis.

name: Authority for private suits for wrongs and claims against the United States
description: That Elias C. Boudinot ... be, and he is hereby, authorized to bring suit in the Court of Claims against the United States Government, to recover what may be due to him in justice and equity for the loss inflicted upon him by reason of said seizure ...
guidance: Congress may authorize individual claimants to sue the United States in Court of Claims for specific wrongs arising from federal actions.

name: Specific appropriations and recoupment from Indian annuities for damages
description: The Secretary of the Treasury ... authorized and directed to pay Henry Warren ... the sum of fifteen thousand eight hundred and sixty-seven dollars and fifty cents ... and that the Secretary of the Interior be ... directed to retain, out of any annuities due or to become due the Comanche and Kiowa Indians, the sum of eleven thousand eight hundred and fifty-two dollars and fifty cents, and from any annuities due or to become due the Cheyennes the sum of four thousand and fifteen dollars, and cover the same into the Treasury in accordance with treaty stipulations between said Indian tribes and the United States.
guidance: Congress can appropriate funds for private claims and direct recoupment from tribal annuities consistent with treaty terms.

name: National application statutory content requirements (35 U.S.C. 111(a))
description: An application for patent shall be made in writing to the Director and shall include a specification as prescribed by section 112, a drawing as prescribed by section 113, and an oath or declaration as prescribed by section 115. The application must be accompanied by the fee required by law; fee, oath/declaration, and 1+ claims may be submitted after the filing date within prescribed periods and conditions.
guidance: Failure to submit required fee/oath/claims within prescribed period results in abandonment. The filing date is the date a specification, with or without claims, is received in the USPTO (subject to later statutory/PLT amendments described).

name: Provisional application requirements (35 U.S.C. 111(b))
description: A provisional application shall include a specification as prescribed by section 112(a) and a drawing as prescribed by section 113; a claim is not required in a provisional application.
guidance: Provisional apps: fee may be submitted after filing date within prescribed period; filing date is when specification (with or without claims) is received; provisional will be regarded as abandoned 12 months after filing if no timely request to treat it as a nonprovisional is made; provisional applications are not examined for patentability and are not entitled to priority under certain statutory provisions.

name: Filing date definition (post-PLT/AIA context)
description: The filing date of an application is the date on which a specification, with or without claims, is received in the USPTO; for design patents the filing date is when the specification including at least one claim and any required drawings are received.
guidance: PLTIA (Dec 18, 2013) changed filing-date requirements for nonprovisional applications (see MPEP §§601.01 and 601.01(f)); nonprovisional utility and plant apps filed on/after that date may receive a filing date without claims or drawings, but design patent filing date rules remain stricter.

name: Continuing application categories and statutory bases
description: Applications filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a) include original nonprovisional utility, plant, design, divisional, continuation, and continuation-in-part applications filed under 37 CFR 1.53(b), reissue applications under 1.53(b), and design CPAs under 1.53(d). Continuing applications are filed under the conditions in 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, 365(c), or 386(c) and 37 CFR 1.78.
guidance: See MPEP §§201.06 et seq., 201.07, and 201.08 for divisional, continuation, and CIP specifics; see MPEP §211 et seq. for claiming benefit rules.

name: Continuation-in-part (CIP) definition and requirements
description: A continuation-in-part is an application filed during the lifetime of a prior-filed application that repeats some substantial portion or all of the prior-filed application and adds matter not disclosed in the prior-filed application; it must claim benefit of the prior filing under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, 365(c), or 386(c).
guidance: A CIP may only be filed under 37 CFR 1.53(b); it cannot be filed as a CPA. Requirements to claim benefit include same inventor or at least one common joint inventor, filing before patenting/abandonment of the prior application, and containing a specific reference to the earlier filed application (post-2012: reference in ADS). See MPEP §201.08 and §211.

name: Form and content of benefit claims (37 CFR 1.78 / MPEP §211)
description: Any nonprovisional application that claims the benefit of one or more prior-filed applications must contain or be amended to contain a reference to each such prior-filed application identifying it by application number, international application number and date, or international registration number and filing date; the reference must identify whether the later application is a continuation, divisional, or continuation-in-part.
guidance: For applications filed on/after Sept 16, 2012, the specific reference must be included in an application data sheet (ADS) per 37 CFR 1.76(b)(5). See MPEP §211 for procedures to correct/add benefit claims and time limits under 37 CFR 1.78.

name: Stating opinion on grounds for rejection
description: ‘Opinion on grounds for rejection’ is about results of review of the claimed invention conducted by examiner considering requirements for patentability and deficiency in the specification, and applicant’s response to it.
guidance: Examiner should prepare the opinion in advance and participate with it, but must orally explain grounds during interview. Minutes may summarize the purpose of the grounds for rejection; applicant's argument in response shall be described.

name: Product/device claims: structural/compositional definition and 'use' language
description: Tuotetta tai laitetta koskevissa vaatimuksissa rakenteen tai koostumuksen piirteet määrittelevät keksinnön. Tuote- tai laitevaatimuksessa esitetty käyttötarkoitus ... tulkitaan siten, että laite soveltuu kyseiseen käyttötarkoitukseen. Näin ilmaistu käyttötarkoitus ei ole sinänsä tunnetusta tekniikasta erottava piirre. Käyttötarkoitus otetaan kuitenkin huomioon rakenteen piirteiden tulkinnassa.
guidance: A product 'for use' is interpreted as suitable for that use but the use alone does not confer novelty; if a known product could be used for that purpose (even if not stated), it destroys novelty. If a known product is unsuited for the stated use, it is not novelty-destroying. Product-by-process is allowable but product must have structural difference; a new manufacturing method alone does not guarantee product novelty. Medical first and second medical use forms are treated specially (first/second medical use).

name: Method and use claims: functional/technical features
description: Menetelmää tai käyttöä koskevat vaatimukset kohdistuvat toimintaan. Menetelmävaatimuksessa keksinnölle tunnusmerkillisiä piirteitä ovat ... toimenpiteitä tai toimintoja koskevat tiedot. Käyttövaatimuksessa ilmoitetaan se erityinen tarkoitus, johon tuotetta tai menetelmää käytetään. ... käyttövaatimuksessa ilmaistu tuotteen käyttötarkoitus rinnastetaan toiminnalliseksi piirteeksi, joka määrittää keksintöä.
guidance: In method claims functional steps and operations are treated as technical features; if the claimed use only reflects a technical effect inevitably resulting from other method steps it may not limit the claim. When method concerns product manufacturing, differences in starting materials, final product or at least one process step relative to known processes can make the method new; the product's claimed use only limits scope insofar as the product must be suitable for that use.

name: Closest prior art (lähin tekniikan taso) selection
description: Lähinnä tekniikan tasoa edustaa julkaisu, josta tunnetaan sellainen yhdistelmä keksinnön piirteistä, että se muodostaa lupaavimman lähtökohdan kehitystyössä, joka voisi johtaa keksintöön. ... Lähimmän tekniikan tason tulisi palvella samaa tarkoitusta tai saada aikaan sama vaikutus kuin vaatimuksen kohteena oleva keksintö tai edustaa ainakin samaa tai läheistä tekniikan alaa.
guidance: Select the reference that requires the fewest structural/functional changes to reach the claimed invention and serves similar purpose; if multiple candidates exist, analysis may be run separately for each; lack of inventive step on any one analysis suffices to refuse.

name: Expungement: claim, targets, timing, and scope
description: New claim: the mark has never been used on some or all of the goods or services; not an abandonment claim and does not evaluate intent to commence use.
guidance: Targets Section 1, 44, and 66 registrations. Can be filed between 3–10 years post-registration. Focuses on never having been used for listed goods/services.

name: Claims must particularly point out and distinctly claim (35 U.S.C. § 112 second paragraph)
description: The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the applicant regards as his invention.
guidance: Although the statute places claims within the specification, claims are treated as a distinct part of the application and must clearly delineate the patentee's monopoly.

name: Enablement evaluated as of the filing date
description: Enablement must be established only as of the date the inventor filed for her patent.
guidance: Subsequent technical developments do not enlarge the scope of what the original disclosure had to enable; an applicant can claim subject matter later shown to be broader if the original disclosure enabled the claimed invention as understood on the filing date (Phillips Petroleum v. U.S. Steel example).

name: Claims covering inoperable species are invalid unless specification teaches how to distinguish operable embodiments
description: Patent claims covering many embodiments that include inoperable species are invalid unless the specification teaches, or skilled artisans can be presumed to know, how to distinguish the embodiments that work from those that do not.
guidance: Cited cases (In re Cavallito) and Chisum commentary explain invalidity where broad claims sweep in numerous inoperative compounds; applicant must either teach how to identify operative species or be presumed to have enabled them.

name: Claims cannot claim beyond the specification
description: A claim that 'reads beyond' the specification or is outside the specification cannot be maintained; claims must be supported by the specification.
guidance: Historic cases (quoted language) show that claims must derive aid from the specification; claiming subject matter outside the disclosure is impermissible.

name: Pioneer patent status confers broader claim construction and broader range of equivalents
description: Pioneer patents (early, fundamental inventions) are often entitled to a broad range of equivalents and broader claim construction because of sparse prior art.
guidance: Courts have held pioneer patents receive broad protection (citing Graver Tank and other authorities); breadth of claims does not necessarily justify rejection for vagueness if prior art is limited.

name: Improvement patents and Jepson claim format
description: Improvement patents are those claiming an improvement on earlier patents; Jepson claims are a claim drafting format that expressly recognizes the preamble portion as prior art and claims the improvement.
guidance: Jepson claims are a specific preamble format; the article uses 'improvement patent' more loosely to include patents later found dominated by earlier patents. Improvement patents are contemplated by the statute (35 U.S.C. § 101 examples).

name: Doctrine of equivalents — general principle
description: Doctrine of equivalents permits a finding of infringement where the accused device does not literally read on the claims but is equivalent — performing substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result (interchangeability notion).
guidance: Graver Tank language about 'insubstantial change' and interchangeability underlies the doctrine; courts examine scope and content of prior art and the ordinary skill in the art to determine equivalency (Great Northern, Thomas & Betts).

name: Reverse doctrine of equivalents (defense to infringement)
description: Even where an accused device literally falls within the claim language, it may not infringe if it operates in a substantially different way and does not appropriate the patentee's contribution (reverse doctrine of equivalents).
guidance: Cases (e.g., Graver Tank discussions, SRI/Mead examples) find noninfringement under reverse doctrine when the accused device functions in a substantially different way; application is fact-intensive and rarely invoked successfully.

name: Relation between enablement and infringement (reverse doctrine of equivalents / claim scope)
description: Enablement doctrine (breadth of disclosure) and infringement doctrines interact — enablement can influence how broadly claims are construed and whether equivalents apply; conversely, infringement defenses can consider whether accused device required substantial additional research over disclosure.
guidance: Some courts suggest addressing limits of enablement at the infringement stage via reverse doctrine of equivalents (Hogan, Texas Instruments, etc.), but reverse doctrine is rarely used and has limited appeal as a general solution.

name: Operability/principle-of-operation as factor in infringement
description: Courts consider whether accused devices operate on the same principle or in a substantially different way when deciding infringement; different functioning can support noninfringement even if literal claim language is implicated.
guidance: Cases (Leesona, Precision Metal, Mechanical Plastics) show that devices serving similar purposes but functioning substantially differently may avoid infringement; courts examine principle of operation as part of equivalence analysis.

name: Definition and rules of contributory infringement (furnishing parts, machines, or specially adapted articles)
description: Contributory infringement is intentional aid or cooperation in transactions that collectively constitute complete infringement. Examples: furnishing one part of a patented combination intending it be assembled with other parts and used; furnishing a machine useful only for making a patented article with intent that it be so used; furnishing articles for a patented machine intending they be operated on by it; furnishing a machine or composition particularly adapted to perform a patented process intending that it be so used.
guidance: The part furnished must be an element of the claimed combination. Sending parts abroad for incorporation may avoid U.S. contributory liability in some cases. If the article or machine has substantial non-infringing uses and the supplier did not intend or know of infringing use, there is no contributory liability; but if the supplier knew or intended the infringing use, he cannot escape liability by showing the property also has non-infringing uses. Case law examples illustrate these distinctions.

name: Role of patent attorneys / scope of attorney services
description: Typically, we prepare the description and claims for you (called a specification) and after obtaining your approval and making any adjustments we attend to all the paperwork for submitting an application to the UK Patent Office. We keep a detailed diary for your application and seek your instructions in good time before various deadlines and significant-cost-incurring matters arise. We deal with all the formalities and correspondence with the UK Patent Office, keep you informed and seek your comments as required at each stage. We can also advise on many related matters.
guidance: Patent attorneys handle drafting, filing, prosecution, diary management and correspondence; they charge professional time (usually hourly) and may offer additional advisory services.

name: Statutory patentability requirements
description: To be patentable an invention must meet all the statutory requirements for patentability: novelty, utility, and non-obviousness.
guidance: Claims are crafted to meet these requirements; enablement and disclosure doctrines operate alongside these statutory requirements during prosecution.

name: Enablement (35 U.S.C. §112) / disclosure sufficiency
description: The disclosure must be sufficient to enable someone skilled in the relevant art to make and use all the embodiments of the invention encompassed by the claims.
guidance: Enablement can be applied loosely: a specification describing one working example may be sufficient; disclosure of an inventive concept or principle can suffice even if not every embodiment is described. Examples: Gillette (conceptual disclosure upheld), Selden (overbroad disclosure narrowed).

name: Claims define scope (specification vs claims)
description: Claims define the patentee's technological territory (analogous to metes and bounds), while the specification is used to determine patentability and enablement.
guidance: Claims usually encompass more than the material in the specification; courts and examiners treat specification and claims as serving different functions in establishing scope and enforceability.

name: Burden on Patent Office examiner for non-enablement
description: The examiner must point to something in the prior art indicating that some claimed embodiments are impossible or would require additional information; absent such evidence, broad claims may be allowed.
guidance: Patent Office policy places the burden of disproving enablement on the examiner to avoid leaving claim scope to individual examiners' technological forecasting; courts narrow claims later if necessary.

name: Doctrine of equivalents (function-way-result / Graver Tank test)
description: If there is no literal infringement, courts ask whether the accused product performs the same function, in substantially the same way, to achieve substantially the same result, and may find infringement under the doctrine of equivalents.
guidance: Apply after literal infringement question; examples include International Nickel (magnesium equivalence) and Graver Tank formulation; courts stretch claim language 'on proper occasions' after exhaust of interpretive aids.

name: Literal infringement analysis
description: The first step in infringement analysis is to determine whether the challenger’s product falls squarely within the literal language of the patentee’s claims.
guidance: If literal infringement is found, plaintiff succeeds unless defenses (e.g., reverse equivalents) apply; if not, move to equivalents analysis.

name: Blocking patents / subservient patents and mutual exclusion
description: Two patents can 'block' each other when a broad patent dominates and a narrower patent claims an improvement; each may require a license from the other to practice the full technology.
guidance: Court may declare a patent subservient; although subservient patentees still gain bargaining leverage and can limit dominant patentee damages, blocking patents complicate freedom-to-operate and licensing negotiations.

name: Prosecution history estoppel
description: Claims or subject matter surrendered during prosecution cannot later be recaptured under the doctrine of equivalents.
guidance: Prosecution history estoppel is a constraint on stretching claim breadth via equivalents; ties allowable equivalents to what was given up during prosecution.

name: Prior art limits on stretching claims/equivalents
description: Courts are constrained by the prior art when 'stretching' claim language under the doctrine of equivalents; an applicant cannot claim what is in the prior art.
guidance: Equivalents cannot be used to take subject matter lying in the prior art; prior art serves as an outer boundary for permissible claim expansion.

name: Product vs process claims and new-use patents
description: Product claims (composition of matter) are typically broader; a newly discovered use for a known product can often be protected by process claims directed to applying Old Product X to New Application Y.
guidance: Dawson Chemical illustrates protecting a new application via a process patent; encourages drafting process claims to capture new uses even when the product itself is unpatentable.

name: Patenting purified/natural products (product claims in biotech/chemistry)
description: Purified versions of naturally occurring products are often claimed as patentable 'new' things when transformed into a useful commercial or therapeutic form, though controversy exists.
guidance: Cases like Parke-Davis suggest purified natural products may be patentable; biotechnology cases (Genentech, Scripps/Genentech) show jurisdictional and doctrinal complexity; European Patent Office may reject broad species claims (Leder & Stewart transgenic mammals example).

name: Tension between enablement and doctrine of equivalents
description: There is an inherent tension: enablement suggests limiting claims to what the specification enables, while the doctrine of equivalents permits expanding scope beyond literal claim language; courts sometimes apply equivalents even where enablement would counsel otherwise.
guidance: Authors note conflict and recommend reconciling doctrines to avoid permitting claim scope beyond what disclosure supports; specific examples show inconsistency across cases.

name: Drafting strategy to capture inventions and new uses
description: Applicants often draft claims broadly (e.g., claiming principle/concept or all non-human transgenic mammals) or draft process claims to protect new uses of known compounds.
guidance: Broad drafting can be allowed during prosecution absent prior-art proof of non-enablement (burden on examiner); courts and EPO may later narrow; examples include Leder & Stewart transgenic mice claims and Rohm & Haas new-use process claim.

name: Printer/publisher/time statements; author's name not required
description: By statute the name of the printer and publisher must be printed on every book; it is not necessary that the author's name appear to secure statutory rights.
guidance: In practice the publisher's imprint and date are often required for specific statutory provisions (and for pieces of music and engravings), but omission of the author's name does not defeat an author's claim to copyright.

name: Supplemental replies restricted and not a matter of right
description: A reply that is supplemental to a reply that is in compliance with § 1.111(b) will not be entered as a matter of right except as provided in paragraph (a)(2)(ii).
guidance: The Office may enter a supplemental reply only if it is clearly limited to: (A) Cancellation of a claim(s); (B) Adoption of the examiner suggestion(s); (C) Placement of the application in condition for allowance; (D) Reply to an Office requirement made after the first reply was filed; (E) Correction of informalities (e.g., typographical errors); or (F) Simplification of issues for appeal. A supplemental reply will be entered if filed during the period when action by the Office is suspended under § 1.103(a) or (c). If a supplemental reply is not approved for entry, its contents must be included in a proper response to a subsequent Office action.

name: Replies must distinctly and specifically point out errors and address every ground
description: The reply must be reduced to a writing which distinctly and specifically points out the supposed errors in the examiner’s action and must reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the prior Office action.
guidance: The reply must present arguments pointing out the specific distinctions believed to render the claims patentable over any applied references. A general allegation that the claims define a patentable invention without specifically pointing out how the language of the claims patentably distinguishes them from the references does not comply with this requirement. The reply must appear throughout to be a bona fide attempt to advance the application or the reexamination proceeding.

name: Amendments in reply must show patentable novelty and avoidance of references
description: In amending in reply to a rejection of claims in an application or patent under reexamination, the applicant or patent owner must clearly point out the patentable novelty which he or she thinks the claims present in view of the state of the art disclosed by the references cited or the objections made.
guidance: The applicant or patent owner must also show how the amendments avoid such references or objections.

name: Requirement of identical claims in merged proceedings and remedy if not identical
description: When proceedings are merged, the patent owner is required to maintain identical claims in both files while the proceedings remain merged.
guidance: If claims are not identical at the time the merger decision is drafted, an Office action will be issued concurrently with the merger decision containing a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) as indefinite, and will require a patent owner amendment to place claims in identical form. Patent owner must respond per 37 CFR 1.111 and include remarks setting forth the basis for any new or amended claims; third-party requester may comment on such amendments per 37 CFR 1.947.

name: Public acquiescence as substitute evidence of validity
description: Where no judgment sustaining the patent can be offered, or where such judgment is of doubtful value, the deficiency may be supplied by proof of a public acquiescence in the claims of the patent of sufficient definiteness and duration to afford a reasonable presumption of its validity.
guidance: Acquiescence is a voluntary submission, against interest, to an asserted right. Proofs include exclusive possession and exercise of the right after grant (manufacture, repeated sales, licensing), long undisputed use with public acquiescence, acceptance by the public, and use/sale prior to application. Such evidence can justify a provisional injunction even if some doubt of validity remains; special facts may, however, take a case out of the general rule.

name: Public acceptance and use before patent application
description: The use and sale of the invention by the plaintiff before he applied for a patent, and the acquiescence of the public in his exclusive claims, is to be regarded as evidence of patentability and of recognition of the plaintiff's claim.
guidance: Courts consider acceptance by the public and long undisputed use as important indicia. Sufficient acquiescence will support injunctive relief even where the patent has not been finally adjudicated valid.

name: The breadth of the claims (Wands factor A)
description: The breadth of the claims.
guidance: Claim scope is a primary factor: broader claims that attempt to cover large classes (e.g., millions of antibodies) demand more disclosure. See Amgen v. Sanofi where claims covering a vast number of antibodies, but disclosing only 26 sequences, weighed against enablement. See also MPEP § 2164.08 for fuller discussion of scope/breadth.

name: The level of predictability in the art (Wands factor E)
description: The level of predictability in the art.
guidance: Predictable arts require less disclosure to enable practice across claim scope; unpredictable arts (e.g., certain biotechnology areas) require more specific guidance and examples. See MPEP § 2164.03 for discussion of predictability and amount of direction.

name: The existence of working examples (Wands factor G)
description: The existence of working examples.
guidance: Presence of working examples in the specification is evidence supporting enablement. However, a few examples may suffice only if the specification also discloses a general quality or commonality that reliably enables the whole claimed class; otherwise, limited examples supporting a very broad claim may be insufficient (see Amgen). See MPEP § 2164.02.

name: The quantity of experimentation needed (Wands factor H)
description: The quantity of experimentation needed to make or use the invention based on the content of the disclosure.
guidance: Evaluate how much trial-and-error, screening, or experimentation would be necessary for a skilled artisan to practice the full scope of the claims in view of the disclosure. If the required experimentation is more than reasonable, enablement fails. See MPEP § 2164.06.

name: Definition of lack of enablement
description: A conclusion of lack of enablement means the specification, at the time of filing, would not have taught one skilled in the art how to make and/or use the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
guidance: This legal standard is applied by assessing the evidence for each Wands factor as of the filing date. See In re Wright, 999 F.2d 1557, 1562.

name: Reasonable experimentation depends on nature of the invention and the art (Amgen guidance)
description: The specification may require a reasonable amount of experimentation and what is reasonable depends on the nature of the invention and the underlying art.
guidance: The Supreme Court in Amgen recognized that a few examples can suffice if the specification discloses a general quality running through the class that gives it a peculiar fitness for the purpose, but when claims attempt to monopolize a vast class (e.g., millions of antibodies) and practicing the claim requires screening each candidate, lack of enablement is likely. Examiners should compare the number and representativeness of examples to claim breadth and consider whether additional screening or undue experimentation would be necessary.

name: Required elements of a proper rejection
description: Each rejection must: specify which claims are rejected; clearly explain each ground of rejection; cite supporting references when applicable; and, when practicable, indicate how the rejections might be overcome.
guidance: These elements ensure the applicant can meaningfully respond; failure to include them can render the action defective.

name: Standard for making final rejections
description: Final rejection may be made on the second or subsequent examination, subject to limits.
guidance: A final rejection is improper if the examiner introduces new grounds not necessitated by claim amendments or by information disclosure statements filed with required fees. Before making a final rejection, a 'clear issue should be developed between the examiner and applicant,' and the examiner must repeat all applicable grounds and clearly state supporting reasons. Final actions must include the appropriate form paragraphs (7.39–7.42) notifying applicants of appeal rights and options.

name: Handling claims copied from existing patents
description: When claims are copied from existing patents, the examiner must determine whether corresponding patent claims are also unpatentable under the asserted grounds.
guidance: If the rejection ground would also render the patent's claims unpatentable, the Office action must be approved by the Technology Center Director.

name: Citing and explaining references when pertinence is not apparent
description: When the relevance of a cited reference to a claim is not obvious, the examiner must explain why the reference is pertinent.
guidance: This is part of the examiner's duty to 'cite the best references' and to communicate clear reasoning so applicants can respond effectively.

name: Post-grant amendments
description: The Protocol provides for post-grant amendments if an Applicant applies in writing and pays the prescribed fee on condition that the amendment falls wholly within the scope of the claims before an amendment.
guidance: Amendments after grant are permitted only when requested in writing, the prescribed fee is paid, and the amended subject-matter does not extend beyond the scope of the originally granted claims.

name: Claims: methods of treatment and multiple dependent claims
description: Provisions on drafting claims involving methods of treatment and multiple dependent claims have been included.
guidance: New rules address how to draft and treat claims directed to therapeutic methods and permit/clarify multiple dependent claim formats according to the Protocol's provisions.

name: Permitted assistance for completing mechanical means (Bloxam v. Elsee)
description: An inventor may be assisted by an engineer to complete the mechanical means for carrying his intentions into effect; additions made by that person will belong to the employer who may include them in the specification as part of his own invention.
guidance: Although the inventor must have the original idea, it is established (Bloxam v. Elsee) that skilled assistance employed expressly to complete mechanical contrivances does not defeat the employer's claim to the invention; the employer may incorporate the assistant's additions into the specification and claim them.

name: Examples concerning essential features (Claims Annex)
description: Illustrative examples to determine which features are essential for defining claim scope.

name: Graham factual inquiry — scope and content of the prior art
description: Determining the scope and content of the prior art by obtaining a thorough understanding of the invention disclosed and claimed (reading the specification and claims) and giving the claims the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.
guidance: Once claim scope is determined, decide what to search for and where to search. The search should cover the claimed subject matter and disclosed features which might reasonably be expected to be claimed. Although a rejection need not be based on a teaching/suggestion to combine, a preferred search will look for such references if they exist. See MPEP §§ 904, 904.02, 904.03 and § 2111 for related guidance.

name: Graham factual inquiry — differences between the claimed invention and the prior art
description: Ascertaining the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art requires interpreting the claim language and considering both the invention and the prior art as a whole.
guidance: Interpret claims per MPEP § 2111 and consider the totality of the claimed invention and reference teachings (see MPEP § 2141.02). All claim limitations must be considered in comparing to the prior art.

name: Broadest reasonable interpretation of claims
description: The scope of the claimed invention must be clearly determined by giving the claims the 'broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.'
guidance: See Phillips v. AWH Corp. and MPEP § 2111. Determination of claim scope precedes searching and comparison to prior art.

name: Rationale: Combining prior art elements to yield predictable results
description: A claim may be obvious where prior art elements are combined according to known methods to yield predictable results.
guidance: This is an exemplified rationale consistent with KSR. The examiner must articulate why the combination would have been predictable and supported by the record. See MPEP § 2143 and § 2144 discussion.

name: Rationale: Applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement
description: Applying a known technique to a known device (method or product) that is ready for improvement to yield predictable results supports obviousness.
guidance: Show the device was 'ready for improvement' and that the application of the technique would predictably produce the claimed result.

name: Rationale: Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art
description: Obviousness may be supported when there is some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art that would have led one of ordinary skill to modify or combine references to arrive at the claimed invention.
guidance: This captures classical TSM-type reasoning; the examiner should articulate the relevant teaching/suggestion/motivation and explain the path from prior art to claimed invention. See MPEP § 2143.01.

name: Examiners must explain why differences between prior art and claims would have been obvious
description: Prior art references need not teach every claim limitation, but the examiner must explain why the differences would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill.
guidance: The mere existence of differences does not establish nonobviousness (Dann v. Johnston). The gap between prior art and claim cannot be so great as to render the claim nonobvious; provide articulated reasoning supporting the bridge.

name: Applicant reply / traverse requirements
description: Applicants must distinctly and specifically point out alleged errors in the Office action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection per 37 CFR 1.111(b).
guidance: An effective traverse to factual findings must include a reasoned statement explaining why the Office erred; mere assertions that the examiner failed to establish a prima facie case or unsupported claims that reliance on common knowledge lacks documentary evidence are not substantively adequate. If applicant does not properly traverse, the examiner may repeat the rejection and make the next action final (see MPEP § 706.07(a)).

name: Complete specification must not claim a different invention than provisional
description: Provisions added make clear that a complete specification which describes or claims an invention other than that described in the provisional specification, and that such other invention forms part of an application made by the opponent in the interval between the filing of the provisional specification and the giving of the complete specification, is a ground (for action/objection).
guidance: Prevents applicants from changing the invention between provisional and complete specifications to the prejudice of third parties who filed intervening applications.

name: Application filing requirements under 37 CFR 1.53(b)
description: The filing date of an application filed under this section is the date on which a specification as prescribed by 35 U.S.C. 112 containing a description pursuant to § 1.71 and at least one claim pursuant to § 1.75, and any drawing required by § 1.81(a) are filed in the Patent and Trademark Office. No new matter may be introduced into an application after its filing date.
guidance: Filing fee and an oath/declaration are required by 37 CFR 1.51(b) for a complete application but may be filed after the filing date upon payment of the surcharge in 37 CFR 1.16(f). 37 CFR 1.53(b) is the default application rule (exceptions: national stage 1.495, provisional 1.53(c), CPA design 1.53(d)). A continuing application may be filed under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, or 365(c) and 37 CFR 1.78(a).

name: Recommended practice for claims and preliminary amendments
description: Applicant should file a new set of claims as the original claims of the continuing application instead of filing a copy of the claims from the prior application and a preliminary amendment.
guidance: Preliminary amendments present on the filing date are part of the original disclosure, but preliminary amendments may not be reflected in the published application unless also submitted through the EFS. To have a publication contain only desired claims, file the continuation/divisional with a new specification containing only the desired set of claims.

name: Publication considerations for continuing applications
description: Any utility or plant patent application that will be published pursuant to 35 U.S.C. 122(b) should be filed under 37 CFR 1.53(b) with a specification (including the claims) and drawings that the applicant would like to have published because the Office will generally publish the specification (including the claims) and drawings as filed.
guidance: Preliminary amendments may not be reflected in the patent application publication unless the amended specification is also submitted via EFS. Filing a continuation with a new specification containing the desired claims is strongly recommended to control what is published and to preserve potential provisional rights under 35 U.S.C. 154(d).

name: Incorporation by reference rules (37 CFR 1.57 and 1.78)
description: An applicant may incorporate by reference a prior application by including an explicit statement in the specification that specifically enumerated prior application(s) are 'hereby incorporated by reference.' For applications filed on or after September 21, 2004, a claim under 35 U.S.C. 120 and 37 CFR 1.78 is considered an incorporation by reference as to inadvertently omitted material subject to 37 CFR 1.57(a).
guidance: For apps filed on/after Sept 21, 2004, applicants are encouraged to provide an explicit incorporation by reference statement. An incorporation by reference statement added after filing is not effective because no new matter can be added after the filing date. Mere reference to another application/publication is not an incorporation for 35 U.S.C. 112 purposes.

name: Interlocutory appeals and claim-construction clarity (Markman orders)
description: H.R. 1908 provides the Federal Circuit jurisdiction over interlocutory decisions (Markman orders) in which the district court construes the claims of a patent as a matter of law.
guidance: Purpose is to clarify claim scope early in litigation and make patent litigation more efficient by enabling appellate review of claim construction before final judgment.

name: Limits on reassertion of issues and discovery abuse in administrative proceedings
description: The bill prohibits a party from reasserting claims in court that it raised in post-grant review and requires the PTO to prescribe rules for abuse of discovery or improper use of the proceeding.
guidance: Aimed at preventing tactical or abusive serial litigation (claim-splitting) and overbroad discovery in administrative challenges, thereby protecting patent owners from repeated attacks while allowing a meaningful administrative check on patent validity.

name: Combination claims: infringement only when full combination used
description: Every patent stands upon its subject-matter, and accordingly the question of infringement depends upon the use of that which is covered by the patent. A patent may be for a new combination, whether the particular parts or things constituting that combination be new or old. But where the patent is for a combination, and not for several and distinct improvements, it is no infringement to use any of the parts or things which go to make up the combination, if the combination itself be not used.
guidance: If the claim is to the combination as such, defendants may use individual elements without infringement so long as the claimed combination is not employed.

name: Novelty of multiple claimed improvements / whole-patent risk
description: Formerly it was necessary that the whole of the improvements claimed as such should be new; and if the novelty of any one of them failed, the action could not be sustained — the patent might be void on account of partial failure of the whole consideration on which it was granted.
guidance: This doctrine rests on the idea the consideration (novelty of all parts) was entire; subsequent statutes (Act of July 4, 1836 and later) recognize defenses and permit that a patent be deemed valid for so much as is truly the invention of the patentee if material and definitely distinguishable, unless the specification was knowingly made too broad to defraud the public.

name: Severability / statutory carve-out for materially distinct parts
description: A more recent statute has provided that the patent shall be deemed good and valid for so much of the invention or discovery as shall be truly and bonâ fide the invention or discovery of the patentee, if it is a material and substantial part of the thing patented, and is definitely distinguishable from the other parts which the patentee had no right to claim, notwithstanding the specification may be too broad, if it was so made by mistake, accident or inadvertence, and without any wilful default or intent to defraud or mislead the public.
guidance: Leaves former doctrine applicable where the claim was made too broad wilfully or with intent to deceive; courts will separate valid, distinguishable, material parts when made innocently.

name: Utility requirement and false suggestion
description: If any thing claimed as essential turn out to be useless, the patent is voidable, provided it was known to the patentee, at the time of enrolling his specification, to be useless, because he misleads the public by representing it to be useful.
guidance: If a part was later discovered not to be useful, that alone does not invalidate the patent unless there was a false suggestion at the time of grant. A patent for an entire machine useful on the whole remains valid even if some parts are useless, so long as there is no false suggestion.

name: Method-only claims require reduction to practice / new substance
description: The method and the mode of doing a thing are the same, and it is impossible to support a patent for a method only, without having carried it into effect, and produced some new substance. 'Principle reduced into practice' means a practice founded on principle — the thing done or made.
guidance: Purely abstract methods are insufficient; the inventive concept must be embodied in a manufacture or practical application to be patentable.

name: Step 2B main question
description: Does the claim recite additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception?
guidance: Examiners should first identify whether there are any additional elements (features/limitations/steps) recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception(s), then evaluate those additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether they contribute an inventive concept (i.e., amount to significantly more than the judicial exception(s)). This evaluation is made with respect to the considerations the Supreme Court has identified as relevant to the eligibility analysis (see MPEP § 2106.05(a)-(h)).

name: Identify additional elements (carryover from Step 2A Prong Two)
description: Carry over identification of the additional element(s) in the claim from Step 2A Prong Two.
guidance: Examiners should reuse their identification of additional elements from Step 2A Prong Two as the starting point for Step 2B analysis.

name: Evaluate additional elements individually and in combination
description: Evaluate additional elements both individually and as an ordered combination to determine whether they amount to significantly more than the judicial exception.
guidance: Consider whether elements that are individually known may, when arranged in a non-conventional and non-generic combination, provide an inventive concept (e.g., BASCOM: installation of a filtering tool at a specific remote location with customizable features). The inventive-concept inquiry requires more than recognizing each claim element, by itself, was known in the art.

name: Use MPEP §2106.05(a)-(h) considerations (not a weighing test)
description: Apply the considerations introduced in Part I.A and discussed in MPEP § 2106.05(a) through (h) to the additional elements.
guidance: Many considerations overlap and more than one may be relevant. It is not important how elements are characterized or how many considerations apply; rather, evaluate the significance of the additional elements relative to applicant's invention and whether they encompass an inventive concept. Not all considerations will be relevant to every element or claim.

name: Outcome: claim as a whole amounts to significantly more (Pathway C) or not
description: If the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the exception itself, the claim is eligible (Step 2B: YES) at Pathway C; if not, the claim is not patent-eligible (Step 2B: NO) and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101.
guidance: Step 2B determines whether the claim as a whole adds an inventive concept. If there are no meaningful limitations that transform the exception into a patent-eligible application, the claim is not eligible and an ineligibility rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 should be made (see MPEP § 2106.07 for formulating rejections).

name: Consideration: Improvements to the Functioning of a Computer or Other Technology
description: Consider whether the claim 'purport(s) to improve the functioning of the computer itself' or 'any other technology or technical field.'
guidance: This consideration — the search for a technological solution to a technological problem — is relevant in Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B. Case law examples include DDR Holdings, Enfish, McRO, Visual Memory, Amdocs, and others. Determining an improvement may involve consultation of the specification to identify technical problems and unconventional technical solutions expressed in the claim.

name: Computer-specific limitation: claim scope must require computer implementation
description: For a method claim to improve computer functionality, the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim must be limited to computer implementation.
guidance: A claim whose entire scope can be performed mentally cannot be said to improve computer technology (Synopsys). Likewise, claims covering embodiments that can be practiced verbally or by telephone cannot improve computer technology (RecogniCorp).

name: Examples of improvements and non-improvements (use as evidentiary guidance)
description: Court-provided examples indicate what may or may not show an improvement in computer functionality or other technology.
guidance: Examples that may show improvement (non-exhaustive): modification to hyperlink protocol (DDR Holdings); inventive distribution of functionality within a network to filter content (BASCOM); halftone rendering method; unconventional distributed network architecture; programmable memory system; detailed techniques for transmitting images; particular server structures for organized images; specific software programming/design for menus; improved virus scanning profiles; improved user interfaces; particular interfaces for 3D spreadsheets; software license restriction methods. Examples that may not be sufficient (non-exhaustive): generating restaurant menus with functionally claimed features; accelerating analysis solely via general-purpose computer speed; mere automation of manual processes; recording/transmitting/archiving digital images with conventional technology; affixing a barcode without technical details; instructions to display information without how to achieve it; improvements to information stored (not database functionality); arranging GUI information that merely assists users.

name: Damages versus account of profits — election timing
description: A patent owner may seek damages or an account of profits; both remedies are usually claimed in the alternative in the particulars of claim and the election is made only after infringement has been found.
guidance: Claim both alternatives; election occurs post-determination of infringement.

name: Damages — compensatory principle and measures
description: Generally, damages are compensatory, not punitive. If the patentee sells/manufactures products, it may claim lost sales and ancillary item losses; if the patentee licenses the patent, damages are usually a royalty rate based on comparable licences; where the patentee neither manufactures nor licenses, the court will determine a notional royalty applying the user principle.
guidance: The general rule is to put the injured party in the same position it would have been in but for the wrong. The burden of proof lies with the claimant but damages are assessed liberally.

name: Revocation grounds (UK)
description: Under UK law, five grounds for revocation by a third party: Nonpatentability (not novel/inventive or excluded subject-matter), Nonentitlement, Insufficiency (specification doesn't enable skilled person), Added matter (subject-matter extends beyond originally filed content), Unallowable post-grant extension (impermissible amendment after grant).
guidance: No standing required to bring a revocation claim in the UK.

name: Declaratory relief (UK) — scope and Arrow declarations
description: Statutory provision allows declarations of noninfringement by any party; courts have broad inherent jurisdiction to make declarations that serve a useful purpose. Arrow declarations can confirm that an applicant's product/process was known or obvious at a relevant date.
guidance: Arrow declarations are used when divisional applications or shielding subject matter threaten the applicant; successful declaration provides a defence to future infringement claims because claims cannot be both valid and infringed if product/process was known or obvious at priority date.

name: Search and seizure (saisie-contrefaçon) mechanism (France)
description: Ex parte search-and-seizure orders allow a bailiff to enter defendant premises, describe accused product/process, seize samples and take copies of documentation evidencing materiality/origin/scope of infringement; claimant has 31 days to launch proceedings or the seizure is void and materials returned.
guidance: No discovery/disclosure in French system, so this measure is heavily used (performed in >80% of infringement proceedings) and evidence obtained can often be used in other jurisdictions.

name: France — recovery of fees
description: The winning party can claim reimbursement of attorneys' fees, but the grant and amount are within the court's discretion; usually the amount awarded ranges between 20% and 70% of attorneys' fees.
guidance: No fixed statutory rule for determining amounts; discretion leads to variability.

name: France — defendant-initiated relief options
description: Defendants can initiate invalidity actions where they show an interest; grounds include lack of novelty, inventive step, industrial application, insufficiency, added matter, or undue extension. Declaratory noninfringement actions proceed in two phases: an amicable phase inviting the patentee's opinion, then a judicial phase by summons if needed.
guidance: FRAND-specific contractual breach claims (breach of ETSI declaration) have been recognized by French courts; procedural prerequisites (amicable step) apply for noninfringement actions.

name: EPO problem-solution approach usage (Netherlands)
description: Dutch courts apply established EPO case law, most importantly the problem-solution approach for assessing inventive step: determine closest prior art, establish objective technical problem, and consider if the claimed invention would have been obvious to the skilled person.
guidance: EPO decisions are persuasive and often relied upon by Dutch courts when assessing validity.

name: Statements are not admissions of unpatentability
description: Statements in the detailed explanation will NOT be construed as an admission of unpatentability; they indicate that the patent owner is requesting the Office consider whether certain issues may be raised by each item of information with respect to specific claims.
guidance: Patent owners may identify specific patentability issues (e.g., anticipation, obviousness, written description, enablement) in the explanation to provide focused review and explicit consideration of potential issues on the record.

name: Correction of factual information requires additional supporting items
description: If the request includes an item of information limited to correction of factual information (e.g., foreign priority or domestic benefit claim, common ownership), the request should also include one or more additional items of information that potentially show the patentability of the claims depends on the factual information to be corrected.
guidance: Example: To correct an effective filing date by claiming benefit of a parent patent, include the parent patent and an intervening reference, and explain how the intervening reference may be applied to the claims if the effective filing date remains unchanged, and explain how the patent owner is entitled to the corrected factual information (e.g., how each claim limitation is supported by the parent). If merely deleting a benefit/priority claim, an explanation of entitlement to a new effective filing date may not be required.

name: Do not combine optional patentability-argument with required detailed explanation
description: Requests that combine the detailed explanation under 37 CFR 1.610(b)(5) with the optional discussion under 37 CFR 1.610(c)(3) often have lengthy patentability arguments with little explanation of how items apply to claim limitations, risking a finding of noncompliance.
guidance: If the patent owner submits the optional content, the Office strongly recommends presenting it under separate subheadings (e.g., 'Optional Explanation under 37 CFR 1.610(c)(3)'). Combining discussions can cause the Office to find the required explanation was not provided and lose the filing date.

name: Three-month statutory decision period (SNQ determination)
description: Within three months after the filing date of a request for supplemental examination, the Office will determine whether a substantial new question of patentability (SNQ) affecting any claim is raised by any of the items of information properly presented in the request.
guidance: The determination will generally be limited to review of the items identified in the request as applied to the identified claims, will be based on the claims in effect at the time of determination, and will become part of the official patent record. The examiner should take up a request about six weeks after filing; if the three-month period ends on a weekend or federal holiday, the certificate should issue by the preceding business day.

name: Standard for determining SNQ
description: The standard for determining whether an item of information raises a SNQ is the same as set forth in MPEP § 2242 for ex parte reexaminations: whether there is a substantial likelihood that a reasonable examiner would consider the item important in determining patentability.
guidance: Determination is generally limited to the items of information identified in the request with respect to the identified claims. The supplemental examination certificate containing the determination becomes part of the official record.

name: Determination limited to identified items and claims
description: The determination will generally be limited to the item(s) of information identified in the request as applied to the identified claim(s) of the patent; if the patent owner wants consideration of an item with respect to multiple claims, each claim must be identified and explained.
guidance: If the patent owner fails to request consideration of certain claims in view of an item of information, the owner is not entitled to a determination for that item with respect to those claims. The determination is based on claims in effect at time of determination.

name: Amendment paper submission in reexamination
description: A proposed amendment in an ex parte or an inter partes reexamination proceeding is made by filing a paper directing that proposed specified changes be made to the patent specification, including the claims, or to the drawings.
guidance: An amendment paper may be submitted as an accompaniment to a request by the patent owner in accordance with § 1.510(e), as part of a patent owner statement under § 1.530(b), or, where permitted, during prosecution pursuant to § 1.550(a) or § 1.937.

name: Fee deficiency notices and correction time periods
description: If excess claims fees required by 37 CFR 1.20(c)(3) and (c)(4) are not paid with the presentation of the excess claims, a Notice of Defective Paper will be issued requiring correction of the defect (fee deficiency).
guidance: In third-party requested reexaminations, set a one-month period (form PTOL-475) to correct the defect. In patent owner requested or Director ordered reexaminations, set a two-month period (form PTO-2311). An extension of time to correct may be requested under 37 CFR 1.550(c). If unpaid within the period, prosecution will be terminated under 37 CFR 1.550(e). If unpaid in response to a final Office action, notify owner of fee deficiency in the advisory action.

name: Examiner consideration of submitted matter
description: Once reexamination is ordered, any submissions properly filed and served in accordance with 37 CFR 1.530 and 1.535 will be considered by the examiner when preparing the first Office action.
guidance: Consideration of proposed amendments to the specification including claims will be guided by 1.530(d)-(j). Consideration of the patent owner’s statement guided by 1.530(c). Consideration of requester’s reply guided by 1.535. Issues not previously presented but within scope will be treated in the Office action; issues outside the scope should be treated pursuant to 1.552(c). For handling of new matter see MPEP § 2270.

name: Conduct of ex parte reexamination proceedings (general)
description: After the times for filing the statement and reply have expired, reexamination will be conducted according to procedures established for initial examination under sections 132 and 133, and will be conducted with special dispatch.
guidance: The patent owner may propose any amendment and new claims to distinguish the invention from prior art cited under section 301 or in response to an adverse decision; no proposed amended or new claim enlarging the scope of a claim will be permitted. Proceedings (including appeals) are to be concluded with special dispatch within the Office (35 U.S.C.305).

name: Scope of ex parte reexamination (37 CFR 1.552)
description: Claims in an ex parte reexamination proceeding will be examined on the basis of patents or printed publications and, with respect to subject matter added or deleted in the reexamination proceeding, on the basis of the requirements of 35 U.S.C.112.
guidance: Claims will not be permitted to enlarge the scope of the claims of the patent. Issues other than those indicated in paragraphs (a) and (b) (i.e., patentability based on patents/printed publications and 35 U.S.C.112 for added/deleted matter) will not be resolved in reexamination; if raised, they will be noted by the examiner and the patent owner may consider filing a reissue application to have such issues considered. Any statement of the patent owner of record may be used after a reexamination proceeding has been ordered to determine the proper meaning of a patent claim when applying patents or printed publications.

name: Markush claim examination rules (MPEP § 803.02 III.A)
description: Following election, the Markush claim will be examined fully with respect to the elected species and further to the extent necessary to determine patentability; where a claim reads on multiple species, only one species needs to be taught or suggested by the prior art for the claim to be anticipated or rendered obvious.
guidance: If the Markush claim is not allowable, the provisional election is given effect and examination is limited to the Markush claim and claims to the elected species, with claims drawn to species patentably distinct from the elected species held withdrawn. If applicant amends the Markush claim to exclude species anticipated/obvious over prior art, the amended claim will be reexamined; finality and entry of amendments are governed by MPEP §§ 706.07(a), 714.13, and 37 CFR 1.116 rules.

name: Mutual exclusivity test for species restriction (MPEP § 806.04(f))
description: Where two or more species are claimed, a requirement for restriction to a single species may be proper if the species are mutually exclusive. Claims to different species are mutually exclusive if one claim recites limitations disclosed for a first species but not a second, and the second recites limitations disclosed only for the second and not the first.
guidance: Expressed another way: to require restriction between claims limited to species, the claims must not overlap in scope. Overlap means shared limitations or scope; absence of mutual exclusivity counsels against restriction for that reason alone, but other factors (e.g., patentable distinctness, burden) still matter.

name: Patentable distinctness criterion
description: Species are patentably distinct if they are not obvious variants of each other; if the examiner determines species are not obvious variants, they are patentably distinct.
guidance: Determination of patentable distinctness is fact-based and can be contested by applicant; if species are held patentably distinct, claims directed to nonelected species may be withdrawn from consideration following election.

name: Provisional election procedure and scope
description: An election of a single disclosed species (or a single grouping of patentably indistinct species) may be required as a provisional election conditioned on a generic claim being non-allowable; the election serves as the starting point for examination.
guidance: The provisional election is implemented in the first action when appropriate; if the elected species is rejected (anticipated/obvious), the provisional election is given effect and examination is limited to claims reading on the elected species. Applicants may elect a species with traverse and argue lack of burden or improper restriction.

name: Effect of prior art on Markush/Group claims (anticipation/obviousness)
description: Where a Markush claim lists alternatives, the presence of the prior art disclosing one alternative is sufficient to anticipate or render the entire Markush claim obvious.
guidance: Cited authority: Fresenius USA, Inc. v. Baxter Int'l, Inc. — 'the entire element is disclosed by the prior art if one alternative in the Markush group is in the prior art.' Thus only one species need be taught or suggested by prior art to defeat a Markush claim.

name: Withdrawal and reexamination consequences for non-elected species
description: Claims drawn to species patentably distinct from the elected species will be held withdrawn from further consideration when a Markush/provisional election is given effect; if applicant later amends to exclude species rendered obvious, the claim will be reexamined to the extent necessary.
guidance: If applicant overcomes the prior art rejection by amending to exclude the offending species, the amended Markush claim will be examined again; if applicant obtains allowance of a generic claim, applicant is entitled to consideration of claims to additional species that depend from or require all limitations of the allowable generic claim under 37 CFR 1.141.

name: Definition and legal background of Markush claims
description: A 'Markush' claim recites a list of alternatively useable members; the listing of specified alternatives is referred to as a Markush group or grouping.
guidance: Historical and case law references supporting this definition include In re Harnisch, Ex parte Markush (Comm'r Pat. 1924), and Abbott Labs v. Baxter Pharmaceutical Products, Inc. See MPEP § 2117 for further treatment.

name: 707.07(d)-Language To Be Used in Rejecting Claims
description: 707.07(d)-Language To Be Used in Rejecting Claims

name: 716.02(d)-Unexpected Results Commensurate in Scope With Claimed Invention
description: 716.02(d)-Unexpected Results Commensurate in Scope With Claimed Invention

name: 716.03(a)-Commercial Success Commensurate in Scope With Claimed Invention
description: 716.03(a)-Commercial Success Commensurate in Scope With Claimed Invention
guidance: Table of contents entry only; no substantive text on this page.

name: Burden of proof (clear and convincing evidence)
description: The OED Director has the burden of proving alleged violations by clear and convincing evidence. Respondent must prove any affirmative defense by clear and convincing evidence. 37 C.F.R. § 11.49.
guidance: Standard of proof for both prosecution and defensive affirmative claims in USPTO disciplinary proceedings; decisive finding must be supported by clear and convincing proof of misconduct.

name: Factor 6: Strength/Weakness of the Petition
description: Whether the petition presents a strong prima facie case of unpatentability (adequate claim-element-by-element mapping to prior art, adequate articulation of grounds, and a Graham-style analysis), or conversely whether the petition is 'weak'.
guidance: Factor 6 considers whether the petition is sufficiently detailed and persuasive: it must identify grounds for unpatentability, explain which references are relied on and how they map to each claim limitation, and provide supporting evidence (e.g., expert testimony). Mere attorney argument that a petition is 'weak' is insufficient absent demonstration of specific mapping or analytical deficiencies. If references were not considered during prosecution and the petition identifies that, this supports institution because it can show examiner error. Patent Owner attacks that fail to point to inadequate mappings or lack of grounds do not overcome the petition. The Board looks for an element-by-element explanation and evidence to support a prima facie case under Graham.

name: Offer multiple options and pursue a joint hypothesis
description: Provide alternative approaches and collaborate with the examiner to find an agreeable path to allowance.
guidance: Multiple Options: Give the examiner different strategy options (e.g., different proposed claim amendments). This gives the examiner an opportunity to determine which approach would likely work best. Joint Hypothesis: Find a 'yes' path together by jointly identifying workable changes or arguments that address the examiner's concerns.

name: Specification may control generality of claims but cannot contradict letters patent
description: The specification can limit or control the generality of the patent's terms, but if there is a clear repugnancy between the description in the specification and the invention stated in the letters patent, the patent is void because the statute is not complied with.
guidance: The rule allowing specification to control the patent does not extend to cases of inconsistency between them. (Illustration: The King v. Wheeler where patent stated invention not described in specification.)

name: Two objects of the specification
description: The specification has two objects: (1) to make known how to construct/use the invention so artisans can make and use it after patent expiry; (2) to put the public in possession of what the patentee claims so as to ascertain novelty and warn potential users of infringement.
guidance: These twin objects inform the rules of construction and the requirements of sufficiency and clarity in drafting. The specification must enable practice after expiration and disclose what is claimed to avoid misleading the public.

name: Describe subject-matter so public can know the claim (first rule)
description: A specification must describe the subject-matter — what the patentee claims to have invented — so as to enable the public to know what his claim is.
guidance: Language need not be technical or scientifically accurate but must not mislead and must show with reasonable certainty what is intended to be claimed. Whole specification must be read in connection; phrases standing alone should not be singled out. If the invention is left ambiguous and uncertain, the patent is void. (Wyeth v. Stone; Lowell v. Lewis.)

name: Written description must distinguish old from new
description: When the patentee uses what is old, the specification must distinguish between what is old and what is new and point out in what the invention consists.
guidance: If the specification mixes old and new without distinguishing and thereby appears to claim the whole as new, the patent may be broader than the invention and void. The patentee should, if using known elements, either omit them or designate them as old, or expressly disclaim them. (Dixon v. Moyer; Carpenter v. Smith; Davis v. Palmer.)

name: Constrict claims to be co-extensive with actual discovery
description: A specification should be construed, consistently with the fair import of language, so as to make the claim co-extensive with the actual discovery; patentees will be presumed not to intend to claim things they know to be in common use unless language requires it.
