guidance: Construction should not extend claim beyond the true invention; the court should adopt interpretation that gives effect to the exact nature and extent of the claim as apparent in the whole instrument. (English Court of Common Pleas rule; Haworth v. Hardcastle.)

name: Describing old matters: general reference allowed if not ambiguous
description: It is not always necessary to describe things that are old in detail; things generally known or in common use may be referred to in general terms provided they create no ambiguity and are accompanied by an intelligible description of what is new.
guidance: When describing an improvement, the former machine should be set forth sufficiently to show what the patentee engrafts his improvement upon, and the patentee should disclaim the old and state distinctly the improvement claimed. Failing to do so risks making the patent appear to claim the whole machine. (Dixon v. Moyer; Godson on Patents.)

name: Avoid vagueness in manner of describing invention
description: A common defect is vagueness or ambiguity in the manner of description which makes it difficult or impossible to determine what the invention is (distinct from ambiguity in words).
guidance: Examples: directions that leave it uncertain whether several listed materials are to be treated together or separately (lead/minium/red lead); claiming a whole class of substances when in fact only one works will mislead the public and render the specification ambiguous. (Turner v. Winter; Ryan v. Goodwin.)

name: If the specification professes to produce results it does not, patent is void
description: If the patent professes to make or produce particular substances or effects by the directed process and the process, as directed, does not produce what is professed, the patent is void.
guidance: Illustration: a specification claiming to make white lead by the same process as produces something else — if it does not in truth produce white lead, the patent is void. (Turner v. Winter; Ashurst, J.'s observation.)

name: Generic claims over materials: permissible if combination is new and patentee disclosed his own materials
description: If the patentee states the substances he uses and there are still other substances that will produce the effect, a generic description that claims the class is not void for ambiguity or over-breadth provided the combination is new in respect to all substances referred to.
guidance: The key is that the combination must be new and the specification must honestly present what the patentee used; courts will consider the intention as expressed on the face of the specification and the state of knowledge at the time. (Ryan v. Goodwin; Crossley v. Beverly.)

name: Fee deficiency notification and correction
description: If excess claims fees required by 37 CFR 1.20(c)(3) and (c)(4) are not paid with presentation of excess claims, a Notice of Defective Paper (PTOL-2069) will be issued.
guidance: PTOL-2069 sets a one-month time period to correct the defect; an extension may be requested under 37 CFR 1.956. If unpaid within the response period, prosecution of the reexamination proceeding will be terminated under 37 CFR 1.957(b) or limited under 37 CFR 1.957(c) to effect the “abandonment” set forth in 37 CFR 1.20(c)(5).

name: Consequences when patent owner fails to respond (37 CFR 1.957)
description: If the patent owner fails to file a timely, appropriate or complete response in an inter partes reexamination, prosecution may be terminated or limited depending on whether any claims were found patentable.
guidance: (A) If no claims are found patentable, prosecution will be terminated and the Director will issue and publish a certificate concluding reexamination under §1.997 (NIRC). (B) If at least one claim is found patentable, further prosecution will be limited to the claim(s) found patentable at that time and to any claims added thereafter which do not expand the scope of those patentable claims; claims under rejection/objection may be withdrawn and canceled upon publication of the certificate. The ACP will set periods for patent owner response and third party comments under 37 CFR 1.951.

name: Right of Appeal Notice (RAN) and appeal consequences
description: Where the patent owner fails to take timely appeal actions after issuance of a RAN, or where appeal is dismissed, consequences vary with whether claims were found patentable at time of failure to act.
guidance: If no claim found patentable at failure, NIRC issued. If at least one claim was found patentable and third party requester does not appeal or fails to continue appeal, prosecution should be terminated (NIRC). If third party appellant continues appeal, prosecution is limited to claims found patentable at time of failure to act. Third party may appeal withdrawal of a rejection stated in RAN as a final decision favorable to patentability (see 37 CFR 41.61(a)(2)).

name: Third party failure to timely comment on a patent owner response
description: If a third party requester does not timely file written comments on a patent owner response, any subsequent submission of comments on that response will be refused consideration; the loss of commenting right applies only to that specific response.
guidance: If the patent owner’s response was incomplete and later completed, the third party may file comments on the completed response. However, where completion required only payment of a fee (other than an excess claims fee to support an amendment), the requester may not file comments after fee submission. Failure to timely appeal causes loss of appellate rights as appellant, though the requester may still act as respondent or enter the appeal under certain rules.

name: Examiner withdrawal of a ground of rejection — general guidelines
description: If the examiner withdraws a ground of rejection at any time in the prosecution of the inter partes reexamination, distinct treatments depend on origin of rejection and whether claims were amended.
guidance: (A) Where rejected originally by examiner, withdraw should be clearly stated as decision favorable to patentability; third party’s next comments may propose the withdrawn rejection as a 'rejection proposed by the third party requester' and may appeal withdrawal in RAN. (B) Where rejection was proposed by third party and claims not amended, treat issue as a rejection proposed by third party that examiner refuses to adopt. (C) Generally where claims amended and examiner withdraws a ground previously proposed by third party, this is not a refusal to adopt (rejection never proposed as to amended claims); third party may re-propose the rejection as to amended claims and may appeal if RAN issued. (D) If claim amended by adding a dependent claim previously subjected to a proposed requester rejection and the examiner withdraws that rejection as to the amended claim, treat as a refusal to adopt the requester’s previously proposed rejection.

name: Drawings or photographs
description: Drawings or photographs;
guidance: Include clear drawings or, where permitted, photographs that fully disclose the claimed design from the necessary viewpoints. Ensure images meet USPTO form/quality requirements.

name: Permissible additional specification statements
description: In addition to the figure descriptions, the following types of statements are permissible in a design patent specification: a description of the appearance of portions of the claimed design which are not illustrated in the drawing disclosure (i.e., 'the right side elevational view is a mirror image of the left side'); description disclaiming portions of the article not shown, that form no part of the claimed design; statement indicating that any broken line illustration of environmental structure in the drawing is not part of the design sought to be patented; and description denoting the nature and environmental use of the claimed design, if not included in the preamble.
guidance: Use these permitted statements to: (1) note mirrored views, (2) disclaim unclaimed parts, (3) clarify broken-line environmental elements are not claimed, and (4) state the nature/environmental use if not in the preamble. These help avoid overclaiming or ambiguity.

name: Broken lines to show environment and disclaim them when appropriate
description: Statement indicating that any broken line illustration of environmental structure in the drawing is not part of the design sought to be patented;
guidance: Use broken lines in drawings to depict environment/unnclaimed structure and include an explicit statement that such broken-line elements are not part of the claimed design to avoid unintentional claim scope.

name: Avoid vague/general descriptions when claiming broad rights
description: Description must not be vague and general. When a patentee attempts to secure a right of an extensive nature, the description of the process must not be vague and general.
guidance: A sweeping claim requires particular description of how to achieve it; general references (e.g., 'same as ordinary apparatus') are insufficient (Booth v. Kennard).

name: Precisely describe materials and avoid overly general class terms
description: A specification, in describing materials and ingredients required for carrying the invention into effect, must not employ general terms which cover what is unsuitable as well as what is suitable.
guidance: If you claim a class of materials, identify which members are suitable; you cannot leave the public to test which members work (Turner v. Winter; Stevens v. Keating).

name: Do not claim classes containing unsuitable or dangerous members without definition
description: If a claimed class (e.g., 'earthy sulphites' or 'alkaline and earthy sulphites') contains members that are poisonous or unsuitable, the claim is too wide or vague unless the specification defines the suitable members.
guidance: Either limit the claim to suitable members or expressly identify which within the class are proper (Bailey v. Roberton).

name: State most suitable proportions within patentee's knowledge
description: A person who takes out a patent for an invention consisting of the use of known materials in new proportions, though bound to state the most suitable proportions within his knowledge, is not bound to limit his claim to the precise proportions recommended by him in his specification.
guidance: Disclose best-known proportions but claims need not be strictly confined to the exact numbers given; evidence and case law guide boundaries (Patent Type Founding Co. v. Richard).

name: Additions in complete specification must relate to the original invention
description: The additions must strictly relate to the invention as it stood at the date of the application. The introduction of new heads into the specification or an extension of the subject-matter of the original invention will not be permitted.
guidance: You may incorporate refinements discovered after the provisional filing only insofar as they are within the scope of the originally claimed invention (Penn v. Butler; Haley v. Roberton).

name: Need not set forth every possible application of a principle
description: An inventor who obtains a patent for the useful application of a principle is not to be called on to set forth every mode of applying it. It is sufficient if he shows some of its useful applications, those applications being the best illustrations of the invention known to him.
guidance: Disclose illustrative, practical applications known to you; but a general claim cannot later cover applications/improvements unknown at the date of specification (Neilson v. Harford; Badische Anilin und Soda Fabrik v. Levinstein).

name: Do not describe processes including wholly ineffectual options as producing the claimed result
description: If a specification describes several processes or combinations and affirms they will produce a certain result, and some one of the processes or combinations is wholly ineffectual and useless, the patent will be bad even if the mistake would be at once observed by an ordinary workman.
guidance: Ensure that every method/combo you assert produces the claimed result is actually operative; including an inoperative variant can invalidate the entire specification (Simpson v. Holliday).

name: Corresponding specifications in a family of patents and priority/priority dates
description: A family of patents (same invention filed in multiple countries) may yield corresponding specifications; priority rights under the Paris Convention mean related filings can establish earlier effective dates for patent documents in the family.
guidance: Where a U.S. patent claims benefit of earlier foreign or domestic filings, the prior-art date of the U.S. patent may be that earlier filing date (see MPEP § 2154.01(b), § 2136 et seq.). Examiners should trace priority chains across family members to determine earliest effective dates.

name: Required contents of remarks accompanying an amendment
description: Per MPEP §714.16, remarks accompanying an amendment that corrects an error in the patent must fully and clearly state: (A) why the amendment is needed; (B) why the proposed amended or new claims require no additional search or examination; (C) why the claims are patentable; and (D) why they were not presented earlier.
guidance: This is required whenever an amendment to correct an error affects disclosure, claim scope, or adds a claim. The remarks must be complete and clear so the examiner can determine compliance with reissue requirements.

name: Corrections not requiring physical amendment still treated as amendments
description: Correcting an error after allowance that does not include an amendment of the specification or claims (e.g., filing a certified copy of an original foreign application) is nevertheless an amendment of the patent for reissue purposes.
guidance: Even when no physical amendment is entered, the requirements of 37 CFR 1.312 and related reissue rules must be met because the correction is treated as an amendment of the patent.

name: Treatment when a reexamination or PTAB trial certificate issues while reissue pending
description: If a reexamination certificate or PTAB trial certificate is to be issued for a patent while a reissue application is pending and will not be merged, the examiner will not act on the reissue application until the certificate issues and publishes; thereafter, the Office resumes examination and typically gives the patent owner two months to amend reissue claims based on the concluded proceeding.
guidance: Claims canceled by the certificate are treated as claims lost in litigation. Further prosecution is generally limited to claims narrower than those canceled; claims equal or broader in scope are generally deemed surrendered and will be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 251 and may be subject to estoppel (see MPEP §2308.03).

name: Exceptions allowing broader claims after a certificate
description: Broader claims in a reissue application may be presented despite a certificate canceling claims when: (a) the broader claims can be patentable despite the canceled claims (e.g., have an earlier effective filing date or can be sworn behind), and (b) the broader claims could not have been presented in the reexamination or PTAB trial.
guidance: Criterion (a) examples: reissue claims supported by a parent application giving an earlier effective date, or subject matter that can be sworn behind. Criterion (b) example: claims directed to a distinct invention broader than all claims during reexamination/PTAB trial. If all patent claims were canceled, petitions (37 CFR 1.183 or 1.182 depending on context) may be required to proceed; see MPEP for petition procedure.

name: Proceeding when all patent claims are canceled by a certificate
description: Even where all patent claims were canceled by a reexamination certificate or a PTAB trial certificate, the reissue application can proceed to correct the 35 U.S.C. 251 “error” of presenting unpatentable claims, subject to petitions and guidance.
guidance: If claims were canceled in a reexamination certificate, the patent owner must file a petition under 37 CFR 1.183 to waive 37 CFR 1.570 and/or 1.997(d) as appropriate; if canceled in a PTAB trial certificate, file a petition under 37 CFR 1.182. A petition is grantable if reissue claims are narrower than canceled claims or satisfy the exceptions described for presenting broader claims (earlier effective date, cannot be sworn behind, or could not have been presented in the other proceeding). Matters may be forwarded to OPLA for resolution.

name: Requirements for suggesting an interference (37 CFR 41.202) in a reissue
description: An applicant (including a reissue applicant) suggesting an interference must: (1) identify the application or patent that is the subject of the suggested interference; (2) identify all claims believed to interfere; (3) propose one or more counts and show correspondence of claims to counts; (4) explain in detail why the applicant will prevail on priority; (5) if a claim has been added/amended to provoke an interference, provide a claim chart showing written description support; and (6) for each constructive reduction to practice for which benefit is sought, provide a chart showing where the disclosure provides such reduction to practice.
guidance: Provide sufficient detail (claim charts, correspondence) to satisfy 37 CFR 41.202 and the case law cited (e.g., In re Keil, In re Dien). These materials substantiate the basis for the suggested interference and priority assertions.

name: Using a reissue application to provoke an interference: conditions and limits
description: A reissue application may be employed to provoke an interference if it (A) adds copied claims not present in the original patent, (B) amends claims to correspond to those of the patent/application with which an interference is sought, or (C) contains at least one error appropriate for reissue (not directed solely to provoking an interference).
guidance: For situations (A) and (B), the reissue oath/declaration must assert that applicant erred in failing to include claims of the proper scope in the original application and identify the claims added to provoke the interference. The subject matter of copied/amended claims must be supported by the original patent disclosure under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph. A reissue applicant cannot present added/amended claims to provoke an interference if the claims were deliberately omitted from the original patent (for reissues filed before Sept 16, 2012). Timing limits apply (e.g., pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 135(b) and two-year rule under 35 U.S.C. 251) — see MPEP §715.05 and §1412.03.

name: Explanation of support for claim changes
description: Each claim amendment must be accompanied by an explanation of the support in the disclosure of the patent for the amendment (support for changes, insertions and deletions) as required by 37 CFR 1.530(e).
guidance: Failure to submit the explanation will generally result in a notification that the amendment is not completely responsive prior to final rejection (see MPEP § 2266.01). Amendments submitted after final rejection without explanation will not be entered. Patent owner should also point out what is changed in the 'Remarks' portion of the amendment.

name: Amendment of a new claim previously presented
description: An amendment of a new claim must present the entire text of the new claim containing the amendatory material, and it must be underlined throughout the claim; it cannot contain bracketing or other indication of what was in the previous version.
guidance: Because changes are made vis-a-vis the original patent, the amended new claim shows only the changes from the original patent (underlined) and not any bracketed deletions from prior new-claim versions. Patent owner must point out what is changed in 'Remarks' and provide support explanation per 37 CFR 1.530(e).

name: Excess claims fees for claims added during reexamination
description: 37 CFR 1.20(c) establishes excess claims fees for: (c)(3) each independent claim in excess of three and in excess of the number of independent claims in the patent; (c)(4) each claim (dependent or independent) in excess of twenty and in excess of the number of claims in the patent being reexamined. Amounts differ for small vs other than small entities.
guidance: Fees must be paid with the request or when claims are later presented; if not paid, fees must be paid or the claims canceled prior to expiration of the time set in a Notice of Fee Deficiency (PTOL-475) to avoid abandonment. Examples illustrate fee application. Effective for amendments filed on or after Dec 8, 2004. If unpaid, notice PTOL-475 with one-month SSP issued; extension possible under 37 CFR 1.550(c). Failure to pay may result in termination under 37 CFR 1.550(e).

name: Conduct of reexamination proceedings and limit on enlarging claims
description: Reexamination will be conducted according to procedures for initial examination (sections 132 and 133). The patent owner may propose any amendment or new claim to distinguish the invention from cited prior art or to respond to adverse patentability decisions, but 'No proposed amended or new claim enlarging the scope of a claim of the patent will be permitted in a reexamination proceeding' (35 U.S.C. 305).
guidance: Proceedings (including appeals) are to be conducted with special dispatch. See 37 CFR 1.550 for conduct of ex parte reexamination proceedings; result is issuance of an ex parte reexamination certificate under § 1.570.

name: Handling of amendments submitted after final rejection
description: An amendment submitted after final rejection that fails to comply with requirements (e.g., lacks claim status or explanatory support) will not be entered.
guidance: Form paragraph use: after final rejection such amendments should not be entered and patent owner informed by advisory Office action (PTOL-467). Informal amendments submitted after final rejection are treated as not entered.

name: Clerical cross-references for related amendment handling
description: For clerical handling and special cases (merged proceedings; amendments where prior reexamination certificate or reissue exists; handling dependent claims), refer to specific MPEP sections (e.g., § 2270, § 2670, § 2283, § 2285, § 2295, § 2260.01).
guidance: When an amendment is made in a pending reexamination where a prior certificate/reissue exists, italicized text of certificate/reissue is treated as if originally present and bracketed text treated as never present; present amendments accordingly (see MPEP § 2295/§ 2285 guidance).

name: Value of a favorable international search report (ISR)
description: A favorable international search report (and any supplementary ISR) strengthens the applicant's position vis-à-vis national/regional Patent Offices and makes arguments for grant more convincing.
guidance: Use favorable ISRs strategically to support national phase prosecution; unfavorable reports may prompt claim amendment or abandonment to save costs.

name: Required elements of an international application
description: Any international application must contain: request, description, claim(s), one or more drawings (where necessary for understanding), and abstract.
guidance: Detailed information on each element is provided in following paragraphs; missing elements may lead to irregularities or loss of filing date.

name: Order of elements in application
description: Elements must be arranged in the following order: request, description, claim(s), abstract, drawing(s) (if any). Any sequence listing part of the description must be provided as a separate electronic file (XML).
guidance: Strict ordering is required; sequence listings have specific filing format requirements (XML).

name: Mandatory indications in the Request
description: The request must contain the title of the invention; identify the applicant, normally the inventor, and the agent (if any); the filing constitutes designation of all Contracting States; the request should also contain, where applicable, a priority claim, choice of competent ISA, and reference to any relevant earlier search; the request must be signed.
guidance: Detailed box-by-box instructions for filling the request form are provided later; ensure language of request complies with language rules (5.013).

name: Non-infringement (all-elements rule)
description: The accused product or process does not infringe because it does not meet every element of any asserted patent claim (the all-elements rule).
guidance: Strategies include identifying missing claim elements, arguing for a narrow claim construction, technically distinguishing the accused product from the claimed invention, and using prosecution history to limit claim scope.

name: Patent invalidity (patentability defenses)
description: Defenses based on failure to meet patentability requirements under U.S. law (e.g., §§101, 102, 103, 112 and improper inventorship).
guidance: Common theories: §101 subject-matter ineligibility (Alice/Mayo), §102 anticipation (single prior reference discloses all claim elements), §103 obviousness (combination of references), §112 written description/enablement/indefiniteness challenges, and challenges based on improper inventorship. Use prior art searches, claim construction, and expert evidence to support invalidity.

name: Prior use and public disclosure (including 35 U.S.C. §273 prior user rights)
description: Showing the accused technology was publicly disclosed or in use before the patent filing date can defeat infringement claims or provide a statutory prior-user defense.
guidance: 35 U.S.C. 273: provides a defense to infringement (not invalidity) for commercial internal use occurring at least 1 year before the patent filing; the right has limited scope and is generally not transferable except with the business. Documentation of dates and uses is critical.

name: Patent misuse
description: Patentee impermissibly extends the patent monopoly beyond its lawful scope (e.g., tying arrangements), which can render enforcement improper.
guidance: Claims of misuse require showing that the patentee’s licensing or enforcement practices violated patent-policy limits; remedies and standards vary by jurisdiction and facts.

name: Early case assessment
description: Initial evaluation of the merits and risks of a patent suit to guide strategy and resource allocation.
guidance: Key tasks: understand the scope of allegations, evaluate potential risks, preserve relevant evidence, and identify weak points in the plaintiff’s case. Early factual and technical investigations (e.g., claim charts, prior art scoping) are essential.

name: Prospective limitation of malpractice liability (37 C.F.R. § 11.108(h)(1))
description: A practitioner may not make an agreement prospectively limiting the practitioner's liability to a client for malpractice unless the client is independently represented in making the agreement.
guidance: Scrutinize contractual language that purports to waive or limit future malpractice claims; if such language exists, confirm whether the client had independent representation at the time and whether the limitation complies with §11.108(h)(1). Example: added clause 'will not ever be held accountable nor sued for damages' breached the rule where client lacked independent counsel.

name: Moral duties extend to animals
description: Animals are included under compassion's protecting aegis; beasts have moral claims and are not outside moral consideration.
guidance: Critiques the European/Cartesian view that beasts have no rights; points out linguistic and cultural artifices that dehumanize animals. Argues for extending moral sympathy and legal protection to animals, and cites cross-cultural evidence (Indian, Chinese, ancient Greek altars) that compassion for animals has historical support.

name: Failure To Particularly Point Out And Distinctly Claim (Indefinite)
description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which applicant regards as the invention.
guidance: Rejection must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.02 or 7.103.2 and followed by one or more applicable form paragraphs (7.34.02 - 7.34.11) or supply a full explanation of the deficiency. Whenever possible, identify particular terms/limitations rendering the claim indefinite and explain why. If one of ordinary skill can determine the scope, this rejection is not appropriate. See MPEP §§ 2171-2174.

name: ¶ 7.34.02 Terminology Used Inconsistent with Accepted Meaning
description: Where applicant defines a claim term contrary to its ordinary meaning, the written description must clearly redefine the term and set forth the uncommon definition so as to put one reasonably skilled in the art on notice.
guidance: Cite Process Control Corp. v. HydReclaim Corp. Provide the applicant's assigned meaning (bracket 3) and the accepted meaning (bracket 4). Support accepted meaning with appropriate references (e.g., textbook/dictionary). Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.34.01 and used only where specification does not clearly redefine the term.

name: ¶ 7.34.03 Relative Term - Term of Degree Rendering Claim Indefinite
description: A relative term of degree appearing in a claim that is not defined by the claim or the specification, and for which one of ordinary skill in the art would not be reasonably apprised of scope, renders the claim indefinite.
guidance: Explain which parameter/quantity/limitation in the claim is rendered indefinite (bracket 3). This paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.34.01.

name: ¶ 7.34.04 Broader Range/Limitation And Narrow Range/Limitation in Same Claim
description: A broad range or limitation together with a narrower range/limitation falling within the broad range in the same claim is considered indefinite because the metes and bounds are unclear.
guidance: Insert broader range/limitation (bracket 2) and the narrow range/limitation (bracket 3) and note whether the narrow language is exemplary or required. Cite Ex parte Wu and related decisions. Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.34.01.

name: ¶ 7.34.05 Lack of Antecedent Basis in the Claims
description: Claim recites a limitation without sufficient antecedent basis in the claim, rendering the scope indeterminate.
guidance: Insert limitation lacking antecedent basis (bracket 2) and identify location in the claim (bracket 3). Use only in aggravated situations where lack of antecedent basis makes claim scope indeterminate. Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.34.01.

name: ¶ 7.34.06 Use Claims
description: Claims that provide for the use of something but do not set forth any steps involved in the method/process are unclear and indefinite; a mere recitation of a use without active steps may not be a proper process claim under 35 U.S.C. 101.
guidance: Insert what is being used (bracket 2). See MPEP § 2173.05(q) and authorities (Ex parte Dunki, Clinical Products v. Brenner). Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.34.01.

name: ¶ 7.34.07 Claims Are a Literal Translation
description: Claims that are narrative, indefinite, and appear to be literal translations from a foreign document (with grammatical/idiomatic errors) fail to conform to current U.S. practice.
guidance: Use when claims are poorly written/translated. Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.34.01.

name: ¶ 7.34.08 Indefinite Claim Language: 'For Example'
description: The phrase 'for example' in a claim renders the claim indefinite because it is unclear whether the limitations following the phrase are part of the claimed invention.
guidance: Cite MPEP § 2173.05(d). Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.34.01.

name: ¶ 7.34.09 Indefinite Claim Language: 'Or The Like'
description: The phrase 'or the like' renders claims indefinite because it includes elements not actually disclosed, making scope unascertainable.
guidance: Cite MPEP § 2173.05(d). Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.34.01.

name: ¶ 7.34.10 Indefinite Claim Language: 'Such As'
description: The phrase 'such as' renders a claim indefinite because it is unclear whether the limitations following are part of the claimed invention.
guidance: Cite MPEP § 2173.05(d). Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.34.01.

name: ¶ 7.34.12 Essential Steps Omitted
description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as incomplete for omitting essential steps; omission amounts to a gap between steps.
guidance: Recite the omitted steps (bracket 2) and give rationale for considering the omitted steps critical or essential. Preceded by form paragraph 7.30.02 or 7.103.

name: ¶ 7.34.13 Essential Elements Omitted
description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as incomplete for omitting essential elements; omission amounts to a gap between elements.
guidance: Recite omitted elements (bracket 2) and provide rationale for considering them critical or essential. Preceded by form paragraph 7.30.02 or 7.103.

name: ¶ 7.34.14 Essential Cooperative Relationships Omitted
description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, for omitting essential structural cooperative relationships of elements, creating gaps in necessary structural connections.
guidance: Recite omitted structural cooperative relationships (bracket 2) and give rationale for their criticality. Preceded by form paragraph 7.30.02 or 7.103.

name: ¶ 7.34.15 Rejection Under 35 U.S.C. 112, Pro Se
description: For pro se applicants: claim(s) are narrative, replete with indefinite/functional/operational language; structure must be clearly and positively specified, organized to present a complete operative device, and claims must be in one-sentence form.
guidance: Use to explain deficiencies in pro se-filed claims; note format of cited patents as examples. Preceded by applicable form paragraphs.

name: ¶ 7.35 Rejection, 35 U.S.C. 112, 2nd Paragraph - Omnibus Claim
description: Claim rejected as indefinite because it fails to point out what is included or excluded by the claim language; the claim is an 'omnibus' type (e.g., 'A device substantially as shown and described').
guidance: Precede rejection with form paragraph 7.30.02. No further explanation necessary; see MPEP § 1302.04(b) for cancellation by examiner's amendment upon allowance.

name: ¶ 7.35.01 Trademark or Trade Name as a Limitation in the Claim
description: A claim containing a trademark/trade name as a limitation does not comply with 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, because trademarks identify source, not the goods, creating uncertain claim scope.
guidance: Insert trademark/trade name (bracket 2) and specify the material/product identified (bracket 3). Cite Ex parte Simpson (218 USPQ 1020). Preceded by applicable form paragraphs.

name: ¶ 706.03(o) New Matter — Examiner Alert
description: New matter (subject matter not disclosed in the original application) added after filing may be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 132; examples include adding unsupported subject matter, adding specific percentages/compounds after a broader disclosure, or omitting a method step.
guidance: See MPEP §§ 2163.06-2163.07(b), § 608.04(c), In re Wertheim. Examiner must detect new matter in amended cases and object under 35 U.S.C. 132; use form paragraph 7.28 to object to new matter added to the specification. If new matter added affects claims, also use 7.31.01 (112, first paragraph) for claims.

name: ¶ 7.28 Objection to New Matter Added to Specification
description: The amendment filed is objected to under 35 U.S.C. 132 because it introduces new matter into the disclosure; identify added material not supported by original disclosure.
guidance: Applicant required to cancel new matter in reply. Use form paragraph 14.22.01 in reissue applications. In bracket 2, identify new matter by page/line/drawing and provide explanation addressing any applicant statements that subject matter was described on filing; include unresolved questions raising doubt as to possession at time of filing. If new matter added to claims, reject under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph (7.31.01) rather than this paragraph.

name: ¶ 706.03(x) Reissue — Scope and Bar
description: 35 U.S.C. 251 forbids granting a reissue enlarging the scope of the claims of the original patent unless applied for within two years of grant; reissue claims broader than original may be rejected as barred.
guidance: Interpretation applies to any claim broader in any respect. Reissue applications by assignee that enlarge scope may be rejected, but courts have allowed corrective actions in some circumstances (In re Bennett). Defective reissue oath can be ground for rejecting all claims in reissue application. See MPEP Chapter 1400.

name: ¶ 706.04 Rejection of Previously Allowed Claims
description: A claim noted as allowable shall thereafter be rejected only after the proposed rejection is submitted to the primary examiner for consideration and approval; full faith should be given to prior examiner's actions absent clear error or new art.
guidance: Use Form Paragraph 7.50 to indicate withdraw of allowability and identify newly discovered references. Great care in authorizing rejection; do not adopt entirely new approach or new search merely hoping to find new grounds. See Ex parte Grier and Amgen v. Hoechst Marion Roussel guidance.

name: Specification requirements (35 U.S.C. 112 — written description/enablement framing)
description: The specification must contain a written description of the invention and the manner and process of making and using it, and enablement (as recast by amended subsection headings: e.g., ‘(a) IN GENERAL.—The specification…’).
guidance: Statutory text restructures section 112 into labeled subsections (a)–(f); language revisions emphasize inventor/joint inventor perspective in the enablement/written description phrasing and reorganize claim/claim-form rules (form; dependent references; multiple dependent claims; elements in combination).

name: Defense is not a general license — scope limited
description: The defense is not a general license under all claims of the patent; it extends only to the specific subject matter for which a qualifying commercial use has been established, but includes variations in quantity/volume and improvements that do not infringe additional specifically claimed subject matter.
guidance: Scope of protection is narrowly tailored to the particular subject matter and uses proven.

name: Scope of inter partes review (§311(b))
description: A petitioner may request cancellation of one or more claims only on a ground that could be raised under §§102 or 103 and only on the basis of prior art consisting of patents or printed publications.
guidance: IPR is limited to patentability challenges based on patents/printed publications under novelty/obviousness grounds.

name: Petition content requirements (§312(a))
description: A petition may be considered only if: (1) accompanied by payment of fee; (2) identifies all real parties in interest; (3) identifies in writing and with particularity each claim challenged, the grounds for challenge to each claim, and the evidence supporting the grounds, including (A) copies of patents/printed publications relied upon and (B) affidavits/declarations if relying on expert opinions; (4) provides other information as the Director may require; and (5) provides copies of required documents to the patent owner or designated representative.
guidance: Petitions must be detailed and documentary; service on patent owner required; Director may require additional information.

name: Institution threshold for IPR (§314(a))
description: The Director may not authorize IPR to be instituted unless the Director determines that the information in the petition and any response shows there is a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail with respect to at least one of the claims challenged.
guidance: Statute establishes a 'reasonable likelihood' threshold for institution (lower than ultimate proof standard).

name: Amendment of the patent during IPR (§316(d))
description: During an instituted IPR, the patent owner may file one motion to amend to (A) cancel any challenged patent claim, and/or (B) for each challenged claim propose a reasonable number of substitute claims. Additional motions may be permitted jointly to materially advance settlement or as permitted by regulation. An amendment may not enlarge the scope of claims or introduce new matter.
guidance: Patent owner is given a narrow, regulated opportunity to amend claims; amendments cannot broaden claim scope or add new matter; information submitted in support of amendments becomes public prosecution history.

name: Final written decision and certificate (§318)
description: If an IPR is instituted and not dismissed, the PTAB shall issue a final written decision on patentability of any challenged claim and any new claim added under §316(d). Where final decision issued and appeals exhausted/terminated, Director shall issue and publish a certificate canceling any claim finally determined unpatentable, confirming any claim determined patentable, and incorporating any new/amended claim determined patentable.
guidance: Final PTAB decisions are implemented by official certificates that alter patent claims and status.

name: Intervening rights for amended/new claims (§318(c))
description: Any amended or new claim determined to be patentable and incorporated into a patent following IPR shall have the same effect as specified in §252 for reissued patents regarding the rights of persons who made/purchased/used or imported the subject matter or prepared substantially therefor before issuance of the certificate.
guidance: Amendments can create intervening rights protecting earlier users from certain infringement claims.

name: Statutory categories requirement (35 U.S.C. 101)
description: First, the claimed invention must be to one of the four statutory categories. 35 U.S.C. 101 defines the four categories of invention: processes, machines, manufactures and compositions of matter.
guidance: The latter three categories define 'things' or 'products' (must exist in some physical or tangible form for those categories) while the first category defines 'actions' (a series of steps or acts). See MPEP § 2106.03 for detailed information. It is not necessary to identify a single category so long as the claim falls into at least one. Non-limiting examples of claims not directed to any statutory category include information/data per se, software/computer program per se when claimed as a product without structural recitations, and transitory signal transmissions. If the claim as a whole does not fall within any statutory category (Step 1: NO), a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 must be made.

name: Judicial exceptions and 'significantly more' requirement (Alice/Mayo framework)
description: Second, the claimed invention also must qualify as patent-eligible subject matter, i.e., the claim must not be directed to a judicial exception unless the claim as a whole includes additional limitations amounting to significantly more than the exception. The judicial exceptions are abstract ideas, laws of nature and natural phenomena (including products of nature).
guidance: Use the Alice/Mayo two-part test: (1) determine whether the claims are directed to a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon); (2) if so, determine whether additional elements individually or in combination amount to significantly more (the search for an 'inventive concept'). Integration of an exception into a practical application or an improvement in technology can render claims eligible. See MPEP §§ 2106.04 and 2106.05 for detailed guidance and controlling case law (Alice, Mayo, Diehr, etc.).

name: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) of the claim
description: Establish the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim as a whole prior to examining a claim for eligibility.
guidance: BRI sets the boundaries of coverage sought by the claim and influences whether the claim covers subject matter beyond the four statutory categories or encompasses exceptions. Claim construction affects whether a claim is to a statutory category and whether it is directed to a judicial exception. If the BRI encompasses non-statutory embodiments (e.g., carrier waves), the claim may fail Step 1. Examiners should point out the BRI and may recommend amendment to narrow the claim if appropriate. See MPEP § 2111 for more on determining BRI; cases such as Mentor Graphics, Synopsys, Enfish illustrate how interpretation affects eligibility.

name: Step 1 (Eligibility Step 1) — whether claim is to a statutory category
description: Evaluate whether the claim as a whole is to a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter under 35 U.S.C. 101.
guidance: For non-process categories verify the claim recites physical or tangible form. Examples and clarifying definitions: machine = concrete thing consisting of parts or devices; manufacture = tangible article given new form, quality, property or combination; composition of matter = combination of two or more substances. If the claim's BRI covers statutory and non-statutory embodiments, the claim fails Step 1. Best practice: recommend amendments to narrow claims to statutory embodiments where possible.

name: Step 2A (Eligibility Step 2A) — whether claim is directed to a judicial exception
description: Determine whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon (a judicial exception).
guidance: Consider abstract idea groupings (e.g., mathematical concepts, certain methods of organizing human activity, mental processes), 'tentative abstract ideas', laws of nature, natural phenomena, and product-of-nature issues. Use doctrinal analyses such as 'markedly different characteristics' and consider whether the claim integrates the exception into a practical application. See MPEP § 2106.04 and its subparts for examples and explanatory tests.

name: Step 2B (Eligibility Step 2B) — whether claim amounts to 'significantly more' (inventive concept)
description: If the claim is directed to a judicial exception, determine whether additional elements, individually or as an ordered combination, add significantly more than the exception (i.e., provide an inventive concept).
guidance: Consider whether the additional elements effect an improvement to the functioning of a computer or other technology; whether the claim is tied to a particular machine or transforms an article into a different state or thing (particular transformation); whether elements are well-understood, routine, conventional activity (which weigh against eligibility); whether other meaningful limitations exist; beware of mere instructions to apply an exception or insignificant extra-solution activity. See MPEP § 2106.05 and subparts (2106.05(a)-(h)) for detailed guidance, examples, and case law.

name: Three eligibility pathways (Pathway A/B/C) and when to apply streamlined analysis
description: Use three pathways to reach eligibility conclusions: Pathway A (self-evident eligibility/streamlined), Pathway B (claim not directed to a judicial exception), Pathway C (claim directed to a judicial exception but recites significantly more).
guidance: Pathway A: claims that fall within a statutory category and whose eligibility is self-evident may be found eligible using a streamlined analysis (see MPEP § 2106.06). Pathway B: claims to a statutory category that are not directed to a judicial exception are eligible without Step 2B. Pathway C: claims directed to an exception that recite additional limitations amounting to significantly more are eligible. If uncertain about applicability of a streamlined analysis, examiners are encouraged to conduct the full Alice/Mayo analysis. If not eligible under any pathway, reject under 35 U.S.C. 101.

name: Physical/tangible form requirement and examples of non-statutory product claims
description: For machine, manufacture, and composition of matter categories, eligible subject matter must exist in some physical or tangible form; claims to intangible collections of information or software 'detached from any medium' may not fall within statutory categories.
guidance: Examples of non-statutory product claims: data per se, computer program per se (software per se) claimed without structural recitations, transitory signal transmissions (propagating electrical or electromagnetic signals), and expressly excluded items such as humans per se. A product claimed only as code or instructions detached from a medium lacks physical embodiment and is not in a statutory category. See Digitech, Nuijten, Microsoft v. AT&T, In re Ferguson for case examples.

name: Claims whose BRI covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments — examiner practices
description: If the BRI of a claim covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments, the claim embraces non-statutory subject matter and fails Step 1.
guidance: When this occurs, it is best practice for the examiner to (1) point out the BRI, (2) recommend an amendment that would narrow the claim to statutory embodiments if possible, and (3) apply appropriate rejection (use form paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01 where Step 1: NO). Examples: machine-readable medium claims whose BRI includes carrier waves should be rejected. See Mentor Graphics v. EVE-USA, In re Nuijten for examples.

name: Machine-or-transformation and other tests as evidentiary clues (not separate tests)
description: The machine-or-transformation test is an important clue to eligibility but should not be used as a separate test; it should be considered as part of the integration/significantly more determination in the Alice/Mayo analysis.
guidance: Similarly, the pre-Alice 'useful, concrete, and tangible result' test and the 'special purpose computer' rationale are superseded or limited by more recent Supreme Court precedent. Examiners should treat such tests as evidentiary guidance when assessing whether a claim integrates an exception into a practical application or recites significantly more.

name: 101 is a threshold test — apply other statutes (102, 103, 112) as needed
description: 35 U.S.C. 101 is only a threshold inquiry; even if an invention qualifies under §101, it must still satisfy the other statutory requirements for patentability (35 U.S.C. 102, 103, and 112).
guidance: Examiners are reminded to make a complete examination under 102 (novelty), 103 (nonobviousness), and 112 (written description/enablement/definiteness), as well as utility and other requirements. Use these statutes as additional tools to ensure the claim meets conditions for patentability.

name: Streamlined analysis criteria (MPEP § 2106.06) — when eligibility is self-evident
description: Eligibility may be found via a streamlined analysis when it is self-evident that the claim is not directed to a judicial exception or clearly integrates an exception into a practical application.
guidance: Streamlined analysis is appropriate when the eligibility of the claim is self-evident or when the claim clearly improves technology or computer functionality. If eligibility is not self-evident, conduct full Alice/Mayo analysis. See MPEP § 2106.06(a)-(b) for details and examples.

name: Office action practice: identify selected counterpart
description: If a claim is rejected as ineligible, it is a 'best practice' for the examiner to identify the selected counterpart in the Office action if the record is not already clear.
guidance: This practice assists the applicant in responding and clarifies how the examiner is interpreting the claim.

name: Appropriate characteristics must be possessed by the claimed product
description: Characteristics chosen for the markedly different analysis must be possessed by the claimed product because the claim must define the invention to be patented.
guidance: Examiners identify such characteristics by looking at what is recited in the claim and what is encompassed within the broadest reasonable interpretation (e.g., a claim to 'deoxyribose' conveys structural characteristics; a claim to 'isolated gene B' requires reliance on BRI to determine sequence or encoded protein). Unclaimed characteristics cannot contribute to eligibility (Roslin).

name: Phenotypic characteristic examples
description: Phenotypic characteristics (functional and structural) may be considered in the analysis.
guidance: Examples include shape, size, color, and behavior of an organism (Roslin). Note that unclaimed phenotypic differences generally cannot make a claimed subject matter markedly different if they are not claimed.

name: Examples of products having markedly different characteristics
description: Court-identified examples where claimed nature-based products had markedly different characteristics and were eligible.
guidance: Chakrabarty: genetically modified bacterium that could degrade multiple hydrocarbons and contained additional plasmids (changed function and structure) — eligible. Myriad: cDNA that retained exons but had different nucleotide sequence (lacking introns) — eligible as distinct from naturally occurring DNA.

name: Step 2B — Search for an inventive concept (definition)
description: After determining a claim is directed to a judicial exception, the search for an 'inventive concept' asks whether additional claim elements amount to 'significantly more' than the judicial exception itself.
guidance: An inventive concept cannot be furnished by the unpatentable law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea itself; it is furnished by an element or combination recited in the claim in addition to the judicial exception (Alice; Mayo).

name: Consider additional elements individually and in combination
description: Evaluating whether additional elements provide an inventive concept requires considering those elements both individually and as an ordered combination to ensure the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more.
guidance: Consideration in combination is important because elements that are conventional individually may amount to significantly more when arranged non-conventionally (Rapid Litigation Mgmt. v. CellzDirect; BASCOM). The claim must be considered as a whole (Diamond v. Diehr).

name: Limitations that have qualified as 'significantly more' (non-exhaustive list)
description: Certain types of additional limitations have been found by courts to qualify as 'significantly more' when recited with a judicial exception.
guidance: Court-identified qualifying limitations include: (i) improvements to the functioning of a computer (DDR Holdings); (ii) improvements to any other technology or technical field (Diehr); (iii) applying the judicial exception with, or by use of, a particular machine arranged in a specific way (Eibel Process); (iv) effecting a transformation or reduction of an article to a different state or thing (Diehr); (v) adding a specific limitation beyond well-understood, routine, conventional activity or adding unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application (BASCOM); and (vi) other meaningful limitations beyond generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment (e.g., an immunization step integrating data comparison into a specific process) (Classen).

name: Drawings, specimens, and models where applicable
description: He shall accompany the whole with drawings and written references, where the nature of the case admits of drawings, or with specimens of the ingredients, and of the composition of matter, sufficient in quantity for the purpose of experiment... And such inventor shall, moreover, deliver a model of his machine, provided, the secretary shall deem such model to be necessary
guidance: Where practicable drafts and specimens must be provided; models are required at Secretary's discretion. Drawings and specimens support enablement and the court-admissibility of claims.

name: Requirement to distinguish improvement from prior art and confine patent to new parts
description: If it be for an improvement in an existing machine, he must, in his patent, distinguish the new from the old; and confine his patent to such parts only as are new; for if both are mixed up together, and a patent is taken out for the whole, it is void
guidance: Patent drafter must clearly identify and limit claims to the inventor's contribution; claiming the whole machine when only an improvement was invented risks invalidation for overclaiming.

name: Patent cannot be for an effect only; must claim manner/means
description: A patent can in no case be for an effect only, but for an effect produced in a certain manner, or by a peculiar operation
guidance: Claims directed purely to results without specifying how the result is produced are insufficient; invention must be defined by the method or structure producing the effect.

name: Scope of infringement for combination patents vs separate machines
description: A patent may be for a new combination of machines to produce certain effects... in such a case, the patent being for the combination only, it is no infringement of the patent to use any of the machines separately, if the whole combination be not used
guidance: Infringement of a combination patent requires use of the claimed combination as a whole; using only parts not covered by combination claim may not infringe. Conversely, if patent claims several distinct improvements in aggregate, using any one improvement may infringe depending on claim language and judicial interpretation.

name: Substantive statements required in oath/declaration (37 CFR 1.63(b))
description: In addition to paragraph (a) requirements, the oath/declaration must: (1) identify the application to which it is directed; (2) state that the person making the oath/declaration has reviewed and understands the contents of the application, including the claims, as amended by any amendment specifically referred to in the oath/declaration; and (3) state that the person acknowledges the duty to disclose to the Office all information known to be material to patentability as defined in 37 CFR 1.56.
guidance: The oath/declaration functions as an affirmation that the inventor has reviewed and understands the application and acknowledges disclosure duties; failure to include these statements can make the oath/declaration defective and trigger requirements for supplemental filings or notifications.

name: Addresses and foreign priority information in oath/declaration (37 CFR 1.63(c))
description: Unless such information is supplied on an ADS in accordance with 37 CFR 1.76, the oath/declaration must also identify: (1) the mailing address, and the residence if different, of each inventor; and (2) any foreign application for patent (or inventor's certificate) for which a claim for priority is made pursuant to 37 CFR 1.55, and any foreign application having a filing date before that of the application on which priority is claimed, by specifying the application number, country, day, month, and year of its filing.
guidance: If all foreign applications were filed within 12 months of the U.S. filing date, applicant is required only to recite the first such foreign application of which priority is claimed. If the information is omitted, form paragraphs (e.g., 6.05, 6.05.08) may be used to notify applicant that the oath/declaration is defective for omission of foreign application identification.

name: Preliminary amendments and new matter; supplemental oath/declaration requirement
description: If a preliminary amendment is present on the filing date and the oath/declaration does not refer to the preliminary amendment, applicant must ensure the preliminary amendment does not contain new matter; if it does, applicant must provide a supplemental oath/declaration under 37 CFR 1.67 referring to the preliminary amendment. Failure to submit such a supplemental oath/declaration removes safeguards implied in the oath/declaration requirements.
guidance: Applicants can avoid needing an oath referring to a preliminary amendment by incorporating amendments into the specification (including a new set of claims) when filing. Applicants are strongly encouraged to avoid submitting preliminary amendments to minimize Office burden and avoid delays. During examination, an examiner may require a supplemental oath/declaration, an amendment that cancels the unsupported subject matter, or a request for reconsideration.

name: Identification and treatment of new claims not originally claimed (supplemental oath requirement)
description: If a claim is presented for matter not originally claimed or embraced in the original statement of invention in the specification, a supplemental oath or declaration is required (37 CFR 1.67; see MPEP § 603).
guidance: When new claim matter is presented, applicant must submit supplemental oath/declaration referencing the new matter. For applications filed prior to certain rule changes, a surcharge may be required when supplemental oath references preliminary amendments (see MPEP discussion).

name: Statutory categories requirement (§ 101)
description: Whoever invents or discovers any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter ... may obtain a patent therefor (35 U.S.C. § 101). The claimed subject matter must fall into at least one of these four categories.
guidance: The four-category language is the explicit scope of patentable subject matter; if a claim covers material not found in any of the four categories it falls outside § 101 even if new and useful. Historical context and precedent inform the meaning of each category.

name: Process (statutory) requires acts or steps
description: A 'process' is a mode of treatment of certain materials to produce a given result; it is an act, or a series of acts, performed upon the subject-matter to be transformed and reduced to a different state or thing.
guidance: Cited authorities (Cochrane v. Deener, Gottschalk v. Benson, In re Kollar, NTP v. RIM) hold that a process must be carried out (i.e., recite acts/steps). Merely describing a product by reference to the process that made it (product-by-process) does not make the claim a 'process' for § 101 purposes.

name: Product-by-process claims remain product claims (do not convert to process)
description: A product-by-process claim defines a product at least in part by the method or process by which it is made; such claims are still directed to the ultimate product, not the underlying process.
guidance: Even if a claim recites an encoding process, that recitation does not transform a claim to the resulting signal into a process claim; the claim must be considered as to the product it covers.

name: Claim construction is a threshold legal question
description: Claim construction is a question of law reviewed de novo and must be resolved before or as part of the § 101 analysis; understanding claim scope can determine whether the claim fits a statutory category.
guidance: Interpret whether claim terms (e.g., 'signal') require a physical carrier and whether dependent claims add physical limitations. Courts construe claims to determine if some physical carrier is required or if the claim could cover abstract data.

name: State Street guidance — focus on essential characteristics and utility but still must fit a statutory category
description: Courts should look to the essential characteristics and practical utility of the subject matter rather than be preoccupied with pigeonholing among the four categories; nonetheless the subject matter must fall into at least one statutory category.
guidance: If it is clear a claim satisfies a statutory category, courts need not decide which one; however, where a claim may fall into none, the court must analyze each statutory category.

name: Printed matter doctrine / information-on-medium requires functional relationship
description: When the only difference between prior art and a claimed storage medium is the information stored thereon (printed matter), the stored information lacks patentable weight unless there is a new functional relationship between the printed matter and the substrate.
guidance: Claims to information encoded on a tangible medium may be patentable if the information imposes a physical organization or functional improvement (Lowry). Otherwise, the doctrine often operates under § 103 to reject such claims as obvious.

name: Abstract idea exclusion (algorithmic/mathematical principles)
description: Abstract mathematical algorithms or principles (e.g., conversion algorithms) that are so general as to cover known and unknown uses are not patentable subject matter (Gottschalk v. Benson; Parker v. Flook).
guidance: Even useful algorithms may be unpatentable if the claim effectively covers an abstract idea without being tied to a statutory category or a specific physical application; presence of a physical manifestation may affect analysis.

name: Standard of review for § 101 and claim construction
description: Whether a claim is valid under § 101 is a question of law reviewed de novo; claim construction is likewise a question of law reviewed de novo on appeal.
guidance: Appellate review treats these legal determinations without deference, so precise articulation and analysis of claim terms and statutory meaning is critical.

name: Apparatus claims vs. signal claims: apparatus that generates signals may be patentable
description: While transitory signals themselves may be unpatentable, apparatus (machines) that generate, receive, process, or store signals can be patentable as machines.
guidance: Claim drafting that recites physical structure (devices, encoders, storage media) rather than just the transient signal can place the subject matter within a statutory category.

name: Broad claim scope when claims specify only informational content
description: Claims that limit only the informational content (e.g., 'a signal encoded in accordance with a given encoding process') without tying the claim to a particular physical medium or structural features may be read to cover intangible strings of data or many forms of carriers.
guidance: Such breadth can create § 101 vulnerability; claim drafters should consider adding physical or structural limitations to avoid claims that purport to cover abstract or purely informational entities.

name: Utility (new and useful) remains a separate limitation relevant to § 101 analysis
description: The statutory requirement that an invention be 'new and useful' informs whether claimed subject matter is sufficiently concrete and direct in its benefit to qualify as patent-eligible (Brenner v. Manson; In re Fisher).
guidance: Claims whose only contribution is information content without a functional technological effect may fail utility or be treated via printed matter/obviousness doctrines; court distinguishes between useful technological applications and mere abstract information.

name: Clarity and distinctness of specification and claims
description: The validity of a patent materially depends upon the accuracy and distinctness with which the invention is stated in the specification; when a patentee states and sums up the particulars of his invention in his specification and his patent covers them, he is confined to such summary.
guidance: Courts cannot reject a claim that the patentee asserts as his own in the specification; but if something included in the patent is not new, the patent may be void. The patentee cannot afterwards broaden beyond what is summed up in the specification.

name: Novelty of claimed subject-matter
description: If any part which the patentee claims in his specification as his invention is not new (even if of slight value), and is included in the patent, the patent may be void.
guidance: A claim that covers matter already in public use or known is fatal. The inventor's honest mistake about being first does not save the claim. (Act of 1837 provides a limited mitigation—see separate entry.)

name: Lack of inventive concept (Alice step two)
description: Even if a claim is directed to an abstract idea, it is ineligible unless the claim recites an 'inventive concept' sufficient to transform the idea into a patent-eligible application.
guidance: Repeated holdings state claims lacked an inventive concept because they merely implemented the abstract idea on generic technology or used routine steps (e.g., 'with no inventive concept'; 'claims lacked an inventive concept because the recited amplification and detection steps were "well-understood, routine and conventional."').

name: Routine, conventional, well-understood techniques do not supply an inventive concept
description: Steps that employ known, routine, or well-understood techniques (even if combined with a new discovery) do not contribute an inventive concept for eligibility purposes.
guidance: Examples: amplification and detection steps characterized as routine; using "well-known ASR technology" for speech recognition; recited compression/encryption/storage steps that give functional results without technical detail. Courts frequently find no inventive concept where the claim merely instructs to apply conventional techniques to an abstract idea or natural law.

name: Mental processes/entirely in-the-mind steps are ineligible
description: Claim steps that can be performed entirely in the human mind or are essentially mental processes are treated as abstract and ineligible.
guidance: Holdings include claims characterized as 'mental process' steps (e.g., recognizing words and storing results in report fields; interpreting a written social-media statement) and other examples such as calculating scores, comparing sequences, or making determinations that are essentially mental acts.

name: Generic computer implementation does not make an idea patent-eligible
description: Applying an abstract idea to the Internet or a generic computer (e.g., 'applying these concepts to internet traffic') is insufficient to confer eligibility unless the claim recites a specific technological improvement.
guidance: Cases: claims using a 'persistent identifier' for targeted marketing, or 'applying these concepts to internet traffic' were held abstract; 'applying these concepts to internet traffic does not take the patent outside of the realm of an abstract idea.' Mere computer implementation or use of networked devices is insufficient.

name: Claims that improve computer technology or solve a technical problem may be eligible
description: Claims that are tied to a particular technological improvement or solve a problem rooted in computer technology can be found not directed to an abstract idea and thus may be eligible.
guidance: Examples where courts denied dismissal: a computer application upgrade that solved a problem in digital distribution by generating unique installation patches for release channels; transcription error recognition claims that 'recite[d] specific methods for navigating and editing dictation transcripts' and thus 'improve[d] the functionality of speech recognition devices.' Such claims include specific technical means, not merely abstract ideas implemented on a computer.

name: Specific limiting rules tied to a technical field can weigh toward eligibility
description: Claims that recite detailed, field-specific processing rules or feature extraction methods tied to digital image processing (or other technical domains) may be found to recite more than an abstract idea.
guidance: Example: photographic subject determination claims requiring 'extraction of both structural and semantic saliency features, and 'integrating' those features' were described as 'tied to digital image processing' and alleged to be 'unconventional' in the field—supporting a conclusion they might claim a technological improvement.

name: Automating human activities using generic computing often remains abstract
description: Claims that merely automate tasks previously performed by humans (e.g., replacing human labor with computer processing) are often characterized as directed to an abstract idea absent a specific technical innovation.
guidance: Example: claims described as 'using a computer, instead of human labor, to combine two types of data to form machine code' were held directed to an abstract idea with no inventive concept.

name: Specification must supply technical detail showing how results are achieved to support eligibility
description: Claims that state functional results without technical detail describing how to achieve those results are vulnerable to §101 invalidity for lacking an inventive concept.
guidance: Court holdings reference claims that 'obtain[ed] functional results' (e.g., 'determining a parameter, selecting a compression algorithm, applying that algorithm, and storing the resulting data') but provided 'no technical detail describing how to achieve those results' and were thus ineligible.

name: Insufficient factual development on unconventionality can preclude immediate dismissal
description: When the complaint or specification alleges that a claimed process was unconventional in its field, courts may deny motions to dismiss to allow factual development on whether the claims contain an inventive concept.
guidance: Examples: courts denied dismissal where plaintiffs alleged a novel approach or that the claimed module operated in an unconventional way (e.g., home social newsfeed generation, photographic feature integration), noting that 'factual development regarding just how unconventional or innovative this application was at the time might impact the Section 101 inquiry.'

name: Claim construction and expert evidence can affect the §101 analysis (but absence may not block early resolution)
description: While claim construction or expert testimony can be important, courts have held that a §101 decision can be appropriate early if the patent and pleadings show the claim is plainly directed to an abstract idea and lacks an inventive concept; conversely, lack of proposed constructions or expert support can permit dismissal.
guidance: Example: the Cleveland Clinic Foundation decision noted the appellant provided no proposed constructions or expert testimony that would change the eligibility analysis, supporting summary dismissal. Conversely, other decisions preserved claims where technical specificity or allegations might preclude early resolution.

name: Claims narrowly describing particular technical implementations may survive §101 at pleading stage
description: When claims recite concrete technical limitations describing how to achieve improved functionality, courts may decline to dismiss on eligibility grounds pending factual development.
guidance: Instances where courts denied motions: claims that contained 'specific limiting rules' or described a 'specific method of producing guidance information for capturing an image' that was 'not necessarily conventional or generic'—these claims proceeded for further development rather than being dismissed as abstract.

name: Limitations on grounds for validity challenges (102/103)
description: A petitioner who challenges claims on a ground raised under section 102 or 103 (as in effect on the day prior to enactment) may support such ground only on the basis of: (i) prior art described by section 102(a) (pre-enactment); or (ii) prior art that discloses the invention more than 1 year prior to the patent application date in the United States and would be described by 102(a) if the disclosure had been made by another before the inventor.
guidance: Challenges under 102/103 in a transitional proceeding are limited to specific categories of prior art (pre-enactment 102(a) style disclosures or certain >1 year U.S. disclosures); this constrains reliance on other forms of prior art or later statutory formulations.

name: Statutory definition of 'covered business-method patent'
description: For purposes of the transitional program, a 'covered business-method patent' means a patent that claims a method or corresponding apparatus for performing data processing operations utilized in the practice, administration, or management of a financial product or service, except that the term shall not include patents for technological inventions.
guidance: The definition focuses on data-processing claims tied to financial products/services and expressly excludes 'technological inventions'; regulators must provide criteria to distinguish technological inventions.

name: Auto-classification tool functionality and explainability
description: Auto-classification tool leveraging machine learning to classify patent documents using the Cooperative Patent Classification (CPC) system; can suggest CPC symbols, identify claimed subject matter for refinement, and includes indicators linking suggested CPC symbols to specific portions of the document.
guidance: Tool should suggest CPC codes, identify claimed subject matter, provide explainability by linking suggestions to text segments, integrate feedback with existing classification processes, and support expansion to broader classification requirements.

name: Contents required in a 35 U.S.C. 103 (obviousness) rejection
description: When making a 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection, the examiner should set forth: (A) the relevant teachings of the prior art relied upon (with specific citations where appropriate); (B) the differences between the claim and the applied reference(s); (C) the proposed modification(s) of the applied reference(s) necessary to arrive at the claimed subject matter; and (D) an explanation why one of ordinary skill in the art at the time would have been motivated to make the proposed modification.
guidance: To establish a prima facie case of obviousness, the examiner must show (1) some suggestion or motivation to modify or combine references (in the references or in common knowledge), (2) a reasonable expectation of success, and (3) that the references (alone or combined) teach or suggest all claim limitations. The teaching/suggestion and reasonable expectation must be found in the prior art and not based on applicant's disclosure. Cite In re Vaeck and see MPEP §§2141–2144.09 for examples and decision law.

name: Provisional rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/103 (copending applications)
description: A provisional rejection of obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/103 is appropriate where copending applications have different effective filing dates and a common assignee or a common inventor, because the earlier filed copending application, if patented, would constitute prior art under 102(e).
guidance: Provisional rejection alerts applicant that an actual rejection may follow if one application issues and gives applicant opportunity to respond. It may be overcome by: (A) arguing patentability; (B) combining subject matter into a single application claiming 35 U.S.C. 120 benefit and abandoning copending apps (subject to 112/120 support requirements); (C) filing a 37 CFR 1.132 showing derivation; (D) filing a 37 CFR 1.131 showing earlier invention date; or (E) filing a continuation after Nov. 29, 1999 that shows common ownership per amended 103(c). A terminal disclaimer cannot overcome certain provisional situations (see In re Bartfeld). Confidentiality under 35 U.S.C. 122 must otherwise be maintained.

name: Provisional double patenting and conflict between copending applications
description: If the claims of the copending application conflict with claims of the instant application, a provisional double patenting rejection should also be made (use paragraphs 8.30 and 8.32).
