guidance: Examples in the MPEP illustrate when provisional double patenting rejections and provisional 102(e)/103 rejections apply. If inventions are commonly owned and requirements are met, some rejections may be overcome (e.g., terminal disclaimers), subject to statutory/precedential limitations.

name: Examination of continuing application claiming 35 U.S.C. 120 benefit
description: An application claiming the benefit of a prior-filed copending national or international application under 35 U.S.C. 120 must name as an inventor at least one inventor named in the prior-filed application, and the prior filed application must disclose the named inventor's invention claimed in at least one claim of the later-filed application in the manner required by 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
guidance: So long as at least one inventor is in common and other requirements are met, the Office will permit a claim for 35 U.S.C. 120 benefit without additional submissions. The examiner must examine the earlier-filed application to determine common inventorship and 120 requirements when necessary (e.g., when intervening references appear).

name: 35 U.S.C. 103(c) — Disqualification of prior art for common ownership
description: Subject matter developed by another which qualifies as prior art only under one or more of subsections (e), (f), and (g) of section 102 shall not preclude patentability under 103 where the subject matter and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.
guidance: Effective Nov. 29, 1999 the amendment expanded disqualification to include prior art under 102(e) for applications filed on or after that date. 103(c) applies only to obviousness determinations under 103 and does not affect anticipatory prior art under 102. The burden to establish disqualification (i.e., common ownership) is on the applicant (or patentee) once the examiner establishes a prima facie case of obviousness. See MPEP §706.02(l) for procedural details.

name: Definition of 'common ownership' for 103(c)
description: 'Commonly owned' means wholly or entirely owned (100%) by the same person, persons, or organization at the time the claimed invention was made; less than 100% ownership of subject matter or the claimed invention means common ownership does not exist.
guidance: Common ownership requires actual ownership or a legal obligation to assign both the subject matter and the claimed invention at the time the claimed invention was made. A license where basic ownership rights are retained does not defeat common ownership. Moral or unenforceable obligations do not evidence common ownership. Determination is fact-specific; see examples in MPEP (parent/subsidiary scenarios, joint ventures, government inventor rights).

name: Naturally occurring DNA segments are unpatentable
description: “A naturally occurring DNA segment is a product of nature and, as such, cannot be patented.” (Supreme Court holding in Association for Molecular Pathology v Myriad Genetics.)
guidance: The Court ruled that isolated human genes that are naturally occurring are not patent-eligible. The decision prompted the USPTO to instruct examiners to reject product claims drawn solely to naturally occurring nucleic acids or fragments, whether isolated or not. The opinion was short and case-specific, and commentators warned it gives limited guidance for other biotech situations.

name: USPTO examiner guidance rejecting isolated genomic DNA product claims
description: Following Myriad, the USPTO issued a memo instructing examiners to reject product claims drawn solely to naturally occurring nucleic acids, or fragments of them, whether isolated or not.
guidance: Practitioners should expect immediate changes at the USPTO in examination practice: product claims to genomic DNA must be re-evaluated, and applicants should consider claim drafting strategies that rely on non-naturally occurring constructs or functional/technical limitations.

name: Jurisdictional differences allow isolated-gene patents in some countries
description: Australia, Canada and Japan allow the patenting of human genes provided they are isolated and the patent application explains how the genes are useful.
guidance: Because countries differ on whether isolated genes are patentable, patent-seeking entities must tailor IP strategies by jurisdiction—filing claims and drafting specifications to meet local standards for patent-eligibility and utility.

name: Uncertainty about scope of Myriad for other DNA constructs and biological molecules
description: There are many other types of DNA constructs that are patented, such as short nucleotide probes and primers and iRNA constructs; it is unclear whether or how Myriad will be applied to other areas of biotechnology, such as proteins and antibodies, or to other pharmaceutical products isolated from natural sources.
guidance: The decision drew a bright line between 'naturally occurring DNA' and 'cDNA' but left ambiguity for many synthetic or semi-synthetic constructs; practitioners should expect years of further case law and USPTO/Federal Circuit guidance, and draft claims cautiously to emphasize human-made aspects or technical applications.

name: Portfolio management: revisit, maintain, abandon or renegotiate patent assets
description: Companies that already hold patents over genes will need to revisit their portfolios and consider abandoning patents rather than pay fees to maintain hollow IP rights; businesses that have licensed-in patent rights may want to renegotiate royalty rates.
guidance: Post-Myriad, firms must audit their holdings, evaluate claim strength under new subject-matter standards, and make economic decisions about maintenance, enforcement, licensing terms, and potential divestment of weakened assets.

name: Pre-issuance communications as evidence of knowledge
description: Pre-issuance letters advising defendants of a pending patent application have been found relevant to willfulness inquiries because they can show that defendants had some knowledge of the eventual patent's scope.
guidance: Communications before patent issuance (e.g., warning letters about pending applications) can be used by patentees to establish knowledge and support enhanced damages claims.

name: Merits objections vs confidentiality/privilege objections
description: Objections going to the merits include challenges that a request is overly broad, unduly vague or ambiguous, burdensome and oppressive, seeks non-discoverable information on expert witnesses, or is not calculated to lead to admissible evidence. By contrast, claims of trade secret, business-sensitive/confidential information, attorney-client privilege, or attorney work product do not go to the merits but to characteristics of the responsive information.
guidance: Differentiate objections carefully: confidentiality/privilege objections are treated differently and generally are not considered waived even if other merits objections are forfeited.

name: Sanctions available for failure to provide disclosures or discovery
description: The Board may impose a variety of sanctions, pursuant to 37 CFR § 2.120(g) and Fed. R. Civ. P. 37(b)(2), including striking pleadings, refusing to allow support or opposition for claims/defenses, drawing adverse inferences, prohibiting introduction of designated matters in evidence, and entering judgment against the disobedient party; the Board will not hold contempt or award expenses including attorneys' fees.
guidance: Sanctions must be appropriate to the misconduct; consult TBMP § 527.01 for further information and the limitations on awards of fees and contempt.

name: Reasonable number of substitute claims
description: In reviewing a motion to amend, the patent owner must demonstrate the amendment proposes a reasonable number of substitute claims (35 U.S.C. §316(d); 37 C.F.R. §42.121).
guidance: This is one of the statutory/regulatory gatekeeping requirements (cited together with the other three requirements). The Board cites Lectrosonics (precedential) for guidance on motions to amend. No specific numeric ceiling is given on the page; reasonableness is evaluated in context.

name: Amendment responds to a ground of unpatentability involved in the trial
description: The amendment must respond to a ground of unpatentability involved in the trial (35 U.S.C. §316(d); 37 C.F.R. §42.121).
guidance: A proposed substitute claim must be tailored to address the adjudicated grounds. The Board evaluates whether the new claim scope bears on the grounds asserted in the IPR.

name: Amendment does not enlarge claim scope or introduce new subject matter
description: The amendment must not seek to enlarge the scope of the claims of the patent or introduce new subject matter (35 U.S.C. §316(d); 37 C.F.R. §42.121).
guidance: Board reviews both whether the amendment broadens the claims and whether it adds matter beyond the originally filed disclosure; this is a statutory/regulatory requirement cited in Lectrosonics.

name: Proposed claims supported in the original disclosure (no new matter / written description)
description: The proposed substitute claims must be supported in the original disclosure of the patent (35 U.S.C. §316(d); 37 C.F.R. §42.121).
guidance: This is the written-description/new-matter requirement. The Board examines whether the specification as filed provides adequate support for the claim language; lack of support can justify denial of a motion to amend.

name: Indefiniteness standard (Nautilus reasonable certainty)
description: Claims are indefinite if they fail to 'inform, with reasonable certainty, those skilled in the art about the scope of the invention' (Nautilus, Inc. v. Biosig Instruments, Inc.).
guidance: The Board applies Nautilus and related USPTO guidance (USPTO Memorandum on Indefiniteness Under 35 U.S.C. §112 in AIA Post-Grant Proceedings, MPEP 2173.05(e)). Example on this page: a comparative term like 'typical grocery store sugar' can render claims indefinite if it admits multiple reasonable meanings and no 'informed and confident choice' is available among them.

name: Comparative claim terms must be well-defined for comparisons
description: If a claim compares a property of the claimed invention to a comparator (e.g., 'more completely and consistently dissolved in comparison to the use of typical grocery store sugar'), the comparator must be sufficiently definite so a person of ordinary skill can make the required comparison.
guidance: The Board will find such comparative claim language indefinite if the comparator term is ambiguous in scope (multiple plausible definitions, brand-to-brand variance, no numerical standard) such that no 'informed and confident choice' exists. The decision analyzes particle-size distributions and shows that brand variance of EFG sugar made the comparator ambiguous.

name: Enablement under 35 U.S.C. §112(a)
description: Proposed substitute claims must be enabled by the patent disclosure; petitioners may challenge lack of enablement as a ground for unpatentability (35 U.S.C. §112(a) / enablement issues raised in the proceeding).
guidance: The Board considers evidence and expert testimony regarding whether the specification enables the full scope of the proposed claims. The decision discusses enablement in connection with challenges and reference teachings (e.g., arguments that Thijssen is non-enabling for the claimed context).

name: Obviousness analysis: teach/suggest, motivation to combine, and reasonable expectation of success
description: To show obviousness, the petitioner must demonstrate (1) the cited references teach or suggest the claim limitations, (2) a person of ordinary skill would have been motivated to combine the references, and (3) a person of ordinary skill would have had a reasonable expectation of success in doing so.
guidance: The Board applies the Graham framework (and weighs evidence accordingly). The decision applies this standard to combinations (e.g., Cooper combined with Thijssen and conventional practices) and explains why the Board found the necessary teaching/suggestion, motivation, and reasonable expectation of success for certain proposed claims.

name: Level of ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA)
description: The Board identifies and adopts a level of ordinary skill in the art for the proceeding, which frames how a person of ordinary skill would understand disclosures, claim terms, and combinations.
guidance: The decision maintains the level of skill set in the Institution Decision (experience/education in the food industry sufficient to understand sugar particle size and screening). Parties may dispute the identified level; the Board may ask parties to brief the issue. The PHOSITA definition informs indefiniteness, enablement, and obviousness analyses.

name: Objective indicia (secondary considerations) and nexus requirement
description: Objective indicia to be considered include long-felt but unmet need, commercial success, copying, praise, skepticism, and unexpected results. To use such evidence, the patentee must show a nexus between the evidence and the claimed features (nexus presumption applies in limited circumstances).
guidance: The Board evaluates objective indicia critically: commercial success requires a defined market and a showing that sales represent a substantial portion of that market; sales figures alone are insufficient without market context. A nexus presumption may apply when the evidence is tied to a specific product that is coextensive with the claims (Fox Factory), but without such linkage the patentee must demonstrate direct ties. Copying requires proof of access and similarity (internal documents, photos, disassembly) and praise should specifically relate to claimed features; mere assertions or incorporation-by-reference citations are insufficient.

name: Anticipation and effect of unchallenged institution findings
description: If petitioners present convincing evidence of anticipation at institution and the patent owner fails to respond or rebut in later briefing, the Board may maintain its institution findings that a reference anticipates original claims.
guidance: The decision adopts prior Institution Decision findings regarding Cooper's anticipation of original claims where Patent Owner did not submit a Preliminary Response; absence of contrary evidence or arguments can lead the Board to adopt earlier determinations.

name: Procedural/evidentiary rule for submissions and incorporation by reference
description: Parties must support assertions with specific discussion of exhibits; merely directing the Board to review exhibits without incorporation or argument can violate rules and be unpersuasive (37 C.F.R. §42.6(a) / incorporation by reference constraints).
guidance: The Board criticized Patent Owner for directing the Board to review exhibits on its own (violation of rules on incorporation by reference). For objective indicia like praise, the party must tie exhibits to claim features and discuss them in the brief; otherwise the exhibits carry little persuasive weight.

name: Nonobviousness of a genus can be supported by species data when trend allows extension
description: The nonobviousness of a broader claimed range may be supported by evidence based on unexpected results of a species or narrower range if one of ordinary skill would be able to determine a trend allowing reasonable extension of the probative value.
guidance: Limited exemplification can support a genus if data show a trend that reasonably predicts similar results across the genus (In re Kollman). Conversely, isolated or unrepresentative species data that do not permit reasonable extrapolation are insufficient (In re Lindner).

name: Affidavit/declaration must compare claimed subject matter with closest prior art
description: An affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 must compare the claimed subject matter with the closest prior art to be effective to rebut a prima facie case of obviousness.
guidance: Comparisons should determine number and importance of claim limitations in common with references (In re Burckel; In re Merchant). Deviations from reference disclosures should be explained (In re Finley) or noted and evaluated (In re Armstrong).

name: Nexus required between claimed invention and evidence of commercial success
description: An applicant asserting commercial success to support nonobviousness bears the burden of proof of establishing a nexus between the claimed invention and the evidence of commercial success.
guidance: The PTO relies on applicants to provide hard evidence of commercial success and nexus because the examiner lacks means to gather such evidence (In re Huang; In re GPAC; In re Paulsen). Nexus denotes a factually and legally sufficient connection (Demaco).

name: Commercial success must be derived from the claimed invention (not advertising or extraneous factors)
description: Commercial success alleged must be directly derived from the invention claimed, and not the result of heavy promotion, advertising, purchaser ties, or other business events extraneous to the merits of the invention.
guidance: Conclusions that increased sales are due to the invention require evidentiary support; inventor opinions are insufficient (In re Mageli; In re Huang). Licensing or advertising may inflate apparent success for reasons unrelated to unobviousness (Pentec; EWP Corp. v. Reliance). Examiners must scrutinize causation.

name: In design cases, nexus between commercial success and design is especially difficult
description: Establishing a nexus between commercial success and the claimed design is especially difficult; evidence must clearly attribute success to the design rather than brand recognition, improved performance, or other factors.
guidance: Design patents require clear attribution of sales/market acceptance to the design itself (Litton Systems v. Whirlpool). Examiners should require tight causal linkage.

name: Discovery and application of a natural law or force may be patentable as applied
description: The discovery and application of a new force or law of nature, as a means of producing an effect or result in matter never before produced, may in some cases be the subject of a patentable invention.
guidance: Clarifies limitation: a law of nature cannot be appropriated in the abstract, but if an inventor produces a practical effect by applying the law, he may appropriate that application (i.e., claim the application insofar as others practicing it would be piracy).

name: Appropriation/scope test — piracy of the original invention
description: The truth, law, property, or quality of matter, which, by reason of its application, enters into the essence of an invention, may be appropriated, to the extent of every application which, according to the principles of law and the rules of logic, is to be deemed piracy of the original invention.
guidance: This is the test for how far an inventor's appropriation reaches: any later application that effectively copies or 'pirates' the original invention's application of a law/property is within the inventor's claim. Examples throughout (hot-air blast, steam application) show application to varied apparatus still may be piracy if same effect by same agent.

name: Permitted breadth of general claims applying known properties or laws
description: Inventions which consist in the application of the known qualities of substances extend the appropriation of the inventor to those qualities in the same manner and in the same sense.
guidance: Examples: Walton's use of india-rubber to give elasticity to card backs — patent held to cover giving elasticity and flexibility by india-rubber however applied; evaporating sugar by forcing air through liquid — any apparatus applying the same law to same purpose may practise the same invention. But caution: appropriation is confined to the inventor's application, not the abstract law.

name: Distinction between form-only inventions and principle-based inventions
description: When the patent is a patent for form, or particular arrangement, or for the apparatus devised to accomplish a particular effect, changes in these respects will be changes in the subject-matter of the invention; but in cases where the invention has a characteristic or an aggregate of characteristics, independent of particular form ... changes in these things amount only to the substitution of one equivalent for another.
guidance: Rule for claim drafting and claim construction: determine whether the invention is the particular form/arrangement (narrow claim) or the underlying characteristic/principle (permits broader claim covering equivalents). Use this to assess infringement and claim breadth.

name: Selling element (iv): Practitioner was not publicly disciplined
description: Reciprocal discipline may be defeated if the practitioner can argue that he or she was not publicly censured, publicly reprimanded, placed on probation, disbarred, suspended or disciplinarily disqualified by the state.
guidance: This is a procedural/technical ground: if the practitioner shows the state did not actually impose public discipline of the sort claimed, reciprocal discipline should not be imposed. The practitioner still bears the clear-and-convincing evidentiary burden to prove this.

name: State licensure confers disciplinary jurisdiction regardless of location of misconduct
description: A lawyer admitted to practice in a jurisdiction is subject to that jurisdiction's disciplinary authority regardless of where the lawyer's conduct occurs (citing Middlesex, ABA Model Rule 8.5, New Jersey Rule 8.5).
guidance: Licensure in the state provides authority to discipline for conduct occurring elsewhere; ignorance of the scope of disciplinary jurisdiction is not an excuse. The Office rejects claims that misconduct occurring in another state deprives the licensing state of jurisdiction.

name: Timeliness of Protest (When Should the Protest Be Submitted)
description: Except where accompanied by the written consent of the applicant, a protest must be submitted prior to the date the application was published under 37 CFR 1.211 or the mailing of a notice of allowance under 37 CFR 1.311, whichever occurs first.
guidance: Protests should be filed as soon as possible after learning of the application to maximize consideration. A protest submitted after mailing of a notice of allowance may still be considered if it clearly anticipates or renders claims obvious, but likelihood of consideration decreases as allowance approaches. Special rules apply for reissue applications (see reissue-related criterion).

name: Petitions decided by the Deputy Commissioner who oversees the Office of Petitions (MPEP §1002.02(b))
description: A long list of specific petition types are assigned to the Deputy Commissioner (Office of Petitions/Patent Legal Administration/MPEP staff) for decision.
guidance: Enumerated items include (but are not limited to): petitions to revive abandoned applications based on unintentional delay (37 CFR 1.137); petitions under §1.183 for waiver/suspension of rules; petitions invoking supervisory authority under §1.181; petitions for unintentionally delayed foreign or domestic priority/benefit claims (§1.55(e), §1.78); petitions to defer issuance (1.314); express abandonment after issue fee (1.313(c)(3)); petitions relating to patent term adjustment and restoration; petitions relating to filing date and conversions between provisional/nonprovisional; petitions to change entity status (1.28/1.29); petitions to issue corrected patents (1.322(b)); petitions to expunge/expunge assignment info (1.59/1.182) and many others (items 1–50 listed in the MPEP). See MPEP §1002.02(b) for the full enumerated list.

name: Definition of 'practice before the Office' in patent matters
description: Practice before the Office in patent matters includes, but is not limited to, preparing and prosecuting any patent application; consulting with or giving advice to a client in contemplation of filing a patent application or other document with the Office; drafting the specification or claims of a patent application; drafting an amendment or reply to a communication from the Office that may require written argument to establish the patentability of a claimed invention; drafting a reply to a communication from the Office regarding a patent application.
guidance: Cites 37 C.F.R. § 11.5(b)(1). The Court found drafting patent applications, drafting responses to Office Actions, and advising clients on patentability are acts that constitute practice before the Office. Mere transcription of a client's words may not constitute practice, but rephrasing or adding legal analysis does.

name: Unauthorized practice of law before the USPTO
description: Only practitioners registered under § 11.6 are permitted to prosecute patent applications of others before the Office or represent others in any proceedings before the Office; representing or providing the types of services defined as practice before the Office when not authorized constitutes unauthorized practice.
guidance: Cites 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.6, 11.10, 11.5, and case law (e.g., In re Amalgamated Dev. Co., In re Herren). Advising inventors on patentability, preparing patent applications (including specifications and claims), and preparing and filing amendments are examples of practicing law. Distinction: pure typing/transcription may be permissible; adding legal rephrasing/opinion is not.

name: Failure to respond to lawful demand for information (RFIs)
description: A practitioner, in connection with a disciplinary matter, shall not knowingly fail to respond to a lawful demand or request for information unless disclosure is protected (e.g., privileged). 'Knowingly' means actual knowledge.
guidance: Cites 37 C.F.R. § 11.801(b) and § 11.1. Courts note limits to attorney-client privilege (identity of client generally not protected). A general, unsupported claim of privilege (without a privilege log) is insufficient.

name: Evidentiary standard — clear and convincing evidence
description: The OED Director must establish violations of the USPTO disciplinary rules by clear and convincing evidence in these proceedings.
guidance: The decision repeatedly applies the 'clear and convincing' standard when evaluating claims (e.g., dishonesty, criminal acts, misrepresentation). Where evidence is lacking or only shows negligence, the rule may not be found violated.

name: 102(e) for 111(a) applications claiming priority to prior U.S. provisional or nonprovisional
description: For 111(a) applications that claim priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) to a prior U.S. provisional or claim the benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 of a prior nonprovisional, the prior art dates under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) are the earlier effective U.S. filing dates, assuming the earlier-filed application has proper support for the subject matter as required by 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or 120.
guidance: Assess proper written support (see 35 U.S.C. 112 first paragraph) in the earlier-filed application when relying on its date. Examples illustrate dates.

name: All references of an IA filed on/after Nov 29, 2000 and published in English get IA filing date as 102(e) date
description: All references, whether the WIPO publication, the U.S. patent application publication or the U.S. patent, of an international application filed on or after November 29, 2000, designated the U.S., and published in English under PCT Article 21(2) have the 35 U.S.C. 102(e) prior art date of the international filing date or earlier effective U.S. filing date.
guidance: If the IA properly claims priority to an earlier-filed U.S. provisional or nonprovisional, the 102(e) date becomes that earlier U.S. filing date, provided the earlier-filed application has proper support for the relied-upon subject matter.

name: Provisional 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection over copending U.S. patent application
description: If an earlier filed, copending, and unpublished U.S. patent application discloses subject matter which would anticipate the claims in a later-filed pending U.S. application with a different inventive entity, the examiner should determine whether a provisional 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection of the later-filed application can be made.
guidance: A provisional 102(e) rejection may also be made if the earlier filed pending application has been published as redacted (37 CFR 1.217) and the subject matter relied upon is not supported in the redacted publication of the patent application. Use form paragraph 7.15.01 when making such a provisional rejection.

name: How to overcome a provisional 102(e) rejection
description: A provisional rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) can be overcome in the same manner that a 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection can be overcome.
guidance: It may also be overcome by abandoning the applications and filing a new application containing the subject matter of both, or by showing under 37 CFR 1.132 that any invention disclosed but not claimed in the copending application was derived from the inventor of this application, or by an appropriate showing under 37 CFR 1.131. The rejection may not be overcome by filing a terminal disclaimer (In re Bartfeld).

name: Form paragraph 7.15.01 required language for provisional rejection (common assignee or inventor)
description: Form paragraph 7.15.01 should be used to provisionally reject claims under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as being anticipated by a copending application having a common assignee or at least one common inventor.
guidance: The paragraph explains basis: earlier effective U.S. filing date of copending application would constitute prior art if published/patented, identifies possible rebuttals (derivation under 37 CFR 1.132, 1.131), and notes that terminal disclaimers do not overcome the rejection. Examiner notes specify use and related form paragraphs (e.g., 7.12 vs 7.12.01) to determine applicable 102(e) date.

name: Consideration of priority/benefit claims when determining 102(e) date
description: In determining the 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date, consider priority/benefit claims to earlier-filed U.S. provisional applications under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), U.S. nonprovisional applications under 35 U.S.C. 120 or 121, and international applications under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121 or 365(c) if the subject matter used to make the rejection is appropriately supported in the relied-upon earlier-filed application's disclosure (and any intermediate application(s)).
guidance: Do NOT consider foreign priority claims under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) and 365(a) for establishing 102(e) dates. Ensure proper support in the chain of priority/benefit claims per statutory requirements (112/119/120).

name: Permissible scope of amendments in a reissue
description: The patentee may redescribe his invention in an amended specification and is not rigidly confined to prior wording; he may include whatever was suggested or substantially indicated in the original, provided it was properly embraced in the invention as actually made and perfected.
guidance: Differences in description and claims are not dispositive so long as identity of the subject-matter is preserved; the description may be varied and claims restricted or enlarged within that range. The drawings and model may show what was 'substantially indicated.'

name: Use of expert testimony when technical terms are present
description: Where the specification and claim (original or reissued) employ technical terms or terms of art, the court may hear testimony of scientific witnesses to aid in ascertaining the true meaning of the language employed.
guidance: Testimony of scientific witnesses may be indispensable in some cases; both parties have a right to examine such witnesses and it is error to reject essential expert testimony. Cases: Bischoff v. Wethered; Betts v. Menzies.

name: Commissioner may correct errors of his own earlier examination
description: If an error or mistake in allowance/restriction was made by the commissioner himself (e.g., suggesting a narrowed claim), the commissioner has authority to grant a reissue correcting that error under special circumstances.
guidance: Example: when the commissioner wrongly suggested a restricted claim and later it is discovered no legal objection existed, surrender and reissue restoring the original claim were allowed (Davidson syringe example; Morey v. Lockwood).

name: Statutory listing requirement (21 U.S.C. § 355(b)(1)(A)(viii))
description: An NDA holder must submit “the patent number and expiration date of each patent for which a claim of patent infringement could reasonably be asserted if a person not licensed by the owner engaged in the manufacture, use, or sale of the drug,” and the listed patent must (I) “claim the drug for which the applicant submitted the application and is a drug substance (active ingredient) patent or a drug product (formulation or composition) patent” or (II) claim a method of using such drug.
guidance: OBTA (2021) amended the provision and added explicit language that certain other patent information “shall not be submitted,” thereby setting both a floor and a ceiling for listable patents; Congress intended the amended language to codify FDA regulations (21 C.F.R. § 314.53(b)(1)). Treat the statutory text as imposing two distinct requirements: (a) a patent be one for which a claim of infringement could reasonably be asserted, and (b) it must additionally be a patent that actually ‘claims the drug’ (as further defined elsewhere).

name: Meaning of 'claims' (35 U.S.C. § 112(b) / patent law)
description: A patent 'claims' subject matter by the claim language that 'particularly point[s] out and distinctly claim[s] the subject matter which the inventor ... regards as the invention' (35 U.S.C. § 112(b)); claims and the specification read together define the invention.
guidance: For listing purposes, 'claims' should be interpreted according to patent-law claim construction principles: the court must look to what the patent particularly points out and distinctly claims, not simply whether a product would infringe the claim. Do not conflate the statutory word 'claims' with the separate concept of infringement.

name: OBTA's 'drug-substance/drug-product' limitation
description: The OBTA added that a patent that 'claims the drug for which the applicant submitted the application' must be 'a drug substance (active ingredient) patent or a drug product (formulation or composition) patent.'
guidance: This legislative change narrows listable patents to typical drug-substance or drug-product patents (or method-of-use patents). Patents that fall outside those categories are not to be submitted per the OBTA language ('shall not be submitted'). The court noted this language but did not have to reach every consequence of it in the decision.

name: Delisting counterclaim scope (§ 355(j)(5)(C)(ii)(I))
description: If the patent owner sues after receiving a paragraph IV notice, the applicant may assert a counterclaim seeking an order requiring the holder to 'correct or delete' the patent information submitted on the ground that the patent does not claim (aa) the drug for which the application was approved or (bb) an approved method of using the drug.
guidance: The counterclaim is a limited but potent remedy because a successful delisting can convert a paragraph IV to a paragraph I (or otherwise eliminate the 30‑month stay). A generic applicant cannot bring a delisting action outside this counterclaim context.

name: Combination-product treatment does not convert device subparts into 'the drug'
description: Approval of a combination product via an NDA (because the product's primary mode of action is that of a drug) does not make every component of the combination product a 'drug.' Device components retain their identity as device parts.
guidance: For listing, the patent must claim the part that made the product approvable as a drug (i.e., the active ingredient/ drug-substance). Use the SMDA framework: determine primary mode of action and treat constituent parts according to their identities; inclusion in an NDA does not transform device patents into drug patents for listing purposes.

name: Claim construction applies to listing inquiry (but formal Markman not always required)
description: When determining what a patent 'claims' for listing/delisting, courts apply patent claim construction principles (Markman).
guidance: A full Markman hearing is not required in every case; courts may adopt reasonable claim constructions on the pleadings for purposes of deciding a delisting question, citing precedent (e.g., Jazz Pharms., Aatrix). Still, the statutory requirement that claims 'particularly point out and distinctly claim' remains controlling.

name: Claims must particularly point out the specific approved active ingredient (not generic/overbroad 'active drug')
description: A claim that merely requires the presence of 'an active drug' (i.e., any active ingredient) is too broad to 'particularly point out and distinctly claim' the specific drug approved in an NDA (which identifies a specific active ingredient and often concentration).
guidance: For listing, courts expect claims to identify the specific active ingredient (and, where relevant, the formulation parameters that were the basis for approval). Broad, unspecified active‑ingredient language does not satisfy the statutory requirement to 'claim the drug for which the applicant submitted the application.'

name: Drug v. device functional/structural distinction (what makes something a 'drug')
description: A drug is distinguished from a device in that a drug 'furnishes pharmacological activity' and achieves its primary intended purpose through chemical action or metabolization; devices are characterized more by their purely mechanical nature.
guidance: Use the chemical-action/metabolization touchstone (Bacto‑Unidisk; Genus Med.; Ipsen) to decide whether a claimed invention is a drug-substance/product or a device; only patents to the drug-substance/product side will generally be listable as 'claiming the drug.'

name: First-inventor-to-file priority (priority determined by filing date)
description: Transition from first-to-invent to a first-inventor-to-file system in which the filing date determines priority rather than an earlier date of conception.
guidance: Under first to file, once the inventor files information with the Patent Office, he has a priority date that is both secure and public. The filing date is what will determine priority, not a purported date of conception, making it much harder for thieves to claim earlier invention dates. This harmonizes U.S. practice with the rest of the world and provides greater certainty for innovators.

name: Complete application contents (nonprovisional) (§ 1.51(b))
description: A complete application filed under § 1.53(b) or § 1.53(d) comprises: (1) a specification as prescribed by 35 U.S.C. 112 including a claim or claims (see §§ 1.71–1.77); (2) the inventor's oath or declaration (see §§ 1.63 and 1.64); (3) drawings, when necessary (see §§ 1.81–1.85); and (4) the prescribed filing fee, search fee, examination fee, and application size fee (see § 1.16).
guidance: Applicants are encouraged to file an information disclosure statement in nonprovisional applications (§§ 1.97 and 1.98); no IDS may be filed in a provisional application.

name: Application language requirement (§ 1.52(b)(1)-(2))
description: The application and any amendments or corrections must comply with paper/format requirements and be in the English language or be accompanied by a translation into English and a statement that the translation is accurate.
guidance: The specification (including abstract and claims) and amendments must have lines 1.5 or double spaced, use a nonscript font (e.g., Arial, Times Roman, Courier, preferably font size 12), capital letters should be at least 0.3175 cm (0.125 in) high but may be no smaller than 0.21 cm (0.08 in) (e.g., font size 6), and the text should be a single column.

name: Claims and abstract placement and page numbering (§ 1.52(b)(3)-(5))
description: The claim(s) must commence on a separate physical sheet or electronic page. The abstract must commence on a separate physical sheet or electronic page or be submitted as the first page of the patent in certain proceedings. Pages of the specification (including claims and abstract) must be numbered consecutively starting with 1, centrally located above or preferably below the text.
guidance: These rules have exceptions for reissue and reexamination/supplemental examination proceedings.

name: Paragraph numbering in specification (§ 1.52(b)(6))
description: Paragraphs of the specification (other than claims or abstract) may be numbered at filing and should be individually and consecutively numbered using Arabic numerals, at least four numerals enclosed in square brackets (e.g., [0001]) including leading zeros.
guidance: Paragraph numbers and enclosing brackets should appear to the right of the left margin as the first item in each paragraph before the first word, and should be highlighted in bold. (Text references a required gap equivalent to ... ; formatting guidance truncated in chunk.)

name: FTO field limitation (claims focus)
description: Field: claims characterize and limit the scope.
guidance: Advice: choose the 'Claims' field when doing FTO searches because claims define the enforceable scope that can block practice in a jurisdiction.

name: Patentability: no date/geographic/field limits
description: Limitation: No date limit: any prior art can block you. No geographic limit: any prior art can block you. No Field limitation: any prior art disclosed in the description is sufficient to destroy novelty.
guidance: Advice: for patentability searches choose 'Alive or Dead' and search 'All publications'; use 'Full Text' (search description/objects, not only claims) because disclosure anywhere in the document can anticipate novelty.

name: Field limitation summary for FTO vs patentability
description: No field limitation: Full Text (patentability). Field limitation: Claims (FTO).
guidance: Use Claims field when limiting to enforceable scope (FTO). Use Full Text when doing novelty searches where any disclosure suffices to destroy novelty.

name: Filter and view document features
description: Filter: allows to filter the result of a search (three options by default, possibility to add). View document: allows clicking on the title to view a particular family and focus on claims of a member.
guidance: Use filters to narrow results and 'View document' to inspect family member claims; filters and views improve triage efficiency.

name: Rule 22 – Determination of value-based fee for the infringement action
description: Method for the Court to determine the value-based portion of fees for infringement claims and required payments/adjustments.
guidance: Value-based fee initially paid on claimant's assessment; if judge-rapporteur determines higher value, remaining fees due within 10 days; Court reimburses overpaid fees if value is lower.

name: Rule 371 – Time periods for paying court fees
description: When fixed and other fees must be paid, proof of payment requirements, and special rules for urgent cases and value-based fees.
guidance: Fixed fees are paid on lodging; proof of payment provided with pleading. In urgency, representative must pay within period set by Court and filing may be deemed effective if paid within that period. Value-based fee paid per claimant's assessment; if judge-rapporteur determines higher value remaining fees due within 10 days; overpayments reimbursed. If Application for legal aid is lodged, ordinary timing rules may not apply.

name: Priority applies only to subject matter actually disclosed
description: Priority is limited to the subject matter actually disclosed in the provisional; claims in a later non‑provisional are only entitled to the provisional date to the extent their claim elements are supported by that disclosure.
guidance: When drafting provisional content, be explicit in disclosing every feature you might later claim; failure to disclose a claim element means losing priority for that element (and potential exposure to intervening prior art).

name: Treat provisional disclosure like a non‑provisional specification
description: Draft the provisional as if it were a non‑provisional spec: every claim element you might ever want should appear in some form in the provisional.
guidance: Include figures, alternative embodiments, numerical ranges, and the rationale for novelty. The article emphasizes 'the cost of writing a fat provisional is small compared to the cost of losing priority.'

name: Include figures, alternative embodiments, and numerical ranges
description: A strong provisional should include drawings, alternative embodiments, numerical ranges, and explanatory framing (e.g., 'why this is novel').
guidance: Concrete disclosures (figures and multiple embodiments) increase the likelihood that later claim elements will be supported; avoid sparse narrative-only filings.

name: The Disclosure Trap: avoid filing 'thin' provisionals
description: Many provisionals are filed too thin (e.g., a short 4‑page narrative), which creates risk that later non‑provisional claims won't be supported and priority will be lost.
guidance: Antipattern example: founder files a brief narrative provisional and later spends thousands on a non‑provisional with claims; examiner cites a reference and the new claims lack support in the provisional. Counter this by richer initial disclosure.

name: Multiple provisionals allowed and useful
description: You can file additional provisional applications during the 12‑month window and later consolidate them into a single non‑provisional that claims priority to all of them.
guidance: If your invention evolves, file updated provisionals at milestones. Multiple provisionals are relatively cheap and can be used to capture development over the year; the non‑provisional can claim priority to each provisional that supports its subject matter.

name: Prima facie case when claimed and prior art products are structurally or compositionally identical
description: Where the claimed and prior art products are identical or substantially identical in structure or composition, or are produced by identical or substantially identical processes, a prima facie case of either anticipation or obviousness has been established.
guidance: Cites In re Best, In re Spada: When the PTO shows a sound basis for believing the products are the same, the applicant has the burden to show they are not. The prima facie case can be rebutted by evidence showing the prior art products do not necessarily possess the characteristics of the claimed product. Example cases: Titanium Metals Corp. v. Banner (composition within claimed ranges can anticipate even if properties not disclosed).

name: Inherency presumption for claimed properties/functions when structures are substantially identical
description: When the structure recited in the reference is substantially identical to that of the claims, claimed properties or functions are presumed to be inherent.
guidance: If the prior-art structure would necessarily perform the claimed function, inherency can establish anticipation. Applicant must show the prior art would not perform the method or have the property (e.g., in re Schreiber, failure to specify dimensions undermined applicant's declaration). See MPEP § 2113 for product-by-process burden of proof.

name: Composition claims — identical composition implies same properties
description: If the prior art teaches the identical chemical structure, the properties applicant discloses and/or claims are necessarily present; 'Products of identical chemical composition can not have mutually exclusive properties.'
guidance: Cites In re Spada: virtual identity of monomers and procedures sufficed for a prima facie case of unpatentability despite claimed differences in tackiness vs hardness. Applicant needs evidence to show different properties despite identical composition.

name: Printed matter — nonfunctional printed matter does not distinguish products
description: Where the only difference between a prior art product and a claimed product is printed matter that is not functionally related to the product, the printed matter will not distinguish the claimed product from the prior art.
guidance: Critical question: does any new and unobvious functional relationship exist between the printed matter and the substrate? Cites In re Ngai, In re Gulack. Example: differing instruction content does not avoid anticipation if the instructions are not functionally related.

name: Process-of-use claims — new uses of old structures can be patentable only in narrow circumstances
description: Discovery of a new use for an old structure based on unknown properties might be patentable as a process of using; however, if the claim is directed to a result or property of the old composition/structure, the claim is anticipated.
guidance: Cites In re Hack, In re May, In re Tomlinson: Finding a new property of an old composition (e.g., nonaddictive property) does not necessarily constitute a patentable new use if the references disclosed the composition for related results. Claims reciting new compounds or unexpected properties may be patentable with evidence of unexpected results.

name: Product-by-process claims — patentability determined by the product, not the recited process
description: Product-by-process claims are limited by and defined by the process but determination of patentability is based on the product itself; if the product is the same as or obvious from a prior-art product, the claim is unpatentable even if made by a different process.
guidance: Cites In re Thorpe, Amgen v. Roche: courts approve use of 35 U.S.C. 102/103 rejections for product-by-process claims. In infringement analysis, however, a product-by-process claim is infringed only by a product made by the recited process. Office should consider structure implied by process steps when relevant (In re Garnero).

name: Apparatus claims must be structurally distinguishable from the prior art
description: Claims directed to an apparatus must be distinguished from the prior art in terms of structure rather than function; apparatus claims cover what a device is, not what it does.
guidance: Cites In re Schreiber, Hewlett-Packard v. Bausch & Lomb. Functional recitations alone do not satisfy structural distinctions; examiners should look for structural limitations.

name: Manner of operating the device does not differentiate an apparatus claim if structural elements are taught by the prior art
description: A recitation regarding the manner in which a claimed apparatus is intended to be employed does not differentiate the claimed apparatus from a prior-art apparatus if the prior art teaches all the structural limitations of the claim.
guidance: Cites Ex parte Masham: use/intent recitations (e.g., 'for mixing flowing developer material') are immaterial if the structural elements are present in the prior art; amount of submersion or intended use often immaterial to structure.

name: A prior-art device that performs all claimed functions still may not anticipate if there is any structural difference
description: Even if the prior art device performs all the functions recited in the claim, a structural difference can prevent anticipation; means-plus-function limitations are met only by corresponding structures in the specification or equivalents.
guidance: Cites In re Ruskin, In re Donaldson, In re Robertson: courts may construe claims to require specific separate elements (e.g., three fastening elements) and find no anticipation if prior art lacks that structure. Consider means-plus-function claim construction rules (see MPEP §§2181–2186).

name: Computer-implemented functional claim limitations — broad coverage and obviousness considerations
description: Functional claim language not limited to a specific structure covers all devices capable of performing the recited function; the term 'computer' is broad and not limited absent specific definition; broadly claiming automation of a manual function often does not distinguish over the prior art.
guidance: Cites In re Paulsen, Leapfrog v. Fisher-Price, KSR, Muniauction: a 'computer' can include calculators if specification supports broad interpretation; implementing known functions on a general-purpose computer can be obvious if predictable; adapting existing devices with commonplace electronics or Internet/browser technologies can be obvious. See MPEP §§2143, 2144.04 for obviousness rationales.

name: Material or article worked upon does not limit apparatus claims
description: Expressions relating the apparatus to contents thereof during intended operation and inclusion of material or article worked upon by the claimed structure do not, without more, impart patentability to apparatus claims.
guidance: Cites Ex parte Thibault, In re Young, In re Casey: the manner a machine is used or the article it forms is not germane to patentability of the machine itself. This line of cases applies to machinery claims, not product or kit claims.

name: Materials manipulated in a process must be considered in process patentability
description: The materials on which a process is carried out must be accorded weight in determining the patentability of a process.
guidance: Cites Ex parte Leonard: All claim limitations, including materials, must be considered when weighing differences between claimed invention and prior art for obviousness (see MPEP §2143.03).

name: Novel or nonobvious starting material or end product can affect process obviousness — no per se rules
description: A process yielding a novel and nonobvious product may nonetheless be obvious; conversely, a process yielding a well-known product may be nonobvious. Obviousness requires a fact-specific analysis of the claimed subject matter as a whole.
guidance: Cites In re Ochiai, In re Brouwer, TorPharm v. Ranbaxy and illustrative cases: treat product limitations as material limitations in process claims; consider all claim limitations; no automatic per se rules — analyze case-by-case (examples given where processes were found obvious or patentable depending on context and presence/absence of novel catalysts or microorganisms).

name: Prior art is presumed operable/enabling when it expressly anticipates or makes obvious all elements
description: When a reference relied on expressly anticipates or makes obvious all elements of the claimed invention, the reference is presumed to be operable; burden on applicant to rebut presumption.
guidance: Cites In re Sasse and MPEP §716.07: examiners may presume operability of prior-art references that teach all claim elements; applicant must provide facts to rebut (e.g., showing inoperability).

name: Efficacy is not required for prior art enablement
description: A prior art reference provides an enabling disclosure and thus anticipates a claimed invention if it describes the claimed invention in sufficient detail to enable one of ordinary skill to carry it out; proof of efficacy is not required.
guidance: Cites Impax Labs. v. Aventis Pharm.: enabling disclosure is about ability to make/use without undue experimentation, not proof that the invention works as claimed. See MPEP §2122.

name: 35 U.S.C. 102 rejections may be supported by secondary evidence showing reference is operable
description: A 35 U.S.C. 102 rejection can be made even if the primary reference does not itself teach how to practice the invention; secondary evidence (other patents or publications) can be cited to show public possession/enabling disclosure.
guidance: Cites In re Donohue and MPEP §2131.01: examiners may combine references or cite secondary references to establish that the primary reference was enabling for the claimed subject matter.

name: Compounds and compositions — enabling prior art requires one skilled in the art to be able to make/synthesize
description: For compounds and compositions, an enabling prior art disclosure requires that one of ordinary skill in the art be able to make or synthesize the claimed compound/composition without undue experimentation.
guidance: This section begins the discussion on what constitutes enabling prior art for compounds and compositions (see following MPEP text and cited cases for application). Evidence of methods or corroborating patents/publications may be necessary to show enablement.

name: Preserve privilege—no waiver by production (FRE 502(d))
description: Pursuant to Federal Rule of Evidence 502(d), disclosure (including production) of information that a party later claims should not have been disclosed because of a privilege shall not constitute a waiver of any claim of attorney-client privilege, work product, or other ground for withholding production.
guidance: Model protects against broad waiver across proceedings when producing under the Order.

name: Redaction of privileged or legally protected matter
description: Any Producing Party may redact matter it claims is subject to privilege, work product, legal prohibition, or other immunity; redacted pages shall be marked “REDACTED” and the basis specified; an unredacted version shall be preserved.
guidance: Model suggests inserting specifics for redaction of privileged matter from native electronic files; protected data redaction rules follow (see next entries).

name: FWD outcomes by invalidity challenge type
description: Success at FWD varies by statute: §§101, 102, and §112 (written description/enablement) had relatively high rates (53–73%) of invalidating all challenged claims, while §112 indefiniteness (23%) and §103 (44%) were less likely to invalidate all claims in the sample.
guidance: Because petitions often assert multiple grounds, claims can be sustained under one ground but invalidated under another; small sample sizes for many categories warrant caution in interpretation.

name: Comparison of PTAB (PGR) vs district court on §112 challenges
description: Claims challenged under §112 have higher survival at the PTAB (PGR) than in district court: e.g., indefiniteness survival 89% at PTAB vs 40% in district court; written description 82% vs 63%; enablement 84% vs 71% (based on included data).
guidance: This is notable because the PTAB uses a lower burden of proof (preponderance) vs district court (clear and convincing), suggesting procedural/venue differences and case-selection effects influence outcomes; sample sizes and case selection should be considered.

name: Burden of proof difference between PTAB and district court
description: PTAB invalidity findings use the preponderance of the evidence standard while district court uses clear and convincing evidence for patent invalidity.
guidance: Despite the lower PTAB standard, PGR §112 challenges showed higher claim survival at PTAB than district court in the dataset; practitioners must weigh this counter-intuitive empirical result when choosing venue.

name: Distinction: assignment of contract vs assignment of claim (section 3477)
description: There is a manifest distinction between assignment of a Government contract (prohibited by §3737) and an assignment of a claim for money due under the contract (not prohibited if properly made under §3477).
guidance: However, an assignment of claims that is in substance a transfer of the contract (e.g., assignment of all claims with power to collect plus recital that it is 'further continuing collateral security' and a mortgage on property) will be treated as an assignment of the contract within §3737 and invalid. An assignment need not be formal or express; courts look to facts and circumstances indicating intent. §3477 is broad and embraces all claims against the Government; assignments not made as prescribed are declared 'absolutely null and void' as against the Government, but payments actually made to an assignee under an informal/unrevoked power of attorney will be valid as between the parties and accounting officers must allow disbursing officers credit.

name: Textual consistency across versions
description: Compare different published versions (Nilus, Lutostansky, Butmi, Retcliffe-Goedsche) for additions, deletions, and changes in wording and claims—e.g., Nilus adding '929 years before the birth of Christ', transformation of 'the sages' into 'the government of the Jews', and Butmi's change from future-terror to past-assassination phrasing.
guidance: Examine parallel passages, note chronological changes (pre- and post-revolution edits), and treat abrupt insertions or politically convenient alterations as strong evidence of fabrication or later tampering. Use side-by-side comparisons and document how changes serve political aims.

name: Dissemination networks and financial/propaganda incentives
description: Analyze how the texts spread (countries, periodicals, emigrant agents) and the motives of those spreading them (commercial gain, political activism, loss of prior patronage as with Black Hundreds émigrés seeking income).
guidance: Map publication dates, languages, and outlets; look for repeated republication by the same networks or for anonymous embellishers. Financial or opportunistic motives for spread weaken claims of authenticity.

name: Primary-source corroboration and documentary evidence
description: Seek independent primary documents (letters, official records, photographed facsimiles) that corroborate claims—e.g., the reproduced letter from Grand Duke Michael to Lutostansky shown in the book.
guidance: Authenticate such supporting documents separately (provenance, archival records, paper/ink dating where possible). Even supportive primary items must be evaluated for context and possible forgery or misattribution.

name: Internal contradictions and implausible chronological claims
description: Spot internal logical contradictions or historically implausible assertions (such as a political plan devised '929 years before the birth of Christ') and use them as indicators of fabrication.
guidance: Cross-check historical claims with established scholarship and timelines; mark manifest anachronisms or numerically specific but unsupported claims as warning signs.

name: Foreign registration considered equivalent to patenting for 35 U.S.C. 102(d)
description: Registration of a design abroad is considered equivalent to patenting under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) and 35 U.S.C. 102(d), whether or not the foreign grant is published.
guidance: If the foreign applicant has received protection in the foreign country, a claim for priority will vest if the U.S. application is timely filed. To avoid statutory bars under 35 U.S.C. 102(d)/172, the U.S. design patent application must be filed within six (6) months of the foreign filing. The MPEP includes a table listing country-specific dates which can be used for 102(d) purposes (e.g., date of registration/grant, filing date, publication date) and notes that foreign laws vary.

name: 35 U.S.C. 102(a) rejection (form paragraph ¶ 15.11)
description: The claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(a) as being clearly anticipated by [1] because the invention was known or used by others in this country, or patented or described in a printed publication in this or a foreign country before the invention thereof by the applicant for patent.
guidance: Use bracket [1] to identify the reference applied against the claimed design. Include applicable Examiner Notes where present.

name: 35 U.S.C. 102(b) rejection (form paragraph ¶ 15.12)
description: The claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(b) as being clearly anticipated by [1] because the invention was patented or described in a printed publication in this or a foreign country, or in public use or on sale in this country more than one (1) year prior to the application for patent in the United States.
guidance: Insert the reference in bracket [1] and explain basis (publication date, public use, or on sale) supporting the one-year statutory bar.

name: 35 U.S.C. 102(c) rejection (form paragraph ¶ 15.13)
description: The claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(c) because the invention has been abandoned.
guidance: Use when abandonment is the basis for rejection; include supporting facts.

name: 35 U.S.C. 102(d)/172 rejection (form paragraph ¶ 15.14)
description: The claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(d), as modified by 35 U.S.C. 172, as being clearly anticipated by [1] because the invention was first patented or caused to be patented, or was the subject of an inventor’s certificate by the applicant, or his/her legal representatives or assigns in a foreign country prior to the date of the application for patent in this country on an application for patent or inventor’s certificate filed more than six (6) months before the filing of the application in the United States.
guidance: Insert the foreign reference in bracket [1]. Ensure the timing and issuance facts meet the >6 month and prior-grant requirements before making this rejection.

name: 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection (form paragraph ¶ 15.15)
description: The claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as being clearly anticipated by [1] because the invention was described in a patented or published application for patent by another filed in the United States before the invention thereof by the applicant for patent.
guidance: Insert reference in bracket [1]. For determining the 102(e) effective date, follow American Inventor's Protection Act rules and the Examiner Notes for form paragraphs 7.12/7.12.01 when appropriate (consider international application dates and continuations).

name: 35 U.S.C. 102(f) rejection (form paragraph ¶ 15.16)
description: The claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(f) because applicant did not himself invent the subject matter sought to be patented.
guidance: Use when derivation or inventorship issues indicate the applicant is not the original inventor; include supporting facts and references to required statements.

name: 35 U.S.C. 102(g) rejection (form paragraph ¶ 15.17)
description: The claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(g) because, before the applicant's invention thereof, the invention was made in this country by another who had not abandoned, suppressed or concealed it.
guidance: Use when another party in the U.S. made the invention earlier and did not abandon/suppress/conceal. Include necessary facts to support the priority finding.

name: Identical claim: common assignee (¶ 15.24.05)
description: The claim is directed to the same invention as that of the claim of commonly assigned copending application No. [1]. The issue of priority under 35 U.S.C. 102(g) and possibly 35 U.S.C. 102(f) of this single invention must be resolved.
guidance: Since the USPTO normally will not institute an interference between commonly owned applications or a patent and an application, the assignee is required to state which entity is the prior inventor of the conflicting subject matter. A terminal disclaimer has no effect in this situation. Failure to comply will result in abandonment of this application.

name: Explanation of rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(a),(b),(d),(e) (¶ 15.15.01)
description: The shape and appearance of [1] is identical in all material respects to that of the claimed design.
guidance: This paragraph should be included after the applicable 102 rejection to explain the basis of the rejection; insert the claimed design reference in bracket [1] and identify the claimed design. Explain how material identity in shape and appearance supports anticipation.

name: Provisional 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection — design disclosed but not claimed in another application with common inventor/assignee (¶ 15.15.02)
description: The claim is provisionally rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as being anticipated by copending Application No. [1] which has a common [2] with the instant application. This is a provisional rejection based upon a presumption of future publication or patenting of the copending application.
guidance: Suggested ways to overcome: (A) show derivation under 37 CFR 1.132; (B) show a date of invention prior to the reference under 37 CFR 1.131; (C) perfect priority under 35 U.S.C. 119 by filing certified priority documents meeting 35 U.S.C. 112 first paragraph requirements; or (D) perfect priority under 35 U.S.C. 120 by amending spec or filing ADS under 37 CFR 1.76/1.78(a) and establishing enablement/description per 35 U.S.C.112. This rejection may not be overcome by filing a terminal disclaimer (In re Bartfeld). Include bracket insertions for application and inventor/assignee as noted.

name: 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection — design disclosed but not claimed in a patent (¶ 15.15.04)
description: The claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as being anticipated by patent [1]. Based upon the different inventive entity and the earlier effective U.S. filing date of the reference, it constitutes prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(e).
guidance: Suggested ways to overcome are similar to provisional copending-application rejections: derivation showing, proof of earlier invention, perfecting priority under 119 or 120 with certified documents, and meeting 35 U.S.C. 112 requirements. This rejection may not be overcome by a terminal disclaimer (In re Bartfeld). Use brackets to insert patent number(s).

name: Nonobviousness requirement for designs (35 U.S.C. 103(a))
description: A claimed design that meets the test of novelty must additionally be evaluated for nonobviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103(a).
guidance: Apply the Graham v. John Deere factual inquiries (scope/content of prior art; differences between claimed and prior art; level of ordinary skill; objective evidence/secondary considerations). Consider design-specific precedents and the overall appearance test for design patent obviousness.

name: Graham factual inquiries applied to design patents
description: The basic factual inquiries guiding evaluation of obviousness are: (A) determining the scope and content of the prior art; (B) ascertaining the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art; and (C) resolving the level of ordinary skill in the art; (D) evaluating objective evidence of nonobviousness (secondary considerations).
guidance: Use these inquiries as the framework for assessing prima facie obviousness of design claims, supplemented by design-specific case law.

name: Differences between prior art and claimed design — overall appearance test
description: In determining patentability under 35 U.S.C. 103(a), it is the overall appearance of the design that must be considered. The mere fact that there are differences between a design and the prior art is not alone sufficient to justify patentability.
guidance: All differences between the claimed design and the closest prior art reference should be identified in any rejection under 103(a). If differences are de minimis or inconsequential from a design viewpoint, the rejection should state so. Case citations: In re Leslie, In re Lamb.

name: Form paragraphs for 35 U.S.C. 103(a) rejections and rationale
description: Use provided form paragraphs to state 103(a) rejections and prefatory/rationale language (¶ 15.18, ¶ 15.70, ¶ 15.67, ¶ 15.19).
guidance: ¶ 15.18: single-reference 103(a) rejection wording; ¶ 15.19: multiple-reference 103(a) rejection wording ('The claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over [1] in view of [2]'). ¶ 15.70 preface: 'It would have been obvious to a designer of ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made to [1].' ¶ 15.67 provides rationale about unobviousness in overall appearance (not minute details). Insert explanations and supporting facts into the brackets as directed.

name: Concepts relating to certain business practices
description: Claims directed to business practices such as generating menus, generating a second menu from a first and sending it to another location, taking orders from restaurant customers, structuring a sales force or marketing company, using advertising as an exchange/currency, or algorithms for business optimization.
guidance: Courts have described such claims as directed to abstract ideas — e.g., adding conventional computer components to well-known business practices does not make them patent-eligible. Representative cases: Enfish-era examples including claims described as “generating menus … or taking orders from restaurant customers,” In re Ferguson (structuring a sales force), Ultramercial v. Hulu (advertising as currency), In re Maucorps (algorithm for visit scheduling). The guidance emphasizes that merely implementing business practices on generic computers or adding conventional components is not enough.

name: Concepts relating to managing human behavior
description: Claims that address methods of managing or influencing human behavior, such as storing user-selected spending limits and notifying users (budgeting/tracking financial transactions), filtering content, or mental processes a specialist should follow.
guidance: Courts have treated such concepts as abstract ideas because they are methods of organizing human activity (e.g., Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One Bank—tracking transactions to determine preset spending limits; BASCOM—filtering content as an abstract idea though eligibility turned on step 2B analysis). Examples include rules for user behavior monitoring and mental processes (In re Meyer). The guidance notes similarity to other methods of organizing human activity found abstract.

name: Concepts relating to tracking or organizing information
description: Claims directed to filtering, classifying, collecting, analyzing, encoding/decoding, organizing, receiving/screening/distributing, or otherwise structuring information (including tailoring content based on user data or navigation data).
guidance: Courts have repeatedly characterized such information-management concepts as abstract ideas (e.g., BASCOM—filtering content; Intellectual Ventures v. Capital One—customizing web pages; TLI Communications—classifying and storing digital images; Electric Power Group—collecting/analyzing/displaying results; RecogniCorp—encoding/decoding images; Digitech—organizing through mathematical correlations; Intellectual Ventures v. Symantec—email screening/distribution). The guidance highlights that information is intangible and that collecting/analysing/presenting information without more is within the realm of abstract ideas.

name: Concepts relating to data comparisons performable mentally or analogous to human mental work
description: Claims that involve obtaining, collecting, comparing, or mapping intangible data and determining validity or differences—steps that a human could perform mentally or with pen and paper (e.g., verifying credit-card validity by comparing transaction data; comparing genetic sequences to identify alterations; anonymous loan shopping comparisons).
guidance: If the claimed data-comparison steps can be performed in the human mind or with routine pen-and-paper techniques, courts have found them to be abstract mental processes (e.g., CyberSource—map of transactions to verify validity; University of Utah v. Ambry Genetics—comparing BRCA sequences; Mortgage Grader—anonymous loan shopping). The guidance notes that claims not requiring network or computer implementation may read on purely mental performance and thus be ineligible.

name: Concepts relating to organizing or analyzing information performable mentally or analogous to human mental work
description: Claims that recite converting, translating, recognizing, analyzing, or otherwise organizing information in ways that read on mental processes (e.g., translating functional descriptions to hardware descriptions, data recognition and storage, detecting misuse by collecting/analyzing access logs).
guidance: Courts have found such claims abstract where the steps could be performed mentally or are equivalent to longstanding human practices (Synopsys v. Mentor Graphics—translating circuit descriptions; Content Extraction—data collection/recognition/storage; FairWarning—collecting/analyzing access logs and notifying). The guidance stresses that merely invoking computer-based tools in the specification is insufficient if the claims themselves do not require computer implementation or otherwise add meaningful technological improvements (distinguishing from claims that improve computer functionality).

name: Concepts described as ideas having no particular concrete or tangible form
description: Claims reciting conceptual frameworks or building-block ideas without a particular concrete application or tangible form (e.g., using advertising as currency, determining prices via organizational/product hierarchies, assigning hair designs to balance head shape).
guidance: Courts have characterized such high-level conceptual frameworks as abstract ideas because they lack concrete/tangible application and are basic conceptual building blocks for organizing information (Ultramercial—advertising as currency; Versata—determining price with hierarchies; In re Brown—hair-cutting allocation). The guidance shows that abstractness can arise even when practical steps are recited if the claim is essentially a non-concrete conceptual scheme.

name: Mathematical relationships/formulas (judicial exception)
description: Mathematical concepts including algorithms, mathematical relationships, formulas, and calculations are treated as judicial exceptions (abstract ideas or akin to laws of nature).
guidance: The guidance explains that courts have long regarded mathematical formulas and algorithms as non-statutory exceptions (e.g., Benson, Flook, Diehr). Mathematical procedures are treated as abstract ideas; whether a claim that uses a formula is patent-eligible depends on whether additional claim elements amount to significantly more than the abstract mathematical concept (see Alice/Mayo framework). Examples include converting binary-coded decimals, formulae for alarm limits, and mathematical hedging formulas.

name: Concepts relating to a mathematical relationship or formula
description: Claims that recite or are rooted in a specific mathematical formula or relationship (e.g., Arrhenius equation for cure time in Diehr).
guidance: Courts have treated specific mathematical formulas as judicial exceptions (Diehr noted an Arrhenius equation as an exception like a law of nature). The guidance reiterates that asserting a mathematical relationship alone is not sufficient for patent eligibility; the presence of a formula calls for careful step-two analysis to determine whether the claim adds an inventive concept beyond the mathematical relationship.

name: Concepts relating to performing mathematical calculations
description: Claims that involve calculating, manipulating numeric values, generating derived values, or organizing information through mathematical correlations (e.g., life-insurance policy value calculations, data manipulation using mathematical formulas).
guidance: Courts have found claims directed to mere mathematical computation or manipulation to be abstract (Bancorp—policy value calculations as mere computation; Digitech—manipulating existing information with formulas to create new forms). Representative examples include algorithms for visit-optimization, algorithms for detecting abnormal conditions by calculation, and other calculation-based processes. The guidance emphasizes that mathematical calculation alone does not render a claim patent-eligible absent additional limitations that provide a specific, practical application or technological improvement.
