name: Enablement requirement — make and use without undue experimentation
description: A conclusion of lack of enablement means that, based on the evidence regarding each of the enablement factors, the specification, at the time the application was filed, would not have taught one skilled in the art how to make and/or use the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
guidance: Determination is reached by weighing all factual considerations (Wands factors). The examiner must consider relevant evidence as a whole and base any nonenablement conclusion on that evidence. Citations: In re Wright; In re Wands.

name: How to make the claimed invention — one method may suffice if correlated
description: If the specification discloses at least one method for making and using the claimed invention that bears a reasonable correlation to the entire scope of the claim, the enablement requirement is satisfied; failure to disclose other methods does not render the claim invalid.
guidance: For unstable/transitory intermediates, the applicant need not teach how to make a stable or isolatable form. The availability of starting materials or apparatus is a key issue—if a required apparatus or chemical is not readily available, sufficient disclosure of it is required. Cases: In re Fisher; In re Breslow; In re Ghiron; In re Howarth.

name: How to use the claimed invention — known modes and dosage
description: If a statement of utility connotes how to use and the art recognizes standard modes of administration, 35 U.S.C. 112 is satisfied. Dosage or method of use need not be specified if one skilled in the art could obtain such information without undue experimentation.
guidance: When a claim is limited by a particular use, enablement is evaluated based on that limitation. If multiple uses are disclosed and at least one is enabled, the specification may be enabling for the claimed invention. Cases: In re Johnson; In re Hitchings; In re Brana; In re Vaeck.

name: Working examples — presence, prophetic examples, and weight
description: Compliance with enablement does not turn on whether an example is disclosed. Examples may be working (based on performed work) or prophetic (based on predicted results). The specification need not contain an example if the disclosure otherwise enables without undue experimentation.
guidance: Lack of a working example is a factor to be considered, especially in unpredictable arts, but should never be the sole reason for rejecting a claim. A single working example can preclude a rejection stating nothing is enabled, though the presence of only one working example can be a factor in assessing whether the claimed scope is broader than enabled. Cases: Gould v. Quigg; Re Borkowski; Re Brana.

name: Correlation between in vitro/in vivo models and claimed uses
description: An in vitro or in vivo animal model example constitutes a working example only if it 'correlates' with a disclosed or claimed method of use; lack of correlation means the example does not constitute a working example.
guidance: Whether a model correlates depends on the state of the prior art; if a model is recognized to correlate, it should be accepted unless the examiner has evidence it does not. Examiner bears initial burden to give reasons for lack of correlation and must weigh evidence for and against correlation. Rigorous exact correlation is not required if probative evidence supports reasonable correlation. Case: In re Brana; Cross v. Iizuka.

name: Claimed genus — representative examples and genus-wide enablement
description: For a claimed genus, representative examples together with a statement applicable to the genus may ordinarily be sufficient if one skilled in the art would expect the genus could be used without undue experimentation. Proof of enablement for other members of the genus is required only when adequate reasons are advanced to show inability to extrapolate.
guidance: Examiner must provide adequate reasons if asserting a genus is not enabled. See MPEP §2164.02(III).

name: Predictability of the art vs. amount of guidance required
description: The amount of guidance or direction needed in the specification is inversely related to what is known in the prior art and the predictability in the art; nascent or unpredictable technologies require more specific and useful teaching to be enabling.
guidance: In unpredictable arts (e.g., many chemical reactions, physiological activity), disclosure of a single species usually will not support broad genus claims; in predictable arts (mechanical, electrical), a single embodiment may provide broad enablement. Cite: In re Fisher; In re Marzocchi; In re Vickers; In re Soll; Chiron v. Genentech.

name: Burden on the examiner to establish a reasonable basis for nonenablement
description: Before analyzing enablement, the examiner must construe the claims and select meanings for ambiguous terms; to make a rejection, the examiner has the initial burden to establish a reasonable basis to question enablement and explain why the disclosure is insufficient.
guidance: The examiner must explain why it doubts the truth or accuracy of supporting disclosure and back up assertions with acceptable evidence or reasoning. Minimal requirement per In re Bowen: give reasons explaining uncertainty. Examiners should present the best case in the first Office action and identify enabled allowable subject matter early (compact prosecution principles). Cases: Genentech v. Wellcome; In re Wright; In re Marzocchi; In re Bowen.

name: Enablement determination must be based on the evidence as a whole — no personal opinion
description: The examiner must weigh all evidence—specification, applicant submissions (declarations, affidavits, references), and evidence/reasoning presented in the rejection—and decide if the claimed invention is enabled based on the weight of the record, not personal opinion.
guidance: Applicant may submit declarations under 37 C.F.R. 1.132 or cite references; such evidence must be commensurate with the specification and the claimed scope. Declarations and submissions carry weight proportionate to factual support they provide. Cases: In re Brandstadter; In re Buchner; In re Alton.

name: Examples of missing information — identify essential missing elements
description: Doubt about enablement often arises because information is missing about one or more essential claim elements or relationships which a skilled person could not develop without undue experimentation; examiner should specifically identify what is missing and why it is needed.
guidance: When asserting missing information, examiner should explain how the missing data prevents enabling the full claim scope and supply references if possible to support a prima facie case. See MPEP §2164.06(a).

name: Electrical/mechanical claims and broad claim language risk
description: Enablement serves to prevent claims broader than the disclosed invention. Broad claim language is used at the peril of losing claims that cannot be enabled across the full scope—lack of details for embodiments (e.g., electronic sensors) can render claims nonenabled for those embodiments.
guidance: Examples include claims that cover mechanical and electronic embodiments where specification lacks disclosure for one type (e.g., electronic side impact sensors) — the specification must apprise how to make and use such embodiments or claims may fail enablement. Cases: MagSil Corp. v. Hitachi; Auto. Techs. Int'l, Inc. v. BMW.

name: Weight and sufficiency of applicant-submitted evidence (declarations, FDA submissions)
description: Applicant may submit declarations, affidavits, or regulatory submissions to rebut a prima facie case of lack of enablement; such evidence must convincingly show that one skilled in the art could make and use the claimed invention at the filing date and must be commensurate with the claimed scope.
guidance: Examiner should compare steps, materials, and conditions in applicant's evidence with those in the application to ensure they are commensurate in scope and were supported by the specification as filed and what was well-known at filing. FDA submissions may be considered but their standards differ from USPTO enablement requirements. Cases: In re Brandstadter; Scott v. Finney; In re Alton; In re Buchner.

name: Materiality standard — what is 'material to patentability'
description: Material information is information that is 'material to the patentability' of the invention claimed — think of 'material' as something that calls into question the novelty of the claimed invention or might render it obvious.
guidance: References MPEP and 37 CFR 1.56(b); includes anything a reasonable examiner would be substantially likely to consider important in deciding whether to allow an application. Case law example: Bristol-Myers Squibb Co. v. Rhone-Poulenc Rorer, Inc. (article not prior art found material to enablement).

name: Cross-citing prior art across related applications
description: Determine at filing whether a new US application is related to previously filed foreign or US applications; if related, cross-reference for purposes of filing IDSs in the group of related cases (cross-citing prior art).
guidance: Relevant regulations: 37 CFR 1.57(b) and MPEP 2001.05. Relatedness is often indicated by a priority claim to the same foreign application; in the absence of priority claims, relatedness can be shown by common inventors/assignee or similar subject matter (MPEP 2001.06(b)). Cross-citing ensures prior art uncovered in one case is considered in related cases.

name: Mere plan, system, or intent cannot patentize old acts
description: Calling a thing a 'system' or 'plan' (i.e., the intent combined with an act) does not make old, known acts patentable; a system properly means a combination of many things acting together, and if the thing done is not new, intent cannot make it patentable.
guidance: A claim for the exclusive right to perform an act that was often done before cannot be supported by labeling it a system or plan. The patent must cover a new combination or contrivance, not merely an intention to use an old method for a particular purpose.

name: Evidence of fraud, incomplete disclosure, or improper claiming (15th & 13th section matters)
description: Under the statutes the defendant may give evidence that the plaintiff's description and specification do not contain the whole truth relative to the invention; that the patentee was not the original and first inventor; that he had unjustly obtained the patent; or that the patentee claimed more than he had a right to claim as new.
guidance: The 15th section lists matters admissible under the general issue; the 13th section contemplates correction where a patentee claims more than his right and the Commissioner may cause a new patent to be issued to the inventor for the same invention (limited scope).

name: Patent as a monopoly — strict construction principle
description: Every patent is a monopoly and must be strictly confined to the case excepted; nothing justifies the monopoly except the natural right of property in the products of a person's labor and ingenuity.
guidance: Because patents derogate common right, courts and the Commissioner should strictly construe scope and only allow patents when the statutory and equitable justifications exist. This underlies cautious refusal where the claimed subject is not truly inventive or new.

name: Final rejection on first action following Request for Continued Examination (RCE, 37 CFR 1.114)
description: Claims may be finally rejected in the first action following the filing of the RCE (with a submission and fee under 37 CFR 1.114) when all the claims in the application after entry of the submission under 37 CFR 1.114 and any entered supplemental amendments (A) are identical to, patentably indistinct from, or have unity of invention with the claims in the application prior to the entry of the submission under 37 CFR 1.114 (in other words, restriction (including lack of unity of invention) would not have been proper if the new or amended claims had been entered prior to the filing of the RCE), and (B) would have been properly finally rejected on the grounds and art of record in the next Office action if they had been entered in the application prior to the filing of the RCE under 37 CFR 1.114.
guidance: Both the pre- and post-RCE claim sets must be essentially the same in unity/patentable distinctness and the record must support that a final rejection would have been proper in the next action absent the RCE. The paragraph emphasizes that an RCE is not a vehicle to obtain continued examination on a different invention.

name: PTAB factors for weighing prior constructions
description: The PTAB considers exemplary factors in determining the 'appropriate weight' to give a prior claim construction: (1) the similarities between the record in the district court or the ITC and the record before the Board; (2) whether the prior claim construction is final or interlocutory; (3) whether the terms construed by the district court or ITC are necessary to deciding the issues before it; and (4) the facts and circumstances of each case.
guidance: Source: Patent Trial and Appeal Board Consolidated Trial Practice Guide (Trial Practice Guide) at 47 (Nov. 2019). These factors should be addressed in briefing to explain why a prior construction should or should not be given weight.

name: Use intrinsic and extrinsic evidence to support departure or adoption
description: Accentuate helpful intrinsic and extrinsic evidence (specification, prosecution history, expert testimony, dictionaries) that the district court or the ITC may have ignored or given short shrift.
guidance: PTAB applies Phillips: consider claim language, specification, prosecution history, and extrinsic evidence. Where the PTAB endorses a prior construction it often quotes and adopts the prior tribunal's reasoning or independently examines the specification and experts (e.g., MediaTek v. NTT; Lab. Corp. v. Quest).

name: Anchor arguments to claim construction canons (first principles)
description: Arguments should be grounded in basic canons of claim construction: consistency with claim language and specification, avoidance of importing limitations from the specification, and not excluding preferred/claimed embodiments.
guidance: PTAB 'departs' from prior constructions that violate basic rules (e.g., importing limitations or creating redundancy). Demonstrating that a prior construction contradicts these tenets is an effective way to evade it; showing compliance helps secure adoption (see Juniper Networks v. Packet Intel; Renesas v. Broadcom). File history arguments may be persuasive given PTAB expertise.

name: PTAB is not bound by prior constructions
description: Prior constructions from other courts based on the Phillips standard do not bind the PTAB; the PTAB can and has found prior constructions wanting and adopted different constructions.
guidance: PTAB will deviate when prior constructions violate claim construction rules, import limitations, exclude embodiments, or are otherwise flawed (examples: Juniper Networks; Renesas). Emphasize such flaws if seeking deviation.

name: Picture claim definition
description: A picture claim is a narrow claim that closely tracks a specific commercial embodiment - so close that a literal reading of the claim looks like a verbal photograph of the actual product. Every detail of the actual implementation is in the claim.

name: Narrow claim enforceability advantages
description: Counter-intuitively, the narrowest claim in a portfolio is often the most enforceable. It has the lowest risk of invalidation (because it incorporates many limiting details that prior art lacks), the clearest infringement read (because it tracks the real product), and the lowest doctrine-of-equivalents complications.
guidance: Use narrowness as a tool: include many limiting details that distinguish from prior art to reduce invalidation risk and make infringement determinations clearer; expect fewer doctrine-of-equivalents disputes.

name: Picture claims are insurance, not offense
description: You do not enforce a picture claim against a competitor. You use it as the survivor when the broad independent claims are challenged in IPR or litigation.
guidance: Treat picture claims as fallback claims that remain after broader claims are invalidated. They can still cover your own product (useful for proving secondary considerations) and may cover a competitor that copied you, but the primary role is survivability in post-grant or litigation proceedings.

name: How to write a picture claim (level of detail)
description: Take your prototype. Describe every meaningful component, every interface, every data field, every numerical range you actually use. Put it all in one claim.
guidance: Be exhaustive: expect the claim to be very long (the article says 'three pages long' and 'read like an instruction manual'). Include concrete implementation details and actual numeric ranges rather than abstract functional language; verbosity and length are acceptable and intentional for picture claims.

name: Use dependent claims as a ladder
description: In a typical 20-claim application, claim 1 is the broad 'moonshot' claim, claims 2-10 progressively narrow, and the final dependent claim is essentially the picture claim.
guidance: Draft a spectrum of dependent claims from broad to extremely narrow so a court can 'stop at any rung' — the ladder provides incremental fallbacks if broader claims are attacked. Ensure each dependent step meaningfully narrows the scope toward the picture claim.

name: Picture claims help damages
description: Damages experts use the smallest-saleable-patent-practicing-unit framework. A claim that closely tracks the product makes it easier to argue the claimed invention drives demand for the product, which raises the royalty base.
guidance: When calculating royalties or negotiating damages, a picture claim that maps to the commercial product can strengthen arguments about the contribution of the claimed features to product value and support a larger damages base.

name: Risk of having only picture claims
description: A portfolio of only picture claims gives competitors a roadmap to design around.
guidance: Do not rely solely on picture claims; maintain both broad claims (to deter design-arounds and capture inventive scope) and picture claims (as unkillable survivors). Balance 'scare' value and survivability in claim portfolio design.

name: AI and Big Data — sufficient disclosure for algorithm/data inventions
description: Sufficient disclosure requirements for algorithm/data-related inventions.
guidance: Algorithm- and data-related inventions must meet disclosure requirements (enablement/written description) appropriate to the technology — e.g., sufficient detail about algorithms, models, data, training processes, parameters, or workflows so a skilled person can implement the claimed solution. The 2026 revision explicitly emphasizes disclosure sufficiency for AI/data inventions.

name: Inventiveness assessment applies to the claimed technical solution as a whole
description: The claimed technical solution should be subject to the inventiveness assessment test in its entirety, rather than a test of inventiveness of certain technical features.
guidance: When assessing inventive step, examiners must evaluate the claimed invention as an integrated technical solution — avoid isolating or dissecting only particular features for inventiveness. This principle affects claim drafting and how prior art is compared to the claim in its whole.

name: Three-step test for inventiveness (problem–solution approach)
description: CNIPA uses a three-step approach similar to the EPO's problem–solution method to assess inventive step.
guidance: The three steps are: (1) determine the closest prior art; (2) determine the distinguishing features and the technical problem actually solved; (3) determine whether the claimed invention is obvious to a person skilled in the art. Examiners should follow these sequential steps when evaluating inventive step; the approach emphasizes identification of the actual technical problem and distinguishing features rather than hindsight reasoning.

name: Patentable subject-matter exclusions (Article 25)
description: Certain categories are excluded from patentability under Article 25.
guidance: The listed non-patentable subject matter includes: scientific discoveries; rules and methods for mental activities; methods for diagnosis and treatment of diseases; animal and plant varieties; substances obtained by means of nuclear transformation; and designs that are mainly used for marking patterns/colors/combinations on plane prints. Applicants should frame claims to avoid falling squarely within these excluded categories or show technical character where applicable.

name: Utility model scope and inventiveness standard
description: Utility models cover product shape, structure, or combinations and (post-2024 amendments) are subject to inventiveness examination with a lower bar than invention patents.
guidance: Utility model protection is distinct from invention patents and applies to structural/shape aspects of products. While utility models now undergo inventiveness examination, the threshold is lower than for invention patents — practitioners should consider strategic filing choices (utility model vs invention patent) and draft claims consistent with the scope and inventiveness expectations for utility models in China.

name: Detail required for stating rejections (pertinency and manner of applying prior art)
description: The first Office action must be sufficiently detailed that the pertinency and manner of applying the cited prior art to the claims in each rejection is clearly set forth therein.
guidance: Explicitly explain why cited patents/printed publications are pertinent and precisely how they are applied to each claim; show mapping between prior art and claim limitations so the rejection is understandable and defensible.

name: Incorporation and review of requester-supplied materials
description: Where the request for reexamination includes material such as a claim chart to explain a proposed rejection, the examiner may bodily incorporate the claim chart (or other material) within the Office action.
guidance: If incorporating requester materials, the examiner must carefully review them to ensure any items incorporated in a statement of the rejection clearly and completely address the patentability of the claims; do not blindly adopt requester charts without verification.

name: Explaining reasons for patentability or allowance
description: If the examiner concludes in any Office action that one or more of the claims are patentable over the cited patents or printed publications, the examiner should indicate why the claim(s) is/are clearly patentable in a manner similar to that used to indicate reasons for allowance (MPEP §1302.14).
guidance: When finding claims patentable, provide clear reasons and supporting references (or point to record portions that establish patentability) analogous to allowance explanations so the basis for patentability is on the record.

name: Use of patent owner statements (37 CFR 1.501(a)(2)) when relied upon
description: If any statement of the patent owner submitted pursuant to 37 CFR 1.501(a)(2) is relied upon in the detailed explanation, requester must have explained how that statement is being used to determine the proper meaning of a patent claim in connection with prior art applied to that claim.
guidance: When examiner relies on a patent-owner statement, check that requester provided an explanation of how that statement informs claim meaning relative to applied prior art; that explanation will be considered in drafting the Office action and in determining claim scope.

name: Disclaimers and dedications by patent owner
description: A patent owner may disclaim or dedicate to the public the entire patent term (all claims), the entire term of any complete claim, or the terminal part of the term of the entire patent (but not a terminal part of only some claims) (35 U.S.C. § 253).
guidance: A fee (set by regulation) is paid, the PTO publishes notice in the Official Gazette and prints copies for attachment to printed patents. Typical motivations: substantial question as to validity, duplicate coverage ('double patenting') requiring terminal disclaimer so patents expire same day (terminal disclaimer effective only for obviousness-type double patenting).

name: Reissue requirements under 35 U.S.C. § 251
description: A patent may be reissued by the PTO upon surrender of the original patent if, through error without deceptive intention, it is deemed wholly or partly inoperative or invalid (35 U.S.C. § 251).
guidance: Common bases for reissue: (1) claims too narrow or too broad; (2) inaccuracies in disclosure; (3) incorrect naming of inventors; (4) failure to claim foreign priority correctly; (5) failure to refer properly to a copending application. The reissue oath/declaration must set forth the error(s). Reissue must claim the same general invention and may not add new matter or recapture surrendered subject matter. Claims may be broadened only if the reissue is filed within two years of issuance and signed by the inventor; after two years claims may only be narrowed (if not being broadened, assignee may sign). Reissue files are public; protests allowed; examiner may consider de novo all patentability issues. When reissued, cancellations are bracketed and additions italicized. Intervening rights may arise for parties who practiced subject matter not covered by original claims but covered by reissued claims.

name: Reexamination procedure and limits
description: If reexamination is ordered, the patent owner may file within two months a Patent Owner's Statement showing why claims are patentable and present narrowing amendments; the requester (other than owner) may reply within two months (37 C.F.R. §§ 1.530, 1.535). After the statement period, reexamination proceeds ex parte similar to prosecution; appeals from final rejection are available. In reexamination, claims may only be narrowed, although new claims no broader than the original claims may be added.
guidance: On completion, the PTO issues a Notice of Intent to Issue a Reexamination Certificate and then the Reexamination Certificate. The certificate will: (a) cancel unpatentable claims; (b) confirm patentable claims; (c) incorporate amended or new patentable claims; (d) make approved changes in the description; (e) include any statutory disclaimer filed; (f) refer to unamended claims held invalid on final holding by another forum on non-patent/printed-publication grounds; (g) refer to any claims not reexamined; (h) be mailed to patent owner and requester; (i) refer to dependent claims determined patentable. Reexamination files are public; any interested person may file citations during reexamination. Citations received after reexamination ordered are entered after completion and require a new request if further consideration is desired. Intervening rights can arise from reexamination (35 U.S.C. § 307(b)).

name: Acts that satisfy §1400(b) (what constitutes 'in the district')
description: For venue the focus is on whether the act occurred in the district, not whether the act constitutes infringement. Acts satisfying §1400(b) include making, using, offering for sale, selling an accused product or process in the district; inducing another to make/use/sell in the district; and contributing in the district to another's making/using/selling.
guidance: 'Making' means manufacturing or assembling; 'using' means actual use (not mere possession). 'Selling' has been historically ambiguous—some jurisdictions required a formal sale under the UCC, others required solicitation plus demonstrations; GATT-implementing legislation expanded acts (e.g., offer to sell) that may satisfy venue. For inducement/contributory claims, venue is appropriate only where the alleged inducer or contributor acted.

name: Presumption of validity and burden of proof to show invalidity
description: A patent is presumed valid (35 U.S.C. § 282); each claim is presumed valid independently. The burden on a party challenging validity is to show, by clear and convincing evidence, that the patent is invalid.
guidance: Courts are not bound by the PTO's decision to issue a patent but give deference to the agency. If a challenger presents no evidence different from that reviewed by the examiner, the challenge is difficult. The challenger’s task is easier if material evidence not considered by the PTO is presented, but the legal burden of proof remains unchanged.

name: Publicity/character of original discipline (whether publicly imposed)
description: An explicit ground is whether any argument exists that the practitioner was not publicly censured, publicly reprimanded, placed on probation, disbarred, suspended or disciplinarily disqualified (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(iv)).
guidance: Respondent may assert that the state action was not of the type claimed, but must establish that fact by clear and convincing evidence.

name: Specificity requirement for claims of false evidence or statements
description: Allegations that false statements or false evidence were used in the state proceeding must be specific (identify particular misleading statements/documents) to show infirmity of proof.
guidance: Generic or conclusory claims that witnesses were 'manipulative' or documents were 'not representative' fail to meet the clear-and-convincing threshold.

name: Federal preemption defense (Sperry and Kroll limits)
description: A claim that state discipline is preempted by federal law (e.g., federal patent practice) is governed by Sperry v. State of Fla.; state control over law practice within its borders persists except to the limited extent necessary for federal objectives.
guidance: Discipline related to federal matters (e.g., patent practice) is not per se preempted; preemption applies only where state action conflicts with federal objectives. Precedent (Kroll) supports that state discipline need not be preempted where it does not attempt to exclude practice before the USPTO.

name: Current statutory/MPEP restriction standard (35 U.S.C. §121; MPEP §803)
description: An application may properly be required to be restricted to one of two or more claimed inventions only if: (1) they are able to support separate patents and they are either independent or distinct; and (2) search and examination of the entire application involves a serious burden (MPEP §803).
guidance: This is the Office's baseline practice intended to balance granting reasonable breadth of protection in a single patent against the burden on the USPTO of examining multiple inventions in a single application. Implementation involves identifying separate inventions, grouping claims, stating reasons, and requiring an election to prevent abandonment.

name: PCT Unity of Invention (PCT Rule 13) (as a candidate standard)
description: PCT Rule 13.1: 'The international application shall relate to one invention only or to a group of inventions so linked as to form a general inventive concept.' Under Option 2 the unity concept is applied so that multiple inventions constitute a single inventive concept if there is a technical relationship among the claimed inventions involving one or more of the same or corresponding 'special technical features.'
guidance: Under USPTO-modified Option 2, any purported special technical/common feature must also comply with 35 U.S.C. §112, first paragraph (in addition to novelty and non-obviousness). Where necessary in large applications, the applicant will be invited to identify a reference claim to facilitate determining 'same or corresponding' features. If no response to an invitation to pay additional fees, current PCT practice searches the first mentioned invention; the study notes public preference for allowing applicants to choose a 'main' invention and for abandonment (not defaulting to the first mentioned) if no response is received.

name: Scope of IPRs and PGRs
description: An inter partes review ("IPR") or post-grant review ("PGR") is a proceeding designed to allow a Petitioner to attack the validity of one or more claims of an issued patent. These proceedings only examine validity and do not adjudicate infringement or award damages, injunctions, or other remedies.
guidance: They were created by the American Invents Act (AIA). Use these proceedings as a faster, cheaper alternative to district court litigation when the goal is to attack validity only.

name: IPR eligibility and timing when AIA claims exist
description: For IPRs, all patents are eligible and there is no general deadline for filing. However, if the target patent has at least one AIA claim, one must wait to file a Petition until the later of nine months after issuance (or re-issuance) or termination of any PGR on the patent.
guidance: Coordinate strategy across available post-grant options and watch for overlapping PGRs that can delay IPR filing.

name: Petition scope and word limits; required petition contents
description: A Petition may only attack one patent. Petitions have word limits: 14,000 words for IPRs and 18,700 words for PGRs. The Petition must set forth: the grounds for standing, the claim(s) attacked, the statutory grounds for the attack, how the claims are to be construed, and how/why the construed claim is unpatentable. The Petition must also identify the real parties-in-interest, related matters, lead and back-up counsel, and service information. The Petition is typically supported by one or more declarations of technical experts and supporting exhibits.
guidance: Structure the petition to hit each required element within the word limits and attach supporting declarations/exhibits; any omission can jeopardize institution.

name: Motions to amend and burdens
description: The Patent Owner has the option to propose substitute claims via a Motion to Amend. Motions to Amend are only reached if a given claim is found unpatentable and the PTAB grants very few motions to amend. Rules (amended Jan 2021) state that the Patent Owner 'bears the burden of persuasion to show, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the motion to amend complies' with statutory/regulatory requirements; and the Petitioner 'bears the burden of persuasion to show, by a preponderance of the evidence, that any proposed substitute claims are unpatentable.' The Board may exercise discretion to grant or deny only for reasons supported by readily identifiable and persuasive evidence of record.
guidance: Anticipate that motions to amend are difficult to win; if representing a Patent Owner, prepare persuasive evidence for compliance; if representing a Petitioner, prepare to attack substitute claims' patentability.

name: Final Written Decision contents and timing
description: Within three months of the Oral Hearing the panel issues its Final Written Decision, which addresses all bases and all claims raised in the Petition as well as patentability of any proposed amended claims. Final Written Decisions typically address claim construction (when necessary), weight given to experts’ opinions, fact-findings regarding scope and content of prior art, the Panel’s judgment on disputed evidence, and reasoning behind the Board’s conclusion as to patentability.
guidance: Craft the record and evidentiary support to influence claim construction, expert weight, and prior-art fact findings that will be recited in the Final Written Decision.

name: Complete explanation for each new ground of rejection
description: For each new ground of rejection, a complete explanation supporting the rejection must be provided with a proper reference to the applicable statute, prior art references relied upon, and the claim numbers of the claims that are subject to the rejection in the examiner’s answer.
guidance: New grounds must include statute citation, cited references, and claim numbers; must be prominently identified in the 'Grounds of Rejection to be Reviewed on Appeal' section under 'New Grounds of Rejection' (may use form paragraph 12.256).

name: Presume all rejected claims are on appeal; maintain rejections unless overcome
description: Examiners are not to make any determination whether fewer than all of the rejected claims are identified by the appellant as being appealed. The Board will presume that all of the rejected claims are on appeal; therefore, the examiner will treat all pending, rejected claims as being on appeal, and maintain all of the rejections set forth in the Office action from which the appeal is taken, unless appellant has overcome the rejection.
guidance: Appellant can overcome by persuasive arguments, acceptable terminal disclaimer, or evidence. If appellant requested abeyance or did not present argument on a rejection in the brief, the examiner should maintain the rejection and identify that the appellant has not argued it.

name: Example: new calculations, structures, or portions relied upon can create new grounds
description: Citing new calculations (e.g., overlapping ranges identified/calculated for the first time), citing a different structure in support of structural obviousness, or pointing to a different portion of a reference or claim limitation may create a new ground of rejection.
guidance: Such factual additions or reliance on different facts/portions that alter the basis/facts supporting a rejection have been held to constitute new grounds (e.g., In re Kumar; In re Wiechert; In re Waymouth).

name: Situations not considered new grounds
description: There is no new ground of rejection when the basic thrust of the rejection remains the same such that an appellant has been given a fair opportunity to react; a change in discussion or rationale without new evidence or new statutory basis does not necessarily constitute a new ground.
guidance: Specific non-new examples include: citing a different portion of a reference to elaborate upon previously cited material; rejections applied to claims added/amended under 37 CFR 1.116/41.33 when advisory action indicated which individual rejections would apply (applicant was advised); and use of references merely to support what was already asserted as 'well-known' in the art (see MPEP § 2144.03).

name: Use of form paragraphs and required structure in examiner's answer
description: The examiner's answer should follow established form-paragraph structure (e.g., ¶12.249 Examiner’s Answer Cover Sheet; ¶12.254 Grounds of Rejection to be Reviewed on Appeal; ¶12.255 Restatement of Rejection; ¶12.256 New Grounds of Rejection - Heading; ¶12.257 Withdrawn Rejections; ¶12.261 Response to Argument; ¶12.279 Conclusion/¶12.279.01 Conclusion raising new grounds; ¶12.279.02 Dismissal following new grounds).
guidance: Use the specified form paragraphs where applicable, populate bracketed fields appropriately (dates, claim numbers, conferees, signatures), and follow examiner notes on when to use particular paragraphs and insertions (e.g., when notice of appeal filed on or after January 23, 2012). Conclude answers containing new grounds with form paragraph 12.279.01 to notify applicant of reply period and include required TC Director approval.

name: Board exchanges and preliminary opinions during re-examination
description: During the re-examination proceeding there may be multiple exchanges; letters from the board will set out the board’s preliminary opinions on the patentability of claims subject to re-examination and any proposed amendments made by the patentee.
guidance: Final determinations on patentability are reserved until issuance of a certificate of re-examination.

name: No enlargement of claim scope in re-examination amendments
description: No amendment or new claim shall enlarge the scope of a claim of the patent (subsection 48.3(2) of the Patent Act).
guidance: This is taken to mean any proposed claim must, at a minimum, include all features of the broadest independent claim of the patent — a proposed claim may not broaden protection in some respects even if narrowed in others.

name: Legal equivalence of re-examination determinations
description: Determinations of a re-examination board are functionally equivalent to a decision of the Commissioner of Patents under section 40 of the Patent Act; they are a re-determination of validity of claims within the circumstances set out in sections 48.1 to 48.5.
guidance: The board must be satisfied the patentee is not 'by law' entitled to a claim to cancel it; the same criteria apply to decisions not to incorporate amendments, with the additional requirement that an amendment not enlarge the scope of a claim.

name: Outcomes in certificate of re-examination
description: Upon completion the re-examination board will issue a certificate of re-examination which may: cancel any claim determined unpatentable; confirm any claim determined patentable; or incorporate any proposed amended or new claim determined patentable.
guidance: A decision letter outlining the reasons accompanies the certificate; registration certificate attaches the certificate to the patent and a new cover page is generated and stored in electronic files and the Canadian Patent Database.

name: Effect of canceling an independent claim
description: If a certificate indicates an independent claim is cancelled, this removes the scope of protection afforded by the claim but does not mean the text of the independent claim is no longer considered part of any dependent claim that refers to it.
guidance: Cancellation is a removal of scope, not necessarily textual deletion from dependent claim references.

name: Retroactive and conditional effects of re-examination certificate
description: Effects set out in subsection 48.4(3): (a) if some claims cancelled, patent deemed issued in corrected form from grant date; (b) if all claims cancelled, patent deemed never to have been issued; (c) amended or new claims effective from date of certificate for unexpired term.
guidance: Invalidity is retroactive, but addition/amendment of claims only gives rights for remaining term. Effects do not apply until appeal period expires, and if appealed only apply to extent reflected in final judicial judgment (subsection 48.4(4)).

name: Grounds for 'defective or inoperative' patent
description: Pursuant to subsection 47(1) a patent is 'defective or inoperative' where, due to some error, the original patent failed to fulfil the applicant’s intent upon grant. Two primary reasons: (1) insufficient description and specification; and (2) the patentee having claimed more or less than they had a right to claim as new.
guidance: This relates to scope of protection or quality of description; does not equate to defects in compliance with the Act and Rules for validity purposes.

name: Insufficient description and specification indicators
description: A patent defective for insufficient description/specification lacks textual/graphical matter or includes wrong matter contrary to inventor intent, e.g., failure to accurately claim or describe the invention, claim subcombinations, include dependent claims, or claims to different categories of invention.
guidance: Such failings could indicate reissue is appropriate if they show the patent does not express applicant intent.

name: Claiming more or less than entitled
description: A patent is defective for claiming more or less when the claims protect more or less subject-matter than the patentee intended; errors in description/drawings can cause this defect.
guidance: Reissue may be appropriate to correct scope mismatches if they meet subsection 47(1).

name: Same invention requirement for reissue
description: Any amended description/specification in reissue must be directed to the 'same invention ... for which the original patent was granted' (subsection 47(1)). All matter in a reissued patent must find support somewhere in the original patent's description, drawings or claims.
guidance: No requirement for identical inventive concept; matter inferable from original description/drawings/claims or admitted prior art is acceptable.

name: Retroactive effect and maintenance fees for reissued patent
description: Effect of reissue is retroactive and rights exist with respect to the reissued patent as if they had been in effect as of the original grant date (subsection 47(2)). No additional maintenance fees apply to an application for reissue; maintenance fees remain payable on the original patent until it reissues, then on the reissued patent under the same due dates as the original patent.
guidance: A reissued patent may not be withdrawn after it has been issued in favour of the original patent. Pending actions unaffected to the extent their claims are identical in scope.

name: Domestic industry requirement (two prongs)
description: To satisfy domestic industry in a patent case, complainant must demonstrate significant US activity related to at least one claim of each asserted patent (19 U.S.C. § 1337(a)(3)). There are two elements: the economic prong and the technical prong.
guidance: Economic prong: requires significant US activities (production/manufacture, R&D, licensing) related to products that practice the asserted patent; quantitative analysis required (Lelo). Technical prong: economic activities must be related to the asserted patent and the patented article must practice at least one claim (Alloc).

name: Pre-suit investigation and complaint factual pleading requirements
description: Because Section 337 is a fact-pleading venue, a detailed pre-suit investigation is required and the complaint must contain detailed factual allegations, including claim charts for all patent claims asserted.
guidance: Investigation should analyze importation, domestic industry, and remedy issues. Complaint must include detailed infringement claim charts and contentions, a description (with evidence) of domestic industry, detailed information regarding proposed remedy, and background materials; a separate public interest statement is required. Drafting takes weeks/months and often portions filed under seal.

name: Service and institution mechanics; Notice of Investigation (NOI)
description: A complainant need not serve respondents unless requesting temporary relief. If the Commission institutes an investigation, it serves the complaint and publishes a Notice of Investigation (NOI) in the Federal Register describing allegations, parties, and assigned ALJ.
guidance: The NOI sets the actual scope of accused products using plain language; read the NOI carefully to determine the investigation scope and which imported products fall within asserted claims (19 C.F.R. § 210.10(b)(1)).

name: Enablement and well-established utility requirement for chemical-substance/biotech inventions
description: For chemical substances (including genes) the description requirements involve a well-established utility and enablement: a person skilled in the art must be able to make and use the claimed invention as of the filing date, and the utility should be clearly and sufficiently stated since the claimed substance cannot be used without clear description.
guidance: Court decisions cited (e.g., 2007HEO5116) support strict enablement and utility; mere discovery of existence of a natural product generally insufficient.

name: Claim content for genes and DNA fragments — sequence specificity
description: A gene and a DNA fragment should be described by specifying the sequence thereof. Use of expressions like 'a sequence having ~% homology with a specific reference sequence' in the claim is not permitted in principle unless the description provides solid evidence that variants with that homology contain the same activity.
guidance: Claims should be sequence-specific; broad homology-based claim language rarely accepted without supporting description and evidence (case law referenced).

name: Claiming structural genes by amino acid sequence
description: A structural gene may be described in a claim by specifying the amino acid sequence of the protein encoded by the gene.
guidance: Protein amino-acid sequence can serve to define the corresponding gene in claims.

name: Genetic variants — disclosure of position and content
description: When expressions such as 'deletion', 'substitution' or 'addition' are used in relation to a sequence, the position and the content of those variants should be specifically disclosed. If specific examples of genetic variants are provided, it may be permitted to define claims by limiting function and scope of variants, but merely describing hybridization conditions is insufficient to specify scope.
guidance: High specificity required for variant claims; functional-limited variant claims permitted only with concrete supporting examples.

name: Protein and recombinant protein claim description
description: A protein and a recombinant protein should be described by specifying the amino acid sequence or the nucleic acid sequence of the structural gene encoding the protein.
guidance: Sequence-based description is the norm for protein-related claims.

name: Protein variants — position/content disclosure and exceptional function-based claims
description: When claiming protein variants using terms like 'deletion', 'substitution', 'addition', the position and content must be clearly described. Under exceptional circumstances, if there are specific and sufficient examples of a protein variant in the description, it is permitted to describe the invention by limiting the function of the protein and the scope of the variant.
guidance: Function-based variant claims allowed only as exceptions supported by concrete exemplification.

name: When protein sequence cannot be specified — alternate claim descriptors
description: If a protein cannot be specified by its amino-acid sequence, it may be described in the claim by limiting all of functions, physicochemical properties, origin/source, and method for producing the protein; in this case there must be reasonable grounds for why the protein cannot be specified by sequence.
guidance: Non-sequence descriptors are acceptable only with justification and clear functional/physicochemical characterization.

name: Plant-variety claims filed before Sept 30, 2006 — asexual reproduction requirement
description: For applications relating to plant invention filed before September 30, 2006, a plant variety capable of asexual reproduction is the only patentable subject matter among plant varieties, and it is required to describe the method of asexual reproduction in the claim.
guidance: Temporal/legal cutoff: earlier-filed plant applications have specific claim/form requirements under prior law (Article 31 of Old Patent Act).

name: Unity of invention in biotechnology — depends on shared technical feature and contribution over prior art
description: Whether unity of invention is fulfilled depends on the degree of disclosure of prior arts and whether claimed items share a same or corresponding special technical feature that makes a contribution over prior art. Examples show lack of unity when claims share only origin or unrelated functions, and unity when claims share a common structural/functional motif not known in prior art.
guidance: Examine common technical features and whether they materially contribute over prior art (examples 1–5 illustrate application).

name: Pharmacological-effect disclosure requirement (pharmaceutical inventions)
description: The pharmacological effect of a medicinal-use invention should be described in the original specification to support its medical use. Principally, pharmacological effect should be supported by clinical tests; animal or in-vitro tests can substitute clinical tests in some inventions. Specification should disclose test results or describe in great detail how the substance shows effect unless the mechanism was clearly known before filing.
guidance: Pharmacological data or detailed mechanism description is required to support medicinal-use claims; selection inventions must state effects clearly for skilled persons.

name: Cosmetics — objective evidence for claimed effects
description: Effects of cosmetics should be confirmed by objective documents such as sensory panel test results; functional cosmetics with biochemical or physical effects require objective documentation and detailed description to prove functional effect.
guidance: Sensory tests, biochemical/physical measurements, and other objective evidence expected for cosmetics/function claims.

name: Claims drafting for medicinal use — product recitation and specific pharmacological effect
description: A medicinal-use invention should be recited as a product invention. Comprehensive descriptions like 'medicine' or 'therapeutic agent' are not allowable; the medicinal use should be stated as a pharmacological effect such as diagnosis, therapy, improvement (relief), treatment or prevention. Specification by pharmacological mechanism is allowed if a skilled person recognizes the mechanism as a specific pharmacological effect.
guidance: Claims must specify the therapeutic effect or disease target rather than generic terms; mechanism-based claim language allowed only when it unambiguously indicates a specific medicinal use.

name: Novelty of differently-stated but identical inventions
description: Two inventions stated differently in claims but having the same purpose and effect are deemed identical (examples: device for manufacturing medicines vs. simple processes for manufacturing; medicine vs. directions for medicine; mixture vs. process for manufacturing mixture).
guidance: Substance and purpose/effect, not claim wording alone, determine novelty equivalence.

name: Different combination of the same elements is not infringement
description: Using the same elements in a different combination (i.e., differently combined or comprising only a portion of the claimed elements) is not an infringement.
guidance: Text: "To make or use or sell a combination in which the same elements are differently combined, or a combination which comprises only a portion of these elements... is not an infringement." Cited: Pattee v. Moline Plow Co.; Byam v. Eddy; Rowell v. Lindsay. Court looks to whether the arrangement/plan of cooperation is preserved.

name: Use of equivalents infringes combination claims
description: A combination patent is infringed if equivalents of claimed elements are used in place of the claimed elements.
guidance: Text: "That a combination is infringed if equivalents are used" (Dederick v. Whitman Agricultural Co., Wheeler v. Morris, Reay v. Rajmor). Courts apply the doctrine of equivalents to combination claims.

name: All claimed elements must be used to infringe (general rule)
description: A combination is not infringed unless all its elements, as claimed, are used (whether essential or not).
guidance: Text: "That a combination is not infringed unless all its elements, as they are claimed, are used..." (Boyer v. Schultz Belting Co.; American Bell Tel. Co. v. Spencer). Numerous exceptions and qualifications follow in the treatise.

name: Using less than all elements may infringe if omitted parts are new to same inventor
description: Using fewer than all claimed elements does not infringe unless the elements used were new and patentable to the same inventor (i.e., those elements are themselves the patentee's invention).
guidance: Text: "That a combination is not infringed by the use of less than all its elements unless the elements used were new and patentable to the same inventor" (Thoens v. Israel). Also discussed in context of when sub-parts are separate inventions.

name: Omission of an element that performs an independent function may avoid infringement
description: If one claimed element is omitted and that omitted element performed a function of its own not discharged by remaining elements, the omission may avoid infringement.
guidance: Text: "That a combination is not infringed if one of its elements is omitted where the omitted element performs a function of its own not discharged by the remaining elements" (Tobey Furniture Co. v. Colby). Courts examine whether omitted element is functionally essential.

name: A combination-patent does not, by itself, protect individual old elements
description: A patent claiming only a combination does not protect elements of which it is composed if those elements are old; such elements are the public's property unless separately claimed as new.
guidance: Text: "A patent claiming a combination only does not protect the elements of which it is composed. If these are old, they are already the property of the public..." (Rowell v. Lindsay; Lee v. Blandy). Emphasizes necessity to distinctly claim separate inventions (elements or sub-combinations).

name: Patented element used as component of new combination can be infringement
description: The use of a patented invention as an element in a new combination is an infringement of the patent covering that element.
guidance: Text: "That the use of a patented invention as an element in a new combination is an infringement" (Cleveland v. Towle). If an element itself is claimed and patented, incorporation into new combinations can give rise to liability.

name: Presumption that each claim has a unique scope
description: Each claim in a patent is presumed to have a unique scope.
guidance: This presumption underlies claim interpretation: no two claims should cover the same subject matter. It promotes clarity and reduces ambiguity across a patent's claim set.

name: Dependent claims must be more limiting than independent claims
description: Dependent claims must be more limiting than the independent claims they refer to.
guidance: Dependent claims are interpreted to provide additional specific limitations and thus define a subset of the independent claim. Example given: an independent claim for a bicycle frame with dependent claims specifying materials or handlebar design — the dependent claims should be narrower.

name: Claims must not be interpreted to cover identical subject matter
description: Claims cannot be interpreted to cover the same subject matter.
guidance: Interpreting two claims as coextensive contradicts the doctrine; claim language should be read so as to avoid rendering one claim redundant with another.

name: Courts should not import limitations from one claim into another
description: Courts should not import limitations from one claim into another.
guidance: When construing claims, courts should avoid reading a limitation appearing only in a dependent claim into the broader independent claim, because that would improperly narrow the independent claim and undermine claim differentiation.

name: Use of the doctrine in patent examination and litigation
description: The doctrine is primarily applied in patent litigation and during the patent examination process.
guidance: Practitioners use it to argue for broader interpretations of claims (e.g., in defending against infringement) or to support particular constructions during prosecution. It is a tool during claim construction disputes before courts or examiners.

name: Purpose: promote clarity and prevent ambiguity in claim sets
description: The doctrine is designed to promote clarity and prevent ambiguity in patent claims.
guidance: By treating claims as having distinct meanings, the doctrine helps delineate the scope of protection and reduces interpretive overlap that could create uncertainty for patent owners and third parties.

name: Prohibition on broadening dependent claims by importing independent-claim features
description: Dependent claims cannot be broadened to include features from independent claims.
guidance: Contrary to some misunderstandings, dependent claims are not meant to be used to enlarge the scope of an independent claim by importing elements; they are intended to add limitations, not broaden.

name: Relation to claim construction and other doctrines (e.g., Doctrine of Equivalents)
description: Claim differentiation is a principle that guides the claim construction process and is distinct from doctrines like the Doctrine of Equivalents.
guidance: While claim differentiation directs how literal claim language is read (ensuring distinct scopes), the Doctrine of Equivalents addresses infringement when an accused product falls outside the literal claim language but is equivalent in substance. Use claim differentiation when construing literal scope; use equivalence doctrines for non-literal infringement issues.

name: Practical examples illustrating proper application
description: Hypothetical examples demonstrate how dependent claims should form narrower subsets of independent claims.
guidance: Example: an independent claim for a 'vehicle' and a dependent claim for an 'electric vehicle' — the dependent claim must be interpreted as a specific subset. Another example: bicycle frame with dependent claims for material or handlebar design. These examples show how to read dependent claims as adding limitations.

name: Prior patent defense: identity and public issuance/date
description: When novelty is denied on the ground of a prior patent, two questions arise: (1) whether the plaintiff's invention is identical with or included in the prior patent; (2) whether the prior patent was duly issued and publicly accessible before the plaintiff's conception.
guidance: The defendant's primary evidence is the prior patent itself, construed alongside the plaintiff's patent; courts often use experts to compare claims and specifications. The defendant must show the prior patent was a public document under the issuing country's law and that it was published/made accessible before the plaintiff's inventive act. Certified copies from patent offices are prima facie evidence of existence, date, and contents; where foreign patents have different regimes (secret vs public), the defendant must prove which category applies. Re-issues, file wrappers, and similar materials have limitations and do not always show operative dates or reductions to practice.

name: Types and admissibility of evidence (certified copies, drawings, parol, experts)
description: Permissible evidence includes certified copies of patents/specifications/drawings, specimens, sketches/drawings, witness testimony, experts, practical mechanics; but some items (e.g., file wrappers, title-page imprint) have limited probative value.
guidance: Certified patent office copies are prima facie proof of issue, date, and contents. Where copies are unobtainable, parol proof of publication and contents may be admitted but is weaker and subject to scrutiny. Experts are routinely used to explain/compare patent claims and to testify whether a disclosure enables practice. Negative evidence (witnesses who would have known but did not) and silence can create presumptions but yield to positive proof. Courts treat different evidence types with varying weight; documentary authenticated evidence is strongest.

name: Statutory categories requirement (Step 1)
description: First, the claimed invention must be to one of the four statutory categories: processes, machines, manufactures and compositions of matter (35 U.S.C. 101).
guidance: Defines ‘process’ (actions or series of acts) and explains that machines, manufactures, and compositions are physical/tangible 'things.' For product claims (machines/manufactures/compositions) the claimed subject matter must exist in some physical or tangible form. Non-limiting examples of claims not falling in the categories include information/data per se, computer program per se (software per se), transitory signals/carrier waves, and subject matter excluded by statute (e.g., humans per se under AIA). If the BRI of a claim covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments, the claim fails Step 1; examiners should point out the BRI and recommend narrowing amendments when possible.

name: Judicial exceptions exclusion / Alice‑Mayo two‑part framework
description: Second, the claimed invention must not be directed to a judicial exception (abstract ideas, laws of nature, natural phenomena) unless the claim as a whole includes additional limitations amounting to significantly more than the exception.
guidance: The MPEP adopts the Alice/Mayo two-part test: (1) determine whether claims are directed to an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon (Step 2A); (2) if so, determine whether the claim recites additional elements that amount to significantly more (Step 2B) — the 'search for an inventive concept.' The Alice/Mayo test is the only test to use for §101. The machine‑or‑transformation test is a helpful clue, not a separate test. Do not evaluate eligibility by 'useful, concrete, and tangible result' or by utility; do not treat mere recitation of concrete components or field‑of‑use as dispositive.

name: Establish Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) before eligibility analysis
description: Before examining a claim for eligibility, the examiner must establish the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim as a whole.
guidance: BRI sets the boundaries of coverage sought and influences whether a claim covers non-statutory subject matter or a judicial exception. Claim construction affects Step 1 and both parts of the Alice/Mayo test. Examples (Mentor Graphics, Synopsys, Enfish, Amdocs) show how different constructions can change eligibility findings. When BRI covers non‑statutory embodiments, reject and recommend amendment to narrow scope. See MPEP §2111 for BRI details.

name: Eligibility Step 1 procedural determination
description: Step 1 asks: Is the claim to a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter (after BRI and review of disclosure)?
guidance: If claim as a whole does not fall within any statutory category (Step 1: NO) reject under 35 U.S.C. 101 (use form paragraphs 7.05/7.05.01). If claim falls within one or more categories (Step 1: YES), proceed to Step 2A to determine whether it is directed to a judicial exception. If amendment could make claim statutory, examiner should recommend amendment and may proceed to Pathways A/B/C analysis for eligibility of the amended claim.

name: Step 2A — Whether claim is directed to a judicial exception
description: Identify whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon.
guidance: Claims directed to nothing more than abstract ideas, natural phenomena, or laws of nature are not eligible. The examiner should identify the particular exception implicated and analyze whether the claim is 'directed to' that exception (considering claim limitations and BRI). See MPEP §2106.04 and cited case law (Diehr, Alice, Mayo, Benson, Flook, Chakrabarty, etc.).

name: Abstract idea groupings and tentative abstract ideas
description: Classify and identify abstract ideas by recognized groupings and identify tentative abstract ideas when appropriate.
guidance: MPEP provides example lists and groupings of abstract ideas and notes that some concepts may be tentatively considered abstract pending analysis. Examiners should use these groupings and examples to help identify whether a claim recites an abstract idea, but apply full Alice/Mayo analysis rather than rely solely on grouping labels.

name: Markedly different characteristics analysis (products of nature)
description: For claims involving natural products, analyze whether the claimed subject matter has markedly different characteristics from the naturally occurring counterpart.
guidance: If the claimed product exhibits markedly different characteristics (structure, function, or other properties) from what exists in nature, it may not be a judicial exception and may be eligible. Use the 'markedly different characteristics' test and applicable case law (e.g., Myriad) to assess whether a claimed composition or organism is a product of nature or a patent‑eligible human-made invention.

name: Step 2B — Whether claim recites additional elements amounting to 'significantly more' (inventive concept)
description: If claim is directed to a judicial exception, determine whether additional claim elements, individually or in combination, transform the nature of the claim into a patent‑eligible application (i.e., whether they amount to significantly more than the exception).
guidance: The 'significantly more' inquiry looks for an inventive concept beyond the judicial exception. MPEP §2106.05 enumerates categories of considerations (improvements to technology, particular machine, particular transformation, whether elements are conventional/routine, other meaningful limitations, etc.) to determine if 'significantly more' exists.

name: Particular machine limitation
description: Recitation of a particular machine in the claims can support eligibility if the machine is specific and confines the claim beyond a generic computer.
guidance: Claims tied to a particular machine may limit the claim's scope sufficiently to amount to significantly more; however, merely reciting a generic computer or 'special purpose' computer is often insufficient. Evaluate whether the machine is particular and plays a meaningful role in implementing the claimed invention (§2106.05(b)).

name: Particular transformation (machine‑or‑transformation consideration)
description: A claimed transformation of a particular article to a different state or thing can support eligibility.
guidance: The machine‑or‑transformation test is a useful clue to eligibility: a particular transformation of an article can indicate that the claim poses patent‑eligible subject matter. But do not treat M‑O‑T as a separate test; consider it within the Alice/Mayo framework (see §2106.05(c)).

name: Well‑understood, routine, conventional activity does not confer eligibility
description: If the additional elements beyond the judicial exception are well‑understood, routine, or conventional in the field, they do not amount to significantly more.
guidance: Examiners must assess whether claimed additional elements merely recite conventional activity known in the art — if so, they cannot supply the inventive concept required at Step 2B (§2106.05(d)). Case law and MPEP examples illustrate when conventional features fail to transform an abstract idea into a patent‑eligible invention.

name: Mere instructions to apply an exception are insufficient
description: Claiming only instructions to apply a judicial exception (e.g., 'apply the algorithm') does not render the claim patent‑eligible.
guidance: If additional claim language simply tells a practitioner to implement an abstract idea or law of nature without more (no technical implementation or meaningful limitations), it is not 'significantly more' (§2106.05(f)).

name: Field of use or technological environment limitations alone are insufficient
description: Limiting the claim to a particular field of use or technological environment, by itself, does not make an otherwise abstract claim eligible.
guidance: A claim cannot be rendered nonabstract merely by reciting that it is implemented on the Internet or in a particular field; need meaningful technical improvement or other significantly more features (§2106.05(h)).

name: Streamlined analysis and eligibility pathways (Pathways A, B, C)
description: Use the flowchart pathways to determine eligibility: Pathway A (streamlined/self‑evident eligibility), Pathway B (falls within statutory category and not directed to judicial exception), Pathway C (directed to exception but recites significantly more).
guidance: If eligibility is self‑evident, examiners may use a streamlined Pathway A analysis (§2106.06). Pathway B applies when Step 1 = YES and Step 2A = NO (no exception). Pathway C applies when Step 1 = YES, Step 2A = YES, and Step 2B = YES (significantly more). If uncertain about streamlined analysis, perform full Alice/Mayo analysis. Claims not eligible under any pathway should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101.

name: Complete examination — use of other statutory provisions
description: Regardless of a §101 rejection or eligibility finding, the examiner should complete examination of each claim under other patentability requirements (35 U.S.C. 102, 103, 112, utility, inventorship, and non‑statutory double patenting).
guidance: §101 is a threshold inquiry but not the sole tool for patentability determinations; novelty, nonobviousness, and specification requirements may be applied to address deficiencies that §101 does not resolve (see Bilski and related citations).

name: Formulating and supporting §101 rejections and evaluating applicant responses
description: Use established form paragraphs and procedural practices when making §101 rejections and when evaluating applicant responses.
guidance: MPEP provides guidance on formulating and supporting rejections for lack of subject matter eligibility, recommended form paragraphs (e.g., 7.05, 7.05.01), how to evaluate applicant arguments/evidence, and how to clarify the record (§2106.07). Examiners should explain reasons for the rejection, identify the judicial exception, provide claim analysis under Alice/Mayo, and note recommended claim amendments when appropriate.

name: Motivation to combine prior art
description: A replacement or combination of an element from one cited reference with an element from another is supported when prior art suggests benefits (e.g., reduce device volume, reduce time) and there is no particular technical difficulty in making the replacement.
guidance: Courts look for sufficient motivation in the prior art (e.g., explicit disclosures of advantages) and absence of technical difficulty; if an element of a cited reference includes all constitutional elements of a claim and prior art suggests benefits, combination to reach the claim can be considered obvious.

name: Significance required for numerical limitations
description: A claimed numerical limitation (e.g., a concentration threshold) must have a recognized critical significance or show a remarkable effect within vs outside the claimed range to support inventiveness.
guidance: If the claim differs from prior art only by a numerical range, the specification must provide grounds, rationale, embodiments, or evidence showing a remarkable difference in effect tied to that numerical limit; absent such grounds, the numerical limitation alone is insufficient to establish inventiveness.

name: Product-by-process vs product claim inventive test
description: A product-by-process claim (defining a product by how it is made) may lack inventiveness if the completed product has no difference in structure or effect from a prior-art product; conversely, a process (manufacturing) claim can be inventive if the process feature is non-obvious and yields a distinguishable or remarkable effect.
guidance: Examine the completed product's structure/effect compared to prior art — if identical, product-by-process claim may fail. For process claims, determine whether the claimed process step(s) (e.g., 'fixing an ion exchange film to flow frames before stacking') could be easily derived and whether they produce a notable technical advantage.

name: First-to-file identity test (Article 36(1))
description: If an earlier-filed cited reference claim includes all the features of a later-filed claim and only adds an additional feature, and that additional feature is not an essential basic element, the earlier (narrower) claim can be deemed identical to the later (broader) claim, making the later-filed claim unpatentable under the first-to-file rule.
guidance: Assess whether common features can be separated from the additional feature and whether the additional feature is essential to the invention; if not essential and the earlier claim covers the common features, treat the inventions as identical for first-to-file purposes.

name: Specification description requirements for Markush-type claims (Article 42(3))
description: A Markush-type medicinal claim does not violate description requirements merely because some selective elements are not described as specific embodiments in the specification, provided a person of ordinary skill could understand and practice the effect of the invention from the specification and such effect can be fully expected.
guidance: Focus on enablement and sufficiency: if the spec allows the skilled person to carry out the invention and reasonably expect the claimed effect, missing specific embodiments of each Markush option do not automatically render the claim deficient.

name: Denied obviousness when combination requires abandoning core means
description: Ease in combining cited references is denied if deriving the claimed invention would require substantially modifying the structure of a cited reference to the extent of abandoning the means by which that reference solves its problem.
guidance: If combining a 'well-known' technology with a reference would destroy the core solution or create structural interference (e.g., wedge-inserting devices interfering with each other), the combination is not a straightforward derivation and obviousness may be denied.

name: Change of use requiring structural change can defeat obviousness
description: When the claimed device differs in use (and corresponding structure/strength/size) from the cited reference, shifting the use in an obviousness combination may not be feasible if it requires accompanying changes in the entire structure.
guidance: If deriving the claimed invention from a cited reference would necessitate substantial structural alterations tied to a different use (e.g., converting a cosmetic bottle to a chiropractic massager), a person of ordinary skill would not easily conceive that change and inventiveness may be upheld.

name: Statutory categories (35 U.S.C. 101)
description: 35 U.S.C. 101 defines four categories: processes, machines, manufactures and compositions of matter. The latter three define 'things' or 'products' while the first defines 'actions' (a series of steps or acts).
guidance: When determining whether a claim falls in a statutory category, verify the claim is to a process (method/series of acts) or to a physical/tangible machine, manufacture, or composition of matter. See MPEP §2106.03 for authoritative definitions and examples.

name: Broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim as a whole
description: It is essential that the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim be established prior to examining a claim for eligibility. The BRI sets the boundaries of the coverage sought by the claim and will influence whether the claim seeks to cover subject matter that is beyond the four statutory categories or encompasses subject matter that falls within the exceptions.
guidance: Determine applicant's invention by reviewing the entire disclosure and construing claims under BRI (see MPEP §2111). Claim interpretation affects Step 1 and both prongs of the Alice/Mayo test; if BRI covers non-statutory embodiments recommend amendments narrowing the claim.

name: Alice/Mayo two-part test (Step 2)
description: Step 2 (the Alice/Mayo test) is a two-part test: Step 2A — determine whether the claims are directed to an abstract idea, a law of nature or a natural phenomenon (a judicial exception). Step 2B — if so, determine whether the claim recites additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception.
guidance: The Alice/Mayo two-part test is the only test that should be used to evaluate eligibility. The second part is described as the 'search for an "inventive concept"'.
