The machine-or-transformation test may be considered as part of the 'integration' or 'significantly more' determination but is not a separate test.

name: Pathways A, B, and C for eligibility (flowchart)
description: Three pathways to eligibility are identified: Pathway A (claims falling within a statutory category whose eligibility is self-evident — streamlined analysis), Pathway B (claims within a statutory category and not directed to a judicial exception — Step 2A: NO), and Pathway C (claims within a statutory category, directed to a judicial exception, but reciting additional elements that amount to significantly more — Step 2B: YES).
guidance: If a claim could have been found eligible at Pathway A but is subjected to further analysis, it may still be eligible at B or C. If not eligible at any pathway, the claim is patent ineligible under 35 U.S.C. 101. Examiners uncertain whether to use streamlined analysis are encouraged to conduct a full eligibility analysis.

name: Eligibility Step 1: Whether a claim is to a statutory category
description: Step 1 asks: Is the claim to a process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter? Evaluation of this step should be made after determining what applicant has invented and construing the claims in accordance with BRI.
guidance: If a claim as a whole does not fall within any statutory category, it fails Step 1 and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101. If the BRI covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments, the claim embraces non-statutory subject matter and fails Step 1; best practice is to point out BRI and recommend narrowing amendments.

name: Examples of product claims that are not statutory
description: Non-limiting examples of claims that are not directed to any statutory category include: products that do not have a physical or tangible form (e.g., information/data per se or a computer program per se claimed as a product without structural recitations); transitory forms of signal transmission (signals per se); and subject matter expressly prohibited from patenting (e.g., humans per se).
guidance: Product claims must have physical or tangible form to fall within machine/manufacture/composition categories. Software expressed as code detached from any medium or an intangible collection of information may be non-statutory.

name: Abstract ideas — groupings, examples, and tentative abstract ideas
description: Abstract ideas encompass concepts such as certain methods of organizing human activity, mathematical formulas, and mental processes. The MPEP provides groupings and examples to help identify when claims do or do not recite abstract ideas, and notes some 'tentative' abstract ideas where further analysis is needed.
guidance: Use the MPEP examples and groupings (2106.04(a)(1)-(3)) to determine whether a claim recites an abstract idea; consider whether claimed steps are merely mental processes or fundamental economic practices, or if they integrate an idea into a practical application.

name: Laws of nature, natural phenomena & products of nature — 'markedly different characteristics' analysis
description: For claims implicating laws of nature, natural phenomena, or products of nature, assess whether the claimed subject matter exhibits markedly different characteristics compared to the natural product or phenomenon as found in nature.
guidance: If the claim recites a product of nature, examine whether it has been markedly altered or provided with distinctive characteristics by human intervention (see MPEP §2106.04(b)-(c)).

name: Step 2B subfactor: Improvements to computer functioning or other technology
description: One indication of 'significantly more' can be that the claim provides an improvement to the functioning of a computer or to any other technology or technical field.
guidance: Assess whether the claim's limitations improve computer or technological functionality (not merely use generic computer components to perform the abstract idea). See MPEP §2106.05(a) and case examples (e.g., Enfish, McRO).

name: Step 2B subfactor: Particular machine
description: Recitation of a particular machine can weigh in favor of eligibility if the machine is specific and integral to the claim rather than a generic computer or token recitation.
guidance: Distinguish between claims that tie the exception to a specific, claimed machine and those that merely recite a conventional computer. See MPEP §2106.05(b).

name: Step 2B subfactor: Particular transformation (machine-or-transformation relevance)
description: Particular transformation of an article by the claimed process (the 'transformation' prong of the machine-or-transformation test) can support a finding of 'significantly more.'
guidance: The machine-or-transformation test is an important clue and should be considered as part of the 'integration' or 'significantly more' determination, but it is not a separate eligibility test. See MPEP §2106.05(c).

name: Step 2B subfactor: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity
description: If the additional elements are well-understood, routine, conventional activities previously known in the field, they do not amount to 'significantly more.'
guidance: Examiners should evaluate whether claim limitations are merely generic or conventional steps that add nothing inventive. See MPEP §2106.05(d) and case law indicating routine/conventional elements are insufficient.

name: Step 2B subfactor: Other meaningful limitations
description: Other meaningful limitations beyond mere implementation of the exception — e.g., specific non-conventional steps or details that transform how the exception is applied — can contribute to a 'significantly more' finding.
guidance: Consider limitations that impose meaningful bounds on the claim or provide technical benefits; see MPEP §2106.05(e).

name: Step 2B subfactor: Mere instructions to apply an exception
description: Claims that are effectively 'mere instructions to apply an exception' (e.g., telling a user to apply an abstract idea) do not add 'significantly more.'
guidance: Such claim language is insufficient to confer eligibility; examine whether the claim adds technical implementation details beyond instruction-level recitations. See MPEP §2106.05(f).

name: Streamlined analysis — Eligibility is self-evident
description: If a claim's eligibility is self-evident (i.e., clearly not directed to an exception or clearly amounts to significantly more), examiners may use a streamlined analysis (Pathway A).
guidance: When eligibility is self-evident, a streamlined finding of eligibility at Pathway A is appropriate. If uncertain, conduct the full Alice/Mayo analysis to promote consistency.

name: Streamlined analysis — Clear improvement to a technology or computer functionality
description: A claim that shows a clear improvement to a technology or to computer functionality can be eligible via a streamlined analysis.
guidance: Use MPEP §2106.06(b) examples and case law to determine whether the improvement is clear enough to warrant streamlined treatment (e.g., improvements recognized in Enfish, McRO).

name: 35 U.S.C. 101 is a threshold test — consider other patentability requirements
description: 35 U.S.C. 101 is not the sole tool for determining patentability; 35 U.S.C. 112, 35 U.S.C. 102, and 35 U.S.C. 103 provide additional tools to ensure claims meet the conditions for patentability.
guidance: Even if a claim is eligible under §101, it must still meet novelty, nonobviousness, enablement/written description, utility, inventorship, and other requirements. Examiners should complete examinations under 102, 103, 112, and utility/double-patenting considerations as applicable.

name: Conditions for claiming a “grace period for not losing novelty”
description: To claim the 6-month novelty grace period, disclosure must have occurred within six months before application, applicant must submit statement to CNIPA within two months after learning of disclosure with supporting materials, the disclosed solution must be directly/indirectly derived from applicant/inventor, and disclosure was without applicant’s consent.
guidance: (Case No. 5W135853 Integrated Bracket Floating Breakwater Bracket)

name: Consideration of parameter characteristics in technological inspiration
description: For claims with specific parameter features, if closest prior art has same components and similar parameters and provides guidance on parameter selection, and patent spec doesn't show the parameters yield significantly better effects, the parameters are routine choices.
guidance: (Case No. 4W117515 Method for producing knot yarn and vortex nozzle)

name: Examination of inventiveness for claims with parameter relationships in optical lenses
description: For optical imaging systems designed with software, judge creativity by retracing design process; consider whether creative work determined initial structure and parameter constraints. Classify parameters into those with inevitable linkage and those without; linkage implications affect whether parameters can be fixed or change during optimization.
guidance: (Case No. 4W115749 Camera Optical Lens)

name: Understanding of “Created Words” in claims
description: Terms in claims are generally understood with meanings commonly used in the technical field. For made-up words without common meaning, interpret objectively based on claim limitations, description of the technical problem, and technical effects in the specification; patent examination files are references for scope understanding.
guidance: (Case No. 4W117583)

name: Understanding the scope of protection of process claims
description: For method claims, if a skilled person can determine that a certain process step is implicitly defined by other steps through overall understanding of process flow and connections, then even if not in claim text it should be considered part of scope of protection.
guidance: (Case No. 4W117474 Preparation of Acrylic Acid)

name: Claims should be based on the description — support determination based on intended technical problem
description: Whether a claim is supported by the description should be determined based on the technical problem the invention intends to solve, using background, objectives, technical problem/beneficial effects, and specific implementation content, not on the technical problem actually solved in inventive step analysis.
guidance: (Case No. 1F678174 Preparation Method of Hydroxymethylfurfural)

name: Understanding the “generalization of claims” in support judgments
description: When judging support, clarify the technical problem the patent intends to solve and then assess whether claim generalization departs from the technical means and problem as disclosed in the specification.
guidance: (Case No. 5W135482 A power tool)

name: Interpreting “amendment timing” and claim text in consolidated hearings
description: When two invalidation requests are heard together and the patentee submits amendment text timely for one request but not the other, the amendment text that meets timing should be used for the combined hearing to maintain consistency of examination text.
guidance: (Case No. 5W132976/5W133604 A rotating opening and closing base structure and air purifier)

name: Amendment requirements for claim scope narrowing
description: Amendments must not add new technical content beyond original disclosure; narrowing claim scope is permitted but must be supported by the original application.
guidance: General principle reflected across claim/amendment decisions. (Implied across claims-related cases)

name: Determination of added subject-matter when amending claims
description: Amendments are disallowed if they introduce technical content that a skilled person could not derive directly and unambiguously from the original disclosure; the support requirement is assessed in light of the technical problem and the original description.
guidance: Applied in support and amendment cases (referenced in multiple case points).

name: Determine correspondence between sales page and product on shopping website
description: If a shopping website assigns unique product codes to items, there is generally a strict correspondence between sales page and physical product identified by code unless evidence shows platform rules violated; burden of proof lies with party claiming mismatch.
guidance: (Case No. 5W132976/5W133604 A rotating opening and closing base structure and air purifier)

name: Examination of cases involving conflicts between design patents and copyrights
description: When petitioner claims work was made into animated video and publicized and thus patentee had access, first examine relevance between work and video, relationship of copyright holder and publisher, similarity of static/dynamic images and timing; then determine whether release constitutes disclosure per platform mechanisms—if public before application date, patentee had access.
guidance: (Case No. 6W127201 Milk Dragon Fan)

name: Structural-alteration criterion
description: A claimed molecule may be patent-eligible if its chemical structure is meaningfully altered from the naturally occurring counterpart (the Federal Circuit's rationale permitting cDNA-like claims because of structural change).
guidance: Evaluate whether extraction or synthetic manipulation changes chemical structure (e.g., removal of introns in cDNA) and whether such structural changes are sufficiently distinct to support eligibility — noting the Supreme Court's ambiguous treatment of this rationale in Myriad.

name: Information/content sameness criterion
description: If the claimed molecule embodies the same nucleotide 'coding information' as the native molecule, it may be treated as a product of nature (Justice Thomas’s emphasis in Myriad).
guidance: Assess whether the claim essentially captures the same informational template/process (coding sequence) as found in nature; be aware this approach conflicts with structural tests and produces indeterminate results when structure and information diverge.

name: Preemption of downstream innovation
description: A central policy rationale for §101 exclusions is to avoid claims that preempt future uses and downstream technologies — the 'storehouse of knowledge' concern.
guidance: Analyze whether the claim would block future inventive activity or practical applications that would otherwise be available to all; heavy preemption risk argues for exclusion or narrowing of claims under §101 (as in Mayo/Alice reasoning).

name: §112 disclosure / commensurability as claim-limiting tool
description: Disclosure doctrines (§112) and commensurability requirements can limit overly broad product claims and may be more appropriate than a categorical §101 exclusion.
guidance: Where claims are broad or foundational, consider whether specification and claim scope are commensurate; use §112 to constrain claim breadth rather than importing a sweeping §101 rule in every case.

name: Claim breadth, disclosed embodiments, and cumulative-improvement factors
description: Commentators propose multi-factor tests (claim breadth, number of disclosed embodiments, likelihood of cumulative improvements) to determine whether a claim is 'fundamental' or overbroad.
guidance: Use these indicia as proxies for preemption risk and ‘fundamentality’; the author recognizes merit in such multi-factor approaches but cautions about their problematic application to material/product claims.

name: Functional-attributes versus structural-claims distinction
description: Courts often conflate discussion of a material’s 'qualities' (functional attributes) with the patent claim, but claims typically assert structures, not mere properties.
guidance: Avoid treating statements about natural qualities as if the patent directly claims those qualities; analyze the claim language to see whether it claims a structure/composition or merely tries to monopolize a property or natural quality.

name: Inventive concept requirement (Mayo/Alice step-two) applied to products
description: After identifying a 'building-block' or natural product, analyze whether the claim contains an 'inventive concept' sufficient to transform it into patent-eligible subject matter.
guidance: Recognize the article's critique that it's unclear what constitutes an 'inventive concept' for tangible compositions (unlike specialized hardware/software examples); courts must articulate concrete indicia for product cases.

name: Use other doctrinal levers rather than broad §101 exclusions (policy-driven, invention-by-invention approach)
description: The author suggests the possible need for a more granular, invention-specific policy lever (e.g., refined §112, §103, or guidelines) instead of expansive §101 rejections to police fundamental product claims.
guidance: Consider tailoring remedies—claim construction, §112 disclosure limits, novelty/obviousness analyses, and specific statutory rules—before resorting to categorical §101 exclusions that are difficult to administrate for products.

name: Lead compound selection (chemical cases)
description: Obviousness based on structural similarity requires identification of some motivation that would have led a person of ordinary skill to select and modify a known compound (a 'lead compound') to achieve the claimed compound.
guidance: The 'lead compound' concept may be applied flexibly — any known compound might serve as a lead compound for obviousness purposes (Eisai). Structural similarity can supply the reason to modify; an expectation of similar properties (in light of the totality of the prior art) can be sufficient even without an explicit prior-art teaching. A lead compound used for obviousness need not be one pharmaceutical chemists would pick for development (e.g., could be inactive) but there still must be some reason to start with it beyond mere existence (Altana, Altana/Teva; Altana/compound 12).

name: Reason to modify and reasonable expectation of success (chemistry)
description: To show obviousness of a claimed chemical compound, there must be both a reason to modify a prior art compound and a reasonable expectation of success in making the claimed compound.
guidance: Procter & Gamble v. Teva: even if a prior-art compound is presumed an appropriate lead, there must be evidence that the modifications would have been routine and that one of ordinary skill would have expected success. Lack of routine modifications or reasonable expectation of success supports nonobviousness. Unexpected results (e.g., superior potency, lower toxicity) can rebut a prima facie obviousness showing.

name: Predictability and the skill of the ordinary artisan
description: Obviousness rationales depending on known techniques assume the results would have been predictable to one of ordinary skill; if application would have been beyond that skill, the claim is not obvious.
guidance: KSR cautions that if the actual application of the technique would have been beyond the skill of one of ordinary skill in the art, then using the technique would not have been obvious. Always tie predictability findings back to Graham factual inquiries; include any additional facts necessary to explain the conclusion of obviousness. 'If any of these findings cannot be made, then this rationale cannot be used to support a conclusion that the claim would have been obvious.'

name: Specification and related parts interpret the Claims
description: The entire specification, with the drawings, model, oath, and title, are to be considered as interpreting the Claims.
guidance: Explanations contained in the specification are to be taken as the inventor's own interpreter of the meaning of his Claim and of the essential qualities of the invention protected by his patent; the whole specification may and should be looked at to learn from the description of the invention (cases cited: Mathews v. Iron Clad Mfg. Co., Ex parte Holt, Bruce v. Mader, etc.).

name: Clear and explicit Claim language controls
description: Where a Claim is clear and explicit its language controls its meaning, without referring to the specification.
guidance: If terms are clear, the claim must be construed by its words; the specification cannot enlarge a clear claim (cites Rich v. Close).

name: Claims may be restricted by the descriptive parts but never enlarged
description: In construing Claims by descriptive portions, the scope of the Claims may often be restricted, but can never be enlarged.
guidance: Claims must be limited to the invention communicated to the public; liberal construction requires interpreting other patent parts broadly but cannot expand Claims beyond what the description legitimately supports.

name: General words limited by the real nature of the invention
description: General words in a description or Claim are to be limited by the real nature of the invention.
guidance: A Claim's generality is trimmed by the actual invention described in the specification and by the real nature and purpose of the invention (Fischer v. Hayes and related authorities).

name: A general Claim is limited to the invention described in the specification
description: A general Claim will be limited to the invention described in the specification.
guidance: Although a Claim may read broadly, it is confined to the invention as described; inventor may abandon parts of described matter and Claims cannot be stretched beyond the described disclosure.

name: Claims are not necessarily limited by drawings when specification shows broader invention
description: Claims are not limited by drawings when the specification shows that the real invention was broader.
guidance: If the specification demonstrates a broader conception, drawings do not confine the Claim to the precise figures shown (Hamilton v. Ives example).

name: When Claim requires no explanation, use ordinary meaning; otherwise investigate history and art
description: If the Claim requires no explanation, the court expounds it by the ordinary meaning of its words. If explanation is required, the entire field of inquiry (history of the art, inventor statements, other facts) is open to determine the true invention.
guidance: When claim ambiguous, seek what the plaintiffs claimed as their invention by looking to specification and external evidence of the inventor's view (Rich v. Close; other notes).

name: Combination claims construed broadly to support the combination
description: A Claim for a combination is to be construed liberally in order to support the combination, even though another Claim is made for a special arrangement of the same elements.
guidance: But limitations imposed by inventor (especially after rejection) act as disclaimers and must be strictly construed in favor of the public; if a combination is shown old, claim may be read as covering particular elements employed (Be parte Marsh; Sargent v. Hall; other cites).

name: A combination Claim includes everything expressed or necessarily implied to be material
description: A Claim for a combination includes everything which is either expressed or necessarily implied to be material to the combination.
guidance: All claimed elements are regarded as material in construing the patent; however, if a claimed element is expressly disclaimed, the claim cannot be construed to cover it (Thompson v. Gildersleeve; Shaver v. Skinner Mfg. Co.).

name: Cannot eliminate an expressly claimed element or treat a claimed useless element as immaterial
description: The courts cannot, by construction, eliminate a claimed element of a combination simply because it is practically useless.
guidance: Claimed elements must be treated as material; construction cannot excise a claimed element on the ground of practical uselessness (Williams v. Stolzenbach and authorities).

name: Claims for principles/forces interpreted as claims for the instrument or operation applying them
description: A Claim for the principle or force employed in an invention will be interpreted, if possible, as a Claim for the instrument or operation by which the force is applied to its appropriate object.
guidance: Courts prefer to limit abstract principle claims to concrete means/devices when specification indicates such; see Union Paper Bag Co. v. Nixon and related notes.

name: Functional claims construed to cover the device performing the function
description: A Claim for a function, where the specification describes the device or apparatus which performs it, will be construed as intended to cover such apparatus or device.
guidance: Functional language is read in light of the specification's described means; use cases: Albany Steam Trap Co. v. Felthousen and others.

name: Result/effect claims construed as means if specification supports
description: A Claim for a result or effect will be considered as a Claim for the means by which the effect is produced, if the specification, as a whole, is open to that interpretation.
guidance: If the specification describes means for achieving the result, the claim can be read as limited to those means (Palmer v. Galling Gun Co.; Henderson v. Cleveland Co-operating Stove Co.).

name: A Claim for an entirety (multi-part instrument/process) is not divisible by construction
description: A Claim for an entire instrument or process consisting of several steps or divisible parts cannot usually be divided by construction so as to cover the independent members separately.
guidance: Unless the specification indicates the inventor intended separate claims for parts, a whole claim stands as a unit (National Car Brake Shoe Co. v. Lake Shore & Michigan Southern R.R. Co.; Evans v. Kelly).

name: Two separate Claims cannot be construed together as one to support each other
description: Two apparently separate Claims cannot be construed as one Claim and be thus supported by each other.
guidance: Each claim must stand on its own terms; courts will not merge separate claims to save invalid ones (Seymour v. McCormick and related citations).

name: 'Substantially as described' and 'as herein described' refer to the specification
description: The phrase 'substantially as described' (and similar phrases like 'as herein described') in the Claim signifies much or little as the patentee evidently designed and refers the Claim to the specification for fuller statement.
guidance: Such phrases are always supposed incorporated and relate only to material features of the invention; they enable a claim that on its face covers only a function/result to be construed by the described means (Seymour v. Osborne, Matthews v. Schoneberger).

name: Title and names construed in connection with specification and drawings
description: The names and terms used by the patentee are to be construed in view of the entire specification and drawings; the title should agree with the specification but does not control.
guidance: Title is taken in connection with the specification and drawings and is given a liberal construction; title alone does not control claim scope (Foye v. Nichols; Goodyear v. Railroad examples).

name: Drawings construed by the specification; drawings cannot change the character of the invention
description: Drawings are to be construed by the specifications; but drawings cannot be used to change the character of the invention described in the specification.
guidance: Drawings may aid or illustrate, and may be interpreted by the model, but they cannot be used to alter the descriptive disclosure; they can also demonstrate that the claimed machine is not the one for which it issued in some cases (Burrall v. Jewett; Hancock Inspirator Co. v. Jenks).

name: Claims cannot be enlarged by correspondence or proceedings before the Patent Office
description: The Claims of a patent cannot be enlarged by the correspondence of the inventor with the Patent Office, nor by the proceedings pending the application.
guidance: While the specification may aid construction, the claims remain limited to what was legitimately communicated and cannot be expanded by subsequent prosecution history beyond that disclosure (general principle stated in the treatise).

name: Claim 1 importance / claim-level targeting
description: Claim 1 is an independent claim and typically the broadest and most important claim; objections on claim 1 hit the core of the application.
guidance: FERs that explicitly target claim 1 with 3(d) (or novelty/inventive step) indicate examiners are striking the application's core. Analysis should distinguish objections 'on claim 1' vs. objections without specified claims because FER vagueness can obscure claim-level targeting.

name: FER specificity vs ambiguity
description: First Examination Reports (FERs) vary in specificity: some directly indicate which claims are objected to, others simply state 'claims fail to satisfy' without specifying claim numbers.
guidance: Ambiguous FER language is an anti-pattern for claim-level analysis; trend toward more specific FERs over time improves ability to attribute objections to particular claims. Analysts should code FERs as 'objection including claim 1', 'objection not directed at claim 1', or 'objection without specific claims'.

name: Ambiguity/limitations of available data (coding and measurement)
description: FER quality varies over time; earlier FERs often vague, later FERs more specific. Data truncation (e.g., Indian data truncated to 2012 at the time of collection) and missing final decisions for many FERs limit inference.
guidance: Researchers should document coding rules, sample restrictions (e.g., PCT July priority month), and account for censoring when interpreting trends in FER prevalence, claim-level attribution, and grant rates.

name: Third‑party observations — eligibility and content
description: Third parties may, anonymously if so desired, file observations under the PCT which ... should exclusively refer to prior art relevant to the novelty and/or inventive step of the invention claimed in the international application.
guidance: Observations are to be submitted electronically to the IB using WIPO's online tool between international publication and 28 months from the priority date. They may be filed in any language of publication and the cited prior art may be in any language. See WIPO 'ePCT Third Party Observations' guide. The applicant is notified by the IB and may file comments within 30 months from the priority date. Any third‑party observations/comments will be made available for public inspection.

name: IPER completion — same criteria and scope as WO‑ISA; searched claims only
description: The IPER is drafted in the same way as the WO‑ISA; a positive or negative opinion will be given for all claims, taking into account arguments/amendments submitted by the applicant. The same criteria apply as to the WO‑ISA with respect to examination issues.
guidance: The IPER will only be established for claims which have been searched (as indicated in the WO‑ISA); any amended claims that are directed to subject‑matter not searched will not be considered and an indication will be made in Section III of the IPER (non‑establishment of opinion), with reasons on the separate sheet. See Rule 66.1(e).

name: Request to examine different sets of claims for different elected States — not accepted
description: Filing different sets of claims for different elected States or different (main and auxiliary) requests based on different sets of claims is not accepted under the PCT.
guidance: Examining multiple co‑pending requests is time‑consuming and contrary to PCT intention; auxiliary requests are not provided for. If a preferred request is clear (e.g., main request), the WO‑IPEA/IPER is established on that request with a remark that treatment of different requests is not provided under the PCT. If unclear, the applicant is asked (preferably by telephone) to furnish one set only or state which set should be used. If no reply and applicant insists on plurality, WO‑IPEA/IPER drawn up on the first set with a remark recorded under Section I.

name: Request to examine certain claims only — not accepted
description: A request by the applicant to establish the IPER for certain claims only (without formally restricting the set of claims) is not accepted.
guidance: The IPER is established on the claims on file and can only be restricted by the examiner (e.g., lack of unity, unsearched claims, clarity, added subject‑matter). A restriction at the applicant's request would be contrary to Art.35(2), which states the IPER relates to 'each claim'. Applicants are informed that unless a restricted set of claims is filed the IPER will be established for all claims.

name: Title — brevity and alignment with description/claims
description: The title must be short and precise and should first state the title of the invention as appearing in the request (Rule 5.1(a)).
guidance: The examiner should review the title in light of the description and claims and any amendments thereto to ensure the title is concise and gives a clear and adequate indication of the subject of the invention. If amendments change claim categories, the examiner should check whether a corresponding amendment to the title is needed (may not go beyond disclosure as filed). See ISPE Guidelines for further provisions.

name: Patent Prosecution Highway (PPH) — eligibility and basis
description: The PPH enables an applicant whose claims have been determined to be patentable/allowable to have a corresponding application filed with a PPH partner office processed in an accelerated manner while allowing offices to exploit available work results.
guidance: Under the PPH pilot programme a PPH request can be based on the latest PCT work product (WO‑ISA or IPRP/IPER) established by one of the PPH partner offices as ISA or IPEA (PPH based on PCT work products), or on national work products indicating patentable/allowable claims (PPH based on national work products). Procedures/requirements for filing PPH requests are available from partner offices' websites. Irrespective of PPH, applicants may request accelerated examination under the EPO PACE programme at any time.

name: Nexus requirement between claimed invention and evidence
description: For an evidentiary declaration to be relevant, there must be a nexus between the invention as claimed and the evidence provided in the declaration.
guidance: Examples: a SMED may demonstrate how one of ordinary skill in the art would interpret a specification that describes a technological improvement to show the claimed invention is patent-eligible; the examiner must determine whether the SMED improperly supplements the specification and whether a nexus exists before weighing the evidence.

name: Legal conclusions vs factual bases
description: An opinion as to the legal conclusion itself (e.g., that the claim is eligible or ineligible) is not entitled to weight, while the underlying factual basis for the opinion may be persuasive.
guidance: Declarants should provide factual evidence and the factual basis for expert conclusions (state of the art, test results, specific structural/operational details) rather than mere legal opinions.

name: SMEDs can demonstrate how a claim is not a judicial exception or is integrated into a practical application
description: A SMED may demonstrate that a claim does not recite a judicial exception, identify when a judicial exception is integrated into a practical application, or demonstrate that a claim amounts to significantly more than a judicial exception.
guidance: Use factual evidence (expert testimony, objective data, explanation of how claimed elements effect a practical application) to show integration into a practical application under Alice Step 2 (e.g., the additional elements apply/use the exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis). Examiners should evaluate nexus and non-supplementation before relying on these showings.

name: Types of factual showings that can rebut Step 2 rejections (illustrative scenarios)
description: Specific factual showings that may be persuasive under Alice Step 2 include: (a) evidence that claimed limitations cannot practically be performed in the human mind; (b) evidence the claim improves the functioning of a computer or another technology; (c) objective comparative testing showing superior performance of a claimed architecture; (d) evidence that claimed rules enable automation of tasks previously subjective to humans; (e) evidence that additional claim elements effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis; and (f) evidence that an unconventional arrangement of conventional elements provides technical advantages.
guidance: The memo provides multiple hypotheticals illustrating each type (e.g., distributed network monitoring that cannot be done in the human mind; self-referential table improving storage and retrieval; neural network architecture with objective comparative testing; animation automation supported by trade articles; prophylaxis schedule adjustment that lowers disease risk; remote ISP filtering arrangement providing efficient operations). In each case, examiner must ensure no improper supplementation and a nexus exists before weighing the evidence under the preponderance standard.

name: Desjardins precedent and what counts as 'something more' under Alice
description: Improvements in computational performance, learning, storage, data sets and structures, and changes to system architecture (how information flows) can constitute patent-eligible technological advancements under the Alice framework when properly shown.
guidance: The memo cites the precedential ARP decision In re Desjardins and emphasizes that Section 101 remains a gatekeeper but must be applied properly; §§102/103/112 remain the proper inquiries for defining claim scope. When evaluating 'something more,' consider how the invention is applied, how it operates, and what it accomplished (architectural/system-level changes are particularly probative).

name: ¶ 7.37.08 Unpersuasive Argument: Arguing Limitations Which Are Not Claimed
description: If applicant relies on features not recited in the rejected claim(s), those features should not be read into the claims; claims are interpreted in light of the specification but limitations from the specification are not read into the claims.
guidance: In bracket 1, recite the features applicant relies upon but which are not recited in the claims. Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.37.

name: ¶ 7.37.09 Unpersuasive Argument: Intended Use
description: A recitation of the intended use of the claimed invention must result in a structural difference between the claimed invention and the prior art to patentably distinguish; if the prior art structure can perform the intended use, it meets the claim.
guidance: Briefly restate applicant’s arguments about intended use in bracket 1. Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.37.

name: ¶ 7.37.10 Unpersuasive Argument: Limitation(s) in Preamble
description: A preamble is generally not accorded patentable weight where it merely recites the purpose of a process or intended use of a structure and the body of the claim stands alone; recitations in the preamble will not be given patentable weight absent structural dependence.
guidance: In bracket 1, state the preamble recitation applicant is arguing about. Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.37. Cite In re Hirao and Kropa v. Robie.

name: ¶ 7.37.11 Unpersuasive Argument: General Allegation of Patentability
description: Applicant’s arguments that amount to general allegations that the claims define a patentable invention fail to comply with 37 CFR 1.111(b) because they do not specifically point out how claim language patentably distinguishes from references.
guidance: Use when applicant's response is a general assertion of patentability without specific comparison to cited art. Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.37.

name: ¶ 7.38.01 Arguments Persuasive, Previous Rejection/Objection Withdrawn
description: Applicant’s arguments, see [1], filed [2], with respect to [3] have been fully considered and are persuasive. The [4] of [5] has been withdrawn.
guidance: Bracket instructions: identify pages/lines of applicant remarks (bracket1), file date (bracket2), claims/figures/specification (bracket3), the rejection/objection being withdrawn (bracket4), and the new ground(s) or subject matter (bracket5). Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.37.

name: ¶ 7.38.02 Arguments Persuasive, New Ground(s) of Rejection
description: Applicant’s arguments do not comply with 37 CFR 1.111(c) because they do not clearly point out the patentable novelty which they think the claims present in view of the art or show how amendments avoid such references or objections. Applicant’s arguments, filed [2], are persuasive; the rejection has been withdrawn but a new ground(s) of rejection is made in view of [5].
guidance: Must identify applicant arguments (bracket1), filing date (bracket2), claims at issue (bracket3), statutory basis for previous rejection (bracket4), and the basis for the new ground(s) of rejection (bracket5). Precede with form paragraph 7.37.

name: Drawings‑only limitation
description: The use of colour or greyscale is strictly limited to the drawings. The Notice is unambiguous that the use of colour or greyscale in the description, claims, or abstract is inadmissible.
guidance: If the description, claims or abstract are filed with colour, those elements will be converted to black and white for publication. Applicants must therefore confine colour to the drawings themselves.

name: Advisory: avoid referring to colours in text ("Don't Say Red")
description: Applicants are advised not to refer to colour‑specific features of the drawings in the description, claims or abstract (e.g. stating a component is "beige" or "yellow"), since colour specifications may not always be reliably and objectively identifiable.
guidance: Do not make claim or description language depend on colour-based distinctions. Instead, describe features by structure, material, position, or other non-colour attributes to avoid clarity/sufficiency problems.

name: Relative Term - Term of Degree Rendering Claim Indefinite
description: The term “[1]” in claim [2] is a relative term which renders the claim indefinite. The term “[1]” is not defined by the claim, the specification does not provide a standard for ascertaining the requisite degree, and one of ordinary skill in the art would not be reasonably apprised of the scope of the invention.
guidance: Examiner Note: In bracket 3, explain which parameter, quantity, or other limitation in the claim has been rendered indefinite by the use of the term appearing in bracket 1. This form paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.34.01.

name: Broader Range And Narrow Range/Limitation in Same Claim Indefiniteness
description: A broad range or limitation together with a narrow range or limitation that falls within the broad range or limitation (in the same claim) is considered indefinite since the resulting claim does not clearly set forth the metes and bounds of the patent protection desired.
guidance: Explains risk where broad language is followed by 'such as' and then narrow language (may be exemplary or required). Cite MPEP § 2173.05(c) and decisions (Ex parte Wu, Steigewald, Hall, Hasche). Examiner Note: insert broader and narrower ranges in brackets; may be modified to fit other instances. Must be preceded by 7.34.01.

name: Lack of Antecedent Basis in the Claims
description: Claim [1] recites the limitation [2] in [3]. There is insufficient antecedent basis for this limitation in the claim.
guidance: Examiner Note: In bracket 2, insert the limitation which lacks antecedent basis (e.g., 'said lever' or 'the lever'). In bracket 3, identify where the limitation appears. Use ONLY in aggravated situations where lack of antecedent basis makes scope indeterminate. Must be preceded by 7.34.01.

name: Use Claims (claiming a 'use' without steps) Indefinite / 35 U.S.C. 101 Issue
description: Claim [1] provides for the use of [2], but since the claim does not set forth any steps delimiting how this use is practiced, it is unclear what method/process applicant is intending to encompass. A claim is indefinite where it merely recites a use without any active, positive steps delimiting how this use is practiced.
guidance: Such a recitation can be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 as not being a proper process claim. Example cases: Ex parte Dunki; Clinical Products, Ltd. v. Brenner. Examiner Note: 'such as' may render claim indefinite (see MPEP § 2173.05(d)). Must be preceded by 7.34.01.

name: Modifier of 'Means' Lacks Function (Means-Plus-Function Defect)
description: The word 'means' is preceded by the word(s) '[2]' attempting a 'means' clause to recite an element as a means for performing a specified function; however, since no function is specified by the word(s) preceding 'means,' it is impossible to determine equivalents of the element as required by 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph.
guidance: Examiner Note: In bracket 2 insert what is being used (e.g., 'the monoclonal antibodies of claim 4'). See MPEP § 2173.05(q). Must be preceded by 7.34.01. Additional guidance: words before 'means' must convey a function (e.g., 'latch means' is definite; 'conduit means' is indefinite).

name: Claims Are a Literal Translation (Narrative/Grammatical Indefiniteness)
description: The claims are generally narrative and indefinite, failing to conform with current U.S. practice. They appear to be a literal translation into English from a foreign document and are replete with grammatical and idiomatic errors.
guidance: Use this form paragraph when claims are narrative in form and indefinite. Must be preceded by 7.34.01.

name: Indefinite Claim Language: 'For Example'
description: The phrase 'for example' renders the claim indefinite because it is unclear whether the limitations following the phrase are part of the claimed invention.
guidance: See MPEP § 2173.05(d). Must be preceded by 7.34.01.

name: Indefinite Claim Language: 'Or The Like'
description: The phrase 'or the like' renders the claim(s) indefinite because the claim(s) include(s) elements not actually disclosed (those encompassed by 'or the like'), thereby rendering the scope of the claim(s) unascertainable.
guidance: See MPEP § 2173.05(d). Must be preceded by 7.34.01.

name: Indefinite Claim Language: 'Such As'
description: The phrase 'such as' can render the claim indefinite because it is unclear whether the features introduced by such language are merely exemplary or required features of the claims.
guidance: This rejection must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.02 or 7.103. (Related to broader/narrow language issues.)

name: Essential Steps Omitted (35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph - method gaps)
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as being incomplete for omitting essential steps, such omission amounting to a gap between the steps. The omitted steps are: [2].
guidance: This rejection must be preceded by 7.30.02 or 7.103. In bracket 2, recite the steps omitted and give rationale why omitted steps are critical/essential.

name: Essential Elements Omitted (35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph - structural gaps)
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as being incomplete for omitting essential elements, such omission amounting to a gap between the elements. The omitted elements are: [2].
guidance: This rejection must be preceded by 7.30.02 or 7.103. In bracket 2, recite omitted elements and rationale for criticality.

name: Essential Cooperative Relationships Omitted (structural relationships missing)
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as being incomplete for omitting essential structural cooperative relationships of elements, such omission amounting to a gap between the necessary structural connections. The omitted structural cooperative relationships are: [2].
guidance: This rejection must be preceded by 7.30.02 or 7.103. In bracket 2, recite omitted cooperative relationships and rationale for considering them critical or essential.

name: Rejection Under 35 U.S.C. 112, Pro Se (narrative claims from pro se applicants)
description: Claim [1] rejected as failing to define the invention in the manner required by 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph. The claim(s) are narrative in form and replete with indefinite language; structure must be clearly and positively specified and claims must be in one-sentence form.
guidance: Useful for pro se filings where claims are disorganized/narrative. Note format of claims in cited patents. Use when pro se deficiencies make scope indefinite.

name: Unclear Whether Recited Structure/Material/Acts Preclude Application of 35 U.S.C. 112, Sixth Paragraph
description: The claim limitation '[1]' uses 'means for' or 'step for' or a non-structural term coupled with functional language, but is modified by some structure, material, or acts recited in the claim. It is unclear whether the recited structure, material, or acts are sufficient for performing the claimed function because [2].
guidance: Provide bracketed explanations: (1) recite limitation in bracket 1, (2) explain why it is unclear whether limitation invokes 112 sixth paragraph. May be used when ambiguous; must be preceded by 7.30.02 and 7.34.01.

name: Unclear Whether Claim Limitation Invokes 35 U.S.C. 112, Sixth Paragraph When 'Means for' Not Used
description: Applicant asserts that claim element '[1]' invokes 112 sixth paragraph, but it is unclear because [2]. Applicant may amend to include 'means for' or 'step for' (properly modified) or present sufficient showing that the claim recites insufficient structure, material, or acts to preclude application of 112 sixth paragraph.
guidance: Examiner Note: Use in reply situations where applicant argued invocation of sixth paragraph though phrase 'means for' isn't used. Must be preceded by 7.30.02 and 7.34.01. See MPEP § 706.07(a) for final action guidance.

name: No Disclosure or Insufficient Disclosure of Corresponding Structure for Means-Plus-Function (112 Sixth Paragraph)
description: Claim element '[1]' invokes 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph. However, the written description fails to disclose the corresponding structure, material, or acts for the claimed function. [2]
guidance: Applicant should either (a) amend the specification to expressly recite the corresponding structure/material/acts and link them to the function without introducing new matter, or (b) state on the record what corresponding structure/material/acts (implicitly/inherently set forth) perform the function. In brackets, recite limitation and explain insufficiency. Must be preceded by 7.30.02 and 7.34.01. See 37 CFR 1.75(d) and MPEP §§ 608.01(o), 2181.

name: Fails To Clearly Link or Associate Disclosed Structure to Function (Means-Plus-Function Linkage)
description: Claim element '[1]' invokes 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph. However, the written description fails to clearly link or associate the disclosed structure, material, or acts to the claimed function such that one of ordinary skill would recognize what performs the claimed function. [2]
guidance: Applicant may: (a) amend claim to avoid sixth paragraph interpretation, or (b) amend written description to expressly recite or clearly link corresponding structure/material/acts to function (without new matter), or (c) state on the record where the corresponding structure is set forth in spec. In brackets, recite limitation and explain why linkage is unclear. Must be preceded by 7.30.02 and 7.34.01. See 37 CFR 1.75(d) and MPEP §§ 608.01(o), 2181.

name: Omnibus Claim Rejection (Fails to Particularly Point Out and Distinctly Claim)
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as being indefinite in that it fails to point out what is included or excluded by the claim language. This claim is an omnibus type claim.
guidance: Use to reject 'omnibus' type claims (example: 'A device substantially as shown and described.'). Must be preceded by 7.30.02 or 7.103. No further explanation necessary. See MPEP § 1302.04(b) for cancellation by examiner's amendment upon allowance.

name: Trademark or Trade Name as a Limitation in the Claim
description: Claim [1] contains the trademark/trade name [2]. Where a trademark or trade name is used in a claim as a limitation to identify or describe a particular material or product, the claim does not comply with 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph because trademark identifies source, not goods.
guidance: Claim scope is uncertain since trademark does not identify/describe the goods. Example: Ex parte Simpson. Examiner Note: insert trademark/trade name and where used in claim in bracket 2.

name: Specification Only Implicitly/Inherently Discloses Structure for Means-Plus-Function (Objected To)
description: Claim element '[1]' invokes 112 sixth paragraph. The written description only implicitly or inherently sets forth the corresponding structure/material/acts that perform the claimed function.
guidance: Per 37 CFR 1.75(d) and MPEP §§ 608.01(o), 2181, applicant should: (a) amend claim to avoid sixth paragraph interpretation; or (b) amend spec to expressly recite corresponding structure/material/acts and link them to function (without new matter); or (c) state on the record what corresponding structure/material/acts (implicitly/inherently set forth) perform the function. In bracket 1 recite limitation invoking sixth paragraph.

name: Claim Limitation Interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112, Sixth Paragraph (identify corresponding structure)
description: Claim limitation '[1]' has been interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, because it uses a non-structural term '[2]' coupled with functional language '[3]' without reciting sufficient structure. The non-structural term is not preceded by a structural modifier. [4]
guidance: Since limitation invokes sixth paragraph, claim is interpreted to cover the corresponding structure described in the specification that achieves the claimed function, and equivalents. Examiner must identify corresponding structure in spec (bracket 6) and provide references. Applicant may amend or present argument. Provide bracketed items: limitation, non-structural term, functional language, explanation why non-structural, claim numbers containing limitation, corresponding structure references. See Supplementary Examination Guidelines (76 FR 7162).

name: Objection to New Matter Added to Specification (35 U.S.C. 132(a))
description: The amendment filed [1] is objected to under 35 U.S.C. 132(a) because it introduces new matter into the disclosure. The added material not supported by the original disclosure is: [2]. Applicant is required to cancel the new matter in the reply.
guidance: Examiner Note: Not to be used in reissue applications (use 14.22.01). In bracket 2 identify new matter by page/line/drawing figures and provide explanation addressing applicant's support and unresolved questions. If new matter is added to claims, also make a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph (form paragraph 7.31.01). See MPEP § 2163 and §§ 608.04.

name: Possession of the claimed invention — factors to consider
description: Whether the specification shows that applicant was in possession of the claimed invention is ... a factual determination reached by considering a number of factors.
guidance: Factors to be considered include the level of skill and knowledge in the art, partial structure, physical and/or chemical properties, functional characteristics alone or coupled with a known or disclosed correlation between structure and function, and the method of making the claimed invention. Disclosure of any combination of such identifying characteristics that distinguish the claimed invention from other materials and would lead one of skill in the art to the conclusion that the applicant was in possession of the claimed species is sufficient. (See Eli Lilly, In re Hayes, etc.)

name: Functional/method disclosure may suffice in mature arts
description: In most technologies which are mature ... a written description question should not be raised for claims present in the application when originally filed, even if the specification discloses only a method of making the invention and the function of the invention.
guidance: Example: Disclosing a microprocessor capable of performing certain functions is sufficient when one skilled in the art would understand what is intended and know how to carry it out (In re Hayes). An inventor is not required to describe every detail in a mature art.

name: Higher specificity required in emerging or unpredictable arts
description: For inventions in emerging and unpredictable technologies, or for inventions characterized by factors not reasonably predictable ... more evidence is required to show possession.
guidance: Disclosure of only a method of making the invention and the function may not be sufficient to support a product claim other than a product-by-process claim. Where the process has actually been used to produce the product, product-by-process written description may be satisfied; otherwise additional proof of operability or ability to carry out the process is required. (See Fiers v. Revel; Amgen.)

name: Partial-structure disclosure insufficient without additional characterization
description: Disclosure of a partial structure without additional characterization of the product may not be sufficient to evidence possession of the claimed invention.
guidance: In chemical and biological arts (e.g., genes), conception requires the inventor be able to define the compound so as to distinguish it, or describe how to obtain it, or provide physical/chemical properties or other characteristics; defining solely by principal biological property (e.g., encoding erythropoietin) is insufficient. Reduction to practice may be the only corroborating evidence. (See Amgen; Burroughs Wellcome.)

name: Genus claims: support via representative species or identifying characteristics
description: The written description requirement for a claimed genus may be satisfied through sufficient description of a representative number of species ... or by disclosure of relevant, identifying characteristics, i.e., structure or other physical and/or chemical properties, by functional characteristics coupled with a known or disclosed correlation between function and structure, or by a combination of such identifying characteristics.
guidance: A “representative number of species” means the species which are adequately described are representative of the entire genus. When there is substantial variation within the genus, one must describe a sufficient variety of species to reflect that variation. Disclosure of only one species may be adequate only if it “indicates that the patentee has invented species sufficient to constitute the gen[us].” Cases (Enzo Biochem, Noelle v. Lederman, In re Curtis, etc.) illustrate when one species suffices and when it does not.

name: Specification cannot support expansive claim language merely by describing one embodiment
description: A specification cannot always support expansive claim language and satisfy the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112 “merely by clearly describing one embodiment of the thing claimed.”
guidance: The issue is whether a person skilled in the art would understand applicant to have invented, and been in possession of, the invention as broadly claimed. If the specification teaches only one particular method and there is no evidence it contemplates a more generic method, broader claims may be invalid (LizardTech v. Earth Resource Mapping).

name: Examiner initial burden and required findings for rejection
description: The examiner has the initial burden of presenting evidence or reasoning to explain why persons skilled in the art would not recognize in the original disclosure a description of the invention defined by the claims.
guidance: In rejecting a claim, the examiner must set forth express findings of fact which should: (A) Identify the claim limitation at issue; and (B) Establish a prima facie case by providing reasons why a person skilled in the art at the time of filing would not have recognized that the inventor was in possession of the invention as claimed in view of the disclosure. A general allegation of “unpredictability in the art” is not sufficient. (See Wertheim.) When appropriate, suggest amendments to the claims which can be supported by the application’s written description, being mindful of the prohibition against addition of new matter.

name: Support for new or amended claims and priority claims
description: To comply with the written description requirement ... or to be entitled to an earlier priority date or filing date under 35 U.S.C. 119, 120, or 365(c), each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure.
guidance: When an explicit limitation is not present in the written description whose benefit is sought, it must be shown that a person of ordinary skill would have understood at the time of filing that the description requires that limitation. Inherency must be established by clear extrinsic evidence (not probabilities). If support is lacking, an amended/new claim must be rejected or priority denied. (See Hyatt v. Boone; In re Robertson; In re Wright; In re Robins.)

name: Claims must include elements described as essential
description: Furthermore, each claim must include all elements which applicant has described as essential.
guidance: If an element which applicant describes as essential or critical is not claimed, a new or amended claim must be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) as lacking adequate written description. (See Johnson Worldwide Assoc. Inc. v. Zebco Corp.; Gentry Gallery v. Berkline Corp.; Tronzo v. Biomet.)

name: Complete patentability determination and clear communication
description: Office personnel must complete the patentability determination under all the relevant statutory provisions of title 35 of the U.S. Code.
guidance: After analyzing the claimed invention under 101, 112, 102, and 103, review all proposed rejections and their bases to confirm correctness before imposing any rejection. The Office action should clearly communicate the findings, conclusions, and reasons which support them, and when possible offer helpful suggestions on how to overcome rejections.

name: Distinguish written description issues from new matter objections
description: A written description requirement issue generally involves whether the subject matter of a claim is supported by the disclosure of an application as filed. The claim should not be rejected or objected to on the ground of new matter.
guidance: The concept of new matter is properly employed as a basis for objection to amendments to the abstract, specification or drawings attempting to add new disclosure to that originally presented. While the test or analysis of description requirement and new matter issues is the same, the examining procedure and statutory basis for addressing these issues differ. See MPEP § 2163.06.

name: Objective standard for written description sufficiency
description: An objective standard: “does the description clearly allow persons of ordinary skill in the art to recognize that he or she invented what is claimed.”
guidance: Under Vas-Cath, to satisfy the written description requirement, an applicant must convey with reasonable clarity to those skilled in the art that, as of the filing date sought, he or she was in possession of the invention, and that the invention is whatever is now claimed. Possession may be shown by describing an actual reduction to practice, showing the invention was 'ready for patenting' (drawings or structural chemical formulas), or by describing distinguishing identifying characteristics sufficient to show possession. Subject matter need not be literally described in haec verba; implicit or inherent support may suffice if a skilled artisan would understand it.

name: Typical circumstances where written description issues arise
description: A description requirement issue can arise in a number of circumstances where it must be determined whether the subject matter of a claim is supported in an application as filed.
guidance: Most typically the issue arises when: I) an amendment affects a claim (claim amendments or specification amendments), II) reliance on filing date of a parent application under 35 U.S.C. 120, or III) reliance on priority under 35 U.S.C. 119. Rejection of an original claim for lack of written description should be rare due to a strong presumption that the specification as filed is adequate. (See In re Wertheim.)

name: Purchase of materials/elements does not convey right to make or use combination (general rule) with one exception
description: A purchaser of the materials of which an article consists, or of the elements of which it is combined, obtains thereby no right to make and use the article, or to unite the elements and employ them in the combination, although the vendor is the owner of the patent in which the combination or the article is claimed. To this rule there is one exception.
guidance: Exception stated immediately after: "The sale of any object which can be used only in constructing a patented article, or in practising a patented art, is presumed to have been intended both by the buyer and seller for that specific use; and when the seller is the owner of the patent for the article or art, his act of sale confers a license on the purchaser to employ the object for that purpose." (text cites cases and explains the presumption).

name: Sale by patentee who constructs and sells a machine conveys the right to use that specific machine to fullest practical extent
description: The sale by a person who has the full right to make, sell, and use such a machine carries with it the right to the use of that machine to the full extent to which it can be used in point of time. ... He conveyed his whole right to it — his whole right to the use of it.
guidance: Authorities (Mitchell v. Hawley; Blanchard v. Whitney) are cited to support that when the patentee himself builds and sells a machine, the purchaser gets the use-rights as if the patent had never claimed that specific sold article — the patentee has 'parted with' his exclusive right in that particular item. This supports the general principle that sale by owner conveys broad use-rights for that specific article.

name: Teaching/Suggestion/Motivation requirement to modify or combine prior art
description: To reject a claim based on this rationale, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries. Then, Office personnel must articulate the following: (1) a finding that there was some teaching, suggestion, or motivation, either in the references themselves or in the knowledge generally available to one of ordinary skill in the art, to modify the reference or to combine reference teachings; (2) a finding that there was reasonable expectation of success; and (3) whatever additional findings based on the Graham factual inquiries may be necessary, in view of the facts of the case under consideration, to explain a conclusion of obviousness.
guidance: Must explicitly state these findings in the rejection; if any cannot be made, the rationale cannot support obviousness. Examples: combining Asano with an electronic sensor; updating password device with bioauthentication. Reference case law (DyStar, Kahn, KSR) as needed.

name: Reasonable expectation of success is required
description: Where there is a reason to modify or combine the prior art to achieve the claimed invention, the claims may be rejected as prima facie obvious provided there is also a reasonable expectation of success.
guidance: Expectation of success refers to the likelihood that the combination/modification would meet claim limitations. It can be shown implicitly via prior art teachings but should be indicated explicitly in the rejection. Cite Elekta v. ZAP, Intelligent Bio-Sys., In re Merck examples.

name: Indefinite claim limitations cannot be disregarded
description: A claim limitation which is considered indefinite cannot be disregarded. If a claim is subject to more than one interpretation, at least one of which would render the claim unpatentable over the prior art, the examiner should reject the claim as indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) and should reject the claim over the prior art based on the interpretation that renders the prior art applicable.
guidance: Do not base a prior art rejection on speculative or unreasonable claim interpretations. If appropriate, make both an indefiniteness rejection and a prior art rejection to avoid piecemeal appeals (Ex parte Ionescu, In re Steele).

name: Limitations lacking support in original specification must still be considered
description: When evaluating claims for obviousness, all the limitations of the claims must be considered and given weight, including limitations which do not find support in the specification as originally filed (i.e., new matter).
guidance: Do not ignore negative or other limitations absent from the original spec when assessing prior art (Ex parte Grasselli, In re Miller). Consider whether the limitation is part of properly construed claim scope.

name: Dependent claims and claim scope relationships
description: If an independent claim is nonobvious under 35 U.S.C. 103, then any claim depending therefrom is nonobvious. However, this may not apply if a dependent claim is not properly dependent or has a later effective filing date.
guidance: Consider effective filing dates on a claim-by-claim basis and ensure proper dependency; consult MPEP §§ 608.01(n), 2133.01, and 2152.01 for effective filing date issues.

name: Clarity of the Record Pilot best practices
description: Analysis of the Clarity of the Record Pilot identified best practices in interview summaries, reasons for allowance, and claim interpretation.
guidance: Launch follow-on pilots to identify how examination practices impact clarity; adopt identified best practices to improve record clarity.

name: Understand the Training Process
description: Document training paradigms (supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement), training data, loss functions, optimization algorithms, hyperparameters, staged training, pruning, and which parts of networks are trained or fixed.
guidance: Training details can affect eligibility (training claims sometimes easier to show eligible), enforceability (detection/split-infringement issues), and enablement. Interview prompts: 'What loss function(s) are used?' 'What optimization algorithm?' 'What hyperparameters?' 'Are parts trained separately or jointly?'

name: Understand the Process at Inference Time
description: Describe inputs and outputs during inference, the enabling architecture, improvements resulting from inference, whether trained models are updated at inference, and whether input data distributions change over time.
guidance: Clarify how inference is carried out, how outputs are made usable, whether models are retrained or updated online, and whether combining models or multi-network arrangements are employed; these support claim drafting on inference and enablement.

name: EPO Drafting Considerations (technical problem/solution)
description: When filing to the EPO, clearly define the technical problem and the technical solution; features related to the technical solution may be required in the claims.
guidance: EPO treats computational models/algorithms as abstract per se; to obtain a patent, show application to solve a technical problem in a field of technology. Draft specification and claims to emphasize technical application and include technical features in claims where appropriate.

name: Japanese Enablement and Support Requirements
description: JPO expects specification to enable creation of a learned model achieving a certain degree of accuracy; disclose relationships between input and output data used in training.
guidance: Provide concrete relationships (e.g., correlations) between features and outputs and evidence or explanation supporting the claimed accuracy; avoid only high-level or vague feature descriptions that fail support/enablement.

name: Chinese Claim/Description Guidance
description: Chinese Guidelines require considering claims as a whole; show algorithmic adjustments that provide technical effects; written description should show how technical features interact and include practical application (input/output).
guidance: Draft claims and spec to present technical features collectively, include input parameters and outputs tied to specific technical areas, and explain interactions between features. Objective user-experience improvements should be grounded in technical implementations.

name: Drafting to Prevent or Overcome §101 Rejections
description: Draft AI applications to show patent-eligible subject matter by integrating any alleged judicial exception into a practical application and by claiming AI-specific architecture or training elements.
guidance: Use USPTO examples (e.g., Example 39) as guidance: emphasize technical improvements, specific implementations, and avoid purely abstract high-level claims. Show how claims improve computing/technical fields (efficiency, accuracy, speed, resource use) and avoid preemption.

name: Claiming Strategies (architecture, training, problem/solution)
description: Employ claim types such as architecture claims, training claims, and problem/solution claims to capture AI-specific innovations and enhance eligibility/enforceability.
guidance: Architecture and training claims can emphasize tangible technical elements; problem/solution claims tie claim scope to a technical problem and practical effect. Consider inclusion of architectural details, training steps, loss functions, data flows, and interactions with devices/endpoints in claims.

name: Problem/Solution Support in Specification
description: Explicitly set out the technical problem and the concrete technical solution in the specification to support claims and to satisfy foreign office expectations.
guidance: Document how claimed features solve the technical problem, how features interact to produce effects, and, where possible, quantify improvements (accuracy, speed, resource usage).

name: Drafting to Withstand Appellate/CAFC Scrutiny
description: Prepare specifications and claims with sufficient technical specificity and factual record to defend subject-matter eligibility and other challenges on appeal.
guidance: Do not rely solely on USPTO guidance (not precedential); anticipate Federal Circuit focus on concrete technical improvements and avoid conflating novelty with eligibility. Provide factual allegations of technical improvement where appropriate.

name: Cloud-Based / As-a-Service (aaS) Documentation Paragraph
description: Include specification language addressing cloud-based implementations and documentation practices for aaS deployments to clarify how the claimed invention operates when remotely implemented.
guidance: Documenting cloud interactions, endpoints, and data flows in the specification supports enablement and helps with detectability/enforcement where the core operation is remote or distributed.

name: Avoid Claiming Features Likely Disclosed Publicly
description: Be cautious claiming features that are very likely to be disclosed in competitors’ public documents or standards, which can affect enforceability and trade-secret strategy.
guidance: If features are standard-compliant or publicly documented, consider different claim scopes or focusing on combinations/implementations that produce technical improvements.

name: Demonstrate Non-Preemptive Technical Improvements
description: Show how claimed innovations enhance computing systems or AI systems (efficiency, accuracy, speed, resource use) in a manner that does not preempt fundamental methods or abstract ideas.
guidance: Provide concrete implementation details and measurable or concrete effects; avoid overly broad claim language that could be characterized as preemptive.

name: Leverage USPTO Examples and PTAB Decisions with Caution
description: Use USPTO PEG examples (e.g., Example 39) and PTAB informative decisions (e.g., Ex Parte Hannun) as drafting guidance but recognize they are not precedential in court.
guidance: USPTO materials can illustrate claim/spec drafting approaches that succeeded at the Office, but litigation outcomes are governed by Federal Circuit and Supreme Court precedent—draft to survive both examination and judicial scrutiny.

name: Monitor Recent Case Law and District Court Trends
description: Be aware district courts have shown mixed results on computer/AI eligibility; many AI-related patents were invalidated early, but outcomes vary based on claim specificity and alleged technical improvement.
guidance: Use case examples (e.g., Smart Systems, Athena Diagnostics, Singular Computing, Applied Predictive Techs., Kaavo) to inform drafting: courts favor claims with plausible technical improvements and specific implementations; pleadings with factual allegations of improvement may survive early dismissal.

name: Brazil: novelty requires single-document disclosure; inventive step may combine documents
description: Under Brazilian law, to prove lack of novelty it is necessary that all elements of the claimed invention be disclosed in a single document; for inventive step it is possible to submit several pieces of prior art to prove lack of inventive step.
guidance: Article 11 defines state of the art as everything made accessible to the public prior to filing date by any means, in Brazil or abroad. Administrative practice indicates documents with restricted circulation (e.g., internal factory documents or exchanges between two companies) are not considered accessible to the public.

name: Treatment of later‑filed applications on identical invention
description: Where more than two patent applications are filed on the identical invention, the examiner shall defer examination for later-filed applications until the prior-filed application has been processed or has been laid-open or registered. However, where the later-filed application can be rejected based on the same ground as the prior-filed application, the examiner can start examination.
guidance: Detailed start-of-examination rules depend on: identicalness of applicants, disclosure status (laid-open/not laid-open). Table summarizes outcomes (e.g., if identical applicants & prior filed laid-open => examination conducted; if identical applicants & prior not laid-open => examination conducted with Article 36(1) rejection notified, patentability determined after confirming claims of prior-filed application; if different applicants and prior not laid-open => examination deferred until disclosure). Examiner must apply Article 36(1) when finalizing decision after prior-filed's claim scope determined.

name: Examination after prior-filed application processed
description: When the prior-filed application is examined or laid open or registered after examination on later-filed applications is deferred, the examiner may conduct examination on later-filed application but shall make the final decision applying Article 36(1) once the scope of claim of the prior-filed application is determined.
guidance: Examiner may start examination but final patentability decision must account for prior-filed claim scope (Article 36(1)).

name: Procedure and contents of written decision to reject an application
