description: Where applicant fails to overcome grounds for rejection, examiner shall make a decision to reject in writing with rationale attached. The written decision shall include application number, title of invention, name and address of applicant and agent, date of notice of grounds for rejection, text of decision and its rationale, date of decision to reject, and examiner's sign and seal.
guidance: Commissioner delivers certified copy; decision confirmed when cannot be revoked (e.g., no appeal, trial decision supporting rejection). Examiner shall indicate determination on applicant's amendment where notified grounds were still not overcome and list issuable items in the written argument. If any claim contains grounds for rejection in multi-claim application, reject the application. Examiner shall not base rejection on unreasonable rationale other than already-notified grounds; to rely on new prior art examiner must notify that fact as a ground for rejection.

name: Second patent to same person for same invention unlawful
description: After one patent has issued, a second patent to the same person for the same invention, though with broader claims, is unlawful.
guidance: Consolidated Roller-Mill Co. v. Coombs (1889), 39 Fed. Rep. 25.

name: Foreign narrow patent does not preclude broader domestic patent
description: A foreign patent with narrow claims does not prevent obtaining a domestic patent for a broader invention.
guidance: Faure v. Bradley (1888), 44 O. G. 945.

name: Where none of combination elements are new, patentees limited to form shown in drawings
description: Where none of the elements of a combination are new or claimed separately and other similar combinations are in use, patentee is limited to the form of the elements shown by his drawings.
guidance: Heine Safety Boiler Co. v. Smith F.W.H. & P. Co. (1889), 47 O. G. 1634.

name: Examiner may require definite, intelligible claims but not hinder appeals
description: An examiner can require that claims be definite and intelligible, but cannot in any manner hinder the applicant from obtaining his full rights on appeal.
guidance: Ex parte Rogers (1889), 49 O. G. 1361.

name: Applicant's oath about amendment not conclusive
description: The applicant's oath that matter claimed by an amendment was part of the original invention is not conclusive; the Office may inspect the whole application to determine the question.
guidance: Ex parte Regan (1888), 45 O. G. 689.

name: Appeal routes: oath, merits, functional claim
description: Appeal from rejection for want of a proper oath lies to the examiners-in-chief; an objection to a claim as functional is not a rejection and appeal to examiners-in-chief does not lie; functional claims are necessarily indefinite.
guidance: Ex parte Boyer (1889); Ex parte Barrett (1888).

name: Meaning of 'Invention' [Sec. 12]
description: "An idea of an inventor which permits in practice the solution to a specific problem in the field of technology"; an invention may be or may relate to a product or process.
guidance: The invention must enable a practical solution to a specific technical problem; treat product and process equally as possible inventions when drafting claims and description.

name: Non‑Patentable: Plant and Animal Varieties / Essentially Biological Processes
description: Plant and animal varieties or essentially biological processes for the production of plants or animals are not patentable, except man‑made living micro‑organisms.
guidance: Biotech filings should focus on man‑made microorganisms or technical processes that fall outside 'essentially biological' exclusions where possible; consider alternative claim drafting strategies.

name: Contents of Patent Specification
description: Patent specification should include Drawings, Abstract, Claim(s), and Description.
guidance: Ensure each section is complete: claims define scope, description supports and enables claims, drawings illustrate embodiments, and abstract summarises invention for publication. Thoroughly read and understand the specification before filing or prosecuting.

name: Novelty Test: Feature Analysis
description: Novelty is tested by feature analysis — compare each claimed feature against prior art items to see if all features are disclosed.
guidance: Create feature tables to map claim elements to prior art (example provided for a watering device). If any single prior art lacks a claimed feature, novelty may be retained.

name: Complete specification and claims
description: A complete specification must describe the invention in detail and set out a list of claims which define the scope of protection sought under the patent.
guidance: A complete patent application must be drafted and filed by a patent attorney. Claims determine infringement and scope; the applicant should ensure the specification supports the claims. File within 12 months of the provisional filing date.

name: Enablement (Scope of Disclosure)
description: How much must the specification teach to support the claims?
guidance: Industry-specific standards: Pharmaceuticals: single working example often supports claims to closely related compounds. Biotechnology: following Amgen v. Sanofi, structural genus claims require full-scope enablement. Software: functional claiming widely accepted; structural detail rarely required. Mechanical: drawings and one embodiment usually sufficient. Quality marker: Are the disclosed embodiments representative of the claimed scope under the relevant industry standard?

name: Written Description
description: Does the specification show the inventor 'possessed' the claimed invention at filing?
guidance: Quality marker: Continuation claims drafted years after filing should be scrutinized for whether the original specification supports the new claim language. Late-added genus claims or claims targeting competitor products are red flags indicating weak written description support.

name: Doctrine of Equivalents (DOE) and Reverse DOE
description: Court-applied scope-modulating tools that expand or contract claim scope beyond literal claim language.
guidance: Quality implications: Pioneer patents claim broad equivalents reach; quality requires that pioneer status be genuine. Improvement patents are vulnerable to reverse DOE, so quality requires that the patent represent a substantial advance over the prior art. Use of DOE should be assessed in light of patent's role (pioneer vs improvement).

name: Subject-Matter Eligibility (35 U.S.C. 101)
description: The Mayo/Alice framework dramatically affects eligibility for software, biotech, diagnostics, and related claims.
guidance: Quality markers: Software claims that recite generic computer implementation of an abstract idea are low quality (Alice-vulnerable). Diagnostic claims that recite a natural correlation plus conventional steps are low quality (Mayo-vulnerable). High-quality eligibility-sensitive claims include specific technical implementations or non-conventional combinations that avoid abstract-idea/nature-based rejections.

name: Software industry calibration
description: Industry-specific calibration for software: lower written description bar and widespread functional claiming, but vulnerability under eligibility doctrine.
guidance: Quality requires technical specificity to survive Alice; quality marker: claims tied to a particular technical improvement (not merely an abstract result). Even with a lower written-description bar, claims should be drafted to show concrete technical implementation details to avoid eligibility rejections.

name: Biotechnology industry calibration
description: Biotechnology requires a high enablement and written description bar, especially for structural/genus claims.
guidance: Quality marker: Representative species supporting genus claims and disclosure of structural-functional correlation. Following cases like Amgen v. Sanofi, broad structural genus claims need full-scope enablement — failure to provide representative embodiments or structure/function linkage is a quality defect.

name: Pharmaceuticals industry calibration
description: Pharmaceutical patents have distinct enablement/written-description/utility concerns; single working examples may support close compound claims but method claims face eligibility scrutiny.
guidance: Quality marker: Compound claims with strong structural support are high quality. Method-of-treatment claims face evolving eligibility issues; supporting pharmacological data and demonstrated utility strengthen quality and reduce vulnerability to challenge.

name: Semiconductors industry calibration
description: Semiconductor patents confront cumulative-technology concerns and therefore require claim scope that permits design-around.
guidance: Quality requires defined scope that permits design-around and avoids overbroad, performance-only claiming. Quality marker: claims tied to specific processes or structures rather than generic 'improved performance' language.

name: Operative test: Identify technological regime (industry)
description: For any patent, first evaluate whether the application correctly identifies the technological regime (industry).
guidance: If the application misidentifies its industry, the chosen doctrinal calibrations (PHOSITA, enablement expectations, written-description norms, eligibility risks) will be misapplied and weaken the patent. Look for explicit characterization of industry and whether claimed subject matter fits that regime's typical standards.

name: Operative test: PHOSITA skill-level calibration
description: Assess whether the PHOSITA skill level is appropriately calibrated for the technological regime.
guidance: Check prosecution and specification language for assertions about routine skill, required background knowledge, and whether the claim drafting assumes a low- or high-skilled PHOSITA. Mischaracterization is a quality defect (e.g., treating biotech as low-skill).

name: Operative test: Enablement disclosure meets industry-specific bar
description: Evaluate whether the enablement disclosure satisfies the industry-specific enablement standard.
guidance: Compare the specification's embodiments and examples to the enablement expectations for the relevant field (e.g., representative species for biotech, working examples for pharma, implementation details for software). Lack of representative embodiments relative to claimed breadth indicates poor quality.

name: Operative test: Claim breadth proportionate to written-description standard
description: Determine whether claim breadth is proportionate to the written-description standard applicable in the industry.
guidance: Large genus claims must be supported by disclosure that shows possession across the breadth claimed. Scrutinize continuation or broadened claims added years after filing for insufficient written-description support or 'targeting competitors' red flags.

name: Operative test: Anticipate eligibility challenges relevant to field
description: Check whether the application anticipates subject-matter eligibility challenges that commonly arise in its field.
guidance: For software, watch for claims that merely recite abstract ideas implemented on generic computers. For diagnostics, watch for claims that merely recite natural correlations plus conventional steps. High-quality drafting will include technical implementation details or inventive concept to mitigate Mayo/Alice risks.

name: Operative test: Prosecution history reflects awareness of industry-specific case law
description: Assess whether the prosecution history demonstrates awareness of and responses to industry-specific case law and prior-art issues.
guidance: Quality prosecution will cite relevant case law, disclose and distinguish material prior art, make appropriate IDS submissions, and show consideration of eligibility decisions and how claim language was adapted accordingly. Absence of such awareness suggests poor lever-calibration and weaker patents.

name: Administrative vs. civil vs. criminal jurisdiction categories
description: The framework distinguishes administrative jurisdiction (validity-related matters such as refusal, invalidation, confirmation of scope of rights, correction, cancellation), civil jurisdiction (civil infringement actions including damages, preliminary injunctions, permanent injunctions; civil copyright infringement), and criminal jurisdiction (criminal infringement of patent, trademark, copyright and design cases).
guidance: Which court and procedure applies depends on the nature of the claim (administrative challenge to register vs. civil enforcement vs. criminal prosecution). Some courts have exclusive jurisdiction over certain categories.

name: Scope of challenges in PGR
description: A petitioner in a post-grant review may request to cancel as unpatentable one or more claims of a patent on any ground that could be raised under paragraph (2) or (3) of section 282(b) (relating to invalidity of the patent or any claim).

name: Requirements of petition (claims, grounds, evidence particularity)
description: The petition identifies, in writing and with particularity, each claim challenged, the grounds on which the challenge to each claim is based, and the evidence that supports the grounds for the challenge to each claim.
guidance: The petition must include copies of patents and printed publications relied upon, and affidavits or declarations if relying on other factual evidence or expert opinions; provide such other information as the Director may require by regulation.

name: Reissue patent limitation for PGR
description: A post-grant review may not be instituted if the petition requests cancellation of a claim in a reissue patent that is identical to or narrower than a claim in the original patent from which the reissue patent was issued, and the time limitations in section 321(c) would bar filing a petition for a post-grant review for such original patent.

name: Institution threshold — more likely than not standard
description: The Director may not authorize a post-grant review to be instituted unless the Director determines that the information presented in the petition, if not rebutted, would demonstrate that it is more likely than not that at least one of the claims challenged in the petition is unpatentable.

name: Patent owner motion to amend (one motion standard)
description: During a post-grant review the patent owner may file one motion to amend the patent in one or more of the following ways: (A) cancel any challenged patent claim; (B) for each challenged claim, propose a reasonable number of substitute claims.
guidance: Additional motions may be permitted upon joint request to materially advance settlement or upon request of the patent owner for good cause shown. An amendment may not enlarge the scope of the claims or introduce new matter.

name: Final written decision and certificate
description: If a post-grant review is instituted and not dismissed, the PTAB shall issue a final written decision with respect to the patentability of any challenged claim and any new claim added under section 326(d). The Director shall issue and publish a certificate canceling any claim finally determined unpatentable, confirming claims determined patentable, and incorporating new or amended claims determined patentable after appeals are final.

name: Intervening rights for amended/new claims
description: Any proposed amended or new claim determined to be patentable and incorporated into a patent following a post-grant review shall have the same effect as specified in section 252 for reissued patents regarding the rights of persons who made, purchased, used, or imported things patented by such claim prior to issuance of the certificate.

name: National stage commencement requirements
description: To commence the national stage, the applicant shall file the national fee (section 41(a)), a copy of the international application (if required), and a translation into English if filed in another language; amendments under article 19 to claims (unless communicated by IB), an oath or declaration complying with section 115, and translations of any annexes to the international preliminary examination report if made in another language.
guidance: Some requirements may be complied with by the date of commencement or by later time fixed by the Director; failure to comply is regarded as abandonment or cancellation of amendments, and a surcharge may be required to accept late compliance.

name: Timing constraints and consequences in national stage
description: The national stage shall commence with expiration of applicable treaty time limits (article 22 or 39), and after national stage commences no patent may be granted or refused before expiration of applicable treaty time limits under article 28 or 41 except with express consent of the applicant.
guidance: Applicant may present amendments to specification, claims, and drawings after national stage commencement; national stage may be commenced early at the express request of the applicant if application is in order and subsection (c) requirements have been complied with.

name: Filing date threshold (35 U.S.C. 111)
description: The filing date of an application shall be the date on which a specification, with or without claims, is received in the United States Patent and Trademark Office.
guidance: 35 U.S.C. 111 and 37 CFR 1.53(b)/(c) govern what papers must be received to accord a filing date; for provisionals, the filing date rules are similarly applied per 37 CFR 1.53(c). If filing date is refused, petition under 37 CFR 1.53(e)(2) with fee (37 CFR 1.17(f)) is required for review.

name: Required contents of an application (35 U.S.C. 111(2))
description: An application shall include: (A) a specification as prescribed by section 112; (B) a drawing as prescribed by section 113; and (C) an oath or declaration as prescribed by section 115.
guidance: The fee, oath or declaration, and one or more claims may be submitted after the filing date within such period and conditions (including payment of a surcharge) as prescribed by the Director; failure to submit within the prescribed period results in abandonment.

name: Timing for submitting copy/translation for reference filing (37 CFR 1.57(a)(1)-(2))
description: If a correspondence address is provided, the applicant will be notified and given a period to file a copy of the specification and drawings, an English translation if needed, and pay the fee and surcharge; if no correspondence address provided, applicant has three months from filing date to file the copy, translation, fee, and surcharge to avoid abandonment.
guidance: Such notices may be combined with 37 CFR 1.53(f) notices (e.g., to provide at least one claim and pay filing fees). Timeframes depend on presence of a correspondence address.

name: Effect on priority/benefit claims for applications filed by reference
description: In a reference filing under 37 CFR 1.57(a), the reference to a previously filed application in an ADS is not sufficient to establish a priority or benefit claim to that previously filed application; the ADS has separate sections for reference filing and priority/benefit claims.
guidance: An application abandoned under 35 U.S.C. 111(c) and 37 CFR 1.57(a)(1) or (a)(2) is treated as having never been filed, precluding priority/benefit claims to that reference unless revived under 37 CFR 1.137 and a copy of the previously filed specification/drawings is submitted.

name: Clarity of claims
description: Claims shall be clear.
guidance: Article 84 EPC; many Guidelines entries address clarity (GL F IV 4.1, GL F IV 4.4, GL F IV 4.6.1, GL F IV 4.14.1). Opposition and appeal case law (CLR II A 1.4) and GL D V 5 discuss clarity objections and their examination.

name: Conciseness of claims
description: Claims shall be concise.
guidance: Article 84 EPC; GL F IV 5 discusses conciseness and number of claims. Conciseness is considered together with clarity and fees (R.45, R.162).

name: Support by the description
description: Claims shall be supported by the description.
guidance: Article 84 EPC; interaction with Article 83 (sufficiency) and Article 123 (amendments) addressed in GL F III 11, CLR II C 8.1/8.2, GL H II (amendments). Support requirement examined in opposition (CLR II A 1.5).

name: Alternatives in a claim
description: How to present alternatives within a claim (multiple embodiments or options).
guidance: GL F IV 3.7 addresses alternatives in a claim and related clarity/support considerations.

name: Conciseness and number of claims (fees consideration)
description: Number and scope of claims must balance conciseness with the need to define protection; some claims incur fees.
guidance: Rules R.45 and R.162 govern claims incurring fees; GL F IV 5 discusses conciseness and number of claims with fee implications.

name: General statements, 'spirit of the invention', claim-like clauses
description: Avoid drafting claim-like clauses that are vague, general statements or refer only to the 'spirit' of the invention.
guidance: GL F IV 4.4 warns against general/claim-like clauses and explains why these may fail clarity/support requirements.

name: Functional features and means-plus-function interpretation
description: Use and interpretation of functional features; rules for 'means for ...' style claims.
guidance: CLR II A 3.4 and GL F IV 4.13.2 cover functional features and interpretation of means-plus-function wording, with case law examples clarifying allowable scope and necessary disclosure.

name: Characterisation by parameter / parameters
description: Characterising an invention by parameters and the use of numerical/technical parameters in claims.
guidance: CLR II A 3.5 and GL F IV 4.11 discuss when parameter-based claim language is acceptable and how parameters must be supported and disclosed to avoid ambiguity or lack of sufficiency.

name: Unspecified features and relative qualities
description: Handling of unspecified features and claims relying on relative qualities (e.g., 'substantially', 'approximately').
guidance: CLR II A 3.6 and CLR II A 6.2 (meaning of terms like 'comprising (substantially)') provide guidance on interpreting relative/unspecified language and pitfalls for clarity/support.

name: Result to be achieved
description: Claims that define an invention by the result to be achieved (functional/result-oriented claiming).
guidance: GL F IV 4.10 and related case law discuss limits on result-to-be-achieved-type claim language and the need for technical features enabling that result.

name: Use claims
description: Special considerations when drafting 'use' claims (e.g., first/second medical use, purpose-limited product claims).
guidance: GL F IV 4.16 and specific case law entries outline the formal and substantive requirements for use claims and purpose-limited product claims.

name: Negative limitations / disclaimers
description: Use and drafting of negative claim limitations (disclaimers) and conditions under which they are allowable.
guidance: GL F IV 4.19 plus Enlarged Board decisions (G 1/03, G 2/03, G 1/04, G 2/10, G 3/14, G 1/16 etc.) and GL H V/GL H IV entries discuss allowable disclaimers, undisclosed disclaimers, and drafting requirements.

name: Reference signs in claims
description: Whether and how to include reference signs (numerical labels referring to drawings) in claims.
guidance: GL F IV 4.18 explains the use of reference signs: they are generally not part of the claimed subject-matter and should be used cautiously to avoid clarity issues.

name: Order of claims
description: Recommended order and logical arrangement of claims in the claim set.
guidance: GL F IV 4.23 gives guidance on appropriate ordering of claims (independent first, then dependent, grouping by category) to improve clarity and examination efficiency.

name: Interpretation of terms such as 'comprising', 'consisting of'
description: Meaning and legal effects of transitional and compositional terms used in claims.
guidance: CLR II A 6.2 explains interpretation of terms like 'comprising (substantially)', 'consisting (essentially) of', and how they affect claim scope and clarity.

name: Claims directed to computer-implemented inventions
description: Specific drafting and clarity issues for computer-implemented inventions and where method steps may be implemented by generic data processing means.
guidance: GL F IV 3.9 and sub-sections (3.9.1, 3.9.2, 3.9.3) cover cases where steps can be implemented by generic processing, where specific devices are defined, and distributed computing environments — with guidance on claim clarity and support.

name: Use of the description/drawings to define unclear terms
description: When and how the description and drawings may be used to establish definitions for terms that are unclear in the claims.
guidance: GL B III 3.2.3 describes the extent to which examiners/searchers may rely on description/drawings to interpret unclear claim terms (especially during search and examination).

name: Clarity objections in opposition and limitation/revocation proceedings
description: How clarity of claims is examined and objected to during opposition, limitation, and revocation procedures.
guidance: CLR II A 1.4, GL D V 5, GL D X 4.3 and GL H IV 4.3/4.4 entries address procedural scope for raising clarity objections in opposition/limitation proceedings and the standards applied.

name: Lack of support vs insufficient disclosure
description: Distinguishing lack of support for claims (Article 84/123 issues) from insufficient disclosure (Article 83) and how amendments interplay with these grounds.
guidance: GL F IV 6.3/6.4 and CLR II C 8.x entries discuss the difference between support and sufficiency objections and relevant case law on amendment limits and remedial measures.

name: Claims incurring fees and formal content requirements
description: Formal rules regarding claims that incur fees and the necessary claim content for filing/fees (e.g., R.40, R.43, R.45, R.49).
guidance: Rules R.40, R.43, R.45, R.49 and R.57 govern date of filing, form and content of claims, fees, and formal examination aspects; these procedural rules affect claim drafting and prosecution strategy.

name: What to search for
description: The search should target the claimed subject matter and disclosed features reasonably expected to be claimed, not only literal claim limitations.
guidance: Although a rejection need not be based on a teaching or suggestion to combine, a preferred search is directed to finding references that provide such a teaching or suggestion if they exist (see MPEP §904.02).

name: Claim interpretation — broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI)
description: Claims must be given the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification when determining claim scope for search and comparison purposes.
guidance: Apply Phillips v. AWH and MPEP §2111 principles in construing claim language before comparing to prior art; ensure scope determination is clear in the record.

name: Ascertaining differences between claimed invention and prior art
description: Interpret claim language and compare the claimed invention as a whole to the prior art to identify differences.
guidance: Consider both the invention and the prior art as a whole (see MPEP §2141.02). All claim limitations must be considered in the analysis.

name: Use of common sense and examiner expertise
description: Common sense and the examiner’s scientific/technical competence may inform what would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill, even if not explicitly taught in a particular reference.
guidance: While record support is required, examiners may employ reasoned explanations that use common sense or their expertise to explain why a claimed combination would have been obvious (see DyStar, Perfect Web).

name: Rationales to support rejections (exemplary list A–G)
description: Exemplary rationales that may support a conclusion of obviousness include: (A) combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results; (B) simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results; (C) use of known technique to improve similar devices in the same way; (D) applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement to yield predictable results; (E) 'obvious to try' — choosing from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions with a reasonable expectation of success; (F) known work in one field prompting predictable variations in same or different fields; (G) some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art to modify or combine references.
guidance: The list is exemplary, not exhaustive. See MPEP §2143 and §2144 for further discussion and examples illustrating each rationale. The key is clearly articulating why the claimed invention would have been obvious.

name: Requirement for articulated reasoning (no conclusory statements)
description: Rejections on obviousness cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements; there must be articulated reasoning with a rational underpinning supporting the legal conclusion of obviousness.
guidance: Provide explicit explanation linking factual findings to the legal conclusion (KSR quoting In re Kahn). Avoid conclusory labels — explain why prior art would have motivated or made the claimed combination predictable.

name: Step 1 — Whether the amendment narrowed the literal scope of the claim
description: The first question in a prosecution history estoppel inquiry is whether an amendment filed in the PTO has narrowed the literal scope of a claim.
guidance: If the amendment was not narrowing, prosecution history estoppel does not apply. (Cites Pioneer Magnetics v. Micro Linear.) This is a threshold factual/legal determination to be resolved before proceeding to reasons for the amendment.

name: Festo presumption of surrender (scope surrendered by a patentability-related narrowing amendment)
description: When a narrowing amendment is found to have been made for a reason relating to patentability, Festo imposes the presumption that the patentee surrendered all territory between the original claim limitation and the amended claim limitation.
guidance: This is a rebuttable presumption; the patentee bears the burden to show that the particular alleged equivalent was not surrendered. If the patentee fails to rebut, prosecution history estoppel bars reliance on the doctrine of equivalents for that claim limitation.

name: Patentee's burden to rebut the Festo presumption (general statement)
description: The patentee must show that 'at the time of the amendment one skilled in the art could not reasonably be expected to have drafted a claim that would have literally encompassed the alleged equivalent.' (Festo VIII, 535 U.S. at 741.)
guidance: The Supreme Court enumerated three ways to overcome the presumption; the patentee must prove at least one of them. The court treats the ultimate rebuttal determination as a question of law for the court to decide, though underlying factual issues may exist.

name: Interaction of Warner-Jenkinson and Festo presumptions (procedure)
description: The Warner-Jenkinson presumption (that an unexplained narrowing amendment was for a substantial reason related to patentability) and the Festo presumption (that such an amendment surrenders all territory between original and amended limitations) operate together in sequence.
guidance: Procedure: (1) Determine if amendment narrowed claim; (2) if so, determine whether amendment was for patentability (Warner-Jenkinson presumes yes if reason not in record); (3) if patentability-related, apply Festo presumption of surrender; (4) allow patentee to attempt rebuttal via the three Festo criteria; (5) if unsuccessful, estoppel bars DOE; if successful, proceed to equivalence merits.

name: Timing: One-year pre-filing or pre-disclosure requirement
description: (a)(2) such commercial use occurred at least 1 year before the earlier of either (A) the effective filing date of the claimed invention; or (B) the date on which the claimed invention was disclosed to the public in a manner that qualified for the exception from prior art under section 102(b).
guidance: The one-year gap was part of the House compromise with universities; it helps ensure the prior user did not derive the invention from the patentee and that the prior user was the earlier party to invent (assuming reasonable diligence by patentee). Critics argued the one-year limit can deny rights to clear first inventors; some earlier proposals required shorter gaps or reduction to practice.

name: End-result concept (subject matter vs useful end result)
description: Subsection (d) and (a)(1)/(d) use the concept of a 'useful end result' and imply the 'subject matter' protected by §273 is a process or tool used to make another product, not the final consumer product itself.
guidance: The 'end result' language implies prior-user protection attaches to processes/tools and their produced results; e.g., a product-by-process claim may allow extension to a finished consumer product, but normally final consumer products that are publicly sold become prior art.

name: Counting claims for fee calculation
description: In estimating fees for a request for examination, the number of claims shall be counted by each claim regardless of whether claims are independent or dependent; a dependent claim is counted as one even if dependent on more than two claims.
guidance: Specific counting rules for scenarios: (①) if request for examination filed at same time as filing or no amendment before request, count initial claims; (②) if amendments before request, count final claims after amendment; (③) if request and amendment submitted simultaneously, count claims at time of amendment submission; (④) if claims increased after request, additional fees are based on increased claims regardless of deleted claims. Examples provided in text.

name: If admitting use but claiming agency or license, disclose principal / license terms
description: Where the defendant admits use but excuses it by acting as agent or under license, the answer must disclose the principal or show that the license warrants the use made.
guidance: An assertion of agency must name the principal; a license defence must show the license's scope covers the acts complained of. Otherwise the admission may be treated as an admission of infringement.

name: Markman four-factor test — Historical test
description: Apply the historical test: examine whether the issue (as analogous to an 18th-century cause) was traditionally tried at law (and thus to a jury) or at equity/court; then determine whether the particular issue must go to the jury to preserve the substance of the common-law right as it existed in 1791.
guidance: Two-part historical analysis: (1) was the cause/issue tried at law in 1791 (patent infringement actions were), and (2) was the specific component (e.g., claim construction or enablement) historically a jury question such that leaving it to the judge would abridge the Seventh Amendment protection. The Note emphasizes searching for direct historical analogues (specifications, terms of art) and finds little evidence of jury participation in specification/term-definition historically; for enablement the Note argues history supports jury determination because enablement was tried to juries in the relevant period.

name: Markman four-factor test — Functional considerations
description: Assess which decisionmaker (judge or jury) is functionally better suited to resolve the issue based on the nature of the question (technicality, need for credibility assessments, factual determinants, judges' training in interpreting written instruments).
guidance: For claim construction the Court found judges better suited due to training and the textual/interpretive nature of the task; for enablement the Note emphasizes many factual determinations (scope of disclosure, level of ordinary skill, adequacy of incorporated documents, credibility of witnesses) and argues the jury is better positioned to resolve enablement. Consider whether the task is closer to statutory/document construction (judge) or to factfinding/credibility determinations (jury).

name: Markman four-factor test — Uniformity of treatment
description: Consider the need for uniformity, predictability, and stare decisis: whether treating the issue as a question of law (judge) better serves public notice and consistency across cases.
guidance: The Supreme Court gave weight to uniformity in assigning claim construction to judges to avoid a 'zone of uncertainty.' The Note counsels evaluating whether an incorrect determination in one case will materially affect other parties (collateral estoppel, settlement consequences). For enablement, the Note argues the need for uniformity is less than for claim construction because enablement rulings are less likely to be given preclusive effect before final judgment.

name: Wands factors for undue experimentation
description: Eight non-exhaustive factors to determine whether the experimentation required by the specification is 'undue': (1) the quantity of experimentation necessary, (2) the amount of direction or guidance presented, (3) the presence or absence of working examples, (4) the nature of the invention, (5) the state of the prior art, (6) the relative skill of those in the art, (7) the predictability or unpredictability of the art, and (8) the breadth of the claims.
guidance: Courts apply these In re Wands factors in toto; no single factor is dispositive. Use them to evaluate whether the specification permits practice of the claimed invention without undue trial-and-error. The Note cites Wands as the standard framework for enablement review.

name: Elements required to apply collateral estoppel to claim construction
description: To apply collateral estoppel to a prior claim construction, four requirements must be satisfied: (1) the issue must be identical to one previously decided; (2) the issue must have been actually litigated; (3) the issue must have been essential to a final judgment in the prior litigation; and (4) the party against whom estoppel is asserted must have had a 'full and fair opportunity' to litigate the issue previously.
guidance: Post-Markman practice has produced questions about preclusive effect of district-court claim constructions (which may be decided prior to final judgment). The Note explains that collateral estoppel will be more readily applied to claim construction than to enablement because claim construction can be final after a Markman hearing, whereas enablement typically lacks a separate final ruling prior to judgment.

name: Claim construction as a legal question post-Markman
description: Under Markman v. Westview Instruments, Inc., claim interpretation (construction) is allocated to judges as a question of law; judges, not juries, decide the acquired meaning of patent terms.
guidance: The Note explains the Supreme Court's reasons (historical practice, judges' interpretive skills, functional considerations, and need for uniformity). Post-Markman practice: judges hold claim-construction (Markman) hearings, often consider extrinsic evidence, and issue constructions that shape trial and appeal strategy. Courts may hold Markman hearings before or during trial; the Federal Circuit has not entertained interlocutory appeals from these hearings in practice.

name: Evaluating whether the additional elements are well-understood, routine, conventional activity
description: When making a determination whether the additional elements in a claim amount to significantly more than a judicial exception, the examiner should evaluate whether the elements define only well-understood, routine, conventional activity.
guidance: Key points examiners must consider: (1) Being known in the art does not necessarily make an element conventional—novel/obvious inquiries are separate from eligibility (e.g., Enfish illustrates known features can be non-conventional if they provide technical improvements). (2) A factual determination is required to support a conclusion that an additional element (or combination) is well-understood, routine, conventional activity (Berkheimer), but a prior-art search is not always necessary; examiners may rely on what courts or those in the art recognize and on the specification’s own statements. The examiner should conclude based on their expertise that an element is widely prevalent or in common use in the relevant industry; if not, the element will generally favor eligibility (example: glucose-sensing earring vs. routine blood glucose monitoring). The factual determination must be expressly supported in writing (see MPEP § 2106.07(a)); appropriate forms of support include: (a) citation to the specification or applicant statements, (b) citation to relevant court decisions, (c) citation to publications showing conventionality, or (d) official notice by the examiner. (3) Even if individual elements are conventional, their combination may amount to an inventive concept (Diamond v. Diehr; Rapid Litigation; BASCOM). A rejection should be made only if the examiner, relying on expertise, can conclude in Step 2B that the additional elements do not amount to significantly more. See MPEP § 2106.07(a) for how to support conclusions on the record.

name: Computer functions courts have recognized as well-understood, routine, conventional when claimed generically
description: The courts have recognized certain generic computer functions as well-understood, routine, and conventional functions when recited at a high level of generality or as insignificant extra-solution activity.
guidance: Examples the courts have treated as routine when claimed generically: (i) receiving or transmitting data over a network (e.g., using the Internet to gather data; utilizing an intermediary computer to forward information); (ii) performing repetitive calculations (e.g., recomputing or readjusting values); (iii) electronic recordkeeping (e.g., creating/maintaining shadow accounts; updating activity logs); (iv) storing and retrieving information in memory; (v) electronically scanning or extracting data from a physical document (e.g., OCR); and (vi) a web browser’s back-and-forward button functionality. Caveat: this listing does not mean all computer functions are routine or that a generic computer implementation is necessarily ineligible—cases like DDR Holdings, Amdocs, and BASCOM show that specific arrangements or technical improvements can render claims eligible. Courts have found ineligible claims where the claim as a whole is nothing more than generic computer functions implementing an abstract idea (human-analog). Conversely, eligible claims can arise when generic components in combination perform non-generic, technical functions.

name: Laboratory techniques courts have recognized as well-understood, routine, conventional when claimed generically
description: In the life sciences, courts have identified common laboratory techniques as well-understood, routine, conventional activities when recited at a high level of generality or as insignificant extra-solution activity.
guidance: Examples include: (i) determining the level of a biomarker in blood by any means; (ii) using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) to amplify and detect DNA; (iii) detecting DNA or enzymes in a sample; (iv) immunizing a patient against a disease; (v) analyzing DNA to provide sequence information or detect allelic variants; (vi) freezing and thawing cells; (vii) amplifying and sequencing nucleic acid sequences; and (viii) hybridizing a gene probe. These techniques, when claimed only generically, may be treated as routine and not contribute an inventive concept unless there is more specificity or an unconventional application/arrangement.

name: Other activities courts have recognized as well-understood, routine, conventional when claimed generically
description: Beyond computer and lab functions, courts have treated certain everyday activities as routine when recited at a high level of generality or as insignificant extra-solution activity.
guidance: Examples include: (i) recording a customer’s order; (ii) shuffling and dealing a standard deck of cards; (iii) restricting public access to media by requiring a consumer to view an advertisement; (iv) presenting offers and gathering statistics; (v) determining an estimated outcome and setting a price; and (vi) arranging a hierarchy of groups, sorting information, eliminating less restrictive pricing information, and determining the price. As with other categories, being on this list does not automatically make every claim ineligible—context, specificity, and integration into a practical application matter.

name: Other meaningful limitations (beyond linking to a technological environment)
description: The claim should add meaningful limitations beyond generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment to transform the judicial exception into patent-eligible subject matter.
guidance: Meaningful limitations can arise from considerations in MPEP § 2106.05(a)-(d) when they amount to significantly more than the judicial exception or integrate it into a practical application. Examples: Diamond v. Diehr (use of Arrhenius equation integrated into an automated rubber-molding process — steps like installing rubber, measuring temperature, and automatically opening the press limited the mathematical equation to a practical application); Classen (analysis + a specific immunization step integrated the abstract analysis into a tangible treatment). By contrast, Alice found that recitation of a generic computer implementation merely linked an abstract idea to a technological environment and did not meaningfully limit it. Examiners must evaluate additional elements both individually and in combination—an element that is not enough alone may nonetheless be meaningful in combination (Diehr, BASCOM). For treatment/prophylaxis claims, overlap exists with Step 2A Prong Two considerations (see MPEP § 2106.04(d)(2)). When appropriate, examiners should explain on the record why additional elements meaningfully limit the judicial exception.

name: Mere instructions to apply an exception (the 'apply it' rule)
description: A determination whether additional elements are merely instructions to implement a judicial exception (i.e., 'apply it') or do more than recite using the exception.
guidance: Claims that merely state the judicial exception and add words that effectively say 'apply it' (or equivalent) do not render the exception patent-eligible. The Supreme Court requires that additional elements do 'more than simply stat[e] the [judicial exception] while adding the words ‘apply it’' (Alice quoting Mayo). Examples: Mayo—measuring metabolite levels was merely an instruction to apply the law of nature because measurement could be done by any means; Alice—recitation of a generic computer implementation was a mere instruction to apply an abstract idea; Benson—process for converting BCD to binary had no meaningful practical application except in connection with a computer. Requiring more than mere instructions does not mean claims must be narrow to be eligible: courts have found some broad claims eligible (e.g., McRO; Thales Visionix) and some narrow claims ineligible (e.g., Ultramercial; Electric Power Group). Examiners should beware of §101 analyses that turn on drafting (the 'draftsman’s art') and evaluate whether claimed additional elements supply a meaningful inventive concept beyond mere implementation.

name: Inventive step evaluation on claimed technical solution as a whole
description: Whether an invention possesses inventiveness is determined in relation to the claimed invention; the evaluation should be conducted on the technical solution defined by the claims, i.e., the entire technical solution, rather than a single technical feature.
guidance: Technical features that contribute to prior art or produce unexpected technical effects should be included in the claims; otherwise, even if described in the specification, they will not be considered in evaluating inventiveness. Features that do not contribute to solving the technical problem generally will not affect inventiveness even if included in the claims. Example: adding conventional/irrelevant features (housing shape, screen size) that do not contribute to the technical solution won't confer inventive step.

name: Sufficiency of disclosure (Article 26(3))—what is required
description: Specifications must disclose enough detail (e.g., key indicators, causal relationships, validation data) for a person skilled in the art to determine that the solution can solve the technical problem claimed.
guidance: Example: A cancer-prediction application failing to specify which blood/biochemistry indicators are key, their weights, causal links to prediction, or validation data was held non-compliant with Article 26(3). Lack of proof that the solution improves accuracy means insufficient disclosure.

name: Bitstream subject-matter exclusion (simple bitstreams not patentable)
description: If the subject matter of a claim relates only to a simple bitstream, then the claim falls under rules and methods for intellectual activities (Article 25(1)(ii)) and is not subject to patent protection.
guidance: Examples: claims that merely define a bitstream by listing syntax elements (e.g., 'A bitstream, characterized in that it includes syntax element A, syntax element B…') or that are titled as a 'method for generating a bitstream' but only define the bitstream content are non-patentable.

name: Specification drafting requirements for bitstream inventions
description: The specification of an invention patent application containing a bitstream generated by a specific video coding method should clearly and completely describe that specific video coding method so that a person skilled in the art can implement it.
guidance: If the subject relates to storing/transmitting the bitstream or a computer-readable medium, the specification should include corresponding description to support those claims.

name: Claim drafting guidance for bitstream/storage/transmission/media claims
description: Patent applications that include bitstreams generated by a specific video coding method can be drafted as claims for storage methods, transmission methods, and computer-readable storage media, and such claims should generally be based on claims related to the specific video coding method or include all features of those methods.
guidance: Example claim set shows method/device/media claims anchored to a video encoding method claim, with subsequent storage/transmission/media claims referencing the method or including its features.

name: Purpose of obviousness-type double patenting (ODP)
description: ODP 'is intended to prevent a patentee from obtaining a time-wise extension of patent for the same invention or an obvious modification thereof' and 'prevents an inventor from securing a second, later expiring patent for an invention covered by a patent that was filed at the same time.'
guidance: ODP applies where claims of a later-expiring patent are not patentably distinct from claims of an earlier-expiring, commonly owned patent. Terminal disclaimers are the usual remedy to overcome an ODP rejection. (Citations: In re Lonardo; AbbVie.)

name: How to determine which patent is 'later-expiring' for ODP
description: An ODP determination requires identifying which patent is the later-expiring patent, because ODP invalidates a later-expiring patent that claims an obvious variation of an earlier-expiring patent.
guidance: When patents have term adjustments/extensions (PTA or PTE), the appropriate expiration date to use must be determined (see separate metrics for PTA and PTE). The chosen expiration date controls which patent is 'later-expiring' and thus whether ODP applies.

name: Effect of finding ODP (scope of invalidation/remedy)
description: If asserted claims of a later-expiring patent are obvious variations of an earlier patent's claims and no terminal disclaimer is filed, the later claims are unpatentable under ODP.
guidance: Non-asserted claims that are not shown to be obvious variations remain entitled to their full statutory term, including PTA, unless separately found to be later-filed obvious variations. Invalidating only an 'adjustment period' would be tantamount to granting a retroactive terminal disclaimer and is improper if not raised and treated in the proceedings.

name: Derivation petition requirements (35 U.S.C. 135(a))
description: A petition to institute a derivation proceeding must state with particularity the basis for finding that a named inventor in the earlier application derived the claimed invention from an inventor named in the petitioner’s application, and without authorization filed the earlier application; must be filed within one year of the first publication by the earlier applicant of a claim to the same or substantially the same invention; must be made under oath; and must be supported by substantial evidence.

name: Timeliness and feasibility as institution factors
description: The Board may consider whether the review can be completed timely and may decline to institute a proceeding it determines it cannot complete in time.
guidance: Example refusal: petition that seeks review of several hundred claims based on a thousand references where resolving patentability would require compelled testimony of dozens of foreign non-party witnesses.

name: Scope of authorization when instituting
description: When instituting a trial, the Board will streamline issues by authorizing the trial only on the challenged claims for which threshold standards are met and will identify, on a claim-by-claim basis, the grounds on which the trial will proceed.
guidance: Any claim or issue not included in the authorization is not part of the trial.

name: Contents required in a motion to amend
description: Motions to amend must comply with content requirements in §§ 42.121(b) / 42.221(b): include a claim listing, show requested changes clearly, and describe how the original disclosure and any relied-on prior application support each claim added or amended.
guidance: A patent owner may not enlarge claim scope or add new matter; replacement claims should be identified as proposed substitute claims with all changes clearly discussed; must set forth support in original disclosure and any application for which benefit of filing date is sought.

name: Procedural requirements for proposed amendments
description: A motion to amend must be accompanied by the proposed amendment; claims filed by amendments should be substitute claims and must clearly state whether each claim is original, cancelled, replaced by proposed substitute, proposed substitute for X, or proposed new claim.
guidance: Amendments must clearly state where the specification and drawings support all limitations in proposed substitute claims; if the Board cannot determine support, the motion may be denied.

name: Statement of patentably distinct features
description: Motions to amend should clearly state the patentably distinct features for proposed substitute claims.
guidance: This aids the Board in determining whether the amendment narrows the claims and whether the amendment is responsive to the grounds of unpatentability.

name: Distinction between description and specification/claim (act of 1836)
description: The act of 1836 prescribed that the inventor should 'particularly specify and point out that which he claimed to be his own invention or discovery' — establishing the Claim (specification) as distinct from the Description.
guidance: This distinction is central for re-issue law: 'description' = detailed delineation for public use; 'specification' (or 'claim') = the specific statement of what is claimed. Re-issues relate differently to defects in each part.

name: Grounds for re-issue (defective/insufficient description or excessive claim)
description: Re-issues were limited to cases where a patent was 'inoperative or invalid, by reason of a defective or insufficient description or specification, or by reason of the patentee claiming in his specification, as his own invention, more than he had, or shall have, a right to claim as new.'
guidance: Two principal grounds: curing defective/insufficient disclosure (description/specification) and correcting an excessive claim. Historically courts have differed about whether re-issue can enlarge claims; modern view: enlargements only when actual inadvertent mistake exists.

name: Re-issue cannot be used to broaden claims except for bona fide mistake; delay may bar re-issue
description: A re-issue for the purpose of enlarging and expanding the Claim of a patent was not comprised within the literal terms of the law except where an actual mistake had occurred; an unreasonable delay in applying for a re-issue indicates the allegation of inadvertence or mistake is a mere pretence.
guidance: Re-issues for claim enlargement should be exception, not rule. Courts condemn using re-issue to capture later developments (waiting until others make improvements and then expanding). Miller v. Brass Co. and related commentary stress bona fide inadvertence as necessary and warn against abuse due to delay or sleeping on rights.

name: Character and amount of evidence varies with claim and alleged incredibility
description: The character and amount of evidence needed to support an asserted utility will vary depending on what is claimed and whether the asserted utility appears to contravene established principles and beliefs.
guidance: Assess utility requirements in light of the claim scope and whether the asserted use appears 'incredible' in view of current scientific understanding (Ex parte Ferguson; In re Gazave; In re Chilowsky). More extraordinary claims may require more persuasive support.

name: Credibility varies with type of claimed therapeutic effect (symptom treatment vs cure)
description: Claims to treat or cure diseases with no prior cures warrant careful review; assertions of usefulness for treating symptoms may require modest evidence, while assertions of 'curing' a disease may require significantly greater evidentiary support.
guidance: Assess credibility in light of state of the art at the time of invention; consider expert affidavits with sound reasoning as often sufficient to establish a reasonable expectation of success for challenging disease conditions (In re Sichert; In re Jolles; Ex parte Ferguson).

name: Inventor must contribute to conception
description: To be an inventor, a person must contribute to the conception of the invention; contribution to conception is the threshold question in determining inventorship, and merely suggesting a desired result (without means) does not make one an inventor.
guidance: Reduction to practice is generally irrelevant to inventorship except in rare simultaneous-conception-and-reduction situations (Fiers v. Revel). For chemical compounds, conception must be of the specific claimed compounds (Board of Education v. American Bioscience; Ex parte Smernoff). See MPEP § 2138.04–.05 for evidence required to establish conception or reduction to practice.

name: Joint inventorship standards (35 U.S.C. 116)
description: When an invention is made by two or more persons jointly, they shall apply for patent jointly. Joint inventors need not have worked together physically, need not have made the same type or amount of contribution, and need not contribute to every claim — contribution to at least one claim suffices.
guidance: There must be some quantum of collaboration or connection (e.g., collaboration, common direction, one inventor building on another’s report) — mere complete lack of contact is insufficient (Kimberly-Clark v. Procter & Gamble). Partial contributions that are original and significant qualify. Contribution to a means-plus-function element can make one a joint inventor as to that claim (Ethicon Inc. v. United States Surgical). See MPEP § 2109.01 and § 602.09 for correction procedures.

name: Inventorship 'by another' and differing inventive entities
description: Inventorship is 'by another' when there are different inventive entities and at least one inventor is not in common between the applications; special practice applies for first-to-file (AIA) versus pre-AIA cases.
guidance: Follow MPEP § 2153.01(a) for FITF (AIA) cases and MPEP § 2136.04 for pre-AIA cases. Determine whether inventive entities differ and whether an inventor is in common when assessing issues like derivation or benefit claims.

name: § 11.106 Confidentiality of information
description: A practitioner shall not reveal information relating to representation unless client gives informed consent, disclosure is impliedly authorized to carry out the representation, disclosure is permitted by specific exceptions, or disclosure is required by other provisions. Practitioner may reveal information to prevent death/substantial bodily harm, prevent client from engaging in inequitable conduct before the Office or crime/fraud reasonably certain to result in substantial injury to another when client used practitioner's services, to secure legal advice about compliance, to establish claim/defense on behalf of practitioner, or to comply with other law/court order. A practitioner shall disclose to the Office information necessary to comply with duty of disclosure provisions.
guidance: Lists six exceptions where disclosure may be reasonable; also notes implied authorization to reveal information to the extent necessary to carry out representation; ties to duty of disclosure to the Office.

name: § 11.115 Safekeeping property
description: A practitioner shall hold property of clients or third persons separate from practitioner's own property. Funds must be kept in separate accounts in proper jurisdictions; other property must be identified and safeguarded. Complete records preserved for five years after termination. Advance fees must be deposited into client trust account and withdrawn only as earned or expenses incurred. Promptly notify clients upon receipt of funds/property, deliver funds/property client is entitled to, and render accounting upon request. When multiple claimants claim interests, property must be kept separate until dispute resolved and undisputed portions promptly distributed.
guidance: Extensive recordkeeping requirements: receipt/disbursement journals; ledger records per client; copies of retainer/compensation agreements; accountings; bills; records showing disbursements; equivalents of checkbook registers, bank statements, canceled checks; records of electronic transfers with authorizing person and confirmations; monthly trial balances and quarterly reconciliations; copies of client file portions related to trust transactions. Client trust account safeguards: authorized signatories limited to practitioner or persons under direct supervision; receipts deposited intact; withdrawals by check payable to named payee or authorized electronic transfer only. Records may be maintained electronically if printable. Lawyers' records meeting state requirements deemed compliant; rules for firms employing patent agents also stated.

name: Determine whether the invention already exists / avoid public disclosure before filing
description: According to U.S. patent law, an invention cannot be patented if the claimed invention was described in a printed publication, on sale, available to the public, or in public use before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
guidance: Maintain confidentiality — do not publicly disclose, offer for sale, or otherwise make the invention public prior to filing, because such disclosures can be prior art that bars patentability.

name: Scope: apply only to nature-based product limitations
description: The markedly different characteristics analysis should be applied only to the nature-based product limitations in the claim to determine whether the nature-based products are 'product of nature' exceptions.
guidance: Because a nature-based product can be claimed by itself or as one or more limitations of a claim, care should be taken not to overly extend the markedly different characteristics analysis to products that when viewed as a whole are not nature-based.

name: When to perform or skip the analysis for naturally occurring limitations
description: If the nature-based product limitation is naturally occurring, there is no need to perform the markedly different characteristics analysis because the limitation is by definition directed to a naturally occurring product and thus falls under the product of nature exception.
guidance: However, if the nature-based product limitation is not naturally occurring (for example due to some human intervention), then the markedly different characteristics analysis must be performed to determine whether the claimed product limitation is a product of nature exception.

name: Application to product claims
description: Where the claim is to a nature-based product by itself, apply the markedly different characteristics analysis to the entire product; where the claim is to a nature-based product produced by combining multiple components, apply the analysis to the resultant combination; where the claim includes a nature-based product in combination with non-nature-based elements, apply the analysis only to the nature-based product limitation.
guidance: Examples: a claim to 'a Lactobacillus bacterium' -> analyze entire bacterium (Chakrabarty). A probiotic composition comprising Lactobacillus and milk -> analyze the mixture (resultant combination). A yogurt starter kit comprising Lactobacillus in a container with instructions -> analyze only the Lactobacillus; container and instructions evaluated separately in Prong Two/Step 2B. See Funk Bros. Seed Co. example where only bacterial mixture was analyzed.

name: Application to product-by-process claims
description: For a product-by-process claim, the analysis turns on whether the nature-based product in the claim has markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart.
guidance: Refer to MPEP § 2113 for more information on product-by-process claims; focus remains on the characteristics of the claimed nature-based product as recited by the claim.

name: Standard for determining 'markedly different' characteristics
description: To be 'markedly different', a characteristic must be changed compared to the naturally occurring counterpart and cannot be an inherent/innate characteristic or an incidental change. The inventor must have caused the claimed product to possess at least one characteristic that is different from that of the counterpart.
guidance: If there is no change in any characteristic, the claimed product is a product of nature exception. If there is a change in at least one characteristic and that change was produced by the inventor's efforts/influences, then the change will generally be considered a markedly different characteristic such that the claimed product is not a product of nature exception. See Myriad discussion that incidental changes from isolation are not enough.

name: Positive examples: products found to have markedly different characteristics
description: Court examples of products held to have markedly different characteristics and thus not products of nature.
guidance: Chakrabarty: genetically modified Pseudomonas bacterium with additional plasmids and the functional ability to degrade multiple hydrocarbons (structural and functional changes). Myriad: claimed full-length cDNA of BRCA1—structural difference (exons only) though same protein-encoding function—held not a product of nature. These illustrate that structural and/or functional changes produced by the inventor can support eligibility.

name: Negative examples: products lacking markedly different characteristics
description: Court examples where claimed products lacked markedly different characteristics and were treated as products of nature (ineligible).
guidance: Myriad: isolated genes—incidental structural differences from isolation were insufficient because sequences otherwise identical to natural genes. Ambry Genetics: synthetic primers matched natural nucleotide sequences and retained innate DNA functions (binding), so not markedly different. In re Marden: ductility of vanadium was inherent and not a characteristic conferred by a new combination/chemical change. Roslin: cloned farm animals were genetic copies of donors; unclaimed phenotypic differences could not render them markedly different. These illustrate anti-patterns (innate characteristics, incidental changes, unclaimed differences).

name: Fundamental Economic Practices
description: Claims that recite fundamental economic practices (ways of organizing human economic activity) are directed to unpatentable abstract ideas.
guidance: Examples and case law: hedging to ‘protect against risk’ (Bilski v. Kappos, 561 U.S. 593) — hedging is a “fundamental economic practice” and an unpatentable abstract idea; methods allowing suppliers/consumers to minimize risk from market demand fluctuations; Bancorp Services v. Sun Life (claims for managing a stable value protected life insurance policy were an attempt to patent the abstract idea of managing such a policy and using well-known calculations); other examples include mitigating settlement risk (Alice v. CLS Bank), rules for conducting a wagering game (In re Smith), financial instruments designed to protect against investment risk (In re Chorna), offer-based price optimization (OIP Techs. v. Amazon), local processing of payments for remotely purchased goods (Inventor Holdings v. Bed Bath Beyond), using an external marking on mail to communicate sender/recipient/contents (Secured Mail Solutions v. Universal Wilde), and placing an order based on displayed market information (Trading Technologies v. IBG). Courts treat these subject matters as abstract ideas under Alice/Mayo.

name: Mental Processes — general definition
description: A mental process (thinking) that can be performed in the human mind, or by a human using pen and paper, is considered an abstract idea.
guidance: Authoritative citations: CyberSource v. Retail Decisions; Gottschalk v. Benson; Mayo; Parker v. Flook. The grouping includes observations, evaluations, judgments, and opinions and applies to product and process claims alike. Courts consider methods that are the equivalent of human mental work to be unpatentable abstract ideas (‘basic tools of scientific and technological work’). Examiners should use the subsequent points A–D to guide determination of whether a claim recites a mental process.

name: A. Claim with limitation(s) that cannot practically be performed in the human mind does not recite a mental process
description: If the claim contains limitations that humans cannot practically perform mentally (the human mind is not equipped to perform them), the claim does not fall into the mental-process abstract-idea grouping.
guidance: Cases/examples where claims were not mental processes because they could not practically be performed mentally: SRI Int’l v. Cisco (collection/analysis of network data using network monitors and packet analysis), SiRF Tech. (GPS pseudorange calculations to determine receiver position and time), Synopsys (specific multi-step data encryption manipulation), Research Corp. Techs. (pixel-by-pixel halftone rendering requiring manipulation of computer data structures). Examiners should identify limitations that a human cannot practically perform and treat those claims as not reciting a mental process.

name: B. Claim that encompasses a human performing the step(s) mentally with or without a physical aid recites a mental process
description: If the claim recites limitations that can practically be performed in the human mind — even if a physical aid (pen and paper, slide rule) may be used — the limitation falls within the mental-process grouping and is an abstract idea.
guidance: Courts do not distinguish between purely mental acts and those aided by simple physical tools; the use of a physical aid does not negate the mental nature (Benson; Synopsys). Examples: CyberSource (constructing a map of credit card numbers could be done by writing transaction lists), Flook (computations performable by pencil and paper), University of Florida Research Foundation v. GE (analysis/manipulation described as performed mentally with pen and paper flowsheets and charts), Symantec (message screening steps performable mentally or with pen and paper). Examiners should consider whether claimed steps can be performed by a human mentally (possibly with simple aids) and, if so, treat them as mental processes.

name: C. A claim that requires a computer may still recite a mental process
description: Claims implemented on a computer can nonetheless recite a mental process if the underlying claimed concept can be performed mentally (or with pen and paper); computer implementation alone does not avoid abstraction.
guidance: Supreme Court/BCA cases: Benson (algorithm performable mentally but implemented in computers was an abstract idea); Mortgage Grader (anonymous loan shopping could be performed by humans without a computer). Examiners should carefully consider the broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the specification to determine whether the applicant is simply claiming a concept performed 1) on a generic computer, 2) in a computer environment, or 3) using a computer as a tool — in those situations the claim is considered to recite a mental process. Example subpoint — Performing a mental process on a generic computer: Voter Verified (voting/verifying/submitting votes described as human cognitive actions despite computer implementation); Versata (determining a price using general purpose computer hardware). If the specification describes the claimed invention as a concept performed in the human mind and computer steps are generic, treat as abstract.

name: D. ‘Mental processes’ is a type of abstract idea that can appear in product and process claims
description: The term ‘mental processes’ refers to a category of abstract ideas and is not limited to statutory claim types; product (systems, media) and process claims can both recite mental-process-type abstract ideas.
guidance: Example: Versata (product claims to computer systems and computer-readable media were identified as reciting mental-process-type abstract ideas). Examiners should understand that the classification focuses on the nature of the idea, not whether the claim is a process or a product.

name: Novelty — separate comparison (no combining for novelty)
description: When determining novelty, the examiner shall compare each claim of the application separately with the relevant technical contents disclosed in each item of the prior art, rather than with a combination of the contents disclosed in several items of the prior art or with a combination of several technical solutions disclosed in one reference document.
guidance: Novelty assessment uses single-item comparisons; combining disclosures is not appropriate for novelty rejection.

name: JPO — claim specification and interpretation
description: The examiner specifies the claimed invention based on the claim, taking the description, drawings and common general knowledge at the time of filing into consideration in interpreting the meanings of words in the claims.
guidance: Examiner should always consider the matter or terms described in the claims and should not ignore them; interpretation uses claim text plus description/drawings/common general knowledge.

name: JPO — inventive step assessment procedure (primary/secondary prior art and 4-step reasoning)
description: The examiner selects the prior art most suitable for the reasoning (the 'primary prior art') and determines whether it is possible to reason that a person skilled in the art would easily arrive at the claimed invention from the primary prior art by following steps (1)–(4): (1) determine if reasoning is possible using secondary prior art or common general knowledge to cover differences; (2) if impossible, conclude inventive step exists; (3) if possible, comprehensively assess factors supporting inventive step; (4) if after (3) reasoning is impossible, conclude inventive step exists, otherwise conclude it does not involve an inventive step.
guidance: Do not regard a combination of two or more independent pieces of prior art as the primary prior art; use the primary/secondary framework and the staged reasoning described.

name: CNIPA — three-step obviousness test
description: Usually the following three steps are followed: (1) determining the closest prior art; (2) determining the distinguishing features of the invention and the technical problem actually solved; (3) determining whether or not the claimed invention is obvious to a person skilled in the art starting from the closest prior art and the technical problem actually solved, i.e., whether there exists a technical motivation in the prior art to apply the distinguishing features to the closest prior art.
guidance: If such a technical motivation exists, the invention is considered obvious and lacks prominent substantive features.

name: Algorithms tied to computer internal structure or performance are technical
description: If the algorithm in the claim has specific technical relationships with the internal structure of computer systems, realizes improvement of internal performance of computer systems, or improves hardware computing efficiency or execution effects (reducing data storage/transmission, improving hardware processing speed), then algorithmic features shall be considered to functionally support technical features and contribute to the technical solution.
guidance: Such algorithmic contributions should be factored into inventiveness assessment.

name: Business-method features requiring technical adjustments are technical
description: If the implementation of features of rules and methods for business in a claim requires an adjustment or improvement of technical means, then the business-method features and the technical features functionally support each other and their contribution to the technical solution shall be considered in inventiveness examination.
guidance: Look for required technical modifications as a sign that business-method features contribute technically.

name: JPO — enablement requirement (Article 36(4) JPA)
description: The description must be clear and sufficient to enable any person ordinarily skilled in the art to which the invention pertains to work the invention. The examiner determines the enablement requirement for each claim; if a skilled person cannot understand how to carry out the claimed invention on the basis of the description, drawings and common general technical knowledge at filing, the description is insufficient.
guidance: If carrying out the invention would require trials and errors or complicated experimentation beyond what a skilled person should reasonably be expected to do, enablement is not satisfied.

name: JPO — support requirement (Article 36(6)(i) JPA)
description: A claimed invention shall be disclosed in the description. The purpose is to prevent a patent for an invention not disclosed to the public; the examiner determines whether the statements in the claims satisfy the support requirement by comparing the claimed invention and the invention stated in the description, examining substantial correspondence.
