guidance: Substantial correspondence centers on whether a skilled person would recognize that the problem to be solved would be actually solved by the disclosure; claims that exceed the extent of disclosure fail support requirement.

name: JPO — violation type: generic claim with only specific embodiments
description: A violation exists where a claim is directed to a generic concept but embodiments only of a part of more specific concepts encompassed by the generic concept are stated in the description in a manner that only the specific concepts can be carried out, and there is a well-founded reason that other specific concepts encompassed are not clearly/sufficiently enabled.
guidance: Both conditions (i) generic claim/only specific embodiments, and (ii) well-founded reason that other variants are not enabled, must apply to find this enablement violation.

name: JPO — product function presumed from AI requires embodiment or substitution
description: Inventions of a product presumed to have a certain function because of AI cannot satisfy the description requirements without an embodiment in which evaluation on the function is made using a product actually made, unless an estimation result by AI can be a substitution for an evaluation on a product actually made.
guidance: Empirical evaluation often required when claiming product functionality established via AI inference.

name: CNIPA — claims supported by description and limits on generalization (Article 26.4)
description: The claims shall be supported by the description and define the extent of protection sought clearly and concisely. The technical solution for which protection is sought in each claim shall be a solution that a skilled person can reach directly or by generalization from the contents sufficiently disclosed. Generalization of claims shall not go beyond the scope of contents disclosed in the description.
guidance: Allow generalization to equivalents/obvious variants only where a skilled person can reasonably predict same properties/uses; speculative generalizations whose effects are difficult to determine are not allowed.

name: CNIPA — functional feature and pure functional claim limits
description: A technical feature defined by function in a claim is construed as embracing all means capable of performing the function. Whether such functional definition can be supported by the description shall be examined; if embodiments only show a particular way and a skilled person would not appreciate that other alternative means could perform the function, then embracing other alternative means is not allowed. Pure functional definition is not permitted.
guidance: If the description merely vaguely states alternatives without enabling how they might be used, function-based claiming is disallowed.

name: CNIPA — claims for computer programs and apparatus mapping to program modules
description: Claims of computer-program inventions may be process claims or product/apparatus claims. Claims must be supported by the description and represent the technical solution in its entirety, outlining essential technical features rather than only functions/effects. Where an apparatus claim corresponds step-for-step to program flow, components are regarded as program modules and the apparatus claim is treated as program module architecture rather than entity hardware.
guidance: Careful claim drafting needed to reflect whether claimed components are hardware or program-module abstractions; examiner will treat module-based apparatus claims accordingly.

name: Claims for inventions containing algorithmic/business features (CNIPA)
description: Claims shall be supported by the description and shall record the technical features, the algorithmic features or features of rules and methods for business that functionally support each other or have an interaction relationship with the technical features, and shall define the extent of patent protection in a clear and concise manner.
guidance: Claims must explicitly include the interacting algorithmic/business features together with the technical features; clarity and concision required.

name: Thesis I — Prevenient grace necessary for the beginning of faith (de fide)
description: Prevenient grace is absolutely necessary not only for faith's increase but for the very beginning of faith; faith is 'the gift of God' and the first impulse to believe is an effect of prevenient grace.
guidance: Supported by Scripture (e.g. John VI 'No man can come to me, except the Father draw him') and Tradition; condemned Semipelagian claims that the beginning of faith is a natural act of the will.

name: Rejection of Semipelagian intermediate claims
description: Semipelagianism taught that the beginning of faith depends on the will (initium fidei), that nature can merit grace by 'meritum de congruo', and that free-will after justification can secure final perseverance unaided; these positions were condemned by the Second Council of Orange and repudiated by the Church.
guidance: The Church judged such compromises unacceptable; historical and patristic evidence (e.g. Augustine, earlier Fathers) is marshaled to show prevenient grace precedes any natural beginning of faith or meritorious natural disposition.

name: Foreign-language prior art translations
description: Portola Packaging may not prohibit reexamination over a complete and accurate translation of that foreign language prior art reference.
guidance: If a reexamination request explains why a more complete and accurate translation of the same foreign language prior art reference teaches what is required by the patent claims, it may be appropriate to rely on that foreign language prior art reference to order and/or conduct reexamination.

name: Office action wording when rejection withdrawn under Portola Packaging
description: If a rejection in the reexamination has previously been issued and that rejection is withdrawn to comply with In re Portola Packaging, the Office action withdrawing such rejection should state the withdrawal and that no patentability determination of the claims has been made in the reexamination proceeding.
guidance: Use the template phrasing: 'The rejection(s) based upon _______ is/are withdrawn in view of In re Portola Packaging, Inc., 110 F.3d 786, 42 USPQ2d 1295 (Fed. Cir. 1997). No patentability determination of the claims of the patent in view of such prior art has been made in this reexamination proceeding.'

name: Ability to correct foreign priority or domestic benefit during reexamination
description: The patent owner may correct the failure to adequately claim foreign priority or domestic benefit in a patent to be reexamined during the reexamination proceeding in accordance with the section's guidelines; renewal of previously made claims of priority/benefit is not necessary during reexamination.
guidance: Design applications cannot claim the benefit of a provisional application. Specific petitions, fees, and supporting documents may be required depending on the filing dates and circumstances (see the detailed rules below).

name: Submitting for first time both foreign priority claim and certified copy — general rule
description: The patent owner may obtain the right of foreign priority where it is necessary to submit for the first time both the claim for priority and the certified copy, but certain petitions may be required depending on the filing date of the application which matured into the patent.
guidance: When required, a grantable petition under 37 CFR 1.55(e) must be filed in the application that matured into the patent; a separate letter must be filed in the reexamination proceeding identifying the concurrently filed petition and application number. Decisions and supporting ADS or other materials will be placed in the reexamination file.

name: Requirements when the patent matured from an application filed on or after September 16, 2012 (foreign priority restoration)
description: If the patent matured from an application filed on or after Sept 16, 2012, the patent owner must file in the file of the application which matured into the patent: (a) a grantable petition for an unintentionally delayed priority claim under 37 CFR 1.55(e); (b) an application data sheet identifying the foreign application (37 CFR 1.76(b)(6)) unless previously submitted; (c) a certified copy of the foreign application unless previously submitted or an exception applies; (d) the petition fee (37 CFR 1.17(m)); and (e) a statement that the entire delay was unintentional.
guidance: In the reexamination proceeding, file a separate letter notifying the Office that items (a)-(e) are concurrently being filed in the application file. When a decision on the petition is rendered, a copy of the decision and any ADS determined to meet requirements will be placed in the reexamination file.

name: Claiming domestic benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 — general correction during reexamination
description: The patent owner may correct failure to adequately claim benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 of an earlier filed copending U.S. patent application during reexamination; for patents which matured from applications filed on/after Nov 29, 2000, a grantable petition for an unintentionally delayed benefit claim under 37 CFR 1.78(e) must be filed.
guidance: The petition and attachments (except certain specification amendments) must be filed in the file of the application which matured into the patent, and a letter must be filed in the reexamination proceeding notifying the Office of the concurrent filing. Decisions and ADS placed in reexamination file when petition decided.

name: Requirements for claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 for applications filed on or after September 16, 2012
description: If the patent matured from an application filed on or after Sept 16, 2012, the patent owner must file in that application's file: (a) a grantable petition for an unintentionally delayed benefit claim under 37 CFR 1.78(e); (b) an application data sheet including the reference required by 35 U.S.C. 120 and 37 CFR 1.78(d)(2) unless previously submitted; (c) the petition fee (37 CFR 1.17(m)); and (d) a statement that the entire delay was unintentional.
guidance: In the reexamination, file a letter notifying the Office that items (a)-(d) are concurrently being filed in the application file. When a decision on the petition is rendered, a copy will be placed in the reexamination file, and if granted, the ADS determined to meet requirements will be placed in the reexamination file.

name: Requirements for claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 for applications filed before September 16, 2012
description: If the patent matured from an application filed before Sept 16, 2012, the patent owner must file in the application file: (a) a grantable petition under 37 CFR 1.78(e); (b) unless an amendment in the reexamination is chosen, an ADS including the required reference to the prior-filed application (37 CFR 1.76(b)(5)); (c) the petition fee; and (d) a statement that the delay was unintentional.
guidance: Alternatively, the patent owner may file, in the reexamination proceeding, an amendment inserting the required reference into the specification first sentence(s) following the title as set forth in 37 CFR 1.78(h). A notifying letter must be filed in the reexamination. Decisions and ADS placed in reexamination file when petition decided.

name: Restoring benefit of a provisional application where filing of the subsequent application was delayed (37 CFR 1.78(b))
description: A grantable petition to restore the benefit of a provisional application under 37 CFR 1.78(b), with required attachments including an ADS meeting 1.78(b), must be filed in the file of the application which matured into the patent (the subsequent application); a letter must be filed in the reexamination proceeding notifying the Office of the concurrent filing.
guidance: When a decision on the petition is rendered in the subsequent application file, a copy of the decision and any ADS determined to meet requirements will be placed in the reexamination proceeding file. Design applications cannot claim provisional benefit.

name: Purpose and content expectations of the examiner's first Office action in reexamination
description: The examiner’s first ex parte action on the merits should be the primary action to establish the issues between the examiner and the patent owner and should be sufficiently detailed to enable the second action to be properly made a final action.
guidance: First action should caution the patent owner to make a complete response because the next action is expected to be final; caution that 37 CFR 1.116(b) will be strictly enforced after final action; include a detailed statement of the pertinency and manner of applying cited prior art to each claim; if claim charts were submitted, the examiner may incorporate them but must carefully review them; the first action should respond to substance of arguments raised under 37 CFR 1.510, 1.530, and 1.535 and treat inappropriate arguments per 37 CFR 1.552(c). If relying on a patent owner statement under 1.501(a)(2), the requester must explain how that statement is being used to determine claim meaning.

name: Handling of dependent claims in reexamination (2260.01)
description: If an unamended base patent claim has been rejected, canceled, or is no longer subject to reexamination due to adjudication in court, any claim undergoing reexamination which is directly or indirectly dependent thereon should be confirmed or allowed if the dependent claim is otherwise allowable and should not be objected to or rejected merely because it depends on a rejected or canceled patent claim.
guidance: No requirement should be made to rewrite the dependent claim in independent form. If a new base claim (other than original patent base claim) has been canceled in reexamination, a claim which depends thereon should be rejected as indefinite. If a new base claim or amended patent claim is rejected, a dependent claim should be objected to if it is otherwise patentable and a requirement made for rewriting the dependent claim in independent form.

name: Form and content specifics for Office actions (2262)
description: The examiner’s first Office action should state the examiner’s position and be so complete that the second Office action can properly be final. The first Office action must be sufficiently detailed to set forth pertinency and manner of applying cited prior art to the claims; claim charts may be incorporated but must be reviewed; subsequent actions must address patent owner responses to previous actions.
guidance: If examiner concludes claims are patentable over cited prior art, indicate why similar to allowance (MPEP § 1302.14) and refer to record portions that clearly establish patentability. Normally, title changes are unnecessary; if needed, notify patent owner early. Examiner may indicate a telephone conference with patent owner’s representative may result in placing the proceeding in condition for NIRC; when conferences occur, actions must be properly signed/initialed by conferees per policy (see MPEP § 2271.01).

name: Division of specification into Description and Claim and their functions
description: A specification has two parts: the Description (to communicate the invention to the public) and the Claim (to define the limits of the exclusive right).
guidance: The Description may include broader contextual material and explanations; the Claim enumerates essential characteristics and refers to the Description for fuller explanation. The Claim is the measure of the patent; courts will not search the specification to supply definiteness the Claim should provide.

name: Claims must particularly and distinctly define the invention
description: Claims must point out particularly and distinctly the invention to be secured; the Claim is the measure of the patent and must define essential characteristics.
guidance: While the Description explains, the Claim delimits; a Claim cannot be vague. Both Description and Claims are required; the Claim may need to be specific and well-defined to supplement the Description (see Ex parte Skinner, Smith v. Murray).

name: Both Description and Claims required in a specification
description: A valid specification requires both a Description and at least one Claim; the Description alone is not sufficient under current statute—claims must supplement the description.
guidance: The primary object is description, but the Claim must specifically and distinctly define the invention. The patent office assumes specification parts will conform to statutes and rules; failure to include both may render application defective (see Ex parte Crandall).

name: Anticipate claim chart mapping (SEP drafting)
description: When drafting patents likely to become SEPs, anticipate that claims will be mapped to the standard via claim charts.
guidance: Draft claims and specification so that mapping to standard-essential elements is clear and defensible in licensing and litigation.

name: Use standard's terminology in patent drafting
description: Employ terminology from the relevant standard in the specification and claims where appropriate.
guidance: Using standard terminology facilitates claim-charting and reduces disputes over what constitutes essential subject matter.

name: Cover both upstream and downstream implementations
description: Draft claims to encompass both upstream (e.g., chipset) and downstream (e.g., device) implementations of the standard.
guidance: Broad coverage helps capture real-world implementations and supports portfolio licensing strategies.

name: Capture mandatory features of the standard (avoid optional features)
description: Focus claims on mandatory features of the standard and avoid drafting only for optional features which are less likely to be essential.
guidance: Mandatory-feature coverage increases the likelihood of essentiality determinations; optional-feature claims are weaker candidates for SEP status.

name: Provide claim charts showing essentiality (licensing best practice for SEP owners)
description: SEP owners should provide claim charts demonstrating how claims map to the standard and why they are essential.
guidance: Claim charts are a primary way to establish essentiality and support licensing demands and litigation positions.

name: Document the negotiation process (licensing best practice for implementers)
description: Maintain records of communications, offers, and rationale during licensing discussions.
guidance: Documentation supports an implementer’s defense against injunctions and FRAND-related claims of bad faith.

name: SEP litigation strategy for patent owners: establish essentiality with claim charts
description: In litigation, patent owners should establish essentiality through clear claim-chart evidence mapping claims to the standard.
guidance: Strong essentiality evidence supports damages claims and defenses against challenges to enforceability.

name: SEP litigation strategy for patent owners: file counter-claims against unwilling licensees
description: Patent owners may file counter-claims (e.g., for breach of contract or infringement) against implementers that refuse to license on FRAND terms.
guidance: Counter-claims can be part of a broader enforcement strategy, but must be balanced against antitrust and forum-selection considerations.

name: SEP litigation strategy for patent owners: seek licensing in established jurisdictions
description: Bring licensing claims in jurisdictions known for established SEP jurisprudence (e.g., UK, China).
guidance: Choice of forum can materially affect remedies and FRAND determinations; forum-shopping risks include anti-suit and anti-anti-suit injunctions.

name: SEP litigation strategy for implementers: challenge essentiality
description: Implementers should challenge whether asserted patents are actually essential to the standard.
guidance: Invalidating essentiality or narrowing claim scope can reduce licensing exposure and damages.

name: Pictures/drawings may constitute an enabling disclosure
description: Pictures and drawings may be sufficiently enabling to put the public in possession of the article pictured and thus may be used to reject claims to the article.
guidance: The picture must show all the claimed structural features and how they are put together. Drawings can constitute description for anticipation 'by drawings alone as well as by words.' See In re Bager and MPEP § 2125 (drawings as prior art).

name: Later factual references can sometimes be relied on even if they postdate filing
description: In certain circumstances, references cited to show a universal fact need not be available as prior art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention; later publications may be cited to show facts such as that undue experimentation would have been required, a parameter was critical or not, a specification statement was inaccurate, inoperation or lack of utility, or indefiniteness.
guidance: Such post-effective-filing-date factual evidence may be used to illuminate specific factual questions (e.g., enablement, criticality) but it is impermissible to use later factual references to determine whether the application met the written-description or enablement requirements under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) as of the filing date. See In re Wilson, Corneil, Rainer, Marzocchi, Langer, Koller, and Amgen v. Sanofi.

name: Tax strategies are treated as prior art under AIA section 14
description: For novelty and nonobviousness under 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103, any strategy for reducing, avoiding, or deferring tax liability (a 'tax strategy') shall be deemed insufficient to differentiate a claimed invention from the prior art.
guidance: The term 'tax liability' covers liabilities under federal, state, local, or foreign law. The provision took effect Sept 16, 2011 and applies to applications pending or filed on/after that date and patents issued on/after that date. There are two statutory exclusions (see next rubric entries). Examiner treatment parallels printed-matter limitations (MPEP § 2112.01).

name: Exclusions to AIA section 14 (tax strategy provision)
description: Two exclusions: (1) the provision does not apply to that part of an invention that is a method, apparatus, technology, computer program product, or system used solely for preparing a tax or information return or other tax filing (including recording/transmitting/organizing data related to such filing); (2) the provision does not apply to that part that is used solely for financial management, to the extent it is severable from any tax strategy or does not limit the use of any tax strategy by any taxpayer or advisor.
guidance: If claim limitations fall within these exclusions (e.g., software solely enabling tax filing), such limitations may be given patentable weight; otherwise limitations directed to a tax strategy must be treated as within the prior art.

name: Examination procedure for claims relating to tax strategies
description: When examining claims related to tax strategies, follow a procedure: construe the claim per MPEP § 2111 et seq., analyze 35 U.S.C. 101 and 112 in accordance with current guidance (unaffected by sec. 14), identify any limitations relating to a tax strategy (noting exclusions), and evaluate the claim for 102/103 treating tax-strategy limitations as within the prior art.
guidance: Form paragraph 7.06.01 may be used to indicate claim limitations interpreted as tax strategies. Treating tax-strategy limitations as within the prior art is analogous to treatment of printed-matter limitations (MPEP § 2112.01).

name: Form paragraph 7.06.01 wording for tax-strategy limitation
description: Template paragraph to indicate a claim limitation interpreted as a tax strategy is being treated as within the prior art and insufficient to differentiate the claim from the prior art.
guidance: Includes Examiner Note instructing to recite the claim limitation in bracket 1 and insert claim numbers in bracket 2; see MPEP § 2124.01 for more information.

name: Treatment of computer-implemented methods involving tax strategies
description: A computer-implemented method that is novel and non-obvious is not affected by the tax-strategy provision even if used for a tax purpose; however, a prior-art computer-implemented method does not become non-obvious merely by implementing a novel tax strategy. Claim limitations solely directed to enabling tax filing or to financial management (when severable) should be given patentable weight; limitations directed to a tax strategy should not.
guidance: Analyze claims for 35 U.S.C. 101 and 112 as usual; do not give patentable weight to tax-strategy limitations for purposes of 102/103 analysis.

name: Drawings and pictures as prior art
description: Drawings and pictures can anticipate claims if they clearly show the structure which is claimed; origin of the drawing is immaterial and unintended or unexplained features in a utility patent drawing can still be relied upon.
guidance: Evaluate drawings for what they reasonably disclose and suggest to one of ordinary skill in the art. See In re Mraz and In re Aslanian; see MPEP § 2121.04 for drawings as 'enabled disclosures.'

name: Scope of a patent reference that is a 'patent' but not a 'publication' — use of the specification
description: When a patented document is used as a patent (not as a publication), the examiner may rely on any information provided in the specification which relates to the subject matter of the patented claims when making a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(a) or pre-AIA 102(a),(b) or (d).
guidance: Unclaimed details in the specification germane to the claimed invention can be relied upon; courts have held that 'invention ... patented' includes all disclosed aspects. See Ex parte Ovist, In re Kathawala. Note In re Fuge's limited holding ('at the least, the scope ... embraces everything included in the claim').

name: Provisional rights for applicants prior to grant
description: Where an applicant knows their invention or industrial design is being commercially used by another without prior use right, the applicant may notify in writing the user of the filing, specifying filing date and publication date so that the user shall terminate or continue such use. For layout-designs commercially exploited by the person with registration right or licensee before grant, if aware of another's commercial use, they may notify the user of their registration right to terminate or continue use.
guidance: Allows applicants to assert provisional interests before grant by notifying alleged infringers; may underpin later compensation claims per Article 131 and provisional rights rules.

name: Ensure limits on repeat filings do not unduly harm legitimate applicants
description: Design repeat-filing limits to distinguish abusive continuation practice from good-faith further prosecution or necessary refinement.
guidance: Recognize industries (e.g., pharmaceuticals, biotech) that file early and legitimately refine claims; allow mechanisms (narrow exceptions, higher fees, or limited continuations) for such cases. Use appeal processes (PTAB, Federal Circuit) as an alternative avenue for applicants who reach repeat-filing limits.

name: Mere exercise of ordinary creativity of a person skilled in the art
description: Common improvements based on general applications of known art, reasoning based on known physical properties, or referring to other technical fields to solve a known problem fall into ordinary creativity and typically negate inventive step.
guidance: Includes selecting optimal material from known materials, optimizing numerical ranges, replacing with equivalents, workshop modification of design, partial removal of features, and simple change of use. If differences between claimed and cited inventions fall only into these categories, inventive step is usually denied unless another ground supports it.

name: Partial removal of technical features
description: A claimed invention is not considered inventive if omission of some technical features known in the prior art simply removes the related function/effect and is obvious to the skilled person; but inventive step may be acknowledged when omission does not affect or enhances function.
guidance: Evaluate whether omission merely removes functionality or whether it unexpectedly improves or leaves function intact. Example: omitting a water-soluble silicate from toothpaste to cut cost removes the protective effect and is non-inventive.

name: Simple change and limitation of use of the invention
description: A claim that merely changes the use of a known invention, or imposes a simple further restriction of such use without exhibiting any advantage, is not considered inventive.
guidance: If a new use is naturally expected from prior properties (e.g., reusing synthetic oil as cutting oil because its lubricating properties change slowly), inventive step is negated.

name: Advantageous effects to be considered
description: If an effect derived from matters defining a claimed invention is advantageous compared to a cited invention, it supports affirmatively the inventive step.
guidance: Remarkable advantageous effects not foreseeable by a skilled person from the state of the art can rebut a prima facie obviousness finding. Particularly important in unpredictable fields (selection inventions, chemical). Examiner may rely on inventor's assertions and experimental evidence if the effect is inferable from the description and drawings; unsupported assertions should not be considered. Case law references cited.

name: Determining inventive step of an invention including numerical limitations
description: Experimental selection of an optimal numerical range from known art is normally ordinary creativity; inventive step is possible if the limited numerical range produces a remarkably improved effect across the boundary.
guidance: Criteria for significance: (1) significance required regarding any part of range if claimed invention is a continuation of cited invention; (2) if inventions solve different problems with qualitatively different effects, significance is not required. To acknowledge significance, there must be a remarkable change across the boundary and (a) technical meaning of the numerical limitation described in detail, and (b) embodiments or supplemental materials proving the range is critical—ideally objective experimental results covering the range. Examples given where numeric limits without explanation are technically meaningless.

name: Determining inventive step of a parameter invention
description: A parameter invention introduces a non-standard parameter (mathematical correlation of parameters) as an essential element; inventive-step determination must consider the technical meaning and function caused by the parameter.
guidance: First determine subject matter from description/drawings/common knowledge. If the parameter is merely a different expression or weakly linked to effect, inventive step denied. If parameter functions like a numerical limitation, those criteria apply. Examiner may raise reasonable doubt and must state grounds concretely; if parameter is standard/common, these special criteria are not applied. Also, if converting measurement/definitions makes claimed and cited inventions similar, novelty/inventive step may be lacking.

name: Determining inventive step of a product invention described by its manufacturing process
description: When a product is claimed by a manufacturing method, the examiner should determine inventive step by comparing the product itself (composition/properties) with publicly known products, not by considering the manufacturing method.
guidance: The object to be protected is the product itself; the manufacturing method/apparatus need not be considered for novelty/inventive-step assessment. If the product shows remarkable property changes due to the method (demonstrated in description), inventive step may be acknowledged based on product characteristics. Examples provided (seat-belt belt coupling, cannaf tea inorganic content).

name: Claim for a design: distinctness and specificity
description: A Claim for a design must be as distinct and specific as a Claim for any other invention, if the nature of the design will permit. Nothing beyond the configuration or ornamentation, which constitutes the invention, must be mentioned in the Claim; neither the qualities of the substance upon which the design is imposed, nor the mechanical functions which the substance may thus be enabled to perform, being any part of the design itself.
guidance: The Claim may be a verbal description of essential features or by reference to drawings indicating lines and figures. Different designs cannot be embraced in a single Claim; Claims for distinct designs cannot be joined unless so dependent as to come within usual joinder rules. Use of the phrase 'as shown and described' limits the patent to the exact design.

name: Claim for an improvement: must distinguish from prior art
description: An improvement is an invention essentially distinct from the original art or instrument to which it pertains; and a Claim for an improvement must, therefore, not only define the improvement, like any other new invention, but also fully and accurately distinguish between it and the old invention.
guidance: The Claim should confine itself entirely to the characteristics of the improvement, embracing nothing not necessarily connected with it. If mention of features of the original is required for precise definition, the language must make clear those original features are not claimed. An applicant may be required to explicitly distinguish the old and new, but need not acknowledge the old as old in doing so.

name: Improvement claims cannot improperly broaden to original art
description: A Claim for an improvement must be limited to the improvement itself and cannot be a Claim for the whole art or instrument when the advance is only an improvement.
guidance: A Claim that attempts to claim the whole original art as well as the improvement is invalid. Two or more distinct improvements cannot be joined in one Claim; if several associated improvements are claimed and one is old, the entire combined Claim may be void.

name: Improvement claim must show distinction in the Claim itself
description: It is not sufficient that persons skilled in the art can distinguish the improvement from the original invention; the Claim itself must show it.
guidance: The Claim must demonstrate the distinguishing features by its terms (not rely solely on expert evidence). Fair construction may permit implied limitation, but the Claim language must indicate the improvement is what is claimed.

name: Generic (genus) vs specific (species) claims: scope relations
description: A generic invention represents essential characteristics of a group; a patent for the genus always covers the species. An invention consisting in the use of a class of substances for a certain purpose is generic as to the use of a particular substance of that class.
guidance: A subsequent inventor of a species holds rights subject to generic inventor's rights; an inventor of a species may obtain a patent covering the genus unless another previously conceived the same fundamental idea and is using diligence in reducing it to practice. Generic claims do not cover different functions or results beyond their terms.

name: Joining generic and specific claims
description: Where an invention has only the common characteristics, its description supports only a generic Claim; if it also has special qualities, its description will support both specific and generic Claims.
guidance: Both a generic and a specific Claim may be inserted where description supports both. The phrase 'substantially as described' in a Claim confines the Claim to the generic or specific invention described. Several species described under a genus does not permit aggregating separate specific Claims into one Claim to create a generic Claim.

name: Specific claim limits patent even if description is generic
description: A Claim for a species limits the patent to that species, though the Description covers a generic invention.
guidance: A specific Claim does not convert into a generic protection simply because the description is broader; specific wording governs scope.

name: When a Claim is defective
description: A Claim is defective when it fails to define the real invention with sufficient completeness and precision, or when it claims more than belongs to the invention.
guidance: A defective Claim that overreaches is absolutely void; defects may be remedied by re-issue, and overbroad Claims are also curable by disclaimer. Presence of a void Claim in a patent does not affect valid Claims unless there is evident intent to mislead or unreasonable delay in filing a disclaimer.

name: Patent Office's settled Claim language determines validity and scope
description: The Claim is to define what the Patent Office, after due examination, has ascertained to be the real discovery of the inventor, and it must be amended or withdrawn according to the judgment of the officers to whom this duty is committed.
guidance: Once the PTO settles Claim terms by its decision, the courts will not disturb it or enlarge/narrow it by construction. The PTO has a duty to secure correct statement of Claims before allowing issue.

name: Specification signature and formal presentation
description: The specification must be signed by the inventor, or by his executor or administrator, and the signature must be attested by two witnesses, each signing his full name, legibly written. The Description and Claims, and all amendments, must be written in a clear and readable hand on one side of the paper only; and all interlineations and erasures must be marked in marginal or foot notes on the same sheet.
guidance: A wide left margin (legal-cap paper with numbered lines) is recommended. Signatures and attestations are formally required; under later statutes the drawing may be signed by inventor or authorized agent.

name: Drawings must correspond in essential characteristics with the specification
description: The drawings filed must correspond with the specification in all the essential characteristics of the invention.
guidance: Drawings are another method of portraying the same invention; discrepancies between verbal and pictorial descriptions may create ambiguity rendering the patent void. Use reference figures/letters in drawings tied to the Description and Claims so verbal and pictorial representations illustrate each other.

name: Drawing content rules for classes of inventions
description: Drawings must exhibit every feature of the invention covered by the Claims. For an art, every stage or sub-process capable of illustration must be shown; in a machine or manufacture, disclose all essential parts in their proper places; the drawings of an improvement must exhibit the improvement itself disconnected and also sufficiently of the old structure to show connection; a design must be shown by drawing or photograph depicting all distinctive characteristics.
guidance: Drawings need not be working-drawings nor on an operative scale. They are not intended as construction blueprints beyond showing essential attributes sufficient for a skilled mechanic to create and employ the invention.

name: Model filing and model requisites
description: A model is not required until the Patent Office orders it; when required, a model must clearly exhibit every feature of the invention which forms the subject of a Claim but should not include any other matter unless necessary for representation.
guidance: A working model is often desirable to enable examiners to understand operation. Models must be neatly and substantially made of durable material (metal preferred unless material is essential feature). Size, finish and other minor requisites correspond to PTO regulations; the sufficiency of a model is conclusively determined by the Commissioner. A model filed when not required is returned.

name: Focus on the claim 'as a whole' and the claimed advance
description: At step one courts must evaluate the claim's character 'as a whole' and assess 'the focus of the claimed advance over the prior art' to determine if the claim is directed to excluded subject matter.
guidance: Do not improperly dissect claims into isolated portions when determining what the claim is directed to; focus on the claim language itself to identify the claimed advance (citing Diehr, Intell. Ventures I v. Erie, ChargePoint).

name: Improvement in computer technology versus using computers as tools
description: Claims that are 'necessarily rooted in computer technology' and that solve problems specifically arising in computer networks may be non-abstract (DDR Holdings exception); by contrast, claims that use computers merely as tools to automate conventional human activity are abstract.
guidance: Assess whether the claim's focus is an improvement in computers as tools (which may weigh toward eligibility) or an independently abstract idea that merely uses computers as tools (which fails step one).

name: Step two — inventive concept requirement ('significantly more')
description: At step two, courts search for an inventive concept—an element or combination of elements sufficient to ensure the patent in practice amounts to significantly more than a patent upon the ineligible concept itself.
guidance: The inventive concept can arise from unconventional features or improvements in technology, but must go beyond restating the abstract idea or claiming conventional computer functionality (citing Alice, Mayo, SAP).

name: Do not 'dissect' claims into eligible and ineligible elements
description: Courts should not read out or ignore claim elements labeled 'abstract' when assessing the claim; Diehr instructs that claims are not to be dissected into eligible and ineligible elements.
guidance: At both steps, the proper analysis considers claim elements together (and as an ordered combination) rather than wholesale excising portions of the claim.

name: Proper scope of the 'abstract idea' characterization
description: When identifying the abstract idea, courts must avoid defining it too broadly (sweeping in concrete computer operations not historically deemed abstract) or too narrowly (failing to credit technical benefits and the claimed advance).
guidance: Mischaracterizing the abstract idea (either overbroadly or overly narrowly) can lead to incorrect conclusions; courts should credit technical benefits and focus on the claimed advance over the prior art (citing Diehr, Alice, and criticisms of Federal Circuit practice).

name: Form paragraph 7.12.fti — Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e): Patent Application Publication or Patent to Another with Earlier Filing Date (post-AIPA/AIPA rules)
description: (e) the invention was described in (1) an application for patent, published under section 122(b), by another filed in the United States before the invention by the applicant ... or (2) a patent granted on an application for patent by another filed in the United States before the invention ... except that an international application filed under the treaty shall have the effects ... only if the international application designated the United States and was published in English.
guidance: Use only if the reference is: (a) a U.S. patent or publication of a U.S. application filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a); (b) a U.S. patent issued from, or a U.S. or WIPO publication of, an international application (PCT) if the international application has an international filing date on or after November 29, 2000; or (c) a U.S. patent issued from, or a WIPO publication of, an international design application that designates the U.S. Consider benefit claims to earlier-filed U.S. provisionals under 119(e) and to nonprovisionals/international applications under 120/121/365(c)/386(c) only if the subject matter used to make the rejection is appropriately supported in the earlier application(s). Do NOT consider foreign priority claims under 119(a)-(d), 365(a)/(b), or 386(a)/(b). To rely on an international filing date under pre-AIA 102(e), the PCT must (1) be filed on or after Nov 29, 2000, (2) designate the U.S., and (3) have been published in English by WIPO under PCT Article 21(2); otherwise treat the reference under 102(a) or 102(b) as of its publication date.

name: Form paragraph 7.12.01.fti — Pre-AIPA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) (PCT international filing date prior to Nov 29, 2000)
description: (e) the invention was described in a patent granted on an application for patent by another filed in the United States before the invention ... — pre-AIPA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) applicable when reference is a U.S. patent resulting from an international application filed before Nov 29, 2000.
guidance: Use only when the reference is a U.S. patent issued from a national stage of, or continuing application claiming benefit to, an international application having an international filing date prior to Nov 29, 2000. Determine the reference's pre-AIPA 102(e) date as the date the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 371(c)(1),(2) and (4) were fulfilled for national stage patents; consider benefit claims to earlier-filed provisionals and nonprovisionals only if supported by the earlier disclosure; do NOT consider foreign priority claims.

name: Form paragraph 7.15.fti — Rejection template for pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a), (b), and (g)
description: Template: 'Claim(s) [1] is/are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 [2] as being [3] by [4].'
guidance: In bracket 2 insert the appropriate paragraph letter(s) of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 in parentheses. In bracket 3 insert either '--clearly anticipated--' or '--anticipated--' with an explanation at the end of the paragraph. In bracket 4 insert the prior art relied upon. This rejection must be preceded by form paragraph 7.07.fti and appropriate other paragraphs (7.08-7.14) or by form paragraph 7.103. If 102(e) is also applied, follow with the appropriate 7.15.01/7.15.02/7.15.03 form paragraph. For applications with filing date on/after March 16, 2013 claiming priority to earlier application, 7.06 must precede.

name: Form paragraph 7.15.01.fti — Provisional rejection under pre-AIA 102(e) when copending application has common assignee/applicant/joint inventor
description: Claims are provisionally rejected under pre-AIA 102(e) as being anticipated by a copending application which has a common assignee, common applicant, or at least one common (joint) inventor. The provisional rejection is based on a presumption of future publication or patenting of the copending application.
guidance: The copending application must have a common assignee, applicant (35 U.S.C. 118), or at least one common (joint) inventor. The provisional rejection may be overcome by: a showing under 37 CFR 1.132 that any invention disclosed but not claimed in the copending application was derived from the inventor of this application; or by an appropriate showing under 37 CFR 1.131(a). It may not be overcome by filing a terminal disclaimer. Use 7.12.fti to determine the copending application's 102(e) date unless the copending application is a national stage PCT with international filing date prior to Nov 29, 2000 (then use 7.12.01.fti). If the claims would have been obvious over the copending application, use form paragraph 7.21.01.fti. If identical subject matter issues exist under 35 U.S.C. 101 or nonstatutory double patenting, use form paragraphs 8.30-8.39 as appropriate.

name: Form paragraph 7.15.02.fti — Rejection under pre-AIA 102(e) when reference has common assignee/applicant/joint inventor
description: Claim(s) are rejected under pre-AIA 102(e) as being anticipated by [reference]. The applied reference has a common [assignee/applicant/joint inventor] with the instant application and, based upon its pre-AIA 102(e) date, constitutes prior art.
guidance: Use this when the patent or patent application publication is prior art under pre-AIA 102(e) and has a common assignee, applicant (35 U.S.C. 118), or joint inventor. Apply the rules of 7.12.fti (AIPA) or 7.12.01.fti (pre-AIPA) to determine the reference's 102(e) date. Consider benefit claims to earlier-filed provisionals/nonprovisionals only if supported in the earlier disclosure. Patent application publications may only be used if preceded by 7.12.fti. If the reference is a PCT publication with international filing date prior to Nov 29, 2000, or that did not designate the U.S. or was not published in English, do not treat it as 102(e); instead apply 102(a) or (b) as of its publication date.

name: Form paragraph 7.15.03.fti — Rejection under pre-AIA 102(e) when no common assignee or inventor
description: Claim(s) are rejected under pre-AIA 102(e) as being [clearly anticipated/anticipated] by [reference] where the patent or patent application publication has an earlier filing date and is not required to have a common assignee or inventor.
guidance: Must be preceded by 7.12.fti or 7.12.01.fti. Insert either '--clearly anticipated--' or '--anticipated--' with explanation. If the reference is a PCT publication with international filing date prior to Nov 29, 2000, or if it did not designate the U.S. or was not published in English, do not treat as 102(e); apply 102(a) or (b) as of publication date.

name: Form paragraph 7.19.fti — Rejection under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f) when applicant not the inventor
description: Claim [1] is/are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f) because the applicant did not invent the claimed subject matter. [2]
guidance: Must be preceded by paragraphs 7.07.fti and 7.13.fti or by paragraph 7.103. In bracket 2 insert an explanation of the supporting evidence establishing that applicant was not the inventor. See MPEP §2137.

name: Benefit-claim and provisional-support rules for determining 102(e) dates
description: In determining a reference’s pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date, consider benefit claims to earlier-filed U.S. provisional applications under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), and to earlier-filed U.S. nonprovisional and international applications under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, 365(c), or 386(c) only if the subject matter used to make the rejection is appropriately supported in the relied upon earlier-filed application's disclosure (and any intermediate application(s)).
guidance: Do NOT consider foreign priority claims under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d), 365(a)/(b), or 386(a)/(b). A reference is entitled to the benefit of a provisional filing date only if at least one of the claims in the reference is supported by the written description of the provisional application in compliance with pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph (35 U.S.C. 112(a)). See cited Federal Circuit decisions (Dynamic Drinkware; Amgen v. Sanofi) for precedent.

name: Obviousness evaluation framework under 35 U.S.C. 103 (Graham/KSR guidance)
description: Apply the Graham framework (scope and content of prior art; differences between claimed invention and prior art; level of ordinary skill; secondary considerations) and the flexible approach endorsed by the Supreme Court in KSR v. Teleflex. The KSR decision rejected a rigid application of the teaching-suggestion-motivation (TSM) test and emphasized a commonsense inquiry.
guidance: Examiners should: (1) not limit analysis to the specific problem the patentee identified; (2) recognize that a person of ordinary skill may be led to combine elements from prior art even if those elements addressed different problems; (3) consider 'obvious to try' in appropriate contexts; and (4) avoid rigid rules that deny recourse to common sense. However, invoking 'common sense' to supply a missing limitation must still be supported by evidence and a reasoned explanation, especially when the missing limitation goes to the heart of the invention (see Arendi v. Apple and other cited cases). For AIA-applicable cases use 'before the effective filing date of the claimed invention' as the relevant time; for pre-AIA use 'at the time of the invention.'

name: Cancellation of all claims is abandonment
description: The cancellation of all the claims in an application is an abandonment of the application/invention.
guidance: Specific authority cited (Lasscell). Cancellation that leaves no claims is effectively an abandonment to the public.

name: Second application for part of an invention disclosed in a pending application is a continuation as to two-years' public use
description: When a second application is made for part of an invention disclosed in a former and still-pending application, the later is a continuation of the former insofar as the two-years' public-use question is concerned.
guidance: Cited authority: Graham v. McCormick and related decisions; partial claiming can preserve the earlier date for specific issues.

name: File-wrapper signature and control until seal affixed
description: Until the file-wrapper is signed and the application forwarded to the Issue Division the case is still under the examiner's control; until the seal is affixed the patent is not complete and the Commissioner may in extreme cases withhold the seal.
guidance: Affixing the seal gives finality; withholding the seal should be rare and limited to clear violations (manifestly old claims, fraud, illegality).

name: Interference proceedings determine priority of invention (first-to-invent with due diligence)
description: An interference is instituted to determine the priority between rival inventors who claim substantially the same patentable invention; the law awards a single patent to the party who first conceived the invention and reduced it to practice, provided he used due diligence in reduction to practice.
guidance: Interference procedure is the contested proceeding for deciding priority (see §586). It is declared between applications (not merely applicants) and focuses on which invention was first produced; title issues may remain separate from the interference outcome (Hibbard v. Richmond and historical notes).

name: Interpretation (Linguistic Meaning)
description: Determining what the claim words communicate as a matter of language (ordinary or technical word meaning).
guidance: Focuses on ordinary meaning and technical/term-of-art meanings; drafting should aim to resolve linguistic ambiguities through definitions, consistent usage, or reliance on art-recognized meanings.

name: Defined claim terms
description: Claim terms (especially novel or coined terms) are explicitly defined in the specification.
guidance: Explicit definitions reduce interpretation disputes; include definitions for invented terminology or uncommon uses to anchor linguistic meaning.

name: Consistent terminology across claims and specification
description: The same terms are used consistently in claims and throughout the specification.
guidance: Inconsistent usage creates interpretive ambiguity; consistent term selection and application across the document improve linguistic clarity.

name: Glossary or definition section in specification
description: A dedicated section that defines key terms used in the claims and specification.
guidance: Provides a clear source for linguistic meaning; especially helpful for coined terms, terms used idiosyncratically, or when distinguishing ordinary vs. technical meanings.

name: Inconsistent use of the same term across claims (quality defect)
description: The same lexical item is used with differing meanings or in differing ways across claims or between claims and specification.
guidance: Leads to linguistic ambiguity; can be cured by consistent drafting or by explicit notice of different meanings.

name: Multiple plausible linguistic interpretations (quality defect)
description: Claim language admits two or more plausible ordinary-language readings absent clarifying definitions.
guidance: Creates interpretation-stage vulnerability; drafting should eliminate homographs, equivocal phrasing, and other sources of multiple plausible readings.

name: Reliance on prosecution-history disclaimers to narrow ambiguous language (quality defect)
description: Using prosecution statements to narrow claims rather than clarifying claim language itself.
guidance: Relying on prosecution-history disclaimers indicates linguistic-stage failure and can produce undesirable binding positions; better to resolve ambiguity in the specification or claim text.

name: Specification clearly identifies the technical contribution ('real invention')
description: The specification explicitly and coherently explains the technical contribution the inventor regards as the invention.
guidance: Anchoring the 'real invention' helps courts choose construction theories that map claim scope to the disclosed contribution; include explicit statements of technical advancement and inventive features.

name: Working examples representative of claimed scope
description: The specification contains working examples that illustrate embodiments representative of the scope claimed.
guidance: Representative examples help courts determine whether the claim scope tracks the disclosed invention; include examples that reflect the range of intended coverage without creating ambiguity about limits.

name: Proper means-plus-function indication when desired
description: When claiming by function, indicate means-plus-function structure appropriately so that the scope is tied to corresponding structure in the specification.
guidance: If a means-plus-function claim is intended, draft the claim and specification to satisfy the statutory/ doctrinal requirements so courts construe the claim against disclosed structure; if not intended, avoid phrasing that invites 112(f) treatment.

name: Express references to embodiments as illustrative vs. limiting
description: Explicitly state whether embodiments/examples are illustrative and not limiting (or specify when they are limiting).
guidance: Avoid ambiguous statements that force courts to infer whether embodiments limit claim scope; clear disclaimers reduce construction disputes about embodiment scope.

name: Specification-claim mapping: claims map cleanly onto disclosed embodiments
description: Claims correspond in a clear, non-conflicting way to the specification's disclosed embodiments.
guidance: A clean mapping reduces construction conflicts; ensure claim elements have support in the specification and that the scope of claims is representatively reflected by embodiments.

name: No mismatch between specification scope and claim scope (construction-conflict marker)
description: Absence of contradictions between what the specification discloses and the language/coverage of the claims.
guidance: Mismatches are red flags that invite judicial construction to reconcile the conflict; avoid scope gaps where the specification implies a narrower or different invention than claimed.

name: Anticipate Broadest Reasonable Construction (BRC) during prosecution
description: Drafting and prosecution strategy should recognize that examiners apply BRC and that prosecution may expand claim scope during examination.
guidance: Anticipate BRC by drafting narrower supportive disclosure when necessary, argue for narrower interpretations with specification support, and use prosecution to establish positions that will limit later constructions if desired.

name: Avoid creating estoppels that conflict with desired construction
description: Avoid making prosecution or specification statements that will later estop the patentee from arguing a desired construction in litigation.
guidance: Be strategic in admissions, claim amendments, and argument; where narrowing is necessary, document rationale and be mindful of downstream binding effects.

name: Tier 1 — Linguistic Quality (operational test)
description: Evaluate whether claims are linguistically clear: defined terms, consistent terminology, and absence of obvious linguistic ambiguities.
guidance: If Tier 1 passes, the claim is linguistically clean; still evaluate Tier 2 because construction theory may nonetheless create unpredictability.

name: Tier 2 — Construction Quality (operational test)
description: Evaluate whether the specification and prosecution support a coherent construction theory (the 'real invention' is identifiable, examples are representative, embodiments-claim relationships explicit, and prosecution history coherent).
guidance: Patents that satisfy Tier 2 in addition to Tier 1 are construction-resistant; failing Tier 2 means exposure to contested theories of construction despite linguistic clarity.

name: Operative Quality Test (seven-point checklist)
description: A consolidated checklist: (1) claim terms defined or settled, (2) consistent terminology, (3) lack of obvious linguistic ambiguities, (4) specification identifies the 'real invention', (5) working examples representative of claimed scope, (6) relationship between embodiments and claims explicit, (7) prosecution history supports a single coherent construction theory.
guidance: A patent passing all seven tests is described as having high construction-resistance; use this checklist when reviewing issued patents for litigation risk or during drafting to improve construction predictability.

name: Watch for construction-conflict markers
description: Identify markers that predict construction disputes: specification-claim mismatches, ambiguous embodiments, undefined key terms, and prosecution history inconsistencies.
guidance: These markers indicate vulnerability in Markman proceedings; prioritize remediation (amendments, clarifying affidavits, prosecution arguments) where possible.

name: Commercial or Legal Interactions (abstract idea grouping)
description: “Commercial interactions” or “legal interactions” include agreements in the form of contracts, legal obligations, advertising, marketing or sales activities or behaviors, and business relations.
guidance: Claims reciting commercial/legal interactions are often directed to abstract ideas. Example: buySAFE (transaction performance guaranty — creating a contractual relationship was found to be an abstract idea). Other examples include managing a stable value protected life insurance policy (Bancorp), processing insurance claims under an insurance policy (Accenture), tax-free real estate exchanges (Fort Properties), hedging (Bilski), mitigating settlement risk (Alice), arbitration (In re Comiskey), using advertising as an exchange/currency (Ultramercial), structuring a sales force or marketing company (In re Ferguson), algorithms for visit optimization (In re Maucorps), offer-based price optimization (OIP Techs. v. Amazon), processing applications through a dealer/bank clearing-house (Dealertrack), and processing applications for financing (Credit Acceptance). Examiner guidance: treat such claims as within the “methods of organizing human activity”/abstract idea grouping when appropriate and analyze under the subject matter eligibility framework.

name: Mental Processes — general rule (abstract idea grouping)
description: The courts consider a mental process (thinking) that “can be performed in the human mind, or by a human using a pen and paper” to be an abstract idea. Mental processes include observations, evaluations, judgments, and opinions.
guidance: Authoritative citations: CyberSource, Benson, Mayo, Parker v. Flook. Examiners should recognize that methods which can be performed mentally or with simple physical aids are ‘basic tools’ and are unpatentable abstract ideas. When a claim’s limitations are of the nature of mental processes (observations, evaluations, judgments, opinions) and are recited at a high level of generality, treat them as abstract ideas and proceed with the eligibility framework.

name: Mental Processes — A: Limitations that cannot practically be performed in the human mind are not mental processes
description: A claim with limitation(s) that cannot practically be performed in the human mind does not recite a mental process.
guidance: If the human mind is not equipped to perform the claimed limitation(s), the claim may not fall in the mental-process grouping. Examples of claims not reciting mental processes: GPS receiver calculating pseudoranges to estimate distance and time (SiRF Tech.), detecting suspicious activity using network monitors and analyzing network packets (SRI Int’l), a specific multi-step data encryption method involving manipulation of data structures (Synopsys), and rendering a halftone image by pixel-by-pixel comparison against a blue noise mask that outputs a modified computer data structure (Research Corp. Techs.). Examiner guidance: evaluate whether the claim limitations could practically be performed mentally; if not, do not treat them as mental-process abstract ideas.

name: Mental Processes — B: Claims that encompass human performance mentally (with or without physical aid) recite mental processes
description: A claim that encompasses a human performing the step(s) mentally, with or without a physical aid (e.g., pen and paper), recites a mental process.
guidance: Use specification and claim language to determine whether claimed steps are performable mentally. The use of physical aids (pencil/paper, slide rule) does not negate the mental nature — it only accounts for memory/capacity variation. Examples: constructing a map of credit card numbers that can be made by writing down transactions (CyberSource); computations performable by pencil and paper (Flook). Examiner guidance: if a limitation can practically be performed by a person mentally or with simple aids, treat it as a mental-process abstract idea.

name: Mental Processes — C: Claims that require/mention a computer may still recite a mental process
description: Claims that require a computer may nonetheless recite a mental process depending on how the claim/specification recites the concept.
guidance: Examiners must carefully interpret the claim and specification to determine if the invention is merely a concept performed on a generic computer, performed in a computer environment but analogous to human cognitive actions, or merely using a computer as a tool to perform a mental process. Sub-categories and examples: 1) Performing a mental process on a generic computer — Voter Verified, Versata (claims directed to determining price were abstract despite use of general-purpose hardware). 2) Performing a mental process in a computer environment — Symantec (electronic post office analogized to human mail handling), FairWarning (rules-based detection of misuse analogous to human fraud detection). 3) Using a computer as a tool to perform a mental process — Mortgage Grader (anonymous loan shopping concept could be performed by humans), Berkheimer (parsing/comparing data at high level). Examiner guidance: review specification to see if applicant is claiming a human-mental concept merely performed on computers; if so, treat as a mental process.

name: Mental Processes — D: Both product and process claims may recite mental processes
description: Both product claims (e.g., computer system, computer-readable medium) and process claims may recite mental processes; the classification depends on the substance of the claimed concept, not the statutory category.
guidance: Examples of product claims found to recite mental-process-type abstract ideas include: APIs for extracting/processing information from hard copy documents (Content Extraction), computer systems for anonymous loan shopping (Mortgage Grader), computer-readable media for detecting fraud (CyberSource), electronic post offices (Symantec), wide-area real-time electric grid monitoring (Electric Power Group), and storage media implementing pricing methods (Versata). Examiner guidance: do not assume a system or medium claim inherently avoids the mental-process grouping; analyze the underlying concept.

name: Tentative abstract ideas — examiner procedure and TC Director approval requirements
description: A “tentative abstract idea” refers to claim limitations that an examiner believes should be treated as an abstract idea even though they do not fall within the enumerated groupings (mathematical concepts, methods of organizing human activity, mental processes).
guidance: Procedure: 1) If the claim as a whole integrates the tentative abstract idea into a practical application → claim is not directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: NO) → eligible at Pathway B. 2) If the claim as a whole does not integrate into a practical application → claim is directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: YES) → proceed to Step 2B. At Step 2B, if the claim provides an inventive concept (Step 2B: YES) → eligible at Pathway C. 3) If the claim does not provide an inventive concept (Step 2B: NO) → bring application to the Technology Center (TC) director; a rejection of a claim reciting a tentative abstract idea must be approved by the TC director (approval to be indicated in the file record). Office action must identify the previously non-enumerated abstract idea via form paragraph 7.05.017 and include the TC Director’s signature. Examiner guidance: interviews may help; examiner may withdraw or maintain rejection upon considering applicant’s reply; TC Director approval is required only for issuing such a Step 2B rejection.

name: Laws of Nature, Natural Phenomena & Products of Nature (judicial exceptions)
description: Laws of nature and natural phenomena include naturally occurring principles/relations and nature-based products that are naturally occurring or that do not have markedly different characteristics compared to what occurs in nature.
guidance: These categories are judicial exceptions because the manifestations of laws of nature and natural phenomena are ‘‘part of the storehouse of knowledge’’ and not patentable. Examples identified by the courts include: isolated DNA (Myriad), a cloned farm animal (In re Roslin), correlations between DNA regions (Genetic Techs. v. Merial), metabolic correlations (Mayo), correlation of myeloperoxidase and cardiovascular risk (Cleveland Clinic), electromagnetism to transmit signals (O’Reilly v. Morse), bacterial qualities (Funk Bros.), single-stranded primers (Ambry Genetics), chemical principles underlying union of fatty elements and water (Tilghman v. Proctor), existence of cell-free fetal DNA (Ariosa), and genotype–drug risk correlations (Vanda). Examiner guidance: treat such claims as judicial exceptions and apply the subject matter eligibility framework to determine whether additional claim elements integrate the judicial exception into a patent-eligible application.

name: Claims clarity, conciseness and support (Section 3(1C))
description: The claims shall define the matter for which protection is sought; they shall be clear and concise and be supported by the description.
guidance: Explanatory Notes: Claims must be interpretable, not ambiguous, and must have basis in the specification.

name: Abstract purpose (Section 3(1D))
description: The abstract shall merely serve for use as technical information; in particular not for the purpose of interpreting the scope of the protection sought.
guidance: Explanatory Notes: Abstracts are for technical information only and should not be used to construe claim scope.

name: Meaning and interpretation of claims (Section 3(16))
description: The extent of the protection conferred by an ARIPO patent or ARIPO application shall be determined by the terms of the claims; nevertheless, the description and drawings shall be used to interpret the claims.
guidance: Explanatory Notes: Claims define scope but description/drawings assist interpretation.

name: Identify what applicant invented and establish BRI
description: Review the disclosure to identify what applicant considers as the invention (MPEP 2103(I)). This can be brief and should not just reproduce the claim. Establish the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim.
guidance: Section I: summarize applicant's invention in plain terms focused on what the invention accomplishes (examples given: managing Bingo game aspects, performance guaranty, distribution of media by advertising). Emphasize that every claim must be examined individually and the summary should not simply restate the claim language.

name: Step 1 — Statutory category check (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter)
description: Determine whether the claimed invention falls within one of the four statutory categories of invention (process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter).
guidance: Choose A (Yes) or B (No). If No, make a rejection as drawn to non‑statutory subject matter and use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01. If the claim could be amended to fall within a statutory category, it is recommended to continue the SME analysis under that assumption, make the assumption clear in the record, and consider suggesting a potential amendment to applicant that would result in the claim being drawn to a statutory category. If no amendment is possible, conclude SME analysis and continue with other patentability requirements.

name: Step 2A — Is the claim directed to an abstract idea?
description: Determine whether the claim recites a concept similar to those identified by courts as abstract (e.g., fundamental economic practices, certain methods of organizing human activity, ideas themselves, mathematical relationships/formulae). A claim is 'directed' to an abstract idea when the abstract idea is recited (set forth or described) in the claim.
guidance: Choose A (No), B (Yes — but a streamlined analysis is appropriate), or C (Yes — identify the limitation(s) that recite the abstract idea and explain why). Use the case law chart and 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance for assistance. If streamlined (B) is appropriate, a full eligibility analysis may not be needed (see February 2015 Training Slides). If C, explicitly identify the claim elements that set forth the abstract idea and explain why those elements constitute an abstract idea (examples provided in worksheet).

name: Identify claim limitations that recite the abstract idea
description: List the specific claim elements/limitations (steps, components) that set forth or describe the abstract idea and explain why those limitations are considered the abstract idea.
guidance: For each claim, enumerate the elements that embody the abstract idea (example: Bingo example lists elements (i)–(viii) such as input of preselected numbers, storage as a group, assignment of player identifier, retrieval, selection for play, addition of control number, output of receipt, verification via control number). Then explain why the described scheme is an abstract idea (e.g., organizing human activity, can be performed mentally or with a computer).

name: Step 2B — Are there additional elements beyond the abstract idea?
description: Determine whether the claim includes any additional elements (features/limitations/steps) beyond the abstract idea identified in Step 2A.
guidance: Choose 1 (No) or 2 (Yes). If No (no other elements), conclude SME analysis by making a §101 rejection and continue examination under other patentability requirements (use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015). If Yes, list the additional claim elements (e.g., computer with CPU, memory, printer, input/output, program) and continue to evaluate their significance under Step 2B.

name: Evaluate the significance of additional elements (search for an 'inventive concept')
description: Assess whether the additional elements, individually or in combination, confer an 'inventive concept' such that the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the abstract idea.
guidance: Consider how the additional elements relate to what the applicant invented and evaluate them both individually and in combination. Reasons supporting significance can include one or more of the following considerations: improves another technology or technical field; improves the functioning of a computer itself; applies the abstract idea with, or by use of, a particular machine (not a generic computer performing generic functions and not mere instructions to implement the idea on a computer); effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing; adds a specific limitation other than what is well-understood, routine and conventional in the field (i.e., not appending well‑understood routine activities at a high level); adds unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application (not insignificant extrasolution activity such as mere data gathering); adds meaningful limitations amounting to more than generally linking the use of the abstract idea to a particular technological environment. It is not important how many of these considerations apply; evaluate significance relative to applicant's invention.

name: What constitutes insufficient 'additional elements' (anti-patterns)
description: Guidance on common deficient recitations that do not amount to 'significantly more'.
guidance: Examples of insufficient elements include: providing a programmed/generic computer performing generic computer functions; mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer; adding the words 'apply it' or equivalent; appending well‑understood, routine and conventional activities at a high level of generality; adding insignificant extrasolution activity such as mere data gathering. If additional elements are only generic computer components claimed to perform basic storage/retrieval/processing functions, they likely do not add significantly more.

name: Procedural: Suggest potential claim amendments and document assumptions
description: If elements in the disclosure could be added to make the claim eligible, identify those elements and consider suggesting them to applicant; if analyzing under an assumed amendment, make the assumption clear in the record.
guidance: Worksheet fields prompt examiners to identify possible disclosure elements that could be added and to note them in the Office action. If the examiner continues analysis based on an assumed amendment (e.g., to place the claim into a statutory category), explicitly state the assumption in the record and consider proposing specific amendments to applicant. If no amendment is possible, conclude SME analysis and proceed to other requirements.

name: Use official form paragraphs for §101 rejections
description: When concluding that a claim is ineligible under §101, use the designated form paragraphs.
guidance: Use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015 (and 7.05.01 where applicable) available in Custom OACs when making a §101 rejection. Sample rejection language is provided in the worksheet demonstrating how to explain that the claim is 'directed to a judicial exception ... without significantly more' and why additional elements are insufficient.

name: Insignificant application / insignificant extra-solution activity
description: Claim limitations that add only insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., mere data gathering, printing/downloading, or routine physical activity) do not meaningfully limit a judicial exception.
guidance: Cases identify insignificant computer implementation as an example of insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., Fort Props.; Bancorp Servs.). See MPEP § 2106.05(f) for more information. For claim limitations that add insignificant extra-solution activity to the judicial exception (e.g., mere data gathering in conjunction with a law of nature or abstract idea), examiners should explain in an eligibility rejection why they do not meaningfully limit the claim.
