Example rationale: adding a final step of storing data to a process that only recites computing the area of a space (a mathematical relationship) does not add a meaningful limitation to the process of computing the area. See MPEP § 2106.07(a) for formulating rejections.

name: Field of use / technological environment limitations do not alone confer eligibility
description: Limitations that merely indicate a field of use or technological environment in which to apply a judicial exception (i.e., merely linking use of the exception to a particular technological environment) do not amount to significantly more and cannot integrate a judicial exception into a practical application.
guidance: Supreme Court and Federal Circuit precedent (e.g., Parker v. Flook; Bilski; Diamond v. Diehr) show that token or incidental field-of-use limitations (e.g., limiting a formula to petrochemical processes) are insufficient. Contrast: Diehr where specific limitations acted in concert to transform a product. Examples of such inadequate field-of-use/technological-environment limitations include (i) limiting drug administration to a patient population (Mayo), (ii) limiting hedging to commodity providers/consumers (Bilski), (iii) limiting a formula to wheel circumference (Flook), (iv) requiring execution in a computer environment (FairWarning), (v) limiting virus screening to telephone network/Internet (Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec), (vi) limiting collection/analysis/display to power-grid data (Electric Power Group), etc. Examiners should consider 'technological environment' and 'field of use' interchangeable for eligibility analysis and be aware of overlap with insignificant extra-solution activity (see MPEP § 2106.05(g)). For claim limitations that generally link the judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use, examiners should explain in an eligibility rejection why they do not meaningfully limit the claim (e.g., employing generic computer functions in one environment does not add significantly more). See MPEP § 2106.07(a).

name: Streamlined analysis (Pathway A) may be used when eligibility is self-evident
description: Examiners may use a streamlined eligibility analysis (Pathway A) for efficiency when the eligibility of the claim is self-evident (e.g., the claim clearly improves a technology or computer functionality).
guidance: The streamlined analysis yields the same result as the full Alice/Mayo analysis and is not a way to avoid a proper ineligibility finding. If there is doubt about whether the applicant is effectively seeking coverage for a judicial exception, the full Alice/Mayo analysis should be used. A claim that qualifies as eligible after Step 2A (Pathway B) or Step 2B (Pathway C) would also be eligible under the streamlined analysis. The record may simply lack an eligibility rejection or include clarifying remarks where Pathway A is used.

name: Eligibility is self-evident (criteria for Pathway A)
description: A claim is suitable for streamlined review when, viewed as a whole, it clearly does not seek to tie up any judicial exception and its eligibility is self-evident.
guidance: Examples: complex manufactured industrial products or processes with meaningful limitations alongside a judicial exception (e.g., a robotic arm assembly with a control system using certain mathematical relationships); nature-based products that clearly do not attempt to tie up the nature-based product (e.g., artificial hip prosthesis coated with a naturally occurring mineral; cellphone with an electrical contact made of gold). Close calls do not qualify for streamlined analysis and require full analysis. See MPEP § 2106.06(a).

name: Clear improvement to a technology or computer functionality
description: Claims that clearly improve a technology or computer functionality may be eligible without undergoing the full Alice/Mayo analysis because they are not directed to an abstract idea when appropriately claimed.
guidance: Federal Circuit decisions (e.g., Enfish; McRO) illustrate that claims directed to clear technological improvements can be treated as not abstract. When claims clearly improve computer-related technology or other technologies/technological processes, their eligibility may be self-evident and Pathway A or Pathway B may be appropriate. If the improvement is a 'close call' (e.g., BASCOM filtering example), perform the full analysis (Step 2B) to determine whether claims amount to significantly more. See MPEP § 2106.06(b) and § 2106.05(a) for details.

name: Rejections must be based on substantive law and support a prima facie case
description: Eligibility rejections must be grounded in the substantive law under 35 U.S.C. 101 as interpreted by judicial precedent, and a rejection should set forth a prima facie case of ineligibility with clear and specific reasoning.
guidance: Examination guidance, training, and examples discuss substantive law but do not themselves form the basis for rejection. Examiners should review the record as a whole (specification, claims, prosecution history, relevant case law/prior art) before concluding eligibility. The initial burden is on the examiner to explain why a claim is ineligible clearly and specifically so the applicant has sufficient notice and can effectively respond. See MPEP §§ 2106.03–2106.06 and § 2106.07 for further detail.

name: Evaluate each claim on a claim-by-claim basis
description: Eligibility should be evaluated separately for each claim because dependent or related claims may add limitations that change the eligibility determination.
guidance: Even if an independent claim is ineligible, dependent claims may be eligible if they add limitations integrating the judicial exception into a practical application or amount to significantly more. Conversely, dependent claims may be ineligible if they add only the judicial exception without meaningful additional limitations. Examiners must consider each claim on its own merits when forming rejections.

name: Step 1: When a claim does not fall within a statutory category
description: If a claim is determined not to fall within one of the four statutory categories of invention, the rejection should explain why the claim does not fall within a statutory category (Step 1: NO).
guidance: See MPEP § 2106.03 for discussion of Step 1 and the statutory categories. The Office action must provide an explanation sufficiently clear and specific to give applicant notice and enable effective response.

name: Step 2A Prong One — Identify and explain the judicial exception recited in the claim
description: A subject matter eligibility rejection must point to the specific claim limitation(s) that recite the judicial exception and explain why those claim limitations set forth or describe a judicial exception (Step 2A Prong One).
guidance: When the claim describes but does not expressly set forth the judicial exception, the rejection must explain what subject matter the limitations describe and why that described subject matter is a judicial exception. For abstract ideas, the rejection should identify the abstract idea as recited and explain why it falls within one of the groupings of abstract ideas (mathematical concepts, mental processes, or certain methods of organizing human activity) enumerated in MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2). See MPEP § 2106.04 for more information.

name: Step 2A Prong Two — Identify additional elements and evaluate integration into a practical application
description: For Prong Two, the rejection should identify any additional elements recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception and evaluate whether those additional elements integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.
guidance: The evaluation must explain that 1) there are no additional elements, or 2) the claim as a whole, looking at additional elements individually and in combination, does not integrate the judicial exception into a practical application using the considerations in MPEP §§ 2106.04(d), 2106.05(a)-(c) and (e)-(h). Examiners should give weight to all claimed additional elements in Prong Two, even if they represent well-understood, routine, conventional activity.

name: Step 2B — Explain why additional elements do not amount to significantly more
description: For Step 2B, the rejection should explain why the additional elements, taken individually and in combination, do not result in the claim, as a whole, amounting to significantly more than the identified judicial exception.
guidance: If the examiner concludes that certain claim elements recite well-understood, routine, conventional activities, the examiner must expressly support the rejection in writing with one of the four options specified in Subsection III. The rejection should explain for each part of the Step 2 analysis: identifying the exception, identifying additional elements (pointing to specific claim features), and explaining why those additional elements individually and in combination 1) do not integrate the exception into a practical application and 2) do not result in significantly more than the exception. See MPEP § 2106.07(a) and related subsections for required support and explanations.

name: Provide clear, specific explanations in Office actions to enable applicant response
description: When making a rejection, the Office action must provide a sufficiently clear and specific explanation as to why each claim is unpatentable to give applicant notice and enable an effective response.
guidance: A proper rejection forms a prima facie case and allocates the burdens between examiner and applicant. When evaluating applicant responses, examiners must carefully consider all arguments and evidence; if applicant properly rebuts the examiner’s findings, the rejection should be withdrawn or rebutted in the next Office action. Under compact prosecution principles, examiners should also state all non-cumulative reasons and bases for rejecting claims (including 35 U.S.C. 102, 103, 112, utility, inventorship, double patenting) in the first Office action.

name: Avoid conflating § 101 with §§ 102/103/112
description: Eligibility analysis should not import considerations of novelty, nonobviousness, or written description; §§ 102, 103, and 112 are the appropriate statutory tools to address claims that are overly broad or preemptive.
guidance: Critics argued that preemption analysis in Mayo/Alice 'has conflated eligibility with the more rigorous patentability requirements set forth in 35 U.S.C. §§ 102 and 103' and that the eligibility test 'has effectively evolved into a watered-down obviousness analysis.' Several commenters recommended using §§ 102, 103, and 112 to address overly broad claims rather than § 101.

name: Assess claims as a whole rather than 'stripping away' conventional limitations
description: Eligibility analysis should consider the claim in its entirety and not remove or ignore conventional elements as if performing an obviousness analysis.
guidance: Criticism: the Mayo/Alice framework 'fails to consider the claim as a whole, as during an obviousness analysis, but to instead “strip away” what are viewed as conventional limitations.' Commenters urged treating the claim holistically.

name: Use §§ 102/103/112 to address overbroad or vague claiming (preemption concerns)
description: Claims that threaten to preempt downstream innovation should be dealt with via novelty, nonobviousness, enablement, written description, or definiteness analyses rather than by expanding § 101 exceptions.
guidance: Many members of the public argued that 'there are other more robust statutory grounds to address broad claims that “might preempt or prevent access to any underlying concept,” namely, lack of adequate written description, enablement, and definiteness.'

name: Avoid bright-line tests in diagnostics; appreciate diagnostic claim structure
description: Examiners and guidelines should not apply inflexible bright-line rules to diagnostic claims and should take into account how diagnostics are claimed and operate in practice.
guidance: A diagnostics-industry commentator urged examiners to 'guard against application of bright line tests and to “appreciate how diagnostics work and how the claims typically sought in diagnostic medicine differ from decades-old claims held in court decisions to simply recite a law of nature.”'

name: Clarify eligibility of computer-implemented inventions; provide balanced guidance
description: USPTO guidelines should clarify when computer software and computer-implemented claims are patent eligible, while also explaining limits (e.g., that mere recitation of a generic computer cannot transform an abstract idea).
guidance: Some commenters recommended revising guidance to make clear that claims directed to computer software may be eligible; others warned the guidelines should not unfairly tilt toward eligibility. One non-profit recommended MPEP include Alice’s holding that 'mere recitation of a generic computer cannot transform a patent-ineligible abstract idea into a patent-eligible invention.'

name: Clarify and define 'technical solution' / 'technical problem' language
description: The USPTO (and courts) should define what constitutes a 'technical solution to a technical problem' to provide examiners and practitioners with a predictable standard for software and related fields.
guidance: Commenters noted the Federal Circuit's use of 'technical solution/technical problem' and urged the USPTO to clarify this terminology and explain how it should be applied in claims and the specification.

name: Consider economic and sectoral impacts (software and life sciences special concerns)
description: Policy and claim-examination standards should account for industry-specific effects—particularly in life sciences (diagnostics/pharma) and software—on investment, commercialization, and U.S. competitiveness.
guidance: Public comments noted disproportionate impacts: life sciences claim narrowing threatens biopharma incentives and commercialization; software industry is split but some say Alice reduced abusive litigation and improved clarity; harmonization and predictable eligibility were urged to protect domestic industries.

name: Provide guidance on rewriting ineligible claims to be eligible
description: Guidance should include examples or instructions showing how applicants can amend or redraft claims that might be deemed ineligible so they recite patent-eligible subject matter.
guidance: AIPLA and others criticized current examples for failing to show how to revise ineligible claims and recommended guidance that demonstrates concrete claim-drafting strategies to achieve eligibility.

name: Penalty for false assertion of entitlement to fee reduction
description: An entity found to have falsely asserted entitlement to a fee reduction shall be subject to a fine, determined by the Director, of not less than three times the amount that the entity failed to pay as a result of the false assertion.
guidance: Deterrent civil penalty (minimum treble amount of unpaid fee) for false fee-reduction claims; applies whether discovered before or after patent issuance.

name: AIA first-inventor-to-file applicability and effective filing date rule
description: The first-inventor-to-file provisions of the Leahy-Smith America Invents Act (AIA) apply to any application for patent and any patent issuing thereon that contains or contained at any time a claim to an invention that has an effective filing date on or after March 16, 2013. Effective filing date is (A) the actual filing date of the patent or application containing the claim or (B) the filing date of the earliest application for which the patent or application is entitled to a right of priority or benefit under specified sections (e.g., 119, 120, 121, 365, 386).
guidance: Determines whether AIA/first-inventor-to-file rules apply by reference to claim effective filing date and priority/benefit chains; includes cross-references to statutory sections defining priority/benefit.

name: Definitions (35 U.S.C. 100): key terms
description: Statutory definitions include: 'invention' (invention or discovery); 'process' (process, art, or method, including new use of known process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, or material); 'United States' (USA, its territories and possessions); 'patentee' (patentee and successors in title); 'third-party requester' (person requesting ex parte reexamination who is not patent owner); 'inventor' (individual or individuals who invented or discovered the subject matter); 'joint inventor'/'coinventor' (one of the individuals who invented a joint invention); 'joint research agreement' (written contract/grant/cooperative agreement between 2+ persons/entities for experimental/developmental/research work); 'effective filing date' (actual filing date or earliest priority/benefit filing date as applicable); 'claimed invention' (subject matter defined by a claim).
guidance: These statutory definitions govern interpretation throughout title 35 and are necessary to apply novelty, priority, and other patentability rules; note AIA applicability caveats for pre-AIA text.

name: Exceptions for disclosures appearing in applications and patents, and common ownership/joint research agreements (102(a)(2) and 102(c))
description: A disclosure shall not be prior art under subsection (a)(2) if (A) the subject matter was obtained directly or indirectly from the inventor/joint inventor; (B) the subject matter had been publicly disclosed by the inventor (or someone who obtained it from the inventor) before the subject matter was effectively filed; or (C) the subject matter disclosed and the claimed invention were, not later than the effective filing date, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person. Subject matter disclosed and a claimed invention are deemed to have been owned by the same person under a joint research agreement in effect on or before the effective filing date if the disclosed subject matter was developed and the claimed invention made by parties to the agreement, the invention was made as a result of activities within the scope of the agreement, and the patent application discloses or is amended to disclose the parties' names.
guidance: Statutory exclusions to treat certain prior art as non-preclusive where there is common ownership/derivation or joint research agreement relationship; requires disclosure/amendment to name parties for the JRA defense.

name: Biotechnological process special nonobviousness rule (35 U.S.C. 103(b) pre-AIA / exceptions)
description: Upon timely election by the applicant, a biotechnological process using or resulting in a composition of matter that is novel under section 102 and nonobvious under 103(a) shall be considered nonobvious if (A) claims to the process and the composition are contained in the same application or in separate applications having the same effective filing date; and (B) the composition and the process were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person at the time invented.
guidance: Special statutory protection for certain biotech process/composition claim sets allowing a process patent to be treated as nonobvious when tied to a novel composition owned by the same entity; includes rules for claim content and co-ownership, and special term synchronization rules for resulting patents.

name: Common ownership / joint research agreement exception under 103(c)
description: Subject matter developed by another person that qualifies as prior art only under certain subsections of 102 shall not preclude patentability where the subject matter and the claimed invention were, at the time the claimed invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person. For this purpose, common ownership includes inventions made by parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made, where the invention resulted from activities within the scope of the agreement and the application discloses the parties' names.
guidance: Parallels the 102(c) common-ownership/JRA exceptions, applied in nonobviousness analysis to prevent certain otherwise-applicable prior art from negating patentability when ownership/assignment relationships or JRA conditions are met.

name: Specific reference to earlier-filed applications (35 U.S.C. § 120 / 37 C.F.R. § 1.78)
description: The later application must 'contain a specific reference to [each] earlier filed application' to which it purports to claim priority; references must identify prior application numbers and relationships.
guidance: 37 C.F.R. § 1.78 requires identification by application number (series code and serial number) and indication of the relationship (continuation, divisional, or continuation-in-part). The reference must be included in an application data sheet (ADS) or the specification (in the first sentence(s) following the title).

name: Definitions and differences: continuation, divisional, continuation-in-part (CIP)
description: Continuation and divisional applications are both continuing applications based on the same disclosure as an earlier application; they differ in what they claim. A CIP includes new matter.
guidance: Per MPEP citations: continuation = claims directed to the same invention claimed in an earlier application (with possible scope variation); divisional = carved out of an earlier application that disclosed/claimed more than one independent invention and claims one or more (but not all) of the non-claimed independent inventions; CIP = contains all or a portion of the earlier disclosure together with newly added matter not present in the earlier application. Use these distinctions when selecting filing type and claiming priority.

name: Use and meaning of 'parent' and 'original' in priority chains
description: The term 'parent' refers to the immediately preceding application from which a continuing application claims priority; 'original' refers to the first application in a chain of continuing applications.
guidance: MPEP §§ 201.04, 201.04(a) definitions are cited; practitioners should correctly identify and disclose parent vs. original in the priority statements and ADS to avoid confusion about which application is being relied upon.

name: Provisional priority claiming requirements (35 U.S.C. § 119(e)(1))
description: To claim the benefit of an earlier-filed provisional application, an amendment containing the specific reference to the earlier-filed provisional must be submitted during the pendency of the application as required by the Director.
guidance: Although provisional applications cannot themselves be continuation, divisional, or CIP applications, claiming a provisional priority requires the specific reference be timely submitted during pendency. The article cites § 119(e)(1): '[n]o application shall be entitled to the benefit of an earlier filed provisional application … unless an amendment containing the specific reference ... is submitted at such time during the pendency of the application as required by the Director.'

name: Place and form of benefit claims (ADS or specification first sentences)
description: The reference to prior applications must be included in an application data sheet (ADS) or the specification must contain (or be amended to contain) such reference in the first sentence(s) following the title.
guidance: Droplets, Inc. v. E*Trade Bank is cited for the view that the reference 'must be included in an application data sheet …, or the specification must contain or be amended to contain such reference in the first sentence(s) following the title.' Practitioners should ensure the benefit claim is placed in one of these compliant locations.

name: Express identification of relationship (continuation/divisional/CIP) for each prior application
description: When claiming benefit from multiple prior applications, the later application must identify the relationship between each nonprovisional application (i.e., whether the later-filed application is a continuation, divisional, or CIP of the prior-filed application).
guidance: 37 C.F.R. § 1.78(d)(3) language is quoted: the reference should indicate 'the relationship of the applications (i.e., whether the later-filed application is a continuation, divisional, or continuation-in-part ...).' MPEP guidance reiterates that identifying the relationship is necessary to establish copendency across the chain.

name: Permissibility and procedure for amending benefit claims / changing relationships
description: An application may be amended to change its relationship to a prior-filed application (e.g., from CIP to divisional), and the correction of a timely submitted benefit claim is permitted.
guidance: In re Janssen Biotech, Inc. and 37 C.F.R. § 1.78(d)(2) are cited allowing the specification to 'contain or be amended to contain a reference to each such prior-filed application' and identifying relationships. MPEP § 211.03 permits correction of a 'timely submitted benefit claim' by changing relationships (e.g., from 'continuation-in-part' to 'continuation' or 'divisional'). Practitioners should ensure timely submission and follow regulatory procedures when making such amendments.

name: Careful drafting of self-referential language ('this application' / 'present application')
description: Phrases like 'this application' or 'present application' have been interpreted by courts to set forth the priority chain of the present application and can create disclaimers and estoppel if used carelessly.
guidance: Cases such as Santarus v. Par Pharm., Broadcast Innovation v. Charter Commc’ns, and Zenon Envtl. illustrate that courts interpret 'this application is a divisional' or 'this application claims priority to all such previous applications…' in specific ways. The article warns 'present application' is a phrase that should be used lightly, if at all, given possible adverse effects; see also a cited BNA article 'Avoiding the Present (Invention)'.

name: Prohibition/limits on treating provisionals as continuing applications
description: Provisional patent applications cannot themselves be continuation, continuation-in-part, or divisional applications.
guidance: The article explicitly states this limitation and excludes provisional applications from the subsequent application discussion; practitioners must therefore understand that continuation-type filings must be nonprovisional filings claiming benefit from provisionals per §119(e) rules rather than being continuations of provisionals.

name: Effect of restriction on nonelected claims for fee calculation
description: After a requirement for restriction, nonelected claims will be included in determining the fees due in connection with a subsequent amendment unless such claims are canceled.
guidance: An amendment canceling claims accompanying the papers constituting the application will be effective to diminish the number of claims to be considered in calculating the filing fees to be paid. A preliminary amendment filed concurrently with a response to a Notice To File Missing Parts of Application that cancels or adds claims will be taken into account in determining the appropriate fees due in response to the Notice. No refund will be made for claims being canceled in the response that have already been paid for. Money paid in connection with the filing of a proposed amendment will not be refunded by reason of the nonentry of the amendment; unentered claims will not be counted when calculating the fee due in subsequent amendments. Amendments affecting the claims cannot serve as the basis for granting any refund (see MPEP § 607.02 V for refund of excess claims fees). Excess claims fees set forth in 37 CFR 1.20(c)(3) and (c)(4) apply to excess claims presented during reexamination.

name: Interpretation of deposit account authorizations
description: How the Office treats deposit account authorizations to charge various fees.
guidance: A deposit account authorization to charge “the filing fee” is treated as an authorization to charge the applicable fees under 37 CFR 1.16 (the basic filing fee, search fee, examination fee, any excess claims fee, and any application size fee) to the deposit account. An authorization to charge “the basic filing fee” is treated as an authorization to charge the applicable basic filing fee, search fee, and examination fee. Any deposit account authorization to charge the filing fee but not the search fee or examination fee must specifically limit the authorization by reference to one or more of paragraphs (a) through (e) of 37 CFR 1.16. The Office treats such authorizations as received on the date of receipt as defined in 37 CFR 1.6 for refund purposes.

name: Disclosure requirement under 35 U.S.C. 112(a)
description: To obtain a valid patent, the application as filed must contain a full and clear disclosure of the invention in the manner prescribed by 35 U.S.C. 112(a).
guidance: The requirement ensures the public receives something in return for exclusionary rights. All amendments and claims must find descriptive basis in the original disclosure; no new matter may be introduced after filing. Applicant may rely on the specification with original claims and drawings as filed. Examiners should object to language deemed offensive under 37 CFR 1.3 for lack of decorum and courtesy; offensive depictions or caricatures in drawings should similarly be objected to. See MPEP § 714.25 for amendments and papers presented in violation of 37 CFR 1.3.

name: Specification and related parts must commence on separate pages
description: The specification, claims, abstract, and sequence listing (if any) must each begin on separate physical sheets/pages.
guidance: The specification must commence on a separate sheet; each sheet including part of the specification may not include other parts of the application. The claim(s), abstract and sequence listing should not be included on a sheet including any other part of the application. The claim(s) must commence on a separate physical sheet or electronic page (§ 1.75(h)). The abstract must commence on a separate physical sheet or electronic page or be submitted as the first page of the patent in a reissue application or reexamination or supplemental examination proceeding (§ 1.72(b)).

name: Specification text formatting (spacing, font, columns, page/paragraph numbering)
description: Specifications (other than reissue and certain proceedings) must meet spacing, paper-size, font, column, and numbering requirements.
guidance: Specification should be on flexible, strong, smooth, non-shiny, durable, white paper; lines 1 1/2 or double spaced; paper either DIN A4 or 8.5x11 inches with specified margins; text in nonscript type font (e.g., Arial, Times Roman, Courier), preferably font size 12, capitals at least 0.3175 cm high, but may be no smaller than 0.21 cm (font size 6); only a single column of text. Pages of specification (including claims and abstract) must be numbered consecutively starting with 1, centered above or preferably below the text. Paragraphs (other than claims/abstract) may be numbered using Arabic numerals in square brackets (e.g., [0001]) with leading zeros, highlighted in bold, and treated consistently with nontext elements being part of the surrounding paragraph. Paragraph/section headers are not paragraphs and should not be numbered.

name: Language and translation requirements for non-English filings (37 CFR 1.52(d))
description: Nonprovisional and provisional applications may be filed in a language other than English, but specific translation and processing fee requirements apply.
guidance: If a nonprovisional application under 35 U.S.C. 111(a) is filed in a non-English language, an English translation, a statement the translation is accurate, and the processing fee (§ 1.17(i)) are required; if not filed, applicant will be notified and given time to file to avoid abandonment. A provisional application filed in a non-English language does not require an English translation at the provisional stage; see § 1.78(a) for claiming benefit in a later nonprovisional.

name: Chemical and mathematical formulae and tables rules (37 CFR 1.58)
description: Guidance on inclusion of chemical/mathematical formulae, tables, and their placement.
guidance: The specification may contain chemical and mathematical formulae but shall not contain drawings or flow diagrams. The description portion may contain tables, but the same tables should not be included in both the drawings and description portions. Claims may contain tables if necessary to conform to 35 U.S.C. 112 or otherwise desirable. Tables submitted in electronic form must comply with § 1.58(c) and related provisions.

name: Definition/expected scope of 'valuable service'
description: The decision explains that 'valuable service' encompasses a level of expertise enabling a practitioner to prepare and prosecute patent applications and draft specifications or claims of patent applications.
guidance: Evaluation focuses on whether the applicant can independently perform substantive patent-practice tasks that require scientific/technical knowledge, not merely ancillary tasks.

name: Definition of parameters (EPO Guidelines)
description: Parameters are characteristic values, which may be values of directly measurable properties (e.g. the melting point of a substance, the flexural strength of a steel, the resistance of an electrical conductor). The characteristics of a product may be specified by parameters related to the physical structure of the product, provided that those parameters can be clearly and reliably determined by objective procedures which are usual in the art.
guidance: Use this EPO definition to determine whether a feature in your claim is a 'parameter' and therefore subject to the Guidelines' requirements.

name: Parameters must be clearly and reliably determinable by objective procedures usual in the art
description: A critical requirement from the Guidelines is that the parameter 'can be clearly and reliably determined by objective procedures which are usual in the art'.
guidance: When drafting parameter-based claims, ensure the parameter can be measured by objective, well-established procedures in the relevant technical field; otherwise the EPO may object.

name: Clarity — claims must be clear in themselves (Art.84(i))
description: For Article 84 EPC clarity, each parameter needs to meet the requirement that the claims must be clear in themselves when read by the skilled person (not including knowledge derived from the description).
guidance: Do not rely on the description to supply essential measurement details needed to make the claim intelligible to the skilled person.

name: Clarity — measurement method must appear in the claim (Art.84(ii))
description: The method for measuring a parameter (or at least a reference thereto) must appear completely in the claim itself.
guidance: Preferably include the measurement method wording directly in the claim; alternatively, have an explicit reference or text in the description that can be incorporated into the claim during prosecution.

name: Clarity — verifiability by the skilled person (Art.84(iii))
description: An applicant who chooses to define the scope of the claim by parameters needs to ensure that the skilled person can easily and unambiguously verify whether they are working inside or outside the scope of the claim.
guidance: Draft parameter thresholds and measurement instructions so that a practitioner can reproducibly test whether a product or process falls within the claimed scope.

name: Exception — omission acceptable if all methods yield same result within accuracy
description: The requirement may also be met if all the measurement methodologies known in the relevant technical field for determining this parameter yield the same result within the appropriate limit of measurement accuracy.
guidance: Consider providing evidence or argument that alternative measurement methods produce equivalent results to support omission of a specific method from the claim.

name: Practical drafting advice to preserve amendment basis
description: If the claim does not itself include the measurement method, ensure the description includes text that describes the method for measuring the parameter(s) and which can easily be added to the claim during prosecution. Preferably have some text in the description that can be added verbatim to the claims to meet the EPO's strict requirements regarding the basis for any amendments that are made.
guidance: Draft description passages with clear, copy-able measurement protocols and reasonable limits (e.g. upper bounds for open-ended ranges) so you can amend claims later without running afoul of the EPO's amendment-basis rules.

name: Statutory category (Step 1)
description: Evaluate whether the claim falls within a statutory category of invention (process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter) under MPEP 2106.03.
guidance: Apply broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) to claim language; determine whether the claim recites a machine, manufacture, composition, or process (e.g., controller = manufacture/machine). If yes, Step 1 = YES and proceed to judicial-exception analysis.

name: Claim recites a judicial exception (Step 2A Prong One)
description: Determine whether the claim 'recites' or 'sets forth' a judicial exception (law of nature, natural phenomenon, abstract idea) as explained in MPEP 2106.04(II) and the October 2019 Update.
guidance: Identify claim limitations that embody mathematical concepts, mental processes, laws of nature, or nature-based product limitations. Recitation can be explicit functional language (e.g., 'calculate using the Arrhenius equation') and multiple exceptions in a claim are permissible; if any judicial exception is recited, proceed to further analysis.

name: Markedly different characteristics analysis for nature-based products
description: When a claim recites a nature-based product limitation, analyze whether the claimed nature-based product possesses markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart (MPEP 2106.04(c)(I)).
guidance: Apply the analysis to the nature-based product as claimed; for mixtures/combination products, apply to the resultant combination rather than component parts. If components do not occur together in nature, compare the claimed mixture to its individual components. Consider changed structure or changed functional properties (a changed function can evidence markedly different characteristics). If markedly different characteristics exist, the product is not a 'product of nature' exception.

name: Claim must define the invention; unclaimed characteristics not counted
description: Ensure the claimed limitation itself defines the invention and that only characteristics recited or encompassed within the BRI of the claim can contribute to eligibility (In re Roslin, Roche Molecular).
guidance: Examiners should identify characteristics by what is recited in the claim and its BRI. The claim need not explicitly recite a markedly different characteristic so long as the BRI of the claim reflects the claimed product possesses at least one appropriate markedly different characteristic.

name: Combine multiple recited judicial exceptions into a single exception
description: When a claim recites a series of steps or multiple limitations that each embody judicial exceptions, treat the combined recited judicial exceptions as a single judicial exception for further analysis.
guidance: Follow MPEP 2106.04 and 2106.05(II) and October 2019 Update guidance; consolidation simplifies Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B analyses.

name: Step 2B — 'significantly more' / inventive concept
description: Evaluate whether the claim as a whole amounts to 'significantly more' than the recited judicial exception by identifying an inventive concept in the additional elements individually or in combination (MPEP 2106.05).
guidance: Re-assess elements previously deemed insignificant extra-solution activity for whether they are well-understood, routine, conventional (Berkheimer). If additional elements are well-known and generic, they will not supply 'significantly more'. Conversely, specific unconventional tools or meaningful improvements to technology can provide 'significantly more'.

name: Rejection practice note: explain exception and insufficiency of additional elements
description: When issuing a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101, the examiner should identify the exception by pointing to specific claim limitations and explain why they describe an abstract idea/other exception, and explain why additional elements fail to integrate or amount to significantly more.
guidance: If relying on the conclusion that an additional element is well-understood, routine, conventional (Berkheimer Option 1), the rejection should cite support for that conclusion in the specification or other record evidence.

name: Improvements-to-technology and 'other meaningful limitations' consideration
description: To find that a claim 'integrates' an exception by virtue of an improvement to technology or other meaningful limitations, there must be a technical explanation in the specification and the claim must reflect the asserted improvement.
guidance: Examiners should evaluate specification and claim together; do not perform improvements analysis with reference to whether claim elements are conventional (that is excluded at Step 2A Prong Two). Examiners are not expected to make qualitative judgments on the merits of an asserted improvement except where a person of ordinary skill would clearly understand the claim/specification do not show an improvement.

name: Claim interpretation under Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI)
description: Interpret claim terms under the BRI standard consistent with the specification (MPEP 2111); preambles do not limit claims unless the preamble supplies a positive limitation.
guidance: Use the same claim interpretation across eligibility and other patentability requirements. When a limitation is drafted as 35 U.S.C. 112(f) means-plus-function, apply the appropriate three-prong test and corresponding-structure limitation to BRI.

name: Means-plus-function limitations under 35 U.S.C. 112(f)
description: If a claim limitation satisfies the three-prong test for 112(f), its BRI is limited to the structure, material, or acts disclosed in the specification and equivalents (MPEP 2181).
guidance: When 112(f) applies, the limitation will be interpreted as limited to the disclosed corresponding structure (e.g., ARCXY thermocouple) and that interpretation should be used for eligibility, novelty, obviousness, and other analyses; prior art must show the same structure or equivalents to anticipate or render obvious the claim.

name: Eligibility Step 1 — statutory category
description: Is the claim to a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter (i.e., one of the four statutory categories)?
guidance: Evaluate after determining what applicant has invented by reviewing the entire application disclosure and construing claims under the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI). If the claim as a whole does not fall within any statutory category (Step 1: NO), the claim is non‑statutory and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101. If the claim falls within one or more statutory categories (Step 1: YES), proceed to determine whether it is eligible at Pathway A or requires further analysis at Step 2A for judicial exceptions. Examples: transitory signals (propagating carrier waves) are non‑statutory even if physical; a machine‑readable medium whose BRI includes carrier waves should be rejected under §101.

name: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) and review of disclosure
description: Before applying eligibility steps, determine what the applicant has invented by reviewing the entire disclosure and construing claims according to the BRI.
guidance: Evaluation at each eligibility step should be made after determining the applicant's invention via whole‑application review and BRI. If the BRI covers non‑statutory embodiments, point out the BRI and recommend narrowing amendments. See MPEP §2111 for more on BRI. Use Form paragraphs 7.05/7.05.01 when making an eligibility rejection arising from Step 1 failures.

name: Claims whose BRI covers both statutory and non‑statutory embodiments
description: If a claim's BRI embraces both statutory and non‑statutory embodiments, the claim embraces non‑statutory subject matter and fails Step 1.
guidance: Such claims should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 for failing to claim statutory subject matter. It is best practice for the examiner to point out the problematic BRI and recommend an amendment, if possible, to narrow the claim to statutory embodiments. Example: a 'computer readable medium' claim that can read as a compact disc (statutory) or a carrier wave (non‑statutory) is properly rejected.

name: Eligibility Step 2A — directed to a judicial exception
description: After finding a claim within a statutory category, determine whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon).
guidance: Step 2A is the first part of the Alice/Mayo framework. If the claim as a whole is not directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: NO) it is eligible at Pathway B and the eligibility analysis ends. If it is directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: YES), further analysis at Step 2B is required to determine whether the claim amounts to 'significantly more' than the exception. Evaluate Step 2A after BRI and whole‑application review.

name: Step 2A two‑prong inquiry — Prong One (recitation) vs Prong Two (integration)
description: Prong One: does the claim recite (set forth or describe) a judicial exception? Prong Two: if it recites an exception, do the additional elements integrate the exception into a practical application?
guidance: Treat Prong One as identification of whether the claim 'recites' an exception (either by explicitly setting it forth or by describing the concept). If Prong One is met, Prong Two examines whether additional claim elements transform/integrate the exception into a practical application so that the claim is not 'directed to' the exception. If additional elements do not integrate the exception into a practical application, the claim is directed to the exception (Step 2A: YES) and proceeds to Step 2B. See MPEP §2106.04(d)(2) for how to evaluate 'integration into a practical application.'

name: Step 2A Prong One — distinguish 'recites' from 'involves'
description: Determine whether the claim 'recites' an abstract idea/law of nature/natural phenomenon (i.e., sets it forth or describes it) rather than merely involving such a concept.
guidance: Examples: a claim stating 'elements that operate in accordance with F=ma' sets forth (recites) a law of nature and meets Prong One; a claim to a teeter‑totter (lever) merely involves the principle of mechanical advantage but does not recite it and thus does not meet Prong One. Examiners should identify specific claim limitation(s) believed to recite an exception and then determine whether those limitations fall within the judicial exception categories. See MPEP §2106.04(a),(b),(c) for details.

name: Handling claims that recite multiple judicial exceptions
description: Apply the same eligibility analysis regardless of how many judicial exceptions are recited; avoid parsing into multiple exceptions unless they are distinct.
guidance: If multiple distinct exceptions are present (e.g., one limitation is a law of nature and another is an abstract idea), examiners may select one exception and perform the analysis on that selected exception for efficiency. If analysis shows additional elements integrate or amount to significantly more than the selected exception, the claim is eligible. If multiple exceptions are not clearly distinct, treat them together as a single judicial exception for Prong Two and Step 2B. When possible, identify the claim as reciting the multiple types (e.g., mental steps + mathematical calculation) in the record to clarify analysis.

name: Abstract idea groupings (enumerated approach)
description: To identify abstract ideas, use the Office's enumerated groupings: (1) mathematical concepts; (2) certain methods of organizing human activity; and (3) mental processes.
guidance: This grouping approach distills relevant case law into clear categories for examination instead of relying solely on case comparisons. Examiners should (1) identify the specific claim limitation(s) believed to recite an abstract idea, and (2) determine whether those limitations fall within at least one grouping. If so, Prong One is satisfied and Prong Two analysis follows; if not, the claim does not recite an abstract idea and the abstract‑idea analysis concludes (except in rare circumstances). Note: software and business methods are not categorically excluded, and software is not automatically an abstract idea merely because it involves mathematical calculations. See MPEP §2106.04(a)(2) and cited cases (Enfish, McRO, Thales).

name: Procedure when claim fails Step 1 or Step 2A due to exceptions
description: If a claim fails Step 1 (not a statutory category) or fails Step 2A (directed to a judicial exception without integration), the examiner should make the appropriate 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection and follow form‑paragraph and best practice guidance.
guidance: Use form paragraphs (e.g., 7.05 and 7.05.01) for Step 1 rejections. When a claim fails due to lack of additional elements integrating the exception, recommend amendments if possible that could resolve eligibility. If claim embraces non‑statutory embodiments but might be amended to statutory embodiments, proceed to analyze whether the amended claim would be eligible at Pathway A, B, or C and recommend amendments as a best practice.

name: Nature-based product eligibility categories
description: Nature-based products are those products derived from natural sources that require closer scrutiny to determine whether they are an exception. They fall into two categories: 1. Eligible nature-based products have markedly different characteristics from any naturally occurring counterpart. They are not judicial exceptions. 2. Ineligible nature-based products are either: (i) naturally occurring, or (ii) not naturally occurring but do not have markedly different characteristics from any naturally occurring counterpart. They are 'product of nature' exceptions.
guidance: Use this binary classification to determine whether a nature-derived claim limitation potentially falls within the 'product of nature' judicial exception. If classified as ineligible (a product-of-nature exception), proceed to Step 2B to consider 'significantly more.'

name: Markedly different characteristics analysis is part of Step 2A
description: The markedly different characteristics analysis is used to determine if a nature-based product is a 'product of nature' exception. Thus, the markedly different characteristics analysis is part of Step 2A, i.e., it helps answer the question of whether a claim is directed to an exception.
guidance: Treat the analysis as the mechanism within Step 2A to decide whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception (law of nature/natural phenomenon/product of nature). If Step 2A determines the claim is not directed to an exception, eligibility is satisfied (unless another exception exists).

name: Use the markedly different characteristics analysis to identify 'products of nature'
description: If the nature-based product has markedly different characteristics, it is not an exception. The claim is eligible (Step 2A: NO), unless the claim recites another exception. If the nature-based product does not have markedly different characteristics, it is a 'product of nature' exception, and thus the claim is directed to an exception (Step 2A: YES). Proceed to Step 2B to analyze whether the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the exception.
guidance: Apply this rule to classify the claim outcome of Step 2A. Remember to consider other claim elements only after a product is found to be an exception (i.e., in Step 2B).

name: Do not over-extend the markedly different characteristics analysis (when not to apply)
description: Care should be taken not to overly extend the markedly different characteristics analysis. The streamlined eligibility analysis applies if the claim is directed to an invention that clearly does not seek to tie up any judicial exception. E.g., the artificial hip prosthesis coated with a naturally occurring mineral, or the plastic chair with wooden trim.
guidance: Avoid unnecessary markedly-different comparisons for claims that obviously do not attempt to monopolize natural products. Also: process claims are not subject to the markedly different characteristics analysis, except where a process claim is drafted in such a way that there is no difference in substance from a product claim to a nature-based product (e.g., the 'method of providing an apple').

name: Analyze only the nature-based product limitations
description: Do not apply the markedly different characteristics analysis to claim limitations that are not nature-based.
guidance: For multi-element claims, isolate and analyze only the nature-derived limitation(s) for markedly different characteristics. Example: in 'probiotic composition comprising a mixture of Lactobacillus and milk in a container' analyze the 'mixture of Lactobacillus and milk' but not the container (the container is evaluated later in Step 2B if needed).

name: Purification alone does not create markedly different characteristics absent structural or functional change
description: Example: Purified amazonic acid is structurally and functionally identical to the naturally occurring acid in the leaves; because there are no different characteristics, there are no markedly different characteristics.
guidance: When a claim is to a purified form, examine whether purification caused structural or functional changes. If purification only isolates the natural material without changing characteristics, treat it as a product-of-nature exception (see sample rejection).

name: Claims encompassing naturally occurring embodiments are likely product-of-nature exceptions
description: If the claim encompasses naturally occurring antibodies (or other nature-derived embodiments) with no meaningful structural or functional distinction, there is no marked difference and the claim is a 'product of nature' exception.
guidance: Check claim breadth: if at least some embodiments within the claim are indistinguishable from naturally occurring products, then the claim may be directed to a judicial exception. Narrowing to specific sequences/structures that differ may avoid the exception.

name: If a nature-based product is found to be an exception, proceed to Step 2B to evaluate 'significantly more'
description: When the nature-based product does not have markedly different characteristics and is thus a 'product of nature' exception, proceed to Step 2B to analyze whether the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the exception.
guidance: Evaluate additional claimed elements (non-nature-based limitations) under Step 2B to determine whether they add an inventive concept or other features that transform the claim into a patent-eligible application of the exception.

name: Process claims focused on practical application may not be directed to the nature-based product exception
description: A method claim that recites administering a nature-based product to treat disease (e.g., 'method of treating breast or colon cancer, comprising administering an effective amount of purified amazonic acid') can be not directed to the nature-based product exception because the claim focuses on a process of practically applying the product rather than tying up the product itself.
guidance: When evaluating method/process claims that mention nature-based products, determine whether the claim is directed to the nature-based product or to a practical application; if the latter, Step 2A may find no exception and the claim may be eligible.

name: Use appropriate rejection form paragraphs and explain rejections with nature-based analysis
description: When rejecting claims under 35 U.S.C. 101 as directed to a product-of-nature exception without significantly more, use form paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015. Example language explains that the claimed product is not markedly different from its naturally occurring counterpart and that no additional elements add 'significantly more.'
guidance: Follow USPTO form paragraph practice for consistent office actions. Include factual findings about structural/functional similarities or differences and explain why additional claim elements do or do not supply 'significantly more.'

name: Formalities examination for disclosure exception claims
description: Upon an application indicating the purport of claiming disclosure exception, the examiner conducts formalities examination on whether the application is submitted within the statutory period (12 or 6 months) and whether the disclosure was made by a person with the right to obtain a patent.
guidance: The office issues a notice to correct deficiencies when: (i) discloser differs from filer/inventor; (ii) application filed after statutory period; (iii) wrong disclosure date or type or incorrect supporting information; (iv) submitted documents insufficient to prove relevant facts. Failure to amend within designated period invalidates the Article 30 claiming proceeding (the filing remains effective).

name: International applications — declaration and evidence rules
description: For international (PCT) applications deemed filed to KIPO, a person can declare exceptions to lack of novelty in PCT Request Box No. VIII(v); that declaration is deemed to meet application cover-sheet requirements if a document proving the relevant facts is legitimately submitted within 30 days from the reference date under Article 200.
guidance: Where such declaration and supporting evidence are submitted within the specified period, the international application shall be examined as if it included a regular domestic claiming of exceptions to lack of novelty (refer to PCT Rule 4.17). For national phase entries, similar timing applies relative to the national entry reference date.

name: Scope of 'state of the art' for inventive-step analysis
description: The 'state of the art' at filing includes the inventions referred to in Article 29(1), common general knowledge, and other publicly known technical matters; it also relates to all information relevant to the technical field described in the claims, including ordinary methods to conduct daily work and experiments.
guidance: Consider both explicit prior-art disclosures and routine/common techniques when assessing whether a claimed invention would have been obvious to the person skilled in the art.

name: General principles for determining inventive step (claim-by-claim, combination of references)
description: Determine whether the invention described in each claim could have been easily made by a person skilled in the art based on prior-art reference(s) prior to filing; if yes, that claim lacks inventive step. Determination is to be made for each claim separately.
guidance: When there are multiple claims, make the inventive-step determination claim-by-claim. Notifying applicants of lack of novelty is different from notifying lack of inventive step, but an examiner may notify both together if novelty is lacking.

name: Myriad: Genomic DNA is not patentable; cDNA is patentable
description: Genomic DNA (gDNA) is NOT patentable — even when isolated and purified from the human genome. Complementary DNA (cDNA) IS patentable — cDNA is synthetically created by reverse-transcribing mRNA and does not include introns.
guidance: Key test: is the claimed molecule meaningfully different in structure or function from what exists in nature? Examples: genomic DNA (isolated from body) ❌ not patentable; cDNA ✅ patentable. Synthetic genes (optimized codons) ✅; gene with inserted regulatory elements ✅. Avoid relying on 'isolation' alone — show synthetic origin or structural changes.

name: Mayo two-step test for diagnostic methods (§101/Alice framework)
description: Step 1: Is the claim directed to a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea? Step 2: If yes, do the additional elements in the claim amount to 'significantly more' than the exception itself?
guidance: Diagnostic claims often fail Step 2 because measurement and comparison steps are 'well-understood, routine, and conventional.' The framework was applied in Mayo and extended via Alice. Use this test to analyze diagnostic method claims.

name: Elements that can make diagnostic method claims survive Mayo
description: To survive Mayo, diagnostic method claims should include elements that amount to 'significantly more' than a natural law or correlation.
guidance: Examples of survivable elements: a novel, non-obvious biomarker; an unconventional measurement technique that is not routine in the field; a treatment step that goes beyond merely observing and applying the natural correlation; specific clinical decision algorithms. Anti-pattern: claims that only observe a correlation and use routine lab steps are likely invalid.

name: Synthetically created or engineered molecules are patentable when sufficiently different
description: cDNA sequences, synthetic genes with optimized codons, engineered proteins with modified amino acid sequences, chimeric antibodies, and fusion proteins can be patent-eligible if they are not found in nature.
guidance: Emphasize human engineering and provide sequence comparisons, structural data, and functional assays showing differences from natural counterparts. Claim both structure and functional consequences where appropriate.

name: Novel compositions and formulations are patentable
description: Novel drug-antibody conjugates (ADCs), pharmaceutical formulations with improved properties, and nanoparticle delivery systems for biologics are examples of patent-eligible compositions.
guidance: Draft claims to capture the inventive combination or improved properties (stability, bioavailability, delivery characteristics). Provide experimental support and examples in the specification.

name: Genetically modified organisms (GMOs) and engineered organisms can be patentable
description: Transgenic plants and animals with inserted genes conferring new traits, engineered microorganisms producing novel compounds or functions, and CRISPR-modified organisms can be patent-eligible when claimed to reflect human engineering.
guidance: Claim the genetic modifications and their functional effects; careful claim drafting is needed to avoid §101 issues. Note licensing/ownership issues (e.g., CRISPR patent wars) may affect commercialization.

name: Categories facing §101 challenges: naturally occurring molecules
description: Naturally occurring molecules—genomic DNA sequences, naturally occurring proteins/peptides/antibodies isolated from human or animal sources, and natural metabolites/biomarkers—face §101 patent-eligibility challenges.
guidance: Avoid claims that only isolate/purify naturally occurring items. To claim related subject matter, show structural or functional attributes that are engineered/novel versus naturally occurring.

name: Categories facing §101 challenges: diagnostic correlations based on natural laws
description: Methods claiming only the observation that biomarker X correlates with disease Y, or diagnostic methods using routine measurement techniques to apply a natural correlation, are vulnerable under Mayo.
guidance: Add concrete application steps (treatment decisions, novel measurement approaches, specific clinical algorithms) and demonstrate why steps are not 'well-understood, routine, and conventional.' Personalized medicine selection methods must themselves be novel and non-routine.

name: CRISPR-specific eligibility: engineered components and delivery systems
description: Claims directed to engineered CRISPR components (synthetic guide RNAs, modified Cas9 proteins), engineered CRISPR delivery systems (viral vectors, nanoparticles), and methods of using CRISPR to edit specific genes in specific cell types are patent-eligible; claims to the naturally occurring bacterial CRISPR system are not.
guidance: Draft claims around engineered sequences, protein modifications, delivery technologies, and specific applications. Be mindful of existing patent ownership and licensing needs (e.g., multiple groups hold patents with differing scopes).

name: Stem cells and cell lines: patentable modifications vs natural origins
description: Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), differentiated cells produced through novel protocols, and genetically modified stem cell lines are patent-eligible; embryonic stem cell lines isolated directly without modification and methods using conventional techniques face eligibility challenges.
guidance: Claim the reprogramming/modification steps and resulting functional differences. For methods, show that culturing or isolation steps are innovative and not merely routine, otherwise they may fail under Mayo.

name: Claim drafting strategy: emphasize structural differences in composition claims
description: For composition of matter patents, the specification and claims should explicitly describe how the claimed molecule is structurally different from any naturally occurring counterpart and include supporting data.
guidance: Include sequence comparisons, structural data, and functional assays demonstrating difference. Use precise claim language reciting engineered features and provide examples in the specification to counter §101 challenges.

name: Claim drafting strategy: avoid 'isolated' or 'purified' language alone
description: Post-Myriad, claiming a molecule as merely 'isolated' or 'purified' is insufficient to confer patent eligibility.
guidance: Claims must recite structural modifications, synthetic origin, or functional characteristics that do not exist in nature. Anti-pattern: relying on 'isolated from the body' wording without demonstrating marked differences.

name: Claim drafting strategy: for diagnostics, add concrete application steps
description: To survive Mayo, diagnostic method claims should include treatment steps, novel measurement techniques, or specific clinical decision algorithms that go beyond simply observing and applying a natural correlation.
guidance: Draft claims that tie the biomarker measurement to a concrete, non-routine clinical action or an inventive measurement approach. Provide specification evidence of technical challenges overcome and clinical utility.

name: Claim drafting strategy: use the specification to establish non-obviousness
description: Because Mayo turns on whether additional claim elements are 'well-understood, routine, and conventional,' the specification should explain technical challenges, unexpected results, and why the claimed method was not obvious to skilled practitioners.
guidance: Document experimental hurdles, comparative data, and unexpected benefits in the specification to support both §101 and non-obviousness arguments.

name: Claim drafting strategy: file both composition and method claims
description: For engineered biologics, consider filing both composition claims (covering the molecule itself) and method claims (covering how it's made or used) because one claim type may survive when the other faces §101 challenges.
guidance: Use method claims as fallback territory and ensure methods include inventive steps beyond routine techniques. Coordinate claim scope to maximize protection while reducing §101 risk.

name: License-fee evidence: apportionment when only some claims infringed
description: Where a license fee is established with reference to the entire patent, and only certain claims are infringed, the master must apportion the license fee according to the value of the claims, if possible, unless the remaining claims are merely structural; burden of proof on plaintiff to show value of infringed claims.
guidance: Master must try to allocate an established license fee to the infringed claims rather than applying it whole-cloth when only some claims are at issue (cases: Willimantic Thread Co. v. Clark Thread Co.).

name: Presumption that all pending, rejected claims are on appeal
description: Examiners are not required to determine whether fewer than all rejected claims are identified as being appealed. The Board will presume all rejected claims are on appeal except those canceled by amendment.
guidance: Treat all pending, rejected claims as being on appeal and maintain rejections unless appellant has overcome them. If appellant did not argue a rejection or requested it be held in abeyance, identify that the appellant did not argue it.

name: Identification of how final rejection applies to amended/added claims
description: Where amendments after final action are entered for appeal purposes, the examiner must identify (in an advisory action) how one or more individual rejections set forth in the final rejection would be used to reject the added or amended claim(s).
guidance: Provide clear mapping of prior rejections to amended claims so the record shows how the rejections would apply.

name: Examiner reevaluation and withdrawal of unsupported rejections
description: The examiner should reevaluate their position in light of arguments presented and expressly withdraw any rejections not adhered to in the 'WITHDRAWN REJECTIONS' subsection.
guidance: If all rejections of an independent claim are withdrawn while others remain, note the change of status. If dependent claims' rejections change, note those changes and advise applicant of options (e.g., rewrite dependent claim in independent form under 41.33(b)(2) before the time in 90.3).

name: Warning for non-statutory double patenting (NSDP) rejections not argued
description: If claims are rejected on the ground of non-statutory double patenting and the rejection was not addressed in the appeal brief, include a warning (¶ 12.278) explaining that the appeal may be dismissed by a court or the Court may summarily affirm the NSDP rejection.
guidance: In bracketed text, insert the claim numbers subject to NSDP. Explain jurisdictional risks and the need for a terminal disclaimer prior to judicial review if the rejection is not overcome.

name: Substitute examiner's answer on remand (further consideration of a rejection)
description: The examiner may furnish a substitute examiner's answer in response to a remand by the Board for further consideration of a rejection (37 CFR 41.50(a)). Appellant must within two months either request reopening (reply under 1.111) or maintain the appeal (reply brief under 41.41) to avoid dismissal of the appeal as to the remanded claims.
guidance: A substitute examiner's answer may set forth a new ground of rejection subject to the same TC Director approval requirements. Use form paragraph 12.285 for substitute answers on remand and include reasons supporting the rejections. TC Director must approve substitute answers setting new grounds.

name: Claim indefiniteness from lack of antecedent basis
description: A claim is indefinite when it contains words or phrases whose meaning is unclear (e.g., referring to 'said lever' or 'the lever' where no earlier recitation or limitation of a lever appears, or where two different levers are recited earlier making it unclear which is meant).
guidance: Examples: referring to 'said aluminum lever' when only 'a lever' was recited earlier is indefinite because it is uncertain which lever is referenced. If two different levers are recited earlier, later recitation of 'said lever' is unclear. Case citation: In re Packard, 751 F.3d 1307. Examiner should identify such ambiguities as indefiniteness under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre‑AIA 112, second paragraph).

name: Reasonable ascertainability by a person skilled in the art negates indefiniteness
description: A claim is not indefinite if its scope would be reasonably ascertainable by those skilled in the art, even absent explicit antecedent wording.
guidance: If skilled artisans can reasonably determine what the claim refers to, lack of explicit antecedent wording does not render the claim indefinite. Example: 'controlled stream of fluid' provided reasonable antecedent basis for 'the controlled fluid' (Ex parte Porter, 25 USPQ2d 1144). Examiners must assess whether the claim language, taken as a whole, apprises one of ordinary skill of its scope.

name: Examiner should suggest constructive corrections for antecedent problems
description: Antecedent problems are typically drafting oversights and examiners should identify and suggest corrections in a positive, constructive way so minor problems can be easily corrected.
guidance: The examiner's role is to ensure claim language complies with statutory requirements but to expend effort proportionately—identify minor antecedent oversights for applicant correction. However, even if correctable, indefiniteness is not automatically unobjectionable merely because it could have been fixed (In re Hammack, 427 F.2d 1384).

name: Terms lacking antecedent basis in the specification are not necessarily indefinite
description: The absence of a term in the specification as an antecedent does not by itself render the claim indefinite; there is no requirement that claim wording must match the specification verbatim.
guidance: Applicants have latitude in defining the invention by their chosen claim terms so long as those terms define the invention with reasonable clarity and precision. Examiners should evaluate whether the claim terms, even if not mirrored in the spec, still convey definite scope to skilled artisans.

name: Additional elements in the claim body absent from the preamble do not per se cause indefiniteness—consider the claim as a whole
description: A claim is not per se indefinite simply because the body of the claim recites elements not appearing in the preamble; the totality of claim limitations and their interaction must be considered to determine whether the claim apprises one of ordinary skill of its scope.
guidance: Assess the claim in its entirety to determine the inventor's contribution to the art and whether the notice function of 35 U.S.C. 112 is satisfied. Example: In re Larsen—preamble omitted a linear member that appeared in the body; the court reversed the examiner's rejection after finding the claim as a whole was sufficiently definite.

name: Aggregation / substitution leading to obviousness
description: If modification or substitution of elements does not lead to structural difficulties and the functional effect of new elements is not regarded as greater than the summed effects of the prior art references, the claimed invention falls within an aggregation and is therefore denied inventive step.
guidance: Example: substituting a spindle from prior art reference 2 for the spindle of prior art reference 1 — if no structural difficulties and no greater functional effect, treat as aggregation. Examiner should assess whether summed effects are merely additive rather than producing a remarkable effect.

name: Aggregation in multiple-reference combinations
description: When a claimed invention corresponds to a combination of elements disclosed across multiple prior art references, if the combination does not lead to particular difficulties nor produce any remarkable difference in functional effect, the aggregation is considered obvious to a person skilled in the art.
guidance: Example: combining an injection molding machine, a vacuum chamber, and a mold fastening system — if combination is straightforward and effect unremarkable, it is obvious. Examiner should evaluate whether the combination causes particular technical difficulties or a remarkable synergistic effect.

name: Synthetic determination of inventive step
description: Inventive step determination should consider synthetically the objective, technical configuration, and functional effect of an invention described in a claim — i.e., the uniqueness of the objective and the remarkableness of the effect as a whole, mainly based on the difficulty of technical configuration.
guidance: Do not readily conclude lack of inventive step if applicant offers written arguments claiming non-obviousness; consider other supportive factors (teaching away, secondary evidence, etc.).

name: Law restrictions irrelevant to inventive step
description: Implementation prohibitions or legal restrictions on the technical content of the claimed invention (domestically or abroad) are not taken into consideration when determining inventive step.
guidance: Example: a lottery-drawing method prohibited by law is still assessed on technical difficulty alone and considered obvious if technically straightforward, despite legal prohibition.

name: Assess prior art by whole disclosure (no cherry-picking)
description: When determining obviousness in view of prior art, the examiner should base the decision on matters a person skilled in the art can reasonably recognize from the whole disclosure of the prior art, rather than certain parts which might unfairly constitute a ground for lack of inventive step.
guidance: If an applicant presents other prior art that contradicts parts of the disclosure or makes them unclear, the examiner should comprehensively determine whether a skilled person can easily arrive at the claimed invention by considering the prior art as a whole.

name: Article 29 — identity of invention requirement
description: The invention described in the claims of the present application should be completely or substantially identical to an invention or utility innovation described in the original specification of another application for Article 29(3)-(4) to apply.
guidance: Even if the matters in the original specification of another application are later omitted by amendment, Article 29(3,4) is implemented. Examiner must assess substantial identity.

name: Treatment of prior-filed vs later-filed applications with domestic priority (common disclosure rules)
description: When relying on inventions disclosed in the original specification of a prior-filed application that formed the basis for a domestic priority claim and a later-filed application, (a) inventions commonly disclosed in both are deemed another application filed on the filing date of the prior-filed application and apply under Article 29(3,4); (b) inventions solely in the later-filed application's original specification are deemed filed on the later-filed application's date; inventions solely in the prior-filed application's original specification but not in later-filed are not applied under Article 29(3,4).
guidance: A prior-filed application is deemed withdrawn if not laid open after certain periods (e.g., 1 year 3 months) — timing affects lay-open status. If invention was newly described via amendment, these rules do not apply. Examples clarify which inventions can be relied upon.

name: Special rules for international (PCT) applications and translations
description: When 'another application' is an international application, 'laid open' may include international publication under PCT Article 21. The scope of inventions applied under Article 29 varies depending on filing dates (pre/post Dec 31, 2014 / Jan 1, 2015).
