For applications filed on/after Jan 1, 2015, if the applicant fails to submit a Korean translation within the specified period under Article 201(4), the international application may be deemed withdrawn and cannot be relied upon as another application.
guidance: Where international applications claim domestic priority, inventions disclosed in the specification/claims/drawings submitted at the international filing date and translations determine the extent of enlarged novelty application. Examiner must pay attention to whether translations exist and which documents were submitted at which filing date.

name: Patentable subject matter — medical treatments (treating the human body)
description: Methods of medical treatment are not excluded from patentable subject matter and can be patented.
guidance: Apotex v Sanofi-Aventis (HCA majority) confirms methods of medical treatment can be patentable. Policy debates exist (access vs incentive), but medical-use method claims may be within scope of patentability; infringement and s117 (contributory infringement) issues remain relevant.

name: Usefulness / utility (s 7A)
description: An invention must be useful: the complete specification must disclose a specific, substantial and credible use for the invention, and disclose it sufficiently for a person skilled in the art to appreciate that use.
guidance: Raising the Bar (2012) amendments inserted s 7A defining 'useful' as requiring a specific, substantial and credible use disclosed in the complete specification, and sufficient disclosure so the skilled person can appreciate that use. This is a stricter test than pre-2012 where utility was met by showing the invention worked as claimed; commercial viability is not required but specificity is. Note US practice differs (utility not examined pre-grant in the same way).

name: Specification / description requirements (provisional and complete specifications)
description: A patent specification must disclose the invention clearly and completely enough for a person skilled in the relevant art to perform it; the complete specification must disclose the best known method and end with claims.
guidance: Provisional specification must be clear and complete enough for performance by the skilled person. Complete specification (s 40) must disclose the invention sufficiently, disclose the best method known to the applicant, and conclude with claims. The complete specification must enable the specific, substantial and credible use (post-Raising the Bar).

name: Claims content and formal requirements
description: Claims define the scope of monopoly and must be clear, succinct, supported by the specification, and relate to one invention only.
guidance: s 40(3)-(4) require claims to be clear and succinct and supported by matter disclosed in the specification; claims must not be broader than the contribution to the art described. Each claim is considered on its own merits (invalidity of one claim does not necessarily invalidate others). Claims must relate to one invention only. Aim is to prevent claims obtaining monopoly beyond the disclosed contribution.

name: Claim construction principles
description: Claims should be given a purposive construction and construed according to ordinary principles of written documents, read in light of the specification and common general knowledge.
guidance: Do not import limitations from the body of the specification that are not reproduced in the claim. Read the specification as a whole; body of specification can qualify or define expressions in a claim where appropriate. If claim language is ambiguous, it is permissible to resort to the body of the specification for clarification. The specification must be construed in light of common general knowledge extant before the priority date. Purposive (not purely literal) construction applies.

name: Agents and salesmen may be enjoined and treated as principals if evidence supports it
description: Though a defendant may claim to be an agent, he will be treated as a principal if the infringing article bears his name and other evidence points to him as primarily responsible; actual agents who sell infringing articles on behalf of their maker or owner are also liable to an injunction.
guidance: Courts look to substance over form; agents with active roles in sales/distribution can be enjoined even without ownership interest (Maltby v. Bobo; Steiger v. Heidelberger).

name: No misrepresentation of multiple competent means
description: If a patentee 'represents several things as competent to produce a specific effect, when only one will answer, that is bad.'
guidance: The specification must not claim multiple alternatives as effective when only one actually works; presenting useless alternatives can invalidate the patent or be viewed unfavourably by courts.

name: Patent may fail if part of claim is not new
description: There are authorities that where a patent is granted for several things, and one of them is not new, the patent 'fails in toto.'
guidance: Courts have sometimes held that inclusion of non‑novel elements among claimed items can invalidate the whole grant, though holdings vary by case.

name: Who may appeal (eligibility)
description: An applicant for a patent, any of whose claims has been twice rejected, may appeal from the decision of the primary examiner to the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (35 U.S.C. 134; 37 CFR 41.31(a)(1)). Patent owners in ex parte reexamination and certain reexamination scenarios may also appeal (37 CFR 41.31(a)(2)-(3)).
guidance: The "twice rejected" limitation need not be limited to the particular application (e.g., a rejection in a parent application and a subsequent rejection in a continuing application suffices). Appeals cannot be filed while prosecution is under an RCE; a notice of appeal cannot be entered with an RCE until the application is under a rejection. Distinguish pre- and post-November 29, 1999 reexamination filing rules for patent owners (different triggering events for appeal). See Ex Parte Lemoine and cited statutes/regulations for examples.

name: Scope of the appeal and presumption of affected claims
description: An appeal, when taken, is presumed to be taken from the rejection of all claims under rejection unless cancelled by an amendment filed and entered by the Office (37 CFR 41.31(c)).
guidance: If appellant does not cancel claims they do not wish to appeal and also fails to provide argument in the appeal brief directed to those claims, any challenge to that ground of rejection is waived and the Board may affirm those rejections. Waiver of challenges (including nonstatutory double patenting rejections) may have jurisdictional consequences for later judicial review. To avoid unintended waiver, either amend to cancel claims not appealed or present argument addressing rejected claims in the brief.

name: Interplay with amendments filed on or after final action (37 CFR 1.116)
description: If appellant files an amendment, a notice of appeal and an appeal brief on the same date after the mailing of a final action, 37 CFR 1.116 applies: such an amendment is not entered as a matter of right and may be admitted only under specified conditions.
guidance: An after-final amendment filed with a notice and brief may be admitted if it cancels claims or complies with form requirements, presents rejected claims in better form for consideration on appeal, or amends the specification upon a showing of good and sufficient reasons why it was not earlier presented. See MPEP §1.116 discussion for admission standards.

name: Pre-Appeal Brief Review Request Pilot Program requirements
description: Upon filing a notice of appeal, an appellant may request a Pre-Appeal Brief Review (pilot) by filing the request with the notice and before filing an appeal brief; the request (excluding the form) may not exceed five total pages and must be accompanied by arguments in a separate paper entitled 'Pre-Appeal Brief Request for Review'.
guidance: Program specifics: Form PTO/AIA/33 may be used; the request must be filed with the notice of appeal and prior to the appeal brief; requests are limited to appealable (not petitionable) matters; an after-final amendment may not accompany the request (any such amendment causes the request to fail content requirements). A request that fails to comply cannot be corrected and refiled because it must be filed on the same date as the notice. If a notice of appeal, pre-appeal request, and an RCE are filed the same day, the RCE controls and the pre-appeal request will not be considered. Upon receipt of a compliant request, a panel (including at least a supervisor and the examiner of record) reviews the arguments, may reopen prosecution, and issues one of four possible decisions: (A) application remains under appeal; (B) prosecution reopened (may include proposed amendment); (C) application allowed on existing claims; (D) request dismissed for non-compliance. No interviews are permitted during the review and the applicant may not attend. Filing the pre-appeal request may extend the time to file an appeal brief until the panel decision is mailed; after a panel decision the appeal-brief deadline is reset (one month from decision or balance of original two-month period, whichever greater) and is extendible under 37 CFR 1.136.

name: Treatment of dictionaries and extrinsic aids in appeal briefing
description: For purposes of appeal, dictionaries are not classified as 'Evidence' and appellants and examiners are permitted to cite dictionaries in briefs and examiner’s answers (37 CFR 41.30 and related discussion).
guidance: Excluding dictionaries from 'Evidence' allows their use in briefs without triggering the restrictions of 37 CFR 41.33(d)(2). This treatment is consistent with precedent (e.g., Phillips v. AWH Corp.) that courts may consult dictionaries to understand ordinary meanings and claim construction so long as the dictionary does not contradict the patent specification. Examiners may likewise refer to dictionaries without automatically creating a new ground of rejection.

name: Product-by-process limitation weight
description: A product-by-process limitation (e.g., 'cast in one piece') carries no patentable weight unless it is shown to impart any difference in structure from a product made otherwise.
guidance: If the limitation does not change the product’s structure, it cannot distinguish the claim over prior art merely because of the described process.

name: Scope of § 315(e)(2) estoppel defined by petition
description: Estoppel under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2) is defined by the petition’s content — the petition, not the institution decision, defines the scope of the IPR for estoppel purposes.
guidance: Including a claim/ground in the petition can result in estoppel even if the Board denied institution on that ground; a petitioner should seek remand (e.g., under SAS) if institution error needs correction.

name: Alice/Mayo § 101 eligibility — abstract idea/mental process
description: Claims directed to collection/comprehension of information and indication of results, performable in the human mind and executed on a generic computer in its normal manner, are directed to an abstract idea and fail step one of Alice/Mayo.
guidance: Show specifically how asserted evidence (e.g., documents) alters the eligibility finding and include such evidence in the joint appendix to avoid forfeiture on appeal.

name: Cancellation of claim before final decision affects standing to appeal
description: If a challenged claim is finally cancelled in a co-pending proceeding before the PTAB’s final written decision, the patent owner lacks standing to appeal the Board’s unpatentability determination as to that claim.
guidance: Cancellation prior to the final decision eliminates the concrete interest necessary to pursue appeal for that claim.

name: Motion-to-amend responsiveness requirement in IPRs
description: A substitute claim in a motion to amend need only include at least one limitation that directly responds to a ground of unpatentability; the patentee may include other non-substantive amendments in the proposed substitute claim.
guidance: 37 C.F.R. § 42.121 does not require every amendment in the substitute claim to be directly responsive so long as at least one narrowing responsive limitation is present.

name: PTAB not bound to accept argument-based disclaimer in IPR
description: The Board is not required to treat a patent owner’s statements in an IPR as a binding disclaimer for determining claim scope — the PTO need not accept disclaimer-by-argument in the same IPR proceeding.
guidance: A disclaimer in an IPR is binding in later proceedings but not necessarily in the IPR itself; patentees should use the motion-to-amend process rather than rely on argument-based disclaimer.

name: District-court stay standard — good cause and case-specific factors
description: A district court grants or denies stays pending PTAB proceedings based on factors including whether the stay will simplify issues, stage of litigation (e.g., claim construction completed, discovery stage), timing and diligence in filing IPRs, prejudice to plaintiff, and potential for delay.
guidance: Courts weigh early-stage litigation, lack of scheduling/trial date, and potential simplification in favor of a stay; speculative simplification, advanced stage, or prejudice (including imminent patent expiry) weigh against a stay.

name: PTAB analysis may inform indefiniteness determinations in district court
description: A district court may rely on the PTAB’s ability to analyze a claim term in light of prior art and prosecution statements to conclude the term is not indefinite.
guidance: Use prosecution history and PTAB analyses as evidence of a term’s meaning; PTAB’s engagement with the claim term can support definiteness findings.

name: Recovery of costs despite partial PTAB invalidations
description: A plaintiff who loses some patents in PTAB reviews but prevails on other asserted patents in district court may still recover costs if those remaining victories suffice to support an award.
guidance: Invalidation or withdrawal of some patents does not necessarily defeat entitlement to costs for successful litigation on remaining claims.

name: Inter Partes Review — Contents of Petition
description: Per 37 C.F.R. §42.104 the Petition must (a) establish petitioner standing, (b) identify relief requested, and (c) identify for each challenged claim: the challenged claim; statutory basis (102/103) and cited patents/printed publications; claim construction; why claim is unpatentable with element-by-element support; exhibit numbers and specific portions relied upon.
guidance: Petition must also identify real party in interest, related matters, counsel, and service information; may include statement of material facts; attach exhibits and English translations with affidavits. Petition limited to 60 double-spaced 14-point font pages (IPR). Use claim charts (single-spaced) to be concise. For §112(f) limitations, identify corresponding specification structure/material/acts.

name: Inter Partes Review — Claim Construction Expectation
description: Rules appear to require construing full breadth of each claim term, but USPTO applies 'broadest reasonable construction in light of the specification', giving plain meaning unless inconsistent with the specification; detailed constructions only needed for terms with special meanings.
guidance: Alternative proposed constructions are permissible; for means/step-plus-function limitations, identify corresponding specification portions. Consider effect of proposed constructions on later litigation and estoppels.

name: Inter Partes Review — Fee
description: USPTO fee for filing an IPR petition depends on number of challenged claims: $27,200 for up to 20 claims; $600 additional per claim over 20. No small or micro entity discount.
guidance: Dependent claims can be counted as multiple claims for fee purposes if claims they depend from are not challenged; multiple dependent claims counted as a single claim under some interpretations. Fees substantially higher than prior reexamination; consider staged fee structure changes in future rulemaking.

name: Inter Partes Review — Patent Owner Estoppel/Limitations on Subsequent USPTO Actions
description: If a claim is canceled as part of the final judgment in an IPR, the patent owner will be precluded from taking action in the USPTO inconsistent with that judgment, including obtaining a claim not patentably distinct from a finally refused or canceled claim or obtaining an amendment that was denied during the trial proceeding.
guidance: Prevents patent owner from getting a second bite at the apple for lost claims or denied amendments; patentably distinct claims can be pursued in continuing or reissue applications. Substantive amendments or new claims may give rise to intervening rights under 35 U.S.C. §318(c) and doctrine of equitable intervening rights.

name: Post-Grant Review — Applicability
description: As of September 16, 2012, PGR is available for any issued patent that either (1) includes claims subject to the new §§ 102 and 103 (generally patents with earliest effective filing date on/after March 16, 2013) or (2) is eligible for the transitional post-grant review for business method patents.
guidance: PGR broadens available bases for challenge but is limited to patents within the new statutory regime or transitional program; evaluate eligibility before choosing PGR vs IPR.

name: Post-Grant Review — Basis of Petition
description: A PGR petition can challenge claims on any basis available under 35 U.S.C. §§ 282(b)(2) or (3): §§ 101, 102, 103, 112 (except best mode), and/or 251. Inequitable conduct is not a basis.
guidance: PGR allows broader challenges than IPR; consider whether broader grounds justify PGR despite higher fees and earlier filing deadline.

name: Post-Grant Review — Contents of Petition
description: Per 37 C.F.R. §42.204 the Petition must (a) establish standing, (b) identify relief requested, and (c) identify for each challenged claim: challenged claim; statutory basis (101/102/103/112/251) and cited patents/printed publications; claim construction; why claim is unpatentable with element-by-element support; exhibits and specific portions relied upon.
guidance: Petition must identify real party in interest, related matters, counsel, and service info; attach exhibits and English translations with affidavits. Petition limited to 80 double-spaced 14-point font pages (PGR). Claim charts encouraged. For §112(f) limitations identify corresponding specification portions.

name: Post-Grant Review — Claim Construction Expectation
description: As in IPR, rules appear to require construing full breadth of claim terms but USPTO will apply 'broadest reasonable construction in light of the specification' and give plain meaning unless inconsistent; detailed constructions only where terms have special meaning.
guidance: Alternative constructions permissible; consider claim construction impact on institution and later litigation. Patent owner statements from court or USPTO proceedings may be submitted but considered only after institution.

name: Post-Grant Review — Threshold Standard for Institution
description: Board will institute PGR if the Petition, unrebutted, demonstrates that it is 'more likely than not that at least one of the claims challenged in the Petition is unpatentable.'
guidance: This is a higher standard than IPR's 'reasonable likelihood'. Applied claim-by-claim and ground-by-ground. Board may rarely institute under alternative standard for novel/unsettled legal questions of broad importance.

name: Post-Grant Review — Estoppels (Petitioner/Real Party/Privies)
description: Estoppols apply on a claim-by-claim basis once final decision of the Board is issued; because PGR covers broader grounds, the resulting estoppols are broader (apply to any arguments that were raised or reasonably could have been raised under §§ 101, 102, 103, 112 (except best mode), and/or 251).
guidance: Broader estoppels counsel caution when choosing PGR: a PGR that addresses only 102/103 may still preclude later arguments under other statutes that reasonably could have been raised.

name: Transitional Post-Grant Review for Business Method Patents — Applicability/Who Can File/Qualifying Patents
description: Transitional PGR permits petitioners to request PGR of certain patents directed to business methods that are otherwise ineligible for PGR; specifics include eligibility criteria for 'business method' patents.
guidance: If a single claim meets the transitional standard, the entire patent can be subject to PGR; during prosecution consider separating business-method-like claims into separate continuations to limit exposure.

name: Trial Process — Petition (procedural role during trial)
description: The Petition is the primary document presenting petitioner's arguments and evidence; the rest of the trial may focus on patent owner counter-arguments and petitioner's rebuttals rather than re-establishing the petition basis.
guidance: Draft a thorough, concise Petition with claim charts and supporting evidence; consider withholding limited information only with awareness of risks (e.g., claims not included in trial, deadline effects).

name: Trial Process — Institution of Trial; Scope of Institution
description: Board may institute trial for all or some claims and on all or some grounds; institution is claim-by-claim, ground-by-ground, and the proceeding is generally limited to instituted claims/issues unless new issues are raised by supplemental information or claim amendments are filed.
guidance: Petitioners should consider which claims/grounds they want included because estoppols and scope are tied to instituted items; claim selection affects strategy and cost.

name: Recommendations — Forum Selection
description: Because standards of review, claim construction, and presumption of patentability differ between Board trials and federal court, petitioners should evaluate which forum best suits their arguments (e.g., broader constructions and lower burdens may favor Board).
guidance: Consider substantive and tactical advantages of IPR/PGR vs district court (burden of proof, claim construction standards, speed, discovery differences) when deciding where to challenge.

name: Recommendations — Early Planning and Preparation
description: Trials move quickly with discovery, testimony, and depositions within short windows; petitioners should prepare discovery, witnesses, e-discovery plans, mandatory disclosures, and other trial materials before filing; patent owners must mobilize promptly at first sign of petition.
guidance: Petitioners have a preparation advantage; litigants should identify experts, custodians, search terms, and draft potential claim amendments or replacement claims early (outline by initial conference).

name: Recommendations — Claim Construction Considerations
description: Petitioner must construe challenged claims in the Petition; proposed constructions can affect subsequent litigation, licensing, and estoppel exposure.
guidance: Carefully consider proposed claim constructions and how they will influence later disputes and negotiations; avoid constructions that inadvertently harm broader strategy.

name: Requirements of a terminal disclaimer (per 37 CFR 1.321)
description: A terminal disclaimer is a statement filed by an owner (in whole or in part) of a patent or patent to be granted used to disclaim or dedicate a portion of the entire term of all claims of a patent. The formal requirements are set forth in 37 CFR 1.321.
guidance: Sample terminal disclaimer forms and further filing/treatment guidance are provided in MPEP § 1490. Examiners and applicants should follow 37 CFR 1.321's content and procedural requirements (including required provisions limiting enforceability to the period of common ownership or per joint research agreement when applicable).

name: Withdrawal of a terminal disclaimer before issuance
description: If a terminal disclaimer is filed in an application and the claims are later canceled or shown to be patentably distinct from the reference claims, the terminal disclaimer may be withdrawn before patent issuance by filing a petition under 37 CFR 1.182 requesting withdrawal of the recorded terminal disclaimer.
guidance: A terminal disclaimer may not be withdrawn after patent issuance. See MPEP § 1490, subsection VIII, for full withdrawal procedure and considerations.

name: Definition and threshold for common ownership (35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) and pre-AIA 103(c)(1))
description: Applications or patents are 'commonly owned' under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) if they were wholly owned by the same person(s) or organization(s) not later than the effective filing date of the claimed invention; under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c)(1) common ownership is determined at the time the claimed invention was made.
guidance: Common ownership requires 100% ownership of the subject matter that would otherwise be prior art and 100% ownership of the claimed invention. Partial ownership (<100%) does not establish common ownership for these exceptions. See MPEP § 717.02(a) and MPEP § 2146.02 for detailed definitions and evaluation guidance.

name: Joint research agreement criteria for treating references as commonly owned (35 U.S.C. 102(c) and pre-AIA 103(c))
description: Subject matter disclosure and a claimed invention can be treated as commonly owned under the joint research agreement provisions if the disclosure was developed and the invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the relevant date, the claimed invention resulted from activities within the scope of that agreement, and the application discloses (or is amended to disclose) the names of the parties to the agreement.
guidance: The CREATE Act (pre-AIA 103(c)) and 35 U.S.C. 102(c) have similar requirements but differ in timing: 102(c) is keyed to effective filing date; CREATE Act focuses on the date the invention was made and applies only to obviousness (not anticipation or double patenting). Definitions: 'joint research agreement' = written contract/grant/cooperative agreement among two or more persons for experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention. See MPEP §§ 2146 and 717 for more details.

name: Determining invention priority (when required and when not)
description: A determination of priority is not required when two inventions are commonly owned as set forth in 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c)(1).
guidance: Where common ownership applies, the earlier invention cannot be used as prior art against the later, so priority determinations are unnecessary. However, when the provisions do not apply, examiners may require identification of the prior inventor under 37 CFR 1.78(g) or other rules; failure to comply with such a requirement may result in abandonment unless conflicting claims are eliminated.

name: 37 CFR 1.78(g) requirements for identifying ownership/prior inventor
description: If an application (or patent under reexamination) and at least one other application naming different inventors are owned by the same party and contain patentably indistinct claims, and there is no record statement indicating common ownership on the relevant date, the Office may require the applicant/assignee to state whether the claimed inventions were commonly owned or to indicate which named inventor is the prior inventor.
guidance: Form paragraphs (e.g., 8.27.aia, 8.27.fti, 8.28.aia, etc.) may be used to require this information. The assignee must comply to avoid abandonment unless conflicting claims are eliminated. If the assignee asserts common ownership under the relevant statute, no further priority determination is required.

name: Doctrine preventing multiple patents to the same invention (double patenting principle)
description: Claims in commonly owned applications of different inventive entities may be rejected for double patenting to prevent an organization from obtaining two or more patents with different expiration dates covering nearly identical subject matter; claims must be patentably distinct, not merely different in form.
guidance: Cited precedent (In re Zickendraht; In re Christensen) supports that more than mere formal differences are required for entitlement to a second patent. Examiners should apply nonstatutory double patenting doctrine when claims lack patentable distinctness.

name: Effect and scope of the CREATE Act (treatment of non-commonly owned joint research agreement references)
description: The CREATE Act (Public Law 108-453) permits an applicant or patentee who is party to a joint research agreement to disqualify certain prior art that is otherwise available only under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e),(f),(g) for purposes of obviousness, thereby allowing non-commonly owned patents/applications subject to a qualifying joint research agreement to be treated as commonly owned for obviousness determinations under pre-AIA 103(c)(2).
guidance: To invoke CREATE, conditions must be met: (A) later invention not anticipated by earlier; (B) claimed invention made by/on behalf of parties to the joint research agreement in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; (C) invention resulted from activities within the scope of the agreement; (D) the patent application discloses/amends to disclose names of the parties. CREATE applies only to obviousness (not to anticipation or double patenting) and focuses on the date the invention was made (unlike 35 U.S.C. 102(c)). See MPEP § 2146.02 for more detail.

name: Computer program listing length and placement (>60 and ≤300 lines)
description: A computer program listing of over sixty (60) lines and less than three hundred and one (301) lines must, if submitted as part of the specification, be positioned at the end of the specification and before the claims, in accordance with 37 CFR 1.96(b).
guidance: Applicant is required to cancel the paper listing and either incorporate the listing in a text file submitted via EFS‑Web or on compact disc in compliance with 37 CFR 1.96, or insert the computer program listing after the detailed description but before the claims. Use the specified form paragraph whenever a paper printout of >60 and ≤300 lines is included and was filed on/after September 8, 2000. A computer program listing of more than three hundred lines will not be printed in any patent application publication or patent (37 CFR 1.96(c)).

name: Full statement of position with citations
description: The brief must set forth arguments and the basis therefor, with citations of the statutes, regulations, authorities and parts of the record relied upon.
guidance: Essential that the Board be provided with a brief fully stating the position of the appellant with respect to each ground so that no search of the Record is required. The brief should not incorporate or reference previous responses. A statement which merely points out what a claim recites will not be considered an argument for patentability.

name: Summary of claimed subject matter (37 CFR 41.37(c)(1)(iii))
description: A concise explanation of the subject matter defined in each of the rejected independent claims, referring to the specification in the Record by page and line number or by paragraph number, and to drawings by reference characters.
guidance: For each independent claim (and dependent claims argued separately) that contains a means-plus-function or step-plus-function under 35 U.S.C. 112(f), the concise explanation must identify the structure, material, or acts in the specification corresponding to each claimed function with specific references. Reference to the patent application publication does not satisfy this paragraph.

name: Separate headings/subheadings for each ground of rejection and for separately-argued claims
description: Each ground of rejection must be argued under a separate heading which clearly identifies the ground being contested. For multiple claims under the same ground, claims may be argued separately, as a group, or as a subgroup, but must be placed under subheadings identifying the specific claim(s) by number.
guidance: If appellant groups claims, the Board may select a single claim from the group and decide on that basis. Failure to separately argue claims which appellant has grouped together constitutes a waiver of any argument that the Board must consider the patentability of any grouped claim separately. Appellant must use a subheading for each claim for which separate consideration is desired. Examples of possible heading/subheading formats are provided.

name: Claims appendix requirements (37 CFR 41.37(c)(1)(v))
description: An appendix containing a copy of the claims involved in the appeal is required.
guidance: The copy should be a clean copy and should not include markings such as brackets or underlining except for claims in a reissue application and certain reexamination proceedings. The copy should be double-spaced and the appendix should start on a new page. See MPEP §§ cited for reissue/reexamination specifics.

name: 608.01(a)-Arrangement of Application
description: Required arrangement/order of parts of the application (specification, claims, drawings, abstract, etc.).

name: 608.01(o)-Basis for Claim Terminology in Description
description: Requirement that claim terminology be supported by the description/specification.

name: 608.01(s)-Restoration of Canceled Matter
description: Rules for restoring matter previously canceled from the specification/claims.

name: 608.02(e)-Examiner Determines Completeness and Consistency of Drawings
description: Role of the examiner in determining whether the drawings are complete and consistent with the specification and claims.

name: 608.04-New Matter
description: Standards and handling for new matter (matter not present in the specification, claims, or drawings on the application filing date).

name: 608.04(a)-Matter Not Present in Specification, Claims, or Drawings on the Application Filing Date
description: Definition and consequences of matter not present on the filing date (new matter).

name: Anticipation requires every element in a single prior art reference
description: “A claim is anticipated only if each and every element as set forth in the claim is found, either expressly or inherently described, in a single prior art reference.”
guidance: To reject a claim as anticipated the disclosure must teach every element required by the claim under its broadest reasonable interpretation. The identical invention must be shown in as complete detail as is contained in the claim. Elements must be arranged as required by the claim, but identity of terminology is not required (not an ipsissimis verbis test). (Verdegaal Bros.; Richardson v. Suzuki; In re Bond; MPEP §2114 citations).

name: Claim to alternatives is anticipated if any alternative is in the prior art
description: When a claim covers several structures or compositions, either generically or as alternatives, the claim is deemed anticipated if any of the structures or compositions within the scope of the claim is known in the prior art.
guidance: Example: claim listing multiple year-date formats was anticipated by a system offsetting only two-digit formats (Brown v. 3M).

name: Exception A — Use extra references to prove the primary reference contains an enabled disclosure
description: Extra references and extrinsic evidence can be used to show that the primary reference has an enabled disclosure when the claimed composition or machine is disclosed identically by the reference.
guidance: If the primary reference teaches all claim elements but does not teach how to make or use them, other references that teach methods of making or demonstrating enablement may be cited to show the prior art placed the invention in the public's possession (In re Samour; In re Donohue). Motivation to combine is not required when the primary reference itself teaches all elements.

name: Exception B — Use extra references or extrinsic evidence to explain meaning of terms in the primary reference
description: Extrinsic evidence may be used to explain but not to expand the meaning of terms and phrases used in the reference relied upon as anticipatory of the claimed subject matter.
guidance: If the meaning of a claim/reference term cannot be determined from intrinsic evidence alone, extrinsic evidence (depositions, declarations, technical literature) may be consulted to ascertain how a person of ordinary skill would have understood the term at the relevant time (In re Baxter Travenol Labs.; Actelion v. Mylan; Teva v. Sandoz).

name: Reference that clearly names a species anticipates that species regardless of number of other species named
description: When the species is clearly named in a reference, the species claim is anticipated no matter how many other species are additionally named.
guidance: Comprehensiveness of listing does not negate that the specifically named compound is 'described' (Ex parte A; In re Sivaramakrishnan).

name: Generic disclosure anticipates a species only if the species can be 'at once envisaged'
description: A generic disclosure will anticipate a claimed species when a person of ordinary skill reading the reference would 'at once envisage' the claimed arrangement, combination, or specific compound from the disclosure.
guidance: Whether one of ordinary skill would 'at once envisage' depends on factual aspects including how large the genus is, whether substituent classes are limited, presence of preferred embodiments, and ability to draw the specific structural formula or write the name of each compound (Sanofi‑Synthelabo; Kennametal; In re Petering; In re Schauman). If the reference requires selecting and combining various alternatives from broad lists such that many permutations exist, anticipation will not be found.

name: When selection from lists is required, anticipation only if classes are sufficiently limited/well‑delineated
description: If arriving at the claimed compound requires selecting various substituents from lists of alternatives in a generic formula, anticipation can only be found if the classes of substituents are sufficiently limited or well delineated so that the specific compound is 'at once envisaged.'
guidance: Look to preferred embodiments and the number/limits of substituents to determine whether the limited class permits exact envisaging (Ex parte A; In re Petering; In re Schauman).

name: A specific prior art example within a claimed range anticipates the range
description: When a claim covers a range of values or compositions, the claim is anticipated if the prior art discloses one of the specific points within that claimed range.
guidance: Example: a prior-art data point falling within a claimed compositional range anticipates (Titanium Metals Corp. v. Banner; UCB v. Actavis Labs.).

name: Overlapping/touching prior‑art ranges anticipate only if disclosed with 'sufficient specificity'
description: If the prior art teaches a range that overlaps or touches the claimed range but provides no specific example within the claimed range, anticipation depends on whether the prior disclosure presents the claimed range with 'sufficient specificity' — a fact‑dependent inquiry.
guidance: Consider narrowness of claimed range, any evidence of criticality, predictability, and whether one of ordinary skill would expect material differences across the ranges (ClearValue; Atofina). If not sufficiently specific, examiner may use a combined 102/103 approach and must provide reasons for both anticipation and a reasoned statement regarding obviousness (Ex parte Lee). See MPEP §2144.05 for obviousness of ranges.

name: Nonanalogous art or teaching away does not defeat anticipation
description: Arguments that the alleged anticipatory prior art is 'nonanalogous art' or 'teaches away from the invention' are not germane to a rejection under section 102.
guidance: A reference may be directed to a different problem or field yet still anticipate if it explicitly or inherently discloses every claim limitation. Disparaging statements or teaching away in the reference do not negate that it discloses the claimed subject matter (Twin Disc; Celeritas; State Contracting & Eng'g; Upsher‑Smith Labs.; Atlas Powder Co.).

name: Examiner should be prepared to explain claim and prior art interpretations
description: Examiners should be prepared to explain how the applied prior art is being interpreted, how the claims are being interpreted, and how the applied art discloses each limitation of the claims for which the art is being relied upon.
guidance: Clear articulation of mapping between claim limitations and prior art elements helps productive discussion.

name: Submit proposed responses and amendments before interview when applicable
description: Where applicable, applicants should submit a proposed response in advance of the interview to allow examiners sufficient time to prepare and conduct a well organized interview.
guidance: Any proposed response should include all proposed amendments to specification, claims and drawings, citations to spec support for amendments, citations to reference portions to be discussed, additional evidence, and a brief summary of arguments. A fully 37 CFR 1.111-compliant submission is unnecessary prior to the interview.

name: Be thoroughly conversant with the case record
description: Both the examiner and the applicant should be thoroughly conversant with the specification, claims, relevant prior art, all grounds of rejection, relevant arguments and issues currently of record in the application.
guidance: Thorough familiarity is necessary to identify allowable subject matter and meaningfully advance prosecution.

name: Provide real-world examples to aid examiner understanding
description: Applicants should be prepared to identify 'real world' applications of the claimed invention to assist in enhancing the examiner's understanding of the claimed invention.
guidance: Concrete application examples can clarify claim scope and inventive concept for examiners.

name: Provide introductory summary when a new examiner joins
description: If an examiner of record participating in the interview is new to the case, at the beginning of the interview, applicant should provide the new examiner an introductory summary/discussion of the invention, referencing the claims, specification and figures, to the extent necessary.
guidance: A concise orientation brings new examiners up to speed and makes the interview productive (MPEP 713.01 V).

name: Identify specification support for proposed claim amendments
description: When proposing claim amendments, both the examiner and the applicant should identify support in the specification for the proposed claim amendments.
guidance: Explicitly linking amendments to spec support reduces later written-record problems and §112 issues.

name: Ensure mutual understanding of claim language and scope
description: Consider addressing claim language, semantics, conjunctions, punctuation, etc.; consider reading a claim out loud; consider diagramming the elements of the claim and their interrelationships to determine claim scope.
guidance: Practical techniques (reading aloud, diagramming) help parties converge on claim meaning and avoid misunderstandings.

name: Examples of suitable interview summary content
description: Suitable interview summary comments capture the thrust of issues/arguments raised in an interview using concrete references (example items include: applicant argued a reference combination does not render the invention obvious with pinpoint citations; applicant argued examiner's claim-term interpretation is unreasonably broad with specification citations; agreement that material incorporated by reference is necessary and applicant must amend specification; specific proposed amendment discussed with detailed edits and limitations noted).
guidance: Use precise statements with citations to specification pages/columns/lines and identify specific claim limitations, statutory bases (§112, §101, obviousness), and actions required. These examples illustrate the level of specificity required to be 'suitable' (see Example A list).

name: Examples of unsuitable interview summary content
description: Unsuitable interview summary comments are vague and do not capture the thrust of the issues/arguments (examples: 'Issues of Anticipation/Obviousness were discussed'; 'Agreement was (or was not) reached because the claims are found patentable (or unpatentable)'; generic restatements that do not identify specifics).
guidance: Avoid one-line or generic summaries that omit citations, specific claim language, or the nature of the dispute. The 'unsuitable' list provides anti-patterns to avoid in interview summaries.

name: ¶ 7.14.aia — Pre-AIA 102(g) Priority of Invention
description: (g)(1) during the course of an interference another inventor establishes priority that before such person’s invention the invention was made by such other inventor and not abandoned, suppressed or concealed; (g)(2) before such person’s invention the invention was made in this country by another inventor who had not abandoned, suppressed, or concealed it. Consider conception, reduction to practice, and reasonable diligence.
guidance: A rejection under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) is appropriate in an application/patent examined under the AIA only if the application/patent contains or contained a claim to an invention having an effective filing date (35 U.S.C.100(i)) before March 16, 2013 or a specific reference under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, or 365(c) to a patent/application that contains such a claim. Must be preceded by form paragraphs 7.07.aia and 7.08.aia as appropriate, or by 7.103. Insert appropriate bracketed material (claim numbers, whether clearly anticipated/anticipated, prior art relied upon).

name: ¶ 7.15.01.aia — Provisional Rejection, 35 U.S.C.102(a)(2) (copending app with common assignee/applicant/joint inventor)
description: Claim(s) [1] is/are provisionally rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) as being anticipated by copending Application No. [2] which has a common [3] with the instant application. The copending application would constitute prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) if published under 122(b) or patented under 151; rejection is based on presumption of future publication or patenting.
guidance: May be overcome by: (1) showing under 37 CFR 1.130(a) that subject matter in the copending application was obtained directly/indirectly from the inventor/joint inventor (102(b)(2)(A)); (2) showing under 37 CFR 1.130(b) of a prior public disclosure (102(b)(2)(B)); or (3) a statement under 35 U.S.C.102(b)(2)(C) establishing common ownership/assignment/joint research agreement. Must be preceded by 7.07.aia. This rejection may not be overcome by filing a terminal disclaimer (In re Bartfeld). Insert bracketed info (claims, application no., common relationship, explanation).

name: ¶ 7.15.02.aia — Rejection, 35 U.S.C.102(a)(2) (common assignee/applicant/joint inventor)
description: Claim(s) [1] is/are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) as being [2] by [3]. The applied reference has a common [4] with the instant application and, based upon the earlier effectively filed date of the reference, constitutes prior art under 102(a)(2).
guidance: This rejection may be overcome by: (1) a showing under 37 CFR 1.130(a) that the reference's subject matter was obtained from the inventor/joint inventor (102(b)(2)(A)); (2) a showing under 37 CFR 1.130(b) of a prior public disclosure (102(b)(2)(B)) if the same invention is not being claimed; or (3) a statement under 35 U.S.C.102(b)(2)(C) establishing common ownership/assignment/joint research agreement. Use only in AIA applications (filed on/after March 16, 2013) and must be preceded by 7.03.aia and 7.12.aia. If the reference issued/published before the effective filing date it also is applicable under 102(a)(1). Insert bracketed items (claim numbers, anticipated/clearly anticipated, prior art relied upon, common relationship). Address statutory double patenting (8.30–8.32) and nonstatutory double patenting (8.33–8.39) when relevant. Precedence by 7.06 required for priority to pre-March 16, 2013 filings.

name: ¶ 7.15.03.aia — Rejection, 35 U.S.C.102(a)(2) (no common assignee/inventor required)
description: Claim(s) [1] is/are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) as being [2] by [3].
guidance: Used to reject over a U.S. patent, U.S. patent application publication, or WIPO patent application publication with an earlier prior art date under 102(a)(2) where the reference is not required to have a common assignee or inventor. Use only for applications filed on/after March 16, 2013 examined under AIA 102/103 and precede with 7.03.aia and 7.12.aia as required. Insert bracketed items (claim numbers, anticipated/clearly anticipated with explanation, prior art).

name: ¶ 7.18.aia — Rejection, Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C.102(g)
description: Claim [1] rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) as being [2] by [3].
guidance: Use this form paragraph only for an application or patent being examined under the AIA if it contains or contained a claim to an invention having an effective filing date (35 U.S.C.100(i)) before March 16, 2013 or a specific reference under 120, 121, or 365(c) to any patent/application that contains such a claim. Must be preceded by 7.14.aia or 7.103. Insert bracketed items (claim numbers, anticipated/clearly anticipated with explanation, prior art relied upon).

name: AIA 35 U.S.C.102(b)(1)(A) — Grace Period Inventor-Originated Disclosure Exception
description: A disclosure which would otherwise qualify as prior art under 102(a)(1) is not prior art if the disclosure was (1) one year or less before the effective filing date of the claimed invention; and (2) by the inventor or a joint inventor, or by another who obtained the subject matter directly or indirectly from the inventor or joint inventor.
guidance: Whether a disclosure is inventor-originated requires case-by-case treatment depending on whether it is apparent from the disclosure itself or the application specification that it is inventor-originated. A disclosure is not prior art under 102(a)(1) if it: (1) was made one year or less before the effective filing date; (2) names the inventor or joint inventor as an author or inventor; and (3) does not name additional persons as authors on a printed publication or joint inventors on a patent. If the publication names additional authors/inventors beyond those in the application, it may not be apparent. Applicants may include a 37 CFR 1.77(b)(6) statement in the specification to identify grace period inventor-originated disclosures; the statement must convey the same information required in a 37 CFR 1.130(a) declaration. The Office provides a mechanism (affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.130) to establish that a disclosure is not prior art due to a 102(b) exception. The one-year grace period is extended to the next business day if it would otherwise end on a weekend or federal holiday.

name: AIA 35 U.S.C.102(b)(1)(B) — Inventor-Originated Prior Public Disclosure Exception
description: A disclosure which would otherwise qualify as prior art under 102(a)(1) is excepted as prior art if: (1) the disclosure was made one year or less before the effective filing date; and (2) the subject matter disclosed had been previously publicly disclosed by the inventor, a joint inventor, or another who obtained the subject matter directly or indirectly from the inventor or joint inventor.
guidance: The exception focuses on whether the 'subject matter' of the intervening disclosure had been previously publicly disclosed by the inventor/joint inventor (or someone who obtained it therefrom). There is no requirement that the mode of disclosure be the same; the previous disclosure need not be verbatim. However, the subject matter in the prior art relied upon must be the same 'subject matter' as previously publicly disclosed by the inventor — the exceptions do not apply if the only differences are insubstantial, trivial, or obvious. If an intervening disclosure includes both subject matter previously disclosed by the inventor and new subject matter, only the inventor-originated portions (e.g., A, B, C) are excepted; the new portions (e.g., D) remain prior art. Examples: species/genus distinctions — if inventor disclosed a species, a later publication of a genus that encompasses it may be excepted; converse may not. The exception's applicability is determined without comparing the subject matter to the claimed invention — it pertains to whether the intervening reference's subject matter had been previously publicly disclosed by the inventor. Applicants can establish applicability via affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.130 (see MPEP §2155.02/2155.03).

name: Office action when applicant's rebuttal insufficient
description: If, after evaluating the evidence, the examiner is still not convinced that the claimed invention is patentable, the next Office action should include a statement to that effect and identify the reason(s) (e.g., evidence of commercial success not convincing, the commercial success not related to the technology, etc.).
guidance: Identify specific reasons why proffered secondary evidence fails to overcome the prima facie case. See Demaco Corp. v. F. Von Langsdorff Licensing Ltd. and MPEP § 716.01; see MPEP § 2144.08 II.B. for guidance on sufficiency of rebuttal evidence.

name: Direct and indirect comparative tests are probative
description: Evidence of unexpected properties may be in the form of a direct or indirect comparison of the claimed invention with the closest prior art which is commensurate in scope with the claims.
guidance: See In re Boesch and MPEP §§ 716.02(d)-716.02(e). Proper comparative testing (commensurate in scope) can rebut prima facie obviousness; direct comparative testing often required to show unexpected results.

name: Intermediate patentability via end-product unexpected properties
description: The patentability of an intermediate may be established by unexpected properties of an end product when one of ordinary skill would reasonably ascribe to the claimed intermediate the 'contributing cause' for such unexpectedly superior activity or property.
guidance: Applicant must identify cause of the unexpectedly superior activity in the end product and establish a nexus between the intermediate and the end product (In re Magerlein).

name: Weighing unexpected and expected evidence
description: Evidence of unexpected results must be weighed against evidence supporting prima facie obviousness in making the final determination of obviousness of the claimed invention.
guidance: Unexpected properties must have significance equal to or greater than expected properties to rebut obviousness (In re May; In re Nolan; In re Eli Lilly). See MPEP § 716.01(d) on weighing evidence.

name: Unexpected results must be commensurate in scope with claims
description: The objective evidence of non-obviousness must be commensurate in scope with the claims which the evidence is offered to support; the showing must be reviewed to see if results occur over the entire claimed range.
guidance: Examples: In re Clemens (tests at only high 'elevated' temps insufficient when claims cover lower temps); In re Grasselli (tests limited to sodium not commensurate with broader claims).

name: Nonobviousness of a genus supported by species under circumstances
description: The nonobviousness of a broader claimed range or genus can be supported by evidence based on unexpected results from testing a narrower range or species if one of ordinary skill can determine a trend allowing reasonable extension of probative value.
guidance: See In re Kollman and In re Lindner for limits; limited exemplified species insufficient unless data show trend or extension is reasonable.

name: Affidavit/declaration must compare with closest prior art
description: An affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 must compare the claimed subject matter with the closest prior art to be effective to rebut a prima facie case of obviousness.
guidance: Comparison of claimed invention with each cited reference to determine number and relative importance of claim limitations usually yields the closest single prior art reference (In re Burckel; In re Merchant). Deviations from reference disclosures should be explained (In re Finley; In re Armstrong).

name: Commercial success requires nexus to claimed invention
description: An applicant asserting commercial success to support nonobviousness bears the burden of proof of establishing a nexus between the claimed invention and the evidence of commercial success.
guidance: PTO relies on applicant to provide hard evidence of commercial success and nexus (In re Huang; In re GPAC; In re Paulsen). Nexus means a factually and legally sufficient connection (Demaco).

name: Affidavit language alone insufficient to show nexus
description: An affidavit or declaration attributing commercial success to a product 'constructed according to the disclosure and claims' does not establish nexus because it lacks evidence that sold product corresponds to the claimed invention.
guidance: See Ex parte Standish: provide concrete evidence linking claimed features to commercial success.

name: Commercial success must be derived from claimed invention, not marketing or extraneous factors
description: Determine that alleged commercial success is directly derived from the invention in a marketplace where consumers choose on objective principles, and not the result of heavy promotion, advertising, brand loyalty, favorable licensing conditions, or other business events.
guidance: Conclusive statements attributing sales to the invention are little weight (In re Mageli; In re Noznick). Inventor's opinion insufficient to demonstrate nexus (In re Huang). Consider alternative explanations such as advertising, market shifts, licensing economics (Pentec; EWP Corp.; Hybritech example where advertising still allowed nexus).

name: Commercial success must flow from functions/advantages disclosed or inherent
description: Commercial success must flow from the functions and advantages disclosed or inherent in the specification; success of embodiments may not be attributable to modifications by others.
guidance: Evidence must show success ties to claimed features or inherent properties (In re Vamco Machine & Tool).

name: Application must be in condition for examination at filing (conditions for examination)
description: The application must be in condition for examination at the time of filing. This means the application must include specified items (see list).
guidance: Required items include: (1) basic filing fee, search fee, and examination fee (37 CFR 1.16); (2) application size fee if >100 sheets (37 CFR 1.16(s)); (3) an executed oath or declaration (37 CFR 1.63); (4) a specification (37 CFR 1.52) containing a description (37 CFR 1.71) and claims (37 CFR 1.75); (5) a title and an abstract (37 CFR 1.72); (6) drawings (37 CFR 1.84); (7) electronic submissions of sequence listings, large tables, or computer listings via EFS in ASCII text if applicable (37 CFR 1.821(c)/(e), 1.96); (8) foreign priority claim under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) identified in the executed oath/declaration or application data sheet if applicable; (9) domestic benefit claims under 35 U.S.C. 119(e),120,121, or 365(c) in compliance with 37 CFR 1.78 (specific reference placement rules and translation statement for benefit to non-English provisional applications) if applicable; (10) English translation and accuracy statement plus processing fee if specification in non-English (37 CFR 1.52(d), 1.17(i)); (11) no preliminary amendments present on the filing date; and (12) no petition under 37 CFR 1.47 for a non-signing inventor. For design applications, comply with 37 CFR 1.151-1.154. Applicant should also provide a suggested classification by class/subclass on the transmittal letter, petition, or application data sheet (37 CFR 1.76(b)(3)).

name: Updated preexamination search and accelerated examination support documents required for claim amendments
description: For any amendments to the claims (including any new claim) that is not encompassed by the preexamination search and accelerated examination support documents previously filed, applicant is required to provide updated preexamination search and accelerated examination support documents that encompass the amended or new claims at the time of filing the amendment.
guidance: Failure to provide such updated support documents at time of filing the amendment will cause the amendment to be treated as not fully responsive and not to be entered (see MPEP § 708.02(a) subsection VIII.D.). Form paragraphs 7.70.AE and 7.71.AE must be included in every Office action (other than notice of allowance) for applicable special-status applications.

name: Prioritized Examination (37 CFR 1.102(e)) requirements and limitations
description: A request for prioritized examination under 37 CFR 1.102(e) must comply with the paragraph and be accompanied by the prioritized examination fee under § 1.17(c), the processing fee under § 1.17(i), and, if not already paid, the publication fee under § 1.18(d).
guidance: An application for prioritized examination may not contain or be amended to contain more than four independent claims, more than thirty total claims, or any multiple dependent claim. Prioritized examination will not be accorded to international applications that have not entered the national stage under 35 U.S.C. 371, design applications, reissue applications, provisional applications, or reexamination proceedings. A request for prioritized examination may be filed with an original utility or plant nonprovisional application that is complete as defined by § 1.51(b), with any fees due under § 1.16 paid on filing. If the application is a utility application, it must be filed via the Office's electronic filing system. The request for prioritized examination must be present upon filing of the application and must also comply with paragraph (e)(1) or (e)(2).

name: Definition: behaviors characterizing a 'patent troll'
description: A party that does one or more of the following: purchases a patent (often from a bankrupt firm) and then sues another company claiming infringement; enforces patents against purported infringers without intending to manufacture the patented product or supply the patented service; enforces patents but has no manufacturing or research base; focuses solely on enforcing patent rights; or asserts patent infringement claims against non-copiers or against a large industry of non-copiers.
guidance: The term is pejorative and definitions are contested; related labels include patent holding company (PHC), patent monetization entity (PME), patent assertion entity (PAE), and non-practicing entity (NPE). Whether an entity is called a 'troll' can depend on its conduct and public perception.

name: Bad-faith infringement-threat indicators (Vermont Consumer Protection Act)
description: Vermont's law indicates bad faith where threat letters show lack of specificity of the alleged infringement, settlement demands or damage claims that include excessive licensing fees, and unreasonably short deadlines for payment.
guidance: The Vermont statute gives recipients of threat letters the right to counter-sue in state court; similar state statutes or enforcement actions (e.g., FTC settlement vs MPHJ) can impose penalties for deceptive or abusive demand-letter campaigns.

name: Risk indicator: software and business-method patents are especially vulnerable
description: Software patents (and business-method patents) are described as particularly prone to abuse because software is inherently conceptual and claim scope can be hard to define; statistics show software patents litigate at higher rates.
guidance: Practitioners should treat such patents as higher risk for assertion and heightened scrutiny when clearing freedom-to-operate.

name: Defensive tactic: patent infringement insurance
description: Insurance products are available to help protect companies from the cost of defending against infringement claims.
guidance: Insurance can manage financial risk though coverage terms and costs vary.

name: Policy recommendation: clearer patents and higher novelty/non-obviousness standards
description: Government reports recommend policies to foster clearer patents with a high standard of novelty and non-obviousness, reduce disparity in litigation costs between patent owners and technology users, and increase the adaptability of the system to new technologies and business models.
guidance: Stronger examination standards, clearer claim drafting, and litigation-cost reforms are proposed levers to reduce abusive assertions.

name: Infringement under 35 U.S.C. § 271(f)(2)
description: To show infringement under Section 271(f)(2), the plaintiff must prove each of the following more likely than not: (1) the defendant actually supplied the components from the United States into a foreign country or caused them to be supplied from the United States to a foreign country; (2) the defendant knew or should have known that the components were especially made or adapted for use in a product that infringes a claim of the patent; (3) those components have no substantial non-infringing use; and (4) the defendant intended for the components to be combined into that product.
guidance: It is not necessary to find that the components actually were combined into an infringing product, only that the defendant intended the components to be combined into a product that would have infringed the patent if combined in the United States. Relevant authorities: 35 U.S.C. § 271(f)(2); WesternGeco v. ION, Microsoft v. AT&T, Cardiac Pacemakers v. St. Jude, Waymark v. Porta Sys., Rotec v. Mitsubishi. (Use these elements when instructing the jury.)

name: Defendant’s burden to prove invalidity (clear and convincing evidence)
description: The defendant must prove by clear and convincing evidence that each asserted claim is invalid.
guidance: This burden never changes regardless of whether a prior art reference was considered during prosecution. Practice note: if the PTO did not have all material facts, the challenger’s burden may be easier to sustain and it may be appropriate to instruct the jury to evaluate whether evidence is materially new and consider that when determining whether invalidity is proven by clear and convincing evidence. Authorities: Microsoft v. i4i; Sciele Pharma v. Lupin.

name: Invalidity of independent vs dependent claims
description: Independent claims stand alone and do not refer to other claims; dependent claims refer to and include all elements of the claim(s) to which they refer plus additional elements. The jury must evaluate invalidity on a claim-by-claim basis.
guidance: Even if an independent claim is invalid, dependent claims are not automatically invalid — evaluate separately. However, if you find a dependent claim is invalid, then you must find the independent claim from which it depends is also invalid. Provide examples identifying differences between specific independent and dependent claims. Citations: Comaper v. Antec, Callaway v. Acushnet, Ormco v. Align Tech.

name: Person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA) for invalidity analysis
description: Invalidity is determined from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art in the field of the claimed invention as of the time of the invention or the effective filing date.
guidance: Instruct the jury on how to characterize the POSITA (education, experience, typical skills) because that perspective governs what the POSITA would understand from prior art when assessing anticipation or obviousness. Cite 35 U.S.C. § 103; KSR; Continental Can v. Monsanto.

name: Anticipation — general rule
description: To prove anticipation, the defendant must show by clear and convincing evidence that the claimed invention is not new because each element in the claim is present in a single prior art item and arranged/combined in the same way as recited in the claim.
guidance: You may not combine two or more items of prior art to find anticipation. In determining whether elements are present, consider what a POSITA would have understood from reviewing the particular prior art reference. If parties dispute whether an item is prior art, instruct accordingly. Cite numerous Fed. Cir. authorities and practice notes on inherency where applicable.

name: Prior public knowledge (pre-AIA)
description: A claim is invalid if the invention defined in the claim was publicly known by others in the United States before the invention by the patentee (pre-AIA §102(a) context).
guidance: If there is a factual dispute about date of invention or priority date, instruct the jury on how to determine cutoff dates. Cite pre-AIA statutory sections and relevant cases (e.g., Minn. Mining v. Chemque, Woodland Trust).

name: Prior public use (pre-AIA) — definition and factors
description: A claim is invalid if the invention was publicly used by others in the United States before the relevant cutoff date. A public use requires (1) accessibility to the public or commercial exploitation in the U.S., and (2) readiness for patenting.
guidance: Consider factors: nature of public activity, public access, confidentiality obligations on observers, commercial exploitation (even if specifics kept secret), testing/experimentation circumstances, absence of concealment. Secret use by a third party is not public unless public or employees had access. If pre-AIA §102(b) is at issue, instruct that readiness for patenting requires reduction to practice or sufficiently detailed drawings/descriptions enabling a POSITA to make or use the invention. Cite Pfaff, Barry v. Medtronic, Clock Spring, and others.

name: Prior public use (AIA) — worldwide public use
description: Under the AIA, a claim is invalid if the claimed invention was in public use anywhere in the world before the effective filing date.
guidance: Factors similar to pre-AIA public use apply (public access, confidentiality, testing circumstances). Commercial exploitation anywhere in the world may qualify even if the specifics of the invention were kept secret. Invention must also have been ready for patenting (reduction to practice or adequate descriptions). Cite 35 U.S.C. §102(a)(1) and practice notes.

name: Printed publication as prior art
description: A claim is invalid if the invention was described in a printed publication (maintained in tangible form) that was sufficiently accessible to persons interested in the subject matter before the relevant cutoff date.
guidance: ‘Printed publication’ includes printed pages, electronic files, microfilm, photographs, internet publications, photocopies, issued patents, and published patent applications as of their publication date. Accessibility means persons interested and ordinarily skilled exercising reasonable diligence could locate it. The disclosure must be enabling (complete enough to enable a POSITA to use the invention without undue experimentation). Cite 35 U.S.C. §102(a)/(b) (pre-AIA) and §§102(a)(1)/(a)(2) (AIA), and related cases. Include practice-note instruction on accessibility when disputed.

name: Prior invention (pre-AIA) — earlier inventor by others in U.S.
description: A claim is invalid if the invention was invented by another person in the United States before the patentee (pre-AIA §102(a)/(g) context). The defendant must show by clear and convincing evidence that (1) the third party reduced to practice a product/method with all claim features before the patentee’s invention, or (2) the third party conceived first and exercised reasonable diligence to later reduce to practice.
guidance: The defendant must also prove the prior product/method was sufficiently developed that a POSITA would recognize it would work for its intended purpose. The defense may be negated if the prior invention was abandoned, suppressed, or concealed. If priority of invention is submitted to the jury additional instructions on conception, reduction to practice, and diligence are required. Cite Teva v. AstraZeneca, Rosco v. Mirror Lite, Dow Chem. v. Astro-Valcour, and related authorities.

name: Prior patent as prior art (pre-AIA)
description: A claim is invalid if the invention was disclosed in a prior patent issued before the applicable cutoff date (pre-AIA context).
guidance: If anticipation or obviousness is based on a prior filing date (e.g., earlier-filed patent application), use the specific instructions addressing prior-filed applications and effective filing dates (see Section 6.8 cross-reference). Provide factual identification of the prior patent(s) admitted into evidence and relevant dates.

name: Burden of proof for internet disclosure (Netherlands civil procedure)
description: Under the Netherlands Code of Civil Procedure (Article 177) the burden of proof that information was disclosed on the Internet rests with the party that makes the claim; that party must submit sufficient evidence.
guidance: Claimant must present documentary/evidentiary support (prints, server logs, etc.) to establish online disclosure.

name: Drawings required when invention admits representation
description: Drawings are required by statute to be furnished by applicants in all cases wherein the invention admits of representation by drawings.
guidance: Statutory requirement is only that they be signed by applicant or attorney-in-fact, but Patent Office rules require drawings to show every feature of the invention covered by the claims. For improvements on old machines, drawings must exhibit the invention itself disconnected from the old structure and also another view showing so much of the old structure as will suffice to show the connection. Rules describe numerous other characteristics which must be carefully followed to secure favorable action.

name: Right to amend specifications and statutory notice on rejection
description: The right to amend applications is of great value; although not expressly established by statute originally, statutes (since 1870 and continuing) require that whenever any claim is rejected the Commissioner should notify the applicant and furnish information useful in judging the propriety of altering his specification.
guidance: The present statute on the subject is substantially identical with the 1870 provision: rejection triggers notice and information to assist the applicant in considering amendment.

name: Handling a matter without adequate preparation (37 C.F.R. § 10.77(b))
description: A practitioner shall not handle a legal matter without preparation adequate in the circumstances.
guidance: Examples of inadequate preparation: failing to produce sufficient evidence to substantiate claimed mailings to the PTO; failing to supply adequate evidence in support of a petition for revival; filing informal status enquiries instead of required formal petitions to revive applications.

name: Dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(4))
description: A practitioner shall not engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation.
guidance: Specific examples: falsely representing to the PTO or clients that responses, amendments, or payments were mailed/received; falsely claiming not to have received Notices of Allowance or other PTO communications. Such false statements to the PTO or clients support discipline under this provision.

name: Reissue oath/declaration must state patent is wholly or partly inoperative or invalid
description: The reissue oath/declaration filed with this application is defective because it fails to contain the statement(s) required under 37 CFR 1.175 as to applicant's belief that the original patent is wholly or partly inoperative or invalid.
guidance: Use when applicant fails to allege that the original patent is inoperative or invalid and/or fails to state the reason (defective specification/drawing or claiming more/less than the right). In the Office action, point out the specific defect and follow with form paragraph 14.14.

name: Rejection — 35 U.S.C. 251: Broadened claims after two years
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 251 as being broadened in a reissue application filed outside the two year statutory period.
guidance: A claim is broader in scope than the original claims if it contains within its scope any conceivable product or process which would not have infringed the original patent; broadened if broader in any one respect even though narrower in others. Identify and explain claim limitations that broaden scope. See MPEP §§ 706.03(x) and 1412.03.

name: Rejection — 35 U.S.C. 251: Broadened claims filed by assignee
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 251 as being improperly broadened in a reissue application made and sworn to by the assignee. The application for reissue may be made and sworn to by the assignee of the entire interest only if the application does not seek to enlarge the scope of the claims of the original patent or (for reissue applications filed on or after September 16, 2012) the application for the original patent was filed by the assignee of the entire interest under 37 CFR 1.46.
guidance: A claim is broader in scope if it contains any conceivable product/process not covered by the original patent. Identify limitations that broaden scope and explain. See MPEP §§ 706.03(x) and 1412.03.

name: Rejection — 35 U.S.C. 251: New matter added to patent
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 251 as being based upon new matter added to the patent for which reissue is sought. The added material which is not supported by the prior patent is as follows: [2]
guidance: In bracket 2, provide page and line numbers and explanation. Also make a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (pre‑AIA 112, first paragraph) if new matter is added to claims or specification affecting claims. If new matter added to specification not affecting claims, make an objection under 35 U.S.C. 132 using form paragraph 7.28.

name: Amendments to reissue must comply with 37 CFR 1.173(b)
description: Applicant is notified that any subsequent amendment to the specification and/or claims must comply with 37 CFR 1.173(b). In addition, for reissue applications filed before September 16, 2012, when any substantive amendment is filed in the reissue application, which amendment otherwise places the reissue application in condition for allowance, a supplemental oath/declaration will be required. See MPEP § 1414.01.
guidance: Use in first Office action to advise proper manner of making amendments and need to file supplemental oath/declaration before allowance (for pre‑2012 filings). Improper amendments will be called out with a shortened statutory period for reply (one month or thirty days, whichever longer).

name: Rejection — Pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 251: No error without deceptive intention (external knowledge)
description: Claims [1] rejected under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 251 because this application was filed before September 16, 2012 and error 'without any deceptive intention' has not been established. In view of the judicial determination in [2] of [3] on the part of applicant, a conclusion that any error was 'without deceptive intention' cannot be supported. [4]
