guidance: Use to point out judicial determinations of fraud/inequitable conduct/violation of duty of disclosure. Provide citation/location in opinion where determination is set forth. Do not use in applications filed on or after Sept. 16, 2012.

name: Rejection — Pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 251: No error without deceptive intention (evidence in application)
description: Claims [1] rejected under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 251 because this application was filed before September 16, 2012 and error 'without any deceptive intention' has not been established. In view of the reply filed on [2], a conclusion that any error was 'without deceptive intention' cannot be supported. [3]
guidance: Use when admissions or evidence in the application's record indicate fraud/inequitable conduct. Admissions must be explicit and unequivocal. Do not use in applications filed on or after Sept. 16, 2012.

name: Terminal disclaimer directed to particular claim(s) (not acceptable)
description: It is directed to a particular claim or claims, which is not acceptable, since 'the disclaimer must be of a terminal portion of the term of the entire [patent or] patent to be granted.' See MPEP § 1490.
guidance: Must be preceded by form paragraphs 14.24/14.25 AND 14.26. Provide example of proper terminal disclaimer language using form paragraphs 14.27.04.fti or 14.27.04.1.

name: Recapture prohibition in reissue (impermissible recapture)
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 251 as being an impermissible recapture of broadened claimed subject matter surrendered in the application for the patent upon which the present reissue is based. A broadening aspect is present in the reissue which was not present in the application for patent. The record shows that the broadening aspect relates to claimed subject matter that applicant previously surrendered during prosecution.
guidance: Explain specifics why recapture exists, omitted/broadened claim limitations providing the 'broadening aspect', and where in the original application the narrowed claim scope was presented/argued to obviate a rejection/objection. See MPEP § 1412.02 and cited case law (Greenliant, Mostafazadeh, North American Container, Pannu, Hester, etc.).

name: Meaning of 'Related but Distinct' inventions
description: Related inventions are those disclosed as connected in design, operation, or effect (e.g., combination and subcombination, process and product). Related inventions are 'distinct' if the inventions as claimed are not connected in at least one of design, operation, or effect and at least one invention is PATENTABLE (novel and nonobvious) OVER THE OTHER.
guidance: Distinctness may require a two-way test in some situations (see MPEP § 806.05(c) and § 806.05(j)). Decisions use the terms with varying meanings—read carefully.

name: When restriction is proper (overall criterion)
description: Restriction is proper only if claims can support separate patents and the claimed inventions are either independent or distinct.
guidance: If search and examination of all claims can be made without serious burden, the examiner must examine them on the merits even if they include claims to independent or distinct inventions.

name: Two specific criteria for restriction between patentably distinct inventions
description: (A) The inventions must be independent or distinct as claimed; and (B) There would be a serious search and/or examination burden on the examiner if restriction is not required.
guidance: Both criteria must be demonstrated to support a restriction requirement; see MPEP § 803.02 and § 808.

name: Rejoinder of process claims upon allowance of product
description: When claims to a product and to a process of making and/or using the product are presented, applicant may be required to elect product or process; if applicant elects product and the product claim(s) become allowable, withdrawn process claims that depend from or otherwise require all the limitations of the allowable product claim will be considered for rejoinder.
guidance: All claims to a nonelected process invention must depend from or otherwise require all limitations of the allowable product claim for rejoinder to occur. Upon rejoinder, the restriction requirement between elected product and rejoined process(es) will be withdrawn. Preserve 35 U.S.C. 121 rights by not canceling nonelected claims before rejoinder occurs.

name: When examiner should not invite an election
description: Examiner should not invite applicant to elect any group of species that would clearly be rejectable as an improper Markush grouping or under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) if presented in a separate claim.
guidance: Do not require provisional election between species that are not patentably distinct or when no serious burden exists.

name: Determining When Subject Matter Was Effectively Filed Under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(d)
description: A U.S. patent, U.S. patent application publication, or WIPO published application is prior art under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) with respect to any subject matter described in the document as of either its actual filing date or the filing date of a prior application to which a priority or benefit claim is made.
guidance: A document is 'entitled to claim' priority/benefit if it: (1) contains a priority/benefit claim to the prior application; (2) was filed within the applicable filing period (copending or within 12 months as applicable); and (3) has a common inventor or same applicant. For 102(d) prior art purposes, the Office need not evaluate whether any claim is actually entitled to priority/benefit under 35 U.S.C. 119/120/121/365/386. A prior-filed application relied upon must describe the subject matter but need not meet 35 U.S.C. 112(a) enablement. The AIA eliminates the Hilmer doctrine; foreign priority dates (earliest such application that describes the subject matter) can make a U.S. patent document effectively filed earlier.

name: Prior Art Exception Under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(B) (Inventor or Inventor-Originated Prior Public Disclosure Exception to 102(a)(2))
description: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(B) provides that a U.S. patent document which would otherwise qualify as prior art under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) may be disqualified as prior art if the subject matter disclosed had been previously publicly disclosed by the inventor, a joint inventor, or another who obtained the subject matter directly or indirectly from the inventor or joint inventor, before the date the subject matter relied upon was effectively filed.
guidance: The exception focuses on the 'subject matter' previously publicly disclosed; there is no requirement that mode of disclosure be the same or verbatim. If inventor previously disclosed A,B,C and intervening U.S. patent document discloses A,B,C,D, only D is available as prior art. Genus/species examples apply as in 102(b)(1)(B). Determination of applicability does not involve comparing the claimed invention to either disclosure; it concerns whether the intervening document's subject matter was previously publicly disclosed by the inventor (or person who obtained it from the inventor). See MPEP §§2155.02 and 2155.03 for affidavits/declarations.

name: Exceptions to the disclaimer (situations where owner does not disclaim the terminal part)
description: "In making the above disclaimer, the owner does not disclaim the terminal part of the term of any patent granted on the instant application that would extend to the expiration date of the full statutory term ... in the event that said prior patent later: expires for failure to pay a maintenance fee; is held unenforceable; is found invalid by a court of competent jurisdiction; is statutorily disclaimed in whole or terminally disclaimed under 37 CFR 1.321; has all claims canceled by a reexamination certificate; is reissued; or is in any manner terminated prior to the expiration of its full statutory term as presently shortened by any terminal disclaimer."
guidance: List of seven specific events that, if later occurring to the prior patent, mean the terminal disclaimer will not bar extension of term to the full statutory expiration. The form requires these exceptions to be explicitly acknowledged.

name: Described-but-unclaimed matters in use cannot be claimed after unreasonable delay
description: Where matters have been described but not claimed in the original patent, and have gone into use by others, they cannot be claimed in a re-issue after unreasonable delay.
guidance: If an inventor described subject matter in the specification but omitted it from the claims, and third parties have used that matter, the inventor may be barred from later claiming it by reissue if there has been an unreasonable delay. (Cases cited: Wooster v. Handy, Brainard v. Cramme, etc.)

name: No fixed statute of limitation; 'reasonable time' standard governs delay
description: There is no precise limit of time for applying for reissue; the amendment must be made within a 'reasonable time' determined by the courts from all circumstances.
guidance: Complex specifications and ambiguous claims may justify greater indulgence. Courts assess whether delay was avoidable and whether it prejudiced others; unreasonably long or avoidable delay can preclude reissue.

name: Reissue may be made in any form necessary to secure the actual invention
description: When an amendment by reissue is allowable it can be made in any form and to any extent necessary to render the patent effective for the original invention.
guidance: The language of the specification can be varied indefinitely; new claims may be added or old claims divided and restated to achieve protection for the invention, so long as no new matter is introduced that was absent from the original description.

name: Reissue must not introduce patentable matter absent from original description
description: New patentable matter not substantially indicated by the original specification may not be introduced by reissue.
guidance: Reissue cannot be used to claim an invention that was not present in the original disclosure (in fact and function). Such additions render the reissue invalid to the extent they introduce new matter.

name: New claims may be added from the old specification if omission was by mistake and patentee not estopped
description: A re-issue may contain new claims based on the old specification if such claims were omitted by mistake and the patentee has not been estopped from amending.
guidance: Courts allow adding claims that were present in the original disclosure but omitted by mistake, provided there has been no estoppel or prejudice to others; citations include Combined Patents Co. v. Lloyd and Swift v. Whisen.

name: Reissue cannot change the invention by narrowing one claim and expanding another
description: A re-issue cannot change the invention by narrowing a claim in one part and expanding it in another.
guidance: Reissue must be consistent overall; selectively narrowing and expanding can amount to changing the invention and render the reissue improper. (Gage v. Kellogg cited.)

name: Unwarranted expansion of claims in reissue is void
description: A re-issue that unwarrantably expands the claims is void.
guidance: Attempting to broaden claim scope beyond what the original patent permitted (especially to cover prior art or third‑party use) will invalidate the reissue or the expanded claims. (Uoe v. Knap and others.)

name: Original cannot be broadened to include matter anticipated by prior devices
description: The original patent cannot be broadened by re-issue so as to include matter anticipated by prior devices.
guidance: If broadened claims read on prior art (matter anticipated), the re-issue is improper. Courts will not permit reissue to reach subject matter anticipatory of prior devices. (Ives & Millers, Hartford Spring & Axle Co. cited.)

name: Inexact reissue claims that naturally expand the invention are void
description: An inexact claim in the re-issue which, if naturally construed, would expand the invention is void.
guidance: Claims in the reissue must be precise and not ambiguous in a way that would enlarge the patent monopoly beyond what the original disclosure justified. (Tyler v. Galloway cited.)

name: Reissue cannot create a new and substantially different invention or produce different effects
description: A re-issue cannot contain any change in the original specification or claim whereby a new and substantially different invention results, or different effects are produced.
guidance: If the claimed changes would result in a different inventive concept or new operative effects, the reissue is invalid. (Salamander Felting Co. v. Haven cited.)

name: Divisional reissues must be confined to inventions indicated in the original specification and be patentable separately
description: Reissue divisions must be for distinct inventions embraced in the original, not merely different applications of the same invention under the same genus; each division must claim a complete invention in itself.
guidance: Divisions should reflect separable, patentable subject matter that was indicated in the original disclosure; mere variants or alternative applications within the same genus do not justify separate divisional reissues. (Ex parte Herr, Ex parte Sexton, etc.)

name: Specification and claims of reissue may differ in wording if they claim nothing beyond what was present in the original (in fact and function)
description: The specification and claims of the re-issue may differ from those of the original provided they claim nothing except what was present, both in fact and function, either in the original drawings or model.
guidance: Different language in the reissue is acceptable so long as the reissued claims are consistent with the original disclosure and do not introduce substantively new subject matter. (Stephenson v. Second Avenue R.R. Co. cited.)

name: Divisional reissues may each claim the part in separate condition and in combination with others
description: Each reissue division may claim its own part in its separate condition and also as connected with the others; one division may describe the whole invention to explain the claimed portion.
guidance: Divisions should enable public understanding of the separated device's application; describing the whole machine for context is permissible, but that description does not expand what the patent actually covers beyond the claims.

name: Complete file history reflecting reasons for allowance
description: The file history should clearly reflect the reasons why the application was allowed and should be complete so the record 'speaks for itself.'
guidance: Examiners must ensure the file history is complete to facilitate evaluation of patent scope and strength and to help avoid or simplify subsequent litigation. See MPEP § 1302.14, subsection I. When allowing a claim based on an interpretation not readily apparent from prosecution, set forth in the reasons for allowance the claim interpretation applied (especially after an interview). Ensure reasons do not place unwarranted interpretations, broad or narrow, upon the claims.

name: Make of record specific 35 U.S.C. 112 issues discussed in interviews
description: Examples of 35 U.S.C. 112 issues that should be made of record after an interview include why a term is or is not sufficiently clear, inconsistency with the specification, whether 112(f) is invoked and corresponding structure identification, and any claim amendments discussed.
guidance: Document why a term is/is not clear; why it is/is not inconsistent with the specification; whether it invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre‑AIA 112, sixth paragraph) and, if so, identify corresponding structure/material/acts in the specification; record any claim amendments proposed to resolve ambiguities.

name: Specification should serve as a glossary; claim terms need clear support/antecedent basis
description: The specification should ideally serve as a glossary to the claim terms so that the examiner and the public can clearly ascertain the meaning of the claim terms; claim terms must find clear support or antecedent basis in the specification per 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1).
guidance: If the specification does not provide needed support or antecedent basis, object under 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1) and require applicant to amend the description or claims (without introducing new matter). Glossaries in the spec are a helpful device. See MPEP § 608.01(o) and § 2181, subsection IV.

name: Avoid internal inconsistencies between claims and specification or among claims
description: A claim may be indefinite when a conflict or inconsistency between the claimed subject matter and the specification disclosure renders the scope of the claim uncertain, or when inconsistencies among claims render scope uncertain.
guidance: Examine for internal inconsistency examples (cases cited such as In re Cohn, In re Anderson, and Tvngo Ltd. v. LG Elecs.). Dependent claims that contradict independent claims can make the disputed phrase indefinite. Consider specification, other claims, and prosecution history to clarify meaning.

name: Meaning of every term should be apparent at filing
description: The meaning of every term used in a claim should be apparent from the prior art or from the specification and drawings at the time the application is filed; claim language must not be 'ambiguous, vague, incoherent, opaque, or otherwise unclear.'
guidance: Claims are given the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification during examination. Applicants may use new terminology, but terms must be made clear and precise so the metes and bounds of the claimed invention can be ascertained. When the specification states the intended meaning, examine using that definition (cases: Packard, Morris, Prater, Zletz).

name: Balance requirement for clarity with language and science limitations
description: The requirement for clarity and precision must be balanced with the limitations of the language and the science; claims should be as precise as the subject matter permits.
guidance: New terms are permissible and often desirable, particularly for evolving technologies. If language is not as precise as subject matter permits, the examiner should provide reasons for indefiniteness and suggest alternatives that would avoid rejection (Packard). The standard is reasonable precision in context.

name: Terms used contrary to ordinary meaning must be redefined in the written description
description: If an applicant uses a term contrary to its ordinary meaning, the written description must clearly redefine the term so as to put one skilled in the art on notice of the redefinition.
guidance: Applicant may act as own lexicographer, but the written description must clearly redefine the claim term (cases: Process Control Corp. v. HydReclaim; Hormone Research Foundation v. Genentech). Until redefinition is clear, a 112(b) rejection is appropriate; consult technical dictionaries where relevant (MPEP § 2111.01).

name: Reference to a variable object or undefined positional relationships may render claim indefinite
description: Claims that define limitations by reference to an object whose relationship is not sufficiently defined (e.g., positional relationships to a user of unspecified height) may be indefinite.
guidance: When elements have two or more plausible constructions and the examiner cannot ascertain positional relationships, the claim may be indefinite (cases: Ex parte Miyazaki, Ex parte Brummer). By contrast, 'so dimensioned as to be insertable through the space between the doorframe of an automobile and one of the seats' was definite (Orthokinetics).

name: Approximations like 'about' must be interpreted in context
description: Determining the range encompassed by the term 'about' requires consideration of the context in the specification and claims; 'about' may be definite or indefinite depending on the disclosure and prior art.
guidance: Examples: a stretch rate 'exceeding about 10% per second' was definite because measurable; 'at least about' was held indefinite where close prior art and no guidance existed (W.L. Gore; Amgen v. Chugai). Examine whether the specification gives guidance to measure the approximation.

name: 'Similar' and 'type' can render claims indefinite
description: Use of terms like 'similar' (e.g., 'or similar apparatus') and the addition of 'type' to otherwise definite expressions can extend scope and render the claim indefinite if intended scope is unclear.
guidance: Examples: 'similar apparatus' was held indefinite (Ex parte Kristensen); 'ZSM-5-type' aluminosilicate zeolites held indefinite where 'type' was unclear and dependent claims fell outside the genus (Ex parte Attig).

name: Subjective terms require an objective standard in the specification
description: When a subjective term is used in the claim (e.g., 'aesthetically pleasing', 'comparable', 'superior'), the examiner should determine whether the specification supplies an objective standard for measuring the term; otherwise the claim may be indefinite.
guidance: Claim scope cannot depend solely on the unrestrained subjective opinion of an individual. If no objective boundary is provided, rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) is appropriate (Datamize; Interval Licensing). Applicants may overcome by amending or providing evidence that PHOSITA can ascertain the meaning.

name: Avoid putting both narrow and broader numerical ranges in the same claim
description: Use of a narrow numerical range that falls within a broader range in the same claim may render the claim indefinite when the boundaries are not discernible (e.g., 'between 45 and 78 C, preferably between 50 and 60 C').
guidance: Preferences and examples belong in the specification or in dependent claims. If it is unclear whether the narrower range is a limitation, make a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b). Dependent claims narrowing a range from an independent claim are acceptable.

name: Open-ended numerical ranges should be analyzed for definiteness
description: Open-ended ranges (e.g., 'at least 20% sodium') must be checked for internal consistency with other claim language (e.g., dependent claims that sum to 100% excluding the 'at least' component).
guidance: Analyze percent bases and inclusivity. A theoretical >100% content across components is not per se indefinite. Consider whether the claim meaning is clear in context (cases: In re Kroekel, In re Kirsch, In re Mochel).

name: Examples or preferences ('for example', 'such as') belong in the specification, not claims
description: Description of examples or preferences should be in the specification rather than the claims; if stated in claims, they may lead to confusion over intended scope.
guidance: The mere use of 'such as' or 'for example' in a claim does not by itself render it indefinite, but many fact-specific examples (listed in MPEP) have been held indefinite. Use caution and analyze whether the example in the claim is being used as a limitation.

name: Provide antecedent basis for claim terms; avoid unclear 'said'/'the' references
description: A claim is indefinite when it contains words or phrases whose meaning is unclear because there is no earlier recitation or it is unclear which previous element is being referenced (lack of antecedent basis).
guidance: If 'said lever' or 'the lever' lacks earlier recitation, the claim may be indefinite. However, failure to provide explicit antecedent basis does not always render a claim indefinite if the scope is reasonably ascertainable by PHOSITA (Ex parte Porter). Inherent components have antecedent basis in recited elements (Bose v. JBL). Examiners should suggest corrections to antecedent problems.

name: When only nominal damages are recoverable
description: Nominal damages are the only recovery when the plaintiff fails to prove an established license fee or depreciation in value of exclusive use, or when the proof does not establish a proper measure of actual damages. Nominal damages are also proper in several specific situations enumerated by the courts.
guidance: Situations giving rise to only nominal damages include: (a) plaintiff claims a close monopoly but did not preserve it and no license fee is proved (Burdell v. Denig); (b) open, cheap, and equally useful methods exist and no license fee proved; (c) only certain claims of little importance were infringed; (d) only the making of an article without sale or use; (e) plaintiff misled defendant; (f) plaintiff's device not stamped or due notice not given; (g) only one claim valid and no license fee proven. Juries cannot lawfully award more than nominal damages where evidence supports only nominal damages — such a verdict is fatal and requires new trial. Cases: Blake v. Greenwood Cemetery; Carter v. Baker; Whittemore v. Cutter; McComb v. Brodie; Johnson v. Boot; others cited in text.

name: Structural support required for software-based means-plus-function limitations
description: A means-plus-function limitation that corresponds to software per se (i.e., only supported by software and not by an algorithm and the computer or microprocessor programmed with the algorithm) should be deemed indefinite and rejected under § 112, ¶ 2.
guidance: Do not construe the limitation as covering pure software implementation absent corresponding structure disclosed in the specification. A claim that includes such a limitation is not necessarily directed to software per se as a whole if other structural limitations exist, but the means-plus-function limitation itself requires corresponding structure (e.g., algorithm and programmed device) or it is indefinite.

name: Examiners must establish a clear record when asserting indefiniteness
description: Examiners should carefully provide a complete and accurate picture of the Office’s consideration and must clearly explain all actions taken during prosecution, avoiding mere conclusions that a term is indefinite.
guidance: When rejecting under § 112, ¶ 2, provide findings and reasons supporting the rejection. MPEP § 2173.05 gives examples of rationales (functional claim limitations, relative terminology, lack of antecedent basis, etc.). A clear record enhances prosecution clarity and benefits public notice.

name: Office action must set forth specific term and why metes and bounds are unclear
description: An Office action rejecting under § 112, ¶ 2 must identify the specific term or phrase deemed indefinite and explain in detail why that term renders the metes and bounds of the claim unclear.
guidance: Provide sufficient information for applicant to prepare a meaningful response (explain what is indefinite and why, and, where practicable, indicate how indefiniteness may be resolved). Claims are given their broadest reasonable interpretation during prosecution to facilitate clarifying claims at the application stage. Quote: 'Because claims delineate the patentee’s right to exclude...' (to emphasize public notice).

name: Focus on statutory threshold clarity rather than stylistic improvements
description: The examination focus under § 112, ¶ 2 is whether claim language meets the statutory threshold of clarity and precision, not whether the examiner prefers alternate wording.
guidance: If language satisfies § 112, ¶ 2 but could be made clearer, suggest improved claim language rather than issue an indefiniteness rejection. When more information is needed to ascertain meaning, consider a requirement for information under 37 CFR 1.105 (see MPEP § 704.10).

name: Practice compact prosecution: identify all grounds and state claim interpretation
description: In the initial review and first Office action, examiners should review claims for compliance with all statutory requirements and identify all applicable grounds of rejection, stating how ambiguous claim terms are being interpreted when applying prior art.
guidance: Reject each claim on all reasonable grounds (e.g., § 112 ¶ 2 and § 102/§ 103 based on examiner's interpretation) to avoid piecemeal examination. When rejecting over prior art, state on the record how the claim term or phrase is being interpreted with respect to the applied art.

name: Attempt interview when indefiniteness is sole issue; make interview record explicit
description: If indefiniteness is the only outstanding issue, examiners should attempt to resolve it through an interview before issuing a rejection, and the substance of any interview must be made of record.
guidance: Interviews can clarify broadest reasonable interpretation, meaning of claim limitations, scope of preamble language, functional language, intended use language, and means-plus-function limitations. Record examples: why term is/is not sufficiently clear, consistency with specification, why § 112, ¶ 6 is/ is not invoked and identification of corresponding structure, any claim amendments discussed.

name: Provide claim interpretation in reasons for allowance when record is unclear
description: When the prosecution record does not make clear the examiner’s reasons for allowing a claim, the examiner may set forth such reasoning in reasons for allowance pursuant to 37 CFR 1.104(e).
guidance: Reasons for allowance improve the quality and reliability of issued patents by clarifying why the claim is allowable (e.g., the claim interpretation applied relative to prior art). However, avoid placing unwarranted broad or narrow interpretations upon the claims.

name: When invoking § 112, ¶ 6, state the basis and identify corresponding structure
description: If a claim limitation is interpreted as invoking § 112, ¶ 6 (means/step‑plus‑function), the Office action should state that the limitation is being treated under ¶ 6 and explain why, and identify the corresponding structure in the specification.
guidance: Explain when non‑'means for' language (e.g., 'module for') is treated under ¶ 6 (functional term coupled to non‑structural word). If corresponding structure is not clearly identifiable, still attempt to identify the structure most closely associated with the means-plus-function limitation to facilitate a prior art search. When allowing such a claim, indicate that ¶ 6 was applied and clarify the associated structure if not apparent in the specification.

name: Written description requirement for computer-implemented functional claims
description: To satisfy § 112, ¶ 1 written description, the specification must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail that one skilled in the art can reasonably conclude the inventor possessed the claimed invention, including for computer‑implemented functional claims.
guidance: Generic claim language or claiming in purely functional terms without describing species that achieve the function may fail written description (Ariad, LizardTech). For computer‑implemented inventions, determine whether the specification discloses the computer and the algorithm (necessary steps/flowcharts) that perform the claimed function in sufficient detail such that one skilled in the art could program the disclosed computer to perform the claimed function (e.g., Hayes example where algorithmic steps were described). If not, make a § 112, ¶ 1 written description rejection. See MPEP §§ 2161.01–2163.07(b).

name: Enablement requirement for computer-implemented functional claims (undue experimentation/Wands factors)
description: The specification must enable the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation; assess enablement using the Wands factors.
guidance: Consider the Wands factors: (1) breadth of the claims; (2) nature of the invention; (3) state of the prior art; (4) level of skill in the art; (5) predictability in the art; (6) amount of direction provided by the inventor; (7) existence of working examples; (8) quantity of experimentation needed. Functional claim language that is broad because it is not limited to particular structure may raise enablement concerns — the claim scope must be commensurate with the disclosure. Examples: Sitrick (spec enabled video games but not movies); Auto. Techs. (failure to disclose how to make an electronic side impact sensor). See MPEP §§ 2161.01, 2164.01(a)–2164.08(c).

name: Patentability considerations for computer-implemented functional claim language
description: Functional claim language that covers all devices capable of performing a recited function may be anticipated or obvious if the prior art inherently or predictably performs that function, and the term 'computer' should be given its broadest reasonable meaning consistent with the specification.
guidance: If prior art discloses a device capable of inherently performing the claimed function, a § 102 or § 103 rejection may be appropriate. A claim using 'computer' is not limited to a particular kind of computer unless modified or defined in the specification (In re Paulsen). Implementing a known function on a general‑purpose computer may be obvious if it is a predictable use of prior art elements; adapting existing processes to Internet/browser tech has been found obvious. See MPEP §§ 2112, 2114 and KSR-related guidance (Examination Guidelines Update).

name: Means-plus-function (¶6) applies only to purely functional limitations lacking structure
description: Means-plus-function claiming applies only to purely functional limitations that do not provide the structure that performs the recited function.
guidance: Per Phillips, determine whether claim language provides structural meaning; if it does not, treat under § 112, ¶ 6 and require disclosure of corresponding structure in the specification. Refer to MPEP § 2173.05 and relevant case law when making this determination.

name: Support for substitute claims / motion to amend authorization
description: Authorization to file an additional motion to amend may be denied where the patent owner 'facially cannot meet one of the requirements (e.g., no support for the new claims)'.
guidance: Denying authorization where the patent owner lacks support for new claims increases efficiency and prevents unnecessary opposition briefing and Board decision-writing. The Board will evaluate whether the patent owner meets the requirements for proposed substitute claims before authorizing filing of a motion to amend.

name: CBM nexus requirement to financial product or service
description: Under the rules, the petitioner must demonstrate that the patent for which review is sought is a covered business method patent — i.e., that the patent claims a method or corresponding apparatus for performing data processing or other operation used in the practice, administration, or management of a financial product or service, and which is not a technological invention.
guidance: Demonstration is claim-based. The rules do not limit which claims may be challenged to only those directed specifically to the covered business method; petitioner should articulate how the claims satisfy the statutory definition.

name: Procedure for request for judgment and determination of trial subjects
description: The party requesting judgment must file a request for judgment form stating the purpose and reasons (Article 140(1) Korean Patent Act); the subject of the trial is determined by those entries, not independently by KITAB or court.
guidance: Each claim and each accused invention become distinct subjects of the trial; entries in the request define the trial scope. The confirmation trial resembles a lawsuit seeking to confirm the right to prohibit and damages arising from infringement.

name: Claim-by-claim determination when multiple claims exist
description: Where a patented invention has multiple claims, the composition of the accused invention that is the object of the freely usable technology determination differs for each claim; results may differ claim-by-claim.
guidance: Determinations must be made for each relationship between each individual claim and the accused invention (e.g., 'for the relationship between the accused invention and Claim 1, the accused invention is freely usable technology').

name: Specifying accused invention by claim (per-claim specification method)
description: Plaintiff or the requester should be allowed to specify only the compositional elements to be compared to each claim when there are one or more accused inventions.
guidance: Permitting per-claim specification avoids dismissal when extraneous/mistakenly specified elements (e.g., C") would otherwise render the accused invention unspecified or incorrectly implemented. Example: Claim1 = A+B → specify A'+B'; Claim2 = A+B+C → specify A'+B'+C'.

name: Allowance of multiple accused inventions in a single confirmation trial
description: It is suggested that multiple accused inventions be allowed in a single trial to confirm the scope of a patent; merging requests for convenience essentially conducts multiple trials concurrently.
guidance: Merging requests does not require combining per-claim specifics into one specification; plaintiff may still specify accused inventions by claim even if trials are merged.

name: Requirement to add claim to provoke interference
description: The examiner may, pursuant to 35 U.S.C. 132(a) and 37 CFR 41.202(c), require an applicant to add a claim that would interfere with the claim of another application or patent.
guidance: The claim the examiner proposes to have added must (1) be patentable to the applicant, and (2) be drawn to patentable subject matter claimed by another applicant or patentee. The requirement may be made to obtain a clearer definition of the interfering subject matter or to establish whether the applicant will pursue claims to the interfering subject matter. When requirement is based on a published application with allowed claims or a patent, the examiner must identify that published application or patent.

name: Discretionary principles for requiring an interfering claim
description: Given the cost and complexity of interferences, a requirement to add a claim under 37 CFR 41.202(c) should not be lightly made. Before making the requirement, the examiner should consult with an IPS. The following principles should guide the examiner's discretion.
guidance: Principles: (A) Generally do not suggest an interference if examination is not otherwise completed. (B) The required claim must not encompass prior art or otherwise be barred. (C) The application must provide adequate support under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) for the subject matter of the required claim. (D) A claim should not be required when the applicant expressly states the commonly described subject matter is not the applicant's invention. (E) A claim based on a claim from a published application should not be required unless the claim from the published application has been allowed. Examples provided illustrate application of these principles (e.g., pre-AIA 102(b) prior art, time-bar situations, attribution to another inventor, genus/species relationships).

name: Use and content of form paragraph to require adding claim (Form ¶23.04)
description: Form paragraph 23.04 may be used to require an applicant to add a claim to provoke interference.
guidance: The required claim must be copied exactly in the form. Applicant is given TWO (2) MONTHS from mailing date to add the claim; refusal to add will operate as concession of priority for the subject matter of the required claim but will not abandon the application. Extensions may be granted under 37 CFR 1.136(a) but cannot carry the reply beyond the six-month statutory maximum (35 U.S.C. 133). If interference would be with a patent, applicant must also comply with 37 CFR 41.202(a)(2)–(a)(6). Examiner notes indicate bracketed insertions (e.g., published application number or patent number) and other drafting instructions.

name: Common ownership and election of priority
description: An administrative patent judge may decline to declare, or the Board may issue judgment in, an interference between applications or patents that are commonly owned.
guidance: Interference is rarely appropriate between two applications or an application and patent that belong to the same owner. The owner should determine priority and is obligated under 37 CFR 1.56 to inform the examiner which application or patent is entitled to priority. The examiner may require an election of priority; the owner must eliminate commonly claimed subject matter by canceling claims, disclaiming patent claims, amending application claims, or filing a reissue to amend patent claims. Examples (e.g., post-merger applications, co-inventor disagreements) illustrate application.

name: Requirement to show priority under 37 CFR 41.202(d)(1)
description: Whenever an application has an earliest constructive reduction-to-practice later than the apparent earliest constructive reduction-to-practice for a patent or published application claiming interfering subject matter, the applicant must show why it would prevail on priority.
guidance: If no showing has been filed and the applicant's earliest constructive reduction-to-practice is later, the examiner must require a showing of priority because an insufficient showing (including none) can trigger a prompt judgment against the applicant (see 37 CFR 41.202(d)(2)). The showing must, if unrebutted, support a determination of priority in favor of the party making the showing. When testimony or production necessary to show priority is not available without authorization under §41.150(c) or §41.156(a), the showing must include any necessary interrogatories/requests/deposition requests and a detailed proffer of expected responses and relevance.

name: Relationship to 37 CFR 1.131 affidavits
description: Ordinarily an applicant may use an affidavit under 37 CFR 1.131 to overcome a rejection under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) or 102(e); however, an exception arises when the reference is a patent or a published application that has claims directed to the same patentable invention.
guidance: When the reference contains claims directed to the same patentable invention as the application claims being rejected, priority is determined in an interference and the applicant must make the priority showing under 37 CFR 41.202(d) instead of using a 1.131 affidavit. The examiner should consider whether an interference would be possible at the time the affidavit would be submitted; if not (e.g., published claims significantly modified or not in condition for allowance), a 1.131 affidavit may be permitted.

name: Suspension of related examinations and minimizing adverse effects
description: Although the examiner may not act in a patent or application directly involved in an interference, examination may continue in related cases, including benefit files; suspension of related cases may be necessary in certain circumstances.
guidance: Once examination is completed, the examiner should consult with an IPS to determine whether and how further action should proceed. Suspension may be necessary if claims would be barred by a loss in the interference. Steps to minimize the effect (e.g., on patent term adjustment) should be considered: require restriction under 35 U.S.C. 121 to claims that do not interfere so they can issue, while the applicant files a divisional for interfering claims which may be suspended.

name: Adding additional parties to an interference
description: During the course of an interference, if the examiner discovers other applications or patents of parties that claim the same invention but are not already involved, the examiner should consult with an IPS and prepare a referral of the suggested interference to the Board.
guidance: Prepare the referral in the same way as an initial referral; consult IPS for scope and explanation why the additional files claim same invention.

name: Examiner responsibilities after an interference (judgment effect within the Office)
description: A Board judgment disposes of all issues that were, or by motion could have properly been, raised and decided. Jurisdiction over an application returns to the examiner once the interference has terminated.
guidance: If there is a recommendation for further action in the judgment, the examiner must reopen prosecution to consider the recommendation, enter any recommended rejection, and maintain the rejection unless overcome by amendment or new evidence. In the first action after termination, the examiner should make of record all references not already of record which were pertinent to preliminary motions and discussed in the decision on motion. An interference judgment resolves priority between parties but does not prevent the examiner from making rejections in further examination. Adverse judgment against a claim is final Office action; if no claim remains allowable, issue a notice of abandonment. Form paragraph 23.02 may be used to resume ex parte prosecution.

name: Adding or amending claims during an interference
description: A party may file a motion during the interference to add or amend a claim; a patentee may file a reissue application in support of such a motion.
guidance: A copy of the paper adding or amending the claim will be placed in the official record of the application but not entered. The examiner may enter the added claim or amended claim into the application only if, and only to the extent, authorized by the Board (typically in the decision on the motion). The decision authorizing entry does not prevent the examiner from rejecting the claim during further prosecution.

name: Conciseness of claims (Rule 7(1))
description: The requirement that the claims should be concise refers to the claims in their entirety as well as to the individual claims.
guidance: Undue repetition of words or an undue multiplicity of claims of a trivial nature may be considered non-compliant. Claims may be objected to as lacking conciseness when unduly multiplied or duplicative; claims should not be presented in a way that obscures the matter for which protection is sought. Individual claims may be objected to as lacking conciseness if they contain long recitations or unimportant details that render the scope indefinite. The reasonable number of claims depends on the nature and facts of each case and the interests of the relevant public.

name: Number of claims — avoid undue multiplicity (Rule 7(1))
description: The number of claims must be considered in relation to the nature of the invention the applicant seeks to protect.
guidance: Undue repetition or a multiplicity of trivial claims that make it unduly burdensome to determine the matter for which protection is sought may be objected to. Alternatives within a single claim should not make it unduly burdensome to determine subject matter. Identical or nearly identical claims that cover the same thing may be objected to, but small wording changes that change scope slightly should not usually be objected to.

name: Support in description (Rule 7(1))
description: The claims 'shall be fully supported by the description.' There must be a basis in the description for the subject matter of every claim and the scope of the claims must not be broader than justified by the description and drawings.
guidance: Support must relate to the features of the claimed invention; vague statements or assertions without technical content provide no basis. An examiner should raise an objection of lack of support only if there are well-founded reasons; where raised, reasons should, where possible, be supported by a published document.

name: Clear and complete disclosure (Rule 7(1))
description: Subject matter of each claim must be supported by the description and drawings 'in a manner sufficiently clear and complete for the invention to be carried out by a person skilled in the art.'
guidance: Disclosure must enable the invention to be carried out as of the international filing date without undue experimentation. A person skilled in the art may use general knowledge to supplement the application. Reasonable trial and error is permissible, but not 'undue experimentation.'

name: Factors for undue experimentation
description: Factors to be considered in determining whether undue experimentation is needed.
guidance: Consider: (i) breadth of the claims; (ii) nature of the invention; (iii) general knowledge of the skilled person; (iv) level of predictability in the art; (v) amount of direction in the application, including prior art references; (vi) amount of experimentation required. Also consider character of experimentation (routine vs beyond routine). Representative examples plus explanation of how they apply to the claim scope may suffice.

name: Sufficiency commensurate with the claims
description: Extent of permissible generalization from examples must be judged in light of prior art; a claim should not be so broad as to go beyond the invention nor so narrow as to deprive the applicant of a just reward.
guidance: Obvious modifications, uses and equivalents of described embodiments should not be questioned. Generic claims may be acceptable if there is fair support in the description and no reason to suppose the invention cannot be carried out across the claimed field. If information is insufficient to enable extension to parts of the claimed field, the examiner should invite evidence or require restriction of the claim.

name: Relationship of claims to disclosure (Rule 7(1))
description: Claimed invention must be fully supported by the description and drawings, showing the applicant only claims what was recognized and described on the filing date.
guidance: Claims are inconsistent with the disclosure if an essential element for function/operation is missing from the claim, or if there are contradictions between claims and description, or if the scope covers areas not recognized by the applicant. Examples: a fuel oil composition claim omitting an additive described as necessary would lack support.

name: Functional claiming — alternatives and limits
description: A claim may define a feature in terms of its function even where only one example is given if the skilled person would appreciate other means to achieve that function.
guidance: If the description conveys that a function is to be carried out in a particular way with no intimation of alternatives, then a claim embracing other means may not comply with support. Mere vague statements that other means 'may' be adopted may not be sufficient unless reasonably clear what they are and how to use them.

name: Characterisation of chemical compounds by parameters
description: Characterization solely by parameters may be appropriate in certain cases.
guidance: Such characterization is fully supported only when sufficient identifying characteristics show the applicant recognized and described the claimed invention at filing (e.g., partial structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics coupled with known correlation between structure and function).

name: Interpretation of claims
description: Claims should be interpreted in view of the description, drawings and general knowledge of the skilled person; special meanings given in the description should be used.
guidance: Claims should not be limited by examples in the description; if description gives a term a special meaning, that definition should be used for claim interpretation and the examiner should, if possible, require claim amendment to make the meaning clear in the claim wording alone. Claims should be read attempting to make technical sense and may depart from strict literal wording for that purpose.

name: Further requirements: enablement and technical character
description: In addition to the four basic requirements, the invention must be such that it can be carried out by a person skilled in the art, and must be of 'technical character' — relating to a technical field, concerned with a technical problem, and having technical features definable in the claim.
guidance: Examiners should assess technical character independently of novelty/inventive step; if no technical character, reject under Section 3(10).

name: Priority under Paris Convention
description: The Paris Convention establishes a 'right of priority' enabling an IP applicant to claim priority of an earlier application filed up to 12 months previously for patents and utility models, and up to six months previously for trademarks and industrial designs.
guidance: Priority date is the filing date of the earlier application and is critical for determining novelty and prior art.

name: Prior art definition
description: All information disclosed to the public about an invention, in any form, before a given date; information on prior art assists in determining whether the claimed invention is new and involves an inventive step.
guidance: Prior art analysis is central to novelty and inventive-step determinations by patent examiners.

name: Preamble limiting effect (MPEP 2111.02)
description: Determine whether the preamble limits the claim: when the preamble only states a purpose or field of use it does not limit the claim; if the preamble gives 'life, meaning and vitality' it may be construed to further limit the claim.
guidance: Example: a preamble merely stating field/purpose does not add limitations (so no additional limitations beyond the abstract idea); but where the claim states the calculation is performed by 'the computer' referencing the preamble computer, the preamble 'gives life' and is limiting (see MPEP 2111.02).

name: Significantly more analysis (Step 2B): individual elements and ordered combination
description: After identifying an exception, analyze whether any additional element or combination of elements recited in the claim amounts to 'significantly more' than the judicial exception (Step 2B: YES/NO).
guidance: Conduct the Step 2B analysis for each abstract idea individually (if multiple are present) and consider both elements individually and as an ordered combination. The ordered combination can sometimes provide the required 'significantly more' where individual elements would not.

name: Limiting to a particular technological environment/field-of-use is insufficient
description: Simply limiting the abstract idea to a particular technological environment (e.g., graphical user interface) or field of use does not by itself amount to 'significantly more.'
guidance: Cites Flook and other case law: restricting use of an abstract idea to a GUI or particular environment is not enough unless the claim recites meaningful additional limitations beyond mere environmental application.

name: Ordered combination that improves technology or effects transformation can be significantly more
description: When additional limitations, taken as an ordered combination, recite a specific application that improves the functioning of a computer or another technological field or effect a transformation of an article into a different state or thing, the claim may amount to 'significantly more.'
guidance: Examples: scaling and relocating text in overlapping windows improves the computer's basic display function (thus significantly more); integrating the Arrhenius equation into a computer-controlled rubber-molding press that repeatedly measures temperature and opens the press when cured both improves precision rubber molding and effects transformation of raw rubber into a cured product (Diehr example).

name: High-level recitation of known, well-understood, routine, conventional activities weighs against eligibility
description: Claim elements that merely recite well-understood, routine, and conventional computer functions (e.g., accessing a database, performing calculations, initiating a timer) do not add meaningful limitations.
guidance: If the claim is limited to computer implementation but the computer is only used for generic tasks that are routine and conventional, that computer implementation will not transform the abstract idea into eligible subject matter.

name: Multiple abstract ideas require separate Step 2B analyses
description: If a claim recites multiple abstract ideas, perform the Step 2B analysis for each abstract idea individually until ineligibility for one is shown or eligibility for all is shown.
guidance: The rubber-molding example explains that with multiple abstract ideas (mathematical relationship and mental steps), Step 2B must be conducted for each abstract idea in turn.

name: Examiner action guidance: how to state rejections or allowances
description: When issuing a rejection, the examiner should identify the judicial exception by pointing to the claim elements (e.g., the formula, generating and scaling steps) and explain that those elements are abstract and why additional limitations do or do not amount to significantly more; if eligible, remarks may be added to an Office action or reasons for allowance indicating the claim recites exceptions but is eligible due to additional limitations.
guidance: Examples in the text instruct examiners to: point to specific claim steps that are the exception (e.g., mathematical algorithm), explain similarity to court-found abstract ideas, note whether preamble limits the claim, and explain why additional limitations fail to add significantly more (e.g., mere data gathering, field-of-use, generic computer functions) or why they do (ordered combination that improves technology).

name: Due cause / legitimate descriptive use defence
description: Use of a generic or descriptive word element for an informative purpose (e.g., indicating presence of spa facilities) can amount to due cause and may negate claims of unfair advantage or likelihood of confusion with an earlier mark's reputation.
guidance: Evaluate whether the element performs an informative purpose and whether it takes undue advantage of an earlier mark; if clearly descriptive and used to inform consumers, due cause may apply.

name: Acquired distinctiveness (Article 7(3) / evidence requirements)
description: Claims of distinctiveness acquired through use must be substantiated; the Board may remit the case to the Cancellation Division solely to examine acquired distinctiveness if required.
guidance: Provide robust evidence of market exposure, duration, geographic scope, nature of use within the Community; isolated declarations or attendance lists without detailed provenance are insufficient.

name: Use outside the Community not prima facie sufficient
description: Evidence of use in third countries (outside the Community) is not sufficient to show use in the Community; the applicant must prove effective use inside the Community in the same fashion as claimed.
guidance: Provide concrete proof of Community use (sales, advertising, geographic spread) rather than attendance by Community nationals at events abroad.

name: Alice two-step patent-eligibility test
description: The Supreme Court’s two-step test: first ask whether a claim is 'directed to' an ineligible concept (abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon); second, if so, ask whether, setting aside the ineligible principle, the patent contains 'additional elements' that 'transform' the claim into a 'patent-eligible application' of the underlying principle.
guidance: Showing that the patent recites 'well-understood, routine, [and] conventional activity' is one way to show that the patent does not qualify as an application of the underlying, ineligible principle. (Cites: Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank Int’l; Mayo Collaborative Servs. v. Prometheus.)

name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity (Alice step two)
description: Whether a patent involves well-understood, routine, or conventional activity is treated by the Federal Circuit as a question of fact.
guidance: That factual determination can depend on evidence such as trial testimony about the state of the art and may therefore raise disputes of fact that can require a jury trial (Berkheimer v. HP). It is used to assess whether claimed 'additional elements' provide an inventive concept.

name: Claim specificity versus prior-art comparison in Alice step two
description: Some Federal Circuit decisions emphasize the specificity of the claims themselves (their concrete, discrete implementation) rather than how the claimed invention compares to previously known technology when resolving step two.
guidance: Courts have sometimes refused to consider evidence of novelty or nonobviousness when deciding step two, instead pinning rulings on claim breadth or specific claim limitations (e.g., Bascom, Two-Way Media, Affinity Labs). This approach resembles claim construction and treats the issue more as a legal determination about claim scope than a fact-driven inquiry into the state of the art.

name: Determination of what a claim is 'directed to' (Alice step one)
description: Step one asks whether a patent claim is 'directed to' an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon; determining what a claim is 'directed to' can look like the legal task of claim construction.
guidance: The Federal Circuit has instructed that comparing the claimed invention to prior precedent is a key method for deciding the question (e.g., Enfish). Some district courts treat Alice Step One as a 'purely legal question' and may decide it based solely on intrinsic evidence; other courts have relied on extrinsic sources (textbooks, treatises) indicating a more fact-driven analysis.

name: 'Fundamental economic practice' standard invites factual inquiry
description: Courts have written that a patent recites an abstract idea when it claims 'a fundamental economic practice long prevalent in our system of commerce,' a standard that invites inquiry into historical/practical facts.
guidance: Because this standard asks whether a practice is 'longstanding,' courts and judges have looked to extrinsic evidence and factual determinations (see Solutran; CardioNet dissent noting relevance of extrinsic evidence).

name: Laws of nature and natural phenomena eligibility involves factual questions
description: Determining whether a claim involves a law of nature or a natural phenomenon requires determining whether the claimed subject matter exists in the world without human intervention.
guidance: Myriad illustrates invalidation when claimed DNA sequences 'existed in nature before' discovery; courts have relied on witness testimony and extrinsic evidence to determine whether claimed subject matter is natural (e.g., Myriad; American Axle; BRCA litigation).

name: Anticipation as a question of fact (and element-by-element comparison)
description: The Federal Circuit has repeatedly described anticipation as a question of fact — often because anticipation requires finding each element of the claimed invention in a single prior art reference (an element-by-element factual comparison).
guidance: Appellate opinions state anticipation is a factual question (Brown v. 3M; In re Gleave; Microsoft v. Biscotti), but many subsidiary issues (e.g., whether a reference is a 'printed publication') are treated as legal questions. The element-by-element comparison is analogous to the fact question of infringement, which juries typically decide.

name: Written description requirement (§112) — possession and support
description: Written description polices claim breadth by ensuring the inventor actually invented what the patent claims: (1) it prevents adding claims not supported by the original disclosure; (2) it invalidates patents when the specification indicates the inventor was not in possession of the claimed invention.
guidance: Illustrative cases: Gentry Gallery (original application described an 'essential element' limiting claimed subject matter), Eli Lilly (specification disclosed rat insulin sequence but claimed human insulin). The Federal Circuit (Ariad en banc) treats written description as a question of fact; the inquiry 'depends on the nature of the invention and the amount of knowledge imparted to those skilled in the art' and typically involves documentary comparison, expert testimony, and a person-of-ordinary-skill perspective—much like claim construction. Written-description issues often reach juries and are reviewed deferentially on appeal, in contrast to de novo review of claim construction.

name: Enablement requirement (§112) (relation to written description)
description: Enablement is the companion requirement in §112 that ensures the specification teaches how to make and use the claimed invention (i.e., enables a person of ordinary skill in the art).
guidance: Enablement is described as written description’s 'close cousin'—both derive from §112 and overlap in function—though the page only begins the enablement discussion here. Enablement inquiries likewise involve technical documentary evidence and may raise mixed law-fact issues.

name: Statutory categories of invention
description: The four statutory categories of invention under 35 U.S.C. § 101 are Process, Machine, Manufacture, or Composition of Matter and improvements thereof.
guidance: Claims that do not fall within these categories are not eligible for patenting. Identification of one particular category is not necessary for eligibility; a claim may satisfy more than one category (e.g., bicycle may be both machine and manufacture). Analyze based on the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim as a whole. If a claim covers both eligible and ineligible subject matter, reject under §101.

name: Broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) and claim-as-a-whole analysis
description: Analyze claims under the broadest reasonable interpretation and consider the claim as a whole in the eligibility determination.
guidance: Use BRI when determining whether a claim fits a statutory category and when performing judicial-exception analysis. Keep in mind what the applicant considers to be the invention.

name: Failure to claim within a statutory category → rejection
description: If, under the broadest reasonable interpretation, a claim covers an invention that does not fall within the four statutory categories, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. § 101 must be made.
guidance: Explain why the claimed invention does not satisfy any of the categories (see MPEP 2106(I) for definitions). Use Form ¶¶ 7.04, 7.05, 7.05.01; use Form ¶ 7.04.01 for human organisms.

name: Signals per se are not statutory categories (ineligible)
description: Transitory, propagating signals (signals per se) are not within the four statutory categories and are therefore ineligible subject matter (In re Nuijten).
guidance: Under BRI, a computer readable media (CRM) may cover an ineligible signal per se unless the specification provides a special definition distinguishing storage media from transmission media. If the specification is silent, acceptable claim amendments include excluding the signal embodiment (e.g., adding 'non-transitory'), but 'non-transitory' is not required. It is not acceptable to add 'physical' or 'tangible' or to add 'storage' absent support in the original disclosure.

name: Basic judicial-exception analysis (claim directed to exception or practical application)
description: Determine whether the claim as a whole is directed to a judicial exception (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea) and whether the exception has been practically applied.
guidance: Analyze all elements/steps to see if the exception is practically applied. A claim directed to a practical application may be eligible. Determine whether the claim covers all substantial applications of the exception and thereby forecloses future innovation. A claim directed solely to the exception itself is not eligible.

name: Product-claim (machine/manufacture/composition) flowchart analysis
description: Five-step product claim analysis: (1) Does the claim meet definitions of process, machine, manufacture or composition? (2) If a process, follow process analysis. (3) Does the claim recite an abstract idea, law of nature or natural phenomenon? (4) Is the claim as a whole directed to a practical application of the exception? (5) Does the claim cover substantially all practical applications of the exception?
guidance: If the claim recites a judicial exception but is directed to a practical application (evidence: man-made tangible embodiment with a real-world use), proceed; if it covers substantially all practical applications (forecloses innovation), deem ineligible. If not drawn to an eligible subject matter, reject under 35 U.S.C. § 101 (use Form ¶¶ 7.04, 7.05, 7.05.01). See MPEP 2106(II)(A).

name: Process-claim analysis: laws of nature vs. abstract ideas
description: For process claims that include a law of nature as a limitation, use the three essential inquiries (MPEP 2106.01). For other process claims, use factors relating to abstract idea determination (including Bilski factors/Machine-or-Transformation guidance).
guidance: Select the appropriate analysis path depending on whether the claim includes a natural principle limitation; see Interim Guidance for Determining Subject Matter Eligibility for Process Claims in View of Bilski v. Kappos and 2012 Interim Procedure for process claims involving laws of nature.

name: Three essential inquiries for laws of nature (process claims)
description: 1) Is the claim directed to a process (an act or series of acts or steps)? 2) Does the claim focus on use of a law of nature/natural phenomenon/naturally occurring relation or correlation (i.e., is the natural principle a limiting feature)? 3) Does the claim include additional elements/steps that integrate the natural principle into the claimed invention such that it is practically applied and amount to significantly more than the natural principle itself?
guidance: Ask also: Is the claim more than a law of nature + the general instruction to simply 'apply it'?

name: Natural principle as a claim limitation (definition and examples)
description: A natural principle is the handiwork of nature and occurs without the hand of man; includes correlations that exist apart from human action (e.g., relationship between blood glucose levels and diabetes).
guidance: Examples of methods that focus on natural principles include diagnosing a condition based on naturally occurring correlations, or identifying disease using a naturally occurring relationship between a substance and disease. Claims that do not include such limitations (e.g., administering a man-made drug, treating by medical procedure, new use for a known drug) need not use this analysis.

name: Inquiry 3 Part I – Integration evaluation (factors that weigh in favor)
description: When assessing whether additional elements/steps integrate the natural principle into the claimed invention, consider whether: the steps relate to the natural principle in a significant way; the steps impose a meaningful limit on claim scope; the steps include a machine or transformation that implements the principle.
guidance: It is not necessary that every step show integration. If additional elements/steps do not integrate the natural principle, there is no practical application and the claim fails.

name: Inquiry 3 Part II – 'Amounts to significantly more' evaluation (factors that weigh in favor)
description: Factors indicating the claim amounts to significantly more than the natural principle itself: the steps do more than describe the principle with general instructions to apply it; the steps narrow claim scope so others are not foreclosed; the steps add a novel or non-obvious feature; the steps include a new use of a known substance.
guidance: These factors support finding a patent-eligible practical application of a natural principle.

name: ‘Amounts to significantly more’ evaluation (factors that weigh against)
description: Factors weighing against the claim amounting to significantly more include: the steps are well-understood, purely conventional or routine; the steps are those that must be taken by others to apply the principle; the steps are recited at a high level of generality such that substantially all practical applications are covered.
guidance: If the claim amounts to no more than recognizing the law of nature (routine/high-level steps), the claim should be rejected.

name: Process claims – abstract ideas determination
description: A claim that attempts to patent an abstract idea per se is ineligible; determine eligibility by weighing factors that indicate whether the claim represents a practical application of an abstract idea or the abstract idea itself.
guidance: The factors include inquiries from the machine-or-transformation test as a useful investigative tool, but not determinative. Not every factor will be relevant; no factor is conclusive by itself; weight accorded varies with facts and technology; factors are not exclusive.

name: Abstract-idea factors that weigh against eligibility
description: Factors against eligibility include no recitation of machine or transformation, or an insufficient recitation (machine is nominal, generic, merely an object, or tangential to steps). Claims that are merely statements of a general concept (cover both known and unknown uses, can be performed without apparatus) weigh against eligibility.
guidance: Examples of insufficiency: machine recited only generically covering any machine; transformations that only change position/location; 'article' is a general concept; claim only states a problem to be solved or is disembodied/imperceptible.

name: Transitional phrase (definition and role)
description: A transitional phrase, in United States patent law, is a phrase that links the preamble of a patent claim to the specific elements set forth in the claim which define what the invention itself actually is.
guidance: The transitional phrase acts as a limitation on the claim, indicating whether a similar device, method, or composition infringes the patent if it contains more or fewer elements than the claim in the patent. The article notes there are three kinds of transitional phrases: open, closed, and hybrid.

name: Closed transition ("consisting of")
description: A closed transition usually uses the words "consisting of." Use of this phrase limits the preamble to exactly what follows and nothing more.
guidance: Example: a claim for a pencil with the closed transition "consisting of" followed by a cylinder of writing material and a casing means a third party who adds an eraser would not be infringing. Use of a closed transition makes it easier for competitors to design around the claim (they may add elements and avoid infringement), but it may help the patent owner avoid prior art that would otherwise block the patent from issuing.

name: Open transition ("comprises" or "comprising")
description: An open transition usually uses the word "comprises" or "comprising." This is the broadest form of transition, as it does not limit the preamble to whatever elements are identified in the claim.
guidance: Example: if the pencil claim used "comprising" instead of "consisting of," the pencil-plus-eraser would be infringing (assuming validity). Open transitions broaden claim scope and make it easier to capture products or methods that include additional, unrecited elements.

name: Hybrid transition ("consisting essentially of")
description: A hybrid transition uses the phrase "consisting essentially of." The effect is to leave the claim open to include additional elements, but only if those additional elements do not materially affect the basic and novel characteristics of the claimed combination.
guidance: Example: a pencil with an added eraser might still not infringe, but additions that are non-material to claimed functions (e.g., a fin or non-functional button) would still infringe. This phrasing can help avoid prior art while remaining broad enough to capture imperfect attempts to copy the patented device.

name: Claims define the scope of the patent
description: Patent claims are the numbered sentences at the end of the patent that define the invention and the patent owner's exclusive rights; only claims can be infringed (not the written description or drawings).
guidance: Each claim must be considered individually. The words of the claims define the scope of exclusive rights, and the same claim meaning must be used for infringement and invalidity determinations.

name: Judge's role in claim construction
description: The judge will determine the meaning of claim language that must be interpreted and will provide those meanings to the jury; the jury must accept and use the court's constructions when deciding infringement and invalidity.
guidance: Read any stipulations and the court's constructions aloud. Citations: Teva; Phillips; Markman family of cases. Emphasize jury must follow judge's claim meanings even if they disagree.

name: Cutoff Date (pre-AIA vs AIA) and prior art pool
description: Defines Cutoff Date: pre-AIA law may have different Cutoff Dates depending on subsection of §102; under the AIA the Cutoff Date is the effective filing date of the claimed invention. Different claims in a patent may have different Cutoff Dates.
guidance: If claims have different Cutoff Dates and those dates are disputed, the jury may need instructions on how to determine the Cutoff Date(s) and on differences in the pool of available prior art for each claim. Practice Note explains pre-AIA variances (date of invention or one year before filing/effective priority) and AIA definitions.

name: Direct infringement—burden and mental state immaterial
description: A defendant is liable for direct infringement if the plaintiff proves by a preponderance of the evidence that the defendant made, used, imported, offered to sell, or sold the invention defined in at least one claim during the patent term. Knowledge of the patent or intent to infringe is immaterial to direct infringement.
guidance: Cites 35 U.S.C. § 271(a) and cases (Commil, Medtronic, Global-Tech, etc.). Instruction emphasizes the 'more likely than not' standard for direct infringement.

name: Literal infringement—all claim elements must be present
description: A patent claim is literally infringed only if the accused product or method includes each and every element (or method step) recited in that patent claim, applying the court's claim constructions.
guidance: Determine literal infringement separately for each asserted claim. The same accused element may satisfy more than one claim element. If any element is missing, there is no literal infringement. (Cites cases such as Limelight, Hutchins, Gen. Mills.)

name: Infringement under claim transitional language ('comprising'/'consisting of'/'consisting essentially of')
description: Explains meanings of common transitional phrases in claim preambles: 'comprising' means including the following but not excluding others; 'consisting of' means including the following and excluding others; 'consisting essentially of' means including the following and possibly unlisted components that do not materially affect the invention.
guidance: If accused product/method includes all claim elements but also additional components, 'comprising' still permits literal infringement; 'consisting of' would preclude literal infringement if additional components exist; 'consisting essentially of' permits additional components only if they do not materially affect the invention. (Cites relevant case law.)

name: Literal infringement of means-plus-function and step-plus-function claims
description: To establish literal infringement of a means-plus-function or step-plus-function limitation, the plaintiff must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that the accused product/method (1) performs the recited function, and (2) includes structure or step that is identical or equivalent to the corresponding structure/step described in the patent specification/drawings.
