guidance: First decide whether the accused product/method has any structure/step that performs the specific function; if not, no infringement of that limitation. If it does, determine whether that structure/step is the same as or equivalent to the structure recited in the specification. Equivalence is decided from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art; insubstantial differences or performing substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result are indicators of equivalence. Citations: 35 U.S.C. § 112 and Federal Circuit authority (Williamson, Brilliant Instruments, etc.).

name: Doctrine of equivalents—when to apply and equivalence tests
description: If the accused product/method does not literally infringe, the jury must decide whether it infringes under the doctrine of equivalents by having components/steps equivalent to missing claim elements. Equivalence can be shown by demonstrating an element is insubstantially different from the claimed element or that it performs substantially the same function, in substantially the same way, to achieve substantially the same result.
guidance: The jury may consider whether persons of ordinary skill at the time would have known of interchangeability, though known interchangeability is not required. If a claim is literally infringed, no need to resort to the doctrine of equivalents; the doctrine is available only if one or more claim elements are not literally met. The same accused component may satisfy more than one claim element, and multiple accused components may together satisfy a single claim element. (Cites Warner-Jenkinson, Graver Tank.)

name: Limitations on doctrine of equivalents—prosecution history estoppel
description: Prosecution history estoppel can bar application of the doctrine of equivalents for claim elements surrendered during prosecution by argument or amendment made for reasons related to patentability; if the court determines prosecution history estoppel applies, the jury should be instructed that the doctrine of equivalents cannot be applied to specified claim elements.
guidance: This instruction should be given only if the court has determined prosecution history estoppel applies as a matter of law. The court should list the elements on a claim-by-claim basis for which equivalents are barred; those elements must be literally present for infringement. (Cites Festo and related authority.)

name: Limitations on doctrine of equivalents—dedication to the public (subject matter dedication)
description: If the court determines, as a matter of law, that certain subject matter has been dedicated to the public, the doctrine of equivalents cannot be applied to those claim elements; those elements must be literally present for infringement.
guidance: This instruction should be given only if the court has made the dedication-to-public determination. The court should list the elements on a claim-by-claim basis that cannot be found by equivalents. (Cites SanDisk, Pfizer, PSC Computer Prods., Toro, Johnson & Johnston.)

name: Practice note: Distinguish theories of infringement
description: To avoid jury confusion, distinguish claims alleged to be infringed directly versus indirectly, literal infringement versus doctrine of equivalents, and induced infringement versus contributory infringement.
guidance: Consider presenting related instructions (e.g., joint infringement and inducement) back-to-back and in a way that highlights differences in theories, required evidence, and specific findings jurors must make.

name: Grounds for extension / eligibility criteria (Article 54-3; Article 92-3(1)(v))
description: Grounds designated by Ordinance include: (1) a need to extend the patent term because the patent was registered after four years from the filing date or three years from the date of request for examination, whichever is later; (2) a specification of the period of request for extension and an explanation that the period of delay attributable to the applicant is reduced (with evidential document); and (3) other necessary items to prove the ground for extension.
guidance: The application must explain and document the relevant delay periods and any reductions in applicant-attributable delay; evidential documents must be attached for each claimed ground.

name: Higher Success Rates
description: ~10% higher allowance rates for PPH applications.
guidance: PPH applications tend to have higher allowance rates, reflecting reliance on prior allowable claims from a partner office. This metric supports choosing PPH when allowance probability improvement is desired.

name: Requirement: allowability in first office
description: Office of first examination has determined at least one claim allowable.
guidance: A favorable ruling (at least one allowable claim) from the first office is a precondition to request PPH; you must supply evidence of that allowability (e.g., office action or allowance notice) when filing the PPH request.

name: Requirement: claim correspondence
description: Claims in second office must 'sufficiently correspond' to allowable claims.
guidance: Claims need not be identical but should sufficiently correspond in scope/limitations to the allowable claims from the first office. A claim correspondence table is required to explain how claims map between offices.

name: Filing steps and required documents
description: Required filing items: 1) File PPH request with the second office; 2) Submit copies of office actions from first office; 3) Submit copies of allowed claims from first office; 4) Provide claim correspondence table; 5) Submit search information.
guidance: Follow the enumerated procedural steps precisely. The claim correspondence table and search information are critical evidentiary documents; missing or inadequate documentation can lead to denial of PPH status.

name: Strategic consideration — When NOT to use PPH
description: Avoid PPH when initial application has narrow claims you don't want; when you want to delay examination; when initial application was incompletely examined.
guidance: Do not request PPH if adopting the allowable claims would be strategically undesirable (e.g., they narrow claim scope you want to keep), if you prefer to defer examination for business reasons, or if the first-office examination is incomplete or unreliable.

name: Comparison with other acceleration options
description: Comparison table elements: PPH (First action ~5 months, $0 fee, requires allowable claims in another office); Track One (~12 months total, $4,200, <30 claims); Accelerated Examination (~12 months, $140, requires pre-exam search + statement); First Action Interview (timeline varies, $0, must request within 60 days of FAOM).
guidance: Choose acceleration route based on desired timeline, cost tolerance, and eligibility constraints (e.g., claim count limits, required prior search/statement). PPH is often lowest-cost if eligibility is met, but other tracks may better fit specific needs.

name: Limitation: claim divergence and dependency on foreign examination quality
description: Requires correspondence of claims (cannot have claims dramatically different); initial office of examination must conclude examination favorably first; quality of underlying foreign examination affects PPH outcome.
guidance: PPH's effectiveness is contingent on the substantive thoroughness and conclusions of the first-office examination; if the foreign examination is superficial or the claims diverge substantially, the second office may not accept PPH or may still issue substantial rejections.

name: More Like This Document (MLTD) AI search
description: Use an AI search that finds documents similar to those examiners are studying by using title, abstract, claim(s), description, CPC, and examiner citation data to calculate similarity.
guidance: Enable Patent Examiners to perform MLTD searches to retrieve potentially relevant prior art; public demonstration previewed at PPAC meeting (Aug 2022). Link provided for more information.

name: Claims define the invention (bedrock principle)
description: The claims of a patent define the invention that is protected; claim construction begins with the actual words of the claims.
guidance: Always start analysis with the claim language. Do not assume the specification replaces the claims as the definition of the invention.

name: Ordinary and customary meaning to a person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA)
description: A claim term's meaning is the meaning it would have to a person of ordinary skill in the art in question at the time of the invention (effective filing date).
guidance: Read disputed terms in the context of the particular claim and the entire patent. Use the POSITA viewpoint as the primary interpretive lens.

name: Time frame for construing claim meaning
description: Claim terms are to be given the meanings they would have had at the effective filing date of the application, not at the patent issue date.
guidance: Do not adopt methodologies that anchor claim meaning to the patent issue date (Texas Digital approach criticized).

name: Intrinsic evidence is the most reliable source
description: Intrinsic evidence—the claims, the specification, and the prosecution history—is the primary and most reliable source for claim construction.
guidance: Specification characterized as 'the single best guide' to meaning; consult intrinsic record first and give it greatest weight.

name: Specification as primary guide and potential lexicography/disavowal source
description: The specification must be consulted to determine whether the inventor expressly defined terms (was his own lexicographer) or disclaimed/disavowed claim scope; the specification can define terms expressly or by implication.
guidance: If the specification defines a term or shows clear disavowal of scope, that inventor-intended meaning is dispositive.

name: Prosecution history is intrinsic but often less useful
description: The prosecution history functions similarly to the specification for claim construction but may be less useful because prosecution can introduce ambiguities arising from negotiation between PTO and applicant.
guidance: Consider prosecution history for context, but recognize its limitations and potential lack of clarity.

name: Expert testimony must be supported and not merely conclusory
description: Conclusive assertions by experts are particularly suspect; expert declarations regarding claim construction should be supported by documentary evidence.
guidance: Avoid relying on unsupported expert conclusory statements; corroborate with intrinsic documents and objective extrinsic materials where needed.

name: No rigid formula or mandated sequence of sources
description: There is no 'magic formula,' catechism, or rigid algorithm for claim construction and courts are not barred from considering any particular sources or required to analyze them in a specific sequence.
guidance: However, courts must 'attach the appropriate weight' to various sources and cannot let extrinsic evidence contradict claim meaning that is unambiguous from the intrinsic record.

name: Do not import extraneous limitations from the specification into claims
description: It is improper to read limitations into the claims from the specification; claims should not be limited to particular embodiments unless there is clear indication.
guidance: Examples in the specification are primarily to teach how to make/use the invention and to satisfy best mode; they should not be automatically read as limiting the claim scope.

name: Do not limit a claim to a disclosed embodiment absent clear intent
description: Limiting a claim to a single disclosed embodiment is improper unless the specification or prosecution history makes clear that the patentee intended that limitation (explicit or implicit disavowal).
guidance: The mere fact that only one embodiment is disclosed, or that a feature appears in all embodiments, does not by itself justify narrowing a broadly worded claim.

name: Claim differentiation doctrine
description: Differences among claims can be a useful guide; the presence of a dependent claim that adds a limitation gives rise to a presumption that the limitation is not present in the independent claim.
guidance: Use claim differentiation as a tool to infer relative scope between independent and dependent claims, but weigh it against the intrinsic record.

name: Avoid importing functional limitations implying unrecited structure
description: Do not include functional limitations in a claim if those functional limitations imply structure that is not recited in the claim, except when intentionally focusing on functional properties.
guidance: If functional language is used, be aware it might suggest unrecited structure; draft carefully when functional claiming is intended.

name: Means-plus-function considerations and sufficiency of structure recitation
description: A claim term may or may not invoke means-plus-function treatment; certain words (e.g., 'baffle') can be a sufficient recitation of structure and thus not be treated as a 'means' limitation.
guidance: Analyze whether the claim language supplies sufficient structure; if means-plus-function applies, construe under 35 U.S.C. §112(f) and limit to corresponding disclosed structure.

name: Attach appropriate weight to intrinsic vs extrinsic evidence
description: While courts may consider a variety of sources, they must give greatest weight to intrinsic evidence and avoid letting extrinsic sources change meanings established by the intrinsic record.
guidance: Weigh sources contextually; do not let extrinsic evidence override clear claim meaning present in the specification and claims.

name: Drafting recommendation: include dependent claims reciting structure/functions
description: Include dependent claims that more specifically recite the structure and/or functions of elements recited in the independent claims (invoke the 'claim differentiation' doctrine).
guidance: Use dependent claims to preserve narrower fall-back positions and to create claim-differentiation-based arguments about scope.

name: Drafting recommendation: explicitly define important claim terms in the specification
description: If you desire that a word in the claim cover a particular structure, state that desire in the specification; explicitly define the word so it has the intended meaning.
guidance: Provide explicit definitional language and examples (sample language provided in report). This helps ensure a POSITA would understand the intended meaning from the specification.

name: Drafting recommendation: use different words in different independent claims when desired
description: Consider using different words in different independent claims to describe the same invention because a claim term is construed consistently wherever used; same word across claims will have same meaning.
guidance: Varying terminology across independent claims can preserve alternative claim scopes that might otherwise be collapsed by consistent term usage.

name: Drafting recommendation: ensure dictionary definitions for important words are not too limiting
description: For important words (technical words or words describing relationships/characteristics), make sure the dictionary definition of that word is not too limiting; define in spec if necessary.
guidance: Proactively define claim terms in the specification to avoid adverse reliance on narrow dictionary definitions during construction.

name: Litigation strategy: argue different independent claims separately
description: Argue different independent claims separately unless those claims have the exact same patentable features.
guidance: Treat each independent claim as potentially having distinct scopes and implications; do not rely on a one-size-fits-all argument for all independent claims.

name: Appellate review and deference debate
description: There is disagreement about whether the Federal Circuit should give deference to trial court claim constructions because claim construction may involve subsidiary factual determinations better resolved by the trial court.
guidance: Be aware of the ongoing debate (Judge Mayer dissent) advocating deference to trial courts on factual components; appellate strategy should account for possible de novo review or arguments for deference where factual findings were central.

name: Three classes of controversies that affect the monopoly
description: Controversies affecting the monopoly take three forms: (1) dispute over legal existence of the monopoly (patentability); (2) dispute over existence of monopoly in favor of the patentee (title); (3) dispute over the character/scope of matters embraced by the monopoly (scope/claim construction).
guidance: Any controversy fitting one of these forms is a patent law case for federal jurisdictional purposes.

name: Form and scope of injunction
description: An injunction must be appropriately tailored in form and scope to the injury and the rights protected, not broader than necessary.
guidance: Scope determined by patent claims, the conduct enjoined, and equitable considerations.

name: Signature, Oath/Declaration/POA handling and limits on signing for clients
description: Practitioner must ensure valid client signatures on Oaths, Declarations, and Powers of Attorney and must not improperly sign a client's name or file documents claiming client signature without proper authorization.
guidance: The engagement letter here purported to accept facsimile, typed between hash marks, email signatures and granted a limited power to sign government patent forms; yet the respondent placed clients' electronic signatures on some applications. Guidance: obtain clear, documented client authorization and avoid forging or otherwise placing client signatures without explicit, informed consent; ensure any limited POA is used only within its lawful bounds and accuracy is confirmed.

name: Board’s range of sanctions for discovery misconduct
description: For failure to provide disclosures or discovery, the Board may impose a variety of sanctions rooted in Fed. R. Civ. P. 37(b)(2), including striking pleadings, refusing to allow support or opposition of claims/defenses, drawing adverse inferences, prohibiting introduction of designated matters, and entering judgment against the disobedient party.
guidance: The Board will not hold any person in contempt or award expenses, including attorneys' fees, to any party. See TBMP § 527.01 for further information. (Cites: Fed. R. Civ. P. 37; 37 CFR § 2.116).

name: Request for grant — form and required contents
description: Request for grant shall be filed on a form drawn up by the EPO; printed forms made available free by authorities under Article 75(1). The request shall contain a petition for grant, the title of the invention (clear, concise, technical; exclude fancy names and indicating claim categories), and name/address/nationality of the applicant.
guidance: Names of natural persons to be family name before given name(s); names of legal entities by official designations; addresses must satisfy postal delivery requirements and include relevant administrative units and house number if any. It is recommended to indicate telegraphic/teletype address and telephone number. If a representative is appointed, their name and address must be included (further content follows in next Rule text).

name: Form of claim determines statutory subject-matter
description: The Office distinguishes between claims by their form (e.g., data structure per se, computer program per se, physical memory storing software, method/process, device/manufacture) when determining whether subject-matter is within the definition of 'invention' in section 2 of the Patent Act.
guidance: A claim that is in form a data structure or computer program per se is generally non-statutory (disembodied). A claim directed to a physical memory storing software or to a device operating the method is in form a statutory manufacture or device, but may still fail if the inventive contribution is non-statutory. Examine whether claimed non-statutory elements limit the technological nature of a statutory element; perform a contribution analysis comparing discrete elements to the prior art.

name: Graphical user interface (GUI) claims
description: A GUI per se is directed to excluded subject-matter by its form; even if generated by a computer program, the claim may still be objected to under section 2 of the Patent Act.
guidance: A method claim that includes statutory steps (e.g., displaying graphical elements and dynamically retrieving information) which together provide a technological solution (e.g., dynamic querying to keep control options current) can be statutory. If the method steps operate together to provide a unitary technological result and are novel/inventive over the prior art, the method may be patentable. If the method is patentable, corresponding device or memory claims that implement the method may also be allowable.

name: Data structures per se are non-statutory
description: The Office considers a data structure to be an abstract idea or plan for organizing data items and not to include the physical medium upon which it is stored; a data structure per se is disembodied and not an invention within section 2 of the Patent Act.
guidance: For a data structure to affect patentability it must in some way limit the technological nature of a statutory element in the claim. A claim defining a data structure alone is directed to non-statutory subject matter by its form. A computer-implemented method using the data structure that changes the technological character of a step (e.g., prioritizing packets using the structure) may be statutory if novel and inventive. A physical memory storing data does not alter the technological character of the memory unless the stored data is part of executable code that renders the computer more efficient or reliable.

name: Physical memory storing data versus executable code
description: A claim to a physical memory is a statutory manufacture in form, but the nature of the stored content matters: data stored on the memory does not alter the technological character of the memory, whereas executable computer code that makes the computer more efficient may do so.
guidance: If the inventive contribution is merely the data, the memory claim may include a discrete non-statutory element and be objected to under section 2 after contribution analysis. If the memory stores executable code that imparts a technological effect (e.g., improves efficiency, reliability), that software-on-physical-memory element can be a statutory contribution.

name: Databases and database management systems (DBMS)
description: A database is interpreted as solely a collection of information and a database per se is disembodied and not an invention within section 2. A database management system is generally understood to be a computer program and thus a computer program per se is not statutory.
guidance: A claim to a physical memory storing a DBMS defines a statutory manufacture in form, but the inventive contribution must alter the technological character of a statutory element. A claim to a system or server that includes software means that provide new technological functionality (e.g., load-tracking control server distributing requests according to server load and synchronizing during light load) can be statutory if the software is novel and inventive.

name: Contribution analysis for mixed statutory/non-statutory claims
description: Where a claim includes both statutory elements (machines, memories, methods) and non-statutory elements (data structures, databases, signals, programs per se), the examiner should perform a contribution analysis to determine whether the claim as a whole contains a statutory contribution.
guidance: Non-statutory features are treated as discrete elements of the claim. If the inventive aspect is non-statutory, object under section 2 of the Patent Act. If the combination of elements (including statutory elements modified by software) provides a technological solution that is novel and inventive, the claim may be allowable.

name: Computer-aided design (CAD) programs and methods
description: CAD programs are specialized computer programs used as tools by designers and may comprise a technological contribution; methods of designing may be viewed as schemes or mental processes which are disembodied and not a practical invention.
guidance: Inventions related to CAD usually focus on the CAD program functionality as a tool. If the CAD method provides a technological solution to a practical problem (e.g., hierarchical optimisation that reduces operations and avoids false minima), the computer-implemented method can be statutory. A CAD program per se (computer program claim) is defective in form unless tied to a statutory medium or device that embodies a technological contribution.

name: Requirement for implementation detail to show technological contribution
description: When claimed steps are essentially known calculations or procedures, merely performing them on a computer does not necessarily provide a statutory contribution; explicit details of how the computer performs the operations or how a technological obstacle is overcome may be required.
guidance: If the sequence of operations to perform the calculations would have been self-evident to a person skilled in the art, there is no technological innovation in enabling the computer to perform them and an objection under section 2 is appropriate. Where implementation details show the computer performs operations in a novel way that overcomes a technical obstacle, these should be claimed to support patentability.

name: Signals (electromagnetic and acoustic) are non-statutory
description: The Office regards electromagnetic and acoustic signals and waveforms to be forms of energy and not material products; claims to signals per se do not constitute statutory subject-matter within section 2 of the Patent Act.
guidance: Signals are transitory in nature. Once information in a signal has been stored on a physical medium it is more appropriately referred to as data; however, claims defining a physical medium storing a signal or waveform are considered indefinite under section 27(4). Methods, processes, machines or manufactures involved in generation, transmission, reception, or processing of signals may be patentable if other patentability criteria (novelty, inventiveness, technological contribution) are satisfied.

name: Device/transceiver claims that include software-enabled encoding
description: A device claim (e.g., a transceiver) that recites means for encoding, transmitting and decoding where some means relate to hardware and others to software may be statutory if the software-enabled encoding modifies technological character and provides a technical advantage (e.g., high-rate transmission while minimizing interference).
guidance: If the software-enabled encoding is novel and inventive, the overall device claim can be allowable because the claim does not include a discrete non-statutory element; evaluate novelty and inventive step of all defined elements in combination.

name: Claims including higher life forms may be salvageable by purposive construction
description: A claim not directed to a higher life form per se but including a higher life form within its scope (e.g., as a component of a composition, as a use) may, depending on purposive construction, be statutory subject-matter.
guidance: For example, a claim to 'an animal feed comprising X' construed as the use of X is likely statutory even if X is a higher life form. When construed as X or a product comprising X, the claim will be non-statutory if X is a higher life form. Where X has been processed by significant chemical or physical modification, the claim may be construed as a manufacture and be statutory.

name: Organs and tissues generally non-statutory
description: Organs and tissues (whether of plant or animal origin) are generally not considered to be manufactures or compositions of matter for purposes of section 2 of the Patent Act.
guidance: Organs and tissues are typically created by complex processes with elements requiring no human intervention and do not consist of ingredients combined or mixed together. Claims directed to organs or tissues should be treated accordingly under subject-matter analysis.

name: Sufficiency of an Office action under 35 U.S.C. § 132
description: Section 132 ensures that an applicant 'at least be informed of the broad statutory basis for [the rejection of] his claims, so that he may determine what the issues are on which he can or should produce evidence.' Section 132 is violated when a rejection is so uninformative that it prevents the applicant from recognizing and seeking to counter the grounds for rejection.
guidance: An Office action must provide enough information specific to the application to place the applicant on notice of the basis for rejections so the applicant can recognize and counter them. The mere inclusion of boilerplate language does not render an Office action insufficient if it still contains enough application‑specific information. (Cites Chester v. Miller and MPEP references.)

name: Reply requirements under 37 CFR 1.111(b) — specificity and completeness
description: The reply must 'distinctly and specifically point out the supposed errors in the examiner's action and must reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the prior Office action.'
guidance: Replies must present arguments pointing out the specific distinctions believed to render the claims patentable over applied references. A general allegation that the claims define a patentable invention without specific explanation does not comply. The reply must appear to be a bona fide attempt to advance the application. Matters challenging examiner reliability/pertinence are appropriate in a 1.111 reply, not via 1.181 petition.

name: Limits on supplemental replies (37 CFR 1.111(a)(2))
description: A reply that is supplemental to a compliant reply will not be entered as a matter of right except as provided; the Office may enter a supplemental reply only if clearly limited to certain categories (e.g., cancellation of claims, adoption of examiner suggestions, placing application in condition for allowance, reply to an Office requirement made after the first reply, correction of informalities, or simplification of issues for appeal).
guidance: A supplemental reply will be entered if filed during a period when Office action is suspended under §1.103(a) or (c).

name: Amendment requirements in reply to a rejection (37 CFR 1.111(c))
description: When amending in reply to a rejection, the applicant must 'clearly point out the patentable novelty which he or she thinks the claims present in view of the state of the art disclosed by the references cited or the objections made' and show how the amendments avoid such references or objections.
guidance: Amendments must make it clear how the changed claim language overcomes the cited art/objections.

name: Patent document organization (four main parts)
description: A patent specification is a legal document that follows a standard organizational format. The typical patent consists of four main parts: Front page(s), Drawings, Specification and Claims.
guidance: Use the conventional structure so examiners and searchers can find information; ensure each part is present and clearly separated (front pages, drawings, specification, claims).

name: Summary of the Invention
description: Briefly describes solutions to the problems and advantages over the prior art as discussed in the background section.
guidance: Often mirrors the broadest independent claim; use it to provide a concise presentation of the inventive concept without introducing limiting language.

name: Drawings (as part of the submission)
description: Drawings are one of the main parts of the patent and support the detailed description and claims.
guidance: Provide clear drawings referenced in the description; use consistent figure numbering and include enough views/detail to support claimed features.

name: Claims define legal scope (format and formality)
description: The numbered claims at the end define the scope of legal protection. Each claim must be a single sentence.
guidance: Draft claims carefully to capture desired scope; claims must be numbered and comply with formal requirements (single-sentence claim structure). Include dependent and independent claims as appropriate to provide fallback positions.

name: Abstract length and purpose
description: A 150-word maximum summary of the technical disclosure on a separate sheet, used by searchers to evaluate relevance.
guidance: Keep within the word limit and summarize the technical disclosure clearly for search and classification purposes; do not use the abstract to add limiting technical detail that would affect claim interpretation.

name: Use consistent terminology
description: Use consistent terminology throughout the specification.
guidance: Consistent terms reduce ambiguity between description and claims and help avoid inadvertent narrowing of scope due to inconsistent phrasing.

name: Disclose multiple embodiments
description: Disclose multiple embodiments of the invention.
guidance: Providing several embodiments and variations helps support broad claim scope and provides fallback positions if certain claim scopes are rejected. Make sure embodiments illustrate alternative implementations.

name: Avoid statements that limit scope
description: Avoid statements that explicitly or implicitly limit the invention (examples: 'the invention must,' 'the invention requires').
guidance: Such absolute or mandatory language can be used to construe and narrow claim scope; prefer permissive language and present features as examples or options rather than requirements.

name: Include features for fallback claim limitations
description: Include all features that may be used as fallback claim limitations.
guidance: Ensure the specification describes features that you may later use to narrow claims during prosecution; anticipate possible rejections and provide descriptive support for dependent claims and claim amendments.

name: Negative expressions in claims
description: Claims containing negative expressions such as 'not being...', 'not having...', 'not requiring...' may be objectionable under subsection 27(4) of the Patent Act because claims should generally set forth what the invention is or does, and not what it is not or does not do, unless there is no positive way to describe it.
guidance: Avoid negative claim language unless no positive way exists. Dependent claims that effectively cancel or negate features of a preceding claim and thereby make the dependent claim broader than the preceding claim are objectionable under subsection 63(4) of the Patent Rules.

name: Completeness of claims (sufficiency/operability)
description: To define the invention distinctly and in explicit terms, sufficient elements must be recited for operability; the inventive features must appear in each claim.
guidance: In compositions, a claim must define a minimum of two ingredients, at least broadly. Claims failing to recite sufficient elements are indefinite and contrary to subsection 27(4) of the Patent Act.

name: Reference to charts, tables and graphs
description: Reference to charts, tables or graphs in claims may be permitted where the invention is very complex and it is practically impossible or extremely cumbersome to define relationships precisely without such references.
guidance: If a chart/table is brief and concise (about 5-10 lines), the applicant may be required to enter it into the claims (subsection 62(1)). Use references to large/complex tabulations only where reproduction in the claim would be impractical.

name: Scope of claim relative to description
description: A claim may be as narrow as the applicant wishes within the scope of the invention disclosed, but must not be broader than the invention as described or supported by the description.
guidance: Claims should be given the meaning and scope normally used in the relevant art unless the description explicitly gives a special meaning. Claims covering subject-matter outside the scope of the described invention should be objected to for failing to satisfy section 60 of the Patent Rules.

name: Ranges within broader described ranges
description: No objection is made to claims directed to narrower ranges that fall within a broader range described in the description even if the narrow range is not specifically shown in the description.
guidance: If the broad claim is anticipated by prior art, the narrower claim will also fall unless restricting to the narrower range produces a new and unobvious result or effect.

name: Dependent claim formal requirements
description: Section 63 permits claims to refer to one or more other claims to define an invention more narrowly by adding further characteristics; a dependent claim must state the additional features claimed and must only refer to preceding claims by number.
guidance: Claims referring to other claims to avoid repetition must not become ambiguous or contravene subsection 27(4). A claim referring to more than one claim must refer to those claims in the alternative only (subsection 63(3)); common phrasing: '…according to any one of claims…'. Examiner should object where there is uncertainty which part of a preceding claim is referred to or where cross-category referencing creates ambiguity.

name: Page numbering of claims
description: Pages of the claims must be numbered consecutively and run continuously from the last page of the description so that the pages of the specification as a whole are numbered consecutively (subsection 50(1) of the Patent Rules).
guidance: Transitional provisions apply for certain filing dates (see section 193 for category 3 applications).

name: Definition and patentability of combinations
description: A combination is a union of elements or process steps cooperating to produce a unitary and practical result that is not the sum of the known characteristics of the elements or steps. A patentable combination is where elements cooperate in an unexpected manner or in a known way to give an unobvious result or effect.
guidance: Subcombinations (parts of a combination) may be claimed. Claims to combinations are allowable if they meet Patent Act and Rules requirements.

name: Exhaustive combinations (scope limits)
description: Claims must not exceed the scope of the invention by going further than the protection to which the inventor is entitled; generally, inventor entitled to claim the invention and its immediate and cooperating environment.
guidance: Claims to larger environments or downstream combinations are objectionable unless the overall combination produces new and unexpected results amounting to further invention (which may require restriction under section 36).

name: Product claims: acceptable definitions
description: A product may be defined by structure, by the process by which it is made (product-by-process), or by physical or chemical properties; mixtures of these forms are possible.
guidance: The most explicit and definite product claims define the product by structure; where structure is known, it should be given in the claim (subsection 27(4) requirement to distinguish new product).

name: Means claims (functional claiming)
description: A 'means' claim defines part of an invention as a means or mechanism for performing an act rather than reciting the element performing the action.
guidance: Claims composed of more than one statement of old means can be allowable if there is invention in the new combination. A single statement of means is objectionable as indefinite (subsection 27(4)). A claim is also objected to if it contains a broad means statement at the point of invention that embraces all possible means (merely restates the problem). Examiner should indicate in detail why a means claim is indefinite. Examples illustrate unacceptable 'means for...' and acceptable claims reciting structure.

name: Guidelines for use claims incorporating steps
description: Use claims are permitted and use claims incorporating method steps are acceptable provided the use is clearly identified and not a method of medical treatment.
guidance: If the claim is complete and understandable without method steps, the claim as a whole is acceptable; method steps serve only to restrict a previously recited use.

name: Markush claims (genus claims)
description: A Markush claim (a genus expressed as 'selected from the group consisting of...') is allowable in chemical cases provided it is clear that the alternatives possess at least one property in common mainly responsible for their function in the claimed relationship.
guidance: Markush format may occasionally be used in mechanical/electrical fields. A Markush should generally cover a group of two or more different materials/elements/compounds with a common functional property; examples given (solvent selected from alcohol, ether, acetone).

name: Definition of 'machine', 'manufacture', and 'composition of matter'
description: Machine: mechanical/physical embodiment of functions where parts cooperate to accomplish an effect; Manufacture: broadly a non-living mechanistic product or process of making technical articles; Composition of matter: physical/chemical substances, compounds and compositions including combinations of ingredients.
guidance: Machines may be claimed as device/apparatus/system. Manufactures are articles made by physical labour or mechanical power (often modern industrial production). 'Composition' implies ingredients perceptible in space and mass; scope limited to avoid redundancy with 'machine' and 'manufacture'.

name: Examples of practitioner misconduct that support discipline
description: Specific acts and omissions cited as the factual basis for discipline include: failing to communicate Notices to File Missing Parts, failing to communicate Office Actions in a timely manner, failing to respond to Office Actions resulting in abandonment, filing non‑compliant amendments (constructive election of another invention), billing for fees not paid to the USPTO, invoicing for more claims than filed, accepting payment without filing (trademark), and over‑charging client for USPTO fees.
guidance: These concrete examples illustrate the types of conduct that violate the cited professional responsibility rules (communication, diligence, thoroughness, safekeeping of funds). The Order also notes mitigation (restitution in form of goods, cooperation, temporary cessation of taking new clients).

name: 102(b)(1)(A) grace period inventor disclosure exception
description: A disclosure which would otherwise qualify as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) is not prior art if: (1) it was made one year or less before the effective filing date of the claimed invention; and (2) it was made by the inventor or a joint inventor, or by another who obtained the subject matter directly or indirectly from the inventor or joint inventor.
guidance: See MPEP §§ 2153.01(a) and related discussion. Office personnel will not apply a disclosure as prior art if it is apparent from the disclosure itself that it is by the inventor or joint inventor (e.g., names the inventor as author and does not name additional authors). If not apparent, applicant may submit evidence (e.g., affidavit/declaration). Applicants may identify grace period disclosures in the specification per 37 CFR 1.77(b)(6) to expedite examination.

name: Mechanisms to overcome a 102(a)(1) or 102(a)(2) rejection — benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 120
description: Overcome a rejection by submitting a benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 120 within the time period set in 37 CFR 1.78 by providing the required reference to a prior application in a corrected application data sheet under 37 CFR 1.76 and by establishing that the prior application satisfies the enablement and written description requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(a), or filing a grantable petition to accept an unintentionally delayed benefit claim under 37 CFR 1.78.
guidance: See MPEP § 211 et seq. This requires showing the earlier application satisfies 112(a) (enablement and written description).

name: Mechanisms to overcome a 102(a)(1) or 102(a)(2) rejection — benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) (provisional)
description: Submit a benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) within the time period set in 37 CFR 1.78 by providing the required reference to a prior provisional application in a corrected ADS under 37 CFR 1.76 and by establishing that the prior provisional satisfies the enablement and written description requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(a), or file a grantable petition to accept an unintentionally delayed benefit claim under 37 CFR 1.78.
guidance: See MPEP § 211 et seq. Establishing 112(a) support in the provisional is required.

name: Mechanisms to overcome a 102(a)(1) or 102(a)(2) rejection — foreign priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d)
description: Submit a claim to priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) within the time period set in 37 CFR 1.55 by identifying a prior foreign application in a corrected ADS under 37 CFR 1.76 and by establishing that the prior foreign application satisfies the enablement and written description requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(a), or file a grantable petition to accept a delayed priority claim under 37 CFR 1.55.
guidance: The foreign priority filing date must antedate the reference and be perfected; perfected filing requires filing a certified priority document (and English translation if necessary) per 37 CFR 1.55(g). See MPEP §§ 213 - 216.

name: Form paragraph 7.15.aia — Rejection 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1)/102(a)(2)
description: Claim(s) [1] is/are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102 [2] as being [3] by [4].
guidance: Examiner Notes: Use only for applications filed on or after March 16, 2013 under AIA 102/103; must be preceded by 7.03.aia and 7.07.aia (may be preceded by 7.08.aia). Use only for specified reference types (U.S. patent under 151, U.S. patent application publication under 122(b), or WIPO publication with earlier effective filing date). Include explanation if using 'anticipated' vs 'clearly anticipated'. For priority-claiming applications filed before March 16, 2013 must be preceded by 7.06.

name: Form paragraph 7.15.01.aia — Provisional rejection 102(a)(2) (copending application with common assignee/applicant/joint inventor)
description: Claim(s) [1] is/are provisionally rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) as being anticipated by copending Application No. [2] which has a common [3] with the instant application. Based upon the earlier effective filing date of the copending application, it would constitute prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) if published or patented.
guidance: This provisional rejection may be overcome by: (1) showing under 37 CFR 1.130(a) that subject matter was obtained from the inventor/joint inventor (102(b)(2)(A)); (2) showing under 37 CFR 1.130(b) of a prior public disclosure (102(b)(2)(B)); or (3) a statement under 102(b)(2)(C) establishing common ownership or JRA. This rejection may not be overcome by filing a terminal disclaimer (In re Bartfeld). Use only for AIA-examined apps filed on/after March 16, 2013 and must be preceded by 7.03.aia.

name: Form paragraph 7.18.aia — Rejection pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g)
description: Claim [1] rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) as being [2] by [3]. (Addresses priority of invention and interference-type determinations.)
guidance: Use only for applications/patents examined under AIA 102/103 that contain or contained a claim to an invention having an effective filing date before March 16, 2013 or a specific reference under 35 U.S.C. 120/121/365(c) to such a claim. Must be preceded by 7.14.aia or 7.103.

name: Claim construction as a whole (broadest reasonable interpretation)
description: For Each Claim, Determine What the Claim as a Whole Covers. Each claim must be separately analyzed and given its broadest reasonable interpretation in light of and consistent with the written description.
guidance: Consider the entire claim including preamble language and the transitional phrase. The examiner should evaluate each claim to determine if sufficient structures, acts, or functions are recited to make clear the scope and meaning of the claim, including the weight to be given the preamble. Limitations may not be imported into the claims from the specification. Case citations: In re Morris; Bell Communications Research v. Vitalink; Corning Glass Works v. Sumitomo.

name: Preamble and transitional phrase treatment
description: The entire claim, including preamble and the transitional phrase (e.g., 'comprising', 'consisting essentially of', 'consisting of'), must be considered in claim construction and support analysis.
guidance: 'Comprising' is open-ended and allows unrecited elements; 'consisting essentially of' occupies a middle ground and, absent clear specification, may be construed equivalent to 'comprising' for 102/103 purposes. If applicant contends exclusion by 'consisting essentially of', applicant bears burden to show additional steps/components would materially change characteristics. See Genentech v. Chiron; PPG Industries v. Guardian Industries; In re De Lajarte.

name: Review entire application for support
description: Review the claims and the entire specification, including specific embodiments, figures, and sequence listings, to understand how applicant provides support for the various features of the claimed invention.
guidance: Also review original claims, abstract, drawings when assessing means-plus-function support. Determine field of invention and level of skill in the art; consider inverse correlation between level of skill and specificity required. Well-known information need not be described in detail. See Wang Labs. v. Toshiba; Hybritech v. Monoclonal Antibodies.

name: Written description standard: possession of claimed invention
description: Determine whether there is sufficient written description to inform a skilled artisan that applicant was in possession of the claimed invention as a whole at filing.
guidance: Possession may be shown by actual reduction to practice, clear depiction in drawings, structural chemical formulas, or any description of sufficient, relevant, identifying characteristics so a skilled person would recognize possession. The inquiry is factual and case-by-case. See Purdue Pharma v. Faulding; Pfaff v. Wells Electronics.

name: Evidence types that can show possession
description: Possession may be evidenced by reduction to practice, detailed drawings, structural/chemical formulas, sequence data, deposits, or identifying characteristics (sequence, structure, binding affinity, molecular weight, etc.).
guidance: Examples: description of constructing an embodiment or performing a process that meets claim limitations; deposit of biological material per 37 CFR 1.801 et seq.; restriction maps, mRNA isolation and expression. Drawings alone can provide written description in appropriate cases. See Cooper v. Goldfarb; Vas‑Cath; UMC Elecs.; Enzo Biochem; Noelle v. Lederman.

name: Function-only definitions are generally insufficient
description: A definition by function alone does not suffice to describe certain claimed subject matter (e.g., coding sequences, chemical compounds) because it indicates what the gene/compound does rather than what it is.
guidance: Function combined with known correlation to structure may suffice in some arts; absent such correlation, function-only disclosure is little more than a wish. See Eli Lilly; Fiers; In re Wilder; Fonar (software exception).

name: Chemical and small-molecule inventions require precise definition
description: An adequate written description of a chemical invention requires a precise definition by structure, formula, chemical name, or physical properties, not merely a plan to obtain the chemical.
guidance: If the specification only discloses assays or methods for identifying compounds without disclosing which compounds achieve the claimed effect, the written description requirement may not be met. See Univ. of Rochester v. G.D. Searle; examples in Fonar.

name: Means-plus-function (35 U.S.C. 112, para. 6) support requirement
description: If a claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112, para. 6 (means- or step-plus-function), it must be interpreted to cover the corresponding structure, materials, or acts in the specification and equivalents.
guidance: The examiner must consider the original disclosure in summary, detailed description, claims, abstract, and drawings. Means-plus-function is adequately described if (1) the written description links particular structure/materials/acts to the function, or (2) one skilled in the art would know what structure/materials/acts perform the function. Rejection under 112, para. 2 cannot stand where 112, para. 1 support exists for means-plus-function recitations. See In re Noll; Supplemental Examination Guidelines; MPEP §2181.

name: Analysis approach for claims to a single species or embodiment
description: For each claim drawn to a single embodiment or species: (A) determine whether the application describes an actual reduction to practice; (B) if not, determine whether there is a reduction to drawings or structural chemical formulas sufficiently detailed; (C) if not, determine whether the invention is set forth in distinguishing identifying characteristics sufficient to show possession.
guidance: If a complete structure is disclosed, the written description requirement is satisfied for that species and a 112, para. 1 rejection must not be made. If complete structure is not disclosed, evaluate whether other identifying characteristics (partial structure, properties, function with known correlation, method of making) would lead skilled artisan to conclude applicant was in possession. See Fields v. Conover; Eli Lilly; In re Wilder.

name: Factors to consider when assessing possession
description: Consider multiple factors: level of skill and knowledge in the art, partial structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics (with known correlation to structure), method of making the claimed invention, and any combination of identifying characteristics that distinguish the claimed invention.
guidance: The determination is factual and depends on art maturity and predictability; disclosure of any combination of such identifying characteristics that would lead one of skill in the art to conclude possession is sufficient. See Eli Lilly; Capon v. Eshhar.

name: Effect of art maturity and predictability on disclosure required
description: The description needed to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112 varies with the nature and scope of the invention and with the scientific/technologic knowledge already in existence; mature, predictable arts require less detailed disclosure than emerging, unpredictable fields.
guidance: In mature technologies where knowledge/skill is high, a written description question generally should not be raised for claims present when originally filed, even if specification discloses only method and function (e.g., microprocessor programming). In contrast, for unpredictable or emerging technologies, more evidence is required; product-by-process claims are satisfied when the process has actually been used to produce the product, but mere description of a process without clear performability may be insufficient. See In re Hayes Microcomputer; Fiers; Amgen.

name: Language and format required when rejecting claims
description: Where a claim is refused for any reason relating to the merits it should be 'rejected' and the ground of rejection fully and clearly stated, and the word 'reject' must be used.
guidance: The examiner should designate the statutory basis by express reference to a section of 35 U.S.C. in the opening sentence of each ground of rejection; explain why rejected as broader than enabling disclosure, point out where indefiniteness resides, or specify elements lacking for incompleteness. Avoid omnibus rejections and grouping claim pluralities unless equally applicable.

name: Unpersuasive Argument: Limitation(s) in Preamble
description: A preamble is generally not accorded patentable weight where it merely recites the purpose of a process or the intended use of a structure and where the body of the claim can stand alone.
guidance: See In re Hirao and Kropa v. Robie. Precede with form paragraph 7.37.

name: State when claims are allowable
description: When claims are allowable, the examiner should state that the claims are allowable in the Office action.
guidance: Designate status clearly (see heading 'State When Claims Are Allowable [R-2]'). Further procedural detail appears elsewhere in the MPEP.

name: Specification must state specific improvement and be limited to it
description: Where the patent is for an improvement of a machine (or an improved machine) the specification must state in what the improvement specifically consists and the claim must be limited to such improvement.
guidance: If the terms are so obscure or doubtful that the court cannot say which particular improvement is claimed and to what it is limited, the patent is void for ambiguity; if it covers more than the improvement it is void for being broader than the invention. (See Barrett v. Hall.)

name: Do not claim prior art as new; distinguish new from old
description: A specification that includes what has been invented before without showing that the patentee does not claim it will render the patent broader than his invention and therefore void; courts cannot reject part of a claim, so any claimed matter that is not new invalidates the patent.
guidance: The patentee must state what he claims as new and what he admits to be old; if the description mixes old and new and does not distinctly ascertain what is claimed, the patent will be void. (Carpenter v. Smith; Lowell v. Lewis; Moody v. Fiske.)

name: Constrain claim to be coextensive with actual discovery
description: A specification should be construed, consistently with the fair import of the language, so as to make the claim coextensive with the actual discovery; patentees are presumed not to intend to claim things already in use.
guidance: Literal words may be limited by context (ejusdem generis, state of knowledge, surrounding phrases) so as not to include unrelated matters; courts should avoid forced constructions that extend claims beyond the facts. (Court of Common Pleas rule; Crossley v. Beverly; Winans v. Providence R.R.)

name: Affirmatively state what is new and negatively what is old
description: The usual form is to state affirmatively the patentee's new features, and, when using anything old, to state negatively that he does not claim that thing.
guidance: Patentee is not confined to precise wording, but should sum up and distinguish the invention. Good drafting practice is to describe the whole subject and then point out the parts which are old and those which constitute the improvement. (Wyeth v. Stone; Godson on Patents.)

name: Describe existing (old) apparatus sufficiently and disclaim it, then state the improvement
description: When claiming an improvement, the prior apparatus or machine should be set forth sufficiently to make known what the patentee engrafts his improvement upon; he should disclaim the invention of the old parts and state his improvement distinctly.
guidance: Failure to identify the old parts and then state clearly what is added can render the specification defective (illustrated by Nichols v. Ross and Holmes v. L. & N.W.R.W.). The specification should show how the patentee's additions differ from the old structure.

name: Avoid vagueness in the manner of describing the invention
description: A common defect is vagueness or ambiguity in the description that makes it difficult or impossible to determine what the invention is (distinct from mere ambiguous terms).
guidance: Examples: directions that leave uncertain which materials are to be treated (Turner v. Winter); claiming an entire machine by inserting unnecessary parts or numbers (King v. Arkwright). If a whole class is claimed but only one member works, the specification misleads. The specification must enable the public to know what is claimed.

name: Generic claims and variations: disclose best modes but claiming equivalents is permitted
description: If a particular effect can be produced in several modes, it is sufficient for the patentee to state the modes he contemplates as best; claiming variations (substitutes of a like character) will not render the claim void so long as the combinations claimed are substantially new.
guidance: The patentee may claim substitutes or alternative modes of carrying out the invention provided he has invented them or they are substantially new; broad/generic claims are acceptable when they are coextensive with the invention. (Phillips on Patents; Ryan v. Goodwin — matches example.)

name: Ambiguity as to scope (e.g., size, range) invalidates claims
description: If the specification leaves it uncertain whether the claim is for any size (or other broad scope) or only particular sizes/types, that uncertainty can render the specification bad.
guidance: Example: a cable-holder claim uncertain whether for one cable of whatever size or for holders adaptable to different sizes was held defective. (Hastings v. Brown.)

name: Courts give liberal construction to patents to protect real inventors when possible
description: If, taking the specification as a whole, the court can perceive the exact nature and extent of the claim, it should adopt an interpretation that gives full effect to the inventor's rights rather than defeat them for minor ambiguity.
guidance: Principle expressed as ut res magis valeat quam pereat: ambiguities should, where reasonable, be resolved to preserve valid claims provided the invention's nature and extent are discernible from the specification as a whole. (Ryan v. Goodwin and related authorities.)

name: Language of filing
description: Applicants must file their patent application, including the specification, in the official language of the country of filing (or English where permitted). The language of filing is used as the language of the proceedings and for any amendments.
guidance: If filed in a language other than an official/authorized language, a translation of the specification (title, abstract, claims, description and drawings) must be filed within a specified period or upon request of the patent office.

name: Documents and information required for filing
description: Specific documents and information that must accompany a patent filing (e.g., specification, claims, abstract, drawings, applicant details, priority documents where relevant).
guidance: Requirements vary by AMS; the Guidelines list required filing documents per AMS and note that failure to provide required documents may affect filing date or require completion within set periods.

name: Priority claims from multiple applications
description: Rules for claiming priority from multiple earlier applications (including order, evidence, and effect on entitlement).
guidance: Guidance on formalities for claiming priority and documentation required to support multiple priority claims is provided (see Question 6).

name: Medical methods, surgical/therapeutic and diagnostic method exclusions
description: Whether methods for treatment of humans/animals by surgery, therapy or diagnosis are excluded from patentability and how such claims are treated.
guidance: Chapter 5.2.7 explains national positions and permissible claim drafting (e.g., use claims, medical use claims) across AMS.

name: Clarity requirements for claims and description
description: Conditions necessary for clarity of the invention in claims and description; claims must be clear and supported by description and drawings.
guidance: Chapter 7 (7.1–7.11) lists clarity conditions, prohibited terms, rules for drawings, multiple dependencies, one-part/two-part claim forms, multiple independent claims, use claims, product-by-process claims, ranges, limitations, disclaimers, and imprecise terms.

name: Rules for drawings and figures in relation to clarity
description: Standards for drawings and figures to support claims and description with respect to clarity requirements.
guidance: Chapter 7.3 specifies formatting, labelling, and how drawings interact with descriptions and claims to meet clarity.

name: Multiple dependencies and multiple independent claims
description: Permissibility and treatment of multiple dependent claims and multiple independent claims in the same application.
guidance: Chapters 7.4 and 7.6 explain limitations, allowable forms and how such claims affect fees, unity and clarity assessments.

name: Support requirement — claims must be supported by description and drawings
description: Claims (independent and dependent) need to be supported by disclosure in the description and drawings; lack of support is a ground for objection.
guidance: This principle is emphasised in Chapter 7 and reiterated in Chapters on sufficiency and amendments; amendments to claims may require corresponding description amendments (Chapter 7.14 / 13.4).

name: Definition of novelty and novelty test
description: Definition of 'novelty' and the tests applied to determine whether claimed subject-matter is novel.
guidance: Chapter 10.1–10.2 set out novelty definitions and approaches including absolute novelty, state of the art, technical equivalents and combination attacks (Chapter 10.3 series).

name: ASPEC work-sharing procedures and requirements
description: Procedural rules for requesting ASPEC acceleration/work-product sharing, required documents (written opinion/IPER/WO/ISA reports), and eligibility criteria (including at least one allowable claim).
guidance: Chapters 14.3 and 14.4 set out ASPEC and PCT-ASPEC request procedures, documents required, local agent requirements, claims correspondence table, e-ASPEC options, and country-specific quirks (tables listing AMS requirements).

name: Foreign language reference translation completeness
description: If a foreign-language prior art reference was cited/discussed previously but never completely and accurately translated into English, a reexamination request that provides a complete and accurate translation explaining how the reference meets claim requirements may justify reliance on that reference in reexamination.
guidance: The requester should explain why a more complete and accurate translation actually teaches what is required by the patent claims; Portola Packaging does not necessarily prohibit reexamination when a fuller translation establishes prior art content.

name: Required notices when terminating/withdrawing under Portola Packaging
description: When prosecution is terminated or rejections withdrawn to comply with In re Portola Packaging, the Office must include specific language in Notices of Intent to Issue Ex Parte Reexamination Certificate or in Office actions withdrawing rejections.
guidance: Example required wording for termination: 'The prosecution of this reexamination is terminated based on In re Portola Packaging, Inc., 110 F.3d 786, 42 USPQ2d 1295 (Fed. Cir. 1997). No patentability determination has been made in this reexamination proceeding.' Example wording for withdrawn rejections: 'The rejection(s) based upon _______ is/are withdrawn in view of In re Portola Packaging, Inc., ... No patentability determination of the claims of the patent in view of such prior art has been made in this reexamination proceeding.'

name: Content requirements for first and subsequent Office actions
description: The examiner’s first Office action on the merits should clearly establish the issues between the examiner and patent owner and be sufficiently detailed to permit a proper final action subsequently.
guidance: The first action must set forth pertinency and manner of applying cited prior art to each claim; if the request includes claim charts, the examiner may incorporate them but must carefully review to ensure incorporated items clearly and completely address patentability. Subsequent actions must address all patent owner responses. If claims are found patentable, the examiner should indicate why in a manner similar to reasons for allowance (MPEP §1302.14) and may refer to record portions establishing patentability. The first action should caution the patent owner that a complete response is required because the next action is expected to be final and that 37 CFR 1.116(b) requirements will be strictly enforced after final action.

name: Use of patent owner statements in claim interpretation
description: If the examiner relies upon a patent owner statement submitted under 37 CFR 1.501(a)(2) in the detailed explanation, the reexamination requester must explain how that statement is being used to determine the proper meaning of a patent claim in connection with prior art applied to that claim.
guidance: That explanation will be considered by the Office in drafting the Office action to determine the scope of the claims subject to reexamination; reliance on such statements must be explicit and supported.

name: Requirements for patent owner replies to Office actions
description: Replies must be written and must distinctly and specifically point out supposed errors in the examiner’s action, reply to every ground of objection/rejection, and present arguments showing specific distinctions believed to render the claims patentable over applied references.
guidance: A reply must appear to be a bona fide attempt to advance the application or reexamination to final action. A general allegation that the claims define a patentable invention without specific argument does not comply. In amending, the applicant must clearly point out the patentable novelty and show how amendments avoid references or objections.

name: Supplemental reply entry conditions
description: Supplemental replies are not entered as a matter of right except in limited categories; the Office may enter a supplemental reply only when it is clearly limited to specified subjects or filed while Office action is suspended.
guidance: Categories (37 CFR 1.111(a)(2)(i)) permitting entry include: (A) cancellation of claim(s); (B) adoption of examiner suggestions; (C) placement in condition for allowance; (D) reply to an Office requirement made after the first reply was filed; (E) correction of informalities (typographical errors); (F) simplification of issues for appeal. A supplemental reply filed during a suspension period (§1.103(a) or (c)) will be entered.

name: General procedural rules under 37 CFR 1.550 (conduct of ex parte reexamination)
description: Ex parte reexaminations are to be conducted with special dispatch, provide minimum response periods, and include rules on what submissions are permitted and how participation of third‑party requesters is limited.
guidance: Key points: (a) proceedings conducted with special dispatch and will result in issuance of ex parte reexamination certificate under §1.570; (b) patent owner given at least 30 days to respond to any Office action and may submit statements, proposed amendments, or new claims to place patent in allowable condition; (c) extensions only for sufficient cause with petition fee; (d) failure to file timely/appropriate response leads to terminated prosecution and issuance of certificate per last Office action; (e) reexamination requester will be sent copies of Office actions and its active participation ends with the reply under §1.535 — no further submissions will be considered except as permitted by §§1.510, 1.535, or entered prior to order for reexamination per §1.525; (f) documents filed after order must meet requirements of §1.501(a); (g) documents filed by either party must be served on the other per §1.248 or may be refused consideration.

name: Literal infringement of means-plus-function claims (§112, ¶6)
description: To establish literal infringement of a means-plus-function patent claim, [the patent holder] must prove two things: (1) that the accused device employs a structure [act] identical or equivalent to the structure [act] described in the patent, and (2) that the relevant structure [act] in the accused device performs the identical function specified in the claim.
guidance: Where the structures are not identical, the patent holder must prove by a preponderance (more probable than not) that the accused structure is equivalent to the disclosed structure. Two structures are equivalent if a person of ordinary skill in the art would consider the differences insubstantial. Determine whether the accused structure performs the identical function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result, or whether persons of ordinary skill would have considered the structures interchangeable at the time of patent grant. Note: §112, ¶6 requires identical, not equivalent function; equivalence under §112, ¶6 and the doctrine of equivalents are not coextensive.

name: Inducing patent infringement — elements
description: A party induces patent infringement if it purposefully causes, urges, or encourages another to infringe. To prove inducement, the patent holder must prove it is more probable than not that: (1) the alleged infringer actively encouraged or instructed another person on how to [use a product or perform a process] in a way the jury finds infringes the patent claims; (2) the alleged infringer knew of the patent; (3) the alleged infringer knew or should have known that the encouragement or instructions would induce infringement; and (4) the other person infringed the patent.
guidance: The patent holder must prove specific intent to induce infringement — knowingly inducing infringement, not merely knowingly inducing acts that constitute infringement. There must be proof of a direct infringement for each instance of indirect infringement. (See 35 U.S.C. §271(b).)

name: Enablement requirement (sufficiency to make and use)
description: A patent claim is invalid if the specification does not disclose sufficient information to enable one skilled in the field to make and use the claimed invention. The alleged infringer must prove it is highly probable that the claim was not enabled.
guidance: Patents are written for persons skilled in the art and need not state what such persons would likely know. The need for some experimentation does not necessarily mean lack of enablement. Factors to consider for undue experimentation include: (1) quantity of experimentation necessary; (2) amount of direction or guidance in the patent; (3) presence or absence of working examples; (4) nature of the invention; (5) state of the prior art; (6) relative skill of those in the art; (7) predictability of the art; and (8) breadth of the claims. (See In re Wands and cited authorities.)

name: Best mode requirement
description: If the inventor knew of a best way, or 'mode,' of making and using the claimed invention when filing the application, the specification must contain a description of that mode.
guidance: Determining best mode involves two questions: (1) At filing, did the inventor know of a mode of making or using the invention that the inventor considered better than any other (a subjective inquiry)? If no, stop — no best mode failure. (2) If yes, does the patent contain a description of that best mode sufficient to enable a skilled person to carry it out without undue experimentation (an objective enablement inquiry)? If both are proven highly probable, the claims are invalid. The purpose is to ensure full disclosure to the public.

name: Anticipation — novelty (public use/known or previously published)
description: A claim is anticipated (not new) if all of its requirements existed in a single device or method that predates the claimed invention, or were described in a single prior publication or patent that predates the claimed invention. The alleged infringer must prove it is highly probable the claim was anticipated.
guidance: The disclosure in the prior reference need not use the same words as the claim, but all claim requirements must be present, either stated or necessarily implied, such that someone of ordinary skill could make and use the claimed invention. Ways to show anticipation include: prior public knowledge or use in the U.S., prior patent or printed publication anywhere in the world (if reasonably accessible), prior issued U.S. patent or published U.S. patent application (subject to applicable dates). If invention date is disputed, the jury must determine the date of invention.

name: Statutory bars (timeliness / one-year bars)
description: A patent may be invalid if the applicant failed to meet statutory timing provisions — i.e., certain events occurred more than one year before the patent application filing date (statutory bars). For invalidity by a statutory bar, all claim requirements must have been present in a single prior art reference dated more than one year before the application.
guidance: Ways to show statutory bar (choose applicable): prior printed publication anywhere in the world more than one year before filing (reasonably accessible to interested persons); public or commercial use in the U.S. more than one year before filing (not primarily experimental use); sale or offer for sale in the U.S. more than one year before filing where the claimed invention was ready for patenting (actually built or sufficiently detailed drawings/descriptions); or a foreign patent application filed more than one year before the U.S. application. The prior reference disclosure need not use the same words as the claim but must disclose all requirements in enough detail to enable a skilled person to make and use the claimed invention. (See 35 U.S.C. §102(b), Pfaff, etc.)

name: Obviousness (non‑statutory invalidity under Graham/KSR)
description: A claim is invalid as obvious if the claimed invention would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the field of the invention at the relevant time. Even if no single prior art reference anticipates, the combination of prior art may render the claim obvious.
guidance: Do not determine obviousness with hindsight; put yourself in the position of a person of ordinary skill at the time. Consider whether there was a reason that would have prompted such a person to combine prior art elements as the claimed invention does (teachings, suggestions, motivations may come from written references or the ordinary skill knowledge, or from the nature of the problem). Additional factual inquiries: (1) level of ordinary skill in the art; (2) scope and content of the prior art (what references are pertinent/analogous); (3) differences between the claimed invention and the prior art. Consider whether the innovation applied a known technique used to improve a similar device/method, or whether it would have been obvious to try (a small number of predictable options with reasonable expectation of success). Also consider secondary factors tending to show nonobviousness (e.g., commercial success, long-felt need, unsuccessful attempts by others, copying, unexpected results, acceptance/licensing, prior art criticizing the invention) and factors tending to show obviousness (e.g., independent invention by others). The asserted invalidity must be proven highly probable by the party asserting it.

name: Establish a prima facie case with clear articulation
