description: The key to supporting any rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 is the clear articulation of the reason(s) why the claimed invention would have been obvious; analysis supporting a rejection should be 'made explicit'.
guidance: Rejections cannot be sustained with mere conclusory statements; there must be articulated reasoning with some rational underpinning (citing KSR, In re Kahn). The examiner must explain why a person of ordinary skill would have found the invention obvious, and link factual findings to the legal conclusion.

name: Resolve the Graham factual inquiries
description: The examiner must resolve the Graham inquiries (scope and content of the prior art; differences between prior art and claims; level of ordinary skill; and objective indicia/secondary considerations) before applying obviousness rationales.
guidance: Any additional factual findings based on the Graham inquiries that are necessary in view of the facts of the case must be made and explained to support a conclusion of obviousness.

name: Rationale A — Combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results
description: To use this rationale, examiner must find (1) prior art included each claimed element (not necessarily in a single reference); (2) one of ordinary skill could have combined the elements by known methods and each element performs the same function as separately; (3) a person of ordinary skill would have recognized that the results were predictable; and (4) any additional Graham-based findings necessary to explain obviousness.
guidance: The rationale is that all claimed elements were known and their combination yields nothing more than predictable results (KSR). If any of these findings cannot be made, this rationale cannot support obviousness. Examples illustrate 'predictable results' requirement and situations where combining fails (Adams, Omeprazole, Crocs, Sundance). Examiners must identify a reason that would have prompted combination.

name: Rationale G — Teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art to modify or combine
description: Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art that would have led one of ordinary skill to modify the prior art reference or combine teachings to arrive at the claimed invention may support obviousness.
guidance: Per Ball Aerosol, explicit teaching of a motivation to combine in the prior art is not always required; the court's analysis must be explicit and may rely on inferences, common sense, and ordinary ingenuity — but the examiner must articulate the chain of reasoning linking prior art to the claimed combination.

name: Consider teachings that 'teach away' as evidence against obviousness
description: If the prior art teaches away from the claimed modification or combination, this weighs against an obviousness finding.
guidance: Examples (Adams, Puno/DePuy, Crocs) show that when prior art discourages the proposed change or points to disadvantages, combination may be nonobvious even if elements are present in the prior art. Examiners must identify and explain such teach-away evidence when present.

name: Require reasonable expectation of success/ability to optimize
description: A reasonable expectation of success and the technical ability to optimize parameters (if claimed invention rests on optimization) are relevant to whether an invention would have been obvious.
guidance: Ecolab and In re O'Farrell underscore that absent the expectation of success or the ability to optimize within ordinary skill, obviousness may not be supported. Examiners should explain whether optimization was within ordinary skill and whether an expectation of success existed.

name: Written description requirement (§112)
description: Section 112 requires that the specification contain a written description of the invention. An adequate written description “reasonably conveys to those skilled in the art that the inventor had possession of the claimed subject matter as of the filing date.” (Ariad).
guidance: Applied in contexts including claims to genera, claims with negative limitations, and claims that assert only one of multiple solutions disclosed. The newsletter reviews how courts analyze sufficiency (possession) as distinct from but related to enablement; factual circumstances and state of the art matter. Examples and cases: Ariad, Boston Scientific, Santarus, Crown Packaging.

name: Disclosing a genus of compounds
description: “[A] sufficient description of a genus requires the disclosure of either a representative number of species falling within the scope of the genus or structural features common to the members of the genus so that one of skill in the art can ‘visualize or recognize’ the members of the genus.” (Ariad).
guidance: No bright-line rule for how many species or how much detail is necessary; depends on invention and state of the art. Functional descriptions of a genus may be insufficient if the specification lacks definitions, examples, or criteria to identify members without guess-and-check (Boston Scientific). Functional claim language can meet written description only if an established correlation between structure and function is disclosed or known in the art. Courts give weight to whether the specification gives guidance for identifying working members of the genus.

name: Support for negative claim limitations
description: Negative claim limitations (expressly excluding subject matter) are adequately supported when the specification describes a reason to exclude the relevant limitation.
guidance: Per Santarus, written-description support for a negative limitation need not rise to the level of disclaimer; describing disadvantages of the excluded subject matter can suffice (example: no-sucralfate limitation supported by specification statements and incorporated material). There is a judicial split in reasoning: Judge Newman observed that a reason to exclude may not always be necessary (negative limitations can arise during prosecution to distinguish prior art). Be aware of both the panel rule and concurring/dissenting views.

name: Claims covering one of multiple disclosed solutions
description: When a specification discloses multiple concurrent solutions to related problems, written description issues may arise if claims cover just one solution but that solution is not disclosed independently from the others.
guidance: Key question: does the specification (including original claim language) demonstrate possession of an embodiment that achieves the claimed improvement without requiring the other solution? Per Crown Packaging (citing Revolution Eyewear), it is not automatically invalid to claim only one of related solutions; invalidity arises if the spec shows the solutions must be practiced together or does not disclose the single-solution embodiment. Courts will examine whether the specification teaches the solutions as independent ways to achieve the benefit or as necessarily combined.

name: Enablement of the full scope of claims (open-ended ranges)
description: The specification must enable one of ordinary skill to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation; it must contain sufficient disclosure to enable an ordinarily skilled artisan to make and use the entire scope of the claimed invention at the time of filing.
guidance: Prevent inadequate disclosure and overbroad claiming. A broad claim scope (e.g., asserting much larger performance or ranges than demonstrated at filing) is invalid if the specification does not provide a reasonable expectation that the full claimed scope can be achieved without undue experimentation (Magsil example: specification showed 11.8% change but claims asserted far larger changes achieved only years later; court affirmed lack of enablement). Later advances in the field do not cure a lack of enablement at filing. Policy: enablement prevents overbroad claims and preserves incentives for follow-on inventions.

name: Definiteness requirement (claims must particularly point out and distinctly claim)
description: Section 112 requires that the specification “conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter” of the invention—the definiteness requirement.
guidance: Definiteness can be implicated where the specification fails to provide adequate disclosure of the structure corresponding to claimed functions (interplays with means-plus-function analysis). Failure to set forth adequate disclosure may be treated as failure to particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention. Cases such as Noah Systems illustrate how definiteness and corresponding-structure disclosure overlap for functional claim elements.

name: Means-plus-function (112(f)) for computer-implemented limitations — corresponding structure / algorithm
description: An element expressed as a means or step for performing a specified function is construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof. When the claimed function entails particular programming, the specification must disclose an algorithm for performing the claimed function.
guidance: If the function is one any general-purpose computer can perform in a generic way (e.g., processing, receiving, storing), disclosure of a general-purpose computer may suffice. If the function requires particular programming, the spec must disclose an algorithm (which may be expressed as a mathematical formula, prose, flow chart, or other understandable terms). Partial disclosure of an algorithm supporting some but not all claimed functions may be treated as if no algorithm was disclosed for definiteness purposes (Noah Systems). The disclosure must identify the method for performing the function even if a skilled artisan might otherwise glean it from other sources.

name: Claim form and related §112 provisions under the AIA
description: The AIA (effective for applications filed on/after Sept. 16, 2012) revised Section 112 to a subsection format and set out claim-form rules: (c) claims may be independent, dependent, or multiple dependent; (d) dependent claims must reference a previous claim and specify a further limitation; (e) multiple dependent claims must refer in the alternative only to more than one prior claim, cannot serve as a basis for another multiple dependent claim, and are construed to incorporate by reference all limitations of the particular claim considered.
guidance: The addition of subsection headings under the AIA will likely end the practice of referring to Section 112 paragraph numbers (e.g., 112 ¶1, ¶6). Practitioners should follow the formal claim-drafting constraints for dependent and multiple dependent claims in prosecution and drafting.

name: Best mode disclosure and its post-AIA treatment
description: Section 112 continues to require that the specification “set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor … of carrying out the invention.”
guidance: The AIA (Leahy-Smith America Invents Act) eliminated failure to disclose the best mode as a ground for invalidity in litigation: under amended §282, failure to disclose best mode cannot be a basis for canceling or holding a patent claim invalid or unenforceable. Best mode remains a formal requirement in patent applications and can be the basis for PTO rejection during prosecution, but not a post-grant invalidity defense.

name: Micro entity qualification elements (37 C.F.R. § 1.29 / MPEP § 509.04)
description: In order to qualify as a micro entity, patent applicants must certify that: (1) the applicant qualifies as a small entity as defined in § 1.27; (2) neither the applicant nor the inventor nor a joint inventor has been named as the inventor or a joint inventor on more than four previously filed patent applications; (3) neither the applicant nor the inventor nor a joint inventor, in the calendar year preceding the calendar year in which the applicable fee is being paid, had a gross income ... exceeding three times the median household income for that preceding calendar year; and (4) neither the applicant nor the inventor nor a joint inventor has assigned, granted, or conveyed, nor is under an obligation by contract or law to assign, grant, or convey, a license or other ownership interest in the application concerned to an entity that ... had a gross income ... exceeding three times the median household income for that preceding calendar year.
guidance: See generally 37 C.F.R. § 1.29; MPEP § 509.04. The page emphasizes applicants must make these specific factual certifications in writing to claim micro entity fees.

name: Concise description of asserted relevance required
description: 37 CFR 1.290(d)(2) requires a concise description of the asserted relevance of each item identified in the document list; this is a statement of facts regarding the submitted evidence and not itself evidence.
guidance: The concise description should set forth facts explaining how the item is of potential relevance to examination. It may be narrative or a claim chart and is most effective when it draws the examiner’s attention to specific relevant pages, lines, figures, or paragraphs.

name: Concise description must be more than bare statements
description: At a minimum, a concise description of relevance must be more than a bare statement that the document is relevant (e.g., 'Document 1 is relevant' is insufficient).
guidance: Annotated/highlighted copies alone are not proper concise descriptions. Avoid mere form paragraphs or general opposition statements. Focused descriptions (intro plus claim chart mapping portions to claim elements) are appropriate; verbose narratives that merely repeat claim charts or approach the length of the documents are discouraged.

name: Maintain a permissive institution threshold for inter partes reviews
description: The bill raises the initiation threshold to where the Director must find 'a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail with respect to at least one of the claims challenged in the petition.' The existing standard asks whether a petition raises a 'substantial new question of patentability.'
guidance: Preserve the existing 'substantial new question of patentability' standard because (as noted) the majority of inter partes reexaminations initiated under the current standard have been ultimately deemed meritorious; a stricter/unclear standard risks rejecting legitimate petitions at the outset without sufficient inquiry.

name: Plant patent claim formalities
description: The claim shall be in formal terms to the new and distinct variety of the specified plant as described and illustrated, and may also recite the principal distinguishing characteristics. More than one claim is not permitted.
guidance: Applies to plant patent claims: single claim only; must formally claim the new distinct variety and may include principal distinguishing characteristics (see § 1.164).

name: Reissue application required contents
description: An application for reissue must contain the same parts required for an application for an original patent, complying with all the rules relating thereto, and in addition, must comply with the requirements of the rules relating to reissue applications.
guidance: Specifically, the entire specification including the claims and the drawings of the patent must be furnished (copy of printed patent in double-column format), and copies of any disclaimer, certificate of correction, or reexamination certificate issued in the patent must be included (see § 1.171 and § 1.173(a)). No new matter may be introduced.

name: Reissue specification and drawing copy requirements
description: The entire specification, including the claims, of the patent for which reissue is requested must be furnished in the form of a copy of the printed patent, in double column format, each page on only one side of a single sheet of paper. Applicant must submit a clean copy of each drawing sheet of the printed patent at filing.
guidance: If the drawing copy complies with § 1.84, no further drawings required. The Office will not transfer drawings from the patent file to the reissue application; copies of certain issued certificates/disclaimers must be included (see § 1.173(a)(1)-(2)).

name: Amending the specification (text) in reissue
description: Changes to the specification, other than to the claims, must be made by submission of the entire text of an added or rewritten paragraph, including markings pursuant to paragraph (d), except that an entire paragraph may be deleted by a statement deleting the paragraph without presentation of the text.
guidance: Must identify the precise point where any added or rewritten paragraph is located; follow special rules for large tables, program listings, and sequence listings (see § 1.173(b)(1)(i)-(ii)).

name: Claim status and support for claim changes
description: Whenever there is an amendment to the claims, there must be supplied, on pages separate from the pages containing the changes, the status (i.e., pending or canceled), as of the date of the amendment, of all patent claims and of all added claims, and an explanation of the support in the disclosure of the patent for the changes made to the claims.
guidance: Provide a clear claim status list and a support explanation to show basis in the original disclosure for each change (see § 1.173(c)).

name: Marking convention for changes in reissue
description: The matter to be omitted by reissue must be enclosed in brackets; and the matter to be added by reissue must be underlined.
guidance: Markings apply to specification and claims (excluding certain large tables and listings per the rule) and are mandatory when changes are made by incorporation or amendment paper (see § 1.173(d)).

name: Office-requested amendment for correspondence
description: The disclosure must be amended, when required by the Office, to correct inaccuracies of description and definition, and to secure substantial correspondence between the claims, the remainder of the specification, and the drawings.
guidance: If the Office determines inconsistencies exist, applicant must amend the disclosure to align claims, specification, and drawings (see § 1.173(f)).

name: Inventor's oath/declaration requirements for reissue
description: The inventor’s oath or declaration for a reissue application must, in addition to complying with other oath requirements, specifically identify at least one error pursuant to 35 U.S.C. 251 being relied upon as the basis for reissue and state that the applicant believes the original patent to be wholly or partly inoperative or invalid by reason of a defective specification or drawing, or by reason of the patentee claiming more or less than the patentee had the right to claim in the patent.
guidance: If the reissue seeks to enlarge claim scope, the oath/declaration must identify a claim sought to be broadened. The oath/declaration must be executed by each inventor or, in certain circumstances, by an assignee per the rule; supplemental oaths required if errors not previously covered are corrected (see § 1.175). Variations exist for pre-AIA filings (see § 1.175 (pre-AIA)).

name: Multiple reissue applications rules
description: If applicant files more than one application for the reissue of a single patent, each such application must contain in the first sentence of the specification a notice stating that more than one reissue application has been filed and identifying each reissue application by relationship, application number and filing date.
guidance: Each claim of the patent being reissued must be presented in each reissue application as amended, unamended, or canceled with the same claim numbers. The same claim may not be presented in its original unamended form for examination in more than one of the multiple reissue applications. The Office may suspend action, merge applications, or refuse issuance of an application that contains only unamended claims and does not correct an error (see § 1.177).

name: Intentional delay is not 'unintentional' — examples
description: A delay resulting from a deliberately chosen course of action on the part of the applicant is not 'unintentional' within 37 CFR 1.137(b).
guidance: Examples of deliberate decisions that preclude finding unintentional delay include: (A) applicant does not consider claims patentable over outstanding references; (B) applicant does not consider allowed/patentable claims of sufficient breadth/value to justify expense; (C) applicant does not consider any patent sufficiently valuable; (D) applicant does not consider any patent to maintain an interest; (E) applicant remains interested but seeks to defer fees and prosecution expenses. A later change of mind does not convert an intentional abandonment into an unintentional delay.

name: 35 U.S.C. § 112, fifth paragraph (multiple dependent claim construction)
description: "A multiple dependent claim shall be construed to incorporate by reference all the limitations of the particular claim in relation to which it is being considered."
guidance: The plain statutory text communicates that a multiple dependent claim is the equivalent of several single dependent claims; each alternative must be construed with the limitations of the particular claim to which it refers. This supports treating each alternative version of a multiple dependent claim as a separate dependent claim for patentability analysis.

name: 37 C.F.R. § 1.75(c) (multiple dependent claim construction and fee treatment)
description: "[A] multiple dependent claim shall be construed to incorporate by reference all the limitations of each of the particular claims in relation to which it is being considered." and "For fee calculation purposes . . . a multiple dependent claim will be considered to be that number of claims to which direct reference is made therein."
guidance: Regulatory language mirrors § 112(5) and expressly ties fee calculation to each referenced claim, implying each alternative is treated separately (e.g., a multiple dependent claim referring to two independent claims is charged as two dependent claims). Use this to justify separate analysis of each alternative dependency.

name: 35 U.S.C. § 282 (presumption of independent validity of each claim)
description: "Each claim of a patent (whether in independent, dependent, or multiple dependent form) shall be presumed valid independently of the validity of other claims; dependent or multiple dependent claims shall be presumed valid even though dependent upon an invalid claim."
guidance: Section 282 requires treating the validity (patentability) of each claim independently. Reading § 112(5) to allow one invalidated version of a multiple dependent claim to invalidate all versions would conflict with § 282. Thus, presumption of validity supports separate consideration of each alternative dependency.

name: USPTO / MPEP guidance on multiple dependent claims
description: MPEP § 608.01(n)(I)(B)(4): a multiple dependent claim "does not contain all the limitations of all the alternative claims to which it refers, but rather contains in any one embodiment only those limitations of the particular claim referred to for the embodiment under consideration," and "a multiple dependent claim must be considered in the same manner as a plurality of single dependent claims."
guidance: Examiner guidance explicitly instructs treating multiple dependent claims as multiple single dependent claims. The MPEP provides examples (e.g., canceling one base claim while another remains results in the corresponding version being canceled/confirmed separately) — use these practice examples when evaluating/prosecuting multiple dependent claims.

name: Preponderance of the evidence standard in IPR
description: In inter partes review, the petitioner must establish unpatentability by a preponderance of the evidence.
guidance: When assessing claims (including multiple dependent claims), the Board determines unpatentability based on whether the petitioner has met the preponderance burden. If petitioner fails to show unpatentability of a particular version (e.g., the version depending from claim 1), that version should be found not unpatentable even if another version (e.g., depending from claim 2) was shown unpatentable.

name: Legislative history and international treaties (PCT Rule 6.4) support
description: PCT Rule 6.4 and the legislative adoption in Public Law 94-131 show the U.S. provision was intended to mirror PCT treatment: dependent claims (including multiple dependent) are construed to include the limitations of the particular claim in relation to which they are considered.
guidance: Legislative history and international harmonization (PCT Rule 6.4) corroborate reading § 112(5) to require per-alternative construction and analysis. Cite the legislative adoption when arguing for or interpreting multiple dependent claims.

name: Case-law principle: address claims individually where scopes materially differ
description: Where claims differ in scope in an aspect material to the analysis, those claims must be addressed individually (citing Dayco Products).
guidance: If different alternative dependencies produce materially different claim scopes, the tribunal must evaluate patentability for each scope separately rather than grouping them. Prior cases (Dow Chemical, Dayco) emphasize independent treatment and presumption of validity, and indicate courts/tribunals should not treat multiple dependent claim versions as a unit without analysis of each.

name: Board/tribunal practice caution: prior decisions do not imply blanket invalidation
description: A prior Board or court statement finding a multiple dependent claim invalid may have been directed only to particular asserted alternatives and not to all alternative dependencies.
guidance: Do not infer that earlier decisions invalidating a multiple dependent claim applied to all versions unless the decision explicitly addressed each alternative; analyze the decision's scope to determine which versions were actually considered. Rely on the record to establish which alternative dependencies were before the tribunal.

name: 37 CFR 1.111(b) — Applicant reply/required traverse
description: Applicant must distinctly and specifically point out the supposed errors in the Office’s action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the Office action. The reply must present arguments pointing out the specific distinction believed to render the claims patentable over any applied references.
guidance: If applicant disagrees with factual findings, an effective traverse must include a reasoned statement explaining why the applicant believes the Office has erred as to the factual findings. A mere statement that the Office has not established a prima facie case or that reliance on common knowledge is unsupported by documentary evidence is not substantively adequate under 37 CFR 1.111(b). Examiners may repeat the prior rejection and make the next Office action final if traverse is inadequate (see MPEP §706.07(a)).

name: Consideration of applicant’s rebuttal evidence
description: Office personnel should consider all timely rebuttal evidence submitted by applicants when reevaluating any obviousness determination.
guidance: Rebuttal evidence may include secondary considerations (e.g., commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others) and evidence of unexpected results. Examples of applicant demonstrations include: (A) one of ordinary skill could not have combined the claimed elements by known methods (technological difficulties); (B) elements in combination do not merely perform the same function they perform separately; (C) the results of the claimed combination were unexpected. Once rebuttal evidence is presented, the Office should reconsider the obviousness determination in view of the entire record, review all rejections and bases for continued viability, and clearly communicate findings and conclusions. Follow MPEP §706.07(a) and MPEP §2145; consider affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132 per MPEP §716–§716.10.

name: Substantive content of the prior art (what the prior art teaches/supports)
description: Assess the substantive content of prior art with respect to issues like availability of inoperative devices, whether the prior art must be enabling, broad disclosures vs preferred embodiments, and admissions.
guidance: See MPEP §2121–§2129 for relevant case law. Examiner must evaluate whether the prior art would have taught, suggested, or made enabling the claimed subject matter to a person of ordinary skill.

name: Pre-AIA §103(c) — applicant burden to show conditions apply
description: An applicant subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 who wants to rely on pre-AIA §103(c) benefits bears the burden of establishing that the subject matter used in a §103 rejection and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, owned by or subject to assignment to the same person.
guidance: For joint research agreement benefits under pre-AIA §103(c) (applicable to certain pending dates), the applicant must establish: (A) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on/before the invention date; (B) the invention was made as a result of activities within the scope of that agreement; and (C) the application discloses or is amended to disclose the parties to the agreement. See MPEP §706.02(l)(1)–(l)(2) and cited case law (e.g., Ex parte Yoshino, In re Bartfeld).

name: Analogous art requirement for use in §103 rejections
description: To rely on a reference under 35 U.S.C. §103, the reference must be analogous prior art to the claimed invention.
guidance: A reference is analogous if: (1) it is from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention (even if addressing a different problem); or (2) it is reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor. 'Reasonably pertinent' means the reference would have logically commended itself to an inventor addressing the problem. Examiner may include a statement of understanding of the problem and should consider the specification and inferences a person of ordinary skill would draw. See KSR, In re Bigio, In re Icon Health & Fitness, and In re Klein for guidance and tests. Applicant arguments that a reference is nonanalogous should be fully considered in light of the specification.

name: Analogy in the design arts — same general use requirement
description: For design patents, a prior design is of the type claimed if it has the same general use as that claimed in the design application.
guidance: Court and Board decisions (e.g., In re Rosen, Ex parte Pappas, In re Butera) illustrate when furniture designs or feed bunk designs are analogous or nonanalogous depending on general use and designer's scope of knowledge. See MPEP §1504.03 for more.

name: Differences between prior art and claimed invention — consider claim and prior art as whole
description: Ascertaining differences between the prior art and the claims requires interpreting claim language and considering both the invention and the prior art references as a whole.
guidance: The §103 inquiry is whether the claimed invention 'as a whole' would have been obvious, not whether individual differences would have been obvious. See relevant claim interpretation law (MPEP §2111–§2116.01) and cases (Stratoflex, Schenck, In re Hirao) illustrating how admitted unobvious portions can make the combination nonobvious when viewed as a whole.

name: Do not distill the invention to a 'gist' or 'thrust' — respect 'as a whole' requirement
description: Reducing an invention to a single gist or thrust disregards the statutory requirement to analyze the subject matter 'as a whole.'
guidance: Avoid narrowing consideration to one advantage or isolated limitation (see W.L. Gore, Bausch & Lomb, Jones v. Hardy, Panduit). Examiners must consider all claim limitations and the entire claimed combination.

name: Applicants alleging discovery of a problem source must provide substantiating evidence
description: Applicants who claim they discovered the source of a problem must substantiate that allegation with evidence.
guidance: Substantiation may be by affidavit or declaration or by clear and persuasive assertions in the specification. Unsubstantiated attorney argument is insufficient (see In re Wiseman, In re Kaslow). Examiners should require appropriate support for such allegations.

name: Intentional/deliberate abandonment precludes 'unintentional' finding
description: A delay resulting from a deliberately chosen course of action on the part of the applicant (e.g., concluding claims are unpatentable, deferring prosecution/fees, deciding patent has insufficient value) is not 'unintentional' within 37 CFR 1.137(b).
guidance: Examples of deliberate courses of action that preclude unintentional delay include: (A) applicant does not consider claims patentable over references; (B) applicant does not consider allowed/patentable claims of sufficient breadth to justify expense; (C) applicant does not consider any patent of sufficient value to justify expense; (D) applicant does not consider any patent of sufficient value to maintain interest; (E) applicant seeks to defer fees and prosecution expenses. A subsequent change of mind does not convert a prior deliberate decision into 'unintentional.'

name: Prior use by others (one person) can defeat novelty
description: Prior use or knowledge by any other person (not the applicant) is sufficient to defeat a claim of being the inventor, unless excluded by other statutory limitations.
guidance: The term 'others' in the statute was intended to mean any person other than the patentee; a single prior user can be enough if the use/knowledge was in a manner accessible to the public.

name: Construction of a patent claim is a question of law for the court
description: "The construction of a patent, including terms of art within its claim, is exclusively within the province of the court."
guidance: The Court holds claim construction is a legal determination for the judge (not the jury). The opinion affirms that interpreting the words in the claim to determine scope is a judicial function and must be decided as a matter of law. (See also Winans v. Denmead: first issue is construing the letters-patent — question of law.)

name: Distinction between claim construction (law) and infringement (fact)
description: "The first is a question of law, to be determined by the court, construing the letters-patent... The second is a question of fact, to be submitted to a jury."
guidance: Patent cases have two separable elements: (1) construing the patent (judge) and (2) determining whether a defendant's product/process falls within that construction (jury on infringement). Courts must 'lay down to the jury the law which should govern them' on factual issues once construction is judicially determined.

name: Where no direct antecedent exists, compare to earlier practices and draw best analogy
description: When the old practice provides no clear answer, the modern practice should be compared to earlier practices whose allocation to court or jury is known, and the best analogy drawn.
guidance: Use precedent and analogical reasoning (Granfinanciera, Tull) to classify 'mongrel' practices. The Court compares modern claim construction to historical practices (e.g., construction of specifications, land patents) to determine allocation.

name: Specification must enable; claims define the scope of the invention
description: A patent contains a specification describing the invention 'in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to make and use the same.' 35 U.S.C. §112. Claims 'particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the applicant regards as his invention.'
guidance: Specification (enablement/description) and claims (particular pointing-out) serve different functions. Claims 'define the scope of a patent grant' and must be construed to determine what is covered. Claims cover machines, manufactures, compositions, or processes — not abstract functions or scientific explanations.

name: Judges are better positioned than juries to construe technical patent terms
description: A judge, from his training and discipline, is more likely to give a proper interpretation to highly technical patents than a jury and is in a better position to ascertain whether an expert's proposed definition fully comports with the instrument as a whole.
guidance: Functional considerations favor judicial construction: judges have training in interpreting documents, can perform sophisticated analysis of the patent 'as a whole,' ensure internal coherence between claims and specification, and apply specialized doctrines developed by courts and the Patent Office.

name: Distinguish documentary construction from 'evidence in pais' (physical identity issues)
description: Bischoff held that it is not the construction of the instrument, but the character of the thing invented (its outward embodiment), which may be sought by evidence in pais and presented to a jury.
guidance: When the dispute concerns the physical identity or characteristics of an accused device (outward embodiment), expert evidence to the jury on identity/diversity is appropriate. By contrast, the legal interpretation of documentary terms (the claim language) remains for the court.

name: Credibility disputes alone are rarely sufficient to convert construction into a jury issue
description: There could be a case in which a simple credibility judgment would suffice to choose between experts... But our own experience with document construction leaves us doubtful that trial courts will run into many cases like that.
guidance: Even when experts offer competing meanings, courts expect that resolution typically requires sophisticated analysis of the patent as a whole, subsuming credibility into legal interpretation. Simple credibility determinations are exceptional and do not generally warrant submission of claim construction to a jury.

name: Public policy: clarity of patent limits is essential for innovation and public notice
description: The limits of a patent must be known for the protection of the patentee, the encouragement of the inventive genius of others and the assurance that the subject of the patent will be dedicated ultimately to the public.
guidance: Ambiguity about claim scope creates a 'zone of uncertainty' that discourages invention. Judicially consistent claim construction helps provide notice to the public and protect both patentees and potential innovators; this policy supports treating construction as a legal issue.

name: Additional applicable fees (size/claims/RCE)
description: If applicable, pay application size fee (specification/drawings exceed 100 sheets, 37 CFR 1.16(s)), excess independent claim fee (independent claims > 3, 37 CFR 1.16(h)), excess claim fee (claims > 20, 37 CFR 1.16(i)), and, if requesting prioritized examination for an RCE, the RCE fee (37 CFR 1.17(e)).
guidance: Include these fees at filing if they apply; warnings will be shown if required fees are unchecked.

name: DOCX requirement to avoid Non‑DOCX surcharge
description: The specification, claims, and abstract for a new utility nonprovisional patent application must be filed in DOCX format in order to avoid a Non‑DOCX surcharge (up to $400).
guidance: Applicants may also optionally submit an Auxiliary PDF of their application, but must upload it in the appropriate space to avoid the Non‑DOCX surcharge.

name: Particular treatment and prophylaxis consideration (Step 2A Prong Two)
description: A claim reciting a judicial exception is not directed to the judicial exception if it also recites additional element(s) demonstrating that the claim as a whole integrates the exception into a practical application; one way to demonstrate such integration is when the additional elements apply or use the recited judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition.
guidance: Explanation and examples (Vanda Pharm. v. West-Ward): using a law of nature to effect a safer treatment (e.g., genotyping assay + dose adjustment) can render claims not 'directed to' the judicial exception at Step 2A. Examples of treatments/prophylaxis include acupuncture, administration of medication, dialysis, organ transplants, phototherapy, physiotherapy, radiation therapy, surgery, immunization steps that lower risk of later disease (Classen).

name: Claim limitation must affirmatively recite an action that effects treatment or prophylaxis
description: To qualify as a 'treatment' or 'prophylaxis' limitation, the claim limitation must affirmatively recite an action that effects a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition.
guidance: Positive examples: 'administering amazonic acid to a patient', 'administering a course of plasmapheresis to a patient.' Non-examples: intended use or field-of-use language (e.g., 'prescribing a topical steroid to a patient with eczema' is not positive because it does not require actual use), mere recitations that a product is a 'pharmaceutical composition' or that a device 'is operable to dispense' are not affirmative treatment limitations.

name: Inventive concept definition (Step 2B): additional elements must amount to 'significantly more'
description: An 'inventive concept' is furnished by an element or combination of elements recited in the claim in addition to (beyond) the judicial exception, and is sufficient to ensure the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception itself.
guidance: The inventive concept cannot be supplied by the unpatentable law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea itself. Evaluate whether additional elements, individually or in combination, provide significantly more than the judicial exception so that the claim amounts to eligible subject matter.

name: Consider additional elements both individually and in combination
description: Evaluating whether additional elements amount to an inventive concept requires considering them both individually and in combination to ensure they amount to significantly more than the judicial exception itself.
guidance: Consideration in combination is important because individually conventional elements can amount to significantly more when non-conventionally arranged (e.g., BASCOM: remote installation of filtering tool with customizable features). Courts consider claim elements 'as a whole' (Diamond v. Diehr).

name: Conventionality / routine character is relevant but distinct from novelty/obviousness
description: Although courts evaluate conventionality of an additional element in eligibility analysis, the search for an inventive concept is not a novelty (§102) or obviousness (§103) determination.
guidance: Lack of novelty under §102 or obviousness under §103 is 'of no relevance' to the §101 question of whether a claim falls within patent-eligible categories. The inventive concept inquiry is distinct: an inventive concept can be found in a non-conventional and non-generic arrangement of known, conventional pieces (e.g., BASCOM, Rapid Litigation Mgmt. v. CellzDirect). Patentability under §§102/103 is neither required for nor dispositive of §101 eligibility.

name: Effecting a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing
description: A claimed process that effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing can supply an inventive concept.
guidance: Example: transformation of raw, uncured synthetic rubber into precision-molded products (Diehr). See MPEP § 2106.05(c).

name: Adding a specific limitation beyond well-understood, routine, conventional activity or adding unconventional steps that confine the claim
description: Adding a specific limitation other than well-understood, routine, conventional activity in the field, or adding unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application, may supply an inventive concept.
guidance: Example: non-conventional and non-generic arrangement of computer components for filtering Internet content (BASCOM) — the arrangement, though consisting of known components, was non-conventional and provided significantly more. See MPEP § 2106.05(d).

name: Use judicial decisions as analytic examples when conducting the 'significantly more' analysis
description: When conducting the Step 2B significantly more analysis, courts' approaches (e.g., Alice, BASCOM, DDR, Diehr, Vanda, Mayo) provide models for: identifying additional elements, considering elements individually, and considering them as an ordered combination.
guidance: Alice: identified additional elements (computer functions/hardware), found them well-understood/routine and the combination added nothing significantly more. BASCOM: emphasized evaluating arrangement in combination, where non-conventional arrangement of known elements supplied an inventive concept. Use these case analyses to guide claim parsing and weighing of elements.

name: Photographs — when black and white photos are allowed
description: Photographs (including photocopies) are not ordinarily permitted but will be accepted if they are the only practicable medium for illustrating the claimed invention (e.g., electrophoresis gels, blots, autoradiographs, cell cultures, histological sections, animals, plants, in vivo imaging, thin layer chromatography plates, crystalline structures, and ornamental effects in design applications).
guidance: Photographs must be of sufficient quality that all details are reproducible in the printed patent; if the subject admits illustration by drawing, the examiner may require a drawing instead. Black and white photographs submitted in lieu of ink drawings must comply with 37 CFR 1.84(b) and no petition/fee is required for black and white photographs; only one set of photographs is required.

name: Views — number, type, grouping, and placement
description: The drawing must contain as many views as necessary to show the invention; views may be plan, elevation, section, or perspective; detail views on larger scale may be used.
guidance: All views must be grouped together and arranged on the sheet(s) without wasting space, preferably upright, clearly separated from one another, and must not be included on sheets containing the specification, claims, or abstract. Views must not be connected by projection lines and must not contain center lines (except as specified); waveforms may be connected by dashed lines to show relative timing.

name: Numbering of views and single-view rules
description: Different views must be numbered in consecutive Arabic numerals starting with 1, independent of sheet numbering, and in the order they appear if possible. Partial views forming one complete view must use the same number followed by a capital letter.
guidance: View numbers must be preceded by the abbreviation "FIG.". If only a single view is used in an application to illustrate the claimed invention, it must not be numbered and "FIG." must not appear. Numbers/letters identifying the views must be simple, clear, not enclosed, and larger than numbers used for reference characters.

name: 37 CFR 1.703(a)(5) — longer-than-four-months after a final decision by the Board or a federal court
description: The period is the number of days, if any, beginning on the day after the date that is four months after the date of a final decision by the Patent Trial and Appeal Board or by a federal court in an appeal under 35 U.S.C. 141 or a civil action under 35 U.S.C. 145 (where at least one allowable claim remains) and ending on the mailing date of either an action under 35 U.S.C. 132 or a notice of allowance under 35 U.S.C. 151, whichever occurs first.
guidance: Key definitions: 'allowable claims remain in the application' means at least one pending claim not withdrawn and not subject to rejection/objection; examples (A–C) illustrate allowable vs. objected claims. For a Board decision to count, it must sustain or reverse rejections on appeal (or in limited cases a remand may be deemed a decision). A 'final decision' means last decision in the review by the Board (or federal court) that does not require further applicant action to avoid termination; a decision containing a new ground of rejection under 37 CFR 41.50(b) is not 'final' for this purpose.

name: 37 CFR 1.703(e) — periods for successful appeal
description: The period of adjustment under 37 CFR 1.702(e) is the sum of the number of days, if any, from the date jurisdiction passes to the PTAB under 37 CFR 41.35(a) (or 41.31 for earlier regimes) and ending on the date of a final decision in favor of the applicant by the Board or a federal court in an appeal under 35 U.S.C. 141 or a civil action under 35 U.S.C. 145.
guidance: Federal Circuit precedent (SawStop; Chudik) requires both (1) reversal of an adverse determination of patentability and (2) issuance of the patent 'as a result of that reversal' for the adjustment to apply. A claim that issues only after substantive post-appeal prosecution/amendment that materially changes the claim may not satisfy 'issued under a decision in the review reversing an adverse determination of patentability.'

name: Accurate drafting that captures novelty
description: Write patent applications that accurately capture an invention’s new and novel nature to firmly protect it against later claims.
guidance: Emphasis on drafting that reflects the invention's novel aspects precisely—this is presented as key to preventing later challenges and securing robust protection.

name: Presumption against fraud; doubtful claims construed in patentee's favor (ut res magis valeat quam pereat)
description: Fraud is never to be presumed; in doubtful cases the patentee is presumed to intend to claim no more than his actual invention. The maxim ut res magis valeat quam pereat guides construction toward supporting a claim if it can be done without violating principle.
guidance: If after fair construction doubt remains whether a claim is broader than the invention, adopt the rule favorable to the patentee; but where a claim manifestly admits of no construction but an invalidly comprehensive one, the rule does not apply.

name: Patent protects fair fruits of actual invention, not a broader monopoly
description: The Patent Law establishes no monopoly beyond the fair fruits of actual invention; it protects the real inventor in the enjoyment of what he first produced, and recognizes as substantive inventions changes introducing new characteristics, results, or advantages.
guidance: The law proceeds on encouraging inventive activity while limiting appropriation to the inventor's actual contribution; known properties and laws remain common property except as applied in the inventor's claimed subject-matter.

name: When specification includes old matter, two inquiries determine overclaiming
description: To determine whether the patentee has included in his claim anything that existed before, inquire (1) whether he makes use of anything not new, and (2) whether that thing, according to the fair import of his language, is represented to be part of the invention claimed.
guidance: The first is a question of evidence; the second invokes principles of construction. If claim is doubtful, apply presumption against overclaiming; if claim clearly includes old matter, the patent is unsupported.

name: Patent may remain valid pro tanto after real invention is ascertained
description: Where a claim is broader or narrower than the real invention, provisions of the law may allow a patent to remain valid pro tanto, after the real invention of the party has been judicially ascertained.
guidance: This mitigates harsh consequences of over- or under-claiming by allowing partial validity anchored to the actual invention.

name: Substantive arguments to raise in POR
description: Common substantive challenges include missing claim elements, claim construction disputes, status of references as prior art, anticipation arguments (including inherency), and obviousness arguments (show motivation to combine, sufficient explanation, and address secondary indicia of non-obviousness).
guidance: POR should comprehensively address anticipation and obviousness theories — attack motivation, reasoning, and present affirmative evidence of non-obviousness (secondary indicia). Use factual development and expert support where appropriate.

name: Remand to consider amendment
description: There is no obligation resting on the Board to consider new or amended claims submitted while it has jurisdiction of the appeal. However, a proposed amendment filed after the date of filing of a brief to either cancel claims (where cancellation does not affect the scope of any other pending claim), or to rewrite dependent claims into independent form may be remanded for consideration by the examiner. If the proposed amendment is in effect an abandonment of the appeal, the appeal will normally be dismissed by the Board.
guidance: See MPEP §1206. Board may remand for limited classes of post-brief amendments; amendments that abandon the appeal generally result in dismissal.

name: Board decision options: affirm, reverse, remand (37 CFR 41.50(a))
description: The Board, in its decision, may affirm or reverse the decision of the examiner in whole or in part on the grounds and on the claims specified by the examiner. The Board may also remand an application to the examiner. The affirmance of a rejection on any of the grounds specified constitutes a general affirmance except as to any ground specifically reversed.
guidance: When a substitute examiner's answer follows a remand, appellant must within two months either reopen prosecution (request prosecution be reopened under §1.111) or maintain the appeal (file a reply brief under §41.41). Actions taken affect whether the appeal is withdrawn/maintained.

name: Partial amendment + rehearing handling
description: If an appellant files an appropriate amendment/new evidence as to less than all claims rejected under 41.50(b), and requests rehearing as to the remainder, the examiner will not consider the claims for which rehearing was requested. The request for rehearing will be considered by the Board after prosecution with respect to the first group of claims is terminated.
guidance: Argument as to claims rejected by the Board not accompanied by appropriate amendment/new evidence will be treated as a request for rehearing as to those claims.

name: Treatment when examiner is reversed in whole
description: A complete reversal of the examiner’s rejection brings the case up for immediate action by the examiner. The examiner should not regard such a reversal as a challenge to make a new search to uncover other and better references; the second examiner should give full faith and credit to the prior examiner’s search.
guidance: If examiner has specific knowledge of references indicating nonpatentability of appealed claims, they should submit the matter to the TC Director or CRU Director for authorization to reopen prosecution under 37 CFR 1.198; such requests for rehearing by the examiner must state with particularity points misapprehended and are limited to new arguments based on recent relevant decisions. All examiner rehearing requests require approval by the TC/CRU Director and Deputy Commissioner for Patent Examination Policy before mailing.

name: Consequences if examiner sustains rejections in whole or in part
description: If the examiner is sustained in whole or in part and claims require action, proceedings may be considered terminated in certain circumstances (e.g., dismissal of appeal), but where claims are allowed or the nature of the decision requires further action by the examiner, prosecution continues as required.
guidance: See 37 CFR 41.35 for jurisdictional end points; examiner must follow applicable MPEP guidance (e.g., §1214.06) when further action is required.

name: Provisional patent (patent-pending) considerations
description: If you have a provisional patent (patent pending), it is possible to begin negotiating with licensees, although reduced royalties are likely to be a condition of the contract.
guidance: Consider licensing the invention as a 'trade secret' or include a provision that also covers trade secrets so the licensee cannot use the invention if a patent isn't eventually granted. Be explicit about contingencies if a patent application fails, changes in claim scope, and how that affects royalties/rights.

name: Preparing to initiate licensing (procedural readiness)
description: If you still need to patent your IP, you may choose to work with an online service provider so that you'll be ready to initiate future patent license agreements.
guidance: Use filing services or templates to secure provisional/design/utility patents and assemble documentation necessary for valuation and negotiation (e.g., prosecution history, claim scope, commercialization plans) before engaging licensees.

name: Challenger limitation: no participation after filing
description: Patent challenger generally cannot participate in the reexam after filing of initial request.
guidance: This limits challengers' ability to respond to amendments or newly added claims during prosecution, ceding procedural control to patent owner and examiner.

name: Common early large-volume claim additions
description: Common for Patent Owners to add large volume of claims before first office action.
guidance: Filing preliminary amendments or many new claims early is a frequent owner tactic to reshape claim scope and create fallback positions.

name: Broader claim interpretation standard (BRI) risk
description: Jeopardizes validity of issued patent, given broader claim interpretation standard (BRI).
guidance: EPRx applies broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI), which may increase vulnerability of claims compared to district court claim construction standards.

name: Consider damages impact of potential amendments
description: Is damages impact from potential amendments palatable?
guidance: Owners must evaluate whether narrowing or changing claims during EPRx will materially reduce infringement damages or enforcement leverage.

name: Amend at the first Office Action; add narrowing new claims
description: Take advantage of the opportunity to amend claims: amend at the first Office Action, rather than waiting; even if maintaining the original claims, add amended versions as new claims; add new claims (must be narrowing compared to original claims).
guidance: Early, narrowing amendments can preserve rights and present fallback claim sets to the examiner.

name: Provide declaration evidence when appropriate
description: Provide declaration evidence when appropriate.
guidance: Affidavits/declarations can support patentability positions, rebut art, or establish facts relevant to claim amendments.

name: Identification of international application (Box I)
description: The applicant should clearly identify the international application by its international application number, international filing date and title, as provided for in Box No. I. If a new title has been established by the International Searching Authority, that title should be indicated.
guidance: Use the prescribed date format (refer to paragraph 5.061); when multiple priority claims exist, indicate the earliest priority filing date as the priority date; a file reference (≤25 characters) may be added (see paragraph 5.017).

name: Authority limitations/conditions that exclude search
description: If the Authority finds that carrying out the supplementary search is entirely excluded by a limitation or condition in its Agreement with IB (other than Article 17(2) limitation), it will declare the request not to have been submitted and notify applicant and IB; if not entirely excluded, it may restrict the search to certain claims and indicate this in the report.
guidance: Consult the Authority's Agreement (ISA/IPEA agreements and Annex SISA) for the scope and any exclusions (see paragraph 8.041).

name: Required content of Section 8 disclosure
description: Disclosure must set out 'detailed particulars' of corresponding foreign applications—examples include country name, application number, status of such applications, objections raised, orders passed on grounds of novelty or patentability, amendments made to specifications and claims, claims allowed, search and examination reports, and other prosecution details.
guidance: Ayyangar Report envisaged comprehensive disclosure (objections, orders, amendments) to aid proper examination. Under Section 8(2) the Controller may request these prosecution particulars; the earlier Rules expressly allowed summons of examination reports/dockets. An anti-pattern is supplying only basic bibliographic patent identifiers while omitting prosecution history or objections.

name: Use of foreign prosecution information as an examination criterion
description: Disclosure of foreign prosecution status and particulars is 'one of the criteria for evaluating and approving a patent application' and assists examiners in assessing novelty, inventive step and claim scope.
guidance: Timely, detailed foreign prosecution information improves patent quality and helps prevent frivolous grants and evergreening. Anti‑pattern: treating Section 8 disclosures as mere formalities or relying solely on limited databases, which can perpetuate information asymmetry and lower examination quality.

name: Claim clarity / public notice
description: Lack of clarity in patent claims increases costs because it makes understanding the invention and determining what prior art to search for more difficult; unclear terms can perpetuate lack of clarity in new claims and lead to disparate beliefs about litigation outcomes.
guidance: Clarity reduces USPTO information costs and helps patentees, potential licensees, competitors, and courts assess scope and validity. Even if only a portion of patents require detailed claim construction, a mostly costless interpretive-rule change that minimizes notice problems is worthwhile. Examples and citations show effects on negotiations, settlement likelihood, and investor behavior.

name: Broadest reasonable construction (BRC) rule in prosecution
description: The USPTO applies the broadest reasonable construction rule during prosecution (claims given their broadest reasonable interpretation), which tends toward broader claim meanings and thus broader prior art searches.
guidance: BRC may increase prior-art search breadth and lead to over-rejection during prosecution; it can also produce claim meanings during prosecution that differ from later litigated meanings. Examples include BPAI and dictionary-driven constructions (e.g., Motoyama). The article critiques using BRC in litigation.

name: PHOSITA / ordinary-meaning rule during prosecution
description: Claims should be given their ordinary meaning to a person having ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA) at the time of filing, which fixes claim meaning to an ascertainable reference and aligns with examiners' understanding.
guidance: Applying PHOSITA in prosecution promotes clearer, more consistent claim meanings, reduces the risk that issued patents perpetuate vagueness, and leverages examiners' skill rather than dictionary expedients. Examples (Motoyama, American Academy) illustrate how ordinary-meaning readings would yield different outcomes.

name: Consistency between prosecution and litigation
description: Differing interpretive standards between the USPTO and courts cause harms: uncertainty, increased litigation costs, repeated preparation after reversals, and potentially inconsistent claim meanings.
guidance: If courts sometimes construe claims more broadly than examiners did, parties' expectations diverge, leading to broken settlements and expensive litigation (e.g., Eolas, Phillips discussions). The Markman hearing and resulting construction are often the most important and costly part of patent cases.

name: Use of specification for context but caution against importing limitations
description: Courts should use the specification for contextual understanding of claim terms but must avoid improperly importing limitations from the specification into the claims.
guidance: Phillips (Fed. Cir. en banc) encouraged reliance on the specification for context while acknowledging the difficulty in distinguishing permissible interpretation from impermissible limitation. The specification is a primary source, but its use must preserve claim scope where appropriate.

name: Dictionary definitions should not be primary source in litigation
description: Relying on dictionary definitions as the first source of claim meaning was criticized (Phillips), because it led some courts to give broader meanings than the USPTO had used during prosecution.
guidance: Courts should avoid treating dictionaries as dispositive; instead, look to intrinsic evidence (claim language, specification, prosecution history) and use dictionaries only where appropriate. Overreliance can produce overly broad constructions and poor public notice.

name: Presumption in favor of narrower meaning to preserve validity
description: Where there is an equal choice between a broader and a narrower meaning of a claim, adopt the narrower meaning because it best serves the notice function and helps preserve patent validity.
guidance: This interpretive presumption supports limiting ambiguous claims to avoid ensnaring unwary infringers and aligns with long-standing justifications for narrow construction in litigation where claims cannot be amended (Athletic Alternatives, other citations).

name: Avoid using BRC in litigation
description: Applying the broadest reasonable construction rule in litigation is ill-advised because it conflicts with the presumption favoring narrower meanings and would be likely to invalidate patents by reading them broadly against prior art.
guidance: Two primary reasons: (1) it conflicts with the policy of adopting narrower meanings to preserve validity and public notice; (2) BRC is designed to reject claims and so would improperly increase the risk that true inventions are invalidated in litigation where claims cannot be amended.

name: Risk of over- or under-inclusion (ensnaring and undercoverage)
description: Ambiguous or improperly construed claim terms can both ensnare unintended products (too broad) and fail to cover inventions the patentee intended (too narrow).
guidance: Case examples: Motoyama (BPAI’s broad dictionary reading made 'electronic mail' cover unrelated data packets over the Internet while excluding local-network email the applicant intended) and In re American Academy (broad reading of 'user computer' to include mainframes). These show practical harms from poor constructions.

name: Preserving validity vs. rejection efficiency tradeoff
description: While BRC may be acceptable during prosecution to reject weak applications (because amendments are possible), applying a rule aimed at rejecting patents in litigation (where claims cannot be amended) is contrary to the Patent Act’s directive that novel and nonobvious inventions be patentable.
guidance: Narrow construction in litigation serves to preserve validity; BRC's primary purpose of over-rejecting is inconsistent with adjudicative settings. The article emphasizes using PHOSITA during prosecution to limit invalidation risk.

name: Issuing more patents under PHOSITA may have benefits
description: Applying PHOSITA in prosecution could lead to more patents issuing (narrower claims are likelier to be valid), and issuing more patents could increase searchable prior art that helps invalidate weak patents later.
guidance: Although issuing more patents could be seen as overprotective, it may be beneficial because published or issued patents become prior art and improve the body of searchable prior disclosures; supporting recommendations in Part VI may further limit issuance of undesired patents.

name: Clarity (Art. 84)
description: Clarity (Art. 84) of claims and specification is a formal requirement.
guidance: Part F provides guidance on assessing clarity and claim drafting requirements under Article 84 EPC.

name: Recorded terminal disclaimer cannot be nullified after patent or reexamination certificate issues
description: After a patent or reexamination certificate issues, a recorded terminal disclaimer will not be nullified; mechanisms to correct patents (certificate of correction, reissue, reexamination, IPR, PGR, CBM) are not available to withdraw or nullify the effect of a recorded terminal disclaimer.
guidance: Public policy disfavors restoring to the patent owner what was dedicated to the public. Certificate of Correction (35 U.S.C. 255) is limited to clerical/typographical/minor mistakes and corrections that do not constitute new matter or require reexamination. Reissue (35 U.S.C. 251) cannot be used to withdraw a terminal disclaimer because reissue cannot extend the unexpired part of the original patent term and recapture principles bar restoring disclaimed term. Case law cited: In re Jentoft; Altoona Publix Theatres v. American Tri-Ergon Corp.; In re Yamazaki; Ball Corp. v. United States; Ex parte Anthony; In re Dinsmore. Also nullification would improperly enlarge the vertical scope of claims (Board remarks).

name: Focus on structure, not method of use
description: You should absolutely focus on structure, not on the method of use. Differences in the method of use will only come into play if you are claiming a new and nonobvious method of using, which is typically not the case.
guidance: In majority of cases protect the device/apparatus (structural features); don't rely on use-differences unless you are claiming a distinct method claim.

name: 37 C.F.R. 1.75(e) Jepson claim template (regulatory guidance)
description: (e) Where the nature of the case admits, as in the case of an improvement, any independent claim should contain in the following order: (1) A preamble comprising a general description of all the elements or steps of the claimed combination which are conventional or known, (2) A phrase such as 'wherein the improvement comprises,' and (3) Those elements, steps, and/or relationships which constitute that portion of the claimed combination which the applicant considers as the new or improved portion.
guidance: This is the CFR-referenced template describing Jepson-format claims. The article notes the rule but warns against following it blindly; use only where truly appropriate.

name: Avoid Jepson claims in most circumstances
description: Claiming done as Rule 75(e) suggests is known as writing a claim in Jepson format ... No patent attorney in their right mind would follow this suggestion. A Jepson claim is not something that you must employ and it comes with significant disadvantages with only the most nuanced of advantages that present in a very rare circumstance.
guidance: Jepson claims create admissions and limitations that can harm claim scope and prosecution options. The author strongly recommends avoiding Jepson claims except in rare, specific situations.

name: Jepson preamble elements are treated as prior art / claim limitations
description: When using the format of Rule 75(e) the preamble is considered to positively and clearly include all the elements or steps recited therein as a part of the claimed combination. Therefore, the elements or steps recited in the preamble become a part of the claim and do in fact act as limitations.
guidance: Using Jepson format is 'taken as an implied admission that the subject matter of the preamble is the prior art work of another' (MPEP 2129). This can expand the universe of prior art considered against the claim and limit scope.

name: Draft claims positively with proper antecedent basis
description: Positive introductions avoid admissions. Example claim (from '860 patent) shows each piece introduced separately with proper antecedent basis (i.e., 'a' or 'an' the first time introduced and 'the' or 'said' when subsequently discussed).
guidance: Write claims in traditional format with clear antecedent basis, introducing elements neutrally (no statements that elements are 'known' or part of the prior art). This preserves flexibility and avoids inadvertent admissions.

name: Jepson format can trigger means-plus-function interpretation
description: Jepson claim meet means plus function claiming! Means plus function claiming is not evil per se, but is far more nuanced than inventors and newbies are ready to handle.
guidance: Be cautious: Jepson structure and terse descriptions of the improvement may lend themselves to means-plus-function analysis, which imposes additional limitations (e.g., limiting scope to corresponding structure in the specification).

name: Jepson claims can and should be rewritten into traditional format
description: There is absolutely no reason why a Jepson claim could not be re-written into traditional format.
guidance: If possible, re-draft improvements in traditional claim format that avoid admissions and state elements positively. See linked drafting guides for basic claiming and method claims.

name: Do not self-represent on claim format choices; consult trained professionals
description: Inventors who seek to represent themselves beware! ... Jepson claims should be avoided in all but rare circumstances. Leave Jepson claiming to the trained professionals. Please do not attempt this at home!
guidance: Because Jepson and claim-format choices have long-term, potentially irreversible prosecution consequences, seek experienced patent counsel rather than DIY drafting.

name: Termination of proceedings
description: Situations in which proceedings on an earlier application are 'terminated' for purposes of 35 U.S.C. 120 (so that a later-filed application must be filed before termination to be copending).
guidance: Proceedings terminate when (A) issue fee is not paid and application is abandoned for failure to pay (date of due payment is termination date), (B) application in interference loses as to all claims (proceedings terminated as of date appeal/review was due), (C) decision by the Board terminates proceedings, and (D) a decision by the court terminates proceedings. 'Before' means 'not later than.' See MPEP § 711.02(c).

name: Showing required for nonreceipt of an Office action (petition basis)
description: What evidence a practitioner must submit to support a claim that an Office communication was never received (for withdrawing a holding of abandonment).
guidance: Must include a practitioner statement that the Office communication was not received and attest that a search of the file jacket and docket records indicates nonreceipt. Attach a copy of the docket record where the communication would have been entered and reference it (e.g., docket report showing replies for the relevant dates). Stronger proof may be required if practitioner has history of not receiving Office actions. Evidence of nonreceipt of other communications not directly tied to the reply-to-avoid-abandonment action will not necessarily warrant withdrawal. See Delgar v. Schulyer and MPEP guidance.

name: Required reply for abandonment after a final action
description: What constitutes the required reply in a nonprovisional application abandoned for failure to reply to a final Office action.
guidance: Required reply under 37 CFR 1.113 must include cancellation of, or appeal from, the rejection of each claim so rejected. Acceptable replies for petition purposes include: (A) a Notice of Appeal and appeal fee; (B) an amendment under 37 CFR 1.116 that cancels all rejected claims or otherwise prima facie places the application in condition for allowance; (C) filing an RCE with submission and fee under 37 CFR 1.114 (for utility/plant applications); or (D) filing a continuing application under 37 CFR 1.53(b) (or CPA under 1.53(d) for certain older cases). When an amendment is proposed, the Office may route the case to the Technology Center to determine if the amendment places the application in condition for allowance; if not, the petition may be denied and PTOL-303 used to notify the Office of Petitions.

name: Terminal disclaimer requirements for revival petitions
description: When a terminal disclaimer must accompany a petition to withdraw the holding of abandonment or a petition to revive, and how the term dedication is calculated.
guidance: A petition to revive under 37 CFR 1.137(d) in certain design applications and utility/plant applications filed before June 8, 1995 must be accompanied by a terminal disclaimer and fee under 37 CFR 1.321 dedicating a terminal part of the patent term equivalent to the period of abandonment (or the lesser of the abandonment period and any period extending beyond 20 years from U.S. filing/earliest priority). The terminal disclaimer must also apply to any patent on a continuing application that claims benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120/121/365(c). Provisions do not apply where revival is sought solely for copendency with later applications filed on/after June 8, 1995, to lapsed patents, or to reexamination proceedings. A terminal disclaimer is sometimes required when Office treats an untimely petition on merits to avoid granting patent term extension under 35 U.S.C. 154(b) due to prosecution delay caused by abandonment, because abandonment is a per se failure to exercise due diligence.

name: Enhanced documentation of claim interpretation
description: Pilot focus: enhanced documentation of claim interpretation.
guidance: Examiners should document claim interpretation explicitly when terms could be construed multiple ways. This is a core Pilot emphasis to ensure the record shows how terms were interpreted during prosecution.

name: More precise reasons for allowance
description: Pilot focus: more precise reasons for allowance.
guidance: Specify reasons for allowance with precision, particularly when prior art rejections were overcome. Reasons should make clear how claims meet statutory requirements and why rejections no longer apply.

name: Identify specific limitations distinguishing claims over prior art
description: Best practice to identify the specific claim limitations that distinguish the claims from prior art.
guidance: When overcoming prior art, the record should call out the particular limitations that distinguish the claims; do not rely on generalized statements. This supports transparency and reduces future ambiguity.

name: Appropriate and clear patentability determinations for every pending claim throughout prosecution
description: Quality metric: deliver appropriate and clear patentability determinations for every pending claim throughout prosecution.
guidance: The USPTO aims for an impeccable work product where each pending claim has a properly documented and clearly explained patentability determination at each stage of prosecution.

name: Drafter practice — submit applications with clear claim scope
description: Implication for drafters: submit applications with clear claim scope.
guidance: Understanding examiner practices helps drafters present claims that reduce ambiguity; clear claim scope makes examiner interpretations less likely to vary.

name: Drafter practice — use precise language anticipating examiner interpretations
description: Implication for drafters: use precise language anticipating examiner interpretations.
