guidance: Choose wording that minimizes potential multiple constructions and anticipate how examiners may read claim terms to reduce need for later clarification.

name: Drafter practice — provide claim charts in responses showing how amendments overcome rejections
description: Implication for drafters: include claim charts in responses that show how amendments overcome rejections.
guidance: Providing clear mappings between amended claim language and prior art or rejection grounds helps the record show why rejections are overcome and supports precise allowance reasoning.

name: Claim drafting techniques and methodologies
description: Learn claim drafting techniques and methodologies aimed at drafting the all-important claims that determine the scope and coverage of protection.
guidance: Practical exercises and personal feedback are used to develop the capacity to formulate credible sets of claims.

name: Specification drafting (description, summary, background/abstract)
description: Training covers drafting the specification including the description, summary and background/abstract for inventions.
guidance: Tutor-led modules and practical exercises focus on drafting clear, complete specifications that support claims.

name: Analysis of inventions
description: Participants learn how to analyse inventions to identify inventive features and draftable subject matter.
guidance: Analysis skills feed into claim and specification drafting exercises and strategic filing decisions.

name: Phase 1 — Drafting basics (modules & outcomes)
description: Fundamentals of drafting claims and the specification via tutor-led study of online modules: Fundamentals of Patent Drafting, Parts of a Patent Application, Relevance of Claim Drafting: Types of claims, Designing claims, Drafting a Description, Performing Drawings.
guidance: Participants complete practical exercises to assess background and description of inventions and formulate credible sets of claims and specifications.

name: Phase 2 — Geneva workshop topics
description: Workshop sessions cover: Fundamentals of Patent Law and Specification Structure; Making the Most Out of the Inventor Interview; An Expert Approach to Claim Drafting – Functional Analysis; Strategic Drafting in Specific Technology Areas; Drafting for Different Jurisdictions; Thinking Ahead: Drafting Enforceable Claims.
guidance: Face-to-face workshop combines theory and practice to develop skills in drafting claims and specifications covering a comprehensive scope of protection.

name: Phase 3 — Mentoring and advanced exercises
description: Follow-up mentoring focused on reinforcing skills from Phases 1 and 2 through advanced patent drafting exercises and discussions tailored to participants' technical fields.
guidance: Expert-guided practical exercises include: Claim Drafting in View of Prior Art; Amending Claims and Draft Specification; Claim Drafting for Chemistry/Biology; Claim Drafting for Electronics/Mechanics; direct interaction and hands-on advice from instructors.

name: Practical outcome: ability to draft enforceable, comprehensive protection
description: Participants should gain the capacity to draft enforceable claims and specifications that provide a comprehensive scope of protection.
guidance: Emphasis on drafting enforceable claims, functional analysis, anticipating jurisdictional differences, and thinking ahead to enforceability.

name: Identification of the 'actual invention' (CIPO current guidelines)
description: The 'actual invention' is identified as either a single element or a combination of elements that provide a solution to a problem; the claim must be limited to or narrower than an actual invention that meets the physicality standard and relates to the manual or productive arts.
guidance: Elements that are essential in the applicant's intention but have no material effect on the working of the 'actual invention' (superfluous limitations) may not form part of the 'actual invention'. The requirement that a claim be limited to or narrower than an actual invention means the claim must place the fences around the entirety of an actual invention or some part of an actual invention; claims that fence subject-matter not part of an actual invention may fail subsection 27(4) clarity requirements.

name: Limitations of segregating to 'inventive contribution' alone
description: Previous CIPO practice that segregated and assessed only the 'inventive contribution' (the combination of claim elements not taught by prior art) was invalidated by courts because the proper object of assessment is 'the subject matter defined by the claim' rather than an inventor's characterization of the invention.
guidance: Examiners and practitioners should not isolate only the novel elements and ignore the claim as defined; the claim must be assessed consistent with case law (see Re Amazon.com Inc.).

name: MOPOP guidance on considering essential elements that cooperate
description: In identifying the actual invention, it is appropriate to consider solutions evident to a person skilled in the art on reading the specification, and the actual invention must consider all essential elements (as purposively construed) that cooperate together to achieve the solution.
guidance: For claims with a single essential element, analysis focuses on whether that element achieves the solution; for claims with multiple essential elements, analysis must consider any combination of those elements that cooperate to achieve the solution. The actual invention is not necessarily limited to the inventive aspect alone and may include known elements that cooperate.

name: Exhaustive combination and claim clarity (subsection 27(4) interaction)
description: A claim must place the fences properly around the actual invention or part thereof; claims that define subject-matter beyond the immediate and cooperating environment of the invention ('exhaustive combinations') may be rejected for lack of clarity (subsection 27(4)) or unity.
guidance: Practically, examiners sometimes raise unity-style objections under subsection 27(4) for claims that contain multiple inventive concepts or where the inventive concept is unclear. MOPOP references (e.g., 16.07.01 and 21.07.01) address related examiner practice.

name: Treatment of mere aggregations under obviousness (section 28.3)
description: Mere aggregations should be identified as a defect under section 28.3 of the Patent Act as being obvious; separate prior art documents may be cited to show that each individual part is known in the prior art.
guidance: Where claimed subject-matter is a mere aggregation, the examiner can rely on multiple prior art sources to show each element was known and thus render the claim obvious. This shows how patentability (novelty/obviousness) of parts can be assessed separately where there is no synergy.

name: Definition and effect of 'counterpart foreign patent application'
description: A counterpart foreign patent application exists where a priority claim is made in either application to the other, or the U.S. and foreign disclosures are substantively identical.
guidance: Communications from foreign offices that list family members (including U.S. patents or English-language patents) may be treated as the foreign office citing the U.S./English patent for purposes of 1.97(e)(1) if 1.97 and 1.98 are complied with.

name: Including prior art patent numbers in the specification
description: Generally do not include prior art patent numbers in the spec.
guidance: Cite prior patents in the IDS instead. Listing them in the specification creates an admission that they are prior art, which can later constrain claim construction or feed obviousness rejections.

name: Content of the Summary of the Invention
description: Provide a short summary that mirrors the independent claims at a high level, using the same terminology.
guidance: Avoid characterizing 'the invention' as a single monolith; instead characterize 'a method,' 'a system,' or 'an apparatus.' Keep the summary concise and aligned with claim language to avoid inadvertent limiting statements.

name: Structure and content of the Detailed Description
description: The Detailed Description should be the longest part of the spec and walk through the figures one by one.
guidance: For each figure describe what is shown, what it does, how components interact, and what variations are possible. Use phrases like 'in some embodiments...' to disclose alternatives and embodiments. Ensure interactions and variations are described to support claim scope and enablement.

name: Filing date: specification (with or without claims) suffices for nonprovisional (non-design) applications
description: The filing date of a nonprovisional application (other than a design) is the date on which the USPTO receives a specification, with or without claims.
guidance: An application filed without any claims will prompt OPAP to issue a notice giving the applicant a time period to submit at least one claim to avoid abandonment. Importantly, an application will not be placed on an examiner's docket unless and until the application includes at least one claim.

name: No change to filing date requirements for design applications
description: For a design patent application the filing date remains the date on which the Office receives the specification (including at least one claim) and any required drawings.
guidance: Design applications must still include required drawings to obtain a filing date.

name: No new matter in claims or drawings submitted after filing date
description: Any claim and any drawing submitted after the filing date of an application may not contain new matter.
guidance: Post-filing additions are limited to what is supported in the originally filed specification/drawings; practitioners should ensure post‑filing submissions do not introduce new subject matter.

name: Reference filing (filing by reference to a previously filed application)
description: A nonprovisional application may be filed by reference (in the ADS or PLT Model International Request Form) to a previously filed application indicating that the specification and any drawings are replaced by the reference to the previously filed application.
guidance: If filed by reference, OPAP will issue a notice giving the applicant a time period within which to submit an English-language copy of the specification and drawings from the previously filed application to avoid abandonment. The English-language copy will be used as the specification and drawings of the application filed by reference. As with other filings, the application will not be placed on an examiner's docket unless and until it includes a specification including at least one claim.

name: Scope of claim: whole machine vs. improvement (patent limited to actual improvement)
description: If a specific machine already exists and the patentee merely added an improvement, the patentee cannot claim the whole machine; the patent extends only to the actual improvement, not to the pre-existing machine.
guidance: Examples: adding the patented lever to a watch does not permit patenting the whole watch; improvements to steam engines likewise limited. The patenter’s right cannot exceed what he actually invented.

name: Combination-claims and aggregation of previously separate operations
description: Where a patent claims a whole machine that combines several distinct operations or stages, it is not sufficient that the specific assembled machine did not exist before; if the different effects were previously produced in separate machines or by substantially the same application of machinery, combining them will not sustain a patent for the whole machine.
guidance: Juries must decide whether the principles (modes of operation) are new or whether the machine is only an aggregation of known elements producing no substantially different result. Whittemore/wood-carding example: identify distinct stages and compare to prior separate machines.

name: Estoppel from expressly waived claim in the specification
description: 'the patentee must be held to be estopped from asserting a claim which is expressly waived on the record.'
guidance: If the specification expressly disclaims a substance or class of use, the patentee cannot later claim that subject-matter; the specification serves to inform the public what may be safely done during the patent term without infringing. (Applied to a patentee who declared his invention 'did not extend to the use' of a particular substance.)

name: Scope of a 'new combination' claim excludes use of individual old materials alone
description: 'any one may use any one or all of the materials forming the composition, provided he does not use them in the combination patented.'
guidance: Where the patent claims a new combination of previously known ingredients, third parties may lawfully use individual ingredients or other combinations (including the old combination with a formerly essential ingredient) so long as they do not practice the patented combination itself. Infringement inquiry asks whether defendant used the plaintiff's combination 'substantially according to their patent.' (See friction-match examples.)

name: Presence or insignificance of an omitted ingredient determines infringement
description: Whether defendant's product 'contain[s] that substance as a principal ingredient, in conformity with the prescribed formula, or whether they are made without it or with so inconsiderable a portion of it as to be substantially according to plaintiff's patent.'
guidance: When a claimed composition omits an ingredient used in prior art, courts look to whether defendants actually include that ingredient (or include it only in trivial amounts) to decide if their product is substantially the patented composition. Factual finding on presence/quantity is decisive.

name: Substitution by a natural or composite article may fall within claims if specification's language so covers it
description: If a defendant uses an article (e.g., borax) which is composed of ingredients the specification claims (acid + alkali), it may be 'exactly the same thing' as claiming the separate ingredients; conversely, if the article is used merely for a different function (e.g., as a flux), that may not be infringement.
guidance: Examine whether the specification's words cover the composite/natural article in substance. If the language 'conveys the same meaning' as describing component acids/alkalies, infringement may be found; but if the article operates in a different way (flux vs acid/alkali role), it may be outside the patent. (Discussed in Martin's cement/borax context.)

name: Construction of patent claims must adhere to what the specification actually explains
description: 'In order to decide this (the infringement), we must first determine for what invention the patent, as explained by the specification, is taken out.'
guidance: Claim scope is determined by construing the specification: what the patentee explained and distinguished (e.g., Heath patent limited to 'carburet of manganese' in that state and mode). Courts will not read the claim broader than the invention as described in the specification; differences in wording that nevertheless 'convey the same meaning' may be treated as the same.

name: Direct infringement requires use in the mode described; indirect (colorable) variation depends on substitution of equivalents
description: Direct infringement: using the substance 'in the mode described in the specification.' Indirect infringement: 'if a defendant substitutes for a part of a plaintiff's invention some well-known equivalent...he would probably be considered as only making a colorable variation.'
guidance: Literal (direct) infringement needs the defendant to practice the claimed mode/state. Indirect infringement can exist where a defendant makes a colorable variation by substituting a known equivalent that accomplishes the same result; courts examine whether the substitution was intentionally imitative or effectively the same in result and operation.

name: Use of a natural product in its natural state may not infringe a patent limited to an artificial product, but processing/revivification can infringe
description: '...the right of the patentee was restricted to the use of artificial precipitated oxides of iron, and that the user by defendants of a natural product known as bog ochre in its natural state...was no infringement; but...the revivification of the natural product was an infringement.'
guidance: Determine whether the patentee's claim is limited to an artificial/prepared form; if so, mere use of a naturally occurring substance that performs the same function may be noninfringing, whereas applying the patentee's claimed processing (revivification or adaptation) to a natural product can be infringement.

name: True and first inventor / origin of the invention
description: The patentee must be the 'true and first inventor': he must not have obtained the invention from another person (unless imported from abroad), nor derived it from a printed book or from a patent specification published domestically or introduced from abroad.
guidance: This requirement addresses the inventor's provenance: if the claimed inventor obtained the invention from someone else or from public printed sources, that will defeat the patentee's claim to be 'true and first' and undermine validity.

name: Identification of patent and every claim for which reexamination is requested (37 CFR 1.915(b)(1))
description: The request must identify the patent by patent number and every claim for which reexamination is requested.
guidance: Although not required, it is strongly suggested to also state the patentee and patent title to prevent mis-typing errors in the patent number. Clearly identify each claim the requester wants reexamined.

name: Statement pointing out each substantial new question and detailed explanation of pertinency (37 CFR 1.915(b)(3))
description: The request must contain a statement pointing out each substantial new question of patentability based on the cited patents and printed publications, and a detailed explanation of the pertinency and manner of applying the patents and printed publications to every claim for which reexamination is requested.
guidance: The request must identify each substantial new question of patentability and each proposed ground of rejection separately. For each identified question/ground, explain how the cited documents are applied to meet or teach the patent claim limitations to establish the substantial new question or proposed ground. The request must apply all cited prior art to the claims requested for reexamination. See MPEP §§2616–2617 for examples.

name: Copy of entire patent and related documents; formatting (37 CFR 1.915(b)(5))
description: Submit a copy of the entire patent including the front face, drawings, and specification/claims (in double column format) for which reexamination is requested, and a copy of any disclaimer, certificate of correction, or reexamination certificate issued in the patent. All copies must have each page plainly written on only one side of a sheet of paper.
guidance: Provide the printed patent reproduced on one side of paper in double-column format; present drawing pages and front page as in the printed patent. Include prior disclaimers/certificates as part of the patent record.

name: Meaning of 'plant' for plant patents
description: The term 'plant' has been interpreted to mean 'plant' in the ordinary and accepted sense and not in the strict scientific sense and thus excludes bacteria; it does not include asexual propagating material, per se.
guidance: Case citations (e.g., In re Arzberger; Ex parte Hibberd) support this interpretation. Use ordinary botanical meaning when evaluating claims and disclosures.

name: Terminal disclaimer for obviousness-type double patenting
description: The filing of a terminal disclaimer may be used in appropriate situations to overcome an obviousness-type double patenting rejection based on claims to the asexually reproduced plant (35 U.S.C. 101) and the same plant in an application under 35 U.S.C. 161.
guidance: Where claims in different applications raise obviousness-type double patenting concerns, examiners and applicants should consider terminal disclaimers as an available remedy.

name: Plant patent rights and term (35 U.S.C. 163)
description: Rights associated with a plant patent include rights associated with a utility patent and the 'right to exclude' with additional terms provided in 35 U.S.C. 163. A plant patent issuing from an application filed after June 7, 1995 has a term which expires 20 years after the filing date (or earlier claimed filing date).
guidance: Plant patent applications will be published pursuant to 35 U.S.C. 122(b). Consider effective filing date and any claimed priorities under 120/121/365(c). See MPEP §2701 for term calculations.

name: Specification sections and ordering (37 CFR 1.163(c))
description: The specification should include, in order when applicable: Title; Cross-reference to related applications; Statement regarding federally sponsored research; Latin name of genus and species; Variety denomination; Background; Brief summary; Brief description of drawing; Detailed botanical description; A single claim; Abstract of the disclosure.
guidance: Each section should be preceded by an appropriate heading in upper case; inclusion of Latin name and variety denomination facilitates registration and database compilation (see ADS usage).

name: Single-claim requirement and claim form (37 CFR 1.164)
description: The claim shall be in formal terms to the new and distinct variety of the specified plant as described and illustrated, and may also recite the principal distinguishing characteristics. More than one claim is not permitted.
guidance: A plant patent is granted only on the entire plant. A method claim in a plant patent application is improper. Example proper claim: 'A new and distinct variety of hybrid tea rose plant, substantially as illustrated and described herein.'

name: Examination standards: statutory provisions and search
description: Plant applications are subject to the same examination process as any other national application; statutory provisions regarding patentable subject matter, utility, novelty, obviousness, disclosure, and claim specificity apply (35 U.S.C. 101, 102, 103, and 112), with the sole exception set forth in 35 U.S.C. 162.
guidance: Examiners develop prior art via searches of patent classification and nonpatent literature and may obtain advisory reports from the Agricultural Research Service (ARS). The ARS report is advisory and placed in the file but not a printed paper in the Office.

name: Office action content and restrictions (claim/title/advertising)
description: The action on the application will include matters as in other patent applications; the claim language must be directed to the 'new and distinct variety of plant' (the entire plant), and the title must relate to the entire plant, not to its flower or fruit.
guidance: Do not permit claims directed only to flower or fruit separate from the plant. Remove unwarranted advertising or laudatory expressions from the specification and objectionable background drawings (e.g., signs with nursery names). Examiner may amend language (e.g., insert 'tree' after 'apple'). Use form paragraphs (e.g., 16.04, 16.08) for rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102/112.

name: Foreign filing more than 12 months before U.S. filing
description: A claim for priority under 35 U.S.C.119(a)-(d) cannot be based on an earlier foreign application if that application was filed more than 12 months prior to the U.S. application filing date.
guidance: Use form paragraph 2.23 to notify applicant. However, where a provisional filing and a later complete foreign filing exist (e.g., British provisional vs complete), entitlement may be based on the complete specification if within one year; note how printed heading will reflect claimed priority for subject matter not disclosed in provisional.

name: No certified copy filed despite claim
description: Where priority is claimed but no certified copy of the foreign application has been filed, applicant has not complied with 35 U.S.C.119(b) requirements.
guidance: Use form paragraph 2.25 to require that applicant file the certified copy and provide application-specific details in the notice.

name: Examiner's treatment when encountering an intervening reference
description: If an examiner finds a reference with an effective date between the foreign filing date and the U.S. filing date, the examiner rejects claims considered unpatentable over that reference unless priority papers are of record demonstrating entitlement to the foreign date.
guidance: If papers are not yet filed, applicant may argue or submit papers; form paragraph 2.19 ('Overcome Rejection by Translation') may be used. If papers are filed but not in English, require an English translation with a statement of accuracy. If papers are in file and examiner determines applicant entitled to the date, withdrawal of the rejection is appropriate; otherwise repeat the rejection with reasons.

name: Translation requirement and accuracy statement
description: When foreign papers are not in English and are presented for the purpose of overcoming a reference or determining entitlement to a foreign filing date, a translation into English is required together with a statement that the translation is accurate.
guidance: When examiner requires filing of papers, translation should be required at the same time. If no translation is present, the examiner may reject unpatentable claims and require an English translation to determine entitlement to the date.

name: Identity of invention and sufficiency examination
description: The most important aspect of determining right of priority is whether the U.S. and foreign applications disclose the same invention; the foreign application may be considered as if filed in the U.S. on the foreign date, but must be examined for sufficiency of disclosure under 35 U.S.C.112 and for basis of the claims sought.
guidance: An applicant may be entitled to the foreign filing date for some claims but not others; entitlement may come from different foreign applications for different claim sets. Examiners must study the foreign papers to determine identity and sufficiency.

name: Form paragraph usage and examiner notifications
description: Specific form paragraphs (e.g., 2.19, 2.21, 2.22, 2.23, 2.24, 2.25, 2.26, 2.27) are prescribed for acknowledging papers, notifying applicants of defects, and explaining examiner actions regarding foreign priority papers.
guidance: Use the appropriate form paragraph based on the situation: untimely claims, inconsistent or missing oath/declaration references, certified copies filed but no claim, foreign filing more than 12 months earlier, claimed date not earliest, no certified copy filed, acknowledgement of papers placed in record, and acknowledgment in parent application, respectively.

name: Patent application filing fees and claim surcharges
description: Separate fees apply for filing national and international patent applications; fees differ for electronic filing vs paper and include surcharges for claims beyond a specified number (e.g., fees for 'up to ten patent claims' and additional-claim fees).
guidance: Paper filing may be charged at 150% of the electronic filing fee. Specific fee numbers (e.g., 311000, 311050, 311100) identify amounts for up-to-ten-claim filings and per-additional-claim fees.

name: Publication, translation and correction fees
description: Publication of translations or corrections (e.g., for European patent claims/specifications) is subject to fees; some legacy items remain applicable for earlier European patents.
guidance: Specific fee numbers (313800–313820 etc.) indicate amounts; note historical applicability footnotes for certain European patents published before given dates.

name: Utility patent rights and term
description: As with all utility patents in the United States, a biological patent provides the patent holder with the right to exclude others from making, using, selling, or importing the claimed invention or discovery in biology for a limited period of time - for patents filed after 1998, 20 years from the filing date.
guidance: Defines the fundamental exclusionary right conferred by U.S. utility patents and the statutory term for post-1998 filings.

name: Basic patentability requirements (novelty, inventive step/non-obviousness, industrial applicability/utility)
description: Patentability generally requires that a technical solution be (1) new, (2) involve an inventive step, and (3) be industrially applicable / useful.
guidance: These baseline requirements apply to biological inventions as to other technologies; the article lists them as the standard patentability elements used to evaluate claims.

name: Patentability of isolated and manipulated cells (including human cells) contingent on transformation/novelty
description: Isolated and manipulated cells — even human cells — can be patented. The U.S. PTO issued patents claiming primate and human embryonic stem cells; immortalized cell lines have been patented (e.g., Moore-related patents).
guidance: Biological material removed from a human can become patentable when it has been studied, manipulated, or 'immortalized' so that it differs functionally from the naturally occurring material.

name: Gene patent criteria and limits (isolated sequences, known function; post-Myriad constraints)
description: A gene patent is a patent on a specific isolated gene sequence, its chemical composition, the processes for obtaining or using it, or combinations of such claims. Historically, U.S. patents on genes were granted on isolated gene sequences with known functions. In 2013 (Association for Molecular Pathology v. Myriad Genetics), the Supreme Court held that a naturally occurring DNA segment is a product of nature and not patent eligible merely because it has been isolated; synthesized DNA sequences (e.g., cDNA) may still be eligible.
guidance: Claims directed to naturally occurring DNA sequences are vulnerable under the product-of-nature doctrine; claims to non-naturally occurring, synthetically created sequences or to methods using sequences may have different fates. The article emphasizes that gene patents have been used to claim isolated sequences, diagnostic uses, and altered sequences.

name: Scope of patent claims: compositions, processes, uses, combinations (including genomes, cell lines, transgenic animals)
description: Biological patents have claimed a wide range of subject matter: isolated compositions, processes for obtaining or using biological material, entire genomes, cell lines, genetically modified organisms (e.g., the Oncomouse), and methods for making recombinant proteins.
guidance: When drafting or evaluating biological patent claims, consider the claim category (composition, method, use, organism) because different categories are treated differently under patent-eligibility jurisprudence and PTO practice.

name: Reliance on precedent and litigation history to determine eligibility and scope
description: Key court decisions (Parke-Davis v. Mulford; Diamond v. Chakrabarty; Moore litigation; Association for Molecular Pathology v. Myriad Genetics) have materially shaped what biological subject matter is patentable and how claims are interpreted and enforced.
guidance: Analysis of patentability for biological inventions must account for controlling case law and Federal Circuit/Supreme Court holdings; historical practice (e.g., broad gene patents, stem cell patents) has been modified by later decisions.

name: Explanation requirements for 35 U.S.C. 112 first paragraph rejections
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, the Examiner’s Answer shall explain how the first paragraph is not complied with, including, as appropriate, how the specification and drawings do not (a) describe the subject matter defined by each rejected claim, (b) enable one skilled in the art to make and use the claimed subject matter, and (c) set forth the best mode contemplated by the appellant.
guidance: Provide claim-specific explanations tied to the specification/drawings; identify deficiencies in written description, enablement, and best mode as applicable.

name: Explanation requirements for 35 U.S.C. 112 second paragraph rejections
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, the Examiner’s Answer shall explain how the claims do not particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter regarded as the invention.
guidance: Provide concrete reasons showing lack of clarity/definiteness in claim language and how it fails the second paragraph requirements.

name: Explanation requirements for 35 U.S.C. 102 rejections (anticipation)
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102, the Examiner’s Answer shall explain why the rejected claims are anticipated, pointing out where all of the specific limitations recited in the rejected claims are found in the prior art relied upon in the rejection.
guidance: Point to explicit locations in the prior art where each limitation appears; be specific (page/figure/line) rather than conclusory.

name: Explanation requirements for 35 U.S.C. 103 rejections (obviousness)
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103, the Examiner’s Answer shall state the ground of rejection, point out where each of the specific limitations recited in the rejected claims is found in the prior art relied upon, identify the differences between the rejected claims and the primary reference, and explain why it would have been obvious to modify the primary reference to arrive at the claimed subject matter.
guidance: Specify the combination rationale and motivation to combine; identify claim-to-reference correspondences and differences and explain the reasoning that supports obviousness.

name: Feature-by-feature claim-to-art comparison when correspondence is unclear
description: When there may be questions about how claim limitations correspond to features in the prior art, the examiner should compare at least one rejected claim feature-by-feature with the prior art, aligning the claim language side-by-side with references to specific page/line numbers, drawing reference numbers, and quotations from the prior art as appropriate.
guidance: Use a side-by-side alignment with citations and quotations to remove ambiguity about how each claim limitation is met by the art (see MPEP guidance).

name: Claim: object and function
description: Object of the claim is not to aid the description but to ascertain what is claimed as new; claim is a means of clearly presenting the subject-matter of the patent.
guidance: Claims define the monopoly; drafter must focus claims on delimiting novel subject-matter rather than restating the specification.

name: Claim must distinguish old from new
description: Claims must distinguish between the old and the new; need not describe old in detail; not presumed to cover well-known articles.
guidance: Claims should be drafted to make the novel aspects clear; background does not need exhaustive description in the claims.

name: Claim ambiguity rules
description: Ambiguous claims that cover a whole class of subjects of which only one answers are problematic; where each method answers, claim not ambiguous.
guidance: Avoid drafting claims that overbroadly cover classes where only some members perform the invention; clarity prevents indefiniteness challenges.

name: Claims and abstract principles
description: Claims must not be for an abstract principle; must be for a principle embodied in a particular organism/machine/method; claim for an abstract principle invalid because it prevents subsequent invention.
guidance: Claims should recite concrete applications or structures; purely abstract claims are invalid.

name: Claims for machines vs processes/products
description: A claim for a machine will not cover a process and vice versa; though clumsily worded a claim may cover both process and product in some cases.
guidance: Drafters must choose claim categories carefully; mixed drafting can create uncertainty as to scope.

name: Claims to variations and combinations
description: Claims for variations in application of a general principle must be drafted appropriately; for a combination, how claim scope is determined; for an applied principle, claims will cover similar methods.
guidance: When claiming combinations or variant applications, specify the essential cooperative elements or the manner of application to bind equivalents as appropriate.

name: Claim sufficiency and judicial construction
description: Sufficiency of claims is decided by the court; construction of patent/claim by court (and sometimes jury), judged liberally; principles of construction listed.
guidance: Claim construction doctrines matter heavily in litigation; courts construe claims in light of specification and prosecution history.

name: Omission of essential elements fatal
description: Omission from the specification of what is essential is fatal; omission of an ingredient or step in a well-known process may in some cases be patentable if it affects degree of benefit only.
guidance: Ensure the specification discloses all essential elements required for practicing the claimed invention; missing essentials can render the patent invalid.

name: Principles/theories not patentable; application can be
description: A mere principle or law of nature is not patentable; the requisites for patenting a 'principle' are discussed; a claim for an abstract principle is invalid; where an inventor describes a mode of application, applied principles may be patentable and will cover similar methods.
guidance: Claims should recite practical application/implementation of underlying principles rather than claiming the principle itself.

name: Infringement: acts that constitute infringement
description: Infringement consists in making, using, or vending; punishable by action at law; includes making patented machine, using patented process (subject to exceptions), and selling articles made by a patented machine in certain circumstances.
guidance: Analyze accused activity against each claim element; consider process, product, and machine claims separately and together.

name: Sale of materials and articles produced by patented machine
description: Sale of the materials of a patented machine is not per se an infringement; sale of articles produced by a patented machine is not necessarily an infringement; whether product sale infringes depends on claim coverage (process vs product).
guidance: Focus on claim scope: if patent claims the product, sale may infringe; if only the machine is claimed, sale of products may not infringe absent process/product claims.

name: Infringement of combination claims
description: Infringement of a combination claim depends on whether the accused device or process practices the combination; may turn upon use of equivalents; where parts of a combination are novel, the combination may be infringed even if components individually differ.
guidance: Assess presence of all claim elements or their equivalents; missing an essential cooperative element may avoid infringement.

name: Proportions and essential ingredients in process claims
description: Where the proportions of ingredients are essential, there is no infringement to vary them; varying essential proportions may avoid infringement.
guidance: Claims that specify critical proportions can limit scope; accused products with materially different proportions may avoid infringement.

name: Court vs jury roles
description: Court's province to construe letters-patent and decide whether claims are explicit; jury to pass on use of mechanical equivalents, novelty, sufficiency of specification (under proper instructions), and questions of infringement and utility in many cases.
guidance: Litigation strategy must account for mixed questions of law and fact; prepare for claim construction hearings and jury trials.

name: Repugnancy between title and description
description: Repugnancy between the title of the patent and the description of the specification is fatal.
guidance: Ensure consistency between the claim/title and the specification to avoid invalidity for repugnancy.

name: Application contents (petition, declaration, specification, drawings, claims)
description: Patents/applications must be accompanied by a petition, declaration, and specification; the specification should contain a declaration of authorship, a description of the invention illustrated with necessary drawings, and claims of the inventions or combinations claimed as new.
guidance: Specifications and drawings are often required in duplicate; the specification must be limited to one invention in some colonies; signatures, attestation by witnesses, and place and date of signature may be required; where the applicant acts by agent a power of attorney may be used.

name: Amendments of specifications (limits and procedure)
description: Amendments of the specification may be made by leave of the Registrar (subject to appeal to the Court); no amendment is to be allowed that will make the specification, as amended, claim an invention substantially larger than, or substantially different from, the invention originally claimed.
guidance: Leave to amend is conclusive except in case of fraud; amendments may be applied for and opposed by any person; amendments may also be permitted by Court/judge during actions.

name: Remedy where patentee has overclaimed by mistake
description: If it is proved that by mistake, accident, or inadvertence the patentee claimed something of which he was not the inventor, the patent shall be deemed valid for so much of the invention as shall actually be his own; a Commissioner may, if satisfied the error arose from inadvertence and not fraud, and upon surrender and filing of an amended specification, grant a new patent for the unexpired term.
guidance: Treble damages remain recoverable for unlawful users of the patentee's patented invention that legitimately falls within his true claim; fees (e.g., £10) may be payable on such regrants.

name: Disclaimers and memoranda of alteration
description: Patentees are at liberty, with leave of the appropriate officer, to enter disclaimers or memoranda of alteration; fees are payable on each such application.
guidance: Disclaimers and memoranda allow the patentee to correct/surrender parts of the claim or specification; fees vary by colony.

name: Single-invention limitation and claims
description: The specification must be limited to one invention; every patent is to be granted for one invention only, but may contain more than one claim; no objection can be taken on the ground that it covers more than one invention in some jurisdictions.
guidance: Procedural rules may require limitation to a single invention for the formal application even if multiple claims are drafted to define scope.

name: Substantial New Question of Patentability for Subsequent Requests
description: In order for a second or subsequent request for ex parte reexamination to be granted, a substantial new question of patentability must be raised by the art (patents and/or printed publications) cited in the second or subsequent request for reexamination.
guidance: See MPEP § 2240 for discussion on whether a substantial new question of patentability is raised by the prior art cited in a later request; second requests are decided on the claims in effect at time of determination (37 CFR 1.515(a)).

name: Housekeeping Amendment to Make Claims Identical
description: Where the claims are not the same in both files at time of merger, the decision will give the patent owner one month to provide an amendment to make the claims the same in each file.
guidance: The patent owner must not address patentability in a housekeeping amendment. If the required identical-amendment is not timely submitted, any claim that does not contain identical text in all merged proceedings should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as indefinite.

name: Timing for Decision on Merging or Staying Reissue and Reexamination
description: A decision whether to merge the reissue application and reexamination or to stay one of the proceedings will not be made prior to the mailing of an order to reexamine pursuant to 37 CFR 1.525 and the expiration of the statement-reply period following the order.
guidance: Determination on the request must not be delayed because of a copending reissue application due to 35 U.S.C. 304 and 37 CFR 1.515 requiring determination within three months of the request filing. After reexamination order and statement-reply period, CRU SPRS or TC QAS should notify OPLA promptly that proceedings are ready for consideration of merger. If reissue patent issues prior to determination, reexamination should be based on reissue claims presented as a 'clean copy' (use form paragraph 22.05).

name: Descriptive language limits — impermissible content
description: Identify and act on descriptive language in specifications that is impermissible or functional rather than ornamental.
guidance: Descriptive/specification language that describes functional uses or matters unrelated to the design may be objected to or rejected under 35 U.S.C. 171 or 35 U.S.C. 112 depending on how claims are worded. Example: language describing converting a shipping container into an aquarium with branding/illumination may be impermissible.

name: Specificity requirement for licensing/notice letters (willful infringement)
description: Recipients of licensing letters will not be exposed to liability for willful infringement unless the letter clearly states the acts that allegedly constitute infringement and identifies each particular patent claim believed to be infringed.
guidance: Aimed at discouraging vague demand letters that create willfulness liability risk; reduces incentives for opportunistic licensing letters and potential treble damages threats absent claim/act specificity.

name: Same venue rules for declaratory judgment and infringement cases
description: The Committee determined that the same venue rules shall apply for both patent declaratory judgment cases and patent infringement cases.
guidance: This change addresses prior application of different standards in declaratory judgment contexts and aims for parity between claim types.

name: Interlocutory appeals of claim construction (Markman) — district court certification
description: Section 8 amends 28 U.S.C. §1292(c)(2) to give district court judges discretion to certify Markman claim construction orders for interlocutory review; when such orders are certified, the Federal Circuit must decide the appeal.
guidance: Transfers discretion from Federal Circuit to district court judge to determine whether and when an interlocutory appeal of claim construction would best promote case resolution. The district court may also stay the case pending appeal. Rationale: district judges are best positioned to know when the case is ready for appellate claim construction resolution; intended to reduce costs and increase predictability given high reversal rates on claim construction.

name: Inequitable conduct — codified standard and safeguards (new 35 U.S.C. §298)
description: Section 12 inserts a new §298 that codifies and clarifies the doctrine of inequitable conduct: (a) requires proof by clear and convincing evidence; (b) defines 'material' as information a reasonable examiner would consider important in deciding whether to allow the patent application (non-cumulative information important in deciding whether to allow the patent); (c) permits intent to deceive to be inferred but not solely on the basis of gross negligence or on materiality alone; (d) requires that inequitable conduct claims be pled with particularity under Rule 9(b); (e) grants the court discretion to fashion appropriate remedies, which can include holding one, more than one, or all claims unenforceable and/or denying equitable relief such as injunctions.
guidance: Addresses problems of multiple materiality standards, inference of intent from materiality alone, and the all-or-nothing remedy. Aims to balance applicants’ duty of candor with not chilling meaningful disclosures to the USPTO. Pleading and evidentiary requirements should reduce harassment via over-pleading inequitable conduct defenses.

name: When relying on potential infringement liability, show concrete plans creating substantial risk of suit
description: If a party relies on potential infringement liability as the basis for standing, it 'must establish that it has concrete plans for future activity that creates a substantial risk of future infringement or [will] likely cause the patentee to assert a claim of infringement.' (JTEKT Corp.)
guidance: Provide detailed plans for future conduct (specific products, customers, timelines, design/material choices) and explain why those plans create a substantial risk of infringement or would likely provoke suit. Vague development plans or generalized business intent do not suffice.

name: Whether the method involves or is executed by a particular machine or apparatus (machine-or-transformation clue)
description: "The machine-or-transformation test is a useful and important clue, and investigative tool, for determining whether some claimed inventions are processes under § 101." A "machine" is a concrete thing (broadly interpreted to include electrical, electronic, optical, acoustic devices); an "apparatus" can include a machine or group of machines.
guidance: Relevant considerations: the particularity or generality of the elements of the machine or apparatus (specific identification weighs toward eligibility); for computer-implemented processes a general purpose computer may be sufficiently "particular" when programmed to perform the process steps because such programming creates a special purpose computer (citing In re Alappat); however, "adding a 'computer-aided' limitation ... without more, is insufficient" where claims are silent as to how/extent/significance of the computer (DealerTrack). To qualify as a particular machine, the claim must clearly convey that the computer is programmed to perform the steps. If the claim is so abstract and sweeping that performing it would cover substantially all practical applications of a judicial exception, the machine is not sufficiently particular.

name: Machine/apparatus subfactor: Whether the machine's involvement is extrasolution activity or a field-of-use
description: The extent to which (or how) the machine or apparatus imposes meaningful limits on execution of the claimed method steps.
guidance: Use of a machine that contributes only nominally or insignificantly to execution of the method (e.g., in a data gathering step or in a field-of-use limitation) weighs against eligibility. Limiting an abstract idea to one field of use or adding token post-solution components does not make the concept patentable (citing Bilski, Cybersource).

name: Whether performance of the claimed method involves an application of a law of nature
description: An application of a law of nature may represent patent-eligible subject matter even in the absence of a particular machine or transformation. If such an application exists, the claims are less likely to be drawn to an abstract idea.
guidance: When a natural principle is a limiting element, evaluate whether the claim applies that principle in a particular, practical way rather than preempting the principle itself. See MPEP § 2106.01 for more guidance.

name: Law-of-nature subfactors (particularity, subjective determination, extrasolution)
description: Where an application of a law of nature is present, consider: (a) the particularity or generality of the application (broad applicability across many fields weighs against eligibility); (b) whether the claimed method recites an application solely involving subjective determinations (ways to think about the law) — such recitations weigh against eligibility; (c) whether the application's involvement is extrasolution activity or a field-of-use (nominal contribution weighs against eligibility).
guidance: Claims that would monopolize a natural force or scientific fact or claim every mode of accomplishing an effect are problematic (citing O'Reilly v. Morse, The Telephone Cases). Applications that are sensorially verifiable and not merely opinion are more likely to weigh in favor of eligibility.

name: Whether a general concept (principle/theory/plan/scheme) is involved in executing the steps of the method
description: The presence of such a general concept can be a clue that the claim is drawn to an abstract idea.
guidance: Relevant factors: (a) extent to which use of the concept would preempt its use in other fields; (b) extent to which the claim is abstract/sweeping covering known and unknown uses and any machinery; (c) extent to which the claim would cover all possible solutions to a problem (statement of problem vs specific solution); (d) whether the concept is disembodied or well-instantiated (instantiated concepts weigh in favor). A concept that is not well-instantiated weighs against eligibility (citing Bilski, Diehr, Research Corp., DealerTrack, Ultramercial).

name: Making the determination of eligibility (weighing factors; examiner documentation)
description: Each relevant factor should be weighed to determine whether the method is claiming an abstract idea by covering a general concept or whether it is limited to a particular practical application. The presence or absence of a single factor will not be determinative.
guidance: If factors indicate the method claim is not merely covering an abstract idea, the claim is eligible under 35 U.S.C. 101 and must be further evaluated under 102, 103, and 112. If factors indicate the claim attempts to cover an abstract idea, the examiner will reject under 35 U.S.C. 101, providing clear rationale and specifically pointing out the factors relied upon so the applicant can respond. The examiner's conclusion must be based on the evidence as a whole. Under compact prosecution, each claim should be reviewed for compliance with every statutory requirement in the initial review and Office personnel should state all non-cumulative reasons and bases for rejecting claims in the first Office action.

name: Establish on the Record a prima facie case
description: USPTO personnel should review the totality of the evidence (e.g., specification, claims, relevant prior art) before concluding whether the claimed invention is statutory or within an exception. "The examiner bears the initial burden … of presenting a prima facie case of unpatentability."
guidance: If the record suggests it is more likely than not that the claimed invention would be considered a practical application of an abstract idea, physical phenomenon, or law of nature, then USPTO personnel should not reject the claim. After identifying and explaining in the record the reasons why a claim is for an abstract idea/law/natural phenomenon with no practical application, the burden shifts to the applicant to amend or show why the claim is eligible (citing In re Oetiker, In re Brana).

name: Subject Matter Eligibility Analysis of Process Claims Involving Laws of Nature — essential three inquiries (MPEP § 2106.01)
description: After determining what applicant invented and establishing the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claimed invention, conduct the following three inquiries on the claim as a whole: (1) Is the claimed invention directed to a process (an act or series of acts or steps)? (2) Does the claim focus on use of a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or naturally occurring relation or correlation (is the natural principle a limiting feature)? (3) Does the claim include additional elements/steps or a combination that integrate the natural principle into the claimed invention such that the natural principle is practically applied and the claim amounts to significantly more than the natural principle itself?
guidance: If Inquiry 1 is No, this analysis is not applicable (see MPEP § 2106 for products). If Inquiry 2 is No, analyze instead whether an abstract idea is claimed (MPEP § 2106). If Inquiry 3 is No (i.e., the claim is no more than the natural principle plus instructions to apply it), the claim is not patent-eligible and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101. The guidance emphasizes integration of the natural principle into a practical application and that mere application without significantly more is insufficient.

name: Necessity to adapt the description to amended claims
description: If the claims of a European patent are amended during opposition or examination proceedings and the amendment introduces an inconsistency between the amended claims and the description, is it necessary, to comply with the requirements of the EPC, to adapt the description to the amended claims so as to remove the inconsistency?
guidance: Common practice before the EPO is to adapt the description (often at the end of opposition proceedings) so it is in line with the maintained/amended claims. The article frames this as the central question referred to the Enlarged Board of Appeal in G 1/25 and gives the practical example of a description that still discloses embodiments that fall outside the scope of newly-limited claims.

name: Legal basis — Article 84 EPC (clarity/support) as a ground for adaptation
description: One line of case law derives a need to adapt the description from Article 84 EPC, i.e. requirements of clarity and support of the claims in the description.
guidance: Some Boards have treated Article 84 (alone or combined with other provisions) as providing the requisite legal basis for requiring adaptation of the description where inconsistencies arise. The article notes this is the more commonly-followed line of case law.

name: Legal basis — Rule 42 EPC (content of the description) as a ground for adaptation
description: Rule 42 EPC (content of the description) is cited in case law as another provision supporting adaptation of the description to match amended claims.
guidance: Rule 42 has been used (sometimes together with Article 84) to justify amending the description so that it does not describe embodiments outside the scope of the maintained claims. The article lists Rule 42 as among the sources invoked by the traditional approach.

name: Common practice and timing for description adaptation
description: In practice, descriptions are usually adapted to the maintained/amended claims at the end of opposition proceedings, and similarly during later stages of examination where claims are amended.
guidance: The article states this is routine practice: to amend the description so it does not disclose embodiments that are outside the scope of the allowed/maintained claims. This pragmatic timing (typically at the conclusion of proceedings) is important for docketing and client advice.

name: Circumstances that give rise to inconsistency between claims and description
description: Inconsistency arises where amended (usually narrowed) claims exclude embodiments that the original description continues to disclose, for example where the description indicates the invention includes embodiments that are no longer within the scope of the maintained claims.
guidance: Identifying such passages is the first step: if the description still describes features/embodiments broader than the amended claims, practitioners commonly consider adapting or deleting those passages to avoid inconsistency. The article uses the example from T 0697/22 involving a narrower definition of an 'organic binder' in the maintained claims than in the description.

name: Effect of an inconsistent description on claim interpretation (UPC authority)
description: Case law (e.g., UPC Hamburg decision AGFA NV v Gucci Sweden AB) has held that a broader description inconsistent with maintained claims cannot be used to interpret more limited claims to the patentee's benefit.
guidance: This indicates that, at least in some courts, an inconsistent description will not expand claim scope; however, the treatment of such inconsistencies varies and does not resolve whether adaptation is required under the EPC. Practitioners should consider both national/court authority and EPO practice.

name: Referral questions to the Enlarged Board of Appeal (G 1/25)
description: The referral G 1/25 poses three specific questions: (1) is it necessary under the EPC to adapt the description to amended claims after amendments create inconsistency; (2) if so, which EPC provision(s) necessitate such adaptation; (3) would the answers differ if the amendment occurred during examination/examination-appeal proceedings?
guidance: The outcome of these questions will determine whether the traditional practice continues to be legally required or whether the more recent decisions denying a legal basis prevail. The article highlights that the Enlarged Board's decision will be decisive for boards' and departments' practice at the EPO.

name: Civil limitation period for counterfeiting actions
description: Civil proceedings for counterfeiting are time-barred after five years with effect from the date of the alleged acts.
guidance: Five-year limitation applies to civil claims under these provisions.

name: Publication contents for applications
description: Organization shall publish for each application: application number, filing date, graphical/photographic representations, products, applicant name and address, priority claimed, and agent name/address.
guidance: Publication ensures transparency and enables oppositions/third-party awareness.

name: Legal date of registration and issuance of certificate content
description: Legal date of registration is the filing date; once registration is completed owner is issued a certificate containing registration number, filing number, filing date, Locarno class, products, owner name/address, and validly claimed priority; Organization shall attach graphical/photographic representations to the certificate.
guidance: Certificate formalizes rights and includes representations for clarity of scope.

name: Rule 131 declarations must be truthful (no antedating by false declaration)
description: The Rule 131 declaration at issue was prepared to antedate a patent cited as prior art; the declaration must truthfully represent reduction to practice and factual demonstrations asserted to antedate prior art.
guidance: Practitioners must ensure any Rule 131 declaration genuinely supports the factual assertions (e.g., that the inventor reduced the invention to practice on specified dates and demonstrated the claimed features). Preparing or filing a declaration containing untrue assertions to antedate prior art risks inequitable conduct and unenforceability of resulting patents.

name: Doctrine of Equivalents — function-way-result test
description: "a patentee may invoke [the doctrine of equivalents] to proceed against the producer of a device if it performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to obtain the same result" (Graver Tank formulation).
guidance: Apply an element-by-element inquiry asking whether the accused product performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result. Example: Graver Tank (manganese silicate held equivalent to magnesium silicate because operation and result were substantially identical). Consider whether persons reasonably skilled in the art would have known of the interchangeability of the unclaimed elements with the claimed ones.

name: All Elements Rule
description: "[E]ach element contained in a patent claim is deemed material to defining the scope of the patented invention, and thus the doctrine of equivalents must be applied to individual elements of the claim, not to the invention as a whole."
guidance: Evaluate equivalence on an element-by-element basis (not by overall invention similarity). This limits broad 'overall similarity' arguments and requires demonstration of an equivalent for each claimed element omitted or altered in the accused device.

name: Prosecution History Estoppel — general principle
description: A patentee may be estopped from invoking the doctrine of equivalents for subject matter intentionally disclaimed or surrendered during prosecution; historically a patentee cannot recapture intentionally disclaimed subject matter.
guidance: Where an applicant disclaims or narrows claim scope to obtain allowance, courts may bar claiming equivalents that lie within what was surrendered. Historical cases (Leggett, Union Metallic Cartridge, Hurlbut) establish that disclaimers during prosecution can limit later equivalence claims.

name: Warner-Jenkinson presumption and patentee's burden to show reason for amendment
description: The Court placed the burden on the patentee to establish the reason for an amendment required during prosecution; when no reason for amendment could be established, courts should presume the applicant had a substantial reason related to patentability and thus bar the doctrine of equivalents as to that element.
guidance: Patentees must explain the reason for claim amendments; absent a satisfactory explanation, a presumption bars equivalents for the amended element. That presumption is rebuttable by providing appropriate reasons, but the Court did not clearly define what counts as a 'substantial reason related to patentability.'

name: Festo foreseeability-and-reasonableness test for amended claims (exceptions to complete bar)
description: Festo permits recapture of equivalents for amended claim elements in limited situations: where the equivalents were unforeseeable at the time of the amendment; where the rationale underlying the amendment bears only a tangential relation to the equivalent in question; or where there are other reasons suggesting the patentee could not reasonably have been expected to describe the insubstantial substitution.
guidance: If an equivalent was unforeseeable (e.g., later-developed technology) or impractical to describe with reasonable claim language (example: analogous DNA sequences encoding similar proteins), Festo allows applying doctrine of equivalents despite an amendment. Courts should analyze foreseeability to a person of ordinary skill at time of amendment and whether the amendment's stated rationale actually relates to the accused equivalent.

name: Scope of surrendered subject matter (Exhibit Supply rule and Festo exceptions)
description: "By the amendment [the patentee] recognized and emphasized the difference between the two phrases and proclaimed his abandonment of all that is embraced in that difference." (Exhibit Supply) — the difference between original and amended claims is generally abandoned.
guidance: While Exhibit Supply supports treating the difference as abandoned, Festo carves out exceptions (unforeseeable equivalents, tangential rationale, other reasons). Courts must start with the presumption of surrender for narrowed claims but then assess whether any Festo exception allows recapture of particular equivalents.

name: Foreseeability as a bar to equivalence (policy rationale)
description: If an equivalent was foreseeable to a person of ordinary skill in the art, the patentee should be held responsible for failure to claim that equivalent; the doctrine should not protect inadvertence or failure to claim foreseeable alternatives.
guidance: Policy balancing: foreseeability supports strong notice function — foreseeable equivalents should be claimed, otherwise public cannot rely on claim boundaries. This rationale underlies limiting equivalence for amended claims when equivalents were foreseeable at the time of amendment.

name: Flexible bar vs. Complete bar (approaches to prosecution history estoppel)
description: Two competing approaches: the 'flexible bar' (availability of equivalents after amendment depends on nature and purpose of amendment — effect can range from great to small to zero) versus the 'complete bar' (amendment to an element precludes any DOE claim on that element).
guidance: Federal Circuit at times embraced a 'flexible bar' (Hughes I), then moved toward a 'complete bar' en banc; Festo reconciled by limiting complete bar to situations where patentee cannot explain reason for amendment and allowing recapture under specified exceptions. Practitioners should understand which approach a court applies and how Festo constrains a blanket complete-bar rule.

name: Equivalence inquiry factor: knowledge of interchangeability by persons skilled in the art
description: An important factor in determining equivalence is whether persons reasonably skilled in the art would have known of the interchangeability of the unclaimed elements with the claimed ones.
guidance: Assess technical interchangeability and contemporaneous understanding in the art. Evidence about whether POSITA would have expected the substitute to be interchangeable bears on both equivalence under Graver Tank (supports equivalence) and on foreseeability-based estoppel analysis (may support bar).

name: Doctrinal purpose: balancing protection of patent rights and public notice
description: Patent law serves two functions: incentives for innovators (protection) and notice to the public of claim boundaries (certainty). The proper application of the doctrine of equivalents and prosecution history estoppel should balance these competing functions.
guidance: Interpretive tests (all elements rule, foreseeability, presumption for amendments, Festo exceptions) should be applied with this balance in mind: preserve reasonable protection against copyists while ensuring the public can discern claim scope with workable certainty.

name: Addition of 'And Described' to Claim (Form ¶ 15.64)
description: When adding "-- and described --" to the claim after "shown," indicate the reason and whether the wording "must be" or "has been" is appropriate.
guidance: Examiner Note: In bracket 1, insert reason. In bracket 2, insert --must be-- or --has been--.

name: Reproductions must be complete, clear, and comply with Hague Rule 9 / Part Four
description: Every design application must include a reproduction (drawing or photograph) of the claimed design; the drawing or photograph constitutes the entire visual disclosure of the claim and must be a clear and complete depiction of the design applied to the article designated in the title, with nothing left to conjecture.
guidance: Formal requirements for reproductions for nonprovisional international design applications are set forth in Hague Agreement Rule 9 and Part Four of the Administrative Instructions (see 37 CFR 1.1026). Drawing requirements in 37 CFR 1.84 do not apply except as provided (see 37 CFR 1.1061(b)). Reproductions must comply with Rule 9 and Part Four; amended reproductions submitted directly to the Office are subject to review under 37 CFR 1.1026.

name: Object and require consistency where views are inconsistent
description: When inconsistencies are found among the views, the examiner should object to the reproductions and request that the views be made consistent.
guidance: Pursuant to Hague Agreement Rule 9(4), a Contracting Party may refuse effects of the international registration if reproductions are not sufficient to fully disclose the industrial design. When inconsistencies are of such magnitude that the overall appearance is unclear, the claim should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b) as nonenabling and indefinite (see MPEP § 1504.04, subsection I).

name: Use and description of broken/dotted lines or coloring to indicate non-protected matter (35 U.S.C. 112 considerations)
description: When using broken or dotted lines or coloring in a reproduction to indicate matter shown for which protection is not sought, applicants are encouraged to include an explanation of the purpose of the broken or dotted lines or coloring in the description to avoid uncertainty as to the scope of the claimed design.
guidance: Applicants are encouraged not to simply rely on a description to indicate matter not forming part of the design but to also identify the matter by broken/dotted lines or coloring. Presence of undescribed broken lines or color that renders the scope unclear may lead to rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b). Use form paragraphs such as 29.21 where undescribed broken lines or color render the scope unclear.

name: Rejection for undescribed broken lines (Form ¶ 29.21) — 35 U.S.C. 112(b)
description: The claim is rejected for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention as required in 35 U.S.C. 112(b) when reproductions include broken lines that are not described in the specification and the scope of the claimed design cannot be determined.
guidance: Use form paragraph 29.21 where presence of undescribed broken lines or coloring makes the claim indefinite; explain the figures and specify which broken lines are undescribed (insert figure references and specifics).

name: Final decree and requirement of account
description: A final decree is one which terminates the litigation by awarding profits, damages, and other permanent relief; a final decree for plaintiff cannot be granted where an account is necessary until the account has been taken by the master and reported to and accepted by the court.
guidance: Final decrees for defendants can be entered at conclusion of hearing when any one of defendant's defenses is sustained; the court will dismiss the bill rather than decide claims solely to establish precedent.

name: Compliance with 37 CFR 1.530(d)-(j)
description: Any proposed amendment to the specification and/or claims in reexamination must comply with 37 CFR 1.530(d)-(j), be formally presented pursuant to 37 CFR 1.52(a) and (b), and contain any fees required by 37 CFR 1.20(c).
guidance: If an amendment does not comply, a supplemental paper correctly proposing amendments is required. A shortened statutory period for response (ONE MONTH or THIRTY DAYS, whichever is longer) will be set; failure to timely correct will result in the amendment being held not appropriate and consequences under 37 CFR 1.957(b) or (c).

name: Excess claims fees applicability
description: Excess claims fees specified in 37 CFR 1.20(c) (implementing 35 U.S.C. 41(a)(2)) apply to excess claims proposed to be added to a patent during a reexamination proceeding: the independent-claims fee applies for each independent claim in excess of three and in excess of the number of independent claims in the patent under reexamination; the total-claims fee applies for each claim in excess of twenty and in excess of the number of claims in the patent under reexamination.
guidance: Fees differ by entity status (micro/small/other). Fees are due only for 'new' (excess) claims resulting from the amendment; revising existing claims without adding new claims does not incur a fee. A claim disclaimed under 35 U.S.C. 253 or canceled in a previous certificate is not considered for fee calculation. If excess claims fees are not paid with the presentation, a Notice of Defective Paper (PTOL‑2069) will be issued with a one‑month time for correction; failure to pay may result in termination (37 CFR 1.957(b)) or limitation (37 CFR 1.957(c)). Examples in the text illustrate calculation.

name: Limitations on submission of prior art by third party requester
description: After the inter partes reexamination order, the third party requester may only cite additional prior art if filed as part of comments under §1.947 or §1.951(b) and limited to prior art that: (1) is necessary to rebut a finding of fact by the examiner; (2) is necessary to rebut a response of the patent owner; or (3) for the first time became known or available to the third party requester after filing the request.
guidance: Prior art under (3) must be accompanied by a statement explaining when it first became known/available and a discussion of pertinency to at least one claim. Submission of new art does not, by itself, permit a newly proposed rejection unless the patent owner has presented an amendment or new claims that necessitate the rejection. New proposed rejections based on newly presented art must comply with MPEP §2617 and the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 311 (pertinency and explanation of how the art is applied). Substituting new art to replace art originally advanced (i.e., changing the theory for unamended claims) is not permitted as a rebuttal of an examiner finding.

name: Examiner withdraws a ground of rejection — treatment and requester options
description: If the examiner withdraws a ground of rejection at any time, specific guidelines apply depending on whether the rejection was examiner-initiated or originally proposed by the third party requester, and depending on whether claims have been amended.
guidance: Examples: (A) Withdrawal of an examiner-initiated rejection should be stated as a decision favorable to patentability; the requester may propose the withdrawn rejection as a 'rejection proposed by the third party requester' in its next comments and may appeal the withdrawal as a final decision favorable to patentability if a Right of Appeal Notice (RAN) is later issued. (B) If the examiner withdraws a rejection previously proposed by the requester as to unamended claims, treat the issue as a rejection proposed by the requester that the examiner refuses to adopt. (C) If claims have been amended, withdrawal of a previously proposed requester rejection is generally not treated as a refusal to adopt (since the rejection was not proposed as to amended claims), but the requester may propose the rejection anew as to the amended claims. (D) If a claim is amended merely to include a dependent claim previously subjected to a requester rejection and the examiner withdraws the ground, that is a refusal to adopt the requester’s previously proposed rejection of the dependent claim.

name: Consequences for unpaid excess claims fees
description: If the excess claims fees required by 37 CFR 1.20(c)(3) and (c)(4) are not paid with the presentation of the excess claims, a Notice of Defective Paper (PTOL‑2069) will be issued setting a one‑month time period to correct the defect; an extension may be requested under 37 CFR 1.956. If unpaid within the time period, the prosecution of the reexamination proceeding will be terminated under 37 CFR 1.957(b) or limited under 37 CFR 1.957(c), as appropriate.
guidance: PTOL‑2069 is the form used for fee deficiency notices. Failure to pay may result in cancellation of claims or other adverse consequences; timely payment avoids abandonment.

name: Narrow claim construction after patent expiration
description: Once the patent expires, a narrow claim construction is applied (see MPEP §2258, subsection I.G. 'Claim Interpretation and Treatment').
guidance: This is a substantive assertion about claim interpretation post‑expiration; examiners and practitioners should consult MPEP §2258.I.G for details on how claim interpretation/treatment differs when a patent has expired.

name: Standard of review for claim construction and indefiniteness
description: Claim construction is a question of law and receives de novo review on appeal; claim indefiniteness is a legal conclusion implementing 35 U.S.C. § 112, and is reviewed de novo.
