guidance: Cited authorities: Markman v. Westview Instruments, Inc., 517 U.S. 370, 390–91 (1996); Teva Pharms. USA, Inc. v. Sandoz, Inc., 574 U.S. 318, 325 (2015); Atmel Corp. v. Info. Storage Devices, Inc., 198 F.3d 1374, 1378 (Fed. Cir. 1999) ('A determination of claim indefiniteness is a legal conclusion ...'). Courts should apply de novo review to the legal question of indefiniteness, while recognizing any subsidiary factual findings may have separate standards.

name: Viewpoint of a person skilled in the art (POSITA)
description: Indefiniteness is decided from the viewpoint of persons skilled in the field of the invention; claims must inform such persons about the scope of the invention with reasonable certainty.
guidance: Example case-specific POSITA definition here: 'at least a master’s degree in computer science or a related field, or a bachelor’s degree ... plus two years of relevant experience, with experience in computer graphics, computer-aided design, solid modeling, or geometric modeling.' (District court agreed definition cited by parties.)

name: Definiteness requirement (Nautilus 'reasonable certainty' standard)
description: Under 35 U.S.C. § 112, claims, viewed in light of the specification and prosecution history, must inform those skilled in the art about the scope of the invention with reasonable certainty; the requirement mandates clarity but recognizes absolute precision is unattainable.
guidance: Primary authority: Nautilus, Inc. v. Biosig Instruments, Inc., 572 U.S. 898, 910 (2014): 'inform those skilled in the art about the scope of the invention with reasonable certainty.' Courts must read claims in context (intrinsic record) to assess reasonable certainty.

name: Proper sources for claim construction: intrinsic and extrinsic evidence
description: Courts should look first to the intrinsic record—the words of the claims themselves, the remainder of the specification, and the prosecution history—and may consult extrinsic evidence (expert testimony, technical dictionaries, state of the art) to inform meaning.
guidance: Authority: Phillips v. AWH Corp., 415 F.3d 1303, 1314 (Fed. Cir. 2005) (en banc). Extrinsic evidence can explain technical terms and the state of the art but does not override intrinsic evidence.

name: Function of claims versus specification
description: Claims define the patent right and provide legal notice of the boundaries of the monopoly; the specification teaches and describes the invention. Claims need not duplicate the detailed technical description in the specification.
guidance: Cited: Ariad Pharms., Inc. v. Eli Lilly & Co., 598 F.3d 1336, 1347 (Fed. Cir. 2010) ('Claims define and circumscribe, the written description discloses and teaches.'); In re Vamco Mach. & Tool, Inc., 752 F.2d 1564, 1577 n.5 (Fed. Cir. 1985) (claims are legal documents defining scope). Use specification to interpret claims, but claims remain the metes and bounds of the right.

name: Incorrect 'unanswered questions' or 'claim language standing alone' test is an improper standard
description: A standard that declares a claim indefinite if there exist any 'unanswered questions' or if alleged ambiguities are not resolved 'in the claim language, standing alone' is incorrect.
guidance: Courts must not require that every technical question raised by an expert be answered within the literal claim language; instead, claims are read in light of the specification and prosecution history to determine how a POSITA would understand them. The district court erred applying an 'unanswered questions' test in this case.

name: Role and limits of expert testimony in claim construction
description: Expert testimony may be used to explain terms of art, the meaning of technical terms, and the state of the art, but it cannot be used to establish the proper or legal construction of the claim language itself.
guidance: Authority: Teva Pharms., 574 U.S. at 332 (quoting Winans v. N.Y. & Erie R.R. Co., 62 U.S. 88, 100–01 (1859)). Experts inform the factual record about technology; legal claim construction remains the court's task.

name: Weight and relevance of prosecution history and examiner amendments
description: Prosecution history—including examiner rejections and applicant amendments resolving rejections—bears on claim meaning and definiteness; an examiner's withdrawal of an indefiniteness rejection after claim amendment is a relevant fact in construing claims and assessing indefiniteness.
guidance: Example: examiner initially rejected claims for indefiniteness and required specific amendments; applicant amended claims in consultation with examiner and the examiner withdrew the indefiniteness rejection and allowed the claims. Courts should consider such prosecution events rather than ignoring them.

name: Prior art and established approaches can inform definiteness
description: When the general approach is sufficiently well established in the art and referenced in the patent (e.g., Watson and Delaunay methods), that background can render claim language definite because a POSITA would understand the claimed improvement in that context.
guidance: Authority: Presidio Components, Inc. v. Am. Tech. Ceramics Corp., 875 F.3d 1369, 1377 (Fed. Cir. 2017). Use of well-known prior art in the specification and claims may clarify terms that otherwise appear terse.

name: Certainty required: reasonable, not absolute; patents addressed to skilled artisans
description: The definiteness requirement demands clarity sufficient to apprise skilled artisans of the claimed scope with reasonable certainty; it does not require absolute precision in all cases and patents are addressed to those skilled in the art (not the general public).
guidance: Cited: Nautilus, 572 U.S. at 909–10; Carnegie Steel Co. v. Cambria Iron Co., 185 U.S. 403, 437 (1902). Courts should balance competing concerns and apply a standard of reasonableness in light of the subject matter.

name: Procedure for obtaining publication dates of references
description: Requests to determine earliest publication or first distribution dates should be made to STIC in the examiner's Technology Center.
guidance: For U.S. publications, STIC staff can obtain the day and month claimed by the copyright owner; similar information for foreign publications can be obtained through correspondence but may take longer.

name: Examiner review criteria and grounds for exception to national defense classification
description: When assigning an IPC/CPC classification code that corresponds to national defense codes, the examiner shall determine whether to treat the application as national defense-related. In principle such applications need to be treated as national defense-related, but exceptions exist.
guidance: Grounds for exception include: applicant has no address or business in the Republic of Korea; application does not fall under major defense materials specified in the Defense Acquisition Program Act; subject not among weapons systems specified in enforcement decrees; prior art identical or similar has already been disclosed; claimed invention is not related to national security/military secrets; application was incorrectly classified initially but was laid open to public before change. If difficult to determine, the examiner may consult the Director of the Emergency Affairs Subsection, the applicant, or a military expert.

name: Conditions and procedures for permission to file overseas (United States example)
description: Where the Korean government grants permission to file a banned application overseas (currently limited to the United States by bilateral agreement), permission is issued in writing after consultation with DAPA and subject to specified conditions and procedural requirements.
guidance: Conditions include: (1) the specification content shall be clear and specific enough to examine the application in the United States; (2) the right to claim damages caused by confidentiality in the United States shall be waived except for damages due to use/disclosure by the United States without permission. Procedural steps: submit written request Form No.21; if permission granted, applicant must attach two copies of application documents, copy of permission, copy of representative's personal info and security clearance to the US application and submit those documents to DAPA; designate a representative who holds US security clearance; immediately notify DAPA of the US application number and filing date. The bilateral agreement limits filing to Korea and the United States under the confidentiality agreement.

name: Permissibility of negative limitations under 35 U.S.C. 112(b)
description: The current view of the courts is that there is nothing inherently ambiguous or uncertain about a negative limitation; so long as the boundaries of the patent protection sought are set forth definitely, albeit negatively, the claim complies with the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph).
guidance: Negative limitations are not per se indefinite. The examiner/ drafter should evaluate whether the negative wording nonetheless sets clear boundaries for the claim scope. Older case law criticized certain negative limitations, but modern precedent accepts negative limitations that define clear boundaries. See examples and cases cited (In re Schechter, In re Wakefield, In re Barr).

name: Avoid claiming by exclusion (indefiniteness risk)
description: A negative limitation that attempts to claim the invention by excluding what the inventors did not invent (i.e., defining the invention primarily in terms of what it is not) can render the claim indefinite.
guidance: Watch for phrasing that effectively claims by exclusion rather than describing the invention. Example of problematic language: 'R is an alkenyl radical other than 2‑butenyl and 2,4‑pentadienyl' (In re Schechter) — held to be indefinite because it attempted to claim by excluding unclaimed matter. Where the negative limitation simply excludes a few known alternatives that are clearly defined in the disclosure, it may be acceptable; where it merely says 'other than' undefined or numerous alternatives, risk of indefiniteness increases.

name: Definiteness requirement applied to each recited negative limitation
description: Each recited limitation — including negative limitations — must itself be definite. If the negative limitation is definite, the claim may be allowable despite being phrased negatively.
guidance: Evaluate the definiteness of each negative phrase individually. Example: the limitation 'said homopolymer being free from the proteins, soaps, resins, and sugars present in natural Hevea rubber' was considered definite because each referred characteristic was definite (In re Wakefield). Similarly, 'incapable of forming a dye with said oxidized developing agent' was held definite where the boundaries were clear (In re Barr).

name: Negative limitations must have basis in the original disclosure (written description support)
description: Any negative limitation or exclusionary proviso must have basis in the original disclosure; without such basis, the negative limitation fails the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (pre‑AIA 112, first paragraph).
guidance: If the specification positively recites alternative elements, those alternatives may be explicitly excluded in the claims (In re Johnson; Ex parte Grasselli). The examiner should look for explicit support in the original filing for excluding specific elements or features. If the negative limitation is not supported by the specification, the claim should be rejected under the written description requirement; see MPEP § 2163–§ 2163.07(b) for further discussion.

name: Positive recitation of alternatives permits later exclusion
description: Where the specification describes alternative features or elements positively, the applicant may later exclude those alternatives in the claims via negative limitations.
guidance: Support can be inferential where the specification describes 'the whole' such that it 'necessarily described the part remaining' — court authority (In re Johnson) supports that a description of alternatives can provide basis to exclude particular alternatives. Ex parte Grasselli and related authority confirm that explicit positive disclosure of alternatives is a sound basis for exclusion in claims.

name: Applicant need not articulate advantages/disadvantages to exclude alternatives
description: An applicant is not required to explain the advantages or disadvantages of alternative features in the specification in order to later exclude those alternatives in the claims.
guidance: The Federal Circuit has held that describing alternative features without discussing pros/cons does not preclude later excluding options in claims (Inphi Corp. v. Netlist, Inc.). Drafting practice: you do not need to describe why an excluded alternative is inferior to have support for excluding it, but you must still have sufficient disclosure to show possession of the claimed subject matter.

name: Mere silence in the specification generally does not provide basis for a negative limitation (but may in special circumstances)
description: The mere absence of a positive recitation in the specification is not generally sufficient to support a negative claim limitation; silence will not generally suffice to support a negative claim limitation.
guidance: However, where the disclosure would reasonably convey to a person skilled in the art that the inventor possessed the claimed subject matter, a negative limitation may be supported even without explicit positive recitation. Ex parte Parks noted lack of literal basis may not establish a prima facie lack of descriptive support. Novartis Pharms. Corp. v. Accord Healthcare, Inc. (quoting Ariad) emphasizes that the disclosure must 'reasonably convey[] to those skilled in the art that the inventor had possession of the claimed subject matter as of the filing date.' Consider whether a skilled artisan would understand from context that the negative limitation is necessarily present.

name: Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) where negative limitation lacks written‑description basis
description: Any claim containing a negative limitation which does not have basis in the original disclosure should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (pre‑AIA 112, first paragraph) for failing to comply with the written description requirement.
guidance: When examining or drafting, if you cannot identify adequate support in the original disclosure for a negative limitation, apply a written description rejection. Cross‑reference MPEP §2163–§2163.07(b) for detailed written‑description analysis and examples. Document why the claimed exclusion is unsupported and provide references to the specification (or lack thereof).

name: Specification Must Be Enabling to Persons Skilled in the Art
description: The relative skill of those in the art refers to the skill level of those in the technological field to which the claimed invention pertains. Where different arts are involved in the invention, the specification is enabling if it enables persons skilled in each art to carry out the aspect of the invention applicable to their specialty.
guidance: If two distinct technologies are relevant, disclosure is adequate only if a person of ordinary skill in each technology could practice the invention from the disclosure. See In re Naquin; Ex parte Zechnall (disclosure enabling if electronic computer art cooperates with fuel injection art).

name: Examiner Must Specifically Identify Missing Information for Enablement Rejections
description: When doubt about enablement arises because information is missing about one or more essential claim elements or relationships between elements, the examiner should specifically identify what information is missing and why the missing information is needed to provide enablement.
guidance: The examiner's Office action should state which essential elements/relationships lack disclosure and explain why the missing information is necessary to avoid undue experimentation.

name: Enablement Must Be Commensurate with Claim Breadth
description: Enablement serves the dual function of ensuring adequate disclosure and preventing claims broader than the disclosed invention. Broad claim language risks losing any claim that cannot be enabled across its full scope.
guidance: When claims are broad, examiners should assess whether the specification provides sufficient direction to enable the full claimed scope. Examples: MagSil (broad resistance-change claim not enabled across claimed scope); Auto. Techs. (claim interpreted to include electronic sensors where spec lacked electronic detail). Challenge claims that encompass areas not supported by the specification.

name: Block Diagrams and Functional Labels Alone May Be Nonenabling
description: A disclosure presented as block diagrams (hollow rectangles functionally labeled and interconnected) may be insufficient if there is no indication whether parts are off-the-shelf or must be specifically constructed or modified, and if there are no details on interconnection, timing, and control to obtain the claimed operations.
guidance: Functional block diagrams without specifics about the identity, construction, interconnection, timing, or control of components can justify a 35 U.S.C. 112 rejection. See In re Gunn; In re Donohue; In re Ghiron; In re Scarbrough. Examiners should challenge functional-only block diagrams when more than routine experimentation would be required to implement the blocks.

name: Device Disclosures May Require Details of Complex Component Construction and Operation
description: An adequate disclosure of a device may require details of how complex components are constructed and perform the desired function; mere generic naming and overall function may be insufficient.
guidance: If complex elements are described only generically and it is not routine to adapt known elements to the claimed system, the disclosure may be nonenabling. See In re Scarbrough (complex elements known to perform broadly recited functions in different systems must be shown adaptable for the applicant's system with only reasonable experimentation).

name: Microorganisms and Biological Deposits: Availability Requirement for Enablement
description: Patent applications involving living biological products (e.g., microorganisms) present unique availability questions. A public deposit can provide an acceptable means of meeting written description and enablement; a deposit must be made prior to issue but need not be made prior to filing.
guidance: Examiners must consider scope of claim limitations (e.g., species vs strains). Depositing representative strains may not enable a claim to an entire species if the verbal description does not enable making other members of the species. See In re Argoudelis; In re Lundak; Ex parte Jackson. See MPEP §§ 2402–2411.03 for deposit rules.

name: Chemical/Drug Enablement: Limited Examples and Unpredictability Can Defeat Enablement
description: In unpredictable arts such as antisense genetics, limited examples and an assertion of broad applicability may be insufficient; enablement must be commensurate with the breadth claimed.
guidance: Courts have found nonenabling disclosures when (1) the amount of direction and number of working examples are narrow compared to claim breadth, (2) the art is highly unpredictable, and (3) substantial experimentation would be required to extend to claimed scope. See Enzo Biochem (antisense), In re Wright (vaccine across RNA viruses), In re Goodman (plant expression). Conversely, detailed direction and working examples can support enablement (PPG, In re Wands, In re Bundy). Examiners should weigh examples, unpredictability, and guidance in spec.

name: Computer-Related Inventions: Apply Combined Skilled-in-the-Art Standard
description: When a claimed invention involves computer programming and another technology, the level of skill of persons in both technologies is the appropriate criterion for enablement analysis.
guidance: Examiners should recognize that knowledge of persons skilled in both technologies is required to determine sufficiency. See In re Naquin; In re Brown; White Consol. Indus. v. Vega Servo-Control.

name: Referencing Prior Art Documents and Commercial Availability
description: Commercial availability of an identified prior art computer system is relevant to enablement, but merely citing technical publications or patents is insufficient unless it is clear which parts of the cited material would enable construction and how they interconnect. Prior art patents relied upon must have publication dates earlier than the application’s effective filing date.
guidance: Post-filing patents/pubs are not evidence of what was known at filing and cannot be used to show state of the art. Examiners should require applicants to show how cited prior art would enable the claimed invention (which parts, how interconnected). See In re Forman; In re Budnick; In re Gunn.

name: Consider all claim limitations; cannot disregard printed matter
description: USPTO personnel must consider all claim limitations when determining patentability of an invention over the prior art. Since a claim must be read as a whole, USPTO personnel may not disregard claim limitations that include printed matter.
guidance: Cites In re Gulack and Diamond v. Diehr. The examiner must treat printed matter as a claim limitation in the overall claim construction analysis; do not ignore printed matter when comparing to prior art.

name: Printed matter — threshold: limitation directed to content of information
description: A limitation is printed matter only if it claims the content of information.
guidance: This is the first step of printed matter analysis (In re DiStefano). If the limitation is directed to content, proceed to determine whether it is functionally or structurally related to its substrate.

name: Functional relationship test for printed matter
description: Printed matter and associated product must be in a functional relationship to be given patentable weight; a functional relationship can be found where the printed matter performs some function with respect to the product or the product performs some function with respect to the printed matter.
guidance: Examples: indicia on a measuring cup indicating volume (In re Miller); a hatband whose physical arrangement of numbers satisfies a claimed algorithm (Gulack). If such a new and nonobvious functional relationship exists, give patentable weight to the printed matter (In re Lowry, In re Ngai, In re Gulack).

name: Evidence against functional relationship (support-only printed matter)
description: No functional relationship exists where a product merely serves as a support for printed matter or where the claim as a whole is directed to conveying a message/meaning to a human independent of the substrate.
guidance: Examples/anti-patterns: hatband images not arranged in sequence (Gulack); deck of playing cards with images (In re Bryan); measuring tape with unrelated wiring information; kit containing chemicals plus general printed instructions that are unrelated to that specific set (In re Ngai). If printed matter and product do not depend on each other, printed matter lacks functional relationship.

name: Functional relationship must be new and nonobvious to carry patentable weight
description: Once a functional relationship between printed matter and product is found, the relationship must be new and nonobvious for the printed matter to be given patentable weight.
guidance: Even if a functional relationship exists (e.g., color-coded indicia indicating expiration date), the claim may be anticipated or obvious if prior art teaches the claimed invention or combination of references shows it.

name: Machine-readable media: evaluate programming-system relationship
description: When determining the scope of a claim directed to a computer-readable medium containing programming, examine the relationship between the programming and the intended computer system to determine functional relationship.
guidance: If the programming performs some function with respect to the intended computer system (e.g., attribute data objects facilitating retrieval), a functional relationship exists and the claimed artifact is given patentable weight (Lowry). If the medium merely supports information directed to a human reader (e.g., batting averages, music tracks), no functional relationship exists. Claims reciting executable code that embody an abstract idea must also be evaluated for eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 101 (see MPEP § 2106).

name: Anticipation/obviousness OK when prior art appears identical though silent on inherent characteristic
description: A rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 can be made when the prior art product seems identical to the claimed composition except the prior art is silent as to an inherent characteristic, because a prior art product that inherently possesses each claimed limitation anticipates the claim.
guidance: Cites In re Best and related reasoning: a single reference can anticipate even if it does not state the characteristic explicitly, if the characteristic is necessarily present.

name: Once examiner shows inherency, burden of production shifts to applicant
description: When a reference teaching a product appearing substantially identical is made the basis of a rejection and the examiner presents evidence or reasoning to show inherency, the burden of production shifts to the applicant to prove the prior art products do not necessarily or inherently possess the characteristics of the claimed product.
guidance: Cites In re Best and In re Fitzgerald. Applicant must present objective evidence to rebut (e.g., comparative data, specific dimensions/tests). Declarations lacking essential factual specifics (e.g., Schreiber) may fail to rebut.

name: Product/apparatus claims: substantially identical structure/composition implies properties/functions presumed inherent
description: Where claimed and prior art products are identical or substantially identical in structure or composition, or are produced by identical or substantially identical processes, a prima facie case of anticipation or obviousness is established and claimed properties/functions are presumed inherent.
guidance: Cites In re Best, In re Spada, Titanium Metals Corp. Applicant bears burden to show the prior art product does not possess the characteristics; examples include chemical composition matches or structural identity.

name: Product claims: nonfunctional printed matter does not distinguish over otherwise identical prior art
description: Where the only difference between a prior art product and a claimed product is printed matter that is not functionally related to the product, the content of the printed matter will not distinguish the claimed product from the prior art for patentability purposes.
guidance: Cites In re Ngai, In re Gulack, In re Miller, In re Xiao, In re Bryan. Court rationale: permitting such distinctions would allow perpetual patenting by adding new instruction sheets or labels unless a new and nonobvious functional relationship exists.

name: Process claims: prior art device may anticipate method if device inherently performs method in normal operation
description: Under inherency principles, if a prior art device, in its normal and usual operation, would necessarily perform the method claimed, then the method is anticipated by the prior art device.
guidance: Cites In re King and In re Best. When prior art device is the same as the device described in the specification for carrying out the claimed method, it can be assumed the device will inherently perform the claimed process. Applicant must introduce evidence (e.g., demonstrating differences) to rebut.

name: Process-of-use claims: new and nonobvious uses of old structures may be patentable, but mere discovery of new property may not
description: The discovery of a new use for an old structure based on unknown properties might be patentable as a process of use; however, when the claim recites using an old composition/structure and the 'use' is directed to a result or property of that composition/structure, the claim is anticipated if the prior art composition/structure is the same.
guidance: Cites In re Hack and In re May. Applicants relying on unexpected properties must show they are nonobvious and unexpected; a mere finding of a previously unknown property does not necessarily make a new use patentable.

name: Product-by-process claims: scope defined by structure implied by steps, not by the manipulations
description: Product-by-process claims are not limited to the manipulations of the recited steps but are limited to the structure implied by those steps.
guidance: Implication: when evaluating novelty/obviousness of product-by-process claims, focus on the structural identity resulting from the process; see MPEP § 2113 for further guidance on burden and analogous issues.

name: First filings and subsequent filings
description: First filings are applications filed without claiming priority of another previous filing; all other applications are subsequent filings (usually within one year of the first filing).
guidance: Where first-filing statistics are incomplete, the report assumes domestic national filings are equivalent to first filings and treats PCT filings as subsequent filings. Note this is an approximation except where patent-family data allow precise counts.

name: Step 2B: Do additional elements amount to an inventive concept (significantly more)?
description: Step 2B asks: Does the claim recite additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception(s)? Examiners should answer this by first identifying additional elements (features/limitations/steps) recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception(s), and then evaluating those additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether they contribute an inventive concept (i.e., amount to significantly more than the judicial exception(s)).
guidance: Evaluation is made with respect to considerations the Supreme Court identified and discussed in the MPEP (§2106.05(a)-(h)). This is not a weighing test; it is important to evaluate the significance of the additional elements relative to the invention and determine whether they encompass an inventive concept. If the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the exception, the claim is eligible (Pathway C). If not, the claim is not patent-eligible and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101.

name: Outcome rule: Pathway C eligibility vs 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection
description: If the claim as a whole recites significantly more than the exception, the claim is eligible (Step 2B: YES) at Pathway C. If the claim as a whole does not amount to significantly more than the judicial exception, the claim is not patent-eligible (Step 2B: NO) and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101.
guidance: When concluding there is no inventive concept, formulate an ineligibility rejection per MPEP §2106.07. If there is an inventive concept, the eligibility analysis is complete.

name: 2106.05(a): Improvements to functioning of a computer or other technology
description: In determining patent eligibility, examiners should consider whether the claim 'purport(s) to improve the functioning of the computer itself' or 'any other technology or technical field.' This consideration is the search for a technological solution to a technological problem and may be evaluated at Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B.
guidance: This consideration has support in case law (e.g., Enfish, McRO, DDR Holdings, Amdocs). If an asserted improvement is to conventional computer functioning or technology, the specification must provide technical explanation of how to implement the invention so that a person of ordinary skill would recognize the improvement. Improvements that are merely assertions without technical detail are insufficient. The examiner should analyze both the specification and the claim to ensure the claim reflects the disclosed improvement.

name: Specification must provide technical explanation showing asserted improvement
description: If it is asserted the invention improves conventional functioning of a computer or technology, a technical explanation as to how to implement the invention should be present in the specification so that one of ordinary skill in the art would recognize the claimed invention as providing an improvement.
guidance: The specification need not explicitly use the word 'improvement,' but must describe the invention such that the improvement is apparent to one of ordinary skill. Conclusory statements asserting an improvement without necessary detail are insufficient (e.g., contrast McRO (sufficient explanation) with Affinity Labs (insufficient details)).

name: Claim must reflect the disclosed improvement; evaluate the claim 'as a whole'
description: After finding the specification discloses an improvement, ensure the claim itself reflects that improvement: the claim must include the components or steps of the invention that provide the improvement (though it need not literally recite the improvement phrase). Evaluate the full scope of the claim under the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) and evaluate the claim 'as an ordered combination.'
guidance: Do not oversimplify claims or ignore specific claim requirements. A claimed improvement must be present in the claim scope; mere recitation of generic computer components may be insufficient even if the specification describes improvements (see Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec).

name: Improvement may arise from one or more additional elements or their combination
description: The improvement can be provided by one or more additional elements, or by additional element(s) in combination with the recited judicial exception.
guidance: Analyze claims as a whole for unconventional, non-generic arrangements of elements (e.g., BASCOM installation/location/combination example). See Diamond v. Diehr and Finjan/Finjan-related discussion in MPEP §2106.04(d).

name: Computer-limited scope requirement and mental-steps/telephone/verbal embodiments
description: For a method claim to improve computer functionality, the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim must be limited to computer implementation; a claim whose entire scope can be performed mentally cannot be said to improve computer technology.
guidance: If a claimed process covers embodiments that are performable without a computer (e.g., verbally or by telephone), it cannot improve computer technology (see Synopsys; RecogniCorp). Ensure claim scope excludes purely mental or non-computer implementations when asserting computer-functionality improvement.

name: Examples the courts have indicated may show an improvement in computer-functionality
description: The guideline lists illustrative examples of improvements courts have found persuasive (e.g., modification of hyperlink protocol for dual-source hybrid webpage; inventive distribution of functionality to filter Internet content; methods of rendering halftone images; distributed network architectures reducing congestion; memory systems configurable by processor type; technical details for transmitting images; particular server structures storing organized images; particular software programming/menus; methods generating security profiles; improved user interfaces; interfaces for navigating 3D spreadsheets; licensed-software operation restrictions).
guidance: These examples (enumerated i–xii in the MPEP) are illustrative, not exhaustive, and show the kinds of unconventional technical solutions courts have recognized as improvements. Use these as analogies when assessing whether a claimed element(s) plausibly provides a technological improvement.

name: Examples the courts have indicated may NOT be sufficient to show an improvement
description: The guideline lists illustrative examples courts have found insufficient to show an improvement in computer-functionality (e.g., functionally claimed restaurant menus; accelerating analysis solely by general-purpose computer speed; mere automation of manual processes; recording/transmitting/archiving images with conventional tech; affixing barcodes without technical details; instructions to display information without how-to limitations; improving stored information quality rather than database functionality; arranging GUI information to assist users).
guidance: These examples (enumerated i–viii) indicate shades of insufficient technical contribution: merely using generic computer capabilities, asserting speed gains due solely to a general-purpose computer, or claiming results without technical means to achieve them will typically fail to supply an inventive concept. Compare claim specifics to these examples when deciding insufficiency.

name: Definition of 'practice of law' (Massachusetts standard)
description: The practice of law includes directing and managing the enforcement of legal claims and the establishment of the legal rights of others, where it is necessary to form and to act upon opinions as to what those rights are and as to the legal methods which must be adopted to enforce them, the practice of giving or furnishing legal advice as to such rights and methods and the practice, as an occupation, of drafting documents by which such rights are created, modified, surrendered or secured (quoting In re Hrones).
guidance: Crafting a sophisticated civil rights lawsuit, causing commencement and directing prosecution of the lawsuit, and drafting pleadings that create or modify rights all fall within this definition and therefore constitute practicing law in Massachusetts.

name: Pro hac vice admission cannot be presumed without application
description: No pro hac vice admission will be offered by the court without an attorney first requesting it; it is unreasonable to expect admission without having sought it and satisfied prerequisites such as recruiting local counsel and filing necessary supporting documentation.
guidance: Routine grant of such motions assumes the applicant has met procedural prerequisites. A claim that pro hac vice admission was 'pending' is unsupported if the practitioner never filed the motion or did not demonstrate diligent efforts to obtain local counsel. Lack of evidence of 'diligent effort' to find local counsel precludes finding the expectation reasonable.

name: Proof of 'diligent effort' required when claiming inability to find local counsel
description: When a practitioner claims he could not find local counsel (to support a claim that admission pro hac vice was not possible), he must produce evidence depicting the 'diligent effort' he undertook to find such counsel.
guidance: Absent concrete evidence of effort, assertions that it was 'virtually impossible' or that counsel could not be found are insufficient to show a reasonable expectation of admission; tribunals will reject conclusory statements without supporting proof.

name: Judicially developed exceptions to Section 101
description: The Supreme Court has long held that Section 101 contains implicit exceptions: 'laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas,' when claimed as such, are not patentable.
guidance: These three types of nonpatentable discoveries are sometimes called the judicially developed exceptions to patent-eligible subject matter. Historical treatment of these exceptions has varied over time and affects scope of eligibility.

name: Alice/Mayo two-step test — Step 2: inventive concept requirement
description: Under the second step of the Alice/Mayo test, if the claims are directed to an ineligible concept, then the invention is not patentable unless the patent claims have an inventive concept.
guidance: Step 2 considers the elements of each patent claim, both individually and as an ordered combination, in determining whether they contain additional aspects that 'transform the nature of the claim' into a patent-eligible application of an ineligible concept.

name: Conventionality/Generic-computer implementation cannot supply inventive concept
description: Claim limitations that are conventional, routine, and well understood, such as implementing an abstract idea on a generic computer, cannot supply an inventive concept.
guidance: This principle means simply reciting conventional technology or routine steps (e.g., using a generic computer) will not transform an abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter; courts evaluate both individual elements and ordered combinations for an inventive contribution.

name: Supreme Court examples of ineligible claims (illustrative precedents)
description: The Supreme Court invalidated patents as ineligible under Section 101 in several notable cases: a business method for hedging price-fluctuation risk (Bilski v. Kappos, 2010); a method for calibrating drug dosage (Mayo v. Prometheus, 2012); isolated human DNA segments (Ass'n for Molecular Pathology v. Myriad Genetics, 2013); and a computer-implemented method of mitigating settlement risk in financial transactions (Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank, 2014).
guidance: These decisions illustrate applications of the judicial exceptions and the Alice/Mayo framework and show that certain business methods, natural products, and certain computer-implemented methods have been treated as ineligible, leading to narrower eligibility in software, business methods, and biotechnology.

name: Interplay of Section 101 with other patentability requirements
description: Section 101 defines the types of inventions that may be patented but is only one statutory gate; eligible subject matter must also meet other legal requirements such as novelty, enablement, and nonobviousness.
guidance: A claimed invention must satisfy Section 101 and the other statutory requirements—failure on any ground can defeat patentability; policy or legislative changes to Section 101 do not alter these other requirements.

name: Enumerated substantive defenses to infringement actions
description: Defenses permitting judgment for the defendant include that the plaintiff's specification and claim "does not contain the whole truth relative to his invention ... or ... contains more than is necessary to produce the described effect" (concealment or addition made to deceive), that the patentee was not the "original and first inventor or discoverer" of the thing or a substantial part claimed, that it "had been described in some public work anterior" to the patentee, that it "had been in public use or on sale with the consent and allowance of the patentee before his application," that the patent was "surreptitiously or unjustly obtained" from another who was reasonably diligent, or that an alien patentee failed for eighteen months to put the invention on sale.
guidance: These are multiple substantive grounds that can render a patent unenforceable in a damages action; proof must show the stated facts (e.g., prior publication, prior use/sale, fraud, lack of originality).

name: Court powers when plaintiff's claim embraces more than actual invention
description: If the plaintiff fails on the ground that his specification of claim "is embraced more than that of which he was the first inventor," but the defendant used any part "justly and truly specified and claimed as new," the court may adjudge and award costs as may appear just and equitable.
guidance: Even when an overbroad claim causes plaintiff to fail, courts can award equitable costs where defendant infringed a legitimately claimed subset.

name: Recording of pre-December 15, 1836 patents and documents
description: Any person in possession or interest in a patent issued prior to Dec 15, 1836 (or assignments executed/recorded prior) may, without charge, present them to the Commissioner to have them recorded anew with descriptions, specifications, claims, and drawings; the Commissioner shall transcribe authenticated copies into record books; where drawings were not originally annexed, a drawing verified by oath may be filed or copied.
guidance: Owners of pre-fire patents can have records reconstructed and entered anew to restore the evidentiary record.

name: Right to make disclaimer for overbroad claims
description: Whenever a patentee has by inadvertence, accident, or mistake claimed more than he was the original or first inventor of, he (or his administrators, executors, assigns) may make a disclaimer of such parts not claimed to be held by virtue of the patent, stating extent of interest; the disclaimer shall be in writing, attested by witnesses, recorded in the Patent Office on payment of ten dollars, and thereafter taken as part of the original specification to extent of interest. Such disclaimer shall not affect actions pending at the time except as relates to unreasonable neglect or delay in filing the same.
guidance: Disclaimers can narrow asserted scope to remove overclaims; formal execution, fee, and recordation are required; timing relative to suits matters for costs and relief.

name: Revision and restriction of claims on additions/improvements and reissues
description: Whenever application is made for adding a newly discovered improvement to an existing patent, or a patent is returned for reissue, the specification of claim annexed shall be subject to revision and restriction in the same manner as original applications; the Commissioner shall not add the improvement nor grant the reissue until the applicant has entered a disclaimer or altered the specification of claim in accordance with the Commissioner's decision; applicant dissatisfied has the same remedy and privileges as in original applications.
guidance: Claims for improvements or reissues are examined and may be restricted; applicants have appeal/remedy channels analogous to originals.

name: Initial filing completeness and accuracy
description: The initial filing must include a detailed description of the invention, claims defining the scope of protection sought, and any necessary drawings or diagrams; a correct filing date and application number are assigned which establish priority.
guidance: Ensure the application is complete and accurate at filing to avoid delays or rejections. The filing date is critical as it establishes priority; include all necessary documents and well-drafted claims and drawings to minimize later problems.

name: Substantive patentability criteria (novelty, inventive step, industrial applicability)
description: During substantive examination the JPO assesses whether the invention meets legal requirements for patentability: novelty, inventive step, and industrial applicability.
guidance: Draft claims and description to emphasize what is new and inventive and how the invention is industrially applicable. Anticipate and address likely prior art and obviousness lines in the specification and prosecution strategy.

name: Thorough, well-reasoned responses to office actions
description: Responses should address each of the examiner’s objections in detail and may include amended claims, additional technical details, or legal/technical arguments to overcome objections.
guidance: Craft responses that are clear, point-by-point, and supported by citations or evidence where appropriate. Collaboration with a patent attorney is recommended to frame persuasive legal and technical arguments.

name: Amendments must avoid new matter
description: Amendments are allowed to clarify or narrow claims, but JPO regulations prohibit adding new matter not disclosed in the original application.
guidance: When amending, ensure all changes are directly supported by the original disclosure. Draft the initial application with possible fallback positions to facilitate later claim amendments without risking added matter objections.

name: Strategic claim amendment practices
description: Amendments can include narrowing claims to avoid prior art, clarifying ambiguous language, or providing additional details to support patentability.
guidance: Amend strategically to preserve patent scope while overcoming rejections; avoid unnecessary narrowing. Ensure amendments are consistent with prosecution strategy across jurisdictions if pursuing international protection.

name: Harmonizing filings across jurisdictions
description: When seeking protection in multiple jurisdictions, align claims and descriptions while addressing each office’s specific requirements and legal standards.
guidance: Be aware of differences (e.g., strict no-new-matter policies at EPO and JPO versus broader amendment practices at the USPTO). Tailor amendments and claim language to each jurisdiction while keeping global consistency.

name: Early and comprehensive prior art searching
description: Conduct thorough prior art searches before filing to identify obstacles and draft stronger claims.
guidance: A proactive search informs claim drafting, anticipates examiner objections, and helps craft arguments differentiating the invention. Consider professional search firms for deeper or non-English prior art.

name: Detailed and clear application drafting
description: A high-quality initial application should contain detailed descriptions, well-defined claims, and supporting drawings to reduce the likelihood of objections.
guidance: Provide embodiments, examples, and technical details enabling a skilled person to reproduce the invention; include fallback claim sets and embodiments to facilitate later prosecution without adding new matter.

name: Timely and strategic responses to office actions
description: Respond promptly and strategically to office actions, carefully reviewing objections and making necessary amendments or arguments.
guidance: Delays can limit options and weaken positions; coordinate response strategy with counsel to balance claim breadth and likelihood of allowance.

name: Addressing novelty objections
description: To overcome novelty rejections, provide detailed arguments that clearly distinguish your invention from cited prior art.
guidance: Highlight unique features and technical differences with examples or data. If necessary, amend claims to focus on distinguishing elements supported by the original disclosure.

name: Managing amendments without introducing unsupported information
description: When amending claims or description, ensure all changes are supported by the original disclosure and do not introduce new technical information.
guidance: Draft the original filing with embodiments and fallback language to facilitate permissible amendments later. Review amendment chains to ensure they trace back to original passages.

name: What examiners read first (order of review)
description: When opening a new application, examiners typically read in this order: (1) the abstract, (2) the independent claims, (3) the figures, (4) the detailed description as it relates to the independent claims.
guidance: A clear, accessible abstract and self-contained independent claims set the tone for examination. Structure front matter so the abstract and independent claims communicate the invention quickly.

name: Do not claim features not described in the specification
description: Claims that recite features not described in the spec cause problems during examination.
guidance: Ensure every claimed element has clear support in the detailed description (avoid adding claim language unsupported by the spec). This prevents enablement/written-description issues and examiner rejections.

name: Avoid unnecessarily long claims with repeated restatements
description: Unnecessarily long claims that restate the same concept waste examiner time and obscure the invention.
guidance: Keep claim language concise and avoid redundant recitations that do not add substantive limitations; clarity and brevity aid examiner understanding.

name: Independent claims should be self-contained and clear
description: Independent claims should be self-contained: a reader should be able to understand the invention from the independent claim alone.
guidance: Avoid claims that require the reader to look up specialized terms in the spec; draft independent claims to stand on their own so an examiner can quickly grasp the claimed invention.

name: Specification should walk through the claims (map spec to claims)
description: The detailed description should make it clear, paragraph by paragraph, where each claim element is described.
guidance: Structure the specification to mirror the claim sequence so an examiner can easily locate support for each claim element.

name: Office action responses: directly engage with cited references
description: Direct engagement with the cited references—quote the passage, explain why it does not teach the claim element—is helpful to examiners.
guidance: Point to exact passages in the prior art and explain differences rather than making broad or vague assertions; specific citations save examiner time and increase persuasiveness.

name: Avoid unhelpful response tactics
description: Arguments that the examiner misunderstood the prior art without specific citations; accusations of bias or unprofessional conduct; restating arguments from the original spec; repeating the same argument across multiple rejections are unhelpful.
guidance: Do not accuse the examiner or rely on unsupported assertions. Tailor arguments to each rejection with citations and fresh reasoning rather than repeating prior text or claims of misunderstanding.

name: Foster mutual understanding (collaborative approach)
description: Examiners and applicants are not adversaries. The examination process works best when both sides communicate clearly about what the claim covers and what the prior art teaches.
guidance: Aim for clear, professional communication; treat interviews and focused responses as tools to achieve mutual understanding and efficient prosecution.

name: Quality indicators summary
description: Quality indicators emphasized by the USPTO Patent Quality Chat: clear claims, well-supported amendments, consistent terminology, accurate figures, and engagement with the substance of the office action.
guidance: Use these indicators as a checklist when preparing applications and responses to improve examination quality and reduce unnecessary correspondence.

name: Number and type of views required
description: The drawing must contain as many views as necessary to show the invention; views may be plan, elevation, section, or perspective; detail views and enlarged views are allowed.
guidance: All views must be grouped together, arranged without wasting space, preferably upright, clearly separated, and not included on sheets with specifications, claims, or abstract. Views must not be connected by projection lines or contain center lines. Waveforms may be connected by dashed lines to show relative timing.

name: Status determination and treatment of citizenship claimants
description: Claimants to citizenship who have applied to citizenship court and been rejected (or pending review) are deprived of privileges; agent investigates and permits them to remain if prima facie just claim exists; long delays are detrimental.
guidance: Investigate claimants per Department rules; permit those with prima facie claims to remain pending final determination; recommend timely settlement of citizenship claims to avoid harm to nation and claimants.

name: Definition of a design (claimed subject matter)
description: In a design patent application, the subject matter which is claimed is the design embodied in or applied to an article of manufacture (or portion thereof) and not the article itself.
guidance: Design consists of visual characteristics/appearance (configuration, surface ornamentation, or combination). Design is inseparable from the article, must be definite, preconceived, capable of reproduction, and not merely chance result of a method. The overall appearance creates the impression on an observer.

name: Single-claim requirement
description: Design patent applications may include only a single claim.
guidance: Claim must be in formal terms to the ornamental design for the article (specifying name) as shown, or as shown and described (37 CFR 1.153). More than one claim is neither required nor permitted.

name: Required elements and arrangement of a design application
description: A design patent application has the elements required of a utility application (see Chapter 600) and should follow the arrangement in 37 CFR 1.154.
guidance: Suggested order: transmittal forms, preamble (name, title, brief description of nature/intended use), cross-references, federally sponsored research statement, description of figures, feature description, single claim, drawings/photographs, executed oath/declaration.

name: Title and preamble requirements
description: The title of the design must designate the particular article (name generally known and used by the public) and the preamble should state applicant name, title of design, and brief description of nature/intended use (37 CFR 1.153, 1.154).
guidance: Title must correspond to claim language; examiner should allow latitude but require amendment only if title/claim are clearly misdescriptive, inaccurate, or unclear. Use of 'or the like' for environment is acceptable; using broad ambiguous titles that broaden the article is objectionable. Amendments to title require antecedent basis and must not introduce new matter.

name: Impermissible specification statements (new matter and improper subject matter)
description: Disclaimers directed to solid-line parts, statements suggesting modifications not illustrated, and descriptions of unrelated function are not permitted in the specification of an issued design patent.
guidance: Such statements may be included in original application to provide antecedent basis for future amendment, but cannot broaden claimed design beyond drawings; including them in issued patent is improper and should be canceled or objected to.

name: Drawings are essential and must comply with 37 CFR 1.84 and 1.152
description: The design must be represented by a drawing that contains a sufficient number of views to constitute a complete disclosure of the appearance of the design; appropriate surface shading should be used; broken lines may be used for visible environmental structure only; color drawings/photographs limited by petition.
guidance: Any detail shown in drawings or photographs deposited with the original application constitutes an integral part of the disclosed and claimed design unless explicitly disclaimed in original papers. Inconsistencies among views should be objected to; severe inconsistencies can render the claim nonenabled under 35 U.S.C. 112.

name: Necessity for good drawings (enablement / sufficiency)
description: The drawing or photograph constitutes the entire visual disclosure of the claim and must be so clear and complete that nothing regarding the design is left to conjecture.
guidance: Insufficient drawings may be fatal to validity under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, and may adversely affect effective filing dates for continuations.

name: Broken lines: environment and boundaries
description: Broken lines commonly disclose environmental structure or define the bounds of the claim; broken lines form no part of the claimed design when used as environment and may be used to indicate boundaries that are not present in reality.
guidance: Broken lines cannot be used to show hidden planes/surfaces, or to indicate lesser importance of a portion. If broken lines cross full-line design, specification must explicitly identify their purpose. Adding non-straight broken-line boundaries may introduce new matter.

name: Claim must show claimed design in full (solid) lines
description: The ornamental design being claimed must be shown in solid lines in the drawing; dotted/broken lines cannot be used to indicate immaterial features of the claimed design.
guidance: There are no portions of a claimed design that are immaterial or unimportant; environmental structure may be in broken lines but claimed subject matter must be in full lines.

name: Effect of detail shown in informal drawings/photographs
description: Any detail shown in informal drawings or photographs deposited with the original application papers constitutes an integral part of the disclosed and claimed design unless a specific disclaimer appears in the original application papers.
guidance: A specific disclaimer in the original application (specification or on drawings/photographs) provides antecedent basis for omission of disclaimed details in later-filed drawings.

name: Overall-appearance test for novelty and nonobviousness
description: In determining the patentability of a design, it is the overall appearance of the claimed design which must be taken into consideration.
guidance: Characteristic feature statements do not substitute for overall appearance analysis; comparisons to prior art consider the total visual impression (see In re Rosen, In re Leslie).

name: 35 U.S.C. 112 considerations (enablement and claim definiteness)
description: The claim defines the subject matter which the applicant regards as the invention (35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph); drawings must enable the claimed design (35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph).
guidance: Unclear or inconsistent figure descriptions/drawings may be objected to or may lead to a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112 as nonenabled; amendments introducing new drawing matter are prohibited.

name: Amendments and new matter prohibition
description: Amendments to title, claim language, drawings, or specification must have antecedent basis in the original disclosure and may not introduce new matter (35 U.S.C. 132; MPEP guidance).
guidance: Adding details, changing configuration/shape, or non-straight broken-line boundaries not present in original disclosure can constitute prohibited new matter and may cause rejection or loss of priority benefit.

name: Benefit of earlier U.S. filing date under 35 U.S.C. 120
description: An application for patent which is disclosed in the manner required by 35 U.S.C. 112 in an earlier-filed application by the same inventor may have the same effect as though filed on the date of the prior application if filed before patenting/abandonment and contains or is amended to contain a specific reference to the earlier filed application (35 U.S.C. 120).
guidance: CIPs that change shape/configuration generally do not get the benefit of the earlier filing date. If the earlier application is fatally defective under 112, later CIPs cannot rely on 120 for benefit. Indicate benefit statements in the first line of the specification when claiming benefit.

name: Right of priority under 35 U.S.C. 119 (foreign priority)
description: No application for design patent shall be entitled to right of priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(b) unless a claim therefor and a certified copy of the original foreign application, specification and drawings are filed before issue fee is paid or at a time during pendency as required by the Commissioner, but not earlier than six months after U.S. filing.
guidance: Certification shall show the date of the application and filing of specification; translations and other information may be required; failure to file required papers can forfeit priority.

name: Design patent overlap with trademark and trademark use limits
description: Design patent and trademark may be obtained on same subject matter; use of trademarks in design patent specifications is permitted under limited circumstances; trademarks alone or coupled with 'type' should not be used in the title.
guidance: Examiners must object to trademarks used in the title; if trademark appears in drawing, the specification must include a statement preceding the claim identifying the trademark material forming part of the claimed design and the name of the owner. Derogatory use of a trademark will result in rejection under 35 U.S.C. 171 as offensive subject matter.

name: Formal description of broken lines required
description: A specific statement must be used to describe broken lines used as environment: '-- The broken line showing of [1] is for illustrative purposes only and forms no part of the claimed design. --' and for boundaries: '-- The broken line(s) which define the bounds of the claimed design form no part thereof. --'
guidance: Insert the appropriate statement in the specification preceding the claim when broken lines are present; ensure brackets replaced with the correct structure names and wording ('must be'/'has been').

name: Basis and scope of international preliminary examination (Rule 66.1 and related)
description: IPE shall be based on the international application as filed, subject to amendments under Article 34 (which may be submitted at time of filing the demand or up to establishment of report), and Article 19 amendments made before or after the demand, unless superseded. Rectification of obvious mistakes authorized under Rule 91.1 may be taken into account. Claims lacking an international search report need not be the subject of IPE.
guidance: Amendments under Article 19 made before the demand are generally taken into account unless superseded; amendments after the demand and Article 34 submissions are taken into account subject to timing rules (see Rule 66.4 bis).

name: Content and notification procedure for the IPEA's written opinion (Rule 66.2)
description: IPEA must notify the applicant in writing where it: (i) considers situations referred to in Article 34(4) exist; (ii) considers any claim should be negative for lack of novelty, inventive step or industrial applicability; (iii) notices defects in form/contents under the Treaty/Regulations; (iv) considers any amendment goes beyond the disclosure as filed; (v) wishes to accompany the report by observations on clarity/support; (vi) considers a claim relates to an invention without an ISR and decides not to examine it; (vii) cannot meaningfully examine due to unavailable nucleotide/amino acid sequence listing.
guidance: The notification must fully state reasons, invite written reply (with amendments where appropriate), and fix a reasonable time limit for reply — normally two months after notification, not less than one month, at least two months if ISR is transmitted simultaneously, and not more than three months unless extended. Time limit may be extended on applicant's request before expiration.

name: Handling of priority documents and translations (Rule 66.7)
description: If IPEA needs a copy of the earlier application whose priority is claimed, the IB shall furnish it on request. If not furnished because applicant failed Rule 17.1 requirements and the earlier application is not otherwise available, the report may be established as if priority had not been claimed. If the priority application is in a different language, IPEA may invite applicant to furnish a translation within two months where validity of the priority claim is relevant; failure may result in report as if priority not claimed.
guidance: Ensures IPEA can assess priority validity; applicant must supply copies/translations when requested to avoid adverse treatment.

name: Form and presentation requirements for amendments (Rule 66.8)
description: When amending description or drawings, applicant generally must submit replacement sheets for every sheet that differs, accompanied by a letter highlighting differences, indicating the basis for amendment in the application as filed and preferably explaining reasons. Deletions or minor changes may use copies provided clarity is maintained. Claims amendments follow Rule 46.5 mutatis mutandis and the submitted set replaces all previously filed claims.
guidance: Replacement sheets must be directly reproducible and accompanied by basis explanation (Rule 46.5(b)(iii)); cancellation of entire sheets should be communicated in a letter preferably explaining reasons. Claim replacement replaces all earlier claims.

name: Invitation to restrict claims or pay additional fees (Rule 68.2)
description: If IPEA finds lack of unity and chooses to invite the applicant to restrict claims or to pay additional fees, the invitation shall: (i) specify at least one possibility of restriction that would comply; (ii) specify reasons why unity is not complied with; (iii) invite compliance within one month from the date of invitation; (iv) indicate amount of additional fees; (v) invite payment of protest fee (where applicable) within one month and indicate amount.
guidance: Invitation must be specific about restriction options, reasons, fee amounts and deadlines; applicant has one month to act on invitation.

name: Procedure for insufficient restriction and determination of main invention (Rule 68.4–68.5)
description: If applicant restricts claims but not sufficiently to comply with unity requirement, IPEA shall proceed as provided in Article 34(3)(c). Where doubt exists as to which invention is main for Article 34(3)(c) purposes, the invention first mentioned in the claims shall be considered the main invention.
guidance: IPEA follows Article 34(3)(c) procedures (which may include partial examination) when restriction insufficient; order of claims determines main invention when ambiguous.

name: Basis, scope and effects to be stated in the international preliminary examination report (Rule 70.1–70.2)
description: The report shall mean the international preliminary examination report. It shall issue on the claims as amended (if amended). If report is established as if priority not claimed or if IPEA considers any amendment goes beyond disclosure as filed, the report shall so indicate and give reasons. If parts of the application were not subject to IPE (e.g., no ISR), the report shall indicate this. The report shall indicate whether rectifications of obvious mistakes were taken into account or not, and state whether a top-up search was made (or not) and its date.
guidance: Report must transparently state the factual and procedural basis on which it was prepared (claims version, priority treatment, treatment of amendments, top-up search status, etc.) and provide reasons where it disregards amendments as going beyond the original disclosure.

name: Language(s) of filing
description: Applicants must file their patent application, including the specification, in the official language of the country of filing (for Cambodia, Lao PDR, Indonesia, Thailand and Viet Nam) and English (for Brunei Darussalam and Singapore). In Malaysia, Myanmar and the Philippines, applicants can choose between the official language and English.
guidance: The language of filing is the language of proceedings; translations of the specification (title, abstract, claims, description and drawings) must be filed within a specified period or upon request if filed in another language. In Myanmar, even if English is selected, office communications are in the country’s official language.

name: Claims requirements
description: The application must contain one or more claims which define the matter for which protection is sought; claims must be clear and supported by the description.
guidance: Claims must define subject-matter in terms of technical features (which may be expressed in mathematical, structural and/or functional terms). Claims must not rely on references to the description or drawings for technical features unless necessary for understanding or to enhance clarity/conciseness.

name: Priority claim invalidity and effect on prior art date
description: A priority claim is invalid if made outside the 12‑month period or if the earlier application was not actually the first application by the applicant for the disclosed subject-matter.
guidance: If the priority claim is invalid, the effective filing date for determining prior art is the local filing date; other causes of invalidity are addressed during substantive examination.

name: Formalities examination required documents and scope
description: Formalities examination checks compliance with formal requirements: request form, applicant/inventor identification, title, description and one or more claims, drawings when necessary, abstract, representative details, priority claim.
guidance: Contents of abstract, description, drawings, title and claims are not closely scrutinized during formalities beyond identifiability; however some AMS may examine initial clarity, multiple dependency, claim priority evaluation, exclusions to patentability or even unity 'a priori' during formalities.

name: Grounds for rejection/abandonment during formalities examination
description: Applications may be deemed abandoned or rejected if required filing documents are missing/erroneous/incomplete/non-compliant, if title/abstract/description/claims are missing, translations are not timely, foreign applicants are unrepresented when required, inventor designation/assignment missing, documents not filed in time, prescribed fees unpaid, or where non-patentable subject matter is present (country-specific).
guidance: Examiners identify deficiencies and invite remedy within defined (possibly extendable) periods; failure to remedy leads to abandonment/rejection.

name: Amendment of application before and during formalities examination
description: Applicants may amend or correct the application/specification of their own initiative or at the request of the office, without affecting the filing date, provided they request to amend in the prescribed manner and within prescribed periods with any required documents/fees.
guidance: Accepted amendments are entered in the application and considered for publication. New matter extending beyond the originally filed disclosure will be rejected; applicants may broaden claims only within the scope of the originally filed disclosure.

name: Assessment of unity of invention (a priori and a posteriori)
description: A patent application must relate to one invention or to a group of inventions linked to form a single general inventive concept; unity is assessed a priori (from claims language) and a posteriori (in view of the prior art).
guidance: Link must be a technical relationship expressed in claims via same/corresponding special technical features. Lack of unity should be determined from properly construed claim language and relevant prior art. Unity is best assessed during substantive examination but should be considered early to avoid unnecessary costs. Avoid narrow/literal approaches; use broad, practical consideration of interdependence. Example: independent claims A+Z, A+Y, Z+Y lack unity a priori if no common subject-matter; A+Z and A+Y have unity a priori while a posteriori lack may arise if A is known in prior art.

name: Fundamental reason for rule against double patenting
description: The fundamental reason for the rule is to prevent unjustified timewise extension of the right to exclude granted by a patent no matter how the extension is brought about; to prevail the appellant has the burden of establishing that the invention claimed is 'independent and distinct' from the invention of the appealed claims.
guidance: Quoting In re Schneller: where allowance of appealed claims would extend patent protection already disclosed and covered by claims of the patent, and there is no terminal disclaimer or mitigating circumstances, the rule against double patenting must be applied.

name: Design/Plant vs Utility double patenting principles
description: Double patenting principles and criteria applied in utility-utility situations generally apply to utility-plant or utility-design situations; double patenting may be raised where applicant filed both utility and plant or design applications.
guidance: Double patenting may be found in design-utility situations irrespective of whether claims involve the same invention or obvious variations. Some cases suggest a two-way obviousness determination is necessary in design-utility cases (Carman Indus.); examine claim scopes (interior construction vs external configuration) and whether they are obvious variations.

name: Difference between double patenting rejection and 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/103(a) prior art rejections
description: A double patenting rejection must rely on comparison with the claims in an issued or to be issued patent, whereas a 102(e)/103(a) rejection relies on what is disclosed (whether or not claimed) in the same issued or to be issued patent.
guidance: Terminal disclaimer cannot obviate a 102(e)/103(a) rejection. For applications pending on or after Nov 29, 1999 and on/after Dec 10, 2004, commonly assigned/owned patents/applications may be disqualified as 102(e) prior art under 103(c)(1). Examiners should make both 102(e)/103 and double patenting rejections when facts support both; omission of one when applicable prevents making next Office action final if the omitted rejection is added later.

name: Avoiding statutory double patenting rejections
description: A statutory double patenting rejection can be avoided by amending the conflicting claims so that they are not coextensive in scope or by canceling the conflicting claims in the pending applications.
guidance: Where conflicting claims are in multiple pending applications, cancel conflicting claims in all but one application to avoid provisional statutory rejections. A terminal disclaimer is not effective against statutory double patenting. Use of a 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit to overcome statutory double patenting is inappropriate.

name: Avoiding nonstatutory double patenting rejections (terminal disclaimer)
description: A rejection based on a nonstatutory type of double patenting can be avoided by filing a terminal disclaimer in the application or proceeding in which the rejection is made.
guidance: Terminal disclaimer practice supported by case law (In re Vogel, Knohl, Griswold, Jentoft, Eckel, Braithwaite). Terminal disclaimers encourage disclosure and earlier expiration of patents. Filing a terminal disclaimer is not an admission of the propriety of the rejection. For commonly owned subject matter, the disclaimer must include a provision that the patent shall be unenforceable if it ceases to be commonly owned (37 CFR 1.321(c)). 37 CFR 1.131 affidavits are inapplicable where claims are directed to substantially the same invention or lack patentable distinctness.

name: Terminal disclaimer mechanics and requirements
description: A terminal disclaimer is a statement filed by an owner to disclaim or dedicate a portion of the entire term of all the claims of a patent; requirements are set forth in 37 CFR 1.321 and sample forms/guidance in MPEP §1490.
guidance: The terminal disclaimer must operate with respect to all claims in the patent; statute does not provide for disclaimer of only specified claim(s). When the claimed invention resulted from a joint research agreement, 37 CFR 1.321(d) sets forth additional requirements. A terminal disclaimer must include commonly-owned provisions when required and may need to extend to continuing applications by its terms.

name: Terminal disclaimer required for nonstatutory double patenting in applications filed on/after June 8, 1995
description: For continuing utility or plant applications filed on or after June 8, 1995 (20-year term regime), a terminal disclaimer under 37 CFR 1.321 is required to overcome a nonstatutory double patenting rejection, even if the application claims benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, or 365(c).
guidance: Reasons: 35 U.S.C. 154(a)(2) sets 20-year patent term rules and 154(b) allows for patent term extensions; 37 CFR 1.321(c)(3) prevents harassment by multiple parties by requiring common ownership provisions.
