Examiners should cite this MPEP section or Official Gazette notice when applicants argue a terminal disclaimer should not be required due to 35 U.S.C. 154 change.

name: Written description requirement applies to Jepson preamble
description: The preamble of a Jepson-style claim must be supported by an adequate written description under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a); the specification must describe an invention understandable to a skilled artisan and show that the inventor actually invented the invention claimed.
guidance: The Federal Circuit in In re Xencor held that even though the Jepson preamble may recite known prior art, the totality of the claim (including the preamble) requires written description support. A patentee cannot avoid the possession requirement by asserting something is well-known in the art.

name: Jepson preamble can be limiting
description: Unlike most claim preambles, a Jepson-style preamble is typically limiting because it recites the conventional or known elements and sets off the purported improvement.
guidance: When the Jepson format is used, the preamble defines the claimed invention and limits claim scope; practitioners should recognize that using a Jepson preamble can therefore narrow or otherwise define claim boundaries.

name: Written description inquiry depends on skill, unpredictability, and newness
description: The amount and content of disclosure necessary to supply an adequate written description varies depending on factors including the level of knowledge of a person of ordinary skill in the art, the unpredictability of the art, and the newness of the technology.
guidance: In unpredictable arts (e.g., life sciences, chemistry) the written description requirements are often more stringent; examiners and courts may look to these factors when assessing whether the Jepson preamble and overall claim have adequate support.

name: Finder of fact may consider patent and extrinsic evidence for written description
description: A written description inquiry for a Jepson claim may consider disclosures in the patent itself and evidence outside the patent to understand what a person of ordinary skill in the art would have known.
guidance: Practitioners should be prepared to rely on or produce extrinsic evidence to establish that preamble material was well-known if the specification alone is insufficient.

name: Jepson claims cannot be used to expand specification by adding preamble content
description: Xencor precludes the use of Jepson-style claims to expand the scope of the written description in the specification by simply including additional information in the preamble and asserting that information is well-known.
guidance: Do not rely on the preamble as a shortcut to claim subject matter not supported by the written description in the specification.

name: Disadvantages of using Jepson format
description: Jepson-style claims have several disadvantages: the preamble is limiting, the format is often taken as an implied admission that the preamble material is prior art, and now the preamble requires adequate written description support.
guidance: These disadvantages should be weighed when deciding whether to draft claims in Jepson format; implied-admission concerns are typically rebuttable only in narrow circumstances (e.g., to avoid a double patenting rejection in a co-pending application).

name: Limited advantages / appropriate uses of Jepson claims
description: Jepson-style claims may still be beneficial in a few specific circumstances, such as distinguishing one claimed invention from another, overcoming or preventing a double patenting rejection for a similar invention, or where U.S. applications originate outside the U.S. and Jepson is common in foreign practice.
guidance: Use Jepson claims sparingly and only when their particular procedural or strategic benefit outweighs the written description and implied-admission risks.

name: Drafting advice: ensure adequate support in specification or extrinsic evidence for preamble limitations
description: Patent practitioners should ensure there is adequate support to satisfy the written description requirement for the preamble of a Jepson-style claim, either in the patent itself or through extrinsic evidence that conclusively establishes the knowledge of a person of ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: Before including limitations in the Jepson preamble, confirm the specification contains sufficient disclosure (examples, working embodiments, descriptions of uses/populations, etc.) or that external art/evidence will establish the asserted prior knowledge.

name: Example of insufficient written description (anti-pattern)
description: An appellate panel found the specification did not adequately describe what patients or diseases can be successfully treated with an anti-C5 antibody or provide a single working example describing treatment with the claimed Fc modifications.
guidance: Lack of concrete examples or descriptions linking claimed elements to their practical application (e.g., which patients/diseases, working examples) can be fatal to written-description support for Jepson preamble limitations.

name: Jepson format structure (37 C.F.R. § 1.75(e))
description: When appropriate for an improvement, an independent claim should contain: (1) a preamble comprising a general description of conventional or known elements or steps, (2) a phrase such as 'wherein the improvement comprises,' and (3) those elements/steps/relationships constituting the new or improved portion.
guidance: Follow the Jepson structure when the nature of the case admits, but remember that using this format carries the written-description and implied-admission considerations described above.

name: Required reply — failure to reply to a final action
description: A reply under 37 CFR 1.113 to a final action must include: (A) a Notice of Appeal and appeal fee; (B) an amendment under 37 CFR 1.116 that cancels all rejected claims or otherwise prima facie places the application in condition for allowance; (C) filing of an RCE under 37 CFR 1.114 (with submission meeting 1.111 and requisite fee) for certain post-June 8, 1995 applications; or (D) filing of a continuing application under 37 CFR 1.53(b) (or CPA under 1.53(d) for design applications).
guidance: If the reply is a proposed amendment under 1.116, the Office of Petitions will normally route the matter to the Technology Center to determine whether the amendment places the application in condition for allowance. Examiners should mark replies 'OK to enter upon revival' when appropriate; otherwise the Office of Petitions will not grant the petition and will use form PTOL-303 to advise.

name: Unintentional delay standard and evidentiary expectations
description: The Office usually relies on the applicant's duty of candor and accepts a statement that 'the entire delay...was unintentional' without further information in the vast majority of 1.137 petitions, but may require additional information where delay exceeds two years or other questions arise.
guidance: An extended delay (>2 years from abandonment) raises doubt and requires additional explanation and supporting facts/correspondence. Deliberate decisions to permit abandonment (e.g., claims unpatentable, insufficient value, defer fees) are not 'unintentional' and cannot be cured by later change of mind or changed circumstances. Submitting an inappropriate/untruthful unintentionality statement can have serious consequences (e.g., inequitable conduct and unenforceability). See examples A–E of deliberate choices that preclude unintentionality.

name: Translation arrangements for unitary patent (claims and languages)
description: Regulation (EU) No 1260/2012 allows patent applications in any language, with a translation into one of the EPO's official languages (EN, FR, DE). The applicant has to translate the patent claims into the two remaining EPO languages.
guidance: Translation costs would be covered for certain EU residents filing in another EU language. No further translation is needed unless required in specific litigation. The European Parliament secured full reimbursement of translation costs for EU-based SMEs, non-profit organisations, universities and public research organisations and a compensation scheme with a ceiling for certain filings.

name: Trial for Correction — permissible corrections
description: A patent holder may file a petition for trial to correct specifications or drawings in any of the following cases: to narrow a claim; to correct a clerical error; or to clarify an ambiguous description.
guidance: Trial for correction is intended to protect a patent invention by providing an opportunity for a patentee to make corrections under the condition that there are no unexpected losses or damages caused to any third parties. However, this shall not apply when a patent opposition is pending before the IPTAB.

name: Trial to Confirm the Scope of Rights
description: A patentee or an interested person may request a trial to confirm the scope of a patent right.
guidance: When filing a petition to confirm the scope of at least two claims in a patent, a petition may be filed for each claim.

name: Section 28.3 (claim-date obviousness requirement)
description: The subject-matter defined by a claim in an application for a patent in Canada must be subject-matter that would not have been obvious on the claim date to a person skilled in the art or science to which it pertains, having regard to (a) information disclosed more than one year before the filing date by the applicant (or derived from the applicant) and (b) information disclosed before the claim date by others.
guidance: Apply the claim-date (priority/earlier filing) for first-to-file system. Note that “information … available to the public” may be broader than information “generally known” in the art. Consider both applicant's own prior disclosures (with one-year bars) and third-party public disclosures before the claim date.

name: Inventive concept must be found in claims (avoid 'spirit of the invention')
description: One should not find 'the inventive concept' or resort to vague notions such as the 'spirit of the invention' outside of the claims; the claims as construed define the monopoly.
guidance: Do not expand the inventive concept beyond properly construed claim language; avoid resurrecting older concepts like 'pith and substance' to broaden claim scope when assessing obviousness.

name: Motivation of the inventor vs. motivation of skilled person
description: “Motivation” may mean why the claimed inventor made the invention, or why a hypothetical skilled person would combine elements of the prior art to arrive at it.
guidance: Ask whether the notional skilled person had a good reason to pursue the combination (i.e., would have had a reasonable expectation of success). Distinguish general motivation (everyone seeking solution) from unique/personal motivation (only the inventor had reason to pursue it).

name: Orange Book listing eligibility and restrictions
description: FDA’s Orange Book records approved drug products, patents covering those drugs, and any regulatory exclusivities. To be eligible for listing, a patent must claim a drug or a method of using a drug for which a claim of patent infringement reasonably could be asserted.
guidance: Eligible patent types include drug substance (active ingredient), drug product (formulation/composition), and method-of-use patents. Patents on packaging, manufacturing processes, metabolites, or intermediates are ineligible for listing.

name: Establishing exception via common ownership (clear and conspicuous statement)
description: A proper submission to establish the prior-art exception based on common ownership is a clear and conspicuous statement that the claimed invention and the subject matter disclosed were, not later than the effective filing date of the claimed invention, owned by, or subject to an obligation of assignment to, the same person.
guidance: Failure to provide the required clear and conspicuous statement (e.g., not filed in a conspicuous manner or not timely) results in the subject matter not being excepted under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C). See MPEP §717.02(b) and form paragraph guidance (¶ 7.20.04.aia).

name: Establishing exception via joint research agreement (JRA) requirements
description: To invoke the JRA exception under 35 U.S.C. 102(c), applicant must (a) amend the specification to disclose the names of the parties to the JRA in accordance with 37 CFR 1.71(g)(1) if not already disclosed, and (b) file a clear and conspicuous statement that the referenced subject matter was developed and the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of one or more parties to a joint research agreement (within the meaning of 35 U.S.C. 100(h)) that was in effect on or before the effective filing date and that the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the JRA.
guidance: Timing/fee rules for the amendment apply (see 37 CFR 1.71(g)(2)). Examples illustrate that the JRA must be in effect on or before the effective filing date and the claimed invention must have been made as a result of activities within the JRA's scope; provisional priority filings before the JRA or JRAs limited to different inventions will defeat the exception (see Examples 1–4).

name: Form paragraph usage and prerequisites for addressing 102(b)(2)(C) issues
description: Specific form paragraphs (¶ 7.20.01.aia, ¶ 7.20.02.aia, ¶ 7.20.04.aia, ¶ 7.20.05.aia, etc.) are prescribed for use in addressing prior-art-exception situations under 35 U.S.C.102(b)(2)(C).
guidance: Common prerequisites include using these form paragraphs only in applications filed on or after March 16, 2013 and where claims are examined under the AIA 102/103, preceding with form paragraph 7.03.aia, and including bracketed identifying information (e.g., identify common assignee or the reference). ¶ 7.20.02.aia must be used in all applications with joint inventors (unless claims clearly restricted to a single invention). Follow Examiner Notes specified in each form paragraph.

name: Illustrative examples of when the JRA exception applies or fails
description: Examples demonstrate the application of the JRA/common ownership rules: (1) JRA in place before effective filing date and invention made within scope = exception may apply; (2) JRA not in effect until after claimed invention effective filing date = exception does not apply; (3) reliance on an earlier provisional filed before JRA means invention effectively filed before JRA and exception fails; (4) JRA limited to different activities/invention means exception does not apply.
guidance: These fact patterns illustrate the importance of effective filing dates, provisional priority chains, and the scope/timing of the JRA in determining eligibility for the exception (see Examples 1–4 in the text).

name: Patentability requirements (novelty, non-obviousness, utility)
description: To be patentable, at least three major requirements in patent law must be satisfied: novelty, non-obviousness, and utility.
guidance: These are the ultimate legal criteria that generated claims must meet; the manuscript suggests training reward models for novelty and non-obviousness (or a joint model) and keeping human-in-the-loop for utility because of scarcity of negative samples. Note: the reward model in the experiments (granted vs pre-grant) is only a preliminary proxy and cannot substitute for full legal determination.

name: Reward based on limiting terms (count of limiting clauses)
description: Reward computed as the sum of counts of limiting terms in the generated claim text (example implementation: reward += text.count('wherein ') + text.count('whereby ') + text.count('where ') + text.count('when ')).
guidance: Limiting clauses (typically indicated by 'wherein', etc.) narrow claim scope and increase likelihood of allowance but decrease likelihood of infringement. The experiment validates that policy models can be controlled to increase or decrease the number of limiting terms; however, more limiting terms often increase claim length and may reduce text quality.

name: Joint reward function (length + limiting terms)
description: Combined reward that enforces an upper bound on length (using max_len and end-of-claim tag) and adds counts of limiting terms to the reward (i.e., length-based reward + sum of limiting term counts).
guidance: Joint rewards can lead the model to prioritize adding limiting terms while respecting length constraints; experiments showed claim length constrained while limiting terms increase. Models may still collapse after extended training; qualitative review needed.

name: Reward model classifying granted vs pre-grant (binary)
description: Train a classification reward model (distilbert-base) with labels granted=1 and pre-grant=0; use classification accuracy or predicted probability as reward for PPO.
guidance: Reward model input tokens are capped at 500 due to model context window. The policy trained to maximize this reward increases the proportion of generated claims predicted as 'granted' (reported granted ratios before/after PPO). Caveat: predictions do not equal actual prosecution or litigation outcomes; the reward model is a proxy and its limitations determine final quality.

name: Presence of <|end of claim|> tag as a generation requirement
description: Generated text must include a specific end-of-claim tag (<|end of claim|>) for the length-based reward to be computed positively; absence after truncation yields zero reward.
guidance: This tag functions as an explicit termination signal for reward computation and truncation handling. Experimental reward code checks for s.find('<|end of claim|>') == -1 to assign zero reward when missing.

name: Limiting terms list (example set)
description: Limiting terms treated as indicators of claim limitations: 'wherein', 'where', 'when', 'whereby' (listed explicitly in the experiments).
guidance: The listed terms are not exhaustive; additional terms can be incorporated in future work. Counting these terms is used as a simple heuristic proxy for claim narrowness in reward design.

name: Balance between claim scope and allowance/infringement
description: A well-crafted patent claim should strike a balance between broader claim scope (more likely to be infringed, less likely to be allowed) and narrower scope (more likely to be allowed, less likely to be infringed).
guidance: Reward design should reflect practitioner intent (maximize allowance probability subject to preferred scope). The manuscript frames this as an objective for RLHF but notes achieving equilibrium is complex and requires human/patent-practitioner involvement.

name: Quality and coherence of generated patent text
description: Text quality tends to decline as claim length increases; longer generated claims often become nonsensical or far-fetched.
guidance: Higher rewards targeted at length or limiting-term counts can lead to a decline in textual quality. The paper emphasizes the need for qualitative human review and notes that policy alignment to a reward model does not guarantee high-quality, legally sound claims.

name: Evaluation metrics and monitoring (reward mean, claim length, number of limiting terms, granted ratios)
description: Key empirical metrics used to evaluate training and policy behavior include reward mean (over training steps), average claim length, number of limiting terms, and the ratio of claims predicted as granted before/after PPO training.
guidance: Plots in experiments include moving averages (window size 100). Comparative tables (e.g., Table 4) show granted/pre-grant counts and ratios for 1,000-row samples before and after PPO to assess efficacy. Use both quantitative metrics and qualitative inspections (appendices) for assessment.

name: Interviews after allowance regarding amendments (37 CFR 1.312)
description: After an application is sent to issue (after a notice of allowance), interviews that involve detailed consideration of claims sought to be entered or prior art should not be given; requests for interviews in such cases should be granted only with specific approval of the Technology Center Director upon a written showing of extraordinary circumstances.
guidance: Applicants are not entitled to greater consideration for informally presented amendments than for formally presented ones; interviews after allowance are tightly constrained.

name: Amendment document sectioning and recommended format
description: Each section of an amendment document (Specification Amendments, Claim Amendments, Drawing Amendments, Remarks) must begin on a separate sheet to facilitate indexing and scanning; recommended order: cover sheet (table of contents), 'Amendments to the Specification', 'Amendments to the Claims', 'Amendments to the Drawings', remarks section, and any drawing sheets.
guidance: Adopt this recommended format to reduce processing time and avoid non-compliant amendments.

name: Amendments to the specification: methods and identification
description: Amendments to the specification (other than claims and certain special appendices) must be made by adding, deleting, or replacing a paragraph; by replacing a section; or by providing a substitute specification. The amendment must unambiguously identify the paragraph or section to be modified by paragraph number, page and line, or other unambiguous method and be accompanied by replacement or new paragraphs as required.
guidance: Replacement paragraphs must include markings to show all changes relative to previous version. Added paragraphs presented in clean form (no underlining). If paragraph numbering exists, maintain or use decimal numbering for inserted paragraphs (e.g., [0071.1]).

name: Claim status identifiers and acceptable alternatives
description: The status of every claim must be identified by one of the status identifiers: (Original), (Currently amended), (Canceled), (Withdrawn), (Previously presented), (New), or (Not entered). The Office may accept alternative wording if the status is accurate and clear.
guidance: Examples of acceptable alternatives (e.g., 'Original Claim', 'Newly added', 'Canceled without prejudice'). The examiner may accept additional variations; acceptance does not require a corrective amendment or notice to applicant.

name: Drawing processing after allowance
description: Drawing submissions without any amendments to the specification and claims after allowance should be forwarded to the Office of Data Management.
guidance: Follow filing instructions for post-allowance drawing-only submissions to ensure proper routing.

name: Examiner's amendments exception (37 CFR 1.121(g))
description: The Office may make examiner's amendments to the specification, including the claims, by specific instructions to insert or delete subject matter at precise locations; examiner's amendments do not need to comply with paragraphs (b)(1), (b)(2), or (c) of 37 CFR 1.121.
guidance: Examiner's amendments are used to expedite prosecution and reduce cycle time; applicant should be aware that such changes may be made without the formal amendment markup requirements applicable to applicant-filed amendments.

name: Use of description and drawings to interpret claims
description: Boards have interpreted the claims in the light of the description and drawings in order to establish whether they were clear and concise.
guidance: Several decisions (e.g. T 456/91, T 860/93) accept that the description may be used to interpret claims; the case law also notes that a patent may be its own dictionary (see II.A.6.3.3). However, this principle is subject to limits described in subsequent entries.

name: Breadth of a term is acceptable if unambiguous to the skilled person
description: The clarity of a claim is not diminished by the mere breadth of a term of art contained in it, if the meaning of such term was unambiguous for a person skilled in the art, either per se or in the light of the description.
guidance: Example: T 456/91 – although an extremely large number of compounds could be used, it was clear from the claims when read in the light of the description which peptides were suitable.

name: Claims must be clear in themselves (no reliance on the description)
description: Article 84 EPC requires that claims must be clear in themselves when read using normal skills, including knowledge of the prior art but not any knowledge derived from the description contained in the patent application or the amended patent.
guidance: Authorities: T 2/80, T 454/89, T 412/03, T 129/13, T 412/02, T 908/04. The requirement means it must be possible to understand the claims without reference to the description; claims should not rely on the description to remove self-contradictions or basic obscurity.

name: Art.69 EPC (interpretation for extent of protection) cannot cure Art.84 clarity defects
description: While Art.69 EPC allows the description to be used to interpret the claims for the purpose of determining extent of protection, it is not concerned with a claim's definition of the matter for which protection is sought (Art.84 EPC).
guidance: Therefore, in examination or opposition an applicant/patentee cannot rely on Art.69 as a substitute for an amendment necessary to remedy a lack of clarity (T 454/89, T 760/90, T 1129/97, confirmed in T 56/04, T 64/03, T 1265/13).

name: Precise definition in the description does not automatically make an unclear claim clear
description: The mere fact that the precise meaning of an unclear term is expressly disclosed in the description but not in the claims does not mean that the claims meet the clarity requirement.
guidance: Authority: T 1129/97 (example: 'low alkyl' defined in description does not cure unclear claim wording). See also T 49/99 and T 623/13.

name: Clarity deficiency in claim wording is not rectified by description or drawings
description: A clarity deficiency in the claim wording is not remedied by the fact that the description and drawings would help the reader to understand the technical subject-matter that the claim was intended to define.
guidance: Authority: T 49/99. The claims themselves must define the subject-matter clearly; supporting material cannot be used to fix ambiguous claim language except as limited by case law (see exception entry).

name: Exceptional allowance where a vague claim term is defined only in the description
description: A vague or unclear term used in the claim and a precise definition only in the description can be allowed only in exceptional cases if the precise definition cannot be incorporated into the claim and the precise definition is unambiguously and directly identifiable by a skilled person from the description.
guidance: Authority: T 56/04 (mutatis mutandis reference to R.29(6) EPC 1973). The board emphasised that an exception is narrow: e.g. a specific value disclosed in the description that could instead have been incorporated into the claim will not justify the exception (T 56/04, T 623/13).

name: Unclear technical feature prevents identification beyond doubt, especially for delimitation from prior art
description: A claim containing an unclear technical feature prevents its subject-matter from being identified beyond doubt; this is particularly problematic if the unclear feature is meant to delimit the claimed subject-matter from the state of the art.
guidance: Authority: T 56/04. Such lack of clarity undermines the claim's function to delimit the monopoly and therefore usually requires amendment rather than reliance on the description.

name: Determination of parameters in claims — need for clarity on how parameters are measured
description: Where a product is characterised by parameters, it must be clear from the claim itself how those parameters are to be determined.
guidance: See II.A.3.5 for detail. However, boards have in some cases justified that the claim need not include the procedure for measuring the parameter (e.g. T 992/02), so whether the measurement method must be in the claim depends on the circumstances and whether the skilled person can determine the parameter unambiguously.

name: Self-contradictory claims remain unclear despite description
description: A claim does not comply with the clarity requirement if it is not, per se, free of contradiction; it must be possible to understand the claims without reference to the description.
guidance: Authorities: T 2/80 and repeated in T 454/89 and others. If a claim is self-contradictory, the description cannot be used to resolve that contradiction for Art.84 purposes.

name: Drafting with IPR/PTAB in mind
description: Inter Partes Review at the PTAB is the dominant patent invalidity venue; patents are challenged under 102 and 103 using printed publications. PTAB applies broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) for unexpired patents, which can yield claim constructions narrower than district courts.
guidance: Anticipate that a petitioner will use prior art printed publications and that claim construction at PTAB will often be broader (BRI) relative to district court. Draft claims and spec to withstand these challenges by clarifying terms and providing fallback claim sets.

name: Use a detailed specification to anchor construction
description: The PTAB defers to clear spec definitions; a claim term defined in the spec is construed accordingly even under BRI.
guidance: Include detailed descriptions and definitions in the spec for critical terms (express lexicography) so the PTAB will construe claim terms consistent with those definitions. Provide examples and embodiments that illustrate intended meanings.

name: Express lexicography for critical terms
description: Use express lexicography for critical terms so that a claim term defined in the spec is construed accordingly by the PTAB.
guidance: Explicitly define key claim terms in the specification and, where appropriate, explain scope and alternatives. Avoid ambiguity in term usage and provide clear anchors that can be relied upon during post-grant review.

name: Do not rely on claim differentiation at the PTAB
description: Claim differentiation is a less powerful tool at the PTAB; do not rely on it to broaden one claim by reference to a narrower one.
guidance: Because PTAB gives limited weight to claim differentiation, draft independent and dependent claims so each stands on its own; provide explicit support in the spec for any broader interpretations rather than depending on differentiation arguments.

name: Include multiple independent claims of varying scope
description: If the petitioner challenges only some claims, the unchallenged claims survive even if the challenged ones do not. Multiple independent claims of varying scope create more pieces that can survive.
guidance: Draft a graduated set of independent claims (broad and narrower independent claims) to increase chances that some claims remain if others are cancelled. Consider claim sets that capture different aspects/variants of the invention.

name: Long, detailed specification to support amendments
description: A long, detailed spec provides anchors for amendments at the PTAB. The PTAB allows amendments only with full spec support; sparse specs limit amendment options.
guidance: Draft comprehensive disclosures and multiple embodiments so that, if amendment is needed in post-grant proceedings, there is clear basis in the spec to add or modify claim language. Provide various fallback examples and explicit linking language.

name: Reissue options and timing
description: The patentee can file a reissue to broaden or narrow claims within 2 years of issuance (broadening) or any time (narrowing).
guidance: Consider timely reissue applications if post-grant analysis shows scope errors. Use reissue to correct claim scope, remembering the 2-year limit for broadening reissues and the differing availability for narrowing reissues.

name: Prosecution choice: broad claims plus narrow backups
description: If only broad claims issue, an IPR challenge that succeeds wipes out the patent. If a graduated claim ladder issued, narrow backups survive.
guidance: Balance pursuing broad claims with issuing narrower dependent or independent backups. Where appropriate, pursue a ladder of claims so that narrower claims persist even if broader claims are cancelled in post-grant proceedings.

name: Argue economically during prosecution
description: Every argument made during prosecution can be cited at the PTAB.
guidance: Avoid excessive or unnecessary argumentation that narrows claim scope or creates admissions. Make only necessary, strategic arguments and preserve flexibility for post-grant defense.

name: File continuations prior to IPR filing
description: Once IPR is filed, the patentee's options for amendment are limited. Pending continuations allow new claims to be drafted to capture the accused product.
guidance: Maintain pending continuations before an IPR is filed so you can pursue additional claim drafting and protect embodiments/products that might otherwise be lost. Use continuations strategically as part of an overall portfolio defense.

name: Anticipate high institution and claim-cancellation rates
description: Modern IPR institution rates are roughly 60%, with ~80% of instituted petitions resulting in cancellation of at least some claims. Drafting must anticipate this challenge.
guidance: Adopt drafting and prosecution strategies (detailed spec, claim ladders, continuations, careful argumentation, evidence collection) that assume a realistic chance of post-grant challenge and partial cancellation.

name: Covered business method (CBM) patent definition (AIA §18)
description: A covered business method (CBM) patent is defined in section 18 of the America Invents Act (AIA) as a patent that "claims a method or corresponding apparatus for performing data processing or other operations used in the practice, administration, or management of a financial product or service," but is not for a "technological" invention.
guidance: The AIA statute provides for CBM review of CBM patents — an administrative proceeding to determine the validity of the patent under review. Congress created CBM review because of concern with "litigation abuse over business method patents." (Section 18 is implemented by USPTO regulations.)

name: CBM patents must relate to monetary matters (regulatory further definition)
description: Under USPTO regulations promulgated pursuant to the statute, a CBM patent is one relating to monetary matters.
guidance: The USPTO regulations further refine the statutory definition; whether a claim 'relates to monetary matters' is a regulatory criterion used to determine CBM status.

name: Technological invention exclusion (regulatory test)
description: A technological invention is defined as one in which "the claimed subject matter as a whole recites a technological feature that is novel and unobvious over the prior art; and solves a technical problem using a technical solution."
guidance: If the claimed subject matter satisfies this test it is considered a technological invention and thus excluded from being a CBM. The technological-invention inquiry is central to distinguishing CBM patents from technological patents.

name: PTAB institution standard for CBM proceedings
description: The standard for whether the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB) will institute a CBM proceeding is whether a petition by an interested party establishes that it is more likely than not that at least one claim of the challenged patent is unpatentable.
guidance: This 'more likely than not' threshold governs institution of CBM review (see 35 U.S.C. § 324). Petitions are ordinarily filed by parties sued for infringement, but standing rules (see separate criterion) can broaden who may file.

name: Claim construction standard for pre-November 13, 2018 IPRs
description: In an inter partes review proceeding based on a petition filed prior to November 13, 2018, the Board interprets claims of an unexpired patent using the broadest reasonable construction in light of the specification in which they appear.
guidance: See 37 C.F.R. § 42.100(b) (2017); Cuozzo Speed Techs., LLC v. Lee, 136 S. Ct. 2131, 2144–46 (2016) (upholding the use of the broadest reasonable interpretation standard). A subsequent amendment to the regulation does not apply to petitions filed before November 13, 2018.

name: Ordinary and customary meaning when no construction necessary
description: If a party asserts that 'no constructions are necessary,' claim terms take on their ordinary and customary meaning that the terms would have to one of ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: Parties may propose that claim terms be given ordinary meaning; the Board will construe terms where necessary (see example where 'rate' was construed).

name: Anticipation under 35 U.S.C. § 102
description: A claim is unpatentable as anticipated under 35 U.S.C. § 102 if a single prior-art reference expressly or inherently describes each limitation set forth in the claim.
guidance: See Perricone v. Medicis Pharm. Corp., 432 F.3d 1368, 1375 (Fed. Cir. 2005); Verdegaal Bros., Inc. v. Union Oil Co. of Cal., 814 F.2d 628, 631 (Fed. Cir. 1987). The Board will compare the claim limitations to the prior-art reference(s) and determine whether each limitation is described. Part-time satisfaction (e.g., a prior-art system that sometimes practices the claimed limitation) can be sufficient to establish anticipation (Hewlett-Packard Co. v. Mustek Sys. Inc., 340 F.3d 1314).

name: Obviousness under 35 U.S.C. § 103 (Graham framework)
description: A claim is unpatentable for obviousness under 35 U.S.C. § 103 if the differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made.
guidance: Apply Graham factors: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between claimed subject matter and prior art; (3) level of skill in the art; (4) objective evidence (secondary considerations). See KSR Int’l Co. v. Teleflex Inc., 550 U.S. 398, 406 (2007). The obviousness inquiry typically requires an analysis of whether there was an apparent reason to combine known elements in the fashion claimed; courts require 'articulated reasoning with some rational underpinning' (In re Kahn, 441 F.3d 977, 988).

name: Requirement to articulate reason to combine references
description: To prevail on obviousness, a petitioner must show why a person of ordinary skill would have been motivated to combine prior art references in the particular manner claimed.
guidance: KSR requires an analysis of 'whether there was an apparent reason to combine the known elements in the fashion claimed by the patent at issue.' Mere conclusory statements are insufficient (In re Magnum Oil Tools Int’l, Ltd., 829 F.3d 1364, 1380). The Board looks for articulated reasoning with a rational underpinning (In re Kahn).

name: Petitioner's burden of proof and particularity requirement
description: In an inter partes review, the petitioner must demonstrate by a preponderance of the evidence that the challenged claims are unpatentable, and the petitioner has the burden from the onset to show with particularity why the patent is unpatentable.
guidance: See 35 U.S.C. § 316(e); 37 C.F.R. § 42.1(d). Petitions must identify 'with particularity... the evidence that supports the grounds for the challenge to each claim' (Harmonic Inc. v. Avid Tech., Inc., 815 F.3d 1356, 1363). The burden never shifts to Patent Owner (Dynamic Drinkware, LLC v. Nat’l Graphics, Inc., 800 F.3d 1375).

name: Part-time practice in prior art can establish anticipation
description: Prior art that only sometimes embodies a claimed method or limitation can nonetheless teach that aspect of the invention and establish anticipation.
guidance: Cited authority: Hewlett-Packard Co. v. Mustek Sys. Inc., 340 F.3d 1314 (Fed. Cir. 2003). The Board analogously applies this principle to software aspects of apparatus claims: the mere fact that a prior-art server might sometimes transmit slower does not negate that it also contains instructions to transmit faster when it does so.

name: Avoid importing additional limitations beyond court construction
description: In construing claim terms and assessing prior art disclosures, one must not improperly import additional limitations into the claim beyond the court's construction.
guidance: Example: Patent Owner attempted to read a requirement that 'each' requested media data element must be sent faster than playback into the Federal Circuit's construction of 'rate'; the Board rejected importing that additional requirement.

name: Board will consider dependent-claim limitations by reference
description: For dependent claims, the Board may rely on analysis provided for corresponding limitations in other claims and petition references; lack of a separate response from Patent Owner on dependent claims does not preclude the Board from finding them unpatentable if the petitioned analysis supports that conclusion.
guidance: The decision reviewed dependent-claim mappings to earlier-analyzed claim limitations and found Carmel disclosed respective limitations when the petition provided the cross-reference analysis.

name: Remedies and post-decision procedural notices
description: If Patent Owner wishes to pursue amendment of challenged claims outside the IPR (e.g., reissue or reexamination) after issuance of a final written decision, specific Notices and obligations apply.
guidance: See April 2019 Notice Regarding Options for Amendments by Patent Owner Through Reissue or Reexamination During a Pending AIA Trial Proceeding (84 Fed. Reg. 16,654 (Apr. 22, 2019)). If filing a reissue application or request for reexamination of the challenged patent, Patent Owner must notify the Board of related matters in updated mandatory notices (37 C.F.R. § 42.8(a)(3), (b)(2)).

name: Establish broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI)
description: The broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim must be established prior to examining a claim for eligibility.
guidance: Examiners should determine BRI before performing eligibility analysis (see MPEP 2106, subsection II). BRI is the baseline for applying the flowchart in MPEP 2106, subsection III.

name: Step 2A Prong One — does the claim recite a judicial exception?
description: Determine whether a claim recites a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon).
guidance: The USPTO distills relevant case law into three enumerated groupings of abstract ideas: mathematical concepts, certain methods of organizing human activity, and mental processes (see MPEP 2106.04(a)). If the claim sets forth or describes such an exception, further analysis is required.

name: Mental process grouping — definition and limits
description: A mental process (thinking) that 'can be performed in the human mind, or by a human using a pen and paper,' is treated as an abstract idea.
guidance: Determine a claim recites a mental process when it contains limitations that can practically be performed in the human mind (e.g., observations, evaluations, judgments, opinions). Do NOT expand this grouping to encompass limitations that cannot practically be performed in the human mind; limitations that encompass AI in a way the human mind cannot practically perform do not fall in this grouping. See AI-SME Update and MPEP examples showing hardware-based limitations that are not mental processes (e.g., uniquely encoded RFID transponder data structures).

name: Distinguish 'recites' vs 'involves' a judicial exception
description: Claims that 'recite' an exception (set forth or describe it) require further eligibility analysis; claims that merely 'involve' an exception (are based on it) may be eligible and not require further analysis.
guidance: Consult MPEP 2106.04, subsection II(A)(1) for the recite vs involve distinction and Ex Parte Linden for PTAB considerations. Use concrete claim language analysis to decide whether the exception is recited (described) or merely involved (based on).

name: Use concrete examples to identify recitation (e.g., Example 39 vs 47)
description: Apply example-based reasoning: a limitation like 'training the neural network' may merely involve an abstract idea, whereas naming specific mathematical algorithms (e.g., backpropagation, gradient descent) can recite a judicial exception.
guidance: Compare USPTO examples: Example 39 (Method for Training a Neural Network for Facial Detection) — limitation 'training the neural network in a first stage using the first training set' does not recite an exception; Example 47 (Anomaly Detection) — limitation specifying backpropagation and gradient descent recites a mathematical abstract idea. Use examples to guide whether claim language describes mathematical relationships/calculations explicitly.

name: Step 2A Prong Two — does the claim integrate the exception into a practical application?
description: After a claim is found to recite a judicial exception, evaluate whether the claim as a whole integrates the recited exception into a practical application.
guidance: Use the considerations in MPEP 2106.04(d) to evaluate whether additional elements integrate the exception into a practical application. Many considerations overlap and multiple may apply. Not all considerations will be relevant to every element or claim.

name: Analyze the claim as a whole and consider interactions
description: When evaluating integration into a practical application, consider all claim limitations and how they interact and impact each other — do not evaluate additional limitations in a vacuum.
guidance: The way additional elements use or interact with the exception can integrate the exception into a practical application. Consider combined effect of limitations rather than isolating them. See MPEP 2106.04(d), subsection III.

name: Improvements consideration — improvement to computer or technology
description: Claims can be eligible if they reflect an improvement to the functioning of a computer or to another technology or technical field, integrating the judicial exception into a practical application.
guidance: Determine whether the claim covers a particular solution to a problem or a particular way to achieve an outcome rather than merely claiming the idea of a solution. Consult the specification to determine whether the disclosed invention improves technology; the specification need not explicitly state the improvement but must describe the invention such that the improvement would be apparent to a person of ordinary skill. The claim itself does not have to explicitly recite the improvement.

name: 'Apply it' consideration — more than mere instructions to implement
description: Evaluate whether additional elements amount to more than a recitation of the words 'apply it' (or equivalent) — mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer are not sufficient.
guidance: Do not oversimplify claim limitations when applying the 'apply it' consideration. This consideration often overlaps with the improvements consideration. Assess whether the claim provides meaningful limiting detail beyond a generic instruction to use a computer to perform the judicial exception. See MPEP 2106.05(f) and warning not to expand 'apply it' too broadly.

name: Particularity vs generality when assessing 'apply it' and improvements
description: Consider the particularity or generality of how the judicial exception is applied: does the claim recite only the idea/outcome, or a particular solution/way to achieve it?
guidance: When evaluating additional elements, consider: (1) whether the claim recites only the idea of a solution or provides details of how the solution is accomplished; (2) whether the claim invokes computers/machinery merely as a tool or purports to improve computer capabilities or existing technology; (3) the particularity or generality of the application. Claims that improve computer capabilities or technology support finding the exception is integrated into a practical application.

name: Avoid oversimplification of claim limitations
description: Examiners must be careful not to oversimplify the claims by looking at them generally and failing to account for the specific requirements of the claims.
guidance: Consider all claim limitations (see MPEP 2106.05(a) and MPEP 2143.03). Overbroad simplification can lead to incorrect 'apply it' conclusions; analyze specific requirements and how they limit the exception.

name: Judicial assignment of claim construction (Markman)
description: Claim construction is a question of law assigned exclusively to judges (the Markman process), separating legal interpretation from factual questions historically reserved for juries.
guidance: The Markman decision (517 U.S. 370 (1996)) requires courts—not juries—to resolve fundamental disputes over claim scope, enhancing judicial efficiency and uniformity. The court observed that 'The construction of a patent, including terms of art within its claim, is exclusively within the province of the court.'

name: Statutory requirement of particularity (35 U.S.C. §112(b))
description: Patent claims must 'particularly point out and distinctly claim' the invention under 35 U.S.C. §112(b).
guidance: This statutory foundation requires clarity so the public can understand the scope of legal monopolies; ambiguity in claim language implicates constitutional and statutory concerns and motivates early construction.

name: Intrinsic evidence controls (Phillips en banc)
description: Intrinsic evidence—the claims, specification, and prosecution history—should control the interpretation of disputed terms.
guidance: Following Phillips v. AWH Corp., courts prioritize intrinsic sources when construing terms. Extrinsic sources are relegated to secondary tools and used only when intrinsic evidence fails to resolve ambiguity.

name: Specification as the 'single best guide' to meaning
description: The patent specification is considered the most reliable indicator of a disputed term's meaning—'the single best guide.'
guidance: Because the specification results from an iterative process between applicant and Patent Office, courts read claims in view of the specification (Phillips v. AWH Corp., 415 F.3d at 1315).

name: Prosecution history can limit claim scope (disclaimer/estoppel)
description: Prosecution history, though less reliable than the specification, helps elucidate how the inventor defined the invention and distinguished it from prior art.
guidance: Vague statements in the prosecution history may influence claim scope under doctrines like prosecution history disclaimer or estoppel; courts consult it to understand how the applicant characterized claim language during prosecution.

name: Evidentiary hierarchy in Markman hearings
description: There is an evidentiary hierarchy that prioritizes the patent’s internal record (claims and specification) over prosecution history and places extrinsic evidence at the bottom.
guidance: This hierarchy structures how courts evaluate competing constructions: start with claims/specification, then prosecution history, and rely on extrinsic materials only as a last resort.

name: Limit and prioritize disputed terms (court management)
description: Courts often limit the number of claim terms subject to construction and focus on those necessary to resolve the case.
guidance: Local rules may cap disputed terms (e.g., N.D. Cal. Patent L.R. 4-3(c) limits to ten terms absent leave of court). Parties should identify materially disputed terms; terms with plain and ordinary meaning and those that do not affect infringement/validity may be excluded from construction.

name: Claim construction narrows discovery scope
description: Once claim terms are construed, parties can narrow document production, deposition topics, and expert reports.
guidance: Early claim construction reduces litigation costs and limits fishing expeditions by focusing discovery on the construed claim scope.

name: Summary judgment commonly follows claim construction
description: After construction, courts frequently grant summary judgment if, under the construed claim scope, the accused device cannot infringe or a claim is invalid.
guidance: Patentees may also seek summary judgment of infringement under a favorable construction; claim construction can be dispositive for both infringement and invalidity motions.

name: Risk of narrowing functional or overly broad claims (§112(f))
description: Courts routinely narrow overly broad or functional claims—especially in software and AI—under §112(f), requiring detailed structural disclosure to support claim language.
guidance: Functional claiming poses heightened risks in high-technology domains; patentees should ensure the specification supplies concrete structure to avoid §112(f) limitations (see Williamson v. Citrix Online).

name: Compulsory licence petition content and evidence
description: A petition to the Board of Trade for an order upon a patentee to grant a licence shall show clearly the nature of the petitioner's interest, the ground(s) upon which he claims relief, and shall state in detail the circumstances of the case, the terms asked for and the purport of the proposed order.
guidance: Petition and examined copy must be left at the Patent Office accompanied by affidavits, statutory declarations and other documentary evidence tendered in proof of alleged default. Forms in Patents Forms H and HI. Petitioner should make out a prima facie case before giving patentee notice.

name: Register entries on sealing and changes of proprietorship
description: Upon sealing of a patent the Comptroller shall enter in the Register of Patents the name, address and description of the patentee as the grantee and the title of the invention. Where a person becomes entitled to a patent or any share or interest by assignment, transmission, or operation of law, a request for entry of his name in the register shall be left at the Patent Office.
guidance: Requests must be signed/made by the claimant or authorised agent; particulars of the assignment/transmission showing manner and parties must be stated; supporting documents must be produced and an examined copy left (or an official/certified copy if matter of record). See Forms L and S.87/S.36 references.

name: Partition and removal of clouds on patent title
description: Partition of a patent right held in tenancy in common can be made by common consent of all owners but not against the will of any owner; equity has jurisdiction to remove a cloud on title consisting of an express or implied assertion of adverse ownership or encumbrance.
guidance: Equitable relief is available to clear title disputes among co-owners or adverse claimants.

name: New rhetoric — Solidity of claims
description: The first tenet of new rhetoric is the solidity of claims: claims must be judged as reasonable, rather than absolute, and grounded in a reality acceptable to the audience.
guidance: Use the Toulmin model: claim (thesis), grounds (support), warrant (reasoning linking claim and grounds). Employ syllogisms for explicit formal reasoning and enthymemes when relying on premises implied by the audience’s beliefs. Claims should be 'real and preferable premises' so an audience can decode and accept them.

name: New rhetoric — Ambiguity and its contexts
description: Language is ambiguous and ambiguity occurs in four contexts: (1) no previous applicable rule because the case is the first to discuss the issue; (2) a previous ruling is subject to more than one meaning; (3) when a previous ruling is claimed to be invalid; and (4) conflict exists between two potentially applicable rules.
guidance: Recognize and articulate ambiguity when analyzing legal texts; ambiguity is inherent to language and affects how claims are perceived and adjudicated.

name: Abstract idea exclusion (judicially recognized exception under §101)
description: The Court held that laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas are implicitly exempted from being patented; abstract ideas cannot be patented because permitting a patent to an abstract idea 'would effectively grant a monopoly over an abstract idea.'
guidance: Determine whether a claim is 'directed to' an abstract idea (e.g., intermediated settlement, risk hedging). If so, examine whether the claim adds something significantly more than the abstract idea itself; mere recitation of a generic computer implementing the idea is insufficient.

name: Clarity versus vagueness of patent claims (vagueness increases litigation)
description: Vague patents, especially those grounded on abstract concepts, increase the likelihood of litigation and can be exploited for rent-seeking behavior.
guidance: Draft claims with clarity and precise scope to reduce downstream litigation risk; courts and commentators note that vague/abstract claims facilitate NPE litigation and judicial uncertainty.

name: For each claim, determine what the claim as a whole covers
description: Claim construction is an essential part of the examination process. Each claim must be separately analyzed and given its broadest reasonable interpretation in light of and consistent with the written description.
guidance: The entire claim must be considered, including preamble language and the transitional phrase. The examiner should evaluate each claim to determine if sufficient structures, acts, or functions are recited to make clear the scope and meaning of the claim, including the weight to be given the preamble (see Bell Communications Research; Corning Glass Works).

name: Interpretation of transitional phrases (comprising / consisting essentially of / consisting of)
description: Transitional term 'comprising' is open-ended (covers recited subject matter alone or in combination with unrecited matter). 'Consisting essentially of' is a middle ground and 'consisting of' is closed.
guidance: By using 'consisting essentially of' a drafter signals openness only to unlisted ingredients that do not materially affect the basic and novel properties; absent a clear indication in the specification or claims of what the basic and novel characteristics actually are, 'consisting essentially of' will be construed as equivalent to 'comprising' for 35 U.S.C. 102/103 purposes (see PPG). If applicant contends exclusion, applicant bears burden of showing introduction of additional steps/components would materially change characteristics (In re De Lajarte).

name: Do not import limitations from the specification into the claims
description: Limitations may not be imported into the claims from the specification.
guidance: While examining support, the absence of definitions or details for well-established terms or procedures should not be the basis for a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a). The preamble's import must be determined by reviewing the entirety of the application to understand what inventors intended to encompass (Pac-Tec; Corning).

name: Review the entire application to evaluate support for claimed elements
description: Prior to determining whether the disclosure satisfies the written description requirement, the examiner should review the claims and the entire specification, including specific embodiments, figures, and sequence listings, to understand how applicant provides support for claimed features.
guidance: Review should be from the standpoint of one of skill in the art at filing and include a determination of the field of invention and level of skill. For some arts, there is an inverse correlation between level of skill and the specificity of disclosure necessary (see Wang Labs.; Hybritech).

name: Determine whether disclosure shows possession of the claimed invention as a whole
description: The examiner must determine whether there is sufficient written description to inform a skilled artisan that applicant was in possession of the claimed invention as a whole at the time the application was filed.
guidance: Possession may be shown by many means (reduction to practice, detailed drawings, structural chemical formulas, or other identifying characteristics). The inquiry is factual and case-by-case (Purdue Pharma; Pfaff).

name: Possession shown by actual reduction to practice
description: Possession may be shown by describing an actual reduction to practice of the claimed invention (constructing an embodiment or performing a process that meets all claim limitations and determining it works for intended purpose).
guidance: Reduction to practice ordinarily provides strong evidence an invention is complete, but is not necessary in every case. For biological materials, a deposit in accordance with 37 CFR 1.801 et seq. may evidence reduction to practice (Cooper v. Goldfarb; UMC Elecs.; Estee Lauder; Mahurkar).

name: Possession shown by drawings or structural chemical formulas
description: Drawings or structural chemical formulas sufficiently detailed may show possession of the claimed invention as a whole.
guidance: Drawings alone can provide a 'written description' (Vas-Cath; Wolfensperger; Autogiro). In chemical claims, generic formulae may indicate what the generic claims encompass and be adequate to describe a claimed genus (Eli Lilly).

name: Biotech-specific identifying characteristics/examples
description: For biomolecules, examples of identifying characteristics that may demonstrate possession include a sequence, structure, binding affinity, binding specificity, molecular weight, and length.
guidance: Disclosure of an antigen fully characterized may provide adequate written description for antibodies claimed by binding affinity if generating the antibody was routine; but if the generation was not possible by conventional technology, antibody claims may lack adequate description (Centocor; Noelle; Falkner; Capon).

name: Chemical invention specificity requirement
description: An adequate written description of a chemical invention requires a precise definition—structure, formula, chemical name, or physical properties—not merely a wish or plan for obtaining the chemical invention claimed.
guidance: Claims directed to chemicals require defining features that distinguish the chemical and describe how to obtain it (Univ. of Rochester v. G.D. Searle).

name: Means-plus-function claim (35 U.S.C. 112(f) / pre-AIA 112, para. 6) support standard
description: If a claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) it must be interpreted to cover the corresponding structure, materials, or acts in the specification and 'equivalents thereof.'
guidance: In considering whether there is 35 U.S.C. 112(a) support for a means-plus-function limitation, examiner must consider original disclosure in summary, detailed description, original claims, abstract, and drawings. Adequacy is met if (1) the written description adequately links particular structure/materials/acts to perform the function, or (2) it is clear one skilled in the art would have known what structure/materials/acts disclosed perform the function (see Aristocrat; Atmel; Biomedino). Note: relying solely on what one skilled in the art could implement is not enough to excuse inadequate disclosure in the specification.

name: Indefiniteness of means-plus-function can trigger written description rejection
description: When a means-plus-function limitation is indefinite due to lack of corresponding structure/materials/acts, then the claim limitation necessarily lacks an adequate written description.
guidance: Thus, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (indefiniteness) for no corresponding structure should also be accompanied by a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) for lack of written description.

name: Genus vs species analysis for claim scope
description: A claim limited to a single disclosed embodiment/species is analyzed as a claim to that single embodiment; a claim that encompasses two or more embodiments/species is analyzed as a genus.
guidance: See MPEP § 806.04(e). The written description inquiry varies with whether the claim is to a species or genus and the nature of the disclosure.

name: Checklist for claims drawn to a single embodiment or species
description: For each claim drawn to a single embodiment/species: (A) determine whether the application describes an actual reduction to practice; (B) if not, determine whether the invention is complete as evidenced by drawings or structural chemical formulas sufficiently detailed; (C) if not, determine whether the invention is set forth in terms of distinguishing identifying characteristics evidenced by other descriptions sufficiently detailed to show possession.
guidance: Follow-up steps: (1) Determine if application describes the complete structure (or acts of a process) of the claimed invention as a whole—complete structure typically satisfies 35 U.S.C. 112(a). (2) If complete structure not disclosed, determine whether other relevant identifying characteristics are disclosed in sufficient detail so a skilled artisan would recognize possession, e.g., in biotech a strong structure-function correlation may allow function+minimal structure to suffice. If disclosure is only goals or results to be achieved, it is insufficient (In re Wilder).

name: Factors to consider in determining sufficiency of written description
description: The determination is factual and multifactorial: consider level of skill and knowledge in the art, partial structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics alone or coupled with known correlation between structure and function, and the method of making the claimed invention.
guidance: Disclosure of any combination of such identifying characteristics that distinguish the claimed invention from other materials and would lead one of skill to conclude applicant was in possession is sufficient (Eli Lilly).

name: Maturity and predictability of the art influences required disclosure
description: In mature technologies where knowledge and skill are high, written description questions should not ordinarily be raised for claims present in the original filing even if the specification discloses only a method of making and the function. In emerging and unpredictable technologies, more evidence is required to show possession.
guidance: Use patents and printed publications in the art to determine whether the art is mature and what level of disclosure is necessary. In unpredictable fields, disclosure of only method and function may not support a product claim other than product-by-process (Fiers; Amgen).

name: Product-by-process claim considerations
description: Where the process has actually been used to produce the product, the written description requirement for a product-by-process claim is clearly satisfied; however, requirement may not be satisfied where it is not clear the acts set forth can be performed or that the product is produced by that process.
guidance: If process steps are not shown to be performable or don't actually produce the product, the product claim may lack written description (Amgen; Fiers).

name: Interference parties and scope
description: An interference involves parties asserting inventorship/priority where claims are to the 'same patentable invention' or otherwise overlap in a count.
guidance: Subject matter that is the basis of an interference is rejected under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) upon conclusion of an interference (unless acts showing prior invention were not in this country). Interference practice operates to the exclusion of ex parte practice under 37 CFR 1.131 when claims are to the same patentable invention.

name: Inventorship/derivation and 35 U.S.C. 101/102(f) requirement
description: 35 U.S.C. 101 requires that whoever invents or discovers the claimed invention must be named as the inventor(s) for a patent to be granted; derivation from another can support a rejection under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f).
guidance: Derivation addresses originality (who invented the subject matter), while priority focuses on who invented first; where derivation can be shown, a 102(f) rejection is proper. (Ex parte Kusko; Price v. Symsek.)

name: US-specific strict examination standards and risks
description: The US has particularly strict design examination standards, especially regarding specification and claim language and the content and quality of drawings; there is sensitivity to adding new matter and difficulty correcting rejected applications once on file.
guidance: Because of these stricter US rules, entering the US with an international application can be risky if the application was not drafted with US requirements in mind; corrections after filing may be difficult or impossible.

name: Definitions relevant to examination (35 U.S.C. 100)
description: Key statutory definitions (e.g., 'invention', 'process', 'United States', 'patentee', 'third-party requester', 'inventor', 'joint inventor', 'joint research agreement', 'effective filing date', 'claimed invention') determine application treatment and rights.
guidance: Effective filing date rules (including priority/benefit dates) and claimed invention definitions are used to determine entitlement and applicable law (AIA vs pre-AIA). See MPEP for applicability nuances (PLTIA impact).

name: Filing-date and requisites of the application (post-PLTIA)
description: For nonprovisional applications filed on/after Dec 18, 2013 (PLTIA/PLT implementation), the filing date (except design) is the date a specification, with or without claims, is received in the Office; drawings are not always required except where necessary for understanding.
guidance: Design applications differ. Inclusion of claims/drawings remains prudent to ensure disclosure satisfies 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and 113; OPAP reviews completeness (fees, oath/declaration, all pages) and issues notices for incomplete filings. Applications without at least one claim may receive an OPAP notice to submit a claim to avoid abandonment; examiners will not docket an application until it includes specification and at least one claim.

name: Handling of obviously informal cases
description: When disclosure is informal or insufficient to permit a complete merits action, examiner may follow specified procedure (reasonable search, include form listing informalities, require revision to idiomatic English, reject informal claims under 35 U.S.C. 112).
guidance: Procedure elements: (A) make reasonable search to extent possible (if incomprehensible, inform applicant that no search was made); (B) include form listing informalities and formal requirements in first Office action (see form paragraph references); (C) require spec revision to idiomatic English and U.S. practice; (D) reject claims failing to define invention per 35 U.S.C. 112—blanket rejection usually sufficient. Examiner should point out informality points; applicant bears burden to revise; multiple obviously informal claims treated as a single claim for fee/exam purposes.

name: Preliminary amendments in informal cases (no new matter)
description: Applicants are urged to submit a preliminary amendment promptly (preferably within 3 months after filing) to correct obvious informalities; amendments must exclude 'new matter'.
guidance: Preliminary amendments filed after filing date do not enjoy original disclosure status; see MPEP § 608.04(b). Amend informalities so disclosure and initial claims are understandable and properly dependent/definite.

name: Use of forms 7.31.01–7.31.04 for claim rejections based on deficiencies
description: When rejecting claims due to disclosure deficiencies as described in form paragraphs (e.g., 7.01/7.02), use the appropriate 7.31.xx form paragraphs for claim rejections.
guidance: Forms provide standardized wording and examiner notes for using rejections tied to disclosure deficiencies.

name: Search duties before examination (MPEP § 704.01)
description: After reading the specification and claims, the examiner searches prior art; the invention should be thoroughly understood before the search. Informal or imperfectly understood cases also receive searches to avoid piecemeal prosecution.
guidance: See Chapter 900 (esp. §§ 904–904.03) for searching details.

name: Examples of information that may be required under 37 CFR 1.105(a)(1)
description: Enumerated examples include: (i) existence of particularly relevant commercial databases known to inventors; (ii) whether a prior-art search was made and what was searched; (iii) copies of non-patent literature/published applications/patents by any inventor that relate to the claimed invention; (iv) literature used to draft the application; (v) literature used in the invention process (e.g., to design around); (vi) identification of what is being improved where claimed invention is an improvement; (vii) identification of any use of the claimed invention known to inventors at filing; (viii) technical information known to applicant concerning related art, disclosure, claimed subject matter, or accuracy of examiner interpretation.
guidance: These examples are illustrative, not exhaustive. Requirements should narrow focus and be reasonably based on examination needs.

name: Components necessary for filing date for nonprovisional applications (37 CFR 1.53(b))
description: The component parts of a nonprovisional application filed under 37 CFR 1.53(b) necessary to obtain a filing date are: a specification as prescribed by 35 U.S.C. 112 and 37 CFR 1.71; a claim as prescribed by 35 U.S.C. 112 and 37 CFR 1.75; and a drawing, if necessary under 35 U.S.C. 113 (first sentence) and 37 CFR 1.81(a).
guidance: If submitted papers are too informal to be given a filing date (e.g., specification is obviously informal or incoherent), the case is held as incomplete and no filing date is granted until corrections are made; the filing date will be the date the corrections are made.

name: Notice and handling of incomplete nonprovisional applications
description: If nonprovisional application papers filed under 37 CFR 1.53(b) do not include required parts or are too informal, OIPE prepares and mails a Notice of Incomplete Application and holds the case as incomplete; no filing date is granted until the incompleteness is corrected.
guidance: Examples of incompleteness include omission of specification, omission of at least one claim (for nonprovisional), or missing drawings if required. Applicants are informed of shortcomings and must correct them to obtain a filing date.

name: Preliminary amendment limitations and fee consequences
description: A nonprovisional application filed under 37 CFR 1.53(b) may be filed with a preliminary amendment limited to the cancellation of claims; any preliminary amendment must comply with 37 CFR 1.121 and include a complete listing of all claims.
guidance: Office strongly recommends filing with the desired set of claims rather than filing then cancelling claims. A preliminary amendment cancelling claims will reduce the number of claims considered in filing fee calculation. No refund will be made once the fee for claims is properly paid even if claims are later cancelled, unless a petition for express abandonment under 37 CFR 1.138(d) is granted.

name: Filing date definition and review of refusal to accord filing date
description: The filing date of the provisional or nonprovisional application is the date of receipt in the Office of the application which includes a specification containing description pursuant to 37 CFR 1.71 and at least one claim (required for nonprovisional applications) pursuant to 37 CFR 1.75, and any drawings required by 37 CFR 1.81(a).
guidance: If items are missing, applicant will be notified and filing date will be the receipt date of the missing parts. Review of a refusal to grant a filing date is by petition with petition fee (37 CFR 1.17). Petitioner should present arguments that items were not missing or that a filing date should be assigned. For properly deposited Express Mail under 37 CFR 1.10, the deposit date may be the filing date; petitions and supporting evidence should be provided to seek review. Petitions on these matters are decided in the Office of the Deputy Commissioner for Patent Examination Policy (MPEP § 1002.02(b)).

name: Informal application definition and correction procedures
description: An application is informal if it is typed on both sides of paper, or is not permanent, legible, or reproducible. OIPE accords a filing date to papers that include a specification and at least one claim (when required) even if they do not comply with rules, and issues a Notice of Informal Application indicating the informality.
guidance: If informalities are timely corrected, the application is given the filing date of the original informal papers. Failure to correct within specified time results in abandonment. The transmittal letter for continuing applications should identify any provisional or parent application information to simplify processing.

name: Computer program listing of >60 and ≤300 lines placement
description: A computer program listing contained in the written specification of more than 60 lines and no more than 300 lines must be positioned at the end of the specification and before the claims.
guidance: Alternatively, incorporate the listing in a text file submitted via EFS-Web or on compact disc in compliance with 37 CFR 1.96, or insert the listing after the detailed description but before the claims. Cancel the in-specification printout if using an electronic submission. See 37 CFR 1.96(b).

name: Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 — judicial exception without significantly more
description: Reject claims that are directed to a judicial exception (law of nature, natural phenomenon, abstract idea) that lack 'significantly more' to transform the exception into patent-eligible subject matter.
guidance: Identify the judicial exception, explain why the claim is directed to it, and identify additional elements and why they do not amount to significantly more (considered separately and in combination). Provide examples: products of nature must be markedly different (e.g., DNA must be markedly different), generic computer implementation is insufficient, routine data-gathering steps do not add meaningful limitations. Use form paragraph 7.05.015 and related MPEP §2106 guidance.

name: Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 — utility lacking
description: Reject claims under 35 U.S.C. 101 when the claimed invention lacks patentable utility.
guidance: Provide a clear explanation of lack of utility (bracketed). See MPEP §§ 706.03(a) and 2105–2107.03 for guidance.

name: Utility rejections under 35 U.S.C. 101 and enablement under 35 U.S.C. 112(a)
description: A claim may be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 for lack of utility and also under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph) if the specification does not support an asserted or well-established utility such that one skilled in the art would know how to use the claimed invention.
guidance: Where enablement is at issue, apply In re Wands (858 F.2d 731) factors and provide undue experimentation analysis (see MPEP §§2164–2164.08(c)). Use appropriate form paragraphs to explain the lack of asserted/well-established utility and reasons for enablement deficiencies.

name: Duplicate claims objection (37 CFR 1.75)
description: When two claims are duplicates or so close that they cover the same thing (despite slight wording differences), object to the duplicate claim under 37 CFR 1.75 as a substantial duplicate of an allowed claim.
