guidance: If one claim is allowable, object to the other as a substantial duplicate. Use form paragraph 7.05.05 (warning) or 7.05.06 (objection) as appropriate. If duplicate claims are not allowable, use the objection paragraph. Insert claim numbers and explanations in brackets as instructed.

name: Formats for utility/credibility findings (Format A/B/C)
description: Use different format templates depending on whether an asserted utility is absent, not specific and substantial, not credible, or multiple utilities have varying credibility/specificity.
guidance: Format A: use when no asserted utility or asserted utility not specific and substantial; Format B: use when asserted utility not credible; Format C: use when multiple utilities exist and none are specific, substantial, and credible. Insert claim numbers and tailored explanations per form paragraph 7.05.06.

name: Notice when prior art applicable under both pre-AIA and AIA
description: When a prior art rejection is made and the determination whether the application is subject to AIA or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102/103 might be incorrect, correction of the statutory basis later will not be treated as a new ground of rejection if the prior art and rationale supporting the rejection are the same under either status.
guidance: Use this form paragraph in Office Actions where a prior art rejection is made in applications with actual filing dates on or after March 16, 2013, that claim priority to applications filed before March 16, 2013. Use only once per Office Action.

name: Claim limitation that relates to a tax strategy deemed prior art
description: A claim limitation that has been interpreted as a tax strategy for reducing, avoiding, or deferring tax liability is treated as within the prior art and insufficient to differentiate the claimed invention from the prior art.
guidance: Recite the claim limitation and identify affected claim numbers in the form paragraph. See MPEP §2124.01 for more information. Use when a limitation reads on a tax strategy (AIA Section 14 implications).

name: Pre-AIA 102(e) — earlier-filed U.S. patent/application by another (AIPA/AIPA/2002 amendments considerations)
description: Under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e), the invention was described in an earlier-filed U.S. patent or patent application publication by another (including certain international applications treated as U.S. filings under statutory conditions), providing a prior art date for the reference.
guidance: Use form paragraph 7.12.fti when the reference is a U.S. patent or publication filed under specific conditions (see enumerated subpoints). Carefully consider benefit/priority claims (119(e), 120, 121, 365(c), 386(c)) and the international filing date conditions (e.g., PCT filing date after Nov 29, 2000). See accompanying examiner notes for conditions and precedences.

name: Ways to overcome a 35 U.S.C. 102(b) rejection
description: A rejection based on 35 U.S.C. 102(b) can be overcome by several means enumerated (A)–(F).
guidance: Options include: (A) Persuasively arguing that the claims are patentably distinguishable from the prior art; (B) Amending the claims to patentably distinguish over the prior art; (C) Perfecting priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or 120 by amending the specification to reference a prior application or by filing an application data sheet under 37 CFR 1.76 containing a specific reference to a prior application in accordance with 37 CFR 1.78(a); (D) Filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 showing prior invention if the reference is not a U.S. patent (or application in the case of a provisional rejection) claiming the same patentable invention (but 1.131 is not acceptable when claims of the reference and application are directed to the same invention or obvious variants; then examiner must consider double patenting or interference); (E) Perfecting a claim to priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) (foreign priority filing date must antedate the reference and be perfected including certified priority document and English translation if necessary and examiner must establish enablement and description under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph); (F) Perfecting priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or 120 by amending the specification or filing an application data sheet as in (C). See MPEP § 715 for 37 CFR 1.131 affidavits.

name: Ways to overcome a 35 U.S.C. 102(a) rejection
description: A rejection based on 35 U.S.C. 102(a) can be overcome by similar approaches to 102(b).
guidance: Typical methods include (A) arguing patentable distinction, (B) amending claims to distinguish, and (C) filing appropriate affidavits/declarations (e.g., under 37 CFR 1.132 showing the reference invention is not by "another"). See MPEP § 715 and § 716.10 for details; where 1.131/1.132 affidavits apply and their limitations.

name: Ways to overcome a 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection
description: A rejection based on 35 U.S.C. 102(e) can be overcome by arguing patentable distinction, amending the claims, or filing appropriate affidavits/declarations.
guidance: Specifically: (A) Persuasively arguing that the claims are patentably distinguishable; (B) Amending the claims to patentably distinguish over the prior art; (C) Filing an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 showing that the reference invention is not by "another" (see MPEP § 715.01(a), § 715.01(c), and § 716.10), or filing under 37 CFR 1.131 as appropriate. Note: provisional 102(e) rejections and certain situations (e.g., derivation) have special limitations (see form paragraphs and case law such as In re Bartfeld).

name: Provisional 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection for copending U.S. applications
description: If a copending U.S. patent application discloses subject matter that would anticipate claims in another pending U.S. application having a different inventive entity, the examiner should determine whether a provisional 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection can be made.
guidance: If (1) at least one common inventor exists between the applications or the applications are commonly assigned and (2) the effective filing dates are different, a provisional rejection of the later filed application should be made because the earlier filed application, if patented or published, would be prior art under 102(e). The provisional rejection is made under 35 U.S.C. 102(e). It can be overcome in the same manner as 102(e) rejections (see MPEP § 706.02(b)), or by abandoning the applications and filing a new application containing the subject matter of both. The provisional rejection cannot be overcome by filing a terminal disclaimer in certain circumstances (see In re Bartfeld). Use form paragraphs 7.15.01 or 7.15.04 as appropriate.

name: Form paragraph 7.15.01 — provisional rejection (pre-/non-published applications)
description: Boilerplate form paragraph for provisionally rejecting a claim under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as anticipated by a copending application with a common assignee or at least one common inventor, where the application being examined was filed before 11/29/00 and not voluntarily published under 35 U.S.C. 122(b).
guidance: Text explains the provisional rejection is based on presumption of future patenting of the copending application. It outlines possible ways to overcome (37 CFR 1.132 or 1.131 showings) and notes that the rejection may not be overcome by filing a terminal disclaimer (In re Bartfeld). Examiner notes provide which circumstances require use of different form paragraphs (e.g., 7.21.01) depending on filing/publication dates and ownership of record.

name: Limits on using 37 CFR 1.131 to avoid interference
description: A 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit is ineffective to overcome a U.S. patent or application publication that claims applicant’s invention when the claims are identical or not patentably distinct such that an interference would exist under 37 CFR 41.203(a).
guidance: Where commonly owned claims are not patentably distinct, terminal disclaimer and 37 CFR 1.130 may overcome a 103 rejection; but 1.131 cannot be used to avoid creation of two patents on the same invention. See case law (In re Clark, In re Hidy, In re Teague, etc.) and MPEP § 718. Form paragraph 7.58 may be used to note such situations.

name: Exhibits need not support all claim limitations if declaration supplies missing parts
description: An accompanying exhibit need not support all claimed limitations, provided that any missing limitation is supported by the declaration itself.
guidance: Examiner must consider the affidavit/declaration and all accompanying exhibits, records and notes in their entirety when reviewing sufficiency. See Ex parte Ovshinsky.

name: Review for prior public use/on-sale and best mode when evaluating 1.131 evidence
description: Examiners must review affidavits/declarations and accompanying evidence to determine whether they show that the claimed invention was 'in public use' or 'on sale' in this country more than one year prior to the effective filing date (statutory bar under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)), and must consider whether reliance on embodiments not disclosed in the application raises a best mode issue under 35 U.S.C. 112.
guidance: Even if an affidavit overcomes the cited reference, applicant's own prior public use or sale may still bar patentability. A best mode rejection should only be made if record, by preponderance of the evidence, establishes that the specification did not set forth the best mode. See MPEP § 2133.03 and § 2165.

name: 37 CFR 1.132: affidavits/declarations traversing rejections must be sworn and responsive
description: When any claim is rejected or objected to, evidence submitted to traverse the rejection on a basis not otherwise provided for must be by oath or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132; the primary examiner must personally review and decide whether such evidence is responsive and presents sufficient facts to overcome the rejection.
guidance: All traversing affidavits/declarations not falling under other specific rules are treated under 1.132. Use form paragraphs 7.65/7.66 and subparagraphs 7.66.01–7.66.05 to comment on sufficiency and to state reasons for insufficiency.

name: Common reasons an affidavit/declaration under 1.132 is insufficient
description: Affidavit/declaration may be insufficient for reasons including: untimely; fails to set forth facts; facts presented are not germane to the rejection at issue; showing is not commensurate in scope with the claims; affiant has never seen the invention before; statements only assert that invention works as intended; refers only to the invention generally and not to individual claims; no evidence of long-felt need; or conclusion that rebuttal evidence fails to outweigh evidence of obviousness.
guidance: Form paragraphs 7.66 and 7.66.01–7.66.05 enumerate these categories and require a detailed explanation of why the affidavit/declaration is insufficient rather than general conclusory statements. See MPEP § 716 for examples and examiner notes.

name: Objective (secondary) evidence of nonobviousness must be considered
description: Affidavits/declarations, when timely presented, containing evidence of criticality or unexpected results, commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, skepticism of experts, etc., must be considered by the examiner in determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103.
guidance: Comparative data in the specification intended to illustrate the claimed invention must be considered. The lack of objective evidence does not weigh in favor of obviousness. Corroboration is not required in 1.131 practice; whether test results are needed to prove utility depends on facts. Cite Graham v. John Deere, Stratoflex, In re Margolis, Miles Labs, and other cases for precedent.

name: Examiner must provide detailed explanations when rejecting entered evidence
description: If an entered affidavit or declaration is deemed insufficient to overcome a rejection, the examiner must set forth the reasons for insufficiency with specific explanations rather than general statements.
guidance: General statements like 'the declaration lacks technical validity' or 'the evidence is not commensurate with the scope of the claims' without supporting explanation are insufficient. Use the form paragraphs and include specific factual or legal defects (e.g., untimely, lacks facts, not commensurate in scope).

name: Method of Determination of Identicalness
description: Determining of applying Article 29 paragraph (3) and (4) refers to whether an invention described in the claimed invention is identical to the invention or utility innovation specified in the description or drawings in another application at its filing (hereinafter referred to as 'prior art reference').
guidance: Procedure: (1) Determine a claimed invention of the present application (same as novelty determination in Chapter 2). (2) Determine the disclosure of the prior art reference from the specification description (including inherent disclosure obvious in light of common general knowledge). (3) Find identicalness and difference by comparing the claimed invention with the prior art reference (do not compare claimed invention with an invention formed by combining more than two prior art references). (4) If no difference between subject matters defining the claimed invention and prior art reference, they are identical; identicalness includes substantial identicalness.

name: Substantial Method of Determination of Identicalness
description: Identicalness of invention is related with determining novelty as well as inventive step (Article 29(2)), disclosure exception (Article 30), enlarged concept of novelty (Article 29(3),(4)), protection of lawful holder of a right, first-to-file, succession to rights, divisional/converted applications and priority claims; the criteria of identicalness shall apply in those cases.
guidance: Apply identicalness criteria consistently across related Articles; determining identicalness relies on comparing subject matter-defining elements of claimed invention and prior art reference. If there is any difference in subject matter, the inventions are not identical. Complete or substantial identity results in being identical to a prior art reference.

name: Application Requirement — Identical Invention determination
description: The identicalness of the invention shall be determined based on whether the claimed inventions in the applications have the same technical ideas (including invention vs utility innovation). Where more than two claims exist, identicalness is determined per claim. Article 36 applies regardless of identicalness of inventors or applicants.
guidance: Determination process: (i) specify inventions disclosed in claims (same as Chapter 2 novelty process); (ii) identify identicalness and differences by comparison; (iii) if no difference in configurations, deemed identical; if differences exist but fall under enlarged concept of novelty (Chapter 4 para 6), deemed the same (including substantial identicalness).

name: Reference date — application with treaty priority
description: The reference date of an application with priority claim under a treaty on an invention disclosed in the specification or drawings of the application serving as the basis of the priority claim shall be the filing date of the application which is the basis of the priority claim. For multiple priority claims, reference date is the earliest filing date among the filing dates of each invention. Markush-type claims may have different reference dates even within the same claims.
guidance: Apply per-invention earliest priority date. Note Markush group considerations.

name: Reference date — domestic priority
description: The reference date of an application with domestic priority on an invention disclosed in the specification or drawings of the application serving as the basis of the prior-filed application shall be the filing date of that prior application. For multiple domestic priority claims, the earliest filing date among each invention applies.
guidance: Same per-invention earliest-date rule as treaty priority; note Markush-type implications as above.

name: Reference date — international applications filed on/before Dec 31, 2014
description: For international patent applications (Republic of Korea designated state) filed on/before Dec 31, 2014, the reference date shall be the filing date of the international patent application on an invention disclosed in the translation of the specification, claims or drawings of the international patent application.
guidance: For international applications considered to be a patent application by decision (Article 214(4)), reference date is filing date of invention disclosed in the translation under Article 214(4) or Utility Model Act Article 40(4). Translation requirement applicable pre-2015.

name: Reference date — international applications filed on/after Jan 1, 2015
description: For international applications (ROK designated state) filed on/after Jan 1, 2015, 'laid open to public inspection' refers to PCT Article 21 international publication; reference date shall be the date of filing the international application on an invention disclosed in the specification or drawings of the international application (no Korean-translation prerequisite).
guidance: When applying Article 29(3) and (4) to international applications claiming domestic priority, inventions disclosed in the specification or drawings submitted at the international filing date are used as the reference for enlarged novelty and identicalness analyses. International applications deemed withdrawn for failure to submit Korean translation under Article 214(4) cannot be relied upon as another application under Article 29(3) and (4).

name: Examination where more than two applications filed on different dates — examiner handling
description: Where multiple applications for the same invention are filed on different dates, only the earliest filing may obtain a patent. Examiners must handle later-filed applications according to applicant identity and publication status of prior-filed applications.
guidance: If applicant and inventor differ and prior-filed application is laid open or registered, Article 29(3) and (4) apply to later-filed application; proviso on enlarged novelty can be flexibly applied even if claims not confirmed. If prior-filed not laid open, postpone examination until it is laid open/registered. If applicants/inventors are same, apply Article 36 proviso and make decision after scope of claims in prior-filed application is confirmed.

name: 102(e) prior art date for patents/publications from IAs filed on or after November 29, 2000
description: All references (WIPO publication, U.S. patent application publication, or U.S. patent) of or claiming the benefit of an IA filed on or after Nov. 29, 2000, designated the U.S., and published in English under PCT Article 21(2) have the 35 U.S.C. 102(e) prior art date of the international filing date or earlier effective U.S. filing date.
guidance: No benefit of the international filing date (nor any U.S. filing dates prior to the IA) is given for 35 U.S.C. 102(e) purposes if the IA was published by WIPO in a language other than English. Use form paragraph 7.12 and follow Examiner Notes to determine the 102(e) date. Consider benefit/priority claims only if subject matter is appropriately supported in earlier disclosures.

name: IA publications not published in English or not designating the U.S.: cannot be applied under 102(e)
description: If an international application was published by WIPO in a language other than English, or did not designate the U.S., the IA publication by WIPO (and certain related U.S. publications/patents) may not be applied as a reference under 35 U.S.C. 102(e).
guidance: Such references may be applied under 35 U.S.C. 102(a) or (b) as of their publication date. If a U.S. publication or patent issued from a continuing application claiming benefit to such an IA, the 102(e) date may be the earliest U.S. filing date after the IA filing date (see Examiner Notes).

name: Determining 102(e) prior art date: consider benefit/priority claims only with proper support
description: In determining the 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date, consider priority/benefit claims to earlier-filed U.S. provisional applications under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), U.S. nonprovisional applications under 35 U.S.C. 120 or 121, and international applications under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121 or 365(c) only if the subject matter used to make the rejection is appropriately supported in the relied-upon earlier-filed application's disclosure (and any intermediate application(s)).
guidance: Do NOT consider foreign priority claims under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) and 365(a). A benefit claim to a U.S. patent of an earlier-filed international application may only result in an effective U.S. filing date as of the date the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 371(c)(1), (2) and (4) were fulfilled (pre-AIPA situations).

name: Use of pre-AIPA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) (form paragraph 7.12.01)
description: If the reference is a U.S. patent issued directly or indirectly from a national stage of, or a continuing application claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 365(c) to, an IA having an international filing date prior to Nov. 29, 2000, apply pre-AIPA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) (form paragraph 7.12.01).
guidance: The prior art date of such a reference is the date the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 371(c)(1), (2) and (4) were fulfilled. Use form paragraph 7.12.01 and associated Examiner Notes to assist determination.

name: Provisional 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection for copending U.S. applications (common inventor/assignee)
description: If at least one common inventor exists between the applications or the applications are commonly assigned and the effective filing dates are different, a provisional 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection of the later-filed application should be made when the earlier-filed copending unpublished U.S. application discloses subject matter that would anticipate the later-filed application's claims.
guidance: Provisional because the earlier-filed application is unpublished; it presumes future publication/patenting of the copending application. Use form paragraph 7.15.01 when making such provisional rejections. The provisional rejection may be overcome by a 37 CFR 1.132 derivation showing or a suitable 37 CFR 1.131 showing; it may NOT be overcome by filing a terminal disclaimer (In re Bartfeld). If claims would have been obvious over the copending application, give obviousness form paragraph (7.21.01).

name: ¶ 7.15 series — general rejection language and variants for 102(a),(b),(g),(e)
description: ¶ 7.15 is a general rejection template: 'Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102[2] as being [3] by [4].' Specific follow-up paragraphs (7.15.02, 7.15.03) cover 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejections where the reference has or does not have a common assignee/inventor.
guidance: Bracket inserts must be filled appropriately (paragraph letter, 'clearly anticipated' vs 'anticipated' with explanation, prior art relied upon). If 102(e) is applied, follow with 7.15.02 or 7.15.03. 7.15 must be preceded by 7.07 and as appropriate other paragraphs or 7.103.

name: Identification of the particular part of the reference relied upon
description: The particular part of the reference relied upon to support a rejection should be identified in the Office action.
guidance: For clarity and proper record, point to the specific disclosure (paragraph, claim, figure) in the reference that supports anticipation or obviousness; follow form paragraph conventions for insertion and explanation.

name: Identicalness determined by claim language
description: The decision whether an invention is identical is determined by the identicalness of the matters described in the claims.
guidance: When multiple claims exist, novelty should be determined for each claim individually.

name: When claim language is clear define as recited
description: When claim language is clear, the claimed invention should be defined as recited in the claim.
guidance: Terminology in claims is interpreted with its general meaning and scope accepted in the technical field, unless the term has a specific meaning explicitly defined in the description. Interpretation should be objective and reasonable, considering technical meaning and a person skilled in the art at filing date.

name: Avoid limiting claims by description/drawings when claim clear
description: If the claim is clearly understandable, an examiner should avoid giving it a limited interpretation solely by referencing the description or drawings.
guidance: Matters not described in the claims but only in the description/drawings should be considered not recited in the claims. Conversely, if matters are recited in claims, they should be considered when interpreting the invention. Examiners may consult description/drawings to understand claim subject matter but must not examine claims by applying subject matter not described in the claims.

name: Claims may be broader than embodiments
description: If claim subject matter is more comprehensive than embodiments in the description, novelty and inventive step must not be determined by interpreting specific embodiments as the claimed invention.
guidance: Examples: generic term 'cream' in claim is not limited to a narrowly disclosed embodiment; 'thin film type probe' claim not limited to a particular tip pattern shown in drawings; rotation direction shown in drawings does not limit a claim that omits rotation direction.

name: Obscure or unclear claim terms — examine clarity first
description: If a term in a claim is obscure or unclear, the examiner should determine whether the claimed invention can be grasped by reference to the description, drawings and common general knowledge at filing.
guidance: If the invention can be grasped, examiner may notify deficiency in description and novelty collectively. If it remains unclear even with those aids, novelty is not conducted and a rejection for deficiency of description should be issued.

name: Product defined by function/characteristic construed broadly
description: When a claim specifies a product by its work, function, property, or characteristic, it should in principle be construed as every product that has that function/characteristic, unless specifically defined otherwise in the description or limited by common general technical knowledge.
guidance: Take CGK into account; some uses of 'function' may be understood to exclude technically implausible members (example: 'means to selectively join plastic materials' would not be read to apply to magnetic materials difficult to join).

name: Limitation of use (product-by-use) construed as product specially suitable
description: Where a claim limits a product by its use, the claimed invention should be interpreted as the product specially suitable for the disclosed use, considering description, drawings, and CGK.
guidance: If a product with all technical characteristics is not appropriate for the claimed use (or needs conversion), it should not be regarded as the product of the claim. If the limitation of use is not actually suitable in view of the specification/drawings/CGK, the limitation may have no impact on defining the claimed invention and thus not affect novelty (example: agricultural use limitation not preventing anticipation by a catalogue-disclosed fabric if not particularly suited).

name: Product-by-process claims: process as definition of structure/properties
description: Manufacturing process recited in a product claim is treated as a means of defining structure or properties of the final product, not as limiting to the process per se.
guidance: Novelty/inventive step should be determined by comparing the product having the structure/properties defined by all claim limitations (including process). If the process affects structure/properties, consider process limitations; if the process only affects efficiency/yield and not product properties, novelty is judged by the final product alone. If identical product can be produced by a different process and prior art shows identical product, the claim is not novel. Where it's difficult to determine effect of process, examiner should issue a notice of rejection stating novelty denied and consider applicant arguments; examiner may solicit written arguments or evidence.

name: Jepson-type claims: preamble included in scope
description: Even for Jepson-type claims (preamble/body division), the invention should be specified as a whole including the preamble because claim type does not change technical scope.
guidance: Elements in the preamble are not automatically considered publicly known merely because they are in the preamble; whether preamble elements were publicly known is a factual matter. It is inappropriate to compare only the body with prior art while ignoring the preamble; the technical idea of the invention as a whole (including preamble) is subject matter for patentability.

name: Publication timing and special cases
description: Certain documents (e.g., manuscripts submitted to journals) are not considered publicly known until their contents are released; catalogues generally count as publications unless not published for special reasons; thesis 'publication date' defined as distribution to public or university libraries after final exam unless earlier public announcement.
guidance: If filing date equals publication date, claimed invention does not lose novelty except when filing time is clearly after time of publication.

name: Method for determining novelty by direct comparison
description: Novelty is determined by comparing the matters defining the claimed invention with matters disclosed in the prior art reference and extracting differences; no difference means not novel.
guidance: Claimed invention is not novel when it is substantially or exactly identical to the prior art disclosure. 'Substantially identical' means no newly produced effect and differences are mere addition/conversion/deletion of well-known/common art that do not practically affect the technical idea.

name: Novelty of inventions with numerical limitations
description: Rules for claims that include numerical limitations: different outcomes depend on how prior art discloses numbers or ranges relative to the claimed numerical limits.
guidance: Four subcases: (1) If prior art has no numerical limitation and claim adds new numbers, invention regarded novel unless the numerical value could be chosen by skilled person or hinted by prior art/CGK (then novelty denied). (2) If claimed numerical range is included in a prior art's range, novelty is not negated automatically — criticality of the range must be shown (technical meaning described in detail; embodiments or supplemental materials proving the range is critical; objective confirmation typically via experimental results covering the range). (3) If claimed range includes a prior art range, novelty can be denied at once. (4) If claimed range differs from prior art range, novelty is generally recognized.

name: Novelty rules for parameter inventions
description: Parameter inventions (applicant creates a new parameter or arithmetic correlation used as an essential claim element) require determining the subject matter from description/drawings/CGK before assessing inventive step and novelty.
guidance: Novelty is determined by interpreting the parameter as part of the claim, but novelty is not established merely because the parameter is novel. Novelty is generally denied if the parameter merely identifies experimentally the nature/characteristics of a publicly known product or is merely a change in expression. If reasonable doubt exists that claimed invention is identical to prior art, examiner may await written arguments or experimental certificates; if doubt unresolved, reject. Examiner must concretely describe grounds for reasonable doubt and may propose ways to overcome rejection. The above rules do not apply when the parameter is standard, commonly used, or easily understandable by a skilled person.

name: Generic vs specific concept comparison
description: When claim and prior art use generic vs specific concepts, their relationship affects novelty: generic claim vs specific prior art, and vice versa.
guidance: ① If claim is generic and prior art is specific (a species), claim is not novel (example: claim to 'metal' anticipated by prior art disclosing Cu). ② If claim is specific and prior art generic, claimed invention generally has novelty, unless the specific embodiment can be directly derived from the generic in view of CGK (then novelty denied).

name: Do not use combinations of multiple prior art for novelty
description: Novelty determination must not be conducted by comparing a claimed invention with a combination of two or more prior art references; combining references is a matter of inventive step, not novelty.
guidance: Exceptions: when a prior art reference cites a separate publication, that separate publication is regarded as part of the prior art reference and may be relied upon for novelty. Dictionaries and references used to interpret cited reference terms may be treated as cited references.

name: Workgroup 2760 training manual standard
description: A training manual (100+ pages) focusing on analyzing the specification and claims, searching, and preparing written reports (office actions) is used to bring new examiners up to speed within ~6 months and to ensure consistent examination.
guidance: Manual contains samples of actions, guidance on handling/responding to amendments, and is distributed to new examiners immediately; used in apprentice training.

name: Quality-improvement initiatives and review measures
description: Continuous quality initiatives include Examiner-Trainers, enhanced training, search improvements, March 2000 initiatives for additional review, and in-process review mechanisms to ensure high-quality examination.
guidance: USPTO's mission is to help customers get patents but examiners must apply statute and rules (35 U.S.C., 37 C.F.R.); examiners must analyze claims, determine if burden of proof for denial is met, and may point out patentable inventions disclosed but unclaimed. Quality initiatives are resource intensive and are continuously updated.

name: Examiner duty to assist applicants and analyze claim scope
description: The patent examiner is tasked with helping the inventor, including pointing out patentable inventions disclosed but not claimed, and with analyzing the scope of claims to determine whether sufficient evidence exists to meet the burden of proof to deny patenting.
guidance: The patent statute presumes entitlement to a patent unless the examiner meets the burden of proof to deny; examiners must balance assistance with proper application of legal standards.

name: Credibility of asserted utility
description: An examiner must determine whether an asserted utility is credible based on the information disclosed in the application; absence of a known cure is not a basis to conclude lack of utility.
guidance: Only claims for which an asserted utility is not credible should be rejected. Credibility is judged from the specification and supporting evidence; modest evidence may suffice to support a claim of treating a symptom, while claims of 'curing' a disease require significantly greater evidentiary support. Expert affidavits indicating a reasonable expectation of success, supported by sound reasoning (e.g., in light of FDA clinical-trial practices), usually suffice to establish credibility. Cite case law examples (In re Jolles, In re Sichert, etc.).

name: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) during prosecution
description: During examination, pending claims must be given their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.
guidance: BRI is applied by the PTO (not the same as court claim construction) to the claim language as understood by one of ordinary skill in the art, taking into account the specification. The standard reduces the chance that issued claims will be interpreted more broadly than justified because applicants can amend during prosecution. BRI does not mean the broadest possible interpretation; the construction must be consistent with ordinary and customary meaning and the specification. Relevant authorities and rule citations (Phillips, In re Am. Acad. of Sci. Tech. Ctr., 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1)).

name: Words of a claim given plain (ordinary and customary) meaning unless inconsistent with the specification
description: Under BRI, claim words are given their plain meaning (ordinary and customary meaning to a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention), unless the specification rebuts that meaning.
guidance: The ordinary meaning may be evidenced by claims, specification, drawings, and prior art, but the specification is the best source—ideally serving as a glossary. If the specification clearly sets a different definition, that special definition controls. Examples (Chef America, In re Zletz) illustrate applying plain meaning and when to follow a spec-defined meaning.

name: Do not import limitations from the specification into the claim
description: It is improper to read limitations from a particular embodiment in the written description into a claim when the claim language is broader than that embodiment.
guidance: While the written description may aid understanding, examiners must avoid narrowing claims by importing unrecited limitations. Exceptions include when claim language invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (means-plus-function), in which case the specification must be consulted to determine corresponding structure, material, or acts and the claim is limited to those equivalents. Case examples (Superguide, Liebel‑Flarsheim, In re Donaldson, In re Marosi, Zletz) illustrate improper importing and proper limits.

name: Means‑plus‑function (35 U.S.C. 112(f)/pre‑AIA 112, 6th para.) construal
description: When a claim element is expressed as means- or step-plus-function, the specification must be consulted to identify corresponding structure, material, or acts, and the element is limited to what is described and equivalents.
guidance: If claim language falls under 112(f), examiners must construe the element in light of the specification’s disclosure of structure/acts/materials. This construal limits the claim to the corresponding disclosure and equivalents. Cite In re Donaldson and MPEP §§ 2181–2186 for procedure and examples.

name: Sources for determining ordinary and customary meaning
description: The ordinary and customary meaning of a claim term may be evidenced by claims themselves, specification, drawings, prior art, and dictionaries; the specification is preferred when clear.
guidance: If the specification clearly defines a term, extrinsic evidence is unnecessary. If ambiguity remains or no ordinary meaning exists, examiners should look to specification and prior art; if no reasonably clear meaning can be ascribed, apply the broadest reasonable interpretation and consider a 35 U.S.C. 112(b) rejection and spec objections under 37 CFR 1.75(d). Case examples include Vitronics, In re Abbott Diabetes Care, and In re Suitco Surface.

name: Applicant as lexicographer (special definitions)
description: An applicant may rebut the presumption of ordinary meaning by clearly setting forth a special definition of a claim term in the specification; such lexicography must be deliberate and sufficiently clear to give notice to one of ordinary skill.
guidance: When the specification provides an explicit definition, that definition controls claim interpretation. The special meaning must be sufficiently clear and deliberate (In re Paulsen, Intellicall). If a special meaning is present, the examiner should acknowledge and identify it on the record. Examples (Toro Co., Old Town Canoe) show where spec definitions govern.

name: Disavowal of claim scope (clear and unmistakable disclaimer)
description: An applicant may narrow the presumed ordinary meaning by clearly disavowing or disclaiming claim scope in the specification, but disavowal must be clear and unmistakable.
guidance: Disavowal can be explicit or, in some cases, implicit where the specification consistently excludes or disparages a feature across all embodiments. If the examiner believes implicit disavowal narrows BRI, the examiner should make that interpretation clear on the record. Examples (SciMed, In re Am. Acad. of Sci. Tech. Ctr., In re Abbott Diabetes Care) illustrate explicit and implicit disavowal.

name: Effect of the preamble on claim scope (structural vs. purpose/use)
description: Whether a claim preamble limits the claim is a case‑by‑case determination based on the entire record; a preamble that recites structural limitations or is necessary to give life and meaning to the claim is limiting, whereas a mere statement of purpose or intended use is not.
guidance: Examiners should review the entire application to determine if preamble language limits structure or merely states purpose. If the body of the claim sets forth all limitations and the preamble only states intended use, the preamble is not a limitation (Pitney Bowes, Rowe v. Dror). However, if the preamble provides structural limitations or the intended use results in a structural/manipulative difference over prior art, the preamble limits the claim (Corning, Kropa, Jansen, In re Cruciferous Sprout Litig.). Evaluate whether prior art capable of performing the recited purpose meets the claim. Use cited cases and hypothetical examples to guide analysis.

name: Examiner decision flow for terms not invoking 112(f)
description: A stepwise process examiners should follow to determine claim term meaning under BRI when 112(f) is not invoked.
guidance: 1) Determine if the term has an ordinary and customary meaning to one of ordinary skill. 2a) If yes, check the specification for a special definition. 2b) If the spec provides a special definition, use it and identify it in the Office action. 2c) If not, apply the ordinary meaning. 3) If no ordinary meaning exists, check the specification for a meaning; if none can be reasonably ascribed after considering spec and prior art, apply BRI as best understood and reject under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) and object to the specification under 37 CFR 1.75(d). Office actions should acknowledge any special definition when used.

name: Plant patent—Latin name and variety denomination
description: Pre-AIA 37 CFR 1.76(b)(3) requests that the plant patent applicant state the Latin name and the variety denomination for the plant claimed.
guidance: The Latin name and variety denomination are usually included in the specification and will be included in any plant patent or publication if included in an ADS or data sheet; inclusion aids the UPOV database compilation and makes that process more efficient.

name: Domestic priority/continuity data in ADS
description: Domestic priority information should include the application number (series code and serial number), the filing date, the status (including patent number if available), and relationship of each application for which a benefit is claimed under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), 120, 121, or 365(c).
guidance: Providing this information in the ADS constitutes the specific reference required by 35 U.S.C.119(e) or 120 and complies with 37 CFR 1.78(a)(3)/(d)(3); if included in the ADS, a specific reference does not otherwise have to be made in the specification (e.g., first sentence). Pre-AIA 37 CFR 1.76(b)(5) does not apply to provisional applications. If continuity data is in the ADS but not in the specification, the patent front page will take the continuity data from the ADS.

name: 2024 USPTO Inventorship Guidance — 'significantly contributed' standard for AI-assisted inventions
description: The 2024 Inventorship Guidance stated AI-assisted inventions could be patented so long as at least one natural person 'significantly contributed' to the claimed invention. It explained this is satisfied if at least one human met all three Pannu elements (significant contribution to conception; not insignificant in comparison with the full invention; more than explaining well-known concepts).
guidance: Human contributions pertaining only to reduction to practice were not sufficient for inventorship. For patents with multiple claims, the 2024 Guidance required a human being to make a significant contribution to each claim. The guidance also acknowledged tools (including AI) 'may perform acts that, if performed by a human, could constitute inventorship under our laws.'

name: Patent-eligible subject matter — Section 101 and judicial exceptions
description: Section 101 allows patents on 'any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter,' but the Supreme Court has recognized judicial exceptions: 'laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas' are not patent-eligible.
guidance: When evaluating whether an AI-related claim is within Section 101, determine whether it is directed to one of the judicial exceptions (e.g., a mathematical formula, mental process) before proceeding to the Alice/Mayo framework.

name: Alice/Mayo two-step test for patent eligibility
description: Step 1: Determine whether the patent claims are 'directed to' an ineligible concept (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea). Step 2: If so, determine whether the elements of each claim contain an 'inventive concept' that transforms the claim into a patent-eligible application of the ineligible concept.
guidance: Claim limitations that are conventional, routine, and well understood—such as implementing an abstract idea on a generic computer—cannot supply the inventive concept. The test has narrowed patent-eligibility in areas like software, business methods, diagnostics, and biotechnology.

name: USPTO 2019/AI Eligibility Guidance — two-prong division of Alice step 1: 'recites' and 'integrates'
description: Under USPTO's framework, step 1 of Alice is divided into two prongs: (1) whether the patent claim 'recites' an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomena; and (2) if so, whether the claim has additional elements that 'integrate' the ineligible concept into a practical application of the judicial exception.
guidance: A claim is patent-eligible if it either does not recite an ineligible concept or if it 'integrates' that concept into a practical application. The AI Eligibility Guidance gives examples: a claim to an application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) for an artificial neural network is eligible because it is directed to specific hardware components and does not recite an abstract idea; a claim on a general method of using a trained neural network to detect anomalies is ineligible (directed to an abstract mathematical/mental process implemented on generic components).

name: Practical application/inventive-concept standard for AI claims — 'improv[ing] the functioning of a computer or ... another technology or technical field'
description: AI inventions may be eligible when they 'integrate' an abstract idea into a practical application by 'improv[ing] the functioning of a computer or improv[ing] another technology or technical field.'
guidance: Examples: a general deep neural network method to analyze speech is ineligible as abstract, but a particular method that separates mixed speech into separate waveforms and recombines them without unwanted sources may be an eligible practical application. Evaluate whether the claim recites technical improvements or specific applications to a technological field.

name: Practical/administrative considerations and stakeholder perspectives
description: Stakeholders differ on how USPTO guidance treats AI: some view the 2025 guidance as providing 'certainty' and consistent with pro-patent policy; others criticize USPTO examples as unrealistic or argue guidance treats trained AI as a 'generic computer' and may make obtaining AI patents unnecessarily difficult.
guidance: When crafting or evaluating guidance/policy, consider (a) clarity and realistic examples, (b) whether claim limitations tied to AI are treated as generic or technical, and (c) how guidance aligns with or diverges from case law (and potential legislative responses).

name: Pointer/motivation requirement from prior art
description: The skilled person needs a pointer or motivation from a realistic starting point that directs them to implement a next step toward the claimed invention.
guidance: A claimed solution is obvious when the skilled person would take the next step either (i) prompted by the pointer or (ii) as a matter of routine, and arrive at the claimed invention. Conditional language, identification of areas for exploration, and calls for further studies cannot count as directional signposts.

name: Would, not could — avoid hindsight
description: The assessment asks whether the skilled person would (not merely could) have arrived at the claimed invention with a reasonable expectation of success.
guidance: It is insufficient to show mere feasibility, existence of techniques to implement a change, a general interest in a target, or a broad research activity. The skilled person must be directed by the prior art and be able to predict success with some confidence appropriate to the field.

name: Clarity requirement under 35 U.S.C. §112(b)
description: Claim clarity is required by 35 U.S.C. §112(b); current PTO policy emphasizes claim clarity (e.g., USPTO glossary pilot program).
guidance: Claims must be sufficiently definite so that their metes and bounds are clear to a person of ordinary skill in the art; the PTO has initiatives to promote clarity.

name: Definition of a Markush claim
description: A Markush-type claim recites alternatives in a format such as 'selected from the group consisting of A, B and C.' The term 'Markush claim' here means any claim that recites a list of alternatively useable species regardless of format.
guidance: While the 'selected from the group consisting of' phrasing is common, the guidelines apply to any enumeration of alternatively usable species.

name: Indefiniteness test for Markush groups (breadth vs indefiniteness)
description: Breadth alone is not indefiniteness, but if a Markush group is so expansive that persons skilled in the art cannot determine the metes and bounds (i.e., cannot envision all members), the claim may be indefinite under 35 U.S.C. §112(b).
guidance: Apply the test whether one of ordinary skill can envision all members; very large or amorphous lists can trigger indefiniteness rejections (citing In re Gardner).

name: Subgenus/genus claims are acceptable if supported
description: Genus, subgenus, and Markush-type claims, if properly supported by the disclosure, are acceptable ways to claim inventions; examiners should not reject Markush-type claims merely because genus claims encompass them (MPEP §2173.05(h)).
guidance: Ensure adequate written description/support for genus/subgenus/Markush groupings in the specification to withstand challenges.

name: Process/combination vs. compound Markush grouping
description: When a Markush group occurs in a claim reciting a process or a combination (not a single compound), it is sufficient if the members of the group are disclosed to possess at least one property in common which is mainly responsible for their function in the claimed relationship; for single-compound claims members ordinarily must belong to a recognized physical/chemical or art-recognized class.
guidance: Different standards apply depending on whether claim is to a compound or to a process/combination — focus on the property responsible for function in process claims; disclose such common properties in the specification when possible.

name: Are Markush claims 'generic' (propriety/test stringency)
description: Present practice holds that claims reciting Markush groups are not generic claims (MPEP §803); this may subject enumerated groups to a more stringent test for propriety of the recited members because enumeration is often used when no appropriate generic language exists.
guidance: Be aware that enumeration invites scrutiny of the propriety of included members; prefer genuine generic language only when appropriate and supported.

name: Improper Markush Grouping prong 1: single structural similarity requirement
description: A claim contains an improper Markush grouping if the species of the Markush group do not share a 'single structural similarity' — i.e., they do not belong to the same recognized physical or chemical class or the same art-recognized class (Supplementary §112 Guidelines; MPEP §803.02).
guidance: Determine whether a 'substantial structural feature' common to members exists and is essential to the claimed use; absence supports an improper grouping rejection (see Harnisch/Hozumi).

name: Improper Markush Grouping prong 2: common use requirement
description: A claim contains an improper Markush grouping if the species do not share a common use — meaning they are not disclosed in the specification or known in the art to be functionally equivalent (Supplementary §112 Guidelines).
guidance: Assess whether the specification or the prior art supports a shared functional use among listed species; lack of such support justifies a grouping rejection.

name: MPEP §803.02 two-prong test (substantial structural feature + common use)
description: MPEP §803.02 explains a Markush grouping is proper when the embodiments share both a common use and a substantial structural feature essential to that use.
guidance: Apply both prongs: (1) substantial structural feature, and (2) common use that flows from that feature. If claim reads on patentably distinct inventions, a provisional election may be made.

name: Claim-as-a-whole analysis approach
description: Analyze the claim as a whole to determine whether the alternative species share a common use and a substantial structural feature essential to that use; if species lack either, or the shared structural feature is not essential to the common use, an improper Markush grouping rejection is appropriate.
guidance: Use Form ¶ 8.40 for improper grouping rejections and provide specific reasons why members do not share the structural feature and common use.

name: Examiner response options and applicant rebuttals
description: Appropriate applicant responses to an improper grouping rejection include amending the claims to include only species that share a single structural similarity and common use, or presenting a sufficient showing that the species in fact share such structural similarity and common use. An election of species can be required to conduct examination.
guidance: Applicants should either narrow claims, provide evidence of shared structure/use, or elect species for examination; examiners may extend search to related species sharing structure/use.

name: Form ¶ 8.40 Improper Markush Grouping Rejection template and examiner notes
description: Form paragraph provides boilerplate rejection language explaining that the improper Markush grouping includes species that do not share both a substantial structural feature and a common use that flows from it, and directs applicant to amend or show sufficiency. Examiner notes instruct to identify claim numbers, explain why members fail the test, and note election timing.
guidance: When issuing such a rejection, the examiner should fill in claim numbers and specific deficiencies; form may only be used after applicant has made an election if an election is appropriate.

name: Case-law guidance and limits (Weber, Harnisch, Hozumi, deGrado)
description: Key cases provide instructive holdings: Weber emphasizes applicants' right to claim inventions and warns against administrative overreach; Harnisch found Markush groupings proper where compounds formed a subgenus with substantial structural similarity and common utility; Hozumi reversed improper grouping where structural feature essential to utility was disclosed; deGrado illustrates appellate procedural interplay.
guidance: Use case law to inform whether a grouping is 'improper' — focus on unity of invention, structural similarity, and disclosed common utility; recognize precedential status and nuances of each case.

name: Markush Clarity Scorecard (practical checklist)
description: Practical categorization of common clarity issues: Reasonably clear items — 'consisting of' vs 'comprising', double inclusion, indefiniteness, subgenus claims, process/combination vs compound claims, portions of chemical compounds. Needs more clarity — 'Are Markush claims generic?' and 'Improper Markush Grouping'.
guidance: Use this quick checklist when evaluating Markush claims to triage clarity issues and identify which require deeper analysis or policy clarification.

name: Pre-filing patentability assessment and prior art searches
description: Conduct thorough patentability searches and analyses to evaluate your invention’s potential for protection.
guidance: Perform comprehensive searches to ensure the application stands out and to inform strategic claim drafting; Yucheng IP Law conducts such searches as part of pre-filing assessment.

name: Document preparation quality: detailed descriptions and sufficient disclosure
description: Prepare comprehensive patent specifications that meet CNIPA’s requirements.
guidance: Provide complete technical details and working examples to avoid insufficient disclosure; include detailed claims and technical drawings where applicable.

name: Strategic claim drafting
description: Develop robust claim strategies to maximize protection while ensuring compliance with Chinese patent law.
guidance: Balance broad protection and compliance with substantive examination standards; use experienced technical experts and patent attorneys for claim wording.

name: Claim Construction for the Case (judge-provided meanings)
description: It is the judge's job to provide to you the meaning of any claim language that must be interpreted. You must accept the meanings the judge gives you and use them when you decide whether any claim has been infringed and whether any claim is invalid. The meaning of the words of the patent claims must be the same when deciding both infringement and invalidity.
guidance: For claim limitations the court has not construed, jurors are to use the plain and ordinary meaning as understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the alleged invention. (Teva v. Sandoz; Phillips; Markman.) The judge will read stipulations and the court's claim constructions to the jury.

name: Construction of Means-/Step-Plus-Function Claims
description: For limitations in means[[step]]-plus-function format, the element does not cover all means/steps that perform the recited function. The court determines the recited function and the corresponding structure/step described in the specification (or an equivalent of that structure/step).
guidance: The jury must use the court's interpretation of the means-plus-function/step-plus-function element when deliberating on infringement and validity. Citations: 35 U.S.C. § 112; Mettler-Toledo; JVW Enterprises; Utah Med. Prods.; Valmont Indus.

name: Infringement—Generally (claim-by-claim assessment)
description: Infringement is assessed claim-by-claim. Patent law gives the owner of a valid patent the right to exclude others from importing, making, using, offering to sell, or selling the claimed invention in the United States during the patent term. Any person or entity that has engaged in those acts without permission infringes the patent.
guidance: When deciding infringement, jurors must compare the accused product/method to the patent claims (not to the plaintiff's product/method). Distinguish direct vs indirect infringement; literal infringement vs doctrine of equivalents; induced vs contributory infringement for indirect theories.

name: Direct Infringement—Knowledge and Intent Immaterial
description: A defendant is liable for direct infringement if the plaintiff proves by a preponderance of the evidence that the defendant made, used, imported, offered to sell, or sold the invention defined in at least one claim during the patent term.
guidance: Direct infringement can occur without knowledge of the patent or intent to infringe. (35 U.S.C. § 271(a); Commil; Medtronic v. Mirowski; Global-Tech; Warner-Jenkinson.)

name: Direct Infringement—Literal Infringement
description: A patent claim is literally infringed only if the defendant’s accused product/method includes each and every element/method step recited in that patent claim.
guidance: Evaluate literal infringement separately for each asserted claim. The same accused element may satisfy more than one claim element. If the accused product/method does not contain one or more elements of a claim, it does not literally infringe that claim. (Limelight; Hutchins; Gen. Mills; Amstar.)

name: Literal Infringement of Means-/Step-Plus-Function Claims
description: To establish infringement of a means-/step-plus-function claim, the plaintiff must prove by a preponderance that (1) the accused part/step performs the recited function, and (2) is identical or equivalent to the structure/step described in the specification for performing that function.
guidance: First decide whether the accused product/method has any structure/step that performs the specified function. If yes, decide whether that structure/step is the same as or equivalent to the structure/step recited in the specification from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill. Equivalence can be shown by insubstantial differences or by performing substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result. If function not performed or structure not same/equivalent, the means-plus-function claim is not infringed. (35 U.S.C. § 112; Williamson; Gen. Protecht; Applied Med. Res.; A1-Site.)

name: Claim Preamble/Transitional Phrases—"Comprising", "Consisting of", "Consisting essentially of"
description: "Comprising" means including the following but not excluding others. "Consisting of" means including the following and excluding others. "Consisting essentially of" means including the following and possibly including unlisted components/steps that do not materially affect the invention.
guidance: If a claim uses "comprising," additional components/steps do not preclude literal infringement. If it uses "consisting of," the presence of additional components/steps means no literal infringement. If it uses "consisting essentially of," additional components/steps are allowed only if they do not negate an element or materially affect the basic and novel properties of the invention. (Shire Dev.; Multilayer Stretch; CIAS; Norian.)

name: Direct Infringement—Doctrine of Equivalents (DOE)
description: If the accused product/method does not literally infringe an asserted claim, the jury must decide whether it infringes under the doctrine of equivalents by having components/steps equivalent to missing claim elements.
guidance: Analyze each individual claim element not literally present and decide whether the accused product/method has an equivalent for that element. Showing equivalence can be by demonstrating insubstantial differences, substantially same function/way/result, or that persons of ordinary skill would have known of interchangeability at the time of alleged infringement (though known interchangeability is not required). The same accused component may satisfy more than one element, and multiple accused components may satisfy one element. (Warner-Jenkinson; Graver Tank; Brilliant Instruments; Crown Packaging; Intellectual Prop. Dev.; Sun Studs; Hughes Aircraft; In re Kelley.) Practice note: if claim is literally infringed, DOE need not be applied; DOE available only for elements not literally met.

name: Actively Inducing Patent Infringement (Inducement to Infringe)
description: To establish that the defendant actively induced infringement, the plaintiff must prove it is more likely than not that (A) a single actor is responsible for direct infringement (all components/steps), and (B) the defendant actively induced those acts of infringement.
guidance: To prove inducement the plaintiff must establish four elements by a preponderance: (1) the defendant aided, instructed, or otherwise acted with intent to cause acts by the alleged direct infringer that would constitute direct infringement; (2) the defendant knew of the patent or showed willful blindness to its existence; (3) the defendant knew, or showed willful blindness, that the actions of the alleged direct infringer would infringe at least one claim; and (4) the alleged direct infringer infringed at least one claim. Willful blindness requires subjective belief of high probability a patent existed and deliberate actions to avoid learning of it. (35 U.S.C. § 271(b); TecSec; Commil; Sanofi v. Watson; Limelight; Global-Tech; Takeda; Info-Hold; DSU Medical; Metabolite; Ferguson Beauregard; Hewlett-Packard.)

name: Infringement by Supply of All or a Substantial Portion of Components Abroad (§ 271(f)(1))
description: To show infringement under §271(f)(1), the plaintiff must prove that: (1) the product as intended to be assembled outside the U.S. included all elements of at least one asserted claim; (2) the defendant supplied (or caused to be supplied) components from the U.S. that made up all or a substantial portion of the invention of that claim; and (3) the defendant specifically intended to induce the combination of those components into a product that would infringe if assembled in the U.S.
guidance: A "substantial portion of components" is a quantitative, not qualitative, assessment; the export of a single component of a multi-component invention cannot create liability under §271(f)(1). Section 271(f)(1) does not apply to method claims because §271(f) requires components be 'supplied.' (35 U.S.C. § 271(f)(1); LifeTechs v. Promega; Cardiac Pacemakers; Microsoft v. AT&T.)

name: Infringement by Supply of Components Especially Made or Adapted for Use Abroad (§ 271(f)(2))
description: To show infringement under §271(f)(2), the plaintiff must prove: (1) the defendant actually supplied or caused components to be supplied from the U.S. into a foreign country; (2) the defendant knew or should have known that the components were especially made or adapted for use in a product that infringes a claim; (3) those components have no substantial non-infringing use; and (4) the defendant intended for the components to be combined into that product.
guidance: It is not necessary that the components actually be combined into an infringing product, so long as the defendant intended the components to be combined into a product that would have infringed if combined in the U.S. For §271(f)(2), a "substantial use" is one that is not occasional, farfetched, impractical, experimental, or hypothetical. (35 U.S.C. § 271(f)(2); WesternGeco; Microsoft v. AT&T; Cardiac Pacemakers; Waymark; Rotec.)

name: Summary of Invalidity Defense (burden and standard)
description: The defendant contends that the asserted claim(s) are invalid. The defendant must prove by clear and convincing evidence that each asserted claim is invalid.
guidance: The jury must determine invalidity claim-by-claim; the instruction will be followed by more detailed invalidity contentions (e.g., anticipation, obviousness).

name: Prior Art Defined (pre-AIA)
description: Prior art includes items received into evidence during trial such as: (1) any product/method publicly known or used by others in the U.S. before the claimed invention was invented; (2) any product/method that was in public use or on sale in the U.S. before the cutoff date; (3) any patents that issued before the cutoff date; (4) any publications having dates of public accessibility before the cutoff date; and (5) any product/method that was made by anyone in the U.S. before the date of invention where the claimed invention was not later abandoned, suppressed, or concealed.
guidance: The instruction identifies the specific prior art items the defendant contends are prior art. Citation: 35 U.S.C. § 102 (pre-AIA).

name: Amendments must not introduce new matter
description: A design claim may be amended by broadening or narrowing its scope within the bounds of the disclosure as originally filed provided it complies with the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a). An amendment to the claim which has no support in the specification and/or drawings as originally filed introduces new matter because that subject matter is not described in the application as originally filed.
guidance: Examples: (A) An amendment changing the configuration of the original design by the addition of previously undisclosed subject matter introduces new matter (In re Salmon). (B) Changing surface appearance by adding previously undisclosed three-dimensional surface treatment (beading, grooves, ribs) is new matter. By contrast, removal of two-dimensional, superimposed surface treatment will not introduce new matter if it is clear the underlying configuration was possessed at filing. Converting originally-disclosed solid lines to broken lines (or vice versa) will not introduce new matter where no new elements are added, but any amendment affecting the claimed design must be evaluated for written description compliance. Preliminary amendments filed with application papers and inclusion of disclaimers in original specification/drawings/photographs are examples of amendments that would not introduce new matter. (See MPEP §§ 1504.04, 1503.02, 608.04(b); 37 CFR 1.121(f)).

name: Drawings define scope; drawings satisfy written description for designs
description: The scope of a design claim is defined by what is shown in full lines in the application drawings. For designs, 'it is the drawings of the design patent that provide the description of the invention.'
guidance: Cited cases: Contessa Food Prods. v. Conagra; Daniels. If features are not desired to be claimed they may be shown in broken lines to exclude them; failure to do so signals inclusion. The written description test is the same for design and utility patents (35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre-AIA 112).

name: Written description sufficiency test (possession standard)
description: The test for sufficiency of written description is whether the disclosure of the application relied upon reasonably conveys to those skilled in the art that the inventor had possession of the claimed subject matter as of the filing date.
guidance: Use an objective inquiry into the four corners of the specification from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art (Ariad). 'Possession as shown in the disclosure' and 'the hallmark of written description is disclosure.' For ornamental designs, the practical question is whether earlier illustrations depict the later-claimed ornamental design (Racing Strollers). The analysis is from the perspective of an ordinary designer; courts have emphasized whether a skilled artisan would recognize the claimed portion as separable or claimable.

name: Evaluate amended claims and priority/continuation claims for written description support
description: A written description issue generally involves whether the subject matter of a claim is supported by the disclosure of an application as filed. This question arises when an amended claim is presented or when a claim for priority/benefit of an earlier-filed application is made.
guidance: A continuation must comply with the written description requirement to be entitled to the parent application's filing date (Owens; Daniels). If the later-claimed design is not reasonably conveyed by the earlier disclosure, the claim should be rejected for lack of written description and will not be entitled to the earlier date (see MPEP §§ 1504.10, 1504.20). Examples: Munchkin v. Luv N’ Care (spout shape not specifically disclosed) illustrates failure to convey possession.

name: Examine the resulting amended design as a whole for written description compliance
description: When an amendment affects the claimed design, the resulting amended design must be evaluated for compliance with the written description requirement; the fact that an amendment only affects features that were originally disclosed does not negate the need to determine whether the amendment complies with the written description requirement.
guidance: Even if elements of the later-claimed design are individually visible in the original disclosure, additional consideration may be required to determine whether the whole later-claimed design was reasonably conveyed to an ordinary designer. In many cases (e.g., converting solid/broken lines) the examiner can determine possession by reviewing drawings; in limited situations further analysis is required. If not reasonably conveyed, reject under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (see Ariad, Daniels, Racing Strollers).

name: Record must be clear; examiner must set forth basis and consider applicant submissions
description: If an examiner determines that an amendment to a design claim is not supported by the original disclosure, the examiner should set forth a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) in the next Office action, specifically identifying the differences or changes made to the claimed design that are not supported in the original disclosure. The Office has the initial burden of establishing a prima facie case for any rejection and must set forth express findings of fact supporting that rejection.
guidance: Do not use a general statement that the amended drawing/specification/title contains new matter. When repeating a rejection after applicant response, review the basis in view of the record as a whole (amendments, arguments, affidavits/declarations). If the record demonstrates written description is satisfied, do not repeat the rejection. If again rejecting, fully respond to rebuttal arguments and properly treat applicant's evidence (In re Alton). Use form paragraphs such as ¶15.51 (35 U.S.C.112(a) rejection) and ¶15.65 where appropriate. Examiner notes in form paragraphs advise specifying what is unsupported and suggesting corrective actions.

name: Application may be fatally defective if definite enabled claim cannot be identified without new matter
description: If an amendment that introduces new matter into the claim is the result of a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b) and it is clear that the disclosure as originally filed cannot support any definite and enabled design claim without the introduction of new matter, the record of the application should reflect that the application is seen to be fatally defective.
guidance: Form paragraph 15.65 may be used to set forth this position. In bracketed text, identify the subject matter which is insufficiently disclosed. This signals that applicant may have no viable way to obtain a valid claim absent new matter.

name: Definiteness (35 U.S.C. 112(b)) evaluated in light of disclosure and prior art
description: Defects in claim language give rise to a rejection under the second paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112(b). The definiteness of the language employed must be analyzed not in a vacuum but in light of the teachings of the prior art and of the particular application disclosure as it would be interpreted by one possessing the ordinary level of skill in the pertinent art.
guidance: A claim may appear indefinite in the abstract but be definite when read with the application disclosure or prior art (In re Moore). There is no per se rule; evaluate facts and circumstances of each application. Use form paragraphs 15.22 and 15.22.02 for 'or the like' style problems. Use ¶15.22.03 when title fails to specify a known article of manufacture.

name: Broadening language in title: 'or the like' / 'or similar article' cautions
description: Use of phrases in the claim such as 'or similar article,' 'or the like,' or equivalent terminology has been held to be indefinite. However, the use of broadening language in the title when directed to the environment of the article embodying the design should not automatically be the basis for a rejection under 35 U.S.C.112(b).
guidance: Ex parte Pappas held such phrases indefinite in some contexts. Examiner notes: ¶15.22.02 should be used where there is another rejection in the Office action; do not use when phrase in the title is directed to the environment of the article. ¶15.69.01 may be used to remove indefinite language by examiner's amendment (with appropriate authorization).

name: Title must identify a known article of manufacture or request additional information
description: The claim should be rejected as indefinite when it cannot be determined from the designation and the drawing what article of manufacture is being claimed (e.g., 'widget' that does not identify a known or recognizable article). If the title of the article is too ambiguous, the examiner should request additional information.
guidance: ¶15.22.03: reject when title fails to specify a known article of manufacture; clarifying the title by specifying the article may introduce new matter (35 U.S.C.132 and 37 CFR 1.121). ¶15.21.01 requests applicant to provide a sufficient explanation of the nature and intended use of the article, and additional helpful information (analogous fields of search, prior art, brochures, co-pending utility application numbers). Submit information as separate paper, not inserted in specification (37 CFR 1.56; 1.97; 1.98).

name: Restriction practice: single claim rule and when to require restriction
description: A design patent application may only have a single claim (37 CFR 1.153(a)). More than one embodiment of a design may be protected by a single claim only if they involve a single inventive concept according to nonstatutory double patenting practice for designs. The examiner will require restriction in each design application which contains more than one patentably distinct design.
guidance: Restriction is required under 35 U.S.C. 121 if multiple designs are patentably distinct. The test for patentable distinctness requires: (A) the embodiments have overall appearances with basically the same design characteristics; and (B) the differences between the embodiments are insufficient to patentably distinguish one design from the other (differences de minimis or obvious to a designer of ordinary skill). Clear admissions by applicant that embodiments are not patentably distinct do not overcome restriction if evidence lacking. Use nonstatutory double patenting analysis (In re Rubinfield).

name: Initial inquiry — nature of the invention
description: The initial inquiry is into the nature of the invention, i.e., the subject matter to which the claimed invention pertains. The nature of the invention becomes the backdrop to determine the state of the art and the level of skill possessed by one skilled in the art.
guidance: Determine what the claimed invention actually relates to before evaluating prior art or skill level; use that definition to scope the pertinent art and skill assessment.

name: Define pertinent art by problem to be solved
description: In general, the pertinent art should be defined in terms of the problem to be solved rather than in terms of the technology area, industry, trade, etc. for which the invention is used.
guidance: Frame the relevant skilled artisan and art by the problem context of the claimed invention to assess enablement and predictability.

name: Enablement standard — must enable a person skilled in the art
