description: 35 U.S.C. 112 requires the specification to be enabling only to a person 'skilled in the art to which it pertains, or with which it is most nearly connected.'
guidance: Assess whether the specification teaches how to make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation by a person of ordinary skill as of the filing date.

name: Examiner must identify missing information when claiming non-enablement
description: When enablement doubt arises because information is missing about one or more essential parts or relationships between parts, the examiner should specifically identify what information is missing and why the missing information is needed to provide enablement.
guidance: Rejections should explain concretely what elements/relationships are unspecified and why a skilled artisan could not fill the gaps without undue experimentation.

name: Block diagram / functional disclosure may be non-enabling without details
description: A disclosure depicted by block diagrams with functional labels can be nonenabling if there is no indication whether parts are off-the-shelf or must be specially constructed, and if the specification lacks details on how parts should be interconnected, timed, and controlled to obtain the claimed operations.
guidance: Challenge components represented as blocks when the specification fails to identify elements, relationships, or how to assemble/adapt complex subassemblies; cite In re Gunn, In re Donohue, In re Scarbrough.

name: Complex component disclosure may require construction details
description: An adequate disclosure of a device may require details of how complex components are constructed and perform the desired function; merely naming complex components generically and stating ultimate functions can be insufficient.
guidance: If adaptation of known complex elements to the claimed system would require extensive development work, the disclosure may be non-enabling (see In re Scarbrough).

name: Biological materials / microorganism deposits and availability
description: For inventions involving living biological products (e.g., microorganisms), availability of the biological material (e.g., via a public depository) can be necessary to meet written description and enablement. A deposit must be made 'prior to issue' though not necessarily prior to filing.
guidance: Consider the scope of the claim (e.g., species vs. strains) relative to what was deposited and whether the verbal description enables production of other claimed members; consult MPEP §2402–§2411.03 and §2411.01 for deposit rules and rejections.

name: Breadth of claims must be commensurate with breadth of enablement
description: The breadth of enablement must be commensurate in scope with the claims. Limited examples or narrow direction compared to broad claims, especially in unpredictable arts, can render claims non-enabling.
guidance: Evaluate number of working examples, predictability of the technology, and amount of direction; examples: Enzo Biochem v. Calgene (antisense overbroad), In re Wright (vaccine claims), In re Goodman (plant cells).

name: Chemical/art-specific consideration: assay difficulty and quantity of examples
description: In the chemical arts, guidance and ease in carrying out an assay to achieve the claimed objectives may be an issue; a very difficult/time-consuming assay needed to identify a claimed compound contributes to the quantity of experimentation analysis.
guidance: Consider assay difficulty/time and whether experiments required are merely routine; quantity of examples is one factor among others (In re Wands).

name: Computer-related enablement — present factual analysis and assess all relevant arts
description: To establish a reasonable basis for questioning adequacy in computer applications, the examiner must present a factual analysis showing that a person skilled in the art would not be able to make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation. When computer programming and another technology are involved, the knowledge of persons skilled in both technologies is the appropriate criteria.
guidance: Focus on each block element's functions and how the specification teaches implementation; if more than routine experimentation would be required to implement a component, challenge it under 35 U.S.C. 112 first paragraph.

name: Block elements more comprehensive than a computer — challenge complex assemblages and timing
description: For systems including a computer plus other hardware/software, scrutinize whether block elements are complex assemblages with differing characteristics requiring precise coordination; without timing charts or sufficient interconnection detail, unreasonable work may be required to achieve claimed functions.
guidance: If disclosure lacks precise operations for microprocessors or timing between elements, there may be a reasonable basis to challenge enablement (see In re Ghiron, In re Scarbrough, In re Brown).

name: Affidavit practice — scrutinize affiant skill and factual support
description: Affidavits used to rebut an enablement challenge must be critically analyzed: assess the skill level/qualifications of the affiant relative to the routineer; affidavits that present conclusions with few supporting facts are weak.
guidance: An affiant with higher-than-routineer skill is less probative; examine factual basis (number of programmers, man-hours, level of skill) supporting claims that routineers could implement the invention (see In re Brandstadter, In re Naquin, In re Morehouse).

name: Permissible clarifications when feature is well known (20.14)
description: An amendment adding a specific feature may be permissible if the applicant convincingly shows that, in the context of the claimed invention, the feature would be so well known to the person skilled in the art that its introduction is an obvious clarification and does not extend the application content.
guidance: Example: specification of helical springs is permissible if drawings interpreted by the skilled person show helical springs or if it is natural practice to use helical springs for the mounting in question.

name: Use of later-filed examples/statements as evidence (20.17)
description: Later-filed examples or statements (even if not allowed into the application) may be considered by the examiner as evidence supporting allowability of claims, e.g., showing that the invention can be readily applied across the claimed field or supporting inventive step.
guidance: When such evidence is used to support a positive conclusion on inventive step or other allowability aspects, the examiner should mention this evidence in the international preliminary examination report (see paragraphs 5.52, 5.53, 13.15).

name: Adding claim-disclosed subject matter into description and support issues (20.20)
description: It is permissible to amend the description to include subject matter that was disclosed in a claim of the application as filed; however, the amended description must still provide the required support for the claims and any contradictions must be resolved by amending claims or description.
guidance: Special care where adding negative limitations to overcome prior art as this may raise lack-of-support issues.

name: Support for claim amendments and handling of negative limitations/disclaimers (20.21 and Appendix A20.21)
description: Any amendment to claims or addition of new claims must be supported by the description as originally filed; each claim limitation must be explicitly or inherently supported. Negative limitations, exclusions, or disclaimers must be examined for new matter issues.
guidance: Divergent practices exist: (A20.21[1]) A negative limitation raises a new matter issue if the excluded subject matter lacks support in the application as filed. (A20.21[2]) A negative limitation or disclaimer with no basis in the application as filed may be permissible to overcome accidental anticipation or to exclude parts for reasons other than novelty (e.g., lack of industrial applicability or insufficient disclosure).

name: Documentation of special search cases (21.26(vi)-(viii))
description: Authorities should document special cases internally such as limitations of search and justification, lack of clarity of the claims, and lack of unity.
guidance: Record rationale for any limitations and noteworthy issues encountered during search/examination.

name: Scope of estoppel after CBM
description: CBM estoppel extends only to grounds actually asserted in the proceeding, and not to grounds that "reasonably could have been asserted."
guidance: This narrower estoppel was touted as an advantage over IPR estoppel; however, caselaw and practice made the practical difference small because IPR estoppel (as applied) also left re-litigation opportunities for non-instituted grounds and claims. See comparisons with 35 U.S.C. §§ 315(e)(2), 325(e)(1)-(2) and relevant Federal Circuit cases.

name: Requirement that at least one claim expressly recite a financial activity (Federal Circuit standard)
description: The Federal Circuit held that the patent must have at least one claim that expressly recites a financial activity element; mere "incidental to" or "complementary to" financial activity is insufficient to make a patent a CBM patent.
guidance: Key decisions: Unwired Planet (vacated Board's broader test), Secure Axcess and related rulings narrowing CBM reach. This limits CBM applicability and reduced new filings.

name: Use of pre-institution disclaimers by patent owners
description: Patent owners can cancel (disclaim) claims that support a challenger's assertion that the patent claims a "Covered Business Method," and a disclaimed claim is treated as if it never existed.
guidance: This strategy allowed owners to end proceedings unilaterally pre-institution (37 C.F.R. § 42.207(e)). Post-institution disclaimers do not have the same effect because eligibility is determined at institution time.

name: Timing rule for eligibility determination
description: CBM eligibility is determined based on the claims of the challenged patent as they exist at the time of the institution decision.
guidance: Consequently, post-institution disclaimers do not affect the Board's CBM eligibility determination; petitioners and owners must consider claim status at institution moment (see J.P. Morgan Chase v. Intellectual Ventures II and Emerson Elec. examples).

name: Partial-institution / non-instituted-grounds estoppel consequences
description: Historically, Final Written Decisions addressed only instituted grounds and claims; non-instituted grounds often were not subject to estoppel, allowing re-litigation of those grounds in district court.
guidance: This practice reduced the practical difference between CBM and IPR estoppel. The Supreme Court's SAS decision (requiring institution on all claims/all grounds) altered the landscape and may expand estoppel scope going forward.

name: Effectiveness metrics for the CBM program (filings, institutions, success rates)
description: Program statistics used to assess CBM's effectiveness: e.g., sharp decline in petitions (36 petitions in FY2018), months with zero filings, increases in denials of institution after Federal Circuit narrowing; high invalidation rates reported for cases reaching Final Written Decision (statistics cited: ~96.7% or ~97% with some claims found unpatentable).
guidance: These metrics feed competing narratives: CBM succeeded in weeding out bad patents vs. CBM collapsed due to narrowings, costs, and practical limitations. Use multiple metrics (filings, institution rates, stay rates, invalidation rates) when evaluating program health.

name: Amendment requirements for adding/replacing Sequence Listing XML
description: Any amendment to a patent application adding an initial submission or replacing a Sequence Listing XML after the filing date must include: (1) a Sequence Listing XML in accordance with §§ 1.831 through 1.834 submitted via EFS or on read-only optical disc; (2) a request to amend the specification to include an incorporation by reference statement identifying the name/date/size of the file (except in certain international-stage filings); (3) a statement that identifies the location of all additions, deletions, or replacements of sequence information relative to the replaced Sequence Listing XML; (4) a statement that indicates the support for the additions/deletions/replacements with specific references to particular parts of the application as originally filed (specification, claims, drawings) for all amended sequence data; and (5) a statement that the replacement Sequence Listing XML includes no new matter.
guidance: When submitting replacements or late additions, include the replacement XML and detailed amendment statements showing locations, support, and an explicit assertion of no new matter; label replacements 'REPLACEMENT MM/DD/YYYY' when on disc.

name: Substitute statement requirement for continuing applications (37 CFR 1.63(d)(1))
description: A newly executed substitute statement under 37 CFR 1.64 is not required in a continuing application that claims the benefit of an earlier-filed application (35 U.S.C. 120, 121, 365(c), or 386(c)) provided a substitute statement under 37 CFR 1.64 was executed by or with respect to such inventor and filed in the earlier-filed application, and a copy of such substitute statement showing the signature or an indication thereon that it was executed is submitted in the continuing application.
guidance: Condition for omission of a newly executed substitute statement: the earlier-filed application must already contain a proper substitute statement and the continuing application must submit a copy showing execution/signature. This applies to continuations/divisionals relying on earlier substitute statements; check signature or clear indication of execution on the copy.

name: Examiner obligations concerning new matter when relying on prior oath/declaration or preliminary amendments
description: Where a copy of the oath/declaration from a prior application was filed in a continuation/divisional application, if the examiner determines that new matter is present relative to the prior application, the examiner should so notify the applicant in the next Office action (preferably the first Office action) and require applicant to delete the benefit claim or redesignate the application as a continuation-in-part.
guidance: Preliminary amendments present on filing date are part of the original disclosure; amendments must comply with 37 CFR 1.121. The Office may require a substitute specification for preliminary amendments. If new matter is present in preliminary amendments, examiner should follow MPEP §§211, 608.04(b), and 714 guidance and notify applicant promptly.

name: CPA eligibility and filing requirements (37 CFR 1.53(d)(1)-(2))
description: A continuation or divisional application may be filed as a Continued Prosecution Application (CPA) under paragraph (d) provided that: (i) the application is for a design patent; (ii) the prior nonprovisional is a design application complete per §1.51(b) (except possibly inventor's oath/declaration for CPAs filed on/after Sept.16,2012) and contains an application data sheet meeting §1.53(f)(3)(i); and (iii) the CPA is filed before the earliest of payment of the issue fee on the prior application (unless a petition under §1.313(c) is granted), abandonment of the prior application, or termination of proceedings on the prior application. The CPA must identify the prior application and disclose/claim only subject matter disclosed in the prior application; it must name the same inventors (except as provided in (d)(4)), include the request for a CPA, utilize the file jacket and contents of the prior application (including specification, drawings and inventor's oath/declaration), be assigned the application number of the prior application for identification purposes, and be a request to expressly abandon the prior application as of the CPA request filing date.
guidance: CPA practice is limited to design applications and has precise timing and content requirements. The CPA is intended to utilize the prior application's file and contents; ensure the CPA request includes the identifying information and only claims prior-disclosed subject matter. CPAs carry specific advantages (see guidance) but also strict no-new-matter rules.

name: No new matter in CPA; substitute specification and amendment handling (37 CFR 1.53(d)(5) and §1.125)
description: Any new change must be made as an amendment to the prior application as it existed prior to filing the CPA. No amendment in a CPA may introduce new matter. Any new specification filed with the CPA request will not be considered part of the original application papers but will be treated as a substitute specification in accordance with §1.125. Substitute specifications that include new matter will be denied entry. Preliminary amendments other than substitute specifications will ordinarily be entered, but any new matter entered must be canceled from the descriptive portion of the specification; claims relying upon such new matter will be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a).
guidance: Applicants should ensure substitute specifications assert no new matter and comply with §1.125(b) requirements (including statement that no new matter is included). If new matter is present, expect cancellation/112(a) rejections. Applicants can petition under §1.182 to remove an amendment from CPA and request it be made a separate application (with a new file and filing date).

name: Handling of substitute specifications or preliminary amendments that contain new matter in a CPA
description: Any substitute specification containing new matter filed with a CPA will be denied entry by the substitute specification or preliminary amendment examiner. Preliminary amendments (other than substitute specification) filed with a CPA request will ordinarily be entered, but any new matter which is entered will be required to be canceled from the descriptive portion of the specification. Any claim(s) which relies upon such new matter for support will be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a). An applicant may file a petition under 37 CFR 1.182 requesting that the amendment be removed from the CPA application file and be accorded status as a separate application (new file and filing date) if appropriate.
guidance: Do not include new matter in substitute specifications for CPAs; if new matter is present, expect denial of entry for substitute spec or cancellation and 112(a) rejections. Petition under §1.182 may be available to seek separate application status for the amendment, but applicants will not automatically receive refunds of fees if petition granted.

name: Description and drawings shall always be consulted to interpret claims for patentability
description: “The description and drawings shall always be consulted to interpret the claims when assessing the patentability of an invention under Articles 52 to 57 EPC, and not only if the person skilled in the art finds a claim to be unclear or ambiguous when read in isolation.”
guidance: When assessing novelty and inventive step, examiners and parties must take the entire disclosure into account. This departs from a practice that consulted the description only when a claim appeared ambiguous in isolation. The decision aligns EPO practice with national courts and the UPC.

name: Article 69 and Article 84 may be applied analogously for patentability purposes
description: The EBA notes that neither Article 69 nor Article 84 EPC provides a fully satisfactory legal basis for interpreting patent claims during patentability assessment, and that the strictly formal answer to whether Article 69(1), second sentence, and Article 1 of the Protocol apply for patentability would be “No”. However, existing case law applies these provisions analogously to patentability.
guidance: Practitioners may rely on Art.69/Protocol and Art.84 reasoning analogously when arguing interpretation for novelty/inventive step, even though Art.69 is primarily about infringement and Art.84 concerns clarity/formal requirements.

name: A finding of clarity is itself an act of interpretation
description: The EBA states that the finding that a claim is clear is in itself an act of interpretation, i.e. the conclusion that a claim is clear cannot be reached without having interpreted the subject-matter of the claim.
guidance: One cannot avoid interpretation by claiming that a claim is ‘clear on its face’; reaching clarity requires interpretive steps and therefore consultation of the description/drawings.

name: Correct response to any unclarity in a claim is amendment
description: EBA: “The correct response to any unclarity in a claim is amendment.” (Reasons 20)
guidance: Examiners are likely to request claim amendments for clarity under Article 84 EPC. Applicants should be prepared to amend claims to remove unclarity, but must balance this against added‑matter constraints (see related rubric).

name: Draft claims with EPO‑proven language and provide fallback positions
description: Applicants should draft their applications with claim language that is – as far as possible – “EPO‑proven” to ensure clarity from the outset. Broad claims should always be accompanied by proper fallback positions, either within the claims themselves or in a general part of the description.
guidance: Strategic drafting reduces the risk that later clarity requests force claim narrowing that cannot be supported by original disclosure, avoiding an “inescapable trap” between clarity and original‑disclosure requirements.

name: Be careful when adapting the description to the claims
description: Now that it is certain that the description will also be taken into account when interpreting the claims in potential opposition proceedings, particular care must be taken when adapting the description to the claims during examination.
guidance: Any addition or deletion to or from the description should be carefully assessed for its implications on claim interpretation. An apparently simple adaptation can change the meaning of a claim term and open attacks for alleged added matter.

name: Interpretation‑first approach can assist patentees defending added‑matter attacks
description: If, for questions of added matter under Art. 123(2) EPC or Art. 100(c) EPC, these provisions require that the subject‑matter be determined, the patent claims must be interpreted consistently with Articles 52 to 57 EPC, i.e., in the light of the description and figures.
guidance: In opposition, patentees may invoke interpretation in light of the description to argue that a term added to a claim is synonymous with wording in the original disclosure; if adhered to, this may reduce findings of inadmissible extension.

name: No detailed method mandated for how to use the description; spectrum of approaches possible
description: The decision states the proposition that the description and drawings shall always be consulted for interpretation, but does not give guidance on how claim interpretation should be conducted on this basis.
guidance: Possible approaches range from a minimalistic position (consider only explicit definitions in the description) to broader functional/systematic approaches giving less weight to claim wording. Near term, EPO practice is expected to be limited to considering definitions or other unambiguous statements in the description, though the existing body of case law may require deeper interpretation in some cases.

name: Practical expectations in prosecution: examiners’ time constraints and tactical opportunities for applicants
description: Given the limited amount of time examiners have to prepare reports, it is unlikely that EPO search and examination reports will routinely prioritize claim interpretation up front. However, the decision gives applicants a legal basis for opening such discussions if helpful.
guidance: Applicants can proactively request interpretation discussions; but expect examiners to be more inclined to require clarity amendments rather than undertake extended interpretative analysis due to resource constraints.

name: Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph — Indefinite (general)
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which applicant regards as the invention.
guidance: Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.02 or 7.103. Follow with one or more specific form paragraphs 7.34.02–7.34.11 as applicable; if none fit, supply a full explanation identifying particular term(s)/limitations causing indefiniteness and why. If one skilled in the art could determine scope, this rejection is not appropriate. See MPEP §§ 2171–2174. Use form paragraph 7.34.15 for pro se applicants.

name: Terminology redefinition inconsistent with accepted meaning
description: Where applicant acts as own lexicographer to redefine a claim term contrary to its ordinary meaning, the written description must clearly redefine the term to put one skilled in the art on notice of the uncommon definition.
guidance: State the meaning assigned by the claim and the accepted meaning. Support examiner's accepted meaning with appropriate references (textbook/dictionary) per MPEP § 2173.05(a). This paragraph must be preceded by 7.34.01 and used only where the specification does not clearly redefine the term.

name: Relative term / term of degree rendering claim indefinite
description: A relative term or term of degree (e.g., 'sufficient', 'substantial') that is not defined by the claim or specification and provides no standard for ascertaining the requisite degree renders the claim indefinite.
guidance: Explain which parameter, quantity, or limitation is rendered indefinite and why. Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.34.01.

name: Broad range and narrow range/limitation within same claim (indefiniteness)
description: A claim that recites a broad range/limitation together with a narrow range/limitation that falls within the broad range (in the same claim) is indefinite because it fails to clearly set forth the metes and bounds of protection desired.
guidance: Insert the broader and narrower recitations and where they appear. May be modified to fit other indefiniteness instances. Must be preceded by 7.34.01. See MPEP § 2173.05(c) and cited Board decisions.

name: Use claims that merely recite a use without steps (indefinite / non-proper process)
description: A claim that provides for the use of [2] but does not set forth steps involved in the method/process is unclear and indefinite; mere recital of a use can render the claim improper as a process claim under 35 U.S.C. 101.
guidance: Insert what is being 'used' and explain deficiency. See MPEP § 2173.05(q) and cited cases. Must be preceded by 7.34.01. If the claim recites a use only, consider rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 as not a proper process claim.

name: Claims are literal translation (grammatical/idiomatic defects)
description: Claims that are generally narrative and indefinite because they are literal translations from a foreign document and contain grammatical and idiomatic errors.
guidance: Point out that claims fail to conform with current U.S. practice. This form paragraph must be preceded by 7.34.01.

name: Essential elements omitted (device claims incomplete)
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, for omitting essential elements such that there is a gap between elements; omitted elements are [2].
guidance: Must be preceded by 7.30.02 or 7.103. Give rationale for why omitted elements are critical/essential and list them. See MPEP § 2172.01.

name: Essential cooperative relationships omitted
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, for omitting essential structural cooperative relationships of elements, amounting to a gap between necessary structural connections; omitted relationships are [2].
guidance: Must be preceded by 7.30.02 or 7.103. Explain why omitted structural cooperative relationships are critical/essential and identify them. See MPEP § 2172.01.

name: Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112 for pro se applicants
description: Claims by pro se applicants that are narrative, indefinite, and functional/operational in language are rejected for failing to define the invention as required; structure must be clearly and positively specified and claims must be in one-sentence form.
guidance: Use form paragraph 7.34.15 for pro se applicants. Note format of exemplary patent claims and specify that structure must present a complete operative device.

name: Trademark or trade name used as claim limitation (indefiniteness)
description: Use of a trademark/trade name in a claim to identify or describe a material/product does not comply with 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph because trademarks identify source, not goods, making claim scope uncertain.
guidance: Insert the trademark/trade name and where used; specify the material/product the trademark is meant to identify/describe. Cite Ex parte Simpson. This form paragraph addresses indefiniteness caused by trademark usage.

name: Duplicate claims — warning and objection procedure
description: When two claims are duplicates or so close in content that they cover the same thing despite slight wording differences, object to the duplicate under 37 CFR 1.75 after allowing one claim (use form paragraphs 7.05.05 for warning; 7.05.06 for objection).
guidance: Use 7.05.05 when duplicate claims are present and not allowable to give applicant chance to correct. If one claim is allowable, object the duplicate with 7.05.06. See MPEP § 706.03(k) and § 804 for double patenting.

name: New matter — objection under 35 U.S.C. 132(a)
description: Amendments that introduce subject matter not disclosed in the original application are objectionable as 'new matter' (35 U.S.C. 132(a)); new matter may include added specific percentages/compounds or omission of method steps.
guidance: Detect and object to new matter in abstracts, specification, or drawings using Form Paragraph 7.28; if new matter is added to claims, also reject under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph (use form paragraph 7.31.01). Identify new matter by page/line/drawing figure, require applicant to cancel new matter in reply, and consider added matter as part of claimed subject matter for other rejections/priors. See MPEP §§ 2163.05–2163.07 and § 608.04.

name: Reissue application limitations (35 U.S.C. 251)
description: 35 U.S.C. 251 forbids granting a reissue that enlarges the scope of claims of the original patent unless applied for within two years from grant; reissue by assignee is limited and claims enlarging scope may be rejected as barred.
guidance: If reissue is applied for within two years (or properly claims benefit), examiner need not consider undue delay. Defective reissue oath may be ground to reject all reissue claims. See MPEP Chapter 1400 and cited cases.

name: Rejection of previously allowed claims — procedural safeguards
description: A claim noted as allowable shall be rejected thereafter only after the proposed rejection is submitted to the primary examiner for consideration and approval; give full faith and credit to prior examiner's search/action unless clear error or new art is found.
guidance: Exercise great care before rejecting a previously allowed claim. Use Form Paragraph 7.50 when withdrawing indicated allowability in view of newly discovered reference(s); any such action requires Primary Examiner signature. See Ex parte Grier and related guidance.

name: Final rejection — requirements and reply limitations (37 CFR 1.113)
description: On second or subsequent examination, the examiner may make a rejection final; the final rejection must repeat or state all grounds of rejection and clearly state reasons supporting rejections; applicant's reply is limited to appeal or specified amendments.
guidance: Before issuing a final rejection, develop a clear issue between examiner and applicant. In a final rejection, the examiner must state all applicable grounds and reasons. Replies to a final action must include cancellation of, or appeal from, each rejected claim; if any claim stands allowed the reply must comply with form requirements. See 37 CFR 1.113 and related MPEP guidance.

name: Form paragraph sequencing and usage requirement
description: Certain form paragraphs must be preceded by specified other form paragraphs (e.g., most 7.34.xx paragraphs must be preceded by 7.34.01 or 7.30.02/7.103); appropriate sequencing and selection of form paragraphs is required when drafting Office actions.
guidance: Follow examiner notes about mandatory precedences and exclusivity (e.g., 7.30.01/7.30.02 used only once in a given action; some paragraphs only to be used where specification does not redefine a term). When no form paragraph fits, supply a full, explicit explanation of the claim deficiency.

name: Applicant provocation requirements (§41.202(a))
description: §41.202(a) restates the requirements of Rules 604, 607, and 608 for applicants provoking an interference.
guidance: §41.202(a)(5) continues practice of looking at the applicant’s specification to determine the meaning of a copied claim (not the specification from which the claim was copied).

name: Requirement to add or copy claims to provoke an interference (§41.202(c))
description: §41.202(c) restates the practice under Rule 605 of requiring an applicant to add a claim to provoke an interference, and adds requirements for applicants copying claims from patents.
guidance: An applicant ordinarily must add a claim (or follow the rule's specific copying requirements) to properly provoke an interference.

name: Standard for declaring an interference (§41.203)
description: §41.203(a) states the standard for declaring a patent interference: the Director uses a two-way unpatentability test to determine whether claimed inventions interfere. §41.203(b) authorizes an administrative patent judge to declare the interference; §41.203(c) permits redeclaration sua sponte or in response to motions; §41.203(d) permits parties to suggest declaration/redeclaration to accommodate files.
guidance: Declaration is governed by a two-way unpatentability test and administrative patent judges have authority to declare or redeclare interferences, including on party suggestion.

name: Claim correspondence and its effect (§41.207(b))
description: §41.207(b) clarifies claim correspondence practice and explicitly states effect: (1) patentability must be determined for claims, not counts; (2) a claim corresponds to the count if the subject matter of the claim would have been anticipated by or obvious (alone or in combination with prior art) in view of the subject matter of the count.
guidance: Assessment of correspondence is based on anticipation/obviousness comparison of claim subject matter against the count's subject matter; patentability determinations remain claim-focused.

name: Step 2A Prong One: Abstract ideas (identify judicial exceptions)
description: Determine whether the claim recites an abstract idea by evaluating whether claim limitation(s) fall within at least one of three groupings of abstract ideas: mathematical concepts; mental processes; and certain methods of organizing human activity.
guidance: See MPEP 2106.04(a). Use examples (e.g., Training a Neural Network Example 39; Livestock Management Example 46 claim 4) to distinguish claims that do not recite abstract ideas.

name: Mathematical concepts (abstract idea grouping)
description: Includes mathematical relationships, mathematical formulas or equations, and mathematical calculations.
guidance: MPEP 2106.04(a)(2)(I). If claim limitations are essentially mathematical relationships/formulas/calculations they may be an abstract idea under Prong One.

name: Mental processes (abstract idea grouping)
description: Concepts that can be performed in the human mind, including observations, evaluations, judgments, and opinions.
guidance: MPEP 2106.04(a)(2)(III). Claims reciting mental processes fall within the abstract idea grouping unless additional elements integrate them into a practical application.

name: Step 2A Prong One: Laws of nature / natural principles
description: Identify whether the claim recites a law of nature or natural phenomenon (judicial exceptions other than abstract ideas).
guidance: See MPEP 2106.04(b) for concepts and products courts have identified as laws of nature/natural phenomena. Use examples (e.g., Julitis Example 29; Controller for Injection Mold Example 45 claim 4) to assess whether a claimed limitation is a law of nature.

name: Step 2A Prong One: Products of nature — Markedly Different Characteristics (MDC) analysis
description: When a claim limitation is to a nature-based product, apply the MDC analysis to determine whether it is a product of nature judicial exception.
guidance: MPEP 2106.04(c). Consider whether changes in structure or function are more than minor/routine: examples include engineered antibodies (Example 16), inactivated/attenuated virus (Example 28), gel/granulated forms (Example 30); functional changes (rate of cell growth, immunogenic effect, taste, glycemic control) may demonstrate MDC.

name: Step 2A Prong Two: Integration into a practical application
description: If a judicial exception is recited, evaluate whether the additional claim elements integrate the exception into a practical application such that the claim is more than drafting to monopolize the exception.
guidance: MPEP 2106.04(d). Use considerations from case law, including "improvements to the functioning of a computer/other technology" and "particular treatment or prophylaxis." Integration requires that additional elements apply, rely on, or use the judicial exception to impose a meaningful limit on the exception.

name: Considerations distinguishing Prong Two vs. Step 2B
description: Differentiate Prong Two (integration into a practical application) from Step 2B (inventive concept): Prong Two asks whether additional elements meaningfully limit/use the exception; Step 2B asks whether those elements amount to significantly more than the exception.
guidance: Use the court‑laid considerations (e.g., whether steps are merely data gathering, whether steps are conventional or merely instructions to apply a natural product) to determine where the claim falls. Examples: data gathering may be 'insignificant extra‑solution activity' (Example 45); a container that merely applies a natural product may not meaningfully limit the exception (Example 44).

name: Example-based indicators of eligibility or ineligibility
description: Illustrative fact-pattern outcomes indicate how the tests are applied: e.g., 'No exception recited → eligible at Step 2A Prong One'; 'additional limitation that does not meaningfully limit the claim → not integrated (Prong Two fails)'; 'mere data gathering or well‑known steps → not significantly more (Step 2B fails)'.
guidance: Slides include 46 examples across technologies (biotech, pharmaceuticals, antibodies, vaccines, business methods, computer/software) showing eligible and ineligible claims consistent with case law (Example 39: facial detection – no exception recited; Example 44: denveric acid variations; Example 45: controller for injection mold demonstrates data gathering vs. integrated control). Consult the indexed examples to see which considerations were applied.

name: Fee for each independent claim in excess of three (and in excess of claims in patent under reexamination)
description: For filing with a request for reexamination or later presentation of each claim in independent form in excess of three and also in excess of the number of claims in independent form in the patent under reexamination, an excess-claim fee applies.
guidance: Formatting requirements referenced near this provision: font size no smaller than 12 point, margins conforming to § 1.52(a)(1)(ii), and sufficient clarity/contrast for OCR. TABLE 3 TO PARAGRAPH (c)(3) and TABLE 4 TO PARAGRAPH (c)(4) give per-claim amounts by entity type (examples elsewhere in the section).

name: Federal Government use license exceptions to small-entity status
description: Claiming small-entity status is not prohibited for persons in an application filed/prosecuted/maintained at no expense to the Government where certain Government use licenses result from Executive Order 10096 or other federal agency action (e.g., 15 U.S.C. 3710d(a) circumstances).
guidance: The section enumerates specific Government-license-derived exceptions that do not bar small-entity status for persons under paragraph (a)(1). Consult the complete section for detailed conditions and limitations.

name: Definition: prosecution history estoppel (file-wrapper estoppel)
description: A doctrine indicating that a person who filed a patent application and then makes narrowing amendments to the application to accommodate the patent law may be precluded from invoking the doctrine of equivalents to broaden the scope of their claims to cover subject matter ceded by the amendments.
guidance: Explains the basic effect: narrowing amendments during prosecution can limit a patentee's ability to assert equivalents for the amended elements. Although primarily a U.S. term, the issue of using prosecution history in claim construction arises in other jurisdictions.

name: Canada: admissibility and rejection of file-wrapper estoppel
description: Patents in Canada are subject to purposive construction; extrinsic evidence is not permitted, and Canadian courts emphatically reject 'file wrapper estoppel'.
guidance: As of Dec 13, 2018, new section 53.1 of the Patent Act makes prosecution history evidence admissible before the Court for the purposes of claim construction. Nevertheless, Canadian jurisprudence generally bars use of negotiations with the Patent Office to establish equivalents or to determine claim scope; no distinction is drawn between literal and substantive infringement when excluding file-wrapper evidence.

name: Germany: general exclusion with limited later nuance
description: The German Federal Court of Justice ruled (2002) that 'issues derived from prosecution history cannot be taken into account in the assessment of the scope of protection of a patent, even with regard to the requirement of legal certainty.'
guidance: A later 14 June 2016 BGH ruling indicated that statements made during prosecution may indicate how the skilled person construes a patent, but such indications 'must not readily be relied on as the sole basis of claim construction' — i.e., limited, non-decisive use is possible.

name: United Kingdom: general discouragement, narrow exceptions
description: UK courts have ruled that use of the examination file in aiding construction of a patent should be discouraged except where the file includes 'objective information about and commentary on experiments'.
guidance: Examiner-file material is generally discouraged as an aid to claim construction in the UK, with limited admissibility when it provides objective factual experimental information.

name: U.S. Federal Circuit (pre-Supreme Court Festo): complete-bar rule
description: The Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit (Nov 2000) set a complete bar rule: a narrowing amendment that is related to statutory requirements for a patent will completely bar the patentee from asserting the doctrine of equivalents for the amended claim element.
guidance: The Federal Circuit stated: (1) an amendment that narrows the scope of a claim for any reason related to statutory requirements will give rise to a complete bar with respect to the amended claim element; (2) a 'voluntary' claim amendment that narrows the scope for a reason related to statutory requirements will give rise to prosecution history estoppel as to the amended element; and (3) an amendment followed by failure to explain the reasons during prosecution can give rise to estoppel.

name: U.S. Supreme Court (Festo): presumptive bar and patentee's rebuttal burdens
description: The Supreme Court overturned the Federal Circuit's complete bar, adopting a presumptive bar approach: narrowing amendments may give rise to prosecution history estoppel, but the patentee can rebut the presumption by showing specific circumstances.
guidance: To overcome the presumptive bar the patentee must establish that: (1) the equivalent was unforeseeable at the time the claim was drafted; (2) the amendment did not surrender the particular equivalent in question; or (3) there was some reason why the patentee could not have recited the equivalent in the claim. The Court emphasized caution in disrupting inventing-community expectations and assigned the burden to patentees to show that the amendment did not surrender particular equivalents.

name: Presumption of truth for applicant's asserted utility
description: A specification disclosure that teaches how to make and use the invention in terms corresponding in scope to the claimed subject matter must be taken as complying with the enabling requirement, and the Office should presume a statement of utility made by an applicant is true.
guidance: Office personnel should not begin by questioning the truth of the statement of utility; instead ask whether there is any reason to question it. Evaluate the logic of the applicant's statements and any evidence cited. If the asserted utility is credible (i.e., believable based on the record or the nature of the invention), a rejection for lack of utility is not appropriate.

name: Initial burden on the Office — prima facie showing and evidentiary support
description: The Office must (A) make a prima facie showing that the claimed invention lacks utility, and (B) provide a sufficient evidentiary basis for factual assumptions relied upon in establishing the prima facie showing.
guidance: The PTO must do more than merely question operability — it must set forth factual reasons that would lead one skilled in the art to question the objective truth of the statement of operability. If the Office cannot develop a proper prima facie case and evidentiary support, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 should not be imposed.

name: Examiner evidentiary requests to substantiate an asserted utility
description: In appropriate situations, the Office may require an applicant to substantiate an asserted utility for a claimed invention when operativeness appears unlikely or the alleged utility appears incredible in view of the art.
guidance: When requesting evidence, the examiner should indicate why the factual record is defective relative to applicant assertions and, where appropriate, specify what type of evidentiary showing can remedy the defect. Requests for additional evidence should be imposed rarely and only if necessary to support scientific credibility of the asserted utility.

name: Applicant's response and burden shift
description: If a proper rejection has been imposed, the burden shifts to the applicant to rebut the prima facie showing using amendments, arguments, or new evidence (e.g., affidavits or declarations under 37 CFR 1.132, or printed publications).
guidance: New evidence must be relevant to the issues raised. Declarations that set forth conclusions without establishing a nexus to supporting evidence, or that merely express opinions, may be of limited probative value. Office personnel must review original disclosure, evidence relied on in the prima facie showing, claim amendments, and any new reasoning or evidence, and must recognize, consider, and respond to each substantive element of the applicant's reply.

name: Evaluation of evidence related to utility — no fixed quantity/character
description: There is no predetermined amount or character of evidence that must be provided to support an asserted utility; the amount and character will vary depending on what is claimed and whether the asserted utility contravenes established scientific principles.
guidance: Applicants do not need to prove utility beyond a reasonable doubt or with statistical certainty. Evidence is sufficient if, considered as a whole, it leads a person of ordinary skill in the art to conclude the asserted utility is more likely than not true. Courts have reversed rejections where applicants provided reasonable evidentiary support.

name: Treatment of claims for difficult or previously untreatable diseases
description: Claims directed to treating or curing diseases for which there have been no previously successful treatments warrant careful review; credibility of asserted utility may be harder to establish where contemporary understanding suggests the task is impossible.
guidance: The absence of a known cure does not automatically mean lack of utility. An assertion that treats a symptom may require modest support; an assertion of 'curing' may require significantly greater evidence. Affidavit evidence from experts indicating a reasonable expectation of success, supported by sound reasoning, usually should be sufficient to establish credibility.

name: Claims must be given their broadest reasonable interpretation
description: During patent examination, pending claims must be given their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.
guidance: The PTO determines scope of claims not solely on claim language but 'in light of the specification as it would be interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art.' Because applicants can amend claims during prosecution, applying the broadest reasonable interpretation reduces the possibility that an issued claim will be interpreted more broadly than justified. Examiners should avoid importing limitations from the specification into the claim that have no express basis in the claim language.

name: Boxing for claims not searched (reasons (i)-(iii))
description: Where claims are not searched for reasons (i) to (iii), box 2 of the first sheet of the international search report is checked and Box No. II on continuation sheet is completed giving details.
guidance: Identify the claims not searched and state the specific reason(s).

name: Treatment of omnibus claims
description: Claims which rely on references to the description or drawings (omnibus claims) are searched and reported upon if they can be given a definite construction.
guidance: If omnibus claims breach Rule 6.2(a) (no reference to the description or drawings except when absolutely necessary), this may be reported in Box No. VII of the written opinion or report for international preliminary examination.

name: Abstract content: summary of disclosure and technical field
description: The abstract should provide a summary of the disclosure as contained in the description, claims and drawings, indicate the technical field, clearly state the technical problem, the gist of the solution, and the principal use(s) of the invention.
guidance: Draft as an efficient scanning tool for searching purposes; each main technical feature mentioned and illustrated by a drawing should be followed by its reference sign in parentheses.

name: Abstract must not contain statements of merits or speculative application
description: The abstract should not contain statements on the alleged merits or value of the claimed invention or on its speculative application; avoid phrases which can be implied, e.g., 'This disclosure concerns', or 'This invention relates to'.
guidance: Remove promotional or speculative language; focus on technical facts.

name: Relationship between documents and claims (claim mapping)
description: Each citation should include a reference to the claims to which it relates; different relevant parts of a cited document should each be related to claims similarly, and the same document may represent different categories with respect to different claims.
guidance: Where necessary, relate specific parts/passages of the cited document to specific claim numbers; exception: 'L' documents and 'A' documents guidance noted elsewhere.

name: Consequences of Refusing to Dance: RPS Declaratory Judgment Rights and Broad Portfolio Suit
description: If the applicant refuses to provide its aBLA, the RPS gains the right to immediately file a declaratory judgment action for infringement, validity, or enforceability of any patent that claims the biological product or its use—potentially asserting the entire relevant portfolio at once.
guidance: Refusal hands procedural initiative to the RPS and risks sprawling, multi-front litigation that the applicant must be prepared to defend without having revealed its process; weigh this against trade-secret protection benefits.

name: Regulatory prohibition on claiming independent/distinct inventions together (37 C.F.R. §1.141)
description: Two or more independent and distinct inventions may not be claimed in one national application, except more than one species may be claimed if there is an allowable generic claim and species claims in excess of one are dependent or include all limitations of the generic claim.
guidance: Allows multiple species only when a generic claim is allowable and species claims beyond one are dependent or include the generic limitations.

name: Restriction proper only if inventions can support separate patents and are independent or distinct (MPEP 803)
description: Claims may properly be required to be restricted to one of two or more claimed inventions only if they are able to support separate patents and they are either independent or distinct.
guidance: Examiner must evaluate whether separate patents are supportable and determine independence/distinctness per related MPEP sections.

name: Compare claimed subject matter to determine distinctness/independence (MPEP 806.01)
description: In questions of double patenting and restriction, the claimed subject matter that is asserted must be compared to determine distinctness or independence.
guidance: Assessment focuses on claim scope and comparison of claim language rather than solely disclosed embodiments.

name: Product/process distinction standard (example guidance)
description: To establish distinction between a product claim and a process claim, the examiner must show that the product as claimed can be used in a materially different process; a process limited to administering Compound X does not encompass applying ice and is not distinct simply because other processes exist.
guidance: Do not treat product/process as distinct unless claim language makes them materially different in claimed scope; analyze what the process claim actually requires.

name: Single embodiment claims defining same essential features — never restrict (MPEP 806.03)
description: Where claims define the same essential characteristics of a single disclosed embodiment, restriction should never be required because the claims are different definitions of the same disclosed subject matter.
guidance: Claims that vary only in breadth/scope over the same embodiment are not distinct inventions for restriction purposes.

name: Provisional election of species for Markush-type claims (MPEP 803.02/808.01)
description: For Markush-type claims encompassing at least two independent/distinct inventions, the examiner may require a provisional election of a single species prior to examination on the merits, using form paragraph 8.01 or 8.02 as appropriate.
guidance: Provisional election narrows initial examination to elected species; non-elected species may be held withdrawn.

name: Examination practice after election for Markush claims (MPEP 803.02)
description: Following election, the Markush-type claim is examined fully with respect to the elected species and further to the extent necessary to determine patentability. If the elected species is rejected as anticipated or obvious, the Markush claim and elected species are rejected and nonelected species are held withdrawn.
guidance: Examiner need not extend search to all nonelected species; provisional election limits examination unless overcome by applicant amendment.

name: If prior art is found on a nonelected species (MPEP 803.02)
description: If prior art is found that anticipates or renders obvious the Markush-type claim with respect to a nonelected species, the Markush claim shall be rejected and nonelected species held withdrawn; the prior art search will not be extended unnecessarily to cover all nonelected species.
guidance: Examiner's search is not required to cover all nonelected species broadly once rejection is found for a nonelected species.

name: Applicant can amend Markush claim to remove problematic species and have reexamination extended (MPEP 803.02)
description: If applicant overcomes a rejection by amending the Markush-type claim to exclude the species anticipated or rendered obvious, the amended Markush claim will be reexamined and examination extended as necessary to determine patentability.
guidance: Applicant amendments can restore broader examination of the Markush claim when prior-art issues are removed.

name: Restriction only when generic claims encompass multiplicity causing unduly extensive/burdensome search (MPEP 808.01/803.02)
description: In applications with only generic claims, restriction cannot be required unless the generic claims recite or encompass such multiplicity of species that an unduly extensive and burdensome search would be necessary to search the entire scope.
guidance: Assess whether burden of full search justifies restriction; do not restrict merely because multiple species are possible.

name: Cannot restrict among already-examined claims after full action on the merits (MPEP 803.02/808.01)
description: Following a first action on the merits of all claims, a later examiner cannot properly require restriction amongst already-examined claims; the Office cannot establish burden after prior full examination to support a new requirement.
guidance: Full faith and credit should be given to prior examiner's search and action unless clear error or new prior art exists.

name: Demarcation — indicate exactly how application is to be restricted (MPEP 814)
description: The examiner must provide a clear and detailed record of the restriction requirement to show the demarcation between restricted inventions so it can be determined whether continuing-application claims are consonant with the restriction and subject to the 35 U.S.C. 121 protection.
guidance: Complete, precise restriction statements are needed for downstream double-patenting/determinations and for applicant/continuation filings.

name: Rejoinder practice applies to national stage applications (MPEP 1893.05(d))
description: For national stage applications filed under 35 U.S.C. 371, if the examiner determines lack of unity and requires election, when all claims drawn to the elected invention are allowable, the nonelected invention(s) should be considered for rejoinder; any nonelected product claim that requires all limitations of an allowable product claim, and nonelected process claims that require all limitations of an allowable process claim, should be rejoined.
guidance: Rejoinder rules extend to national stage/PCT national entry practice; apply unity principles in light of PCT unity for PCT-originated filings.

name: Polynucleotide/nucleotide sequence applications — apply 800 chapter standards (OG Notice)
description: For U.S. national applications filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a), polynucleotide molecules will be subject to the standards for requiring restriction or provisional election of species set forth in MPEP Chapter 800, and will be considered for independence, relatedness, distinction and burden as for any other molecule. For PCTs and national stage filings, unity of invention determination will be made in view of PCT rules; unity exists when molecules, as claimed, share a general inventive concept.
guidance: Apply the same restriction/election/burden standards to nucleotide sequence claims; for PCT-originated filings, use PCT unity principles when assessing national stage claims.

name: Standards for affirmative defenses (selective enforcement and Contract Clause)
description: Selective enforcement: to prevail, Respondent must show (1) she was singled out while similarly situated persons were left untouched, and (2) the prosecution was pursued invidiously or in bad faith (based on impermissible considerations). Contract Clause: to claim impairment, a party must show existence of contract, law impaired the contract, and impairment was substantial; Contract Clause claims typically apply to state legislation and not federal government.
guidance: These defenses require specific proof; mere allegation of others' similar conduct is insufficient without showing investigation/enforcement disparity and invidious motive. Contract Clause defenses are unlikely to succeed against federal regulatory action absent special circumstances.

name: Judicial exceptions — recognized groupings
description: Judicial exceptions include: Abstract Idea: Mathematical Concept; Abstract Idea: Mental Process; Abstract Idea: Certain Methods of Organizing Human Activity; Law of Nature; Product of Nature; Multiple exceptions in same claim; No recited exception.
guidance: Map claimed subject matter to one or more of these groupings (e.g., mathematical calculations → mathematical concept; observation/evaluation → mental process). It is sufficient to identify at least one matching exception for further analysis.

name: Treatment of multiple exceptions (avoid over-parsing)
description: "Unless it is clear that a claim recites distinct exceptions, such as a law of nature and an abstract idea, care should be taken not to parse the claim into multiple exceptions, particularly in claims involving abstract ideas." MPEP 2106.04, subsection II.B.
guidance: If possible, consider limitations together as a single abstract idea rather than separately; when different abstract-idea groupings appear (e.g., mathematical concept + mental process), an examiner may treat them together for Step 2A analysis.

name: Improvement to functioning of a computer or other technology
description: One way to determine integration into a practical application is when the claimed invention improves the functioning of a computer or improves another technology or technical field. See MPEP 2106.04(d)(1) and 2106.05(a).
guidance: The specification must set forth an improvement in technology and the claim itself must reflect the disclosed improvement. If both are present, this supports a finding that the claim is not directed to a judicial exception.

name: Particular treatment or prophylaxis (Prong Two consideration)
description: Particular treatment or prophylaxis is a Prong Two consideration for medical/biotech claims: a claim that applies an abstract idea by identifying a specific patient population and administering a particular treatment may meaningfully limit the abstract idea. See MPEP 2106.04(d)(2).
guidance: Determine whether the claim requires a particular treatment tied to a specific patient population or disease such that the abstract idea is meaningfully limited (e.g., administering Compound X to high-risk patients). Mere generic 'administer an appropriate treatment' is insufficient.

name: Particular machine or particular transformation
description: Claims that recite a particular machine or a particular transformation can integrate an exception into a practical application (traditional 'machine-or-transformation' considerations).
guidance: Assess whether the claim's recited machine/transform is a meaningful, specific implementation rather than a generic invocation of a computer or routine transformation.

name: Mere instructions to apply an exception (MPEP 2106.05(f))
description: MPEP 2106.05(f) provides considerations for determining whether a claim simply recites a judicial exception with the words 'apply it' (or equivalent), i.e., mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer.
guidance: Consider (1) whether the claim recites only the idea of a solution or outcome (no details of how the solution is accomplished); (2) whether the claim invokes computers or other machinery merely as a tool to perform an existing process; and (3) the particularity or generality of the application of the judicial exception. If these point to 'apply it' language, the additional elements likely do not integrate the exception.

name: Field of use / technological environment (MPEP 2106.05(h))
description: Simply confining an abstract idea to a particular technological field or environment (e.g., 'using a neural network' or 'in network traffic') generally does not add an inventive concept.
guidance: A mere statement of field of use or linking to a technical environment is typically insufficient to render a claim eligible unless combined with other meaningful limitations or technical improvements.

name: Step 2B — inventive concept / 'significantly more' analysis
description: This part of the eligibility analysis evaluates whether the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the recited exception, i.e., whether any additional elements, or combination thereof, add an inventive concept to the claim. See MPEP 2106.05.
guidance: Even if Prong Two fails (claim directed to an exception), examine whether unconventional, non-routine additional elements (alone or in combination) provide 'significantly more.' If not, claim remains ineligible.

name: Well-understood, routine, conventional (WURC) activity — Step 2B consideration
description: At Step 2B, previously-identified extra-solution activities should be re-evaluated to determine whether they are well-understood, routine, and conventional in the field (MPEP 2106.05(g)).
guidance: If the additional elements are WURC, they cannot provide an inventive concept. If the claim elements reflect improvements beyond WURC activity, they may supply an inventive concept.

name: Classification of mental processes and mathematical calculations as abstract ideas
description: Mental steps (observation, evaluation, judgment, opinion) and mathematical calculations (e.g., rounding, weighting, backpropagation/gradient descent) are commonly classified as abstract ideas under MPEP 2106.04(a)(2) groupings.
guidance: When claim steps can be practically performed in the human mind or are mathematical concepts, treat those limitations as abstract ideas and proceed with Step 2A/2B analysis accordingly.

name: Assessing claimed remedial or real-time actions as technical improvements
description: Claim recitations of automatic remedial actions (e.g., detecting source address in real time, dropping malicious packets, blocking future traffic) can reflect a technical improvement and may integrate an abstract idea into a practical application if the claim and specification show the improvement.
guidance: Evaluate whether the claimed real-time/remedial steps are specific, technical solutions that improve a technological field (e.g., network security) rather than generic results or field-of-use framing.

name: Patentability requirements (statutory grounds)
description: Claims must define a useful, novel, nonobvious, and enabled invention that has been clearly described in the specification (requirements of 35 U.S.C. 101, 102, 103 and 112).
guidance: The standards of patentability applied in examination must be the same throughout the Office. All requirements for patentability (e.g., patent eligible, useful, novel, nonobvious, enabled, and clearly described as provided in 35 U.S.C. 101, 102, 103 and 112) must be met before a claim is allowed. A claim should not be allowed merely because it recites in detail all features (a 'picture' claim).

name: Early, clear articulation of rejections
description: The goal of examination is to clearly articulate any rejection early in the prosecution process so that the applicant has the opportunity to provide evidence of patentability and otherwise reply completely at the earliest opportunity.
guidance: After the application has been read and the claimed invention understood and a prior art search made, the examiner should review and analyze the application with the prior art and articulate rejections early; the examiner then reviews all evidence before issuing the next Office action.

name: Citation of best references and designation of relied parts
description: In rejecting claims for want of novelty or for obviousness, the examiner must cite the best references at his or her command. When a reference is complex or shows inventions other than that claimed, the particular part relied on must be designated as nearly as practicable.
guidance: The pertinence of each reference, if not apparent, must be clearly explained and each rejected claim specified. Language used in rejecting claims should be unequivocal (see MPEP § 707.07(d)).

name: Treatment of commonly owned or joint-research prior art
description: Subject matter that would otherwise qualify as prior art may be treated as commonly owned or as subject to a joint research agreement (and thus excluded) if the applicant/patent owner provides appropriate statements and disclosures.
guidance: For claims under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2)/102(b)(2)(C) or pre‑AIA 102/103(c), an applicant may provide statements that subject matter and the claimed invention were owned by the same person or were made under a joint research agreement, and must disclose/identify the parties as required. Specific conditions and statements are set out for various statutory provisions.

name: Constructive handling of form defects or missing limitations
description: When the application discloses patentable subject matter but the claims in their present form cannot be allowed because of defects in form or omission of a limitation, the examiner should not stop with a bare objection or rejection.
guidance: The examiner’s action should be constructive and when possible should offer a definite suggestion for correction.

name: Noting patentable subject matter disclosed but not claimed
description: If the examiner is satisfied that patentable subject matter has been disclosed and the record indicates the applicant intends to claim such subject matter, the examiner may note in the Office action that certain aspects or features have not been claimed and that if properly claimed such claims may be given favorable consideration.
guidance: This is advisory language the examiner may include to guide the applicant toward claiming patentable aspects disclosed in the specification.

name: Rejections not based on prior art must be fully developed
description: When a rejection not based on prior art is proper (e.g., lack of adequate written description, enablement, utility, subject matter eligibility, etc.), such rejection should be stated with a full development of the reasons rather than by a mere conclusion.
guidance: Examiners should review each claim for compliance with every statutory requirement during initial review. Deficiencies should be explained clearly and, whenever practicable, indicate how rejections may be overcome and how problems may be resolved. Relevant MPEP sections are cited for specific grounds (e.g., §§ 2104‑2107, 2161‑2174).

name: Rejection of claims copied from a patent
description: When claims corresponding to claims of a patent are presented in an application, the examiner must determine whether the presented claims are unpatentable on any grounds (35 U.S.C. 101, 102, 103, 112, double patenting, etc.).
guidance: If any presented claims are rejectable, they should be rejected. If the ground of rejection would also apply to the corresponding claims in the patent, any Office action including the rejection must have the approval of the Technology Center Director. See MPEP § 1003. Interference and derivation proceedings are addressed in MPEP Chapter 2300 and 37 CFR Parts 41 and 42.

name: Final rejection: when proper and content requirements
description: On the second or any subsequent examination the rejection or other action may be made final; in making such final rejection the examiner shall repeat or state all grounds of rejection then considered applicable and clearly state the reasons in support thereof.
guidance: Reply to a final rejection must include cancellation of, or appeal from, each rejected claim. Before final rejection a clear issue should be developed between examiner and applicant. Examiners should thoroughly search and fully apply references in the first action to bring prosecution to speedy conclusion and to avoid piecemeal examination.

name: Written description as proof of possession
description: Whether the specification shows that applicant was in possession of the claimed invention is a factual determination reached by considering a number of factors.
guidance: Factors include level of skill and knowledge in the art, partial structure, physical and/or chemical properties, functional characteristics alone or coupled with a known or disclosed correlation between structure and function, and the method of making the claimed invention. Disclosure of any combination of such identifying characteristics that distinguish the claimed invention from other materials and would lead one of skill in the art to the conclusion that the applicant was in possession of the claimed species is sufficient. (See Eli Lilly, Capon v. Eshhar, and related cases.)

name: Varying sufficiency depending on nature of the art
description: The description needed to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112 varies with the nature and scope of the invention at issue, and with the scientific and technologic knowledge already in existence.
guidance: In mature technologies where the art is well developed, written description issues are less likely for originally filed claims even if the spec discloses only method of making and function. In emerging or unpredictable technologies more evidence is required to show possession; mere method and function may not support product claims. (Cite: Eli Lilly, Amgen, Fiers, Burroughs Wellcome.)

name: Product‑by‑process disclosure limitations
description: Disclosure of only a method of making the invention and the function may not be sufficient to support a product claim other than a product‑by‑process claim.
guidance: Where the process has actually been used to produce the product, a product‑by‑process claim's written description requirement is clearly satisfied; however, if it's not clear the acts can be performed or the product produced by that process, the requirement may not be satisfied. (See Fiers v. Revel; Amgen.)

name: Partial structural disclosure may be insufficient
description: Disclosure of a partial structure without additional characterization of the product may not be sufficient to evidence possession of the claimed invention.
guidance: E.g., in biotechnology, conceiving a gene requires ability to define it to distinguish it from other materials and describe how to obtain it; defining solely by principal biological property is insufficient. Reduction to practice helps corroborate conception and possession. (See Amgen and Burroughs Wellcome.)

name: Genus support via representative species or identifying characteristics
description: The written description requirement for a claimed genus may be satisfied through sufficient description of a representative number of species, reduction to drawings, or by disclosure of relevant identifying characteristics (structure, properties, or function coupled with a known/disclosed structure‑function correlation).
guidance: A 'representative number of species' must reflect variation within the genus. Where substantial variation exists, describe a sufficient variety of species. One species may suffice only if the disclosure indicates the patentee invented species sufficient to constitute the genus. (Cites: Eli Lilly, AbbVie, Enzo Biochem, Noelle v. Lederman.)

name: Representative number concept and unpredictability
description: Whether disclosed species are representative depends on whether one of skill would recognize that the applicant possessed the common attributes of the genus; in unpredictable arts, one species usually will not support a broad genus claim.
guidance: If representative species are not disclosed, the genus claim must be rejected for inadequate written description. In unpredictable arts, the disclosure must adequately reflect structural diversity or establish a reasonable structure‑function correlation. (Cite: AbbVie, Eli Lilly.)

name: Structure‑function correlation as alternative to enumerating species
description: A reasonable structure‑function correlation, established in the specification or known in the art, can support a genus claim without listing many species.
guidance: Correlations may be inventor‑described or known at filing. Example: disclosure of an amino acid sequence may sufficiently convey possession of nucleic acids encoding it because the genetic code is known. (See discussion citing In re Bell and In re Baird.)

name: Examiner initial burden to justify written description rejection
description: The examiner has the initial burden of presenting evidence or reasoning to explain why persons skilled in the art would not recognize in the original disclosure a description of the invention defined by the claims.
guidance: A description as filed is presumed adequate unless the examiner rebuts the presumption with a reasonable basis. The examiner must identify the claim limitation at issue and establish a prima facie case by providing reasons why a person skilled in the art would not recognize possession in view of the disclosure. A general allegation of 'unpredictability in the art' is insufficient. (See Wertheim.)

name: Requirement that claim limitations be supported in the original disclosure for priority/benefit
description: To be entitled to an earlier priority or filing date under 35 U.S.C. 119/120/365/386, each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure.
guidance: If an explicit limitation is not present in the written description whose benefit is sought, it must be shown that a person of ordinary skill would have understood at filing that the description requires that limitation. (Cite: Hyatt v. Boone; In re Wright.)

name: Consequences when original disclosure lacks support
description: If the originally filed disclosure does not provide support for each claim limitation, or if an essential element is omitted, the claim must be rejected or priority/benefit denied.
guidance: Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre‑AIA 112, para.1) or denial of the priority/benefit claim is appropriate when support is lacking.

name: Complete patentability determination and clear Office action communication
description: Office personnel must complete the patentability determination under all relevant statutory provisions (35 U.S.C. 101, 112, 102, 103) and clearly communicate findings, conclusions, and their bases in the Office action.
guidance: After analyzing the claimed invention under all statutes and reviewing proposed rejections for correctness, only then should any rejection be imposed. The Office action should, when possible, offer helpful suggestions on how to overcome rejections.

name: Manner of showing possession (permissible descriptive means)
description: Possession may be shown by describing the claimed invention with all limitations using words, structures, figures, diagrams, formulas, reduction to practice, drawings, structural chemical formulas, or by describing distinguishing identifying characteristics.
