guidance: Examples: actual reduction to practice; disclosure that invention was 'ready for patenting' (drawings or structural formulas); distinguishing characteristics sufficient to show applicant was in possession. (Cites: Lockwood; Pfaff; Eli Lilly; Amgen.)

name: Subject matter need not be described verbatim but must be reasonably conveyed
description: The subject matter of the claim need not be described literally (in haec verba) to satisfy the description requirement, but the disclosure must reasonably convey possession of the later claimed subject matter.
guidance: If a claim is amended to include subject matter or terminology not present in the application as filed (departure/addition/deletion), the examiner should conclude the claimed subject matter is not described and reject accordingly. (See Vas‑Cath, In re Gosteli, and related discussion.)

name: Typical circumstances raising description issues
description: Written description issues commonly arise in amendments affecting claims, reliance on parent/priority filing dates, interferences, and when an original claim is not sufficiently described.
guidance: Specific examples: (I) amendments to claims or spec must be supported (In re Wright); (II) reliance on 35 U.S.C. 120 requires disclosure in parent application; (III) priority under 35 U.S.C. 119 requires corresponding support in foreign/provisional; (IV) claims corresponding to a count in an interference must be supported; (V) original claims may lack support when defined functionally without how function is performed, or when a broad genus is claimed but spec describes only a narrow species. (Cited cases throughout.)

name: Examiner should suggest claim amendments when appropriate
description: When appropriate, the examiner should suggest amendments to the claims which can be supported by the application's written description, mindful of prohibition against adding new matter.
guidance: Suggest amendments that align with the disclosure but avoid introducing new matter. See Rasmussen for caution about adding new matter to claims or specification.

name: Presumption of adequacy and standard objective test
description: A description as filed is presumed adequate unless sufficient evidence or reasoning rebuts that presumption; the objective test is whether the description clearly allows persons of ordinary skill in the art to recognize that the inventor invented what is now claimed.
guidance: Cite In re Marzocchi for presumption, In re Gosteli and Vas‑Cath for objective standard: the specification must convey with reasonable clarity to skilled artisans that, as of the filing date, the applicant was in possession of the invention as now claimed.

name: Complete and proper recordation of interview substance
description: The complete and proper recordation of the substance of any interview should include at least the following applicable items:
guidance: (A) a brief description of the nature of any exhibit shown or any demonstration conducted; (B) identification of the claims discussed; (C) identification of specific prior art discussed; (D) identification of the principal proposed amendments of a substantive nature discussed, unless already described on the Interview Summary form; (E) identification of the general principal thrust arguments of the applicant and the examiner (need not be verbatim or highly detailed; identification sufficient if general nature/thrust is understandable in file context); (F) a general indication of any other pertinent matters discussed; (G) if appropriate, the general results or outcome of the interview; (H) for interviews via electronic mail, a paper copy of the e-mail contents MUST be made and placed in the file as required by the Federal Records Act in the same manner as Examiner Interview Summary Form, PTOL 413. The Interview Summary form will not be considered complete and proper unless it includes or is supplemented to include all applicable items above.

name: Interviews involving cases sent to issue (post-allowance)
description: After an application is sent to issue (37 CFR 1.312), an interview involving detailed consideration of claims sought to be entered and discussion of prior art to determine allowability should not be given.
guidance: Applicant is not entitled to greater consideration informally than when formally presented; requests for interviews after a notice of allowance should be granted only with Technology Center Director approval and a written showing of extraordinary circumstances.

name: Amendment sections and document structure
description: Each section of an amendment document (e.g., Specification Amendments, Claim Amendments, Drawing Amendments, and Remarks) must begin on a separate sheet to facilitate indexing and electronic scanning.
guidance: Recommended amendment paper format (order): (A) cover sheet/table of contents with application info; (B) 'Amendments to the Specification' (separate sheet); (C) 'Amendments to the Claims' including complete listing of all claims ever presented; (D) 'Amendments to the Drawings'; (E) remarks section (separate sheet); (F) any drawings being submitted including Replacement/New/Annotated sheets.

name: Specification amendments presentation requirements
description: Amendments to the specification (other than claims, computer listings, sequence listings) must be made by adding, deleting or replacing a paragraph, by replacing a section, or by a substitute specification, and must unambiguously identify the location to be modified.
guidance: For paragraph amendments: (i) an instruction identifying location; (ii) full text of replacement paragraph(s) with markings showing changes relative to previous version; added subject matter shown by underlining; deleted matter shown by strike-through (double brackets may be used for five or fewer chars); (iii) full text of any added paragraphs presented without underlining (clean); (iv) deleted paragraph text must not be presented with strike-through or double brackets. If paragraph numbering present, replacement paragraphs should keep or extend numbering (e.g., [0071], [0071.1]). A deleted paragraph can only be reinstated by a subsequent amendment adding the previously deleted paragraph or section.

name: Fundamental factual inquiry: possession as of filing date
description: The fundamental factual inquiry is whether the specification conveys with reasonable clarity to those skilled in the art that, as of the filing date sought, applicant was in possession of the invention as now claimed.
guidance: Assess possession from standpoint of one of ordinary skill as of filing date. Cases: Vas-Cath, AbbVie v. Janssen, In re Smith, In re Wertheim. The inquiry is factual and case-by-case; how close the description must come depends on the nature of the invention and the knowledge imparted to those skilled in the art.

name: Presumption and examiner's initial burden / making a prima facie case
description: There is a presumption that an adequate written description is present in the specification as filed; the examiner has the initial burden, after thorough reading/evaluation, of presenting evidence or reasons why a person skilled in the art would not recognize adequate support for the claimed invention.
guidance: To make a prima facie case the examiner must identify claim limitations that are not adequately supported and explain why the claim is not fully supported by the disclosure. A clear, specific explanation (e.g., that the specification lists each element but lacks adequate description of their combination) can shift burden to applicant. See Wertheim; Hyatt v. Dudas; Stored Value Solutions v. Card Activation Techs.

name: Claim construction and analyze claim as a whole
description: For each claim, determine what the claim as a whole covers; claim construction is essential and each claim must be separately analyzed and given a reasonable interpretation consistent with the written description.
guidance: Consider entire claim including preamble, transitional phrase (comprising / consisting essentially of / consisting of), and body. Determine weight to be given the preamble and do not import limitations from the specification into the claims. Guidance and examples: In re Katz; Lockwood; Bell Communications; Corning Glass Works; Genentech v. Chiron; PPG Indus. v. Guardian Indus.

name: Review entire application to find support for claimed elements
description: Review the claims and the entire specification (including specific embodiments, figures, sequence listings) to understand how applicant provides support for each element or step of the claimed invention.
guidance: Examine how disclosure supports various features; determine field of invention and level of skill. Information well known in the art need not be disclosed in detail. Compare embodiments, figures, and sequence listings to claims. See Rasmussen, Amgen v. Chugai, Wang Labs v. Toshiba.

name: Possession shown by relevant identifying characteristics (biotech/chem specifics)
description: An adequate written description may be shown by description of sufficient, relevant, identifying characteristics (sequence, structure, binding affinity/specificity, molecular weight, length, partial structure, physical/chemical properties, etc.) that would permit a skilled artisan to recognize applicant was in possession of the claimed invention.
guidance: In biotech, structural formulas are convenient but other combinations of identifying characteristics may suffice; examples include unique cleavage, isoelectric points, restriction maps, enzymatic activity comparisons, antibody cross-reactivity. However, function-only descriptions typically will not suffice for compositions (Eli Lilly, Fiers). See Enzo Biochem; Falkner v. Inglis; Capon v. Eshhar; Amgen v. Sanofi; Centocor v. Abbott.

name: Means-(or step-)plus-function limitations: corresponding structure/materials/acts required
description: If a claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre-AIA sixth paragraph), it must be interpreted to cover corresponding structure, material, or acts disclosed in the specification and equivalents thereof; the specification must link particular structure/material/acts to the claimed function or it must be clear to one skilled in the art what disclosed structure performs the function.
guidance: Examine summary, detailed description, original claims, abstract, and drawings for corresponding structure. Two ways to satisfy: (1) written description adequately links/associates particular structure/material/acts to perform the function; or (2) it is clear that one skilled in the art would know which structures perform the recited function. If no corresponding structure is disclosed and the claim is indefinite under 112(b), it also fails 112(a) written description. Cases: Aristocrat Techs.; Atmel; Biomedino; In re Noll. See also MPEP §2181 and Fed. Reg. guidance.

name: Species claims: three-step analysis (A,B,C) for single embodiment/species
description: For each claim drawn to a single embodiment or species, determine (A) whether the application describes an actual reduction to practice; (B) if not, whether the invention is complete as evidenced by reduction to drawings or structural chemical formulas sufficiently detailed to show possession; (C) if not, whether distinguishing identifying characteristics are disclosed in sufficient detail to show possession.
guidance: If complete structure is disclosed, written description is satisfied for that species. If not, evaluate whether other identifying characteristics (partial structure, properties, function+correlation, method of making) are detailed enough for a skilled artisan to recognize possession. If none of (A)-(C) are met, reject claim under 35 U.S.C. 112(a). See Fields v. Conover; Eli Lilly; In re Wilder.

name: Genus claims: representative species or identifying characteristics required
description: For claims drawn to a genus, the written description may be satisfied by sufficient description of a representative number of species (by reduction to practice or drawings) or by disclosure of relevant identifying characteristics (structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics coupled with known correlation) sufficient to show applicant was in possession of the genus.
guidance: Assess whether representative species or species-characterizing features are disclosed so that a person skilled in the art would understand the scope of the genus. See Eli Lilly.

name: Factors to consider in assessing possession
description: Consider multiple factors: level of skill and knowledge in the art, partial structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics alone or with structure–function correlation, method of making, and combinations of such characteristics.
guidance: Use these factors to determine whether disclosed characteristics distinguish the claimed invention from other materials and would lead a skilled artisan to conclude applicant had possession. Consider maturity of the art and reliance on patents/printed publications to determine what is known. In unpredictable arts more evidence is required. See Eli Lilly; Capon v. Eshhar.

name: Product-by-process and unpredictable fields: additional evidence required
description: For product-by-process claims and inventions in unpredictable arts (e.g., certain biological and chemical inventions), disclosure of only a method of making and function may not suffice; where the process has been used to produce the product, written description is satisfied, but if it is unclear that acts can be performed or product produced, the requirement may not be met.
guidance: In unpredictable fields, disclosure of additional characterization may still be insufficient if inventor cannot define or obtain the product; reduction to practice may be the only convincing evidence. See Fiers v. Revel; Amgen v. Chugai; Burroughs Wellcome v. Barr Labs.

name: Newly added or amended claims: applicant must point out original support
description: For newly added or amended claims applicant should show support in the original disclosure for the new or amended claims; an examiner can state that applicant has not pointed out where support exists when support is not apparent.
guidance: A simple statement that applicant has not pointed out where the new/amended claim is supported may be sufficient where support is not apparent; applicant should specifically point out support for any amendments. See Hyatt v. Dudas; MPEP §§ 714.02, 2163.04, 2163.06.

name: Means-plus-function corresponding structure requirement (§112, ¶6)
description: When a claim limitation is in means-plus-function form the specification must disclose corresponding structure, material, or acts sufficient to perform the claimed function and must clearly link or associate that structure to the claimed function.
guidance: The specification need only disclose sufficient structure to perform the function to one of ordinary skill in the art. If the function is not a specific one requiring a special program or algorithm, a general purpose computer with memory may be sufficient corresponding structure (e.g., for the function of storing data). The disclosure must prevent purely functional claiming by providing co-extensive structure as disclosed.

name: Written description requirement (§112, ¶1) — possession
description: The specification must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail that one skilled in the art can reasonably conclude that the inventor had possession of the claimed invention.
guidance: Specifically, the specification must be understandable to a person of ordinary skill and show that the inventor actually invented the claimed invention. Mere statement of a problem or desired result is insufficient; the disclosure must convey constructive possession of the claimed subject matter (illustrated by multiple case examples).

name: Enablement requirement (§112, ¶1) — full scope without undue experimentation
description: The specification must teach those skilled in the art how to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
guidance: Enablement must cover the full breadth of the claims. Even if some embodiments are enabled, claims are invalid if significant portions of the claimed scope require undue experimentation or are not taught by the specification (see AK Steel, Sitrick examples).

name: Functional claim limitations must be supported and commensurate in scope
description: Functional language (describing a problem to be solved or a function/result achieved) must be adequately supported by the written description and commensurate in scope with the enabling disclosure.
guidance: Functional claim limitations that attempt to cover all means or methods of performing a function or solving a problem can render a claim overly broad if the specification does not support or enable that full breadth (per the 2011 Supplementary Guidelines and case law).

name: Cannot claim generically when specification discloses only a particular method
description: A claim that generically covers all ways of achieving a result is invalid if the specification only describes a particular method for achieving that result and does not show the inventor possessed the generic method.
guidance: LizardTech: Claiming all ways of performing DWT-based compression to create a seamless DWT failed because the specification described only a single way (maintaining updated sums). The spec need not spell out every detail, but must include enough to convince a skilled person that the inventor possessed the generic invention.

name: Cannot claim broader species/genus when other species are not shown to be attainable by routine methods
description: Claims to a broader class (e.g., fully-human antibodies) are not supported if the specification discloses only different species (e.g., chimeric/mouse antibodies) and creation of the broader species was not routine or enabled at filing.
guidance: Centocor: Disclosure of a chimeric antibody with desirable properties did not support claiming fully-human antibodies with the same properties where it was not possible with conventional technology to create such fully-human antibodies at the time.

name: Claims added later or broadened during prosecution must be supported by the specification
description: Claims that were not part of the original disclosure (e.g., broader 'spikeless' claims added later) must nonetheless be supported by the specification; absence of such support can render them invalid under written description.
guidance: ICU Med.: Spikeless claims were invalid where the original specification described only valves with spikes; figures and preslit embodiments that facilitate piercing did not demonstrate possession of spikeless valves.

name: Specification teaching away can defeat enablement for portions of claim scope
description: If the specification expressly teaches against an embodiment or discourages certain parameters, that teaching can show that the specification does not enable a claimed embodiment and may require undue experimentation to practice.
guidance: AK Steel: The specification warned that higher silicon content would not wet well, discouraging experimentation and showing lack of enablement for claims covering high-silicon coatings even though other coatings were enabled.

name: Claims must enable all embodiments encompassed by their breadth
description: If the claims are broad enough to cover multiple types of embodiments (e.g., movies and video games), the specification must enable each embodiment within the claim scope.
guidance: Sitrick: Although the spec described an IAIS for video games, it did not teach how to perform analogous substitution/integration in movies. Because movies and video games are technically different, enabling one does not necessarily enable the other; claims covering both require enabling disclosure for each.

name: A specification that discloses multiple problems or multiple solutions may support claims directed to only one
description: When the specification sets out more than one problem or more than one solution to a problem, it is not necessary for every claim to include limitations addressing all disclosed problems/solutions; a claim addressing only one disclosed solution can satisfy written description if the disclosure conveys possession of that claimed solution.
guidance: Revolution Eyewear and Crown Packaging examples: Claims directed to only one of several disclosed solutions (e.g., only the primary-frame magnetic solution; only the sloped chuck wall solution) were found to comply with written description where the spec supported that single solution.

name: Single-means claims are non-compliant with enablement (§112, ¶1) / combination requirement for §112, ¶6
description: A claim drafted as a single means-plus-function limitation with no other limitations (i.e., not an element in a claim for a combination) fails the combination requirement of §112, ¶6 and does not comply with the enablement requirement.
guidance: In re Hyatt: A 'single-means-claim' that embraces every conceivable structure for performing the function is not enabled because the specification only states those structures known to the inventor; means-plus-function limitations must be recited as an element in a combination to be proper under §112, ¶6.

name: For biological sequence claims, actual isolation/characterization may be required to show written description
description: For claims to DNA/proteins, merely describing the protein or antigen may be insufficient; the specification may need to disclose the nucleotide sequence or an isolation/characterization method to demonstrate possession of the claimed nucleic acid.
guidance: Fiers (interference context): Lack of actual isolation/sequencing (or adequate descriptive support) led to failure to prove conception/possession. In some cases disclosure of a well-characterized antigen can suffice if creation of antibodies is routine, but where it was not routine, more specific disclosure is required.

name: General principle: specification need not spell out every detail but must convince skilled artisan and enable without undue experimentation
description: The specification does not have to disclose every detail or every way to achieve the claimed result, but must include enough to convince one of ordinary skill that the inventor possessed the invention and taught how to make and use it across the full claimed scope without undue experimentation.
guidance: Repeated across cases: courts permit some breadth where reasonable extrapolation is routine, but will reject claims that claim all solutions to a problem when spec shows only one solution or that require significant additional inventive work to achieve other species.

name: Priority of invention — first inventor requirement
description: The applicant must establish that he was the first inventor of the claimed improvement; priority is decided by the evidence as to dates and acts of invention.
guidance: Evidence must carry the date of invention prior to the rival claim; testimony, depositions, and contemporaneous acts (reduction to practice, models, use) are evaluated to determine priority.

name: Allegations of surreptitious procurement or misconduct require supporting evidence
description: Charges that a patent was obtained surreptitiously or that evidence was suppressed must be supported by competent evidence; absent such proof, the allegations are disregarded.
guidance: Court will not accept speculative or unsupported accusations of wrongdoing; specific competent proof is required to sustain such claims.

name: Common ownership requirement
description: Actual ownership of the subject matter and the claimed invention by the same individual(s) or organization(s) or a legal obligation to assign both the subject matter and the claimed invention to the same individual(s) or organization(s)/business entity(ies) must be in existence at the time the claimed invention was made in order for the subject matter to be disqualified as prior art. A moral or unenforceable obligation would not evidence common ownership.
guidance: Includes illustrative examples (parent/subsidiary percentages, joint ventures, licenses). License to another does not necessarily make subject matter prior art if same person owned subject matter and invention at the time the invention was made. Common ownership is determined on the facts; an invention is 'made' when conception is complete (Pfaff v. Wells; Mergenthaler v. Scudder; In re Tansel). Common ownership at time of invention may be established irrespective of where invention was made (domestic or abroad).

name: Use of double patenting rejections among commonly owned applications
description: In appropriate circumstances, claims in commonly owned applications of different inventive entities may be rejected on the grounds of double patenting; such rejections can be overcome in appropriate circumstances by the filing of terminal disclaimers.
guidance: This practice prevents extending patent protection improperly while permitting legitimate benefits to inventors/assignees. Double patenting rejections may arise as a result of CREATE Act amendments and are authorized by case law (e.g., In re Bowers). See MPEP § 804 for guidance; terminal disclaimer per 37 CFR 1.321(d) can obviate double patenting rejections.

name: Substantive requirements to invoke CREATE Act safe harbor via JRA
description: To overcome a 35 U.S.C. 103(a) rejection based upon subject matter that qualifies as prior art only under 102(e),(f) or (g) via the CREATE Act, the applicant must: (1) provide a statement that the prior art and the claimed invention were made by or on behalf of parties to a JRA that was in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; and (2) state that the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the JRA.
guidance: The applicant must comply with statute and rules. The application must disclose or be amended to disclose the names of the parties to the JRA (37 CFR 1.71(g)(1)). The statement should be on or begin on a separate sheet and must not be directed to other matters (37 CFR 1.4(c)), and must be signed per 37 CFR 1.33(b). If the examiner disqualifies subject matter under 103(c), the examiner will treat the application and the 102(e)/(f)/(g) prior art as if commonly owned for purposes of 103(a).

name: Scope requirement for JRA safe harbor (activities within scope)
description: Even if a JRA existed prior to the later invention, the claimed invention must have been made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the JRA to qualify for disqualification of the prior art under 103(c).
guidance: Illustrative examples: (a) JRA effective after later invention — cannot invoke 103(c); (b) JRA in effect but limited to different activities/subject matter — cannot invoke 103(c) for inventions outside scope.

name: Content and placement requirements for the required JRA/ownership statement
description: The statement to invoke the prior art disqualification under CREATE must state that the prior art and the claimed invention were made by or on behalf of parties to a JRA that was in effect on or before the claimed invention date, and that the claimed invention was made as a result of activities within the scope of the JRA. The statement should either be on or begin on a separate sheet and must not be directed to other matters (37 CFR 1.4(c)).
guidance: The statement must be signed in accordance with 37 CFR 1.33(b). If the statement is filed in accordance with 103(c) and rules, the examiner will treat the application and the 102(e)/(f)/(g) prior art as commonly owned for 103(a) purposes. Submission remains subject to the rules of practice (37 CFR 1.116, 1.121, 1.312). If an amendment under 1.71(g) is used to disclose JRA parties to invoke safe harbor, timing and fee rules apply (see 1.71(g)(2)).

name: Broadest reasonable interpretation during examination
description: During examination, a claim must be given its broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification because the applicant can amend claims during prosecution and BRI reduces the possibility that an issued claim will be interpreted more broadly than justified.
guidance: Cites In re Yamamoto, In re Zletz, Buszard. Focus inquiry on what would be reasonable from the perspective of one of ordinary skill in the art. See MPEP § 2111 for full discussion. Examiners apply BRI in prosecution (different from post‑issuance court construction).

name: Plain meaning / ordinary and customary meaning of claim terms
description: Under BRI, words of the claim must be given their plain meaning—the ordinary and customary meaning given by those of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention—unless such meaning is inconsistent with the specification.
guidance: Sources evidencing ordinary meaning include the claims, specification, drawings, and prior art; the specification is the best source and may serve as a glossary. The presumption of ordinary meaning may be rebutted only by a clear and intentional special definition in the specification (In re Morris). Applicants may not add a special definition after filing (but may point to a definition already in the filed specification). See MPEP § 2111.01.

name: Determine whether a claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) / pre‑AIA 112 sixth paragraph
description: As part of claim interpretation, examiners should determine whether each limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (or pre‑AIA 112, sixth paragraph). If invoked, the limitation must be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.
guidance: See In re Donaldson Co., and MPEP § 2181 I for more information regarding determining invocation and corresponding structure for means‑ (or step‑) plus‑function claim limitations.

name: Understand difference between prosecution (BRI) and court claim construction
description: Patented claims are not given BRI during court proceedings; courts apply the Nautilus definiteness standard (claims must inform skilled artisans about scope with reasonable certainty). The Office construes claims using BRI to develop a clear prosecution record and to facilitate sharpening and clarifying claims.
guidance: Cite Packard, Morris, Zletz, Buszard. Applicant can amend claims or provide persuasive explanations/evidence to show clarity. Examiners should not conflate court standards with examination practice.

name: Threshold requirements of clarity and precision for definiteness
description: The examiner’s focus is whether the claim meets the statutory threshold requirements of clarity and precision in 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre‑AIA 112 second paragraph), not whether more suitable language exists.
guidance: Allow some latitude in expression provided statutory requirements are satisfied. If patentable subject matter is disclosed and claims define it with required particularity and distinctness, allow them. Examiners may suggest language improvements but should not insist on personal preferences.

name: Totality-of-the‑circumstances analysis: three primary considerations
description: Definiteness must be analyzed in light of: (A) the content of the particular application disclosure; (B) the teachings of the prior art; and (C) the claim interpretation that would be given by one possessing ordinary skill in the pertinent art at the time the invention was made.
guidance: The examiner must consider these factors together rather than in isolation when determining compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(b).

name: Consider the claim as a whole and the notice function
description: In reviewing a claim for compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(b), the examiner must consider the claim as a whole to determine whether it apprises one of ordinary skill in the art of its scope and serves the notice function required by the statute.
guidance: Cite Solomon v. Kimberly‑Clark and In re Larsen: the totality of claim limitations and their interactions determine what the inventor contributed; claims must notify the public what is within and outside patent protection.

name: Indefiniteness arises when more than one reasonable interpretation exists
description: If a person of ordinary skill, reading the claim (under BRI) in light of the specification, would read it with more than one reasonable interpretation, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre‑AIA 112 second paragraph) is appropriate.
guidance: Examiners cautioned not to confuse breadth with indefiniteness: a broad claim can be definite if its scope is clearly defined (genus vs unclear genus examples). See MPEP § 2173.05(h) for Markush issues.

name: Examiner must establish a clear record when asserting indefiniteness
description: When making a prima facie indefiniteness rejection, the examiner should clearly communicate in the Office action the specific findings and reasons supporting the rejection and avoid mere conclusory statements that the claim is indefinite.
guidance: See MPEP § 706.03 and § 707.07(g). Provide detailed explanation of why the term/phrase renders the metes and bounds unclear and, whenever practicable, indicate how the issue may be resolved. Examples and fact‑specific rationales appear in MPEP § 2173.05.

name: Office action must provide sufficient explanation to permit a meaningful response
description: The Office action should identify the specific term/phrase that is indefinite and explain why the metes and bounds are unclear so the applicant can meaningfully respond (explain/submit evidence or amend the claim).
guidance: If the applicant fails to adequately respond to the prima facie case, the examiner may make the indefiniteness rejection final (Packard). Cite Halliburton, Morton Intl. Examiners should point out specifics and suggest ways to resolve the indefiniteness where practicable. See MPEP § 707.07(d).

name: Specification should serve as a glossary; correspondence between specification and claims
description: The specification ideally serves as a glossary to claim terms; claim terms must find clear support or antecedent basis in the specification under 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1) so meaning is ascertainable by reference to the specification.
guidance: If the specification does not provide needed support/antecedent basis, object under 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1). Applicant may be required to amend the description to provide support (without introducing new matter) or amend the claim. See MPEP § 608.01(o) and § 2181 IV.

name: Conflict or inconsistency between claim and specification renders claim indefinite
description: A claim that is clear on its face may nonetheless be indefinite when a conflict or inconsistency with the specification disclosure renders the scope uncertain (internal inconsistency makes claim indefinite).
guidance: Cite In re Moore, In re Cohn, In re Hammack, In re Anderson examples where specification‑claim conflicts caused indefiniteness. No claim may be read independently of its supporting disclosure.

name: Breadth is not indefiniteness; address undue breadth under proper statutes
description: Breadth alone does not equal indefiniteness. A claim can be broad yet definite if its boundaries are clearly delineated. Undue breadth should be addressed under the statutory provision appropriate to the reason it is too broad.
guidance: If too broad because it does not set forth what inventor regards as the invention (evidence outside filed application) → reject under 35 U.S.C. 112(b). If too broad because not supported or enabling → reject under 35 U.S.C. 112(a). If too broad because it reads on prior art → reject under 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103.

name: New terminology must have apparent meaning from specification or prior art
description: The meaning of every term used in a claim should be apparent from the prior art or from the specification and drawings at filing. New terms are permitted but must be made clear and precise so metes and bounds are ascertainable.
guidance: When the specification states the intended meaning for a term, that meaning controls for examination (In re Zletz). Use MPEP § 2181 when new terms implicate means‑plus‑function issues.

name: Directed to a tangible medium
description: A Beauregard claim must be directed to a tangible medium (a computer-readable medium) rather than to abstract information alone.
guidance: Beauregard claims typically recite a floppy disk or CD-ROM as the computer-readable medium and are thus sometimes called 'floppy disk' claims. Framing the claim as an article of manufacture (the medium) is the core formal requirement of the Beauregard format.

name: Contain program instructions or other software-related content
description: The claimed medium must contain program instructions or other software-related content encoded on it.
guidance: Draft claims to explicitly recite that instructions, code, or software content are encoded on the medium so the claim is to the medium-with-instructions rather than to abstract information alone.

name: Comply with 35 U.S.C. § 112 requirements
description: Beauregard claims must be written in a way that complies with 35 U.S.C. § 112 (written description, enablement, and definiteness).
guidance: Ensure the claim language and the specification provide sufficient written description of the instructions and how they operate, enablement of the claimed invention, and definite claim scope to avoid §112 rejections.

name: Specify 'non-transitory' computer-readable media to avoid signal-based rejection
description: Claims should specify 'non-transitory' computer-readable media to avoid rejections based on signal or transitory embodiments.
guidance: Including the term 'non-transitory' in the claim preamble or recitation (e.g., 'a non-transitory computer-readable medium') helps avoid Nuijten-style rejections that treat transitory signals as unpatentable subject matter.

name: Avoid claims that are mere manipulation or reorganization of data
description: Claims that merely recite manipulation or reorganization of data are likely to be held patent-ineligible under Alice/CyberSource principles.
guidance: Do not rely solely on reciting data rearrangement or formatting; include technical improvements, inventive steps, or other aspects that demonstrate more than an abstract idea or mere data processing to strengthen eligibility arguments.

name: Recalibrated examination time assignment
description: An updated method of assigning examination time based on the application’s classification 'picture' and specific application attributes (including overall number of claims, length of the specification, and number of pages in any filed information disclosure statements).
guidance: Implemented FY20 to address time limitations and application complexity; USPTO data show this recalibration supports adequate examination time and improved quality (reflected in FY20→FY23 improvements).

name: Office action compliance rule (any claim error = action noncompliant)
description: When evaluating an Office action, if any single claim has an improper determination under any statute (e.g., an improper rejection was included or a proper rejection was omitted), then the entire Office action is identified as noncompliant.
guidance: If found noncompliant the finding is verified by an OPQA supervisor and sent to the relevant TC for consideration and any appropriate action; conversely, if all claims are treated correctly under every statute, the Office action is compliant.

name: Use of Master Review Form (MRF) to identify root causes
description: OPQA’s Master Review Form collects a plethora of root-cause reasons that drive statutory compliance and quality.
guidance: Focusing training on specific, actionable issues identified by the MRF (e.g., detailed mapping of claims to prior art) is more impactful than broad-topic training (e.g., anticipation/obviousness).

name: Effect of recording: limitations and Office determination (37 CFR 3.54)
description: Recording under § 3.11 is not a determination of the validity of the document or its effect on title; the Office will determine effect when necessary, including whether a party has authority to act in a pending matter.
guidance: This serves as notification that recordation preserves a history of claimed interests but does not itself adjudicate title questions.

name: Evidentiary/discovery complaints must be specific and timely
description: Claims that testimony or exhibits should have been stricken because documents were not provided are inadequate if the complaining party neither requested the documents in discovery nor identifies the specific missing documents.
guidance: When asserting discovery-based error, specify which document(s) were not produced, show that they were material, and explain why they could not have been obtained earlier despite due diligence.

name: Written description requirement (Form ¶ 7.31.01)
description: Claim(s) rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre‑AIA 112, first paragraph, as failing to comply with the written description requirement because the claim contains subject matter which was not described in the specification in such a way as to reasonably convey to one skilled in the art that the inventor(s) had possession of the claimed invention at the time the application was filed.
guidance: This rejection must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.01 or 7.103. In the office action identify (by suitable reference to page and line numbers and/or drawing figures) the subject matter not properly described in the application and provide an explanation of the position. The explanation should include any questions the examiner asked which were not satisfactorily resolved and which raise doubt as to possession of the claimed invention at filing.

name: Enablement requirement (Form ¶ 7.31.02)
description: Claim(s) rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre‑AIA 112, first paragraph, as failing to comply with the enablement requirement because the claim contains subject matter which was not described in the specification in such a way as to enable one skilled in the art to make and/or use the invention.
guidance: This rejection must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.01 or 7.103. If the problem is one of claim scope, use form paragraph 7.31.03. In the office action identify the claimed subject matter for which the specification is not enabling and explain why the specification is not enabling, applying the factors set forth in In re Wands, 858 F.2d 731, 737, 8 USPQ2d 1400, 1404 (Fed. Cir. 1998) as appropriate. The explanation should include any outstanding examiner questions that were not satisfactorily resolved and that raise doubt as to enablement. Where an essential component or step is not recited in the claims, use form paragraph 7.33.01.

name: Scope of enablement / commensurateness (Form ¶ 7.31.03)
description: Claim(s) rejected because the specification, while being enabling for some identified subject matter, does not reasonably provide enablement for other identified subject matter — i.e., the specification does not enable the invention commensurate in scope with the claims.
guidance: This rejection must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.01 or 7.103. Use when the scope of the claims is not commensurate with the scope of the enabling disclosure. In the office action identify the claimed subject matter for which the specification is enabling (by reference to specific portions of the specification) and identify the aspects of the claim(s) for which the specification is not enabling. State which portion(s) of the statutory enablement requirement are implicated (make/use/make and use) and explain why the specification is not enabling, applying In re Wands factors and including any unanswered examiner questions that raise doubt.

name: Scope of enablement for a single means (means‑plus‑function) claim (Form ¶ 7.31.05)
description: Claim(s) rejected because the claim purports to invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre‑AIA 112 sixth paragraph) but fails to recite a combination of elements as required, so it cannot rely on the specification to provide structure/material/acts to support the claimed function; the claim thus recites a function with no limits and covers every conceivable means while the specification discloses at most those means known to the inventor.
guidance: This rejection must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.01 or 7.103. Use only when the claim recites a single element and that element is in means‑plus‑function format; this situation should be rare. The disclosure is not commensurate with the scope of the claim when only inventor‑known means are disclosed but the claim covers all conceivable means for the function.

name: Essential subject matter missing from claims (Enablement) (Form ¶ 7.33.01)
description: Claim(s) rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre‑AIA 112, first paragraph, as based on a disclosure which is not enabling because the disclosure does not enable one of ordinary skill in the art to practice the invention without specified material/step/feature that is critical or essential to the practice of the invention but not included in the claim(s).
guidance: This rejection must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.01 or 7.103. In the office action recite the subject matter omitted from the claims and give the rationale for considering the omitted subject matter critical or essential. The examiner shall cite the statement, argument, date, drawing, or other evidence demonstrating that a particular feature was considered essential by the applicant and is not reflected in the rejected claims. See In re Mayhew, 527 F.2d 1229, 188 USPQ 356 (CCPA 1976).

name: Procedural requirements for form‑paragraph use and office action content
description: Various form paragraphs (e.g., 7.30.01, 7.103, 7.31.01–7.31.05, 7.33.01) must be used in specified sequences and with particular content requirements (e.g., identification of claim numbers, references to pages/lines/figures, insertion of bases and explanations).
guidance: Specific procedural notes include: the statutory paragraph is only required in first actions on the merits and final rejections; form paragraphs 7.30.01 and 7.30.02 are to be used only once in an Office action; rejections under the written description/enablement provisions must be preceded by 7.30.01 or 7.103; bracketed placeholders in form paragraphs must be filled appropriately (pluralize 'Claim' if necessary, insert claim numbers, insert basis/evidence in bracketed spots); identify and explain subject matter deficiencies with suitable page/line/figure references; indicate any unanswered examiner questions that led to doubt. Where the problem implicates other MPEP sections (e.g., essential components, means‑plus‑function, best mode), use the corresponding form paragraph (e.g., 7.33.01 for missing essential subject matter).

name: Payment of required fees
description: The processing fee set forth in 37 CFR 1.17(i), the prioritized examination fee set forth in 37 CFR 1.17(c), and if not already paid, the publication fee set forth in 37 CFR 1.18(d) have been filed with the request. The basic filing fee, search fee, examination fee, and any required excess claims and application size fees are filed with the request or have been already been paid.
guidance: All applicable fees must accompany the Track One request (or have already been paid). References to specific fee provisions: 37 CFR 1.17(i) (processing fee), 1.17(c) (prioritized examination fee), and 1.18(d) (publication fee). Ensure excess-claim and application-size fees are paid where required.

name: Focus on whether a skilled person can read and understand the data (functional disclosure standard)
description: If the purpose of data is to demonstrate the plausibility of a claimed effect, what matters is whether a skilled person would be able to read and understand the data.
guidance: This is a functional perspective suggesting that formal compliance should not override the substantive requirement of enabling and disclosing sufficient information. It is offered as an argument for rethinking rigid formal drawing rules for scientific data.

name: Patent-Eligible Subject Matter (35 U.S.C. §101; Alice/Mayo two-step)
description: What standard determines whether a patent claim is “directed to” a patent-ineligible concept under step 1 of the Supreme Court’s two-step Alice/Mayo framework; and whether patent eligibility (at each step of the Alice/Mayo framework) is a question of law for the court based on the scope of the claims or a question of fact for the jury based on the state of the art at the time of the patent.
guidance: Apply the Alice/Mayo two-step: (1) determine whether the claim is "directed to" a patent-ineligible concept (e.g., natural law); (2) if so, determine whether the claim recites an "inventive concept" sufficient to transform the ineligible concept into patent-eligible subject matter. Courts may treat the two steps differently (majority in American Axle found claims directed to Hooke’s law at step one and lacking an inventive concept at step two). Debates include whether courts improperly conflate enablement/§112 with §101, and whether eligibility is a pure question of law or involves factual inquiries (jury). The article notes splits at the Federal Circuit and Solicitor General interest (CVSG). Example/anti-pattern: treating §101 as a substitute for enablement leads to criticism that the court applied a "Nothing More" test that effectively imports §112 into §101.

name: Means-Plus-Function Claiming (§112(f))
description: Two-step means-plus-function analysis: (1) determine whether a claim limitation is drafted in means-plus-function format; (2) if yes, determine what structure, if any, the specification discloses corresponding to the claimed function.
guidance: For step one, consider presence of the word "means," whether the term would be understood by a person having ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA) as the name for a structure, intrinsic evidence (claims, prosecution history), and extrinsic evidence (dictionaries, expert testimony). If claim does not recite "means," the challenger bears the burden (preponderance of the evidence) to show the limitation fails to recite sufficiently definite structure. A class of structures may suffice (single specific structure not required). Examples from Federal Circuit precedent: "circuit" can connote structure; "user identification module" may not. For software terms (e.g., "code"/"application"), structure may be defined in part by function and by reference to algorithms—absence of algorithmic disclosure can render a claim indefinite. In Dyfan v. Target the court looked to expert testimony and claim context to conclude "code"/"application" connote structure and the "system" limitation was defined by the claim language.

name: Written Description / Corresponding-Structure Requirement (35 U.S.C. §112)
description: Specification must disclose corresponding structure for functional claim elements (including means-plus-function claims); failure to disclose corresponding structure or algorithm (for software-implemented functions) can render claims indefinite under §112(b) or otherwise fail written description/enablement.
guidance: When §112(f) applies, courts examine whether the specification provides adequate corresponding structure (for software, algorithms are often the required structure). District court in Dyfan found no algorithm and held claims indefinite; Federal Circuit reversed on step one but highlighted that absence of corresponding structure is a separate problem. The article highlights the interplay and potential confusion between §112 (enablement/written description) and §101 analyses, including criticisms that courts may incorrectly collapse these requirements.

name: Appellate Review of Patent Jury Verdicts and Claim Construction (O2 Micro duty; Seventh Amendment limits)
description: Whether an appellate court may reverse a jury verdict by sua sponte adopting a new claim construction where the district court declined to construe the term (treating it as plain and ordinary meaning) and the jury resolved infringement facts; and the duty of a district court to resolve fundamental claim term disputes (O2 Micro).
guidance: When parties present a fundamental dispute about claim scope, O2 Micro requires the court to construe the term rather than leaving it to the jury; appellate courts must be cautious about recasting factual issues as claim construction issues post hoc. Olaf Sööt Design v. Daktronics exemplifies the issue where the Federal Circuit's sua sponte construction recast a jury factual finding as a legal issue, leading to reversal. Guidance: ensure district courts resolve claim term disputes to avoid improper jury submissions; appellate reversal based on new constructions risks Seventh Amendment concerns if it effectively supplants the jury's factfinding.

name: Statutory Limits on Inter Partes Review (AIA §311(b))
description: A petitioner in an inter partes review may request cancellation of claims only on grounds that could be raised under §102 or §103 and only on the basis of prior art consisting of patents or printed publications.
guidance: IPR petitions must be grounded solely on novelty/obviousness under §§102/103 and rely only on patents/printed publications as prior art; other grounds or types of evidence are outside the statutory scope. This statutory constraint frames what the PTAB may consider and what expert testimony may legitimately interpret. Practitioners should ensure challenges are framed within these statutory boundaries.

name: Claim Construction and Related Doctrines (prosecution disclaimer; effect on damages; grammar of claims)
description: Various claim-construction principles affecting infringement, damages, and related evidentiary rulings: prosecution disclaimer's effect on limiting claim scope; how claim construction can affect damages calculations and admissibility of expert testimony on damages; and textual/grammatical issues (e.g., construing "and" to mean "or").
guidance: Claim construction can have cascading effects beyond infringement: it can trigger prosecution disclaimer, alter damages assessments, and affect what expert testimony is admissible. The article cites cases addressing prosecution disclaimer, the effect of claim construction on damages and expert admissibility (Apple v. Wi-LAN), and interpretive choices like reading "and" as "or" (Michael Kaufman v. Microsoft). Guidance: analyze intrinsic evidence/prosecution history for disclaimer; anticipate how narrowing or broadening constructions influence damages and expert opinions; be mindful that ordinary grammatical cues may be overridden by technical context or prosecution history.

name: Novelty
description: Requirement that the claimed subject-matter is new over the state of the art.
guidance: Standards and tests to determine novelty, including direct and implicit disclosure analyses.

name: Allowability of amendments – Art. 123(2) and (3)
description: Substantive test for amendments: no added subject-matter (Art.123(2)) and no extension of protection (Art.123(3)).
guidance: Detailed guidance on assessing added matter and whether amended claims extend the scope of protection post‑grant.

name: Technology tutorials (submitted or recorded)
description: Courts may require or encourage a technology tutorial to provide context about highly technical or unfamiliar terms and issues.
guidance: Benefits: (a) may help focus issues and force the parties to avoid extraneous material; (b) can reduce the time needed for claim construction; and (c) gives both parties an equal chance to have the last word. Recorded tutorials can be provided to new judicial clerks and can be part of the appellate record. Tutorials set the stage for argument and may be especially useful before Markman hearings.

name: Patent and claim winnowing (Model Order phased limits)
description: Use a phased process to limit the number of asserted claims and prior art presented, reducing complexity and litigation costs.
guidance: Model Order specifics: Not later than 40 days after the accused infringer produces documents showing operation of accused instrumentalities, plaintiff must serve a Preliminary Election of Asserted Claims asserting no more than ten claims per patent and no more than 32 total claims. Not later than 28 days after the Court issues its Claim Construction Order, plaintiff must serve a Final Election identifying no more than five asserted claims per patent (from the ten) and no more than 16 total claims. The Model Order permits relaxation when only one patent is asserted (increase per-patent limits by 50%, rounding up). Courts may allow adding claims that present unique issues as to liability or damages. Parties encouraged to discuss lower limits based on case-specific factors (commonality among patents, number/diversity of accused products, technology complexity, claim complexity, and other issues).

name: Step-wise limitation of asserted claims across stages
description: Limit asserted claims at multiple stages (before claim construction, after claim construction, and before trial) to allow refinement of theories as the case progresses.
guidance: A step-wise approach lets plaintiffs refine theories through discovery, claim construction, and dispositive motions. Some courts impose initial limits, then further limits after claim construction and before trial; the process should allow plaintiffs opportunity to add claims presenting unique liability or damages issues and should be flexible rather than immutable.

name: Adopt and apply Patent Local Rules (PLRs) to structure claim-construction process
description: Patent-specific local rules establish a standardized timeline and framework for disclosures and submissions leading up to claim construction (Markman) proceedings.
guidance: Purpose: to present the court with a limited set of meaningful disputes, require early notice of infringement and invalidity contentions, counter 'shifting sands' litigation tactics, crystallize theories early, and set natural boundaries for discovery. PLRs typically require early, relatively specific contentions and may set presumptive limits (e.g., number of terms to be construed). PLRs are presumptive and judges may modify them for good cause, but modifications must be consistent with Federal Circuit case law when issues are unique to patent law.

name: Follow a standardized PLR timetable for disclosures and briefing
description: Use a structured schedule for case-management conference, asserted-claims disclosures, invalidity contentions, identification of claim terms, preliminary constructions, joint statements, discovery close, and claim-construction briefing/hearing.
guidance: Typical Northern District of California timetable (example): (1) CMC set by court; (2) Disclosure of Asserted Claims/Infringement Contentions within 10 days of CMC; (3) Invalidity Contentions within 45 days of (2); (4) Identify Claim Terms to be Constr. within 10 days of (3); (5) Preliminary Claim Constructions within 20 days of (4); (6) Joint Claim-Construction Statement within 60 days of (3); (7) Close of Claim-Construction Discovery within 30 days of (6); opening, responsive, reply briefs and Markman hearing spaced with specified day-intervals. Courts may adapt timetable depending on complexity.

name: Adopt an accelerated timeline when appropriate
description: Use a streamlined schedule for less complex cases or when parties jointly agree, potentially eliminating patent-specific initial disclosures and a separate Markman hearing.
guidance: Example accelerated timeline (‘Track B’): produce opinion of counsel within two months after CMC; close fact and expert discovery on accelerated calendar; combine claim-construction and summary-judgment briefs and hearings within compressed intervals (e.g., 5 months after CMC for opening briefs). Decision to accelerate should follow discussion of substantive issues driving the case (technology simplicity, little dispute about structure/function of accused devices).

name: Limit number of claim terms at the Markman hearing (typically ten)
description: Presumptively restrict the number of claim terms presented for construction at the principal Markman hearing to focus on the most significant terms.
guidance: Many courts set a default ten-term limit (parties jointly identify ten terms likely to be most significant, including those that may be case- or claim-dispositive). Courts may require parties to explain why particular terms are significant. The limit can be increased or decreased for good cause; additional terms can be sought in later phases. The ten-term limit avoids peripheral disputes and focuses the court on key issues.

name: Structure claim-construction briefing and oral argument with judge-managed procedures
description: Use joint claim-construction statements, technology tutorials, focused briefing, and (where helpful) hearings combining counsel argument and, rarely, witness testimony; exercise broad judicial discretion to manage timing and process.
guidance: Some courts allow parties to let terms emerge in briefing; others require joint statements. The judge should consider interrelation of claim construction with discovery, summary judgment, and settlement. Courts decide whether to hold a hearing based on whether it will be helpful (e.g., divergent expert perspectives). Practices vary by district and judge; the court’s decisions should promote focused, efficient resolution of claim-meaning disputes.

name: Primacy of intrinsic evidence with controlled use of extrinsic evidence under Teva
description: Claim construction should be grounded in intrinsic evidence (patent document and prosecution history); Teva allows district courts to make subsidiary factual findings based on extrinsic evidence when necessary, but intrinsic evidence prevails where it diverges from extrinsic evidence.
guidance: Teva endorses a hybrid review: subsidiary factual findings are subject to 'clearly erroneous' review while ultimate claim-construction decisions receive de novo appellate review. Where extrinsic evidence is needed, the court should: (1) delineate disputed subsidiary factual questions prior to Markman; (2) conduct focused briefing with supporting expert declarations and evidentiary hearings to create an adequate record; and (3) prepare a careful Markman order explaining the basis for the construction. Courts must exercise due caution in entertaining extrinsic evidence to avoid waste and escalate expert battles.

name: Manage expert testimony and extrinsic evidence for claim construction
description: Early identification and careful management of expert evidence is recommended, with options to limit or structure expert proceedings to prevent unnecessary cost and delay.
guidance: Courts should ask parties early whether they intend to rely on expert testimony and the substance thereof. If fact-finding is planned, focused expert declarations and evidentiary hearings may be used. Court may employ the 'hot tub' method (direct engagement among experts and judge) to sharpen issues and assess credibility. For non-technical/common terms, expert testimony may be less useful and can be limited or disallowed. Judges should weigh the likely benefit against potential for escalating expert battles.

name: Phase discovery in relation to claim construction
description: Tailor fact and expert discovery timing to the needs of claim construction: allow targeted pre-construction discovery about accused products when necessary, but limit discovery on unrelated issues until after claim construction.
guidance: Although claim construction is based on intrinsic evidence, knowledge of accused product structure/function and relevant prior art often informs which claim terms need construction. Many PLRs expressly provide for discovery prior to claim construction, including mandated early disclosures of infringement and invalidity contentions. Courts should discuss potential limits or phasing of pre-claim-construction discovery to avoid wasting resources on damages, willfulness, or other matters that claim construction may render unnecessary. When claim construction is conducted after fact discovery, standard written discovery can be more feasible.

name: Provide post-claim-construction fact and expert discovery as warranted
description: After a claim-construction order, permit additional fact and expert discovery to address issues implicated by the court’s constructions.
guidance: Claim-construction orders may reveal previously uninvestigated features of accused devices; courts commonly set fact discovery to proceed for a period after construction. Inventor depositions for Markman purposes may be initially limited to claim-construction topics, with broader depositions allowed after the Markman process. Expert discovery similarly may follow claim construction to address newly implicated issues.

name: Unity of subject-matter required
description: A patent must possess unity of subject-matter as required by statute; separate distinct inventions should not be claimed together.
guidance: Discusses how unity is determined, treatment of two distinct inventions, several improvements, joint inventions, and consistency with combinations (Index entries: "UNITY" and related sections).

name: Specification must distinguish old from new
description: The specification must distinguish what is old in the art from what is new in the inventor's contribution.
guidance: Guidance on how to describe what is old and what is novel; avoid claiming what is not original and do not mislead the public about novelty (see 'must distinguish what is old from what is new').

name: State the best mode of producing the effect
description: The specification should state the best mode known to the patentee of producing the claimed effect.
guidance: Multiple references (e.g., 'to state the best mode of producing an effect') stress disclosure of the best or preferred method to practise the invention; failure may be ground to invalidate or limit the patent.

name: Amendments & disclaimers allowed by statute
description: Amendments to specifications and disclaimers are permitted by statute under specified conditions.
guidance: Includes statutory processes for amendment and use of disclaimers to narrow claims; procedural guidance and common defects related to amendments are discussed (see 'amendments of, allowed by statute' and 'by disclaimers').

name: Must not claim purely inchoate ideas or elementary principles
description: An inchoate idea, elementary principle, or a discovery in pure science unconnected to practical application is not patentable.
guidance: The treatise gives examples and doctrinal reasoning distinguishing scientific discovery from patentable practical application (see 'cannot be an inchoate idea', 'an elementary principle', 'a science').

name: Claims should be construed in light of the specification and prosecution history
description: Claims should be construed in light of the specification and prosecution history.
guidance: This principle ensures that claims are interpreted in the context of the patent as a whole; see Phillips v. AWH Corp. for emphasis on using specification and prosecution history in claim construction.

name: Different claims should have different scopes
description: Different claims should have different scopes.
guidance: Core statement of claim differentiation: the doctrine prevents treating distinct claims as duplicative in scope; useful both in construction and in drafting to avoid redundancy across claim sets.

name: Narrower claims should not be interpreted so broadly that they encompass the same scope as broader claims
description: Narrower claims should not be interpreted so broadly that they encompass the same scope as broader claims.
guidance: Avoid construing dependent or narrower claims in a way that renders broader claims redundant; such overbroad interpretations can be rejected by courts and may undermine infringement or validity positions.

name: Doctrine is a guideline, not a hard-and-fast rule (case-by-case application)
description: The doctrine is not a hard and fast rule, but rather a guideline that can be applied on a case-by-case basis.
guidance: Courts apply claim differentiation flexibly; litigators should treat the doctrine as a rebuttable presumption rather than an absolute limit. Be ready to show why a particular claim should or should not be differentiated given the specification and prosecution history.

name: Claim construction should consider claim language, specification, and prosecution history
description: The court should consider the language of the claims, the specification, and the prosecution history when construing claims.
guidance: Follow a structured claim construction process: start with the claim language, consult the specification for context, and review prosecution history for disclaimers or amendments that inform scope. The doctrine of claim differentiation is one factor in this multi-part analysis.

name: Infringement analysis must account for differences between claims and the accused product/process
description: Infringement analysis should take into account the differences between the claims and the accused product or process.
guidance: After claim construction, compare each claim element to the accused product or process. Pay attention to distinctions between claims (e.g., element presence/absence or narrower limitations) when assessing infringement.

name: Overbroad interpretation of narrower claims can affect validity (novelty/obviousness)
description: If a narrower claim is interpreted too broadly, it may be found to be invalid for lack of novelty or obviousness.
guidance: Overbroad construction may expose claims to prior art or obviousness attacks. Use claim differentiation to argue for a narrower construction to preserve validity, or conversely, assert that a broad interpretation undermines novelty/obviousness if defending against enforcement.

name: Doctrine can support §112 challenges (clarity/definiteness)
description: The doctrine can be used to argue that a patent is invalid for failing to meet the requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112, which requires that claims be clear and definite.
guidance: Argue that if claim scope is ambiguous or overlaps improperly with other claims, the claim may fail the definiteness or written-description/enablement aspects of §112. Use specification and prosecution history to show lack of clear scope.

name: Drafting — use clear and concise language in claims
description: Use clear and concise language when drafting claims.
guidance: Clarity in claim drafting reduces later contention over scope and helps prevent problematic overlap between claims. Prefer precise terms and avoid unnecessary ambiguity that could invite adverse claim-differentiation or §112 arguments.

name: Drafting — ensure different claims have different scopes and consider differentiation during prosecution
description: Ensure that different claims have different scopes. Consider the doctrine of claim differentiation when amending claims during prosecution.
guidance: When drafting and amending claims, deliberately craft varying scopes among independent and dependent claims. During prosecution, anticipate that narrowing amendments or statements may create differentiation consequences; plan claim sets and remarks to minimize unintended scope concessions.

name: Practical litigation strategy: use the doctrine to argue for narrower interpretations and prepare counterarguments
description: Use the doctrine to argue for a narrower interpretation of claims that are at risk of being invalidated or found not to be infringed. Be prepared to address potential counterarguments based on the doctrine.
guidance: Practical steps: (1) Carefully analyze claims, specification, and prosecution history to understand scope; (2) identify opportunities in the claim set to press differentiation arguments that favor your client; (3) anticipate opposing uses of the doctrine and assemble evidence from the intrinsic record to rebut them.

name: Relevant precedents shaping claim-differentiation analysis (Tandon; Phillips)
description: Key cases: Tandon v. ITC (1985) held that claim differentiation precluded a broad interpretation of a narrower claim that would render a broader claim redundant. Phillips v. AWH Corp. (2005) emphasized construing claims in light of the specification and prosecution history.
guidance: Cite and distinguish these precedents when arguing claim-differentiation points. Use Phillips for the central role of intrinsic evidence and Tandon as an example where differentiation prevailed; examine subsequent Federal Circuit/SCOTUS decisions for refinements.

name: Mathematical/set-theoretic representation of claim scopes (proper subset)
description: The doctrine can be represented mathematically: Scope of Claim A ⊆ Scope of Claim B, and the doctrine requires Scope of Claim A ⊂ Scope of Claim B (proper subset).
guidance: This formalization underscores that a dependent or narrower claim should not be coextensive with a broader claim. Use this conceptual model when explaining differentiation, but remember courts apply contextual legal analysis rather than pure set theory.

name: Obviousness-type double patenting (OTDP) doctrine
description: OTDP (nonstatutory double patenting) prohibits acquiring a second patent on an invention that is an obvious variation on one of the inventor's earlier patents; when later claims are obvious in light of an earlier patent, the second patent is not 'patentably distinct' and is invalid.
guidance: OTDP was developed by courts to prevent evasion of statutory double patenting via slightly varied claim drafting; an OTDP rejection can be overcome via a terminal disclaimer (in contrast to statutory double patenting).

name: Distinction between statutory double patenting and OTDP
description: Statutory double patenting (derived from Section 101) absolutely prohibits a second patent claiming the same invention; OTDP addresses obvious variants not identical inventions.
guidance: Statutory double patenting cannot be cured by a terminal disclaimer, whereas OTDP rejections historically can be obviated by filing a terminal disclaimer.

name: Procedural choices when facing OTDP rejection
description: When an examiner rejects claims based on OTDP, the applicant can either (1) contest the OTDP rejection on its merits (e.g., argue patentable distinctness or amend claims), or (2) avoid the issue via a terminal disclaimer.
guidance: Using a terminal disclaimer sidesteps substantive litigation with the PTO over obviousness but costs a shortened patent term; contesting the rejection may preserve term but can be more burdensome and costly.

name: Use of terminal disclaimers in continuing applications (parent/child relationships)
description: Continuing applications (continuations, CIPs, divisionals) that claim priority to an earlier application can give rise to child patents that have terminal disclaimers so they expire at the same time as the parent patent.
guidance: Terminal disclaimers are often used to align expiration dates among related family members and avoid OTDP rejections in the continuing-application context.

name: Historical judicial justification for terminal disclaimers
description: CCPA decisions from the 1960s held that a terminal disclaimer causing two patents to expire together is 'tantamount ... to having all the claims in one patent' and thus forecloses extension of monopoly, which justified their use to obviate OTDP.
guidance: The Federal Circuit adopted these CCPA holdings; courts have treated terminal disclaimers as a permissible cure for OTDP based on public-policy rationales about preventing extended monopoly.

name: USPTO NPRM proposed enforceability condition (May 2024)
description: USPTO proposed requiring applicants using a terminal disclaimer to agree that enforceability of any disclaimed patent depends on the validity of any patent tied to the disclaimed patent through a terminal disclaimer—if any claim of the referenced patent is held unpatentable or invalid on certain grounds by final decision, the disclaimed patent cannot be enforced.
guidance: The proposal would tie the validity/enforceability of the disclaimed patent to referenced patents (including indirect ties through intermediate patents) so that patents tied by terminal disclaimers would 'stand and fall together' in practice.

name: Scope of NPRM's proposed rule (indirect ties and unidirectionality)
description: The proposed rule would apply when a disclaimed patent is tied indirectly through 'multiple intermediate patents/applications'; it would be 'unidirectional'—the condition applies only to the disclaimed patent and not to referenced patents lacking a terminal disclaimer.
guidance: Example: patent Z tied to Y which is tied to X would be unenforceable if a claim of X is invalidated; conversely, invalidating Z would not affect Y or X under the proposed rule.

name: Alternative RFC proposals (stipulation/admission of obviousness)
description: USPTO's earlier RFC proposed options like requiring applicants to stipulate that claims are not patentably distinct as a condition of filing a terminal disclaimer, or treating the terminal disclaimer as an admission of obviousness so that a family tied by disclaimers would stand or fall together.
guidance: Some argued these approaches conflicted with case law (e.g., SimpleAir v. Google holding a terminal disclaimer is not an admission of obviousness), raising questions about USPTO's regulatory authority to require such stipulations.

name: Policy considerations for and against changing terminal disclaimer practice
description: Proponents argue proposed rule would promote competition, lower cost of challenging groups of patents tied by terminal disclaimers, reduce patent thickets, and improve patent quality; opponents argue USPTO may lack authority, the rule departs from independent-claim validity, will increase prosecution costs, and could harm small inventors.
guidance: Stakeholders (FDA, USPTO, former USPTO leaders, members of Congress) provided competing empirical and policy arguments; the comment period closed with many comments opposing the NPRM.

name: International filing date: conditions for accord
description: The receiving Office shall accord as the international filing date the date of receipt of the international application, provided that at the time of receipt certain requirements under PCT Article 11(1) were satisfied.
guidance: Requirements include at least one applicant being a resident or national of the receiving Office's State, prescribed language, indication that it is intended as an international application, designation of at least one Contracting State, applicant name, a part appearing to be a description, and a part appearing to be a claim. If requirements are not satisfied on initial receipt, applicant is invited to correct within a set time; the filing date becomes the date of the timely correction. If correction not timely made, the RO will notify the applicant that the application is not an international application. If corrections are completely contained in an earlier application (with priority claim and proper incorporation), the initial receipt date may be retained. (See PCT Art. 11, PCT Rules 4.18, 20.3–20.6, 20.4.)

name: Order and numbering of parts and sheets
