description: The elements of the international application are to be arranged in the order: request, description (other than any sequence listing part), claims, abstract, drawings, and sequence listing part (if applicable). All sheets must be numbered in consecutive Arabic numerals using separate series: first series for the request; second for description, claims and abstract; third for drawings; further series for sequence listing.
guidance: Use separate numbering series for different parts (PCT Rule 11.7 and Administrative Instructions Section 207(b)). Only one copy need be filed in the U.S. Receiving Office. Improper order or numbering may be corrected but following the prescribed order aids processing.

name: Description sufficiency (enablement / disclosure)
description: The description shall disclose the invention in a manner sufficiently clear and complete for the invention to be carried out by a person skilled in the art. (PCT Article 5.)
guidance: The description should disclose the invention as claimed so that the technical problem and its solution can be understood and state advantageous effects relative to background art. It should set forth at least the best mode contemplated (where applicable) and indicate how the invention is capable of exploitation in industry and how it can be made and used (or only used if applicable).

name: Best mode disclosure
description: The description shall set forth at least the best mode contemplated by the applicant for carrying out the invention claimed; this shall be done in terms of examples, where appropriate, and with reference to the drawings, if any. (PCT Rule 5.1(a)(v)).
guidance: Where the national law of a designated State does not require best mode, failure to describe the best mode contemplated shall have no effect in that State. The MPEP notes that best mode should be presented in examples and with reference to drawings where applicable.

name: Publication timing for ARIPO utility model application
description: The ARIPO utility model application shall be published as soon as possible—(a) after the expiry of a period of 18 months from the date of filing or, if priority has been claimed, from the date of priority; or (b) at the request of the applicant, before the expiry of the 18-month period and subject to the payment of the prescribed fee.
guidance: If the decision to register the utility model becomes effective before the expiry of the 18-month period, the application shall be published at the same time as the specification. For priority claims, the 18 months is calculated from the original filing date (or earliest priority date if multiple claims).

name: Request for limitation (post-grant amendment) filing and fee
description: At the request of the proprietor, the ARIPO patent or utility model may be limited by an amendment; the request shall be filed in accordance with Implementing Regulations and shall not be deemed filed until the limitation fee has been paid.
guidance: Any amendment to the claims must fall wholly within the scope of the claims before the amendment.

name: Formulation of medical indication/use claims
description: Claims related to medical indications or use claims shall, for the purpose of examination, be drafted in accordance with standard phrases provided (examples include: 'Pharmaceutical composition for the prophylaxis/treatment of Y comprising X', 'Compound X for use as a drug/medicament for the treatment of Y', 'Use of X for the manufacture of a pharmaceutical composition', etc.).
guidance: Distinct sets of standard formulations are provided for first medical indications and second medical indications (e.g., 'Use of X for the manufacture of a medicament for treatment of Y'). Use these standard phrasings in drafting to comply with ARIPO examination practice.

name: Specification absence or ambiguity (uncertainty / indefiniteness)
description: The defendant may show that there is no specification, or that the specification is so ambiguous and unintelligible that the court cannot determine from it what the invention is intended to be patented; in such case the patent is void for ambiguity.
guidance: This is a distinct issue from statutory special matters and can be put in issue by a plea of not guilty; the specification must enable the court and the public to ascertain what is claimed with reasonable certainty.

name: Distinguish new from old; claims must appear with reasonable certainty
description: The patentee must describe, in full and exact terms, what his invention consists of and distinguish what is new from what is old; what is claimed as new must appear with reasonable certainty on the face of the patent, either expressly or by necessary implication.
guidance: If the specification mixes up old and new, or leaves the scope of what is claimed to minute references and conjecture, the patent is void; courts look for reasonable certainty in the claimed subject-matter.

name: Statutory provisos limiting prior-use attack and equitable relief on overbroad claims
description: Provisos: (1) if it satisfactorily appears that the patentee, at the time of application, believed himself to be the first inventor, the patent shall not be held void because of prior foreign use, unless the subject had been previously patented or described in printed publication; (2) if plaintiff fails because his specification/claim embraces more than he invented, but the defendant has used any part truly specified and claimed as new, the court may adjudge costs as just and equitable.
guidance: These provisos moderate the harshness of a strict prior-use/anticipation rule and permit equitable allocation of costs when part of a claim is genuinely new and infringed.

name: Integrate patent attorney oversight early
description: Have a patent attorney review drawings before filing to ensure they comply with rules and actually support the claims and enforcement strategy.
guidance: Attorneys can flag technical issues beyond formatting—e.g., whether the drawings adequately support claim scope. Early review avoids costly corrections, office actions, and can improve enforceability.

name: Recognize business impact of compliant drawings
description: Compliant, professional drawings reduce office actions, speed approvals, and improve credibility with investors and in litigation contexts.
guidance: Treat drawings as strategic assets: first-time acceptance saves time and money, protects filing dates, and reduces risk that unclear drawings will weaken claim scope or invite challenges.

name: Table of contents for amendment sections (section pagination)
description: Amendments to the Specification begin on page 2 of this paper.  Amendments to the Claims are reflected in the listing of claims which begins on page 3 of this paper.  Amendments to the Drawings begin on page 4 of this paper and include both an attached replacement sheet and an annotated sheet showing changes.  Remarks/Arguments begin on page 5 of this paper.  An Appendix including amended drawing figures is attached following page 5 of this paper.
guidance: Provide a clear table-of-contents-like notice at the front of the amendment indicating on which page each amendment category (specification, claims, drawings, remarks/arguments, appendix/attachments) begins and note attached replacement/annotated sheets.

name: Remarks/Arguments must explain nature and basis of amendments
description: In the specification, the paragraphs [0021] and [0045] have been amended to correct minor editorial problems.  The new paragraph [0075.1] added after paragraph [0075] discusses in general terms the features taken from Example 4.  In amended Figure 2, the previously omitted element numeral 13 has been added.  Claims 6-10 and 12-13 remain in this application.  Claims 1-5 and 11 have been canceled.  Claims 7 and 8 have been withdrawn.  The examiner has acknowledged that claims 6 and 9-10 are directed to allowable subject matter.  Claim 7-8 have been withdrawn as the result of an earlier restriction requirement.  Claim 13 adds an additional feature from Example 2 in the specification.  In view of the examiner’s earlier restriction requirement, applicant retains the right to present claims 7-8 in a divisional application … Applicant respectfully requests that a timely Notice of Allowance be issued in this case.
guidance: Provide a Remarks/Arguments section that (a) describes what amendments were made and why (editorial corrections, incorporation of examples, overcoming rejections), (b) identifies claim statuses and examiner acknowledgements (e.g., allowable subject matter), (c) explains procedural matters (restriction/divisional rights), and (d) includes a request (e.g., for Notice of Allowance) where appropriate. Be precise and link claim changes to specification support or examiner communications.

name: Amendments and affidavits/evidence after appeal
description: Amendments filed after filing an appeal and prior to the date a brief is filed may be admitted as provided in § 1.116. Amendments filed on or after the date of filing a brief may be admitted: (1) to cancel claims where cancellation does not affect the scope of any other pending claim, or (2) to rewrite dependent claims into independent form.
guidance: All other amendments filed after the date of filing an appeal will not be admitted except as permitted by §§ 41.39(b)(1), 41.50(a)(2)(i), and 41.50(b)(1). An affidavit or other Evidence filed after filing an appeal and prior to the date of filing a brief may be admitted if the examiner determines it overcomes all rejections under appeal and that good and sufficient reasons why it was necessary and not earlier presented have been made. Other affidavits/evidence filed after appeal will not be admitted except as permitted by listed sections.

name: Appeal brief content and formatting requirements
description: Except as provided, the brief shall contain the following items under appropriate headings and in the order indicated: (i) Real party in interest; (ii) Related appeals, interferences, and trials; (iii) Summary of claimed subject matter; (iv) Argument with respect to each ground of rejection and the basis therefor; (v) Claims appendix.
guidance: Specifics: (i) identify real party in interest by name unless inventors are themselves the real party in interest; (ii) identify related cases by application/patent/appeal/interference/trial number that involve an application or patent owned by the appellant or assignee and may affect the Board decision; (iii) provide concise explanation of subject matter defined in each rejected independent claim with references to the specification in the Record (page/line or paragraph) and drawings by reference characters; if a claim contains a means-plus-function or step-plus-function under 35 U.S.C. 112(f), identify corresponding structure/material/acts in the specification by reference; reference to the patent application publication does not satisfy this requirement; (iv) arguments must explain why the examiner erred, with citations of statutes/regulations/authorities/Record; any arguments or authorities not included in the appeal brief will be refused consideration except as provided in §§ 41.41, 41.47 and 41.52; each ground contested must be argued under a separate heading that reasonably identifies the ground; for grounds applying to multiple claims, claims may be argued separately, as a group, or as a subgroup; failure to separately argue grouped claims constitutes waiver of argument for separate patentability; a statement merely pointing out what a claim recites is not an argument for separate patentability; (v) include an appendix containing a copy of the claims involved.

name: Infirmity of proof standard
description: A showing that there was such infirmity of proof establishing the misconduct as to give rise to the clear conviction that the Office could not, consistently with its duty, accept as final the conclusion on that subject.
guidance: This is a high, narrow standard—practitioner must show proof so lacking that the Office cannot accept the state tribunal's conclusion. Courts/USPTO afford state findings high respect; infirmity claims require clear and convincing evidence.

name: Grave injustice standard
description: A claim that imposition of the same public discipline by the Office would result in a grave injustice.
guidance: Practitioner must prove by clear and convincing evidence that applying identical discipline would produce a grave injustice. This is one of the limited Selling/§11.24(d)(1) defenses and is narrowly construed.

name: Eligibility outcome based on marked differences
description: If the claimed nature-based product exhibits markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart, then the claim does not recite a product-of-nature exception and is eligible at Step 2A (Pathway B) unless the claim recites another exception. If the entire claim is a single nature-based product and a marked difference is shown, no further Step 2B analysis is necessary.
guidance: If the nature-based product lacks markedly different characteristics, it is a product-of-nature exception and requires further analysis in Step 2A Prong Two (integration into a practical application) and possibly Step 2B. For claims including additional elements, examiners should check whether other exceptions are recited and proceed accordingly.

name: Identifying appropriate characteristics for comparison
description: Identify characteristics to compare that are actually possessed by the claimed product, based on the claim language and the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of that claim. Characteristics can be structural, functional, or other properties.
guidance: Characteristics relied on must be recited in the claim or encompassed by the claim's BRI; unclaimed characteristics cannot be used to establish marked differences. Example: a claim to 'deoxyribose' implies structural characteristics (loss of a hydroxyl). For 'isolated gene B' rely on what that term reasonably encompasses (sequence, encoded protein, etc.).

name: Examples of products found to have markedly different characteristics
description: Court examples where claimed products were held to have markedly different characteristics and thus were eligible.
guidance: Chakrabarty: genetically modified bacterium with additional plasmids and ability to degrade multiple hydrocarbons was markedly different and eligible. Myriad: full-length cDNA (exon-only sequence) was structurally distinct from genomic DNA and held not a product of nature.

name: Requirement to follow 37 CFR 1.530 and 1.121 for amendments
description: Any proposed amendment to the description and claims in patents involved in reexamination proceedings must be made in accordance with § 1.530, and 37 CFR 1.121 (manner of making amendments in applications) applies, with specific reexamination provisions.
guidance: Proposed amendments may accompany a request filed by the patent owner (§1.510(e)), be part of a patent owner statement (§1.530(b)), or be filed during prosecution where permitted (§1.550(a) or §1.937). See MPEP § 2250 for manner of making amendments by patent owner and examples of proper claim amendment format; for clerical handling see MPEP § 2270.

name: Form and content requirements for changes to specification other than claims
description: Changes to the specification (other than claims, Large Tables §1.58(c), Computer Program Listing Appendix §1.96(c), Sequence Listing §1.821(c), or Sequence Listing XML §1.831(a)) must be made by submission of the entire text of an added or rewritten paragraph, including markings per paragraph (f), except that an entire paragraph may be deleted by a statement deleting the paragraph without presentation of the paragraph text. The precise point where any added or rewritten paragraph is located must be identified.
guidance: Changes to Large Tables, Computer Program Listing Appendix, Sequence Listing, or Sequence Listing XML must follow their respective rules (§1.58(g), §1.96(c)(5), §1.825, §1.835). All formal requirements for papers other than those set out in section are in §1.52.

name: Status of claims and support for claim changes must be supplied
description: Whenever there is an amendment to the claims pursuant to paragraph (d), there must also be supplied, on pages separate from the pages containing the changes, the status (i.e., pending or canceled), as of the date of the amendment, of all patent claims and of all added claims, and an explanation of the support in the disclosure of the patent for the changes to the claims made by the amendment paper.
guidance: This separate statement demonstrates that claim changes are supported by the original disclosure and clarifies the claim set post-amendment.

name: Markings to show changes (brackets and underlining)
description: Any changes relative to the patent being reexamined which are made to the specification, including the claims, must include the following markings: (1) matter to be omitted must be enclosed in brackets; and (2) matter to be added must be underlined.
guidance: All amendments must visibly show insertions and deletions with these markings; where a portion of the text is amended more than once, each amendment should indicate ALL changes (insertions and deletions) in relation to the current text of the patent under reexamination.

name: Amendment of disclosure may be required to secure correspondence
description: The disclosure must be amended, when required by the Office, to correct inaccuracies of description and definition, and to secure substantial correspondence between the claims, the remainder of the specification, and the drawings.
guidance: Office may require changes to ensure consistency among claims, specification, and drawings; amendments must be relative to the patent specification and drawings in effect as of the date of filing the request for reexamination.

name: Amendments must be relative to patent as of filing date of request
description: All amendments must be made relative to the patent specification, including the claims, and drawings, which are in effect as of the date of filing the request for reexamination.
guidance: You cannot base amendments on intervening changes; the baseline is the patent text in effect on the request filing date.

name: No enlargement of claim scope or introduction of new matter; restrictions for expired patents
description: No amendment may enlarge the scope of the claims of the patent or introduce new matter. No amendment may be proposed for entry in an expired patent. Moreover, no amendment, other than the cancellation of claims, will be incorporated into the patent by a certificate issued after the expiration of the patent.
guidance: This is a strict substantive limitation: amendments are limited to narrowing or clarifying the claims without adding new subject matter or expanding scope; cancellations are permitted even after expiration, but additions/changes will not be incorporated post-expiration.

name: Maintenance, renewal, and incontestability requirements
description: Owners can maintain registrations indefinitely if the registered mark is in use; specific affidavits and renewal filings are required at statutory intervals.
guidance: Between the fifth and sixth years after registration, the owner must file an affidavit attesting to use; to renew, an acceptable affidavit of use and an application for renewal must be filed within one year before the end of each 10-year registration period. Owners on the Principal Register may claim incontestability after five consecutive years of continuous use post-registration.

name: Apply Federal Circuit law to patent-substantive issues
description: When questions involve substantive patent law (e.g., whether a particular claim is the same as or separate from another claim), the Federal Circuit's law governs.
guidance: Although regional-circuit law governs certain procedural questions (like collateral-estoppel procedure), the court applies its own law to substantive patent issues, such as determining whether claims are identical for preclusion purposes.

name: Claim construction process (Phillips/Vitronics)
description: The proper approach to determining claim scope is to look first to the intrinsic evidence: the patent itself (claims and specification) and, if in evidence, the prosecution history.
guidance: Extrinsic evidence (expert testimony, dictionaries, treatises) is less significant than the intrinsic record. Extrinsic evidence may not be used to contradict claim meaning that is unambiguous in light of the intrinsic evidence. Claim construction is ultimately a legal question subject to de novo review on appeal, but subsidiary fact-finding for claim construction is for the trial court to perform (Teva).

name: Role and limits of extrinsic evidence
description: Extrinsic evidence (expert testimony, inventor testimony, dictionaries, treatises) is less significant than intrinsic evidence and cannot be used to contradict an unambiguous claim meaning from the intrinsic record.
guidance: District courts should not rely primarily on extrinsic evidence to define claim scope if intrinsic evidence is dispositive. Treat extrinsic materials as subordinate and use them only to aid construction where intrinsic evidence leaves genuine ambiguity.

name: Limits on preclusion from PTAB findings where legal standards differ
description: Findings underlying an IPR (which applied a preponderance standard) do not necessarily estop a patentee from defending validity of separate claims in district court where the district court requires proof by clear and convincing evidence.
guidance: Collateral estoppel does not apply where the second action involves a different legal standard (B & B Hardware; Grogan). Because IPR uses preponderance while district court requires clear and convincing, factual findings about prior art capabilities in an IPR do not automatically preclude argument or evidence in district court on different claims that were not adjudicated as invalid.

name: Burden of proof differences: IPR vs district court
description: In an IPR, the petitioner must prove unpatentability by a preponderance of the evidence; in district court, a defendant asserting invalidity must prove it by clear and convincing evidence.
guidance: Because the burdens differ, Board findings under the lower standard do not necessarily satisfy the higher district-court standard for separate, unadjudicated claims.

name: Claim scope identity test for collateral estoppel in patent cases
description: For collateral estoppel to bar relitigation of infringement, the scope of the claims in the new action must be materially the same as the claims adjudicated previously; differences that materially alter the infringement question defeat preclusion.
guidance: Determination requires claim construction per Phillips; the district court should perform claim construction (looking first to intrinsic evidence) rather than relying primarily on extrinsic expert charts. If claim scope is unresolved or disputed, summary judgment on collateral estoppel is inappropriate.

name: Requirements for parent application to set effective prior-art date
description: A prior-art parent application must be copendent, have some continuity of disclosure, and be specifically referred to in the patent or published application; continuous disclosure must describe the subject matter relied on as prior art (the disclosure can become narrower in intervening applications but must still exist).
guidance: Paragraph (2) implements these requirements indirectly by requiring the prior application be 'entitled to claim priority or benefit' under section 120 et seq.; enables reliance on earlier fuller disclosures when continuity and specific reference are present.

name: Doctrine of inherency applies to public-availability standard
description: Under inherency, if an element is not expressly disclosed in a prior-art reference, the reference will still be deemed to anticipate a claim if the missing element is necessarily present in the thing described in the reference and would be recognized by persons of ordinary skill; applies to products sold to the public as well as published references.
guidance: Practical example: once a product is sold on the market, any invention inherent to the product becomes publicly-available prior art and cannot be patented.

name: Kaplan: treatment of broad vs. narrow claims and joint inventorship
description: Mere domination of a narrower claim by a broader patent claim does not per se justify a double patenting rejection; the disclosure of a joint invention in a patent cannot be treated as though it were prior art.
guidance: Consider inventorship and why narrower claims were not presented in the earlier patent (e.g., statutory reasons precluding joint inventorship filings prior to 1984). Don't improperly use the patent specification's disclosure as prior art in double patenting analysis; analyze reasons for separate filings and timing.

name: Applicability of double patenting to design and plant situations
description: Double patenting principles applied in utility-utility situations generally apply to utility-plant and utility-design situations; rejection may be made where appropriate.
guidance: Design-utility cases may require a two-way obviousness determination; examine whether claims involve the same invention or obvious variations. Review cited case law (Carman, Thorington, Phelan, Barber, Hargraves) for precedential guidance and consider differences in claimed subject matter (external appearance vs interior construction).

name: Distinction between double patenting and prior art rejections (35 U.S.C. 102/103)
description: A double patenting rejection must rely on a comparison with the claims in an issued or to-be-issued patent, whereas a 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/103(a) rejection relies on what is disclosed in the reference (claimed or unclaimed).
guidance: In 102(e)/103(a) rejections, the reference patent is available for all that it fairly discloses; a terminal disclaimer cannot be used to overcome a 102(e)/103(a) rejection. For commonly owned references, consider 35 U.S.C. 103(c)(1) disqualification rules and other procedural options (co-filing, merging, affidavits under 37 CFR 1.132 or declarations under 37 CFR 1.131 where applicable) as alternatives to invoking prior art effect.

name: Exceptions to 35 U.S.C. 121 prohibition (A–G)
description: Situations where the 35 U.S.C. 121 prohibition does not apply: (A) applicant voluntarily filed multiple applications without an examiner restriction; (B) claims are not consonant with restriction because materially changed; (C) restriction was made subject to nonallowance of generic/linking claims and such claims later allowed; (D) restriction made only in an international application by ISA/IPEA; (E) restriction withdrawn before patent issues; (F) claims of second application are drawn to the 'same invention' as the first; (G) where a restriction was made subject to nonallowance of product and product subsequently allowed, requiring withdrawal of restriction.
guidance: Maintain the line of demarcation between independent and distinct inventions identified in the restriction requirement for consonance. Note that continuation practice where restriction not reinstated may allow reliance on continuity despite earlier restriction language.

name: Avoiding statutory double patenting
description: Statutory double patenting can be avoided by amending conflicting claims so they are not coextensive in scope, canceling conflicting claims in pending applications, or cancelling conflicting claims in all but one pending application for provisional rejections.
guidance: Terminal disclaimers are not effective against statutory double patenting. Use of 37 CFR 1.131 affidavits is inappropriate for statutory double patenting (case law: In re Dunn and progeny).

name: Avoiding nonstatutory double patenting (terminal disclaimer guidance)
description: A nonstatutory double patenting rejection can be obviated by filing a terminal disclaimer in the application or proceeding in which the rejection is made.
guidance: Terminal disclaimers encourage disclosure and earlier filing; filing is not an admission of the rejection's propriety. Terminal disclaimer must operate with respect to all claims in the patent (cannot disclaim term of only specified claims). Where subject matter was commonly owned at the time of invention, disclaimers must include a provision making the patent unenforceable if it ceases to be commonly owned (37 CFR 1.321(c)). Terminal disclaimers cannot overcome 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/103(a) rejections. 37 CFR 1.131 affidavits are inappropriate to overcome nonstatutory double patenting when claims are substantially the same or lack patentable distinctness.

name: Terminal disclaimer formal requirements
description: Requirements for a terminal disclaimer are set forth in 37 CFR 1.321; sample forms and filing/treatment guidance are in MPEP § 1490.
guidance: A terminal disclaimer is a statement filed by an owner to disclaim or dedicate a portion of the entire term of all claims of a patent. Ensure compliance with 37 CFR 1.321 provisions, including special provisions for common ownership and joint research agreements (1.321(c) and (d)).

name: Mandatory terminal disclaimer for continuing applications filed on/after June 8, 1995
description: For continuing utility or plant applications filed on/after June 8, 1995, a terminal disclaimer under 37 CFR 1.321 is required to overcome a nonstatutory double patenting rejection, even if the continuing application claims benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, or 365(c).
guidance: Reasoning: 35 U.S.C. 154(a)(2) provides a 20-year term from earliest claimed filing date, and 154(b) allows term adjustments; to avoid potential term-extension problems and harassment by multiple owners, the terminal disclaimer must include provisions required by 37 CFR 1.321(c)(3) and (d) as applicable. Cite MPEP section or Official Gazette notice when responding to arguments that 37 CFR 1.321 should not be required due to 35 U.S.C. 154.

name: Provisional double patenting practice across multiple pending applications
description: Where a provisional double patenting rejection is made in one of two or more pending applications, the examiner should follow practice in MPEP § 804 subsection I.B.1 to determine in which application an appropriate terminal disclaimer must be filed.
guidance: Provisional rejections should also be made in conflicting applications; claims that differ aside from minor language differences are not considered the same invention, but if differences would have been obvious, terminal disclaimers are effective. Ensure consistency of provisional rejections across related files and coordinate terminal disclaimer filing as required.

name: Inapplicability of 37 CFR 1.131 affidavits to overcome double patenting
description: Use of a 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit (or similar) is inappropriate to overcome either statutory or nonstatutory double patenting rejections when the claims are directed to substantially the same invention or lack patentable distinctness.
guidance: Case law (In re Dunn, Knell v. Muller, and related CCPA decisions) supports that 1.131 is inapplicable where the application claims and the patent claim the same or substantially the same invention. Instead, rely on claim amendments, cancellations, or terminal disclaimers (for nonstatutory) as appropriate.

name: Novelty (definition and exceptions)
description: An invention is new if it is not anticipated by prior art, which consists of everything disclosed to the public anywhere by written or oral disclosure, by use, or by any other way realized before the relevant filing date or validly claimed priority date (Article 2/2).
guidance: Disclosure within one year before filing/priority due to abusive actions by others is disregarded; disclosure at an officially recognized exhibition within six months preceding filing is not taken into account (Implementing Bylaws determine protection provisions).

name: First-to-file rule
description: Where more than one application pertains to the same invention, the patent shall be granted to the owner of the first application that has the earliest priority date (Article 2/6).
guidance: Priority date (including valid priority claims) determines entitlement when multiple filings exist.

name: Required contents of application
description: The application shall contain the title of the invention, a specification, one or more claims, one or more drawings (if any), and an abstract (Article 5/2/1).
guidance: Complete set of documents required for formal filing and examination to proceed.

name: Claims determine scope of protection
description: The claim or claims shall determine the scope of the protection sought; the specification and the drawings may be used to interpret the claims (Article 5/2/3).
guidance: Claims are primary for rights; specification/drawings are interpretive aids.

name: Claim clarity, conciseness and support
description: Claims shall be clear and concise and shall be fully supported by the specification (Article 5/2/4).
guidance: Lack of clarity or support can render claims invalid or rejectable.

name: Abstract purpose limitation
description: The abstract shall merely serve the purpose of technical information and shall not be taken into account for interpreting the application (Article 5/2/5).
guidance: Abstract is informative only and not a substantive interpretive document for claim construction.

name: Priority claim requirements and term
description: Application may contain claim of priority of previous application filed in any State or regional office; must indicate date and filing number and country and produce proof, otherwise priority claim denied; duration of priority shall be twelve Gregorian months (Article 7/1-7/2).
guidance: Strict documentary proof required for priority; 12-month Paris Convention-style priority period.

name: Scope of patent owner's exploitation rights
description: Patent entitles owner to exploit invention: product exploitation includes manufacturing, use, import, sale, or offering for sale; for industrial processes owner also has rights to products directly obtained by using such process and to prevent others from actual use of the process without consent (Article 12/1-12/2).
guidance: Rights cover acts of exploitation broadly; process claims afford rights over direct product of the process as well.

name: Patentee must give public notice of any qualified allowance of public use
description: If a patentee intends to surrender his exclusive right in a qualified manner or for a qualified trade, he should at the time give public notice of the nature and extent of his allowance of the public use.
guidance: Without clear public notice, aquiescence in public use means the patentee no longer claims exclusivity for that use and cannot later seek injunction to restrain extension (example: Wyeth v. Stone discussion on domestic vs foreign trade).

name: Comparison of specifications and identity between patents may be judicial when facts undisputed (but authorities conflict)
description: Where the defendant claims his act is under another patent or that the plaintiff's invention is contained in a patent granted to a third party, the court has been held in many cases to have the exclusive province to pronounce upon identity when the facts are not disputed; however, authorities have conflicted and later decisions (e.g., reversal of Exchequer Chamber in Betts v. Menzies) have recognized that when facts are disputed the matter may require different treatment.
guidance: Cases: Bovill v. Pimm, Betts v. Menzies, Bush v. Fox, Hills v. Evans. The treatise records the historical conflict and ultimate reversal of the Exchequer Chamber decision, illustrating that judicial determination of identity is appropriate only where factual dispute is absent; otherwise, jury issues may be implicated.

name: Definiteness standard under 35 U.S.C. 112(b)
description: A determination of indefiniteness requires whether those skilled in the art would understand what is claimed when the claim is read in light of the specification.
guidance: Evaluate whether a person of ordinary skill in the art would understand the metes and bounds of the claimed invention in view of the specification (citing Power-One; Orthokinetics example). The test is whether the claim informs those skilled in the art of its scope with reasonable certainty (Nautilus for issued patents; see relation to prosecution).

name: Apply broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) consistent with the specification during prosecution
description: During examination, claims are construed by giving them their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification to facilitate sharpening and clarifying claims at the application stage.
guidance: Do not apply the narrower judicial claim construction used in litigation; apply BRI (citing Packard, Buszard, Yamamoto, Zletz). Recognize this can result in a lower threshold for ambiguity than a court's determination. Use BRI to determine whether metes and bounds are clear; if not, reject under §112(b).

name: Threshold requirements of clarity and precision (particularity and distinctness)
description: The examiner’s focus is whether the claim meets the statutory threshold requirements of clarity and precision—i.e., particularity and distinctness required by §112(b), not whether better wording exists.
guidance: Allow claims that define patentable subject matter with the required degree of particularity and distinctness. Permit some latitude in expression when the statutory requirement is nevertheless satisfied. The essential inquiry is whether the claims circumscribe particular subject matter with reasonable clarity and particularity.

name: Contextual analysis: disclosure, prior art, and POSITA understanding
description: Definiteness must be analyzed in light of (A) the content of the application disclosure, (B) teachings of the prior art, and (C) the claim interpretation a person of ordinary skill in the art would give at the relevant time.
guidance: When reviewing claims, consider all three factors together rather than in isolation. The relevant time is before the effective filing date for AIA applications (or at the time of invention for pre‑AIA).

name: Consider the claim as a whole
description: The examiner must view the claim in its entirety and consider the interaction of all limitations to ascertain the inventor’s contribution and whether the claim apprises POSITA of its scope.
guidance: Do not analyze isolated words outside the context of the whole claim; the totality of limitations can resolve apparent ambiguities (citing Larsen).

name: Indefiniteness arises if more than one reasonable interpretation exists under BRI
description: If, under the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification, a person of ordinary skill would read the claim with more than one reasonable meaning, the claim is indefinite.
guidance: If there is more than one reasonable interpretation of a claim term or phrase such that the metes and bounds are unclear, a §112(b) rejection is appropriate (citing Packard, Zletz).

name: Do not equate claim breadth with indefiniteness
description: A broad claim is not necessarily indefinite merely because it covers a wide scope; indefiniteness relates to unclear boundaries, not breadth per se.
guidance: A genus claim that clearly delineates scope can be broad but definite; by contrast, a genus claim that leaves ambiguity as to which species are included is indefinite (see Markush guidance at MPEP §2173.05(h)).

name: Office action content requirement: identify term, explain why, and suggest resolution when practicable
description: An Office action rejecting a claim as indefinite must (1) point out the specific term or phrase deemed indefinite, (2) explain in detail why it renders the metes and bounds unclear, and (3) whenever practicable, indicate how the indefiniteness may be resolved.
guidance: Provide sufficient detail to permit the applicant to prepare a meaningful response. Cite relevant MPEP sections (§706.03, §707.07(g),(d)). Failure of applicant to adequately respond may result in a final rejection.

name: Encourage constructive examiner suggestions but not insistence on preference
description: Examiners are encouraged to suggest claim language to improve clarity/precision but should not insist on their own wording if the applicant’s language satisfies §112(b).
guidance: Offer suggested amendments or wording to help applicant resolve issues, but accept other modes of expression that meet statutory requirements.

name: Applicant options to overcome indefiniteness: amend or provide persuasive evidentiary explanation
description: In response to an indefiniteness rejection applicants may amend the claim or provide persuasive explanation (and evidence as necessary) demonstrating that a POSITA would not find the language unclear.
guidance: Persuasive explanations may include separate definitions, e.g., art‑recognized dictionary definitions, or other intrinsic/extrinsic evidence to show how a skilled artisan would understand the term (citing Packard).

name: Use interviews to attempt resolution when indefiniteness is the only issue
description: When indefiniteness is the only issue, examiners are encouraged to initiate an interview with applicant to discuss claim language, BRI, and possible claim amendments before resorting to a rejection.
guidance: Interviews can clarify meanings and eliminate the need for a §112(b) rejection. The substance of any interview must be made of record and include why a term is/ is not clear, inconsistency with the specification, whether §112(f) is invoked and corresponding structure, and any discussed amendments (citing MPEP §713.04 and 37 CFR 1.2).

name: Provide claim interpretation in Reasons for Allowance when the prosecution record does not make reasons clear
description: If the file record as a whole does not make clear the reasons for allowing claims, the examiner may set forth the claim interpretation applied in a Reasons for Allowance statement pursuant to 37 CFR 1.104(e).
guidance: Setting forth claim interpretation improves quality and reliability of issued patents and aids public understanding. However, avoid placing unwarranted interpretations (either broad or narrow) on the claims (citing MPEP §1302.14).

name: When additional information is necessary, consider a requirement for information under 37 CFR 1.105
description: If the examiner determines more information is necessary to ascertain the meaning of a claim term, a formal requirement for information under 37 CFR 1.105 may be appropriate.
guidance: Refer to MPEP §704.10 for requirements for information and use this procedure when intrinsic evidence is insufficient to resolve claim meaning.

name: Expectation of similar properties may suffice without explicit teaching
description: An expectation of similar properties in light of the prior art can be sufficient to support obviousness even without an explicit teaching in the prior art to isolate or make the claimed compound.
guidance: Cites Aventis: requiring an explicit teaching to purify a stereoisomer is a rigid TSM-style requirement disfavored by KSR. Office personnel may rely on an expectation of similar properties derived from structural similarity or other prior art disclosures.

name: Structural similarity can provide the necessary motivation
description: Obviousness based on structural similarity can be proved by identification of some motivation that would have led one of ordinary skill to select and then modify a known compound.
guidance: It is sufficient to show that the claimed and prior art compounds possess a 'sufficiently close relationship ... to create an expectation, in light of the totality of the prior art, that the new compound will have similar properties' (Eisai). However, there still must be a reason to select and modify the prior art compound, and a reasonable expectation of success when required.

name: Must articulate a reason to modify and a reasonable expectation of success
description: To base an obviousness rejection on modification of a prior art compound, there must be both a reason to modify the starting compound and a reasonable expectation of success in achieving the claimed compound.
guidance: Procter & Gamble and other cases emphasize both prongs: (1) reason to select/modify (may be structural similarity, teachings about properties, market pressures), and (2) reasonable expectation that the routine modification would yield the claimed result. If modification would not have been routine or predictable, obviousness is weak (Procter & Gamble, risedronate).

name: Use of Known Technique To Improve Similar Devices (Methods, or Products) in the Same Way — four required findings
description: To reject a claim based on applying a known technique used to improve similar items in the same way, examiners must articulate: (1) a finding that the prior art contained a 'base' device (method, or product) upon which the claimed invention can be seen as an 'improvement'; (2) a finding that the prior art contained a 'comparable' device that has been improved in the same way as the claimed invention; (3) a finding that one of ordinary skill could have applied the known 'improvement' technique in the same way to the 'base' device and the results would have been predictable; and (4) whatever additional Graham factual findings are necessary.
guidance: Rationale: a method of enhancing a class of devices has been made part of the ordinary capabilities of one skilled in the art based on its teaching in other situations. If any of these findings cannot be made, the rationale cannot support obviousness. (See Altana discussion and numbered list in the text.)

name: Prior art need not be true homologs or isomers to show obviousness
description: Prior art structures need not be true homologs or isomers to render claimed structurally similar compounds prima facie obvious if the similarity of structure and properties is sufficiently close.
guidance: Example: heterocyclic carbamoyloxmino pesticidal compounds where ring atom spacing differences still led court to find one skilled person motivated to make claimed compounds.

name: Methods of using pharmaceutical compositions (excluded)
description: Any method of using pharmaceutical composition is not patentable.
guidance: Procedural/treatment methods directed to medical use are excluded; consider claim drafting alternatives (e.g., composition or Swiss-type/second medical use claims where permitted).

name: Biological materials like organs, tissues, cells, viruses (excluded under Section 3(c))
description: Biological materials such as organs, tissues, cells, viruses etc. and processes of preparing thereof are not patentable under Section 3(c).
guidance: Carefully map claimed subject-matter to statutory wording; recombinant/engineered materials may be treated differently if produced by human intervention.

name: Categories of claims in computer inventions (method/process, apparatus/system, computer program product)
description: Applications may fall under method/process, apparatus/system or computer program product claims; different issues apply to each category.
guidance: Examiners should look at specific aspects per category (see subsequent criteria).

name: Method/process claims for computer-related inventions (technical effect required)
description: The method claim should clearly define the steps involved; it should have a technical effect and solve a technical problem. Claims should incorporate details regarding mode of implementation via hardware or software for clarity.
guidance: Process/method claims should contain a hardware or machine limitation and be defined in relation to particular hardware components to avoid being 'software per se'. Processes carried out under control of a program can be allowable if tied to specific hardware/technical application.

name: Apparatus/system claims for computer-related inventions (constructional hardware features)
description: The apparatus claim should clearly define the inventive constructional hardware features and should incorporate a 'process limitation' defining the specific application (not general application).
guidance: Claims that merely recite functional means corresponding to steps of an excluded method may be rejected. A novel solution involving internal computer operations or particular hardware interactions that produce a technical effect can be patentable.

name: Computer program product claims (not allowable) and exceptions
description: Claims relating to software program products (program on a computer-readable storage medium) are not allowable as they are software per se; claiming instructions encoded on a medium does not affect the issue.
guidance: However, if the new feature requires specific hardware adoption or the invention consists of hardware with software to perform hardware function (embedded systems), patentability may be possible.

name: Examine technical contribution / 'technical character' in software-related inventions
description: It is necessary for the applicant to describe the 'technical contribution' to the prior art when the invention involves software. The technical problem which needs to be solved should be sufficiently described and how the hardware is controlled by the software to overcome the problem.
guidance: The 'technical character' of the invention should be brought out clearly in the claims and specification; focus examination on whether claimed features produce a new technical effect or improvement.

name: Sufficiency and best mode for hardware vs software claims
description: Best mode must be described for hardware; for software-implemented processes provide sequence of steps and flowcharts; source/pseudo/object codes may be included to support sufficiency.
guidance: Failure to disclose best mode or necessary implementation details may lead to insufficiency objections.

name: Development of the Search Strategy
description: How to design a search strategy tailored to the claims and invention.
guidance: Covers use of a Three Person Team (3PT) for searching, considerations for independent/dependent/broad claims, reserving the search, use of controlled language, and selection of search areas (patent literature, classification, non-patent literature).

name: Construction of Specifications, Claims and Claim Types
description: Purpose and principles of construing the specification and claims for examination.
guidance: Covers initial considerations, addressee, role of common general knowledge, rules of construction (plain meaning, read as whole, purposive construction, dictionary principle, reject absurd, technical document approach), and treatment of errors/omissions.

name: Claim Construction and Claim Types
description: Approach to construing claims and considerations for different claim types.
guidance: Includes that claims are legal documents, presumption against redundancy, omnibus claims, Swiss claims, product-by-process, parametric claims, 'for use' wording, open/closed claim language ('comprises/includes/consists of'), reference numerals, relative terms, qualifiers like 'substantially/about/generally', appended claims and claim drafting issues.

name: Specification and Claims to Examine
description: Which documents and versions to examine and how to treat amendments made prior to examination.
guidance: Addressing consideration of amendments, unity (single invention), omnibus claims, provisional specifications, and guidance on claim sets to be examined.

name: Full Disclosure, Sufficiency, Clarity and Support (Section 40 considerations)
description: Requirements for clear and complete disclosure and support for claims under s40 (sufficiency/best method/support).
guidance: Includes that claims must be clear and succinct, s40(2)(a) clear and complete disclosure, s40(3) support for claims, difference between disclosure and support, best method requirement, deposit of micro-organisms, claims defining the invention, and examples of subsections.

name: Claims Define the Invention / Claims are Clear and Succinct
description: Expectation that claims define the invention and must be clear and succinct.
guidance: Guidance on drafting and evaluating clarity and succinctness of claim language and structure.

name: Best Method / Full Description
description: Requirement to disclose the best method known to the applicant for performing the invention.
guidance: Covers date for determining full description, ascertainability of nature of invention, enabling disclosures, effort required to perform, and aspects claimed across different claims.

name: Section 40 Specifications (Historical/Specific Guidance)
description: Detailed guidance on section 40 requirements including what is the invention, full description, claims as fair basis, and sub-tests for fair basis.
guidance: Addresses approach in leading cases (e.g., Lockwood v Doric), consistory clause, essential features, critical analysis requirement, best method, enabling disclosures, relation between described invention and claimed invention, alternatives, claiming by results, reach-through claims, claims to alloys and more.

name: Priority Dates and Filing Dates Issues
description: Detailed treatment of priority date determinations for claims and related complications (convention applications, amended claims, associated applications).
guidance: Guidance on determining priority dates for claims, for convention applications, relation to amended claims and priority documents that are provisional.

name: Definitions in 35 U.S.C. 100: 'claimed invention' (100(j))
description: The term 'claimed invention' is defined as the subject matter defined by a claim in a patent or an application for a patent.
guidance: Used to identify the subject matter to which effective filing date and prior art rules apply.

name: Definition of 'effective filing date' (35 U.S.C. 100(i)(1))
description: For a claimed invention in a patent or application (other than a reissue or reissued patent), the effective filing date is the earlier of: (1) the actual filing date of the patent or application containing the claimed invention; or (2) the filing date of the earliest provisional, nonprovisional, international (PCT), or foreign patent application to which the patent or application is entitled to benefit or priority as to such claimed invention.
guidance: The effective filing date controls whether a disclosure is before or after the claimed invention for prior art purposes. The earlier application must support the claimed invention as required by 35 U.S.C. 112(a). See MPEP § 2152.01 and § 2153.01(a).

name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1) inventor-originated disclosure exception (one-year grace period)
description: Certain disclosures made one year or less before the effective filing date shall not be prior art under 102(a)(1) if: (1) the disclosure was made by the inventor or joint inventor or by another who obtained the subject matter directly or indirectly from the inventor/joint inventor; or (2) the subject matter disclosed had, before such disclosure, been publicly disclosed by the inventor/joint inventor or by another who obtained it directly or indirectly from the inventor/joint inventor.
guidance: This effectively provides a one-year grace period for an inventor-originated disclosure; the grace period is measured from the filing date of the earliest U.S. or foreign patent application to which benefit or priority is properly asserted and which supports the claimed invention under 35 U.S.C. 112(a). The grace period is extended to the next business day if it ends on a weekend or federal holiday (35 U.S.C. 21(b)). See MPEP § 2153 and subsections for details.

name: Who may benefit from the 102(b)(1) grace period
description: The inventor, joint inventor, assignee, obligated assignee, or other party having sufficient interest may file a patent application within the one-year grace period and avoid certain inventor-originated disclosures being prior art.
guidance: Grace-period entitlement is measured relative to the effective filing date and the earliest application to which priority/benefit is claimed that supports the claimed invention (112(a) support). See MPEP § 2153 and §§ 2153.01(a), 2153.02.

name: Measurement of the AIA grace period
description: The one-year grace period in AIA 102(b)(1) is measured from the filing date of the earliest U.S. or foreign patent application to which a proper benefit or priority claim is asserted and the earlier application supports the claimed invention as required by 35 U.S.C. 112(a).
guidance: Differs from pre-AIA 102(b) (which measured from the filing date of the earliest U.S. application). Regulations governing filing dates (e.g., Priority Mail Express deposit, electronic filing) do not alter this statutory measurement; see MPEP §§ 2153.01(a) and 2153.02 for interactions with 37 C.F.R. filing rules.

name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(c) deemed common ownership for joint research agreements
description: Subject matter disclosed and a claimed invention shall be deemed to have been owned by the same person (or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person) for purposes of applying the 102(b)(2)(C) exception if: (1) the subject matter disclosed was developed and the claimed invention was made by, or on behalf of, one or more parties to a joint research agreement that was in effect on or before the effective filing date; (2) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (3) the application discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement.
guidance: The term 'joint research agreement' is defined in 35 U.S.C. 100(h) as a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement between two or more persons or entities for experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention. See MPEP § 2154 and § 2156.

name: Claims in effect govern determination
description: The examiner's determination is based on the claims in effect at the time of the determination; certain amendments (e.g., presented with the request by the owner or filed in pending reexamination) will not be considered when deciding requests.
guidance: No input from the patent owner is considered prior to determination unless the owner filed the request; amendments in reissue or pending reexamination may be excluded per statute and regulation references.

name: Reexamination scope limited to claims requested
description: The Office’s determination and subsequent examination will generally be limited to review of the claims for which reexamination was requested; claims not requested will generally not be reexamined.
guidance: If the Office chooses to reexamine claims not requested, it is permitted to do so; case law (e.g., Sony) shows reexamination can be limited to requested claims.

name: Second or subsequent requests must present a 'different' SNQ
description: A second or subsequent request filed while a first reexamination is pending must provide prior art that raises a substantial new question of patentability that is different from that raised in the pending reexamination for the claims in effect at the time of determination.
guidance: If the second request raises the same SNQ as the pending proceeding, it should be denied; if it raises a different SNQ as to some claims, it may be granted in part; the decision is based on the claims in effect at the time of the determination (37 CFR 1.515(a)).

name: Recapture Category 1 — Omission of Surrender-Generating Limitation (recapture)
description: Reissue claims are broader by entirely omitting surrender-generating limitation(s) and are narrower in unrelated aspect(s): in this case, there is recapture.
guidance: Recapture exists because there is no addition of a new limitation that is related to the surrendered subject matter or if any new limitation related to the surrendered subject matter fails to materially narrow the claim (e.g., only adds what is known in the prior art). Example: original claims directed to ABC; reissue directed to ABD where C was a surrender-generating limitation (added or argued to obtain allowance). Eliminating C broadens into surrendered area; narrowing by D (unrelated to C) will not avoid recapture. See In re Clement, Pannu.

name: Recapture Category 2 — Broader in Unrelated Aspect(s), Narrower in Surrender Area (no recapture)
description: Reissue claims are narrower or equal in scope in the area related to surrendered subject matter and are broader in unrelated aspects: in this case, there is no recapture.
guidance: Example: patent claimed ABCDE; reissue claims ABDE (omitting C) where a different limitation E was the surrender-generating limitation. Omitting C (unrelated to the surrender) and retaining/narrowing the surrender-generating limitation avoids recapture. Reissue can broaden in an aspect not germane to the prior-art rejection while narrowing in the area of surrender (e.g., narrow E to Especific). Also examples such as presenting AC or AB_broadC avoid recapture if they do not attempt to reclaim surrendered subject matter. See Mentor Corp. v. Coloplast; In re Clement.

name: Recapture Category 3 — Retain Surrender-Generating Limitation Unchanged (no recapture)
description: Reissue claims retain surrender-generating limitation(s) without change and are narrower or broader in unrelated aspects: there is no recapture.
guidance: If the limitation that led to surrender (e.g., C) remains unmodified in the reissue claims, changes elsewhere that do not affect the surrendered matter do not constitute recapture. Caveat: if applicant had previously argued that association of added limitation(s) defined over the art (synergy), then omission of either related limitation could be barred. See related discussion on surrender by argument.

name: Recapture Category 4 — Retained but Broadened Surrender-Generating Limitation (may be recapture)
description: Reissue claims retain, in broadened form, the surrender-generating limitation(s): in this case there may be recapture.
guidance: If the retained limitation is broadened (e.g., C -> C_broadened) and that broadened limitation does not materially narrow the reissue claim relative to the original surrendered subject matter (for example, C_broadened is well-known in the prior art or was contained in prior art relied on), a recapture rejection can be made. If the modified limitation nevertheless 'materially narrows' relative to the original claim, recapture may be avoided. See In re Mostafazadeh; In re Youman; guidance that prior-art content used in original prosecution forms the ceiling for material narrowing analysis.

name: Definition of 'Broadened Reissue Claim'
description: A broadened reissue claim enlarges the scope of the claims of the original patent — i.e., is greater in scope than each and every claim of the original patent.
guidance: A claim is broadened if it is broader in at least one respect even though it may be narrower in other respects. A reissue claim that would cover any conceivable product or process that would not have infringed the original patent is broadened. Disclaimed claims (filed before reissue) are not part of the 'original patent' for this test. Case law examples: Vectra Fitness, Tillotson, In re Ruth, In re Rogoff.

name: Two-Year Filing Limit for Broadening Reissue (35 U.S.C. 251(d))
description: No reissued patent shall be granted enlarging the scope of the claims of the original patent unless applied for within two years from the grant of the original patent.
guidance: A broadened claim can be presented within two years from grant. If an intent to broaden is unequivocally indicated in a parent reissue application filed within two years, further broadened claims may be presented in continuation/divisional reissue applications after two years. A reissue filed on the two-year anniversary is timely. Case law: In re Staats, In re Graff, In re Fotland, In re Bennett, In re Doll. Use form ¶14.12 for improper broadened claims filed outside two years; examiner should identify claim limitations that broaden scope.

name: Addition of Process or Article Claims (incl. computer-readable medium) Generally Broadening
description: Adding process claims or article-of-manufacture claims (e.g., functional descriptive material on a computer-readable medium) in a reissue application is generally considered a broadening of the invention.
guidance: Such additions must be applied for within two years of the grant of the original patent (or in an appropriate continuing reissue filed within two years). Example: converting patented process claims into corresponding article claims is generally broadening (Ex parte Wikdahl). See MPEP § 1412.03 and discussion of broadened claims.

name: Dependent Claim Broadened but Not a Broadened Reissue Claim
description: A dependent claim that is broadened in reissue is not a 'broadened reissue claim' if it remains narrower than or equal in scope to any other claim in the patent.
guidance: Because dependent claims incorporate limitations of the claims on which they depend, a dependent claim broadened relative to its patent form is not a broadened reissue claim so long as some other claim in the patent remains as broad as or broader than the reissued dependent claim.

name: New Category of Invention Added in Reissue — Generally Broadening
description: Adding a new category of invention (e.g., adding method claims where only product claims existed) in a reissue application is generally considered broadening.
guidance: However, if the newly claimed method contains every limitation of the original claim(s) (so that infringement of the new claim necessarily results in infringement of the original claim), the addition may not be broadening. Examples and analysis guidance: Ex parte Wikdahl.

name: Examiner Rejection for Recapture — Use of Form ¶14.17 and Required Explanation
description: Reissue claims that recapture surrendered subject matter should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 251 using form paragraph 14.17.
guidance: Examiner Note: In bracket 2, the examiner should explain specifics of why recapture exists — identify omitted/broadened claim limitations that provide the 'broadening aspect', where in the original application the narrowed scope was presented/argued to obviate a rejection/objection, and that the reissue claim is not materially narrowed to avoid recapture. Explain the prima facie analysis for steps 1-3. See MPEP § 1412.02.

name: Illustrative Recapture Patterns (examples to be rejected)
description: Common reissue claim patterns that should be rejected for recapture include: (1) eliminating the surrender-generating limitation; (2) eliminating the SGL and adding a narrowing limitation found not to be materially narrowing; (3) broadening the SGL where the broadened SGL is well known in the art; (4) broadening the SGL and adding another limitation that is not materially narrowing.
guidance: Example shorthand patterns: 1) ABCD eliminates E (SGL). 2) ABCDF eliminates E and adds F which is not materially narrowing. 3) ABCDE broader: E_broader is well known in art. 4) ABCDE broader F: E_broader well known; add F not materially narrowing. Applicant can rebut patterns like 2 and 4 by showing added limitation F materially narrows with respect to surrendered subject matter; applicant should point out specifically which limitation is added and how it materially narrows.

name: Rebuttal Standard for Reissue Applicant — 'Materially Narrow' Requirement
description: A reissue applicant may rebut a recapture rejection by demonstrating that the rejected claim includes one or more limitations that 'materially narrow' the reissue claims in a way that relates to the subject matter surrendered during original prosecution.
guidance: Applicant should explicitly identify the added limitation(s) (e.g., limitation F) and explain how the limitation materially narrows the claims relative to what was surrendered. The examiner evaluates material narrowing relative to surrendered subject matter and prior art used in original prosecution (prior-art ceiling). See flowchart guidance referenced in MPEP § 1412.02.

name: Oath/Declaration Requirements for Broadening Reissue (filed on/after Sept 16, 2012)
description: Any reissue application filed on or after Sept 16, 2012 must be applied for by all of the patentees; the original reissue oath/declaration in a broadening reissue must be signed by all inventors unless the original application was filed under 37 CFR 1.46 by the assignee of the entire interest.
guidance: For broadening reissue applications filed on/after Sept 16, 2012 the inventor’s oath/declaration must identify a specific claim that the application seeks to broaden (37 CFR 1.175(b)); a general statement that 'all claims are broadened' is insufficient. A supplemental oath/declaration is not needed for errors corrected subsequent to the original oath, but a replacement oath/declaration is needed where there was a failure to identify any error that would support reissue; replacement must be signed by all inventors unless original app was filed under 37 CFR 1.46 by an assignee. See MPEP § 1414.

name: Reissue as Vehicle for Correcting Inventorship — Signature, Consent, and Procedural Rules
description: Reissue may correct inventorship (35 U.S.C. 251) with specific requirements for the reissue oath/declaration and signatures, depending on whether the reissue seeks to enlarge claim scope and whether the original application was filed by an assignee under 37 CFR 1.46.
guidance: If reissue does not seek to enlarge claim scope, the reissue oath may be made and sworn to by the assignee of the entire interest under 37 CFR 1.172. An assignee of part interest may not file unless other co-owners join or consent. If a named inventor X is to be deleted and has not assigned rights, X must consent to the reissue (37 CFR 1.172(a)). If inventors are required to sign and an inventor is being deleted, the deleted inventor need not sign; if an inventor is being added, the added inventor must sign the reissue oath/declaration. Where the original application was filed by the assignee under 37 CFR 1.46, the assignee may sign the oath/declaration for reissue filed on/after Sept 16, 2012; otherwise all inventors must sign unless 37 CFR 1.64 substitute statement applies (deceased, incapacitated, refuses, or cannot be found). Examples illustrate required signatures and substitute statements. See MPEP §§ 1412.04–1412.05 and 37 CFR 1.64/1.72/1.175.

name: Applicability to applications/patents with pre‑AIA effective filing dates and certain priority references
description: The provisions of this section apply to any application for patent, and to any patent issuing thereon, that contains, or contained at any time: (1) A claim to an invention that has an effective filing date as defined in § 1.109 that is before March 16, 2013; or (2) A specific reference under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, 365(c), or 386(c) to any patent or application that contains, or contained at any time, a claim to an invention that has an effective filing date as defined in § 1.109 that is before March 16, 2013.
guidance: Apply 1.131(c) only to applications/patents that meet these effective filing date or priority‑reference conditions. If an application has no pre‑AIA effective filing date and no such references, 1.131(c) is not applicable.

name: Convening officer as accuser/prosecutor determined by animus
description: Whether the commander who convened the court is to be regarded as the 'accuser or prosecutor' depends mainly upon his animus in the matter; he may initiate investigation and prefer charges personally and thus be the accuser, or he may properly direct investigation and referral without becoming the accuser in the sense of the article.
guidance: Factors indicating the convening officer is an accuser include personal interest adverse to the accused, adopting another's charges as his own, directing charges despite investigative recommendation against preferring them, and other indicia of personal animus (see C. 2240, May 1896 and multiple R. citations). If claimed, the accused may prove the convening officer's status by affidavit or other evidence.

name: Arrangement of elements and ordering of sheets
description: The elements of the international application must be placed in the following order: the request, the description (excluding the sequence listing part of the description), the claim(s), the abstract and the drawings (if any).
guidance: This ordering is required for the international application to be presented correctly for processing and publication. Sequence listings are treated separately (see ST.26 entry).

name: Writing of text matter — legibility, dark indelible color and minimum character size
description: The request, the description, the claims and the abstract shall be typed or printed in a dark indelible color (Rule 11.9). Graphic symbols, chemical and mathematical formulae and certain characters in the Chinese or Japanese languages may be hand drawn. The text must be printed in letters the capitals of which are not less than 0.28 cm high (Rule 11.9(d)) — approximately 12 point text in Times New Roman.
guidance: Text must be suitable for OCR and reproduction: dark ink, machine-printed where possible, and sufficiently large (≥0.28 cm capitals). Certain technical symbols and some Asian characters may be hand-drawn. Handwritten markings on request form (e.g., check-boxes) need not be objected to if legible.

name: Line numbering sequence — recommendation and when to object (Rule 11.8(a))
description: Rule 11.8(a) strongly recommends that every fifth line of each sheet of the description, and of each sheet of claims be numbered, the numbers appearing in the right half of the left margin, but this is not mandatory. If lines are not numbered or numbered differently there is no basis for objection regarding reasonably uniform publication. The only reason for objection is if numbering appears somewhere other than the left margin or if there is not a clear gap between the numbering and the main text.
guidance: Line numbering is recommended for ease of reference, but ROs should not object unless numbering interferes with the main text or appears outside the left margin area without a clear gap.

name: Handling of sequence variants
description: A primary sequence may be presented and variants (e.g., conservatively modified variants, truncations) discussed without listing every variant separately, provided the primary sequence is listed and variants are properly annotated.
guidance: If a variant meeting length thresholds is disclosed by enumeration anywhere in the application, it must be presented in the Sequence Listing. Examples: 'conservatively modified variants thereof' can be used; implied C-terminal deletions (e.g., deletion of 1–5 residues) need not all be separately listed but should be annotated. Sequences considered essential to understanding or claimed should be included as separate entries. The Office database will only contain the unmodified (listed) sequence, so clear annotation is recommended.

name: Sequence identifier requirement (SEQ ID NO)
description: Each disclosed nucleic acid and/or amino acid sequence must appear separately in the Sequence Listing and be assigned a sequence identifier (e.g., 'SEQ ID NO:'), with identifiers beginning at 1 and increasing sequentially by integers.
guidance: Use of variants of the label (e.g., 'SEQ NO.', 'Seq. Id. No.') is acceptable if it is clear. Sequence identifiers should, where practical, reflect the order in which sequences are discussed in the application. When text or claims discuss a sequence that is set forth in the Sequence Listing, the sequence identifier must be referenced at all occurrences (even if the sequence is enumerated in the text). Fragments (e.g., 'residues 14 to 243 of SEQ ID NO:23') are permissible without separately presenting the fragment in the Sequence Listing.

name: Contents of a 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection (required elements)
description: After indicating that the rejection is under 35 U.S.C. 103, the examiner should set forth in the Office action: (A) the relevant teachings of the prior art relied upon, preferably with reference to the relevant column or page number(s) and line number(s) where appropriate; (B) the difference or differences in the claim over the applied reference(s); (C) the proposed modification of the applied reference(s) necessary to arrive at the claimed subject matter; and (D) an explanation why one of ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made would have been motivated to make the proposed modification.
guidance: Provide specific citations to the prior art (columns/pages/lines) where appropriate. Explicitly state claim/reference differences and the exact modification(s) hypothesized. Explain the motivation to combine/modify in clear factual/legal terms so issues are identifiable early and the applicant can fairly reply.

name: Prima facie obviousness criteria
description: To establish a prima facie case of obviousness, three basic criteria must be met: (1) some suggestion or motivation, either in the references themselves or in the general knowledge available to one of ordinary skill, to modify or combine reference teachings; (2) a reasonable expectation of success; and (3) the prior art reference(s) must teach or suggest all claim limitations.
guidance: The teaching/suggestion to make the claimed combination and the reasonable expectation of success must both be found in the prior art and not based on applicant’s disclosure. See MPEP §§ 2141–2144.09 for decisions and examples. Examiner must support each prong in the record.

name: Examiner burden to provide a convincing line of reasoning
description: The initial burden is on the examiner to provide some suggestion of the desirability of doing what the inventor has done; either the references must expressly or impliedly suggest the claimed invention or the examiner must present a convincing line of reasoning as to why the artisan would have found the claimed invention obvious in light of the references.
guidance: Cite Ex parte Clapp and MPEP §2144–§2144.09 for examples of adequate reasoning. The written rationale should be sufficient so that issues are clear and the applicant can respond; vague or conclusory assertions are insufficient.

name: Clarity of written record and explanation of rationale
description: It is important for an examiner to properly communicate the basis for a rejection so that the issues can be identified early and the applicant can be given fair opportunity to reply. The written record must clearly explain the rationale for decisions made during prosecution because issued patents are presumed valid and examiners cannot normally be compelled to testify about their mental processes.
guidance: Provide explicit reasoning in the Office action; ensure the record is sufficient to support later interpretations of claim scope and to withstand litigation challenges (35 U.S.C. 282, 261).

name: Determination of 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date for patents and application publications
