description: Use the AIPA/2002 amendments (form paragraphs 7.12 / 7.12.01) to determine the 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date of a U.S. patent or of a publication of a U.S. application, considering whether the reference was filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a) or is a U.S. patent issued from, or a U.S./WIPO publication of, an international application with an international filing date on or after November 29, 2000.
guidance: Consider priority/benefit claims to earlier-filed U.S. provisional applications (35 U.S.C. 119(e)), U.S. nonprovisional applications (35 U.S.C. 120 or 121), and international applications (35 U.S.C. 120, 121 or 365(c)) only if the relied-upon earlier-filed application's disclosure appropriately supports the subject matter. Do NOT consider priority/benefit claims to U.S. applications filed before an international application with international filing date prior to Nov 29, 2000. Do NOT consider foreign priority claims under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) and 365(a). If an international application had an international filing date prior to Nov 29, 2000 and did not designate the U.S. or was not published in English by WIPO, it is not prior art under 102(e) but may be applied under 102(a) or (b) as of its publication date.

name: Ways to overcome provisional 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/103 rejections
description: A provisional rejection can be overcome by: (A) arguing patentability over the earlier filed application; (B) combining the subject matter of the copending applications into a single application claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 of the prior applications and abandoning the copending applications (subject to 35 U.S.C. 112(first paragraph) support requirements); (C) filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 showing derivation (that unclaimed invention disclosed in the copending application was derived from the inventor of the other application); (D) filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 showing a date of invention prior to the effective U.S. filing date of the copending application; or (E) for applications filed on/after Nov 29, 1999, showing that the prior art and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, commonly owned or subject to obligation of assignment to the same person.
guidance: Be mindful that combining into a single application may not preserve 35 U.S.C. 120 benefit for claims that lack 112 support in prior applications; see Studiengesellschaft Kohle v. Shell Oil. Terminal disclaimers and 37 CFR procedures may also be relevant where common ownership exists and for double patenting issues.

name: 35 U.S.C. 103(c) disqualification of prior art (when prior art is excluded)
description: Subject matter developed by another person which qualifies as prior art only under subsections (e), (f), and (g) of section 102 shall not preclude patentability under 35 U.S.C. 103 where the subject matter and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.
guidance: 103(c) applies only to obviousness determinations under 35 U.S.C. 103, not to whether subject matter qualifies as prior art under 102. If subject matter qualifies as prior art under any other subsection (e.g., 102(a), 102(b), or 102(e) for certain dates), it will not be disqualified by 103(c). The burden is on the applicant/patentee to establish common ownership at the relevant time. See MPEP §706.02(l)(1).

name: Requirements for a continuing application to claim benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120
description: An application claiming benefit of a prior-filed copending national or international application under 35 U.S.C. 120 must name as an inventor at least one inventor named in the prior filed application, and the prior filed application must disclose the named inventor’s invention claimed in at least one claim of the later-filed application in the manner provided by the first paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112.
guidance: So long as at least one inventor is in common and other 120 requirements are met, the Office will permit a claim for 120 benefit without additional submissions unless examination reveals a need (e.g., intervening reference). Examiner should examine the earlier filed application to determine common inventorship and satisfaction of 112 support for at least one claim of the later application.

name: 35 U.S.C. 102(b) public use or on-sale rejections (evidence requirement)
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(b) based upon a public use or sale of the invention requires that a full explanation of the evidence establishing a public use or sale be provided in the Office action.
guidance: Ensure the Office action (bracket 2) includes a complete explanation of the supporting evidence and precede this form paragraph with the appropriate other form paragraphs as instructed (e.g., 7.07, 7.09, or 7.103).

name: 35 U.S.C. 102(c) abandonment rejections (evidence requirement)
description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(c) because the invention has been abandoned requires insertion of a full explanation of the evidence establishing abandonment of the invention.
guidance: Provide detailed factual support and refer to MPEP §2134 for further guidance. Precede with proper form paragraphs as instructed.

name: 35 U.S.C. 102(f) applicant not inventor (evidence requirement)
description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(f) because the applicant did not invent the claimed subject matter requires an explanation of the supporting evidence establishing that applicant was not the inventor.
guidance: Provide supporting evidence and cite MPEP §2137 for required procedures; precede with required form paragraphs (e.g., 7.07 and 7.13 or 7.103).

name: Petition content and timing
description: Proceedings begin with the filing of a petition that identifies all of the claims challenged and the grounds and supporting evidence on a claim-by-claim basis; the petition must be filed consistent with any statute-required time periods and be accompanied by the evidence the petitioner seeks to rely upon.
guidance: For IPR, PGR, and CBM the patent owner may file a preliminary response within three months of notification of a filing date; petitions should include claim-by-claim grounds and supporting evidence. (References: 35 U.S.C. 135(a), 311(c), § 42.3.)

name: Narrowing of issues at institution
description: Upon institution, the Board will narrow the issues for final decision by authorizing trial only on challenged claims and specific grounds for which threshold standards are met; any claim or issue not included in the authorization will not be part of the trial.
guidance: The Board will identify on a claim-by-claim basis the grounds authorized for trial; dissatisfied parties may seek rehearing for overlooked or misapprehended points (see § 42.71).

name: Right to depose declarants supporting amendments
description: Where a patent owner relies upon new declaration evidence in support of claim amendments, the petitioner will be authorized to depose those declarants and submit observations on the deposition.
guidance: Sequenced discovery anticipates depositions tied to filings; Board will authorize depositions consistent with Scheduling Order and fairness.

name: Receiving or transmitting data over a network
description: Receiving or transmitting data over a network (e.g., using the Internet to gather data) has been recognized by courts as a well-understood, routine, conventional computer function when claimed in a generic manner.
guidance: Case examples: Symantec (utilizing intermediary computer to forward information), TLI Communications (telephone for image transmission), OIP Techs. (sending messages over a network), buySAFE (computer receives and sends information over a network). Caveat: DDR Holdings distinguished claims that specify how Internet interactions are manipulated to yield a desired result (i.e., specifics may avoid being labeled generic). Analyze with other Step 2B considerations.

name: Performing repetitive calculations
description: Using a computer to perform repetitive calculations can be a conventional computer function when recited at a generic level.
guidance: Authorities: Flook (recomputing/readjusting alarm limit values), Bancorp Services v. Sun Life (computer used only for basic repetitive calculations does not impose meaningful limits). If the claimed computation imposes meaningful limits or specific improvements, it may not be merely conventional.

name: Electronic recordkeeping
description: Electronic recordkeeping (e.g., creating and maintaining shadow accounts or updating an activity log) is recognized as well-understood, routine, conventional activity when claimed generically.
guidance: Cited cases: Alice (creating/maintaining 'shadow accounts'), Ultramercial (updating an activity log). Consider whether the claim adds non-generic, meaningful limitations beyond mere recordkeeping.

name: Electronically scanning or extracting data from a physical document
description: Electronically scanning or extracting data from a physical document (e.g., OCR) is a recognized conventional activity when claimed at a high level of generality.
guidance: Case: Content Extraction and Transmission v. Wells Fargo (optical character recognition). Evaluate whether the claim recites specific technical improvements in how scanning/extraction is performed.

name: Web browser back and forward button functionality
description: Browser back/forward button functionality is an example of a well-understood, routine, conventional computer function when claimed generically.
guidance: Case: Internet Patent Corp. v. Active Network. Consider whether the claim adds a non-generic manner of implementing such functionality.

name: Determining the level of a biomarker in blood by any means
description: Determining a biomarker level in blood (by any means) is a life-sciences laboratory technique courts have recognized as well-understood, routine, conventional when claimed generically.
guidance: Authority: Mayo (determination of metabolites), Cleveland Clinic Foundation v. True Health Diagnostics. If the claim ties the measurement to a specific, unconventional application or integrates it into a meaningful limitation, it may be significantly more.

name: Using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) to amplify and detect DNA
description: PCR amplification and detection of DNA is recognized as a conventional laboratory technique when recited generically.
guidance: Cases: Genetic Techs. v. Merial; Ariosa v. Sequenom. Examiners should determine whether there is a non-generic application or unconventional technique that makes the claim significantly more.

name: Detecting DNA or enzymes in a sample
description: Detecting DNA or enzymes in a sample is a well-understood laboratory activity when claimed at a high level of generality.
guidance: Cited authorities: Sequenom; Cleveland Clinic Foundation. Assess whether the claim adds meaningful limitations beyond the generic detection step.

name: Immunizing a patient against a disease
description: Immunizing a patient is a conventional life-sciences activity recognized by courts when claimed generically.
guidance: Case: Classen Immunotherapies v. Biogen IDEC. Consider if the immunization step integrates analysis into a specific and tangible application (which may be meaningful).

name: Analyzing DNA to provide sequence information or detect allelic variants
description: Analyzing DNA to obtain sequence information or detect allelic variants is a recognized conventional laboratory activity when recited generically.
guidance: Authority: Genetic Techs. Evaluate whether claimed analysis is performed in a novel, unconventional manner or integrated into a meaningful application.

name: Amplifying and sequencing nucleic acid sequences
description: Amplifying and sequencing nucleic acids is a well-understood technique when claimed in a generic manner.
guidance: Case: Univ. of Utah Research Foundation v. Ambry Genetics. Assess for specific, unconventional methods or improvements.

name: Hybridizing a gene probe
description: Hybridizing a gene probe is a routine laboratory activity when recited generically.
guidance: Case: Ambry Genetics. Determine whether the claim recites a non-generic application or improvement.

name: Recording a customer’s order
description: Recording a customer's order is an example of other activity courts have found to be well-understood, routine, conventional when claimed generically.
guidance: Case: Apple v. Ameranth. Consider whether the claimed way of recording provides a specific technological improvement.

name: Shuffling and dealing a standard deck of cards
description: Shuffling and dealing a standard deck of cards is a conventional activity when claimed generically.
guidance: Case: In re Smith. Claims that merely recite such conventional activities without more are likely not to add significantly more than an abstract idea.

name: Restricting public access to media by requiring a consumer to view an advertisement
description: Requiring a consumer to view an advertisement to access media has been treated as routine activity when claimed generically.
guidance: Case: Ultramercial v. Hulu. Evaluate whether the claimed mechanism adds meaningful limitation or is mere routine activity.

name: Identifying undeliverable mail items, decoding data, and creating output data
description: Identifying undeliverable mail items, decoding data on those items, and creating output data is an example of activity courts have found routine when recited generically.
guidance: Case: Return Mail, Inc. v. U.S. Postal Service. Examine whether the claim recites specific, unconventional processing that would be significantly more.

name: Determining an estimated outcome and setting a price
description: Determining an estimated outcome and setting a price is an example of routine activity when claimed generically.
guidance: Case: OIP Techs. Analyze whether a claimed specific method of estimation/price-setting provides a meaningful limitation.

name: Arranging a hierarchy of groups, sorting information, eliminating less restrictive pricing information and determining the price
description: Arranging hierarchies, sorting information, eliminating less restrictive pricing info, and determining price are activities courts have recognized as conventional when recited generically.
guidance: Case: Versata Dev. Group v. SAP. Determine whether the claimed combination or arrangement provides a non-conventional technical improvement.

name: Whether the claim recites only the idea of a solution or outcome
description: A claim that recites only the idea of a solution or outcome—failing to recite details of how the solution is accomplished—is equivalent to merely saying 'apply it' and does not provide significantly more.
guidance: Authorities: Electric Power Group (caution against result-focused claims that effectively cover any solution), Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec, Internet Patents Corp. v. Active Network. By contrast, claiming a particular solution or way to achieve the outcome may provide significantly more. Example: Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One (claims describing modifications to underlying XML documents lacked specific steps and were held ineligible). Examiners should look for lack of mechanism, overly result-oriented language, or absence of specific steps as indications the claim merely recites an outcome.

name: Summary of invention statement
description: State whether the examiner disagrees with the summary of invention contained in the brief and, if deficient, explain the deficiency and include a correct summary if necessary.
guidance: If the summary is deficient, explain specifics (¶12.53.02). Include a correct summary when necessary for clear understanding of the claimed invention.

name: Grounds of rejection: explanation requirement
description: For each ground of rejection applicable to the appealed claims, provide an explanation of the ground of rejection or reference to a final rejection or other single prior action for a clear exposition of the rejection.
guidance: Explain each ground fully or point to a single prior action that does. If pointing to a prior action, ensure the prior action fully sets forth the rejection; otherwise supply the full explanation in the answer.

name: 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph explanation
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, the examiner's answer (or single prior action) shall explain how the first paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112 is not complied with, including how the specification/drawings (a) do not describe the subject matter defined by each rejected claim, (b) would not enable one skilled in the art to make and use the subject matter without undue experimentation, and (c) do not set forth the best mode contemplated by the appellant.
guidance: Provide specific references to specification/drawings and explain the deficiency claim-by-claim as appropriate.

name: 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph explanation
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, the examiner's answer (or single prior action) shall explain how the claims do not particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which applicant regards as the invention.
guidance: Identify claim language that is indefinite or fails the 'particular' and 'distinct' requirement and explain why.

name: 35 U.S.C. 102 anticipation explanation
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102, the examiner's answer (or single prior action) shall explain why the rejected claims are anticipated or not patentable under 35 U.S.C. 102, pointing out where all specific limitations recited in the rejected claims are found in the prior art relied upon.
guidance: Point to exact locations in the prior art (page/line/drawing) where each limitation is found.

name: 35 U.S.C. 103 obviousness explanation
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103, the examiner's answer (or single prior action) shall (i) state the ground of rejection and point out where each specific limitation is found in the prior art relied upon, (ii) identify any differences between the rejected claims and the prior art relied on, and (iii) explain how and why the claimed subject matter is rendered unpatentable over the prior art. If based on combination of references, explain the rationale for making the combination.
guidance: Provide a reasoned explanation tying claim limitations to references and rationale for combining teachings when applicable.

name: Limitations on combining individual rejections for amended claims
description: 37 CFR 1.193(a)(2) authorizes rejection in an examiner's answer of a claim that combines limitations previously rejected individually only to the extent that the advisory action identified the specific individual rejection(s) that would be used; combining multiple individual rejections into a new combined rejection (e.g., using A in view of B and C) where that combined rejection was not indicated may constitute a new ground and is not authorized.
guidance: Examples provided: combining claim 1 and 2 may be authorized if advisory action indicated that rejection; combining claims 1,2,3 into a new claim raising new issues may be refused entry.

name: Patentability requirements (overall)
description: To be patentable, an invention must fulfill several requirements that are broadly classified as novelty, inventive step (nonobviousness) and industrial applicability (utility); additionally the claimed subject matter must be eligible for patent protection under the relevant national/regional law.
guidance: All elements must be present in the single reference for lack of novelty; subject-matter eligibility is a threshold that gates further assessment of novelty and inventive step.

name: Novelty (anticipation)
description: Novelty generally requires that the claimed invention must not have been 'made available to the public' before the filing (or priority) date; lack of novelty (anticipation) occurs when all elements/features of a claim are found in a single prior art reference.
guidance: If at least one feature in the claimed invention is not in the single prior art reference, the claim may be novel. Example: a rocking chair claim that omits rocker attachments can be anticipated by a prior chair with four legs if the claimed elements match exactly. Avoid public disclosure before filing; use NDAs to preserve novelty.

name: Generic vs specific claim scope (novelty implications)
description: If a claim recites a generic concept and prior art discloses a specific example included in that generic concept, the prior art can destroy novelty; conversely, a claim to a specific concept may remain novel against prior art only disclosing a broader generic concept if the specific has distinguishing technical features.
guidance: Example: claim to 'conductive material' is anticipated by prior disclosure of 'copper material'; claim to 'copper material' may still be novel against prior disclosure of 'conductive material' if copper has distinguishing technical features (e.g., specific conductivity).

name: Analysis steps for inventive step (common approach)
description: Typical analysis involves determining: (1) the scope and content of the prior art; (2) the differences between the prior art and the claimed invention; and (3) the level of skill of those in the pertinent art.
guidance: Carefully compare claimed steps/features and prior art disclosures. If a person skilled in the art could obviously arrive at the claimed invention from the prior art, the invention is obvious.

name: Problem–solution approach (EPO-style inventive step analysis)
description: The problem–solution approach involves: (1) determining the closest prior art; (2) establishing distinguishing features between the claimed invention and that prior art; (3) formulating the objective technical problem; and (4) considering whether the claimed solution would have been obvious to the skilled person.
guidance: This structured approach is commonly used by the EPO and useful for framing inventive-step arguments and claim drafting to highlight technical effects and inventive contributions.

name: Patentable subject matter / Eligibility (threshold)
description: Subject-matter eligibility determines whether claimed subject matter falls within statutory categories (varies by jurisdiction) or whether it is excluded (laws of nature, abstract ideas, natural phenomena, etc.); only if eligible should novelty/inventive-step be assessed.
guidance: U.S.: positive statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter) but subject-matter limits developed by case law (law of nature, abstract idea, natural phenomenon). Japan: 'creation of a technical idea utilizing a law of nature.' EPC and others list nonpatentable examples rather than a positive definition.

name: Disclosure requirement (purpose and components)
description: In exchange for exclusive rights, patent applicants must sufficiently disclose the invention so the public can practice it after patent expiry; disclosure requirements typically include support/written description, enablement, and clarity, and in some countries a best mode requirement.
guidance: Disclosure ensures the claims are justified by the description and prevents adding new subject matter after filing. Poor initial drafting can preclude later amendment to add needed disclosure.

name: Support requirement / Written description
description: Claims must be supported by the description (written description requirement in the U.S.): there must be a basis in the description for every claim and the scope of claims must not be broader than justified by the description and drawings.
guidance: A claim is supported unless a person skilled in the art would be unable, based on the application as filed, to extend the teaching of the description to the whole claimed field. Draft descriptions to underpin all claim scope you may later pursue.

name: Clarity requirement
description: The disclosure and claims must be clear so that the scope of protection is communicated to others (clarity requirement).
guidance: Clarity problems can lead to rejections or limit enforceability. Draft claims and descriptions with precise language and avoid ambiguity.

name: Required content and form of a public-use petition
description: A petition under 37 CFR 1.292 must be submitted in writing, must specifically identify the application (application number or serial number and filing date), and should include a listing of all affidavits or declarations and exhibits relied on.
guidance: The petition must contain a sufficient description of the subject matter alleged to have been in 'public use' or 'on sale,' including any necessary photographs, drawings, diagrams, exhibits, or flowcharts to enable the examiner to compare the claimed subject matter to the alleged public-use/on-sale subject matter. The petition and accompanying papers must either (A) reflect service on applicant/attorney/agent, or (B) be filed in duplicate if service is not possible.

name: Examiner's prima facie showing standard for public use petitions
description: A prima facie case is established by the petition if the examiner finds that the facts asserted in the affidavit(s) or declaration(s), as supported by the exhibits, if later proved true by testimony taken in the public use proceeding, would result in a statutory bar to the claims under 35 U.S.C. 102(b) alone or in combination with 35 U.S.C. 103.
guidance: To make this determination the examiner must: identify exactly what was in public use or on sale; determine whether it was in use or on sale in this country more than 1 year before the effective filing date; and determine whether the pending claims 'read' on or are obvious over what has been shown to be in public use or on sale. Compare all pending claims with the matter alleged, not just claims identified by petitioner.

name: Petitions alleging obviousness must include prior art/explanation
description: In situations where the petition alleges only that the claims are obvious over subject matter asserted to be in public use or on sale, the petition should include prior art or other information on which it relies and explain how the prior art or other information in combination with the subject matter asserted renders the claims obvious.
guidance: The examiner is not expected to make a search in evaluating the petition. However, if the examiner is aware of prior art which, in his/her opinion, renders the claims obvious over the asserted subject matter, the examiner may determine that a prima facie case is established even if the petition alleged only anticipation under 35 U.S.C. 102(b).

name: Examiner memorandum when prima facie determination made
description: After making a determination, the examiner will forward a memorandum to the Patent Legal Administrator stating findings and decision as to whether a prima facie case has been established.
guidance: Findings should include a summary of alleged facts, a comparison of at least one claim with the device alleged to be in public use or on sale, and any other pertinent facts to aid the Patent Legal Administrator. The report should be prepared in triplicate.

name: Expert evidence may aid in construing patents
description: Expert evidence may aid the court in construing a patent.
guidance: Technical/expert testimony helps courts interpret specifications, claims, and art understood by skilled artisans.

name: Jury decides sufficiency of description; court decides sufficiency of claim
description: Jury determines sufficiency of the description; the court determines sufficiency of the claim.
guidance: Division of responsibility: factual sufficiency of disclosure may be for the jury; legal sufficiency/claim construction is for the court.

name: Doctrine of equivalents (equivalents defined)
description: 'Equivalent' defined; the doctrine of equivalents governs when unclaimed variations infringe.
guidance: Courts define 'equivalent' contextually; use of 'equivalent' language in claims creates interpretive issues (see multiple citations defining 'equivalent').

name: Joinder of generic and specific claims allowed in some circumstances
description: Joinder of generic and specific claims may be permissible.
guidance: Courts address when a generic claim may be joined with specific claims without prejudicing clarity or statutory requirements.

name: Distinction between art and apparatus
description: Courts distinguish between an art (process/method) and apparatus (device/product).
guidance: Different patentability and claim-drafting rules apply to processes versus apparatuses/products.

name: Patent construed as an entirety
description: A patent should be construed as an entirety (specification and claims read together).
guidance: Claims are interpreted in the context of the entire specification and prosecution history; piecemeal construction is disfavored.

name: Claim must distinguish old and new matter
description: A claim must distinguish the old (prior art) from the new (invention).
guidance: Claims should clearly indicate the novel contribution relative to prior art; description must enable this distinction.

name: Infringement by making, sale, or use
description: Infringement may occur by making, selling, or using the patented invention.
guidance: All three types of acts can constitute infringement depending on claim scope and territorial jurisdiction.

name: Patent privilege intended to secure disclosure
description: The patent privilege is intended to secure public disclosure of inventions in exchange for monopoly rights.
guidance: This quid pro quo underlies enablement/written-description requirements and limits on claim scope.

name: Ambiguity in description detrimental
description: Ambiguity in the description of the specification can defeat or limit a patent.
guidance: Specifications must be sufficiently precise; ambiguous wording can narrow claim scope or lead to invalidity.

name: Equivocal words (like 'equivalent') in claims are scrutinized
description: Equivocal terms such as 'equivalent' in claims are subject to close judicial scrutiny.
guidance: Use of imprecise catch-all language can create indefiniteness or interpretive issues; courts look to context and prosecution history.

name: Functional claims
description: Functional claiming is recognized but governed by limits and tests.
guidance: Claims reciting functions must still satisfy statutory requirements and be clear to those skilled in the art; courts have special scrutiny for pure functional claiming.

name: Structural law of a machine (structure controls)
description: The structural law (structure) of a machine is central to patent analysis of machine claims.
guidance: Courts evaluate the structural elements and their cooperation in machines to determine novelty and infringement.

name: Combination of designs and embodiment in drawings
description: Designs can be combined and must be embodied clearly in drawings to be protected.
guidance: Design patents rely on drawings to show claimed appearance; combinations of designs require clear depiction and claim scope.

name: Infringement by co-owners
description: Co-owners may infringe a patent by unauthorized acts; co-ownership does not immunize infringement.
guidance: Ownership structure affects standing and liability; co-owner exploitation may still give rise to infringement claims among co-owners or third parties.

name: Description construed with other parts of the specification
description: Claims and description are construed together with other parts of the specification and relevant records.
guidance: Interpretation is holistic; prosecution history and specification language influence claim scope and meaning.

name: Purpose of Description and Claim
description: The specification's description and the claim have distinct purposes: disclosure vs. defining monopoly scope.
guidance: Courts analyze the description to interpret claims, but claims define legal rights; both must be coherent.

name: Right to all species of a genus
description: The patentee has rights to all species of his disclosed genus under certain doctrines.
guidance: Broad genus claims can be allowed where the specification supports coverage of all species, but written-description and enablement constrain breadth.

name: Patent covers all modes of embodiment
description: A valid patent may cover all modes of embodiment of the claimed invention disclosed in the specification.
guidance: Courts interpret claims to encompass the disclosed embodiments; abstract principles without reduction are not patentable.

name: Principle or abstraction not patentable
description: A mere principle, idea, or abstraction is not patentable absent reduction to practice or specific application.
guidance: Claims to pure principles are invalid; patentability requires application/embodiment or reduction to practice.

name: Result or effect per se not patentable
description: A mere result or effect is not patentable without concrete means to achieve it.
guidance: Patents must claim concrete means/structure/process rather than abstract desired results.

name: Strict construction of letters-patent
description: Patents are subject to strict construction (narrow interpretation) in some doctrines.
guidance: Courts may construe patent claims narrowly against patentees when statutory or equitable reasons require.

name: Re-issue cannot be used to enlarge claims improperly
description: Re-issue will not be granted to improperly enlarge claims beyond original scope.
guidance: Re-issue is remedial but cannot expand monopoly beyond what was claimed/disclosed originally; unreasonable delay in seeking re-issue can invalidate it.

name: Patent extended to cover all modes of embodiment (reiterated)
description: A patent may be interpreted to extend to all modes of embodiment disclosed or fairly within claim scope.
guidance: Claim scope covers disclosed embodiments and equivalents subject to statutory limits; abstract principles alone are excluded.

name: Admissions by applicant constitute prior art
description: A statement by an applicant in the specification or made during prosecution identifying the work of another as 'prior art' is an admission which can be relied upon for both anticipation and obviousness determinations, regardless of whether the admitted prior art would otherwise qualify as prior art under the statutory categories of 35 U.S.C. 102.
guidance: Case law: Riverwood Int’l Corp. v. R.A. Jones & Co., 324 F.3d 1346 (Fed. Cir. 2003); Constant v. Advanced Micro-Devices Inc., 848 F.2d 1560 (Fed. Cir. 1988). If the admitted prior art anticipates the claim but does not qualify as prior art under any paragraphs of 35 U.S.C. 102, the claim may nevertheless be rejected as anticipated by the admitted prior art without citing 35 U.S.C. 102. (Also note caveat regarding same inventive entity—see separate metric.)

name: Examiner must determine whether an 'admission' is another's work or the inventor's own
description: When an applicant identifies subject matter as 'prior art,' the examiner must determine whether that subject matter is the inventor's own work or the work of another.
guidance: In making this determination, the examiner should consider any credible explanation provided by the applicant; in the absence of another credible explanation, examiners should treat the subject matter as the work of another. This determines whether the admission can be used as prior art against the claims.

name: Discussion of prior art in the specification constitutes an admission
description: Where the specification identifies work done by another as 'prior art,' the subject matter so identified is treated as admitted prior art.
guidance: Example: In re Nomiya, 509 F.2d 566 (CCPA 1975) — applicant’s labeling of figures as 'prior art' was held to be an admission that the pictured material was prior art relative to the claimed improvement. Examiners should treat explicit identification in the specification as an admission.

name: Jepson-format claims imply admission that the preamble is prior art (with possible rebuttal)
description: Drafting a claim in Jepson format is taken as an implied admission that the subject matter of the preamble is the prior art work of another.
guidance: Authority: 37 CFR 1.75(e); MPEP §608.01(m); In re Fout, 675 F.2d 297 (CCPA 1982). This implication may be overcome if the applicant gives another credible reason for using Jepson format (see In re Ehrreich, 590 F.2d 902 (CCPA 1979), where use to avoid double patenting was an acceptable explanation). Also, if the Jepson preamble actually describes the inventor’s own work, it should not be used against the claims (see Reading & Bates; Ehrreich).

name: Specification sheet separation and section placement (37 CFR 1.71(f))
description: The specification must commence on a separate sheet; each sheet including part of the specification may not include other parts of the application. The claim(s), abstract, and sequence listing (if any) should not be included on a sheet including any other part of the application.
guidance: Each of these sections (specification, abstract, claims, sequence listings) should begin on a new page because they are separately indexed in the Image File Wrapper; avoid overlap of sections on a single page.

name: Line spacing, font, and column requirements (37 CFR 1.52(b)(2))
description: The specification (including claims and abstract) must have lines that are 1.5 or double spaced; text in a nonscript type font (e.g., Arial, Times Roman, or Courier), preferably font size 12; capital letters at least 0.3175 cm high but no smaller than 0.21 cm; and only a single column of text.
guidance: Text may not be written solely in capital letters. Use readable font sizes; examiners may object for spacing or numerous errors (form paragraphs 6.29–6.31).

name: Page and paragraph numbering
description: Pages of the specification including claims and abstract must be consecutively numbered starting with 1, with numbers centrally located above or preferably below the text. Paragraphs (other than claims or abstract) may be numbered at filing using four numerals in square brackets (e.g., [0001]) with leading zeros and bold brackets.
guidance: Nontext elements are considered part of the surrounding paragraph and should not be independently numbered. Section headers are not considered paragraphs and should not be numbered.

name: 1412.03-Broadening Reissue Claims
description: Broadening Reissue Claims

name: Claims considered for determination
description: The determination should be made on the claims in effect at the time the decision is made (37 CFR 1.515(a)).
guidance: Evaluations of whether a substantial new question of patentability exists must reference the claim set currently in force when the examiner makes the decision; amended/changed claims at the time of decision govern the analysis.

name: Contains an inventive concept (Alice step 2)
description: Whether the claim supplies an "inventive concept" that transforms an abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter — i.e., reciting something significantly more than the abstract idea itself.
guidance: Courts found inventive concept where claims: recited components "in a specific manner for a specifically configured path," recited a "specific arrangement of components and a very specific implementation and structure of the executable program code," recited a "new kind of virus protection," or recited limitations that "improve the functioning of a computer" or constitute a "technical improvement over prior art ways." Courts also note that the fact a claim "adds little to the prior art ... does not mean that the claim lacks an inventive concept vis-à-vis an abstract idea."

name: Claims that improve computer or technological functioning are more likely eligible
description: Claims that are directed to or effectuate an improvement in computer/information technology (not merely using a computer as a tool) are treated as non-abstract or as providing an inventive concept.
guidance: Illustrations: claims that "improve the functioning of [a] computer due to 'user-configured business rules and configurable/application links,'" claims that make synchronization faster, reduce bandwidth/storage, enable synchronization across formats, improve cellular networking, enhance data compression or transmission efficiency, or "improve an existing technological process." Courts repeatedly accept eligibility where the claim solves a problem "rooted in computer technology."

name: Reciting specific physical components or tangible limitations supports eligibility
description: Claims that include concrete physical devices, apparatus elements, or steps requiring physical action (i.e., "activity outside of one's mind") are less likely to be characterized as abstract.
guidance: Cases treated claims as non-abstract where they recited a "piece of exercise equipment," "dispatch and mobile unit," "unmanned aerial vehicles," a "tangible resumption of an interrupted file download," a "new and useful arrangement" of hardware for haptic/vibrotactile devices, or where steps like "detecting the presence of a person at a door, sending a video, and speaking" were required. Courts emphasize physical or apparatus limitations ("specialized equipment" or "physical limitations") as favoring eligibility.

name: Specific arrangement or unconventional combination of known components can supply inventive concept
description: Claims that claim a non-conventional, non-generic arrangement or combination of known pieces can provide the inventive concept needed for eligibility.
guidance: Examples: courts credited claims that recited "a non-conventional and non-generic arrangement of known, conventional pieces," or recited an "unconventional arrangement" that avoided prior-art linkage practices (e.g., add/remove persons via buddy list). Such recitations may be treated as an inventive concept even where individual components are conventional.

name: Recitation of concrete implementation details (software/structure) supports eligibility
description: Claims that recite concrete implementation details (e.g., the "specific implementation and structure of the executable program code") rather than high-level functional results are more likely to be found to contain an inventive concept.
guidance: Cases found eligibility where claims described "a specific arrangement of components and a very specific implementation and structure of the executable program code," or "describe[d] how a solution will be implemented that addresses a business challenge particular to the Internet." The level of claimed specificity and structure is a recurring factor.

name: Problems unique to computer/technical world weigh toward eligibility
description: If the claimed invention addresses a problem that exists only in the technical realm (e.g., Internet, cellular networks, IMS architectures, distinguishing humans from computers), courts view the claim as more likely to be non-abstract.
guidance: Holdings: claims solving issues "created by the design of cellular networks," "a problem that currently exists only within the technical world" (e.g., CAPTCHA), or problems specific to IMS architectures or online gaming have been held not to be directed to abstract ideas.

name: Mathematical formulas or algorithms are suspect but can be eligible when improving technology
description: Claims directed to mathematical formulas or algorithms are often characterized as abstract, but eligibility can be found where the mathematical element is applied to effect a technological improvement.
guidance: Example: some MPEG decoder claims were "directed to no more than a mathematical formula," but the court nonetheless found they did "attempt to improve a technological issue" and thus did not lack an inventive concept. Courts look for application of math/algorithms to solve a technical problem.

name: Claims that limit themselves to a particular technological environment or concrete structure can show inventive concept
description: Limiting claims to a particular technological environment (e.g., cellular communications) or to a particular concrete device/structure can support a finding of inventive concept.
guidance: Examples: claims limited to "cellular communications and the concrete structure of a mobile device," claims reciting "the inclusion of a specific set of 16 cyclic shift intervals," or reciting a dispatch/mobile unit were treated as having inventive concept by virtue of their concrete technological framing.

name: Failure of defendant to show elements are 'well‑understood, routine, conventional' undermines finding of no inventive concept
description: Courts treat evidence about whether claimed limitations are merely well-understood, routine, and conventional as dispositive; absent such evidence, a challenge under step two may fail.
guidance: Example: a court denied summary judgment where defendants "failed to submit any evidence that the claims recited 'well‑understood, routine or conventional activities.'" Thus the party attacking eligibility bears an evidentiary burden on conventionality.

name: Reciting 'how' a solution is implemented (not just the result) favors eligibility
description: Claims that explain 'how' a claimed result is achieved — i.e., specific processes, links, business rules, or component interactions — are more likely to survive §101 scrutiny than claims that assert only an outcome.
guidance: For example, claims that "specif[y] how a solution will be implemented that addresses a business challenge particular to the Internet" or recite "user-configured business rules and configurable/application links" were treated as improving computer functioning and thus non-abstract.

name: Claims solving scaling or architecture-specific networking problems are more likely eligible
description: Claims that propose a novel network structure or approach to transmit/distribute data as the number of participants scales or that address architecture-specific issues (e.g., IMS) are seen as addressing technical problems and not mere abstract ideas.
guidance: Cases found eligibility where claims covered "an innovative network structure for the distribution of data as the number of participants in a computer network is scaled," or where claims solved a "particular technical problem that only existed in wireless communication networks operating under an IMS architecture."

name: Claims that provide tangible improvements to device capabilities are eligible
description: Claims that effect tangible changes in device operation or provide capabilities beyond traditional systems (e.g., controlling device configurations, enabling new detection modalities) support eligibility.
guidance: Examples: volume control claims providing capabilities beyond hardwired systems, POS terminal improvements, or haptic devices notifying users via vibration were held non-abstract because the claims improved device functionality.

name: Limiting to particular data formats, storage/synchronization methods, or bandwidth optimizations supports eligibility
description: Claims that specify particular data-format handling, synchronization methods across formats, or bandwidth/storage optimizations can be treated as technological improvements rather than abstract ideas.
guidance: Instances: claims reciting faster synchronization, reducing bandwidth and storage, enabling synchronization without physical connection, and lossless compression/decompression tied to storage/retrieval were found to improve computer/data-handling technology.

name: Recitation of specialized codes, intervals, or multi-code procedures can indicate specificity/non‑abstractness
description: Claims that require particular codes, numerous access codes, or specific interval sets are treated as reciting specialized procedures rather than generic abstraction.
guidance: Examples: claims using "four different access codes," a "specific set of 16 cyclic shift intervals," or similar particularized procedural limitations were relied upon by courts to conclude the claims recited specialized procedures and thus were not merely abstract.

name: Functional/overbroad claim drafting favors ineligibility when lacking technical detail
description: Claims drafted as broad functional results (e.g., "providing directions") without technical detail or concrete implementation are vulnerable to being characterized as abstract and ineligible.
guidance: In some cases courts found claims covering "providing directions in a natural language" or other high-level functionality to be non-abstract only where the claim also recited particular technical implementations; otherwise broad functional language alone is risky.

name: Use of the term 'invention' in specification
description: Avoid using in the description phrases such as 'the invention is …' and use instead 'an embodiment of the invention' or 'an exemplification of the invention.'
guidance: Describing embodiments as 'an embodiment' promotes broader interpretation of claims; stating 'the invention is X' can unnecessarily narrow claim scope.

name: Avoiding limiting the claims via description/drawings
description: Condition discussions of context, drawings and example operation so that the context does not necessarily become limiting (i.e., part of the invention).
guidance: Be careful with wording and examples so they do not become construed as essential features during prosecution or litigation; take care especially with means-plus-function claims where unnecessary detail in drawings may be later argued as essential.

name: Preferred/optional features description
description: Subject matter or features in dependent claims should be described as preferred or optional embodiments or features; otherwise they may be regarded as 'essential' features.
guidance: Recite advantages of preferred/optional features (useful if amendment becomes necessary). If a claim sets out a preferred feature or range, set out further characteristics or narrower ranges. Note: in the United States practitioners often avoid discussing 'preferred' embodiments because case law affects infringement analysis.

name: Number of embodiments/examples tied to claim scope
description: The number of embodiments or examples required depends on the scope of the claims: many mechanical inventions may need a single embodiment with alternatives; chemical/biological inventions may require many examples.
guidance: Provide sufficient examples to support broad claims, especially in chemistry/biology where evidentiary examples are often necessary.

name: Drawings are key supporting materials
description: The patent drafter is required to prepare good visual supporting materials; some drafters consider drawings the most important part of the application after the claims, particularly in mechanical, electrical and electronic fields.
guidance: Drawings should explain the invention; sometimes they can stand alone with the description confirming what the drawings show.

name: Abstract: purpose and drafting timing
description: The abstract is intended to summarize the essentials of the invention; its main purpose is to aid searching and it should be brief and accurate.
guidance: Often a version of the first paragraph of the summary will work. Prepare the abstract at the end of drafting to avoid disclosing elements not present elsewhere; ask whether every element in the abstract is disclosed in the description and claims—if not, add it or modify the abstract.

name: Abstract should not be used to interpret claims (with US exception)
description: In most countries the abstract delivers technical information and cannot be taken into account to interpret claim scope or patentability; the United States is an exception where abstracts should be drafted broadly to avoid limitation.
guidance: In the U.S., inclusion of reference indicators in the abstract has been found to narrow claim interpretation and should generally be omitted or deleted.

name: Domestic/priority filing timing
description: First filing of a patent application establishes the priority date for the family of foreign applications; clients typically want first filing domestically and as early as possible.
guidance: File early to secure priority; determine whether later foreign filings will claim priority under the Paris Convention within 12 months.

name: Requirement to name actual inventor(s) (35 U.S.C. 115/37 CFR 1.48)
description: An application must include the name of the inventor for any invention claimed in the application (35 U.S.C. 115(a)); the Office presumes named inventors are the actual inventors.
guidance: If an application names a person who is not the actual inventor, remedy via derivation proceeding (35 U.S.C. 135), correction of inventorship under 37 CFR 1.48, or rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 and 115 as appropriate. Applicant should submit a request to correct inventorship under 37 CFR 1.48; absent such a request in rare clear cases, Office personnel should reject claims under 35 U.S.C. 101 and 35 U.S.C. 115 (use Form Paragraph 7.04.02.aia).

name: Form paragraph usage for improper inventorship rejections
description: Use Form Paragraph 7.04.02.aia to reject claims under 35 U.S.C. 101 and 115 for failing to set forth the correct inventorship; use 7.04.101.aia or 7.04.102.aia to state statutory bases.
guidance: Follow bracket insertion instructions (e.g., explain supporting evidence in bracket 1). Precede rejection with required form paragraphs as noted in Examiner Notes.

name: Obviousness assessed as of effective filing date (AIA 35 U.S.C. 103)
description: AIA 35 U.S.C. 103 determines obviousness as of the effective filing date of the claimed invention rather than the date the invention was made.
guidance: This generally aligns practice with pre-AIA use of effective filing date as proxy for invention date, but where evidence of an earlier invention date exists (affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131), differences may arise.

name: Obviousness requires consideration of differences between claimed invention and prior art
description: AIA 35 U.S.C. 103 requires consideration of 'the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art.'
guidance: This follows Graham v. John Deere and Federal Circuit reasoning that 'claims' define the invention; examiners should ascertain differences between prior art and the claims when determining obviousness.

name: Non-enabling disclosures are prior art for obviousness
description: A non-enabling disclosure is still prior art for all it teaches for purposes of determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103.
guidance: Even if a reference does not enable the claimed invention (and thus cannot anticipate under 102), it may still be applied in a 103 obviousness rejection for what it teaches (see Symbol Techs. Inc. v. Opticon Inc.; Beckman Instruments v. LKB Produkter AB).

name: Form paragraph 7.20.02.aia: presumption of common ownership for joint inventors
description: When an application names joint inventors, the examiner presumes that the subject matter of the claims was commonly owned at the time inventions were effectively filed absent evidence to the contrary.
guidance: Applicant must point out inventor and effective filing dates for each claim not commonly owned under 37 CFR 1.56 so examiner can consider applicability of 102(b)(2)(C). Use this paragraph in all post-March 16, 2013 applications with joint inventors (unless claims clearly limited to one invention). Must be preceded by 7.03.aia.

name: 7.23.aia: Test for Obviousness (Graham factors summarized)
description: Factual inquiries for determining obviousness: (1) determine scope and contents of the prior art; (2) ascertain differences between the prior art and the claims at issue; (3) resolve the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; (4) consider objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
guidance: This paragraph may be used in response to arguments regarding applicability of factors for determining obviousness. Use in AIA-examined applications (filed on/after March 16, 2013) and preceded by 7.03.aia.

name: Form paragraph 7.27.aia: combined 102/103 rejection when status ambiguous
description: Use paragraph 7.27.aia to reject claims under 35 U.S.C. 102 (anticipation) and alternatively under 35 U.S.C. 103 (obviousness) when the determination of whether the reference anticipates or makes the claim obvious depends on claim interpretation or other uncertainties.
guidance: This paragraph is NOT intended as a routine substitute for a 102 rejection; use only in specific circumstances (examples provided a–f) such as disputed claim interpretation, inherent properties, genus/species issues, product-by-process equivalence, means-plus-function uncertainty, or overlapping ranges. Must be preceded by 7.07.aia and 7.08.aia and/or 7.12.aia or by form paragraph 7.103; include full explanation of both theories.

name: Determine applicability date (whether application is subject to FITF AIA provisions)
description: Because AIA changes to 102 and 103 apply only to applications filed on or after March 16, 2013, examiners must determine the effective filing date of claimed invention to know whether to apply AIA or pre-AIA provisions.
guidance: Applications filed before March 16, 2013 are governed by pre-AIA 102 and 103 even if an RCE is filed or national stage entered after March 16, 2013. Adding claims via amendment that introduces new matter after that date does not make the application subject to AIA (35 U.S.C. 132(a)). For PCTs and continuity claims, see MPEP § 2159 et seq.

name: Review for Prior Public Use/On-Sale and Best Mode Risks
description: Examiners must determine whether affidavits/declarations and accompanying evidence show that the claimed invention was in public use or on sale in the U.S. more than one year prior to the effective filing date (statutory bar), and whether the evidence indicates failure to disclose the best mode.
guidance: Even if a reference is antedated, applicant's own prior public use/on-sale activities may create a statutory bar under 35 U.S.C. 102(b). If the 1.131 evidence relies on an embodiment not disclosed in the application, consider the best mode requirement and make a best-mode rejection only if preponderance of the evidence shows specification fails to set forth the best mode. See MPEP §§ 2133.03 and 2165-2165.04.

name: Requirement for Oath/Declaration Under 37 CFR 1.132
description: When any claim of an application or a patent under reexamination is rejected or objected to, any evidence submitted to traverse the rejection or objection on a basis not otherwise provided for must be by way of an oath or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132.
guidance: This is the general policy for receiving affidavit evidence traversing rejections or objections. All affidavits/declarations not falling under other specific rules are to be treated under this rule. Use form paragraphs 7.65 or 7.66 and subparagraphs 7.66.01–7.66.05 as appropriate to comment on a 1.132 affidavit or declaration.

name: Form Paragraph 7.66 — Affidavit/Declaration Insufficient
description: Template stating that the affidavit/declaration filed is insufficient to overcome the rejection of specified claim(s) based upon identified grounds, followed by reasons for insufficiency.
guidance: Examiner must state specific reasons for insufficiency (e.g., untimely; fails to set forth facts; facts not germane to rejection; showing not commensurate in scope with claims) and include a detailed explanation. May employ form paragraphs 7.66.01–7.66.05 as appropriate.

name: 7.66.03 — Refers Only to Invention, Not to Claims (Insufficient)
description: Affidavit refers only to the system described in the application and not to the individual claims; does not show that objective evidence of nonobviousness is commensurate in scope with the claims.
guidance: Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.66; provide full explanation if appropriate. Evidence must be commensurate in scope with the claims to be probative.

name: 7.66.04 — No Evidence of Long-Felt Need (Insufficient)
description: Affidavit states the claimed subject matter solved a long-standing problem but provides no showing that others of ordinary skill were working on the problem or that knowledge of the cited references would not have enabled them to solve it.
guidance: Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.66 and include a full explanation if appropriate. Mere assertion of long-felt need without evidence is insufficient (see MPEP § 716.04).

name: Objective Evidence of Nonobviousness Must Be Considered When Timely Presented
description: Affidavits/declarations containing evidence of criticality or unexpected results, commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, skepticism of experts, etc., must be considered in determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103.
guidance: Cites Stratoflex, Graham v. John Deere, In re Palmer, In re Fielder and others. Comparative data in the specification intended to illustrate the claimed invention must be considered. Lack of objective evidence does not weigh in favor of obviousness, but failure to rebut a prima facie case can be dispositive.

name: Allegations of Unexpected Results — Substantive Standard
description: Any differences between the claimed invention and the prior art may result in differences in properties; the key is whether the properties differ to such an extent that the difference is truly unexpected (a marked improvement or difference in kind rather than merely degree).
guidance: Case law examples: In re Merck & Co., In re Waymouth, In re Wagner, Ex parte Gelles. Evidence of greater-than-expected results (including synergism) can support nonobviousness, but applicants must show results greater than those expected from the prior art to an unobvious extent and that the results provide a significant, practical advantage. Greater-than-additive effects are not necessarily sufficient if such effects could have been expected.

name: Effective filing date is of the claimed invention
description: Clarified that the effective filing date is of 'the claimed invention' in the application or patent.
guidance: When determining priority and effective dates, focus on the claimed invention(s) — the effective date pertains to the claims for which entitlement is asserted.

name: Attribution language for secondary considerations
description: Replaced 'DERIVED FROM' with 'ATTRIBUTABLE TO' and replaced 'directly derived from' with 'a result of' in subsection I.
guidance: Use refined attribution language when assessing whether secondary considerations (e.g., commercial success) are attributable to the claimed invention rather than external factors.

name: Recapture / surrendered subject matter guidance
description: Clarified that, in the context of recapture case law, claims are considered canceled if they were replaced by other claims that are more specific than the canceled claims in at least one aspect in order to overcome a rejection; added examples, definitions (SGL), flowchart, and related citations (In re McDonald, In re Youman, In re Mostafazadeh).
guidance: Provides a stepwise framework for analyzing recapture: identify canceled claims, determine whether reissue claims broaden in ways that relate to surrendered subject matter, and apply situational examples; use revised flowchart and cross-references.

name: Claim construction timing and evidence rules
description: Replaced 'the time the invention was made' with 'the relevant time' and emphasized that it is not necessary to identify a single statutory category into which a claim falls so long as it is clear the claim falls into at least one statutory category; included numerous case law citations (Phillips, Salazar, Sisvel, Malvern Panalytical, Actelion, CCS Fitness, Apple v. Corephotonics, Biogen, United Therapeutics, Amgen, etc.).
guidance: Use 'relevant time' for claim construction analyses, consult cited case law for rules on consulting extrinsic evidence and claim meaning, and apply the flexible statutory-category approach when assessing claim eligibility/subject matter classification.

name: Examiners must explain when claim limitations are mere 'apply it' instructions
description: For claim limitations that do not amount to more than a recitation of the words 'apply it' (or an equivalent), such as mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer, examiners should explain why they do not meaningfully limit the claim in an eligibility rejection.
guidance: If limitations merely instruct application of an exception (e.g., implementing on a generic computer), explain why they are not meaningful limitations; see Alice and MPEP §2106.07(a) for formulating subject matter eligibility rejections. Provide claim-specific reasoning showing lack of meaningful limitation.

name: Whether the claim invokes computers or other machinery merely as tools
description: Assess whether the claim invokes a computer or other machinery merely as a tool to perform an existing process (use of general-purpose computers in their ordinary capacity does not add significantly more).
guidance: Using a computer to receive, store, or transmit data, or adding generic computer components to an abstract idea, is insufficient (cites Affinity Labs, TLI Communications, Alice). Claims that improve computer capabilities or existing technology (Enfish, McRO) may provide significantly more. Provide claim-specific analysis showing whether claimed machine usage is conventional or represents a technological improvement. See MPEP §2106.05(a) for improvements to computer functioning.

name: The particularity or generality of the application of the judicial exception
description: Evaluate how particularly the claim confines the judicial exception: broad applicability across many fields or claiming every mode of achieving an effect suggests merely adding 'apply it'; limitations that confine the exception to a particular, practical application may amount to significantly more.
guidance: Broad, result-oriented recitations that do not restrict how the effect is achieved are likely not meaningful limitations (cites Internet Patents Corp., O’Reilly v. Morse, The Telephone Cases). In contrast, combinations that specify how interactions are manipulated to yield a desired result (DDR Holdings, BASCOM, Diehr) can be meaningful. Consider whether limitations integrate the exception into a technical process or are mere field-of-use token additions.

name: Whether the extra-solution limitation is well known
description: Determine if the extra-solution limitation is well-known or conventional, which supports a finding that it is token or insignificant extra-solution activity.
guidance: Cases finding well-known limitations to be token include Bilski (well-known random analysis techniques), Flook, and Intellectual Ventures I v. Erie Indem. Co. (use of a well-known XML tag). If a limitation is known in the field, explain why it does or does not meaningfully limit the claim.

name: Examples of mere data gathering considered insignificant
description: Courts have found the following to be mere data gathering and therefore insignificant extra-solution activity: performing clinical tests to obtain inputs, testing a system for response, presenting offers and gathering statistics, obtaining transaction information via the Internet to verify credit card transactions, consulting/updating an activity log, determining biomarker levels in blood.
guidance: Use these examples (In re Grams; In re Meyers; OIP Technologies; CyberSource; Ultramercial; Mayo) as analogous guidance when evaluating claimed data-gathering steps; explain claim-specific parallels or distinctions.

name: Examples of insignificant application (post-solution or trivial physical steps)
description: Courts have described steps such as cutting hair after determining style or printing/downloading generated menus as insignificant application of an exception.
guidance: See In re Brown and Ameranth for non-precedential examples; explain whether post-solution physical steps are integrated or merely incidental to the claimed inventive concept.

name: Insignificant computer implementation as extra-solution activity
description: Some cases identify insignificant computer implementation (using generic computer functionality) as an example of insignificant extra-solution activity or as a mere instruction to apply an exception.
guidance: See Fort Properties v. American Master Lease, Bancorp Services v. Sun Life, and cross-reference MPEP §2106.05(f) for additional guidance about insignificant computer implementation. Distinguish claims that improve computer functionality (Enfish, McRO) from those that merely use generic computer functions.

name: Examiners must explain when added elements are insignificant extra-solution activity
description: For claim limitations that add insignificant extra-solution activity to the judicial exception (e.g., mere data gathering), examiners should explain in an eligibility rejection why they do not meaningfully limit the claim.
guidance: Provide concrete reasoning (e.g., adding a final storing step to a mathematical formula does not add a meaningful limitation). See MPEP §2106.07(a) for formulating eligibility rejections and consider particular machine, transformation, well-understood/routine/conventional, and field-of-use factors.

name: Field of use and technological environment limitations are not per se inventive
description: Limitations that merely link a judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use (i.e., 'field of use' limitations) do not amount to significantly more than the exception itself.
guidance: The Supreme Court and Federal Circuit (Parker v. Flook, Bilski, Affinity Labs) hold that token field-of-use restrictions (e.g., limiting use to a particular industry or device type) do not confer eligibility. Compare with Diamond v. Diehr where limitations were integrated into a process. Evaluate whether the limitation is integrated into and alters how the claimed steps are performed, rather than being incidental or token.

name: Integration into the claim as a whole vs. token field-of-use additions
description: Assess whether the additional element is integrated into the claim as a whole (meaningfully affects how steps are carried out) rather than merely incidentally limiting the field of use.
guidance: Integrated, specific limitations acting in concert to transform a product/process (Diehr) can make a claim eligible; incidental, token additions (e.g., merely stating a device or audience) do not (Flook, Affinity Labs). Look for changes to the sequence, structure, or functioning caused by the limitation.

name: ER 1.13(b) — Failure to advise client about suspected theft and declarations
description: Respondent violated ER 1.13(b) by failing to advise TASER that Respondent believed one of TASER's employees had stolen the technology giving rise to certain technology and had signed a declaration under oath claiming sole inventorship of the technology.
guidance: A lawyer must advise an organizational client of information reasonably necessary to enable the client to protect its interests.

name: Non-contingent motion to amend (meaning/effect)
description: A “non-contingent” motion to amend means that the panel will not determine the patentability of the original substituted claims, which will be cancelled, and instead the panel will consider the merits of the motion to amend and, if the procedural requirements are met, provide a final written decision on the patentability of the substitute claims.
guidance: If a motion to amend is non-contingent, the Board will evaluate the substitute claims on their merits and may cancel the original claims rather than conditionally keeping them pending the outcome of the motion. The Trial Hearing Order should reflect the non-contingent nature of the motion.

name: Use of appendices and claim listings vs. substantive briefing
description: The motion to amend itself, not the claim listing (discussed below), must set forth the written description support. The appendix (claim listing) may be filed but shall not contain substantive briefing.
guidance: Claim listings and claim charts can be placed in an appendix (which typically does not count toward page limits), but all substantive arguments and evidence supporting a motion to amend — including written-description support — must be in the motion itself, not relegated to an appendix. Courts/Board will not accept substantive briefing hidden in an appendix.

name: 37 C.F.R. § 42.121(b) — written-description support requirement for motions to amend
description: A motion to amend must set forth written description support in the originally filed disclosure of the subject patent for each proposed substitute claim.
guidance: The motion itself must identify where the originally filed patent disclosure supports each proposed substitute claim; merely including a claim listing or chart in an appendix is insufficient to satisfy § 42.121(b). The Western Digital guidance (cited) reinforces that the motion must contain the written‑description support.

name: 37 C.F.R. § 42.23(b) — scope of replies (no new issues)
description: A reply may only respond to arguments raised in the corresponding opposition; a reply that raises a new issue will not be considered.
guidance: Parties should not use a reply to present new substitute claims or new substantive issues beyond responding to the opposition. The Board will not attempt to parse replies to separate proper from improper content; case law (e.g., Intelligent Bio-Systems v. Illumina) supports refusing replies that raise new issues.

name: Oral hearing structure and time allocation
description: The Board modified the Trial Hearing Order to allocate 45 minutes total time to Petitioner and Patent Owner each, and set the order: Petitioner opens on original challenged claims and specified proposed substitute claims; Patent Owner responds; Petitioner may reserve rebuttal time (no more than half its total) and Patent Owner may reserve sur-rebuttal (no more than half its total).
guidance: Parties should plan oral argument within allotted total times and be prepared to address both original challenged claims and any substitute claims the Board has agreed to consider. Rebuttal and sur-rebuttal time is limited to half of a party's total allocated time.

name: Affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(c) to disqualify commonly owned patent for 35 U.S.C. 103
description: When a claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 on a U.S. patent or publication that is not prior art under 102(b) and the inventions are not identical but not patentably distinct and are owned by the same party, the applicant may disqualify the patent/publication as prior art.
guidance: To disqualify the patent/publication the applicant must submit (1) a terminal disclaimer in accordance with § 1.321(c); and (2) an oath or declaration stating current common ownership and that the inventor named in the examined application is the prior inventor under 35 U.S.C. 104 (as in effect on March 15, 2013).

name: Applicability — which applications/patents 1.131 applies to
description: The provisions apply to any application for patent, and to any patent issuing thereon, that contains (1) a claim to an invention that has an effective filing date before March 16, 2013; or (2) a specific reference under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, 365(c), or 386(c) to any patent or application that itself contains a claim with an effective filing date before March 16, 2013.
guidance: Where § 1.130 applies (AIA-era exceptions), § 1.131 applicability is limited only to rejections under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g). See MPEP cross-references for AIA-era practice.

name: Inappropriate — statutory double patenting (F)
description: An affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(a) is inappropriate where the reference patent or application publication claims the same invention and the claimed invention under examination is subject to statutory double patenting.
guidance: See MPEP § 804 for double patenting issues and resolution (terminal disclaimers, etc.).

name: Reference date to be overcome — US patents, US application publications, and international publications
description: The date to be overcome under 37 CFR 1.131(a) is the effective date of the reference (i.e., the date on which the reference is available as prior art). For domestic patents used as references under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) the effective date is the earlier of the actual filing date of the reference U.S. patent or U.S. patent application and the earliest claimed domestic benefit date that the reference is entitled to, but not the foreign priority date.
guidance: In re Hilmer supports that foreign filing date is not the relevant effective date when used as a reference under pre-AIA 102(e). See MPEP §§ 2136‑2136.03 for detailed rules on effective dates.

name: Reference date to be overcome — activities
description: For activities relied on (e.g., public use, sales, knowledge by others), the effective date of the activity used to reject the claims is the date the activity was first known to have occurred.
guidance: See MPEP §§ 2120.02 and 2133.03 for handling activities and determining their effective dates.

name: 7.57.fti — Affidavit/Declaration Under 37 CFR 1.131(a): Ineffective — Heading
description: The filed affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(a) has been considered but is ineffective to overcome the [reference].
guidance: Bracket instructions: insert either '--affidavit--' or '--declaration--' and follow with one or more of form paragraphs 7.58.fti to 7.63.fti or a paragraph setting forth the proper basis for insufficiency (e.g., failure to establish acts performed in this country, scope not commensurate with claims).

name: Review for prior public use/on sale and best mode (715.10)
description: Examiners must review affidavits/declarations and accompanying evidence carefully to determine whether they show that the claimed invention was 'in public use' or 'on sale' in this country more than one year prior to the effective filing date (statutory bar under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)).
guidance: Even if the affidavit antedates the reference, applicant’s own prior public use or sale may create a statutory bar that cannot be overcome by 1.131(a). Where the affidavit relies on an embodiment not disclosed in the application, an examiner must consider whether the best mode requirement is violated and should only make a best mode rejection if the record establishes by a preponderance of the evidence that the specification fails to set forth the best mode contemplated (see MPEP §§ 2165‑2165.04).

name: Use claims lacking active steps may be indefinite
description: A claim that merely recites a 'use' without setting forth any active, positive steps involved in the process generally raises an issue of indefiniteness under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph.
guidance: Example: claim to 'a process for using monoclonal antibodies ... to isolate and purify human fibroblast interferon' held indefinite (Ex parte Erlich). Such 'use' claims that do not purport to claim a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter may also fail 35 U.S.C. 101 (In re Moreton). Consider rejection under 112(b) and/or 101 where appropriate.

name: Claims cannot import specification limitations
