description: Although a claim should be interpreted in light of the specification disclosure, it is generally improper to read limitations contained in the specification into the claims.
guidance: Do not rely on the specification to impart limitations to the claim that are not recited in the claim. See In re Prater and In re Winkhaus for discussion.

name: Use claims may be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 and/or 112
description: It is appropriate to reject a claim that recites a use but fails to recite steps under 35 U.S.C. 101 and 35 U.S.C. 112(b) if the facts support both rejections.
guidance: When facts support both grounds, make both rejections so applicant can address them; cite appropriate form paragraphs for 112(b) (see MPEP §2175).

name: 'Utilizing' or similar step can be definite in some cases
description: Recitation of a step such as 'utilizing' has been held not indefinite where the step is clear in context.
guidance: Example: Ex parte Porter — a claim reciting the step of 'utilizing the nozzle of claim 7' was found not indefinite. Evaluate context and whether the step imparts sufficient meaning.

name: Omnibus claims are indefinite
description: An omnibus claim (e.g., 'A device substantially as shown and described') should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as indefinite for failing to point out what is included or excluded by the claim language.
guidance: See Ex parte Fressola for history/explanation. Use form paragraph 7.35 to reject omnibus claims; see MPEP §1302.04(b) for cancellation upon allowance.

name: Incorporation by reference to figures/tables only when necessary
description: Incorporation by reference to a specific figure or table in a claim is permitted only in exceptional circumstances where there is no practical way to define the invention in words and where incorporation is more concise than duplicating a drawing or table.
guidance: Incorporation by reference is a 'necessity doctrine', not for applicant convenience (Ex parte Fressola). Where possible, claims should be complete in themselves.

name: Reference characters in claims generally don't affect scope
description: Reference characters corresponding to elements recited in the detailed description and the drawings may be used in conjunction with recitation of the same element or group of elements in the claims; generally their presence or absence does not affect claim scope.
guidance: See MPEP §608.01(m) for treatment of reference characters.

name: Chemical formula/compound claims not indefinite absent error
description: Claims to chemical compounds and compositions are not to be considered indefinite or speculative merely because a structure is not fully presented or because corroborating spectroscopic/other data are absent.
guidance: Examples/cases: Ex parte Morton; Ex parte Sobin; In re Fisher reversed a rejection for failure to identify entire structure. Compounds may be claimed by a name understandable to one skilled in the art, by physical/chemical characteristics, or by the process by which they are made (Ex parte Brian). The absence of corroborating data alone is not a basis for indefiniteness.

name: Trademarks/trade names in claims require careful analysis
description: The presence of a trademark or trade name in a claim is not per se improper under 35 U.S.C. 112(b), but the claim must be analyzed to determine how the mark or name is used in the claim.
guidance: A trademark identifies source, not the goods; if used to identify/describe a particular material or product, the claim fails 112(b) (Ex parte Simpson). If present but not intended as a limitation, explain why; if it causes confusion as to scope, reject under 112(b).

name: Process claims shouldn't be rejected solely for defining inherent function of an apparatus
description: Method/process claims should not be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) merely because they define the inherent function of a disclosed machine or apparatus.
guidance: In re Tarczy-Hornoch: an otherwise patentable process claim should not be rejected simply because the application discloses an apparatus that will inherently carry out the recited steps.

name: Compact prosecution: identify all grounds and explain indefinite term interpretation
description: The examiner should review each claim for compliance with every statutory requirement in the initial review and identify all applicable grounds of rejection in the first Office action; when a claim term renders a claim indefinite, the examiner should make an indefiniteness rejection and also any prior-art rejections based on the examiner's interpretation.
guidance: Cite 37 CFR 1.104(a)(1) and MPEP §706. Avoid piecemeal examination; reject each claim on all valid grounds available (see MPEP §707.07(g)). When rejecting over prior art in view of an indefiniteness issue, explicitly state how the claim term is being interpreted relative to the applied prior art (see In re Packard).

name: Approaches for prior art rejection when claim terms are indefinite
description: Two approaches: (1) If uncertainty is not great and at least one interpretation renders claim unpatentable, enter two rejections — indefiniteness under 112(b) and prior art under the interpretation that makes the prior art applicable; (2) If there is great confusion/uncertainty as to interpretation, do not base a 103 rejection on speculation about meaning.
guidance: Approach (1) helps avoid piecemeal examination and gives applicant clearer notice (see Ex parte Ionescu). Approach (2) is supported by In re Steele — do not base a 103 rejection on considerable speculation about claim meaning.

name: 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and 112(b) are distinct requirements
description: Requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (written description/enabling disclosure) and 112(b) (particularity/distinctness) are separate and distinct; insufficient disclosure under 112(a) does not by itself render the claim indefinite under 112(b).
guidance: If the specification discloses that a particular feature is essential to practice of the invention, failure to recite that feature in the claim may support a rejection under 112(a) (In re Mayhew). If a claim is amended to include subject matter not described in the application as filed, reject under 112(a) (In re Simon, In re Panagrossi).

name: 7.34.01 Failure to Particularly Point Out and Distinctly Claim (Indefinite)
description: Form paragraph to reject claims as indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter the inventor regards as the invention.
guidance: Must be preceded by 7.30.02 or 7.103. Follow with one or more of form paragraphs 7.34.02–7.34.10 and/or 7.34.23–7.34.24 as applicable. Identify particular term(s)/limitation(s) rendering claim indefinite and explain why; if scope is ascertainable to one of ordinary skill, do not use this rejection.

name: 7.34.03 Relative Term/Term of Degree Rendering Claim Indefinite
description: A relative term or term of degree (e.g., 'sufficient', 'substantial') that is not defined and provides no standard for ascertaining the requisite degree renders the claim indefinite.
guidance: Explain which parameter or limitation is rendered indefinite. Precede with 7.34.01.

name: 7.34.04 Broad Range and Narrow Range in Same Claim May Be Indefinite
description: A claim reciting both a broad range/limitation together with a narrower range/limitation that falls within it may be indefinite if the claim does not clearly set forth the metes and bounds of the protection desired.
guidance: Explain whether the narrower language is merely exemplary or required; see MPEP §2173.05(c). Precede with 7.34.01.

name: 7.34.10 Indefinite Claim Language: 'Such As'
description: The phrase 'such as' renders a claim indefinite because it is unclear whether limitations following the phrase are part of the claimed invention.
guidance: This form paragraph must be preceded by 7.34.01; may be modified to fit other instances of indefiniteness. See MPEP §2173.05(d).

name: 7.34.08 Indefinite Claim Language: 'For Example'
description: Use of the phrase 'for example' renders the claim indefinite because it is unclear whether the limitations following are part of the claimed invention.
guidance: Must be preceded by 7.34.01. See MPEP §2173.05(d).

name: 7.34.09 Indefinite Claim Language: 'Or The Like'
description: The phrase 'or the like' renders claim(s) indefinite because it includes elements not actually disclosed, making scope unascertainable.
guidance: Must be preceded by 7.34.01. See MPEP §2173.05(d).

name: 7.34.05 Lack of Antecedent Basis
description: Use when a claim recites a limitation without sufficient antecedent basis in the claim language.
guidance: Must be preceded by 7.34.01. In bracket identify the limitation lacking antecedent basis (e.g., 'said lever') and where it appears in the claim.

name: 7.34.12 Essential Steps Omitted
description: Claim rejected for being incomplete due to omission of essential steps, amounting to a gap between steps (process claims).
guidance: Use only in aggravated situations where omission makes scope indeterminate. Precede with 7.30.02 or 7.103 and 7.34.01. Recite omitted steps and rationale for considering them critical/essential (see MPEP §2172.01).

name: 7.34.07/7.34.13 Claims as Literal Translations/Essential Elements Omitted
description: Claims that are narrative and indefinite, appearing to be literal translations with grammatical/idiomatic errors, or claims omitting essential elements, should be rejected as indefinite/incomplete.
guidance: Precede with 7.34.01. For omitted elements, recite omitted elements and explain why they are essential.

name: 7.34.14 Essential Cooperative Relationships Omitted
description: Reject claims that omit essential structural cooperative relationships of elements, creating a gap between necessary structural connections.
guidance: Precede with 7.30.02 or 7.103 and 7.34.01. Recite omitted cooperative relationships and rationale for their essentiality (see MPEP §2172.01).

name: 7.34.15 Rejection Under 35 U.S.C. 112 for Pro Se Applicants
description: Guidance for rejecting claims filed by pro se applicants that are narrative in form and replete with indefinite language; the structure must be clearly and positively specified and claims must be in one-sentence form.
guidance: Use when applicant acts pro se; note claim format expectations and reference patents cited to illustrate claim format.

name: 7.35 Rejection for Omnibus Claim (Form Paragraph)
description: Form paragraph to reject an omnibus type claim under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) as indefinite for failing to point out what is included or excluded by the claim language.
guidance: Must be preceded by 7.30.02 or 7.103. No further explanation necessary for omnibus-type claims. Example: 'A device substantially as shown and described.'

name: 7.35.01 Trademark/Trade Name as a Limitation (Form Paragraph)
description: Claim containing a trademark/trade name used as a limitation to identify or describe a particular material or product does not comply with 35 U.S.C. 112(b).
guidance: Insert trademark/trade name and where used in claim; specify the material/product claimed to be identified/ described by the mark; explain why identification/description is indefinite (see Ex parte Simpson). Precede with 7.30.02 or 7.103.

name: Means-plus-function (35 U.S.C. 112(f)) general guidance
description: Section provides guidelines for examination of 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA 112 sixth-paragraph 'means or step plus function' limitations; BRI for such language is the structure, material or act described in the specification as performing the entire claimed function and equivalents.
guidance: Courts (In re Donaldson, Williamson) require that examiners consider the specification's corresponding structure and apply the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the written description. 112(f) limitations may receive a narrower interpretation than non-112(f) limitations.

name: Presumption that 112(f) applies when 'means' or 'step' used
description: A claim limitation is presumed to invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f) when it explicitly uses the term 'means' or 'step' and includes functional language.
guidance: This presumption is overcome if the limitation includes sufficient structure, material, or acts necessary to perform the recited function (TriMed, Altiris). If examiner decides 'means'/'step' limitation is not treated under 112(f), state reasons in Office action.

name: Presumption that 112(f) does NOT apply when 'means' not used (rebuttable)
description: A claim limitation that does not use the term 'means' will trigger the rebuttable presumption that 35 U.S.C. 112(f) does not apply.
guidance: The presumption is overcome when the claim term fails to recite sufficiently definite structure or recites function without reciting sufficient structure (Williamson; Watts). Examiner should still consider whether the presumption is overcome and may apply 112(f) where appropriate.

name: Three-prong analysis for applying 35 U.S.C. 112(f)
description: Examiners will apply 35 U.S.C. 112(f) to a claim limitation if it meets a 3-prong analysis: (A) uses 'means'/'step' or generic placeholder; (B) is modified by functional language (e.g., 'means for', 'configured to'); (C) is not modified by sufficient structure, material, or acts for performing the claimed function.
guidance: If all three prongs met, treat as 112(f). If claim uses 'means'/'step' but prong (B) or (C) not met, the Office action must explain why 112(f) is not being applied. Explicitly state in Office action when a claim limitation is being interpreted under 112(f).

name: BRI rule for 112(f) limitations
description: The broadest reasonable interpretation of a claim limitation invoking 35 U.S.C. 112(f) is the structure, material, or act described in the specification as performing the claimed function and equivalents.
guidance: Do not disregard the structure disclosed in the specification when rendering a patentability determination (In re Donaldson). 112(f) can lead to a narrower claim construction than non-112(f) claim language.

name: Claim-language-driven application of 112(f)
description: Application of 35 U.S.C. 112(f) is driven by the claim language, not by applicant intent or statements in the specification or prosecution history.
guidance: Examiners must construe claim terms as they would be by one of ordinary skill in the art in light of the specification. Applicants have the opportunity and obligation to define their inventions precisely during prosecution (In re Morris, In re Zletz, Sage Prods.).

name: Avoid inconsistencies between the description and the claims
description: Any inconsistency between the description and the claims must be avoided if it may throw doubt on the extent of protection and therefore render the claim unclear or unsupported under Art. 84.
guidance: Includes simple verbal inconsistencies and inconsistencies regarding apparently essential features not mentioned in the independent claims, as well as cases where part of the subject-matter of the description and/or drawings is not covered by the claims. The EPO Guidelines (F‑IV, 4.3) expect such inconsistencies to be removed or remedied so as not to create doubt about claim scope.

name: Default deletion of embodiments not covered by independent claims (March 2021 approach)
description: Embodiments in the description which are no longer covered by the independent claims must be deleted (…) unless these embodiments can reasonably be considered to be useful for highlighting specific aspects of the amended claims.
guidance: The March 2021 EPO Guidelines required, as a general rule, deletion of inconsistent embodiments; retaining them was an exception only if they legitimately help to highlight aspects of the amended claims. This strict approach is traceable to earlier Board decisions (e.g., T 1808/06).

name: When retaining inconsistent embodiments, they must be clearly and specifically marked (March 2022 requirements)
description: If inconsistent embodiments are not deleted, the fact that an embodiment is not covered by the claims must be prominently stated and must refer to one or more specific embodiments using unambiguous expressions.
guidance: The March 2022 Guidelines leave the choice to applicants whether to delete or mark inconsistent embodiments, but impose conditions for marking: statements must explicitly and unambiguously identify specific embodiments as not falling within the claimed subject-matter. Generic statements at the description start are insufficient; merely replacing terms like "embodiment" or "invention" with "example" or "disclosure" is not enough. Mandatory features of an independent claim may not be presented as optional.

name: Generic disclaimers or superficial edits are insufficient to avoid inconsistency
description: It is not sufficient to make a generic statement that 'embodiments not falling under the scope of the (…) claims are to be considered merely as examples', nor is it sufficient only to replace terms such as 'embodiment' or 'invention' by 'example' or 'disclosure'.
guidance: Applicants must use unambiguous, specific statements referring to particular embodiments when marking them as not covered; otherwise examiners/boards may consider the description inconsistent with the claims and require deletion or amendment.

name: Claims must be clear in themselves; the description cannot be relied on to resolve clarity issues (T 1989/18)
description: Article 84 EPC requires that the claims are clear, i.e. properly define and delimit the subject-matter for which protection is sought in understandable and unambiguous terms. Claims must be clear in themselves when read with normal skills including knowledge about the prior art, but not including any knowledge derived from the description of the application or the amended patent.
guidance: Under this view (Board decision T 1989/18), the description cannot be used to resolve a clarity issue in a claim, nor can it give rise to such an issue if the claim is clear per se. Support (that the claimed subject-matter is described) remains relevant, but clarity assessment should not import descriptive material to make claims clear.

name: Support requirement entails that the entire description should be consistent with the claims (T 1024/18)
description: The requirement in Article 84 EPC of the claims to be supported by the description includes that the description is consistent with the claims not only in some part but throughout.
guidance: According to decision T 1024/18, longstanding Boards' case law requires consistency between the entirety of the description and the claims; embodiments inconsistent with the claims must therefore be deleted or clearly identifiable to the reader. This decision explicitly contradicts the T 1989/18 approach on this point and aligns with the March 2022 EPO Guidelines.

name: German litigation practice: keep original disclosure and add explicit indications when parts are no longer covered
description: For enforcement of an EP patent before German courts, it is in the interest of applicants to ensure that patent descriptions comprise all text as filed and to add indications that certain parts of the original disclosure are no longer covered by the granted claims.
guidance: Under German patent law the description and drawings form the basis for claim construction and file history is not available; German courts tend to consider all originally disclosed embodiments as useful for highlighting aspects of amended claims. Therefore, marking specific parts as not covered (rather than deleting them) is recommended to help courts understand the patentee's and EPO's views on relevance and prior art.

name: Substitute specification and preliminary amendment rules
description: Any new specification filed with the CPA request will not be considered part of the original application papers, but will be treated as a substitute specification in accordance with 37 CFR 1.125; any substitute specification must comply with 37 CFR 1.125(b) (including a statement that the substitute specification includes no new matter).
guidance: A substitute specification containing new matter will be denied entry by the substitute specification or preliminary examiner. Preliminary amendments (other than substitute specifications) filed with a CPA request will ordinarily be entered, but any new matter entered must be canceled pursuant to 35 U.S.C. 132 from the descriptive portion of the specification, and any claim relying on such new matter will be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a). Applicant may petition under 37 CFR 1.182 to have the amendment removed from the CPA file and accorded status as a separate application (new file wrapper and application number), but a refund of the CPA filing fee is not available as a result.

name: Required parts and fees for CPA (including oath/declaration)
description: Under 37 CFR 1.53(d), the specification, claims, drawings, and any amendments entered in the prior nonprovisional application are used in the CPA. A new basic filing fee, search fee, and examination fee are required in accordance with 35 U.S.C. 41 and 37 CFR 1.16. The statutory requirement under 35 U.S.C. 111(a) is a signed oath or declaration; the previously filed oath or declaration (if any) will be considered to be the oath or declaration of the CPA. For CPAs filed on or after September 16, 2012, the oath or declaration must comply with the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 115 as revised.
guidance: Be aware of historic fee rules (no search/exam fees required before Dec 8, 2004) and that a CPA will not be placed on the files for examination until all required parts and fees (including any surcharge) are received.

name: Original disclosure and new matter carryover
description: The original disclosure of a CPA is the same as the original disclosure of the parent non-continued prosecution application and amendments entered in the parent application(s). Any subject matter added by amendment in the parent application which is deemed to be new matter in the parent application will also be considered new matter in the CPA. No amendment filed in a CPA may include new matter.
guidance: Claims or specification portions that were not properly entered in the parent (or that were new matter in the parent) will be treated as new matter in the CPA and can give rise to rejections/cancellations.

name: Instances held to be private indebtedness (examples)
description: Specific examples held to be private indebtedness: claims by a wife against her husband for support; decrees for alimony against officers or soldiers; claims based on separation agreements; claims for taxes due to a foreign commune; debts for telegraph messages or services not operated by the United States; officers' mess or post laundries operated privately.
guidance: Multiple decisions cited (e.g., C.26935; C.6882; P.61, 185) explain that even when services are connected to military life or post facilities, if the United States incurs no obligation, the indebtedness remains private and pay cannot be stopped to satisfy it (C.22200, Oct. 22, 1907/1909).

name: Final judgments treated as conclusive indebtedness
description: After a claim against an officer or soldier has been reduced to a final personal judgment, if no proceedings are pending to set it aside it will be considered by the War Department as an indebtedness beyond dispute.
guidance: An explanation of the nature of the judgment and defenses that could have been presented to the court will not be considered to determine indebtedness in fact (judgment deemed conclusive), although such explanations/defenses may be considered to determine whether failure to satisfy the judgment constitutes a violation of the 61st or 62nd Article of War (citing C.20063, C.26858, etc.). No distinction will be made between contract and tort judgments in this respect.

name: Threshold requirements of clarity and precision
description: The examiner’s focus during examination of claims for compliance with the requirement for definiteness of 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, is whether the claim meets the threshold requirements of clarity and precision, not whether more suitable language or modes of expression are available.
guidance: When satisfied that patentable subject matter is disclosed and claims are directed to such subject matter, examiner should allow claims that define the patentable subject matter with a reasonable degree of particularity and distinctness. Some latitude in manner of expression and aptness of terms should be permitted. Examiners encouraged to suggest improved claim language but should not reject claims merely because they prefer other phrasing if applicant’s language satisfies the statutory requirement.

name: Essential inquiry — claims must circumscribe subject matter with reasonable particularity
description: The essential inquiry is whether the claims set out and circumscribe a particular subject matter with a reasonable degree of clarity and particularity.
guidance: Definiteness must be analyzed in light of the application disclosure, the teachings of the prior art, and the claim interpretation that would be given by one possessing ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made. Claims must apprise one of ordinary skill in the art of their scope and serve the public notice function (what constitutes infringement). Consider the totality of limitations and their interactions when ascertaining scope.

name: Consider the claim as a whole in light of disclosure and prior art
description: In reviewing a claim for compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, the examiner must consider the claim as a whole to determine whether the claim apprises one of ordinary skill in the art of its scope.
guidance: Assess the claim in light of (A) the content of the particular application disclosure, (B) the teachings of the prior art, and (C) the claim interpretation a POSITA would give at the time of invention. Use case law (e.g., Solomon v. Kimberly-Clark; In re Larsen) to support totality analysis.

name: Meaning discernible even if term not used/defined in specification
description: A claim term that is not used or defined in the specification is not indefinite if the meaning of the claim term is discernible.
guidance: Example: Bancorp — components of a compound phrase had well recognized meanings allowing POSITA to infer the entire phrase. If meaning is discernible to POSITA, 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph is satisfied.

name: When indefiniteness rejection is appropriate (inability to ascertain metes and bounds)
description: If a person of ordinary skill in the art could not interpret the metes and bounds of the claim so as to understand how to avoid infringement, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, is appropriate.
guidance: Cite Morton Int’l. However, if applicant’s language satisfies statutory requirements but examiner merely prefers clearer language, suggest improvements rather than reject. Use 37 CFR 1.105 requirement for additional information if necessary (see MPEP § 704.10).

name: No per se rules — context matters (e.g., use of 'such as')
description: The mere use of the phrase 'such as' in the claim does not by itself render the claim indefinite; Office policy is not to employ per se rules to make technical rejections.
guidance: Examples of language held indefinite are fact-specific and listed in MPEP § 2173.05(d). Test for definiteness is whether those skilled in the art would understand what is claimed when read in light of the specification (Orthokinetics). If examiner thinks clarity can be improved (e.g., deletion of 'such as'), they may suggest it but should not pursue a rejection solely on that basis if statutory requirement is met.

name: Office action must provide sufficient explanation to permit meaningful response
description: The Office action must set forth the specific term or phrase that is indefinite and why the metes and bounds are unclear so the applicant can meaningfully respond.
guidance: Explain in detail why a term renders claim scope unclear, and whenever practicable indicate how indefiniteness may be resolved (point out specific term/phrase, explain reasoning, indicate practicable remedies). Note claims are given their broadest reasonable interpretation during prosecution to facilitate sharpening/clarifying the claims (In re Buszard). If examiner later withdraws rejection after applicant argument, explain why the position changed and refer to applicant remarks to clarify the record.

name: Use interviews to resolve indefiniteness before resorting to rejection
description: When indefiniteness is the only issue, attempt resolution through an interview with the applicant before making a rejection.
guidance: Interviews can clarify broadest reasonable interpretation, meaning of claim limitations, scope and clarity of preamble/functional/means-plus-function limitations, etc. Substance of interviews must be made of record in the application. Examples of issues to make of record: why term is/is not sufficiently clear, whether it is inconsistent with the specification, whether it invokes 112, sixth paragraph, and any claim amendments discussed that would resolve ambiguities.

name: Correspondence between specification and claims (support/antecedent basis)
description: The specification should ideally serve as a glossary to the claim terms so the examiner and public can clearly ascertain meaning; correspondence between the specification and claims is required by 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1).
guidance: Exact claim terms are not required in the specification if equivalent terms provide needed guidance so meaning is discernable to POSITA (Bancorp). Glossaries are encouraged. If spec lacks needed support or antecedent basis, object under 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1) and require applicant to amend description or claims (without introducing new matter).

name: Meaning of every term should be apparent (new terminology guidance)
description: The meaning of every term used in a claim should be apparent from the prior art or from the specification and drawings at the time the application is filed.
guidance: Applicants may use new terms (often desirable for new tech), and new terms are not indefinite just because they don't appear in prior art (In re Fisher). The broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification should be applied. If proposed language is not as precise as subject matter permits, examiner should provide reasons to support indefiniteness and suggest alternatives.

name: Relative terminology / terms of degree — provide measurement standard
description: When a term of degree is used in a claim, the examiner should determine whether the specification provides some standard for measuring that degree.
guidance: If the spec does not provide a standard, determine whether POSITA could nevertheless ascertain scope (recognized standard in art, examples, figures). Applicant may overcome indefiniteness by submitting a 37 CFR 1.132 declaration showing examples that meet/do not meet the limitation (Enzo Biochem example). If scope remains unclear when read in light of the specification, rejection is proper. Relative terms used where improvement rests on size/weight require greater criticality in disclosure of a standard.

name: Reference to a variable object may render a claim indefinite
description: A claim may be rendered indefinite by reference to an object that is variable (e.g., sizing relative to a rider of unspecified build).
guidance: Contrast with examples where 'so dimensioned as to be insertable through the space between the doorframe of an automobile and one of the seats' was definite because phrase was as accurate as the subject matter permits. Determine whether the reference provides an ascertainable standard.

name: Specification requirements (35 U.S.C. §112)
description: Specification.
guidance: Statutory requirements for the specification (written description, enablement, best mode (where applicable), and definiteness of claims); governs sufficiency of disclosure and claim clarity; referenced as 'Contents of specification' in index.

name: Claims (statutory and indexing references)
description: Claims are an essential part of the patent and define the scope of the invention (index references: 'Claim').
guidance: Claims must satisfy statutory requirements (patentability, clarity, supported by specification). Reissue and reexamination rules interact with claim scope (e.g., reissue for defective claims, no new matter on reissue).

name: Benefit of earlier filing date; right of priority (35 U.S.C. §§119–121, 365)
description: Benefit of earlier filing date; right of priority; right of priority under treaties and international filings.
guidance: Rules for claiming benefit of earlier U.S. filings or foreign priority under treaty provisions and PCT; affects effective filing date for novelty and obviousness determinations.

name: Derivation proceedings and interferences (35 U.S.C. §135 and pre-AIA interference provisions)
description: Derivation proceedings; (pre-AIA) interferences.
guidance: Procedures to resolve disputes over who first invented or who derived claimed subject matter; derivation replaced interference post-AIA, with specific procedural rules in the statute.

name: Reissue of defective patents (35 U.S.C. §251–253)
description: Reissue of defective patents; disclaimer.
guidance: Allows correction of defective patents (e.g., defective claims) via reissue subject to statutory limits (no new matter; effect on term; intervening rights). Also includes disclaimer provisions.

name: Notice letter requirements, timing, and strategic balance
description: After FDA acceptance acknowledgment, the generic has 20 days to notify the NDA holder/patent owner with a 'detailed statement of the factual and legal basis' for the Paragraph IV certification; the notice must be sufficiently specific.
guidance: Balance: a thorough letter supports good-faith defenses (reduces willful infringement risk) but supplies the brand with a litigation roadmap; a lean letter risks challenge as insufficient. Best practice: cite actual prior art, identify specific claim elements, explain scientific grounds for design-arounds, and run through experienced ANDA counsel.

name: Pre-filing patent landscape analysis and freedom-to-operate (FTO)
description: Comprehensive landscape covers Orange Book and non-Orange Book U.S. patents, prosecution histories/file wrappers, continuations/divisionals, international filings, and prior art; FTO compares proposed formulation/manufacturing/excipients/particle form to claim scope.
guidance: Produce two FTO outputs: (1) a claim-by-claim non-infringement opinion and (2) a design-around analysis suggesting alternatives that maintain BE. A documented, lawyer-signed FTO is primary defense against willful infringement and treble damages; invest heavily in file wrapper review to identify prosecution-history estoppel and other limiting facts.

name: Claim construction, Markman hearings, and Teva v. Sandoz implications
description: Claim construction defines claim scope and controls infringement/non-infringement; Markman hearings are pivotal and, after Teva v. Sandoz (2015), factual findings underlying claim construction are reviewed for clear error on appeal while legal conclusions are reviewed de novo.
guidance: Begin Markman preparation pre-filing; invest in expert witness selection and preparation for district court Markman proceedings; venue selection matters because district courts differ in claim-construction practices and post-Teva factual findings are harder to reverse on appeal.

name: Notice letter drafting as legal brief and pre-filing external counsel review
description: The notice letter should function as an opening legal brief with specific prior art citations, claim element identification, and scientific basis for design-arounds, rather than an administrative checklist.
guidance: Run notice letters through external ANDA litigation counsel; remember confidentiality is not guaranteed once attached to public filings. The level of specificity must balance good-faith defense preparation against giving the brand litigation intelligence.

name: Understand the inventive concept
description: When preparing for your interview, understand the inventive concept.
guidance: Be able to explain what the invention is and how the claims and specification express the inventive concept so discussion can focus on patentability and claim scope.

name: Identify allowable subject matter where appropriate
description: When preparing for your interview, identify allowable subject matter where appropriate.
guidance: Be prepared to point out claim sets or claim elements that are clearly allowable, or to propose claim language that would be allowable.

name: Document specifics regarding each issue discussed
description: The Summary of Interview should contain specifics regarding each issue discussed.
guidance: Record sufficient detail so readers of the file can understand what was discussed, including references, claim terms at issue, and factual or legal points raised.

name: Clearly identify any agreement reached
description: The Summary of Interview should contain clear identification of any agreement reached between the parties.
guidance: State explicitly what was agreed, including whether any claims will be allowable, claim interpretations, priority date determinations, application of case law, next steps, or statutory subject matter conclusions.

name: Record any agreed claim amendment(s)
description: The Summary of Interview should record any agreed upon claim amendment(s).
guidance: Specify the exact claim language agreed upon and link amendments to issues they resolve (e.g., overcoming specific rejections). Agreement examples include allowability, interpretation of claim limitations, priority dates, application of case law, next steps, statutory subject matter, etc.

name: Prefer clear, specific substance in interview summaries (avoid vague statements)
description: Summaries should avoid vague or unclear statements such as 'discussed proposed claim amendments. No agreement was reached.' or 'Agreement was reached because the claims are found patentable.'
guidance: Examples of unclear substance (bad): 'Examiner and practitioner discussed proposed claim amendments. No agreement was reached.'; 'Agreement was reached because the claims are found patentable.' Examples of clear substance (good): Provide factual detail on arguments, citations (e.g., 'See Jones at col. 5, lines 10-20'), state what was agreed or not agreed, identify text to be added to claims, note that an updated search will be conducted, or that certain claims will be allowable pending an updated search.

name: Record specific claim language and specify what prior art is overcome
description: Record the specific claim language agreed upon and specify which prior art is overcome by those amendments or arguments.
guidance: Tie claim text to the prior art references or rejections overcome to make the resolution concrete in the record.

name: BRC-Phillips Convergence
description: Would the examiner's 'broadest reasonable construction' (BRC) and a litigation court's Phillips construction yield substantially similar scopes?
guidance: Compare the scope that would be applied under prosecution (BRC) with the likely Phillips-style construction in litigation. A patent provides high-quality notice when these constructions converge; divergence indicates a notice failure. Consider specific claim terms and how intrinsic evidence and prosecution arguments would be read under each standard.

name: Claim Term Definition
description: Are key claim terms defined explicitly in the specification?
guidance: Explicit definitions (a definitions section or glossary) that give terms operational consequences improve predictability. Lack of definitions or coined terms without definition weakens notice. Definitions should be unambiguous and tied to embodiments where appropriate.

name: Prosecution-Litigation Consistency
description: Has the applicant taken consistent claim-scope positions across prosecution and litigation stages?
guidance: Evaluate prosecution history for clear, consistent claim-scope commitments. Applicant arguments used to obtain allowance that contradict later litigation positions create ambiguity and can bind future construction (prosecution-history estoppel). Consistency between applicant arguments and later litigated positions is a marker of high notice-quality.

name: Embodiment Representativeness
description: Do specification embodiments match the claimed scope (i.e., are embodiments clearly disclosed and representative)?
guidance: High notice quality requires embodiments that reflect the full scope of the claims rather than examples that are narrower or inconsistent. Check whether examples imply a different scope than claim language and whether embodiments are treated as illustrative or limiting.

name: Third-Party Predictability
description: Could a competent third party reading the patent predict whether their planned activity falls within the scope without litigation?
guidance: This is the practical test of notice: would a typical practitioner know from the patent whether an action would infringe? If not, the patent fails the notice-quality test. Consider the clarity of claims, definitions, prosecution statements, and how they would be read by non-adjudicative readers.

name: Specification Supports Notice
description: Does the specification provide support for a clear claim scope through embodiments, prior-art distinctions, definitions, and background?
guidance: Look for: clearly disclosed and representative embodiments; prior art distinguished with specific technical reasons; a definitions section or glossary for novel terms; and background that articulates the invention's scope. Weak or conflicting specification content undermines notice.

name: Claim Drafting Quality (avoid drafting defects)
description: Are claims free from drafting defects that create ambiguity (e.g., functional language without 112(f) treatment, coined terms without definition, multi-word phrases with multiple plausible meanings, inconsistent terminology between independent and dependent claims)?
guidance: Good drafting avoids functional language that invites multiple interpretations unless properly supported and treated under 35 U.S.C. §112(f), defines coined terms, uses consistent phrasing, and ensures dependent claims use terminology consistent with independent claims. Each listed drafting defect is an anti-pattern to notice clarity.

name: Specification Defects (indicia of weak notice)
description: Does the specification contain defects that undermine notice (e.g., embodiments inconsistent with claim language, missing definitions for novel claim terms, background that conflicts with claim scope, examples implying different scope)?
guidance: Identify conflicts between specification text and claim language, absent or vague definitions for novel terms, and background disclosures that narrow or contradict the asserted claim scope. These defects predict litigation ambiguities and notice failure.

name: Mandatory Claim Term Definitions (reform proposal)
description: Require applicants to define key claim terms explicitly in the specification.
guidance: Mandatory definitions would reduce ambiguity, clarify operational meaning, and improve third-party predictability. This reform is both a drafting recommendation and a potential regulatory change to enhance notice.

name: Pre-Grant Public Comment (reform proposal)
description: Allow third parties to flag claim-scope ambiguities before grant.
guidance: A pre-grant comment mechanism would surface latent ambiguities and encourage applicants/examiners to resolve them before issuance, improving the notice function of patents.

name: Strong Notice Marker: Examiner Reasoning Aligned with Applicant Positions
description: Examiner reasoning that aligns with the applicant's claim-scope positions indicates strong notice.
guidance: When examiner statements, rejections, and allowances reflect the same interpretive view the applicant later relies upon, the likelihood of BRC-Phillips divergence is reduced and notice improves.

name: Strong Notice Marker: Consistent Terminology
description: Consistent terminology across claims and the specification supports clear notice.
guidance: Avoid using different words for the same concept or the same words for different concepts across independent/dependent claims and the specification; consistency reduces interpretive ambiguity.

name: Strong Notice Marker: Prosecution History with Explicit Claim-Scope Commitments
description: A prosecution history that contains explicit claim-scope commitments is a marker of good notice.
guidance: Clear statements made during prosecution about what claim terms mean or what is disclaimed increase predictability for third parties and courts.

name: Weak Notice Marker: Coined Terms without Definition
description: Coined terms used in claims but not defined in the specification are a sign of weak notice.
guidance: Undefined coined terms force reliance on later litigation to assign meaning and undermine third-party predictability.

name: Weak Notice Marker: Examiner's BRC Reasoning Differs from Applicant Arguments
description: When an examiner's BRC reasoning diverges from the applicant's claim-scope arguments, notice is weakened.
guidance: Such divergence creates multiple plausible constructions and increases the likelihood of post-issuance disputes and unpredictability.

name: Weak Notice Marker: Inconsistent Terminology
description: Inconsistent terminology across claim sets or between claims and specification indicates weak notice.
guidance: This repeats as an anti-pattern: inconsistent use of terms produces latent ambiguities that courts and third parties will later have to resolve.

name: Weak Notice Marker: Specification Embodiments Narrower than Claim Language
description: When specification embodiments are narrower than the claim language, notice is weakened.
guidance: Narrow examples can suggest limitations not present in the claims or create uncertainty about the intended scope; ensure embodiments are representative or explicitly labeled as illustrative.

name: Factor (a): similarities and material differences between asserted art and prior art in examination
description: (a) [T]he similarities and material differences between the asserted art and the prior art involved during examination;
guidance: Used to guide the first prong of Advanced Bionics: show whether the petition's references are meaningfully different from those before the Examiner. Emphasize distinguishing features (e.g., different disclosure of key claim limitations) to defeat the first-prong match.

name: Material error example: misapprehending or overlooking specific teachings of relevant prior art
description: "An example of a material error may include misapprehending or overlooking specific teachings of the relevant prior art where those teachings impact patentability of the challenged claims." (Advanced Bionics, Paper 6 at 8.)
guidance: Show concrete instances where Examiner missed or misinterpreted teachings (e.g., untranslated protocols or appendices, specific dose disclosures). Use expert declarations and primary-source evidence to demonstrate the oversight and connect it to patentability.

name: Settled expectations factor is contextual and does not rest solely on Patent Owner’s R&D investment
description: The Director’s Memo contemplates 'settled expectations of the parties, such as the length of time the claims have been in force.' The brief argues that a patent owner’s assertion of its own settled expectation (e.g., R&D investment) is insufficient alone to warrant discretionary denial.
guidance: When opposing or supporting discretionary denial, analyze the timing (how long the patent has been in force), whether challengers delayed, and whether expectations truly are 'settled' (market reliance, long issuance), rather than relying solely on self-serving statements about investment. For recent patents and prompt petitions, argue settled expectations weigh against denial.

name: Use clear language when rejecting claims
description: Where a claim is refused for any reason relating to the merits thereof it should be 'rejected' and the ground of rejection fully and clearly stated, and the word 'rejected' must be used. The examiner should designate the statutory basis for any ground of rejection by express reference to a section of 35 U.S.C. in the opening sentence of each ground of rejection.
guidance: If rejected as too broad, give the reason; if indefinite, point out wherein the indefiniteness resides; if incomplete, specify missing elements. Avoid personal comments and expressions of opinion about lack of merit. Do not assert doubts about allowability in the record. Avoid omnibus phrasing and improper grouping of claims.

name: Avoid improperly expressed rejections (omnibus and grouping)
description: An omnibus rejection of the claim 'on the references and for the reasons of record' is stereotyped and usually not informative and should therefore be avoided. A plurality of claims should never be grouped together in a common rejection, unless that rejection is equally applicable to all claims in the group.
guidance: State specific grounds and reasons; avoid boilerplate and grouping that obscures which claims are rejected for which reasons.

name: Answer material traversed by applicant
description: Where the requirements are traversed, or suspension thereof requested, the examiner should make proper reference thereto in his or her action on the amendment. Where the applicant traverses any rejection, the examiner should, if he or she repeats the rejection, take note of the applicant's argument and answer the substance of it.
guidance: Address the substance of applicant’s arguments; if applying prior rejection to new/amended claims, specifically identify the ground (by citing paragraph in former Office letter).

name: Avoid piecemeal examination where possible
description: Piecemeal examination should be avoided as much as possible. The examiner ordinarily should reject each claim on all valid grounds available, avoiding, however, undue multiplication of references.
guidance: Apply major technical rejections (lack of disclosure, undue breadth, indefiniteness, res judicata) when appropriate, fully developing reasons rather than offering mere conclusions. Exceptions permitting limited action include: application too informal, undue multiplicity of claims (no successful election), misjoinder (no successful election), and perpetual motion disclosures. When certain rejections like res judicata or new matter apply, accompany with rejections on all other available grounds.

name: State when claims are allowable and suggest corrective action
description: The examiner should identify any claims which he or she judges, as presently recited, to be allowable and/or should suggest any way in which he or she considers that rejected claims may be amended to make them allowable.
guidance: For pro se applications, examiners may draft one or more claims and indicate they would be allowed if incorporated. If claim is allowable except for form, offer definite suggestions for correction and consider interviews to accelerate agreement on allowable claims. Do not delay allowance of clearly allowable claims once prior art fully developed.

name: Unpersuasive Argument: Novelty Not Clearly Pointed Out
description: Applicant’s arguments fail to comply with 37 CFR 1.111(c) when they do not clearly point out the patentable novelty the claims present in view of the prior art or how amendments avoid such references or objections.
guidance: Require clarity regarding claimed novelty relative to cited art. Use form paragraph 7.37.12.

name: Interview Basics (MPEP §713)
description: Interviews are governed by MPEP 713 and may occur in person, via telephone, video conference, electronic mail, or electronic instant message using USPTO tools; internet email/instant messages/video conferences are not secure and require applicant authorization.
guidance: Typical interviews are ~30 minutes; examiners receive 60 minutes of non-production credit (30 min prep + 30 min interview). Applicants may bring demonstrations/exhibits (not generally admitted into the record unless complying with 37 CFR 1.91). An agenda is not required but is typically requested and should include references, claims, specific rejections, and any proposed amendments or evidence.

name: Recordation and Interview Summaries (MPEP §713.04)
description: Oral discussions must be summarized in writing to conform with 37 C.F.R. 1.2; the interview summary should identify claims discussed, specific prior art discussed, and whether an agreement was reached with description of its nature.
guidance: Both examiner and applicant must draft interview summaries (the applicant need not write a separate summary if the examiner indicates it's unnecessary). Summaries are typically brief; applicants often prefer minimal summaries to limit prosecution history estoppel. No agreements not on the written record will be recognized.

name: Recommendations to Improve Interview Practice: Require Proposed Claim Language
description: Require both applicants and examiners to bring concrete proposed claim language to interviews to focus discussions and provide starting points for resolution.
guidance: Surveys show dissatisfaction with 'ways to overcome the rejection'—requiring draft claim language from both sides would help clarify solutions and how the examiner interprets claims/prior art.

name: Recommendations to Improve Interview Practice: Increase Examiner Non-Production Time
description: Increase non-production time allotment for interview practice (e.g., from one hour to two hours) to reflect actual preparation and documentation needs.
guidance: Increasing allotted time would allow examiners to better review prior art and applicant arguments, and could be paired with requirements for more detailed interview summaries or drafting claims to overcome rejections; extra time could be conditioned on producing more substantive outputs.

name: Must do more than state the law and add 'apply it'
description: To transform an unpatentable law of nature into a patent-eligible application, one must do more than simply state the law of nature while adding the words 'apply it.'
guidance: Claims that merely recite the natural law and tell a practitioner to apply it (e.g., 'measure X and apply correlation Y') are insufficient. See Benson, Parker v. Flook, and the Court’s repeated admonition that 'apply it' alone does not create eligibility.

name: Inventive concept / additional elements required
description: A claimed process that focuses upon the use of a natural law must also contain other elements or a combination of elements (sometimes referred to as an 'inventive concept') sufficient to ensure the patent in practice amounts to significantly more than a patent upon the natural law itself.
guidance: Evaluate whether additional claim features provide practical assurance the claim is an inventive application (e.g., Diehr’s integrated steps added significance). Mere identification of audience, recital of the law, or conventional measurement steps do not constitute the requisite inventive concept.

name: Purely conventional or obvious pre-solution activity is insufficient
description: Purely conventional or obvious pre-solution activity previously engaged in by researchers is normally not sufficient to transform an unpatentable law of nature into a patent-eligible application.
guidance: If claimed steps (apart from the law itself) are well-understood, routine, conventional, or 'insignificant post-solution activity' (e.g., standard measuring techniques, telling a practitioner to do what they already do), they do not make the claim patent-eligible. See Flook and Mayo’s analysis of the 'determining' step.

name: Administering / determining / wherein claim elements can be insufficient
description: Claim elements of the type 'administering' (identifying intended audience), 'determining' (measuring by any process), and 'wherein' (reciting the correlations) may be insufficient where they merely: identify users, recite the natural law, and instruct routine measurement.
guidance: Mayo’s claims reciting these three steps were invalid because (1) administering only picked out an audience, (2) wherein clauses merely informed the audience of the natural laws, and (3) determining instructed routine conventional measurement 'through whatever process the doctor wishes to use.' Such step-types should be scrutinized for conventionality and preemption.

name: Avoid making patent eligibility depend on draftsman's art
description: Patent eligibility must not be allowed to 'depend simply on the draftsman’s art'—courts must look to underlying principles rather than claim phrasing alone.
guidance: If patentability turns solely on how the claim is drafted (e.g., clever wording to recite an application of a law), §101 analysis should identify whether the substance is an attempt to monopolize a law of nature despite form.

name: Whether involvement is extrasolution activity or a field-of-use (for transformations)
description: Whether its involvement is extrasolution activity or a field-of-use; the extent to which (or how) the transformation imposes meaningful limits on execution of the claimed method steps.
guidance: A transformation that contributes only nominally or insignificantly to execution of the claimed method (e.g., in a data gathering step or in a field-of-use limitation) would weigh against eligibility.

name: Particularity or generality of the application (of a law of nature)
description: The particularity or generality of the application of the law of nature: broad applicability across many fields weighs against eligibility.
guidance: Claims that generically recite an effect of a law of nature or 'claim every mode' of accomplishing that effect (monopolizing a natural force or patenting a scientific fact) weigh against eligibility (e.g., O'Reilly v. Morse).

name: Whether claimed method recites application of a law of nature solely involving subjective determinations
description: Whether the claimed method recites an application of a law of nature solely involving subjective determinations (e.g., ways to think about the law of nature).
guidance: Application of a law of nature to a particular way of thinking about or reacting to it weighs against eligibility; observable and verifiable processes weigh in favor.

name: Whether involvement is extrasolution activity or a field-of-use (for laws of nature)
description: Whether its involvement is extrasolution activity or a field-of-use; the extent to which the application imposes meaningful limits on execution of the claimed method steps.
guidance: An application that contributes only nominally or insignificantly to execution of the claimed method (e.g., a data gathering step or field-of-use limitation) would weigh against eligibility.

name: Whether a general concept is involved in executing the steps of the method
description: Whether a general concept (principle, theory, plan, or scheme) is involved in executing the steps of the method: presence can be a clue the claim is drawn to an abstract idea.
guidance: If a general concept is present, evaluate factors such as preemption, abstractness/sweeping scope, whether claim states a problem vs a particular solution, and whether the concept is disembodied or instantiated.

name: Weigh the relevant factors; no single factor is determinative
description: Each of the factors relevant to the particular patent application should be weighed to determine whether the method is claiming an abstract idea or is limited to a particular practical application.
guidance: The presence or absence of a single factor will not be determinative; examiners must consider and weigh all relevant factors to reach a proper determination whether the claim as a whole is drawn to an abstract idea.

name: If not merely an abstract idea, proceed to evaluate other statutory requirements
description: If the factors indicate that the method claim is not merely covering an abstract idea, the claim is eligible under 35 U.S.C. 101 and must be further evaluated under novelty (102), non-obviousness (103), and definiteness/description/enablement (112).
guidance: 35 U.S.C. 101 is a coarse filter; 102/103/112 typically are the primary tools for evaluating patentability unless the claim is truly abstract.

name: If claim is determined to cover an abstract idea, examiner must reject under 35 U.S.C. 101 with clear rationale
description: If factors indicate the method claim is attempting to cover an abstract idea, the examiner will reject the claim under 35 U.S.C. 101, providing clear rationale supporting the determination that an abstract idea has been claimed.
guidance: The examiner must specifically point out the factors relied upon in making the determination so the applicant can make specific arguments in response; the conclusion must be based on the evidence as a whole.

name: USPTO personnel must establish a prima facie case of unpatentability
description: USPTO personnel should review the totality of the evidence (specification, claims, relevant prior art) before reaching a conclusion regarding subject matter eligibility; the examiner bears the initial burden of presenting a prima facie case of unpatentability.
guidance: If the record suggests it is more likely than not that the claimed invention is a practical application of an abstract idea or falls within an exception, then USPTO personnel should not reject the claim; after identifying reasons, the burden shifts to the applicant to amend or show eligibility.

name: Inquiry 2: Does the claim focus on use of a natural principle?
description: Does the claim focus on use of a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or naturally occurring relation/correlation (a 'natural principle') as a limiting feature of the claim?
guidance: If no, the procedure is complete (and analyze for abstract ideas under MPEP §2106). If yes, proceed to Inquiry 3. A claim focuses on a natural principle when it recites a correlation used to make a diagnosis or similar limiting element.

name: Definition and examples of a natural principle
description: A natural principle is the handiwork of nature and occurs without the hand of man (e.g., disinfecting property of sunlight; relationship between blood glucose levels and diabetes; correlations that manifest when a man-made product interacts with a natural substance).
guidance: These examples are illustrative, not limiting. A correlation that is a limiting element of the claim triggers the Inquiry 3 analysis.

name: Inquiry 3: Practical application and preemption (integrating the natural principle)
description: Does the claim include additional elements/steps or a combination of elements/steps that integrate the natural principle into the claimed invention such that the natural principle is practically applied and the claim amounts to significantly more than the natural principle itself?
guidance: If no, reject under 35 U.S.C. 101. The claim must do more than state a natural correlation plus a general instruction to 'apply it'; at least one additional element must apply, rely on, or use the natural principle in a significant way that imposes meaningful limits and prevents preemption of all practical applications.

name: Additional elements must integrate natural principle (not merely appended extrasolution activity)
description: Additional elements or steps must relate significantly to the natural principle to impose a meaningful limit on claim scope and show practical application.
guidance: Elements that are merely appended extrasolution activity (e.g., recording a diagnosis on a chart) or routine conventional activities do not integrate the principle and are insufficient.

name: Additional steps must be sufficient to ensure claim amounts to significantly more than the natural principle (avoid preemption)
description: The additional elements or steps must narrow the claim so that others are not foreclosed from using the natural principle (a basic tool of scientific and technological work).
guidance: Well-understood, purely conventional, or field-of-use limitations are insufficient; a claim that confines reach to particular patent-eligible applications (e.g., a new drug or a new way of using a drug) can be eligible.

name: Appending conventional steps at a high level of generality does not confer eligibility
description: Appended conventional steps, specified at a high level of generality, to a natural principle do not make the claim patent-eligible.
guidance: High-level recitations of known steps that add nothing specific to the natural principle will fail Inquiry 3 (see Mayo).

name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity does not add specificity
description: Steps that amount to instructions that are well-understood, routine, conventional activity previously engaged in by those in the field add nothing specific to the natural principle.
guidance: Such steps are insufficient to render the claim patent-eligible under Inquiry 3.

name: Limitations necessary for all practical applications of the natural principle are insufficient
description: Additional limitations that are necessary for all practical applications of the natural principle (such that everyone practicing the principle would have to perform those steps) would not be sufficient for eligibility.
guidance: If the claimed limitations are effectively required for any use of the principle, the claim can improperly preempt the principle and be ineligible.

name: Step 2A, Prong One: Does the claim recite a judicial exception?
description: Determine whether the claim 'recites' a judicial exception (set forth or described in the claim) such as an abstract idea (mathematical concept, mental process) or law of nature.
guidance: If claim language includes mathematical operations (e.g., STFT, V = fθ(X)) or mental processes (e.g., partitioning into clusters that could be done mentally), the claim recites a judicial exception. See MPEP 2106.04, subsection II.

name: Groupings of abstract ideas (mathematical concepts vs mental processes)
description: Identify which grouping(s) of abstract ideas the claim limitations fall into (e.g., mathematical concepts, mental processes) and treat them appropriately.
guidance: Mathematical concepts include specific transforms and formulas (e.g., STFT, embedding formula). Mental processes include concepts performed in the human mind such as observation, evaluation, judgment, and opinion (e.g., detecting anomalies by human observation). When multiple limitations fall within the same grouping, consider them together as a single abstract idea. See MPEP 2106.04(a)(2) and II.B.

name: Do not parse multiple abstract ideas unless clearly distinct
description: Avoid parsing a claim into multiple separate judicial exceptions unless it is clear the claim recites distinct exceptions (e.g., law of nature and an abstract idea).
guidance: Particularly in claims involving abstract ideas, consider limitations together rather than analyzing separately. See MPEP 2106.04, subsection II.B (discussing Bilski v. Kappos).

name: Step 2A, Prong Two: Integration into a practical application
description: Evaluate whether the claim as a whole integrates the recited judicial exception into a practical application by identifying additional elements beyond the exception and evaluating them individually and in combination.
guidance: Perform (1) identification of any additional elements beyond the judicial exception, and (2) assessment of those elements alone and together to determine if the claim integrates the exception into a practical application. See MPEP 2106.04(d).

name: Improvement to computer or technical field indicates integration
description: One indicator that a claim integrates an exception into a practical application is that the claimed invention improves the functioning of a computer or another technology/technical field.
guidance: To evaluate improvements, the specification must set forth a technical improvement and the claim must reflect that disclosed improvement. See MPEP 2106.04(d)(1) and 2106.05(a). Example: steps that detect source addresses, drop packets, and block future traffic can reflect an improvement in network intrusion detection and thus integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.

name: Generic computer or generic component recitation is insufficient
description: Reciting use of a computer or a generic component (e.g., 'a deep neural network') without details can amount to no more than mere instructions to apply the judicial exception on a generic computer.
guidance: Consider whether the claim: (1) recites only the idea of a solution/outcome without details, (2) invokes computers/machinery merely as a tool to perform an existing process, and (3) is particular or general in its application. If the claim lacks detail about how the component operates to solve a technical problem, it likely represents mere instructions to apply the exception. See MPEP 2106.05(f).

name: Step 2B: Inventive concept / 'significantly more' analysis
description: Evaluate whether the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the recited judicial exception by adding an inventive concept via additional elements or their combination.
guidance: Re-evaluate whether extra-solution activities are well-understood, routine, and conventional in the field (MPEP 2106.05(g)). If additional elements are merely conventional or routine, or are only instructions to implement the exception on generic computers, they do not provide an inventive concept (Step 2B: NO).

name: Claim must reflect the specification's disclosed technical improvement
description: Even if the specification describes a technical improvement, the claim must include limitations that reflect that improvement to avoid being directed to the judicial exception.
guidance: Example: the disclosure may describe an improvement achieved by partitioning embeddings, clustering, and synthesizing signals, but a claim that only requires determining embedding vectors without the other reflective limitations fails to reflect the disclosed improvement and may be ineligible. See MPEP 2106.05(a).

name: Claim interpretation standard: Broadest reasonable interpretation
description: Interpret claim terms according to their broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the specification as understood by one of ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: Terms are presumed to have their plain meaning consistent with the specification (MPEP 2111). For example, 'receiving' a mixed speech signal could encompass receiving via a microphone in a user device or other sensors.

name: Amendments in opposition require a ground of opposition (Rule 80 EPC)
description: Amendments in Opposition should be occasioned by a ground of Opposition (Rule 80 EPC). A lack of clarity under Article 84 EPC is not a ground for Opposition, except in cases where the lack of clarity arises solely as a result of a post-grant amendment (G 3/14).
guidance: Adaptation of the description in opposition is not appropriate unless a new discrepancy between the description and the claims had arisen as a result of a post-grant amendment. T2391/18 confirms that a granted patent cannot be invalidated solely on the grounds that the claims are unclear because the description was not adequately adapted before grant (Article 84 EPC).

name: Amended claims introducing new limitations must be accompanied by adapted description
description: Any amended claims submitted during opposition that include limitations not present in the granted claims should always be accompanied by a corresponding amended description.
guidance: Derived from T2391/18: when claim scope is narrowed or altered by post-grant claim amendments in opposition, the description should be adapted to remove or reconcile discrepancies between claims and description.

name: Do not 'mine' the description for limiting definitions
description: The description of a patent could not be mined for a definition limiting the meaning of the claims.
guidance: T450/20: courts/boards should not take isolated passages from the description to impose limiting definitions on claim terms.

name: Functional language in the description may be used to construe claims
description: It is permissible to use functional language from the description to construe the claims.
guidance: While mining for limiting definitions is disallowed, functional formulations in the description can legitimately inform claim construction (T450/20).

name: Novelty — definition (lack of novelty)
description: For international preliminary examination, the invention, as defined by a claim, lacks novelty if every element or step is explicitly or inherently disclosed within the prior art defined in Rule 64.1, including any features implicit to a person skilled in the art.
guidance: Inherency requires extrinsic evidence showing the missing descriptive matter is necessarily present. Inherency may not be established by probabilities or possibilities. Well-known equivalents not disclosed in a prior art document are not considered when assessing novelty (they are a matter for inventive step). The same considerations apply when producing a written opinion and in selecting documents for the international search report.

name: Prior art disclosure must be enabling to defeat novelty
description: The prior art disclosure must enable a person skilled in the art to carry out the claimed invention; a document that is not enabling for the claimed invention does not necessarily defeat novelty.
guidance: Ordinarily enablement may be inferred for patent documents. For non-patent literature that raises questions as to enablement, the examiner should determine that the prior art would have enabled a person skilled in the art. Knowledge from outside the prior art document may be considered where appropriate (see appendix to Chapter 12). A prior art document not enabling for novelty may still be relied on for inventive step.

name: Methodology for assessing novelty
description: For assessment of novelty the examiner should: (i) evaluate the elements of the claimed invention; (ii) determine if a document forms part of the 'prior art'; (iii) assess whether each and every element or step was explicitly or inherently disclosed in combination by the document to a person skilled in the art on the date of publication.

name: Claim interpretation for novelty (purpose/use statements)
description: When interpreting claims for novelty, statements reciting the purpose or intended use must be evaluated to determine whether the recited purpose/use results in a structural difference (or, for process claims, a difference in steps) between the claimed invention and the prior art. Non-distinctive characteristics of a particular intended use should be disregarded.
guidance: Examples: a substance claimed for use as a catalyst is not novel over the same substance known as a dye unless the use implies a distinguishing form (e.g. additives). A 'mould for molten steel' implies limitations that distinguish it from a plastic ice cube tray.

name: Generic vs specific disclosures for novelty
description: A specific example in prior art that falls within a claimed generic parameter anticipates the generic claim. Conversely, a genus does not always anticipate a species unless the specific example is identified with sufficient specificity in the prior art.
guidance: If the prior art identifies the claimed example with sufficient specificity, that example lacks novelty regardless of other species described.

name: Ranges: specific examples and selection inventions
description: A specific example in prior art within a claimed range anticipates the range. Where prior art discloses a range that touches/overlaps the claimed range but not a specific example within it, novelty must be decided case-by-case; narrow claimed ranges may be selection inventions if not sufficiently disclosed and if unexpected results support them.
guidance: Unexpected results may also render claims unobvious (inventive step).

name: Divergent practices on extrinsic knowledge for novelty (A12.02[1])
description: One practice: the prior document must provide a sufficient disclosure on its effective date (publication date) together with knowledge generally available on that effective date to supply every element/step of the claimed invention to a person skilled in the art.
guidance: Authorities following this practice do not consider knowledge made available after the prior document's publication date when assessing whether it disclosed the claimed invention.

name: Divergent practices on extrinsic knowledge for novelty (A12.02[2])
description: Alternative practice: the prior document must provide a sufficient disclosure on the 'relevant date' of the claim being searched or examined; Authorities following this practice consider knowledge that became available after the publication date but before the relevant date when determining sufficiency of disclosure.
guidance: Authorities differ; those not following these guidelines may still rely on the prior art document for inventive step.

name: Inventive step — definition (non-obviousness)
description: A claimed invention involves an inventive step if, having regard to the prior art, it is not, at the relevant date, obvious to a person skilled in the art. Novelty and inventive step are different criteria: inventive step assesses whether the invention as a whole would not have been obvious to the skilled person in light of the prior art as a whole.
guidance: Multiple items of prior art may be combined in determining inventive step.

name: Assessing combinations and invention as a whole
description: In determining inventive step the invention must be considered as a whole; it is not sufficient to argue that separate features of a combination are known or obvious individually, unless there is no functional relationship (mere juxtaposition).
guidance: Claim should be directed to technical features. Various ways a skilled person may arrive at an invention should be considered.

name: Account for applicant acknowledgements and general knowledge
description: When identifying the contribution of the invention against the art, account should be taken of what the applicant acknowledges to be known; such acknowledgements should generally be regarded as correct unless amended. Also consider further prior art and the general knowledge of the skilled person.
guidance: Prior art used must be enabling for what it teaches; any combination of items of prior art and general knowledge relied upon must provide enablement with respect to the claimed invention.

name: Assessment steps for inventive step (13.08)
description: The following considerations should be applied: (i) determine scope of claimed invention; (ii) determine scope of relevant prior art; (iii) determine the person skilled in the art; (iv) identify differences and similarities between prior art and claimed invention; (v) assess whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious to the skilled person given the prior art and general knowledge.

name: Motivation, reasonable likelihood of success, and problem-solution approach
