description: The invention is obvious if prior art or general knowledge would have motivated the skilled person, with reasonable likelihood of success, to reach the claimed invention by substituting, combining or modifying prior art. One particular way to determine inventive step is the problem-solution approach (see appendix).

name: Examples of obviousness (illustrative guides)
description: Examples where claimed invention should be regarded as obvious include: (a) application of known measures in an obvious way such that at least one way of supplying missing claim features would naturally occur to the skilled person; (b) differences that are merely use of well-known equivalents; (c) a new use of a well-known material employing known properties; (d) substitution of a recently developed material whose properties make it plainly suitable for that use.
guidance: These examples are guides only; the applicable principle is always 'was it obvious to a person skilled in the art?' Examiners should avoid forcing a case into an example that does not clearly apply.

name: Board remand/reversal/affirmance and appellant rights
description: The Board may reverse the rejection (with or without remand to the examiner for further action), remand the appeal to the examiner for further consideration, or affirm the rejection. A final decision on appeal can only be reached when the record is susceptible to meaningful review.
guidance: Appellants under § 41.50(a)(2) may respond to any supplemental examiner’s answer by (1) requesting prosecution be reopened before the examiner by filing a reply under § 1.111 with or without amendment or submission of affidavits (§§ 1.130, 1.131 or 1.132) or other evidence; or (2) requesting the appeal be maintained by filing a reply brief as provided in § 41.41. Many remands result from unclear records (e.g., amendments/additional evidence filed during appeal not clearly considered or merely 'entered' without comment). Limits on post-notice-of-appeal amendments/evidence (see § 41.33) are expected to minimize such occurrences. Upon remand the examiner may determine claims patentable and pass the case to issue.

name: Clean copy requirement for involved claims (§ 41.110(a))
description: Each party must file a clean copy of its involved claims; requirement strikes balance between clarity and cost and does not require clean copies of uninvolved claims.
guidance: A clean copy of any claim to be added should be included with any motion to add the claim (§ 41.110(c)); parties may voluntarily file clean copies of uninvolved claims if easier.

name: Claim annotation requirement and estoppel consequences (§ 41.110)
description: Parties are required to provide annotated claims; claim annotation is vital to efficient contested-case administration to show how the party intends its claim to be read.
guidance: Claim annotation must be complete and accurate; it provides a starting point for opposing parties and the Board. Parties may point out additional support consistent with their annotation. Corrections can be sought via miscellaneous motion (§ 41.121(a)(3)), and prejudice to the opposing party is an important consideration in granting relief. Attempting to avoid prosecution estoppel is not a valid reason to evade clear claim meaning.

name: Enumerated grouping — Mental processes
description: Mental processes: concepts performed in the human mind (including an observation, evaluation, judgment, opinion).
guidance: If the claim limitation can be practically performed in the human mind (or by a human using pen and paper), it may be a mental process. Note that mere recitation 'by a processor' is not sufficient to remove a limitation from the mental processes grouping.

name: Step 2B — Inventive concept (significantly more)
description: Evaluate Step 2B: Does the claim provide an inventive concept, i.e., do the additional element(s) or combination of elements amount to significantly more than the judicial exception in the claim?
guidance: Determine whether the claim recites additional features that add significantly more than the abstract idea (an inventive concept). Mere instructions to apply the exception using a generic computer component (e.g., a generic processor performing data processing) do not supply an inventive concept. If no inventive concept exists, the claim is ineligible.

name: Generic computer component recitation is insufficient
description: The mere nominal recitation of a generic processor or generic computer components does not take claim limitations out of a judicial exception grouping or integrate an abstract idea into a practical application.
guidance: A processor recited at a high level of generality, performing generic computer functions (e.g., 'determining' or 'ranking' by a processor) is no more than instructions to apply the exception on a generic computer and generally fails both Prong Two and Step 2B tests. Use examples where claims recite only a generic processor to justify ineligibility.

name: Processor actions that cannot be performed in the mind
description: If the claimed limitation requires processor actions that cannot be practically performed in the human mind (e.g., tracking how much memory has been allocated to applications), the limitation may not fall within the mental processes grouping.
guidance: Use concrete, technical operations that rely on computer hardware/state (for example, accessing computer memory indicative of application usage) to show the limitation is not a mental process under Prong One, as in the GUI claim example where tracking memory allocation removed the mental-process concern.

name: Rejection drafting under the 2019 PEG
description: When drafting a rejection for an ineligible claim, the rejection should: identify the abstract idea recited in the claim and reference the appropriate enumerated grouping; identify the additional elements and explain why they do not integrate the abstract idea into a practical application; and explain why the additional elements do not provide an inventive concept.
guidance: Follow the new form-paragraph scheme and include a clear explanation addressing why the claim recites a judicial exception, fails to integrate it into a practical application, and fails to provide an inventive concept. A sample rejection under the 2019 PEG is provided on the microsite for reference.

name: Handling pending applications after applicant response
description: If applicant argues in response to an office action that the claims are eligible, examiners should re-evaluate the eligibility of each claim previously rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 in accordance with the 2019 PEG.
guidance: If the claim is now eligible, withdraw the 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection. If still ineligible, update the form paragraph(s) used and ensure the rejection explains why the claim recites a judicial exception, fails to integrate the judicial exception into a practical application, and fails to provide an inventive concept. Examiners should also consider patentability under 35 U.S.C. 102, 103, and 112.

name: Standard of appellate review (fact v. law)
description: Whether a claim is directed to printed matter (patent-eligibility) is a question of law reviewed de novo; anticipation is a question of fact reviewed for substantial evidence.
guidance: Deferential review (substantial evidence) applies to factual findings about anticipation—i.e., ask whether the record contains 'such relevant evidence as a reasonable mind might accept as adequate to support a conclusion.' Legal questions (e.g., printed matter as a §101 issue) get de novo review.

name: Anticipation requirement (claim elements in prior art)
description: A claim is anticipated when a single prior art reference (or product) discloses every limitation of the asserted claim such that the prior art 'anticipates' the claimed invention.
guidance: Prior art products that sometimes embody the claimed characteristics can still anticipate (citing Hewlett-Packard Co. v. Mustek Sys.); use stipulations, admissions, expert testimony, studies, lab notebooks, and exhibits to determine whether each claim limitation is present in the prior art.

name: Printed-matter doctrine (informational content lacks patentable weight)
description: The content of information conveyed by claimed markers (e.g., that a port is suitable for certain pressures/flow) is 'printed matter' not entitled to patentable weight.
guidance: Limitations that merely claim informational content (mental steps to recognize printed matter) do not add patentable weight. Use cases like Praxair and prior Federal Circuit precedent to determine when limitations are merely printed matter.

name: When a marking/marker gets patentable weight (structure vs content)
description: A radiographic marker is entitled to patentable weight only to the extent it constitutes a structural feature that is radiographically discernible, not because of any meaning ascribed to it.
guidance: Distinguish between (1) informational content of a marking (printed matter — no weight) and (2) the physical/structural means by which information is conveyed (may be given weight if it is a structural, radiographically discernible feature). Evaluate whether the claimed advance focuses on the content or the means of conveyance.

name: Letters/typographical markings are ordinarily printed matter
description: A claimed 'radiographic letter' (e.g., radiographic letters etched on a port) is printed matter because a letter intrinsically conveys typographical meaning and is not functionally related to the substrate.
guidance: Absent evidence of a technical/functional effect arising from using a letter (as opposed to other indicia), typographical markings should be treated as informational printed matter and not used to distinguish over prior art (citing In re Marco Guldenaar Holding B.V.).

name: Mental-step limitations implicate printed matter
description: Claim limitations that require a user to recognize or mentally process information (mental steps) may attempt to capture informational content and thus be considered printed matter lacking patentable weight.
guidance: When a claim's limitation consists of 'identifying' information on an x-ray (or similar recognition), analyze whether that step merely recites a mental recognition of printed matter; if so, it does not confer patentable weight (citing Praxair).

name: Evidentiary weight of admissions and stipulations
description: Stipulations and expert admissions (e.g., that titanium ports were radiographically visible before a priority date or that some prior ports 'pass' power-injection testing) can constitute uncontested evidence that forecloses reasonable dispute.
guidance: When admissions/stipulations, corroborated by exhibits (x-rays, lab notebooks, studies), establish a claim limitation in prior art, a court may properly conclude there is no genuine dispute of material fact for a jury, supporting JMOL.

name: Absence of claim-language requirement is dispositive
description: If a purported distinguishing feature (e.g., FDA approval for a particular use) is not required by the claim language or the claim construction, then lack of that feature in the prior art does not mean the prior art fails to anticipate.
guidance: Do not import requirements (like regulatory approval) into claim scope when the claim text and construction do not include them; anticipation is assessed against the claim as properly construed.

name: Definition of a Jepson claim
description: A Jepson claim is a method or product claim where one or more limitations are specifically identified as a point of novelty, distinguishable over at least the contents of the preamble. The preamble makes a statement about the state of the prior art, and then claims an improvement over the prior art.
guidance: Use this format when the claim explicitly separates known/conventional subject matter (preamble) from the claimed improvement. The definition emphasizes that the claimed improvement is presented as distinct from what is stated in the preamble.

name: Jepson claim structure and format
description: A Jepson claim has a specific format: 1) A preamble that identifies conventional/known features of the claimed subject matter; 2) A specific transitional phrase (e.g., "wherein the improvement comprises"); 3) A recitation of the "new or improved" aspects of the claimed subject matter.
guidance: Follow the three-part layout in the claim text. Example wording: "A system for storing information having (...) wherein the improvement comprises:" The transitional phrase should clearly signal which limitations are conventional and which are the improvement.

name: Regulatory template (37 C.F.R. 1.75(e))
description: Improvement patent claims should follow a specific template with three components: 1) A preamble comprising a general description of all the elements or steps of the claimed combination which are conventional or known; 2) A phrase such as "wherein the improvement comprises"; 3) Those elements, steps, and/or relationships which constitute that portion of the claimed combination which the applicant considers as the new or improved portion.
guidance: Cite and conform to 37 C.F.R. 1.75(e) when drafting Jepson-format claims to ensure the claim language matches the regulatory expectation for improvement claims. Use the regulatory phrasing to clearly delineate the known versus new portions.

name: Prior-art admission risk when using Jepson format
description: Drafting a claim in Jepson format is taken as an implied admission that the subject matter of the preamble is the prior art work of another.
guidance: This implied admission can facilitate examiners' or accused infringers' arguments that the improvement is obvious in light of the admitted prior art under 35 U.S.C. § 103(a). Because of this risk, Jepson claim style is seldom used in modern U.S. practice. Consider alternate claim drafting strategies unless the admission is harmless or beneficial.

name: Appropriate circumstances to use Jepson claims
description: Jepson claims may be appropriate when the patentee is attempting to overcome, or prevent, a double patenting rejection, particularly when avoiding double patenting over the patentee's own work.
guidance: When used to avoid double patenting over the patentee's own earlier work, the Jepson format generally causes no deleterious effects. An examiner may also suggest Jepson format to clearly delineate that the patent will only cover the improvement and not the underlying work. Use Jepson only when its benefits (e.g., resolving double patenting issues or complying with an examiner's direction) outweigh the risk of admitting conventional subject matter as prior art.

name: Use of the official application form (G 6003)
description: Please use the official form (Antrag auf Eintragung eines Gebrauchsmusters - G 6003) when applying for a utility model.
guidance: The application must be filed using the official DPMA form; supporting materials (description, drawings, claims) must accompany this form. Formal requirements for application documents are stipulated by the Utility Model Ordinance.

name: Claims must be submitted and determine scope
description: You must also submit claims. The contents of the claims determine the scope of protection of your utility model. Therefore, the wording of the claims is particularly important.
guidance: The claims must contain the technical features that are to be protected. Information about the invention’s purpose or advantages does not meet this requirement. For tips on how to draft the claims, refer to the “Information for Utility Model Applicants” leaflet.

name: Conduct in-depth review of selected patents using front-page information
description: When you select promising patents, inspect front-page metadata (title, abstract, claims, inventor and assignee names) to judge relevance and to find new search leads.
guidance: Suggestions: collect inventor/assignee names as search terms, note surprising terminology or classification numbers, and record how a patent differs from your idea (for later comparison). Use front-page info to decide which patents deserve deeper claim/description comparison.

name: Be mindful of database-specific features (structure/expand/search facets)
description: Different portals offer features such as 'Structure Search', 'Classifications' explorer, expand/view options, funnels/filters, and save/export functions that change how you locate and inspect patents.
guidance: Examples: Lens' 'Structure Search' and classification tree, UI funnel icon to start classification-based searches, 'Expand' view to show abstracts/claims, and save-to-Zotero buttons. Learn and exploit these features for efficient searching.

name: Use of Patentability Report practice
description: Patentability Report practice is not obligatory and should be resorted to only where it will save total examiner time or result in improved quality of action due to specialized knowledge.
guidance: Patentability Reports are appropriate when plural, indivisible inventions are claimed and specialists on each character of the claimed invention treating claims in their specialty will save time or improve quality. Not proper where claims are directed to the same character of invention but differ in scope only. Examples where P.R. is ordinarily not proper: (A) claims related as manufacturing process and product defined by the process; (B) product and process where process merely makes a product with certain characteristics; (C) combination vs subcombination distinguished solely by characteristics of the subcombination. A P.R. that will save total examiner time requires approval of the Director of the Technology Center and the “Approved” stamp on the memorandum requesting the P.R.

name: Goal and nature of examination
description: After reading the application and understanding the claimed invention, the examiner makes a prior art search and reviews the application with the state of the prior art to determine whether the claims define a useful, novel, nonobvious, and enabled invention clearly described in the specification.
guidance: The goal is to clearly articulate any rejection early in prosecution so the applicant can respond; the examiner must review all evidence (including applicant arguments) before the next Office action. If information reasonably necessary for examination should be required from applicant under 37 CFR 1.105, generally make such a requirement prior to or with the first Office action on the merits and follow MPEP § 704.10 et seq. Examiners should not overlook allowing claims that properly define the invention.

name: Rejection requirements under 37 CFR 1.104
description: If the invention is not considered patentable as claimed, the claims (or those considered unpatentable) will be rejected. When rejecting for lack of novelty or obviousness, the examiner must cite the best references at hand and, if a reference is complex or shows other inventions, designate the particular part relied on 'as nearly as practicable.'
guidance: The pertinence of each reference must be clearly explained and each rejected claim specified. Examiner may rely upon admissions by applicant or facts within examiner's knowledge. Subject matter developed by another person that qualifies as prior art only under 35 U.S.C. 102(f) or (g) may be used under 35 U.S.C. 103 unless entire rights were commonly owned or subject to obligation of assignment. Claims precluded by waiver in a published statutory invention registration must be rejected as specified.

name: Constructive handling of form defects or omission of a limitation
description: When patentable subject matter is disclosed and claims are intended to be directed to such subject matter, but are unallowable due to defects in form or omission of a limitation, the examiner should not stop with a bare objection or rejection.
guidance: The examiner's action should be constructive and, when possible, offer a definite suggestion for correction.

name: Rejection on prior art is the most frequent ground (102/103)
description: The most frequent ground of rejection is unpatentability in view of the prior art — either lack of novelty under 35 U.S.C. 102 or obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103.
guidance: Language in rejecting claims should be unequivocal. See MPEP § 707.07(d) for language guidance.

name: Choice of prior art; use best available art
description: Prior art rejections should ordinarily be confined strictly to the best available art.
guidance: Exceptions where other references may be used include: (A) propriety of a 102 or 103 rejection depends on particular interpretation of a claim; (B) a claim is met only in terms by a reference which does not disclose the inventive concept; (C) the most pertinent reference seems likely to be antedated by a 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit/declaration. Avoid merely cumulative rejections and back up exceptions with the best other art available. See MPEP § 707.05.

name: Determining the effective filing date of the application
description: The effective filing date may be the filing date of the application itself or, under certain circumstances, the filing date of an earlier application (parent), provisional, or may be subject to foreign priority rules.
guidance: If claims are fully supported under 35 U.S.C. 112 by an earlier parent U.S. application, the effective filing date equals the earlier filing date. For continuation/divisional/CIP situations see MPEP §§ referenced. If claiming foreign priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) or 365(a), the effective filing date is the filing date of the U.S. application unless other situations apply. If properly claims benefit under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) to a provisional, the effective filing date for claims fully supported by the provisional is the provisional's filing date. See MPEP §§ 1893.03(b), 201.11(a), 1895, 1895.01, 1896 for more.

name: Deciding between 35 U.S.C. 102(a), (b), or (e)
description: Once an examiner finds a printed publication or patent disclosing the claimed invention, the examiner should determine whether the rejection should be made under 35 U.S.C. 102(a), (b), or (e) by comparing the effective filing date of the application with the date of the reference.
guidance: Determination of the effective filing date is prerequisite. See MPEP § 706.02 for details on making the comparison and selecting the proper subsection under 102.

name: Judicial exceptions exclusion (Step 2 principle)
description: Second, the claimed invention must qualify as patent-eligible subject matter — the claim must not be directed to a judicial exception (abstract ideas, laws of nature, natural phenomena/products of nature) unless the claim as a whole includes additional limitations amounting to significantly more than the exception.
guidance: Identify whether claim limitations align with at least one judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon). If the claim is directed to an exception, analyze whether additional elements provide 'significantly more' (an 'inventive concept') per the Alice/Mayo framework.

name: Apply the Alice/Mayo two‑part test (use as the sole framework)
description: Use the Alice/Mayo two‑part test to evaluate eligibility: (1) determine whether the claims are directed to an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon (Step 2A); (2) if so, determine whether the claim recites additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception (Step 2B).
guidance: The Alice/Mayo two‑part test is the only test that should be used. The second part is described as a search for an 'inventive concept.' Conduct Step 2A first; only proceed to Step 2B if Step 2A finds the claim directed to an exception.

name: Pathways A/B/C eligibility flow (streamlined and full analyses)
description: Three pathways to eligibility: Pathway A (self‑evident eligibility — streamlined), Pathway B (claim falls within statutory category and is not directed to a judicial exception), Pathway C (claim falls within statutory category, is directed to a judicial exception, but recites additional elements amounting to significantly more).
guidance: If uncertain whether streamlined analysis (Pathway A) is appropriate, conduct full Alice/Mayo analysis. Claims not eligible under any pathway should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101. Claims that could be eligible under Pathway A but are subjected to full analysis will still be eligible at Pathway B or C if appropriate.

name: Examples of non‑statutory product claims
description: Non-limiting examples of claims that are not directed to any of the statutory categories include: products that do not have a physical or tangible form (e.g., data per se, computer program per se claimed as a product), transitory forms of signal transmission (signals per se), and subject matter statutorily prohibited (e.g., humans per se).
guidance: A product claim to software expressed as code or instructions detached from any medium lacks physical embodiment; such product claims without structural recitations do not fall within statutory categories. Transitory propagating signals lack the concrete structure to be a machine/manufacture/composition.

name: Definitions of the four statutory categories
description: Clarify what each statutory category means: process = act or series of acts (method); machine = concrete thing consisting of parts/devices; manufacture = tangible article given a new form/quality/property by human action; composition of matter = combination of two or more substances or composite articles.
guidance: When determining Step 1, verify claim elements satisfy the relevant category definition (e.g., machines/ manufactures/ compositions require physical/tangible form). It is not necessary to pick a single category if the claim clearly falls within at least one.

name: Claim interpretation can change eligibility outcomes
description: Claim construction (in light of the specification and BRI) can be decisive in determining whether a claim is statutory, directed to an exception, or recites significantly more.
guidance: Use relevant case law examples: interpretations that broaden claims to include non‑statutory embodiments (e.g., carrier waves) can cause Step 1 failure; constructions that require concrete technical limitations can support finding 'not directed to an abstract idea' or provide 'significantly more.' Consider 35 U.S.C. 112(f) functional claim interpretations where applicable.

name: Machine‑or‑transformation test as a clue, not a separate test
description: The machine‑or‑transformation test is an important clue to eligibility but should not be used as a separate test; it should be considered in the 'significantly more' analysis (Step 2B).
guidance: Treat evidence that a claim is tied to a particular machine or effects a particular transformation as supportive of eligibility under Step 2B, but do not treat the test as dispositive on its own.

name: Preemption concern underlies the eligibility analysis
description: The underlying concern driving the Alice/Mayo framework is preemption: patents should not monopolize basic tools (abstract ideas, laws of nature, natural phenomena) such that innovation is impeded.
guidance: While preemption is not a standalone test, consider whether the claim would effectively preempt use of the underlying exception; lack of preemption can support eligibility, while broad preemptive claims weigh against it.

name: Improvements to technology or computer functionality (Step 2B factor)
description: A claim that improves the functioning of a computer or other technology/technical field can supply 'significantly more' and weigh toward eligibility under Step 2B.
guidance: If claim elements produce a technological improvement (not merely an abstract idea implemented on a computer), identify and reference specification portions describing the improvement. Examples include improvements to existing technology or to computer functionality recognized by case law (e.g., Enfish).

name: Particular machine requirement (Step 2B factor)
description: Limiting a claim to a particular machine (or an unconventional use of a machine) can support a finding of 'significantly more' under Step 2B.
guidance: Demonstrate how the claim's machine limitation is specific and meaningful (not merely a generic computer). Generic computer implementation is insufficient.

name: Avoid relying on well‑understood, routine, conventional activity to supply 'significantly more' (Step 2B negative factor)
description: Elements that are well‑understood, routine, conventional activities previously known in the industry do not amount to 'significantly more.'
guidance: If additional claim elements are generic computer functions or commonplace steps, they are unlikely to transform an exception into patent‑eligible subject matter. Examiners should identify and explain why elements are routine/conventional when making a rejection.

name: Other meaningful limitations and non‑generic arrangements (Step 2B considerations)
description: Claims may be eligible if they recite other meaningful limitations or a non‑generic arrangement of known, conventional elements that provide unconventional technical solutions.
guidance: Look for ordered combinations and non‑generic arrangements that achieve an unconventional technical result; cite specification or claim construction that shows the limitation is more than a mere instruction to apply an exception.

name: Mere instructions to apply an exception are insufficient (Step 2B negative factor)
description: Mere instructions to apply an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon (e.g., 'apply the formula') do not supply 'significantly more.'
guidance: Discern whether the claim simply tells practitioners to implement an exception without adding a technical solution; such claims should be treated as ineligible absent additional meaningful limitations.

name: Field of use or technological environment limitations are generally insufficient
description: Limiting an abstract idea to a particular field of use or technological environment (e.g., 'on the Internet' or 'in banking') does not, by itself, make the claim patent eligible.
guidance: Field‑of‑use or environment restrictions should not be credited as providing 'significantly more' unless they contribute a meaningful, technical improvement or unconventional limitation beyond the exception.

name: Streamlined analysis when eligibility is self‑evident (2106.06)
description: If eligibility is self‑evident (claims clearly fall within a statutory category and are plainly eligible), a streamlined analysis (Pathway A) may be used to find claims eligible.
guidance: Use streamlined analysis for clear cases, but if uncertain, perform full Alice/Mayo analysis to promote consistency and correctness. Claims that are arguably eligible under Pathway A but undergo full analysis will be found eligible under Pathway B or C if appropriate.

name: Procedural and recordkeeping guidance for §101 rejections and allowances
description: When making a §101 rejection, use appropriate form paragraphs (e.g., 7.05 and 7.05.01) and explain the BRI or deficiencies; when claims are found eligible, clarifying remarks referencing specification and elements producing improvements may be made on the record (including with a Notice of Allowance).
guidance: Provide clear explanations in the record to aid applicant understanding and prosecution. When recommending amendments to avoid non‑statutory embodiments, explain examples and suggest narrowing language. Clarifying remarks are useful both for allowances and for explaining the rationale for rejections.

name: Identification and labeling of judicial exceptions (no strict bright lines)
description: Judicial exceptions can be described using varied terms (laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract ideas, physical phenomena, products of nature, scientific principles, mental processes, disembodied algorithms). There are no bright lines between exception types; many concepts overlap.
guidance: For §101 analysis, it suffices for the examiner to identify that the claimed concept aligns with at least one judicial exception. Be mindful that certain concepts (e.g., mathematical formulas) can be characterized under multiple exception labels.

name: Conception must occur in the inventor's mind and can create joint inventorship
description: Conception must be done in the mind of the inventor — a definite and permanent idea — and any person sharing in conception of a claimed invention is a joint inventor.
guidance: Case: Bosies v. Benedict; In re VerHoef. Testimony by a noninventor about the meaning of variables in an inventor’s notebook is insufficient to establish conception by the inventor as a matter of law.

name: Broadening Claim (definition)
description: A reissue claim is “broadened” where at least one limitation of the patent claims is either completely eliminated or is only presented in a broader way in the reissue claim relative to the broadest patented claim(s).
guidance: If the reissue claim is not broadened in any respect as compared to the patent claims, the recapture analysis ends; there is no recapture. See MPEP § 1412.03 for further guidance as to the nature of a 'broadening claim.'

name: Canceled Claim (definition)
description: A claim canceled from the original application to obtain the patent for which reissue is being sought.
guidance: In recapture context, claims are considered canceled if they were deleted and not replaced or were replaced by other claims that are more specific than the canceled claims in at least one aspect in order to overcome a rejection in the original prosecution.

name: Surrender Generating Limitation (SGL) / Surrendered Subject Matter
description: An SGL is a 'limitation' presented, argued, or stated to make the claims patentable (in the original application) and 'generates' the surrender of claimed subject matter.
guidance: An SGL can be created by presentation of new/amended claims or an argument/statement by applicant that a limitation defines the invention over the art. A patent owner is bound by arguments relied upon to overcome an art rejection even if the Office adopted a different rationale. An SGL can also be created to obviate rejections on other grounds.

name: Three-step Test for Recapture (overview)
description: Recapture analysis is a three-step process: (1) determine whether and in what respect the reissue claims are broader than the original patent claims; (2) determine whether the broader aspects relate to subject matter surrendered in the original prosecution; (3) determine whether the reissue claims were materially narrowed in other respects so the claims may not have been enlarged and hence avoid recapture.
guidance: If at any step the criterion for 'no recapture' is met, the analysis can stop per the notes in the test. The MPEP cites Clement, North American Container and related case law for this test.

name: Step 1 — Is There Broadening? (examiner duty)
description: Examiner must review each reissue claim for the presence of broadening as compared with the scope of the claims of the patent to be reissued.
guidance: A reissue claim is broadened if some limitation of the patent claims is no longer required in the reissue claim. If no broadening, analysis ends. Examiners should consult MPEP §1412.03 for types of broadening.

name: Step 2A — Did Applicant Surrender Subject Matter?
description: Determine whether applicant surrendered any subject matter in the prosecution of the original application that became the patent to be reissued.
guidance: If an original patent claim limitation now omitted or broadened in the reissue was originally relied upon by applicant to make the claims allowable (by amendment or argument), the omitted limitation relates to surrendered subject matter. Examiner must review prosecution history (including rejections and applicant's arguments) to determine surrender. If applicant did not surrender subject matter, analysis ends — no recapture.

name: Step 2B — Does Broadening Relate to Surrendered Subject Matter?
description: If applicant did surrender subject matter, determine whether any of the broadening aspects of the reissue claims is in the area of the surrendered subject matter.
guidance: Analyze all broadening aspects to see if omitted/broadened limitations are directed to limitations relied upon by applicant in the original application. If the reissue claims are broadened with respect to previously surrendered subject matter, recapture will be present regardless of unrelated narrowing limitations (Mostafazadeh).

name: Argument Alone Can Create Surrender (precision required)
description: Surrender that forms basis for impermissible recapture can occur through applicant arguments alone (even without amendment).
guidance: The argument relied upon must be specific as to the limitation relied upon rather than a general 'boilerplate' statement that the limitations of the claims define over the prior art. Boilerplate or general statements are insufficient to establish surrender. Examples of insufficient boilerplate are provided in the MPEP.

name: Who Can Make the Surrendering Argument (applicant vs examiner)
description: Surrender of claimed subject matter cannot be based solely upon an applicant’s failure to respond to, or failure to challenge, an examiner’s statement made during prosecution; applicant is bound only by applicant’s amendments or positive arguments/statements.
guidance: Examiner's reasons for allowance alone cannot establish surrender. If applicant files comments supporting examiner's reasons, surrender may have occurred; if applicant files counter statements pointing to a different limitation as distinguishing, that different limitation may be the SGL. A general reply supporting allowance will not create surrender (Ex parte Yamaguchi).

name: Step 3 — Material Narrowing Analysis
description: Determine whether the reissue claims were materially narrowed in other respects such that the surrendered subject matter is not entirely or substantially recaptured.
guidance: If reissue claims were materially narrowed relative to the surrendered subject matter (i.e., narrowing limitations relate to what was amended/argued in the original application), recapture may be avoided (Youman, Mostafazadeh). The reissue applicant should point out explicitly what limitation has been added to materially narrow and how it narrows the claims.

name: Situation 1 — SGL Entirely Eliminated (recapture)
description: If an SGL has been entirely eliminated from a reissue claim, then a recapture rejection under 35 U.S.C. 251 may be proper.
guidance: Omission of an SGL, even if accompanied by other limitations making the claim narrower in unrelated aspects, is impermissible recapture (Pannu). A reissue claim that omits the surrender-generating limitation will generally be barred unless there is a new limitation related to the surrendered subject matter that materially narrows.

name: Situation 2 — SGL Modified but Not Entirely Eliminated
description: If an SGL has been retained but made less restrictive (broadened) in the reissue claim, determine whether the retained portion materially narrows the original claims to avoid recapture.
guidance: If the retained portion materially narrows relative to the surrendered subject matter, recapture may be avoided. If the retained portion is well known in the prior art or contained in prior art relied upon in original prosecution, it may not be materially narrowing and recapture exists (Mostafazadeh, Youman).

name: Situation 3 — Material Narrowing in Other Respects Must Relate to Surrendered Subject Matter
description: Even if the SGL is eliminated or not materially narrowed, recapture can be avoided if the reissued claims were materially narrowed in other respects that relate to the surrendered subject matter.
guidance: Narrowing limitations unrelated to the surrendered subject matter are insufficient. The material narrowing must address what was amended or argued by applicant in the original application (Greenliant, Gen. Electric example). Applicant can rebut Office recapture finding by showing such related material narrowing.

name: Comparing Reissue Claims to Canceled Claims (recapture bar)
description: The recapture rule bars the patentee from acquiring, through reissue, claims that are in all aspects the same scope as, or broader in scope than, those claims canceled from the original application to obtain a patent.
guidance: If reissue claims are narrower with respect to the added limitation that defined over the art (i.e., they retain the entirety of the limitation added in original prosecution), there will be no recapture even if the reissue claims are broader in some other, non-surrender-related aspect.

name: Comparing Reissue Claims to Patent Claims (four-part analysis)
description: When reissue claims are both broadened and narrowed versus the patent claims, examine whether the broadening is 'germane to a prior art rejection' (i.e., related to surrendered subject matter) and whether any narrowing is related to the surrender.
guidance: If reissue claims are broader by entirely omitting surrender-generating limitations and only narrowed in unrelated aspects, there is recapture. If reissue claims are narrower or equal in scope in the area related to surrendered subject matter and broader in unrelated aspects, there is no recapture (examples provided).

name: Printed patent copy format and completeness
description: A copy of the printed patent (including specification, drawings, and claims) must be supplied and reproduced on only one side of separate paper; two-sided copies are improper. Any disclaimer, certificate of correction, or reexamination certificate issued in the patent must also be supplied to provide the complete patent.
guidance: The copy must have each page plainly written on only one side. Include drawings, specification, and claims. Copies of any disclaimers, certificates of correction, or reexamination certificates that are part of the patent must be provided so the Office has the complete patent file copy (see MPEP § 2219).

name: Required content: identification of claims and detailed explanation applying cited art (37 CFR 1.510(b)(2))
description: The request must identify every claim for which reexamination is requested and include a detailed explanation of the pertinency and manner of applying the cited prior patents and printed publications to each such claim.
guidance: Provide limitation-by-limitation explanations—ideally in a detailed claim chart—showing how each claimed limitation maps to the teachings of each reference. For each proposed combination explain how each reference is used and provide at least one basis for combining references for obviousness rejections. Quote pertinent teachings and cite page/column/line numbers and figure numbers where appropriate. Avoid lumping claims or proposed combinations together; use clear, specific language (examples of inappropriate and appropriate phrasing are provided in the MPEP). Any failure to provide required explanations will result in a Notice of Failure to Comply and possible withdrawal or need to cure.

name: Prior art limited to patents and printed publications
description: Substantial new questions of patentability in reexamination must be based on prior patents and printed publications (statutory prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102/103).
guidance: Matters such as public use, on-sale, inventorship, 35 U.S.C. 101, 35 U.S.C. 112, conduct by parties, etc., should not be included in the request and will not be considered when making the determination on the request. A cited patent/printed publication cannot be used merely as evidence of alleged public use or on-sale activity; it must be applied directly to claims under appropriate portions of 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103.

name: Obviousness combination requirement (basis for combining)
description: For proposed obviousness rejections, the requester must provide at least one clear basis for combining the cited references and explain why the claim(s) would have been obvious over the proposed combination.
guidance: Preferably quote pertinent teachings from each reference and provide citations to specific pages/cols/lines and figures. Do not lump multiple alternative combinations together without explaining the distinct rationale for each combination. Examples of acceptable and unacceptable phrasing are provided in the MPEP.

name: English translations for non-English references
description: An English language translation of all necessary and pertinent non-English language patents and/or printed publications must be included with the request.
guidance: Translations should cover the portions of the references relied upon so the Office and patent owner can assess the cited material's pertinency and application to the claims.

name: Newness / usefulness (the “new and useful” requirement)
description: The statute authorizes patents on “any new and useful process…,” so claimed inventions must be new and useful to qualify as patentable subject matter.
guidance: The article treats novelty/usefulness as embedded in §101's language; lack of novelty has historically been invoked to reject claims (see discussion of prior cases). Novelty here is discussed as a separate ground (often §102), but the text notes earlier decisions rejected business-method patents on grounds like lack of novelty rather than a categorical business-method bar.

name: Practical limits via other doctrines (novelty, nonobviousness, enablement) rather than categorical exclusions
description: Where the statute is broad, practical limits on overbroad business-method patents have often been imposed through other patentability doctrines (e.g., lack of novelty, obviousness, enablement) rather than an outright business-method ban.
guidance: The article notes that many earlier rejections of business-method patents rested on grounds such as lack of novelty or being mere abstractions; it suggests that, in practice, the legal system often uses these other doctrinal tools to police claims rather than a categorical exclusion. This is guidance for evaluators to consider multiple doctrinal axes when assessing claims.

name: Scope of review (grounds and evidence)
description: IPR is a trial proceeding conducted at the PTAB to review patentability of one or more claims in a patent only on a ground that could be raised under §§ 102 or 103, and only on the basis of patents and printed publications.
guidance: IPR cannot be used to raise other statutory grounds (e.g., §101, §112) or rely on evidence other than patents and printed publications. Petitioners should craft grounds limited to novelty and obviousness and cite patents/printed publications as prior art.

name: Strategic considerations for defending against an IPR
description: Preliminary Response is critical (early dismissal possible); Argue strong patent owner interests; Use Director discretionary denial factors; Amend claims if possible.
guidance: Filing a persuasive Preliminary Response can sometimes prevent institution. Defendants (patent owners) should highlight patent-strength factors, attack the petition's sufficiency under the reasonable-likelihood standard, and consider claim amendments or other motions to preserve claim scope and value.

name: Advantages of IPR as a forum
description: Advantages of IPR: 1. Faster: 18 months or less from filing to final disposition. 2. Cheaper than litigation: Limited discovery. 3. Higher invalidation rates: ~75% of instituted IPRs result in some claims being invalidated. 4. Specialized adjudicators: PTAB judges have technical backgrounds. 5. Standard of review: Preponderance of evidence (district court: clear and convincing).
guidance: These comparative advantages inform the decision to pursue IPR. Weigh speed, cost, and the PTAB's experience against estoppel risks and scope limitations when choosing between IPR and district-court litigation.

name: Caveats about composition bias and sample limitations
description: Empirical conclusions must account for possible compositional changes (e.g., variation in circuits represented, technology mix, plaintiff/defendant types) and Westlaw coverage biases that could skew observed rates of fee awards.
guidance: The paper emphasizes need for larger datasets and further breakdowns (e.g., by claim type or party type) to rule out confounding compositional effects and to increase statistical reliability.

name: Doctrine of Equivalents — role of interchangeability and function
description: Known interchangeability may support a conclusion that the difference between the [part] [step] in the [product] [method] and the claim requirement is not substantial. The fact that a [part] [step] of the [product] [method] performs the same function as the claim requirement is not, by itself, sufficient to show known interchangeability.
guidance: Known interchangeability is supportive but not required to find infringement under the doctrine of equivalents; mere performance of the same function alone is insufficient.

name: Doctrine of Equivalents — limitation by subject matter described but not claimed
description: You may not use the doctrine of equivalents to find infringement if you find that the subject matter alleged to be equivalent to a requirement of the patent claim was described in the [ ] patent but not covered by any of its claims. The subject matter described but not claimed must be specific enough that one of ordinary skill in the art would understand that it was present in the patent.
guidance: Material described in the specification but intentionally not claimed can prevent DOE coverage of that material.

name: Means-plus-function claims — literal scope (§112(6))
description: A means-plus-function requirement only covers the specific [structure] disclosed in a patent specification for performing the claimed function and the equivalents of those specific [structure] that perform the claimed function. A means-plus-function requirement does not cover all possible structures that could be used to perform the claimed function.
guidance: Example: 'means for processing data' is interpreted to cover the actual means disclosed in the patent for processing data and other means equivalent to it, not every possible means (e.g., pencil-and-paper or human brain) unless so disclosed or equivalent.

name: Means-plus-function claims — literal infringement proof steps
description: To decide if [patent holder] has proven that [alleged infringer]’s [product] includes structure covered by a means-plus-function requirement, first decide whether the [product] has any structure that performs the described function. If not, the claim is not infringed. If it does, determine whether that structure is the same as or equivalent to the structure identified in the specification; if same or equivalent, the means-plus-function requirement is satisfied.
guidance: The court (judge) may identify the corresponding structure in the specification. Equivalence requires showing a person of ordinary skill would consider differences not substantial and that the structure was available on the patent grant date.

name: Means-plus-function claims — temporal limitation on equivalents (§112(6) vs DOE)
description: An equivalent structure under §112(6) cannot embrace technology developed after the issuance of the patent because the literal meaning of a claim is fixed upon its issuance. Although an after-arising equivalent may infringe under the doctrine of equivalents, it generally cannot infringe literally under §112(6).
guidance: Under §112(6) the accused device must perform the identical function as recited in the claim element; DOE can be satisfied when the function is only substantially the same. The §112(6) equivalent must have been available as of the patent issuance date.

name: Means-plus-function (method) — step-plus-function adaptation
description: If a claim at issue is a method claim with a limitation written in 'step-plus-function' format, substitute 'acts' for 'structure' and apply the corresponding means-plus-function rules.
guidance: Modify instruction wording for method claims accordingly.

name: Limitations on Doctrine of Equivalents due to claim amendments/statements (prosecution history estoppel)
description: Because [patent holder] made certain claim changes or statements during the patent application process for the [ ] patent, the doctrine of equivalents analysis cannot be applied to the following requirements of the asserted claims: [List requirements on a claim-by-claim basis]. Unless each of these requirements is literally present within the [alleged infringer]’s [product] [method], there can be no infringement of the claim.
guidance: Prosecution history estoppel or related prosecution statements can carve out subject matter from DOE coverage; judge should identify the affected claim limitations.

name: Contributory infringement — elements
description: Contributory infringement exists if: (1) someone other than [alleged infringer] directly infringed a claim of the [ ] patent; and (2) [alleged infringer] supplied an important component of the infringing part of the [product] or [method]; (3) the component is not a common component suitable for non-infringing use; and (4) [alleged infringer] supplied the component with knowledge of the [ ] patent and knowledge that the component was especially made or adapted for use in an infringing manner.
guidance: If there is no direct infringement by anyone, there can be no contributory infringement. The supplier must know of the patent and that the component was specially made/adapted for infringing use.

name: Anticipation (novelty) — all-elements-in-single-reference test
description: A patent claim is invalid if the claimed invention is not new. For anticipation, all of its requirements must have existed in a single device or method or been described in a single previous publication or patent that predates the claimed invention. The description need not use the same words, but all claim requirements must be present either stated or necessarily implied.
guidance: Ways to show anticipation include prior public knowledge/use, prior printed publication or patent anywhere in the world, prior making by someone else, prior issued/published U.S. patent/application, learning the invention from another, or first-inventor disputes (conception and reduction to practice rules). Tailor the applicable list to the case.

name: Statutory bars (one-year bars)
description: A patent claim is invalid if the patent application was not filed within the time required by law (statutory bar). For a statutory bar, all claimed requirements must have been present in one prior art reference dated more than one year before the patent application was filed.
guidance: Examples: printed publication more than one year before filing; public use in the U.S. not primarily experimental; sale or offer for sale in the U.S. more than one year before filing (unless primarily experimental); foreign patent obtained more than one year before U.S. filing. Disclosure need not use exact words but must enable one of ordinary skill to make and use the invention.

name: Obviousness — Graham factors and secondary considerations
description: A patent claim is invalid if the claimed invention would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the field at the time of the application. The determination requires factual findings on: (1) the level of ordinary skill in the field; (2) the scope and content of the prior art; and (3) the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art. Additionally, determine whether any of the following have been established: commercial success, long-felt need, unsuccessful attempts by others, copying, unexpected and superior results, acceptance by others, independent invention, and other evidence tending to show nonobviousness or obviousness.
guidance: The court makes the ultimate legal determination of obviousness based on underlying factual determinations (often made by the jury). Present only the disputed Graham factors to the jury as necessary; secondary considerations (aka objective indicia) should be considered when supported by evidence.

name: Role division between jury and judge on obviousness
description: The court is charged with making the determination as to whether a patent claim was obvious based upon your determination of several factual questions. The ultimate judgment of obviousness is a legal determination for the judge, while the jury may be asked to determine underlying factual issues.
guidance: The jury should be presented with the specific factual issues in dispute (Graham factors); the judge then applies the law to those facts to reach the legal conclusion.

name: Use of bracketed terminology for customization
description: To enhance litigants' ability to customize the Instructions to a particular case, bracketed terminology (e.g., [subject matter], [the Defendant], [claims in dispute]) is provided so parties can find-and-replace case-specific facts.
guidance: Brackets indicate where alternative terminology may be used (e.g., [[product] [method]]). Users should replace placeholders (e.g., 'system' -> 'product') and make appropriate edits for product vs method patents.

name: United States Patents—what a patent is and how it is obtained
description: A patent gives the owner the right to exclude others from making, using, offering to sell, or selling the claimed invention in the United States or importing it. A patent application includes a specification and claims; the Patent Examiner searches prior art and issues Office Actions.
guidance: Explain prosecution history (file wrapper), role of PTO/Patent Examiner, what claims do (define scope), and that jury will be instructed on what constitutes prior art in the case.

name: Literal infringement—each and every claim element required
description: A patent claim is literally infringed only if the accused product/method includes each and every [[element] [method step]] in that patent claim.
guidance: If the accused product lacks one or more claim elements, there is no literal infringement; decide literal infringement claim-by-claim.

name: Doctrine of equivalents—insubstantial differences (function-way-result)
description: A claim is infringed under the doctrine of equivalents if the accused product/method contains the equivalent of each claim element not literally present—i.e., an element that is only insubstantially different, often shown by performing substantially the same function, in substantially the same way, to achieve substantially the same result.
guidance: Plaintiff must prove by a preponderance that equivalents exist for each missing element; jury should be instructed on recognized limitations to the doctrine (see prosecution history estoppel, dedication to public).

name: Limitations on doctrine of equivalents—prosecution history estoppel and dedication to the public
description: Limitations on the doctrine include prosecution history estoppel and subject matter dedicated to the public, which can bar application of equivalents for certain claim scope.
guidance: Provide instructions on how prosecution amendments or statements may limit equivalents; give examples and relevant case citations as needed.

name: Claim construction—general (judge defines claim terms)
description: It is the judge's job to give the meaning of any claim language that must be interpreted; jurors must accept and use those meanings when deciding infringement and invalidity.
guidance: Claims are to be construed the same way for infringement and invalidity; read stipulations and the court's claim constructions to the jury.

name: Claim construction for the case—read court constructions/stipulations
description: [READ STIPULATIONS AND COURT’S CLAIM CONSTRUCTIONS]; the judge provides constructions of disputed terms and of any limitations governed by 35 U.S.C. § 112 ¶ 6 (means-plus-function).
guidance: Cite Teva v. Sandoz, Phillips, Markman, etc., and explain that jurors must follow the court’s constructions even if they disagree.

name: Means-plus-function claims—construction and limiting structure
description: When a claim element is expressed as a 'means' or 'step' for performing a function (35 U.S.C. § 112 ¶ 6), the element covers the structure or steps described in the specification that perform the recited function and equivalents, not all means that perform the function.
guidance: Instruction 2.2 should be given only if the case involves means-plus-function claims; judge should identify the recited function and the corresponding structure/step in the specification (or equivalents) for jury use.

name: Direct infringement—knowledge and intent are immaterial
description: Direct infringement does not require knowledge of the patent or intent to infringe; such mental state is immaterial to the finding of direct infringement.
guidance: This instruction clarifies that direct infringement is a question of whether the accused product/method meets the claim limitations, regardless of defendant's awareness.

name: Infringement under §271(g) (product made by a patented process)
description: A party may be liable for infringement by import, sale, offer for sale, or use of a product made by a patented process (§271(g)).
guidance: Explain the nexus between the product and the asserted process claim and the elements required for §271(g) liability.

name: Claim phrase meanings: 'comprising of', 'consisting of', 'consisting essentially of'
description: Special instructions are provided regarding how to treat transitional phrases such as 'comprising', 'consisting of', and 'consisting essentially of' in claim scope.
guidance: Explain to jurors how each transitional term affects claim scope (open vs closed vs partially open) with examples as needed.

name: Summary of Invalidity Defense—overview
description: The jury must decide whether the defendant has proven that asserted claims are invalid, overcoming the presumption of validity with clear and convincing evidence.
guidance: Invalidity can be based on prior art (anticipation, obviousness), written description/enablement failures, or other statutory bars; instruct on the specific invalidity theories asserted in the case.

name: Prior art—definitions (pre-AIA vs AIA) and what counts
description: Prior art is defined differently under pre-AIA and AIA law: pre-AIA categories (e.g., date of invention, one-year bars) vs AIA (publicly available before effective filing date).
guidance: Practice Note on 'Cutoff Date' explains that Cutoff Date may vary by claim and by pre-AIA vs AIA subsections; jury may need instruction on determining Cutoff Date(s) for each claim.

name: Anticipation—prior public knowledge, public use, on-sale bar, printed publication, prior invention, prior patent, prior U.S. application
description: Anticipation instructions cover many ways a claim can be anticipated: prior public knowledge, prior public use, on-sale bar (including pre-AIA/AIA distinctions), experimental use, printed publications, prior patents, and prior U.S. applications.
guidance: Provide separate sub-instructions for pre-AIA vs AIA contexts where relevant; instruct jurors on elements required to prove anticipation for each category and how to treat experimental uses and printed publications.

name: Obviousness—Graham factors and secondary considerations
description: Obviousness instructions follow Graham v. John Deere: (1) scope and content of prior art, (2) differences between claimed invention and prior art, (3) level of ordinary skill in the art, and (4) secondary considerations (other considerations) such as commercial success, long-felt need, failure of others, etc.
guidance: Explain how jurors should weigh these factors together and the standard for proving obviousness (clear and convincing evidence).

name: Enablement (35 U.S.C. §112)—sufficiency of specification to teach making and using
description: Enablement requires the specification to describe how the invention works and how to make and use it so as to enable others skilled in the art to do so.
guidance: Instruct jurors on what evidence is relevant to enablement (breadth of claim vs enabling disclosure) and burden of proof for invalidity based on non-enablement.

name: Reasonable royalty—smallest salable unit and apportionment
description: Royalties should be based on the 'smallest salable unit' that practices the patent and has close relation to the claimed invention; where that unit contains non-infringing features, damages must be apportioned to the value attributable to the patented technology.
guidance: Entire market value rule (EMV) is a narrow exception: patentee must show the patented feature 'drives the demand' or 'substantially creates the value' of the entire product to recover royalties on entire product revenues.

name: Standard-Essential Patents (SEPs) and FRAND-specific guidance
description: For SEPs, jury should be instructed on the particulars of the patentee's FRAND commitment, on patent law principles, and only on relevant Georgia-Pacific factors; jurors must be instructed on apportionment to the portion of the standard and the claimed invention.
guidance: Do not instruct on irrelevant Georgia-Pacific factors; explain apportionment between value of standard and value of claimed invention (Ericsson, Apple v. Motorola guidance).

name: Apportionment — award only incremental value attributable to the claimed invention
description: Any royalty award must be apportioned to reflect no more than the incremental value that is contributed by the patent(s)-in-suit, distinguished from the value of non-patented elements, manufacturing, business risks, or improvements added by the infringer.
guidance: Identify the smallest saleable patent-practicing unit when appropriate; separate and quantify the portion of value attributable to the patented feature(s) versus other features. Factor and jury instructions must emphasize apportionment as central to accurate damages.

name: Factor One: The incremental value contributed by the invention
description: Determine the incremental value that the claimed invention contributed to the accused product (i.e., the value over and above the best available alternative at the hypothetical negotiation date).
guidance: Focus the factfinder on the incremental contribution of the patented feature to the product's value; exclude value that would have existed absent the patented feature or that is attributable to conventional elements or alternatives.

name: Factor Two: The value contributed by factors other than the claimed invention
description: Identify and quantify value in the accused product that is attributable to non-claimed features, complementary technologies, business practices, or other sources not claimed by the patent(s)-in-suit.
guidance: This factor supports apportionment: the jury should reduce any award to exclude value from non-patented elements or separate contributions from other technologies or patents.

name: Instructions regarding FRAND/SEP contexts
description: When a patent is essential to a standard and subject to a FRAND commitment, the reasonable royalty must reflect only the contribution of the patented technology to the standard's capabilities and must exclude value attributable to the standard as a whole or to other patents incorporated in the standard.
guidance: Juries must apportion awards to exclude value attributable to the ability to practice the standard itself and to other patents. Where applicable (e.g., IEEE commitments), courts should instruct juries on specific FRAND-language considerations (contribution of claimed invention to smallest saleable product, comparable licenses not obtained under threat, etc.).

name: Procedure to calculate running royalty damages
description: To calculate a running royalty: identify total sales revenue of the smallest saleable component practicing the invention; identify the apportioned base (portion attributable to the claimed invention); determine the royalty rate the parties would have agreed to; multiply apportioned base by royalty rate to get total damages.
guidance: Provide jurors with concrete steps and party contentions for each step (e.g., disputed base amount or rate). Emphasize apportionment in identifying the base and require factual support for claimed bases and rates.

name: Affirmative treatment/prophylaxis limitation requirement
description: To qualify as a 'treatment' or 'prophylaxis' limitation the claim limitation must affirmatively recite an action that treats or prevents a disease or medical condition (e.g., 'administering amazonic acid to a patient', 'administering a course of plasmapheresis to a patient').
guidance: If the limitation is merely an intended use, field-of-use limitation, or does not require the substance actually be used by/on the patient (e.g., 'prescribing a topical steroid to a patient with eczema' or labeling a product as a 'pharmaceutical composition'), it is not an affirmative treatment/prophylaxis limitation and cannot integrate a judicial exception under the 'treatment or prophylaxis' consideration.

name: Particularity of treatment or prophylaxis
description: The treatment/prophylaxis limitation must be 'particular,' i.e., specifically identified so it does not encompass all applications of the judicial exception(s).
guidance: Compare a claim reciting 'administering a lower than normal dosage of a beta blocker medication to a patient identified as having the poor metabolizer genotype' (particular) vs 'administering a suitable medication to a patient' (not particular). Examiners may also evaluate related considerations such as mere instructions to apply an exception, and field-of-use/technological environment when assessing particularity.

name: Limitation must not be mere extra-solution activity or field-of-use
description: A claimed treatment/prophylaxis must impose meaningful limits on the judicial exception and must not be merely extra-solution activity (e.g., steps performed only to gather data) or a field-of-use restriction.
guidance: Example contrast: (a) administering vaccines to gather data for a mental analysis (extra-solution, not integrative) vs (c) vaccinating a second group according to the lowest-risk schedule determined by the analysis (integrative, applies the exception). Evaluate with insignificant extra-solution activity and field-of-use/technological environment considerations.

name: Identify additional claim elements beyond the judicial exception
description: Step 2B begins by identifying any and all additional elements (features/limitations/steps) recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception(s).
guidance: Examiners should carry over additional-element identifications from Step 2A Prong Two and use them as the basis for the inventive-concept analysis. Claims must be analyzed individually (each claim may be treated differently).

name: Inventive concept cannot be the judicial exception itself
description: An inventive concept 'cannot be furnished by the unpatentable law of nature (or natural phenomenon or abstract idea) itself.'
guidance: An inventive concept must be an element or combination of elements recited in the claim in addition to the judicial exception that ensures the claim amounts to significantly more than the exception alone (Alice/Mayo precedent).

name: Improvement to the functioning of a computer or other technology
description: Claims that purport to improve the functioning of the computer itself or any other technology/technical field can qualify as 'significantly more' in the §101 analysis.
guidance: When asserting such an improvement, the specification should provide sufficient technical detail to make the improvement apparent to a person of ordinary skill. The claim must reflect the disclosed improvement (though not necessarily by literal language like 'thereby increasing bandwidth'). Evaluate the claim 'as an ordered combination' and avoid oversimplifying. See McRO (automation of animation tasks) and DDR (technological solution to technological problem) examples.

name: Effecting a transformation or reduction of an article to a different state or thing
description: A claimed process that effects a transformation of a particular article to a different state or thing can amount to significantly more.
guidance: Example: transforming raw, uncured synthetic rubber into precision-molded rubber products (Diehr). The transformation must be meaningful and tied to the claimed steps.

name: Adding specific non-conventional limitations that confine the claim to a particular useful application
description: Adding limitations other than well-understood, routine, conventional activity, or adding unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application, can provide an inventive concept.
guidance: Example: BASCOM—non-conventional and non-generic arrangement of computer components for filtering Internet content. The added limitations must be more than generic or high-level recitations of conventional activity.

name: Limitations found insufficient to supply an inventive concept
description: A set of limitation-types that the courts have held are not enough to make a claim 'significantly more' than a judicial exception.
guidance: Includes: (i) adding the words 'apply it' or mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer (Alice); (ii) simply appending well-understood, routine, conventional activities at a high level of generality; (iii) adding insignificant extra-solution activity such as mere data gathering (CyberSource); (iv) generally linking the exception to a technological environment or field-of-use without meaningful limitation (Bilski, Flook). These should not be treated as inventive concepts.

name: Specification must support asserted technical improvements
description: If an applicant asserts that the invention improves conventional computer functioning or technology, the specification must contain sufficient technical explanation such that one of ordinary skill would recognize the improvement.
guidance: A conclusory assertion of improvement in the specification is insufficient. The specification need not literally state the improvement phrase, but must describe details or a technical problem/solution that make the improvement apparent (compare McRO vs Affinity Labs). After finding disclosure of improvement, ensure the claim scope reflects that improvement.

name: Evaluate claims under the broadest reasonable interpretation and as a whole
description: Examiners should review the entire disclosure, construe claims under the broadest reasonable interpretation, and evaluate whether the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception.
guidance: Avoid oversimplifying claims by ignoring specific claim requirements. Consider dependent claims separately — one claim in an application may be ineligible while another dependent claim may recite additional elements that amount to significantly more. Follow the MPEP flowchart (Step 2B leads to YES eligible (Pathway C) or NO ineligible → §101 rejection).

name: Inventor attribution and entitlement (Article 8)
description: The name of the inventor shall be mentioned in the Patent application unless the inventor requests otherwise; rights belong to the inventor or legal successor; if essential elements derived from another person's invention, rights belong to original inventor; joint inventors share rights; mere assistance without inventive contribution does not make one an inventor; where multiple persons independently perform the same invention, the person who files first or claims priority is entitled to the Patent provided application satisfies requirements.
guidance: First‑to‑file rule (subject to priority), and clear standards for who qualifies as inventor.

name: Formal application requirements (Article 11)
description: Application shall be submitted by inventor, registration agent, or person to whom rights devolved and include applicant name, inventor name, agent (if any), declaration justifying applicant's right if not inventor; name of invention, summary, detailed description, one or more claims, and illustrations (if any); abstract for technical info only; description must be sufficient at filing for skilled person to implement; claims must be clear, concise and entirely based on the description; application and attachments in both Arabic and English; applicant must provide requested information within 90 days; amendments permitted if non‑essential; executive regulations determine attachments/dates.
guidance: Strict sufficiency and formal-language requirements; 90‑day reply timelines; claims must be supported by description.

name: Independent claim must state essential elements
description: The independent claim will state the essential elements of the invention. Those essential elements are necessary for achieving the technical effect underlying the solution of the technical problem with which the application is concerned (the problem usually being derived from the description).
guidance: The independent claim should contain all essential elements explicitly described in the description as necessary for the essential functionality of the invention. To achieve the broadest possible protection, the essential elements will be stretched to their greatest reasonable extent, taking into account the essential functionality and prior art.

name: Formulate an inventive-step strategy for all claims
description: For all of the claims (independent and dependent), some argument of – or a strategy for – inventive step should be formulated, for example being nonobvious, or giving rise to an unexpected advantage or effect.
guidance: When drafting claims, consider how each claim (including dependent fallback claims) can be supported with arguments for inventive step/nonobviousness and how claimed features contribute to technical effect.

name: Dependent claims as more particular embodiments / fallback positions
description: Dependent claims will be concerned with more particular embodiments of the invention — that is, a more specific disclosure of the invention than that set out in the independent claim. Some dependent claims should be drafted as 'fallback positions' in case the independent claim is found during prosecution (or litigation) to be not novel or to lack inventive step.
guidance: In brainstorming, identify order of importance of elements (essential and nonessential) taking into account patentability, commercial settings and enforcement possibilities. Draft dependent claims to provide fallback scope if broader claims are defeated.

name: One dependent claim per selected/added element (with exceptions)
description: In general, one dependent claim is drafted per selected or added element. But there are cases (such as in a Markush formula) in which several elements (such as chemical radical values) are selected simultaneously.
guidance: A dependent claim adding an element selected from among a group or further characterizing an element can depend from only those preceding claims that themselves provide an antecedent for that element. A dependent claim adding an extra element does not need an antecedent; it can depend from any preceding claims and may (but need not) have multiple dependency.

name: Use dependency ordering (add elements in decreasing importance)
description: When drafting dependent chains, elements may be added successively in decreasing order of importance.
