guidance: Identify an order of importance for elements and draft dependent claims adding selected values in that order (e.g., A > B > C), producing singular dependency chains when successive selected elements are added.

name: Prefer singular dependency for successive selected elements
description: So far, Claims 1–3 form a dependency chain with only singular dependency, as is recommended when successive selected elements are added.
guidance: When adding successive selected elements, use singular dependency to form clear fallback chains. Multiple dependency can be used for other purposes but may complicate conversion to jurisdictions that disallow it.

name: Multiple dependent claims: permitted/recommended per jurisdiction
description: When, in the following dependent claims, an extra element is added, writing the claim in multiple dependent form is strongly recommended for the EPO, for the reasons explained in section 3.3. The claim set in this example will be appropriate for the EPO and those patent offices that allow multiple dependencies from multiple dependent claims — something not permitted at the USPTO.
guidance: Use multiple dependency in EPO-style sets to offer broader coverage. However, before entering USPTO national phase, deconstruct multiple dependencies into appropriate singular dependencies and prepare US-style claims; otherwise multiple dependencies will not be allowed at the USPTO.

name: Avoid creating a dependency pyramid (anti-pattern)
description: A dependency pyramid (many multiple dependencies whose vertex is Claim 1) is not generally recommended, because it does not offer good fallback positions in the event that the vertex Claim 1 is found not to be novel.
guidance: Beware that multiple dependencies might be erased or transformed by another drafter into claims all depending from Claim 1, creating a pyramid. Structure dependencies to preserve useful fallback positions rather than centralize everything on a single vertex claim.

name: Analyse dependency groups separately for validity and infringement
description: The analysis starts by separating out the different dependency groups (or a dependency chain), each one being formed of a single independent claim and all the claims that depend from it. Each dependency group is then considered separately.
guidance: For validity (novelty/inventive step) and infringement assessments, treat each dependency group independently. Use diagrams of claim scopes vs prior art or accused embodiments to determine which claims are novel/valid or infringed.

name: Do not assume invalidity/infringement results propagate across dependencies
description: Care must be taken not to conclude (wrongly) that invalidity of an independent claim necessarily implies invalidity of all of the claims dependent from it — a relatively frequent mistake made by nonexperts. Similarly, care must be taken not to conclude (wrongly) that infringement of the independent claim implies infringement of all the claims dependent from it.
guidance: Examples: if prior art falls within a dependent claim's scope but outside another dependent claim, some dependent claims may remain novel/valid. If an accused embodiment falls within a dependent claim, it may also fall within broader claims in the chain, but absence from an independent claim means dependent chain claims are not infringed.

name: Two-part test for literal infringement assessment
description: A declaration of infringement involves making two judgments: (i) that at least one prohibited act has been carried out; and (ii) that the 'accused embodiment' associated with that prohibited act falls within the scope of at least one valid claim of the patent.
guidance: Assume the prohibited act is proven; then compare accused embodiment features with claim elements to decide literal infringement. Use dependency/group analysis to simplify: if embodiment outside independent claim, then claims depending from it are not infringed.

name: Brainstorming objectives when starting claim drafting
description: The drafting process typically starts with a brainstorming meeting between the patent drafter and the inventor(s), with the initial objectives of: identifying the invention(s); selecting a claim type for the first independent claim; and choosing a preamble at an appropriate level for the dependency group corresponding to the independent claim.
guidance: Perform brainstorming taking into account specific embodiments, drawings, and the closest prior art. Prioritize elements by commercial importance and patentability to plan fallback claims and enforcement strategy.

name: Draft to permit jurisdictional adaptation (PCT amendments / US conversion)
description: Before the PCT international application enters national/regional phases, use the opportunity under the PCT for amending the claims to fit national requirements. Great care should be taken when drafting a claim set appropriate to the USPTO. If this task is not performed by the same person who drafted the PCT application, they should give specific instructions about the detail underlying the original claim set to a new drafter.
guidance: Prepare sets of claims to be deconstructed or expanded (e.g., deconstruct EPO multiple-dependency claims into USPTO-acceptable singular dependencies). Consider producing separate US-claim variants (broad and narrow dependency chains) to cover intermediate scopes and avoid added-matter/added-claim problems.

name: Control total number of claims to avoid excess fees
description: When adapting claim sets, keep the total number of claims within reasonable limits (ideally no more than 20 in examples given) to avoid extra claim fees (e.g., EPO allows 15 without extra fee at time of writing).
guidance: Use steps to generate claims that cover broadest, narrowest, and intermediate scopes while watching claim count. The example shows converting an EPO set with multiple dependencies into about 20 US-claims to cover a wide range of scopes without excessive fees.

name: Method/process claim drafting considerations (order and 'for' language)
description: In many jurisdictions, the steps in a method claim are presumed to occur in any order, unless otherwise stated. A preamble with 'for' (e.g., 'an apparatus for carrying out the process') may be construed as meaning merely an apparatus suitable for the process in some jurisdictions.
guidance: When drafting method claims, be explicit if sequence matters. For apparatus or product claims with purposive language, recognize that suitability for a purpose may not impose the same limitations as a method step. Consider jurisdictional treatment of use claims (e.g., EPO treats 'use of X as insecticide' equivalent to a process claim; US requires drafting as a process claim).

name: Use Markush groups and consider equivalents to broaden claims
description: When considering an element defined by a term of a preferred embodiment, the patent drafter should think of broader terms and other elements that a person skilled in the art would consider technical equivalents. Sometimes, including alternative elements in a Markush group may help in drafting broader claims.
guidance: Consider broadening from structural to functional terminology where supported. Use Markush groups where appropriate (e.g., C1, C2, C3, C4) and assess support in the description for broader terms and equivalence between variants.

name: Professional tip: edit claims to remove unnecessary words
description: Once you believe you have reasonably captured the essence of the invention, review and re-review the claim to see how many words you can remove from it while still preserving the essence of the invention.
guidance: Involving the inventor in this process can help conceptualize the invention more clearly. Consider whether adjectives or qualifiers (e.g., 'pivotal' mounting) are strictly necessary for claim completeness or can be omitted to broaden scope.

name: Identity, equivalence, and scope of patented inventions
description: Identity exists when the same means produces the same effect — identity of effect, function, and means; equivalence, specific difference, and generic difference determine whether inventions are identical or diverse.
guidance: Identity depends on identity of force, object, and mode of application; absent if one cannot be substituted for another; whether same functions performed in same way; scope of patented inventions is determined by the claims; form and embodiment differences do not necessarily defeat identity.

name: LIX D — Comity principle: first-attaching jurisdiction should carry case; military retention discretion and prerequisites for attachment
description: As a principle of comity, the jurisdiction which first attaches should carry the case to termination. For such jurisdiction to attach, the prisoner should be in custody and charges should have been served with view to trial by court-martial. Military authorities may decline to surrender until claims of the United States satisfied; retention of jurisdiction is discretionary and may be waived (especially for grave charges).
guidance: Citations: G.O.29; various C. and R. opinions (C.10048; 11589; 14042; 17767; numerous others) provide examples and factors for discretion.

name: Voluntary amendments also trigger estoppel
description: Voluntary claim amendments—those not required by the examiner—signal to the public that subject matter has been surrendered and therefore can create prosecution history estoppel.
guidance: Treat voluntary narrowing amendments the same as examiner-required narrowing amendments for estoppel purposes (per Federal Circuit reasoning).

name: Foreseeability test (scope and timing)
description: An equivalent may be excluded if it was foreseeable at the time of application/amendment—if foreseeable, the patentee should have claimed it literally.
guidance: Timing ambiguity: court text is inconsistent whether foreseeability is assessed at time of application or amendment; the author argues it is more logical to apply at time of amendment (the act that triggers estoppel). Foreseeability determinations typically require technical fact-finding (experts); courts may need to decide judge vs jury responsibility and may consider pretrial Festo hearings akin to Markman hearings.

name: Foreseeability test vs Graver Tank tension
description: Foreseeability test conflicts with the historic Graver Tank spirit which allowed recovery for equivalents that may have been known yet not literally claimed; the Court's statement that patentees should draft claims to encompass readily known equivalents appears inconsistent with Graver Tank.
guidance: Recognize doctrinal tension: applying foreseeability strictly may penalize drafting/adversarial realities of prosecution and PTO practice; scholars argue for either overruling Graver Tank or adopting a uniform foreseeability standard irrespective of amendment history.

name: Reasonableness (other-reason) test
description: If it would be unreasonable to expect the patentee to have described the insubstantial substitution in question (some other reason), the patentee can rebut the presumption.
guidance: This is an equitable consideration focused on whether the patentee could reasonably have claimed the equivalent; often implicated in fields like biotech where exhaustive literal claiming is impractical (sequence variants). Lacks bright-line rules and may require factfinder determinations.

name: Who decides foreseeability/rebuttal issues — judge vs jury
description: The Supreme Court and Federal Circuit left ambiguous whether foreseeability and other rebuttal issues are for judge or jury; district courts and commentators differ.
guidance: Options proposed: judge-decided pretrial Festo hearing (to promote consistency) or jury fact-finding (credibility of experts). Expect litigation over the proper allocation; practitioners should prepare both factual records and claim-construction arguments.

name: Practical prosecution implications — drafting diligence
description: Festo IV increases the burden on patent prosecutors to draft claims that literally capture foreseeable equivalents and to document amendment reasons; careless omissions may be unrecoverable.
guidance: Practical strategies recommended: (1) file continuation applications to recapture equivalents supported by original disclosure; (2) appeal rejections rather than amend when valuable claims are at stake; (3) draft comprehensive initial claims to avoid narrowing amendments. Each strategy has costs/tradeoffs.

name: Prosecution strategies that will not preserve equivalents
description: Certain proposed strategies post-Festo are ineffective: filing parallel broad/narrow applications does not preserve equivalents if prosecution history of parents/grandparents is considered; canceling claims still considered abandonment; starting narrow then broadening is not protective.
guidance: Cite Federal Circuit precedent: Mark I Mktg. (parent/grandparent prosecution included), Intermatic (estoppel applies to all claims with same limitation), Diversitech (canceled claims considered abandoned). Practitioners should not rely on these tactics to avoid estoppel.

name: Specifications must agree with the patent
description: Specifications must agree with the letters-patent; repugnancy between them has legal effect.
guidance: Specifications and drawings are construed together with the patent. Courts construe specifications liberally but require that the patent not claim more than described; contradictions or repugnancies are material.

name: Claims / patent scope must not exceed invention
description: A patent cannot be more extensive than the invention; it should contain no more than is necessary.
guidance: Patents are construed with the specification; a patent that attempts to cover distinct inventions or to be broader than described is invalid to that extent. The patent relates back to date of invention but is limited to what was actually invented and described.

name: Extent of description — disclose every thing essential
description: Specifications should describe every thing essential to the invention but need not describe what the patentee is not claiming.
guidance: While some things need not be described, omissions of essential details can invalidate. Slight defects may be fatal; the description should include materials of a machine when necessary and be precise about essential elements.

name: Best mode, experiments and experimental claims
description: A specification must state the best mode and should not require excessive experiments; in some cases experiments may be required to prove operability.
guidance: Patentee must describe the best-known mode; while the specification should not impose undue experimental burden, some practical experimentation in follow-up disclosure may be necessary in complex chemical or experimental arts.

name: Claims to combinations and multiple inventions
description: When several things are described or several improvements claimed, the specification and patent must be construed to determine whether separate patents are required.
guidance: The treatise explains how combinations and improvements may be treated in one patent, when several improvements can be embraced together, and when separate patents are appropriate.

name: Interfering applications and priority of inventors
description: When two applicants claim the same invention, interfering applications procedures determine entitlement to the patent.
guidance: The book discusses caveats, petitions, oaths, and how the Patent Office and courts decide priority and resolve interfering applications, including relevant dates and evidence of conception and reduction to practice.

name: Petition content — identification of claims and relief requested
description: A petition must request judgment against one or more identified patent claims and set forth the precise relief requested for each challenged claim, including identification of the claim.
guidance: In addition to other required notices (e.g., §§ 42.6, 42.8, 42.22, 42.24), the petition must clearly identify which claim(s) are challenged and the precise relief sought.

name: Petition content — statutory grounds identified
description: The petition must identify the specific statutory grounds (e.g., those permitted under 35 U.S.C. 282(b) as modified) on which each challenged claim is attacked.
guidance: For covered business method and post‑grant petitions, the petition must state which statutory grounds support the challenge (if alleging unpatentability other than by prior art, identify the statutory provision and explain the failure).

name: Petition content — claim construction requirement (means/step‑plus‑function)
description: Where the claim contains a means‑plus‑function or step‑plus‑function limitation under 35 U.S.C. 112(f), the petition must identify the specific portions of the specification that describe the structure, material, or acts corresponding to each claimed function.
guidance: Pinpoint the spec language supporting the claimed function(s); this applies in petitions (post‑grant, CBM, derivation) and to proposed substitute claims in motions to amend.

name: Petition content — showing how construed claim is unpatentable
description: The petition must explain how the construed claim is unpatentable under the statutory grounds identified; if based on prior art, specify where each element of the claim is found in the prior art; for other grounds identify the specific part of the claim that fails and explain why.
guidance: Must provide element‑by‑element mappings to prior art when applicable and specific statutory noncompliance explanations for non‑prior art grounds.

name: Motion to amend — permissible scope and denials
description: Any motion to amend may be denied where: (i) the amendment does not respond to a ground of unpatentability involved in the trial; or (ii) the amendment seeks to enlarge the scope of the claims or introduce new subject matter.
guidance: Motions that expand scope or add new matter are improper; amendments should be responsive to trial issues.

name: Motion to amend — required content/support
description: Any motion to amend must include a claim listing (may be in an appendix), show changes clearly, and set forth: (1) the support in the original disclosure of the patent for each proposed substitute claim; and (2) the support in an earlier‑filed disclosure for each claim for which benefit of the earlier filing date is sought.
guidance: Must provide clear support citations to the original disclosure and any earlier disclosures relied upon for priority benefit.

name: Burden of persuasion on motions to amend
description: On any motion to amend: (1) the patent owner bears the burden to show by a preponderance of the evidence that the motion complies with statutory requirements and section requirements; (2) the petitioner bears the burden to show by a preponderance that any proposed substitute claims are unpatentable; and (3) the Board may exercise discretion to grant or deny a motion or to raise a new ground of unpatentability in connection with a proposed substitute claim.
guidance: Both sides carry preponderance burdens; Board discretion may introduce new grounds with notice and opportunity to respond; determinations are on the preponderance of evidence.

name: Covered Business Method (CBM) review — applicability and pendency
description: A CBM patent review is a trial under subpart A and is subject to post‑grant review procedures except for specific sections; claim construction uses the same standard as in a civil action under 35 U.S.C. 282(b) (ordinary and customary meaning as understood by one of ordinary skill and prosecution history). Pendency after institution is normally no more than one year, with possible extension up to six months for good cause.
guidance: CBM petitions are available only for patents claiming data processing or operations used in financial products/services (excluding technological inventions); prior claim constructions from civil actions or ITC that are timely made of record will be considered.

name: CBM — definition of technological invention
description: In determining whether a patent is for a technological invention (and thus excluded from CBM), consider whether the claimed subject matter as a whole recites a technological feature that is novel and unobvious over the prior art and solves a technical problem using a technical solution.
guidance: Assess technological features and technical problem/solution; CBM excludes patents for technological inventions.

name: Derivation petition — content and sufficiency of showing
description: The petition must demonstrate compliance with filing/timing rules and show the petitioner has at least one claim that is (i) the same or substantially the same as the respondent’s claimed invention and (ii) the same or substantially the same as the invention disclosed to the respondent. The petition must show the claimed invention was derived from an inventor named in the petitioner’s application and that the inventor did not authorize the filing of the earlier application. A derivation showing is not sufficient unless supported by substantial evidence, including at least one affidavit addressing communication and lack of authorization that is corroborated.
guidance: Provide sufficient corroborated evidence (including at least one affidavit) demonstrating communication of the derived invention and lack of authorization to file the earlier application.

name: Derivation — claim construction requirement (means/step‑plus‑function)
description: For each of the respondent’s claims to the derived invention, the petition must identify how the claim is to be construed; for means/step‑plus‑function limitations under 35 U.S.C. 112(f), identify the specific portions of the specification that describe the structure, material, or acts corresponding to each claimed function.
guidance: Same pinpointing requirement as in other petition contexts — identify supporting spec passages.

name: Public availability of Board records and publication discretion
description: Board decisions are available for public inspection if rendered in a file open to the public or in a published application; the Office may independently publish any Board decision available for public inspection. A Board decision not otherwise publishable may be published if the Director finds special circumstances and a party does not object within two months on confidentiality/trade secret grounds with specificity.
guidance: Parties must timely object with specific claims of confidential trade secrets to prevent publication; otherwise decisions in public files may be made public.

name: Avoid labeling anything as 'the invention'
description: Refer to embodiments or examples rather than calling a particular disclosure 'the invention.'
guidance: SciMed: If the specification describes a particular embodiment as 'the invention', courts may construe other claims to require that specific structure. Draft to present multiple embodiments and use neutral language like 'embodiments' or 'examples' rather than definitive phrases such as 'the invention.'

name: Define unusual claim terms in the specification
description: Claim terms receive their ordinary meaning to a person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA) in light of the specification.
guidance: Phillips: Do not rely on dictionaries alone to define terms. For unusual or nonstandard terminology, provide explicit definitions in the spec so the intended scope is clear to a POSITA.

name: Avoid functional/nonce language that invites 35 U.S.C. §112(f)
description: Functional language without adequate structural support can trigger means-plus-function treatment even if the word 'means' is not used.
guidance: Williamson: Use specific structural language (e.g., 'processor,' 'circuit,' 'memory') rather than generic/nonce terms ('module,' 'mechanism,' 'unit') when you do not intend a means-plus-function construction. Provide structural detail in the spec to support claimed functional elements.

name: Disclose algorithms for software-related means-plus-function elements
description: When claiming software functions under means-plus-function, the specification must disclose an algorithm (flowchart, pseudocode, or descriptive prose) that performs the claimed function.
guidance: Aristocrat: Do not rely on describing a 'general-purpose computer' alone. Include algorithmic disclosure (flowcharts, pseudocode, or clear prose describing the steps) to provide corresponding structure for software-implemented functions.

name: Ensure definiteness — provide reasonable certainty for claim scope
description: Claim language must be 'reasonably certain' to a POSITA in view of the specification and prosecution history.
guidance: Nautilus: For claim terms that are not standard in the field, the specification should give enough clarity and context so a POSITA can ascertain the bounds of the claim with reasonable certainty. Provide definitions, examples, and context for borderline or ambiguous terms.

name: Draft method claims to avoid divided infringement problems
description: Structure method claims so a single actor performs every step or so that one actor directs or controls the actions of others.
guidance: Akamai: Because divided performance by multiple actors can defeat direct infringement, draft method claims carefully — either concentrate steps so a single actor necessarily performs them, or include claim language and factual support showing how a single actor directs/controls others (e.g., contractual or agency relationships).

name: Address multiple failure modes for software patents separately
description: Software claims face risks under 35 U.S.C. §101 (abstract idea), §112(b) (indefiniteness), and §112(f) (means-plus-function) — each must be addressed in the specification and claims.
guidance: Combine defenses: disclose a concrete technical improvement to support §101; use structural language and corresponding structure to avoid §112(f); provide clear term definitions to satisfy §112(b); include algorithmic flowcharts and descriptions per Aristocrat to supply structure for software functions.

name: Amend surgically and explain reasons to preserve doctrine-of-equivalents
description: Claim amendments during prosecution can create a presumption that the amended element surrenders equivalents for that element.
guidance: Festo: Because amendments can foreclose doctrine-of-equivalents reach, amend only as narrowly as necessary and record clear reasons for the amendment. If an amendment would not save the claim, consider cancelling the claim instead of making sweeping changes that could limit equivalents.

name: Disclose numeric ranges and representative endpoints to support claimed ranges
description: For claims that will rely on numeric ranges, the specification must disclose the range or representative endpoints so the claim is supported.
guidance: In re Wertheim: When you might claim 'between 50 and 100', disclose multiple endpoints (e.g., 30, 50, 75, 100, 150) in the spec to ensure that claimed ranges have adequate written-description/support and to reduce vulnerability to challenges based on lack of range support.

name: Do not rely on asserted distinctions that are merely inherent in the prior art
description: If a claimed feature is inherent in a prior art reference, that prior art can anticipate the claim even if the feature is not expressly disclosed.
guidance: In re Kao: When distinguishing over prior art, rely on actively chosen and expressly disclosed features in the specification rather than features that might be inherent in the cited references. Provide explicit disclosure and argumentation distinguishing the claimed invention from inherent properties of the prior art.

name: Fundamental economic practices or principles
description: Fundamental economic practices or principles include hedging, insurance, and mitigating risks; concepts relating to the economy and commerce may be considered 'fundamental economic practices.'
guidance: The term 'fundamental' is not limited to old or well-known practices; new methods (e.g., price optimization) may be fundamental. Case examples: Bilski (hedging), Bancorp (insurance), OIP Technologies (price optimization), In re Smith (wagering game rules), In re Chorna (financial instruments). The Supreme Court treated intermediated settlement/risk hedging as a 'fundamental economic practice' (Alice). These practices have been found to be abstract ideas when claimed as a series of steps to implement them.

name: Examiner procedure for identifying abstract ideas (Step 2A Prong One)
description: Examiners should determine whether a claim recites an abstract idea by (1) identifying the specific limitation(s) in the claim under examination that the examiner believes recites an abstract idea, and (2) determining whether the identified limitation(s) fall within at least one of the groupings of abstract ideas listed above.
guidance: If identified limitation(s) falls within at least one grouping, it is reasonable to conclude the claim recites an abstract idea in Step 2A Prong One and the claim then requires further analysis in Step 2A Prong Two to determine whether additional elements integrate the abstract idea into a practical application (see MPEP § 2106.04(d)). If the identified limitation(s) do not fall within any grouping, it is reasonable to find that the claim does not recite an abstract idea, concluding the judicial-exception eligibility analysis (claim eligible at Pathway B) unless the claim recites another exception (law of nature or natural phenomenon). Examiners should identify at least one abstract-idea grouping, and preferably identify all groupings to the extent possible if a limitation falls within multiple groupings.

name: Examples of claims that do not recite abstract ideas (non-limiting)
description: Some claims do not recite an abstract idea because they do not recite an abstract idea, even though at some level they may be based on or involve an abstract idea.
guidance: Non-limiting hypothetical examples include: i) a printer comprising a belt, roller, printhead, ink cartridge; ii) a washing machine comprising tub, drive motor, controller, housing; iii) an earring with a sensor for blood glucose and memory; iv) a method for sequencing BRCA1 gene sequences (PCR amplification and sequencing); v) a method for loading BIOS into a local computer system (remote transfer to volatile memory and transferring control); vi) a method of rearranging GUI icons based on usage tracking and moving most used icons; vii) a method of training a neural network for facial detection using staged training sets. These are eligible at Step 2A Prong One (Pathway B) because they do not recite (set forth or describe) an abstract idea.

name: Scope/limits of the 'certain methods' grouping and non-exhaustive nature of groupings
description: The term 'certain' limits the 'methods of organizing human activity' grouping to the enumerated sub-groupings and the groupings are not mutually exclusive; some claim limitations may fall within multiple groupings or sub-groupings.
guidance: Not all methods of organizing human activity are abstract ideas (example: a defined set of steps for combining particular ingredients to create a drug formulation is not a 'certain' method of organizing human activity). The grouping should not be expanded beyond the enumerated sub-groupings except in rare circumstances (see MPEP § 2106.04(a)(3)). If a claim limitation falls within multiple groupings, examiners should identify at least one, preferably all applicable groupings, and then proceed to analyze integration into a practical application in Step 2A Prong Two.

name: Non-obviousness under 35 U.S.C. §103 / Graham factors
description: The element of non-obviousness must be assessed using the Graham factors: (1) scope and content of the prior art, (2) differences between the prior art and the claims at issue, and (3) the level of ordinary skill in the relevant art; secondary considerations (e.g., commercial success, long-felt but unresolved needs, failure of others) may also be relevant.
guidance: The Court reaffirmed Graham as the main test and described it as expansive and flexible. Apply these factors objectively to determine whether the claimed invention would have been obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention.

name: Look to interrelated teachings, marketplace demands, and background knowledge
description: Determining obviousness may require looking to interrelated teachings of multiple patents, the effects of demands known to the design community or present in the marketplace, and the background knowledge possessed by a person having ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: Teachings need not be precise or explicit; implicit directions in the collective prior art and market/design pressures can point a skilled person toward the claimed combination.

name: Avoid granting patents that would occur in the ordinary course without real innovation
description: Granting patent protection to advances that would occur in the ordinary course without real innovation retards progress and may, for patents combining previously known elements, deprive prior inventions of their value or utility.
guidance: Apply a cautious approach when claims are combinations of known elements; ensure the claimed subject matter reflects real innovation beyond expected incremental developments.

name: Obviousness can be found even without clear TSM
description: A claimed invention may be obvious despite the absence of a clear teaching, suggestion, or motivation to combine various prior art references.
guidance: Do not treat lack of an explicit TSM as dispositive for non-obviousness; consider whether the collective prior art and ordinary skill would have led to the claimed invention.

name: Information that must be itemized on return postcard receipts
description: The identifying data on the postcard should include inventor’s name(s); title of invention; number of pages of specification, claims, and sheet(s) of drawing(s); whether the inventor's oath or declaration is included; a list of any additional forms included; and amount and manner of paying the fee.
guidance: A return postcard should itemize all components of the application; failure to itemize each component will mean the postcard will not serve as evidence that any unitemized component was received. Merely writing 'a complete application' will not suffice. The person receiving items at USPTO will check the listing against items submitted and initial any crossed‑off items.

name: Filing date rules for nonprovisional, design, and provisional applications
description: The filing date of a nonprovisional application is the date on which a specification, with or without claims, is received. The filing date for a design patent (except CPA) is the date the specification as prescribed by 35 U.S.C. 112, including at least one claim, and any required drawings are received. The filing date of a provisional application is the date the specification, with or without claims, is received.
guidance: No new matter may be introduced after the filing date. A provisional application filed before Dec 18, 2013 had to include any required drawings to be entitled to a filing date. Continuing applications must meet statutory conditions (35 U.S.C. 120, 121, 365(c), 386(c) and § 1.78).

name: Substantial New Question of Patentability (SNQ) requirement
description: Under 35 U.S.C. 304, the Office must determine whether 'a substantial new question of patentability' affecting any claim has been raised; 37 CFR 1.510(b)(1) requires a request to include 'a statement pointing out each substantial new question of patentability based on prior patents and printed publications.'
guidance: Request must clearly set forth in detail what the requester considers the SNQ to be in view of patents and printed publications and must point out how the questions raised are substantially different from those raised previously in examination. If such a new question is found, reexamination will be ordered. KSR's clarification of obviousness does not alter the SNQ legal standard — simply asking the Office to reexamine previously-applied art based only on KSR (without presenting the art in a new light) will not raise an SNQ.

name: Completeness of the explanation; claim-chart/limitation-by-limitation comparison
description: The mere citation of new patents/printed publications without explanation does not comply with 37 CFR 1.510(b)(2). The requester must explain how each cited reference or combination is applied to all claims the requester considers to merit reexamination.
guidance: Ideally provide a detailed claim chart comparing limitation-by-limitation each claim with the relevant teachings of each reference (see sample request in MPEP § 2214). For proposed obviousness rejections, provide at least one basis for combining references and a statement why the claims would have been obvious over the combination. Preferably quote pertinent teachings with page/column/line/figure citations. The MPEP contains explicit examples of inappropriate language (e.g., lumping claims or alternative combinations) and appropriate language showing precise, claim-by-claim formulations.

name: Examples of appropriate vs inappropriate claim-language formulations
description: The MPEP gives specific examples of inappropriate and appropriate language when asserting anticipation or obviousness against claims.
guidance: Inappropriate examples include lumping multiple alternative rejections together (e.g., 'Claim 1 is unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. 102 as being anticipated by, or in the alternative, under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being obvious over Smith'), or listing multiple alternatives without separate explanations. Appropriate examples are claim-specific statements (e.g., 'Claim 1 is unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. 102 as being anticipated by Smith.' or 'Claim 2 is unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being obvious over Smith in view of Jones.'). Use clear, separate explanations for each claim and each combination.

name: Amendments included in a patent owner’s request
description: Under 37 CFR 1.510(e), a patent owner may include a proposed amendment with a reexamination request, but any such amendment must comply with 37 CFR 1.530(d)–(j) and MPEP § 2250 as to format and requirements.
guidance: If the amendment adds claims, excess claims fees per 37 CFR 1.20(c)(3) and (c)(4) may apply. The decision on whether to order reexamination is based on the wording of the patent claims in effect at the time of the request (i.e., proposed amendments are ignored for the order decision). If reexamination is ordered, subsequent prosecution will be on the basis of claims as amended.

name: Required application documents
description: The patent application must include a set of specific documents.
guidance: The patent application is composed of the following documents: Specification; Claims; Abstract; Drawings (if any); and Sequence listing (only for applications in the biotechnology field). Download the forms for these documents.

name: Original subject-matter jurisdiction (28 U.S.C. §1338(a))
description: Federal district courts have exclusive original jurisdiction of 'any civil action arising under any Act of Congress relating to patents.' Whether a claim 'arises under' is determined by the well-pleaded complaint rule and by the complaint alone.
guidance: Apply Christianson v. Colt Industries and Holmes Group principles: if the plaintiff’s complaint on its face presents a federal patent issue, the case arises under federal patent law. Determine patent jurisdiction solely on the basis of the complaint, not counterclaims.

name: Scheduling order content for patent cases
description: Scheduling orders in patent cases should include dates and deadlines tailored to patent-specific issues to balance efficiency with adequate development of technical issues.
guidance: Recommended scheduling order items include: last date to disclose intention to rely on advice of counsel as a defense; last date to add inequitable conduct allegations without leave; disclosure of invalidity and infringement contentions; close of fact discovery; claim-construction hearing date; close of expert discovery; last date for filing and hearing dispositive motions; schedule for Daubert motions; possibility of staggering expert report deadlines with damages reports due before technical reports; requiring substantial disclosure of damages theories in initial disclosures; and setting an early date for motions to dismiss to narrow the action.

name: Substantive considerations checklist
description: Identify substantive legal and technical issues that affect case complexity and opportunities for early resolution.
guidance: Issues to address: Is the asserting party the named inventor or how were rights acquired? Is there parallel litigation (ITC) or PTAB review? Is there a dispute about structure/function of the accused device? Is technology complex? Are there substantive issues amenable to early resolution (e.g., dispositive claim terms, patent eligibility)? Have asserted patents been litigated or licensed before? Are patents connected to industry standards or subject to FRAND obligations? Have patents been reexamined at the USPTO? Will opinion-of-counsel waiver issues arise? Has litigation counsel been involved in prosecution? Discuss expert witness role limitations and proof plans for indirect infringement, damages theories (reasonable royalty, entire-market-value rule), and whether surveys will be used — all to guide discovery and trial preparation.

name: Managing cooperation and potential for early resolution
description: Encourage early cooperation on discovery scope, electronic discovery, claim-construction scope, and dispute-limitation mechanisms to promote efficiency and early settlement.
guidance: Discuss and consider limits on depositions, document requests, requests for admission, and interrogatories (modifying the 25-interrogatory limit if needed). Address electronic discovery issues early, consider limiting number of claim terms to be construed, require meet-and-confer before bringing discovery disputes, limit discovery disputes requiring court intervention, consider adopting or adapting patent local rules, and plan timing of summary judgment relative to claim construction. Consider mediation early and appoint mediator or initiate selection process.

name: Time period for making benefit claim (U.S. utility/plant applications filed on/after Nov 29, 2000)
description: If the application is a utility or plant application filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a) on or after November 29, 2000, the benefit claim of the prior application under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), 120, 121, or 365(c) must be made during the pendency of the application and within the later of four months from the actual filing date of the later-filed application or sixteen months from the filing date of the prior-filed application. This time period is not extendable and failure to submit the reference within this time period is considered a waiver.
guidance: Cites 37 CFR 1.78(a)(2). Noncompliance = deemed waiver; use examiner form language notifying applicant that the benefit claim was not entered and that petition is required. Applies only to utility/plant apps filed on/after Nov 29, 2000.

name: Exception when benefit claim elsewhere was recognized on filing receipt
description: If an applicant includes a claim to the benefit of a prior application elsewhere in the application but not in the manner specified in 37 CFR 1.78(a) (e.g., in an unexecuted oath/declaration or transmittal letter), and the Office recognized the information as shown by its inclusion on a filing receipt, the Office will not require a petition and surcharge to correct the benefit claim.
guidance: Applicant must still submit the benefit claim in the manner specified by 37 CFR 1.78(a) (amendment to first sentence(s) of the specification or ADS) to have a proper claim. If the information was not recognized (absent on filing receipt), a petition and surcharge are required.

name: Recognition/filing-receipt absence requires petition & surcharge
description: If a benefit claim is included elsewhere in the application but is not recognized by the Office (e.g., absent from filing receipt or located in unconventional locations like the body of the specification), the Office will require a petition and the surcharge under 37 CFR 1.17(t) to correct the benefit claim because the application will not have been scheduled for publication on the basis of such information.
guidance: Distinguishes timely-submitted-but-misplaced claims that were recognized (no petition) vs. those not recognized (petition required).

name: Deleting benefit claims (effects and treatment)
description: Applicants may cancel their claim to priority by amending the specification or submitting a new ADS to delete references to prior applications. The examiner should consider whether any new prior art may now be available if a benefit claim is deleted. Amendments/ADS to delete a benefit claim after final rejection or action are treated under 37 CFR 1.116 (see MPEP §§714.12, 714.13); after allowance treated under 37 CFR 1.312 (see MPEP §714.16). Deletion will not delay publication unless recognized within nine weeks prior to projected publication date.
guidance: Cancellation may be viewed as intentional waiver; if applicant later petitions to accept an unintentionally delayed claim to add benefit back, the Office may refuse if delay was not unintentional. No supplemental declaration necessary to delete claim via ADS.

name: English translation requirement for non-English provisional benefit claims
description: If benefit is being claimed to a provisional application filed in a language other than English, an English language translation of the provisional application and a statement that the translation is accurate are required to be filed in the provisional application (see 37 CFR 1.78(a)(5)(iv)).
guidance: If translation and statement were not filed as required, applicant will be notified in the nonprovisional and given time to file them in the provisional; failure to timely reply will result in abandonment of the nonprovisional. Form paragraph 2.38 may be used to notify applicant.

name: Terminal Disclaimer Practice purpose
description: Continuation/Terminal Disclaimer practice primarily serves to refine claim language.
guidance: Continuation patents with further refinements are an essential part of the patent system and afford the applicant the ability to refine the claim language by, for example, broadening claims, narrowing claims, focusing on different aspects of the invention, accommodating real world infringement conditions or changes to patent law. The current terminal disclaimer practice prohibits abuse of term extension by limiting the term of “child” patents to the term of the parent along with ownership restrictions.

name: Allow iterative claim refinement
description: Applicants must be able to iterate claim language across continuations to obtain 'good' patents; claiming is complex and small details can render claims unenforceable.
guidance: There must be a mechanism for applicants to claim their justifiably earned rights in an optimal fashion while allowing for human error, better understanding of the prior art presented during examination, adaptation to rapid changes in the usage environment and changes in the law. The current system of claim refinements over several continuations may yield only a single enforceable patent after several iterations; without iterations an applicant could only gain rights by perfecting the initial prosecution or engaging in complex (and expensive) maneuvers.

name: Practicality of USPTO-proposed alternatives must be evaluated
description: Suggested mechanisms for addressing terminal disclaimer requirements (combine claims, cancel/amend, argue patentable distinctness, file reissue) must be practicable and not impose unrealistic burdens.
guidance: The letter addresses each USPTO suggestion: (1) combining conflicting claims into a single application is impractical because there is no practical method to combine claims into an already issued patent; (2) canceling or amending conflicting claims forces applicants to accept flaws or eliminate improved claims (a 'Hobsons choice'); (3) arguing patentable distinctness imposes the burden of substantive office actions; (4) reissue is arduous, expensive, requires surrendering the patent, and may be unavailable due to timing constraints.

name: Avoid confiscation of rights across patents
description: Invalidation of a single claim should not automatically strip rights from other claims or related patents in a continuation chain.
guidance: Under the current system, invalidation of any one claim does not render the other claims of that patent or any other patent automatically invalid. Under the proposed rules, an applicant seeking a variety of claim coverage through continuation practice will be subject to confiscation of all of its rights if just one claim in an earlier issued patent in the continuation chain is found to be invalid. Such confiscation is untenable.

name: Rule should not incentivize defensive or inefficient filing strategies
description: Regulatory changes must not force applicants to adopt filing strategies that increase costs and burden examiners, such as filing parent applications with extremely large claim sets.
guidance: The proposed rule may force innovators to file parent applications with extremely large claim sets, increasing initial drafting costs before knowing the scope of the prior art and increasing the burden on the Examiner. Spreading examination across multiple applications currently provides more focused examination and better claims than forcing examination of a very large number of claims in one examination.

name: Identify the judicial exception as recited in the claim (Step 2A)
description: Identify the judicial exception by referring to what is recited (i.e., set forth or described) in the claim and explain why it is considered an exception.
guidance: The rejection should point to the specific claim limitation(s) that recites the judicial exception. Where the claim describes but does not expressly set forth the exception, the rejection must explain what subject matter those limitations describe and why that described subject matter is a judicial exception.

name: Explain why the identified limitation corresponds to a court-identified abstract idea
description: When the examiner determines the claim recites an abstract idea, the rejection should identify the abstract idea as it is recited in the claim and explain why it corresponds to a concept that the courts have identified as an abstract idea.
guidance: Citing to an appropriate court decision that supports the identification is a best practice. Examiners should be familiar with any cited decision and ensure the rejection is reasonably tied to the facts. Examiners should not go beyond those concepts similar to what courts have identified as abstract ideas. See the July 2015 Quick Reference Sheet concepts for examples.

name: Explain why limitations recite a law of nature or natural phenomenon (Step 2A)
description: When the examiner determines the claim recites a law of nature or natural phenomenon, the rejection should identify it as recited in the claim and explain using a reasoned rationale why it is considered a law of nature or natural phenomenon.
guidance: Provide concrete reasoning (e.g., the claimed correlation describes a consequence of natural processes or occurs in nature and exists apart from human action). Use sample explanations where appropriate to show the connection to natural processes.

name: Explain why a claimed product is a product of nature
description: When the claim recites a product of nature, identify the exception as recited in the claim and explain using a reasoned rationale why the product does not have markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart.
guidance: Compare the claimed product to its closest naturally occurring counterpart (e.g., 'X in its natural state') and explain whether there is a marked difference in structure, function, or other properties. If no marked difference is shown in the record, treat as a product of nature exception.

name: Explain why additional elements do not amount to significantly more (Step 2B)
description: Explain the reason(s) that the additional elements taken individually, and also taken as a combination, do not result in the claim as a whole amounting to significantly more than the judicial exception.
guidance: Address the additional elements both individually and in combination. Provide a reasoned rationale for the conclusion and explain why the combination does not meaningfully limit the exception. Remember that a new combination may be eligible (Diehr), so the combination analysis is critical.

name: Explain when additional elements are well-understood, routine, conventional
description: When concluding that particular claim limitations are well-understood, routine, conventional activities in the relevant field, explain why the courts have recognized, or those in the field would recognize, those limitations as such.
guidance: A prior art search is not necessary to resolve this inquiry. The evaluation turns on whether the use was well-understood, routine, conventional activity previously engaged in by those in the field. If determined widely prevalent and conventional, provide a reasoned explanation supporting that conclusion and consider rebuttal evidence to clarify the record.

name: Explain why generic computer components performing generic functions do not add significantly more
description: For claim limitations that recite a generic computer component performing generic computer functions at a high level of generality, explain why these functions do not meaningfully limit the claim.
guidance: Use the July 2015 Update's listing of computer functions courts have recognized as well-understood, routine, conventional when claimed generically. Do not assume all computer functions are conventional. Consider whether generic components in combination perform non-generic functions (e.g., DDR) and thus may be significantly more.

name: Explain why extrasolution activity or field-of-use limitations are insufficient
description: For claim limitations that add insignificant extrasolution activity (e.g., mere data gathering, final storing step) or merely link the exception to a particular technological environment or field of use, explain why they do not meaningfully limit the claim.
guidance: Provide concrete reasoning; examples include storing data after computing a mathematical relationship or limiting an abstract idea to a particular industry (Flook-style) — such limitations often do not add significantly more.

name: Use examples only as illustrative, not as bases for rejection
description: USPTO examples issued with the Interim Eligibility Guidance are illustrative analyses and should not be used as a basis for subject matter eligibility rejections.
guidance: Examples (including hypothetical fact patterns) do not carry the weight of court decisions. Applicants may cite examples in support, but examiners should not require applicants to model claims after the examples to attain eligibility.

name: Make rejections sufficiently clear and specific to enable effective response
description: The Office action must provide an explanation as to why each claim is unpatentable that is sufficiently clear and specific to provide applicant sufficient notice of the reasons for ineligibility and enable the applicant to effectively respond.
guidance: Include the identified judicial exception, the specific additional elements, and the examiner's reasons for why those elements do not amount to significantly more, with a reasoned rationale tied to facts of the case.

name: Rejection only when conclusion is readily apparent to an examiner
description: A rejection should be made only if it is readily apparent to an examiner relying on his or her expertise in the art in the Step 2B inquiry that the additional elements do not amount to claiming significantly more than the judicial exception.
guidance: If not readily apparent, avoid making a § 101 rejection. Where appropriate, explain why the additional elements provide an inventive concept by adding a meaningful limitation.

name: Provide a reasoned rebuttal when maintaining a rejection after applicant challenge
description: If applicant challenges the identification of an abstract idea based on a court case and the challenge is not persuasive, provide an explanation why the abstract idea identified in the claim is similar to the concept in the cited case.
guidance: If the original rejection did not identify a Supreme Court or Federal Circuit decision and applicant challenges the identification, the examiner should point to a case with a similar abstract idea and explain why the claim corresponds to that case. Citation to a supportive case is not a new ground unless the basic thrust of the rejection changes (see MPEP 1207.03(a)).

name: Assess 'specially programmed' or 'particular machine' claims on whether they add significantly more
description: If applicant amends a claim to add a generic computer or generic computer components and asserts special programming or a particular machine, examine whether the added elements provide significantly more than the judicial exception.
guidance: Merely adding a generic computer, generic components, or a programmed computer does not automatically overcome an eligibility rejection (Alice). Analyze whether the added elements meaningfully limit the claim, improve another technology, improve computer functioning, or add unconventional steps confining the claim to a particular useful application.

name: Use court decisions as the primary foundation for identifications and conclusions
description: When identifying abstract ideas or other judicial exceptions and explaining why additional elements are conventional or not, the examiner should rely primarily on court decisions and reasoned rationale tied to facts.
guidance: A chart of court decisions is available on the USPTO website. Ensure any cited decision is directly relevant and not taken out of context; be prepared to explain similarity to the instant claim if applicant challenges the citation.

name: Breadth of the claims
description: The breadth of the claims.
guidance: Listed as factor (A) in MPEP 2164.01(a) / In re Wands. A broader claim scope can increase the risk that the disclosure does not enable the full claimed scope.

name: Quantity of experimentation needed
description: The quantity of experimentation needed to make or use the invention based on the content of the disclosure.
guidance: Listed as factor (H) in MPEP 2164.01(a) / In re Wands. Evaluate how much trial-and-error or routine experimentation would be required from the disclosure to practice the full scope of the claims.

name: Meaning of 'recites' a judicial exception
description: In Step 2A Prong One, a claim 'recites' a judicial exception when the judicial exception is 'set forth' or 'described' in the claim.
guidance: There are two ways an exception can be recited: 'set forth' (explicitly stated, e.g., a mathematical equation) or 'described' (claimed concept expresses the exception without explicit terminology, e.g., 'intermediated settlement'). Examiner should evaluate whether the claim 'sets forth or describes' an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon per MPEP guidance and PEG examples (Examples 37-46, pre-PEG examples).

name: Evaluate recitation of a law of nature / natural phenomenon / product of nature
description: Determine whether the claim sets forth or describes a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or product of nature.
guidance: Follow MPEP 2106.04(b) and (c), including the 'markedly different characteristics' analysis. Use cited examples (Examples 43-45 and pre-PEG examples) to identify these exceptions.

name: Mathematical concepts grouping
description: Mathematical concepts include mathematical relationships, mathematical formulas or equations, and mathematical calculations.
guidance: When determining whether a claim recites a mathematical concept, consider whether the claim actually recites the concept rather than merely being based on or involving a mathematical concept. A mathematical relationship may be expressed in words or symbols (e.g., Arrhenius equation); numerical formulas or textual equivalents (e.g., 'determining a ratio of A to B') fall here; mathematical calculations encompass operations like multiplication or resampling statistics. See Examples 41, 43, 45 and MPEP 2106.04(a)(2)(IV).

name: Mathematical calculations (subcategory)
description: Mathematical calculations are mathematical operations or acts of calculating (e.g., multiplication, exponentiation, statistical analysis).
guidance: A claim need not use the word 'calculating' to be a mathematical calculation; 'determining' or 'performing' may encompass calculations in the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim in light of the specification (see SAP Am., Inc. v. InvestPic, Inc. example).

name: Commercial or legal interactions (subcategory)
description: Covers agreements (contracts), legal obligations, advertising/marketing/sales behaviors, and business relations.
guidance: Examples: transaction performance guaranty, processing insurance claims under a policy, tax-free real estate exchanges, arbitration, marketing techniques like offer-based price optimization, structuring sales forces. See cited cases and MPEP.

name: Mental processes grouping
description: Mental processes are concepts performed in the human mind (e.g., observations, evaluations, judgments, opinions).
guidance: Evaluate whether claim limitations can practically be performed in the human mind; if so, they fall within the mental processes grouping. Considerations: (i) if the limitation cannot practically be performed mentally (e.g., complex GPS pseudorange calculations, manipulation of network packets, specific data encryption, image halftoning), it is not a mental process; (ii) requiring a generic computer does not necessarily prevent classification as a mental process—an examiner should use the broadest reasonable interpretation in view of the specification; (iii) a claim encompassing human performance with pen and paper can recite a mental process. Use cited examples (Electric Power Group, University of Utah, CyberSource, etc.).

name: Claims requiring a computer may still recite mental processes
description: A claim that requires a generic computer can nonetheless recite a mental process if, in broad interpretation, the underlying concept is performable by the human mind and the computer is merely generic or a tool.
guidance: Review the specification to determine whether the invention is described as a concept performed in the mind and merely claimed as performed on a generic computer, in a computer environment, or using a computer as a tool. If so, treat as mental process (see Voter Verified and Mortgage Grader examples).

name: Pen-and-paper aid does not negate mental process
description: If a claim encompasses a human performing steps mentally with the aid of a pen and paper, it recites a mental process.
guidance: The use of a physical aid to assist memory does not change the mental nature of the limitation; however, if the limitation could not practically be performed in the human mind even with pen and paper, it is not a mental process (see CyberSource example).

name: Tentative abstract idea procedure and TC Director review
description: Procedure for handling claims that appear to recite an abstract idea not previously enumerated: TC Director approval is required for subject matter eligibility rejection based on a tentative abstract idea.
guidance: Office action will identify such claims via form paragraph 7.05.017 and include the TC Director’s signature; Patents Management is informed and public notification (e.g., USPTO.GOV/PatentEligibility) follows. Examiner retains authority to withdraw or maintain a rejection after applicant reply; an interview with the TC Director is not required to withdraw the rejection; interviews with the examiner may be conducted to advance prosecution.

name: Step 2A Prong Two: 'integration into a practical application'
description: Prong Two asks whether the claim as a whole 'integrates the recited judicial exception into a practical application' so that the claim imposes a meaningful limit on the exception.
guidance: Mere recitation of an exception (Prong One) does not mean the claim is 'directed to' that exception. Use the considerations identified by the Supreme Court and Federal Circuit (improving technology, effecting a particular treatment/prophylaxis, using a particular machine, particular transformation, etc.) as set out in MPEP 2106.05(a)-(c) and (e)-(h). If the additional limitations impose a meaningful limit (e.g., show an improvement in functioning of a computer or other technology), the claim is eligible at Step 2A; otherwise proceed to Step 2B.

name: Consideration: particular machine or particular transformation and specificity
description: Use of a particular machine or a particular transformation and the specificity of limitations are considerations for integration.
guidance: A 'specific way of achieving a result' is not a standalone consideration, but the specificity of claim limitations is relevant to evaluating use of a particular machine, particular transformation, and whether limitations are mere instructions to apply an exception. Generic computer components (e.g., 'data processing system') are insufficient by themselves to show integration (see CLS Bank example).

name: Claim-as-a-whole analysis (do not evaluate additional limitations in a vacuum)
description: Prong Two requires evaluating the claim as a whole — the judicial exception and additional claim elements together — to determine integration into a practical application.
guidance: Do not assess additional limitations entirely separate from the recited exception; consider how limitations interact and whether together they impose meaningful limits (see Bascom filtering example). If additional limitations are only insignificant extra-solution activity, proceed to Step 2B for conventionality analysis.

name: If an examiner identifies an abstract idea not clearly within enumerated groupings, raise to TC Director
description: When a claim limitation does not fall clearly within the PEG enumerated groupings but case law suggests it is an abstract idea, the examiner should bring the matter to the TC Director.
guidance: Use the 'tentative abstract idea' procedure: TC Director approval for rejection, form paragraph, and public notification steps apply.

name: Do not treat a claim as reciting a mathematical concept if math only appears in specification
description: A claim does not recite a mathematical concept merely because the specification describes a mathematical concept; the mathematical concept must be recited in the claim itself.
guidance: Limitations 'based on' or 'involving' a mathematical concept described in the specification may not suffice to place the limitation in the mathematical concepts grouping unless the math itself is recited in the claim; see Examples 38-39 guidance.

name: Terminal disclaimer requirements (37 CFR 1.321)
description: A terminal disclaimer is a statement filed by an owner (in whole or in part) of a patent or a patent to be granted that is used to disclaim or dedicate a portion of the entire term of all the claims of a patent. The requirements for a terminal disclaimer are set forth in 37 CFR 1.321.
guidance: Sample forms of a terminal disclaimer, and guidance as to the filing and treatment of a terminal disclaimer, are provided in MPEP § 1490. A terminal disclaimer may be used to overcome double patenting rejections by disclaiming the terminal portion of the later patent's term.

name: Terminal disclaimer enforceability provision (37 CFR 1.321(c)(3))
description: 37 CFR 1.321(c)(3) requires that a terminal disclaimer 'include a provision that any patent granted on that application or any patent subject to the reexamination proceeding shall be enforceable only for and during such period that said patent is commonly owned with the application or patent which formed the basis for the rejection.'
guidance: Examiners must ensure the terminal disclaimer filed to obviate a nonstatutory double patenting rejection based on commonly owned conflicting claims includes this enforceability provision. Failure to include it can defeat the disclaimer's purpose.

name: Terminal disclaimer requirements for joint research agreements (37 CFR 1.321(d))
description: 37 CFR 1.321(d) sets forth the requirements for a terminal disclaimer where the claimed invention resulted from activities undertaken within the scope of a joint research agreement.
guidance: When inventions arise from a joint research agreement, filing a terminal disclaimer that includes each one of the conflicting double patenting references is also necessary to avoid ownership problems between parties to a joint research agreement. Use 1.321(d) requirements to craft disclaimers for such cases.

name: Terminal disclaimer required to overcome nonstatutory double patenting for applications filed on/after June 8, 1995
description: A terminal disclaimer under 37 CFR 1.321 is required in an application to overcome a nonstatutory double patenting rejection, even if the application was filed on or after June 8, 1995 and claims the benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, or 365(c) of the filing date of the patent or application which forms the basis for the rejection.
guidance: Because 35 U.S.C. 154(a)(2) sets 20-year patent terms from filing and 154(b) allows for term adjustments, a terminal disclaimer is still necessary to avoid the potential for multiple patents with different expiration dates and harassment of accused infringers. Examiners should cite this MPEP section or the Official Gazette notice when applicants argue a disclaimer is unnecessary due to the change to 35 U.S.C. 154.

name: Common ownership exclusion (35 U.S.C. 103(c)(1)-(2))
description: Subject matter developed by another person, which qualifies as prior art only under one or more of subsections (e), (f), and (g) of section 102, shall not preclude patentability where the subject matter and the claimed invention were, at the time the claimed invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person. For purposes of this subsection, subject matter developed by another person and a claimed invention shall be deemed to have been owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person if: (A) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement that was in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; (B) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (C) the application for patent for the claimed invention discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement.
guidance: The statute shields patentability from certain prior art only when these ownership/agreements conditions are met. Examiners should apply the statutory tests (including the definition of 'joint research agreement') when determining whether a reference is disqualified under 103(c). See MPEP § 706.02(l) for detailed definition of common ownership.

name: Definition of 'joint research agreement' (35 U.S.C. 103(c)(3))
description: For purposes of paragraph (2), the term 'joint research agreement' means a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement entered into by two or more persons or entities for the performance of experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention.
guidance: The agreement must be written and cover experimental/developmental/research work in the claimed invention's field. Examiners must verify that the agreement meets this statutory definition when applying 103(c)(2).

name: Disqualifying a commonly owned patent/published application as prior art (37 CFR 1.130(a))
description: When any claim of an application or a patent under reexamination is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 on a U.S. patent or U.S. patent application publication which is not prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(b), and the inventions are not identical but not patentably distinct, and the inventions are owned by the same party, the applicant or owner may disqualify the patent or patent application publication as prior art by submission of: (1) A terminal disclaimer in accordance with § 1.321(c); and (2) An oath or declaration stating that the application or patent under reexamination and patent or published application are currently owned by the same party, and that the inventor named in the application or patent under reexamination is the prior inventor under 35 U.S.C. 104.
guidance: Examiners should accept this combination (terminal disclaimer + oath/declaration) to disqualify the reference as prior art where the statutory conditions are met. See MPEP for form and procedural handling.

name: When double patenting rejections apply
description: Claims in commonly owned applications of different inventive entities may be rejected on the ground of double patenting to prevent an organization from obtaining two or more patents with different expiration dates covering nearly identical subject matter. Claims may also be rejected on grounds of nonstatutory double patenting in certain non-commonly owned applications that claim inventions resulting from activities undertaken within the scope of a joint research agreement (CREATE Act).
guidance: Apply double patenting where claims are not patentably distinct and would improperly extend patent term or allow multiple patents covering the same invention. Cite case law (e.g., In re Zickendraht; In re Christensen) when appropriate. Use terminal disclaimers or statutory exclusions as applicable to resolve issues.

name: CREATE Act treatment for non-commonly owned inventions (35 U.S.C. 103(c)(2))
description: Pursuant to the CREATE Act, non-commonly owned applications or patents that are subject to a joint research agreement may be treated as if they are 'commonly owned' for determining obviousness if conditions are met. Two inventions come within 35 U.S.C. 103(c)(2) when: (A) the later invention is not anticipated by the earlier invention under 35 U.S.C. 102; (B) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement that was in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; (C) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (D) the application for patent for the claimed invention discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement.
guidance: Examiners should apply these four conditions for applications pending on or after December 10, 2004 (and certain reexaminations) to determine whether a reference is disqualified under 103(c). See MPEP § 706.02(l)(2) and CREATE Act legislative history for context.

name: Check Patent Family Members Across Jurisdictions
description: Family members across jurisdictions provide additional context.
guidance: Investigate family filings (same application filed in multiple countries) to find earlier or more detailed disclosures, different claim scopes, or prosecution outcomes that inform novelty and patentability assessments.

name: Specification must disclose the exact nature and properties of the invention
description: The patentee must inform the public of the exact nature of the manufacture invented; omissions about qualities or results that are claimed will invalidate the grant.
guidance: Do not claim broader qualities or results than can actually be produced; be accurate about capabilities and limitations.

name: If patent claims multiple things, claim only what is truly invented
description: The patentee must not claim more than his invention; if a patent is taken for several things and he fails in any one of them (or claims more than his invention), the specification may be incorrect or the patent void.
guidance: Cases differ: if one claimed item is not new the grant can fail in toto; if one claimed item later proves useless, earlier cases suggest the grant may still be valid. Courts scrutinize whether the specification claims the whole machine when only an improvement was invented (Browne/lace engine, Browne v. Wigley analogues).

name: Distinguish new parts from old (do not monopolize pre-existing subject-matter)
description: Where the patent is for an improvement or addition, the inventor cannot monopolize the whole subject; the specification is incorrect if it contains description of more than the improvement unless it particularly distinguishes the new from the old parts.
guidance: If the invention is a new combination added to existing combinations, describe only the new combinations and how they are added. If prior combinations existed, claim only the additional combinations that are truly new.

name: Method or principle patents must be described with exceptional accuracy
description: If a method is the subject-matter of the patent (i.e., tangible means carrying the method into practice are claimed), the description must be so clear and evident that no experiments are necessary to learn it and to put it in practice as beneficially as the patentee enjoys it.
guidance: Because principles or pure methods are problematic as patent subjects, the specification of any method is governed by the same rigorous rules as for machines/manufactures: enablement without need for inventive trial, full particulars of the tangible means, and clarity of operation.

name: Indicia and examples of unauthorized practice or prejudicial conduct
description: Facts the tribunal treats as evidence of unauthorized practice or prejudicial conduct include drafting complaints and oppositions for pro se plaintiffs, providing legal advice and 'legaliz[ing]' client descriptions, using notations like 'prepared with the aid of [attorney],' drafting substantive filings while not admitted or while suspended, and continuing such conduct after court warnings.
guidance: The tribunal considers documentary notations, witness testimony about the practitioner's drafting and advisory role, failure to obtain pro hac vice admission, failure to disclose suspension, and continued similar behavior after prior warnings as persuasive evidence. Conversely, absence of evidence that the practitioner knew his suspension removed 'admitted' status may mitigate findings on misrepresentation claims.

name: Enablement — make and use by a person of skill
description: The disclosure must explain enough about the invention so that someone skilled in the art can both make and use the invention.
guidance: Purpose: to put the invention into the public domain and thereby advance the technical arts (Invitrogen Corp. v. Clontech Labs.). Ensure the specification teaches how to make and use what is actually claimed.

name: Claim-by-claim enablement (partial enablement possible)
