description: A disclosure can sufficiently enable one or more claims while being insufficient with respect to other claims.
guidance: Enablement is claim-specific; some claims may be enabled and others not (In re Borkowski). Draft claims and specification together to avoid enabled/unenabled mismatches.

name: Undue experimentation prohibition
description: The invention must be described so that it can be made and used without undue experimentation; some reasonable experimentation is tolerable.
guidance: Undue experimentation is a factual, multi-factor inquiry. The specification must teach sufficiently to avoid requiring the public to engage in impermissible trial-and-error to practice the claimed invention.

name: Wands factors for assessing undue experimentation
description: Relevant factors to determine whether undue experimentation is required include: (1) quantity of experimentation necessary; (2) amount of direction or guidance presented; (3) presence or absence of working examples; (4) nature of the invention; (5) state of the prior art; (6) relative skill of those in the art; (7) predictability/unpredictability of the art; and (8) breadth of the claims.
guidance: These factors are illustrative, not mandatory (In re Wands; Amgen v. Chugai). A court need not address all factors to find enablement. Use working examples and clear guidance to reduce risk of undue experimentation (Streck, In re Wands, Amgen).

name: Breadth of claims vs. breadth of disclosure
description: The broader the claims, the more disclosure is needed to enable the full scope of the claimed subject matter.
guidance: Avoid claiming more breadth than the specification supports. Where broad claim scope is desired, include multiple embodiments, variations, and exemplars to support enablement across the claim scope.

name: Complete vs. defective disclosure consequences
description: A completely defective disclosure can lead to a total failure of enablement and invalidation; disclosure failures are sometimes partial but can also be all-or-nothing if lacking the necessary explanation and clarity.
guidance: Because failures can be fatal, err on the side of providing detailed disclosure; incomplete or vague specifications risk claim invalidity.

name: Claims must recite how computer aids the method (more than generic computer elements)
description: To show that a computer aids in improving technology, claims must recite details about how a computer aids the method, the extent to which it aids the method, or the significance of the computer to performance of the method; merely adding generic computer components is insufficient.
guidance: Assess whether the claim includes more than instructions to perform the method on generic components or machinery. If applicant adds a generic computer or generic computer components (including assertions of 'specially programmed' generic computers), the examiner should determine whether those added elements integrate the exception into a practical application or provide significantly more. Mere recitation of a generic computer or conventional computer functions does not automatically overcome an eligibility rejection. See MPEP §2106.05(f) for more on mere instructions to apply an exception. Cases: Alappat (superseded rationale that programming a generic computer renders eligibility); Alice Corp. (mere use of computer to perform existing process insufficient); Ultramercial and TLI (mere recitation of tangible components not necessarily inventive).

name: Particular machine consideration — particularity or generality of machine elements
description: When evaluating whether a claim integrates a judicial exception via a particular machine (Step 2A Prong Two / Step 2B), consider the particularity or generality of the elements of the machine or apparatus; i.e., how specifically the machine can be identified rather than claiming 'any and all machines.'
guidance: A claim that recites a machine with specific, identifiable structure (shape, conductors, components, arrangement) is more likely to integrate an exception into a practical application. Examples: Mackay Radio (specific antenna shape/arrangement), Eibel Process (Fourdrinier machine with defined structure). In contrast, a general-purpose computer that merely applies a judicial exception using conventional computer functions does not qualify as a 'particular machine.' See Ultramercial, TLI, Eon, and the discussion that Alappat's rationale is superseded by Bilski/Alice. Use this factor alongside other considerations (mere instructions, insignificant extra-solution activity, field of use).

name: Particular machine consideration — whether the machine implements the method steps
description: Consider whether the recited machine or apparatus actually implements the claimed method steps (plays an integral role) versus merely being an object on which the method operates.
guidance: If the machine plays a significant part in permitting performance of the claimed method, it may integrate the exception into a practical application or provide significantly more. If the machine only functions as an obvious mechanism to achieve the solution more quickly or merely hosts the steps, it will likely not add significantly more. Example: CyberSource v. Retail Decisions — the Internet was not deemed to perform the fraud detection steps. See MPEP §2106.05(f) and case law (Versata) for when a machine must 'play a significant part' rather than being a mere tool.

name: Particular machine consideration — whether involvement is extra-solution activity or field-of-use
description: Assess the extent to which the machine's involvement imposes meaningful limits on the claim as opposed to being extra-solution activity or a mere field-of-use limitation.
guidance: If the machine contributes only nominally or insignificantly to executing the claimed method (e.g., limited to data-gathering steps or merely describing the source of data), it will not integrate the exception or provide significantly more. Cases: Bilski (field-of-use limitations insufficient), CyberSource (data-gathering steps insufficient). See MPEP §§2106.05(g) & (h) for more on insignificant extra-solution activity and field-of-use considerations.

name: Machine-or-transformation (M-or-T) test — useful clue but not dispositive
description: The machine-or-transformation test is a useful and important clue and investigative tool for determining patent eligibility but is not a stand-alone test; claims must still be evaluated under the Alice/Mayo two-part framework.
guidance: A claim that passes the Alice/Mayo test is eligible even if it fails the M-or-T test. Conversely, a claim that fails Alice/Mayo is ineligible even if it satisfies the M-or-T test. Use the M-or-T test alongside other considerations (mere instructions to apply an exception, insignificant extra-solution activity, field of use) to inform the analysis. See Bilski, McRO, DDR Holdings, and Diehr discussions in MPEP.

name: Particular transformation consideration (transformation of a particular article)
description: Determine whether the claim effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing; such a transformation is a clue to patentability for process claims that do not include particular machines, though it is not a stand-alone test.
guidance: An 'article' includes a physical object or substance that must be particular (specifically identifiable). 'Transformation' means the article has changed to a different state or thing — usually more than simply using the article or changing its location; a new/different function or use is evidence of transformation. Purely mental processes or mere manipulation of abstract data typically are not eligible transformations. Example: Tilghman v. Proctor (transformation of fatty bodies into fat acids and glycerine). Factors relevant to the analysis: (1) particularity vs generality of the transformation (more particular favors eligibility); (2) degree to which the recited article is particular (generic recitation less likely to provide significantly more); (3) nature/extent of change in state or thing (different function/use favors eligibility; mere location change does not); (4) nature of the article transformed (physical/tangible transformations weigh more than intangible/mental); (5) whether transformation is extra-solution activity or field-of-use (transformations that are nominal/insignificant do not provide significantly more). See Gottschalk v. Benson, Diamond v. Diehr, and Mayo discussions; consult MPEP §§2106.05(g) & (h) for related guidance.

name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity consideration (Step 2B)
description: In Step 2B, evaluate whether additional element(s) beyond a judicial exception are well-understood, routine, and conventional activities previously known in the industry; if so (and recited at a high level of generality), they do not amount to 'significantly more.'
guidance: If an additional element (or combination) is specific and unconventional — e.g., confines the claim to a particular useful application of the exception — it favors eligibility (example: DDR Holdings where claims modified conventional hyperlink protocol to dynamically produce a hybrid webpage). If additional elements are merely known and conventional (example: Mayo — measuring metabolite levels by any known process), they do not provide an inventive concept. This consideration overlaps with other Step 2B factors (improvement consideration, mere instructions, insignificant extra-solution activity); evaluate them together. Important points: (a) an element known in the art can still be unconventional or non-routine for eligibility purposes (novelty/obviousness is distinct from eligibility); (b) improvements over conventional functionality may support eligibility even if not novel (Enfish discussion). Use case law (DDR, Mayo, Parker v. Flook) and MPEP §2106.05(d) guidance when applying this factor.

name: Preservation of true free-will (no praemotio ad unum)
description: A system must not make the will inevitably predetermined by God (a _praedeterminatio ad unum_) so that it can no longer be called truly free.
guidance: Text repeatedly objects that an efficacious physical premotion which 'predetermines the will' destroys freedom. The page stresses that liberty resides formally in the will (not merely in the intellect) and that any claimed faculty to resist (potentia dissentiendi/potentia resistendi) must be a real, activatable power, not a chimera (compare the man tied to a chair example).

name: Preservation of moral responsibility (libertas a coactione and libertas a necessitate)
description: The theory must safeguard that the will is not coerced (libertas a coactione) and retains capacity to resist (libertas a necessitate as appropriate), so moral responsibility is meaningful.
guidance: Augustinians claim moral predetermination (praemotio moralis) leaves will free; the critique demands genuine capacity to resist at all times. If efficacious grace removes that capacity, the will's freedom (and moral responsibility) is compromised.

name: Required components of the Request for Reexamination
description: The request must include: (1) a statement pointing out each substantial new question of patentability based on prior patents and printed publications (37 C.F.R. § 1.510(b)(1)); (2) an identification of every claim for which reexamination is requested (37 C.F.R. § 1.510(b)(2)); (3) a detailed explanation of how to apply the prior art to each claim; and (4) a certification of no IPR, PGR, or CBM estoppel (37 C.F.R. § 1.510(b)(2), § 1.510(b)(6)).
guidance: Each element is required by regulation—prepare the claim‑by‑claim explanations and the estoppel certification carefully to avoid rejection.

name: Recommended components of the Request
description: Recommended items include an exhibit list that assigns a unique number to each supporting document and an explanation of how to construe the claims in light of any patent owner statements filed in other proceedings.
guidance: If you cite patent owner statements (e.g., litigation claim construction briefs, PTAB briefs, office action responses), those statements must be filed with the request (37 C.F.R. § 1.510(b)(2)). An exhibit list improves organization and tribunal navigation.

name: Recommended supporting documents (additional evidence)
description: Recommended items include a copy of the patent’s file history, expert declarations, 'librarian' declarations to establish NPL status, claim charts summarizing each proposed rejection, and any litigation claim construction orders.
guidance: These documents are not strictly required but materially strengthen the request and make the examiner’s work easier.

name: Conditions imposed when permission to file in the United States is granted
description: Where permission to file in the US is granted, (1) the specification must be clear and specific to allow examination by US authorities, and (2) the right to claim damages caused by confidentiality of the invention in the US must be waived (except damages from unauthorized US use/disclosure).
guidance: An applicant who files in the US after permission must attach two copies of application documents, a copy of the Korean permission, personal information and security-cleared representative documentation to the Commissioner of the Defense Acquisition Program Administration, and designate a US security-cleared representative to handle patent proceedings.

name: Eligible category: application serving as basis of priority claim under treaties
description: A patent application which serves as the basis of a priority claim under treaties is eligible if a foreign application claiming priority to it is pending before a foreign patent office.
guidance: Limited to cases where a foreign patent application claiming priority is pending abroad.

name: Claims requirement for eligibility
description: The invention that makes the application eligible for expedited examination must be recited in the claims. If the invention is described only in the specification and not claimed, the application is not recognized as eligible.
guidance: Eligibility is assessed based on the claims as amended before the time of determining eligibility. If at least one claim is recognized as eligible, the entire application may be accepted for expedited examination. If eligibility-creating claims are cancelled before determination, the request will not be recognized.

name: Laying-open/publication requirement for third-party practicing basis
description: For the ground that a third party is practicing the claimed invention (Article 61(1)), the application must have been laid open; except for this ground, publication is not required to seek expedited examination.
guidance: If a request based on third-party practice is filed before laying-open and laying-open is imminent, determination of eligibility may be deferred (not dismissed); once laid open, examiner proceeds with expedited examination.

name: Necessity of urgent processing: when required and assessment factors
description: Applications listed under Article 9 are in principle deemed necessary for urgent processing; for other statutory sources (special acts), necessity must be shown. Determination considers (1) relevance to national policies, (2) protection of applicant’s interest, and (3) whether urgent processing is likely to ensure grant of the patent (patentability).
guidance: For factor (3) the requester can submit prior-art search results and an explanation of patentability comparing the claimed invention to prior art; those materials help the examiner decide urgency.

name: Substitution of search results from local IP centers or additional searches
description: Search results produced with support of local IP centers or additional relevant search results may be submitted instead of the self-search process and results, but a contrastive explanation must still be provided in the application.
guidance: Such substitutions are acceptable where they sufficiently explain the search and comparison to the claimed invention.

name: Written description must demonstrate possession
description: The specification must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail that one skilled in the art can reasonably conclude that the inventor had possession of the claimed invention.
guidance: The description may use words, structures, figures, diagrams, and formulas; possession can be shown by reduction to practice, disclosure that the invention was "ready for patenting," or distinguishing identifying characteristics sufficient to show possession. Compliance is fact-based and varies with the nature of the invention (citations: Moba; Vas-Cath; Pfaff; Eli Lilly; Amgen).

name: Enablement: make and use without undue experimentation
description: To satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (enablement), the specification must teach those skilled in the art how to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention without "undue experimentation."
guidance: When assessing undue experimentation, weigh the Wands factors: (1) breadth of the claims; (2) nature of the invention; (3) state of the prior art; (4) level of ordinary skill; (5) level of predictability in the art; (6) amount of direction provided by the inventor; (7) existence of working examples; and (8) quantity of experimentation needed. Examination requires a reasonable basis for questioning enablement; once shown, applicant must rebut with factual demonstration (cites: In re Wands; In re Wright; In re Brown; In re Ghiron; In re Doyle).

name: Scope of claims must be commensurate with enablement
description: The scope of the claims must be less than or equal to the scope of the enablement provided by the specification.
guidance: Broad, functional claim language (not invoking 112(f)) is construed broadly to cover any embodiment performing the function; examiner must ensure the specification enables the full claim scope. Examples: Sitrick (video games vs. movies) and MagSil (resistive-change magnitude) show patentees choosing broad claim language at risk of invalidity if full scope isn't enabled.

name: Cannot rely on ordinary skill to supply novel information
description: The specification need not teach what is well known in the art, but the applicant cannot rely on the knowledge of one skilled in the art to supply information required to enable the novel aspect of the claimed invention.
guidance: The novel aspects of an invention must be enabled in the specification itself; omission of specific starting materials or conditions that are necessary to carry out the invention can render it non-enabled (cites: ALZA; Auto. Technologies; Genentech).

name: Means-(or step-)plus-function limitations require corresponding structure/materials/acts
description: If a claim includes a means- (or step-) plus-function limitation under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (or pre-AIA sixth paragraph), the specification must disclose sufficient corresponding structure, materials, or acts that perform the entire claimed function.
guidance: If no sufficient corresponding structure is disclosed, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or written description may be required; and a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre-AIA second paragraph) must be made in addition to a written description rejection (cites: In re Donaldson).

name: Functional-only descriptions may fail written description
description: An invention described solely in terms of a method of making and/or its function may lack written descriptive support where there is no described or art-recognized correlation between the disclosed function and the structure(s) responsible for it.
guidance: Examples include protein/amino-acid/genetic claims where sequence/function correlation is required; merely rendering a claimed invention obvious does not necessarily satisfy written description (cites: In re Bell; In re Deuel; Eli Lilly; Fonar).

name: Original claims: presumption of adequate written description but still fact-specific
description: There is a presumption that an adequate written description exists when the application is filed, but original claims may still lack adequate written description if essential or critical features are not described with sufficient particularity.
guidance: Examiner has initial burden to present reasons why skilled artisans would not recognize the claim in the disclosure. Even originally-filed claims must be examined to ensure all limitations, especially non-conventional ones, are adequately supported (cites: In re Wertheim; Vas-Cath; cases like Gentry Gallery, Tronzo).

name: New or amended claims must be supported by originally-filed disclosure (no new matter)
description: New or amended claims that introduce elements or limitations not supported by the as-filed disclosure violate the written description requirement and the prohibition against adding new matter.
guidance: Support may be express, implicit, or inherent; correcting obvious errors is permissible when an ordinary artisan would recognize the error and correction. For sequence corrections and biological deposits, post-filing deposits may support corrections only if accompanied by required statements (cites: 35 U.S.C. 132/251; In re Rasmussen; In re Benno; Cubist v. Hospira; 37 CFR 1.801/1.804).

name: Essential or critical features disclosed as essential cannot be omitted from claims
description: If the specification describes a limitation as essential or critical to the invention, omission of that limitation in a claim may render the claim noncompliant with the written description requirement.
guidance: Claims that omit matter disclosed as essential may also be subject to enablement or 112(b)/second paragraph rejections. Cases: Gentry Gallery, In re Sus, Tronzo, and others illustrating that the disclosure can 'make crystal clear' a narrow understanding of a term that cannot be broadened (citations in text).

name: Deposit of biological materials may aid written description but is not a substitute
description: A deposit made under 37 CFR 1.801 et seq. may satisfy written description for claimed biological materials where appropriate, but such a deposit is not a substitute for a complete written description.
guidance: The specification should include as much information about the deposited material as possible to aid examiner comparison with prior art and to permit verification; post-filing deposits can support sequence corrections only with required statements (cites: Enzo Biochem; 54 Fed. Reg. 34,864; In re Lundak).

name: Examiner must establish reasonable basis before enablement rejection; applicant must rebut
description: USPTO personnel must establish on the record a reasonable basis for questioning the adequacy of the disclosure to enable a person of ordinary skill to make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
guidance: Once the examiner has advanced a reasonable basis, the burden shifts to the applicant to rebut and factually demonstrate the disclosure is sufficient. Examiners should provide reasons for questioning enablement and follow with thorough review of prior art and other statutory requirements before completing an Office action (cites: In re Brown; In re Ghiron; In re Doyle; MPEP §§ 2164 et seq.).

name: Functional claim language without invoking 112(f) broadens claim scope and raises enablement/written_description concerns
description: When a claim is not limited to any particular structure for a recited function and does not invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f), the claim language is typically construed broadly to cover any and all embodiments performing that function.
guidance: Because such claims encompass potentially all devices/structures that perform the function, examiners must be concerned whether the disclosure sufficiently enables the full scope; applicants presenting broad claim language must ensure their specification fully enables across that scope (cites: In re Swinehart; AK Steel v. Sollac; In re Moore).

name: Written description and enablement are separate requirements with distinct objectives
description: The written description requirement (demonstrating possession and informing the public of what is claimed) is separate and distinct from the enablement requirement (teaching how to make and use without undue experimentation).
guidance: Both are minimum requirements under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (first paragraph); failure to satisfy either can result in rejection or invalidity. Examiners should assess both independently (cites: Ariad; Vas-Cath; Univ. of Rochester v. G.D. Searle).

name: Prior-art date when reference did not result from or claim benefit of an IA
description: If the potential reference did not result from, nor claim the benefit of, an international application, its pre-AIA 102(e) prior art date is its earliest effective U.S. filing date, taking into account any proper benefit claims to earlier U.S. applications under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or 120.
guidance: For benefit claims, the prior application(s) must properly support the subject matter used to make the rejection in compliance with pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112 (first paragraph) / 35 U.S.C. 112(a). For 119(e) provisional benefit claims see the separate provisional-support requirement.

name: When an international filing date is treated as a U.S. filing date (IA on/after Nov 29, 2000)
description: An international filing date of an international application (IA) filed on or after November 29, 2000 is a U.S. filing date for pre-AIA 102(e) prior art purposes only if: (a) the IA has an international filing date on or after Nov 29, 2000; (b) the IA designated the United States; and (c) the IA was published by WIPO under PCT Article 21(2) in the English language.
guidance: If these three conditions are met, the IA filing date (or an earlier effective U.S. filing date to which the IA properly claims benefit) is the 102(e) date, provided all requirements for benefit claims (119(e), 120, 365(c), 386(c)) and 112 written-description support are satisfied.

name: Benefit-claim subject-matter support requirement (112 compliance)
description: For any benefit claim (35 U.S.C. 119(e), 120, 365(c), 386(c)) used to secure an earlier effective filing date for a reference under pre-AIA 102(e), the subject matter relied upon in the rejection must be disclosed in the earlier-filed application in compliance with pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112 (first paragraph) / 35 U.S.C. 112(a).
guidance: Examiners must verify written-description/support in the earlier application for the specific subject matter used to make the rejection before attributing the earlier filing date to the reference.

name: Provisional (35 U.S.C. 119(e)) benefit — claim-support special rule
description: A benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) to a provisional application gives the potential reference the provisional filing date for 102(e) purposes only if at least one claim of the potential reference is supported by the written description of the provisional application in compliance with pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112 (first paragraph) / 35 U.S.C. 112(a).
guidance: Examiners must check that at least one claim in the reference reads on subject matter supported by the provisional's written description before using the provisional's filing date as the 102(e) date. See MPEP § 2136.03, subsection III for more detail.

name: Particular treatment and prophylaxis (Step 2A Prong Two)
description: A claim reciting a judicial exception is not directed to the judicial exception if it also recites additional element(s) demonstrating that the claim as a whole integrates the exception into a practical application; one way to demonstrate such integration is when the additional elements apply or use the recited judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition.
guidance: Such application or use meaningfully limits the claim by going beyond generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment. Claims qualifying under this consideration are eligible at Step 2A because they are not 'directed to' the recited judicial exception. Examples include administration steps that treat or prevent a disease (e.g., administering a drug in a dose range depending on genotype).

name: Treatment/prophylaxis limitation must affirmatively recite an action that effects treatment or prophylaxis
description: To qualify as a 'treatment' or 'prophylaxis' limitation, the claim limitation must affirmatively recite an action that effects a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition.
guidance: Examples of affirmative limitations: 'administering amazonic acid to a patient', 'administering a course of plasmapheresis to a patient.' Mere intended use, a field-of-use limitation, or a recitation that a product is a 'pharmaceutical composition' are not affirmative treatment/prophylaxis limitations. A step of 'prescribing' is not positive if it does not require actual use by/on the patient.

name: More-than-nominal relationship to the exception
description: The treatment or prophylaxis limitation must have more than a nominal or insignificant relationship to the exception(s).
guidance: Assess whether the claimed treatment meaningfully relates to the recited law/correlation (e.g., administering insulin to reduce risk of ketoacidosis linked to high blood glucose is meaningfully related; administering aspirin in that context is at best nominal). Consider also the 'insignificant extra-solution activity' and 'field of use' considerations when determining meaningful relationship.

name: Inventive concept requirement (Step 2B): additional elements must amount to 'significantly more'
description: An 'inventive concept' is furnished by an element or combination of elements that is recited in the claim in addition to the judicial exception, and is sufficient to ensure that the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception itself.
guidance: The inventive concept cannot be furnished by the unpatentable law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea itself. Evaluating additional elements requires considering them both individually and in combination to ensure they amount to significantly more than the exception.

name: Search for an inventive concept is distinct from novelty/obviousness (§102/§103)
description: The search for an inventive concept should not be confused with a novelty (§102) or non-obviousness (§103) determination; novelty of an element is of no relevance to whether a claim falls within §101 categories.
guidance: Lack of novelty or obviousness does not necessarily indicate that additional elements are routine/conventional, and conversely patentability under §§102/103 is neither required for nor a guarantee of §101 eligibility. Do not substitute §§102/103/112 inquiries for the §101 analysis.

name: Considerations that can indicate 'significantly more' (illustrative list)
description: The Supreme Court has identified several non-exclusive considerations relevant to whether additional elements amount to an inventive concept.
guidance: Examples of limitations courts have found to qualify as 'significantly more' include: (i) improvements to the functioning of a computer; (ii) improvements to any other technology or technical field; (iii) applying the judicial exception with/by use of a particular machine; (iv) effecting a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing; (v) adding a specific limitation other than well-understood, routine, conventional activity or adding unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application; (vi) other meaningful limitations beyond generally linking the use of the exception to a particular technological environment (e.g., immunization step integrating data comparison into a process that lowers disease risk). The list is not exclusive and elements may be analyzed under more than one consideration.

name: Limitations that courts have found insufficient to supply 'significantly more' (illustrative list)
description: Certain types of additions to a claim are generally not enough to qualify as significantly more than a judicial exception.
guidance: Examples of insufficient limitations: (i) adding the words 'apply it' or mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer; (ii) appending well-understood, routine, conventional activities specified at a high level of generality (generic computer functions); (iii) adding insignificant extra-solution activity such as mere data gathering; (iv) generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use. See MPEP §2106.05(f)-(h) for examples and case citations.

name: Physicality/tangibility of additional elements is not determinative
description: Mere physicality or tangibility of an additional element(s) is not a relevant consideration in Step 2B; tangible implementation alone does not guarantee an inventive concept, nor does intangibility doom eligibility.
guidance: A computer is a tangible machine, but reciting a generic computer to implement an abstract idea does not make the claim patent-eligible (Alice). Conversely, improvements that are not defined by physical components may still be eligible (Enfish; McRO). Consult case law examples where physical steps did not supply an inventive concept and where non-physical improvements did.

name: Requirements to obtain reciprocal discipline nunc pro tunc (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(f))
description: Reciprocal discipline may be imposed nunc pro tunc upon request by a practitioner only if the practitioner: (1) promptly notified the OED Director of his or her suspension or disciplinary disqualification in another jurisdiction; (2) establishes by clear and convincing evidence that the practitioner voluntarily ceased all activities related to practice before the Office; and (3) complied with all provisions of § 11.58.
guidance: The effective date of reciprocal discipline applied nunc pro tunc is the date the practitioner voluntarily ceased practice-related activities before the Office and complied with § 11.58. Evidence may include a dated letter to the OED Director (example: letter dated October 10, 2011 notifying the OED Director), Office records supporting the asserted cessation date (example: cessation on October 31, 2009), and a statement of compliance (or prompt compliance upon receipt of final order) with § 11.58. The Office requires clear and convincing evidence for the voluntary cessation claim.

name: Constraints on amendments and supplements
description: Any amendment or supplement must not expand the scope or change the substance of the claimed subject matter and must ensure unity.
guidance: Amendments that expand disclosure or change substance are prohibited; unity of the application must be maintained.

name: Provisional rights to inventions, industrial designs and layout designs
description: Applicants may assert provisional rights against third-party commercial use during pendency and claim remuneration if the right is later granted.
guidance: If applicant knows another is using the invention/design/layout commercially without prior user right, applicant may serve written notice specifying filing and publication dates so the user may terminate or continue use. For layout-designs commercially exploited before grant by the person having the right to registration, they may serve such notice. If user continues use and a Protection Title is later issued, the owner may request remuneration equivalent to licensing fees for the relevant scope and period of use.

name: Eligibility for accelerated substantive examination — third-party and public-interest requests
description: The following persons may request an accelerated substantive examination: Third parties accused of wrongfully copying the subject matter of a patent application; A third party who owns a technology that has subsequently been registered as a patent; The Ministry of Health, in the case of patent applications for medicines acquired by the National Public Health System (SUS); and The State when a national emergency is declared or when there is a public interest in examining a specific request.
guidance: Third parties and public authorities may trigger expedited handling; this can be used both offensively (to challenge or clear a path) and defensively (to obtain certainty). Prepare documentary proof of the claimed relationship (e.g., evidence of copying or ownership, official Ministry/State declarations).

name: Patent Prosecution Highway (PPH) pilot program for accelerated examination
description: A new accelerated substantive examination procedure exists for applications subject to a PPH (Patent Prosecution Highway) pilot program. Since 01/12/2019 a PPH pilot program with standardized requirements and governed by a single regulation (n°252/19) is in force. The Brazilian INPI has signed PPH agreements with numerous patent offices (Japan, Argentina, Colombia, Chile, Costa Rica, Denmark, El Salvador, Ecuador, Nicaragua, Panama, Paraguay, Peru, Uruguay, Europe-EPO, United States, United Kingdom, Dominican Republic, China, Austria, Sweden and South Korea).
guidance: If claims have been allowed/granted by a partner office, consider entering the PPH pilot program and file standardized PPH documentation per Reg. 252/19 to obtain accelerated substantive examination in Brazil. Ensure claims submitted in Brazil correspond to the allowed claims abroad and comply with the program's formal requirements.

name: Backlog reduction plan — operational process and applicant recommendation
description: The plan is based on the mass publication of standardized reports, essentially a list of prior art cited by a foreign office. Applicants are invited to submit the same claims accepted for a counterpart foreign patent and/or supporting arguments used abroad. The Brazilian INPI can also take advantage of the fact that no response to these reports needs to be filed in the event of an abandoned application. Abandoned applications can therefore be rejected without substantive examination.
guidance: Practical advice given: 'file the same claims in Brazil as you would in any other country!' Submitting claims aligned with granted foreign claims and reusing supporting arguments used abroad will speed up grant under the plan. Also be aware that abandoned counterparts may lead to rejection without substantive examination, so monitor family prosecution status.

name: Foreign language prior art — need for complete/accurate translation
description: If a foreign-language prior art reference was cited/discussed in prior prosecution but never completely and accurately translated into English during original prosecution, a reexamination request explaining why a more complete and accurate translation actually teaches what is required by the claims may justify reexamination.
guidance: Portola Packaging does not prohibit reexamination in such circumstances; focus on whether translation now shows teachings required by claims.

name: Completeness of examiner's action — permissible limitations
description: The examiner's action will be complete as to all matters, except where appropriate to limit action due to misjoinder of invention, fundamental defects, and the like; matters of form need not be raised until a claim is found allowable.
guidance: Examiner may focus action on substantive defects as appropriate and defer form issues until allowance.

name: Rejections for novelty/obviousness — cite best references and explain pertinency
description: In rejecting claims for want of novelty or for obviousness, the examiner must cite the best references at his/her command. When a reference is complex or shows inventions other than that claimed, the particular part relied on must be designated as nearly as practicable and the pertinency of each reference must be clearly explained and each rejected claim specified.
guidance: Must make clear which parts of references are relied upon and why they are pertinent to the rejection.

name: Reliance on admissions and examiner's knowledge
description: In rejecting claims the examiner may rely upon admissions by the applicant or patent owner in reexamination, and may rely upon facts within his/her knowledge (permitted by paragraph (d)(2)).
guidance: Admissions in the file and official knowledge can support rejections, subject to the requirements for specificity and support for asserted facts.

name: Reasons for allowance must be set forth if unclear
description: If the examiner believes the record of prosecution as a whole does not make clear his/her reasons for allowing a claim, the examiner may set forth such reasoning in an Office action or separate communication, and the applicant/patent owner may file a statement commenting on those reasons.
guidance: Reasons should be incorporated into actions rejecting other claims or be provided as a separate communication; failure by the examiner to respond to comments does not carry implication.

name: Dependent claims on new base claims — indefiniteness/rewriting requirements
description: If a new base claim (one not appearing in the patent) has been canceled, a claim depending on it should be rejected as indefinite. If a new base claim or an amended patent claim is rejected, a dependent claim should be objected to (if otherwise patentable) and require rewriting the dependent claim in independent form.
guidance: Newly introduced base claims do not enjoy the same protective treatment as original patent base claims.

name: Form and content of first Office action in reexamination
description: The first Office action should be so complete that the second Office action can properly be made final; it must clearly set forth pertinency and manner of applying cited prior art to the claims, respond to the substance of each argument raised by patent owner/requester, and indicate reasons why claims are patentable when appropriate.
guidance: First action must be thorough because of reexamination finality and patent owner inability to file a continuation; treat inappropriate arguments per 37 CFR 1.552(c).

name: Language of proceedings rules
description: At first instance local and regional divisions will use the official language(s) of the hosting member state; the central division will use the language in which the patent was granted (English, French or German). The Court of Appeal follows the first instance language, with exceptions and party agreements possible.
guidance: If a local/regional division provides a choice of language a claimant may choose; however, if the defendant only conducts activities in one member state with multiple official languages, the claimant must start in that region's language. Parties can agree exceptions; language choice affects evidence, pleadings and costs.

name: Where to bring infringement claims (venue rules)
description: Claims for infringement, provisional/protective measures and injunctions, damages or compensation shall be brought before either the local or regional division in the member state where the actual or threatened infringement occurred, or where the defendant has residence or principal place of business (or in absence, place of business). If none apply or the member state has no local/regional division, proceedings will be before the central division.
guidance: Multiple divisions may be competent, providing some forum choice; choice of venue affects applicable language, remedies and tactical considerations.

name: Court fees: fixed and value-based fee structure
description: Court fees include fixed fees and value-based fees. Infringement actions and declarations of non-infringement have fixed court fees of €11,000. Fixed fee for revocation actions is €20,000. Value-based fees apply to infringement/decl. non-infringement claims with value > €500,000: minimum value-based fee €2,500 (action value up to €750,000) up to maximum €325,000 (actions > €50m). Value-based fees do not apply to revocation actions or counterclaims.
guidance: Parties should budget for both fixed and potential value-based fees; the value thresholds and caps materially affect litigation economics for high-value disputes.

name: Depicting transparent materials
description: Elements visible behind transparent surfaces should be shown in light, full lines, not broken lines.
guidance: When illustrating transparent materials (e.g., aquarium, perfume bottle), show behind-the-surface elements with light solid lines so they are visible but not claimed as separate elements via broken lines.

name: Broken-line disclosure (environmental/boundary features)
description: Broken lines may be used to show environment and boundaries that form no part of the claimed design.
guidance: Use broken lines to indicate surrounding environment or boundary elements that are not claimed; these should not be interpreted as claim elements.

name: Indeterminate length indication
description: Use of a separation and a bracket to indicate that, for ease of illustration, the precise length of the molding is not claimed.
guidance: When a part's exact length is not claimed, indicate indeterminate length by showing separation and a bracket to avoid inadvertently claiming a specific length (e.g., picture frame molding).

name: Depicting specific materials
description: Drawings may depict specific materials or ornamental effects when material is relevant to the appearance of the design (e.g., sandal, multi-pocketed storage bag examples).
guidance: If material or texture/ornamental effect is part of the claimed appearance, depict it clearly in the drawings (via shading, stippling, notes, or appropriate views).

name: 35 U.S.C. 112 — Specification requirements (written description, enablement, best mode)
description: The specification shall contain a written description of the invention, and the manner and process of making and using it, in full, clear, concise, and exact terms to enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the invention, and shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor.
guidance: Ensure the specification provides sufficient written description and enablement, and disclose the best mode. Avoid adding new matter in later amendments. Claims must particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter regarded as the invention.

name: Claim form rules under 35 U.S.C. 112
description: A claim may be written in independent or, if the nature of the case admits, in dependent or multiple dependent form. Dependent claims must refer to a previous claim and specify a further limitation; multiple dependent claims reference alternatives and incorporate limitations by reference.
guidance: Draft claims in appropriate dependent/independent forms; multiple dependent claims cannot serve as basis for other multiple dependent claims; understand incorporation-by-reference effects for claim construction.

name: Means-plus-function claim provision (35 U.S.C. 112 paragraph)
description: An element in a claim for a combination may be expressed as a means or step for performing a specified function without recital of structure, material, or acts, and such claim shall be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.
guidance: If using means/step language, ensure the specification discloses corresponding structure/material/acts sufficiently to support the means-plus-function claim; otherwise the claim may be limited or invalid.

name: 35 U.S.C. 132 — Notice of rejection and reexamination
description: Whenever, on examination, any claim is rejected, the Director shall notify the applicant stating the reasons with useful information and references. If applicant persists in the claim, the application shall be reexamined. No amendment shall introduce new matter.
guidance: Provide clear reasons in Office actions; applicants must avoid introducing new matter in amendments; the Director may set regulations for continued examination and fees with small-entity reductions.

name: 37 CFR 1.63 — Inventor contact and foreign application details in oath/declaration
description: Unless supplied on an application data sheet, the oath or declaration must also identify mailing address (and residence if different) of each inventor, and any foreign application for which priority is claimed by specifying application number, country, and filing date.
guidance: Either include this bibliographic information in the oath/declaration or supply it on an ADS; be precise about foreign priority details to support priority claims.

name: 37 CFR 1.84(b) — Photographs in applications
description: Photographs (including photocopies) are not ordinarily permitted but will be accepted if photographs are the only practicable medium for illustrating the claimed invention (examples include gels, blots, cell cultures, histological tissue sections, animals, plants, in vivo imaging, thin layer structures, and ornamental effects in design applications). Photographs must be of sufficient quality for reproducibility in the printed patent.
guidance: Only use photographs when drawings cannot practically depict the subject matter. Be prepared to replace photographs with drawings if the examiner requires it and ensure photographs meet high-quality reproduction standards.

name: Preparation and content rules for bills of costs
description: A party seeking costs is limited to the lesser of its actual costs or the maximum allowable cost; use Form 24 and instructions to prepare a bill of costs.
guidance: Flatten the bill and prepare a combined PDF with vendor invoices to support costs claimed. The Court prefers stipulation on costs; objections are limited to 5 pages. File the bill via CM/ECF Forms and Certificates submenu.

name: Brief cover page content rules
description: Outside cover must include case number (top center), court name, official caption (must exactly match PACER/docketing notice), nature of proceeding and tribunal appealed from (including PTAB judges’ names now encouraged), title of the brief, and counsel contact info (name, address, telephone; other contact info optional).
guidance: Inside cover should include contact information for other counsel if it doesn’t fit on the outside cover and the language of a claim at issue (or on a page immediately after the cover if space requires). Ensure the caption exactly matches the official caption.

name: Standard of proof for unpatentability in IPR
description: Petitioner must show unpatentability by a preponderance of the evidence (see 35 U.S.C. § 316(e)).
guidance: The Board determines whether Petitioner has shown by a preponderance that each challenged claim is unpatentable; claims not shown by a preponderance are sustained. Example: claims 1–6, 10, 11, 14, 17, 19, and 20 were found unpatentable by a preponderance; claim 18 was not.

name: Claim construction standard in IPR (broadest reasonable construction)
description: In an inter partes review, the Board interprets claim terms in an unexpired patent according to the broadest reasonable construction in light of the specification of the patent in which they appear (37 C.F.R. § 42.100(b); Cuozzo).
guidance: Absent any special definitions, give claim terms their ordinary and customary meaning as would be understood by one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention. Any special definitions must be set forth with reasonable clarity, deliberateness, and precision (In re Paulsen). Only terms in controversy need be construed, and only to the extent necessary to resolve the controversy (Vivid Techs.).

name: Open-ended claim language 'comprising' (inclusion of unrecited ingredients)
description: Use of the term 'comprising' permits inclusion of elements in addition to those specified in the claims (In re Baxter; CIAS, Inc. v. Alliance Gaming Corp.).
guidance: When a formulation is recited with 'comprising' and a property is attributed to 'the formulation,' the broadest reasonable construction can include embodiments containing additional, unrecited ingredient(s) that may contribute to the claimed functional property. Example applied: the formulation 'inhibits aggregation' may include additional unrecited ingredients that cause inhibition.

name: Interpretation of functional claim limitations
description: A functional limitation attributing a property to 'the formulation' is read as a property of the formulation as a whole, not necessarily attributable to any particular recited ingredient.
guidance: Do not read a functional property as requiring that a specific recited ingredient (e.g., the aluminum salt) itself perform the function unless the claim language or clear specification text requires it. The property may be satisfied by the combination of recited elements or by additional, unrecited elements.

name: When to import limitations from the specification into claims
description: Do not import limitations from the specification into claims absent clear support; claims are not limited to examples or measurements described in the specification.
guidance: Example: although the specification measures inhibition of aggregation by antigenicity in Example 4, the Board refused to read an 'antigenicity' limitation into the claim because the claim does not require a specific level of immunogenicity and the presence of a polysaccharide-protein conjugate already supplies the immunogenic element. Use specification to inform ordinary meaning but not to add unclaimed numerical or functional thresholds unless claim language requires it.

name: Obviousness framework (Graham factors and KSR)
description: The obviousness inquiry is resolved based on (1) scope and content of the prior art, (2) differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art, (3) level of ordinary skill in the art, and (4) secondary considerations, and requires a reason to combine with a reasonable expectation of success (Graham; KSR).
guidance: A claim is unpatentable if, as a whole, it would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill. Mere knowledge of separate elements in the prior art is insufficient; there must be an articulated reason a skilled artisan would combine the references and a reasonable expectation that the combination would work. Avoid hindsight—using the inventor's disclosure as a blueprint to piece together prior art is improper (KSR; In re Fine; Kinetic Concepts).

name: Inherency in obviousness and modifications
description: A feature that is the necessary and inevitable result of applying the prior art combination may be inherent, but inherency must be established by clear evidence, not just speculation.
guidance: When asserting that a combined reference inherently produces a claimed property (e.g., inhibition of silicone-induced aggregation), the petitioner must show that the property necessarily flows from the combination, supported by evidence or sound expert testimony.

name: Objective indicia / secondary considerations of nonobviousness
description: Evidence such as commercial success, industry praise, long-felt but unsolved need, copying by others, and overcoming failures of others may weigh against obviousness if a nexus to the claimed invention is shown.
guidance: Secondary considerations must be timely raised and supported by admissible evidence showing a nexus to the claimed features. The Board may decline to reach or give weight to secondary considerations if the petitioner has not first established obviousness or if the necessary evidentiary predicate is lacking.

name: Requirement for concrete evidence when asserting obviousness of complex, multicomponent inventions
description: For claims reciting many structural elements (e.g., a 13‑valent conjugate composition), a petitioner must provide evidence that the prior art taught or would have led a skilled artisan to make those specific combinations with a reasonable expectation of success.
guidance: Assertions of a 'natural progression' from smaller to larger valency vaccines are insufficient without evidence that the specific multivalent composition was taught, tested, or would have been expected to work. The Board expects documentation (publications, studies, or convincing expert testimony with factual basis) showing that the exact multi-component arrangement was known or would have been predictably achievable.

name: Litigation – Hatch‑Waxman Act matters by amount at risk (Q45Ba–Q45Bp)
description: Patent litigation specifically under the Hatch‑Waxman/ANDA context, broken down by amount at risk and litigation phases (initial management, discovery/motions/claim construction, trial/appeal, mediation).
guidance: Specialized pharmaceutical litigation category.

name: Litigation – Defending claims of patent infringement by Non‑Practicing Entity (NPE) by amount at risk (Q45Ca–Q45Cp)
description: Defense of patent infringement claims asserted by NPEs, segmented by amount at risk and litigation phases (initial management, discovery, trial, mediation).
guidance: NPE-specific defense workload categories.

name: Examiners' duties and standards for rejection
description: The examiner decides patentability from any data at his command according to rules of courts and Commissioner's judgments; not bound by conclusions of former examiners; must cite references and give reasons in notices of rejection; may reject if invention evidently impracticable.
guidance: Examiners must state grounded reasons and cite references; they are not required to draft claim language for applicant; grounds and references that may be cited are governed by law and practice.

name: Amendment substantive/form limits
description: Amendments to the application may be partial or total and, in form, may be made to any extent; in substance an amendment cannot embrace new matter or enlarge the invention; substitute of a different specific invention for the one claimed is improper.
guidance: Amendments must not introduce new subject-matter; changes that effectively enlarge the invention or substitute a different invention are barred; numerous examples exist (see cited examples).

name: Amendments and claims withdrawn to avoid rejection
description: An amendment cannot include claims once withdrawn to avoid rejection and cannot prejudice intermediate inventors.
guidance: Claims previously withdrawn to avoid rejection cannot later be reinserted via amendment; applicants must be careful not to prejudice third-party rights by tardy amendments.

name: Specification, description, and claim scope
description: The Description and the Claim: the specification (description, drawings, or model) may show patentable matter but only the matter claimed is covered by the patent; where two specifications describe but only one claims, patent issues on the latter; disclaimers must explain the claim and not contradict it.
guidance: Claims define the metes and bounds of the monopoly; the specification supports claims but the patent's enforceable scope is the claims as issued; disclaimers and descriptions must be consistent with claims.

name: Abandonment to the public — grounds and computation
description: Abandonment may occur by express acts or words, cancellation of claims, or unreasonable delay in prosecuting; not by attorney action, not by filing a new application, not by some Patent Office delays/errors; two years' inaction after last action is a common trigger; burden of proof on applicant to show non-abandonment.
guidance: The 'last action' and 'inaction' are specifically defined; suspension of action is distinguished from inaction; computation of time (two years) and consequences are detailed, and Commissioner determinations may be conclusive.

name: Definition and patentability criteria for 'art'
description: An 'art' is defined by essential attributes: it must produce physical effects, may be a force applied, mode of application, or specific treatment of an object; may be new even if apparatus or product is old; must be useful and reduced to practice; mere functional description or mere employment of substances in an old art may not suffice.
guidance: Three classes of art exist with distinctions; combination arts have essentials; identity is shown by identity of product; patenting an art should claim it as an art, not merely as apparatus or product, to cover all modes of practicing it.

name: Claims for art vs. apparatus/product
description: A claim for an art must claim the art itself and not merely the apparatus or product; a patent for an art covers all modes of pursuing it; claims must meet requisite formal and substantive requirements.
guidance: When drafting claims for processes or methods, ensure language captures the art and is not limited inadvertently to a particular apparatus or product unless intended.

name: Burden of proof allocation in patent litigation
description: Burden of proof in patent cases is allocated on issues such as inventive skill, prior use, publication, utility, abandonment, specification fraud/ambiguity, excessive claims, and priority; on defendants to show patentee is not true inventor in appropriate circumstances.
guidance: Parties should prepare proof accordingly: patentees to prove validity and priority; defendants to prove invalidating facts or lack of inventorship, with burdens on specific elements depending on the issue.

name: Definition of 'covered business-method patent' (statutory core)
description: The term 'covered business method patent' means a patent that claims a method or corresponding apparatus for performing data processing or other operations used in the practice, administration, or management of a financial product or service.
guidance: This statutory definition sets the baseline eligibility for section 18 review: the claimed invention must relate to data processing or other operations tied to a financial product or service and may be claimed as methods or corresponding apparatus. The House added 'or other operations' to broaden scope beyond USPTO class 705.

name: Meaning of 'financial product or service'
description: A financial product is, at its most basic, an agreement between two parties stipulating movements of money or other consideration now or in the future; to be eligible for section 18 review, patent claims must only be broad enough to cover a financial product or service.
guidance: Senator Schumer listed extensive examples and emphasized that the patent need not recite a specific financial product or service; it is enough that the claims are broad enough to cover one. The definition is not limited to traditional banking—insurance, brokerages, mutual funds, annuities, and other financial companies fall within the scope.

name: Scope of 'practice, administration, or management' of a financial product or service
description: The phrase 'practice, administration or management' is intended to cover ancillary activities related to a financial product or service, not only patents claiming the product or service itself.
guidance: Examples given include marketing, customer interfaces, website management and functionality, transmission or management of data, servicing, underwriting, customer communications, and back-office operations (e.g., payment processing, stock clearing). The provision therefore reaches patents that claim activities financial in nature, incidental to financial activity, or complementary to it.

name: Breadth expansion via 'or other' and inclusion of 'corresponding apparatus'
description: House amendment changed 'data processing operations' to 'data processing or other operations' and included 'method or corresponding apparatus' in the definition.
guidance: The addition of 'or other' broadens coverage beyond class 705 patents. 'Method or corresponding apparatus' is intended to encompass any claim type (method, system, apparatus, GUI claims, data structure claims, Beauregard claims on storage media, Lowry claims, etc.) so that clever drafting cannot avoid PTO review—form should not trump substance.

name: Improvements or additions are patentable but must be claimed narrowly
description: An addition to or improvement of a manufacture is recognized as a new manufacture in law and may be patented, but the patent must be confined to the addition or improvement itself and not extend to the whole underlying article.
guidance: Lord Mansfield and subsequent cases permit patents for improvements, but if the grant extends to the whole (substratum) it is void (Jessop's case). The improvement must be substantial and useful; if it cannot be used without an existing grant, the patentee must wait to use it against that grant, although he may patent the improvement per se and sell it. Practically: draft claims/specification to focus on the improvement only.

name: Combinations or arrangements of known things
description: A new combination or arrangement of old materials or machines which produces a new effect (new article or a better/cheaper way of making an old article) may be patented; the novelty of the arrangement is the essential quality.
guidance: Even when each part is old and separately in common use, the new compound or effect produced by combining them is what the grant protects. However, the patent must be for the new combination only; claiming the whole machine where only the combination is new will invalidate the patent (Browne/bobbin lace example). The specification must clearly express that the claim is limited to the new combination or application.

name: Specification must clearly confine claim to the new matter
description: Where the patentable subject is an addition, improvement, or new combination, the specification must clearly express that the claim is in respect of that new combination or application only, and not claim merit in the original or old materials.
guidance: Lord Eldon and other authorities required explicit limiting language; failure to confine the claim to the addition/new combination can render the grant invalid. The text emphasizes that the ostensible object of the patent should be the new combined matter and not any part of the old article.

name: Abstract principles or mere methods are not patentable unless embodied in tangible means
description: A mere abstract or philosophical principle cannot be monopolized. A principle carried into practice by tangible means may be patentable, but the patent is, in reality, for the tangible means (substance or machine) enabling the method, not for the principle itself.
guidance: The better opinion cited is that a patent for the application of a principle is as bad as one for the principle itself; courts require a corporeal, substantial thing or a new mode of employing practical art. Cases (Boulton & Watt, Hornblower v. Boulton, King v. Wheeler) are cited. Practically: ensure patents claim concrete apparatus or composition, not a bare principle or broad method.

name: Patents must not claim more than inventor actually invented
description: If a specification describes parts or combinations that existed before, and the patentee only invented a part or an improvement, claiming the whole invented machine or manufacture exceeds what was actually invented and may invalidate the patent.
guidance: The Browne/Heathcote lace machine example shows courts will examine what the inventor actually invented versus what the specification claims. If the patentee 'took up his invention from a point' and then described a whole machine including old parts, his specification may be bad. Draft claims to match the inventor's real contribution.

name: Patent eligibility of genetically modified organisms / microorganisms
description: Chakrabarty held that a genetically engineered bacterium constituted patentable subject matter as a 'composition of matter' or 'manufacture.'
guidance: For claims that involve living organisms, analyze whether the organism is a product of human ingenuity (e.g., genetically altered bacteria, engineered seeds). Chakrabarty supports treating such manmade organisms as eligible; cite Chakrabarty when arguing eligibility for modified biological entities.

name: "Something more" / 'inventive concept' requirement (post-Mayo/Myriad)
description: Post‑Chakrabarty Supreme Court jurisprudence (Mayo, Myriad) requires more than conventional, routine, or well-known activity — courts look for an 'inventive concept' or 'something more' beyond mere isolation/purification or natural correlations.
guidance: Assess whether the claim recites additional inventive features beyond the natural law, natural phenomenon, or routine isolation steps. If the claim merely applies conventional techniques to a natural relationship or to isolated natural products, it risks being held ineligible. The 'something more' inquiry is subjective and fact‑specific; gather evidence showing nonconventionality, inventive steps, or technical improvements.

name: Ineligibility of naturally occurring biological relationships and isolated DNA sequences (Mayo/Myriad holdings)
description: The Supreme Court in Mayo and Myriad found that naturally occurring biological relationships and isolated DNA sequences are not patent eligible.
guidance: When claims recite naturally occurring correlations, laws of nature, or mere isolated native DNA sequences, treat them as vulnerable under Mayo/Myriad. Distinguish claims that add inventive applications or materially different structures from those that simply claim the natural phenomenon or its unaltered sequence.

name: Reexamination Granted — Meaning of Grant
description: An Order Granting Reexamination is not a determination of claim patentability; it indicates the request has established the existence of at least one Substantial New Question (SNQ) of patentability based upon prior patents and/or printed publications.

name: Reexamination Denied — Meaning of Denial
description: An Order Denying Reexamination is not a determination of claim patentability; it is an order denying reexamination of any claims because the Office determined that no SNQ has been established in the request.

name: Appeal to the BPAI — Inter Partes
description: Either party may file a notice of appeal as a proper response to a RAN in an inter partes reexamination.
guidance: If some claims are rejected and some allowed or confirmed as patentable, both parties may appeal those determinations, file appeal briefs, respondent's briefs, and, after the examiner's answer, file rebuttal briefs directed to the examiner’s answer. [MPEP 2674]

name: Effect of Concluded Litigation on Reexamination — Validity Findings
description: A court decision holding that a patent claim is valid will not preclude the Office from continuing to reexamine such claim in an ex parte reexamination proceeding.
guidance: The Office applies the 'broadest reasonable interpretation' of claim language in reexamination because claims may be amended, whereas courts apply a less liberal standard; therefore the Office may find a claim unpatentable even if a court held it valid. [MPEP 2286]

name: Effect of Concluded Litigation on Reexamination — Invalidity Findings
description: A final, non-appealable court decision holding that a patent claim is invalid will preclude the Office from ordering any reexamination proceeding for that claim or will result in termination of any previously ordered reexamination as to that claim.
guidance: [MPEP 2286]

name: Estoppel in Inter Partes Reexamination
description: A final, nonappealable holding in litigation that a patent claim is valid may operate to estop a party from requesting inter partes reexamination of that claim or from maintaining a previously ordered inter partes reexamination of that claim.
guidance: Estoppel may also preclude a party who has obtained an Order Granting Inter Partes Reexamination from asserting invalidity of that claim in litigation under Section 1338 of Title 28 on grounds that such party raised, or could have raised, during that inter partes reexamination if that claim has been finally determined to be patentable in the inter partes reexamination proceeding. [MPEP 2686.04(V)]

name: Notice of Intent to Issue Reexamination Certificate (NIRC)
description: An NIRC is mailed to inform the parties that a reexamination proceeding has been terminated, whether by failure to timely file a required response or by natural resolution of all outstanding issues of claim patentability.
guidance: The NIRC lists the status of all claims that were subject to reexamination, including canceled claims and any claims added during the proceeding that were determined to be patentable, and indicates which claims, if any, were not reexamined. An NIRC may include an examiner’s amendment and must include reasons for confirmation of any patent claims determined to be patentable without amendment, and reasons for allowance of any amended or newly added claims. [MPEP 2287]

name: BRI claim construction standard
description: The BRI standard requires consideration of the “broadest reasonable meaning of [a claim’s] words in their ordinary usage as they would be understood by one of ordinary skill in the art, taking into account whatever enlightenment by way of definitions or otherwise that may be afforded by the written description contained in the applicant’s specification.” Claim words are given their ordinary and customary meaning unless the patent applicant acts as his own lexicographer. The PTO should also consult the prosecution history. While extrinsic evidence is not prohibited, it should be considered secondarily and in a limited manner so that the interpretation is the broadest reasonable interpretation, not just the broadest interpretation.
guidance: Applied by the USPTO in pre-issuance examinations and most post-issuance review proceedings (e.g., traditionally in reexams and AIA trials). Cannot be divorced from the specification and record evidence (Microsoft v. Proxyconn; In re NTP). Cases show the Board/Examiners may interpret terms more broadly under BRI; however, the Board should avoid importing improper limitations from the specification (Papst-Motoren). Examples: PTAB constructions under BRI in PPC Broadband and other PTAB decisions.

name: Phillips claim construction standard
description: Under Phillips, claims are given their ordinary and customary meaning — “the meaning that the term would have to a person of ordinary skill in the art in question at the time of the invention.” Primary reliance is placed on intrinsic evidence (claims, specification, prosecution history); extrinsic evidence is secondary.
guidance: Applied by district courts following the Federal Circuit’s en banc Phillips decision. Phillips reconciled earlier inconsistent precedent (Vitronics, Texas Digital) and clarified intrinsic-evidence-first approach. USPTO has proposed (and in some circumstances adopted) applying Phillips in PTAB proceedings for expired patents or by rulemaking (proposed rule 83 Fed. Reg. 21221).

name: Intrinsic evidence primary; extrinsic evidence secondary
description: Both BRI and Phillips emphasize primary reliance on intrinsic evidence (claim language, specification, prosecution history) to construe claim terms, with extrinsic evidence (dictionaries, expert testimony) considered only secondarily.
guidance: Under BRI extrinsic evidence is allowed but limited and subordinate to intrinsic evidence to ensure the interpretation is the broadest reasonable one. Phillips likewise places extrinsic evidence secondary to intrinsic sources. See Phillips, Vitronics discussion, and PPC cases where specification usage controlled.

name: BRI cannot be narrower than Phillips (relative breadth principle)
description: The broadest reasonable interpretation of a claim term may be the same as or broader than the construction of a term under the Phillips standard. But it cannot be narrower.
guidance: This is summarized in Facebook v. Pragmatus and applied in post-grant litigation: if a PTAB/BPAI construction under BRI is narrower than a Phillips construction, that may be erroneous. Use this as a sanity check when comparing constructions across forums.

name: Effect of patent expiration on claim construction
description: When a patent expires during the pendency of a USPTO proceeding or appeal, the USPTO has sometimes applied a Phillips-type or district-court-type standard instead of BRI; cases show mixed results — in some instances a new (narrower) construction followed expiration, in others the construction remained the same.
guidance: Examples: Papst-Motoren and Ex parte Bowles (BPAI changed construction on expiration and reversed rejections); Rambus (examiner agreed to apply Phillips but found same construction); several PTAB/Federal Circuit cases where expiration led to different treatment. Check MPEP §2258.G and 37 C.F.R. §42.100 for rules on expiration handling.

name: Avoid importing limitations from the specification (no wholesale reconstruction)
description: Decision makers are warned against ‘wholesale reconstruction of the claims by importing limitations into the claims from the specification.’ Importing improper ‘inferential limitations’ from the specification into claims is barred (Papst-Motoren and In re Priest).
guidance: Both PTO and courts must be careful not to read limitations from the specification into claim language; whether a construction imports limitations is a key battleground and can determine outcomes under either standard. Cite examples where BPAI reversed examiner or affirmed rejections based on this principle.

name: Standard of proof for invalidity (evidentiary standard)
description: The PTAB uses a preponderance-of-the-evidence standard to invalidate claims (35 U.S.C. §316(e)), whereas district courts require clear-and-convincing evidence for invalidation (Microsoft v. i4i).
guidance: Empirical work (Schwartz & Seaman) shows different invalidation rates under the two standards (e.g., 38.3% under preponderance vs 27.1% under clear-and-convincing in experiments). This difference, together with the presumption of validity, contributes materially to different outcomes between PTO and courts.

name: Judicial estoppel (doctrinal factors)
description: Judicial estoppel precludes a party from taking a later position clearly inconsistent with an earlier one where (a) the later position is clearly inconsistent, (b) the party persuaded a court to accept the earlier position (so acceptance would create the perception the court was misled), and (c) the party would derive an unfair advantage or impose unfair detriment on the opponent if not estopped.
guidance: Parties should avoid flip-flopping between broad and narrow constructions across tribunals; courts have penalized inconsistent litigation positions (e.g., Source Search Tech. fee award). Judicial estoppel considerations apply even when different claim-construction standards are used, but are particularly salient if both PTAB and courts apply the same construction standard.

name: Director discretion and management of parallel USPTO proceedings
description: The Director has statutory authority (e.g., 35 U.S.C. §315(d)) to determine how to proceed when a patent is involved in multiple USPTO proceedings (IPR, reexam, reissue, derivation). The Director may choose to institute, stay, or decline institution to avoid inconsistent outcomes.
guidance: Practical options include not instituting an IPR where a reexam is pending, staying reexam, or otherwise coordinating proceedings to limit application of different claim-construction standards across concurrent USPTO proceedings. This discretion can reduce occasions for inconsistent constructions within the Office.
