name: Use of prior court constructions by the USPTO (not strictly bound)
description: The USPTO is not strictly bound by district-court claim constructions, though examiners and the Board may adopt or rely on prior court constructions; the Office has sometimes chosen to follow a court’s narrower construction but has noted that it is not bound to accept it.
guidance: Examples: examiners in Guardian Media and Katz reexams accepted prior court constructions (but noted lack of binding effect); BPAI and PTAB sometimes adopt district-court constructions when persuasive. Expect the PTO to treat prior court rulings as informative but not determinative unless rule or regulation requires otherwise.

name: Predictability and fact-specificity of outcomes under BRI vs Phillips
description: Differences in outcomes under BRI and Phillips are fact-specific and hinge on how aggressively the decision maker reads claims in light of the specification and how close that reading comes to importing limitations. The same claim term may be construed the same under both standards or may differ; empirical and case-law evidence shows both possibilities.
guidance: No simple rule reliably predicts which standard will yield broader or narrower construction for a given term. Practitioners must analyze claim language, specification usage (e.g., repeated use of a term to mean encircle), prosecution history, and forum-specific incentives (presumption, burden) to assess risk. Case examples: PPC Broadband (standards outcome-determinative), Rambus and Straight Path (constructions similar despite different standards).

name: What a patent is and how one is obtained
description: Explains that a United States patent is granted by the PTO, gives the patent owner the right to exclude others from making, using, selling, offering to sell, or importing the patented invention in the U.S., and that the patent application includes a specification and claims defining the invention.
guidance: Describes prosecution, the role of the PTO examiner, prior art searching, office actions, prosecution history, and notes that a PTO grant does not conclusively establish validity because the court can find claims invalid based on evidence not considered by the PTO.

name: Patent at issue (identification of claims and parties)
description: Identifies the asserted patent and claims, the parties (patent holder and alleged infringer), the accused products/methods, and what the jury must decide (infringement, invalidity, and damages).
guidance: Template instructions for presenting the patent, specification, drawings and claims to jury; reminds jury that willfulness (if at issue) is a separate finding that should not affect damage award directly.

name: Claim construction / interpretation of claims
description: The judge interprets the meaning of claim language; claims are numbered sentences that set forth requirements (elements/limitations) that define the boundaries of the patent's protection.
guidance: Jury must accept the court's definitions of claim terms and apply those definitions to issues of infringement and invalidity; coordinate with special instructions for means-plus-function claims. Authorities cited: Markman, Phillips, Pitney Bowes, etc.

name: Overview of applicable law — claim-by-claim assessment
description: Infringement is assessed on a claim-by-claim basis; there may be infringement as to one claim but not another. There are different ways a patent may be infringed (direct, contributory, inducement).
guidance: Court may give preliminary overview to focus jury on relevant facts; will provide detailed instructions later. Invalidity may be shown for reasons such as lack of novelty or obviousness; written description and enablement defenses also explained.

name: Infringement — general rule and burden
description: Patent holder must prove, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the requirements for one or more types of infringement (direct, inducement, contributory) are met for an asserted claim.
guidance: Introduces the specific instructions for literal infringement, doctrine of equivalents, inducement, contributory infringement, and willfulness.

name: Direct literal infringement
description: To prove literal infringement, the patent holder must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that the accused product or process meets all of the requirements of a claim (each and every element) and was made/used/sold/imported without permission during the patent term.
guidance: If accused product/method does not have every requirement of the claim, there is no literal infringement. Addresses treatment of dependent claims (dependent claims incorporate all requirements of the claim they reference) and notes that knowledge of the patent or infringement is irrelevant to literal infringement.

name: Means-plus-function claims — literal infringement
description: Means-plus-function claim limitations cover only the specific structure disclosed in the specification for performing the claimed function and the equivalents of those specific structures, not all possible structures that could perform the function.
guidance: Court will identify the corresponding structure in the specification for each means-plus-function limitation. Jury must determine (1) whether the accused product has structure performing the claimed function, and (2) whether that structure is the same as or equivalent to the disclosed structure. Equivalence judged by insubstantial differences or function-way-result as of the time the patent issued.

name: Direct infringement by combined acts of multiple parties
description: When no single party performs all steps of a claimed method but multiple parties together perform every step, the claim is directly infringed only if all steps are performed by or attributable to a single entity.
guidance: An entity is responsible for others' performance when it directs or controls others' performance or when the actors form a joint enterprise. A joint enterprise requires proof of four elements: agreement, common purpose, community of pecuniary interest, and equal right to control/direction.

name: Direct infringement involving system components outside the United States
description: When some system components are located outside the U.S., direct infringement requires that the accused system include every element of the claim and that control of the system was exercised and the benefit of the system was enjoyed in the United States.
guidance: Patent holder must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that control and beneficial use occurred in the U.S. Authorities cited (NTP, Akamai, etc.).

name: Invalidity — general grounds
description: Claims may be invalid for a number of reasons including lack of novelty (anticipation), obviousness, failure to meet the written description requirement, and failure to enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the invention.
guidance: Invalidity is a defense to infringement; the alleged infringer must prove invalidity by clear and convincing evidence. The instructions explain specific doctrines (anticipation, obviousness, written description, enablement, statutory bars).

name: Obviousness — Graham framework and secondary considerations
description: A claim may be invalid as obvious even if no single prior art reference discloses every claim element; the jury must consider (1) scope and content of the prior art, (2) differences between the prior art and the claimed invention, (3) the level of ordinary skill in the art, and (4) objective evidence of non-obviousness (secondary considerations).
guidance: The instruction lays out these sub-questions and directs the jury to weigh evidence such as commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, copying, and other objective indicia. The alleged infringer must prove obviousness by clear and convincing evidence.

name: Damages — general principle
description: If the jury finds infringement of a claim that is not invalid, it must determine money damages to compensate the patent holder for the infringement; damages should put the patent holder in approximately the same financial position it would have been in had the infringement not occurred and must be at least a reasonable royalty.
guidance: Damages are compensatory, not punitive; jury may not award fines or penalties beyond compensation. The court will provide detailed instructions for lost profits, reasonable royalties, and other damage considerations.

name: Glossary / definitions control
description: Technical terms and legal terms used in the instructions have definitions which must be followed and control the jury's deliberations.
guidance: Provides definitions of terms such as abstract, amendment, anticipation, claim, conception, continuations, elements, enablement, infringement, limitation, nonobviousness, office action, prior art, prosecution history, reads on, reduction to practice, reexamination, requirement, royalty, specification, etc., to ensure jurors understand specialized vocabulary used in instructions.

name: Required statements in the oath or declaration (35 U.S.C. 115(b))
description: An oath or declaration shall contain statements that (1) the application was made or was authorized to be made by the affiant or declarant; and (2) such individual believes himself or herself to be the original inventor or an original joint inventor of a claimed invention in the application.
guidance: These two statements are mandatory content elements of the oath/declaration; additional statutory/ regulatory requirements may apply.

name: 37 CFR 1.63(a) specific oath/declaration elements
description: An oath or declaration must: (1) Identify the inventor executing the oath by his or her legal name; (2) Identify the application to which it is directed; (3) Include a statement that the person believes the named inventor to be the original inventor or an original joint inventor of a claimed invention in the application; and (4) State that the application was made or was authorized to be made by the person executing the oath or declaration.
guidance: These regulatory elements implement 35 U.S.C. 115 and must appear in any oath/declaration submitted under 37 CFR 1.63.

name: 37 CFR 1.63(c) competence, review, and duty to disclose
description: A person may not execute an oath or declaration unless that person has reviewed and understands the contents of the application, including the claims, and is aware of the duty to disclose to the Office all information known to the person to be material to patentability as defined in 37 CFR 1.56. No minimum age, but the person must be competent to execute.
guidance: Although the express 'reviewed and understands' wording of pre-AIA 1.63(b)(2)/(3) is not required in AIA-era filings, the declarant must still have reviewed/understood the application and be aware of duty to disclose; competence is required.

name: Additional mandatory contents (where required by designated Contracting Parties)
description: Elements required by certain Contracting Parties (Article 5(2), Rule 7, 37 CFR 1.1021(b)) may include: indications concerning the identity of the creator; a brief description of the reproduction or of the characteristic features of the industrial design; and/or a claim; and pursuant to Rule 8(1), a statement, document, oath or declaration.
guidance: These are mandatory only when a designated Contracting Party requires them; applicants should include them when designating such Contracting Parties to avoid defects.

name: Optional contents of an international design application
description: Optional contents (Rule 7(5), 37 CFR 1.1021(c)) may include: (1) two or more industrial designs subject to prescribed conditions; (2) a request for deferment of publication or immediate publication; (3) any additional mandatory elements even if not required by any designated Contracting Party; (4) prescribed information concerning applicant’s representative; (5) a claim of priority of earlier applications (may be accompanied by a DAS access code); (6) a declaration for Article 11 Paris Convention exhibition; (7) any declaration/statement as specified in Administrative Instructions; (8) a statement identifying information known by applicant to be material to eligibility; and (9) a proposed translation of text matter for recording/publication.
guidance: Inclusion of optional contents can be strategic (e.g., priority claims, translations) but must comply with prescribed formats and possible additional fees (e.g., description exceeding 100 words).

name: DM/1 form content fields (what DM/1 includes)
description: Form DM/1 includes specific spaces to set forth: (1) information concerning the applicant; (2) applicant’s entitlement to file; (3) correspondence address for the IB where multiple applicants and no appointed representative; (4) appointment of a representative; (5) industrial designs and reproductions included; (6) designated Contracting Parties; (7) applicable product and Locarno classification; (8) number of reproductions; (9) a description; (10) a description of the reproductions; (11) identity of the creator; (12) a claim; (13) priority claim; (14) information regarding any international exhibition where designs were shown; (15) exception to lack of novelty; (16) relation with a principal design; (17) request for immediate or deferred publication; (18) reduction of individual designation fee; (19) signature of applicant or representative; and a Payment of Fees section.
guidance: Filling the DM/1 fields as intended reduces the risk of defects and missing mandatory items. Annexes I–V are available for particular Contracting Party-specific submissions.

name: Quality and disclosure sufficiency of reproductions (Rule 9(2) and Rule 9(4))
description: Reproductions shall be of a quality permitting all the details of the industrial design to be clearly distinguished and permitting publication. A Contracting Party may refuse the effects of the international registration if the reproductions in the international registration are not sufficient to disclose fully the industrial design.
guidance: To minimize refusal risk, follow IB guidance 'Guidance on Preparing and Providing Reproductions' (available on WIPO website) and Administrative Instructions. Matter shown but not claimed may be indicated as provided in Admin. Instr.

name: Indicating matter not forming part of the design (Administrative Instructions Section 403)
description: Matter shown in a reproduction but for which protection is not sought may be indicated either in the description referred to in Rule 7(5)(a) and/or by means of dotted or broken lines or coloring. Matter not forming part of the industrial design or product may be shown if indicated in accordance with paragraph (a).
guidance: Use dotted/broken lines or coloring or the description to disclaim elements not claimed, per Admin. Instr. 403, to clarify scope of protection.

name: Filing date antedating by earlier foreign or provisional application
description: The filing date can be antedated by an earlier foreign priority application or provisional application if 35 U.S.C. 119 is met and the foreign application or provisional application “supports” (conforms to 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, requirements) all the claims of the U.S. application.
guidance: See In re Gosteli. A prior application which was not copending with the application at issue cannot be used to antedate a reference (In re Costello). A terminal disclaimer does not overcome a pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection (e.g., In re Bartfeld). See MPEP § 706.02(b) for methods to overcome pre-AIA 102(e) rejections and MPEP § 715 for affidavit/declaration contents.

name: Combination claims in a reference do not prove inventorship of individual elements
description: Claiming of individual elements or subcombinations in a combination claim of the reference does not itself establish that the inventor or at least one joint inventor invented those elements if the elements/subcombinations are not separately claimed apart from the combination.
guidance: The existence of combination claims is not evidence that the inventor invented individual elements or subcombinations unless those elements are separately claimed (In re DeBaun; In re Facius). Examiner should assess whether the reference separately claims the subelements.

name: Inventor must contribute to the conception of the invention
description: The threshold question in determining inventorship is who conceived the invention; unless a person contributes to conception, he is not an inventor.
guidance: Reduction to practice is generally irrelevant for inventorship except in simultaneous conception/reduction contexts. For chemical compounds, conception of specific claimed compounds is required; general knowledge of anticipated properties is insufficient (In re Hardee; Board of Education v. American Bioscience). One who merely suggests a desired result, not the means, is not a coinventor (Ex parte Smernoff). See MPEP §§ 2138.04–2138.05 for evidence needed to establish conception or reduction to practice.

name: Requirements for joint inventorship
description: Joint inventors may apply for a patent jointly even if they did not physically work together, did not contribute the same amount, or did not contribute to every claim; each joint inventor must contribute to the conception of at least one claim.
guidance: There must be some 'quantum of collaboration or connection' (e.g., collaboration, common direction, one inventor seeing and building on another's report). A contributor to one claim suffices. Contributors of a disclosed means for a means-plus-function claim element are joint inventors for that claim unless contribution was merely a reduction to practice of a broader sole inventor concept (35 U.S.C. 116; Ethicon v. U.S. Surgical).

name: Required identifying data on return postcard
description: The identifying data on the postcard should include: (A) applicant’s name(s); (B) title of invention; (C) number of pages of specification, claims (for nonprovisional applications), and sheets of drawing; (D) whether oath or declaration is included; (E) a list of any additional forms included with the application (e.g., application transmittal form, application data sheet, fee transmittal form, and/or provisional application cover sheet); and (F) amount and manner of paying the fee.
guidance: A return postcard should be attached to each patent application for which a receipt is desired. It is important that the return postcard itemize all of the components of the application; otherwise it will not serve as evidence that any component which was not itemized was received by the USPTO.

name: Return postcard must itemize each component to serve as evidence
description: The postcard receipt will not serve as prima facie evidence of receipt of any item which is not adequately itemized on the postcard.
guidance: Merely listing 'a complete application' or 'patent application' is not sufficient. Each separate component (specification including written description, claims and abstract; number of claims; sheets of drawings; pages of oath/declaration; pages of cover sheet for provisional) should be specifically and properly itemized on the postcard. Incorporation by reference to a transmittal letter will not serve as prima facie evidence of receipt of those items.

name: Nonprovisional application filing-date entitlement (37 CFR 1.53(b))
description: The filing date of a nonprovisional application is the date on which a specification as prescribed by 35 U.S.C. 112 containing a description pursuant to § 1.71 and at least one claim pursuant to § 1.75, and any drawing required by § 1.81(a) are filed in the Office. No new matter may be introduced into an application after its filing date.
guidance: A continuing application (continuation, divisional, continuation-in-part) may be filed under specified statutory conditions. If the purported specification is so informal and incoherent that it clearly does not constitute a specification under 35 U.S.C.112 and 37 CFR1.71, the application will not be accorded a filing date until corrections are made.

name: Conversion of nonprovisional to provisional, and provisional to nonprovisional
description: An application filed under paragraph (b) may be converted to a provisional application and accorded the original filing date if accompanied by the processing fee and filed prior to certain events. A provisional may be converted to a nonprovisional and accorded the provisional filing date if conversion is accompanied by required fees and an amendment including at least one claim (unless provisional already contains a claim).
guidance: Conversion does not entitle applicant to refund of fees or application of previously paid fees to the new filing; conversion to nonprovisional may result in patent term being measured from at least the provisional filing date (adverse to applicant). Applicants should consider filing a nonprovisional claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C.119(e) instead of converting.

name: Continued Prosecution Application (CPA) rules (37 CFR 1.53(d))
description: A continued prosecution application (CPA) filed under 37 CFR1.53(d) (design applications only) will be assigned the application number of the prior application for identification purposes. A CPA must identify the prior application, disclose and claim only subject matter disclosed in the prior application, name as inventors the same inventors named in the prior application (subject to limited exceptions), and be filed before specified events (e.g., payment of issue fee, abandonment, termination of proceedings).
guidance: Filing fee, search fee, and examination fee for a CPA are set by §1.16. A CPA may utilize the file jacket and contents of the prior application; no amendment in a CPA may introduce new matter. Filing a CPA constitutes a waiver of confidentiality under 35 U.S.C.122 to the extent members of the public entitled to access to one application may be given similar access to related applications.

name: Incomplete nonprovisional application grounds
description: If nonprovisional application papers filed under 37 CFR1.53(b) do not include at least a specification containing a description and at least one claim and a drawing if necessary under 35 U.S.C.113, or if the papers are too informal to be given a filing date, the case is held as an incomplete application and no filing date is granted until incompleteness is corrected.
guidance: A Notice of Incomplete Application is mailed when nonprovisional application papers are deemed incomplete. Components necessary to obtain a filing date are: specification as prescribed by 35 U.S.C.112 and 37 CFR1.71; a claim as prescribed by 35 U.S.C.112 and 37 CFR1.75; and a drawing if required by 35 U.S.C.113 and 37 CFR1.81(a). Even if components purport to be present, they must satisfy statutory and regulatory requirements; obviously informal/incoherent documents will be unacceptable.

name: Step 2 — Does the remainder of the claim add 'significantly more'?
description: If the claim's inventive concept is a natural law, determine whether the rest of the claim adds 'significantly more' than the natural law itself.
guidance: Actions that are purely conventional, routine, or well-understood do not add 'significantly more' (per Mayo). The analysis purports to view the claim as a whole, but focuses on whether additional steps meaningfully transform or apply the natural law.

name: Conventional or obvious steps cannot rescue a natural law claim
description: The Court found that purely conventional or obvious methods (e.g., well-known methods of determining metabolite levels) do not impart patent eligibility to a claim that centers on a natural law.
guidance: Novelty and nonobviousness concepts from §102/§103 were, for the first time, invoked in the §101 analysis; practitioners should not rely on routine assay steps to confer eligibility.

name: Avoid making the 'law of nature' the central part of the claim
description: Do not draft claims where the natural law (e.g., a correlation between a biomarker and outcome) is the central claimed invention.
guidance: If the claim centers on the natural relationship, it is vulnerable under Mayo. Structure claims to emphasize applied techniques, novel reagents, specific interventions, or inventive steps beyond mere recognition of the relationship.

name: Avoid using solely general 'determining' steps
description: Generic 'determining' or measurement steps presented without technical detail are likely to be considered purely conventional and will not make a claim patent eligible.
guidance: Claims should avoid vague 'determine' language and instead recite specific, novel methods, apparatus, or data-processing steps that materially transform the sample or information in a nonconventional way.

name: Emphasize anything 'out of the ordinary' in the method
description: Highlight and claim features that are not routine or conventional — anything that is out of the ordinary in the assay or method.
guidance: Novel sample-processing steps, specific reagents, nonconventional protocols, or inventive integration steps may help demonstrate that the claim adds 'significantly more' than a natural law.

name: Combine diagnostics with computing or other inventive technology
description: Pairing traditional life-science diagnostics with computing functions (e.g., algorithms that determine correlations based on detected levels) or other technical elements may help avoid Mayo rejections.
guidance: Claims to combined systems/methods that include technical, nonconventional computing steps or inventive data processing can provide the 'significantly more' needed for eligibility; be careful to claim specific technical implementations rather than abstract algorithms.

name: Require greater specificity in assay claims post-Mayo
description: Post-Mayo, diagnostic method claims will require more specificity as to how the assay is performed and what technically differentiates it from routine practice.
guidance: General descriptions of assays are insufficient. Provide concrete parameters, steps, reagents, instruments, thresholds with technical justification, and any novel sample handling or measurement techniques.

name: Rejection, 35 U.S.C. 102(e), No Common Assignee or Inventor
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as being [2] by [3].
guidance: This form paragraph is used to reject over a patent or patent application publication with an earlier filing date that discloses but does not claim the same invention. The patent or publication must have neither a common assignee nor a common inventor. In bracket 2, insert either '--clearly anticipated--' or '--anticipated--' with an explanation at the end of the paragraph. In bracket 3, insert the prior art relied upon. Patent application publications may only be used if this form paragraph was preceded by form paragraph 7.12.01. Patent application publications may only be used if this form paragraph was preceded by form paragraph 7.12.01.

name: Rejection, 35 U.S.C. 102(f) Applicant Not the Inventor
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(f) because the applicant did not invent the claimed subject matter. [2]
guidance: This paragraph must be preceded either by paragraphs 7.07 and 7.13 or by paragraph 7.103. In bracket 2, insert an explanation of the supporting evidence establishing that applicant was not the inventor. See MPEP § 2137.

name: Prima facie case of obviousness: three basic criteria
description: To establish a prima facie case of obviousness, three basic criteria must be met: (1) there must be some suggestion or motivation, either in the references themselves or in the knowledge generally available to one of ordinary skill in the art, to modify the reference or to combine reference teachings; (2) there must be a reasonable expectation of success; and (3) the prior art reference(s) must teach or suggest all the claim limitations.
guidance: The teaching or suggestion to make the claimed combination and the reasonable expectation of success must both be found in the prior art and not based on applicant’s disclosure. See In re Vaeck and MPEP § 2143–§ 2143.03 for decisions pertinent to these criteria.

name: Examiner burden: provide suggestion/motivation or convincing line of reasoning
description: The initial burden is on the examiner to provide some suggestion of the desirability of doing what the inventor has done — either the references must expressly or impliedly suggest the claimed invention or the examiner must present a convincing line of reasoning why the artisan would have found the claimed invention obvious in light of the references.
guidance: A convincing line of reasoning is required where the suggestion is not explicit in the prior art. See Ex parte Clapp and MPEP § 2144–§ 2144.09 for examples of reasoning supporting obviousness rejections.

name: Ways to overcome a provisional 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/103 rejection (A–E)
description: A provisional rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/103 can be overcome by: (A) arguing patentability over the earlier filed application; (B) combining the subject matter of the copending applications into a single application claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 and abandoning the copending applications; (C) filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 showing unclaimed invention disclosed in copending application was derived from the inventor of the other application; (D) filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 showing a date of invention prior to the effective U.S. filing date of the copending application; or (E) for an application filed on or after November 29, 1999, showing that the prior art and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.
guidance: Note: combining applications to claim 35 U.S.C. 120 benefit requires that the earlier application contain a disclosure complying with 35 U.S.C. 112 first paragraph for each claim; a terminal disclaimer under 37 CFR 1.321(c) may be used where appropriate if the earlier application has matured into a patent. See MPEP for details and judicial decisions (Studiengesellschaft Kohle, etc.).

name: Definition of 'commonly owned' for 35 U.S.C. 103(c)
description: The term 'commonly owned' means wholly (100%) owned by the same person(s) or organization(s) at the time the claimed invention was made.
guidance: If either the subject matter or the claimed invention is owned less than 100% by the same entities, common ownership does not exist. For joint ventures, both the application and the reference must have been owned by or subject to assignment to the joint venture at the time the invention was made. A mere license where basic ownership rights are retained does not defeat ownership. Ownership must be actual/enforceable at the relevant time; moral or unenforceable obligations do not suffice.

name: Requirements for claiming 35 U.S.C. 120 benefit (inventorship and disclosure)
description: An application claiming the benefit of a prior filed copending national or international application under 35 U.S.C. 120 must name as an inventor at least one inventor named in the prior filed application. The prior filed application must also disclose the named inventor's invention claimed in at least one claim of the later filed application in the manner provided by the first paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112.
guidance: So long as the applications have at least one inventor in common and the other requirements are met, the Office will permit a claim for 35 U.S.C. 120 benefit without additional submissions from applicants regarding inventorship differences. In addition to normal examination, the examiner must examine the earlier filed application to determine if the earlier and later applications have at least one inventor in common and that the other 35 U.S.C. 120 requirements are met. The claim for 120 benefit will be permitted without examination of the earlier application for disclosure and support of at least one claim of the later-filed application under 35 U.S.C. 112 unless it becomes necessary to do so (for example, because of an intervening reference).

name: Double patenting rejections and terminal disclaimers
description: Where the claims of copending applications conflict, a provisional double patenting rejection should be given. Non-statutory and statutory double patenting rejections, based on subject matter disqualified as prior art under amended 35 U.S.C. 103(c), should still be made as appropriate.
guidance: Double patenting rejections can be overcome by terminal disclaimers (see 37 CFR 1.321(c)). The practice of rejecting claims in commonly owned applications of different inventive entities on the grounds of double patenting has been reinstituted in appropriate circumstances to prevent improper extension of patent protection while permitting legitimate benefits to inventors/assignees. See In re Bowers and MPEP § 804 for details.

name: Substitute Specification Not Entered (nonconforming to 1.125(b)/(c))
description: A substitute specification filed has not been entered because it does not conform to 37 CFR 1.125(b) and (c).
guidance: Insert a statement of why improper (e.g., missing statement of lack of new matter, missing marked-up copy, clean copy not supplied, filed in reissue or reexamination, filed after payment of issue fee, or contains claims). Substitute specifications filed after final action or appeal are governed by 37 CFR 1.116; those filed after mailing of a notice of allowance are governed by 37 CFR 1.312.

name: Application Papers Must Be Legible (formatting and font requirements)
description: The specification (including abstract and claims) and any amendments must have text written plainly and legibly by typewriter or machine printer in a nonscript type font (e.g., Arial, Times Roman, Courier).
guidance: Preferably font size 12; capital letters at least 0.3175 cm (0.125 in) high, but may be no smaller than 0.21 cm (0.08 in) (e.g., font size 6) in portrait orientation; only a single column of text. Presentation must permit direct reproduction of legible copies by photographic, electrostatic, photo-offset, microfilming, or electronic capture (OCR). See 37 CFR 1.52(a) and (b). If illegible, require a legible substitute spec in compliance with 1.52(a),(b) and 1.125.

name: Objective evidence must be considered when timely present
description: Affidavits or declarations, when timely presented, containing evidence of criticality or unexpected results, commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, skepticism of experts, etc., must be considered by the examiner in determining the issue of obviousness of claims for patentability under 35 U.S.C. 103.
guidance: Court holdings (e.g., Stratoflex) require consideration of secondary considerations en route to determination of obviousness; such evidence may give context to circumstances surrounding the origin of the subject matter sought to be patented and may be relevant as indicia of obviousness or unobviousness.

name: Must specifically explain why evidence is insufficient
description: When concluding that an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 is insufficient, the examiner must specifically explain why the evidence is insufficient; general statements such as 'the declaration lacks technical validity' or 'the evidence is not commensurate with the scope of the claims' without supporting explanation are insufficient.
guidance: Use form paragraph as a conclusion to the explanation of insufficiency and precede it by appropriate form paragraph(s) (e.g., form paragraph 7.66). Provide detailed reasons (e.g., data not convincing, lack of nexus, commercial success not related to technology).

name: Nexus requirement for secondary evidence
description: To be of probative value, any secondary evidence must be related to the claimed invention (nexus required).
guidance: The term 'nexus' designates a factually and legally sufficient connection between the objective evidence of nonobviousness and the claimed invention so that the evidence is probative. The weight attached depends on relevance and amount/nature of the evidence. Examiner must determine whether a nexus exists between the merits of the claimed invention and the secondary considerations.

name: Affidavit of applicant vs. disinterested person
description: An affidavit of an applicant as to the advantages of his or her claimed invention, while less persuasive than that of a disinterested person, cannot be disregarded for this reason alone.
guidance: Applicant affidavits should be considered, but examiners should weigh potential bias and factual support; see Ex parte Keyes and In re McKenna for precedent.

name: If examiner remains unconvinced, state reasons in next action
description: If, after evaluating the evidence, the examiner is still not convinced that the claimed invention is patentable, the next Office action should include a statement to that effect and identify the reason(s).
guidance: Identify specific insufficiencies (e.g., commercial success not convincing; commercial success not related to the technology) and cite applicable case law (e.g., Demaco). See MPEP §2145 for guidance on sufficiency of rebuttal evidence.

name: Comparison with the closest prior art is required
description: An affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 must compare the claimed subject matter with the closest prior art to be effective to rebut a prima facie case of obviousness.
guidance: Compare the claimed invention with the disclosure of each cited reference to determine the closest single prior art reference (In re Merchant). Explain deviations from reference disclosure; when testing less than all cited compounds, tests must permit a conclusion respecting relative effectiveness (In re Johnson, In re Payne). When two equally close references exist, showing unexpected results over one will not rebut unless teachings are sufficiently similar.

name: Commercial success must have nexus to claimed invention; consider totality of record
description: Nexus between the claimed invention and evidence of commercial success is required. The totality of the record must be considered when determining whether a claimed invention would have been obvious.
guidance: Evidence/arguments directed to advantages not disclosed in the specification cannot be disregarded; commercial success unconnected to the claimed technology is not probative. Consider all give-and-take of ex parte prosecution (In re Chu, In re Zenitz, Ex parte Sasajima).

name: Review and use of documents cited in the application
description: When the application cites documents in the description, the examiner shall review them to determine whether they provide a starting point for the claimed invention, show the current status of the technology, explain other solutions to the task, or aid understanding of the claimed invention.
guidance: If cited documents are not directly related and merely stated in the description, the examiner shall disregard them. If necessary documents for assessing patentability cannot be acquired by common methods, the examiner shall request submission from the applicant and defer examination until submission.

name: Consideration of foreign-office/search-organization search outcomes
description: If foreign patent offices or search organizations already conducted search regarding the claimed invention, the examiner shall review those search outcomes to determine whether they can be used as relevant prior art.
guidance: Examiners should assess the relevance and appropriateness of foreign search reports when available.

name: Time coverage of search (reference dates)
description: Search should generally cover documents published before the filing date (or priority date for priority-claiming applications). Exceptional extension to documents published after the filing date is allowed in specific circumstances (e.g., Article 29(3)/(4) or Article 36) and when verifying priority validity is impossible at search stage.
guidance: Documents published after filing date may be used as supporting material for confirming incorrectness/incompleteness of the invention rationale or facts. For priority-claiming applications, the basic reference date for the search on each claim is the filing date of the application, but if documents exist between earliest priority date and filing date, examiner should determine reference date per claim and decide which documents to cite; examiner may set priority date per claim when straightforward.

name: General principle of equivalents in search
description: The search will consider prior art incorporating technical features which are equivalents to the technical features of the claimed invention, in light of the description. Equivalent elements are not limited to features explicitly described in the description.
guidance: Example: a claim specifying parts joined by welding is interpreted to include other combining elements such as gluing or riveting unless the invention explicitly limits the feature to welding.

name: Search obligations for dependent claims and claim categories
description: When searching for independent claim(s), the examiner conducts prior-art search for all dependent claims that fall within the identical classification as the independent claim. Dependent claims are interpreted as restricted by all features of the claims on which they depend. When application contains claims of different categories, all must be included in the search.
guidance: If the independent claim's patentability is not questioned, no need to further search or cite documents for dependent claims. If a product claim is clearly novel/non-obvious, no special effort needed to search process claims inevitably resulting in that product or use claims; conversely, if only one category is present, examiner may decide to include other categories in search (examples given for pharmacological composition and method claims).

name: Classification of prior-art relevance (X/Y/A/O/P/E/T/L)
description: Related prior art in search reports can be classified depending on relevance: X = alone destroys novelty/ inventive step; Y = requires combination with others to deny inventive step; A = related but not X or Y; O = oral disclosure/use/exhibition; P = published between international filing date and priority date; E = filed before international filing date but published after; T = documents disclosing principle/theory or published later than priority/filing date; L = may throw doubt on a priority claim or negate claimed invention or determine other contents.
guidance: Use standard categorization (X, Y, A, O, P, E, T, L) when annotating citation sheets and search reports.

name: Understanding the invention for examination purposes
description: Examiner shall clearly understand the subject matter of the claimed invention in light of the specification by considering the problems to be solved, the means for solving the problems, how it differs from background art, and the effects of the invention.
guidance: Examination proceeds based on the specification as originally filed, but should take into account amendments made by the applicant prior to the notice of rejection grounds. See Part V for methods confirming amended specification.

name: Claim construction principle
description: Examiner should construe the claimed invention as recited in a claim. Terms in a claim should be interpreted within the general scope and meaning of the technical field, unless they have a specific meaning explicitly defined in the description.
guidance: Avoid over-interpretation of claims without logical grounds; interpret dependent claims as restricted by antecedent claims.

name: Review of prior-art documents for publication date and technical disclosure
description: Examiner shall determine whether prior-art retrieved can provide grounds for rejection regarding novelty, inventive step, enlarged concept of novelty or first-to-file application; publication date is critical for determining whether it precedes filing/priority date.
guidance: For the enlarged concept of novelty, examiner shall check applicants and inventors of the prior application. Examiner must understand technical issues disclosed in the prior art and be careful not to treat as disclosed matters that are not in those documents or to over-interpret claims without logical support.

name: Reference-date determination for priority-claiming applications (claim-by-claim)
description: If an invention claimed is identical (including substantially identical) to the invention of the application filed in the first country, the reference date shall be the filing date of that first-country application. For inventions not described in the first-country application, the filing date of the claiming application is the reference date. Reference date determination is in principle claim-by-claim.
guidance: For multiple priority claims, earliest filing date among the relevant first-country applications governs for commonly described inventions. Combining technical matters across multiple first-country applications is treated as 'not described' in the first-country application for reference-date purposes. If the first-country application itself claims priority based on an earlier application, it may not be regarded as the 'earliest application' per Paris Convention Article 4C(2), and the examiner should specify reason for non-retroactive application when applicable.

name: Patents interfering definition and non-coextensive claim rule
description: Patents which contain one or more claims in common are interfering patents. A generic claim and an included specific claim that are not co-extensive do not interfere with each other.
guidance: All but one of several interfering patents are necessarily void as to the interfering claim(s), though they may remain valid as to other claims.

name: Action in equity is the prescribed proceeding for adjudicating interfering claims
description: An action in equity is the proper proceeding to adjudicate interfering claims of issued patents in point of relative priority.
guidance: Such an action may be joined with an infringement action where complainant's patent issued first; but if defendant's patent issued first, infringement action cannot be joined with interference. Cross-bills and counterclaims have special limitations under the statute and equity practice.

name: 35 U.S.C. § 103 — non-obvious subject matter
description: A patent may not be obtained if the differences between the subject matter sought to be patented and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which said subject matter pertains.
guidance: Apply the statutory standard by comparing claimed subject matter as a whole to prior art from the perspective of PHOSITA. Consider entire specification when determining obviousness.

name: Claims interpretation — broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with specification
description: During prosecution claims are to be given their reasonable broadest interpretation consistent with PHOSITA’s interpretation of the specification.
guidance: Interpret claim language as PHOSITA would reasonably read it in light of the specification when assessing obviousness and other patentability issues.

name: Graham factors — ascertain differences between prior art and claims
description: Ascertain differences between the prior art and the claims as part of the Graham analysis.
guidance: Explicitly list claim limitations not found in prior art and evaluate whether those differences would have been obvious to PHOSITA.

name: Good-cause / interest-of-justice standard for excusing late action
description: Late actions may be excused only on a showing of good cause or if Board consideration on the merits is in the interests of justice (37 C.F.R. § 42.5(c)(3)).
guidance: Movants must show diligence or other strong justification; mere later discovery of publicly available materials or speculative claims of changed 'evidentiary landscape' (absent clear new evidence) will generally not suffice. The Board will examine when movant knew or should have known the facts and how promptly it acted thereafter.

name: Relevance of public availability of supporting evidence
description: If the evidence a movant relies upon was publicly available prior to filing of the Patent Owner Response (or the petition), that supports a finding that the movant could have timely raised the issue and thus undermines claims of newly discovered grounds.
guidance: Cite dates of public reports, court opinions, and other exhibits; if exhibits predate the responsive filings, the Board will likely find a lack of diligence and waiver.

name: Trial procedure in patent actions (jury, assessor, amendment)
description: Patent suits are tried without a jury unless by leave; an assessor may be called in; the specification may be amended during action; particulars of claim/defence and of breaches/objections must be delivered and may be amended by leave.
guidance: Court may permit amendments and the use of assessors; leave required for jury trial and for adducing evidence of matters not particularized.

name: Particulars required in statements of claim and defence
description: Statements of claim must be accompanied by particulars of breaches (object: to state parts of specification infringed and parts of a machine that infringe). Statements of defence must deliver particulars of objections (prior user, names of prior users, general user, prior publication including books/pages/dates/specification numbers, fraud or misrepresentation, that invention is not properly set out, that specification fails to distinguish old from new, that it does not set out the best method, that patent comprises more than one invention not allowed).
guidance: No evidence is allowed at trial of infringements for which particulars were not delivered except by leave; generality of particulars cannot be objected to at trial; particulars may be amended (even after trial begun) by leave.

name: Amendments and affidavits after appeal standard
description: Section 41.33 (replacing former Rules 116 and 195): (a) Amendments filed after filing an appeal and prior to the brief may be admitted as provided in §1.116; (b) Amendments filed on/after filing a brief may be admitted only to cancel claims (if cancellation doesn't affect scope of other pending claims) or to rewrite dependent claims into independent form; (c) All other amendments after filing an appeal will not be admitted except as permitted by specified sections; (d) Affidavits or other evidence filed after filing appeal and prior to brief may be admitted if the examiner determines they overcome all rejections under appeal and there is a showing of good and sufficient reasons why necessary and not earlier presented.
guidance: Amendments after appeal are tightly limited; treat post-appeal amendments and affidavits as exceptional and follow §1.116 standards for admission.

name: Board decision roles: affirm/reverse/remand and conforming amendment
description: Section 41.50(a)(1),(c): The Board may affirm or reverse the examiner's decision in whole or in part on grounds/claims specified by the examiner, or remand to examiner. The Board’s opinion may explicitly state how a claim on appeal could be amended to overcome a specific rejection; appellant then has the right to amend in conformity with such statement, but the examiner may still reject the amended claim if the rejection constitutes a new ground of rejection.
guidance: Board opinions can provide guidance for conforming amendments to overcome specific rejections; such amendments are permitted but subject to new-ground scrutiny by the examiner.

name: Broadest reasonable construction and pendency goal for interferences
description: Section 41.200(b)-(c): A claim shall be given its broadest reasonable construction in light of the specification of the application or patent in which it appears; patent interferences shall be administered such that pendency before the Board is normally no more than two years.
guidance: Use broadest reasonable claim construction for interference proceedings; Board aims to resolve interferences within ~2 years of pendency when possible.

name: Definitions specific to interferences (counts, involved claim, threshold issue, senior/junior party)
description: Section 41.201: 'Count' defines the interfering subject matter and scope of admissible proofs; 'involved claim' is a claim designated as corresponding to the count; 'senior party' is entitled to presumption of prior invention based on accorded benefit; 'threshold issue' examples include no interference-in-fact, repose, or lack of written description.
guidance: Understand interference-specific terms as they control admissibility of proofs, presumptions, and early threshold motions.

name: Declaration content for interference
description: Section 41.203(b): Notice declaring an interference must identify the interfering subject matter, the involved applications/patents/claims, the accorded benefit for each count, and the claims corresponding to each count.
guidance: Declaration sets the scope of the proceeding and the initial presumptions of benefit and correspondence; parties should review declaration carefully for accuracy.

name: Content and sufficiency of motions in interferences
description: Section 41.208: Substantive motions in an interference must (a) raise a threshold issue, (b) seek to change the scope of interfering subject matter or claim correspondence, (c) seek to change benefit accorded, or (d) seek judgment on derivation or priority. A motion must provide a showing, supported with appropriate evidence, such that, if unrebutted, it would justify the relief sought; the burden of proof is on the movant. To be sufficient when adding/amending a claim or count, the movant must show patentability (claim or count) over prior art.
guidance: Craft motions in interference with a clear legal basis, evidentiary support, and proof of patentability when adding/amending claims or counts; anticipate and meet the movant’s burden.

name: Presumptions regarding priority and claim correspondence
description: Section 41.207: (a) Parties are presumed to have invented in order of dates of their accorded benefit for each count; (a)(2) Priority proof by preponderance except clear and convincing evidence required if earliest constructive reduction to practice is after issue/publication date of an involved patent/application; (b) All claims of a party corresponding to the count are presumed to stand or fall together and challenge requires timely substantive motion; (c) When a motion for judgment of unpatentability against an opponent’s claim on prior art is granted, movant’s claims corresponding to same count will be presumed unpatentable unless movant rebuts.
guidance: Know and plan for presumptions: accorded benefit drives presumptive order of invention; higher evidentiary standard applies if priority date is after certain public dates; challenge claim correspondence timely; anticipate cross-applicability of prior-art judgments.

name: Institution standard under 35 U.S.C. § 314
description: The Board may not authorize an inter partes review to be instituted unless the information presented in the petition and any response shows that there is a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail with respect to at least one of the claims challenged in the petition.
guidance: The Board evaluates the Petition, Preliminary Response, Reply, Sur-Reply, and the evidence of record to determine whether the evidence presented demonstrates a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail in establishing unpatentability of at least one challenged claim. (Text cites 35 U.S.C. § 314 and describes consideration of the record.)

name: Petition particularity requirement (35 U.S.C. § 312(a)(3))
description: A petition must identify 'with particularity . . . the evidence that supports the grounds for the challenge to each claim.'
guidance: Petitioner has the burden from the onset to show with particularity why the patent it challenges is unpatentable. (Cites Harmonic Inc. v. Avid Tech., Inc., and statutory text.)

name: Claim construction standard (Phillips / 37 C.F.R. § 100(b))
description: Claim terms are generally given their ordinary and customary meaning as understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention; look principally to intrinsic evidence (claim language, written description, prosecution history).
guidance: Extrinsic evidence is less significant than the intrinsic record in determining the legally operative meaning of claim language (citing Phillips, DePuy Spine, C.R. Bard). The Board applies the same claim construction standard that would be used in a civil action under 35 U.S.C. § 282(b).

name: Constrict claim construction to what is necessary (Nidec)
description: The Board provides claim construction only to the extent necessary to resolve the controversy presented.
guidance: If resolution of an argument does not require construction of a term, the Board may decline to reach a construction at the institution stage (citing Nidec Motor Corp. v. Zhongshan Broad Ocean Motor Co.). The decision gives examples where the Board did not construe the preamble or dose-term claim language at institution.

name: Definition of a person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA) — applied example
description: A POSITA in this case would have knowledge regarding diagnosis and treatment of angiogenic eye disorders, administration of therapies to treat those disorders, and the ability to understand published results; typically an M.D. or Ph.D. (or equivalent experience).
guidance: Board adopted a prior PTAB definition for consistency; the POSITA definition can influence how claim language and prior art disclosures are interpreted at institution.

name: Obviousness legal framework (Graham factors)
description: A claim is unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. § 103 if differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art are such that the whole would have been obvious to a POSITA at the time of the invention.
guidance: Resolve obviousness using underlying factual determinations: (1) scope and content of prior art; (2) differences between claimed subject matter and the prior art; (3) level of ordinary skill in the art; (4) objective evidence of nonobviousness. (Cites Graham v. John Deere.)

name: Patentable weight of claim limitations
description: A claim limitation (e.g., exclusion criteria) may be entitled to patentable weight and must be considered in the unpatentability analysis.
guidance: Parties may dispute whether a limitation is limiting; the Board may assume for institution that a limitation is entitled to patentable weight and then evaluate whether prior art discloses or makes obvious that limitation.

name: General Plastic discretionary-denial factors (when considering denial under 35 U.S.C. § 314(a))
description: When exercising discretion to deny institution, the Board may consider a set of factors identified in General Plastic.
guidance: The seven General Plastic factors (quoted/used by the Board) are: (1) whether the same petitioner previously filed a petition directed to the same claims of the same patent; (2) whether at the time of filing of the first petition the petitioner knew of the prior art asserted in the second petition or should have known of it; (3) whether at the time of filing of the second petition the petitioner already received the patent owner’s preliminary response to the first petition or received the Board’s decision on whether to institute review in the first petition; (4) the length of time that elapsed between the time the petitioner learned of the prior art asserted in the second petition and the filing of the second petition; (5) whether the petitioner provides adequate explanation for the time elapsed between the filings of multiple petitions directed to the same claims of the same patent; (6) the finite resources of the Board; and (7) the requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 316(a)(11) to issue a final determination not later than 1 year after the date on which the Director notices institution of review. The Board uses these factors to decide whether to deny institution to prevent serial/abusive petitions.

name: Adoption/incorporation of prior PTAB decisions for corresponding limitations
description: The Board may incorporate and adopt reasoning from prior related PTAB decisions when the claims or limitations are identical or substantially identical.
guidance: Example: the Board incorporated reasoning from a prior -00881 Decision to find that many claim limitations were taught by Dixon, then focused only on unresolved differences (the exclusion criteria). The Board may rely on prior findings for portions of analysis.

name: Anticipation vs. obviousness distinction in analysis
description: When prior art does not literally disclose a limitation, the Board considers whether that limitation is obvious in view of the cited references (as opposed to being anticipated).
guidance: The decision notes that many claim limitations were previously found anticipated by Dixon in a related proceeding, but with an additional exclusion-criteria limitation the Board analyzed whether that limitation was taught or obvious over CATT, MACTEL, and PIER.

name: Types of references that may be applied under 35 U.S.C. 102(e)
description: The potential reference must be a U.S. patent, a U.S. application publication (35 U.S.C. 122(b)) or a WIPO publication of an international application under PCT Article 21(2) in order to apply the reference under 35 U.S.C. 102(e).
guidance: If the reference did not result from or claim the benefit of an international application, its 102(e) date is the earliest effective U.S. filing date, taking into consideration any proper benefit claims under 119(e) or 120 if the prior application(s) properly supports the subject matter used to make the rejection in compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.

name: Three-condition test for treating an international filing date as a U.S. filing date under 102(e)
description: An international filing date is a U.S. filing date for 102(e) prior art purposes only if (a) the international application has an international filing date on or after November 29, 2000; (b) it designated the United States; and (c) it was published under PCT Article 21(2) in English.
guidance: If all three conditions are met, the international filing date is the 102(e) prior art date. If the international application properly claims benefit to an earlier-filed U.S. or international application (or provisional), and the earlier application properly supports the subject matter per 35 U.S.C. 112, the earlier filing date may be the effective prior art date.

name: Determining 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date for references that claim benefit/priority
description: The 102(e) date of a reference that claims benefit under 119(e) (provisional) or 120 (earlier U.S. nonprovisional) is the earliest effective U.S. filing date to which proper benefit is claimed, provided the earlier application properly supports the subject matter under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
guidance: Examiners must consider whether benefit/priority claims are properly perfected (e.g., certified priority documents filed, English translations if necessary) and whether the earlier application enables and describes the subject matter used to make the rejection (see 37 CFR 1.55 and 1.78 requirements and MPEP §§ 201.11, 201.13, 706.02).

name: How to overcome a 35 U.S.C. 102(b) rejection
description: A rejection based on 35 U.S.C. 102(b) can be overcome by: (A) persuasively arguing claims are patentably distinguishable; (B) amending claims to be patentably distinguishable; (C) perfecting benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 within the time period set in 37 CFR 1.78(a) (including amending the specification or filing an ADS) and establishing that the prior application satisfies 35 U.S.C. 112(first paragraph); or (D) perfecting benefit under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) by complying with 37 CFR 1.78(a).
guidance: Once a benefit claim is perfected, the rejection must be reconsidered to determine whether the prior art still qualifies as 102(b) or now qualifies under 102(a). See MPEP §§ 201.11 and 706.02 for details.

name: How to overcome a 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection
description: A rejection based on 35 U.S.C. 102(e) can be overcome by: (A) arguing patentable distinctions; (B) amending claims; (C) filing an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 showing the reference invention is not by 'another'; (D) filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 showing prior invention (with limitations); (E) submitting a claim to priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) in time or filing a grantable petition under 37 CFR 1.55(c); or (F) perfecting benefit under 119(e) or 120 within the time periods set in 37 CFR 1.78(a) or filing a grantable petition.
guidance: A 1.131 affidavit is not acceptable if the claims of the reference and the application are directed to the same invention or are obvious variants. If there is a common assignee or inventor between the application and patent, a double patenting rejection must be made. If there is no common assignee/inventor and 102(e) is the only possible rejection, the examiner must determine whether an interference should be declared. See MPEP § 715, § 716.10, § 804, and Chapter 2300.

name: Examiner procedure I — overall flow to determine 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date
description: I. Determine the appropriate 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date for each potential reference by following the guidelines and flow charts: (A) confirm reference type (U.S. patent, U.S. app publication, or WIPO publication under PCT Art 21(2)); (B) determine if reference resulted from or claimed benefit of an international application; (C) if so, apply the three-condition test for treating the IA filing date as a U.S. filing date; (D) treat foreign priority/further rules accordingly.
guidance: If a reference did not result from nor claim the benefit of an international application, its 102(e) date is its earliest effective U.S. filing date, considering proper benefit claims under 119(e) or 120 and compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph. See MPEP § 2136.02 for support considerations.

name: Examples illustrating common 102(e) factual situations
description: Nine examples (Examples 1–9) illustrate common factual situations (only the most common) for determining the 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date of references: Example 1: 111(a) application with no priority/benefit claims; Example 2: 111(a) with benefit claim to prior U.S.; Example 3: 111(a) with 119(a)-(d) priority to a foreign application; Examples 4–9 involve international applications and national stage issues.
guidance: Examples specify that for 111(a) applications with no benefit claims the 102(e) prior art date is the application's actual filing date; for benefit claims the earlier effective U.S. filing date is accorded assuming proper support; and various permutations with IAs depend on filing dates, designation, publication language, and whether the IA is pre- or post-November 29, 2000.

name: Determination of invention based on claim limitations
description: The determination of the invention for which patent protection is sought shall be made based on the limitations recited in each of the claims in accordance with the applicant’s will.
guidance: The description or drawings are considered only when the claims are indefinite or technical terms are ambiguous. The invention should not be determined based on disclosure in the description beyond the limitations of the claims. An abstract cannot be used to decide the protection scope.

name: Claims must be supported by the description (Article 42(4)(i))
description: The claims shall be supported by the description of the invention; an invention recited in claims but not disclosed in the description would be unfair to grant.
guidance: An examiner shall determine whether a person skilled in the art can figure out the subject matters corresponding to the claims from the description. Support is assessed by whether the claimed invention departs from the scope grasped by a skilled person based on the description, not by literal identicalness.

name: Unsupported: claim limitations neither disclosed nor implied
description: Where the subject matters or the limitations of the claims are neither disclosed nor implied in the description of the invention, the claims are not supported.
guidance: Examples: specific numerical limitations in claims absent in description; claims directed to an ultrasonic motor when description only discloses a DC motor (unless description implies other motors and a skilled person could practice with an ultrasonic motor).

name: Unsupported: differing terms causing ambiguous correspondence
description: Where the terms used in the claims are different from those used in the description so that correspondence between description and claims is ambiguous, the claims are not supported.
guidance: Ambiguity in terminology undermines the support requirement; examiner should assess whether a skilled person can bridge the terminology gap.

name: Unsupported: claims recite functions/means without disclosed configuration
description: Where the claims recite means or steps to perform particular functions, but specific configuration corresponding to such means or steps is not disclosed in the description, the claims are not supported.
guidance: Functional recitation without any enabling structural or procedural disclosure can render claims unsupported unless the description enables the skilled person to realize the function.

name: Unsupported: disclosure cannot be extended/generalized to claimed scope
description: Where disclosure of the description cannot be extended or generalized to the scope of the claimed invention based on the level of skill in the art at filing, the claims are not supported.
guidance: Examples: claims defined by technical effects (e.g., energy efficiency) but description only discloses specific means and cannot be generalized; claims reciting many chemical compounds defined by a property when only a few have demonstrated efficacy (collagenase-3 inhibitor example).

name: Unsupported: omission of indispensable features
description: Where claims do not recite the features explained as indispensable to solve the technical problem in the description, the claims are not supported.
guidance: Example: description requires a low-water-content 'cream' as stuffing to prevent moisture transition, but claims recite merely 'cream' (general milk fat substance), omitting the indispensable low-water-content feature.

name: Relation to lack of description provisions
description: Reference to interplay between Article 42(4)(i) (support) and Article 42(3)(i) (lack of description on claims).
guidance: See the section discussing the relation with lack of description on claims for cross-reference when assessing support vs lack of description issues.

name: Clear and concise statement requirement (Article 42(4)(ii))
description: Claims must set forth the claimed invention clearly and concisely so they serve the function of determining protection scope and permit assessment of patentability.
guidance: Whether claims are clear and concise is determined by a person skilled in the art based on the claims in light of the description, drawings, and the level of skill at filing. 'Concise' refers to claim language, not to the idea of the invention.

name: Unclear claim language but clerical error exception
description: If unclear claim language is a mere clerical error and does not lead a skilled person to decide the invention is unclear, and the invention can be easily understood from description/drawings/skill level, it shall not be deemed unclear.
guidance: Examples of clerical errors and handling are provided; examiner should not issue a rejection for clerical errors and may make an ex officio amendment if no other ground exists. If uncertain, notify applicant to allow amendment/argument.

name: Unclear: listing of claim elements without relationships
description: Where each claim element is merely listed but relationships between elements are not recited and therefore the invention is unclear.
guidance: Claims must express relationships among elements (e.g., order, connection, interaction) rather than only listing constituent parts.

name: Unclear: ambiguous category of claimed invention (product vs method)
description: Where the category to which the claimed invention belongs is unclear, the claim is unclear. Category is usually determined by terms at the end of the claim, but may be ambiguous where subject matter hampers identification.
guidance: For products, a variety of expressions can be used to explain structure/function; for methods, various expressions explain method/steps. Determine category from claim wording; if difficult, deem ambiguous.

name: Unclear: excessive claim length or repetition
description: Where claim language is too lengthy, such as repetition of the same matter, so that the subject matter for which protection is sought is not clear and concise.
guidance: Avoid unnecessary repetition and overly long claim phrasing which obscures what is being claimed.

name: Unclear: expressions that make configuration unclear
description: Where claims include expressions which make the configuration of the invention unclear, the claim may be indefinite.
guidance: However, if the unclear expressions' meaning is clearly supported by the description and the invention is deemed clearly defined, the claim is acceptable. Examples of such expressions and how to assess them are provided.

name: Problematic vague qualifiers and optional language
description: Use of arbitrarily additional matter or optional phrases (e.g., 'at one’s will', 'if necessary', 'in particular', 'for example', 'and/or') can render claims unclear or lead to multiple alternative inventions in a single claim.
guidance: Assess whether usage of 'and/or' or similar phrases results in multiple contrasting inventions in one claim and whether the number of claims is proper for the invention's characteristics.

name: Problematic comparative/degree expressions
description: Use of vague comparative or degree expressions (e.g., 'mainly', 'as main process', 'appropriate', 'proper amount of', 'many', 'high', 'most of', 'almost', 'approximately', 'about') can render the claim unclear.
guidance: Such terms should be used carefully and clarified by the specification where necessary to avoid indefiniteness.

name: Problematic negative limitations
description: Use of unclear negative limitations (e.g., 'except for', 'other than') can make the claim indefinite.
guidance: Ensure negative limitations are precise and supported by the disclosure to avoid ambiguity about what is excluded.

name: Problematic numerical limitations without bounds or contradictory ranges
description: Numerical limitations stated without maximum/minimum bounds (e.g., 'more than', 'less than', '0~10') or dual/conflicting numerical ranges in a single claim can render claims unclear.
guidance: Examples include '120-200℃ or more appropriately 150-180℃' — dual ranges in one claim create ambiguity. Provide precise numerical bounds or clarify intent in the description.

name: Unclear due to reuse of same term for different functions
description: Where multiple technical terms of the same expression serving different functions are used in the claims without specifying different functions or indicating corresponding reference numerals, the invention is unclear.
guidance: Differentiate identical expressions used for distinct roles or attach reference numerals to clarify meaning.

name: Unclear due to recitation of irrelevant non-technical matters
description: Where matters irrelevant to the technical configuration (commercial benefits, regions of sale, places of sale, etc.) are recited in claims, the invention is not clear and concise.
guidance: Claims should be limited to technical features relevant to the invention; exclude commercial/market statements from claim language.

name: Unclear when claim defined solely by reference to spec/drawings
description: Where the invention is defined by reference to the description or drawings without reciting the configuration, the claim is unclear and may be invalid unless such reference is inevitable.
guidance: Reference to description/drawings is allowable only if inevitable; otherwise the claim must recite the technical configuration explicitly.

name: Clerical error categories (exceptions to rejection)
description: Certain clerical errors are not deemed to violate clarity/conciseness and should not be a ground for rejection: (i) 'said OOO' lacking antecedent but invention clear when read excluding 'said'; (ii) non-identical but corresponding indicated/indicating terms; (iii) deleted dependent claims but invention still clear when excluding dependencies.
guidance: If such clerical errors are found, examiner should not issue decision to reject and may make ex officio amendment if no other ground exists; if uncertain, notify applicant to allow response. If clerical errors arise from amendments, they should not be a new ground for rejection under Article 51.

name: Handling uncertain clerical cases
description: Where it is unclear that a claim falls under the clerical-error exceptions, the examiner should notify the applicant of such facts and issue notice of ground for rejection rather than making an ex officio amendment or 'Matters to be noted', to give applicant opportunity to respond.
guidance: If after re-examination following applicant's response the claim is deemed to fall under clerical error exception, do not reject and consider ex officio amendment.

name: Markush-type claims acceptable when alternatives share property/function
description: A Markush type claim selecting alternatives from a group does not render the claim indefinite if all inventions configured by selecting an alternative possess a similar property or function.
guidance: Example: A+(one of a, b, or c) is acceptable if A+a, A+b, A+c have similar properties/functions. The same principle applies beyond chemistry (e.g., mechanical, electrical fields).

name: Chemical Markush grouping requirements
description: For chemical substances grouped in a Markush claim, the grouping does not render the claim indefinite if (①) all substances selected share a common property/vitality and (②) they share an important chemical structure or belong to a group deemed one in the art.
guidance: 'Important chemical structure' means a common structural part prominent in most structures; 'group deemed as one' means substances expected by ordinary skill to be identically practiced in the claimed invention (i.e., same result expected whichever is chosen).

name: Functional limitations — allowed only when configuration still clear
description: Claims including functional limitations (reciting function or effect) are not allowable if the configuration is not clear; they are allowable when (①) defining functionally is necessary because the technical idea cannot be clearly set forth only by configuration (e.g., some biotech or computer-related inventions) or (②) the meaning of the functional limitation is clearly specified by the disclosure.
