guidance: Examiner shall determine whether the subject matter is clearly understood by a skilled person in light of the description/drawings and the level of skill at filing; if not, issue rejection under Article 42(4)(ii).

name: Product claims defined by manufacturing method
description: A product claim can define the product by its manufacturing method if the product's configuration is clearly understood from the method limitation; otherwise the claim is indefinite.
guidance: If method-of-manufacture limitation does not make the product's structure/nature understandable even in light of the specification, drawings, and ordinary skill, examiner shall notify ground for rejection. If applicant must define product by process for specific reasons or proves process does not affect product structure/nature, examiner may consider rejection remedied.

name: Composition ratio (%) — technical contradictions render claim unclear
description: For claims reciting composition ratios as percentages, certain technical deficiencies/contradictions render the claimed configuration not exactly stated: (①) sum of maximum ratios <100%; (②) sum of minimum ratios >100%; (③) sum of maximum of one component and minimums of others >100%; (④) sum of minimum of one component and maximums of others <100%.
guidance: Open ('comprising') claims may be clear in some of these cases because unspecified other components can make totals 100%. Examples illustrate when percentage-based claims are indefinite vs acceptable.

name: Parts by weight and composition ratio clarity
description: Describing composition ratio as parts by weight does not require satisfying percentage-sum rules; parts by weight indicate amounts relative to a reference component and are deemed clear even without specifying the reference component.
guidance: Alloy claims are an exception: an alloy claim should set composition ranges that add up to 100% and cannot be specified only by limiting main component; total sum of composition ranges should not be over or under 100% regardless of 'comprising' or 'consisting of'.

name: Alloy claim special rule
description: For alloy claims, the composition ranges of each component should add up to 100%; even open claims ('comprising') are not accepted if the sum of ranges cannot reach 100%.
guidance: Additionally, when claiming alloys, list components and recite composition ranges exactly. See the guidance for invention relating to alloy for further requirements.

name: Claim drafting: independent vs dependent claim discrimination
description: A dependent claim should narrow or add further limitations to specify the independent claim. If a claim does not narrow/add limitations in content, or formally refers to another claim without narrowing, it is not a dependent claim.
guidance: Examples: a claim substituting element A with B in invention of claim 0 does not narrow/specify and thus is not a dependent claim. Article 5(1) of the Enforcement Decree prescribes that dependent claims must substantiate the independent claim by narrowing or adding limitations.

name: Preamble: limitation vs statement of purpose
description: The claim preamble must be read in the context of the entire claim; if the claim body intrinsically sets forth all limitations and the preamble merely states a purpose or intended use, the preamble is not a claim limitation. Conversely, if the preamble's statement of intended use formed the basis for distinguishing the prior art during prosecution (clear reliance), the preamble becomes a limitation.
guidance: Read the entire record (claim body, specification, prosecution history) to determine what the inventors intended. Examples: Pitney Bowes, Kropa, STX (preamble not limiting where body is structurally complete); Jansen and In re Cruciferous Sprout (preamble can be limiting when it specifies an intended recipient/feature); Metabolite and Catalina (prosecution reliance on preamble can convert it to a limitation). During examination determine whether the recited purpose/intent results in a structural or manipulative difference over the prior art; if prior art structures can perform the recited use, they meet the claim unless the prosecution history shows reliance on the preamble.

name: Transitional phrase 'comprising' (open-ended)
description: 'Comprising' (synonymous with including/containing/characterized by) is presumptively open-ended and allows additional, unrecited elements or steps.
guidance: Treat claims using 'comprising' as inclusive: named elements are essential but others may be present. Case examples: Mars, Invitrogen, Genentech, Gillette (claims with 'comprising' may encompass devices with additional elements such as more than three blades). Consider the whole claim context if contrary indications exist.

name: Transitional phrase 'consisting of' (closed)
description: 'Consisting of' excludes any element, step, or ingredient not specified in the claim; a claim depending from a 'consisting of' claim cannot add elements or steps.
guidance: Apply a strong presumption that the clause or claim using 'consisting of' is closed to unrecited elements. When 'consists of' appears in a clause of the claim body there is an especially strong presumption the term is closed to unrecited elements in that clause. Examples: In re Gray, Ex parte Davis. Note factual nuances (e.g., Norian – spatula unrelated to claimed chemicals did not avoid infringement despite a 'consisting of' recitation). Determine what is excluded at the clause level versus the claim-as-a-whole level.

name: Transitional phrase 'consisting essentially of' (middle ground)
description: 'Consisting essentially of' limits the claim to the specified materials or steps and those that do not materially affect the basic and novel characteristic(s) of the claimed invention; occupies a middle ground between 'consisting of' and 'comprising.'
guidance: If the specification does not clearly identify what materially affects the basic/novel characteristics, treat 'consisting essentially of' as equivalent to 'comprising' for prior-art searching and application. If applicant contends exclusion of certain prior art components, the applicant bears the burden to show that the additional elements would materially change the invention. Examples: In re Herz, PPG Industries (court construed 'consisting essentially of' based on specification and evidence), AK Steel (specification indicated silicon limit to define material effect). For method claims, the phrase can limit steps analogously; applicant must establish material change.

name: Other transitional phrases ('having', 'composed of')
description: Transitional phrases such as 'having' and 'composed of' must be interpreted in light of the specification to determine whether the claim language is open or closed.
guidance: Do not apply a fixed presumption for terms like 'having' — interpret contextually. Lampi interpreted 'having' as open in one case, Crystal Semiconductor held it does not create a presumption that the body is open. 'Composed of' may be read as 'consisting of' or 'consisting essentially of' depending on facts and specification (AFG Industries, In re Bertsch). Evaluate intrinsic evidence and prosecution history.

name: Markush group selection and mixtures presumption
description: An element defined by selection from a group of alternatives (a Markush grouping) requires selection from the closed group listed; absent qualifying language, there is a presumption that the Markush group is closed to combinations or mixtures of the listed alternatives.
guidance: If combinations/mixtures are intended, include qualifying language such as 'at least one member' or 'or mixtures thereof' or provide intrinsic evidence to overcome the presumption. Case examples: Abbott Labs; Multilayer Stretch Cling Film (presumption overcome by dependent claim/specification). Evaluate claim wording and specification for evidence of intended openness to mixtures.

name: 'Adapted to/for', 'wherein', 'whereby' clauses and contingent limitations
description: Clauses like 'adapted to/for', 'wherein', and 'whereby' may or may not be limiting depending on the specific facts; contingent limitations (steps or structure required only if a condition precedent occurs) are interpreted differently for method and system claims.
guidance: Analyze whether such clauses impose a required limitation or merely describe an intended result. Courts have held these clauses limiting where they give meaning/purpose to manipulative steps (Griffin), or where 'adapted to' has a narrower, design-based meaning in the written description (Giannelli). 'Whereby' clauses stating a condition material to patentability cannot be ignored (Hoffer), but a 'whereby' that merely expresses the intended result of an already-recited step is not given weight. For contingent limitations: under the broadest reasonable interpretation, a method claim requires only those steps that must be performed (if condition not met, contingent step is not required); a system claim must include structure to perform the function should the condition occur. See Ex parte Schulhauser (PTAB precedential) for method vs system analysis.

name: Printed matter: functional vs nonfunctional and patentable weight
description: Determine whether a claim limitation is directed to printed matter; printed matter is given patentable weight only if there is a new and unobvious functional relationship between the printed matter and the physical substrate (product) or process.
guidance: First decide whether the limitation is printed matter. If so, determine whether printed matter performs a function with respect to the product, or vice versa (e.g., indicia on a measuring cup indicating volume — functional relationship; hatband arranging numbers to satisfy an algorithm — product performs a function with respect to printed matter). If printed matter merely uses the product as a support to convey a message/meaning to humans (e.g., images on a hatband, deck of cards, tables of batting averages on a memory stick), no functional relationship exists and no patentable weight should be given. For kits with instructions unrelated to that particular kit, printed matter lacks functional relationship (In re Ngai). If a functional relationship exists, determine whether it is new and unobvious before giving patentable weight (Lowry, Gulack, Miller, In re DiStefano, In re Kao).

name: Machine-readable media: functional relationship of programming
description: When claims are directed to a computer-readable medium containing programming, evaluate the relationship between the programming and the intended computer system: programming that performs a function with respect to the computer establishes a functional relationship and may be given patentable weight; data/programming that merely conveys information to a human reader does not.
guidance: Examine whether the recorded code/object performs functions that affect the computer system (example: attribute data objects facilitating retrieval/addition/removal in the intended system — functional). If the medium merely stores human-oriented information (batting averages, music tracks), treat it as mere support for information and not functionally related. Additionally, claims to media storing instructions/executable code that recite an abstract idea must be evaluated for 35 U.S.C. 101 eligibility (see MPEP § 2106).

name: Inherency in prior art rejections; burden and factual nature
description: Express, implicit, and inherent disclosures of a prior art reference may be relied on to reject claims under 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103; inherency is a question of fact and may support anticipation or obviousness.
guidance: Evaluate whether a characteristic, result, or structure necessarily flows from the prior art disclosure. Case law (In re Napier, In re Grasselli) supports using inherent teachings in rejections. The examiner should present a factual basis showing that the claimed feature is necessarily present in the prior art reference(s).

name: Discovery of new property does not make old prior art patentable; recognition not required for inherency
description: The mere discovery or characterization of a previously unappreciated property of a prior art composition does not render the old composition patentably new; an inherent feature need not have been recognized at the time of the prior invention — it suffices that the subject matter is in fact inherent in the prior art.
guidance: Do not treat a newly appreciated property or scientific explanation of a prior art embodiment as creating novelty. Courts (Atlas Powder, In re Best, In re Crish) have held that inherent characteristics present in prior art anticipate or render obvious claimed subject matter even if unrecognized. Expert testimony and post-critical-date evidence may be used to show inherency (Schering, Toro, SmithKline). Ensure the record supports that the feature necessarily results from practicing the prior art, not merely possibly or optionally present.

name: Subject-matter jurisdiction for declaratory judgment requires evidence of an immediate, real controversy
description: A declaratory judgment claim must be supported by facts showing an actual controversy of sufficient immediacy and reality; absent such facts, a court lacks subject-matter jurisdiction and the claim must be dismissed.
guidance: Application: Maxwell presented no evidence that he was engaging in activity that would subject him to a patent infringement suit, nor did the record show Midland or Wannop took a position placing Maxwell in a position of choosing between illegal action or abandoning claimed rights. Because those elements were missing, the court held the declaratory-judgment claims were properly dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction.

name: Failure to state a claim upon which relief can be granted
description: A plaintiff must allege sufficient facts to state a claim on which relief can be granted; failure to do so justifies dismissal under the appropriate rule (i.e., Rule 12(b)(6) standards).
guidance: The appellate court affirmed dismissal because Maxwell 'failed to state a claim upon which relief could be granted.' Though the opinion does not recite Twombly/Iqbal language, it treats the absence of necessary substantive allegations (here, for jurisdiction and declaratory relief) as grounds for dismissal.

name: Advancing claims or defenses unwarranted under existing law (37 C.F.R. § 10.85(a)(2))
description: Proscribes knowingly advancing a claim or defense that is unwarranted under existing law.
guidance: Applied where a practitioner pursues positions without legal support. If the practitioner did not know the law barred the claim (because no inquiry was made), the element of knowing advancement is not satisfied.

name: Affirmative defenses pleading and proof requirements (37 C.F.R. § 11.36(c))
description: To raise an affirmative defense in a USPTO attorney-discipline proceeding, the respondent must 'state affirmatively in the answer special matters of defense' and the statement must (1) specify the defense; (2) explain the defense's nexus to the alleged misconduct; and (3) explain the reason it provides a defense.
guidance: Affirmative defenses must be proven by clear and convincing evidence. Generic or unsupported assertions (e.g., 'failure to state a claim' without elaboration) are insufficient and will be rejected.

name: Prioritized examination filing requirements and claim limits (37 CFR 1.102(e))
description: A request for prioritized examination must comply with the paragraph’s requirements and be accompanied by prioritized examination fee (§1.17(c)), processing fee (§1.17(i)), and if not already paid, the publication fee (§1.18(d)). An application for prioritized examination may not contain or be amended to contain more than four independent claims, more than thirty total claims, or any multiple dependent claim.
guidance: Prioritized examination is limited by application type (see exclusions) and annual cap (no more than 15,000 requests per fiscal year). Must also meet the specific filing/timing requirements in e(1) or e(2).

name: Prioritized examination with original nonprovisional application (e)(1) filing content/time limits
description: A request for prioritized examination may be filed with an original utility or plant nonprovisional application under 35 U.S.C. 111(a). The application must include a specification as prescribed by 35 U.S.C. 112 including at least one claim, a drawing when necessary, and the inventor’s oath or declaration on filing (though the oath/declaration may be postponed per §1.53(f)(3) if an ADS meeting conditions is present). Utility applications must be filed via USPTO patent electronic filing system and include filing, search, and examination fees upon filing; plant applications must include their applicable fees. The request must be present upon filing, except applicant may file an amendment to cancel any independent claims in excess of four, any total claims in excess of thirty, and any multiple dependent claim not later than one month from a first decision on the request; this one‑month period is not extendable.
guidance: Strict completeness and fee requirements at filing. The one‑month cure period is non‑extendable; ensure claim counts comply or be prepared to timely amend.

name: Accelerated examination eligibility (general)
description: A new application may be granted accelerated examination status only if it meets the conditions in subsection I (the accelerated examination program requirements). Petitions to make special filed on/after Aug 25, 2006 must meet these revised requirements (except health/age/PPH).
guidance: Refer to the listed items (A–I) below for the detailed filing, claim, search, support‑document, and interview obligations for accelerated examination.

name: Accelerated exam requirement F: single‑invention requirement and election without traverse
description: The claims must be directed to a single invention. If the USPTO determines claims are not directed to a single invention, applicant must make an election without traverse in a telephonic interview. The petition must include a statement that applicant will agree to make such an election without traverse.
guidance: If applicant refuses or cannot be reached, claim 1 may be constructively elected without traverse; ensure claim set unity or be prepared to elect.

name: Accelerated exam requirement H: preexamination search statement and content
description: At filing, applicant must provide a statement that a preexamination search was conducted, including identification of the field of search by CPC group/subgroup (or US class/subclass for designs) and the date of the search. For database searches, provide the search logic or chemical structure/sequence used as a query, the name of the files searched and the database service, and the date of the search.
guidance: A thorough, well‑documented preexamination search is required and must be tied to the claimed invention; insufficient or undocumented searches can cause denial of accelerated status.

name: Preexamination search claim‑coverage requirement H(2)
description: The preexamination search must be directed to the claimed invention and encompass all of the features of the claims, giving the claims the broadest reasonable interpretation.
guidance: Search must match the BRIEST reasonable reading of the claims and cover all claim elements.

name: Preexamination search coverage of disclosed features H(3)
description: The preexamination search must also encompass disclosed features that may be claimed. An amendment to the claims not encompassed by the preexamination search or an updated accelerated examination support document will be treated as not fully responsive and will not be entered.
guidance: Any subsequent claim amendments require an updated search/document that covers the new claim scope at time of filing; otherwise the amendment will not be entered.

name: Accelerated examination support document required (I) — IDS inclusion I(1)
description: At filing, applicant must provide an accelerated examination support document that includes an Information Disclosure Statement (IDS) in compliance with 37 CFR 1.98 citing each reference deemed most closely related to the subject matter of each claim.
guidance: Cite and disclose the most relevant references up front; the support document is central to accelerated prosecution.

name: Support document: mapping claim limitations to references I(2)
description: For each reference cited, the support document must identify all the limitations in the claims that are disclosed by the reference specifying where the limitation is disclosed in the cited reference.
guidance: Provide precise claim‑to‑reference mappings (citations to specific pages/cols/lines/figs) to show where each claim element appears in the prior art.

name: Support document: detailed patentability explanation I(3)
description: The support document must include a detailed explanation of how each of the claims are patentable over the references cited with the particularity required by 37 CFR 1.111(b) and (c).
guidance: Provide claim‑by‑claim, element‑by‑element arguments explaining patentability over the cited art with the required particularity.

name: Support document: concise statement of utility I(4)
description: The support document must include a concise statement of the utility of the invention as defined in each of the independent claims (unless the application is a design application).
guidance: State the practical utility tied to the claimed subject matter for each independent claim.

name: Support document: 35 U.S.C. 112(a) written‑description support showing I(5)
description: The support document must include a showing of where each limitation of the claims finds support under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or first paragraph pre‑AIA 112) in the written description of the specification. If applicable, identify each means‑/step‑plus‑function element invoking 35 U.S.C. 112(f) and the corresponding structure, material, or acts in the specification. If claiming benefit to earlier applications, include where each limitation finds support in each such application where support exists.
guidance: Provide precise citations to the specification (and any priority documents) showing written‑description support for each claim limitation, and identify structure for means‑plus‑function elements.

name: Examiner interview and Office action issuance policy for accelerated exam
description: If the USPTO determines a possible rejection or other issue must be addressed, the examiner will telephone the applicant to discuss the issue and any possible amendment or submission to resolve it. The USPTO will not issue an Office action (other than a notice of allowance) unless either (A) an interview was conducted but did not place the application in condition for allowance, or (B) there is a determination that an interview is unlikely to result in allowance. Prior to mailing any Office action rejecting the claims, the USPTO will conduct a conference to review the rejections.
guidance: Examiners will use interviews and internal conferences to try to resolve issues before issuing rejecting OAs; applicants should be ready to participate in interviews promptly.

name: Reply scope limitations and treatment of non‑responsive amendments
description: A reply to an Office action must be limited to the rejections, objections, and requirements made. Any amendment that attempts to (A) add claims resulting in >3 independent or >20 total claims, (B) present claims not encompassed by the preexamination search or updated support document, or (C) present claims directed to a nonelected invention or an invention other than previously claimed, will be treated as not fully responsive and will not be entered.
guidance: Ensure amendments stay within claim limits and are encompassed by the original (or updated) search/support doc; otherwise they will be rejected as non‑responsive.

name: Requirement to file updated support document for amendments not encompassed
description: For any amendment to the claims (including any new claim) that is not encompassed by the accelerated examination support document, applicant is required to provide an updated accelerated examination support document that encompasses the amended/new claims at the time of filing the amendment. Failure to provide such updated document will cause the amendment to be treated as not fully responsive and not entered. Any IDS filed with an updated support document must comply with 37 CFR 1.97 and 1.98.
guidance: Timing: updated support document must accompany the amendment; do not file late.

name: Doctrine of claim differentiation (definition)
description: The doctrine of claim differentiation is a principle used in patent law that asserts each claim within a patent should be interpreted as having a distinct meaning and scope. Two claims in the same patent will not have identical scope, but instead there is likely an intended difference in scope.
guidance: This is the baseline principle: interpret claims with the presumption that the drafter intended different scope for different claims rather than redundancy.

name: Presumption from dependent claims
description: "The presence of a dependent claim that adds a particular limitation gives rise to a presumption that the limitation in question is not present in the independent claim."
guidance: When a dependent claim adds a limitation, courts will presume the independent claim does not include that limitation. Use this presumption in claim construction and argumentation.

name: Dependent claims construed as more specific/limiting
description: Dependent claims, which rely on independent claims, are interpreted in a way that makes them more specific or limiting than the independent claims they reference.
guidance: Treat dependent claims as narrowing: they should be read to add limitations rather than merely repeat the independent claim.

name: Doctrine prevents redundant narrowing of independent claims
description: The doctrine prevents broader claims from being interpreted so narrowly that dependent claims become redundant.
guidance: Courts use this principle to avoid constructions that would render dependent claims meaningless; illustrated by the example of a broad chemical compound claim and a narrower derivative-from-salicylic-acid claim.

name: Tolerance of similarity when only one reasonable interpretation exists
description: If a claim will bear only one interpretation, similarity will have to be tolerated.
guidance: Where the claim language unambiguously leads to a single meaning, the presumption of differentiation yields to the plain meaning of the claim.

name: Drafting best practices to leverage claim differentiation
description: Use dependent claims to add specific limitations; each dependent claim should add a meaningfully different limitation; this creates a presumption that the broader independent claim does not require those specific limitations; helps prevent narrow constructions of independent claims.
guidance: When drafting, intentionally vary dependent claims to add concrete, meaningfully different limitations so that courts will presume the independent claim is broader. Avoid drafting dependent claims that merely restate or trivially repeat the independent claim.

name: Rebuttal ground: clear disavowal in the specification
description: The presumption can be rebutted by: Clear disavowal in the specification
guidance: If the specification explicitly disavows coverage of an element or meaning, courts will construe claims consistent with that disavowal despite dependent-claim structure.

name: Rebuttal ground: need to give meaning to the claim language as a whole
description: The presumption can be rebutted by: The need to give meaning to the claim language as a whole
guidance: If applying the presumption would render claim language meaningless or fail to give effect to all claim terms, courts may reject the presumption to preserve the claims' overall meaning.

name: Indefiniteness categories (Table 1)
description: A set of fine-grained indefiniteness categories used to classify reasons for rejection under 35 U.S.C. §112(b) and corresponding MPEP sections.
guidance:
Categories (with brief descriptions / MPEP sections):
- Antecedent Basis (2173.05(e)): Claim contains a term referencing an element lacking a clear prior introduction, creating ambiguity what it references.
- Undefined Term (2173.05(a)): A term lacks a clear, accepted and/or unambiguous meaning to a POSITA, making the claim’s scope uncertain.
- Relative Term (2173.05(b)): A relative term (e.g., 'thin,' 'substantial') is used without providing a clear point of comparison, rendering the claim’s scope indefinite.
- Exemplary Phrasing (2173.05(d)): Claim uses 'such as' or similar phrasing, making it unclear whether the listed items are exhaustive or merely examples.
- Functional Claiming (2173.05(g)): Claim recites 'means for' or 'step for' without disclosing adequate corresponding structure, material, or acts in the specification (35 U.S.C. 112(f)/pre-AIA second paragraph).
- Contradicting Limitations (2173): Claim includes an element that contradicts or is inconsistent with other claim limitations.
- Omission of Essential Elements or Steps (2172.01): Claim fails to recite an element, step, or cooperative relationship between elements/steps that is essential to the invention as disclosed.
- Dependence (Other): Claim depends on an indefinite claim.
- Other (-): Catch-all for indefiniteness reasons not covered above.
Note: Some reasons were used only during parsing and filtered out for the final dataset (paper notes greyed-out reasons).

name: Statutory and normative definiteness requirement (35 U.S.C. §112(b) / Nautilus standard)
description: Definiteness requires that every claim is sufficiently clear and unambiguous to enable a person skilled in the art to understand the scope of the invention. Post-Nautilus (2014) standard: claims must inform, 'with reasonable certainty, those skilled in the art about the scope of the invention.'
guidance: Treat 35 U.S.C. §112(b) rejections as the target rejection class. The MPEP provides examiner guidance referenced throughout. Exclude pre-2014 applications to avoid differing legal standards (Nautilus change).

name: Consider only first office action
description: Use only the first office action for each application as it generally establishes the core grounds for rejection.
guidance: Download the first office action and select the latest claim and specification documents preceding that action to avoid introducing issues that appear only in later prosecution rounds.

name: Document download & parsing
description: Download claims, specification, and office action documents from the USPTO Open Data Portal (ODP) in XML and parse to Markdown/JSON for further processing.
guidance: Use the ODP File Wrapper API; parse XML into machine-readable JSON/Markdown to feed LLM parsers and downstream modules.

name: Office action parsing procedure (LLM extraction)
description: Select office action sections containing '112' and prompt an LLM (e.g., Gemma 3 27B) to extract 112(b) rejections into a fixed JSON schema.
guidance: For each rejection, extract: the verbatim text snippet arguing indefiniteness ('reasonText'), a category from Table 1 ('reasonCategory'), and a list of recited phrases ('claimRecitations'). Instruct the LLM to copy verbatim and not paraphrase, extend, or explain. Use fuzzy matching to find occurrences of recited phrases in the claim text.

name: Office action extraction rules (verbatim, granularity, scope)
description: Strict extraction rules for 35 U.S.C. 112(b) rejections (Appendix A): extract verbatim, do not paraphrase, do not mix multiple reasons into one entry; if unsure use 'other'; if none leave 'rejectionReasons' empty.
guidance: Follow the JSON schema exactly. Include every single recitation substring (even repeats/overlaps). Focus solely on 35 U.S.C. 112(b) rejections; ignore 112(a), 102, 103, etc. Prefer inclusive ranges when listing claim numbers. Do not include interpretation statements and do not fix spelling/grammar. Extract fine-grained reasons as separate entries.

name: Sampling of definite claims (balancing)
description: To obtain definite claims, sample claims from applications whose office actions do not contain the term '112(b)'; balance the dataset between definite and indefinite claims.
guidance: Compute average number of indefinite claims per application, then iterate definite applications in random order and sample the same number of claims per application until class balance is achieved, rounding up/down to match per-application counts.

name: Dataset split (application-level)
description: Randomly split applications into train (60%), test (30%), and validation (10%) partitions.
guidance: Perform the split at the application-level (not claim-level) to avoid data leakage; ensure distributional parity (definite/indefinite fractions, independent/dependent claim distribution, category distribution) across splits where possible.

name: Human validation study protocol
description: Manual inspection of a random sample to validate automatic annotations.
guidance: Inspect 50 randomly sampled claims (both definite and indefinite), compare the office action against extracted binary labels, extracted free-form reasoning texts, and assigned categories to estimate annotation accuracy and noise. Use findings to quantify reliability (paper: binary labels all correct; some category noise observed).

name: Primary evaluation tasks
description: Evaluate models on three complementary tasks: (1) binary definite/indefinite classification, (2) multi-label classification of indefiniteness categories, and (3) generation of free-form reasoning for indefiniteness reasons evaluated by an LLM-as-Judge.
guidance: Design systems and metrics to capture not only whether a claim is indefinite, but why — enabling actionable feedback for drafters/examiners.

name: Binary classification metrics & thresholding
description: Use standard binary classification metrics: Precision, Recall, F1-score, AUROC, Accuracy.
guidance: For evaluation, determine a prediction confidence threshold that balances predictions (the paper chooses the threshold such that half of validation claims are predicted as indefinite). Report metrics at that threshold and report AUROC to capture performance across thresholds.

name: LLM agent design & prompting for examination
description: Zero-shot LLM agent prompt for claim examination (Appendix B): instruct the model to dissect the claim, list all potential indefiniteness issues, estimate likelihood using verbalized expressions, and use tools to retrieve related claims and description paragraphs.
guidance: Provide the claim, the set of indefiniteness categories, and two tools: get_claim (retrieve claim by number) and search_description (TF-IDF retrieval of description paragraphs). Allow unlimited interleaved tool calls. Instruct the agent to output JSON matching the office-action-extraction schema, including per-reason confidence, free-form reasoning, a category (Table 1), and claim recitations. Encourage step-by-step reasoning and exhaustive issue listing; ignore novelty/non-obviousness.

name: Disclosure Adequacy for Priority Benefit
description: You will only get an early filing date for claims that are supported by the disclosure in the provisional application.
guidance: Be as complete as possible in the provisional. Consider what will ultimately be claimed in the utility application when drafting the provisional—insufficient disclosure means 'no priority for important claims.' Ensure the provisional's disclosure enables the claimed invention (written description and enablement).

name: No New Matter / Cannot Add New Matter to Provisional
description: New matter cannot be added to a provisional application to create priority for claims that were not supported in the provisional.
guidance: If you need to add material not present in the provisional, you must file a new application; you cannot rely on the provisional to support claims that depend on later-added subject matter. Draft provisionals with anticipated claim scope in mind.

name: Provisional Pitfalls (weak provisional dangers)
description: Common failure modes specific to provisional applications that undermine priority and value.
guidance: Pitfalls listed: A 'throwaway provisional' gives priority for nothing; Insufficient disclosure = no priority for important claims; Cannot add new matter to provisional (must file new application). Avoid filing thin provisionals just to hit a date—quality of disclosure matters for later claims.

name: Sufficiency of disclosure (general)
description: On filing, the application must supply a sufficient disclosure in respect of the invention as claimed with regard to all of the claims.
guidance: If claims define the invention in terms of parameters, the application must include a clear description of the methods used to determine those parameter values unless a PSIA would know which method to use or all methods yield the same result. An examiner finding insufficiency cannot be cured after the fact by adding further examples that introduce added subject-matter; remedy may include restricting claims to embodiments sufficiently described and deleting descriptions of other embodiments.

name: Sufficiency and support of claims linkage
description: Where the disclosure is insufficient to enable a PSIA to carry out the claimed invention, the claims may be too broad to be supported by the description.
guidance: Insufficiency may therefore lead to objections both under sufficiency (enablement) and under support of claims; examiner should consider both requirements together.

name: Disclosure vs clarity distinction
description: There is a balance between lack of clarity and lack of disclosure to be assessed on the merits of each case.
guidance: Ambiguity in claims will lead to lack of disclosure objection if the whole scope of the claim is affected making it impossible to carry out the invention; otherwise a lack of clarity objection is more appropriate.

name: Internet search use and confidentiality caution
description: Search can cover Internet sources (online journals, databases, websites); extent depends on case and systematic internet search may be regularly necessary in some technical fields.
guidance: In information/software fields internet searches often necessary. When searching unpublished applications, take care not to disclose confidential information via search terms — choose keywords that avoid disclosing invention rather than long claim text.

name: Inclusion of analogous fields in search
description: Field of search should, where appropriate, include analogous fields consistent with the description and drawings.
guidance: Determine analogous fields by necessary function or use of claimed invention, not only specific functions indicated. Consider: (i) fields where same/similar structure expected for different use; (ii) fields to which a generic concept pertains; (iii) art within inventor's activity relevant to problem; (iv) fields relevant to function/utility inherent in claimed subject-matter. Extension decision rests on whether a reasonable lack-of-inventive-step objection could be established from likely finds in those fields.

name: Search parameters and coverage (what to search)
description: Search parameters may cover IPC, keywords and drawings; search coverage may include abstracts, claims, title, description and drawings.
guidance: When beginning the search, analyze claims in light of description and drawings to determine subject of the claimed invention; search directed to invention as interpreted with regard to description and with emphasis on inventive concept.

name: Analysis of claims for search direction
description: Examiner first critically analyzes the claims in the light of description and drawings to determine subject of claimed invention.
guidance: Search is directed to the invention defined by the claims as interpreted with due regard to the description/drawings and inventive concept.

name: Full coverage principle (subject-matter scope)
description: In principle and insofar as possible and reasonable the search should cover the entire subject-matter to which the claims are directed or might reasonably be expected to be directed after amendment.
guidance: Economy considerations may justify certain restrictions (e.g., broad claim with many examples where it is not possible to foresee which will be subject of amended claims). Example: if description gives detailed transistor circuit but claims functionally, the search must include that detailed circuit.

name: Handling speculative or unduly wide claims
description: No special search effort beyond what is supported by the description is needed for unduly wide or speculative claims.
guidance: Do not extend to unrelated technologies merely due to broad wording, except where it is probable that extended search could produce a document that establishes lack of novelty or inventive step. If meaningful search of unsupported claim subject-matter can be done without much extra effort and scope is not unduly wide, extend the search.

name: Search of particular claim types and the role of preamble
description: Words of a claim read as a PSIA would understand; in two-part claims preamble is a limitation on scope.
guidance: In some circumstances extend search to technological background including (i) preamble portion before 'characterised by' or 'the improvement comprising'; (ii) state of prior art as explained in introduction of description; (iii) general technological background ('general state of the art'). Consider particular forms such as product-by-process and two-part claims accordingly.

name: Combination claims and sub-combinations search
description: For claims characterised by combinations of elements (A, B and C), the search should be directed to the combination.
guidance: When searching classification units, also search sub-combinations (AB, AC, BC) and individual elements (A, B, C) in those units at the same time. Additional classification units for sub-combinations or individual elements should be searched only if necessary to establish novelty of an element to assess inventive step of the combination.

name: Different categories of claims in search
description: When application contains claims of different categories that comply with unity, all must be included in the search; where only one category present it may be desirable to include others.
guidance: Example: a reference describing a process but only claiming the product might be classified under product subclass; therefore, when searching for a process it may be necessary to search for the product as well. In chemical claims, starting products may form part of the state of the art and need not be searched; intermediate products only when claimed; final products are highly recommended to be searched unless evidently known.

name: Preparation of a written search statement
description: Examiner may prepare a written search statement defining subject of their search as precisely as possible.
guidance: Claims may serve but may need generalisation to cover all aspects and embodiments. Consider exclusions from search and lack of unity; if unity not satisfied, examiner may choose to conduct search on first invention or inventive concept only. Examiner should avoid restricting search unless unavoidable.

name: Determination of the closest prior art
description: The closest prior art is the single reference disclosing the combination of features that constitutes the most promising starting point for development leading to the invention.
guidance: Closest prior art should be directed to similar purpose/effect or belong to same/closely related field, be capable of carrying out claimed function, and be selected based on examiner's interpretation of claims. Examiner should also cite prior art likely to assist in determining sufficiency and support throughout the claimed field.

name: Definition and purpose of a terminal disclaimer (37 CFR 1.321)
description: A terminal disclaimer is a statement filed by an owner (in whole or in part) of a patent or a patent to be granted that is used to disclaim or dedicate a portion of the entire term of all the claims of a patent. The requirements for a terminal disclaimer are set forth in 37 CFR 1.321. Sample forms and guidance are provided in MPEP § 1490.
guidance: Use a terminal disclaimer where appropriate to disclaim the terminal portion of the later patent's term; see 37 CFR 1.321 for formal requirements and MPEP § 1490 for sample forms and filing/treatment guidance.

name: Terminal disclaimer requirement to overcome nonstatutory double patenting for applications filed on/after June 8, 1995
description: A terminal disclaimer under 37 CFR 1.321 is required in an application to overcome a nonstatutory double patenting rejection, even if the application was filed on or after June 8, 1995 and claims the benefit of an earlier filing date under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, or 365(c).
guidance: Examiners should cite this MPEP section or the Official Gazette notice (1202 O.G. 112 (Sept. 30, 1997)) when applicant argues a terminal disclaimer should not be required because of the 20-year patent term rules in 35 U.S.C. 154(a)(2). Reasons include 35 U.S.C. 154(b) patent term adjustments and the enforceability condition required by 37 CFR 1.321(c)(3).

name: 37 CFR 1.321(c)(3) enforceability provision for terminal disclaimers
description: When a terminal disclaimer is filed to obviate a nonstatutory double patenting rejection based on commonly owned conflicting claims, 37 CFR 1.321(c)(3) requires the disclaimer to include a provision that any patent granted on that application shall be enforceable only for and during such period that said patent is commonly owned with the application or patent which formed the basis for the rejection.
guidance: A terminal disclaimer must expressly contain the enforceability limitation to avoid extension-of-monopoly problems; failure to include this provision undermines the purpose of the disclaimer.

name: 37 CFR 1.321(d) requirements for terminal disclaimers involving joint research agreements
description: 37 CFR 1.321(d) sets forth the requirements for a terminal disclaimer where the claimed invention resulted from activities undertaken within the scope of a joint research agreement.
guidance: When the inventions arise from a joint research agreement, the terminal disclaimer must meet the special requirements of 1.321(d) (see MPEP § 1490 for sample forms and further guidance).

name: Conditions for non-commonly owned inventions to be treated as commonly owned under CREATE Act (35 U.S.C. 103(c)(2))
description: Two inventions come within the provisions of 35 U.S.C. 103(c)(2) (for applications pending on or after Dec. 10, 2004, and certain reexaminations) when: (A) the later invention is not anticipated by the earlier invention under 35 U.S.C. 102; (B) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; (C) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (D) the application for the claimed invention discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement.
guidance: These conditions implement the CREATE Act (Public Law 108-453). If all are met the non-commonly owned references may be treated as if commonly owned for 103 purposes, disqualifying them as prior art under certain 102/103 rejections.

name: Form paragraph 8.27: different inventors, common assignee, same invention
description: Use ¶ 8.27 when claim [1] is directed to the same invention as claim [2] of commonly assigned [3]; priority under 35 U.S.C. 102(g) and possibly 102(f) must be resolved. The assignee is required to state which entity is the prior inventor. A terminal disclaimer has no effect in this situation since the basis is priority under 35 U.S.C. 102(f) or (g), not extension of monopoly.
guidance: If the commonly assigned application/patent has an earlier U.S. filing date, also consider a 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection (form paragraphs 7.15.01/7.15.02). Failure to comply will result in abandonment. Do not use this para if one invention would have been obvious in view of the other (use 8.28).

name: Provisional rejection practice (¶¶ 7.15.01, 7.21.01) for copending applications with common assignee/inventor
description: Use provisional rejection paragraphs when the claimed invention is not patentably distinct from disclosure in a copending application with an earlier effective U.S. filing date and the copending application has a common assignee or at least one common inventor. A provisional rejection presumes future publication or patenting of the copending application and may be overcome by showing derivation (37 CFR 1.132), an earlier date of invention (37 CFR 1.131), or that the copending application is disqualified under 35 U.S.C. 103(c).
guidance: Do not use provisional rejection paragraphs for applications pending on or after Dec. 10, 2004 when the copending application is disqualified under 103(c) as prior art in a 103(a) rejection. A provisional 102(e) rejection may not be overcome by a terminal disclaimer (see In re Bartfeld).

name: Guidance on determining prior art dates under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) (AIPA and pre-AIPA rules)
description: When applying 35 U.S.C. 102(e), use the amendments (AIPA, IP/High Technology Technical Amendments Act of 2002) to determine a reference's prior art date, unless the reference is a U.S. patent issued directly or indirectly from an international application with certain international filing date conditions (e.g., prior to Nov. 29, 2000). Pre-AIPA 102(e) rules apply for some references as specified (use form paragraphs 7.12, 7.12.01 and Examiner Notes to assist determination).
guidance: Consider priority/benefit claims to earlier-filed U.S. provisional or nonprovisional applications and international applications under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), 120, 121, or 365(c) when the relied-upon subject matter is appropriately supported in the earlier application's disclosure. Use the detailed Examiner Notes for specific date computations.

name: Timing of Obviousness Determination (effective filing date)
description: AIA 35 U.S.C. 103 determines obviousness before the effective filing date of the claimed invention, rather than as of the time the claimed invention was made.
guidance: This differs from pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103 practice where the Office used effective filing date as a proxy for invention date unless earlier invention date was established (e.g., by affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131). As a practical matter, this distinction affects cases only when pre-AIA 103 is applicable and there is evidence of an invention date prior to the effective filing date.

name: Consideration of 'differences between the claimed invention and the prior art'
description: AIA 35 U.S.C. 103 requires consideration of 'the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art.'
guidance: This language does not change the approach to obviousness determinations: claims are the measure of the invention. The MPEP notes that the Court has equated 'the subject matter sought to be patented' with the claims (Graham v. John Deere). Examiners should ascertain the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue when formulating an obviousness rejection.

name: Manner of invention is irrelevant to patentability
description: Statutory language: 'Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.'
guidance: When applying 35 U.S.C. 103, examiners should not base patentability determinations on how the inventor arrived at the invention; focus is on the claimed invention vs prior art as of the effective filing date.

name: Test for Obviousness — Factual Inquiries (Graham factors)
description: The factual inquiries summarized for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103 are: (1) determining the scope and contents of the prior art; (2) ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue; (3) resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; (4) considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
guidance: This four-part test (the 'Graham factors') should be the basis for the factual background of any obviousness determination. Examiners must apply these inquiries and may use form paragraph ¶ 7.23.aia when appropriate.

name: Formulating and supporting a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103
description: A rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 must be supported by an explanation (rationale) showing why the claimed invention would have been obvious, following MPEP § 2144 and related guidance.
guidance: Examiners should provide an explanation of the rejection (how the references map to the claim limitations and why one of ordinary skill would be motivated to combine or modify references with a reasonable expectation of success). See MPEP § 2144 for guidance on appropriate rationales (implicit disclosure, reliance on scientific theory, common knowledge, etc.).

name: Joint inventors and presumption of common ownership
description: When an application currently names joint inventors, the examiner presumes that the subject matter of the various claims was commonly owned at the time any inventions covered were effectively filed absent evidence to the contrary.
guidance: Applicant is advised of the obligation under 37 CFR 1.56 to point out inventor and effective filing dates for claims not commonly owned so the examiner can consider applicability of 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C). Use ¶ 7.20.02.aia in all applications with joint inventors unless claims are clearly restricted to a single claimed invention.

name: When to use a combined 102/103 rejection (¶ 7.27.aia)
description: A claim may be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102 (anticipation) or, in the alternative, under 35 U.S.C. 103 (obviousness) when appropriate; ¶ 7.27.aia enumerates example circumstances where such paragraph may be used rather than separate rejections.
guidance: Examples include: disputed claim interpretation (one interpretation leads to 102, another to 103); when reference discloses all limitations except a property or function and examiner cannot determine inherent properties but has basis for shifting burden (In re Fitzgerald); genus-species situations where genus disclosure makes a species obvious; product-by-process equivalence questions; means-plus-function equivalence uncertainty; overlapping ranges where reference and claim ranges overlap but reference lacks specific example. Examiners should otherwise make a single rejection under either 102 or 103 whenever possible and must provide full explanation for both alternatives when using ¶ 7.27.aia.

name: Combining references for a 103 rejection (¶ 7.22.aia and supporting guidance)
description: When a claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over a reference as applied to an earlier claim and further in view of another reference, the examiner must precede ¶ 7.22.aia with ¶ 7.21.aia and provide an explanation of the rejection.
guidance: Examiners must explain how the references are combined and why a person of ordinary skill would have been motivated to combine them with a reasonable expectation of success. Cross-reference to MPEP § 2144 for guidance on appropriate rationales and supporting evidence.

name: Restriction on assisting in pension claim evidence
description: In the sense of section 5498 R.S., a retired officer may not assist a regular soldier in obtaining the evidence necessary to support his application for a pension.

name: Claims must define technical features (Rule 43(1) EPC)
description: The claims shall define the matter for which protection is sought in terms of the technical features of the invention.
guidance: Where appropriate, claims should contain a statement indicating the subject-matter designation and those technical features necessary for definition that form part of the prior art, and a characterising portion specifying the technical features for which protection is sought.

name: Present independent claims in the two-part form where appropriate
description: Independent claims very often appear in two-part form: a preamble describing features forming part of the prior art and a characterising part beginning with 'characterised in that' or 'characterised by' specifying the novel features.
guidance: Use the two-part form when it clearly distinguishes known features from the characterising features. The EPC requires this 'wherever appropriate'—the EPO may itself amend claims into two-part form in an intention-to-grant communication. Accepting such amendments can be pragmatic to obtain grant, absent other substantive objections.

name: Reference signs in claims (Rule 43(7) EPC)
description: Where the application contains drawings including reference signs, technical features in the claims shall preferably be followed by such reference signs (in parentheses) if intelligibility is thereby increased; these reference signs shall not be construed as limiting the claim.
guidance: Reference signs' sole function is to increase intelligibility. It is generally sufficient to include the reference sign at the first instance of a feature in each claim rather than every occurrence. Applicants may note in the description that reference signs are non-limiting. EPO practice often treats inclusion of reference signs as mandatory and may insert them; the requirement can be lifted only if claims without them are shown to be clear under Article 84 EPC.

name: Conform the description to the claims (support and consistency; Article 84 and Article 69(1) EPC)
description: A patent can only be granted where the claimed invention is supported by the description. Claims must be interpreted in light of the description, and inconsistencies between description and claims must be avoided.
guidance: If independent claims are amended to introduce limitations, the description must be amended to make clear those formerly-optional features are essential. Subject matter falling outside the scope of the claims (for example after amendments) must be indicated as not part of the claimed invention or deleted. Failure to amend as required can lead to summons to oral proceedings.

name: Handle excluded subject-matter in the description (Article 53 EPC)
description: Any subject-matter excluded from patentability under Article 53 EPC must be removed, reworded so it no longer relates to excluded subject-matter, or prominently marked to make it clear it does not form part of the claimed invention.
guidance: This applies to matter contrary to ordre public or morality, plant or animal varieties and essentially biological processes, and methods of treatment of the human or animal body. If protection is desired for such subject-matter present in the application as filed, consider filing a divisional directed to that subject-matter before the parent application is finally disposed of.

name: Divisional applications timing and strategy
description: If the applicant seeks protection for subject-matter not claimed in the (to-be-granted) application but disclosed in the application as filed, they should consider filing a divisional application directed to that subject-matter.
guidance: Divisional applications must be filed before the earlier patent application is finally granted, refused, abandoned, withdrawn, or deemed to be withdrawn. Use divisionals to preserve claim scope for different subject-matter rather than leaving it in the description only.

name: Statutory Double Patenting (35 U.S.C. 101)
description: Statutory double patenting asks whether the 'same invention' is being claimed twice — i.e., identical subject matter being claimed in two patents/applications.
guidance: Reliable test: Is there an embodiment that falls within the scope of one claim but not the other? Could one claim be literally infringed without literally infringing the other claim? Remedies: Amend or cancel claims. A terminal disclaimer is NOT sufficient to overcome a statutory double patenting rejection. Declarations under 37 CFR 1.131 are NOT sufficient.

name: Non-Statutory Obviousness-Type Double Patenting (ODP-Obviousness)
description: Rejection based on an obviousness analysis that the claimed invention would have been an obvious variation of an invention defined in a claim in a patent (or copending application).
guidance: Any obviousness-type double patenting rejection should make clear: (1) the differences between the examined claim and the claim in the reference patent or copending application, and (2) the reasons for concluding that the claim at issue would have been an obvious variation. Reliance on the specification of a potentially conflicting patent or application is generally prohibited (limited exceptions apply). Declarations under 37 CFR 1.131 are NOT sufficient to overcome such a rejection. Remedies include amending/canceling claims, filing argument/documentary evidence, or filing a proper terminal disclaimer.

name: Written Rejection Content Requirements for ODP-Obviousness
description: Any obviousness-type double patenting rejection based on an obviousness analysis should make clear the differences between the examined claim and the reference claim and the reasons for concluding the examined claim would have been an obvious variation.
guidance: Examiner must articulate both the claim differences and the rationale supporting an obviousness conclusion (i.e., factual findings and reasoning). This distinguishes an ODP-Obviousness rejection from a mere conclusory assertion.

name: Differences Between 35 U.S.C. 103 Analysis and ODP-Obviousness Analysis
description: 35 U.S.C. 103 (obviousness) analysis uses prior art within the meaning of 35 U.S.C. 102; ODP-Obviousness analysis uses claims of a potentially conflicting patent or application (alone or with 102 prior art).
guidance: Reliance on the specification of a potentially conflicting patent/application is generally prohibited in ODP analyses, except for limited uses (e.g., dictionary or claim-support). Understand which source constitutes the 'reference' for the analysis.

name: Proper Uses of Disclosure of a Potentially Conflicting Patent/Application
description: Exceptions to the general prohibition on using the disclosure of a potentially conflicting patent/application include: (1) using it as a dictionary for claim terminology, and (2) portions of the disclosure that provide support for the claims in the potentially conflicting patent/application.
guidance: Examiners should avoid treating the specification of a conflicting patent as prior art except for these limited purposes.

name: Focus on Claims for Double Patenting Analysis
description: Compare the claims of the potentially conflicting patent/application to the examined claims; the use of the specification of the potentially conflicting patent/application is generally prohibited (with limited exceptions).
guidance: The analysis is primarily claim-to-claim; assess literal scope overlap, generic/species relationships, and whether one claim could be literally infringed without infringing the other.

name: ODP-Anticipation — Caution Regarding Generic and Species Claims
description: A generic claim does not usually anticipate a species; overlapping generic claims do not usually anticipate one another.
guidance: Do not infer anticipation simply from broad-to-narrow claim overlap (domination). Where anticipation is not established, consider ODP-Obviousness instead.

name: Domination
description: Domination: Broad or generic claims in one patent fully encompass narrower claims in another patent.
guidance: Domination by itself cannot support a double patenting rejection, but domination does not preclude a double patenting rejection. Examiners must analyze whether the domination actually establishes statutory or non-statutory double patenting per the applicable tests.

name: Double Patenting vs. Art (Prior Art) Rejection Distinction
description: Double patenting compares claims (with limited use of the disclosure of the potentially conflicting patent/application) and can be overcome by a terminal disclaimer (ODP only). An art rejection uses the reference for all it fairly teaches and cannot be overcome by a terminal disclaimer.
guidance: Do not conflate an art rejection with a double patenting rejection; the legal bases, evidentiary sources, and remedies differ.

name: Terminal Disclaimer — Operative Details and Limitations
description: A terminal disclaimer 'must operate with respect to all claims in the patent,' is 'not an admission of the propriety of the rejection,' and is 'effective only with respect to the application identified in the disclaimer, unless by its terms it extends to continuing applications.' A fee is required for each terminal disclaimer filed. A terminal disclaimer is required even in applications filed on or after June 8, 1995.
guidance: Even when patents would expire on the same day, a terminal disclaimer is required to ensure enforceability only as long as they are commonly owned; ensure correct identification of application numbers and payment of fees. Terminal disclaimer effectiveness is limited to the application(s) identified unless it explicitly extends.

name: How to Overcome a Proper Statutory Double Patenting Rejection
description: Statutory double patenting can be overcome by amending the claims or canceling the claims. A terminal disclaimer is NOT sufficient, and declarations under 37 CFR 1.131 are NOT sufficient.
guidance: Because statutory DP is a same-invention/identical-subject-matter problem, only substantive change to the claim set (or cancellation) resolves it.

name: How to Overcome a Proper Non-Statutory Double Patenting Rejection
description: Non-statutory double patenting rejections (all types) may be overcome by amending the claims, canceling the claims, filing argument and/or documentary evidence, or filing a proper terminal disclaimer. Declarations under 37 CFR 1.131 are NOT sufficient.
guidance: Terminal disclaimers are an accepted procedural remedy for ODP but do not address statutory double patenting. When relying on arguments or evidence, ensure the examiner's written rejection criteria (differences and reasons) are addressed.

name: Claim interpretation is a matter of law (judge, not jury)
description: Following Markman v. Westview Instruments, Inc., the Supreme Court held that claim interpretation is a matter of law rather than a question of fact for the jury.
guidance: Courts treat patents like contracts and therefore are best suited to interpret patent language; judges perform claim construction in a Markman hearing which usually defines the scope of the patent either for or against the inventor.

name: Primacy of the claim language (ordinary meaning in light of the invention)
description: The court must analyze the claim language's plain or ordinary meaning and interpret it 'in light of the specifics . . . [of] the invention.'
guidance: The words themselves are the most important source of evidence when defining the scope of the patent; courts start with the language of the claims.

name: Prosecution history informs claim scope
description: Patent history (prosecution history) provides information regarding proceedings prior to patent approval, including applicant representations to the PTO.
guidance: Prosecution history may provide the court with a more in-depth understanding as to the intended scope of the claim and is part of intrinsic evidence considered during claim construction.

name: Limits on extrinsic evidence (Vitronics → Pitney-Bowes → Teva rule evolution)
description: Vitronics stated extrinsic evidence should not be used when intrinsic evidence is sufficient; Pitney-Bowes allowed judges to consult extrinsic evidence even where intrinsic evidence was adequate; the Supreme Court in Teva (2015) clarified the modern approach.
guidance: Current guiding rule (post-Teva): only intrinsic evidence should be used initially; if after intrinsic review the claim terms are still ambiguous, extrinsic evidence can be consulted. If there is a dispute over underlying facts, courts may make secondary factual findings about extrinsic evidence credibility.

name: Appellate standard of review for claim construction (de novo to hybrid clear-error)
description: Federal Circuit originally applied de novo review to claim construction (Cybor en banc), meaning appellate courts reviewed without regard to the lower court's decision; Teva modified this, requiring deference to a trial court's factual findings absent clear error.
guidance: After Teva, appellate courts review legal conclusions de novo but must defer to the lower court's factual findings regarding extrinsic evidence unless clearly erroneous (hybrid standard). This change affected reversal rates and uniformity concerns.

name: Advantages and disadvantages of conducting Markman early (pre-discovery)
description: Conducting a Markman hearing during the pre-discovery phase can limit litigation time and centralize discovery around the court's interpretation.
guidance: Benefits: limiting litigation time, early settlements, decreasing litigation costs, centralizing discovery. Disadvantages: short discovery phases, court interpreting claim language with little information, early constructions may later change making early hearings impractical.

name: Subject matter eligibility strategies (§101)
description: When drafting AI claims, follow the MPEP/Alice-Mayo-style evaluation: determine statutory category, whether claims recite an abstract idea, whether claims are integrated into a practical application, and whether additional elements amount to 'significantly more.' Use three basic strategies: avoid language invoking an abstract idea, include language integrating the claim into a practical application, and include additional elements integral to the invention.
guidance: Avoid steps that sound like mental processes (predict, identify, evaluate), mathematical equations/notation, and words that invoke business/legal activities. To integrate into a practical application, include technology-related steps (e.g., improving model accuracy; reducing model size/parameters/layers; reducing training data; enabling lifelong learning; improving training speed/efficiency; increasing inference speed/efficiency; enabling/optimizing different hardware). To show 'significantly more,' include specific architectural elements, ML-specific steps (encoding/decoding, embedding, performing a convolution), steps that cannot be performed in the human mind, physical sensors or physical transformations, and non-generic hardware.

name: Avoiding means-plus-function/indefiniteness (§112 risk)
description: Avoid drafting claims with non-structural, generic terms (Module; Component; Unit; Element; Mechanism; System; Apparatus) that invite 35 U.S.C. §112(f) interpretation unless the specification provides corresponding structure. Provide more than a repeat of generic terms.
guidance: Prefer more specific AI terms where appropriate (machine learning model, ANN, CNN, GAN, reinforcement learning model). If non-structural terms are used, describe in the specification whether the element is hardware or implemented in software and provide sufficient structural description so the claim is not rejected as indefinite.

name: Training-claim drafting considerations
description: Recognize that training claims can be claimable (per MPEP examples) but may be rejected; tailor training claims to avoid explicit mathematical concepts and support them in the specification as computationally intense and impractical to perform mentally. Consider novel loss functions, dedicated training architectures, and special-purpose hardware in claims.
guidance: Describe training steps in the specification with computational detail, avoid reciting explicit formulas in claims, highlight novel loss functions or training-architecture details, and consider claiming special-purpose hardware (GPU/TPU/accelerator) to overcome 'generic computer' objections.

name: Inference-claim drafting strategies
description: Differentiate inference claims by species: (1) standard ML model performing a novel task, (2) novel ML model performing a standard task, and (3) novel ML model performing a novel task. Tailor claim strategy accordingly: focus on the novel task, explicitly claim what makes the model novel (configurations, layer combinations), or leverage the novel task to allow broader model claiming.
guidance: For (1), emphasize what the novel task is because a generic ML model is unlikely to confer eligibility. For (2), claim the specific configuration or combination of layers that makes the model novel. For (3), recite elements of the novel task to permit more flexible/broad claiming while balancing trade secrets.

name: Architecture-claim drafting
description: Draft architecture claims to recite specific AI architectural components and processing patterns (CNN, RNN, transformer, ensembles) and/or hardware aspects rather than only generic computing components. Architecture claims may focus on a portion of an architecture and be part of a complete claim set including training and inference claims.
guidance: Reference particular machine-like components (CNN, RNN, BERT, GPT) to avoid being considered generic. Claiming architectural elements shows practical application and non-conventionality. Incorporate architectural elements into method steps (e.g., 'performing a neural network convolution') and consider hardware sensors and special compute hardware as claim elements.

name: Problem/solution claim drafting
description: Claims that recite a problem, the technical solution, and the resulting improvement over prior art systems can avoid eligibility rejections even without explicit architecture or training elements.
guidance: Structure claims to identify the problem (e.g., receive a 2D image depicting an obstacle), intermediate technical solution steps (e.g., generate a depth map indicating obstacle distance), and the resulting action or improvement (e.g., navigate while avoiding obstacle using the depth map). Ensure the problem, solution, and result are fully described in the specification to support eligibility arguments.

name: Specification drafting for §101 (use of claim terms in light of spec)
description: Because claim terms are interpreted in light of the specification, include technical definitions and detailed descriptions in the spec for terms that might otherwise be read as abstract (predict, identify, observe, evaluate, encode).
guidance: Provide AI/ML-specific technical definitions (e.g., 'encoding' as representing data in a high-dimensional embedding space) or describe exemplary uses of terms to differentiate from mental processes. Describe a technical problem, the technical solution, and the technology-specific benefits derived from the invention to show integration into a practical application and to support 'significantly more' arguments.

name: Definiteness support and examples (§112(b))
description: To avoid indefiniteness, provide algorithms, descriptions of how functions are performed, what elements perform functions, how exceptions are handled, and examples demonstrating possession of the invention at filing.
guidance: Provide method steps that are performed automatically (rather than relying on user actions) when possible. For well-known/off-the-shelf ML modules, claim terms may avoid invoking §112(f); for specialized ML modules, provide sufficient structural description (algorithms, inputs/outputs, exception handling). Use examples to show possession and enablement.

name: Problem/solution description in specification
description: In the specification, provide a description of the technical problem in the prior art, a description of the technical solution including structure performing each claimed function (algorithms if software), and a description of how the solution yields improvements over existing systems.
guidance: Motivate the solution without conceding too much background as prior art: identify field, provide a generic device/task name, describe implementation problems, describe structure performing claimed functions (and how), provide non-limiting definitions or exemplary uses of AI-specific terms, and describe improvements that are specific and tied to the problem.

name: Responding to §101 office-action rejections (prosecution strategies)
description: Three key response strategies to §101 rejections: (1) argue the claim does not recite a judicial exception, (2) argue the claim is integrated into a practical application, and (3) argue that additional elements (or their combination) add 'significantly more' than conventional solutions.
guidance: These parallel the eligibility-avoidance strategies; implement them with AI-specific tailoring (e.g., emphasize non-abstract architectural/training elements, physical sensors, technical improvements, specific ML operations). When responding, ensure examiner has been walked through the four-step eligibility analysis and the specification supports the chosen strategy.

name: Definiteness requirement under 35 U.S.C. 112(b)
description: Claims must be sufficiently definite to inform the public of the bounds of the protected invention, i.e., what subject matter is covered by the exclusive rights of the patent. During prosecution, claims are given their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.
guidance: The focus is whether the claim meets threshold requirements of clarity and precision so that a person of ordinary skill can ascertain the metes and bounds and avoid infringement. Citation examples: Halliburton, In re Buszard, In re Yamamoto, In re Zletz; see MPEP § 2173.02 and related sections.

name: Examiner's duties when making a prima facie indefiniteness rejection
description: When rejecting a claim as prima facie indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b), the examiner should provide enough information in the Office action to permit applicant to make a meaningful response.
guidance: Examiner should point out the specific term or phrase that is indefinite, explain in detail why it renders the metes and bounds unclear, and, whenever practicable, indicate how the indefiniteness may be resolved. See MPEP § 707.07(d). If applicant does not adequately respond, the examiner may make the rejection final (e.g., Packard).

name: Examination focus: clarity and precision, not preference for wording
description: The focus during examination for compliance with definiteness is whether the claim meets clarity and precision thresholds, not whether more suitable language or modes of expression are available.
guidance: Examiners are encouraged to suggest claim language to improve clarity but should not insist on their own preferences if applicant-selected language satisfies statutory requirement. If more information is necessary, a requirement under 37 CFR 1.105 may be appropriate (see MPEP § 704.10).

name: Applicant remedies for alleged indefiniteness
description: An applicant may resolve ambiguity by amending the claims or by providing a persuasive explanation on the record that a person of ordinary skill would not consider the claim language unclear.
