guidance: In some cases applicant may provide separate definitions (e.g., art-recognized dictionary) or submit evidence (e.g., declaration under 37 CFR 1.132) to show how the ordinarily-skilled artisan would understand the term. If examiner is persuaded, the examiner should indicate in the next Office communication that the previous rejection has been withdrawn and explain what prompted the change (make specific reference to applicant's remarks).

name: Make record clear to limit prosecution history estoppel
description: Examiners should provide explicit reasoning for making or withdrawing any rejection related to 35 U.S.C. 112(b) so the prosecution history clearly reflects the rationale.
guidance: A clear and complete prosecution file record is important because prosecution history estoppel requires that claims be interpreted in light of PTO proceedings. Cite Festo: narrowing amendments made to satisfy Patent Act requirements may give rise to estoppel; examiners should clarify the record to show purpose of amendments or withdrawals.

name: Provide claim interpretation in reasons for allowance when the record is unclear (37 CFR 1.104(e))
description: If the examiner believes the prosecution record does not make clear the reasons for allowing a claim, the examiner may set forth such reasoning in reasons for allowance.
guidance: One purpose is to improve quality/reliability of issued patents by providing a complete file history for public and patentee evaluation and to help avoid or simplify subsequent litigation. When allowing a claim based on an interpretation not readily apparent from the record, set forth the claim interpretation in reasons for allowance. Ensure statements do not place unwarranted broad or narrow interpretations on the claims (see MPEP §1302.14).

name: Use interviews to resolve indefiniteness before rejecting
description: Interviews are an effective examination tool and are encouraged when they can further prosecution, shorten pendency, or benefit examiner/applicant; issues of claim interpretation and clarity may often be resolved via interview.
guidance: Examiners may initiate interviews to discuss broadest reasonable interpretation, meaning of claim limitations, scope of preamble language, functional language, intended use language, means-plus-function limitations, etc. The substance of any interview must be made of record in the application (MPEP §713.04; 37 CFR 1.2). Examples of 35 U.S.C. 112 issues to record include why a term is/is not clear, whether it invokes 112(f) and identification of corresponding structure/material/acts, and any claim amendments discussed.

name: Specification should provide correspondence and antecedent basis for claim terms (37 CFR 1.75(d)(1))
description: The specification should ideally serve as a glossary so examiner and public can ascertain the meaning of claim terms; claim terms must find clear support or antecedent basis in the specification.
guidance: If specification lacks needed support/antecedent basis, object to the specification under 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1) and require applicant to amend description (without introducing new matter) or amend the claim. See MPEP §§608.01(o) and 2181.

name: Claims inconsistent with the specification may be indefinite
description: A claim, although clear on its face, may be indefinite when a conflict between claimed subject matter and the specification disclosure renders claim scope uncertain.
guidance: Court examples (Moore, Cohn, Hammack, Anderson) show that internal inconsistencies between claim language and specification definitions/examples can render claims indefinite. Examiner should consider whether specification teaches or defines terms in a way that contradicts claim meaning.

name: Inconsistencies among claims can render claims indefinite
description: Inconsistencies in the meaning of terms or phrases between claims may make the scope of claims uncertain.
guidance: When a disputed phrase is unclear, a skilled artisan may look to other claims for clarification (Philips v. AWH). Example: Tvngo Ltd. v. LG Elecs. — dependent claims using a phrase in a way that contradicts the independent claim can create indefiniteness.

name: Breadth of a claim is not the same as indefiniteness
description: A broad claim is not indefinite merely because it encompasses wide subject matter, provided the scope is clearly defined.
guidance: A genus claim covering multiple species is broad but not indefinite if the scope is clear. Undue breadth should be addressed under appropriate statutory provisions depending on reason: if claim is too broad because it does not set forth what inventor regards as invention, consider 35 U.S.C. 112(b); if unsupported or not enabled, consider 35 U.S.C. 112(a); if reads on prior art, consider 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103.

name: Meaning of every term should be apparent; balance clarity with limits of language
description: The meaning of every term used in a claim should be apparent from the prior art or the specification and drawings at filing. New terms are permissible but the clarity/precision requirement must be balanced with language and science limitations.
guidance: Applicants need not confine to prior art terminology but must make clear and precise the terms used to define the invention so metes and bounds can be ascertained. When specification states intended meaning, examine using that meaning (In re Zletz). If language is as precise as subject matter permits and apprises skilled artisans of utilization and scope, statute demands no more (see Packard). Examiners should suggest alternatives if language is not as precise as subject matter permits.

name: Relative terminology and terms of degree are not automatically indefinite
description: Use of relative terminology (terms of degree) does not automatically render a claim indefinite; acceptability depends on whether one of ordinary skill would understand what is claimed in light of the specification.
guidance: If a term of degree is used, the examiner should determine whether the specification provides some standard for measuring that degree or whether a recognized standard in the art exists. Examples: Interval Licensing, Hearing Components, Enzo Biochem, Seattle Box. If specification lacks a standard, applicant may overcome rejection with evidence (e.g., 37 CFR 1.132 declaration). Claims are indefinite if scope cannot be understood when read in light of the specification even if a term of degree is used.

name: Approximations (e.g., 'about') must be interpreted in context
description: In determining the range encompassed by terms of approximation such as 'about,' one must consider the context of the term as used in the specification and claims.
guidance: The meaning of 'about' and similar approximations depends on context and the disclosure; examiners should look to specification context, examples, figures, and recognized standards in the art to determine the range encompassed.

name: Statement to invoke joint research agreement (JRA) exception
description: Applicant or patent owner must provide a statement that the disclosure relied on by the rejection and the claimed invention were made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement under 35 U.S.C. 102(c).
guidance: The statement must also assert that the agreement was in effect on or before the effective filing date of the claimed invention, and that the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the joint research agreement. The statement should either be on or begin on a separate sheet and must not be directed to other matters (37 CFR 1.4(c)). The statement must be signed in accordance with 37 CFR 1.33(b). See 37 CFR 1.104(c)(4)(ii)(A).

name: Disclosure or amendment to disclose names of parties to JRA
description: The application for the claimed invention must disclose or be amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement.
guidance: 37 CFR 1.71(g)(1) permits the specification to be amended to disclose the name of each party to the JRA as required by 35 U.S.C. 102(c)(3). If names are not already stated in the application, an amendment is necessary to include them.

name: JRA effective-date and scope requirements
description: The joint research agreement must have been in effect on or before the effective filing date of the claimed invention, and the claimed invention must have been made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the JRA.
guidance: The JRA is not required to be in effect on or before the prior art date of the reference whose subject matter is to be excepted. If the JRA began after the effective filing date, or if the claimed invention was not made within the scope of the JRA, the JRA exception cannot be invoked (illustrated by Examples 1–3).

name: Examples to illustrate proper and improper invocation
description: Concrete examples show when the JRA/common-ownership exceptions will or will not apply (e.g., timing of JRA, scope of JRA activities, ownership allocations).
guidance: Example guidance: (1) If JRA existed prior to the effective filing date and claimed invention was made within JRA scope, the exception can be invoked (Example 1). (2) If JRA goes into effect after the application’s effective filing date, the exception cannot be invoked (Example 2). (3) If JRA exists but is limited to different activities and the claimed invention was not made as a result of activities within JRA scope, the exception cannot be invoked (Example 3). Use these factual distinctions when evaluating eligibility.

name: General Review of Disclosure
description: When an application is apparently ready for allowance, the examiner should review to make certain the whole application meets all formal and substantive (statutory) requirements and that the language of the claims is enabled by, and finds adequate descriptive support in, the application disclosure as originally filed.
guidance: Ensure claims are enabled and have written description support; confine disclosure to the invention claimed (limit summary/descriptive matter to be in harmony with claims); include sufficient background; check antecedent basis for claim terms; renumber claims per 37 CFR 1.126 and prepare examiner’s amendment if order changed; check abstract (limit 150 words) and title (short and specific); erase any pencil notes; review timeliness of amendments. See MPEP §1302.01, §608.01(c),(d), §608.01(o). Use form paragraphs 13.07 and 13.08 where applicable.

name: Ink and Format Requirements for Corrections
description: When correcting originally filed papers of applications with a paper application file wrapper, clean red ink must be used (not blue or black ink).
guidance: Informal corrections are initialed and dated in red ink; formal examiner’s amendments are entered by technical support staff. IFW applications require formal examiner’s amendments for corrections to the body of specification/claims.

name: Formal Examiner’s Amendment Use and Form Paragraphs
description: A formal examiner’s amendment may be used to correct all other informalities in the body of the written portions of the specification as well as all errors and omissions in the claims, but such corrections must be made by formal examiner’s amendment signed by the primary examiner and placed in the file with a copy sent to applicant.
guidance: A formal EA should include form paragraph 13.02 and form paragraph 13.02.01. Use form paragraph 13.02.02 if an extension of time is required. Formal EAs are not to be used in reexamination (use form paragraph 22.06). See MPEP §1302.04.

name: Limit on Examiner Making Substantive Changes Without Applicant Approval
description: No examiner’s amendment, whether formal or informal, may make substantive changes to the written portions of the specification, including the abstract, without obtaining applicant’s approval first.
guidance: Substantive changes to abstract at time of allowance must be by formal EA and require applicant approval. Courts have noted abstract may determine meaning of claims; examiners should review abstract for compliance with 37 CFR 1.72(b) early in prosecution. See Pandrol USA v. Airboss Railway, Hill-Rom v. Kinetic Concepts, and MPEP §1302.04.

name: Priority/Benefit Statements Location Requirement
description: Statements that an application is a division/continuation/continuation-in-part or claims benefit to an earlier filing should appear as the first sentence of the specification or in an application data sheet (with exceptions for design applications).
guidance: Helps ensure entitlement to earlier U.S. effective filing date under 35 U.S.C. §§120,121,365(c),119(e). If such statements appear elsewhere, relocate or make them in an ADS. CPA practice specifics noted (CPA practice eliminated effective July 14, 2003 for utility/plant). See MPEP §1302.04.

name: Title of Invention Specificity
description: Where the title of the invention is not specific to the invention as claimed, the examiner should ensure the title is made specific.
guidance: See MPEP §606.01. Examiner may change title on or after allowance if applicant has not supplied a satisfactory title.

name: Identification of Claims in Examiner’s Amendments
description: To identify a claim, a formal examiner’s amendment should refer to it by the original number and, if renumbered in the allowed application, also by the new number.
guidance: Use both original and renumbered claim numbers in EAs to avoid ambiguity. See MPEP §1302.04(g).

name: Interference Search Requirement
description: Assuming the application is ready for issue, the examiner makes an interference search and notes the date and class and subclasses searched in the file wrapper.
guidance: Inspect pending prints and drawings (or claims if invention not susceptible of illustration) in interference files of relevant subclasses and other pertinent classes to ascertain whether any other applicant is claiming substantially the same subject matter. If search discloses no interfering application, prepare application for issue. Note: interference searches may be required in specific TCs (e.g., Working Group 3640). See MPEP §1302.08 and §2301.01(b).

name: Selection of Claim(s) for Printing in Official Gazette
description: Select claim(s) to be printed according to defined rules: the broadest claim should be selected; ordinarily designate one claim per invention (up to max five if plurality of inventions); do not select a dependent claim unless the independent claim is also printed; for multiple dependent claims, list entire chain for one embodiment; for reissue select broadest claim with changes or broadest additional reissue claim.
guidance: Record the claim number(s) on file wrapper in black ink, separated by commas if multiple; use renumbered patent claim number. See MPEP §1302.09.

name: Format for Recording Claim Numbers and Print Figure
description: When recording the selected claim(s) and print figure, write claim number clearly in black ink; separate multiple claims with commas; refer to claim by renumbered patent claim number; select print figure consistent with the claim and not labeled 'prior art'; 'None' may be written if no figure appropriate.
guidance: Ordinarily select a single figure consistent with the printed claim; do not select a figure labeled prior art. See MPEP §1302.09.

name: Rejection After Allowance and Withdrawal for New Reference
description: A claim noted as allowable shall thereafter be rejected only with approval of the primary examiner. If a new reference is discovered that clearly applies to allowed claims, a memorandum is addressed to the TC Director requesting withdrawal from issue to apply the new reference.
guidance: Memorandum should cite the reference and briefly state its application; submit with reference and file wrapper (if paper). If request approved, TC Director withdraws application and examiner issues an Office action rejecting claims in view of the new reference. If issue fee paid and prosecution reopened applicant may request refund or credit or wait to see outcome. See MPEP §1308.01–.02 and §706.04.

name: Quality Review Program for Examined Patent Applications
description: The Office of Patent Quality Assurance administers a program reviewing the quality of examination of patent applications via randomly selected samples of allowed applications from each examiner, reviewed by Review Quality Assurance Specialists.
guidance: Review may include independent search; excludes applications with Board or court decisions. The reviewer may consult others (not the original examiner). Reviewed applications may be returned to TCs for consideration; if claims are determined unpatentable prosecution is reopened with form paragraph 13.04. Quality Assurance forms/papers are not to be included with Office actions or retained in the file; do not indicate in the record that QA review was conducted. See MPEP §1308.03.

name: Review for prior public use/on sale and best mode issues
description: Examiners must determine whether affidavits/declarations and accompanying evidence show that the claimed invention was "in public use" or "on sale" more than one year prior to the effective filing date (statutory bar under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)). If the 1.131(a) evidence relies on an embodiment not disclosed in the application, the best mode requirement must be considered.
guidance: A best mode rejection should not be made unless the record, taken as a whole, establishes by a preponderance of the evidence that the specification has not set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor (see MPEP §§ 2133.03 and 2165–2165.04).

name: 37 CFR 1.132 affidavits/declarations to traverse rejections
description: When any claim of an application is rejected or objected to, any evidence submitted to traverse the rejection on a basis not otherwise provided for must be by oath or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132. It is the primary examiner's responsibility to review and decide whether such affidavits/declarations and other traversing evidence are responsive and present sufficient facts to overcome the rejection.
guidance: Publications may be evidence of the facts at issue and should be considered to the extent probative and properly submitted. This rule is the general Office policy for receiving affidavit evidence traversing rejections when not covered by other specific rules.

name: Form paragraphs for 1.132 responses and categories of insufficiency
description: Use form paragraph 7.65 (affidavit/declaration effective to withdraw rejection) or 7.66 (insufficient) and form paragraphs 7.66.01–7.66.05 to explain specific reasons an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 is insufficient.
guidance: Reasons for insufficiency categories include: untimely; fails to set forth facts; facts not germane to the rejection; showing not commensurate in scope with claims. Examiner must include detailed explanation of why the affidavit/declaration is insufficient.

name: Reason 7.66.03 — Refers only to invention, not to individual claims
description: An affidavit that refers only to the system described in an application and not to the individual claims does not show the objective evidence of nonobviousness is commensurate in scope with the claims.
guidance: Ensure the affidavit ties evidence to the individual claim limitations; this form paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.66 and accompanied by a full explanation if appropriate.

name: Objective evidence (secondary considerations) must be considered when timely presented
description: Affidavits/declarations containing evidence of criticality or unexpected results, commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, skepticism of experts, etc., must be considered by the examiner in determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103.
guidance: Comparative data in the specification intended to illustrate the claimed invention must be considered. While lack of objective evidence does not weigh in favor of nonobviousness, where a prima facie case of obviousness is established, failure to provide rebuttal evidence is dispositive.

name: Identify the 'Single Sentence Inventive Concept'
description: If you cannot fit the inventive concept into a single sentence, you do not yet have a clean invention.
guidance: Force yourself to write: 'The new thing is that ____ enables ____ by ____.' Use this single-sentence test to clarify and distill the core inventive idea; lack of a concise formulation indicates the concept is not yet well-defined for claiming.

name: Spec first, claims second, then iterate
description: Many practitioners write a complete spec, draft claims from it, then revise the spec to ensure every claim term has antecedent support and every claim element has at least three sentences of context in the spec.
guidance: Draft a comprehensive specification before or alongside claims; after drafting claims, go back and revise the spec so each claim term is grounded (antecedent support) and each claimed element is discussed in multiple sentences (recommendation: at least three sentences) to provide context and bolster written-description/enablement arguments.

name: Disclose generalizations, not just implementations
description: For each implementation choice you made, ask 'what is the general principle here?' and 'what other choices would also work?'
guidance: When describing embodiments, explicitly state the general principle underlying each implementation and provide at least two alternative ways to implement it. Avoid only describing a single concrete implementation; broad disclosure of alternatives supports broader claim scope and reduces enablement/written-description attacks.

name: Watch the 'heart of the invention' trap
description: If the spec repeatedly says 'the heart of the invention is X,' courts may construe every claim as requiring X.
guidance: Do not single out one feature as the 'heart' or essential element of the invention in the specification. Over-emphasizing one feature risks limiting claim construction; instead present the invention holistically and avoid language that makes a particular feature appear mandatory across all claims.

name: Anchor claim terms in defined concepts
description: If your claim uses an unusual term, define it explicitly: 'As used herein, X means Y.'
guidance: Provide explicit definitions in the specification for unusual or newly-coined claim terms. Courts and examiners give weight to explicit definitions, which can guide claim construction and reduce ambiguity. Use clear 'as used herein' language when introducing definitions.

name: Use multiple independent claims
description: A typical strong filing has 3-4 independent claims of different scope and type (method, system, apparatus, computer-readable medium).
guidance: Include several independent claims across claim categories (e.g., method, system/apparatus, computer-readable medium) and at different breadth levels. Treat each independent claim as an 'insurance policy'—if one path is invalidated or limited, others may survive. Vary scope to cover broad territory and valuable sub-regions.

name: Rectangle around the invention (claim scope layering)
description: Imagine the universe of all possible products. The invention occupies a small region. Each claim is a rectangle around some part of that region.
guidance: Draft the broadest claim to cover as much as possible without reading on prior art; draft narrower claims as smaller rectangles inside that broad rectangle to cover higher-value or fallback embodiments. Use this spatial analogy to plan claim scope, overlap, and fallback positions strategically.

name: Consider litigation survivability
description: A claim with 12 elements, each cited in a different prior art reference, will likely face an obviousness challenge. A claim with 6 elements where the inventive concept is concentrated in 2-3 specific elements is harder to attack with a multi-reference combination.
guidance: Assess how easy it would be for an opponent to combine prior art references against your claims. Prefer concentrating the inventive concept into fewer, critical claim elements rather than spreading it thin across many elements, and design claims to reduce vulnerability to obviousness arguments based on combining multiple references.

name: Get foreign counterparts in mind early
description: If you plan to file in Europe, draft with European requirements in mind from the start: avoid US-specific drafting tricks (Markush groupings work differently), keep the spec carefully neutral on prior art, and include problem-solution framing that EPO examiners find natural.
guidance: When global filing is anticipated, adapt drafting tactics to foreign offices' standards (e.g., EPO). Avoid relying on U.S.-centric drafting approaches that may be ineffective or harmful abroad (be cautious with Markush/grouping, prior-art statements, etc.). Include neutral problem-solution statements and other disclosures that harmonize with foreign prosecution practices to preserve flexibility and claim scope internationally.

name: Variant Embodiments Within Scope of Claim
description: Variant Embodiments Within Scope of Claim

name: Caution about correlated patent characteristics and interpretation
description: Many patent metrics are highly correlated (e.g., number of claims, prior art types, number of applications, forward citations) because applicants anticipating value/difficulty tend to draft differently and cite more art.
guidance: Be mindful of common-cause and reverse causation: applicant behavior (more claims, continuations, citations) both reflects and creates perceived value and later citation patterns. Correlations complicate multivariate analysis; small sample sizes further limit statistical power. Use robustness checks and be explicit about causal limitations.

name: Elimination of deceptive-intent requirements
description: Section 16 (subsections (a)–(h)) reinserts language eliminating various deceptive-intent requirements relating to correcting the naming of the inventor, obtaining a retroactive foreign filing license, seeking section 251 reissue, or enforcing remaining valid claims if a claim is invalidated.
guidance: Eliminating deceptive-intent requirements moves the U.S. patent system away from subjective intent focus toward a more objective, evidence-based system that will be cheaper to litigate and more efficient to administer.

name: Section 5(g) submission of patent-owner statements to the Office
description: Section 5(g) modifies section 301 of title 35 to allow any person to submit to the Office the patent owner’s statements in federal court or in any Office proceeding about the scope of the patent’s claims.
guidance: This submission mechanism helps the Office determine whether a patent reads on products or services characteristic of financial institutions (relevant to deciding whether a patent is a covered business-method patent).

name: Form and content requirements of the petition
description: A petition under 37 CFR 1.292 must be submitted in writing, must specifically identify the application to which the petition is directed by application number or serial number and filing date, and should include a listing of all affidavits or declarations and exhibits relied on.
guidance: The petition must contain a sufficient description of the subject matter alleged to have been in public use or on sale, including necessary photographs, drawings, diagrams, exhibits, or flowcharts to enable the examiner to compare the claimed subject matter to the alleged public use/on-sale subject matter. The petition and accompanying papers must either (A) reflect that a copy has been served upon the applicant or applicant’s attorney/agent of record, or (B) be filed with the Office in duplicate if service is not possible. The petition itself should be clearly identified as a “PETITION UNDER 37 CFR 1.292.”

name: Prima facie showing standard for public use/on-sale
description: A prima facie case is established by the petition if the examiner finds that the facts asserted in the affidavit(s) or declaration(s), as supported by the exhibits, if later proved true by testimony taken in the public use proceeding, would result in a statutory bar to the claims under 35 U.S.C. 102(b) alone or in combination with 35 U.S.C. 103.
guidance: To make this determination the examiner must identify exactly what was in public use or on sale, whether it was in use or on sale in this country more than one year before the effective filing date, and whether the pending claims 'read' on or are obvious over what has been shown to be in public use or on sale. Compare all pending claims with the matter alleged to have been in use or on sale, not just those identified by petitioner.

name: Petition requirements when alleging obviousness
description: Where the petition alleges only that the claims are obvious over subject matter asserted to be in public use or on sale, the petition should include prior art or other information on which it relies and explain how the prior art or other information in combination with the subject matter asserted to be in public use or on sale renders the claims obvious.
guidance: The examiner is not expected to make a search of the prior art in evaluating the petition. However, if the examiner is aware of prior art or other information which, in the examiner's opinion, renders the claims obvious over the subject matter asserted to be in public use or on sale, the examiner may determine that a prima facie case is made out even if petition alleged only anticipation under 35 U.S.C. 102(b).

name: Examiner reporting requirements to Patent Legal Administrator
description: After making a prima facie determination, the examiner will forward a memorandum to the Patent Legal Administrator stating findings and decision as to whether a prima facie case has been established.
guidance: Findings should include a summary of the alleged facts, a comparison of at least one claim with the device alleged to be in public use or on sale, and any other pertinent facts to aid the Patent Legal Administrator in conducting the preliminary hearing. The report should be prepared in triplicate and addressed to the Patent Legal Administrator.

name: Review and appeal limitations
description: There is no review from the final decision of the examiner in the public use proceedings except limited supervisory review under 37 CFR 1.181 for clear error.
guidance: A petition under 37 CFR 1.181 requesting Commissioner to vacate the examiner's decision will not be entertained except where there is a showing of clear error. Once the application returns to ex parte status, appellate review under 35 U.S.C. 134 and 141-145 may be had of any adverse rejection of claims resulting from examiner's decisions as to public use or sale.

name: Duty to disclose 'material' information (trade secret/proprietary/protective order context)
description: Inventors and others covered by 37 CFR 1.56(c) and 1.555 have a duty to disclose to the Office information they are aware of which is material to patentability. 37 CFR 1.56(b) states information is material to patentability when it is not cumulative to information already of record and (1) establishes by itself or in combination a prima facie case of unpatentability of a claim; or (2) refutes or is inconsistent with a position the applicant takes in opposing unpatentability or asserting patentability.
guidance: A prima facie case of unpatentability is established when the information compels a conclusion that a claim is unpatentable under the preponderance of evidence standard, giving each claim term its broadest reasonable construction consistent with the specification, before considering evidence to establish a contrary conclusion. The obligation to disclose is the same whether the information is trade secret, proprietary, or subject to protective order.

name: Subject matter eligibility (35 U.S.C. 101)
description: Subject Matter Eligibility: guidance, examples, and training materials related to determining whether claimed subject matter is patent eligible under 35 U.S.C. 101.
guidance: Listed as 'Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance, Examples, and Training' (training modules and guidance referenced). Note: other training materials (e.g., written description materials) may include examples that now require further analysis for subject matter eligibility in view of recent law changes.

name: Examining computer-implemented functional claim limitations (35 U.S.C. 112 compliance)
description: Training focused on how to examine computer-implemented functional claim limitations for compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112.
guidance: Listed as 'Examining Computer-Implemented Functional Claim Limitations for Compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112' with Computer-Based Training (CBT) [posted 3/28/2019] and PowerPoint [posted 3/27/2019].

name: 35 U.S.C. 112(a) — Enablement
description: Training and guidance addressing enablement under 35 U.S.C. 112(a), with focus on electrical/mechanical and computer/software-related claims.
guidance: Computer Based Training (CBT) and PowerPoint: 'Examining Claims for Compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(a): Part II - Enablement = Focus on Electrical/Mechanical and Computer/Software-related Claims' (CBT posted 10/15/2015; PPT posted 10/07/2015).

name: 35 U.S.C. 112(b) — Definiteness and functional language
description: Guidance on ensuring claims are definite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b), including handling functional language and claim clarity.
guidance: Items include 'Enhancing Clarity By Ensuring That Claims are Definite Under 35 U.S.C. 112(b)' (PowerPoint [posted May 20, 2016]) and 'Functional Language Workshop: Claim Interpretation And Definiteness Under 35 U.S.C. 112(b)' (PPT [posted September 8, 2016]). Hands-on examples and worksheets provided (Ultrasonic Surgical Shears, Laundry Detergent, Computerized Color Editing) along with blank worksheets and answer keys.

name: 35 U.S.C. 112(f) — Means-plus-function limitations
description: Standards and procedures for addressing means-plus-function claim limitations under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) in office actions and examination practice.
guidance: Materials: 'Addressing 35 U.S.C. § 112(F) or "Means-plus-Function" Limitations in an Office Action using New Form Paragraphs' Computer Based Training (CBT) [posted March 27, 2018]; Sample Office Action (PDF) and PDF of CBT [posted March 27, 2018]; Instructor-led training PPT and example background/claims and office actions for Chemical (Laundry Detergent), Electrical (Computerized Color Editing System), Mechanical (Ultrasonic Surgical Shears) (all PDFs posted March 27, 2018). Public comments invited to TrainingComments112f@uspto.gov. Also includes 'Supplementary Examination Guidelines for Determining Compliance With 35 U.S.C. 112' (signed January 21, 2011).

name: Functional language worksheets and hands-on examples
description: Practical exercises and worksheets to apply claim-definiteness and functional-language analysis in concrete hypothetical claim sets.
guidance: Hands-On Examples and Functional Language Worksheets include: Example 1 (Ultrasonic Surgical Shears), Example 2 (Laundry Detergent), Example 3 (Computerized Color Editing), Blank worksheets, supporting reference info, and answer keys for each example.

name: Examining functional claim limitations — focus on computer/software-related claims
description: CBT focused on examining functional claim limitations with emphasis on computer/software-related claims.
guidance: Computer Based Training 'Examining Functional Claim Limitations: Focus on Computer/Software-related Claims' [CBT posted June 30, 2015] and PowerPoint [posted June 30, 2015].

name: Broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) and plain meaning of claim terms
description: Training on applying the broadest reasonable interpretation standard and determining the plain meaning of claim terms during examination.
guidance: Computer Based Training (CBT) 'Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) and the Plain Meaning of Claim Terms' [CBT posted March 3, 2015] and PowerPoint [posted March 3, 2015].

name: Completion of examination before contested case (37 CFR 41.102)
description: Before a contested case is initiated, except as the Board may otherwise authorize, for each involved application and patent: (a) examination or reexamination must be completed, and (b) there must be at least one claim that: (1) is patentable but for a judgment in the contested case, and (2) would be involved in the contested case.
guidance: Ensures there is an examinable claim that remains if the contested issue resolves against the party; used to determine readiness for Board contested proceedings.

name: Considerations for merging vs staying — case-by-case analysis
description: The decision on whether to merge the proceedings or stay a proceeding will be made on a case-by-case basis based upon the various proceedings. The status of the reissue application and the reexamination proceeding will be taken into account.
guidance: Examples: (A) reissue about to issue — delay determination until reissue granted and base reexamination on reissue claims; (B) reissue pending — merge narrower reexamination with broader reissue when desirable; (C) reexamination underway — consider status such as appeals or Notice of Intent to Issue a Reexamination Certificate. Cases on appeal or to courts alter merger likelihood.

name: Handling when reissue issues before reexamination determination (use reissue claims as starting point; form paragraph 22.05)
description: If a reissue patent issues before determination on the reexamination request must be made, the determination should normally be delayed until after the granting of the reissue patent; the reexamination, if ordered, would then be on the reissue patent claims rather than the original patent claims.
guidance: Reexamination starting claims must be presented as a 'clean copy' (bracketed words absent, added words not italicized). Where reissue patent has issued, use form paragraph 22.05 to state subsequent proceedings will be based on reissue claims.

name: Submission requirement under 37 CFR 1.114
description: A 'submission' as used in 37 CFR 1.114 includes, but is not limited to, an information disclosure statement (IDS), an amendment to the written description, claims, or drawings, new arguments, or new evidence in support of patentability. If a reply to an Office action under 35 U.S.C. 132 is outstanding, the submission must meet the reply requirements of 37 CFR 1.111.
guidance: A request for suspension of action, an appeal brief or a reply brief (or related papers) will not be considered a submission under 37 CFR 1.114, but the submission may consist of arguments in a previously filed appeal brief or reply brief or incorporate them by reference. Previously filed after-final amendments (whether or not entered) may satisfy the submission requirement. See 37 CFR 1.114(c) and 1.111.

name: Claims giving conditions of application can validly embrace various devices
description: If the conditions of the application of a principle are given and means of making it are furnished, the claim is not necessarily void; the inventor may define conditions which form the limits of his invention, and those conditions may embrace many devices or forms differing from those used by the patentee.
guidance: Example: Neilson's patent (hot blast) was upheld because he gave conditions admitting various heating apparatus. The key is to ascertain and articulate the conditions limiting the asserted invention so the scope is not merely conjectural.

name: Avoid separating the principle from necessary means in drafting (draft to the application by means)
description: To avoid claiming an abstract principle, the specification and claims should use appropriate terms signifying that the application of the principle is claimed as effected by the means used and described by the patentee and by all other means which, applied within the just scope of his conditions, will perform the like office.
guidance: No universal formula of words exists; formularies are of little use. Use language that ties the claimed application to concrete means and to equivalents within the stated conditions. Anti-pattern: drafting broad language that purports to claim a principle irrespective of implementation (e.g., Morse's overly general claim).

name: Process claims must recite the process/means, not merely the desired result
description: A process claim that merely names the result (e.g., 'rendering the system insensible to pain') without specifying anything beyond a well-known, ordinary process (e.g., inhalation of vapor) is not a patentable process; coupling a result to a known means does not create patentability.
guidance: A process must include novel or particular steps or instruments beyond the ordinary function to be patentable. Claiming only the effect produced by old agents and old means is insufficient. Draft process claims to recite the operative steps or new mode of application.

name: Breadth of claim depends on inventor's disclosure and position in order of invention
description: An inventor who gives conditions that admit application of a principle by various means (and who stands in the order of invention to justify such a claim) may legitimately claim the broader application; conversely, a general claim that is unlimited as to conditions (as in Morse) is invalid.
guidance: Assess whether the patentee provided the necessary conditions or rule of action to support a broader claim; if not, the claim should be restricted to what the patentee truly described and enabled.

name: Petition content and filing limits
description: Petitions must include detailed identification of grounds, claim constructions, and where each claim element is found in the prior art; filings are subject to a 14,000-word limit per petition (37 C.F.R. § 42.104(b); 37 C.F.R. § 42.24(a)(1)(i)).
guidance: Do not attempt to incorporate arguments by reference (37 C.F.R. § 42.6(a)(3)). If over the 14,000-word limit, petitioner may seek waiver under 37 C.F.R. § 42.24(a)(2). The petition should stand on its own with detailed identification of grounds and claim constructions, including construction of means-plus-function terms and mapping of elements to prior art.

name: Timing and scope of petitions relative to district-court contentions
description: Practical advice: wait for the patent owner's preliminary infringement contentions from district court to see which claims are asserted before deciding which claims and issues to challenge in an IPR petition.
guidance: Where a district court infringement matter is pending, obtaining the plaintiff's preliminary infringement contentions can inform which claims are actually in dispute and allow a more targeted PTAB petition, avoiding unnecessary challenges and conserving word count.

name: Definition of obviousness-type (nonstatutory) double patenting
description: Under the doctrine of obviousness-type double patenting, the USPTO rejects patentably indistinct claims when the subject applications/patents and the applications/patents whose claims form the basis of the nonstatutory double patenting: (1) have the same inventive entity, at least one common (joint) inventor, a common applicant, and/or a common owner/assignee; or (2) are not commonly owned but are owned by parties to a joint research agreement.
guidance: Explains why obvious variants across same or different patent families may create nonstatutory double patenting rejections and motivates the use of terminal disclaimers to obviate such rejections.

name: Statutory disclaimer recording requirements (§1.321(a))
description: A patentee disclaiming any complete claim(s) or dedicating term must ensure the disclaimer: (1) is signed by the patentee or an attorney/agent of record; (2) identifies the patent and complete claim(s) or term being disclaimed; (3) states the present extent of the disclaimant’s ownership interest; and (4) is accompanied by the fee set forth in §1.20(d).
guidance: Notice of the disclaimer is published in the Official Gazette and attached to printed copies of the specification; the disclaimer is binding on the disclaimant and successors/assigns and must be recorded in the PTO.

name: Enforcement condition for terminal disclaimers filed to obviate nonstatutory double patenting (§1.321(c)(3))
description: A terminal disclaimer filed to obviate nonstatutory double patenting must include an agreement that the subject patent (or any patent granted on its application) shall be enforceable: (i) only for and during such period that it is commonly owned with the reference patent (or any patent granted on the reference application); and (ii) only if the subject patent is not tied and has never been tied directly or indirectly to a patent by one or more terminal disclaimers filed to obviate nonstatutory double patenting in which: (A) a claim has been finally held unpatentable or invalid under 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103 by a Federal court or at the USPTO with all appeals exhausted; or (B) a statutory disclaimer of a claim is filed after any challenge based on 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103 to that claim has been made.
guidance: This proposed additional enforcement agreement is voluntary in the sense it is part of the terminal disclaimer language required for issuance; it does not adjudicate claim validity but conditions enforceability to reduce the burden on challengers who otherwise might need to invalidate multiple tied patents. The terminal disclaimer remains unidirectional (binds only the patent where it is filed).

name: Special enforcement/waiver provision for joint research agreement exceptions (§1.321(d))
description: When the reference patent/application is not commonly owned but was disqualified as prior art because of a joint research agreement, the terminal disclaimer must: (1) comply with b(2)–(4); (2) include signatures as required; and (3) include a provision waiving the right to separately enforce the subject patent and the reference patent and agreeing the subject patent shall be enforceable: (i) only while the subject patent and the reference patent are not separately enforced; and (ii) only if the subject patent is not tied and has never been tied directly or indirectly to a patent by one or more terminal disclaimers filed to obviate nonstatutory double patenting in which (A) a claim has been finally held unpatentable/invalid under 102/103 with appeals exhausted; or (B) a statutory disclaimer of a claim is filed after any challenge under 102/103 to that claim has been made.
guidance: This paragraph tailors the enforcement limitation to cases where the reference was excepted from prior-art status under joint research agreement rules, requiring an express waiver of separate enforcement in addition to the tying/invalidity conditions.

name: Meaning of 'a claim has been finally held unpatentable or invalid'
description: ‘Finally held unpatentable’ refers to a final determination by the USPTO in an AIA trial or a reexamination proceeding that one or more claims are unpatentable after all appeals or appeal rights are exhausted; ‘finally held . . . invalid’ relates to a final decision entered in a Federal court in a civil action holding one or more claims invalid after all appeals or appeal rights are exhausted.
guidance: This definition establishes the trigger condition for the proposed enforceability-limiting agreement in terminal disclaimers (i.e., when tied patents become unenforceable because a tied patent’s claim was finally invalidated over prior art). The proposed agreement cannot be avoided by filing a statutory disclaimer under 35 U.S.C. 253(a) after a 102/103 challenge has been made.

name: Proposed terminal disclaimer is not an admission of obviousness or requirement to stipulate patentable indistinctness
description: The USPTO opted not to propose a rule requiring a stipulation that the claims are not patentably distinct, and the proposed rule does not require treating filing a terminal disclaimer as an admission of obviousness.
guidance: The preamble explains comments received for and against treating terminal disclaimers as admissions; cites case law (e.g., SimpleAir, Motionless Keyboard, Ortho Pharm., Quad Envtl.) that filing a terminal disclaimer is not an admission on the merits. The proposed agreement conditions enforceability but 'does not concern the validity of claims.'

name: Practical alternatives to filing a terminal disclaimer with the proposed agreement
description: Applicants facing a nonstatutory double patenting rejection may avoid filing a terminal disclaimer with the proposed agreement by: (1) combining the conflicting claims into a single application; (2) canceling or amending conflicting claims in the application or the other application; (3) arguing that rejected claims are patentably distinct from the claims of the reference patent/application; or (4) filing a reissue application of the patent whose claims formed the basis to add canceled conflicting claims (provided no new matter is introduced).
guidance: Applicants may also separate patentably distinct claims into another application and file a terminal disclaimer with the proposed agreement only in the application having indistinct claims. If claims are amended after filing a terminal disclaimer so they no longer conflict, an applicant may petition under 37 CFR 1.182 to withdraw the terminal disclaimer prior to issuance to avoid the proposed agreement’s effects.

name: Check applicant interview summary for accuracy
description: Applicant’s summary of what took place at the interview should be carefully checked to determine the accuracy of any argument or statement attributed to the examiner during the interview.
guidance: If an inaccuracy directly affects patentability, point it out in the next Office letter. If claims are allowable for other reasons, examiner should send a letter setting forth his/her version. If record is complete and accurate, place 'Interview record OK' on the paper recording the interview with date and examiner initials.

name: Interviews after application sent to issue are generally not appropriate
description: After an application is sent to issue, an interview that would involve a detailed consideration of claims sought to be entered and discussion of prior art to determine allowability should not be given because the application is technically no longer under the primary examiner's jurisdiction (37 CFR 1.312).
guidance: Amendments presented informally after issuance cannot be demanded as a matter of right; requests for interviews on cases where a notice of allowance has been mailed require Technology Center Director approval and a written showing of extraordinary circumstances.

name: Amendment document sectioning and order
description: Each section of an amendment document (Specification Amendments, Claim Amendments, Drawing Amendments, and Remarks) must begin on a separate sheet to facilitate indexing and electronic scanning.
guidance: Recommended order: (A) cover sheet/table of contents with application info and page locations; (B) 'Amendments to the Specification' (separate sheet); (C) 'Amendments to the Claims' (separate sheet) including complete listing of all claims ever presented; (D) 'Amendments to the Drawings' (separate sheet) describing drawing changes; (E) remarks section (separate sheet); (F) any drawings including Replacement/New/Annotated sheets.

name: Specification amendment methods and identification
description: Amendments to the specification (other than claims, computer listings, sequence listings) must be made by adding, deleting or replacing a paragraph, by replacing a section, or by a substitute specification.
guidance: Amendment must unambiguously identify the paragraph to be modified (paragraph number, page/line, or other unambiguous method) and be accompanied by replacement/new paragraphs. Replacement paragraphs must include markings showing changes; new paragraphs presented in clean form without underlining.

name: Exception for examiner’s amendments
description: Changes to the specification, including the claims, made by the Office in an examiner’s amendment may be made by specific instructions identifying precise insertion/deletion points, and compliance with certain paragraphs of 1.121 is not required for examiner’s amendments.
guidance: Examiner's amendments have special procedural leeway compared to applicant-filed amendments.

name: Must invent and describe some mode of carrying the principle into effect
description: The patentee must have invented and described some mode of carrying the principle into effect; he may or may not have invented new devices, but must show a practical means of effecting the application.
guidance: A specification that simply states a principle without pointing out a mode of conducting the process will be treated as a mere principle and the patent will be invalid. Practitioners should avoid separating the principle from the means of applying it in the specification and claim.

name: Claims that are overly general or claim a principle in the abstract are invalid
description: A claim framed generally for doing something 'by any method' or claiming an art/principle in the abstract is too large and general and cannot be supported as a specification.
guidance: Examples: claims 'for making gas direct from seeds' without method were held too general; claiming an 'art' (e.g., cutting ice by any non-human power) in the abstract is improper and void unless limited to particular machines or methods.

name: Proper claim scope should embrace described means and equivalents performing the same function
description: A valid claim to an application of a principle should be so stated as to embrace directly or by implication the particular means described for the application and all other means which will substantially perform the like office in the application.
guidance: Courts may treat later-invented contrivances that substantially perform the same function as equivalent or substituted means (Neilson's hot-blast pipes were treated as equivalent). But claim scope depends on whole specification and surrounding facts.

name: Disclaimers can narrow claims and limit the patent's scope
description: A patentee may file a disclaimer that limits the original broad claim to a particular described mode, thereby avoiding invalidity for overbreadth but reducing the reach of the patent.
guidance: Courts will enforce the patent as so limited; a disclaimer may prevent assertion that the patent covers all modes of applying the principle, but also precludes asserting broader coverage against defendants (see Seed v. Higgins and later appeals).

name: A technical claim that appears too general may be saved by construing it with the whole specification
description: If a technical claim is apparently open to criticism as too general or abstract, it may be saved by a construction that fairly gathers the patentee's intention from the whole specification (i.e., limiting impliedly to the means shown).
guidance: Courts will consider the specification as a whole to determine whether the patentee intended to claim the principle abstractly or only its application by the described means.

name: Application-of-principle plus mechanical contrivances may be treated as part of the invention (basis for infringement vs improvement)
description: The new application of a principle by mechanical contrivances can be regarded as part of the invention itself, and subsequent different or improved modes of application may, in some views, be considered improvements that could still infringe without the patentee's consent.
guidance: This doctrine is suggested in Foote v. Silsby: variation of the means, even if an improvement, might be treated as an infringement if it performs the same application of the principle, but courts’ application varies with claim language, prior art, and disclaimer.

name: Claims framed as an 'art' or 'principle' rather than a machine or specific method are suspect
description: Claims that purport to claim an 'art' or general principle (for example, 'the art of cutting ice by non-human power') instead of a particular machine or method are improper and usually cannot form the basis of a patent.
guidance: Such language is often surplusage or fatal; the proper subject for a patent is a machine, manufacture, composition of matter, or a specific practical process, not an abstract 'art' without operative limiting detail.

name: Mayo two-prong framework — prong two: 'inventive concept' requirement
description: 'Do the claims contain an "inventive concept" that is sufficient to transform the claimed abstract idea into a patent-eligible application?'
guidance: The second prong examines whether claim elements, individually and 'as an ordered combination,' supply an inventive concept that transforms the ineligible concept into a patent-eligible application. The Court stated that mere instructions to 'apply' an abstract idea are insufficient. Examples: In Alice, the Court found the claims did little more than tell practitioners to implement an abstract idea on a general-purpose computer and thus lacked an inventive concept.

name: 'Significantly more' requirement
description: The Court requires that eligible patent claims must recite 'significantly more' than just the ineligible law of nature (or abstract idea) and routine applications thereof.
guidance: The opinion treats 'significantly more' as a necessary but unelaborated threshold—raising questions about how much additional material is needed. Practitioners must assess whether added claim limitations supply substantive technical contribution beyond the abstract concept and routine practice.

name: Conventional, well-known steps at a high level of generality are insufficient
description: Appending conventional steps (i.e., steps 'well known in the art'), specified only at a high level of generality, does not supply the inventive concept required by Mayo prong two.
guidance: Mayo itself showed that adding conventional, routine activity described in broad terms will not transform an ineligible concept into a patentable application. Avoid high-level recitations of routine industry practices as purportedly inventive claim elements.

name: Improvement to computer functioning or another technology can support eligibility
description: Claims that improve the functioning of the computer itself or effect an improvement in another technology or technical field may be patent-eligible.
guidance: Diehr illustrated that nonconventional application of technology (e.g., using a thermocouple in a particular way to improve rubber curing) supports eligibility. The Alice Court noted claims that 'purport to improve the functioning of the computer itself' or effect technological improvements are more likely to pass Section 101 analysis. Guidance for drafters: tie the invention to concrete technological improvements rather than abstruse business aims.

name: Technological-foundation / 'technological arts' consideration (higher scrutiny for business methods)
description: Claims having a more significant technological foundation are more likely to recite patentable subject matter; by contrast, business-method claims (pure 'business concepts') are more likely to be deemed abstract.
guidance: Although the Federal Circuit previously found the 'technological arts' test unworkable, Alice demonstrates the Court looks to technological aspects—whether claims address a technological problem or improve technology. Practitioners prosecuting business-method claims should consider expressly tying claims to technological improvements to reduce risk of invalidation.

name: Evaluate claims 'as an ordered combination' as well as element-by-element
description: Mayo's second prong examines claim elements individually and 'as an ordered combination' to determine whether the combination supplies an inventive concept.
guidance: Even if individual elements are conventional, their particular ordered combination could supply an inventive concept—but in Alice viewing the claim as a whole still failed to supply the inventive concept. Drafters should consider whether a specific sequence or combination yields a technical improvement.

name: Presence of hardware/computer components does not guarantee eligibility
description: The mere presence of hardware and computerized functions in claims does not ensure patent eligibility if those elements are generic and conventional.
guidance: Alice rejected system and medium claims because they merely recited generic and conventional computer components for implementing the same abstract idea as the method claim. Practitioners should avoid relying on token hardware recitations and instead specify concrete, nonconventional computer/architectural improvements.

name: Prosecution drafting recommendation: lower abstraction and include implementation details
description: Practitioners may need to adopt claim-drafting techniques that target a lower level of abstraction, including incorporating implementation details into claims that illustrate an improvement of the functioning of a computer, technology, or technical field.
guidance: The article recommends incorporating implementation details, describing how the invention improves computer operation or other technology, and avoiding broad, high-level formulations of business methods. These tactical steps can help meet the Mayo 'inventive concept' requirement and fend off Section 101 challenges.

name: Enablement requirement — enable full scope of the claims
description: "If a patent claims an entire class of processes, machines, manufactures, or compositions of matter, the patent’s specification must enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the entire class. In other words, the specification must enable the full scope of the invention as defined by its claims." (Amgen, 143 S.Ct. at 1254)
guidance: Key principle: the specification must enable the full scope of claimed subject matter. Practical implication: when a claim seeks broad coverage (a genus), the specification must provide enabling disclosure across that claimed breadth. Courts will evaluate whether the specification enables "all of what is claimed, not merely a subset."

name: Amount of disclosure — examples plus a disclosed general quality can suffice
description: "The specification does not always need to 'describe with particularity how to make and use every single embodiment within a claimed class.' ... For instance, it may suffice to give an example (or a few examples) if the specification also discloses some general quality . . . running through the class that gives it a peculiar fitness for the particular purpose." (Amgen, 143 S.Ct. at 1254-55)
guidance: Guidance for sufficiency: specific examples can be adequate when paired with disclosure of a general, class-wide quality that reliably enables skilled artisans to make and use the full class. Evaluate whether the disclosed examples + general trait reasonably allow practice across the claimed genus.

name: Experimentation must be reasonable
description: "The specification may call for a reasonable amount of experimentation."
guidance: Permissible amount of follow-on work is limited to "reasonable" experimentation. Courts assess whether the experimentation required to practice the claim is reasonable given the nature of the invention and the underlying art; excessive or undue experimentation indicates lack of enablement.

name: The more claimed, the more must be enabled (claim breadth vs disclosure)
description: "The more one claims, the more one must enable." (Amgen, 143 S.Ct. at 1254)
guidance: Rule of thumb: broader claim scope demands proportionally greater enabling disclosure. Narrow claims covering specific embodiments require less expansive disclosure than claims that assert an entire class or "kingdom" of subject matter.

name: Wands factors are probative in enablement inquiries
description: Although the Supreme Court did not cite Wands, "the Wands factors appear at least probative of the essential inquiry in determining whether one must engage in reasonable experimentation."
guidance: Use the Wands factors (level of ordinary skill, predictability of the art, amount of guidance in the disclosure, presence of working examples, breadth of the claims, nature of the invention, and the quantity of experimentation necessary) as an evidentiary framework to assess enablement's reasonableness and scope. Courts (including CAFC) have applied Wands in evaluating enablement.

name: Written-description requirement (distinct but related)
description: Litigation history shows written description was separately evaluated (juries and courts assessed whether claims were adequately described).
guidance: Treat written description as a separate statutory requirement from enablement. A specification must demonstrate that the inventor possessed the claimed invention (written description) as well as teach how to make and use it (enablement). Procedural note: jury instructions and evidentiary rulings on written description can be pivotal in litigation.

name: Precedent/analogy to prior cases (Morse, Incandescent Lamp, Holland Furniture, Wood & Mineral Separation)
description: The Court analyzed Amgen in light of prior decisions: Morse, Incandescent Lamp, Holland Furniture, and Wood & Mineral Separation; these cases teach that claiming excessively broad subject matter without commensurate enablement fails.
guidance: Analogize to historical precedents that struck down claims attempting 'sovereignty over [an] entire kingdom' of subject matter. Consider lessons from older cases (e.g., that a specification may tolerate some experimentation but reasonableness depends on the invention and prior art).

name: Patent bargain (policy backdrop)
description: Patent bargain: Quid pro quo — Inventor discloses the invention; Inventor receives a limited term of protection. Congress has left the enablement requirement intact.
guidance: Policy reminder: enablement is rooted in the patent bargain — disclosure must be sufficient to justify the granted exclusion. This policy frame informs strictness of enablement analysis, especially for broad claims.

name: Always add general M210/M220 when specific M21/M22 used
description: One of the general codes M210 or M220 is always added to the code record when a specific code from Subset M21: or M22: is assigned.
guidance: Example: a propyl chain not multiply bonded to a heteroatom receives M210 and M213. Prior to 1981, specific codes in Subsets M21/M22 were only assigned if there were no polyvalent chains; from 1981 onward, specific codes are assigned only if chain length is specifically claimed or exemplified. For comprehensive retrieval, search M210 rather than specific chain lengths.

name: Set M4 Basic Group codes and priority assignment
description: M41 codes categorize compounds by general structural class (M411 inorganic/miscellaneous, M412 fused ring heterocyclic, M413 mononuclear heterocyclic, M414 carbocyclic aromatic, M415 alicyclic, M416 aliphatic, M417 incomplete structure disclosed). Only one M41 code is assigned per compound according to an ordered priority.
guidance: Priority: list is ordered; the first applicable code is selected (e.g., fused ring heterocycle takes precedence over aliphatic). Polymers use M423 (not M41). For inorganic salts, OR M411 with the subset code for free acid/base when searching. If M417 assigned, assign basic-group codes for all other compounds claimed or exemplified.

name: M710–M760: interpretations and historical application notes
description: Definitions: M710 New compound/intermediate; M720 Known compound is produced; M730 Compound used in synthetic process; M740 Apparatus; M750 Compound detected/removed; M760 Compound is medium for analysis/diagnosis.
guidance: Notes: M710 normally only for new compounds but from 1979 also used when compounds disclosed but not claimed new; therefore do not rely solely on M710 for novelty searches. M720 includes purification/extraction/separation (including optical isomers). M730 usage expanded post-1981. M750 and M760 consistently applied since ~1979 and include monoclonal antibody diagnostics and important solvents respectively. M740 implies inventive feature is apparatus and reduces emphasis on chemical features.

name: Part N coding precondition: process must be claimed and important
description: To be coded in Part N, a chemical process must be claimed and must be an important feature of the invention.
guidance: Set N0 (general) was used pre-1981; Sets N1–N5 are the more specific replacement. Check claims and whole patent wording to determine novelty/importance of a process (see notes on scope changes in 1979 and 1981).

name: Scope expansion rules for Part N (1979 and 1981 changes)
description: The scope of chemical reactions covered by Part N expanded in 1979 and 1981: earlier Part N codes were only used for processes producing known compounds; after 1979 and 1981 more processes (including those with novel features or novel natural materials) were coded.
guidance: From 1979 processes were coded even if end products were new when the process was claimed. From 1981 onward, Part N codes were assigned to processes having novel features even if all end products are new. Determine process novelty from the entire patent wording, not just claims.

name: Derwent Registry number assignment rules
description: Since 1981, Derwent Registry numbers assigned to starting materials and isolable intermediates, auxiliaries that provide atoms to organic products, auxiliaries limiting the invention, and all catalysts (provided compounds are mentioned in claims/examples and registry numbers exist).
guidance: Registry usage affects subsequent code generation/searchability (see 'Searching With Other Kinds of Codes').

name: Catalyst coding policy and Q421 subfield
description: From 1970 forward, novel catalysts or catalysts produced by novel processes receive fragmentation codes; from 1977 catalysts are searchable via CPI Section N Manual Codes; from 1981 catalysts in claims/examples are assigned to a separate code subfield with Q421.
guidance: If a catalyst is not stated to be novel and not produced by a novel process, only limited codes are assigned (applicable A/B sets, C0–C5 for inorganic elements significant to the catalyst, sets C6/C7 and Subset C81, a Basic Group code from M4, Q421 and M730 where applicable, and C8 for elements absent). Exception: alumina/aluminosilicate catalysts are not coded in A–M because they have specific CPI Section N Manual Codes.

name: Items required for complete and proper recordation of interview substance
description: The complete and proper recordation of the substance of any interview should include at least the following applicable items: (A) brief description of any exhibit shown or demonstration; (B) identification of the claims discussed; (C) identification of specific prior art discussed; (D) identification of principal proposed amendments of a substantive nature discussed; (E) general thrust of principal arguments of applicant and examiner; (F) general indication of any other pertinent matters discussed; (G) if appropriate, the general results or outcome of the interview unless already described in the Interview Summary form.
guidance: The identification of arguments need not be lengthy or elaborate; it is sufficient if the general nature or thrust of the principal arguments can be understood in the context of the application file. Where a complete record of the interview has been incorporated in an examiner's amendment, completion of the Interview Summary form may not be necessary.

name: Head of department generally has no authority to reopen a claim once duly settled
description: Under executive practice, a head of a department is generally not empowered, without specific statutory authority, to reopen a claim or controversy once duly settled by his predecessor; a successor may reopen only for fraud, lack of jurisdiction, manifest error on the face of the proceedings, or newly discovered evidence presented within a reasonable time and sufficient to warrant a new trial in law. Any public officer may, however, correct his own errors and reopen cases decided by himself.
guidance: Authorities and elaboration: Rollins and Presbrey v. U. S. and departmental practice; numerous Comptroller and Attorney General opinions cited (e.g., P. 34, 225, Aug. 1, 1889; 9 Op. Atty. Gen. 34). Reopening based on resolutions or committee reports is permissible for reexamination but such committee views are not binding; the Secretary must follow the statute and his own judgment.

name: Distinction between contractual unliquidated claims and damages founded on neglect or breach
description: Claims for money due on contracts where exact amount is not fixed are technically 'unliquidated damages' but arise from executed agreements and are normally susceptible to accounting; by contrast, claims for unliquidated damages founded on neglect or breach of obligations (not necessarily arising from contract) require extraneous proof and judicial liquidation and are not committed to Treasury accounting officers.
guidance: Quoted summary from Dennis v. U. S.: contractual claims are determinable by vouchers/reports; breach-based claims involve broad investigation and are for the courts (see Power's case, Brannen's case, Cramp & Sons v. U. S.).

name: Conditions for extension of patent term (§ 1.720)
description: The term of a patent may be extended if the patent and application satisfy specified conditions listed in paragraphs (a) through (h).
guidance: Conditions enumerated: (a) the patent claims a product or a method of using or manufacturing a product as defined in § 1.710; (b) the term of the patent has never been previously extended (except for extensions pursuant to §§ 1.701, 1.760, or 1.790); (c) an application for extension is submitted in compliance with § 1.740; (d) the product has been subject to a regulatory review period as defined in 35 U.S.C. 156(g) before commercial marketing/use; (e) the product has received permission for commercial marketing or use and (1) that permission is the first received permission for commercial marketing/use under the provision of law under which the applicable regulatory review occurred, or (2) for patents (other than certain recombinant DNA manufacturing claims), the permission is the first permitted commercial marketing/use of a product manufactured under the process claimed, or (3) special rule for new animal drugs or veterinary biological products addressing food-producing vs non-food-producing animals; (f) the application is submitted within the sixty-day period beginning on the date the product first received permission for commercial marketing/use (with special-case timing language for recombinant-DNA manufacturing claims and certain animal drug situations); (g) the patent term, including any interim extension under § 1.790, has not expired before submission in compliance with § 1.741; and (h) no other patent term has been extended for the same regulatory review period for the product.

name: Patent identification and documentary attachments (§ 1.740(a)(6)-(8))
description: Provide complete identification of the patent and copies of the patent and any post‑grant instruments.
guidance: Include inventor name(s), patent number, date of issue, date of expiration; a copy of the patent including the entire specification (including claims) and drawings; and copies of any disclaimer, certificate of correction, receipt of maintenance fee payment, or reexamination certificate issued in the patent.

name: Applicant's opinion of eligibility and claimed extension length (§ 1.740(a)(12))
description: A statement by the applicant that, in the applicant's opinion, the patent is eligible for extension and the length of extension claimed, including how the length was determined.
guidance: Begin on a new page and include a calculation or explanation of how the applicant computed the claimed extension length.

name: Complete application filing date and minimum elements (§ 1.741(a))
description: A 'complete application' receives a filing date only when certain minimum elements are included; these minimum elements are required to establish a filing date and trigger timing rights.
guidance: The filing date is the date a complete application is received via the USPTO electronic filing system or pursuant to § 1.8(a)(1)(i)(C) and (a)(1)(ii). A complete application must include: (1) identification of the approved product; (2) identification of each Federal statute under which regulatory review occurred; (3) identification of the patent for which extension is sought; (4) identification of each claim of the patent which claims the approved product or a method of using or manufacturing it; and (5) sufficient information to enable the Director to determine under subsections (a) and (b) of 35 U.S.C. 156 the eligibility of a patent for extension. If incomplete, the Office will notify the applicant and petition procedures and fees apply for review of completeness/filing date determinations.

name: Fundamental written description test
description: Does the description clearly allow persons of ordinary skill in the art to recognize that the applicant was in possession of the invention as of the filing date? (e.g., "does the description clearly allow persons of ordinary skill in the art to recognize that he or she invented what is claimed"; Vas-Cath, Gosteli).
guidance: Objective standard: whether the disclosure 'reasonably conveys to the artisan that the inventor had possession at that time of the later claimed subject matter.' Consider entire specification (words, structures, figures, diagrams, formulas).

name: Identifying characteristics sufficient to show possession
description: Disclosure of sufficiently detailed, relevant identifying characteristics (complete or partial structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics coupled with known correlation between function and structure) can show possession.
guidance: Examples for biomolecules: sequence, structure, binding affinity, binding specificity, molecular weight, length, unique cleavage by particular enzymes, isoelectric points, restriction enzyme maps, comparison of enzymatic activities, antibody cross-reactivity. Presence of such distinguishing characteristics that distinguish the claimed invention from others is sufficient.

name: Functional definition limitation
description: A definition by function alone 'does not suffice' to describe a coding sequence or other claimed subject matter unless coupled with known or disclosed correlation between function and structure.
guidance: Function-only recitations are often 'little more than a wish' (Eli Lilly, In re Wilder). In predictable arts where structure-function correlations exist, function + minimal structure may suffice (see Fonar for software).

name: Chemical/structural precision requirement
description: An adequate written description of a chemical invention generally requires a precise definition (structure, formula, chemical name, or physical properties), not merely a wish or plan for obtaining the chemical invention claimed.
guidance: Court examples: Univ. of Rochester v. G.D. Searle held methods/assays without disclosure of actual compounds insufficient to describe claimed methods of selective inhibition.

name: Means-plus-function (35 U.S.C. 112, para. 6) claim support
