description: If a claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112, paragraph 6, it must be interpreted to cover the corresponding structure, materials, or acts described in the specification and equivalents; written description must support the means/step-plus-function limitation.
guidance: Examiner must consider summary, detailed description, original claims, abstract, and drawings in assessing support. Adequacy under para.1 is met if: (1) written description adequately links adequately described particular structure/material/acts to the recited function; or (2) it is clear that one skilled in the art would have known what structure/material/acts perform the recited function. See MPEP §2181 and supplemental guidance.

name: Single embodiment/species analysis procedure
description: For each claim drawn to a single embodiment or species: (A) determine whether application describes an actual reduction to practice; (B) if not, determine whether reduction to drawings or structural formula sufficiently shows possession; (C) if not, determine whether other identifying characteristics sufficiently show possession.
guidance: If a complete structure (or acts of a process) is disclosed, the written description requirement is satisfied for that species and rejection must not be made. See Fields v. Conover for lack of 'full, clear, concise, and exact' description examples.

name: Factors to consider in possession determination
description: Whether the specification shows possession is a factual determination considering multiple factors.
guidance: Factors include level of skill and knowledge in the art, partial structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics alone or coupled with correlation between structure and function, and the method of making the claimed invention. Use patents and prior printed publications to gauge maturity of the art.

name: Genus claim written description (representative species) standard
description: A claimed genus may be supported by sufficient description of a representative number of species by actual reduction to practice, reduction to drawings, or disclosure of relevant identifying characteristics sufficient to show possession of the genus.
guidance: A 'representative number of species' must reflect variation within the genus. When substantial variation exists, more species must be described. Disclosure of only one species supports a genus only if disclosure indicates patentee invented species sufficient to constitute the genus.

name: One-species disclosure may sometimes support genus
description: A disclosure of only one species may support a genus if the disclosure indicates that the patentee has invented species sufficient to constitute the genus or where the specification conveys that broader coverage is intended and enablement/predictability justify it.
guidance: Cite examples: Rasmussen (one method supported 'adheringly applying' genus), Herschler (known chemical compounds in auxiliary use). But LizardTech and Tronzo show a single embodiment often cannot support expansive generic claim language.

name: New/amended claims and priority — examiner applicant burdens
description: For new or amended claims or claims asserting earlier priority/filing date, the examiner has the initial burden to present evidence or reasoning why skilled persons would not recognize in the original disclosure a description of the claimed invention; applicant should show support in the original disclosure for new/amended claims.
guidance: Applicants should specifically point out support for amendments (see MPEP §714.02 and §2163.06). Each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported; absence of explicit limitation requires showing a POSA would understand the description requires that limitation (Hyatt v. Boone).

name: Examiner's required findings when rejecting for lack of written description
description: When rejecting a claim for lack of written description, the examiner must set forth express findings of fact to support the conclusion.
guidance: Findings should (A) identify the claim limitation at issue; and (B) establish a prima facie case by providing reasons why a person skilled in the art at the filing date would not have recognized that the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention. A general allegation of 'unpredictability in the art' is not sufficient.

name: Literal wording not required but amended claims must be supported
description: Subject matter of the claim need not be described literally to satisfy the written description requirement; however, if a claim is amended to include subject matter not present in the application as filed, the claim should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, or benefit of an earlier filing date denied.
guidance: If amended claims involve departure/addition/deletion from original disclosure, the examiner should conclude the claimed subject matter is not described and take appropriate action.

name: Distinction between written description rejection and new matter objection
description: A lack of support in the original disclosure for claimed subject matter is addressed as a rejection under the written description requirement (35 U.S.C.112, first paragraph) or denial of priority; it should not be handled as an objection for new matter.
guidance: New matter objections address amendments that attempt to add disclosure not originally presented; while analysis for both issues is similar, statutory bases and procedures differ (Rasmussen).

name: Requirement that each claim include all elements applicant described as essential
description: Each claim must include all elements which applicant has described as essential or critical in the specification.
guidance: Failure to claim an element the applicant described as essential can be grounds for rejecting new/child claims or denying priority (citations: Johnson Worldwide Associates, Gentry Gallery, Tronzo).

name: Historical/claim-format considerations (business-method claim format as an established claim form)
description: The 'business method claim format' has been used in various forms historically, and some business-method patents present detailed, specific, and well-defined procedures that resemble engineering solutions rather than abstract ideas.
guidance: The article gives examples (e.g., a 2008 patent on valuing private equity investments) to show that some business-method patents are concrete and specific. This historical and technical context is relevant to assessing whether a claimed business method is an impermissible abstraction or a patentable application.

name: Protective order sealing and in-court disclosure procedures (paragraphs 6 & 7)
description: The protective order required designated confidential documents to be submitted to the court in a sealed envelope or other appropriate sealed container with certain markings (paragraph 6) and required notice to opposing counsel and the court prior to any in-court disclosure so the court may determine handling (paragraph 7).
guidance: When documents are subject to protective-order confidentiality, parties must follow the order's sealing and notice procedures before revealing them at trial or filing them under seal; failure to satisfy those procedures can undermine confidentiality claims.

name: Statutory status of higher and lower life forms
description: Lower life forms (e.g., microscopic algae; unicellular fungi; bacteria; protozoa; viruses; transformed cell lines; hybridomas; embryonic, pluripotent and multipotent stem cells) are treated differently from higher life forms (e.g., animals, plants, mushrooms, fertilized eggs and totipotent stem cells). A claim directed to a higher life form per se is generally non-statutory (outside the definition of "invention" in section 2 of the Patent Act).
guidance: Claims that are not directed to a higher life form per se but include a higher life form as a component (e.g., a composition, food product, or a use) may be statutory depending on the essential elements determined by purposive construction. If the claim is construed to be a use (e.g., use of X for animal feed) it will likely be statutory even if X is a higher life form; if construed as X or a product comprising X, it will be non-statutory. A higher life form that has been processed by significant chemical or physical modification may be construed as a manufacture. Examples: (i) claims to a plant or seed are non-statutory, whereas claims to a plant cell or a bacterial host cell transformed with a sequence are statutory; (ii) a transgenic pig claim is non-statutory, but a cell line or the use of the pig for producing odourless manure can be statutory depending on claim construction.

name: Patentability of processes to produce life forms is independent of product statutory status
description: A method or process may be patentable even if the product it produces is non-statutory. The patentability of a claimed process is assessed independently of whether its product is statutory.
guidance: Critical consideration is the degree of human intervention embodied in the claimed process. A process that occurs essentially according to nature with no significant human intervention is not patentable. A process is patent-eligible where at least one step of human intervention is an essential element of the claim. Examples of processes considered to include significant human intervention: producing a lower life form; producing a higher life form (if beyond traditional breeding); producing an organ or tissue via genetic transformation; in vitro culturing/manipulation of cells; processes to separate cells; generating mutants using chemical/physical agents. Example: a process comprising a transformation step followed by breeding and selection was statutory because the transformation step (significant human intervention) was an essential element; the resultant plant claim could nonetheless be non-statutory.

name: Purposive construction to identify essential elements
description: Assessment for patentability must be based on a purposive construction of the claim, not a mere literal interpretation. The essential elements identified by purposive construction determine whether a claim defines statutory subject-matter under section 2.
guidance: When a claim includes multiple steps, the examiner must identify which steps are essential to the inventor's solution of the identified problem. If essential elements are limited to traditional breeding steps (which are not significant human intervention), the claim may be non-statutory even if other, non-essential steps exist in the description. Examiners should determine the problem addressed by the application and the solution as contemplated by the inventor; where necessary, focus on the solution given the greatest emphasis in the description.

name: Bioinformatics — biomolecules versus information
description: Biomolecules (nucleic acids, polypeptides, proteins, peptides) are chemical compounds and claims to them are statutory. Biomolecules that express information through primary structure (sequence) are statutory as compounds. In contrast, information per se (e.g., atomic coordinates representing 3D structure) is non-statutory.
guidance: A claim to a polypeptide defined by its amino acid sequence is statutory. A claim to atomic coordinates of a protein (the coordinates themselves) is non-statutory because they are information. A claim to a protein comprising atomic coordinates (i.e., defining the molecule by coordinates) may be statutory. A computer model of a biomolecule that relies on structural information is not patentable (it equates to a graphical presentation of information); generic computer systems/programs merely configured to generate the model are excluded. However, the mere presence of a computer model of a biomolecule in a method (e.g., an in silico screening method) does not by itself render the method unpatentable—such a method can be statutory if the method as claimed meets other patentability requirements.

name: Dosage regimes and forms — when medical element renders claim non-statutory
description: Claims reciting a dosage regime or prescribed dosage amount may be directed to a method of medical treatment and thus non-statutory. By contrast, dosage forms, pharmaceutical packages or kits (physical items) are considered patentable subject matter.
guidance: Removing the medical aspect of a claim (e.g., recasting as non-medical, cosmetic, diagnostic) may render it acceptable if the description adequately supports the non-medical terminology and the claim can reasonably be understood as non-therapeutic. Use claims and kit/package claims that embody dosage forms may avoid the medical-treatment exclusion if drafted appropriately.

name: Kits and packages — definitions and claim drafting to satisfy clarity (subsection 27(4))
description: A 'package' is one or more components contained within conventional packaging material. A 'kit' is a specific type of package containing two or more components. When a pharmaceutical composition (a single formulated product) is a component in a kit, that unit dose is regarded as one component.
guidance: Claims must be defined distinctly and explicitly in accordance with subsection 27(4) of the Patent Act; the scope must be clear to the person skilled in the art. The term 'kit' must be construed as having a minimum of two components. A subsection 27(4) defect arises where the application defines a kit as consisting of only one component or where the description fails to describe components and the examiner construes the kit as having only one component. If the description or claim unambiguously defines the kit as containing at least two components, no defect exists. Multiple independent product claims (e.g., package, kit, package containing kit) may be present if clarity is preserved.

name: Claims of indefinite scope or ambiguity relating to kits/packages
description: Ambiguous or interchangeable use of 'kit' and 'package' can create a lack of clarity under subsection 27(4). A kit construed as consisting of only one component fails the clarity requirement.
guidance: Where a kit claim only explicitly defines one component, the claim may still comply with subsection 27(4) if there is basis in the description for a second component (e.g., examples of possible second components). Examiners should consider whether the skilled person would understand the kit as containing at least two components in view of the description and common general knowledge.

name: Medical diagnostic methods — structure and examination approach
description: A diagnostic method outlines a sequence of steps to extract diagnostic meaning from data and will often comprise steps to (i) acquire data about an analyte (identifying, detecting, measuring presence/quantity) and (ii) analyze the significance of the acquired data (correlating presence/level to a condition).
guidance: To determine patentability of diagnostic method claims, examiners must apply purposive construction (identify problem, inventor's solution, essential elements). The guidance applies to varied claim forms including direct methods of diagnosing, prognostic or predictive methods, 'use of' claims, kits for diagnosing, device claims (e.g., microarrays), use of compounds where diagnosis informs treatment, and computer-implemented diagnostic methods. The examiner should construe the claimed subject-matter to determine whether it is a diagnostic method per se.

name: Identifying the problem for diagnostic claims: data acquisition vs data analysis
description: Identification of the problem and solution informs purposive construction. For diagnostics, the inventor is generally solving a data acquisition problem and/or a data analysis problem.
guidance: Indicators of a data acquisition problem include disclosure of a novel/non-CGK analyte, a novel/non-CGK combination of biomarkers, a novel/non-CGK means to identify or quantify an analyte, application of a CGK identification means to a non-standard sample/population, performance within specific non-standard constraints (timing), explicit statements that the problem relates to identification/quantification, detailed technical description of acquisition, and emphasis on challenges/deficiencies of prior acquisition methods. Indicators of a data analysis problem include explicit statements that the problem is data analysis, emphasis on discovery of a new correlation between a (known) analyte and a condition with little technical detail on acquiring the analyte, indication that acquisition is CGK, and lack of any explicit indication that practical acquisition problems were solved. Examiners should use these factors to determine which problem is being addressed.

name: Determining the solution to the identified diagnostic problem
description: The solution is the element or set of elements essential to resolving the identified problem. For claims including solutions to more than one problem, examination should focus on one solution (guided by the description and the solution given greatest emphasis).
guidance: Where a data acquisition problem is identified, the solution comprises elements that provide means to acquire data about the analyte. The examiner must determine which claim elements are essential to the inventor's chosen solution and perform purposive construction accordingly; if a different solution must be considered, the analysis should be redone focusing on that solution.

name: Date of filing requirements
description: The date of filing is the date on which documents filed contain: (a) an indication that a European patent is sought; (b) designation of at least one Contracting State; (c) information identifying the applicant; (d) a description and one or more claims in one of the official languages, even if other requirements are not complied with.

name: Requirements for claims
description: The claims shall define the matter for which protection is sought; they shall be clear and concise and be supported by the description.

name: Claiming priority formalities
description: To claim priority the applicant must file a declaration of priority, a copy of the previous application and, if its language is not one of the EPO official languages, a translation in an official language; procedure in Implementing Regulations.
guidance: Multiple priorities permitted; priority covers only elements included in earlier application(s); elements not present among earlier claims can still be covered if the earlier application documents as a whole specifically disclose them.

name: Refusal and grant conditions
description: Examining Division shall refuse if application/invention does not meet requirements; shall decide to grant if they meet requirements provided: (a) applicant approves the text in which it intends to grant; (b) fees for grant and printing are paid within the time limit; (c) renewal and additional fees already due have been paid.
guidance: If fees not paid in due time the application is deemed withdrawn; decision to grant takes effect only when the Bulletin mentions the grant; translations of claims into the two other official languages may be required under Implementing Regulations, with time limits and failure to file leading to withdrawal.

name: Publication of granted patent specification
description: At the time the mention of grant is published, the EPO shall publish a specification of the European patent containing the description, claims and any drawings.

name: Revocation, rejection or maintenance as amended
description: The Opposition Division shall revoke the patent if grounds prejudice maintenance; reject the opposition if they do not; or decide to maintain the patent as amended provided the proprietor approves the text and the fee for printing a new specification is paid within the time limit.
guidance: Failure to pay printing fee leads to revocation; translations of amended claims into the two other official languages may be required and failure to file leads to revocation.

name: Publication of amended specification
description: If a European patent is amended under maintenance, the EPO shall publish a new specification containing the amended description, claims and any drawings simultaneously with the mention of the opposition decision.

name: Possession determination factors
description: Whether the specification shows that the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention is a factual determination reached by considering a number of factors.
guidance: Factors include the level of skill and knowledge in the art; partial structure; physical and/or chemical properties; functional characteristics alone or coupled with a known or disclosed correlation between structure and function; and the method of making the claimed invention. Disclosure of any combination of such identifying characteristics that distinguish the claimed invention from other materials and would lead one of skill in the art to conclude the inventor was in possession is sufficient.

name: Variation with nature and maturity of the art
description: The description needed to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112 varies with the nature and scope of the invention and with the scientific and technological knowledge already in existence.
guidance: Patents and printed publications should be used to determine whether an art is mature and the level of skill. In mature, predictable arts a specification that discloses only a method of making and function often will not raise a written description question for claims present when originally filed. In emerging or unpredictable technologies, more evidence is required to show possession.

name: Method/function disclosure vs product claims (including product-by-process)
description: Disclosure of only a method of making the invention and its function may not be sufficient to support a product claim (other than a product-by-process claim).
guidance: Where the process has actually been used to produce the product, the written description requirement for a product-by-process claim is satisfied. The requirement may not be satisfied where it is not clear that the acts set forth in the specification can be performed, or that the product is produced by that process.

name: Partial structure disclosure limitation
description: Disclosure of a partial structure without additional characterization may not be sufficient to evidence possession of the claimed invention.
guidance: For chemical/biological inventions (e.g., genes), conception requires definition sufficient to distinguish the compound and describe how to obtain it (structure, method of preparation, physical/chemical properties, or other distinguishing characteristics). Defining solely by a principal biological property is generally insufficient.

name: Species claim support (tests a/b/c)
description: A claim to a species must meet required tests (e.g., reduction to practice, reduction to drawings, or disclosure of identifying characteristics) to avoid rejection for lack of adequate written description under 35 U.S.C. 112(a).
guidance: Any species claim that does not meet the test described under at least one of the enumerated bases must be rejected as lacking adequate written description.

name: Genus claim support via representative species or identifying characteristics
description: The written description requirement for a claimed genus may be satisfied through sufficient description of a representative number of species by reduction to practice, reduction to drawings, or by disclosure of identifying characteristics (structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics coupled with structure–function correlation), or combinations thereof.
guidance: A 'representative number of species' must reflect the variation within the genus. Where substantial variation exists, describe a sufficient variety of species. Disclosure of only one species supports a genus claim only if the disclosure indicates the patentee has invented species sufficient to constitute the genus.

name: Representative number and unpredictability
description: Whether a disclosed set of species is 'representative' depends on whether a person skilled in the art would recognize that the inventor possessed the necessary common attributes of the genus; in unpredictable arts, one species will often be insufficient.
guidance: If representative species are not adequately disclosed for a genus, the genus claim must be rejected. Examples: claims to broad antibody genera not supported by disclosure of a single structurally similar antibody when other types exist; conversely, some arts permit a single species to indicate the class if the disclosure clearly conveys that other species are encompassed.

name: Structure–function correlation as sufficiency basis
description: A reasonable structure–function correlation may support a genus where structural features that produce the claimed function are disclosed or are known in the art.
guidance: Such correlations may be established by the inventor's specification or may be known in the art at the filing date. When established, they can permit broader claims without disclosure of every species.

name: Breadth of claims must be commensurate with disclosure
description: A specification cannot support expansive claim language merely by clearly describing one embodiment of the thing claimed; the issue is whether a person skilled in the art would understand the inventor to have invented the invention as broadly claimed.
guidance: If the specification teaches only a particular method/embodiment and gives no reason to generalize, broad generic claims may be invalid under 35 U.S.C. 112. Case examples (e.g., LizardTech) illustrate claims invalidated when only one particular method was disclosed.

name: Support required for new/amended claims and priority/benefit claims
description: To comply with 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or to be entitled to an earlier filing or priority date under 35 U.S.C. 119, 120, 365, or 386, each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure.
guidance: When an explicit limitation in a claim is not present in the written description whose benefit is sought, it must be shown that a person of ordinary skill would have understood at filing that the description requires that limitation. If not supported, new/amended claims must be rejected or benefit/priority denied.

name: Examiner burden and required findings for a written description rejection
description: A description as filed is presumed adequate; the examiner bears the initial burden of presenting evidence or reasoning to rebut that presumption and explain why persons skilled in the art would not recognize the disclosure as describing the claimed invention.
guidance: In rejecting a claim the examiner must set forth express findings of fact including: (A) identification of the claim limitation at issue; and (B) establishment of a prima facie case by providing reasons why a person skilled in the art at the filing time would not have recognized that the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention. A general allegation of 'unpredictability in the art' is not sufficient. When appropriate, suggest claim amendments supportable by the original disclosure, mindful of the prohibition on new matter.

name: Possession test (standard phrasing)
description: Objective standard: 'does the description clearly allow persons of ordinary skill in the art to recognize that he or she invented what is claimed' (i.e., that the inventor was in possession of the invention as now claimed)?
guidance: Possession may be shown by words, structures, figures, diagrams, and formulas that fully set forth the claimed invention, or by reduction to practice or disclosure that the invention was 'ready for patenting' (e.g., drawings or structural formulas).

name: Literal vs non-literal disclosure; prohibition on added matter
description: The subject matter of the claim need not be described literally in haec verba to satisfy the written description requirement; however, if a claim is amended to include subject matter, limitations, or terminology not present in the application as filed (a departure/addition/deletion), the examiner should conclude the claimed subject matter is not described in that application.
guidance: Such conclusions lead to rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or denial of benefit of an earlier filing date as appropriate. Examiners should use new-matter objection procedures where applicable (see MPEP § 2163.06).

name: Essential elements must be claimed or supported
description: Each claim must include all elements which the applicant has described as essential; if the originally filed disclosure does not provide support for each claim limitation, or if an element described as essential is omitted from the claim, the claim must be rejected or benefit/priority denied.
guidance: Case law supports rejection where an essential element described in the specification is not claimed or where new claims attempt to encompass subject matter not supported in the earlier disclosure.

name: Typical procedural circumstances raising written description issues
description: Common situations where written description questions arise include: amendments affecting a claim; reliance on the filing date of a parent application under 35 U.S.C. 120; and reliance on foreign priority or provisional filing date under 35 U.S.C. 119.
guidance: In each context, the claims must be supported by the relevant earlier disclosure 'in the manner required by 35 U.S.C. 112(a)'. The guidance includes examples of courts evaluating 'ipsis verbis' disclosure, blaze marks, and other indicators of sufficient support for benefit/priority claims.

name: Alternative positions by applicant
description: An applicant may, in appropriate cases, take alternative positions with respect to a refusal to register (for example: argue the mark is not merely descriptive, and alternatively claim acquired distinctiveness under § 2(f)).
guidance: It is the applicant’s responsibility to make clear that it is taking alternative positions. See TBMP §§ 309.03 and 311.02(b) for related guidance. Alternative positions mirror the ability of the examining attorney to refuse on alternative grounds; be explicit in presenting alternatives.

name: Guidelines requirement to remove inconsistencies between claims and description
description: The Guidelines require that the applicant remove any inconsistencies by amendment or by deleting inconsistent embodiments or marking them as not falling within the claim scope; and that general statements and claim-like clauses are deleted or amended to avoid claim-like language.
guidance: Since the April 2023 Guidelines update, EPO examiners have taken a harder line on inconsistencies between claims and description. This may lead examiners to amend the description (or require deletion/marking of embodiments) in the Druckexemplar accompanying a Rule 71(3) EPC Communication. Applicants must consider whether to accept examiner's changes or to contest them (possibly by appeal).

name: Article 84 EPC — claims must be clear, concise, and supported by the description
description: Article 84 EPC states that 'the claims shall (i) be clear and concise and (ii) be supported by the description.'
guidance: The Board notes that Article 84 formally places the requirement on the claims rather than on the description or drawings. This underpins questions about whether the Office can require adaptation of the description to match the claims.

name: Delete or amend 'claim‑like' clauses and general statements in the description
description: General statements and claim-like clauses in the description should be deleted or amended to avoid claim-like language.
guidance: The Guidelines explicitly direct deletion or amendment of claim-like language to remove inconsistencies; applicants who retain such clauses risk the Examiner deleting them and potentially facing objections under Article 84.

name: Clarity requirement interpreted as a claim‑focused standard (claims must be clear without resorting to description)
description: A significant body of EPO case law has found that Article 84 places a requirement on the claims only, i.e., that they are clear in themselves without having to resort to the description for an interpretation.
guidance: The Board emphasises that 'legal certainty requires that claims are understood without having to resort to the description.' This interpretation is in tension with EPO practice that requires description adaption; it limits the degree to which the description can be used to resolve claim ambiguity.

name: Support requirement historically required correspondence between claims and description
description: Early case law added that the claims should correspond to, be consistent with and be commensurate with the description.
guidance: Historically this supported adaptation of the description to claims of reduced scope, but that historical approach is now questioned by the Board in light of Article 84's wording.

name: Limits on using Article 69 EPC to justify description adaption
description: Article 69 EPC and its interpretation (that extent of protection is determined by the claims while description/drawings are used to interpret them) have sometimes been used to justify adapting the description to claims of reduced scope.
guidance: The Board is wary of this justification, noting that 'it is not for the Office to harmonise the extent of protection conferred by the European patents [and applications] by bringing the description and/or the drawings of an application or patent in agreement with the amended claims held allowable.' Thus Article 69 should not be used to force harmonisation of description to claims.

name: Question whether inconsistency between description/drawings and claims can lead to refusal under Article 84
description: The Board formulated the question: Is there a lack of clarity of a claim or a lack of support of a claim by the description within the meaning of Article 84 EPC if a part of the disclosure (e.g., an embodiment, an example or a claim‑like clause) is not encompassed by the subject‑matter for which protection is sought ('inconsistency in scope between the description and/or drawings and the claims') and can an application consequently be refused based on Article 84 EPC if the applicant does not remove the inconsistency in scope between the description and/or drawings and the claims by way of amendment of the description ('adaption of the description')?
guidance: This is the core legal question referred for possible further referral to the Enlarged Board; its answer will determine whether refusal for non‑adaptation is permissible and thus whether the Guidelines' approach is consistent with Article 84.

name: Procedural recourse: appeal and referral to the Enlarged Board of Appeal
description: If disagreement arises over Examiner's deletions/amendments (e.g., deletion of claim‑like clauses), an applicant may request an appealable decision on the state of the file and seek Board of Appeal review; the Board may decide to refer the legal question to the Enlarged Board of Appeal.
guidance: A referral to the Enlarged Board would provide much‑needed clarity but would 'inevitably and significantly delay the grant' of the patent. Applicants should weigh the costs/benefits of contesting adaptions versus accepting changes to proceed to grant.

name: Trial for correction (IPTAB)
description: A patent holder may pursue a petition for the correction of a granted patent or utility model for reasons of narrowing a claim, correcting a clerical error, or clarifying an ambiguous description (Article 136 of the Patent Act).
guidance: Permissible corrections are limited to specified grounds; correction procedure is an ex parte IPTAB remedy.

name: Scope of examination in revocation suits (limitation vs nonlimitation theory)
description: There are two theories whether revocation suits are limited to grounds/evidence claimed in the IPTAB trial (limitation theory) or not (nonlimitation theory). The Supreme Court has upheld the nonlimitation theory for inter partes cases: a revocation suit examines substantive or procedural unlawfulness present at the time of the disposition and may consider unlawfulness beyond what was presented at IPTAB.
guidance: Litigants may raise and courts may examine grounds beyond the IPTAB record in inter partes revocation suits; parties should be prepared to litigate broader issues on judicial review.

name: Claim construction principles for infringement analysis
description: To determine patent infringement, interpretation of the scope of claims is required with focus on the language and text stated in the scope of claims (principle of literal interpretation), while also taking into account the descriptions and drawings of the invention and common technical knowledge at the time the application was filed (principle of reference to the descriptions).
guidance: Literal interpretive first; descriptions and common general knowledge used as reference; elements present only in descriptions (not claims) should not be compared against alleged infringing product/process elements.

name: Element-by-element comparison requirement
description: To fall within the protective scope of a patented invention, the defendant’s product or process must include all elements of the patented invention; if only some elements are included and others missing, the product/process does not fall within the protective scope in principle.
guidance: Infringement requires presence of all claim elements (literal infringement) but doctrine of equivalents may apply where elements are not literally identical but are equivalent.

name: Description must be correctly and fully disclosed
description: The invention must be “correctly and fully” described in the description, which according to subsection 1(1) of the Patent Rules is “the part of the specification other than the claims”.
guidance: Claims must be fully supported by the description (section 60 Patent Rules). A description that states the nature of the invention only by reference to the claims is improper and suggests non‑compliance with subsection 27(3) of the Patent Act.

name: Do not describe the invention by reference to the claims
description: It is improper for the description to state the nature of the invention by reference to the claims (e.g. “the problem ... is overcome through the method of claim 1”).
guidance: Such statements must be removed or replaced by explicit description; examples of unacceptable language are provided. Amending the description to include originally filed claim language in a non‑divisional application is permissible (subsection 38.2(2)).

name: Description form per section 56 — required elements
description: The description must include, in manner and order: (a) short precise title (no trademark/coined/personal name); (b) technical field; (c) background art important for understanding/searching/examination; (d) description permitting understanding of technical problem and its solution; (e) concise description of figures; (f) at least one mode contemplated using examples if appropriate; (g) sequence listing if required.
guidance: Subsection 56(2) allows different order if it aids understanding; headings like 'Summary' or 'Detailed Description of Preferred Embodiments' are permitted but broader claim support must be found elsewhere in the description.

name: Headings permitted but cannot limit support
description: Headings such as 'Summary of the Invention' and 'Detailed Description of the Preferred Embodiments' are permitted in Canadian practice.
guidance: Where a heading suggests 'preferred embodiments', support for claims broader than those embodiments must be found in other descriptive parts satisfying subsection 27(3), including enablement and sound prediction support.

name: Pages and pagination formalities
description: Pages of the description, as part of the specification, must be numbered consecutively (subsection 50(1) Patent Rules) and no page of the description may contain the petition, abstract, drawings or claims; each must begin on a new page (section 49 Patent Rules).
guidance: Formatting non‑compliance under sections 13, 47, 48 may be identified by examiners or support staff to expedite allowance; requisitioning compliance is permissible under PCT Article 27.

name: Amendments to description — inclusion of originally filed claims language
description: One amendment always permissible from 'new matter' standpoint is inclusion of the language of the originally filed claims in the description of a non‑divisional application originally filed in English or French.
guidance: General amendment guidance is in chapters 11 and 20; amendments may not add new matter and special attention is required when replacing restrictive language with permissive language.

name: Amendments referencing prior art may introduce new matter
description: Introducing teachings from a prior art document into the description may, depending on circumstances, introduce new matter.
guidance: If specific teachings in prior art are required to enable the invention or to support a sound prediction and it would not have been clear to the skilled person which teachings were necessary as of the claim date, including those teachings may add new matter.

name: Claims must define invention to provide public notice
description: A claim must define the invention so a person skilled in the art will understand where they may and may not go without infringing; claims must be distinct and explicit (section 27(4) Patent Act).
guidance: Claims must be novel (whole claimed subject‑matter not part of state of the art) and specify positively all elements/features necessary to ensure the result set forth in the description. Each claim must be a single sentence.

name: Claim structure (preamble, transitional phrase, body)
description: Claims may be drafted to contain: preamble/introductory phrase, transitional phrase, and body (purview).
guidance: Preamble identifies category; transitional phrase (e.g., 'comprising' vs 'consisting of') indicates open/closed recitation; body lists elements, steps, ingredients, or groups. Any form of claim conforming to section 27(4) and Patent Rules acceptable.

name: Principles of claim construction — essential elements and specification as whole
description: Claims are the starting point for construing a patent; essential elements must be determined and the specification construed as a whole. Analysis is from viewpoint of skilled person with a mind willing to understand.
guidance: Reference to description allowed only to assist understanding of claim terms where terms have a unique meaning; cannot be used to vary claim scope. During examination claims may be amended to remove ambiguity.

name: Plain meaning unless description defines term
description: Language of claims is interpreted by giving each term its plain and usual meaning in the art unless it is clear from the description that a term in the claims is to be given a different meaning.
guidance: Applicants can act as their own lexicographer but must make it clear; inadvisable to redefine terms contrary to well‑known meanings.

name: Clarity requirement — avoid ambiguity and multiple interpretations
description: No speculation should be necessary to determine what is covered by each claim; wording should not be so flexible that several interpretations are possible.
guidance: A claim is indefinite when its precise limits are uncertain. Broadness alone does not make a claim indefinite. Use simple language if possible.

name: Antecedent basis rules
description: When an element is referred to in definite terms without introduction previously, the claim is objectionable under section 27(4) (lack of proper antecedent).
guidance: Implied antecedents permitted where the phrase by definition contains the missing antecedent (examples provided).

name: Avoidance of imprecise or vague expressions
description: Claims should not include vague expressions such as 'thin', 'strong', 'if desired', 'about', 'preferably', etc., unless further defined in clear terms.
guidance: The manual lists commonly used imprecise terms and discusses context where they may be acceptable or indefinite (e.g., 'therapeutically effective amount', 'a major part'). Consider subsection 27(4) and section 60 when such terms appear.

name: Negative limitations caution
description: Claims containing negative expressions ('not being...', 'not having...') may be objectionable because claims should generally set forth what the invention is rather than what it is not, unless no positive way exists.
guidance: Dependent claims that negate features of a preceding claim and become broader are objectionable under subsection 63(4) of the Patent Rules.

name: Completeness of claims — recite sufficient elements for operability
description: To define the invention distinctly and explicitly, sufficient elements must be recited for operability; inventive features must appear in each claim.
guidance: Example: composition claims generally must define a minimum of two ingredients at least broadly; failure to do so can be objected to as indefinite under subsection 27(4).

name: Support requirement — claims fully supported by description
description: A claim must be fully supported by the description as required by section 60 of the Patent Rules; characteristics of embodiments set forth in the claim must be fully set forth in the description.
guidance: Terms used in claims and description must be used in the same sense. Matter in originally filed claims may be added to the description (except for divisional applications with further requirements).

name: Claims should not rely on references to description/drawings except narrowly
description: Generally not acceptable for a claim to contain reference to the description or drawings (subsection 62(1) Patent Rules).
guidance: Exceptions: reference numerals in parentheses (subsection 62(2)) if claim otherwise complete; charts/graphs/tables or complex tests may be referred to if reproducing them in the claim is impractical; sequence listing and biological deposit identifiers may be referenced (subsections 62(3),(4)).

name: Scope of claims relative to disclosure — applicant may draft narrow claims
description: A claim may be as narrow as the applicant wishes within the scope of the invention disclosed.
guidance: Scope must, however, remain supported and enabled by the disclosure.

name: When specification limits claim to a particular mode, mere production may not prove infringement
description: If the specification describes a particular mode of carrying out the invention, mere production of an article with similar results does not necessarily prove use of that specified mode.
guidance: Example: where the specification stated the invention to relate to 'a mode of manufacturing candles by the application of two or more plaited wicks in each candle' and set out the mode at length, the mere production of a candle in which the wicks turned outward in burning was held to be no evidence of infringement. (per totam curiam cited in §314)

name: Superior or improved apparatus does not avoid infringement if it applies the same principle
description: A defendant's apparatus may be a great improvement over what the patentee described, yet still infringe if it applies the same principle as claimed and falls within the specification's scope.
guidance: Neilson: defendant's apparatus was superior but held an infringement because it applied heated air in the close vessel between blowing apparatus and furnace — ‘‘it is the application of heated air ... and therefore ... it would be an infringement of it.’’ (§319)

name: Combination claims: claiming a combination can be valid and use of the same combination may infringe even if components were previously separate
description: A combination of known elements can be the subject of a patent; using that same combination (even if parts were previously separately used) may be infringement, and minor differences in arrangement need not avoid liability.
guidance: Example: patent claiming combination of a blast and an exhaust in ventilating millstones held valid and infringed even though blast and exhaust had been used separately before; use in a mill with different stone rotation was still infringement. (§319)

name: Substantial new question (SNQ) — what raises SNQ
description: The reexamination is granted if a substantial new question of patentability is raised by the request based on patents or printed publications.
guidance: An SNQ exists when cited art presents teaching not present in prior prosecution/previous examinations and a reasonable examiner would consider that teaching important in deciding patentability of the claim(s). Examples in MPEP: a reference teaching a spring-supported extruder at a 30° angle when that teaching was not present in prior prosecution could raise an SNQ for certain claims. Conversely, a reference that is a substantial equivalent of art considered earlier or cumulative will not raise an SNQ.

name: Scope limited to claims identified in request
description: Only claims for which reexamination is requested will be reexamined; claims not requested remain not reexamined.
guidance: If the request does not seek reexamination for certain claims, those claims will not be reexamined (example: 'reexamination has not been requested for claims 5–20; accordingly claims 5–20 will not be reexamined').

name: General conduct rules — applicability of initial examination procedures
description: Inter partes reexamination is conducted according to procedures established for initial examination under sections 132 and 133, except as otherwise provided.
guidance: Patent owner may propose any amendment and new claims except those enlarging claim scope. Except for the reexamination request itself, any document filed by either party shall be served on the other. Office will send requester copies of communications to patent owner. Third party requester has one opportunity to file written comments addressing issues raised by Office action or patent owner response if received within 30 days of service. All proceedings are to be conducted with special dispatch unless Director determines good cause to suspend (35 U.S.C. 314(c); 37 CFR 1.937). All communications directed to merits must be in writing and filed for entry into the record.

name: Required copies under 37 CFR 1.98(a)(2)
description: When submitting references, a legible copy is required for certain categories of documents.
guidance: Required copies include: (1) each foreign patent; (2) each publication or the portion that caused it to be listed (other than U.S. patents and U.S. patent application publications unless required by the Office); (3) for each cited pending unpublished U.S. application, the application specification including the claims and any drawing or that portion that caused it to be listed; and (4) all other information or the portion which caused it to be listed.

name: Scope of inter partes reexamination (37 CFR 1.906)
description: Defines substantive scope and limits of issues that may be resolved in inter partes reexamination.
guidance: Claims will be examined on the basis of patents or printed publications and, with respect to subject matter added or deleted during reexamination, on the basis of 35 U.S.C. 112 requirements. Claims may not be amended to enlarge their scope. Issues other than those indicated (patents/printed publications and 112 for added matter) will not be resolved in inter partes reexamination; if such issues arise they should be noted and patent owner may consider filing a reissue application. Inter partes differs from ex parte in procedural matters (party participation, types/timing of Office actions, estoppel effects, initiation prohibitions) but not in substance to be considered.

name: Obviousness under 35 U.S.C. § 103(a)
description: For a claimed invention to be patentable, the differences between it and the prior art must be such that a relevant artisan at the priority date would not have found the claimed subject matter as a whole obvious. Obviousness is a question of law based on underlying facts including the scope and content of the prior art, differences between the prior art and the claims at issue, the level of ordinary skill, and relevant evidence of secondary considerations.
guidance: Apply Graham v. John Deere and KSR: consider (1) scope and content of prior art, (2) differences between prior art and claims, (3) level of ordinary skill, and (4) secondary considerations. Court reviews legal determinations de novo and factual findings for substantial-evidence support. (See Henny Penny; KSR; Graham.)

name: Nexus may attach to an individual element or to an inventive combination
description: Secondary-consideration evidence may be linked either to an individual claim element or to the inventive combination of known elements.
guidance: When evidence is tied to the combination (and not to a single pre-existing feature), WBIP allows treating 'the claimed combination as a whole' as the nexus for objective evidence. But where evidence 'relate[s] entirely' to a single feature present in the prior art, the WBIP rationale for treating the combination as nexus does not save that evidence from being unhelpful to the obviousness inquiry.

name: Proper petition content and consequences of reserving new theories for reply
description: A petitioner must present its grounds and rationales in its petition; arguments first presented in reply that are 'meaningfully distinct' from the petition may be treated as untimely new contentions.
guidance: If a petitioner could have but did not present an argument in the petition (e.g., that it would have been obvious to modify a prior-art reference to meet a claim limitation), the Board may decline to consider it when raised only in reply. The petitioner is the 'master of its complaint' and cannot rely on reply briefing to introduce new theories. (Cites: Intelligent Bio-Systems; Ariosa; Acceleration Bay; SAS Institute.)

name: Prima-facie analysis at institution/decision stages and specificity for discrete claim limitations
description: A challenge to patentability must reason as to why prior art renders a claimed limitation obvious; absence of disclosure of a specific limitation in the asserted prior art can lead the Board to find the prima-facie case unpersuasive.
guidance: When the Board finds that a claimed limitation (e.g., a 1/8-inch tolerance) is not disclosed by the asserted references, that finding can render secondary-consideration evidence immaterial for that claim subset. A petitioner must explain modifications or optimizations to prior art references in its petition rather than in a late reply. (Illustrated by the Board's handling of the one-eighth-inch limitation in the '834 patent IPR.)

name: Restricted prior-art bases in transitional CBM proceedings
description: A petitioner who challenges claims in a covered business-method patent on a ground raised under section 102 or 103 (as in effect on the day prior to enactment) may support such ground only on the basis of prior art described by section 102(a) (as in effect before enactment) or prior art that (I) discloses the invention more than 1 year prior to the U.S. application and (II) would be described by section 102(a) (pre-enactment) if disclosed by another before the applicant's invention.
guidance: This limits the types of prior art that can be invoked in transitional CBM proceedings to older statutory categories or year-old disclosures satisfying certain conditions.

name: Scope and definition of 'covered business method patent' (CBM)
description: For purposes of the transitional program, 'covered business method patent' means a patent that claims a method or corresponding apparatus for performing data processing operations utilized in the practice, administration, or management of a financial product or service, except that the term shall not include patents for technological inventions.
guidance: Solely for implementing the transitional proceeding, the Director shall prescribe regulations for determining whether a patent is for a technological invention (i.e., exclusions for technological inventions).

name: Alice two-part subject-matter eligibility
description: Apply the two-step Alice/Mayo test: (1) determine whether claims are 'directed to' an abstract idea (e.g., mathematical concepts, mental processes, methods of organizing human activity); (2) if so, determine whether claim elements add an 'inventive concept' that transforms the abstract idea into a patent-eligible application.
guidance: Courts often resolve §101 issues at early stages (motion to dismiss, judgment on the pleadings). Claims that recite only high-level functions performed by generic computing modules are vulnerable. In step two, an inventive concept requires more than well-understood, routine, conventional components or simply applying the abstract idea using generic computer technology.

name: Claims must recite specific technical/AI elements or architecture
description: Claims that lack AI-specific elements or architecture (i.e., only describe high-level goals or outcomes) risk being found directed to abstract ideas.
guidance: Even if the specification mentions neural networks or AI, courts have invalidated claims when the claim language itself does not require or recite those technical elements. Include concrete technical components or configurations in claims rather than generic 'modules' or functional language.

name: Describe specific technical details of analysis in specification and claims
description: Provide concrete, technical details about the exact sort of analysis, algorithms, or architecture rather than broad descriptions of data analysis.
guidance: Courts criticized claims that covered 'history data analysis' broadly without technical specifics; lack of specific technical details can lead to preemption concerns and §101 invalidity. Where possible, claim and describe the particular technical steps or structures used to perform analysis.

name: Claim an improvement to computer/technical field
description: Draft claims to be directed to an actual improvement in computer architecture or another technical field (e.g., improved processor architecture or improved speech-recognition performance).
guidance: Courts have treated claimed improvements to computer architecture (e.g., LPHDR processing elements) as plausibly inventive and sufficient to survive early pleadings. The specification should explain how the invention improves the relevant technical field.

name: Avoid preempting broad methods or mental processes
description: Do not claim concepts so broadly that they would preempt a general method of analyzing data or performing mental processes.
guidance: Courts invalidate claims whose breadth would effectively preempt all methods of performing a particular abstract idea. Tailor claim scope to technical implementations rather than abstract goals.

name: Claims should recite a specific implementation comprising technical elements
description: Where possible, ensure claims are tied to concrete implementations (technical elements, structures, or configurations) rather than abstract descriptions of functionality.
guidance: PTAB and courts have credited claims that recite technical elements (e.g., AI + computer speech recognition) as not 'directed to' an abstract idea. Specific implementation language in claims helps distinguish from abstract idea categorizations.

name: Specification must show how the invention provides a technical improvement
description: The specification should explicitly describe how the claimed invention improves the technical field (performance, simplicity, accuracy, etc.).
guidance: PTAB relied on specification statements (e.g., improved performance using DeepSpeech learning) to find claims directed to a technical improvement. Emphasize empirical or technical advantages over prior art in the specification.

name: Claim detectable features (viewable when product is operated)
description: Draft claims to include features that are visible or discernible when an AI-enabled product/method is operated (UI elements, outputs, intermediate results).
guidance: Detectable features make enforcement feasible because infringement can be observed in product operation or user interfaces. Examples: UI prompting for inputs, displayed intermediate/final AI results, or user-specific criteria used for training.

name: Focus claims on model/architecture elements likely disclosed in competitor materials
description: Target model/architecture aspects (e.g., '7 layer neural network') that competitors may advertise or mention in marketing, allowing detection from public materials.
guidance: Competitor marketing or technical descriptions may overtly describe architecture to compete on features; capturing those elements in claims aids detection without reverse engineering.

name: Be mindful of whether claimed combinations are 'well-understood, routine, and conventional'
description: Evaluate whether the combination of claim elements, especially generic computer components, would be considered conventional as of the invention date.
guidance: Under Alice step two, an inventive concept is not present if the only alleged innovation is applying an abstract idea using conventional components. Courts will examine whether the combination amounts to significantly more.

name: Avoid claiming purely functional/desirable results without concrete means
description: Claims that merely claim desirable outcomes or functions (e.g., 'optimize parameters') without concrete means or technical steps risk being characterized as abstract ideas.
guidance: Draft claims to recite how the desired result is achieved (structures, algorithms, data transformations) rather than only stating the goal.

name: Leverage USPTO examples and PEG guidance where possible
description: Use the USPTO 2019 PEG/MPEP examples as drafting guides; some examples illustrate patent-eligible AI claims (e.g., Example 39: two-stage neural network training to reduce false positives).
guidance: Align claim and specification drafting with examples that the USPTO has labeled patent-eligible to increase chances of passing examiner eligibility review; ensure claims avoid reciting mathematical concepts/mental processes when those are problematic.

name: Think broadly about the inference and datapoints to capture broader infringement
description: When drafting claims, consider what the claimed inference represents and what datapoints could be substituted to perform the same inference, to capture broader infringement beyond a single productized embodiment.
guidance: Different ML architectures can produce similar inferences; scope claims to cover the inference or effect (through concrete technical means) rather than only a single model embodiment so competitors can't easily design around by swapping datapoints or models.

name: Conversion to first-inventor-to-file priority
description: The United States patent system is converted to a first-inventor-to-file system giving priority to the earlier-filed application for a claimed invention; interference proceedings are replaced with derivation proceedings.
guidance: Interference procedures are repealed; derivation proceedings determine whether an earlier-filed applicant was the proper applicant. Various conforming amendments to Secs. 100, 102, 103, 120, 135, and repeal of Secs. 104 and 157 are made to effect the change.

name: Derivation proceeding requirements and timing
description: A derivation proceeding may be requested to determine whether an earlier applicant derived the claimed invention and filed without authorization.
guidance: The request must set forth the basis for finding derivation and be filed within 12 months of the date of first publication of an application for a substantially same claim. The Board issues a final decision; Board decisions may be appealed to the Federal Circuit or to district court under Sec. 146.

name: Entire market value rule (method A for reasonable royalty)
description: A royalty may be based upon the entire market value of the larger apparatus/process incorporating the infringing product/process if the claimed invention's specific contribution over the prior art is the predominant basis for market demand of the larger apparatus/process.
guidance: This limits use of the entire market value rule to situations where the patented feature predominantly drives demand for the whole product/process.

name: Established marketplace licensing method (method B for reasonable royalty)
description: A royalty may be based on other nonexclusive licenses of the patented invention if the claimed invention has been the subject of nonexclusive licenses to a number of persons sufficient to indicate general marketplace recognition, the license was secured prior to filing of the case, and the infringer's use is of substantially the same scope, volume and benefit.
guidance: This method relies on comparable licensing evidence that predates the litigation and matches the infringer's use.

name: Apportionment requirement (method C/backstop for reasonable royalty)
description: If showings under (A) and (B) have not been made, the court shall conduct an analysis to ensure a reasonable royalty is applied only to the portion of the economic value of the infringing product or process properly attributable to the claimed invention's specific contribution over the prior art.
guidance: Designed to prevent overcompensation by requiring apportionment of value attributable to the claimed invention versus preexisting elements.

name: Limitations on willful infringement findings — timing of pleadings
description: A patentee may not plead (and a court may not determine) willful infringement before a court determines that the patent is not invalid, is enforceable, and has been infringed by the infringer.
guidance: Prevents early willfulness claims before threshold issues (validity, enforceability, infringement) have been adjudicated.

name: Required submissions under 35 U.S.C. 371(c)
description: The applicant shall file in the Patent and Trademark Office: (1) the national fee provided in section 41(a); (2) a copy of the international application, and a translation into English if filed in another language; (3) amendments to the claims made under PCT Article 19, and English translation if made in another language; (4) an oath or declaration of the inventor complying with section 115 and relevant regulations; (5) an English translation of any annexes to the international preliminary examination report if made in another language.
guidance: These items are the core documents/fees required to commence and fulfill the U.S. national stage; some may be waived or postponed under specified conditions (see specific entries below). Failure to comply by required times is treated as abandonment unless unavoidable and shown to the Director's satisfaction.

name: Article 19 amendments filed with the International Bureau
description: Claims of an international application may be amended under PCT Article 19 (description and drawings may not). Article 19 amendments (including a complete claim set in English) will be entered by replacing original English claims; if made in another language, applicant must provide an English translation by commencement.
guidance: Article 19 amendments not received by commencement are considered canceled (35 U.S.C. 371(d)). If canceled but desired, they must be offered as preliminary or responsive amendments under 37 CFR 1.121 or 1.111. Form PTO-1390 includes a checkbox to instruct the U.S. DO/EO not to enter Article 19 amendments.

name: Status-identifier specifics for claims entered from PCT amendments
description: Use 'original' for claims presented on the international filing date and not modified; use 'previously presented' for claims added/modified under PCT Articles 19 or 34 that were entered in the national phase; use 'canceled' for claims canceled under PCT amendment that were entered.
guidance: MPEP provides concrete examples illustrating claim-status labeling in various Article 19/34 scenarios (examples 1–4). Proper identification avoids confusion and delays.

name: Post-commencement treatment of amendments and patent grant/refusal timing
description: After an international application has entered the national stage, no patent may be granted or refused thereon before the expiration of the applicable time limit under PCT Article 28 or Article 41, except with the express consent of the applicant. The applicant may present amendments to the specification, claims, and drawings after the national stage has commenced.
guidance: Applicants retain the right to amend during national stage; however, Article 34 amendments made after commencement are not considered in the U.S. national stage and must be submitted as U.S. amendments (e.g., preliminary amendment under 37 CFR 1.121).

name: Possession and exercise of exclusive right (prima facie ground for injunction)
description: To obtain an injunction the plaintiff should generally show long possession and exercise of his exclusive right — a prima facie case of possession and enjoyment of the patent right.
guidance: No fixed period is prescribed; the general principle is that time elapsed between grant and injunction must have been sufficient to permit the patentee to construct and sell articles or machines in conformity with his claim, and to sell them publicly and repeatedly. If plaintiff makes out a prima facie case by possession/enjoyment, that supports granting an injunction until further order.

name: Former recoveries or licenses as proof of possession (subject to non-collusion)
description: Proof of possession may consist of former recoveries or licenses granted to parties who submitted; these can support a claim of possession and enjoyment.
guidance: Such recoveries/submissions will not establish the necessary possession if it appears they were collusively obtained; they need not have been obtained by trial — they remain effective if there was originally a real contest. Example: where many licenses were prepared/granted and parties submitted, court found sufficient use.

name: Core patent-validity requirements referenced for equitable consideration
description: For purposes of equitable relief and the law on patents generally: (1) the invention must be novel; (2) it must be useful; (3) the specification must be intelligible; and (4) the specification must not attempt to claim more than the patentee is strictly entitled to.
guidance: These matters (utility, intelligibility, novelty) are for jury as facts; whether specification attempts to cover too much is a question of law to be considered by courts. A patent that attempts to cover more than its real discovery — e.g., claiming original invention where only a particular combination or application was discovered — may be rendered ineffectual even to the extent it would otherwise be valid. Conversely, valid patents may exist for new combinations/applications of previously used materials if the specification clearly confines claim to that combination/application only.

name: Restrictions on Supplemental Answers Responding to Reply Briefs (When New Ground Allowed)
description: 37 CFR 41.43(a)(2) prohibits a supplemental examiner's answer responding to a reply brief from including a new ground of rejection. After the filing of a reply brief, any new ground of rejection responding to the reply brief must be by way of reopening of prosecution.
guidance: Examples of new issues that give the examiner discretion to provide a supplemental answer (but not to include a new ground) are provided (e.g., arguments that a reference is nonanalogous art or that a particular claim element is not taught). If the examiner intends to include a new ground, prosecution must be reopened with SPE approval and appropriate form language (12.187).

name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.39(b) – presenting claims or defenses not warranted by law
description: Presenting a claim or defense that is not warranted under existing law violates 37 C.F.R. § 10.39(b).
guidance: Advancing legally unwarranted claims or defenses may be discipline-worthy when supported by facts.

name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.85(a)(2) – knowingly advancing an unwarranted claim
description: Knowingly advancing an unwarranted claim is prohibited under 37 C.F.R. § 10.85(a)(2).
guidance: Intentional advancement of claims without basis can support sanction.

name: International Convention / priority right
description: Under the International Convention, subjects/citizens of member states enjoy the same patent advantages as nationals; a person who has made an application in one state enjoys a right of priority for six months (one month longer for countries beyond the sea) for applications in the other states; temporary protection may be granted for articles shown at recognised international exhibitions.
guidance: Priority rights (six months) allow subsequent foreign filings to claim the date of the first filing; check Convention membership and applicable priority term for overseas filings.

name: United States — appeals and interferences
description: If dissatisfied with an examiner's final action, applicant may appeal to the Board of Examiners-in-Chief, then to the Commissioner of Patents, and thereafter (in uncontested cases) to the Supreme Court of the District of Columbia. When two or more applicants claim the same invention, the Commissioner may declare an interference to determine the prior inventor via written proofs; appeals from interference decisions follow similar paths except no appeal to the district supreme court.
guidance: There is a formal multi-level appeals process; interferences resolve priority disputes by written evidence and separate appeal rules.

name: United States — reissue and courts' strictness
description: Provision is made for reissue of a patent in case of insufficient or defective specification or where more was claimed than was new, but courts have recently been severe in dealing with reissued patents and broadly reissued patents are often declared invalid.
guidance: Avoid overreliance on reissue to expand scope; draft original applications carefully to reduce the risk of severe judicial scrutiny of reissues.

name: Austria — description sufficiency and duplicate submissions
description: A description must accompany the petition containing a full, clear, and minute explanation of the invention and claims, to enable all competent persons to manufacture the article according to that specification; if drawings, samples, or models are required for full comprehension, they must be supplied in duplicates (one for Austria, one for Hungary).
guidance: Ensure complete enabling disclosure; supply duplicate physical/drawing material where required for dual-administration territories.

name: Brazil — specification language, one invention rule, and provisional exhibition
description: Applicant must deposit in duplicate a specification in Portuguese together with drawings; application must be limited to one invention; foreigners with patents abroad applying in Brazil within seven months of foreign grant are protected; inventors may publicly exhibit inventions prior to application with permission.
guidance: Translate/prepare Portuguese specification in duplicate and limit claims to a single invention; provisional exhibitions possible with permission; priority-like protection for prompt foreign filers.

name: Principles are patentable only when developed and embodied in a practical application
description: A principle, rule, or truth in mechanics or physics cannot be the subject of a patent in the abstract; it becomes patentable only when it is developed, carried out, embodied, and connected with corporeal substances so as to act and produce effects in some art — i.e., when it is reduced to a process.
guidance: Anti-pattern: attempting to claim an abstract principle or a broad method unconfined to producing a particular product/result will be rejected as it would create overbroad monopolies covering every application of the principle. The safe course is to claim the specific mode/means of applying the principle and the practical result thereby achieved.

name: International Search (IS) — meaningful search and claim drafting
description: The manner of claiming affects whether the ISA can do a meaningful search; limitations on searches and meaningful search definitions are specified.
guidance: Claiming manner affects ability to do meaningful search (5.113); 'meaningful —' referenced (5.113); limitations on search (7.013-7.014); partial search results included where lack of unity (7.017).

name: Omissions and amendments
description: Omission of information from the IA or from publication is treated as an amendment; omission of entire elements or sheets may not be rectifiable; omission specifics for claims, description, drawings are given.
guidance: Omission considered an amendment to IA (10.067); omission of certain info from publication (9.016A, 11.073A); omission of entire elements/sheets not rectifiable (11.034); omission of a sheet of claims/description/drawings references (5.126, 5.110, 5.161).

name: Statutory invention (Patent Act Article 2(1))
description: An 'Invention' means the highly advanced creation of a technical idea using the rules of nature.
guidance: 'Highly advanced creation' is a relative concept (distinguishes Patent from Utility Model) but is not considered in practice when determining whether a claimed subject matter meets the requirements of 'Invention' for patentability.

name: Computer programming language or computer program (non-statutory unless tied to hardware/machine)
description: Computer programs as mere lists of orders are not statutory inventions. But inventions where data processing is specifically executed using hardware (data-processing unit/machine operating with the program), the operating method, or computer-readable media carrying the program are statutory.
guidance: Look for a concrete hardware association, operating method, or novel machine-readable medium to treat software-related claims as statutory.

name: Determining the identity of claimed inventions (novelty assessment)
description: Procedure and principles for defining the invention in claims and finding the identity between claimed invention and cited inventions when determining novelty.
guidance: Includes methods for defining inventions disclosed in claims (general principle and handling special expressions), finding cited inventions (publicly known/worked/published), determining novelty for numerical/parameter-limited inventions, and general considerations. Identity includes substantial identity; do not combine more than two cited inventions when comparing to a single claim.

name: Enlarged concept of novelty (Article 29(3) & (4))
description: Provisions treating inventions described in other applications (prior or subsequent) as if filed on the filing date under certain conditions; includes conditions to meet, guidelines applying proviso, and handling of international applications.
guidance: Covers conditions (another application laid open/published, identity of invention in claims vs initial specification, priority issues), procedure for determining identity, and special rules for international applications and domestic priority claims.
