name: Advantageous effects to be considered (inventive step positive indicators)
description: Consider advantageous effects produced by claimed features when assessing inventive step; beneficial technical effects can support non-obviousness.
guidance: Assess whether claimed advantages are credible, supported by description or evidence, and not merely result of routine optimization.

name: Determination of inventive step of a combination invention
description: Special considerations when the claimed invention is a combination of known elements — whether the combination yields a new technical effect or merely aggregates known features.
guidance: Assess synergy, whether combination yields non-obvious effects, and whether prior art provided motivation to combine.

name: Summary of Claimed Subject Matter Requirement
description: A concise explanation of the subject matter defined in each rejected independent claim, with references to the specification in the Record by page/line or paragraph and to drawings by reference characters. For means-plus-function (35 U.S.C. 112(f)) claims, identify corresponding structure/material/acts in the specification with references.
guidance: Reference to the patent application publication does not satisfy the requirement. Each rejected independent claim must be summarized concisely so the Board can readily see what is being contested.

name: Argument Content and Presentation Requirements
description: Arguments must address each ground of rejection and the basis therefor, with citations to statutes, regulations, authorities, and parts of the Record relied on, explaining why the examiner erred for each contested ground. Each ground contested must be argued under a separate heading that reasonably identifies the ground (e.g., claim number, statutory basis, applied reference).
guidance: Arguments or authorities not included in the brief will be refused consideration by the Board for the present appeal (except as provided in 37 CFR §§ 41.41, 41.47, 41.52). For multiple claims under the same ground, appellant may argue claims separately, as a group, or as a subgroup; failure to separately argue a grouped claim constitutes waiver of an argument that the Board must consider patentability of any grouped claim separately. Mere restatement of what a claim recites is not an argument. The Board may select a single claim from a group to decide the appeal on that basis. New arguments made first at oral hearing are normally not considered.

name: 35 U.S.C. § 314(a) institution standard
description: 35 U.S.C. § 314(a) provides limits on when the Director is permitted to institute an IPR, requiring the Director to first determine that there is a “reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail with respect to at least 1 of the claims challenged in the petition,” but does not enumerate any circumstances or facts under which the Director is required to institute an IPR.
guidance: This statutory 'reasonable likelihood' threshold governs institution on the merits, but does not deprive the Director of discretion to deny institution for other reasons; petitions must still clear this merits threshold if referred to the Board.

name: Whether there have been changes in the law or new judicial precedent since issuance of the claims that may affect patentability
description: The Workload Management Memo lists as a relevant consideration whether there have been changes in the law or new judicial precedent issued since issuance of the claims that may affect patentability.
guidance: A change in law or new precedent that undermines the patent owner’s position may favor institution; conversely, settled later precedent that supports patentability may favor denial. Petitioners should highlight favorable intervening precedent and show why review is appropriate despite prior legal developments.

name: The strength of the unpatentability challenge
description: The Workload Management Memo lists the 'strength of the unpatentability challenge' as a relevant consideration for discretionary denial.
guidance: A persuasive, well-supported merits showing makes institution more likely when discretionary denial is considered; weak or marginal challenges are more vulnerable to denial on discretionary grounds. Emphasize claim charts, clear prior art disclosures, and direct nexus to claim language to demonstrate strength.

name: Settled expectations (length of time claims have been in force) — detailed standard and rebuttals
description: The 'settled expectations' consideration — such as 'the length of time the claims have been in force' — is highlighted as a newly prominent basis for discretionary denial. The Director has said there is 'no bright-line rule' but decisions show a practical pattern: patents >6 years often yield findings of 'strong settled expectations' while patents <6 years often do not.
guidance: Settled expectations is now one of the predominant bases for discretionary denial. However, it is not dispositive; petitioners can rebut settled-expectations concerns by showing facts like lack of commercialization/assertion/marking/licensing in the petitioner’s technology space, evidence of examiner error or overlooked prior art in prosecution, or patent expiry (which may tilt back toward institution). Practitioners should marshal specific factual evidence to rebut settled expectations when challenging older patents (examples: no prior enforcement against petitioner's industry, unexercised patents, prosecution history showing missed prior art).

name: Broadened-claim presentation in reissue after two-year period
description: A broadened claim may be presented in a reissue application after the two year period even though the broadened claim presented after the two years is different than the broadened claim presented within the two year period.
guidance: Reissue practice permits presentation of a broadened claim after the two-year window; examiners/practitioners should be aware that a later broadened claim need not be identical to one presented earlier within the two-year period.

name: Specific reference to parent application in continuation/CIP
description: In a continuation or continuation-in-part application, a specific reference to the parent application must be included in an application data sheet or in the first sentence(s) of the specification.
guidance: Include the required reference to the parent (35 U.S.C. 120/37 CFR 1.78(a)(2)(iii)) to ensure proper benefit claim; to expedite examination, certify at filing that the international application has not been withdrawn when claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 and 365(c).

name: Unity of invention election and rejoinder guidance
description: If an examiner determines that the claims lack unity of invention and requires election of a single invention, when all of the claims drawn to the elected invention are allowable, the claims directed to the nonelected invention(s) should be considered for rejoinder following the guidance set forth in MPEP § 821.04(b).
guidance: Follow MPEP § 821.04(b) for rejoinder procedures when elected claims become allowable and consider rejoinder of nonelected claims accordingly.

name: Certificate of reexamination and effect of terminated reexamination prosecution
description: When the prosecution of a reexamination proceeding is terminated, a reexamination certificate is issued which indicates the status of all claims following the reexamination. Unless prosecution is reopened by the Director, the reexamination proceeding is concluded by the issuance and publication of a reexamination certificate.
guidance: Understand that reexamination termination results in a certificate describing claim status; reopening requires Director action.

name: Reexamination fees: scope and excess-claim fees
description: The fees for a reexamination proceeding include the fees for the request, for addition of claims, for a request for an extension of time, for any appeal, brief, and oral hearing. No fee is required for the issuance of a reexamination certificate. If an amendment is submitted to add claims to the patent being reexamined, excess claims fees may apply.
guidance: When filing amendments that add claims or requesting extensions or appeals in reexamination, assess and pay applicable fees (including excess claims fees) to avoid defects; issuance of the reexamination certificate itself carries no fee.

name: Appropriate correction required for informalities
description: Use this form paragraph to point out minor informalities such as spelling errors, inconsistent terminology, etc., which should be corrected.
guidance: If the informalities render the claim(s) indefinite, use form paragraph 7.34.01 instead to reject the claim(s) under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph.

name: Reference characters must be enclosed within parentheses
description: The claims are objected to because they include reference characters which are not enclosed within parentheses.
guidance: Reference characters corresponding to elements recited in the detailed description of the drawings and used in conjunction with the recitation of the same element or group of elements in the claims should be enclosed within parentheses so as to avoid confusion with other numbers or characters which may appear in the claims. See MPEP § 608.01(m). Use of this paragraph is optional; alternatively correct at allowance by informal examiner's amendment. If lack of parentheses renders the claim(s) indefinite, use form paragraph 7.34.01 to reject under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph.

name: Multiple dependent claim form (alternative only)
description: A multiple dependent claim shall refer to such other claims in the alternative only. A multiple dependent claim shall not serve as a basis for any other multiple dependent claim.
guidance: For fee calculation purposes a multiple dependent claim will be considered to be that number of claims to which direct reference is made therein. Claims in dependent form shall be construed to include all the limitations of the claim incorporated by reference. 35 U.S.C. 112 authorizes multiple dependent claims in applications filed on and after January 24, 1978, as long as they are in alternative form. Cumulative claiming (e.g., 'claims 3 and 4') is not permitted. A multiple dependent claim may refer in the alternative to only one set of claims and may not serve as a basis for another multiple dependent claim either directly or indirectly.

name: Acceptable and unacceptable multiple dependent claim wording
description: Examples of acceptable multiple dependent claim wording (e.g., 'A gadget according to claims 3 or 4...') and unacceptable wording (e.g., cumulative 'claim 3 and 4', references to non-alternative sets, references to two sets of claims for different features, references to another multiple dependent claim).
guidance: Use the provided acceptable examples as templates. Unacceptable forms include 'claim 3 and 4' (conjunctive), referring to numerically succeeding claims in a way that cannot be understood, referencing two sets of claims to different features, or depending from another multiple dependent claim. Such defects should be objected to or handled per form paragraph 7.45.

name: TC technical support staff handling of added multiple dependent claims
description: The Technology Center technical support staff is responsible for verifying compliance with the statute and rules of multiple dependent claims added by amendment and for calculating the amount of any additional fees required.
guidance: Do not enter an amendment containing a new multiple dependent claim or changing dependency before checking whether paid fees cover the amended claims. Contact applicant/attorney to pay additional fees; include a copy of PTO/SB/07 when informing applicant in an insufficient fee situation. Note: OPAP already verifies initial filing fee accuracy.

name: Examiner procedure for claims referring to numerically succeeding claims
description: If any series of dependent claims contains a claim with an improper reference to a numerically following claim which cannot be understood, the claim referring to a following claim should normally be objected to and not treated on the merits.
guidance: However, where a claim refers to a numerically following claim and the dependency is clear both as presented and as it will be renumbered at issue, all claims should be examined on the merits and no objection as to form need be made; examiner will renumber at allowance. Bring unusual problems to supervisor's attention. Examples (A and B) illustrate acceptable handling and renumbering practice.

name: Fee treatment for multiple dependent claims (use of PTO/SB/07)
description: To assist in computation of fees for multiple dependent claims use a 'Multiple Dependent Claim Fee Calculation Sheet' (PTO/SB/07) with PTO/SB/06; OPAP places form in application file when multiple dependent claims are filed.
guidance: If multiple dependent claims are later added by amendment, TC technical support staff will place the form in the file. Calculate total independent and dependent claims for fee purposes on PTO/SB/07 then transfer to PTO/SB/06.

name: Proper dependent claim test / Infringement test
description: The test as to whether a claim is a proper dependent claim is that it shall include every limitation of the claim from which it depends (35 U.S.C. 112, fourth paragraph) or in other words that it shall not conceivably be infringed by anything which would not also infringe the basic claim.
guidance: A dependent claim does not lack compliance simply because there is a question as to the significance of the further limitation or whether it changes scope. Example: if claim 1 recites A,B,C,D, a claim reciting claim 1 with D omitted or replaced is not a proper dependent claim. Examiners are reminded that a dependent claim is directed to the combination of everything recited in base claim plus dependent limitations and must be compared with prior art as if it were an independent claim.

name: Claim form and arrangement rules for dependent claims
description: A series of singular dependent claims is permissible in which a dependent claim refers to a preceding claim which, in turn, refers to another preceding claim. A claim which depends from a dependent claim should not be separated therefrom by any claim which does not also depend from said dependent claim.
guidance: A dependent claim may refer back to any preceding independent claim. Applicant's sequence should generally not be changed. During prosecution, numbering may change; numbering and references should be carefully checked when claims are renumbered upon allowance. Use form paragraph 7.43 to state objection when claim is dependent upon a rejected base claim but would be allowable if rewritten in independent form including all limitations.

name: Antecedent basis / Specification support for claim terminology
description: The meaning of every term used in any of the claims should be apparent from the descriptive portion of the specification with clear disclosure as to its import; in mechanical cases, it should be identified in the descriptive portion of the specification by reference to the drawing.
guidance: While applicant is not limited to nomenclature used in application as filed, appropriate amendment of the specification should be made when new terms are introduced to provide clear support or antecedent basis for new terms. Examiners should ensure terms used in claims presented late in prosecution find clear support/antecedent basis in the description so meaning may be ascertainable per 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1). If not, applicant required to amend description to provide support (without introducing new matter). Use form paragraph 7.44 to object: 'Claimed Subject Matter Not in Specification.' See MPEP § 2111.01 and § 2173.05(a).

name: Completeness of disclosure (enablement and utility)
description: A disclosure in an application, to be complete, must contain such description and details as to enable any person skilled in the art or science to which the invention pertains to make and use the invention as of its filing date.
guidance: Essential novelty must be described in sufficient detail including proportions and techniques where necessary. Specific operative embodiments or examples must be set forth; examples and description should be of sufficient scope to justify the scope of the claims. Markush claims require support for each member. Chemical compounds must be taught how to make. A complete disclosure should include a statement of utility. See MPEP § 2107, § 2107.01, § 2107.02, § 2107.03 and § 2164.06(a) for utility guidance.

name: Incorporation by reference rules (37 CFR 1.57)
description: An incorporation by reference must be set forth in the specification and must (1) express a clear intent to incorporate by reference by using the root words 'incorporat(e)' and 'reference' and (2) clearly identify the referenced patent, application, or publication.
guidance: Subject to conditions, inadvertently omitted portions present in prior-filed applications may be considered incorporated when certain priority/benefit claims are present, but the application must be amended to include the omitted portion within Office-set time (no later than close of prosecution). Applicant must supply a copy of the prior application, English translation if applicable, and identify where the omitted portion is found. 'Essential material' may be incorporated only by incorporation to a U.S. patent or U.S. patent application publication (that does not itself incorporate the essential material) and is limited to material necessary for written description, claims, or means-plus-function structure (35 U.S.C. 112 requirements). Nonessential material may be incorporated by reference to various publications; incorporation by hyperlink or browser executable code is not permitted.

name: Condition for examination requirements (§ 1.704(f))
description: An application filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a) is in condition for examination when it includes a specification (including at least one claim and an abstract (§ 1.72(b))), papers in compliance with § 1.52, drawings (if any) in compliance with § 1.84, any required English translation, Sequence Listing or Sequence Listing XML if applicable, an inventor's oath/declaration or application data sheet with the information in § 1.63(b), basic filing/search/examination fees, any certified copy required by § 1.57(a), and any required application size fee. International applications have analogous requirements per §§ 1.491 and 1.492.
guidance: An application is considered to have papers/drawings/sequence listings in compliance for purposes of paragraph (f) on the filing date of the latest reply (if any) correcting those items that is prior to the date of mailing of either an action under 35 U.S.C. 132 or a notice of allowance under 35 U.S.C. 151, whichever occurs first.

name: Paris Convention right of priority (requirements and effect)
description: If an application is filed in a Paris-Convention country, a later-filed application for the same invention in another Paris country within one year will be entitled to the benefit of the filing date of the first application upon fulfillment of various conditions.
guidance: Patents or published specifications of the later filing countries are required to specify that priority has been claimed and to give the country, date, and number of the priority application; this information aids locating any patent based on the priority application. See MPEP §213 for further detail.

name: Check foreign priority/publication when U.S. reference claims foreign priority
description: When a U.S. patent or U.S. published application being considered as a reference claims the priority of a previously filed foreign application, determine if the foreign application has issued or been published to see if there is an earlier date.
guidance: Examiner should check foreign documents because a foreign patent or publication may have an earlier printed publication date than the U.S. document; that earlier date can affect 35 U.S.C. 102 rejections. Whether a foreign priority application filing date can serve as an 'effectively filed date' under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) is governed by 35 U.S.C. 102(d) (see MPEP § 2154.01(b)).

name: Verify earlier related document contains necessary subject matter
description: Related documents in a family usually have identical disclosures but sometimes contain differences in claims or minor specification differences.
guidance: Examiners should always verify that the earlier related document also includes the subject matter necessary for the rejection before relying on it as a reference.

name: 37 CFR 1.132 evidence formality requirement
description: When any claim is rejected or objected to, any evidence submitted to traverse the rejection/objection on a basis not otherwise provided for must be by way of an oath or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132.
guidance: This rule is the general policy for receiving affidavit evidence traversing rejections or objections that do not fall under other specific rules.

name: Use of form paragraphs 7.65/7.66 for office actions
description: Form paragraph 7.65 (effective to withdraw rejection) and 7.66 (insufficient) and the set 7.66.01–7.66.05 form paragraphs should be used as appropriate to comment on 37 CFR 1.132 affidavits/declarations.
guidance: Each form paragraph contains bracketed fields for insertion (e.g., filing date, affected claims, statutory grounds). When using 7.66, follow with detailed reasons for insufficiency (untimely, fails to set forth facts, not commensurate in scope, etc.).

name: Form paragraph 7.65 — sufficient to overcome rejection
description: Template wording to state that the affidavit/declaration filed on [date] is sufficient to overcome the rejection of claim(s) [x] based upon [statutory grounds/reference].
guidance: Insert appropriate bracketed items; examiner note fields for internal use. Use when the affidavit/declaration adequately rebuts the rejection.

name: Insufficiency reason — invention works as intended
description: Statements that merely affirm the claimed subject matter functions as intended are not relevant to nonobviousness and provide no objective evidence.
guidance: Such conclusory functional statements lack probative value for nonobviousness and require additional factual support.

name: Insufficiency reason — refers only to invention, not claims
description: If the affidavit/declaration refers only to the system described in the application and not to the individual claims, it does not show that objective evidence of nonobviousness is commensurate in scope with the claims.
guidance: Affidavits must address the claimed limitations, not just a general embodiment.

name: Insufficiency reason — no evidence of long-felt need
description: Assertions that the claimed subject matter solved a long-standing problem are insufficient without showing that others of ordinary skill were working on the problem, for how long, and that knowledge of the prior art would not have enabled solving it.
guidance: Provide evidence that others were working and still unable to solve the problem despite knowledge of prior art; mere assertion is inadequate.

name: Comparative data in specification
description: Examiners must consider comparative data in the specification intended to illustrate the claimed invention when reaching a conclusion regarding obviousness.
guidance: See In re Margolis; lack of comparative data can weaken assertions of unexpected results.

name: Presence of an unexpected property as evidence
description: Demonstration of a property present in the claimed invention but not in the prior art (e.g., new therapeutic activity) is evidence of nonobviousness.
guidance: In re Papesch and related cases show unexpected properties can be persuasive but do not automatically mandate patentability; factual support required.

name: Absence of an expected property as evidence
description: Showing a claimed invention lacks a property that prior art would have expected it to have can be evidence of nonobviousness.
guidance: Example: claimed compounds expected to have beta-blocking activity did not, which was unexpected and supported unobviousness (Ex parte Mead Johnson).

name: Direct and indirect comparative testing probative
description: Direct or indirect comparative tests comparing the claimed invention with the closest prior art, commensurate in scope with the claims, are probative of nonobviousness.
guidance: See In re Boesch, Blondel, Fouche for precedents where comparative testing was sufficient to rebut prima facie obviousness.

name: Patentability of intermediates via end-product unexpectedness
description: Patentability of an intermediate may be established by unexpected properties of an end product when one of ordinary skill would reasonably ascribe the intermediate as the contributing cause; applicant must identify the cause and establish a nexus between intermediate and end product.
guidance: Follow In re Magerlein: identify contributing cause of superior end-product property and tie it factually to the claimed intermediate.

name: Use of comparators in patentability assessment (compare claim to original invention)
description: Section 3(d) requires comparison of the new form/claim with the original substance to determine whether the new form shows enhanced efficacy or is merely an obvious/insubstantial modification.
guidance: This comparison-based analysis resembles heightened non-obviousness review and guides courts/examiners to evaluate whether the claimed improvement is substantive relative to the prior product.

name: Statement indicating basis for amendment with specific references
description: Any amendment to sequence data must include a statement that indicates the basis for the amendment, with specific references to particular parts of the application (specification, claims, drawings) as originally filed (required for all amended sequence data in replacement 'Sequence Listing').
guidance: This statement supports that the amendment is supported by the original disclosure; missing or insufficient statements trigger specific deficiency form paragraphs (see ¶24.14, ¶24.16).

name: Form paragraph ¶24.10 — Sequence identifiers (SEQ ID NO:) missing in specification
description: Specific deficiency: nucleotide and/or amino acid sequences appearing in the specification are not identified by sequence identifiers in accordance with 37 CFR 1.821(d). Required response: provide a substitute specification inserting the required sequence identifiers, consisting of a marked-up version, a clean version, and a statement that the substitute specification contains no new matter.
guidance: Use when reference has not been made to the sequence by 'SEQ ID NO:' in the description or claims, even if embedded in the text. Precede with 24.01.

name: Regular nonprovisional application completeness requirements
description: A regular nonprovisional (referred to as 'regular' in Public PAIR) must be complete before examination can commence: at minimum it must contain at least one claim, a specification that discloses the invention, drawings when necessary, and an executed oath or declaration.
guidance: A filing date is assigned when the application is complete (see MPEP 601.01). Incomplete applications delay placement on an examiner's docket.

name: Provisional application requirements and limitations
description: Provisional applications (since 1995) are not examined, expire 12 months after filing, need not include claims or an oath/declaration, but must include a specification that meets written description and enablement and must provide names and residence addresses of inventors.
guidance: To claim benefit of a provisional the later-filed nonprovisional must be filed within 12 months and the claimed subject matter must have support in the provisional and at least one inventor in common. Provisional → nonprovisional conversion via petition under 37 C.F.R. 1.53(c)(3) is an alternative.

name: Reissue application criteria
description: A reissue application corrects an error in a previously-issued patent that makes it wholly or partially invalid or inoperable (mistakes in specification/drawings, inventorship, claims of benefit). No new subject matter may be introduced; claims may be broadened only if reissue is filed within two years of original issue date.
guidance: Reissue is examined similarly to a regular application and often receives priority on an examiner’s docket; there may be a (usually two-month) delay to allow public protests unless shortened by circumstances like litigation.

name: Examiner evaluation criteria during examination
description: When examining claims, the examiner evaluates: patent-eligible subject matter; adequacy of the written description and enablement; clarity and definiteness of claims; and conducts prior art searches for anticipation or obviousness (single reference or combination).
guidance: Where multiple inventions are claimed the examiner can issue a restriction requirement; allowance vs. non-final rejection outcomes depend on these substantive assessments.

name: Examples of Arguments Appropriate for Pre-Appeal
description: Types of arguments that are suited to the limited Pre-Appeal (≤5 pages) review.
guidance: Appropriate Pre-Appeal arguments include: the applied reference is not in fact prior art; the inventive entity is clearly not one to which the reference can be applied; a claim element is clearly not present in the applied art; support in the disclosure is clearly found contrary to a 112(a) rejection (contrary to the rejection’s assertion); no rationale is provided in a 103 rejection; no evidentiary basis for a 103 rationale is provided in the rejection.

name: Argument Ordering and Strategy: Best Argument First
description: Tactical guidance on ordering arguments in Pre-Appeal or Appeal submissions.
guidance: Order arguments with the best argument first. Use a 'Funnel Approach' to structure each issue: Rejection → Claim → Limitation → Why (i.e., identify the rejection at issue, the claim at issue, the limitation at issue, and explain why it is erroneous).

name: Avoid Mere Recitation; Must Argue Separate Patentability
description: What does not qualify as an argument for patentability.
guidance: A statement which merely points out what a claim recites will not be considered an argument for separate patentability of the claim (37 C.F.R. § 41.37(c)(1)(iv)). See also In re Lovin, 652 F.3d 1349 (Fed. Cir. 2011). Parties must explain why the elements recited render the claim patentable over the rejection, not merely repeat claim language.

name: Claim Interpretation Guidance — Deference to PTO Without Express Definition
description: How claim terms are interpreted when the specification lacks express definitions.
guidance: Absent an express definition in the specification, appellants pointing to definitions or usages that conform to their interpretation does not make the PTO's definition unreasonable where the PTO can point to other sources that support its interpretation (In re Morris, 127 F.3d 1048, 1056 (Fed. Cir. 1997)). To control interpretation, include express definitions in the specification.

name: Reject vague or indefinite claim language
description: Examiners should reject vague claim language and force more definite and unambiguous expressions of the invention.
guidance: Under 35 U.S.C. § 112, examiners have statutory authority to reject applications that do not completely and unambiguously describe and enable the claimed invention. Increasing rejections on this ground will incentivize applicants to clarify initial applications (because specification changes can constitute new matter and affect priority). Example/anti-pattern: permitting claims that cover both patentable and non-patentable subject matter (Prater) leads to invalid claims; examiners should notify patentees when claims are too broad and require narrowing (e.g., limit to digital computers).

name: Examiners require disclaimers and applicant definitions when warranted
description: Where an applicant explains that certain prior art does not apply or asserts a specific meaning for a term, the examiner should require a clear disclaimer or require that the definition be reflected in the claims or specification.
guidance: Requiring disclaimers or explicit definitions creates a clearer public record and allows courts to apply disclaimers when construing claims (SanDisk v. Memorex). Trademark practice provides an analogy (examiners routinely require disclaimers for non-protectable words). If definitions or disclaimers are ambiguous, courts will not use them to limit ordinary meaning. Examples: require a disclaimer when applicant distinguishes prior art; require that a declared meaning of a term be placed into the claims or specification.

name: Examiners should take an active role and issue 'reasons for allowance' statements
description: Examiners should compile and state the reasons why particular claims were allowed—documenting which limitations made a claim allowable over the prior art.
guidance: A final 'reasons for allowance' document would explain that a claim was allowed because it included a certain limitation (enhances public notice). If binding on courts, such a document would further improve claim construction consistency. This proposal relies on examiners already knowing reasons for allowance and would not significantly lengthen review if done succinctly.

name: Examiners should police word/phrase interpretation during prosecution
description: Examiners should actively identify ambiguities, explore scope and breadth of language, and impose clarification during prosecution rather than leaving ambiguities unresolved.
guidance: The MPEP and caselaw (In re Zletz) encourage recognition and clarification of ambiguities during prosecution. Doing so increases public notice by producing clearer claim language or explicit disclaimers/definitions in the record. This may involve affirmative statements about the examiner's understanding of what the patent is and is not intended to cover.

name: Do not require examiners to create full claim charts for every application
description: Examiners should not be required to prepare detailed claim charts for every patent application because of the substantial time cost relative to public benefit.
guidance: Creating proper claim charts can take hours or days; with ~4,000 examiners and ~400,000 applications per year, requiring claim charts would impose significant workload increases (even 30 extra minutes each is meaningful). Only a small percentage of patents are litigated, and even then only a subset of claim terms are disputed, so requiring full claim charts is inefficient.

name: Do not require a comprehensive lexicon for every patent; require targeted definitions
description: Applicants should not be forced to provide a complete lexicon defining every word in every claim, because such a requirement is costly and still leaves ambiguity; instead, require definitions or clarifying amendments for terms likely to be disputed.
guidance: A full lexicon for a patent with many claims could require hundreds of definitions and spawn disputes over definitions themselves. Targeted definition requirements—where examiners or applicants identify specific disputed terms and place definitions in the patent—are more cost-effective and improve notice for the terms most likely to be litigated.

name: Enforce written description and enablement requirements (35 U.S.C. § 112)
description: Examiners should more vigorously reject applications that fail to provide sufficient detail in the written specification to describe and enable the claimed invention.
guidance: Stronger enforcement of § 112 will incentivize applicants to produce comprehensive initial specifications, which clarify claim meaning and reduce reliance on prosecution history. Rejecting ill-described applications prevents applicants from using vague claims to obtain unwarranted scope, and because changes to the specification can be new matter, applicants prefer priority and therefore will supply better initial detail. Example: Eli Lilly/regents case where insufficient description invalidated overbroad claims.

name: Require detailed description of preferred embodiments and implementation
description: Applicants should be required (or examiners should insist) to provide more detail on how the invention is implemented in preferred embodiments to clarify what is and is not part of the invention.
guidance: Clear preferred-embodiment descriptions help courts construe ambiguous terms (Globetrotter: specification showed 'preventing' included passive 'no-license' messages). Applicants may resist for fear of limiting claim scope (Honeywell), so examiner pressure is necessary. Marginal cost of accurate descriptions is likely low since applicants understand their inventions.

name: Relax the obviousness standard to allow more prior art to be considered
description: To ensure adequate testing of claims against prior art, the obviousness standard should be relaxed (as KSR did) so examiners can consider more prior art and combinations when evaluating patentability.
guidance: Abandoning the broadest reasonable construction rule risks narrower prosecution-stage interpretations that exclude relevant prior art; relaxing obviousness helps preserve substantive examination against as much relevant prior art as possible. Prior Federal Circuit tests requiring explicit teaching/suggestion/motivation to combine limited examiners' ability to find combinations; KSR's approach permits broader consideration of prior art combination to test validity and define outer claim limits.

name: Permit and encourage examiner-initiated amendments to improve clarity
description: Examiners should be empowered to amend patent applications or require applicant amendments (e.g., to add disclaimers or definitions) when necessary to obtain clear claims.
guidance: Rules (e.g., 37 C.F.R. § 1.121(g) and MPEP § 714(II)(E)) already provide for examiner amendments, though they are rarely used; encouraging such amendments would reverse the trend of applicant-initiated-only amendments and could efficiently produce clearer claims without requiring wholesale new disclosure from applicants. Applicants who disagree can respond and attempt to clarify their intent.

name: Effect and timing of disclaimers on novelty defence and costs
description: If a disclaimer of the improperly claimed part has been filed in the patent office in reasonable time, a defence of want of novelty that attacks only part of the thing patented will not be a complete answer to an action but will prevent recovery of costs.
guidance: No costs can be recovered unless the plaintiff filed a disclaimer of all the part of the thing patented which the original specification should not have claimed before bringing the action. Unreasonable neglect or delay in entering the disclaimer may permit the defence to be admitted as a bar; unreasonable neglect is a question of law for the court. Notices of defence should specify the particular parts intended to be attacked.

name: Technology-specific filtering through prosecution/litigation/licensing
description: The filtering of patents through prosecution, litigation, and licensing systems leaves a small and technologically uneven group of patents that reach judgment; the filtering process itself may be technology specific.
guidance: Interpret outcome distributions as potentially shaped by upstream and midstream selection mechanisms that vary by technology (e.g., prosecutorial claiming strategies, licensing markets, settlement norms).

name: Biotechnology as an anomalous category requiring special scrutiny
description: Biotech patents in the dataset were adjudicated successfully for patentees only 8% of the time and were more likely to be invalidated or found not infringed than other technologies; this anomaly may stem from selection, functional claiming, notable cases (e.g., Myriad), or changes in patentability standards.
guidance: Treat biotech results as a puzzle warranting targeted case studies and expanded samples; consider recent doctrinal shifts and landmark invalidations when interpreting aggregate biotech outcomes.

name: Invention information — definition and determination
description: Invention information is technical information in the total disclosure of a patent document that represents an addition to the state of the art.
guidance: It is determined in the context of the state of the art, using guidance provided by the claims, with due regard to description and drawings. 'Addition to the state of the art' means all novel and unobvious subject matter specifically disclosed in a patent document.

name: Classification of chemical compounds disclosed by general formulae (Steps 1–4)
description: When general formulae (Markush-type) disclose large sets of related compounds, classification is restricted to compounds most useful for searches following a four-step procedure.
guidance: Step 1: Classify all 'fully identified' compounds that are novel and unobvious if they are (i) specifically claimed as such or in a composition, (ii) products of a claimed process, or (iii) derivatives of these. 'Fully identified' means structure is exact name/formula or deducible from preparation from specified reactants (not more than one from a list) AND compound is characterised by a physical property or worked example with practical details. Compounds identified only by empirical formula are not 'fully identified'. Step 2: If no fully identified compounds disclosed (e.g., computer-generated, no experiments), classify only compounds with exact chemical name or developed formula, limited to a single or very small number of groups. Step 3: If only general Markush formula disclosed, classify in the most specific group(s) that cover all or most potential embodiments, limited to a single or very small number of groups. Step 4: In addition to obligatory classification, non-obligatory classification may be made when other compounds within scope of the general formula or compounds from computer-generated models are of interest.

name: Right to publish translations, abstracts, or editions with notes
description: It is asserted that any one is at liberty to print Acts of Parliament and the Bible with notes, or to publish a translation/abstract from original texts and enjoy copyright in that new production.
guidance: This point challenges a prerogative that would prevent annotated or derivative editions; Lord Mansfield admitted an abstract of court records might be published. The prerogative's claimed purpose (prevent mutilation/incorrect printing) does not clearly justify excluding annotated or translated editions.

name: Availability of copies where benefit is claimed in an issued or published document (37 CFR 1.14(a)(1)(v))
description: A copy of the file contents of an unpublished pending application may be provided to any person upon written request and payment of fee if the benefit of the application is claimed under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), 120, 121, or 365 in an application or patent that has issued or published as described.
guidance: Copies provided may include application-as-filed or specific documents in the file; the Office will not provide access to the paper file of a pending application except as provided in paragraphs (c) or (h).

name: Product-of-nature / markedly-different-characteristics requirement
description: Characteristics of claimed subject matter that are innate to naturally occurring material and not markedly different from their natural counterparts render claims directed to a product of nature ineligible.
guidance: If claimed characteristics are 'innate to naturally occurring DNA' or inherent to a natural material (e.g., ductility of vanadium, genetic sequence of DNA, cloned animal genetics), the claims lack 'markedly different characteristics' and are products of nature exceptions (citing Ambry Genetics, In re Marden, In re Roslin). Phenotypic or structural differences that are not claimed are irrelevant. The claimed features must themselves show the marked differences.

name: Integration into a practical application (Step 2A Prong Two) — general
description: After identifying a judicial exception (Step 2A Prong One), evaluate whether the claim as a whole integrates the exception into a practical application; if so, the claim is not directed to the exception and is eligible at Pathway B.
guidance: A claim 'integrates' a judicial exception when the additional elements apply, rely on, or use the exception in a manner that imposes a meaningful limit on the exception rather than merely attempting to monopolize it. The evaluation uses a set of considerations (non-exclusive) and follows the procedure of identifying additional elements and evaluating them individually and in combination (see MPEP § 2106.05 subsections for details). If integration is found, Step 2A concludes (Step 2A: NO). If not, proceed to Step 2B.

name: Improvement in the functioning of a computer or other technology
description: An additional element that demonstrates an improvement to computer functionality or another technology/technical field can show integration of the judicial exception into a practical application.
guidance: Examiners should consult the specification to determine whether disclosure provides sufficient detail for a person of ordinary skill to recognize the improvement; the specification need not explicitly say 'improvement' but must make it apparent. The claim must reflect the components/steps that provide the improvement (it need not recite the improvement in words). This 'improvements' consideration at Step 2A does not consider whether the elements are well-understood, routine, or conventional. Case examples: Enfish, McRO, Visual Memory, Finjan, SRI (see MPEP § 2106.05(a)).

name: Applying or using the judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis
description: Claims that use the judicial exception to effect a particular medical treatment or prophylaxis can integrate the exception into a practical application and thus be not directed to the exception.
guidance: This consideration is distinct and elevated due to cases like Vanda. Claims that include administration/treatment steps that use a natural-law relationship to guide or limit therapy (e.g., genotype-guided dosing to reduce risk) may be eligible at Step 2A because the steps are directed to treating the patient, not merely gathering diagnostic data (contrast with Mayo). Examples of 'treatment' limitations include administration of medication, surgery, dialysis, physiotherapy, phototherapy, organ transplants, acupuncture, radiation therapy, etc.

name: Implementing the judicial exception with, or using it in conjunction with, a particular machine or manufacture integral to the claim
description: An additional element that implements or uses the judicial exception with a specific machine or manufacture integral to the claim may indicate integration into a practical application.
guidance: Evaluate whether the claim recites a particular machine/manufacture that is integral (not merely a generic computer). Specificity of the machine-related limitations is relevant to determine if they meaningfully limit the exception (see MPEP §§ 2106.05(b),(f)). Mere recitation of a generic machine is insufficient; the claim should reflect how the machine is integral to the claimed invention.

name: Applying or using the judicial exception in some other meaningful way beyond a general field link
description: Any additional elements that apply or use the judicial exception in a meaningful way beyond merely linking it to a technological environment can indicate integration into a practical application.
guidance: This is a catch-all for limitations that impose meaningful limits on the exception beyond general field-of-use or environment links. The claim as a whole should be more than a drafting effort designed to monopolize the exception (see MPEP § 2106.05(e)).

name: Generally linking the exception to a particular technological environment or field of use is insufficient (anti-pattern)
description: A claim that merely links the use of a judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use does not integrate the exception into a practical application.
guidance: General field-of-use limitations or merely stating the technological context without meaningful limiting interaction between the additional elements and the exception will not render the claim eligible (see MPEP § 2106.05(h)).

name: Specificity of claimed limitations — not a standalone but relevant
description: Specific ways of achieving a result are not standalone considerations, but the specificity of claim limitations is relevant to evaluations of particular machine, transformation, and mere-instruction-to-apply considerations.
guidance: Claims that lack specificity about how to implement the additional elements (e.g., how to select parameters, monitor variables, or effect steps) may be found to recite only insignificant post-solution activity (see Parker v. Flook). Examiners should consider specificity when applying related considerations (MPEP §§ 2106.05(b),(c),(f)).

name: Procedural method for Prong Two evaluation
description: To evaluate integration into a practical application, identify additional claim elements beyond the judicial exception and evaluate those elements individually and in combination using the listed considerations; not all considerations apply to every claim.
guidance: The analysis is not a weighing test; the number or label of applicable considerations is immaterial. Focus on the significance of the additional elements relative to the applicant’s invention and whether they integrate the exception into a practical application. Examine each claim separately — claims in the same application may yield different eligibility outcomes. For multiple exceptions recited, see MPEP § 2106.04 subsection II.B.

name: Enablement requirement / Practicability
description: The invention related to the claims must be able to be practiced with the embodiments disclosed in the description; if a certain embodiment for practicing the invention related to the claims is deemed different from the embodiment disclosed in the description, the examiner shall notify a ground for rejection citing violation of Article 42(3)(i) of the Patent Act.
guidance: When notifying enablement violations, specify the corresponding claims. If the description pursuant to Article 21(3) is present but not clear/detailed enough for the claimed invention to be practiced, notify under Article 42(3). For applications filed after Jan 1, 2015, propose amendment under Article 46 rather than immediate invalidation; for earlier applications, different consequences may apply.

name: Embodiment disclosure requirements
description: When claims are written generically, state representative embodiments corresponding to the generic description, unless a skilled person can derive details from the generic description.
guidance: Include basic data, comparative embodiments (technically closest to the invention), and alternative embodiments; specify differences between embodiments and show reference numbers for drawings in parentheses after technical terms.

name: Background art disclosure requirement
description: Background art refers to conventional art beneficial for understanding the invention and conducting prior art searches and examination; it shall be disclosed in the description.
guidance: For applications filed after July 1, 2011, failure to disclose related background art is a ground for rejection under Article 42(3)(ii). The background art should be related to the invention defined by the claim limitations, considering technical field, problems, solutions, and effects.

name: Inconsistency or ambiguity in technical terms
description: Where different technical terms are used across the description and claims making the invention difficult to practice, notify rejection under Article 42(3). Where terms in the description and claims do not clearly match or are ambiguous, notify rejection under Article 42(4).
guidance: Undefined or unclear academic/technical terms, or lack of original-language/Chinese-character equivalents when needed, can be ground for rejection under Article 42(3).

name: Notification method and specificity of rejection grounds
description: When notifying rejection for enablement or description-method violations, the examiner shall specify any violation and the corresponding claims (especially for enablement).
guidance: If the description method requirement (Article 21(3)) is violated but the claims can still be practiced, the description may still be considered legitimate. Distinct procedures apply depending on filing date (pre-2015 vs post-2015) regarding amendment proposals under Article 46.

name: Form and numbering of claims
description: Claims shall include at least one claim to be protected; claims must be supported by the description and set forth the invention clearly and concisely (Article 42(4)). Claims may include independent and dependent claims; the number of claims should be reasonable relative to the nature of the invention. Each claim must be entered on a new line and numbered in Arabic numerals in order.
guidance: A claim that refers to another claim must state the number referred to; multiple dependent claims have specific restrictions (cannot serve as basis for other multiple dependent claims). The claim from which another depends should precede it.

name: Recognition of invention/scope determination
description: The invention for which protection is sought is determined by the limitations recited in each claim in accordance with the applicant’s will; the description/drawings are considered only when claims are indefinite or technical term meanings are ambiguous.
guidance: Do not determine protection scope based on the description beyond claim limitations; abstracts cannot be used to decide protection scope.

name: Claims must be supported by the description (support requirement)
description: An examiner determines support by whether a person skilled in the art can figure out that subject matters corresponding to the claim limitations are disclosed in the description; support is judged by whether claims depart from the scope grasped by a skilled person based on the description, not by literal identity.
guidance: Cases lacking support include: (i) claim limitations (e.g., numeric) not disclosed or implied in the description; (ii) claim terms different from description rendering correspondence ambiguous; (iii) claims recite means/steps for functions but no specific configuration is disclosed; (iv) description cannot be extended/generalized to the claimed scope by a skilled person (e.g., claims defined only by technical effects while description shows only specific means). Examiners should consider the level of skill in the art.

name: Inventive concept standard
description: An "inventive concept" is more than merely implementing an abstract idea using "well-understood, routine, [and] conventional activities previously known to the industry."
guidance: Assess whether claim elements, individually and as an ordered combination, provide something beyond conventional computer implementation (see Content Extraction & Transmission LLC v. Wells Fargo Bank, Nat’l Ass’n, 776 F.3d 1343, 1347–48).

name: Conventionality is a factual inquiry (Berkheimer rule)
description: Whether claim elements are "well-understood, routine, or conventional" is often a question of fact; a material dispute of fact over conventionality precludes dismissal or summary adjudication on §101.
guidance: District courts should not resolve such disputes against the non-movant at the 12(b)(6) stage; evidentiary development may be required (see Berkheimer v. HP, Inc., 881 F.3d 1360).

name: Adopt non-moving party’s claim construction on motion to dismiss where appropriate
description: When claim scope is disputed on a Rule 12 motion and the district court has not conducted claim construction, the court should proceed by adopting the non-moving party’s construction for purposes of the motion.
guidance: Follow Aatrix Software, Inc. v. Green Shades Software, Inc., 882 F.3d 1121, 1125; do not resolve disputed claim-meaning questions against the patentee on 12(b)(6).

name: Specific structural/functional claim limitations can supply inventive concept
description: Claims that recite a specific technical solution—i.e., particular arrangements of elements, network structure, or functional limitations that improve computer/network functioning—can constitute an inventive concept sufficient to survive §101 challenge.
guidance: Look for claim language that delineates structure and function and for specification statements tying those features to improved performance (see BASCOM; Enfish; Thales; SRI). Courts should consider whether the claimed arrangement is a technical improvement over prior art ways of arranging systems.

name: Plausible factual allegations tethered to claim limitations defeat dismissal
description: If the complaint plausibly alleges that specific claimed limitations provided new or improved functionality (e.g., reduced cost, improved redundancy, smoother playback), those allegations tethered to claim language create a factual dispute precluding 12(b)(6) dismissal.
guidance: Assess whether alleged benefits are tied to the claim elements (e.g., capacity improvements tied to distribution outside CDN). If so, treat as plausible inventive-concept allegations (see Berkheimer and the opinion's application).

name: Dynamic P2P network structural limitation (as an alleged inventive concept)
description: Claim must include at least one P2P dynamic network with a multiplicity of peer nodes that "consume the same content within a predetermined time" and are "distributed outside controlled networks and/or content distribution networks (CDNs)."
guidance: This structural limitation is alleged to be inventive because it (per the specification) groups peers by simultaneous content consumption to provide smooth playback, avoid stuttering/buffering, improve redundancy, address capacity problems, and reduce CDN costs; courts should treat such structural-functional recitations as potential inventive concepts.

name: Content segmentation based on trace routes (as an alleged inventive concept)
description: Claim requires content segmentation "based on CDN address resolution, trace route to CDN and P2P server manager, dynamic feedback from peers reporting traffic rates between individual peer and its neighbors, round-robin and other server side scheduling/resource allocation techniques."
guidance: The specification and prosecution history describe segmenting using trace routes as a factor for balancing/managing distribution and improving reliability, redundancy, and efficiency. If the claim requires trace-route-based segmentation (and the complaint pleads it does), that limitation can be an inventive concept; courts should not assume trace-route usage is merely conventional without resolving factual disputes.

name: Derivation petition particularity requirement
description: The petition shall set forth with particularity the basis for finding that an individual named in an earlier application as the inventor or a joint inventor derived such invention from an individual named in the petitioner’s application as the inventor or a joint inventor and, without authorization, the earlier application claiming such invention was filed.
guidance: Derivation petitions must plead specific factual detail showing derivation (not mere allegation).

name: Definition of earlier application for derivation purposes
description: For purposes of this section, an application shall not be deemed to be an earlier application with respect to an invention, relative to another application, unless a claim to the invention was or could have been made in such application having an effective filing date that is earlier than the effective filing date of any claim to the invention that was or could have been made in such other application.
guidance: Determination of which application is 'earlier' depends on whether a claim to the invention could have been made with an earlier effective filing date (affects entitlement and timing).

name: PTAB determination standard in derivation proceeding
description: In a derivation proceeding instituted under subsection (a), the Patent Trial and Appeal Board shall determine whether an inventor named in the earlier application derived the claimed invention from an inventor named in the petitioner’s application and, without authorization, the earlier application claiming such invention was filed.
guidance: PTAB evaluates evidence to determine whether derivation occurred and whether the earlier filing was unauthorized; PTAB may correct inventor naming where appropriate.

name: PTAB deferral and stay powers in derivation proceedings
description: The Patent Trial and Appeal Board may defer action on a petition for a derivation proceeding until the expiration of the 3-month period beginning on the date on which the Director issues a patent that includes the claimed invention that is the subject of the petition. The Patent Trial and Appeal Board also may defer action on a petition for a derivation proceeding, or stay the proceeding after it has been instituted, until the termination of a proceeding under chapter 30, 31, or 32 involving the patent of the earlier applicant.
guidance: PTAB may delay or stay derivation proceedings for short statutory periods or while related post-grant proceedings (e.g., IPR/PGR) are pending.

name: Settlement filing and confidentiality in derivation
description: Parties to a proceeding instituted under subsection (a) may terminate the proceeding by filing a written statement reflecting the agreement of the parties as to the correct inventor of the claimed invention in dispute. Unless the Patent Trial and Appeal Board finds the agreement to be inconsistent with the evidence of record, if any, it shall take action consistent with the agreement. Any written settlement or understanding of the parties shall be filed with the Director. At the request of a party to the proceeding, the agreement or understanding shall be treated as business confidential information, shall be kept separate from the file of the involved patents or applications, and shall be made available only to Government agencies on written request, or to any person on a showing of good cause.
guidance: Settlements regarding inventorship must be filed; PTAB will accept settlements consistent with the record and can treat them as confidential business information upon request, with limited disclosure rules.

name: Arbitration option in derivation proceedings
description: Parties to a proceeding instituted under subsection (a) may, within such time as may be specified by the Director by regulation, determine such contest or any aspect thereof by arbitration. Such arbitration shall be governed by the provisions of title 9, to the extent such title is not inconsistent with this section. The parties shall give notice of any arbitration award to the Director, and such award shall, as between the parties to the arbitration, be dispositive of the issues to which it relates. The arbitration award shall be unenforceable until such notice is given. Nothing in this subsection shall preclude the Director from determining the patentability of the claimed inventions involved in the proceeding.
guidance: Arbitration is permitted as an alternative dispute resolution method, but the Director retains authority over patentability issues; awards are binding between parties after notice to Director but not enforceable until filed.

name: Amendment rights before designated Offices
description: The applicant shall be given the opportunity to amend the claims, the description, and the drawings before each designated Office within the prescribed time limit. No designated Office shall grant or refuse a patent before such time limit has expired except with the express consent of the applicant. Amendments shall not go beyond the disclosure in the international application as filed unless national law permits.
guidance: Amendments must be in accordance with national law where the Treaty/Regulations are silent; where translation is required, amendments must be in translation language.

name: Objective and substantive criteria of international preliminary examination
description: The objective of the international preliminary examination is to formulate a preliminary and non‑binding opinion on whether the claimed invention appears to be novel, to involve an inventive step (to be non‑obvious), and to be industrially applicable.
guidance: For PCT purposes: novelty = not anticipated by prior art as defined in the Regulations; inventive step = not obvious to a person skilled in the art at the prescribed relevant date; industrial applicability = can be made or used in any kind of industry (broadest sense). The IPEA shall consider all documents cited in the international search report and may consider additional relevant documents. Any Contracting State may apply additional or different criteria at national phase.

name: Refusal to carry out international preliminary examination
description: If the IPEA considers that the application relates to subject matter on which it is not required to carry out an international preliminary examination, or that the description/claims/drawings are so unclear or claims inadequately supported that no meaningful opinion can be formed on novelty, inventive step, or industrial applicability, the IPEA shall not go into those questions and shall inform the applicant of this opinion and reasons.
guidance: If such situation applies only to certain claims, the IPEA's action applies only to those claims.

name: Contents and limitations of the international preliminary examination report (IPER)
description: The IPER shall be established within the prescribed time limit and form. It shall not contain any statement on whether the claimed invention is patentable under any national law. It shall state, in relation to each claim, whether the claim appears to satisfy the criteria of novelty, inventive step, and industrial applicability as defined for international preliminary examination, accompanied by citation of documents believed to support the conclusion and explanations as circumstances require. It shall also include other observations as Regulations provide.
guidance: If the IPEA finds situations under Article 34(4)(a), the report shall state that opinion and reasons and shall not contain the statements required by paragraph (2). If Article 34(4)(b) situation exists for certain claims, the report will treat those claims accordingly.

name: Amendment rights before elected Offices
description: The applicant shall be given the opportunity to amend the claims, description, and drawings, before each elected Office within the prescribed time limit. No elected Office shall grant or refuse a patent before such time limit has expired except with the express consent of the applicant. Amendments shall not go beyond the disclosure in the international application as filed unless national law permits.
guidance: Amendments must comply with the national law of the elected State in all respects not provided for in the Treaty/Regulations; where translation is required, amendments shall be in the translation language.

name: Chemical and mathematical formulae and tables allowed (but not drawings)
description: The specification, including the claims, may contain chemical and mathematical formulae, but shall not contain drawings or flow diagrams. The description portion may contain tables, but the same tables should not be included in both the drawings and description portion of the specification. Claims may contain tables if necessary to conform to 35 U.S.C. 112 or otherwise desirable.
guidance: Graphical illustrations/flowcharts belong in drawings (see 37 CFR 1.81) and examiners should object to descriptive illustrations in the specification and request drawings when appropriate.

name: Page numbering and line spacing
description: The pages of the specification, including claims and abstract, must be numbered consecutively starting with 1, the numbers being centrally located above or preferably below the text. The lines of the specification and any amendments must be 1 1/2 or double spaced.
guidance: The text must be written in a nonscript type font (preferably font size 12) with capital letters at least 0.3175 cm (0.125 inch) high but no smaller than 0.21 cm (0.08 inch) (font size 6). The text may not be written solely in capital letters and only a single column of text is permitted.

name: Separate sheets for specification elements
description: The specification must commence on a separate sheet. Each sheet including part of the specification may not include other parts of the application or other information. The claim(s), abstract and sequence listing (if any) should not be included on a sheet including any other part of the application. The claim(s) must commence on a separate sheet or electronic page and any sheet including a claim or portion of a claim may not contain any other parts.
guidance: The abstract must commence on a separate sheet and any sheet including an abstract or portion thereof may not contain any other parts of the application.

name: Non-English filing — translation and accuracy statement required (nonprovisional)
description: If a nonprovisional application is filed in a language other than English, an English language translation of the non-English application, a statement that the translation is accurate, and the processing fee set forth in § 1.17(i) are required. If these items are not filed with the application, applicant will be notified and given time to file them to avoid abandonment.
guidance: For provisional applications filed in a non-English language, an English translation is not required at filing but will be required later if benefit is claimed in a later-filed nonprovisional application (see § 1.78(a)).

name: Illustrations/flowcharts in descriptive portion are improper
description: Graphical illustrations, diagrammatic views, flowcharts, and diagrams in the descriptive portion of the specification do not come within 37 CFR 1.58(a) and examiners should object to such descriptive illustrations and request drawings in accordance with 37 CFR 1.81.
guidance: The written description must not contain drawings or flow diagrams. Claims may incorporate by reference to a specific figure or table where practical definition in words is not possible. The description should not duplicate tables that appear in drawings.

name: Specification section order and headings
description: The specification should include the following sections in order (if applicable): title of the invention; cross-reference to related applications; statement regarding federally sponsored research; names of parties to a joint research agreement; reference to Sequence Listing/table/computer program appendix on compact disc and incorporation-by-reference; statement regarding prior disclosures; background of the invention; brief summary; brief description of views of drawings; detailed description; claim(s); abstract; Sequence Listing (if on paper).
guidance: Text of these sections should be preceded by a section heading in uppercase without underlining or bold type. If no text follows, the phrase 'Not Applicable' should follow the heading. Provisional applications are recommended to follow the same format though claims are not required.

name: Application Data Sheet (ADS) controls certain information (post-2012 filings)
description: For applications filed on or after September 16, 2012, if there is a discrepancy between information in an application data sheet and elsewhere in the application, the application data sheet will control except for naming of inventors. The most recent compliant ADS will govern with respect to foreign priority or domestic benefit claims.
guidance: For filings before September 16, 2012, different pre-AIA rules about ADS control apply; naming inventors and citizenship remain governed by specific CFR.

name: Rejection of Claims Copied From Patent
description: When claims corresponding to claims of a patent are presented in an application, the examiner must determine whether the presented claims are unpatentable on any ground(s) (e.g., 35 U.S.C. 101, 102, 103, 112, double patenting).
guidance: If any claims in the application are rejectable, they should be rejected. If the ground of rejection is also applicable to the corresponding claims in the patent, any Office action including the rejection must have the approval of the Technology Center Director (see MPEP § 1003). See MPEP Chapter 2300 and 37 CFR Parts 41 and 42 for interferences/derivation.

name: Final Rejection: Statutory Basis and General Requirements (37 CFR 1.113)
description: On the second or any subsequent examination the rejection or other action may be made final; reply to a final rejection is limited (appeal or restricted amendment options). In making such final rejection, the examiner shall repeat or state all grounds of rejection then considered applicable to the claims and clearly state the reasons in support.
guidance: Replies must comply with 37 CFR 1.114 (or specified paragraphs), including cancellation of or appeal from each rejected claim. Before making final, develop a clear issue between examiner and applicant; perform thorough first-action search and fully apply references; do not make hasty or ill-considered final rejections; balance speedy conclusion with full and fair hearing for applicant.

name: When a Final Rejection Is Proper on Second or Subsequent Action
description: Second or subsequent actions on the merits shall be final, except where the examiner introduces a new ground of rejection that is neither necessitated by applicant’s amendment nor based on information submitted in an IDS filed during the period set forth in 37 CFR 1.97(c) with the required fee.
guidance: Where an IDS with fee is filed within the 1.97(c) period, the examiner may use the information (e.g., a printed publication or evidence of public use) and make the next action final even if claims were not amended, provided no other new ground is introduced. See MPEP § 609.04(b) for IDS specifics. For guidance on what constitutes a new ground, see MPEP § 1207.03(a). Rejections based on art submitted in reply to a 37 CFR 1.105 requirement generally cannot be made final in the next Office action unless necessitated by amendment.

name: Effects of Applicant Amendments That Fail to Show Patentable Novelty
description: If an applicant amends the claims without attempting to show patentable novelty, the examiner should not allow the claims; the claims may be finally rejected if clearly open to rejection on the record.
guidance: Use Form Paragraph 7.40 where an action is made final including new grounds of rejection necessitated by applicant’s amendment. Examiners should ensure that applicant had adequate opportunity to avoid all grounds of rejection before making final.

name: Provisional application characteristics
description: Provisional applications are automatically abandoned after one year; no claims are required; the written disclosure must meet the same requirements as a nonprovisional; provisional applications are not allowed for design patent applications.
guidance: Use provisionals to secure a filing date but remember they are temporary (one year) and the disclosure must still be sufficient to support later claims. Do not use for design patents.

name: Nonprovisional application requirements
description: Nonprovisional applications require at least one claim and a written disclosure that meets the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre- or post-AIA as applicable); such applications are examined for patentability and can result in a patent.
guidance: Ensure at least one properly formatted claim and a specification that satisfies written description and enablement requirements before filing.

name: Originally-filed disclosure contents
description: The originally-filed disclosure must contain the written description, how to make and use the invention, full and definitive terms that convey the invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art, at least one specific embodiment (examples), and at least one independent claim (must begin on a new page).
guidance: Include specific embodiments and concrete terminology that will provide antecedent basis for later claim terms; include at least one independent claim on a new page when appropriate.

name: Written description details
description: The written description should focus on explaining the structures, processes, or compositions of the invention; refer to figures and explain parts by reference numerals; provide clear support/antecedent basis for all terms used in the claims so claim term meanings are ascertainable by reference to the description.
guidance: Use clear element descriptions and link claim terminology to specification text and figures. Provide examples and embodiments that support the full scope you may later claim.

name: Drawings requirements
description: Drawings are part of the disclosure and are required if necessary to understand the invention; a drawing necessary to understand the invention cannot be introduced after the filing date (replacement drawings allowed).
guidance: Provide drawings that show every claimed feature, with as many views as necessary; label and describe parts clearly. Do not plan to add essential drawings after filing.

name: If-a-limitation-is-in-a-claim-it-must-be-in-the-specification
description: If a limitation is in a claim, it must be in the specification: claims define the invention and what aspects are legally enforceable and must conform to the invention as set forth in the remainder of the specification.
guidance: Ensure all claim limitations have clear support in the specification to avoid indefiniteness, lack of written description, or lack of enablement problems.

name: Claims formatting rules
description: Claims should start on a separate sheet with a clear header (e.g., 'Claims:'), be 1.5 or double spaced, each claim must be a single sentence (begins with a capital and ends with a period), amendments must indicate correct status identifiers and show proper editing, and claims should be numbered consecutively in ascending order with original numbering preserved throughout prosecution.
guidance: Follow formal requirements strictly to avoid procedural rejec­tions: one-sentence claims, proper spacing, headers, consistent numbering and clear markings for added/canceled text.

name: Independent claim requirements and role
description: A minimum of one independent claim is required; it has the greatest breadth and scope, sets forth the statutory category of the invention, and typically provides support/basis for dependent limitations.
guidance: Draft independent claim(s) to capture the broadest valid scope you can support in the specification and use dependent claims to add narrowing fallback positions.

name: Dependent claim rules
