description: A dependent claim refers to a preceding claim(s), incorporates by reference all limitations of the claim(s) that precede it, and narrows the scope of the preceding claim. See MPEP §608.01(n) for proper/improper forms of claim dependency.
guidance: Ensure dependent claims properly refer to and incorporate the full scope of the antecedent claim and do not introduce improper reference or replace elements from another claim.

name: Pre-drafting considerations
description: Before writing a claim, identify: what the invention is; the critical elements; how pieces and parts relate; whether you have more than one invention (tangible vs method); and whether there are multiple versions of each invention.
guidance: Map out components/relationships and decide which statutory class(es) to claim (apparatus, machine, composition, method) and whether multiple independent claim strategies are needed.

name: Claim drafting strategic objectives
description: Claims should define an invention that is described, enabled, and within the scope of the specification; aim to obtain the broadest possible valid independent claim(s); consider different categories and scopes of independent claims; add supported limitations to narrow; allow inclusion of some unclaimed elements while excluding others; and recognize that claim construction is ongoing throughout prosecution.
guidance: Plan claim sets strategically (multiple claim types, fallback dependent claims) and be prepared to amend and re-evaluate claim scope during prosecution to optimize enforceable coverage.

name: Claim scope balance (too specific vs too general)
description: Claim scope should avoid being too specific (not valuable) or too general (not patentable).
guidance: Balance breadth to capture commercially valuable subject matter while remaining supportable and patentable in light of prior art and statutory requirements.

name: Claim fees and budgeting
description: Fees depend on the number of claims: e.g., independent claims in excess of 3 incur per-claim fees and each claim in excess of 20 also incurs fees (examples given for micro entity status). Fees are not one-time and must be considered throughout prosecution.
guidance: Budget for excess-claim fees when planning broad claim sets and potential amended claims during prosecution.

name: Claim anatomy: preamble, transitional phrase, body
description: A claim has three main parts: (1) a preamble/introduction, (2) a transitional phrase (e.g., 'comprising', 'consisting of'), and (3) a body reciting the elements of the invention.
guidance: Structure claims clearly into these parts; choose transitional language deliberately to signal open or closed scope.

name: Preamble guidance
description: The preamble defines the statutory category of the invention. As a general rule the preamble does not limit the scope of the claim. Intended use/functional language generally does not contribute to patentability (e.g., 'a boot for exercising' is still a boot). The preamble of a dependent claim must cite the claim from which it depends.
guidance: Use the preamble for statutory classification and avoid relying on preamble-use language to confer patentability limitations unless you intend that effect and have support in the specification.

name: Transitional phrase guidance (comprising vs consisting of)
description: 'Comprising' is open and indicates the invention includes, but is not limited to, the recited elements; 'Consisting of' is closed and limits the invention to only the recited elements. It is common to use both phrases in the same claim to limit different aspects.
guidance: Select transitional phrases intentionally to control claim openness or closedness; mixing phrases can tailor scope for different claim portions. (Source: MPEP §2111.03.)

name: Body of the claim guidance
description: The body sets forth elements, steps, and relationships that define the claimed invention. Limitations should be consistent with the statutory category, use terms with clear support/antecedent basis in the specification, set up antecedent basis for dependent claims, may introduce new elements (e.g., 'further comprises'), and must not employ language that renders the claim indefinite.
guidance: Write clear, supported limitations with proper antecedent basis and consistent terminology; avoid vague or relative terms that could lead to indefiniteness rejections.

name: Examiner's method and claim interpretation (BRI)
description: Examiners analyze claim language using the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI), must understand the invention, determine the metes and bounds of the claims are clear, and if warranted write a clear rejection explaining why the invention is indefinite.
guidance: Draft claims to minimize ambiguity under BRI and be prepared to respond to examiner rejections that challenge clarity/definiteness and to amend claims in prosecution.

name: Common causes of claim indefiniteness
description: Four common reasons for a claim being unclear are: lack of antecedent basis; unclear/relative terminology; exemplary language; and improperly dependent claims.
guidance: Check claim set for these specific issues (provide antecedent basis, define or avoid relative terms, avoid exemplary 'such as' language, ensure proper claim dependency).

name: Antecedent basis problem (example)
description: Example with boot claims: Claim 1 recites 'a boot comprising ... at least one fastening mechanism ...'; Claim 2 recites 'wherein said at least one fastening mechanism comprises a buckle.' Claim 3 then states 'wherein said buckle is plastic.' Claim 3 lacks antecedent basis because 'buckle' was not previously introduced as 'a buckle' in Claim 1 or the specification.
guidance: Introduce element names in the independent claim or ensure the specification provides proper antecedent basis before using 'said [element]' in later claims.

name: Relative terminology problem (example: 'polymer-like')
description: Relative terms (e.g., 'polymer-like') can render a claim indefinite if the specification does not define what is meant by that relative term and prior art does not clarify the scope.
guidance: Avoid undefined relative descriptors; if used, provide precise definition or examples in the specification to give PHOSITA understandable boundaries.

name: Improperly dependent claims (dependency errors)
description: Dependent claims that depend on canceled claims or that improperly refer back (e.g., refer only to a portion of another claim, replace elements from another claim, or reference the apparatus of claim 1 in a way that is not proper) are improper and can render claim structure defective.
guidance: Ensure each dependent claim properly depends on a valid antecedent claim, incorporates all limitations of that claim, and does not attempt to replace or partially refer back to elements in a manner inconsistent with MPEP rules.

name: Claim drafting DOs
description: Recommended practices: 'Particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter regarded as the invention.' Consider drafting claims first then the specification based on claim terms; review both to make necessary additions/corrections so claim terms find support in the specification; review patents issued in your field; ensure each term has proper antecedent basis; think about desired legal protection and tailor claims accordingly.
guidance: Follow these DOs as a checklist when preparing applications: draft clear claims, then ensure the specification supports them; research issued patents in the field for claim language conventions; ensure antecedent basis throughout.

name: Claim drafting cautions / DON'Ts
description: Cautions include: do not use claims covering two statutory classes of invention ('A widget and method for using same...'); do not use terms inconsistently between claims and specification; do not refer back to only a portion of another claim in a dependent claim; do not 'replace' elements from another claim within a dependent claim; do not write multi-sentence claims.
guidance: Avoid these anti-patterns to reduce procedural and substantive rejections: be consistent, adhere to proper dependency form, and keep each claim a single sentence.

name: Search continuation for Markush claims
description: The search and examination of a Markush claim should be continued until either (1) prior art is found that anticipates or renders obvious a species that falls within the scope of a proper Markush grouping that includes the elected species, or (2) it is determined that no prior art rejection of any species that falls within the scope of a proper Markush grouping that includes the elected species can be made.
guidance: The examiner need not extend the search beyond a proper Markush grouping. Continue examination of the Markush claim to determine whether it meets all other requirements of patentability (e.g., 35 U.S.C. 101 and 112, nonstatutory double patenting, and proper Markush grouping).

name: Prohibition on forcing scope narrowing for proper Markush claims
description: An examiner may not seek to require an applicant to limit the scope of a claim that is directed to a proper Markush group to a subset of species that falls within the scope of the claim in the absence of a rejection of the claim for not complying with the requirements for patentability (e.g., 35 U.S.C. 101, 102, 103, and 112, and nonstatutory double patenting).
guidance: This includes actions such as Ex parte Quayle or a Notice of Non-Responsive Amendment—cannot be used to force narrowing without a patentability rejection.

name: Effect of final rejection on provisional election
description: If a claim in a first application recites a proper Markush grouping encompassing patentably distinct inventions, and the claim is rejected over prior art in a proper final rejection, the examiner who required a provisional election need not continue to search the claim; the applicant's election loses its provisional status and is given full effect under 35 U.S.C. 121.
guidance: If a divisional application is later filed claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 of the first application, the 35 U.S.C. 121 shield may be applicable so long as the consonance requirement is met.

name: Refund when additional species embraced by generic claim
description: Whenever claims drawn to an additional species in a transitional application for which applicant paid the fee are no longer withdrawn because they are fully embraced by an allowable generic claim, applicant should be notified that he or she may request a refund of the fee paid for that additional species.
guidance: Determination of when claims to a nonelected species would no longer be withdrawn should be made as indicated in MPEP § 806.04(d), § 821.04, and § 821.04(a).

name: Presumption of independence for nucleotide-sequence claims
description: Polynucleotide molecules defined by their nucleic acid sequence that encode different proteins are structurally distinct and are thus deemed to normally constitute independent and distinct inventions within the meaning of 35 U.S.C. 121.
guidance: Absent evidence to the contrary, each such nucleotide sequence is presumed to represent an independent and distinct invention, subject to restriction per 35 U.S.C. 121 and 37 CFR 1.141 et seq.

name: Types of double patenting rejections
description: There are generally two types: (1) 'same invention' type double patenting rejection based on 35 U.S.C. 101, and (2) 'nonstatutory-type' double patenting rejection based on a judicially created doctrine intended to prevent prolongation of patent term by prohibiting claims in a second patent not patentably distinct from claims in a first patent.
guidance: The focus of DP analysis is on the claims in the multiple patents/applications.

name: Terminal disclaimer as response to nonstatutory double patenting
description: A terminal disclaimer, submitted per 37 CFR 1.321(c) or (d), includes a provision that the patent is enforceable only for and during such period that it is owned by the same party (or parties) that owns the other patents/applications identified in the terminal disclaimer that claim obvious variations of one invention.
guidance: Terminal disclaimer addresses equitable concerns about extending exclusivity; see In re Van Ornum and other cited authorities.

name: Use of charts and AIA/FTI distinctions in double patenting analysis
description: Charts are provided showing treatment of applications/patents having conflicting claims (same invention or patentably indistinct inventions), with FTI (first-to-invent) and AIA versions for use depending on the applicable 35 U.S.C. 102/103 regime of the involved applications/patents.
guidance: Examiners may need to use FTI versions for earlier-filed applications subject to pre-AIA 102/103 and AIA versions for later-filed applications subject to post-AIA 102/103 (or vice versa). Charts show possible rejections if record supports them.

name: Instances where double patenting issue can be raised
description: A double patenting issue may arise between two or more pending applications, between one or more pending applications and a patent, or in reexamination proceedings between the patent claims being reexamined and claims of applications/patents. Double patenting does not relate to international applications not yet in national stage.
guidance: Examiner must determine whether grant of a second patent would give rise to an unjustified extension of rights granted in the first patent.

name: Order and arrangement of application elements
description: The elements of the application, if applicable, should appear in the following order: (1) Utility application transmittal form; (2) Fee transmittal form; (3) Application data sheet (§ 1.76); (4) Specification; (5) Drawings; (6) The inventor's oath or declaration. The specification should include sections in order: title; cross-reference to related applications; statement regarding federally sponsored research or development; names of parties to a joint research agreement; statement regarding prior disclosures by the inventor; background; brief summary; brief description of views of the drawing; detailed description; claims; abstract; sequence listing (if on paper).
guidance: Follow 37 CFR 1.77 ordering. Precede specification section text with uppercase section headings without underlining or bold (see § 1.77(b) & (c)).

name: Computer program listing length and placement rules
description: If a computer program listing is 300 lines or fewer (each line ≤72 characters), it may be submitted either as drawings or as part of the specification. Any listing having more than 60 lines submitted as part of the specification must be positioned at the end of the description but before the claims. A listing of more than 300 lines must be submitted as an appendix (ASCII text via EFS-Web or on compact disc) and will not be printed in the patent.
guidance: If submitted as drawings follow § 1.84. If submitted in the specification, follow § 1.52. Any amendment to a listing in the specification must be made by substitute sheet. Use form paragraphs 6.64.01 and 6.64.02 to notify applicants of noncompliance.

name: Claim Construction—Generally
description: Judge will define the meaning of the patent claims and instruct the jury on claim language; jurors must follow the court’s construction and must not define claims themselves.
guidance: ‘‘It will be my job to tell you what the language of the patent claims means. You must follow my instructions as to the meaning of the patent claims. You are not to define the patent claims yourselves.’’ Use bracketed placeholders to adapt language to product vs. method contexts.

name: Claim Construction for the Case
description: Case-specific construction of claim terms will be provided for the jury to use in comparing accused products/methods to claims.
guidance: Instructions include a section titled 'Claim Construction for the Case' and may include alternate bracketed formulations to be customized to the particular claim terms and dispute in the case.

name: Construction of Means-Plus-Function Claims for the Case
description: Special instruction for construction of means-plus-function (and step-plus-function) claims applicable to the case.
guidance: Includes directions for identifying the corresponding structure/steps in the specification that perform the claimed function and instructs jurors how to apply that construction in infringement analyses.

name: Infringement of 'Comprising,' 'Consisting of,' and 'Consisting Essentially of' Claims
description: Instructions on the different claim-open/closed language effects ('comprising' vs 'consisting of' vs 'consisting essentially of').
guidance: Explains how these transitional phrases affect scope (e.g., 'comprising' is open-ended) and instructs jurors how to apply those meanings when comparing accused products/methods to claims.

name: Direct Infringement—Doctrine of Equivalents
description: A claim is infringed under the doctrine of equivalents if the accused product/method contains an equivalent component/step for each claimed element not literally present; an equivalent is only insubstantially different (e.g., performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result).
guidance: Plaintiff must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that each missing claim element has an equivalent in the accused product/method. Includes limitations discussed elsewhere (prosecution history estoppel; subject matter dedicated to the public).

name: Summary of Invalidity Defense
description: Defendant must prove invalidity of each challenged claim by clear and convincing evidence to overcome the presumption of patent validity; invalidity is a defense to infringement.
guidance: Explains standard of proof differences: infringement by preponderance of the evidence; invalidity by clear and convincing evidence (‘‘highly probable’’ language recommended as a jury-friendly substitute). Practice Note discusses substituting 'highly probable' for clarity.

name: Anticipation—Generally
description: Anticipation (novelty) requires that a single prior art reference disclose every element of the claimed invention such that the claim is not new.
guidance: Includes multiple subtopics explaining forms of prior art and the required proof that a single reference meets all claim limitations.

name: Anticipation—Printed Publication
description: When a printed publication constitutes prior art that anticipates a claim (timing, public accessibility, content disclosure).
guidance: Provides standards for determining whether a document was sufficiently publicly accessible to be a printed publication and whether it discloses all claim elements.

name: Obviousness—Generally (Graham factors)
description: Obviousness is assessed under the Graham framework: scope and content of prior art, differences between claimed invention and prior art, level of ordinary skill in the art, and secondary considerations.
guidance: Instruction 'Obviousness—Generally' frames the analysis and directs jurors to evaluate the four factors and apply them together to determine whether the invention would have been obvious.

name: Obviousness—First Factor: Scope and Content of the Prior Art
description: Consider the scope and content of the prior art relevant to the claimed invention when analyzing obviousness.
guidance: Jurors should identify the prior art references most pertinent to the asserted claims and what they disclose.

name: Obviousness—Second Factor: Differences Between the Claimed Invention and the Prior Art
description: Assess the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art references identified.
guidance: Determine what, if anything, the claimed invention adds beyond the prior art and whether those differences would have been obvious to a POSITA.

name: Identical invention treated as filed on first-country filing date
description: If the invention described in an application claiming a priority under the treaty is identical with the invention described in the application filed in the first country, the invention in the application claiming priority shall be treated as if filed on the filing date of the application in the first country for applying provisions in Articles 29, 36 of the Patent Act.
guidance: This rule is applied when determining the reference date for novelty/inventive step; reference date determination is generally done on a claim-by-claim basis (see related criteria).

name: Reference date determined claim-by-claim (general rule)
description: The reference date for determining patentability shall be determined on a claim-by-claim basis in principle.
guidance: Details follow depending on whether a claim is identical to a first-country disclosure, not described in the first-country application, or involves multiple priority claims. Examiner must apply rules per-claim.

name: Priority claims where the first-country application itself claims priority
description: When the application filed in the first country claims the priority right based on another earlier application, the application shall not be regarded as the 'earliest application' prescribed in Article 4 C(2) of the Paris Convention for the invention described in both the application and the earlier application; the effect of the priority claim shall not be recognized.
guidance: Examination shall not be conducted retroactively to the reference date in such cases, and the examiner shall notify a specific reason for non-retroactive application. If prior art discovered prevents retroactivity between earliest date and filing date of the priority claim, the examiner must state the reason for non-retroactive application in the notice of grounds for rejection.

name: Domestic priority: applicant eligibility
description: A person eligible to claim domestic priority is an applicant of the prior-filed application. If the applicant of the prior-filed application and the applicant of the later-filed application are not the same, the examiner shall request amendments and invalidate the priority claim procedure if the deficiency is not cured. The scope of amendments is limited to correction of obvious errors.
guidance: Whether applicants are the same is determined as of when the domestic priority claim has been filed (cover sheet or amendment time). Examiner must enforce identity of applicants at claim filing time.

name: Domestic priority: one-year filing period
description: The domestic priority claim shall be made within one year from the filing date of the prior-filed application which forms the basis of the domestic priority claim.
guidance: If filed after the statutory period, the examiner requests amendments and invalidates the priority claim procedure if deficiency is not cured; scope of amendment limited to obvious errors and this is stated in the notice.

name: Domestic priority: identical-invention retroactivity and claim-by-claim rules
description: Where inventions claimed in the later application and those stated in the original specification/drawings of the prior-filed application are identical (including 'de facto identical'), the later application shall be deemed to have been filed at the time of the prior-filed application for applying Articles 29, 36 etc.; effects are determined on a claim-by-claim basis.
guidance: For multiple domestic priority claims, when the invention is stated in two or more original specifications of prior-filed applications, the reference date is the earliest filing date. If the claimed invention is not stated in the original specification of the prior-filed application, the filing date of the domestic priority claim is the reference date; combinations of matters from multiple prior-filed applications or with new matter are treated as not stated in the prior-filed original specification.

name: Prior-filed application deemed withdrawn after one year three months
description: Where the inventions stated in the original specification/drawings of the later application and those in the original specification of the prior-filed application are identical, the prior-filed application, which shall be deemed to have been withdrawn when one year and three months has lapsed from the filing date, is regarded to be laid open at the time when the application with the priority claim is laid open or published in the patent gazette for purposes of Article 29(3).
guidance: When the examiner discovers an application under examination has become a basis for a domestic priority claim, he/she shall defer further examination. If the domestic priority claim is invalidated due to formal deficiency, the examiner shall resume examination on the suspended application.

name: Application by a legitimate right holder: statutory requirements (four conditions)
description: To be recognized as an application by a legitimate right holder (Articles 34 and 35), the following must be met: (1) an application by the unentitled person was filed earlier than the application of the legitimate holder; (2) the unentitled person's application is rejected or invalidated in a trial on the ground it was not filed by the entitled person; (3) the application by the legitimate holder is filed within thirty days from the date when the trial decision became conclusive and unappealable; and (4) the scope of the claimed invention in the legitimate holder's application falls within the scope of disclosure of the unentitled person's application.
guidance: Where legitimate-holder filing uses Form (xiv) or arguments during examination, the examiner shall assess legitimacy before other rejection grounds. If examiner doubts conditions (1),(3),(4), deliver notice that filing date shall not be retroactive. If condition (2) not satisfied, examination is deferred until the trial decision is final and conclusive.

name: Effect and scope when application by legitimate right holder is recognized
description: When an application is recognized as legitimate, it is deemed to have been filed at the date when the unentitled person filed. Judgments of patent requirements, period calculations, and related provisions shall be determined as of the unentitled person's filing date. Scope of invention is limited to claimed inventions and those disclosed in the unentitled person's specification/drawings; inventions beyond that scope are not retroactive.
guidance: Example: a third-party application filed between the unentitled person's filing and the legitimate holder's filing shall not cause rejection of the legitimate holder's application because the legitimate holder's filing date is retroactive to the unentitled person's earlier filing. Requests for examination filed after three years from the unentitled person's filing date are valid if filed simultaneously with the legitimate-holder’s application.

name: International (PCT) application treatment and Korean translation requirement
description: An international patent application (PCT) where the filing date is established under the PCT and Korea is designated is treated as a regular patent application filed on the international filing date except for certain exceptional clauses (including enlarged concept of novelty). An international application filed in a foreign language is deemed withdrawn if its Korean translation is not submitted per Article 201 of the Patent Act.
guidance: Effects arising from submission of a translation differ depending on filing date (special rules for applications filed before Dec 31, 2014 vs after Jan 1, 2015) regarding which parts (description, claims, drawings, abstract) are considered originally filed in Korea.

name: Examiner actions and priority treatment for international applications
description: When an international application enters the national phase with Korean translation submitted and claims priority under the PCT, the priority claim is treated as the treaty priority. If the application serving as basis is a Korean application or an international application where Korea is the only designated State, the priority claim is considered domestic. If an international application serves as basis of domestic priority and becomes 'another application' under Article 29(3), it is considered laid open at the time of international publication; scope limited to inventions described as of international filing date and its translation.
guidance: A person claiming disclosure exceptions for an invention claimed in an international application may submit a written statement and evidential documents within 30 days from the reference date even if the purport was not stated in the international application. Korean translations of PCT Article 19/34 amendments submitted within reference date are treated as voluntary amendments under Article 47. Examiner may request copies of documents cited in the ISR/IPER; Commissioner may request submission within a designated period.

name: Special provisions for enlarged concept of novelty for international applications (date-dependent)
description: Special provisions regarding the enlarged concept of novelty apply depending on filing dates of the concerned and 'another application'. For example: (i) where both applications were filed before Dec 31, 2014 (or 'another application' before Dec 31, 2014 but concerned later), an international application relied upon as 'another application' is considered laid open at international publication but scope limited to inventions described in specification/claims/drawings as of the international filing date and its translation; (ii) where both filed after Jan 1, 2015, scope of 'another application' is limited to inventions described in the description/claims/drawings as filed. International applications deemed withdrawn for failure to submit Korean translation per Article 201(4) cannot be 'another application' for enlarged concept.
guidance: Apply transitional/temporal rules carefully to decide scope of prior international applications when judging novelty under expanded concept rules.

name: Form and tailoring of preliminary injunctions
description: A preliminary injunction may contain a general or a limited prohibition, and may issue either alone or in connection with other special orders for relief; when certain claims are disputed, the injunction may be confined to those unquestionably valid; where certain infringing articles cannot be equitably enjoined he may be forbidden to procure others and employ them.
guidance: Injunctions should be fitted to each case to protect the plaintiff without unnecessary injury to the defendant; courts may couple injunctions with orders for a bond, an account, or other terms.

name: Duration and temporal limits of injunctions
description: An injunction remains in force as long as the patent is capable of infringement, unless previously recalled by the court or superseded by other judgment in the suit; it must be directed only against devices constructed while the patent was in force and should be limited to the life of the patent.
guidance: An injunction forbidding use after the patent term effectively extends the patent and is improper. Where the date of expiration is disputed the court will not fix a premature limit but the defendant can move to dissolve when the claimed expiration arrives.

name: Technology area: Software
description: An invention in which data processing is a sufficiently critical element that at least one claim element in the patent consists of data processing—the actual manipulation of data—regardless of whether the code carrying out that data processing is on a magnetic storage medium or embedded in a chip.
guidance: Includes firmware; used as a broad category for regression and descriptive statistics.

name: Technology area: Pure software
description: An invention consisting only of data processing; all claim elements in the patent consist of data processing (with trivial non‑data elements such as generic input/output/storage allowed).
guidance: Subset of software; excludes inventions with meaningful non‑data processing elements.

name: Technology area: Software business method
description: A subset of software patents covering methods for conducting business transactions—narrowly defined here to claims that obviously cover automated generation of customer proposals, advertising, and the use of online catalogs.
guidance: Use a narrow definition to avoid overbroad inclusion of business-related software.

name: Include 'specific features' in claims to show practical application
description: Provide 'specific features' in your patent claims that transform the claims from an ineligible abstract mental process (e.g., 'collecting data, analyzing the data, and displaying results') into an eligible 'practical application' under Alice Step 2A Prong 2.
guidance: Identify and recite claim limitations that do more than state the abstract idea; e.g., the PTAB found that 'downloading the pump configuration files and using them to deliver insulin' were specific features that were not 'insignificant post-solution activity' but an improvement to the operation of an insulin pump. Treat each 'specific feature' individually or in combination as supporting eligibility.

name: Support each claimed 'specific feature' in the Specification as an 'improvement to a technology'
description: Include support in the specification that each recited 'specific feature' is an improvement to technology, which the PTAB used to reverse §101 rejections (i.e., treat features as 'an improvement to the operation' of a device or system).
guidance: Write the specification to explain how claimed features improve conventional, routine, or traditional systems/methods (examples: improved insulin pump operation; higher performance in speech recognition). Ensure the specification links claimed limitations to concrete technological advantages.

name: Recite technological limitations in claims that integrate the abstract idea into a practical application
description: Claims should themselves contain the technological limitation(s) that integrate the abstract idea into a practical application (do not rely on importing unclaimed specification details).
guidance: If an improvement is described in the spec (e.g., 'causing a computer program to enter data into a form'), include that limitation in at least some claims (as Campbell shows: claims with the 'enter data into a form' limitation were eligible while broader claims without it were not). Limitations not present in the claims may not be used to avoid an abstract-idea finding.

name: Include multiple independent and dependent claims as prosecution/appeal backups
description: Draft a variety of claims (broad and narrower) so that if broader claims fail under §101, narrower claims might survive (and vice versa).
guidance: It is a good idea to include multiple independent claims and dependent claims in the appeal as backups in case the PTAB is not persuaded by the broader claim set but is okay with the narrower one.

name: When claims recite mathematical concepts, show how they are integrated into a device or improve it
description: When drafting claims involving mathematical concepts or equations, ensure the claims make clear how those concepts are integrated into a device or other practical application and used to improve that device or otherwise solve a problem in the field.
guidance: Avoid mere mathematical recitation; explain in the specification and claim language how the math is a consequence of device arrangement or used to improve system performance (e.g., Fautz: math used with coil arrangement to improve MR imaging).

name: Avoid bare recitations of mathematical concepts without tying them to systems/implementations
description: Do not claim mathematical concepts in the abstract; tie them to specific systems, components, or practical computing steps to avoid being treated as a judicial exception.
guidance: Claims that merely recite calculations or math at a high level (without showing application to a device/system) are at risk of being 'directed to' an abstract idea.

name: Frame inventions as improving the functioning of a computer (or other device) when appropriate
description: Where possible, describe and claim the invention as an improvement to how a computer or device functions, rather than merely as implementing an abstract concept on a generic computer.
guidance: Frame improvements generally (improving the functioning of a computer) or tie to specific components or operations. Also, capture specific embodiments of those improvements in the claims so some claims are more likely to survive review (Hsu, Kim).

name: Force Examiners to identify specific alleged ineligible concepts under Step 2A
description: During prosecution, require Examiners to specify the particular judicial exception(s) they allege under prong 1 and prong 2 of Step 2A to clarify rejections and aid in response or appeal.
guidance: Request that the Examiner identify the specific ineligible concept(s) present in the claims; clarifying the precise alleged exception can help resolve rejections or narrow issues for appeal (Hannun practice tip).

name: Use Berkheimer to challenge unsupported Step 2B rejections (require factual support)
description: Rely on Berkheimer v. HP: where an Examiner asserts 'no additional elements' or that claim elements are conventional, require factual support rather than conclusory statements.
guidance: If the Examiner's Step 2B position lacks evidentiary support that claimed elements are well-understood, routine, conventional, push back and argue the need for factual basis. PTAB has reversed some unsupported Step 2B findings.

name: Do not import specification limitations into claims; claims control
description: Limitations disclosed only in the specification but not recited in the claims cannot be imported into the claims to avoid a §101 rejection.
guidance: If a specific technical solution is in the specification but not claimed, you cannot rely on it for claim eligibility—capture such solutions in claim language (Hsu).

name: Generic computer components (processor, memory) are insufficient to make claims patent-eligible
description: Reciting a generic 'processor' or 'memory' performing claimed steps does not typically integrate an abstract idea into a practical application; such generic recitations may be treated as mere implementation on a general-purpose computer.
guidance: Claims that merely use standard computer components to perform abstract ideas are vulnerable; instead, recite how the components are specially configured or how the arrangement provides a technical improvement (Kavis, Kim).

name: Claims should not be described at a high level of generality when asserting an inventive concept
description: If computer-related limitations are described only at a high level of generality and are well-understood, routine, or conventional, they will likely fail to provide an inventive concept under Step 2B.
guidance: Provide specific, concrete claim language and supporting specification showing how elements differ from routine practice; avoid generic, high-level functional language (Kavis Step 2B guidance).

name: Ensure proper prior-art comparison in obviousness (Section 103) rejections
description: For 103 rejections, the Examiner must properly compare the prior art to the specific recited language of the claims; failure to do so can lead to reversal.
guidance: When responding to 103 rejections, point out where the Examiner's comparison is deficient or fails to account for specific claim limitations (Hsu example where 103 rejections were reversed).

name: When mathematical calculations arise from device arrangement and improve system performance, emphasize that connection
description: If the claimed mathematical calculations are a consequence of a device's physical arrangement and used to improve the system (e.g., coil arrangement in MR imaging), emphasize that the claims solve a technical problem and are not mere abstract math.
guidance: Document and claim how the math is applied by the device and how that application improves operation; this supported eligibility in Ex Parte Fautz (citing Thales Visionix).

name: Device/apparatus claims may be more likely to be eligible than corresponding method claims
description: Apparatus claims that recite a device 'configured to' perform claimed steps and are shown to be 'special-purpose improved machines' may survive §101 where broadly phrased method claims fail.
guidance: Include both method and device claims; show in the specification and claim language that device claims improve machine operation (Kim: device claims were eligible while method claims were not).

name: Avoid claiming steps that can be performed mentally or with pen and paper
description: If a claim recites steps that can practically be performed in the human mind or with pen and paper (e.g., simple selection or comparison steps), those steps may support a finding of a mental process abstract idea.
guidance: Draft claims to include computerized, non-mental limitations or special hardware/processing steps that make performance by a person impractical; otherwise the claim may be directed to a mental process (Kim, Kavis).

name: Capture specific algorithmic/solution details in dependent claims when they provide the improvement
description: If particular algorithmic choices or metrics (e.g., Jaccard Distance, Kullback-Leibler divergence) are the basis for an improvement, include those specifics in at least some claims so those claims may be treated as practical applications.
guidance: Hsu showed that only claims reciting the specific solutions (the particular disambiguation methods) were found to be practical applications—so include dependent claims that recite the concrete solution details.

name: Sufficiency of description is a question of fact for the jury (subject-matter experts)
description: The sufficiency of the Description is a question of fact, to be investigated by experience, elucidated by evidence, and decided by a jury. Only persons skilled in the art are usually capable of judging whether delineations are correct, complete, and intelligible.
guidance: Prepare factual evidence and expert testimony when asserting or defending sufficiency. Courts may nonetheless resolve pure legal constructions of claim language as questions of law.

name: Scope of patent: claims must particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention
description: It is the office of the Claim to define the limits of that exclusive use which is secured to the inventor by the patent. The statutes require that he shall particularly point out and distinctly claim the part, improvement, or combination which he claims as his invention or discovery.
guidance: Claims must conclude the specification and be specific and distinct for every separate subject matter claimed. They define the public boundary between allowed and disclaimed subject matter; vague or absent claims render the application deficient.

name: Product vs process coverage: if product cannot be recognized apart from process, patent may cover it only when made by that process
description: Unless a product is so described that it can be recognised apart from the description of the process of making it, the patent will cover it only when made by that process.
guidance: When drafting, either (a) describe the product so it is recognizable independently, or (b) limit the claim to the product produced by the specified process. If both product and machine/process are described, product description may suffice even if the machine is useless.

name: Graham factual inquiry — differences between claimed invention and prior art
description: Ascertaining the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art requires interpreting the claim language and considering both the invention and the prior art as a whole.
guidance: Interpret claims per MPEP §2111; consider both claimed limitations and the prior art collectively (see MPEP §2141.02). The mere existence of differences does not establish nonobviousness (Dann v. Johnston).

name: Determine claimed scope with broadest reasonable interpretation
description: The scope of the claimed invention must be clearly determined by giving the claims the 'broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.'
guidance: Apply claim construction principles (Phillips v. AWH and MPEP §2111) before searching and before comparing to prior art. The determined scope drives what is searched and what prior art is pertinent.

name: Search scope — what to search for
description: The search should cover the claimed subject matter and should also cover the disclosed features which might reasonably be expected to be claimed.
guidance: Although a rejection need not be based on a teaching or suggestion to combine, a preferred search is directed to finding references that provide such teaching/suggestion if they exist. Follow MPEP §904 et seq.

name: Ascertaining differences — interpret claim language and consider whole
description: Ascertaining differences requires interpreting claim language (see MPEP §2111) and considering both the invention and the prior art as a whole.
guidance: Document how specific claim limitations map (or do not map) to prior art disclosures. Consider whole-claim comparisons rather than isolated elements.

name: Rationales to support obviousness rejections — known technique used to improve similar devices
description: Use of known technique to improve similar devices (methods, or products) in the same way supports obviousness.
guidance: Demonstrate that the technique was known and that POSA would have had a reasonable expectation of improvement when applied to the claimed device.

name: Applicant reply requirements (37 CFR 1.111(b))
description: Applicant must distinctly and specifically point out the supposed errors in the Office's action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the Office action; the reply must present arguments pointing out the specific distinction believed to render the claims patentable.
guidance: Provide a reasoned statement explaining why the applicant believes the Office erred substantively as to the factual findings. Mere assertions that a prima facie case has not been made, without documentary support, are substantively inadequate and will not rebut the rejection under 37 CFR 1.111(b).

name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) common ownership/joint research requirements
description: To rely on pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) to overcome a rejection based on prior art that qualifies only under certain subsections of pre-AIA 102, the applicant must establish: (A) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; (B) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities within the scope of that agreement; and (C) the application discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement.
guidance: These disqualifications apply only to subject matter that qualifies as prior art solely under pre-AIA 102(e), (f), or (g) when used in a pre-AIA 103(a) rejection. See MPEP §§2146, 2146.01, 2146.02 for requirements and examples.

name: Marking and publication when application is subject to a concurrent use proceeding
description: When approved for publication, an application entitled to registration subject to a concurrent use proceeding is marked: 'SUBJECT TO CONCURRENT USE PROCEEDING WITH _______________. APPLICANT CLAIMS EXCLUSIVE RIGHT TO USE THE MARK IN THE AREA COMPRISING ________________.'
guidance: The first blank fills with involved application/registration numbers or names/addresses if no registration; the second blank with the geographic area and any limitations. If application is based on a prior Board decision and a new proceeding is unnecessary, it is instead marked: 'REGISTRATION LIMITED TO THE AREA COMPRISING ______________ PURSUANT TO CONCURRENT USE PROCEEDING NO. _______. CONCURRENT REGISTRATION WITH ______________.' The Board will publish in the Official Gazette and send notices (including web links) to applicant and excepted users (37 C.F.R. §§ 2.80, 2.99(b)-(d)).

name: Which applications and registrations are 'involved' and how unpublished/conflicting applications are treated
description: Involved applications/registrations include the concurrent use application(s); every conflicting unrestricted application identified in the concurrent use application(s) that was filed prior to the concurrent use filing date; registrations identified in the concurrent use application(s) as being owned by listed exceptions; and every registration claimed by the concurrent use applicant unless there is no conflict.
guidance: If an identified application has not yet been published or cleared opposition, it is included as a common law user rather than an applicant; the Board may suspend the proceeding until the unpublished application is abandoned or published and survives opposition and then add it. The Board inquires whether parties own other conflicting apps/regs and will add them where appropriate. If a party owns a conflicting unrestricted application filed after the concurrent use application, the examining attorney will suspend action on that subsequent unrestricted application pending disposition of the concurrent use application; if the concurrent use application matures, it will be cited under § 2(d) against the subsequent unrestricted application. If the later-filed applicant amends to seek concurrent registration and it clears publication without opposition, it may be added to the proceeding. See TBMP § 1104 and notes.

name: Procedure for obviously informal cases
description: When it is impractical to give a complete action on the merits because of an informal or insufficient disclosure, follow a limited procedure: (A) make a reasonable search based on what can be understood; (B) point out informalities and drawing deficiencies via attachments; (C) require specification revision to idiomatic English and U.S. practice; (D) reject informal claims as failing to define the invention under 35 U.S.C. 112.
guidance: If disclosure is incomprehensible to preclude a reasonable search, clearly inform applicant no search was made. Treat multiple obviously informal claims as a single claim for fee and examination purposes. Urge preliminary amendments (preferably within 3 months) but exclude new matter.

name: Search obligations and prior examiner deference
description: After reading the specification and claims, the examiner searches the prior art; the invention should be thoroughly understood before a search. When acting on an application previously acted on by another examiner, give full faith and credit to the previous examiner's search and action unless there is a clear error or knowledge of other prior art.
guidance: Do not take an entirely new approach or make a new search merely in hope of finding something; see MPEP § 904–904.03 and MPEP § 719.05 for guidance on prior examiner's work.

name: Types of information that may be required under 1.105
description: Examples include: particularly relevant commercial databases known to inventors; whether a search was made and what was searched; copies of non-patent literature/patents/publications related to claimed invention; information used to draft the application or in the invention process; identification of what is being improved; identification of any use of the claimed invention known at filing; technical information known to applicant concerning related art, disclosure, claimed subject matter, or facts pertinent to patentability.
guidance: Requirements may seek factual information only (not opinions), and may be presented as interrogatories, stipulations, or specific questions. A reply stating information is unknown or not readily available may be accepted as complete.

name: Scope: factual information and reasonable basis
description: Information required must be factual and reasonably necessary to properly examine or treat the matter; there must be a reasonable basis that the information would aid examination. The scope should be narrowly defined and based on the examiner's reasonable basis.
guidance: 1.105 is not a substitute for examiner search—examiner must still make their own search per MPEP § 704.01 and § 904 et seq. The reasonable necessity criteria is met when (A) claimed subject matter cannot be adequately searched by class/keyword, or (B) the application file or lack of relevant prior art suggests applicant likely has relevant information.

name: Examples of information reasonably required (detailed list)
description: Non-exhaustive examples: (A) name/citation of relevant indexed journal or treatise; (B) trade name of goods/services embodying claimed subject matter; (C)-(D) citations/copies of advertising or journal articles; (E)-(F) trade names/providers/analyses of competing goods/services; (G) identification of pending/abandoned applications by inventor or assignee disclosing similar subject matter; (H) reply to a protest under 37 CFR 1.291; (I) explanation of technical material in a publication; (J)-(L) identification of changes in reformatted continuing applications, mark-ups for CIPs, comments on new Federal Circuit decisions; (M)-(S) publication dates, derivation questions, art related to applicant's invention, accuracy of examiner's analysis, means-plus-function support clarifications; (S) interrogatories or stipulations about common technical features, support for means/steps-plus-function claims, portions of disclosure providing written description/enablement, meanings of claim terms, portions corresponding to admitted prior art, facts related to public use or sale.
guidance: Use these examples to narrowly focus requirements. Where support for a means-plus-function claim is unclear, inquiry may lead to rejections under 35 U.S.C. 112 (written description/definiteness) if support cannot be shown.

name: General rule on expungement of information (37 CFR 1.59)
description: Information in an application will not be expunged except as provided in 37 CFR 1.59(b). Information forming part of the original disclosure (written specification, claims, drawings, preliminary amendments specifically incorporated in an executed oath/declaration) will not be expunged from the file wrapper.
guidance: An applicant may request expungement of other information by filing a petition under 37 CFR 1.59(b) with the required fee and establishing to the Director's satisfaction that expungement is appropriate.

name: Domicil of emancipated minor requires animus manendi
description: An emancipated minor's domicil is determined like any other person's: there must be an animus manendi. A temporary residence adopted solely to secure a cadet appointment is not effective to change domicil.
guidance: R.56,473, Aug. 1888. Scrutinize claimed residences intended solely to qualify for appointment.

name: Industrial Applicability / Utility
description: The invention must be capable of industrial application or provide a specific, substantial, and credible utility.
guidance: Traditional formulation applies to AI-generated inventions as well—claims should demonstrate real-world applicability. The work reiterates the standard wording (industrial applicability/utility) used across jurisdictions.

name: Submission deadline for documents proving Article 30 applicability (domestic)
description: The applicant shall submit documents proving the fact that the provision of Article 30 applies to the invention, within thirty days of the date of filing.
guidance: Documents must be timely submitted within 30 days of filing to support the Article 30 claim.

name: Grounds for notice to correct defects in Article 30 claims
description: Notwithstanding the submission of the written intention, the office gives the applicant a notice to correct defects when: (a) the discloser is different from the filer/inventor; (b) the application is filed more than 12 months (6 months pre-2012) after the disclosure date; (c) wrong disclosure date/type or incorrect information on supporting documents; (d) submitted documents are not enough to prove the relevant fact.
guidance: These enumerated defects trigger a formal notice to correct; if not corrected within the designated period, the Article 30 claiming procedure may be invalidated.

name: Scope of the 'state of the art' for inventive step
description: The state of the art includes inventions referred to in Article 29(1), common general knowledge, and other publicly known technical matters, including ordinary methods for daily works and experiments.
guidance: All relevant technical information in the field of the claimed invention at filing time is part of the state of the art.

name: Per‑claim assessment of inventive step
description: When there are two or more claims in an application, the determination of inventive step should be made for each claim separately.
guidance: Examiners must evaluate inventive step claim‑by‑claim; refusals should point to the specific claim and the reasons.

name: Sequencing: novelty determination before inventive step
description: Determination of novelty should come first; inventive step determination is distinct and based on whether claimed invention could have been easily made even if novel.
guidance: If an invention is not novel, examiner may nonetheless notify reasons for refusal on inventive step, but novelty is assessed first (citing Supreme Court decision).

name: Examiner's comprehensive approach to inventive step
description: Examiner shall consider the overall state of the art, the purpose, technical structure, advantageous effects, applicant's opinion, and focus on the difficulty of the technical structure to comprehensively determine inventive step.
guidance: Key considerations: (1) whether cited prior art provides motivation, (2) whether differences are mere exercise of ordinary creativity, (3) whether claimed invention has advantageous effects over cited art.

name: Procedure to determine inventive step (four steps)
description: (1) Specify the claimed invention (same as novelty). (2) Specify cited inventions (from viewpoint of person skilled in art). (3) Choose closest cited invention and clearly identify differences; treat structurally combined elements as one integrated unit. (4) Determine whether the claimed invention could have been easily made in view of cited inventions or common general knowledge before filing.
guidance: The selection of the closest cited invention and accurate comparison (especially integrated structural elements) is critical to the analysis.

name: Selection of cited inventions – technical field relevance
description: A cited invention should, in principle, be selected from the same technical field or a reasonably relevant technical field to the problem, effect, and use of the claimed invention; technical field can be inferred from effects or functions of claim elements.
guidance: Prior art from different fields can be cited when it might be applied to solve the problem or used by a skilled person; relevance, similarity of problem, and similarity of function/operation are considered.

name: Probable cause/motivation grounds for obviousness
description: Strong grounds that a skilled person would be led to the claimed invention include suggestions shown in cited disclosures, close similarity of problem to be solved, close similarity of function/work/operation, and close relevance of technical fields.
guidance: These factors support an obviousness conclusion when they would have motivated a skilled person to combine or adapt prior teachings.

name: Suggestions in cited disclosures as evidence of motivation
description: Suggestions shown in the disclosures of the cited inventions relevant to a claimed invention can be strong grounds for determining that a skilled person would have been led to the claimed invention.
guidance: Implicit or explicit teachings that point toward the claimed modification/support a finding of obviousness.

name: Close similarity of problem as ground for combining prior art
description: If the technical problems of claimed and cited inventions are closely similar, that can be a strong ground for determining that a skilled person would combine cited inventions and arrive at the claimed invention.
guidance: Examiner assesses whether problems are sufficiently similar or whether common technical sense makes the combination obvious even across fields.

name: Close similarity of function/work/operation as ground
description: A close similarity in function, work, or operation between claimed and cited inventions (or between cited inventions) can be a well‑founded ground that a skilled person would reach the claimed invention.
guidance: Application of a known functional part from one device to another with similar operation may be considered obvious.

name: Substantive requirements of the international application
description: Lists the mandatory elements of the international application (basic registration/application reference, applicant name and address, appointment of representative if any, indication of goods and services, mark representation and indications, designations, priority claims, signatures and certification by Office of origin).
guidance: Explains the content of the application form and each item (Items 1–13): how to fill name/address/e-mail/correspondence address; rules for several applicants; preferred language for correspondence; Item 5 (basic application/registration) requirements; Item 6 (priority) and supporting documents; Item 7 (the mark) including special kinds of marks, color claims and standard character marks; Item 9 miscellaneous indications (transliteration, translation, disclaimers, verbal elements, descriptions); Item 10 goods and services (classification, indications); Item 11 designations; Item 12 applicant signature; Item 13 certification and signature by the Office of origin. Includes fee calculation sheet guidance (how fees are computed on filing).

name: The Mark: representation, color and special kinds
description: Requirements for the representation of the mark in the international application, including special types (figurative, sound, position, hologram etc.), claims to color, and use of standard characters.
guidance: Explains when a mark must be represented graphically, how to indicate color(s) claimed, when to submit reproductions or descriptions for non-visual marks, and how verbal elements and disclaimers should be indicated. Provides examples and notes on equivalence and transcription for multilingual filings.

name: Designations and subsequent designations
description: Procedural and substantive rules for designating Contracting Parties in the international application and for presenting subsequent designations after registration.
guidance: Specifies entitlement to make subsequent designations, official forms and required items (MM2 etc.), language of subsequent designation, how to indicate goods/services for the designation, interaction with seniority claims and declarations (EU specifics), and recording/publication of subsequent designations and their effects (date of subsequent designation; periods of protection; possible refusals by designated Offices).

name: Recording, publication and contents of the International Register and Gazette
description: What information is recorded in the International Register and published in the WIPO Gazette of International Marks, and the legal effects of such recording and publication.
guidance: Describes contents (holder, mark, goods/services, designations, priority, dates, recorded changes such as limitation/renunciation/cancellation, replacement notifications and seniority claims), the language(s) of publication/registration, legalization of extracts, and how published information creates public notice to third parties.

name: Petition to Director for denial of reexamination (37 CFR 1.515(c), 1.181)
description: A petition to the Director under 37 CFR 1.515(c) and 1.181 to challenge a denial of reexamination must be filed within one month of the mailing date of the decision denying the request for reexamination. Extensions of time to file such a petition may only be sought by a petition under 37 CFR 1.183 with appropriate fee to waive the time provisions of 37 CFR 1.515(c).
guidance: Decisions on petitions under 37 CFR 1.515(c) are final and not appealable. 37 CFR 1.515(c) applies only to challenging a basis for denying reexamination, not to challenging a basis for granting reexamination. If an order grants reexamination as to some claims but finds no SNQ for others, a third-party requester may petition under 1.515(c) within one month to reconsider the determination as to the claim for which no SNQ was found.

name: Patent owner statement timing (37 CFR 1.530)
description: Except as provided in § 1.510(e), no statement or other response by the patent owner in an ex parte reexamination shall be filed prior to determinations under § 1.515 or § 1.520; premature statements will not be acknowledged or considered and will be returned or discarded.
guidance: When reexamination is ordered under 35 U.S.C. 304 the order will set a period of not less than two months for the patent owner to file a statement and any narrowing amendments; extensions may be requested under 37 CFR 1.550(c). Any statement must clearly point out why the patent claims are believed patentable considering the cited prior art alone or in reasonable combination.

name: Amendments must comply with 37 CFR 1.530(d)-(j)
description: Any proposed amendment to the description and claims in patents involved in reexamination proceedings must be made in accordance with § 1.530 (and comply with formal presentation requirements in 37 CFR 1.52(a) and (b)).
guidance: Amendments submitted must include required fees (37 CFR 1.20(c)) and follow the specific rules for specification, claims, and drawings as set out in 1.530(d)-(j). Noncompliant amendments may be held inappropriate or not entered; see form paragraphs PTOL-22.12/22.13 and instructions for informing the patent owner and time to correct informalities.

name: Specification amendment format (37 CFR 1.530(d)(1))
description: All amendments to the specification (other than claims) must be made by submission of the full text of any paragraph to be changed, with markings showing changes (single brackets for deletions and underlining for additions), and the precise point in the specification where the change is to be made must be indicated.
guidance: The exception allowing deletion of an entire paragraph by statement alone is permitted, but presenting the full text aids entry. Underlining for added paragraphs must be the complete text. Markings are made vis-a-vis the original patent, not relative to prior amendments. Indicate precise insertion point to avoid delays in issuance of reexamination certificate.

name: Claim status requirement (37 CFR 1.530(e))
description: Whenever there is an amendment to the claims, the submission must supply, on separate pages, the status (pending or canceled) as of the date of the amendment of all patent claims and of all added claims, and an explanation of the support in the disclosure for the changes to the claims.
guidance: Failure to submit claim status will generally result in an informal notification (MPEP § 2266.02) and amendments submitted after final rejection will not be entered. The explanation of support addresses the merits; failure to provide it will likewise lead to notification and possible non-entry.

name: No enlargement of claim scope; no new matter (37 CFR 1.530(j) and related)
description: No amendment may enlarge the scope of the claims of the patent or introduce new matter; no amendment may be proposed for entry in an expired patent. Amendments that broaden claims should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 305.
guidance: The test for enlargement is the same as for reissue applications under 35 U.S.C. 251 (see In re Freeman and MPEP § 2258). For handling of new matter see MPEP § 2270. Amendments are normally entered if timely and rule-compliant, but do not become effective in the patent until the reexamination certificate is issued.

name: Amendment of new claims (presentation and remarks)
description: An amendment of a new claim previously presented in the reexamination must present the entire text of the new claim containing the amendatory material and must be underlined throughout; the presentation cannot contain bracketing or other indication of what was in the previous version.
guidance: Because changes are made vis-a-vis the original patent, the amended new claim does not show prior-version differences; the patent owner must point out what changed in the 'Remarks' portion of the amendment. As required by 37 CFR 1.530(e), each change must be accompanied by explanation of support in the disclosure for the change.

name: Distinction: meritum de condigno versus meritum de congruo
description: Condign merit (meritum de condigno) gives a strict claim in justice to reward; congruous merit (meritum de congruo) gives only a quasi-claim based on equity or decency.
guidance: Explains that the two are not species of one genus but analogous; some scholastics (Dominicus Soto, Becanus) rejected 'meritum de congruo' due to ambiguity of 'equity' but the text defends the term. Discusses historical Semipelagian debate and Augustine's nuanced recognition that justifying faith of the sinner is not entirely without merit (contextualizing congruous merit).

name: Legitimacy of a scientific hypothesis
description: Forming a hypothesis is a legitimate scientific act even when founded on slight grounds, provided it is tentative and useful to guide inquiry; hypotheses need not claim proof but must be admissible and discussable.
guidance: Examples given: Gilbert's hypothesis that the earth is a magnet; suggestions that the brain is a voltaic pile; Gall's localisation attempts. A hypothesis may be valuable by opening a promising path of inquiry even if verification is difficult. Verification requires observation and experiment; hypotheses should be judged by their capacity to be rendered discussable and amenable to inquiry rather than by immediate conformity to inductive proof.

name: Description inherently involves classification and resemblance
description: To describe an observed fact is necessarily to assert a resemblance between that fact and other things; description therefore always introduces elements beyond the bare sensation.
guidance: Example: saying 'I see something white' not only reports a sensation but classifies it by resemblance to the category 'white.' Recognize that any descriptive statement contains conceptual additions (classificatory claims) that must be evaluated and cannot be treated as raw perception.

name: Technological quality: minimum word count of independent claims
description: Proxy for patent scope/technical content: the minimum word count across all independent claims of a patent.
guidance: Included as an alternative measure of technological quality / patent scope in regressions (Table 4, col. d) to test whether narrowing/widening of claim length explains commercial value changes.

name: Patent scope proxies (number of claims and backward citations)
description: Patent scope and relation to prior art proxied by total number of claims and total number of backward citations.
guidance: Included as controls in patent-level regressions to account for patent breadth and dependence on prior art; used to argue the CAFC effect is not driven by simple changes in claim counts or backward citations.

name: Appeals-rate logistic model (test for anticipation / timing)
description: Logistic model of whether a case was decided by an appellate court, including circuit indicators, post-CAFC indicators by circuit, number of claims, assignment indicator, tech fixed effects, owner_defendant, home_circuit, and year fixed effects.
guidance: Used to test whether CAFC timing/direction was anticipated (if so, rates of appeals would not change). Figure 2 and regression results show a substantial nationwide increase in appeals after CAFC, inconsistent with anticipation. Model specification and interpretation are provided.

name: Robustness and alternative-explanation checks
description: Tests to rule out that CAFC effect on commercial value is driven by changes in technological quality, patent scope, scientific progress, or regional R&D/PhD supply.
guidance: Specific robustness regressions control for forward citations, citations to scientific publications, minimum independent claim word count, PhDs per million population, and R&D per capita. Authors also construct alternative CAFC indices with different control sets (year FE only; with patent characteristics; with litigation characteristics) and show similar patterns; Hausman tests fail to reject equality of coefficients across specifications. Additional robustness: excluding patents from circuits showing largest CAFC shifts to test sensitivity to selection.

name: Identify abstract ideas as recited and tie to abstract-idea groupings
description: When the examiner determines the claim recites an abstract idea, the rejection should identify the abstract idea as it is recited in the claim and explain why it falls within one of the groupings of abstract ideas (mathematical concepts, mental processes, or certain methods of organizing human activity) enumerated in MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2), or follow the tentative abstract idea procedure.
guidance: Identify the abstract idea as recited in claim language and explain why it falls within a grouping. If the limitation does not fall within the enumerated groupings, use the 'tentative abstract idea' procedure (MPEP § 2106.04(a)(3)). While not required, the explanation may cite an appropriate court decision that supports the identification, but examiners should be familiar with any cited decision and avoid relying upon language taken out of context or non-precedential decisions unless facts match uniquely. See USPTO court-decision chart at www.uspto.gov/PatentEligibility. Sample language: identify the recited limitation and explain why it is a mental process, mathematical concept, or method of organizing human activity.

name: Identify laws of nature or natural phenomena as recited and explain rationale
description: If the claim recites a law of nature or a natural phenomenon, the rejection should identify that law or phenomenon as recited in the claim and explain using a reasoned rationale why it is considered a law of nature or natural phenomenon.
guidance: Explain using a reasoned rationale why the recited subject matter is a law of nature or natural phenomenon. See MPEP § 2106.04(b). Sample: 'The claim recites the correlation of X, and X is a law of nature because it describes a consequence of natural processes in the human body.' When the claim describes but does not expressly set forth the exception, explain what subject matter is described and why it is an exception.

name: Identify products of nature and perform markedly different characteristics analysis
description: When the claim recites a product of nature, the rejection should identify the exception as recited in the claim and explain using a reasoned rationale why the product does not have markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state.
guidance: Refer to how the product of nature is recited in the claim and compare to the closest naturally occurring counterpart to determine if there are markedly different characteristics (MPEP § 2106.04(b),(c)). Sample: 'X was isolated from naturally occurring Y. Because there is no indication in the record that isolation resulted in a marked difference in structure, function, or other properties as compared to its counterpart, X is a product of nature exception.'

name: Explain why additional claim elements do not integrate the exception or add significantly more (Step 2A Prong Two & Step 2B)
description: After identifying the judicial exception, identify any additional elements recited in the claim beyond the exception and explain why they do not integrate the exception into a practical application and do not add significantly more to the exception. The explanation should address additional elements both individually and in combination.
guidance: Evaluate additional elements individually and in combination when determining whether the claim as a whole recites eligible subject matter. Remember that a new combination of known steps may be eligible (Diamond v. Diehr). Address whether additional elements meaningfully limit the exception. See MPEP §§ 2106.04(d) and 2106.05 for considerations. Provide reasoned rationale so applicant can respond; when appropriate, explain why additional elements do integrate the exception or provide an inventive concept by adding a meaningful limitation. If concluding certain limitations are well-understood, routine, conventional in the relevant field, support that conclusion per Subsection III.

name: Treatment of generic computer components and insignificant extra-solution activity
description: For claim limitations that recite a generic computer component performing generic computer functions at a high level of generality, examiners can explain why these generic computing functions do not meaningfully limit the claim. Similarly, limitations that add insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., mere data gathering, storing data, or linking to a technological environment) often do not integrate the exception into a practical application.
guidance: Explain why generic computing functions (e.g., using the Internet to gather data) or insignificant extra-solution activity do not add a meaningful limitation. Keep in mind case law (e.g., DDR Holdings where generic components in combination performed non-generic functions and were eligible; Parker v. Flook where field-of-use limitation was insufficient). See MPEP §§ 2106.05(f),(g),(h) for examples. Provide concrete explanation (e.g., storing data does not meaningfully limit computing a mathematical relationship; placing a product of nature in a test tube is merely a nominal extra-solution component).

name: Evidentiary requirements and treatment of eligibility as question of law with possible factual issues
description: The courts consider eligibility a question of law, and generally do not require 'evidence' to find a claim recites a judicial exception; however, underlying factual issues (e.g., whether additional elements are well-understood, routine, conventional) may arise and when asserting such routine/conventional character the examiner must support that assertion in writing.
guidance: At Step 2A Prong One, a reasoned rationale is sufficient and no evidence (publications/affidavits) is required to find a claim recites a judicial exception. At Step 2A Prong Two/Step 2B, evidence is not required except when asserting that additional limitations are well-understood, routine, or conventional; in that case, the examiner must support the conclusion in writing using one of the Subsection III options (A)-(D). Cite relevant precedents that describe whether the issue is law or involves factual findings (Rapid Litig. Mgmt.; Berkheimer; etc.).

name: Use appropriate form paragraphs and required ordering/content for 35 U.S.C. 101 rejections
description: Use specified form paragraphs (7.04.01, 7.05, 7.05.01, 7.05.016, and 7.05.017 where applicable) when making 35 U.S.C. 101 rejections, and follow the required ordering and content instructions for each form paragraph.
