guidance: Form paragraph 7.04.01 (Statement of Statutory Basis) must precede first use of 35 U.S.C. 101 in first actions/final rejections. Use 7.05 (Rejection, 35 U.S.C. 101 - heading) and follow it with a detailed explanation using 7.05.01, 7.05.016, 7.05.017, etc., as applicable. 7.05.016 is for claims directed to a judicial exception without significantly more and must identify whether claims are directed to a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea and explain the recitation, why it is an exception, why additional elements fail to integrate into a practical application, and why additional elements do not amount to significantly more. If the judicial exception is a tentative abstract idea, include form paragraph 7.05.017 and the TC Director's signature. Follow examiner notes for bracketed content and ordering.

name: Suggest specification-based claim amendments to overcome eligibility rejections (best practice)
description: In the event a rejection is made, it is a best practice for the examiner to consult the specification to determine if there are elements that could be added to the claim to make it eligible, and identify those elements in the Office action and suggest them as a way to overcome the rejection.
guidance: When appropriate, identify elements from the specification that could be included in claims to provide meaningful limitations or inventive concepts and explicitly suggest such amendments in the Office action to help applicant overcome the rejection.

name: When a foreign patent limits the domestic term
description: To limit the term of the domestic patent by a foreign patent, the inventions covered by the two patents must be identical and the foreign patent must take effect before the issue of the domestic patent (the controlling date is the issue/publication date of the foreign patent).
guidance: The foreign patent limits the domestic whether the foreign protection was open or secret; a domestic patent is not limited by a foreign patent unless the latter claims and describes the same invention; the rule also applies when a U.S. patent covers several inventions separately patented abroad (Gramme Elec. Co.; Holmes Electric Protective Co.; Ex parte Siemens).

name: Subject matter issues are appropriately addressed
description: Subject matter issues include: lack of statutory subject matter or utility (section 2 and subsection 27(8) of the Patent Act); inadequate description of the invention (subsection 27(3) of the Patent Act, section 56 of the Patent Rules); introduction of new subject matter (section 38.2 of the Patent Act); lack of unity (section 36 of the Patent Act, and section 88 of the Patent Rules); and lack of support for claims (section 60 of the Patent Rules).
guidance: Examiners must identify and address statutory subject matter defects, utility, sufficiency of description, added/new matter, unity and claim support, citing the correct statutory authority in reports.

name: Search and/or examination is reserved when appropriate
description: Search and/or examination may be reserved (completely or partially) when deficiencies in the specification make it impractical to issue a comprehensive report.
guidance: Situations justifying reservation include: specification too insufficient/unclear to search; claims directed solely to non-statutory subject matter; claimed subject matter not supported by the specification as filed; missing sequence listing preventing search; lack of unity; introduction of new subject matter (new subject matter is not examined). When reservation is used, the extent and reason must be clearly stated in the examiner's report. In lack of unity cases, inform applicant to elect one group linked by a single general inventive concept and limit further examination to that election.

name: A correct search strategy is adopted
description: A correct search strategy, where a meaningful search can be carried out: identifies the inventive concept(s) underlying the claims; includes a first-to-file search of Canadian patent documents; makes effective use of available search results; includes a supplemental/top up or comprehensive search, as required; and pays regard to the amount of searching that is reasonable and practicable.
guidance: Details: perform first-to-file searches in Canadian patent documents (including non-laid-open) to identify novelty and overlap issues, aiming to identify documents filed/published in five years prior to filing date; for PCT national phase, consider PCT search results and IPRP/IPER when available; conduct comprehensive searches when no PCT ISR and no adequate foreign family search results; otherwise a first-to-file search may suffice. Supplemental/top-up searches should be used when examiner knowledge suggests additional prior art likely exists. When performing searches, rely on sufficient breadth to identify documents relevant to novelty and inventive step, use appropriate search fields and methods prioritizing fields with highest probability of finding relevant documents, and document the search strategy in the search record according to office practice. Note: do not search claimed embodiments not properly supported by the specification as filed.

name: Novelty, obviousness and double patenting are appropriately addressed
description: If the examiner has reasonable grounds to believe that the invention is anticipated or obvious: the most relevant prior art is listed in the references section of the examiner's report; a summary of the relevant teachings of the prior art is provided; each lack of novelty defect is identified under section 28.2 of the Patent Act; and each obviousness defect is identified under section 28.3 of the Patent Act. Double patenting issues must also be identified when appropriate.
guidance: When search fails to reveal pertinent references, state that. Assess each claim against prior art, with emphasis on independent claims; level of detail for dependent claims may vary by number of claims, prosecution stage and nature of limitations. For double patenting: identify conterminous or obviousness double patenting defects if same invention is claimed in pending application and issued Canadian patent to same applicant; identify defects under section 44 if necessary. Where overlap exists between copending applications, warn applicant in the report and maintain warning while overlap exists; when one co-pending application becomes allowable/granted, mark the other as containing a double patenting defect. Note: if an issued patent or co-pending application can be cited as prior art under section 28.2 or 28.3, separate overlap/double patenting defect need not be identified.

name: Application formalities are appropriately addressed
description: Application formality defects include: lack of clarity of the claims (e.g., subsection 27(4) of the Patent Act, subsection 62(1), sections 63, 61 and 51 of the Patent Rules); drawings not furnished or not clear; description formalities such as unidentified trademarks, incorrect page numbering, incorporations by reference and inadequate publication details; title not short and precise; abstract not a concise summary; sequence listing not in correct format.
guidance: Clarity matters do not extend to minor defects of grammar or spelling which do not lead to ambiguity (i.e., which would not give rise to a defect under subsection 27(4)). An examiner should not delay allowance merely to clean up trivial language defects.

name: All defects are identified in a sufficiently informative manner
description: Sufficient detail is always provided when identifying a defect so that the applicant can understand the defect and determine an appropriate response.
guidance: Include: reference to correct authority basis (Patent Act, Patent Rules or jurisprudence); appropriate explanation, particularly for obviousness or lack of clarity; indicate relevant passages of the application and prior art when appropriate; identify defective claims; identify groups and rationale for lack of unity defects; at second or subsequent report stages, address applicant's amendments and arguments when defects continue. Note: explanation may include a suggestion of a remedy, but must not dictate any specific remedy.

name: Format of examiner's report is clear and content is accurate
description: Written communications include matters of form, where appropriate: all information is accurate including agent contact information, application number, owner, title, classification, applicant reference number, examiner name and examiner telephone number; the basis of the report is clearly identified.
guidance: Report should clearly identify: any reservations to search/examination; the unity group elected by the applicant; the applicant's latest amendment; the number of claims; requisitions (sections 85, 86 and 94) clearly identified by a bullet in headers; citations correctly identified with sufficient detail to retrieve the document; content presented in logical order; search record present and complete; and a report for a private inventor may be more detailed and written in plain language.

name: Distinguish claims 'directed to' a judicial exception
description: Thus distinguishes claims that are “directed to” the recited judicial exception from claims that are not “directed to” the recited judicial exception.
guidance: A judicial exception is not eligible subject matter; if a claim is directed to the judicial exception it requires further analysis under the Alice/Mayo framework. If a claim contains only the judicial exception (or merely recites another judicial exception), it is insufficient to integrate the exception into a practical application and is not eligible. Examiners should make appropriate rejections (see MPEP § 2106.07) and it is a best practice to recommend an amendment that would resolve eligibility if possible.

name: Additional elements must 'transform' exception into patent-eligible application
description: For a claim reciting a judicial exception to be eligible, the additional elements (if any) in the claim must “transform into a patent-eligible application of the judicial exception, either at Prong Two or in Step 2B.”
guidance: If there are no additional elements in the claim, then it cannot be eligible. If additional elements merely recite another judicial exception, that is insufficient (e.g., adding one abstract idea to another does not render the claim non-abstract). Examiners should evaluate whether additional elements integrate the exception into a practical application or amount to significantly more.

name: Recommend amendment when claim lacks additional elements
description: If there are no additional elements in the claim, then it cannot be eligible.
guidance: After making the appropriate rejection (see MPEP § 2106.07 for formulating a rejection for lack of eligibility), it is a best practice for the examiner to recommend an amendment, if possible, that would resolve eligibility of the claim.

name: Apply same eligibility analysis regardless of number of exceptions
description: Examiners should apply the same eligibility analysis to all claims regardless of the number of exceptions recited therein.
guidance: Unless it is clear a claim recites distinct exceptions (e.g., a law of nature and an abstract idea), care should be taken not to parse the claim into multiple exceptions, particularly in claims involving abstract ideas. If possible, treat the claim for Prong Two and Step 2B purposes as containing a single judicial exception.

name: When exceptions are distinct, select one exception to analyze
description: In some claims, the multiple exceptions are distinct from each other (e.g., a first limitation describes a law of nature and a second limitation recites an abstract idea).
guidance: For examination efficiency, examiners should select one of the exceptions and conduct the eligibility analysis for that selected exception. If the analysis indicates the claim recites additional element(s) that integrate the selected exception into a practical application or amount to significantly more than the selected exception, then consider the claim patent eligible. If not, consider the claim ineligible. (See University of Utah Research Foundation v. Ambry Genetics.)

name: Do not parse multiple abstract ideas; consider together when possible
description: In claims reciting multiple abstract ideas (same or different groupings) or multiple laws of nature, examiners should not parse the claim.
guidance: Identify multiple concepts (e.g., mental steps and mathematical calculation) in Step 2A Prong One to make the record clear, but where possible consider the limitations together as a single abstract idea for Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B rather than analyzing separate abstract ideas individually.

name: Identify specific claim limitations that recite an abstract idea (two-step identification)
description: Examiners should determine whether a claim recites an abstract idea by (1) identifying the specific limitation(s) in the claim under examination that the examiner believes recites an abstract idea, and (2) determining whether the identified limitation(s) fall within at least one of the groupings of abstract ideas listed above.
guidance: If the identified limitation(s) fall within a grouping, reasonable to conclude the claim recites an abstract idea in Step 2A Prong One and the claim then requires further analysis in Step 2A Prong Two to determine whether additional elements integrate the abstract idea into a practical application. If the identified limitations do not fall within any of the groupings, reasonable to find the claim does not recite an abstract idea and the analysis concludes at Pathway B, unless the claim recites another exception (e.g., law of nature).

name: If limitation falls within a grouping -> proceed to Step 2A Prong Two
description: If the identified limitation(s) fall within at least one of the groupings of abstract ideas, it is reasonable to conclude that the claim recites an abstract idea in Step 2A Prong One.
guidance: The claim then requires further analysis in Step 2A Prong Two to determine whether any additional elements in the claim integrate the abstract idea into a practical application (see MPEP § 2106.04(d)).

name: If limitation does not fall within any grouping -> eligible at Pathway B
description: If the identified limitation(s) do not fall within any of the groupings of abstract ideas, it is reasonable to find that the claim does not recite an abstract idea.
guidance: This concludes the abstract idea judicial exception eligibility analysis (Pathway B), except in rare circumstances discussed in MPEP § 2106.04(a)(3). The claim is thus eligible at Pathway B unless it recites and is directed to another exception (such as a law of nature or natural phenomenon).

name: Groupings are not mutually exclusive; identify all applicable groupings
description: The groupings of abstract ideas are not mutually exclusive; some claims recite limitations that fall within more than one grouping or sub-grouping.
guidance: Examiners should identify at least one abstract idea grouping, but preferably identify all groupings to the extent possible if a claim limitation is determined to fall within multiple groupings, and proceed with the analysis in Step 2A Prong Two.

name: Separate reciting an abstract idea from merely involving one (Prong One caution)
description: While all inventions at some level embody, use, reflect, rest upon, or apply laws of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract ideas, not all claims recite an abstract idea.
guidance: The Step 2A Prong One analysis requires a claim to recite (i.e., set forth or describe) an abstract idea in Prong One before proceeding to the Prong Two inquiry about whether the claim is directed to that idea, thereby separating claims that recite abstract ideas from those that merely are based on or involve an abstract idea.

name: Examples of claims that do not recite abstract ideas (non-limiting hypotheticals)
description: Non-limiting hypothetical examples of claims that do not recite (set forth or describe) an abstract idea include specific device or method claims.
guidance: Illustrative examples provided: (i) a printer comprising a belt, roller, printhead, and ink cartridge; (ii) a washing machine with tub, drive motor, controller and housing; (iii) an earring with a glucose sensor and memory; (iv) a method for sequencing BRCA1 gene sequences (amplify and sequence); (v) a method for loading BIOS into a local computer system from remote memory; (vi) a method of rearranging icons on a GUI based on usage; (vii) a method of training a neural network with staged training sets. These examples show claims that do not recite abstract ideas and are eligible at Step 2A Prong One (Pathway B).

name: Mathematical concepts grouping definition
description: The mathematical concepts grouping is defined as mathematical relationships, mathematical formulas or equations, and mathematical calculations.
guidance: The Supreme Court and Federal Circuit have identified many concepts within this grouping (e.g., converting binary-coded decimal, Arrhenius equation, mathematical formula for hedging). When determining whether a claim recites a mathematical concept, consider whether the claim recites the mathematical concept or merely limitations that are based on or involve it. A limitation merely based on or involving a mathematical concept may not fall into the grouping if the mathematical concept itself is not recited in the claim. Mathematical concepts need not be expressed in symbols; words operating on data can serve the same purpose (e.g., “determining a ratio of A to B”).

name: Mathematical relationships indicators and examples
description: A mathematical relationship is a relationship between variables or numbers and may be expressed in words or using mathematical symbols.
guidance: Examples include: (i) relationship between reaction rate and temperature (Arrhenius equation); (ii) conversion between binary-coded decimal and pure binary; (iii) relationship between radio activity and antenna conductor arrangement; (iv) organizing/manipulating information through mathematical correlations. If a claim recites such relationships it likely falls in the mathematical concepts grouping.

name: Mathematical formulas or equations indicators and examples
description: A claim that recites a numerical formula or equation will be considered as falling within the “mathematical concepts” grouping.
guidance: Textual expressions of formulas (e.g., “determining a ratio of A to B” or “calculating force by multiplying mass by acceleration”) also count. Examples: electromagnetic standing wave formulas; the Arrhenius equation; a formula for computing an alarm limit; a mathematical formula for hedging.

name: Mathematical calculations indicators and examples
description: A claim that recites a mathematical calculation, when given its broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the specification, will be considered as falling within the “mathematical concepts” grouping.
guidance: Mathematical calculation means performing a mathematical operation or using mathematical methods to determine a variable or number (e.g., determining, performing, calculating). Examples include resampled statistical analysis to generate distribution, calculating an alarm limit, converting geospatial coordinates, managing insurance policy values via calculations, algorithms for optimization, and calculating differences between local and average values.

name: Errors of fact must be actual factual errors that warrant dismissal
description: Alleged factual errors must be genuine mistakes in the Final Order's factual findings, not a mix of chronology, opinion, or mis-statements of procedural history.
guidance: Requesters must identify specific factual errors showing the decisionmaker erred (e.g., overlooked or mischaracterized testimony or documentary evidence in a way that affects the outcome). The Director is not obligated to reference every piece of evidence in the Final Order; claiming 'concealment' when the testimony was considered is insufficient. Repeating prior factual arguments that were adjudicated does not meet the standard.

name: Overall three-question process for §101
description: After determining what applicant invented and establishing the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim in accordance with MPEP §2103, walk through the three questions in the flowchart to determine whether the claim is drawn to patent-eligible subject matter.
guidance: If not eligible at any stage, the claim is prima facie ineligible and should be rejected using revised form paragraph 7.05.13. Use MPEP §2103 for claim interpretation; state all non-cumulative reasons in the first Office action under compact prosecution.

name: Question 2: Judicial exception present?
description: Does the claim recite or involve one or more judicial exceptions (abstract ideas, laws of nature/natural principles, natural phenomena, and natural products)?
guidance: If no, claim is patent-eligible. If yes, or unclear, proceed to Question 3. Examples of natural products include chemicals derived from nature (antibiotics, fats, oils, etc.), foods, metals/minerals, natural materials (rocks, soils), nucleic acids, organisms, proteins/peptides, and substances found in or derived from nature. If in doubt that claim recites something similar to a natural product, proceed to Question 3.

name: Question 3: Claim as a whole significantly different?
description: Does the claim as a whole recite something significantly different than the judicial exception(s)?
guidance: If the claim recites an abstract idea, analyze using MPEP §2106(II) only. Otherwise, perform the factor-based analysis in Part II. If the totality of relevant factors indicates the claim is not significantly different, reject under 35 U.S.C. 101 using revised form paragraph 7.05.13; if it is significantly different, the claim is patent-eligible.

name: Use of MPEP §2106(II) for abstract ideas
description: There is no change to examination of claims reciting an abstract idea; they should continue to be analyzed for subject matter eligibility using the existing guidance in MPEP §2106(II).
guidance: If a claim recites an abstract idea (even if combined with other judicial exceptions), do not apply the factor-based 'significantly different' analysis here; follow MPEP §2106(II) guidance, including evaluation of practical application factors.

name: Factor a) product claim markedly different
description: Claim is a product claim reciting something that initially appears to be a natural product, but after analysis is determined to be non-naturally occurring and markedly different in structure from naturally occurring products.
guidance: To satisfy, identify differences between the recited product and naturally occurring products and evaluate whether those differences together rise to the level of a marked difference in structure. Not all changes (e.g., mere isolation) rise to marked differences. Marked differences may be structural and/or functional; being produced by routine manipulation does not preclude weighing toward eligibility (e.g., cDNA, hybrid plants).

name: Factor b) meaningful limits on claim scope
description: Claim recites elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) that impose meaningful limits on claim scope, i.e., the elements/steps narrow the scope of the claim so that others are not substantially foreclosed from using the judicial exception(s).
guidance: Examples: specific dosages, time frames, patient types, or other limitations that confine use to a particular application. If elements meaningfully limit scope, they weigh toward eligibility.

name: Factor c) elements significantly related to the exception
description: Claim recites elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) that relate to the judicial exception in a significant way, i.e., the elements/steps are more than nominally, insignificantly, or tangentially related to the judicial exception(s).
guidance: Elements that integrate, manipulate or materially change the judicial exception (not merely mention it) favor eligibility.

name: Factor d) more than general instructions
description: Claim recites elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) that do more than describe the judicial exception(s) with general instructions to apply or use the judicial exception(s).
guidance: Claims that only include high-level instructions to apply a natural principle weigh against eligibility; concrete, specific steps weigh toward eligibility.

name: Factor e) particular machine or transformation
description: Claim recites elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) that include a particular machine or transformation of a particular article, where the particular machine/transformation implements one or more judicial exception(s) or integrates the judicial exception(s) into a particular practical application.
guidance: See MPEP 2106(II)(B)(1) for explanation of machine-or-transformation factors. A specific machine/transformation that meaningfully integrates the exception favors eligibility.

name: Factor f) more than well-understood, routine, conventional
description: Claim recites one or more elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) that add a feature that is more than well-understood, purely conventional or routine in the relevant field.
guidance: If additional elements perform non-routine functions or are themselves novel/non-conventional, they weigh toward eligibility. Prior routine use of components for different purposes does not automatically make the claim conventional for the claimed application.

name: Factor g) product claim not markedly different
description: Claim is a product claim reciting something that appears to be a natural product that is not markedly different in structure from naturally occurring products.
guidance: If the recited product is structurally (and functionally) not markedly different from its natural counterpart, this factor weighs against eligibility (e.g., purified product structurally identical to natural form).

name: Factor h) high-level generality covering all practical applications
description: Claim recites elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) at a high level of generality such that substantially all practical applications of the judicial exception(s) are covered.
guidance: Claims drafted so broadly that they foreclose substantially all uses of the natural principle/product weigh against eligibility.

name: Factor i) elements required to apply the exception
description: Claim recites elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) that must be used/taken by others to apply the judicial exception(s).
guidance: If the additional elements dictate how others must perform the exception (i.e., are effectively required to practice it), this weighs against eligibility; if alternatives exist, this factor may not be satisfied.

name: Factor j) additional elements are well-understood, conventional, routine
description: Claim recites elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) that are well-understood, purely conventional or routine in the relevant field.
guidance: If the extra elements are routine/conventional in the relevant art, they are unlikely to render the claim significantly different and weigh against eligibility.

name: Factor k) insignificant extra-solution activity
description: Claim recites elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) that are insignificant extra-solution activity, e.g., are merely appended to the judicial exception(s).
guidance: Merely tacking on trivial activities that do not meaningfully integrate the exception or confine its use should not render the claim eligible; such activity weighs against eligibility.

name: Factor l) mere field of use
description: Claim recites elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) that amount to nothing more than a mere field of use.
guidance: Limiting use of a judicial exception to a particular field or environment without adding substantive limitations is insufficient to make the claim significantly different.

name: Marked-difference inquiry (Chakrabarty-centered)
description: For natural products, analyze whether the claimed product is a non-naturally occurring product of human ingenuity that is 'markedly different' from naturally occurring products.
guidance: Myriad reaffirmed reliance on Chakrabarty's criterion: identify differences between the recited product and naturally occurring counterparts, then evaluate whether differences together rise to a marked structural difference. Mere recitation of words like 'isolated' or routine manipulation may not create a marked difference. Structural differences that also produce functional differences strengthen the case for marked difference (e.g., chemically modified molecules, cDNA, engineered organisms).

name: Use of other statutory provisions and compact prosecution
description: §101 is not the sole tool for determining patentability; where a claim encompasses a judicial exception such as a natural product, sections 102, 103, and 112 provide additional tools for ensuring patentability. Under principles of compact prosecution, Office personnel should state all non-cumulative reasons and bases for rejecting claims in the first Office action.
guidance: Examiners should include non-redundant rejections under other statutes where appropriate to provide a complete prima facie case of unpatentability.

name: Revised form paragraph 7.05.13 usage and explanation
description: Revised form paragraph 7.05.13 should be used when rejecting claims that recite or involve a law of nature, natural principle, natural phenomenon, or natural product for lack of subject matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 101. This form paragraph must be preceded by form paragraphs 7.04 and 7.05.
guidance: In bracket 2 of the paragraph, identify the judicial exception(s) recited or involved and explain why the element(s)/step(s) in addition to the judicial exception(s) do not result in the claim as a whole reciting something significantly different. Explain why the claim features do not add significantly more and/or fail to show a marked difference; show why features are extra-solution activity, mere field-of-use, or conventional/routine. The explanation must be sufficient to establish a prima facie case.

name: Appeal Statistics (Allowance After Appeal)
description: The examiner’s rate of allowance after an appeal is filed (how often appeals result in allowance rather than proceeding to PTAB).
guidance: If allowance after appeal is relatively high, appealing (instead of filing an RCE) may avoid unnecessary claim narrowing. If allowance after appeal is low, the appeal is likely to go to the PTAB — consider client comfort with delay due to PTAB backlog and weigh against filing an RCE to potentially reach agreement earlier. Use allowance and RCEs-per-patent rates together when making the decision.

name: Use Markush structures to claim a broad genus
description: Markush structures allow inventors to claim a wide range of structurally related compounds under a single patent claim, covering a broad genus rather than listing each variation separately.
guidance: Use Markush groupings to strengthen scope of protection and reduce risk of design-arounds; useful when protecting lead molecules and related analogs. Balance breadth with adequate disclosure and support.

name: Meet 35 U.S.C. § 112 requirements (written description, enablement, definiteness)
description: Markush claims must satisfy written description, enablement, and definiteness under 35 U.S.C. § 112.
guidance: Ensure the specification provides sufficient disclosure to show possession of the claimed genus (written description), enables a person skilled in the art to make and use the full scope (enablement), and defines claim scope with required definiteness. Be aware the USPTO examines Markush claims with these statutory criteria in mind.

name: Follow USPTO guidelines for Markush claims (unity and disclosure of alternatives)
description: USPTO guidance emphasizes unity of invention and that each alternative in a Markush group must be sufficiently disclosed.
guidance: Consult and follow the USPTO's specific guidance on Markush claims when drafting and prosecuting claims. Demonstrate why the alternatives form a unitary invention and provide disclosure/support for each alternative to avoid rejections.

name: Ensure the specification describes all members of the group adequately
description: The specification should adequately describe the members of the claimed group so that the claim scope is supported and enabled.
guidance: Provide representative examples, experimental data, or clear enabling disclosure for the range of claimed alternatives. Lack of adequate description for group members can lead to § 112 rejections.

name: Avoid overly broad or speculative groupings that are not enabled
description: Do not claim speculative or overly broad groupings where the specification does not enable or support the full claimed scope.
guidance: If alternatives are speculative or their properties are unpredictable across the claimed genus, narrow the claim or add supporting disclosure. Overbroad claims risk rejections for lack of enablement or written description.

name: Avoid grouping insufficiently similar alternatives to prevent restriction requirements (35 U.S.C. § 121)
description: If alternatives in a Markush group are not sufficiently similar, examiners may issue a restriction requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 121, forcing division of the application.
guidance: Group alternatives that are chemically and functionally related. If dissimilar alternatives must be claimed, expect potential restriction and plan prosecution strategy (e.g., divisional applications).

name: Anticipate increased scrutiny in international prosecution (unity and formal differences)
description: Markush claims often receive greater scrutiny during international prosecution where unity of invention and formal claim requirements may differ.
guidance: Review foreign patent offices' practices and WIPO resources when planning Markush claims for international filing. Tailor claims or prepare supporting arguments to meet differing unity and formal requirements abroad.

name: Record claim(s) selected for printing — general rule
description: Examiners preparing a non-IFW application for issue are to record the number of the claim selected for printing in the Official Gazette in the box labeled 'PRINT CLAIM' on the face of the file wrapper, or if IFW application, on the Issue Classification sheet.
guidance: When recording, write the claim number clearly in black ink; if multiple claims are selected, separate numbers with commas; refer to the renumbered patent claim number rather than the original application claim number.

name: Selection rules for claim(s) to print
description: The claim or claims should be selected in accordance with these instructions: (A) The broadest claim should be selected. (B) Examiners should ordinarily designate but one claim on each invention, although when a plurality of inventions are claimed in an application, additional claims up to a maximum of five may be designated for publication. (C) A dependent claim should not be selected unless the independent claim on which it depends is also printed. In the case where a multiple dependent claim is selected, the entire chain of claims for one embodiment should be listed. (D) In reissue applications, the broadest claim with changes or the broadest additional reissue claim should be selected for printing.
guidance: Follow the listed subpoints; ensure consistency between claims selected and figure selected for printing.

name: Authority to state reasons for allowance (37 CFR 1.104(e))
description: If the examiner believes that the record of the prosecution as a whole does not make clear his or her reasons for allowing a claim or claims, the examiner may set forth such reasoning. The reasons shall be incorporated into an Office action rejecting other claims or be the subject of a separate communication; applicant may file a statement commenting.
guidance: Stating reasons for allowance is not mandatory, but examiners are urged to ensure the application file contains a complete and accurate picture of the Office’s consideration. The practice formalizes existing authority and provides applicants opportunity to comment. Failure to respond to applicant comments does not create any implication.

name: Content requirements for a Statement of Reasons for Allowance
description: Where specific reasons are recorded, care must be taken to ensure statements are accurate, precise, and do not place unwarranted interpretations on the claims. Each statement should include at least (1) the major difference in the claims not found in the prior art of record, and (2) the reasons why that difference is considered to define patentability over the prior art if either is not clear in the record.
guidance: Statements need not enumerate all reasons; where many reasons exist, stating major or important reasons may suffice, but couch appropriately. Avoid stock paragraphs or meaningless/uninformative statements. It is improper to use the statement to attempt to narrow a claim by providing a special definition not supported in the description.

name: When to add Reasons for Allowance — illustrative indicators
description: Illustrative examples when a statement should likely be added include: (A) claims allowed on the basis of one/some of a number of arguments/affidavits where a statement is necessary to identify which were persuasive (appeal brief, ordinary reply, affidavit under 37 CFR 1.131 plus arguments under 102/103); (B) first action issue of a noncontinuing or continuing application where differences are not discussed elsewhere; (C) withdrawal of a rejection for reasons not suggested by applicant; (D) allowance after remand from the Board; (E) allowance coincident with citation of newly found references that are very close to the claims but claims considered patentable thereover; (F) where reasons are of record but unclear or spread throughout file history; (G) allowance based on a claim interpretation not readily apparent; (H) allowance following court decision.
guidance: These guidelines are illustrative—not exhaustive—and intended to aid the examiner's judgment whether the record 'as a whole' makes clear the reasons for allowance.

name: Examples of suitable and unsuitable statement content
description: The manual provides concrete examples of suitable statements (e.g., primary reason is inclusion of a specific limitation, telephonic interview agreed amendment, claims deemed nonobvious improvement, grant of effective filing date) and examples of unsuitable content (e.g., vague mechanical descriptions without explanation, 'main reasons are applicant’s remarks', blanket assertions of novelty/nonobviousness without support).
guidance: Do not include matter not relating directly to reasons for allowance. Unsuitable statements include those that are unclear, conclusory, or that attempt to create definitions or broad legal positions not supported by the record.

name: Scope-of-license proof: acts must be within conferred authority
description: A defendant relying on a license must show that his acts were performed under the authority conferred and not in antagonism to the patent or under a license from a different patent.
guidance: If acts exceed the license's scope the licensee is an infringer; plaintiff must rebut claims of authority by denying existence or by counter evidence, or by showing defendant's acts fall outside conferred authority.

name: PGR petition content requirements (35 U.S.C. 322(a))
description: A petition filed under 35 U.S.C. 321 may be considered only if it: (1) is accompanied by the fee; (2) identifies all real parties in interest; (3) identifies in writing and with particularity each claim challenged, the grounds for each challenge, and the evidence supporting each challenge (including copies of relied-upon patents/printed publications and affidavits/declarations if relying on other factual evidence or expert opinions); (4) provides other information the Director may require by regulation; and (5) provides copies of documents required under (2)-(4) to the patent owner or representative.
guidance: The petition must give the Office and patent owner clear, particularized legal and factual bases and supporting exhibits for each challenged claim; failure to meet these elements bars consideration.

name: Institution standard for PGR (35 U.S.C. 324(a))
description: The Director may not authorize a post-grant review to be instituted unless the Director determines that the information in the petition, if unrebutted, would demonstrate that it is more likely than not that at least one of the claims challenged is unpatentable.
guidance: This is a 'more likely than not' threshold for institution, requiring the petition to present sufficient persuasive evidence on at least one claim.

name: Limitation re: reissue patents (35 U.S.C. 325(f))
description: A PGR may not be instituted if the petition requests cancellation of a claim in a reissue patent that is identical to or narrower than a claim in the original patent when the time limitations in 35 U.S.C. 321(c) would bar filing a petition for the original patent.
guidance: Reissue substitutions cannot be used to evade the original PGR filing-time bar.

name: Motion to amend standards and public disclosure (35 U.S.C. 326(a)(9))
description: Regulations will set forth standards and procedures for allowing the patent owner to move to amend the patent to cancel a challenged claim or propose a reasonable number of substitute claims, and ensure any information submitted in support of an amendment is made public as part of the prosecution history.
guidance: Amendment requests are limited in scope, must not introduce new matter, and support materials become public record.

name: Motion to amend: single motion and limits (35 U.S.C. 326(d))
description: During a PGR the patent owner may file a single motion to amend to cancel any challenged claim and/or propose a reasonable number of substitute claims; additional motions may be permitted for settlement or for good cause; an amendment may not enlarge the scope of claims or introduce new matter.
guidance: Motions to amend are tightly constrained: limited in number, cannot broaden claims, and may be allowed later only under specific circumstances.

name: Final written decision and certificate (35 U.S.C. 328(a)-(b))
description: If a PGR is instituted and not dismissed, the PTAB will issue a final written decision on patentability of challenged claims and any new claim added; after appeal time or termination of appeals, the Director will issue and publish a certificate canceling any claim finally determined unpatentable, confirming any claim determined patentable, and incorporating new or amended claims determined patentable.
guidance: The final decision and implementing certificate effect changes on the patent record, including cancellation or incorporation of amended claims.

name: Effect of new or amended claims (35 U.S.C. 328(c))
description: Any proposed amended or new claim determined patentable and incorporated into a patent following a PGR will have the same effect as specified in 35 U.S.C. 252 for reissued patents regarding rights of prior users, purchasers, or importers.
guidance: Successful amended/new claims have statutorily defined retroactive/legal effects similar to reissue.

name: IPR claim construction standard: broadest reasonable interpretation (37 C.F.R. § 42.100(b))
description: A claim in an unexpired patent shall be given its broadest reasonable construction in light of the specification in which it appears.
guidance: The Office applies broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) for claim construction in IPRs, consistent with historic PTO practice and justified by the opportunity to amend claims during IPR; cited precedents include Yamamoto and In re Am. Acad. of Sci.

name: IPR petition content: standing and particulars (37 C.F.R. § 42.104(a)-(b))
description: A petition must demonstrate standing: certify the patent is available for IPR and that the petitioner is not barred or estopped; the petition must identify each claim challenged, the specific grounds for each challenge, how claims are to be construed, why the claims as construed are unpatentable under the identified grounds, and exhibit numbers and citations to supporting evidence.
guidance: Petitions must present precise, claim-by-claim legal/factual bases and exhibit citations; facially improper standing may be denied without reaching merits.

name: Disclosure of self-search results (number of prior arts)
description: For expedited examination, more than four searched prior arts closest to the claimed invention shall be disclosed. However, where special conditions exist, such as no relevant prior arts are found in the new technical field, less than three search results may be disclosed.
guidance: If the searched prior art is directly related to the technical field or all components of the claimed invention, the description of the search result shall be recognized as appropriate. Additional search results from local IP centers may be submitted instead of self-search processes and results. Self-search results suffice if an examiner can easily comprehend them; strict adherence to Annexed Form no.5 wording is not required. Antipattern: omitting mandatory search-results content (see 'inappropriately disclosed' below).

name: Contrastive explanation content and scope
description: In the contrastive explanation, the similarities, differences and contrastive analysis between each claim of the application for expedited examination and the closest prior art document to the concerned claim shall be described consecutively.
guidance: Contrastive explanations of all independent claims shall be described; contrastive explanation of dependent claims may be left out. If an independent claim's contrastive explanation is not disclosed but involves the same components as another disclosed independent claim (but in a different category), the undisclosed independent claim may be deemed appropriately described based on the disclosed one.

name: Specification of third-party practicing conditions (Article 4(1))
description: A person requesting expedited examination under Article 4(1) (third party's practicing of the invention per Article 61(1) of the Patent Act) shall specify the condition under which a third party practiced the claimed invention or utility model in a written explanation.
guidance: Provide evidential documents that detail how/when a third party practiced the invention; complement orders will be issued if the evidence is insufficient.

name: Requests made on multiple grounds
description: A request for expedited examination can be made on multiple grounds; if the requester holds at least one ground for request, the examiner shall not invalidate the request and shall determine and proceed with expedited examination.
guidance: If a ground claimed is insufficient but another ground exists among those submitted, proceed based on any valid ground. If a ground not claimed is obvious or explained enough, it may be considered, but determination is generally based on grounds indicated in the explanation.

name: Special-case timing rules (deferral, divisional applications, pre-start requests)
description: Various special timing rules apply: (i) For applications filed before June 30, 2001 and requested by third party, defer determination for three months after filing. (ii) For divisional applications of a parent requested for expedited examination, the start time for the divisional (if not itself requested) is calculated based on the date of request for examination on the original application. (iii) If expedited request is made after examination has started and the application is eligible, treat as if requested and conduct expedited examination.
guidance: For divisional applications requested for expedited examination, start according to earlier examination order between divisional and original. For prior-filed applications claiming domestic priority, in many cases requests may be invalidated unless priority is withdrawn per guidance.

name: Infringement must relate to the precise invention claimed
description: Acts of manufacture, use, or sale must relate to the precise invention as claimed; the accused product/process must be identical in effect, function, and mode of operation to the claimed invention to constitute infringement.
guidance: Apparent exceptions for machine patents (where employing the structural law may appropriate the whole idea) are in reality applications of the requirement that the accused thing embody the essential structure/idea; see sections and cases referenced regarding machine patents and equivalents (§900 and notes).

name: Using part of a patented invention is not infringement unless it appropriates the invention
description: Employing a distinct part of a patented invention is not an infringement unless that part itself constitutes an infringement or is an essential/operative equivalent of the claimed invention.
guidance: If the part used embodies the essential parts or equivalents of the claimed invention or, in machines, embraces the complete expression of the structural law, use may be infringement; see Sessions v. Romadka (1884) and related notes (§900, §926).

name: Patent marking/notice obligation to prevent ignorant infringement
description: The law imposes on the patentee an obligation to notify the public of their claims (e.g., stamping 'patented' with the patent date on the article or its package); failure to mark may bar recovery of substantial damages against persons not otherwise notified of the patent.
guidance: For functional arts the patent specification discloses practice; for tangible articles, marking allows the public to learn the invention from the article itself. See statutory/duty-to-stamp discussion and cases referenced (§902/Infringement through Ignorance').

name: Amendment affecting a claim
description: An amendment to the claims or the addition of a new claim must be supported by the description of the invention in the application as filed. An amendment to the specification (e.g., a change in the definition of a term used both in the specification and claim) may indirectly affect a claim even though no actual amendment is made to the claim.
guidance: Case citation: In re Wright, 866 F.2d 422. Examiner must ensure any claim amendment is supported by originally filed disclosure; look for explicit, implicit, or inherent support.

name: Reliance on filing date of parent application under 35 U.S.C. 120
description: Claims in a U.S. application are entitled to the benefit of the filing date of an earlier filed U.S. application if the subject matter of the claim is disclosed in the manner provided by 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, in the earlier application.
guidance: Citations: Tronzo v. Biomet, In re Scheiber. Examiner must determine whether earlier application discloses claimed subject matter with adequate written description for priority entitlement.

name: Reliance on priority under 35 U.S.C. 119
description: Claims in a U.S. application are entitled to the benefit of a foreign priority date or the filing date of a provisional application only if the corresponding foreign or provisional application supports the claims in the manner required by 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
guidance: Citations: In re Ziegler; Kawai v. Metlesics; In re Gosteli. Evaluate foreign/provisional disclosures for written description support before granting priority.

name: Support for a claim corresponding to a count in an interference
description: In an interference, the claim corresponding to a count must be supported by the specification in the manner provided by 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph; earlier applications relied upon for benefit must likewise meet 112 requirements for the subject matter of the count.
guidance: Citations: Fields v. Conover (broad generic disclosure insufficient for a specific compound); Hyatt v. Boone. When interference benefit is claimed, ensure earlier app meets written description for the count.

name: Statement of rejection requirements (what to include in a written-description rejection)
description: When rejecting a claim for lack of written description, the examiner must set forth express findings of fact supporting the conclusion, including (A) identification of the claim limitation(s) at issue; and (B) establishment of a prima facie case by providing reasons why a person skilled in the art at filing would not recognize that the inventor was in possession of the invention as claimed in view of the disclosure.
guidance: A general allegation of unpredictability is insufficient. A simple statement pointing out where support is lacking may suffice for new/amended claims. Cite Hyatt v. Dudas; suggest claim amendments where appropriate, mindful of prohibition on adding new matter (see Rasmussen).

name: Changes to the scope of claims must be supported by original disclosure
description: To comply with the written description requirement or to be entitled to an earlier priority date under 35 U.S.C. 119, 120, or 365(c), each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure.
guidance: See MPEP §2163. Applies to broadenings, narrowings, numerical range changes, and terminology changes; examine original disclosure for express/implicit/inherent support.

name: Broadening claim — omission of a limitation
description: Omission of a limitation can raise whether the inventor had possession of a broader, more generic invention. A claim that omits an element the applicant described as essential/critical does not comply with the written description requirement.
guidance: Citations: Gentry Gallery v. Berkline; Johnson Worldwide v. Zebco; Tronzo v. Biomet; In re Wilder. If specification describes a feature as 'the only possible location' or 'essential,' omission will likely fail. Compare In re Peters where a limitation was nonessential.

name: Addition of a generic claim (genus supported by species)
description: A genus claim may be supported by sufficient description of a representative number of species; a single species supports a genus only when disclosure indicates the patentee invented species sufficient to constitute the genus. If the genus exhibits substantial variation, a sufficient variety of species must be described to reflect that variation.
guidance: Citations: Enzo Biochem; In re Curtis; In re Rasmussen; In re Herschler; In re Smythe; Tronzo; In re Gosteli. Examine whether the disclosed species are 'representative' and whether operability across genus would be predicted by ordinary artisans.

name: Narrowing or subgeneric claim (introducing unsupported limitations)
description: Introducing claim changes that narrow claims by adding elements or limitations not supported by the as-filed disclosure violates 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph. Subgeneric recitations may or may not be acceptable depending on factual communication to skilled artisans.
guidance: Citations: Fujikawa v. Wattanasin; In re Ruschig; Ex parte Ohshiro; In re Lukach; Ex parte Sorenson; In re Smith; In re Wilder. 'Laundry list' disclosures are insufficient to reasonably lead to every species; decide each case on facts.

name: Relationship of written description requirement to new matter
description: Lack of written description generally arises with respect to claim subject matter. If applicant amends or attempts to amend abstract, specification or drawings to add content not described in the application as filed, new matter issues arise. Information present in any one part of the original application may be added to any other part without introducing new matter.
guidance: Statutory prohibitions: 35 U.S.C. 132 (no new matter in pending application) and 35 U.S.C. 251 (no new matter in reissue). If added content is not in original filing, treat as new matter and object/reject as appropriate.

name: Treatment of new matter (examiner actions)
description: If new subject matter is added to the disclosure (abstract, specification, drawings), the examiner should object to the introduction of new matter under 35 U.S.C. 132 or 251 and require applicant to cancel the new matter. If new matter is added to claims, reject claims under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph - written description requirement.
guidance: Cite In re Rasmussen. Examiner should still consider subject matter added to claims when making prior art rejections since applicant may overcome the new matter rejection. If specification amended to add new matter that affects claim limitations, reject the claims under 112 para. 1.

name: Review of new matter objections and/or rejections
description: A rejection of claims for new matter is reviewable by the Board of Patent Appeals and Interferences (BPAI), whereas an objection and requirement to delete new matter is subject to supervisory review by petition under 37 CFR 1.181. If both claims and specification contain new matter and there has been both a rejection and objection, the issue is appealable and should not be decided by petition.
guidance: Use appropriate procedural route depending on whether action is an objection (petitionable) or rejection (appealable).

name: Claimed subject matter not disclosed in remainder of specification
description: Claims as filed are part of the disclosure; if an originally filed claim discloses material not disclosed elsewhere in the specification, applicant may amend the specification to include the claimed subject matter.
guidance: Cite In re Benno. Use Form Paragraph 7.44 when originally claimed subject matter lacks proper antecedent basis (see MPEP §608.01(o)).

name: Step 1 – statutory category check
description: Determine whether the claim is directed to a statutory category (e.g., composition of matter, manufacture, process).
guidance: All example analyses begin by confirming Step 1: YES when claims are directed to a statutory category (composition of matter, manufacture, or process). If Step 1 is NO the analysis ends; otherwise proceed to the nature-based product exception analysis (Step 2A).

name: Use markedly different characteristics analysis for nature-based products (Step 2A)
description: For nature-based products, determine whether the claimed subject matter is directed to a judicial exception (product of nature) by assessing whether the claimed product has 'markedly different characteristics' from its naturally occurring counterpart.
guidance: If the claimed nature-based product lacks markedly different characteristics it is an exception (Step 2A: YES); if it has such differences, it is not directed to the exception (Step 2A: NO). The guidance is illustrated across multiple examples (purified small molecules, proteins, nucleic acids, bacteria, mixtures, compositions).

name: Structural differences can show a marked difference
description: Changes in chemical or physical structure relative to the natural counterpart (e.g., different chemical substitution, removal/addition of groups, altered crystalline form, different glycan) can establish a marked difference.
guidance: Examples: 5-methyl amazonic acid (addition of methyl group) and deoxyamazonic acid (hydroxyl replaced by hydrogen) are structural changes that render claims eligible; purified Antibiotic L in tetrahedral crystals or with a high-mannose N-glycan is structurally distinct from the natural form; peptides with ≥90% identity but containing at least one non-natural substitution are structurally different.

name: Functional differences can show a marked difference
description: Differences in biological or pharmacological function between the claimed product and its natural counterpart can demonstrate a marked difference.
guidance: Examples: 5-methyl amazonic acid stimulates hair growth in addition to treating cancer; recombinant Antibiotic L expressed in yeast has lower immunogenicity and different half-life; genetically modified Pseudomonas containing extra plasmids degrades multiple hydrocarbons. Functional changes rise to the level of a marked difference even if structural changes accompany them or not.

name: Combinations that create a non-natural structure can be eligible
description: Claims limited to compositions where naturally occurring substances are physically joined into a non-natural structure can have markedly different characteristics and be eligible.
guidance: Example: a pharmaceutical composition comprising a core of amazonic acid enveloped by a layer of natural polymeric material produces a non-natural structure with different in vivo behavior (colonic release) and thus qualifies as not a product of nature (Step 2A: NO).

name: Product-by-process claims are construed by the structure implied, not limited to process steps
description: During examination, product-by-process claims are limited to the structural characteristics of the product implied by the recited steps, not to the recited manipulations themselves.
guidance: Example: a claim 'A composition comprising an acid produced by a process which comprises: providing amazonic acid; and replacing the hydroxyl group...' is interpreted as the product deoxyamazonic acid; if that product is structurally different from the natural counterpart, claim can be eligible.

name: Claims that encompass both natural and non-natural embodiments risk ineligibility
description: A claim that covers embodiments that are identical to natural products as well as changed embodiments may fail the marked difference test because some embodiments will lack marked differences.
guidance: Example: a broad claim to 'Antibiotic L' that encompasses naturally occurring hexagonal-pyramidal crystal form and non-natural tetrahedral crystals is ineligible because at least some embodiments are identical to what exists in nature (Step 2A: YES). Limiting claims to only the non-natural forms can cure eligibility problems.

name: Method claims focused on practical application can be eligible without marked-difference analysis
description: Claims directed to a practical application or process of using a nature-based product (e.g., method of treating a disease) can be not directed to the product-exception even though they recite a nature-based product.
guidance: Examples: methods of treating colon or breast cancer by administering amazonic acid are analyzed as claims focused on a process of practical application and are therefore not directed to the nature-based product exception (Step 2A: NO); the markedly different characteristics analysis need not be applied in such cases.

name: Vectors comprising heterologous sequences create non-natural combinations and can be eligible
description: Claims to vectors that combine a natural nucleic acid with heterologous sequences (sequences not naturally co-occurring in the organism) are limited to non-natural combinations and thus are not products of nature.
guidance: Example: a vector comprising SEQ ID NO:1 and a heterologous nucleic acid (e.g., viral promoter) results in different genetic structure/expression and qualifies as not a product of nature.

name: Claims limited by sequence identity plus non-natural substitution can be eligible
description: Limiting nucleic acid or peptide claims to sequences having a specified identity to a natural sequence AND containing at least one non-naturally occurring substitution can establish marked difference.
guidance: Example: claims to nucleic acids or peptides with ≥90% identity to a natural sequence but containing at least one substitution not known to occur in nature are treated as structurally different and eligible.

name: Apply broadest reasonable interpretation when analyzing claims
description: Analyze claims for eligibility under their broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the specification; interpret claim scope to determine whether it covers natural embodiments or is limited to non-natural variants.
guidance: All claim example analyses state they are 'analyzed for eligibility in accordance with their broadest reasonable interpretation' — examiners should construe claims broadly to determine whether the claim as written encompasses natural products, and then apply Steps 2A/2B accordingly.

name: Scope of claimed design — overall visual appearance
description: The scope of the claim encompasses the design’s visual appearance as a whole and the visual impression it creates; do not cover a broad general design concept.
guidance: Consider all figures in the patent and all visual features of the design as a whole rather than isolated portions. (Page 22)

name: Solid lines vs broken lines in drawings
description: All matter depicted in solid lines contributes to the overall appearance of the design and is part of the claim; features shown in broken lines and described as disclaimed are excluded from the claimed design.
guidance: Failure to show features in broken lines signals inclusion of such features in the claimed design. Functional features illustrated in solid lines are part of the claimed design based on their contribution to visual appearance. (Page 22)

name: Effect of specification and prosecution history on claim scope
description: The drawings are supplemented by the written description and the prosecution history may limit the claimed design.
guidance: Insert case-specific descriptions of any limitations resulting from the description or prosecution history when applicable. (Page 19-22)

name: Direct infringement — ordinary observer/overall appearance test
description: To determine infringement, compare the overall appearances of the accused design and the claimed design using the judge’s claim construction; if, in view of the prior art, the overall appearance of the accused design is substantially the same as the claimed design, find infringement.
guidance: Focus on the overall appearance, not individual features. Minor differences should not prevent a finding of infringement. Familiarize yourself with the prior art before making comparisons. (Page 25)

name: Anticipation — identical in all material respects
description: A design is anticipated if a single prior art reference is 'identical in all material respects' to the overall visual impression of the claimed design; a design that is not new is anticipated.
guidance: Defendant must prove anticipation by clear and convincing evidence. Minor differences do not necessarily preclude anticipation, but the prior reference must be substantially the same in overall visual impression. (Page 31)

name: Obviousness (design) — combination of references and Graham-like factors
description: A claimed design is invalid as obvious if a designer of ordinary skill would have combined a primary reference with a closely related secondary reference to create the same overall visual appearance as the claimed design. The primary reference must teach a specific design (not merely a concept).
guidance: Evaluate five factors: (1) scope and content of prior art relied on; (2) differences between claimed design and prior art; (3) level of ordinary skill in the art at the time; (4) whether the ordinary observer would find the two designs substantially the same; and (5) any additional considerations indicating obviousness or not. Defendant must prove obviousness by clear and convincing evidence. (Page 35-36)

name: Burden of proof distinctions
description: Different issues require different proof standards: infringement is decided by a preponderance of the evidence; invalidity (anticipation, obviousness, etc.) and willful infringement require proof by clear and convincing evidence (where specified).
guidance: Apply the specified standards (preponderance vs clear and convincing) when evaluating evidence for each claim/defense. (Pages 24, 29, 28)

name: Prosecution history estoppel (general principle)
description: Prosecution history (proceedings between applicant and patent office from filing to issuance) can limit claim scope and is relevant to claim construction and assessment of infringement under the doctrine of equivalents.
guidance: Prosecution history estoppel is one of the factors that limit the application of the doctrine of equivalents and takes priority when there is a conflict between the two principles.

name: Amendment-based estoppel
description: Estoppel that arises when an applicant makes a narrowing amendment to a claim during prosecution.
guidance: A narrowing amendment made to satisfy patentability requirements may give rise to an estoppel that is presumed to have surrendered the scope between the pre‑amendment and post‑amendment claim. This presumption can be overcome if the justification for the amendment has only a tangential relationship to the equivalent in question.

name: Argument-based estoppel
description: Estoppel that arises from arguments or representations made to the patent examiner that relinquish claim breadth even without an actual claim amendment.
guidance: Unmistakable declarations to the patent office in favor of patentability, whether necessary to obtain allowance or not, can prevent the patentee from later claiming the surrendered subject matter under the doctrine of equivalents.

name: Festo framework and consequences
description: Supreme Court's Festo decision articulated the doctrine's applicability and set standards for when prosecution history estoppel applies.
guidance: Key points from Festo: (1) every restricting change made to fulfill the Patent Act may give rise to an estoppel; (2) an unexplained narrowing amendment is presumed to have been made to satisfy the Patent Act; (3) estoppel is not an absolute bar to the doctrine of equivalents; (4) the applicant is presumed to have surrendered the scope between pre- and post-amendment claims; (5) it is the applicant's burden to show that a particular equivalent was not surrendered.

name: Estoppel via foreign prosecution statements (when considered)
description: Statements made to foreign patent offices may be considered to establish prosecution history estoppel under certain conditions.
guidance: Courts may consider foreign prosecution statements when: (1) the statement was made in an official procedure where the patentee had incentive to be careful; (2) the patents are related and/or contain identical claims; and (3) the remark was unrelated to distinctive elements of foreign patent law.

name: Scope and temporal limits of estoppel across patents
description: How estoppel based on one prosecution can affect other patents or claims and its temporal limitations.
guidance: Prosecution history estoppel based on arguments or amendments to a single claim may be used to limit the reach of later claims in the same invention and adjacent patents. Conversely, estoppel generally may not apply to patents granted prior to the conduct that gave rise to the estoppel.

name: Examples of claim amendments that narrow scope
description: Common amendment practices that narrow an independent claim and may trigger estoppel.
guidance: Typical narrowing amendments include adding new technical features from the specification into the independent claim, and rewriting a dependent/subordinate claim as a new independent claim—both change the scope of the original independent claim.

name: Effect of estoppel on infringement analysis (limits doctrine of equivalents)
description: Prosecution history estoppel can preclude using the doctrine of equivalents to prove infringement.
guidance: Estoppel may bar a patentee from arguing that accused devices/practices are equivalent to claimed elements, affecting direct infringement and equivalent‑theory infringement; the doctrine of equivalents remains a separate path to protect IP (e.g., in federal litigation or ITC exclusion), but its breadth is narrowed by estoppel doctrine.

name: Burden of proof to rebut estoppel
description: Who must demonstrate whether an equivalent was surrendered during prosecution.
guidance: The patentee/applicant bears the burden to show that a particular equivalent was not surrendered by an amendment or argument; absent such a showing, narrowing amendments are presumed to have been made for patentability reasons and to have surrendered intervening claim scope.

name: What Is A Covered Business Method?
description: Covered Business Method (CBM) patents are methods, apparatuses, or operations used in the practice, administration or management of a financial product or service. CBM patents exclude “technological inventions,” which claim a novel and non-obvious technological feature that solves a technical problem using a technical solution.
guidance: Use this definition to determine whether a challenged patent falls within the CBM class (financial product/service focus). Exclude patents that claim technological inventions that solve technical problems with technical solutions.

name: Grounds for Review / Invalidity Basis
description: The petitioner must assert that at least one claim of the challenged patent is directed to a covered business method and that the claim is invalid under the statutory grounds of patentability, such as anticipation, obviousness, or lack of written description.
guidance: CBM challenges may be based on statutory bases including (as noted) 35 U.S.C. §101 (subject matter), §103 (obviousness), §112 (written description/enablement). Ensure the petition ties the asserted statutory grounds to the claim language and provides supporting evidence.

name: Filing Requirements
description: The petitioner must file a petition for CBM review with the PTAB, providing specific information about the challenged patent, the grounds for invalidity, and any supporting evidence.
guidance: Prepare a petition that includes identification of challenged claims, detailed explanations of grounds, citations to prior art/evidence, and any necessary declarations. Procedural compliance and completeness are essential for institution considerations.

name: Effects / Remedies if Claims Found Unpatentable
description: If the PTAB determines that one or more claims of the patent are unpatentable, those claims may be cancelled or amended.
guidance: CBM provides a mechanism to cancel or require amendment of challenged claims. Use CBM strategically when the goal is claim cancellation or clearing freedom-to-operate issues for financial/ business-method-related patents.

name: Enablement requirement for prior art disclosure
description: For a disclosure to constitute prior art for novelty and obviousness analyses, the disclosure must enable one of ordinary skill in the art to comprehend and make the invention.
guidance: Assess whether the prior disclosure provides sufficient detail (enablement) to practice the claimed invention; prior art need not teach well-known skills.

name: Mere instructions to apply an exception ('apply it')
description: Determine whether the additional elements are nothing more than a recitation of the judicial exception plus words that instruct to 'apply it' (or equivalents such as implementation on a generic computer). Such recitations do not render the claim eligible.
guidance: Supreme Court cases (Alice, Mayo, Benson) show that simply adding words to apply an abstract idea or law of nature—especially by reciting a generic computer—does not provide an inventive concept. Examiners should explain why alleged additional elements do not meaningfully limit the exception and should consider overlaps with other Step 2B considerations (particular machine/transformation, well-understood/routine/conventional activity). Note that requiring more than 'mere instructions' does not mean claims must be narrow; some broad claims have been held eligible (e.g., McRO, Thales Visionix), and some narrow claims ineligible (e.g., Ultramercial, Electric Power Group).

name: Reciting only the idea or outcome (result-oriented claiming)
description: Claims that recite only the idea of a solution or the desired outcome—failing to recite details of how the solution is accomplished—are equivalent to saying 'apply it' and do not supply significantly more.
guidance: If claim limitations attempt to cover any solution to an identified problem without restricting how the result is achieved or describing mechanisms, they likely do not add significantly more (see Electric Power Group; Intellectual Ventures v. Symantec). By contrast, claiming a particular solution or a particular way to achieve an outcome can provide significantly more. Example: claims that describe modifying an XML document but provide no specific steps were held ineligible (Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One).

name: Particularity versus generality of application
description: Assess whether the claim confines the judicial exception to a particular, practical application (which may provide significantly more) versus claiming broad applicability across many fields (which likely does not).
guidance: Broad claims that generically recite an effect or claim every mode of accomplishing that effect are likely equivalent to adding 'apply it' (see Internet Patents Corp. v. Active Network; O’Reilly v. Morse). Limitations that confine the exception to a particular practical application and are integrated into the claim's steps (e.g., Diehr; BASCOM's filtering tool at a specific location with customizable features) have been found meaningful. A common sign of a non-meaningful limitation is an absence of integration into the claim as a whole (token or incidental additions).

name: Insignificant extra-solution activity (pre- and post-solution)
description: Determine whether additional elements amount to insignificant 'extra-solution' activity—incidental pre-solution or post-solution steps that are nominal or tangential to the claimed invention and do not add an inventive concept.
guidance: Extra-solution activity includes things like data gathering before the claimed process or outputting results after it (e.g., printing). The Supreme Court (Flook, Mayo) and subsequent cases treat such insignificant activities, particularly when well-understood or conventional, as not transforming an unpatentable principle into a patentable process. Examiners should evaluate other Step 2B considerations (particular machine/transformation, well-understood/routine/conventional, field-of-use) when determining insignificance. If an extra-solution activity is not integrated or is merely nominal, explain on the record why it does not meaningfully limit the exception.

name: Factors for analyzing extra-solution activity
description: When evaluating whether an additional element is insignificant extra-solution activity, consider whether the limitation is well-known, significant, or merely necessary data gathering/output.
guidance: 1) Well-known: If the extra-solution element is well known (e.g., standard analysis techniques, common XML tags), it may be token extra-solution activity (Bilski; Flook; Intellectual Ventures v. Erie Indem.). 2) Significance: Does the limitation impose meaningful limits on the claim (if not, it may be insignificant; see Ultramercial; Apple v. Ameranth). 3) Necessary data gathering/output: If all uses of the recited judicial exception require the data gathering or outputting, that activity is likely insignificant (Mayo; OIP Technologies). Use these factors plus case examples to justify an eligibility rejection.
