name: Field of use / technological environment limitations
description: Limitations that merely link the judicial exception to a particular field of use or technological environment (e.g., 'apply this formula in petrochemical processes' or 'on a cellular telephone') typically do not amount to significantly more.
guidance: Parker v. Flook illustrates that limiting an abstract idea to a particular field is a classic token limitation; more recent cases (Affinity Labs) show that limiting an abstract idea to a device class or environment (e.g., cell phones) often fails to add an inventive concept. A key question is whether the limitation is integrated into the claim to change how the steps are performed (Diehr) versus an incidental or token field-of-use statement. Examples include limiting drug administration to a patient class (Mayo), limiting hedging to commodity providers/consumers (Bilski), or specifying that a process runs on the Internet (FairWarning; Ultramercial).

name: Claim construction standard (Phillips/§282/37 C.F.R. §42.100(b))
description: Use the same claim construction standard as in a civil action under 35 U.S.C. § 282(b): construe claims according to the ordinary and customary meaning understood by a POSITA in the context of the specification, prosecution history, other claims, and extrinsic evidence. Phillips v. AWH Corp., 415 F.3d 1303 (Fed. Cir. 2005) (en banc) applies.
guidance: The specification is usually dispositive and the single best guide to claim meaning. Extrinsic evidence (expert testimony, dictionaries, treatises) is less significant than the intrinsic record. If an inventor acts as lexicographer, the specification must set forth that definition with reasonable clarity, deliberateness, and precision (Renishaw; Poly‑Am.). Only those claim terms in controversy need to be construed, and only to the extent necessary to resolve the controversy (Realtime Data v. Iancu).

name: Constricted construction of disputed claim terms only as needed
description: Only those claim terms that are in controversy need to be construed, and only to the extent necessary to resolve the controversy.
guidance: The Board will not construe every term; it construes particular terms when parties dispute their meaning or when necessary to resolve obviousness/anticipation disputes. Adopt constructions that align with intrinsic record and controlling court constructions when appropriate.

name: Adoption of prior court claim construction when persuasive
description: The Board may adopt a district court's claim construction if it better aligns with the specification and the parties do not meaningfully dispute it.
guidance: Example: the Board adopted the district court’s construction of 'user profile' as 'a collection of settings and information associated with a user' because it fit the specification and Petitioner did not object. Parties' concessions in hearing or briefs may influence adoption.

name: Construction of specific claim term 'user profile'
description: For this patent, 'user profile' is construed as 'a collection of settings and information associated with a user.'
guidance: The Board favored the district court construction over a narrower dictionary-style proposal because the specification described dedicated user folders and hierarchical directories consistent with settings/information associated with a user; Petitioner expressly agreed to the district court's construction at oral argument.

name: Construction of specific claim phrase 'the first group of video information being configured to allow a user to edit'
description: This limitation is construed to mean at least that a user can modify which video information is a part of the first group of video information (i.e., user can edit membership of the group).
guidance: If a party proposes a reasonable construction and the opposing party does not meaningfully contest it, the Board may adopt that construction for purposes of the proceeding.

name: Mapping prior art to individual claim limitations
description: Petitioner must account for each claim limitation by showing that prior art either expressly discloses the limitation or would have rendered it obvious in combination.
guidance: The Board reviews each limitation (including preamble when limiting) and examines whether prior-art references disclose or would have suggested that element; dependent claims are assessed in light of their parent claims. If an asserted reference fails to disclose a limitation, petitioner may rely on other references or combinations to fill the gap.

name: Weighing expert testimony and credibility of witnesses
description: The Board evaluates the credibility and weight of expert declarations and testimony when experts disagree about facts (e.g., what a reference discloses or whether a reference is publicly available).
guidance: Credibility determinations may be based on consistency with documentary evidence, reasoned explanations, and whether claimed factual positions are contradicted by explicit language in the cited references. The Board may discount expert testimony that is inconsistent with the intrinsic record or that lacks persuasive explanation.

name: Determination of claim priority/effective filing date
description: Assess priority chain and whether claims are entitled to the asserted earlier priority dates; effective filing date affects which version of statutes applies (AIA vs pre-AIA) and which prior art is relevant.
guidance: If claims are not entitled to an earlier priority date, the AIA versions of sections (e.g., 35 U.S.C. § 103) may apply. The Board may rely on findings from related proceedings about entitlement to priority when evaluating applicable prior art.

name: Subject-matter limitation: products only (Germany)
description: Processes and methods cannot be protected by a Gebrauchsmuster, only products can.
guidance: This distinguishes the German Gebrauchsmuster from patents; the German utility model protects product-type inventions but excludes process/method claims.

name: Statutory requirements for computer-implemented inventions
description: The statutory requirements for computer-implemented inventions are the same as for all inventions, including subject matter eligibility and utility (35 U.S.C. 101), novelty (35 U.S.C. 102), nonobviousness (35 U.S.C. 103), definiteness (35 U.S.C. 112(b) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C.112, second paragraph), and the three separate and distinct requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C.112, first paragraph. Claims with computer-implemented functional limitations may invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre-AIA sixth paragraph).
guidance: See MPEP §§ 2106, 2107, 2161, 2181. Even if not construed under 112(f), functional language must be evaluated for written description and enablement under 112(a).

name: Written description requirement (35 U.S.C.112(a))
description: The specification must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail that one skilled in the art can reasonably conclude that the inventor had possession of the claimed invention at the time of filing.
guidance: Purpose is to ensure claim scope does not overreach inventor’s contribution. This requirement is separate from enablement. Case law: Ariad, Reiffin, LizardTech, Rivera. See MPEP §§ 2162-2163.07(b).

name: Genus/species support for written description
description: There is no special rule for supporting a genus by disclosure of a species; whether a genus is supported depends on the state of the art and the nature and breadth of the genus. Disclosure of species is sufficient if it conveys to one of ordinary skill that the inventor possessed the genus.
guidance: Consider the state of the art and whether disclosed species provide adequate support for claimed genus. See Hynix Semiconductor and related cases.

name: Risk of generic or functional claim language
description: Original claims that are generic or functional (or both) often fail written description because functional claims may claim a desired result without describing species that achieve that result.
guidance: An adequate written description of a genus requires more than a generic statement of boundaries. Cases: Ariad, Enzo Biochem, Fiers, Eli Lilly. Examiners should scrutinize functional/genus claims for sufficient disclosure of species or structure.

name: Requirement to disclose algorithm/steps for computer-implemented functional claims
description: For software-related functional claim limitations, the algorithm or steps/procedure for performing the computer function must be described with sufficient detail so that one of ordinary skill can understand how the inventor intended the function to be performed.
guidance: An algorithm may be expressed as a mathematical formula, in prose, as a flowchart, or in any manner that provides sufficient structure. It is not sufficient merely that one skilled in the art could write a program to achieve the function; the specification must explain how the inventor intends to achieve the function. See Finisar, Vasudevan; see MPEP §§ 2163.02 and 2181 IV.

name: Interrelationship of hardware and software disclosure
description: Determination of sufficiency of disclosure for computer-implemented inventions requires inquiry into both disclosed hardware and disclosed software because of their interrelationship and interdependence.
guidance: Critical inquiry: does the disclosure reasonably convey to those skilled in the art that the inventor possessed the claimed subject matter as of the filing date. See Vasudevan Software v. MicroStrategy and Ariad.

name: Means-plus-function (35 U.S.C.112(f)) corresponding structure requirement
description: For means- (or step-) plus-function limitations under 112(f) or pre-AIA sixth paragraph, the specification must provide sufficient corresponding structure, materials, or acts that perform the entire claimed function; otherwise the applicant has failed to particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention (112(b) or pre-AIA second paragraph).
guidance: If insufficient corresponding structure is disclosed for a 112(f) limitation, make a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) and also under 112(b). See In re Donaldson and MPEP § 2181 II.B.2(a).

name: Enablement requirement (35 U.S.C.112(a))
description: The specification must teach those skilled in the art how to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
guidance: All questions of enablement are evaluated against the claimed subject matter as a whole; focus on whether everything within the scope of the claim is enabled. See In re Wright, In re Wands, and MPEP §§ 2164-2164.08(c).

name: Wands factors (factors for undue experimentation)
description: When assessing undue experimentation, consider (1) breadth of the claims; (2) nature of the invention; (3) state of the prior art; (4) level of one of ordinary skill; (5) level of predictability in the art; (6) amount of direction provided by the inventor; (7) existence of working examples; and (8) quantity of experimentation needed.
guidance: The undue experimentation determination is a conclusion reached by weighing these factual considerations (In re Wands). Use them to justify an enablement rejection when appropriate.

name: Claims must be commensurate with enablement (scope <= enablement)
description: The scope of the claims must be less than or equal to the scope of the enablement provided by the specification; broad claim language chosen by the patentee is at the peril of losing claims that cannot be enabled across their full scope.
guidance: Case examples: Sitrick (claims covering movies and video games without enabling movies), MagSil (broad resistive-change claims not enabled across scope). Examiners should ensure specification enables the full scope claimed.

name: Functional claim language not invoking 112(f) is broadly construed
description: When a claim is not limited to particular structure for performing a function and does not invoke 112(f), functional claim language is typically construed broadly to cover any and all embodiments that perform the recited function, raising concern whether disclosure enables the full scope.
guidance: Because such claims encompass all devices/structures performing the function, ensure disclosure sufficiently enables the full scope; otherwise make enablement rejection. See In re Swinehart, AK Steel, In re Moore.

name: Specification need not disclose well-known art but must enable novel aspects
description: The specification need not teach what is well known in the art; however, the applicant cannot rely on the knowledge of one skilled in the art to supply information required to enable the novel aspect of the claimed invention when that enabling knowledge is not in the art.
guidance: Cases: ALZA, Auto. Technologies, Genentech, Idenix. Use supplementation by known art cautiously; the novel aspects must be enabled in the specification itself.

name: Written description may be satisfied by originally-filed claims or other portions
description: A satisfactory written description may be found in originally-filed claims or any other portion of the originally-filed specification, but that does not mean all originally-filed claims have adequate written support; the specification must be examined to assess support.
guidance: See In re Koller, In re Gardner, In re Wertheim. Examiners must verify that originally-filed material indeed conveys possession of claimed subject matter.

name: Ways to show possession for written description
description: Possession may be shown by describing the claimed invention with all limitations using words, structures, figures, diagrams, formulas, actual reduction to practice, disclosure showing invention was 'ready for patenting', distinguishing identifying characteristics, or, for biological materials, an appropriate deposit.
guidance: Examples and cases: Lockwood, Pfaff, Eli Lilly, Amgen, Enzo Biochem. For biological deposits follow 37 CFR 1.801 et seq.; deposit is not a substitute for a written description and written description of deposited material should be as complete as possible.

name: Rejections for lack of written description or enablement
description: A rejection under 35 U.S.C.112(a) (written description) or 35 U.S.C.112(a) (enablement) must be made when the specification does not provide adequate disclosure to demonstrate possession or to enable the full scope of the claim.
guidance: Examiners should establish a prima facie case, conduct thorough prior art review and examination on merits for other statutory requirements prior to completing an office action that includes such a rejection. See MPEP §§ 2163, 2164, 2181.

name: Specification support for new claims
description: A continuation application is a new application that claims priority to an earlier application and shares the same disclosure...so long as the spec supports the new claims.
guidance: You may pursue different claim scopes years after the original filing without losing the earlier priority date only if the original specification provides support for the new claim language; do not attempt to claim subject matter not supported by the parent disclosure.

name: Distinguish CIP vs. continuation vs. divisional (priority and new matter effects)
description: A continuation has the same disclosure as the parent. A continuation-in-part (CIP) adds new matter; new claims supported by the new matter only get the CIP filing date. A divisional pursues claims to subject matter restricted out of the parent.
guidance: Because CIPs introduce new matter and create complicated priority date issues, many strategists prefer continuations and divisionals when possible; choose the vehicle that preserves desired priority dates and minimizes complexity.

name: Use continuations to shift claim type
description: The parent might claim a method. The continuation can claim the apparatus. A second continuation can claim the computer-readable medium. A third can claim a system of multiple devices.
guidance: Drafting successive continuations to claim different claim categories (method, apparatus, medium, system) lets you reach different potential infringers/defendants; plan claim diversification across continuations.

name: Use continuations to test new legal/theory framings (e.g., 101 technical improvements)
description: Spec written in 2020 might support a 101-eligible 'technical improvement' framing that did not feel necessary at the time. A 2027 continuation can pursue claims with that framing if the spec contains the seeds.
guidance: Continuations allow delayed pursuit of alternative claim theories or eligibility framings as case law or enforcement needs evolve; ensure the original disclosure contains the basis for any later-applied theory.

name: Confinement (punishment) does not automatically remove line-of-duty status
description: It is a part of military duty to submit to punishment; a soldier is not necessarily out of the line of duty when in confinement, and if an injury received during confinement was a casualty of the service not incurred by his own fault, his pension claim should not be prejudiced.
guidance: Cited authorities support pension allowance where confinement-related injuries are not due to the soldier's own negligence or fault (R. 41, 2 Op. Atty. Gen.; G. 3063; others).

name: Interior Department discretion in line-of-duty determinations
description: The Interior Department ordinarily decides for itself whether, for pension purposes, a death or disability was incurred in the line of duty.
guidance: Administrative agencies exercise factfinding discretion in each claim.

name: Surgeon General authority for artificial limbs under section 4787
description: Section 4787, R. S., and related acts provide that artificial limbs shall be issued in cases of injury in line of duty; the Surgeon General is specifically designated as the authority to pass on the question of whether the disability was incurred in line of duty for this purpose.
guidance: Decisions: C. 2221, Dec. 16, 1908 and Jan. 16, 1909. Also, Surgeon General's regulations are auxiliary to the statute and do not divest persons of rights to prosecute claims (R. 49, 225, July, 1885).

name: When Article 84 may be examined in opposition proceedings
description: Compliance with Article 84 EPC may be examined only when, and to the extent that, the amendment introduces non-compliance with Article 84 EPC.
guidance: The Enlarged Board ruled (G 3/14) that the 'conventional' approach applies: claims may be examined for Article 84 only to the extent the amendment itself gives rise to a lack of clarity. The rationale includes that Article 84 is not a ground of opposition and amendment should not open the door to broad re-examination of clarity by third parties.

name: Relationship between Article 84 and opposition grounds (Article 100) / Article 101(3) requirement
description: Lack of compliance with Article 84 EPC may not be used as a ground of opposition (Article 100 EPC); however where an amendment is made in opposition or appeal proceedings the patent must 'meet the requirements of the EPC' (Article 101(3) EPC).
guidance: Although Article 84 is not a ground of opposition, when claims are amended during opposition the requirement of clarity must nonetheless be considered to the extent the amendment creates non-compliance. This point is consistent with G 9/91 regarding requirements applying to maintained amended patents.

name: Introduction of a complete dependent claim into an independent claim
description: An amendment consisting of striking out the original independent claim and then writing out the previous dependent claim in full (i.e. introduction of the features of a complete dependent claim) should not be subject to any examination for clarity under Article 84 EPC.
guidance: The Enlarged Board concluded that such amendments are effectively drafting the dependent claim in independent form and therefore do not open Article 84 scrutiny in opposition proceedings.

name: Introduction of elements from a dependent claim that are simple alternatives or deletion of optional features
description: Amendments based on an embodiment expressed as an alternative in a dependent claim, or involving deletion of wording from a dependent claim thereby narrowing its scope, or involving the deletion of optional features, are to be treated the same as introduction of a complete dependent claim and are not open to Article 84 examination.
guidance: Example: if a dependent claim specifies 'substantially concave or convex, optionally having a radius of curvature of at least 10 mm', amending to specify a 'substantially concave surface' (a simple alternative together with deletion of an optional feature) will avoid Article 84 scrutiny.

name: Amendments that disconnect previously linked features are examinable for clarity
description: Amendments which disconnect features from other features to which they were previously linked in a dependent claim are open to examination under Article 84 EPC.
guidance: Example: if a dependent claim specifies a 'substantially concave surface having a radius of curvature of at least 10 mm', amending to specify merely a 'substantially concave surface' (thus removing the radius-of-curvature link) may be examined for clarity. Such amendments may also give rise to added-subject-matter issues depending on circumstances.

name: Three strands of case law on clarity examination (contextual standard)
description: Case law developed three approaches: (1) the 'conventional' approach—clarity examined only to the extent it arises out of the amendment; (2) an extended 'arising out of' approach—where clarity problems concealed in dependent claims are highlighted by amendment; and (3) a diverging/wider approach—allowing broader examination of clarity after amendment.
guidance: The Enlarged Board analysed these strands and endorsed the 'conventional' approach (approach 1), rejecting the wider approaches. This decision provides authoritative guidance on which prior decisions are consistent or inconsistent with G 3/14.

name: Practical example guidance (surface / radius of curvature scenarios)
description: Specific examples illustrate when clarity can or cannot be examined: (a) claim 1 refers to a surface and claim 2 specifies 'substantially flat' → amending claim 1 to 'substantially flat surface' (introduction of the complete dependent claim feature) cannot be examined for clarity; (b) dependent claim listing alternatives including an optional radius → selecting one alternative and deleting an optional feature avoids scrutiny; (c) removing a radius limitation that was linked to the feature can attract clarity examination.
guidance: These examples show application of the rule to common drafting patterns and highlight where disconnection of linked features triggers Article 84 scrutiny. The discussion also notes potential overlap with added-subject-matter concerns.

name: Consequences when clarity cannot be raised during opposition
description: Where a patentee seeks to rely on a feature from a dependent claim which is inherently unclear, even if lack of clarity cannot be raised as a ground, the EPO is likely to give that feature a broad meaning.
guidance: A broadly interpreted unclear feature may prevent establishing a useful distinction over the prior art. Decision T 1459/05 is cited as an example where the Board gave an unclear feature a broad meaning — the Enlarged Board cited that decision despite disagreeing with its overall approach to Article 84 examination.

name: Policy rationale limiting clarity scrutiny after amendment
description: Amendment should not open a door to allow third parties to scrutinise a patent thoroughly for compliance with all the requirements of the EPC; therefore clarity examination is limited to amendment-caused issues.
guidance: The Enlarged Board acknowledged it is not optimal that patents may be granted with claims that do not comply with Article 84 EPC but emphasised the legislature's choice not to make Article 84 a ground of opposition. Practically, amendments arise in a high proportion of oppositions (~70%), so the limitation prevents broad re-litigation of clarity on many amended patents.

name: Motivation to combine references
description: There must be a reason an ordinary artisan would have been motivated to combine the prior art teachings (references) to arrive at the claimed invention.
guidance: Motivation may come from explicit statements in references (e.g., Baselga ’96 specifically teaching paclitaxel as a chemotherapeutic to combine with rhuMAb HER2), preclinical data suggesting potentiation/synergy, or the general knowledge of POSITA. Consider contemporaneous statements, citations, and clinical-trial plans as evidence of motivation.

name: Secondary considerations (objective indicia) and nexus requirement
description: Objective indicia such as long-felt but unmet need, praise, unexpected results, and commercial success may support nonobviousness, but their probative weight requires establishing a nexus between the evidence and the novel aspects of the claimed invention.
guidance: Apply In re Huai-Hung Kao: if the objective evidence results from something other than what is both claimed and novel, there is no nexus. Examples: commercial success must be tied to the claimed features; unexpected results must be attributable to the claimed invention rather than other causes.

name: Use appropriate baseline for claimed clinical endpoints
description: When assessing claims reciting clinical outcomes (e.g., 'an amount effective to extend the time to disease progression'), identify the proper comparison baseline (e.g., no treatment or a specific comparator).
guidance: The Board noted that the proper analysis of 'extend the time to disease progression' is to compare the claimed combination to no treatment in some contexts, and also evaluated comparisons to paclitaxel alone when relevant. Ensure claim construction and the record determine the correct comparator.

name: Evidentiary value of comparative numerical data (e.g., response rates, median TTP)
description: Numerical results in prior art (e.g., % response, median time to progression) can be used to support expectation of clinical improvement or to show a claimed benefit relative to known treatments.
guidance: Use contemporaneous clinical data and drug labeling (e.g., TAXOL PDR median TTP) to compare to reported results in the art (e.g., Baselga ’96 reporting 5.1 months TTP). Recognize surrogate endpoints (response rate) were often used as proxies for endpoints like TTP in early-phase trials; weigh accordingly.

name: Terminal disclaimer condition for untimely petition to withdraw abandonment (post-June 8, 1995)
description: Where a petition to withdraw the holding of abandonment is untimely in a utility or plant application filed on or after June 8, 1995, the Office may treat the petition on its merits only if it is accompanied by a terminal disclaimer dedicating to the public a terminal part of the term of any patent granted that would extend beyond 20 years from the filing date (or earliest 35 U.S.C. 120/121/365(c) benefit).
guidance: The terminal disclaimer must also apply to any patent granted on any application that claims the benefit of the filing date under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, or 365(c). Such a terminal disclaimer is required to avoid granting patent term extension under 35 U.S.C. 154(b) due to prosecution delay caused by treatment of the application as abandoned. (MPEP text)

name: Reply to a final action (nonprovisional applications)
description: For abandonment due to failure to reply to a final action, the reply required for a petition to revive must comply with 37 CFR 1.113 and include cancellation of, or appeal from, the rejection of each claim so rejected.
guidance: Permissible replies include (A) a Notice of Appeal and appeal fee; (B) an amendment under 37 CFR 1.116 that cancels all rejected claims or otherwise prima facie places the application in condition for allowance; (C) filing an RCE (37 CFR 1.114) accompanied by a submission and fee for utility/plant apps (post-June 8,1995); or (D) filing a continuing application under 37 CFR 1.53(b) (or CPA under 1.53(d) in limited cases). If a proposed amendment is filed, the Office of Petitions may route it to the Technology Center to determine if the amendment places the application in condition for allowance; if not, the petition will not be granted.

name: What does not qualify as 'unintentional' or 'unavoidable' delay — deliberate decisions
description: A delay resulting from a deliberately chosen course of action (e.g., applicant deliberately permits abandonment because claims are unpatentable, insufficient commercial value, to defer fees, or similar deliberate choices) is not 'unintentional' within 37 CFR 1.137(b) and precludes revival under either standard.
guidance: Change of mind after deliberate abandonment does not make the prior delay 'unintentional' (see In re Maldague, In re Application of G). Specific examples listed: (A) applicant does not consider claims patentable; (B) applicant considers allowed claims too narrow; (C) applicant considers patent not worth expense; (D) applicant not interested in obtaining patent; (E) applicant seeks to defer fees and expenses.

name: What does not constitute proper notification of change of correspondence address
description: The following do NOT constitute proper notification of a change in correspondence address: (A) mere inclusion of a different address in a paper filed for another purpose without mention of an address change; (B) notification on a paper listing plural applications as affected (except under Customer Number practice); or (C) lack of notification or belated notification to the USPTO of the change.
guidance: Proper, timely, and conspicuous notification is required to support claims of unavoidable delay due to address changes.

name: Notice and content for Non‑Compliant Amendments (Form PTOL‑324)
description: When an amendment fails to comply with 37 CFR 1.121, the Office will notify the applicant by a Notice of Non‑Compliant Amendment (Form PTOL‑324) identifying the non‑compliant section, required items for compliance, and reasons for non‑compliance.
guidance: The type of amendment determines whether a reply period is given and whether the reply may consist only of the corrected section (e.g., a complete claim listing) instead of the entire amendment. See the enumerated amendment‑type rules for specific time periods and consequences.

name: Time periods and treatment for preliminary amendments present on filing date
description: A preliminary amendment present on the filing date that is non‑compliant will prompt OPAP to send a notice giving a two‑month time period for reply; extensions available under 37 CFR 1.136(a).
guidance: Failure to reply to the OPAP notice will result in abandonment of the application. Reply must include either a substitute specification under 37 CFR 1.125 (if amendment to the specification) or a complete claim listing under 37 CFR 1.121(c) (if amendment to the claims).

name: Amendment of replacement paragraphs/sections (amendment of amendments)
description: When a replacement paragraph or section of the specification is to be amended, it should be wholly rewritten and the original insertion canceled.
guidance: Present a marked‑up version using underlining to indicate added subject matter and strike‑through to indicate deletions. Matter canceled by amendment can be reinstated only by a subsequent amendment presenting the canceled matter as a new insertion. A claim canceled by amendment may be reinstated only by a subsequent amendment presenting the claim as a new claim with a new claim number.

name: Definition and publication effects of preliminary amendments
description: A preliminary amendment is one received on or before the mail date of the first Office action (37 CFR 1.115). For applications filed on/after Sep 21, 2004, a preliminary amendment present on filing date is part of the original disclosure; amendments filed after the filing date are not part of the original disclosure.
guidance: Preliminary amendments must comply with 37 CFR 1.121 (complete claim listing; each section begins on a separate sheet). Preliminary amendments to the specification (other than claims) may require a substitute specification in compliance with 1.121(b)(3) and 1.125 to be usable for publication. Filing a preliminary amendment is not recommended because changes may not be reflected in the patent application publication if technical preparations have begun. If present on filing date and containing subject matter not in the originally filed spec/drawings, applicant must file a supplemental oath/declaration under 37 CFR 1.67 referring to the preliminary amendment.

name: When preliminary amendments may be disapproved by the Director
description: A preliminary amendment in compliance with § 1.121 will be entered unless disapproved by the Director. It will be disapproved if it seeks cancellation of all claims without presenting any new or substitute claims, or if it unduly interferes with preparation of a first Office action.
guidance: Factors in disapproval for undue interference: (i) state of preparation of first Office action as of receipt date; (ii) nature of changes to specification or claims. Entry will not be disapproved under 37 CFR 1.115(b)(2) if filed no later than: (A) three months from filing date under § 1.53(b); (B) three months from national stage entry under § 1.491; (C) three months from filing date of a CPA under § 1.53(d) for design apps; or (D) last day of any requested suspension period under § 1.103. These time periods are not extendable.

name: Factors justifying denial of entry of a preliminary amendment
description: Entry may be denied when two conditions are met: (A) examiner has devoted significant time preparing an Office action before receipt; and (B) entry would require significant additional time to prepare the Office action.
guidance: Examples of amendment content that may cause denial because they would require significant additional time: amends the claims; adds numerous new claims; amends the specification to change scope of claims; amends specification raising a new matter issue; includes arguments; includes an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131/1.132; includes evidence traversing rejections from a prior Office action in the parent application. This list is not exhaustive. Examiner should obtain SPE approval before denying entry.

name: Petition content: statutory grounds and claim construction
description: Petition must specify the statutory grounds for the petition (e.g., IPR – 35 U.S.C. §§ 102 or 103; PGR – 35 U.S.C. §§ 101, 102, 103, 112, or 251) and must show how the PTAB should construe each claim (Phillips-type approach, not broadest reasonable construction).
guidance: Explicitly identify the ground(s) and state the proposed claim construction under the Phillips framework. Explain how the construed claim is unpatentable under the cited statutory ground(s).

name: Petition content: element-by-element mapping to prior art with exhibit citations
description: Petition must explain where each claim element is found in the prior art—typically paragraph form (prior practice is claim charts)—and include specific citations to exhibit numbers for the supporting evidence. (37 C.F.R. §§ 42.104, 42.204)
guidance: Provide claim charts or clear paragraph-by-paragraph mappings; cite exhibits precisely (e.g., Ex1006). Avoid conclusory statements without exhibit references.

name: Institution standard: IPR reasonable likelihood
description: "The Director may not authorize an inter partes review to be instituted unless the Director determines that the information presented in the petition ... shows that there is a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail with respect to at least 1 of the claims challenged in the petition." (35 U.S.C. § 314(a))
guidance: Prepare evidence/arguments to meet the 'reasonable likelihood' threshold for at least one challenged claim; institution is discretionary and depends on the petition plus any preliminary response.

name: Institution standard: PGR more-likely-than-not (and novel legal question)
description: "The Director may not authorize a post-grant review to be instituted unless the Director determines that the information presented in the petition ... would demonstrate that it is more likely than not that at least 1 of the claims challenged in the petition is unpatentable." (35 U.S.C. § 324(a)) — may also be satisfied if petition raises a novel or unsettled legal question important to other patents or applications.
guidance: For PGR, show >50% likelihood of unpatentability or present an important novel legal issue; tailor the petition accordingly.

name: Patent Owner Preliminary Response (POPR): scope and limits
description: Patent owner may file a POPR within three months of PTAB’s notice according a filing date. POPR is limited to stating reasons why PTAB should not institute trial; may present supporting evidence including new testimonial testimony; may not include any amendment; may disclaim challenged claims (37 C.F.R. §§ 42.107, 42.207).
guidance: Patent owners can present evidence to defeat institution but cannot amend. If disclaimed, claim preclusion applies (precedential authority cited).

name: Motion to amend claims: limits and support requirement
description: Patent owner may file a motion to amend instituted claims (typically due three months after institution). A motion to amend may not enlarge claim scope or add new matter and must clearly identify support for the amended claims in the original patent disclosure (35 U.S.C. §§ 316(d)(3), 326(d)(3); 37 C.F.R. §§ 42.121(a), 42.221(a)). Motions to amend are limited to 25 pages (37 C.F.R. § 42.24(a)(1)).
guidance: Provide explicit citations to original disclosure for each amended limitation; adhere to page limits. Consider pilot program options and related studies (USPTO MTA Study).

name: Final written decision: timing and permissible outcomes
description: PTAB must enter a final written decision no later than one year after instituting trial; Director may extend by not more than 6 months for good cause (35 U.S.C. §§ 316(a)(11), 326(a)(11)). In an IPR, PTAB may cancel claims as anticipated (§102) or obvious (§103). In PGR, PTAB may cancel claims for §102/103, §101, §112, or §251 grounds. PTAB may cancel all or some reviewed claims or incorporate new/amended claims determined to be patentable (35 U.S.C. §§ 318(a)-(b), 328(a)-(b)).
guidance: Prepare for a final decision within statutory deadline; motions to amend and evidentiary records should support desired final outcomes.

name: Re-issue is a continuation of the original and governed by same law
description: A re-issued patent is a new statement (continuation) of the contract between the public and the patentee and is to be interpreted by the same rules as an original patent; rights arising under it are governed by the law in force when the original was granted.
guidance: Patentability of what is claimed in the re-issue is determined by the state of the art as of the original application's date. The motive for obtaining a re-issue is generally unimportant unless there is actual fraud.

name: Limits on amendment of description and claims same as if inventor applied
description: The limits within which the original description and claims may be amended in a re-issue, and the consequences of prior disclaimer or abandonment, are the same as if the application had been made by the inventor.
guidance: Amendments cannot exceed the permissible scope (as determined by law and the original disclosure); previous disclaimers or abandonments affect what may properly be reclaimed or broadened in the re-issue.

name: Enablement requirement (35 U.S.C. 112(a))
description: Compliance with the enablement requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph) depends on whether one skilled in the art can make and use the invention without undue experimentation.
guidance: Whether the disclosure teaches how to make and use the invention in terms corresponding in scope to the claims; only an enabling disclosure is required, not demonstration of complete safety or all embodiments. The amount of required guidance depends on the nature of the invention, prior art, and predictability of the art.

name: Enablement when claim limited by a particular use
description: When a compound or composition claim is limited by a particular use, enablement of that claim should be evaluated based on that limitation.
guidance: If claim expressly recites a use, examiner should assess whether the specification enables that recited use (see In re Vaeck).

name: Enablement when claim not limited by a recited use / multiple disclosed uses
description: When a compound/composition claim is not limited by a recited use, any enabled use that reasonably correlates with the entire scope of the claim is sufficient to preclude an enablement rejection. If multiple uses are disclosed, an enablement rejection must explain why the specification fails to enable each disclosed use.
guidance: If any disclosed use is enabled when multiple uses are present, the application is enabling for the claimed invention; a rejection must be supported with explanations and evidence as to lack of enablement for each use.

name: Working vs. prophetic examples
description: An example may be 'working' (based on work actually performed) or 'prophetic' (describing predicted results rather than work actually conducted).
guidance: Claims/specification should assist readers in differentiating working and prophetic examples (prophetic examples should use future or present tense rather than past). The presence or absence of examples does not by itself determine enablement; prophetic examples are not per se non-enabling, but must not be misrepresented.

name: Effect of absence of working examples / single working example
description: Lack of working examples or lack of evidence that the claimed invention works should never be the sole reason for rejecting claims for nonenablement; a single working example can preclude a rejection that 'nothing is enabled.'
guidance: While a single working example may prevent a blanket non-enablement rejection, it should not automatically allow broad claim scope without analysis — examiner must evaluate whether extrapolation from that example to the full claimed scope would require undue experimentation and must explain why extrapolation is or is not reasonable.

name: Representative examples for a claimed genus
description: For a claimed genus, representative examples together with a statement applicable to the genus as a whole will ordinarily be sufficient if one skilled in the art would expect the claimed genus could be used without undue experimentation.
guidance: Proof of enablement for other members of the genus is required only where the examiner advances adequate reasons showing a skilled person could not use the genus as a whole without undue experimentation. Sometimes a few examples plus a general quality 'running through' the class can suffice (Amgen v. Sanofi citing Incandescent Lamp).

name: Examiner's initial burden to question enablement and claim construction
description: Before analyzing enablement, the examiner must construe the claims and, for unclear terms, select and state the intended definition and scope in the Office action.
guidance: To make a rejection, examiner has initial burden to establish a reasonable basis to question enablement and must give reasons explaining the uncertainty; must back up assertions with acceptable evidence or reasoning and provide specific technical reasons (In re Wright, In re Marzocchi, Genentech v. Wellcome).

name: Compact prosecution / presenting best rejection early
description: Under compact prosecution principles, the first Office action on the merits should present the best case with all relevant reasons, issues, and evidence for an enablement rejection so applicant can rebut and so subsequent actions may be made final where appropriate.
guidance: If examiner recognizes claim limitations that would render claims enabled, those should be communicated to applicant as early as possible so enabled, allowable subject matter is identified promptly.

name: Determination of enablement based on the evidence as a whole; applicant's burden to rebut
description: Once examiner establishes a reasonable basis to question enablement, burden shifts to applicant to present persuasive arguments and suitable proofs that one skilled in the art could make and use the claimed invention using the application as a guide.
guidance: Applicant may submit 37 CFR 1.132 affidavits/declarations or cite references; evidence need only be convincing by a preponderance standard. Examiner must compare any post‑filing declarations' experimental steps to the specification to ensure commensurate scope and then weigh all evidence without relying on personal opinion (In re Brandstadter, In re Buchner, Pac. Biosciences v. Oxford Nanopore).

name: Quantity and quality of experimentation (undue experimentation / Wands factors)
description: The quantity of experimentation needed to practice the invention is one factor (undue experimentation) but reasonableness depends on nature of the invention and underlying art; extensive routine experimentation may be permissible if sufficient direction is provided.
guidance: Time and expense are factors but not controlling; difficulty and complexity of assays or of components may make experimentation undue in some arts (examples: Telectronics — held reasonable despite time/cost; Amgen — lack of enablement where claim scope required screening millions of candidates). The specification may call for a reasonable amount of experimentation; quantity of examples is only one factor.

name: Identify missing information for enablement rejections
description: If enablement doubt arises because information is missing about one or more essential claim elements or relationships between parts, the examiner should specifically identify what information is missing and why it is needed to provide enablement.
guidance: Examiners should state which essential information is lacking and explain why a skilled artisan could not develop that information without undue experimentation; references should be supplied if possible to support a prima facie case (MPEP § 2164.06(a)).

name: 'Same invention' requirement for reissue (Parker & Whipple rule)
description: Only 'the same invention' can be covered by a reissued patent; the Supreme Court defined this as whatever invention was described in the original letters patent and appears therein to have been intended to be secured thereby.
guidance: This meaning excludes basing a reissue claim solely on a model or drawing or on materials not appearing in the original letters patent as intended to be secured. Models, drawings, and descriptions cannot alone support a reissue claim unless the original letters patent's description shows the invention was intended to be secured originally.

name: Sub‑combination claiming in reissue (same function requirement)
description: A sub‑combination may be claimed in a reissue if it was shown in the original as performing the same function, even if it was claimed in the original only as part of a larger combination.
guidance: A sub‑combination that is shown to perform a substantially different function in the reissue than it could perform in its original environment cannot be legally claimed in a reissue; the functional identity in original environment is decisive.

name: Separate claim to a single device previously claimed only in combination
description: A single device previously claimed only in combination may be made the subject of a separate claim in a reissue provided the device was a new and useful invention of the patentee, could have been separately claimed in the original, and appears in the original to have been intended to be secured thereby.
guidance: This permits carving-out single elements when the original supports it by showing the element as an intended invention.

name: Equivalents and scope broadening in reissue (Miller v. Brass rule)
description: Whether a reissue may describe an equivalent of an original element and claim broadly enough to cover that equivalent depends on the application of Miller v. Brass Co.; such reissue may be sustained if applied for promptly after the original patent grant.
guidance: The right to obtain such a reissue is lost by long lapse of time after the date of the original and before the reissue application.

name: Liberal construction to preserve reissues (limits)
description: Reissue patents are not to be held void for want of identity where a liberal construction of the original and reissue documents can avert that result; courts will modify claims by construction to make them conform to propriety where reasonable.
guidance: This remedial inclination cannot be relied on when a patent was surrendered and reissued solely to broaden its claim and the broadened claim is void for lack of novelty and identity. The claims of the reissued patent will be given their intended effect.

name: Grantees' election between original and reissued patent rights
description: Grantees may either continue to hold their rights under the original patent after it is surrendered and reissued by the patentee or may take corresponding rights under the reissued patent; they have a choice.
guidance: This can theoretically lead to a single invention being patented in one part of the U.S. while free in another. In practice patentees/assignees seldom surrender claims worth retaining, and grantees often ratify broadened reissues. Statutory change could require all assignees/grantees to join in surrender to avoid such disparities.

name: Whether an element is more than mere instructions to apply an exception
description: Determine whether an element (or combination of elements) is more than mere instructions to apply an exception (e.g., mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer).
guidance: Examiners should explain why limitations that are merely instructions to 'apply it' do not meaningfully limit the claim in an eligibility rejection. Examples and case law are used to show when recitations (such as implementing on a generic computer) do not add significantly more (e.g., Alice). For claim limitations that do not amount to more than a recitation of the words 'apply it', examiners should explain why they do not meaningfully limit the claim and consult MPEP § 2106.07(a) for formulating rejections.

name: Field of use and technological environment limitations
description: Assess whether additional elements do more than generally link the judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use; mere field-of-use limitations do not make a claim patent eligible.
guidance: A claim cannot be made eligible simply by limiting the formula or abstract idea to a particular technological use (Diamond v. Diehr; Parker v. Flook; Bilski). Token or incidental field-of-use limitations (e.g., limiting administration of a drug to a particular patient population; specifying commodity providers/consumers; limiting a formula to a specific type of object) do not add an inventive concept (Mayo; Bilski; Flook). The key distinction is whether the field-of-use limitation is integrated into the claim as a whole and alters how steps are performed (Diehr’s integrated process vs Flook’s non-integrated limitation). Recent cases (Affinity Labs) show that merely confining an abstract idea to a device class (e.g., cellular telephones) is insufficient. Examiners should look for absence/presence of integration and consult examples (Diehr integrated steps vs Flook token field-of-use) to determine whether the limitation adds significantly more.

name: Assignment of 'all my rights' implies no warranty of title
description: An assignment of 'all the rights of the assignor' in the patented invention contains no implied averment as to the nature or scope of the interest conveyed and therefore implies no warranty that the assignor owned the entire right.
guidance: Such conveyance transfers whatever interest the assignor then had, subject to prior conveyances; assignee cannot claim implied perfect title where instrument limited to assignor's existing rights (see Tumbull v. Weir Plow Co.).

name: Assignments of part rights and of improvements: scope and acceptance rules
description: An assignment of part (e.g., 'one third of the full and exclusive right') in a specification about to be filed carries the stated fractional interest in all patentable devices described and claimed; an assignee may accept a different patent in lieu of the one agreed to if he acts on such acceptance and is estopped from claiming the other.
guidance: Assignments purporting to cover future improvements/devices included in a specification can vest proportional interest; courts have enforced acceptance and estoppel doctrines (see Puetz v. Bransford; Topliff v. Topliff).

name: Presumption that 'means' or generic placeholders invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f)
description: Examiners will apply 35 U.S.C. 112(f) to a claim limitation that uses the term 'means' or generic placeholder associated with functional language, unless that term is (1) preceded by a structural modifier, defined in the specification as a particular structure or known by one skilled in the art, that denotes the type of structural device (e.g., 'filters'), or (2) otherwise modified by sufficient structure or the claimed function.
guidance: Also applies analogously to 'step for' unless modified by sufficient acts. Applicant may rebut this presumption by adding sufficient structure/material/acts in the claim; the USPTO will consider the presumption rebutted until such modifying language is deleted.

name: Three-prong check for whether coupled term denotes structure
description: To determine whether a word, term, or phrase coupled with a function denotes structure, examiners may check whether: (1) the specification provides a description sufficient to inform one of ordinary skill in the art that the term denotes structure; (2) general and subject matter specific dictionaries provide evidence the term is recognized as a noun denoting structure; and/or (3) the prior art provides evidence the term is an art-recognized structure to perform the claimed function.
guidance: See Ex parte Rodriguez (precedential). Use these sources to decide whether the term conveys structural meaning to a POSITA.

name: Element-by-element determination of 112(f) applicability
description: It is necessary to decide on an element by element basis whether 35 U.S.C. 112(f) applies. Each claim must be independently reviewed to determine the applicability of 35 U.S.C. 112(f) even where the application contains substantially similar process and apparatus claims.
guidance: Claims should not be interpreted as means- or step-plus-function solely because other claims use that form; interpret each limitation in context of the claim language and specification.

name: Corresponding structure must be disclosed in the specification
description: The corresponding structure (or material or acts) of a means- (or step-) plus-function limitation must be disclosed in the specification itself in a way that one skilled in the art will understand what structure (or material or acts) will perform the recited function.
guidance: If no disclosure of structure/material/acts exists, the claim fails 35 U.S.C. 112(b). The disclosure may be implicit or inherent if clear to those skilled in the art; however, a bare statement that known techniques can be used does not disclose structure (Biomedino).

name: Written description/enablement requirements still apply
description: Invocation of 35 U.S.C. 112(f) does not exempt an applicant from compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (written description/enablement) and 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (definiteness) (or pre-AIA corresponding paragraphs).
guidance: Means-plus-function language can be used but claims must still accurately define the invention and the specification must adequately disclose sufficient structure. Use In re Donaldson, In re Knowlton, Atmel, and related cases as guidance.

name: Ambiguous or inconclusive 3-prong analysis leads to examiner determination and applicant opportunity
description: A claim may be indefinite when the 3-prong analysis for determining whether the limitation should be interpreted under 112(f) is inconclusive because of ambiguous words in the claim. Examiner should determine whether the words recite sufficiently definite structure; applicant can present arguments or amend claims to clarify whether 112(f) applies.
guidance: Examiner must consider claim language, specification, and how a POSITA would understand the language in light of disclosure.

name: Computer-implemented 112(f) limitations require disclosure of an algorithm
description: For a computer-implemented 35 U.S.C. 112(f) claim limitation, the specification must disclose an algorithm for performing the claimed specific computer function, or else the claim is indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b).
guidance: The disclosed structure is the special purpose computer programmed to perform the disclosed algorithm (not merely a general purpose computer). See NetMoneyIN, Aoyama, WMS, Aristocrat, Noah Systems and related cases.

name: General purpose computer alone is usually insufficient
description: A general purpose computer or microprocessor can serve as structure only where the claimed function is 'coextensive' with a microprocessor itself (rare circumstances such as 'receiving', 'storing', 'processing'). All other computer-implemented functions require disclosure of an algorithm.
guidance: EON Corp., Katz, Ergo Licensing. If only a general purpose computer is disclosed without special programming/algorithm, treat as pure functional claiming and likely indefinite.

name: Algorithm sufficiency judged by POSITA skill level; acceptable forms of algorithm disclosure
description: An algorithm is a finite sequence of steps for solving a logical or mathematical problem or performing a task. Applicant may express the algorithm in any understandable terms including as a mathematical formula, in prose, in a flow chart, or 'in any other manner that provides sufficient structure.'
guidance: Adequacy is determined in view of what one of ordinary skill in the art would understand as sufficient to define the structure and make claim boundaries understandable. See Finisar, Intel, In re Dossel, Typhoon Touch.

name: When multiple functions are recited, specification must disclose structure/algorithm for all functions
description: Where a means-plus-function limitation performs multiple identifiable functions, the specification must disclose adequate corresponding structure (algorithm) to perform all of the claimed functions; disclosure that covers only some functions is treated as if no algorithm was disclosed.
guidance: Williamson, Noah, Media Rights and related cases: failure to disclose an algorithm for one of multiple functions renders the limitation indefinite.

name: Mere references to 'software', 'logic', or black-box components are insufficient
description: Mere reference to a general purpose computer with appropriate programming, or simply reciting 'software' without providing detail about how to accomplish a specific software function, or referencing an undefined component (e.g., 'access control manager'), 'logic', or 'code' (black box), is not an adequate disclosure of corresponding structure.
guidance: There must be some explanation of how the computer or computer component performs the claimed function; see Blackboard, NetMoneyIN, Finisar.

name: Means-plus-function limitation limits claim to disclosed implementation mode (hardware/software) and equivalents
description: By choosing to use a means-plus-function limitation and invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f), applicant limits that claim limitation to the disclosed structure, i.e., implementation by hardware or the combination of hardware and software, and equivalents thereof.
guidance: Examiner should not construe the limitation as covering pure software implementation if the disclosure points to hardware or hardware/software combination. If only software is disclosed without algorithm, the limitation is indefinite.

name: If unclear whether supporting structure or algorithm is adequate, appropriate rejection is under 112(b)
description: If it is unclear whether there is sufficient supporting structure or whether the algorithm is adequate to perform the entire claimed function, it is appropriate to reject the claim under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (or pre-AIA 112 second paragraph).
guidance: When rejected as indefinite for lacking corresponding structure/algorithm, the claim will also likely lack written description under 112(a); examiner should consider enablement and written description MPEP sections.

name: Insufficiency of specification disclosure results in failure of 112(b) and written description
description: If there is no disclosure of structure, material or acts for performing the recited function, the claim fails to satisfy the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(b). Such insufficiency is closely related to failure to satisfy the written description (35 U.S.C. 112(a)).
guidance: Cited cases: Atmel, Biomedino, Budde, Cardiac Pacemakers, Aristocrat, In re Noll. Examiner should assess whether specification demonstrates possession and enables the full scope of claimed invention (see MPEP §§2161.01, 2163.03, 2164.08).

name: Not all claim amendments are 'narrowing' — estoppel depends on narrowing nature
description: The real issue is whether an amendment was 'narrowing,' and not all amendments are narrowing amendments; estoppel arises from narrowing amendments.
guidance: Deputy Solicitor Wallace and others noted some Federal Circuit decisions find amendments not narrowing; section 112 (second paragraph) amendments can still be narrowing. Parties disputed how to define 'narrowing' and whether that term is workable.

name: Exhibit Supply implied-disclaimer principle
description: When an applicant narrows a claim, he gives up everything in between what was claimed and the prior art, and that this acts as an implied disclaimer.
guidance: Wallace repeatedly cited the 1942 Exhibit Supply case to support the proposition that narrowing amendments create an implied disclaimer and put the public on notice; this was used to justify estoppel against equivalents for narrowed subject matter.

name: Estoppel from §112 second paragraph and enablement-related amendments
description: Estoppel could arise even where a claim was not amended to avoid the prior art (e.g., some §112, second paragraph amendments could be 'narrowing'); amendments made in response to enablement rejections should properly invoke estoppel.
guidance: Parties argued that amendments for reasons other than patentability (e.g., to address written-description/enablement problems) may nevertheless narrow the claim scope and produce estoppel implications.

name: Distinction between literal infringement and equivalents in practice
description: Many patent cases are decided on literal infringement, and courts must consider when doctrine of equivalents is needed as opposed to literal claim scope.
guidance: Neustadt pointed to statistics (31 Federal Circuit cases favoring patent holder; most on literal infringement) to suggest doctrine of equivalents is not the predominant route; Justices asked how often equivalents are decisive.

name: Means-plus-function claiming as a strategic patent-drafting choice to preserve equivalents
description: Applicants may attempt to rely on means-plus-function claiming to achieve equivalents where the doctrine of equivalents might otherwise be limited by estoppel.
guidance: Justice Breyer asked whether applicants could use §112 sixth paragraph claiming to preserve equivalents, indicating the interplay between claim-drafting technique and later infringement doctrines is a factor in evaluating patent scope.

name: ¶ 7.14.aia Pre-AIA 102(g), Priority of Invention
description: (g)(1) during the course of an interference conducted under section 135 or section 291, another inventor involved therein establishes ... that before such person’s invention thereof the invention was made by such other inventor and not abandoned, suppressed, or concealed; or (2) before such person’s invention thereof, the invention was made in this country by another inventor who had not abandoned, suppressed, or concealed it. In determining priority consider dates of conception, reduction to practice, and reasonable diligence.
guidance: A rejection on pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) is appropriate in an application examined under the AIA first-to-file provisions only if the application also contains or contained at any time (1) a claim having an effective filing date before March 16, 2013, or (2) a specific reference under 120, 121, or 365(c) to any patent or application that contains such a claim. Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.07.aia.

name: ¶ 7.15.aia Rejection, 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1)/102(a)(2)
description: Claim(s) [1] is/are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102 [2] as being [3] by [4].
guidance: Examiner Note: Use only in AIA applications filed on or after March 16, 2013 and examined under amended 35 U.S.C. 102/103; must be preceded by form paragraph 7.03.aia. Fill brackets with claim numbers, whether (a)(1) or (a)(2), whether '--clearly anticipated--' or '--anticipated--' with explanation, and the prior art relied upon. Preceding paragraphs required: either 7.07.aia and 7.08.aia and 7.12.aia as appropriate, or 7.103. For claims claiming priority to pre-March 16, 2013 applications include form paragraph 7.06.

name: ¶ 7.15.01.aia Provisional Rejection, 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) - Common Assignee/Common Applicant/Joint Inventor
description: Claim(s) [1] is/are provisionally rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) as being anticipated by copending Application No. [2] which has a common [3] with the instant application. The copending application would constitute prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) if published under 35 U.S.C. 122(b) or patented under 35 U.S.C. 151. This provisional rejection is based upon a presumption of future publication or patenting of the copending application. [4].
guidance: May be overcome by: (1) showing under 37 CFR 1.130(a) that subject matter was obtained from the inventor/joint inventor (102(b)(2)(A)); (2) showing under 37 CFR 1.130(b) of a prior public disclosure (102(b)(2)(B)); or (3) statement under 102(b)(2)(C) re common ownership/assignment or joint research agreement. Terminal disclaimer cannot overcome this rejection (In re Bartfeld). Examiner Notes: Use only for AIA-filed applications; must be preceded by 7.03.aia. Copending application must have a common assignee, common applicant (35 U.S.C. 118) or at least one common inventor. If claims would be obvious over the other copending application use 7.21.01.aia. Insert appropriate bracket contents (claim numbers, application number, assignee/applicant/joint inventor, explanation). Under 35 U.S.C. 101 two patents cannot issue on identical subject matter; related form paragraphs (8.30, 8.32, 8.27.aia, 8.33, 8.34-8.39) may be used. For priority to pre-March 16, 2013 applications precede with 7.06.

name: ¶ 7.15.02.aia Rejection, 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2), Common Assignee/Applicant/Joint Inventor(s)
description: Claim(s) [1] is/are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) as being [2] by [3]. The applied reference has a common [4] with the instant application. Based upon the earlier effectively filed date of the reference, it constitutes prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2).
guidance: Might be overcome by (1) showing under 37 CFR 1.130(a) that subject matter was obtained from the inventor/joint inventor (102(b)(2)(A)); (2) showing under 37 CFR 1.130(b) of a prior public disclosure (if same invention not being claimed) (102(b)(2)(B)); or (3) statement under 102(b)(2)(C) (common ownership/assignment or joint research agreement). Examiner Notes: Use only in AIA applications (post-Mar 16, 2013) and must be preceded by 7.03.aia. Reference must be U.S. patent under 151, U.S. patent application publication under 122(b), or WIPO publication with earlier effective filing date. If published before effective filing date, also applies under 102(a)(1). Fill bracket instructions: claim numbers, whether '--clearly anticipated--' or '--anticipated--', prior art, and indicate --assignee--/--applicant--/--joint inventor-- in bracket 4. Must be preceded by 7.12.aia. Related double patenting and claim-distinctness considerations (form paragraphs 8.30-8.39) apply. For priority to pre-Mar 16, 2013 include 7.06.

name: ¶ 7.15.03.aia Rejection, 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2), No Common Assignee or Inventor(s)
description: Claim(s) [1] is/are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) as being [2] by [3].
guidance: Examiner Note: Use only in AIA applications filed on/after March 16, 2013 examined under amended 35 U.S.C. 102/103; must be preceded by 7.03.aia. This is used to reject over a U.S. patent, U.S. patent application publication or WIPO publication with an earlier prior art date under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) where the reference is not required to have a common assignee/inventor. If any of these was published before effective filing date, also applicable under 102(a)(1). Fill bracket contents per instructions (claim numbers, anticipated/clearly anticipated, prior art). Must be preceded by 7.12.aia.

name: ¶ 7.18.aia Rejection, Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g)
description: Claim [1] rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) as being [2] by [3].
guidance: Examiner Note: Use only for applications/patents being examined under amended 35 U.S.C. 102/103 (preceded by 7.03.aia) and MUST contain or have contained a claim having an effective filing date before March 16, 2013 or a specific reference under 120, 121, or 365(c) containing such a claim. Fill bracket contents: claim numbers, whether '--clearly anticipated--' or '--anticipated--' with explanation, and prior art relied upon. This rejection must be preceded either by 7.14.aia or by 7.103.

name: 2106-Patent Subject Matter Eligibility (Step 1 and Step 2 Analyses)
description: Includes Eligibility Step 1: The Four Categories of Statutory Subject Matter; Eligibility Step 2A: Whether a Claim is Directed to a Judicial Exception; Eligibility Step 2B: Whether a Claim Amounts to Significantly More.
guidance: Subsections list analysis for abstract ideas, laws of nature/natural phenomena, markedly different characteristics, integration into a practical application, and Step 2B considerations such as improvements to computer/technology, particular machine, transformation, well-understood routine activity, mere instructions to apply an exception, insignificant extra-solution activity, field of use and technological environment, and streamlined analyses where eligibility is self-evident or shows clear improvement to technology.

name: 2106.04(a) Abstract Ideas and related groupings/examples
description: Subsection addresses abstract ideas: examples of claims that do not recite abstract ideas, abstract idea groupings, and tentative abstract ideas.
guidance: Provides examiner guidance and examples to identify abstract ideas vs. non-abstract claims; helps determine whether claim is directed to an abstract idea in Step 2A.

name: 2106.05-Eligibility Step 2B: Whether a Claim Amounts to Significantly More
description: Step 2B considers whether claim limitations provide 'significantly more' than the judicial exception itself.
guidance: Subparts specify meaningful limitations including improvements to computer/technology (2106.05(a)), particular machine (2106.05(b)), particular transformation (2106.05(c)), well-understood routine conventional activity (2106.05(d)), other meaningful limitations (2106.05(e)), mere instructions to apply an exception (2106.05(f)), insignificant extra-solution activity (2106.05(g)), and field of use/technological environment (2106.05(h)).

name: 2111-Claim Interpretation; Broadest Reasonable Interpretation
description: Guidance on claim interpretation using the broadest reasonable interpretation standard.
guidance: Subsections cover plain meaning (2111.01), effect of preamble (2111.02), transitional phrases (2111.03), 'Adapted to/for/Wherein/Whereby' and contingent clauses (2111.04), and functional vs nonfunctional descriptive material (2111.05).

name: 2141-Examination Guidelines for Determining Obviousness Under 35 U.S.C. 103
description: Guidance on obviousness analysis including scope and content of prior art, differences between prior art and claimed invention, level of ordinary skill in the art, and the legal concept of prima facie obviousness.
guidance: Includes examples of basic requirements of a prima facie case (2143), suggestion/motivation to modify (2143.01), reasonable expectation of success (2143.02), consideration that all claim limitations must be considered (2143.03), supporting a rejection under 103 (2144) including reliance on implicit disclosure, scientific theory, common knowledge, precedent, overlapping ranges, equivalence, suitability, and close structural similarity for chemical compounds.

name: 2154-Provisions Pertaining to Subject Matter in a U.S. Patent or Application Effectively Filed Before the Effective Filing Date of the Claimed Invention
description: Guidance on prior art under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) 'U.S. Patent Documents' and related issues such as WIPO published applications, determining effective filing dates, and requirement that reference 'names another inventor'.
guidance: Subsections: 2154.01 Prior Art Under AIA 102(a)(2) 'U.S. Patent Documents' (including 2154.01(a)-(d)), and 2154.02 Prior Art Exceptions under 102(b)(2) to AIA 102(a)(2) (sections (a)-(c) covering inventor-originated disclosure, inventor-originated prior public disclosure, and common ownership/obligation of assignment).

name: Patent application formal/essential elements
description: Requirements for a valid patent application including inventor identification, successor in title, protection of legitimate holder, and references required in filings.
guidance: Specifies documentary requirements and evidentiary proof for inventor and ownership claims.

name: Claims: recognition and support by description
description: Claims must be supported by the description; claims should be drafted so that the invention is recognized and supported by the specification.
guidance: Includes sections 'Recognition of Invention', 'Claims supported by Description of Invention' and examples of unacceptable claim-scope not supported by disclosure.

name: Claims must be clear and concise
description: Claims should provide a clear and concise statement of the invention.
guidance: Includes guidance on clarity, definiteness, avoiding ambiguous terms, and meeting statutory claim form requirements.

name: Matters necessary for specification of invention (claim content requirements)
description: Identify matters deemed necessary for the specification of the invention that must be included in claims or described sufficiently in the specification.
guidance: Addresses essential technical features that must be claimed or disclosed to properly define the invention.

name: Claim drafting requirements and deferral of submission of claims
description: Rules and best practices for drafting claims and the system allowing deferral of submission of claims in certain circumstances.
guidance: Contains concrete drafting rules and the special procedure for deferring claims under specified conditions.

name: Novelty (Article 29 etc.)
description: Novelty requirement and methods for determining whether the claimed invention is new in light of prior art and disclosure exceptions.
guidance: Includes understanding of provisions, determination methods, disclosure exceptions and how to treat data-only differences and inherent disclosures.

name: Inventive step (non-obviousness) — general principles
description: Principles and methods for determining inventive step: define closest prior art, person having ordinary skill in the art, problems solved by the invention, and how to reason to assess obviousness.
guidance: Explains general principles and concrete methods of determining inventive step (see Chapter 3, Part III); examiners should evaluate whether reasoning from prior art and common general knowledge would lead to the claimed invention.

name: Treatment when difference is only in data contents
description: If the only difference between the claimed invention and the closest prior art is data contents, novelty or inventive step cannot be affirmatively inferred.
guidance: Examples show that merely changing the subject-matter of the data (e.g., student vs racehorse records) does not create novelty when structure/processing is the same.

name: Special application types: divisional, converted, and priority-claim applications
description: Requirements, procedures, effects and examination considerations for divisional applications, converted applications, and applications claiming priority under treaty or domestically.
guidance: Covers requirements for filing, effects on priority and scope, and related examination instructions.

name: Examination criteria by technology (tech-specific requirements)
description: Technology-specific examination criteria and disclosure requirements for fields such as biotechnology, pharmaceuticals and cosmetics, food, functional drinking water, chemical compounds, alloys, polymers, textiles, architectural design, and computer-related inventions.
guidance: Each technology chapter provides requirements for the description/claims and for patentability specific to the technology; e.g., nucleic acid/amino acid sequences, deposit requirements for biological material, and special considerations for computer-related inventions.

name: Prohibition on new matter for amendments filed with 37 CFR 1.17(r) / 37 CFR 1.114
description: In view of 35 U.S.C. 132, no amendment considered as a result of payment of the fee set forth in 37 CFR 1.17(r) (or entered pursuant to 37 CFR 1.114) may introduce new matter into the disclosure of the application.
guidance: The submission may comprise an IDS, an amendment to the written description, claims or drawings, new substantive argument and/or new evidence, but any amendment determined to contain new matter should be treated as a reply under 37 CFR 1.111 that contains new matter (see MPEP § 706.03(o)). If applicant seeks to add new matter, the procedure in 37 CFR 1.114 is not available and the applicant must file a continuation-in-part under 37 CFR 1.53(b). Also, an RCE cannot be used to obtain continued examination on the basis of claims that are independent and distinct from previously claimed and examined claims (i.e., cannot switch inventions; see 37 CFR 1.145).

name: Definition and sufficiency of 'submission' under 37 CFR 1.114/1.129
description: A 'submission' includes, but is not limited to, an information disclosure statement (IDS), an amendment to the written description, claims, or drawings, new arguments, or new evidence in support of patentability.
guidance: If a reply to an Office action under 35 U.S.C. 132 is outstanding, the submission must meet the reply requirements of 37 CFR 1.111. An appeal brief or reply brief (or related papers) is not a submission, although arguments from an appeal/reply brief may be incorporated by reference or resubmitted.
