Previously filed amendments after final (entered or not) may satisfy the submission requirement. Arguments entered after final that were not persuasive may nonetheless satisfy the submission requirement if they are responsive within the meaning of 37 CFR 1.111.

name: Entry and processing of amendments upon proper RCE
description: If conditions for filing an RCE are satisfied, previously filed unentered submissions, amendments filed with the RCE, and amendments filed prior to the mailing of the next Office action will normally be entered and the application forwarded to the examiner.
guidance: Absent specific instructions, all amendments filed as of the date the RCE is filed are entered in the order filed. Applicants are encouraged to file all amendments no later than the RCE filing to avoid disapproval of entry under 37 CFR 1.111(b). Consider filing a suspension of action under 37 CFR 1.103(c) with the RCE if additional time is needed for a supplement (e.g., affidavit/test data). RCE filers do not need to pay excess claims fees previously paid; new claims in excess of previously paid-for claims will require payment under 37 CFR 1.16.

name: Novelty (Article 54)
description: Novelty — an invention is considered new if it does not form part of the state of the art.
guidance: Determines the absolute novelty requirement against prior art; critical for assessing whether claimed subject-matter is new at filing or priority date.

name: Filing requirements of the European patent application (Articles 75–83 et seq.)
description: Filing of the European patent application and requirements of the European patent application — formal content and documents to be submitted on filing (designation, disclosure, claims, abstract, drawings where applicable).
guidance: Specifies what must be included at filing (e.g., request, description, claims, drawings), how divisional applications are treated, designation of States, and other formalities that determine filing date and admissibility.

name: Disclosure of the invention / Sufficiency (Article 83 and related)
description: Disclosure of the invention — the European patent application must disclose the invention in a manner sufficiently clear and complete for it to be carried out by a person skilled in the art.
guidance: Sufficiency of disclosure is a substantive requirement; inadequate disclosure can be a ground for refusal or revocation and limits the allowable scope of claims and amendments.

name: The claims (Article 84 and related)
description: The claims — claims must define the matter for which protection is sought and be clear and concise and supported by the description.
guidance: Claims determine the extent of protection; Article 84 and implementing rules govern clarity, conciseness and support by the description; claim drafting must satisfy these for grant and to avoid objections during examination and opposition.

name: Priority right and claiming priority (Articles 87–89)
description: Priority right — conditions and effect of claiming priority from an earlier application under the Paris Convention; how priority is claimed and effects on novelty and filing date.
guidance: Rules determine the priority date and thus what is prior art; procedural requirements for claiming priority (timing, documents) are critical to secure priority.

name: Language of filing and proceedings; translations; publication language (Article 14)
description: Languages of the European Patent Office — official languages are English, French and German; applications must be filed in one of these languages or accompanied by a translation within time limits; translations of claims into the two other languages must be included for the specification.
guidance: Specifies filing-language options and mandatory translations; if required translation is not filed in time, document may be deemed not received; grants and publications rules depend on language of proceedings.

name: Refusal or grant; publication of specification (Part IV headings)
description: Refusal or grant — after examination the Examining Division shall decide to refuse or grant the European patent; on grant the specification is published in the language of proceedings with claim translations.
guidance: Grant triggers national effects in designated States; refusal can be appealed; publication formalities (translations) determine enforceability and rights in Contracting States.

name: Effect of revocation and extent of protection (Articles 68–70 and Protocol on Article 69)
description: Effect of revocation — rules on consequences of revocation; extent of protection — Article 69 (and its Protocol) prescribes that the extent of protection is to be interpreted as a balance between literal claim wording and the description, providing fair protection and reasonable certainty.
guidance: Protocol cautions against extremes (strict literalism vs claims as mere guidelines) and mandates an intermediate interpretation combining fair protection for patentee with reasonable certainty for third parties.

name: Authentic text and translations of patent documents (Articles 68, 14, etc.)
description: Authentic text of a European patent application or European patent — rules on which language/text is authentic and requirements for translations of the specification and claims into other official languages.
guidance: Authenticity and required translations affect enforceability and interpretation; entries in Register made in three languages, but language of proceedings is authentic in case of doubt.

name: Beauregard claim
description: In United States patent law, a Beauregard claim is a claim to a computer program written in the form of a claim to an article of manufacture: a computer‑readable medium on which are encoded, typically, instructions for carrying out a process.
guidance: Explains history and uncertainty: originated in In re Beauregard (1995). Historically faced the 'printed matter' doctrine; practice evolved to recite 'non‑transitory' computer‑readable media after In re Nuijten. Supreme Court decisions (e.g., Alice) and Federal Circuit decisions (e.g., CyberSource) can make Beauregard claims unpatentable if the underlying method is not patent‑eligible. EPO and UK practice differ (EPO allows computer program claim forms; UK practice has shifted with case law). Also notes practical decline in use as distribution moved from physical media to network delivery.

name: Exhausted‑combination claim
description: An exhausted‑combination claim comprises a claim (usually a machine claim) in which a novel device is combined with conventional elements in a conventional manner (e.g., a conventional PC containing a novel microprocessor).
guidance: Discusses doctrinal status (Federal Circuit held doctrine outdated in 1984) but notes potential practical significance for royalty base and exhaustion issues (Quanta assumed older precedents). Embedding a non‑satisfying machine‑or‑transformation element in a combination may be used tactically to appear to meet that test.

name: Functional (means‑plus‑function / step‑plus‑function) claim
description: A functional claim expresses a technical feature in functional terms (e.g., 'means for converting a digital electric signal into an analog electric signal' or 'step for converting...') and is governed by statutes and case law of the filing jurisdiction.
guidance: In the U.S., governed by 35 U.S.C. §112, paragraph 6: such claim elements are construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents. Extensive analysis and complex case law exist; scope is limited to disclosed corresponding structure. Practitioners still use this style when the specification supports it, but it requires careful support in the specification and carries interpretive limits.

name: Jepson claim
description: In U.S. practice, a Jepson claim is a method or product claim where one or more limitations are specifically identified as a point of novelty, distinguishable over at least the contents of the preamble (e.g., '...wherein the improvement comprises:').
guidance: Useful to call examiner's attention to a point of novelty without argument or amendment; was used to avoid double patenting in some contexts. But Jepson claims plainly admit that the preamble subject matter is prior art, which can facilitate obviousness arguments under 35 U.S.C. §103; thus they are seldom used in modern U.S. practice.

name: Markush claim / Markush structure
description: Mainly used in chemistry: a Markush claim or structure is a claim with multiple 'functionally equivalent' chemical entities allowed in one or more parts of the compound (format often 'selected from the group consisting of A, B and C').
guidance: Used to claim alternatives/groups of chemical constituents considered equivalent for the invention. Can result in a very large number of possible compounds, creating searching/indexing challenges; specialized databases are used to search Markush structures. USPTO prescribes the proper format ('selected from the group consisting of A, B and C'). Regulatory/proposed changes to use of Markush claims have been considered historically.

name: Product‑by‑process claim
description: A product‑by‑process claim is directed to a product defined by its process of preparation (e.g., 'Product obtained by the process of claim X').
guidance: EPO practice: interpret as 'Product obtainable by the process of claim...' and permissible only if the product is patentable as such and cannot be sufficiently defined by composition/structure or other testable parameters. In the U.S., PTO practice has allowed product‑by‑process claims even for products that can be sufficiently described, but case law (e.g., Abbott Labs. v. Sandoz, 2009) makes such claims disadvantageous: to prove infringement the patentee must show both product and process elements, while invalidation may rely only on product elements in prior art. Distinguish protection conferred from pure process claims.

name: Requirement to remove "inconsistencies" after claim amendments (EPO Guidelines F-IV 4.3)
description: The 2021 revision of the EPO Guidelines F-IV 4.3 (i) - (iii) requires adapting the description after claim amendments to remove 'inconsistencies' between the description and the amended claims, based on an expanded interpretation of the support requirement of Article 84 EPC.
guidance: This is the EPO Guidelines' stated practice that has triggered controversy; the page notes it is an expanded interpretation of the support requirement and has led to conflicting Board of Appeal decisions.

name: Adaptation needed only if inconsistency makes claim language unclear (T 2194/19 approach)
description: An inconsistency or contradiction between description and claims justifies adaptation only if parts of the description make the language of the claims unclear; otherwise not justified when the language of the claims is clear in itself.
guidance: T 2194/19 equates 'inconsistency' and 'contradiction' and ties the requirement to the clarity requirement of Article 84 in combination with support. Practical implication: do not require deletion of unclaimed embodiments unless the Division shows they make the claims unclear.

name: Burden of proof on the Examining Division to show inconsistency causes doubt
description: The Examining Division must explain why the inconsistency it requires the applicant to remove would make the language of the claims unclear; mere absence of coverage of an embodiment by the claims is insufficient.
guidance: The Division must make a specific showing that the inconsistency 'causes doubt' about claim language; hypothetical or potential doubts ('could cause') are not enough.

name: EPO's interpretation invoking a 'precise determination' of scope (T 3097/19 critique)
description: T 3097/19 shifts rationale from support to an interpretation of the first sentence of Article 84 calling for a 'precise determination' of the scope of protection, which the author considers to go far beyond the clarity requirement.
guidance: This approach conflicts with settled case law that claims may be broad without violating clarity; be wary of Boards invoking an elevated 'precision' standard to justify description adaptation.

name: Claims must mention all essential features — requirement for claims, not description (GL F-IV 4.3 (ii), T 32/82)
description: It is established case law that a claim must mention all essential features. This is a requirement for the claims, not for the description.
guidance: Do not conflate claim content obligations with requirements to rewrite the description; essential-feature requirements should be addressed in claim drafting rather than by wholesale deletion from the description.

name: Deleting unclaimed embodiments creates prosecution-estoppel/disclaimer risks (national courts' consensus)
description: The EPO's objective in deleting unclaimed embodiments may be to create the equivalent of a disclaimer or prosecution estoppel preventing a patentee from recapturing ground; national courts have generally rejected such overreaching consequences (Pemetrexed and many national decisions).
guidance: Do not assume that deleting embodiments during prosecution will prevent broader claim interpretation by national courts; litigation outcomes may still allow broader constructions or equivalents.

name: Claim interpretation in examination should be broadest possible and without relying on the description (T 2502/19 principle)
description: Claims should be taken by themselves and tested against the broadest possible or objectively reasonable construction which would occur to the skilled reader; Article 84 does not require reliance on other parts of the application documents.
guidance: Because examination claim interpretation is independent of the description, adapting the description is often irrelevant to clarity under Article 84; focus on claim drafting and clarity rather than description redaction for examination purposes.

name: Prohibition of words like 'substantially'/'approximately' (GL F-IV 4.7) can cause new-matter problems
description: The ban on words such as 'substantially' and 'approximately' required by Guidelines F-IV 4.7 can create issues: if an Examining Division deletes 'substantially' but the description never discloses the strict form, this may be considered inadmissible new matter.
guidance: Be careful when responding to objections that call for removing such qualifiers; deletion may change the claimed subject-matter scope and create Article 123(2) issues.

name: Purpose of Rule 132 declarations
description: “When any claim of an application or a patent under reexamination is rejected or objected to, any evidence submitted to traverse the rejection or objection on a basis not otherwise provided for must be by way of an oath or declaration under this section.” 37 CFR 1.132
guidance: The rule gives applicants a way to provide evidence to overcome a ground of rejection or an objection. Note: affidavits are rare; the term 'declaration' used. All declarations not falling within specific rules are to be treated under this rule (MPEP 716). Office practice allows submission even where no rejection of record in some cases.

name: Examiner must acknowledge declaration in next office action
description: If the examiner determines the declaration meets formal requirements, the examiner must consider it on the merits and explain in the next office action why it is sufficient or insufficient to overcome the traversed rejection(s).
guidance: Where sufficient, comments should be consistent with guidelines for statements of reasons for allowance (MPEP 1302.14): e.g., 'The declaration is sufficient to overcome the rejection...'. Where insufficient, the examiner must specifically explain why: e.g., 'The declaration is insufficient to overcome the rejection because ...' General unsupported statements like 'lacks technical validity' or 'not commensurate with the scope of the claims' without explanation are insufficient. MPEP 716.01(A),(B); 37 CFR 1.68.

name: Weighing evidence — preponderance standard
description: The ultimate determination of patentability must be based on consideration of the entire record based on a preponderance of the evidence standard.
guidance: Examiner must make a 'fresh' consideration of the rejection when a rule 132 declaration is properly submitted. The rejection should be maintained where a preponderance of all the evidence indicates the claimed subject matter is unpatentable. 'Preponderance' means 'more likely than not.' MPEP 716.01(d).

name: Unexpected results — required showing
description: To rebut a prima facie case of obviousness, a declaration establishing unexpected results should present a comparison with the closest prior art, under substantially the same conditions except for the allegedly novel features, and show results that are actually unexpected and of statistical and practical significance.
guidance: Details the declaration should include: description of what was tested (must compare to closest prior art), description of test conditions (commensurate with claim scope), test results for both claimed invention and closest prior art, and analysis of results (MPEP 716.02(e)). Precisely what was done should be recited (steps, materials, results). Conclusory statements without showing actual test results for both the prior art and claimed invention are insufficient. The unexpected property must be due to claimed features (not unclaimed), and scope of showing must be commensurate with claim scope. Applicant is not required to compare to hypothetical combination products suggested by examiner's combination of references (MPEP 716.02).

name: Commensurate-in-scope requirement
description: Evidence (e.g., test conditions/results) must be commensurate in scope with the scope of the claimed subject matter.
guidance: Example: claims reciting broad temperature ranges only allow evidence commensurate with the particular claim scope; evidence showing unexpected results only at temperatures higher than the broad claim may be commensurate only with a narrower dependent claim. See In re Clemens; MPEP discussion.

name: Sufficiency of applicant's disclosure under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (enablement)
description: Evidence must support that a person of skill in the art would have been able to make and use the claimed invention based on the disclosure without undue experimentation.
guidance: Evidence used to supplement a specification that appears deficient must establish that the information needed to make the specification complete would have been known to those of ordinary skill in the art (MPEP 716.09).

name: Establishing inherent disclosure in the application
description: Rule 132 declarations may be used to establish inherency where a claim is amended to recite a limitation not explicitly recited in the original application, or where a continuing application recites something not expressly mentioned in the parent case and benefit of the parent filing date is necessary.
guidance: Examiner will evaluate whether the declaration presents facts that affirmatively establish the purported inherent feature is necessarily present; mere possibility is insufficient. MPEP 2112 and discussion in slides.

name: Materiality of parts in combination claims
description: The patentee makes all the parts of a combination material, when he claims them in combination and not separately.
guidance: When a claim recites elements only as a combination, each element is material to infringement analysis. This rule is subject to exceptions where patentability depends on a particular form; e.g., a shoe last made in two sections may infringe a patent for a last of same shape made in three sections.

name: Patentee deemed to claim all forms copying the invention absent disclaimer
description: The patentee, having described his invention and shown its principles, and claimed it in that form which most perfectly embodies it, is, in contemplation of law, deemed to claim every form in which his invention may be copied, unless he manifests an intention to disclaim some of these forms.
guidance: This principle supports a broad application of equivalents, especially for combination patents; a clear disclaimer in the specification can limit coverage.

name: Interchangeability/radical unfitness test
description: Interchangeability usually requires change of form to fit the thing interchanged to its new environment; non-interchangeability involves such radical unfitness for a proposed position and function as cannot be removed by any change of form.
guidance: If a proposed substitute would require only reasonable form changes to perform the claimed function, interchangeability may support equivalence; but radical inability to function in the claimed position negates equivalence.

name: Filing Too Early
description: A provisional filed before you have actually figured out the invention buys you priority for a half-baked idea. You then spend the next year evolving the invention - and your non-provisional claims will not be supported by the provisional. Wait until you can describe the invention in detail.
guidance: Do not file a provisional until you can describe the invention in sufficient detail to support later non‑provisional claims; avoid 'half‑baked' disclosures that will not provide adequate written description/enablement for later claim scope. If you plan to rely on a provisional, ensure it discloses the embodiments and variations you may later claim.

name: Disclosing Only the Commercial Embodiment
description: If you only describe the version you sell, your competitors can design around with minor variations. Disclose alternatives - different materials, different geometries, different orderings, different control schemes. The spec is your safety net.
guidance: Draft the specification to include multiple embodiments, variations, and alternative implementations (materials, geometries, orderings, control schemes, etc.) to broaden claim support and reduce design‑around risks. Treat the spec as a safety net for claiming variations beyond the commercialized product.

name: Letting the Inventor Write the Claims
description: Even technical inventors who can write a perfectly clear textbook chapter typically cannot write good claims. Claims have arcane drafting conventions (single‑sentence, antecedent basis, specific transitional phrases) and strategic considerations (claim differentiation, claim hierarchy, infringement‑detectability). Hire a patent attorney or registered agent.
guidance: Have claims drafted or reviewed by an experienced patent attorney or registered agent who understands claim drafting conventions and prosecution strategy. Inventors can provide technical content, but claim language and strategy are specialized and strategic.

name: Failing to Update Inventorship
description: Inventorship is who actually conceived the claimed subject matter, not who paid for the work or who manages the team. Wrongly listing inventors can invalidate the patent. Reassess inventorship after each claim amendment.
guidance: Determine inventorship based on conception of the claimed subject matter and update the inventor list whenever claims change during drafting or prosecution. Consult counsel to correct inventorship promptly when necessary to avoid invalidity risk.

name: Skipping the Search
description: Filing without a prior art search is filing blind. A $1,500 search before filing routinely surfaces references that, had they been known, would have led to a different (and stronger) claim strategy.
guidance: Conduct a prior art search (or budget for one) before filing to inform claim scope and strategy. Use search results to shape disclosures and claims, reducing the risk of avoidable rejections or weak claim drafting.

name: Claims breadth and scope
description: Whether the reach of the patent (technically covered in the patent 'claims') is as broad as possible, given the state of prior developments in the field.
guidance: One claim should be as broad as possible. Guidance covers drafting the main (independent) claim, drafting dependent claims, additional sets of claims, the effect of prior art on claims, technical requirements of claims, sample claims, common misconceptions regarding claims, and a checklist for drafting claims.

name: Quality of applicant's prosecution of correspondence with the PTO
description: How an applicant handles correspondence with the patent office (responses to office actions, amendments, petitions, etc.).
guidance: Includes what to do when you receive an Office Action, format for amending specification and claims, drafting the remarks, typing and filing the amendment, consequences if first amendment doesn't result in allowance, petitions (e.g., petition to make special), and Request for Continued Examination (RCE).

name: Novelty (35 U.S.C. §102)
description: Requirement #3 for a utility patent: the invention must be novel (not anticipated by prior art).
guidance: Treated together with patentability searching and analysis of prior art; influences claim breadth and drafting strategy.

name: Preliminary work before preparing patent application
description: Do preliminary work—sketches, naming parts, and flowcharts—before preparing the patent application and drafting the specification and drawings.
guidance: Includes checklists for application draft and a sample specification; emphasizes preparing sketches and naming parts first to ease drafting and claim preparation.

name: Claim drafting techniques and checklists
description: Techniques for drafting independent and dependent claims, additional sets of claims, and use of claim-drafting checklists.
guidance: Covers drafting the main independent claim, dependent claims, handling prior art, technical claim requirements, example claims, and a 'Checklist for Drafting Claims.'

name: Responding to Office Actions and amendment practice
description: What to do when you receive an Office Action, format for amending the specification and claims, drafting the remarks, typing and filing the amendment, and strategies if the first amendment doesn't result in allowance.
guidance: Includes a sample Office Action, step-by-step response guidance, and examples of drafting remarks and amendments; covers appeals and pre-appeal brief request procedures.

name: Use and limits of AI in patent drafting
description: Discussion of USPTO guidance and the use of artificial intelligence to draft the specification and claims.
guidance: The 22nd edition covers USPTO guidance on using AI in patent applications and includes specific sections 'Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) To Draft the Specification' and 'Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) To Draft Claims'—presumably discussing benefits and caveats.

name: Pre-drafting inventor analysis (questions to ask)
description: Prior to writing claim(s) answer these questions: What is the invention? What are the elements that make up the invention? How do the elements relate to one another? Do you have more than one invention? Tangible: Apparatus, machine, composition. Method: Making or Using. Are there multiple embodiments of the same invention?
guidance: Use these questions to identify separate inventions, elements, relationships, and embodiments before drafting claims. Classify whether the invention is product (apparatus/composition) or method (process).

name: Legal requirement: at least one claim that particularly points out and distinctly defines the invention
description: A nonprovisional patent application must have at least one claim particularly pointing out and distinctly defining the invention.
guidance: Ensure at least one properly drafted independent claim in the application that meets statutory requirements for definiteness and distinctness.

name: Claim form: independent vs dependent
description: A claim may be written in independent or dependent form. An independent claim is a standalone claim that contains all the limitations necessary to define an invention. A dependent claim must refer to a claim previously set forth and must further limit that claim.
guidance: Draft independent claims to stand alone and dependent claims to add further limiting features; ensure dependencies properly refer to earlier claims and actually narrow them.

name: Dependent claims incorporate limitations by reference
description: A claim in dependent form incorporates by reference all the limitations of the claim to which it refers.
guidance: When drafting dependent claims, rely on incorporated limitations from the parent claim and add only additional limitations; be careful with partial references.

name: Claims must be fully supported and enabled by the disclosure
description: Claims must be fully supported and enabled by the disclosure.
guidance: Ensure the specification supplies adequate written description and enablement for each claimed limitation and for the full scope claimed to avoid 35 U.S.C. §112 rejections.

name: Order claims by scope (broadest first)
description: Claims should be arranged in order of scope so the first claim presented is the broadest.
guidance: Place broad independent claims early in the claim set and narrower dependent claims after them to reflect logical narrowing and facilitate examination.

name: Consistent terminology between specification and claims
description: Consistent terminology should be used in both the patent disclosure and the claims.
guidance: Use the same terms (avoid synonyms) across the specification and claims to prevent ambiguity and support antecedent basis; reconcile any terminology mismatches before filing.

name: Claim must conform to the specification and provide antecedent basis
description: A claim defines the invention and what aspects are legally enforceable. Must conform to the invention as set forth in the remainder of the specification. Terms and phrases used in the claims must find clear support or antecedent basis in the description so that the meaning of the terms in the claims are clearly understood by reference to the description.
guidance: Review claims against the specification to confirm every claimed element has clear disclosure and antecedent language; add necessary specification language if a claim term lacks support.

name: Select appropriate claim category (product vs method)
description: Types of claims: Product claims are directed to elements that can be active (device/apparatus/machine) or non-active (composition of matter or article of manufacture) or a combination. Method (process) claims describe a series of acts or steps for performing a function or accomplishing a result.
guidance: Decide which statutory class best captures the invention and draft claim types accordingly; avoid mixing statutory classes improperly in one claim.

name: Claim structure: preamble, transitional phrase, claim body
description: A claim in a utility application or patent has three parts: 1) Preamble provides context and may or may not limit the claim; 2) Transitional phrase establishes whether the claim is open, closed or partially open; 3) Claim body recites the limitations (structure and/or acts) necessary to define the invention.
guidance: Ensure each claim contains and properly uses these three parts; structure the body to recite clear limitations that define the inventive contribution.

name: Preamble guidance (avoid functional limiting language)
description: Every claim needs a preamble. The general rule is that the preamble of a claim does not limit the scope of the claim, but try and stay away from functional language. Try: “A shovel…” Instead of: “A shovel for digging…”
guidance: Draft preambles as simple noun phrases when possible to avoid unintentionally limiting the claim; avoid phrasing that reads as functional when the structure is what matters.

name: Transitional phrase choice and meanings
description: Common transitions: “comprising”, “consisting essentially of”, and “consisting of.” “Comprising” means the invention includes but is not limited to the elements identified in the claim. “Consisting essentially of” limits the scope to specified materials or steps 'and those that do not materially affect the basic and novel characteristic(s)'. “Consisting of” is closed and limits the invention to the recited elements.
guidance: Choose transitions deliberately: use 'comprising' for open-ended claims (most common), 'consisting of' to close the claim, and 'consisting essentially of' for intermediate scope; avoid non-standard transitions that may invite interpretation issues.

name: Claim body clarity: recite limitations in clear, full, concise terms
description: The claim body should recite the limitations (structure and/or acts) in clear, full, concise terms necessary to define the invention.
guidance: Use precise structural terms for apparatus claims and clear step language for method claims; avoid vague or purely functional language unconnected to structure or steps that perform the function.

name: Avoid antecedent ambiguity
description: A lack of clarity could arise where a claim refers to 'said lever' or 'the lever' where the claim contains no earlier recitation or where two different levers are recited earlier and it's unclear which is intended.
guidance: Check claims for multiple similarly named elements and supply distinct identifiers or clarifying language to avoid confusion about which element is referenced.

name: Use dependent transitions correctly: 'further comprising' vs 'wherein'
description: When adding a component you use 'further comprising' and then explain how the component is connected or relates with components already introduced. When further describing something that has already been introduced you use 'wherein.'
guidance: Use 'further comprising' to add structural or step elements; use 'wherein' to specify characteristics or relationships of previously introduced elements; follow conventional transition usage for clarity and correct claim scope.

name: Focus on the inventive concept (novelty, non-obviousness, utility)
description: Focus on the inventive concept: What features set the invention apart from prior inventions? A claimed invention must be novel, non-obvious and have utility. A Patent is not a marketing brochure.
guidance: Identify the core inventive features that distinguish over prior art and center claims on those features rather than marketing descriptions; determine whether there are multiple inventive features to claim separately.

name: Consider claim drafting costs versus desired coverage
description: Consider how much you can afford to spend on claims. Independent in excess of 3 = $115 per (micro entity); Total claims in excess of 20 = $25 per (micro entity). Claim fees for small entity are double micro entity. Not just at time of filing, but during prosecution. What is your desired Patent Scope end state? Broadest possible valid claim? (longer prosecution) Claims with range of claim scopes? (high claim costs).
guidance: Balance budget constraints against desired claim breadth and number of independent claims; plan claim strategy (broad first, fallback narrower claims) mindful of filing and prosecution fees.

name: Balance specificity and generality (avoid too specific or too general claims)
description: Claims that are too specific may not be valuable; claims that are too general may not be patentable. Strive to introduce all components and characterizations necessary for the invention to work and be different from the public domain.
guidance: Draft claims that capture the inventive concept broadly enough to be valuable but with enough limiting features to distinguish over prior art; prepare fallback dependent claims to cover narrower options.

name: Claim drafting DOs (best practices)
description: Do: Consider drafting your specification first and then your claims based on terms used in the specification; think about what legal protection you want and tailor your claims accordingly; look at the claims in patents issued in your field; particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter regarded as the invention; review and reconcile both the specification and claims so claim terms find support; check for antecedent basis issues within the claims; ensure dependent claims further limit the claim from which they depend (35 U.S.C. 112(d), MPEP 608.01(n)).
guidance: Follow these best practices to reduce formal and substantive rejections: align spec and claims, use field precedent for claim drafting style, and verify dependencies and antecedent basis before filing.

name: Claim drafting Cautions (avoid these pitfalls)
description: Cautions: Do not use claims covering multiple statutory classes of invention (e.g., “A widget and method for using same…”). Do not use non-standard transitional phrases (may raise interpretation questions). Do not use terms inconsistently between claims and/or specification. Do not refer back to only a portion of another claim in a dependent claim. Do not use a dependent claim to remove/replace an element from the claim it depends on. Do not use language that merely suggests, makes optional and thus does not limit the claim. Avoid negative limitations unless clearly supported by the disclosure. Do not use functional language unconnected to structure or steps. Do not use terms in the claim that are unsupported by the specification. Do not use trademarks or tradenames in the claims; use generic terms instead.
guidance: Avoid combining statutory classes in one claim, use standard transitions and consistent terminology, ensure dependent claims properly narrow and do not contradict parent claims, support negative limitations in the spec, avoid functional-only language without structure, and replace trademarks with generic descriptors.

name: Assessment of other rejection types (§102, §103, §112)
description: Check whether the event (Alice) affected other rejection grounds (novelty §102, non-obviousness §103, and §112 clarity/enablement). The expectation is that Alice should not affect these because it clarified subject-matter eligibility, not novelty or obviousness.
guidance: Estimate analogous DID specifications for §102/§103/§112 rejection rates and their examination uncertainty. Look for discontinuous jumps or persistent changes post-event; absence of statistically significant jumps supports the claim that Alice specifically affected §101 and not other grounds. Rely on USPTO compact prosecution policy (examiners issue all grounds in first action) when interpreting substitution arguments.

name: Regression specification and controls
description: Standard regression elements recommended/used: include time fixed effects (Month x Year or Half Year), technology fixed effects (USPC), and possibly examiner fixed effects; include covariates such as avg number of independent claims, avg word count in claims, avg examiner variance, number of examiners, number of applications, avg applications per examiner, and variance in abstractness.
guidance: Report observations, R-squared, and use robust standard errors. Choose fixed effects that capture seasonality and technology heterogeneity (month-year and USPC are used here). When adding many covariates, monitor changes in magnitude and significance of main treatment terms to assess robustness and potential multicollinearity.

name: Treating the Application As a Technical Paper
description: Patent specifications are legal documents. They have specific drafting conventions (single-sentence claims, antecedent basis, particular transitional phrases) that conflict with technical writing norms.
guidance: Inventors who write the spec like a journal article create cleanup work for the attorney and often hide the inventive concept under technical detail. Follow legal drafting conventions rather than academic/technical prose.

name: Including Marketing Claims
description: "Best in class," "industry-leading," "groundbreaking," "revolutionary" - these are not patent terms.
guidance: Marketing language cannot help patentability and may hurt: an opponent can quote such language to argue issues (e.g., external motivation/long‑felt need) if obviousness is contested. Marketing language has no place in a specification.

name: Claiming Your Goal Instead of Your Mechanism
description: Claiming a goal (e.g., "a system for reducing network latency") without specifying how invites attacks under §101 (abstract idea) and §112 (enablement).
guidance: Draft claims to recite the mechanism by which the result is achieved; the mechanism is what is patentable rather than a high-level goal.

name: Failing to Disclose Alternatives
description: Over‑specification of one concrete choice in the prototype (material, geometry, ordering, parameter value) creates design-around opportunities for competitors.
guidance: Every concrete choice should be accompanied by disclosure of alternatives that would also work—this reduces design‑around risk and preserves broader claim scope.

name: Inconsistent Terminology
description: Calling the same thing different names across the specification (e.g., "the widget," "the device," "the component," "the unit") creates ambiguity.
guidance: Pick one term per concept and use it everywhere to avoid ambiguity in claim interpretation and specification clarity.

name: Antecedent Basis Errors
description: The first time a concept appears in a claim, use "a" or "an." On every subsequent reference, use "the."
guidance: Switching terms ("a widget" then "said widget" then "the widget") is fine but inconsistent; forgetting to introduce a term properly can create §112(b) rejections. Maintain correct antecedent basis throughout claims.

name: Putting Limitations in the Preamble
description: The preamble of a claim may or may not be limiting, which makes it risky to place distinguishing features there.
guidance: Put your distinguishing features in the body of the claim where they are unambiguously limitations rather than relying on the preamble.

name: Wrong Inventorship
description: Inventors are those who conceived the claimed subject matter. People who only provided guidance (CEOs, advisors, contractors without conception) are not inventors.
guidance: Incorrect inventorship can render a patent unenforceable until corrected. Determine inventorship carefully based on conception of the claimed inventions.

name: Ignoring International Strategy
description: Decisions made for the U.S. filing (claim style, embodiments disclosed, prior art admissions) affect PCT and national-phase filings.
guidance: Make U.S. filing decisions with international prosecution strategy in mind to avoid foreclosing options abroad or creating conflicts in later filings.

name: Not Filing Continuations
description: Letting the parent application issue without a pending continuation can foreclose future claim scope.
guidance: Keep at least one continuation pending while the patent family remains commercially relevant to preserve the ability to pursue additional claim scope later.

name: Disclosure requirement (sufficiency of disclosure)
description: The patent application must disclose the invention sufficiently clearly and completely that a person skilled in the art can carry out the invention.
guidance: Ensure the description supports the full scope of the claims; avoid leaving claims that cannot be practiced. Disclosure must enable reduction to practice where required by jurisdiction.

name: Typical parts of a patent application
description: A patent application typically includes a request, description, claims, drawings, abstract and must follow the applicable application format.
guidance: Follow required formalities for each jurisdiction. Order of drafting may vary but consider drafting claims early to focus the description and embodiments around the claim scope.

name: Theory of the patent claim (role and structure)
description: Claims are sets of sentences that define the invention being protected; they determine the scope of exclusive rights conferred by a patent.
guidance: Understand parts of a claim (preamble, body, characterizing portion), grammar and conventions (two-part form, transitional phrases), and how claim language maps to potential infringing acts.

name: Broad and narrow claims (claim scope layering)
description: Use a combination of broad claims to maximize coverage and narrow claims to increase allowance prospects and fallback positions.
guidance: Balance breadth with patentability. Broad claims must still be supported by disclosure and withstand prior art; include dependent and fallback claims to preserve value during prosecution.

name: Claim grammar and word choice
description: Use clear, consistent, and jurisdiction-appropriate claim wording, paying attention to transitional phrases like 'comprising' and their intended effect (open/closed).
guidance: Include description language to clarify whether terms like 'comprise' are intended to be inclusive. Avoid ambiguous or inconsistent terminology between claims and description.

name: Alternative elements, Markush and functional claims
description: Draft claims that allow alternative elements (Markush groups) and functional language where appropriate, while complying with jurisdictional rules on clarity and support.
guidance: Use Markush claims for chemical/compound alternatives; be cautious with functional/means-plus-function language because many jurisdictions construe such claims narrowly and require corresponding disclosure.

name: Independent and dependent claims; claim sets
description: Organize claim sets with independent claims defining principal scopes and dependent claims adding further limitations as fallbacks.
guidance: Consider the number and structure of independent claims permitted by the jurisdiction, use dependent claims to preserve fallback positions, and avoid unnecessary duplication. Multiple dependent claims have special rules/costs.

name: Multiple dependent claims
description: Multiple dependent claims refer to more than one previous claim and are governed by specific formal and fee rules in many jurisdictions.
guidance: Use multiple dependent claims sparingly and in compliance with local rules (fees, format). Consider drafting alternatives if jurisdiction disallows or penalizes multiple dependency.

name: Avoid unnecessary limitations
description: Do not introduce limitations into claims that are not essential to distinguish over the prior art or to practice the invention.
guidance: Unnecessary limitations narrow protection and provide easy workarounds for competitors; use careful drafting to capture the inventive concept broadly while retaining support.

name: Ensuring the description supports the claims (original disclosure/new matter)
description: The description must provide support for the claimed subject matter; amendments adding new matter not originally disclosed are not allowed.
guidance: When drafting and amending, ensure the claimed scope has basis in the original disclosure; carefully document embodiments and alternatives to preserve amendment latitude.

name: Drafting a description: title, technical field, background and summary
description: The description should include a clear title, technical field, background art describing prior problems, and a summary of the invention highlighting advantages and core inventive concept.
guidance: The background should disclose closest prior art and problems solved; the summary should make the inventive contribution clear and align with claim language so description supports claim scope.

name: Drafting embodiments and examples
description: Provide detailed embodiments and examples that illustrate how to practice the invention and variants that fall within the claimed scope.
guidance: Include sufficient detail (materials, parameters, methods) for enablement and consider covering alternatives and fallback variants to preserve claim breadth.

name: Drafting drawings
description: Prepare drawings of appropriate types with reference indicators and a suitable level of detail to illustrate embodiments and aid claim interpretation.
guidance: Coordinate reference numerals between drawings and description; decide whether inventor-provided drawings are sufficient and supplement where necessary to show inventive features.

name: Use of multiple claim types for the same invention
description: Include different claim types (product, process/method, use, apparatus) for the same inventive concept to maximize protection and enforcement options.
guidance: Draft parallel claim sets (device+method) when appropriate, and ensure the description supports each claim type with enabling disclosure.

name: Amendments and prosecution practice
description: Respond to office actions, draft responses, perform interviews, and manage amendments, paying attention to deadlines, appeals, divisional/continuation/CIP filings and opposition proceedings.
guidance: Prepare principled amendment strategies that preserve value, justify claim changes with support in the original disclosure, and use interviews to resolve examiner objections when possible.

name: Sufficient specificity for range anticipation
description: When a prior-art reference discloses a range that touches or overlaps the claimed range, anticipation requires that the reference disclose the claimed subject matter with 'sufficient specificity' to constitute anticipation under the statute; this is a case-by-case determination.
guidance: Consider whether the reference teaches the narrow claimed range with sufficient specificity (e.g., lack of evidence of criticality across the range supports anticipation — ClearValue) or whether the claimed range is shown to be critical and the reference's broader range does not clearly disclose the species (Atofina). If insufficient specificity exists, the reference might not anticipate but could be relevant to obviousness. If unclear, a combined 35 U.S.C. 102/103 rejection is permitted and the examiner must provide reasons for anticipation and a reasoned statement regarding obviousness. See MPEP § 2144.05 for obviousness of ranges.

name: Nonanalogous art or teaching away not relevant to anticipation
description: Arguments that a reference is nonanalogous art, teaches away, or addresses a different problem are not germane to a § 102 anticipation analysis; a reference may anticipate even if it disparages or teaches away from the invention.
guidance: Anticipation focuses on whether the reference explicitly or inherently discloses every claim limitation. Teaching away or different field/context does not prevent anticipation (see Twin Disc, Celeritas, Atlas Powder, Upsher-Smith).

name: Sale of product made by secret process
description: Another’s sale of a product produced by a secret process can be a § 102(a) public use only if the process can be determined by examining the product.
guidance: If inspection of the sold product would not reveal the process, secret use coupled with sale does not create a public-use bar for the process claim.

name: Pre-AIA § 102(b) one-year grace period rule
description: Under pre-AIA § 102(b), an invention is barred if patented, described in a printed publication, in public use, or on sale more than one year prior to the U.S. application date; the one-year grace period is extended to the next working day if it would otherwise end on a holiday or weekend.
guidance: The time bar is measured from the U.S. filing date. Continuation-in-part filings get the child filing date for claims not supported by the parent. See In re Katz, Paperless Accounting v. BART, and MPEP § 706.02 for effective filing date issues.

name: Caveat emptor: licensee's duty to investigate licensor's title
description: The doctrine of caveat emptor is rigidly applied: it is the licensee's duty to ascertain before purchase whether the licensor has a good title to convey.
guidance: Licensees who fail to investigate cannot later claim broader rights than licensor had; courts will enforce that the licensee takes the interest subject to existing limitations.

name: License coverage of patent extensions — presumption and burden of proof
description: A license is presumed to cover only the original term of the patent; one who claims that it covers an extended term must prove it.
guidance: Courts construe license language against coverage of extensions unless language is clear (cases cited: Hodge v. Hudson River, Pitts v. Hall, Clum v. Brewer indicating explicit language is required to include extensions).

name: Repudiation: licensee may repudiate and then challenge validity for future use but not avoid past royalties on completed sales
description: If the licensee repudiates the license (ceases to claim its protection), as to his future exercise of privileges he may defend on the ground the patent is invalid; after such repudiation he may also dispute validity in actions against him for license fees for the past making or use of the invention, but not for royalties on completed sales.
guidance: When a license expressly admits patent validity and precludes impairment of that admission, the licensee cannot attack validity during the term. Repudiation changes estoppel posture — careful transactional drafting advised.

name: Two-step subject matter eligibility test
description: There are two criteria for determining subject matter eligibility and both must be satisfied: (1) the claimed invention must be directed to one of the four statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter), and (2) the claimed invention must not be wholly directed to subject matter encompassing a judicially recognized exception (laws of nature, physical phenomena, abstract ideas).
guidance: Use the two-step analysis to evaluate claims. Both steps must be considered; if Step 1 is not met the claim is ineligible, but Step 2 should still be conducted if an amendment might cure the defect.

name: Claims that cover both statutory and non-statutory embodiments
description: A claim that covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments (under the broadest reasonable interpretation in view of the specification and a person of ordinary skill) embraces non-statutory subject matter and fails Step 1.
guidance: Example: machine readable media that could encompass a compact disc (statutory) or a carrier wave (transitory signal, non-statutory) should be rejected under §101. If claim could be amended to remove the non-statutory embodiment, still perform Step 2.

name: Practical application principle
description: A claim that is limited to a particular practical application of a judicial exception (i.e., how the exception is applied in a real world product or process) may be patent-eligible; a practical application is not merely the result achieved but concrete application showing integration into real-world use.
guidance: Evaluate the claim as a whole. Evidence of practical application (tangible structure, integration of law-of-nature into steps) indicates the subject matter is not abstract. See Ultramercial v. Hulu example.

name: Product claims — tangible embodiment requirement
description: If a claimed product (machine, manufacture, composition) does not recite tangible limitations under the broadest reasonable interpretation, it may wholly embrace a judicial exception; tangible structural limitations are evidence of a particular practical application.
guidance: Examples: A machine 'comprising a plurality of structural elements' that work together shows tangible embodiment and likely eligibility; a machine claiming only the operating principle (e.g., 'operates in accordance with F=ma') without structural elements would be ineligible. Non-transitory tangible computer-readable media with structural limitations can be eligible.

name: Preemption evaluation for product claims
description: After identifying a practical application, evaluate whether the claim impermissibly covers substantially all practical applications of the judicial exception; if so, it is not patent-eligible.
guidance: If claim covers only one limited application, it is more likely eligible. Consider scope and whether others could make use of the underlying concept in other practical applications.

name: Process (method) claims must be limited to a particular practical application
description: A process claim to be statutory must be limited to a particular practical application so that it does not simply claim an abstract idea or preempt all uses of a law of nature or physical phenomenon.
guidance: The machine-or-transformation test remains a useful investigative tool but is not the sole test (Bilski). Recitation of structure or transformative steps often supports eligibility; however, mere field-of-use or token post-solution components do not save a claim (Flook).

name: Factor: involvement of a particular machine or apparatus
description: Whether the method involves or is executed by a particular machine or apparatus is a key factor: claims tied to a particular machine are less likely to be abstract.
guidance: Assess particularity (specific identifiable machine vs 'any machine'), whether the machine is programmed to perform the claimed steps (programming can create a special purpose machine), and whether the machine's role imposes meaningful limits. Citations: Bilski, In re Alappat, Ultramercial, DealerTrack v. Huber.

name: Evaluating applicant's response to a §101 rejection
description: A proper response may amend or add claim limitations that integrate the natural principle into the process/product (practical application) and limit the claim beyond the principle plus routine steps; persuasive arguments may show the additional steps add 'significantly more' or are not routine/conventional.
guidance: Examples: constructing a sanitizing device using UV light with integrated steps (not simply 'expose to sunlight'); adding novel testing or treatment steps beyond routine blood testing. Demonstrating steps are not conventional can be persuasive. Refer to 2012 Interim Procedure for further examples.

name: Computer-implemented claims — significance of programming and specificity
description: Merely adding a 'computer-aided' limitation or reciting a general purpose computer is insufficient to render an abstract idea patent-eligible unless the claim clearly conveys that the computer is programmed to perform the claimed steps (creating a special purpose computer) or otherwise shows meaningful technical implementation.
guidance: Claims must indicate how a computer aids the method, the extent of the computer's role, or the significance of the computer to performance; silent or generic recitation of a computer will weigh against eligibility (DealerTrack v. Huber).

name: Field-of-use and 'insignificant extra-solution activity' guidance
description: Field-of-use limitations (e.g., 'for use with a machine' or 'for transforming an article') and insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., generic data-gathering) do not impose meaningful limits on the claim and do not make an abstract idea patent-eligible.
guidance: Distinguish meaningful structural/operational limitations from mere environment or conventional pre/post-solution activity. Such insignificant elements should not be treated as conferring patent eligibility (citing Bilski, Parker v. Flook, Cybersource).

name: Statement content for JRA disqualification (37 CFR 1.104(c)(5)(ii)(A)-(B))
description: To invoke JRA‑based disqualification under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c)(2), the applicant/patent owner must provide: (A) a statement that the subject matter and the claimed invention were made by or on behalf of the parties to a JRA (within 35 U.S.C. 100(h) and § 1.9(e)) that was in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made and that the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the JRA; and (B) the application for the claimed invention discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the JRA.
guidance: Both content elements are required: the factual statement about who made the inventions and that the invention resulted from activities within the JRA, plus disclosure (or timely amendment) of the JRA party names in the application.

name: Options to overcome provisional 103(a) rejection (copending applications)
description: A provisional 103(a) rejection based on provisional prior art under pre‑AIA 102(e) can be overcome by: (A) arguing patentability over the earlier filed application; (B) combining subject matter into a single application claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 and abandoning copending applications (subject to 112/enablement concerns); (C) filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 showing derivation; (D) filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(a) showing date of invention prior to the provisional 102(e) date; or (E) for applications pending on or after Dec. 10, 2004, showing common ownership at time invention was made or that subject matter is disqualified under pre‑AIA 103(c).
guidance: Each option has legal/formal prerequisites (e.g., 1.132 derivation evidence, 1.131 date of invention proof, 35 U.S.C. 120 benefit requirements and 35 U.S.C. 112 compliance). Combining applications may affect entitlement to earlier filing dates (Studiengesellschaft Kohle v. Shell Oil).

name: Use of terminal disclaimer and affidavits for interfering subject matter
description: Where applications claim interfering subject matter (37 CFR 41.203(a)), a terminal disclaimer and an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(c) may be used to overcome a 103(a) rejection in a common ownership situation if the earlier application has been published or matured into a patent.
guidance: See MPEP § 718 for guidance on interfering subject matter and proper use of terminal disclaimers/affidavits.

name: Definition of 'biotechnological process' for 103(b)
description: For purposes of 103(b), a 'biotechnological process' means: (A) a process of genetically altering or otherwise inducing a single‑ or multi‑celled organism to (i) express an exogenous nucleotide sequence, (ii) inhibit, eliminate, augment, or alter expression of an endogenous nucleotide sequence, or (iii) express a specific physiological characteristic not naturally associated with the organism; (B) cell fusion procedures yielding a cell line that expresses a specific protein (e.g., monoclonal antibody); and other enumerated biotech process types.
guidance: Process claims must fall within the statutory definition to qualify for 103(b) treatment.

name: Inventive step for dosage regimen/dose
description: Inventive step may be acknowledged only for a specific dosage regimen and dose which are deemed to be worthwhile to be protected as a patent due to prominent or heterogeneous effect for which a person skilled in the art cannot expect.
guidance: Evaluate claimed dosage/regimen in light of closest prior art; inventive step requires an unexpected/prominent or qualitatively heterogeneous effect not predictable from prior art. Examples: (Ex1) small once-daily 1 mg dose refused where prior art taught 0.5–2.5 mg and predicted valid effect; (Ex2) monthly high-dose (150 mg) could be inventive if it shows unexpectedly striking differences (e.g., bone density improvement) that are not predictable merely because higher dose often increases bioavailability.

name: Inventive step for polymorphic/crystalline forms
description: Invention of crystal with claims stating compounds of specific crystal having different form of crystal from the compound in cited document is deemed to have the inventive step if it has different effect qualitatively or quantitatively with the compound in cited document.
guidance: Recognize that different polymorphs can affect solubility, safety, stability, etc.; inventive step is present if the new crystal form exhibits qualitatively different effects or substantially different quantitative effects. The effect should be stated in the specification; if doubtful, prove by submitting trusted documents (e.g., comparative studies) after filing date.

name: Requirement to state effect of polymorph in description
description: The effect of a claimed polymorphic crystal form should be stated in the description of the crystal form invention, not merely reported by comparison with cited documents.
guidance: If effect is doubtful, applicants should provide proof (comparative studies, trusted documents). Lack of clear statement/proof can lead to refusal on inventive-step grounds.

name: Requirement to evaluate food inventions for public safety
description: In examining an invention directed to food, it is necessary to determine whether the food is harmful to the health of the public, and unique matters including how to describe sensory effects and functional effects of a healthy food should be considered.
guidance: Food is readily accessible and ingested repeatedly; examiners must scrutinize safety and whether description/claims appropriately limit intended use. Food taken as medicine is excluded.

name: Physiochemical/mechanical analysis requirements for sensory features
description: Methods, devices, requirements, etc. for physiochemical or mechanical analysis should be stated specifically in the description to support the sensory feature according to analysis results.
guidance: Examples of analysis devices: colorimeter/spectrophotometer (color), GC/electronic nose (scent), electronic tongue/refractometer/pH meter (flavor), viscometer/texture analyzer/rheometer/amylograph (viscosity/texture). Include sufficient detail so results support claimed sensory features (example: Brix change measured by refractometer to support increased sweetness).

name: Treatment of publicly known functional raw material
description: If effective dose of a functional raw material or ingredient is publicly known and sufficient to identify its function, a mixture including it may be deemed to include the effect without re-proving.
guidance: Define 'functional raw material publicly known' (e.g., declared by Minister, separately recognized raw materials, or functions published domestically/internationally). Ensure the known effective dose is clearly relevant to the claimed composition.

name: Claims: usage limiting a health functional food is a claim element
description: If the subject matter recited in a claim is a health functional food, the usage limiting the food is considered as a claim element.
guidance: Be aware that usage limitations may be interpreted as claim elements; but a mere different usage does not necessarily guarantee novelty if composition is identical to prior art (see Supreme Court precedent).

name: Claims of use must be expressed by objectives, not by quality
description: For a use invention of a health functional food, its usage shall be specifically described by objectives to be achieved through the quality, not by the quality itself.
guidance: Examples: 'for improvement of hyperlipidemia', 'for drop in blood sugar' are acceptable objective-style usage descriptions. Avoid limitiations stated as 'quality' (e.g., 'having activating antagonism for binding receptor') which specify function/mechanism rather than an intended use and may not be construed as a use invention.

name: Differences between food-usage and medicinal-use claims
description: Health functional food usage may be stated in terms of types of function helpful to the human body, but food claims should not be drafted as medicinal treatment claims (e.g., 'to treat taurine deficiency disease' is unclear for food).
guidance: Claims that effectively claim therapeutic treatment may be deemed unclear or inappropriate for food; draft usage limitations consistent with food (general functional benefits) rather than medical treatment.

name: Determination when both food and pharmaceutical claims filed
description: If both health functional food and medicinal product are filed in one application, it shall be determined separately whether each can be harmful to public health.
guidance: For pharmaceutical composition claims examine per medicinal guidelines; for food composition consider food safety. A compound with great effect may still be unpatentable as food if harmful to humans even though patentable as a pharmaceutical.

name: Functional drinking water: need for objective proof of claimed properties
description: For inventions of functional drinking water (e.g., electrolyzed reduced water, hexagonal water, magnetized water), it is necessary to satisfy description requirements including statement of medical effect, statement of maintaining magnetic state, and to submit objective tests/measuring methods when not acceptable as common technical knowledge.
guidance: If claims are limited to parameters like pH, ORP, active hydrogen, etc., the process and beneficial effects must be stated and supported; where assertions are not consistent with common technical knowledge, reliable test results must be submitted. Notes caution against unsupported theories (e.g., pyramid-produced hexagonal water) without scientific proof.

name: Industrial applicability and 'uncompleted invention' in functional water
description: A manufacturing device or method for producing a claimed functional water without test reports/evidence that the water is actually produced is considered an uncompleted invention which is impossible to accomplish.
guidance: Do not accept purely theoretical processes or empirical rules without scientific proof. Require evidence that the claimed product can be made and has the claimed properties.

name: Chemical compound: disclosure of representative embodiments for generic claims
description: For inventions relating to a new chemical compound, embodiment specifying technical means shall be disclosed. Where the claim is recited generically, representative embodiment(s) shall be disclosed by a group.
guidance: If no representative embodiments are provided for a Markush/genus-type claim and a skilled person cannot recognize other species, examiner shall notify lack of support. Provide representative examples across the claimed scope when claiming classes of compounds.

name: Claims must be supported by the description
description: If a claim (e.g., Markush-type compound group) is not clearly supported by the description so a person skilled in the art can recognize the claimed members, the examiner shall present grounds for rejection for lack of support.
guidance: Provide reasons when rejecting and consider amendment to description or claims to align scope with disclosed embodiments.

name: Clarity requirements for chemical compound claims
description: If a chemical compound is specified by name or structural formula the claim is clear; if necessary, physical/chemical property or preparation can be used to define the invention. Expressions like 'alkyl' or 'aryl' without carbon number may be acceptable if the variety can be introduced based on the chemical framework, but unspecified 'substituted …' or vague terms like 'derivative'/'homologous series' must clearly identify scope.
guidance: Consider whether unspecified substituents or vague group terms render the invention unsupported or not reproducible; specify carbon numbers or embodiments where necessary to preserve clarity and enablement.

name: Novelty: compound defined by characteristics, salts, purity
description: A compound defined by specific characteristics that is identical to a well-known compound specified by name or structural formula lacks novelty. A known compound's conventional salt is substantially identical and lacks novelty. Simple purity improvement of a known compound lacks novelty.
guidance: Assess whether the claimed compound is distinguishable by distinct natural properties beyond mere purity or salt form.

name: Novelty rules for preparation/method claims
description: If the claimed preparation method is the same as prior art and merely limited by use, it is deemed to lack novelty. If the claimed preparation uses starting material produced by a particular preparation but other conditions are equivalent to prior art, the claimed preparation may lack novelty.
guidance: Examine method claims for whether they produce a substantially same compound or rely on different, non-obvious process steps; use limitations alone are insufficient to establish novelty.

name: Inorganic compound inventions: microstructure and property specification
description: For inorganic compounds, even with same name/formula, physical properties or configuration including microstructure (crystal form, unit surface area of particles, etc.) can differ; subject matter may not be specified by name/formula alone.
guidance: Claims should include specific properties to enable identification of microstructure; determine whether the specific property can be expected to result from the claimed adoption/combination of components given the level of technology.

name: Product-by-use (use-limited product) claim construction and novelty
description: When a chemical compound is claimed with a 'for ~' use limitation (e.g., 'Compound Z for Y'), the limitation may be construed as indication of utility only and the claim read as the compound without use limitation.
guidance: Consequently, a use-limited product claim may lack novelty if the compound itself is disclosed in prior art. Drafters should consider alternative claim formats (e.g., second medical use-style claims where permissible) to capture new therapeutic uses.

name: Seventeenth Defence: Denial of a Legal Title in the Plaintiff
description: Attacks the plaintiff’s legal title to the patent — a denial that his interest in the patented invention is sufficient to enable him to maintain an action at law.
guidance: This defence targets defects in the legal ownership/assignment/territorial rights (patentee, assignee, grantee enforcing within territory). Matters of corporate capacity, infancy, coverture, misjoinder/non-joinder are not part of this defence but are available in abatement. Equitable interests cannot be asserted in a legal action to defeat the record owner’s claims. (Examples/cases cited to illustrate limits.)

name: Eighteenth Defence: Denial that the Art or Instrument Employed by the Defendant is Covered by the Patent
description: Denial that the art or article employed by the defendant is covered by the plaintiff’s patent — i.e., the idea or means embodied in the defendant’s invention is not identical with or included in the idea embodied in the plaintiff’s claimed invention.
guidance: This is not merely a denial of identity: an original invention may be infringed by an improvement. The defence must show the defendant’s invention excludes the patented invention in every form to avoid liability; if the defendant’s device uses the plaintiff’s invention alone or as an element or foundation (even if combined with improvements), infringement may still be found. (Cites §¶ and cases discussing identity vs. inclusion.)

name: Photographs vs ink drawings: when photographs allowed and restrictions
description: Black-and-white photographs may be filed in lieu of ink drawings only if the photographs are the only practicable medium for illustrating the claimed invention (37 CFR §1.84(b)(1)).
guidance: Photos cannot be combined with black-and-white line drawings in one design application (see MPEP 1503.02). If photographs are submitted instead of ink drawings, the photos should not show any environmental structure.

name: Written disclaimers not permitted in issued design patents
description: Written disclaimer statements are not permitted in issued design patents, but are temporarily allowed in a pending design application to enable future amendments.
guidance: Therefore, the most effective way to avoid claiming a particular design feature or element is to show such feature in broken or dashed lines rather than rely on a written disclaimer for the issued patent.

name: Disclosure requirements for AI inventions — general
description: EPC Guidelines update disclosure requirements for AI inventions (F-III, 3), underlining the importance for patent applications claiming inventions relating to AI to disclose the mathematical methods and the training datasets to the extent needed to reproduce the technical effect over the whole range claimed.
guidance: The Guidelines state that applicants should disclose mathematical methods and training datasets to the extent necessary to reproduce the claimed technical effect across the claimed scope.

name: Disclosure of training dataset characteristics when effect depends on them
description: If the technical effect is dependent on particular characteristics of the training dataset used, those characteristics that are required to reproduce the technical effect must be disclosed unless the skilled person can determine them without undue burden using common general knowledge.
guidance: Applicants must disclose dataset characteristics necessary to reproduce the technical effect over the whole range claimed, except where such characteristics can be derived by the skilled person from common general knowledge without undue burden.

name: Primary reliance on intrinsic evidence
description: Courts will consider intrinsic evidence first when conducting claim construction. Intrinsic evidence refers to materials submitted as part of the patent application: the patent application itself (claims, summary, written description), prosecution history (written or oral communications with the examiner), previous related patents and their prosecution history, and prior art referenced in the patent application.
guidance: Intrinsic evidence is given significant weight because it points to the applicant’s thought process. Claims must be read in view of the specification; specifications are the best guide and may contain special meanings or internal disclaimers. Prosecution history plays a role but may be ambiguous due to negotiation with the examiner.

name: Use extrinsic evidence only for background and education
description: Extrinsic evidence includes dictionary definitions, encyclopedias/engineering dictionaries, journals or scientific treatises, testimony from the patent applicant, and expert testimony.
guidance: Extrinsic evidence is useful to educate the court and explain technology or what a person of ordinary skill in the art would understand at the effective filing date. However, it should not be substituted for intrinsic evidence and carries the risk of altering claim meaning or expanding scope if misapplied.

name: Ordinary meaning to a person of ordinary skill in the art (Phillips)
description: Under Phillips v. AWH Corp., each claim term must be given 'the meaning that the term would have to a person of ordinary skill in the art in question at the time of the invention' (the effective filing date); that meaning is the 'ordinary meaning' baseline for claim construction.
guidance: The ordinary meaning is an objective baseline but may not always be the proper construction if intrinsic evidence shows a different meaning. Timing is important—use materials contemporaneous with the effective filing date to determine the level of skill and meaning.

name: Read claims in view of the specification
description: Claims must be read in view of the specification; specifications are highly relevant and are the best guide to the meaning of a disputed term.
guidance: Specifications may define special meanings for terms or contain internal disclaimers that govern construction. Reliance on the specification is a central part of intrinsic-evidence-based analysis.

name: Prosecution history and disclaimers affect claim scope
