description: Amendments and statements made during prosecution (prosecution history) can result in disclaimers and influence how courts interpret claim language.
guidance: Courts will consider prosecution history to the extent it clarifies what the applicant disclaimed or amended, but prosecution history sometimes lacks clarity because it reflects negotiation with the examiner and may be more ambiguous than the application or grant.

name: Extrinsic evidence cannot override intrinsic evidence
description: Although courts generally permit extrinsic evidence, it should not be used as a substitute for a careful reading of the claims and the specification.
guidance: Because extrinsic sources are not written with the particular patent in mind, there is a risk they could be used improperly to change claim meaning; courts therefore treat extrinsic evidence as secondary and for background only.

name: Correct minor mistakes in claim language; major corrections require PTO
description: Courts may correct minor mistakes and typos in claim language where there is no reasonable debate as to the correction, but major errors generally must be corrected by the Patent Office.
guidance: Correction is permitted only where the proper correction is obvious and undisputed; otherwise, the Patent Office must address substantive changes.

name: Prefer claim interpretation that preserves validity when interpretations are equally plausible
description: The Phillips court indicated claims should be construed in a way that preserves patent validity when two equally viable interpretations exist, choosing the one that preserves validity.
guidance: This principle typically applies only when the intrinsic record supports two equally reasonable constructions—courts will favor the construction that keeps the patent valid.

name: PTO claim construction rule (37 CFR 42.100) aligns certain proceedings with Phillips
description: As of November 2018, the USPTO adopted 37 CFR 42.100 to bring claim construction rules for IPR, PGR, and CBM proceedings in line with Phillips; prior civil or ITC claim construction decisions properly entered into the record may be considered by the PTO.
guidance: This rule applies to petitions filed after its adoption; it replaces the broadest-reasonable-interpretation (BRI) standard for those proceedings but BRI remains for petitions filed earlier and for reexaminations and reissues.

name: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) standard (historical PTO standard)
description: Under the old BRI standard the PTO gave claims their broadest possible interpretation and required challengers to show the claim was being interpreted more broadly than a court would; claimed words were given their ordinary and customary meaning unless the applicant defined terms in the specification.
guidance: BRI tended to increase the possibility that claims would be interpreted to encompass prior art and thus be cancelled. Extrinsic evidence could be considered but intrinsic evidence was favored even under BRI. BRI remains applicable for some earlier-filed proceedings and reexaminations.

name: Meet-and-confer and narrowing disputed terms to streamline hearings
description: Courts typically require parties to meet and confer to determine which claims are actually in dispute; if parties agree on constructions, the hearing may be unnecessary or may focus only on disputed terms.
guidance: Identifying and stipulating to constructions can save time and money; some courts request a specific identification of disputed claims to streamline proceedings.

name: Evaluate prior art against the broadest reasonable interpretation of claims
description: Carefully evaluate and explain to the applicant the scope of the claims, particularly the broadest claims; pick out the broadest claim(s) and measure the materiality of prior art against a reasonably broad interpretation.
guidance: Avoid mistakenly evaluating prior art in light of the gist or a narrower interpretation of the invention; focus on whether prior art is material to the broadest claim interpretation.

name: Assess materiality from viewpoint of closest prior art
description: It may be useful to evaluate the materiality of prior art or other information from the viewpoint of whether it is the closest prior art or other information.
guidance: A withheld reference may be highly material when it discloses a more complete combination of relevant features, even if those features appear in other references. Consider whether a reference provides a more complete combination of elements claimed (Semiconductor Energy Laboratory v. Samsung).

name: Submit information about prior uses and sales even if experimental or uncertain
description: Submit information about prior uses and sales even if it appears they may have been experimental, not involve what is specifically claimed in the invention, or not encompass a completed invention.
guidance: Case law (TransWeb v. 3M, Hycor Corp. v. Schlueter Co., LaBounty) supports submitting such information; better to disclose and let the Office weigh materiality.

name: Obvious to Try
description: The Federal Circuit has narrowed "obvious to try": the prior art must (a) identify a finite number of identified, predictable solutions, (b) suggest the inventor's chosen solution, and (c) provide a reasonable expectation of success.
guidance: Show that the prior art did not present a finite/predictable set, did not single out the claimed solution, or did not create a reasonable expectation that the chosen option would work. Example: if prior art lists five candidates and the inventor chose the third, "obvious to try" should apply only if there was reasonable expectation that the third would work.

name: Determine broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim (consider 112(f))
description: Determine the broadest reasonable interpretation of each claim; remember to consider whether the claims invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f).
guidance: BRI step includes checking whether claim terms (e.g., 'unit') are generic placeholders that trigger 112(f). If 112(f) applies, interpret the limitation to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents. (See MPEP 2181.)

name: Written description requirement under 35 U.S.C. 112(a)
description: The specification as filed must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail so that one of ordinary skill in the art can reasonably conclude that the inventor had possession of the claimed invention at the time of filing.
guidance: If the disclosure only restates functional language or uses generic placeholders without sufficient structural detail, it may fail 112(a). Use Form Paragraphs 7.30.01 and 7.31.01 for rejections. Example: generic 'capturing unit' or 'analyzing unit' without structure is insufficient.

name: 112(f)/means-plus-function invocation and corresponding structure requirement
description: If a claim uses 'means' or a substitute (e.g., 'unit') that is a generic placeholder modified by functional language and lacks sufficiently definite structure, it invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f).
guidance: Such claim elements must be interpreted to cover the corresponding structure, materials, or acts described in the specification and 'equivalents thereof.' If the specification does not disclose corresponding structure, those limitations lack written description support and may be indefinite under 112(b).

name: Computer-implemented functional limitations require algorithmic/corresponding structure disclosure
description: For computer-implemented specialized functions recited functionally, the disclosure must include corresponding structure — i.e., a general purpose computer or component plus the algorithms that perform the claimed functions.
guidance: Merely asserting that one of ordinary skill could devise an algorithm is insufficient for written description. Flowcharts or generic unit names without algorithms or instruction-level disclosure may fail to demonstrate possession. If missing, claim may also be indefinite under 112(b).

name: Analyze written description support in the earlier (provisional) application for benefit claims
description: When a later application claims benefit of an earlier filing date, evaluate whether the earlier-filed application provides adequate 112(a) support for each claim limitation that purports to receive the earlier date.
guidance: If the earlier disclosure is sparse (e.g., generic 'units' without structure), claims in the later application are not entitled to the earlier filing date. Examiner should notify applicant that benefit is not proper (use Form Paragraphs 2.09 and 2.10) and perform prior art search based on the actual filing date.

name: Analyze written description support in the non-provisional specification
description: Examine whether the non-provisional specification provides sufficient structure, embodiments, or detail to support each claim limitation.
guidance: Non-provisional disclosure that identifies concrete structure (e.g., a digital camera, CPU programmed with APIDQ instructions, specific network interface) can provide 112(a) support and satisfy corresponding-structure requirements for 112(f) elements.

name: Claim scope must be commensurate with the disclosure (numerical ranges and broad genus claims)
description: Claim limitations (including numerical ranges like 'at least 90%') must be supported by the specification; the claim's BRI determines its scope (e.g., 'at least 90%' reads up to 100%).
guidance: If the specification only shows up to 97%, a claim covering up to 100% lacks written description support and should be rejected under 112(a). Consider narrowing or limiting to disclosed species to remedy.

name: Amendments that introduce new technical matter are improper (new matter prohibition)
description: Amendments that add specifics not present in the original disclosure (e.g., adding 'Gaussian high pass filter' when not originally disclosed) constitute new matter.
guidance: Such amendments lack written description support and add new matter; reject under 112(a) and advise applicant. Use sample rejection language; recommend applicant may change application relationship to CIP or delete benefit claim.

name: Structural claim terms versus functional placeholders (impact on 112(f))
description: Terms that recite sufficiently definite structure (e.g., 'filter') generally do not invoke 112(f), whereas generic placeholders like 'unit' often do.
guidance: If a term is structural, claim is not limited to the corresponding structure in the specification and covers all appropriate equivalents; nonetheless, written description support is still required to show possession of the claimed structural function.

name: Examiner actions when later-filed claims are not entitled to earlier filing date
description: When claims are not supported by the earlier filing, the examiner should notify applicant and proceed based on the actual filing date.
guidance: Notify using form paragraphs (e.g., 2.09, 2.10), perform prior-art search as of actual filing date, and may use intervening references in rejections until applicant corrects the benefit claim or shows entitlement.

name: Triggers for evaluating the propriety of a benefit claim
description: Evaluate entitlement to an earlier filing date when there is a reason to question the adequacy of support in the earlier application.
guidance: Typical triggers include an intervening prior art reference, significant broadening of later-filed claims, or when the earlier application appears substantially less substantial than the later-filed application. Best practice: verify benefit claim when such circumstances arise.

name: Distinguish written description, enablement, and indefiniteness analyses
description: Written description concerns possession; enablement concerns ability to make and use without undue experimentation (Wands factors); indefiniteness under 112(b) can arise when functional claim elements lack corresponding structure.
guidance: Be prepared to discuss enablement issues raised by Wands factors though this workshop focuses on written description. Example: the specification may be enabling (one of ordinary skill could implement) but still fail written description if inventor did not show possession of the full claimed scope.

name: Amendments may remove 112(f) invocation but can broaden scope and create written description problems
description: Adding structural language (e.g., specifying a 'central processing unit having a memory with instructions stored therein') can avoid 112(f) but may broaden claim to cover all ways of performing the function.
guidance: If the specification only discloses a particular species (e.g., APIDQ) and indicates that species is critical, the broader amended claim may still lack written description support. Remedy: limit the claim to the disclosed species.

name: Original claims do not automatically provide written description support for themselves
description: Merely reproducing a claim limitation in the specification or pointing to an original claim does not necessarily satisfy written description unless the claim itself conveys sufficient information to show possession.
guidance: Evaluate on a case-by-case basis; do not assume that an original claim, by its wording, constitutes adequate written description of structural detail or algorithms.

name: Relative terms (e.g., 'about') are judged in context for definiteness
description: Use of relative terms like 'about' does not automatically render a claim indefinite; context and the state of the art determine whether the term is definite.
guidance: Consider specification examples and state of the art (see MPEP 2173.05(B)(II)). In the example, 'about a 95% accurate image detection rate' is sufficiently definite to be allowable.

name: 112(f) limitations unsupported by corresponding structure may render claim indefinite under 112(b)
description: If a functionally claimed element invokes 112(f) but the specification lacks corresponding structure, the limitation may be both unsupported under 112(a) and indefinite under 112(b).
guidance: Cross-check for both written description and definiteness problems and cite appropriate MPEP guidance and prior training where necessary.

name: Dependent-claim limitations can cure broad independent-claim deficiencies if limited to disclosed species
description: Limiting dependent claims to the disclosed species (e.g., specifying APIDQ in dependent claim) can make a dependent claim commensurate with the specification even if the independent claim is too broad.
guidance: Use dependent claim amendments to tie scope to disclosed embodiments; e.g., Amended Claim 2 limited to APIDQ was supported by the non-provisional specification and remedied scope issues.

name: Worksheet procedure for examining written description support
description: Use a stepwise worksheet: (1) determine BRI (and 112(f) invocation); (2) analyze whether each claim limitation has adequate written description support in the provisional; (3) analyze support in the non-provisional; (4) identify unsupported features. Order of provisional vs non-provisional analysis can vary.
guidance: Document which features are unsupported and prepare appropriate rejections/notifications. The workshop provides blank worksheet fields for each original and amended claim.

name: Provide clear examiner notification and sample rejection language
description: When concluding lack of entitlement to a benefit or lack of written description, the examiner should use clear form paragraph language and indicate applicant options.
guidance: Examples in the workshop include a sample Form Paragraph notifying lack of benefit (based on failure to comply with 112(a)) and sample rejections for lack of written description (7.30.01/7.31.01). Recommend options for applicant: cancel new matter, convert to CIP, or delete benefit claim.

name: Continuations and divisionals follow same written-description-benefit rules as provisionals
description: When a later application is a continuation or divisional, only those claims supported under 112(a) by the parent are entitled to the parent's filing date.
guidance: Apply the same analysis as for provisional-based benefit claims; see MPEP 211.05 for sufficiency of disclosure in prior-filed applications.

name: Fintiv Factor 4: Overlap between issues raised in the petition and in the parallel proceeding
description: Assesses whether the petition presents the same or substantially the same claims, grounds, arguments, and evidence as are before the district court. Substantial overlap raises concerns of inefficiency and risk of conflicting decisions.
guidance: Degree of overlap is highly fact dependent. Petitioners can mitigate duplication/conflict concerns by stipulations (e.g., not pursuing the same grounds in court if PTAB is instituted); broader stipulations (not pursuing any ground raised or that could have been reasonably raised in an IPR under § 102/103 on printed publications/patents) are more persuasive. Panels have accepted broad stipulations as tipping this factor strongly in favor of institution (see Sand Revolution, Sotera).

name: Primary prior art selection and whole-reference comparison
description: When combining prior art references, select a primary prior art and compare it against the claimed invention as a whole, then examine secondary prior art to overcome differences in a logical fashion.
guidance: The POSA would naturally start from one prior art reference (primary prior art) as a whole and then combine the whole or particular element(s) from another prior art reference (secondary prior art). Depending on which reference is selected as primary, the elements or context of combination may change, altering incentives or obstructions and the conclusion on inventive step. The proposal recommends that judgments and examinations explicitly select a primary prior art and proceed in this order.

name: Avoid abstract element-by-element combination
description: Do not examine or combine elements of prior art references in overly abstract terms beyond the comparison stage; combine elements as disclosed in the prior art when assessing combination.
guidance: Abstracting specific elements of prior art references is acceptable to the extent necessary to determine correspondence with abstract claim features, but such abstracting should stop at the comparison stage and should not extend to the combination stage. POSA should combine elements in the state disclosed in the prior art (though simple design changes may be permitted).

name: Prohibition of hindsight-driven combinations
description: Avoid constructing combinations by extracting claim-corresponding elements from multiple prior art references centered around nothing, which gives the impression of hindsight analysis.
guidance: The traditional method risks hindsight by enumerating matching elements across multiple references; instead, examination should reflect how a POSA (who lacks knowledge of the claimed invention) would naturally analyze references.

name: Specific pleading of motivation to combine
description: Those alleging lack of inventive step (petitioner) must clearly allege the incentive or the form of combination in detail and discharge the burden of proof thereof.
guidance: Petitioner must allege specifically how and why prior art references would be combined; this allows the patentee to defend by claiming obstructive factors in response. Courts/examiners should require concrete allegations of inducement for combination.

name: Collective assessment of motivation factors
description: Factors such as related technical field, hint of prior art combination, commonality of problem, or functional/application commonality must be considered together to determine whether there is sufficient motivation to combine.
guidance: Do not conclude motivation to combine merely because one factor (e.g., technical relatedness) is present; especially technical relatedness often functions as a de minimis condition and rarely suffices alone. Examine whether the motivation specifically leads to combination with the claimed invention.

name: Examine problem/function/application concretely (not overly abstract)
description: When assessing commonality of problem or function/application among prior art references, avoid treating these concepts in overly abstract or generic terms that artificially create commonality.
guidance: Even where problems/functions are similar, numerous possible combinations or partial differences may limit a specific path to the claimed invention; examiners must test whether the commonality specifically leads to the claimed combination.

name: Distinguish aggregation (mere listing) from meaningful combination
description: If the claimed invention is merely an aggregation (enumeration/listing) of technical features without functional relationship, it is obvious and lacks inventive step.
guidance: KIPO/JPO/EPO/USPTO guidelines emphasize: a simple aggregation (each element disclosed but no function/application relationship) is within ordinary innovation. The examiner must assess whether elements interact functionally or simply sum their separate effects.

name: POSA perspective: examine prior art references as single inventions
description: A person of ordinary skill in the art (POSA), lacking knowledge of the claimed invention, would examine each prior art reference as a single invention and consider any combination thereof, rather than pre-selecting isolated elements tailored to the claim.
guidance: It is unnatural for POSA to extract and recombine isolated elements centered around the claimed invention; instead analysis should reflect how references are disclosed and practiced as wholes.

name: USPTO 'predictable results' criterion for combination rejections
description: To reject a claim for obviousness based on combining prior art, it must be found that the references include each claimed element, POSA could have combined them by known methods, and POSA would have recognized that the results were predictable.
guidance: USPTO formulation requires predictable results of combination as part of the obviousness rationale (citing Anderson’s Black Rock v. Pavement Salvage example).

name: Examination focus on relationship of function or application
description: The focus of inventive step examination should be on the relationship of function or application among claimed elements; lack of functional relationship supports obviousness.
guidance: Common to multiple guidelines: examine whether technical features relate functionally or in application; if not, combination may be deemed obvious even if each element is known.

name: Comparison-first then secondary art to overcome differences
description: In assessment, first identify differences between primary prior art and the claimed invention, then examine secondary prior art for whether it logically overcomes those differences.
guidance: This ordered approach reduces hindsight and better reflects how POSA would combine references to address a specific shortfall in the primary reference.

name: Abstraction allowed for correspondence assessment but not for combination
description: Abstract the specific prior art elements only to the extent needed to determine correspondence with claim features; do not use such abstraction to justify combining references.
guidance: Court should avoid converting a specific disclosed feature into a generic function and then use that genericization to claim that combination was obvious (example given where 'attachment means' was abstracted to 'part that has the function of a gasket' and other disclosed specifics were ignored).

name: KIPO guideline on simple enumeration
description: KIPO: where claims of a combination invention merely 'enumerates (lists) the technical features or a simple combination (simple collection)', which cannot be recognized as a technically meaningful combination, each technical feature would be considered obvious thereby denying inventive step unless other evidence exists.
guidance: KIPO Example: mere substitution/modification between cited inventions that does not create structural difficulties or remarkable functional difference leads to denial of inventive step as aggregation.

name: Plaintiff's alternative claim for usual royalties and excess damages
description: Patentee may claim the amount they would usually receive for executing the patented invention (royalty) as damages; in addition, damages exceeding that amount may be claimed where appropriate (court may consider infringer's intent/gross negligence).
guidance: Article 128(5)-(6): statutory structure permits claiming a standard royalty and also seeking higher damages with court's consideration of culpability in awarding excess.

name: Special technical features — definition and role
description: Special technical features are the particular technical feature(s) in a claim that define the contribution the claimed invention as a whole makes over the prior art.
guidance: Identify the special technical features of each invention, then determine whether a technical relationship exists between inventions that involves these special technical features. Corresponding (not necessarily identical) special technical features across claims can provide the required link (e.g., metal spring vs rubber block providing resilience).

name: Permissible combinations of claims (forms of claiming linked inventions)
description: Certain combinations of independent claims in different categories may be included in one application if they belong to a single general inventive concept (examples include product + process for manufacture + use; process + apparatus designed for process; etc.).
guidance: The guidelines list six forms (i)-(vi) illustrating allowable combinations: multiple independent claims of same category; product + process specially adapted to manufacture it; product + use; product+process+use; product+process+apparatus specifically designed for the process; process+apparatus specifically designed for the process. These examples are not exhaustive — other combinations are permissible if they share a single general inventive concept.

name: 'Specially adapted' / 'specifically designed' does not automatically create unity
description: Expressions like 'specially adapted' or 'specifically designed' in claims do not necessarily imply a single general inventive concept linking claims.
guidance: For a process to be 'specially adapted' it must actually result in the claimed product (i.e., be suited to making the claimed product accessible). For an apparatus to be 'specifically designed' it must be suitable for carrying out the process and the contribution it makes over the prior art should correspond to that made by the process. It is irrelevant whether the apparatus could be used for other processes or the process by other apparatus.

name: Unity for intermediate and final products
description: Unity may be present between intermediate and final products when they (i) share the same essential structural element (basic chemical structures the same or intermediate incorporates essential element), and (ii) are technically closely interrelated (final product manufactured directly from intermediate or separated by a small number of intermediates containing the same essential element).
guidance: Unity can exist even when structures are unknown (e.g., intermediate known, final unknown) provided sufficient evidence shows technical interrelation. Different intermediates used in different processes may be claimed provided they have the same essential structural element. Intermediates separated by a non‑new intermediate breaks unity. Families of intermediates/final products should correspond compound-for-compound where applicable; family congruence need not be absolute. Other activities/effects of intermediates do not necessarily prejudice unity.

name: Alternatives and unity within single claims (including Markush groupings)
description: Alternative forms of an invention may be claimed in plural independent claims or within a single claim; the same unity criteria apply and lack of unity may exist within a single claim. For Markush groupings unity exists if the alternatives are of a similar nature.
guidance: For chemical Markush groupings, alternatives are 'similar' if (i) all alternatives share a common property or activity, and (ii) a common structure is present (a significant structural element shared) or all alternatives belong to a recognized class of compounds expected to behave similarly. A small shared portion can be sufficient if it is structurally distinctive in view of the prior art. If at least one Markush alternative is not novel, unity should be reconsidered.

name: Examiner's practical approach and discretion
description: Examiners should avoid narrow, literal or academic approaches to unity; consider the practical degree of interdependence of alternatives in relation to the state of the art revealed by the search report and give the benefit of doubt to the applicant.
guidance: Do not raise or persist in unity objections where unnecessary (especially if no further search is required). If common matter of independent claims is well known and remaining subject-matter differs with no unifying novel concept, objection is justified. Each case should be considered on its merits.

name: Search Examiner actions on lack of unity during search
description: Search Examiners may note and report lack of unity by drawing up a partial search report based on those parts of the application relating to the first‑mentioned invention; they may not refuse for lack of unity or require claim limitation but must inform applicant of additional search fees if they wish other inventions searched.
guidance: Applicant may pay further search fees within a stipulated period to have other inventions covered in the search report. The Search Examiner's partial search report records the lack-of-unity findings for later substantive examination.

name: Substantive Examiner responsibilities when lack of unity arises
description: Final responsibility for deciding whether the application meets unity rests with the Substantive Examiner, who will generally follow the search opinion but must consider applicant arguments and may order further search or require deletion/limitation of claims.
guidance: If applicant paid further fees and requested refund, Substantive Examiner will order refund where appropriate. If applicant did not seek searches of other inventions, the application proceeds on the searched invention. Examiner should invite applicant to elect which invention prosecution should proceed on and may require excision/amendment or divisional filings for other inventions.

name: Principles of examination — focus on substantive content and special technical features
description: To determine unity, examine whether substantive contents of the technical solutions in the claims belong to a single general inventive concept by checking for same or corresponding special technical features that make the claimed inventions technically interrelated.
guidance: Determination is made primarily on the basis of claims, referring to description/drawings if necessary. The order or form of claims does not affect unity determination. Generally consider unity among independent claims; normally do not object between independent and its dependent claims, except where a dependent is in form but actually independent.

name: Timing of unity determination (before or after search)
description: For some applications unity can be decided before search (when inventions obviously lack unity), but for many applications determination requires consideration of prior art and can only be made after search.
guidance: If a first independent claim is denied novelty/inventive step after search, re‑determine whether the remaining independent claims belong to a single general inventive concept. Obvious lack of unity (no same/corresponding technical features or only customary means) can be determined pre-search.

name: Three-step approach to examining unity (practical procedure)
description: A recommended approach when unity is not obviously lacking: (1) compare first invention with relevant prior art to identify its special technical feature; (2) determine whether the second invention contains same or corresponding special technical features; (3) conclude unity if such same/corresponding features exist, otherwise conclude lack of unity.
guidance: This stepwise method underlies the examiner examples and practical assessments; it emphasizes identification of contribution over prior art as the linchpin for interrelation between claimed inventions.

name: Non-obvious (35 U.S.C. § 103)
description: A patentable invention must involve an inventive step — it must not be an obvious improvement to a person skilled in the art.
guidance: Patent prosecution and claim drafting should focus on demonstrating technical differences and unexpected benefits. Obviousness analysis is fact‑intensive and often disputed.

name: Adequately described (enablement / written description)
description: A patent application must teach others how to make and use the invention; the disclosure must be sufficiently detailed.
guidance: Draft applications with enabling examples, embodiments, and sufficient detail to support the full scope of claimed subject matter. Lack of adequate description can lead to rejection or invalidation.

name: Suitability for patent: want to license the technology
description: Patents are easier to license because claims define the scope; trade secret licensing requires disclosure to licensees and introduces additional risk.
guidance: If monetization via licensing is part of the business model, patents typically facilitate transactions and valuation.

name: Who may petition for post-grant review (eligibility / bars)
description: A person who is not the owner of a patent may file a petition for post-grant review unless: (a) before filing the petition the petitioner or real party-in-interest filed a civil action challenging the patent; or (b) the petitioner (or real party-in-interest or privy) is estopped from challenging the claims on the grounds identified.
guidance: PGR does not include the IPR one-year-served limitation; estoppel and prior civil action bars still apply.

name: Content of petition — identification of challenge (IPR specific required elements)
description: For each challenged claim the petition must identify: (1) the claim; (2) the specific statutory grounds under 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103 and the patents or printed publications relied upon for each ground; (3) how the challenged claim is to be construed (including identification of corresponding specification portions for 112(f) limitations); (4) how the construed claim is unpatentable and where each element is found in the prior art; and (5) exhibit numbers of supporting evidence and the relevance/identification of specific portions relied upon.
guidance: The Board may exclude or give no weight to evidence where a party fails to state its relevance or to identify specific supporting portions.

name: Content of petition — identification of challenge (PGR specific required elements)
description: For each challenged claim the petition must identify: (1) the claim; (2) the specific statutory grounds permitted under 35 U.S.C. 282(b)(2) or (3) on which the challenge is based; (3) how the claim is to be construed (including 112(f) identification); (4) how the construed claim is unpatentable (for prior-art grounds, specify where each element is found; for other grounds, identify the specific part of the claim that fails and explain why); and (5) exhibit numbers and relevance with specific portions identified.
guidance: As with IPR, the Board may exclude evidence lacking a stated relevance or specific citations.

name: Board institution discretion and partial institution
description: When instituting review, the Board may authorize review to proceed on all or some of the challenged claims and on all or some of the grounds of unpatentability asserted for each claim. At any time prior to institution, the Board may deny some or all grounds for some or all challenged claims; denial of a ground is a decision not to institute on that ground.
guidance: Institution can be partial (claims/grounds) and the Board may narrow institution before formally instituting a trial.

name: Motion to amend — one motion and timing
description: A patent owner may file one motion to amend a patent, but only after conferring with the Board. Unless a due date is provided by Board order, the motion must be filed no later than the filing of the patent owner response.
guidance: The motion to amend may be denied if it does not respond to a ground of unpatentability or if it seeks to enlarge claim scope or introduce new matter.

name: Content requirements for motion to amend claims
description: A motion to amend must include a claim listing, show changes clearly, and set forth: (1) the support in the original disclosure for each claim added or amended; and (2) the support in any earlier-filed disclosure for any claim for which benefit of that filing date is sought.
guidance: Demonstrating written description/support in the original disclosure (and earlier disclosures where priority is asserted) is required to justify claim amendments.

name: Effect of Aqua Products on burden for motions to amend
description: Aqua Products held that the PTO had not adopted a rule placing the burden of persuasion on the patent owner for the patentability of amended claims; the Board will determine whether substitute claims are unpatentable by a preponderance of the evidence based on the entirety of the record.
guidance: Following Aqua Products, the USPTO memorandum (Guidance on Motions to Amend in view of Aqua Products) directs the Board to assess substitute claims using the record; Lectrosonics clarifies that ordinarily the burden of persuasion will lie with the petitioner to show proposed substitute claims are unpatentable by a preponderance of the evidence.

name: Lectrosonics motion-to-amend requirements: responsiveness and scope limits
description: Motions to amend must respond to a ground of unpatentability involved in the trial; proposed substitute claims may not enlarge the scope of the claims or introduce new subject matter.
guidance: The Board allowed additional claim limitations to address §101 or §112 issues if necessary, but rejects substitute claims that broaden scope or add new matter; motions should be tailored to address trial issues.

name: Lectrosonics motion-to-amend requirements: claim listing, reasonable number, page limits, duty of candor
description: The PTAB set out requirements including: a claim listing for substitute claims; reasonable number of substitute claims; default page limits for motion briefing and for submission of testimony/evidence; and the duty of candor.
guidance: Follow procedural and content requirements (provide clear claim listings, observe page limits, limit number of substitutes to reasonable counts, and ensure candor in filings). Failure to comply may prejudice the motion.

name: Showing examiner error material to patentability under § 325(d)
description: When a petition presents the same/substantially same art or arguments, the petitioner can overcome § 325(d) denial only by showing the Office erred 'in a manner material to the patentability of challenged claims' (examples: misapprehending or overlooking specific teachings of prior art, or an error of law such as claim construction that impacts patentability).
guidance: Petitioners should explain clearly 'how or why the Examiner erred' (Puma) and identify material prosecution errors (Oticon example where an examiner failed to consider a reference). General assertions are insufficient.

name: IPR estoppel under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2): grounds petitioner raised or reasonably could have raised
description: A petitioner that files an IPR resulting in a final decision 'may not assert in district court ... that the claim is invalid on any ground that the petitioner raised or reasonably could have raised during that [IPR].'
guidance: Estoppel applies to 'grounds' (not simply specific evidence). Courts evaluate whether a ground was reasonably available during the IPR; if so, the petitioner may be estopped from asserting that ground later in litigation.

name: Not original/first inventor or prior use (notice required)
description: Notice required where defendant claims the patentee was not the original and first inventor/discoverer of a material and substantial part of the thing patented (this embraces prior use, prior knowledge, and related claims).
guidance: This provision is broad and intended to cover all alleged prior use/knowledge in the U.S. before the patentee's alleged inventive act; statutes evolved to include prior use concepts and the disclosure of names/residences of those alleged to have used/knew the invention.

name: Defences admissible under the general issue without notice — excessive_claim
description: Defence: That the claim is excessive and has not been cured within reasonable time by a disclaimer.
guidance: May be presented under the general issue without notice; relates to overbroad claims and corrective disclaimers.

name: Defences admissible under the general issue without notice — ambiguous_claim
description: Defence: That the claim is ambiguous.
guidance: Claim ambiguity is a defense that can be raised under the general issue without notice.

name: Office approach: enumerated groupings for identifying abstract ideas
description: The Office uses an approach that distills relevant case law into enumerated groupings of abstract ideas to facilitate examination, shifting examiners' focus from reliance on individual judicial cases to applying a broad body of case law across technologies and claim types.
guidance: The enumerated groupings are rooted in Supreme Court and Federal Circuit precedent (see MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2)). This represents a departure from a former case-comparison approach. Examiners should apply these groupings generally rather than relying solely on comparisons to individual cases.

name: Examiner procedure to determine whether a claim recites an abstract idea
description: Examiners should (1) identify the specific limitation(s) in the claim that the examiner believes recite an abstract idea, and (2) determine whether those limitation(s) fall within at least one of the enumerated abstract-idea groupings.
guidance: If the identified limitation(s) fall within a grouping, conclude the claim recites an abstract idea in Step 2A Prong One and proceed to Step 2A Prong Two to analyze whether additional claim elements integrate the abstract idea into a practical application (see MPEP § 2106.04(d)). If the limitation(s) do not fall within any grouping, conclude the claim does not recite an abstract idea and the Step 2A analysis ends (Pathway B), unless another judicial exception (e.g., law of nature) is present. Preferably identify all applicable groupings when a limitation falls within multiple groupings.

name: Abstract idea grouping: Mathematical concepts (grouping definition)
description: The mathematical concepts grouping is defined as mathematical relationships, mathematical formulas or equations, and mathematical calculations.
guidance: Supreme Court and Federal Circuit decisions have repeatedly identified these concepts as abstract ideas (examples: Benson, Flook, Diehr, Bilski, Alice). When determining membership in this grouping, consider whether the claim recites a mathematical concept or merely involves or is based on one. A claim need not use mathematical symbols to recite a mathematical concept; textual descriptions operating on data can serve the same purpose (e.g., 'determining a ratio of A to B').

name: Abstract idea grouping: Mental processes
description: Mental processes are concepts performed in the human mind, including observation, evaluation, judgment, and opinion.
guidance: Claims that recite concepts that can be performed in the human mind may fall into this grouping. Note that a limitation that could be practically performed in the human mind may also overlap with the mathematical concepts grouping (e.g., performing mathematical calculations that could be done mentally).

name: Consequence of grouping membership and next steps
description: If a claim limitation falls within at least one abstract-idea grouping, conclude that the claim recites an abstract idea (Step 2A Prong One) and perform further analysis in Step 2A Prong Two to determine whether additional elements integrate the abstract idea into a practical application.
guidance: Step 2A Prong Two examines whether the claim as a whole is directed to the abstract idea or instead integrates it into a practical application (see MPEP § 2106.04(d)). If the Prong Two analysis shows integration into a practical application, the claim may be eligible; otherwise the claim proceeds to the broader Alice/Mayo framework for patent-ineligibility analysis.

name: If limitations do not fall within any grouping, claim does not recite an abstract idea
description: If the identified limitation(s) do not fall within any of the enumerated groupings, it is reasonable to find the claim does not recite an abstract idea, concluding the abstract-idea eligibility analysis at Step 2A Prong One (Pathway B), unless another judicial exception is present.
guidance: If another judicial exception (e.g., law of nature or natural phenomenon) is implicated, follow MPEP §§ 2106.04(b) and 2106.04(c) for Step 2A analysis. Otherwise, the claim is eligible at Step 2A Prong One.

name: Claim recites a mental process
description: Claims that are essentially mental processes (e.g., analysis or manipulation of data that can be performed mentally or with pen and paper) are abstract ideas and can be ineligible under §101.
guidance: Examiners should look to the specification to determine whether claimed steps are described as being performable mentally (examples: CyberSource (listing transactions), Flook (computations by pencil and paper), University of Florida Research Foundation v. General Electric (pen and paper methodologies), Symantec (screening messages that can be performed by a human)). If the claim limitations can be performed mentally, they qualify as a mental process-type abstract idea.

name: A claim that requires a computer may still recite a mental process
description: Claims can recite a mental process even if claimed as being performed on a computer; the fact that a computer is recited does not automatically avoid the mental process exception.
guidance: Evaluate the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim in light of the specification. Review whether the specification describes the invention as a concept performed in the human mind and the applicant is merely claiming that concept: (1) on a generic computer, (2) in a computer environment, or (3) using a computer as a tool. In such situations, the claim is considered to recite a mental process.

name: Tentative abstract ideas (non-enumerated exceptions)
description: In rare circumstances, a claim limitation may be treated as an abstract idea even though it does not fall within the enumerated groupings (mathematical concepts, certain methods of organizing human activity, mental processes); such a limitation is a 'tentative abstract idea.'
guidance: Evaluate the claim under the eligibility framework: if the claim integrates the tentative abstract idea into a practical application → Step 2A:NO → eligible at Pathway B. If not integrated → Step 2A:YES → proceed to Step 2B: if claim provides an inventive concept → eligible at Pathway C; if not → bring application to Technology Center (TC) director. A Step 2B rejection based on a tentative abstract idea requires TC director approval (to be reflected by form paragraph 7.05.017 and TC Director signature). Interviews with the examiner may help; TC Director interview not required to withdraw or maintain such a rejection but TC approval is required for issuance of the rejection.

name: Claims describing natural abilities/processes are not always laws of nature
description: Not every claim that describes a natural ability or process necessarily recites a law of nature or natural phenomenon; claims focused on applications or particular process steps may be eligible.
guidance: Examples: Rapid Litigation Mgmt. v. CellzDirect (fractionating/recovering/cryopreserving hepatocytes found eligible because not merely observing a property), methods of treating cancer with chemotherapy and methods of producing a new compound are not per se laws of nature when the claim is focused on applied treatment or manufacturing steps. Such claims proceed to Prong Two (Step 2A Prong Two) if another exception applies.

name: Integration into a practical application can overcome a law of nature exception
description: Even if a claim recites a law of nature or natural phenomenon, the claim may still be eligible if it integrates the exception into a practical application.
guidance: Example: Vanda — claims reciting a natural relationship between genotype and drug response were held eligible because they included a tailored treatment step that applied the relationship in a practical manner. This is equivalent to finding eligibility at Step 2A Prong Two (Pathway B).

name: BRI and nature-based product limitations may encompass eligible and ineligible embodiments
description: Under the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI), a nature-based product limitation may encompass both embodiments that are markedly different (eligible) and embodiments that lack markedly different characteristics (products of nature).
guidance: When BRI encompasses both eligible and ineligible products, examiners should point out the BRI and recommend narrowing amendments, if possible, to claim embodiments that are not products of nature. Examiners should consider whether the streamlined eligibility analysis (MPEP § 2106.06) is appropriate for inventions that clearly do not seek to tie up judicial exceptions.

name: Streamlined eligibility analysis for clear non-tie-up cases
description: If a claim recites a nature-based product limitation but is directed to an invention that clearly does not seek to tie up any judicial exception, the examiner should consider the streamlined eligibility analysis.
guidance: Refer to MPEP § 2106.06; in such cases it may not be necessary to conduct the markedly different characteristics analysis.

name: Subject matter summary
description: the subject matter of the patent/application
guidance: Provide a concise description of the claimed invention's field and high-level features (e.g., 'Formulation and trading of risk management – Methods, systems, computer readable media') to enable quick topical comparison with pending applications.

name: Eligibility conclusion (eligible/ineligible)
description: whether the claims were eligible or ineligible (note that a finding applies to all claims in the patent/application unless otherwise noted)
guidance: Indicate the court's ultimate determination for the claims (eligible or ineligible). If the court specified claim-level outcomes, identify which specific claims were held eligible/ineligible (e.g., 'claims 1, 5-6 ineligible; claims 2 & 7 eligible').

name: Case-level claim detail notes
description: notation when the court’s eligibility determination applies to some claims but not others (e.g., '’479: asserted claims 33-34. ’510, ’720, and ’375: all claims.')
guidance: When a court's decision identifies claim-specific outcomes, record those specifics (claim numbers and which claims were affected) so examiners can compare specific claim language rather than relying on blanket statements.

name: Fact-specificity reminder
description: It is important to remember that each case turns on its own facts. Therefore, the mere fact that a pending application may be similarly classified to a patent or an application in this chart, or have similar subject matter, does not necessarily indicate an eligibility issue. Identification of a judicial exception in a claim merely indicates further analysis for eligibility should be conducted.
guidance: Use the chart as a starting point for further analysis rather than as a dispositive determination; similarity in classification or subject matter signals that an examiner should perform a detailed eligibility analysis on the particular claim language and facts of the application.

name: Definition of 'information material to patentability' (37 CFR 1.555(b))
description: Information is material when it is not cumulative and (1) is a patent or printed publication that establishes, alone or in combination, a prima facie case of unpatentability of a claim; or (2) refutes or is inconsistent with a position the patent owner takes in opposing an unpatentability argument or asserting patentability.
guidance: A prima facie case is established when the information compels a conclusion that a claim is unpatentable under the preponderance of the evidence standard, giving each claim term the broadest reasonable construction consistent with the specification, and before considering evidence to establish a contrary conclusion.

name: Document copy requirements (37 CFR 1.98(a))
description: Parties submitting documents cited in the patent or parent applications must supply legible copies: (1) each foreign patent, (2) each publication or the portion causing it to be listed (other than U.S. patents and U.S. patent application publications unless required), (3) for each cited pending unpublished U.S. application, the application specification including claims and drawings or the portion causing it to be listed, (4) all other information or portion causing it to be listed.
guidance: The 1.98(d) exception does not apply to ex parte and inter partes reexamination proceedings because reexamination does not rely on the patent for an earlier effective filing date.

name: Limits on discussions with non-patent owners (procedural vs merits)
description: Examiners may discuss only strictly procedural matters with parties who are not the patent owner; matters that can be obtained by reading the public file are procedural and may be discussed to the extent shown in the file, while matters not available in the file are considered merits and may not be discussed.
guidance: Examples: (A) information obtainable from reading the file is procedural; (B) matters not in the file are merits and may not be discussed. Questions regarding interpretation of claim limitations are merits — examiner may only quote the Office action and not further discuss. Parties not the patent owner should be referred to CRU SPRS or TC QAS for procedural questions beyond the file.

name: Special dispatch and interview pre-submission requirements (35 U.S.C. 305)
description: Pursuant to statutory 'special dispatch' in reexamination proceedings, preliminary steps are required to structure interviews for efficiency: patent owner should contact examiner to indicate issues and, if interview is granted, submit informal written statement and copies of proposed claims at least three working days prior.
guidance: These materials should be transmitted directly to the examiner (fax or hand-carried) to avoid delays; informal copies considered by the examiner will become part of the record attached to the PTOL-474. The one-hour guideline is based on the expectation that claims in a reexamined patent will already define the invention sufficiently; extensions require petition showing sufficient cause.

name: Difference identification between claim and cited document
description: Identify specific points at which the invention of Claim 1 and the cited invention differ (e.g., presence of front-and-rear and left-right fuzzy decision-making systems and the specific steps (1)～(6)).
guidance: List the concrete technical feature(s) that are not specified in the cited document. The examiner's analysis compares the claim's steps/features with those disclosed in D1 and explicitly states the 'Difference' before evaluating its significance.

name: Presence of advantageous technical effect supporting inventive step
description: Determine whether the claimed differences yield an advantageous effect (e.g., improved reliability and accuracy of stability/fall-direction judgment; improved operational efficiency of hardware).
guidance: Explain how the effect is produced (e.g., fusion of sensors + fuzzy algorithm yields better judgment; padding weight parameters to target sizes improves hardware efficiency). Use demonstrated/argued effects to support non-obviousness when prior art lacks such effect.

name: Absence of prior-art suggestion / not a design variation
description: Evaluate whether there is any basis in cited documents to assume the claimed technical matter is a mere 'design variation' or routine design choice from the prior art.
guidance: If no prior art suggests the specific algorithmic or structural feature and it is not common general knowledge, treat it as non-trivial. Examiners explicitly state when 'there is also no basis for assuming that the technical matter in question is "design variation, etc." from the cited document.'

name: Assessment of obstructive factors
description: Consider whether any non-obvious 'obstructive factor' exists that would prevent a skilled person from applying prior-art teaching to reach the claimed invention.
guidance: Examiners note absence of obstructive factors as supporting obviousness; presence of obstructive factors or unexpected technical difficulty supports inventive step.

name: Subject-matter eligibility for software-related inventions (JPA Article 29(1) analysis)
description: Determine whether claimed information processing is implemented by specific means (co-operation of software and hardware) such that the claimed apparatus constitutes a technical creation utilizing a law of nature and thus falls under 'invention'.
guidance: Look for recited concrete means (storage means, reception means, simulation and output means, etc.) and whether software processing is specifically implemented using hardware resources. If so, conclude the claim is technical (JPO example: business plan design apparatus).

name: Enablement / sufficiency of disclosure (Article 36(4)(i) / 36(6)(i))
description: Decide whether the description discloses the invention such that a person skilled in the art can make and use the invention (e.g., can generate the claimed estimation model using a generally used ML algorithm and appropriate training data).
guidance: Even if precise correlations are not shown, examiners may accept that common general technical knowledge permits a skilled person to obtain the estimation model. Check that inputs/outputs, training-data types, and implementation modes are described sufficiently for reproduction.

name: Claims supported by the description (support requirement)
description: Assess whether the claims are supported by the detailed description and do not extend beyond what the description discloses (i.e., whether the skilled person can obtain the claimed technical solution from the description).
guidance: Examiners check that the claimed technical solution is derivable from the description and that the description 'sets forth the invention in a manner sufficiently clear and complete' to satisfy statutory support provisions (CNIPA/JPA examples).

name: Concrete implementation of functional claim elements
description: When claims recite functional modules (e.g., 'model generation means', 'feature value obtainment means'), determine whether the description provides sufficient concrete implementation (algorithms, data types, processing steps) to carry out those functions.
guidance: Examiners accepted claims where the description explained what web advertisement data and mention data are, how mention evaluation values can be obtained, and that general ML algorithms (neural networks) with training data can generate the model. Lack of concrete implementation may risk insufficiency.

name: Use the two-step Mayo/Alice framework
description: Apply the two-step Mayo/Alice framework: (1) determine whether the claim is directed to an unpatentable law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea; (2) if so, determine whether the claim includes an 'inventive concept' sufficient to transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application.
guidance: Cite Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank and Mayo Collaborative Servs.; perform both steps sequentially and explicitly. Step 1 asks what the claim is 'directed to'; step 2 asks whether an inventive concept exists that transforms the abstract idea into a patent-eligible application.

name: Identify the 'focus of the claimed advance' at step one
description: At step one, ask 'what the patent asserts to be the focus of the claimed advance over the prior art,' focusing on the language of the asserted claims considered in light of the specification.
guidance: Follow TecSec, Inc. v. Adobe Inc.; base the directed-to inquiry on claim language and specification rather than generalized characterizations. The claimed focus (not merely the field) controls the analysis.

name: Claims directed to results/effects that are abstract ideas
description: A claim is directed to an abstract idea if it claims a result or effect that itself is the abstract idea and merely invokes generic processes and machinery rather than a specific means or method that improves the relevant technology.
guidance: Use Smart Sys. Innovations and Elec. Power Grp. reasoning: if the claimed advance is a goal/result implemented by generic components, treat it as an abstract idea. Example: 'producing a resultant digital image ... enhanced with said second digital image' characterized as an abstract idea of enhancing one picture with another.

name: Conventional components performing basic functions do not supply inventiveness
description: Recitation of well-known, routine, conventional components (e.g., image sensors, lenses, analog-to-digital converters, memory, generic processors) that perform only their basic functions at a high level of generality does not render a claim patent-eligible.
guidance: If the claim lists commonplace components and they 'perform only their basic functions' or are recited at a high level of generality, that supports ineligibility (see In re TLI Commc’ns and Alice step two analysis). Demonstrating the components were 'well-known and conventional' weighs against finding an inventive concept.

name: Inventive concept requirement at step two
description: At step two, the claim must include an 'inventive concept' — meaning elements or combination that transform the abstract idea into a patent-eligible application, rather than merely invoking well-understood, routine, conventional components.
guidance: Mere novelty/allowance in prosecution or the fact that conventional hardware is 'vital' to implementation does not satisfy step two (see SAP Am. v. InvestPic, Two-Way Media). The claimed features must add more than routine, conventional activity.

name: Novelty/allowance/prosecution history are separate from eligibility
description: Novelty (§102), obviousness (§103), and allowance over prior art in prosecution do not, by themselves, establish §101 eligibility.
guidance: Follow Diehr and SAP Am.: demonstrate that even if claim elements are novel or were allowed over references, eligibility requires analysis under Alice; novelty is not sufficient to confer eligibility.

name: Mismatch between specification detail and claim breadth undermines eligibility
description: If the specification describes particular detailed configurations as the inventive advance but the asserted claims are drafted broadly (e.g., claiming a simpler or more generic configuration), that breadth mismatch supports a finding that the claim is directed to an abstract idea rather than the specific technical improvement.
guidance: Use this to test whether the claim actually captures the specific improvements disclosed; the presence of detailed embodiments in the spec does not save broadly drafted claims that cover only the abstract idea.

name: Conventional components 'behave as expected' supports ineligibility
description: If the recited physical components behave exactly as expected according to their ordinary use, this supports finding no inventive concept under Alice step two.
guidance: Cite In re TLI: look for whether claimed components do anything unconventional or whether they simply execute their routine functions.

name: Courts may determine §101 eligibility at the Rule 12(b)(6) pleadings stage
description: Patent eligibility under §101 can be resolved at the pleadings stage when the claim language and intrinsic record (and judicially noticeable facts) make the §101 issue clear.
guidance: See Genetic Techs., Affinity Labs: courts can consider the patent specification and other exhibits; they need not accept allegations that contradict the intrinsic record. However, careful consideration of what facts are judicially noticeable is required.

name: Use of long-standing or well-known practices evidences abstraction
description: Demonstrated, long-standing practices in the relevant field (e.g., photographers using multiple pictures to enhance each other for over a century) support that the claimed idea is an abstract practice rather than a patentable technological improvement.
guidance: When historical or field practice is undisputed or judicially noticeable, it can be considered at the pleadings stage to show the idea is conventional or abstract (Affinity Labs, district court reliance).

name: Redetermination when amendments occur post-determination
description: If an applicant amends a specification or claims after a determination on expedited examination but before examination is initiated, the examiner may instruct corrections to the expedited request and re-determine whether to permit expedited examination considering the corrections.
guidance: An examiner may grant a correction order designating a period up to one month at his discretion to allow applicant correction prior to re-determination.

name: Expedited exam without re-determination when correspondence provided
description: Where an applicant submits an explanation comparing all claims (including amended ones) with prior art cited in a foreign office notification, or correspondence explanation with claims recognized patentable by a foreign office or by international search/examination, expedited examination shall be conducted without re-determination.
guidance: Providing full correspondence/explanations that show claims alignment with recognized patentable claims avoids the need for re-determining expedited status.

name: Utility model expedited examination eligibility
description: An application for utility model registration requested for examination upon filing and then requested for expedited examination within two months from filing is eligible for expedited examination; patent applications are not eligible under this clause.
guidance: Utility models have 10-year term and tend to be for shorter lifecycle tech; however, divisional/converted utility model applications cannot claim the parent's filing date and cannot be requested for expedited examination based on those requirements.

name: Determination when search report from authorized institute is submitted
description: For applications whose search report is submitted by an authorized prior art search institute, the examiner shall make a determination on expedited examination; where the claims to be examined are identical with the claims in the prior art search report, a request for expedited examination shall be recognized.
guidance: If the search report does not meet the guideline for writing reports (see below) and cannot be used, the examiner shall make a correction order within the designated period and may reject the expedited request if not corrected.

name: Divisional applications relying on parent search report
description: Where expedited examination is determined on a parent application based on an authorized prior art search report and all claims of a divisional application in the parent's search report have already been examined, a request for expedited examination for the divisional can be filed without an additional prior art search.
guidance: Applicant should submit a contrastive explanation indicating all claims of the divisional are identical with the parent's pre-division claims and a written explanation that the prior art search results for the divisional are included in the parent's report. If examiner finds search results on divisional claims are not indicated, a correction order will be issued; failure to correct can lead to rejection of the expedited request.

name: Handling amended specifications after prior-art search request
description: If prior art search was commissioned and the specification was later amended before filing the request for expedited examination (so the search was conducted on pre-amended claims), and then a search report is re-submitted at time of filing a request after a correction order, the examiner shall make a determination on expedited examination.
guidance: Where grounds for request change due to prior art search after correction order, the examiner decides on legitimacy of the ground for change. Applicants must indicate date of request for prior art search and name of the authorized institute in corrected documents so the examiner can designate the search institution and upload the report. Prior art search reports for expedited examination are due within one month (super-expedited: 10 days); failure to submit within time after correction orders triggers further correction orders and potential rejection.

name: Appropriateness of amendments during reconsideration
description: Amendments made within 30 days from filing an appeal shall correspond to those necessitated by the final rejection and must be within the scope of the matters described in the originally filed specification or drawings.
guidance: Scope of claim amendments within 30 days is limited to: (1) narrowing the scope by restricting or deleting a claim or adding an element; (2) correcting clerical errors; (3) clarifying ambiguous description; (4) reinstating claims before amendment or certain amendments in accordance with Article 47(3) exceptions. Criteria for evaluating scope/requirements of amendments refer to Chapter 2 of Part 4 of the Examination Guidelines.

name: Comparison baseline for evaluating successive amendments
description: The baseline for evaluating whether an amendment introduces new matter or narrows scope depends on the procedural history (e.g., amendment I/II/III/IV); comparisons use either the originally filed application or the most recently entered amendment depending on circumstances.
guidance: Examples: (i) If decision to reject came after notice of non-final rejection based on amendment II and applicant files amendment III with appeal, new matter (Article 47(2)) is compared to the originally filed specification, while Article 47(3) amendment requirements are evaluated against amendment II — scope narrowing is determined by comparing corresponding claims between amendment II and amendment III. Similar comparison rules apply for other scenarios (decision after final rejection, refusal to enter amendment, etc.).

name: Protection for isolation processes and uses of natural substances (Oman)
description: Omani law excludes natural substances from patentability but does not apply that exclusion to processes of isolating those natural substances from their original environment; the law also does not exclude the use itself where it constitutes an invention.
guidance: This carve-out means isolating processes and inventive uses of known natural substances can be protected—evaluate claims for process vs product scope.

name: Omission of formerly essential element expands the Claim
description: That when an element formerly claimed as essential is omitted, the Claim is expanded.
guidance: Phillips v. Risser (1885): omission of an essential element broadens the scope and is improper.

name: Re-issue lawful if actual nature of combination unchanged
description: If the actual nature of the combination is unchanged the re-issue may vary widely from the original in its statement of the invention as well as in its Claims.
guidance: Non-essential parts erroneously described may be omitted; equivalents may be introduced if equivalence is pointed out in the re-issue specification. (See Treatise discussion and Gill v. Wells (1874)).

name: If non-essential was claimed as essential, mistake may be irremediable
description: That if non-essential features were, however, claimed as an essential element the mistake is irremediable.
guidance: Cross-references to earlier sections indicate that where the original claim treated a non-essential part as essential and it was claimed as such, the error cannot (necessarily) be cured by re-issue.

name: Where original describes two equivalent elements, re-issue may claim either alone
description: That where the original patent describes and claims two elements, either of which is the equivalent of both, the re-issue may claim either alone.
guidance: Donbar v. White (1881) and related authorities: where elements are equivalents, individual claiming in re-issue is permitted.

name: Re-issued combination may embrace sub-combinations shown in original
description: When the original patent describes and claims only the combination, but substantially sets forth any or all of the various sub-combinations in model, drawings, or specifications, these may be claimed in the re-issue, if not before abandoned or disclaimed, provided they originated from the inventive genius of the same inventor.
guidance: Christman v. Rumsey (1879), The Com Planter Patent, Jenkins v. Stetson (1887), and others support claiming sub-combinations that were sufficiently indicated in the original.

name: Re-issue may claim sub-combinations even if language differs
description: The re-issue need not describe sub-combinations in the exact language of the original, but may contain a more full and exact description of the same invention; identity of sub-combination as to elements and cooperative law must be preserved.
guidance: A re-issue for sub-combinations is sustained when the original indicated those sub-combinations as practically operative and the re-issue indicates how each may be used.

name: Timeliness supports re-issue for sub-combinations (six-month rule)
description: That where the sub-combinations claimed in the re-issue were shown in the original and the re-issue is applied for within six months after the grant of the original, inadvertence or mistake need not be specially proved; the speedy application is sufficient evidence.
guidance: Jenkins v. Stetson (1887), 82 Fed. Rep. 398: speedy application (within six months) creates presumption supporting re-issue claims for sub-combinations.

name: Re-issue may embrace individual elements of a combination
description: The re-issue of a patent for a combination may embrace such of its essential elements as are substantially indicated in the original specification, drawings, or model, and were the inventions of the same inventor.
guidance: Every element of a combination is an operative means and may be a distinct invention; re-issue can secure exclusive use of each separately claimed element if adequately indicated originally.

name: When form not material, re-issue may claim all forms or restrict to one member of a class
description: But when form is not made material by the original description, the re-issue may claim all forms of the element; or when the original describes an element as consisting in a class of acts or substances, the re-issue may confine the element to any single member of that class.
guidance: Gong Bell Mfg. Co. v. Clark (1878); St Louis Stamping Co. v. Quinby (1879) provide illustrations.

name: Cannot claim new groupings not described as sub-combinations
description: The right to bring individual elements within the operation of the patent by re-issue does not authorize the inventor to claim in it any grouping of elements which the original did not describe as a sub-combination.
guidance: Re-issue must respect groupings/sub-combinations that were indicated in the original; inventing new groupings in re-issue is impermissible.

name: Elements shown only as connected portions in drawings cannot be later claimed as inventions
description: Elements shown in the original drawings only as a connected portion of the mechanism, and so described, cannot be claimed on the re-issue as an invention.
guidance: Ives v. Sargent (1887) and related authority: mere depiction as part of larger mechanism is not sufficient to later claim that part as separate invention.

name: Re-issue cannot cover separate elements after unreasonable delay
description: That a combination-patent cannot re-issue to cover the separate elements after unreasonable delay.
guidance: Archer v. Amd (1887), Bantz v. Frantz (1882): undue delay in seeking separate-element claims can bar re-issue for them.

name: Generic/species relation limits re-issue (generic may embrace one species)
description: In the re-issue of a generic patent, the species which the original describes and which might have appropriately been claimed therein may be protected; but if the specification of the original generic patent describes two or more species, one only can be claimed in the re-issue.
guidance: A generic invention is distinct from each species; only one species may be joined with the genus in a single patent; Joinder rules and limitations discussed (JBe parte McClintock etc.).

name: Specific patent cannot re-issue to claim the genus (except narrow exception)
description: A patent for a specific invention cannot re-issue to embrace the generic; exception: where inventor described and claimed the genus in his application but was compelled (without fault) to accept a patent for the specific invention alone, he may amend to insert the genus.
guidance: Re-issue cannot be used to expand a specific patent to cover the whole genus unless original application circumstances justify it (see Ex parte Waters, Ex parte Ewart, and Treatise discussion).

name: Process and apparatus/product relations determine whether re-issue may claim apparatus or product
description: Besides the art itself, the re-issue may in certain cases cover the apparatus it employs or the product in which it results, where these were invented by the same inventor, sufficiently described originally, and neither abandoned nor disclaimed; the right depends on their relation to the art and the propriety of joining them in the original patent.
guidance: If the process cannot be performed without the apparatus mentioned, or the product uniformly follows employment of the process, the inventions are inseparably connected and re-issue may cover product or apparatus (Treatise discussion).

name: Drawings define enforceable scope
description: The ornamental features illustrated in the drawings define the enforceable scope of a design patent in the same way that claims define the enforceable scope of a utility patent.
guidance: Ensure drawings clearly and accurately depict the novel ornamental features you wish to claim because those drawings (not separate claim text) determine what is claimed and enforceable.

name: Clarity and detail
