description: Drawings must be sufficiently clear and detailed to accurately represent the claimed design and must depict every design feature the applicant wishes to claim.
guidance: Include shape, configuration, ornamental design, surface ornamentation, and surface textures as necessary. Omissions or unclear depiction may prevent proper claiming of features.

name: Black-and-white default; color permitted with petition
description: Drawings are traditionally black-and-white line drawings; color drawings may be submitted only if necessary to illustrate the claimed design properly and require USPTO approval.
guidance: Submitting color requires a petition and additional fee. If color drawings are submitted, include specification language such as: "The patent or application file contains at least one drawing executed in color. Copies of this patent or patent application publication with color drawing(s) will be provided by the Office upon request and payment of the necessary fee."

name: Solid vs broken (dashed) lines usage
description: Solid lines depict all parts of the design claimed by the applicant; broken or dashed lines illustrate portions of the design not claimed.
guidance: Use broken lines to show context or unclaimed surrounding environment (e.g., showing the rest of an article in broken lines when only an element is claimed). Note that some foreign jurisdictions do not allow broken lines, meaning dashed-line features in a U.S. application may need to be shown as solid lines in foreign counterparts.

name: Permissible graphic forms and restrictions
description: Photographs and computer-generated drawings are allowed if they meet USPTO clarity, detail, and reproducibility requirements; photographs may be used when they are the only practicable medium.
guidance: Do not combine photographs with black-and-white line drawings in the same design application. Photographs should not show environmental structure (i.e., extraneous background/context that is not part of the claimed design). Ensure high reproducibility and clarity for non-line art media.

name: Ensure claim limitations match court-found elements and level of generality
description: Examiners should ensure the claim limitations before the examiner are the same as those found to be well-understood, routine, conventional by the courts and recited at the same high level of generality.
guidance: It is not enough that the additional elements are similar to elements at issue in cited cases; they must be recited in the same manner/level of generality. Court decisions discussed in MPEP § 2106.05(d) do not imply that all computer functions are well-understood/routine/conventional, nor that a generic computer component performing a generic computer function is necessarily ineligible. See MPEP § 2106.05(f) and cases such as DDR Holdings for examples where generic components in combination can be 'significantly more.'

name: Form paragraph usage for 35 U.S.C. 101 rejections
description: Prescribed form paragraphs must be used in examining and writing rejections based on 35 U.S.C. 101 and related subject-matter eligibility determinations.
guidance: Use form paragraphs 7.04.01, 7.05, and 7.05.01 for rejections based on failure to claim an invention within statutory categories. Use 7.04.01, 7.05, and 7.05.016 for rejections based on claims directed to a judicial exception without providing an inventive concept/significantly more (Step 2B). If the judicial exception is a 'tentative abstract idea' (does not fall within MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2) groupings), also use 7.05.017 and include the TC Director's signature. Form paragraph 7.04.01 must precede first use of 35 U.S.C. 101 in all first actions and final rejections. Follow local Examiner Notes for ordering and accompanying text.

name: Contents required in form paragraph 7.05.016 (nonstatutory, judicial exception)
description: The rejection must state that the claimed invention is directed to [exception] without significantly more and explain why the exception is not integrated into a practical application and why additional elements do not amount to significantly more.
guidance: Bracketed items: [1] identify whether the claim is directed to a law of nature, natural phenomenon (including a product of nature), or an abstract idea; [2] recite what the claims recite as the judicial exception; [3] explain why the judicial exception is not integrated into a practical application; [4] identify additional elements and explain why, separately and in combination, they do not add significantly more (e.g., merely storing/retrieving info in memory are well-understood/routine/conventional computer functions). Include discussion of data gathering as insignificant extra‑solution activity or putting a product of nature into a generic container as nominal/token extra‑solution activity.

name: TC Director approval and contents for form paragraph 7.05.017 (tentative abstract idea)
description: Use 7.05.017 when treating a 'tentative abstract idea' as an abstract idea; TC Director approval and signature are required.
guidance: In bracket 1, justify why the claim limitation(s) is/are being treated as an abstract idea even though they do not fall within the groupings in MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2) (e.g., explain why the limitation is among the 'basic tools of scientific and technological work'). In bracket 2, insert the TC Director's signature. Also explain identification of the exception (how it is recited and why it is an exception) and why the combination of additional elements fails to integrate the exception into a practical application.

name: Examiner duties when evaluating applicant’s response to eligibility rejection
description: After identifying reasons why a claim is directed to a judicial exception without significantly more, the burden shifts to the applicant to amend the claim, present persuasive arguments, or submit evidence; examiners must carefully consider all of applicant's arguments and evidence rebutting the rejection.
guidance: If applicant amends, determine the amended claim’s broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) and re-perform the subject-matter eligibility analysis. If applicant's amendment, evidence, or arguments persuasively establish eligibility, the rejection should be withdrawn. If an additional element alone does not integrate the exception, it may still do so in combination with other elements (generic computer components can in combination perform non-generic functions).

name: Appropriate examiner rebuttals and reconsideration triggers when maintaining rejection
description: If applicant properly challenges examiner findings but the examiner deems it appropriate to maintain the rejection, the examiner must provide a rebuttal in the next Office action and may need to provide additional support or explanations.
guidance: Examples: (1) If applicant challenges a tentative abstract idea based on a court case and not persuasive, explain why the abstract idea is similar to the concept in the cited case. (2) If applicant presents specific argument/evidence that additional elements are not well-understood/routine/conventional, reevaluate and, if maintaining, consider whether evidence should be provided to support the rejection; if official notice was taken and challenged, provide items (A)-(C) or an affidavit/declaration. (3) If applicant adds a generic computer or claims 'specially programmed', look to whether the added elements integrate the exception into a practical application; merely adding a generic computer/programming does not automatically overcome eligibility rejections (see Alice and OIP Techs.). (4) If applicant argues lack of preemption, reconsider Step 2A (improvement to functioning of a computer/technology) and Step 2B (inventive concept in combination).

name: Clarifying the record when claims are found eligible
description: When claims are deemed patent eligible, the examiner may make clarifying remarks on the record to explain the rationale and assist applicant understanding.
guidance: Clarifying remarks can reference the portion of the specification describing claimed improvements and note claim elements producing that improvement. Remarks can be made during prosecution or with a notice of allowance. Clarifying explanations (e.g., BRI) are useful to help applicant respond to rejections (example: explain that a computer-readable medium claim's BRI covers a carrier wave and suggest narrowing amendments).

name: Initial steps for utility examination
description: Office personnel must follow procedures when reviewing applications for compliance with the utility requirement: read the claims and supporting written description, determine what applicant has claimed including specific embodiments, and ensure the claims define statutory subject matter.
guidance: If at any time it is readily apparent that the claimed invention has a well-established utility, do not impose a rejection based on lack of utility. Ensure claims define a process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, or improvement thereof.

name: Specific and substantial utility requirement and credibility assessment
description: A claimed invention must have a specific and substantial utility; utilities that are 'throw-away', 'insubstantial', or 'nonspecific' do not satisfy 35 U.S.C. 101.
guidance: Credibility is assessed from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art in view of the disclosure and any other evidence of record (e.g., test data, affidavits/declarations, patents, printed publications). An applicant need only provide one credible assertion of specific and substantial utility for each claimed invention to satisfy the requirement.

name: When to reject for lack of utility and concurrent 112(a) rejection
description: If the applicant's asserted specific/substantial utility is not credible, or no assertion is made and there is no readily apparent well-established utility, reject the claims under 35 U.S.C. 101 for lack of utility and under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre-AIA 112, first paragraph) for failure to teach how to use the invention.
guidance: The 112 rejection imposed with a 101 rejection should incorporate by reference the grounds of the corresponding 101 rejection. The examiner should shift the burden to the applicant to (i) explicitly identify a specific and substantial utility and (ii) provide evidence that a POSITA would have recognized that the identified utility was well-established at the time of filing. Ensure adequate nexus between evidence and the properties of the claimed subject matter as disclosed in the application as filed.

name: Requirements for a prima facie showing of no specific/substantial/credible utility
description: A prima facie showing that a claimed utility is not specific/substantial or not credible must establish that it is more likely than not that a POSITA would not consider the asserted utility specific/substantial/credible.
guidance: The prima facie showing must contain: (i) an explanation clearly setting forth the reasoning used to conclude the asserted utility is not specific/substantial or credible; (ii) support for factual findings relied upon; and (iii) an evaluation of all relevant evidence of record, including utilities taught in the closest prior art. Where no utility is disclosed or well-established, the showing need only establish that applicant has not asserted a utility and that on the record there is no known well-established utility.

name: Examiner response to applicant rebuttal and withdrawal of rejections
description: If applicant satisfactorily rebuts a prima facie rejection based on lack of utility, the examiner must withdraw the 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection and the corresponding 35 U.S.C. 112 rejection.
guidance: When applicant responds, the examiner should review the original disclosure, evidence relied upon in establishing the prima facie showing, any claim amendments, and any new reasoning or evidence. The examiner must recognize, fully consider, and respond to each substantive element of the applicant's response; only where the totality of the record continues to show lack of specific/substantial/credible utility should the rejection be maintained.

name: Effective filing date for CIP claims determined claim-by-claim
description: The effective filing date of a claimed invention is determined on a claim-by-claim basis and not an application-by-application basis in continuation-in-part (CIP) situations.
guidance: Any claim that is fully supported in the parent application has the parent's effective filing date; any claim that contains limitations only supported by the CIP has the CIP filing date. Prior art with a critical date more than one year prior to the child filing date will bar claims that have the child filing date (e.g., Paperless Accounting v. BART; Santarus; Studiengesellschaft Kohle v. Shell).

name: Permissible ways to overcome a pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) rejection
description: A rejection based on pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) can be overcome by: (A) persuasively arguing that the claims are patentably distinguishable from the prior art; (B) amending the claims to patentably distinguish over the prior art; (C) submitting and perfecting a benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 120 within the time period set in 37 CFR 1.78 (or filing a petition under 1.78), and establishing that the prior application satisfies enablement/written description requirements; or (D) submitting and perfecting a benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) (or filing a grantable petition under 1.78).
guidance: For (C) applicants filed on/after 9/16/2012 should file a corrected ADS under 37 CFR 1.76 referring to the prior application; pre-9/16/2012 applicants may amend the specification or file a corrected ADS. Establishment of benefit requires meeting enablement and written description per 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre-AIA 112 first paragraph). PLTIA (effective 12/18/2013) may allow restoration of provisional benefit in some circumstances (see MPEP §§211, 211.01(a)). If the prior art qualifies under 102(a) after benefit perfection, see MPEP § 2132.01.

name: On-sale bar: impermissible sale or offer more than one year before effective filing date
description: An impermissible sale has occurred if there was a definite sale, or offer to sell, more than one year before the effective filing date of the claimed invention and the subject matter of the sale or offer fully anticipated the claimed invention or would have rendered the claimed invention obvious.
guidance: Ferag AG v. Quipp and other cases demonstrate that a sale/offer more than one year prior can trigger the on-sale bar if it anticipates or combines to make the claim obvious. The on-sale bar can operate alone or in conjunction with 35 U.S.C. 103.

name: Abstract ideas are not patentable
description: Claims that are 'abstract ideas' — e.g., an abstract strategy for hedging and investment — are not patentable subject matter under §101.
guidance: If the claimed invention is mainly an abstract strategy or idea (as the Court found Bilski's claims to be), it should be excluded from patentability. Look for whether the claim adds practical application or merely recites an abstract concept.

name: Statutory definition of 'process' (§100(b)) governs
description: §100(b) defines 'process' as 'process, art or method' and includes a new use of a known process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, or material; the Court held that the doctrine of noscitur a sociis should not be used to narrow this statutory definition.
guidance: When assessing whether a claim is a 'process', rely on the statutory definition in §100(b) rather than attempting to narrow the meaning by association with neighboring words.

name: Nucleotide Sequences
description: MPEP section 803.04: Restriction practice guidance specific to claims involving nucleotide sequences.

name: Determination of Distinctness or Independence of Claimed Inventions
description: MPEP section 806: Overall framework for determining whether claimed inventions are distinct or independent for restriction purposes.

name: Compare Claimed Subject Matter
description: MPEP section 806.01: The comparative analysis of claim scope/subject matter to determine distinctness or independence.

name: Genus and/or Species Inventions
description: MPEP section 806.04: Rules for analyzing genus (generic) claims versus species (specific) claims when considering restriction.

name: Reasons for Holding of Independence or Distinctness (Species)
description: MPEP section 808.01 and 808.01(a): Specific reasons or factual findings supporting a holding that claims are independent or distinct, including species-specific considerations.

name: Indicate Exactly How Application Is To Be Restricted
description: MPEP section 814: Requirement that the restriction statement should indicate precisely how the application is to be restricted (which claims/inventions are grouped).

name: Treatment of Claims Held To Be Drawn to Nonelected Inventions
description: MPEP section 821: How claims determined to be directed to nonelected inventions are to be treated (including after election and traversal scenarios).

name: Program cost categories
description: Total program or operating costs are reported by detailed cost categories such as Personnel Services and Benefits; Travel and Transportation; Rent, Communications, and Utilities; Printing and Reproduction; Contractual Services; Training; Maintenance and Repairs; Supplies and Materials; Equipment not Capitalized; Insurance Claims and Indemnities; Depreciation, Amortization, or Loss on Asset Dispositions.
guidance: Financial reporting must present direct and allocated amounts by these categories (dollars in thousands shown). These categories align to budget object classes and support the Schedule of Spending and Statement of Budgetary Resources reconciliation.

name: Claim scope determination (claim construction and infringement inquiries)
description: The courts must conduct two inquiries: the determination of the scope of the claims, as a matter of law, and the factual finding of whether the properly construed claims encompass the accused structure.
guidance: Focus on the elements of the individual claim rather than the invention as a whole; claim scope is a legal question and whether the accused device meets that scope is a factual determination (see McGill Inc. v. John Zink Co.).

name: Literal infringement
description: Literal infringement is found when the words of the claim literally read on the accused subject matter and such subject matter embodies the essential characteristics of the invention defined by the claim.
guidance: If the accused matter falls clearly within the claim based on the claim language, infringement is established and inquiry ends (Graver Tank). Literal infringement requires each claim limitation to be present exactly. Literal copying is rare; most disputes turn on equivalents.

name: Requirement that every claim limitation be found exactly or by substantial equivalent
description: To establish infringement of a patent every limitation set forth in a claim must be found in the accused product or process exactly or by a substantial equivalent.
guidance: Analysis focuses on individual claim limitations rather than the invention as a whole (Johnston v. IVAC Corp.; Pennwalt).

name: Additional functions defense
description: A defense asserts that the accused device performs additional functions not found in the patented device.
guidance: Performing additional functions does not by itself preclude a finding of equivalence; the reference point is the limitations and functions described in the claims (Federal Circuit precedent).

name: Prosecution history estoppel (limitation on doctrine of equivalents)
description: Material representations or claim amendments made during prosecution that alter claim scope can bar the patentee from recapturing through equivalence coverage surrendered to obtain the patent.
guidance: If coverage was given up to avoid prior art (statements or amendments), the patentee cannot later use equivalence to recover that surrendered scope (Loctite; Mannesmann Demag; Diversitech example where canceled broader claim scope could not be regained).

name: Prior art limitation on equivalents
description: There can be no infringement under the doctrine of equivalents if the asserted scope of equivalency would encompass the prior art.
guidance: Determine whether a hypothetical claim that literally covered the accused device would have been allowable over the prior art; if it would not (i.e., would read on prior art or be obvious), then equivalence cannot be used to obtain that coverage. Patentee bears the burden of showing the sought range of equivalents will not encompass prior art (Wilson Sporting Goods; We Care v. Ultra‑Mark).

name: Technological advances limitation
description: Extensive technological advances affecting all claimed functions that result in multiple departures from literal readability may be too great to support a holding of infringement under the doctrine of equivalents.
guidance: An 'embellishment' made possible by advances may sometimes be protected by the doctrine, but where totality of change is large, equivalence may not apply (Texas Instruments; Datascope/Hughes Aircraft discussion).

name: Focus on claim elements (not invention as whole)
description: In determining both literal infringement and equivalence, the focus must be on the elements of the individual claim rather than the invention as a whole.
guidance: Claims define the metes and bounds of protection; analyzing the accused device must map to each claim limitation (Pennwalt Corp.).

name: Purpose of the doctrine — equitable protection against 'verbalism' and piracy
description: The doctrine was devised to provide equity and prevent 'pirating' of the patentee's invention where there is no literal infringement but liability is appropriate.
guidance: Courts emphasize that denying equivalence in appropriate cases would render patent protection 'hollow and useless' by rewarding insubstantial changes that avoid literal claim language (Graver Tank; Hormone Research Found.; Hughes Aircraft discussion). This purpose guides a balanced application but does not override estoppel and prior art limits.

name: Treaty/Article 21 claim interpretation standard (PHT draft)
description: Article 21: 'The extent of protection conferred by the patent shall be determined by the claims, which are to be interpreted in the light of the description and drawings.' Claims 'shall be so interpreted as to combine fair protection for the owner of the patent with a reasonable degree of certainty for third parties.'
guidance: Claims should not be confined to strict literal wording, nor be so loose as to extend protection to what the owner contemplated but did not claim; interpret claims in light of specification and drawings to balance fairness and certainty (text of draft PHT art.21(1)(a)-(b)).

name: Independent Inventions
description: Inventions as claimed are independent if there is no disclosed relationship between the inventions, that is, they are unconnected in design, operation, and effect.
guidance: If two or more inventions are independent and there would be a serious search and/or examination burden on the examiner if restriction is not required, applicant should be required to restrict the claims presented to one of such independent inventions. Examples: (A) two different combinations not disclosed as capable of use together having different modes of operation, functions and effects (e.g., an article of apparel and a locomotive bearing); (B) process and apparatus where the apparatus cannot be used to practice the process (a specific molding process vs. a molding apparatus that cannot practice it). Form paragraphs 8.20.02 and 8.20.03 may be used to restrict between independent, unrelated inventions and between an unrelated product and process.

name: Species — Independence/Distinctness and Restriction Permissibility
description: Where there is no disclosure of a relationship between species, they are independent inventions; a restriction is permissible if there is a patentable difference between the species and a serious search/examination burden would result if restriction is not required.
guidance: If a relationship between species is disclosed, the disclosed relation must be discussed and reasons advanced showing the relation does not prevent restriction. Election of species should not be required between species considered clearly unpatentable (obvious) over each other; group species considered clearly unpatentable over each other. Election of species may be required prior to a search in some cases (e.g., species claims with no generic claims, or species plus generic/Markush claims). See MPEP §§ 803, 808.01(a), 803.02, 809.02(a), and 809.

name: Election of Species Required — Identification and Reply Requirements
description: Where restriction between species is appropriate, the examiner should send a restriction letter (or telephone requirement) identifying generic claims (or indicating none present), clearly identify each disclosed species (or exemplary ones), and require applicant to elect a single disclosed species under 35 U.S.C. 121.
guidance: Identify species preferably by figures or examples; if not, state mechanical means, material, or other distinguishing characteristics; if inconvenient to identify individual species, claims may be grouped by species. Provide reasons why species are independent or distinct. A complete reply must include a proper election and a listing of all claims readable on the election (including any claims subsequently added). Election may be with or without traverse; to preserve petition rights, election must be with traverse and traversal must be timely presented in the election reply (failure to timely traverse loses right to petition under 37 CFR 1.144). If only generic claims are presented, restriction cannot be required unless the generic claim encompasses such multiplicity of species that an unduly extensive search would be necessary. If applicant presents species claims after an Office action on only generic claims with no restriction, the Office may require election of a single species for examination. See form paragraph 8.01 and detailed examiner notes (bracket insertions and reasons).

name: Restriction Between Linked Inventions — When to Require and Form Paragraph 8.12
description: Where an application includes otherwise properly divisible inventions that are linked by a claim which, if allowable, would require rejoinder, the examiner should require restriction (written or telephoned). Use form paragraph 8.12 when linking claim is other than a genus claim linking species inventions.
guidance: Form paragraph 8.12 identifies the linking claim(s), the inventions linked, and states that the restriction requirement as to the linked inventions is subject to nonallowance of the linking claim(s). Upon indication of allowability of linking claim(s), restriction is withdrawn and claims depending from or requiring all limitations of the allowable linking claim will be rejoined and fully examined per 37 CFR 1.104. Applicant should be advised about possible provisional statutory/nonstatutory double patenting rejections in divisional applications when divisional claims are anticipated by or include all limitations of the allowable linking claim. Examiner notes: include bracket insertions and references to related form paragraphs (8.45, 8.46, 8.47).

name: Telephone Restriction Practice
description: If an examiner determines a restriction requirement should be made, the examiner should draft the requirement and telephone the attorney/agent to request an oral election, with or without traverse, and arrange a second call generally within 3 working days to allow consideration.
guidance: If attorney/agent objects or fails to respond, mail a restriction requirement referencing the unsuccessful call. When an oral election is made, incorporate into the next Office action a formal restriction requirement including date of election, attorney/agent name, and a complete telephone interview record, followed by a complete action on the elected invention (including linking/generic claims if present). No telephone communication is needed if the requirement is complex, applicant is pro se, or examiner knows an election will not be made by telephone. Use form paragraphs 8.23, 8.23.01, 8.23.03 for telephonic election/attempts/no-telephone-permitted. Telephone practice is not permitted where no valid power of attorney is of record (use form 8.23.03). If telephonic election causes belief that C* classification picture is incorrect, examiner should submit a C* classification challenge and document the internal “Telephonic Restriction and Election Summary” (not mailed) with required details. Telephone restriction practice is limited to examiners with negotiation authority or with prior supervisory approval.

name: Indicate Exactly How Application Is To Be Restricted — Recordkeeping/Clarity Requirement
description: The examiner must provide a clear and detailed record of the restriction requirement to provide a clear demarcation between restricted inventions so it can be determined whether claims in a divisional are consonant with the restriction requirement and therefore subject to the prohibition against double patenting rejections under 35 U.S.C. 121.
guidance: Clear demarcation supports later determinations of consonance and double patenting. Use appropriate form paragraphs and fully document species/groups, reasons for restriction, claims corresponding to each group, election details, and any classification challenges. See MPEP § 804.01 and related case law (e.g., Geneva Pharms., Inc. v. GlaxoSmithKline PLC).

name: Design specification components
description: A design application primarily includes: a set of representations illustrating the article; a 'Definitive Statement' setting out features for which protection is claimed; an 'Explanatory Statement' (optional except for IC layouts); and a 'Brief Statement of Features' published with a representation.
guidance: Prepare clear representations and statements to define scope of protection; explanatory statement optional except where required.

name: Representations requirement
description: Representations (commonly drawings but may be photographs) must properly depict the features of the design as applied to the article being protected.
guidance: Ensure representations accurately show the design features to avoid ambiguity in the claimed scope.

name: Patent specification requirements
description: The patent specification is a technical and legal document drafted to protect an invention and is normally accompanied by drawings which help to explain the invention.
guidance: A complete specification must describe the invention in detail and set out claims defining the scope of protection.

name: Scope limitation: patent covers what is disclosed
description: A patent application can only cover that which is disclosed in the accompanying specification.
guidance: If developments or modifications go beyond the initial disclosure, a second filing will be necessary to include those changes in the subject matter claimed.

name: Contents required for a national application (35 U.S.C. 111(a))
description: An application must include a specification as prescribed by section 112, a drawing as prescribed by section 113, and an oath or declaration as prescribed by section 115.
guidance: The application shall be accompanied by the fee required by law. The fee, oath or declaration, and one or more claims may be submitted after the filing date within a prescribed period and under conditions (including surcharge). Failure to submit within that period causes abandonment. The filing date is when a specification, with or without claims, is received by the USPTO.

name: Filing date rules and PLTIA effect
description: The filing date of an application is the date on which a specification, with or without claims, is received in the USPTO; for design patents the filing date requires the specification including at least one claim and any required drawings (35 U.S.C. 171(c)).
guidance: Effective Dec 18, 2013 (PLTIA), nonprovisional applications (except design) filed on/after that date are no longer required to include at least one claim or any drawings to receive a filing date. A nonprovisional filed under 111(a) on or after Dec 18, 2013, may be filed by reference to a previously filed application (foreign, international, provisional, or nonprovisional) (see 35 U.S.C. 111(c)).

name: Conversion of provisional application to nonprovisional (37 CFR 1.53(c))
description: A provisional application filed under paragraph (c) may be converted to a nonprovisional application and accorded the original filing date of the provisional application.
guidance: Conversion requires the processing fee, must be filed prior to abandonment/payment of issue fee/expiration of 12 months, must include at least one claim as prescribed by 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (unless provisional already contains one), and must include filing, search, and examination fees for the nonprovisional plus any surcharge if basic filing fee or oath/declaration absent on the original filing date. Conversion may adversely affect patent term (term of any patent issuing measured from at least the filing date of the provisional resulting from conversion); applicants are advised to consider claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) instead to avoid adverse patent term impact.

name: Purpose and scope of 37 CFR 1.57(b) (incorporation by reference for inadvertently omitted material)
description: 37 CFR 1.57(b) provides that if all or a portion of the specification or drawings were inadvertently omitted from an application, and the application contains a claim for priority/benefit that was present on the filing date, and the omitted portion is completely contained in a prior-filed application, the claim for priority/benefit shall be considered an incorporation by reference of the prior-filed application as to the omitted portion.
guidance: The rule is a safeguard allowing inadvertently omitted material to be added by amendment if conditions are met. It does not require an express incorporation-by-reference statement in the later application.

name: Conditions and requirements for adding omitted material under 37 CFR 1.57(b)
description: To add omitted material under 37 CFR 1.57(b) the following must be met: (A) application filed on or after Sept 21, 2004; (B) the specification or drawings were inadvertently omitted; (C) a claim under 37 CFR 1.55 (foreign priority) or 1.78 (benefit) was present on the filing date; (D) the omitted portion must be completely contained in the prior-filed application; (E) applicant must file an amendment to include the omitted portion within any Office-set time, but no later than close of prosecution as defined by 37 CFR 1.114(b) or abandonment; (F) if the application is not otherwise entitled to a filing date, applicant must file a petition under 37 CFR 1.53(e); (G) applicant must supply a copy of the prior-filed application (except where the prior-filed application is filed under 35 U.S.C. 111); (H) applicant must supply an English translation of any non-English prior-filed application; and (I) applicant must identify where the omitted portion can be found in the prior-filed application.
guidance: All conditions are required; failure of any may render the amendment noncompliant. Where OPAP issues a Notice of Omitted Item(s), respond within the time set (commonly two months) and identify the amendment as under 37 CFR 1.57(b).

name: Status of claims statement (37 CFR 1.192(c)(3))
description: A statement of the status of all the claims in the application, or patent under reexamination, i.e., for each claim in the case, appellant must state whether it is cancelled, allowed, rejected, etc.; each claim on appeal must be identified.
guidance: Included to avoid confusion about which claims are on appeal and their precise wording, especially where post-final amendments were sought. State status as appellant understands it so disagreements can be resolved before Board decision.

name: Status of amendments statement (37 CFR 1.192(c)(4))
description: A statement of the status of any amendment filed subsequent to final rejection, i.e., whether or not the amendment has been acted upon by the examiner, and, if so, whether it was entered, denied entry, or entered in part.
guidance: This statement should reflect the appellant's understanding. It ensures clarity about post-final amendments and helps the examiner and Board resolve disagreements about claim status.

name: Summary of invention (37 CFR 1.192(c)(5))
description: A concise explanation of the invention defined in the claims involved in the appeal, required to refer to the specification by page and line number, and, if there is a drawing, to the drawing by reference characters.
guidance: Preferably read the appealed claims on the specification and any drawing. Providing page/line references and drawing characters helps the Board quickly determine where the claimed subject matter is described.

name: Argument detail for 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph (37 CFR 1.192(c)(8)(i))
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, the brief must contain an argument which specifies the errors in the rejection and how the first paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112 is complied with, including how the specification and drawings, if any, support compliance.
guidance: Specify the errors in the §112 first paragraph rejection and indicate how the disclosure supports the claim limitations. Include citations to specification page/line and figures as appropriate.

name: Argument detail for 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph (37 CFR 1.192(c)(8)(i)/(ii))
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, the brief must contain an argument which specifies the errors in the rejection and how the claims particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which applicant regards as the invention.
guidance: Explain how each claim satisfies the definiteness/claiming requirements and specify why the rejection is erroneous with reference to claim language and the record.

name: Argument detail for 35 U.S.C. 102 rejections (37 CFR 1.192(c)(8)(iii))
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102, the brief must contain an argument which specifies the errors in the rejection and why the rejected claims are patentable under 35 U.S.C. 102, including any specific limitations in the rejected claims which are not described in the prior art relied upon in the rejection.
guidance: Identify the particular claim limitations not found in the cited prior art and explain why those omissions render the rejection in error. Specify the claim(s) for which no argument was provided if applicable.

name: Argument detail for 35 U.S.C. 103 rejections (37 CFR 1.192(c)(8)(iv))
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103, the brief must contain an argument which specifies the errors in the rejection and, if appropriate, the specific limitations in the rejected claims which are not described in the prior art, and an explanation how such limitations render the claimed subject matter unobvious over the prior art. If based on a combination of references, the argument must explain why the references, taken as a whole, do not suggest the claimed subject matter and why features disclosed in one reference may not be properly combined with features disclosed in another.
guidance: A general argument that all limitations are not described in a single reference does not satisfy the requirements. Provide claimed-to-prior-art comparisons and reasoning why the combination would not have been made or would not produce the claimed invention.

name: Argument requirement for other grounds (37 CFR 1.192(c)(8)(v))
description: For each rejection not falling under subparagraphs (i) to (iv), the argument should specify the specific limitations in the rejected claims, if appropriate, or other reasons, which cause the rejection to be in error.
guidance: Some grounds (e.g., 35 U.S.C. 101 nonstatutory subject matter) may not require citing particular claim limitations; instead explain why the rejection is erroneous with appropriate legal and factual support (example: Ex parte Hibberd).

name: Amendments filed with or after appeal (37 CFR 1.116 / 1.195)
description: An amendment filed after final rejection but before jurisdiction passes to the Board may be entered if it conforms to 37 CFR 1.116; amendments introducing new matter, necessitating a new search, adding claims without canceling corresponding rejected claims, or raising new issues will not be entered. New affidavit/evidence must be in a separate paper and is governed by 37 CFR 1.195.
guidance: Entry of amendments after final rejection is not a matter of right. Examiners must respond to nonentered amendments and indicate the status of each claim of record or proposed. If a paper clearly places the application in condition for allowance, it should be entered and Notice of Allowability sent. Amendments received after jurisdiction has passed to the Board should not be considered by the examiner unless remanded by the Board.

name: Time limits for filing application claiming priority (general)
description: A person who intends to claim priority under the treaty shall file a patent application within one year from the filing date of the first application which forms the basis of the priority claim.
guidance: This is reflected in Article 54(2) and specific time calculations follow Paris Convention rules.

name: Specific time periods: one year (patent/utility model) and six months (design)
description: Within one year from the filing date of the first application if priority claim is based on a patent application or utility model registration; within six months if based on a design registration.
guidance: Time period is calculated from the day after the filing date of the first application in accordance with Article 4C(2) of the Paris Convention. If the last day falls on an official holiday/closed day, filing may be done the next business day.

name: Documents required to substantiate priority and submission deadline (1 year 4 months)
description: A person who claimed priority must submit to the Commissioner of KIPO documents specified (e.g., certified copies of the first application's specification and drawings or prescribed written statements) within one year and four months from the earliest priority date (or in designated countries the application number may suffice).
guidance: Failure to submit required evidential documents within the period voids the priority claim.

name: Examiner may request Korean translation of evidential documents; two-month period
description: Where the examiner (as Commissioner of KIPO) requires submission of a Korean translation of the evidential documents to determine patentability (e.g., where prior art may exist between priority date and filing date), the applicant must submit the Korean translation within the designated period of two months, extendable.
guidance: If translation is not submitted within the period, the examiner can invalidate the proceedings for the concerned priority claim. Translations are reference materials; amendments to translations are permitted even if they substantially change contents.

name: Substantive requirement — first application must be regular
description: The first application filed in one of the treaty countries shall be regular; the relevant law of the country determines regularity. Whether the first application remains pending does not affect the priority claim — withdrawal, abandonment, invalidation, or rejection does not negate the priority effect.
guidance: Even if the first application cannot yield a patent in its country, priority claim remains effective.

name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(5) (frivolous litigation) / obligation to avoid frivolous claims
description: Practitioner must not bring frivolous infringement suits or ITC proceedings; such conduct is prejudicial to the administration of justice.
guidance: Allegation: bringing suits and ITC proceedings without sufficient pre-filing investigation or that were frivolous supports discipline under §10.23(b)(5).

name: Controversies between parties claiming under different patents are federal
description: That a controversy between parties claiming under different patents and involving the scope of either patent is within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Federal courts, see Garver v. Bement (1888), 69 Mich. 149.
guidance: Inter-patentee boundary disputes implicate federal jurisdiction.

name: Purely contractual patent-related cases not federal
description: That a case based entirely on contract is not a patent case within the jurisdiction of the Federal courts, see Brooklyn Watch Globe Co. v. Leach (1888), 35 Fed. Rep. 8; Williams v. Star Sand Co. (1888), 35 Fed. Rep. 369.
guidance: Focus on the substantive nature of the claim determines federal jurisdiction.

name: Licensee claiming prior use must state details in notice/answer
description: That where a licensee, in defence to an action for royalties, claims that the patent is invalid on the ground of prior use, he must in his notice or answer state where and by whom the use was made, see Hat Sweat Mfg. Co. v. Reinoehl (1886), 40 Hun (N. Y.), 47.
guidance: Obligations of specificity apply to prior-use defenses in pleadings.

name: Patent not multifarious for asserting several equivalent substances
description: That a patent is not multifarious because it asserts that a number of different substances may be used as equivalents, see Celluloid Mfg. Co. v. Frederick Crane Chemical Co. (1888), 36 Fed. Rep. 110.
guidance: Claims allowing equivalent materials do not necessarily render a specification multiplicious.

name: Prior patent enabling skilled mechanic to make present device sustains defense
description: That if the description in a prior patent would enable any good mechanic to make the present device from the one there described, the defence is sustained, see United States Bung Mfg. Co. v. Independent Bung & Bushing Co. (1887), 64 Blatch. 406.
guidance: A prior patent's enabling disclosure can anticipate later claims if it teaches how to make the asserted invention.

name: Use of patent owner written statements in reexamination (§301)
description: Written statements of the patent owner filed in a proceeding before a Federal court or the USPTO regarding claim scope may be cited in a reexamination proceeding to determine the proper meaning of a patent claim.
guidance: Such written statements and related materials “shall not be considered by the Office for any purpose other than to determine the proper meaning of a patent claim.” The Committee explained these additions are intended to counteract patent owners offering differing interpretations of prior art in different proceedings, and specifically not to serve as a basis for institution of a reexamination.

name: Effect of treaties on patent rights and examination
description: Treaties duly concluded and promulgated have the same effect as domestic law; patent treaties to which Korea is a party should be referred to in examination because they may contain more detailed provisions than domestic Patent Act.
guidance: Example: Paris Convention allows priority claims even if first application was for utility model or design; examiners should recognize priority claims accordingly even if domestic law text is narrower.

name: Scope of power of agent (Article 6)
description: An agent empowered to conduct patent-related proceedings by a principal domiciled/with business in Korea may perform only expressly authorized acts. Enumerated acts include: (1) to convert, abandon or withdraw a patent application; (2) to abandon a patent; (3) to withdraw application for registering extension of patent term; (4) to withdraw a petition; (5) to withdraw a request; (6) to claim or withdraw a priority; (7) to file a petition for trial under Article 132-17; (8) to appoint a sub-agent.
guidance: These acts require express authorization; the provision also applies to patent administrators. Agents must be authorised in writing for these powers.

name: Representation for two or more persons (Article 11)
description: When two or more persons jointly perform a patent-related proceeding, each shall represent all, except for particular acts: converting/abandoning/withdrawing an application, withdrawing an application for registering extension of patent term, withdrawing a petition, withdrawing a request, claiming/withdrawing priority, filing petition for trial. If they appoint a representative and notify the Office/Board, only the appointed representative may represent all; appointment must be proved in writing.
guidance: The proviso requires written proof of appointment. The enumerated exceptional acts require unanimous consent or appointment of a representative to be performed on behalf of all.

name: Requirements of a bill in equity for infringement actions (introductory)
description: A bill in equity in actions for infringement must disclose the substantial groundwork of the case and contain averments (i.e., the claim must set forth the facts and legal basis).
guidance: The chunk begins this section and indicates the bill must state the substantive allegations necessary to ground equitable relief; further specifics follow in the treatise beyond this excerpt.

name: Prohibition on technical-opinion testimony absent pertinent-art expertise
description: A witness not qualified in the pertinent art may not testify as an expert as to anticipation, the nature of the claimed invention, what a prior art reference discloses, whether asserted claims read on the prior art reference, or obviousness (including motivation to combine).
guidance: Underlying factual questions (scope/content of prior art, differences between claimed invention and prior art, motivation to combine references) require technical expertise and are improper subjects for a patent-law expert lacking such expertise. Admission of such testimony 'serves only to cause mischief and confuse the factfinder.'

name: Limits on experts opining on legal conclusions
description: Experts should not be permitted to instruct the jury on the applicable law or to give opinions on ultimate legal issues (e.g., the court's role in claim construction and ultimate legal determinations).
guidance: Testimony designed to instruct the jury on the law or to usurp the court’s role in legal conclusions is inadmissible. Courts have repeatedly cautioned against patent lawyers testifying as to proper claim interpretation or ultimate questions of infringement/validity without proper technical qualification.

name: Perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA)
description: Patent claims are construed and questions such as what a prior art reference discloses or whether a claim would have been obvious are determined from the perspective of one of ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: Courts must evaluate disclosures, claim scope, and obviousness through the POSITA lens. A witness who is actually of ordinary skill in the art may be qualified to explain technical matters to the factfinder.

name: When obviousness may be resolved as a matter of law
description: Where the content of the prior art, the scope of the patent claim, and the level of ordinary skill in the art are not in material dispute, and the obviousness of the claim is apparent in light of these factors, summary judgment (or JMOL) is appropriate because the ultimate judgment is a legal determination.
guidance: If underlying factual inquiries are undisputed and the combination would have been obvious to a POSITA, courts may decide obviousness as a matter of law rather than leave it to the jury.

name: Implementation that is the 'work of the skillful mechanic' is not inventive
description: Applying known techniques to improve or adapt prior art in an expected way is the work of a skillful mechanic, not of an inventor, and thus may render a claim obvious.
guidance: If incorporation of a known feature from one reference into another involves only routine work by a designer of ordinary skill, that supports a finding of obviousness (Hotchkiss / Sakraida reasoning).

name: Prima Facie Case of Eligibility (examiner burden)
description: A prima facie case of eligibility requires the examiner to explain why a claim or claims are unpatentable clearly and specifically, so that applicant has sufficient notice and is able to effectively respond.
guidance: The examiner’s burden is met by clearly articulating the reason(s) why the claimed invention is not eligible, for example by providing a reasoned rationale that identifies the judicial exception recited in the claim and why it is considered an exception, and that identifies the additional elements in the claim (if any) and explains why they do not amount to significantly more than the exception. This rationale may rely, where appropriate, on the knowledge generally available to those in the art, on the case law precedent, on applicant’s own disclosure, or on evidence. Sample rejections satisfying this burden are found in the training materials (worksheets for Examples 5–8).

name: Identify the judicial exception recited in the claim and explain why it is an exception
description: When asserting a claim is directed to a judicial exception, the examiner must identify which exception is implicated by the claim language and explain why that concept is an exception under controlling case law.
guidance: Provide a reasoned rationale that identifies the judicial exception recited in the claim and why it is considered an exception; tie the claimed concept to judicial descriptors or court-identified abstract ideas rather than labeling without explanation.

name: Identify claim additional elements and evaluate 'significantly more'
description: For claims that recite a judicial exception plus additional elements, examiners must identify those additional elements and explain why they do or do not amount to 'significantly more' than the judicial exception itself.
guidance: Apply Supreme Court and Federal Circuit considerations (illustrated in Examples 21–25) to determine whether the additional elements integrate the exception into a practical application or otherwise add an inventive concept. Explain reasoning clearly so applicant can respond.

name: Use of case law, training materials, applicant disclosure, or evidence to support rationale
description: Examiners may base their eligibility rationale on knowledge generally available to those in the art, judicial precedent, the applicant’s own disclosure, or other evidence.
guidance: Cite relevant case law (see Appendix 3 index), refer to training worksheets and examples (Appendix 1 and training materials), and where appropriate, point to applicant disclosure or proffered evidence to substantiate why a claim element is well-understood, routine, or conventional.

name: Apply streamlined analysis when appropriate
description: The July 2015 Update identifies a 'streamlined' analysis path and provides examples (26 & 27) illustrating its application.
guidance: Use streamlined analysis in cases where the claim clearly is not directed to a judicial exception or where other simplifications are appropriate per the Update; consult Examples 26 & 27 for illustration of situations where the streamlined approach applies.

name: Determine when a claim is not directed to any judicial exception
description: Part of the eligibility determination is concluding that a claim is not directed to a judicial exception; Examples 23 & 27 illustrate claims found not directed to any judicial exception.
guidance: If the claim, when properly assessed, is not similar to court-identified exceptions or otherwise does not recite an exception, then eligibility can be found without further Alice-step analysis. Explain why the claim is not directed to an exception with reference to claim language and examples/case law.

name: Fundamental Economic Practices (abstract-idea descriptor)
description: Concepts relating to the economy and commerce, such as agreements between people in the form of contracts, legal obligations, and business relations (labeled 'Fundamental Economic Practices').
guidance: Examples include creating a contractual relationship, hedging, mitigating settlement risk, processing loan information, tax-free investing, and displaying an advertisement in exchange for access to copyrighted media. Use these examples when assessing whether a claim recites a fundamental economic practice.

name: An Idea 'Of Itself' (abstract-idea descriptor)
description: An idea standing alone such as an uninstantiated concept, plan or scheme, as well as a mental process that 'can be performed in the human mind, or by a human using a pen and paper.'
guidance: Examples include obtaining and comparing intangible data, data recognition and storage, organizing information to store and transmit, diagnosing by performing clinical tests and thinking about results, and other purely mental processes. Assess whether the claim merely recites an uninstantiated idea or mental process.

name: Certain Methods of Organizing Human Activity (abstract-idea descriptor)
description: Concepts relating to interpersonal and intrapersonal activities such as managing relationships or transactions between people, social activities, advertising/marketing/sales, and managing human mental activity.
guidance: Examples include structuring a sales force or marketing company, managing an insurance policy, managing a game of bingo, meal planning, and other organizational/practical human-activity methods. Use these examples to evaluate whether a claim's concept fits this descriptor.

name: Mathematical Relationships/Formulas (abstract-idea descriptor)
description: Mathematical concepts such as algorithms, mathematical relationships, mathematical formulas, and calculations.
guidance: Examples include an algorithm for converting binary coded decimal to pure binary, formulas for computing alarm limits, formulas describing electromagnetic phenomena, Arrhenius equation, algorithms for computing prices and financial analyses, and calculating differences between local and average data values. Determine whether the claim's core is a mathematical concept and evaluate integration into practical application or additional elements.

name: VC expectations by stage and sector
description: A common thread: most VCs do not ask for patents but expect them in deeptech. A 'patent pending' status with a serious provisional often suffices for seed-stage; for Series A in hardware/biotech, they expect issued or near-issued claims with credible scope.
guidance: Match IP activity to fundraising milestones: provisional/pending is often acceptable at seed; for later rounds in capital-intensive or deeptech sectors, have issued or near-issued claims with credible claim scope to satisfy diligence.

name: File provisional now, decide later
description: If unsure, file a thoroughly-disclosed provisional. Twelve months gives you time to test the product, talk to investors, and decide whether to go non-provisional. Provisionals cost a few thousand dollars and preserve all options.
guidance: Use a well-drafted provisional to preserve priority while you validate the market; ensure the provisional is thoroughly disclosed (not a thin placeholder) so it supports later claims if you convert to a non-provisional.

name: Co‑founders and inventorship
description: If two co-founders both contributed to the invention, both are inventors. Inventorship is determined by who conceived the claimed subject matter, not who paid for the work or owns the company. Get assignments executed early.
guidance: Determine inventorship by contribution to the claimed invention (not ownership or payment), list all true inventors, and secure assignments and documentation early to avoid later disputes and chain-of-title problems.

name: National stage: commencement and required submissions (35 U.S.C. 371(c))
description: Upon commencement of the national stage the applicant shall file in the Patent and Trademark Office: (1) the national fee provided in section 41(a); (2) a copy of the international application and an English translation if filed in another language (unless not required or already communicated); (3) amendments to the claims made under article 19 and translations if in another language (unless already communicated); (4) an oath or declaration of the inventor complying with section 115 and PTO regulations; and (5) an English translation of any annexes to the international preliminary examination report if in another language.
guidance: These items are required by the date of commencement of the national stage unless the Director fixes a later time. Failure to comply is regarded as abandonment (or cancellation of Article 19 amendments). Director may require a surcharge to accept late national fee or oath/declaration. Applicant may present amendments to specification, claims and drawings after national stage commencement; applicant may request earlier commencement if the application is in order.

name: Tax strategies deemed within the prior art (AIA §14)
description: For purposes of evaluating an invention under 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103, any strategy for reducing, avoiding, or deferring tax liability shall be deemed insufficient to differentiate a claimed invention from the prior art. Exclusions apply for inventions used solely for preparing tax returns or purely financial-management technology to the extent severable.
guidance: Claims directed to tax strategies are treated as lacking novelty/obviousness distinction from prior art; craft claims to recite patent-eligible technological improvements or fall into statutory exclusions.

name: Transitional program for covered business method patents (AIA §18)
description: Establishes a transitional post-grant review proceeding for covered business method (CBM) patents, to be implemented by Director regulations and employing post-grant review standards/procedures with specified exceptions and limitations (e.g., who may petition, prior-art limitations). Defines CBM patents as those claiming methods/apparatus for data processing or operations used in financial product/service practice, administration, or management, excluding patents for technological inventions.
guidance: CBM review has special standing and scope rules (e.g., petitioner requirement related to being sued), venue/appeal/stay considerations for civil litigation apply, and Director must issue regs to determine 'technological invention' status. Use caution when asserting/defending CBM patents.

name: Limitation on issuing patents directed to human organisms (AIA §33)
description: Notwithstanding any other law, no patent may issue on a claim directed to or encompassing a human organism.
guidance: Ensure claims do not attempt to claim human organisms; such claims are statutorily forbidden.

name: ADS bibliographic headings — domestic benefit information (1.76(b)(5))
description: Domestic benefit information includes the application number, filing date, status (including patent number if available), and relationship of each application for which a benefit is claimed under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), 120, 121, 365(c), or 386(c).
guidance: Providing this information in the ADS constitutes the specific reference required by 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or 120 and § 1.78; continuity data for the patent front page will be taken from the ADS. This does not apply to provisional applications.

name: Random audits of post-registration proof of use declarations
description: Conduct random audits of 'proof of use' (post-registration maintenance affidavits) under 37 C.F.R. §§ 2.161(h) and 7.37(h) to improve the integrity of the Trademark Register by cancelling registrations with unsubstantiated use claims and removing unsupported goods/services.
guidance: FY2019: over 5,000 files audited; in 62% of audited registrations, either a response deleting goods/services was filed or registration cancelled. In audited files, 78% of registrants were represented by an attorney and 22% were pro se. Goal: reduce unsubstantiated use claims and improve register accuracy.

name: Use of government funding and the risk of grant fraud allegations
description: When government grants are involved, false statements about ownership or project scope can lead to grant‑fraud investigations and criminal exposure.
guidance: The narrative shows the NSF freezing grant money and a criminal investigation/charge for alleged grant fraud; auditors will compare grant forms, ownership claims, and actual assignments — discrepancies can trigger administrative and criminal actions.

name: Use of sequence identifiers in description, claims, and drawings
description: When the description or claims discuss a sequence that is set forth in the Sequence Listing XML, the sequence must be referenced by its sequence identifier preceded by “SEQ ID NO:” (or the like) in the text of the description or claims; when a sequence is presented in a drawing, reference must be made by sequence identifier either in the drawing or in the Brief Description of the Drawings where the correlation is clear.
guidance: Sequence identifiers used in text/drawings must correspond to the identifiers assigned in the Sequence Listing XML (§ 1.832(a)). This is required even if the sequence is also embedded in the specification or claims. Use of SEQ ID NO: is a shorthand and does not change 35 U.S.C. 112 requirements. When multiple sequences appear in a drawing, ensure the correlation between drawing items and their SEQ ID NOs is clear (e.g., list in Brief Description).

name: Sequence identifiers do not alter 35 U.S.C. 112 requirements
description: Use of sequence identifiers throughout the specification and claims provides a shorthand but does not alter the statutory disclosure or claim requirements under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or 112(b).
guidance: Do not assume sequence identifiers relieve any written description, enablement, or claim definiteness obligations—these remain governed by 35 U.S.C. 112; identifiers merely simplify reference.

name: Routine optimization / result-effective variable doctrine
description: The determination whether a claimed parameter is a result-effective variable is part of a broader routine optimization analysis: 'where the general conditions of a claim are disclosed in the prior art, it is not inventive to discover the optimum or workable ranges by routine experimentation.'
guidance: Even if a prior-art reference does not disclose a specific parameter for the claimed subject matter, the Board may consider whether that parameter would have been recognized as result-effective; if so, optimization of that parameter is normally obvious. (Citations: In re Aller, In re Antonie, E.I. DuPont, Applied Materials.)

name: Expectation-of-success standard (reasonable, not absolute)
description: An expectation of success for obviousness 'need only be reasonable, not absolute.'
guidance: Unpredictability in the art does not preclude obviousness if there was a reasonable probability of success; prior art showing some successes for components can support a reasonable expectation for combined claims. (Citations: Pfizer v. Apotex, Univ. of Strathclyde discussion.)

name: Prior-art references not limited to working examples
description: A prior art reference is not limited to its specific working examples.
guidance: Board may rely on the general teachings of a reference even when the reference does not exemplify every claimed embodiment; courts will accept that the disclosure of a composition as 'immunogenic' implies immunogenicity rather than requiring explicit experimental exemplars for every serotype. (Cites In re Mills; applied in analysis of GSK-711 and Merck-086.)

name: Motions to amend under §316(d) and 37 C.F.R. §42.121 — patentability inquiry
description: A patent owner’s motion to amend (proposing substitute claims) may be denied if the proposed claims are not independently patentable (e.g., are unpatentable as obvious over the prior art).
guidance: The Board must assess whether proposed substitute claims would have been patentable, including analyzing every recited limitation (for example, functional/result limitations like a claimed '2-log increase' in IgG). Denial is reviewed under the APA for arbitrary and capricious agency action.

name: Agency explanation requirement for motions to amend (reasoned basis enabling review)
description: When denying a motion to amend, the Board must provide a 'reasoned basis' sufficient to enable meaningful judicial review and to prevent the court from supplying reasons the agency did not give.
guidance: The Board must set forth a sufficiently detailed explanation on issues made material by governing law; conclusory statements without analysis of claimed limitations (e.g., ignoring a recited 2‑log IgG result limitation) fail to meet this requirement and warrant remand.

name: Requirement to analyze all claim limitations including result-limiting functional language
description: The Board must consider whether the incorporation of claimed elements would satisfy not only compositional elements but also any recited functional/result limitations (e.g., immunogenicity metrics such as 'more than a 2-log increase above baseline in serum IgG').
guidance: A decision that ignores that a proposed claim requires a specified quantitative result (and fails to analyze whether the prior art would have rendered that result reasonably expected across the recited serotypes) is unsupported by substantial evidence and warrants remand.

name: Remand / vacatur when Board fails to support determination with substantial evidence
description: If the Board’s determination that proposed claims are unpatentable is not supported by substantial evidence (or the Board fails to address material claim limitations), the appellate court will vacate and remand for further consideration.
guidance: Remand is appropriate where Board decisions are silent or conclusory on critical points (e.g., Sanofi Decision’s silence on why proposed claims 48 and 49 would have been obvious given their 2‑log requirement).

name: USPTO statutory authority over practitioner conduct (35 U.S.C. §§ 2(b)(2)(D), 32)
description: The Director and USPTO have statutory authority to regulate recognition and conduct of practitioners and to suspend or exclude persons from practice for incompetence, disreputability, or gross misconduct (35 U.S.C. § 32; 35 U.S.C. § 2(b)(2)(D)).
guidance: This jurisdiction is broad and applies to practitioners engaged in patent, trademark, and other non-patent matters; claims that § 32 applies only to patent matters are rejected based on the statutory scheme and precedent (Kroll v. Finnerty; Haley v. Lee; 37 C.F.R. § 11.19(a)).

name: Jurisdictional challenges may be raised at any time
description: Subject-matter jurisdiction arguments are not forfeited by failure to raise them earlier and may be raised at any time.
guidance: Citing Cotton and related authorities, jurisdiction is a threshold issue that can be raised even on reconsideration, though a properly supported jurisdictional claim must still have merit to succeed.

name: Claim must disclose and reflect an improvement to technology
description: The specification should disclose sufficient details such that one of ordinary skill in the art would recognize the claimed invention as providing an improvement, and the claim itself must reflect the improvement in technology.
guidance: Important considerations: whether the claim covers a particular technical solution or way to achieve a desired outcome rather than merely claiming the idea of a solution; whether the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) is limited to computer implementation. See MPEP § 2106.05(a) for further principles and examples. Case guidance: a claimed process that can be performed without a computer cannot be characterized as an improvement in a computer (Synopsys, Inc. v. Mentor Graphics Corp., 839 F.3d 1138 (Fed. Cir. 2016)). Mere automation of manual processes or increasing speed solely from a general-purpose computer's capabilities is not sufficient (FairWarning IP v. Iatric Sys., 839 F.3d 1089; Credit Acceptance Corp. v. Westlake Services, 859 F.3d 1044). Claims that are only conventional implementations on generic components are also insufficient to show an improvement (Affinity Labs v. DirecTV; TLI Communications v. AV Auto.).

name: Mere automation or conventional computer implementation is insufficient
description: Mere automation of manual processes, increasing speed solely due to a general-purpose computer, or implementing conventional activity on generic computer components does not show an improvement in computer-functionality or other technology.
guidance: Cases: FairWarning IP, Credit Acceptance, Affinity Labs, TLI Communications. Examiners should look beyond mere use of computer components to determine whether the claim adds a technical improvement.

name: Resolve improvement question early in Alice/Mayo analysis
description: Examiners are encouraged to resolve whether a claim improves computer-functionality or other technology as early as possible in the eligibility analysis (Step 2A or 2B).
guidance: A claim that is directed to a clear improvement (e.g., Enfish) could be found eligible at Pathway A (streamlined Step 2A) or at Pathway B as not being directed to an abstract idea. Even if an improvement is not clear enough for Step 2A, it may still contribute to eligibility in Step 2B as part of the inventive concept analysis. See Amdocs v. Openet for an example where an unconventional distributed network architecture contributed to eligibility at Step 2B.

name: Claim must recite the abstract idea to be directed to it
description: If a claim is based on or involves an abstract idea but does not recite (set forth or describe) anything similar to a judicially-identified abstract idea, then the claim is not directed to an abstract idea.
guidance: Step 2A requires a claim to recite an abstract idea in order to be directed to that idea. Judicial decisions: Enfish (self-referential table was based on but not directed to an abstract idea), DDR Holdings (modifying hyperlink protocol not directed to abstract idea), Trading Techs. (graphical UI improvement not directed). Non-limiting hypothetical examples of claims that do not set forth an abstract idea: a printer with mechanical components; a washing machine with controller; an earring glucose sensor with memory; a BRCA1 sequencing PCR method; a BIOS loading method that transfers BIOS from remote memory to local volatile memory and transfers control.

name: Claim that recites an abstract idea may nonetheless be directed to an improvement
description: If a claim recites an abstract idea, but the claim as a whole is directed to an improvement (or otherwise clearly does not seek to tie up the abstract idea), then the claim is not directed to an abstract idea.
guidance: The presence of additional elements demonstrating an improvement can shift the focus from the abstract idea to a technical improvement. Types of improvements courts have recognized and cases: McRO (automatic lip synchronization and facial animation), Enfish (self-referential table improvement), Research Corporation (blue noise mask plus steps that improved computer functioning). Non-limiting hypothetical examples: surgical shears with pressure regulator to limit force; robotic arm assembly with sensor and control for smooth motion; autofocus camera with algorithm and drive mechanism; internal combustion engine with exhaust gas recirculation controlled by a processor.

name: Rely on concepts identified in cases, not judicial descriptors
description: When determining whether a claimed concept is similar to a concept the courts have identified as an abstract idea, examiners should rely on the concepts identified in the cases rather than the judicial descriptors themselves.
guidance: Associations between concepts and judicial descriptors (e.g., 'fundamental economic practices') are not mutually exclusive and some concepts may map to multiple descriptors (e.g., hedging in Bilski). Use the case law concepts as the analytic anchor rather than labels.

name: Category: Concepts relating to mitigating risks
description: Concepts for mitigating risks (e.g., intermediated settlement or settlement risk mitigation) have been identified as abstract ideas.
guidance: Example: Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank (claims to intermediated settlement and creating 'shadow' account records were held directed to the abstract idea of intermediated settlement). Other examples include financial instruments designed to hedge risk (In re Chorna).

name: Enablement / adequate public disclosure
description: The public must be put in possession of the manufacture in a way as ample and beneficial as the patentee enjoys it.
guidance: A method, if claimed, must be described so clearly and evidently that no experiments are necessary to learn it and put it into practice as beneficially as the patentee enjoys it.

name: Caveat content and filing procedure
description: A caveat for an incomplete invention must set forth the design and purpose thereof, and its principal and distinguishing characteristics, and is filed on payment of twenty dollars and preserved in secrecy.
guidance: If another application that may interfere is made within one year, the commissioner shall deposit the description/specifications/drawings/model in confidential archives and mail notice to the caveat filer, who then has three months to file his description/specifications/drawings/model; if specifications of claim interfere, like proceedings follow as in interfering applications.

name: Grounds and procedure for reissue / renewal of patent (defective/insufficient specification)
description: Whenever a patent is inoperative or invalid by reason of a defective or insufficient description or specification, or by claiming more than the inventor had a right to claim as new, and the error arose by inadvertence/accident/mistake without fraudulent intention, the Commissioner may, upon surrender of the patent and payment of fifteen dollars, cause a new patent to be issued for the same invention for the residue of the original term in accordance with the corrected description and specification.
guidance: In case of death or assignment, executors/assignees have similar rights. The reissued patent and corrected specification have the same legal effect for actions subsequently arising as though originally filed in corrected form. The patentee may also annex descriptions of newly-invented improvements by like proceedings and fee.

name: Revision/restriction of claims on reissue or addition of improvements
description: When application is made for addition of a newly-discovered improvement or for correction and reissue, the specification of claim annexed to every such patent shall be subject to revision and restriction in the same manner as original applications; the Commissioner shall not add improvements nor grant reissue until the applicant has entered a disclaimer or altered his specification of claim in accordance with the Commissioner's decision.
guidance: If dissatisfied with the Commissioner's decision, the applicant has the same remedies and privileges as in original patent-application proceedings.
