name: Scope of claims on reissued patents (no obligation to claim everything originally claimed)
description: On reissue the patentee is not required to claim in the renewed patent all things which were claimed in the original patent; he may omit parts and retain what he deems proper.
guidance: Statutes and case law permit restricting or altering claims on reissue if original claims were excessive; the Commissioner may require disclaimers or alterations.

name: Conditions to be entitled to an international filing date
description: Article 11(1), Rule 20.1, Rule 20.2 — The RO must accord an international filing date if: (i) applicant does not obviously lack the right to file at that RO (residence/nationality considerations); (ii) application is in a prescribed language; (iii) the application contains at least: (a) indication it is intended as international, (b) a request constituting designation of a Contracting State, (c) name of applicant (sufficiently identifying), (d) a part appearing to be a description, (e) a part appearing to be a claim or claims.
guidance: Name may be misspelled or incomplete so long as identity can be established; see paragraph 6.005 for full conditions.

name: Language-mix rules for accord of filing date
description: Article 11(1)(ii), Article 11(1)(iii), Rule 12.1, Rule 20.1(c)/(d) — For accord of filing date, in most ROs the requirement is met if the description and claims are in a language accepted by the RO; other elements not in that language may be corrected later without affecting filing date.
guidance: A translation must be furnished where the filing language is not accepted by the ISA and/or not a language of publication. In some Offices Rule 20.1(c) is incompatible with national law, in which case all elements must comply with Rule 12.1 before a filing date is accorded (see Annex C for details).

name: Presumption that claims differ in scope
description: No two claims in the same patent should be interpreted to cover the same thing. It is presumed that each claim in a patent is different in scope and meaning from all other claims.
guidance: Use this presumption when construing multiple claims: treat independent and dependent claims as having different scope unless clear evidence indicates otherwise. This is the basic rule of claim differentiation expressed on the page.

name: Doctrine tends to produce broader claim constructions
description: Application of the doctrine generally results in broader constructions of patent claims, because it is most commonly used to prevent defendants from limiting a broad genus claim to the range of embodiments actually disclosed or more explicitly recited in other claims.
guidance: When faced with an argument that a broad (genus) claim should be read narrowly to match specific embodiments recited elsewhere in the patent, invoke claim differentiation to support a broader construction. This is commonly used defensively by patentees and plaintiffs in litigation to resist narrowing interpretations.

name: Limitation on patentees using the doctrine to broaden claims
description: However, this doctrine cannot be used by the patentee to broaden claims.
guidance: Do not allow patentees to expand claim scope beyond what the claim language permits by relying on claim differentiation as a tool to enlarge claim coverage; the doctrine is not a vehicle for expanding claim scope beyond its proper construction.

name: Prohibition on importing limitations from other claims into an independent claim
description: It is improper for courts to read into an independent claim a limitation explicitly set forth in another claim.
guidance: Avoid importing limitations: courts should not construe an independent claim to include limitations that appear only in dependent claims. See cited authority: Environmental Designs, Ltd. v. Union Oil Co., 713 F.2d 693, 699 (Fed. Cir. 1983).

name: Lack of inventive concept
description: Even if a claim is directed to an abstract idea, it must include an 'inventive concept' — additional limitations that transform the idea into patent-eligible subject matter.
guidance: Courts routinely find no inventive concept where the claims merely apply the abstract idea using generic computer, telephonic, or network components, routine or well‑understood activity, or conventional implementation. The inventive-concept inquiry looks for meaningful limitations beyond the abstract idea itself.

name: Preemption / risk of monopolization concern
description: Claims should not be so broad as to preempt the abstract idea itself or monopolize fundamental practices.
guidance: Courts consider whether the claim would effectively prevent others from using the abstract idea and whether the claim sets meaningful boundaries. Lack of specificity that risks monopolization weighs against eligibility.

name: Claim specificity / sufficient structure required
description: To transform an abstract idea into patentable subject matter, claims must ground the idea in specific structure, unique components, or particularized implementation rather than vague 'rules engines' or general directives.
guidance: Examples: a 'rules engine' described only as general instructions, or a component that 'can be configured' to perform a function, is insufficient. Claims that fail to describe how components are customized or how they operate do not provide the specificity courts require.

name: Novelty/nonobviousness does not determine §101 eligibility
description: A claim's novelty or nonobviousness under §§102/103 does not make it patent-eligible under §101.
guidance: Courts repeatedly explain that even if an invention is novel and nonobvious, if it only implements an abstract idea using conventional technology it may still be ineligible under §101.

name: Limiting claims to a particular technological environment is often insufficient
description: Simply stating that an abstract idea is implemented in a mobile, Internet, cloud, or interactive television environment does not necessarily confer eligibility.
guidance: Courts have held that a technological-environment limitation does not save claims where the implementation uses conventional components and does not solve a computer-specific problem.

name: Dependent claims must supply meaningful limitations
description: Dependent claims that add only routine or unspecified limitations (e.g., no details about types, sources, or actions) do not typically provide the inventive concept necessary to overcome §101 rejections.
guidance: Courts have found dependent claims unhelpful where they do not specify what is collected, where from, or what specific actions follow a match, or where they merely recite additional generic steps.

name: Claims must describe how claimed solution improves technology
description: Courts look for recitations showing that the claimed invention provides a concrete technological improvement (e.g., changes how computers operate, optimizes interfaces, new searching/analysis/encryption techniques).
guidance: Assertions of hypothetical benefits (e.g., massive scale-up, reduced expense, privacy improvements) that are not recited in the claims themselves will not establish eligibility.

name: Using longstanding business practices is abstract
description: Claims that merely implement traditional business methods, economic strategies, or conventional commercial transactions (coupons, discounts, booking/tracing shipping, intermediated transactions) are treated as abstract ideas.
guidance: Courts cite examples where the claimed systems merely digitize or automate business practices without inventive technological improvements.

name: Claims framed as information collection/organization are often abstract
description: Claims that claim gathering, storing, labeling, normalizing, or organizing data (e.g., containerized data, searchable containers, data normalization, indexing) are frequently deemed abstract absent specific technological improvements.
guidance: Courts analogize such claims to libraries, ledgers, folders, time-cards and emphasize that implementing these practices on a computer without specific improvements does not confer eligibility.

name: Claims should not be judged solely by the alleged 'genius' of the idea
description: Even clever or creative ideas are not automatically patent-eligible if they claim an abstract idea implemented in a conventional way.
guidance: Courts note that patent law does not grant protection for all 'inspirations of genius' absent the requisite inventive concept and specificity.

name: Improvements limited to a particular machine must show meaningful modification
description: Simply limiting an abstract idea to a machine or particular device (e.g., elevator computer, mobile device) does not save the claim unless the limitation meaningfully changes how the machine operates.
guidance: Courts reject arguments that tying an idea to a particular machine is dispositive if the claimed machine is a generic computer performing conventional tasks.

name: No requirement that described apparatus be the best possible
description: It is not necessary that the apparatus described should produce the greatest amount of benefit; it is sufficient if persons acquainted with the art would construct an apparatus productive of some benefit.
guidance: The specification need not claim the optimal embodiment; a working, beneficial embodiment that a skilled person can build suffices.

name: Distinguish what is new and what is old
description: The specification must inform the public what is new and what old.
guidance: Clearly identify novel features versus previously known elements. Failure to do so may lead to the patent being construed as claiming the whole apparatus or parts that are old.

name: Avoid ambiguous or generic terms that mislead
description: If the terms in which the description of the subject is expressed be ambiguous...the grant would be invalid. Use of generic terms where only one species works (e.g., 'fossil salt' vs 'sal gem') can make the specification bad.
guidance: Be precise in naming materials and limits. Examples: claiming 'any other substance' can be fatal if the embodiment only works with a narrower set; technical terms with nonstandard meanings should be explained.

name: Specification should warn the public what is prohibited and teach the invention
description: The specification is to warn the public of what is prohibited, and to teach them the invention.
guidance: Claims/description should clearly demarcate the patentee's exclusion (what the public must avoid) and provide teaching sufficient for use by others.

name: Common defects in specifications (summary list)
description: The specification is bad, when: 1. The terms are ambiguous. 2. Necessary descriptions are omitted. 3. Parts claimed are not original. 4. Things are put in to mislead. 5. The drawings are incorrect. 6. One of different ways, or different ingredients named, fails. 7. One of several effects specified is not produced. 8. The things described are not the best known to the patentee.
guidance: Use this checklist when reviewing a specification. Each item is illustrated by cases in the text (e.g., ambiguous 'fossil salt', omitted necessary steps, misleading extra parts, failing species in a claimed class).

name: US Special Rules of Practice for US-designated IDAs
description: IDAs that designate the US must comply with specific US rules under 37 C.F.R. §§ 1.1001–1.1071.
guidance: Key US requirements: include a specification and a claim; claim language must fit US design law (see 37 C.F.R. §§ 1.1024 and 1.1025); IDAs designating the US can include no more than one claim directed to only one independent and distinct design (37 C.F.R. §§ 1.1025 and 1.1064); cannot request deferment of publication when designating the US (37 C.F.R. § 1.1028); must include an oath or declaration for US filing (37 C.F.R. § 1.1021(d)(3) and § 1.1067(b)); corrections by IB must be sent to USPTO before applicable (37 C.F.R. § 1.1065).

name: Claim Language Form Requirement
description: The claim language must be in the form of an 'ornamental design' of the subject article 'as shown' or 'as shown and described' for US-designated IDAs.
guidance: Draft the claim to conform to the specified formulation (37 C.F.R. § 1.1025) to avoid formal defects and ensure compatibility with US design practice.

name: Particularity vs. Result-Oriented Recitation (consideration under 'apply it')
description: Whether the claim merely recites the idea of a solution or outcome (result-oriented, functionally stated) without details of how the solution is accomplished.
guidance: Claims that attempt to cover any solution to an identified problem with no restriction on how the result is accomplished and no description of the mechanism do not integrate a judicial exception into a practical application (equivalent to 'apply it'). By contrast, claiming a particular solution or a particular way to achieve a desired outcome may integrate the exception into a practical application. Cases: Electric Power Group (caution against claims so result-focused as to cover any solution), Intellectual Ventures/Capital One (XML example: merely using abstract idea in context of XML without specifying how), Internet Patents Corp. v. Active Network (maintaining state of data without mechanism described).

name: Particularity/Generality of the Application of the Judicial Exception (consideration under 'apply it')
description: How particular or general is the claimed application of the judicial exception across fields of endeavor and modes of accomplishing the effect.
guidance: A claim with broad applicability across many fields that generically recites an effect or claims every mode of accomplishing that effect may amount to merely adding 'apply it' and not provide meaningful limitations (O’Reilly v. Morse, The Telephone Cases, Internet Patents Corp.). Limitations that confine the exception to a particular, practical application may amount to significantly more (BASCOM: specific ISP‑located filtering tool with per‑user customization).

name: Insignificant Extra‑Solution Activity
description: Whether additional elements add more than insignificant extra‑solution activity to the judicial exception; 'extra‑solution activity' are activities incidental to the primary process/product (pre‑solution or post‑solution) that are nominal or tangential additions.
guidance: Insignificant extra‑solution activity (e.g., mere data gathering, routine post‑solution output) does not amount to an inventive concept, particularly when well‑understood or conventional (Parker v. Flook; Mayo). Examiners should consider overlap with particular machine/particular transformation and field-of-use/technological environment considerations; however, well‑understood/routine/conventional is evaluated in Step 2B and should not be considered in Step 2A Prong Two. Examiners should explain in rejections why such elements do not meaningfully limit the claim (see MPEP §2106.07(a)). Examples of extra-solution activity: pre‑solution data gathering (e.g., obtaining credit card transaction info), post‑solution output (e.g., printing a report), testing to obtain inputs, presenting offers and gathering response statistics. Cases: Flook (post‑solution alarm limit adjustment), Mayo (measuring metabolites), OIP Technologies (presenting offers and gathering statistics), CyberSource (verifying transactions).

name: Factors for Determining Insignificant Extra‑Solution Activity
description: Considerations to decide if an additional element is insignificant extra‑solution activity.
guidance: Examiners may consider: (1) Whether the extra‑solution limitation is well known — token or conventional activities (cases: Bilski, Flook, Intellectual Ventures/Erie). Note overlap with well‑understood/routine/conventional (not to be used in Step 2A Prong Two). (2) Whether the limitation is significant — does it impose meaningful limits on the claim so it is not nominally/tangentially related (cases: Ultramercial v. Hulu, Apple v. Ameranth). This factor is considered in Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B. (3) Whether the limitation amounts to necessary data gathering and outputting — i.e., all uses of the recited judicial exception require such data gathering or output (cases: Mayo; OIP Technologies). This is considered in Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B.

name: Field of Use and Technological Environment
description: Whether additional elements do more than generally link the use of a judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use.
guidance: Limiting an abstract idea to a particular field of use or adding token post‑solution components does not make the concept patentable (Parker v. Flook; Bilski). A claim cannot be made eligible simply by acquiescing to limiting the formula's reach to a particular technological use (Diamond v. Diehr). Examiners should treat mere field‑of‑use/technological environment limitations as not providing significantly more than the judicial exception. Example: Flook — mathematical formula applied in a catalytic chemical process was insufficient to render patentable.

name: Domestic priority and foreign priority via ADS constitute required claims
description: Providing domestic or foreign priority information in an ADS constitutes the specific reference/claim for priority required by statute/rule.
guidance: Domestic priority information furnished in ADS (application number, filing date, status, relationship) constitutes the specific reference required by 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or 120 and § 1.78(a)(2) or (a)(5). Foreign priority information in ADS constitutes the claim for priority required by 35 U.S.C. 119(b) and 37 CFR 1.55(a). Note: 37 CFR 1.76(b)(5) and (b)(6) do not apply to provisional applications.

name: Contents of the International Search Report (ISR)
description: The international search report contains citations of documents considered to be relevant (PCT Rule 43.5 & Admin. Instr. Sec. 503), classification of the subject matter (PCT Rule 43.3 & Admin. Instr. Sec. 504), and an indication of the fields searched (PCT Rule 43.6).
guidance: Citations of particular relevance must be specially indicated (Admin. Instr. Sec. 505). Citations of certain special categories must be indicated (Sec. 507). Citations not relevant to all claims must be related to the specific claim numbers (Sec. 508). If only certain passages are relevant, identify page/column/lines (PCT Rule 43.5(e)).

name: Box 2 / Box No. II — Limitation of the subject of the international search
description: The report must indicate whether any claims are unsearchable for specified reasons and identify the claims and reasons when limitations are applied.
guidance: Three categories where such limitations may arise are: (A) claims not required to be searched by the ISA (see MPEP §1843.02); (B) claims where a meaningful search cannot be carried out (see MPEP §1843.03); (C) multiple dependent claims not complying with PCT Rule 6.4(a). If limitations applied, check Box 2 and complete Box No. II with details.

name: Box 5 — Abstract contents and form
description: The abstract must be a summary of the disclosure in the description, claims, and drawings; indicate the technical field, clearly state the technical problem, the gist of the solution, and principal uses; include applicable chemical formulae (PCT Rule 8.1).
guidance: Abstract should be as concise as disclosure permits (preferably 50–150 words in English). It must not contain statements on alleged merits or speculative applications. Each main technical feature mentioned and illustrated by a drawing should be followed by a reference sign in parentheses (PCT Rule 8.1(d)). On the ISR first sheet indicate approval of text or enter a newly established abstract and state the defect (e.g., too long, missing). Applicant may submit modifications within one month from mailing of the ISR (PCT Rule 38.3).

name: Box C — Documents considered to be relevant (three components)
description: Completion of Box C involves (A) the citation category, (B) the citation plus identification of relevant passages where appropriate, and (C) identification of relevant claim numbers.
guidance: Keep multiple citations showing the same inventive elements to a minimum. When citing a document, clearly indicate the portions most relevant. Use the continuation sheet if necessary and check the 'Further documents listed...' box.

name: Citation category — A (state of the art)
description: Category 'A' indicates a document that defines the state of the art and does not prejudice novelty or inventive step.
guidance: For 'A' citations it is generally not necessary to indicate relevant claims unless there is a good reason (e.g., clear lack of unity and relevance only to particular claims).

name: Citation category — P (intermediate documents)
description: Category 'P' is used for documents published between the filing date of the application being searched and the date of priority claimed (or on the very day of earliest priority); 'P' is accompanied by relevance symbol (e.g., 'P,X').
guidance: Use when a document falls into the intermediate publication timeframe per PCT Article 2(xi)(b).

name: Citation identification and relationship to claims
description: Identify any document according to WIPO Standard ST.14. Each citation should include a reference to the claims to which it relates (Admin. Instr. Sec. 508), except 'L' and generally 'A' documents (unless reasons exist).
guidance: If different parts of a cited document are relevant to different claims, relate each relevant part to the specific claims. The same document may have different categories relative to different claims (example formatting provided).

name: Written Opinion — scope and timing
description: The ISA shall, at the same time as it establishes the ISR (or the Article 17(2)(a) declaration), establish a written opinion as to whether the claimed invention appears to be novel, to involve an inventive step (non‑obvious), and to be industrially applicable, and whether the international application complies with the Treaty/Regulations to the extent checked by the ISA (PCT Rule 43bis.1).
guidance: The written opinion shall contain other observations as provided by the Regulations, notify the applicant of defects, fully state reasons for the opinion (per Rules 66.1bis and 66.2(b)), and invite a written reply with amendments where appropriate (PCT Rule 66.2(c)). If a demand for international preliminary examination is filed, the written opinion may be treated as the written opinion of the IPEA (subject to Rule 66.1bis conditions).

name: Specification and claim drafting subsection labeling
description: The specification paragraphs are renumbered as subsections (a) In General, (b) Conclusion, (c) Form, (d) Reference in Dependent Forms, (e) Reference in Multiple Dependent Form, and (f) Element in Claim for a Combination, with corresponding changes in textual references.
guidance: Structural/formatting changes that clarify subsection headings and the labeling of claim-related provisions; impacts how specification text and claim rules are cited and applied.

name: Entire market value rule limitation
description: Unless the claimant shows that the patent’s specific contribution over the prior art is the predominant basis for market demand for an infringing product or process, damages may not be based upon the entire market value of the products or processes involved that satisfy that demand.
guidance: Prevents using the entire market value of a multi-component product unless the patented feature drives consumer demand (predominant basis test).

name: Increased damages for willful infringement and required proof
description: A court that has determined that the infringer has willfully infringed may increase the damages up to three times the amount of damages found or assessed under subsection (a). A court may find willful infringement only if the patent owner presents clear and convincing evidence that (A) after receiving written notice from the patentee alleging acts of infringement with particularity and identifying each claim and accused product/process, the infringer, after reasonable opportunity to investigate, thereafter performed one or more of the alleged acts; (B) the infringer intentionally copied the patented invention with knowledge it was patented; or (C) after being found by a court to have infringed, the infringer engaged in conduct not colorably different and resulted in a separate finding of infringement.
guidance: Creates a heightened standard (clear and convincing evidence) and specifies permitted grounds for finding willfulness, including a particularized pre-suit notice requirement as one route to willfulness.

name: Procedures and limitations for written statements submitted
description: A party submitting written statements shall include any other documents, pleadings, or evidence from the proceeding that address the patent owner’s statements or the claims; such statements shall not be considered for any purpose other than to determine the proper meaning of the claims that are the subject of a request in a proceeding ordered pursuant to section 304 or 313; materials subject to a protective order shall be redacted.
guidance: Limits the use of submitted written statements to claim-construction purposes in specified proceedings and requires inclusion of related materials and redaction where subject to protective orders.

name: Reexamination — Director determination of substantial new question within three months
description: Within three months after the owner of a patent files a request for reexamination, the Director shall determine whether a substantial new question of patentability affecting any claim is raised by the request, with or without consideration of other patents or printed publications. The existence of a substantial new question is not precluded by prior citation or consideration by the Office.
guidance: Imposes a three-month gatekeeping timeframe for Director to decide whether reexamination is warranted and clarifies that prior citation does not bar finding a substantial new question.

name: Post-grant review — who may file and scope
description: A person who is not the patent owner may file a petition for cancellation seeking to institute a post-grant review proceeding to cancel as unpatentable any claim of a patent on any ground that could be raised under paragraphs (2) or (3) of section 282(b). The Director shall establish fees.
guidance: Limits petitioners to non-owners and allows challenges on statutory invalidity grounds; requires fee-setting by the Director.

name: Director's gatekeeping and nonreviewable institution decision
description: The Director shall determine if the petition and evidence establish a substantial question of patentability for at least one claim and may initiate post-grant review if sufficient grounds exist. The Director shall notify parties in writing within 60 days and any such determination to institute or deny is not reviewable.
guidance: Gives the Director final, nonappealable authority to institute post-grant review within a 60-day decision window.

name: Amendment of patent during post-grant review — scope and limits
description: In response to a challenge, the patent owner may file one motion to amend to cancel any challenged claim, propose substitute claims for each challenged claim, or amend drawings/other than claims. Additional motions allowed only for good cause. An amendment may not enlarge the scope of the claims or introduce new matter.
guidance: Allows limited amendment options but forbids broadening or adding new matter; extra amendments require good cause.

name: Final decision, effect, and issuance of certificate after post-grant review
description: If the proceeding is instituted and not dismissed, the PTAB shall issue a final written decision on patentability of any challenged claim and any new claim added. If final and appeal time expired or appeal terminated, the Director shall issue and publish a certificate canceling any claim finally determined unpatentable and incorporating any new claim determined patentable. New claims incorporated have the same effect as set forth in section 252 for reissued patents regarding prior users.
guidance: Specifies final written decision requirement, administrative certificate process, and legal effect of incorporated new claims on prior users.

name: Discovery and Inspection Mechanisms (Germany-specific)
description: Availability and scope of mechanisms to retrieve evidence from the opposing party or third parties, including inspection and seizure powers under national law implementing the EU Enforcement Directive.
guidance: Claimant must show a likelihood of infringement and must exactly specify documents/areas for inspection and justify why disclosure/inspection is important and why no other means exist. Successful inspections permit counsel-eyes-only access, expert reports, sample seizure, and copying of evidence; inspection orders can be appealed by the defendant.

name: Factor 4 – Likelihood of Prevailing on the Merits
description: Evaluate the jurisdiction’s historical tendency (e.g., perceived patentee-friendliness) and evidentiary standards—whether claimants can succeed on substantiated, concrete indications without fully proving every element under a submission/production evidence principle.
guidance: In jurisdictions perceived as patentee-friendly (Germany), claimants may win based on substantiated indications if defendants cannot contest with similar substantiation. Use local success-rate data where available when estimating merits.

name: FRAND / SEP considerations
description: In SEP/FRAND disputes, defendants can raise FRAND defenses that may limit injunctions or tailor relief to FRAND royalties; courts need only decide whether a patentee’s offer is FRAND and need not set global FRAND terms.
guidance: German courts adhere closely to ECJ Huawei v ZTE requirements; outcome may limit injunctions but still allow information and damages/account claims. FRAND case law varies across German courts (Mannheim, Munich, Dusseldorf).

name: 2234-Entry of Amendments
description: Procedures governing entry of amendments to the patent claims/specification during reexamination.

name: 2260.01-Dependent Claims
description: Treatment and considerations specific to dependent claims in reexamination Office actions.

name: Three-month determination deadline
description: Within three months after the filing date of a request for supplemental examination, the Office will determine whether a substantial new question of patentability affecting any claim of the patent is raised by any of the items of information presented in the request.
guidance: The determination will generally be based on the claims in effect at the time and become part of the official record. If the three-month period ends on a Saturday, Sunday, or federal holiday in D.C., the certificate should issue by the preceding business day. Examiners should take up the request roughly six weeks after filing and must complete the determination within the statutory three-month period.

name: Scope of review limited to identified items and claims
description: The determination will generally be limited to a review of the item(s) of information identified in the request as applied to the identified claim(s) of the patent.
guidance: If the patent owner wants consideration of an item with respect to multiple claims, the request must identify each claim and include the required detailed explanation for each claim. The Office will generally not initiate supplemental examination for claims that were not requested.

name: Requirement for separate, detailed explanation for each claim (37 CFR 1.610(b)(5))
description: The request must include a separate, detailed explanation of the relevance and manner of applying each item of information to each claim of the patent for which supplemental examination is requested.
guidance: If the patent owner fails to explain how any item may be applied to a claim, the owner is not entitled to supplemental examination of that claim. A notice of a noncompliant request should be mailed where required. Example: request that only explains application to claims 1–5 but requests examination of claims 1–10 will not entitle determination for claims 6–10.

name: Examiner discretion to analyze items across requested claims
description: While the Office will generally analyze an item only with respect to the claim(s) identified by the patent owner, the examiner has the discretion to determine whether any of the items properly submitted raise an SNQ affecting any of the claims for which supplemental examination is requested.
guidance: The examiner may analyze items in a manner other than that provided by the patent owner, including considering multiple items against multiple claims. However, the patent owner is not entitled to a determination for claims lacking the required explanation.

name: Effect of finding an SNQ — reexamination may be ordered
description: If the examiner determines that an SNQ affecting a patent claim has been raised by at least one of the items, reexamination will be ordered under 35 U.S.C. 257.
guidance: Once reexamination is ordered, the Office may, in its sole discretion, reexamine claims other than those for which supplemental examination was requested (35 U.S.C. 303(a)). If claims are amended by a certificate or reissued patent after reexamination is ordered, reexamination should be on the basis of the claims as amended.

name: Procedure for domestic benefit / priority corrections (example guidance)
description: When a request includes a claim of missing domestic benefit plus an intervening reference, the examiner will first determine whether the intervening reference raises an SNQ if the effective filing date remains unchanged.
guidance: If the reference would raise an SNQ absent correction, the examiner may preliminarily consider entitlement to the earlier filing date, but final entitlement generally is made in the resulting reexamination proceeding where appropriate amendments and petitions can be filed. If the intervening reference does not raise an SNQ, the domestic benefit correction will not be further considered on the merits.

name: Handling when only factual correction information is provided
description: If the only information in the request is correction of factual information that does not itself raise an SNQ, the supplemental examination certificate will state no SNQ is raised and the reasons will indicate that no additional items showing dependency of patentability on the corrected fact were included.
guidance: Example: a lone parent-patent copy and explanation showing claim support without an intervening reference will typically result in a conclusion that no SNQ is raised.

name: Effect of federal court decisions on supplemental examination
description: A non-final federal court decision concerning validity/unenforceability has no binding effect on the Office's determination of whether an SNQ exists; the Office will make its determination without awaiting court decisions. A final federal court decision (after all appeals) upholding invalidity or unenforceability is controlling on the Office and the Office will not examine claims finally held invalid or unenforceable.
guidance: If claims requested to be examined have been finally held invalid or unenforceable, those claims will not be examined and the supplemental examination may be limited or not conducted. If a supplemental examination certificate inadvertently issued but a final holding of invalidity/unenforceability is brought to the Office's attention prior to the certificate's issuance, the certificate will be vacated; if the final holding occurs after electronic issuance to IFW/Patent Center, the certificate will not be vacated.

name: Content requirements for the Reasons for SNQ Determination (reasons document)
description: The reasons document must explain, for each item of information, why each item does or does not raise an SNQ and identify the claims affected or not affected.
guidance: Where an item raises an SNQ, include: (1) a statement that the item raises an SNQ and identification of claims affected; (2) where appropriate, statement that the item does not raise an SNQ and identification of claims not affected; (3) a brief statement of the basis for the determination. Use form paragraph 28.01 as the heading for the reasons document. If an item affects less than all requested claims, identify the claims not affected and provide basis.

name: Scope of material claims and chemical equivalents
description: If the invention claimed is for the use of a particular metallic substance (e.g. carburet of manganese in definite proportions), the use of different substances (e.g. coal-tar and oxide of manganese) will not infringe unless such substances were known equivalents at the date of the specification.
guidance: The Court considered whether at the date of the patent persons acquainted with the subject knew coal-tar and oxide of manganese would be chemical equivalents; a discovery made after the patent date may itself be the subject of a new patent. If the specification truly limits the invention to a particular substance and no equivalent was known at the date, there is no evidence of infringement (cases: Heath et al.).

name: Composition proportions and claim breadth for alloys
description: When an inventor states the most suitable proportions of ingredients for a composition (e.g. an alloy), another person will not be allowed to evade the patent by employing somewhat different proportions.
guidance: Claims to compositions that specify particular proportions will be construed to cover those proportions and closely similar ones if the inventor has stated them as the suitable proportions known to him (case: Muntz v. Foster and Collins). Evidence about purity of metals and practicability of following earlier directions is relevant to distinguishing prior compositions.

name: Evidence standard for proof of ability to apply specification
description: The question is whether the witnesses satisfy that the specification gives the public the means of making a machine or product as claimed so that an ordinary workman of competent skill could execute an order by following the directions given.
guidance: If the jury believes a workman could not execute the order without inventing, then the specification is insufficient. The jury must assess credibility and whether testimony makes out the plaintiff's proposition.

name: Rejection for non-identical claims (35 U.S.C. 112, para. 2)
description: If an amendment to make the claims the same in each file is required by the merger decision but is not timely submitted, any claim that does not contain identical text in all of the merged proceedings should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, paragraph 2, as indefinite.
guidance: Failure to submit identical claim text across merged files can lead to indefiniteness rejections for lack of particular pointing out of the invention.

name: Procedure when reissue issues before or after reexamination decision
description: If a reissue patent will issue before the determination on reexamination must be made, determination should normally be made after granting the reissue patent and based on the reissue patent claims; if reissue issues after reexamination is ordered, subsequent proceedings in the reexamination will be based on the reissue patent claims.
guidance: Reissue claims must be presented as a 'clean copy' in the reexamination proceeding (no bracketed/italic markup); Form paragraph 22.05 may be used in Office action to note proceedings are based on reissue claims.

name: CPA subject matter limitation (37 CFR 1.53(d)(2)(ii))
description: A CPA discloses and claims only subject matter disclosed in the prior application.
guidance: No amendment in a CPA may introduce new matter or matter that would have been new matter in the prior application. Any new specification filed with the CPA request will be treated as a substitute specification under § 1.125 and is not part of the original application papers.

name: No new matter in CPAs; handling substitute specifications (37 CFR 1.53(d)(5) and § 1.125)
description: Any new change must be made in the form of an amendment to the prior application as it existed prior to the filing of a CPA. No amendment in a CPA may introduce new matter. Any new specification filed with the CPA request will be treated as a substitute specification in accordance with § 1.125.
guidance: A substitute specification must comply with § 1.125(b) and be accompanied by a statement that it includes no new matter. A substitute specification containing new matter will be denied entry by the examiner. Any new matter which is entered will be required to be canceled pursuant to 35 U.S.C. 132 from the descriptive portion of the specification, and any claims relying on such new matter will be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph. Applicant may file a petition under 37 CFR 1.182 requesting that the substitute specification or preliminary amendment be removed from the CPA file and treated as a separate application, but a refund of the CPA filing fee is not available simply because such a petition is granted.

name: Grounds of Rejection — General Explanation Requirement
description: The following ground(s) of rejection are applicable to the appealed claims. [1].
guidance: In bracket 1, explain each ground of rejection clearly and completely as set forth in paragraphs (i)-(vi) (see separate items for statutory-specific explanation requirements).

name: Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph — Examiner's Explanation
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, the examiner’s answer shall explain why the first paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112 is not complied with, including, as appropriate, how the specification and drawings, if any, (a) do not describe the subject matter defined by each of the rejected claims, and/or (b) would not enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the subject matter defined by each of the rejected claims without undue experimentation including a consideration of the undue experimentation factors set forth in MPEP § 2164.01(a).
guidance: Explain specifically where the written description or enablement is deficient and address undue experimentation factors.

name: Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph — Examiner's Explanation
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, the examiner’s answer shall explain why the claims do not particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which “applicant” regards as the invention.
guidance: Identify the claim language deficiencies that render the claims indefinite or not distinct.

name: Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102 — Examiner's Explanation
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102, the examiner’s answer shall explain why the rejected claims are anticipated or not patentable under 35 U.S.C. 102, pointing out where all of the specific limitations recited in the rejected claims are found in the art relied upon in the rejection.
guidance: Point to exact locations in the prior art that disclose each claim limitation.

name: Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 — Examiner's Explanation
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103, the examiner’s answer shall state the ground of rejection and point out where each of the specific limitations recited in the rejected claims is found in the prior art relied on in the rejection, shall identify any difference between the rejected claims and the prior art relied on (i.e., the primary reference) and shall explain why it would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person of ordinary skill in the art to have modified the primary reference to arrive at the claimed subject matter.
guidance: Identify the differences and provide a rationale for the obviousness of combining or modifying the primary reference to reach the claimed invention.

name: Feature‑by‑feature comparison for 102/103 questions
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103 where there may be questions as to how limitations in the claims correspond to features in the prior art, the examiner, in addition to the requirements of (iii) and (iv), shall compare at least one of the rejected claims feature-by-feature with the prior art relied upon in the rejection. The comparison shall align the language of the claim side-by-side with a reference to the specific page or column, line number, drawing reference number and quotation from the reference, as appropriate.
guidance: Provide side-by-side alignment of claim language and exact prior art citations/quotations to show correspondence or lack thereof.

name: Findings of Patentability — General Explanation Requirement
description: The following findings of patentability, i.e., determinations of inapplicability of a proposed rejection, are applicable to the appealed claims. [1].
guidance: In bracket 1 explain each determination of inapplicability of a proposed rejection, or refer to the RAN if it clearly and completely sets forth the determination and complies with paragraphs (i)-(vi) (see below for statutory specifics).

name: Determination of Inapplicability — 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph
description: For each determination of inapplicability of a proposed rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph; the examiner’s answer shall explain how the first paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112 is complied with, including, as appropriate, how the specification and drawings, if any, (a) do describe the subject matter defined by each of the claims proposed for rejection, and/or (b) would in fact enable any person skilled in the art to make and use the subject matter defined by each of the claims proposed for rejection without undue experimentation.
guidance: Explain with specificity how the written description and enablement requirements are satisfied; address undue experimentation factors where appropriate.

name: Determination of Inapplicability — 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph
description: For each determination of inapplicability of a proposed rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph; the examiner’s answer shall explain how the claims do particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which “applicant” regards as the invention.
guidance: Show how claim language is definite and adequately delineates the invention.

name: Determination of Inapplicability — 35 U.S.C. 102
description: For each determination of inapplicability of a proposed rejection of the appealed claims under 35 U.S.C. 102; the examiner’s answer shall explain why the claims proposed for rejection are not anticipated and patentable under 35 U.S.C. 102, pointing out which limitations recited in the claims proposed for rejection are not found in the prior art relied upon in the proposed rejection.
guidance: Identify the missing limitations in the prior art and explain why those omissions render the proposal inapplicable.

name: Determination of Inapplicability — 35 U.S.C. 103
description: For each determination of inapplicability of a proposed rejection of the appealed claims under 35 U.S.C. 103; the examiner’s answer shall point out which limitations recited in the patentable claims are not found in the prior art relied upon in the proposed rejection, shall identify the difference between the patentable claims and the prior art relied upon by the third party requester and shall explain why the claimed subject matter is patentable over the prior art relied on by the third party requester. If the third party requester’s proposed rejection is based upon a combination of references, the examiner’s answer shall explain the rationale for not making the combination.
guidance: Explain which claim elements are absent from or not suggested by the prior art and why an asserted combination would not have been rationally made.

name: Feature‑by‑feature comparison for third‑party proposed 102/103 rejections
description: For each third party requester proposed rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103 where there are questions as to how limitations in the claims define over features in the prior art even after the examiner complies with the requirements of (iii) and (iv), the examiner shall compare at least one of the claims proposed for rejection feature-by-feature with the prior art relied on in the proposed rejection. The comparison shall align the language of the claim side-by-side with a reference to the specific page or column, line number, drawing reference number, and quotation from the reference, as appropriate.
guidance: Provide direct side-by-side comparison and exact citations/quotations to resolve correspondence questions.

name: Board Decision Content and Effect
description: The Board may affirm or reverse each decision of the examiner on all issues raised on each appealed claim, or remand the reexamination proceeding to the examiner for further consideration. The reversal of the examiner’s determination not to make a rejection proposed by a third party requester constitutes a decision adverse to the patentability of the claims and will be set forth in the decision as a new ground of rejection under paragraph (b).
guidance: Affirmance of a rejection on any specified grounds constitutes a general affirmance of the examiner’s decision on that claim except as to any ground specifically reversed; remands and new grounds have specified procedural consequences.

name: Licensee cannot dispute validity while licence continues; exceptions
description: A licensee during the continuance of the licence cannot set up that the invention was not new or useful, or that the patentee was not the first inventor, or that the specification is insufficient; but where a specification's claim is susceptible of two constructions, licensee may insist on the construction making it good.
guidance: Non-challenge clauses are generally effective; however, claim construction issues may favour licensee under ambiguous wording. After licence determination, licensee may be able to challenge validity in suits for injunction to restrain infringement.

name: Filing/specification does not automatically dedicate described parts to the public
description: A description in an applicant's specification of a machine or part, unaccompanied by notice that he has rights in it or desires to secure title, is not necessarily a dedication to the public; the patentee may surrender and amend specification or claim to cure defects.
guidance: Battin v. Taggert reversed lower-court instruction that description alone is dedication. Reissue and amended specifications under statutory remedies can validate claims within the scope of the original invention; surrender/reissue remedies limit what passes to the public.

name: Surrender and reissue effects on rights and suits
description: A surrender of the patent to the commissioner that extinguishes the patent (legal cancellation) prevents reliance on that patent after the surrender; reissue affects subsequent suits but not antecedent suits which depend on the patent's existence at commencement.
guidance: Courts treat surrender as extinguishing the original title; reissued patents must be for the same invention substantially and cannot claim a new and different invention. Monetary recoveries under the original patent are not automatically recoverable upon surrender.

name: Avoid incentivizing overfiling and 'junk' applications
description: Criticism that first-to-file incentivizes racing to the Patent Office and filing numerous low-quality/dead-end applications, thereby unnecessarily burdening both the USPTO and small inventors.
guidance: Supporters counter with international experience (Europe, Canada) suggesting transition does not increase junk applications; this is presented as a contested empirical claim to be considered.

name: Predictability, certainty, and transparency of priority determinations
description: Priority based on filing date/public disclosure rather than subjective private records (e.g., secret inventor notebooks) provides a clear, objective rule.
guidance: Advocates claim this predictability strengthens investor confidence because all will know as soon as an application is filed whether it is likely to have priority over others.

name: Conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. §10.23(b)(4))
description: Engaging in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation by, inter alia, making changes to the [application], pre-filing and during prosecution, without his client's knowledge or authorization (charged under 37 C.F.R. §10.23(b)(4)).
guidance: Examples given: unilaterally altering application drawings/claims (e.g., replacing parallel perforations with diverging/angled perforations) without adequately informing the client; misleading client about the content/scope of claims; ALJ found such behavior to constitute deceit/misrepresentation. The decision cites dictionary definitions (e.g., 'deceit' = 'dishonest behavior'; misrepresentation includes oral/written conduct and concealment); non-disclosure or concealment may have the effect of a misrepresentation.

name: Combination claims vs separate inventions
description: It is often necessary to decide whether the patentee claims a combination of several things, or the distinct invention of several things, or both. ... one circumstance that will always be decisive ... is, that one or more of them is not new.
guidance: If any element of a claimed set is not new, the court must consider whether the patent can be sustained for the combination only. A patent for a combination of three things cannot at the same time be a patent for a combination of any two of them. The subject-matter defined as the combination governs; sub-portions less than the whole cannot be treated as the claimed subject-matter.

name: Enablement: describe manner and process in full, clear, exact terms
description: The statute requires the patentee to describe 'the manner and process of making, constructing, using, and compounding his invention or discovery, in such full, clear, and exact terms, avoiding unnecessary prolixity, as to enable any person skilled in the art or science ... to make, construct, compound, and use the same; and in case of any machine, he shall fully explain the principle and the several modes in which he has contemplated the application of that principle ... and shall particularly specify and point out the part, improvement, or combination which he claims as his own invention or discovery.'
guidance: Specification must enable a person skilled in the art to practice the invention from the specification alone; for machines the principle and modes of application must be explained; the claimed part/improvement must be particularly specified and pointed out.

name: Tighter Standards on Amendments
description: Further clarification of the boundaries of permissible amendments during substantive examination, particularly relating to addition of new technical features, combination of embodiments, and extraction of features from examples.
guidance: Emphasizes application of Article 33 (added matter): any amendment must be clearly and directly derivable from the original disclosure. Practical consequences: claim drafting at the filing stage becomes more critical; relying on broad, generic disclosure to support later narrowing amendments may be risky. The Guidelines suggest intermediate generalizations introduced during prosecution can trigger added-matter objections; such objections may become more common.

name: Increasing Attention to Support and Clarity
description: Stronger emphasis on the support requirement and clarity of claims during examination.
guidance: Examiners are encouraged to examine whether claims are fully supported by the description; assess whether functional features are sufficiently defined; and review whether technical terms are clearly explained. For foreign-origin applications (especially translated from English), extra care is required to ensure the description supports the claims and that functional language and technical terminology are clearly and unambiguously presented.

name: Practical Drafting & Prosecution Recommendations for Overseas Applicants
description: Actionable suggestions for foreign applicants to improve examination outcomes under the revised Guidelines.
guidance: Draft with potential Chinese examination standards in mind, especially regarding technical effects. Avoid relying solely on functional claim language. Ensure sufficient fallback positions are explicitly disclosed in the description. Pay attention to translation quality and adaptation (not just literal accuracy). Overall, claim drafting at filing stage is critical to withstand stricter amendment and support scrutiny; anticipate that small clarifications in the Guidelines can influence day-to-day examination practice (stricter formal compliance, more structured inventiveness analysis, closer scrutiny of claim wording).

name: Form and contents of patent; grant scope and term
description: Patents shall be issued in the name of the Secretary of the United States under the Patent Office seal, signed by the Secretary and countersigned by the Commissioner, and recorded with descriptions/specifications/drawings; each patent shall contain a short description or title correctly indicating its nature and design, and shall grant to applicant (and heirs, administrators, executors, assigns) for a term not exceeding fourteen years the full and exclusive right and liberty of making, using, and vending the invention or discovery, referring to specifications annexed, and specifying what the patentee claims as his invention or discovery.
guidance: Specifies formalities and the maximum statutory term (14 years) under this act.

name: Specification enabling requirement (written description; manner and process)
description: Before any inventor shall receive a patent, he shall deliver a written description of his invention and of the manner and process of making, constructing, using, and compounding the same, in such full, clear, and exact terms, avoiding unnecessary prolixity, as to enable any person skilled in the art or science to which it appertains to make, construct, compound and use the same.
guidance: For machines, the inventor must fully explain the principle and several modes of applying that principle and particularly specify and point out the part, improvement, or combination claimed as his own invention or discovery.

name: Notice and process when specification/claim is defective or anticipation exists
description: When examination shows the applicant was not the original and first inventor, or part of the claimed subject had been invented/discovered/patented/described before, or the description is defective/insufficient, the Commissioner shall notify the applicant and give brief information and references useful in deciding to renew, withdraw, or alter the specification to narrow claims to what is new.
guidance: Applicant may withdraw and relinquish claim to the model to receive back $20 (part of duty) by filing written notice; if applicant persists, he must re‑swear and may obtain decision of a board of examiners upon payment and process.

name: Reissue for inadvertent defects or overclaiming; fee and effect
description: Where a patent is inoperative or invalid by reason of defective/insufficient description/specification or because the patentee claimed more than he had right to claim, if error arose by inadvertence/accident/mistake without fraudulent intention, the Commissioner, upon surrender of patent and payment of $15, may cause a new patent to be issued to the inventor for the residue of the unexpired period in accordance with corrected description and specification; similar right vests in executors/assignees.
guidance: Reissued patent with corrected specification shall have same legal effect in actions thereafter as though originally filed in corrected form; patentee may likewise annex a subsequently invented improvement to the original patent on payment of $15 and proper proceedings.

name: Drawing disclosure is incorporated into the claim ('as shown' / 'as shown and described')
description: The drawing in a design application is incorporated into the claim by use of the claim language 'as shown.' The drawing disclosure can be supplemented by narrative description in the specification; such description is incorporated into the claim by 'as shown and described.'
guidance: Treat the combination of drawings and any descriptive text as defining the scope of the claimed design when assessing compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112.

name: Determine scope under 35 U.S.C. 112 (second paragraph) before enablement (first paragraph)
description: Any analysis for compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112 should begin with a determination of whether the claims satisfy the requirements of the second paragraph before moving on to the first paragraph. A determination of the scope of protection sought by the claim must be made because the drawing disclosure and any narrative description are incorporated into the claim.
guidance: First identify the scope of the claimed design (what is being claimed) — then determine whether the disclosure enables a designer of ordinary skill to make an article having that shape and appearance. If the visual disclosure is inadequate to determine scope, the claim may fail both paragraphs.

name: Scope limited to surfaces shown in full lines and any written description; title does not define scope
description: The scope of a claimed design is understood to be limited to those surfaces or portions of the article shown in the drawing in full lines in combination with any additional written description in the specification. The title does not define the scope of the claimed design but merely identifies the article.
guidance: Assume the claim protects what is shown and described; if visible portions are not shown they are prima facie not part of the claim. Use MPEP §1503.01 guidance and case law (e.g., In re Zahn).

name: Descriptive statements for flat, unornamented visible surfaces
description: While it is not necessary to show in the drawing those visible surfaces that are flat and devoid of surface ornamentation, they should be described in the specification by way of a descriptive statement if they are considered part of the claimed design. Such descriptive statements may not be used to describe visible surfaces which include structure that is clearly not flat.
guidance: Use descriptive statements cautiously: they are acceptable for flat, unornamented surfaces but not to define complex/three-dimensional visible structure that is not shown in the drawings (Philco Corp. v. Admiral Corp.; MPEP §1503.02).

name: When drawings/specification omit visible parts, examiner should state omitted parts form no part of claim
description: Applications in which the title defines an entire article but the drawings and specification fail to disclose portions or surfaces of the article that would be visible either during use or on sale will not be considered to violate 35 U.S.C. 112 if those omitted surfaces form no part of the claimed design. Examiners should include a statement in the first Office action indicating that the surfaces or portions not shown are understood to form no part of the claimed design (form paragraph 15.85).
guidance: Insert form paragraph 15.85 (Undisclosed visible surface(s)/portion(s) not forming part of the claimed design) to notify applicant that unshown visible areas are considered outside the claim scope.

name: When rejecting under 35 U.S.C. 112 for drawing deficiencies, identify specific deficiencies and suggest cures
description: When a claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first and second paragraphs, as nonenabling and indefinite due to an insufficient drawing disclosure, examiners must specifically identify in the Office action what the deficiencies are in the drawing. A mere statement that the claim is nonenabling and indefinite due to poor quality of the drawing is not sufficient.
guidance: Point out the portions of the drawing that are insufficient to permit understanding of the shape and appearance, and, if possible, suggest how the rejection may be overcome (form paragraphs 15.21 and 15.20.02 may be used).

name: Inconsistencies between drawing views and resulting actions
description: When inconsistencies between the views of the drawings are so great that the overall appearance of the design is unclear, the claim should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first and second paragraphs, as nonenabling and indefinite. Otherwise, inconsistencies between drawing views will be objected to and correction required by applicant.
guidance: If inconsistencies render the design's overall appearance unclear, issue a 112 rejection specifying all inconsistencies; if not, object and require correction (see MPEP §1503.02).

name: Narrative descriptions cannot rely on vague 'variations' or 'equivalents' absent drawings
description: If a description in the specification refers to embodiments or modified forms not shown in the drawing, or includes vague and nondescriptive words such as 'variations' and 'equivalents,' or a statement indicating that the claimed design is not limited to the exact shape and appearance shown in the drawing, the claim should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first and second paragraphs, as nonenabling and indefinite.
guidance: Such descriptions fail to enable a designer to make the other embodiments without additional drawing views and fail to particularly point out/stringently claim those shapes; use form paragraph 15.21 to reject for these reasons.

name: Suggested responses to overcome 35 U.S.C. 112 rejections for drawings
description: It is suggested that applicant may submit large, clear informal drawings or photographs which show the unclear areas in order that the examiner may determine if the claim may be clarified without adding new matter. Alternatively, applicant may disclaim the areas by converting them to broken lines and amend the specification to state that the broken-line portions form no part of the claimed design.
guidance: In bracketed text, identify unclear areas; provide applicants the option of supplying clearer drawings/photos or disclaiming via broken lines (form paragraph 15.20.02).

name: Abstract ideas / mathematical formulas as judicial exceptions
description: A mathematical formula (e.g., the Arrhenius equation) is an exception like a scientific principle or natural phenomenon and is non-statutory subject matter.
guidance: Claims directed to mathematical formulas, algorithms, or similar abstract concepts are treated as judicial exceptions and are not patent eligible per se. See Diehr, Benson, Flook, Mackay, Bilski, and related case law. If a claim recites such an exception, it is directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: YES) and requires further analysis in Step 2B to determine whether the claim recites a patent-eligible application of the exception. Examples include algorithms for converting binary coded decimal to pure binary (Benson), formulas for computing alarm limits (Flook), and mathematical formulas for hedging (Bilski).

name: Concepts involving performing mathematical calculations can be abstract
description: Claims that involve generating values, calculating policy or investment values, manipulating numerical results, or organizing information through mathematical correlations may be directed to abstract ideas of performing mathematical computations.
guidance: Courts have found claims abstract where they describe mere mathematical computation or manipulation of data (e.g., Bancorp, Digitech). Examiners should look to the specification to determine whether claimed determinations are 'mere mathematical computation' and consider these as abstract ideas under Step 2A (requiring Step 2B if the claim is otherwise directed to a judicial exception). Examples include calculating surrender value credits (Bancorp) and organizing existing information into a new form via mathematical formulas (Digitech).

name: Products of nature exception for nature-based products
description: When a law of nature or natural phenomenon is claimed as a physical product, it is often treated as a 'product of nature' exception and can be ineligible unless it possesses markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart.
guidance: Products of nature include both naturally occurring products and non-naturally occurring products that are structurally identical to natural counterparts. Synthetic replication does not automatically confer eligibility (Ambry Genetics; Myriad). The key is whether the claimed nature-based product possesses markedly different characteristics from any naturally occurring counterpart. If a claim recites a nature-based product limitation, examiners should use the markedly different characteristics analysis (MPEP §2106.04(c)) to evaluate whether the limitation is a product of nature exception. Examples: isolated genes, primers, cloned animals, genetically modified bacteria (Chakrabarty, Roslin, Myriad, Ambry).

name: Markedly different characteristics analysis (part of Step 2A)
description: The markedly different characteristics analysis compares the nature-based product limitation to its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state to determine whether the product is a 'product of nature' exception.
guidance: Markedly different characteristics can be expressed as the product’s structure, function, and/or other properties and are evaluated on a claim-by-claim basis. If the nature-based product limitation has markedly different characteristics, the claim does not recite a product of nature exception (Step 2A: NO) at Pathway B unless another exception is present; if it does not, the limitation is a product of nature exception (Step 2A: YES) and the claim requires Step 2B analysis to determine whether additional elements add significantly more. For claims that are only a single nature-based product, showing a markedly different characteristic obviates further analysis (no Step 2B needed).

name: When to apply the markedly different characteristics analysis — product-in-combination and product-by-process claims
description: When the claim recites a nature-based product in combination with non-nature-based elements, or is a product-by-process claim, the analysis focuses on the nature-based product limitation's characteristics.
guidance: For a nature-based product in combination with non-nature elements (e.g., a yogurt starter kit comprising Lactobacillus plus container/instructions), analyze only the nature-based product limitation for markedly different characteristics; other elements are considered in Step 2B if the nature-based product is a product of nature. For product-by-process claims, the question is whether the nature-based product in the claim has markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart (see MPEP §2113).

name: Identifying and evaluating characteristics for 'markedly different'
description: Markedly different characteristics may be expressed as differences in structure, function, and/or other properties, and must be evaluated based on what is recited in the claim.
guidance: Compare the claimed nature-based product limitation to the selected naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state on the basis of structure, function, and other properties recited in the claim. If the nature-based product limitation is naturally occurring, no markedly different characteristics analysis is needed because it is by definition a naturally occurring product. If the limitation is not naturally occurring (e.g., modified by human intervention), perform the analysis to determine whether it possesses markedly different characteristics sufficient to avoid the product-of-nature exception.

name: Broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) considerations and claim narrowing
description: Under BRI, a nature-based product limitation may encompass both eligible and ineligible products; examiners should consider BRI and recommend narrowing amendments where appropriate.
guidance: Because the BRI of a claim may cover embodiments that lack markedly different characteristics, a claim may be directed to a product of nature under Step 2A. If a claim is directed to products both with and without markedly different characteristics, examiners should point out the BRI and, where possible, recommend an amendment to narrow the claim to embodiments that are not directed to products of nature or that are otherwise eligible. Example: a claim to 'a cloned giraffe' may have a BRI encompassing cloned giraffes with and without markedly different characteristics; examiners should identify this and suggest narrowing amendments in Office actions.

name: Streamlined eligibility analysis when claims do not seek to tie up exceptions
description: If a claim that recites a nature-based product limitation clearly does not seek to tie up any judicial exception, consider whether the streamlined eligibility analysis in MPEP §2106.06 is appropriate.
guidance: For claims that recite nature-based products but are clearly directed to inventions that do not attempt to preempt the use of the judicial exception, examiners may apply a streamlined eligibility analysis and may not need to perform the full markedly different characteristics analysis. Examiners should consider this approach where appropriate to avoid unnecessary analysis.

name: When to construe claim terms (Nidec/Vivid)
description: Only terms 'that are in controversy, and only to the extent necessary to resolve the controversy' need to be explicitly construed.
guidance: Board may decline to construe terms not necessary to resolve the proceeding. See Nidec Motor Corp. v. Zhongshan Broad Ocean Motor Co., 868 F.3d 1013, 1017 (Fed. Cir. 2017) (quoting Vivid Techs., Inc. v. Am. Sci. & Eng’g, Inc., 200 F.3d 795, 803 (Fed. Cir. 1999)).

name: Use of specification to supply express definitions
description: A patent specification may provide an express definition of a claim term, which controls claim construction.
guidance: If the specification expressly defines a term, the Board will apply that definition (here, the ’248 patent expressly defines 'treat'/'treatment'). Dependents can support constructions (e.g., a dependent claim reciting reduced hemorrhages supports that 'treating' includes partial alleviation).

name: Specific construction applied: 'treating a coagulopathy'
description: Construed as 'prophylaxis and/or therapy and/or cure of this coagulopathy' which includes partial alleviation of symptoms, for any duration of therapeutic efficacy.
guidance: Applied based on the intrinsic evidence and the express definition in the specification (Ex. 1001, 5:19–26) and support from dependent claim 16.

name: Burden and standard of proof in IPR final written decision
description: The petitioner must demonstrate unpatentability of challenged claims by a preponderance of the evidence in the inter partes review.
guidance: This is the statutory IPR burden applied by the Board in determining patentability in its Final Written Decision under 35 U.S.C. § 318(a).

name: Institution standard: reasonable likelihood of prevailing
description: At institution, the Board determines whether the information presented in the petition establishes a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail in challenging at least one claim.
guidance: If reasonable likelihood is shown, the Board may institute an inter partes review as to the challenged claims (referenced here as basis for institution in Paper 15, Decision on Institution).

name: Obviousness legal framework (Graham and KSR)
description: A claim is unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. § 103 if differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention. The question is resolved using underlying factual determinations: (1) scope/content of the prior art; (2) differences between claimed subject matter and the prior art; (3) level of ordinary skill; and (4) objective evidence (when available).
guidance: Apply an 'expansive and flexible approach' to obviousness; combination that yields only predictable use of prior art elements is likely obvious. See Graham v. John Deere Co., 383 U.S. 1 (1966); KSR Int'l Co. v. Teleflex, Inc., 550 U.S. 398 (2007).

name: Obviousness requires motivation to combine and reasonable expectation of success
description: Obviousness requires more than showing the prior art contains separate references covering each limitation; it requires that a person of ordinary skill would have selected and combined those prior art elements in the normal course of research and development to yield the claimed invention, and have a reasonable expectation of success.
guidance: See Unigene Labs., Inc. v. Apotex, Inc., 655 F.3d 1352, 1360 (Fed. Cir. 2011). Reasonable expectation of success need only be reasonable, not absolute (Pfizer, OSI Pharms distinctions discussed). Hindsight must be avoided.

name: Anticipation (§102) — prior art disclosure requirement
description: Anticipation requires that a single prior art reference disclose every limitation of the claimed invention (i.e., claim elements are found in the prior art reference).
guidance: If established, a claim is unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. § 102 (e.g., §102(b) ground based on Stafford was pleaded). The Board may decide anticipation grounds but need not if other grounds dispose the case.

name: Nexus requirement for objective indicia (ClassCo/Fox Factory/Brown & Williamson)
description: A patentee must establish a nexus between the objective evidence and the merits of the claimed invention; nexus is presumed only when the patentee shows the asserted objective evidence is tied to a specific product that embodies the claimed features and is coextensive with them.
guidance: Patentee bears burden to establish nexus; presumption shifts burden to challenger to rebut. 'Coextensive' means the product is essentially the claimed invention (unclaimed features must be insignificant). Evidence must be reasonably commensurate with the scope of the claims. See ClassCo, Fox Factory, Brown & Williamson, Rambus, Campbell Soup, and related Federal Circuit authority.

name: Coextensiveness / commensurate-in-scope standard
description: For a presumption of nexus, the marketed product must embody the claimed features and be coextensive with them; 'coextensive' means the product is the invention disclosed and claimed and unclaimed features are insignificant.
guidance: The Board assesses whether objective indicia evidence is reasonably commensurate with the scope of the claims (Fox Factory; Campbell Soup discussion).

name: Use and weight of objective indicia evidence
description: Even strong objective indicia may be insufficient to overcome a strong prima facie showing of obviousness; objective indicia may often be most probative but do not necessarily determine outcome.
guidance: Board evaluates nexus, commensurateness, and probative weight; examples: industry adoption, praise, or clinical trial activity must be tied to claimed invention to be given substantial weight.

name: Admissions in specification as evidence for obviousness
