description: Admissions or statements in the patent's specification may be relied upon when assessing whether claims would have been obvious.
guidance: Board may consider specification statements that indicate predictability or expectations of substitutions (citing Koninlijke Philips NV v. Google LLC).

name: Dependent claims can inform claim construction
description: A dependent claim recitation can support a construction of a broader independent claim (e.g., Claim 16's recitation that expression 'reduces and/or prevents hemorrhages' supports that 'treating' includes partial alleviation).
guidance: Use dependents to interpret scope and meaning where intrinsic evidence supports doing so.

name: Written-description requirement (§112, ¶1)
description: The specification must contain a written description of the invention and of the manner and process of making and using it, in full, clear, concise, and exact terms.
guidance: The specification must describe the invention sought to be patented; because claims are part of the specification, what is described in the original claims is necessarily described in the original specification. Problems arise when claims are changed relying on the original specification: the issue is whether the originally filed specification describes what is in the new claims. It is not necessary to describe word-for-word what is in the new claims; it need only convey to those skilled in the art that the inventor invented what is in the new claims. Determination is case-by-case with little precedential value for fact-specific decisions.

name: Claims must be as definite as possible
description: Claims define the metes and bounds of the patent's exclusionary power and must be presented as definite as possible.
guidance: Whether a claim is sufficiently definite is determined in light of the relevant prior art and the particular application. A claim is not necessarily indefinite because it defines the invention by function or by product-by-process rather than by structure. See cases like Amgen v. Chugai and others.

name: Claim construction (meaning of claim terms)
description: Determining what the words in a claim mean (claim construction) is a question of law for the court; determining whether the construed claim covers the accused product/process is a question of fact.
guidance: Courts look to the patent's specification (written description, drawings, other claims), the prosecution history (file wrapper), and possibly extrinsic evidence (expert testimony). Words may mean their ordinary meaning to one skilled in the art or, if the inventor acts as his/her own lexicographer, a different meaning. Extrinsic evidence may help construe claim language but is not used to vary claim terms. Means-plus-function language is construed to include only structure, material, or acts (and their equivalents) described in the specification as performing the claimed function (35 U.S.C. §112 ¶6).

name: Literal infringement requirement
description: A claim is literally infringed if each properly construed claim element reads on the accused product or process.
guidance: For means-plus-function elements, literal infringement occurs only when the accused product/process (a) employs means identical to those disclosed in the specification to perform the identical function, or (b) employs a means that is the structural equivalent of the means disclosed to perform the identical function. Example: a claim reciting a solid rod attaching blades would not literally read on a fan with a hollow rod because the solid-rod element is absent. Product-by-process claims read on products made by the identical process.

name: Promotional bills, grand claims, and panoramas
description: Bills proclaimed 'an entire new Melo-Drama', 'A SPLENDID PANORAMA, Painted by the First Artists', and highly specific cast/lists; sensational billings promised extraordinary feats (e.g., Madame Gobert's advertised lifts).
guidance: Use bold, detailed bills and panoramas to advertise novelty and attract crowds. However, be aware that extravagant claims invite scrutiny; misleading or impossible promises may undermine credibility when exposed (audiences and critics note trickery).

name: Purposive construction and claim interpretation principle
description: Purposive construction is performed by the court to objectively determine what the person skilled in the art would, as of the date of publication of the patent application and on the basis of the particular words or phrases used in the claim, have understood the applicant to have intended to be the scope of protection sought.
guidance: Free World Trust and Whirlpool continue to guide the courts; purposive construction principles enumerated in Free World Trust. Note difference between judicial construction (claims adjudicated in court are fixed, result of negotiation with the Patent Office, and benefit from presumption of validity under subsection 43(2) of the Patent Act) and examination (claim language may change during prosecution). Examiners should be 'alive to the possibility that a patent claim may be expressed in language that is deliberately or inadvertently deceptive' (e.g., claiming an 'art' or 'process' that may be a mathematical formula and therefore not patentable subject matter).

name: Claim date definition
description: The 'claim date' of a claim in an application or patent is the filing date of the application in Canada, unless there is a priority claimed; in that case the claim date is the filing date of the earliest priority application which supports the subject matter of the claim.
guidance: Used when assessing priority and novelty support.

name: Correction of obvious errors during examination
description: During examination, obvious errors should be corrected whenever identified.
guidance: The manual notes that the courts have addressed the date for claim construction rather than enablement and that obvious errors found during examination should be corrected.

name: Suppliers to subcontractors — certified copy of contract and bond upon affidavit (XX C 12)
description: The act of August 13, 1894 is believed to protect persons furnishing labor or materials to subcontractors as well as to the original contractor; a party who has furnished material to a subcontractor should be given a certified copy of the contract and bond upon filing the affidavit required by the act.
guidance: When suppliers to subcontractors file the statutory affidavit, supply authenticated copies of contract and bond for their use in pursuing claims; courts may ultimately decide scope but administrative practice favors providing copies. (G. 1908, Jan. 4, 1896.)

name: Amendments under 37 CFR 1.116/41.33 and non-new-ground treatment
description: If an amendment filed under 37 CFR 1.116 or 41.33 adds or amends claims and the advisory action indicates which individual rejection(s) from the action on appeal would be used to reject the added or amended claims, then (1) the appeal brief must address the rejection(s) of the added or amended claim(s) and (2) the examiner’s answer may include the rejection(s) of the added or amended claims; such rejection(s) in the examiner’s answer would not be considered a new ground of rejection within the meaning of 37 CFR 41.39.
guidance: Example: canceling a claim and incorporating its limitations into a dependent claim (or rewriting as a new independent claim) so that the appealed claim contains the canceled claim's limitations does not create a new ground if applicant was given fair opportunity to react and the advisory action advised which rejections apply. This provision does not change entry practice under 1.116/41.33 — those rules still control whether the amendment is entered; 41.39(a)(2) only permits inclusion of a rejection in an answer, it does not affect entry entitlement.

name: Definition and treatment of 'individual rejections'
description: An 'individual rejection' is a rejection identified by its statutory basis and the references/combination relied upon (e.g., claim 1 rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102 based on Reference A; claim 2 rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 based on Reference A in view of Reference B; claim 3 rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 based on Reference A in view of Reference C).
guidance: When amendments combine limitations from different original claims, rejections that correspond to those identified 'individual rejections' (e.g., A in view of B) may be appropriate and not new grounds provided the applicant was advised in the advisory action that such rejections would be applied to amended claims. However, if an amended claim raises a new issue beyond those identified (i.e., a genuinely new ground), then the amendment may properly be refused entry.

name: Citing a different portion of a reference that merely elaborates (DBC example)
description: If the examiner’s answer cites a different portion of an applied reference that goes no farther than, and merely elaborates upon, what was previously cited, then such citation does not constitute a new ground of rejection.
guidance: Illustrative case: In re DBC — Board cited an Example in a translation that elaborated upon the abstract's generic disclosures (same claim limitations) and the court held this was not a new ground because it 'goes no farther than, and merely elaborates upon, what is taught by the abstract.'

name: Failure to timely reply to a new ground results in sua sponte dismissal
description: If appellant fails to timely file a reply under 37 CFR 1.111 or a reply brief in response to an examiner’s answer that contains a new ground of rejection, the appeal will be sua sponte dismissed as to the claims subject to the new ground of rejection.
guidance: Examiners normally will not make determinations as to the sufficiency of a reply to a new ground once jurisdiction passes to the Board. If the appeal is dismissed by the Board, the examiner should follow MPEP § 1215 for subsequent procedure.

name: Identify corresponding structure/material/acts for means-plus-function limitation
description: If one skilled in the art would be able to identify the structure, material or acts from the description in the specification for performing the recited function, then the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre-AIA 112, second paragraph) are satisfied.
guidance: Apply the 'one skilled in the art' analysis (Atmel; Dossel). Examiner should determine whether the specification disclosure, possibly combined with claims, would permit a POSITA to recognize the structure underlying the recited function (examples: computer + algorithm recognized as a general-purpose computer implementation).

name: Require amendment when corresponding structure not identifiable
description: If one skilled in the art would not be able to identify the structure, material or acts from the specification for performing the recited function, applicant must amend the specification to contain the material incorporated by reference, including the clear link or associated structure, material or acts to the function recited in the claim (see 37 CFR 1.57(d)(3)).
guidance: Applicant should include only the relevant portions of the referenced document corresponding to the means-/step-plus-function limitation to keep the specification concise.

name: Means-plus-function indefiniteness often implicates written description and enablement
description: A means- (or step-) plus-function limitation found indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) for failure to disclose sufficient corresponding structure may also lack adequate written description and may not be sufficiently enabled to support the full scope of the claim under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (pre-AIA first paragraph).
guidance: Examiners should consider whether the disclosure enables a POSITA to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention (see sections MPEP §2161.01, §2164.08). Ariad (genus/function claims) emphasizes demonstrating possession of a functionally-defined genus by describing sufficient species.

name: Consider entire original disclosure for written description/enablement
description: In assessing 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (written description/enablement) support, examiners must consider the summary, detailed description, original claims, abstract, and drawings.
guidance: Cite and consider relevant authorities (In re Mott; In re Anderson; Hill-Rom; In re Armbruster; Vas-Cath; In re Wolfensperger) — the full original filing may provide support even if not explicit in one section.

name: Mere restatement of function in specification is insufficient
description: Merely restating a function associated with a means-plus-function limitation in the specification, without more description of the means that accomplish the function, is insufficient to provide corresponding structure for definiteness and written description.
guidance: Cite cases (Noah; Blackboard; Aristocrat) — specification must describe the means/structure, not just restate the claimed function.

name: Claims' terms and phrases must have clear support/antecedent basis in description
description: 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1) requires that terms and phrases used in the claims find clear support or antecedent basis in the description so that their meaning may be ascertainable by reference to the description.
guidance: When the written description implicitly or inherently sets forth corresponding structure, the examiner should either (A) have applicant amend to expressly recite the structure/material/acts, or (B) state on the record what structure/material/acts perform the function — but avoid adding prohibited new matter.

name: Duty to 'link or associate' structure to function (quid pro quo)
description: Structure disclosed in the specification is 'corresponding' structure only if the specification or prosecution history clearly links or associates that structure to the function recited in the claim (B. Braun / 35 U.S.C. 112(f) 'quid pro quo').
guidance: Even if a POSITA could write software to perform a function, absent a clear link in the specification/prosecution history the software may not be treated as corresponding structure (Medical Instrumentation v. Elekta example).

name: Single means claims do not invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f) and are problematic
description: A single means claim (means-plus-function limitation as the only limitation of a claim) cannot invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f) because that provision applies to 'an element in a claim for a combination.' Such single-means claims are not limited to the structure/material/acts disclosed in the specification and thus may cover every conceivable means to perform the function, making them potentially nonenabling under 35 U.S.C. 112(a).
guidance: Cite In re Hyatt — single-means claims that read on subject matter not enabled by the specification should be rejected under 112(a). Distinguish multiple functional limitations (each is a separate element).

name: Interpret multiple functional limitations as separate 112(f) elements
description: When a claim uses a generic placeholder (e.g., 'system') to recite a series of functions, each function should be interpreted as a separate section 112(f) limitation.
guidance: Example: a 'system configured to extract' and 'system configured to compare' — treat as two separate elements invoking 112(f) where 'system' serves as a non-structural placeholder.

name: Examiner must state when 35 U.S.C. 112(f) is being applied and identify corresponding structure
description: When an examiner interprets a claim limitation under 35 U.S.C. 112(f), the Office action should specify that determination and indicate what the specification identifies as the corresponding structure.
guidance: If corresponding structure is not clearly identifiable, the Office action should still attempt to identify the structure most closely associated with the means-/step-plus-function limitation to facilitate a prior art search. If applicant disagrees, they may present showing or amend claims.

name: Presumptions and 3-prong analysis for invoking 112(f)
description: A claim limitation that explicitly uses 'means' with functional language triggers a presumption that 35 U.S.C. 112(f) applies; conversely, lack of the term 'means' triggers a presumption it does not. These presumptions are rebuttable and examiners should apply them along with the 3-prong analysis.
guidance: Establish the record for the presumption and 3-prong analysis; state the interpretation in the Office action so applicant/public are notified and can respond or amend to avoid 112(f) interpretation.

name: On allowance, indicate 112(f) interpretation and associated structure
description: When allowing a claim that was treated under 35 U.S.C. 112(f), the examiner should indicate in the reasons for allowance that the claim was interpreted under 112(f) and clarify the associated structure if not previously made of record.
guidance: Helps public notice and clarifies claim scope.

name: Prior art application to means-plus-function requires identical function and sound basis for equivalence
description: Applying prior art to a means-/step-plus-function limitation requires that the prior art element perform the identical function specified in the claim; if the prior art only teaches identity of function, the examiner bears the initial burden to show the prior art structure or step is the same as or equivalent to the corresponding structure/material/acts described in the specification.
guidance: If the prior art teaches the identical structure but is silent about performing the claimed function, a reasonable presumption of inherent performance may be appropriate, but examiner must provide a 'sound basis for believing' the prior art structure would be capable of performing the claimed function (see MPEP §2114 and In re Spada).

name: Even if nonequivalence is shown, examiner must consider obviousness (35 U.S.C. 103)
description: A finding of nonequivalence preventing anticipation does not preclude a determination that the claimed means-/step-plus-function limitation is obvious from the prior art; the examiner must still perform a 103 analysis.
guidance: Alternative grounds of rejection may be appropriate; examiner may apply 102/103 where appropriate despite equivalence issues.

name: Specification silence on equivalents can shift burden to applicant
description: Where the specification is silent as to what constitutes equivalents and the examiner has made a prima facie case of equivalence, the burden is on the applicant to show that a prior art element which performs the claimed function is not an equivalent.
guidance: Cite In re Mulder and In re Noll; applicant's explanations should be consistent with the specification disclosure.

name: Scope of 'equivalents' depends on how element is described in specification
description: An equivalent embraces more than the specific elements described in the specification for performing the function but less than any element that performs the function; scope varies depending on whether specification limits to particular embodiments or describes broader equivalence.
guidance: If only one embodiment is described, corresponding structure may be limited to that embodiment and equivalents thereof (NOMOS). If the disclosure is so broad as to encompass any and all structures, then 'equivalents' cease to limit claim scope and claims must be read accordingly.

name: Applicants may amend claims to avoid 112(f) interpretation
description: In response to an Office action invoking 35 U.S.C. 112(f), applicant may (1) present a sufficient showing to establish that the claim limitation recites sufficient structure to avoid interpretation under 112(f), or (2) amend the claim to recite sufficient structure (or otherwise avoid the limitation).
guidance: Amendments might include reciting specific structure/material/acts or narrowing the functional language; see MPEP §2187 for form paragraphs.

name: When making a prior art search for means-plus-function limitations, attempt to identify corresponding structure
description: To facilitate a prior art search, Office actions should identify the corresponding structure for the claimed function; if not clearly identifiable, the examiner should attempt to identify the most closely associated structure in the specification.
guidance: This helps locate prior art and clarifies for applicant what is being compared; if multiple disclosed implementations exist, clarify which supports the limitation (see subsection II.B).

name: Complete application contents
description: A complete application for a patent contains: (a) A request for grant of a patent, accompanied by the prescribed fee; (b) A description of the invention (should describe at least one way of carrying out the invention claimed, with examples where appropriate, and with reference to the drawings, if any); (c) One or more claim(s) (the claims define the scope of protection and should be supported by the description); (d) Any drawing(s) referred to in the description or any claim(s); (e) An abstract of the invention (summary used in publication of the patent application).
guidance: Reference: Section 25 and 2.1.1. All items must be attached in the Specifications tab when filing (2.3.2).

name: Claims: structure and content
description: Claims define the matter for which protection is sought and shall be in terms of the technical features of the invention (expressed in structural, functional or mathematical terms). Claims shall be written either: (a) in two parts (first part indicating features that are part of prior art; second part introduced by words like 'characterised in that' followed by features defining the invention), or (b) in a single statement reciting a combination of elements or steps.
guidance: Claims should be supported by the description (2.2.7–2.2.8).

name: Claims should not rely on description or drawings
description: Claims shall not rely, in respect of the technical features of the invention, on references to the description or drawings, unless such a reference is necessary for understanding of the claim or enhances clarity/conciseness.
guidance: Avoid incorporating material by reference unless necessary (Rule 19(9), 2.2.9).

name: Number of claims and excess-claim fees
description: Applicants are encouraged to keep the number of claims reasonable. Claims in excess of 20 attract a fee per claim at the search and/or examination phase and for issuance of certificate of grant.
guidance: Be strategic about claim drafting to avoid additional fees (2.2.6).

name: Form and presentation of drawings
description: Drawings must be submitted as a separate set of documents commencing on a fresh sheet; each drawing/figure should be clearly numbered consecutively in Arabic numerals (independent of sheet numbering).
guidance: Drawings generally must be black, white or grayscale (no colour), should not contain textual matters, and features should be denoted by reference signs mentioned in the description or claims. Drawings should be scalable so that reduction to 2/3 keeps details distinguishable (2.2.14–2.2.17). See Rules 21 and 23 for details.

name: Abstract: form, length and figure indication
description: The abstract is a separate document forming the same series as the description and claims, placed immediately after the claims. It must be as concise as the disclosure permits and normally not contain more than 150 words. If the specification contains drawings, the applicant must indicate on the abstract the figure intended to be published (up to two figures), or indicate 'No Figure'.
guidance: For applications lodged on/after 14 Feb 2014 the abstract no longer needs to commence with a title. The text of the abstract must be identical between the attached document and the abstract text field in Patents Form 1; where chemical/mathematical formula or tables cannot be captured, enter 'Refer to abstract attached' (2.2.18–2.2.25).

name: Title of invention requirements
description: The title is a formal requirement and must be short, precise and indicate the matter to which the invention relates. The Registrar may reframe the title if it fails to comply. Because the title will be published, avoid disclosing too many details.
guidance: Applicants can edit auto-populated titles when claiming an earlier filing date; changes may be made by Patent Examiners during search/examination (2.3.8).

name: Marked-up vs clean copies and claim corrections after Dec 2019
description: When requesting correction of a specification or making corrections to claims, the request shall be accompanied by both marked-up and clean copies of the proposed correction. From 1 Dec 2019, if corrections have been made to claims, a marked-up copy and a clean copy of the full set of claims must be submitted, and amendments/corrections should be reflected similarly in both copies.
guidance: Follow Chapter 5.1.12 for accepted formats of marked-up and clean copies (11.8.13, 11.8.25).

name: Placement and numbering of sequence listing in filing (for certain filing dates)
description: For applications with date of filing from 26 May 2022 to 30 Jun 2022: if sequence listing is intended to form part of the description, it must be placed immediately after the description and before the claims and be numbered independently from the description and claims; the page count for each item must be indicated under the checklist in Patents Form 1 and the sequence listing page count included in the page count for the description.
guidance: A new document type 'sequence listing (specification)' exists for attaching sequence listings to Patents Form 1 (2.2.36–2.2.38).

name: Identification of prior application and relationship
description: Benefit claims under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, 365(c), and 386(c) must identify the prior application by application number, by international application number and international filing date, or by registration number and international filing date under 37 CFR 1.1023, and indicate the relationship between the applications (whether the instant application is a continuation, divisional, or continuation-in-part of the prior nonprovisional application).
guidance: See 37 CFR 1.78; identification must include both the prior application identifier and the specific relationship type. For international design applications that become nonprovisional, identifying by the nonprovisional application number is preferable.

name: Proper phrasing of benefit claim in specification
description: Where the reference to a prior nonprovisional application appears in the specification (permitted for applications filed before September 16, 2012), a proper benefit claim must state the relationship and filing date, e.g., “this application is a continuation of prior Application No. ---, filed ---.”
guidance: A benefit claim that merely states “this application claims the benefit of Application No. ---, filed ---” or “is a continuing application of Application No. ---, filed ---” does not comply with 35 U.S.C. 120 and 37 CFR 1.78 because it fails to state the required relationship (continuation, divisional, or continuation-in-part).

name: Location and form of benefit claim (ADS vs. specification) by filing date
description: For applications filed on or after September 16, 2012 the reference must be included in an application data sheet (ADS). For applications filed prior to that date, the benefit claim must appear either in the ADS or in the first sentence(s) of the specification following the title (or as an amendment to the first sentence(s) of the specification).
guidance: See MPEP § 211.02; if benefit claim appears elsewhere but was recognized on the filing receipt, petition may not be required, but the claim must still be submitted in the manner specified by 37 CFR 1.78 (ADS or spec as applicable).

name: Exclusive nature of relationship terms (continuation/divisional/CIP)
description: To specify the relationship between applications, applicant must specify whether the application is a continuation, divisional, or continuation-in-part of the prior application; the terms are exclusive and an application cannot be, for example, both a continuation and a divisional or both a continuation and a continuation-in-part of the same application.
guidance: When claiming benefit to an entire chain of prior-filed nonprovisionals, the relationship for each link in the chain must be specified (e.g., “this application is a continuation of Application No. C, filed ---, which is a continuation of Application No. B, filed ---, which is a continuation of Application No. A, filed ---”).

name: Provisional application reference requirements and relationship omission
description: When a nonprovisional application filed on or after September 16, 2012 claims the benefit of one or more provisional applications under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), the reference must be included in an ADS. For applications filed prior to that date the reference must be in an ADS and/or the first sentence(s) of the specification. The relationship term (continuation/divisional/CIP) is not required and should not be specified when claiming the benefit of a prior provisional under 35 U.S.C. 119(e).
guidance: If an applicant states that the later application “is a continuation” of a provisional or otherwise mixes 119(e) and 120 language, it may create ambiguity as to whether benefit is sought under 119(e) or 120; claiming benefit to a provisional under 120 is not recommended because it can affect patent term measurement under 35 U.S.C. 154(a)(2). Also, design applications cannot claim benefit of provisional applications.

name: Consequences of incomplete or improper benefit claim
description: Any benefit claim that does not both identify a prior application by its application number and specify a relationship between the applications will not be considered to contain a specific reference as required by 35 U.S.C. 120 and may not be recognized by the Office.
guidance: If not recognized, the claim may not be included on the filing receipt and publication may not be scheduled on the basis of the prior application’s filing date. If the time period set forth in 37 CFR 1.78 for submitting the required reference has expired, applicant must submit a petition under 37 CFR 1.78 and pay the petition fee under 37 CFR 1.17(m) to accept an unintentionally delayed claim.

name: When petition and fee are required vs. not required to correct benefit claim
description: If the reference required by 35 U.S.C. 120 and 37 CFR 1.78 is not submitted within the required time period, a petition for an unintentionally delayed claim under 37 CFR 1.78 and the petition fee under 37 CFR 1.17(m) are required to add the benefit claim. However, a petition and fee are not required where the reference was previously submitted within the time period but not in the location specified by 37 CFR 1.78 (e.g., was included in an oath/declaration or transmittal letter) provided the information concerning the benefit claim was recognized by the Office (as shown on the first filing receipt).
guidance: Even when a petition is not required because the Office recognized the claim, the applicant must still submit the required reference in the proper manner (ADS or amendment to first sentence(s) of specification as applicable). See MPEP § 211.03.

name: Correcting a filing receipt with missing/incorrect benefit information
description: If applicant receives a filing receipt with missing or incorrect benefit claim information, applicant may request a corrected filing receipt, but the Office will not grant such a request to include a benefit claim unless the proper reference to the prior application is included (i) in an ADS for applications filed on or after September 16, 2012 or (ii) in the first sentence(s) of the specification or an ADS for applications filed prior to September 16, 2012, within the time period required by 37 CFR 1.78 (with some exceptions).
guidance: If the proper reference was previously submitted, the request should indicate where/when it was submitted. Applicants should promptly review their filing receipts to avoid the need for a petition and associated fee.

name: Deleting benefit claims and effects
description: Applicants may delete a benefit claim: for applications filed on or after September 16, 2012 by filing a corrected ADS deleting the reference; for applications filed prior to that date by amending the specification or submitting a supplemental ADS. A deletion of a benefit claim may be considered as evidence that the applicant intentionally waived the benefit claim.
guidance: Examiner should consider whether any new prior art may now be available if a benefit claim is deleted. Amendments or ADSs deleting benefit claims filed after final rejection or after allowance are treated under 37 CFR 1.116 or 1.312 respectively. If the applicant later files a petition to accept an unintentionally delayed claim after cancellation, the Office may refuse to accept it because the cancellation may show the delay was intentional.

name: Sufficiency of disclosure in prior-filed application (35 U.S.C. 112(a) requirement)
description: To be entitled to the benefit of the filing date of an earlier-filed application, the later-filed application must be an application for a patent for an invention which is also disclosed in the prior application; the disclosure in the prior application must provide adequate support and enablement for the claimed subject matter in compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (except for the best mode requirement).
guidance: The disclosure of the prior-filed application must provide adequate written description and enablement to permit one of ordinary skill in the art to make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation. See Transco Prods. and case law citations.

name: Provisional application support requirements (New Railhead precedent)
description: Under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), the written description and drawing(s) (if any) of the provisional application must adequately support and enable the subject matter claimed in the nonprovisional application that claims the benefit of the provisional application.
guidance: In New Railhead Mfg. v. Vermeer Mfg. Co., the court held that the provisional specification must contain a written description sufficient under 35 U.S.C. 112¶1 to enable an ordinarily skilled artisan to practice the invention claimed in the nonprovisional. Lack of adequate support in the provisional can result in the nonprovisional not being entitled to the provisional’s filing date (with attendant invalidity risks under 35 U.S.C. 102/102(b)).

name: Claims in provisional not required but later claims must be supported
description: A claim is not required in a provisional application; however, for a claim in a later-filed nonprovisional application to be entitled to the benefit of the provisional filing date, the provisional’s written description and drawings (if any) must adequately support and enable the subject matter of that later claim.
guidance: If the provisional does not adequately support the claim limitations present in the later-filed nonprovisional (e.g., a specific structural limitation), the nonprovisional is not entitled to the provisional filing date and the patent can be vulnerable to intervening prior art.

name: Classification of patents granted after search and examination
description: All subject matter covered by the claims of a patent document must be classified as invention information along with any novel and unobvious constituents or components (subcombinations) of the claimed subject matter. Classification should be based on the subject matter of each claim as a whole and on each inventive embodiment within a claim. Any unclaimed subject matter in the disclosure that is novel and unobvious must also be classified as invention information. It is desirable to classify or index any additional information complementing the invention information if useful for search.
guidance: For granted patents, treat claims and novel/unobvious disclosed elements as invention information; include novel subcombinations. Also consider classifying complementary additional information where useful.

name: Classification of searched but unexamined patent documents (e.g., published applications)
description: All claimed subject matter that appears to be novel and unobvious in view of the search results must be classified as invention information along with any novel and unobvious constituents or components (subcombinations) of the claimed subject matter. Any unclaimed subject matter in the disclosure that appears to be novel and unobvious in view of the search results must also be classified as invention information. It is desirable to classify or index any additional information complementing the invention information if useful for search.
guidance: Use the search results to determine novelty/unobviousness for classification decisions on published but unexamined applications; treat items that appear novel/unobvious as invention information.

name: Claims Considered in Making the Determination
description: 2816.01: Claims Considered in Making the Determination

name: Sufficiency of disclosure / enablement (35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph)
description: Specification must provide an enabling disclosure so one skilled in the art could make and use the claimed invention; once examiner establishes a prima facie case of lack of enablement the burden falls on applicant to present persuasive arguments and suitable proofs.
guidance: Evidence supplementing an apparently deficient specification must show the missing information would have been known to those of ordinary skill in the art. Affidavits or declarations aiming to show sufficiency are generally not acceptable to establish facts the specification should recite (see In re Buchner, In re Smyth).

name: Affidavit/declaration to disqualify commonly owned patent (37 CFR 1.130)
description: When a claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 based on a U.S. patent or published U.S. application that is commonly owned and not prior art under 102(b), the applicant/owner may disqualify that patent/publication as prior art by satisfying the conditions of 37 CFR 1.130.
guidance: Required submissions: (1) terminal disclaimer per 37 CFR 1.321(c); and (2) an oath/declaration stating current common ownership and that the inventor named in the application/patent under reexamination is the prior inventor under 35 U.S.C. 104. The inventions must not be patentably distinct; the named inventor must have invented the claimed subject matter prior to the actual invention date of the reference. The affidavit/declaration may be signed by inventors, attorney/agent of record, or assignee(s). Limitations: certain foreign dates cannot be used to establish prior invention (see subsections A–C). A U.S. patent that anticipates the claimed subject matter cannot be disqualified under 37 CFR 1.130 or 1.131.

name: Sufficiency of invention and specification limits (claims limited by description)
description: An improvement is to be confined by the specification and description; claims are interpreted in view of what the specification states (e.g., limited to cast-iron guns because the specification mentioned cast iron).
guidance: Treadwell v. Parrott: claim confined to cast-iron guns because the specification limited the invention to that material; thus claims must be read in light of the specification's expressed scope.

name: Proper claim drafting: overly broad or imprecise claims can forfeit patentability
description: Claims that improperly describe the invention or hazard the patentable quality (e.g., claiming the mode of using a caisson rather than the specific machine) can render an otherwise new invention unpatentable.
guidance: Caisson example: the patentee's broad claim to the mode of construction risked the patent because the apparatus and parts of the claimed method were already known; claims should accurately and narrowly describe the inventive contribution.

name: Third‑party submissions: timing and content requirements (Intellectual Ventures)
description: Allow third parties to submit prior art any time after publication and before a notice of allowance (and in reexamination), conditional on (a) identifying the claim elements each reference is relevant to, and (b) identifying specific wording/figures in the prior art relevant to each claim element (not merely whole claims).
guidance: To avoid examiner/applicant burden, disallow arguments or permit only minimal explanations pointing to relevance.

name: Applicant pre‑filing searches improve application quality
description: Applicants' knowledge of closest prior art before filing results in improved patent applications with clearer claim scope and reduced pendency.
guidance: Incentivize pre‑filing searches and enable applicants to draft claims with better distinction from prior art.

name: Examiners should read entire IDS and specification before search
description: Examiners should read all prior art references in the IDS and the entire specification — not just claims — before conducting a search.
guidance: Assess whether current time and count systems are commensurate with this expectation and adjust examiner accounting if necessary.

name: Pre‑search interview between applicant and assigned examiner (3M)
description: Permit applicants to conduct an interview with the assigned examiner after the examiner has read the application but prior to any search, limited to mutual understanding of claim term interpretation for search and prosecution scope.
guidance: Require a pre‑search interview summary; allow filing claim amendments resulting from the interview; restrict patentability discussion under 35 U.S.C. 102/103.

name: Quality examination: proper interpretation and application of closest prior art
description: Quality examination requires the proper interpretation and application of the closest prior art to the claims and clear statements for rejection and allowance.
guidance: Ensure rejections/allowances include technical reasoning, not mere word matches; provide standards to interpret claim terms and articulate technical basis.

name: Rejection/allowance must explain technical reasoning (no conclusory statements)
description: Rejection and allowance must explain the examiner’s technical reasoning; conclusory, unsupported statements are unacceptable.
guidance: Require detailed explanation linking claim elements to prior art and technical rationale for conclusions.

name: Standards for citing portions of references and detailed citations
description: Create standards for examiners to identify portions of cited references that are relevant, and in office actions provide specific citations indicating which elements in cited references correspond to each claim term.
guidance: This reduces ambiguity (e.g., whether identical wording is used for identical/different purposes) and helps applicants understand examiner positions.

name: Reject inadequately described claims and require antecedent basis
description: Reject claims that are inadequately described; require antecedent basis for amended claims and encourage active amendment suggestions by examiners.
guidance: Promote clear claim drafting and examiner assistance to guide applicants toward allowable claim scope.

name: Technical accuracy and avoid word‑matching without technical explanation
description: Finding the closest art does not mean it is properly understood or applied; the cited reference must actually disclose or suggest the claim limitation and not be relied on solely due to word matching.
guidance: Identify improper instances of superficial word matching; require technical explanation for why a reference meets a limitation.

name: Acknowledge varying application complexity and adjust resources
description: Not all applications are equal; develop objective criteria to categorize applications by complexity and allow differing examiner time allotments and counts accordingly.
guidance: Criteria may include technology, specification length, number of examples, references cited, and claim scope; permit applicant petition and examiner interview regarding category assignment.

name: Tiered examination based on objective complexity criteria (GSK)
description: Differentiate applications by objective criteria (technology, spec length, working examples, references, claim scope) into tiers (e.g., 1 high complexity, 3 low) and allocate counts/time accordingly; allow applicant petition and interview for category assignment.
guidance: Adjust application fees for more complex cases and provide sufficient examiner time to perform comprehensive searches for complex applications.

name: Presumption from phrase 'means for' or 'step for'
description: The claim limitation is presumed to invoke 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph when it explicitly uses the phrase 'means for' or 'step for' and includes functional language.
guidance: That presumption is overcome when the limitation further includes the structure necessary to perform the recited function. See TriMed, Inc. v. Stryker Corp., 514 F.3d 1256, 1259-60 (Fed. Cir. 2008). If applicant uses the phrase in the preamble, a §112, second paragraph rejection may be appropriate where it is unclear whether the preamble is reciting a means-plus-function limitation or merely stating intended use.

name: Presumption against §112(6) when phrase absent
description: A claim limitation that does not use the phrase 'means for' or 'step for' will trigger the rebuttable presumption that 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph does not apply.
guidance: This is a strong presumption not readily overcome (Phillips v. AWH Corp.; Lighting World v. Birchwood Lighting). It may be overcome if the limitation uses a non-structural term (a nonce word or verbal construct that is effectively a substitute for 'means for').

name: Three‑prong test for invoking §112(6)
description: Examiners will apply 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph to a claim limitation if it meets the following 3-prong analysis: (A) the claim limitation uses the phrase 'means for' or 'step for' or a non-structural term; (B) the phrase or non-structural term is modified by functional language; and (C) the phrase or non-structural term is not modified by sufficient structure, material, or acts for achieving the specified function.
guidance: Apply all three prongs; if all met, treat the limitation as means-/step-plus-function. If not met, explain why in the Office action. See MPEP § 2181.

name: First prong — determining non-structural vs structural usage
description: When the claim limitation does not include 'means for,' examiners should determine whether the presumption that §112(6) does not apply is overcome by a non-structural term (a term simply a substitute for 'means for').
guidance: Even if a term is broad, if persons of ordinary skill understand it as the name for the structure that performs the function, §112(6) will not apply (Lighting World; Apex; CCS Fitness; Watts). Examples of structural terms found not to invoke §112(6) are provided in MPEP. The list of non-structural terms is illustrative, not exhaustive.

name: Applicant options when examiner does not find invocation
description: If the examiner has not interpreted a claim limitation as invoking 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph and an applicant wishes it to be treated under §112(6), applicant must either: (A) amend the claim to include the phrase 'means for' or 'step for'; or (B) rebut the presumption that §112(6) does not apply by showing that the limitation is written as a function to be performed and does not recite sufficient structure, material, or acts.
guidance: Case authority: Watts v. XL Systems; Masco Corp. v. United States. Conversely, if applicant used 'means for' but did include structure, the examiner should explain why §112(6) is not being applied.

name: Second prong — functional modification requirement
description: The phrase 'means for' or the non-structural term must be modified by functional language — i.e., the element is set forth, at least in part, by the function it performs rather than by specific structure, material, or acts.
guidance: If the term 'means' is not linked to a specific function, §112(6) may not be invoked. For method claims, §112(6) is implicated only when steps-plus-function without acts are present; mere 'ing' verbs do not automatically convert steps into step-plus-function clauses. See York Prod.; Caterpillar; O.I. Corp.

name: Determining whether a term denotes structure — three checks
description: To determine whether a word, term, or phrase coupled with a function denotes structure, examiners should check whether: (1) the specification provides a description sufficient to inform one of ordinary skill in the art that the term denotes structure; (2) general and subject matter specific dictionaries provide evidence that the term has achieved recognition as a noun denoting structure; and (3) the prior art provides evidence that the term has an art-recognized structure to perform the claimed function.
guidance: This three-part analysis is from Ex parte Rodriguez (precedential). Use these sources to assess whether a term is structural or non-structural in context.

name: Element-by-element application of §112(6)
description: It is necessary to decide on an element-by-element basis whether 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph applies; not all terms in a means-plus-function clause are limited to what is disclosed in the written description and equivalents, since §112(6) applies only to the interpretation of the means or step that performs the recited function.
guidance: Each claim must be independently reviewed even where process and apparatus claims use substantially similar language (O.I. Corp.). Do not assume that language in one claim governs another.

name: Office action content when treating or not treating under §112(6)
description: Where a claim limitation meets the 3-prong analysis and is being treated under 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, the examiner will include a statement in the Office action that the claim limitation is being treated under §112(6). If a claim limitation uses 'means for' or 'step for' but the examiner determines that either the second or third prong is not met, the examiner must include a statement in the Office action explaining the reasons why the claim limitation is not being treated under §112(6).
guidance: Transparency in the Office action is required so applicants understand the reasoning and can respond appropriately. See MPEP § 2181 subsection VI.

name: Use of §112, second paragraph rejection when unclear
description: In the event that it is unclear whether the claim limitation falls within the scope of 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph may be appropriate.
guidance: Be alert to ambiguity that prevents a clear determination under the 3-prong test; §112 second paragraph addresses definiteness issues.

name: §112(6) does not excuse compliance with §112 paragraphs 1 and 2
description: Invocation of 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph does not exempt an applicant from compliance with the written-description and definiteness requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112, first and second paragraphs.
guidance: Means-plus-function claiming requires adequate specification disclosure of corresponding structure; failure to do so can result in §112(2) indefiniteness or written description failures (Donaldson; Knowlton).

name: Computer-implemented means-plus-function — general vs specific functions
description: For a computer-implemented means-plus-function claim limitation, a general purpose computer is usually sufficient as corresponding structure for performing a general computing function (e.g., 'means for storing data'), but the corresponding structure for performing a specific function must be more than simply a general purpose computer or microprocessor.
guidance: When the claimed function requires a specific implementation, the specification must disclose the algorithm needed to transform the general purpose computer into a special purpose computer capable of performing that specific function. Cases: Katz; Aristocrat; Finisar; WMS Gaming.

name: Algorithm disclosure requirement for computer-implemented functions
description: To claim a computer-implemented means-plus-function and avoid pure functional claiming, the specification must disclose the algorithm that transforms the general purpose computer into the special purpose computer designed to perform the disclosed algorithm.
guidance: An algorithm may be expressed as a mathematical formula, in prose, in a flow chart, or any other understandable terms that provide sufficient structure. Applicant need not provide source code, but must disclose the algorithmic steps (Aristocrat; Finisar; WMS Gaming).

name: Use Claims (recitation of a use without steps)
description: Claim [1] provides for the use of [2], but, since the claim does not set forth any steps involved in the method/process, it is unclear what method/process applicant is intending to encompass. A claim is indefinite where it merely recites a use without any active, positive steps delimiting how this use is actually practiced. Claim [3] is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 because the claimed recitation of a use, without setting forth any steps involved in the process, results in an improper definition of a process.
guidance: In bracket 2 insert what is being used (e.g., 'the monoclonal antibodies of claim 4' for a method for using monoclonal antibodies to purify interferon). See Ex parte Dunki and Clinical Products v. Brenner; see MPEP §2173.05(q). This form paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.34.01.

name: Claims Are a Literal Translation
description: The claims are generally narrative and indefinite, failing to conform with current U.S. practice. They appear to be a literal translation into English from a foreign document and are replete with grammatical and idiomatic errors.
guidance: Use this form paragraph to indicate claims are narrative/indefinite due to literal translation; must be preceded by form paragraph 7.34.01.

name: Modifier of 'Means' Lacks Function (35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph)
description: Regarding claim [1], the word 'means' is preceded by the word(s) '[2]' in an attempt to use a 'means' clause to recite a claim element as a means for performing a specified function. However, since no function is specified by the word(s) preceding 'means,' it is impossible to determine the equivalents of the element, as required by 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph.
guidance: Words preceding 'means' must convey a function. Example: 'latch means' is definite because 'latch' conveys the function 'latching' (i.e., 'means for latching' makes sense). 'Conduit means' is indefinite since 'conduit' has no functional connotation. In such cases use this form paragraph and precede with 7.34.01.

name: Essential Steps Omitted (35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph)
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as being incomplete for omitting essential steps, such omission amounting to a gap between the steps. The omitted steps are: [2].
guidance: This rejection must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.02 or 7.103. In bracket 2 recite the steps omitted from the claims and give the rationale for considering them critical or essential.

name: Essential Elements Omitted (35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph)
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as being incomplete for omitting essential elements, such omission amounting to a gap between the elements. The omitted elements are: [2].
guidance: This rejection must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.02 or 7.103. In bracket 2 recite the elements omitted from the claims and provide rationale for considering them critical or essential.

name: Rejection, 35 U.S.C. 112, 2nd Paragraph - Omnibus Claim
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as being indefinite in that it fails to point out what is included or excluded by the claim language. This claim is an omnibus type claim.
guidance: Use this paragraph to reject an 'omnibus' type claim. No further explanation necessary. This rejection must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.02 or 7.103. See MPEP §1302.04(b) for cancellation by examiner's amendment upon allowance. Example: 'A device substantially as shown and described.'

name: Duplicate Claims (substantial duplicate under 37 CFR 1.75)
description: When two claims in an application are duplicates, or else are so close in content that they both cover the same thing, despite a slight difference in wording, it is proper after allowing one claim to object to the other claim under 37 CFR 1.75 as being a substantial duplicate of the allowed claim.
guidance: Form paragraphs 7.05.05 (warning) and 7.05.06 (objection) may be used. 7.05.05 advises applicant that if claim [1] is found allowable, claim [2] will be objected to as a substantial duplicate; use when duplicate claims are present but not allowable to give opportunity to correct. If duplicate claims are not allowable, use 7.05.05; if allowable, use 7.05.06.

name: New Matter (35 U.S.C. 132) - No amendment shall introduce new matter
description: No amendment shall introduce new matter into the disclosure of the invention. In amended cases, subject matter not disclosed in the original application is sometimes added and a claim directed thereto; such claims are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
guidance: New matter includes addition of unsuppported subject matter, adding specific percentages/compounds after a broader original disclosure, or omission of a step from a method. See Waldemar Link v. Osteonics, In re Rasmusson, MPEP §§2163.05-2163.07(b) and §§608.04-608.04(c). Examiner must be alert to detect new matter; use 35 U.S.C. 132 as basis for objection to amended abstract, specification, or drawings. If new matter added to claims, use 7.31.01 rejection rather than 7.28 objection.

name: Objection to New Matter Added to Specification (Form Paragraph 7.28)
description: The amendment filed [1] is objected to under 35 U.S.C. 132 because it introduces new matter into the disclosure. The added material which is not supported by the original disclosure is as follows: [2].
guidance: Applicant required to cancel the new matter in reply. Not for reissue applications (use 14.22.01). In bracket 2 identify new matter by page/line numbers and/or drawing figures and explain why not described in the specification as filed, addressing any applicant statements and unresolved questions raising doubt as to possession at filing. If new matter affects claims, also make rejection under form paragraph 7.31.01; if new matter added only to a claim, do not use this paragraph but use 7.31.01.

name: Reissue (35 U.S.C. 251) - enlargement of claim scope barred after 2 years
description: 35 U.S.C. 251 forbids granting a reissue 'enlarging the scope of the claims of the original patent' unless applied for within two years from the grant of the original patent. Such a bar is absolute.
guidance: Claims broader in any respect than original patent claims may be rejected as barred by 35 U.S.C. 251. When reissue applied for within two years, examiner does not go into the question of undue delay. A defective reissue oath is ground for rejecting all claims in the reissue application. Note reissue applications are 'special' and remain so even without prompt reply. See MPEP Chapter 1400 and applicable case law (e.g., In re Bennett).

name: Rejection of Previously Allowed Claims
description: A claim noted as allowable shall thereafter be rejected only after the proposed rejection has been submitted to the primary examiner for consideration of all the facts and approval of the proposed action.
guidance: Give full faith and credit to prior examiner's search/action unless clear error or other prior art is known. Examiner should not take an entirely new approach or make a new search merely hoping to find something. When rejecting a previously allowed claim, point out in the letter that the claim was previously allowed using Form Paragraph 7.50.

name: Caveat confidentiality and interference notice
description: Caveats are filed in confidential archives and preserved in secrecy. If another person applies within one year for a potentially interfering patent, the Commissioner must deposit the application materials in confidential archives and mail notice to the caveat filer, who then has three months to file a full description, specification, drawings, and model to avail of the caveat.
guidance: If, in the Commissioner's opinion, the specifications of claim interfere, like proceedings may be had as in interfering applications.

name: Reissue for defective/insufficient specification or over-claiming (upon inadvertence)
description: If a patent is inoperative or invalid by reason of defective/insufficient description/specification or claiming more than inventor had a right to claim, and the error arose by inadvertence, accident, or mistake without fraudulent intention, the Commissioner may, upon surrender of the patent and payment of $15, issue a new patent for the same invention for the residue of the unexpired term according to the corrected specification.
guidance: Reissue may be obtained by inventor or, in case of death/assignment, by his executors/administrators/assignees. The reissued patent has same legal effect as if originally filed in corrected form.

name: Permitted defenses to infringement actions
description: Defendant may prove: the specification does not contain whole truth relative to invention; contains more than necessary to produce described effect; concealment or addition intended to deceive; patentee was not original/first inventor of the thing or substantial part claimed; the invention had been described in public work anteriorly; in public use or on sale with patentee's consent before application; that patentee surreptitiously or unjustly obtained patent from another who was diligently perfecting it; or that an alien patentee failed to put the invention on sale in U.S. within 18 months of patent date.
guidance: If defendant relies on prior invention/knowledge/use, he must state names and places of residence of witnesses he intends to prove possessed prior knowledge; if defenses established judgment rendered for defendant with costs.

name: Court discretion when plaintiff overclaims
description: If plaintiff's specification or claim embraces more than he was first inventor of, but defendant had used or violated any part of the invention truly and justly specified and claimed as new, court may adjudge and award costs as appear just and equitable.
guidance: Courts have flexibility to award equitable costs based on what parts were truly claimed and infringed.

name: Re-recording of pre-December 15, 1836 patents and assignments
description: Persons in possession or interest in patents or assignments issued/executed prior to Dec 15, 1836 may, without charge, present them to the Commissioner to be recorded anew together with descriptions, specifications of claim, and drawings; Commissioner must transcribe/copy into record books.
guidance: Clerks of U.S. judicial courts shall transmit authenticated copies to the Commissioner; certified copies of such records/drawings are prima facie evidence in courts without proof of loss of originals; patents/assignments not recorded anew will not be received in evidence after June 1 unless so recorded and a drawing deposited and verified.

name: Procedure for disclaimer of overbroad claims
description: When a patentee, through inadvertence, accident, or mistake, has claimed more than he was the original/first inventor of, patentee (and successors) may make a written disclaimer of such parts not claimed, attested by witnesses and recorded in Patent Office on payment of $10, stating extent of interest.
guidance: Such disclaimer becomes part of the original specification to extent of the interest possessed by disclaimant and those claiming under him; disclaimer does not affect pending actions except as relates to unreasonable neglect/delay in filing the same.

name: Revision/restriction of claims for additions and reissues
description: Applications to add newly discovered improvements to existing patents or when patents are returned for correction/reissue shall have specifications/claims subject to revision and restriction like original applications; Commissioner will not add improvement or grant reissue until applicant enters disclaimer or alters specification/claim per Commissioner's decision.
guidance: Applicant dissatisfied with Commissioner's decision has same remedy/privileges/proceedings as in original applications.

name: Valid patent scope when inventor mistakenly claims others' matter (without fraud)
description: When by mistake, accident, or inadvertence and without intent to defraud, a patentee claims as original/first inventor any material/substantial part of thing patented of which he was not first inventor, the patent shall be deemed good and valid for so much of the invention as is truly and bona fide his own, provided that part is material/substantial and definitively distinguishable from the other parts wrongly claimed.
guidance: Patentee (or successors) may maintain suit for infringement of bona fide part; however, plaintiff shall not recover costs unless he had entered at the Patent Office, prior to commencement, a disclaimer to all parts claimed without right.

name: Numbering and form requirements for claims and paragraphs
description: Numbering of claims and numbering of paragraphs must follow Office practice.
guidance: Claims and specification paragraphs must be numbered in accordance with the Office formatting rules (see 1.52, 1.75, 1.126, 1.125). Claims commence on a separate sheet or electronic page per formatting rules (see 1.52(b)(3), 1.75(h)).

name: Claims must conform to invention and specification
description: Claims must conform to the invention and specification.
guidance: Claim language and scope must be supported by and consistent with the disclosed invention and the specification; claims not so supported are objectionable or subject to rejection (see 1.75(d)).

name: Priority, effective filing date, and related filing-date rules
description: Effective filing date of a claimed invention and related filing date/priority rules.
guidance: Rules determine effective filing dates for claims (under AIA and pre-AIA rules), priority claims, and related consequences for patentability (see 1.109 and related provisions).

name: Supplemental Examination — voluntary disclosure to improve patent quality
description: A new "Supplemental Examination" administrative proceeding encourages the voluntary and proactive disclosure of information that may be relevant to patent prosecution for the Office to consider, reconsider, or correct.
guidance: Voluntary disclosure by patentees serves to strengthen valid patents while narrowing or eliminating patents or claims that should not have been issued. Use of the proceeding by patent owners is to be encouraged. The Director should implement the authority in a way that maximizes its potential to improve patent quality and reduce uncertainty about scope, validity, or enforceability.

name: Supplemental Examination — referral for alleged fraud and limits on PTO authority
description: Subparagraph (c) provides that if, during supplemental examination or reexamination, a court or administrative agency advises the PTO that it has determined a fraud on the Office may have been committed in connection with the patent, the Director shall refer the matter to the Attorney General.
guidance: The provision is not intended to impose any obligation on the PTO beyond those it already undertakes, nor to make the PTO an investigative or adjudicative body. Referral decisions are to be made by the Director (not delegated to examiners or other agents). A referral does not relieve the Director of the obligation to conclude the supplemental examination or reexamination so that any invalid claims can be properly cancelled.

name: Non-patentability of human organisms (Weldon amendment)
description: Language adopted: "None of the funds appropriated or otherwise made available under this Act may be used to issue patents on claims directed to or encompassing a human organism."
guidance: This provision codifies long-standing USPTO practice that any claim which can reasonably be construed as directed to a member of the species Homo sapiens at any stage (including embryo, fetus, infant, child, adolescent, adult) is non-patentable. The amendment is intended to provide unequivocal congressional backing for the policy, and to apply regardless of how the organism was produced (e.g., IVF, somatic cell nuclear transfer, parthenogenesis). It also explains that the term "human organism" includes human-animal hybrid organisms but does not include non-human organisms that merely incorporate human genes.

name: USPTO practice: rejection when claim 'encompasses' a human being (MPEP 2105)
description: MPEP 2105: "If the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claimed invention as a whole encompasses a human being, then a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 must be made indicating that the claimed invention is directed to nonstatutory subject matter."
guidance: In practice, examiners advise applicants that a claim construed to include a human being will be rejected and typically suggest an amendment adding the qualifier 'non-human' to avoid this ground of rejection. Although MPEP does not expressly address claims directed to human embryos, examiners treat such claims as directed to a human being and reject them as non-statutory subject matter.

name: Scope exclusions — stem cells, genes, tissues, methods, drugs, devices remain unaffected
description: The amendment should not be construed to affect claims directed to or encompassing subject matter other than human organisms, including but not limited to cells, tissues, organs, stem cells, stem cell lines, genes, hormones, proteins, substances, methods for creating/modifying/treating human organisms, drugs or devices.
guidance: Congressional statements and contemporaneous administrative letters stress that stem cells are not 'organisms' and that existing patents on stem cells, genes, and many biotechnology products and methods are not intended to be affected. Testimony from experts (e.g., NIH Director, industry scientists) supports the distinction that pluripotent stem cells are not organisms; the amendment and report language seek to preserve existing patent rights in these areas.

name: ¶ 7.05.016 — Nonstatutory (Directed to a Judicial Exception without an Inventive Concept/Significantly More)
description: For claims directed to a judicial exception (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea) that do not include significantly more, use 7.05.016 to describe the exception, why it is an exception, why it is not integrated into a practical application, and why additional elements do not add significantly more.
guidance: Use 7.05.016 preceded by 7.05. This paragraph is for use with all product (machine, manufacture, composition) and process claims. Fill brackets as follows: (1) bracket 1 — identify whether the claim(s) are directed to a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea; (2) bracket 2 — identify the exception by referring to how it is recited in the claim and explain why it is considered an exception (e.g., refer to the enumerated abstract idea grouping in Section I of the 2019 PEG and give examples such as 'the Arrhenius equation...' or 'series of steps instructing how to hedge risk...'); for products of nature explain lack of marked difference (e.g., 'naturally occurring DNA segment ... not markedly different'); (3) bracket 3 — explain why the exception is not integrated into a practical application (examples: generic computer elements merely implementing the abstract idea; data gathering steps are insignificant extra-solution activity; placing a product of nature into a generic container like a test tube is a nominal or token extrasolution component); (4) bracket 4 — identify additional elements and explain why, separately and in combination, they do not add significantly more (an 'inventive concept') — e.g., storing and retrieving information in memory are well-understood, routine, conventional computer functions as recognized by court decisions listed in MPEP § 2106.05(d).

name: Requirement to accompany 7.05.016 with 7.05.017 for non-enumerated abstract ideas
description: If the recited abstract idea does not fall within the enumerated groupings of abstract ideas in the 2019 PEG, 7.05.016 should be accompanied by 7.05.017 because TC Director approval is required to treat a non-enumerated limitation as an abstract idea.
guidance: Examiner Note: For claims that recite a limitation that does not fall within the enumerated groupings of abstract ideas, 7.05.016 should be accompanied by 7.05.017. 7.05.016 alone may be used for enumerated abstract ideas, laws of nature, and natural phenomena; for non-enumerated abstract ideas, TC Director approval is required and must be documented with 7.05.017.

name: ¶ 7.05.017 — TC Director Approval for Non-Enumerated Abstract Idea
description: When treating a tentative/non-enumerated claim limitation as an abstract idea, obtain TC Director approval and use 7.05.017 to document the justification and signature.
guidance: 7.05.017 must be preceded by 7.05.016. Use it to state that the identified claim limitation(s) does/does not fall within the enumerated groupings in Section I of the 2019 PEG but are being treated as an abstract idea, and provide the justification in bracket 1. The rejection must include the TC Director's signature in bracket 2 to evidence approval. Examiner Note: approval from the TC Director is required to treat a tentative abstract idea as an abstract idea. In bracket 1 provide justification (for example, explain why the limitation is among the 'basic tools of scientific and technological work').

name: Explain integration into a practical application and when additional elements are insufficient
description: When asserting that a claim is not integrated into a practical application, specifically explain why additional elements fail to meaningfully limit the judicial exception and why they do not add significantly more.
guidance: Provide concrete explanations: e.g., generically recited computer elements 'do not add a meaningful limitation' because they merely implement the abstract idea on a computer; data-gathering steps required to use a naturally occurring correlation are 'insignificant extra-solution activity'; placing a product of nature into a generic container (test tube) is a token extra-solution component. For additional elements, explain why they, separately and in combination, do not amount to an 'inventive concept' (examples: storing and retrieving information in memory are routine and conventional). Reference court decisions listed in MPEP § 2106.05(d) where appropriate.

name: Scope of use — applicability to all claim types and exclusions
description: 7.05.016 applies to all product and process claims directed to judicial exceptions; existing procedures for claims directed to or encompassing a human organism or limited by the Atomic Energy Act remain unchanged.
guidance: 7.05.016 is for use with all product (machine, manufacture, composition of matter) and process claims, and for all claims directed to a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea. No changes have been made to form paragraphs for rejections based on a claim directed to or encompassing a human organism or to procedures limited by the Atomic Energy Act — continue to follow MPEP §§ 706.03(a)(II) and 706.03(b) for such claims.

name: Trigger for § 112(f) interpretation
description: When an element or step is claimed only by its function, § 112(f) interpretation is required.
guidance: Application of § 112(f) is driven by the claim language (not applicant intent). § 112(f) is a claiming style permitted only for claims that recite a combination of elements (not single-element claims). Analyze each limitation/element individually; if a limitation claims only a function and no sufficient structure/material/act is recited, interpret that limitation under § 112(f).

name: MPEP 2181 three-prong test for identifying § 112(f) limitations
description: Apply § 112(f) to a claim limitation if it meets the following 3-prong test: (A) the claim limitation uses the term “means” or “step” or a term used as a substitute for “means” that is a generic placeholder (also called a nonce term or a non-structural term having no specific structural meaning) for performing the claimed function; (B) the term “means” or “step” or the generic placeholder is modified by functional language, typically, but not always linked by the transition word “for” (e.g., “means for”) or another linking word or phrase, such as "configured to" or "so that"; and (C) the term “means” or “step” or the generic placeholder is not modified by sufficient structure, material, or acts for performing the claimed function.
guidance: If all three prongs are satisfied, interpret the limitation under § 112(f). If the test is not met, interpret the limitation under its plain meaning in light of the specification (MPEP 2111). When in doubt, establish a reasoned position on the record explaining the analysis (words of the claim, specification, state of the art) so applicant may respond.

name: Presumption when 'means' or 'step' is absent
description: A claim limitation that does not use the term “means” or “step” creates a rebuttable presumption that the claim limitation is not interpreted under § 112(f).
guidance: This presumption is rebutted when the limitation recites function without reciting sufficient structure/material/acts to entirely perform that function (e.g., a generic placeholder like 'device' coupled with a function). When rebutted, document that § 112(f) is being applied (use FP 7.30.06). Note that this presumption is rarely overcome for process claim limitations that do not use the word 'step.'

name: Presumption when 'means' or 'step' is present
description: A claim limitation that explicitly uses the term “means” or “step” creates a rebuttable presumption that the claim limitation is interpreted under § 112(f).
guidance: This presumption is rebutted when the limitation recites sufficient structure/material/acts to entirely perform the recited function (for example, 'a printer means for printing' where 'printer' is a recognized structure). When rebutted, document that § 112(f) is not being used (use FP 7.30.07). Remember § 112(f) is pertinent only where a function is recited.

name: Distinction between means-plus-function and step-plus-function
description: 'Means-plus-function' limitations refer to structural elements and can appear in product or process claims; 'step-plus-function' limitations recite a step in purely functional terms and will appear in process claims.
guidance: Step-plus-function limitations are rare because inclusion of action words (specific acts) typically rebuts the presumption that § 112(f) applies. Courts have not extended the generic-placeholder doctrine to 'step' as readily as to 'means'; treat step analyses accordingly.

name: Establishing the Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI)
description: Establish the BRI of both § 112(f) and non-§ 112(f) claim limitations before examining for patentability.
guidance: The BRI of a § 112(f) limitation is limited to what is disclosed in the specification (structure) and equivalents that perform the recited function.
