The BRI of a non-§ 112(f) limitation is its plain meaning in light of the specification (unless a special definition/disclaimer applies). After establishing BRI, proceed to examine §§ 101, 102, 103, 112, and non-statutory double patenting.

name: Where to record claim interpretation in an Office action
description: Discussion of § 112(f) should appear toward the beginning of an Office action under the 'CLAIM INTERPRETATION' heading; § 112(f) controls interpretation but is not a basis for a rejection by itself.
guidance: Address § 112(f) when a limitation is first interpreted under it (typically in the first Office action or when the limitation is first introduced). Once established on the record, repetition is unnecessary unless the interpretation changes. Use the Claim Interpretation heading also for other clarifying claim-interpretation remarks or special definitions.

name: Use of new form paragraphs to make § 112(f) interpretation on the record
description: New form paragraphs assist examiners in establishing § 112(f) claim interpretation and explaining presumptions: FP 7.30.05 (BRI under § 112(f), three-prong test, presumptions); FP 7.30.06 (§ 112(f) invoked despite absence of 'means'); FP 7.30.07 (§ 112(f) not invoked despite presence of 'means'); plus FP 7.30.03.h (Claim Interpretation Header) and FP 7.30.03 (Statutory Basis).
guidance: Select the appropriate FP(s) via the Claim Interpretation tab in OACS/OC. When invoking § 112(f) without 'means', include FP 7.30.06 and identify the claim(s)/limitation(s); when 'means' is present but rebutted, include FP 7.30.07 and identify the limitation(s). Use FP 7.30.05 to state the three-prong test and presumptions. Examiners can append brief explanatory remarks after the form paragraph inserts (e.g., 'In this application the recited "module" for printing has no structural meaning').

name: Content and level of explanation to include
description: Office actions should provide sufficient explanation whenever prosecution positions and claim-interpretation decisions can be clarified for applicant and the public.
guidance: Beyond inserting form paragraphs, consider adding reasons why particular subject matter is allowable, whether priority documents provide support, identifying terms not given their plain meaning, noting unsupported breadth of claim terms, and identifying § 112(f) language. If multiple instances of the same generic placeholder occur, a single clarifying statement may address all instances and list claims where § 112(f) interpretation applies.

name: Proper responses by applicant to avoid § 112(f) interpretation
description: An appropriate applicant response to avoid interpretation under § 112(f): amend the claim limitation to clearly recite a definite structure, material, or act that entirely performs the recited function; or present a sufficient showing that the limitation already recites such a structure/material/act.
guidance: If applicant amends to add a named structure or demonstrates that the claim already recites sufficient structure/acts, the presumption that § 112(f) applies may be rebutted; the examiner should then document the rebuttal (e.g., FP 7.30.07) and re-evaluate BRI and patentability accordingly.

name: Proper responses by applicant to obtain § 112(f) interpretation
description: An appropriate applicant response to obtain interpretation under § 112(f): amend the claim limitation to remove the structure/material/act that performs the recited function; or present a sufficient showing that the claim does not recite any structure/material/act that entirely performs the recited function.
guidance: If applicant removes or shows absence of structure performing the function, the limitation may meet the three-prong test and be interpreted under § 112(f); examiners should document invocation (FP 7.30.06) and limit BRI to specification-disclosed structure and equivalents.

name: Limitation-by-limitation analysis with illustrative examples
description: § 112(f) analysis is performed on a limitation-by-limitation basis; examples illustrate common outcomes (e.g., 'knife blade' is a named structure -> not § 112(f); 'means for cutting' -> § 112(f) and limited to spec-disclosed spoon-with-knife-blade; 'device for cutting' (generic placeholder) -> § 112(f); 'knife blade means for cutting' (means present but structure recited) -> presumption rebutted -> not § 112(f)).
guidance: Use concrete examples from the specification when explaining why a limitation meets or fails the three-prong test. Identify specific claim language in the Office action and, where helpful, include short explanatory remarks showing how the specification supports the structural disclosure (e.g., motor disclosed for 'mechanism...for rotating', spring disclosed for 'unit ... for biasing').

name: Limit preservation/discovery to relevant and necessary information (proportionality)
description: Preservation or discovery of Protected Data should be limited in scope to that which is relevant and necessary to support any party’s claim or defense.
guidance: Limiting scope minimizes conflicts of law and impacts on data subjects; courts and parties should employ proportionality to minimize conflicts with Data Protection Laws.

name: Examination guidelines for applying references under 35 U.S.C. 102(e)
description: Determine the appropriate 102(e) date for each potential reference by following stepwise guidelines: verify reference type, check international application relationship, and apply date rules depending on international filing characteristics.
guidance: I. (A) Potential reference must be U.S. patent, U.S. application publication (35 U.S.C. 122(b)), or WIPO publication of international application under PCT Article 21(2). (B) Determine if reference resulted from or claimed benefit of an international application; if yes, proceed to (C). (C) If resulted from/claimed benefit of an international application: (1) If international filing date on/after Nov 29, 2000 AND designated the U.S. AND published under PCT Art 21(2) in English, then international filing date is a U.S. filing date for 102(e) purposes (and may be bridged to earlier applications if appropriate and supported under 35 U.S.C. 112); (2) If filed on/after Nov 29, 2000 but did not designate the U.S. or was not published in English under PCT Art 21(2), do not treat international filing date as U.S. filing date—apply as 102(a)/(b) by publication date or 102(e) as of any later U.S. filing date that properly claimed benefit; (3) If international filing date prior to Nov 29, 2000, apply pre-AIPA provisions (e.g., for U.S. patents, 102(e) date is earlier of completion of 371(c)(1),(2),(4) or filing date of later-filed U.S. application that claimed benefit; U.S. application publications/WIPO publications directly resulting from international apps filed before Nov 29, 2000 are never applied under 102(e) but may be 102(a)/(b) by publication date; etc.); (4) Be aware that a WIPO publication may have an earlier 102(a)/(b) date even if a related U.S. patent/application does not have an earlier 102(e) date. (D) Foreign applications' filing dates claimed via 35 U.S.C. 119/365 may not be used as 102(e) dates; international filing dates claimed as foreign priority under 365(a)/(b) are likewise not usable as 102(e) dates. II. Examples (nine illustrative examples) are provided to illustrate common factual situations for determining 102(e) dates; use examples only as illustrations, not definitive rules for all fact patterns.

name: Enablement: practise from the specification alone
description: To describe the invention in such a manner as to enable the public to practise it, from the specification alone.
guidance: Statutory requirement: describe 'the manner and process of making, constructing, using, and compounding his invention or discovery, in such full, clear, and exact terms, avoiding unnecessary prolixity, as to enable any person skilled in the art... to make, construct, compound, and use the same.' Must also 'fully explain the principle and the several modes' and 'particularly specify and point out the part... which he claims.' Enablement is judged as a question of fact for a jury in many cases.

name: Use full, clear, and exact terms; avoid unnecessary prolixity
description: The patentee must describe 'in such full, clear, and exact terms, avoiding unnecessary prolixity,' so as to enable a skilled person to make and use the invention.
guidance: This includes explaining the principle and the modes of applying it, and identifying the part or combination claimed. Overly prolix or vague language that obscures how to make or use the invention risks insufficiency.

name: Purpose and scope of new part 41 and related changes
description: Provide new interference rules in a new part 41 of 37 CFR; provide Subpart A to consolidate general provisions relating to the Board and make them consistent across proceedings; delegate authority from the Director to the Chief Administrative Patent Judge for petitions and limited disqualifications; provide Subpart B rules for ex parte appeals; limit amendments filed on or after filing a brief; change format and content of appeal brief; provide Subpart C rules for inter partes reexamination appeals; provide Subpart D general rules for contested cases (interferences and ownership); provide Subpart E rules specific to patent interferences; clarify when there is an interference-in-fact, how claims correspond to a count, and how benefit of earlier applications is accorded; require applicants adding a claim to provoke an interference to provide additional details; clarify that a two-way unpatentability test is used to determine whether claimed inventions interfere.
guidance: The preamble states these changes are interpretive rules or rules of agency practice and procedure (5 U.S.C. 553(b)(A)) and thus prior notice and comment were not required. The changes relate solely to procedure for filing and prosecuting patent applications, appeals to the Board, and contested cases.

name: § 1.55 - Claim for foreign priority; Office may require earlier filings
description: The Office may require the claim for priority and the certified copy of the foreign application be filed earlier than provided when: (i) application becomes involved in an interference (see § 41.202); (ii) necessary to overcome the date of a reference relied upon by the examiner; or (iii) deemed necessary by the examiner. An English translation of a non-English foreign application is not required except when involved in an interference, necessary to overcome a reference, or specifically required by the examiner. If translation is required, it must be filed together with a statement that the translation is accurate.
guidance: Priority documentation and translations may be required sooner when interference or prior-art handling demands it; translation requires a certification of accuracy.

name: § 1.112 - Reconsideration before final action
description: After reply by applicant or patent owner to a non-final action and any comments by an inter partes reexamination requester, the application or patent will be reconsidered and again examined. Applicant (or patent owner and requester in reexam) will be notified if claims are rejected or favorable decisions made. Applicant may reply with or without amendment unless the Office action is made final, an appeal has been taken, or specified final/closing notices have been given.
guidance: Standard reconsideration and reply rules apply; examine the specifics for exceptions such as final actions or appeals (see §§ 1.113, 1.116, 41.31, etc.).

name: § 1.116 - Amendments and affidavits or other evidence after final action and prior to appeal
description: After a final rejection but before or on the same date of filing an appeal: (1) amendments may cancel claims or comply with form requirements; (2) amendments presenting rejected claims in better form for appeal may be admitted; (3) amendments touching merits may be admitted upon showing good and sufficient reasons why necessary and not earlier presented. Admission or refusal does not relieve appeal condition or save from abandonment. Specific restrictions apply in inter partes reexamination and ex parte reexamination regarding cancellations affecting other pending claims and after right of appeal notice. Affidavits or other evidence may be admitted upon a showing of good and sufficient reasons. After decision on appeal, amendments, affidavits and other evidence can only be made as provided in §§ 1.198 and 1.981, or to carry into effect a recommendation under § 41.50(c).
guidance: Admittance of post-final amendments/evidence requires justification and may be limited by reexamination or appeal status; see referenced sections for special constraints.

name: § 1.197 - Return of jurisdiction from the Board; termination of proceedings
description: Jurisdiction over an application or patent under ex parte reexamination passes to the examiner after a decision by the Board upon transmittal of the file, subject to appellant’s right of appeal or other review, for further action as required to carry into effect the Board decision. Proceedings on an application are considered terminated by dismissal of an appeal or failure to timely file appeal to the court or a civil action except where claims stand allowed or further action by the examiner is required. The date of termination is the date of dismissal or expiration of time for appeal; if appeal/civil action filed, termination is when such proceedings terminate (e.g., issuance of mandate).
guidance: Transmittal triggers examiner jurisdiction for carrying out Board decisions; termination definitions tie to appeal filing dates and dispositions.

name: Patent owner’s statement content requirement (37 CFR 1.530(c))
description: Any statement filed by the patent owner shall clearly point out why the subject matter as claimed is not anticipated or rendered obvious by the prior art patents or printed publications, either alone or in any reasonable combinations.
guidance: Where the reexamination request was filed by a third party requester, any statement filed by the patent owner must be served upon the requester in accordance with § 1.248. Lack of proof of service can cause the statement to be considered inappropriate and may be denied consideration (see MPEP § 2267).

name: Manner of making specification amendments (37 CFR 1.530(d)(1))
description: Changes to the specification, other than to the claims, must be made by submission of the entire text of an added or rewritten paragraph including markings pursuant to paragraph (f) of this section, except that an entire paragraph may be deleted by a statement deleting the paragraph without presentation of the text of the paragraph.
guidance: The precise point in the specification where the added or rewritten paragraph is located must be identified. All paragraphs added must be submitted as completely underlined. All bracketing and underlining is made in comparison to the original patent (not relative to prior amendments). Blocked paragraphs are assigned letter/number and a caret indicates insertion point — formatting/page layout need not be a concern.

name: Claim status and support requirement (37 CFR 1.530(e))
description: Whenever there is an amendment to the claims, there must be supplied, on pages separate from pages containing the changes, the status (pending or canceled) as of the date of the amendment of all patent claims and of all added claims, and an explanation of the support in the disclosure of the patent for the changes to the claims made by the amendment paper.
guidance: Failure to submit claim status will generally result in an informal response to the patent owner prior to final rejection; failure to set forth the support may lead to the amendment not being entered (especially if submitted after final rejection).

name: Required markings for amendments (37 CFR 1.530(f))
description: Any changes relative to the patent being reexamined which are made to the specification, including the claims, must include the following markings: matter to be omitted must be enclosed in brackets; matter to be added must be underlined.
guidance: Markings are made relative to the original patent and are used later to show exact additions/deletions in the reexamination certificate (underlined matter printed in italics; brackets printed as inserted).

name: Amendment substantive limits — no enlargement / no new matter / expiration rules (37 CFR 1.530(j))
description: No amendment may enlarge the scope of the claims of the patent or introduce new matter. No amendment may be proposed for entry in an expired patent; moreover, no amendment other than cancellation of claims will be incorporated into the patent by a certificate issued after expiration.
guidance: Amendments do not become effective until the reexamination certificate is issued and published. If a patent expires during reexamination, all amendments to claims and added claims are withdrawn (diagonal line placed across amended/new claims) and reexamination proceeds on the unamended claims. Examiner should cancel rejected/objected claims so certificate issuance does not attempt to incorporate amendments after expiration.

name: Formal paper and electronic submission requirements (37 CFR 1.52(a)-(b))
description: All papers to become part of USPTO permanent records must be on specified paper (A4 or 8.5x11 inches), certain margins, written on one side in portrait, legible machine-printed permanent dark ink, sufficient clarity/contrast for reproduction; no holes recommended; electronic submissions must comply with Office’s electronic filing system requirements.
guidance: Specifications (except reexamination) should be 1½ or double spaced, nonscript font (e.g., Arial, Times Roman, preferably 12), single column; claims and abstracts must begin on separate physical sheets/pages. English language requirement or accompanied by accurate translation.

name: Importance of interpreting the specific SSO/ETSI IPR Policy with evidentiary support
description: The decision provides insight into the importance of looking to the specific standard setting body’s IPR Policy at issue and providing evidence for interpreting that policy.
guidance: When making or defending FRAND/SSO-related claims, ground arguments in the precise language of the applicable IPR policy and marshal record evidence (testimony, contemporaneous documents) to support an interpretation.

name: Patent misuse / competition-law claims against SEP owners require showing more than traditional enforcement
description: Competition law claims asserted against SEPs may not prevail when patent owners have followed traditional patent enforcement and licensing strategies or even if they breach a FRAND commitment. Rather, there must be something more egregious or deceptive with the particular patent owner’s conduct to give rise to competition law claims required to address harm to competition beyond harm addressed by patent or contract remedies.
guidance: To assert antitrust or patent-misuse claims tied to SEP conduct, plead and prove conduct that causes competitive harm beyond ordinary patent enforcement or contractual FRAND breaches (e.g., deception, coercion producing market-wide harm). Examples the court considered (and rejected) included alleged requirements to take worldwide licenses, using threats of foreign injunctions to coerce licensing, disparate licensing terms, and nondisclosure of pool royalties — but these alone may not suffice without additional evidence of competitive harm.

name: Administrative bodies (e.g., ITC) may review claim construction and SEP issues
description: The U.S. International Trade Commission (ITC) determined to review in part an ALJ’s decision concerning claim construction and standard essential patent (SEP) issues (337-TA-613).
guidance: Expect administrative tribunals to engage with SEP and claim-construction questions; strategy and evidence for SEPs should account for both district court and administrative processes and potential interlocutory or remand review.

name: OPQA error definition and classification (clear errors)
description: Errors are defined as unreasonable failures by the patent examiner to reject patent claims for one or more reasons provided in the patent laws, or when an examiner incorrectly rejects patent claims (known internally as clear errors).
guidance: OPQA records why a determination had an error and which area of patent law the examiner did not follow. These error identifications feed components 1 and 2 of the composite metric. Accurate and consistent error classification is critical because OPQA-derived inputs heavily influence corps-wide accuracy rates and supervisor bonuses.

name: Preemption/wholly preempt test
description: Claims that 'wholly preempt' the use of an unpatentable element (e.g., a mathematical algorithm or natural phenomenon) are invalid because they effectively claim the unpatentable element itself.
guidance: Assess whether a claim 'effectively preempts all uses' of a naturally occurring correlation or abstract idea. The analysis differs where a diagnostic inference is embedded in a specific treatment regimen (may preempt less) versus purely observational claims (may wholly preempt).

name: Abstract idea category (ambiguous meaning)
description: 'Abstract idea' is an ambiguous, undefined term; one possible meaning is the opposite of 'concrete' or 'tangible.' The machine-or-transformation test may proxy for this meaning but is imperfect.
guidance: Because 'abstract idea' is vague, courts have used multiple clues (e.g., transformation, preemption, mental steps) to decide whether a claim is an abstract idea. Beware that natural phenomena may be concrete in some senses and thus not neatly equated with 'abstract ideas.'

name: Mental processes exclusion ('determine and infer' claims)
description: Claims that recite purely mental steps — e.g., determining a measurable fact (biomarker) and inferring a diagnosis or treatment decision — can fall into the excluded category of 'mental processes' and be unpatentable.
guidance: Distinguish between claims that are 'only mental steps' and claims that include antecedent transformative steps. In Prometheus the 'wherein' inference clauses were mental steps, but the claim as a whole passed §101 because prior transformative steps were present.

name: Transformative steps can save otherwise-mental claims
description: Inclusion of transformative, physical steps (e.g., administering a drug, obtaining and processing a biological sample, growing cells) can render a claim patent-eligible even if it includes mental inference steps.
guidance: Courts have treated steps like 'determining the level of a metabolite' or 'growing transformed cells' as 'inherently transformative' and sufficient to satisfy machine-or-transformation. However, such transformative steps may be disregarded if they amount to 'insignificant post-solution activity' or are merely conventional/data-gathering.

name: Whether transformative steps relied on are 'well-known' or conventional
description: If the claimed transformative steps used to satisfy machine-or-transformation are themselves conventional or 'well-known', their presence may not justify patent eligibility.
guidance: The petition in Mayo highlighted concern about claims that rely on 'well-known methods' (e.g., administering drugs, testing blood) to meet the transformation test. Courts may scrutinize whether such conventional steps genuinely add inventive character or merely serve as a drafting device.

name: Claims-drafting maneuvers and their limits
description: Redrafting claims to add explicit physical steps (e.g., 'obtaining a sample', 'determining a sequence') can sometimes convert an invalid 'determine-and-infer' claim into a patent-eligible one, but courts may find such maneuvers inadequate if they are merely formalistic.
guidance: Although the Federal Circuit suggested adding antecedent transformative steps could save some claims, precedent warns that courts may disregard attempts that amount to trivial additions or drafting tricks that do not change the substance of what is claimed.

name: How broadly a diagnostic inference can be claimed (scope/preemption assessment)
description: A key question is how broadly one may claim a diagnostic inference without impermissibly preempting underlying natural correlations; claims tied to specific regimens may avoid wholesale preemption.
guidance: Evaluate whether substitution of different biomarker thresholds or different treatments would avoid infringement. If a claim would prevent all uses of a correlation, it's more likely to be deemed to 'wholly preempt' and be invalid.

name: Minimalist or 'coarse filter' approach to subject-matter exclusions
description: An alternate posture assigns a minimal role to §101 exclusions (abstract ideas, natural phenomena, laws of nature), treating §101 as a 'coarse filter' and relying more heavily on §§102/103/112 to police overbroad claims.
guidance: This approach downplays §101 and emphasizes that patent-eligibility should be a low bar, leaving detailed substantive rejections to other doctrines. Research Corp. articulated such a tone.

name: Use of precedent phrases and multi-factor balancing
description: Courts lean on a litany of precedent formulations (e.g., 'manifestly abstract', 'does not preempt all uses', 'utilize natural correlations in a series of specific steps') and balance multiple clues rather than apply a single rigid test.
guidance: Assessment often synthesizes machine-or-transformation, preemption concerns, whether claim recites concrete transformative steps, whether steps are conventional, and whether the claim is essentially an abstract mental process or product of nature. Examples: Prometheus, AMP v. USPTO, Diehr, Bilski.

name: Unity of invention (Art. 82 EPC; Rule 44 EPC)
description: The European patent application shall relate to one invention only, or to a group of inventions so linked as to form a single general inventive concept. A group of inventions fulfils unity only when there is a technical relationship among them involving one or more of the same or corresponding special technical features (features which define a contribution over the prior art).
guidance: The determination whether inventions form a single general inventive concept is made without regard to whether the inventions are claimed in separate claims or as alternatives within a single claim. The EPO uses a detailed procedure for assessing unity (see EPO Examination Guidelines Part F – Chapter V). Unity objections and divisional/partial filing issues arise if this requirement is not met.

name: Strategies to reduce claim count (drafting techniques acceptable at the EPO)
description: Practical drafting techniques to conform a US-style claim set to EPO practice and avoid excess-claim fees and objections.
guidance: Suggested measures: reduce the number of claims to 15; use multiple dependencies (allowed at the EPO) to shorten claim lists; combine dependent claims by using wording such as 'preferably', 'optionally', 'in particular'; transfer some claims into the description as 'claim clauses'. These techniques help avoid fees and simplify conformity to EPO expectations.

name: Fine-grained empirical details corroborate compassion
description: Various separate matters of detail in experience and literature provide supporting evidence for compassion being the moral source.
guidance: Schopenhauer lists multiple small empirical confirmations (examples from texts, practices) that cumulatively strengthen the claim; evaluators should consider breadth of supporting data, not rely on single anecdotes.

name: Compassion extends beyond humans to all living beings
description: Compassion does not stop with human beings but includes all living things; this universality supports its claim as the fundamental moral incentive.
guidance: Assess whether an account of morality can account for moral intimations toward animals and plants; universality of motive strengthens its plausibility as fundamental.

name: Graham v. Deere factual inquiries
description: When analyzing prior art under 35 U.S.C. 103, consider the Graham factors: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between the prior art and the claimed invention; (3) level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; (4) objective evidence relevant to obviousness.
guidance: These four factual inquiries (see MPEP 2141 (II)) must be considered and supported with findings of fact when making an obviousness rejection.

name: Address findings of fact and provide a rationale for combining/modifying references
description: Any 103 rejection must address findings of fact and then provide a rationale for combining or modifying the references relied upon.
guidance: Each rejection must contain an explicit rationale clearly explaining why it would have been obvious to combine or modify the teachings of the references. Each included claim must be explicitly addressed in the rejection, although it is not necessary to rewrite the entire rejection for each claim. (See MPEP 2143.)

name: Optimization within prior-art conditions or routine experimentation
description: Routine optimization (e.g., adjusting concentrations, temperatures) generally will not support patentability unless an articulated rationale shows why routine optimization would have led to the claimed invention with a reasonable expectation of success.
guidance: Provide findings of relevant facts and underpinning reasoning in sufficient detail. The presence of a result-effective variable can be a motivation to optimize, but examiners must explain why routine optimization would have been performed and successful. See MPEP 2144.05 (II).

name: When relying on legal precedent, show application to the facts and not rely solely on case law
description: Case law can supply a line of reasoning to support an obviousness finding, but the examiner must show how that line of reasoning applies to the facts of the application at hand and case law should not be the sole basis for obviousness.
guidance: Provide fact-specific explanation tying the precedent to the claimed limitations. Common TC1600 examples include automating a manual activity, changes in size/shape/sequence of adding ingredients, purifying an old product. See MPEP 2144.04.

name: Tie the selected rationale to the facts of the case and each claimed limitation
description: An obviousness rejection must explain why the invention as a whole and the limitations of each included claim would have been obvious over the cited prior art, and must explain how the selected rationale applies to the facts of the case.
guidance: Clear, fact-specific rejections permit applicants, examiners, and reviewers to understand the basis for rejection. Examiners should explain that at least one particular rationale applies and map that rationale to the claim limitations. (Summary and multiple example slides.)

name: Amendment does not broaden independent claim
description: The amendment does not broaden the scope of the independent claim in any aspect.
guidance: The amendment must be narrowing or at least not broaden the independent claim(s); broadening amendments are disallowed under this program request.

name: Parts & materials-specialized business expedited eligibility
description: An application filed by a parts·materials-specialized business may be accepted as being 'practiced or prepared to be practiced' for expedited examination without submission of the usual evidential documents.
guidance: Relevancy between the parts·materials-specialized business and the claimed invention shall be determined based on proving documents (business license, etc.) enclosed in the expedited-examination request form and, if necessary, by referring to KIAT information networks. If relevancy cannot be checked/confirmed, the examiner shall propose a supplement. For joint applications where one applicant is a parts·materials-specialized business, the request is accepted provided names match; evidential documents should be the original confirmation or a certified copy.

name: General Patent Prosecution Highway (PPH) eligibility
description: An applicant who received a positive decision that at least one claim is allowable from an Office of First Filing (OFF) may request expedited examination at KIPO for a corresponding application that includes claims identical to the allowable claims or claims narrowed by restricting or adding limitations.
guidance: Participating countries are listed and may change; check KIPO homepage. From Jan 1, 2014, requirements were eased: if the earliest priority date of the corresponding application and the concerned KIPO application are the same, the application may be eligible. Specific cases include mutual priority claim situations and national-phase/PCT situations. The PPH allows KIPO to utilize prior art search and examination results from OFF.

name: PPH claim allowability and correspondence requirements
description: For PPH, claims in the corresponding application must have been decided allowable by the participating patent office, and all claims of the concerned KIPO application must correspond to those allowable claims (substantially identical or narrowed by added limitations).
guidance: Claims indicated allowable include those in a written decision to grant or, absent that, claims indicated allowable in the most recent office action or decision to reject. If allowability is not explicitly indicated due to absence of a ground for rejection, the requester should explain the reason in writing. Where claim categories differ, they are not corresponding; mere differences in translation or claim types (independent/dependent) can be deemed substantially the same. Claim correspondence is determined based on a claim correspondence table that the requester must submit.

name: PPH evidential document requirements and translation rules
description: A requester for expedited examination under PPH must submit specified evidential documents: copy of the claims (including the allowable claims), a copy of the examination-related notification from the participating office, copies of prior arts relied upon (non-patent docs must be provided), and an explanation on correspondence between each claim and the allowable claims.
guidance: If the examiner can obtain documents via public networks (AIPN, PAIR, PVS online, etc.), submission may be unnecessary. Documents in languages other than Korean or English must be accompanied by translations unless the examiner can obtain Korean/English translations via networks. The written explanation on claim correspondence is mandatory in all cases and should indicate grounds for correspondence (e.g., literal translation, minor translation differences).

name: PCT-PPH eligibility requirements
description: Under PCT-PPH, a KIPO application is eligible where an international search or international preliminary examination on a corresponding international application (performed in a participating country) includes claims meeting requirements for novelty, inventive step, and industrial applicability, and all claims of the concerned KIPO application correspond to those claims.
guidance: Eligible cases include national-phase applications, applications claiming priority based on the corresponding international application, divisional applications, and applications sharing priority. 'Correspond to' includes substantially identical claims and claims further limited by added limitations; mere translation or claim-type differences are acceptable. Claim correspondence is determined by a submitted claim correspondence table and written explanation.

name: PCT-PPH evidential documents and handling of international opinions
description: Requesters for PCT-PPH must submit a copy of the claims recognized to meet requirements in the international search/exam, a copy of the written opinion or international preliminary examination report, copies of prior art cited in those documents (non-patent docs must be provided), and an explanation on correspondence between all claims and those recognized in international proceedings.
guidance: If 'opinions on an international application' (Box VIII) indicate ambiguity or unclear claims, the requester must explain that the concerned KIPO claims are not affected—this may include responses to those opinions or amendments addressing irregularities. If such explanations are missing, examiner may order amendments. Documents in languages other than Korean/English require translations unless obtainable via public networks (Patentscope etc.).

name: Determination / redetermination and amendment effects on expedited status
description: Determinations on expedited examination made under agreements with foreign offices are not notified to requester unless the request is rejected. If, after determination but before examination starts, the applicant amends claims/specification such that claims are not included in prior comparisons or are not substantially identical to claims recognized as allowable/meeting requirements, the examiner may order corrections and re-determine whether to permit expedited examination.
guidance: An examiner may grant a correction order with a period up to one month at their discretion. If an applicant submits explanations comparing all claims (including amended ones) with prior-art or allowable claims, or submits correspondence explanations for claims meeting international requirements, expedited examination shall be conducted without re-determination. Examiners can order supplementation where explanations are insufficient.

name: Rule 4.2 Communication With Person Represented By Counsel
description: In representing a client, a practitioner shall not communicate about the subject of the representation with a person the practitioner knows to be represented by another practitioner in the matter, unless the practitioner has the consent of the other practitioner or is authorized to do so by law, rule, or a court order.
guidance: Includes an explicit exception for communications with government officials who are otherwise represented but have authority to redress grievances, provided the practitioner first discloses their identity and that they represent a party with a claim against the government (see attached disclosure language).

name: Rule 7.4 Communication Of Fields Of Practice And Specialization
description: (a) A practitioner may communicate the fact that the practitioner does or does not practice in particular fields of law. (b) A registered practitioner who is an attorney may use designations such as 'Patents,' 'Patent Attorney,' 'Patent Lawyer,' 'Registered Patent Attorney,' or similar; a registered practitioner who is not an attorney may use 'Patents,' 'Patent Agent,' 'Registered Patent Agent,' or similar. Unless authorized by § 11.14(b), a registered patent agent shall not hold himself or herself out as being qualified or authorized to practice before the Office in trademark matters or before a court. (d) A practitioner shall not state or imply that a practitioner is certified as a specialist in a particular field of law unless (1) certified by an organization approved by an appropriate state authority or accredited by the ABA, and (2) the name of the certifying organization is clearly identified in the communication. (e) An individual granted limited recognition under § 11.9 may use the designation 'Limited Recognition.'
guidance: Permits truthful statements of fields and specific patent-related designations for registered practitioners, but restricts misrepresentations of specialization and cross-practice claims; requires identification of certifying organization when claiming specialist status.

name: Criterion A for requiring information for prior art (search limitations)
description: The examiner’s search and preliminary analysis demonstrates that the claimed subject matter cannot be adequately searched by class or keyword among patents and typical sources of non-patent literature.
guidance: Often applies in new areas of technology without established classification or where class art diverges substantially from the claimed subject matter.

name: Example Q/R: Clarification of means-plus-function support
description: Clarification of the correlation and identification of what structure, material, or acts set forth in the specification would be capable of carrying out a function recited in a means or steps plus function claim limitation.
guidance: If applicant cannot identify specification support, examiner may conclude there is no such support and make appropriate rejections under 35 U.S.C. 112 (written description/definiteness).

name: Example S: Interrogatories or stipulations of facts known to applicant
description: Use of interrogatories or stipulations to obtain facts known to the applicant (e.g., common technical features shared among claims; support in the disclosure for means/steps-plus-function claims; portions of disclosure providing written description/enablement; meaning of claim terms; which claim portions correspond to admitted prior art; specific utility by claim).
guidance: Interrogatories must be factual in scope and clearly set forth; stipulations can clarify uncontroverted matters. Use form paragraphs 7.105.01 and 7.105.02 where appropriate.

name: Factors for appropriateness prior to first action
description: Factors: (A) claimed subject matter in newly established art area without developed prior art pool; (B) whether applicant submitted an IDS; (C) whether specification background adequately describes background; (D) whether related documents by inventor/assignee not submitted are found; (E) whether non-patent literature is referred to but copy not supplied; (F) background describes information as known or conventional but examiner unfamiliar and can't find it.
guidance: Consider these when deciding to issue a requirement before the first action on the merits.

name: Format of the requirement (must state basis, scope, and form expected)
description: The requirement must clearly indicate that a requirement under 37 CFR 1.105 is being made, the basis for the requirement, and what information is being required. Requirements should specify the particular art area involved, and the particular claimed subject matter within such art area, in which the information is required.
guidance: The requirement should also indicate the form the required information is expected to take (citations/copies, identification of collections, answers to questions, etc.). Generally prepare requirement as a separate document (preferable to including within an Office action). The requirement should state why it was made and how the information is necessary to examination. Interrogatories and stipulations may be used.

name: Use of prescribed form paragraphs when preparing requirements
description: Specific form paragraphs (e.g., ¶ 7.104.02; ¶ 7.105; ¶ 7.105.01; ¶ 7.105.02; ¶ 7.106–¶ 7.121; ¶ 7.122–¶ 7.126) should be used when preparing a requirement for information.
guidance: Form paragraphs include headings, specimen interrogatories/stipulations, and many tailored request templates (domain of search, level of skill, background description, products embodying invention, art suggested by applicant, lists of keywords, database citations, copies of referred art, publications authored by inventors, art relied upon for prior art description, art relied upon for development/drafting, results of prior art search, product names incorporating claimed invention/prior art, details of improvements over prior art, etc.). Use appropriate bracketed insertions and examiner notes per each form paragraph.

name: ¶7.106 Domain of Search (form paragraph guidance)
description: The information is required to extend the domain of search for prior art; limited amounts of art available within the Office are generally found in specified class/subclasses which describe the art; a broader range of art to search is necessary.
guidance: Insert description of art claimed but not found in the classification system; precede with ¶7.105 and follow with ¶7.122–¶7.126 as appropriate.

name: ¶7.117 Art Relied Upon for Drafting Claimed Subject Matter (form paragraph guidance)
description: Provide the title, citation and copy of each publication that was relied upon to draft the claimed subject matter and a concise explanation of the reliance placed on that publication in distinguishing the claimed subject matter from the prior art.
guidance: Limited to documents actually relied upon; for means/steps-plus-function claims identify specific page/line numbers supporting claimed structure/acts.

name: ¶7.119–¶7.121 Product/prior-art and improvement detail requests (form paragraph guidance)
description: Requests for names of products/services incorporating the claimed invention (¶7.119), names of products/services incorporating disclosed prior art (¶7.120), and details of improvement over the prior art (¶7.121) including specific elements providing improvements.
guidance: Use to identify real-world implementations and to obtain applicant's explanation of claim-to-art improvement.

name: Claims drafting and scope of protection
description: Claims determine the extent of protection; they must be based on the specifications and clearly and precisely define the subject matter, avoiding expressions leading to uncertainties (Article 25 and Article 41).
guidance: Claims may be independent (protect essential technical characteristics) or dependent (include features of previous claims). In invention claims, after the preamble the expression 'characterized by' must define essential technical features. Multiple independent claims are allowed if connected by the same inventive concept; claims of different categories (product/process/apparatus) should show interconnection when appropriate using linking phrases. For utility models the main independent claim must fully characterize the elements, positions and interconnections; dependent claims may describe optional complementary elements or variations that don't change unity or operation.

name: Priority rules (unionist priority and internal priority)
description: Unionist priority (Paris Convention) allows a 12-month priority period from first filing abroad; internal priority within Brazil allows a later Brazil filing to claim priority from an earlier Brazil filing by the same applicant within one year (Article 17).
guidance: Priority is admitted only for subject matter disclosed in the previous application; new matter is not covered. Both earlier and subsequent applications must contain complete technical content. A divisional application cannot serve as basis for claiming priority. Internal priority does not extend time limits for claiming unionist priority abroad.

name: Patent term, grant, and formalities (term, publication, letters patent)
description: Invention patents: 20 years from filing; utility models: 15 years from filing (Article 49). A patent is granted after application approval and proof of payment, with issuance of letters patent (Article 38).
guidance: Payment and proof must be made within 60 days of granting (Article 38(1)); patent deemed granted on date of publication (Article 38(3)). Letters patent must contain number, title, nature, inventor name, holder identification and address, term of validity, specifications, claims, drawings, and priority data (Article 39). Patents are territorial; valid only in countries granting protection (Article 4 bis of Paris Convention). Historical Article 40 provided minimum-term protections linked to INPI delay but was declared unconstitutional and later revoked; backlog and long prosecution times have practical term implications.

name: Administrative nullity proceedings (grounds and timing)
description: The patent's nullity will be declared administratively when any legal requirement has not been met; specifications and claims do not comply with Articles 24 and 25; subject matter extends beyond original application content; or essential formalities were not met during processing (Law No. 9,279, art. 50). Nullity proceedings may be filed at authority's initiative or by any person with legitimate interest within six months from grant (Article 51), and may also be filed at any time during the patent's term by INPI or any person with legitimate interest (Article 56).
guidance: Administrative procedure: holder notified to provide a statement within 60 days (art. 52); INPI issues an opinion and notifies holder and claimant to provide statements within 60 days (art. 53). Note that Article 50's breadth has been criticized as potentially allowing nullity for formal noncompliances; Patent Law Treaty limits invalidation for certain formal defects in absence of fraud.

name: Claims interpretation and process/product overlap
description: Claims define and limit protection and are interpreted in view of specifications and drawings (Article 41). Process patents cover products obtained directly by a patented process; if possessor/owner cannot prove different process, process patent infringement is presumed (Article 42(2)).
guidance: Draft claims to clearly capture both product and process aspects where appropriate; ensure specs support any product-by-process or process claims to avoid invalidity or unenforceability.

name: Utility model drafting specifics
description: For utility models, after 'characterized by' all elements constituting the model must be defined with their positions and interconnections. The set of arrangements and forms responsible for best use must be fully characterized in a single independent main claim.
guidance: Utility models may include complementary optional elements or variations in dependent claims that don't change unity/operation; a flat structured model may admit a dependent claim describing a secondary three-dimensional shape arising from flat structure.

name: Relevant prior art for the international search
description: For Article 15(2), relevant prior art consists of everything made available to the public anywhere in the world by written disclosure (including drawings/illustrations) capable of assisting in determining novelty and inventive step, provided the making available occurred prior to the international filing date. Written disclosures that refer to oral disclosures, use, exhibition etc shall be separately mentioned in the international search report when the making available occurred prior to the filing date. Published applications/patents whose publication date is same as or later than but whose filing date (or claimed priority date) is earlier than the international filing date and which would have been relevant if published prior to the filing date shall be specially mentioned in the search report.
guidance: Search reports must note prior art timing nuances; both publication and filing/priority dates matter for relevance.

name: Fields to be covered by the international search
description: The international search shall cover all technical fields and be carried out on the basis of all search files which may contain material pertinent to the invention. Not only shall the art in which the invention is classifiable be searched but also analogous arts regardless of classification. Whether arts are analogous should be considered in light of the necessary essential function or use of the invention. The international search shall also embrace subject matter generally recognized as equivalent to the subject matter of the claimed invention for all or certain features.
guidance: Search scope is broad: include analogous arts determined by essential function/use and equivalents to claimed subject matter.

name: Orientation of the international search
description: International search shall be made on the basis of the claims, with due regard to the description and drawings and with particular emphasis on the inventive concept towards which the claims are directed. As far as possible and reasonable, the search shall cover the entire subject matter to which the claims are directed or to which they might reasonably be expected to be directed after amendment.
guidance: Claims are primary but description/drawings and conceivable amended claim scope must be considered.

name: Definition/list of 'national patent documents'
description: Subject to paragraphs, 'national patent documents' shall include: (i) patents issued in and after 1920 by France, former Reichspatentamt of Germany, Japan, former Soviet Union, Switzerland (French/German only), UK, USA; (ii) patents issued by FRG, PRC, Republic of Korea, Russian Federation; (iii) patent applications published in/after 1920 in those countries; (iv) inventors' certificates issued by former Soviet Union; (v) utility certificates issued by France and published applications for utility certificates; (vi) such patents/applications in any other country after 1920 as are in English/French/German/Spanish and in which no priority is claimed, provided the national Office places these at disposal of each ISA.
guidance: Specifies which national patent collections must be included in minimum documentation; language and date criteria apply.

name: Contents and language requirements of the international search report
description: The international search report shall be dated and indicate the date on which the international search was actually completed and the filing date of any earlier application whose priority is claimed (or earliest among them). It shall contain classification at least according to the International Patent Classification, effected by the ISA. Every international search report and any declaration under Article 17(2)(a) shall be in the language in which the international application is to be published, provided that if a translation of the application into another language was transmitted and the ISA so wishes, the report and declaration may be in the language of that translation; further language exception rules apply where translations furnished under Rule 12.4 are not accepted by the ISA.
guidance: Reports must state completion date, priority filing dates, IPC classification, and be in the publication language (with specified translation exceptions). Also must identify the ISA, application number, applicant name and filing date.

name: Base claims on the most exact experiments
description: «il a toujours soin de justifier la nomenclature dont il fait usage, & de suivre les rapports qui doivent se trouver entre les idées & les mots qui les représentent.» (and earlier: "établir, par les expériences les plus exactes, les faits qui doivent servir de base aux connoissances chimiques")
guidance: Experimental facts should be the foundation of chemical knowledge: design and report precise, repeatable experiments; use experimental results to justify theoretical claims. Emphasize exact measurement and empirical grounding rather than speculation.

name: Public acquiescence as indicia of invention
description: Public acquiescence in the inventor's rights over an extended period is a strong circumstance to prove invention.
guidance: Longstanding acceptance of the inventor's exclusive rights (e.g., no competing claims or challenges over time) supports inventive character.

name: Markedly different characteristics analysis (overview)
description: The markedly different characteristics analysis compares the nature-based product limitation to its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state. Markedly different characteristics can be expressed as the product’s structure, function, and/or other properties, and are evaluated based on what is recited in the claim on a case-by-case basis.
guidance: If the analysis indicates that a nature-based product limitation does not exhibit markedly different characteristics, then that limitation is a product of nature exception. If the analysis indicates that a nature-based product limitation has markedly different characteristics, then that limitation is not a product of nature exception. If the nature-based product is naturally occurring, no analysis is necessary because it by definition falls under the product-of-nature exception.

name: Identify appropriate characteristics for analysis
description: Identify the characteristics of the claimed nature-based product to compare to the counterpart; appropriate characteristics must be possessed by the claimed product and are determined from the claim language and its broadest reasonable interpretation.
guidance: Characteristics may be explicitly recited in the claim or apparent from the broadest reasonable interpretation (e.g., chemical name, 'isolated gene B'). Unclaimed characteristics cannot be relied upon. Consider what the claim defines and what is encompassed by that definition when identifying characteristics.

name: Examples of characteristics that do NOT establish marked difference (case examples)
description: Court examples where changes were incidental/not enough, or where claimed differences were unclaimed/innate and thus insufficient.
guidance: Myriad isolated genes: isolation-induced incidental structural changes (loss of covalent bonds) were not enough because genes remained otherwise identical. Ambry primers: single-stranded primers corresponded exactly to natural sequences and exploited innate binding function of DNA; thus lacked markedly different characteristics. Roslin clones: clones were genetic replicas; unclaimed phenotypic differences did not make them markedly different. Marden: inherent ductility was not given by applicant and thus not markedly different.

name: Search for an inventive concept (Alice/Mayo Step 2B – overview)
description: After determining a claim is directed to a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon), determine whether the claim integrates the exception into an 'inventive concept' so that the claim amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception itself.
guidance: An inventive concept cannot be furnished by the unpatentable judicial exception itself. It must be an element or combination of elements recited in the claim in addition to the judicial exception and be sufficient to ensure the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more. Consider additional elements both individually and as an ordered combination.

name: Consideration of claim elements individually and in combination
description: Evaluating additional elements requires assessing both their individual contribution and their combined effect to determine whether they amount to significantly more than the judicial exception.
guidance: Although an element may not be significantly more on its own, a non-conventional, non-generic arrangement of individually known elements may provide an inventive concept (e.g., BASCOM; CellzDirect). Claims must be considered as a whole (Diehr).

name: Considerations that courts have found to qualify as 'significantly more'
description: Limitations that courts have found, when recited with a judicial exception, to qualify as 'significantly more' (non-exhaustive list).
guidance: Includes (i) improvements to functioning of a computer (DDR Holdings example); (ii) improvements to any other technology/technical field (Diehr thermocouple example); (iii) applying the judicial exception with, or by use of, a particular machine arranged in a particular way (Eibel/Fourdrinier example); (iv) effecting a transformation/reduction of an article to a different state or thing (Diehr rubber example); (v) adding specific limitations other than well-understood, routine, conventional activity or adding unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application (BASCOM non-conventional arrangement); (vi) other meaningful limitations beyond generally linking the exception to a technological environment (Classen immunization example).

name: Examples of limitations found NOT to be 'significantly more'
description: Limitations courts have held insufficient to transform a claim directed to a judicial exception into patent-eligible subject matter.
guidance: Includes: (i) merely adding the words 'apply it' or equivalent instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer (Alice); (ii) appending well-understood, routine, conventional activities at a high level of generality (generic computer implementation) (Alice); (iii) adding insignificant extra-solution activity such as mere data gathering (CyberSource); (iv) generally linking the judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use (Bilski, Parker v. Flook).

name: Physicality/tangibility of additional elements is not dispositive
description: Mere physical implementation or tangibility is not, by itself, an inventive concept; nor is the absence of physicality dispositive against eligibility.
guidance: The fact that a computer is a tangible machine does not automatically render a claim patent-eligible; courts have warned that counting tangibility alone would let applicants claim any principle by reciting a computer. Conversely, improvements that are not defined by physical components can still be eligible if they improve an existing technological process (Enfish, McRO).

name: How courts conduct the Step 2B analysis (examples)
description: Illustrative stepwise approach courts have used in analyzing inventive concept under Alice and related cases.
guidance: Example (Alice): identify additional claim elements (hardware/software steps), consider them individually (are they well-understood, routine, conventional?), then consider them as an ordered combination (do they add something substantially more?). Example (BASCOM): district court identified elements as generic, but Federal Circuit emphasized considering the unconventional arrangement of components together to find an inventive concept.

name: Adding claims to inventions by inventors not named (amendment permitted)
description: Pending nonprovisional applications will be permitted to be amended by complying with 37 CFR 1.48 to add claims to inventions by inventors not named when the application was filed as long as such inventions were disclosed in the application as filed.
guidance: 37 CFR 1.48 permits correction of inventorship where the correct inventor(s) were not named in an application for patent. The amendment cannot introduce new matter; added claims must be supported in the original disclosure.

name: Supplemental oath or declaration filed after allowance
description: Supplemental oaths and declarations covering the claims in the application may be filed after allowance as a matter of right.
guidance: When received they will be placed in the file by the Office of Data Management but their receipt will not be acknowledged. They should not be filed or considered as amendments under 37 CFR 1.312 since they make no change in the wording of the papers on file.

name: Anticipation requires all claim limitations in a single prior reference
description: A prior reference anticipates only if it discloses the claimed subject matter, including all limitations; anticipation law does not permit filling in missing limitations simply because a skilled artisan would immediately envision them.
guidance: Cite Nidec: cannot fill in missing limitations. Examiner must establish a prima facie case of anticipation (In re Oetiker) and show that the reference discloses the claimed dosages/ratios/components (e.g., Mark, Olive/Walnut Nutrient Analyses). References that are non‑operable or out of temporal context may be improper bases for anticipation.

name: Specification and prosecution history may make claim elements limiting or non‑limiting
description: Whether claim language (e.g., 'dosage', 'casings providing controlled delivery') is limiting depends on the specification and prosecution history; the specification's statements that elements are or are not limiting affect patentability and anticipation analyses.
guidance: The court and PTO relied on statements that 'the specification states that these claim elements are not limiting' to deny patentability here; applicants should ensure the specification supports their intended limiting construction and preserve arguments during prosecution (see Gulack, Trivascular references cited).

name: Prosecution disclaimer can narrow claim scope and avoid prior‑art overlaps
description: A prosecution disclaimer (e.g., disavowing single‑source compositions such as olives or walnuts) can limit the scope of the claims and bear on anticipation and eligibility.
guidance: If applicant disclaimed single‑source products during prosecution, the Board and court may treat references to single‑source products as outside the claimed scope; ensure prosecution statements are clear and preserved for appeal if relied upon.

name: Substantial evidence standard for affirmance of PTAB findings
description: PTAB findings (e.g., that references show dosages within claimed ranges or that additional limitations are known) are reviewed for support by substantial evidence in the record.
guidance: The Federal Circuit affirmed where the Board's factual findings were supported by substantial evidence (e.g., nutrient analyses showing amounts within claim limits). Challenging parties must point to record evidence that undermines the Board's factual findings.

name: Product‑of‑nature doctrine (§101): claimed composition must be markedly different or involve a transformation
description: Claims directed to natural products are ineligible under §101 unless the claimed composition is shown to be a transformation of a natural product or to have properties not possessed in nature, or unless the claim adds 'significantly more' to the natural product under Mayo/Alice framework.
guidance: Applicant must show evidence that claimed mixtures (e.g., intermixture of lipids from different sources, dosages, casings) change functionality or confer synergy. The decision held applicant failed to show transformation or properties not in nature. Use USPTO examples (e.g., Example 28) for analogies: reciting specific carriers/structures that change physical characteristics can help.

name: Mayo two‑step framework applies: identify natural product then determine 'significantly more'
description: §101 analysis should (1) determine whether claims are directed to a natural product/phenomenon and (2) determine whether the additional elements amount to 'significantly more' than the natural product.
guidance: Court here considered whether 'dosage' and 'casings providing controlled delivery' change functionality (step one) and whether the claims confer a patent‑eligible inventive concept (step two). Applicants should present evidence and reasoning on both steps.

name: Functional claim limitations can confer patentability if they change function/characteristics
description: Limitations such as 'dosage' and 'casings providing controlled delivery' may render a claim patent‑eligible if they change how the natural material functions (i.e., change physical characteristics or confer new properties).
guidance: The court and Board examined whether such limitations existed in nature or were merely described but non‑limiting. Applicants should ensure the specification describes asserted novel functional effects and provide supporting data or expert testimony.

name: Intermixture from different sources must be shown to be structurally or functionally distinct
description: Asserting that an 'intermixture of lipids from different sources' makes a composition non‑natural requires evidence that such intermixtures are structurally different from and have properties not possessed by single‑source natural oils.
guidance: Provide scientific publications, PHOSITA testimony, or experimental evidence showing synergy, altered phytochemical delivery, oxidative stability differences, or other altered properties (the applicant claimed five publications and four PHOSITA testimonies in this case).

name: Prior art references must disclose required components and contextual limitations, not just ranges
description: When claims require specific carriers, binders, casings, or combination elements (e.g., 'one or more carriers selected from starches, sugars, granulating agents, binders and disintegrating agents'), a nutrient analysis that only reports fatty acid amounts may be insufficient to show disclosure of those components.
guidance: The Board reversed as to some claims where examiner failed to show that references disclosed the recited carriers. Examiners must point to disclosure of particular components; applicants can attack anticipatory references for lack of that disclosure.

name: Serving‑size measurements in references are not automatically equivalent to claimed 'dosage'
description: Whether a reference's 'serving' or nutrient‑density measurement qualifies as the claimed 'dosage' depends on context and PHOSITA understanding; a serving may be merely a way to measure nutrient density rather than a dosage.
guidance: Submit PHOSITA testimony or specification context to show that 'serving' does not equate to 'dosage' as claimed; challenge the Board's reliance on nutrient analyses used as dosages if record evidence supports a contrary interpretation.

name: Holistic claim construction: cannot excise subordinate clauses from main clause
description: Claims must be read in context; divorcing a main clause from subordinate clauses (e.g., ignoring the subordinate 'wherein' clauses that define 'dosage') is improper and can distort claim scope.
guidance: Cite claim construction precedents (Gulack, Trivascular). Ensure arguments maintain the contextual linkage between clauses; emphasize that the main clause's 'dosage' is informed by subordinate numeric or relational limitations.

name: Product‑by‑process claims evaluated on product identity
description: A product‑by‑process recitation (e.g., oils 'obtained from' certain nuts) does not necessarily avoid rejections if the claimed product is identical to a natural product; the identity of the product controls patentability, not merely the process language.
guidance: Funk Bros. and related authority: combinations that do not change nature/utility are not patentable. If product‑by‑process claims produce a product compositionally identical to a natural oil, §101/§102 issues remain.

name: Use USPTO Subject Matter Eligibility Examples as comparative guidance
description: USPTO examples (e.g., Example 28 distinguishing a vaccine with a generic carrier vs. a list of specific carriers that change characteristics) can guide analysis of whether recited carriers/casings change physical characteristics and thus confer eligibility.
guidance: Compare claim language to USPTO examples; reciting specific classes of carriers or structures that demonstrably alter characteristics may help under §101. However, ensure the examples are applied correctly and are factually supported in the specification/record.

name: Definition and scope of 'practice before the Office' (37 C.F.R. § 11.5(b))
description: 'Practice before the Office' includes any law-related service connected with presentation to the Office relating to a client's rights, privileges, duties, or responsibilities under laws or regulations administered by the Office, including preparing documents in contemplation of filing and communicating with and advising a client concerning matters pending or contemplated to be presented before the Office (37 C.F.R. § 11.5(b)).
guidance: Examples treated as 'practice' include drafting responses to Office actions, counseling clients on prosecution strategy, advising about legal significance of Office correspondence, and strategizing about filings. Whether someone is 'practicing' is fact-specific and central to unauthorized-practice claims.

name: Requirement for unity of invention (37 CFR 1.475(a))
description: A national stage application shall relate to one invention only or to a group of inventions so linked as to form a single general inventive concept. The requirement is fulfilled only when there is a technical relationship among those inventions involving one or more of the same or corresponding special technical features.
guidance: The expression 'special technical features' means those technical features that define a contribution which each of the claimed inventions, considered as a whole, makes over the prior art. The determination is made without regard to whether the inventions are claimed in separate claims or as alternatives within a single claim (see 37 CFR 1.475(e)). Begin lack-of-unity actions in national-stage applications with the specified heading and follow with the appropriate form paragraphs (e.g., 18.19 or 18.20).

name: Determination of unity without regard to claim format (37 CFR 1.475(e))
description: The determination whether a group of inventions is so linked as to form a single general inventive concept shall be made without regard to whether the inventions are claimed in separate claims or as alternatives within a single claim.
guidance: Do not let claim drafting format (separate claims vs alternatives within a single claim) dictate unity; analyze technical features and contribution over prior art.

name: Permitted combinations of different categories of invention (37 CFR 1.475(b))
description: A national stage application containing claims to different categories of invention will be considered to have unity of invention if the claims are drawn only to one of these combinations: (1) product & process specially adapted for manufacture of that product; (2) product & process of use of that product; (3) product, process specially adapted for manufacture, and a use; (4) process & apparatus/means specifically designed for carrying out the process; (5) product, process specially adapted for manufacture, and apparatus/means specifically designed for carrying out the process.
guidance: If claims fall outside these permitted combinations, unity may not be present (see 37 CFR 1.475(c)). When making restriction requirements between product/apparatus and process, follow guidance about rejoinder (form paragraph 8.21.04) and reconsider restriction if elected claims are allowable.

name: Markush-group chemical alternatives: criteria for 'similar nature'
description: When a single claim defines alternatives of a Markush group, the alternatives are regarded as being of a similar nature where (A) all alternatives have a common property or activity; AND (B) (1) a common structure is present (a significant structural element is shared by all alternatives); OR (B)(2) if common structure cannot unify, all alternatives belong to a recognized class of chemical compounds in the art.
guidance: ‘Significant structural element’ refers to a common chemical structure occupying a large portion of structures, or a small but structurally distinctive portion essential to the common property in view of prior art. ‘Recognized class’ means expectation from the art that members will behave similarly and be substitutable one for another to achieve the intended result.

name: Description defect — inadequate written description (PCT Article 6)
description: Claim [1] objected to under PCT Article 6 because the claim [2] not fully supported by the description. The application, as originally filed, did not describe: [3]
guidance: Identify the claim(s) and the subject matter not described in the application as filed. Use to object if claims claim matter not originally described.

name: Description defect — non-enabling disclosure (PCT Article 5)
description: Claim [1] objected to under PCT Article 6 because the claim [2] not fully supported by the description. The description does not disclose the claimed invention in a manner sufficiently clear and complete for the claimed invention to be carried out by a person skilled in the art as required by PCT Article 5 because: [3]
guidance: Identify claimed subject matter not enabled and explain why it is not enabled. Insert relevant details in bracket 3.

name: Description defect — failure to disclose best mode (PCT Rule 5.1(a)(v))
description: Claim [1] objected to under PCT Article 6 because the claim [2] not fully supported by the description. The description fails to set forth the best mode contemplated by the applicant for carrying out the claimed invention as required by PCT Rule 5.1(a)(v) because: [3].
guidance: Identify claim(s), verb forms, and insert the objection and reasons in bracket 3.

name: Claims — defect in form or contents
description: Claim [1] contain(s) the following defect(s) in the form or contents thereof: [2]
guidance: Pluralize 'claim' if needed and identify the technical deficiency in bracket 2 (e.g., antecedent basis, indefiniteness, formal defects).

name: Claims objectionable — indefiniteness (PCT Article 6)
description: Claim [1] objected to under PCT Article 6 as lacking clarity because claim [2] indefinite for the following reason(s): [3]
guidance: Insert specific reasons for indefiniteness in bracket 3. Ensure claim numbering and verb forms are correct in brackets 1 and 2.

name: Election of species in national stage (18.20)
description: This application contains claims directed to more than one species of the generic invention. These species are deemed to lack unity of invention because they are not so linked as to form a single general inventive concept under PCT Rule 13.1. Applicant is required to elect a single species to which the claims shall be restricted if no generic claim is finally held to be allowable.
guidance: Reply must identify the claims readable on the elected species; an argument that a claim is allowable or that all claims are generic is non-responsive unless accompanied by an election. Upon allowance of a generic claim, applicant is entitled to consideration of additional species written in dependent form or requiring all limitations of an allowed generic claim. Identify species in bracket 1 and each generic claim by number or insert 'NONE'.

name: Requirement for election and rules for traversal (37 CFR 1.143; right to petition 1.144)
description: The reply must include (i) an election of a species or invention to be examined even though the requirement may be traversed (37 CFR 1.143) and (ii) identification of the claims encompassing the elected invention. The election may be made with or without traverse. To preserve a right to petition, the election must be made with traverse. If the reply does not distinctly and specifically point out supposed errors in the restriction requirement, the election shall be treated as an election without traverse. Traversal must be presented at the time of election.
guidance: If traversing on the ground that inventions have unity, applicant must provide reasons and may submit evidence or identify evidence of obvious variants or admissions. Evidence or admissions provided may be used by the examiner in a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) of the other invention. Failure to timely traverse results in loss of right to petition under 37 CFR 1.144. If claims are added after election, applicant must indicate which are readable on the elected invention or species.

name: Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 305 — claim enlarges scope of patent
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 305 as enlarging the scope of the claim(s) of the patent being reexamined. A claim enlarges the scope where it is broader than any claim of the patent. A claim is broader if it contains any conceivable product or process which would not have infringed the original patent; broadened if broader in any one respect even if narrower in others.
