guidance: Identify the claim limitations considered to broaden the scope and explain why (insert in bracket 2). See MPEP § 2258 for further guidance.

name: Proposed amendments in reexamination must comply with 37 CFR 1.530(d)-(j) and formal presentation (37 CFR 1.52)
description: Any proposed amendment to the specification and/or claims in this reexamination proceeding must comply with 37 CFR 1.530(d)-(j), must be formally presented pursuant to 37 CFR 1.52(a) and (b), and must contain any fees required by 37 CFR 1.20(c).
guidance: Advise patent owner of proper manner of making amendments in a reexamination proceeding; use in order granting reexamination and/or first Office action.

name: Preliminary_amendment_entry_rules_37_CFR_1.115
description: Preliminary amendments (received on or before mail date of first Office action) will be entered unless disapproved by the Commissioner. They may be disapproved if they unduly interfere with preparation of the first Office action.
guidance: Factors for disapproval include the state of preparation of the first Office action as of receipt and the nature of changes to specification/claims that would result from entry. Certain filing timing (e.g., within 3 months of filing date, national stage entry, CPA filing date, or last day of suspension requested under 1.103) protects entry and these periods are not extendable.

name: Second_or_subsequent_supplemental_reply_entry_rules_37_CFR_1.111
description: A second (or subsequent) supplemental reply will be entered unless disapproved; it may be disapproved if it unduly interferes with an Office action being prepared in response to the previous reply.
guidance: Consider state of preparation of the responsive Office action and nature of changes to specification/claims that entry would cause. Applicants encouraged to include complete reply in first reply to avoid supplemental replies.

name: Examples_of_changes_justifying_denial_of_entry
description: Entry may be denied if the amendment/reply: (A) amends the claims; (B) adds numerous new claims; (C) amends the specification to change scope of claims; (D) amends spec raising new matter; (E) includes arguments; (F) includes affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131/1.132; or (G) includes evidence traversing prior rejections.
guidance: This list is not exhaustive; any situation meeting the two-condition test may support denial. Obtain SPE approval before denying.

name: Immediate_inspection_checklist_for_amendments
description: All amended applications forwarded to the examiner should be inspected immediately to determine: (A) proper signature; (B) filing within statutory/shortened period or time limit; (C) full responsiveness and compliance with 37 CFR 1.121; (D) whether changes warrant transfer; (E) whether application is special; (F) if claims suggested for interference copied; (G) traversal of restriction requirement; (H) use of non-permanent 'easily erasable' paper; (I) applicant-cited references; (J) terminal disclaimer filed; (K) addition of matter involving security.
guidance: Immediate inspection prevents abandonment and allows timely notification of deficiencies if sufficient time remains.

name: Post-final_interview_policy
description: One personal interview by applicant may be entertained after final action if circumstances warrant; ordinarily only one request should be granted, though in exceptional circumstances examiner may initiate a second if it would materially assist allowance.
guidance: Encourage applicants to include a range of claim alternatives (broad to detailed) by time of filing or at least by first reply to alleviate post-final difficulties.

name: Improvement in the functioning of a computer or other technology/technical field
description: An important consideration is whether the claimed invention improves the functioning of a computer or other technology or technical field.
guidance: Examiners should evaluate the specification to determine if the disclosure provides sufficient details such that one of ordinary skill in the art would recognize the claimed invention as providing an improvement. The specification need not explicitly state the improvement but must describe the invention so the improvement would be apparent to a person of ordinary skill. If the specification asserts an improvement in a conclusory manner (bare assertion without necessary detail), the examiner should not find the claim improves technology. The claim must be evaluated to ensure it reflects the disclosed improvement (it need not recite the improvement in words like “thereby increasing the bandwidth”). Under the 2019 PEG, the Step 2A “improvements” analysis determines whether the claim pertains to an improvement to the functioning of a computer or other technology without reference to whether it is well-understood, routine, or conventional. Consideration applies equally across technologies (computer-implemented, life sciences, etc.). Examiners are generally not expected to make qualitative judgments on the merits of the asserted improvement; if the examiner concludes no improvement, the burden shifts to applicant to provide persuasive evidence (e.g., 37 C.F.R. § 1.132 declaration) showing what the specification conveys to one of ordinary skill. Examples cited: CellzDirect, Rapid Litigation Management, Finjan, Diehr, Trading Technologies.

name: Applying/using a judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis
description: A claim can integrate a judicial exception into a practical application by applying or using the judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition.
guidance: This consideration covers applying abstract ideas, laws of nature, or natural phenomena to effect treatments (e.g., acupuncture, administration of medication, dialysis, transplants, phototherapy, physiotherapy, radiation therapy, surgery). In assessing this consideration, evaluate the particularity of the treatment, whether the treatment has more than a nominal relationship to the exception, and whether the limitation is merely extra-solution activity or a field-of-use. Examples include Classen Immunotherapies, Vanda, and vaccination/genotype administration scenarios.

name: Particularity of the treatment or prophylaxis limitation
description: The treatment or prophylaxis limitation must be “particular,” i.e., specifically identified so that it does not encompass all applications of the judicial exception(s).
guidance: If the administration step is specific (e.g., administering a lower-than-normal dosage of a beta blocker to patients with a specific genotype), it can integrate a mental-process exception into a practical application. By contrast, a generic administration step such as “administering a suitable medication” is not particular and does not integrate the exception. Use concrete claim language to determine particularity.

name: Whether the limitation has more than a nominal or insignificant relationship to the exception
description: The treatment/prophylaxis limitation must have more than a nominal or insignificant relationship to the recited judicial exception(s).
guidance: Example: a claim reciting treating blood glucose >250 mg/dl with insulin has a meaningful connection to the law of nature (treats ketoacidosis risk) and integrates the exception; treating such a patient with aspirin (not known to treat ketoacidosis) has at best a nominal connection and does not integrate the law of nature. Evaluate whether the claimed treatment meaningfully applies the recited exception to address the identified condition.

name: Whether the limitation is merely extra-solution activity or a field-of-use
description: The treatment or prophylaxis limitation must impose meaningful limits on the judicial exception and cannot be merely extra-solution activity or a field-of-use restriction.
guidance: Example: Steps that only administer vaccines to gather data for a later mental-analysis step are extra-solution activity and do not integrate the exception. However, a subsequent step that applies the analyzed information (e.g., vaccinating a second group according to a newly determined lowest-risk schedule) applies the exception and integrates it into a practical application. Determine whether the claimed limitation does more than serve as a necessary precursor for using the exception.

name: Effecting a particular transformation or reduction of an article
description: Claim limitations that effect a particular transformation or reduction of an article are considerations that may indicate integration into a practical application.
guidance: Evaluate whether the claimed steps change the state or identity of an article in a way that meaningfully limits the judicial exception per MPEP guidance and examples. Use cited examples in the PEG for analogous fact patterns.

name: Specificity of claim limitations (relevance to evaluation)
description: Specificity of claim limitations is relevant to the evaluation of many considerations (e.g., use of a particular machine, particular transformation, whether limitations are mere instructions to apply an exception), though specificity alone is not a stand-alone consideration in Step 2A Prong Two.
guidance: Assess how specifically the claim limitations describe the implementation, machine, transformation, or steps. Specific, detailed limitations that reflect an asserted improvement or particular application are more likely to integrate an exception than vague or generic recitations. The specification may make the improvement apparent even if the claim does not use explicit ‘improvement’ language.

name: Consider the claim as a whole (evaluate limitations together)
description: Prong Two analysis considers the claim as a whole: the judicial-exception-containing limitations and the additional elements must be evaluated together to determine whether the claim integrates the judicial exception into a practical application.
guidance: Do not evaluate additional limitations in isolation or in a vacuum; examine how limitations interact and impact each other. Example: Bascom — filtering installed at an ISP server remote from end-users with customizable filtering features, considered together with other limitations, produced an improvement in technology. The analysis should address the combined effect of limitations on integration.

name: Requirements for a prima facie case of subject-matter ineligibility (examiner burden)
description: The examiner bears the initial burden to establish a prima facie case of ineligibility by explaining why a claim is ineligible clearly and specifically so the applicant has sufficient notice and can effectively respond.
guidance: When practicable, examiners should indicate how subject-matter eligibility rejections might be overcome. A Step 2B rejection should: (1) identify the judicial exception recited in the claim and explain why it is considered an exception (Step 2A Prong One); (2) for abstract ideas, explain why a specific limitation falls within one of the enumerated groupings (mathematical concepts, mental processes, certain methods of organizing human activity) or use the 2019 PEG 'tentative abstract idea' procedure; (3) for laws of nature/natural phenomena, identify the law/phenomenon recited and explain why; (4) evaluate and explain why additional elements individually and in combination do not integrate the exception into a practical application using the 2019 PEG considerations (Step 2A Prong Two); and (5) explain why the additional elements do not result in significantly more at Step 2B. If the examiner concludes certain elements are well-understood, routine, conventional, the examiner must expressly support the rejection with one of the four options specified in the Berkheimer Memorandum. Once the examiner satisfies the initial burden, the burden shifts to the applicant to rebut with argument or evidence (37 C.F.R. § 1.132); examiners must carefully consider all applicant arguments and evidence and provide a rebuttal in the next Office action if maintaining the rejection. See MPEP § 2106.07 for formulation guidance and MPEP 716.01 and 37 C.F.R. § 1.132 for evidence submission procedures.

name: Submission requirement — what counts as a submission
description: A 'submission' includes, but is not limited to, an information disclosure statement, an amendment to the written description, claims, or drawings, new arguments, or new evidence in support of patentability.
guidance: If reply to an Office action under 35 U.S.C. 132 is outstanding, the submission must meet the reply requirements of 37 CFR 1.111. A submission may consist of arguments in a previously filed appeal brief or reply brief, or incorporate them by reference. Previously filed after-final amendments (entered or unentered) may satisfy the submission requirement.

name: Opposition — grounds and scope of examination
description: Opposition to the grant of a patent may be made on a number of grounds, including that the patent claims an invention that falls under prior art within Japan or a foreign country at the time of the patent application's filing. A panel will examine only the claims to which an opposition is filed and will conduct the examination on the basis of the reasons and evidence pleaded by the demandant; however, the panel may examine reasons not pleaded in ex officio proceedings.
guidance: Panel’s invocation of ex officio examination must consider public interest, purpose of process, delays, and possible accurate determination. If grounds established, panel must rule patent revoked; revocation has retroactive effect (patent deemed never to have existed).

name: Trial for correction — purpose and allowed corrections
description: A patentee may file a request for a trial for correction to correct the claims, description or drawings of the patent. Article 126(1) provides that corrections may be limited to: restriction of the claims, correction of errors or mistranslations, clarification of any ambiguous statement, or rewriting a claim that cites the preceding claim so that it does not cite the preceding claim.
guidance: Trials for correction are ex parte documentary proceedings. Corrections are usually preventive to guard against invalidation or to clarify ambiguous parts. A request for correction may not be filed during certain pending proceedings (with some prescribed exceptions) and may not be filed after revocation. If request does not correspond to permitted purposes, chief judge notifies patentee and allows submission of a written opinion; failure may lead to disapproval.

name: Effects of allowed corrections
description: If a decision is made to allow a correction (either as a result of a trial or a request for correction) and that decision has become final and binding, the following are deemed to have been made based on the corrected claims, descriptions or drawings with retroactive effect: the filing and publication of the patent application; the examiner’s decision or a trial or appeal decision to the effect that the patent is to be granted; and the registration of the patent right.
guidance: Successful corrections have retroactive effect; strategize corrections carefully because they can change the effective scope and history of the patent.

name: Trials for invalidation — standing and inter partes nature
description: Interested persons may file a request for a trial for invalidation if they wish to invalidate a patent; trials for invalidation are inter partes trials involving a demandant (interested person) and demandee (patentee). Only an 'interested person' may file, determined case-by-case (examples: person being sued for infringement, a manufacturer of the same kind of product, persons claiming a legitimate right to obtain a patent).
guidance: Assess standing carefully; evidence of being sued or commercial overlap may qualify. Trials conducted by panels of three or five administrative patent judges.

name: Grounds for invalidation (Article 123(1) exhaustive list)
description: Reasons for invalidation are limited to the statutory reasons under Article 123(1)(i)–(viii): (i) patent granted on an application with amendment not complying with Article 17-2(3) (amendments must be within original disclosure); (ii) patent granted in violation of Articles 25, 29, 29-2, 32, 38, or 39(1)–(4) (conditions for patentability, enjoyment of rights by foreign nationals, unpatentable inventions, joint applications, prior application issues); (iii) patent granted in violation of a treaty; (iv) patent granted on an application not complying with requirements in Article 36(4)(i) or 36(6) re statements of detailed explanation or claims; (v) matters stated in foreign-language application documents are not within scope of foreign-language documents; (vi) patent granted on application filed by a person without right to grant (except where transfer registered); (vii) after grant, patentee falls into category not permitted enjoyment of patent right or patent comes to violate a treaty; (viii) corrections of description/claims/drawings obtained in violation of provisos to Article 126(1), Article 126(5)–(7) (as applied mutatis mutandis) or provisos to Article 120-5(2) or Article 134-2(1). No other reasons outside statutory provisions constitute grounds.
guidance: Grounds are exhaustive — craft invalidation requests strictly within statutory items. For example, include arguments on added matter, violations of patentability (novelty/ inventive step), entitlement, procedural/treaty violations, or improper corrections when applicable.

name: Patentee written reply and request for correction in invalidation trials
description: After a demandant files a request for invalidation, a patentee may submit written replies and file a request for correction to protect their patent rights. Corrections may include restriction of claims and clarification of ambiguous statements. A request for correction must identify purpose, must not add new matter, must not substantially expand or change scope of claims, and must fulfill requirements for independent patentability.
guidance: Time limits apply: corrections generally must be filed within the time limit for submitting a written reply (first opportunity) or after chief judge provides advance notice of a trial decision. Corrections that become final affect original registration retroactively.

name: Advance notice of a trial decision
description: The panel will provide parties and intervenors with advance notice of a trial decision when the panel is ready to make a trial decision following oral proceedings and in cases where a reason for trial is approved or a request for correction is not approved. The advance notice contains the same matters as the final decision, including conclusions, reasons, determination of appropriateness of corrections, and validity of all claims.
guidance: Advance notice allows patentee to file a request for correction or amend corrected materials; it was established to avoid 'catch-ball' situations with the IP High Court. The panel will not provide advance notice in certain cases (e.g., patentee opts out, no corrections filed and claims found valid, or all requested corrections approved). If patentee requests correction after advance notice, demandant may respond.

name: ¶ 7.85 Amendment Under 37 CFR 1.312 Entered
description: The amendment filed on [1] under 37 CFR 1.312 has been entered.
guidance: Use for amendments under 1.312 that do not affect the scope of the claims (may be signed by primary examiner) and for amendments entered under 1.312 which do affect the scope of the claims (requires signature of supervisory patent examiner). See MPEP § 714.16.

name: ¶ 7.87 Amendment Under 37 CFR 1.312 Not Entered
description: Form paragraph to notify applicant that an amendment under 37 CFR 1.312 has not been entered.
guidance: Specify the reasons for non-entry in the appropriate bracket (e.g., 'The amendment changes the scope of the claims.').

name: ¶ 7.97 Claims Allowed
description: Claim [1] allowed.
guidance: Use to indicate allowance of specific claim(s).

name: ¶ 7.106 Domain of Search
description: The information is required to extend the domain of search for prior art. Limited amounts of art related to the claimed subject matter are available within the Office, and are generally found in class [1] and subclasses [2], which describe [3]. A broader range of art to search is necessary to establish the level of knowledge of those of ordinary skill in the claimed subject matter art of [4].
guidance: Must be preceded by 7.105 and followed by 7.122–7.126. In bracket 4 insert description of art claimed but not found in classification system.

name: ¶ 7.117 Art Relied Upon for Drafting Claimed Subject Matter
description: In response to this requirement, please provide the title, citation and copy of each publication that was relied upon to draft the claimed subject matter. For each publication, provide a concise explanation of the reliance placed on that publication in distinguishing the claimed subject matter from the prior art.
guidance: Must be preceded by 7.105 and followed by 7.122–7.126. Limited to documents actually relied on.

name: ¶ 7.120 Names of Products or Services Incorporating Disclosed Prior Art
description: In response to this requirement, please provide the names of any products or services that have incorporated the disclosed prior art [1].
guidance: Must be preceded by 7.105 and followed by 7.122–7.126. In bracket 1 specify attributes of the prior art that most closely approximate the claimed subject matter to narrow focus of reply.

name: ¶ 7.121 Details of Improvement Over the Prior Art
description: In response to this requirement, please state the specific improvements of the subject matter in claims [1] over the disclosed prior art and indicate the specific elements in the claimed subject matter that provide those improvements. For claims expressed as means or steps plus function, provide specific page and line numbers within the disclosure which describe the claimed structure and acts.
guidance: Must be preceded by 7.105 and followed by 7.122–7.126.

name: After one year and four months only clerical corrections permitted (no additions/changes)
description: Amendments of a priority claim after one year and four months has elapsed shall be permitted only when correcting clerical errors in the indication of the priority claim; changing/specifying/adding the first application is not allowed. However, withdrawal of all or part of priority claims in multiple claims remains allowed.
guidance: Statutory period is strict: additions or specification of the first application after 1 year 4 months are not allowed; examiner may allow only clerical amendments.

name: Substantive examination: grant retroactive filing date per-invention if identical
description: If the invention described in the application claiming priority is identical to the one in the first application (as shown by specification/drawings), the examiner shall examine patentability based on the retroactive filing date of the first application; if not identical, examine based on the filing date of the application claiming priority.
guidance: When rejecting without granting a retroactive filing date, the examiner must describe why retroactivity was not granted along with the grounds for rejection. Examiner may request translations of evidential documents when prior art search shows intervening prior art.

name: Identicalness standard: claims need match the disclosure of first application (not necessarily identical claims)
description: Identicalness does not require the claims of both applications to be identical; rather the invention described in the claims of the later application must be identical to the invention described in the specification or drawings of the first application (apply Article 29(3) standard).
guidance: Inventions are deemed identical in specific situations: (i) later app filed for part of the first app, (ii) later apps based on divisionals of the first app, (iii) single later app filed based on more than two first applications. Priority can be recognized by invention (i.e., per-invention).

name: Treatment of multiple priority claims (multiple first applications)
description: For applications with multiple priority claims, the examiner should not automatically reject for being based on two or more first applications; if inventions are not identical, examiner can cite violation (Article 45). Applicant may divide the application and retain priority for each divided application. Examiner examines based on earliest filing date of each invention.
guidance: If a claimed invention combines subject matter separately described only in different first applications (e.g., combining 'a' from A and 'b' from B), the invention is examined based on the actual filing date of the later (Korean) application (no retroactivity). If the earliest-filed priority among multiple is withdrawn, the examiner must determine whether the newly earliest-filed application can serve as the priority basis per Paris Convention.

name: Prior-art search and choice of filing date for patentability examination
description: If prior art (Article 29 or Article 36 prior-filed application) is not found between the filing date of the first application and the filing date of the priority-claiming application, examine patentability based on the filing date of the first application; if prior art exists, compare to determine whether the later invention is described in the first application.
guidance: Examiner may request translations of evidential documents and compare documents to determine whether to apply retroactive filing date per invention.

name: Special rules for US-based priority claims: continuation-in-part (CIP) handling
description: Where priority is based only on a US CIP and only the CIP specification was submitted as evidential documents, the examiner shall examine inventions based on the filing date without granting retroactivity; if the original application specification/drawings are submitted, follow other CIP guidelines. If an invention is only described in the CIP, the patentability date is the CIP filing date.
guidance: If subject matter is described in both original and CIP and the Treaty-filed application is within one year of the original, subject matter described in both takes the original's filing date; subject matter only in CIP takes CIP's filing date. If the Treaty-filed application is filed after one year from the original, retroactivity for the original may not be available.

name: Special rules for US-based priority claims: provisional vs non-provisional
description: Whether a provisional application serves as the basis for priority depends on the USPTO's issuance of evidential documents certifying priority (e.g., priority documents, certified copy of original application). If no non-provisional is filed after the provisional, the provisional serves as the basis; if a non-provisional is filed claiming benefit, the provisional may be the basic application for priority and the priority period starts from the provisional filing date.
guidance: Examiner should determine which US application the USPTO treated as the basis for priority by checking issued evidential documents; differences in the type of provisional affect which application is the basic application.

name: Failure to submit evidential documents within one year and four months causes loss of priority effect
description: If evidential documents certifying priority are not submitted within one year and four months from the earliest filing date, the priority claim shall lose its effect. Evidential documents means more than the specification/drawings alone.
guidance: Examiner shall request amendment and invalidate the priority claim procedure if documents are not submitted within the statutory period; procedural error cannot be cured after the period. For international patent applications, however, KIPO may allow submission of evidential documents after entering the national stage and accept them if submitted in response to the amendment request.

name: Purport/policy of domestic priority claim
description: Domestic priority claim allows protection for inventions developed from a prior-filed application to further specify, improve, or add to the prior-filed application; inventions identical to the prior-filed application are deemed filed on the prior filing date while newly added improvements are deemed filed on the later filing date.
guidance: This provision prevents irrational rejection of improvements as 'same invention' or improper addition of new matter—supports protection of follow-on refinements while preserving correct filing-date treatment per subject matter.

name: Working examples and claimed genus
description: For a claimed genus, representative examples together with a statement applicable to the genus as a whole will ordinarily be sufficient if one skilled in the art would expect the claimed genus could be used in that manner without undue experimentation.
guidance: Proof of enablement for other members of the genus is required only where the examiner advances adequate reasons to establish that a person skilled in the art could not use the genus as a whole without undue experimentation. In some instances a few examples plus disclosure of a 'general quality ... running through' the class may suffice (citing Amgen v. Sanofi and Incandescent Lamp).

name: Scope of required enablement varies with predictability (single species vs genus)
description: A single embodiment may provide broad enablement in predictable arts (e.g., mechanical/electrical), but in unpredictable arts (e.g., many chemical reactions, physiological activity) the disclosure of a single species usually does not provide adequate basis to support generic claims.
guidance: Consider the predictable/unpredictable nature of the art when evaluating whether disclosure of one species enables the full claimed genus. Case law examples include In re Vickers, In re Cook, In re Soll, In re Fisher, and related decisions.

name: Examiner must construe claims and establish a reasonable basis to question enablement
description: Before any enablement analysis, the examiner must construe the claims and, for ambiguous terms, select and explicitly state the meaning intended to be used in examination.
guidance: To make an enablement rejection, the examiner has the initial burden to establish a reasonable basis to question enablement and explain why the disclosure is doubted (citing Genentech v. Wellcome; In re Wright; In re Marzocchi). The examiner must back up assertions with acceptable evidence or reasoning inconsistent with the contested statements and provide specific technical reasons (In re Bowen).

name: Compact prosecution: present best case in first Office action and identify allowable subject matter early
description: In accordance with compact prosecution, if an enablement rejection is appropriate the first Office action on the merits should present the best case with all relevant reasons, issues, and evidence.
guidance: Providing the best rejection in the first action allows applicant to rebut and prevents unnecessary follow-up and expansion that could delay finality. If examiner recognizes limitations that would render claims enabled, the examiner should note such limitations to applicant early and identify enabled, allowable subject matter.

name: Enablement determinations are based on the evidence as a whole; applicant's burden to rebut
description: Once examiner establishes a reasonable basis to question enablement, the burden falls on applicant to present persuasive arguments, supported by suitable proofs where necessary, that one skilled in the art could make and use the claimed invention using the application as a guide.
guidance: Applicant's evidence need not be absolute but must be convincing by a preponderance of the evidence. Declarations or affidavits under 37 C.F.R. § 1.132 are evidence but their weight depends on factual support (citing In re Brandstadter; In re Buchner; In re Alton). Examiner must weigh specification, applicant‑supplied evidence, and evidence relied on in the rejection and decide based on the evidence, not personal opinion.

name: Quantity of experimentation / undue experimentation analysis
description: A specification may call for a reasonable amount of experimentation to make and use a claimed invention; reasonableness depends on the nature of the invention and the underlying art.
guidance: Consider the Wands factors: the quantity, quality, and predictability of guidance; time and expense; routine nature of experiments; necessity of difficult assays; and whether extensive screening is required. Time and expense are factors but not controlling. Examples: Telectronics (time/expense alone not undue), Amgen v. Sanofi (need to screen millions of antibodies deemed undue), In re Ghiron (functional block diagrams insufficient).

name: When missing essential information, examiner should identify what is missing and why
description: Doubt about enablement commonly arises because information is missing about one or more essential claim elements or relationships between elements which one skilled in the art could not develop without undue experimentation.
guidance: The examiner should specifically identify what information is missing and explain why that information is needed to provide enablement. This includes pinpointing essential parts or relationships and supplying references if possible to support a prima facie case (see MPEP § 2164.06(a)).

name: Enablement serves to prevent claims broader than disclosure
description: Enablement ensures adequate disclosure and prevents claims broader than the disclosed invention; broad claim language is used at the peril of losing any claim that cannot be enabled across its full scope.
guidance: Examiners should be mindful that overly broad functional language or genus claims that extend beyond what the specification enables can be rejected for lack of enablement; the specification must teach how to make and use the claimed subject matter commensurate with claim scope (examples and case law referenced).

name: Indefinite limitations must be considered
description: A claim limitation which is considered indefinite cannot be disregarded.
guidance: If a claim is subject to more than one interpretation and at least one interpretation would render the claim unpatentable over the prior art, the examiner should reject the claim as indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (or pre‑AIA §112 second paragraph) and should reject the claim over the interpretation that renders the prior art applicable. Do not rely on speculative assumptions about meaning; where no reasonably definite meaning can be ascribed, the claim is indefinite (not obvious).

name: A rationale different from applicant’s is permissible
description: It is not necessary that the prior art suggest the combination to achieve the same advantage or result discovered by applicant.
guidance: Motivation to combine may arise from the general problem confronting the inventor rather than the specific problem solved by the inventor. Prior art use of a compound for a different purpose does not preclude finding its use prima facie obvious for the claimed purpose if the references motivate that use (In re Lintner, In re Dillon examples).

name: Omission of an element but retention of its function indicates nonobviousness
description: The omission of an element while retaining the element's function is an indicia of unobviousness.
guidance: Example: In re Edge — prior art eliminated a transparent protective layer, but the claimed invention retained the protective function via a different structure; this retention of function despite omission supported nonobviousness.

name: Scope of repeal (whole or partial)
description: The judgment of repeal may embrace the whole patent, ... or may include only the particular inventions which are covered by the rival patent and are found by the court to have been first invented by the rival patentee. Both patents are equally before the court for judgment and either may be repealed ... to any extent which may be necessary in order to secure to the party claiming under the prior inventor ... the unqualified enjoyment of the monopoly to which he is entitled.
guidance: Court may cancel an entire patent when the adversary's inventive genius produced the entire patentable subject-matter, or may cancel only those claims/inventions that conflict; remedies are tailored to secure the prior inventor's effective monopoly. (Cites: various interference/annulment cases.)

name: Copies requirement for cited non-U.S. and non-stored items (37 CFR 1.98(a)(2))
description: Legible copies are required for certain cited items in order for them to be considered by the Office.
guidance: Required copies include: (i) each cited foreign patent; (ii) each cited publication or the portion that caused listing (other than U.S. patents and U.S. patent application publications unless the Office requires them); (iii) for each cited pending unpublished U.S. application, the application specification including the claims and any drawings, or the portion which caused it to be listed (unless the cited pending U.S. application is stored in IFW); and (iv) all other cited information or the portion which caused listing. Failure to provide required copies will cause the IDS not to be considered.

name: Amendment of specification (timing and limits)
description: The specification may be amended before sealing, after sealing, or even during action. The leave of the Comptroller must be obtained in each case, and where an action is pending, the permission of the Court is required to apply for such leave.
guidance: In no case is an amendment to be allowed which would make the amended specification claim an invention substantially different from that in the original specification; leave to amend is conclusive as to the right to amend (sect. 18).

name: Amendment during action — limitation on damages recovery
description: If amendment is allowed during an action, patentees cannot recover damages in the action unless they satisfy the court that the claim was framed in good faith and with reasonable skill and knowledge.
guidance: This practical limitation reduces opportunistic broadening of claims during litigation.

name: Limitation of patent to one invention (statutory)
description: Limitation of patent to one invention made statutory, with a proviso that it shall not be competent in an action or other proceeding to object to a patent on the ground that it comprises more than one invention (sect. 33).
guidance: This statutory rule both narrows claims and prevents certain procedural attacks in litigation.

name: Claims must particularly point out and distinctly claim
description: Claims are inserted to conform to the statutory requirement that the patentee shall "particularly point out and distinctly claim the part, improvement, or combination which he claims as his invention." "The claims measure the invention."
guidance: A distinct and formal claim is necessary to ascertain the scope of the patented invention; a patent grants no exclusive right except to what is distinctly claimed.

name: What a claim covers (subject matter)
description: A claim covers and secures a process, a machine, a manufacture, a composition of matter, or a design, and never the function or result of either.
guidance: Claims may cover whole inventions or only parts/sub-processes/combinations. The specification may contain multiple claims for whole, parts, and sub-combinations; each claim must satisfy invention, novelty, and utility.

name: Claims must be definite so the public understands scope
description: All claims are required to be definite, so that the public may know what they are prohibited from doing during the existence of the patent and what they are to have at the end of the term.
guidance: Degree of particularity may be reached in various modes: e.g., a machine claim is sufficient if co-extensive with the machine; a part of a machine must be clearly indicated; combination claims should state constituent devices and use the word "combination."

name: Combination claims may be result-oriented but raise fact issues
description: A claim may declare that it "covers so much of the described mechanism as effects a particular specified result," without specifying the parts themselves.
guidance: In such cases it is a question of fact for court determination which parts effect that result and are therefore covered by the claim.

name: Process and product must be separately claimed
description: A process and its product, though securable by separate claims in one patent, cannot be covered by one claim.
guidance: A product having definite characteristics may be described and claimed by those characteristics independent of the process; but if a product claim is framed in terms of the process, nothing infringes it unless produced by that process. (Discussed via Plummer v. Sargent and related authorities.)

name: Product claims framed by process language are limited to that process
description: If a product claim is set forth in the terms of the process (e.g., "ornamented by the application of oil and heat, substantially as described"), then no product made otherwise will infringe.
guidance: A product claim should describe product characteristics to avoid limiting the claim to a single process of manufacture.

name: Material-specific claims must specify the material
description: Where an invention consists of an article made of a specific material, the claim must specify that material and will be void if it generalizes by words that cover materials useless for the purpose as well as the specific material described.
guidance: Do not use overly broad material language that sweeps in nonfunctional or useless materials.

name: Claims are independent and may vary in validity within one patent
description: Each claim is considered as setting forth a complete and independent invention; some claims in a specification may be valid while others are invalid for lack of particularity, invention, novelty, or utility.
guidance: If narrower claim adds an unpatentable element it is void; where possible, claims should be construed to differ rather than to be identical because applicants normally would not repeat the same claim unnecessarily.

name: If all claims are void the patent is void
description: If all the claims of a patent are void (for want of particularity, invention, novelty, utility, or other reason), the patent itself is void, even though valid claims might have been supported by the descriptive part.
guidance: Invalidity is a legal inference from failure to give statutory particularity, not dependent on inventor's intent.

name: Claims broader than the described invention are void
description: Any claim which is broader than the described invention is void, even where the described invention is valuable and could have supported a valuable claim.
guidance: Claims must be co-extensive with what is described and intended to be secured; overbroad claiming is fatal to those claims.

name: Logical hierarchy: class, order, genus, species, variety
description: Inventions are divisible into classes, orders, genuses, species, and varieties; every invention belongs to a variety, species, genus, etc., whether or not it is the first in that group.
guidance: A patent that stands at the head of its genus may properly have a generic claim and a specific claim; Patent Office practice requires a separate application for each species for separate patents but allows generic claims appropriately placed.

name: Statutory particularity is jurisdictional for Commissioner authority
description: The statutory requirements relevant to particularity in descriptions and claims are conditions precedent to the Commissioner's authority to issue letters patent; if issued without conformity, the document is void.
guidance: Invalidity of issued patents on inadequate specifications cannot be cured by showing the inadequacy arose from ignorance rather than fraud. Insufficient specification is a defence available by special plea or under equity rules.

name: Conformity of specification to statutory requirements is a fact question
description: Whether the specification and claims conform to statutory particularity requirements is a question of fact for a jury in law actions or for a chancellor in equity; it is a question of evidence, not of construction.
guidance: Courts will assess factual evidence to determine adequacy rather than resolving it as a pure construction issue.

name: Multiple patents for different parts of one extensive machine permissible
description: Two or more related patents may lawfully be granted for different parts of one extensive machine; in such cases the whole machine should be described and pictured in each specification so the patents differ only in their claims.
guidance: However, plurality of patents cannot be granted for different uses of the same invention; all uses inherent in or described as part of the invention are covered by a single patent.

name: Only one valid original patent per inventor per invention; identity determined by claims
description: Only one valid original patent can be granted to an inventor on one invention; when multiple similar original patents exist, identity or non-identity is determined by comparing the claims and finding whether they are co-extensive.
guidance: Claims are co-extensive if they cover the same combination (same number, same parts, same features). Claims specifying different combinations or omitting features are not co-extensive. The order of applications (dates) controls in determining junior vs senior rights.

name: Claim construction principle: claims control; cannot read-in unclaimed elements
description: To construe letters patent is to determine precisely what inventions they cover; nothing described is secured unless covered by a claim, and no element not mentioned in a claim can be read into it even if it appears in the specification.
guidance: A claim narrower than the actual invention cannot be broadened by construction; a claim broader than permitted by the state of the art cannot be narrowed by construction contrary to its language. Newly discovered uses not indicated in the patent cannot affect claim construction. Construction depends on the claims and established claim-construction rules.

name: Support Independent Inventors (accessibility and affordability)
description: Support independent, micro-, and small-entity inventors to ensure the system is accessible and affordable.
guidance: Measures include pro bono collaborations, StART training, Customer Ambassador program, considering patent small claims court to reduce litigation costs, avoiding fee-based barriers (e.g., to encourage DOCX), and tailoring AIA discretionary-denial guidance to consider unique challenges faced by independent inventors.

name: Collect and analyze PTAB/examination data to learn from invalidations
description: Collect outcomes and mine data to understand why PTAB finds claims unpatentable and to identify improvements.
guidance: Automate data collection of PTAB outcomes (already implemented), enable data mining to find trends (e.g., missed prior art, inconsistent legal application), and study results to guide examiner training and system improvements.

name: Abstract idea — mathematical formulas and related concepts
description: Mathematical formulas (e.g., Arrhenius equation) and similar concepts are judicial exceptions (abstract ideas) and thus non‑statutory subject matter.
guidance: Recognize mathematical formulas and related information‑processing concepts as abstract ideas (citing Diehr, Benson, Flook, Mackay, Bilski). Examples include algorithms for binary conversion (Benson), formulas for alarm limits (Flook), electromagnetic standing wave formulas (Mackay), and mathematical formulas for hedging (Bilski). If a claim is directed to such an abstract idea, it is a judicial exception (Step 2A: YES) and requires further Step 2B analysis to determine whether the claim recites a patent‑eligible application.

name: Laws of nature and natural phenomena — general rule
description: Laws of nature and natural phenomena (naturally occurring principles/relations and nature‑based products that are naturally occurring or not markedly different from what occurs in nature) are judicial exceptions to patent eligibility.
guidance: The basic tools of scientific/technological work (laws of nature, scientific principles, natural phenomena, products of nature) are not patentable. Examples include isolated DNA, cloned animals, correlations between biomarkers and disease, electromagnetism for transmission, and naturally occurring chemical principles (citing Funk Bros., Chakrabarty, Myriad, Mayo, etc.). If a claim recites a law of nature or natural phenomenon, treat it as a judicial exception (Step 2A: YES) and proceed to Step 2B to examine whether the claim recites a patent‑eligible application.

name: Products of nature — when a claimed product is an exception
description: When a law of nature or natural phenomenon is claimed as a physical product, it is treated as a 'product of nature' exception if the product is naturally occurring or lacks markedly different characteristics from a natural counterpart.
guidance: Products of nature include both naturally occurring products and human‑made products that are structurally identical to natural counterparts. Examples: isolated DNA (Myriad), primers (Ambry), cloned animals (Roslin). Non‑naturally occurring products are not automatically eligible simply because of human intervention; the key is whether they possess markedly different characteristics from any naturally occurring counterpart.

name: Markedly different characteristics analysis — purpose and outcome
description: The markedly different characteristics analysis (part of Step 2A) determines whether a claimed nature‑based product is a product of nature exception by comparing claimed product characteristics to its natural counterpart.
guidance: If the nature‑based product has markedly different characteristics (structure, function, and/or other properties) from its natural counterpart, then the limitation is not a product of nature exception and the claim is not directed to a product of nature (Step 2A: NO) unless another exception is present. If it does not exhibit markedly different characteristics, the limitation is a product of nature (Step 2A: YES) and further Step 2B analysis is required to determine eligibility.

name: Claims reciting a nature‑based product plus non‑nature elements
description: If a claim includes a nature‑based product limitation in combination with non‑nature elements (e.g., container, instructions), perform the markedly different characteristics analysis only on the nature‑based product limitation; evaluate other elements in Step 2B if the nature‑based product is a product of nature.
guidance: For example, for a 'yogurt starter kit comprising Lactobacillus in a container with instructions', analyze Lactobacillus for markedly different characteristics. The container and instructions are not part of the markedly different characteristics analysis but may be considered as additional elements when assessing whether the claim recites significantly more (Step 2B). Cite Funk Bros. as an example where only the bacterial mixture was analyzed.

name: Product‑by‑process claims — focus on product characteristics
description: For product‑by‑process claims, the analysis depends on whether the claimed nature‑based product has markedly different characteristics from its natural counterpart.
guidance: Determine whether the claimed product (regardless of the process language) exhibits markedly different characteristics; consult MPEP § 2113 for additional product‑by‑process guidance.

name: BRI and amendment recommendation best practices
description: Under the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI), a nature‑based product limitation may encompass both eligible and ineligible embodiments; examiners should point out BRI issues and recommend narrowing amendments where appropriate.
guidance: If a claim's BRI would encompass embodiments that are products of nature and embodiments that have markedly different characteristics, treat the claim as directed to a product of nature (Step 2A: YES) and, if rejecting under Step 2B for lack of inventive concept, it is best practice to identify the BRI and recommend claim amendments to narrow the claim to eligible embodiments when possible (citing Roslin).

name: Were all 35 U.S.C. 101 Statutory Double Patenting rejection(s) in compliance?
description: Were all the 35 U.S.C. 101 Statutory Double Patenting rejection(s) in compliance? Yes or No
guidance: If a 101 Statutory Double Patenting rejection was made in the Office action being reviewed, the answer must be updated to either Yes or No. i. If 'Yes', go to question 7. ii. If 'No', continue to question 3. The determination of compliance is based on the rejection properly identifying the claim(s) and being supported by sufficient evidence to support the rejection of the claim(s). Consult the statutory compliance standard and scenarios.

name: Identify claim(s) with non-compliant 101 Statutory Double Patenting rejection(s)
description: Each claim discussed individually as a basis for the noncompliance in an 'Explanation of Noncompliance' section in addition to those dependent claims which inherit the noncompliance must be listed.
guidance: The noncompliance is directed to limitations introduced in (check only one): a. Only the independent claim(s); b. Only the dependent claim(s); c. Both the independent claim(s) and dependent claim(s). This question is to identify the type of claim which is the root of the noncompliance (where the basis is first introduced in the claim tree). Only one box may be selected. Examples illustrate how to choose a/b/c.

name: 101 Noncompliance reason — Failure to properly identify claims/statute (5a)
description: 5a: The rejection(s) does not properly identify the rejected claim(s) and/or identify the correct basis.
guidance: When either the claim(s) or the statute is the basis of the noncompliance, this box should be checked. Do not use this box to capture when the reviewer believes the claims were improperly rejected on the merits (use 5b for insufficient evidence). If the examiner improperly made the rejection provisional instead of non-provisional (or vice versa), check 5a. Do not check 5a when the reviewer determines the rejection should have been made under Nonstatutory Double Patenting (raise as omitted instead). If additional claims should have been included in the grounds of rejection, raise as an omitted 101 SDP rejection, not 5a.

name: 101 Noncompliance reason — Insufficient evidence (5b)
description: 5b: The rejection(s) does not provide sufficient evidence to support that the claimed invention is directed to the same invention.
guidance: If 5b is checked, then the basis for lack of sufficient evidence must be identified by checking at least one of 5bi-5bii. Only comments directed to the basis for noncompliance based on lack of sufficient evidence should be included. The write up should avoid rhetorical questioning and should not be personalized.

name: 101 Insufficient evidence subcriteria — no explanation (5bi)
description: 5bi: The rejection(s) fails to provide any explanation supporting the claim(s) being of the same scope (e.g., limitation matching between claim sets).
guidance: If checked, the Explanation of noncompliance related to lack of sufficient evidence must describe the basis for lack of evidence. The reviewer should provide an explanation consistent with the box checked, avoid rhetorical questioning, and not personalize the assessment.

name: 101 Insufficient evidence subcriteria — insufficient explanation (5bii)
description: 5bii: The rejection(s) fails to provide a sufficient explanation supporting the claim(s) being of the same scope (e.g., limitation matching between claim sets).
guidance: Provide explanation of noncompliance related to lack of sufficient evidence consistent with boxes checked under 5b; the write up should be an assessment of the work product and avoid rhetorical questioning or personalization.

name: 101 Additional Information/Feedback — unreasonable claim interpretation (6b)
description: 6b: The noncompliance is the result of an unreasonable claim interpretation.
guidance: Check 6b when the basis for noncompliance is based on a limitation which was improperly construed and/or given patent significance. Do not check 6b if the rejection provides no indication of how the claims are being interpreted. Only check when the rejection provides guidance/indication of interpretation that is unreasonable.

name: Characteristics of 101 Statutory Double Patenting rejection(s) — limited claim lumping
description: The rejection(s) addresses substantially all claims individually and only groups claims together that are of substantially similar scope (i.e. limited claim lumping).
guidance: These boxes represent characteristics that may be exemplified in rejections made under 35 U.S.C. 101 Statutory Double Patenting. The reviewer should check all boxes that apply to the office action reviewed. 'Substantially' and 'reasonably' permit reviewer judgment. Checking a characteristic does not reflect on accuracy/effectiveness — only indicates presence.

name: Characteristics of 101 — reasonably pinpoints where substantially all limitations are met
description: The rejection(s) reasonably pinpoints where substantially all limitations are met by the conflicting claim(s).
guidance: Check when the rejection points to where claim limitations are met by the conflicting claim(s).

name: Characteristics of 101 — statements of patentable weight included
description: Statements of patentable weight are included, particularly when patentable weight is not being given to any of the following: Intended use limitations, Preamble, Claim language that suggests or makes optional some structure or steps.
guidance: Indicate presence of patentable weight statements, especially when patentable weight is being denied for items like preamble or intended use.

name: Characteristics of 101 — claim interpretation stated
description: The rejection(s) sets forth a claim interpretation that points out how the examiner is interpreting the claim/term/phrase for purposes of the rejection(s) (e.g. BRI, special definitions).
guidance: Indicate when the office action shows the examiner's interpretation (broadest reasonable interpretation or special definition) used for the rejection.

name: Characteristics of 101 — included appropriate suggestions to overcome rejection(s)
description: The Office action included appropriate suggestions to overcome rejection(s) (not general FP language or indication of claims with allowable subject matter).
guidance: Check when action provides concrete suggestions to overcome the rejection (not generic or only pointing to allowable subject matter).

name: Were all Nonstatutory Double Patenting rejection(s) in compliance?
description: Were all the Nonstatutory Double Patenting rejection(s) in compliance? Yes or No
guidance: If a Nonstatutory Double Patenting rejection was made in the Office action being reviewed, the answer must be updated to either Yes or No. The determination of compliance is based on the rejection properly identifying the claim(s) and being supported by sufficient evidence. Consult statutory compliance standard and scenarios. If 'Yes' go to question 7; if 'No' continue to question 3.

name: Identify claim(s) with non-compliant Nonstatutory Double Patenting rejection(s)
description: Each claim discussed individually as a basis for the noncompliance in an 'Explanation of Noncompliance' section in addition to those dependent claims which inherit the noncompliance must be listed.
guidance: The noncompliance is directed to limitations introduced in (check only one): a. Only the independent claim(s) b. Only the dependent claim(s) c. Both the independent claim(s) and dependent claim(s). This identifies the root of noncompliance in the claim tree; examples illustrate choice.

name: Nonstatutory DP Noncompliance reason — Failure to identify claims/statute (6a)
description: 6(a): The rejection(s) does not properly identify the rejected claim(s) and/or correct basis.
guidance: When either the claim(s) or the statute is the basis of the noncompliance, this box should be checked. Do not use this box to capture failures of evidentiary support (use 6(c)). If the examiner improperly made the rejection provisional instead of non-provisional (or vice versa), check 6(a). Do not check when the reviewer believes the rejection should have been made under 35 U.S.C. 101 Statutory Double Patenting (raise as omitted 101).

name: Nonstatutory DP Noncompliance reason — insufficient evidence (6c) with five sub-items
description: 6(c): The rejection(s) does not provide sufficient evidence to support that the claimed invention is not patentably distinct. If checked, identify basis by selecting at least one of 6ci-6cv.
guidance: Subitems: i. improperly relied on anticipation when should have relied on obviousness; ii. improperly relied on obviousness when should have relied on anticipation; iii. improperly concluded not patentably distinct without either anticipation or obviousness analysis (absent any claim matching/analysis); iv. improperly relied on the instant specification as basis; v. Other. Provide explanation consistent with boxes checked; avoid rhetorical questioning and personalization.

name: Nonstatutory DP Additional Info/Feedback — noncompliance due to unreasonable claim interpretation (7a)
description: 7a: The noncompliance is the result of an unreasonable claim interpretation.
guidance: Check 7a when the basis for noncompliance is based on a limitation which was improperly construed and/or given patent significance. Only check when the rejection provides some guidance or indication of how the claim limitation is being construed so as to read on the prior art; do not check when the interpretation cannot be determined.

name: Characteristics of Nonstatutory Double Patenting rejection(s) — limited claim lumping
description: The rejection(s) addresses substantially all claims individually and only groups claims together that are of substantially similar scope (i.e. limited claim lumping).
guidance: Check characteristics that apply. 'Substantially' and 'reasonably' permit reviewer judgment; checking indicates presence of characteristic, not accolade-worthiness.

name: Characteristics of Nonstatutory DP — reasonably pinpoints where limitations are met
description: The rejection(s) reasonably pinpoints where substantially all limitations are met by the conflicting claim(s).
guidance: Check when the rejection reasonably identifies where claim limitations map to the conflicting claim(s).

name: Characteristics of Nonstatutory DP — patentable weight statements included
description: Statements of patentable weight are included, particularly when patentable weight is not being given to Intended use limitations, Preamble, or Claim language that suggests or makes optional some structure or steps.
guidance: Indicate presence of statements discussing patentable weight.

name: Characteristics of Nonstatutory DP — claim interpretation stated
description: The rejection(s) sets forth a claim interpretation that points out how the examiner is interpreting the claim/term/phrase for purposes of the rejection(s).
guidance: Check when the office action indicates the claim interpretation used (e.g., BRI, special definition).

name: Characteristics of Nonstatutory DP — included appropriate suggestions to overcome rejection(s)
description: The Office action included appropriate suggestions to overcome rejection(s) (not general FP language or indication of claims with allowable subject matter).
guidance: Check when concrete suggestions to overcome the rejection are provided.

name: Other rejections — were all 'Other' rejection(s) in compliance?
description: Were all the 'Other' rejection(s) in compliance? Yes or No
guidance: If a rejection was made that is not otherwise covered in the MRF, update answer to Yes or No. Determination based on rejection properly identifying the claim(s), the statute (including subparagraphs) and being supported by sufficient evidence to support the conclusion of obviousness. Consult statutory compliance standard and scenarios. If 'No', select one of: Attention Needed or Noncompliant.

name: Identify claim(s) with non-compliant 'Other' rejection(s)
description: Each claim discussed individually as a basis for the noncompliance in an 'Explanation of Noncompliance' section in addition to those dependent claims which inherit the noncompliance must be listed.
guidance: The noncompliance is directed to limitations introduced in (check only one): a. Only the independent claim(s); b. Only the dependent claim(s); c. Both the independent claim(s) and dependent claim(s). Examples illustrate selection.

name: MRF Omitted Rejection 35 U.S.C. 102 standard (anticipation)
description: A claimed invention should have been rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102 when the invention is anticipated (or is 'not novel') over a disclosure that is available as prior art. To reject a claim as anticipated by a reference, the disclosure must teach every element required by the claim under its broadest reasonable interpretation.
guidance: This is the standard reviewers must apply when proposing an omitted 102 rejection. The omitted rejection must identify claims for which an omitted 102 rejection is proposed and provide a thorough description of the omitted rejection.

name: Omitted 102 — identify claims and whether directed to independent/dependent/both
description: Identify the claim(s) where a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102 was omitted and indicate if the omitted rejection(s) is directed to Only the independent claim(s), Only the dependent claim(s), or Both.
guidance: List each claim proposed for an omitted 102 rejection. Do not list claims that have a compliant rejection even if covered by the omitted rejection. Each claim listed must be specifically addressed in the 'Give a thorough description' box.

name: Omitted 102 — give a thorough description of the omitted rejection(s)
description: A complete proposed rejection for each claim listed must be provided. For each claim, the statute, subparagraph and evidence supporting the rejection must be clearly identified.
guidance: The proposed rejection should not be personalized and should reflect a thorough analysis of how the prior art applied anticipates the claimed invention.

name: MRF Omitted Rejection 35 U.S.C. 103 standard (obviousness)
description: A claimed invention should have been rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 when the invention is obvious subject matter. To support the conclusion that the claimed invention should have been rejected as directed to obvious subject matter, the proposed rejection should articulate a prima facie case of obviousness.
guidance: Findings of fact should be supported by sufficient evidence in the prior art. The rejection should articulate how the prior art is to be modified to arrive at the claimed invention. The reasoning/rationale should be taught by the prior art applied or provided by the reviewer in a convincing line of reasoning.

name: Omitted 103 — identify claims and whether directed to independent/dependent/both
description: Identify the claim(s) where a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 was omitted and indicate if the omitted rejection(s) is directed to Only the independent claim(s), Only the dependent claim(s), or Both.
guidance: List each claim for which an omitted 103 rejection is proposed; do not list claims that have a compliant rejection even if covered by the omitted rejection. Each claim listed must be specifically addressed in the 'Give a thorough description' box.

name: Omitted 103 — give a thorough description of the omitted rejection(s)
description: A complete proposed omission for each claim must identify statute/subparagraph, evidence, and articulate a prima facie case of obviousness with supporting findings of fact and rationale.
guidance: Explain how prior art would be modified to arrive at the claimed invention; provide convincing line of reasoning taught by or based on prior art. The proposed rejection should not be personalized.

name: Reading prior art before drafting
description: Before drafting, the drafter must understand the closest prior art.
guidance: A claim drafted without this understanding is likely either too broad (anticipated by art the drafter did not see) or too narrow (incorporating limitations that were not necessary to distinguish the actual prior art).

name: Independent claim drafting
description: The independent claim is the most important sentence in the patent. Drafting it requires answering: What is the minimum combination of elements that distinguishes the invention from prior art? What is the broadest accurate way to describe each element? In what order do the elements interact? Who performs the steps (for method claims)?
guidance: Compose the independent claim to capture the essential, minimal distinguishing combination while using the broadest accurate language; ensure clarity on element interaction order and actor for method claims.

name: Dependent claims strategy
description: Dependent claims should narrow on dimensions that are independently meaningful.
guidance: Examples of meaningful narrowings include: restricting a generic element to a particular species ("wherein the polymer is polyethylene"); adding an optional feature ("further comprising a temperature sensor"); specifying a numerical range ("wherein the temperature is between 50 and 80 degrees C"); specifying a particular application or use case; specifying a particular ordering of steps.

name: Summary section guidance
description: Summary: Mirror the independent claims at high level.
guidance: Use the summary to present the invention in broad terms corresponding to the independent claims to aid understanding and provide support for claim scope.

name: Detailed description of embodiments
description: Detailed Description: The bulk of the spec; walk through figures and embodiments.
guidance: Thoroughly describe embodiments and refer to figures; provide sufficient detail to support claimed features and to avoid functional language unsupported by structure.

name: Claims as the legally operative section
description: Claims: The legally operative section.
guidance: Draft claims carefully—their precise wording determines legal rights and enforcement; ensure claim language is supported by the specification.

name: Common claim types and structures
description: Common claim types: Apparatus, Method, System, Composition — each has typical phrasing/structure (examples provided).
guidance: Use appropriate claim templates: e.g., Apparatus claim: "An apparatus comprising: ..."; Method claim: "A method comprising: ..."; System claim: "A system comprising: ..."; Composition claim: "A composition comprising: 50-70% by weight of A; ..." Adjust language to match the invention type.

name: Place limitations in correct clause
description: Limitations in the preamble that should be in the body.
guidance: Avoid putting essential limitations only in the preamble if they are necessary to claim distinctiveness; place limitations in the claim body where appropriate to ensure proper antecedent and clarity.

name: Support functional language with structure
description: Functional language without supporting structure.
guidance: When using functional claim language, ensure the specification supplies structural support or examples to satisfy written description and enablement requirements.

name: Avoid unsupported negative limitations
description: Negative limitations without spec support.
guidance: Do not include negative claim limitations (e.g., "wherein the device does not include X") unless the specification provides clear support for excluding the feature.

name: Support numerical limits with spec ranges
description: Numerical limits not supported by ranges in the spec.
guidance: Ensure that specific numerical limits in claims are supported by ranges or examples in the specification to avoid lack-of-support issues.

name: Statement of precise relief requested for each claim challenged
description: Provide a statement of the precise relief requested for each claim challenged.
guidance: For each claim you challenge, state exactly what relief you seek (e.g., cancellation of the claim, amendment, specific claim constructions leading to unpatentability). This statement frames the requested outcome for each challenged claim.

name: Identification of the specific claim(s) challenged
description: The statement must identify the following: (1) The claim.
guidance: Clearly identify claim numbers (or language) being challenged so the Board and patent owner can unambiguously know which claims are at issue.

name: Identification of specific statutory grounds (35 U.S.C. 282(b)(2) or (3))
description: The statement must identify the specific statutory grounds permitted under 35 U.S.C. 282(b)(2) or (3) on which the challenge to the claim is based.
guidance: Specify the exact statutory basis for each challenged claim (e.g., anticipation, obviousness, written description, enablement, indefiniteness) as permitted by the cited provisions.

name: Claim construction and corresponding specification disclosure (including 35 U.S.C. 112(f) means/step-plus-function)
description: How the challenged claim is to be construed. Where the claim to be construed contains a means-plus-function or step-plus-function limitation as permitted under 35 U.S.C. 112(f), the construction of the claim must identify the specific portions of the specification that describe the structure, material, or acts corresponding to each claimed function.
guidance: Provide your proposed constructions for the claim elements. For 112(f) limitations, identify the particular specification passages that disclose the structure/material/acts that correspond to each claimed function; failure to identify supporting specification text may undermine the construction.

name: Explanation why the construed claim is unpatentable under identified grounds
description: How the construed claim is unpatentable under the statutory grounds identified in paragraph (b)(2) of this section. Where the grounds for unpatentability are based on prior art, the petition must specify where each element of the claim is found in the prior art. For all other grounds of unpatentability, the petition must identify the specific part of the claim that fails to comply with the statutory grounds raised and state how the identified subject matter fails to comply with the statute.
guidance: When alleging unpatentability: (a) if based on prior art, map each claim element to specific portions of the prior art references (with citations); (b) for other statutory grounds (e.g., enablement, written description, indefiniteness), identify the exact claim text and explain how it fails to meet the statutory requirement. General or conclusory assertions without element-by-element mapping or specific identification are insufficient.

name: Exhibits: identification of exhibit numbers and statement of relevance
description: The exhibit number of the supporting evidence relied upon to support the challenge and the relevance of the evidence to the challenge raised, including identifying specific portions of the evidence that support the challenge.
guidance: List exhibit numbers for each piece of supporting evidence and explain how each exhibit supports particular claim elements or arguments, pointing to specific pages/lines/figures. Note: the Board may exclude or give no weight to evidence where a party has failed to state its relevance or to identify specific portions of the evidence that support the challenge.

name: Claims are the starting point and basis for assessing patentability
description: “The claims are the starting point and the basis for assessing the patentability of an invention under Articles 52 to 57 EPC.”
guidance: Claims form the primary reference for patentability assessment, but they do not stand alone; interpretation must proceed from the claim language as the basis for analysis.

name: Description and drawings shall always be consulted to interpret the claims
description: “The description and drawings shall always be consulted to interpret the claims when assessing the patentability of an invention under Articles 52 to 57 EPC, and not only if the person skilled in the art finds a claim to be unclear or ambiguous when read in isolation.” (EBA headnote)
guidance: The EBA rejects the approach that the description/figures are only relevant where a claim is ambiguous. Practitioners and examiners must therefore routinely refer to the description and figures when construing claim terms for patentability assessments. This resolves divergent Board of Appeal case law and aligns EPO practice with national courts and the UPC.

name: Definitions or similar information in the description are relevant to claim interpretation
description: Referral question: 'May a definition or similar information on a term used in the claims which is explicitly given in the description be disregarded when interpreting the claims to assess patentability and, if so, under what conditions?'
guidance: Given the EBA's conclusion that the description and drawings must always be consulted, explicit definitions in the description are prima facie relevant when construing claim terms. The article notes the question was referred, but does not set out detailed conditions under which such a definition could be disregarded; practitioners should therefore treat descriptively provided definitions as influential in claim construction.

name: Examiners should carry out high-quality clarity examination under Article 84 EPC
description: The EBA notes the 'importance of the examining division carrying out a high quality examination of whether a claim fulfils the clarity requirements of Article 84 EPC.'
guidance: Because examiners are now expected to consult the description/drawings as part of routine claim interpretation, there may be an increase in clarity objections. Applicants should anticipate greater scrutiny of claim wording and consider clearer claim drafting and consistency with the description to avoid objections.

name: Follow UPC jurisprudence that description/drawings are explanatory aids
description: The EBA's approach is consistent with the UPC Court of Appeal statement that 'the description and drawings of a patent must always be used as explanatory aids for the interpretation of the patent claim and not only to resolve any ambiguities in the patent claim' (UPC_CoA_335/2023).
guidance: This alignment reinforces a harmonised approach across EPO and UPC practice; litigators and prosecutors should expect similar interpretative treatment in UPC proceedings and adjust drafting/litigation strategies accordingly.

name: 37 CFR 1.951(a) — Patent owner one‑time submission after ACP
description: After an Action Closing Prosecution (ACP), the patent owner may once file written comments limited to the issues raised in the Office action closing prosecution and may include a proposed amendment to the claims (subject to §1.116 admission criteria).
