guidance: Comments must be filed within the time set for response in the ACP. If the submission addresses issues not raised in the ACP, it will be returned or expunged; no additional opportunity absent a granted petition under 37 CFR 1.183 waiving the one‑opportunity limitation.

name: Requirement to identify and develop issues prior to ACP
description: Examiner and parties should recognize that reexamination may result in final cancellation of claims and that the patent owner cannot continue the proceeding by refiling or RCE; accordingly, all issues (including presentation of evidence under 37 CFR 1.131 and 1.132) should be identified and developed prior to the ACP.
guidance: This is to ensure the record is fully developed before the one‑opportunity post‑ACP limitations apply.

name: Treatment and limits on amendments submitted after ACP
description: Multiple amendments submitted after the ACP: all except the first will be returned without consideration. A patent owner cannot, as a matter of right, amend claims rejected in the ACP, add new claims after ACP, nor reinstate previously canceled claims without satisfying 37 CFR 1.116(b), except in narrow exceptions (canceling claims, adopting examiner’s suggestions, removing issues for appeal, or requiring only cursory review).
guidance: If entry of a proposed amendment would withdraw a ground of rejection or indicate additional claims patentable, the amendment generally raises new issues requiring more than cursory review; examiner must indicate new grounds and address any third‑party comments.

name: Right of Appeal Notice (RAN) — nature and timing
description: Upon considering post‑ACP comments or upon expiration of the time for such comments, the examiner shall issue a RAN (unless prosecution is reopened). The RAN is a final action comprising a final rejection and/or final decision favorable to patentability, identifying status of each claim and setting a one‑month time period to appeal.
guidance: No amendment can be made in response to the RAN in inter partes reexamination; if no notice of appeal is filed, prosecution will be terminated and the Director will issue a certificate under §1.997 in accordance with the RAN.

name: Limitations on post‑RAN amendments and evidence (statutory/regulatory restrictions)
description: No amendment other than canceling claims (where such cancellation does not affect scope of other pending claims) can be made in an inter partes reexamination proceeding after the RAN except as provided in 37 CFR 1.981 or permitted by 37 CFR 41.77(b)(1); furthermore, no affidavit or other evidence can be submitted after the RAN except as provided in 37 CFR 1.981 or 41.77(b)(1).
guidance: An amendment filed after the RAN will not be entered absent a grantable 1.183 petition; examiner may reopen prosecution to accept amendment and issue a new ACP.

name: Prior art qualification under sections 28.2 and 28.3
description: Canada places no blanket restriction on types of references or activities that can be prior art; instead sections 28.2 and 28.3 require the reference or activity to meet certain criteria (e.g., public availability before disclosure deadline) before it can be considered in an anticipation or obviousness analysis.
guidance: If the statutory criteria are met, the reference or activity can be considered prior art in an anticipation and/or obviousness analysis. The form or medium of disclosure (printed, digital, any language) is irrelevant so long as the subject-matter became available to the public in Canada or elsewhere. See also rules on disclosure deadlines, claim dates, and exceptions for applicant disclosures.

name: Co-pending Canadian patent applications can be anticipatory
description: A co-pending Canadian patent application (even if not yet published) can be anticipatory if that other patent document has a claim date that precedes the claim date of the subject claim in question.
guidance: Under paragraph 28.2(1)(d), a pending application may invalidate a later claim where its claim date is earlier. Co-pending applications' claim dates are therefore relevant when determining anticipation.

name: Anticipation test (Apotex v Sanofi): disclosure and enablement from a single reference/activity
description: To be anticipatory, a single prior art reference or activity must both disclose the claimed subject matter and enable the claimed subject matter (the PSA may supply common general knowledge).
guidance: Anticipation requires a single reference or activity providing disclosure and enablement such that performing it would necessarily result in infringement of all essential claim elements. The test applies across technologies and types of patents. See Apotex v Sanofi; Aux Sable; Hoffmann‑La Roche v Sandoz.

name: Disclosure requirement specifics (essential elements and inherent disclosure)
description: The prior art must disclose the essential elements of the claim; exact description is not required and inherent disclosure is possible where old/known subject matter is necessarily present in the prior art.
guidance: A generic genus does not anticipate a later specific selection claim unless performing the generic necessarily infringes the specific claim. Conversely, a specific selection can anticipate a later general claim if performing the specific necessarily infringes the general. Case examples: Abbott, Shire, Swist v MEG Energy, Valence v Phostech.

name: Enablement requirement for anticipation
description: The prior art must be sufficiently detailed to enable a PSA to perform the claimed invention without the exercise of inventive ingenuity or undue experimentation (the PSA can rely on common general knowledge).
guidance: Obvious errors/omissions that a skilled person could readily correct do not defeat enablement. Threshold for 'undue burden' depends on the field — in fields with routine trials the threshold is higher; routine trials generally are not undue, but prolonged/arduous experimentation is undue. See Apotex v Sanofi (para 37).

name: Claim construction: purposive & informed approach
description: Claims are construed in an informed and purposive manner as of the date the patent was published or laid open to public inspection; the PSA and common general knowledge are used to give words meaning and to distinguish essential from non-essential elements.
guidance: A single construction is completed per claim and applied equally to infringement and validity. Claims should not be construed overly technically or literally, nor expanded by vague 'spirit' concepts. The specification and PSA common general knowledge inform construction, but extrinsic evidence like inventor notebooks and prior art are generally inadmissible except as allowed by statute (section 53.1(1)) or specific exceptions. Presumption that all elements are essential can be rebutted based on inventor's intentions and PSA understanding. See Free World Trust, Whirlpool, MOPOP s12.02.02e.

name: Person skilled in the art (PSA) and common general knowledge
description: The PSA is a notional person (or team) of ordinary competence, skill, and knowledge in the relevant field, reasonably diligent but unimaginative, and with a 'mind willing to understand' the specification; their common general knowledge informs claim construction, anticipation, and obviousness analyses.
guidance: The PSA is taken generously (not the most skilled nor the least qualified). Common general knowledge includes what PSAs generally know at the claim date and may include information passed informally (discussions), attitudes, trends, expectations, and sometimes patents, but not all public-domain information. The field's technical complexity affects PSA definition (e.g., 'rocket science patents'). See Janssen-Ortho, Whirlpool, Apotex v Sanofi.

name: Obviousness/sanity check: Sanofi four-step test
description: Obviousness is assessed claim-by-claim using the Sanofi four-step test: (1) identify the PSA and common general knowledge; (2) identify the inventive concept (or construe it); (3) identify differences between the state of the art and the inventive concept; (4) decide whether those differences would have been obvious to the PSA (inventive step).
guidance: The Sanofi test is the canonical framework in Canada (derived from UK Windsurfing/Pozzoli jurisprudence). There is no 'prima facie' concept in Canada; multiple prior art pieces can form a 'mosaic' for the state of the art, including foreign-language and non-analogous references, but courts must still consider whether the PSA would have combined them. See Apotex v Sanofi and related case law.

name: Identity of the inventive concept
description: Determine the inventive concept of the claim (the 'solution taught by the patent'); if not readily apparent, construe it using the claims and, if necessary, the specification, taking care not to improperly narrow or expand the claim by reading the spec.
guidance: Construing the inventive concept is distinct from but related to claim construction. Using the specification is allowed when the inventive concept isn't apparent from the claims, especially for chemical/bare-formula claims, but avoid imputing optional dependent claim limitations into independent claims. One inventive concept may flow through all claims; overlap is expected. See Shire, Mylan, Tetra Tech examples.

name: Secondary considerations (objective indicia)
description: Courts and examiners may consider secondary (contextual) factors as instructive in the obviousness inquiry, including commercial success, industry conduct/failed attempts, long-felt need, conventional wisdom, and imitation.
guidance: Secondary considerations are not determinative by themselves but can be persuasive. Evidence must be tied to the inventive concept (commercial success attributable to claimed invention). Examples of admissible evidence: financial/sales data, awards, competitor actions. Be cautious filing commercially sensitive evidence in prosecution because Canadian Patent Office cannot impose confidentiality orders.

name: Evidence and admissibility limits for claim construction and prosecution
description: Generally extrinsic evidence (inventor notebooks, prior art, contemporary documents) is not admissible for claim construction, except statutory exceptions such as section 53.1(1) communications with the Patent Office.
guidance: Section 53.1(1) allows written communications between applicant and the Canadian Patent Office to be admitted to rebut representations about claim construction. Otherwise, rely on claims, specification, and PSA common general knowledge for construction.

name: Practical prosecution and validity considerations
description: Practical recommendations for searching, prosecution, responding to examiner objections, and court pleadings: use commercial search tools, search competitor portfolios, place watches, challenge examiners who fail to apply the Sanofi test properly, consider claim amendments, and plead all prior art when litigating (no opposition procedure in Canada).
guidance: Commercial search tools yield broader results than free tools. When challenging examiner obviousness objections, applicants can argue failure to properly apply the four-step Sanofi test and may amend claims. In court, pleadings must expressly include all prior art intended to be relied upon; new prior art requires amended pleadings. Note Canada lacks an opposition procedure; validity is challenged in courts.

name: March-in appeals and abeyance (35 U.S.C. 203(b))
description: A determination under this section shall have administrative appeals procedures established by regulation; any adversely affected party may, within sixty days, file a petition in the U.S. Court of Federal Claims to review the determination on the record. In cases under paragraphs (1) and (3) of subsection (a), the agency’s determination shall be held in abeyance pending exhaustion of appeals or petitions.
guidance: Provides judicial review rights and mandates abeyance for certain march-in determinations while appeals proceed.

name: Proper identification of product/service/organization when using marks
description: If proper identification of the product, service, or organization identified by a mark or trade name is omitted from the specification and such identification is deemed necessary, the examiner should hold the disclosure insufficient and reject claims based on identification merely by mark or trade name.
guidance: If a product cannot otherwise be defined, an amendment defining the process of its manufacture may be permitted unless such amendment would introduce new matter; such amendments must be supported by satisfactory showings establishing the specific nature or process of manufacture.

name: Examiner requirement when subject admits illustration but none furnished (37 CFR 1.81(c))
description: Whenever the nature of the subject matter admits of illustration by a drawing and the applicant has not furnished such a drawing, the examiner will require its submission and give at least two months for compliance.
guidance: Drawings submitted after filing may not be used to overcome insufficiency or to supplement original disclosure for claim interpretation; requirement should be clearly indicated as under 37 CFR 1.81(c).

name: Drawings submitted after filing cannot cure insufficiency or supplement disclosure
description: Drawings submitted after the filing date may not be used (i) to overcome any insufficiency of the specification due to lack of enabling disclosure or (ii) to supplement the original disclosure for purpose of interpreting claim scope.
guidance: Applicants should include necessary drawings at filing when required; late drawings may be limited in use.

name: Views: number, arrangement, and separation
description: Drawings must contain as many views as necessary to show the invention; views (plan, elevation, section, perspective) must be grouped together, arranged without wasting space, clearly separated, and not included on sheets with specifications/claims/abstract.
guidance: Views must not be connected by projection lines and must not contain center lines. Detail views and exploded views rules apply (exploded views embraced by bracket; place in brackets when on same sheet as another figure).

name: Office action must provide clear explanation and sufficient notice
description: When making a rejection, the Office action must provide an explanation as to why the claim is ineligible, which must be sufficiently clear and specific to provide applicant sufficient notice of the reasons for ineligibility and enable the applicant to effectively respond.
guidance: The action should explain why the claim is ineligible in a way that allows applicant to identify grounds and respond; worksheets and examples emphasize clarity and specificity as a threshold requirement.

name: Point to specific claim words that recite the judicial exception and explain why
description: Does the rejection point to words of the claim that recite (set forth or describe) the judicial exception? Is there an explanation of why those words are a judicial exception?
guidance: The Office action should cite particular claim language and provide reasoning (not mere conclusory labeling) explaining why those words correspond to the identified judicial exception.

name: Apply the Mayo/Alice two-part framework
description: Use the two-part analysis for claims directed to laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas: (1) determine whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception; (2) if so, determine whether additional elements amount to 'significantly more' than the exception.
guidance: Workshop assumes participants are familiar with the two-part analysis; the exemplary Office action demonstrates stepwise application (identify abstract idea, then evaluate additional elements).

name: Address preemption concerns
description: Consider whether the claim would 'preempt' all uses of the purported abstract idea; preemption is the concern driving the abstract-idea exception.
guidance: Examiners should analyze whether the claims tie up the broad concept or leave alternative techniques open; applicant arguments may show alternative implementations (e.g., different methods of calculating benefit or different transfer mechanisms) to rebut preemption concerns.

name: Consider Machine-or-Transformation (M-or-T) test as a useful clue
description: The Machine-or-Transformation test is a 'useful and important clue' for determining patent eligibility and should be considered where appropriate (e.g., whether the claim is tied to a particular machine).
guidance: Applicant arguments may rely on M-or-T to show eligibility (e.g., claim recites a particular computer system integral to the invention); examiners should weigh this alongside Alice/Mayo analysis.

name: Evaluate whether recited computer elements are merely generic or a claimed special-purpose machine
description: Assess if the computer components recited at a high level of generality merely perform generic computer functions (and thus add nothing) or if the claim ties those components to particular programmed functions rendering a special-purpose machine.
guidance: Exemplar notes that 'generic computer components recited as performing generic computer functions...amount to no more than implementing the abstract idea' but also acknowledges precedent (In re Alappat) that a programmed general-purpose computer can be a special-purpose computer; analysis must be specific to the claim.

name: Assess whether dependent claim limitations provide 'significantly more'
description: Evaluate dependent claim limitations (e.g., kiosk with interactive display, network connector, smart card dispenser) to determine whether they, alone or in combination with independent claim limitations, provide significantly more than the judicial exception.
guidance: Applicant argues that dependent elements describe a distributed computing environment producing a nonroutine action (ejection of a debit card) and that a new combination of known elements may be patentable even if constituents are known (Diamond v. Diehr). Examiners should analyze whether the combination produces a technical improvement or merely an extra-solution activity.

name: Ensure the Office action links claimed features to the legal standards/case law
description: The rejection should explain how claim features relate to judicially-identified abstract ideas and cite relevant caselaw or guidance (e.g., Alice, Bilski, Mayo, Diehr, Alappat) where that linkage is informative.
guidance: The exemplary rejection maps the concept to court-identified concepts (intermediate settlement, risk hedging) and discusses how those precedents inform the conclusion. Examiners should show the analogy and provide supporting explanation.

name: Language of the Statement of claim / language of the proceedings
description: Language of the Statement of claim; language of the proceedings when Contracting Member States designate EPO official languages
guidance: Language selection for the statement of claim and for proceedings is a hot topic: where Contracting Member States designate one or more EPO official languages for local/regional divisions, practitioners must observe the designated language(s) and related translation requirements.

name: Alice two-step framework (patent-eligibility)
description: Under Alice, first determine whether the claims at issue are directed to a patent-ineligible concept; if so, search for an 'inventive concept' sufficient to ensure the patent amounts to significantly more than the ineligible concept.
guidance: Quoted guidance: 'We must first determine whether the claims at issue are directed to a patent-ineligible concept.' If the claims are directed to an abstract idea, proceed to search for elements or combinations that provide significantly more (Alice, 573 U.S. at 217-18; Mayo). This two-step framing is the backbone of the eligibility analysis and guides use of MPEP §§ 2106.04–.05.

name: MPEP Step 2A — Prong One (does the claim recite a judicial exception)
description: Prong One asks: does the claim recite an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon? (MPEP §2106.04(II)(A)(1)).
guidance: The Step 2A Prong One analysis 'requir[es] a claim to recite (i.e., set forth or describe) an abstract idea in Prong One before proceeding to the Prong Two inquiry.' If the claim does not recite a judicial exception under Prong One, do not proceed to Prong Two or Step 2B.

name: MPEP Step 2A — Prong Two (integration into a practical application)
description: Prong Two asks: does the claim recite additional elements that integrate the judicial exception into a practical application? (MPEP §2106.04(II)(A)(2)).
guidance: Only after a determination under Prong One that a judicial exception is recited do you evaluate whether additional elements 'integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.' If, at Prong Two, 'the claim as a whole is not directed to a judicial exception,' the eligibility analysis concludes.

name: MPEP Step 2B — inventive concept (significantly more)
description: Step 2B is a search for an 'inventive concept'—elements or combinations that are 'sufficient to ensure that the patent in practice amounts to significantly more than a patent upon the [ineligible concept] itself.'
guidance: Assess whether additional claim elements provide 'significantly more' than the abstract idea (Alice; Mayo). Consider whether any combination of elements rises to the level of an inventive concept beyond generic computer implementation.

name: Evaluate the character of the claims as a whole
description: The 'directed to' inquiry looks to the character of the claims as a whole, not merely whether the claims involve a patent-ineligible concept in isolation (Enfish).
guidance: Do not resolve eligibility by isolating individual limitations at a high level of generality—consider how the elements work together to achieve improvements (Enfish, 822 F.3d at 1335–39). Panels/examiners should avoid overly cursory analyses that characterize claims too generally.

name: Claims reflecting improvements to computer functionality or another technological field may be patent eligible
description: Claims that are directed to an improvement in the functioning of a computer, or an improvement to other technology or technical field, can integrate an abstract idea into a practical application and be patent eligible (Enfish; McRO).
guidance: Assess whether the claim limitations themselves reflect the disclosed improvement (e.g., improving how a machine learning model operates by protecting prior-task performance while learning new tasks). Mere presence of an abstract idea does not preclude eligibility if the claim as a whole embodies a technological improvement.

name: Generic linking to a technological environment/field of use is insufficient
description: Claims that 'generally link[] the use of a judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use' are not patent eligible (MPEP §2106.05(h); Affinity Labs; Elec. Power Grp.).
guidance: Distinguish between (a) merely stating a field-of-use or applying an abstract idea in a conventional technological environment and (b) reciting claim limitations that produce a technological improvement. The former fails Prong Two/Step 2B.

name: Specification assertions alone are insufficient to establish eligibility
description: Statements in the specification asserting improvements are insufficient, by themselves, to support a patent-eligibility determination absent a subsequent determination that the claim itself reflects the disclosed improvement (MPEP §2106.05(a)).
guidance: Cite and evaluate specification passages (e.g., claims that 'allow the model to preserve performance on earlier tasks') but require that the claim language actually captures that improvement. Reliance solely on spec assertions without claim-level reflection is inadequate (see Intellectual Ventures I LLC v. Symantec Corp.).

name: Avoid equating machine learning with per se unpatentable algorithms or treating claims as 'generic computer components'
description: Panels/examiners should not categorically exclude AI innovations by equating any machine learning with an unpatentable 'algorithm' or by treating remaining elements as mere 'generic computer components.'
guidance: The decision warns against high-level generalization that would render many AI innovations unpatentable. Apply precedent (Enfish, McRO) carefully and explain reasoning when acting sua sponte. Use concrete claim-level analysis rather than broad characterizations of ML.

name: Use §§102, 103, and 112 as the traditional tools to limit patent protection
description: Sections 102 (novelty), 103 (nonobviousness), and 112 (written description/claims) are the traditional and appropriate statutory tools to limit patent protection to its proper scope.
guidance: The Panel emphasizes these statutory provisions should be the focus of examination to police improper claims scope; §101 analysis should not be a substitute for robust application of §§102,103,112 where appropriate.

name: Claims Must Find Basis in Original Disclosure
description: MPEP 608: Claims must be supported by and find basis in the original disclosure of the application.
guidance: Drawings cannot be used to add new claim-supporting matter after filing; they must support claims as filed. Page flags this as a required consideration under MPEP 608.

name: Original Disclosure Requirement for Filing
description: MPEP 608: The original disclosure at filing must meet statutory requirements (i.e., support and enablement).
guidance: This underscores that drawings included at filing (and their content) form part of the original disclosure; they must therefore be adequate to support later claims and avoid new matter issues.

name: Who Is Responsible for Pointing Out and Distinctly Claiming the Invention in a Patent Application?
description: Related FAQ topic: responsibility for pointing out and distinctly claiming the invention (applicant’s duty).
guidance: While not limited to drawings, the page notes this related question because drawings may be used to point out and illustrate claimed features; ultimately the applicant (through the specification and claims) is responsible for distinctly claiming the invention.

name: Can New Terms Be Introduced in Patent Claims After the Initial Filing?
description: Related FAQ topic: whether new terms may be introduced into claims post‑filing.
guidance: Ties back to the no‑new‑matter rule: introducing new terms that would add matter not supported in the original disclosure (including drawings) is impermissible. Page lists this as a related FAQ to drawing/disclosure rules.

name: EPO Guidelines requirement to amend description in line with the claims (H‑V 2.7; F‑IV 4.3(iii))
description: The EPO Guidelines for Examination require applicants to amend the description of a European patent application in line with the scope of the allowable claims (H‑V, 2.7 and F‑IV, 4.3(iii)).
guidance: Under the current Guidelines applicants are required either to delete subject matter no longer covered by the claims or explicitly state that the offending subject matter does not fall under the scope of the invention. The post notes this requirement has become 'rather draconian' in recent years and that examiners continue to require conformity with these Guidelines despite conflicting Board of Appeal decisions.

name: Article 84 EPC — claims must be clear, concise and supported by the description
description: Article 84 EPC stipulates that the claims 'shall be clear and concise and be supported by the description.' It is often cited as legal support for requiring description amendments.
guidance: Some Boards/Examiners rely on Article 84 to require deletion or amendment of description passages; however, decisions such as T 1989/18 and T 1444/20 have held that Article 84 cannot justify removing description matter where the claims are clear in and of themselves without recourse to the description.

name: F‑IV.4.4 — deletion/amendment of claim-like clauses
description: The Guidelines state 'claim-like clauses must also be deleted or amended to avoid claim-like language prior to grant since they otherwise may lead to unclarity on the subject-matter for which protection is sought' (F‑IV.4.4).
guidance: The Board in T 1444/20 found that if the claims of the main request are clear without reference to the description, the mere presence of claim-like clauses in the description that are not part of the claims cannot affect clarity; therefore deletion may not be warranted. The Guidelines' categorical requirement to always remove such clauses was criticised as inconsistent with that reasoning.

name: Rule 42(1)(c) EPC — description must disclose the invention as claimed
description: Rule 42(1)(c) EPC requires that the description must disclose the invention as claimed in such terms that the technical problem and its solution can be understood.
guidance: The Board in T 1444/20 did not accept that this provision translates into a requirement to remove passages of the description that disclose embodiments which are not claimed, particularly where the technical problem solved by the claims can be clearly understood from the description.

name: Clarity test — are claims clear in and of themselves without reference to the description?
description: A practical test applied by Boards: determine whether the claims are clear in and of themselves (i.e., without needing recourse to the description).
guidance: If claims are clear on their own, the presence of claim-like or redundant passages in the description that are not part of the claims cannot affect claim clarity, and deletion of such passages may be unnecessary. T 1989/18 and T 1444/20 support this principle; it directly contradicts a blanket application of the Guidelines' amendment requirement.

name: Deletion warranted only where description passages cause lack of clarity or contradiction with the claims
description: Description passages should be deleted or amended when they give rise to unclarity about the subject-matter for which protection is sought, or when they are contradictory to the claims.
guidance: T 1444/20 emphasises that deletion is not justified merely because content is 'redundant' or not claimed; deletion is more defensible where the description causes lack of clarity or contains subject-matter inconsistent with the claims. Boards have differed on whether and when such contradictions require deletion.

name: Distinguish redundant versus contradictory subject-matter when assessing need for amendment
description: There is a legal and practical distinction between redundant (unclaimed but not conflicting) and contradictory (inconsistent with the claims) subject-matter in the description.
guidance: T 1444/20 concerned deletion of redundant subject-matter and found deletion unnecessary where claims remain clear; by contrast T 1989/18 and T 1024/18 relate to contradictory subject-matter. This distinction affects whether Rule 42/48 or Article 84 can be used to justify amendment or deletion.

name: Claims
description: Claims: At least one claim required.
guidance: Claims define the scope of legal protection sought; a non-provisional utility application must include at least one claim.

name: Definiteness
description: Definiteness: Particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention.
guidance: Claims must be sufficiently definite to inform the public of the bounds of the claimed invention.

name: Patent prosecution process
description: After filing, the application is examined by a patent examiner who determines whether the claims meet patentability requirements. The examiner issues office actions (typically rejecting some or all claims), and the applicant responds with arguments and/or amendments. This back-and-forth continues until the application is allowed or finally rejected.
guidance: Prosecution is an iterative process of office actions and applicant responses. Success depends on persuasive arguments, claim amendments, and meeting procedural requirements until allowance or final rejection.

name: Patentability requirements (examiner assessment)
description: The examiner determines whether the claims meet patentability requirements.
guidance: The page notes the examiner's role in assessing patentability but does not enumerate specific tests; in practice patent offices evaluate novelty, inventive step/non‑obviousness, and industrial applicability/usefulness among other requirements.

name: Definition of novelty / prior art
description: An invention is new if it is not anticipated by prior art. Prior art constituted by everything disclosed to the public anywhere by written or oral disclosure, by use, or by any other way before the relevant filing date or claimed priority date.
guidance: Public disclosure within one year before filing/priority may be disregarded if due to abusive actions against the applicant; disclosure at an officially recognized exhibition within six months preceding filing is not taken into account (Implementing Bylaws determine protection provisions).

name: Content of application
description: Application shall contain the title of the invention, a specification, one or more claims, one or more drawings (if any), and an abstract.
guidance: Specification must disclose the invention sufficiently clearly and completely for a person skilled in the art to carry it out. Claims determine scope of protection; specification and drawings may be used to interpret claims. Claims must be clear, concise, and fully supported by the specification. Abstract serves only technical information and shall not be used to interpret the application.

name: Careful framing of 'need' and background
description: Avoid broad need statements in the background that characterize the invention in overly general terms (e.g., 'the idea of network-controlled charging stations').
guidance: Describe the specific problem being solved (for example, needing to program each charging station individually, leading to inflexibility and extra work) rather than making broad, high-level need statements; an overly broad background can be used to invalidate the patent under broad claim interpretations.

name: Avoid claims that merely 'collect and compare known information'
description: Claims that perform only collecting and comparing known information, without requiring a step based on the comparison, are often found ineligible under §101.
guidance: If possible, draft claims to perform a step based on the comparison or to include additional, concrete actions (e.g., immunization step in Classen) so the claim does something with the comparison; emphasize any post-comparison action to support eligibility.

name: Claim a specific improvement in computing-device capabilities
description: Claims should be directed to a specific improvement in computing devices (a specific manner of performing a function) rather than to an abstract idea with computers used as generic tools.
guidance: Articulate claims with enough specificity at Alice step one to show they are not directed to an abstract idea; focus on how particular claim elements provide a technical improvement (e.g., a specific manner of displaying a limited set of information) rather than only claiming a desirable result.

name: Disclose technical problems in the specification and how the invention solves them
description: The specification should describe technical problems in prior user interfaces (or other computer systems) and explain how the claimed invention solves those problems with improved technology.
guidance: Claim the structure and/or process for the improvement, not just the result. Be specific about how particular claim elements improve functioning of the computer system (examples: saving user navigation steps, improving usability on small screens).

name: Do not claim data structures alone—tie data to tangible use
description: Data structures or profiles (e.g., a device profile) by themselves are not necessarily statutory; claiming only data may be treated as non-tangible.
guidance: Claim use of the profile (a method or device that uses the profile) or claim a tangible, non-transitory medium storing the data structure. Ensure a claim uses the data to solve a technical problem rather than merely existing as data.

name: Avoid claiming only information-based results without inventive means
description: Claims that define a desirable information-based result (collecting, analyzing, and displaying information) in general terms, without limiting inventive means of achieving the result, are likely to fail §101.
guidance: Include inventive technological elements or specific means for performing the functions; do not leave the claim as a high-level goal. Emphasize particular technical mechanisms that perform the collection/analysis/display in a non-conventional way.

name: Characterize technical problem/solution in technical terms and include non-business examples
description: When drafting/specifying, characterize the problem and solution in technical infrastructure terms and provide examples that are not solely business-related.
guidance: Avoid focusing exclusively on the business problem; include examples that show how the claimed invention addresses a technical issue in computer networks or systems (e.g., integration of data across sites, navigation in 3D spreadsheets). This helps analogize to favorable cases (Enfish, Core Wireless, DDR).

name: Prosecution and argument strategies to oppose §101 rejections
description: Multiple tactics can be used to challenge examiner §101 rejections and unfavorable characterizations of claims as abstract ideas.
guidance: Strategies include: attack the identification of the abstract idea (ensure the rejection is tied to the case facts and avoid language taken out of context); argue claims recite a technical solution to a technical problem; point to generation of new information (analogy to Enfish); emphasize user interactivity and improved data presentation (analogy to Core Wireless); point to a particular inventive technological process (distinguish from Electric Power); use guidance/memos (McRo, Enfish, Berkheimer) and training materials; argue that the examiner's broad/simplified characterization (collect/analyze/display) is unreasonable; and press for a narrower, claim-specific abstraction in the §101 analysis.

name: Challenge broadest reasonable interpretation and oversimplification
description: Argue that the examiner's or court's characterization of a claim as an overly broad abstraction (e.g., 'collecting information, analyzing it, and displaying certain results') is unreasonable and improperly removes claim detail.
guidance: Demonstrate how claim elements provide more than the caricature used to compare the claim to abstract-idea cases; show that Enfish, McRo, DDR, etc., were decided on specific claim-level improvements and that similar specifics exist in your claims.

name: Situations where ‘obvious to try’ is improperly equated with obviousness (Kubin’s two classes)
description: Two classes of situations where equating ‘obvious to try’ with obviousness is erroneous: (1) when ‘obvious to try’ would require varying all parameters or trying each of numerous possible choices until one possibly arrived at a successful result, where the prior art gave either no indication of which parameters were critical or no direction as to which of many possible choices is likely to be successful; and (2) when ‘obvious to try’ was to explore a new technology or general approach that seemed promising, where the prior art gave only general guidance as to the particular form of the claimed invention or how to achieve it.
guidance: Cite Kubin: these classes limit application of obvious-to-try. If a case fits either class, obvious-to-try reasoning is not appropriate. Examples: broad unexplored fields, numerous unconstrained parameters, or prior art providing only general guidance (not specific, finite options).

name: Known work in one field prompting predictable adaptation to same or different field — five required findings
description: To reject a claim based on the rationale that known work in one field would prompt a predictable variation for use in the same or different field, Office personnel must articulate: (1) that the prior art included a similar or analogous device (method, or product); (2) that design incentives or market forces would have prompted adaptation; (3) that the differences between claimed invention and prior art were encompassed in known variations or a known principle; (4) that one of ordinary skill could have implemented the claimed variation and it would have been predictable; and (5) any additional Graham factual findings necessary for the case.
guidance: The rationale is that design incentives/market forces could have prompted predictable variation. If any of these findings cannot be made, this rationale cannot support an obviousness conclusion. Examples: Dann, Leapfrog, KSR, Catan illustrate application of these findings.

name: Routine application of conventional methods to a known product can support obviousness when success was predictable
description: When prior art discloses a product (e.g., a polypeptide) and conventional, routine methods in the art (e.g., sequencing, isolation techniques) would have allowed obtaining the claimed product, a skilled artisan would have had a reasonable expectation that the claimed product could be obtained.
guidance: Kubin example: Valiante disclosed the polypeptide and Sambrook disclosed conventional methods for sequencing/isolating the nucleic acid; the Board found a reasonable expectation of successfully obtaining the claimed nucleic acid. Examiners should articulate the specific conventional methods and why they would have produced the claimed invention with reasonable predictability.

name: Anatomy of a Claim
description: Introductory phrase / preamble; Transitional phrase ("comprising," "consisting of," etc.); Body / elements; Multiple types: independent, dependent, multiple dependent.
guidance: Understand and teach the distinct structural parts of a claim and the available claim types; emphasize correct use of preambles and transitional language to control scope.

name: Claim Drafting Choices
description: Open vs. closed transitions; Means-plus-function vs. structural; Method vs. apparatus vs. system; Genus vs. species; Markush groupings; Negative limitations.
guidance: Highlight the strategic tradeoffs among drafting options (scope, prosecution and enforcement risks, indefiniteness/§112 issues). Practice choosing transitions and claim formats appropriate to disclosure and enforcement goals.

name: Specification Drafting (required components)
description: Specification encompasses drawings, written description, and claims: Title of invention; Cross-reference to related applications; Statement regarding federally sponsored research; Background of the invention; Brief summary; Brief description of drawings; Detailed description; Claims; Abstract.
guidance: Teach how each element supports claim scope and §112 requirements (written description/enablement), and how to draft statements (e.g., cross-refs, government support) that comply with procedural rules.

name: Capstone / Practical Exercises
description: Students typically draft a complete patent application; practice claim drafting exercises; respond to mock office actions; conduct prior art search; draft licensing agreements; present patent strategy.
guidance: Use hands-on projects to integrate drafting and prosecution skills; include simulated prosecution and client-facing tasks (licensing, strategy presentation) to mirror practice.

name: Industry-Specific Considerations
description: Pharma/biotech (Hatch-Waxman, BPCIA, ANDA); Software (Alice/Mayo, copyright overlap); Mechanical/electrical; Standard-essential patents (FRAND).
guidance: Address sector-specific laws and case law that affect claim drafting and prosecution strategy; tailor exercises to domain-specific issues (e.g., enablement in biotech, eligibility in software, SEP licensing).

name: Qualifications and Duties of Examiners-in-Chief
description: Examiners-in-chief shall be persons of competent legal knowledge and scientific ability; their duty is, on written petition of the appellant, to revise and determine upon the validity of adverse decisions of examiners upon applications for patents and re-issues, and in interference cases; when required by the Commissioner, they shall hear and report upon claims for extensions and perform other like duties assigned.
guidance: Sets qualification standard (legal + scientific competency) and appellate/review responsibilities for senior examiners. [See Revised Statutes, Section 482.]

name: Costs Limitation Where Patentee Falsely Claims Originality
description: When judgment or decree is rendered for infringement of part of a patent in which it appears the patentee in his specification claimed to be the original and first inventor of any material or substantial part of the thing patented of which he was not the original and first inventor, no costs shall be recovered unless the proper disclaimer has been entered at the Patent-Office before the suit was brought.
guidance: Adverse-costs rule to discourage erroneous or false originality claims; requires pre-suit disclaimer to preserve costs. [See Revised Statutes, Section 973.]

name: Specification Requisites: Written Application and Enabling Disclosure
description: Before receiving a patent the inventor shall make application in writing to the Commissioner and file in the Patent-Office a written description of the invention and of the manner and process of making, constructing, compounding, and using it in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art or science to which it pertains to make, construct, compound, and use the same; in case of a machine, explain its principle and the best mode contemplated of applying that principle so as to distinguish it from other inventions; particularly point out and distinctly claim the part, improvement, or combination which he claims as his invention; the specification and claim shall be signed by the inventor and attested by two witnesses.
guidance: Contains written-application, enablement, best mode, written-claiming, signature, and witness-attestation requirements—fundamental for statutory sufficiency of the specification and claims. [See Revised Statutes, Section 4888.]

name: Content of request — required elements (37 CFR 1.510(b))
description: Any request for reexamination must include: (1) a statement pointing out each substantial new question of patentability based on prior patents and printed publications; (2) identification of every claim for which reexamination is requested and a detailed explanation of the pertinency and manner of applying the cited prior art to every claim (and, if appropriate, how claims distinguish over cited prior art); (3) a copy of every patent or printed publication relied upon accompanied by English translations of necessary parts of non‑English documents; (4) a copy of the entire patent (front face, drawings, specification/claims) in double column format, with each page plainly written on only one side; (5) a certification that a copy of the request filed by a person other than the patent owner has been served in its entirety on the patent owner at the address in § 1.33(c), with name and address of party served (or duplicate copy supplied if service not possible).
guidance: The statement of SNQ should clearly point out why reexamination is warranted. Cited prior art should be listed on a Form PTO-1449/PTO/SB/08A/08B or equivalent. Copies and translations are required so the examiner can fully consider materials. The request should apply the cited prior art to every claim requested; requesters may not argue the references do not raise an SNQ in the request itself (i.e., the request must assert an SNQ). If the patent owner files no statement under 37 CFR 1.530(b), then the requester cannot file later replies under 1.535.

name: Patent copy formatting requirements
description: A copy of the entire patent including front face, drawings, and specification/claims (in double column format) must be provided, and all copies must have each page plainly written on only one side of a sheet of paper.
guidance: Printed patent pages should be reproduced as they appear in the printed patent. Two-sided copies are not proper. Any disclaimers, certificates of correction, or reexamination certificates that are part of the patent must also be supplied.

name: Proper scope of collateral challenges
description: Collateral attacks on the factual findings, credibility determinations, or negotiated nature of the state proceeding are not an appropriate vehicle to avoid reciprocal discipline under § 11.24.
guidance: Claims that the state decision was motivated by resource conservation, negotiation artifacts, or lack of OED Director personal knowledge do not, by themselves, satisfy the Selling factors; the respondent must meet the statutory exceptions with clear and convincing evidence.

name: Number of independent claims
description: A count of allowed independent claims for each patent.
guidance: Used as a proxy for patent scope; expected to be positively correlated with litigation. Note complication: applicants may include narrow/overlapping independent claims, so additional independent claims don't always increase scope. Examples: method, computer-readable medium, system independent claims; high-value inventions often have overlapping independent claims. Fee note: applicants are charged fees for independent claims in excess of three (currently $420 per claim).

name: Functional claiming
description: Indicator for whether any of the claims have a functional limitation, operationalized by presence of the phrases 'means for' or 'step for'.
guidance: Functional claim language lets drafters rely on specification for scope, sometimes making claims less clear; expected (in some models) to be positively associated with litigation or petitions. Note measurement caveat: functional limitations may exist without those phrases; conversely presence of phrases may not always indicate a functional limitation, but the study uses these phrases as the coding rule.

name: FAOM Allowance (First-Action On the Merits allowance)
description: Indicator for whether the patent was allowed on the first action on the merits (first-action allowance).
guidance: Litigated patents are less likely to have FAOM allowances; FAOM may indicate well-drafted or narrow claims, which could reduce litigation through reduced uncertainty or reduced value. Include as a prosecution-quality indicator.

name: Petitioner burden to identify unpatentability with particularity
description: “In an [inter partes review], the petitioner has the burden from the onset to show with particularity why the patent it challenges is unpatentable.” (citing Harmonic Inc. v. Avid Tech., Inc.; 35 U.S.C. § 312(a)(3)).
guidance: Petition must identify with particularity the evidence that supports the grounds for the challenge to each claim. The petition should map claim limitations to prior art and present supporting evidence (e.g., declarations, alignments). Failure to identify evidence with particularity can defeat institution.

name: Obviousness standard under 35 U.S.C. § 103 (Graham factors)
description: A claim is unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. § 103(a) if the differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art. The question is resolved by underlying factual determinations including: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art; (3) level of ordinary skill in the art; and (4) objective evidence of nonobviousness, if any. (Graham v. John Deere Co.).
guidance: Obviousness analyses must address each Graham factor; show where each claim limitation is taught or suggested by prior art and explain the differences and why a POSA would have been motivated to bridge them.

name: KSR guidance on 'obvious to try' and predictability
description: KSR instructs that when there is a design need or market pressure and a finite number of identified, predictable solutions, it may be obvious to try known options — and success following predictable options can indicate obviousness. KSR also states that an improvement is barred from patentability if it is merely the predictable use of prior art elements according to their established functions.
guidance: Explain why the combination falls within a ‘finite, predictable’ set of solutions or why the claimed improvement is more than predictable use. Show why a POSA would pursue the known option(s) rather than relying on hindsight.

name: Claim construction standard in IPR
description: Claims in an IPR are construed using the same standard as in a civil action under 35 U.S.C. § 282(b): in accordance with the ordinary and customary meaning to one of ordinary skill in the art and the prosecution history. The specification is highly relevant and usually dispositive. (37 C.F.R. § 42.100(b); Phillips; In re Abbott Diabetes Care).
guidance: The Board will construe only those terms that are in controversy and only to the extent necessary to resolve the controversy (Realtime Data; Vivid Techs.). If claim terms are not disputed for institution purposes, express constructions may be unnecessary.

name: Mapping claim limitations to the prior art with supporting evidence
description: To meet the petitioner's burden at institution, the petition must show that each limitation of a challenged claim is taught or rendered obvious by the asserted references, using factual evidence (e.g., reference paragraphs, sequence alignments, expert declarations).
guidance: Provide explicit citations and demonstrative evidence (sequence alignments, tables, experiment results, expert testimony) that show how each claim limitation is present in or suggested by the prior art; courts/Board expect concrete linkages rather than conclusory assertions.

name: When combining references, address claim-specific functional/limitation requirements
description: If a claim requires a specific function or tropism (e.g., muscle tropism for claim 8), the petitioner must explain why the combined teachings would yield that particular functional property, not just some general improvement.
guidance: Demonstrate that the asserted combination would provide the claimed function (e.g., cite data showing muscle transduction or explain why the modification specifically enhances muscle targeting), or identify where the prior art links the modification to the required function.

name: Institution decision standard: reasonable likelihood of prevailing
description: Under 35 U.S.C. § 314(a) the Board institutes review if the petitioner shows a reasonable likelihood that it would prevail with respect to at least one of the claims challenged. The Board applies SAS and relevant rules (37 C.F.R. § 42.108(a)).
guidance: Petition should present the strongest grounds with coherent evidence and argumentation. The Board may focus its institution analysis on the strongest ground(s) and limit its discussion accordingly; institution is not a final determination of patentability.

name: Use of specification and prosecution history as primary guides for claim meaning
description: The specification is the single best guide to the meaning of a disputed claim term and prosecution history is relevant to claim construction.
guidance: When interpreting claim terms or arguing what a POSA would have understood, rely on the patent's specification and prosecution history to frame meanings and limits; avoid constructions contrary to the specification unless clearly supported.

name: 0600 — Parts, Form, and Content of Application
description: 600 Parts, Form, and Content of Application
guidance: Standards for required parts of an application, form and content requirements (specification, claims, drawings, oath/declaration).

name: Evaluation implementation and reproducibility practices
description: Use standard libraries (scikit-learn for classification/clustering, Sentence-Transformers evaluators for retrieval/similarity, HuggingFace Datasets for data loading), fixed random seeds, deterministic inference, and document all evaluation hyperparameters for reproducibility.
guidance: Inference config: batch size 64, max sequence length capped at 8192 tokens. Preprocess texts by combining title, abstract, and first claim and filter to not exceed token cap. Report single-run deterministic scores on fixed test sets and use external validation, ablations, and robustness analyses to assess generalization.

name: Structural robustness tests (input-format robustness)
description: Evaluate robustness to missing document components (abstract or claims), removal of separator tokens, and title-only inputs to assess practical deployment resilience.
guidance: Findings: removing separator tokens (noSEP) has negligible effect (~99.8% retention); removing one section (abstract or claims) causes minor degradation (~98.8% retention); title-only input causes substantial drop (~88.5% retention). Use these tests to understand how input formatting impacts embedding quality.

name: Use of a patent attorney (representation)
description: An applicant may be represented by a patent attorney. Use of a patent attorney is recommended (especially for drafting claims and prosecution) but not mandatory for domestic applicants; foreign applicants without domicile in Finland must have an EEA‑resident representative.
guidance: Patent attorneys help evaluate patentability pre-filing, draft claims to provide business‑appropriate protection, and manage prosecution. PRH maintains a register of authorized patent attorneys via the industrial property attorney board.

name: Reissue patents as prima facie evidence (jurisdiction, breadth, identity)
description: Reissue letters patent are prima facie evidence of their own validity with respect to (1) the Commissioner's jurisdiction to treat the original as proper subject for reissue, (2) facts bearing on broadened reissue after lapse of time, and (3) that the reissue does not claim a different invention than the original.
guidance: Presumptions are based on the Commissioner's assumed jurisdiction and knowledge of law; reissue is prima facie as to these three points.

name: Element-by-element objective inquiry
description: The determination of equivalence should be applied as an objective inquiry on an element-by-element basis.
guidance: Apply equivalence to each individual claim element rather than to the accused product or process as a whole; preserve some meaning for each claim element so the doctrine does not 'enlarge the patent beyond the scope of its claims.' This preserves the definitional and public-notice functions of claims.

name: Prosecution history estoppel — availability and limits
description: Prosecution history estoppel continues to be available as a defense to infringement.
guidance: If a patentee demonstrates an amendment required during prosecution had a purpose unrelated to patentability, the court must consider that purpose and estoppel may be avoided. Where the patentee cannot establish such a purpose, the court should presume the amendment was made for reasons related to patentability and apply prosecution history estoppel to bar equivalents for that element. Estoppel has historically been tied to amendments made to avoid the prior art or render claims patentable.

name: Means-plus-function (§112, ¶6) claims — restrictive construction
description: § 112, ¶ 6 provides that a 'means' claim 'shall be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.'
guidance: Section 112, ¶ 6 was enacted as a targeted cure (in response to Halliburton) and functions restrictively: it narrows the literal breadth of means-plus-function claim language to the corresponding structure in the specification and its equivalents. The statutory reference to 'equivalents' in ¶6 is prophylactic and does not negate the doctrine of equivalents where there is no literal infringement.

name: Avoid vitiation — preserve claim element meaning
description: Ensure application of the doctrine is not allowed such broad play as to effectively eliminate that element in its entirety.
guidance: Courts must be vigilant that invoking equivalence for an element does not 'vitiate' the element or erase its scope; maintaining some independent meaning for each claim element is necessary to protect the notice and definitional functions of claims.

name: Choice of linguistic test should be probative
description: The particular linguistic framework used to determine 'equivalence' is less important than whether the test is probative of the essential inquiry.
guidance: Triple identity (function-way-result) and insubstantial differences tests are available; different tests may be suited to different fact patterns. The key question is whether the accused product or process contains elements identical or equivalent to each claimed element. Focus on probative value and element-level analysis rather than rigid adherence to a particular verbal formula.

name: Procedural allocation and safeguards (judge vs jury; summary judgment; verdict form)
description: The Court declines to definitively decide whether equivalence is for judge or jury; prior cases support jury factfinding, but courts determine legal limits.
guidance: District courts must decide legal issues (e.g., prosecution history estoppel, whether a theory would vitiate a claim element) and are obliged to grant partial or complete summary judgment or judgment as a matter of law where no reasonable jury could find equivalence. Special verdicts and interrogatories on each claim element are recommended to facilitate reviewability and uniformity. Federal Rules (56, 50, 49) provide means to resolve legal issues pre- or post-trial.

name: Patent scope should not exceed inventor's disclosure
description: It is basic to the grant of a patent that the scope of a patent should not exceed the scope of invention.
guidance: Courts and the Patent Office should restrain claim breadth to what the inventor actually invented and taught in the specification; avoid granting broad claims that cover embodiments well beyond the patent's disclosure.

name: Enablement and written description constraint (35 U.S.C. §112)
description: The specification must contain a written description and enablement in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to make and use the invention, and must set forth the best mode.
guidance: Adequacy of disclosure is measured as of the filing date; failure to disclose best mode or to enable the claimed scope can invalidate or limit claims (illustrated by Genentech/Scripps and other cases). Enablement doctrine should limit claim breadth to what is actually taught.

name: Restrict overly broad pioneer patents
description: Pioneer patents are often granted broad scope that can block subsequent inventors; there is frequently no justification for the breadth granted and upheld.
guidance: Patent Office and courts should pay close attention to what the pioneer inventor actually disclosed and what was already in the public domain; trim claims to reflect the actual contribution and avoid blocking follow-on innovation.

name: Prefer process (or product-by-process) claims for purified natural products and obvious variants
description: Product patents on purified forms of natural substances or on structurally obvious variants can block subsequent recombinant or improved processes/products.
guidance: Granting process patents or product-by-process claims is more consistent with enablement and better reflects what the inventor actually achieved; this reduces blocking of improvements (illustrated by Parke-Davis/adrenalin and Scripps/Genentech).

name: Patent Office scrutiny of claims vis-à-vis public domain and specification
description: The Patent Office should pay closer attention to the inventor's specification and the broad nature of what was already known and in the public domain when deciding claim scope.
guidance: Restrict allowed claim scope accordingly to avoid granting monopolies over what was already part of public science or what the inventor did not actually teach.

name: Obviousness and prior publications should limit claim breadth
description: Claims that would be obvious in light of prior publications or prior art should be rejected; prior publication can render claims obvious and prevent overly broad patents.
guidance: Use obviousness analysis to deny broad, prospect-like patents (example: rejection of an overly broad gene expression patent because inventors published results prior to the claimed invention).

name: Tailor scope doctrines to preserve incentives for subsequent improvements
description: Scope doctrines can be used to approximate an optimal patent breadth that preserves incentives for both pioneers and subsequent improvers.
guidance: Doctrinal modifications (narrowing of broad claims, use of reverse equivalents, strict adherence to disclosure) should be applied judiciously and primarily to a small number of pioneering breakthroughs to retain incentives for initial inventions while protecting follow-on innovation.

name: Accelerated Examination Program — eligibility and filing requirements
description: To receive accelerated treatment under the Accelerated Examination Program, applicants must file a petition to make special under 37 CFR 1.102 entitled 'Advancement of examination' and meet certain conditions.
guidance: Key requirements include: (1) the application must be filed via EFS-Web with a petition to make special along with (a) required petition fee or (b) a statement that the claimed invention is directed to environmental quality, development or conservation of energy resources, or counter terrorism; (2) the application must be complete and in condition for examination; (3) the application must contain three or fewer independent and twenty or fewer total claims, and must not contain any multiple dependent claims; (4) the claims must be directed to a single invention; (5) the petition must include a statement agreeing to have an interview; (6) applicant must provide a statement that a pre-examination search was conducted that meets certain requirements; and (7) applicant must provide an accelerated examination support document that satisfies certain requirements. See MPEP § 708.02(a). URL: http://www.uspto.gov/patents/process/file/accelerated/index.jsp

name: Green Technology Pilot Program — eligibility and filing requirements
description: A pilot permitting accelerated examination for applications pertaining to clean technologies (environmental quality, energy conservation, renewable energy, greenhouse gas emission reductions) via a petition to make special under 37 CFR 1.102.
guidance: Key requirements include: (1) the application must be filed before Dec. 8, 2009; (2) the application must contain three or fewer independent claims and twenty or fewer total claims, and must not contain any multiple dependent claims; (3) the claims must be directed to a single invention that materially enhances the quality of the environment; (4) the petition must include a statement explaining how the materiality standard is met if it is not clear on its face from the application disclosure; (5) the petition must be filed via EFS-Web; and (6) the petition must be accompanied by a request for early publication and the publication fee. An initial classification requirement was removed on May 21, 2010 to allow more inventions to qualify. Support document: Not Required. URL: http://www.uspto.gov/patents/init_events/green_tech.jsp

name: Terms of degree / relative terms
description: Even if the specification uses the same term of degree as in the claim, a rejection is proper if the scope of the term is not understood when read in light of the specification; when relative terms are used where the improvement rests entirely upon size or weight of an element, the adequacy of disclosure of a standard is of greater criticality.
guidance: Evaluate whether the specification supplies an objective standard for the degree/relative term; rejections under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) are proper when scope is unclear. Example cases: In re Wiggins. If the term's boundaries are not discernible, require amendment or further disclosure.

name: Reference to a variable object
description: A claim may be indefinite by reference to an object that is variable (e.g., reciting relationships to an unspecified user or rider of unspecified build).
guidance: Determine whether the claim specifies the positional/measurement relationship or a known standard. Examples: Ex parte Miyazaki (printer/user height indefinite), Ex parte Brummer (bicycle rider of unspecified build indefinite), Orthokinetics (pediatric wheelchair 'so dimensioned' held definite because as accurate as subject matter permits).

name: Use of 'about' (approximations)
description: The range encompassed by the term 'about' depends on the context of the specification and claims; 'about' can be definite if the limitation can be clearly assessed (e.g., measurable via stopwatch) but may be indefinite where there is close prior art and no indication of range.
guidance: Consider specification context, prosecution history, prior art, and whether a POSITA can determine the covered range. Example: Ortho-McNeil Pharm. v. Caraco; W.L. Gore (stretch rate 'exceeding about 10% per second' definite), Amgen (problems with 'at least about' where no guidance).

name: Use of 'similar' (vague comparative terms)
description: Terms like 'similar' in claim recitations are indefinite if it is unclear what apparatus or structure the applicant intended to cover.
guidance: Look to the specification to see if 'similar' is defined or exemplified; absent that, find the claim indefinite. Examples: Ex parte Kristensen (no clarity for 'similar apparatus'), Ex parte Pappas (design claim 'similar structure' indefinite).

name: Addition of 'type' to an expression
description: Adding 'type' (e.g., 'ZSM-5-type') can extend scope and render a claim indefinite if it is unclear what 'type' conveys, especially when dependent claims fall outside the asserted genus.
guidance: Check whether 'type' is defined or supported; examples: Ex parte Copenhaver, Ex parte Attig. If unclear, rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) may be proper.

name: Subjective terms
description: Facially subjective claim language (e.g., 'aesthetically pleasing', 'unobtrusive manner', 'comparable', 'superior') may render claims indefinite where the specification supplies no objective standard for measuring the scope.
guidance: Require an objective standard in the specification or evidence that a POSITA can ascertain the meaning; applicant may amend to remove the subjective term or provide evidence/definitions. Cases: Datamize (aesthetically pleasing indefinite), Interval Licensing (unobtrusive manner indefinite), Ex parte Anderson. Note: some subjective terms may still be definite if the spec supplies sufficiently clear boundaries.

name: Narrow and broader ranges in the same claim
description: A single claim that includes both a broad range and a narrower range may be indefinite when the claim's boundaries are not discernible (e.g., 'between 45 and 78°C, preferably between 50 and 60°C').
guidance: Prefer placing examples/preferences in the specification or in dependent/other independent claims. If it's unclear whether the narrower range is a limitation, make a 35 U.S.C. 112(b) rejection. Dependent claims reciting narrower ranges are acceptable (e.g., claim 1: 70-150 ohms; claim 2: 70-100 ohms).

name: Open-ended numerical ranges
description: Open-ended ranges (e.g., 'at least 20%') must be carefully analyzed for definiteness, particularly with dependent claims that could create apparent contradictions.
guidance: Check whether dependent claim recitations create ambiguities (e.g., nonsodium ingredients summing to 100% seeming to exclude 'at least' sodium). Note that theoretically impossible compositions in claim language are not necessarily indefinite (subject matter that cannot exist cannot anticipate or infringe). See In re Kroekel, In re Kirsch, In re Mochel.

name: Exemplary claim language ('for example,' 'such as')
description: Describing examples or preferences belongs properly in the specification rather than the claims; using phrases like 'for example' or 'such as' in claims may lead to confusion about scope.
guidance: The mere use of 'such as' or 'for example' does not by itself render a claim indefinite, but examine factually. Examples of problematic phrasing include 'R is halogen, for example, chlorine' and 'material such as rock wool or asbestos.' Apply MPEP § 2173.02 guidance when making 35 U.S.C. 112(b) rejections.

name: Lack of antecedent basis
description: A claim is indefinite when it contains words or phrases whose meaning is unclear due to missing antecedent basis (e.g., referring to 'said lever' when no earlier recitation of a lever exists).
guidance: Consider that antecedent problems are typically correctable drafting oversights; examiners should identify and suggest corrections in a constructive manner. However, failure to provide an antecedent basis can render a claim indefinite (In re Packard). The absence of explicit antecedent wording does not always render a claim indefinite if the scope is reasonably ascertainable (Ex parte Porter, Bose Corp.). Also, omission of elements from a preamble does not per se make a claim indefinite if the claim body apprises a POSITA of scope (In re Larsen).

name: Reference to limitations in another claim
description: Referring to a preceding claim to define a limitation (e.g., 'the product produced by the method of claim 1') is an acceptable claim construction and not necessarily indefinite.
guidance: Such references are acceptable unless the reference format causes confusion. Examine dependent claims for compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(d)/pre-AIA §112 fourth paragraph. See Ex parte Porter and MPEP guidance. If reference causes confusion, a 35 U.S.C. 112(b) rejection may be proper.

name: Functional limitations
description: A claim term is functional when it recites a feature by what it does rather than by what it is; functional language is not per se improper, and 35 U.S.C. 112(f) expressly authorizes means/step-plus-function claiming, but purely functional limitations that provide no structure may be indefinite.
guidance: Evaluate functional limitations in context (specification disclosure and POSITA knowledge). Consider whether the limitation (1) provides a clear indication of scope, (2) sets well-defined boundaries or only states a problem/result, and (3) would allow a POSITA to know what structure or steps are encompassed. Permit functional language when structure or examples are present (In re Schreiber, In re Barr, In re Venezia). Beware of claims that merely recite a problem/result or encompass all means to achieve a result (Ariad, Hyatt, Datamize). Applicant remedies include adding quantitative metrics, providing formulas and examples, supplying general guidelines, or amending to recite structure.

name: Alternative limitations / Markush groups
description: Claims reciting a list of alternatives (Markush group) are generally acceptable when formatted as a closed group ('consisting of'), but an open list ('comprising'/'consisting essentially of') may be indefinite because it is unclear what other alternatives are intended.
guidance: Follow MPEP § 706.03(y), § 2117, and § 803.02 for Markush treatment. If the claim intends to encompass combinations or mixtures, include qualifying language (e.g., 'at least one member' or 'or mixtures thereof'). Breadth by itself is not indefiniteness (In re Gardner), but overly expansive groups that prevent POSITA from discerning metes and bounds may be indefinite. Consider election and restriction issues per Markush practice.

name: Prohibition on leasing mineral/phosphate lands and mining permissions
description: Under the act of July 28, 1892 and related decisions, the Secretary of War has no authority to lease mineral or phosphate lands or to grant permission to locate and work mineral claims on a military reservation by lease or license; 'mineral lands' includes lands chiefly valuable for building stone.
guidance: Requests to work minerals on reservations should be denied absent specific congressional authorization.

name: Inventive step for polymorphic (crystalline) forms
description: An invention claiming a compound with a specific crystal form (polymorph) that differs from a prior-art crystal form is considered to have inventive step if it has a clearly different qualitative effect compared to the prior art, or if it has a clearly different quantitative effect compared to the prior art regardless of qualitative effect.
guidance: The specification should state the effect clearly even if no comparative test data with the prior art are provided. If the claimed effect is doubtful, it must be proven concretely by submitting evidence such as comparative test data trusted by the applicant/patentee after filing date. (See Supreme Court verdict 2010HU2865.)

name: Specification of microstructure/properties for inorganic compounds
description: For inorganic compounds where name and formula are identical but microstructure (e.g., crystal form, unit surface area) differs, the subject matter cannot be specified by name/formula alone; specific property that helps expect the microstructure must be stated.
guidance: Even if microstructure is not technically explained, if a specific property is stated in the specification, reviewers must evaluate the actual compound from that property. To determine inventive step for a preparation of an inorganic compound with specific feature, review of the specific property shall be included in the claim regardless of whether the property is explicitly stated in the claim. Determine whether it is reasonable to expect that the compound with the stated specific property can be produced by adopting/combining the components at the level of technology.

name: Construction of product-by-use claims ('compound for ~')
description: A chemical compound claim limited by wording 'for ~' (e.g., 'Chemical compound Z for Y') is construed as merely indicating utility and is read as the chemical compound without the use limitation (e.g., 'Chemical compound Z').
guidance: When 'for~' only indicates utility, the limitation does not create a distinct product-by-use; claim construction treats it as the compound per se.

name: Novelty of use-limited chemical compound claims
description: If a chemical compound claimed with a use limitation is disclosed in the prior art (without the use limitation), the use-limited claim is deemed to lack novelty.
guidance: Example: 'Chemical compound Z for killing insects' is read as 'Chemical compound Z' and lacks novelty if 'Chemical compound Z' was already disclosed in prior art.

name: Inventive step for selection inventions (selection from a genus)
