description: A selection invention claiming specific species selected from a generic prior-art disclosure is only inventive if the selected species all have different (qualitatively or quantitatively) effects from the prior art.
guidance: If specific compounds are merely selected from a wide range without demonstration of favorable or unexpected effects, the selection lacks inventive step. Conversely, if the selected compounds have unexpected favorable properties not disclosed or expected from prior art, inventive step may be acknowledged.

name: Evidence standard for claimed enantiomer effects
description: Differences in some effects of an enantiomer versus a disclosed racemate are sufficient to support inventive step; discoverability by simple tests does not negate inventive step.
guidance: Even if it is well known that a specific enantiomer has better medicinal effect, it may still be non-obvious that the claimed enantiomer has the better effect if prior publications did not make that specific enantiomer's use clear. Provide comparative data/evidence where effect is in doubt.

name: Inventive step for catalysts with novel composition
description: If no catalyst is disclosed with the same or similar composition for the intended reaction, the claimed catalyst is deemed to have inventive step by comparing its effect with the case without catalyst.
guidance: Demonstrate catalytic effect relative to no catalyst to support inventive step when composition is novel for the reaction.

name: Alloy invention must specify alloying components and composition ranges
description: Because alloy properties vary with element composition, an alloy invention must limit alloying elements and the composition range of each element to specify claims; structure, property, or use may be claim elements.
guidance: If claims only recite elements without composition ranges, the claim may fail to particularly point out the invention. Examples and exceptions are discussed (see sections on special cases).

name: Description requirements for numerical composition limitations (grounds & embodiments)
description: When a numerical limitation to a composition range is stated in claims, the grounds and embodiment for that numerical limitation should be described in the specification, except where it is recognized the alloy can be specified and carried out easily.
guidance: Limits of maximum and minimum must be clear; ambiguous terms not allowed. Describe reasons for numerical limits, significant effect across the whole range, and concrete reasons for synergy between components. Failure to disclose may force trial-and-error reproduction and fail Article 42(3) requirements.

name: Embodiment representation requirement for alloy claims
description: An embodiment that has a composition range consistent with and included in the composition range recited in the claims satisfies the disclosure requirement; at least one such embodiment is required to represent the claimed invention.
guidance: If embodiments omit essential alloying elements or include elements not recited in claims (except inevitable impurities), they do not represent the claimed invention. Specific content of each alloying element should be specified in embodiments; simply stating ranges without specific content may be insufficient.

name: Specificity of claimed alloy effects
description: Effects of an alloy invention should be specifically stated, including unique effects intended to be accomplished; abstract or subjective expressions are insufficient.
guidance: Concrete statement of effects aids assessment of inventive step and sufficiency; vague claims about improved performance without quantified or otherwise concrete disclosure are inadequate.

name: Manufacturing method disclosure for alloy products
description: If the claimed invention is a product alloy, the manufacturing method (melting, casting, heating, machining, plating, etc.) should be stated in detail in the specification so a person skilled in the art can reproduce the alloy, unless it is possible to manufacture the alloy by a normal method (in which case simple statement may suffice).
guidance: Different manufacturing approaches (smelting/refining vs machining/finishing) can be distinct inventions; lack of method detail can render patent rights unenforceable.

name: Claim requirement — composition range limitation for alloy claims
description: Claims for alloys should specify composition ranges of each alloying element; reciting only alloying elements without ranges normally fails to particularly point out the invention, except in special cases (homogeneous solid solutions, amorphous alloys, commercial alloys with known composition, or alloys in industrial standards).
guidance: When issuing rejection for lack of particularity regarding composition range, the examiner should state reasonable grounds in detail after reviewing the whole specification. Examples of acceptable claim phrasing are provided.

name: Recitation of allowable impurity ranges in alloy claims/specification
description: Impurities should not be treated as elements of the alloy unless defined as impurities in the specification or known as impurities by common general knowledge; allowable ranges of impurities that significantly affect property or use should be specified (often upper limits like '0.3 wt% or less').
guidance: Although not necessary to limit every impurity, those that materially impact the alloy's properties should be clearly specified in the description and, where appropriate, in claims.

name: Method to determine identity when composition/structure overlap
description: When claimed and prior-art alloys have identical composition and structure, they are substantially identical even if perceived properties differ; overlapping composition ranges may be considered identical, though a selected composition can be patentable if it has critical meaning.
guidance: If composition and structure are identical, differences in perceived property or omitted use disclosures do not create novelty. Selection from a disclosed range may be patentable only where the selected sub-range has critical and demonstrable significance (e.g., unexpected technical effect). Case law examples illustrate these points.

name: Definition of 'consisting essentially of'
description: “The transitional phrase ‘consisting essentially of’ limits the scope of a claim to the specified materials or steps ‘and those that do not materially affect the basic and novel characteristic(s)’ of the claimed invention.” (MPEP 2111.03)
guidance: Use 'consisting essentially of' when you want a middle ground between fully open and fully closed claim scope. It permits additional elements only if they do not materially affect the invention's basic and novel characteristics. Example: “A cleaning composition consisting essentially of ingredients X, Y, and Z” allows minor additives that don’t significantly change cleaning properties but excludes major components that alter fundamental nature.

name: Comprising: open-ended transitional phrase
description: “Comprising” is open-ended and allows for additional, unrecited elements.
guidance: Use 'comprising' to keep claim scope broad and permit elements or steps beyond those recited. For claim construction and infringement analysis, it does not exclude other components. Note: For prior art searching, MPEP treats 'consisting essentially of' as equivalent to 'comprising' (see related rule).

name: Consisting of: closed transitional phrase
description: “Consisting of” is closed and excludes any element not specified in the claim.
guidance: Use 'consisting of' when you intend to limit the claim strictly to the recited elements or steps and to exclude any unrecited elements. Recommended wording from MPEP: 'Consisting of limits only recited elements.' Avoid 'consisting of' if you want to allow incidental or non-material additives.

name: Specification must define basic and novel characteristics
description: The specification should define the basic and novel characteristics of the invention (MPEP 2111.03).
guidance: To make 'consisting essentially of' meaningful, identify and describe in the specification which characteristics are basic and novel so that determinations about material effect can be made. Failure to do so can create ambiguity in claim scope.

name: Method claim steps must not materially affect novel characteristics
description: MPEP 2111.03 indicates that method claim steps must not materially affect the basic and novel characteristics when 'consisting essentially of' is used for steps or materials.
guidance: When drafting method claims using 'consisting essentially of' (or interpreting them), evaluate whether additional steps would materially alter the invention's novel characteristics; if so, those steps are excluded. Drafting should make clear which characteristics are protected from material alteration.

name: Scope of claim is defined by choice of transitional phrase
description: Transitional phrases (e.g., comprising, consisting essentially of, consisting of) define the scope of a claim (MPEP 2111.03).
guidance: Select the transitional phrase deliberately to achieve the intended breadth or narrowness of the claim. Be aware that each phrase carries different presumptive effects on inclusion/exclusion of unrecited elements and can affect infringement, validity, and prior art considerations.

name: Use 'consisting essentially of' for 'middle ground' composition claim format
description: MPEP guidance: 'Consisting essentially of' is the transitional phrase for a middle ground composition claim format.
guidance: Employ this phrase when you want to allow minor/non-material additives in a composition claim while excluding changes that would alter fundamental properties. Ensure specification support for what is non-material versus material to the invention's basic and novel characteristics.

name: Prior patent (pre-AIA §102(a),(b))
description: [The Defendant] contends that claim ___ is invalid because the invention was patented by [third party] before the Cutoff Date.
guidance: A patent claim is invalid if the invention was patented in the U.S. or a foreign country by another person before it was invented by the patentee or more than one year before the patentee filed the U.S. patent application (pre-AIA timing rules). If date of invention or priority is in dispute, the jury should be instructed on how to determine date of invention; otherwise instruct on the statutory Cutoff Date.

name: Prior patent (AIA §102)
description: [The Defendant] contends that the claimed invention was patented in the United States or a foreign country before the effective filing date (AIA Cutoff Date).
guidance: Under the AIA, a claim is invalid if the invention was patented abroad or in the U.S. before the effective filing date of the claimed invention. If there is factual dispute whether a patent disclosure originated from the inventor or from another who derived it from the inventor, instruct jury on §102(b)(1) exceptions and related doctrines (derivation, prior public disclosure by inventor, etc.).

name: Prior U.S. application / published patent document (pre-AIA §102(e)/(pre-AIA) and AIA §102(a)(2))
description: [The Defendant] contends that the claim is invalid because the invention was described in a published U.S. patent application or patent filed by another person before the invention was made by the patentee or before the effective filing date.
guidance: Pre-AIA: invalid if described in a published U.S. patent application or U.S. patent filed by another before the patentee's invention. AIA: invalid if described in a published U.S. patent application (or published PCT designating U.S.) that was effectively filed before the effective filing date. If disputes exist about derivation, ownership, or exceptions under §§102(b)(2) and (c), instruct the jury accordingly. Determine effective filing dates per statute (see §102(d)).

name: Obviousness—general (Graham/KSR framework)
description: [The Defendant] contends that claim(s) are invalid because the claimed invention(s) are 'obvious.' A claimed invention is invalid as obvious if it would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art as of the Cutoff Date.
guidance: Obviousness is a mixed question of law and fact; beware of hindsight and do not use the patent as a road map for combining prior art. The challenger must prove obviousness by clear and convincing evidence. Consider the Graham factors: (1) scope and content of prior art; (2) differences between the claimed invention and prior art; (3) level of ordinary skill; (4) secondary considerations. Perform separate analyses for each asserted claim.

name: Second Graham factor: differences between the claimed invention and the prior art
description: Analyze relevant differences between the prior art and the claimed invention from the view of a person of ordinary skill in the art as of the Cutoff Date.
guidance: Determine the impact of differences on obviousness of the invention as a whole (not merely a portion). May consider inferences and creative steps a POSITA would have employed. Combination of known elements that yields predictable results supports obviousness; unexpected/unpredictable results or references that teach away support nonobviousness. A claim is not proven obvious merely by showing each element was independently known; must consider whether there was a reason at the time to combine teachings and whether there was a reasonable expectation of success. If alleging inherency, instruct carefully: inherency may supply an element only if it is the natural result of explicit prior art disclosure and cannot be established by mere probabilities or possibilities.

name: Inherency in obviousness analyses
description: Inherency may supply a claim element missing from the explicit disclosure of a prior art reference only if that element is present in, or the natural result of, the combination of explicitly disclosed elements.
guidance: Do not find inherency based on probabilities or possibilities. The inherent element must be the natural result of the prior art disclosure; unexpected inherent properties are relevant. Tailor any inherency instruction to the evidence admitted; give only if properly raised and supported.

name: Fourth Graham factor / Secondary considerations (objective indicia)
description: Other considerations that may help determine obviousness include commercial success, long-felt need, failed attempts by others, copying, unexpected results, praise or surprise by others, and licensing for the invention.
guidance: No single factor is dispositive; must consider the invention as a whole. Secondary considerations are relevant only if there is a nexus between the consideration and the claimed invention. The court should carefully assess admissibility and materiality of such evidence and instruct the jury only when supported by evidence and a sufficient nexus exists.

name: Written-description requirement (35 U.S.C. §112)
description: [The Defendant] contends that the claim(s) lack adequate written description. A patent must contain a written description of the product or method claimed to ensure the applicant actually invented the claimed subject matter.
guidance: Defendant bears the burden by clear and convincing evidence. The specification must describe each and every limitation of a patent claim in sufficient detail (exact words not required). The specification must show POSITAs would recognize that the inventor possessed the subject matter claimed as of the effective filing date. Written-description is fact-based and considered claim-by-claim. Factors to consider: nature and scope of the patent claims; complexity, predictability, and maturity of the technology; existing knowledge in the field; and scope and content of the prior art. If inadequate, the claim is invalid.

name: Damages—general standard
description: If you find infringement and the asserted claims are not invalid, determine amount of damages to compensate the Plaintiff; Plaintiff must prove each element of damages by a preponderance of the evidence.
guidance: Damages must be adequate to compensate the Plaintiff for the infringement but cannot be punitive or include added interest sums. The damages award cannot be less than a reasonable royalty. Only consider damages if you find one or more asserted claims both not invalid and infringed. The instructions on damages do not indicate any view on the merits.

name: Date damages begin (notice and marking rules; §287(a))
description: The start date for damages depends on whether the parties agreed on a start date, or whether Plaintiff provided effective notice (marking or direct notice).
guidance: If stipulated, use the agreed date. If disputed, damages start on the date Plaintiff first notified Defendant of its claim. Notice can be (1) public marking (mark substantially all products with patent number or provide marking via labels or a website) — begins when marking began; or (2) direct specific notice to the Defendant — begins when Defendant received notice. If Plaintiff neither properly marked products nor provided direct notice before suit, Plaintiff can recover damages only after filing date of the lawsuit. See §287(a) and related case law for nuances (licensee marking rules, internet marking, etc.).

name: Statutory classes of patentable subject-matter
description: The statute enumerates classes of subjects held to be patentable: machinery (machines), manufactures (fabrics or substances made by the art or industry of man, not being machinery), compositions of matter, and arts (processes). The subject-matter of a patent should be one invention or discovery.
guidance: Treat a claimed invention as falling within one of these classes; the statutory language and the singular phrasing ('invention or discovery' not 'inventions or discoveries') indicate a patent should have a single subject-matter. Where classification is unclear, determine if the thing is a machine, a vendible manufacture, a composition, or an art (process of making).

name: Definition of 'manufacture'
description: A 'manufacture' has been defined as 'something made by the hands of man' and more generally as 'any new combination of old materials, constituting a new result or production, in the form of a vendible article, not being machinery.'
guidance: Focus on whether the claimed thing is a vendible article produced by combining materials into a new result; vendibility (marketable commodity) and the new result are key. Examples include medicines, stoves, telescopes; avoid classifying tools/parts used primarily as elements of machinery as 'manufactures' unless sold and used separately as merchantable commodities.

name: Unity test: the inventor's objective (common purpose)
description: The object which the inventor proposes to accomplish is the main guide to determine whether his subject-matter is a unit. If several distinct inventions are brought together for a purpose which can only be effected by their union, that indicates unity. If the patent claims both the combination and the distinct purposes each invention can perform separately, multiple subject-matters are embraced.
guidance: Analyze the specification/claims to see whether the inventor treats the items as modes for achieving one object (supporting unity) or as separate inventions each serving independent purposes (pointing to multiplicity).

name: Coverage of parts vs coverage of combination
description: If the patentee describes several distinct and independent parts intended to be used in combination and is the first inventor of each, the patent covers the parts as well as the combination and the use of any one part by another is infringement. But if the patentee is not the inventor of the several things used in the combination and the combination itself is the true subject-matter, use of some of those things not amounting to the same combination is no infringement.
guidance: Determine whether the patentee claims and invented each constituent part; where only the combination is his invention, infringement requires substantially the same combination. This affects claim drafting and enforcement strategy.

name: Specification accuracy and limitation to stated invention
description: When a patentee in his specification states and sums up the particulars of his invention, and his patent covers them, he is confined to such summary; courts cannot reject the claim, and if anything included in that summary is not new the patent is void (even if that part is slight or unimportant).
guidance: Draft the specification and claims with precision and distinctness. Overbroad or imprecise summaries that claim non-novel matter can vitiate the entire patent. The specification should 'fully explain the principle and the several modes' of application.

name: Requirement to disclose the principle and several modes
description: A clause in the Patent Acts requires that the inventor in his specification 'fully explain the principle and the several modes, in which he has contemplated the application of that principle or character, by which it may be distinguished from other inventions.'
guidance: Include full explanation of the inventive principle and the different modes of applying it; this both enables unity claims for multiple modes and supports enforceability. Use the specification to show alternatives and modes that the inventor contemplates as part of the single invention.

name: Voidness risk when patent includes non-original claimed matter
description: If a patent covers particulars claimed as the inventor's and any such claimed part is found not to be his invention (i.e., not new), the patent is void; the inclusion of non-original matter in the patent can render it invalid in its entirety unless statute remedies apply for inadvertent mistakes.
guidance: Claims must avoid including matters not original to the patentee. The Act of 1837 provides limited relief where, by mistake or inadvertence, a patentee claims material not his own, allowing validity for so much as is truly his only if it is material and definitely distinguishable. Nevertheless, careful claim drafting and prior-art searches are crucial.

name: Clarity of the Record Pilot — record clarity criteria
description: Pilot goal: identify and refine best practices for enhancing the clarity of the prosecution record with respect to claim interpretation, reasons for allowance, and interview summaries; encourages examiners to initiate pre-search interviews as needed.
guidance: Clarity of prosecution documents (claim interpretation language, clear reasons for allowance/rejection, interview summaries) is a quality objective. Best practices identified by the pilot inform examiner training and are intended to improve the persuasiveness and durability of office actions.

name: Abstract idea identification and grouping guidance
description: When the examiner determines the claim recites an abstract idea, the rejection should identify the abstract idea as it is recited in the claim and explain why it falls within one of the groupings of abstract ideas (mathematical concepts, mental processes, or certain methods of organizing human activity) enumerated in MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2).
guidance: Alternatively, provide justification under the 'tentative abstract idea' procedure if the limitation does not fall within enumerated groupings. The explanation may cite appropriate court decisions that support the identification but examiners should be familiar with cited decisions, avoid going beyond enumerated concepts, and avoid relying on non-precedential decisions unless facts uniquely match. Sample: 'The claim recites the step of comparing collected information to a predefined threshold, which is an act of evaluating information that can be practically performed in the human mind. Thus, this step is an abstract idea in the "mental process" grouping.'

name: Laws of nature and natural phenomena identification
description: When the examiner determines the claim recites a law of nature or a natural phenomenon, the rejection should identify the law of nature or natural phenomenon as it is recited in the claim and explain using a reasoned rationale why it is considered a law of nature or natural phenomenon.
guidance: See MPEP § 2106.04(b) for more information. Sample: 'The claim recites the correlation of X, and X is a law of nature because it describes a consequence of natural processes in the human body, e.g., the naturally-occurring relationship between the presence of Y and the manifestation of Z.'

name: Product of nature identification and markedly different characteristics analysis
description: When the examiner determines the claim recites a product of nature, the rejection should identify the exception as it is recited in the claim and explain using a reasoned rationale why the product does not have markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state.
guidance: See MPEP § 2106.04(b) and § 2106.04(c) for the markedly different characteristics analysis. Sample: 'The claim recites X, which as explained in the specification was isolated from naturally occurring Y. X is a nature-based product... Because there is no indication... that isolation of X has resulted in a marked difference... X is a product of nature exception.'

name: Explain why additional elements do not add 'significantly more' (Step 2B)
description: For Step 2B, the rejection should explain why the additional elements, taken individually and in combination, do not result in the claim amounting to significantly more than the identified judicial exception.
guidance: When particular claim limitations are concluded to be well-understood, routine, conventional activities, the examiner must expressly support that conclusion in writing with one of the evidentiary options (A)-(D). Address additional elements both individually and in combination; a new combination of known steps may be eligible, so the examiner must consider combinations (Diamond v. Diehr). See MPEP § 2106.05 for more detail.

name: Generic computer functions and computer-implemented claims
description: For claim limitations that recite a generic computer component performing generic computer functions at a high level of generality, examiners can explain why these generic computing functions do not meaningfully limit the claim.
guidance: Keep in mind courts have found computer-implemented processes to be significantly more than an abstract idea where generic computer components are able in combination to perform functions that are not merely generic (e.g., DDR Holdings). See MPEP § 2106.05(f) for information about generic computing functions the courts have found to be mere instructions to implement an exception on a computer, and § 2106.05(d) for well-understood, routine, conventional activities.

name: Insignificant extra-solution activity and general linking to a technological environment
description: For claim limitations that add insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., mere data gathering) or that generally link the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use, explain why they do not meaningfully limit the claim.
guidance: Examples: adding storing data to a mathematical computation does not add a meaningful limitation; placing a naturally occurring product into a generic container (test tube) is merely a nominal extra-solution component. Limiting an abstract idea to a particular industry may be insufficient (Parker v. Flook). See MPEP §§ 2106.05(g) and 2106.05(h).

name: Best practice: consult and cite the specification to suggest claim amendments
description: In the event a rejection is made, it is a best practice for the examiner to consult the specification to determine if there are elements that could be added to the claim to make it eligible and, if so, identify those elements in the Office action and suggest them as a way to overcome the rejection.
guidance: This practice assists compact prosecution and gives applicants clear directions for overcoming eligibility rejections.

name: Evidentiary requirements — no evidence needed for Step 2A Prong One
description: When performing the analysis at Step 2A Prong One, it is sufficient for the examiner to provide a reasoned rationale identifying the judicial exception recited in the claim and explaining why it is considered a judicial exception; there is no requirement to rely on external evidence such as publications or affidavits to find that a claim recites a judicial exception.
guidance: Cited cases show courts have identified abstract ideas without relying on evidence. Cf. Affinity Labs v. Amazon, OIP Techs. v. Amazon, Content Extraction & Transmission v. Wells Fargo.

name: Evidentiary support option (B): court decisions
description: Support may be a citation to one or more court decisions discussed in MPEP § 2106.05(d) that note the well-understood, routine, conventional nature of the additional element(s).
guidance: Ensure the claim limitations before the examiner are the same as those found to be well-understood, routine, conventional by the courts and recited at the same high level of generality. It is not enough that the elements are merely similar. Court decisions cited do not imply all computer functions are conventional; examiners must be careful in comparisons.

name: Form paragraphs and required wording for §101 rejections
description: Use specified form paragraphs for §101 rejections: form paragraphs 7.04.01, 7.05, 7.05.01, and 7.05.016 (and 7.05.017 when a tentative abstract idea is involved).
guidance: ¶7.04.01 (Statement of Statutory Basis, 35 U.S.C. 101) must precede the first use of 35 U.S.C. 101 in all first actions and final rejections. ¶7.05 is a heading and must be preceded by 7.04.01 and followed by detailed explanation using appropriate paragraphs (e.g., 7.05.01, 7.05.016). ¶7.05.016 is for claims directed to a judicial exception without significantly more and applies to product and process claims; it requires filling brackets: [1] identify law of nature/natural phenomenon/abstract idea; [2] identify the exception as recited in the claim and why considered an exception (identify grouping for abstract ideas); [3] explain why combination of additional elements fails to integrate the exception into practical application; [4] explain why additional elements are insufficient to amount to significantly more. For tentative abstract ideas, include 7.05.017 and obtain the TC Director's signature.

name: Williamson standard — words understood as name for structure
description: "The standard is whether the words of the claim are understood by persons of ordinary skill in the art to have a sufficiently definite meaning as the name for structure."
guidance: Presumption that lack of the word "means" avoids §112(f) was weakened by Williamson; a claim term that does not use the word "means" can still invoke §112(f) if it fails to recite sufficiently definite structure. Evaluate whether POSITA would view the claim term as a structural name; if not, §112(f) may apply.

name: Functional language as candidates for §112(f)
description: Terms that precede "configured to," "adapted to," or present participles ("-ing" words) may be candidates for functional interpretation.
guidance: When drafting, stop to identify terms that may be considered functional. Such wording increases the risk the claim term will be treated as function-only and thus subject to §112(f). Consider recasting into structural language where possible.

name: Claim-level features must themselves connote structure
description: If a term does not itself connote structure, determine whether the claim itself provides sufficient features to connote structure.
guidance: Adding structural detail into the claim (e.g., interactions between components, elements like "processor" + "memory" + modules) can in some cases avoid §112(f). Care: adding features can narrow claim scope and enable design-arounds; balance breadth vs structural detail.

name: Specification and figures must provide structural detail
description: If the claim and claim terms do not connote structure, determine whether the specification and figures provide a detailed definition and description such that POSITA concludes the term connotes structure.
guidance: Describe how components are connected, what data is passed, and what operations each component performs. Showing how components operate together (not merely listing functions) helps impart structural character to functional terms.

name: If no structure identified, claim invokes §112(f) and must map to corresponding structure
description: "If we are unable to identify any corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification, the claim term is indefinite."
guidance: Once a term is treated as means-plus-function under §112(f), claim construction requires identification of the corresponding structure, material, or acts disclosed in the specification; failure to do so leads to indefiniteness under §112(b).

name: For computer-implemented functions, disclose more than a general-purpose computer
description: "Because these functions are computer-implemented functions, moreover, the structure disclosed in the specification must be more than a general purpose computer or microprocessor."
guidance: To be definite, the specification must disclose an algorithm for performing the claimed computer-implemented function. Algorithms can be expressed as mathematical formulae, prose, flow charts, or other sufficiently specific forms. Mere statement that a general-purpose processor performs the function is insufficient.

name: Algorithm disclosure requirement
description: The specification must disclose an algorithm for the claimed function; the algorithm may be expressed as mathematical formula, prose, flow chart, or any manner providing sufficient structure.
guidance: When claiming functions performed by software or hardware, include concrete algorithms, flowcharts, pseudocode, or detailed procedural descriptions in the specification to identify corresponding structure and avoid indefiniteness.

name: Caution with 'processor'—may invoke §112(f) in some contexts
description: Many practitioners consider "processor" to connote structure, but the PTAB and courts have found instances where "processor" was interpreted to invoke §112(f), particularly if the claimed features cannot be performed by a general purpose processor.
guidance: If features cannot be performed by a general‑purpose processor, invoking "processor" risks §112(f). PTAB cases (Ex Parte Lakkala, Ex Parte Erol, Ex Parte Smith, Ex Parte Cadarso) show the Office may raise new grounds of rejection based on §112(f) for claims using "processor." Consider reciting processor+memory+modules and describing modules in the spec (e.g., modules stored on memory and executable by processors) to reduce risk.

name: Drafting trade-offs: add structural interaction vs claim scope
description: One way to save a claim from §112(f) interpretation may be to add more structure directly into the claim, where possible; but including superfluous features can adversely impact claim scope and invite design-arounds.
guidance: Weigh the benefit of adding structure against narrowing claim scope. Where possible, add interaction details that impart structure without unnecessarily limiting inventive scope (e.g., reciting relationships between processor and memory, or modules stored in memory and executable by processors).

name: Five-step Federal Circuit analysis for functional claim language
description: Court-provided steps: (1) identify term being claimed functionally, (2) determine whether the term is understood by one of ordinary skill in the art to connote structure, (3) if no, determine whether the claim itself provides sufficient features to connote structure, (4) if no, determine whether specification and figures provide detailed definition and description that POSITA concludes connotes structure, (5) if no, conclude that the claim invokes §112(f) and determine if the claim is definite under §112(b).
guidance: Use this analysis as a checklist when evaluating claim language during drafting or prosecution to decide whether the term will be treated as means-plus-function and whether the specification supports corresponding structure to avoid indefiniteness.

name: If a term is treated as means-plus-function, identify corresponding structure/material/acts in the spec
description: When a term is determined to be a means-plus-function element, attempt to construe the disputed claim term by identifying the corresponding material, acts, or structure described in the specification to which the claim term will be limited.
guidance: Map each claimed function to specific passages, figures, algorithms, modules, or structural components in the spec. Absent such mapping, claims will be indefinite under §112(b).

name: Scope and statutory basis of Priority Mail Express filing date benefits
description: The statutory authority for granting a filing date based on date of deposit for Priority Mail Express® correspondence is 35 U.S.C. 21(a); the specific rule is 37 CFR 1.10. 35 U.S.C. 21(a) is limited to correspondence deposited with USPS; 37 CFR 1.10 is limited to Priority Mail Express® Post Office to Addressee service.
guidance: There is no similar provision or benefit for correspondence deposited in International Express Mail. Use 35 U.S.C. 21(a) and 37 CFR 1.10 when evaluating petitions and filing date claims.

name: Petition to accept unintentionally delayed foreign priority claim (37 CFR 1.55(e))
description: To correct an unintentionally delayed foreign priority claim, file a grantable petition under 37 CFR 1.55(e) in the file of the application which matured into the patent to be reexamined.
guidance: Required items include: (a) an application data sheet, oath, or declaration (unless previously submitted or exception in 37 CFR 1.55(h) applies); (b) the petition fee per 37 CFR 1.17(m); and (c) a statement that the entire delay was unintentional. The Director may require additional information if the unintentionality is in question; petitions filed more than two years after the due date require additional explanation of the circumstances. In the reexamination proceeding, file a separate letter notifying the Office that the petition and attachments are being concurrently filed in the application file. When a decision is rendered in the application file, a copy of the decision and, if granted, the application data sheet (as determined to meet 1.55(e)) will be placed in the reexamination file. See MPEP §214.02.

name: Claiming domestic benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 (applications filed on/after Sept 16, 2012)
description: For a patent to be reexamined that matured from an application filed on/after Sept 16, 2012, the patent owner must file in the file of the application which matured into the patent: a grantable petition under 37 CFR 1.78(e), required application data, fee, and statement of unintentional delay.
guidance: Required items: (a) grantable petition for an unintentionally delayed benefit claim (37 CFR 1.78(e)); (b) an application data sheet including the reference required by 35 U.S.C. 120 and 37 CFR 1.78(d)(2) (37 CFR 1.76(b)(5)), unless previously submitted; (c) petition fee per 37 CFR 1.17(m); (d) a statement that the entire delay between the due date and filing was unintentional (with additional explanation required if >2 years after due date). In the reexamination proceeding, file a separate letter notifying the Office that items (a)-(d) are being concurrently filed in the application file. When a decision under 37 CFR 1.78(e) is rendered in the application file, a copy of the decision and, if granted, the application data sheet determined to meet 1.78(e) will be placed in the reexamination file. See MPEP §211.04.

name: Claiming domestic benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 (applications filed before Sept 16, 2012)
description: For patents that matured from applications filed before Sept 16, 2012, similar petition and filing requirements apply, but the patent owner may either file an application data sheet in the application file or file an amendment in the reexamination inserting the required reference in the first sentence(s) of the specification following the title (per 37 CFR 1.78(h)).
guidance: Required: (a) grantable petition under 37 CFR 1.78(e); (b) unless the patent owner files the amendment in the reexamination, file an application data sheet including the reference required by 35 U.S.C. 120 and 37 CFR 1.78(d)(2); (c) petition fee 1.17(m); (d) statement that entire delay was unintentional (with extra explanation if >2 years). If the patent owner chooses to file the amendment in the reexamination, the amendment must insert the required reference in the first sentence(s) of the specification per 1.78(h). In the reexamination, file a letter notifying concurrent filing. When decision is rendered, copies of decision and any application data sheet determined to meet requirements will be placed in the reexamination file. See MPEP §211.04.

name: Claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) (provisional) for applications filed on/after Sept 16, 2012
description: To correct failure to claim benefit under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) for a patent matured from a utility or plant application filed on/after Sept 16, 2012, file a grantable petition under 37 CFR 1.78(c) in the file of the application which matured into the patent.
guidance: Required: (a) grantable petition under 37 CFR 1.78(c); (b) an application data sheet including the reference required by 35 U.S.C. 119(e) and 37 CFR 1.78(a)(3) to the prior provisional application (unless previously submitted); (c) petition fee per 37 CFR 1.17(m); (d) a statement that the entire delay between the due date and filing was unintentional (extra explanation required if >2 years). File a separate letter in the reexamination proceeding notifying that these items are being concurrently filed. When decision is rendered in the application file, a copy of the decision and, if granted, the application data sheet determined to meet requirements will be placed in the reexamination file. See MPEP §211.02 and §211.04.

name: Claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) (provisional) for applications filed before Sept 16, 2012
description: For patents matured from utility or plant applications filed before Sept 16, 2012, the patent owner must either file the application data sheet in the application file or file an amendment in the reexamination inserting the required provisional reference in the first sentence(s) of the specification per 37 CFR 1.78(h).
guidance: Required: (a) grantable petition under 37 CFR 1.78(c); (b) unless filing the amendment in the reexamination, an application data sheet including the reference required by 35 U.S.C. 119(e) and 37 CFR 1.78(a)(3); (c) petition fee 1.17(m); (d) statement that the delay was unintentional (additional explanation if >2 years). If the patent owner does not choose to file the application data sheet in the application file, an amendment inserting the reference in the first sentence(s) of the specification in the reexamination is acceptable. In the reexamination, file a letter notifying concurrent filing; when decision rendered, copies placed in reexamination file. See MPEP §211.04.

name: Restoring benefit of a provisional application where subsequent filing was delayed (37 CFR 1.78(b))
description: To restore the benefit of a provisional application when filing of the subsequent nonprovisional application was unintentionally delayed, file a grantable petition under 37 CFR 1.78(b) in the file of the subsequent application which matured into the patent to be reexamined.
guidance: Required: grantable petition and any required attachments including an application data sheet meeting 1.78(b) requirements, filed in the subsequent application file. File a separate letter in the reexamination proceeding notifying the Office that the petition and attachments are concurrently filed in the application (identify application number). Design applications cannot claim the benefit of provisional applications. When a decision is rendered in the application file, a copy of the decision and, if granted, the application data sheet determined to meet 1.78(b) will be placed in the reexamination file. See MPEP §211.01(a), subsection II.

name: First Office action completeness and content requirements
description: The examiner’s first Office action in reexamination must be a complete statement of the examiner's position and sufficiently detailed so the second action can properly be made final.
guidance: The action must clearly set forth the pertinency and manner of applying the cited prior art to each rejected claim. If the request included material such as claim charts, the examiner may incorporate them but must carefully review them to ensure they clearly and completely address patentability. The first action should respond to the substance of each argument raised by the patent owner and requester (37 CFR 1.510, 1.530, 1.535) and treat inappropriate arguments per 37 CFR 1.552(c). If the examiner relies on a patent owner statement (37 CFR 1.501(a)(2)) to interpret claim meaning, the requester must explain how that statement is used. The first action should caution the patent owner that a complete response is necessary because the next action is expected to be final, and that 37 CFR 1.116(b) will be strictly enforced after final action; form paragraph 22.04 is appropriate.

name: Priority document and translation obligations
description: If the IPEA needs a copy of the earlier application whose priority is claimed, the IB shall furnish such copy on request. If the copy is not furnished because applicant failed to comply with Rule 17.1, or the priority document is not available, the international preliminary examination report may be established as if the priority had not been claimed (PCT Rule 66.7(a)).
guidance: If the earlier application is in a language other than a language of the IPEA and the validity of the priority claim is relevant, the IPEA may invite the applicant to furnish a translation within two months; failure allows establishment of the report as if priority not claimed. The IB may translate the priority document into English.

name: Procedural model: oppositional model (burden on petitioner)
description: Use an oppositional model: burden on the petitioner to show a claim is not patentable, rather than requiring PTO to meet a burden each time new information is presented.
guidance: This model is favored by PTO as allowing speedier adjudication and avoiding the interminable delays seen in inter partes reexam where PTO must reassess repeatedly.

name: Estoppel from PGR proceedings
description: A party that brought a post grant review proceeding is estopped from raising in any subsequent PTO or ITC proceeding or civil action any claim against that patent that it did raise in the post grant proceeding or that it could have raised in a second-window proceeding.
guidance: Applies could-have-raised estoppel to prevent relitigation of issues; raises policy questions when second-window scope is narrow.

name: Definition and requirements of 'properly filed'
description: A petition is 'properly filed' when delivered and accepted in compliance with applicable filing rules; time deadlines for filing must be complied with.
guidance: This term of art is informed by Artuz v. Bennett, Pace v. DiGuglielmo, and Allen v. Siebert: delivery/acceptance and rule compliance are required even if particular claims may be procedurally barred.

name: File-wrapper immunity for program participants
description: Prosecution records generated under the PTO search-and-patentability program are inadmissible to construe patent claims in later proceedings (file-wrapper immunity).
guidance: Immunity is essential to make the voluntary program attractive and to permit candid communication between applicants and examiners without fear that prosecution statements will later narrow claim construction. PTO may issue regulations identifying material eligible for immunity, including materials from failed attempts, to prevent deterrence of participation.

name: Technology-area classification procedure
description: Assign each patent a single primary technology area (mechanical, electronics, chemistry, biotechnology, software, optics) focusing primarily on claim language, aided by written description and drawings; identify secondary technology areas when another technology forms an additional integral part of the claims.
guidance: Roughly one-third of patents had a secondary technology; primary areas are mutually exclusive; when necessary consult technical dictionaries/encyclopedias/Internet but only rarely.

name: Software business-method subset definition
description: Define 'software business methods' as a narrow subset of software patents whose claims obviously cover automated generation of customer proposals, advertising, financial techniques, use of online catalogs, and similar business-transaction techniques.
guidance: Do not include computer-controlled manufacturing methods in the business-method category; because business-method is a subset of software, treat it appropriately in regressions (cannot co-include with broader software unless substituting categories).

name: Industry classification procedure
description: Assign patents to industry categories that focus on the business use of the patent and the industry of the patent owner; use claim language, written description, and extrinsic evidence (especially the Internet) to determine the industry category.
guidance: Technology and industry classifications differ: technology refers to nature of invention while industry refers to owner/use; in some cases (e.g., biotechnology) the same term may be used for both, but they are not identical.

name: Statutory standard under 35 U.S.C. 251
description: The error upon which reissue is based must be one which causes the patent to be 'deemed wholly or partly inoperative or invalid, by reason of a defective specification or drawing, or by reason of the patentee claiming more or less than he had a right to claim in the patent.'
guidance: Non-substantive corrections — spelling, grammar, typographical, editorial or clerical errors — that do not cause the patent to be deemed wholly or partly inoperative or invalid under 35 U.S.C. 251 do not provide a basis for reissue; such corrections may be made via a certificate of correction (see MPEP §1481). Non-substantive corrections may be included in a reissue only where a qualifying 35 U.S.C. 251 error is already present.

name: Common bases for filing a reissue application
description: The most common bases for filing a reissue application are: (A) the claims are too narrow or too broad; (B) the disclosure contains inaccuracies; (C) applicant failed to or incorrectly claimed foreign priority; and (D) applicant failed to make reference to or incorrectly made reference to prior copending applications.
guidance: These four categories summarize frequent factual/legal errors giving rise to reissue. Each has its own sub-rules and potential alternatives (e.g., certificates of correction or petitions) discussed elsewhere in the section.

name: Error based on scope of claims (adding narrower claims / claiming less or more than entitled)
description: A reissue error may be directed solely to the failure to previously present narrower claims, which are being added by reissue. The omission of a narrower claim from a patent can render a patent partly inoperative by failing to protect the disclosed invention to the full extent allowed by law. This permits submission of additional claims that are narrower in scope than the preexisting patent claims, without any narrowing of the preexisting patent claims.
guidance: Examples and limits: a reissue applicant can retain broad independent claims while adding new dependent (narrower) claims. However, an applicant's failure to timely file a divisional application covering non-elected inventions following a restriction requirement is NOT considered an error correctable by reissue (see MPEP §1412.01). Case law: In re Tanaka (omission of narrower claim), In re Wilder (attorney's failure to appreciate scope can be correctable), and Medrad (error may be 'any error that causes a patentee to claim more or less than he had a right to claim').

name: Evidence from foreign/prosecuting offices for Priority Right applications
description: In the event that the substantive examination is conducted to an Application with a Priority Right, the Minister may request required documents ... such as certified copies of letters relevant to results of substantive examination in other countries; certified copies of Patent documents granted abroad; certified copies of decisions for refusal or invalidation; and other prescribed documents.
guidance: Applicants with priority claims should be prepared to produce certified foreign prosecution/examination documents; these may influence grant or refusal.

name: Patent certificate as proof of right and scope defined by claims
description: A Patent Certificate is a proof of right on Patent. The right of Patent ... is determined its scope of protection based on Invention described in claims.
guidance: Certificate proves the patent right; claims define the scope of protection.

name: Grounds for refusal of divisional applications
description: The Minister refuses: (a) a divisional Application that is filed elapsing the duration as referred to in Article 38 section (2); (b) a claim or claims expanding the scope of protection in a divisional Application ...; and/or (c) an invention which is not a unity of the original Application.
guidance: Divisionals filed late, with expanded scope, or lacking unity with the original application are subject to refusal.

name: Appeal on correction after grant: deadlines and permissible corrections
description: Appeal petition ... is filed within 3 (three) months ... The correction ... must be limited to: limitation on the scope of claim(s); correction for mistranslation of the description; and/or clarification on the unclear and ambiguous content of the description. Correction ... is not beyond the scope of Invention as filed.
guidance: Post-grant correction appeals must be filed within 3 months and are limited to narrowing claims, mistranslation fixes, or clarifications that do not extend the original scope.

name: Inventive step (Article 56 EPC)
description: An invention shall be considered as involving an inventive step if, having regard to the state of the art, it is not obvious to a person skilled in the art.
guidance: This is the statutory non-obviousness test under Art.56 EPC; assessment requires identification of the state of the art and the skilled person and a determination whether the claimed solution would have been obvious.

name: Problem and solution approach (CLR I D 2)
description: Case-law topic: the problem-and-solution approach for assessing inventive step.
guidance: EPO case law standard methodology for inventive-step assessment: (i) determine closest prior art, (ii) establish objective technical problem, (iii) consider whether the claimed solution is obvious in view of the prior art.

name: Determination of the technical problem (CLR I D 4.1)
description: Case-law topic: how the technical problem is determined in inventive-step proceedings.
guidance: Addresses identification of the technical effect and derivation of the objective technical problem from the closest prior art and the claimed effect.

name: Alleged effect not a feature of the claims (CLR II C 3.2)
description: Case-law topic: consequences when a claimed technical effect is not actually a feature of the claims.
guidance: If the alleged effect relied upon for inventive step is not derivable from the claim features, it cannot generally be used to support inventive step.

name: Article 83 EPC and clarity of claims (CLR II C 8.2)
description: Case-law topic: sufficiency of disclosure (Art.83 EPC) and clarity issues that may affect assessment.
guidance: While primarily about sufficiency/clarity, these aspects can bear on inventive-step assessment if the invention is not clearly or sufficiently disclosed.

name: Broad claims (GL F IV 4.22)
description: Guidance topic: examination of unusually broad claim scope.
guidance: Guidance on when broad claim language may be objectionable or how breadth interacts with novelty/ inventive-step assessment.

name: Content of the description (R.42 EPC)
description: Rule: requirements for the description part of a European patent application.
guidance: Proper disclosure in the description is necessary to support claims and can affect how technical features are understood in inventive-step analysis.

name: Contribution to a single claim suffices for joint inventorship
description: A joint inventor or coinventor need not make a contribution to every claim of a patent; a contribution to one claim is enough.
guidance: The contributor of any disclosed means of a means-plus-function claim element is a joint inventor as to that claim unless the contribution was only a reduction to practice of the sole inventor’s broader concept. There is no requirement that all inventors be joint inventors of the subject matter of any one claim. (Ethicon Inc. v. United States Surgical Corp.) See MPEP § 602.09 and § 602.01(c) et seq. for correction of inventorship.

name: Claims must be given their broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) in light of the specification
description: During patent examination, the pending claims must be 'given their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.'
guidance: The PTO determines claim scope not solely on claim language but by giving claims their broadest reasonable construction as would be interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art, taking into account the specification. BRI is applied during prosecution (not in court) because applicants can amend claims; BRI reduces the possibility claims later issue with wider-than-justified scope. BRI is not the broadest possible interpretation — it must be consistent with ordinary/customary meaning and the specification. (Phillips; In re Am. Acad. of Sci. Tech. Ctr.; In re Yamamoto; In re Zletz, et al.)

name: Words of a claim must be given their plain meaning unless inconsistent with the specification
description: Under BRI, words of the claim must be given their plain meaning, unless such meaning is inconsistent with the specification.
guidance: Plain meaning = ordinary and customary meaning given by those of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention; best sources include the claims themselves, the specification, drawings, and prior art. The specification is the best source when it serves as a glossary. Applicant can rebut the presumption by clearly setting forth a different definition in the specification. Examples and case law illustrate when plain meaning applies or is rebutted (Morris; In re Zletz; Chef America; etc.).

name: Means-plus-function (35 U.S.C. 112(f)) elements are limited to corresponding structure/material/acts in the specification and equivalents
description: When an element is claimed using means- (or step-) plus-function language, the specification must be consulted to determine the structure, material, or acts corresponding to the function recited in the claim.
guidance: The claimed element is construed as limited to the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof. Cite In re Donaldson and MPEP § 2181–2186.

name: Ordinary and customary meaning determined from specification, drawings, claims, and prior art; extrinsic evidence rarely needed when specification is clear
description: The ordinary and customary meaning of a term is the meaning that the term would have to a person of ordinary skill in the art as of the effective filing date; it may be evidenced by claims, specification, drawings, and prior art.
guidance: When the specification is clear about scope and content of a claim term, there is no need to turn to extrinsic evidence. Prior art usage must be consistent with specification. Case law (e.g., 3M; In re Suitco Surface; Vitronics; In re Abbott Diabetes Care) supports relying on the specification where clear.

name: Applicant may act as lexicographer (special definitions in the specification)
description: The applicant may rebut the presumption of ordinary meaning by clearly setting forth a special definition of a claim term in the specification that differs from its ordinary meaning.
guidance: Special definitions must be provided 'with reasonable clarity, deliberateness, and precision' and set out in the patent disclosure so one of ordinary skill is on notice of the change. Where an explicit definition is provided, that definition will control. (In re Paulsen; Intellicall; Toro Co.; Old Town Canoe; Multiform Desiccants; MPEP § 2173.05(a)).

name: Applicant may disavow or disclaim claim scope only by clear and unmistakable statements
description: Applicant may rebut plain meaning by clearly disavowing the full scope of a claim term in the specification, but disavowal must be 'clear and unmistakable.'
guidance: Disavowal may be express or in some cases implied (e.g., repeated, consistent depiction with disparaging remarks about alternatives). If examiner believes implicit disavowal narrows BRI, the examiner should make the interpretation clear on the record. (SciMed; In re Am. Acad. of Sci. Tech Ctr.; In re Abbott Diabetes Care.)

name: Examiner decision flow for determining meaning of claim term not invoking 35 U.S.C. 112(f)
description: Follow a decision flow: determine whether a claim term has an ordinary and customary meaning to those of ordinary skill; if yes, check whether the specification provides a special definition; if no special definition, apply ordinary meaning; if special definition exists, use it.
guidance: If a claim term does not have an ordinary and customary meaning, examiner should check the specification for a meaning. If no reasonably clear meaning emerges from specification and prior art, apply the broadest reasonable interpretation and reject the claim under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) and object to the specification under 37 CFR 1.75(d). If the specification provides a meaning, the examiner should use that meaning and may acknowledge/identify the special definition in the Office action.

name: Effect of preamble is determined case-by-case; preamble may be limiting or not
description: The determination of whether a preamble limits a claim is made on a case-by-case basis in light of the facts in each case; there is no litmus test.
guidance: If the preamble, read in context of the entire claim, recites limitations or is 'necessary to give life, meaning, and vitality' to the claim, then it should be treated as a limitation. If the claim body fully sets forth all limitations and the preamble merely states purpose or intended use, it is not a limitation. Examiners must evaluate whether preamble recitations of purpose or intended use result in a structural (or manipulative for process claims) difference from the prior art; if so, the preamble limits. Case examples: Catalina Marketing; Bell Communications Research; Pitney Bowes; Corning Glass; Jansen; Rowe; STX; In re Otto; In re Sinex; In re Schreiber; In re Cruciferous Sprout Litig.

name: Antecedent basis requirement (general)
description: Antecedent basis refers to the requirement that all words in a claim must be explained in the specification so that the words can be clearly understood.
guidance: If a claim term is not explained in the specification, the claim can be rejected or invalidated for being indefinite. Example: using the word “valve” in a claim requires the detailed description to explain whether that is a liquid valve or a heart valve if the context does not make it clear.

name: Use 'a' to introduce a term and 'the' to refer to it (within the claim)
description: A claim is supposed to introduce a term with the letter 'a' (or 'an'). After the term is introduced, the claim should refer to that term with the word 'the'.
guidance: Example: 'A tripod for supporting a camera, the tripod comprising: a first leg, a second leg, and a third leg.' Introducing the tripod initially as 'the tripod' would be indefinite. See also guidance on using A, THE, and SAID in claims. During prosecution, fixing 'a/the' issues is often a simple matter (e.g., change 'the' to 'a').

name: Avoid ambiguous references to multiple parts
description: When multiple instances of a part exist (e.g., first leg, second leg, third leg), referring later to 'the [part]' is ambiguous and may lack antecedent basis.
guidance: Claims must identify whether 'the leg' refers to the first, second, or third leg. Failure to identify which instance is meant can lead to indefiniteness rejections.

name: Express antecedent basis in the specification (specification-level requirement)
description: A claim term or concept must be discussed or shown in the patent application (specification/drawings) to have express antecedent basis.
guidance: If the legs of a tripod are never discussed or shown, a claim reciting 'legs' may be indefinite because there is no express antecedent basis. The drafter can sometimes argue implied antecedent basis (e.g., that all tripods have legs), but the goal is to provide express antecedent basis for all claim terms in the specification rather than rely on implication.

name: Do not rely on implied antecedent basis where avoidable
description: While an applicant may argue that a term has implied antecedent basis in the specification (e.g., common knowledge that all tripods have legs), relying on implied antecedent basis raises avoidable issues.
guidance: Best practice in drafting is to expressly explain claim terms in the specification so examiners and courts have clear antecedent basis; relying on implied basis creates unnecessary disputes during prosecution or litigation.

name: Be specific when terms are ambiguous without contextual definition
description: When a term's meaning cannot be determined from the claim context or the detailed description, the specification must define or describe it.
guidance: Example: if a claim uses 'valve' and the context doesn't indicate whether it is a liquid valve or a heart valve, the detailed description should explain which is meant to avoid indefiniteness.

name: Sanctions for discovery failures
description: USPTO regulations do not specifically provide sanctions for discovery failures, but under Fed. R. Civ. P. 37 a court may, among other things, 'direct that the matters embraced in the order or other designated facts be taken as established for purposes of the action' or 'prohibiting the disobedient party from supporting or opposing designated claims or defenses, or from introducing designated matters into evidence.'
guidance: Tribunals may employ exclusionary and deeming sanctions (e.g., deeming RFAs admitted, precluding evidence) modeled on Fed. R. Civ. P. 37; sanctions should be proportionate and justified by the discovery misconduct.

name: Adverse inference from discovery non-production (discretionary)
description: A court may draw an adverse inference that failure to timely correct deficient discovery responses indicates the withheld information would have supported the opposing party's claims, but such inferences are discretionary and may be declined.
guidance: When seeking adverse inferences, demonstrate the significance of the missing discovery and the respondent's culpability; be aware the tribunal may choose lesser sanctions (e.g., evidence preclusion, deeming RFAs) instead of an adverse inference on the merits.

name: Explanation of support for claim amendments
description: Each claim amendment must be accompanied by an explanation of the support in the disclosure of the patent for the amendment (support for insertions and deletions).
guidance: Required by 37 CFR 1.121(b)(2)(iii). Failure to provide explanation will generally result in non-entry before final rejection; such amendment after final rejection will not be entered.

name: Amendments must not introduce new matter or be in expired patents
description: No amendment may introduce new matter, and no amendment may be made in an expired patent. No reissue may enlarge the scope of the claims unless applied for within two years from the grant of the original patent (35 U.S.C. 251).
guidance: 37 CFR 1.121 and 35 U.S.C. 251. See MPEP § 1412.03 for time limitation on enlarging scope. If amendments would constitute new matter, reissue is improper.

name: All amendments made relative to patent as of reissue filing date
description: All amendments must be made relative to the patent specification (including claims and drawings) which is in effect as of the date of filing of the reissue application.
guidance: 37 CFR 1.121(b)(6). If there was a prior change to the patent (prior reexamination, prior reissue, certificate of correction), the first amendment must be made relative to the patent as changed; subsequent amendments must still be made vis-a-vis the patent specification in effect as of filing, not relative to the prior amendment.

name: Proper format examples for specification and claim amendments
description: Example formats: replace a paragraph by providing full paragraph with underlining/bracketing and point out location (e.g., 'Replace the paragraph beginning at column 4, line 23 with the following: ...'); for claim amendment present entire claim with underlining/bracketing and show dependency changes.
guidance: Follow the provided examples: 'Claim 6 (Amended). The apparatus of claim [5] 1 wherein the [first] second...' ; when changing dependencies it's proper to make an original claim dependent upon a later-filed higher-numbered claim.

name: Amendment of 'new claims' (previously added) rules
description: An amendment of a 'new claim' must present the amended 'new claim' containing the amendatory material and completely underlining the claim; the presentation cannot contain bracketing or other indication of what was in the previous version.
guidance: Applicant must point out what is changed in the 'Remarks' portion of the amendment. Each change must be accompanied by an explanation of the support in the disclosure as required by 37 CFR 1.121(b)(2)(iii).

name: Effect of reissue on original patent rights
description: Upon issue of the reissued patent the surrender of the original patent takes effect, and the reissued patent has same effect in law as if originally granted in the amended form; however, where claims are identical, reissue does not affect pending actions or abate causes of action.
guidance: Per 35 U.S.C. 252 and MPEP discussion: reissue treated as if original patent had been granted in amended form; courts may provide equitable terms for continued manufacture/use where preparations were made prior to grant of reissue.

name: Certificate of Correction for applicant's mistake (35 U.S.C. 255 / 37 CFR 1.323)
description: When a mistake of a clerical/typographical nature or of minor character not the fault of the Office appears in a patent and showing is made that it occurred in good faith, the Commissioner may, upon payment of required fee, issue a certificate if the correction does not constitute new matter or require reexamination.
guidance: 37 CFR 1.323. The fee is set in 37 CFR 1.20(a) (except inventorship correction fees under 1.20(b)). Mistakes affecting claim scope typically require reissue rather than certificate of correction.

name: Caution on multiple dependent-from-multiple-dependent (multi-multi) claims
description: A multiple dependent claim, dependent from a multiple dependent claim (multi-multi), will not be subjected to a substantive examination (from the application filed on or after April 1, 2022) (Art. 36(6)(iv)).
guidance: An amendment to remove multi-multi dependency as a response to an Office Action will lead to a final office action. Avoid filing multi-multi dependencies after the effective date; consider drafting alternatives to multi-multi dependency to save fees without risking prosecution problems.

name: Computer program / software eligibility
description: "Computer program" is an eligible product invention, even if it is not stored in a medium (since 2002). "Computer software," "Data structure," etc., are as well (products considered equivalent to a computer program).
guidance: Patent eligible inventions categories listed: "Product", "Process" (so-called "simple method"), "Process for producing a product". See JPO guidelines for details on claiming software-related inventions.

name: Voluntary amendment timing and benefits (use claims / software)
description: Voluntary amendment can be filed before 1st Office Action. Examination guidelines amended in 2016 for the use claims especially of Foods improved the chances of grant.
guidance: Consider voluntary amendment of computer software claims or limitations with intended use prior to the first OA to improve grant chances. File timely before first OA.

name: Support requirement (Article 36(6)(i))
description: "A claimed invention shall be disclosed in the description" (Article 36(6)(i)). The examiner will compare the claimed invention with the invention disclosed in the description to determine whether the support requirement is satisfied.
guidance: “Substantial” support for the claimed invention should be found in the description. The object of the invention is considered in the comparison. See JPO guideline references provided.

name: Types of violation of support requirement (examples)
description: Four types of violation include: (3) Over-broad or over-generalized claims; (4) No recitation of elements necessary for solving the problems discussed in the specification.
guidance: Examples given: (Type 3) Claiming many types of compound R while description only discloses specific examples R1–R3; (Type 4) Claim recites a 'force adjusting unit' but description only discloses a mechanism that increases force as speed increases while the object is to prevent exceeding speed limit. These illustrate why claims may lack substantial support.

name: Recommended responses to support-requirement rejections
description: Before amending embodiments, consider arguments that the specification discussion can be generalized to the claimed scope in light of common general knowledge at the filing date; consider submission of experimental results.
guidance: Amendment to the embodiment might be reasonable in some cases, BUT first attempt explanatory arguments and/or evidence. Use experimental data to support broader claim scope when appropriate. (Tip 4)

name: Clarity requirement (Article 36(6)(ii))
description: "A claimed invention for which a patent is sought shall be clear" (Article 36(6)(ii)).
guidance: Terms such as "about," "approximately," "substantially," "essentially," "especially," "for example," "etc.," "preferably," and "suitably" would be rejected. Use SI units (m, km, g, kg). Imperial units (inch, feet, yard, pound, ounce) will be rejected.

name: Formal application content: identification of approved product
description: A complete identification of the approved product as by appropriate chemical and generic name, physical structure or characteristics.
guidance: 37 CFR 1.740(a)(1): Identification must enable the Director to determine whether the patent claims the approved product or a method of using/manufacturing it.

name: Formal application content: copy of patent (specification, claims, drawings)
description: A copy of the patent for which an extension is being sought, including the entire specification (including claims) and drawings.
guidance: 37 CFR 1.740(a)(7): Entire patent copy required as part of the application package.

name: Formal application content: copy of disclaimers, corrections, reexamination certificates
description: A copy of any disclaimer, certificate of correction, receipt of maintenance fee payment, or reexamination certificate issued in the patent.
guidance: 37 CFR 1.740(a)(8): Include any documents that affect patent term or claim scope.

name: Formal application content: statement that patent claims the approved product and listing/showing of applicable claims
description: A statement that the patent claims the approved product, or a method of using or manufacturing the approved product, and a showing which lists each applicable patent claim and demonstrates the manner in which at least one such patent claim reads on the approved product, method of use, and/or method of manufacturing.
guidance: 37 CFR 1.740(a)(9): At most a showing explaining three claims is required (one product, one method of use, one method of manufacture) but every claim that claims the approved product/method/manufacture must be listed. Guidance provides examples: use of variables/substituents for generic chemical claims, reference to column/line numbers and drawing refs for means-plus-function claims, and use of an element-by-element claim chart for devices; show relevant equivalents where appropriate.

name: Formal application content: statement of regulatory dates per product type (35 U.S.C.156(g) info)
description: A statement of the relevant dates and information pursuant to 35 U.S.C. 156(g) to enable HHS or Agriculture to determine the applicable regulatory review period, with specific date types required for different product categories (human drug/biologic, new animal drug, veterinary biological product, food/color additive, medical device).
guidance: 37 CFR 1.740(a)(10): For human drugs/biologics include IND effective date and number, NDA/PLA submission date and number, NDA approval date; for animal drugs include dates for major tests or exemptions, NADA submission and approval dates; for veterinary biologicals include authority to prepare experimental product date, license application submission date, license issuance date; for food/color additives include major test initiation date, petition submission and Federal Register publication date; for devices include IDE effective date or clinical investigation start date, PMA or PDP submission date and approval date. If no regulatory event clearly reflects testing/approval commencement, applicant should claim dates and provide reasonable bases and substantiation.

name: Formal application content: statement of claimed eligibility and length of extension with calculation
description: A statement that in the opinion of the applicant the patent is eligible for the extension and a statement as to the length of extension claimed, including how the length of extension was determined.
guidance: 37 CFR 1.740(a)(12): Applicant must show how claimed extension length was calculated and indicate whether statutory caps (14-year or five-year limits under specified subsections) apply.

name: Complete application for filing date (37 CFR 1.741): required elements
description: A complete application for filing date purposes must include: identification of the approved product; identification of each Federal statute under which regulatory review occurred; identification of the patent for which an extension is being sought; identification of each claim of the patent which claims the approved product or method of using/manufacturing it; sufficient information to enable the Director and HHS/Ag to determine eligibility, rights derived, and length of regulatory review period; and a brief description of marketing applicant activities and significant dates.
