guidance: 37 CFR 1.741(a)(1)-(6): These requirements are mandated by 35 U.S.C.156 and must be satisfied within the 60-day filing period for establishment of the filing date. The Office will consider statutory requirements satisfied where sufficient information is provided to act on the application even if further information may later be desired.

name: Showing how patent claims read on the approved product (claim chart guidance)
description: The showing should clearly demonstrate how the product, method of use and/or method of manufacture claim reads on the approved product; where appropriate use variables/substituents mapping for generic chemical claims, reference to column/line and drawing numbers for means-plus-function claims, or an element-by-element claim chart for devices.
guidance: MPEP examples: for generic chemical structure claims list variables/substituents corresponding to approved product; for "means for"/112(f) claims reference patent text and drawings and describe equivalents; for medical devices, a claim chart describing element-by-element correspondence is helpful.

name: Preliminary amendment definition and disapproval factors (37 CFR 1.115)
description: A preliminary amendment is received on or before the mail date of the first Office action (§ 1.104) and will be entered unless disapproved by the Commissioner. A preliminary amendment may be disapproved if it unduly interferes with preparation of a first Office action.
guidance: Factors considered for disapproval include (i) the state of preparation of the first Office action as of the receipt date (§ 1.6) and (ii) the nature of changes to the specification or claims that would result from entry of the preliminary amendment.

name: Entry of second (or subsequent) supplemental replies (37 CFR 1.111)
description: A second (or subsequent) supplemental reply will be entered unless disapproved by the Commissioner, but may be disapproved if it unduly interferes with an Office action being prepared in response to the previous reply.
guidance: Factors to consider mirror those for preliminary amendments: state of preparation of the responsive Office action at receipt and the nature of any changes to specification or claims resulting from entry. Applicants are encouraged to include a complete reply in the first reply to prevent supplemental replies.

name: Types of content that may satisfy 'requires significant additional time'
description: Entry may require significant additional time if the amendment or reply: (A) amends the claims; (B) adds numerous new claims; (C) amends the specification to change claim scope; (D) amends the specification raising new matter; (E) includes arguments; (F) includes an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 or 1.132; or (G) includes evidence traversing rejections from a prior Office action.
guidance: This list is illustrative; other situations satisfying the two-prong test may also justify denial of entry. SPE approval is required before denying entry.

name: Lack of arguments in response — Form paragraph 7.95.01
description: When an applicant's reply lacks arguments, applicant should submit an argument under the heading 'Remarks' pointing out disagreements with the examiner’s contentions and must discuss the references applied against the claims.
guidance: Applicant must explain how the claims avoid or distinguish from the cited references. This paragraph supports treating an otherwise bona fide but argument-deficient reply as nonresponsive and requesting completion.

name: Claims presented with no attempt to point out patentable novelty
description: In amended cases where no attempt is made to point out the patentable novelty, the claims should not be allowed (see 37 CFR 1.111 and MPEP § 714.02).
guidance: An amendment failing to point out the patentable novelty may be held not fully responsive and a time period set to furnish a proper reply; however, if claims as amended are clearly open to rejection on the record, a final rejection should generally be made.

name: Immediate inspection checklist for filed amendments
description: Actions by applicant, especially those filed near the end of the reply period, should be inspected immediately to determine whether they are completely responsive and to prevent abandonment.
guidance: Examiner should check: (A) proper signature (MPEP § 714.01(a)); (B) filed within statutory/shortened period (MPEP § 710–§ 710.05); (C) fully responsive and complies with 37 CFR 1.121 (MPEP §§ 714.03–714.04); (D) whether changes warrant transfer (MPEP § 903.08(d)); (E) if application is special (MPEP § 708.01); (F) if interference-suggested claims were copied (MPEP § 2305); (G) traversal of restriction requirement (MPEP § 818.03(a)); (H) use of nonpermanent paper (MPEP § 714.07); (I) applicant-cited references (MPEP § 707.05(b), § 1302.12); (J) terminal disclaimer filed (MPEP §§ 508.01, 804.02, 804.03, 1490); (K) added security related matter (MPEP § 115).

name: Recommended applicant practices to ease after-final prosecution
description: Applicants are advised to include at filing or no later than the first reply claims varying from the broadest claim to the most detailed claim they are willing to accept to alleviate difficulties encountered after final rejection.
guidance: Ordinarily only one personal interview after final should be entertained, with a second permitted only in exceptional circumstances if it would materially assist in placing the application in condition for allowance.

name: Interpretation–construction distinction
description: Separate the question of what the claim language linguistically means (interpretation) from the question of what legal effect or scope the claim should have (construction).
guidance: Treat interpretation as addressing factual linguistic meaning (what people in the art actually understand the language to communicate) and construction as the normative decision about whether the linguistic meaning should govern patent scope; use this distinction as a conceptual tool to expose the real sources of dispute and to frame policy debates cleanly.

name: Distinguish linguistic uncertainty from legal/policy uncertainty
description: Do not assume that uncertainty over patent rights primarily stems from ambiguity in claim language; uncertainty often arises from judges' normative disagreements over whether to follow linguistic meaning.
guidance: Recognize that most prominent claim-construction disputes are methodological (textualism vs anti-textualism) rather than genuine disputes about linguistic content; thus efforts to refine linguistic tools will often not resolve the core problem.

name: Limitations of linguistic tools
description: Better or more sophisticated linguistic analysis cannot by itself resolve methodological disagreements about claim scope.
guidance: Because many disputes are about whether the linguistic meaning should govern (a policy choice), sharper linguistic techniques will be of limited help; scholars and judges should avoid presenting policy choices as technical linguistic inevitabilities.

name: When courts should look beyond the text (vagueness / construction zone)
description: Courts must look beyond the claim text only in the limited circumstance where the claim is genuinely vague and the dispute falls within the 'construction zone.'
guidance: If true vagueness exists, policy considerations necessarily come into play and courts should acknowledge and resolve them; avoid treating that narrow category as proof that courts should routinely ignore claim text.

name: Proper sources for discerning claim meaning
description: Courts may consult internal and external evidence—specification, prosecution history, dictionaries, and expert testimony—to discern what claim language means to those skilled in the art.
guidance: Cases differ on the preferred order and weight of these sources (see Phillips, Telegenix, Multiform); for technical terms the specification is often the best source, while other authorities (dictionaries, experts) may be appropriate depending on context.

name: Do not conflate linguistic meaning with the patentee’s invention
description: A difference between the linguistic meaning of claim text and the patentee's conception of the invention is not itself a linguistic ambiguity.
guidance: Avoid the rhetorical move of treating every divergence between written claims and the 'real' invention as textual ambiguity; many so-called 'ambiguities' reflect a normative choice about whether to enforce patentee-drafted text.

name: Anti-textualist proposals are policy arguments (not linguistic necessities)
description: Arguments for looking to the 'real' invention (or abolishing claims) are fundamentally normative: they aim to produce narrower, less patentee-favorable scopes to correct biased drafting incentives.
guidance: Anti-textualist scholars should state these normative goals openly rather than masking them as inevitable consequences of linguistic indeterminacy; doing so clarifies the true debate and invites explicit policy adjudication.

name: Account for patentee drafting incentives and bias
description: Patentees have an incentive to draft claims broadly and self-servingly, which motivates proposals to discount claim text in favor of a neutral judge's conception of the invention.
guidance: Consider these incentive effects when evaluating methodological proposals, but treat them as policy tradeoffs that must be justified normatively rather than as proof of textual indeterminacy.

name: Institutional allocation: legal question vs factual question
description: Claim interpretation involves factual elements (what PHOSITA understand) but has been doctrinally classified (Markman) as a 'purely legal' question for appellate resolution.
guidance: Recognize the mixed nature: while interpretation implicates factual inquiry, there are normative and doctrinal reasons to treat claim-construction methodology as primarily a legal (appellate) question to promote doctrinal consistency and settle methodology at the appellate level.

name: Standard of review and deference issues
description: There is debate whether claim construction should be reviewed de novo on appeal or receive deference to district-court factual findings.
guidance: Weigh competing arguments: de novo review supports uniform methodology from appellate courts; some scholars advocate deference for factual predicates (expert evidence) and a hybrid approach may be appropriate depending on documentary vs factual sources.

name: Claims are the measure of the patent grant (public notice function)
description: Patent claims, not specifications, ordinarily define the bounds of the patentee's rights and serve the public-notice function.
guidance: Respect the default rule that claim language frames and resolves issues of interpretation; any departure (e.g., equity-based narrowing) requires explicit normative justification.

name: Doctrine of equivalents is a narrow exception to the claim-as-written rule
description: A court may find infringement under the doctrine of equivalents when an accused product differs only insubstantially from the claimed invention.
guidance: Treat the doctrine as a limited judicial tool rather than a license to routinely override claim text; its availability does not justify broad anti-textualist approaches.

name: Resolve vagueness candidly to avoid empty interpretations
description: When courts face genuine vagueness, they should acknowledge that claim text cannot resolve the issue and that policy considerations will decide outcomes.
guidance: Failure to do so produces empty 'interpretations' that leave outcomes to juries or hidden reasoning; explicit recognition of the policy choice leads to clearer, more accountable decisions.

name: Argue claim-construction methodology overtly on policy grounds
description: Both textualists and anti-textualists should make explicit normative arguments for their preferred methodologies rather than cloaking them as purely linguistic conclusions.
guidance: Open normative debate fosters clearer conceptual analysis and better scholarly engagement; it prevents the rhetorical concealment of policy choices behind claims of linguistic inevitability.

name: Search based on actual U.S. filing date
description: Examiners should search all applications based on the actual U.S. filing date of the application rather than on the filing date of any parent U.S. application for which priority is claimed.
guidance: Because of the 20-year patent term and possible cancellation of priority claims, examiners should cite all material prior art having an effective filing date after the filing date of the U.S. parent application but before the actual filing date of the application being examined.

name: Completeness and clarity of examiner's action on formal matters
description: Forms listing informalities (PTO-948 and PTO-152) should be mailed with the examiner's first action; any additional formal requirements desired should be included in the first action. When a formal requirement is made in an examiner's action indicating allowable subject matter, the action should call attention to 37 CFR 1.111(b) and state that a complete reply must either comply with all formal requirements or specifically traverse each requirement not complied with.
guidance: The examiner's action should be complete as to all matters, except in appropriate circumstances (misjoinder, fundamental defects), where the action may be limited to matters then before further action. Matters of form need not be raised until a claim is found allowable.

name: Language and conduct when rejecting claims
description: Where a claim is refused for any reason relating to the merits, it should be 'rejected' and the ground of rejection fully and clearly stated; the word 'reject' must be used. The examiner should designate the statutory basis for any ground of rejection by express reference to a section of 35 U.S.C. in the opening sentence of each ground of rejection.
guidance: If rejected as broader than the enabling disclosure, state the reason; if rejected as indefinite, point out wherein the indefiniteness resides; if incomplete, specify lacking elements. Avoid personal language and expressions of opinion about applicant. Identify any claims judged allowable and suggest amendments to make rejected claims allowable. Avoid omnibus rejections and grouping multiple claims unless the rejection is equally applicable to all claims in the group.

name: Answer all material traversed
description: An examiner must provide clear explanations of all actions taken during prosecution. Where requirements are traversed or suspension requested, make proper reference in the action on the amendment. Where applicant traverses any rejection and examiner repeats the rejection, the examiner should take note of applicant's argument and answer the substance of it.
guidance: If applicant's arguments are persuasive and the previous rejection is withdrawn, the examiner must provide in the next Office communication the reasons for the withdrawal by referring specifically to the page(s) and line(s) of applicant's remarks forming the basis. It is not acceptable to merely indicate that all of applicant's remarks form the basis. Form paragraphs 7.38.01, 7.38.02, 7.37-series may be used where applicable. If a rejection of record is applied to a new/amended claim, specifically identify that ground (e.g., by citation of the paragraph in the former Office letter).

name: Nature of the patented invention and its commercial embodiment
description: The nature of the patented invention; the character of the commercial embodiment of it as owned and produced by the licensor; and the benefit of those who have used the invention
guidance: Describe how the invention is implemented commercially and document benefits realized by users to support claims about the invention's value and the appropriate royalty base.

name: Ground for revocation: invention claimed is subject of prior grant
description: Patent may be revoked if a claim in the patent to be revoked is identical to a claim in a patent of earlier priority date and the earlier claim is valid.
guidance: Priority date/earlier valid claims are determinative; overlapping identical claims can be invalidated.

name: Ground for revocation: invention not useful (lack of utility)
description: Patent may be revoked if invention is not useful — i.e., it will not work or will not provide the desired result in the specification. Practical or commercial utility is not required; utility judged against state of the art at patent date.
guidance: Demonstrable operability is required; if invention does not perform as claimed, utility ground may succeed.

name: Ground for revocation: insufficient description (lack of sufficiency/enablement)
description: If the invention is not sufficiently described in the specification — the complete specification must describe an embodiment of each claim so as to enable those skilled in the art to practise the invention 'without making further invention' — the patent can be revoked.
guidance: Description must be fair, sufficiently detailed and not unnecessarily difficult to follow; sufficiency is judged on the merits of the specification (case law cited).

name: Ground for revocation: claim not clearly defined and/or not fairly based
description: Two independent grounds: (i) the scope of any claim is not sufficiently and clearly defined; (ii) the claim is not fairly based on matter disclosed in the specification (see s.10).
guidance: Fairly based means the monopoly sought should be no broader than justified by disclosed matter; patentee should not claim more than the disclosure warrants.

name: Contributory infringement — five elements
description: [Alleged infringer] is liable for contributory infringement if the patent holder proves by a preponderance of the evidence that: (1) [alleged infringer] sells, offers to sell, or imports within the United States a component of a product, or apparatus for use in a process, during the time the patent is in force; (2) the component or apparatus has no substantial, noninfringing use; (3) the component or apparatus constitutes a material part of the invention; (4) [alleged infringer] is aware of the patent and knows that the products or processes for which the component has no other substantial use may be covered by a claim of the patent or may satisfy a claim under the doctrine of equivalents; and (5) that use directly infringes the claim.
guidance: Each requirement must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. § 271(c); Aro; Ricoh; Alloc; Mentor; Hewlett‑Packard; Preemption Devices.

name: § 271(f)(1) — supply of components from U.S. for combination abroad (active inducement)
description: To prove § 271(f)(1) liability (active inducement of foreign combination), patentee must prove by a preponderance that: (1) accused supplies (or causes to be supplied) components from the United States to a place outside the United States that make up all or a substantial portion of the invention of any claim; (2) accused takes action intentionally to cause another outside the United States to assemble the components; (3) accused knows of the patent and knows the encouraged acts constitute infringement; and (4) the encouraged acts would constitute direct infringement if carried out in the United States.
guidance: If accused believed the acts would not constitute infringement in the U.S. or that the patent was invalid, cannot be liable for inducement. Instruction should address willful‑blindness only when that theory is asserted. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. § 271(f); Cardiac Pacemakers; Microsoft v. AT&T; Liquid Dynamics; Pellegrini; NTP; Union Carbide; Waymark.

name: § 271(f)(2) — supply of components from U.S. for combination abroad (contributory foreign infringement)
description: To prove § 271(f)(2) liability, patentee must prove by a preponderance that: (1) accused supplies (or causes to be supplied) a component from the United States to a place outside the United States; (2) the only substantial use for the component is in a product that would infringe the patent if the combination had occurred in the United States; (3) accused is aware of the patent and knows the component has no other substantial use and may be covered by a claim of the patent (literally or under doctrine of equivalents); and (4) accused intends for the component to be used in a product that would directly infringe the claim if used in the United States.
guidance: Authorities and commentary similar to §271(f) generally; statute cited is 35 U.S.C. §271(f).

name: § 271(g) — sale/import/use in U.S. of product made abroad by patented process
description: Accused is liable for direct infringement if patent holder proves by a preponderance that accused, without authorization, imports, offers to sell, sells, or uses within the United States a product made outside the United States by a process that, if performed in the United States, would infringe the claim literally or under the doctrine of equivalents.
guidance: Exception: if the product has been materially changed by an additional process or has become a trivial and nonessential component of another product, there is no infringement. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. §271(g); Bayer v. Housey; Ajinomoto v. ADM.

name: Direct infringement where one or more system components located outside the U.S.
description: Direct infringement requires that the accused system include every element recited in the claim. If some (but not all) elements are located outside the United States, the patent holder must prove by a preponderance that the control of the system was exercised and the benefit of the system was enjoyed in the United States (i.e., the place where the system as a whole is put into service).
guidance: Focus is on place where control is exercised and beneficial use obtained. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. §271(a); NTP v. Research in Motion.

name: Prior art (for patents with effective filing date before March 16, 2013)
description: Prior art includes items publicly known, used, offered for sale, or references (publications/patents) that disclose the claimed invention or elements of it. To be prior art, the item must have been made, known, used, published, or patented either before the invention was made (or an earlier inventor date) or more than one year before the filing date. Prior art does not include the inventor's own publication less than one year before the date of invention. Special limitations may apply under subsections of 35 U.S.C. §102.
guidance: Authorities: statutory and case law; precise date rules and exceptions must be applied based on the patent's effective filing date and the applicable version of §102.

name: Anticipation (novelty) — claim invalid if present in single reference
description: To prove anticipation (lack of novelty), alleged infringer must show by clear and convincing evidence that all requirements of the claim were present in a single previous device, method, printed publication, or patent (an 'anticipating prior art' reference). The prior art need not use the same words, but must disclose all claim elements either expressly or impliedly to a person of ordinary skill.
guidance: Anticipation is determined claim‑by‑claim. Where the date of invention is disputed, jury must determine conception/reduction to practice and diligence. Authorities: applicable pre‑AIA §102 law; supporting cases and procedural guidance in instructions.

name: Petition content requirement (claim-by-claim invalidity and prior art grounds)
description: In its request, the petitioner must explain why each claim is invalid and show what previous publication or combination of publications render the claim invalid. Each set of invalidating art is a 'ground' of invalidity.
guidance: Petitions should identify the specific claim(s), articulate why each is invalid, and cite the prior art references or combinations relied on. Petitioners may assert multiple grounds for each claim.

name: Types of allowable grounds (anticipation and obviousness)
description: Typical grounds asserted include anticipation and obviousness over prior art. Each anticipatory reference or combination of art for obviousness is considered one asserted ground of invalidity.
guidance: Anticipation requires a single reference that teaches all elements of a claim; obviousness typically relies on combinations of references. The article observes the board finds obviousness challenges more persuasive than anticipation challenges.

name: Counting methodology for statistical analysis
description: Each anticipatory reference or combination of art for obviousness is considered one asserted ground. Only when board decisions were unclear as to the number of grounds asserted does analysis use numbers from the original petitions instead of board decisions.
guidance: Be explicit about whether statistics are aggregated by petition, by claim, or by asserted ground; use original petitions to resolve ambiguities in board opinions.

name: Distinction between 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103
description: Under 35 U.S.C. 102 the claim is anticipated by the reference (no question of obviousness); the reference must teach every aspect of the claimed invention explicitly or implicitly (features not directly taught must be inherently present). Under 35 U.S.C. 103 the reference teachings must be modified to meet the claims and the modification must have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art as of the relevant time (effective filing date for AIA, time of invention for pre-AIA).
guidance: Keep distinction in mind when making rejections; see MPEP §§ 2131-2146 and 2150-2159.04 for guidance on patentability determinations under 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103.

name: Selecting proper 35 U.S.C. 102 paragraph (AIA vs pre-AIA)
description: Once a printed publication or patent is found to disclose the claimed invention, the examiner should determine whether the rejection should be under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) or (a)(2) (AIA) or under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a), (b), or (e).
guidance: Determine the effective filing date of the claimed invention (see MPEP § 2139.01 for pre-AIA and MPEP § 2152.01 for AIA) and the issue/publication date of the reference (see MPEP §§ 2124, 2126, 2128-2128.02, and 2152.02-2154.02(c)). See MPEP § 2152.05 for whether to apply 102(a)(1) or (a)(2). Use form paragraph 7.03.aia or 7.03.fti in Office actions to indicate which regime applies.

name: Presumption that prior art references are operable/enabling
description: When a reference expressly anticipates or makes obvious all elements of the claimed invention, the reference is presumed to be operable. Once such a reference is found, the burden shifts to the applicant to rebut the presumption of operability.
guidance: In re Sasse and In re Antor Media Corp. support this presumption. An examiner making a proper prima facie case of anticipation need not conduct an inquiry into whether the prior art is enabling; applicant must submit rebuttal evidence of nonenablement. See MPEP § 716.07 for related guidance.

name: Proof of efficacy not required for prior art enablement
description: A prior art reference provides an enabling disclosure if it describes the invention in sufficient detail to enable one of ordinary skill to carry out the claimed invention; proof of efficacy is not required.
guidance: Cited case: Impax Labs. Inc. v. Aventis Pharm. Inc. (proof of efficacy not required for anticipation). See MPEP § 2122 for discussion of utility in the prior art.

name: Plant-related enablement (growing/cultivating requirement)
description: When claims are drawn to plants, the reference combined with prior art knowledge must enable one of ordinary skill to reproduce the plant (i.e., grow/cultivate it); pictures alone may be insufficient if key grafting or propagation information is missing.
guidance: Cases: In re LeGrice (rose pictures insufficient), Ex parte Thomson (commercial seed availability may make disclosure enabling), In re Elsner (combination of publication identifying plant + foreign sale + asexual reproducibility can create a statutory bar). See MPEP § 2152.02(d) for foreign sales under AIA.

name: Pictures/drawings may constitute enabling disclosure
description: Pictures and drawings may be sufficiently enabling to put the public in possession of the article pictured and may be used to reject claims to the article if the picture shows all the claimed structural features and how they are put together.
guidance: Origin of the drawing is immaterial; drawings in design or utility patents can anticipate or render obvious. Evaluate drawings for what they reasonably disclose to one of ordinary skill (In re Bager; Jockmus v. Leviton; In re Mraz; In re Aslanian). Proportions in drawings not to scale have little evidentiary value.

name: Tax strategies deemed within the prior art (AIA §14 guidance)
description: Under AIA section 14, any strategy for reducing, avoiding, or deferring tax liability ('tax strategy') shall be deemed to be within the prior art for purposes of novelty and nonobviousness under 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103; applicants cannot rely on novelty/non-obviousness of a tax strategy to distinguish claims from prior art.
guidance: Two exclusions: (1) parts of inventions used solely for preparing a tax or information return (including recording/transmitting/organizing data related to such filing) and (2) parts used solely for financial management to the extent severable from any tax strategy. This provision applies to applications/patents pending, filed, or issued on or after Sept. 16, 2011. Follow the examination procedure: (1) construe claim (MPEP § 2111 et seq.), (2) analyze 35 U.S.C. 101 and 112, (3) identify limitations relating to a tax strategy and note exclusions, (4) evaluate the claim under 102/103 treating tax-strategy limitations as prior art. Form paragraph 7.06.01 may be used.

name: Treatment of computer-implemented methods vis-à-vis tax-strategy provision
description: A genuinely novel and non-obvious computer-implemented method for manipulating data is not affected by the tax-strategy provision merely because it is used for a tax purpose; however, a prior-art computer-implemented method does not become non-obvious simply by implementing a novel tax strategy. Claim limitations solely enabling filing of income tax returns or assisting with managing finances should be given patentable weight, except limitations directed to a tax strategy should not be given patentable weight.
guidance: Apply the four-step examination guidance for tax strategies and consider whether claimed computer-implemented features are severable from tax-strategy limitations.

name: Clerical processing and entry of compliant amendments
description: The reexamination clerk handles most initial clerical processing. CRU SPE or TC QAS provides oversight. Amendments complying with 37 CFR 1.530(d)-(j) will be entered for purposes of reexamination in the reexamination file. New matter claim amendments must be canceled; new matter drawings ordinarily are not entered.
guidance: For merged reissue-reexamination proceedings see MPEP §2283 and §2285. Where an amendment enlarges claim scope, it may be entered but appropriate claims will be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 305.

name: Panel review conference requirement before final rejection
description: When the examiner determines the proceeding is ready for final rejection, the examiner formulates a draft preliminary decision specifying which claims to reject/allow and reasons, informs the CRU SPE or TC QAS, who convenes a panel review conference. Conference members review claim patentability pursuant to MPEP §2271.01. If the conference confirms the preliminary decision, the final rejection is issued and signed by the examiner with two conferees initialing; if not confirmed, the examiner reevaluates and issues an appropriate action.
guidance: Panel review provides quality control and confirmation prior to issuing a final rejection in reexamination.

name: All changes are made vis-à-vis the patent to be reissued
description: In accordance with 37 CFR 1.173(g), all amendments in the reissue application must be made relative to (i.e. vis-à-vis) the patent specification in effect as of the date of the filing of the reissue application. The patent specification includes the claims and drawings.
guidance: If there was a prior change to the patent (via reexamination certificate, prior reissue, certificate of correction, PTAB trial certificate, etc.), the first amendment of the subject reissue application must be made relative to the patent specification as changed by the prior proceeding. All subsequent amendments must be made relative to the patent specification in effect as of the date of filing of the reissue application, not relative to any prior amendment.

name: Presentation format for amending original patent claims
description: For changes to the claims, submit a copy of the entire patent claim with the amendments shown by underlining and bracketing.
guidance: Example: 'Amend claim 6 as follows: Claim 6 (Amended). The apparatus of claim [5] 1 wherein the [first] second piezoelectric element...' If the dependency of any original patent claim is to be changed by amendment, it is proper to make that original patent claim dependent upon a later-filed higher-numbered claim.

name: Cancellation of claims
description: To cancel an original patent claim, in writing, direct cancellation of the patent claim (e.g., 'Cancel claim 6'). To cancel a new claim previously added in the reissue, direct cancellation in writing (e.g., 'Cancel claim 15').
guidance: Simple written direction to cancel the specific claim is required.

name: Amendment of a new claim (previously presented in reissue)
description: An amendment of a 'new claim' must be done by presenting the amended new claim containing the amendatory material, and completely underlining the claim, including the claim number.
guidance: The presentation cannot contain any bracketing or other indication of what was in the previous version of the claim (because changes are vis-à-vis the original patent). Applicant must point out what is changed in the 'Remarks' portion of the amendment. Per 37 CFR 1.173(c), each change made in the claim must be accompanied by an explanation of the support in the disclosure of the patent for the change.

name: Presentation when making amendments in a reissue of a previously reissued patent (reissue of a reissue)
description: When a copy of a first reissue patent is presented as the specification of a second reissue application, additions made by the first reissue will already be printed in italics and should remain in such format.
guidance: Applicants need only present additions to the specification/claims in the second reissue as double underlined text. Subject matter to be deleted from the first reissue patent should be presented in the second reissue application within sets of double brackets.

name: Providing proper format for reissue specification
description: Where a reissue application has not been prepared in the indicated manner, the examiner may obtain from applicant a clean copy of the reissue specification prepared in the indicated form, or a proper submission of a previously improperly submitted amendment.
guidance: If deletions from the original patent are small, the reissue application can be prepared for issue by putting bracketed inserts at appropriate places and numbering added claims. When applicant submits a clean copy or proper submission of an earlier improper amendment, a supplemental reissue declaration should not be provided because format correction does not correct a 35 U.S.C. 251 error in the patent.

name: Examiner's amendment and reissue oath/declaration requirements
description: When necessary to amend the reissue application to place it in condition for allowance, the examiner may (A) request applicant provide the amendments, or (B) make the amendments with applicant's approval by a formal examiner's amendment.
guidance: If changes are made by formal examiner's amendment, the entire paragraphs or claims being amended need to be presented with appropriate markings. The exception for an examiner's amendment in 37 CFR 1.121(g) does not apply to examiner's amendments in reissue applications. For applications filed on/after Sept 16, 2012, if additional defects/errors are corrected after filing the reissue oath/declaration, a supplemental oath/declaration is not required; however if all previously identified errors are no longer relied upon, applicant must explicitly identify an error being relied upon for reissue (conspicuously and clearly, complying with 35 U.S.C. 251). For filings before that date, a supplemental oath/declaration will be required to correct an 'error' under 35 U.S.C. 251; examiner should telephone applicant to request the supplemental oath/declaration.

name: Design reissue fees and claim limitations
description: Design reissue application fee is set forth in 37 CFR 1.16(e). A search fee (1.16(n)) and an examination fee (1.16(r)) are also required.
guidance: The additional fees in 1.16(h) and 1.16(i) do not apply for a design reissue application because more than one claim is not permitted in a design application pursuant to the last sentence of 37 CFR 1.153(a). The fee for issuing a design reissue patent is set forth in 37 CFR 1.18(b).

name: Multiple design reissue applications and restriction/divisional practice
description: A design reissue application can be filed based on the 'error' of failing to include a design for a patentably distinct segregable part or subcombination of the claimed design, if filed within two years of issuance (considered a broadening).
guidance: Restriction will be required under 37 CFR 1.176(b); the added segregable part will be held constructively non-elected and withdrawn. Examiner should suggest filing a divisional design reissue application directed to constructively non-elected subject matter. Action in original reissue will be suspended pending divisional. If divisional found allowable, a petition under 37 CFR 1.183 is required to waive 1.153 to permit rejoining of designs into single claim for issuance. Filing is improper if original application included the segregable part and a restriction was made but applicant failed to file a divisional before issue of original application.

name: Printed reissue patent heading and printing conventions
description: The specifications of reissue patents will be printed to show changes over the original patent text by enclosing any material omitted by the reissue in heavy brackets [ ] and printing material added by the reissue in italics.
guidance: The printed reissue patent specification will carry the Office-added heading: 'Matter enclosed in heavy brackets [ ] appears in the original patent but forms no part of this reissue specification; matter printed in italics indicates the additions made by reissue.' Examiners should ensure specification is in proper form for printing, carefully check entry of all amendments so changes directed by applicant are accurately printed. Matter added by amendment in the reissue that is later canceled should be crossed through, not bracketed. All claims of the original patent should appear in the reissue patent, with canceled patent claims being enclosed in brackets.

name: Effect of reissue under 35 U.S.C. 252
description: Upon issuance of the reissued patent, surrender of the original patent takes effect; every reissued patent shall have the same effect and operation in law as if originally granted in the amended form, with certain continuity for substantially identical claims.
guidance: Reissue does not abridge rights of persons who, prior to reissue, made, purchased, offered to sell, used, or imported the patented thing; courts may provide for continued manufacture/use/sale or equitable terms for investments made before the grant of the reissue. The reissued patent, to the extent its claims are substantially identical to the original patent, constitutes a continuation with effect from the date of the original patent.

name: Factors indicative of an experimental purpose
description: Courts have considered a number of factors in determining whether a claimed invention was the subject of a commercial offer for sale primarily for purposes of experimentation.
guidance: These factors include: (1) necessity for public testing; (2) amount of control over the experiment retained by the inventor; (3) nature of the invention; (4) length of the test period; (5) whether payment was made; (6) whether there was a secrecy obligation; (7) whether records of the experiment were kept; (8) who conducted the experiment; (9) degree of commercial exploitation during testing; (10) whether the invention reasonably requires evaluation under actual conditions of use; (11) whether testing was systematically performed; (12) whether the inventor continually monitored the invention during testing; and (13) nature of contacts made with potential customers. Case law: Allen Eng’g Corp. v. Bartell Indus., Inc., quoting EZ Dock v. Schafer Sys., Inc.; Electromotive Div. of GM v. Transportation Sys. Div. of GE (customer awareness critical). No single factor or combination is necessarily determinative; examiner must assess scope and length of activity relative to experimental purpose and subject matter.

name: Experimental use ends upon actual reduction to practice
description: Experimental use means perfecting/completing an invention to the point of determining that it will work for its intended purpose; experimental use ends with an actual reduction to practice.
guidance: If examiner concludes applicant considered invention 'complete,' awaiting approvals (e.g., Underwriters' Laboratories) will not normally overcome this. Lack of modifications resulting from alleged experimentation is evidence (though not conclusive) that activity was not experimental. Modifications/refinements that did result must be features of the claimed invention to have probative value. Cases: RCA Corp. v. Data Gen.; InterRoyal; Skil Corp.; In re Theis.

name: Completeness of the invention as a bar to experimental exception
description: If the inventor considered the invention to be 'complete' prior to activity alleged as experimental, that activity will not normally be considered experimental use.
guidance: Examiner should evaluate whether evidence shows the inventor was satisfied invention was complete. Evidence that alleged experimental activity did not lead to specific modifications supports that the activity was commercial rather than experimental. Any modifications arising from experimentation must be part of the claimed invention to be probative.

name: Identify specific limitation considered directed to abstract concept
description: Identify specific limitation that is considered directed to abstract concept.
guidance: Limitations must be mapped to one of three Enumerated Groupings. Examiners should identify the specific claim limitation(s) that recite the judicial exception rather than treating an entire claim generically.

name: Map limitations to Enumerated Groupings
description: Limitations must be mapped to one of three Enumerated Groupings (mathematical concepts; certain methods of organizing human activity; mental processes).
guidance: Use the enumerated groupings rather than relying on case-by-case comparisons. The 2019 PEG shifts examiners' focus to these groupings, which synthesize Supreme Court and Federal Circuit precedent, to produce consistent results across technologies and claim types.

name: Claim 'recites' a judicial exception (Step 2A – Prong One)
description: Determine whether claim recites a judicial exception. A claim 'recites' a judicial exception when the judicial exception is 'set forth' or 'described' in the claim.
guidance: Set forth: claims clearly state the judicial exception (e.g., explicitly state a mathematical equation). Describe: the concept can be identified even if not explicitly named (e.g., recitation of intermediated settlement without using those words). Distinct claim elements can be treated separately, but examiners should not inappropriately parse claims; consider limitations together to avoid separate abstract-idea calculations.

name: Integration into a practical application (Step 2A – Prong Two)
description: Determine whether the identified judicial exception is integrated into a practical application (i.e., the claim as a whole integrates the exception into a practical application).
guidance: Key considerations include whether the claimed invention improves the functioning of a computer or other technology and whether the specification provides sufficient detail such that one of ordinary skill would recognize the improvement. Test for practical application: (1) evaluate the specification to see if the disclosure shows an improvement (the specification need not explicitly state the improvement but it must be apparent to a person of ordinary skill; conclusory assertions are insufficient); (2) ensure the claim reflects the disclosed improvement by including components or steps that provide the improvement (the claim need not explicitly state 'thereby increasing X' to reflect the improvement). Improvements in the judicial exception itself (e.g., a better economic concept) do not count as improvements in technology.

name: Applying judicial exception to particular treatment or prophylaxis (medical claims)
description: A claim can integrate a judicial exception into a practical application by applying or using the judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition.
guidance: Test for practical application in this context: (1) Particularity — the treatment or prophylaxis must be 'particular' and not encompass all applications of the exception; (2) Relationship — the treatment/prophylaxis limitation must have more than a nominal or insignificant relationship to the exception(s); (3) Not extra-solution or field-of-use — the limitation must impose meaningful limits and cannot be mere extra-solution activity or a field-of-use restriction.

name: Significantly more analysis (Step 2B)
description: Determine whether claim elements beyond the judicial exception, individually and in combination, amount to 'significantly more' than the judicial exception itself.
guidance: If additional elements do not integrate the exception into a practical application under Step 2A Prong Two, consider whether the additional elements provide 'significantly more' under Step 2B. The examiner should explain why the additional elements, taken individually and in combination, do not result in the claim amounting to significantly more than the exception.

name: USPTO examiner's duty to establish a prima facie case
description: For a 101 rejection, the examiner must explain and support each step of the 101 analysis (Step 2A Prong One, Step 2A Prong Two, and Step 2B) to establish a prima facie case.
guidance: Step 2A Prong One: the rejection should identify the judicial exception by referring to what is recited (set forth or described) in the claim and explain why it is considered an exception. No requirement exists for the examiner to provide additional external support (publications, affidavits) for the conclusion that a claim recites a judicial exception. Step 2A Prong Two: the rejection should identify additional elements beyond the exception and evaluate integration into a practical application using the PEG considerations, explaining that either there are no additional elements or that those elements do not integrate the exception. Step 2B: the examiner should explain why additional elements do not amount to significantly more.

name: Role and interpretation of examples and case law
description: Use of hypothetical examples and the shift from case-comparison to enumerated groupings in the 2019 PEG.
guidance: Examples are illustrative and should be interpreted based on their fact patterns; a claim need not mirror an example to be eligible. The October update steers examiners away from direct case-by-case comparisons toward applying the enumerated groupings synthesized from Supreme Court and Federal Circuit precedent. The PEG's examples facilitate consistent examination across technologies, but different fact patterns may yield different outcomes; analyze claims under the broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the specification.

name: Domestic benefit information (ADS bibliographic data)
description: Domestic benefit information includes the application number, filing date, status (including patent number if available), and relationship of each application for which a benefit is claimed under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), 120, 121, or 365(c).
guidance: Providing this information in the ADS constitutes the specific reference required by 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or 120 and § 1.78 and need not otherwise be made part of the specification.

name: Patent Law Treaty (PLT) and PCT forms satisfy ADS requirements
description: Presentation of a priority/benefit claim in the PLT Model International Request Form or the PCT Request Form satisfies the requirement in § 1.55 or § 1.78 for presentation of such claims in an ADS; presentation of the name of the applicant in certain PLT forms satisfies § 1.46 ADS requirement.
guidance: If a PCT Request Form is submitted in an application under 35 U.S.C. 111, it must be accompanied by a clear indication that treatment of the application as under 35 U.S.C. 111 is desired.

name: Specification section ordering and headings format
description: The specification should include sections in order (if applicable): Title; Cross-reference to related applications; Statement re federally sponsored research; Names of parties to joint research agreement; Incorporation by reference statements; Statement re prior disclosures; Background; Brief summary; Brief description of drawings; Detailed description; Claims; Abstract; and Sequence Listing (when required). Section headings should be in uppercase and without underlining or bold type.
guidance: Specific incorporation-by-reference rules for ASCII files, XML sequence listings, and large tables reference other MPEP sections (§§ 1.52(e)(8), 1.96(c), 1.821(c), 1.831(a), 1.58(c)).

name: Claiming benefit to a prior-filed provisional under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) — filing-time limitation
description: A nonprovisional application must be filed not later than twelve months after the provisional filing date to claim benefit under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), subject to paragraph (b) (delayed filing restoration).
guidance: Alternatively, a later application may be entitled to claim the provisional benefit via 35 U.S.C. 120/121/365(c) of a subsequent application filed within that 12-month period.

name: Cross-references limitation in ADS
description: Cross-references to other related applications may be made when appropriate, but cross-references to applications for which a benefit is not claimed under title 35 must not be included in an ADS (§ 1.76(b)(5)).
guidance: Include only applications for which you are claiming the statutory benefit in the ADS.

name: Certified copy and translation requirement for foreign-originated international applications
description: Where benefit is claimed under 35 U.S.C. 120/121/365(c)/386(c) to an international application or international design application that designates but did not originate in the United States, the Office may require a certified copy of such application together with an English translation if filed in another language.
guidance: Be prepared to supply certified copies/translations when claiming benefit to such foreign-originated international applications.

name: Case timing (medians and variability)
description: Median times and distribution to key events such as claim construction hearing, trial, preliminary injunction, permanent injunction (e.g., median preliminary injunction 3.8 months, permanent 11.6 months).
guidance: Compare median and boxplot dispersion across districts to budget time and money, and to set client expectations; use district-specific timing for scheduling and flat-fee planning.

name: Invalidity basis categorization
description: Classification of patent invalidity findings by statutory basis (e.g., 101 Subject Matter, 102 Anticipation/Novelty, 103 Obviousness, 112 Definiteness/Enablement/Written Description) and metrics over time/district.
guidance: Track temporal and district trends in invalidity bases (e.g., §101 invalidations) to refine claim drafting, prosecution strategy, and defense planning.

name: Case resolution taxonomy and distribution
description: Lex Machina generates a resolution for each case (e.g., terminated cases 2009-2016: 74.6% settled, 15.3% procedural outcomes, 6.1% claimant wins, 4.0% claim defendant wins).
guidance: Use resolution distributions to set realistic client expectations about settlement likelihood and to allocate resources toward litigation vs settlement efforts.

name: Use of timing analytics for strategy and budgeting
description: Lex Machina recommends using timing analytics to inform counsel and client decisions (e.g., budgeting for claim construction takes less time in Central/Northern Districts of California than in E.D.Tex or D.Del).
guidance: Apply district-specific timing and variability to set flat fees, schedule conflicts, and to advise clients about likely litigation timelines and cash-flow impacts.

name: Required contents of the translation for entry into the national phase (PCT Article 22 vs 39)
description: Under PCT Article 22: description, claims (if amended, both as originally filed and as amended, if applicant wishes amendments to form the basis for proceedings, together with any statement under PCT Article 19(1)), any text matter of drawings, abstract. Under PCT Article 39(1): description, claims, any text matter of drawings (if any of those parts has been amended, both as originally filed and as amended by the annexes to the IPRP Chapter II and claims amended under PCT Article 19, if applicant wishes these amendments to form the basis), abstract.
guidance: If only one translation (of original or amended parts) is furnished the Office will invite the applicant to furnish the missing translation within a reasonable time; failure may lead to deemed withdrawal. If translation of claims amended under PCT Article 19 is not furnished in due time, only those claims will be disregarded (PCT Rule 49.5(c‑bis)) and the international application will not be considered withdrawn (see footnote 1). Additional specific elements (e.g. Rule 13bis deposit references, sequence listings, statements under Article 19(1) and letters under PCT Rule 46.5(b)) must be furnished in an EPO official language when applicable (EP.03). When EPO acts as elected Office additional annexes to the IPRP (Chapter II) must be translated.

name: Page fee calculation rules and timing
description: Page fee is based on the international application as published: pages of the description, claims and drawings counted, plus one page in total for bibliographic data and abstract. Amended claims under PCT Article 19 and/or Article 34 are also considered part of the international publication and must be taken into account unless applicant indicates otherwise.
guidance: If parts of description/claims are amended on entry, the amended pages replace equivalent pages of the published international application and form the basis for calculating the page fee. Special rules apply if the international application was not published in an official EPO language and amendments are filed on entry. Pages amended after expiry of the 31‑month time limit are not counted. Page fees are not refunded if number of pages is reduced during proceedings (EP.05b). Completion of section 6 of Form 1200 helps to indicate which documents will form the basis for proceedings and compute the page fee correctly.

name: Failure to provide application in condition for examination within eight months (37 CFR 1.704(c)(13))
description: If an application is not in condition for examination as defined in paragraph (f) within eight months from filing (or national-stage commencement), PTA is reduced by days beginning the day after the eight-month date and ending on the date the application is in condition for examination.
guidance: Applicant must supply required elements (specification with at least one claim and abstract, compliant papers/drawings/sequence listings, oath/declaration or ADS with required info, and required fees) within eight months or face PTA reduction.

name: Condition for examination — what must be present (37 CFR 1.704(f))
description: An application filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a) is in condition for examination when it includes a specification (including at least one claim and an abstract), papers in compliance with § 1.52, drawings if any in compliance with § 1.84, any required English translation, sequence listings if applicable in compliance with §§ 1.821–1.825, the inventor's oath/declaration or an application data sheet containing § 1.63(b) information, the basic filing fee (§ 1.16(a) or (c)), the search fee (§ 1.16(k) or (m)), the examination fee (§ 1.16(o) or (q)), any required certified copy of a previous application, and any application size fee required under § 1.16(s).
guidance: For international applications, condition for examination is entering the national stage as defined in § 1.491(b) and meeting analogous requirements and fee payments under § 1.492. Correcting papers/drawings/sequence listings before the date of mailing of either an action under 35 U.S.C. 132 or a notice of allowance will be considered for purposes of being in condition for examination.

name: Improvements to another technology or technical field
description: Claim limitations that improve a technology or technical field (outside general-purpose computing) can be 'significantly more.'
guidance: Examples: Diamond v. Diehr — use of the Arrhenius equation to improve rubber-molding process control; SiRF Technology v. ITC — GPS receiver software using a mathematical formula to improve position determination in weak-signal environments.

name: Applying the judicial exception with, or by use of, a particular machine
description: Reciting application of the judicial exception by a particular, specially claimed machine (with specific structural/functional details) can demonstrate 'significantly more.'
guidance: Example: Mackay Radio & Telegraph v. Radio Corp. of America — a mathematical formula employed using a particular type of antenna with details such as shape, conductors, length, and angle. Note: a general-purpose computer that applies a judicial exception using conventional computer functions has not been found to qualify as a particular machine.

name: Adding a specific limitation other than what is well-understood, routine and conventional in the field
description: Reciting specific, unconventional limitations or steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application (beyond well-understood, routine, conventional activity) can be 'significantly more.'
guidance: Example: DDR Holdings, LLC v. Hotels.com, L.P. — claims recited automatic identification of a host web page, retrieval of 'look and feel' information, and generation of a hybrid web page combining merchant information with host look-and-feel, which differed from conventional hyperlink behavior and amounted to significantly more than an abstract idea.

name: Other meaningful limitations beyond generally linking to a technological environment
description: Limitations that do more than generally tie a judicial exception to a technology—i.e., meaningful concrete steps or structure—can constitute 'significantly more.'
guidance: Example: Diamond v. Diehr — beyond the Arrhenius equation, the claim recited installing rubber in a press, closing the mold, constantly measuring temperature, recalculating cure time, and opening the press at the proper time; these meaningful limitations limited the claim to practical application and were not an attempt to patent the mathematical equation.

name: Appending well-understood, routine and conventional activities specified at a high level (insufficient)
description: Adding conventional industry activities, recited at a high level of generality, does not convert a judicial exception into patent-eligible subject matter.
guidance: Examples: Mayo v. Prometheus — claim recited a natural correlation plus instructing a doctor to measure metabolite levels 'using any known process'; Alice Corp. — requiring a generic computer to perform routine functions (creating/maintaining shadow accounts, obtaining data, adjusting balances, issuing automated instructions) was insufficient because those were well-understood, routine, conventional activities.

name: Generally linking the judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use (insufficient)
description: Limitations that only generally tie an abstract idea or other judicial exception to a field of use or to use with computers/networks, without meaningful additional limitations, are insufficient to make the claim 'significantly more.'
guidance: Examples: Bilski v. Kappos — claims describing hedging in commodities/energy markets merely linked the concept to those markets without meaningful limits; Parker v. Flook — limiting a mathematical formula to petrochemical/oil-refining industries did not impose meaningful limits; buySAFE Inc. v. Google, Inc. — using a computer to receive/send information over a network simply attempted to limit an abstract idea to a computer environment.

name: Examiner should immediately inspect amendments
description: Actions by applicant, especially those filed near the end of the period for reply, should be inspected immediately upon filing to determine whether they are completely responsive to the preceding Office action so as to prevent abandonment of the application.
guidance: All amended applications forwarded to the examiner should be inspected at once to determine: (A) proper signature (MPEP § 714.01(a)); (B) filed within statutory/shortened period or time limit (MPEP § 710–§ 710.05); (C) fully responsive and complies with 37 CFR 1.121 (MPEP § 714.03 and § 714.04); (D) whether changes warrant transfer (MPEP § 903.08(d)); (E) whether application is special (MPEP § 708.01); (F) if claims suggested for interference have been copied (Chapter 2300); (G) traversal of a restriction requirement (MPEP § 818.03(a)); (H) use of non-permanent ("easily erasable") paper (MPEP § 714.07); (I) applicant-cited references (MPEP § 707.05(b) and § 1302.12); (J) terminal disclaimer filed (MPEP § 804.02, § 804.03, and § 1490); (K) any security-related matter added (MPEP § 115). If amendment is inadequate and sufficient time remains, applicant should be notified and warned to complete reply (see MPEP § 714.03).

name: Examiner action and explanation when amendment not entered
description: If a proposed amendment does not place the case in better form for appeal or in condition for allowance, the examiner should promptly inform applicant and the refusal should not be arbitrary.
guidance: The amendment should be given sufficient consideration to determine if claims are in condition for allowance or if appeal issues are simplified. Ordinarily specific deficiencies need not be discussed, but if the amendment raises new matter, the examiner should identify the subject matter that constitutes new matter. If amendment presents new issues requiring further consideration/search, provide explanation. Reasons for non-entry should be concise: (A) amendment would not avoid rejections and thus not place case in condition for allowance or for appeal; (B) amendment raises new matter; (C) amendment presents new issues requiring further consideration/search; (D) amendment presents additional claims without canceling finally rejected claims and thus does not place case in better condition for appeal. Examiners should indicate status of each claim of record or proposed and which proposed claims would be entered on filing of an appeal if filed in a separate paper.

name: Amendments after allowance governed by 37 CFR 1.312 (no right to amend)
description: No amendment may be made as a matter of right after mailing of the notice of allowance; any amendment must comply with 37 CFR 1.312 and be filed before or with payment of issue fee to be considered.
guidance: Amendments after allowance may be entered on recommendation of the primary examiner approved by the Director (delegated to SPE). Examples of 'amendments' include (A) specification amendment, (B) change in drawings, (C) amendment to claims, (D) change in inventorship, (E) submission of prior art, (F) petition to correct spelling of inventor's name, (G) petition to change order of inventors, etc. An amendment under 1.312 must be filed on or before the date the issue fee is paid (except where required by Office of Patent Publication). Entries that merely correct formal matters without changing scope or that cancel claims may be entered by primary examiner; other amendments require SPE approval. If amendment is non-compliant with 1.121 but would otherwise be recommended, examiner may enter and correct non-compliance via examiner's amendment. See MPEP § 714.16 and § 714 generally.

name: Considerations for entering amendments under 37 CFR 1.312
description: Amendments after allowance should be considered only where they are needed for proper disclosure/protection and require no substantial additional work by the Office.
guidance: The Technology Center Director may set policy regarding trivial informalities. Consideration of an amendment under 1.312 cannot be demanded as a matter of right. For amendments affecting disclosure, scope of any claim, or adding a claim, remarks accompanying the amendment must fully and clearly state: (A) why the amendment is needed; (B) why the proposed amended or new claims require no additional search or examination; (C) why the claims are patentable; and (D) why they were not presented earlier. The requirements of 37 CFR 1.111(c) (pointing out patentable novelty) apply. Examiner may recommend entry only if these showings are satisfactory and entry would not require substantial Office work.

name: UK Patent Box calculation process (claim steps)
description: Process: calculate qualifying income by identifying revenue streams from qualifying patents; calculate the profit generated from this qualifying income; calculate residual profit by deducting routine profit made from routine business activities; calculate the Patent Box profit by deducting any profits derived from branding or marketing attributes; then use the HMRC formula to calculate the corporate tax deduction.
guidance: Companies must calculate their qualifying Patent Box profit and then apply a specific formula in their tax computation to calculate the deduction, and take the tax deduction as a benefit in their CT600 corporate tax return. Detailed HMRC guidance/manual (CIRD) should be followed for the precise steps and apportions.

name: Treatment of exclusive licences
description: Income generated from exclusive licences will be qualifying income on both sides of the agreement (licensor and licensee), subject to specific conditions concerning the meaning of exclusivity.
guidance: Check conditions on exclusivity in the legislation to determine when both parties may claim. Anti-avoidance rules will scrutinize arrangements that grant exclusivity for the sole purpose of achieving Patent Box eligibility.

name: Provide a legible copy of the patent to be reexamined (and related certificates)
description: Include a copy of the patent to be reexamined including any disclaimer(s), certificate(s) of correction or prior reexamination certificate(s).
guidance: Provide a legible copy of the entire patent (front face, drawings, specification/claims in double column format), each page plainly written on only one side. Illegible copies are not accepted. For non-English references provide translations of relevant portions.

name: Provide a clear Statement of a Substantial New Question of Patentability (SNQ)
description: For each SNQ, state concisely the new technological teaching provided by at least one patent or publication cited for that SNQ, and explain how it presents a new, non-cumulative teaching for the claims at issue.
guidance: Identify what the new technological teaching is or how the reference is presented in a 'new light' for every claim for which reexamination is requested. Provide citations to specific portions of references. Do not attempt to identify every claim limitation as the new teaching (this can obscure the SNQ). State whether the reference was previously considered and to what extent. Provide SNQ statements separate from the detailed proposed rejections. See MPEP §§2216/2616.

name: Identify every claim for which reexamination is requested
description: Provide an identification of every claim that is the subject of the reexamination request.
guidance: Clearly state which claims are applicable to each proposed rejection; do not use phrases like 'at least claims 1 and 2.' Proper claim identification is part of filing-date compliance.

name: State clearly each and every Proposed Rejection
description: Do NOT lump multiple proposed rejections based on different grounds; state each proposed rejection explicitly.
guidance: Separate anticipation (35 U.S.C. 102) explanations from obviousness (35 U.S.C. 103) explanations; separate alternative primary/secondary teachings; avoid 'and/or' and footnote 'suggestions' of other rejections. Group multiple claims under the same ground where appropriate (e.g., 'claims 1-4, 6, 8, and 12 should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(b) as anticipated by Smith'). For patent-owner requests, clearly state which references apply to which claims and identify what elements are or are not shown.

name: Provide a Detailed Explanation for each Proposed Rejection or Application of the Art
description: For each proposed rejection (or, for patent owners, each application of the art), provide a separate, detailed explanation showing how the references apply to every claim limitation.
guidance: For every limitation: (1) point out how the reference meets/teaches the limitation, or (2) for patent-owner requests state that the limitation is not covered, or (3) admit the limitation is known where applicable. For dependent claims, show how prior art applies to added limitations and refer to explanations of base claims. For obviousness, explain what the primary reference teaches, what it fails to teach, how other prior art supplies missing limitations, and why a person of ordinary skill would combine them (provide a reason). Use either a claim chart OR prose (not both), keep explanations consistent with the proposed rejection, and include only the claims and references listed in the proposed rejection. Ensure an explanation only addresses anticipation when the basis is 102 and only addresses obviousness when the basis is 103.

name: Claim chart vs narrative: provide one clear format
description: The detailed explanation must be in claim chart or prose (narrative) format — do not provide both.
guidance: Providing both inflates length and risks inconsistencies; pick one format and be consistent.

name: Clearly state the statutory basis for each proposed rejection and avoid vague groupings
description: Identify whether references are applied under 35 U.S.C. 102 or 35 U.S.C. 103 and explain each proposed rejection separately.
guidance: Do not conflate 102 and 103 explanations; avoid statements like 'Reference A also makes Claim 1 obvious' without detailed obviousness reasoning. Avoid alternate cumulative references grouped with 'and/or' — separately explain each combination you propose (e.g., A in view of C; B in view of C), and avoid headings that suggest additional unexplained rejections.

name: Organize submission with clear headings and include required items under clear headings
description: Inclusion of required items (fee, SNQ statement, claim identification, detailed explanation, copies of references, etc.) with appropriate and clear headings simplifies review.
guidance: Clear headings help USPTO support staff, examiners, patent owners, and the public and reduce likelihood of defect identification or denial of reexamination.

name: When to examine entitlement to priority (intervening references / AIA FITF context)
description: The subject matter of the application is not examined to determine entitlement to the priority of the foreign filing date unless such determination is required for patentability reasons (e.g., when an intervening reference by the inventive entity is found with an effective date between the foreign filing date and the U.S. filing date under the AIA FITF provisions).
guidance: If an intervening reference is found, examiner may reject claims as unpatentable without paying attention to priority date if certified copy not yet filed. Applicant may argue or file foreign papers to overcome rejection. Examiner may require foreign papers (and repeat or continue the rejection as appropriate). Form paragraph 2.19 may be used (Overcome Rejection by Translation).

name: Translation requirement for non-English certified copy
description: When an English language translation of a non-English language foreign application is required, the translation must be that of the certified copy (of the foreign application as filed) submitted together with a statement that the translation of the certified copy is accurate.
guidance: If applicant files the certified copy to overcome an intervening reference, the translation should be required at the same time. Examiner may reject unpatentable claims and require an English translation if the certified copy is not in English and no translation is present. See 37 CFR 1.55 and MPEP §§ 215 and 216.

name: Examiner action after certified copy and translation are filed
description: If the certified copy and translation (if necessary) are filed to overcome the date of a reference, the examiner is to study the certified copy (and translation) to determine if the applicant is entitled to the priority date. If entitled, the rejection is withdrawn; if not entitled, repeat the rejection stating reasons.
guidance: If certified copy is already in file when an intervening reference is found, study it; if entitlement is shown, do not rely on the reference (may cite to applicant on form PTO-892); if not, reject unpatentable claims with explanation.

name: Examine foreign application for identity of invention and sufficiency under 35 U.S.C. 112
description: The most important aspect of the examiner’s action pertaining to a right of priority is the determination of the identity of invention between the U.S. and the foreign applications. The foreign application must be examined for sufficiency of the disclosure under 35 U.S.C. 112 as well as to determine if there is a basis for the claims sought.
guidance: A nonprovisional application may be entitled to the filing date of the foreign application for some claims and not others; applicant may rely on multiple foreign applications for different claims. For UK provisional specifications, note that they need not contain a complete disclosure under 35 U.S.C. 112; if insufficient, reliance may be had on a complete specification if presented, which would be treated as a different application.

name: 35 U.S.C. 119(b)(1) identification requirements for priority
description: No application for patent shall be entitled to this right of priority unless a claim is filed identifying the foreign application by specifying the application number on that foreign application, the intellectual property authority or country in or for which the application was filed, and the date of filing the application, at such time during the pendency of the application as required by the Director.
guidance: Director may consider failure to file a timely claim as a waiver and may establish procedures (including fees) to accept unintentionally delayed claims; Director may require certified copy, translation, and other information (certified by foreign authority) showing dates of application and specification filings.

name: Incorporation by reference relief under 37 CFR 1.57(b) — threshold rule
description: Subject to conditions and requirements, if all or a portion of the specification or drawings is inadvertently omitted from an application, but the application contains a claim under 37 CFR 1.55 or 1.78 that was present on the filing date, and the inadvertently omitted portion is completely contained in the prior-filed application, the claim under 37 CFR 1.55 or 1.78 shall be considered an incorporation by reference of the prior-filed application as to the omitted portion.
guidance: 37 CFR 1.57(b) provides a safeguard for inadvertent omissions allowing later amendment to add omitted material if it is completely contained in a prior-filed application; see also MPEP § 608.01(p) for explicit incorporation statements.

name: CLEARLY DEFINE CLAIM TERMS IN THE SPECIFICATION
description: A patentee may be his or her 'own lexicographer and/or may disavow claim scope,' but to do so, the 'patentee must clearly express that intent in the written description.' M.P.E.P. § 2111. Explicit definitions in the specification can be used strategically to assign a special (narrow) definition that avoids known prior art or excludes an inapplicable plain-and-ordinary meaning.
guidance: Although drafters often avoid explicit definitions to evade unnecessarily limiting claims, in appropriate situations lexicography should be used to define terms narrowly. The specification is the single best guide to claim meaning (see Abbott). Even where not in definitional format, the specification may define terms by implication (see In re Chaganti; In re Suitco Surface). Anti-pattern: omitting definitions and thereby allowing claim terms to be construed more broadly under BRI.

name: USE TERMS TO EXPLAIN THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN CLAIM ELEMENTS
description: When drafting claims, use language (antecedent basis, relative terms like 'other') to show that different claim elements refer to distinct items and to prevent improper conflation of elements.
guidance: Appropriate use of antecedent basis and relative terms can demonstrate that elements are separate and should not be merged by an examiner. Example: Microsoft Corp. v. Proxyconn — 'two other computers' recited independently plus the word 'other' denotes a further level of distinction, undermining an interpretation that collapses those computers into the caching computer. Draft claims to make relationships explicit to avoid unreasonable constructions.

name: RELY ON SPECIFICATION TO LIMIT REACH OF BRI
description: Even absent explicit definitions, read claim language in light of the specification as one of ordinary skill would; the specification often provides the best ammunition against an unreasonable, overly broad PTO construction under BRI.
guidance: Argument strategy: point to specification teachings, embodiments, and contextual language (including non-exhaustive lists or phrasing that shows boundaries) to show that a proposed broad construction is unreasonable. Cases: In re Abbott Diabetes Care (spec read in light of specification), In re Chaganti (specification undermined PTAB interpretation). Note that terms defined by implication in the spec can defeat PTO constructions that include features contrary to the spec's embodiments.
