name: CITE OTHER CLAIM LIMITATIONS TO SHOW A PROFFERED CONSTRUCTION IS ILLOGICAL
description: Use other express claim limitations to demonstrate that an overly broad construction would create illogical results or render other claim limitations redundant.
guidance: Show that construing a term to include features already recited elsewhere makes those recitations redundant (Apple v. Ameranth). Use the claim's full language and clauses to demonstrate that the examiner/PTAB construction conflicts with how the claim reads (D'Agostino example regarding 'single merchant'). Examples include PPC Broadband (continuity member language) and D'Agostino. Strategy: point to internal claim structure and express recitations to argue unreasonableness.

name: USE DEPENDENT CLAIMS AND CLAIM DIFFERENTIATION TO GIVE FURTHER CONTEXT
description: Include dependent claims that add features or restrictive language to provide fallback positions and to guide interpretation of terms in independent claims via the doctrine of claim differentiation.
guidance: Dependent claims can (a) create fallback claim scope and (b) set inner boundaries for terms in independent claims because if a proposed construction of an independent claim would nullify dependent claims, claim differentiation creates a presumption that such a construction is improper (Marine Polymer Techs. v. HemCon). Draft dependent claims intentionally to provide contextual anchoring against broad BRI constructions.

name: Patent disseizor claims and time limits
description: A person claiming to be the true owner (patent disseizor) may demand the court to grant the patent to themselves; claims (and partial claims) can be performed within two years from publication of patent grant, or if malicious intent, until the end of patent protection.
guidance: Proceedings and final decisions are registered and published on the Bulletin and generate effect against bona fide third parties as of registry date. Changes of ownership may terminate third-party licenses; transitional non-monopolized licenses may be ordered by court on equitable terms.

name: Consequences for third-party licensees when ownership changes
description: Upon change of patent ownership under these rules, third parties’ license rights regarding the patent and other recognized rights expire with registry of the change; prior bona fide users may be entitled to a non-monopolized license from the true patentee.
guidance: Prescribed time periods to claim such rights differ: two months for individuals already known as true patentee on the registry and four months for the patent receiver, counting from Office notification of registration. Terms issued should be reasonable and may be modeled on compulsory license provisions; malicious actors are excluded.

name: Remuneration and factors for calculating worker's rate
description: If employer claims full rights the worker can demand a reasonable amount; if employer claims partial rights and uses the invention, the worker can demand payment. In calculating the rate, consider the economic evaluability of the invention, the worker’s job in the business, and the business’s contribution to the invention.
guidance: Employer cannot avoid payment by alleging invention not worth protection unless a court confirms nonpatentability. Method of payment should follow agreement between parties; rate tariff and arbitration procedures for disputes are determined by regulation. Payments and methods are separately determined for multiple workers.

name: Employer obligation to apply for patent when claiming full rights and exceptions
description: If employer claims full rights they are obliged to file the first patent application to the Office, unless filing is avoided for business interests; exceptions where obligation vanishes include (a) invention becoming independent, (b) worker consents not to file, (c) protecting company secrets.
guidance: Worker may personally apply if invention becomes independent. If the employer does not file within the time period determined by the worker, the invention acquires independent status. Employer may file applications abroad and reserve non-monopolized rights for a fee; employer must facilitate worker obtaining patents in countries where employer does not wish to obtain patent, timely to preserve priority.

name: Joinder where broader relief embraces others (Article 56)
description: Cases may be joined when there is identity of parties and cause of action but the relief sought in one case, being broader, embraces the relief sought in the other cases (Article 56 CPC).
guidance: This provides for joining related claims even where requests differ in scope, so long as one encompasses the other.

name: Judge's case management powers (Article 139 I–X)
description: The judge must ensure equal treatment, reasonable duration, prevent dilatory acts, determine coercive measures, promote resolution by parties, extend procedural terms and change evidence order, exercise police power, order personal presence, determine procedural compliance, and notify public bodies in repeated individual claims.
guidance: These powers authorize active judicial management to promote efficiency, fairness, and timeliness in patent cases; Article 139 sole paragraph limits term extensions to before the regular term ends.

name: Genus-species predictability test (unpredictable arts)
description: Where predictability is in question, the affidavit or declaration must show as much as the minimum disclosure required by a patent specification to furnish support for a generic claim; showing a single species may not ordinarily withdraw a rejection based on a reference disclosing a species.
guidance: The test is whether species completed by applicant provide an adequate basis to infer that the invention has generic applicability; more species may be required for large/unpredictable genera (cases: In re Shokal, Mantell, Rainer, DeFano, Clarke).

name: Review for prior public use, on-sale bar, and best mode
description: Examiners must review affidavits/declarations and accompanying evidence to determine whether they show that the claimed invention was in public use or on sale in the U.S. more than one year prior to the effective filing date (statutory bars). Also, if the 1.131 evidence relies on an embodiment not disclosed in the application, the best mode requirement must be considered.
guidance: Even if an affidavit overcomes a reference, prior public use or on-sale activities may create a statutory bar that cannot be overcome under 1.131 (see MPEP § 2133.03). A best mode rejection should be made only where the record, by a preponderance of the evidence, shows the specification fails to set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor (see MPEP § 2165–2165.04).

name: 37 CFR 1.132 affidavits — traversing rejections and scope
description: Affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132 may be received to traverse rejections based on a U.S. patent which substantially shows but does not claim the same patentable invention, foreign patents, printed publications, facts within the personal knowledge of an Office employee, allegations about mode or capability of operation, inoperative or non-utility contentions, or objections that the alleged invention is frivolous or injurious to public health or morals.
guidance: Primary examiner personally reviews whether a 1.132 submission is responsive to the rejection and presents sufficient facts to overcome it. The enumerated grounds in the rule are exemplary; affidavits falling outside other specific rules should be treated under 1.132. Use MPEP form paragraphs (7.65–7.66 and subparagraphs) when commenting on 1.132 affidavits.

name: Unity of invention — categories and combinations
description: An application may claim inventions in categories such as (1) a product, (2) a process for obtaining the product, (3) an apparatus or means specially designed for carrying out the process, or combinations thereof (e.g., product + process, product + apparatus + process specially adapted for manufacture).
guidance: If claims contain claims to more or less than one of the combinations set forth, unity of invention might not be present. The determination whether a group of inventions forms a single general inventive concept shall be made without regard to whether the inventions are claimed in separate claims or as alternatives within a single claim. When multiple products/processes/uses are claimed, the first invention of the category first mentioned in the claims and the first recited invention of each other related category will be considered the main invention.

name: Determination of unity before the International Searching Authority (ISA)
description: Before establishing the international search report, the ISA will determine whether the international application complies with the requirement of unity of invention.
guidance: If the ISA considers the application lacks unity it shall inform the applicant and invite payment of additional fees (PCT Rule 40). The applicant is given a time period in accordance with PCT Rule 40.3 to pay additional fees. If no additional fees are paid, the international search will be performed only on the invention first mentioned (“main invention”) in the claims. Lack of unity may be evident before or after considering prior art (e.g., a discovered document may show a linking claim lacks novelty or is clearly obvious), in which case ISA may raise lack-of-unity objection.

name: Determination of unity before the IPEA and options on lack of unity
description: Before issuing any written opinion or IPER, the IPEA will determine unity of invention. If IPEA finds lack of unity it may (1) issue opinion/IPER indicating lack of unity without inviting restriction or additional fees (no IPE on inventions not previously searched), (2) invite applicant to restrict claims or pay additional fees within a non-extendable time limit, or (3) if applicant fails to restrict/pay, issue an opinion/IPER on the main invention and indicate facts.
guidance: If doubt exists as to which invention is main, the invention first mentioned in the claims and previously searched by an ISA shall be considered the main invention. Lack of unity may be evident before or after consideration of prior art (e.g., discovery of a document showing generic/linking claim lacks novelty or is obvious).

name: National stage fees: basic, search, examination, excess-claim and other surcharges
description: A schedule of fees applies to international applications entering the U.S. national stage: basic national fee, search fee (varies depending on prior ISA/IPER findings and which ISA performed search), examination fee, excess claim fees (per independent claim over 3; per claim over 20), multiple dependent claim fee, application size fee, surcharge for late payments, fee for late English translations, and fees for additional pages.
guidance: Tables specify amounts by entity status (micro/small/other). If fees for excess claims or multiple dependent claims are not paid with the basic national fee or on later presentation, they must be paid or the claims canceled by amendment prior to the expiration of the Office-set time period in any notice of fee deficiency to avoid abandonment. Surcharge applies when filing the search/exam fee or oath after national stage commencement. Application size fees are imposed for specifications/drawings exceeding thresholds (and per additional 50 sheets or fraction). Specific conditional zero-fee situations exist where an IPER or ISA written opinion states criteria of novelty, inventive step, and industrial applicability have been satisfied for all claims.

name: Translation and sequence listing rules for national stage
description: Translations and translated annexes/amendments must be furnished by the 30‑month deadline; sequence listing translation requirements differ by international filing date.
guidance: A translation into English of PCT Article 19 claim amendments and any annexes to an international preliminary examination report must be furnished not later than 30 months from the priority date; otherwise such amendments/annexes are considered canceled (except annex translations may be submitted later with processing fee). For international filing dates before July 1, 2022, a sequence listing need not be translated if PCT Rule 12.1(d) & PCT Rule 5.2(b) conditions met. For filing dates on or after July 1, 2022, an English translation is required for any Sequence Listing XML containing non‑English language values for any language‑dependent free text qualifiers (see §§ 1.831–1.834). Verification of translations may be required when filed if considered necessary.

name: Interpretation–Construction Distinction (conceptual tool)
description: The interpretation-construction distinction separates determining linguistic meaning (interpretation) from giving legal effect (construction).
guidance: Use this distinction to identify whether a dispute is about semantic meaning (solvable by linguistic evidence) or about normative legal effect (requires policy arguments). Avoid conflating the two: many claim disputes presented as linguistic are actually normative construction disputes.

name: Use of intrinsic evidence (specification, whole patent context) in interpretation
description: The patent specification and the remainder of the patent document are relevant contextual evidence for discerning linguistic meaning of claim terms.
guidance: Contextual reading of claims with the specification (e.g., subject-matter focus, grammar, how terms are used elsewhere in the patent) often resolves ambiguities; but this is an inquiry about ordinary linguistic usage rather than an argument that claims must be read to match the patentee's inventive contribution.

name: Use of extrinsic evidence (dictionaries, expert testimony, translators)
description: Dictionaries, encyclopedias, expert testimony, technical translators and other extrinsic sources can be used as proxies to determine how the intended audience would understand claim language.
guidance: Extrinsic evidence is appropriate for unfamiliar languages or technical jargon; such sources are proxies for usage patterns and the understanding of a person of ordinary skill in the art. But extrinsic evidence is secondary to intrinsic evidence when intrinsic context is available.

name: Plain and ordinary meaning / dictionary definitions as interpretive tools
description: Courts and commentators often appeal to 'plain meaning' or dictionary definitions to determine claim term meaning.
guidance: Dictionaries can provide evidence of conventional meaning but are proxies for deeper linguistic usage; overreliance or overstatement of 'plainness' may mischaracterize disputes that are actually normative. Use dictionaries as one piece of evidence, not the sole determinant.

name: Person of Ordinary Skill in the Art (POSITA) as interpretive audience
description: Interpretation often seeks the understanding that a person of ordinary skill in the art would have of claim terms.
guidance: Expert testimony and technical evidence help establish this audience's understanding; patent claims are written for POSITA, so their conventions and jargon matter in discerning linguistic meaning.

name: Invention-centered (anti-textualist/pragmatic) vs text-centered (textualist) approaches
description: Competing normative theories of construction: some argue claims should be construed according to the patentee's actual invention (invention-centered / anti-textualist / pragmatic textualism), while others argue for fidelity to the claim text (textualism).
guidance: Recognize this as a policy disagreement about what legal effect claim language should have; choosing between them is a constructional decision, not purely interpretive. Each approach carries different implications for patent scope and judicial role.

name: Distinguish construction from application (legal scope vs fact application)
description: Construction determines, as a matter of law, what the patentee's legal monopoly covers; application is the subsequent step of comparing an accused product to that legal scope.
guidance: Courts should construe claims (legal meaning) before applying that construction to the facts. But the fact that a court chooses a particular legal scope does not prove that this is the linguistic meaning of the term.

name: Interpretation is objective and resists radical indeterminacy claims
description: The linguistic meanings of legal texts are not radically indeterminate; linguistic communication works, and interpretation yields objective answers when evidence is available.
guidance: Reject the Critical Legal Studies-style claim that 'law means whatever judges say'; interpretative questions are factual in nature even if hard in practice. Empirical indicators like reversal rates do not in themselves prove semantic indeterminacy.

name: Use of grammar and ordinary usage conventions in resolving meaning
description: Grammar and ordinary rules of usage (including reading the claim in the context of surrounding sentences) are valid interpretive tools.
guidance: Apply grammatical analysis and ordinary-language reading to discern which sense of an ambiguous term fits the claim context (example: identifying 'manufacture' as a process in Merrill v. Yeomans).

name: Anti-textualist caution: do not conflate linguistic context with the patentee's inventive contribution
description: Using the specification as linguistic context (to discern ordinary usage) differs from the anti-textualist move that interprets claims according to the patentee's inventive contribution or what the patentee 'justly' has a right to.
guidance: Avoid reasoning that because the inventor only conceived certain embodiments the claim must be limited to them; that is a constructional/invention-centered normative move, not a purely interpretive one.

name: Recitation of relative dimensions without different performance
description: Where the only difference between the prior art and the claims is a recitation of relative dimensions and a device having the claimed relative dimensions would not perform differently, the claimed device is not patentably distinct.
guidance: See Gardner v. TEC Systems, Inc.; structural changes must produce different function or result to be patentable.

name: Purifying an old product
description: Purer forms of known products may be patentable, but mere purity by itself does not render the product unobvious; purified materials are novel vis-à-vis impure materials, but unobviousness depends on other factors.
guidance: Factors include whether the claimed compound/composition has the same utility as related prior-art materials and whether the prior art suggests the particular form/structure or methods of obtaining it. See In re Bergstrom, In re Cofer, Ex parte Gray, Ex parte Stern. Applicant bears burden to show unexpected properties or that prior art did not provide methods to obtain the purified form.

name: Obviousness of overlapping or close ranges
description: When claimed ranges overlap or lie inside ranges disclosed by the prior art, a prima facie case of obviousness exists; ranges that are close enough that one skilled in the art would expect similar properties may also be prima facie obvious.
guidance: See In re Wertheim, In re Woodruff, In re Geisler, Titanium Metals Corp. of America v. Banner. Consider whether prior-art numeric language (e.g., 'about') creates an overlap. If prior art range is extremely broad (genus-like), additional analysis may be required (see In re Baird, In re Jones). Multiple references can collectively disclose a 'range.'

name: Establishing a prima facie case of obviousness (Graham factors)
description: A proper obviousness analysis involves (A) determining the scope and content of the prior art; (B) ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims; (C) determining the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; and (D) evaluating any evidence of secondary considerations.
guidance: If a prima facie case is established, the burden shifts to applicant to come forward with rebuttal evidence/argument. See Graham v. John Deere and cases such as In re Bell, In re Rijckaert, In re Oetiker.

name: Ascertain differences between the closest disclosed prior art species/subgenus and the claimed species/subgenus
description: Identify the closest disclosed species/subgenus in the prior art and compare it to the claimed species/subgenus; make explicit findings on similarities/differences including structure, chemical properties, and utilities.
guidance: In re Stratoflex: focus on whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious. Examiners should compare structures and properties and document the comparison.

name: Determine whether one of ordinary skill would have been motivated to select the claimed species/subgenus
description: Considering prior-art findings (scope/content, differences, skill level), determine whether it would have been obvious to make the claimed invention as a whole — i.e., to select the claimed species/subgenus from the disclosed genus.
guidance: Focus on teachings in the prior art: (a) size of the genus; (b) express teachings that point to selection; (c) teachings of structural similarity; (d) predictability of the technology. Consider express suggestions to select or references that refer to one another (Merck v. Biocraft, In re Kemps).

name: Consider the size of the genus when evaluating species obviousness
description: The size of the prior art genus bears on whether a claimed species would have been envisioned by one skilled in the art, but size alone cannot support obviousness; the totality of circumstances matters.
guidance: Small, highly constrained genera (e.g., only 20 compounds with few variations) may render species obvious (In re Petering, In re Schaumann); broad genera may not. Evaluate number of species, variability, and other contextual factors.

name: Consider express teachings and structural similarity in motivating selection
description: If the prior art expressly teaches a reason to select the claimed species/subgenus or discloses a 'typical', 'preferred', or 'optimum' species structurally similar to the claimed species, that may provide motivation to select the claimed species.
guidance: Structural relationships (homologs, preferred species) often motivate selection because similar structures usually have similar properties (Dillon, Deuel). Point to explicit cross-reference between prior-art disclosures when present.

name: Notice of allowance — issuance and final fee deadline
description: When an examiner has reasonable grounds to believe a patent application complies with the Patent Act and Patent Rules, the Commissioner will notify the applicant via a notice of allowance and require payment of the final fee no later than four months after the date of the notice; failure to pay within that period results in deemed abandonment under paragraph 132(1)(f) of the Patent Rules.
guidance: The final fee includes a basic fee, a fee per page of specification/drawings in excess of 100 (excluding electronic sequence listing pages), and an excess claim fee for each claim in excess of 20 not already paid when requesting examination. See CIPO Patent Fees for amounts.

name: Final fee composition and excess claim fee calculation
description: The final fee is composed of the basic fee, a fee for each page of the specification and drawings in excess of 100 (other than pages of a sequence listing submitted electronically), and an excess claim fee for each claim in excess of 20 that was not already paid when requesting examination.
guidance: To calculate the excess claim fee, the Office looks at the maximum number of excess claims in the application from the date of the request for examination until the application is allowed. Example: if requested with 26 claims (6 excess), amendments raise to 30 (10 excess), later to 18 (maximum unchanged), the maximum during the period is 30 so excess claim fees are charged for 10 excess claims; if 6 were already paid, the notice requires payment for 4 additional excess claims.

name: Conditional notice of allowance — scope, examples of minor defects, and reply consequences
description: Where an examiner believes the application contains only certain minor defects which, if corrected, would allow the application, the Commissioner will issue a conditional notice of allowance indicating the outstanding minor defects and requiring satisfactory amendments or arguments.
guidance: Examples of minor defects include failing to meet margin requirements; failing to meet line spacing or font size; failure to have petition/abstract/description/claims each begin on a new page; failure to consecutively number pages; inclusion of drawings in petition/abstract/description/claims; trademarks included without identification; incorporation of documents by reference; references to documents not available to the public; failure to comply with sequence listing requirements; failure to comply with drawing requirements. The notice requires amendments to address defects and payment of the final fee within four months. If the applicant does not reply in good faith and the final fee is not paid, the application is deemed abandoned under paragraph 132(1)(g).

name: Content and structure requirements for a Final Action report
description: A Final Action is a particular type of examiner's report containing a requisition under subsection 86(5), prominently labelled FINAL ACTION (or 'Décision finale'), and indicating rejection under subsection 86(3) (or subsection 199(1) where applicable). The preamble should identify in broad terms the defects leading to rejection and which claims are defective or allowable.
guidance: The report should be drafted to make the point of disagreement clear, set out the applicant's position as understood by the examiner, and the examiner's reasoning for concluding the application does not comply despite applicant arguments. Where relevant, the report should include: a summary of the application emphasizing relevant claims; identification of any allowable claims; identification and discussion of relevant prior art; summary of relevant prior prosecution; discussion of legal/jurisprudential/administrative considerations central to the dispute; comprehensive grounds for rejection including rebuttal of applicant's arguments; and a brief summation recapitulating grounds for rejection. It may be beneficial to divide the report into sections with clear headings. To the extent practical, the Final Action should be understandable independently of other reports or responses so that interested persons (applicant, Patent Appeal Board, Commissioner, Court) can readily understand the dispute and reasoning.

name: Purpose of definiteness requirement
description: The primary purpose of the definiteness requirement for claim language is to ensure that the scope of the claims is clear so that the public is informed of the boundaries of what constitutes infringement of the patent.
guidance: Use this policy objective to guide whether claim language is sufficiently clear; focus on public notice of claim boundaries.

name: Indefiniteness standard (person of ordinary skill)
description: Claims are found indefinite only where a person of ordinary skill in the art could not determine the metes and bounds of the claims.
guidance: Assess whether a POSITA would be able to ascertain claim scope; if POSITA would read a claim with more than one reasonable interpretation, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112 second paragraph is appropriate.

name: Broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the specification
description: Give a claim its broadest reasonable interpretation, and review the claim as a whole in light of the specification (other claims and the written description) as understood by one of ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: Do not analyze claim terms in a vacuum; consider the application disclosure, teachings of the prior art, and claim interpretation by POSITA at time of invention (cites MPEP 2173.02, 2173.05(a), 2143.03).

name: Multiplicity of reasonable interpretations → rejection
description: If the language of a claim, considered as a whole in light of the specification and given its broadest reasonable interpretation, is such that a person of ordinary skill would read it with more than one reasonable interpretation then a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, is appropriate.
guidance: Where claim subject to more than one interpretation and at least one interpretation would render the claim unpatentable over the prior art, examiner should (1) reject the claim as indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112 second paragraph, and (2) reject the claim over the prior art based on the interpretation that renders the prior art applicable.

name: Means-plus-function limitation without corresponding structure
description: Claims that recite a means-plus-function limitation without disclosing corresponding structure in the specification can be held indefinite.
guidance: Identify lack of corresponding structure in spec for means/step-plus-function language (see Halliburton/Biomedino examples); if absent, 112 second paragraph rejection appropriate.

name: Numeric limitation lacking disclosed measurement method
description: A claim that includes a numeric limitation without disclosing which of multiple methods of measuring that number should be used may be indefinite.
guidance: If multiple reasonable measurement methods exist and spec doesn't indicate which to use, consider 112 second paragraph rejection (see Honeywell).

name: Subjective or purely opinion-dependent terms
description: Use of terms that are completely dependent on a person's subjective opinion can render a claim indefinite.
guidance: If a term's meaning turns entirely on subjective judgment and POSITA cannot ascertain boundaries, pursue an indefiniteness rejection (see Datamize).

name: Lack of proper antecedent basis
description: When it is unclear whether a particular limitation refers to an element previously presented, a claim should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112 second paragraph as being indefinite for failing to point out and distinctly claim the invention.
guidance: Reject where antecedent basis is missing and scope is not reasonably ascertainable; provide constructive suggestions for correction. Rarely, lack of explicit antecedent basis may not render claim indefinite if reasonably ascertainable (see Energizer).

name: Claim term not used/defined in specification and not discernible
description: If a claim term is not used or defined in the specification and the meaning of the claim term is not discernible, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112 second paragraph would be appropriate.
guidance: If term is not used/defined but meaning is discernible by POSITA, do not make a 112 rejection; instead make an objection under 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1) to the specification for lack of support/antecedent basis (example: 'surrender value protected investment credits' was discernible and not indefinite).

name: Applicant-defined terms (lexicographer) must still be clear to POSITA
description: Applicants may define claim terms in the written description and be their own lexicographers, but the provided definition must itself be clear and precise to one of ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: Even if a definition is given in spec, if that definition's broadest reasonable interpretation results in more than one meaning, an indefiniteness rejection is appropriate; check for inconsistencies between claim and specification disclosures.

name: Examiners should not use per se rules for technical rejections
description: Office policy is not to employ per se rules to make technical rejections; examiners should not be interpreted as discouraged from making appropriate 112 second paragraph rejections when evidence exists.
guidance: Avoid blanket/formulaic rejections; examine context. Examples: minor wording changes (use of 'the' vs 'a') when claim otherwise clear should not be a per se rejection.

name: Provide explanatory analysis in the record
description: Any rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112 second paragraph should include an analysis as to why the language, phrase(s) and term(s) used render the claim vague and indefinite.
guidance: Explain how and why claim language is unclear; provide examples and reasoning to help applicant respond; if withdrawal of rejection occurs after traversal, explain what prompted change citing specific argument or authority; if traversal not persuasive, maintain rejection and explain why not persuasive.

name: Ambiguity from similarly worded multiple elements
description: Indefiniteness may arise when a claim includes similarly worded structural elements and it is unclear whether recitations refer to the same or distinct elements (e.g., 'a translator controller' vs 'the linear translator').
guidance: If ambiguous whether later recitation is same element or different, issue 112 second paragraph rejection; if initial phrasing had used clearer antecedent ('a translator controller' then 'the controller') the issue might not arise.

name: Evaluate definiteness by threshold of clarity and particularity
description: Examination should focus on whether the claims meet the threshold requirements of clarity and precision — whether the claims set out and describe a particular subject matter with a reasonable degree of clarity and particularity.
guidance: Do not assess whether more suitable language exists; focus on whether claim language permits POSITA to determine scope with reasonable certainty.

name: Strip Out Adjectives
description: Most adjectives in claims are limiting and unnecessary. "A user-friendly graphical interface" - delete "user-friendly." "A high-performance processor" - delete "high-performance." Each adjective is something an accused product can lack.
guidance: Avoid non-functional, descriptive adjectives that narrow claim scope. When an adjective is not required to distinguish prior art or define the invention's operation, remove it. Examples: remove "user-friendly," "high-performance." Anti-pattern: relying on marketing adjectives to define elements.

name: Functional Claiming Carefully
description: Reciting elements by what they do (rather than what they are) is broader - but invokes 112(f) risk in U.S. practice.
guidance: To gain breadth while minimizing 112(f) (means-plus-function) risk, pair functional language with one or more concrete structural recitations (example: "a sensor configured to detect X, the sensor comprising Y"). Balance functional phrasing with structural detail and ensure the spec supports the functions/structures recited.

name: Genus, Not Species
description: If your invention works with springs, do not claim "a coil spring." Claim "a biasing element" - and disclose, as alternatives, coil springs, leaf springs, elastomer pads, gas springs. Each species disclosure supports a genus claim.
guidance: Claim broader categories (genus) rather than specific species when appropriate, and in the specification disclose multiple representative species as alternatives to support the genus. Practical tip: disclose examples of different species to provide written-description support for the genus claim.

name: Avoid Numerical Limits Unless Necessary
description: "At least 50% by weight" is a hard limit; an accused product at 49.9% does not infringe. If the number is not load-bearing for novelty, leave it out.
guidance: Exclude precise numeric limits unless required to distinguish prior art or define a necessary functional boundary. If numerical limits are needed, disclose ranges and multiple endpoints in the spec to allow claim flexibility. Be mindful that single-point numbers create hard, often unnecessary boundaries.

name: Watch Out for "Configured To" vs. "For"
description: "A processor for performing X" may invoke 112(f) post-Williamson; "a processor configured to perform X" plus a clear algorithmic disclosure in the spec is safer. The choice has scope consequences.
guidance: Choose phrasing carefully: "for" can be interpreted as functional language that triggers 112(f) under current case law; "configured to" is often preferable but requires accompanying disclosure (e.g., algorithmic steps) to support the claimed functionality. Consider how courts have interpreted the phrasing in your jurisdiction and ensure the spec provides concrete support.

name: Avoid Describing the Environment as a Limitation
description: A claim to a widget that says "for use in an automobile" - is the automobile a limitation? Maybe. If you do not need the automobile to distinguish prior art, do not include it.
guidance: Do not include environmental or intended-use language that could be read as a claim limitation unless necessary. Only recite environment or field-of-use when it is essential to novelty or operability; otherwise omit to preserve broader scope.

name: Use Open Transitional Language
description: "Comprising" admits additional unrecited elements. "Including" is treated similarly. "Consisting of" closes the claim. Default to comprising.
guidance: Prefer open transitional phrases (e.g., "comprising," "including") to allow additional, unrecited elements and maximize infringement scope. Use closed transitions (e.g., "consisting of") only when you intentionally want to exclude additional elements. Be explicit about transition terms because they determine openness/closedness of the claim.

name: Do Not Be Afraid of a Long Spec to Support Short Claims
description: Disclosure costs little; claim breadth is determined at the time of drafting and frozen. A 60-page spec supporting a 4-line claim is a fine outcome.
guidance: Invest in a detailed specification to support broad, concise claims. Extensive disclosure (examples, embodiments, species) can be used to justify broad claim language and to fend off written-description and enablement challenges later. Practical trade-off: longer spec is inexpensive compared to losing claim scope.

name: Beware Negative Limitations
description: "Wherein the device does not include X" must be supported in the spec by an explicit statement that X is absent. Santarus v. Par (Fed. Cir. 2012). Without spec support, the negative limitation is a 112(b) problem.
guidance: If you draft claims that exclude features (negative limitations), ensure the specification expressly supports the absence of the excluded feature. Cite/consider controlling case law (e.g., Santarus v. Par) showing that unsupported negative limitations can be indefiniteness or 112(b) problems. Anti-pattern: adding negatives in claims without corresponding spec language.

name: The Genus-Species Trade-Off in Biotech
description: In biotech, broad genus claims face heightened written-description scrutiny (Amgen v. Sanofi, 2023, on enablement). The lesson generalizes: in unpredictable arts, breadth must be earned by extensive disclosure of representative species and a unifying structural feature.
guidance: In unpredictable technical fields (especially biotech), claim breadth requires substantial representative disclosure and identification of a unifying structural/functional feature to satisfy written description and enablement. Support genus claims with many species examples and clear explanation of why the genus is enabled. Be mindful of recent case law (e.g., Amgen v. Sanofi) when asserting broad claims in such arts.

name: Support for targeted fee increases only when tied to examiner/examination resources
description: PPAC supports certain fee increases (e.g., excess claims, IDS, RCE tiering, AIA trial fees) only when there is confidence additional revenue will support examination quality or directly offset USPTO costs.
guidance: If fees increase, ensure funds are dedicated to examiners' time, tools, or processes that improve patent reliability; seek public assurance that fee increases will not be diverted.

name: Excess claims fee conditional support
description: PPAC is supportive of excess claims fee increases with the caveat that the public wants certainty that increased fee revenue will be spent on examination and/or giving examiners more time to evaluate expanded claim sets.
guidance: If imposing excess-claim fees, dedicate funds to provide examiners with additional time/resources to examine excess claims.

name: Photographs that could be illustrated by drawings
description: Photographs of the claimed invention that are capable of illustration by other means, such as ink drawings, should not be used if they are illegible after scanning.
guidance: OPAP may object to photographs that could be replaced by line drawings and which are illegible after scanning. See 37 CFR 1.84(b). Where possible, supply clear line drawings instead of photographs or supply higher-quality images that scan legibly.

name: Final rejection immediately following an RCE (37 CFR 1.114)
description: Claims of an application for which a Request for Continued Examination (RCE) has been filed may be finally rejected in the action immediately subsequent to the filing of the RCE where all claims after entry of the 1.114 submission (A) are drawn to the same invention claimed in the application prior to the entry, and (B) would have been properly finally rejected on the grounds and art of record in the next Office action if entered prior to the filing of the RCE.
guidance: Apply same principles as first-action final rejections (MPEP § 706.07(b)). Use appropriate form paragraph (e.g., 7.42.09). Note statutory and practice limitations (e.g., not made final if new ground necessitated by intervening law changes).

name: Transitional after-final practice (37 CFR 1.129(a))
description: Applicants in applications (other than reissue or design) pending at least two years as of June 8, 1995 (effective filing date June 8, 1993 or earlier) are entitled to have a first submission entered and considered on the merits after final rejection if the first submission and the fee under 37 CFR 1.17(r) are filed prior to filing an appeal brief and prior to abandonment. The finality of the final rejection is automatically withdrawn upon timely filing and payment. A second submission and fee are similarly permitted once more.
guidance: A 'submission' includes IDS, amendments to specification/claims/drawings, new substantive arguments, or new evidence but may not introduce new matter (35 U.S.C. 132). The transitional practice is only available to applications filed on or before June 8, 1995 and is not available for reissue/design applications or reexamination proceedings. Use Form Paragraph 7.41.01 to notify applicant. IDS previously refused because of 1.97(c)/(d) noncompliance may be treated as timely if compliant with 1.98 and fee rules (with special handling for submissions filed on/after 6/8/05 per 1.97(e)/1.17(p)).

name: Post-final amendments and affidavits/evidence entry criteria (before/during appeal)
description: Proposed amendments filed after a final rejection but prior to filing a brief will not be entered if they: (a) raise new issues requiring further consideration/search, (b) raise the issue of new matter, (c) do not place application in better form for appeal by materially reducing/simplifying issues, or (d) present additional claims without canceling a corresponding number of finally rejected claims. Affidavits or other evidence filed after final must show 'good and sufficient reasons' why the evidence is necessary and was not earlier presented (37 CFR 1.116(e)), and may be refused entry under appeal rules (37 CFR 41.33).
guidance: PTOL-303 sections list specific not-entered reasons and reference 37 CFR 1.116 and 41.33(a)/(d)(1). If affidavit/evidence is entered, examiner must explain status of claims after entry. Amendments not in compliance with 37 CFR 1.121 should be handled with PTOL-324 Notice of Non-Compliant Amendment.

name: Divided infringement definition
description: Scenarios where a single entity does not perform every element of a claim, but different entities perform different steps of a claim.
guidance: Examples include customers performing critical steps (e.g., a doctor performing a collection or diagnostic step, or a server user modifying a webpage). The concept is especially relevant as end-user sophistication and web/mobile/cloud technologies increase the likelihood of multi-actor performance.

name: Inducement (§271(b)) can apply without a single direct infringer (Akamai/McKesson ruling)
description: The Federal Circuit held that inducement under §271(b) does not require a single, direct infringer — knowingly inducing performance of each claim limitation, regardless of who performs it, can constitute inducement.
guidance: Per the combined en banc decision (Akamai Tech. v. Limelight Networks and McKesson Tech. v. Epic Systems), entities cannot be immunized merely because they delegated steps to others.

name: Use transformative treatment step to capture divided actors and avoid §101 risk
description: In some cases (e.g., personalized medicine diagnostics involving data gathering, analysis, correlation, and treatment by different entities), adding a transformative treatment step may allow claims performed by divided entities to avoid dismissal under §101.
guidance: This technique can enable protection of previously unpatentable or narrowly-drafted claims by ensuring the claim recites a transformative act, but must be balanced against claim breadth and validity risks.

name: Industries most affected
description: Software, business methods, diagnostics, and biotechnology are particularly impacted due to common use of method claims and multi-actor implementations.
guidance: As cloud/mobile/web technologies and personalized medicine grow, the likelihood of divided-infringement scenarios increases; practitioners in these fields should pay special attention to claim drafting and enforcement strategy.

name: Policy and dissent perspectives (cautionary context)
description: Dissenting judges argued that patentees can usually draft claims to capture a single-party infringer and that expanding inducement liability is a judicial creation with uncertain policy consequences.
guidance: Awareness of dissenting views is important because they reflect potential avenues for future legal challenge and underscore that the decision is contentious and may be narrowed or reversed.

name: Unexpected results must be supported by evidence (not argument)
description: A showing of unexpected results must be based on evidence, not attorney argument, conclusory statements, or speculation.
guidance: Comparative data or factual support is required; conclusory statements (e.g., claiming unusually low immune response without comparative data) are insufficient to overcome a prima facie case of obviousness. See Dillon, In re Mayne, and MPEP § 716.02 - § 716.02(g).

name: Nexus requirement between proffered evidence and the claimed invention
description: To be entitled to substantial weight, applicant should establish a nexus between the rebuttal evidence and the claimed invention; objective evidence of nonobviousness must be attributable to the claimed invention.
guidance: The PTO relies on the applicant to provide hard evidence of commercial success or other secondary considerations (In re Huang). Evidence of commercial success for articles not covered by the claims is not probative (Paulsen). Applicant bears the burden of establishing nexus; examiners should consider whether evidence is commensurate in scope (Kulling, Grasselli).

name: Commensurateness of evidence in scope with the claimed invention
description: Evidence must be reasonably commensurate in scope with the claimed invention; however, applicant need not show unexpected results across the entire claimed range.
guidance: Evidence that a compound/composition possesses superior properties in one of a spectrum of common properties can suffice if a skilled artisan could reasonably extend the probative value (Chupp, Clemens). One test may be insufficient where no adequate basis exists to conclude other claimed compounds would behave similarly (Lindner, Grasselli, Greenfield).

name: Do not import unclaimed specification limitations into claims
description: Although claims are interpreted in light of the specification, limitations from the specification are not read into the claims if they are not recited in the claims.
guidance: See In re Van Geuns, Constant v. AMD, and related case law. Results or limitations discussed only in the specification may be germane to patentability of an embodiment but not to the claims if not claimed.

name: Prior art must be enabling to support a conclusion of obviousness for compounds
description: A conclusion of obviousness based on structural relationships between compounds requires that the references relied upon, together with the knowledge of a person skilled in the art, be enabling so as to put the public in possession of the claimed invention.
guidance: If the prior art fails to disclose or render obvious a method for making a claimed compound at the time the invention was made, this may overcome a presumption of obviousness (Hoeksema, Le Grice, Grose). Applicant may bear the burden of producing evidence that the reference would not enable a skilled artisan to produce the claimed compounds.

name: Deliberate course of action is not unintentional
description: A delay resulting from a deliberately chosen course of action on the part of the applicant does not become "unintentional" within the meaning of 37 CFR 1.137(b).
guidance: Examples of deliberate reasons that will not be considered unintentional include: (A) applicant does not consider claims patentable over references in an outstanding Office action; (B) applicant does not consider allowed/patentable claims of sufficient breadth to justify expense; (C) applicant does not consider any patent of sufficient value to justify expense; (D) applicant does not consider any patent of sufficient value to maintain interest; (E) applicant seeks to defer patent fees and prosecution expenses though remains interested in eventual patent. Case law (In re Application of G; In re Maldague) supports that a deliberate choice remains intentional even if the applicant later changes their mind.

name: Items required for a grantable petition (general PTO/SB/64)
description: NOTE: A grantable petition requires the following items: (1) Petition fee; (2) Reply and/or issue fee; (3) Terminal disclaimer with disclaimer fee - required for all utility and plant applications filed before June 8, 1995; and for all design applications; and (4) Statement that the entire delay was unintentional.
guidance: The form PTO/SB/64 enumerates these required items; fees vary for small entity vs other than small entity (see 37 CFR 1.17(m) and claim small entity under 37 CFR 1.27). The reply may have been filed previously or be enclosed with the petition; issue/publication fees likewise may be previously paid or enclosed.

name: Small entity fee claim and fee amounts
description: Petition fee (and terminal disclaimer fee when applicable) have small entity and other-than-small-entity amounts; the form provides fields to indicate small entity claim (37 CFR 1.17(m); see 37 CFR 1.27).
guidance: Applicants claiming small entity status should indicate it on the form; fee amounts differ depending on entity status. Failure to pay correct fee may affect grantability.

name: USPTO may request additional information when unintentionality is in question
description: The United States Patent and Trademark Office may require additional information if there is a question as to whether either the abandonment or the delay in filing a petition under 37 CFR 1.137(b) was unintentional (MPEP 711.03(c), subsections (III)(C) and (D)).
guidance: Including a simple statement that the entire delay was unintentional accelerates treatment, but applicants should be prepared to submit supporting factual statements or evidence if the Office questions the claim of unintentional delay.

name: Incorporate desired amendments into initial specification
description: To avoid preliminary amendments, applicants should incorporate any desired amendments into the text of the specification (including a new set of claims) at filing, even for continuations or divisionals; a new specification reflecting parent amendments may be submitted together with a copy of the oath/declaration from the previous application, provided no new matter is included.
guidance: Specific references to prior applications required by 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or 120 and 37 CFR 1.78(a) for applications filed on/after Sept 16, 2012 may be submitted in an Application Data Sheet (ADS) rather than in a preliminary amendment; if submitted in a preliminary amendment, a substitute specification is not required if only a benefit claim is added or amended.

name: Appendices and program listings printing rules
description: Appendices, other than those containing sequence listings or certain tables, are not printed if they are contained on pages located after the claims. Computer program listings may be printed if included in the specification before the claims, but program listings provided on compact disc per 37 CFR 1.96(c) and 1.52(e) are not printed as part of the patent or patent application publication.
guidance: If multiple claim sets exist, pages after the first set of claims may be treated as appendices and not printed. Place critical material before the claims to ensure printing.

name: Requirement: proprietor of a granted patent protecting the product
description: You must be the proprietor of a granted patent protecting the product in question.
guidance: The patent must be granted (not merely applied for) and must effectively protect the specific product for which the SPC is sought—i.e., the product falls within the scope/claims of the patent.

name: Implicit constraint: not all patents are eligible
description: Only 'some patents' are eligible for an SPC—eligibility is constrained by product type, patent coverage, and regulatory approval status.
guidance: Before pursuing an SPC, confirm that the patent claims cover the marketed product and that the regulatory approval qualifies for SPC purposes; eligibility assessments are case-specific.

name: Minimum filing requirements — direct national application
description: Minimum requirements for securing a filing date (and priority date): (a) the name and address of the applicant; (b) the name and address of the inventor; (c) a specification comprising a description, claims and any necessary drawings; and (d) the country and filing date of any earlier application whose priority is claimed.
guidance: Preferable (but not essential) to file: priority serial number and IPC symbol (file within 3 months), state of incorporation/nationality of applicant, an abstract, an Appointment of Agent form, and if applicant is not inventor a statement explaining derivation of rights (assignment/employment). These additional items (f–i) may be filed later during preliminary examination. No requirement to file assignment from inventor to applicant.

name: Patent Prosecution Highway (PPH) eligibility and requirements
description: PPH is available to expedite Malaysian prosecution based on favourable examination results of a corresponding JP, EP, CN or PCT application (reference application) by JPO, EPO or CNIPA.
guidance: Conditions: corresponding relationship (priority/common PCT); one or more claims of reference application indicated as allowable by first Patent Office; claims in Malaysian application sufficiently correspond to allowed claims; normal examination has been requested; if examination request filed previously, examination has not yet started. Required documents: relevant office actions or latest office action containing allowable claims or Written Opinion/IPRP, the claims deemed allowable, any non-patent prior art cited, English translations where applicable. Documents accessible via AIPN/DAS/Patentscope need not be submitted (list suffices). Machine translations admissible; MyIPO may request accurate translation if insufficient. If reference application unpublished, documents must be submitted. MyIPO will decide within two weeks; if accepted, allocated to Examiner and any office action issued within three months; applicant must respond within two months. Final decision on grant should be obtainable within six months of submitting PPH request.

name: ASPEC (ASEAN Patent Examination Cooperation) processing requirements
description: ASPEC allows participating offices to consider search and examination reports of a corresponding application from another participating office to advance prosecution out of turn until grant.
guidance: Requirements: corresponding applications (priority/common PCT); a copy of the search report and examination report from the other office plus the claims covered; at least one claim determined allowable; documents filed in English or with verified English translations. No official fee payable.

name: Utility innovation certificate requirements and limits
description: Utility innovation defined as any innovation creating a new product or process or improvement capable of industrial application; there is no requirement for an inventive step.
guidance: Filing requirements and prosecution procedure similar to patents. Utility innovation may have only one claim and maximum term is 20 years from filing. Renewal beyond 10 and 15 years from filing is dependent on completing an extension procedure with evidence of commercial or industrial use in Malaysia or a satisfactory explanation of non-use.

name: Enablement and Written Description (35 U.S.C. § 112) — high-level requirement
description: The application must teach a POSITA how to make and use the claimed compounds without undue experimentation and must demonstrate possession of the claimed invention at filing.
guidance: This requirement encompasses providing synthetic routes, starting materials, characterization data, and utility. Lack of enablement or written description can lead to rejections, especially for broad genus claims.

name: Compound Claims (Per Se Claims)
description: Claims that recite the chemical structure itself (e.g., 'A compound of Formula I... or a pharmaceutically acceptable salt thereof').
guidance: Compound claims provide the broadest protection — they cover the compound for any use. If a competitor makes the patented compound for any purpose, they infringe. Use these to obtain broad core protection.

name: Method of Use Claims
description: Claims to methods of using the compound to treat diseases or achieve specific results (e.g., 'A method of treating Type 2 diabetes comprising administering...').
guidance: These claims can extend protection by covering therapeutic uses discovered later. They are useful when different indications or treatment regimens are developed after the compound patent is filed.

name: Method of Making Claims
description: Claims that recite synthetic routes or processes for preparing the compound (e.g., reacting A with B in presence of a catalyst).
guidance: Useful when a novel or improved synthesis exists. They won't prevent others from making the compound by different methods, but can protect proprietary manufacturing processes.

name: Markush Structures: Claiming Chemical Genus
description: A Markush claim defines a core chemical structure with variable groups (R1, R2, etc.) that can be independently selected from defined lists, allowing a single claim to cover a family of related compounds.
guidance: Markush claims can cover thousands or millions of theoretical compounds and are strategic when you have tested a subset of compounds but want broader protection. Draft carefully to define core and substituent lists logically.

name: USPTO Requirements for Markush Claims
description: USPTO requires that all members of a Markush genus share a common use and a substantial structural similarity.
guidance: If a Markush claim is too broad or substituents yield compounds with different uses/properties, the examiner may issue a restriction requirement forcing election of a subgenus. Ensure substituent lists create compounds that are structurally cohesive and directed to the same utility.

name: Genus Claims (Broad Coverage) — strategic risk
description: Genus claims cover a broad class of compounds (via Markush or general descriptions) and provide wide protection but face higher risks of enablement and written description rejections.
guidance: Risk: USPTO may reject genus claims if insufficient examples or if POSITA couldn't make all claimed compounds without undue experimentation. Consider supporting genus claims with many examples, SAR, predictive rationale, or rely on dependent species claims as fallback.

name: Species Claims (Narrow but Strong)
description: Claims reciting specific individual compounds actually synthesized and characterized (e.g., 'The compound 2-(4-methoxyphenyl)-5-chlorobenzimidazole...').
guidance: Easier to defend on enablement/written description grounds but provide narrower protection. Use species claims to protect leads; they are more likely to survive prosecution if a genus is challenged.

name: Strategic Approach: Claim Both Genus and Species
description: Include independent genus claims for broad coverage and dependent/species claims for specific preferred compounds actually made and tested.
guidance: If the genus is rejected as too broad, species claims can still issue, protecting lead compounds. This 'belt-and-suspenders' approach balances maximized coverage with defensibility.

name: Enablement Requirement — what USPTO looks for
description: The specification must enable a POSITA to make and use the claimed compounds without undue experimentation.
guidance: USPTO looks for: working examples (synthetic procedures), starting materials (commercially available or easily synthesized), reaction conditions (temperatures, solvents, catalysts, times), purification methods (chromatography, recrystallization, distillation), and characterization data (NMR, mass spec, melting point, etc.). To avoid enablement rejections for a large genus, provide multiple working examples covering different regions of the Markush structure, general synthetic schemes, and literature citations for known reactions.

name: Written Description Requirement — demonstrating possession
description: You must demonstrate possession of the claimed invention at the time of filing; for chemical compounds this generally means you actually made the compound or described it with sufficient specificity.
guidance: Problem scenario: claiming a genus of 1,000 compounds but synthesizing only 5 may trigger rejection. Solutions: describe SAR explaining how substituents affect properties, provide a predictive model/rationale, include prophetic examples illustrating compounds across the genus, and include characterization for representative members.

name: Prior Art Searching for Chemical Structures
description: Search chemical structures (not just keywords) using specialized databases and structure-search techniques to determine novelty and scope of prior claims.
guidance: Use structure-based search tools: SciFinder (CAS), Reaxys, PubChem, and USPTO databases. Search types: exact structure match, substructure search (core scaffold), similarity search (Tanimoto coefficient thresholds e.g., >0.85), and Markush search to determine if your compound falls within prior Markush claims. Remember: a compound can be disclosed by an older Markush claim even if it was never actually made.

name: Pharmaceutical Layered Patent Strategy (primary vs secondary patents)
description: Pharmaceutical companies layer patents to maximize exclusivity: core API patent plus secondary patents covering polymorphs, salts, prodrugs, formulations, methods of use, metabolites, etc.
guidance: Primary (API) claims provide strongest protection but expire first. Secondary patents (polymorphs/crystal forms, salts/prodrugs, formulations/delivery systems, methods of use, metabolites) can extend effective exclusivity and create patent thickets. Draft secondary claims thoughtfully to avoid obviousness and enablement pitfalls.

name: Common USPTO Rejection: Enablement — Genus Too Broad
description: Rejection scenario: specification provides only a few examples but claims a genus of tens of thousands of compounds; applicant has not enabled full scope without undue experimentation.
guidance: How to overcome: narrow genus claims, add dependent claims covering subgenuses with more examples, argue that standard synthetic techniques allow routine variation of substituents, provide detailed synthetic schemes showing how to make any member of the genus, and add working examples across the claim scope.

name: Common USPTO Rejection: Written Description — No Possession of Full Genus
description: Rejection scenario: applicant hasn't demonstrated possession of the full claimed genus (e.g., described only A, B, C but claims A–Z).
guidance: How to overcome: describe structural features common to all claimed compounds and explain why they are expected to share claimed properties, provide SAR data, include prophetic examples illustrating compounds throughout the genus, and offer rationale/predictive models supporting possession.

name: Prohibition on submitting false, fraudulent, or misleading information (37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)(1) & (b)(2))
description: "Submitting a document that includes false, misleading, fictitious, or fraudulent information or representations violates 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)(1)." This includes false or misleading domicile information, attorney information, signatory information, applicant information, or claims of use (or intent to use).
guidance: Also violates §11.18(b)(2) when documents are submitted without reasonable inquiry into factual basis, evidentiary support, or in an effort to circumvent USPTO rules. Examples include fabricated deadlines, fake registration certificates, or false fee quotes described in the case.

name: Reasonable inquiry / evidentiary support for factual assertions (37 C.F.R. § 11.18)
description: Practitioners must undertake a reasonable inquiry into factual bases for averments in trademark documents and have evidentiary support for assertions; submitting documents without reasonable inquiry may violate § 11.18.
guidance: The rule applies to domicile, use claims, signatory information, and other facts. Circumventing rules or submitting documents without inquiry can be an improper purpose under §11.18(b)(2).

name: Effective filing date of a claimed invention (pre‑AIA)
description: The effective filing date is the actual filing date of the U.S. application unless one of the exceptions (A),(B),(C) applies: (A) continuation/divisional with proper 35 U.S.C. 120/365(c) benefit — effective date is earliest filing date in chain; (B) continuation‑in‑part (CIP) — claims not supported by parent have effective date equal to new application filing date, while claims fully supported by earlier parent have parent's effective filing date; (C) proper claim of benefit under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) to a provisional — effective date is the provisional filing date for claims fully supported by the provisional under 35 U.S.C. 112 first paragraph.
guidance: Actual international filing date is the U.S. filing date for applications that entered the national stage under 35 U.S.C. 371. The foreign priority document filing date is not the claim’s effective filing date for pre‑AIA 102 purposes, although foreign priority dates may be used to overcome certain references. See MPEP §§ 1893.03(b), 211.01(c), 1895, 1895.01, 1896 for related rules. For CIPs, carefully determine which claims are fully supported by the earlier parent application and which are new.

name: Continuation/divisional/CIP/benefit claim rules for prior‑art dating
description: If an application is a continuation or divisional and meets 35 U.S.C. 120/365(c) requirements, claimed subject matter gets the earliest filing date in the chain. For CIPs, claims not supported by the parent get the new application's actual filing date; claims fully supported by the earlier parent get the parent's effective filing date. Benefit claims under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) to provisionals may give provisional dates for supported claims.
guidance: When determining whether a reference is prior art, examiners must determine whether the subject matter relied upon is supported in the earlier application(s). Do not treat foreign priority dates as the effective filing date for pre‑AIA 102 purposes (though they may be used in other contexts). See MPEP § 2139.01 and related sections (1893.03(c), 211.01(c), 1895).

name: Provisional benefit and support requirement under 35 U.S.C. 119(e)
description: A reference or claim is entitled to the benefit of a provisional application's filing date only if at least one of the claims in the reference is supported by the provisional application's written description in compliance with pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph (now 112(a)).
guidance: Case law (Dynamic Drinkware; Amgen v. Sanofi) requires that the provisional provide adequate written description support for the claim relied upon. Examiners must assess compliance with the written description requirement when attributing provisional dates to references. See MPEP ¶ 7.12.fti Examiner Note 2 and cited cases.

name: Form paragraphs and required usage/order when making pre‑AIA 102 rejections
description: Use the specified MPEP form paragraphs (¶ 7.06, ¶ 7.07.fti, ¶ 7.08.fti–¶ 7.15.fti, etc.) when issuing rejections under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102; particular paragraphs must precede others and some are to be used only once per Office action.
guidance: Examples: ¶ 7.06 (Notice re prior art available under both pre‑AIA and AIA) must be used in all Office Actions when a prior art rejection is made in an application with an actual filing date on/after Mar 16, 2013 that claims priority to an earlier filing; ¶ 7.07.fti (Statement of Statutory Basis) is quoted in first actions on the merits and final rejections and is to be used only once in an Office action; ¶ 7.08.fti–¶ 7.14.fti correspond to the specific 102(a)–(g) paragraphs and must be preceded by ¶ 7.07.fti as indicated. Follow the Examiner Notes on when and how each form paragraph may/must be used and their required sequencing.

name: Statutory paragraph‑specific form paragraph mapping and prerequisites (¶ 7.08.fti–¶ 7.14.fti)
description: There are distinct form paragraphs for each pre‑AIA 102 paragraph: ¶ 7.08.fti for 102(a), ¶ 7.09.fti for 102(b), ¶ 7.10.fti for 102(c), ¶ 7.11.fti for 102(d), ¶ 7.12.fti for 102(e) (with detailed Examiner Notes), ¶ 7.13.fti for 102(f), ¶ 7.14.fti for 102(g). Each must be used in the correct context and with required precedents (e.g., ¶ 7.07.fti).
guidance: Follow the Examiner Notes under each form paragraph for when it must be preceded by ¶ 7.07.fti, when it may be preceded by ¶ 7.08.fti/¶ 7.09.fti/etc., and special sub‑rules within ¶ 7.12.fti concerning PCT/publication/language/benefit claims. Use the exact statutory quotation where required in first actions on the merits and final rejections, and do not repeat once‑only paragraphs multiple times in an Office action.

name: Software patents policy
description: 'Software per se' is excluded from patentability; claims comprising embedded software in a system or in a specific step of a method are usually accepted.
guidance: Computer-implemented inventions can be patentable if tied to a system or method; standalone software should be protected by copyright rather than patent. Uruguay references specific statutory exclusion ('software per se').

name: Markush claims
description: Markush claims may be admitted if they meet the requirements for patentability (novelty, inventive step and industrial application), present a sufficient support in the specification, and properly characterize representative compounds of the various embodiments.
guidance: Chemical/pharmaceutical claim drafting should ensure adequate support in the description and proper characterization of representative compounds to satisfy examination guidelines (Uruguay explicitly accepts Markush claims with sufficient support).

name: Inventive step (non-obviousness) standard
description: An invention shall be deemed to have inventive step if, for a person skilled in the relevant technical matter, it would not be obvious or derived in an evident manner from the state of the prior art.
guidance: Examiners assess whether claimed advances would be obvious to a skilled person in view of prior art. Apply standard country practice and supporting evidence where inventive contribution is close to known techniques.

name: Claim drafting — preamble and technical characteristics
description: Claims shall be formulated with a preamble indicating the object of the invention and the required technical characteristics for defining the elements claimed that combined form part of the state of the prior art.
guidance: Draft claims to clearly separate known/prior-art features (preamble or first part) from the novel/characterizing features (characterized part) as adapted to PY PTO practice. Ensure the preamble and characterizing portions together define the claimed invention.

name: Clarity and support of claims
description: Claims should be clear, the first claim should be independent and include relevant features; other claims should be subordinated. Claims should have support in the specification as filed originally when the application was filed in Paraguay.
guidance: Avoid vague expressions (e.g., 'about', 'effective amount') and unquantified qualifiers. Include dependent claims as needed. There is no formal limit to the number of claims but they must correspond to the nature of the invention and be supported by the original filing.

name: Method and process claims patentability
description: Methods and process claims are considered patentable in Paraguay.
guidance: Draft method/process claims with clear steps and technical effect; they are treated as patentable subject matter provided other patentability requirements are met.

name: Required filing documents (Paraguay)
description: Required documents: a) Power of Attorney certified by Notary Public within 60 days; b) Complete name and address of applicant; c) Complete name and address of inventor; d) Inventor's assignment certified by Notary Public within 90 days; e) Certified copy of priority document and Spanish translation within 90 days; f) Title, Specification, abstract, drawings and claims in Spanish.
guidance: Timely file all formal documents and Spanish translations per deadlines to avoid formal objections or loss of rights; ensure notarization and certified copies where specified.

name: Examiner interviews
description: Interviews with examiners are allowed in practice and are very helpful during prosecution in Paraguay. Examiner interviews are allowed and are helpful to overcome office actions.
guidance: Use interviews to clarify claim scope, present arguments, and negotiate allowable claim language; schedule and prepare written records where possible.

name: Claim amendments — no new matter
description: Patent applicants can amend the application claims if requested by the PY PTO examiner or to answer an office action; new subject matter cannot be incorporated at any stage, neither in the Specification nor in the claims.
guidance: Amend only to correct errors or respond to objections; ensure any amendment is fully supported by the original filing to avoid adding new matter and potential invalidity.

name: Exclusive rights conferred by patent
description: The patent grants exclusive rights to exploit the invention: for a product, prevent third parties from fabricating, using, offering for sale, selling or importing; for a procedure, prevent use of the procedure and acts of use, offering for sale, sale or import of products directly obtained through the procedure.
guidance: Draft claim scope to align with anticipated enforcement goals; understand that unauthorized acts beyond exceptions may be considered infringing.

name: Statute of limitations for patent claims
description: The action for infringement shall be subject to limitation in two years as from the date that the owner becomes aware of the infringement, or four years since the infringement was last committed, between them the one that expires first.
guidance: Prompt monitoring and enforcement are required; choose filing timing carefully relative to discovery of infringement and last infringing act.

name: Damages and litigation costs (patents)
description: Patent owner may claim compensation for damages; 'punitive damages' are not provided. Losing party will have to pay attorney’s fees of the counterparty, and the amount will be set by the Judge.
guidance: Calculate expected recoverable damages under local law and be prepared for judge-determined attorney fee awards rather than statutory multipliers or punitive awards.

name: Famous and well-known marks protection
description: Famous and well-known marks are protected according to the Paris Convention and TRIPS Agreement rules.
guidance: Claim fame/well-known status where applicable to seek broader protection and prevent dilution or exploitation of notoriety.

name: Trademark statute of limitations
description: Trademark infringement actions can be started during the period the trademark is being infringed and until two years after the last infringement act.
guidance: Be mindful of the two-year window following last act for bringing claims; track ongoing infringement to preserve rights.

name: Trademark damages and litigation costs
description: Trademark owner may claim compensation for damages; 'punitive damages' are not provided. The losing party is obliged to support the attorney fees determined by the Judge: between 5% and 20% of the amounts discussed in court. If no monetary amount is involved, Judges usually fix attorney fees considering complexity and duration.
guidance: Estimate likely attorney fee awards and consider economic scale of the dispute; statutory punitive damages are not available.

name: Claims as a disclaimer
description: A claim practically operates as a disclaimer of everything described in the specification except what is expressly claimed; the drafter must avoid including matter beyond the invention or omitting what might have been claimed.
guidance: Keep claims within the true boundary of the invention; do not inadvertently restrict rights by leaving out things you wish to secure. (Discussion referencing Harrison v. Anderston Foundry Co.; Jackson v. Wolstenhulme.)

name: Real object of a claim
description: The real object of a claim 'is not to claim anything which is not mentioned by the specification, but to disclaim something' — the claim specifies what the patentee excludes from the public domain.
guidance: Compose claims to identify precisely the novel subject-matter and to disclaim what is not claimed; always construe claims with reference to the whole specification (Plimpton v. Spiller quoted).

name: Insert distinct claim for what is comprised
description: It is long practice to insert in specifications the distinct claim of what is said to be comprised in the patent; anything not comprised in the claim falls open to the public.
guidance: If a specification describes multiple inventions but claimant confines the claim to one, the others are given to the public — therefore claim explicitly each invention you wish to protect.

name: Claims must show clearly what is intended
