description: Claims ought to show clearly what it is intended to be claimed; ambiguous wording that leaves it unclear whether parts or combinations are claimed can render the patent invalid.
guidance: Particular attention to framing: make it manifest whether you claim a novel combination or individual parts (Rowcliff v. Morris; Fairbairn v. Household). Avoid ambiguous grammatical or structural constructions.

name: Combination claim sufficiency tied to enablement
description: A claim for a combination will not be deemed too vague when there is proof that a competent workman can make the combination from the specification without experiment.
guidance: Ensure the specification enables a skilled person to make the claimed combination; if enablement requires experiment, the claim may be considered vague (Edison & Swan United Electric Light Co. v. Woodhouse).

name: Reference to drawings can cure over‑general description
description: If the description is initially too general, referring to particular figures in the drawings and claiming the invention as described with reference to those figures can make the specification sufficient.
guidance: Use drawings and explicit cross‑references to them to clarify general descriptions and to support claims (Daw v. Eley; Russell v. Cowley; Thomas v. Welch).

name: Claims do not substitute for a full description
description: The claim is not intended to aid the description, but to ascertain the extent of what is claimed as new; a sufficiently precise description is required separately from general expressions in the claim.
guidance: Do not rely on broad claim language to supply what the description omits; ensure the description enables the invention even if the claim contains general terms (Kay v. Marshall; Lister v. Leather).

name: When all parts are old, claim the new combination only
description: If all parts of an invention taken separately are old, the patentee must limit the claim to the new combination rather than claiming the old parts themselves.
guidance: Avoid claiming individual elements that are known; narrow the claim to the inventive combination (Lister v. Leather; Seed v. Higgins).

name: Improvement obvious on specification face may sometimes be protected without claim mention (older patents)
description: For patents granted before certain statutory changes, where an improvement is clearly manifested on the face of the specification it may be protected even if not mentioned in the claim; conversely omission can lose protection for processes specifically omitted from the claim.
guidance: Be cautious relying on older precedents; modern practice requires explicit claiming of novel features but historical cases (Nordenfeldt v. Gardner; Jackson v. Wolstenhulme) illustrate limited exceptions.

name: Claims must not cover too much (over‑claiming kills the patent)
description: An inventor should beware of claiming more than he is strictly entitled to; attempting to cover too much may render the whole patent invalid even if a narrower part would be valid.
guidance: Limit claims to what you can support by novelty and description; an over‑broad claim that includes known matter can vitiate the whole (Hill v. Thompson; example of claiming a principle vs a specific mode).

name: Avoid claiming a general principle when only a particular mode is novel
description: If an inventor claims a principle in addition to a method of carrying it into effect and the principle was known, the patent will be invalid; restricting the claim to the particular mode or proportions may have preserved validity.
guidance: When novelty is in a particular implementation (e.g., specific proportions, specific mechanical arrangement), claim that mode rather than the abstract principle (examples: lime in smelting, chair self‑adjusting leverage, Rex v. Cutler).

name: If subordinate claim is not new, patent may fail
description: If the specification claims a novel combination forming an entire machine and also claims a subordinate combination which is not new, the patent cannot stand.
guidance: Avoid mixing novel and non‑novel subordinate claims that could be held to extend monopoly improperly (cited examples in text).

name: Do not claim broad classes of materials without showing suitability
description: Claiming an entire class (e.g., 'all peroxides of manganese' or 'all qualities of hard woven canvas') when only specific members work will be held to claim too much and may invalidate the patent.
guidance: Identify and describe the particular members of a class that are suitable; if multiple market variants exist but not all work, give guidance or limit the claim to avoid overbreadth (Gaudy v. Reddaway; Kurtz v. S—).

name: Avoid vague, speculative, or hypothetical claims
description: A patentee will not be allowed to make wide hypothetical or speculative claims based on conjecture or to claim matters of which he was ignorant at the date of the patent; law will not permit claiming more than the inventor has actually invented.
guidance: Restrict claims to what has been actually demonstrated or reasonably known at filing. Do not claim every possible variant (shapes, gases, acids) unless the inventor actually conceived and enabled them (Tetley v. Easton; Sterns v. A— examples).

name: Prefer restricting claim to verified processes/materials
description: It is safer for patentees to confine themselves specifically to one good thing that they have found by actual trial to answer the purpose than to include everything.
guidance: A narrowly and well‑supported claim is more likely to be upheld and to prevent trivial attempts at imitation; courts will protect real inventions against colourable variants or equivalents where appropriate (Crossley v. Potter guidance).

name: Appendant claims to old matter are risky and often useless
description: An appendant claim to something old (e.g., old means of firing applied to a new product) may not vitiate a patent but is generally inadvisable because it is either useless or threatens invalidation if read expansively.
guidance: Avoid including claims to known, ancillary elements unless clearly appendant and necessary; such claims can be useless if construed narrowly and dangerous if construed broadly (British Dynamite Co. v. Krebs discussion).

name: Read the specification as a whole; construe claims in context
description: You must always construe a claim with reference to the whole context of a specification; every claim must be read and construed with reference to the specification and not as an isolated sentence.
guidance: Frame claims so their language, when read together with the specification, produces a clear and defensible scope (Plimpton v. Spiller; Edison & Swan v. Woodhouse).

name: Interpretation considers state of knowledge at filing
description: A specification will be construed with reference to the state of knowledge at the time it was prepared; it should not be held invalid because later discoveries make its language broader than originally intended.
guidance: Describe inventions with respect to contemporaneous understanding; do not expect to claim materials unknown at filing merely because later science shows your words could encompass them (Badische Anilin case; naphthylamine example).

name: Defective amendment
description: A proposed amendment to the description and claims which does not comply with 37 CFR 1.530(d)-(k) will be retained in the file but will not be considered.
guidance: Exception: where the only defect in the amendment is that it enlarges the scope of the claims of the patent or introduces new matter, such an amendment will be considered and a rejection will be made in the next Office action. New matter amendments to the disclosure will be required to be canceled and claims containing new matter will be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112. New matter to drawings is ordinarily not entered. An amendment that enlarges the scope of the claims will be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 314(a). See MPEP §§ 2234, 2250, 608.04.

name: Entry of amendments (effect and new matter handling)
description: Where an amendment is submitted in proper form and otherwise appropriate, the amendment will be entered for purposes of the reexamination proceeding though the amendment does not have legal effect until the certificate is issued.
guidance: Any “new matter” amendment to the disclosure (35 U.S.C. 132) will be required to be canceled and claims containing new matter will be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112. A “new matter” amendment to the drawing is ordinarily not entered. Where an amendment enlarges the scope of the claims of the patent, the claims will be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 314(a). For merged proceedings see MPEP §§ 2686.01 and 2686.03.

name: Reconsideration after patent owner response and third party comments
description: After response by the patent owner and any third party comments, the patent under reexamination will be reconsidered and parties will be notified of claims rejected, claims found patentable, and any objections or requirements.
guidance: The patent owner may respond to such Office action with or without amendment, and the third party requester may provide comments after the patent owner’s response. If the patent owner’s response contains an amendment, the examiner will consider whether the amendment raises issues of 35 U.S.C. 112 and/or broadening of claims under 35 U.S.C. 314. Reconsideration continues until ready for closing prosecution, at which point the examiner will issue an Action Closing Prosecution (ACP).

name: Options for Office action to issue (ACP, NIRC, non-ACP) depending on parties’ responsiveness
description: The examiner has discrete options depending on whether the patent owner responded and whether third party comments were timely: issue NIRC if no patent owner response and all claims are rejected; issue ACP if at least one claim is patentable; issue incomplete-response action, Notice of Defective Paper, ACP, or a new non-closing Office action depending on completeness/formality/readiness; handle third party comments that exceed permitted scope under MPEP § 2666.05.
guidance: Specifics: (A) No timely patent owner response: (1) if all claims rejected issue NIRC; (2) if at least one claim free of rejection issue ACP (with statements on limitation of proceeding). Examiner may still issue supplemental OA if new info warrants a new rejection. (B) Timely patent owner response but no timely requester comments: options include incomplete-response action (MPEP § 2666.30), Notice of Defective Paper (MPEP § 2666.50), ACP if ready, or a new office action not closing prosecution (MPEP § 2671.01). (C) Timely response and timely comments: similar handling plus procedures for improper or out-of-scope comments (MPEP § 2666.05). (D) Expedited RAN issuance possible under 37 CFR 1.953(b) if criteria satisfied; see MPEP § 2673.02.

name: Criteria for issuing an Action Closing Prosecution (ACP)
description: An ACP is issued when the patent owner’s response is complete and defect-free and the proceeding is ready for closing prosecution.
guidance: Proceeding is ready for closing prosecution if all claims are determined to be patentable, all claims are determined to be rejected, or some claims are determined patentable and some rejected. After an ACP, requirements of 37 CFR 1.116(b) will be strictly enforced and amendments after an ACP require a showing of good and sufficient reasons why they were not earlier presented.

name: Treatment when examiner withdraws a rejection
description: When the examiner withdraws a ground of rejection originally initiated by the examiner, such withdrawal should be clearly stated as a decision favorable to patentability with respect to the withdrawn rejection.
guidance: If the examiner withdraws a ground of rejection previously proposed by the third party requester (e.g., based on patent owner’s argument or evidence), the examiner should treat the issue as a rejection proposed by the third party requester that the examiner refuses to adopt. If claims have been amended and the examiner withdraws a ground previously proposed by the third party requester as to the original claims, generally this is not a refusal to adopt the requester’s rejection (since it was never proposed as to amended claims), but the requester may re-propose the rejection as to amended claims. If the patent owner fails to respond to actions leading to a RAN and a RAN is issued, the third party requester may appeal such withdrawals as final decisions favorable to patentability (see 37 CFR 41.61(a)(2)). Special handling applies where a dependent claim is amended in certain ways.

name: Patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101 (Alice two-step)
description: Under Alice, the Section 101 analysis proceeds in two parts: Alice Step 1 considers 'whether the claims at issue are directed to … patent-ineligible concepts' (e.g., abstract ideas, laws of nature, natural phenomena). If the claims are directed to ineligible subject matter, Alice Step 2 requires a 'search for 'an inventive concept – i.e., an element or combination of elements that is sufficient to ensure that the patent in practice amounts to significantly more than a patent upon the [ineligible concept] itself.''
guidance: Alice Step 1 is generally treated as a question of law resolvable on intrinsic evidence; Alice Step 2 asks whether the claim contains something 'significantly more' than the ineligible concept. Courts apply these steps sequentially; case law (Alice, Mobile Acuity, Simio) should be cited when framing arguments.

name: Specificity of factual allegations to defeat 12(b)(6)
description: Allegations in the complaint intended to avoid a §101 motion must be specific; conclusory allegations will be disregarded, and allegations unsupported by or that contradict the patent's written description cannot defeat a motion to dismiss.
guidance: Amendments adding well-pled, specific facts (as in Aatrix) can preclude dismissal; but mere conclusory statements that a claim is unconventional or inventive are insufficient. Cite AI Visualize and Aatrix for examples where courts rejected conclusory pleading.

name: Showing an inventive concept (Alice Step 2) — nonconventionality requirement
description: To survive Alice Step 2, the patent must recite an inventive concept that is 'something significantly more' than the abstract idea — i.e., an element or combination that is not conventional, routine, or well-understood.
guidance: Whether an element is conventional can involve questions of fact (Berkheimer). Plaintiffs should plead facts explaining why the claimed features are unconventional; defendants should argue conventionality and show why alleged facts do not preclude dismissal.

name: Electric Power principle for computer-implemented inventions
description: A patent claim that can be reduced to the basic concepts of 'collecting, analyzing, and presenting information using ... conventional operations of generic computer components' cannot survive Section 101.
guidance: When drafting pleadings or responding, parties should map claimed elements to the 'collecting/analyzing/presenting' abstraction to argue ineligibility; plaintiffs should instead allege how the claim improves computer functionality beyond that template.

name: Defendant's burden and approach when identifying a representative claim
description: If a defendant chooses to identify a representative claim, it must show that the challenged claims 'are 'substantially similar and linked to the same' ineligible concept.'
guidance: Defendants should be clear and steadfast in explaining why a particular claim(s) is representative because the burden to justify representativeness lies with the defendant. Provide a persuasive, coherent theory tying claims to the same ineligible concept to overcome the presumption of validity.

name: Specific showing required to justify discovery or claim construction delay
description: To avoid dismissal on the ground that claim construction or discovery is needed before resolving Section 101, a patentee must identify specific details supporting that need.
guidance: A patentee must do more than 'conclusorily assert[] it needs discovery' — it must propose a specific claim construction and explain why the dispute must be resolved before Section 101 can be decided. Defendants should seek to rebut by showing construction/discovery would be irrelevant or futile.

name: Tactical advice: plaintiffs may plead improvements in computer functionality
description: Plaintiffs may provide robust factual allegations explaining why the claimed invention recites an improvement in computer functionality that goes beyond mere speed and efficiency, or otherwise recites an inventive concept.
guidance: Such allegations, if specific and consistent with the specification, can strengthen opposition to a 12(b)(6) §101 motion (Aatrix and related cases are examples where amended pleadings avoiding conventionality led to reversal of dismissal).

name: Tactical advice: defendants should highlight plaintiff silence and inconsistencies
description: Defendants should emphasize where plaintiffs fail to contest representativeness, fail to explain why discovery or claim construction is needed, or fail to clearly explain why claims go beyond an abstract idea.
guidance: Highlighting a plaintiff's silence can support an argument for early, sweeping dismissal; defendants should be prepared to show why asserted gaps justify deciding Section 101 at the pleading stage.

name: Evidentiary basis required for implicit findings and 'inherent' steps
description: When the Board treats certain claim limitations as 'inherent' or makes implicit factual findings, it must explain the evidentiary basis for those determinations.
guidance: Rovalma criticized the PTAB for failing to 'sufficiently lay out the basis for its implicit findings' (e.g., inherent completion of method steps). Lack of explanation of the evidentiary basis supports remand so the Board can develop and articulate its reasoning.

name: Supplemental information submitted within one month of institution (37 C.F.R. § 42.123(a))
description: A party may file a motion to submit supplemental information if the request for authorization is made within one month of the date the trial is instituted and the supplemental information is relevant to a claim for which trial has been instituted.
guidance: Beyond the regulatory threshold, practitioners should argue that the supplemental information does not change the asserted invalidity grounds or that the petitioner reasonably could not have submitted the information with the petition. Request authorization within 30 days and explain relevance (for example, an expert declaration clarifying a claim term).

name: Definition of 'covered business method patent'
description: Includes 'a method or corresponding apparatus' and is intended to encompass all claim types (method, system, apparatus, GUI, data structure (Lowry), storage-medium (Beauregard), etc.). Patent qualifies regardless of claim type or structure; clever drafting should not avoid PTO review.
guidance: Coverage extends to any claim that is in substance a business method; form should not trump substance. However, patents for 'technological inventions' are excluded (see technological invention exception).

name: Technological invention exception (out of scope for business-method proceeding)
description: Excludes 'patents for technological inventions'—patents whose novelty turns on a technological innovation over the prior art, concerned with a technical problem solved with a technical solution, and which require the claims to state the technical features the inventor desires to protect.
guidance: Not intended to exclude patents that merely use known technology to accomplish a business process. Mere recitation of computer hardware, networks, software, memory, databases, scanners, display devices, ATMs, point-of-sale devices, or other known technologies does not make a patent a technological invention. Combining known technology to perform data processing operations is not sufficient to invoke the exception.

name: Scope of 'financial product or service' and ancillary activities covered
description: Amendment covers not only financial products and services but also the 'practice, administration and management' of a financial product or service; intended to capture ancillary activities related to financial products/services.
guidance: Ancillary activities include, without limitation, marketing, customer interfaces, Web site management and functionality, transmission or management of data, servicing, underwriting, customer communications, and back office operations (e.g., payment processing, stock clearing). A patent need not recite a specific financial product/service; claims only need be broad enough to cover a financial product/service.

name: When a patent is deemed to 'relate to' a financial product/service
description: To meet the requirement, the patent claims must only be broad enough to cover a financial product or service; if a patent claims a general online marketing method that could be applied to marketing a financial product/service, it would be deemed to cover one.
guidance: If a patent holder alleges a financial product/service infringes its patent, that patent shall be deemed to cover a financial product/service for purposes of the amendment regardless of explicit claim language.

name: Section 32 — voluntary amendments limited until examination request
description: "Section 32 sets forth that voluntary amendments to patent applications are only possible as long as the applicant files them until the moment in which the examination is requested."
guidance: This creates a trade-off: the sooner an applicant requests examination (to obtain a faster grant), the sooner the window for voluntary amendments closes. Applicants should weigh the benefit of faster prosecution against the need for time to amend claims/specification. This concern was highlighted as a practical issue to resolve if examination timelines are shortened.

name: Show Specific Technical Benefits
description: Name specific technical benefits in claims.
guidance: Identify and claim measurable technical benefits such as faster search times within a database, smaller memory requirements, more dynamic information filtering, more efficient information processing, reduced network bandwidth usage, improved security/encryption, or improved error correction. Quantify when possible.

name: Use Structured UI Approaches
description: Claims should require a specific GUI structure and prescribed functionality directly related to the GUI structure to solve a user-interface problem.
guidance: Draft claims that recite a specific graphical user interface structure and tie functionality to that structure. Emphasize how the GUI structure solves a particular user-interface technical problem (e.g., preserving look-and-feel, improving interaction efficiency).

name: Avoid Pure Method Claims
description: Avoid claims that are pure abstract mental processes or un-tethered methods; tie methods to specific machines or transformations of data.
guidance: Tie method claims to specific machines, show data transformation into a different state, and avoid claim language that reads on human mental performance. Prefer machine-tied or technical-effect-focused claim language.

name: Identify the Technical Problem Clearly in the Specification
description: Clearly identify the technical problem in the specification.
guidance: Explicitly state the technical problem the invention addresses in the written description so that claim scope and patentability can be tied to solving that problem during prosecution or litigation.

name: Describe the Solution in Technical Terms
description: Describe the solution in technical terms (algorithms, data structures).
guidance: Use technical descriptions such as algorithms, data structures, and implementation details (not just high-level functional statements) to show how the invention achieves the claimed improvements.

name: Include Flow Diagrams and Pseudocode
description: Include flow diagrams and pseudocode in the specification.
guidance: Provide flow diagrams, pseudocode, and implementation-level figures to support that the solution is a technical implementation and to reduce the risk that claims are viewed as abstract.

name: Draft Claims That Require Specific Computer Architecture
description: Draft claims that require specific computer architecture.
guidance: Draft independent/dependent claims that recite specific computer architecture details (processors, memory arrangements, data paths) rather than generic computing elements to demonstrate a technological solution and avoid §101 vulnerability.

name: Avoid Mental-Step Language in Independent Claims
description: Avoid mental-step language in independent claims.
guidance: Do not draft independent claims in a manner that reads on human mental processes. Use concrete machine-oriented language and structural limitations instead of abstract, mental-step phrasing.

name: Include Dependent Claims with Hardware Specifics
description: Include dependent claims with hardware specifics.
guidance: Add dependent claims that narrow independent claims by specifying particular hardware elements, sensors, processors, memory architectures, or other physical limitations that strengthen the technological character of the claim set.

name: Consider Apparatus Claims with Structural Detail
description: Consider apparatus claims with structural detail.
guidance: Draft apparatus or system claims that recite structural components and their interconnections or operations to provide an alternative to method claims and emphasize tangible, technical aspects.

name: Draft Beauregard Claims for Software Products (non-transitory medium)
description: Draft Beauregard claims for software products (with non-transitory medium).
guidance: Include claims directed to a computer-readable medium storing instructions (Beauregard claims) as another claim category; ensure the claim language ties the stored program to concrete technical effects rather than abstract functionality.

name: Include Narrow Fallback Claims Tied to Specific Technical Effects
description: Include narrow fallback claims tied to specific technical effects.
guidance: Draft fallback claim(s) narrowly limited to particular technical effects or implementation details to preserve enforceable scope if broader claims are found ineligible.

name: Litigation Strategy for §101 Challenges
description: A patent owner defending against a §101 challenge should identify technological innovations required by the claims and contend that the claims require more than generic software/computer elements.
guidance: In litigation, emphasize technical innovations present in the claims, argue the claims require more than generic elements, present factual evidence of technical improvements, and rely on factual questions where appropriate (e.g., Berkheimer).

name: Cite and Analogize to Key Federal Circuit Cases
description: Invoke specific Federal Circuit cases finding similar claims eligible and distinguish from cases finding similar claims ineligible.
guidance: Use precedent such as DDR Holdings (look-and-feel preservation), Enfish (self-referential database table), McRO (specific animation rules), Berkheimer (inventive concept can be a factual question), Cellspin Soft (pleading-stage challenges), and Trading Tech (GUI for trading) to analogize to your claims and support eligibility arguments.

name: Use Examiner Interviews and Account for Examiner/Art-Unit Variability
description: §101 rejections generally are not applied consistently between art units and examiners; examiners may share thoughts on §101 rejections during interviews — use this opportunity.
guidance: Engage in interviews with examiners to learn their §101 concerns, tailor claim amendments and arguments to the examiner's perspective and the art unit's practice, and document technical explanations revealed during interviews to support eligibility positions.

name: Enablement Requirement (Manner and Process of Making and Using)
description: The specification shall describe the manner and process of making and using the invention in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to make and use the invention (the enablement requirement).
guidance: Enablement is a distinct statutory requirement under 35 U.S.C. 112(a). The inquiry asks whether a person skilled in the art could make and use the claimed invention based on the disclosure. The MPEP emphasizes that a disclosure can be enabling without necessarily describing the invention in the written‑description sense. Examples: a specification might disclose methods enabling certain formulations (broadly defined functional ingredients) but not describe any specific formulation in a way that satisfies written description.

name: Specification Must Describe the Invention Completely (Full, Clear, Concise, Exact Terms)
description: The specification must provide a complete description of the invention and of the manner and process of making and using it in such 'full, clear, concise, and exact terms' as to enable one skilled in the art to make and use the invention.
guidance: This is the statutory language from 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and the pre‑AIA first paragraph and underlies both the written description and enablement inquiries. Practitioners should ensure the specification contains sufficient detail across embodiments to permit practice of the invention and to support the claimed scope. MPEP repeatedly cites this statutory standard when explaining the three separate requirements.

name: Scope Commensurate with Disclosure
description: Claim scope must be commensurate with the disclosure; the written description must support the breadth of the claimed invention.
guidance: The MPEP and cited cases make clear that claims cannot properly be given a scope broader than what the specification demonstrates the inventor possessed. Examiners and practitioners should evaluate whether the specification provides support for the breadth of claims (possession of claimed subject matter). The page cites examples (e.g., functional vs. specific disclosures, software examples) and refers to MPEP sections on 'possession of the invention' and 'scope commensurate with disclosure.'

name: Extent of exemplification required where claims cover a broad field
description: A single example may suffice, but where the claims cover a broad field, the application is not usually regarded as satisfying Art. 83 unless the description gives a number of examples or describes alternative embodiments or variations extending over the area protected by the claims.
guidance: Assess on facts and evidence of each case; some very broad fields may be sufficiently exemplified by limited examples, but usually multiple examples or alternatives are needed to support broad claim scopes. (See also F‑IV, 6.3; Art. 83; Rule 42(1)(e))

name: Requirement to enable performance over the whole area claimed
description: The application must contain, in addition to the examples, sufficient information to allow the person skilled in the art, using common general knowledge, to perform the invention over the whole area claimed without undue burden and without needing inventive skill.
guidance: This is required particularly when only limited examples are provided; applicant must enable substantially any embodiment falling within the ambit of the claim. (Case: T 727/95)

name: Intrinsic limitations from a sensible reading of claims
description: When assessing sufficiency the intrinsic limitations that a sensible reading imposes on the subject‑matter of the independent claims must be taken into consideration.
guidance: The skilled person will exclude any embodiment that is meaningless and not consistent with the teaching of the application; sensible claim reading can therefore narrow the practical scope for sufficiency analysis. (Case: T 521/12)

name: Establish broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim as a whole before eligibility analysis
description: The broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim must be established prior to examining a claim for eligibility because BRI sets the boundaries of the coverage sought by the claim and influences whether the claim seeks to cover subject matter beyond the statutory categories or encompasses judicial exceptions.
guidance: BRI affects both Step 1 (statutory category) and Step 2 (Alice/Mayo analysis). Examiners should construe the claim in light of the entire disclosure and apply BRI consistently (examples: Mentor Graphics, Synopsys, Enfish). If BRI covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments, the claim fails Step 1. See MPEP § 2111 for more on claim interpretation and examples in the text (e.g., carrier waves in machine-readable medium claims).

name: Eligibility Step 1 — Claim falls within one of the four statutory categories
description: Determine whether the claim as a whole is to a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter (35 U.S.C. 101).
guidance: Processes are acts or series of acts (methods). Machines, manufactures, and compositions of matter generally must have physical or tangible form. Product claims that are intangible (data per se, software per se) or transitory signals (carrier waves) do not fall within the three product categories. If claim's BRI includes non-statutory embodiments, reject under § 101 and recommend amendment to narrow scope to statutory embodiments. Use form paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01 when appropriate. See MPEP § 2106.03.

name: Eligibility Step 2A — Determine whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception
description: Identify whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon (i.e., a judicial exception).
guidance: Judicial exceptions include abstract ideas (mathematical formulas, certain methods of organizing human activity, mental processes), laws of nature, natural phenomena, products of nature, scientific principles, and similar concepts. There are no bright-line boundaries; it is sufficient to identify that the claimed concept aligns with at least one judicial exception. The examiner should identify the specific claim limitation(s) that may recite the exception. See MPEP § 2106.04.

name: Eligibility Step 2B — Whether the claim recites additional elements amounting to significantly more
description: If the claim is directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: YES), determine whether the claim recites additional elements, either individually or in combination, that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception.
guidance: This is the search for an 'inventive concept' and is assessed by considering whether added limitations transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application (practical application). The machine-or-transformation test is an important clue to the 'significantly more' determination but should not be used as a separate test. See MPEP § 2106.05.

name: 2106.05(a) — Improvements to the functioning of a computer or to any other technology or technical field
description: A claim that improves an existing technology or the functioning of a computer can supply 'significantly more' and therefore be eligible.
guidance: Examiners should consider whether the claim elements provide a technical improvement beyond the judicial exception (examples: Enfish — self‑referential table that improved database technology; McRO — rules of a particular type that improved an existing technological process). If the claim's additional elements are tied to a technological improvement, eligibility is more likely. See MPEP § 2106.05(a).

name: 2106.05(b) — Particular machine
description: Recitation of a particular machine or apparatus (as more than a generic computer) may supply significantly more.
guidance: Claims tied to a specific, particular machine (not a generic 'computer') can indicate a practical application of an exception. However, mere recitation of generic computer components (a 'general purpose computer') typically is insufficient (see TLI, In re Alappat history). Examiners should evaluate whether the machine limitation meaningfully limits the claim beyond the judicial exception. See MPEP § 2106.05(b).

name: 2106.05(d) — Well-understood, routine, conventional activity
description: If the additional claim elements are well-understood, routine, or conventional activities previously known in the field, they typically do not amount to significantly more.
guidance: Examiners should determine whether the additional elements add anything inventive beyond applying the judicial exception with conventional steps or components. Mere use of routine data gathering, generic computer implementation, or conventional activity will not confer eligibility. See MPEP § 2106.05(d).

name: 2106.05(e) — Other meaningful limitations (non-generic arrangement / unconventional combination)
description: Limitations that supply meaningful constraints — such as unconventional technical solution, non-generic arrangement, or an innovative ordered combination of known elements — may amount to significantly more.
guidance: Examiners should identify whether the claim recites an unconventional technical solution to a technological problem (example: Amdocs where construction of 'enhance' required distributed field enhancements). A non-generic arrangement of known, conventional elements can change the claim's character. See MPEP § 2106.05(e).

name: 2106.05(f) — Mere instructions to apply an exception
description: Limitations that simply instruct practitioners to apply an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon (e.g., 'apply the formula') do not supply significantly more.
guidance: Claims that add only generic instructions to implement an exception (e.g., 'apply this mathematical formula') fail to transform the exception into a patent-eligible application. Such 'mere instruction' limitations are insufficient under Step 2B. See MPEP § 2106.05(f).

name: 2106.05(g) — Insignificant extra-solution activity
description: Claim elements that add insignificant post‑solution or ancillary activity (data collection, certain conventional pre/post steps) do not supply significantly more.
guidance: Activities that are incidental to the solution of the abstract idea (or that occur after solving it) and that amount to no more than data-gathering, insignificant pre/post-solution steps, or conventional activity should not render the claim eligible. See MPEP § 2106.05(g).

name: 2106.05(h) — Field of use and technological environment limitations
description: Limiting an abstract idea to a particular field of use, or reciting a technological environment (e.g., 'over the Internet') does not, by itself, make the claim eligible.
guidance: An abstract idea does not become nonabstract merely by limiting the invention to a particular field or technological environment. Examiners should look for meaningful limitations beyond a mere field‑of‑use restriction. See MPEP § 2106.05(h).

name: The Alice/Mayo two-part test is the controlling framework (use only this test for eligibility)
description: The Supreme Court's Alice/Mayo two-part test (identify whether claims are directed to a judicial exception; if so, determine whether additional elements amount to significantly more) is the only test that should be used to evaluate eligibility under examination.
guidance: Other tests (e.g., machine-or-transformation) serve as clues for the 'significantly more' inquiry but must be considered within the two-part framework. Examiners should not use superseded tests like 'useful, concrete and tangible result' as the eligibility standard. See MPEP § 2106 summary and discussion.

name: Pathways A/B/C to eligibility (streamlined analysis vs. full Alice/Mayo analysis)
description: Three pathways to finding eligibility: Pathway A — claims within statutory category with self-evident eligibility (streamlined); Pathway B — claims within statutory category and not directed to judicial exception (Step 2A: NO); Pathway C — claims within statutory category, directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: YES), but recite additional elements amounting to significantly more (Step 2B: YES).
guidance: If a claim is clearly eligible under Pathway A, a streamlined analysis is appropriate; otherwise, conduct full Step 2A/2B analysis. If unsure whether streamlined analysis applies, perform full analysis. If claim fails all pathways, reject under 35 U.S.C. § 101. See MPEP subsection III and §§ 2106.04–2106.06.

name: Streamlined analysis — Clear improvement to technology or computer functionality
description: Claims that clearly improve computer functionality or any other technology can be found eligible under the streamlined pathway.
guidance: If the claim plainly claims a technological improvement, the examiner may conclude eligibility under streamlined analysis (Pathway A). However, document the specific improvements and supporting specification passages. See MPEP § 2106.06(b).

name: Identify judicial exceptions by examples and labels (no bright lines)
description: Judicial exceptions may be described variously (abstract ideas, laws of nature, natural phenomena, products of nature, mental processes, mathematical algorithms, disembodied concepts). There are no bright lines between types; a concept may fall under more than one label.
guidance: For analysis it is sufficient to identify that the claimed concept aligns with at least one judicial exception and to identify the specific claim limitation(s) implicated. Use case law examples to support the identification. See MPEP § 2106.04.

name: Preemption concern as the underlying consideration
description: The underlying concern driving the two-part framework is preemption — preventing monopolization of basic tools of scientific and technological work (abstract ideas, laws of nature, natural phenomena).
guidance: While preemption is not a standalone test, courts examine whether a claim would preempt substantially all uses of the exception; demonstrations of non-preemption (meaningful limitations, particular machines/transformations, improvements) support eligibility. Examiners should consider preemption in Step 2B analysis and cite relevant cases. See MPEP discussion and cited cases (e.g., Mayo, Alice, Ariosa, Rapid Litigation Management).

name: Formulating a rejection for lack of subject matter eligibility
description: When making a § 101 rejection, the examiner must articulate why the claim is directed to a judicial exception and why any added elements do not amount to significantly more.
guidance: The rejection should identify the judicial exception and the specific claim limitations implicated, provide a reasoned explanation (including BRI), cite relevant case law and MPEP sections, and, where applicable, use model/form paragraphs. If the claim could be amended to be statutory, recommend amendments. See MPEP § 2106.07(a) for procedural guidance.

name: Evaluating applicant's response to a § 101 rejection
description: When applicant responds (arguments, amendments, evidence), the examiner must evaluate whether the response overcomes the reasoned rejection by addressing directed-to-exception (Step 2A) or showing additional elements amount to significantly more (Step 2B).
guidance: Consider whether proposed amendments meaningfully narrow the claim to statutory embodiments or add limitations that materially change the claim's character. Evaluate new evidence or expert declarations that bear on whether elements are conventional. If response fails, maintain rejection with explanation; if persuasive, withdraw rejection and consider clarifying remarks. See MPEP § 2106.07(b).

name: Clarifying the record when issuing eligibility findings
description: Examiners may make clarifying remarks on the record whether the claim is found eligible or ineligible to explain rationale, cite specification support, and aid applicant understanding.
guidance: When eligible due to an improvement in technology, the examiner can reference parts of the specification and note claim elements that produce the improvement. When issuing a rejection, explaining the BRI and suggesting narrowing amendments aids prosecution. Clarifying remarks may be made at any point during prosecution, including with a notice of allowance. See MPEP § 2106.07(c).

name: Claims that encompass both statutory and non-statutory embodiments fail Step 1
description: If the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim covers both statutory embodiments and non-statutory embodiments, the claim as a whole does not fall within a statutory category and fails Step 1.
guidance: In such cases a § 101 rejection should be made for failure to claim statutory subject matter; examiners should point out the BRI and recommend amendments to narrow the claim to statutory embodiments if possible. Example: machine-readable medium claims that encompass carrier waves. See MPEP § 2106.03 and illustrative cases (Mentor Graphics, Nuijten).

name: When an item may be contained within the body of the request
description: If the information to be considered, reconsidered, or corrected is not, at least in part, contained within or based on a supporting document submitted with the request, then the discussion within the body of the request will be considered the item of information.
guidance: Example: a discussion applying 35 U.S.C. 101 to a claim, wholly contained in the body of the request and not based on a supporting document, counts as an item. However, if the body merely reproduces a supporting document, a separate copy must be provided and the supporting document will be counted as the item.

name: Supplemental examination limited to whether request raises an SNQ
description: Supplemental examination is limited to determining whether the information properly submitted as part of the request raises a substantial new question of patentability (SNQ) (35 U.S.C. 257(a)).
guidance: An item limited to correction of factual information alone may not raise an SNQ. To raise an SNQ based on factual correction (e.g., correction of a foreign priority/benefit claim), the request should include additional item(s) (such as intervening references) that would cause patentability to depend on the correction. If no SNQ is raised, the proceeding concludes with issuance of a supplemental examination certificate indicating no SNQ and no reexamination is ordered.

name: Office will consider only items submitted by patent owner
description: When analyzing a request, the Office will only consider the item(s) of information provided by the patent owner and will not initiate supplemental examination of the patent in view of any item not requested by the owner.
guidance: Prior art of record not properly submitted as items will, in general, not be considered except to determine whether submitted items are cumulative. Requests that effectively ask reconsideration of all claims solely in view of factual corrections without listing each prior art item are improper and fail to meet requirements (e.g., 37 CFR 1.610(b)). See MPEP § 2811 for required elements of a request.

name: Step 1 — statutory category (process/composition/etc.)
description: Determine whether the claim recites a statutory category of invention (e.g., process, composition of matter, machine, manufacture).
guidance: If the claim recites a statutory category (for example, 'a method of detecting JUL-1' is a process), proceed to analyze whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception. Example: 'The claim recites a series of steps ... Thus, the claim is directed to a process.'

name: Identify whether claim is directed to a judicial exception
description: Assess whether the claim (or claim limitation) is directed to a judicial exception such as a law of nature, natural phenomenon, product of nature, or abstract idea.
guidance: Point to the claim limitation(s) and explain why they constitute an exception (e.g., correlation between a biomarker and a disease is a law of nature; mental steps/critical thinking can be an abstract idea). Example guidance for rejections: 'identify step c as an exception by pointing to it in the claim and explaining why it is an exception, that the recited correlation is a law of nature ... and/or that the critical thinking step is an abstract idea.'

name: Markedly different characteristics analysis for nature‑based products
description: For claims reciting nature‑based products, evaluate whether the claimed product has 'markedly different characteristics' from its naturally occurring counterpart (changes in structure, function, or other characteristics).
guidance: Consider structural, functional, or other characteristic changes (e.g., granulation to defined particle sizes, addition of pectin to form a gel, altered organoleptic properties, encapsulation for controlled release). If the claim is focused on a process rather than the product, the markedly different characteristics analysis on recited nature‑based product limitations may not be necessary.

name: Broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) to identify natural counterpart
description: Apply the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim to identify the appropriate naturally occurring counterpart for comparison.
guidance: Example: A claim to 'texiol and water' under BRI may cover the naturally occurring sap, so the analysis compares the claimed mixture to that naturally occurring material. Use BRI when determining whether the claim covers what exists in nature.

name: Insignificant pre‑solution/data‑gathering activity
description: Determine whether claimed additional steps are merely data‑gathering or other insignificant pre‑solution activity that do not add meaningful limitations beyond the exception.
guidance: High‑level steps such as 'obtaining a sample' or 'detecting using any generic antibody' are often well‑understood, routine, and conventional and count as insignificant pre‑solution activity (mere instruction to 'apply' the exception). Example: 'Obtaining a sample ... is well‑understood, routine and conventional ... amounts to insignificant presolution activity.'

name: Physical/tangible element alone does not confer eligibility
description: The mere recitation of a physical or tangible element (e.g., a sample, a device, a step of administering a drug) does not automatically make a claim eligible if it is otherwise directed to an exception.
guidance: Cite Alice: 'the mere physical or tangible nature of additional elements ... does not automatically confer eligibility on a claim directed to an abstract idea.' Examiners should explain why physical elements are insufficient if they are routine or conventional.

name: When to skip markedly different product analysis
description: If the claim as a whole is focused on a process (practical application) rather than on a nature‑based product, it may not be necessary to perform the markedly different characteristics analysis on recited nature‑based product limitations.
guidance: Example: claims directed to methods of treating or applying a product (e.g., administering antibodies to treat a disease) may be analyzed as processes, and examiners can focus on whether the process limitations recite a judicial exception rather than analyzing the product limitations' marked differences.

name: Office action / reasons for allowance drafting guidance
description: When issuing a rejection or reasons for allowance, identify the specific claim limitation(s) considered an exception and clearly explain why, and then explain why additional elements do or do not amount to significantly more.
guidance: If the record would benefit from clarification, add remarks to an Office action or reasons for allowance indicating the basis (e.g., that a peptide is a 'product of nature' because it 'lacks markedly different characteristics' or that a recited unconventional limitation confines the exception to a particular useful application). For rejections, 'identify the additional elements and explain why they do not amount to significantly more ... because they merely add data gathering and well‑understood, routine and conventional activities.'

name: Examples of what counts as 'markedly different' or 'significantly more' (illustrative factors)
description: Concrete factual indicia that can support finding markedly different characteristics or significantly more include: changes in organoleptic properties, controlled release behavior, defined particle size distribution (X10/X90), presence of non‑natural additives (e.g., pectin), use of a non‑conventional reagent (e.g., porcine antibody for human protein detection), and unconventional delivery devices (e.g., coated microneedle array).
guidance: Use the specification and factual record (e.g., sensory panels, known prior uses, prevalence in the field) to support findings. If evidence shows the recited formulation or reagent was not routinely used for the claimed purpose at filing, that supports eligibility.

name: Averment that the invention was new, useful, and not on sale or public use before application
description: The declaration should aver the subject-matter was 'new and useful', 'not known or used before the plaintiff's invention or discovery', and 'not at the time of his application for a patent in public use or on sale with his consent or allowance.'
guidance: These are essential elements of the plaintiff's title and must be pleaded to support a claim for infringement.

name: Requirements for correction under 37 CFR 1.48(c) (adding inventors for previously unclaimed subject matter)
description: If a nonprovisional discloses unclaimed subject matter by persons not named as inventors when an executed declaration was first filed, the application may be amended under 37 CFR 1.48(c) to add claims and name correct inventors. Amendment requires: (1) request setting forth desired inventorship change; (2) statement from each person being added that addition is necessitated by amendment of the claims and that the inventorship error occurred without deceptive intention; (3) an oath or declaration by each actual inventor as required by §1.63 or as permitted by §§1.42, 1.43, or 1.47; (4) processing fee under §1.17(i); and (5) written consent of any assignee of the original named inventors.
guidance: Any claims added must be supported by the disclosure as filed and cannot add new matter. Use of appropriate form paragraphs (e.g., 2.13.02, 2.13h) when deficiencies exist.

name: Declaration of possession and claim to be true and first inventor
description: An application must contain a declaration to the effect that the applicant is in possession of an invention, and that he (or one or more joint applicants) claims to be the true and first inventor(s) of the invention, and must be accompanied by either a provisional or complete specification.
guidance: Declaration is a required component of the application; accompaniment by specification (provisional or complete) is mandatory.

name: Complete specification contents and form
description: A complete specification must particularly describe and ascertain the nature of the invention and in what manner it is to be performed, must commence with the title and must end with a distinct statement of the invention claimed, and must be accompanied by drawings if required.
guidance: Emphasises particularity and sufficiency of disclosure: must teach how to perform the invention and include a clear claim; format requirements (title, end with claims).

name: Opposition to grant — permitted grounds and time limit
description: Any person may at any time within two months from the date of advertisement of acceptance give notice of opposition to the grant of the patent on the ground that the applicant obtained the invention from him, or that the invention has been patented in this country on an application of prior date, or that the complete specification describes or claims an invention other than that described in the provisional specification (and such other invention is subject of an intervening application by the opponent), but on no other ground.
guidance: Opposition is tightly circumscribed to named grounds and must be given within two months; procedures for hearing and law officer determination are set out; law officer may obtain expert assistance.

name: Limitation on amendments — no enlargement or substantive change
description: No amendment shall be allowed that would make the specification, as amended, claim an invention substantially larger than, or substantially different from, the invention claimed by the specification as it stood before amendment.
guidance: Core substantive limitation: amendments cannot broaden or change the claimed invention materially; leave to amend conclusive except in case of fraud.

name: Limitation on damages after amendment
description: Where an amendment by way of disclaimer, correction or explanation has been allowed, no damages shall be given in any action in respect of the use of the invention before the amendment unless the patentee establishes to the satisfaction of the Court that his original claim was framed in good faith and with reasonable skill and knowledge.
guidance: Protects defendants from retroactive damages when claims are narrowed unless patentee acted in good faith and with competence in original drafting.

name: Particulars in infringement proceedings — delivery and consequences
description: In an action for infringement the plaintiff must deliver particulars of the breaches complained of with his statement of claim (or by court order), and the defendant must deliver particulars of objections with his defence; if the defendant disputes validity he must state grounds and, if want of novelty, time and place of prior publication or user alleged; evidence of unparticularised allegations is inadmissible without leave; particulars may be amended; taxation of costs will take particulars into account.
guidance: Strict particularisation requirements govern evidence admissibility and cost consequences; ensures parties provide specifics of allegations early.

name: Court may consider evidence of the actual invention and state of the art when construing claims
description: In the progress of a trial the state of the art, the surrounding circumstances in which the inventor was placed, the previous existence of some things mentioned or referred to in the patent, will all be likely to be developed on the evidence; and these facts may materially affect the construction to be given to the claim. The judge must gather as he goes along; informing himself upon the evidence, and observing what facts are controverted, and what facts are not controverted, which bear upon the meaning of the claim, in reference to its extent.
guidance: If facts material to construction are not left in doubt on the evidence, the construction will be given to the jury absolutely; but if the evidence requires a finding of facts by the jury, the construction will be given to them conditionally. The court should receive and watch evidence and apply it to construction, but must take care that evidence is not allowed to supply positive omissions which would render the specification defective. (§§457, 463)

name: Prior existence of matter mentioned affects extent of claim; patentee presumed not to claim things known in use
description: If it is manifest, on the face of the terms in which the patentee has described his invention, that he has included something of which he was not the inventor, his patent cannot be allowed to cover it. The degree or extent to which that thing was known before, its great familiarity and constant use for analogous purposes, will be important elements in the question whether the patentee has claimed it as of his own invention.
guidance: This consideration supports the rule that the patentee is to be presumed not to intend to claim things which he must know to be in use; specifications should be read so, consistently with the fair import of language, as to make the claim coextensive with the actual discovery or invention. (§§458–459)

name: Novelty is a prerequisite and is a question of fact
description: The novelty of the invention is a prerequisite to validity of the patent and is a question of fact to be determined from the evidence.
guidance: Even if the claimed thing is new, the court must decide whether it is the kind of invention the law recognizes as patentable (see also §468).

name: If specification on its face shows inclusion of known matter, patent cannot cover that matter
description: If it is manifest on the face of the specification that the patentee has included something of which he was not the inventor, his patent cannot be allowed to cover it.
guidance: Where it is doubtful whether he has so included it, the extent to which that thing was known and in use will be important in deciding whether he intended to claim it. This supports presumption against claiming known public matter. (§458)

name: Filing fees, payment policies, and discounts
description: Fee structure and payment rules relevant to filing and prosecution.
guidance: Examples provided: Filing Fee (inclusive of 5 claims) — Small Entity Php 2,000; Big Entity Php 4,320. Excess claims fee per claim Php 180 (small) / Php 360 (big). First and Second Publication fees (Php 920/960 depending on category). Issuance fees listed; 'FILE NOW and PAY LATER' option (pay within one month from filing). Plus 1% Legal Research Fund. Student/Youth filer discount: 75% off fees for filers 21 years and below. Annual fee schedules include on-time payment, late payment, 50% surcharge for publication fee late payment, and 1% Legal Research Fund components.

name: Patent/Utility Model/Industrial Designs Women Incentive Package ('Juana Invent/UM/ID')
description: Special incentive to support women inventors and eligible small entities.
guidance: Waiver of filing fees in favor of 1,000 qualified applicants for: filing fees for Invention/UM/ID applications; filing fees for excess claims/additional embodiments for ID; first publication fee; and priority fee, if any. All other fees are to be paid by the applicant. Eligibility: Philippine nationals only or Philippine micro-, small-, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) only.

name: Particular configuration and method can defeat 'abstract idea'
description: Claims that specify a particular configuration of sensors and a particular method of using raw sensor data to more accurately calculate position and orientation are not directed to an abstract idea.
guidance: Example: claims reciting an inertial tracking system with a particular configuration of inertial sensors and a particular method of using the raw data were held not abstract (Visual Memory v. NVIDIA). Anti-pattern: purely high‑level descriptions of tracking without particular sensor configuration or specific data‑processing steps.

name: Non-abstract improvement in computer functionality
description: Claims that effect a non-abstract improvement in computer functionality (rather than claiming the abstract idea generally) are patent-eligible.
guidance: Example: claims directed to computer security/monitoring systems that improve computer functionality were held eligible. Focus drafts on how the invention improves specific computer capabilities or fixes a computer‑specific problem.

name: Claims tied to improved user interfaces or small-screen functioning
description: Claims that improve the functioning of computers in specific contexts (for example, improved display interface for small screens) are not directed to an abstract idea.
guidance: Example: improved display interface for small screens (Core Wireless). Show how the claimed interface overcomes constraints of the device environment.

name: Read the claims as a whole
description: The eligibility inquiry requires that the claims be read as a whole rather than dissected into isolated elements.
guidance: Example: claims for navigating three‑dimensional electronic spreadsheets were found non‑abstract when read as a whole. Anti-pattern: evaluating only individual steps in isolation and ignoring their combined contribution.

name: Generic/recitation of routine steps indicates lack of inventive concept
description: Claims that recite only generic steps (e.g., creating a base version, creating a new version, and determining changes) and nothing more are likely to lack an inventive concept and be ineligible.
guidance: Example: spreadsheet change‑tracking claims were ineligible for reciting only generic versioning steps. Guidance: include non‑generic elements or show how the steps are tied to a specific technological implementation.

name: Examine the patent's 'claimed advance' at Alice step one
description: At step one, courts examine the patent's 'claimed advance' to determine whether the claims are directed to an abstract idea or to a specific technological improvement.
guidance: Example: Ancora — courts look to what the patent asserts it advances. Drafting tip: clearly state the claimed advance in the specification and claims to frame step‑one analysis favorably.

name: Software can constitute non-abstract computer improvements
description: Software that effects a technological improvement to computer technology can render claims non-abstract; improvements need not be hardware‑only.
guidance: Example: software that changes computer behavior (Ancora) was recognized as capable of improving computer technology. Emphasize how software elements materially change computer operation or solve a computer‑specific problem.

name: Overlap between step one and step two considerations
description: Courts recognize overlaps between Alice step one (directed to) and step two (inventive concept) considerations; some factual questions relevant to step two may influence step one.
guidance: Example: court notes overlaps and remands when factual issues on inventive concept exist (Data Engine). Be prepared to present factual record on whether claim limitations are routine or conventional.

name: Machine‑or‑transformation (MOT) test remains relevant in some contexts
description: Even if claims are argued to be abstract, satisfying the machine‑or‑transformation test (e.g., where a computer plays a significant role in real‑time data capture/transmission) can support eligibility.
guidance: Example: claims involving real‑time data capture/transmission satisfied MOT arguments (Helios). Use evidence showing specific machine involvement or a transformation of an article into a different state.

name: Limiting claims to a particular technological field supports eligibility
description: Claims limited to a particular technological field or particular form of a technology (e.g., electronic trading with an intuitive grid display) can be not directed to an abstract idea.
guidance: Example: click‑based trading limited to electronic trading with a technological improvement was eligible. Avoid overbroad functional language that would cover non‑technological implementations.

name: Claims 'rooted in computer technology' to overcome internet-centric problems
description: Claims rooted in computer/network technology that address problems specifically arising in the Internet or computer context are likely eligible.
guidance: Example: solutions rooted in computer technology to overcome Internet‑centric problems (business intelligence automatic agent, remote access portal). Show how the claimed features are necessarily tied to computer/network constraints.

name: Specific, non‑generic devices/systems as meaningful limitations
description: Reciting particular non‑generic devices or trusted systems (e.g., a repository that is a 'trusted system' using digital certificates) can supply an inventive concept and support eligibility.
guidance: Example: digital rights management claims requiring a 'trusted system' and digital certificates. Anti-pattern: reciting a generic 'computer' or 'server' without specific structure or function.

name: Avoid claiming preemption of every application of an idea
description: Claims should not be so broad as to preempt all applications of an abstract idea; narrowly claiming a particular way of performing a function helps eligibility.
guidance: Example: a claim covering only one specific way to calculate an average power did not attempt to preempt every application. Draft claims to carve out a particular implementation rather than monopolize a concept.

name: Specificity that places meaningful boundaries on the inventive concept
description: Claims described with particular steps and parameter determination that place meaningful boundaries are less likely to be abstract and more likely to have an inventive concept.
guidance: Example: image scanning claims that determine parameters and apply them to operate a scanner; court found sufficient specificity. Include concrete parameter values/relationships and how they are used.

name: Claims that 'do more' than an analog counterpart can be eligible
description: Claims that do more than a traditional analog counterpart (e.g., provide proof of delivery and content, not just proof of mailing) may avoid being abstract.
guidance: Example: electronic message delivery claims providing proof of delivery and content. Show additional technical functionality uniquely enabled by the electronic implementation.

name: Problem specifically arising in the technological realm indicates eligibility
description: Claims that address problems that specifically arise in the realm of computers/networks (not long‑prevalent human processes) are more likely to be eligible.
guidance: Example: claims reducing host processing demand or addressing network congestion in defined environments. Identify why the problem is intrinsic to the technology and how the claim addresses it.

name: Factual questions regarding conventionality/inventive concept may require remand
description: Where there are underlying factual disputes (e.g., whether limitations are conventional or provide an inventive concept), courts may remand to the district court rather than resolve §101 on the pleadings.
guidance: Example: Data Engine remanded some claims because of factual questions. Build factual record (expert declarations, prior art comparisons) to counter assertions of conventionality.

name: Written description and enablement requirement (Act of July 4, 1836, §6)
description: Before any inventor shall receive a patent ... he shall deliver a written description of his invention or discovery, and of the manner and process of making, constructing, using and compounding the same, in such full, clear, and exact terms, avoiding unnecessary prolixity, as to enable any person skilled in the art or science to which it appertains ... to make, construct, compound, and use the same.
guidance: For machines: 'he shall fully explain the principle and the several modes in which he has contemplated the application of that principle ... and shall particularly specify and point out the part, improvement, or combination, which he claims as his own invention or discovery.' Accompany the description with drawings/written references where applicable, or with specimens for compositions of matter; descriptions and drawings to be signed by the inventor and attested by two witnesses; furnish a model where a representation by model is possible. The description must enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the invention from the specification itself.

name: Specification may control generality but repugnancy voids the patent
description: The rule allowing the letters-patent to be controlled by the specification cannot extend to a case where the terms of the former are inconsistent with those of the latter; if there is a clear repugnancy between the description of the invention in the specification and the invention stated in the letters-patent, the patent will be void.
guidance: If the patent issues for an invention not described in the specification, the statute is not complied with; the specification cannot be used to justify a patent that claims something different from what is described.

name: Patents construed liberally to ascertain nature and extent of claim
description: Patents are to be construed liberally and not subjected to a rigid interpretation; the nature and extent of the invention claimed is to be ascertained from the fair sense of the words employed.
guidance: While courts take a liberal view to give effect to inventor's rights and promote useful arts, liberal construction is balanced against statutory requisites that protect the public. Do not rely on overly technical narrow reading when the claim's nature is otherwise apparent.

name: Two primary objectives of a specification
description: The specification has two objects: (1) to make known the manner of constructing the machine (if a machine) so as to enable artisans to make and use it after expiration; (2) to put the public in possession of what the party claims as his own invention so as to ascertain if he claims anything already known and to warn innocent purchasers or users of potential infringement.
guidance: Draft the specification both to enable post-expiration practice and to clearly notify the public of the patentee's claim boundaries to avoid misleading or overbroad claims.

name: Describe the subject-matter claimed with reasonable certainty
description: To describe the subject-matter, or what the patentee claims to have invented, so as to enable the public to know what his claim is. It must appear with reasonable certainty what the party intends to claim.
guidance: Language need not be highly technical but must not mislead; the whole specification should be read in connection (words standing alone not singled out). If the claim is left ambiguous or uncertain so that the court cannot, without conjecture, gather the invention, the patent is void. Use clear statements and, where possible, explicit claim language or specific pointing-out of claimed parts.

name: Distinguish clearly between what is old and what is new
description: The statute requires the patentee to give a written description which involves, where the patentee uses what is old, distinguishing between what is old and what is new; he is required to point out in what his invention or discovery consists.
guidance: If the description mixes old and new without showing the patentee does not claim the old parts, the patent may be broader than the invention and therefore void. Be explicit about prior art and the novel contributions; identify which parts are admitted old and which parts are claimed as new.

name: Improvement patents must state specifically what the improvement is and be limited to it
description: If the patent be for an improved machine, or for an improvement of a machine, it must state in what the improvement specifically consists, and it must be limited to such improvement.
guidance: A general statement that the machine is 'an improvement' without stating particulars is insufficient and can render the patent void for ambiguity. Clearly define the improvement and limit claims to that improvement.

name: Cannot include pre-existing (not-new) matter in claim — if any claimed part is not new, patent is void
description: Whatever appears to be covered by the claim of the patentee as his own invention must be taken as part of the claim; courts cannot reject any part of the claim; and therefore if it turns out that anything claimed is not new, the patent is void.
guidance: Do not claim old elements as if they were novel; ensure claims are supported by specification and avoid claiming the exclusive use of known machinery. If a claimed element is shown not to be new, the entire patent claim may be invalidated.

name: When an RCE is appropriate
description: An RCE comes into play when dealing with a Final Office Action. An RCE makes sense when an applicant has received a Final Office Action and desires to make further claim amendments and/or arguments.
guidance: In particular, if the contemplated claim amendments would require the examiner to perform a further search of the prior art (or at least cause the examiner to feel that way), then an RCE would be suitable. Sometimes, conducting an examiner interview prior to filing a response may be useful in determining whether an RCE is warranted.

name: When an RCE is unnecessary
description: Not all Final Office Actions require an RCE. If the examiner has indicated that certain claims would be allowable, then you may simply file an after-final response taking the allowable subject matter.
guidance: An RCE might also be unnecessary if you are considering only narrowing claim amendments. For example, filing an after-final response with an AFCP request may be an option. It will be up to the Examiner to choose whether they will entertain such an after-final response.

name: Use of examiner interviews and strategic amendments
description: With the proper use of examiner interviews and strategic claim amendments and arguments, you might be able to get your patent application allowed without unnecessary filings.
guidance: Conducting an examiner interview prior to filing a response may be useful in determining whether an RCE is warranted; strategic claim amendments and arguments may avoid the need for an RCE or increase the chance of allowance after filing one.

name: USPTO correspondence with regulatory agency for eligibility information
description: When the Office has no clear reason to deny eligibility (or expects informalities will be corrected), the Office sends a first letter to the regulatory agency requesting information regarding eligibility, accompanied by a copy of the application.
guidance: The letter does not request determination of the regulatory review period. The regulatory agency reply typically verifies whether product underwent regulatory review, whether marketing permission was first permitted commercial marketing/use or first under the claimed process, whether the application was filed within 60 days after approval, and any other information relevant to eligibility.

name: Prioritized examination (track) — fee and limitations
description: A prioritized examination fee of $4,800 is established for filing a request for prioritized examination of a nonprovisional utility or plant application. In addition to this fee, the normal filing, search, examination (including applicable excess claims and application size fees), processing fee, and publication fee are due.
guidance: Director may prescribe conditions and limits by regulation. Until regulations are prescribed, no prioritized application may contain/amend to more than 4 independent claims or more than 30 total claims. The Director may not accept more than 10,000 prioritization requests in any fiscal year until regulations set another limit.

name: Reward payable where soldier is charged or administratively found a deserter
description: A reward may be paid either where the soldier has been charged with desertion, or where, though not charged, it is determined administratively that the soldier was a deserter in fact; where not charged, claimant must show deserter in fact to claim reward.

name: Military preliminary locating reduces civilian's reward share
description: If military authorities perform preliminary locating/work and the claimant only effects arrest/confinement/delivery, claimant may be entitled only to a portion of the reward to be determined by the Secretary of War (e.g., $25 deemed ample in one case).

name: Improvements to any other technology or technical field
