description: Improvements in technology beyond mere computer functionality may demonstrate patent eligibility; claims directed to an improvement in a technological process (rather than to an abstract idea) can be eligible under 35 U.S.C. 101.
guidance: Claims should describe how the claimed invention improves the existing technology (e.g., McRO: particular rules that enabled automation of specific animation tasks). To show an improvement, claims must recite details regarding how a computer aids the method, the extent to which the computer aids the method, or the significance of a computer to performance. Merely adding generic computer components or instructions to perform the method on generic machinery is not sufficient. Examples of sufficient improvements include particular computerized methods for rubber molding (Diehr), new telephone/server combos (TLI), improved downloading for streaming (Affinity Labs v. DirecTV), improved digital compression (DDR Holdings), new data-generating measurement devices (Electric Power Group), specific sensor configurations (Thales Visionix), specific structured GUIs (Trading Techs), and improved biomedical preservation processes (CellzDirect). Examples of insufficient improvements include commonplace business methods on general-purpose computers (Alice), routine laboratory techniques, gathering/analyzing/displaying information by conventional techniques (TLI), high-level delivery of broadcast content to portable devices, general email screening on generic computers, and selecting existing content/functions from known options (Affinity Labs). See MPEP § 2106.05(a) and § 2106.05(f) for more on mere instructions to apply an exception.

name: Particularity or generality of the elements of the machine/apparatus
description: When considering whether a claimed machine provides significantly more than a judicial exception, assess the degree to which the machine in the claim can be specifically identified (not any and all machines).
guidance: Specific recitation of particular machine structure (e.g., antenna shape/length in Mackay Radio; Fourdrinier machine components in Eibel Process) can indicate a particular machine. By contrast, a general purpose computer that applies an exception using conventional computer functions does not qualify as a particular machine (Ultramercial; TLI). Merely reciting concrete or tangible components is not an inventive concept. If an applicant adds a generic computer or generic components and asserts they make the claim 'specially programmed' or a 'particular machine,' the examiner should determine whether the added elements provide significantly more than the judicial exception; adding generic computer components or programming to perform generic functions does not automatically overcome eligibility rejections. See MPEP § 2106.03 and related case law.

name: Whether the machine implements the steps of the method (integral use)
description: Determine if the machine is used integrally to achieve performance of the claimed method (plays a significant part in permitting the claimed method to be performed) rather than merely being an object on which the method operates.
guidance: If the machine cannot perform the claimed method steps (e.g., the Internet cannot itself perform fraud detection steps in CyberSource), mere recitation of the Internet or other machines as data sources or objects will not provide significantly more. Additional elements that invoke computers or machinery merely as tools to perform an existing process generally will not be significantly more. See CyberSource and Versata (machine must permit performance, not solely speed up an obvious solution). See MPEP § 2106.05(f).

name: Whether machine involvement is extra-solution activity or field-of-use
description: Assess the extent to which the machine or apparatus imposes meaningful limits on the claim versus contributing only nominally or insignificantly to execution of the claimed method.
guidance: Use of a machine solely for data-gathering steps, or as a field-of-use limitation, typically does not provide significantly more (Bilski; CyberSource). If the machine contributes only nominally to the execution of claimed steps, it will not render an otherwise ineligible claim eligible. See MPEP §§ 2106.05(g) & (h).

name: Transformation factor: degree to which the recited article is particular
description: Assess whether the transformation is applied to a specifically identified article versus a generically recited article; transformations of generically recited articles are less likely to provide significantly more.
guidance: A transformation limited to particular, specifically identifiable articles is more likely to provide significantly more; transformations claimed over 'any and all' articles are less persuasive. Specific identification of the article supports eligibility.

name: Transformation factor: whether transformation is extra-solution activity or field-of-use
description: Determine whether the claimed transformation merely limits the claim to a particular field-of-use or is nominal/insignificant to executing the claimed method.
guidance: If the transformation contributes only nominally (e.g., merely administering a drug as a field-of-use limitation in Mayo), it will not provide significantly more. See Mayo analysis where Supreme Court found administering the drug was only a field-of-use limitation and insufficient to confer eligibility. See MPEP §§ 2106.05(g) & (h).

name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity consideration
description: Assess whether additional elements are well-understood, routine, conventional activities previously known to the industry; if so (and recited at a high level), they do not favor eligibility.
guidance: If additional elements are specific limitations beyond what is well-understood/routine/conventional (e.g., unconventional steps confining the claim to a particular useful application), then they favor eligibility (DDR Holdings example). If additional elements are merely well-known routine activities (e.g., measuring metabolites by any known process in Mayo), they will not amount to an inventive concept. This consideration overlaps with improvement, mere-instruction, and insignificant-extra-solution considerations. See MPEP § 2106.05(d) and case law (DDR Holdings; Mayo; Parker v. Flook).

name: Evaluative point: an element known in the art can still be unconventional/non-routine
description: Known-in-the-art elements are not automatically routine; novelty/obviousness is separate from eligibility — elements known in the art can still be unconventional in how they are used and thus favor eligibility.
guidance: Examiners should not conflate novelty/obviousness with eligibility. Example: Enfish claims reflected an improvement in database technology (self-referential table features) that were considered unconventional for purposes of eligibility even though anticipated by a prior art reference. Thus, an element taught in the prior art can still be non-routine in context and favor eligibility.

name: Apply Alice/Mayo two-step test for all claims
description: All claims must be evaluated using the two-part Alice/Mayo framework: Step 2A — determine whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception; Step 2B — determine whether the claim recites significantly more than the exception.
guidance: If a claim is not directed to an exception at Step 2A or amounts to significantly more at Step 2B, it is eligible. If it is directed to an exception at Step 2A and does not amount to significantly more at Step 2B, it is ineligible. Use other Step 2B considerations (mere instructions, insignificant extra-solution activity, field of use) to inform the analysis. See Alice/Mayo decisions and MPEP guidance.

name: Step 2B considerations to evaluate 'significantly more'
description: When assessing whether claimed elements provide significantly more than a judicial exception, consider: mere instructions to apply an exception, insignificant extra-solution activity, field of use/technological environment, and the definition/role of a 'machine.'
guidance: Examiners may find it helpful to evaluate MPEP § 2106.05(f) (mere instructions to apply an exception), § 2106.05(g) (insignificant extra-solution activity), and § 2106.05(h) (field of use/technological environment) in determining whether an element or combination of elements makes a claim significantly more than the judicial exception. Also consider MPEP § 2106.03 for the definition of 'machine.'

name: Applicability date and coverage (ST.26 requirement)
description: For applications (including national stage and reissue) having a filing date, or international filing date for national stage, on or after July 1, 2022, disclosures of one or more nucleotide and/or amino acid sequences as defined in 37 CFR 1.831(b) must include a Sequence Listing XML as a separate part of the specification (i.e., must comply with 37 CFR 1.831 through 1.835).
guidance: This applies even if the new application claims benefit/priority to earlier applications filed before July 1, 2022 (continuations, CIPs, provisionals where applicable, PCT national stage under 35 U.S.C. 371, reissue filed on/after July 1, 2022). Determine applicability by the filing or international filing date as described.

name: Statement of basis for amendment
description: An amendment that adds an initial Sequence Listing XML must include a statement indicating the basis for the amendment with specific references to particular parts of the application as originally filed (specification, claims, drawings) for all sequence data (37 CFR 1.835(a)(3)).
guidance: The statement should identify paragraphs or drawing sheets where the sequences were originally disclosed and, for replacements or edits, identify the specific sequences being added/modified and their original locations.

name: Support statement for amended sequence data
description: When submitting additions, deletions, or replacements in a Sequence Listing XML, applicant must include a statement indicating the support for the changes with specific references to parts of the application as originally filed for all amended sequence data (37 CFR 1.835(b)(4) and 1.835(a)(3) analogously).
guidance: Cite paragraphs, claims, or drawing sheets that provide the basis/support for each amended sequence entry to show amendment is within original disclosure.

name: Improper ASCII .txt Sequence Listing submissions when XML required and available relief
description: If an applicant mistakenly submits an ASCII .txt Sequence Listing in an application filed on or after July 1, 2022 when a Sequence Listing XML is required, the earlier .txt listing may be used to support a compliant Sequence Listing XML only in limited circumstances (e.g., relying on 37 CFR 1.57(b) if a prior filed application contains a compliant Sequence Listing present on its filing date, or via a grantable petition under 37 CFR 1.182 if no proper benefit/priority claim exists).
guidance: Relief under 1.57(b) requires a compliant earlier listing in an application to which proper benefit/priority is claimed and that the earlier listing was present on that filing date. A petition under 1.182 requires showing the ASCII listing's sequence information and submitting a compliant Sequence Listing XML plus statements that no new matter is introduced; any ASCII .txt listing relied on will be retained in the record for retention purposes.

name: Requirements for a petition or response relying on an earlier Sequence Listing
description: When relying on an earlier Sequence Listing (e.g., under 1.57(b)) or filing a petition under 1.182 to justify a later-submitted compliant Sequence Listing XML, applicant must submit: (1) a compliant Sequence Listing XML; (2) a statement identifying where the omitted portion can be found (e.g., identifying nucleotide/amino acid sequence information in the earlier listing); (3) identification of the sequences relied upon; (4) a statement that the Sequence Listing XML does not introduce new matter; and (5) a statement that the portion was inadvertently omitted if claiming 1.57(b) relief.
guidance: Availability of relief under 1.57(b) precludes filing a grantable petition under 1.182 seeking the same relief. Ensure all required statements and citations to the earlier filed material are precise.

name: Essential requirements for a successful restoration request
description: For the request to restore the right of priority to be successful: the international application must contain a priority claim to an earlier application and must have been filed within two months from the date the priority period expired; the request must state reasons for failure; any applicable fee must be paid; and, if required, supporting declaration/evidence must be provided (Rules 26bis.1(a), 26bis.3).
guidance: If the priority claim was not present at filing, it must be added within two months from expiry in accordance with Rule 26bis.1(a). Fee payment must be made before expiration of the time limit (fee payment time may be extended up to two months under Rule 26bis.3(d)). If evidence is required, it should preferably accompany the request but may be furnished upon invitation.

name: Declarations that may be included in Box No. VIII (i)–(v)
description: For the purposes of national law in one or more designated States, the applicant may include the following declarations under Rule 4.17 in Boxes VIII(i) to (v): (i) declaration as to identity of the inventor; (ii) declaration as to the applicant’s entitlement, as at the international filing date, to apply for and be granted a patent; (iii) declaration as to the applicant’s entitlement, as at the international filing date, to claim priority of the earlier application; (iv) declaration of inventorship (only for purposes of designation of the United States); (v) declaration as to non-prejudicial disclosures or exceptions to lack of novelty.
guidance: These are the only declarations permitted in Boxes VIII(i)–(v). If included, the relevant standardized wording must be used.

name: Prohibition on dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
description: It is professional misconduct for a practitioner to engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation.
guidance: Specific instances include falsely representing to a client that a filing was made, claiming to have served documents when not done, or accepting fees for work not performed.

name: Obvious-to-try is improper when it would require exploring a new technology or general approach with only general guidance
description: Second Kubin class: obvious-to-try is improper 'when what was “obvious to try” was to explore a new technology or general approach that seemed to be a promising field of experimentation, where the prior art gave only general guidance as to the particular form of the claimed invention or how to achieve it.'
guidance: If the prior art provides only broad or speculative guidance about a new field or approach (no specific, predictable solutions), do not base obviousness on 'obvious to try.' Examples: Kubin discussion; Rolls‑Royce (fan blade) — nothing in prior art suggested the specific change, so it would not have presented itself as an option.

name: Reasonable expectation of success (predictability requirement)
description: A finding of reasonable expectation of success is required for obvious-to-try and many obviousness rationales; unpredictability or unexpected results can overcome a prima facie case of obviousness.
guidance: Examiners must evaluate whether, at the time of the invention, a person of ordinary skill would have had a reasonable expectation that the claimed approach would work. Lack of predictability, serendipitous discoveries, or unexpected therapeutic advantages (examples: Takeda, Ortho‑McNeil, Sanofi) support nonobviousness. Conversely, routine methods or predictable application of known techniques (examples: Morella/Sambrook sequencing and isolation leading to Kubin rejection) can support a reasonable expectation of success.

name: Known work in one field may prompt predictable variations in another (design incentives / market forces) — five required findings
description: To reject based on adaptation of known work from one field to another, Office personnel must resolve Graham factual inquiries and articulate the following findings: (1) prior art included a similar or analogous device/method/product; (2) design incentives or market forces would have prompted adaptation; (3) differences between the claimed invention and prior art were encompassed in known variations or principles in the prior art; (4) one of ordinary skill, in view of the incentives/forces, could have implemented the claimed variation and it would have been predictable; and (5) any additional Graham-based findings necessary to explain obviousness.
guidance: The rationale is that market/design pressures could have prompted predictable variation. If any of these findings cannot be made, this rationale cannot support obviousness. Examples: Dann (data processing analogy), Leapfrog (combining older mechanical toy with modern electronics), KSR (pedal assembly adaptation). Examiners must explicitly state and support each of the five findings when relying on this rationale.

name: Teaching, Suggestion, or Motivation (TSM) to modify or combine — required findings
description: To reject a claim based on a motivation-to-combine rationale, Office personnel must resolve Graham factual inquiries and articulate: (1) a finding that there was some teaching, suggestion, or motivation (in the references or general knowledge) to modify or combine; (2) a finding that there was a reasonable expectation of success; and (3) whatever additional Graham-based findings are necessary to explain the conclusion of obviousness.
guidance: This rationale supports the conclusion that a person of ordinary skill would have been motivated to combine teachings to achieve the claimed invention with a reasonable expectation of success. If any of these findings cannot be made, TSM cannot support an obviousness rejection. Case law: DyStar, In re Kahn, and discussion in Perfect Web illustrating how TSM and common sense interact under KSR.

name: Resolve Graham factual inquiries before applying obviousness rationales
description: Before applying any of the above rationales (obvious-to-try, cross-field adaptation, TSM, common sense), Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries (scope and content of the prior art; differences between the prior art and the claims; level of ordinary skill in the art; and objective indicia/secondary considerations) and make any additional factual findings necessary in the case.
guidance: The MPEP repeatedly instructs examiners to place the inquiry 'in the context of the subject matter at issue' and to make explicit Graham findings. Many of the listed rationales are contingent on those factual findings; examiners must articulate them in the record with supporting evidence and reasoning (examples throughout the cited decisions: KSR, Abbott, Takeda, Perfect Web).

name: Timing and circumstances of claim/claim-withdrawal conduct (pre-trial dropping of claims)
description: Maintaining numerous asserted claims until shortly before trial and then dropping patents or claims without warning (particularly close to trial) can be unreasonable, prejudicial, and reflective of substantive weakness—supporting fees in some cases.
guidance: The District of Delaware Hatch-Waxman example: maintaining 35 asserted claims until two weeks before trial and then dropping patents two business days before trial was found 'unreasonable, prejudicial' and supported a fees award.

name: Supply of file elements where ISA ≠ IPEA
description: When the ISA and IPEA are not the same, elements are supplied as follows: demand by applicant; request/description/drawings/claims by the International Bureau; ISR or Article 17(2)(a) declaration and written opinion by the International Bureau; translations required under Rule 55.2 by the applicant (subject to paragraph 18.11 exception); Article 19 amendments by IB transmission or applicant; sequence listings by ISA if same-office IPEA else by applicant; Article 34(2)(b) amendments by applicant; copies of documents cited in ISR not available in IPEA databases by the ISA; priority document by IB; translation of priority document by applicant (subject to invitation).
guidance: Follow the listed allocation of responsibility to ensure the IPEA receives all necessary material for examination.

name: Implicit substantive criteria: sufficiency of disclosure and technical character
description: In addition to novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability, the examiner should be aware the invention must be such that it can be carried out by a person skilled in the art (Article 5) and must relate to a technical field, be concerned with a technical problem and have technical features definable in the claim (Rule 5.1(a)(i), 5.1(a)(iii), 6.3(a)).
guidance: These requirements are implicitly contained in the Treaty and Regulations and relevant to evaluating inventive step and industrial applicability; advantageous effects may be relevant when determining inventive step.

name: Cases where no further written opinion is required
description: If the same Authority acts as both ISA and IPEA and a demand has been filed before the ISA written opinion is prepared, no written opinion is required and the examiner may immediately establish the international preliminary examination report if: (i) the claimed invention satisfies Article 33(1) criteria (novelty, inventive step, industrial applicability); (ii) the application complies with PCT form and contents; (iii) clarity/support requirements met or examiner does not wish to make observations; (iv) no amendment goes beyond the disclosure in the application as filed; (v) all claims relate to an invention in respect of which an ISR is being established and an IPE report is being established for all claims; and (vi) where applicable, sequence listing is available so a meaningful IPE can be carried out.
guidance: If the IPEA does not treat the ISA written opinion as its first written opinion, the same rule applies if criteria (i)–(vi) are satisfied.

name: Priority document and translation handling
description: Where the international application claims priority and the examiner needs the priority document, the examiner should request the International Bureau to furnish a copy. If the priority document is not in a language of the IPEA, the examiner may invite the applicant to furnish a translation.
guidance: If the requested priority document or translation has not been timely furnished, the examiner may establish the IPE report as if the priority has not been claimed and indicate this in the report.

name: Rarity of interference proceedings and legal clarity timeline
description: Interference proceedings at the PTO that are used to resolve disputes regarding patent rights are rare and represent only a tiny fraction of patent filings; there is an established, century-old body of law on First to Invent and it will take years or decades for similar clarity to develop on First to File.
guidance: Claims of improved certainty from first-to-file should be tempered by the time required for new doctrines and case law to develop. Cost-benefit analysis should include transitional legal uncertainty.

name: Transitional review for business-method patents (Section 18)
description: Section 18 creates a new and different administrative review process (a transitional review/temporary pilot) for certain business-method patents, especially financial-services-related patents, allowing post-grant administrative review of those patents.
guidance: Supporters say this provides an inexpensive, faster alternative to litigation and targets low-quality business-method patents often exploited by trolls; opponents claim it creates a special class of patents, retroactively targets validated patents, and may harm small innovators. Policy design must consider scope, pilot parameters, retroactivity, and constitutional arguments.

name: Identification of every claim and detailed explanation applying prior art (37 CFR 1.510(b)(2))
description: An identification of every claim for which reexamination is requested and a detailed explanation of the pertinency and manner of applying the cited prior art to every such claim is required.
guidance: The request must apply all cited prior art to each claim for which reexamination is requested, explaining how the cited documents meet or teach the claim limitations to establish the identified SNQ or proposed ground of rejection. If relying on any patent owner statement under § 1.501(a)(2), the request must explain how that statement is used to determine claim meaning in connection with the prior art. The detailed explanation should be limitation-by-limitation (claim charts are recommended). Do not lump claims, documents, or combinations together without separate explanations. For obviousness rejections, provide at least one basis for combining references and explain why the claim would have been obvious over that combination (preferably quoting pertinent teachings with page/column/line/figure citations). Examples of inappropriate language (e.g., using 'and/or', lumping multiple references without specific mappings) are provided and should be avoided.

name: Copy of the entire patent for which reexamination is requested (37 CFR 1.510(b)(4))
description: A copy of the entire patent including the front face, drawings, and specification/claims (in double column format) and any disclaimer/certificate/correction must be supplied, with each page plainly written on only one side.
guidance: The printed patent can be used to provide abstract, drawings, specification, and claims for the request; reproduce the printed patent on one side of paper only (two-sided copies are not proper). Any disclaimers, certificates of correction, or reexamination certificates that are part of the patent must be supplied to provide the complete patent.

name: Scope of permissible bases: prior patents and printed publications only
description: Substantial new questions of patentability must be based on patents and printed publications; questions based on public use, on sale, conduct by parties, 35 U.S.C. 101, 112, inventorship, etc., should not be included and will not be considered.
guidance: A prior art patent or printed publication cannot be used merely as evidence of alleged public use, on sale, or insufficiency of disclosure — it must be applied directly to claim grounds under 35 U.S.C. 102/103 or relate to application of other patents/printed publications. Admissions and affidavits may be used in limited circumstances (see separate rubric entries).

name: Completeness of the explanation applying prior art (I. EXPLANATION MUST BE COMPLETE)
description: The mere citation of new patents/printed publications without explanation does not comply with 37 CFR 1.510(b)(2); requester must present an explanation of how the cited references are applied to all claims considered to merit reexamination.
guidance: Provide a claim-by-claim application of each cited reference (claim charts recommended), explaining how each reference or combination is used. Do not include background references not used to support an SNQ. Examples of inappropriate phrasing and appropriate phrasing are provided to clarify acceptable specificity. If the request is nonetheless readily understood, it may be accepted despite certain deficiencies, but lack of explanation will ordinarily trigger a Notice of Failure to Comply.

name: Requirements for showing obviousness grounds (combinations) in the request
description: For proposed obviousness rejections, the requester must provide at least one basis for combining the cited references and explain why the claim(s) would have been obvious over the proposed combination.
guidance: Preferably quote the pertinent teachings in the references with specific citations (page/column/line/figure). The explanation must not lump references together; if multiple references are combined, explain separately how each reference contributes to the combination and the rationale for the combination.

name: Patent Validity Analysis
description: Evaluating the strength and validity of asserted patents (e.g., prior art, claim scope).
guidance: Validity analysis is offered to inform enforcement or defense decisions.

name: Claim Construction
description: Drafting and arguing claim construction positions to define the scope of patent claims.
guidance: Claim construction is a highlighted litigation activity, central to infringement and validity disputes.

name: Joint research agreement conditions for 103(c) disqualification
description: For purposes of 103(c), subject matter developed by another person and a claimed invention shall be deemed to have been owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person if: (A) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement that was in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; (B) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (C) the application for patent for the claimed invention discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement.
guidance: The term 'joint research agreement' means a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement entered into by two or more persons or entities for performance of experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention. All three conditions must be satisfied for the 103(c) exclusion based on a joint research agreement.

name: Definition of 'commonly owned' for 103(c)
description: The term 'commonly owned' means wholly owned by the same person(s) or organization(s) at the time the invention was made; common ownership requires 100% ownership of both the subject matter/reference and the claimed invention.
guidance: If ownership is less than 100% for either the reference or the claimed invention, common ownership does not exist. Examples illustrate parent/subsidiary, joint venture, partial ownership, and licenses. A license where basic ownership rights are retained does not defeat ownership. The requirement prevents obtaining ownership after the invention to disqualify prior art.

name: Examiner procedure regarding 35 U.S.C. 120 benefit claims
description: An application claiming the benefit of a prior filed copending national or international application under 35 U.S.C. 120 must name as an inventor at least one inventor named in the prior filed application, and the prior filed application must disclose the named inventor's invention claimed in at least one claim of the later filed application as provided by 35 U.S.C. 112 first paragraph.
guidance: So long as the applications have at least one inventor in common and other requirements are met, the Office will permit a claim for 35 U.S.C. 120 benefit without additional submissions regarding inventorship differences. The examiner must examine the earlier filed application to determine common inventorship and other 120 requirements and may permit the 120 claim without examining the earlier application's disclosure/support unless necessary (e.g., intervening reference).

name: Reinstated practice of double patenting rejections among commonly owned applications
description: In view of 35 U.S.C. 103(c), the Director has reinstated in appropriate circumstances the practice of rejecting claims in commonly owned applications of different inventive entities on the grounds of double patenting.
guidance: Such double patenting rejections can be overcome in appropriate circumstances by filing terminal disclaimers; this practice is judicially authorized (e.g., In re Bowers). Use MPEP § 804 and 37 CFR 1.78(c) for further guidance.

name: Recapture doctrine caution in reissue applications
description: For reissue applications, the doctrine of recapture may prevent the presentation of claims in the reissue application that were amended or cancelled from the application which matured into the patent for which reissue is being sought, if the claims were amended or cancelled to distinguish the claimed invention from 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/103 prior art which was not able to be excluded under 35 U.S.C. 103(c) in the application that issued as a patent.
guidance: If an examiner determines recapture may apply in the reissue application, consultation with the Office of Patent Legal Administration should be initiated via the Technology Center Special Program Examiner.

name: Combination claims must set forth general elements and arrangement
description: A claim for a general combination consisting of several sub-combinations is valid where the general elements in combination and arrangement are set forth in the specification.
guidance: Example: A sewing-machine claim comprising (1) mechanism for forming the stitch, (2) mechanism for holding cloth, (3) feeding mechanism was upheld because all these general elements and their arrangement were set forth in the specification.

name: Do not over-emphasize machine vs. combination distinction
description: Too much stress should not be laid upon the distinction between a machine and a combination; courts will construe according to the substance of the claim and specification.
guidance: Court guidance warns against rigidly separating 'machine' from 'combination' when construing patent claims.

name: Claims only cover what the specification describes (process vs arrangement)
description: Where the specification describes an arrangement or configuration but not the process of performing it, the claim will not be held to cover the un-described process; it covers the arrangement/structure as described.
guidance: Example: Booth v. Garelly — ornamental design claim covered arrangement of colored threads as producing ornamentation, not the unwritten winding process.

name: Specification enablement and best mode (section 26 of 1870)
description: Specification must be a written description of the manner and process of making, constructing, compounding, and using the invention 'in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms' as to enable any person skilled in the art to make, construct, compound, and use it; in case of a machine, explain the principle and the best mode contemplated of applying that principle, so as to distinguish it from other inventions.
guidance: Also requires particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the part, improvement, or combination claimed; specification and claim must be signed by inventor and attested by two witnesses. This is statutory mandatory language.

name: Notification and assistance when claim rejected
description: When a claim is rejected on examination, the commissioner must notify the applicant briefly stating reasons for rejection and provide information and references useful in judging whether to renew the application or alter the specification; if applicant persists, the commissioner must order re-examination.
guidance: Statutory duty to give reasons and helpful references; persistence triggers re-examination procedures.

name: Reissue abuse doctrine (factual standard)
description: Surrendering valid patents and obtaining reissues with expanded or equivocal claims where the original patent was neither inoperative nor invalid and the specification neither defective nor insufficient is an abuse of the reissue privilege and the reissue is void.
guidance: Case law (Burr v. Duryee / Judge Grier) condemns reissues that expand protection to cover prior/future inventions by elastic phrasing; courts will invalidate such reissues.

name: Patent document components
description: Patent documents typically include the following elements: title, bibliometric information, patent classification code, citations, abstract, drawings, detailed description, and claims.
guidance: Although format and content may vary by jurisdiction, include these elements when preparing patent corpora or when using patents as input for models; these elements are integral components of the patenting process and publicly accessible once a patent is issued.

name: Prefer claims for subject classification
description: Claims are more specific and legally representative of the invention and thus more discriminative for patent subject classification than abstracts.
guidance: When training classifiers, prefer claims as input rather than abstracts: models fine-tuned on claims outperformed abstract-based models by roughly 3–7% across section/class/subclass levels in reported experiments.

name: Token counting / language-modeling corpus metric
description: Count tokens using a consistent tokenizer (the paper uses tiktoken with the GPT-4o tokenizer) to measure corpus size and to compute claim length statistics.
guidance: Use the same tokenizer for dataset and model tokenization statistics so token-based cutoff lengths and statistics are comparable across experiments.

name: Structural complexity (subordinate clause ratio)
description: Structural complexity is determined by the ratio of subordinate clauses to the total number of sentences.
guidance: Extract subordinate-clause counts (authors used spaCy) and report this ratio as a measure of grammatical/structural complexity of claims; higher ratios indicate more syntactically complex claims.

name: Syntactic tree depth
description: Syntactic tree depth is computed using a constituency parser and measures the depth of the syntactic parse tree of the main independent claim; higher values indicate more deeply nested grammatical structures.
guidance: Report syntactic tree depth to capture nesting/complexity that may affect model performance on generation and parsing tasks.

name: Detecting reward-model overfitting / suspiciously high reward accuracy
description: Rewarding accuracy achieving exceptionally high scores (e.g., >98% during DPO) can indicate overfitting to superficial patterns rather than meaningful quality distinctions.
guidance: Investigate high reward accuracy as a red flag: check whether the reward model is exploiting simple heuristics (e.g., claim length, presence of specific legal terms) and not capturing substantive technical/legal quality.

name: Common claim-generation anti-patterns
description: Observed low-quality outputs include: an excessively long overloaded independent claim, redundancy in dependent claims, and frequent overuse of terms such as 'wherein' and 'configured to'.
guidance: Use these anti-patterns as qualitative error categories when auditing generated claims; aim for concise independent claims, minimal redundancy in dependencies, and varied syntactic phrasing where appropriate.

name: Affidavit ineffective when there is no patentable distinction between claims (same patentable invention)
description: A 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit is ineffective to overcome a U.S. patent or patent application publication not only when there is verbatim correspondence between claims but also where there is no patentable distinction between the respective claims (i.e., the application and reference claim the 'same patentable invention').
guidance: Interference rules (37 CFR 41.203(a)) define 'same patentable invention'; an applicant cannot use 1.131 to avoid an interference and obtain two patents to the same invention. Where common ownership and non-patentable-distinct claims exist, other tools (e.g., terminal disclaimer, 1.130 affidavits) may be applicable for 35 U.S.C. 103 situations. See In re Clark, In re Hidy, etc.

name: Review for prior public use/on sale statutory bars and best mode concerns
description: Examiners must determine whether affidavits/declarations and accompanying evidence show the claimed invention was in public use or on sale in this country more than one year prior to the effective filing date (which would constitute a statutory bar under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)); where 1.131 evidence relies on an embodiment not disclosed in the application, the examiner must consider the best mode requirement.
guidance: Even if an affidavit overcomes a reference-based rejection, prior public use/on-sale activities cannot be overcome via 1.131. A best mode rejection should not be made unless the record, taken as a whole, establishes by a preponderance of the evidence that the specification fails to set forth the best mode. See MPEP §§ 2133.03 and 2165–2165.04.

name: 37 CFR 1.132 affidavits/declarations traversing rejections must be responsive and sufficient
description: When any claim is rejected or objected to, evidence to traverse the rejection on a basis not otherwise provided for must be by oath or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132. The primary examiner is responsible to personally review and decide whether a 1.132 affidavit/declaration is responsive to the rejection and presents sufficient facts to overcome it.
guidance: This rule is the catch-all for affidavit evidence not covered by other specific rules. Use form paragraphs (e.g., 7.65, 7.66 and 7.66.01–.05) to comment on sufficiency or insufficiency. Examiners should ensure the affidavit specifically addresses the rejection being traversed.

name: Form paragraph guidance for noting effectiveness or insufficiency
description: Form paragraph 7.65 may be used when a 37 CFR 1.132 affidavit/declaration is sufficient to overcome a rejection; form paragraph 7.66 (and subparagraphs) should be used when the affidavit/declaration is insufficient to overcome the rejection, with instructions on inserting filing date, affected claims, and the rejection being overcome.
guidance: Form paragraph templates give exact wording and examiner notes for Office actions (e.g., what to insert in each bracket). Use these to ensure consistent Office action language when admitting or refusing affidavits under 1.132/1.131.

name: Statutory subject-matter and pre‑grant bars
description: That any person who has invented or discovered any "new and useful art, machine, manufacture or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof" may obtain a patent, provided the thing is "not known or used by others in this country, and not patented or described in any printed publication in this or any foreign country, before his invention or discovery thereof, and not in public use or on sale for more than two years prior to his application, unless the same is proved to have been abandoned."
guidance: This language sets both the categories of patentable subject-matter (art, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, and improvements) and the novelty/public‑use/on‑sale time bars. Any analysis of patentability should start from these statutory categories and the requirement that the claimed subject was not previously known, used, published, or on sale beyond the statutory grace period.

name: Definition of 'art' (process/method)
description: The term 'art' was intended to embrace inventions where apparatus or materials may not be the essence of the discovery, but where that essence consists in using apparatus or materials in new processes, methods, or relations, so as to constitute a new mode of attaining an old result; or a mode of attaining a new result; or an entirely new process of making or doing something which has not been made or done before.
guidance: An 'art' covers novel modes of applying existing materials/apparatus (e.g., new relations/order/position of known elements). Examples include new dyeing/tanning methods and the printing-on-both-sides bank-note example (new application of letter-press and copperplate for added security). When the novelty lies in a new method of application rather than new apparatus/substance, claim as an art/process.

name: Proper characterization and claiming (process vs machine/manufacture)
description: Whether the subject-matter of a particular patent is a process (an improvement in an art) or a new manufacture/machine/composition is often decisive; an invention that is in substance a new process but is claimed as a machine or manufacture may be invalid.
guidance: Draft the specification and claims to reflect the essential nature of the invention. The Kay v. Marshall example shows that claiming a process invention as machinery (e.g., claiming altered placement of rollers rather than the process of maceration + short reach spinning) can doom a patent. If the real invention is a process, describe it as such (steps, sequence, conditions) to avoid losing protection by mischaracterization.

name: Combination patents vs patents for parts
description: The word 'machine' in the statute includes new combinations of machines, as well as new organizations of mechanism for a single purpose. In such cases the thing patented is the combination, not the separate machines.
guidance: Carefully draft claims to indicate whether protection is sought for the combination as a whole or for individual parts. The question of whether a claim is for a combination only or for specific parts as well is one of claim construction on the patent and specification.

name: Consequences of unskilful claim/specification construction
description: If an inventor describes or claims the invention in an improper form (e.g., claims a machine when the real invention is a process, or vice versa), the patent may be invalid or narrower than intended. Such unskilful construction may forfeit rights to the real invention.
guidance: Draft claims and specifications carefully to encompass the real invention. The Corning/Le Roy examples illustrate that an ambiguously constructed instrument can lead courts to construe the patent too narrowly (e.g., as a machine rather than a process), allowing defendants to introduce evidence that should otherwise be excluded.

name: Patenting an improvement on an existing patent
description: There may be a patent for an improvement of a machine that is itself the subject of an existing patent; a patent including the subject-matter of a patent still in force is valid if the improvement only is claimed in the specification.
guidance: An improvement patent can coexist with an earlier patent covering the base machine, but practical enforcement may be subject to expiration timing, licensing, or purchase of the original patented machine. When prosecuting improvement claims, confine claims to the improvement to avoid invalidity for double-patenting or overlap.

name: Importance of distinguishing process and product when preparing specification
description: A careful discrimination between an improved process and an improved machine, manufacture, or composition of matter is essential when preparing a specification; the discrimination must be guided by the nature of the invention and its essential character.
guidance: Before drafting, analyze whether novelty lies in (a) the agency/steps (process), (b) the apparatus/principle (machine), or (c) the article's properties (manufacture/composition). If both process and product are novel, consider claiming both, with directions enabling construction of suitable machinery where needed.

name: Claim construction rule to secure the real invention
description: The general rule of construction is that the real invention is to be beneficially secured to the patentee, if the terms of his specification will admit of it; hence construction of claims will aim to give effect to the inventor's real discovery within the words used.
guidance: Courts will construe claims to secure the inventor's real invention when the specification's language permits. Nevertheless, sloppy or ambiguous claim language that ties novelty improperly (e.g., to a particular apparatus instead of the process) risks narrowing protection.

name: Examples as illustrative guidance (use of prior cases)
description: Concrete cases illustrate application of these principles: printing bank-notes by printing on both sides (new application of old materials = art); spinning macerated flax (process vs machine claim failure when misclaimed); casting iron rollers by imparting rotary motion (novel mode); Crane's hot blast with anthracite producing cheaper/better iron (process/manufacture interplay).
guidance: Use case examples as templates when analyzing analogous inventions: identify whether novelty is in steps/agency, apparatus principle, combination, or resulting properties; map the facts to precedent to decide claim scope and drafting strategy.

name: Definition of a Design
description: The claimed subject matter is the design embodied in or applied to an article of manufacture — i.e., the visual characteristics/appearance presented to the eye.
guidance: Design may concern configuration (shape), surface ornamentation, or both. A design is inseparable from the article, must be definite and preconceived, capable of reproduction, and not merely the chance result of a method. Case law (e.g., In re Zahn) supports these points.

name: Ornamentality Requirement / Statutory Subject Matter
description: 35 U.S.C. 171 requires a new, original and ornamental design for an article of manufacture; subject matter must be ornamental, not purely functional or offensive.
guidance: Design claims that are merely functional or derogatory/offensive may be rejected as improper subject matter. Ornamentality is judged from the appearance; functional/structural features are not considered part of design patentability.

name: Distinction Between Design and Utility Patents
description: Design patents protect appearance; utility patents protect function/workings. Many procedural and substantive differences exist.
guidance: Key differences to consider include: term (14 years from grant for design vs 20 years from filing for utility), no maintenance fees for designs, single claim only in design, mandatory restriction practice in designs, no PCT coverage for designs, foreign priority period (6 months for designs v. 1 year for utility provisional), no provisional benefit for designs, RCE unavailable for designs, CPA practice and publication differences. Use this list to determine applicable practices and deadlines.

name: Elements of a Design Patent Application
description: A design application must include the arrangement and elements set forth in 37 CFR 1.154: transmittal form, fee form, application data sheet, specification, drawings/photographs, and executed oath/declaration.
guidance: A claim in proper form and an adequate drawing or photograph are essential elements. Follow the order and section headings recommended in 37 CFR 1.154 and the MPEP guidance.

name: Specification — Title and Preamble Requirements
description: The title must designate the particular article; preamble may state applicant name, title of design, and brief description of nature and intended use.
guidance: Title must correspond to the claim; if title and claim do not correspond, object under 37 CFR 1.153. Titles must not be directed to less than the claimed design shown in full lines. Titles describing combinations or multiple parts must clearly define them as a single entity (e.g., 'set', 'pair', 'assembly'). Amendments to the title must have antecedent basis and not introduce new matter.

name: Specification — Figure Descriptions and Descriptive Matter
description: A brief description of the drawing figures is ordinarily sufficient; additional descriptive statements are permissible in limited forms but generally not required.
guidance: Permissible statements (if present in the original filing) include: description of unillustrated portions, disclaimers of portions not claimed, statements explaining broken lines, statement of nature/intented use, and a 'characteristic features' statement. Descriptive matter added after filing that constitutes new matter is not permitted.

name: Characteristic Feature Statement — Use and Limits
description: Applicant may include a 'characteristic feature' statement identifying a feature considered novel, but this does not determine patentability.
guidance: If used, phrase as 'The characteristic feature of the design resides in [ ... ]'. Such statements may later serve to limit claims but examiners must assess patentability based on the overall appearance, not only the stated feature.

name: Design Claim Form and Content
description: Design applications may include only a single claim, which should be in formal terms to the ornamental design for the article 'as shown' or 'as shown and described' (if descriptive matter is in the specification).
guidance: Claim language must correspond to the title and be consistent with specification terminology. The claim defines the subject matter the applicant regards as the invention (35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph). Examiners should permit reasonable latitude in claim language but object if language is clearly misdescriptive or indefinitive.

name: Full Lines vs Broken Lines in Drawings
description: Full (solid) lines show the claimed design; broken lines can show environment or boundaries but may not be used to denote portions of lesser importance.
guidance: Broken lines may illustrate environment or indicate bounds of a claim; they may not show hidden planes/surfaces not visible through opaque materials, nor be used to claim that parts are immaterial. Where broken lines are used for multiple purposes, the specification must explicitly state their purpose(s). Addition of certain broken-line boundaries may be new matter if not clearly derivable from the original disclosure.

name: Drawing Requirement and Centrality
description: A drawing or photograph is an essential element of a design application and constitutes the entire visual disclosure of the design; it must be clear and complete so nothing is left to conjecture.
guidance: Drawings must comply with 37 CFR 1.84 and 1.152 and include sufficient views to disclose the complete appearance. Inconsistencies among views should be objected to; severe inconsistencies may render the claim nonenabling and indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112.

name: Photographs in Lieu of Drawings
description: Photographs are permitted only under restrictions and must not disclose environmental structure; photographs and ink drawings may not be combined on the same formal submission.
guidance: Photographs must be limited to the claimed design and avoid showing environment. Mixing media (photograph + ink drawing) on the same formal drawing is prohibited. If photographs are used, ensure they comply with 37 CFR 1.152 and do not create ambiguity about claimed subject matter.

name: Drawing Corrections Prior to Appeal
description: Outstanding drawing deficiencies must be corrected before an appeal of the design claim proceeds; appeals without corrected drawings may be dismissed or denied.
guidance: Use form paragraph language requiring corrected drawings in reply to Office action to avoid abandonment. Final rejections may include direction that drawings be corrected prior to appeal (Ex parte Bevan).

name: Necessity for Good Drawings — Enablement and Filing Date Impact
description: Because the drawing is the whole disclosure, good drawings are critical; insufficient drawings may be fatal to validity and can adversely affect effective filing date of continuations.
guidance: Examiners should require appropriate shading, sufficient views, and consistency. Insufficient drawings can trigger 35 U.S.C. 112 rejections (first paragraph — nonenablement) and definite claims under 112 second paragraph.

name: Claim Construction — Overall Appearance Standard
description: Patentability (novelty/nonobviousness) of a design is judged on the overall visual appearance of the claimed design as compared to prior art, not on individual functional elements.
guidance: Characteristic feature statements notwithstanding, the examiner must compare total appearance to prior art (see In re Rosen, In re Leslie). Rejections for novelty/nonobviousness should be framed in terms of overall appearance.

name: Priority and Benefit Rules Specific to Designs
description: Design applications have distinct priority/benefit rules: foreign priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) is 6 months for designs; design applications may not claim benefit of a provisional under 35 U.S.C. 119(e).
guidance: Be mindful of shorter priority periods for designs versus utility applications and the unavailability of provisional/1-year benefit provisions for design filings. The PCT does not apply to design patents.

name: Use of Trademarks in Design Applications
description: Trademarks may be used in specifications/drawings only under limited circumstances; use in the title is improper.
guidance: If trademark material forms part of a claimed design drawing, include a statement preceding the claim identifying the trademark material and the owner. Examiners should object to trademarks in the title and require deletion. Derogatory uses of trademarks may result in rejection as offensive subject matter.

name: (CTFR) Final rejection
description: Any second or any subsequent Office action (may include grounds of objections, rejections, and/or other requirements) from the examiner that is made final indicating that the examiner intends to close prosecution.
guidance: At a final rejection, applicant no longer has the right to amend the application unless the amendment merely cancels claims or complies with a formal requirement made earlier. Use this to determine whether prosecution is being closed and what types of amendments remain available.

name: (A...) Amendment
description: Amendment filed by the applicant in response to an Office action issued by the examiner.
guidance: A reply to an Office action may or may not include an amendment to the claims and/or written description. Look for amendments attached to replies to see claim or specification changes.

name: (CLM) Claims
description: Look for the most recent copy of claims to see if any amendments have been made.
guidance: Always refer to the latest claims document in the file to determine current claim language and scope; claim status may change over multiple Office actions and replies.

name: (REM) Remarks (applicant's reply arguments)
description: This is the arguments/remarks portion of applicant’s reply to an Office action.
guidance: Applicant’s reply must distinctly and specifically point out the supposed errors in the examiner's action and must reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the prior Office action in order to entitle applicant to reconsideration or further examination. The arguments/remarks must point out the specific distinctions believed to render the claims, including any newly presented claims, patentable over any applied references. Use REM to assess the applicant's legal and factual responses and whether they preserve rights to further examination.

name: 35 U.S.C. § 101 rejections (subject matter/utility)
description: Rejections made under 35 U.S.C. § 101 are based on non-statutory subject matter or lack of utility.
guidance: Non-statutory subject matter includes abstract ideas, laws of nature, and natural phenomena. A lack of utility under § 101 is similar to a lack of Industrial Applicability (IA) in an international application. Use §101 entries to determine if the examiner finds the claimed subject matter outside patent-eligible categories or lacking practical utility.

name: Graham Factors
description: (1) Determine the scope and content of the prior art; (2) Ascertain the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art; (3) Resolve the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; and (4) Consider objective indicia of non-obviousness (i.e., secondary considerations).
guidance: Use this four-part analytical framework as the foundation for any obviousness analysis; factual findings on these points are required to support a prima facie conclusion of obviousness.

name: Nexus Requirement for Secondary Considerations (MPEP 716.01(b))
description: To be given substantial weight, evidence of secondary considerations must be relevant to the claimed subject matter and there must be a factually and legally sufficient connection (nexus) between the evidence and the claimed invention.
guidance: Examiners must determine nexus and, if they find evidence insufficient to rebut prima facie obviousness, must specifically set forth facts and reasoning justifying that conclusion. Case examples: Hearing Components (nexus shown by licensing fee drop after expiration) and Muniauction (nexus lacking where evidence was not coextensive with claims).

name: KSR Rationale — Combining Prior Art Elements (required findings)
description: To reject based on combining prior art elements, Examiners must find (1) prior art included each claimed element (not necessarily in one reference); (2) one of ordinary skill could have combined the elements by known methods and each element in combination performs the same function as separately; (3) one of ordinary skill would have recognized the results of the combination were predictable; and (4) whatever additional Graham-based findings are necessary.
guidance: A proper rejection must resolve the Graham factual inquiries and articulate these findings — mere conclusory statements are insufficient.

name: KSR Rationale — Simple Substitution (required findings)
description: For rejection by simple substitution, Examiners must find (1) a prior art device differing from the claimed device by substitution of components; (2) the substituted components/functions were known in the art; (3) one of ordinary skill could have substituted the known element and the results would have been predictable; and (4) any additional Graham-based findings necessary.
guidance: The examiner must supply reasoned analysis showing substitution was predictable; mere assertion of substitution without explanation fails to establish prima facie obviousness.

name: All Claim Limitations Must Be Accounted For
description: If just one claim limitation is not accounted for by the examiner's rejection, the examiner has failed to present a prima facie case of obviousness.
guidance: In responses, show any uncaptured limitation or that the examiner has not shown the missing limitation is present or would be supplied by common sense/inherency without evidence.

name: No Per Se Rules — Fact-Specific Analysis Required
description: Per se rules that eliminate the need for fact-specific analysis flout §103 and case law; reliance on per se rules of obviousness is legally incorrect and must cease.
guidance: Demand claim-by-claim, fact-specific comparison to prior art; do not allow administrative convenience or board-sanctioned per se rules to substitute for required analysis (In re Ochiai).

name: Expectation of Success (must be shown for obviousness)
description: Obviousness requires that a person of ordinary skill would have had a reasonable expectation of success in achieving the known goal; evidence showing no reasonable expectation of success may support nonobviousness.
guidance: Ensure the expectation-of-success analysis matches the actual claimed goal and not a different, less-challenging one (see Institut Pasteur v. Focarino).

name: Clarification of patent-eligibility for tax strategy patents
description: Clarify the treatment of tax strategy patents under the patent statutes.
guidance: Included to address uncertainty and litigation surrounding patents that claim tax strategies; intended to provide clearer boundaries on patentability in this domain.

name: Result as a test of invention
description: The production of a new and useful result (the 'result' achieved) is a test of invention.
guidance: Courts consider whether the claimed invention produces an effect or result beyond the predictable outcome of known elements; a new useful result supports patentability of a combination.

name: Specifications — statutory and substantive requirements
description: Specifications must conform to statutory requirements: must agree with the patent; drawings annexed are part of the specification; they have two objects; rules exist for preparing specifications.
guidance: Follow statutory/formal rules when drafting specifications; include necessary drawings; ensure specification aligns with the claims/patent and satisfies the office's procedural rules.

name: Alice two-step inquiry
description: Perform the two-step Alice/Mayo analysis: (1) determine whether the claims are directed to a patent-ineligible concept (laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract ideas); (2) if so, consider the elements of each claim individually and as an ordered combination to determine whether they contain an 'inventive concept' sufficient to ensure the patent amounts to significantly more than the patent-ineligible concept itself.
guidance: Quote formulation from Alice: first determine whether the claims are directed to an ineligible concept; if so assess the claim elements both individually and 'as an ordered combination' to determine whether they possess an 'inventive concept' that is 'sufficient to ensure that the patent in practice amounts to significantly more than a patent upon the [ineligible concept] itself.' (Alice, 573 U.S. at 217–18; Mayo, 566 U.S. at 72). Use this two-step framework as the governing eligibility test.

name: Look to the focus of the claimed advance over the prior art
description: Determine the claim's character 'as a whole' by looking at the focus of the claimed advance over the prior art to decide whether the claim is directed to excluded subject matter.
guidance: Use the 'focus of the claimed advance' test (Koninklijke KPN v. Gemalto, quoted in the opinion). Ask whether the asserted advance is a specific technological improvement or merely the abstract idea implemented in a new context.

name: Software/ML-specific focus test: improvement in computer capabilities vs using computers as a tool
description: For software (including machine learning) claims, determine whether the claims focus on 'the specific asserted improvement in computer capabilities' or instead on a process that 'qualifies as an abstract idea for which computers are invoked merely as a tool.'
guidance: If the claimed invention is simply using conventional computer/ML techniques as a tool to perform an abstract process, it is likely directed to an abstract idea (quoting Finjan/ Kon. KPN language cited in the opinion). Evaluate whether the specification/claims describe an improvement in computer functionality itself.

name: Generic ML techniques and generic computing are conventional (do not confer eligibility)
description: Claims that rely on applying 'any suitable machine learning technique' (e.g., neural networks, support vector machines, regressions, decision trees, gradient boosted trees, Bayesian networks) and generic computing hardware are treated as using conventional technology and do not, by themselves, make claims patent eligible.
guidance: The opinion emphasizes that the patents' repeated statement that 'any suitable machine learning technique' may be used and that 'generic computing devices' suffice supports finding the ML and computing aspects conventional. Cited language: patents describing a list of typical ML techniques and stating use of generic processors/ computing devices. See also cited precedent that generic steps of implementing calculations on a regular computer do not transform an abstract idea into a patent-eligible invention (In re Board of Trustees of Leland Stanford Junior Univ. and others).

name: Iterative training and dynamic updates inherent to machine learning are not a technological improvement
description: Limitations reciting iterative training, dynamic adjustment, or updating models in response to real-time data are, by their nature, intrinsic to machine learning and therefore do not necessarily supply an inventive concept.
guidance: Recentive's own admissions that 'the way machine learning works is the inputs are defined, the model is trained, and then the algorithm is actually updated and improved over time' support treating such steps as routine/incidental. Thus, merely claiming iterative training or real-time updating (without more) is unlikely to show an inventive concept.

name: Claims must disclose how the results are achieved; functional claiming is insufficient
description: A claim that only functionally describes results (e.g., 'generate optimized schedules' or 'unearth useful patterns') without delineating how to achieve those results in a non-abstract way is insufficient for patentability.
guidance: The opinion cites that claims which 'do not sufficiently describe how to achieve [stated] results in a non-abstract way' and that 'functional claim language, without more, is insufficient' (citing IBM v. Zillow, Two-Way Media, Intell. Ventures, Elec. Power Group). The patent should explain a specific implementation or method by which the purported improvement is achieved.

name: Collecting and processing information is an abstract idea
description: Claims that principally collect information (even if limited to particular content categories) and process it fall within the realm of abstract ideas.
guidance: The opinion notes precedent treating information collection as abstract (Electronic Power Group, Internet Pats. Corp., OIP Techs., Content Extraction, Digitech). Be wary of claims framed as 'collecting information and performing routine analysis' without a specific technical improvement.

name: Speed and efficiency improvements via generic computers are not enough
description: Claims that simply perform a task faster or more efficiently than humans by applying generic computers or generic ML techniques do not make the claims patent eligible.
guidance: Cite authority that increased speed/efficiency from applying computers (without improved computer techniques) does not create eligibility (Content Extraction; DealerTrack; Customedia). Distinguish cases where specific computer techniques produced a technological improvement (e.g., McRO).

name: Step-two requirement: inventive concept must be 'significantly more' than abstract idea
description: At step two, the claim must include an element or combination of elements that transforms the abstract idea into a patent-eligible application—more than merely stating the abstract idea and adding 'apply it.'
guidance: Use Alice and Mayo language: the claim must include an 'inventive concept' sufficient to transform the claimed abstract idea into something 'significantly more' (Alice, Trinity, SAP Am., Broadband iTV). Mere recitation of using ML to dynamically generate outputs is insufficient unless the claim identifies how that use produces a technological improvement.

name: Plausibility at pleading stage and futility of amendment
description: On a motion to dismiss, a patentee must plausibly allege facts that, if true, would show an inventive concept; dismissal is appropriate where the complaint fails to identify claim terms requiring construction or to allege facts that could alter the §101 analysis, and denial of leave to amend is appropriate if amendment would be futile.
guidance: The opinion affirms dismissal where Recentive failed to propose amendments or identify factual issues that would alter the §101 analysis, and quotes district-court standards that dismissal is proper when a plaintiff fails to identify specific claim constructions or facts needing development before §101 resolution (Recentive, Trinity). When asserting eligibility at pleading stage, plead specific structural/implementation details showing inventive concept.

name: Patents claiming only the application of generic ML to a new data environment are ineligible
description: Claims that 'do no more than claim the application of generic machine learning to new data environments, without disclosing improvements to the machine learning models to be applied,' are patent ineligible under §101.
guidance: This is a central holding of the opinion: courts should not allow patents that simply apply conventional ML as a tool in a new domain unless the patent discloses an improvement to the ML technology or a specific technical implementation that provides a technological advance.

name: Avoid identifying defects for the first time in a Final Action
description: While occasionally necessary, identifying a defect for the first time in a Final Action is generally not desirable.
guidance: If a major defect (anticipation, obviousness, lack of utility, non-statutory subject-matter, insufficiency, etc.) was overlooked in prior prosecution, a further regular requisition identifying the defect is most likely necessary so the applicant has opportunity to respond prior to rejection. If a new, significant defect was introduced by applicant amendments made in response to the previous report, the examiner must exercise judgement whether a Final Action is appropriate. However, where a new defect is readily understandable and easily fixed (e.g. missing antecedent, incorrect claim numbering), it may not be necessary to delay rejection. Do not ignore an identified defect to simplify the Final Action; decide whether the defect requires a further report under subsection 86(2) of the Patent Rules or can be included in a Final Action.

name: Final Action preamble: identify defects and claim status
description: The preamble of the report should identify, in broad terms, the defects that have led to the rejection and which claims are considered defective and which are allowable.
guidance: State which claims are central to the impasse and clearly identify any aspects of the claims that are central to the dispute.

name: Final Action content: recommended sections and information
description: Although layout can be tailored, the following information should be provided where relevant: a summary of the application emphasizing relevant claims; identification of any allowable claims; identification of relevant prior art and discussion of pertinent teachings; summary of relevant prior prosecution; discussion of legal/jurisprudential/administrative considerations central to the dispute; grounds for rejection with comprehensive analysis including rebuttal of applicant arguments; and a brief summation recapitulating the grounds for rejection.
guidance: It may be beneficial to divide the report into sections with clear headings. Provide sufficient background (including applicant arguments) so the Final Action can be followed without referring to other documents.

name: Patent owner preliminary response (waiver and effects)
description: A patent owner may elect to waive the patent owner preliminary response. No adverse inference will be taken by such an election. Moreover, a patent owner may file a statutory disclaimer of one or more challenged claims to streamline the proceedings. Where no challenged claims remain, the Board would terminate the proceeding. Where one or more challenged claims remain, the Board’s decision on institution would be based solely on the remaining claims.
guidance: Once a trial is instituted, the Board may decline to consider arguments set forth in a preliminary response unless they are raised in the patent owner response. See In re Nuvasive (explaining that a patent owner waives an issue presented in its preliminary response if it fails to renew the issue in its response after trial is instituted).

name: General Plastic factors for follow-on petitions
description: Non-exclusive factors the Board will consider when exercising discretion on instituting inter partes review, especially for 'follow-on' petitions challenging the same patent as previously challenged:
guidance: The General Plastic factors include: (1) whether the same petitioner previously filed a petition directed to the same claims of the same patent; (2) whether at the time of filing of the first petition the petitioner knew of the prior art asserted in the second petition or should have known of it; (3) whether at the time of filing of the second petition the petitioner already received the patent owner’s preliminary response to the first petition or received the Board’s decision on whether to institute review in the first petition; (4) the length of time that elapsed between the time the petitioner learned of the prior art asserted in the second petition and the filing of the second petition; (5) whether the petitioner provides adequate explanation for the time elapsed between the filings of multiple petitions directed to the same claims of the same patent; (6) the finite resources of the Board; and (7) the requirement to issue a final determination not later than 1 year after the Director notices institution of review. General Plastic factors are not dispositive or exclusive and are part of a balanced assessment including merits. The Board also considers relationships among different petitioners and may weigh additional factors (e.g., events in other proceedings).

name: Parallel/multiple petitions guidance and required disclosures
description: One petition should be sufficient in most situations; multiple petitions against the same patent at or about the same time may place substantial burden and raise fairness, timing, and efficiency concerns. Two petitions may be necessary rarely (e.g., large number of asserted claims, priority date disputes); three or more petitions by a petitioner is unlikely to be appropriate.
guidance: If a petitioner files two or more petitions challenging the same patent, the petitioner should identify (1) a ranking of the petitions in the order it wishes the Board to consider the merits, and (2) a succinct explanation of differences between the petitions, why those differences are material, and why the Board should institute additional petitions. A separate paper providing this explanation is limited to the purpose and no more than 5 pages when filed with each petition. The Board encourages use of a table to identify similarities/differences. Patent owners may respond in preliminary responses (or separate 5-page papers) explaining why the Board should not exercise discretion to institute more than one petition, including by proffering stipulations that limitations are not disputed or certain references qualify as prior art. Panels may request additional papers in limited circumstances for petitions submitted before this Guide; after publication petitioners are expected to justify multiple petitions in the first instance.

name: Content and form of decision on whether to institute (all-or-none rule and analysis)
description: When instituting a trial, the Board will either (1) institute as to all claims challenged in the petition and on all grounds in the petition, or (2) institute on no claims and deny institution. The Board will not institute on fewer than all claims or all challenges in a petition.
guidance: The Board generally will provide analysis of the strengths and weaknesses of all challenges in the petition to guide the parties for trial. The Board retains the discretion to deny institution of the petition as a whole under 35 U.S.C. §§ 314(a) and 325(d) even when the petition includes at least one claim that otherwise meets the criteria. If a panel determines the petition meets standards for institution for fewer than all challenges, or deficiencies affect only a portion of challenges (e.g., failure to provide a § 112(f) construction), the panel will evaluate all challenges and may deny the entire petition in the interests of efficient administration and integrity of the patent system. Where no trial is instituted, the Board expects to provide a short statement as to why standards were not met (though not necessary in all cases).
