The Board’s determination on institution is final and nonappealable.

name: Burden of persuasion and evidentiary standard for substitute claims
description: Following Aqua Products, a patent owner does not bear the burden of persuasion to demonstrate the patentability of substitute claims presented in a motion to amend. Rather, the burden of persuasion ordinarily will lie with the petitioner to show that any proposed substitute claims are unpatentable by a preponderance of the evidence.
guidance: The Board may justify any finding of unpatentability by reference to evidence of record (e.g., when a petitioner ceases to participate). Ultimately, the Board determines whether substitute claims are unpatentable by a preponderance of the evidence based on the entirety of the record, including any opposition by the petitioner. If the entirety of the evidence of record is in equipoise, the Board will grant the motion to amend and the Office will issue a certificate incorporating those claims into the patent.

name: Contents and support required in a motion to amend
description: Any motion to amend must comply with the content requirements of 37 C.F.R. §§ 42.121(b) or 42.221(b): include a claim listing, show the changes being sought clearly, and describe how the original disclosure of the patent and any relied-upon prior application supports each claim that is added or amended.
guidance: The claim listing may be in an appendix. A patent owner may not enlarge the scope of the claims or add new matter (35 U.S.C. §§ 316(d)(3), 326(d)(3)). When replacing an original claim with a new claim, identify the proposed substitute claim and specify the original claim it replaces, clearly identifying all changes relative to the original claim. A patent owner should identify specifically the features added to each substitute claim and any proposed constructions for new claim terms. Although not required, patent owners may offer arguments on patentability and may support them with expert testimony (e.g., to show what a person of ordinary skill would have known and to explain significance of added features). Motions should clearly state patentably distinct features for proposed substitute claims to aid the Board in determining whether the amendment enlarges claims and if it is responsive to grounds of unpatentability. Under 37 C.F.R. § 42.11 all parties have a duty of candor, which includes the patent owner’s duty to disclose information of which the patent owner is aware that is material to the patentability of substitute claims if not already of record.

name: Limits on number and scope of substitute claims
description: The number of substitute claims must be 'reasonable.' There is a presumption that only one substitute claim would be needed to replace each challenged claim.
guidance: This presumption may be rebutted by a demonstration of need. Motions to cancel claims will generally be permitted even late in the proceeding, as will motions to amend to correct simple and obvious typographical errors. Amendments should clearly state where the specification and drawings support all limitations in the proposed substitute claims; if the Board cannot determine support, the motion may be denied.

name: Opposition to a motion to amend — scope and evidence
description: A petitioner will be afforded an opportunity to fully respond to a patent owner's motion to amend. No authorization is needed to file an opposition to a motion to amend. Petitioners may respond to new issues and include evidence responsive to the amendment.
guidance: This includes submission of new expert declarations or additional prior art directed to the proposed substitute claims. The grounds of unpatentability that can be raised in response to proposed substitute claims are not limited by 35 U.S.C. § 311(b); the Board may consider other grounds (including § 101 and § 112) as to proposed substitute claims.

name: Final decision timing and scope
description: For IPR, PGR, and CBM proceedings, the Board will enter a final written decision not more than one year from the date a trial is instituted, except that the time may be extended up to six months for good cause. The timeline may be adjusted in case of joinder.
guidance: The Board expects that a final written decision will address the issues necessary for resolving the proceeding. In derivation proceedings, although not required by statute, the Board expects to provide a final decision not more than one year from institution, deciding whether an inventor in the earlier application derived the claimed invention and filed without authorization.

name: Willing witness factor (convenience of witnesses)
description: The willing witness factor examines where witnesses with relevant and material information are located and whether they are willing to testify.
guidance: A court should consider which employees or third parties possess relevant, material information (including hardware, server-side, or software aspects where relevant). The district court here found five Apple employees in Austin knowledgeable about accused products and weighed that against transfer. A party asserting those witnesses are irrelevant must show why (e.g., by tying the asserted claim scope to only software features).

name: Scope-of-claims relevance inquiry
description: The court should assess the scope of the asserted claims and the information in possession of identified employees to determine whether hardware or server-side functionality is relevant to infringement.
guidance: Even if a party argues the case is limited to software, the district court may find hardware or server-side functionality potentially relevant after examining claim scope and employee knowledge. Appellate review is deferential on these fact-intensive determinations.

name: Interviews after notice of appeal: general rule and exceptions
description: One interview after final rejection is normally permitted (the time from mailing of final rejection through filing of an appeal brief). However, no interviews will be granted from the filing of a request for pre-appeal review through issuance of a decision on the request. Except in unusual situations, no interview is permitted after the appeal brief is filed.
guidance: Interviews after an examiner’s answer and prior to payment of the appeal forwarding fee are likely to confuse the record and are not permitted except in unusual circumstances (e.g., appellant wishes to cancel all appealed claims and proceed to issue with claims previously indicated as allowable, or where the examiner is convinced some claims are in condition for allowance). Requests for interviews on cases under Board jurisdiction require specific approval of the Technology Center Director upon a written showing of extraordinary circumstances to justify remand.

name: Treatment of dictionaries and 'Evidence' on appeal
description: For purposes of appeal, 'Evidence' does not encompass dictionaries, which may be cited before the Board. Evidence is defined to exclude dictionaries so appellants and examiners may refer to dictionaries in briefs and examiner answers without treating those references as evidence.
guidance: Excluding dictionaries from 'Evidence' allows the Board and tribunals to consult dictionaries as aids to understanding; case law (e.g., Phillips v. AWH) supports consultation of dictionaries when construing claim terms.

name: Summary of claimed subject matter requirements
description: A concise explanation of the subject matter defined in each of the rejected independent claims, referring to the specification in the Record by page and line number or paragraph number, and to the drawings by reference characters. For claims with means-plus-function (35 U.S.C. 112(f)), the concise explanation must identify the structure, material, or acts described in the specification corresponding to each claimed function with specific record references.
guidance: Reference to the patent application publication does not satisfy this paragraph. Each rejected independent claim must be summarized; dependent claims argued separately must also have the corresponding identification.

name: Argument content and structure
description: The arguments of appellant with respect to each ground of rejection, and the basis therefor, with citations of the statutes, regulations, authorities, and parts of the Record relied on. The arguments shall explain why the examiner erred as to each ground of rejection contested by appellant.
guidance: Each ground of rejection contested must be argued under a separate heading reasonably identifying the ground (e.g., claim number, statutory basis, applied reference). For grounds applying to multiple claims, appellant may argue separately, as a group, or as a subgroup; failure to separately argue grouped claims is a waiver of separate patentability arguments. A statement merely pointing out what a claim recites is insufficient. Except as provided in §§ 41.41, 41.47 and 41.52, any arguments or authorities not included in the appeal brief will be refused consideration by the Board for the present appeal.

name: Duty to address every ground of rejection (waiver rule)
description: An appellant’s brief must present arguments responsive to every ground of rejection stated by the examiner in the Office action from which the appeal has been taken (as modified by any advisory action and/or pre-appeal brief conference decision). If a ground of rejection is not addressed in the brief, appellant has waived any challenge to that ground and the Board may summarily sustain it.
guidance: Appellant cannot rely on asserting a ground is 'clearly improper' without explaining why the examiner erred; requesting that a rejection be held in abeyance (e.g., non-statutory double patenting) does not meet 37 CFR 41.37(c)(1)(iv) and will be treated as a waiver. The Board may decide appeals as to grouped claims on a single selected claim if appellant groups claims together.

name: Evaluate whether claims are directed to improvement in computer functionality
description: Determine whether the claims are directed to an improvement to computer functionality versus being directed to an abstract idea, recognizing that software improvements may be logical structures and processes rather than particular physical features (Enfish)
guidance: Use precedent like Enfish and McRO when assessing eligibility, particularly for claims related to machine learning or AI. Software can make non-abstract improvements to computer technology just as hardware can; eligibility determinations should turn on whether the claims are directed to an improvement to computer functionality versus an abstract idea.

name: Evaluate specification for disclosed technological improvement
description: The specification should be evaluated to determine if the disclosure provides sufficient details such that one of ordinary skill in the art would recognize the claimed invention as providing an improvement in the functioning of a computer, or an improvement to other technology or a technical field.
guidance: The specification need not explicitly set forth the improvement, but it must describe the invention such that the improvement would be apparent to one of ordinary skill. Conversely, a conclusory bare assertion of an improvement without necessary detail is insufficient.

name: Require that the claim reflects the disclosed improvement
description: If the specification sets forth an improvement in technology or a technical field, the claim must be evaluated to ensure that the claim itself reflects the disclosed improvement — i.e., the claim includes the components or steps of the invention that provide the improvement described in the specification.
guidance: The claim does not need to explicitly recite the improvement (e.g., “thereby increasing the bandwidth of the channel”), but examiners must verify the claim includes the components or steps that provide the improvement. Consider the claim "as a whole" and under the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) to determine whether the claim reflects the disclosed improvement.

name: Evaluate claims as an ordered combination / as a whole
description: When determining whether a claim reflects an improvement, look at the claim 'as a whole' — in other words, evaluate the claim as an ordered combination without ignoring the requirements of the individual steps.
guidance: Be careful to avoid oversimplifying the claims by looking at them generally and failing to account for the specific requirements of the claims. Do not evaluate claims at an inappropriately high level of generality such that meaningful technical limitations are dismissed without adequate explanation (see Ex Parte Desjardins warning).

name: Do not dismiss additional elements as mere 'generic computer components' without analysis
description: Examiners should not dismiss additional claim elements as mere generic computer components without considering whether such elements confer a technological improvement to a technical problem, especially for improvements to computer components or the computer system.
guidance: Consider whether claimed computer/system elements meaningfully contribute to the technological improvement; Desjardins and other precedents show that elements previously characterized as generic may nonetheless be part of an improvement.

name: Specification conclusory statements about improvement are insufficient
description: If the specification explicitly sets forth an improvement but only in a conclusory manner (i.e., a bare assertion of an improvement without the detail necessary to be apparent to a person of ordinary skill in the art), the examiner should not determine that the claim improves technology or a technical field.
guidance: Look for the substantive description enabling a POSITA to appreciate the improvement; mere assertions or boilerplate claims of improvement do not satisfy this requirement.

name: Use related considerations (particular machine; mere instructions to apply) to assist improvement determination
description: The improvement consideration overlaps with other § 101 considerations, specifically the particular machine consideration and the 'mere instructions to apply an exception' consideration; evaluation of those considerations may assist examiners in determining whether a claim satisfies the improvement consideration.
guidance: Cross-reference MPEP § 2106.05(b) and § 2106.05(f) when relevant to assess whether claimed elements provide an actual technological solution rather than mere instructions to implement an abstract idea.

name: Step 2A Prong One / Prong Two analysis — allow Prong Two to integrate exceptions into practical application
description: Even if Step 2A Prong One finds the claims recite an abstract idea (e.g., a mathematical concept), Step 2A Prong Two may determine that the specification identifies improvements and that the claims, taken as a whole, integrate the judicial exception into a practical application such that the claims are outside the enumerated judicial exception.
guidance: Evaluate whether the claims, when read in light of the specification, integrate the exception into a practical application (as in Ex Parte Desjardins where claims addressing catastrophic forgetting were deemed to integrate the exception at Prong Two).

name: Examples of claims that improve technology (non-exhaustive precedential list)
description: Claims that improve technology or a technical field and are not directed to a judicial exception include precedential examples such as Enfish (self-referential data structure), McRO (automatic lip synchronization and facial animation), Visual Memory (enhanced computer memory), Finjan (virus scanning improvements), SRI (network monitoring/suspicious activity detection), and Ex Parte Desjardins (ML training improvements and data-structure-like adjustments).
guidance: Use these cases as illustrative examples of how claims can be found to be technological improvements; additional examples are provided in MPEP § 2106.05(a).

name: Improvements to component/system performance via ML parameter adjustments
description: Improvements to computer component or system performance based upon adjustments to parameters of a machine learning model associated with tasks or workstreams may show an improvement in computer functionality.
guidance: Claims reciting adjustments in values to a plurality of performance parameters while preserving prior values (as in Desjardins) can reflect improvements tantamount to how the machine learning model itself would function in operation and therefore not be subsumed in an identified mathematical calculation.

name: Claims that recite a technological solution to a technological problem are 'more than apply it' instructions
description: Claims that specify how interactions or components are manipulated to yield a desired result — i.e., recite a technological solution to a technological problem — have been found to be more than merely instructing to apply an abstract idea or to use a law of nature (DDR Holdings, BASCOM, Thales Visionix).
guidance: Look for claim limitations that recite how the technological result is achieved (specific configurations, manipulations, or methods) rather than mere high-level goals; such specific technological solutions may overcome the 'apply it' or 'mere instructions' rejections.

name: Consider full claim scope under BRI when determining whether claim reflects improvement
description: The full scope of the claim under the broadest reasonable interpretation should be considered to determine if the claim reflects an improvement in technology or a technical field.
guidance: Do not rely solely on selected phrasing; consider how the claim limitations as a whole would be interpreted under BRI to assess whether they capture a particular solution or way of achieving a desired outcome rather than merely an idea or outcome.

name: Forms for corrections, amendments and types of changes
description: Specific forms must be used for different corrections and recordals.
guidance: To change specification (description/claims/drawings/sequence listing): Patents Form 13 or Form CM4. To change abstract: Patents Form 13 or Form CM4. To rectify errors on Patents Form 37: Form CM4. To change name/address/agent details after international phase: Form CM2. To register transfer of ownership (assignment): Form CM8. For correction of error generally, refer to Chapter 11.8.

name: Format and submission requirements for pre-grant amendments
description: From 1 Apr 2017, both marked-up and clean copies of amended sheets are required for online submission; from 1 Dec 2019, if amendments or corrections have been made to claims, a marked-up and clean copy of the full set of claims must be submitted.
guidance: Amendments/corrections should be based on the latest set of specifications on record (including earlier same-day submissions or pending requests). The amendment request should set out reasons for amendments and any supporting evidence; it is highly encouraged to indicate the basis for amendments with references to particular parts of the application as filed. The Patent Examiner may request such basis during examination. Examples of accepted marked-up and clean copy formats are provided.

name: Scope and limitations of supplementary examination
description: For supplementary examination, the Patent Examiner will review specific grounds only.
guidance: Grounds include support, relatedness of claims, morality, methods of medical treatment or diagnosis, double patenting, and no added matter. From 30 Oct 2017, the Patent Examiner will also determine whether the invention defined in each claim constitutes patentable subject matter and, if not, will state full reasons in a written opinion. Note: applicants may no longer request supplementary examination reports for applications with date of filing on or after 1 Jan 2020 and divisional applications lodged on or after 1 Jan 2020.

name: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation
description: During examination, a claim must be given its broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification as it would be interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: Words of the claim must be given their plain meaning unless inconsistent with the specification; the plain meaning is the ordinary and customary meaning to those of ordinary skill at the time of the invention. The specification is the best source for determining claim-term meaning and can serve as a glossary; the presumption of ordinary meaning may be rebutted if the applicant clearly sets forth a different definition in the specification. See MPEP § 2111 for full discussion.

name: Different Standard During Examination vs. Post-Issuance
description: Claims under examination are construed under a different standard than issued patents: there is no presumption of validity and claims are given their broadest reasonable interpretation.
guidance: Because the patent record is still in development, a lower threshold of ambiguity is applied during prosecution. A claim should be rejected under §112, ¶2 if, after BRI, its metes and bounds are not clear (e.g., a person of ordinary skill would read it with more than one reasonable interpretation). Examiners should not conflate claim breadth with indefiniteness: breadth alone is not indefiniteness if the scope is clearly defined.

name: Determine Invocation of 35 U.S.C. §112, Sixth Paragraph
description: Examiners should determine whether each claim limitation invokes §112, ¶6 (means-plus-function or step-plus-function) or not.
guidance: If a limitation invokes §112, ¶6, it must be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof. See PART 1, section III.C for more information.

name: Functional Language — Scope and Definiteness
description: For functional language (defining an item by what it does rather than by physical characteristics), consider whether the claim: (1) gives a clear-cut indication of the scope covered; (2) sets forth well-defined boundaries rather than only stating a problem to be solved or result to be obtained; and (3) would enable one of ordinary skill to know from the claim terms what structure or steps are encompassed.
guidance: Functional language is not intrinsically improper, but unlimited functional claiming that lacks recited structure/material/steps may be indefinite or fail §112, ¶1 written description/enablement. Examples of problematic functional limitations include claims that merely describe a problem or an outcome. Examiner determinations are context-dependent (specification disclosure and knowledge of one skilled in the art are key).

name: Remedies for Ambiguous Functional Claiming
description: To resolve possible ambiguities in functional claiming, applicants may (1) recite a quantitative metric rather than a qualitative functional feature; (2) show that the specification provides a formula for calculating a property along with examples that meet and do not meet the limitation; (3) show the specification provides general guidelines and examples sufficient to teach one of ordinary skill when the limitation is satisfied; or (4) amend the claims to recite the particular structure that performs the function.
guidance: These actions can be used in prosecution to rebut indefiniteness rejections and to clarify claim metes and bounds on the record.

name: Terms of Degree — Definiteness Standard
description: For terms of degree (e.g., 'substantially free of'), examiners should consider whether the specification provides some standard for measuring the recited degree or whether one of ordinary skill in the art could ascertain the scope (for example, by a standard recognized in the art).
guidance: A claim reciting a term of degree should not be held indefinite if the specification provides examples or teachings that can be used to measure the degree even without precise numerical measurement (e.g., a drawing figure providing a standard).

name: Subjective Terms — Need for Objective Standard
description: For subjective terms (e.g., 'aesthetically pleasing'), examiners should consider whether the specification provides some objective standard for measuring the scope of the claim; if the claim requires unrestricted subjective judgment, it may be rejected as indefinite.
guidance: To overcome indefiniteness for terms of degree or subjective terms, an applicant may provide evidence (e.g., a 37 CFR §1.132 declaration) that one of ordinary skill can ascertain the meaning from the specification, or amend the claim to remove such terms.

name: Markush Group Definiteness
description: A Markush claim (e.g., 'selected from the group consisting of...') may be rejected under §112, ¶2 if one of ordinary skill cannot determine the metes and bounds of the group.
guidance: Indefiniteness can arise if the examiner cannot envision all members of the Markush group or if the species do not share a single structural similarity or a common use (not functionally equivalent). To overcome such a rejection, an applicant may provide evidence that the members share a single structural similarity or common use.

name: Dependent Claims — §112, Fourth Paragraph Compliance
description: When examining a dependent claim, Examiners should determine whether the claim complies with §112, ¶4: it must contain a reference to a previous claim in the same application, further limit the claimed subject matter, and include all the limitations of the previous claim.
guidance: If these requirements are not met, the Examiner should reject the claim under §112, ¶4. To overcome the rejection, amend the claim to properly reference the previous claim, further limit the subject matter, or include all limitations.

name: Means-Plus-Function Claim Invocation Criteria
description: A claim is presumed to invoke §112, ¶6 if it recites 'means for' or 'step for' and includes functional language; if it does not use these phrases, there is a strong rebuttable presumption that §112, ¶6 does not apply.
guidance: Examiners should consider that a non-structural term (e.g., 'mechanism') associated with functional language may invoke §112, ¶6 unless (1) it is preceded by a structural modifier, defined in the specification or known in the art as a particular structure, or (2) it is modified by sufficient structure or material for achieving the recited function. The guidelines set three criteria to apply §112, ¶6: (1) use of 'means for'/'step for' or a non-structural term without a structural modifier; (2) the term is modified by functional language; and (3) the term is not modified by sufficient structure/material/acts for achieving the function.

name: Unclear Invocation — Reject as Indefinite
description: When it is unclear whether a claim invokes §112, ¶6, Examiners should reject the claim under §112, ¶2 as being indefinite.
guidance: Such a rejection requires the applicant to respond by explaining why the language is definite or by amending the claim; rejections must clearly identify the indefinite language and thoroughly explain the reasoning.

name: §112, Sixth Paragraph — Written Description Link Requirement
description: To ensure that a §112, ¶6 limitation complies with §112, ¶2, the written description must clearly link or associate the corresponding structure, material, or acts to the claimed function.
guidance: The specification must disclose the corresponding structure/material/acts; for computer-implemented means-plus-function limitations, the specification must disclose an algorithm (e.g., mathematical formula, flow chart, or textual description) for performing the function. Merely stating that a function is performed by a computer or processor without disclosing an algorithm is insufficient.

name: Examiner Practice — Err on Side of Rejection to Clarify Record
description: The guidelines encourage Examiners to be more critical in evaluating claims for indefiniteness and to err on the side of making rejections because such a rejection requires the applicant to explain or amend, thereby clarifying claim boundaries prior to issuance.
guidance: Expect a short-term increase in §112, ¶2 rejections. Rejections must clearly identify the language causing indefiniteness and thoroughly explain the reasoning. Examiners should avoid piecemeal examination and reject each claim on all valid grounds as appropriate (see MPEP references).

name: Drafting and Prosecution Recommendations for Applicants
description: Recommended applicant actions during drafting and prosecution to avoid or overcome indefiniteness rejections.
guidance: Recommendations: (1) provide guidance in the specification for terms of degree or subjective terms; (2) decide whether to invoke §112, ¶6 and ensure claim language matches intent and the specification discloses corresponding structure/material/acts; (3) ensure algorithms are adequately disclosed for computer-implemented means-plus-function limitations; (4) ensure Markush limitations and dependent claims comply with guideline requirements; (5) consider personal interviews with Examiners to resolve §112, ¶2 rejections; (6) consider filing Rule 132 Declarations to rebut rejections (e.g., to show one of ordinary skill could determine metes and bounds, provide examples in/out of scope); and (7) carefully review Examiner claim constructions for accuracy.

name: Establishing a Clear Record and Compact Prosecution
description: When resolving indefinite claim language, actions should focus on establishing a clear record, providing sufficient explanation in Office Actions, and practicing 'compact prosecution'.
guidance: Office Actions should identify problematic language and explain reasoning; compact prosecution aims to resolve issues efficiently and minimize unnecessary statements that could create estoppel. See PART 1 Step 3 and MPEP references for procedures.

name: Use of Evidence and Declarations to Rebut Indefiniteness
description: Applicants may use evidence (e.g., 37 CFR §1.132 Declarations) to show that the meaning of claim language can be ascertained by one of ordinary skill in the art when reading the specification.
guidance: Such evidence can include examples of items within and outside the claimed scope, demonstrations that the specification provides measurement standards/formulae, or other factual showing to rebut Examiner assertions of indefiniteness.

name: Specification as Primary Source of Claim Meaning
description: The specification should be used as the primary source for interpreting claim terms and for providing standards or definitions to clarify terms.
guidance: When the specification sets a clear path to claim language (e.g., defining terms, providing examples or formulas), the scope of claims is more easily determined and public notice is best served. Applicants may expressly define terms in the specification to rebut ordinary meaning.

name: Functional Claiming Anti-Patterns and Examples
description: Examples where functional or qualitative language has been held indefinite or problematic (illustrative anti-patterns).
guidance: Illustrative problematic phrases include: 'fragile gel' defined functionally without clear degree, phrases reciting outcomes such as 'of such size and contour as to prevent substantial sagging or offsetting during a normal or commercially useful life', and qualitative mixtures characterized by buyer-desired standards like 'commercially uniform'. These examples show that terms describing only outcomes or subjective commercial preferences can create indefiniteness or failure to adequately define structural characteristics.

name: Contents required by 35 U.S.C. 111(a)
description: An application for patent under 35 U.S.C. 111(a) shall include (A) a specification as prescribed by section 112, (B) a drawing as prescribed by section 113, and (C) an oath or declaration as prescribed by section 115. The application shall be accompanied by the fee required by law. The fee, oath or declaration, and one or more claims may be submitted after the filing date within periods and conditions prescribed by the Director; failure to submit them within such prescribed period results in abandonment.
guidance: Filing date is the date on which a specification, with or without claims, is received at the USPTO. Applicants may submit fee/oath/claims after filing under prescribed conditions (may require surcharge). If not timely submitted, application is regarded as abandoned.

name: Definition of filing date and no new matter rule
description: The filing date of an application (nonprovisional) is the date the specification, with or without claims, is received in the Office. No new matter may be introduced into an application after its filing date.
guidance: For design patents the filing date generally requires the specification as prescribed by 35 U.S.C. 112 including at least one claim and any required drawings. Continuing applications must comply with the conditions in sections 120/121/365(c)/386(c) and § 1.78 to claim earlier dates.

name: Complete application components (37 CFR 1.51 / 1.53)
description: A complete (nonprovisional) application comprises: (1) a specification as prescribed by 35 U.S.C. 112, including claim(s); (2) the inventor's oath or declaration; (3) drawings, when necessary; and (4) the prescribed filing fee, search fee, examination fee, and application size fee.
guidance: A complete provisional application under § 1.53(c) comprises a cover sheet identifying it as provisional, a specification under 35 U.S.C. 112(a), drawings when necessary, and the prescribed filing and application size fees. Applicants are encouraged to file an IDS in nonprovisional applications (see § 1.97 and § 1.98); IDSs are not permitted in provisional applications.

name: Preferred arrangement and headings of the specification
description: Preferred order of arrangement for a specification (each heading in upper case without underlining or bold): (A) Title of the invention; (B) Cross-reference to related applications; (C) Statement regarding federally sponsored research or development; (D) Names of parties to a joint research agreement; (E) Reference to a Sequence Listing/table/program listing appendix on compact disc and incorporation-by-reference; (F) Statement regarding prior disclosures by an inventor; (G) Background of the invention (including (1) Field of the invention and (2) Description of related art); (H) Brief summary of the invention; (I) Brief description of the several views of the drawing; (J) Detailed description of the invention; (K) Claim(s) (commencing on a separate sheet); (L) Abstract of the Disclosure (commencing on a separate sheet); (M) Sequence Listing if on paper.
guidance: These headings are the preferred layout suggested for applicant use; see MPEP § 608.01(a) for more detail. If an Application Data Sheet (ADS) is used, data in the ADS need not be duplicated elsewhere except in particular historical circumstances.

name: Completion after filing for missing elements (fees, claims, oath/declaration) (37 CFR 1.53(f))
description: If an application accorded a filing date lacks the basic filing fee, search fee, examination fee, at least one claim, or the inventor's oath/declaration, the applicant (if a correspondence address is provided) will be notified and given time to submit the missing items to avoid abandonment. If no correspondence address is provided, applicant has three months from filing date to supply missing items.
guidance: The inventor's oath/declaration may be postponed until the application is otherwise in condition for allowance if (i) the application is an original non-reissue containing an ADS identifying each inventor by legal name and mailing address, and (ii) oaths/declarations are filed no later than the date the issue fee is paid. This postponed timeframe is not extendable under § 1.136.

name: Provisional application drafting guidelines
description: A provisional application should preferably conform to the arrangement guidelines for nonprovisional applications. The specification must comply with 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and refer to drawings where necessary for understanding the invention. Unlike nonprovisional applications, provisional applications do not require claims or an oath/declaration.
guidance: Use the preferred nonprovisional layout for clarity and to maximize usefulness of the provisional. Because the Office does not conduct substantive examination of provisionals, IDSs are unnecessary and will not be accepted.

name: Required filing documents for Brazilian applications
description: A Brazilian application requires a request form, the specifications, claims, abstract, and drawings (in Portuguese as noted).
guidance: If claiming priority under the Paris Convention, a certified copy of the priority document with a simple Portuguese translation must be provided within prescribed time (commonly 90 days). If the applicant is not the inventor, an assignment or inventor’s release may be required (simple copy with translation can be filed within about 3 months). Drawings and sequence listings (if applicable) should be included at filing, as missing drawings cannot be added later.

name: Language and translation requirements
description: The official language for patents in Brazil is Portuguese; a Brazilian patent application must be filed in Portuguese or accompanied by a Portuguese translation.
guidance: At minimum the title, abstract, and claims must be in Portuguese at filing. If the specification is initially in another language, INPI allows a short window (usually 30 days after filing) to submit the full Portuguese translation. It is recommended to have the full application in Portuguese at filing to avoid issues.

name: Electronic filing and payment procedure (e-INPI / GRU)
description: Brazil uses an electronic filing system (e-INPI); applicants must create an e-INPI account and pay the filing fee via a GRU (government payment form).
guidance: Once the fee is paid and forms completed online, the application can be submitted. The filing date is accorded once INPI receives the documents and payment. Missing required elements (like claims or drawings) may trigger a notice to correct deficiencies; failing to correct timely can lead to dismissal.

name: Substantive examination process and Office Actions
description: Once examination is requested and the application published, an INPI examiner will review formal requirements and patentability (novelty, inventive step, industrial application) and may issue Office Actions.
guidance: Common issues include clarity or breadth of claims, adequacy of disclosure, and patentability over prior art. Applicants typically have 90 days to respond to an Office Action (extendable once for 60 days upon petition). Responses may include arguments or amendments; multiple Office Actions can be issued until objections are overcome or final refusal is issued.

name: PCT national phase filing requirements and documents
description: To enter the national phase in Brazil, submit a copy of the International Application (PCT publication), Portuguese translation of the PCT application (at least specification and claims), any amendments with translations, and accompanying documents like drawings/sequence listings.
guidance: At the time of national phase filing, Brazil requires the title, abstract, and claims in Portuguese. If the PCT specification was in another language, Brazil allows a short 60-day extension after national phase filing to submit the full Portuguese translation of the description. Filing is via e-INPI and the national phase application receives a Brazilian application number.

name: Summary of Claimed Subject Matter
description: A concise explanation of the subject matter defined in each of the rejected independent claims, with references to the specification in the Record by page and line number or paragraph number, and to the drawing by reference characters, if any.
guidance: For claims containing means-plus-function or step-plus-function recitations under 35 U.S.C. 112(f), the concise explanation must identify the structure, material, or acts described in the specification corresponding to each claimed function with precise references. Reference to the patent application publication does not satisfy this requirement.

name: Argument — Structure, Citations, and Separate Headings
description: The arguments of appellant with respect to each ground of rejection, and the basis therefor, with citations of the statutes, regulations, authorities, and parts of the Record relied on; explain why the examiner erred as to each ground contested.
guidance: All arguments and authorities an appellant wishes the Board to consider for the present appeal should be included in the brief (except as allowed by §§41.41, 41.47, 41.52); arguments or authorities not included will be refused consideration by the Board for purposes of the present appeal. Each ground of rejection contested must be argued under a separate heading that reasonably identifies the ground (e.g., claim number, statutory basis, applied reference). For multiple claims under the same ground, appellant may argue separately, as a group, or as a subgroup; failure to separately argue a grouped claim is a waiver of separate-patentability argument. A mere statement of what a claim recites is not an argument for patentability.

name: Format, Identification, and Optional Materials
description: The brief should start each required item on a separate page and the brief, as well as every other document relating to an appeal, should indicate the Technology Center number and application or reexamination control number.
guidance: Only one copy of the appeal brief is required. The rule specifies minimum items but an appellant may include additional material such as list of references, table of contents, table of cases, copies of evidence entered by the examiner, etc. While not required, the Office strongly encourages an evidence appendix (copies of declarations, evidence of secondary considerations) or, at minimum, clear identification in the brief of the evidence relied upon with the date of entry into the Image File Wrapper so the Board can consider the proper evidence and avoid confusion. An example format: (A) Identification page; (B) Table of Contents; (C) Real party in interest page(s); (D) Related appeals page(s); (E) Summary of claimed subject matter; (F) Argument; (G) Claims appendix.

name: Means/Step-Plus-Function (35 U.S.C. 112(f)) Identification Requirement
description: For any claim containing a means-plus-function or step-plus-function recitation as permitted by 35 U.S.C. 112(f), the concise explanation of the claimed subject matter must identify the structure, material, or acts described in the specification corresponding to each claimed function with precise references.
guidance: Reference must be to the specification in the Record by page and line number or paragraph number, and to the drawing by reference characters; mere reference to the patent application publication does not satisfy the requirement.

name: USPTO 2019 Guidance — Alice Step 2A Prong 2 (practical application)
description: A claim that recites a judicial exception is not 'directed to' that exception if the exception is integrated into a practical application of the judicial exception.
guidance: If the judicial exception is integrated into a practical application, the claim is not directed to the exception under Step 2A and need not proceed to Step 2B. If not integrated, proceed to Step 2B (inventive concept). The Guidance supplies examples; PTAB decisions often analyze whether limitations integrate the exception into a practical application.

name: Alice Step 2B — inventive concept (significantly more)
description: After finding a claim directed to a judicial exception under Step 2A, determine whether additional claim elements provide an 'inventive concept' that is significantly more than the judicial exception (consider elements individually and as an ordered combination).
guidance: Federal Circuit often resolves eligibility at Step 2B; look for technical improvements, unconventional arrangements, or elements not well-understood, routine, and conventional. Berkheimer held that whether elements are 'well-understood, routine and conventional' is a question of fact.

name: Practical application evidence — technical integration and improvements
description: To show a practical application (Prong 2) or an inventive concept, claim elements should integrate the judicial exception into a technological solution — e.g., improve computer functionality, provide a technological solution to a technical problem, or produce a specific technological result.
guidance: PTAB and Federal Circuit look for specifics: how the technology is integrated, what technical problem is solved, and quantifiable or described technological benefits (improved efficiency, reduced storage, improved operating efficiency). Mere automation or generic computer implementation is insufficient.

name: Specificity in claims and specification supports eligibility
description: Claims and specification should include concrete details about structures, integration, timing, or other technical features rather than high-level descriptions.
guidance: Practice tips: include multiple specific features tied to the problems of the environment; describe how technology provides the improvement; tie recited advantages to technology rather than mere economic efficiencies. The PTAB reversed some rejections where claims contained limitations addressing problems in a specific hybrid trading environment (e.g., timer mechanism).

name: Ordered combination analysis (individual elements vs. combination)
description: Even if individual claim elements are routine or abstract, the ordered combination of elements may provide an inventive concept — but courts/PTAB will scrutinize whether the combination is merely conventional automation.
guidance: Do not assume ordered combination alone saves eligibility; show that the combination yields a non-generic technical improvement or solves a technical problem in a way not previously known. The PTAB has found ordered combinations insufficient when they simply link abstract ideas to computer use without improving computer function.

name: Claims that are directed to improvements in computer functionality are more likely eligible
description: Claims that specify an improvement in how computers operate (particular manner of summarizing/presenting information, improved data structures, non-generic arrangement of components) can be considered non-abstract and eligible.
guidance: Cases like Enfish and others are cited where claims were held directed to an improvement in computer functionality rather than an abstract idea; show specificity in claim language to capture that improvement.

name: Economic practices and market activity claims are likely 'methods of organizing human activity'
description: Claims reciting fundamental economic practices (trading derivatives, intermediated settlement, basic market operations) are typically grouped as methods of organizing human activity and thus treated as abstract ideas under the Guidance.
guidance: When claims recite economic practices, focus drafting on technological features that integrate the economic practice into a practical application (e.g., technical mechanisms addressing hybrid electronic/paper environments). PTAB noted that core trading operations are 'basic concepts' akin to intermediated settlement.

name: Use specification to define claim terms and show technological character
description: Examiner and PTAB analyses frequently rely on specification statements to interpret claim elements (e.g., 'workflow stages' characterized as human activity vs. technical identifiers).
guidance: Draft specification to describe technical meaning, structure, and integration of claimed elements. Specifications that describe implementation details and technological advantages help arguments for practical application and inventive concept.

name: Demonstrate technological advantages, not only economic efficiencies
description: Advantages recited in the specification and claims should be tied to technological improvements (improving computer function, removing communication advantages, reducing storage redundancy), not merely to economic benefits.
guidance: PTAB and USPTO guidance emphasize that showing technological improvements supports practical application findings; statements of advantage should be tied to claim elements and implementation details.

name: Framing a 35 U.S.C. 103(a) rejection — procedural requirements (¶ 7.21)
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over [2].
guidance: This paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.20 or 7.103. An explanation of the rejection applying the Graham v. Deere test must follow this form paragraph. If reliance is on prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(e), apply AIPA rules to determine prior art date unless the reference is a U.S. patent issued from an international application with filing date prior to November 29, 2000 (use pre-AIPA 102(e) only in the narrow circumstances described). If the applicability of the rejection prevents disqualification under 103(c), follow with form paragraph 7.20.01. Use 7.21.01 for provisional 103(a) rejections based on copending applications.

name: Provisional 35 U.S.C. 103(a) rejection for copending application (¶ 7.21.01)
description: Claim [1] provisionally rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as obvious over copending Application No. [2] which has a common [3] with the instant application; based upon the earlier effective U.S. filing date of the copending application, it would constitute prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) if published or patented.
guidance: This provisional rejection is based on presumption of future publication/patenting of the copending application. It may be overcome by showings under 37 CFR 1.132 (derivation), 37 CFR 1.131 (date of invention), or by showing the copending application is disqualified under 35 U.S.C. 103(c). Use this paragraph when copending application has earlier U.S. filing date and common assignee or at least one common inventor. Apply AIPA guidance for determining 102(e) dates; do not use this paragraph in applications pending on/after Dec 10, 2004 when copending application is disqualified under 103(c). If the claimed invention is also claimed in the copending application, consider obviousness double patenting using paragraphs 8.33 and 8.37, and other related rejections as appropriate.

name: 103(a) rejection where reference has common assignee or inventor (¶ 7.21.02)
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being obvious over [2]; the applied reference has a common [3] with the instant application and constitutes prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) based on its earlier effective filing date.
guidance: This rejection might be overcome by (1) showing under 37 CFR 1.132 that any invention disclosed but not claimed in the reference was derived from the applicant's inventor; (2) showing an earlier date of invention under 37 CFR 1.131; or (3) filing an oath/declaration under 37 CFR 1.130 stating current common ownership and that the named inventor is the prior inventor under 35 U.S.C. 104, together with a terminal disclaimer under 37 CFR 1.321(c). The reference could also be disqualified under 35 U.S.C. 103(c). Apply AIPA rules for 102(e) date where applicable. Insert --assignee-- or --inventor-- in bracket 3 and explanation of obviousness in bracket 4.

name: Combining references — 35 U.S.C. 103(a), further in view (¶ 7.22)
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over [2] as applied to claim [3] above, and further in view of [4].
guidance: This paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.21. An explanation applying the Graham v. Deere test must follow. If relying on prior art under 102(e), apply AIPA rules to determine reference dates as specified in 7.12/7.12.01 guidance.

name: Graham v. Deere test for obviousness (¶ 7.23)
description: The factual inquiries set forth in Graham v. John Deere Co. that are applied for establishing a background for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103(a): (1) determining the scope and contents of the prior art; (2) ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue; (3) resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; (4) considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
guidance: An explanation applying Graham must follow 103(a) rejections. Use these four factual inquiries as the framework for the rationale of obviousness rejections and for responding to applicant arguments invoking Graham.

name: When to use combined 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103(a) rejection (¶ 7.27)
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102([2]) as anticipated by or, in the alternative, under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as obvious over [3].
guidance: This paragraph is NOT intended to be commonly used as a substitute for a single appropriate rejection; use a single rejection under 102 or 103 when possible. Circumstances where this paragraph may be used include: (a) claim interpretation dispute where one interpretation supports 102 and another supports 103; (b) reference discloses all limitations except a property or function and examiner cannot determine inherent possession (In re Fitzgerald); (c) genus discloses small genus placing claimed species in public possession (In re Schaumann); (d) product-by-process issues where product appears same though produced by different process (In re Marosi, In re Thorpe); (e) means-plus-function/equivalency uncertainty (see §§2183-2184); (f) overlapping ranges where reference lacks specific example within claimed range (Ex parte Lee). If claim interpretation renders claims indefinite, consider 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph. A full explanation should follow this form paragraph. Precede by appropriate form paragraphs (7.07 and 7.08–7.14, 7.20 or 7.103).

name: Prioritize prior-art-based examination; develop non-prior-art rejections fully (706.03)
description: The primary object of examination is to determine whether claims are patentable over the prior art; this should not be relegated while undue emphasis is given to nonprior art or 'technical' rejections. Effort should be concentrated on truly essential matters, minimizing/eliminating effort on technical rejections which are not critical.
guidance: Where a major technical rejection is proper (e.g., lack of proper disclosure, undue breadth, utility), state the rejection with a full development of reasons rather than a mere conclusion with stereotyped language. If using form paragraphs in an office action, incorporation reduces chance of misunderstanding as to grounds of rejection.

name: Use of 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection heading and following specificity (¶ 7.05)
description: Use the heading 'Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 because' — this heading-only paragraph must be followed by one of form paragraphs 7.05.01–7.05.03 or another appropriate reason.
guidance: Explain the rejection following recitation of the statute and use the appropriate specific subparagraph(s). This paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.04 in first actions and final rejections.

name: Utility requirement under 35 U.S.C. 101 (¶ 7.05.02)
description: The claimed invention lacks patentable utility. [1]
guidance: In bracket 1, provide explanation of lack of utility. See MPEP §§706.03(a) and 2105–2107.03 for supporting guidance and law.

name: Utility rejections under 35 U.S.C. 101 and enablement under 35 U.S.C. 112 (¶ 7.05.04)
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 because the claimed invention is not supported by either a [2] asserted utility or a well established utility. Claim [4] also rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, where the specification would not enable one skilled in the art to make or use the claimed invention.
guidance: Where the specification would not enable one skilled in the art, or other reasons support an enablement rejection, make a separate 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph rejection using the Wands factors (In re Wands) and an undue experimentation analysis (see MPEP §§2164–2164.08(c)). Use Format A, B, or C as appropriate: Format A insert '--specific and substantial--' for lack of asserted utility; Format B insert '--credible--' for lack of credible asserted utility; Format C for multiple utilities where none are 'specific and substantial' or 'credible' — insert combined wording and address each utility.

name: Board of examiners review when specifications/claim modified (7th section)
description: If the specification and claim shall not have been so modified as, in the opinion of the Commissioner, shall entitle the applicant to a patent, he may on appeal, and upon request in writing, have the decision of a board of examiners who may reverse the Commissioner.
guidance: This affords an administrative review mechanism when the Commissioner thinks modifications might entitle the applicant to a patent; it is part of the internal remedial structure distinct from judicial appeal.

name: What constitutes 'public disclosure' for anticipation
description: Public disclosure encompasses certain kinds of knowledge, use, publication, description, and sale that make the invention available to the public as prior art.
guidance: Assess whether the prior act conveyed the invention to the public in a way that would enable persons of ordinary skill to practice the claimed invention. Public disclosure can occur via publications, sales, uses, or other disseminations of information.

name: Inherent anticipation standard (necessity of inherently present limitations)
description: A claim is inherently anticipated if every element is either expressly or inherently present in a single prior-art reference; inherency requires that the missing limitation is necessarily present in the reference, not merely possibly or conjecturally present.
guidance: Prove inherency with clear evidence that the unstated limitation necessarily follows from the prior art as would be recognized by persons of ordinary skill. Expert testing/demonstrations that reliably reproduce the inherent result are persuasive; mere conjecture or speculation is insufficient. Patentee failure to rebut repeatable testing evidence can support a finding of inherency. Case: In re Omeprazole (majority finding inherency based on consistent expert re-creation; dissent emphasized 'necessarily present' standard).

name: Mutual mistake in contract wording permits compensation for extra work
description: Where mutual error in contract wording caused contractor to perform work not intended to be covered, and facts establish contractor's claim, he is entitled to compensation for the extra work performed.
guidance: Contractor not estopped by his conduct if facts support claim (C. 22238, Oct. 24, 1907).

name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1) — grave injustice (iii)
description: Practitioner must clearly and convincingly show a genuine issue of material fact that imposition of identical discipline by the Office would result in a grave injustice.
guidance: The grave injustice inquiry focuses on whether the severity of the punishment 'fits' the misconduct—that the state's sanction was so ill-fitted that imposing it federally would be unjust. It does not concern timing (e.g., seeking nunc pro tunc relief); the respondent must argue that the underlying sanction itself was inappropriate. Prior voluntary stipulations by respondent undercut this claim.

name: Standard of proof: clear and convincing evidence
description: Any claim to prevent reciprocal discipline (or to obtain a different result) must be supported by clear and convincing evidence of a genuine issue of material fact.
guidance: This is a higher-than-preponderance but lower-than-beyond-a-reasonable-doubt standard; courts and the USPTO apply it strictly in reciprocal-discipline contexts. The respondent must produce strong, credible evidence to overcome the presumption.

name: Duties during suspension and for nunc pro tunc eligibility (§ 11.58)
description: Practitioner must comply with the duties enumerated in 37 C.F.R. § 11.58, including promptly notifying clients of suspension, filing notices of withdrawal for pending matters where required, and ceasing all activities related to practice before the Office.
guidance: Specific examples referenced: § 11.58(b)(1)(ii) (notify clients of suspension) and § 11.58(b)(1)(i) (file notice of withdrawal for pending trademark applications). Failure to perform these duties undermines claims of voluntary cessation and eligibility for nunc pro tunc relief.

name: Limited Claim on Public-Domain Works (Removal of References)
description: The Project Gutenberg Literary Archive Foundation owns a compilation copyright in the collection of Project Gutenberg electronic works. Nearly all the individual works in the collection are in the public domain in the United States. If an individual work is unprotected by copyright law in the United States and you are located in the United States, we do not claim a right to prevent you from copying, distributing, performing, displaying or creating derivative works based on the work as long as all references to Project Gutenberg are removed.
guidance: You may freely copy/distribute/modify public-domain works in the U.S. without complying with the full Project Gutenberg license provided you remove all references to Project Gutenberg; otherwise you must comply with the Foundation's terms. This distinguishes compilation/trademark rights from individual-work public-domain status.

name: BRI covering statutory and non-statutory embodiments
description: A claim whose broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) covers both statutory and non‑statutory embodiments embraces subject matter that is not eligible for patent protection and therefore is directed to non‑statutory subject matter (Step 1: NO).
guidance: When the BRI encompasses non‑statutory embodiments (e.g., machine‑readable media that can encompass transitory carrier waves), a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 is appropriate. It is a best practice for the examiner to point out the BRI and recommend an amendment, if possible, to narrow the claim to embodiments that fall within a statutory category. See examples (In re Nuijten; Mentor Graphics v. EVE‑USA).

name: Step 1: Claim must fall within statutory category
description: Determine whether the claim as a whole falls within one or more statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter) (Step 1: YES); if clearly not within one of the four categories (Step 1: NO), reject under 35 U.S.C. 101.
guidance: When rejecting under Step 1, use form paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01 per MPEP §706.03(a). If the claim fails Step 1 but applicant’s disclosure indicates the claim could be amended to fall within a statutory category, proceed to determine whether such an amended claim would be eligible at Pathway A, B, or C and recommend amendment if possible.

name: Identification of judicial exceptions
description: Judicial exceptions include abstract ideas, laws of nature, and natural phenomena (and related terms such as products of nature, scientific principles, mental processes), and these are not patent eligible.
guidance: There are no bright lines between types of exceptions; many concepts can fall under multiple exceptions. For eligibility analysis it is sufficient for the examiner to identify that the claimed concept (the specific claim limitation(s) believed to recite an exception) aligns with at least one judicial exception. See cited Supreme Court and Federal Circuit precedent (Alice, Myriad, Mayo, etc.).

name: Step 2A: Directed to a judicial exception (recite vs involve)
description: Step 2A asks whether the claim is directed to a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea — i.e., whether such an exception is recited (set forth or described) in the claim. A claim is directed to an exception when that exception is recited in the claim.
guidance: Different language ('set forth' vs 'describe') indicates different ways an exception may be recited. Examiners must consider the claim as a whole and distinguish between claims that recite an exception (require further analysis at Step 2B) and claims that merely involve or are based on an exception (eligible and do not require further analysis). Examples: 'A machine comprising elements that operate in accordance with F=ma' (recites law of nature → Step 2A: YES) versus a teeter‑totter claim that merely involves the law of the lever (Step 2A: NO).

name: Treatment of multiple or parsed exceptions
description: Care should be taken not to parse a recited exception into multiple exceptions unless clearly distinct; steps that manipulate information via a series of mental steps should be treated as a single abstract idea for analysis.
guidance: If a claim recites multiple exceptions (even if not distinct), it is directed to at least one judicial exception (Step 2A: YES) and thus requires further analysis at Step 2B. See RecogniCorp v. Nintendo as example where multiple abstract ideas led to Step 2B analysis.

name: How to determine if a claimed concept is an abstract idea
description: Examiners should determine whether a claim recites an abstract idea by (1) identifying the claimed concept (specific claim limitation(s) believed to be an abstract idea), and (2) comparing the claimed concept to concepts previously identified as abstract ideas by the courts.
guidance: If the claimed concept is similar to previously identified abstract ideas, it is reasonable to conclude the concept is an abstract idea (Step 2A: YES). If it is not similar and there is no basis to conclude it is an abstract idea, find that the claim is not directed to an abstract idea (Step 2A: NO) and eligible at Pathway B unless it recites another exception.

name: Claims directed to improvements in computer functionality/technology are not abstract
description: Some inventions that claim improvements in computer functionality or other technology are not abstract and therefore may be eligible at Step 2A (or via streamlined Pathway A), provided they are appropriately claimed.
guidance: Federal Circuit examples include Enfish (self‑referential table), McRO (automatic lip synchronization using rules), and Visual Memory (enhanced memory system). Examiners must give the claim its BRI, evaluate specification and claim together, and require that the specification disclose sufficient detail so a person of ordinary skill would recognize the improvement. The claim itself must reflect the improvement (covering a particular solution or way to achieve an outcome rather than the mere idea). See MPEP §2106.05(a) for further discussion.

name: When claimed improvement is insufficient
description: A claim does not reflect an improvement to computer‑functionality or technology if the claimed process can be performed without a computer, if it merely automates conventional activity, or if improvements arise solely from using a general‑purpose computer or conventional components.
guidance: Federal Circuit authorities (e.g., Synopsys v. Mentor Graphics; FairWarning; Credit Acceptance; Affinity Labs; TLI Communications) indicate that mere automation, speed increases due only to generic computers, or conventional implementation on generic components are insufficient to show an improvement. Examiners should consult MPEP §2106.05(a) for cases and further examples.

name: Resolve improvements early and consider in full Alice/Mayo analysis
description: Examiners are encouraged to resolve whether a claim improves computer functionality or other technology as early as possible in the eligibility analysis, since such an improvement may render the claim eligible at Pathway A or Pathway B.
guidance: If improvement is clear (e.g., Enfish), the claim could be found eligible at Pathway A under a streamlined analysis or at Pathway B as not directed to an abstract idea. If not clear in Step 2A, the improvement may still contribute to eligibility in Step 2B. See MPEP §2106.06(b) and §2106.05(a).

name: Surface shading — prohibited and recommended techniques
description: Solid black surface shading is not permitted except to represent the color black or color contrast; oblique line shading must be used to show transparent, translucent, and highly polished or reflective surfaces.
guidance: Contrast in materials may be shown by using line shading in one area and stippling in another; this technique allows a claim to broadly cover contrasting surfaces without limiting to specific colors or materials, provided the appearance does not patentably depart from the illustrated visual appearance.

name: Use of broken lines — permitted purposes
description: Broken lines may be used to disclose environmental structure related to the claimed design and to define the bounds of the claim; structure not part of the claimed design but necessary to show the environment may be represented in broken lines.
guidance: Unclaimed subject matter must be described as forming no part of the claimed design or of a specified embodiment thereof. A boundary line may be shown in broken lines if it is not intended to form part of the claimed design. Applicant may choose broken-line boundaries where the boundary does not exist in reality.

name: Broken lines — crossing full lines and disclosure clarity
description: When broken lines cross over the full-line showing of the claimed design, the purpose of those broken lines must be explicitly identified in the specification so that the scope of the claim is clear.
guidance: If broken lines crossing over the design are defined as environment, the surface beneath is part of the claimed design; if defined as boundaries, the area within broken lines is not part of the claimed design. If broken lines obscure clear understanding, include separate figure(s) showing the claimed design without the broken lines. Do not use surface shading on unclaimed subject matter shown in broken lines to avoid confusion.

name: Form paragraph 15.50.02 — Description of Broken Lines
description: The following statement must be used to describe the broken lines on the drawing: '-- The broken line showing of [1] is for the purpose of illustrating [2] and forms no part of the claimed design. --' (Insert name of structure and whether showing portions of the article or environment.)
guidance: This statement must be inserted in the specification preceding the claim to clarify the role of broken lines.

name: Objectionable use of broken lines
description: Dotted lines or broken lines used for environmental structure should not cross or intrude upon the representation of the claimed design, since they may obscure the claimed design and render the disclosure indefinite (35 U.S.C. 112).
guidance: When such intrusion occurs, require separate figures or appropriate amendments to clarify the claimed design.

name: Surface treatment — evidentiary effect and amendments
description: A disclosure of surface treatment in a design drawing or photograph will normally be considered prima facie evidence that the inventor considered the surface treatment integral to the claimed design.
guidance: Amendments canceling two-dimensional surface treatment or reducing it to broken lines will be permitted if it is clear applicant had possession of the underlying configuration without the surface treatment. Removal of three-dimensional surface treatment that is integral to the configuration (e.g., beading, grooves, ribs) will introduce prohibited new matter.

name: Examination prerequisites — statutory requirements for design patents
description: In design patent applications ornamentality, novelty, nonobviousness, enablement and definiteness are necessary prerequisites to grant of a patent; inventive novelty/unobviousness resides in ornamental shape/configuration or surface ornamentation applied to an article of manufacture.
guidance: Novelty/nonobviousness determinations generally require searches in pertinent design classes and mechanical classes, and consultation of catalogs, trade journals and available foreign patent databases. If statutory requirements are not met, examiner must set forth basis for rejections in detail in Office action. If claim is patentable but formal matters remain, issue Ex parte Quayle actions (allowability subject to formal corrections).

name: Statutory subject matter under 35 U.S.C. 171 — types of designs
description: The language 'new, original and ornamental design for an article of manufacture' includes at least: (A) a design for an ornament, impression, print, or picture applied to or embodied in an article of manufacture (surface indicia); (B) a design for the shape or configuration of an article of manufacture; and (C) a combination of the first two categories.
guidance: A picture standing alone is not patentable; the distinguishing factor is embodiment of the design in an article of manufacture. Claims to picture/print per se should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 171 as nonstatutory subject matter.

name: Procedures for examining computer-generated icon applications
description: Review the entire disclosure to determine what is claimed and whether the design is embodied in an article of manufacture; review drawings for depiction of a computer screen/monitor/display panel or portion; ensure sufficient number of views and compliance with 37 CFR 1.84; review title and specification for characteristic feature statements.
guidance: Titles like 'computer icon' are inadequate; titles must indicate embodiment (e.g., 'computer screen with an icon'). If drawing does not depict embodiment, reject under 35 U.S.C. 171; if disclosure suggests embodiment, suggest amendments. Indicate all formal objections under 37 CFR rules and upon applicant reply enter amendments and reassess entire record. Withdraw rejection if applicant establishes embodiment by a preponderance of evidence (In re Oetiker).

name: Treatment of type fonts and changeable icons
description: Type fonts historically have been granted design patents and should not be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 171 solely because modern typesetting is computer-generated. Computer-generated icons that change in appearance during viewing may be claimed by showing sequential views; the transitional process/period is not part of the claimed design.
guidance: Include a descriptive statement in the specification describing the transitional nature and that the process/period of transition forms no part of the claimed design; examples of acceptable descriptive statements are provided in the guidelines.

name: Trademark application content and required documents
description: An application must include: application form with applicant identity; representation of trademark; list of goods/services; proof fee paid; technical specifications for collective/guarantee marks; proof of priority fee payment if claimed; transliteration into Latin alphabet if letters other than Latin used.
guidance: Only one trademark per application; classification per Nice Agreement; applicant may divide application; spelling/obvious mistakes may be corrected; regulatory details determined by regulation.

name: Priority right — who and time limits
description: Nationals of Paris Convention/WTO member states or persons domiciled/operating there enjoy priority for filing in Turkey within six months following initial filing for identical goods/services; supporting priority certificate from competent authority is mandatory; failure to use within period forfeits priority.
guidance: Also includes provisions for exhibition-based priority, first-to-file among simultaneous exhibitors, and rules for multiple priority claims (earliest valid priority date governs).

name: Written description support for a claimed species
description: Possession of a claimed species may be shown by disclosure of an actual reduction to practice, drawings, a complete description of structure, physical and/or chemical properties, functional characteristics coupled with a known or disclosed correlation between structure and function, or a combination of such identifying characteristics that distinguish the claimed invention from other materials and lead one of skill in the art to conclude possession.
guidance: Disclosure of any combination of identifying characteristics that distinguish the claimed invention is sufficient. In mature predictable arts, a method-of-making and function disclosure may be enough to support product claims; in emerging or unpredictable arts, more evidence is required. Disclosure of only a method of making and the function may be insufficient for a product claim (except product-by-process where the process actually produced the product). Partial structure without additional characterization may be insufficient. Reduction to practice corroborates conception; if acts in the specification cannot be performed or product not shown to be produced, written description may not be satisfied. (Cited authorities: Eli Lilly; Fiers; Amgen; Burroughs Wellcome.)

name: Written description support for a claimed genus
description: A claimed genus may be supported by description of a representative number of species, reduction to drawings, or disclosure of relevant identifying characteristics (structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics with a structure-function correlation), or combinations thereof, sufficient to show applicant was in possession of the genus.
guidance: A 'representative number of species' must reflect the variation within the genus; where there is substantial variation, a sufficient variety of species must be described. For unpredictable arts, one species will generally not support a broad genus unless the disclosure indicates that the inventor invented species sufficient to constitute the genus or a reasonable structure-function correlation is established (either in the specification or known in the art). Examples where single-species disclosure was insufficient or sufficient are discussed (AbbVie; Enzo; Noelle; Rasmussen; In re Herschler; In re Smythe). If representative species are not disclosed, the genus claim must be rejected for lack of adequate written description.

name: Objective standard for compliance (possession test)
description: Does the description clearly allow persons of ordinary skill in the art to recognize that the inventor had possession of what is now claimed?
guidance: The inquiry asks whether the specification conveys with reasonable clarity to those skilled in the art that, as of the filing date sought, applicant was in possession of the invention as now claimed. Possession can be shown by words, structures, figures, diagrams, formulas, actual reduction to practice, or by showing the invention was 'ready for patenting' (e.g., drawings or structural formulas). (Cited authorities: In re Gosteli; Vas-Cath; Lockwood; Pfaff; Eli Lilly; Amgen.)

name: Each claim limitation must be supported
description: To comply with the written description requirement or to be entitled to an earlier priority/filing date, each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure.
guidance: When an explicit limitation is not present in the written description, it must be shown that a person of ordinary skill would have understood at the filing date that the description requires that limitation. Each claim must include all elements the applicant described as essential.
