If the original disclosure does not provide support for each limitation, or an element described as essential is omitted from the claim, the claim (or priority/benefit claim) must be rejected/denied.

name: Examiner initial burden to challenge written description adequacy
description: The examiner must have a reasonable basis and present evidence or reasoning by a preponderance of evidence explaining why persons skilled in the art would not recognize in the original disclosure the invention defined by the claims.
guidance: The examiner must set forth express findings of fact supporting the lack of written description conclusion. These findings should (A) identify the claim limitation at issue; and (B) establish a prima facie case by providing reasons why a person skilled in the art at the time would not have recognized that the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention in view of the disclosure. A general allegation of 'unpredictability in the art' is not sufficient. When appropriate, examiners should suggest claim amendments that can be supported by the application, mindful of the prohibition on introducing new matter.

name: Amendments/new claims must be supported in original disclosure
description: When filing an amendment, an applicant should show support in the original disclosure for new or amended claims.
guidance: Applicants should specifically point out the support for any amendments to disclosure. Examiners should not reject on 'new matter' grounds when the issue is one of written description (but should follow MPEP §2163.06 for new matter objections). If claim language departs from the disclosure of the application as filed, the examiner should conclude the claimed subject matter is not described in that application, resulting in rejection or denial of benefit/priority as appropriate. (See MPEP §§714.02 and 2163.06.)

name: Situations that typically raise written description issues
description: Written description issues commonly arise in: amendments affecting a claim; reliance on the filing date of a parent application under 35 U.S.C. 120; reliance on foreign priority or provisional filing dates under 35 U.S.C. 119; claims corresponding to a count in an interference; original claims that may be insufficiently described; and indefiniteness re means/step-plus-function limitations.
guidance: Each circumstance has particular considerations (e.g., an amendment to claims must be supported by the original description; claims relying on earlier filing dates must be disclosed in earlier applications in the manner provided by 35 U.S.C. 112(a)). Examples and cases are cited for each typical circumstance.

name: Original claim may lack written description (functional and broad genus claims)
description: An original claim may lack written description support when it defines the invention in functional language specifying a desired result but the disclosure fails to sufficiently identify how the function is performed, or when a broad genus claim is presented but the disclosure only describes a narrow species with no evidence the genus was contemplated.
guidance: Mere appearance of words in the specification or claim does not necessarily satisfy the requirement; the specification must describe the claimed invention so that one skilled in the art can recognize what is claimed. (Cited authorities: Ariad v. Eli Lilly; Enzo Biochem v. Gen-Probe.)

name: Subject matter need not be described in haec verba, but departures indicate lack
description: The subject matter of the claim need not be literally described using the same terms in order to satisfy the written description requirement, but if a claim is amended to include subject matter, limitations, or terminology not present in the application as filed—i.e., involving a departure from, addition to, or deletion from the disclosure—the examiner should conclude the claimed subject matter is not described in that application.
guidance: This conclusion results in rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre-AIA 112, first paragraph) or denial of the benefit of a prior filing/priority date, as appropriate.

name: Means- (or step-) plus-function limitations and corresponding structure
description: A limitation expressed in means- or step-plus-function language shall be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof. If the specification fails to disclose sufficient corresponding structure, materials, or acts that perform the entire claimed function, the limitation is indefinite.
guidance: Such indefiniteness arises because the applicant has failed to particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention as required by 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (or pre-AIA 112, second paragraph). Examiners should assess whether sufficient corresponding structure/acts are present in the specification to support the claimed function.

name: Effect of voluntary stipulation/consent to sanction
description: A practitioner's voluntary stipulation to facts and to the sanction in the state proceeding (including drafting and signing the stipulation with counsel) undermines claims of due process deprivation or grave injustice.
guidance: Courts and the USPTO treat voluntary agreements resolving state discipline as strong evidence that the sanction was freely and properly imposed; this history makes it difficult for the practitioner to show Selling exceptions.

name: First-Action Allowance
description: A small fraction of applications are allowed on first action - a quality signal for both drafter and case.
guidance: Aim for clean specifications and well-supported claims to maximize this likelihood, even though it remains uncommon (under 10% in most art units). First-action allowance is an aspirational quality target but will vary by art unit.

name: Average Number of Office Actions
description: The mean number of office actions to allowance varies by art unit (typically 1.5 to 3).
guidance: Drafting choices that reduce this number (clearer claims, narrower initial claim scope) save prosecution costs but may sacrifice claim breadth. Track this metric to estimate prosecution cost and to evaluate drafting tradeoffs.

name: Claim Length
description: Empirical studies find that shorter independent claims are correlated with broader scope — and with higher rates of being cited and litigated. The mean independent claim length is around 100–130 words.
guidance: Aim for the lower end of claim-word counts without sacrificing definiteness. Long independent claims can signal narrower scope or drafting problems; balance brevity with clarity/definiteness.

name: Claim-Word Count vs. Specification-Word Count Ratio
description: Strong patents tend to have long specifications supporting short claims. A spec-to-independent-claim ratio above 100:1 is a quality signal.
guidance: A high spec:claim ratio indicates robust support; the opposite (long claims, short spec) often reflects narrow drafting under spec constraints and can hurt patent strength. Ensure the specification provides adequate support for claim breadth.

name: Colorable constitutional challenge requires identification of property-rights or retroactivity concerns
description: To press a constitutional challenge to the PTO's denial of IPR institution, petitioners must identify the kind of property rights or retroactivity concerns that might give rise to a colorable constitutional claim.
guidance: Absent an identified property-right or retroactivity problem, a petitioner cannot establish the constitutional basis necessary to show a clear and indisputable right to relief. The court here held petitioners failed to identify such rights/concerns, and for that reason the constitutional argument did not support mandamus.

name: Patent as prima facie evidence (patentee performed inventive act / inventorship)
description: The patent is prima facie evidence that the patentee or his assignor performed the inventive act resulting in the alleged invention.
guidance: To overthrow this evidence the defendant must prove by conclusive testimony that some specific person other than the alleged inventor conceived the invention, that the alleged inventor obtained knowledge of it, and procured a patent falsely claiming it. Evidence such as admissions, declarations of others uncontradicted by the patentee, company records, or proof of immediate adoption after learning can be used to show nonperformance by the patentee.

name: Proof required to show patentee did not perform the inventive act
description: To rebut the presumption that the patentee performed the inventive act, the defendant must prove by conclusive testimony that (1) some specific person other than the alleged inventor conceived the invention, (2) the alleged inventor obtained knowledge of that invention, and (3) the alleged inventor procured a patent falsely claiming it as his own.
guidance: Evidence admissible includes testimony of the true inventor, contemporaneous descriptions/models, admissions by the patentee, declarations of others uncontradicted by the patentee, company records, and proof of immediate adoption after learning. No proof of actual bad faith is necessary; piracy in fact suffices.

name: Preliminary examination trigger conditions
description: The Registrar will proceed to conduct a preliminary examination on your application when the filing fee is paid and claims are submitted within the specified time periods.
guidance: The page notes specific time limits for payment and claims (see separate metrics). Preliminary examination is a formal check before substantive search/examination.

name: Misspelled words amendable ex‑officio
description: Obvious misspellings in violation of Korean grammar may be corrected ex‑officio (example: 'Semiconducter' → 'Semiconductor').
guidance: Typical editorial misspellings in the description or claims; must be obviously incorrect and corrected to the intended term.

name: Citations to deleted claims — correcting antecedent references
description: Where a deleted claim is cited and only one antecedent claim exists, or where deleted claims are cited among remaining claims, antecedent references should be adjusted ex‑officio to point to surviving antecedent claims (examples provided).
guidance: Change citation targets so antecedent references remain valid and clear; only where the correct antecedent is obvious.

name: Dependent claim subject matter mismatch — convert form to match antecedent
description: If a dependent claim cites a claim of a different category (e.g., method dependent on apparatus), the dependent claim may be reworded ex‑officio to match the citing claim type (example given: change 'A method according to claim 1' to 'An apparatus according to claim 1').
guidance: Only when the intended subject‑matter is evident from the disclosure.

name: Combining dependent claim into cited claim (and deleting duplicates)
description: If a dependent claim is combined into the cited claim (e.g., Claim 1 becomes 'including A and B') the original dependent claim should be deleted ex‑officio to avoid duplication.
guidance: Ensure deletions are obvious housekeeping and do not alter claim scope beyond correcting redundancy.

name: Obvious wrong claim citation amendable ex‑officio
description: If it's obvious that a claim cites the wrong antecedent claim, the citation may be corrected to the correct antecedent (examples provided).
guidance: Correction only when the intended antecedent is unambiguous from the file.

name: Principle: do not change claim scope by ex‑officio amendment
description: Ex‑officio amendment must not change the scope of the claims; if there is any possibility that claim terms may be construed to a different meaning, ex‑officio amendment should not be made.
guidance: Be conservative — even slight ambiguity that may affect claim construction prohibits ex‑officio amendment.

name: Applicant intention must be clear principle
description: Even if an obvious error is apparent, if the applicant's intention is not clearly understood from the specification and written arguments, ex‑officio amendment is not permitted.
guidance: Example: where a claim cites only deleted claims and multiple antecedent claims exist and it's not obvious which was intended, do not amend ex‑officio.

name: Replacing main drawing by ex‑officio amendment
description: Where the applicant did not or wrongly establish a main drawing that explains the claimed invention, the examiner can replace the main drawing ex‑officio by another that better explains the subject matter of the claimed invention.
guidance: Replacement must not introduce new technical matter; use to improve clarity of original disclosure when a better existing drawing in the file is available.

name: Preparation required of examiner before interview
description: Examiner shall read the claimed invention, review patentability requirements and specification deficiencies with preparation comparable to substantive examination, and prepare documents such as prior art search results, minutes of interview, and additional papers.
guidance: State results of preview of grounds for rejection in the minutes to guide discussion during interview.

name: Presumption of nexus and burden shift
description: “then a nexus is presumed and the burden shifts to the party asserting obviousness to present evidence to rebut the presumed nexus.”  Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp. v. Philip Morris Inc., 229 F.3d 1120, 1130 (Fed. Cir. 2000).
guidance: If evidence of objective indicia is shown to be coextensive/commensurate in scope with the claimed invention, a presumption of nexus arises and the challenger must rebut it with evidence showing lack of nexus or that the indicia are attributable to something else.

name: Coextensiveness / commensurate-in-scope requirement
description: Coextensive “mean[s] that the product is the invention disclosed and claimed. . . . A product is essentially the claimed invention when, for example, the unclaimed features amount to nothing more than additional insignificant features.”  Campbell Soup Co. v. Gamon Plus, Inc., 10 F.4th 1268, 1276–77 (Fed. Cir. 2021).
guidance: Objective-indicia evidence (e.g., a commercial product or clinical candidate) must be essentially the claimed invention — unclaimed differences must be insignificant — or else the evidence is not commensurate in scope and cannot support a presumption of nexus.

name: Objective indicia categories to consider
description: Patent Owner relies on objective evidence of “(1) long-felt need for an effective gene therapy for hemophilia B and failure of others; (2) industry praise and copying; and (3) unexpectedly superior efficacy”.
guidance: When evaluating secondary considerations, identify which indicia are asserted (e.g., long‑felt need, praise/copying, unexpected results) and assess whether each is supported and tied to the claimed invention.

name: Nexus requirement tying objective indicia to what is claimed and novel
description: Where objective indicia “result[ ] from something other than what is both claimed and novel in the claim, there is no nexus to the merits of the claimed invention.” (citing Merck & Cie v. Gnosis S.P.A., 808 F.3d 829, 837 (Fed. Cir. 2015)).
guidance: Objective evidence directed to a feature that was already in the prior art (not the claimed novelty) cannot establish a nexus supporting non‑obviousness. The evidence must be tied to the novel features of the claims.

name: Weighing objective indicia in context of the claimed invention as a whole
description: “Ultimately, the fact finder must weigh the [objective indicia] evidence presented in the context of whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious to a skilled artisan.”  (citing Lectrosonics, Inc. v. Zaxcom, Inc., IPR2018-01129, Paper 33 at 33 (PTAB Jan. 24, 2020) (precedential)).
guidance: Secondary considerations are not assessed in isolation; they are considered together with the Graham factors and the claimed invention as a whole to determine obviousness.

name: Industry praise and copying must be commensurate and specific
description: Petitioner notes Patent Owner does not identify any specific evidence of copying beyond the adoption of the “Padua” designation; court agrees praise in the relied references was primarily directed to FIX‑R338L (a prior‑art component) and not commensurate with the claim.
guidance: Evidence of praise or copying should specifically tie adoption/praise to the claimed invention as a whole; mere terminology adoption or praise for a component known in the prior art is insufficient to establish nexus.

name: Long‑felt need / failure of others must relate to claimed invention
description: Patent Owner asserts Factor IX Padua was a “game‑changer” and industry adoption (including ongoing clinical trials) is evidence of satisfying the long‑felt need; Board found such evidence may be directed at the variant rather than the claimed combination and thus not commensurate with claim 1.
guidance: Evidence that a need existed and was unmet can support non‑obviousness only if the evidence is linked to the claimed invention (not merely to an element that was already known).

name: Unexpected results — need for proper comparative baseline and comparable studies
description: Patent Owner asserts a 9‑fold increased activity of FIX‑R338L compared to wild‑type FIX was surprising relative to prior art showing 2–6 fold increases; Board found comparisons unpersuasive because results came from different types of studies (recombinant vs gene therapy) and lacked head‑to‑head comparison.
guidance: To support unexpected results, show a convincing, head‑to‑head comparison to the closest prior art using comparable methods/data; differences in study types (in vitro vs in vivo) can undermine claimed unexpectedness.

name: Preponderance of the evidence standard for petitioner in IPR obviousness
description: We find that Petitioner has shown by a preponderance of the evidence that the combinations ... teach the limitations of claim 1 ... and that a person of ordinary skill would have been motivated to combine the references ... with a reasonable expectation of success.
guidance: The challenger must prove obviousness by a preponderance of the evidence: show that prior art teaches claim limitations and that motivation and reasonable expectation to combine existed.

name: Claim construction influences disclosure and obviousness analysis
description: Under the adopted construction, “treating” a coagulopathy includes partial alleviation of symptoms, for any duration of therapeutic efficacy; thus Manno’s report of ten weeks without bleeding counted as “treating.”
guidance: How terms are construed can determine whether prior art satisfies claim limitations — adopt and apply constructions explicitly in the obviousness inquiry.

name: Evidence of clinical adoption must be commensurate with claim scope (example: capsid/promoter breadth)
description: Petitioner argued AMT‑061 cannot provide evidence of objective indicia because it is not coextensive with the challenged claims (AMT‑061 uses a specific AAV5 capsid while the claims cover use of any AAV capsid), and claims permit many changes (promoters, capsids, FIX variants).
guidance: When claims are broad (e.g., any capsid, many promoters, wide sequence identity ranges), evidence limited to a single implementation (one capsid, one promoter) may not be commensurate in scope and thus insufficient to establish nexus.

name: Sufficiency of evidence and weight of a weak nexus
description: In summary, Patent Owner does not meet its burden to show a presumption of nexus or show a nexus ... Weighing the evidence and arguments presented, we determine that even if there is some nexus, it is weak.
guidance: Even when some connection exists between evidence and the claimed invention, the Board weighs the strength of the nexus; a weak or attenuated nexus will not overcome a showing of obviousness.

name: Filing-date determination and sufficiency of Fedwire confirmation under 35 U.S.C. §312(a) and 37 C.F.R. §42.103(a)
description: Whether Fedwire confirmation of payment constitutes sufficient evidence of payment for establishing a petition filing date was a central question in Toshiba America (IPR2021-00330) and the subject of POP review.
guidance: Panels may require evidence that a wire transfer was 'accepted by the Treasury' or that the payment was 'immediate, final and irrevocable.' General descriptions of Fedwire functionality may be insufficient; specific evidence about the petitioner's wire transfer is persuasive. Compliance with USPTO published instructions for wire transfers and proof of initiation on the claimed date can support an earlier filing date. Pre-established deposit accounts with the USPTO can avoid receipt-timing issues tied to wire transfers.

name: Multiple embodiments permitted only if single inventive concept / patentably indistinct
description: Multiple embodiments of a single inventive concept may be included in the same design application only if they are patentably indistinct. Embodiments that are patentably distinct from one another do not constitute a single inventive concept and thus may not be included in the same design application.
guidance: Cite: In re Rubinfield, In re Platner. Examiner should determine whether embodiments are patentably indistinct before retaining them in one application. If retained, disclosure of plural embodiments does not justify more than a single claim; the claim must be in formal terms (see MPEP §1503.01 III).

name: Combination vs subcombination / change in scope test
description: A design claim covers the entire design as a whole and does not extend to any individual part or portion thereof; embodiments directed to a design as a whole (combination) and individual parts (subcombinations) may not be included in a single application if the appearances are patentably distinct. Designs of different scope may be included only if they are patentably indistinct.
guidance: The difference in scope must be minor and not a patentable distinction; the scope differences must be obvious over one another under 35 U.S.C. 103 without the aid of analogous prior art. If the difference in scope impacts the overall appearance so as to distinguish designs, separate claims (and thus separate applications) are necessary.

name: Pre‑AIA oath/declaration extra contents and foreign priority disclosure (pre‑AIA 37 CFR 1.63(b)(2)/(c)(2))
description: Pre‑AIA oaths/declarations had to state that the person reviewed and understands the application contents and acknowledged duty to disclose (37 CFR 1.63(b)(2)/(b)(3)). They also had to recite all foreign applications for which priority is claimed, including application number, country, and filing date.
guidance: For pre‑AIA filings, include full foreign priority information unless supplied on an ADS. See MPEP §602.03 for defective oaths/declarations guidance.

name: Overlapping, Approaching, and Similar Ranges
description: When claimed ranges overlap or lie inside ranges disclosed by the prior art, a prima facie case of obviousness exists; ranges that are merely close (approaching) can also support a prima facie case.
guidance: Cited cases: In re Wertheim; In re Woodruff; In re Geisler; In re Bergen. Overlapping endpoints can be sufficient, and non-overlapping but close numerical differences may be insufficient to show patentability absent criticality or unexpected results (see Titanium Metals Corp. of America v. Banner; In re Aller; In re Becket; In re Dreyfus). A single claimed value within a prior art 'range' disclosed across multiple references can still be presumed obvious (Iron Grip Barbell Co. v. USA Sports). Consider whether prior art range is so broad as to be analogous to a genus (see In re Baird). See also MPEP § 2144.08 for broad range discussion.

name: Articulated Rationale Required for Routine Optimization Rejections
description: To properly support a rejection based on routine optimization, the examiner must make factual findings and present the underpinning reasoning, explaining why it would have been routine to arrive at the claimed invention and why a person of ordinary skill would have had a reasonable expectation of success.
guidance: Cases: In re Stepan; In re Van Os; Arendi S.A.R.L. v. Apple. After KSR, 'obvious to try' can be a valid rationale when there is a design need/market demand and a finite number of predictable solutions. References to 'common sense' cannot substitute for reasoned analysis without articulated rationale and evidentiary support.

name: Rebuttal — Showing That the Prior Art Teaches Away
description: A prima facie case of obviousness may be rebutted by showing that the prior art, in any material respect, teaches away from the claimed invention.
guidance: Cases: U.S. v. Adams; Depuy Spine v. Medtronic; Allergan v. Sandoz. Teaching away is especially strong where prior art undermines the reason for combining elements. Demonstrating teaching away requires showing the prior art would have discouraged one of ordinary skill from the claimed approach (see In re Geisler for discussion of when a reference does not teach away). See MPEP § 2145 X.D. for further discussion.

name: Rebuttal — Very Broad Prior Art Range May Weigh Against Obviousness
description: If the prior art discloses a very broad range that encompasses members with dissimilar characteristics, that disclosure may not invite optimization and can weigh against maintaining an obviousness rejection.
guidance: Case: Genetics Inst. v. Novartis (disclosure of 68,000 protein variants where claimed truncated proteins vary enormously in structure). See MPEP §§ 2131.02, 2131.03, and 2144.08 for additional discussion.

name: Obviousness of Species When Prior Art Teaches Genus — Examination Guidance
description: When a single prior art reference discloses a genus encompassing the claimed species but not the particular species, Office personnel should search for additional prior art and, if none is found, evaluate factors to determine whether a single-reference 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection is appropriate.
guidance: Office should attempt to find additional prior art to show that the differences between the primary reference and the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious. If additional prior art is not found, consider whether the claimed species or subgenus would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill at the relevant time (see further subsections for factors). This guidance applies regardless of AIA or pre-AIA timing rules (see header note).

name: 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1) grace-period exception
description: A disclosure made one year or less before the effective filing date of a claimed invention shall not be prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) if: (1) the disclosure was made by the inventor or joint inventor or by another who obtained the subject matter disclosed directly or indirectly from the inventor or a joint inventor; or (2) the subject matter disclosed had, before such disclosure, been publicly disclosed by the inventor or a joint inventor or by another who obtained the subject matter disclosed directly or indirectly from the inventor or a joint inventor.
guidance: The Office treats the term 'disclosure' broadly to encompass the documents and activities enumerated in 35 U.S.C. 102(a) (patented, printed publication, public use, on sale, otherwise available to the public). See MPEP § 2153 et seq. for additional guidance.

name: 37 CFR 1.130(b) – affidavit/declaration of prior public disclosure
description: When any claim is rejected, an applicant or patent owner may submit an affidavit or declaration to disqualify a disclosure as prior art by establishing that the subject matter disclosed had, before such disclosure was made or before such subject matter was effectively filed, been publicly disclosed by the inventor or a joint inventor or another who obtained the subject matter disclosed directly or indirectly from the inventor or a joint inventor.
guidance: The affidavit/declaration must identify the subject matter publicly disclosed and provide the date such subject matter was publicly disclosed. If the prior disclosure was in a printed publication, a copy must accompany the affidavit (37 CFR 1.130(b)(1)). If not in a printed publication, the affidavit must describe the subject matter with sufficient detail and particularity to determine what was publicly disclosed (37 CFR 1.130(b)(2)).

name: Time limitation: 37 CFR 1.130(c) – one-year grace period
description: The provisions of 37 CFR 1.130 are not available if the rejection is based upon a disclosure made more than one year before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
guidance: A disclosure made more than one year before the effective filing date is prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) and cannot be excepted under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1). Note: 1.130 may still be relevant for certain 102(a)(2) situations described at MPEP § 2155.06.

name: Scope of applications/patents to which 37 CFR 1.130 applies
description: The provisions apply to any application for patent, and to any patent issuing thereon, that contains (or contained) a claim with an effective filing date on or after March 16, 2013; or which contains a specific reference under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, 365(c), or 386(c) to any patent or application that contains (or contained) such a claim.
guidance: In short, 1.130 applies to AIA (first‑inventor‑to‑file) applications as defined in the MPEP and 35 U.S.C. 100 (note).

name: 37 CFR 1.130 not available if disclosure >1 year before effective filing date
description: If the rejection is based upon a disclosure made more than one year before the effective filing date of the claimed invention, 37 CFR 1.130 cannot be used to except that disclosure under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1).
guidance: This rule is restated multiple times and cross‑references MPEP § 2152.01 for determining effective filing date.

name: Evaluation criteria for 37 CFR 1.130(b) submissions (identifying prior public disclosure)
description: For 1.130(b), the affidavit or declaration must identify the subject matter publicly disclosed and the date of public disclosure; if the prior disclosure was a printed publication a copy must be provided, otherwise the submission must describe the subject matter with sufficient detail and particularity to determine what was publicly disclosed on that date.
guidance: Office personnel will assess whether the description and evidence are sufficiently specific and probative to show the claimed subject matter was publicly disclosed by the inventor/joint inventor prior to the intervening disclosure.

name: Form paragraph use and required content when 1.130 is effective
description: Use form paragraph 7.67.aia when an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.130 is sufficient to overcome the rejection; the paragraph includes brackets to identify whether affidavit or declaration, subsection (a) or (b), filing date, affected claims, the specific reference disqualified, and an explanation of how the submission provides evidence of reliance on an exception in 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1) or (2).
guidance: Examiner notes specify that form paragraph 7.67.aia should be used only for applications filed on or after March 16, 2013, examined under AIA 102/103, and must be preceded by form paragraph 7.03.aia.

name: Invoking 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) (common ownership / joint research agreement) – statement requirement
description: To except subject matter in a reference under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C), an applicant must provide a proper statement indicating common ownership or obligation to assign not later than the effective filing date of the claimed invention, or comply with CREATE Act / joint research agreement requirements.
guidance: If the applicant fails to provide required statements or required specification amendments (e.g., naming parties to the joint research agreement), the attempt to invoke 102(b)(2)(C) is ineffective and form paragraph 7.20.05.aia should be used to inform applicant what is missing. The applicant may alternatively rely on 37 CFR 1.130(a) or 1.130(b) showings.

name: De novo claim construction when no fact findings
description: Claim construction should be reviewed de novo where there are no fact findings implicated (citing Imes, Teva, Markman, Phillips).
guidance: Panel's failure to review claim construction de novo is reversible error; where nothing in the case implicates deference to fact findings, the court must independently determine ordinary meaning and scope of claim terms.

name: Plain words of the claims and prosecution interpretation control
description: The plain language of the claims, together with the inventor's interpretation during prosecution, must be given effect and cannot be disregarded.
guidance: Terms like “dosage” (here argued to mean a specified amount for administration) are limiting when specification, examples, tables, and prosecution statements show a specific meaning; examiner/court cannot treat such terms as non-limiting contrary to prosecution history.

name: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) must align with PHOSITA
description: The BRI applied by the PTO/Board must be consistent with how a person having ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA) would understand the claim terms (In re Cortright).
guidance: Claim constructions that conflict with PHOSITA testimony or analogous patents are improper; BRI cannot be divorced from skilled-worker evidence on meaning.

name: Structural limitations (e.g., 'intermixture') are substantive
description: Structural recitations such as “intermixture of lipids from different sources” are structural limitations that can make a claimed composition a patentable 'composition of matter' rather than a product of nature.
guidance: Structural character (not mere discovery of a natural phenomenon) supports patent eligibility (citing Garnero, Gulack). The existence of an intermixture requirement precludes treating the claim as simply a natural product.

name: Prosecution disclaimer binds claim scope
description: Prosecution statements or disclaimers (e.g., disclaiming a 'single source') are binding and must be considered when construing claims and assessing novelty/eligibility.
guidance: Panel/Board must not ignore undisputed prosecution disclaimers; disclaimer that claims are not single-source impacts both §101 and §102 analyses.

name: Anticipation requires the reference to necessarily practice the claimed invention
description: A reference anticipates only if it necessarily discloses the claimed subject matter — it must function as claimed, not merely possibly or arguably (distinguishing §102 from §103 analyses).
guidance: References that 'may' but do not necessarily disclose a limitation (e.g., specific dosages, casings providing controlled delivery, intermixture arranged as claimed) cannot be used to show anticipation; the Board may not 'fill in' missing limitations.

name: Board/examiner may not fill in missing claim limitations
description: The PTAB or examiner cannot supply missing claim elements or 'optimize' a prior-art reference to meet claim limitations (Nidec, Lindemann).
guidance: Decisions that infer or invent unstated limitations in prior art to reach anticipation are improper; part-to-part relationships and specific arrangements must be present in the reference itself.

name: §101 analysis is separate from §§102/103
description: The §101 patent-eligibility inquiry is distinct from novelty and obviousness analyses; one must not import §102/§103 reasoning wholesale into §101 (Mayo, Alice, Rapid, Classen).
guidance: If claim language as a whole is not directed to an ineligible concept, the §101 inquiry ends; applying anticipation/novelty reasoning to eligibility is reversible error.

name: §101 step one: determine whether claim is directed to a patent-ineligible concept
description: At step one, the court asks whether the claim is directed to an ineligible concept (laws of nature, natural products, abstract ideas); if not, eligibility is satisfied.
guidance: Features not found in nature (e.g., dosage limitations, casings providing controlled delivery, intermixtures) can take a claim out of the realm of natural products at step one—no further 'inventive concept' analysis is needed.

name: §101 step two: 'inventive concept' as 'significantly more' when required
description: If step one points to a patent-ineligible concept, step two asks whether the claimed elements, individually or as an ordered combination, add an 'inventive concept' sufficient to transform the claim into patent-eligible subject matter (Mayo/Alice).
guidance: Courts must consider the claims 'on the whole' (Diehr, Rapid) and evaluate whether limitations like controlled dosage, controlled delivery casings, and specified intermixtures confer significantly more than a natural law/product.

name: Functional printed matter or instructions should not be conflated with natural products
description: Functional or instructional aspects combined with an alleged natural product should not automatically cause the claim to be characterized as a natural product.
guidance: When claims include functional structure (e.g., casings that control delivery) those functional structures may contribute to eligibility rather than render the claim ineligible as a mere natural product.

name: Ordinary meaning of claim terms determined de novo in temporal context
description: The ordinary meaning of claim terms should be determined as a matter of law, de novo, and in the temporal context of the application (Markman, Phillips, Teva).
guidance: Courts must interpret terms like 'lipid', 'source', and 'dosage' according to their plain and contextual meaning at the time of filing, not by later-evolved or strained interpretations.

name: Part-to-part arrangement and 'arranged as in the claim' requirement
description: A prior-art reference must disclose the part-to-part relationships and arrangement 'as in the claim' to anticipate; mere disclosure of components is insufficient (Nidec, Lindemann).
guidance: References that list components or ranges but do not teach the claimed intermixture, dosage arrangement, or casing-delivery relationship cannot be held to anticipate.

name: Consideration of scientific evidence and PHOSITA testimony for structural/functional differences
description: Scientific publications and PHOSITA declarations showing that extraction, mixing, or encapsulation materially change physical/chemical properties are relevant to novelty and eligibility and must be considered.
guidance: Empirical evidence that manipulated mixtures have properties not found in nature supports non-natural character of claimed compositions and undercuts conclusions that claims are indistinguishable from natural products.

name: Claims must be considered 'as a whole' for eligibility and cannot be dissected
description: The eligibility inquiry requires considering the claimed combination in its entirety rather than excising or ignoring limitations.
guidance: Excising limitations such as 'providing controlled delivery' or 'dosage' from the analysis (i.e., 'mutilating the claims') is improper and may render the analysis legally deficient (Gulack, Diehr).

name: Prosecution and examiner admissions about lack of natural counterpart are highly relevant
description: Admissions in the prosecution record or by the examiner that there is no naturally occurring counterpart to claimed combinations are significant evidence of structural distinction from natural products (Myriad, Chakrabarty).
guidance: Such admissions should weigh against treating the claim as directed to a natural product; they support eligibility if the claimed combination has no natural counterpart.

name: Prior art must enable claimed limitations (e.g., 'dosage') to anticipate
description: Enablement in the prior art is required for anticipation; a reference’s mere disclosure of ranges or non-specific data does not necessarily enable specific dosage limitations.
guidance: A reference that does not teach how to achieve the claimed dosage for relevant populations or contexts cannot be relied upon to anticipate—enablement and functional disclosure matter (Perricone, Elsner).

name: Evidence of post-filing scientific publications and expert declarations can corroborate inventive concept and public-health importance
description: Scientific studies and expert declarations showing that claimed formulations solve long-felt problems, alter properties, or have large public-health benefits are relevant to demonstrating the significance and nonobviousness/importance of an invention.
guidance: While not dispositive of eligibility, substantial corroborating scientific evidence and PHOSITA testimony should be weighed in assessing whether claimed subject matter adds 'significantly more' or is structurally distinct from natural products.

name: Claims reciting dosage, controlled delivery, and specified ratios can confer patent-eligibility or inventive concept
description: A claim that combines formulation, explicit dosage limitations, casings that provide controlled delivery, and specified intermixture ratios may be sufficiently distinct from natural products and confer eligibility or an inventive concept.
guidance: Courts should recognize combinations of structural and functional limitations (e.g., dosage + controlled delivery + intermixture) as potentially patent-eligible without collapsing the analysis into novelty or obviousness reexamination.

name: Advantageous effects compared to prior art
description: If an effect achieved by matters defining a claimed invention is advantageous in comparison with an effect of a prior art reference, it is taken into consideration as a fact to affirmatively support its inventive step.
guidance: Under Article 29(2), if the claimed invention could have been easily made from the prior art, a patent may not be granted; however, when an advantageous effect compared to the prior art reference is so remarkable that it could not have been foreseen by a person skilled in the art from the state of the art, the inventive step may not be denied (Supreme Court Decision cited). If an invention is made by collecting/improving publicly known/practiced arts, inventive step is generally not recognized except where it is difficult to collate the arts and achieve a new advantageous effect more than expected, or where a new technical method is added (Supreme Court Decision cited).

name: Numerical limitation (range) inventive-step criteria
description: An invention that defines indispensible elements by specific numerical values is generally not inventive if the numerical range is the result of routine optimization, but may be inventive if the claimed numerical range yields a more advantageous effect across the whole limited range than prior art.
guidance: Critical significance of a numerical range requires: (1) a remarkable change in effect across the boundary of the numerical limitation, and (2) satisfaction of conditions: (a) technical meaning of the numerical limitation described in the specification, and (b) embodiments or supplemental materials proving the upper and lower limits are critical. Generally, experimental results objectively confirming criticality across the entire range are required. Examples: a 12x screw-rotation limitation with no technical explanation is meaningless; a 0.01-0.7% iron-oxide range without remarkable effect is not inventive; conversely, ranges that greatly improve quality/economic efficiency may be inventive (Supreme Court Decision cited).

name: Parameter invention inventive-step criteria
description: A parameter invention (creating a non-standard parameter, mathematically parameterizing correlations between parameters, and using it as an essential claim element) should have its inventive step determined only after the subject matter is defined from the description, drawings, and common knowledge; the functions/characteristics caused by the parameter must be considered.
guidance: Examiner should first consider whether introducing the parameter has technical meaning. If the parameter is merely a different expression or confirms intrinsic features and the cause-effect relation to effect is weak, inventive step is denied. If treated as a numerical limitation, apply numerical-limitation criteria. Even where conversion/difficulty complicates comparison to prior art, the examiner may raise concrete grounds of reasonable doubt and propose solutions; if parameter is standard/common, the special parameter criteria do not apply. Reasonable doubt cases include: conversion based on different definitions/measurement methods, evaluating prior-art parameters under the applicant's measurement method making them similar, or embodiments in the description identical to prior art. If conversion makes claimed invention similar/identical to prior art, novelty and inventive step are not recognized.

name: Product-by-process claim inventive-step determination
description: For product claims described by their manufacturing process, the claim should be construed to define the product (structure/properties) obtained by the process; novelty and inventive step are determined by comparing the product so defined with publicly known products.
guidance: If the manufacturing process affects the structure or properties of the product, inventive step is determined for the product having those structure/properties. If the process only affects manufacturing efficiency or yield (not the product's structure/properties), the process limitations should not be considered and inventive step is determined by the final product itself. Where the structure/properties cannot be understood from the process alone, the examiner shall define the scope in light of the whole specification (embodiments, experimental data, drawings) and, if necessary, issue a rejection stating lack of inventive step over prior art that discloses the same/similar product. If prior art discloses a similar manufacturing process, it can be inferred that the same/similar product results and the examiner should define the product scope accordingly and issue rejection. Examples: JACEOSIDIN extraction steps (product interpreted as JACEOSIDIN itself); belt coupling device where process affects structure and thus must be compared as product with that structure; polarizing film example where process yields specific product properties and should be considered.

name: Combination invention inventive-step criteria
description: A combination invention (gathering technical features disclosed in prior art as a whole to solve a technical problem) must be considered as a whole; inventive step should not be negated merely because each claimed element is known individually. Determination relies on the technical idea and structural combination of elements and the unique effect of the whole.
guidance: When assessing combination inventions, consider difficulty in forming the structurally combined elements as a whole (problem-solution approach) rather than assessing isolated elements. Examiner may combine more than two prior-art references, but only where a person skilled in the art could easily combine them at the filing date. The examiner should consider whether prior art gives motivation/suggestion to combine (explicit teaching, inherent from the technical problem, or part of common general knowledge). Combining well-known technology with another is normally obvious, except where the combination yields an advantageous (synergistic) effect. If the claimed combination yields only juxtaposition/aggregation without special difficulty or synergistic effect, inventive step may be denied. Care: needing many prior-art references to make the combination may indicate hindsight or an invalid rejection. Examples include web game separate-download feature and counting securities via image sensor (combination of two prior references deemed obvious).

name: Nature and scope of the patent monopoly determined by legal interpretation of the letters-patent
description: The character and scope of a patent privilege is determined by the construction given to the letters-patent; the patented invention is the art or instrument which the patent really describes and claims according to its true legal interpretation, not necessarily what the inventor thought he discovered.
guidance: All rights of the patentee and the public's rights depend on the meaning which the law attaches to the language of the patent; interpreting letters-patent imposes vast responsibility on the tribunal and demands industrial skill and knowledge.

name: Interpretation of letters-patent is a matter of law for the court
description: Whether claims are valid or invalid, whether they embrace a given invention, and what the actual nature of the invention is are questions of law for the court to be decided upon inspection of the instrument itself.
guidance: Evidence may be received to explain technical terms or facts necessary to comprehend the language, but such extraneous evidence cannot directly control the legal construction. The court must declare the meaning; the jury may decide factual questions (e.g., sufficiency of the specification as enabling).

name: General rule: patents to be liberally construed in favor of the inventor
description: The fundamental rule requires that a patent and each of its parts be liberally interpreted in favor of the patentee; patents are property and every presumption of law supports their validity.
guidance: Doubtful points should be resolved so as to support the patentee's claims; the specification should be read in a liberal spirit and, if possible, construed to sustain the patent rather than defeat it.

name: Liberal construction consists in giving words legitimate meanings to reflect the true invention
description: A liberal construction interprets terms so as to protect the actual invention: give each word or phrase one of its legitimate meanings that makes the whole claim or description correspond most accurately with the essential characteristics of the true invention.
guidance: This approach recognizes that claims and descriptions are often unskilfully drawn; courts should apply meanings that effectuate the intention of the parties and sustain the patent where consistent with the specification and drawings.

name: Claims construed by reference to the specification, drawings, and state of the art
description: A claim is to be construed liberally by the specifications, drawings, and state of the art to determine its true scope.
guidance: If possible, claims should be construed to sustain all that the patentee has invented; construction should be such as persons skilled in the art would give, using specification and drawings to interpret ambiguous claim language.

name: Patent language must be applied as persons skilled in the art would understand it
description: In construing patents the court should interpret the instrument as persons skilled in the art would, applying its words to its subject-matter.
guidance: Technical meaning and the inventor's intended use are relevant; courts should remember that specification and claims are often unskilfully drafted and should interpret them in light of the art so as to effectuate the invention rather than defeat it.

name: Scope Annex (Rule 45bis.7(e)) — contents and citation practice
description: Formally, the explanations under Rule 45bis.7(e) are part of the SISR (Form PCT/SISA/501) and are contained in an annex called the 'Scope Annex'. The Scope Annex will concentrate on the documents cited in the SISR, but in some circumstances it might be appropriate to raise objections based on documents cited in the ISR.
guidance: If a document cited in the ISR can be used as a Y document for inventive step for some dependent claims in the Scope Annex, it may be necessary to cite it again in the SISR as a Y document for those claims and provide argumentation in the Scope Annex. The examiner may choose to base objections only on documents cited in the ISR if expedient. If objections correspond to those raised in the WO-ISA from the main ISA, a mere reference to the WO-ISA objections will suffice. Examiners should generally avoid an explicit re‑evaluation or negative comment on reasoning given in the WO-ISA, keeping in mind differences in national law.

name: Rule 20.6 sheets — missing parts or elements can be furnished later
description: If parts of the application or an entire element (e.g., all description or all claims) were omitted, they may be furnished later without affecting the international filing date provided the missing parts were completely contained in the priority document and subject to Rules 4.18 and 20.6(a).
guidance: The examiner checks whether the receiving Office's assessment of the 'completely contained' criterion was correct. See GL/PCT‑EPO H‑II for impact on the IPER.

name: Consequences of a restriction of the search for Chapter II examination
description: If the search covered only some claims or part of claims (restriction of search or declaration that no search is possible), only the subject‑matter which has been searched (as indicated in the ISR/WO‑ISA) can be the object of the international preliminary examination. It should always be made clear which claims have been examined.
guidance: After a restriction or declaration of no search, the applicant’s reply may challenge the ISA’s findings, but the IPEA has no responsibility for actions taken by the ISA and there is no provision in the PCT for an IPEA review or appeal against such an ISA decision. Written arguments about completeness of the search are not to be treated as communication with the IPEA unless the reply contains a complaint against the findings at the search stage when the EPO acted as ISA (see GL/PCT‑EPO C‑IX, 4).

name: Compact prosecution / Complete first Office action
description: Examiners should state all reasons and bases for rejecting claims in the first Office action; deficiencies should be explained clearly, particularly when they serve as a basis for a rejection.
guidance: Whenever practicable, examiners should indicate how rejections may be overcome and how problems may be resolved. Where a rejection not based on prior art is proper (lack of adequate written description, enablement, or utility, etc.) such rejection should be stated with a full development of the reasons rather than by a mere conclusion. Failure to follow this approach can lead to unnecessary delays in prosecution.

name: Determine what invention is sought
description: Prior to focusing on statutory requirements, examiners must determine what precisely the inventor or joint inventor has invented and is seeking to patent, and how the claims relate to and define that invention.
guidance: Examiners will review the complete specification, including the detailed description, any specific embodiments disclosed, the claims, and any specific, substantial, and credible utilities. After understanding the invention, the examiner will conduct a prior art search and then determine statutory compliance.

name: Claim analysis: analyze each limitation and correlate to disclosure
description: Claims define the property rights provided by a patent and require careful scrutiny; examiners should identify and evaluate each claim limitation and correlate each limitation to the specification.
guidance: For processes, limitations define steps; for products, discrete structures or materials. Correlate limitation to all portions of disclosure that describe it, regardless of means- or step-plus-function language. Consider the claim as a whole (do not dissect), and give claim terms their plain meaning as understood by one of ordinary skill in the art. See MPEP §§2111 et seq. for additional guidance.

name: Claim construction: broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI)
description: Claims are to be given their broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the supporting disclosure during prosecution.
guidance: Grammar and plain meaning generally dictate claim scope. Positive limitations from the specification cannot be read into a claim that does not itself impose that limitation. Give means- or step-plus-function limitations their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with all corresponding structures/materials/acts described in the specification and their equivalents.

name: Language types that may raise questions as to limiting effect
description: Certain claim language may raise questions whether it is limiting: (A) statements of intended use or field of use (preamble), (B) 'adapted to'/'adapted for' clauses, (C) 'wherein'/'whereby' clauses, (D) contingent limitations, (E) printed matter, (F) terms with associated functional language.
guidance: Whether particular language is a limitation depends on the specific facts of the case. See MPEP §§2111.02–2111.05 for how to determine limiting effect.

name: Determine compliance with 35 U.S.C. 101 (Patentable Subject Matter)
description: Determine whether the claimed invention falls within one of the four statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter) and whether the claim is directed to patent-eligible subject matter and not a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon).
guidance: There are two criteria: (a) claim must fall within a statutory category; (b) claim must not be directed to a judicial exception unless the claim as a whole includes additional limitations amounting to significantly more than the exception (see Alice framework). Avoid focusing solely on 35 U.S.C. 101 to the detriment of 102/103/112 analyses.

name: 35 U.S.C. 101: Four requirements interpretation
description: 35 U.S.C. 101 has been interpreted as imposing four requirements: (i) only one patent may be obtained for an invention (no double patenting), (ii) inventors must be identified appropriately, (iii) claimed invention must be eligible for patenting, and (iv) claimed invention must be useful (utility).
guidance: See MPEP §2104 for discussion. Each requirement must be evaluated as part of the patentability determination.

name: Naming of inventor / inventorship correctness
description: Inventor(s) must be the applicant (for applications filed before Sept. 16, 2012) or must be identified in applications filed on/after that date; incorrect inventorship can lead to rejections under 35 U.S.C. 101/115 or pre-AIA 102(f).
guidance: In rare cases where application clearly does not name correct inventorship and applicant has not filed correction under 37 CFR 1.48, examiner should reject claims accordingly. See MPEP §2109 and §602.01(c).

name: 35 U.S.C. 112(b) / Definiteness and 'particularly point out and distinctly claim'
description: 35 U.S.C. 112(b) requires claims to set forth the subject matter the inventor regards as the invention and to particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention; indefiniteness is judged in light of the disclosure.
guidance: An application is deficient under 112(b) if evidence outside the application shows the inventor regards the invention as different from what is claimed. Claims must set out and define the invention with reasonable precision and particularity; claims, interpreted in light of the disclosure, must reasonably apprise a person of ordinary skill of the invention.

name: Specific 112(b) topics (new terminology, ranges, functional/alternative limitations, etc.)
description: Specific topics that commonly raise 35 U.S.C. 112(b) issues include new terminology, relative terminology, numerical ranges and amounts, exemplary claim language ('for example', 'such as'), lack of antecedent basis, reference to limitations in another claim, functional limitations, alternative limitations, negative limitations, product-by-process claims, 'use' claims, omnibus claims, reference to figures/tables, chemical formulas, trademarks in a claim, mere function of a machine, prolixity, multiplicity, double inclusion, etc.
guidance: See MPEP §§2173 et seq. and related subsections for examination and form paragraphs. Breadth is not indefiniteness per se; analyze in view of specification.

name: Adequate written description (35 U.S.C. 112(a))
description: The specification must reasonably convey to those skilled in the art that the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention as of the date of invention.
guidance: Examiners should evaluate whether the disclosure provides support for the claimed subject matter. Consider typical circumstances where written description issues arise, burden on examiner, relationship to new matter, and how changes to scope of claims impact written description.

name: Means-plus-function (35 U.S.C. 112(f)) and analogous treatment
description: A claim limitation may be interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) even if it does not use the word 'means' when it uses a generic placeholder coupled with functional language without reciting sufficient structure; conversely, 'means' or 'step' may not invoke 112(f) if sufficient structure/materials/acts are recited.
guidance: When 112(f) applies, the limitation is interpreted to cover the corresponding structure/materials/acts described in the specification and equivalents. Use the three-prong test in MPEP §2181. Provide form paragraph rejections where disclosure of corresponding structure is lacking, or where it's unclear whether 112(f) applies. Applicant may amend claims or clarify the record; mere assertions of intent are insufficient.

name: Determine compliance with 35 U.S.C. 102 (novelty / anticipation)
description: Review claimed invention against prior art; if no differences exist between the claimed invention and prior art, the claim lacks novelty and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102.
guidance: Consider what constitutes prior art (printed publications, patents, public use, on sale, foreign/domestic applications), the date of availability, level of public accessibility, admissions as prior art, and whether references are enabling. See MPEP §§2126–2160 for detailed guidance.

name: Determine compliance with 35 U.S.C. 103 (obviousness)
description: After identifying differences between the claimed invention and prior art, assess whether those differences render the claimed invention obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: Evaluate level of ordinary skill, legal concept of prima facie obviousness, suggestion or motivation to modify references, reasonable expectation of success (is required), consideration of all claim limitations, implicit disclosure, reliance on scientific theory or common knowledge, secondary considerations (objective indicia), and obviousness of ranges/species. See MPEP §§2141–2146 and related subsections. Use appropriate form paragraphs.

name: Minimizing or disingenuous explanations undermine credibility
description: Attempts to excuse or minimize misconduct (claiming ignorance of illegality or downplaying conduct) are problematic and detract from assertions of responsibility and candor.
guidance: Explanations that appear evasive or inconsistent with admissions (e.g., admitting Ambien is prescribed yet claiming ignorance of illegality) reduce the persuasive value of the applicant's statement and support denial.

name: Existing royalty is a legal lien on the patented article
description: An existing royalty on a patented article is in the nature of a legal lien upon it, to be paid off before it can be safely used, and is also an element properly entering into the price to be paid for it, if purchased.
guidance: As a result, when the United States purchases a patented article for public works it should pay a price estimated by intrinsic value augmented by probable royalties (P. 141, 358, Dec. 1890; C. 8321, Aug. 20, 1900; 17647, Mar. 10, 1905). The article is sold subject to the royalty claim.

name: Contracting when contractor's proposed work may infringe requires indemnity and bond
description: Where a bidder proposes to use a machine that is subject to suit for patent infringement, the United States should require a clause that: if legal proceedings arise against the United States during execution, the contractor shall hold the United States harmless and refund all expenses, damages and outlays; and if proceedings cause delay, the United States may employ others to complete the work and claim extra costs from the contractor.
guidance: Cites decisions (C. 725, Dec. 1894; 4558, July 1898; 23546, July 3, 1908). Also practical drafting language and indemnity/bonding for government contracts are advised.

name: Act of June 25, 1910: compensation right and limits for patentees whose patents are used by US
description: The act of June 25, 1910 gives to a bona fide patentee a right to recover reasonable compensation for an article patented by him which is used by the United States, but enables the United States to avail itself of any and all defenses which might be pleaded by a defendant in an action for infringement; it also provides that benefits shall not inure to a patentee who, at the time of making his claim, is in the employment or service of the United States and made the device during his employment; the act applies to assignees as well.
guidance: Cites statute and decision (C. 27038, July 15, 1910). Practical implication: claim process exists but limited by statutory defenses and employee-exclusion.

name: Unauthorized Practice of Law (UPL) prohibitions and examples
description: Practitioners must not hold themselves out as attorneys when they are not, must avoid dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation, and must not engage in conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (see 37 C.F.R. §§ 10.23(b)(4), 10.23(b)(5), 10.31(d)(1), 10.89(c)(6)).
guidance: Example: In re Campbell (USPTO Apr. 29, 2014) — a patent agent who represented a client in non-patent criminal and civil matters and claimed to be a 'federal attorney' was excluded from USPTO practice. Avoid misrepresenting status or acting outside authorized scope.

name: Certificates After Issuance and Their Effect on Prior Art
description: Certificates issued after patent grant (reexamination certificates, certificates of correction, post-grant review/inter partes review/derivation certificates) affect the patent record and prior art dates in specified ways.
guidance: Reexamination certificates indicate changes to the specification/claims; changes may not enlarge claim scope; prior art dates remain those of the reexamined patent. Certificates of correction are part of the original patent and do not change prior art dates. PTAB post-grant review or inter partes review certificates issued following final decisions will cancel or confirm claims and incorporate any new/amended patentable claims—these certificates are published and affect the patent record. Derivation certificates can cancel claims if PTAB determines derivation. See 35 U.S.C. 254–255, 307, pre-AIA 316, and related MPEP sections.

name: Use of Patent Family and External Databases for Determining Corresponding Foreign Documents
description: When a corresponding foreign patent or application might establish an earlier date, examiners should search family members and external databases (Derwent World Patents Index, INPADOC, Chemical Abstracts) to locate earlier publications or grants.
guidance: Derwent, INPADOC, and Chemical Abstracts (CAS) can show family members, cross-references, and abstracts; CAS abstracts chemical patents and references one family member in full. Chemical Abstracts access procedures via STIC are provided. Checking family members can reveal earlier printed publication dates or issue dates that affect effective prior art dates (e.g., earlier foreign publication predating a U.S. filing date). See MPEP § 2154.01(b) for determinations related to foreign priority claims.

name: Corresponding Specifications in a Family and Priority Right Considerations
description: Patents in different countries for the same invention form a family and priority rights (Paris Convention) allow later filings within one year to claim benefit of earlier filing dates; corresponding specifications may be identical, translations, or differ (e.g., continuation-in-part).
guidance: When evaluating a U.S. patent or published application that claims foreign priority, determine whether the foreign application issued or published earlier — this can provide an earlier effective date. Use 35 U.S.C. 102(d) to decide whether a foreign priority can be used as an 'effectively filed' date. Duplicate or translated specifications may be cited; content questions are settled based on the specification actually used as the reference. See MPEP § 213 and § 2154 for priority and effective-date rules.

name: Claim Analysis for Search: Variant Embodiments, Equivalents, and Analogous Arts
description: Search must be driven by careful analysis of the claims, identifying variant embodiments within claim scope, potential equivalents, and analogous arts relevant to the claimed invention.
guidance: Analyze claim language and disclosure to determine scope and embodiments to search. Consider doctrine of equivalents and analogous arts where appropriate. Use claim analysis to select classification areas, keywords, and search strategies; see MPEP guidance sections on how to search and analyze claims for search planning.

name: Cooperative Patent Classification (CPC) Scheme and Classification Approach
description: Approach to classification in CPC: use CPC titles, definitions, guidance headings, notes, and combination sets; CPC symbols must represent claimed subject matter and certain CPC entries may carry warnings or guidance.
guidance: Examiners should use CPC titles, references within titles, notes, warnings, and guidance headings found in CPC schemes to determine proper classification. CPC definitions and combination sets can direct search scope. A C* (C-Star) binary designation is used at the family level to mark CPC symbols that are representative of the claimed subject matter — these influence routing/assignment.

name: General Guidelines Governing Assignment of Nonprovisional Design and Plant Applications
description: Applications are generally assigned based on where the application would have an original classification if the claims were in a patent, following rules/principles of classification (MPEP § 903.07) and various assignment criteria.
guidance: Key points: (A) assignment follows classification principles as much as possible; (B) criteria for original classification are in MPEP § 903.07; (C) read claims in light of the disclosure (claimed disclosure) and avoid deciding on the 'real invention' beyond the record; (D) choose the OR subclass as the most indented subclass of the first subclass array; (E) location of the U.S. patents constituting the prior art is generally controlling; (F) ordinarily cannot assign to a class that includes one element of a claimed combination only — treat the claim in its entirety; (G) an examiner seeking transfer may perform searches of both classes and include results in the transfer record.

name: Insignificant extra-solution activity / insignificant application
description: Claim limitations that add only insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., mere data gathering in conjunction with a law of nature or abstract idea) do not meaningfully limit a judicial exception.
guidance: Some cases have identified insignificant computer implementation as an example of insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., Fort Props.; Bancorp Servs.). Examples cited: cutting hair after first determining the hair style (In re Brown); printing or downloading generated menus (Ameranth). For claim limitations that add insignificant extra-solution activity, examiners should explain in an eligibility rejection why they do not meaningfully limit the claim (for example, storing data added to a process that only recites computing a mathematical relationship does not add a meaningful limitation). See MPEP § 2106.05(f) for more information.

name: Examples of field-of-use/technological-environment limitations that are insufficient
description: Court-cited examples of limitations that merely confine an abstract idea to a particular environment or audience and thus fail to make the claim eligible.
guidance: Examples (i–x) include: (i) administering 6-thioguanine to a particular patient population (Mayo); (ii) identifying participants as commodity providers/consumers (Bilski); (iii) limiting C = 2πr to wheels (Flook); (iv) specifying monitoring audit log data occurs in a computer environment (FairWarning); (v) virus screening used within a telephone network or the Internet (Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec); (vi) limiting collecting/analyzing/displaying information to power-grid data (Electric Power Group v. Alstom); (vii) informing doctors to apply a law of nature for genetic polymorphism detection (Genetic Techs. v. Merial); (viii) budgeting implemented using broad communication medium (Internet/telephone) (Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One); (ix) advertising-as-currency used on the Internet (Ultramercial v. Hulu); (x) requiring computer/network/online transaction limitations for guaranteeing performance (buySAFE v. Google). Examiners should explain why such limitations do not meaningfully limit the claim when asserting ineligibility.

name: Streamlined analysis (Pathway A) for self-evident eligibility
description: For efficiency, examiners may use a streamlined eligibility analysis (Pathway A) when the eligibility of the claim is self-evident (e.g., the claim clearly improves a technology or computer functionality).
guidance: The streamlined analysis yields the same result as the full Alice/Mayo test; it is not a way to avoid an ineligibility finding. If there is doubt whether applicant seeks coverage of a judicial exception, the full analysis should be conducted. The record may simply reflect eligibility by absence of a rejection or clarifying remarks. See flowchart in MPEP § 2106, subsection III.

name: Eligibility is self-evident — examples and bounds
description: A claim may be self-evidently eligible if, when viewed as a whole, it clearly does not seek to tie up any judicial exception (e.g., clearly improves technology or is a complex manufactured industrial product).
guidance: Examples: a robotic arm assembly with a control system that uses mathematical relationships but does not tie up the math; a nature-based product claim that does not attempt to tie up the nature-based product (artificial hip prosthesis coated with a naturally occurring mineral); claimed products including only ancillary nature-based components (cellphone with gold contact). Claims that are a 'close call' should undergo the full eligibility analysis (see BASCOM example).

name: Clear improvement to technology or computer functionality
description: Claims that are directed to clear improvements in computer-related technology or other technological processes may be not abstract and thus may avoid the full eligibility analysis.
guidance: Federal Circuit examples: Enfish (self-referential table for database — eligible at Step 1), McRO (automatic lip synchronization and facial animation — eligible at Step 1). If claims clearly improve technology/computer functionality, they may qualify for Pathway A or be found not directed to an abstract idea at Step 2A. If unclear ('close call'), perform the full Alice/Mayo analysis (see BASCOM and related discussion).

name: Rejections must be based on substantive law and review the record as a whole
description: Eligibility rejections must be based on the substantive law under 35 U.S.C. §101 as interpreted by judicial precedent; examiners should review the record as a whole before concluding ineligibility.
guidance: Examination guidance, training, and examples explain the law but are not themselves a basis for rejection. Examiners should consider the specification, claims, prosecution history, relevant case law, and prior art. Eligibility determinations are claim-by-claim; dependent claims may differ from independent claims. See MPEP §§ 2106.03–2106.06 for substantive law discussion.

name: Prima facie case requirement for eligibility rejections
description: When more likely than not that a claim fails eligibility criteria (Step 1 NO and/or Step 2B NO), examiners should formulate a rejection that sets forth a prima facie case of ineligibility under the substantive law.
guidance: The initial burden is on the examiner to explain clearly and specifically why a claim is ineligible so the applicant has sufficient notice to respond. The rejection must provide a reasoned explanation that supports the examiner's conclusion.

name: Step 2A Prong One — identify the judicial exception
description: A subject matter eligibility rejection should point to the specific claim limitation(s) that recite the judicial exception and explain why those limitations set forth or describe a judicial exception (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea).
guidance: Where the claim describes but does not expressly set forth the judicial exception, the rejection must explain what subject matter those limitations describe and why that described subject matter is a judicial exception. When the examiner determines a claim recites an abstract idea, the rejection should identify the abstract idea as recited in the claim and explain why it falls within one of the groupings of abstract ideas (mathematical concepts, mental processes, or certain methods of organizing human activity) per MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2). See MPEP § 2106.04 for more on Step 2A.

name: Step 2A Prong Two — identify additional elements and evaluate integration
description: For Prong Two, the rejection should identify any additional elements beyond the judicial exception and evaluate whether those elements integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.
guidance: The examiner must specifically point to claim features/limitations/steps beyond the identified judicial exception and evaluate the integration using considerations set forth in MPEP §§ 2106.04(d), 2106.05(a)-(c) and (e)-(h). Examiners should give weight to all claimed additional elements in Prong Two, even if those elements represent well-understood, routine, conventional activity.

name: Step 2B — explain lack of inventive concept (significantly more)
description: For Step 2B, the rejection should explain why the additional elements, taken individually and in combination, do not result in the claim as a whole amounting to significantly more than the identified judicial exception.
guidance: If the examiner concludes that certain claim elements are well-understood, routine, conventional activities in the field, the examiner must expressly support the rejection in writing with one of the four options specified in Subsection III. See MPEP § 2106.05 et seq. for guidance on searching for an inventive concept.

name: Point to specific claim limitations when making a rejection
description: When making a subject matter eligibility rejection, the Office action must point to specific claim limitation(s) that recite the judicial exception and explain why each claim is unpatentable with sufficient clarity and specificity to enable applicant to respond.
guidance: After establishing the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim, evaluate eligibility of each claim as a whole using MPEP § 2106. The rejection must be sufficiently clear and specific to provide applicant notice and enable effective response. See MPEP § 2111 for claim interpretation guidance.

name: Three-question eligibility framework (Questions 1-3)
