description: Stepwise analysis: (1) Is the claim directed to a statutory category (machine, manufacture, composition, or process)? (2) Does the claim recite a judicial exception (law of nature, natural principle, natural phenomenon, natural product, or abstract idea)? (3) Does the claim, as a whole, recite something significantly different than the judicial exception?
guidance: If answers to Questions 1–2 are 'yes' (statutory category and judicial exception recited), evaluate Question 3 using the listed factors (a–l). For claims reciting an abstract idea, analyze under MPEP §2106(II) (see separate metric). Examples in the guidance show applying Questions 1–3 to composition, manufacture, process claims and mixed claims (e.g., primers, amplification methods, diagnostic methods).

name: Factor a) Markedly different (product claims)
description: For product claims, whether the claimed natural product(s) are 'markedly different' from what exists in nature (structurally or functionally).
guidance: If the natural product is not markedly different (e.g., isolated nucleic acids whose sequence and function remain as in nature; naturally occurring bacteria not altered), factor a) is not satisfied and weighs against eligibility. Example: primers whose genetic sequence and function are unchanged are not 'markedly different' (Myriad).

name: Factor b) Claim limitations meaningfully narrow scope (avoid substantial foreclosure)
description: Whether elements in addition to the judicial exception meaningfully narrow the claim scope so that others are not substantially foreclosed from using the judicial exception in other ways.
guidance: Satisfied when specific limits (temperatures/times, particular use/application, choice of synthetic vs natural source, etc.) prevent coverage of substantially all uses of the exception. Example: heating/cooling cycles in an amplification method narrow scope; specifying synthetic white light (vs sunlight) limits scope. If only a field-of-use is claimed (e.g., 'use sunlight to treat mood disorder') and substantially forecloses others, b) is not satisfied.

name: Factor c) Elements relate to the judicial exception in a significant way
description: Whether claim elements in addition to the judicial exception relate to it in a significant, non-insignificant manner (e.g., physical integration or direct manipulation).
guidance: Satisfied when additional elements materially integrate or manipulate the natural product/principle (e.g., combination forms a structure into which natural products are physically integrated; heating/cooling steps directly manipulate DNA). Examples: cardboard body + ignition fuse integrate calcium chloride and gunpowder physically; thermal cycling directly manipulates DNA.

name: Factor d) More than mere instructions or description
description: Whether additional claim elements do more than describe the judicial exception or give general instructions to use/apply it (i.e., claim recites a specific practical application).
guidance: Satisfied when the claim as a whole recites a concrete application (e.g., use of a particular antibody and flow cytometry to detect a misfolded protein) rather than a high-level instruction to 'apply' the principle. Unsatisfied when the step is merely 'expose to sunlight' or other general instruction.

name: Factor e) Machine-or-transformation
description: Whether the claim recites a machine or a transformation (the presence of which can weigh toward eligibility).
guidance: If no machine or transformation is recited, factor e) is not satisfied. The guidance checks for a recited machine or transformative act as part of eligibility analysis.

name: Factor f) Additional elements are more than well-understood, purely conventional or routine
description: Whether the additional elements contribute something inventive beyond what is well-understood, routine, or conventional in the relevant art.
guidance: Satisfied when the specification/record shows the additional elements are not routine (e.g., a newly created antibody that is not conventional). Unsatisfied when the claimed steps or elements are conventional (e.g., routine heating/cooling in PCR, routine use of antibodies generally).

name: Factor h) Claim recited at a high level of generality covering substantially all practical applications
description: Whether the claimed elements are recited so broadly that the claim covers substantially all practical applications of the judicial exception.
guidance: Satisfied (weighs against eligibility) when claim language is high-level and covers substantially all applications (e.g., broadly claiming 'expose to white light' without meaningful limits). Not satisfied when specific steps or parameters limit the claim so not all applications are covered (e.g., specified distances/times/filters).

name: Factor i) Claimed elements required to use the judicial exception
description: Whether the claimed elements are required to use or apply the natural products/principle (i.e., everyone using the exception must use the claimed elements).
guidance: If claimed elements are not required (others can practice the exception by other means), i) is not satisfied. Example: use of a particular antibody or Taq polymerase is not required to amplify DNA generally; others may use different enzymes or methods.

name: Factor k) Additional elements are a significant part of the claim (integrated, not merely appended)
description: Whether additional elements form an integrated, meaningful part of the claim rather than being merely appended or insignificant extras.
guidance: Satisfied when additional elements integrate the judicial exception into a practical application (e.g., elements form a structure physically integrating natural products, or steps directly manipulate natural products). Unsatisfied when elements are mere appendages that do not integrate the exception.

name: Claims reciting both an abstract idea and a natural product: apply MPEP §2106(II)
description: When a claim recites an abstract idea in addition to a natural product or other judicial exception, the analysis should follow the guidance in MPEP §2106(II) for abstract-idea claims, including how a practical application of another exception affects eligibility.
guidance: The guidance controls whether the claim qualifies as eligible subject matter when an abstract idea is present. Example: a claim whose only step is 'comparing sequences' (an abstract mental process) and recites a wild-type nucleotide sequence should be analyzed under MPEP §2106(II) and was held ineligible in relevant case law (Myriad/AMP).

name: Use of revised Form Paragraph ¶7.05.13 for §101 rejections involving laws of nature/natural phenomena/natural products
description: When rejecting claims under 35 U.S.C. 101 for reciting or involving a law of nature, natural principle, natural phenomenon, or natural product, use revised form paragraph 7.05.13 (preceded by form paragraphs 7.04 and 7.05).
guidance: Form paragraph text: 'the claimed invention is not directed to patent eligible subject matter. Based upon an analysis with respect to the claim as a whole, claim(s) [1] do not recite something significantly different than a judicial exception. The rationale for this determination is explained below: [2]'. Examiner Note: use this paragraph where claims have a law of nature/natural principle or natural phenomenon (e.g., a natural product) as a claim limitation.

name: Ground: Specification attached lacks claims and amendment period elapsed (Article 11(5-2))
description: Where a specification which does not include the claims is attached to a patent application filed by the lawful holder of a right and the amendment period under Article 42(2)(ii) has already elapsed.
guidance: Late submission of claims after specified amendment period is not acceptable.

name: Ground: Request for examination attached to specification lacking claims (Article 11(15))
description: Where a patent applicant has submitted a request for examination on a patent application attached with a specification which does not include the claims.
guidance: Requests for examination must be accompanied by claims; absence renders request illegitimate.

name: 35 U.S.C. § 314(a) reasonable likelihood standard
description: “The Director may not authorize an inter partes review to be instituted unless the Director determines that the information presented in the petition ... and any response ... shows that there is a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail with respect to at least 1 of the claims challenged in the petition.”
guidance: Statutory threshold for institution based on merits; quoted verbatim from § 314(a). This remains the merits standard separate from the Director's discretion whether to institute on discretionary grounds.

name: Consequences of patent owner failure to file timely/appropriate response (37 CFR 1.957(b)/(c))
description: If no claims are found patentable and the patent owner fails to file a timely and appropriate response, prosecution will be terminated and the Director will issue and publish a certificate concluding the reexamination (NIRC). If claims are found patentable and the patent owner fails to respond timely, further prosecution will be limited to claims found patentable at the time and to claims added thereafter that do not expand scope.
guidance: The examiner will issue an Action Closing Prosecution (ACP) indicating withdrawn/canceled claims and setting periods for response and third‑party comments under 37 CFR 1.951. See MPEP §§ 2671.02 and 2671.03.

name: Right of Appeal Notice consequences
description: If the patent owner fails to make a timely appeal after issuance of a Right of Appeal Notice, or a timely appeal is dismissed, consequences depend on whether any claim was found patentable: (A) If no claim was found patentable → NIRC issued immediately. (B) If at least one claim was found patentable and third‑party requester does not appeal → prosecution terminated and NIRC issued. (C) If at least one claim patentable and third‑party appellant continues appeal → claims limited to those found patentable at time of failure.
guidance: If the third‑party appellant continues appeal while the patent owner fails, non‑patentable claims are withdrawn pending cancellation on issuance of NIRC.

name: Failure of third party to timely comment after patent owner response
description: Where a third party requester does not timely file written comments on a patent owner response, any subsequent submission of comments on that response will be refused consideration.
guidance: The failure applies only to that specific response; the third party retains rights to comment on future patent owner responses. If the original response was incomplete and later completed by the owner, the third party may file comments within 30 days from service of the supplemental/complete response, except where completion only involved payment of a fee (other than excess claims fee). See MPEP § 2666.40.

name: Handling defective submissions for both parties
description: Where both the patent owner response and third party comments are defective, a PTOL‑2069 should be completed for each party setting forth the defects; copies of both completed forms are sent to all parties.
guidance: If defect limited to signature/claim format/obvious defect, CRU technical support staff may issue PTOL‑2069 prior to forwarding to the examiner; otherwise examiner is responsible for obtaining needed corrections.

name: Response to Notice of Defective Paper — content and comment rights
description: Parties are given one month or 30 days (whichever is longer) from mailing date of the notice to correct the defect. If corrected submission is directed solely to form and does not go to the merits, the other party may not comment on the correction.
guidance: If correcting a defective amendment or paying an excess claims fee that brings claims into the proceeding, after correction the third party may comment and prior arguments become relevant. Any discussion of the merits included with the defect correction must be set forth separately and clearly identified as merits; otherwise the submission may be returned and the party given one additional opportunity to correct the defect without intermixed merits discussion.

name: Page limits and 'Response Is Too Long' (37 CFR 1.943)
description: Where the length of the patent owner submission exceeds that permitted by 37 CFR 1.943, the submission is improper and may be expunged (or the owner given options).
guidance: Examiner will mail a Notice permitting the owner to (A) submit a redrafted response within the page limit or (B) file a copy of the supplemental response with pages redacted to satisfy page limits. The Notice sets 15 days to respond. If no response, submission will not be considered and prosecution may be terminated or limited. Certain pages are excluded from the 1.943 page limits (table of contents, table of case law, pages of the claims (not claim charts), claims appendix, and specific brief sections limited to required information). Affidavits/declarations that include opinion/argument are counted toward page limits; factual declarations and exhibits generally are not counted unless they include argument.

name: Panduit Factor 1 — Demand for the patented product
description: To satisfy Panduit Factor 1, the patentee must show "demand for the patented product." The first factor "considers demand for the product as a whole," while the second factor considers demand for particular limitations or features of the claimed invention.
guidance: Patentee may use any relevant evidence to show demand, including sales of embodying products, the accused infringer’s decision to continue selling despite risk of infringement, and the patented feature's promotion or significance. Sales of the infringing product can be used but may require showing comparable sales prices; if products are not sufficiently similar, customers might not transfer demand. The inquiry ties damages to specific claim limitations to ensure forfeits are commensurate with value of patented features.

name: Market-share theory as an alternative to proving no acceptable substitute
description: A patentee may meet Panduit Factor 2 under a market-share theory: lost profits may be awarded "if the patentee shows an established market share in lieu of the absence of acceptable noninfringing alternatives and, at the same time, meets the three other Panduit factors."
guidance: Courts have relied on evidence such as past business practices investing in market development, testimony about loss of business and prior customer relationships, head-to-head competition, real sales losses, and national recognition to support market-share claims. Market-share theory requires demonstrating an established market position plus the other Panduit factors (demand, ability to meet demand, amount of profits).

name: 35 U.S.C. 288 (pre‑AIA) variation
description: Whenever, without deceptive intention, a claim of a patent is invalid, an action may be maintained for the infringement of a claim of the patent which may be valid. The patentee shall recover no costs unless a disclaimer of the invalid claim has been entered at the Patent and Trademark Office before the commencement of the suit.
guidance: Historical/pre‑AIA wording emphasizing 'without deceptive intention'; editor notes indicate applicability distinctions based on filing dates and AIA transition.

name: 35 U.S.C. 291: Relief for owner of a patent derived by another (derived patents)
description: The owner of a patent may have relief by civil action against the owner of another patent that claims the same invention and has an earlier effective filing date, if the invention claimed in such other patent was derived from the inventor of the invention claimed in the patent owned by the person seeking relief.
guidance: Filing limitation: action must be filed only before the end of the 1‑year period beginning on the date of issuance of the first patent containing a claim to the allegedly derived invention and naming an individual alleged to have derived such invention as inventor or joint inventor. Editor notes specify applicability to AIA first‑to‑file transitional provisions and effective dates.

name: 35 U.S.C. 301: Citation of prior art and written statements to the Office
description: Any person at any time may cite to the Office in writing prior art consisting of patents or printed publications believed to bear on the patentability of any claim, or statements of the patent owner filed in proceedings where the owner took a position on claim scope. If the person explains the pertinence and manner of applying the prior art or statements to at least one claim, the citation and explanation shall become part of the official file.
guidance: Written statements must include other documents/pleadings from the proceeding that address the statement. Limitations: such written statements/additional information are to be considered by the Office only to determine proper meaning of a patent claim in proceedings ordered under sections 304, 314, or 324. If subject to protective order, redactions are required. Upon written request, the identity of the person citing may be kept confidential in the patent file.

name: 35 U.S.C. 303: Director's determination on reexamination requests
description: Within three months following filing of a request for reexamination under §302, the Director will determine whether a substantial new question of patentability affecting any claim is raised by the request, with or without consideration of other patents or publications. The Director may on his own initiative determine whether a substantial new question is raised.
guidance: A record of the Director's determination will be placed in the official file and a copy mailed to owner and requester. A determination that no substantial new question has been raised is final and nonappealable; upon such a determination the Director may refund a portion of the reexamination fee.

name: 35 U.S.C. 304: Reexamination order and patent owner statement
description: If the Director finds a substantial new question of patentability under §303(a), the determination will include an order for reexamination. The patent owner will be given a reasonable period, not less than two months from the date of the determination being mailed/given, to file a statement including any amendment to the patent and new claim(s) proposed for consideration in the reexamination. If the owner files such a statement, he must promptly serve a copy on the person who requested reexamination. Within two months of service, the requester may file and have considered a reply to any statement filed by the patent owner.
guidance: Ensures opportunity for owner and requester to present statements/amendments; sets minimum reply periods and service obligations.

name: 35 U.S.C. 305: Conduct of reexamination proceedings (current AIA‑applicable)
description: After the times for filing the statement and reply under §304 have expired, reexamination will be conducted according to procedures established for initial examination under §§132 and 133. In reexamination, the patent owner may propose any amendment to the patent and new claim(s) to distinguish the claimed invention from prior art cited under §301 or in response to an adverse decision. No proposed amended or new claim enlarging the scope of a claim will be permitted. All reexamination proceedings, including appeals to the PTAB, will be conducted with special dispatch within the Office.
guidance: Editor note: Applicable to patents issuing from applications subject to first‑inventor‑to‑file provisions of the AIA; pre‑AIA variant exists. Cross‑references to examination procedures §§132–133 and appeal routing.

name: 35 U.S.C. 305 (pre‑AIA) conduct provisions
description: If Director finds a substantial new question of patentability, order for reexamination includes similar opportunities for owner to file statements and propose amendments/new claims to distinguish from cited prior art; no proposed amendment/new claim enlarging scope permitted; proceedings (including appeals to Board of Patent Appeals and Interferences) will be conducted with special dispatch.
guidance: Older procedural references (Board of Patent Appeals and Interferences) are retained for patents/applications not subject to AIA first‑to‑file; editorial notes clarify applicability.

name: 35 U.S.C. 307: Certificate of patentability, unpatentability, and claim cancellation
description: In a reexamination proceeding, when appeal time has expired or appeals have terminated, the Director will issue and publish a certificate canceling any claim finally determined to be unpatentable, confirming any claim determined to be patentable, and incorporating into the patent any proposed amended or new claim determined to be patentable.
guidance: Any proposed amended/new claim incorporated into a patent following reexamination has the same effect as specified in §252 for reissued patents regarding rights of prior users or those who made/purchased/used/imported items covered by such claim or made substantial preparation prior to the issuance of the certificate.

name: Claims define extent of protection
description: In a patent or patent application, the claims define, in technical terms, the extent of the protection conferred by a patent or the protection sought in a patent application.
guidance: Claims are sentences that define the invention and play the central role in patent litigation: they are the metes and bounds of the patentee's exclusive right. Draft claims carefully because they determine infringement and validity disputes.

name: Independent vs dependent claims
description: Independent claim: stands alone and defines the broadest scope sought. Dependent claim: references an earlier claim and adds further limitations.
guidance: Dependent claims inherit all limitations of their parent and are organized in a hierarchy. A typical patent has 1–4 independent claims and many dependent claims. Use dependent claims to add fallback positions and narrower claim scopes.

name: Product (apparatus/machine/composition) claims
description: Product claims (also called apparatus, machine, composition of matter, manufacture) cover physical things.
guidance: Use product claims to protect tangible inventions and structural features. Draft element-by-element in the body to delineate the physical components or composition.

name: Method / process claims
description: Method or process claims cover a series of steps or actions.
guidance: Draft clear step language and the order/relationship between steps if order is material. Consider infringement patterns (performing steps) and potential for divided infringement issues.

name: Means-plus-function claims (U.S.)
description: Means-plus-function claims recite a function performed by undisclosed structure and are construed under 35 U.S.C. §112(f) (or pre-AIA §112 paragraph 6) as covering the corresponding structure in the specification and equivalents.
guidance: If invoking means-plus-function style, ensure the specification discloses adequate structure corresponding to the claimed function; otherwise the claim may be limited or indefinite. Be aware of how courts limit scope to disclosed structure and equivalents.

name: Beauregard claims (computer-readable medium claims)
description: Beauregard claims (U.S.) recite a computer-readable medium storing instructions (used in software-related patents).
guidance: These claims attempt to claim software by reciting a medium with program instructions. Jurisdictional case law and patentability rules for software should be considered when using this claim form.

name: Markush claims (chemistry combinatorial claiming)
description: Markush claims, used in chemistry, recite a closed group of alternatives (e.g., a list of substituents).
guidance: Use Markush format to claim a group of chemical alternatives; ensure the alternatives form a patentably relevant and supported group under the specification and practice-specific rules.

name: Jepson claims
description: Jepson claims recite known elements in the preamble and the improvement in the body.
guidance: Jepson claims can admit the preamble subject matter as prior art, which may be undesirable in U.S. practice. They are rare in the U.S. for that reason.

name: Swiss-type claims (historical second medical use)
description: Swiss-type claims were used (formerly at the EPO) for second medical use claims and are generally disused now.
guidance: Recognize historical claim formats may be obsolete or replaced by newer claim drafting approaches in particular jurisdictions.

name: Claim construction standard (U.S.: Phillips v. AWH)
description: Claims are interpreted by courts during litigation; in the U.S., claim terms get their ordinary meaning to a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention, in light of the specification and prosecution history (Phillips v. AWH, Fed. Cir. 2005, en banc).
guidance: When drafting, use specification language to shape how a POSITA will understand claim terms, and be mindful of prosecution history statements that can later affect construction. Consider prosecution and specification language to support desired interpretations.

name: Claim indefiniteness (35 U.S.C. §112(b) and Nautilus)
description: Under 35 U.S.C. §112(b), a claim must 'particularly point out and distinctly claim' the invention. Nautilus v. Biosig (2014) established that a claim is indefinite if its scope is not reasonably certain to a person of ordinary skill in the art in light of the specification and prosecution history.
guidance: Draft claims with clear boundaries and supported definitions; vague or ambiguous terms risk invalidation for indefiniteness under the reasonably-certain standard.

name: Feature-level mapping between claim features and prior-art passages
description: Novelty assessment requires intricate matching between specific features of a patent claim and passages in the prior art.
guidance: Models should identify which passages in a prior-art document disclose individual claim features (fine-grained mapping), rather than only producing a claim-level label. This mapping supports transparent explanations of why features are novel or anticipated.

name: Joint retrieval and abstract reasoning evaluation paradigm
description: Propose shifting evaluation to a joint retrieval and abstract reasoning task at the feature level, requiring models to identify specific passages that disclose claim features and to identify which features make a claim novel.
guidance: Evaluation should measure both the retrieval quality (are the correct passages found?) and the reasoning/abstraction quality (does the system correctly judge which features are novel based on retrieved evidence?). The final claim-level novelty decision should be derived from feature-level results.

name: Dataset with fine-grained, feature-level prior-art references (FiNE-Patents)
description: FiNE-Patents: a dataset of 3,658 first patent claims annotated with fine-grained, feature-level prior art references extracted from European Search Opinion (ESOP) documents.
guidance: Use or compare against FiNE-Patents for training/evaluation when available; annotations are feature-level links to ESOP passages, facilitating passage retrieval and novel-feature identification tasks. Release of dataset enables reproducibility and research into transparent patent analysis.

name: Type-volume (word count) and page limits for petitions, motions, oppositions, and replies
description: Specify word counts or page limits (type-volume) for petitions, motions, oppositions, and replies and identify what is excluded from the counts.
guidance: Specific limits: Petition requesting inter partes review: 14,000 words; Petition requesting post-grant review: 18,700 words; Petition requesting covered business method patent review: 18,700 words; Petition requesting derivation proceeding: 14,000 words. Motions (excluding motions to amend): 15 pages. Motions to amend: 25 pages. Replies to patent owner responses to petitions: 5,600 words. Replies to oppositions (excluding replies to oppositions to motions to amend): 5 pages. Replies to oppositions to motions to amend: 12 pages. Word counts/page limits include any statement of material facts in support but exclude table of contents, table of authorities, certificate of service or word count, exhibits, appendix, or claim listing. Patent owner preliminary responses and patent owner responses use the same word counts as the petition; oppositions follow the same page limits as corresponding motions.

name: Claim construction standard for unexpired patents
description: For claims in an unexpired patent that will not expire before a final written decision is issued, the claim shall be given its broadest reasonable construction in light of the specification of the patent in which it appears.
guidance: Amendments proposed to 37 CFR 42.100(b), 42.200(b), and 42.300(b). The Office will add clarifying instructions in the Office Patent Trial Practice Guide regarding how a petitioner may determine which standard to apply in the petition.

name: Filing supplemental information from co-pending litigation
description: Parties may file claim construction orders and other papers from co-pending litigation as supplemental information when relevant to the proceeding.
guidance: Parties may file such papers to support motions, oppositions, or replies. Parties may also seek leave to file a motion to submit supplemental information pursuant to § 42.123, but such papers must be relevant to a claim for which the trial has been instituted. Petitioners historically have included such papers with petitions; patent owners have proffered district court claim constructions with preliminary responses or patent owner responses.

name: No categorical limitation on number of invalidity grounds; institution discretion
description: The Office declines to place a limitation on the number of grounds that a petitioner may present in a petition.
guidance: The Office will use word counts for major briefing to allow parties to structure arguments as they deem best (including claim charts). The Office retains discretion under 35 U.S.C. 314(a) and 324(a) whether to institute a trial and to focus the trial on grounds meeting threshold standards and reasonably decidable within statutory timeframes. Additionally, patent owners bear a duty to support affirmative factual statements with evidence—unsupported statements will be given little or no weight.

name: Publication of registration — required information (industrial design)
description: The Organization shall publish for each certificate: registration number; filing number; filing date; Locarno class; title of the design; company name or owner name and address; creator name and address (unless requested omitted); validly claimed priority; priority date/country/earlier application number; agent name/address (if applicable); and registration date.
guidance: Implementing regulations determine procedures for publication.

name: Border measures on request — detention and proof requirements
description: On written application supported by proof of right, customs may detain goods the applicant claims to be counterfeit; public prosecutor, applicant and importer shall be immediately informed of detention.
guidance: Detention lifted ipso jure within 10 working days if applicant fails to provide proof of interim measures or of application to competent national judge and requisite guarantees; applicant may obtain names/addresses/quantity of sender/importer/recipient notwithstanding professional secrecy rules; owner/importer/recipient may suspend detention on payment of security deposit where decision to suspend free movement is not taken by judicial authority or independent administration.

name: Doctrine of Equivalents (general rule)
description: The doctrine of equivalents is a legal rule that allows a court to hold a party liable for patent infringement if the infringing device or process does not fall within the literal scope of a patent claim but is nevertheless equivalent to the claimed invention.
guidance: Judicially created rule allowing a patentee to assert infringement even if an accused product or process does not literally infringe; serves to 'temper unsparing logic and prevent an infringer from stealing the benefit of the invention.' The doctrine enlarges patent protection beyond literal claim scope.

name: Element-by-Element Application
description: The doctrine of equivalents analysis is applied to individual claim limitations, not to the invention as a whole.
guidance: For each claim limitation, ask whether the accused device has an equivalent — you cannot treat the claim as a monolithic whole when assessing equivalence.

name: Insubstantial Difference Test (Warner-Jenkinson)
description: Whether the difference between the feature in the accused device and the limitation literally recited in the patent claim is 'insubstantial.'
guidance: The Warner-Jenkinson (1997) formulation focuses on whether the difference is insubstantial; if so, the element may be equivalent despite lack of literal coverage.

name: Ensnarement Doctrine
description: A patentee may not assert 'a scope of equivalency that would encompass, or ensnare, the prior art.'
guidance: Equivalence cannot be asserted in a way that would effectively claim what was already in the prior art — courts will limit equivalents to avoid giving the patentee undue coverage over prior art.

name: Public Dedication Rule
description: A patentee may not invoke the doctrine of equivalents to recapture subject matter disclosed but not claimed in a patent.
guidance: If the specification discloses variants or embodiments that were not claimed, those may be considered dedicated to the public and cannot be reclaimed via equivalence.

name: All-Elements Rule
description: Each limitation in a claim must have an equivalent in the accused device or process; you cannot read out a claim limitation entirely.
guidance: Equivalence requires a correspondence for every claim limitation; failure to identify an equivalent for even one limitation defeats an equivalents-based infringement finding.

name: UK — Improver Questions / Actavis Test
description: Modern UK approach (Actavis v. Eli Lilly, 2017): - Does the variant achieve substantially the same result in substantially the same way? - Would it be obvious to the skilled person? - Would the skilled person have concluded the patentee intended strict compliance with the literal meaning?
guidance: This tripartite test refines equivalence by adding an obviousness inquiry and an assessment of whether the skilled person would construe the claim as strictly limiting; used post-Actavis to determine if a variant falls within claim scope by equivalence.

name: Strategic Drafting to Maximize Doctrine Protection
description: Drafting and prosecution practices to enlarge or preserve equivalents coverage.
guidance: Recommended practices include: avoid unnecessary narrowing during prosecution; cover obvious variants in dependent claims; disclose alternatives in the specification (but don't dedicate them); avoid arguments that create prosecution history estoppel. These steps help preserve room to argue equivalence later.

name: Defensive Strategies to Minimize Equivalents Impact
description: Tactics defendants and challengers should use to defeat or limit an equivalents-based claim.
guidance: Search prosecution history for amendments/arguments that give rise to estoppel; identify surrendered subject matter; find disclosed-but-unclaimed variants (public dedication); and locate prior art that would be ensnared by a broad equivalence claim.

name: Claim Limitations at Filing
description: Applications must meet limits at filing: no more than 4 independent claims, no more than 30 total claims, and no multiple dependent claims.
guidance: Amendments may be filed at the time of the request to ensure compliance with these limits; ensure claim count and dependency structure are in compliance before requesting Track One.

name: When Track One Is the Right Choice
description: Track One is particularly useful when applicants need early patent issuance for commercial milestones, have a defined embodiment requiring quick protection, expect near‑term licensing/diligence/fundraising, or plan continuation filings for broader claims.
guidance: Industries commonly using Track One include biotech, pharma, medical devices, polymer science, engineering, and software. Align Track One use with product timelines and portfolio strategy.

name: Portfolio and Continuation Strategy Considerations
description: Consider how Track One fits within a broader portfolio strategy, especially if pursuing continuation filings or parallel applications.
guidance: Because Track One prosecution is fast and claim expansion during Track One is impractical, applicants often secure narrow protection early and pursue broader claim scopes in continuations.

name: Licensee exceeding license may be sued as infringer or for breach
description: If the licensee uses the patented invention beyond the limits of the license or in any unauthorized way, there has been a violation of a right secured to the patentee and the licensee may be sued either under the contract or as an infringer.
guidance: When a licensee exceeds express covenants or granted scope, remedies include infringement litigation or breach of contract claims. (Goodyear v. Union India Rubber Co.; Pope Mfg. Co. v. Owsley.)

name: A licensee who takes license with full knowledge of adverse claims cannot later attack licensor's patent
description: A licensee taking his license with full knowledge of the adverse claims against the patent, and enjoying the benefit of his license, cannot then attack the licensor's patent.
guidance: Acceptance with knowledge and enjoyment of benefits generally estops the licensee from subsequently denying validity; this supports stability of license arrangements. (Jones v. Burnham; Parkhurst v. Kinsman cited.)

name: Board decision outcomes and nonfinality when remand included (37 CFR 1.196(a),(e))
description: The Board may affirm or reverse the examiner's decision in whole or in part on the grounds and claims specified, or remand the application to the examiner; a decision that includes or allows a remand is not a final decision.
guidance: Affirmance of the rejection of a claim on any grounds specified constitutes a general affirmance except as to grounds specifically reversed. After proceedings on remand, the Board may enter an order making its decision final or render a new decision based on all appealed claims as appropriate. Board decisions sometimes set forth a new ground of rejection.

name: Examiner actions when sustained in whole or in part (post-Board affirmance)
description: When the Board affirms a rejection (in whole or part), various examiner actions may follow depending on claim relationships and what stands allowed or rejected.
guidance: Examples: if an independent claim is rejected and a dependent claim is allowed only because it depends on the rejected claim, examiner should either (1) convert dependent claim into independent form by examiner's amendment, cancel claims where rejection affirmed and issue application, or (2) set a one-month time limit for applicant to rewrite the dependent claim in independent form (no 1.136(a) extension). If no reply, cancel appropriate claims and issue application with the allowed claims only. Use suggested notice language (form paragraph 12.20). If uncorrected formal matters remain, take appropriate action but prosecution is otherwise closed.

name: Termination of proceedings and consequences (37 CFR 1.197(c))
description: Proceedings are considered terminated by dismissal of an appeal or failure to timely file an appeal to court or civil action, except where claims stand allowed or nature of decision requires further examiner action; the date of termination is the date the appeal is dismissed or time to appeal expires.
guidance: If court review time (plus allowance for mail) has passed without review, the examiner must take up the application. If a civil action or appeal has been filed, proceedings are considered terminated when that action is terminated (e.g., receiving mandate). In ex parte reexamination, a reexamination certificate should be issued as appropriate.

name: Statutory text: 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph
description: “The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the applicant regards as his invention.”
guidance: This is the textual statutory requirement that underlies definiteness analysis; all claim drafting and examination for indefiniteness is measured against this requirement.

name: Primary purpose of definiteness
description: “The primary purpose of the definiteness requirement for claim language is to ensure that the scope of the claims is clear so that the public is informed of the boundaries of what constitutes infringement of the patent.”
guidance: When assessing definiteness, consider whether the public can determine the claim boundaries; clarity as to scope is the core policy goal.

name: Claims must be precise, clear, correct and unambiguous
description: “An essential purpose of patent examination is to fashion claims that are precise, clear, correct, and unambiguous. Only in this way can uncertainties of claim scope be removed, as much as possible, during the administrative process.”
guidance: Examiners should work to remove uncertainties in claim scope during examination; applicants should draft to achieve these qualities.

name: Two separate requirements under 35 U.S.C. 112 second paragraph
description: “…the claims must set forth the subject matter that applicants regard as their invention; and the claims must particularly point out and distinctly define the metes and bounds of the subject matter that will be protected by the patent grant.”
guidance: Distinguish between (a) claiming what the inventor regards as the invention and (b) defining clear metes and bounds of protection.

name: Test for definiteness (POSITA in light of specification)
description: “The test for definiteness under 35 U.S.C. § 112, second paragraph, is whether 'those skilled in the art would understand what is claimed when the claim is read in light of the specification.'”
guidance: Read claims in view of the disclosure; apply the understanding of a person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA) as of the filing date.

name: Analyze definiteness in context (three-part lens)
description: “Definiteness of claim language must be analyzed, not in a vacuum, but in light of: (A) the content of the particular application disclosure; (B) the teachings of the prior art; and (C) the claim interpretation that would be given by one possessing the ordinary level of skill in the pertinent art at the time the invention was made.”
guidance: Always consider specification disclosure, prior art teachings, and POSITA understanding together when evaluating indefiniteness.

name: If claim amenable to two or more plausible constructions
description: “If claim is amenable to two or more plausible constructions, applicant is required to amend claim to more precisely define metes and bounds of claimed invention or claim is indefinite under § 112, ¶ 2.”
guidance: When multiple plausible meanings exist, examiners should require amendment (or issue a 112(2) rejection) rather than assume a narrower meaning.

name: When a claim is subject to more than one interpretation and at least one renders unpatentable
description: “Where the claim is subject to more than one interpretation and at least one interpretation would render the claim unpatentable over the prior art, examiner should reject the claim as indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, and should reject the claim over the prior art based on the interpretation of the claim that renders the prior art applicable.”
guidance: Examiner should (A) issue a 112(2) rejection and (B) enter a prior-art rejection based on the interpretation that would make the claim unpatentable.

name: Importing limitations from the specification
description: “Limitations appearing in the specification but not recited in the claim should not be read into the claim. . . . Claims must be interpreted 'in view of the specification' without importing limitations from the specification into the claims unnecessarily.”
guidance: Do not inject unrecited spec limitations into claim scope; use specification to inform meaning but not to rewrite claim scope.

name: Examiners must state reasons when making 112(2) rejection
description: “If upon review of a claim in its entirety, the examiner concludes that a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, is appropriate, such a rejection should be made and an analysis as to why the phrase(s) used in the claim is ‘vague and indefinite’ should be included in the Office action.”
guidance: Office actions must explain why language is vague/indefinite, citing specific claim phrases and reasoning.

name: Explain whether rejection is indefiniteness or failure to claim what applicant regards as invention
description: “If a rejection is based on 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, the examiner should further explain whether the rejection is based on indefiniteness or on the failure to claim what applicants regard as their invention.”
guidance: Differentiate and explicitly state the basis—indefiniteness (scope unclear) vs. failure to claim applicant's invention (doesn't claim subject matter applicant regards as invention).

name: No per se rules — fact specific inquiry
description: “Office policy is not to employ per se rules to make technical rejections. Examples of claim language which have been held to be indefinite set forth in MPEP § 2173.05(d) are fact specific and should not be applied as per se rules.”
guidance: Avoid categorical black-letter rules; analyze each claim on its facts and context.

name: Breadth is not the same as indefiniteness
description: “Breadth of a claim is not to be equated with indefiniteness.”
guidance: A broad claim can still be definite; undue breadth may be addressed under other statutes (e.g., 102/103, enablement), not automatically under 112(2).

name: Relationship between 112(2) rejections and art rejections
description: “When making a rejection over prior art in these circumstances, it is important for the examiner to point out how the claim is being interpreted.”
guidance: When issuing art rejections where interpretation matters, clearly state the claim construction used and, if ambiguity exists, consider separate 112(2) and art rejections as appropriate.

name: Do not base art rejection on speculation about meaning
description: “[A] rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 should not be based on considerable speculation about the meaning of terms employed in a claim or assumptions that must be made as to the scope of the claims.”
guidance: If claim interpretation is highly uncertain, avoid relying on speculative constructions for obviousness rejections.

name: Suggesting claim language vs rejecting
description: “Examiners are encouraged to suggest claim language to applicants to improve the clarity or precision of the language used, but should not reject claims or insist on their own preferences if other modes of expression selected by applicants satisfy the statutory requirement.”
guidance: If applicant's wording meets 112(2), examiner should suggest improvements without issuing a rejection based on stylistic preferences.

name: Product-by-process claims are proper
description: “A product-by-process claim, which is a product claim that defines the claimed product in terms of the process by which it is made, is proper.”
guidance: Product-by-process format is acceptable; evaluate definiteness in light of statutory and case law guidance.

name: Reference to limitations in another claim is acceptable
description: “A claim which makes reference to a preceding claim to define a limitation is an acceptable claim construction which should not necessarily be rejected as improper or confusing under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph.”
guidance: Referencing earlier claims (e.g., 'product produced by the method of claim 1') is permissible, provided the referenced claim is clear and not ambiguous.

name: References to cancelled claims
description: Example: Claim 1 cancelled; Claim 2 refers to product produced by method of claim 1 — “Claim 2 should [be] rejected under 35 USC 112 2nd using FP 7.34.01 and then examined under remaining statutes.”
guidance: A claim depending on a canceled claim is defective and should be rejected under 112(2) (lack of antecedent/definition) and examined for other statutory problems.

name: Dependent claim must further limit the independent claim
description: Example: Claim 1 recites full SEQ ID; Claim 2 recites fragment — Claim 2 should be objected to for not further limiting claim 1 pursuant to 37 CFR 1.75(c).
guidance: A dependent claim that is broader than its independent claim (i.e., does not further limit) is improper in form and should be objected to or amended to proper dependent or independent form.

name: Single claim mixing product and process (product + use) is indefinite
description: “A single claim which claims both an apparatus and the method steps of using the apparatus is indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph.”
guidance: Do not combine apparatus and usage steps in a single claim; separate apparatus and method claims are appropriate.

name: ‘Use’ claims lacking essential steps are indefinite
description: “Attempts to claim a process without setting forth any steps involved in the process generally raises an issue of indefiniteness under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph.”
guidance: Claims that merely recite a 'use' without active steps (e.g., 'use of X to isolate Y') may be indefinite; consider alternative rejections under 101 or 112 for missing essential steps.

name: Preamble effect: preamble can be sufficient in process claims
description: Example: 'A method of treating diabetes comprising administering compound X to a subject in need thereof.' — This claim is considered complete with respect to 35 USC 112 2nd paragraph; no requirement that a preamble need be repeated in a final 'wherein' clause.
guidance: A preamble that states intended use/field does not necessarily render the claim indefinite; analyze completeness in context.

name: Use of exemplary language ('for example', 'such as') can create indefiniteness
description: Example: 'A composition comprising Product X and a protease, for example, chymotrypsin.' — Because protease (generic) and chymotrypsin (specific) are not identical in scope, the phrase 'for example' raises the question as to which term is required by the claim; 'the phrase "for example" renders the claim indefinite because it is unclear whether the limitations following the phrase are part of the claimed invention.'
guidance: Avoid ambiguous 'exemplary' phrasing in claims; if used, clarify whether the example is limiting or illustrative, otherwise 112(2) rejection may be warranted.

name: Claims using 'derivative thereof' require clear definition
description: Examples 5A–5C: Claims reciting 'SEQ ID NO:1 or a derivative thereof' may be indefinite if 'derivatives' are not clearly defined in the specification or prior art; but if derivatives are well known or defined, a 112(2) rejection may not be warranted.
guidance: If claiming 'derivative' or similar open-ended terms, ensure the specification or common knowledge supplies adequate boundaries; otherwise issue 112(2) rejection.

name: ‘Derived from’ may be acceptable if supported by specification
description: Example: 'neural stem cells derived from a spinal cord.' If the specification teaches isolation/derivation from spinal cord, no 112(2) issue arises despite broad claim.
guidance: Context and specification support can make broad 'derived from' language definite.

name: Chemical claims: lack of full structure does not automatically render indefinite
description: “A claim to a chemical compound is not indefinite merely because a structure is not presented or because a partial structure is presented. Chemical compounds may be claimed by a name that adequately describes the material to one skilled in the art. A compound of unknown structure may be claimed by a combination of physical and chemical characteristics. . . . A compound may also be claimed in terms of the process by which it is made without raising an issue of indefiniteness.”
guidance: Evaluate chemical claims in light of whether POSITA can ascertain the claimed compound from names, characteristics, or process descriptions; missing structure alone is not dispositive.

name: Undefined variables in chemical formulae are indefinite
description: Example 7A: Claim with formula where variable 'Z' is not defined in the claim or specification — 'Reject Claim 1 under 35 U.S.C 112 2nd paragraph.'
guidance: If variables in a claimed formula are not defined or bounded in the specification, issue 112(2) rejection; if spec defines variable (Example 7B), no rejection is warranted.

name: Functional claim language acceptable when boundaries set
description: “A functional limitation is an attempt to define something by what it does, rather than by what it is ... There is nothing inherently wrong with defining some part of an invention in functional terms. Functional language does not, in and of itself, render a claim improper.”
guidance: Assess functional limitations by context, specification support, and POSITA knowledge. Functional language that sets definite boundaries (e.g., known chemical functional definitions) may be allowable.

name: Numerical ranges: nested narrow range within broad range in same claim is indefinite
description: “Use of a narrow numerical range that falls within a broader range in the same claim may render the claim indefinite when the boundaries of the claim are not discernible. ... A broad range or limitation together with a narrow range or limitation that falls within the broad range or limitation (in the same claim) is considered indefinite, since the resulting claim does not clearly set forth the metes and bounds of the patent protection desired.”
guidance: Avoid claiming overlapping/nested ranges in the same claim; disclose ranges properly in spec and claim boundaries clearly.

name: Parentheses: permitted when synonymous, problematic when mixing scopes
description: Example 13: 'glycerol (glycerin)' permitted because terms are identical in scope. Example 14: 'protease (chymotrypsin)' problematic because generic and specific terms differ in scope — 'the use of parentheses raises the question as to which term is required by the claim.'
guidance: Use parentheses only when the parenthetical term is an exact synonym; mixed-scope parentheses can create indefiniteness and merit 112(2) rejection.

name: Use of trademarks in claims is improper
description: Example 15: Claim reciting 'Velcro attachment' — trademarks identify source, not goods; 'a trademark or trade name is used to identify a source of goods, and not the goods themselves. Thus, a trademark or trade name does not identify or describe the goods associated with the trademark or trade name.'
guidance: Do not use trademarks/trade names as claim limitations to identify materials/products; such usage is improper and should be objected to/rejected.

name: Actions on Petitions to the Director — Patent matters (categories and counts)
description: Counts of actions on patent petitions to the Director broken out by petition nature: acceptance of late assignments, late issue fees, late priority papers, access; certificates of correction; deferment of issue; entity status change; filing date restorations; maintenance fees; revivals; Rule 47 (37 CFR 1.47); supervisory authority; suspend rules; withdrawal from issue; late claim for priority; withdraw as attorney; matters not provided for (37 CFR 1.182); make special; patent term adjustment/extension; and totals.
guidance: Tables show annual counts; readers should consult footnotes and CFR references for procedural standards governing each petition type.

name: Re-issue vs separate patent where matter inseparable
description: If new matter is inseparable from that already patented (i.e., cannot be separately claimed), a later patent covering it must fail and re-issue of the original may be the proper remedy.
guidance: Where the later patent covers matter already protected by the prior patent (especially where the later claim is generic or broad), the later grant may be void; re-issue doctrine applies and in some cases the inventor must seek re-issue rather than a new patent. Authorities: Derby and other cases; re-issue considerations discussed in §§ 687-692, cross-referenced.

name: Single structural similarity — recognized class criterion
description: Members share a 'single structural similarity' when they belong to the same recognized physical or chemical class or the same art‑recognized class (i.e., the art expects members will behave similarly in the claimed invention).
guidance: Practical test: each member could be substituted for another with the expectation of achieving the same intended result. Example: various fasteners for a disposable diaper may be an art‑recognized class because prior art shows substitutability to achieve repositionable/refastenable function. Note: existence of such a recognized class can tend to prove equivalence and, if one member is anticipated, may render the group unpatentable absent convincing evidence of non‑equivalency (In re Ruff).

name: Single structural similarity — substantial structural feature for chemical compounds
description: When alternatives are chemical compounds not in a recognized class, they may still be proper if they share a substantial structural feature essential to a common use, and the use flows from that feature.
guidance: Assess claimed compounds as wholes (do not break down into elements of substituents). Example: coumarin core common to dyes (Harnisch) or phosphoric acid diester backbone with common antimycotic activity (Hozumi). The structural feature must be substantial and disclosed as essential to the utility.

name: Evaluative lens: treat claimed compounds as wholes
description: In determining propriety of a Markush grouping, each compound must be considered as a whole and not broken down into elements or components.
guidance: Avoid focusing only on the variable moiety defined by Markush language; instead examine whether the overall molecules share the required substantial structural similarity and common use. Decisions are fact‑specific and case‑by‑case (Harnisch, In re Jones).

name: Improper Markush grouping — examiner rejection procedure (Form Paragraph 8.40)
description: When species do not share a single structural similarity or a common use, reject the claim as containing an improper Markush grouping using Form Paragraph 8.40.
guidance: Form paragraph language should be used; bracketed insertions must be completed (bracket 1: claim numbers; bracket 2: description of the Markush group; bracket 3: explanation why the alternatives fail the two prongs). Explain why alternatives are not in a recognized class and/or not functionally equivalent, and/or why they do not share a substantial structural feature and associated common use. Note: if an election of species requirement is appropriate, use this form only after applicant has made an election.

name: Suggestions to applicant for overcoming improper Markush rejection
description: Examiners should suggest how applicant may overcome an improper Markush grouping rejection.
guidance: Examples: suggest a proper Markush grouping based on the specification, or suggest that applicant present each alternative (or grouping of patentably indistinct alternatives) in a series of independent or dependent claims. Do not suggest any grouping that clearly would not meet 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or would clearly lack adequate written description if presented in a separate claim.

name: Indefiniteness under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) for Markush claims
description: If a person skilled in the art cannot determine the metes and bounds of a Markush claim because they cannot envision all of the members, the claim is indefinite and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b).
guidance: Apply 112(b) when a boundary cannot be drawn separating embodiments encompassed by the claim from those that are not. See also MPEP §2173.05(h). This rejection is in addition to any improper Markush grouping rejection.

name: Maintaining, overcoming, and reconsidering improper Markush grouping rejections
description: The improper Markush grouping rejection should be maintained until the claim is amended to include only members that share a single structural similarity and a common use, or the applicant presents convincing arguments that the members do share these features.
guidance: If applicant fails to overcome the rejection, maintain it. However, when all claims are otherwise in condition for allowance, the examiner should reconsider the propriety of the rejection and withdraw it if, in light of the prior art and record, the alternatives do in fact share a single structural similarity and common use. No Markush claim may be allowed until improper grouping is overcome or withdrawn and all other conditions of patentability are satisfied.

name: 35 U.S.C. 102 — Definition of novelty/prior art
description: A person is entitled to a patent unless the claimed invention was patented, described in a printed publication, in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public before the effective filing date of the claimed invention, or was described in an issued patent or published application effectively filed before the effective filing date.
guidance: MPEP quotes statutory language and editor notes applicability to AIA vs pre‑AIA filings. This is the baseline novelty/prior art standard examiners apply when assessing novelty.

name: 35 U.S.C. 102 — Exceptions for disclosures in patents/applications and common ownership
description: A disclosure in a patent or application is not prior art under subsection (a)(2) if (A) the subject matter was obtained from the inventor; (B) the subject matter had been publicly disclosed by the inventor before the patent/application was effectively filed; or (C) the subject matter and the claimed invention were owned by the same person or subject to obligation of assignment to the same person.
guidance: Apply these exceptions and consider the common ownership provision, including the related joint research agreement conditions: (1) subject matter developed by parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the effective filing date, (2) invention made as a result of activities within the scope of the joint research agreement, and (3) patent application discloses or is amended to disclose the parties to the joint research agreement.

name: 35 U.S.C. 102 — Effective filing date of patents and published applications as prior art
description: For determining whether a patent or application is prior art under subsection (a)(2), the effective filing date is the actual filing date, or if entitled to priority/benefit under listed sections, the earliest such application's filing date that describes the subject matter.
guidance: When assessing whether an issued patent or published application is prior art, determine whether the patent/application claims benefit/priority to earlier filings; use the earliest effective filing date for subject matter described therein as the relevant prior art date.

name: 35 U.S.C. 103 — Obviousness standard
description: A patent may not be obtained if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date to a person having ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: Patentability under 103 is assessed by considering whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious to a PHOSITA. The manner in which the invention was made does not negate patentability. The MPEP also cites statutory variations (pre‑AIA language) and special biotechnological process provisions (see subsection regarding composition/process claims owned by same person).

name: Biotechnology/process‑composition exception under 35 U.S.C. 103(b) (pre-AIA phrasing included)
description: Under subsection (b) (editor note: applicable language for certain filings), a biotechnological process using or resulting in a composition of matter that is novel and nonobvious may be considered nonobvious if claims to the process and composition are contained in the same application or separate applications having the same effective filing date, and both were owned by the same person at the time invented.
guidance: If these conditions are met, a patent issued on a process must also contain claims to the composition of matter used or made by that process. This statutory carve‑out modifies obviousness analysis for biotech process/composition claim sets and includes ownership/assignment conditions.

name: Require return of property captured in raids when claimed to preserve peace
description: "I made it known that all horses thus obtained must be returned when claimed, and this has been done."
guidance: Establish and enforce clear rules that property taken in raids must be returned upon claim to reduce cycles of retaliation and maintain order.

name: Institution standard — reasonable likelihood of prevailing
description: The Board may deny institution if the Petition fails to establish a reasonable likelihood that Petitioner would prevail in showing unpatentability of the challenged claims.
guidance: The prior Decision denied institution because the Petition did not sufficiently show Mitchell meets the limitation 'propagating failure information by the detecting node to each node of the other nodes...'. The Decision evaluated whether Petitioner presented sufficient evidence and explanation to meet the reasonable-likelihood threshold.

name: Whether the Board engaged in implicit claim construction
description: Determine whether the Board implicitly construed the disputed claim limitation (here, 'propagating failure information by the detecting node to each node of the other nodes') and, if so, whether that implicit construction was correct.
guidance: The Director/DRP reviews whether the original panel's analysis effectively construed the claim even if not labeled a 'claim construction.' The DRP found there was an implicit construction and that it was proper in this case.

name: Plain and ordinary meaning may be inadequate (O2 Micro standard)
description: A determination that a claim term 'needs no construction' or has the 'plain and ordinary meaning' may be inadequate when the term has more than one 'ordinary' meaning or when reliance on a term's 'ordinary' meaning does not resolve the parties' dispute.
guidance: When parties disagree about the meaning of claim language, simply stating 'plain and ordinary meaning' is insufficient; the Board may need to resolve the dispute (and that resolution may amount to claim construction).

name: Claim language controls — read 'each node' / 'all other nodes' broadly
description: When claim language recites 'each node' or 'all other nodes' without limiting language, those terms should be read broadly to encompass all nodes (upstream and downstream), unless the specification or prosecution history requires otherwise.
guidance: The DRP agreed the claim words ('each node'/'all other nodes') do not specify upstream/downstream and thus support a construction including all nodes. The presence of 'each'/'all' was read literally to include every node traversed by the set of links.

name: Use of specification and prosecution history in claim construction
description: Consult the specification and prosecution history to resolve claim-meaning disputes; statements in the specification and applicant's prosecution remarks can support a broad or narrow construction.
guidance: The specification's description of propagating a remote fault indication to 'the other nodes' and prosecution statements describing 'sending a failure information message to all the other nodes' supported the DRP's broad construction. Prosecution distinctions (e.g., contrasting Grenier's single-selector-node behavior) also inform construction.

name: Petition must map each claim element to prior art (37 C.F.R. § 42.104(b)(4))
description: A petition must 'specify where each element of the claim is found in the prior art patents or printed publications relied upon.'
guidance: The Board is not required to develop undeveloped arguments for a petitioner. If a petitioner fails to make clear mappings or to develop an argument in the Petition, the Board may disregard implied or undeveloped positions. The Decision cites 37 C.F.R. § 42.104(b)(4) and admonishes that arguments cannot be buried or only hinted at.

name: Sufficiency to extend prior-art teaching — must explain obviousness of extension
description: To rely on a prior-art reference that teaches a narrower practice (e.g., downstream-only propagation), a petitioner must provide sufficient reasoning showing why a person of ordinary skill would have found it obvious to modify or extend that teaching to cover the claimed broader practice (e.g., propagation to each/all nodes).
guidance: The prior Decision found Petitioner's showing insufficient to extend Mitchell's downstream-only propagation to the claim's requirement of propagation to each/all nodes. Petitioner must explain the rationale for the extension and why it would have been obvious.

name: One-instance showing can suffice for unpatentability (precedential case law), but must be presented timely
description: Federal Circuit precedent recognizes that a single instance that meets the plain language of a claim can be sufficient to render the claim unpatentable.
guidance: Petitioner cited cases (Hewlett‑Packard, Unwired Planet, etc.) in the Request, but because those legal arguments were not presented in the original Petition/Prelim. Resp., the original panel could not have misapprehended them. Legal standards can be dispositive but must be argued in the record before the deciding panel.

name: Scope of Director Review / Delegated Review Panel
description: Director Review (or delegated DRP review) is limited to the issues the Director ordered reviewed — here, (1) whether the Board engaged in an implicit claim construction and if so whether correct; and (2) whether the Board properly considered Petitioner's argument that Mitchell reads on the propagating-failure limitation.
guidance: The DRP's authority and analysis conform to the Director's order; review is focused on the ordered questions and does not expand to newly-raised arguments outside the scope or not properly before the original panel.

name: Rosen/Durling two-step test for design-patent obviousness
description: Durling outlines a two-step analysis for design obviousness: (1) identify a primary (Rosen) reference whose design characteristics are 'basically the same' as the claimed design by discerning the visual impression of the design as a whole; (2) if a satisfactory primary reference exists, determine whether an ordinary designer would have modified the primary reference, using secondary references, to create a design with the same overall visual appearance as the claimed design.
guidance: Step one is a threshold: without a Rosen reference that is basically the same, the obviousness inquiry ends. Step two examines whether the modifications are suggested and would preserve the overall visual impression.

name: Rosen primary-reference requirement ('basically the same')
description: There must be 'a reference, a something in existence, the design characteristics of which are basically the same as the claimed design' to support a holding of obviousness (Rosen / citing Jennings).
guidance: This is the mandatory starting point under Durling—courts look for a single reference that creates essentially the same visual impression as the claimed design; failure to identify such a reference is dispositive under precedent applied by the Board and this Court.

name: Subdivided first-step analysis (visual-impression articulation)
description: To assess whether a Rosen reference exists, a tribunal must (1) discern the correct visual impression created by the patented design as a whole; and (2) determine whether there is a single reference that creates 'basically the same' visual impression.
guidance: Challengers should articulate the claimed design's overall visual impression and identify how a reference matches it; the Board may identify specific element differences (e.g., wheel-arch shape, door cut line, protrusion, sculpting, creases, inflection/concavity lines) to explain why impressions differ.

name: Types of human feedback available in patent prosecution
description: Human feedback types that can be derived from patent/prosecution data: (a) preference ratings, (b) summarizations, (c) corrections, (d) demonstrations, and (e) specific reward signals (drafting intent).
guidance: Examples: (a) granted vs rejected/pre-grant as preference ratings; (b) abstracts as summarizations; (c) revised claims indicating corrections such as fixing antecedent-basis errors; (d) dependent claims as demonstrations of how independent claims derive dependents; (e) reward signals like desired claim length or number of limiting terms to reflect drafting intent. The study focuses on (a) and (e) due to resource limits.

name: Reward function: claim length control
description: Define a reward function that encourages generation of claims of a specified length (broader vs narrower scope control). The reward is based on generated text length relative to a maximum length threshold.
guidance: Implemented reward pseudocode: truncate generated text to max_len; if no end-of-claim tag then reward = 0; else reward = 1 + len(s)/float(max_len). The paper experiments with max_len values (e.g., 512, 1024) and tracks training reward progression, average claim length, and side effects (e.g., limiting terms count). Rationale: shorter claims tend to be broader (higher infringement risk), longer claims may avoid anticipation and obviousness rejections but are narrower.

name: Reward function: limiting terms count (e.g., 'wherein')
description: Define a reward function that counts occurrences of limiting terms/clauses (such as 'wherein') in a claim and rewards more occurrences to encourage narrower, more allowable claims.
guidance: Rationale: limiting clauses typically narrow claim scope and can increase allowance likelihood. The experiment counts limiting terms to compute rewards; tradeoffs are noted (more limiting terms -> higher chance of allowance but narrower scope and lower infringement probability). The paper discusses legal nuance (some 'wherein' clauses may not be limiting if they merely state intended results).

name: Joint reward combining claim length and limiting terms
description: Combine the length-based and limiting-terms reward functions into a single joint reward to control both length and scope simultaneously.
guidance: The joint reward in experiments is a composition of the two rule-based reward functions. The paper notes that joint rewards can also combine learned reward models and rule-based functions, but each component should be validated separately before combining.

name: Use only claim one (first claim) as text target
description: Restrict dataset and model focus to the first claim (claim 1) of patent documents for tractability and interpretability.
guidance: Reasoning: reduces data volume for quicker iterations and clearer proof-of-concept; AIPCO datasets were constructed by joining AIPD category metadata with PatentsView claim-one text. Experiments and examples (generated claims) are all for claim one.

name: Dataset construction: AIPCO (AIPD + PatentsView) by AI component
description: Construct training datasets by combining AIPD (AI patent identifiers) with PatentsView claim text to form eight component-specific datasets: AIPCO-ML, AIPCO-EVO, AIPCO-NLP, AIPCO-SPEECH, AIPCO-VISION, AIPCO-KR, AIPCO-PLANNING, AIPCO-HARDWARE.
guidance: AIPD provides doc identifiers and AI component labels but not text; PatentsView supplies claim text and crosswalks. The paper provides counts and average lengths for granted vs pre-grant per component. Practical note: PatentsView DB dump inspected lacked claim text; the author assembled datasets via downloadable tables and crosswalks.

name: Office Action datasets are valuable but limited in current availability
description: Office actions (examiner rejections and rationale) are an ideal source of explicit human feedback (rejections, affected claims, prior art) but existing office-action datasets lack coverage/connectivity to the AIPD data and often lack the claim text needed for language model training.
guidance: The Office Action Research Dataset covers many office actions (2008–2017) but doesn't align well with AIPD and lacks claim text; Patent Examination Data System has similar limitations. The paper therefore uses granted/pre-grant status rather than office action content for RM training, while noting office actions as future enhancement.

name: Controllability requirement: model should reflect drafting intent
description: Generative models should be controllable to reflect patent drafting intents such as favoring broader scope or higher allowance probability (via length, limiting term usage, etc.).
guidance: The paper motivates reward functions and RM design by the need to encode drafting preferences (e.g., shorter claims for broader scope vs longer claims to avoid anticipation). It shows experiments demonstrating the model can be steered toward different drafting intents using reward functions and PPO.

name: Implementation detail: explicit end-of-claim tag required for reward calculation
description: The reward functions rely on the presence of a specific tag '<|end of claim|>' to detect claim termination; absence of this tag after truncation yields zero reward.
guidance: In the claim-length reward implementation, generated text is truncated to max_len and only if the '<|end of claim|>' tag is present is the length-based reward computed (otherwise reward=0). This is both an anti-pattern guard (discourages overlong incomplete outputs) and an implementation requirement.

name: Use of broad claims
description: Claims drafted broadly to maximize litigation reach.
guidance: Broad claims suggest applicant incentives to capture competitors rather than accurately reflect inventive contribution; check whether breadth is supported by disclosure and whether claim scope maps to specific embodiments.

name: Functional/result-oriented claim language
description: Claims that define inventions by function or result rather than structural detail.
guidance: Functional language is a marker of low-quality drafting unless properly tied to 35 U.S.C. §112(f)/means-plus-function treatment and corresponding structure in the specification; avoid uncabined functional claiming without support.

name: Continuation chains targeting later-developed competitor products
description: Continuation practice used to draft claims after competitors commercialize products, i.e., post-hoc claim drafting.
