description: A specification should describe the invention with reasonable certainty so others can know whether they violate the patent and, after expiry, can make machines correctly; but courts give a liberal construction to sustain inventors if practicable.
guidance: Reasons: Act of Congress requires particular specification and pointing of the part claimed; public must be able to know the scope. Courts should encourage ingenuity by protecting legitimate inventions, yet not allow monopolies of what belonged to others or the public.

name: Establish the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim
description: Establish the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim.
guidance: Construe the claim in accordance with BRI before performing the eligibility analysis; record the BRI in Section I so subsequent determinations (e.g., whether the claim recites an abstract idea) reflect that interpretation.

name: Determine whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea (Step 2A)
description: A claim is 'directed' to an abstract idea when the abstract idea is recited (i.e., set forth or described) in the claim. Courts have found concepts such as fundamental economic practices, certain methods of organizing human activity, ideas themselves (standing alone), or mathematical relationships/formulae to be abstract ideas.
guidance: Choose A, B, or C: A) No — claim does not recite a concept similar to those found abstract; conclude SME and continue with other patentability requirements. B) Yes but streamlined analysis appropriate — eligibility is self-evident and a full analysis not needed. C) Yes — identify the limitation(s) that recite the abstract idea and explain why those limitations are an abstract idea; then continue with Step 2B. Assistance: refer to case law chart and 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance discussions.

name: Use streamlined analysis if eligibility is self-evident
description: Yes, but the streamlined analysis is appropriate as the eligibility is self-evident, and a full eligibility analysis is not needed.
guidance: Apply streamlined analysis when applicant's claimed invention, as explained in Section I, is not focused on the abstract idea and the claim clearly does not attempt to tie up an abstract idea such that others cannot practice it. Refer to February 2015 Training Slides for examples of when streamlined analysis is appropriate. Conclude SME analysis and proceed with other patentability considerations.

name: Identify claim limitation(s) that recite the abstract idea and explain why
description: If the claim is directed to an abstract idea, identify the limitation(s) in the claim that set forth or describe the abstract idea and explain why the recited subject matter is an abstract idea.
guidance: List the specific claim elements that recite the abstract idea and provide reasons why those limitations are considered abstract (e.g., they recite a fundamental economic practice, a method of organizing human activity, an idea standing alone, or a mathematical relationship/formula). Continue to Step 2B after identification.

name: Presence of additional elements beyond the abstract idea (Step 2B - threshold)
description: Are there any additional elements (features/limitations/step) recited in the claim beyond the abstract idea identified above?
guidance: Choose 1 or 2: 1) No — if there are no other elements, conclude SME analysis by making a §101 rejection (use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015). Consider whether disclosure contains elements that could be added to render the claim eligible and identify them for possible suggestions to applicant. 2) Yes — list the claim elements in addition to the abstract idea and continue with evaluation of their significance.

name: Evaluate significance of additional elements — search for an inventive concept
description: Identifying additional elements and evaluating their significance involves the search for an 'inventive concept' in the claim.
guidance: Consider all identified additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the abstract idea. Reasons supporting significance can include one or more of the following: improves another technology or technical field; improves the functioning of a computer itself; applies the abstract idea with, or by use of, a particular machine (not a generic computer performing generic functions; not adding the words 'apply it'); effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing; adds a specific limitation other than what is well-understood, routine and conventional in the field (not appending well-understood, routine, and conventional activities at a high level of generality); adds unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application (not insignificant extrasolution activity such as mere data gathering); adds meaningful limitations that amount to more than generally linking the use of the abstract idea to a particular technological environment.

name: Conclude whether the claim amounts to 'significantly more' (Step 2B conclusion)
description: Decide whether the additional elements, individually or in combination, result in the claim amounting to significantly more than the abstract idea.
guidance: If yes, state why the additional elements amount to significantly more and conclude SME analysis (then continue with other patentability requirements). If no, conclude SME analysis by making a §101 rejection and continue with other patentability requirements (use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015). If appropriate, clarify the record with remarks explaining how the claim both recites an abstract idea and nevertheless amounts to significantly more due to particular elements.

name: Suggest amendments and record assumptions when applicable
description: If the claim could be amended to fall within a statutory category or include elements that might make it eligible, identify and consider suggesting those elements to applicant; make any assumptions clear in the record.
guidance: If no amendment is possible, conclude SME analysis and continue examination under other patentability requirements. If analyzing under an assumption (e.g., claim amended to a statutory category), explicitly record that assumption in the Office action. Identify elements from the disclosure that might be added to the claim to achieve eligibility and propose them to applicant where appropriate.

name: Materiality — 'but for' standard for non-disclosure cases
description: Information is material if 'but for' the failure to disclose or misrepresentation, the PTO would not have allowed one or more claims — i.e., more likely than not the PTO would have refused one or more claims had it been aware of the withheld/true information.
guidance: To decide, use the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim(s) under consideration and apply the more-likely-than-not standard as the PTO would. If this standard shows PTO would not have allowed claims, the withholding/misrepresentation is material even if the claims might still be invalid in the lawsuit; defendant still bears overall burden to prove inequitable conduct by the highly probable standard. (Therasense).

name: Damages — general standard and purpose
description: If accused device/method infringes any valid asserted claims, determine damages to compensate the plaintiff. Plaintiff must prove each element of damages, including amount, by a preponderance of the evidence (more likely than not). Damages must compensate plaintiff to put it in about the same financial position it would have been in absent the infringement; damages may not be punitive or include interest as an extra addition.
guidance: A damage award cannot be less than a reasonable royalty. Instructions about damages do not indicate which party should win; they are guidance if jury finds for plaintiff. (Cites 35 U.S.C. § 284 and Federal Circuit precedent.)

name: Date damages begin — Alternate B (disputed notice date, product claims)
description: If the date of notice is disputed, plaintiff must prove by preponderance that defendant was actually notified on the date alleged. Notice can be given either by (1) public marking (marking substantially all products with 'patent'/'pat' and patent number or internet marking), which starts damages when marking began, or (2) specific notice to defendant about alleged infringement, which starts damages when defendant received that notice.
guidance: If plaintiff and licensees did not properly mark substantially all products and did not notify defendant specifically before suit, plaintiff can only recover damages after filing date. Internet marking is acceptable if labeling links to a posting connecting product to patent number. If adequacy of marking is at issue, additional instructions required. (Cites 35 U.S.C. § 287 and case law.)

name: Phased claim winnowing (limits on asserted claims and prior art)
description: Adopt a phased process to limit the number of asserted claims, prior art references, claim terms to be construed, and accused products—typically with initial 'preliminary election' and later 'final election' stages.
guidance: Follow the Federal Circuit Advisory Council Model Order (example): Preliminary Election no more than 10 claims per patent and total 32 claims (not later than 40 days after certain document production); Final Election not later than 28 days after Claim Construction Order identifying no more than 5 claims per patent and total 16 claims. Parties may propose lower/higher limits based on case-specific factors (commonality, number/diversity of accused products, technology complexity). Courts should ensure opportunity to add claims presenting unique liability/damages issues.

name: Identification of disputed claim terms and meet-and-confer
description: Require parties to identify to each other the claim terms they propose to be construed and the intrinsic/extrinsic evidence they intend to rely upon, then confer.
guidance: This step narrows disputed terms, focuses issues, and prevents last-minute changes, but meeting and conferring may extend the time needed for claim construction.

name: Joint claim-construction statement submission
description: Require a joint claim-construction statement listing stipulated constructions, each side's proposed constructions for disputed terms, and the evidence (intrinsic and extrinsic) on which they rely.
guidance: Helps focus disputes, provides the court a roadmap for briefing, reduces repeated changes in positions, and aids judicial efficiency. May leave some disputes unresolved, delaying parties' ability to evaluate merits; phased approaches can mitigate.

name: Claim-construction briefing procedures (page limits/simultaneous briefing)
description: Adopt briefing rules such as page limits and simultaneous opening and opposing briefs without replies to constrain and structure claim-construction submissions.
guidance: Such procedures can reduce unnecessary material and speed resolution, but may prevent parties from fully addressing each other's arguments if meeting/conferring was inadequate. Courts should choose procedures mindful of fairness and thoroughness.

name: Preliminary claim construction for preliminary injunction motions
description: Preliminary injunction motions usually require a preliminary construction of at least the key claim terms implicated by the injunctive relief request.
guidance: Because injunctions hinge on likely success on the merits, courts should identify and construe terms needed to assess infringement and validity at the preliminary stage.

name: Step-wise winnowing (before construction, after construction, before trial)
description: Apply staged limitations: initial limits on asserted claims before claim construction, further limits following claim construction, and final trimming before trial.
guidance: Allows plaintiffs to refine theories as discovery and construction proceed while controlling complexity and preserving ability to add claims with unique issues. Courts should ensure the process is not arbitrary and preserves parties' rights.

name: Pleading requirements for infringement and willfulness
description: Pleadings must state infringement adequately; willful infringement claims implicate issues such as opinions of counsel and related privilege considerations.
guidance: Courts should evaluate sufficiency of pleadings; willfulness allegations may require particular facts supporting a claim of deliberate or reckless behavior and affect discovery (e.g., opinions of counsel). Privilege issues must be handled carefully.

name: Factors affecting likelihood of settlement for case categories
description: Recognize categories of patent cases with differing settlement prospects and identify factors (e.g., strength of claims, damages exposure, complexity) that affect settlement likeliness.
guidance: Use case categorization to prioritize settlement resources and tailor mediation strategies; consider whether early claim construction, damages narrowing, or phased proceedings will encourage settlement.

name: Patentable subject-matter requirement
description: Every patent must satisfy the requirement for patentable subject-matter (also called patent eligibility or the requirement for 'an invention'); the claimed invention must be the sort of thing that could lead to a patent.
guidance: Most systems define subject-matter negatively (things are patentable unless excluded by statute or case law). Once subject-matter is satisfied, assessment turns to fact-specific criteria such as novelty, non-obviousness, industrial applicability, and sufficient description. If subject-matter is not satisfied, the application fails irrespective of those other considerations.

name: Mayo/Alice two-step test for eligibility
description: Step 1: Determine whether the claims at issue are directed to a patent-ineligible concept (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea). Step 2: If so, consider the elements of each claim individually and as an ordered combination to determine whether the additional elements transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application — i.e., whether there is an 'inventive concept' sufficient to ensure the patent amounts to significantly more than a patent upon the ineligible concept itself.
guidance: This is the uniform subject-matter test the Supreme Court endorsed in Alice, generalized from Mayo. Evaluate both individual claim elements and their ordered combination; search for an 'inventive concept.'

name: Generic computer implementation does not salvage an abstract idea
description: Merely requiring generic computer implementation — e.g., adding 'apply it' with a generic computer and generic computer functions — fails to transform an abstract idea into a patent-eligible invention.
guidance: The Alice Court explicitly held that claims drawn to intermediated settlement that merely required a data processing system, communications controller, and data storage unit (generic computer components) were ineligible. Claim drafters must do more than append conventional computing elements.

name: Diehr principle — using an otherwise unpatentable equation to solve a technological problem
description: Diamond v. Diehr supports patentability where an otherwise unpatentable equation is used to 'solve a technological problem' and 'improve an existing technological process.'
guidance: The Alice opinion characterizes Diehr as patentable for that reason, suggesting claims that integrate mathematical formulas into technological solutions can be eligible if they produce a practical technological improvement.

name: Mathematical algorithms/manipulation of data without physical device are suspect
description: A process that employs mathematical algorithms to manipulate existing information to generate additional information may be patent-ineligible if it recites an ineligible abstract process of gathering and combining data and does not require input from a physical device.
guidance: As illustrated by Digitech v. Electronics for Imaging, such claims are likely to fail Step 2 unless they include additional limitations that amount to significantly more than the abstract idea/algorithm itself.

name: Pre-emption as the underlying policy test
description: The principle underlying the exclusions (laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract ideas) is pre-emption: patents should not 'swallow' basic tools of innovation by monopolizing them.
guidance: When assessing eligibility, consider whether the claim would pre-empt use of the basic idea or tool across fields; prevention of pre-emption supports exclusion.

name: Claim analysis: individual elements and ordered combination
description: Claims should be evaluated both element-by-element and as an ordered combination to determine whether the claim transforms an ineligible concept into a patent-eligible application.
guidance: Step Two explicitly requires this two-pronged claim analysis; inventive concept may arise from the arrangement/combination of elements even if individual elements are conventional.

name: Practical drafting implication: integrate building blocks into 'something more'
description: To pass the two-step test, claims should integrate otherwise unpatentable building blocks (abstract ideas, laws of nature) into an inventive application — 'something more' — rather than claiming the building block itself.
guidance: Draft claims to show how the claimed elements combine to produce a technical effect, solution to a technological problem, or a meaningful improvement in computer or other technology; avoid purely abstract formulations with only conventional implementation steps.

name: Compliance with 35 U.S.C. 101 — invention must be 'useful'
description: The Office must examine each application to ensure compliance with the 'useful invention' or utility requirement of 35 U.S.C. 101; to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 101 an applicant must claim statutory subject matter and show that the claimed invention is 'useful' for some purpose either explicitly or implicitly.
guidance: This is the overarching requirement. Application of the utility element is the focus of the guidelines. See MPEP § 2107 for detailed examination guidance.

name: Specific utility
description: A 'specific utility' is specific to the subject matter claimed and can 'provide a well-defined and particular benefit to the public.' A general statement that a compound 'may be useful' or has 'useful biological properties' is not sufficient to define a specific utility.
guidance: Office personnel should distinguish disclosures that identify a specific use/application from mere indications that the invention 'may prove useful.' Examples of insufficient specificity: treating 'unspecified disorders', calling a polynucleotide simply a 'gene probe' without identifying a DNA target, or broadly alleging 'diagnostic utility' without specifying the condition. Conversely, disclosing a specific biological activity and reasonably correlating it to a disease condition suffices.

name: Substantial utility
description: 'Substantial' utility requires that an asserted use show the claimed invention has a significant and presently available benefit to the public — an immediate, well-defined, real-world use; utilities that require further research to identify or confirm a real-world context are not 'substantial.'
guidance: Accept reasonable uses that provide public benefit; do not require that products/services be currently available to the public. Examples of non-substantial utilities (require further research): (A) basic research into properties/mechanisms; (B) method of treating an unspecified disease; (C) assay for/identifying material that itself has no specific/substantial utility; (D) method of making a material that itself lacks specific/substantial/credible utility; (E) claim to an intermediate product for making a final product that has no specific/substantial/credible utility.

name: Credible utility / not 'incredible'
description: An asserted utility must be credible; an invention that is 'inoperative' (does not operate to produce the claimed results) is not 'useful.' To violate 35 U.S.C. 101, the claimed device must be totally incapable of achieving a useful result.
guidance: Rejections on 'incredible' or 'speculative' utility are rare and fact-specific. Partial success or crude/perfect embodiments do not establish total incapacity; a small degree of utility can be sufficient. Office personnel should not label an asserted utility 'incredible' unless facts clearly support a lack-of-utility rejection. Examples of 'incredible' claims (fact specific): perpetual motion machines, cold fusion, uncharacterized compositions claimed to cure many cancers, methods contradicting known science.

name: One credible asserted utility suffices
description: An applicant need only make one credible assertion of specific utility for the claimed invention to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 101 and 35 U.S.C. 112; additional statements of utility, even if not credible, do not render the claimed invention lacking utility.
guidance: If a properly claimed invention meets at least one stated objective, utility is established. Examples/case law: Raytheon v. Roper; In re Gottlieb. Examiners should not penalize inventions for extra non-credible utility statements.

name: Applicant statements alone cannot be sole basis for lack of utility rejection
description: Statements made by the applicant in the specification or during prosecution cannot, standing alone, be the basis for a lack-of-utility rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 or 35 U.S.C. 112.
guidance: Applicants may include statements whose technical accuracy is not easily confirmed if those statements are not necessary to establish patentability. Examiners should not require applicants to strike nonessential utility statements, nor should examiners read unclaimed results or limitations into a claim.

name: Examiner procedure — determine if asserted or well-established utility exists
description: Upon initial examination, the examiner should review the specification to determine if there are statements asserting that the claimed invention is useful for any particular purpose; a complete disclosure should identify a specific and substantial utility for the invention.
guidance: A statement of specific and substantial utility should fully and clearly explain why the applicant believes the invention is useful and enable one ordinarily skilled in the art to understand the belief (e.g., explain purpose or how the invention may be used). If an applicant rebuts a prima facie 101 lack-of-utility rejection satisfactorily, withdraw the 101 rejection and corresponding 112(a) rejection.

name: Mandatory contents of a nonprovisional/utility application (US) and PCT application
description: In the United States, a nonprovisional patent application must include claims, an abstract, a description, an oath or declaration and, in most cases, drawings. A PCT international application must contain: a request; a description; one or more claims; one or more drawings, where drawings are necessary; and an abstract.
guidance: A provisional application need not include claims. A utility application is the application that includes claims. Ensure required parts are present and in an acceptable language (or accompanied by translation).

name: Office action: scope and priority
description: An office action represents the government’s official position on the pending patent application and may address almost any aspect of the application; the most important parts touch upon the basic questions related to the patentability of the pending claims.
guidance: Inform the client immediately when an office action arrives and explain the patent office’s findings.

name: Enablement rejections and rebuttal methods
description: The examiner may question whether the description provides sufficient disclosure for an ordinary person skilled in the art to understand and practice the invention (enablement rejections).
guidance: Rebut by showing where the description discloses the allegedly missing subject matter, argue that the missing matter was sufficiently known in the prior art and not necessary for enablement, or amend claims to remove the contested feature.

name: Obviousness (inventive step) rejections and rebuttals
description: If the examiner finds that a combination of prior art discloses the claimed invention and that a person of ordinary skill would be motivated to combine them, the examiner will reject the claim for obviousness.
guidance: Rebut by arguing examiner misunderstood cited references, misunderstood the applicant’s invention or claims, arguing lack of motivation to combine, showing secondary indicia, or amending claims to recite nonobvious features.

name: Client involvement and strategic choice over claim amendments
description: The patent drafter should explain draft responses to the client and give the client the opportunity to choose among amendment options, balancing narrower claims overcoming prior art against business objectives and enforceability.
guidance: Clients may know which claim elements are critical to business; narrowing can overcome examiner objections but may make it easier for competitors to design around. Counsel clients on tradeoffs.

name: No new matter in amendments
description: When amending the application, a universal rule in most jurisdictions is that no new matter (new subject matter) beyond that originally disclosed as of the filing date may be added (except to remedy obvious mistakes). The same rule applies to claims, description and drawings.
guidance: Ensure all amendments are supported by original disclosure; determine original disclosure carefully when drafting and when preparing amendments to avoid introducing new matter that could invalidate or render amendments inadmissible.

name: Interpretation: determine the linguistic meaning
description: Interpretation is the task of determining the linguistic meaning of text—the understanding of the text by the intended audience at the time the patent is written.
guidance: Use the intended audience's understanding (often scientists and competitors in the relevant field) at the filing date as the reference point. The linguistic meaning is a factual question separable from legal consequences. Example: the linguistic meaning of a claim will generally be how a "person skilled in the art" would understand the claim language at the filing date.

name: Use person of ordinary skill in the art as interpretive standard
description: The linguistic meaning of a claim is ordinarily the understanding of a person working in the same field as the patentee (often called a 'person skilled in the art') at the time of filing.
guidance: Filing date approximates the temporal reference. Focus on how those in the field would understand the claim language qua language (not their conception of the invention).

name: Do not rely on patentee's unexpressed intent for linguistic meaning
description: Linguistic meaning does not depend on the patentee's unexpressed intent.
guidance: Patentee's broad intent (to claim as much as courts will allow) renders reliance on unexpressed intent circular and unhelpful for interpretation. Avoid treating internal patentee motivations as the linguistic meaning.

name: Do not equate linguistic meaning with patentee's invention or legal entitlement
description: Interpretation refers to how a person skilled in the art understands the claim language, not to that person's understanding of the patentee's invention or what the patentee is 'entitled' to monopolize.
guidance: Basing interpretation on the patentee's invention or entitlement is circular because legal entitlement is itself the construction outcome. Keep interpretation and construction analytically separate.

name: When construing claims, decide the weight to give linguistic meaning and select alternative lodestars if needed
description: Judges must first decide how much weight to give to linguistic meaning; if they do not give it weight (or if it runs out), they must adopt an alternative point of reference (e.g., patentee's inventive idea).
guidance: Be explicit about the normative justification for the choice of lodestar. If choosing the linguistic meaning, be prepared to fill gaps for vague terms; if choosing another reference, acknowledge the normative reasons for overriding textual meaning (e.g., skepticism about deference to patentee-drafted claims).

name: Filing date as temporal anchor for linguistic meaning
description: Because a patent is generally written just before it is filed, the filing date provides a reasonable approximation of the date by which the linguistic meaning is determined.
guidance: Use evidence of usage as of the filing date to evaluate how a person skilled in the art would have understood the claim language.

name: Patent examiners perform construction when assessing entitlement to issue
description: Although the PTO historically claimed examiners 'interpret' claims and courts 'construe' them, examiners are effectively constructing legal effect when they decide whether a patent is legally entitled to issue.
guidance: Recognize that PTO decisions about claim scope for examination purposes implicate constructional judgments (legal effect), not merely neutral linguistic interpretation.

name: Step 2B: Whether additional elements contribute an 'inventive concept'
description: Step 2B asks: Does the claim recite additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception?
guidance: Examiners should identify additional elements beyond the judicial exception(s) and evaluate those additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether they contribute an inventive concept (i.e., amount to significantly more). This evaluation is made with respect to the considerations the Supreme Court identified as relevant and discussed in MPEP § 2106.05(a)-(h). The evaluation is not a weighing test; focus on the significance of the additional elements relative to the invention and whether the claim as a whole encompasses an inventive concept.

name: Claim-by-claim analysis (do not conflate similar claims)
description: Examiners should examine each claim for eligibility separately, based on the particular elements recited therein.
guidance: Claims should not be judged to automatically stand or fall with similar claims in an application; a dependent claim may be eligible due to additional elements even if the independent claim is ineligible.

name: Step 2B outcomes: Pathway C eligibility or 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection
description: If the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the exception, the claim is eligible (Step 2B: YES) at Pathway C; if not, the claim is not patent-eligible (Step 2B: NO) and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101.
guidance: When a claim is ineligible, see MPEP § 2106.07 for guidance on how to formulate an ineligibility rejection. The eligibility analysis is concluded at Step 2B once the determination is made.

name: Improvements to the functioning of a computer or other technology
description: Consider whether the claim 'purport(s) to improve the functioning of the computer itself' or 'any other technology or technical field.'
guidance: This consideration looks for a technological solution to a technological problem. The specification should provide a technical explanation of how to implement the asserted improvement such that one of ordinary skill would recognize it. Conclusory assertions of improvement without necessary detail are insufficient. The claim must reflect the disclosed improvement (may include components or steps providing the improvement), though the claim need not literally recite the improvement phrase. Evaluate the claim 'as an ordered combination' and avoid oversimplifying. Improvement consideration overlaps with other considerations (particular machine, mere instructions to apply an exception). The judicial exception alone cannot provide the improvement; additional elements or their combination can.

name: Computer-functionality improvement requires computer-limited scope
description: For a method claim to improve computer functionality, the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim must be limited to computer implementation.
guidance: A claim whose entire scope can be performed mentally or without a computer cannot be said to improve computer technology (see Synopsys; RecogniCorp). Claims that cover both computer and non-computer embodiments cannot be treated as improving computer technology unless limited to computer implementation.

name: Examples that may or may not show improvements in computer-functionality
description: Courts have listed specific examples that may show an improvement in computer functionality and examples that may not be sufficient.
guidance: Examples that may show improvements include (i) modification of hyperlink protocol to produce hybrid webpages (DDR Holdings), (ii) inventive distribution of functionality within a network to filter Internet content (BASCOM), (iii) method of rendering halftone images, (iv) distributed network architecture reducing congestion (Amdocs/Openet), (v) programmable memory system configurable by processor type (Visual Memory), (vi) technical details for transmitting images over cellular networks or appending classification info (TLI Communications), (vii) particular server structure for organized digital images (TLI Communications), (viii) particular programming/design to create menus (Ameranth), (ix) methods generating security profiles improving virus protection (Finjan), (x) improved selectable application summary UIs (Core Wireless), (xi) specific interface/implementation for 3D spreadsheets (Data Engine), (xii) specific method of restricting software operation within a license (Ancora). Examples that may NOT be sufficient include (i) generating restaurant menus with functionally claimed features (Ameranth), (ii) accelerating analysis solely from a general-purpose computer (FairWarning), (iii) mere automation of manual processes using generic computers (Credit Acceptance; LendingTree), (iv) recording/transmitting/archiving digital images with conventional tech (TLI Communications), (v) affixing a barcode without technical details (Secured Mail Solutions), (vi) instructions to display two sets of information without how to achieve result (Interval Licensing), (vii) improving information stored in a database (BSG Tech), (viii) arranging transactional information on a GUI to help traders process faster (Trading Technologies). Use these as illustrative guidance, not exhaustive rules.

name: Required filing components
description: A typical filing includes: Title; Abstract; Background of the invention; Detailed description; Claims; Supporting illustrations.
guidance: These are the core sections to prepare. Ensure the detailed description and illustrations enable the full scope of the claims and that the background frames the problem without admitting away patentable distinctions.

name: Apparatus claims
description: Apparatus claims — protect the physical device.
guidance: Draft apparatus claims to capture the structural elements and their relationships, including critical geometries, materials, and configurations that distinguish from prior devices. Ensure the written description supplies structure for any claimed elements to avoid §112 problems.

name: Method claims
description: Method claims — safeguard how the device is used.
guidance: Draft clear stepwise methods with necessary limitations to avoid overbreadth yet preserve enforceability. Consider practicability (who performs steps) and potential inducement/contributory infringement theories when claiming methods of use.

name: System claims
description: System claims — tie the device into broader workflows or infrastructure.
guidance: Use system claims to capture the device plus other components (e.g., networks, servers, sensors) and their interactions. System claims can broaden reach beyond the physical device and can be useful against integrated solutions or platforms.

name: Method-of-treatment claims (claim type)
description: Method of treatment claims — how the device treats patients (limited applicability).
guidance: Method-of-treatment claims can be powerful but are subject to special risks (see method-of-treatment limitations). Use them only where appropriate and consider practitioner-immunity and eligibility challenges.

name: Method-of-manufacturing claims
description: Method of manufacturing claims — how the device is made.
guidance: Claiming manufacturing steps can protect novel production processes and may be kept as trade secrets if disclosure is undesirable, but patenting can block competitors. Draft with sufficient detail to satisfy §112 enablement and written-description requirements.

name: Key drafting objectives for claims
description: A well-drafted claim: survives examination, withstands invalidity challenges, reads cleanly on competitor products, and supports multiple infringement theories (direct, induced, contributory).
guidance: Draft claims to balance breadth and robustness: include fallback dependent claims, avoid vague functional language without structure, and ensure the specification supports each claim scope. Anticipate common invalidity theories and draft around them.

name: Consequences of poor claim drafting (anti-patterns)
description: A poorly drafted claim invites office actions, creates narrowing amendments, and faces claim construction rulings reducing commercial value.
guidance: Avoid drafting traps that force narrowing amendments (e.g., overly functional language, incomplete enablement); consider how prosecution history may be used in claim construction and enforceability disputes.

name: Method-of-treatment limitations and risks
description: Method-of-treatment claims face §101 patent-eligibility scrutiny under Mayo; practitioner immunity (35 U.S.C. §287(c)) shields physicians from liability for using patented surgical/medical procedures; EPO excludes certain treatment claims under Article 53(c).
guidance: When drafting treatment claims, evaluate eligibility risks (Mayo/Alice framework) and applicability in foreign jurisdictions (e.g., EPO exclusion). Consider drafting alternatives (device/system claims or diagnostics framed to avoid judicial exceptions) and assess enforcement practicalities given practitioner immunity.

name: Mixed hardware/software claim drafting
description: Pair specific structural elements with software functions; avoid using 'module' or 'means' terms without providing enabling structure; consider 35 U.S.C. §112(f) (means-plus-function) implications.
guidance: For claims that mix hardware and software, explicitly describe the structural implementation of software functions in the spec to avoid indefinite or construed-limited means-plus-function treatment. Use concrete data flows, interfaces, and algorithms where possible to show enabling structure.

name: Regulatory coordination with FDA
description: Coordinate patent strategy with FDA 510(k) or PMA submissions; device class (I, II, III) affects prosecution timing.
guidance: Align disclosure timing and claim scope with regulatory filings—e.g., avoid premature public disclosures that could jeopardize patents; factor in longer PMA timelines for Class III devices when planning enforcement and commercialization. Use regulatory milestones to prioritize claims and expenditures.

name: Anticipation risk (prior art devices)
description: Common rejection: anticipation by prior-art catheters/devices with minor structural differences.
guidance: Carefully analyze prior devices and draft claims/description emphasizing distinguishing geometries, materials, or functional benefits. Provide fallback claim scopes and detailed descriptions of novel features to overcome anticipation rejections.

name: §112 written-description/enablement issues for novel aspects
description: Common rejection: §112 written description or enablement rejections for novel aspects such as geometries or materials.
guidance: Ensure the specification describes and enables the full claimed scope, including detailed descriptions of novel geometries, dimensions, tolerances, and material compositions. Include examples, ranges, and embodiments to support broad claim language.

name: §101 challenges for diagnostic/algorithmic methods
description: Common rejection: §101 rejections for diagnostic methods under Mayo/Alice frameworks.
guidance: When claims implicate diagnostic methods or algorithms, draft to emphasize technical improvements, specific machine implementations, or concrete steps tied to physical devices to reduce abstract-idea scrutiny. Consider alternative claim types (apparatus/system) to capture inventions.

name: Specific national adaptations for PCT national phase (agent, deemed complete specification, priority document rules, dates and publication)
description: Various national modifications apply when processing a PCT national phase: section 9(b) does not apply; the applicant must be represented by an agent appointed within prescribed time; section 10 applies only on compliance with 43E; section 16(2) applies to PCT time limits; certain sections (e.g., 30(1),(5),(6), 32(5), 38, 43(3),(4)) are modified or do not apply; the description, claims, drawings and abstract in Article 3(2) of the PCT shall be deemed to be a complete specification; priority document requirements per Rule 17.1 and section 35(2) are addressed; the international filing date is the national filing date for national phase purposes; publication under Article 21 opens the national phase to public inspection once applicant complied with 43E; other mappings for corrections and amendments are specified.
guidance: These enumerated mappings determine which national sections apply or are displaced for PCT-derived national-phase applications and how filing/priority/publication dates are treated.

name: Amendments to provisional and complete specifications (scope limits and procedure)
description: An applicant or patentee may apply to amend provisional or complete specification, setting out nature and full reasons. Applications open to public inspection must be advertised. Any person may oppose; commissioner/registrar determines whether and on what conditions amendment is allowed. Provisional specification amendments are allowed for corrections/obvious mistakes but must not introduce new matter or matter not in substance disclosed. No amendment of a complete specification that becomes open to public inspection after acceptance shall be allowed if it would introduce new matter or a claim not fairly based on pre-amendment disclosure, or include any claim not wholly within scope of a pre-existing claim. Supplementary disclosure may be allowed in narrow circumstances before acceptance published, but priority of new matter is the date of supplementary disclosure. Amendments during court proceedings must be made to the court; amendments violating section provisions may be set aside by commissioner or court.
guidance: Strict prohibition on introducing new matter; public inspection/acceptance freezes allowable scope; opposition and judicial review routes preserved.

name: Cancellation of 'licences of right' endorsement
description: A patentee may apply for cancellation of endorsement. Registrar may cancel where balance of renewal fees payable if not endorsed is paid and registrar satisfied there is no existing licence or all licensees consent. Persons claiming preclusion by contract at endorsement may apply within prescribed period for cancellation; on cancellation patentee must pay balance of renewal fees or patent will lapse. Similar treatment applies for patents of addition. Cancellation restores rights/liabilities as if endorsement had not been made.
guidance: Cancellation requires clearing financial differences and resolving third-party contract claims; statutory safeguards for interested persons.

name: Policy balancing: patent incentives versus public access and follow-on innovation
description: The Court and commentators considered whether denying patents on isolated genes would undercut incentives for companies to perform costly gene discovery work.
guidance: When evaluating patent policy or a specific patent claim, weigh incentives for upstream discovery (companies' ability to recoup investment and be motivated to find genes) against harms to downstream research, clinical testing, and public access created by exclusivity.

name: Step 2A: Judicial Exception (Exception Presence/Type)
description: Determine whether the claim recites a judicial exception (e.g., Abstract Idea, Product of Nature, Law of Nature) or no exception. The table's Step 2A: Exception column indicates this for each example.
guidance: This criterion identifies whether the claimed subject matter is a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon/product of nature). Table entries include values like 'Abstract Idea', 'Product of Nature', 'Law of Nature', 'None', and 'n/a' for examples where not applicable.

name: Step 2A: MDC Analysis (Characteristics of the Exception)
description: Identify the characteristic(s) of the judicial exception at issue (e.g., function/activity; chem/phys property; structure or form; transformation; phenotype). The table's Step 2A: MDC Analysis column lists these characteristics for each example.
guidance: Used to articulate why a claim is considered to recite the exception by specifying how the exception manifests (for example, 'function/activity, structure or form', 'chem/phys property', 'phenotype', 'transformation'). This helps map a claim's elements to the kind of judicial exception analyzed in Step 2A.

name: Step 2B: 'Significantly More' Considerations
description: Evaluate whether additional claim elements, individually or as an ordered combination, provide 'significantly more' than the judicial exception itself. The table's Step 2B column identifies which considerations apply for each example.
guidance: This is the §101 second-part inquiry: consider whether the claim adds an inventive concept/meaningfully more beyond the exception. The table annotates which considerations (see separate listed considerations) apply to each example to show why it either passes or fails Step 2B.

name: Improving computer
description: Consideration that a claim element or limitation 'improving computer' can weigh in favor of eligibility under Step 2B.
guidance: The index flags examples where the claim was considered to 'improv[e] computer' as a potentially meaningful limitation supporting eligibility; typically contrasted with generic computer implementation which is not enough.

name: Improving another technology
description: Consideration that a claim element 'improving another technology' can support a finding of significantly more under Step 2B.
guidance: If the claim's additional elements improve a technology other than computers (i.e., provide a technological solution), this is treated as a meaningful limitation favoring eligibility in the table's annotations.

name: Limitation that is well-understood, routine, and conventional (WURC)
description: A negative/signifying consideration: claim limitations that are 'well-understood, routine, and conventional' (often illustrated as 'generic computer performing generic computer functions') weigh against finding 'significantly more'.
guidance: The index repeatedly flags 'limitation that is well-understood, routine, and conventional (generic computer performing generic computer functions)' to indicate why many computer-implemented claims fail Step 2B. Presence of WURC limitations typically supports a non-eligible result.

name: Limitation that is not well-understood, routine, and conventional (non-WURC)
description: A positive/signifying consideration: claim limitations that are not well-understood, routine, and conventional can support finding 'significantly more'.
guidance: The table marks examples where limitations were specifically identified as not WURC; such limitations may be considered improvements or meaningful additions and thus support eligibility under Step 2B.

name: Mere instructions to 'apply it'
description: Consideration that mere instructions to 'apply' an abstract idea or law of nature (i.e., directing use without adding meaningful limitation) do not supply 'significantly more'.
guidance: The index highlights examples where claims merely instruct to implement/apply the exception (e.g., 'apply it'), indicating such claims fail Step 2B because they add no meaningful limitation beyond the judicial exception.

name: Transformation
description: Consideration that a physical transformation or change can be a meaningful limitation (e.g., transformation of an article/state) supporting eligibility.
guidance: The MDC Analysis/Step 2B columns annotate examples where transformation (physical change) was relevant; physical transformations can weigh in favor of eligibility when they are central to the claim's added elements.

name: Requirement for unity of invention
description: An international application shall relate to one invention only or to a group of inventions so linked as to form a single general inventive concept. The requirement is fulfilled only when there is a technical relationship among those inventions involving one or more of the same or corresponding special technical features. The determination shall be made without regard to whether the inventions are claimed in separate claims or as alternatives within a single claim.
guidance: The expression 'special technical features' means those technical features that define a contribution which each of the claimed inventions, considered as a whole, makes over the prior art. When claims are directed to multiple categories (product, process, apparatus, use), the first invention of the category first mentioned and the first recited invention of each other category related thereto will be considered the 'main invention'. If no additional fees are paid timely, the international search/examination will be based on the main invention (PCT Article 17(3)(a), 37 CFR 1.475(d)). Follow form paragraphs (e.g., 18.05-18.07) when making lack-of-unity actions.

name: Markush group alternatives — similar nature criterion
description: When a single claim defines alternatives of a Markush group, the requirement of technical interrelationship and same or corresponding special technical features is considered met when the alternatives are of a similar nature.
guidance: For chemical-compound Markush groupings, alternatives are regarded as of similar nature where (A) all alternatives have a common property or activity; and (B) either (1) a common structure is present (a significant structural element is shared by all alternatives) OR (2) all alternatives belong to a recognized class of chemical compounds in the art. 'Significant structural element' may occupy a large portion of structures or be a structurally distinctive portion in view of prior art and be essential to the common property/activity. 'Recognized class' means expectation from knowledge in the art that members will behave similarly (interchangeable for intended result). The fact alternatives are differently classified should not alone justify lack of unity.

name: Unity between intermediate and final products
description: Unity is present between intermediate and final products when two conditions are fulfilled: (A) the intermediate and final products have the same essential structural element (basic chemical structures are the same OR chemically closely interrelated with the intermediate incorporating an essential structural element into the final product); and (B) the intermediate and final products are technically interrelated (final product is manufactured directly from the intermediate or separated by a small number of intermediates all containing the same essential structural element).
guidance: Unity may be accepted even when structures are unknown (e.g., one known intermediate and a final product of unknown structure) if there is sufficient evidence that they are technically closely interrelated (e.g., intermediate contains same essential element). Different intermediate products used in different processes for the same final product may be accepted if they share the same essential structural element. Intermediates and final products shall not be separated by an intermediate which is not new. If the same application claims different intermediates for different structural parts of the final product, unity is not present. When families of compounds are claimed, each intermediate should correspond to a compound claimed in the final family, but families need not be absolutely congruent.

name: Preparation content for invitation to pay additional fees
description: On Form PCT/ISA/206 the examiner should indicate number of inventions claimed, which particular claims cover each invention, explain why the application lacks unity, and state total amount of additional fees required.
guidance: Claims found to be unsearchable under PCT Article 17(2)(b) are excluded; unsearchable claims include: (A) subject matter not required to be searched by ISA (see MPEP §1843.02); (B) claims for which a meaningful search cannot be carried out (MPEP §1843.03); (C) multiple dependent claims not complying with PCT Rule 6.4(a) (MPEP §1843.03). Use appropriate form-paragraphs and provide clear identification of groups/claims using Roman numerals or species identifiers as required.

name: Form paragraphs and headings for lack of unity actions
description: Standardized form paragraphs (e.g., 18.05–18.07.03c, 18.06, 18.06.01, 18.06.02) provide headings, group listings, and specified language for declaring lack of unity and identifying groups of claims (groups I, II, III etc.).
guidance: Begin all lack-of-unity actions during the international phase with the required heading (¶18.05 / ¶18.07). Use form paragraphs to list groups of claims and categories (product/process/apparatus/use) and to explain why groups lack the same or corresponding technical feature. Use examiner notes in each form paragraph for insertion instructions and examples. For applications with claims to different categories, unity may still exist only for certain allowed category combinations (see 37 CFR 1.475(b) and enumerated combinations such as product + process specially adapted to manufacture it, product + use, process + apparatus, etc.).

name: Patent statutory compliance metrics — 35 U.S.C. 112 (written description/claims)
description: Percentage metric that measures examiner compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112 (including 112(a),(b) and 112(f)) requirements.
guidance: Monitors adequacy of written description, claim definiteness, and claim support decisions; used as part of the statutory compliance scorecard.

name: Definition of 'information material to patentability' in reexamination (37 CFR 1.555(b))
description: Information is material if it is not cumulative and either (1) it is a patent or printed publication that establishes, by itself or in combination, a prima facie case of unpatentability of a claim; or (2) it refutes or is inconsistent with a position the patent owner takes in opposing an Office argument of unpatentability or in asserting patentability.
guidance: A prima facie case of unpatentability is established when the information compels a conclusion that a claim is unpatentable under the preponderance of the evidence standard, giving each term its broadest reasonable construction consistent with the specification, and before considering any contrary evidence submitted to establish patentability.

name: Required copies for documents cited in IDS (37 CFR 1.98(a) compliance)
description: To comply with 37 CFR 1.98(a) as to documents cited in the patent or its parent applications, the party must supply legible copies as required by 1.98(a)(2): (1) each foreign patent; (2) each publication or the portion which caused it to be listed, other than U.S. patents and U.S. patent application publications unless required by the Office; (3) for each cited pending unpublished U.S. application, the application specification including the claims and any drawing or the portion causing it to be listed; (4) all other information or the portion which caused it to be listed.
guidance: The exception in 1.98(d) does not apply to ex parte and inter partes reexamination proceedings. Parties should provide copies (or required portions) to avoid rejection of the submission on formal grounds.

name: Interview procedures: pre-interview materials, duration, limitations on frequency
description: If patent owner desires to initiate an interview, contact examiner and, if interview granted, file at least three working days prior an informal written statement of issues to be discussed and an informal copy of any proposed claims (unless waived). Duration of the interview will not exceed one hour unless a petition under 37 CFR 1.182 shows sufficient cause for more time. Only one interview may be requested after an Office action and prior to filing the response to that action, absent good cause.
guidance: Preliminary materials (fax or hand-carried) help structure the interview and are made of record as attachments to the Interview Summary form PTOL-474. Examiner may extend interview duration at examiner’s discretion. A second interview requires showing of good cause explaining why the information could not have been presented sooner, mindful of the statutory mandate for 'special dispatch.' See MPEP §713.09 for standards.

name: Number of claims per patent indicator
description: Indicator measuring the number of claims contained in a patent (claims index), normalised within cohort. Number and content of claims determine the legal boundaries and breadth of a patent, and can reflect expected market value.
guidance: Claims counts vary by patent office rules (historical one-claim rule in Japan) and by fee structures (EPO excess claims fees changed in 2008). The claims indicator is sensitive to truncation because claims can be dropped/redefined during examination; recent cohorts may show artificially higher means if still under examination. Compare across offices and over time with caution and account for institutional/fiscal rules affecting claim counts. The index is winsorized and normalised as above.

name: Minimum sample rules for reporting averages by economy or field
description: When reporting average indices by economy/field, OECD sets minimum sample sizes: e.g., average by economy is provided only for economies with more than 200 patents reporting the NPL/claims index in 2009, and for forward citations an economy needs more than 100 patents reporting the index in 2004.
guidance: Apply minimum-observation thresholds to avoid unstable averages; report the number of observations supporting each average. For small economies or sparse fields, suppress or flag averages and provide caveats.

name: Abuse-of-discretion review for verdict form design
description: The verdict form is reviewed for an abuse of discretion; district courts have broad authority and discretion in controlling the conduct of a trial, including the form by which juries return verdicts.
guidance: A district court abuses its discretion when its exercise of discretion is guided by an erroneous legal conclusion. Courts should ensure verdict forms allow the jury to announce the ultimate legal result of each claim. (Cites: R.R. Dynamics; Koon.)

name: Verdict form must announce ultimate legal result of each claim
description: The 'key' to a general verdict is whether the jury announces the ultimate legal result of each claim.
guidance: If the verdict form asks an overly broad question (e.g., whether defendant infringed 'any' asserted claims) it may fail this test. The form should break out infringement at least patent-by-patent (or more narrowly claim-by-claim if appropriate) so the jury's unanimous determination on each cause of action is clear. (Discusses Zhang v. Am. Gem Seafoods and Jazzabi v. Allstate.)

name: Factors making a settlement agreement non-comparable
description: A settlement/license may be non-comparable (and thus of minimal probative value) when its scope of patent rights is far greater than the asserted patents, when it resolves global litigation across multiple claim types (patent, antitrust, trade-secret, tort), or when it does not actually license the asserted patents.
guidance: Expert testimony relying on such a settlement as a 'check' or 'ballpark' must meaningfully account for differences in scope; failure to do so weakens probative value and increases unfair prejudice. Emphasis of large settlement figures to the jury can be especially prejudicial.

name: § 101 'directed to an abstract idea' inquiry (eligibility)
description: A claim may be held patent-ineligible under § 101 if it is directed to an abstract idea; the court applies the governing § 101 framework (including assessing whether the claims are directed to an abstract idea).
guidance: District courts' grant/denial of summary judgment on § 101 is reviewed de novo; identification of abstract idea requires careful analysis of claim language and may be dispositive of invalidity. (The opinion reversed the district court's non-abstract finding for claims 6 and 7 of the ’332 patent.)

name: Means-plus-function (§ 112 ¶6) two-step analysis
description: Step 1: Determine whether the claim term is in means-plus-function format; absence of the word 'means' creates a rebuttable presumption that § 112 ¶6 does not apply. Step 2: If § 112 ¶6 applies, determine whether the specification discloses adequate corresponding structure for the claimed function.
guidance: The presumption may be overcome if the challenger shows the claim term fails to recite sufficiently definite structure or recites function without sufficient structure. Generic nonce terms (e.g., 'unit', 'module', 'mechanism', 'device') often do not connote structure and may invoke § 112 ¶6. If § 112 ¶6 applies, remand to the district court is appropriate to determine corresponding structure in the first instance. (Cites Williamson, Diebold Nixdorf, MPEP §2181.)

name: Plain meaning, lexicography, and disclaimer in claim construction
description: Claim language has its ordinary meaning unless the patentee acts as lexicographer or disavows claim scope in the specification or prosecution history; absent lexicography or disavowal, courts should not depart from plain meaning.
guidance: To import limits into a claim or depart from plain meaning, there must be clear expressions of intent in the specification or prosecution history. (Cites GE Lighting Sols.)

name: Remand where district court must make factual findings on corresponding structure
description: When an appellate court determines a claim term invokes § 112 ¶6, the matter of whether the specification discloses adequate corresponding structure is a factual/intrinsic-record determination for the district court.
guidance: Appellate courts should remand such issues for the district court to conduct the § 112 ¶6 step-two analysis in the first instance rather than resolve corresponding-structure questions on appeal.

name: Petition must-haves (content requirements)
description: Every Petition must identify the Petitioner, real-parties-in-interest, counsel; include a statement of the precise relief requested; and a full statement of the reasons for the relief requested (detailed explanation of why the claims are invalid).
guidance: IPR/PGR/CBMR petitioners must include prior art (patents/printed publications) analysis for 102/103; PGR/CBMR must include analysis of 101 and 112 where applicable. Petitions must set forth any claim constructions needed to interpret the claims. CBMR requires additional analysis showing the patent is a CBM and that petitioner has been charged with infringement.

name: Institution standards (IPR vs PGR/CBMR)
description: IPR institution standard: reasonable likelihood that petitioner would prevail on at least one challenged claim. PGR/CBMR institution standard: more likely than not that at least one challenged claim is unpatentable.
guidance: These institution standards determine the burden the petitioner must meet at the Petition phase; institution decisions are accompanied by a Scheduling Order and start the one-year clock for Final Written Decision (subject to limited extensions).

name: Section 112 issues in IPR/PGR
description: Section 112 issues cannot be raised in an IPR. However, Section 112 can arise in IPR when determining earliest effective filing date for prior art application and in the context of whether PGR applies.
guidance: Prior to SAS, PTAB sometimes refused to institute IPRs on claims indefiniteness under 112; post-SAS the Board cannot selectively institute some claims and refuse others on that basis. Consider 112 implications when establishing effective filing dates and applicable prior art.

name: Patent Owner Preliminary Response (POPR) timing and effect
description: Any POPR is due within three months of a Notice of Filing Date Accorded (not petition filing date). Rules now allow Patent Owners to submit new testimonial evidence with the Preliminary Response.
guidance: For institution decisions, the Board will find any dispute of material fact in favor of Petitioner. POPR should therefore focus on legal arguments against institution (statutory bars, estoppel, incomplete petition, failure to meet thresholds) and on highlighting weaknesses in prior art or claim elements.

name: POPR substantive arguments to defeat institution
description: Patent Owner may argue statutory bars (e.g., one-year window for IPR, lack of being sued/charged for CBMR, estoppel), that petition is incomplete (e.g., missing claim constructions), or that petition fails to meet institution thresholds.
guidance: Consider arguing that prior art lacks a material element of the claims, teaches away, or does not qualify as prior art. Board has discretion to deny institution based on redundancy or prior consideration by the Office.

name: General Plastic non-exclusive factors
description: Factors to consider for discretionary denial (General Plastic): (1) whether same petitioner previously filed a petition on same claims; (2) knowledge of asserted prior art at time of first petition; (3) whether petitioner received POPR or Board decision on first petition; (4) length of time between learning of prior art and filing second petition; (5) explanation for time elapsed between filings; (6) finite resources of the Board; (7) requirement to issue final determination within 1 year of institution (35 U.S.C. §316(a)(11)).
guidance: These are non-exclusive; weigh them when considering follow-on petitions to anticipate discretionary denial.

name: Motion to amend claims timing and standard
description: Motion to Amend Claims is currently due with the Patent Owner Response. A single Motion to Amend may be filed as of right; additional motions require a showing of 'good cause.' The Phillips claim construction standard will be used for proposed substitute claims in a motion to amend.
guidance: PTAB designated Lectrosonics as precedential regarding motion to amend practice; shape amendment strategy around one motion as of right and the evidentiary record needed to support substituting claims.

name: Best practices — Appeal Briefs
description: Effective Appeal Briefs: present only the strongest arguments; strategically group claims to highlight strongest arguments; develop facts to show how law applies; understand burden of proof; define key claim terms; support arguments with evidence; understand difference between appealable and petitionable issues; use Summary of Claimed Subject Matter.
guidance: Work with judges' expectations: focus, organization, and evidentiary support increase chances of success in ex parte appeals.

name: Best practices — Reply Briefs
description: Effective Reply Briefs: use to respond to points raised in Examiner's Answer; do not reiterate arguments presented in Appeal Brief; do not raise new arguments not responsive to Examiner's Answer; do not separately argue claims for the first time in a Reply Brief.
guidance: Keep reply focused and strictly responsive to avoid waiver and preserve appropriate scope for appeal.

name: Best practices — Petition drafting
description: Dos and don'ts for petitions include number and presentation of grounds, use and content of expert declaration, consider impact of claim construction change, and other strategic matters.
guidance: Roundtable suggestions emphasize strategic drafting to meet institution thresholds, careful selection and presentation of prior art, and well-supported expert declarations.

name: Meaning of 'Independent' and 'Distinct'
description: Defines 'independent' inventions as unrelated (no disclosed relationship in design, operation, or effect) and describes 'related but distinct' inventions (disclosed as connected in design, operation, or effect but nevertheless distinct if claimed inventions are not connected in at least one of design, operation, or effect and at least one is patentable over the other).
guidance: Gives examples (combination and subcombination, process and apparatus, process and product) and explains that 'distinct' permits division among dependent/related inventions; warns that case law uses terms variably and decisions must be read carefully. References MPEP §§ 806.05(c), 806.05(j), 806.06, 808.01 for examples and two-way tests.

name: When Restriction Is Proper
description: A requirement for restriction may be proper only if the claimed inventions each could support separate patents and they are either independent or distinct as claimed.
guidance: Two-prong test: (A) inventions must be independent or distinct, and (B) there would be a serious burden on the examiner if restriction is not required. If the search/examination of all claims can be made without serious burden, the examiner must examine them on the merits even if they cover independent or distinct inventions. See MPEP § 803 and § 803.01.

name: Markush Claims — Unity and Provisional Election
description: Markush-type claims recite alternatives (e.g., 'selected from the group consisting of A, B, and C'); members should ordinarily belong to a recognized class, and unity exists where members share a common utility and a substantial structural feature essential to that utility.
guidance: If Markush members are few or closely related so the entire claim can be searched without serious burden, examiner must examine all members. If a Markush claim encompasses at least two independent/distinct inventions, examiner may require a provisional election of a single species prior to examination. Use form paragraphs 8.01 or 8.02 as appropriate. After election, the Markush claim is examined with respect to the elected species; if elected species is unpatentable, claim and elected species are rejected and non-elected species held withdrawn. If elected species is allowable, examination of the Markush claim is extended as necessary. See MPEP § 803.02 and § 809.

name: Rejoinder Between Product and Process Inventions
description: Process claims that were withdrawn for being non-elected may be rejoined to an allowable product claim only if they depend from or otherwise require all the limitations of the allowable product claim.
guidance: Upon rejoinder of such process claims, the restriction between elected product and rejoined process(es) is withdrawn. Applicants are encouraged to present dependent process claims early to facilitate rejoinder. Amendments after allowance or final rejection have special treatment (37 CFR 1.312, 1.116). If process claims would raise new issues after rejoinder, applicant may be offered opportunity to cancel process claims or file an RCE. See MPEP § 821.04(b).

name: BRI standard for claim construction in IPR
description: The USPTO may use the 'broadest reasonable interpretation' (BRI) standard to construe patent claims during IPR proceedings; the Supreme Court held that the PTO has rulemaking authority to adopt BRI and that the adoption of BRI for IPRs is a reasonable exercise of that authority.
guidance: BRI is applied consistent with the specification; the Court said construing claims under BRI 'helps to protect the public' and is supported by past practice. The opinion acknowledged that BRI may produce outcomes different from district-court Phillips constructions and found that such inconsistency is acceptable given the agency's regulatory design. Practitioners should expect that claim terms in IPR will be given their broadest reasonable construction consistent with the specification, which can be outcome-determinative.

name: Phillips/plain-and-ordinary-meaning standard in district courts
description: District courts construe claims using the Federal Circuit's Phillips standard (plain and ordinary meaning), which is intended to be narrower than the PTAB's BRI standard.
guidance: Because Phillips is narrower, claims that survive under Phillips may still be found unpatentable under BRI. The Supreme Court in Cuozzo did not resolve how district courts should treat prior PTAB constructions; district courts vary—some treat PTAB constructions as further intrinsic evidence, others give them no weight. When claims are amended in an IPR, that IPR may become part of the prosecution history and may be intrinsic evidence for Phillips constructions.

name: Chevron deference to USPTO rulemaking
description: When a statute is ambiguous about a procedural rule (here, which claim-construction standard to use in IPR), courts apply Chevron's two-step framework; if ambiguity exists, the agency's reasonable interpretation is entitled to deference.
guidance: The Court found the AIA did not unambiguously direct one standard over the other (step one) and therefore evaluated whether USPTO's choice was reasonable (step two). The Court concluded the USPTO's adoption of BRI was a reasonable exercise of its rulemaking authority and thus warranted deference.

name: IPR is more like agency reexamination than litigation
description: IPR proceedings share attributes with both examination and litigation, but in significant respects they are more like specialized agency proceedings aimed at reexamining earlier agency decisions.
guidance: Factors supporting the 'agency' view: no presumption of validity in IPR; limited claim amendments; USPTO can continue proceedings after settlement; USPTO can defend PTAB decisions in court. Factors supporting the 'litigation' view: adversarial nature, discovery, briefs, and oral argument. Practitioners should frame strategy recognizing this hybrid character—IPR procedures and goals differ from district-court litigation.

name: Burden of proof differences (IPR vs litigation)
description: IPR challenges must prove unpatentability by a preponderance of the evidence (35 U.S.C. §316(e)), whereas in district-court litigation patent claims enjoy a presumption of validity and invalidity must be proven by clear and convincing evidence (35 U.S.C. §282).
guidance: The lower evidentiary burden in IPRs contributes to a higher rate of claim invalidation. Parties should consider the differing burdens when deciding whether to pursue IPR vs district-court invalidity strategies.

name: When Phillips construction may be used in IPRs (district-court-type construction)
description: A recent rule change (effective May 2, 2016) permits a 'district court-type claim construction' (Phillips/plain-and-ordinary-meaning) in IPRs when certain conditions are met: either party may request such a construction within 30 days of filing the petition if the challenged patent will expire within 18 months of the petition's filing date (37 C.F.R. §42.100(b)).
guidance: This provides a narrow avenue for using Phillips in IPRs for patents near the end of term. Parties should monitor deadlines and file timely requests when applicable.

name: Prosecution bar for recipients of AEO
description: Absent written consent from the Producing Party, any individual who receives access to AEO (or optionally AEO/source code) information shall not be involved in prosecution of patents or patent applications relating to the subject matter of the highly confidential technical information.
guidance: ‘Prosecution’ includes directly or indirectly drafting, amending, advising, or otherwise affecting the scope or maintenance of patent claims (original prosecution, reissue, reexamination, etc.). Prosecution does not include representing a party challenging a patent before an agency. The Prosecution Bar begins when access is first received and ends two (2) years after final termination of the action. It may be appropriate to require an 'Ethical Wall' for counsel who receive AEO information. Parties may also limit access of Designated House Counsel to AEO/source code under certain circumstances.

name: Federal Circuit rule: any narrowing amendment creates estoppel
description: The Federal Circuit's rule (as described) holds that any narrowing amendment, regardless of the reason for it, creates prosecution history estoppel.
guidance: Under this formulation, courts treat any amendment that narrows claim scope as creating a bar to asserting the doctrine of equivalents for the narrowed element, even if the amendment was made for form/clarity reasons rather than to avoid prior art. Criticized as harsh/retroactive by opponents.

name: Foreseeability / unforeseeability as an equitable exception
description: A limited exception may allow equivalents where the accused device or change was unforeseeable at the time of the claim/prosecution, i.e., patentee could not reasonably have claimed against that variant.
guidance: Consider whether the alleged equivalent was reasonably foreseeable to the patentee at the time of claim drafting/prosecution; if unforeseeable and patentee could not reasonably have claimed it, courts may afford limited relief despite narrowing amendment (but this invites litigation over foreseeability).

name: Claims must be read in light of prosecution history; prosecution history gives public notice
description: Claims are interpreted in accordance with their prosecution history; the prosecution record tells the public what was surrendered and what remains allowed — 'The patent tells you what you can't do, but more importantly, it tells you what you can do.'
guidance: When construing claims and deciding equivalents, courts must analyze the prosecution history to understand the patentee's amendments, arguments, and the public notice those give; patentees should be aware that prosecution statements can limit claim scope.

name: Distinction between literal infringement and doctrine of equivalents; courts' practical focus
description: Literal infringement (textual claim coverage) remains central; many patentee successes are based on literal infringement rather than doctrine of equivalents (example given: 27 of 31 Federal Circuit preliminary-injunction cases in 2000 were literal).
guidance: Evaluate literal claim coverage first; doctrine of equivalents is a supplemental, fact-intensive inquiry and is the focus when accused devices avoid literal wording. Statistical trends may affect litigation strategy but do not change legal standards.

name: Means-plus-function protection (§112 ¶6) as a drafting/protection tool for equivalents
description: 35 U.S.C. §112, paragraph 6 allows claiming an element by function and provides protection for structures that perform that function described in the specification or their equivalents.
