guidance: Patent drafters can use §112(6) (means-plus-function) drafting to claim functionally and obtain statutory equivalents for identified structures in the spec; courts will construe such claims according to §112(6) limits (structure in spec and equivalents).

name: Claim drafting guidance: draft broadly but precisely; avoid unnecessary narrowing amendments
description: Patentees should draft claims as broad as reasonably supported by the specification, use available drafting tools (e.g., §112(6)), and avoid narrowing amendments where possible because amendments may reduce enforceable scope and lead to estoppel.
guidance: Practical advice from advocates: (1) draft broad initial claims but support them in the spec; (2) resist narrowing amendments unless necessary; (3) if amendment is made, carefully document the reason in prosecution to preserve the ability to rebut presumptions of estoppel; (4) weigh tradeoffs of appeal vs amending (delay vs estoppel risk).

name: Amendments for form/clarity (e.g., 111/112 objections) can still narrow and create estoppel
description: Even when amendments are made to address form (35 U.S.C. §111) or clarity/written-description (35 U.S.C. §112) objections, such amendments may have the effect of narrowing the claim and thereby create prosecution history estoppel.
guidance: When analyzing an amendment, courts must look beyond the examiner's stated basis and the applicant's stated intent to determine whether the net effect was a narrowing that would reasonably be understood by the public as a disclaimer; applicants should document that amendments were solely stylistic/clarifying where appropriate.

name: Validate essentiality with technical and legal experts
description: Engage technical and legal experts to validate essentiality; automated dashboards help but do not replace manual review.
guidance: Combine automated tools with domain experts — technical reviewers validate whether claims truly read on standard-essential features and legal experts assess declaration/claim scope and enforceability.

name: Prioritize claims to avoid overcrowded SEP clusters
description: Prioritize claims that avoid overcrowded SEP clusters to reduce licensing friction.
guidance: When drafting or prosecuting claims, target areas with fewer competing declared SEPs to improve monetization potential and decrease licensing disputes and friction.

name: Balance breadth with high-value claims
description: Balance breadth with high-value claims; optimize portfolios for monetization, not just declaration volume.
guidance: Rather than maximizing declaration counts, combine technical breadth with a set of targeted, high-value claims that drive licensing leverage and commercial returns.

name: Avoid skipping patentability searches (filing risk)
description: Skipping patentability searches increases invalidation risk and weakens licensing positions.
guidance: Do not file without a thorough patentability search; early identification of prior art or overlapping SEPs allows claim drafting and prosecution strategies that withstand later challenges.

name: Board consideration of amendments filed during jurisdiction
description: The Board is not obligated to consider new or amended claims filed while it has jurisdiction over the appeal; however, certain proposed amendments (e.g., canceling claims without affecting scope of others or rewriting dependent claims into independent form) may be remanded for examiner consideration.
guidance: See MPEP § 1206 for when remand for amendment is appropriate. The Board can refuse to consider claim changes made during its jurisdiction except in limited circumstances.

name: Board decision outcomes – affirmance, reversal, remand, and new grounds
description: The Board may affirm or reverse the examiner's decision in whole or in part on the grounds specified by the examiner, may remand the application to the examiner, and may include a new ground of rejection in its opinion.
guidance: Affirmance of rejection on any specified grounds constitutes general affirmance for that claim except as to any specifically reversed ground. A new ground of rejection is designated as such and is not final for judicial review; appellant has two months to either reopen prosecution (amend/submit new evidence) or request rehearing under § 41.52 addressing the new ground with particularity. Remands included in Board decisions are not final for judicial review; after remand proceedings conclude the Board may adopt its earlier decision as final or render a new decision.

name: Final rejection — meaning and implications
description: A 'final rejection' from the USPTO is issued on or after a second office action and is considered a closure of prosecution by the examiner; the application is considered closed and no patent is issued after the final rejection.
guidance: The term 'final' is a misnomer — you still have multiple procedural avenues (RCE, AAF, AFCP, appeal, continuation, etc.) to continue prosecution or challenge the rejection. Final rejections indicate the examiner believes there is a clear patentability issue (e.g., unresolved objections from earlier actions). Understand whether the rejection truly forecloses your claims or whether targeted amendments/arguments can address it.

name: 35 U.S.C. § 101 – Subject Matter Eligibility
description: Claims may be rejected as abstract ideas, natural phenomena, or laws of nature. This is particularly common with software and biotech patents.
guidance: Treat §101 rejections as legally and factually complex given evolving case law and USPTO guidance. Responses often require tying claims to a practical application or technical improvement, using USPTO examples/guidance, and amending claims to include concrete steps (avoid broad, functional language). Supporting evidence (declarations) or examiner interviews can strengthen the response.

name: 35 U.S.C. § 102 – Novelty
description: A rejection under §102 means the claimed invention is not new and is already disclosed in prior art.
guidance: Address §102 by distinguishing the claimed features from the asserted prior art or by amending claims to recite novel limitations. Demonstrate that no single prior-art reference discloses all claim elements.

name: 35 U.S.C. § 103 – Obviousness
description: Even if a claim is novel, it may be deemed obvious in light of multiple prior art references.
guidance: Counter §103 rejections by arguing non-obviousness through teaching-away, unexpected results, technical advantages, or through claim amendments that add inventive limitations. Use factual showings and legal arguments to rebut combinations asserted by the examiner.

name: 35 U.S.C. § 112 – Specification and claim issues
description: This includes inadequate written descriptions, lack of enablement, or indefinite claim language.
guidance: Respond by amending the specification or claims to add detail, clarification, or support (e.g., add examples, clarify terms). For indefiniteness, narrow or rephrase claim terms. AAFs are often effective for straightforward §112 issues.

name: Amendment After Final (AAF)
description: Submit an AAF to make amendments after a final rejection; an AAF does not involve USPTO fees but gives the examiner a limited time to review the application.
guidance: AAF is cost-effective for quick, straightforward amendments (especially to resolve simple issues such as §112 claim language problems). Because examiner review time is limited, AAFs are best for narrow, easily-addressed objections rather than complex claim-redrafting or substantive new arguments.

name: After Final Consideration Pilot (AFCP) — eligibility and limits
description: File an AFCP request (often together with an AAF) to give the examiner additional time to consider the AAF under the pilot program, subject to eligibility conditions.
guidance: Conditions for AFCP eligibility: (1) you must have been issued a final rejection; (2) you must have filed an AAF; (3) your AAF must amend at least one independent claim without broadening the claim; and (4) you must agree to a telephone interview if required. Note the additional time given to the examiner is still limited; AFCP is useful when a narrow amendment to an independent claim may overcome the rejection and you are willing to participate in examiner communications.

name: Advisory action (post-AAF outcome)
description: If an AAF does not resolve outstanding issues, the patent examiner issues an advisory action which may include basic or additional information regarding the review.
guidance: When you receive an advisory action, options include abandoning the application, abandoning and filing a new application, filing an RCE to reopen examination, or filing an appeal. Choose based on cost, likelihood of success, and strategic goals (e.g., claim scope you want to preserve or pursue in a continuation).

name: Strategies for overcoming §101 rejections
description: Because §101 rejections often assert that the invention is a judicial exception (e.g., an abstract idea), responses should be strategic and supported by law and facts.
guidance: Tactical approaches include: (a) Focus on Practical Application — emphasize how the invention improves a technical field or computer functionality; (b) Use USPTO Guidance — cite the USPTO’s Subject Matter Eligibility guidance (e.g., 2019 PEG and updates) and relevant examples/decisions; (c) Amend with Specificity — add concrete steps tying the abstract idea to real-world use; (d) Avoid Overgeneralization — remove overly broad functional claim language that could trigger 101 issues; (e) Highlight Inventive Concept — argue the implementation is inventive and not routine/conventional. Supporting evidence such as declarations and examiner interviews can strengthen §101 arguments.

name: Examiner interviews and their strategic impact
description: Examiner interviews are informal discussions that can clarify the examiner’s reasoning and expectations and often lead to constructive amendments or avoid written responses.
guidance: Benefits include clarifying ambiguous claim language, understanding the examiner’s interpretation of prior art, testing potential amendments before formal submission, and discussing eligibility under §101 or obviousness under §103. Schedule interviews soon after a final rejection to potentially save time and obtain more favorable outcomes. Note: AFCP may require agreement to a telephone interview.

name: Life science examples for eligibility analysis
description: Use of life-science example claims and hypothetical scenarios as teaching tools for applying eligibility guidance in fact-specific situations.
guidance: The USPTO produced new life science examples that provide exemplary subject matter eligibility analysis under 35 U.S.C. 101 of hypothetical claims and claims drawn from case law. The examples are intended as a teaching tool to assist examiners and the public in understanding how the Office would apply the eligibility guidance in certain fact-specific situations.

name: Transportation appropriation covers transport of materials and personnel for military business
description: Appropriation for 'Transportation of the Army' may bear expenses such as transportation of baggage of officers on military duty, movement of units to expositions when treated as military, transport of cadets, transport of insane prisoners to government hospitals, dredging to enable landing of troops and supplies, salvage claims on government property transported in private vessels, carriage hire incident to official calls, and similar military-necessity transports.
guidance: Multiple examples listed (C.10587; C.10825; C.10863; C.20052; C.21602; C.17725; C.26396; C.25821). But the line is sometimes discretionary and depends on whether the Secretary regards the trip as public business.

name: Scope and limits of PURs (claim‑by‑claim and changes permitted)
description: PUR applies on a claim‑by‑claim basis. Prior user may make changes so long as they do not relate to the inventive concept of the patent (see Kobold Corporation et al v NCS Multistage Inc, 2021 FC 1437).
guidance: Courts will permit evolution of the prior user's embodiment provided changes do not encroach on the inventive concept protected by the patent; scope is therefore limited to what the prior use effectively covered per claim.

name: Anti‑double‑patenting and purposive construction for obviousness‑type double patenting
description: Same applicant: No two patents shall issue with claims to the same invention or claims that are not patentably distinct. For obviousness‑type double patenting, claims are given a purposive construction based on reading the specification through the eyes of the skilled person, taking into account common general knowledge.
guidance: If the claims of the existing patent, as understood by the person skilled in the art in light of CGK on the claim date and the teachings of the specification as a whole, anticipate or render obvious the claims of the application being examined, the claims are not patentably distinct.

name: Three-condition framework for S.3(d) applicability
description: From the section's wording, three conditions must be satisfied for S.3(d) to apply: (1) what is claimed must be a 'mere discovery'; (2) it must be a new form of a known substance; and (3) such claimed substance does not bring about increased efficacy over the known substance.
guidance: If any of the three conditions are not met, S.3(d) should not apply. Use these sequentially to assess whether S.3(d) bars patentability.

name: Markush claim definition
description: A 'Markush' claim recites a list of alternatively useable members. The listing of specified alternatives within a Markush claim is referred to as a Markush group or Markush grouping. Claim language defined by a Markush grouping requires selection from a closed group 'consisting of' the alternative members.
guidance: Treatment of claims reciting alternatives is not governed by the particular format used (e.g., 'selected from the group consisting of A, B, and C' or 'A, B, or C'); any claim that recites alternatively usable members, regardless of format, should be treated as a Markush claim. See cited cases (Ex parte Markush; Abbott Labs v. Baxter; Amgen v. Amneal).

name: Common use requirement
description: Members of the Markush group must share a common function or use when disclosed in the specification or known in the art to be functionally equivalent in the context of the claimed invention.
guidance: Common use may be shown by the specification or prior art; absence of common use supports an 'improper Markush grouping' rejection.

name: Improper Markush grouping rejection procedure
description: When an examiner determines the species of a Markush group do not share a single structural similarity or common use, the claim may be rejected as containing an 'improper Markush grouping'. Such a rejection is on the merits and may be appealed to the PTAB.
guidance: Use Form Paragraph 8.40 for improper Markush grouping rejections. The form paragraph should state why the alternatives fail the two-prong test and provide specifics (insert claim numbers, describe the improper Markush group(s), and explain why requirements are not met).

name: Content required in improper Markush grouping rejection
description: An improper Markush grouping rejection must explain why the alternatives are not all members of the same recognized class and/or why they are not functionally equivalent and have a common use, and/or why (for chemical compounds) they do not share both a substantial structural feature and a related common use.
guidance: Include bracketed specifics per Form Paragraph 8.40: claim numbers, description of Markush group(s), and the factual/legal reasons the group is improper. If election of species is appropriate, wait until after applicant has made an election before using this form paragraph.

name: Examiner suggestions to overcome rejection
description: Examiners should include suggestions for how the applicant may overcome an improper Markush grouping rejection.
guidance: Suggested actions include proposing a proper Markush grouping based on the specification or requiring applicant to set forth each alternative (or grouping of patentably indistinct alternatives) in a series of independent or dependent claims. Examiner should not suggest any grouping that would clearly lack adequate written description under 35 U.S.C. 112(a).

name: Indefiniteness under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) when metes and bounds unclear
description: If a person skilled in the art cannot determine the metes and bounds of the Markush claim due to an inability to envision all members of the Markush grouping, the claim is indefinite and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b).
guidance: This is a separate ground; see MPEP §2173.05(h) for related discussion. Rejection under improper grouping and 112(b) may both be appropriate where boundaries cannot be drawn.

name: Maintaining, overcoming, and reconsidering improper grouping rejection
description: An improper Markush grouping rejection should be maintained until the claim is amended to include only members sharing a single structural similarity and common use, or the applicant presents convincing arguments that the group members share such similarity and use.
guidance: Even if applicant does not overcome the rejection, when all claims are otherwise in condition for allowance the examiner should reconsider the propriety of the rejection and withdraw it if warranted by the record and prior art. No Markush claim can be allowed until the improper grouping rejection is overcome or withdrawn and all other conditions satisfied.

name: Case-by-case evaluation and illustrative examples
description: The propriety of Markush groupings must be decided on a case-by-case basis; examples (Harnisch, Dams, Hozumi, PCT example) illustrate application of the two-prong test and how to weigh common structural features and common use.
guidance: Use the cited cases to guide factual analyses: focus on the commonality across alternative embodiments, the specification disclosure of common properties/utility, and whether the claimed feature is essential to the utility. Examples show how to apply principles when claims are broad or when alternatives vary in functional groups.

name: Format neutrality of Markush treatment
description: The treatment of claims reciting alternatives is not governed by the particular wording or format used to recite the alternatives; any claim that recites alternatively usable members should be treated as a Markush claim.
guidance: Whether the alternatives are presented as a 'group consisting of', as 'A, B, or C', or in chemical formula form, the same substantive tests (single structural similarity and common use) apply.

name: Selection of drawing figure and representative claim for Official Gazette
description: An appropriate drawing figure is to be indicated for printing on the certificate cover sheet and in the Official Gazette. In addition, a representative claim which has been reexamined is to be indicated for publication in the Official Gazette.
guidance: Select the broadest claim. Examiners should ordinarily designate but one claim on each invention; in reexamination the examiner must select only one claim. A dependent claim should not be selected unless the independent claim from which it depends is also printed; special rules apply for multiple dependent and reissue claims.

name: Recording claim numbers and renumbering rule
description: When recording this information in the box provided, enter the claim number clearly; if multiple claims are selected, separate claim numbers by commas; the claim designated must be referred to by using the renumbered patent claim number rather than the original claim number if different.
guidance: Follow the renumbering as reflected in the reexamination file; be precise to avoid misidentification on the certificate/Official Gazette.

name: Handling when all claims are canceled — confirmation contact
description: Prior to canceling the claims and issuing the NIRC, the examiner should telephone the patent owner to inquire if a timely response, timely appeal, etc., was filed ... so as to make certain that a timely response has not been misdirected within the Office.
guidance: If the patent owner indicates no such filing or cannot be reached, proceed to issue a NIRC terminating prosecution. If contacted, make the telephone interview of record as attachment to the NIRC.

name: Drafting examiner's amendment canceling all claims
description: If the proceeding is to be concluded by the cancellation of all claims, the examiner will issue a NIRC action, and as an attachment to the NIRC, the examiner will draft an examiner's amendment canceling all live claims in the reexamination proceeding. In the examiner's amendment, the examiner should point out why the claims have been canceled.
guidance: Provide specific explanatory statements (examples are provided in MPEP) referencing the Office action dates, Board decisions, and applicable CFR and MPEP sections.

name: Treatment of multiple dependent claims in reexamination
description: For the purpose of the NIRC, the addition of a claim of the multiple dependency is viewed as adding a new claim ... the deletion of a claim of the multiple dependency is viewed as canceling the claim deleted.
guidance: For certificate printing and the Examiner's checklist, additions/deletions of multiple dependency elements are often treated as amended claims (printed in amended form), while new dependency-based claims may be designated as 'new' and deleted ones as 'canceled'; provide clear mapping of pre- and post-reexamination designations (examples given in MPEP).

name: Claim status reporting on Examiner's checklist
description: Complete Examiner's checklist items to indicate which patent claims are confirmed, amended, canceled, dependent on amended, and new claims patentable.
guidance: Follow the specific entries and example formatting in the MPEP to populate checklist items (e.g., Patent claims confirmed: 1, 5, 7; Patent claims amended: 2, 3, 4 and 6; New claims patentable: 8).

name: Reexamination reminder — amendment formatting and multiple amendments
description: All amendments to the description and claims must conform to requirements of 37 CFR 1.530(d)-(j). If a portion of the text is amended more than once, each amendment should indicate all of the changes (insertions and deletions) in relation to the current text in the patent under reexamination.
guidance: Follow MPEP § 2250 for specific marking and presentation requirements; examiner's amendment must meet the same rules.

name: Reexamination reminder — reasons for patentability required
description: Reasons for patentability and/or confirmation are required for each claim found patentable.
guidance: Provide clear reasons in an attachment to the NIRC explaining why the claims are patentable over cited patents or publications; see guidance below for forms and phrasing.

name: Reexamination reminder — amended/new claims may not enlarge scope
description: An amended or new claim may not enlarge the scope of the patent claims.
guidance: Ensure all claim amendments narrow or maintain scope relative to the patent as issued; see MPEP § 2250.

name: Reexamination reminder — effects when patent expired during proceeding
description: If the patent has expired, all amendments to the patent claims and all claims added during the proceeding must be withdrawn. Further, all presently rejected and objected-to claims are canceled by examiner's amendment.
guidance: Include a statement in the examiner's amendment withdrawing such changes (sample language provided in MPEP).

name: Reasons for patentability and/or confirmation preparation
description: In the attachment to the NIRC, the examiner should indicate why the claims found patentable in the reexamination proceeding are clearly patentable over the cited patents or printed publications.
guidance: Set forth reasons similar to those used for allowance in an application (see MPEP § 1302.14). May use form PTOL-476 or form paragraph 22.16 ('Statement of Reasons for Patentability and/or Confirmation'). Where the record is clear, examiner may refer to particular portions of the record which establish patentability. Any comments by the patent owner must be labeled and will be placed in the reexamination file.

name: Designation and terminology for confirmed vs patentable claims
description: Original patent claims that are found patentable in a reexamination proceeding are generally to be designated as 'confirmed' claims, while new claims and amended patent claims are generally to be designated as 'patentable' claims.
guidance: For purposes of setting forth reasons, the examiner may use 'patentable' to refer to any claim that defines over the cited patents or printed publications; there is no need to separate 'confirmed' and 'patentable' categories when stating reasons.

name: Effect of certificate canceling all claims and rare reissue exception
description: If a certificate issues and publishes which cancels all of the claims of the patent, no further Office proceedings will be conducted with regard to that patent or any reissue application or reexamination request directed thereto.
guidance: In rare situations where a reissue application is copending, the patent owner may file a petition under 37 CFR 1.183 requesting waiver of 37 CFR 1.570(d) to address claims pending in the reissue application; such petition must be accompanied by a paper cancelling any claim within the scope of the claims canceled by the certificate and explaining why remaining claims are patentable over canceled claims.

name: Unauthorized Practice of Patent Law (37 C.F.R. § 11.505)
description: A practitioner shall not practice law in a jurisdiction in violation of that jurisdiction's regulations; the USPTO is a 'jurisdiction' for purposes of § 11.505. Only practitioners registered under § 11.6 are permitted to prosecute patent applications of others before the Office.
guidance: Activities constituting practice before the Office include reviewing/drafting responses to Notices/Office Actions, making arguments about patentability, drafting/revising patent applications (specifications, claims, drawings), advising on patent strategy, preparing CIPs and PCT filings. Prior USPTO precedents (Wengrovsky, Gaudio) show trademark practitioners providing such services can be disciplined for unauthorized patent practice.

name: Burden of Proof for Affirmative Defenses (37 C.F.R. § 11.49)
description: Practitioners have the burden of proving any affirmative defense by clear and convincing evidence.
guidance: Failure to produce clear and convincing evidence supporting affirmative defenses (waiver, laches, unclean hands, estoppel, constitutional claims, statutory overreach, etc.) will result in rejection of those defenses.

name: Due Process Requirements in Disciplinary Proceedings
description: Due process requires reasonable notice of charges and a meaningful opportunity to be heard, including presenting evidence, testifying, cross-examining witnesses, and presenting argument.
guidance: Participation in hearings with opportunity to present and challenge evidence generally satisfies due process; claims that constitutional due process was violated must be adequately pleaded and developed, and unsupported or undeveloped constitutional assertions may be deemed waived.

name: Definition and Evidence of 'Practice Before the Office' (37 C.F.R. § 11.5)
description: 37 C.F.R. § 11.5 defines 'practice before the Office' and identifies activities that constitute practice in patent matters (see § 11.5 and § 11.5(b)(1)).
guidance: The record may include testimony, invoices, documents showing performance of tasks such as drafting patent applications, responding to Office actions, preparing claims, and advising on prosecution strategy; such evidence supports findings of practice before the Office even if the practitioner did not sign filings.

name: Varying breadth of claims
description: Varying the breadth of claims can offer insurance against arguments that a patent is invalid based on the prior art.
guidance: Drafting claims of differing scope (broad independent claims plus narrower dependent claims) helps defend against prior art discovered later (e.g., during infringement litigation) that might destroy the broad claim but not the narrower ones.

name: Independent claim should specify essential features
description: An independent claim should typically specify the essential features needed to define the invention.
guidance: Although standards vary by office, features implied by generic terms may not need explicit recitation (e.g., a bicycle claim need not mention wheels). Where patentability depends on a technical effect, include all technical features essential for that effect. Claims must be clear and directed to the heart of the invention.

name: Process claims must necessarily lead to the claimed product
description: If a claim is directed to a process for producing a product X, the process claimed should be such that, when carried out reasonably by a person skilled in the art, it necessarily leads to product X as its end result.
guidance: If the claimed process does not inevitably produce the claimed product, there is internal inconsistency and lack of clarity in the claim.

name: Product claims for well-known kinds may identify product and modifications
description: In the case of a product claim, if the product is of a well-known kind and the invention lies in modifying it, it is typically sufficient that the claim clearly identifies the well-known product and specifies what is modified and how.
guidance: Similar considerations apply to apparatus claims; clearly identify the known product and the modifications that embody the inventive contribution.

name: Draft a combination of broad independent and narrower dependent claims
description: Patent drafters commonly prepare a combination of broad and narrow claims by first drafting the broadest independent claim and then drafting dependent claims covering various narrower scopes.
guidance: Dependent claims act as a practical fallback if prior art defeats a broad independent claim; narrower dependent claims may still allow the applicant to obtain useful protection and commercial advantage.

name: Dependent claim format signals dependency and reduces repetition
description: A dependent claim is one that 'depends from' another claim and refers to a parent claim (e.g., 'The apparatus of Claim 1, further comprising...'), which includes everything from the parent claim plus whatever is newly recited.
guidance: This format makes the dependent claim more concise by avoiding repetition of the whole parent claim. Dependent claims tend to be considerably shorter than independent claims.

name: Dependent claims are always narrower than the claim from which they depend
description: Dependent claims can only add elements or limitations to the claim from which they depend; they cannot subtract or broaden the parent claim.
guidance: Example of improper dependent claim: a dependent claim that states 'wherein the light is not attached to the pencil' would subtract an essential element and is therefore improper. Dependent claims must not extend the scope of protection of the corresponding independent claim.

name: Three permitted ways for a dependent claim to state additional features
description: Immediately after the reference to another claim, a dependent claim states at least one additional feature by: (i) adding at least one new element (typically 'further comprising E'); (ii) selecting at least one element from a broader element in the parent claim (typically 'wherein E is E1') or further characterizing an element; or (iii) a combination of (i) and (ii).
guidance: Examples: adding a light to a pencil (further comprising); narrowing 'light' to 'LED light' (wherein); or both adding and narrowing.

name: Dependent claims must refer back to at least one previous claim and cannot refer forward
description: All dependent claims must refer back to at least one previous claim and they cannot refer forward to a subsequent claim.
guidance: Arrangement and numbering must ensure clear dependency (claim trees help visualize relationships).

name: Group and arrange dependent claims to enable ready reckoning and construction
description: Dependent claims should be grouped together in the most appropriate way possible so that their association and meaning can be readily understood.
guidance: The arrangement must enable a ready reckoning and construction of related claims and their meaning; use logical groupings to simplify understanding and later amendments.

name: Dependent claims serve as a prosecution fallback and can be converted to independent claims
description: Dependent claims reflect the 'fallback' position: if an examiner finds prior art that denies patentability to a broad independent claim but not to a dependent claim, the applicant may obtain a patent by cancelling the rejected independent claim and drafting a new independent claim by combining limitations from the allowable dependent claim.
guidance: Examples are provided showing renumbering and amendment formats (deleted words strikethrough, new words underlined). Amendment procedures vary by jurisdiction; dependent claims may be renumbered and amended to become independent when client approves.

name: Dependent claims can support a broader interpretation of independent claims
description: A dependent claim can be used to support a broader interpretation of an independent claim by clarifying that the independent claim can cover alternatives beyond what the dependent claim specifies.
guidance: Example: Claim 1 recites 'a box' and dependent Claim 2 recites 'wherein the box is wooden'; the dependent clarifies but also implies Claim 1 could be wooden or nonwooden. This can help arguments about support/enablement, although an opponent might argue lack of support for alternatives.

name: Dependent claims with two-part and Markush independent claims
description: When a dependent claim depends on an independent claim written in the two-part format (separated by 'characterized in that'), the dependent claim includes everything in both parts and the 'characterized by' phrase is unnecessary (though permissible). For Markush independent claims, a dependent claim may define a narrower subset of the Markush group.
guidance: Examples include two-part claims for writing devices and Markush group narrowing for chemical claims (selecting specific R groups). Dependent claims narrow the broader set by specifying members of the Markush group.

name: Multiple dependent claims: format and interpretation
description: A multiple dependent claim refers to more than one claim in the alternative (e.g., 'the apparatus of Claim 1 or Claim 2' or 'of one of Claims 1 and 2'), meaning it depends from either claim but not both.
guidance: The body of a multiple dependent claim must narrow the claim(s) from which it depends. A multiple dependent claim covers embodiments that satisfy any one of the parent claims to which it refers.

name: Permissible and impermissible phrasing for multiple dependent claims
description: Many expressions are accepted to refer to more than one claim in the alternative (e.g., 'according to Claim 1 or Claim 2', 'as in any of the preceding claims in which...'). Wording that would cause the claims to become cumulative is not permitted (e.g., 'according to Claims 1 and 2', 'according to Claims 1–3', 'as in Claims 1, 2 and/or 3').
guidance: Avoid cumulative formulations that would improperly broaden or combine claims; use alternative phrasing to limit dependency to alternatives.

name: Pros and cons of multiple dependent claims including fee implications
description: Multiple dependent claims usually reduce the countable number of claims, which can affect client decisions because claim fee structures differ by office.
guidance: In the US, multiple dependent claims trigger extra fees and are uncommon; at the EPO they may save fees due to countable claim numbering. Using multiple dependent claims may also facilitate certain amendments (e.g., in the EPO) but excessive use (multiple-multiple dependencies) can complicate comprehension.

name: Multiple-multiple dependent claims permissibility varies by jurisdiction
description: Some jurisdictions (e.g., EPO, Japan) permit multiple-multiple dependent claims (a multiple dependent claim serving as a basis for another multiple dependent claim), while others (e.g., United States, Republic of Korea) do not.
guidance: Be cautious when drafting multiple-multiple dependencies; check local rules to ensure permissibility and to avoid drafting claims that will be disallowed.

name: Claim sets can be reasoned about using set theory and Venn diagrams
description: Claims establish boundaries of technical subject matter (peripheral claiming); their relationships (independent vs dependent) can be illustrated by set theory (subsets, overlaps) and Venn diagrams to show scopes and embodiments.
guidance: Use set representations to visualize how dependent claims form subsets of independent claims, how dependency chains and dependency pyramids arise, and how specific embodiments map into claim scopes. This assists drafting and later interpretation.

name: Analyze claim dependency relationships to assess validity and infringement
description: Analysis of dependency relationships among patent claims is helpful to patent examiners assessing validity (novelty, inventive step) and to judges when validity of granted patents is challenged, and it is also helpful when assessing infringement.
guidance: Use claim trees, dependency charts and scope diagrams to identify which claims may remain novel in light of prior art and which claims an accused product might infringe; examples illustrate situations where some dependent claims remain novel while independent claims do not.

name: Ways to overcome a provisional 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection (options A–E)
description: The rejection can be overcome by: (A) arguing patentability over the earlier filed application; (B) combining the subject matter of the copending applications into a single application claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 and abandoning the copending applications; (C) filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 showing derivation; (D) filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(a) showing a date of invention prior to the effective U.S. filing date of the copending application; or (E) for applications pending on or after December 10, 2004, showing that the prior art and the claimed invention were owned by the same person (or subject to obligation of assignment) at the time the invention was made, or that the subject matter is disqualified under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) (joint research agreement).
guidance: Note for (B): a claim in a subsequently filed application relying on a combination of prior applications may not get the benefit of an earlier filing date under 35 U.S.C. 120 if the earlier filed application does not contain a disclosure which complies with 35 U.S.C. 112 for the claim. See Studiengesellschaft Kohle and MPEP cross-references. For (C) and (D) see MPEP §§ 715.01(a), 715.01(c), 716.10 and 715. For (E) see MPEP § 2146. Where interfering subject matter under 37 CFR 41.203(a) is claimed, a terminal disclaimer and an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(c) may be used to overcome a 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection in common ownership situations if the earlier filed application has been published or matured into a patent (see MPEP § 718).

name: Form paragraph 7.06: Notice re prior art available under both pre-AIA and AIA
description: In the event the determination of the status of the application as subject to AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 (or as subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103) is incorrect, any correction of the statutory basis for the rejection will not be considered a new ground of rejection if the prior art relied upon, and the rationale supporting the rejection, would be the same under either status.
guidance: Examiner Notes: (1) This form paragraph must be used in all Office Actions when a prior art rejection is made in an application with an actual filing date on or after March 16, 2013, that claims priority to, or the benefit of, an application filed before March 16, 2013. (2) This form paragraph should only be used ONCE in an Office action.

name: Form paragraph 7.20.02.fti: Joint inventors, common ownership presumed
description: This application currently names joint inventors. In considering patentability of the claims under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a), the examiner presumes that the subject matter of the various claims was commonly owned at the time any inventions covered therein were made absent any evidence to the contrary. Applicant is advised of the obligation under 37 CFR 1.56 to point out inventor and invention dates of each claim that was not commonly owned at the time a later invention was made.
guidance: Examiner Note: This paragraph must be used in all applications with joint inventors (unless the claims are clearly restricted to only one claimed invention, e.g., only a single claim is presented).

name: Form paragraph 7.21.fti: Rejection, Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a)
description: Claim [1] is/are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over [2].
guidance: Examiner Notes: (1) This paragraph must be preceded by either form paragraph 7.20.fti or 7.103. (2) An explanation of the rejection must follow this form paragraph (see MPEP § 2144). (3) If the rejection relies upon prior art under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e), use pre-AIA 102(e) as amended by the AIPA to determine the reference's prior art date unless the reference is a U.S. patent issued directly/indirectly from an international application with an international filing date prior to Nov 29, 2000 — see related guidance. (4) If the applicability of this rejection prevents the reference from being disqualified under 103(c), form paragraph 7.20.01.fti must follow. (5) If this rejection is a provisional 103(a) rejection based upon a copending application that would comprise prior art under 102(e) if patented or published, use form paragraph 7.21.01.fti instead. (6–7) Instructions for bracket entries.

name: Form paragraph 7.21.01.fti: Provisional rejection template (common assignee/applicant/joint inventor)
description: Claim [1] is/are provisionally rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being obvious over copending Application No. [2] which has a common [3] with the instant application. Based upon the earlier effective U.S. filing date of the copending application, it would constitute prior art under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) if published or patented. This provisional rejection ... is based upon a presumption of future publication or patenting of the copending application.
guidance: This paragraph is used to provisionally reject claims not patentably distinct from disclosure in a copending application having an earlier U.S. filing date and a common assignee, common applicant (35 U.S.C. 118), or at least one common joint inventor. Do not use when copending application is disqualified under 103(c). Use pre-AIA 102(e)/pre-AIPA 102(e) rules to determine prior art date as appropriate. If claimed invention is fully disclosed in copending application, use paragraph 7.15.01.fti. Insert claim numbers, application number, and specify --assignee--, --applicant--, or --joint inventor-- in brackets. This provisional rejection might be overcome by 37 CFR 1.132, 1.131(a), or showing disqualification under 103(c). If not patentably distinct, make provisional obviousness double patenting rejection using form paragraphs 8.33 and 8.37. Additional rejection under 7.21.fti should be made when (a) evidence indicates the copending application is also prior art under 102(f) or (g); and (b) the copending application has not been disqualified under 103(c).

name: Form paragraph 7.21.02.fti: Rejection using reference with common assignee/applicant/joint inventor
description: Claim [1] is/are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being obvious over [2]. The applied reference has a common [3] with the instant application. Based upon the earlier effective U.S. filing date of the reference, it constitutes prior art under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e).
guidance: This rejection might be overcome by: (1) a showing under 37 CFR 1.132 that any invention disclosed but not claimed in the reference was derived from the inventor of this application; (2) a showing of a date of invention for the claimed subject matter prior to the effective U.S. filing date of the reference under 37 CFR 1.131(a); or (3) an oath or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(c) stating current common ownership and that the inventive entity named is the prior inventor under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 104 (as in effect on March 15, 2013), together with a terminal disclaimer under 37 CFR 1.321(c). This paragraph should not be used if the reference qualifies as prior art under 102(a) or (b) or is disqualified under 103(c).

name: Form paragraph 7.22.fti: Rejection, pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a), further in view of
description: Claim [1] rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over [2] as applied to claim [3] above, and further in view of [4].
guidance: Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.21.fti. An explanation of the rejection must follow (see MPEP § 2144). If the rejection relies upon prior art under pre-AIA 102(e), follow the AIPA/prior art date determination rules described elsewhere. Insert appropriate bracketed references and explanation of how the additional reference is applied.

name: Test for obviousness (Graham factors)
description: The factual inquiries for establishing a background for determining obviousness under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) are summarized as follows: 1. Determining the scope and contents of the prior art. 2. Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue. 3. Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art. 4. Considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
guidance: This form paragraph (7.23.fti) may be used, if appropriate, in response to an argument regarding the applicability of the factors for determining obviousness. See MPEP § 2144 for requirements to explain the combination and rationale when rejecting under 103(a).

name: Refund of search fee and excess claims fee (37 CFR 1.138(d))
description: To obtain refund of the search fee and excess claims fee under 37 CFR 1.138(d), the petition and declaration of express abandonment must be submitted before an examination has been made of the application.
guidance: The date on any certificate of mailing or transmission under § 1.8 is not taken into account for determining whether the petition was filed before examination. If not filed before examination, the Office will not refund except as provided in § 1.26. A petition under 1.138(d) will be denied if PALM shows status higher than 031 on or before the filing day; technical preparations for publication generally begin four months prior to projected publication date. Form PTO/SB/24B is recommended; facsimile to Pre-Grant Publication is recommended.

name: Form use and purposes (PTO/SB/24, 24A, 24B)
description: Form PTO/SB/24 may be used for filing a letter of express abandonment; PTO/SB/24A for petition under 1.138(c) to avoid publication; PTO/SB/24B for petition under 1.138(d) to obtain a refund of search fee and excess claims fee.
guidance: Forms include required fields and signature blocks; use of the specific form suited to the requested relief is recommended to avoid delays. The MPEP reproduces these forms and recommends their use.

name: Content limits for concise description of relevance
description: At a minimum, a concise description must be more than a bare statement that the document is relevant (e.g., 'Document 1 is relevant' is insufficient). A copy merely annotated or highlighted will not be deemed a proper concise description.
guidance: Avoid verbosity; be focused. A concise description that includes a short field-intro plus a claim chart mapping document portions to claim elements is likely acceptable. Descriptions that merely repeat information in a claim chart or that approach the length of the documents themselves are not likely to be considered 'concise.' Descriptions that appear to be mere form paragraphs opposing a general class of inventions are non-compliant.

name: Examples of compliant versus non-compliant concise descriptions
description: MPEP provides narrative and claim-chart examples showing compliant content (factual mappings to claim elements, pointing to specific pages/lines/figures) and non-compliant content (statements asserting obviousness or that a claim is unpatentable).
guidance: Use the examples as templates: indicate which claim elements are disclosed by which parts of a publication and cite precise pages/lines/figures. Avoid bolded-style argument language that concludes unpatentability or obviousness.

name: Participation in training and Quality Enhancement Meetings (QEMs)
description: Pilot participants are expected to attend Pilot-specific group training and QEMs covering Pilot introduction, claim interpretation, interview summaries, and reasons for allowance.
guidance: At the start of the Pilot participants attended training on clarifying the record (modules listed). During QEMs participants discuss and develop best practices and may receive additional training.

name: Enhance clarity of Office actions for selected cases
description: Examiners should enhance the clarity of Office actions for selected cases as part of the Pilot activities.
guidance: Selected Office actions are to be modified to include clearer claim interpretations, interview summaries, or reasons for allowance to test the impact of enhanced recordation.

name: Representation and sufficiency of views
description: The design must be represented by a drawing that complies with § 1.84 and must contain a sufficient number of views to constitute a complete disclosure of the appearance of the design.
guidance: Views should disclose the complete appearance of the claimed design and may include front, rear, top, bottom and sides. Perspective views are suggested for three-dimensional designs and, if clearly understood, may obviate the need to illustrate the same surfaces in other views. Views that are merely duplicative or flat and include no surface ornamentation may be omitted if the specification explicitly states so (e.g., one side shown and the other stated as identical or mirror image; bottom may be omitted if stated flat and unornamented). If inconsistencies among views make the overall appearance unclear, the examiner should object and, if so severe, the claim should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112 (first and second paragraphs). Sectional views solely showing internal construction or functional features are unnecessary and may be objected to; sectional views may be included only when exterior contour is not apparent and no internal construction is attempted. When sectional views are added during prosecution, check for antecedent basis for hatching per 37 CFR 1.84(h)(3).

name: Use and description of broken lines
description: Broken lines may be used to show visible environmental structure or to define bounds of the claim but may not be used to show hidden planes/surfaces or to indicate that a portion is of less importance in the design.
guidance: Unclaimed subject matter (environment) may be shown in broken lines and must be described as forming no part of the claimed design or of a specified embodiment. A broken-line boundary may be used to define the bounds of a claimed design, but any broken-line boundary other than a straight broken line may constitute new matter. Broken lines must not be used to show hidden planes and surfaces that cannot be seen through opaque materials. Broken lines should not intrude upon or cross the showing of the claimed design and should not be heavier than full lines. If broken lines cross over full lines, the specification must explicitly identify their purpose (e.g., distinguishing broken-line bounds from broken-line environment), and when broken-line environment obscures the claimed design a separate figure showing the broken lines must be included. Use the prescribed statement to describe broken lines in the specification: “The broken line showing of [1] is for the purpose of illustrating [2] and forms no part of the claimed design.” See also form paragraphs 15.50–15.50.05.

name: Sectional views and internal-construction depictions
description: Sectional views presented solely to show internal construction or functional/mechanical features are unnecessary and may lead to confusion as to the scope of the claimed design and should be objected to under 35 U.S.C. 112 (second paragraph).
guidance: Sectional views may be included only where the exact contour or configuration of the exterior surface of a claimed design is not apparent from the views and no attempt is made to illustrate internal construction. If sectional hatching is added during prosecution, determine whether there is antecedent basis in the original disclosure for the material shown in hatching (37 CFR 1.84(h)(3) and MPEP § 608.02). See cited authorities (Ex parte Tucker; Ex parte Kohler; Ex parte Lohman) for examples.

name: Photographs and color-drawing rules
description: Drawings are normally required in black ink on white paper; photographs are acceptable only when the invention cannot be illustrated in an ink drawing or is shown more clearly in a photograph. Color photographs/drawings have special petition requirements.
guidance: Photographs submitted in lieu of ink drawings must comply with 37 CFR 1.84(b) and must be limited to the design claimed for the article (must not disclose environmental structure). Only one set of black-and-white photographs is required. Color photographs and color drawings may be submitted only with a grantable petition under 37 CFR 1.84(a)(2); a grantable petition must: explain that color is integral to the claimed design, include the fee (37 CFR 1.17(h)), include three sets of the color photos/drawings, and include an amendment to the specification inserting a statement that the file contains at least one drawing/photograph executed in color. If informal color photos/drawings are filed for filing-date purposes, applicant must later submit the petition/fee/sets/statements to treat them as formal. Photographs and ink drawings must not be combined as the formal visual disclosure in one application. If photographs are not of sufficient quality to reproduce all details, objections will be raised and no patent will be issued until acceptable photographs are submitted and approved. If color photographs/drawings are filed originally, color is considered an integral part of the claimed design; omission of color later may be permitted only if underlying configuration without color is clear from the application (see In re Daniels).

name: Necessity for clear, complete drawings (fatal if insufficient)
description: The drawing or photograph constitutes the entire visual disclosure of the claim and must be so clear and complete that nothing regarding the design sought to be patented is left to conjecture; an insufficient drawing may be fatal to validity under 35 U.S.C. 112 (first paragraph).
guidance: Emphasize high quality execution as to clarity and completeness. An insufficient drawing may also negatively affect the effective filing date of a continuing application. Use form paragraph 15.48 and related MPEP guidance to notify applicants when drawings are inadequate and to require corrections or replacement sheets as appropriate.

name: Statute of limitations and limits on damage claims (trademarks)
description: IP Statute (1996) specifically regulates statute of limitations for IP infringement actions as 5 years. Civil Code (2002) establishes 3 years for lawsuits seeking damages. Courts are unsettled on whether 3 or 5 years applies. Statute of limitations for filing invalidity lawsuit is 5 years from date registration is granted.
guidance: Be conservative and file claims promptly; monitor court treatment of the conflict between statutes.

name: Calculation of damages (trademarks)
description: Damages can be calculated based on (i) lost profits, (ii) profits made by the defendant, or (iii) reasonable royalties, whichever is more favorable for the plaintiff.
guidance: Prepare financial and accounting evidence to support the most favorable measure for the claimant.

name: Patentable subject matter requirements
description: Patents are granted for inventions corresponding to products or methods fulfilling the requirements of novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability (Article 14 of Decision 486).
guidance: Ensure specification and claims support novelty, inventive step, and industrial applicability.

name: Markush claim practice (pharma patents)
description: Markush claims are an acceptable claim format in Colombia. Examiners frequently request limiting the scope of Markush formulas to a reasonable generalization of the examples.
guidance: Be prepared to justify breadth of Markush groups and to narrow during prosecution if requested.

name: Software patents (Colombia)
description: Software as such (lines of code) is non-eligible subject-matter, but inventions providing a technical contribution, complying with patentability requirements and claimable as a product or process can be patentable.
guidance: Frame software-related inventions in terms of technical contributions and tangible product/process steps.

name: Clarity of claims (claim drafting recommendations)
description: Avoid functional characteristics and results to be achieved when drafting claims. Article 30 of Decision 486 requires clear and concise claims, entirely supported by the description.
guidance: Ensure claims are supported directly by specification text; limit functional claiming and always provide enabling description.

name: Method and process claim drafting
description: For methods, key point is to have the inventive steps well defined and characterized. Examiners usually request execution details in the claims (environmental or processing conditions and materials).
guidance: Include concrete execution parameters and materials in claims and description to satisfy examiner requests.

name: Patent application formalities (required items)
description: Specification; one or more drawings (if necessary); title; one or more claims; abstract; power of attorney; payment of fees; copy of applicable genetic resources access contract (if claimed products/methods developed from such resources); copy of traditional knowledge access contract (if applicable); copy of biological deposit certificate (if applicable); copy of assignment; status of foreign patent applications for same subject-matter (if available). Items marked with an asterisk are requested to obtain a filing date; remaining items can be filed later.
guidance: Ensure asterisked items are filed to obtain a filing date; avoid presenting multiple unrelated inventions in one application to prevent restriction/election requirements.

name: Single invention requirement / restriction practice
description: A patent application shall only contain one invention or a group of closely related inventions. Otherwise, a restriction requirement requesting an election will be made.
guidance: Structure claims to present a single inventive concept or closely related group; be prepared to elect and file divisionals if needed.

name: Examiner interviews (patents)
description: Examiner interviews are allowed and easy to obtain (simply request a meeting at the CPO office). Interviews are highly recommended as they are useful in many cases to facilitate prosecution and grant.
guidance: Use interviews to clarify claim scope and expedite resolution of objections.

name: Claim amendments practice
description: Provisional applications are not available under Andean Decision 486. Voluntary claim amendments are possible anytime during prosecution and in any case before a final decision. If the patent is rejected, claims can be amended by filing a Reconsideration Action. Amendments cannot extend the original scope of the invention and must find support in the specification.
guidance: Ensure all amendments are fully supported by the original disclosure; plan claim amendment strategy during prosecution to avoid over-broadening.

name: Divisional practice (CPO Resolution 3719)
description: Divisionals may be filed at any time during prosecution, even after a non-final rejection. Parent claim sets must explicitly carve out the divisional's claimed subject matter. Claims in parent and divisional can be further amended after filing. Specification of the divisional should be adapted to reflect subject-matter divided out. Divisionals from divisionals are not allowed.
guidance: When filing divisionals, ensure parent claims carve out divisional subject matter and adapt the divisional specification; plan family strategy given no chain divisionals.

name: Infringement scope and literal infringement rule (patents)
description: If the patent protects a product, the owner can prevent third parties from importing, using, manufacturing, offering for sale or selling the product. For method patents, the owner can prevent third parties from using the method or performing acts involving products obtained directly through the protected method. A patent will be infringed if any of its claims read on an allegedly infringing product or process. Only literal infringement is contemplated under Andean Decision 486; doctrine of equivalents has not been recognized, though judges may expand interpretations equitably.
guidance: Draft claims carefully to cover intended infringing scenarios; do not rely on doctrine of equivalents as a primary enforcement theory.

name: Trigger for issuing a trial certificate
description: The Office will not issue a trial certificate (e.g., canceling all claims) relating to a patent at issue in an AIA proceeding until after either: (1) the deadline for filing a notice of appeal to the Federal Circuit has passed without an appeal (63 days after a FWD or 63 days after a decision on rehearing), or (2) all decisions or determinations in relation to an appeal to the Federal Circuit regarding the patent are finally resolved.
guidance: Issuance of a trial certificate signifies completion of an AIA proceeding and automatically lifts a stay entered pending completion.

name: Reissue: statutory error requirement (35 U.S.C. § 251)
description: 35 U.S.C. § 251 requires an 'error' for reissue; the error requirement is satisfied by a patent owner's failure to previously present narrower claims (e.g., In re Tanaka).
guidance: No admissions as to patentability of original claims are required. The oath may include a statement about an error related to failure to earlier present narrower claims (see MPEP 1414(II)). A reissue proceeds through examination similar to an original patent application and may be stayed.

name: Ex parte reexamination: substantial new question (SNQ) requirement (35 U.S.C. § 303)
description: The Director must determine whether a request for reexamination raises 'a substantial new question [SNQ] of patentability affecting any claim of the patent concerned.'
guidance: SNQ is not raised if the question of patentability was already decided in an earlier concluded examination or review (MPEP 2242(I)). Once an SNQ is established for existing claims, a SNQ is not needed for new or amended claims. The reexamination request should be decided on the wording of the patent claims in effect at the time (MPEP 2221).

name: Limitations on SNQ in light of AIA trial FWD
description: SNQ cannot be a question raised in a ground already decided in a FWD. A later-filed request must have an SNQ different than that addressed in the FWD. SNQ cannot be established based on new questions raised in relation to amended claims proposed during reexamination.
guidance: Prior to issuance of a FWD, an SNQ may be established based on a question raised in a ground presented in an AIA petition (MPEP 2242(I)). If granted, the Office may stay the reexamination pending the FWD.

name: Reissue vs. reexamination — procedural and substantive scope differences
description: Reexamination results in issuance of a certificate in the original patent, whereas reissue issues a new patent. Reissue may address all patentability requirements (35 U.S.C. §§ 101, 102, 103, 112); reexamination generally addresses only §§ 102 and 103, and § 112 only in limited circumstances for newly added subject matter. Reexamination must be based on patents and printed publications (35 U.S.C. §§ 301, 302).
guidance: § 315(b) one-year bar triggered by service of an infringement complaint may apply to a reexamined patent even if reexamination involves amended claims.

name: Director/Board authority to stay/suspend parallel proceedings
description: The Director has authority to determine approach regarding stays of a reissue or ex parte reexamination during the pendency of an AIA trial (35 U.S.C. §§ 315(d), 325(d)). The Director has authorized the Board to enter orders to effect a stay, transfer, consolidation, or termination of parallel Office proceedings involving the same patent (37 CFR §§ 42.3(a), 42.122(a), 42.222(a)).
guidance: The Board ordinarily will stay a parallel Office proceeding where good cause exists; good cause may exist if an ongoing AIA proceeding addresses the same or overlapping claims.

name: Non-limiting stay factors: same or overlapping claims
description: Whether claims challenged in a related AIA proceeding are the same as or depend directly or indirectly from claims at issue in the concurrent parallel proceeding.
guidance: This is a non-limiting factor; overlapping claim scope supports a stay because the AIA proceeding may address the same issues.

name: Non-limiting stay factors: effect of amendments across proceedings
description: Whether amending claim scope in one proceeding would affect claim scope in another proceeding.
guidance: Amendments that would affect parallel proceedings weigh in favor of a stay to prevent conflicting claim sets.

name: Motion to lift stay after FWD — meaningful amendments standard
description: If a patent owner files a motion to lift a stay after a FWD, the Board typically will lift the stay, absent reasons not to. The Board typically will lift a stay if the patent owner proposes amendments in a reissue or reexamination in a meaningful way not previously considered by the Office.
guidance: Meaningful amendments include those that narrow the scope of claims considered in an AIA proceeding or otherwise attempt to resolve issues identified in a FWD.

name: Office practice during Federal Circuit appeals — reexamination
description: Patent owners do not have the option to abandon ex parte reexamination proceedings; once started, reexaminations proceed with special dispatch to completion (35 U.S.C. § 305). After the Office determines to lift a stay (or that a stay is inappropriate), reexamination typically continues to completion notwithstanding a Federal Circuit appeal of a FWD on the same patent.
guidance: If the Office identifies allowable subject matter or determines claims unpatentable, it typically will issue a NIRC and reexamination certificate even if a relevant Federal Circuit appeal is ongoing, unless the patent owner timely files a notice of appeal in the reexamination for Board review.

name: Scope and breadth of claims
description: Patents should not be so broad that they claim fundamental, widely-used behaviors; overly broad patents make 'everyone... guilty of infringement.' Crawford's patent appeared to cover many common Internet activities (upgrades, online purchases, cloud storage).
guidance: Evaluate claim breadth carefully — broad, vague claims that cover common practices are problematic and more likely to be accused of improper grant or to chill innovation.

name: Patent corresponds to a real invention (substance over form)
description: A distinction exists between a 'patent' and a genuine 'invention' — many software patents are seen by engineers as not reflecting actual inventive engineering (described by one engineer as 'mungo mumbo jumbo').
guidance: Favor patents tied to concrete technical contributions or implementations rather than abstract descriptions; examine technical substance, not just legalistic claim language.

name: Software patent eligibility and changing legal standards
description: Historically the patent office resisted software patents (viewed like language/copyright), but federal court decisions in the 1990s shifted this, triggering a 'flood of software patents.'
guidance: When evaluating a software patent, consider the controlling judicial and PTO standards at the time of prosecution — changes in case law can affect whether a claim should have been allowed.

name: Tailoring to specific case issues and eliminating superfluous/confusing instructions
description: The litigants must tailor these instructions to the specific issues in their particular case and to eliminate superfluous or confusing instructions.
guidance: Edit the templates to reflect the parties' claims, defenses, and the actual evidence; remove any instructions irrelevant to the case or wording that could confuse the jury.

name: When unity is fulfilled (PCT Rule 13.2: special technical features)
description: Unity is fulfilled only when there is a technical relationship among those inventions involving one or more of the same or corresponding special technical features. 'Special technical features' means those technical features that define a contribution which each of the claimed inventions, considered as a whole, makes over the prior art.
guidance: Determination is made on the contents of the claims interpreted in light of the description and drawings. Whether a technical feature is 'special' must be considered with respect to novelty and inventive step. The standard can be applied a priori or a posteriori depending on prior-art findings.

name: Determination not affected by manner of claiming (PCT Rule 13.3 / 37 CFR 1.475(e))
description: The determination whether a group of inventions forms a single general inventive concept shall be made without regard to whether the inventions are claimed in separate claims or as alternatives within a single claim.
guidance: Objections can arise within a single claim if it contains distinct embodiments that are not linked by a single general inventive concept. Conversely, merely claiming alternatives within a single claim does not prevent a unity determination; the substance governs, not claim drafting form.

name: Dependent claims allowance (PCT Rule 13.4)
description: Subject to Rule 13.1, it is permitted to include in the same international application a reasonable number of dependent claims, claiming specific forms of the invention claimed in an independent claim, even where the features of any dependent claim could be considered as constituting in themselves an invention.
guidance: If the independent claim avoids the prior art and satisfies unity, dependent claims do not typically give rise to a lack-of-unity objection even if a dependent claim contains a further patentable invention (examples provided).

name: Permissible combinations of claim categories (37 CFR 1.475(b) / MPEP list)
description: An application containing claims to different categories of invention will be considered to have unity if the claims are drawn only to certain combinations (e.g., product + process specially adapted to manufacture product; product + process of use; process + apparatus specifically designed to carry it out; product + process + apparatus combinations).
guidance: The emphasis differs per combination: (A)/(C) emphasize the product, (B) emphasizes the process. The 'specially adapted' and 'specifically designed' language requires corresponding contributions over the prior art (see detailed guidance).

name: Initial unity determination and reconsideration after search
description: The method for determining unity is intended to be applied even before the commencement of the international search; where a search is made, an initial determination (assuming claims avoid the prior art) may be reconsidered based on search results.
guidance: Examiners should make an initial practical assessment but must be prepared to alter unity findings when prior art shows common matter is known.

name: Unity objections within single claims and alternatives
description: Alternative embodiments contained within a single claim may give rise to lack of unity if the claim contains distinct embodiments not linked by a single general inventive concept.
guidance: PCT Rule 13.3 does not prevent objecting to alternatives in a single claim on grounds of clarity, conciseness, or fee considerations; examiners should watch for distinct unlinked embodiments.

name: Combination of numerous independent claim sets across categories accepted only exceptionally
description: While a single set of independent claims according to permitted category-combinations is permissible, the ISA is not required to accept a proliferation of such sets (e.g., multiple independent claims across product/process/use/apparatus) except exceptionally.
guidance: Examiners should guard against claim proliferation that multiplies independent sets across categories unless a single general inventive concept clearly links them.

name: Objection does not normally arise for compositionally unrelated combined elements in one claim
description: An objection of lack of unity does not normally arise if the combination of a number of individual elements is claimed in a single claim (as opposed to distinct embodiments).
guidance: Single-claim combinations are acceptable even if the elements individually seem unrelated, provided the overall claimed combination has unity.

name: Eligibility — types of applications eligible for Track One
description: Original nonprovisional utility and plant patent applications filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a) that have no more than 4 independent claims, no more than 30 total claims, and no multiple dependent claims, and filed on or after September 26, 2011, are eligible.
guidance: The term 'original application' includes first filings and continuing applications (continuation, continuation-in-part, divisional). Reissue applications are not eligible.

name: Requirements for an application to be in condition for examination
description: A proper request for prioritized examination requires that the application include a specification as prescribed by 35 U.S.C. 112 including claim(s), any required drawings, an inventor’s oath/declaration or signed ADS, and the required fees (filing, search, examination, prioritized examination fee and processing fee).
guidance: Requests will be acted upon once the application has met all formal requirements so it is ready for examination (see MPEP 708.02 VIII.C). Failure to submit required items on the date of filing will cause the request to be dismissed. Other informalities (e.g., compliance with 37 C.F.R. 1.52, English-language specification, excess claims fee) will delay a decision but will not cause dismissal.

name: Events that terminate prioritized examination special status
description: Prioritized examination status remains until one of several listed events occurs.
guidance: Events include: (i) filing a petition for extension of time to extend time for filing a reply; (ii) filing an amendment that causes >4 independent claims, >30 total claims, or a multiple dependent claim; (iii) filing a request for continued examination (RCE); (iv) filing a notice of appeal; (v) filing a request for suspension of action; (vi) mailing of a notice of allowance; (vii) mailing of a final Office action; (viii) abandonment of the application; (ix) examination completed as defined in 37 C.F.R. 41.102.

name: Preliminary amendment policy for Track One applications
description: A preliminary amendment filed in an application that includes a Track One request will not result in dismissal of a pending request or termination of special status if already granted, provided the amendment does not cause the application to contain more than four independent claims, more than thirty total claims, or a multiple dependent claim.

name: Consequences of failing to respond timely
description: A party that fails to respond within the allowed time, and cannot show excusable neglect, may be found on motion to compel to have forfeited its right to object to the discovery requests on their merits.
guidance: Merits objections include claims of irrelevance, over-breadth, vagueness, burden/oppression, or lack of likely admissible evidence. Privilege/confidentiality/work-product objections are not merits objections and are treated differently. Courts have discretion; parties should attempt to determine why no response was made before moving to compel.

name: RCE practice after court review is limited
description: The procedure set forth in 37 CFR 1.114 is not available after the filing of a Notice of Appeal to the Federal Circuit or the commencement of a civil action, unless the appeal/civil action is terminated and the application is still pending.
guidance: If an RCE is filed in an application that underwent court review, the examiner should bring the application to the SPE or special program examiner to determine if the RCE is proper. Termination of an unsuccessful appeal or civil action generally results in abandonment unless the application contains allowed claims or the court's mandate directs further Office action. See MPEP § 1216.01.

name: When rejecting for novelty/obviousness cite best references and explain pertinence (37 CFR 1.104(c)(2))
description: In rejecting claims for want of novelty or for obviousness, the examiner must cite the best references at his or her command. When a reference is complex or shows inventions other than that claimed, the particular part relied on must be designated as nearly as practicable. The pertinence of each reference, if not apparent, must be clearly explained and each rejected claim specified.
guidance: For 35 U.S.C. 103 rejections, set out how a reference is modified or how plural references are combined. Include particular figures/pages/paragraphs when necessary.

name: Examiner may rely on applicant admissions and facts within Office knowledge (37 CFR 1.104(c)(3))
description: In rejecting claims the examiner may rely upon admissions by the applicant (or patent owner in reexamination), and may rely upon facts within his or her knowledge pursuant to paragraph (d)(2).
guidance: When relying on facts within Office employee's personal knowledge, the data must be as specific as possible and may require an affidavit to support the data (subject to contradiction).

name: Use of third-party-developed subject matter as prior art and joint research agreement treatment (37 CFR 1.104(c)(4)-(3)(i-iii))
description: Subject matter developed by another person which qualifies as prior art only under 35 U.S.C. 102(e),(f) or (g) may be used as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 103 against a claimed invention unless the entire rights to the subject matter and the claimed invention were commonly owned at the time the claimed invention was made.
