guidance: To overcome a 103 rejection based on 102(e)/(f)/(g) prior art via 103(c)(2), the applicant must provide a statement that the prior art and the claimed invention were made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement (as defined) that was in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made, and that the invention was made as a result of activities within the scope of that agreement; define 'joint research agreement' per the regulation.

name: Reasons for allowance must be stated when record unclear (37 CFR 1.104(e))
description: If the examiner believes the record of prosecution does not make clear his or her reasons for allowing a claim, the examiner may set forth such reasoning; reasons shall be incorporated into an Office action rejecting other claims or be the subject of separate communication. The applicant may file a statement commenting on the reasons for allowance within a specified time.
guidance: Failure by the examiner to respond to any such applicant statement does not give rise to any implication. Provide clear reasoning to maintain transparency.

name: Office actions must include necessary elements and use PTOL-326 for summary
description: Under current procedure the examiner signifies on Office Action Summary Form PTOL-326 certain information including period set for reply, attachments, and a 'Summary of Action' describing the position on all claims; attachments (e.g., Notice of References Cited) are part of the Office action.
guidance: One of form paragraphs 7.100, 7.101, or 7.102 should conclude all actions. Office actions should notify reasons for rejection/objection per 35 U.S.C. 132, include particular figures/pages/paragraphs of references when necessary, and set out how references are modified/combined for 103 rejections. Include application number, 4-digit art unit, examiner's name, and encourage inclusion of the 4-digit confirmation number on every paper filed.

name: Enumerated non-patentable subject-matter (Section 3(10)(h))
description: Section 3(10)(h) lists items that shall not be regarded as inventions: (i) discoveries, scientific theories and mathematical methods; (ii) aesthetic creations; (iii) schemes, rules and methods for performing mental acts, playing games or doing business, and programs for computers; (iv) presentations of information.
guidance: This is an explicit exclusion list that includes 'programs for computers' among other categories. Whether a specific subject-matter falls within an exclusion depends on interpretation and application to the claimed matter (see the 'as such' limitation below).

name: 'As such' limitation on exclusions and effect for software patents
description: Section 3(10)(i) states that paragraph (h) (the exclusions) shall exclude patentability only to the extent to which an ARIPO patent application or ARIPO patent relates to such subject-matter or activities 'as such'.
guidance: The 'as such' qualifier narrows the exclusion: subject-matter that involves or implements excluded items but goes beyond them (e.g., a computer program producing a technical effect) may still be patentable. The page notes that this wording allows ARIPO to grant software patents, since the exclusion does not categorically ban software-related inventions unless they are claimed 'as such'. Practitioners should draft claims and descriptions to emphasize technical features or industrial applicability to avoid being treated as excluded 'as such'.

name: Patentability requirements (35 U.S.C. §§101, 102, 103, 112)
description: An examiner must assess whether claimed inventions meet statutory requirements: subject matter/utility (35 U.S.C. §101), novelty (35 U.S.C. §102), non-obviousness (35 U.S.C. §103), and disclosure/written-description/enablement (35 U.S.C. §112).
guidance: The paper emphasizes that lack-of-novelty (§102) and obviousness (§103) rejections require comparison with prior art and thus require examiners to conduct prior art searches; obviousness rejections are especially time-consuming because they may require combining multiple references and articulating why the combination would make the claim obvious. If the examiner fails to set forth a basis of rejection, the application must be allowed.

name: Post-issuance patent quality/value proxies (renewal, forward citations, generality)
description: Measures used to proxy patent value and quality: incidence of patent renewal at 4 and 8 years, forward-looking citations normalized by number of claims, and patent generality score (1 minus Herfindahl index of technological concentration of forward citations).
guidance: Renewals indicate commercial value (sample renewals: 4-year ~0.886, 8-year ~0.716). Forward citations and generality indicate scholarly/technological impact and breadth. The paper tests whether patents issued by time-constrained examiners are lower on these proxies (finding decreases). Forward citations are corrected/truncated by technology and results are robust to inclusion of technology-by-year fixed effects.

name: 102(e) prior-art from copending applications with common assignee/inventor
description: A copending application with an earlier filing date that discloses the claimed invention (but has not been published under 35 U.S.C. 122) constitutes prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) if the copending application has either a common assignee or at least one common inventor.
guidance: Use form paragraph guidance (e.g., 7.12/7.12.01/7.15.02). This rejection may be overcome by a showing under 37 CFR 1.132 that any invention disclosed but not claimed in the reference was derived from the inventor of this application (thus not 'by another') or by an appropriate showing under 37 CFR 1.131. Insert appropriate bracket language (e.g., --assignee-- or --inventor-- in bracket 3). See Examiner Notes for further application rules.

name: Determination of 35 U.S.C. 102(e) effective date (AIPA vs pre-AIPA)
description: Use 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as amended by the American Inventors Protection Act (AIPA) and IP/High-Tech Technical Amendments to determine the copending application's prior art date, unless the copending application is based (directly or indirectly) on an international application having an international filing date prior to November 29, 2000.
guidance: If the copending reference is a national stage of an international application or a continuing application claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120/121/365(c) to an international application with an international filing date prior to Nov. 29, 2000, use pre-AIPA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) (form paragraph 7.12.01). See Examiner Notes for form paragraphs 7.12 and 7.12.01 to determine the 102(e) date; consider priority/benefit claims under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), 120, 121, 365(c) only when the relied-upon earlier application appropriately supports the subject matter used for the rejection. Do NOT consider foreign priority claims under 119(a)-(d) and 365(a) for the 102(e) date.

name: Overcoming 102(e)/103 rejections involving copending applications
description: A rejection based on a copending application may be overcome by: (1) a showing under 37 CFR 1.132 that the invention disclosed but not claimed in the reference was derived from the inventor of this application; (2) a showing of an earlier date of invention for the instant application under 37 CFR 1.131; or (3) where applicable, an oath/declaration under 37 CFR 1.130 that the application and reference are commonly owned and the inventor is prior, together with a terminal disclaimer under 37 CFR 1.321(c).
guidance: Also possible: show that the copending application is disqualified as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 103(c). For provisional 103(a) rejections, the rejection is a presumption of future publication/patenting of the copending application; annotate bracketed explanation of obviousness when using provisional form paragraphs (e.g., 7.21.01).

name: Use of form paragraphs and required bracket insertions
description: When using form paragraphs (e.g., 7.15.02, 7.21.01, 7.21.02), include the appropriate bracket insertions (e.g., claim number, reference, --assignee-- or --inventor--, and explanation of obviousness or particulars supporting findings).
guidance: Examiner Notes accompanying form paragraphs specify what to insert in each bracket and when the paragraph should or should not be used (e.g., preceding paragraphs 7.12 or 7.12.01 required for 7.15.02).

name: Compare claimed subject matter to determine distinctness/independence
description: In determining double patenting and restriction questions, it is the claimed subject matter that is considered and must be compared to determine distinctness or independence of alleged inventions.
guidance: General principles: (A) If inventions are independent (no disclosed relation), restriction to one is ordinarily proper. (B) If inventions are related as disclosed but distinct as claimed, restriction may be proper. (C) If inventions are related as disclosed and not distinct as claimed, restriction is never proper. See MPEP §806.01 and §802.01 for criteria for patentably distinct inventions.

name: Species may be independent or related (genus/species analysis)
description: Species under a claimed genus may be independent (not connected in design, operation, or effect under the disclosure) or related; if independent, restriction between species may be proper; if related, restriction analysis must consider both election-of-species practice and other restriction practice.
guidance: If species are related (e.g., intermediate and final products), distinctness must be shown (no overlap in scope, not obvious variants, and intermediate product useful other than to make final product) to sustain restriction. See MPEP §806.04(b) and §806.05(j).

name: Definition and characteristics of a generic claim
description: A generic claim should read on each illustrated species and generally require no material element additional to those required by the species claims; each species claim must require all limitations of the generic claim.
guidance: Once a generic claim is allowable, species claims that require all limitations of the generic claim will ordinarily be allowable; when species claims do not require all generic limitations, see MPEP §821.04(a). Rejoinder of previously non-elected species may be required when a generic claim becomes allowable.

name: Claims limited to species and terminology (claim vs species)
description: Claims themselves are never species; a claim may be limited to a single disclosed embodiment (a specific species) or may encompass multiple embodiments (a generic/genus claim). Species refers to the different embodiments of the invention.
guidance: Species may be independent or related as disclosed. Proper restriction practice depends on this characterization (see MPEP §806.04 and related subsections).

name: Restriction between mutually exclusive species
description: Restriction to a single species may be proper when two or more species are claimed and they are mutually exclusive (claims do not overlap in scope).
guidance: Mutually exclusive: one claim recites limitations disclosed for first species but not second, and vice versa; equivalently, claims must not overlap in scope to require restriction between species. Use MPEP §806.04(f).

name: Species must be patentably distinct from each other
description: When requiring restriction among plural species, the examiner should group species considered clearly unpatentable over each other; species must be patentably distinct (not obvious variants and not overlapping in scope) to be separately patentable.
guidance: If a generic claim is allowable, applicant may claim additional species in the same application per 37 CFR 1.141 and MPEP §806.04. Investigate closely when species are voluntarily presented in separate applications to determine whether double patenting rejection is appropriate (see MPEP §804.01, §804.02).

name: Generic claim filed after issuance of species — obviousness-type double patenting
description: If a generic claim is presented after the issuance of a patent claiming one or more species within the scope of the generic claim, the Office may reject the generic claim on grounds of obviousness-type double patenting when certain common-inventor/assignment conditions exist.
guidance: Such rejections may be overcome by filing a terminal disclaimer. Consider 35 U.S.C. 103(c)(2)-(3) joint research agreement exceptions and MPEP §804 guidance; see case law (In re Goodman; In re Braithwaite) for examples.

name: Combination vs subcombination distinctness criteria (two-way distinctness and reasons)
description: To support restriction between combination and subcombination inventions, both two-way distinctness and reasons for insisting on restriction are necessary: (A) the combination as claimed does not require the particulars of the subcombination as claimed for patentability (novelty/unobviousness); and (B) the subcombination can be shown to have utility either by itself or in another materially different combination.
guidance: Also require evidence of a serious search burden if restriction not required (separate classification/status/field of search). Examples: (I) subcombination essential to combination -> no restriction; (II) subcombination not essential and has separate utility -> restriction may be proper. Use form paragraph 8.15 and conclude with appropriate form paragraph (e.g., 8.21).

name: Subcombinations usable together — distinctness and restriction practice
description: Two or more claimed subcombinations disclosed as usable together in a single combination are usually restrictable when the subcombinations do not overlap in scope and are not obvious variants, and at least one subcombination can be shown separately usable.
guidance: To support restriction where plural subcombinations are claimed along with a combination including particulars of at least two subcombinations, show two-way distinctness and reasons for restriction (serious search burden evidence). If elected combination is later found allowable, reconsider restriction and rejoin allowable subcombinations per MPEP §821.04. Use form paragraph 8.16 for subcombinations usable together.

name: Withdrawal of restriction and rejoinder when claims are allowable
description: Upon determining that all claims directed to an elected combination invention are allowable, the examiner must reconsider the propriety of the restriction requirement; if combination is allowable in view of patentability of at least one subcombination, withdraw restriction and rejoin the subcombination claims.
guidance: If a subcombination is elected and found allowable, nonelected claims requiring all the limitations of the allowable claim will be rejoined in accordance with MPEP §821.04. Applicant is advised that claims presented in a continuation/divisional that are anticipated by or include all limitations of an allowable claim may be subject to provisional double patenting rejections.

name: Disclosure requirement for benefit claims (general)
description: To be entitled to the benefit of the filing date of an earlier-filed application, the later-filed application must be an application for a patent for an invention which is also disclosed in the prior application; the disclosure in the prior application and in the later-filed application must be sufficient to comply with the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) except for the best mode requirement.
guidance: The disclosure of the prior-filed application must provide adequate support and enablement for the claimed subject matter of the later-filed application in compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (written description and enablement). Case law cited: Transco Products, Inc. v. Performance Contracting, Inc., and others. Use form paragraphs 2.09 and 2.10/2.11.01 or 2.38–2.40 where claims are not adequately disclosed or enabled.

name: Provisional application benefit (35 U.S.C. 119(e)) — written description and enablement
description: Under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), the written description and drawing(s) (if any) of the provisional application must adequately support and enable the subject matter claimed in the nonprovisional application that claims the benefit of the provisional application.
guidance: The provisional must 'contain a written description of the invention and the manner and process of making and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms,' to enable an ordinarily skilled artisan to practice the invention (New Railhead Mfg. v. Vermeer Mfg. Co.). A claim is not required in a provisional, but the provisional's specification/drawings must adequately support later claims; if not, the later nonprovisional is not entitled to the provisional filing date (example: New Railhead facts and holding). Ensure provisional provides (1) written description of subject matter of the claims and (2) enabling disclosure permitting one of ordinary skill to make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation.

name: Claim support from provisional — no claim requirement but sufficiency requirement
description: Although a provisional application need not contain claims, for a later nonprovisional claim to obtain the provisional filing date, the provisional's written description and drawings must adequately support and enable the claimed subject matter.
guidance: If a claim in the nonprovisional is not adequately supported by the provisional, the nonprovisional is not entitled to the provisional's filing date; if that earlier filing date is necessary to overcome a reference or for interference, ensure provisional disclosure adequately provides both written description and enablement for the claim(s).

name: Continuation-in-part entitlement — partial benefit for disclosed subject matter only
description: A continuation-in-part (CIP) may include matter not disclosed in the prior-filed application, but only those claims in the CIP that are directed solely to subject matter adequately disclosed in the parent nonprovisional are entitled to the benefit of the parent's filing date.
guidance: Claims reciting features first introduced in the CIP obtain only the CIP's filing date. If the prior application is fatally defective for insufficient disclosure to support allowable claims, a CIP cannot obtain the parent's benefit for newly supplied matter. Case citations: In re Chu; Transco Products v. Performance Contracting; In re Van Lagenhoven.

name: Continuous chain requirement for earliest benefit under 35 U.S.C. 112(a)
description: If there is a continuous chain of copending nonprovisional applications, each copending application must disclose the claimed invention of the later-filed application in the manner provided by 35 U.S.C. 112(a) for the later-filed application to be entitled to the earliest filing date in the chain.
guidance: Every link in the chain must satisfy written description and enablement requirements (except best mode). Recent case: Regents of the University of Minnesota v. Gilead Scis., Inc. (2023).

name: Enablement to 'use' the invention required for benefit (In re Hafner)
description: A claim in the later-filed application is not entitled to the benefit of the earlier filing date if the disclosure of the prior-filed application does not enable one skilled in the art to 'use' the claimed invention.
guidance: The previously filed application must satisfy all requirements of the first paragraph of 35 U.S.C.112, including sufficient description to enable one skilled in the art to use the invention (In re Hafner).

name: Consequences when prior application is fatally defective
description: If the prior application is found fatally defective for insufficient disclosure to support allowable claims, a later-filed CIP to supply the deficiency is not entitled to the benefit of the first application's filing date.
guidance: Only claims in the CIP directed solely to subject matter adequately disclosed in the parent get the parent's filing date; claims to newly introduced features get only the CIP filing date. Historical cases: Hunt Co. v. Mallinckrodt Chemical Works and others. Use appropriate rejections under 35 U.S.C.102 where claims entitled only to later dates read on prior art/public disclosures.

name: Use of form paragraphs for examiner communications (2.09, 2.10, 2.10.01)
description: When a later-filed application's claim for benefit is acknowledged but applicant has not complied with one or more conditions for receiving the benefit under the relevant statutes, the examiner should use heading form paragraph 2.09 and follow with one or more of form paragraphs 2.10–2.11.01 or 2.38–2.40 depending on circumstances.
guidance: Form paragraph 2.10: 'Disclosure of Prior-Filed Application Does Not Provide Support for Claimed Subject Matter' — insert prior-application number and explain lack of support/enablement, and list specific claims not entitled to benefit if only some claims are affected. Form paragraph 2.10.01: use when continuation/divisional contains new matter and applicant must delete benefit claim or change relationship to continuation-in-part; include examples of matter not disclosed. Examiner notes provide bracket insertion instructions and contextual use guidance.

name: Critical reference date for patents/application publications when claiming benefit
description: Determine when an issued patent, patent application publication under 35 U.S.C.122(b), or application deemed published under 35 U.S.C.122(b) is available as a reference under 35 U.S.C.102(a)(2) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C.102(e) as of a prior provisional or nonprovisional application's filing date.
guidance: See MPEP §§2154.01(b) and 2136.03 for discussion; the critical date analysis affects whether earlier publications/patents are prior art with respect to benefit dates.

name: Certified copy and translation requirements for foreign priority (37 CFR 1.55(f),(g),(i))
description: The Director may require a certified copy of the original foreign application (and translation if not in English). Certified copies must be filed within specified timeframes (generally within the later of four months from actual U.S. filing or sixteen months from foreign filing for 111(a) applications) or a petition with showing of good and sufficient cause is required.
guidance: Exceptions: certified copy requirement satisfied if a prior-filed U.S. nonprovisional (for which benefit is claimed) contains the certified copy and is identified; participating intellectual property offices under priority document exchange agreements may permit the Office to obtain the copy directly (paragraph (i)). If translation is required, it must be filed with a statement of accuracy. Interim copies clearly labeled and accompanied by cover sheet may be filed under paragraph (j) with later certified copy.

name: Special statements for applications affected by March 16, 2013 effective date (kin to AIA)
description: If a nonprovisional application filed on or after March 16, 2013 claims priority to a foreign application filed prior to that date and also contains (or ever contained) a claim to an invention with an effective filing date on or after March 16, 2013, the applicant must provide a statement to that effect within specified time limits (generally within the later of four months from actual filing, four months from national stage entry, sixteen months from prior foreign filing, or upon presentation of a first claim with such effective date).
guidance: Applicant is not required to provide the statement if they reasonably believe based on available information that the nonprovisional does not and did not at any time contain such a claim. This helps determine whether certain priority/effective-date rules apply to the application.

name: Non-extendable time periods subject to limited statutory/regulatory overrides
description: The time periods set forth for priority claims, certified copies, and related procedures are not extendable except as provided by specific statutes or rules (e.g., 35 U.S.C.21(b), PCT Rule 80.5, Hague Agreement Rule 4(4)).
guidance: Applicants must adhere to the time limits unless a statutory/regulatory provision explicitly allows extension or a petition under specified provisions is granted.

name: Apportionment principle in lost-profits analysis
description: Damages must be commensurate with the value of the patented features; apportionment requires tying damages to specific claim limitations.
guidance: The court in Mentor Graphics found that the Panduit factors 'incorporate apportionment' because requiring demand for both the product as a whole and absence of non-infringing alternatives ties damages to the worth of patented features. This is the judiciary's method of ensuring lost-profits awards reflect the inventive contribution rather than the value of an entire multi-feature device.

name: Step 1 — Statutory category requirement (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter)
description: Step 1: Is the claim directed to one of the four patent-eligible subject matter categories: process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter? The subject matter of the claim must be directed to one of the four subject matter categories.
guidance: If it is not, the claim is not eligible for patent protection and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101. If the claim plainly fails Step 1 but could be amended to fall within a statutory category, Step 2 should still be conducted. Use the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) in light of the specification and one skilled in the art when determining whether a claim encompasses non-statutory embodiments.

name: Process (definition and scope)
description: Process — an act, or a series of acts or steps. (Quoted: 'A process is a mode of treatment of certain materials to produce a given result. It is an act, or a series of acts, performed upon the subject-matter to be transformed and reduced to a different state or thing.')
guidance: Case law examples cited: Gottschalk v. Benson; NTP, Inc. v. Research in Motion; Minton v. Natl. Ass’n. of Securities Dealers. See also 35 U.S.C. 100(b) and Bilski v. Kappos. Use these authorities to characterize claimed methods/processes.

name: Machine (definition and scope)
description: Machine — a concrete thing, consisting of parts, or of certain devices and combination of devices. Includes mechanical devices or combinations of mechanical powers and devices to perform some function and produce a certain effect or result.
guidance: Case law example cited: Burr v. Duryee; Corning v. Burden. Treat claimed apparatus or device combinations as machines when concrete physical parts are recited.

name: Manufacture (definition and scope)
description: Manufacture — an article produced from raw or prepared materials by giving to these materials new forms, qualities, properties, or combinations, whether by hand labor or by machinery.
guidance: Case law example cited: Diamond v. Chakrabarty (quoting Am. Fruit Growers v. Brogdex). Use this standard when the claimed subject is an article created from materials.

name: Composition of matter (definition and scope)
description: Composition of matter — all compositions of two or more substances and all composite articles, whether the results of chemical union or mechanical mixture, or gases, fluids, powders or solids.
guidance: Case law example cited: Chakrabarty. Apply when claims recite chemical or material compositions or composite articles.

name: Non-statutory examples (items that are not directed to statutory categories)
description: Non-limiting examples of claims that are not directed to one of the statutory categories include: (i) transitory forms of signal transmission (e.g., a propagating electrical or electromagnetic signal per se), (ii) a human per se, (iii) a legal contractual agreement between two parties, (iv) a computer program per se, (v) a company, (vi) a mere arrangement of printed matter, and (vii) data per se.
guidance: Cited cases: In re Nuijten; AIA; In re Ferguson; Gottschalk v. Benson; In re Miller; Digitech Image Tech. If the broadest reasonable interpretation of a claim encompasses such non-statutory embodiments, the claim should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101. Example: machine-readable media that can encompass a carrier wave or transitory signal should be rejected if BRI includes the transitory form.

name: Step 2 — Judicial exceptions (laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract ideas)
description: Step 2: Does the claim wholly embrace a judicially recognized exception, which includes laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas? Claims directed to nothing more than abstract ideas, natural phenomena, and laws of nature are not eligible for patent protection.
guidance: Court precedents: Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank; Association for Molecular Pathology v. Myriad; Bilski v. Kappos; Diamond v. Diehr; Parker v. Flook; Gottschalk v. Benson. The guidance notes that the exceptions have also been described by other terms (e.g., 'physical phenomena,' 'scientific principles,' 'mental processes,' 'disembodied mathematical algorithms'). Use these authorities to identify judicial exceptions.

name: Inventive concept / 'significantly more' analysis
description: If a claim is directed to a judicial exception, analyze whether the elements of the claim, considered both individually and as an ordered combination, are sufficient to ensure that the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the exception itself — i.e., whether there is an 'inventive concept.'
guidance: This analysis asks whether the claim is for a particular application of an abstract idea/natural phenomenon or is the abstract idea/natural phenomenon itself. Authorities: Alice Corp.; Mayo Collaborative Serv. v. Prometheus; Diehr. Methods and products employing exceptions to perform a real-world function may still be patentable if the claim as a whole is 'significantly more.'

name: Prima facie case requirement and burden shifting
description: USPTO personnel should review the totality of the evidence (specification, claims, relevant prior art) and must reach a conclusion whether it is more likely than not that the claimed invention either falls outside one of the enumerated statutory classes or within one of the judicial exceptions. The examiner bears the initial burden of presenting a prima facie case of unpatentability.
guidance: Cited authorities: In re Oetiker (examiner initial burden), In re Brana (burden shifts to applicant after examiner explains why claim is an exception without significantly more). If the record suggests the claim is 'significantly more' than an exception, examiners should not reject. After identifying and explaining reasons the claim is for an exception without significantly more, the burden shifts to applicant to amend or show eligibility.

name: Acts deemed as infringement of a registered geographical sign
description: The following uses of a registered geographical sign shall be considered infringement: a) Any direct or indirect commercial use of the registered geographical sign or emblem in relation to products within the scope of the register or comparable products to exploit the reputation where they do not carry the properties specified in the register; b) Any deceptive use, replicas or associative use about the place of origin or translation of the geographical sign even if accompanied by expressions such as 'style', 'type', 'method', 'as produced in'; c) Any use of false or misleading indication or description about the origin or properties specified in the geographical sign register on packaging, promotional material or any written material related to the product; ç) Any deceptive use of the emblem of registered geographical sign.
guidance: Those who have the right to use the geographical sign may request a claim by notifying the registrant via notary and filing suit if not accepted within three months. In case of serious risk of harm, precautionary rulings may be sought regardless of time limits. Lack of presentation of registration record on product does not exclude infringement but is considered in fault evaluation. Where an application is published, the applicant may appeal to the Court for acts of infringement; if the aggressor was informed of the application and acts in bad faith, infringement may be accepted prior to publication.

name: Proper use of drawings and photographs under patent rules (37 C.F.R. § 1.84(b))
description: Photographs are not ordinarily permitted in utility patent applications unless they are the 'only practicable medium for illustrating the claimed invention.'
guidance: Petitions to accept photographs must justify that photographs are the only practical medium and often require accompanying amendments to the specification; failing to meet these requirements can result in petition denial and rejection of the application.

name: Use of Known Technique To Improve Similar Devices (Methods, or Products) — Required Findings
description: (1) a finding that the prior art contained a “base” device (method, or product) upon which the claimed invention can be seen as an “improvement;” (2) a finding that the prior art contained a “comparable” device (method, or product that is not the same as the base device) that has been improved in the same way as the claimed invention; (3) a finding that one of ordinary skill in the art could have applied the known “improvement” technique in the same way to the “base” device (method, or product) and the results would have been predictable to one of ordinary skill in the art; and (4) whatever additional findings based on the Graham factual inquiries may be necessary, in view of the facts of the case under consideration, to explain a conclusion of obviousness.
guidance: Rationale: a method of enhancing a particular class of devices has become part of the ordinary capabilities of one skilled in the art based on teaching of such improvement in other situations. If any of these findings cannot be made, the rationale cannot be used to support obviousness. The Supreme Court in KSR noted that if the actual application would have been beyond the skill of one of ordinary skill, then using the technique would not have been obvious.

name: Applying a Known Technique to a Known Device Ready for Improvement — Required Findings
description: (1) a finding that the prior art contained a “base” device (method, or product) upon which the claimed invention can be seen as an “improvement;” (2) a finding that the prior art contained a known technique that is applicable to the base device (method, or product); (3) a finding that one of ordinary skill in the art would have recognized that applying the known technique would have yielded predictable results and resulted in an improved system; and (4) whatever additional findings based on the Graham factual inquiries may be necessary, in view of the facts of the case under consideration, to explain a conclusion of obviousness.
guidance: Rationale: when a particular known technique is part of the ordinary capabilities of the skilled artisan and the base device was ready for improvement, applying the technique producing predictable results can support obviousness. If any of these findings cannot be made, the rationale cannot be used.

name: Withdrawal from issue — petitions and Office-initiated withdrawal
description: Applications may be withdrawn from issue for further action upon petition by the applicant (with fee per § 1.17(h) and showing of good and sufficient reasons) or at the Office's initiative. A petition is not required if a request for continued examination (§ 1.114) is filed prior to payment of the issue fee.
guidance: If Office withdraws application from issue and later allows it again, a new notice of allowance is issued. Once issue fee paid, Office will not withdraw on its own initiative except for: (1) Office mistake; (2) violation of § 1.56 or illegality; (3) unpatentability of one or more claims; or (4) interference or derivation proceeding. Applicant petitions after payment are limited to specific reasons.

name: Statutory disclaimers and terminal disclaimers requirements
description: A patentee or applicant may disclaim any complete claim(s) or dedicate to the public the entire term or any terminal part of the term. A disclaimer/terminal disclaimer to be recorded must be signed, identify the patent and claim(s) or term being disclaimed, state the present extent of ownership interest, and be accompanied by the fee in § 1.20(d).
guidance: A terminal disclaimer filed to obviate judicially created double patenting must: comply with signature, specification of portion disclaimed, statement of ownership interest, fee, and include provisions waiving separate enforcement and that the patent will be enforceable only during periods when commonly owned with the application/patent forming the basis for double patenting. Special rules apply for double patenting arising from activities under joint research agreements (see paragraph d). Editor notes indicate different applicability for pre- and post-September 16, 2012 filings.

name: Windsurfing / Sanofi four-step approach
description: A four-step approach to determine obviousness: (1) identify the notional 'person skilled in the art' and their relevant common general knowledge; (2) identify the inventive concept of the claim or, if that cannot readily be done, construe the claim; (3) identify differences between the state of the art and the inventive concept/claim as construed; (4) viewed without knowledge of the alleged invention, do those differences constitute steps which would have been obvious to the person skilled in the art or require any degree of invention?
guidance: Adopted by the Supreme Court of Canada (Sanofi). The Court warned against an overly rigid application; the approach is useful and flexible. Failure to recite the exact words is not necessarily error; use as a structured inquiry rather than a compulsory formula.

name: Compare differences between prior art and inventive concept
description: Identify what, if any, differences exist between the matter cited as forming part of the state of the art and the inventive concept of the claim or the claim as construed.
guidance: This is the third step in Windsurfing/Sanofi; clearly list distinguishing features to assess whether they require invention.

name: Obviousness assessed without knowledge of the alleged invention
description: Viewed without any knowledge of the alleged invention as claimed, determine whether the identified differences would have been obvious to the skilled person or require invention.
guidance: Sanofi step four; avoids hindsight bias by asking whether the skilled person, lacking the inventor's insight, would arrive at the invention directly and without difficulty.

name: Cripps question: led directly and without difficulty
description: Would the skilled person, in the light of the state of the art and common general knowledge at the relevant date, have come 'directly and without difficulty' to the claimed solution?
guidance: A strict test often quoted in cases; if answer is 'Yes' the invention is obvious. Related to 'plain as day' / 'crystal clear' formulations.

name: Apply Sanofi with flexibility to New Act patents but focus on claims
description: Sanofi's test can be applied to 'New Act' (s.28.3) patents but the statute emphasizes assessing the 'subject-matter defined by a claim'; courts have reconciled Sanofi with claim-focused analysis.
guidance: Where claims are properly construed (especially combination claims), determining inventive concept may be unnecessary; still ensure the obviousness inquiry respects statutory language limiting consideration to claim subject-matter.

name: Completeness of examiner’s action — permitted limitations (§1.104(b))
description: The examiner’s action will be complete as to all matters, except that in appropriate circumstances (e.g., misjoinder of invention, fundamental defects), the action may be limited to such matters before further action is made.
guidance: Matters of form need not be raised by the examiner until a claim is found allowable.

name: Requirement to cite best references and explain pertinence for novelty/obviousness rejections (§1.104(c)(2))
description: In rejecting claims for want of novelty or for obviousness, the examiner must cite the best references at his or her command; when a reference is complex or shows other inventions, the particular part relied on must be designated as nearly as practicable.
guidance: The pertinence of each reference, if not apparent, must be clearly explained and each rejected claim specified.

name: Reasons for allowance — examiner explanation and applicant comment (§1.104(e))
description: If the examiner believes the record of prosecution does not make clear the reasons for allowing a claim, the examiner may set forth such reasoning in an Office action or separate communication; the applicant or patent owner may file a statement commenting on the reasons for allowance within a specified time.
guidance: The reasons shall be incorporated into an Office action or be the subject of a separate communication. Failure by the examiner to respond to any comment does not give rise to any implication.

name: Effective filing date of a claimed invention (§1.109)
description: The effective filing date for a claimed invention (other than reissue) is the earliest of: (1) the actual filing date of the patent/application containing the claim; or (2) the filing date of the earliest application for which the patent/application is entitled to priority or benefit under 35 U.S.C. 119, 120, 121, 365, or 386.
guidance: For reissue applications or reissued patents, the effective filing date for a claimed invention is determined by deeming the claim to have been contained in the patent for which reissue was sought.

name: Reply to a non-final Office action — must distinctly and specifically point out errors (§1.111(b))
description: To be entitled to reconsideration or further examination, the applicant/patent owner must reply in writing which distinctly and specifically points out the supposed errors in the examiner’s action and must reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the prior Office action.
guidance: The reply must present arguments pointing out specific distinctions believed to render the claims patentable over applied references. A general allegation that the claims define a patentable invention without specifically pointing out how the language patentably distinguishes them does not comply. The reply must appear to be a bona fide attempt to advance the application.

name: Supplemental replies — limited entry as matter of right (§1.111(a)(2))
description: A reply that is supplemental to a compliant reply will not be entered as a matter of right except as provided; the Office may enter a supplemental reply if it is clearly limited to certain topics.
guidance: Permitted supplemental reply matters include: cancellation of claim(s); adoption of examiner suggestions; placement of the application in condition for allowance; reply to an Office requirement made after the first reply was filed; correction of informalities (e.g., typographical errors); simplification of issues for appeal. A supplemental reply will be entered if filed within a specified period during which action by the Office is suspended under § 1.103(a) or (c).

name: Amendments in reply must clearly point out patentable novelty (§1.111(c))
description: In amending in reply to a rejection, the applicant or patent owner must clearly point out the patentable novelty believed to be present in the claims in view of the state of the art disclosed by cited references or objections.
guidance: Applicant must also show how the amendments avoid such references or objections.

name: Final rejection or action — repetition of all grounds and statement of reasons (§1.113(b))
description: On the second or any subsequent examination the rejection or other action may be made final; in making such final rejection the examiner shall repeat or state all grounds of rejection then considered applicable and clearly state reasons in support.
guidance: Reply to a final rejection is limited to appeal or to amendment as specified in § 1.114 or § 1.116. Reply to a final rejection must include cancellation of, or appeal from, each rejected claim; if any claim stands allowed, reply must comply with any form requirements or objections.

name: Request for continued examination (RCE) timing and content (§1.114(a)-(d))
description: If prosecution is closed, an applicant may request continued examination by filing a submission and the fee (§1.17(e)) prior to the earliest of: payment of the issue fee (unless a petition under §1.313 is granted); abandonment; or filing a notice of appeal to Fed. Cir. or commencement of a civil action under 35 U.S.C. 145/146 (unless terminated).
guidance: Prosecution closed means application is under appeal, last Office action is final, a notice of allowance, or action that otherwise closes prosecution. A 'submission' includes IDS, amendment to specification/claims/drawings, new arguments, or new evidence. If timely filed, the Office will withdraw finality of any Office action and enter and consider the submission. Appeal/case briefs are not considered submissions. Section excludes provisional, certain pre-1995 applications, design applications, international design applications, and patents under reexamination.

name: Amendments and affidavits/evidence after final action and prior to appeal (§1.116)
description: After a final rejection/other final action but before or on the same date as filing an appeal or related dates, amendments may be admitted under specified conditions and affidavits or other evidence may be admitted upon showing good and sufficient reasons why they are necessary and were not earlier presented.
guidance: Permitted: (1) amendment canceling claims or complying with form requirements; (2) amendment presenting rejected claims in better form for appeal may be admitted; (3) amendment touching merits may be admitted upon showing of good and sufficient reasons. Admission/refusal does not relieve application from its condition as subject to appeal or abandonment. Special limitations apply to inter partes reexamination and ex parte reexamination proceedings: e.g., in inter partes reexamination no amendment other than canceling claims (that do not affect scope of other pending claims) can be made after right of appeal notice except as provided in §1.981 or §41.77(b)(1). Similarly, affidavits/evidence in inter partes reexam after right of appeal notice generally cannot be made except as provided.

name: Standard of proof in IPR: preponderant evidence
description: Mylan failed to demonstrate by preponderant evidence that the challenged claims were unpatentable as obvious over a combination of prior-art references.
guidance: The PTAB's determination of unpatentability in an inter partes review is evaluated under the preponderance‑of‑the‑evidence standard; a challenger must show that invalidity is more likely than not.

name: Unexpected results as a persuasive secondary consideration
description: Evidence that the claimed invention produced unexpected results may overcome a prima facie obviousness showing.
guidance: The Board determined that Biogen presented sufficient evidence of unexpected results to overcome Mylan's obviousness challenge (see PTAB findings cited on the page). The court's summary reports this as the Board's basis for upholding patentability on obviousness grounds.

name: 35 U.S.C. 103 Obviousness standard
description: A patent may not be obtained if the differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: Patentability is not negated by the manner in which the invention was made. These are the baseline statutory criteria for obviousness determinations under 35 U.S.C. 103(a).

name: 35 U.S.C. 103(b) — Biotechnological process/composition special rule
description: Upon timely election by the applicant, a biotechnological process using or resulting in a composition of matter that is novel under section 102 and nonobvious under subsection (a) shall be considered nonobvious if (A) claims to the process and composition are in the same application or in separate applications having the same effective filing date, and (B) the composition and process were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.
guidance: If a patent issues on the process, it must also contain claims to the composition used/made by that process or expire on the same date as the patent claiming the composition. The statute defines 'biotechnological process' to include (A) genetically altering or inducing organisms to express/alter nucleotide sequences or express specific physiological characteristics, (B) cell fusion producing cell lines expressing a specific protein, and (C) methods of using products produced by such processes.

name: 35 U.S.C. 103(c) — Common ownership/joint research agreement exception
description: Subject matter developed by another person that qualifies as prior art only under certain subsections of 102 shall not preclude patentability where, at the time the claimed invention was made, the subject matter and the claimed invention were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.
guidance: For this exception to apply the claimed invention must have been made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; the invention must result from activities within the scope of the agreement; and the patent application must disclose or be amended to disclose the names of the parties to the agreement. 'Joint research agreement' is defined as a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement between two or more persons/entities for performance of experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention.

name: Importance of priority right for novelty/inventive step
description: The priority right assumes importance if subject matter relevant to the determination of novelty or inventive step (non-obviousness) of the claimed invention: (i) has been disclosed within the meaning of Rule 64.1 on or after the priority date claimed and before the international filing date; or (ii) forms part of the content of an application or patent within the meaning of Rule 64.3 that was published on or after that date but filed earlier than the international filing date or claimed the priority of an earlier application filed prior to the international filing date.
guidance: In such cases the examiner must satisfy himself that the priority date(s) claimed may be accorded to the appropriate parts of the international application and, where appropriate, consider the validity of any priority date claimed under Rule 64.3 (see also Rule 70.10). When considering priority date, bear in mind matters in paragraphs 6.03–6.05.

name: Establishing priority: documents taken as a whole
description: To establish a priority date, it is sufficient that the documents of the previous application taken as a whole specifically disclose the elements of the invention, even if not all elements are found among the claims in the previous application.
guidance: The description and any claims or drawings of the previous application should be considered as a whole, except do not take into account subject matter found solely in that part of the description referring to prior art or in an explicit disclaimer.

name: Specific disclosure requirement for priority
description: The disclosure in the priority document must be specific; mere implication or broad/general reference to elements is insufficient for priority to a detailed embodiment.
guidance: Exact correspondence is not required; it is enough that, on a reasonable assessment, there is in substance a disclosure of the combination of all the important elements of the claim.

name: Examiner access to priority document and translations
description: If the examiner needs a copy of the priority document, the IB supplies it unless the IB has not yet received it. If the priority document is not in an ISA/IPEA language, the examiner may invite the applicant to furnish a translation within two months of the invitation.
guidance: Any written opinion established while there is still time to furnish the priority document or translation may proceed as if the priority had been validly claimed; however, if the document or translation is not timely furnished, further written opinion or international preliminary examination report may proceed as if the priority had not been claimed. No designated Office may disregard a priority claim before giving the applicant an opportunity to furnish the priority document within a reasonable time, and no DO may disregard the claim if the document is available from a digital library per Administrative Instructions.

name: Competent authority to decide rectification
description: The competent authority (receiving Office, International Bureau, ISA or IPEA depending on circumstances) determines whether an alleged mistake is obvious and thus rectifiable.
guidance: Rule 91.1(b) allocation: (i) mistake in request or its correction — receiving Office; (ii) mistake in description/claims/drawings or their correction — ISA (unless IPEA competent); (iii) mistake in description/claims/drawings or amendment under Article 19/34 where demand for IPE has been made and not withdrawn and IPE start date passed — IPEA; (iv) mistake in other documents submitted to RO/ISA/IPEA/IB — that Office/Authority/Bureau as applicable. If an authority receives a request it is not competent to authorize, it transmits it to the appropriate authority and informs the applicant; it may instead inform the applicant to send it to the competent authority.

name: Aim and scope of 'meaningful search' and limits on absence of search
description: The aim of the ISA and IPEA is to issue international search reports and international preliminary reports on patentability that are as complete as possible. 'Meaningful search' should be read to include a search that within reason is complete enough to determine whether the claimed invention complies with substantive requirements (novelty, inventive step, industrial applicability) and/or sufficiency, support and clarity requirements of Articles 5 and 6.
guidance: A finding of 'no meaningful search' should be limited to exceptional situations in which no search at all is possible for a particular claim (for example, where description, claims, or drawings are totally unclear). To the extent description/claims/drawings can be sufficiently understood, a search should be performed, recognizing non-compliance may affect the extent of the search.

name: Plant/animal varieties and essentially biological processes (exclusion nuances)
description: Plant and animal varieties may be excluded from search, but transgenic plants, genetically modified non-human animals and methods of making such inventions would be searched and examined.
guidance: Whether a process is 'essentially biological' is a question of degree depending on the extent of technical intervention by man; significant technical intervention (e.g., application of growth-stimulating substance) would not be excluded. Microbiological processes and products thereof are not excluded; the term covers industrial processes using microorganisms and processes for producing microorganisms (e.g., by genetic engineering). Products of microbiological processes (including plasmids and viruses) may be searched and claimed; propagation of such products is to be construed as a microbiological process.

name: Status of claims (appellant brief)
description: A statement of the status of all the claims in the proceeding (e.g., rejected, allowed or confirmed, withdrawn, objected to, canceled). If the appellant is the owner, identify the rejected claims whose rejection is being appealed; if a requester, identify claims for which the examiner made a favorable determination being appealed.
guidance: Must clearly identify which claims are at issue and why; used by Board to determine appeal scope.

name: Summary of claimed subject matter (appellant brief)
description: A concise explanation of the subject matter defined in each independent claim involved in the appeal, with references to the specification by column/line and to drawings by reference characters. For each independent claim (and dependent claims argued separately) identify every means-plus-function and step-plus-function limitation under 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, and set forth corresponding structure, material, or acts in the specification with page/line and drawing references.
guidance: Must precisely map claim limitations to specification/drawings; means/step-plus-function limitations require explicit identification of corresponding disclosure; this is essential to Board consideration.

name: Claims appendix (appellant brief)
description: An appendix containing a copy of the claims to be reviewed on appeal.
guidance: Include the exact claim language as appendix material for Board review.

name: Respondent brief: required content items
description: Respondent brief must contain items under appropriate headings and in order: (i) Real party in interest; (ii) Related appeals and interferences; (iii) Status of claims (accept or dispute with particularity if disputing); (iv) Status of amendments (accept or dispute with particularity); (v) Summary of claimed subject matter (accept or dispute with specification/drawing references); (vi) Issues to be reviewed (accept or dispute; may present counter statement; requester respondents may not propose new grounds); (vii) Argument accepting or disputing appellant’s contentions with citations; (viii) Evidence appendix; (ix) Related proceedings appendix; (x) Certificate of service.
guidance: If disputing appellant statements, errors must be specified with particularity; each issue/argument treated under separate heading; evidence appendix must only include entered evidence; respondent brief shall not include new or non-admitted amendment/affidavit/evidence.

name: Board decisions: possible dispositions
description: The Board may affirm or reverse each decision of the examiner on issues raised on each appealed claim, or remand the reexamination proceeding to the examiner for further consideration.
guidance: Reversal of examiner’s determination not to make a requester-proposed rejection constitutes a new ground of rejection (see next items).

name: Owner options after Board new ground of rejection
description: Within one month of the decision, owner must either (1) reopen prosecution by filing an amendment or new evidence relating to the claims so rejected, or (2) request rehearing by the Board addressing the new ground and stating with particularity points believed misapprehended or overlooked and all other grounds for rehearing.
guidance: Reopen prosecution response must be an amendment or new evidence (or both) directed to the new ground; requesting rehearing must be timely and specific.

name: Filing claim information: clean and annotated copies
description: Within 14 days of initiation, each party must file a clean copy of its involved claims and, if a biotechnology material sequence is a limitation, a clean copy of the sequence. Within 28 days of initiation, each party must file annotated copies: (1) for claims with limitations illustrated in a drawing or sequence, indicate in bold-face between braces where each limitation is shown; (2) for means-plus-function or step-plus-function limitations under 35 U.S.C. 112(6), indicate in bold-face between braces the specific portions of the specification that describe corresponding structure, material, or acts.
guidance: Accurate annotation linking claim limitations to the disclosure is mandatory; motions to add/amend claims must include clean copy, claim chart showing written-description locations, and annotated claims when applicable.

name: Statement of material facts and claim chart requirement
description: Papers requiring factual statements must include a statement of material facts with each material fact separately stated as a numbered sentence with specific citations to record portions that support the fact. The Board may require that the statement be a separate paper. Claim charts must be used in support of any paper requiring comparison of a claim to something else (another claim, prior art, or a specification) and must accompany the paper as an appendix; claim charts are not a substitute for argument.
guidance: Any material fact not specifically denied is considered admitted in oppositions/replies. Ensure claim charts and numbered factual statements accompany motions and are well-cited.

name: Motions: types and burden of proof
description: Types: substantive motions (e.g., to redefine scope of contested case, change benefit accorded, judgment in contested case), responsive motions (e.g., to amend/add a claim, change inventorship), and miscellaneous motions. The party filing the motion has the burden of proof to establish entitlement to requested relief.
guidance: File motions consistent with any required notice of relief; burden rests on movant; choose correct motion type and provide supporting material.

name: Claiming variations without minute directions is acceptable
description: It is sufficient for the patentee to state the modes which he contemplates as best, and his claim will not be void, as too vague or comprehensive, although he claims the variations from those modes as being equally his invention, without describing the manner of producing those variations.
guidance: For machines, the statute requires specification of the principal and the several modes contemplated, but the patentee need not enter into minute description of every possible formal variation; indicating which variations he claims beyond his preferred modes suffices.

name: Distinction between claim construction (law) and enablement (fact)
description: Whether the specification discloses what the invention is is a question for the court (construction of the patent); whether it sufficiently describes the mode of carrying the invention into practice (enablement) is a question for the jury.
guidance: Courts construe the scope and meaning of the claim as a matter of law; juries (or fact-finders) decide whether a skilled mechanic could make the thing from the directions given. Example: description of rib thickness in a cotton-gin: sufficiency to make a proper rib is a factual question for those skilled in the art.

name: Ambiguity that cannot be elucidated invalidates patent irrespective of motive
description: Where ambiguity exists in the specification to such a degree that it cannot be elucidated, it is immaterial whether it had its origin in the mala fides of the patentee, or in haste or incompetency; ambiguity or claiming too much is the vital test of validity, not motive.
guidance: Courts focus on the sufficiency and clarity of the specification itself; intent or explanations about why ambiguity arose do not save an otherwise unclear claim.

name: Over-fullness (introducing useless/unnecessary matter) can vitiate the patent
description: If things wholly useless and unnecessary are introduced into the specification, as if they were essential, although terms are intelligible and necessary description present, the patent may be declared void.
guidance: English authorities presume such useless insertions were intended to overload and cloud the description to mislead the public and conceal the real invention. Examples: listing ingredients not needed to make the claimed article may void the patent.

name: Improvement patents must clearly limit claim to the improvement, not entire prior machine
description: The description of an improvement, when an improvement is the real subject-matter, should be made in such a manner as will clearly show that the improvement only is claimed by the patentee; if a machine substantially existed before, the patent should be confined to his improvement.
guidance: Even if the effect is the same, the patentee's claim should not encompass the whole pre-existing machine. If the combination in all its parts is entirely new (producing well-known effects), then the whole machine may be claimed as new.

name: When claiming parts of a machine, specify and point them out
description: Where the invention embraces only one or more parts of a machine (e.g., a coulter of a plough), the part or parts claimed must be specified and pointed out so that constructors, other inventors, and the public may know how to make the invention and what is withdrawn from general use.
guidance: Clear pointing out prevents overbroad claims that would unduly restrict prior art or the public's use of the rest of the machine.

name: Greater particularity required when claiming both a new ingredient and a combination
description: Where both a new ingredient and a combination of old ingredients embodied in the same machine are claimed, greater particularity is required, since the patentee's property consists not only in the new ingredient but also in the new combination.
guidance: It is essential the invention be fully described so its precise nature is known to the public; be explicit about both the ingredient and the claimed combination.

name: Sufficiency requirements for a combination of old ingredients
description: In a claim for a combination where all ingredients are old and the invention consists entirely in a new combination of old ingredients producing a new and useful result, 'such combination is sufficiently described, if the ingredients of which it is composed are named, their mode of operation given, and the new and useful result to be accomplished pointed out, so that those skilled in the art, and the public, may know the extent and nature of the claim.'
guidance: Describe components, how they operate together, and the new useful effect so skilled artisans can understand the claim's scope.

name: Recital of prior use when claiming an improvement is necessary
description: If the invention be an improvement and be claimed as such, but nothing is said of any previous use of which the proposed use is an improvement, the patent may be construed as a claim of entire and original discovery; hence the necessity for reciting what had formerly been done and describing a different mode as the improvement claimed.
guidance: Recite prior art or prior modes to show the claim is a narrower improvement rather than a sweeping discovery. Failure to do so can render the patent void or overbroad.

name: Machine patents must explain the principle and several modes of application
description: For any machine, the patentee 'shall fully explain the principle, and the several modes in which he has contemplated the application of that principle or character by which it may be distinguished from other inventions; and shall particularly specify and point out the part, improvement, or combination, which he claims as his own invention or discovery.'
guidance: The 'principle' means the peculiar structure and mode of operation. The patentee should state the device he deems best and also all other modes of producing the same effect he intends to claim. Minute instructions for every variation are unnecessary, but indicating what variations are claimed is required.

name: Claims must not be mere abstract principles—need practical application
description: The patentee may have discovered a principle of science or law of nature, but he cannot patent it by mere statement; he must give it a practical application to some useful purpose and the specification must show the application of the principle to such special purpose by its incorporation with matter to produce a practical result.
guidance: Care must be taken to describe the principle embodied in a particular organization of matter for a purpose; otherwise the claim risks being declared non-patentable as an abstract function or principle.

name: Mandatory components of an application (35 U.S.C. 111)
description: Such application shall include— (A) a specification as prescribed by section 112; (B) a drawing as prescribed by section 113; and (C) an oath or declaration as prescribed by section 115.
guidance: The filing date is the date the specification, with or without claims, is received. The fee, oath or declaration, and 1 or more claims may be submitted after the filing date within a prescribed period and under conditions (including surcharge); failure to submit them within the prescribed period results in abandonment.

name: Provisional application content and limits
description: A provisional application must include a specification as prescribed by section 112(a) and a drawing as prescribed by section 113; a claim is not required in a provisional application.
guidance: A complete provisional application must include the cover sheet required by § 1.51(c)(1) (or ADS) identifying it as provisional and providing inventor name(s), residence, title, attorney/agent name and reg. no., docket, correspondence address, and government contract info if applicable. Provisional applications are regarded as abandoned 12 months after filing if not converted or relied upon, are not entitled to priority under 35 U.S.C. 119/365/386, and no IDS may be filed in a provisional application.

name: Definition of filing date
description: The filing date of an application is the date on which a specification, with or without claims, is received in the United States Patent and Trademark Office.
guidance: For design patents (except continued prosecution), the filing date is when the specification (including at least one claim) and any required drawings are received. No new matter may be introduced after the filing date.

name: Complete application under 37 CFR 1.51
description: A complete application (filed under §1.53(b) or (d)) comprises: (1) a specification as prescribed by 35 U.S.C. 112, including claims; (2) the inventor’s oath or declaration; (3) drawings, when necessary; and (4) the prescribed filing, search, examination, and application size fees.
guidance: A complete provisional application under §1.53(c) comprises a cover sheet (per §1.51(c)(1)), a specification as prescribed by 35 U.S.C. 112(a), drawings when necessary, and prescribed fees. Applicants are encouraged to file an IDS in nonprovisional applications but not in provisionals.

name: Arrangement and contents of the specification
description: Preferred order: (A) Title; (B) Cross-reference to related applications; (C) Statement regarding federally sponsored research or development; (D) Names of parties to joint research agreement; (E) Incorporation by reference statements; (F) Statement regarding prior disclosures by inventor; (G) Background of the invention (field and related art); (H) Brief summary of the invention; (I) Brief description of the drawings; (J) Detailed description of the invention; (K) Claim(s) (commencing on a separate sheet); (L) Abstract of the disclosure (commencing on a separate sheet); (M) Sequence Listing if present.
guidance: These are suggested headers (upper case, without underlining/bold). If an Application Data Sheet (ADS) is used, data in the ADS need not be repeated elsewhere (with limited exceptions). See MPEP §608.01(a) for details.

name: Completion of application subsequent to filing (missing fees/claims/oath)
description: If an application accorded a filing date lacks basic filing, search, or examination fees, at least one claim, or inventor's oath/declaration, the applicant will be notified and given time to supply these to avoid abandonment; timing differs if applicant provided correspondence address.
guidance: Conditions allow postponement of inventor's oath until issue fee date when certain ADS and identification criteria are met. Specific periods are set forth in §1.53(f)(1)-(3).

name: Continued prosecution application requirements
description: A continued prosecution (nonprovisional) application (continuation or divisional) may be filed under conditions: identify the prior application; disclose and claim only subject matter disclosed in the prior application; name same inventors (with limited exceptions); include request that it utilize the prior application's file jacket and contents to constitute the new application.
guidance: A continued prosecution application uses the prior application's number for identification, may waive confidentiality to extent of file access, must be filed before payment of issue fee/abandonment/termination of prior proceedings, and may not introduce new matter. See §1.53(d).

name: Condition for examination (required papers and fees)
description: An application filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a) is in condition for examination when it includes a specification (including at least one claim and an abstract), papers in compliance with § 1.52, drawings (if any) in compliance with § 1.84, any required English translation, a sequence listing in compliance with §§ 1.821–1.825 (if applicable), the inventor's oath/declaration or an application data sheet per § 1.63(b), the basic filing fee (§ 1.16(a) or (c)), the search fee (§ 1.16(k) or (m)), the examination fee (§ 1.16(o) or (q)), any certified copy required by § 1.57(a), and any application size fee under § 1.16(s).
guidance: International applications in national stage must include analogous items and fees (see § 1.491(b) and § 1.492). Papers/drawings/sequence listings corrected prior to mailing of an action under 35 U.S.C. 132 or a notice of allowance are considered in compliance as of the filing date of the latest correcting reply.

name: Exemplary (non-exhaustive) list of applicant actions/inactions that interfere with Office processing (37 CFR 1.704(c) overview)
description: 37 CFR 1.704(c)(1)–(c)(14) set forth actions or inactions by an applicant that interfere with the Office’s ability to process or examine an application and specify how much PTA is reduced for each; the list is exemplary, not exhaustive.
guidance: Office may also reduce PTA on the basis of other conduct that interferes with processing under authority of 35 U.S.C. 154(b)(2)(C)(iii). Examples of infrequent but interfering conduct are given (e.g., meritless petitions for reconsideration, extensions for interference settlement negotiations that do not settle, claim scope changed to match examiner allowance more than six months earlier than allowance date). Applicants must refrain from actions that prevent or interfere with processing.

name: Non-statutory double patenting rejections as proxy for claim broadening
description: Patent examiners may reject a claim if the same inventor has disclosed 'patentably indistinct' claims in a previous application. This non-statutory (obviousness-type) double patenting rejection is taken as a proxy for 'claim broadening' or 'claim tailoring' (as opposed to claiming new and distinct uses of the original invention).
guidance: If applicants use continuations to draft claims that read on standards, expect more non-statutory double-patenting rejections for SEP continuations filed after standard publication than before. Construct matched samples (same year, art unit, examiner), restrict to continuations with full examination histories, estimate linear probability models (outcome=double patenting rejection ×100). Cluster standard errors by patent family. See Table 4 and accompanying notes for implementation details and sample exclusions (e.g. exclude continuations filed before 2008 or disposed after June 2017).

name: Claim-language convergence measured by Jaccard similarity
description: Measure similarity of claims across pairs of applications linked to the same standard via a Jaccard index: number of common keywords in the claims divided by total keywords, multiplied by 100.
guidance: Compare Jaccard similarity for post-standard continuations (J_post) versus pre-standard parent applications (J_pre). Retain pairs where both continuations and parents have at least 10 keywords and drop pairs where the two continuations claim priority to the same parent. Use OLS regressions, pair fixed effects, and controls (filing year effects, art-unit-by-examiner effects, log number of independent claims, words per independent claim). Interpret greater post-publication similarity as evidence that applicants draft claims to cover standards (see Table 5).

name: Interpretation of double patenting rejection statistics
description: Non-statutory double patenting rejections often occur when an applicant seeks to change the scope of an earlier claim (e.g., expanding it by removing limitations); use these rejections as evidence of claim modification rather than wholly new claims.
guidance: Compare rates for post-standard SEP continuations versus matched non-SEP continuations and pre-standard SEPs. Report percentage-point differences and relative increases with baseline probabilities (e.g., post-standard SEPs ~8 percentage points more likely; 15% increase relative to 50% baseline).

name: Theoretical criteria linking late claiming to litigation likelihood
description: Theoretical mechanisms: (i) plaintiffs more likely to assert patents for which infringement is easily proved (for SEPs, infringement typically argued by comparing claims to the standard); (ii) litigation more likely when stakes are higher, and patentees may invest in late claim drafting for more valuable inventions.
guidance: Use these mechanisms to motivate empirical tests relating continuation status and filing lag to litigation outcomes; consider selection versus causal interpretation when continuations remain associated with higher litigation even after conditioning on filing lag.

name: Policy remedies to limit opportunistic continuation practice
description: Potential policy options include adjusting USPTO fee schedules, adopting rules to limit lengthy continuation 'chains', adopting intervening-user rights to protect pre-adopters, and relying on prosecution laches in courts to render patents unenforceable for unreasonable delays. SSOs could also adopt clearer IP policies.
guidance: Evaluate trade-offs: policies might reduce opportunism but could lead to vaguer original claims or last-minute filings. Consider how interventions interact with applicants' incentives, and note empirical difficulty predicting counterfactual behavior.

name: Recognize other tools that delay claim drafting
description: Continuations are not the only way to delay claim drafting; applicants may use provisional applications, requests for continued examination (RCEs), divisionals, or deferred examination in other jurisdictions.
guidance: When assessing delay and its effects, account for these alternative mechanisms and consider cross-jurisdictional differences where continuations are not available. Further research recommended to study combined use of these tools.

name: Graham factual inquiries (core framework)
description: The objective analysis for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103 is based on the Graham v. John Deere factual inquiries: (A) determining the scope and content of the prior art; (B) ascertaining the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art; and (C) resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
