guidance: Also evaluate objective evidence/secondary considerations (commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, unexpected results) and weigh such evidence case-by-case. The Graham factors control the obviousness inquiry and may be reordered in particular cases.

name: Claim interpretation: broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with specification
description: The scope of the claimed invention must be clearly determined by giving the claims the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.
guidance: Read the specification (including claims) to understand what the applicant has invented (see MPEP §904 and Phillips v. AWH).

name: Rationale: simple substitution of one known element for another
description: Obviousness may be supported by a simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results.
guidance: Substitution that yields only predictable results can render claims obvious (KSR examples). Examiner should explain why substitution would have been made by a person of ordinary skill.

name: Applicant reply obligations under 37 C.F.R. 1.111(b)
description: Applicants must timely, distinctly, and specifically point out supposed errors in Office actions and reply to every ground of objection and rejection; replies must present arguments pointing out the specific distinction believed to render the claims patentable.
guidance: An effective traverse of a rejection based on factual findings must include a reasoned statement explaining why the Office erred. Mere assertions that a prima facie case is not established or that common knowledge is unsupported are insufficient; examiner may repeat rejection and make next action final (see MPEP §706.07(a)).

name: Prima facie case requirements (general)
description: To establish a prima facie case of obviousness, the examiner must show a reasoned basis (rationale) for why the claimed invention would have been obvious and account for all claim limitations; reasonable expectation of success may be required depending on rationale.
guidance: See MPEP §2142–§2143 for examples: suggestion/motivation to modify, reasonable expectation of success, and consideration of all claim limitations. The mere existence of differences between prior art and invention does not establish nonobviousness.

name: Categories of prior art under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1)
description: Prior art documents and activities that may preclude patentability include: patented, described in a printed publication, in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
guidance: Documents/activities used to determine novelty/nonobviousness include issued patents, published applications, non-patent printed publications, evidence of public use, sale activity, or other availability. See MPEP §§ 2152.02(a)–(f).

name: Effective filing date of a claimed invention (35 U.S.C. 100(i))
description: The effective filing date is the earliest of: (1) the actual filing date of the patent or application containing the claimed invention; or (2) the filing date of the earliest application for which the patent or application is entitled to a right of priority or benefit under 35 U.S.C. 119, 120, 121, 365, or 386.
guidance: The one-year grace period in AIA 102(b)(1) is measured from the filing date of any U.S. or foreign patent application to which the patent/application is entitled to benefit or priority. Effective filing date is determined claim-by-claim. See MPEP § 2152.01.

name: Anticipation: what 'described' means for printed publications/patents
description: To anticipate under AIA 102(a)(1) or (a)(2), a prior art document must disclose 'each and every element of the claimed invention' either explicitly or inherently, and the elements must be 'arranged or combined in the same way as in the claim.'
guidance: Additionally the prior art must enable a person of ordinary skill in the art to make the invention without undue experimentation (enablement-from-POA viewpoint). There is no requirement that the prior art meet the 'how to use' requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a). Prior art that enables one species can anticipate a broader claim. See cases cited (Gleave, Eli Lilly, Vas-Cath, etc.) and MPEP § 2152.02(b).

name: On sale criteria under AIA 102(a)(1)
description: On sale activity will bar patentability if the claimed invention was the subject of a commercial sale or offer for sale (not primarily for experimental purposes) and ready for patenting; under AIA the sale must have made the invention available to the public.
guidance: Contract law principles determine whether a commercial sale/offer occurred. Enablement inquiry is not applicable to whether an invention is 'on sale.' Secret sales among parties under confidentiality do not qualify as making the invention available to the public. See Pfaff and MPEP § 2133.03.

name: Claim-by-claim effective filing date vs application-by-application AIA applicability
description: Effective filing dates are determined on a claim-by-claim basis (different claims may have different effective filing dates), while the determination of whether pre-AIA or AIA 35 U.S.C. 102/103 applies is made on an application-by-application basis.
guidance: See MPEP § 2152.01 and § 706.02 for interplay between claim-level effective filing dates and application-level applicability of pre-AIA vs AIA statutory regimes.

name: Identification of New Matter by Examiner
description: When objecting, identify the added material that is not supported by the original disclosure by page and line numbers and provide an appropriate explanation of the position.
guidance: Explanation should address any applicant statements supporting possession in the specification as filed and include any unresolved questions that raise doubt as to possession of the claimed invention at the time of filing. If new matter is entered into the claims or affects the claims, treat the new matter as part of claimed subject matter for other rejections.

name: New Matter Consequences for Claims (35 U.S.C. 112 / written description)
description: If the new matter has been entered into the claims or affects the scope of the claims, the affected claims should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph) for reciting elements without support in the original disclosure.
guidance: If new matter is added to the claims, or affects them, make a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) using form paragraph 7.31.01. If new matter is added only to a claim, do not use Form Paragraph 7.28 (which is for specification amendments) — instead reject the claim using 7.31.01. New matter must be considered part of the claimed subject matter for purposes of any other appropriate prior art or 35 U.S.C. 112 rejection.

name: Review/Appeal of Examiner's Holding of New Matter
description: Where the new matter is confined to amendments to the specification, review of the examiner's requirement for cancelation is by petition; where alleged new matter is introduced into or affects the claims (necessitating their rejection), the matter is appealable and should not be considered on petition.
guidance: Refer to MPEP § 2163.06 for additional guidance on petition vs appeal treatment.

name: Statements Required When Adding or Replacing Sequence Listings After Filing
description: When adding or replacing a Sequence Listing (ASCII or XML) after the filing date via the USPTO electronic filing system, specific accompanying statements and requests are required.
guidance: When adding (37 CFR 1.825(a)) include: request to have amendment entered using incorporation by reference (if desired), a statement that submission does not include new matter (1.825(a)(4)), and a statement identifying the basis for the amendment with specific references to parts of the application as originally filed (1.825(a)(3)). When replacing (1.825(b) or 1.835(b)) include: statement of no new matter, statement identifying basis for amendments with specific references to original parts (spec., claims, drawings), and statement identifying location of deletions/replacements/additions (1.825(b)(3)-(5) / 1.835(b)(2)-(5)).

name: Order and Structure of Application Elements (37 CFR 1.77)
description: The elements of the application, if applicable, should appear in the following order: utility application transmittal form; fee transmittal form; application data sheet (§ 1.76); specification; drawings; inventor's oath or declaration. The specification should include sections (if applicable) in this order: title; cross-reference to related applications; statement regarding federally sponsored research; names of parties to a joint research agreement; incorporation by reference paragraph for ASCII/XML files; statement regarding prior disclosures; background; brief summary; brief description of drawings; detailed description; claims; abstract; and Sequence Listing (if applicable).
guidance: Text of the specification sections should be preceded by a section heading in uppercase and without underlining or bold type. See § 1.77(b) and related subsections for details on what to include (e.g., incorporation by reference statements for ASCII/XML files).

name: Indefinite Claim Language: "For Example"
description: Regarding claim [1], the phrase "for example" renders the claim indefinite because it is unclear whether the limitation(s) following the phrase are part of the claimed invention.
guidance: Cite MPEP § 2173.05(d). This form paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.34.01.

name: Broader Range/Limitation And Narrow Range/Limitation in Same Claim
description: A broad range or limitation together with a narrow range or limitation that falls within the broad range or limitation (in the same claim) may be considered indefinite if the resulting claim does not clearly set forth the metes and bounds of the patent protection desired.
guidance: Explain whether the narrower language is (a) merely exemplary (and thus not required) or (b) a required feature. Use when the claim recites both broad recitation [2] and narrower statement [3] in the same claim. Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.34.01.

name: Indefinite Claim Language: "Or The Like"
description: Regarding claim [1], the phrase "or the like" renders the claim(s) indefinite because the claim(s) include(s) elements not actually disclosed (those encompassed by "or the like"), thereby rendering the scope of the claim(s) unascertainable.
guidance: Cite MPEP § 2173.05(d). This form paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.34.01.

name: Indefinite Claim Language: "Such As"
description: Regarding claim [1], the phrase "such as" renders the claim indefinite because it is unclear whether the limitations following the phrase are part of the claimed invention.
guidance: Cite MPEP § 2173.05(d). This form paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.34.01.

name: Essential Steps Omitted
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as being incomplete for omitting essential steps, such omission amounting to a gap between the steps. The omitted steps are: [2]
guidance: This rejection must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.02 or 7.103. In bracket 2, recite the steps omitted from the claims. Give the rationale for considering the omitted steps critical or essential, explaining the basis for concluding the inventor regards the omitted matter as essential.

name: Claims Must Be Structurally Clear and One-Sentence
description: The claim(s) are narrative in form and replete with indefinite language. The structure which goes to make up the device must be clearly and positively specified. The structure must be organized and correlated in such a manner as to present a complete operative device. The claim(s) must be in one sentence form only.
guidance: Use format of claims in cited patents as examples. Narrative/multisentence claims or claims lacking organized correlated structure may be indefinite and subject to rejection.

name: Failure To Particularly Point Out and Distinctly Claim - Omnibus Claim
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as being indefinite in that it fails to point out what is included or excluded by the claim language. This claim is an omnibus type claim.
guidance: This rejection must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.02 or 7.103. Use to reject an 'omnibus' type claim (example: "A device substantially as shown and described."). No further explanation is necessary. In bracket 2, recite the steps omitted from the claims when applicable.

name: Essential Elements Omitted
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as being incomplete for omitting essential elements, such omission amounting to a gap between the elements. The omitted elements are: [2]
guidance: This rejection must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.02 or 7.103. In bracket 2 recite the omitted elements and give rationale explaining why the inventor regards the omitted matter as essential.

name: Presumption that 35 U.S.C. 112(f) Applies When 'Means' or 'Step' Is Used
description: A claim limitation is presumed to invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f) when it explicitly uses the term 'means' or 'step' and includes functional language.
guidance: The presumption is overcome when the limitation further includes the structure, material or acts necessary to perform the recited function. If an examiner finds that 'means' is used but prong (B) or (C) of the 3-prong analysis is not met, the Office action must explain why a limitation using 'means' or 'step' is not being treated under 35 U.S.C. 112(f). Cite TriMed, Altiris and other precedent.

name: Presumption that 35 U.S.C. 112(f) Does Not Apply When 'Means' Not Used (Rebuttable)
description: A claim limitation that does not use the term 'means' will trigger the rebuttable presumption that 35 U.S.C. 112(f) does not apply.
guidance: Examiners should nonetheless consider whether the presumption is overcome (i.e., the claim term fails to recite sufficiently definite structure or else recites function without sufficient structure). Cite Phillips, CCS Fitness, Personalized Media. Even without 'means', terms can be construed under 112(f) if they are generic placeholders or otherwise lack structural meaning (e.g., 'module', 'mechanism for').

name: Three-Prong Analysis to Determine Invocation of 35 U.S.C. 112(f)
description: Examiners will apply 35 U.S.C. 112(f) to a claim limitation if it meets the following 3-prong analysis: (A) the claim limitation uses the term 'means' or 'step' or a term used as a substitute for 'means' that is a generic placeholder; (B) the term is modified by functional language (typically linked by 'for' or similar); and (C) the term is not modified by sufficient structure, material, or acts for performing the claimed function.
guidance: If a claim limitation meets all three prongs, it should be treated under 112(f). If unclear whether limitation falls within 112(f), a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) may be appropriate. The examiner must expressly state in the Office action when a 35 U.S.C. 112(f) interpretation is applied. If the limitation uses 'means' but prongs (B) or (C) are not met, explain why 112(f) is not applied.

name: Functional Modification Requirement (Prong B)
description: The term 'means' or 'step' or the generic placeholder must be modified by functional language (typically linked by 'for' or another linking word or phrase such as 'configured to' or 'so that').
guidance: A function must be recited within the claim limitation; the mere use of 'means' with no associated function rebuts invocation. A statement of function only in the preamble is generally insufficient. For process claims, step-plus-function is implicated only when steps plus function without acts are present.

name: Sufficient Structure/Material/Acts Rebuttal (Prong C)
description: The term 'means' or generic placeholder must not be modified by sufficient structure, material, or acts for achieving the specified function in order to invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f). If the claim itself recites sufficient structure or acts, 112(f) does not apply.
guidance: Structural modifiers (e.g., 'detent mechanism', 'circuit') or explicit acts may impart sufficient structure. Use case law (Envirco, Rodime, Cole, Unidynamics) to assess whether the recited language supplies sufficient structure. If a structural modifier further describes the generic placeholder, it may avoid 112(f) treatment; conversely, non-structural modifiers will not.

name: How To Determine Whether a Term Denotes Structure
description: To determine whether a word, term, or phrase coupled with a function denotes structure, examiners may check whether: (1) the specification provides a description sufficient to inform one of ordinary skill that the term denotes structure; (2) general and subject-matter-specific dictionaries provide evidence that the term has achieved recognition as a noun denoting structure; and/or (3) the prior art provides evidence that the term is an art-recognized structure to perform the claimed function.
guidance: Apply Ex parte Rodriguez (precedential) and relevant Federal Circuit precedent. Consider whether common art usage or the specification gives the term structural significance (e.g., 'filters', 'circuit', 'brakes').

name: Examiner Office Action Requirements When Applying 112(f)
description: A determination that a claim is being interpreted according to 35 U.S.C. 112(f) should be expressly stated in the examiner's Office action.
guidance: If the examiner determines 'means' is used but prong (B) or (C) is not met, the Office action must explain why the limitation is not being treated under 112(f). If 112(f) is asserted and applicant objects, applicant may present a showing of sufficient structure or amend the claim to recite sufficient structure to avoid 112(f).

name: Applicant Options in Response to 112(f) Finding
description: In response to an Office action finding that 35 U.S.C. 112(f) is invoked, applicant may: (1) present a sufficient showing to establish that the claim limitation recites sufficient structure to perform the claimed function; or (2) amend the claim limitation to avoid interpretation under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (e.g., by reciting sufficient structure).
guidance: If applicant does not want the limitation interpreted under 112(f), they must either add structure in the claim or rebut the presumption by showing the limitation already recites sufficient structure. If unclear whether 112(f) applies, a rejection under 112(b) may be appropriate.

name: Process Claims and Step-Plus-Function Caution
description: For process claims, step-plus-function treatment is implicated only when steps plus function without acts are present; merely using '-ing' verbs like passing, heating, reacting, transferring etc. does not automatically create step-plus-function limitations.
guidance: Avoid overbroadly converting typical process language into step-plus-function limitations. Cite O.I. Corp., Baran and related precedents. The claimed function must lack associated acts to be step-plus-function.

name: Detectability
description: Consider how detectable the claimed invention is in a competitor’s product or process. To enforce a patent, the patentee must show a competitor infringes every element of at least one claim; hard-to-detect elements make enforcement more difficult.
guidance: Inventions tied to front-end, customer-visible features that are easily detectable are good candidates for patents. Back-end functionality or internal processes that are not accessible to end users require analysis of whether the element can be detected through reasonable efforts and whether secrecy can be maintained. Up-front claim-scope analysis and drafting to maximize enforceability is recommended.

name: RCE must include required fee and submission
description: A request for continued examination under 37 CFR 1.114 must include the fee set forth in 37 CFR 1.17(e) and a submission as required by 37 CFR 1.114.
guidance: If the fee and/or submission is missing the RCE is improper; consequences vary (e.g., withdrawal of appeal and abandonment, or passing to issue on allowed claims). Examiner should use the appropriate form paragraph (e.g., 7.42.16) to notify applicant. In some circumstances a submission filed with an improper RCE should not be entered, except in narrow situations (see exception below).

name: RCE filed after appeal but without submission/fee — abandonment if no allowed claims
description: If an RCE was filed after appeal to the Board but the request lacks the fee and/or required submission, and no claim is allowed, the proceedings as to the rejected claims are terminated and the application is abandoned (see form paragraph 7.42.10).
guidance: Use form paragraph 7.42.10 to withdraw the appeal and hold the application abandoned where appropriate. See MPEP § 1215.01.

name: RCE filed after appeal including submission but lacking fee — submission not entered; pass to issue on allowed claims
description: If an RCE filed after appeal includes a submission but lacks the fee required by 37 CFR 1.17(e), the submission has not been entered (see 37 CFR 1.116(c)). Since proceedings as to rejected claims are terminated, the application will be passed to issue on allowed claim(s) (form paragraph 7.42.13).
guidance: Insert claim numbers and cancel dependent claims as appropriate. If formal matters outstanding, use form paragraph 7.42.14 to require corrections within shortened statutory period.

name: Appeal Dismissed - Allowed Claims, Formal Matters Remaining
description: If applicant fails to file a brief within the time prescribed by 37 CFR 41.37(a), the appeal stands dismissed and proceedings as to the rejected claims are considered terminated; application will be passed to issue on allowed claim [1] provided the listed formal matters are corrected within a shortened TWO MONTH statutory period to avoid abandonment.
guidance: Use when notice of appeal filed on or after Jan 23, 2012. Note: form paragraph should only be used if formal matters cannot be handled by examiner’s amendment (MPEP § 1215.04). Extensions of time may be granted under 37 CFR 1.136. Insert description of formal matters in bracket 2 and identify allowed claims per bracket guidance.

name: Period For Seeking Court Review Has Lapsed
description: The period under 37 CFR 90.3 for seeking court review of the PTAB decision [1] has expired and no further action taken by appellant; proceedings as to the rejected claims are terminated and the application will be passed to issue on allowed claim [2] provided listed formal matters are promptly corrected; applicant must correct within a shortened TWO MONTH statutory period to avoid abandonment.
guidance: Insert decision rendering date and identify formal matters to be corrected in bracket 3. Extensions under 1.136 may be granted. Prosecution otherwise closed.

name: Requirement for Rewritten Specification
description: Interlineations or cancellations made in the specification or amendments to the claims which could lead to confusion and mistake during issue and printing require that identified portions of the specification or claims be rewritten before passing the case to issue.
guidance: See 37 CFR 1.125 and MPEP § 608.01(q). Specific discussion of sections required to be rewritten must be set forth. See form paragraph 6.28.01 for substitute specification.

name: Defective Reissue Oath/Declaration - No Statement of Defect in the Patent
description: The reissue oath/declaration is defective because it fails to contain the statements required under 37 CFR 1.175 as to applicant’s belief that the original patent is wholly or partly inoperative or invalid, or fails to state the reason (defective specification,drawing, or claiming more/less than patentee had the right to claim).
guidance: Use when applicant fails to allege that the original patent is inoperative or invalid and/or fails to state the reason of defect. In bracket 1 point out the specific defect using the language of the regulation. Form paragraph 14.14 must follow.

name: Eligibility requirements for reexamination
description: Requirements for reexamination: an application has not been invalidated, withdrawn or abandoned; has been rejected (excluding rejection after reexamination); has not requested an appeal trial against decision to reject; and declares intention to request reexamination with amendment of the specification, drawing(s), or claims. 'Amendment' includes substantial and non-substantial changes to the specification.
guidance: Checklist to confirm a valid reexamination request; appeal pending or certain other statuses bar reexamination.

name: Overlapping applications by same applicant—handling when related to an interference
description: Examiners should not consider ex parte questions which are pending before the Office in inter partes proceedings involving the same applicant. The better practice is to reject claims in an application related to another application in interference over the counts of the interference and, if such claims are not canceled in the outside application, suspend prosecution of the outside application pending final determination of priority in the interference. If the applicant wishes to prosecute the outside application and presents good reasons, prosecution should be continued.
guidance: When related claims are at issue in an interference, prefer rejection over consideration ex parte. If applicant shows good cause to proceed, follow precedent (e.g., Ex parte Bullier, In re Seebach, In re Hammell) and MPEP §2300 guidance.

name: Claims whose BRI covers statutory and non-statutory embodiments
description: A claim whose broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments embraces subject matter that is not eligible for patent protection and therefore is directed to non-statutory subject matter (Step 1: NO).
guidance: Such claims fail Step 1 and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101; best practice is for the examiner to point out the BRI and recommend an amendment, if possible, to narrow the claim to those embodiments that fall within a statutory category. Example: machine-readable media whose BRI encompasses transitory carrier waves should be rejected as non-statutory (see In re Nuijten; Mentor Graphics v. EVE-USA).

name: If claim is not within statutory categories (Step 1: NO)
description: If a claim is clearly not within one of the four enumerated categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter), then a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 must be made indicating the claim is directed to non-statutory subject matter.
guidance: Use form paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01 and see MPEP § 706.03(a). However, if the disclosure suggests the claim could be amended to fall within a statutory category, proceed to analyze whether such an amended claim would be eligible at Pathway A, B, or C, and recommend amendment if possible.

name: Step 2A: Determine whether a claim is directed to a judicial exception
description: Step 2A asks whether the claim is 'directed to' a law of nature, natural phenomenon (product of nature), or an abstract idea. A claim is directed to a judicial exception when a judicial exception is recited (set forth or described) in the claim.
guidance: Recitation can occur in different ways (explicit discrete language or broader description). If the claim as a whole is not directed to an exception (Step 2A: NO), it is eligible at Pathway B. If directed to an exception (Step 2A: YES), proceed to Step 2B to determine whether the claim amounts to significantly more than the exception.

name: Distinguish claims that 'recite' an exception from those that merely 'involve' one
description: Examiners should distinguish claims that recite an exception (which require further eligibility analysis) from claims that merely involve an exception (which are eligible and do not require further eligibility analysis).
guidance: Consider the claim as a whole. Example: a claim explicitly reciting F=ma recites a law of nature (directed to an exception); a teeter-totter claim that does not recite the law of the lever merely involves the natural principle and is eligible without further analysis.

name: Avoid parsing a recited exception into multiple exceptions
description: Unless it is clear that the claim recites distinct exceptions, care should be taken not to parse a recited exception into multiple exceptions, particularly for abstract ideas.
guidance: For example, a series of mental steps manipulating information should be treated as a single abstract idea rather than multiple separate abstract ideas. However, if a claim recites multiple exceptions, it is directed to at least one judicial exception and must be analyzed in Step 2B.

name: How to identify an abstract idea in the claim
description: Examiners should determine whether a claim recites an abstract idea by (1) identifying the claimed concept (the specific claim limitation(s) the examiner believes may be an abstract idea), and (2) comparing that claimed concept to concepts previously identified by the courts as abstract ideas.
guidance: If the claimed concept is similar to one or more court-identified abstract ideas, it is reasonable to conclude the concept is an abstract idea (Step 2A: YES) and proceed to Step 2B. If not similar and no basis exists to conclude it is an abstract idea, find the claim not directed to an abstract idea (Step 2A: NO), unless another exception is recited.

name: Claims directed to improvements in computer functionality or other technology are not abstract
description: Inventions that pertain to improvements in computer functionality or other technologies are not abstract when appropriately claimed and may be eligible at Step 2A.
guidance: Federal Circuit examples include Enfish (self-referential database), McRO (automatic lip synchronization using particular computer-implemented rules), and Visual Memory (enhanced computer memory system). When claiming an improvement, the specification should disclose sufficient details such that one of ordinary skill recognizes the claimed invention as providing an improvement, and the claim itself must reflect the improvement in technology. Examiners must give the claim its BRI and evaluate both claim and specification; consider whether the claim covers a particular solution or merely the idea of a solution, and whether the BRI is limited to computer implementation. See MPEP § 2106.05(a) for more.

name: What does not show an improvement to computer-functionality or technology
description: Certain features do not demonstrate an improvement in computer functionality or other technology even if computer-related: e.g., processes that can be performed without a computer, mere automation of manual processes, speed increases that stem solely from general-purpose computer capabilities, or conventional implementation on generic components.
guidance: Federal Circuit guidance: if a claimed process can be performed mentally or without a computer (Synopsys v. Mentor Graphics), it cannot be characterized as an improvement in a computer. Mere automation or implementation on generic components/machinery (Affinity Labs; TLI Communications; FairWarning; Credit Acceptance) is insufficient. Examiners should consider these cases and MPEP § 2106.05(a) for further examples and discussion.

name: Resolve computer/technology improvement question early where possible
description: Although whether a claim improves computer-functionality or other technology may be considered in either Step 2A or Step 2B, examiners are encouraged to resolve this question as early as possible in the eligibility analysis.
guidance: A clear improvement (e.g., Enfish) could be found eligible at Pathway A under the streamlined analysis or at Pathway B as not being directed to an abstract idea. If the improvement is not clear enough for Step 2A, it may nonetheless contribute to eligibility in Step 2B. Use the streamlined procedures in MPEP § 2106.06(b) as appropriate.

name: Were all the 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection(s) in compliance?
description: Determine whether each 103 rejection properly identifies the claim(s), the statute/subparagraph (as appropriate), and is supported by sufficient evidence to establish a prima facie case of obviousness.
guidance: Answer Yes or No. Consult the statutory compliance standard and scenarios for guidance. If No, continue to detailed questions identifying the noncompliant claims and reasons.

name: Failure to properly identify rejected claim(s) and/or statute (103 §4(a))
description: The rejection does not properly identify the rejected claim(s) and/or identify the correct statute/subparagraph.
guidance: This box is for failures in identification only. Do not use this box when the problem is lack of evidentiary support (use 4(c)). Do not use to capture omitted rejections—raise omitted rejections separately. Explanations should avoid rhetorical questions and personalization; explain basis for noncompliance tied to identification failures.

name: Findings of fact not properly articulated and/or evidenced (103 §4(c)(i))
description: The rejection's findings of fact (mapping of claim limitations to prior-art teachings) are incomplete or missing (e.g., missing limitation).
guidance: When the teachings relied on are not found within the references, check this box. If checked, one of 4(c)(i)(A)1-3 and one of 4(c)(i)(B) or (C) must also be checked. The finding of facts is directed to correlation of claim limitations to teachings in the references.

name: No citation/mapping to prior art for the missing limitation (103 §4(c)(i)(B))
description: The rejection provides no guidance or citation mapping between the claimed limitation and the applied prior art for the limitation that is the basis for noncompliance.
guidance: This box captures failures to provide any citation/mapping guidance. Degree of correlation is not considered—focus solely on whether guidance exists. Examples: (1) rejection points to a figure but no teaching for limitation C — if some correlation was provided to primary ref, don't check; (2) rejection asserts limitation B is taught by Jones but provides no correlation — check this box.

name: Rejection does not adequately articulate how prior art is modified (103 §4(c)(ii))
description: The rejection fails to clearly articulate how the primary reference is being modified to arrive at the claimed invention.
guidance: Box captures insufficient articulation of the modification step(s). Consult compliance standard and scenarios for fact patterns that rise to noncompliance.

name: Rejection lacks a proper reason/rationale/motivation for modification (103 §4(c)(iii))
description: The rejection does not articulate an appropriate reason, motivation, or rationale for modifying the prior art to arrive at the claimed invention.
guidance: If no persuasive reason or rationale is articulated, check this box. Sub-bases include: prior art does not support the combination (nonanalogous/teaches away), impermissible hindsight, or no articulated reason present. Further checks capture those sub-reasons.

name: Prior art does not support the asserted combination / nonanalogous art or teaches away (103 §4(c)(iii)(1))
description: The prior art applied does not support the claimed combination (e.g., nonanalogous art or art that teaches away from the asserted modification).
guidance: Use when there would be no reason to make the asserted modification. This includes art being nonanalogous, teaching away, or modification would destroy the reference being modified.

name: Explanation of noncompliance guidance (103)
description: How the reviewer should write the explanation of noncompliance (scope, tone, specificity).
guidance: Comments must be limited to the basis for noncompliance (e.g., failed identification or insufficient evidence). Avoid rhetorical questions and personalization. When lack of sufficient evidence is asserted, identify each claim and claim limitation forming the basis, explain how the reference fails to meet the limitation(s), or why an interpretation is inappropriate if correlation exists.

name: Additional Data/Feedback: improper reliance on inherency (103 §5(a))
description: Check when the rejection relies on inherency to meet a claim limitation and that reliance is asserted to be improper.
guidance: Only check when the rejection provides an explicit assertion that limitations are met by inherency and that assertion is improper. Do not check when inherency is only implied and not expressly relied upon.

name: Additional Data/Feedback: non-compliance due to unreasonable claim interpretation (103 §5(c))
description: The non-compliance is the result of an unreasonable claim interpretation used by the examiner.
guidance: Check only when the rejection provides some guidance or indicates how the limitation is being construed so as to read on the prior art and that construction is unreasonable. If the claim interpretation is not discernible, do not check this box.

name: Characteristic: addresses substantially all claims individually (103 characteristics)
description: The rejection addresses substantially all claims individually and only groups claims together that are of substantially similar scope (limited claim lumping).
guidance: Check when the rejection treats claims individually where appropriate and limits claim grouping to substantially similar-scope claims.

name: Characteristic: reasonably pinpoints where limitations are met (103 characteristics)
description: The rejection reasonably pinpoints where substantially all limitations are met by the prior art (e.g., written specification; drawings).
guidance: Check when the rejection points to precise locations where the reference teaches the claim limitations. Do not check when the rejection refers to large portions of the reference or generally to a figure.

name: Characteristic: includes pasted pertinent figures with annotations (103 characteristics)
description: The rejection includes pasted pertinent figures with annotations (as appropriate) which pinpoint where limitations are met by the prior art.
guidance: Check when pasted annotated figures meaningfully aid in mapping claim limitations to the prior art.

name: Characteristic: goes beyond pinpointing by summarizing how/why limitations are met (103 characteristics)
description: The rejection goes beyond pinpointing by summarizing how/why the limitations are met by the prior art or reciting terminology from the prior art to equate terminology with the claims.
guidance: If this box is checked, the 'reasonably pinpoints' box should also be checked. This indicates the rejection not only maps but explains how/why the mapping supports the limitation.

name: Characteristic: statements of patentable weight included (103 characteristics)
description: Statements of patentable weight are included, particularly when patentable weight is not being given to intended use limitations, preamble, or claim language that suggests or makes optional some structure or steps.
guidance: Check where the rejection sets forth whether patentable weight is (or is not) being given to particular claim language elements.

name: Characteristic: sets forth claim interpretation used (e.g., BRI) (103 characteristics)
description: The rejection sets forth a claim interpretation that points out how the examiner is interpreting the claim/term/phrase for purposes of the rejection (e.g., BRI, special definitions).
guidance: Check when the office action includes explicit claim interpretation relevant to the rejection.

name: Characteristic: included detailed technical analysis (103 characteristics)
description: The office action included detailed technical analysis regarding the invention and/or the applicability of the prior art.
guidance: Check where meaningful technical analysis supports why the prior art does (or does not) meet the claim limitations.

name: Characteristic: included appropriate suggestions to overcome rejections (103 characteristics)
description: The Office action included appropriate suggestions to overcome rejection(s) (not general FP language or mere indication of claims with allowable subject matter).
guidance: Check when the OA provides concrete, actionable suggestions for overcoming the rejection, not just boilerplate.

name: Were all the 35 U.S.C. 112(a) Enablement rejection(s) in compliance?
description: Determine whether each 112(a) enablement rejection properly identifies the claim(s), the statute, and is supported by sufficient evidence to support the conclusion of lack of enablement.
guidance: Answer Yes or No. Use statutory compliance standard and scenarios for assistance. If No, proceed to identify noncompliant claims and bases.

name: Identify claims with non-compliant 112(a) Enablement rejection(s)
description: List each claim discussed individually as a basis for the noncompliance and identify whether the noncompliance is directed to limitations introduced in independent claims, dependent claims, or both.
guidance: List each claim and indicate the claim type where the basis of noncompliance first appears in the claim tree (only one of independent/dependent/both). Include dependent claims that inherit the noncompliance.

name: Was another compliant 112(a) Enablement rejection applied? (112(a) Q3)
description: For claims identified as having a noncompliant 112(a) rejection, indicate whether another compliant 112(a) enablement rejection was applied to those claims.
guidance: If every listed claim also has another compliant basis, answer Yes; if even one does not, answer No. An individual claim may have multiple bases for rejection.

name: 112(a) basis: rejection based on scope of enablement (112(a) §4(b)(i))
description: The rejection was based on scope of enablement (examples include unclaimed essential subject matter and single means claims).
guidance: Examples: MPEP 2164.08(c), 2172.01 for unclaimed essential subject matter; MPEP 2164.08(a) for single means claims.

name: Additional Information/Feedback (112(a) enablement) — unreasonable claim interpretation (112(a) §5(c))
description: The non-compliance is the result of an unreasonable claim interpretation.
guidance: Check when claim construction used in the enablement analysis is unreasonable and is the root cause of noncompliance.

name: Additional Information/Feedback (112(a) enablement) — 112(f) related (112(a) §5(d))
description: The 112(a) rejection(s) is 112(f) related.
guidance: Indicate when the enablement rejection issue ties to 112(f) functional claim elements and corresponding structure/equivalents issues.

name: Characteristics of 112(a) Enablement rejection(s)
description: Checklist of characteristics that may be exemplified in enablement rejections (address claims individually, Wands analysis, claim interpretation, legal analysis, suggestions to overcome).
guidance: Check all applicable boxes. Presence of a characteristic indicates presence, not effectiveness. For example: addresses substantially all claims individually; provides citations to relevant portions of spec and a thorough Wands-factor discussion; sets forth claim interpretation; includes detailed legal analysis; includes appropriate suggestions to overcome rejections; or none of the above.

name: Were all the 35 U.S.C. 112(a) Written Description rejection(s) in compliance?
description: Determine whether each 112(a) written description rejection properly identifies the claim(s), the statute, and is supported by sufficient evidence to support the conclusion of lack of written description.
guidance: Answer Yes or No. Use statutory compliance standards and scenarios for assistance. If No, continue to identify noncompliant claims and provide reasoning.

name: Identify claims with non-compliant 112(a) Written Description rejection(s)
description: List each claim discussed individually as a basis for the written description noncompliance and indicate whether the noncompliance is directed to limitations introduced in independent claims, dependent claims, or both.
guidance: Determine the type of claim where the limitation first appears in the claim tree and check only one of independent/dependent/both. Include dependent claims that inherit the noncompliance; provide examples to illustrate.

name: 600 Parts, Form, and Content of Application
description: Parts, Form, and Content of Application
guidance: TOC entry — includes requirements for specification, claims, drawings, oath/declaration, and formalities.

name: 1500 Design Patents
description: Design Patents
guidance: TOC entry — guidance specific to design patent examination, claims, drawings, and requirements.

name: Patent must be for one invention only (claims allowed)
description: Every patent may be in the form in the First Schedule and shall be granted for one invention only, but may contain more than one claim; it shall not be competent in an action or other proceeding to object to a patent on the ground that it comprises more than one invention.
guidance: It may be hard to decide what constitutes 'one invention' vs more; the examiner is not required to report specially on this point but may report that the specification has not been prepared in the 'prescribed manner' if necessary. A claim is not necessary in a provisional specification (sect. 5(5)).

name: Patent description's practical purpose
description: The purpose of the description in the patent is not to disclose the commercially relevant technology, but to provide a context in which the legal limits of the claim acquire meaning.
guidance: Regulatory efforts should recognize that formal patent text serves legal delimitation more than tech transfer; forcing longer formal disclosures may not increase practical dissemination of know-how.

name: Timing of filing — wait for maturity
description: Whether an immature invention is provisionally protected by a caveat or not, it should not be made the subject of an application for a patent until it reaches maturity; an immature- based patent may be too weak or narrow and may weaken later patents on matured inventions.
guidance: Strategic guidance: delay filing until the invention is sufficiently mature to support broad and valuable claims.

name: Particularity in descriptions and claims as conditions precedent to validity
description: Particularity in descriptions and claims are conditions precedent to validity.
guidance: Specifications and claims must meet particularity requirements as a prerequisite for patent validity; be specific and particular in describing invention and claims.

name: Questions of sufficiency of particularity are questions of fact
description: Questions of sufficiency of particularity of descriptions and claims are questions of fact and not of law.
guidance: Factual inquiry (often jury or factfinder) determines whether particularity is sufficient; expect evidentiary presentation.

name: Claims to be construed in light of the descriptions
description: Claims are to be construed in the light of the descriptions (specification).
guidance: When interpreting claim language, courts will read claims in context of the specification to ascertain the invention's scope.

name: Construction of claims in light of prior state of same art
description: Claims are construed in the light of the prior state of the same art.
guidance: Prior art context informs claim scope — claim language interpreted against what was known in the relevant art.

name: Construction of functional claims
description: There are principles governing construction of functional claims (claims that define an invention by the function performed).
guidance: Functional claim construction requires careful analysis (text references present but detailed guidance may be elsewhere in the chapter).

name: Generic claims and specific claims
description: Distinction between generic claims and specific claims (heading present).
guidance: Choice between generic (broad) and specific (narrow) claim drafting has strategic and validity implications; see chapter for elaboration.

name: Proper liberality and breadth of construction
description: Proper liberality of construction and breadth of construction as governed by extent of use of the patent are principles for interpreting patent claims.
guidance: Courts should be reasonably liberal in construing claims but breadth will be limited by actual use, specification disclosure, and public notice considerations.

name: Construction in light of application papers and contemporaneous statutes
description: Claims and letters patent may be construed in the light of application papers and contemporaneous statutes; questions of construction are generally questions of law.
guidance: Use prosecution history and contemporaneous statutory context as interpretive aids; ultimate claim construction is a legal determination.

name: Automatic verification of goods and services lists in trademark examination
description: Implement automatic verification of goods and services lists during examination of the claimed mark, improving accuracy of automatic terminology checks and providing visual representations of verification results.
guidance: Integrate terminology checks and visualization to increase examiner efficiency and reduce classification/terminology errors.

name: Apply MPEP 2103-2106.07(c) combined eligibility analysis
description: The USPTO’s subject matter eligibility guidance, found in the Manual of Patent Examining Procedure (MPEP) sections 2103-2106.07(c), applies to all technologies, including AI inventions. The guidance combines the criteria for eligibility into a single analysis addressing statutory categories and judicial exceptions.
guidance: Use the MPEP framework to determine whether a claim falls within one of the four statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter) and whether it is directed to a judicial exception (abstract ideas, laws of nature, natural phenomena). Apply the combined/single analysis consistently to AI-related claims.

name: Step 2A, Prong One — does the claim recite an abstract idea?
description: Determine whether a claim recites an abstract idea as the first part of the Step 2A Alice/Mayo inquiry.
guidance: Identify whether claim limitations map to judicially-recognized abstract ideas (e.g., mathematical concepts, certain methods of organizing human activity, mental processes). If the claim recites an abstract idea, proceed to Prong Two; if not, eligibility can be found at this stage.

name: Distinguish 'involves' vs 'recites' an abstract idea
description: Differentiate between claims that merely involve an abstract idea and those that recite an abstract idea, because the latter require further eligibility analysis.
guidance: Claims that merely involve abstract ideas may be treated as per se eligible, whereas claims that recite the judicial exception must undergo the Alice/Mayo.Step 2A analysis. Drafting should aim to avoid language that causes a claim to be characterized as reciting an abstract idea when possible.

name: Recognize groupings of abstract ideas
description: Abstract ideas are grouped by the USPTO into mathematical concepts, certain methods of organizing human activity, and mental processes.
guidance: When analyzing claims, map limitations to these groupings to determine if an abstract idea is present (e.g., feature extraction/comparison may be a 'mental process' or 'mathematical concept'). Use this mapping to anticipate Step 2A outcomes.

name: Hardware-specific or physical-device claims are more likely eligible
description: Claims that recite specific hardware or physical structures (e.g., an ASIC with a particular neuronal array and synaptic circuits) can be found eligible as falling within a statutory category (machine) and not reciting a judicial exception.
guidance: Draft claims to include concrete physical components or device structures where appropriate; emphasize physical architecture to support eligibility at Step 1 and Prong One analyses.

name: Claims that improve computer or other technology support practical application
description: A key consideration for eligibility is whether the claim demonstrates an improvement in the functioning of a computer or another technology or technical field.
guidance: Show that the claimed invention provides a particular solution to a problem or a specific way to achieve a desired outcome (e.g., rule-based system improving animation processes). Emphasize technical improvements rather than abstract goals.

name: Avoid claiming merely the use of a generic computer or generic ML model
description: Claims that simply instruct to apply an abstract idea using a generic computer component or a generic machine learning model are often ineligible.
guidance: The guidance cites examples where methods that rely on a generic machine learning model to perform an abstract process were found ineligible as 'mere instructions to apply the exception using a generic computer component.' To avoid this anti-pattern, include technical specifics about implementation, structure, or training.

name: Add specific technical details (structure, training, implementation) to support eligibility
description: Adding claim limitations that recite specific architectures, training techniques, data discretization methods, or implementation details can transform an otherwise ineligible claim into an eligible one.
guidance: Examples show that claims which recite a particular manner of training/using a neural network, a particular neural network architecture, or specific implementation details were found to integrate the abstract idea into a practical application. Include such specifics in claims and specification where possible.

name: Use 'meaningful limits' in claim scope (practical/particular limits)
description: Claims that include meaningful, particular limits (e.g., a recited specific compound in a treatment) are more likely to be viewed as practical applications rather than abstract ideas.
guidance: When appropriate, narrow claims by reciting particular compounds, steps, or contextual limits that tie the claim to a concrete application or improvement in technology.

name: Focus claim drafting on specific solutions, not abstract ideas
description: Claims should describe a particular solution or a specific way to achieve the desired outcome rather than broadly claiming the idea of the solution.
guidance: Emphasize actionable technical steps, device features, or trained-model particulars that show how the invention achieves the result. Avoid high-level goal language that merely states an objective.

name: Document technological improvements in the specification
description: The specification should clearly describe how the claimed invention improves existing technological processes to support a practical application finding.
guidance: Explicitly describe technical advantages, improvements to computer functionality or other technology, and concrete implementation details in the written description to help overcome eligibility rejections.

name: Method of invention creation (use of AI) is not relevant to subject matter eligibility
description: Whether AI was used to create the invention is not considered in the subject matter eligibility analysis; the guidance focuses on claim language and technical content.
guidance: Do not rely on or argue eligibility based on the fact that AI assisted in conception; instead, ground eligibility arguments in claim limitations and technical improvements recited in the claim and specification.

name: Leverage USPTO examples and monitor case law
description: Use the USPTO’s new eligibility examples (Examples 47–49) and prior examples to frame claims and prosecution strategies, and stay current with Federal Circuit decisions interpreting eligibility.
guidance: Study the provided examples (e.g., ASIC for ANN, discretization and ANN anomaly detection, speech signal processing, personalized medical treatment examples) to model claim drafting and anticipate examiner analysis; keep abreast of court decisions for evolving interpretations.

name: Written description: inventor must show 'possession' as of filing
description: The specification must demonstrate that the inventor was 'in possession' of the claimed invention as of the filing date; a genus can be disclosed either by a representative number of species or by structural features common to the genus so a skilled person can 'visualize or recognize' members of the genus (Ariad standard).
guidance: In life sciences, this is demanding where genera encompass vast numbers of compounds. Case examples include AbbVie (invalidated despite >300 antibodies) and Juno (invalidated with two embodiments). Use the Ariad two-prong approach when evaluating whether the specification shows possession. If the specification lacks representative species or common structural features, written-description support is at risk.

name: Genus disclosure can be supplemented by background knowledge when genus is well-known
description: Where a genus is 'already well explored' and techniques for producing the relevant functionality are 'well known,' the specification can be read in light of the background knowledge in the art to find a representative number of species—particularly where the well-known techniques are not the core invention (Ajinomoto / In re Herschler / In re Fuetterer principle).
guidance: Apply when the claimed invention is the use of a known genus rather than the genus itself. Courts will consider prior-art disclosures and common general knowledge to supply the missing species/teachings. Key conditions: (1) genus well explored in the art; (2) techniques to produce the claimed functionality are well known and routine; (3) those techniques are not the inventive aspect. Cite supportive precedent (Ajinomoto, Herschler, Fuetterer, Erfindergemeinschaft).

name: Enablement: teach making and using the full claimed scope without undue experimentation
description: The specification must teach persons of ordinary skill how to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation, and enablement must be commensurate with the scope of the claim (Amgen principle).
guidance: For genus claims this usually requires sufficient guidance to make and use the entire class. Where making or screening members would require extensive time, effort, or expense (undue experimentation), enablement may fail (see Amgen, Baxalta, Idenix). Evaluate the quantity and quality of examples, protocols, and predictive guidance in the specification against the likely burden on a skilled artisan.

name: Claim scope (functional/use-limited vs. full-genus-for-any-purpose) affects enablement rigor
description: Claims directed to a specific therapeutic use (method-of-use) are narrower in functional scope than claims that claim an entire genus for any and all purposes; narrower functional limits can reduce the enablement burden.
guidance: Teva distinguishes method-of-use claims (only humanized anti-CGRP antibodies to treat headache) from broad composition claims covering an entire genus for all uses. If the claimed function is limited and evidence indicates all members of the genus achieve that function, a practitioner may not need to enable making every genus member for every purpose. When drafting, emphasize functional limits to reduce enablement exposure; when litigating, argue (or challenge) whether the functional limitation truly narrows the inventive scope.

name: Evidence that all genus members perform the claimed function
description: Enablement/written-description support can be met if specification data and testimony permit a reasonable factfinder to conclude that all members of the claimed genus perform the claimed therapeutic function.
guidance: Courts will look to experimental data in the specification, expert testimony, prior-art teachings, and admissions (including opposing party statements in IPR/prosecution) to determine whether a skilled artisan would understand the entire genus is effective for the claimed use. Absent such evidence, enablement and possession may fail; affirmative experimental showing in the spec strengthens validity.

name: Anti-pattern: no disclosed compounds or lack of knowledge in the art undermines written description
description: If the patent discloses no compounds that could be used in the claimed methods and there is no evidence such compounds were known, written-description support is weak or absent (University of Rochester / Ariad caution).
guidance: Avoid claiming methods that require compounds not illustrated or otherwise supported by the specification or the common general knowledge. If the specification provides no enabling examples or the art does not establish that such compounds were known, courts have invalidated claims for lack of written description.

name: Routine/established techniques cited in specification help both written description and enablement
description: Explicitly stating that members 'may be made by any method known in the art' and citing established prior-art methods for producing the claimed compounds can support both possession and enablement when those techniques are routine.
guidance: Draft specifications to reference routine methods and include procedural detail or citations to standard protocols. The court in Teva relied on explicit disclosure of humanization methods and the routine nature of humanization; where techniques are truly routine, less experimental work may be required to practice the claim.

name: Practical drafting and litigation strategy for life-sciences method-of-use/genus claims
description: Practitioners should tailor claim drafting, specification disclosure, and litigation arguments to the framework distinguishing novel genera from uses of well-known genera — e.g., emphasize use-limited claims, include representative examples and data, disclose routine methods, and document the state of the art.
guidance: When drafting: (a) include at least one representative example with data; (b) disclose routine methods and cite prior art; (c) consider claiming the method/use rather than the full genus for broad protection while reducing enablement risk. When defending: marshal specification data, expert testimony, and prior-art evidence showing genus well-known and techniques routine. When attacking: show insufficiency of representative examples, lack of background knowledge, or undue experimentation required to practice full scope.

name: Claim construction standard in IPRs — BRI (Cuozzo)
description: The Supreme Court upheld the USPTO's regulation requiring the PTAB to apply the Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) standard in IPR proceedings.
guidance: BRI affects how claims are interpreted in AIA proceedings and impacts institution/outcome strategy for parties.

name: Enablement limits on functional claiming (Amgen)
description: Functional claims to antibodies based on what they bind to can be invalid under 35 U.S.C. § 112 for lack of enablement if undue experimentation is required to make and use the full scope.
guidance: Functional/means/way claiming can be vulnerable to enablement attacks; applicants should provide sufficient disclosure to avoid undue experimentation.

name: Scope of assignor estoppel (Minerva)
description: Assignor estoppel prohibits inventors from challenging their patents after assignment, but its scope is limited to situations where the assignor's invalidity claim contradicts explicit or implicit representations made in the assignment.
guidance: Assignor estoppel does not apply in certain situations (e.g., claims to future inventions, legal developments rendering representations irrelevant, or claim changes post-assignment); parties should analyze estoppel carefully.

name: Continuation application as an alternative
description: Filing a continuation application creates a new application with potentially new claims and a new examination instead of an RCE.
guidance: Consider continuation when you want to pursue different claim scope or strategies while preserving the parent priority date; continuations involve fresh examination and can be strategic for claim portfolio management.

name: Statutory cause of action under 26 U.S.C. § 7431(a)(1)
description: "If any officer or employee of the United States knowingly, or by reason of negligence, discloses any return or return information with respect to a taxpayer in violation of any provision of section 6103, such taxpayer may bring a civil action for damages against the United States in a district court..."
guidance: To state a claim the plaintiff must show (1) disclosure of 'return' or 'return information'; and (2) that the disclosure was in violation of §6103; and (3) that the disclosure was made knowingly or by reason of negligence. The petition emphasizes that §7431(a) makes disclosure wrongful if 'knowingly or negligently' made and that a plaintiff need only plead the elements of the statutory claim (Hrubec v. Amtrak).

name: 37 CFR 1.132 — affidavits/declarations traversing rejections
description: When a claim is rejected or objected to, any evidence submitted to traverse the rejection on a basis not otherwise provided for must be by oath or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132.
guidance: Primary examiner is responsible to review and decide whether 1.132 submissions are responsive and present sufficient facts to overcome the rejection. This rule serves as general policy for affidavit evidence traversing rejections not covered by other specific rules.

name: Form paragraph 7.66 (insufficient to overcome rejection)
description: Template: 'The [affidavit/declaration] under 37 CFR 1.132 filed [date] is insufficient to overcome the rejection of claim [#] based upon [statutory grounds] as set forth in the last Office action because:' followed by specific reasons.
guidance: After the template, set forth detailed reasons for insufficiency (e.g., untimely, fails to set forth facts, facts not germane, not commensurate with claim scope). Include detailed explanation and appropriate sub-form paragraphs (7.66.01–7.66.05) as needed.

name: 7.66.03 — Refers only to invention, not claims (insufficient)
description: Affidavit refers only to the system described in an application and not to the individual claims, failing to show that objective evidence is commensurate in scope with the claims.
guidance: An affidavit must tie objective evidence to the claim scope; if it does not, it is insufficient. Provide full explanation when invoking this reason.

name: Design patent specification arrangement
description: The following order or arrangement should be observed in framing a design patent specification: (1) Preamble stating name of the applicant, title of the design, and a brief description of the nature and intended use of the article; (2) Cross-reference to related applications; (3) Statement regarding federally sponsored research or development; (4) Description of the figure or figures of the drawing; (5) Feature description; (6) A single claim.
guidance: Do not use this form paragraph in an international design application.

name: Special status for environmental-quality inventions
description: The USPTO will accord "special" status to patent applications for inventions which materially enhance the quality of the environment by contributing to the restoration or maintenance of air, water, and soil.
guidance: Petition under 37 CFR 1.102 must state that special status is sought because the invention materially enhances environmental quality; no fee required. If the disclosure is not clear on its face, the petition must be accompanied by a statement under 37 CFR 1.102 explaining how the materiality standard is met. Materiality cannot be mere speculation about hypothetical end-user applications nor be satisfied by a minor aspect of the claim.

name: Special status for energy-related inventions
description: The USPTO will accord "special" status to patent applications for inventions which materially contribute to (A) discovery/development of energy resources or (B) more efficient utilization and conservation of energy resources.
guidance: Examples for (A) include fossil fuels, hydrogen, nuclear, solar; (B) includes inventions reducing energy consumption in combustion systems, industrial equipment, household appliances. Petition under 37 CFR 1.102 must state how the invention materially contributes to category (A) or (B); no fee required. If not clear on the face, petition must include a statement under 37 CFR 1.102 explaining how materiality is met. Materiality cannot be speculative or rely on minor aspects of the claimed invention.

name: Special status for inventions countering terrorism
description: USPTO will accord "special" status to patent applications for inventions which materially contribute to countering terrorism.
guidance: Petition under 37 CFR 1.102 must state that special status is sought because the invention materially contributes to countering terrorism; no fee required. If the application disclosure is not clear, petition must include a statement under 37 CFR 1.102 explaining materiality. Materiality does not permit speculation about hypothetical end-user application nor reliance on minor aspects of the claimed invention. Examples of technologies may include detecting/identifying explosives, aircraft sensors/security systems, vehicular barricades/disabling systems.

name: Single-invention requirement and election without traverse (I(F))
description: The claims must be directed to a single invention. If USPTO determines claims are not directed to a single invention, applicant must make an election without traverse in a telephonic interview; petition must include statement agreeing to such election.
guidance: If applicant refuses to elect without traverse, petition will be denied; telephone restriction practice will be followed; election may be made at time of filing petition.

name: Preexamination search requirements (I(H))
description: At filing applicant must provide a statement that a preexamination search was conducted, identifying field of search by U.S. class/subclass and date; for database searches include search logic/chemical structure/sequence used, file name(s), database service, and date.
guidance: Search must involve U.S. patents and patent application publications, foreign patent documents, and non-patent literature unless applicant justifies with reasonable certainty that no more pertinent references would be found in an eliminated source. Search must be directed to the claimed invention, encompass all claim features (broadest reasonable interpretation), and also encompass disclosed features that may be claimed. A foreign patent office search report will not satisfy this requirement unless it meets the preexamination search requirements. Statements supporting the petition must be made in good faith (see 37 CFR 1.56 and 10.18).

name: Accelerated examination support document requirements (I(I) items 1–6)
description: At filing applicant must provide an accelerated examination support document (AESD) that: (1) includes an IDS compliant with 37 CFR 1.98 citing each reference deemed most closely related to subject matter of each claim; (2) for each cited reference, identifies all claim limitations disclosed by the reference and where disclosed; (3) includes a detailed explanation of how each claim is patentable over cited references with the particularity required by 37 CFR 1.111(b) and (c); (4) includes a concise statement of utility of the invention as defined in each independent claim (unless design application); (5) shows where each claim limitation finds support under first paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112 in the written description (and in any priority applications); and (6) identifies any cited references that may be disqualified as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 103(c).
guidance: An AESD that fails to encompass amended/new claims will render those amendments not fully responsive and not entered. IDS filed with an updated AESD must comply with 37 CFR 1.97 and 1.98.

name: Initial examiner action timing and interview-first practice (III)
description: Once granted special status the application will be docketed and taken up expeditiously (e.g., within two weeks). If an examiner determines an issue must be addressed, the examiner will telephone the applicant to discuss amendments/submissions prior to issuing an Office action. The USPTO will not issue an Office action (other than notice of allowance) unless: (A) an interview was conducted but did not result in allowance, or (B) a determination is made that an interview is unlikely to result in allowance. Prior to mailing any Office action rejecting claims, the USPTO will conduct a conference to review the rejections.
guidance: Telephone restriction practice applies if claims not to single invention; applicant must make election without traverse in telephonic interview. If an Office action other than allowance or final is mailed, it will set a shortened statutory period of one month (30 days or longer) with no extensions; failure to timely reply results in abandonment.

name: Reply limitations and amendment entry rules (IV)
description: A reply to an Office action must be limited to the rejections, objections, and requirements made. Any amendment that would (A) add claims resulting in more than three independent claims or more than twenty total claims; (B) present claims not encompassed by the preexamination search or an updated AESD; or (C) present claims directed to a non-elected invention or an invention other than previously claimed will be treated as not fully responsive and will not be entered.
guidance: For any amendment to claims not encompassed by the AESD, applicant must provide an updated AESD that encompasses the amended/new claims at time of filing; failure to do so causes the amendment to be not entered. All replies/papers must be filed electronically via EFS-Web; if not, final disposition may occur later than 12 months.

name: Definition of Final Rejection (37 C.F.R. § 1.113)
description: “On the second or any subsequent examination or consideration by the examiner the rejection or other action may be made final, whereupon applicants' reply is limited to appeal in the case of rejection of any claim (§ 1.191), or to amendment as specified in § 1.114 or § 1.116. ... In making such final rejection, the examiner shall repeat or state all grounds of rejection then considered applicable to the claims in the application, clearly stating the reasons in support thereof.”
guidance: Finality limits applicant responses (appeal or limited amendments). Examiner must state and repeat grounds and reasons; applicant replies must comply with §1.114 or §1.116 or appeal. Use this regulatory text to identify when an Office Action is truly final and what reply options remain.

name: Purpose and proper use of Final Rejection
description: The Patent Office introduced the final rejection to conclude prosecution as quickly as possible and discourages switching subject matter in successive amendments or switching between disparate sets of references in successive actions.
guidance: Interpret final rejections as an efficiency tool; applicants should aim to present comprehensive claims and responses in the first Action to avoid unnecessary switching of issues that invite finality. When drafting initial responses, aim to address and avoid all grounds of rejection to limit risk of final rejection.

name: Available responses to a Final Action (five paths)
description: To respond to a final Action an applicant may: (1) file a 'response after final' to argue for allowance without amending claims; (2) file an 'amendment and response after final under 37 C.F.R. § 1.116'; (3) re-file as a continuation application under 37 C.F.R. § 1.53; (4) appeal to the Board under 37 C.F.R. § 1.191; or (5) abandon the application.
guidance: Consider and weigh these mutually exclusive/alternative routes based on the facts: closeness to allowance, desire to avoid narrowing (estoppel), cost/time tradeoffs, and the presence of allowed or objected claims.

name: Handling claims that are objected-to or allowed in a Final Action
description: Objected-to claims contain allowable subject matter plus formality; rewriting an objected claim in independent format (inserting limitations and removing dependency) will generally overcome the objection; if allowed claims are of sufficient breadth applicant may pay issue fees to obtain an earlier patent, or pursue rejected claims in a continuation.
guidance: Decide whether to take immediate allowance (cost/benefit: issue and maintenance fees, presence of infringers, breadth of coverage) or to continue prosecution for broader protection. Cancel rejected claims without prejudice and pursue them in a continuation if appropriate.

name: Appeal eligibility and timing (35 U.S.C. §134 / 37 C.F.R. §1.191)
description: An applicant may appeal any claim in a pending application that has been twice rejected. The applicant must file a timely Notice of Appeal within three months (extensions up to six months with fees are available) and pay the separate appeal fee.
guidance: Appeal is an option when prosecution has stalled and narrowing is undesirable; weigh the time and expense against RCE/continuation strategies. Ensure the timeliness of Notice of Appeal and payment of required fees.

name: Appeal Brief formal content and argument requirements (37 C.F.R. §1.192)
description: An Appeal Brief must include specified items in order (real party in interest; related appeals; status of claims; status of amendments; summary of invention; issues; grouping of claims; argument; appendix). In 'grouping of claims' appellant must group claims that stand or fall together; in 'argument' appellant must provide factual and legal bases with citations.
guidance: Strictly follow formal requirements; group claims thoughtfully to allow a representative claim to be decided; provide legal authority and specific arguments (do not rely solely on familiar prosecution-style arguments). Noncompliance may lead to rejection of the brief and dismissal.

name: Board decision outcomes and post-decision options
description: The Board may affirm, reverse, remand, or take other actions. If reversed, the case is forwarded to the examiner for action and the examiner is discouraged from doing a new search; if affirmed, applicant may abandon, continue prosecution via continuation, petition for rehearing, seek a civil action under 35 U.S.C. §145, or appeal to the Federal Circuit.
guidance: Anticipate possible outcomes and plan next steps (e.g., obtain narrower immediate protection while pursuing broader claims by continuation and appeal). Consider timing and cost of further appeals or civil actions.

name: Abandonment as a deliberate option
description: An applicant may explicitly abandon the application under 37 C.F.R. § 1.138 or allow it to lapse by failing to reply within statutory periods (three-month shortened period plus three-month extension up to six months).
guidance: Use abandonment when the invention is not worth further prosecution (e.g., unpatentable over cited references, narrow little-value claims, or cost reasons). Be mindful of deadlines to avoid inadvertent abandonment.

name: Strategy considerations in choosing a post-final course
