description: Evaluate whether examiner understands the invention and cited references (consider interview), whether narrowing will be acceptable, whether an RCE is cost-effective if close to agreement, and whether an appeal is appropriate after all reasonable amendments are exhausted.
guidance: Use interviews to clear misunderstandings; prefer RCE when close to agreement; pursue appeal only after exhausting reasonable amendments and considering cost/time tradeoffs; consider continuation to obtain some protection quickly while pursuing broader claims.

name: Techniques to avoid a Final Rejection
description: Advanced planning can help avoid final rejections: include independent claims of varying scope (broad and narrow) at filing, conduct prior art searches pre-filing, and when submitting newly identified prior art in an IDS consider amending pending claims to avoid anticipation.
guidance: Draft initial claim sets with fallback scopes and perform good pre-filing searches. Use timely IDS and claim drafting to minimize likelihood of a second-action final rejection.

name: Examiner reasons for allowance and cautions (post-allowance statements)
description: If the record does not make clear the reasons for allowing a claim, the examiner should provide specific reasons for allowance; each statement should include at least (1) the major difference in the claims not found in the prior art of record, and (2) why the claim is considered patentable over the prior art if not clear in the record. Care must be taken to ensure statements are accurate and not unduly broad or narrow due to possible estoppel effects.
guidance: Carefully review any examiner reasons for allowance because statements become part of file history and may create estoppel; if disagree, submit remarks before or with payment of the issue fee to clarify the prosecution record.

name: Amendments after Notice of Allowance (37 C.F.R. § 1.312) — limits and entry criteria
description: No amendment may be made as a matter of right after mailing of a Notice of Allowance. Any amendment must be filed before or with payment of the issue fee and may be entered on recommendation of the primary examiner and approval by the Commissioner. Examiners may enter only formal corrections or formal claim matter changes that do not change claim scope; substantive amendments require justification and may be refused.
guidance: Avoid needing post-allowance amendments by being diligent earlier in prosecution. If substantive change is necessary before issue, include required remarks explaining why the amendment is needed and why no additional search or examination is required.

name: Required showing for substantive post-allowance amendments (MPEP § 716.14)
description: For substantive amendments after allowance applicant must fully and clearly state reasons showing (1) why the amendment is needed; (2) why the proposed amended or new claims require no additional search or examination; (3) why the claims are patentable; and (4) why they were not presented earlier.
guidance: Provide comprehensive remarks addressing each required element. Failure to do so may result in refusal to enter the amendment. Ensure amendments do not materially change disclosure or require substantial PTO work.

name: Inventive step: disregard features not contributing to technical solution
description: Features that do not contribute to the solution of a technical problem generally do not affect the assessment of inventive step of an invention, even if written into the claims.
guidance: Applicants should (1) challenge examiner's identified technical problem if inappropriate, (2) rely on specification disclosures or submit experimental data to rebut the examiner, and (3) ensure specifications clearly explain relationship between each technical feature and the technical effects achieved. Revision may increase rejections where applicants add non-contributing features to claims.

name: Addition of examination criteria and illustrative examples for AI-related inventions
description: Expanded examination standards and illustrative examples for AI, big data, etc., including clarifications on scope (title change), examination principles, public order and morality, inventiveness, and implementability; follows approaches in CNIPA 2024 Trial Guidelines for AI-related inventions.
guidance: Key points included: (1) examine claims (and where necessary specifications); (2) new public_order_and_morality criteria under Article 5(1) — inventions that in data collection/tagging/recommendation/decision-making violate law, public order, morality, or harm public interest are not patentable; (3) illustrative morality examples (facial recognition for marketing; autonomous vehicle model using gender/age for collision choice) showing rejection; (4) added illustrative examples for inventive step in AI contexts (application-scenario-only differences usually lack inventiveness; substantive algorithm/model modifications that achieve technical effects may support inventiveness); (5) implementability/disclosure expectations for AI models (must describe necessary modules, model hierarchy/connections, training steps and parameters, integration with application domain, input/output data settings) to address “black box” concerns.

name: Examination criteria for inventions involving bitstreams
description: New Section: claims directed merely to a simple bitstream, or where substantially all content other than the subject matter refers solely to a simple bitstream, are considered "rules and methods for intellectual activities" and not patentable; however, video encoding/decoding methods that generate a specific bitstream, storage/transmission methods for such bitstream, and computer-readable media storing programs to generate the bitstream may be patentable.
guidance: Requirements include: (1) for implementability, the specification must describe the specific encoding/decoding method clearly and completely so a skilled person can implement it; (2) claim drafting guidance: claims may be method, apparatus, and computer-readable storage medium claims and should generally be drafted referencing the specific video encoding method (examples of acceptable claim formats provided).

name: Chemical and mathematical formulas/tables allowed but no drawings/flow diagrams in specification
description: The specification, including the claims, may contain chemical and mathematical formulae, but shall not contain drawings or flow diagrams. The description may contain tables, but the same tables should not be included in both the drawings and the description portion of the specification. Claims may contain tables if necessary to conform to 35 U.S.C. 112 or otherwise desirable.
guidance: If descriptive illustrations such as graphs or flowcharts appear in the descriptive portion, examiners should object and request drawings under 37 CFR 1.81.

name: Page numbering, line spacing, and font size/character requirements
description: Pages of the specification including claims and abstract must be numbered consecutively starting with 1, numbers centrally located above or preferably below the text. Lines of the specification and any amendments must be 1 1/2 or double spaced. Text must be in a nonscript type font (e.g., Arial, Times Roman, Courier), preferably 12 pt, with capital letters at least 0.3175 cm (0.125 in) high but no smaller than 0.21 cm (0.08 in); text may not be written solely in capital letters.
guidance: These formatting conventions ensure legibility and consistent reproduction; follow them to avoid objections and needs for substitute papers.

name: One-sided pages and separate sheets for application parts
description: All application papers must be plainly written on only one side of a sheet. The specification must commence on a separate sheet; each sheet including part of the specification may not include other parts of the application. Claims, abstract, and Sequence Listing (if on paper or as PDF image) should not be included on a sheet with other parts; claims must commence on separate sheet or electronic page and not contain other parts; abstract must commence on a separate sheet.
guidance: Keep each application component on separate sheets/pages to conform with 37 CFR requirements and enable proper processing and publication.

name: Non-English language application translation requirements
description: Nonprovisional application filed in a language other than English requires an English translation, a statement that the translation is accurate, and the processing fee set in § 1.17(i) (if not filed with the application the Office will notify and give time to file). Provisional applications filed in another language do not require an English translation for the provisional itself, but a translation and statement must be submitted if claiming benefit in a later nonprovisional per § 1.78(a).
guidance: Translations must be literal and accompanied by a statement of accuracy and a signed request to use the translation for examination. If idiomatic changes are needed, a preliminary amendment may be filed provided no new matter is introduced. Failure to timely file translation and statements will result in abandonment of the nonprovisional application or loss of the benefit claim.

name: Infirmity of proof inquiry (Selling element (ii) / §11.24(d)(1)(ii))
description: Whether there was such an infirmity of proof establishing the conduct as to give rise to the clear conviction that the Office could not, consistently with its duty, accept the state's conclusion.
guidance: This is a difficult showing. Deference is given to the state factfinder; credibility determinations generally receive deference. Mere disagreement with findings, claims of evidentiary errors, or complaints about weight of evidence do not ordinarily establish infirmity of proof. Respondent must show an infirmity so substantial that accepting the state sanction would be inconsistent with the USPTO's duty.

name: Form paragraph usage limitation when new ground of rejection introduced
description: This form paragraph should not be used, and a final rejection is improper, where there is another new ground of rejection introduced by the examiner that was not necessitated by amendment to the claims nor based on information submitted in an information disclosure statement filed during the period set forth in 37 CFR 1.97(c) with the fee set forth in 37 CFR 1.17(p).
guidance: Do not make a final rejection using the form paragraph if the examiner introduces a new ground of rejection that is not a consequence of applicant amendment or an IDS timely filed with the appropriate fee. (Original wording preserved.)

name: Conditions for making first action final in a continuing or substitute application
description: For a new application, claims may be finally rejected in the first Office action when (A) the new application is a continuing application of, or a substitute for, an earlier application, and (B) all claims of the new application (1) are identical to, patentably indistinct from, or have unity of invention with, the claims in the earlier application ... and (2) would have been properly finally rejected on the grounds and art of record in the next Office action if they had been entered in the earlier application.
guidance: Both prongs A and B must be met to make a first-action final in a continuation/substitute file. This prevents improper finality where claims or context changed such that earlier prosecution would not have supported final rejection.

name: Transitional after-final practice under 37 CFR 1.129(a) — eligibility and effect
description: An applicant in an application ... that has been pending for at least two years as of June 8, 1995 ... is entitled to have a first submission entered and considered on the merits after final rejection ... if the first submission and the fee set forth in § 1.17(r) are filed prior to the filing of an appeal brief and prior to abandonment of the application. The finality of the final rejection is automatically withdrawn upon the timely filing of the submission and payment of the fee set forth in § 1.17(r).
guidance: Submission includes IDS, amendment to specification/claims/drawings, new substantive argument, or new evidence; no amendment resulting from payment of fee may introduce new matter (35 U.S.C. 132). The transitional after-final practice applies only to applications filed on or before June 8, 1995 (and other date-specific requirements described). Use form paragraph 7.41.01.fti to notify applicant of eligibility.

name: Regulations — detailed formal requirements for international applications (Table of Contents)
description: The Regulations (Table of Contents) include Rules on: The Request (Form and Contents); The Description; The Claims; The Drawings; The Abstract; Expressions, etc., not to be used; Terminology and Signs; Physical Requirements of the International Application; Language of the International Application and Translations for the Purposes of International Search and International Publication; Submission by the Applicant of Documents Relating to Earlier Search; Unity of Invention; Inventions Relating to Biological Material; Nucleotide and/or Amino Acid Sequence Listings; The Transmittal Fee; The International Filing Fee; The Search Fee; Extension of Time Limits for Payment of Fees; The Priority Document; The Applicant; The Competent Receiving Office; International Filing Date; Preparation of Copies; Transmittal of the Record Copy and Translation; Transmittal of the Search Copy, Translation and Sequence Listing; Receipt of the Record Copy by the International Bureau; Receipt of the Search Copy by the International Searching Authority; Checking by, and Correcting before, the Receiving Office of Certain Elements of the International Application; Correction or Addition of Priority Claim; Correction or Addition of Declarations, Indications, etc.
guidance: Regulations provide comprehensive procedural and form requirements for international applications (see enumerated Rule headings). The Table of Contents itself signals the breadth of formal and content requirements applicants and Offices must follow.

name: Required contents of initial application
description: A duly accomplished request containing the name and address of the applicant or, where the applicant is not the designer, a statement indicating the origin of the right to the industrial design, and an indication of the kind of article of manufacture to which the design shall be applied; a description containing title, applicant name, brief description of views, statement of characteristic feature (if any), and a claim; drawings of different views showing the complete appearance including the applicant's signature; payment of required fees at filing; appointment of agent if applicant is not a resident of the Philippines.
guidance: Lists specific elements (request, description items 1–5, drawings, fees, agent appointment) that must be present for an application to be accepted.

name: Special form and order of description
description: The description must contain, in order: (a) Title of the design; (b) Name of Applicant with first name, middle initial, last name (if natural person); (c) Detailed description of the different views/figures of the drawings; (d) Statement of characteristic features, if any; and (e) Claim.
guidance: The description must follow the prescribed order and include the listed elements.

name: Claim wording and number
description: The claim shall be in formal terms of the ornamental design using the terms: '(specifying name) substantially as shown and described' or '(specifying name) substantially as shown'. More than one claim is neither required nor permitted.
guidance: Only a single claim permitted; use the specified phrasing.

name: Use of broken lines in drawings
description: Unclaimed environmental structure may be shown only in broken lines when necessary; broken lines should not obscure or confuse the claimed design and should not be heavier than lines depicting the claimed design. If broken lines intrude upon the claimed design they should be shown in a separate figure.
guidance: Use broken lines sparingly and in compliance to avoid confusing the claimed subject matter.

name: Filing date elements for industrial design
description: The filing date shall be the date on which the Office received in English or Filipino: (a) a request indicating registration is sought; (b) description; (c) a single claim; (d) a representation of the article or pictorial representation; (e) payment of required fees at filing; (f) appointment of agent if applicant is non-resident.
guidance: All listed elements must be present to accord a filing date.

name: Margins and page numbering
description: Margins must be: Top 2–4 cm, Left 2.5–4 cm, Right 2–3 cm, Bottom 2–3 cm. Margins must be blank without unnecessary text. Pages of abstract, description and claims shall be numbered consecutively with Arabic numerals appearing in the central portion of either top or bottom margins.
guidance: Follow precise margin and page numbering specs to avoid formality objections.

name: Plants or animals patentable when not confined to a particular variety
description: Plants or animals are patentable provided that the technical feasibility of the invention is not confined to a particular plant or animal variety.
guidance: A claim that does not individually claim specific plant varieties is not excluded even though it may embrace plant varieties; subject-matter of a claim covering but not identifying plant varieties is not a claim to a variety or varieties.

name: Claim covering plant varieties without identification is not a variety claim
description: A claim wherein specific plant varieties are not individually claimed is not excluded from patentability even though it may embrace plant varieties.
guidance: In the absence of identification of a specific plant variety in a product claim, the claimed subject-matter is neither limited nor directed to a variety or varieties.

name: Products of microbiological processes may be patented per se
description: The product of a microbiological process may also be patentable per se (product claim). Propagation of the microorganism itself is to be construed as a microbiological process; consequently the microorganism can be protected per se as a product obtained by a microbiological process.
guidance: The term microorganism includes bacteria, plasmids, viruses, unicellular fungi (including yeasts), algae, protozoa and human/animal/plant cells. However, product claims for plant or animal varieties cannot be allowed even if produced by a microbiological process.

name: Diagnostic method definition (four phases)
description: To determine whether a claim is directed to a diagnostic method it must include method steps relating to all of the following phases: (i) the examination phase (collection of data); (ii) comparison of data with standard values; (iii) finding of any significant deviation (a symptom); (iv) attribution of the deviation to a particular clinical picture (deductive medical/veterinary decision phase).
guidance: If any of these essential phases are missing and are essential for the invention, they must be included in the independent claim. Some steps (e.g. comparison implying finding) may be implicit; phase (iv) is normally an intellectual exercise and not technical unless a device reaches diagnostic conclusions.

name: Search fields — patent text (abstract, claims, title, document text)
description: Text fields include AB (abstract), AAB (alerting abstract), DAB (documentation/extended abstract), CLM (claims), TI (title), TX (all fields + text), and others.
guidance: Claims are the legal text describing the patent. Use field codes to target specific text fields; e.g., TI searches both Derwent and original titles. About 88% of records have Alerting abstracts; some pre-1970 or certain countries may not have abstracts.

name: Alice two-step eligibility discipline
description: Step 1: Is the claim directed to an abstract idea? Step 2: Does the claim recite an 'inventive concept' that amounts to significantly more?
guidance: You cannot avoid Step 1 by clever drafting. You can win Step 2 by tying the claim to a specific technical improvement. Treat the Alice two-step as a drafting discipline rather than an unpredictable doctrine.

name: Anchor the claim in a technical problem
description: The opening of your specification should describe a technical problem in the operation of a computer (latency, memory footprint, packet loss, indexing inefficiency, security vulnerability). Not a business problem. Not 'users find it hard to...'. A computer problem.
guidance: Explicitly frame the invention as solving technical/computer-operational issues. Use concrete problems (e.g., latency, memory footprint) rather than user/business-facing descriptions to support §101 arguments and examiner citation.

name: Avoid pure result-oriented language
description: Avoid claiming only the result (e.g., 'A method for predicting customer churn' is suspect).
guidance: Prefer phrasing that recites how the result is achieved: e.g., 'A method for predicting customer churn comprising training a gradient-boosted decision tree on a feature set including session timing residuals...' The closer the claim stays to the result only, the closer it is to an abstract idea.

name: Include a hardware-tied embodiment
description: Even if the invention is fundamentally algorithmic, include at least one claim that recites concrete hardware: a specific sensor, a specific accelerator, a particular memory architecture.
guidance: Use a machine-tied claim to invoke the 'machine prong' rhetorically (historic Bilski test). Concrete hardware elements can help resist §101 rejections and show claimed subject matter affects machine functioning.

name: Write the §101 argument into the specification (Technical Improvements paragraph)
description: Before the detailed description, include a paragraph titled 'Technical Improvements' that explicitly catalogs how the claimed system improves the functioning of a computer (e.g., 'reduces query latency by 40%,' 'eliminates the need for a roundtrip to the database server').
guidance: Examiners and judges quote these paragraphs. Explicitly state measurable/technical improvements to support Step 2 inventive-concept arguments and to make it easier for examiners/judges to find technical significance.

name: Avoid 'black box' claims; disclose sufficient architecture
description: A claim that recites 'a model trained to...' without describing the architecture invites both §101 (abstract idea) and §112 (enablement) rejections.
guidance: Recite enough of the model architecture and implementation detail that a skilled person could implement it. Provide architecture, training procedure, storage details, and hardware context to reduce risk of 101/112 rejections.

name: Complete Application (601.01)
description: Complete Application / Content of Provisional and Nonprovisional Applications (601).
guidance: Describes what constitutes a complete application for obtaining a filing date. Subtopics include: 601.01(a) Nonprovisional applications filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a); 601.01(b) Provisional applications filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(b); 601.01(c) Conversion to or from a Provisional Application; 601.01(d) Application Filed Without All Pages of Specification; 601.01(e) Nonprovisional Application Filed Without at Least One Claim; 601.01(f) Applications Filed Without Drawings; 601.01(g) Applications Filed Without All Figures of Drawings. (Guidance: each listed circumstance affects whether a filing date is accorded and what corrections/replacements are permitted.)

name: Specification / Disclosure — Arrangement and Content (608.01)
description: Specification and disclosure requirements, including arrangement of the application and required specification parts (608.01).
guidance: Enumerates required specification elements: 608.01(a) Arrangement of Application; 608.01(b) Abstract of the Disclosure; 608.01(c) Background of the Invention; 608.01(d) Brief Summary of Invention; 608.01(f) Brief Description of Drawings; 608.01(g) Detailed Description of Invention; 608.01(h) Mode of Operation of Invention; 608.01(i) Claims; 608.01(j) Numbering of Claims; 608.01(k) Statutory Requirement of Claims; 608.01(l) Claims Present on the Application Filing Date; 608.01(m) Form of Claims; 608.01(n) Dependent Claims; 608.01(o) Basis for Claim Terminology in Description; 608.01(p) Completeness of Specification; 608.01(q) Substitute or Rewritten Specification; 608.01(r) Derogatory Remarks About Prior Art in Specification; 608.01(s) Restoration of Canceled Matter; 608.01(t) Use in Subsequent Application; 608.01(v) Marks Used in Commerce and Trade Names; 608.01(w) Copyright and Mask Work Notices. Guidance covers how these parts must be presented, statutory/format requirements for claims, how claim terminology must be supported by the description, handling of incomplete or substitute specifications, and limitations on derogatory remarks about prior art.

name: New Matter (608.04)
description: Rules regarding new matter — matter not present on the application filing date (608.04).
guidance: Includes 608.04(a) Matter Not Present in Specification, Claims, or Drawings on the Application Filing Date; 608.04(b) New Matter by Preliminary Amendment; 608.04(c) Review of Examiner’s Holding of New Matter. Guidance covers what constitutes new matter, the prohibition on introducing new matter after filing, how preliminary amendments may inadvertently add new matter, and procedures for contesting or reviewing an examiner's new-matter holding.

name: Proper submission to establish common ownership
description: A proper submission to establish common ownership may be a clear and conspicuous statement that the claimed invention and the subject matter disclosed were, not later than the effective filing date of the claimed invention, owned by, or subject to an obligation of assignment to, the same person.
guidance: The statement must be conspicuous and identify the common assignee (see form paragraph notes). Failure to provide this required statement means the reference is not excepted under 102(b)(2)(C). Applicant may instead attempt to overcome a 102(a)(2) rejection via exceptions under 37 CFR 1.130(a) (obtained from inventor) or 1.130(b) (prior public disclosure affidavit/declaration).

name: Proper submission to establish a joint research agreement (JRA)
description: A proper submission to establish a JRA may include (a) an amendment to the specification to disclose the names of the parties to the JRA (per 37 CFR 1.71(g)), and (b) a clear and conspicuous statement that the subject matter in the prior art was developed and the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of one or more parties to a JRA which was in effect on or before the effective filing date of the claimed invention, and that the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the JRA.
guidance: If the applicant fails to supply the required amendment or statement (e.g., missing names or proof that the JRA was in effect by the effective filing date, or that the invention was made within the scope of the JRA), the attempt to except the reference is ineffective and examiner should use the form paragraph addressing missing requirements (see ¶7.20.05.aia).

name: ¶ 7.20.02.aia — Joint Inventors, Common Ownership Presumed
description: Form paragraph stating that an application currently names joint inventors and the examiner presumes claims' subject matter was commonly owned at the effective filing time absent evidence to the contrary.
guidance: Advises applicant of obligation under 37 CFR 1.56 to point out inventor and effective filing dates of any claim not commonly owned so that examiner may consider applicability of 102(b)(2)(C). Examiner notes: use only in apps filed on/after March 16, 2013 where claims examined under AIA 102/103; must be preceded by 7.03.aia; use in all applications with joint inventors unless claims are clearly restricted to a single claimed invention.

name: 37 CFR 1.131(c) — Affidavit or declaration to disqualify commonly owned patent as prior art
description: When a claim is rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103 in view of a U.S. patent or publication that is not prior art under pre-AIA 102(b), and the inventions are not patentably distinct and are owned by the same party, the applicant/patent owner may disqualify the patent/publication as prior art by submitting (1) a terminal disclaimer per 1.321(c), and (2) an oath/declaration that the application/patent under reexamination and the reference are currently owned by the same party and that the inventor named is the prior inventor under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 104.
guidance: This provision applies to applications/patents with claims having effective filing dates before March 16, 2013 (with specific cross-reference date rules). The affidavit/declaration may be signed by inventor(s), attorney/agent of record, or assignee(s) of entire interest. Terminal disclaimers only overcome nonstatutory double patenting; cannot be used for statutory double patenting. The phrase 'prior inventor under 35 U.S.C. 104 as in effect on March 15, 2013' carries limitations on where a date of invention can be established (NAFTA/WTO date limits). A U.S. patent or publication that anticipates the claimed subject matter cannot be disqualified under pre-AIA 103(c) or 1.131(c). See MPEP §§ 804.03 and 2146-2146.03 for related subject matter.

name: Pleading patent extensions
description: When a patent has been extended by a special Act of Congress and the suit is based partly or wholly on that extension, the declaration must state the legal effect of the Act and specially show the particular space of time covered.
guidance: Extensions are statutory and exceptional; plead the extension statute and the precise extended term relied upon for the claim's time frame.

name: Statement of infringement (what to allege)
description: The statement of infringement should allege that the defendant, without any license, did make, or did use, or did sell the subject of whatever claim(s) the plaintiff intends to prosecute, that the infringement occurred within the territory covered by plaintiff's title and during the time plaintiff held title, contrary to U.S. statutes.
guidance: Allegation of any one of making/using/selling is sufficient to state a cause of action but will not support proof of the others; therefore a plaintiff should allege as many types of infringement as he expects to be able to prove.

name: Chemical-patent special rules: narrower scope, harder enablement, easier nonobviousness
description: Chemical inventions often require more detailed disclosure (enablement) and thus yield narrower claim scope, while unpredictability can make nonobviousness easier to establish if unexpected properties are shown.
guidance: Supported by case law (In re Papesch; In re Bundy) and doctrinal commentary: close structural similarity to prior art raises an obviousness presumption that may be rebutted by evidence of new and unexpected properties; but broad chemical claims need greater support.

name: Markush claim grouping requirement
description: A Markush claim grouping of chemical compounds is allowable only where the grouped substances share a community of chemical and physical characteristics justifying their inclusion.
guidance: Quoted: In re Schechter — such claims allowed 'where the substances grouped have a community of chemical and physical characteristics ... and such inclusion is not repugnant to the principles of scientific classification.' Guides claim drafting for compound families.

name: Obviousness analysis in unpredictable arts (presumption and rebuttal)
description: Structural similarity to prior art raises a presumption of obviousness in chemical cases, but evidence that a claimed compound exhibits new and unexpected properties can overcome that presumption.
guidance: In re Papesch cited; practical implication is that showing unexpected properties is a powerful strategy to withstand obviousness attacks in chemical/biotech cases.

name: Enablement/support for broad chemical claims must be substantial
description: Broad claims in chemical arts require correspondingly greater specification support; lack of precise descriptions of analogs may still suffice in some cases but courts examine unpredictability and data.
guidance: Examples include In re Bundy and Studiengesellschaft Kohle; guidance for prosecutors and litigators on the level of experimental detail and exemplification needed.

name: Trade-off between claim breadth and enablement in chemical art
description: Because chemical inventions are unpredictable, claim breadth tends to be narrower (to satisfy enablement) but this same unpredictability can make it easier to establish nonobviousness for valid inventions.
guidance: Explains why chemical patents are 'easier to obtain, but narrower in scope' — a key consideration in portfolio strategy and policy analysis.

name: 'Prospect' function of patents and limitations of patent scope
description: Patents may function as a 'prospect' for future development, but many patents are not broad enough to serve this function fully — leaving independent alternative routes open.
guidance: Case examples (Standard Oil, Dow, Solvay) and commentary on when patents block or leave open independent routes; bears on how courts interpret claim scope and on antitrust issues.

name: Enablement and obviousness rules reflect unpredictability in claims and prosecution strategy
description: Doctrinal rules (enablement, obviousness) are applied differently depending on predictability: unpredictable fields impose stricter enablement but may ease nonobviousness findings; predictable fields allow broader claims with different proof burdens.
guidance: Summarizes repeated examples across the chunk (chemical unpredictability, catalytic chemistry, polymer patents) and directs claim drafters to tailor disclosure and claim breadth to the art's predictability.

name: Fallacies of Simple Inspection (à priori fallacies)
description: Propositions embraced as self-evident or accepted without proof (or with only intrinsic verisimilitude), i.e., conclusions taken as requiring no external evidence.
guidance: Watch for tacit acceptance of claims as 'self-evident' or derived from intuition alone. Manifestations include mistaking ideas for realities (treating properties of our conceptions as properties of things), personifying abstractions (treating names as distinct entities), inferring truth from conceivability, or assuming that what we find easiest to conceive is likeliest true. Examples discussed: popular superstitions, Cartesian and Leibnitzian metaphysical moves, and historical scientific errors. Practical caution: do not accept intuitions as proof; seek empirical or argumentative support.

name: Fallacies of Observation
description: Inductive fallacies where the facts on which induction proceeds are erroneous (mal-observation, non-observation, or false inference from intermediate marks).
guidance: Treat as failures in ascertainment of facts. When evaluating inductive claims, check whether observations were accurately made or whether inferences from marks are warranted. Errors can be direct (bad observation) or indirect (erroneous inference about observed marks). Remedy: improve empirical ascertainment and inspect intermediate signs for their probative value.

name: Patent publication content and correction policy
description: PRH's patent application publication (A1 etc.) and patent publication (B1 etc.) include description, claims, drawings and abstract; PRH makes correction publications free-of-charge if the error was made by PRH or should have been noticed by PRH before publication.
guidance: PRH publishes a range of kind codes (A1, A8, A9, B1, B2, B3, B8, B9). Corrected publications and republications are possible in specific situations (e.g., maintenance after opposition, limitation). Fees may apply for corrected translations provided by proprietor for EP validations.

name: Primary focus of search: claims and inventive concept
description: Lähtökohtaisesti PRH tutkii hakemuksen käsittelyn aikana yhden keksinnön tai yhtenäisen keksintöryhmän. Uutuustutkimus kattaa lähtökohtaisesti sen, mikä on esitetty patenttivaatimuksissa. Hakijan on tärkeää ymmärtää ydinkeksintö (inventive concept).
guidance: Search is primarily directed to the subject‑matter of the claims, but the examiner also uses the description and drawings to identify the problem solved and to interpret unclear terms.

name: Limiting the search for unclear/overbroad claims
description: Epäselvien ja erityisen laajojen vaatimusten kohdalla tutkimus voidaan kohdistaa siihen, mitä on selitysosan perusteella toteutettavissa. Uutuustutkimus voidaan suorittaa osittaisena, jos itsenäiset patenttivaatimukset määrittelevät keksinnön kohteen kohtuuttoman epäselvästi tai laajasti. Kompleksihakemukset käsitellään erikseen.
guidance: If search is limited PRH will justify restriction in an interim decision stating which claims/parts were searched and why; claims left unsearched are recorded in the search report.

name: Supplementing novelty search after prosecution events
description: Uutuustutkimusta täydennetään hakemuskäsittelyn myöhemmässä vaiheessa, jos siihen on tarvetta esim. patenttivaatimusten muutosten vuoksi. Myös julkistukset, jotka tulivat saataville tutkimuksen jälkeen, on otettava huomioon.
guidance: If amendments introduce new matter or narrow/expand claims, a new/search supplement may be performed and a new search report issued where appropriate.

name: Conditions to claim priority under 35 U.S.C. §120
description: Under 35 U.S.C. §120, a later application is entitled to adopt the filing date of a 'parent' application when (1) both applications disclose the same invention; (2) both applications are filed by the same inventor; (3) both applications are simultaneously co-pending; (4) the earlier application meets the disclosure requirements of 35 U.S.C. §112; and (5) the later application contains a specific reference to the earlier application.
guidance: Court precedents (e.g., Sampson v. Ampex Corp. (1971)) and CCPA/Patent Office practice interpret these conditions; failure to meet them can deny priority benefit.

name: Effect of policy changes (1995 patent-term change; 1999 publication rule)
description: Policy reforms: 1995 changed patent term from 17 years from issue to 20 years from application date; 1999 mandated publication of most applications after 18 months (with opt-out for US-only filings).
guidance: 1995 reduced incentives for 'submarine' strategies by making extended pendency trade off against lost term; 1999 publication reduced secrecy benefits but did not eliminate strategic uses (applicants can still alter claims in continuations). Empirically test pre/post changes and analyze shifts in continuation composition (e.g., reduced overall use; CAPs shifted toward less-important patents).

name: PCT handling and search/examination standards at PRH
description: PRH acts as an international PCT authority (ISA/IPEA). Search is executed with the same tools and databases as the European Patent Office (EPO). PRH also searches/examines non-technical features and unclear claims to cover jurisdictional differences.
guidance: Different examiners handle PCT and national priority applications, resulting in a second search and opinion for quality and coverage. Consulting examiner is mandatory in all PCT applications (see Quality Control Processes).

name: Enablement (35 U.S.C. 112(a))
description: The specification must teach a person of ordinary skill to make and use all embodiments encompassed by the claims, without undue experimentation.
guidance: Examiners should rigorously enforce enablement against claims that 'stretch beyond' disclosed ground, particularly in cumulative-technology fields. Use enablement to reject genus claims that the disclosure does not actually enable across their asserted breadth.

name: Acceptability of Broad Scope for Discrete Inventions
description: For inventions that do not function as inputs to follow-on innovation, broad scope is generally tolerable because there is little risk of blocking subsequent improvers.
guidance: Claim breadth should match the experimental difficulty of identifying the invention (justifying high reward). There is particular value in claiming compounds by structural genus where the disclosed examples support generalization.

name: Representative Working Examples for Discrete Inventions
description: High-quality discrete-invention claims are clear in scope and supported by representative working examples.
guidance: Drafters should include representative exemplars that enable the claimed scope; absence of such examples weakens justification for broad genus claims.

name: Strict Enablement in Cumulative Technologies
description: Examiners should apply enablement strictly in cumulative-technology fields, rejecting genus claims that exceed the inventor's actual contribution.
guidance: Because many actors build on shared components, claims that purport to cover broad functional classes without commensurate disclosure should be narrowed or denied.

name: Use of Reverse Doctrine and Narrowing Claim Construction as Safety Valves
description: Reverse doctrine of equivalents and narrowing claim construction serve as essential safety valves in cumulative fields to preserve room for independent improvement.
guidance: Courts and examiners should use these tools to prevent pioneer patents from foreclosing reasonable design-arounds and subsequent innovation.

name: Scope-Quality Marker: Permit Independent Improvement
description: A key marker of scope quality in cumulative technologies is whether the claims permit independent improvement or create a blocking bottleneck.
guidance: Evaluate whether enforcement of the claim would foreclose reasonable design-arounds and follow-on inventive activity.

name: Chemical Product vs. Process Patent Distinction
description: Chemical inventions present a hybrid: product (specific compound) patents are typically discrete and can sustain broader scope; process patents tend to be cumulative and require narrower scope and strict enablement.
guidance: Treat product claims and process claims differently: product genus claims may be acceptable if structurally supported, while process claims that would block multiple downstream uses should be narrowly drawn and carefully enabled.

name: Chemical Product Claims: Synthesis Route Disclosure
description: Chemical product claims should disclose at least one synthesis route enabling all claimed embodiments.
guidance: Quality marker: ensure the patent discloses a synthesis (process) that enables practicing the claimed compound across its asserted scope; lack of synthesis disclosure undermines genus claims.

name: Genus Claims in Chemistry Require Representative Species
description: Genus claims must be supported by representative species; the number, structural diversity, and disclosed properties of species should justify the genus.
guidance: Examiners should look for species diversity and representative examples sufficient to make the generalization credible to a person of ordinary skill.

name: Science-Based Technologies: High Scope-Quality Concern
description: In science-based technologies (biotechnology, modern software), first-applier risk of 'controlling a broad array of improvements' is particularly acute, creating the highest scope-quality concerns.
guidance: Apply strict enablement standards especially for biotechnology genus claims (cf. Amgen v. Sanofi reasoning). Be wary of claiming broad functional results without structural-functional correlation.

name: Disfavor Functional/Result-Oriented Claiming in Science-Based Fields
description: Functional/result-oriented claiming should be heavily disfavored in science-based technologies unless the specification teaches a structural-functional correlation.
guidance: Only allow result-oriented claims when the disclosure shows how structure maps to the claimed function across the claimed scope; otherwise require structural limitations or narrower claims.

name: Scope-Quality Marker: Full-Range Enablement of Genus
description: Quality marker for science-based fields: does the disclosure enable the claimed genus across the full scope, or does it merely identify one species and claim the genus?
guidance: If disclosure only enables one species, claiming the whole genus is a scope-quality failure unless further support is provided.

name: Pioneer-Patent Discipline (Breadth Proportionate to Disclosure)
description: Patents claiming pioneer status must support their breadth with proportionate disclosure; a pioneer patent backed by a single embodiment is a quality red flag.
guidance: The greater the purported leap from the prior art, the greater the disclosure required to justify broad claim scope.

name: Genus-Species Proportionality
description: Claims to a genus must be supported by enough species to make the generalization credible to a person of ordinary skill.
guidance: Assess the number of species, their structural diversity, and disclosed properties as indicators of whether genus claiming is justified.

name: Cross-Industry Borrowing Caution
description: Doctrines developed in one industry (e.g., chemical/pharmaceutical broad genus claiming or broad doctrine-of-equivalents reach) should not transfer reflexively to other fields like software or biotech without re-evaluating the cumulative-vs-discrete analysis.
guidance: Apply industry-specific analysis rather than transplanting doctrinal norms wholesale; consider how the technology's innovation and follow-on dynamics differ.

name: Applicant Burden for Genus Claims
description: The burden of proving enablement should rest on the applicant for genus claims.
guidance: Examiners should require representative examples spanning the claimed genus; 'paper claims' untethered to working examples are presumptive scope-quality failures.

name: Representative Examples Requirement
description: Examiners should require representative examples spanning the claimed genus for broad claims.
guidance: Absence of representative examples should lead to rejection or narrowing; reasonable doubt about enablement should resolve against the applicant for broad claims.

name: Paper Claims as a Presumptive Failure
description: 'Paper claims' untethered to working examples are presumptive scope-quality failures.
guidance: Claims that assert broad coverage without experimental or structural support should be viewed skeptically and subjected to strict enablement scrutiny.

name: Operative Scope-Quality Test — Technological Regime Identification
description: Ask: What technological regime governs (discrete / cumulative / chemical / science-based)?
guidance: Identifying the regime guides which substantive standards (e.g., strict enablement vs. toleration of breadth) to apply when assessing claim scope.

name: Operative Scope-Quality Test — Support by Disclosed Embodiment-Set
description: Ask: Does the disclosed embodiment-set support the claimed scope under that regime's standards?
guidance: Compare the disclosure to the claim breadth: number/diversity of examples, synthesis routes, and structural-functional correlations are pertinent.

name: Operative Scope-Quality Test — Foreclosure of Independent Improvement
description: Ask: Would enforcement of this claim foreclose reasonable independent improvement?
guidance: If enforcement would create blocking or bottleneck effects in the relevant innovation ecosystem, scope should be narrowed.

name: Operative Scope-Quality Test — Clarity of Outer Boundaries / Design-Aroundability
description: Ask: Are the claim's outer boundaries clear enough to permit design-around?
guidance: Ambiguous outer limits that chill follow-on work or inhibit reasonable design-arounds signal poor scope quality; prefer clear boundaries or narrower claims.

name: Operative Scope-Quality Test — Breadth Proportionate to Contribution
description: Ask: Is the breadth proportionate to the inventor's demonstrated contribution to the art?
guidance: Large claimed breadth requires commensurate demonstrated inventive contribution and supporting disclosure; otherwise breadth should be constrained.

name: Refusal to enter amendment within 30 days after filing an appeal
description: According to Article 174 (applicable mutatis mutandis to Article 51), refusal to enter amendment within 30 days from the filing of an appeal shall fall under any of the followings: ① Where the amendment does not comply with requirements for amendment under Article 47(2)-(3) of the Patent Act; ② Where new grounds for rejection are deemed to be arisen from the amendment (“deletion of claim(s)” excluded among amendments according to Article 47(3), subparagraph 1-4).
guidance: Note: Where grounds for rejection previously notified are not overcome by the amendment within 30 days from filing an appeal, and no new reasons arise from the amendment, the amendment shall be accepted but the original decision stands. If previous grounds are not overcome and new grounds do arise from the amendment, the amendment shall be refused to be entered and review proceeds based on the specification before the amendment.

name: Baseline for evaluating introduction of new matter vs scope-narrowing depending on stage
description: When evaluating appropriateness of an amendment (e.g., whether introduction of new matter under Article 47(2) or requirement under Article 47(3) are met), the comparison baseline depends on the procedural posture: compare with the originally filed specification/drawings for new matter (Article 47(2)); compare with the specification/drawings of the immediately prior amendment for Article 47(3) (i.e., to determine whether scope of claims is narrowed).
guidance: Applied scenarios: (a) If decision to reject is made after issuance of a notice of grounds for non-final rejection and applicant files later amendments on appeal, evaluate Article 47(2) against the originally filed documents and Article 47(3) against the earlier amendment (amendment II). Specifically, determine narrowing by comparing corresponding claims between amendment II and amendment III (or IV as applicable). (b) If refusal to enter occurred before an appeal, evaluate under the presumption that an appeal against refusal is filed unless applicant indicates otherwise. The evaluation baseline changes when combining amendments on appeal (finalize combined amended portions when comparing).

name: Criteria for issuing a notice of grounds for rejection at reconsideration
description: According to Article 174(2) applicable mutatis mutandis to Article 63, criteria for issuing a notice of grounds for rejection at the reconsideration process include: (1) Where amendments within 30 days after filing an appeal violate Article 47(2) or (3) or new rejections are necessitated by amendments (excluding deletion of claim(s)), the amendments shall be refused to be entered and review be based on a specification before the amendment; (2) Where amendments within 30 days after filing an appeal do not include reasons for refusal but new grounds are identified during reconsideration, grounds for rejection shall be issued.
guidance: Further detail: If grounds for rejection existed before the first notice at examination stage, issue a notice of non-final rejection; if grounds occur with amendment made in response to a first notice, issue a notice of final rejection necessitated by amendment; if both non-final and final grounds exist, issue non-final; if amendments responding to examiner's report do not address prior grounds, original decision shall stand without additional notification.

name: Requirements for ex-officio re-examination (time-wise and substantive)
description: (1) Time-wise: If establishment of right is neither registered after grant nor the application withdrawn/abandoned, the examiner can revoke the granted patent ex-officio and reexamine. (2) Substantive: Examiner must find obvious grounds for rejection (excluding certain matters such as background art description requirement, description of claims, and unity violations). The granted patent must be obviously invalidated on that ground, not merely possibly invalidated.
guidance: Obviousness standard: 'obvious grounds for rejection' means sufficiently clear that the examiner may re-open examination; trivial or speculative grounds are insufficient.

name: Procedural notes for conducting ex-officio re-examination
description: Procedural safeguards include consultation among three concerned persons (including a director of an examination division or head of a part) before notifying the applicant of revocation, and issuing a first office action based on the obvious ground as early as possible (within 7 days maximum) so applicant can file written argument. Applicant may amend specification or drawings within the scope of the specification as filed.
guidance: Additional notes: if a decision to reject is to be made based on a ground notified before revocation, applicant must be notified again to submit written argument; ex-officio re-examination is not permitted for improper background-art description, improperly formulated claims, or lack of unity; if the patent is registered or withdrawn/abandoned before notification, revocation is deemed not made; amendments made before revocation shall not be dismissed; if relevant information is submitted before registration, examiner should review whether obvious ground exists based on those documents.

name: Target application criteria for suggesting amendments
description: An examiner can suggest amendments for an application meeting the following requirements: ① the invention should be understandable; ② sufficient prior art search is made (except where lack of description prevents search); ③ the claimed invention has a technical feature distinguished from prior art.
guidance: Recommendations: focus on suggesting a proper scope of a patent rather than overcoming lack of description requirements. Amendments should be simple and clear; for unrepresented applicants provide more detailed suggestions.

name: Guidelines for suggesting amendments for novelty and inventive step
description: An examiner may suggest amendments for novelty and inventive step in the following cases: ① Where dependent claims are allowable, suggest adding a technical element from the allowable dependent claim to the claim needing amendment while explaining the reason. ② Where no claim is allowable but the description discloses a technical element which would differentiate from prior art, suggest adding that element from the description to the claim and explain. ③ Where a dependent claim is allowable but a technical element in the description would give a more reasonable scope than the dependent claim, the examiner may suggest adding the described element to the claim (may suggest both alternatives and indicate technical elements rather than redrafting claims in detail).
guidance: Includes multiple illustrative examples showing: selecting elements from an allowable dependent claim; selecting elements from description when no claim is allowable; selecting elements that provide better scope than patentable dependent claims. Examiner should explain technical effect and recommend which elements to add to overcome lack of inventive step.

name: How to suggest amendment for indefinite claims
description: Amendment may be suggested to overcome rejection for indefinite claims (e.g., delete vague terms or replace with specific ranges disclosed in the description).
guidance: Example: advice that deleting the word 'high-speed' or amending it to 'speed ranging from ㅇㅇ to ㅇㅇ' as described in the specification would render the claim patentable.

name: Inappropriate suggestions of amendment (anti-patterns)
description: Examples of inappropriate suggestions include: (1) suggesting amendment to patentable claims (i.e., advising to add a patentable dependent claim's feature into independent claim when that would undermine a currently patentable dependent claim); (2) excessively narrowing the scope of a claim; (3) ambiguous suggestions lacking specificity; (4) suggestions that may raise new grounds for rejection (e.g., introducing ambiguous relationships between elements); (5) it is not appropriate to suggest introduction of new matter or broadening a claim when notifying grounds for final rejection necessitated by amendment.
guidance: Where suggestions risk creating new grounds for rejection, be more conservative (e.g., suggest adding a feature to an intermediate dependent claim rather than directly to the independent claim). Avoid suggesting amendments that would broaden claims or introduce new matter at final rejection stage.

name: Transition phrases and claim scope
description: In evaluating novelty or inventive step, the examiner should consider which type of transition phrase, such as “consisting of,” “comprising,” “characterized by,” or “consisting essentially of” is used in the claims. The subject matter to be searched depends on the type of transition phrase used.
guidance: PCT ISPE GL §5.20-5.23 apply mutatis mutandis; treat “comprising” as open-ended and “consisting of” as closed-ended; choice of transitional phrase affects the boundaries of the claimed subject-matter and search scope.

name: Means-plus-function claims
description: Claims expressed as means-plus-function should be treated according to established PCT guidance.
guidance: PCT ISPE GL §5.25 apply mutatis mutandis (i.e., apply PCT guidance for interpretation and support of means-plus-function claim elements).

name: Product and apparatus limitations in process claims
description: When a claim relates to a process for producing the product of the invention, the process as claimed should, when carried out reasonably by a PSIA, necessarily result in that particular product; otherwise there is internal inconsistency and lack of clarity.
guidance: Examiners should ensure the process steps as claimed lead to the claimed product; internal inconsistencies between product and process features render claims unclear.

name: Inconsistency between claims and description
description: Claims must be consistent with the description; amendments to claims should be supported by and consistent with the description and drawings.
guidance: PCT ISPE GL §5.29-5.30 apply mutatis mutandis; if claim amendments are made to meet clarity, corresponding description amendments may be required; avoid inconsistency that broadens claim scope beyond description.

name: Clarity requirement — meaning clear to PSIA from claim wording alone
description: The meaning of the terms of a claim must be clear for a Person Skilled in the Art (PSIA) from the wording of the claim alone. Clarity must be analysed in light of the application disclosure, prior art teachings, and PSIA interpretation at the time the invention was made; if a PSIA can determine claim boundaries with reasonable certainty, the claim complies.
guidance: Breadth is not equivalent to lack of clarity; examiner considers disclosure and context; references to PCT ISPE GL paragraphs on clarity (5.32-5.33).

name: Independent claim must specify essential features
description: An independent claim should clearly specify all essential features needed to define the invention, except insofar as such features are implied by generic terms used.
guidance: Example: a claim to a “bicycle” need not mention wheels; ensure essential features are present or clearly implied.

name: Clarity applies to individual claims and the claim set as a whole
description: Requirement that the claims should be clear applies both to individual claims and to the set of claims as a whole, irrespective of product, process or product-by-process claims.
guidance: Examine both singular claims and how claims interact; ensure no internal contradictions across claim set (PCT ISPE GL references).

name: Claims defining products by reference to other products/use relationships require precision
description: Where a claim for an apparatus or a product seeks to define the invention by reference to features of the use to which the apparatus or product is put, lack of clarity can result (especially when defining by relationship to a second product not part of the claimed invention).
guidance: May need to reword (e.g., use “connectable” instead of “connected”), or claim the combination (e.g., “engine with a cylinder head”); permissibility of defining dimensions/shape of first product by reference to second product allowed in some cases (example: number-plate bracket).

name: Use of imprecise terms — case-by-case assessment
description: A claim that includes vague or equivocal wording which leaves reader in doubt as to scope should be objected to for lack of clarity. Terms like “substantially”, “about”, “more or less”, “approximately” may be objectionable depending on circumstances.
guidance: Examine whether such terms prevent unambiguous distinction from prior art; raise novelty/inventive-step objections if ‘about’ prevents clear distinction; ‘comprising’ allowed as open-ended, ‘consisting of’ closed-ended, ‘characterised by’ allowed in two-part claims.

name: Disclaimers and negative limitations
description: Subject-matter of a claim may be limited by disclaimers, negative limitations, or exclusions (e.g., “free of water”). Negative limitations are not per se ambiguous if each recited limitation is clear; negative limitation is unclear if it attempts to claim by excluding what was not invented rather than reciting what was invented.
guidance: Negative limitations can be used to meet novelty; examples given where exclusions are clear; ensure negative limitation's boundaries are definite.

name: Multiple dependent claims — format and allowance
description: Dependency of claims is allowed; multiple dependent claims (referring to more than one other claim) are allowed in the AMS. A multiple dependent claim includes all limitations contained in the claim(s) to which it relates. Dependent claims should be grouped together practically to enable association.
guidance: Patent office may follow alternative guidelines: (a) multiple dependent claim referring to more than one claim should do so only alternatively and cannot form a basis for other multiple dependent claims; or (b) may allow alternative or cumulative references and allow multiple dependent claims to form basis for other multiple dependent claims.

name: Use claims — equivalence to process claims for examination
description: Use claims are allowed in most AMS (with specified country exceptions); for examination, a use claim in form “the use of substance X as an insecticide” is regarded as equivalent to a process claim “a process of killing insects using substance X.”
guidance: Do not interpret such a use claim as directed to the substance per se as an amplifying circuit or to building processes; note country-specific exceptions (e.g., Lao PDR and Viet Nam, Indonesia limited to new products).

name: Use of ranges (e.g., dosage) in claims
description: Use of ranges in claims is explicitly allowed in some AMS under prescribed conditions. A specific example in the prior art that falls within a claimed range anticipates the range claimed.
guidance: If prior art discloses a range that overlaps the claimed narrow range, novelty must be decided case-by-case; narrow selection ranges may still be novel/inventive if evidence (e.g., unexpected results) shows selection produces effects within that narrow range; see Chapter 11 for inventive step considerations.

name: Use of limitations and disclaimers in claims (reprise)
description: Subject-matter of a claim may be limited by disclaimers or negative limitations to meet novelty; negative limitation is acceptable where each recited limitation is clear; mere absence of a positive recitation is not a basis for exclusion.
guidance: Negative limitations should not be used to try to claim by excluding what applicant did not invent; ensure clarity of each excluded element; examples included.

name: Claims must be supported by the description and drawings (support requirement)
description: Claims (independent and dependent) must be fully supported by the description; there must be a basis in the description for the subject-matter of every claim and the claims' scope may not be broader than justified by the description and drawings.
guidance: A claim is regarded as supported unless PSIA would be unable to extend teaching to whole claimed field using routine methods; vague statements or assertions without technical content do not provide basis; raise objection of lack of support only if well-founded and, where possible, supported by published documents; treat clarity/support separate from novelty/inventive step/industrial applicability.

name: Amendment of claim must be supported by description when made to meet clarity
description: Amendment of a claim should be supported by the description and be clear and concise to meet clarity requirement.
guidance: When claims are amended for clarity, ensure description is amended as necessary (PCT ISPE GL §5.29). Avoid introducing added subject-matter.

name: Factors to consider for undue experimentation
description: When determining whether undue experimentation is required to carry out the claimed invention, consider: (i) breadth of the claims; (ii) nature of the invention; (iii) general knowledge of a PSIA; (iv) level of predictability in the art; (v) amount of direction provided in the application (including references to prior art); and (vi) amount of experimentation required to carry out the claimed invention on the basis of the disclosure.
guidance: See PCT ISPE 5.48–5.51 for more details; use these factors to decide whether disclosure enables PSIA without undue experimentation.

name: Contents of the international application
description: An international application shall contain, as specified in this Treaty and the Regulations, a request, a description, one or more claims, one or more drawings (where required), and an abstract.
guidance: The abstract merely serves the purpose of technical information and cannot be taken into account for any other purpose, particularly not for the purpose of interpreting the scope of the protection sought. (Article 3(2)-(3))

name: Claim drafting standards
description: The claim or claims shall define the matter for which protection is sought. Claims shall be clear and concise. They shall be fully supported by the description.
guidance: Claims must be consistent with and supported by the description; clarity and conciseness are expressly required. (Article 6)

name: Conditions for accord of international filing date
description: Receiving Office shall accord an international filing date if, at time of receipt: (i) applicant does not obviously lack the right to file there; (ii) application is in the prescribed language; (iii) the application contains at least: (a) an indication that it is intended as an international application, (b) designation of at least one Contracting State, (c) name of the applicant as prescribed, (d) a part that appears to be a description, (e) a part that appears to be a claim or claims.
guidance: If any of these are missing, the receiving Office invites correction within prescribed time; upon compliance the filing date may be the date of receipt of correction. Filing date confers effect of a regular national application in each designated State. (Article 11(1)-(4))

name: Amendment subordinate to original application
description: An amendment, however extensive in substance or complete in form, must always be subordinate to, and connected with the original application.
guidance: Two distinct applications cannot qualify or support each other. A later application describing the same invention as an earlier one is not regarded as an amendment to the earlier; the earlier stands unaffected and may be amended and allowed without reference to the later. An amendment of one portion does not always change the rest except insofar as construing the whole together modifies the meaning of unaltered portions. A Claim may be amended without affecting the Description, or the Description without influencing the Claims, or the drawings/model without revising the specification.

name: Amended claims require applicant's signature
description: Amended Claims may be inserted into an application by the attorney only with the signature of the applicant.
guidance: An attorney has no right to substitute a clean draft of a specification (or claims) signed and sworn to by the attorney alone; if done it must be erased (see Sheridan v. Latos (1883)).

name: Definition — matter of form
description: A matter of form is one that relates to the fitness of the application for an examination on its merits, or involves merely some rule of Office practice.
guidance: Examples: joinder questions, claim intelligibility, whether a claim is functional (these are treated as matters of form in various cases). Appeals on matters of Office practice are appealable only to the Commissioner.

name: Admission of new evidence during appeal requires remand
description: If evidence is admitted during an appeal to support the applicant's claims against references or to vary factual issues concerning patentability, the whole case must be remanded to the examiner so that he may pass upon it in its new condition.
guidance: This preserves the examiner's primary fact-finding role and ensures issues of fact are first resolved at the Office level before final appellate adjudication.

name: Claims and specification clarity / readability
description: The claim should be described the technology in a correct and concise way; it should be readable by a lay person.
guidance: Drafting claims and specification clearly is really important for jury trials; the interviewee noted Apple's claims are easy to read while Samsung's are difficult regardless of technical level. Ease of reading helps juries and affects litigation outcomes.

name: Identify abstract idea as recited and justify grouping (abstract idea specifics)
description: When the examiner has determined the claim recites an abstract idea, the rejection should identify the abstract idea as it is recited (i.e., set forth or described) in the claim, and explain why it falls within one of the groupings of abstract ideas (mathematical concepts, mental processes, or certain methods of organizing human activity) enumerated in MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2).
guidance: If the limitation does not fall within those groupings, use the 'tentative abstract idea' procedure (MPEP § 2106.04 IV) and provide justification. Optionally cite appropriate court decisions that support the identification of the abstract idea, but examiners should be familiar with cited decisions and ensure the rejection is reasonably tied to the facts. Avoid relying on non-precedential decisions unless the facts match uniquely. A sample explanation is provided (e.g., comparing collected information to a threshold is a 'mental process').

name: Identify law of nature or natural phenomenon as recited and provide reasoned rationale
description: When the examiner determines the claim recites a law of nature or a natural phenomenon, the rejection should identify it as recited in the claim and explain using a reasoned rationale why it is considered a law of nature or natural phenomenon.
guidance: Provide a factual explanation tying the claim language to natural consequences or occurrences (examples: a correlation X that describes a consequence of natural processes; something that occurs in nature and exists apart from human action). See MPEP § 2106.04(b) for more information and sample explanations.

name: Identify product of nature exceptions and analyze markedly different characteristics
description: When the examiner has determined the claim recites a product of nature, the rejection should identify the exception as recited in the claim and explain using a reasoned rationale why the product does not have markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state.
guidance: Compare the claimed product to its closest naturally occurring counterpart and explain lack of marked differences in structure, function, or properties. Provide examples (e.g., isolated DNA segment conveying same genetic information). See MPEP § 2106.04(b)-(c) for guidance on the markedly different characteristics analysis.

name: Rejection only when conclusion is readily apparent; explain rationale for applicant response
description: A rejection should be made only if it is readily apparent to an examiner relying on the examiner's expertise that the additional elements do not integrate the exception into a practical application and do not amount to significantly more than the recited judicial exception.
guidance: When making a rejection, explain the rationale underlying the conclusion so that applicant can effectively respond. Conversely, when appropriate, explain why the additional elements do integrate an exception into a practical application or provide an inventive concept by adding a meaningful limitation. It is a best practice to consult the specification to identify elements that could be added to make the claim eligible and suggest them in the Office action.

name: Generic computer components and generic computing functions guidance
description: For claim limitations that recite a generic computer component performing generic computer functions at a high level of generality, examiners can explain why these generic computing functions do not meaningfully limit the claim.
guidance: Keep in mind courts have held that combinations of generic computer components can sometimes be 'significantly more' (e.g., DDR Holdings). Refer to MPEP § 2106.05(f) for examples of generic computing functions that courts have found to be mere instructions to implement an exception on a computer and to MPEP § 2106.05(d) for well-understood/conventional activities considerations. Explain why the recited computer elements are merely generic implementation if so.

name: Insignificant extra-solution activity and mere field-of-use limitations
description: For claim limitations that add insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., mere data gathering) or that generally link use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use, examiners should explain why they do not meaningfully limit the claim.
guidance: Provide examples and reasons (e.g., storing data to a process of computing area does not add meaningful limitation; placing a product of nature in a test tube is nominal token activity). Cite relevant precedent (Parker v. Flook) and MPEP subsections 2106.05(g) and 2106.05(h). Explain that merely employing well-known computer functions or limiting use to one environment typically is insufficient.

name: Evidentiary standard: no evidence required for Step 2A Prong One
description: When performing the analysis at Step 2A Prong One, it is sufficient for the examiner to provide a reasoned rationale identifying the judicial exception recited in the claim and explaining why it is considered a judicial exception; there is no requirement to rely on external evidence.
guidance: Court decisions have identified abstract ideas without relying on evidence. Thus for Step 2A Prong One, examiner need not cite publications, affidavits, or declarations to find that a claim recites a judicial exception. Cite supporting case law listed in the guidance if helpful.

name: Support Option B: citation to court decisions showing conventional nature
description: An examiner may cite one or more court decisions that note the well-understood, routine, conventional nature of the additional element(s) to support the rejection.
guidance: Ensure the claim limitations before the examiner are the same as those found conventional by the courts and recited at the same high level of generality. It is not sufficient that elements are merely similar. Court decisions cited do not imply all computer functions are conventional; courts have sometimes found generic computer combinations to be significantly more (DDR Holdings).

name: Use of form paragraphs for 35 U.S.C. 101 rejections and required structure
description: Use specified form paragraphs (e.g., 7.04.01, 7.05, 7.05.01, 7.05.016, and 7.05.017) for rejections based on failure to claim statutory categories or directed to a judicial exception without an inventive concept/significantly more.
guidance: 7.04.01 (Statement of Statutory Basis) must precede the first use of 35 U.S.C. 101 in first actions and final rejections. 7.05 is a heading-only paragraph that must be preceded/followed by specific content. 7.05.016 must identify the type of exception, how it is recited, why it is not integrated into a practical application, and why additional elements do not add significantly more. If the exception is a 'tentative abstract idea' use 7.05.017 in addition and include TC Director signature. Follow the Examiner Notes for bracketed content and sequencing (see page text for bracket instructions and examples).

name: Use of 'step[s] for' language signals intent to invoke §112, ¶6
description: In the context of method claims, the use of the term 'steps for' signals the drafter’s intent to invoke §112, ¶6.
guidance: Federal Circuit: 'the use of the term 'steps for' signals the drafter’s intent to invoke §112, ¶6.' Practitioners should treat explicit 'step[s] for' phrasing as a strong indicator that step-plus-function analysis may be appropriate when construing method claims.

name: §112, ¶6 only implicated when steps consist of functions without acts
description: Even where the drafter employs the 'step for' language, §112, ¶6 is implicated only when steps plus function without acts are present.
guidance: Court will apply §112(f) only if the claimed step recites a function and contains no acts — mere 'step for' language alone is not sufficient. Evaluate whether the limitation describes an act (physical deed) versus a pure function.

name: Limitations that recite acts are not step-plus-function limitations
description: A claimed step that comprises an act (e.g., 'holding the lever in a position', 'operably connecting the lever and the dial') is not a step-plus-function limitation because it includes an act that precludes §112, ¶6 treatment.
guidance: Identify verbs/phrases that describe concrete actions (holding, connecting, moving, placing, etc.). If the limitation can be construed as an act, do not treat it as a functional-only step under §112(f). The article uses 'holding' and 'operably connecting' as examples of acts.

name: Limitations that recite only functions may trigger step-plus-function treatment
description: A limitation phrased as performing a function (e.g., 'transmitting a force') can be a step-plus-function limitation because 'transmitting' is a function rather than an act (per the Court of Claims' characterization).
guidance: Assess whether the limitation contains any descriptive act or only functional language. If only functional language remains and 'step[s] for' is present (or it can be shown there are no acts), then §112(f) may apply. Note: Federal Circuit reversed the Court of Claims on the 'transmitting' step in this case, illustrating factual/contextual uncertainty.
