name: Absent 'step[s] for' language, courts will not apply §112, ¶6 without showing no act exists
description: Where the claim drafter has not signaled intent to invoke §112, ¶6 by using the 'step[s] for' language, the court will not construe a limitation as step-plus-function without a showing that the limitation contains nothing that can be construed as an act.
guidance: To avoid §112(f) limitation by inference, patentees can avoid 'step(s) for' phrasing and include descriptive acts in method steps. Conversely, challengers seeking §112(f) treatment must demonstrate the absence of any act in the limitation.

name: Interpretation should avoid disrupting patentees' settled expectations
description: The Federal Circuit referenced Festo to emphasize that decisions should not 'disrupt patentees’ settled expectations regarding the scope of their claims' and therefore construe §112, ¶6 narrowly when not clearly invoked.
guidance: Courts will be cautious about importing §112(f)-style limitations into claims absent clear indicia (explicit 'step[s] for' or lack of acts). Use of precedent and policy considerations can be invoked to argue for or against applying step-plus-function treatment.

name: Directed to an abstract idea (Alice Step 1 / Prong One)
description: Whether the claim is 'directed to' an abstract idea (e.g., collecting, analyzing, manipulating, displaying information; mental processes; fundamental economic practices; mathematical concepts; certain methods of organizing human activity; communications).
guidance: Examples in the document: 'collecting, displaying, and analyzing information'; 'the broad concept of communicating information wirelessly, without more, is an abstract idea'; claims that capture only information or high-level concepts are often found to be directed to abstract ideas. PTAB/Fed. Cir. decisions classify many data-processing and business-practice claims under this rubric.

name: Inventive concept / Alice Step 2 (or Revised Step 2A Prong Two / Step 2B)
description: Whether the claim recites an 'inventive concept' that transforms the abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter — i.e., limitations that are significantly more than well-understood, routine, conventional activity.
guidance: Guidance and cases: an inventive concept can be 'found in the non-conventional and non-generic arrangement of known, conventional pieces' (Berkheimer); factual allegations/declarations can show claims are not routine/conventional (Aatrix). If the only additional features are generic computer components or routine data-handling, no inventive concept exists.

name: Improvement to computer or other technology (Step 1 non-abstract)
description: Claims that are 'directed to an improvement in computer functionality' or solve a technological problem (improve speed, accuracy, usability, memory function, security, etc.) may not be abstract at Alice Step 1.
guidance: Fed. Cir. precedents cited: Enfish (self-referential database), DDR Holdings, Trading Technologies (GUI addressing speed/accuracy/usability), Koninklijke (error checking in data transmission), and cases finding enhanced memory systems or network security improvements. The claim must show specifics of the technological improvement, not merely add conventional components.

name: Specificity of claim limitations vs. high-level results
description: Claims that provide specific steps/structure for achieving a result (a 'way to achieve it') rather than claiming only a desired result are more likely to be eligible.
guidance: Document: 'Claims directed to an improvement ... have specificity required to transform a claim from one claiming only a result to one claiming a way to achieve it.' Lack of detail about how high-level functions are done leads to ineligibility.

name: Recitation of only generic computer components is insufficient
description: Simply reciting generic computer hardware (processor, storage device, server, receiver, standard components) does not make an abstract idea patent eligible.
guidance: Multiple decisions: standard components 'are not sufficient to transform abstract claims into patent-eligible subject matter.' Examiners and courts frequently reject claims where the only added elements are routine computer implementation.

name: Claims performable by a human mind (mental processes) are abstract
description: If claims, when construed broadly, can be performed in the human mind (collecting, comparing, making determinations), they fall into the mental-process category of abstract ideas.
guidance: Examples: coupon fraud detection by comparing data, collecting/comparing information, methods of organizing human activity. PTAB and courts have found such claims abstract when they essentially describe observation, evaluation, and judgment steps.

name: Mathematical algorithms and mathematical concepts are abstract
description: Claims that recite mathematical algorithms, calculations, mapping coordinates, or pure mathematical concepts are treated as abstract ideas unless integrated into a practical application.
guidance: Document: 'Claims recite mathematical concepts and thus abstract ideas under Prong One of the Guidance.' 'Merely calling for a mathematical algorithm to be performed more efficiently ... is not patent eligible.' Use of mathematical output in a concrete application (e.g., controlling a machine, producing an image used to drill) can render eligible.

name: Natural laws / natural principles usage
description: Claims 'directed to the utilization of a natural law' (e.g., Hooke's law, methods of detecting body temperature based on natural principles) implicate Mayo-type exclusion if the claim simply applies the law without more.
guidance: If a claim employs a natural law, courts ask whether the claim integrates that law into an inventive concept or merely uses it in a conventional way. Non-conventional measurement/technique supported by the specification may favor eligibility (Kukkonen example).

name: Preemption analysis — limit claim scope to avoid broad preemption
description: Whether claim limitations and specific structure prevent broad preemption of all ways to achieve the abstract idea is relevant; claims that would preempt all approaches are more likely to be ineligible.
guidance: McRO noted that specific structure of claimed rules would prevent broad preemption; courts consider whether limitations meaningfully restrict use of the abstract idea.

name: Improving user interface or presenting information in a specific structured way
description: Claims that require a 'particular manner of summarizing and presenting information' or a specific, structured GUI that solves identified problems can be non-abstract.
guidance: DDR Holdings and Trading Technologies examples: requirements for a specific structured GUI paired with prescribed functionality that resolves problems in prior art support Step 1 eligibility.

name: Evidence and factual allegations may prevent dismissal on §101
description: Plausible factual allegations and supporting evidence (e.g., declarations, specification details) that an asserted claim contains inventive concepts can preclude dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6) on §101 grounds.
guidance: Aatrix: court held district court improperly dismissed where plaintiff's factual allegations could show inventive concept; examiners and courts should provide reasoning/evidence when finding components 'routine' or 'well-understood.'

name: Dependent claims vs. independent claims — factual questions may arise
description: Dependent claims that add specific limitations may raise factual disputes about whether they contain limitations directed to an arguable inventive concept even when independent claims are found ineligible.
guidance: Berkheimer/Berkheimer-type fact questions: the Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment on dependent claims where specification suggested dependent claims might contain unconventional inventive concepts (e.g., reducing redundancy in object storage).

name: LLM response-generation quality criteria
description: Evaluate generated OA responses on readability/structure, legal-argument depth, specific claim references, technical explanation, and hallucination risk.
guidance: Observed model behaviors: PatentGPT-J-6B often created continuous text blocks with repetition and limited legal depth; Llama 2 improved structure and technical rebuttal but may hallucinate; GPT-3.5 focused on term elucidation and adaptability; GPT-4 provided comprehensive coverage, suggested claim amendments, balanced legal/technical strategies, and used placeholders to reduce hallucination risk.

name: Content required in a prior art citation
description: The prior art submitted under 35 U.S.C. 301 is limited to written prior art consisting of patents or printed publications and must include an explanation of how the submitted art is pertinent and applicable to the patent and why it bears on patentability of any claim.
guidance: At minimum include a broad statement of pertinency/applicability to the claims (e.g., statement that art was made of record in a related application). Preferred to include copies of cited patents/publications and necessary English translations, identification of the patent (number, issue date, patentee), and cover sheet with documents firmly attached. Affidavits or declarations may accompany citations to explain contents or dates; patent owners may include affidavits of commercial success or enablement challenges tied to a cited document. A prior art citation must be directed to patents/printed publications and must not include issues not directed to such documents (e.g., 35 U.S.C. 112 arguments, public use assertions, or statements about the patent owner's conduct). If such extraneous issues are present, the citation should not be entered and should be handled per MPEP §2206.

name: Explanation of pertinency and manner of applying cited art
description: A prior art citation must contain at least some broad statement of the pertinency and applicability of the art submitted to the patentability of the claims of the patent for which the citation is made.
guidance: For reexamination requests, 37 CFR 1.510 requires a detailed explanation pointing out each substantial new question of patentability and the manner of applying cited prior art to every claim for which reexamination is requested; the requester may also point out how claims distinguish over cited art.

name: Ex parte reexamination — basic characteristics
description: Any person can request ex parte reexamination at any time during enforceability; prior art considered is limited to patents or printed publications; a substantial new question of patentability must be present; the actual reexamination proceeding is ex parte if ordered; decision on request must be made no later than 3 months from filing; proceedings proceed with special dispatch; scope and claim amendment limits apply.
guidance: Additional specifics: claims cannot be enlarged by amendment; reexamination normally conducted to conclusion and issuance of a reexamination certificate unless prosecution reopened by Director; reexamination and patent files are open to public (with electronic access via IFW/PAIR).

name: 37 CFR 1.510 — Required content of a request for ex parte reexamination
description: A request must include: (1) a statement pointing out each substantial new question of patentability based on prior patents and printed publications; (2) identification of every claim for which reexamination is requested and a detailed explanation of pertinency and manner of applying the cited prior art to every claim; (3) a copy of every patent or printed publication relied upon, with English translations of necessary parts of non‑English documents; (4) a copy of the entire patent (front face, drawings, specification/claims) and any disclaimers/certificates; (5) a certification that a copy of the request has been served on the patent owner if requester is not the owner; and (6) payment of the reexamination fee (37 CFR 1.510(b)).
guidance: Copies must be plainly written on one side of sheet. If appropriate, requester may point out how claims distinguish over cited art. The Director will send a copy of the request to the owner if requester is not owner. Use of transmittal form PTO/SB/57 is available but not mandatory.

name: Substantial new question of patentability standard
description: Reexamination will be ordered only if the Office determines that a 'substantial new question of patentability' is presented based on prior patents or printed publications (35 U.S.C. 303(a) and 37 CFR 1.510).
guidance: The reexamination statute was amended (e.g., 2002) to expand what qualifies as a substantial new question in specific situations; see MPEP §2242 POLICY IN SPECIFIC SITUATIONS for details. Request must point out each substantial new question and explain how cited art applies to every claim at issue.

name: Limitations on reexamination scope and rejections
description: Prior art considered during reexamination is limited to prior art patents or printed publications applied under the appropriate parts of 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103; certain limitations exist as to the kind of rejections which may be made in reexamination (claims cannot be broadened by amendment).
guidance: Reexamination prosecution is similar to regular examination but with notable differences including special reexamination forms and time periods for special dispatch. See MPEP §§2254–2294 for handling during proceedings.

name: Reexamination of a reexamination — treatment of prior certificate changes
description: A reexamination request filed on a patent for which a reexamination certificate already issued is to be considered based on the patent as modified by the previously issued reexamination certificate (i.e., claims as modified by certificate are the operative claims for the new request).
guidance: When new reexamination file is received, TC clerk must incorporate certificate changes into the reexamination specification prior to forwarding to examiner. Examiner should review the entry to ensure all certificate changes were entered. Any amendment that merely re‑adds italicized (certificate) text already present is improper (informal) and should be handled under 37 CFR 1.530 and MPEP §2266.02. Each reexamination of a reexamination must be reviewed by a TC Special Program Examiner and a TC paralegal.

name: Permissible status information (definition and limits)
description: Status information of an application means only the following information: (A) whether the application is pending, abandoned, or patented; (B) whether the application has been published; (C) the application number or the serial number plus any one of the filing date of the national application, the international filing date, or the date of entry into the national stage; and (D) whether another application claims the benefit of the application and corresponding status information for that application (per 37 CFR 1.14(a)(2) and related text).
guidance: Only these enumerated items may be communicated to the public even where an application is identified; other continuity data (e.g., whether application is CIP/continuation/divisional, abandonment date, issue date) may remain confidential unless specifically authorized.

name: Access to unpublished pending applications whose benefit is claimed
description: A copy of the file contents of an unpublished pending application may be provided upon written request and payment of the fee if the benefit of the application is claimed under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), 120, 121, 365(c), or 386(c) in an application that has issued as a U.S. patent or has published as a statutory invention registration or application publication (per 37 CFR 1.14(a)(1)(v)).
guidance: A copy of the application-as-filed or a specific document in the pending application's file may also be provided under the same conditions. The Office will not provide access to the paper file of a pending application except as provided in paragraphs (c) or (i).

name: Scope and content of the examiner's determination on the request
description: The examiner's determination whether a substantial new question of patentability is raised is based on the claims in effect at the time of determination; the determination becomes part of the official file and is mailed to the patent owner and requester.
guidance: Amendments will not be considered when deciding requests if they: (1) were presented with the request by the patent owner, (2) were filed in a pending reexamination where the certificate has not been issued, or (3) were submitted in a reissue application on which no reissue patent has been issued. The decision's object is to grant or deny an order for reexamination (not to make a final determination of unpatentability). The decision should discuss ALL patent claims to inform the patent owner so a response may be made; the examiner should indicate initial positions on issues identified in the request to allow comment by the patent owner and requester. The examiner should limit discussion to whether a substantial new question has been raised and should not reject claims in the order for ex parte reexamination.

name: Definition and threshold for 'substantial new question of patentability' (SNQ)
description: A reexamination is ordered if the prior art patents and printed publications cited raise a substantial new question of patentability affecting any claim of the patent; the term is developed case-by-case with case law guidance.
guidance: If the prior art patents and printed publications raise a SNQ as to at least one claim, then SNQ is present unless the same question of patentability has already been decided by (A) a final holding of invalidity after all appeals, or (B) by the Office in a previous examination or pending reexamination of the patent. Only one claim need present a SNQ to order reexamination. No prima facie case of unpatentability need be found to grant an order for reexamination. A denial may be petitioned to the Director under 37 CFR 1.181 within one month of mailing of the examiner's determination refusing reexamination; denial is final and nonappealable if no timely petition or if petition decision affirms refusal; partial refund of fee may be made when no SNQ is found (37 CFR 1.26(c)).

name: Requests filed after reissue of the patent
description: If a request for reexamination is filed on a patent after a reissue patent for that patent has issued, reexamination will be denied because the original patent has been surrendered.
guidance: To reexamine a reissued patent, a new request must be filed based on the specification and claims of the reissue patent. If a reissue patent issues after the filing of a request for reexamination (see merge rules in MPEP § 2285).

name: Criteria for deciding second or subsequent requests during a pending reexamination
description: When a second or subsequent ex parte reexamination request is filed while a first ex parte reexamination is pending, whether to order depends on the prior art cited by the later requester and whether it raises a substantial new question of patentability different from that raised in the pending proceeding.
guidance: If the later requester includes prior art that raised the SNQ in the pending reexamination, the second/subsequent request should be denied. If the later request raises a different SNQ or addresses new/amended claims proposed under 37 CFR 1.530(d) in the pending proceeding, reexamination may be ordered to permit examination of the entire patent package. The second/subsequent request should be determined on its own merits. In aggravated situations where the second/subsequent request appears filed for harassment (and a petition is granted), prosecution on the second/subsequent reexamination may be suspended. Merger of a second/subsequent request with an already pending proceeding that would unduly prolong conclusion is disfavored due to the requirement of special dispatch.

name: Succession of patent rights upon death or insanity (section 4896)
description: "When any person, having made any new invention or discovery for which a patent might have been granted, dies before a patent is granted, the right of applying for and obtaining the patent shall devolve on his executor or administrator... in as full manner and on the same terms and conditions as the same might have been claimed or enjoyed by him in his lifetime; and when any person having made any new invention or discovery... becomes insane before a patent is granted, the right... shall devolve on his legally appointed guardian, conservator, or representative in trust for his estate..."
guidance: Covers both death and insanity; legal representatives may make the application and the required oath or affirmation "shall be so varied in form that it can be made by them." The statutory language was amended to specify that the insane-person provision covers applications already on file or thereafter made. Also provides that foreign executors/administrators (where inventor was not domiciled in the U.S.) may apply if their authority is proved by certificate of a U.S. diplomatic or consular officer.

name: Specification, description, and claim requirements (R.S. §4888, as amended 1915)
description: "Before any inventor or discoverer shall receive a patent... he shall file in the Patent Office a written description of the same, and of the manner and process of making, constructing, compounding, and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art or science... to make, construct, compound, and use the same; and in case of a machine, he shall explain the principle thereof, and the best mode in which he has contemplated applying that principle, so as to distinguish it from other inventions; and he shall particularly point out and distinctly claim the part, improvement, or combination which he claims as his invention or discovery. The specification and claim shall be signed by the inventor."
guidance: Codifies enablement, best mode (for machines), and requirement to particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention; signature by inventor required. These are substantive patentability/formal requisites used to evaluate sufficiency of an application/specification.

name: Remedy for patent owners against government use; limitations (Court of Claims Act, June 25, 1910)
description: "Whenever an invention described in and covered by a patent of the United States shall hereafter be used by the United States without license of the owner... such owner may recover reasonable compensation for such use by suit in the Court of Claims: Provided, however, That said Court of Claims shall not entertain a suit... where the claim for compensation is based on the use by the United States of any article heretofore owned, leased, used by, or in the possession of the United States: Provided further, That... the benefits of this Act shall not inure to any patentee who, when he makes such claim is in the employment or service of the Government... nor shall this Act apply to any device discovered or invented by such employee during the time of his employment or service."
guidance: Creates a right to recover reasonable compensation for uncompensated government use, but excludes claims where the U.S. already owned/used the article, permits government defenses available in infringement actions, and excludes patentees who are government employees (and their assignees) and inventions made during employment.

name: Antitrust judgments and tolling of limitations (Antitrust Act §5 and related)
description: A final judgment or decree in any criminal prosecution or suit brought by or on behalf of the United States under the antitrust laws that a defendant has violated such laws shall be prima facie evidence against such defendant in any other suit under said laws; whenever any suit or proceeding is instituted by the United States to prevent, restrain, or punish violations of any of the antitrust laws the running of the statute of limitations in respect of each and every private right of action arising under said laws... shall be suspended during the pendency thereof.
guidance: Provides evidentiary effect to governmental judgments and suspends statute of limitations for related private antitrust claims during pendency of government actions; affects timing and evidentiary strategy in antitrust litigation tied to patent licensing or conduct.

name: How to draft the specification and initial drawings
description: Instructions for drafting the patent specification and preparing required drawings.
guidance: Covers content and form of the written description and drawings needed to support claims (chapter listed in table of contents).

name: Now for the legalese : the claims
description: How to write patent claims — the legal definitions of the invention — including structure and scope considerations.
guidance: Practical guidance on claim drafting, claim scope, and claim language (chapter listed in table of contents).

name: Your application can have children
description: Use of continuations, divisionals, and continuations-in-part to derive additional applications from an earlier filing.
guidance: Explains family practice and procedural options to expand or preserve claim scope (chapter listed in table of contents).

name: Combination-Subcombination distinctness
description: Inventions are distinct if it can be shown that (1) the combination as claimed does not require the particulars of the subcombination as claimed for patentability, and (2) the subcombination has utility by itself or in other materially different combinations (MPEP § 806.05(c)).
guidance: Use form paragraph 8.15 for combination-subcombination restriction. In bracket 3 specify limitations of the claimed subcombination not required by the claimed combination or evidence supporting the conclusion. In bracket 4 suggest separate utility other than used in the combination. The examiner must suggest an example of separate utility; if applicant rebuts with facts, the burden shifts to the examiner to document a viable separate utility or withdraw the requirement. See also MPEP § 806.05(c) and § 821.04 for rejoinder practice.

name: Subcombination essential → not distinct (no restriction)
description: Where a claimed combination requires the details of a separately claimed subcombination (the combination 'requires' the specific characteristics of the subclaim), there is usually no evidence that the combination is patentable without those details; the inventions are not distinct and a restriction must not be made or maintained (MPEP § 806.05(c) I).
guidance: If the combination, as amended or originally claimed, requires all limitations of the subcombination, do not require restriction. If evidence claim ABbr is deleted or amended to require Bsp, the prior restriction should not be maintained. See MPEP § 806.05(c) and § 821.04 on rejoinder.

name: Subcombination not essential → distinctness and restriction proper
description: If the combination as claimed does not require the details of the subcombination and the subcombination has separate utility, the inventions are distinct and restriction is proper provided reasons exist for insisting upon restriction (e.g., serious search or examination burden) (MPEP § 806.05(c) II).
guidance: Diagram as ABbr (broad) vs Bsp (specific); omission of details in ABbr is evidence the combination does not rely on specific limitations of Bsp. Restriction requires demonstration of reasons to insist (see evidence like separate classification, different field of search, status, or non-prior-art issues). Use form paragraph 8.15 and conclude with form paragraph 8.21.

name: Subcombinations usable together — distinctness criteria
description: Two or more claimed subcombinations, disclosed as usable together in a single combination, and which can be shown to be separately usable, are usually restrictable when the subcombinations do not overlap in scope and are not obvious variants (MPEP § 806.05(d)).
guidance: To support restriction, show distinctness and reasons to insist on restriction. Each subcombination is distinct if (A) the combination does not require the particulars of the subcombination for patentability and (B) the subcombination can be shown to have utility either by itself or in another materially different combination. Use form paragraph 8.16; examiner must show one subcombination has utility other than in the disclosed combination and may suggest examples; if applicant rebuts, burden shifts to examiner.

name: Process and apparatus for its practice — distinctness
description: Inventions are distinct if either (1) the process as claimed can be practiced by another materially different apparatus or by hand, or (2) the apparatus as claimed can be used to practice another materially different process (MPEP § 806.05(e)).
guidance: Use form paragraph 8.17 for restriction between process and apparatus. Examiner Note suggests using examples such as (a) materially different apparatus, (b) process can be practiced by hand, (c) apparatus used to practice a materially different process. The examiner must provide reasonable examples that recite material differences; if applicant rebuts, examiner must document another materially different process/apparatus or withdraw the requirement. Conclude with form paragraph 8.21 and include form paragraph 8.21.04 when appropriate for notice of potential rejoinder.

name: Burden of proof and shifting burden on examples/alternative uses
description: The burden is on the examiner to provide examples or show that a subcombination or invention has utility other than in the disclosed combination; if applicant provides facts or convincing evidence that the examiner's suggested use cannot be accomplished, the burden shifts to the examiner to document another viable alternative use or withdraw the restriction requirement (various sections: MPEP § 806.05(c),(d),(e),(f),(g),(h)).
guidance: Examples suggested by the examiner need not always be documented, but must be reasonable. When applicant elects a subcombination and claims thereto are found allowable, any dependent claims requiring all limitations of the allowable subcombination will be examined per 37 CFR 1.104; consider rejoinder practice per MPEP § 821.04.

name: Rejoinder practice when elected claims are allowable
description: Upon determining that all claims directed to an elected combination invention are allowable, the examiner must reconsider the propriety of the restriction requirement; if a subcombination is allowable, non-elected claims requiring that subcombination must be rejoined (MPEP § 806.05(d), § 821.04).
guidance: If a claim to Bsp is allowable, any claims requiring Bsp, including combination claims such as ABsp, must be considered for rejoinder. Rejoined claims will be fully examined for patentability under 37 CFR 1.104; withdrawn process claims not commensurate in scope with an allowable product/apparatus claim will not be rejoined. Use form paragraph 8.21.04 to notify applicant of potential rejoinder and double patenting implications.

name: Claim scope: distinguish apparatus from principle
description: A patentee must not claim a mere principle broadly; the patent is for the particular method or apparatus described in the specification (e.g., Kneller claimed apparatus by which causing evaporation is effected, not the abstract principle).
guidance: Courts construe claims with the specification: where the specification describes a particular apparatus or method, the monopoly extends to that described method/apparatus, not to the general underlying principle. Claiming the principle rather than the concrete means is 'very dangerous.'

name: Specification must accurately describe all new parts and how they operate
description: Every part of the invention which is new must be accurately described as to the manner in which it is to operate (Felton v. Greaves: failure to describe that one roller should be smooth rendered the specification insufficient).
guidance: Describe novel elements and their mode of operation with sufficient detail to show how they perform the claimed function. Omitting essential operational detail for new parts risks invalidity.

name: Do not omit necessary descriptions or conceal practical limitations
description: A specification that omits necessary descriptive matter or misleads about practical limits (e.g., claiming use with substances for which the device is unfit) can be fatal (Clegg retort and other cases).
guidance: Do not overstate the range of applicability; describe practical limits and relevant materials as understood at the time. If the patentee knows the invention is only suitable for certain materials or configurations, disclose that rather than implying universal applicability.

name: Avoid false breadth claims like 'other materials' or 'any other substance'
description: Generic phrases such as 'other materials may be used' or 'any other substance' do not necessarily save a deficient specification and have in cases been nearly fatal (Clegg's gas-retort; 'other materials' did not assist the description).
guidance: If claiming applicability to other materials, indicate which and on what basis; do not rely on broad catch‑alls to cure lack of specificity.

name: Point out the plainest, most practicable method; do not mislead about ease of practice
description: It is the patent-holder's duty to point out the plainest and most easy way of producing what is claimed; if the specification implies a laborious process when a simple purchased ingredient will do (Seidlitz powder case), the public is misled.
guidance: Disclose the practical method you use and avoid suggesting unnecessarily elaborate procedures if simpler, commonly-available alternatives exist. The specification should not cause the public to incur unavailing expense.

name: Do not claim known public matter as new; claim only the true improvement
description: If a specification claims, in addition to the patentee's discovery, something already made public (e.g., exclusion of starch known earlier), the patent may be void (Campion v. Benyon).
guidance: Clearly distinguish and, if necessary, disclaim pre-existing public elements; frame claims to cover the genuine novel contribution (the improvement), not matters already public.

name: If a claimed part later proves useless, patent may still stand
description: Where a patent describes several things and one, thought useful when filed, is later found useless (e.g., a brush in a shearing machine), the grant remains good in law provided the specification was not misleading as to essentials (Lewis v. Marling).
guidance: Claims for multiple aspects are not automatically void if one aspect is later shown useless; however, the patentee must not have represented that the useless part was essential or misled the public.

name: Core Principle: specification is rarely changeable
description: The specification can rarely be changed during prosecution, so the applicant only gets one opportunity to explain how the invention works; claims must be read in light of the specification and a carefully drafted specification is therefore particularly important for later claim construction in litigation.
guidance: Draft the specification to anticipate future claim construction and litigation; treat the specification as the primary record that will constrain claim interpretation. Avoid relying on the idea that prosecution amendments will fix missing disclosures.

name: Plan for future claim combinations
description: Provide a drafting structure that supports later combining of claim elements and dependencies so you can pursue different claim scopes during prosecution and litigation.
guidance: Techniques: file multiply dependent claims and/or include a 'numbered embodiments' section to provide clear basis for later combinations. Draft originally-filed claims that can be re-used as fallback positions.

name: Draft with litigation and invalidation in mind
description: Draft the specification and claims anticipating enforcement and possible invalidation challenges; avoid language or characterizations that could unintentionally limit claim scope or admit prior art.
guidance: Do not make statements that limit scope unnecessarily (e.g., overly definitive descriptions); avoid characterizing the prior art in a way that admits elements as known. Favor wording that preserves alternative claim constructions and avoids narrowing admissions.

name: Avoid 'patent profanity' (limiting language/phrases)
description: Certain common phrases and words can be read as limiting and shrink claim scope if used carelessly in the specification or claims.
guidance: Avoid or use carefully: 'the invention is' / 'the present invention', 'must' / 'essential' / 'critical' / 'necessary', 'always' / 'every' / 'only', and 'preferred' when it functions to limit rather than merely identify a preferred embodiment. Phrase descriptions to avoid unintended limitations.

name: Provide a strong written description
description: Ensure the specification supplies robust written-description support for the full breadth of the claims.
guidance: Include multiple embodiments and examples that cover the breadth of the claimed invention; use pictures, diagrams, and formulas where helpful; provide explicit definitions for ambiguous or novel terms to establish support for claim scope.

name: Drafting for standard-essential patents (SEP) considerations
description: When drafting patents likely to be asserted as standard-essential, tailor the specification and claims to facilitate mapping to standards and implementations.
guidance: Anticipate how a claim chart will map patent features to the standard; use the standard's terminology where possible; cover both upstream and downstream implementations; capture mandatory features of the standard explicitly so the patent can be mapped to required elements.

name: Fintech-specific drafting strategy
description: For financial-technology inventions, draft to emphasize technical improvements and avoid claims that read as purely financial methods (which risk Alice rejections).
guidance: Tie claimed methods to specific computer architectures and document network, security, or efficiency improvements. Avoid claiming pure financial transactions or only financial improvements; show how the invention achieves a technological solution.

name: Avoid added matter (EPO particular concerns)
description: Ensure that every claimed feature has explicit original-filed support and avoid intermediate generalizations that could create added-matter issues under EPO practice.
guidance: Provide explicit basis for each claim feature in the original filing; avoid intermediate generalizations (i.e., extracting and claiming aspects that were only disclosed in combination without basis); consider numbered embodiments to show how features can be combined; be careful with adjectives (e.g., 'low-power' might not support a claim to 'less than 5 watts'). Write claims and disclosure so originally-filed claims can serve as fallback positions.

name: §112(a) written description and enablement
description: The specification must provide a 'written description of the invention, and of the manner and process of making and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to which it pertains, or with which it is most nearly connected, to make and use the same.'
guidance: If an inventor 'claims a lot but describes or enables a little,' the claims can be invalidated (Bonito Boats; Amgen). Courts invalidate AI-related claims that recite features without sufficient detail about operation and function (Impact Engine v. Google). Enablement/written description failures can result from disclosing only certain examples while claiming a broader genus (Amgen).

name: Avoid black-boxing AI features (generic 'machine learning'/'neural networks')
description: Claims that recite AI-related features merely as 'machine learning', 'deep learning', 'neural network', or other high-level terms without elaborating implementation details risk §112 invalidation.
guidance: Example: Impact Engine’s 'compiler' described only as a box in a figure was insufficient. Listing terms like 'reinforcement learning' or 'semi-supervised learning' without substantive disclosure can render claims non-enabled (hypothetical Claim 2 analysis).

name: Genus-species enablement risk post-Amgen
description: A specification that discloses only certain examples may not enable an entire claimed genus; under Amgen, failure to enable the full scope of claims can invalidate genus claims.
guidance: Amgen emphasized that disclosing only certain examples can force a POSITA into 'painstaking experimentation' to make other embodiments. Courts may be more willing to challenge broad genus claims after Amgen.

name: Means-plus-function (§112(b), §112(f)) coverage limitation
description: Means-plus-function claim elements are limited to the 'means ... or the equivalent of the structures, material, or acts described in the patent specification.'
guidance: WMS Gaming; drafters may be tempted to use means-plus-function to avoid specificity, but doing so limits the claim to structures actually disclosed (and equivalents) in the spec and risks narrow construction.

name: Software corresponding-structure requirement: step-by-step algorithm
description: For software means-plus-function claims, the corresponding structure cannot be a general-purpose computer; special programming or a step-by-step algorithm must be disclosed as the corresponding structure.
guidance: Ergo Licensing/CareFusion requires disclosure of an algorithm when special programming is required. Courts have invalidated claims where only a general-purpose computer or an abstraction was cited as structure (Aristocrat; Ergo).

name: Impermissible black-box algorithms under §112(b,f)
description: Disclosing only inputs and outputs or naming an abstract component (an 'access control manager', 'compiler', etc.) without a concrete algorithm is insufficient for §112(b,f) and renders the claim indefinite.
guidance: Augme Technologies (no algorithm beyond inputs/outputs), Blackboard (access control manager = black box), and Finisar (rephrasing function) show courts demand algorithmic detail rather than functional restatement.

name: Functional source code must be demonstrably operational
description: Citing actual source code may satisfy algorithm disclosure requirements, but the code must be functional and demonstrably implement the claimed function.
guidance: In Media Rights Tech. v. Capital One, cited C++ code was non-functional and therefore insufficient; expert testimony showed the code only returned error messages.

name: Claims reciting broad machine-learning methods without detail likely non-enabled
description: Claiming that a module uses 'semi-supervised learning' or 'reinforcement learning' without describing how to implement those methods can cover more embodiments than the specification enables and lead to invalidation under §112(a).
guidance: Hypothetical Claim 2: reciting reinforcement/semi-supervised learning without details presents the same problems as Starrett and Amgen — a POSITA would need undue experimentation.

name: Means-plus-function scope may be limited to specification disclosures
description: Even if algorithmic detail is provided, means-plus-function limitations risk being construed to the particular structures and algorithms disclosed in the specification, narrowing claim scope.
guidance: Takeaway: disclosing details can save claims from indefiniteness but may tighten their scope to the disclosed implementations (risk of limiting effect of means-plus-function claims).

name: Fundamental inventive step test
description: When determining inventive step, decide whether the claimed invention could have been easily made by a person skilled in the art based on prior art references prior to filing. If yes (alone or by combining references), the claim lacks inventive step.
guidance: This is the core obviousness test: compare claimed invention to prior art(s) from the point of view of a person skilled in the art.

name: Per-claim determination
description: When there are two or more claims in an application, the determination of inventive step should be made for each claim individually.
guidance: Each claim's features must be separately assessed against prior art.

name: Examiner's comprehensive consideration
description: The examiner shall consider the overall state of the art, the purpose, technical configuration, advantageous effects of the invention, and applicant arguments to comprehensively determine inventive step, focusing on the difficulty of the technical configuration.
guidance: Pay attention to applicant arguments and assess inventive step in light of the specific purpose and effectiveness of the claimed invention.

name: Three focal considerations for inventive step
description: Determination should consider (1) whether prior art provides motivation to arrive at the claimed subject matter, (2) whether the difference is a mere exercise of ordinary creativity, and (3) whether the claimed invention has advantageous effects over prior art.
guidance: Focus mainly on (1) motivation from prior art and (2) mere exercise of ordinary creativity, while considering (3) advantageous effects as supportive of inventiveness.

name: Procedure for determining inventive step (steps)
description: Procedure: (1) specify the claimed invention (same as novelty), (2) specify scope and content of prior art references (same as novelty), (3) choose the closest prior art and clearly identify differences comparing combined elements as a whole, (4) determine whether the claimed invention could have been easily made by a person skilled in the art in view of prior art/common general knowledge.
guidance: When comparing combined elements, treat the invention's combination as a whole rather than separated elements.

name: Selection of prior art reference (same or relevant technical field)
description: A prior art reference used for comparison should, in principle, be selected from the same technical field as or from a reasonably relevant technical field to the problem, effect, and use of the claimed invention.
guidance: Same technical field typically refers to the industrial field of application but also includes fields inferred from effects/functions of elements. Prior art in different fields may be used if it can be applied to other technical fields or used in solving the claimed problem.

name: Teach-away caution
description: If a prior art description teaches away from the technical idea of the claimed invention, exercise care in selecting it as a prior art reference.
guidance: However, even if a prior art teaches away, it may still be relied upon if other aspects (field relevance, similarity of function/operation) support arriving at the claimed invention (with examples combining two prior art references).

name: Probable cause or motivation grounds
description: Strong grounds that a person skilled in the art would have been led to the claimed invention include suggestions in prior art disclosures, close similarity of problem to be solved, close similarity of function/work/operation, and close relevance of technical fields.
guidance: These grounds support that the claimed invention would have been arrived at from the prior art.

name: Close similarity of a function, work, or operation
description: If close similarity exists in function/work/operation between claimed invention and prior art(s), there can be a well-founded ground that a person skilled in the art would have arrived at the claimed invention.
guidance: Example: applying a particular filter structure from an automobile filter to a home filtering apparatus when functions/operations match.

name: Close relation of technical fields
description: Publicly known technical means from a related technical field can be strong grounds that a person skilled in the art could have easily made the claimed invention.
guidance: Example: structures used for gloves may be applied to socks due to relation of fields.

name: Simple change or limitation of use
description: A claim consisting merely of a use of a known invention or a further simple restriction of such use, without any advantageous effect, is not inventive.
guidance: Example: reusing a synthetic oil as cutting oil when recycling would be naturally expected from delayed lubricating property change.

name: Advantageous effects supporting inventive step
description: If an effect achieved by features defining a claimed invention is advantageous compared to prior art, it supports inventive step — especially if the effect is remarkable and unforeseeable by a person skilled in the art.
guidance: Courts have recognized that unexpected advantageous effects can overcome a prima facie obviousness; this is particularly important in unpredictable fields (selection inventions, chemical inventions). Examiner may consider applicant experiment evidence or arguments if effects are inferable from description/drawings; unsupported assertions should not be considered.

name: Publication of applications (35 U.S.C. 122(b))
description: Subject to exceptions, each application shall be published promptly after expiration of 18 months from the earliest filing date for which benefit is sought; an applicant may request earlier publication.
guidance: Director establishes procedures. The Director's determination to release or not release information concerning a published application is final and nonreviewable. An applicant can request nonpublication at filing and may rescind such request; filing certain foreign applications without timely notice can cause abandonment unless delay shown unintentional. Redacted copies may be submitted when corresponding foreign filings are less extensive; section 154(d) does not apply to claims lacking enabling description in the redacted publication.

name: Access categories for public availability (37 CFR 1.14(a)(1))
description: Records associated with patent applications may be available to the public in specific situations: (i) patented applications and statutory invention registrations; (ii) published abandoned applications; (iii) published pending applications; (iv) unpublished abandoned applications that are identified or relied upon; (v) unpublished pending applications whose benefit is claimed; (vi) unpublished pending applications that are incorporated by reference or otherwise identified; (vii) cases where a petition for access or a power to inspect is required.
guidance: Each category has distinct procedural and fee requirements (e.g., copies upon request and payment under §1.19(b)); redacted copies may limit content for published pending applications if a redacted publication was used. The Office will not provide access to the paper file of a pending application except as provided in paragraphs (c) or (h).

name: Definition/limits of 'status information'
description: Status information means only: (A) whether the application is pending, abandoned, or patented; (B) whether it has been published; (C) the application number or serial number plus a filing/entry date; (D) whether another application claims the benefit of the application (with specified status information for those applications).
guidance: Requesters should be directed to PAIR or FIU for status inquiries. PALM Intranet is used internally to verify and determine status. The rule applies only to subsequent and not prior applications in a chain.

name: Owner's rebuttal brief scope and prohibition on new evidence
description: The rebuttal brief of the owner may be directed to the examiner’s answer and/or any respondent brief. The rebuttal brief of the owner shall not include any new or non-admitted amendment, or an affidavit or other evidence.
guidance: Limit owner rebuttal to responses to answer/respondent briefs; do not introduce new/amended claims or new affidavits/evidence (see 37 CFR 1.116 and 41.63 for exceptions/timing).

name: Board decision authority and new grounds of rejection
description: The Patent Trial and Appeal Board, in its decision, may affirm or reverse each decision of the examiner on all issues raised on each appealed claim, or remand the reexamination proceeding to the examiner for further consideration. The reversal of the examiner’s determination not to make a rejection proposed by the third party requester constitutes a decision adverse to the patentability of the claims ... which will be set forth in the decision of the Patent Trial and Appeal Board as a new ground of rejection under paragraph (b) of this section.
guidance: Board may enter new grounds; reversals of examiner’s refusals to adopt requester rejections become new grounds adverse to patentability.

name: Owner options after Board new ground of rejection and one-month deadline
description: When the Board makes a new ground of rejection, the owner, within one month from the date of the decision, must exercise one of the following two options to avoid termination of the appeal proceeding as to the rejected claim: (1) Reopen prosecution by filing an amendment and/or new evidence; or (2) Request rehearing by the Board under § 41.79, stating with particularity the points believed to have been misapprehended or overlooked.
guidance: Owner has one non-extendable month to choose between reopening (extensions under 1.956 available) or requesting rehearing (no extensions). Responses must be timely and sufficiently particular.

name: NIRC issuance when no new grounds and no party action
description: If no action has been taken by any party to the appeal and at least two weeks after the time for action has expired, the CRU support staff will notify the examiner that the proceeding is ready to be concluded. The examiner will take up the reexamination proceeding for action by issuing a Notice of Intent to Issue Inter Partes Reexamination Certificate (NIRC) in accordance with MPEP § 2687, which will terminate the prosecution of the reexamination proceeding.
guidance: NIRC indicates status of all claims as result of Board decision and includes statements cancelling claims as appropriate; special handling guidance exists for dependent claims (e.g., converting dependent claims to independent form or cancelling) with specified time periods and extension rules.

name: Restriction on filing both rehearing and reopening for same decision
description: Where the Board applies new ground(s) of rejection to at least one claim, the patent owner may file either a response requesting a reopening of prosecution relating to the new ground(s) of rejection or a request for rehearing under 37 CFR 41.79(a)(2) of the new ground(s) of rejection based on the same record. In other words, patent owner may not file both a response requesting a reopening of prosecution and also a request for rehearing under 37 CFR 41.79(a) for the same decision. A patent owner may also not file both a request for rehearing and a conditional request to reopen in the event that the request for rehearing is denied. If such an improper conditional request to reopen prosecution is received, then the submission will be treated as a request to reopen prosecution under 37 CFR 41.77(b)(1).
guidance: Do not submit conflicting/conditional filings; conditional reopenings are treated as reopenings and may have adverse procedural consequences (e.g., termination of appeal to newly rejected claims).

name: Protection limited to well-specified parts vs speculative matter
description: If certain articles are well specified and others are only mentioned in the specification as speculative matter (not intended as perfect instruments), the speculative parts cannot be protected and may be infringed with impunity; but infringement of the well-specified parts cannot be excused.
guidance: Example: Mr. Watt inserted imperfect articles as speculative; those cannot be monopolised. Inventors must be careful to identify what parts they actually claim as perfected.

name: Scope of combination patents and partial use
description: Where a patent is for combinations and proportions producing a new effect, the use of any of the ingredients singly, or in partial combination omitting some, may not be covered as such; yet if a partial combination or differently proportioned composition produces substantially the same result, it may constitute an infringement.
guidance: Determination depends on the nature of the claim: patents for a new combination are distinct from patents on individual ingredients or processes; slight departures that nevertheless reproduce the claimed effect can be infringing.

name: Burden of proof and required evidence by the patentee
description: The plaintiff must be prepared to prove material allegations: that the invention in all parts to which the patent applies is new and useful, that he is the inventor, and that the specification is sufficient in law. A plaintiff must give some evidence to show what his invention was (slight evidence is sufficient to make a prima facie case), after which the defendant must falsify the specification or the claim.
guidance: Sufficiency: experienced and intelligent men versed in the art who have never heard of the invention is good prima facie evidence of novelty; but if one witness states prior use the novelty is destroyed. Slight evidence of operation in the manner specified may suffice to shift burden.

name: When specification defects or concealment affect litigation
description: If it is alleged that the patentee intended to conceal the invention or made an obscure specification (e.g., to prevent foreigners using it), that fact is admissible and may undermine the patentee's claim; the patentee admitted an obscure specification to avoid disclosure may be disadvantaged.
guidance: Courts will examine the specification by reading it in for validity; palpable variance between specification and title may be fatal on the face of the record.

name: Priority claim and supporting documents
description: The applicant must attach to his application, or submit within six months, (a) a written statement specifying the date and number of the earlier filing, the country and the name of the applicant; and (b) a certified copy of the earlier application. Where there are two or more earlier applications, priority may be based only on the earliest application.
guidance: Failure to submit these items in due time results in loss of the benefit of the priority right; any item received more than six months after filing shall be declared inadmissible. Priority has the effect of deeming the application filed on the first application's filing date for protection conditions.

name: Inventive step (not obviousness)
description: An invention involves an inventive step if, having regard to the state of the art, it is not obvious to a person skilled in the art. Assessment asks whether it would have been obvious at the filing date, compared with the state of the art, to arrive at a result within the scope of the claim.
guidance: 'Obvious' means something that does not go beyond the normal progress of technology but follows plainly or logically from the prior art — i.e., something which does not involve the exercise of any skill or ability beyond that to be expected of the person skilled in the art.

name: Description: general part requirements (Patent Regulations, Section 4(1))
description: The description must comprise a general part illustrating the scope of application of the invention and the technique upon which it is based, i.e., the state of the art. Presentation of the state of the art must include references to literature known to the applicant, and must present the special features of the invention over the state of the art, as well as the means necessary for achieving them. This presentation must conform to the presentation given in the claims.
guidance: If the invention cannot be industrially exploited, this must be stated. The general part should make clear how the invention differs from and improves upon the cited prior art.

name: Description: specific part requirements (Patent Regulations, Section 4(2))
description: The description must include a specific part describing the invention in detail, primarily by giving examples or embodiments and possibly referring to a drawing. The invention must be illustrated with examples so that the claims can be considered substantiated.
guidance: If drawings are included, provide a list of figures as an introduction to the specific part. Examples/embodiments should enable the skilled person to carry out the invention and substantiate the claimed scope.

name: Presentation when multiple independent and dependent claims are present (Patent Regulations, Section 5)
description: If the claims contain several independent claims, the inventions corresponding to them are to be presented in the description as specified in Section 4. Subject matter of dependent claims must be presented in the description to such extent as is necessary for the claim to be understood.
guidance: Include embodiments corresponding to dependent claims (the specific part is normally sufficient). Ensure each independent claim is supported by the description.

name: Claims must disclose special characteristics necessary for intended effect (Patent Regulations, Section 13)
description: Each claim must disclose those special characteristics that are necessary for achieving the intended effect.
guidance: Claims should contain the essential technical features that produce the alleged technical effect; lack of these may render claims unsupported or unclear.

name: Clarity/searchability of claims (PRH guideline C.1.3)
description: Claims must be clear and searchable (Patents Office guidance on clarity/searchable claims).
guidance: See PRH Search and Examination Guidelines C.1.3 for specifics on drafting clear, examinable claims and avoiding ambiguity that hampers search and examination.

name: Grounds for revocation/invalidity (Sections 25 and 52)
description: A patent may be revoked or declared invalid if: (1) the patent relates to an invention that does not satisfy the statutory requirements (Sections 1, 1a, 1b or 2); (2) the description is not sufficiently clear to enable a person skilled in the art to carry out the invention; (3) the patent contains subject matter not included in the application as filed; or (4) the scope of protection was extended after the relevant notice (Sections 25(1) and 52(1)).
guidance: These statutory grounds are the key legal criteria applied in oppositions and invalidity actions; ensure examination and claim amendments avoid added matter and extension of scope.

name: Requirement to identify specific facts or information for Rule 56(d) relief
description: A nonmovant must "identify any specific information that would create a genuine dispute of material fact" to justify deferral or denial of summary judgment under Rule 56(d).
guidance: General or vague claims of pending discovery or unspecified defenses will not support 56(d) relief. Courts require specificity as to which facts are expected to be uncovered and how they are material to opposition.

name: Required contents of patent application cover sheet (Article 42)
description: A patent application cover sheet must state: (1) name and domicile of the applicant (or name and place of business if a corporation); (2) name and domicile/place of business of an agent if represented (and firm name/place and designated patent attorney if agent is a patent firm); (3) the title of the invention; (4) the name and domicile of the inventor.
guidance: The cover sheet should also indicate applicant code, priority claim, claim on grace period disclosure exception, and request for examination. The cover sheet must be accompanied by a specification, drawings if necessary, and an abstract.

name: Specification composition requirement
description: A specification filed with an application must contain the description of the invention and the claims, necessary drawings, and an abstract (claims may be submitted later by amendment within prescribed periods).
guidance: The specification serves as both the right document (defining scope) and a technical disclosure for third parties; follow Chapters 3 and 4 (descriptions and claims) for preparation guidance.

name: Title of the invention: brevity, conciseness, identity
description: The title of the invention must be written briefly and concisely according to the subject matter of the invention and shall be identical in the application cover sheet and the specification.
guidance: Avoid ambiguous or wordy titles. Do not include personal names, trademarks, nicknames, expressions indicating only abstract functions, or the word 'patent'. Where multiple categories (product, process, device, use) are claimed, use a concise title encompassing them (e.g., 'Paper, manufacturing process and manufacturing device thereof'). Amend title if claims change; examiners may suggest proper titles or amend ex officio in limited cases. An inappropriate title is not generally a ground for rejection except where clearly inappropriate.

name: Drawings: when required and preparation standard
description: Drawings may be attached when necessary for explanation of the claimed invention; they must be prepared according to the guideline for drawings (Annexed Form No. 17 of Enforcement Rules).
guidance: Where drawings are difficult to prepare per the form (e.g., crystal structures, fibers, oscilloscope results), pictures may replace drawings if they clearly can be laid open in the Official Gazette; grayscale or color accepted if unavoidable. For utility model registration, drawings must be included (failure = illegitimate application returned). Irrelevant drawings may be indicated and notified; attachment errors that do not affect practice may be treated as references but not as grounds for rejection. Submitting new drawings by amendment may constitute adding new matter; examiners must be cautious.

name: Enablement requirement (Article 42(3)(i))
description: The description of the invention shall be written clearly and fully so that any person skilled in the art can easily practice the invention based on ordinary skill, the specification and drawings at the time of filing, without adding special knowledge or undue trial and error.
guidance: Enablement means a skilled person fully understands and reproduces the invention using routine skill at filing. The 'invention to be practiced' is interpreted as the invention recited in the claims; disclosure only in the description but not in the claims does not trigger Article 42(3)(i).

name: Subject of practicing the invention (claims-centered)
description: The invention that must be enabled is the invention recited in the claims; if an invention is disclosed only in the description but not claimed, lack of enablement for that unclaimed matter does not violate Article 42(3)(i).
guidance: Examiner assessment focuses on whether a person skilled in the art can practice the claimed invention as defined by the claims.

name: Enablement for product inventions
description: For product inventions recited in the claims, the description must contain clear and full explanations enabling a skilled person to produce the product; generally the manufacturing method needs to be fully described unless the product can be manufactured based on spec and drawings with ordinary skill.
guidance: Describe roles and functions of each special technical feature. Also describe how to use the product unless use is obvious from spec/drawings and ordinary skill.

name: Relationship of enablement and claim support (Articles 42(3) vs 42(4)(i))
description: Article 42(3) (enablement) applies where a skilled person may not easily reproduce the claimed invention based on the description; Article 42(4)(i) (lack of support) applies where the claimed invention is not disclosed in the description or is outside the scope of what the description discloses to a skilled person.
guidance: Determine whether claims are supported by the description by assessing if the subject matter of the claims is disclosed in the description for a skilled person. If description cannot be generalized to claimed scope, claims are not supported.

name: Genus-species support rules
description: If claims recite a genus but the description only discloses species and the genus cannot be clearly recognized from species, Article 42(4)(i) applies; conversely, if description discloses only a specific embodiment and other embodiments in the generic claims cannot be easily practiced, Article 42(3) also applies.
guidance: Apply Article 42(4)(i) or 42(3)(i) depending on whether the issue is lack of disclosure of the genus or lack of enablement of other embodiments within the genus; examples given for molding methods and oxygen-absorbing compositions illustrate these points.

name: Markush/grouping support requirement
description: Where a Markush grouping is used in claims but the description only discloses embodiments for some constituents and not others so that a skilled person cannot easily practice the rest, an examiner shall notify rejection under Article 42(3).
guidance: If embodiments for the other members of the group are not disclosed in sufficient detail, lack of enablement/support will be found (example: nitration of substituted benzenes where only one substituent's behavior is disclosed).

name: Consistency of terms between description and claims
description: If terms used in the description and the claims do not clearly match, the examiner shall notify a ground for rejection citing violation of Article 42(4)(i) because the claim is not supported by the description.
guidance: Ensure terminology in claims and description align so a skilled person recognizes the claimed subject matter in the description.

name: Citing best references and explaining pertinence
description: In rejecting claims for want of novelty or for obviousness, the examiner must cite the best references at his or her command. When a reference is complex or shows or describes inventions other than that claimed by the applicant, the particular part relied on must be designated as nearly as practicable. The pertinence of each reference, if not apparent, must be clearly explained and each rejected claim specified.
guidance: Cite patent numbers/dates/names (or publication numbers/dates/names for applications); identify specific pages/parts for foreign docs or printed publications; clearly explain how each reference pertains to each rejected claim.

name: Reliance on admissions and examiner's personal-knowledge facts
description: In rejecting claims the examiner may rely upon admissions by the applicant, or the patent owner in a reexamination proceeding, as to any matter affecting patentability and, insofar as rejections in applications are concerned, may also rely upon facts within his or her knowledge pursuant to paragraph (d)(2) of this section.
guidance: If a rejection is based on facts within an Office employee's personal knowledge, the data shall be as specific as possible and the reference must be supported, when called for by the applicant, by the affidavit of such employee, subject to contradiction/explanation by applicant affidavits.

name: Use of subject matter qualifying as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(e),(f),(g) and joint research agreement rule
description: Subject matter which is developed by another person which qualifies as prior art only under 35 U.S.C. 102(e), (f) or (g) may be used as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 103 against a claimed invention unless the entire rights to the subject matter and the claimed invention were commonly owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person at the time the claimed invention was made.
guidance: Defines when subject matter is deemed commonly owned via joint research agreements (three-part test: agreement in effect on/before date invention made; invention result of activities within scope; application discloses or is amended to disclose parties). To overcome a 103 rejection based on such art, applicant must provide a statement that the parties were in a qualifying joint research agreement and the invention resulted from activities within its scope.

name: Reasons for allowance must be stated when unclear
description: If the examiner believes that the record of the prosecution as a whole does not make clear his or her reasons for allowing a claim or claims, the examiner may set forth such reasoning.
guidance: Reasons for allowance should be incorporated into an Office action rejecting other claims or sent as a separate communication; the applicant/patent owner may file comments within a specified time. Failure to respond does not imply anything.

name: Types of first action (ACP vs. rejection action)
description: Where all of the patent claims are found patentable in the first action, the examiner will issue an Action Closing Prosecution (ACP). Where the examiner determines that one or more of the patent claims are to be rejected, the first Office action on the merits will be similar to a first action on the merits in an application (or ex parte reexamination) where a rejection is made.
guidance: Even when following application-style format, inter partes reexamination practice must be followed: use inter partes forms, set special time periods, use inter partes form paragraphs, and send copies to both patent owner and third party requester.

name: Content standard for first Office action (establish issues)
description: The examiner’s first Office action will be a statement of the examiner’s position, and it should be sufficiently complete so that the second Office action can be an Action Closing Prosecution (ACP). It is intended that the first Office action be the primary action to establish the issues which exist.
guidance: First action should be comprehensive and address all prior art patents/printed publications; set forth each ground of rejection/objection and the supporting reasons; specify determinations favorable to patentability and reasons for refusing to adopt requester-proposed rejections; respond to each argument in the request under 37 CFR 1.915. If incorporating a claim chart, carefully review to ensure incorporated items clearly and completely address patentability.

name: Incorporation and review of requester materials (claim charts)
description: Where the request for reexamination includes material such as a claim chart to explain a proposed rejection ... the examiner may bodily incorporate the claim chart (or other matter) within the Office action.
guidance: Examiner must carefully review any incorporated claim chart or material to ensure that items incorporated in a statement of the rejection clearly and completely address the patentability of the claims.

name: Dependent claim handling when base claims canceled or amended
description: If an unamended base patent claim (i.e., a claim appearing in the patent) has been rejected or canceled, any claim undergoing reexamination which is directly or indirectly dependent thereon should be indicated as patentable if it is otherwise patentable. The dependent claim should not be objected to nor rejected merely because it depends upon a rejected or canceled original patent claim.
guidance: No requirement for rewriting the dependent claim in independent form. If a new base claim has been canceled in reexamination, a claim which depends thereon should be rejected as indefinite. If an amended base patent claim or a new base claim is rejected, a claim dependent thereon should be objected to if it is otherwise patentable, and a requirement should be made for rewriting the dependent claim in independent form as appropriate.

name: Examiner Duties under MPEP §707.07(f)
description: When reviewing and acting on an applicant's response, the examiner must provide clear explanations of actions taken, a complete application file history, and substantive answers to traversed requirements (MPEP § 707.07(f); 37 C.F.R. § 1.112).
guidance: Specific duties include: make proper reference to amendments when requirements are traversed and answer their substance; if repeating a rejection, note applicant's argument and answer its substance; if applying a prior rejection to new/amended claims, specifically identify that ground (cite original rejection); if asserted advantages are insufficient, state reasons in the record; if withdrawing a rejection, state reasons and cite relevant pages/lines of applicant remarks. Failure to perform these duties can render an action incomplete and petitionable.

name: Drafting the Petition: Structure and Emphasis
description: The petition should be short and structured—Introduction, Facts, Argument, Request for Relief—and should focus on demonstrating the challenged office action is facially incomplete while expressly avoiding substantive review of rejections.
guidance: Introduction should request Group Director find the action incomplete and instruct issuance of a new complete office action; state petition is not seeking review on merits. Facts should summarize the applicant's most recent filing and the office action omissions with page citations. Argument should cite the relevant statute/regulation/MPEP authorities (notably MPEP § 707.07(f)) and apply completeness requirements to demonstrated omissions. Request for Relief should ask withdrawal of the challenged office action and instruction to the examiner to issue a new complete office action examining all claims and addressing all remarks.

name: Request for Relief Content
description: The petition's request should ask that the current office action be withdrawn and that the Group Director instruct the examiner to issue a new complete office action that examines all claims and fully addresses all applicant remarks and arguments.
guidance: A granted petition usually results in vacating the challenged action and issuance of a replacement office action with a shortened statutory response time; the replacement may be non-final or final. A grant often results in some patent term adjustment (PTA) accrual.

name: Grounds for invalidity of utility models
description: Utility models shall be declared invalid if they (a) are not new, lack inventive step, or are not industrially applicable; (b) are not registrable under Article 4 (e.g., prohibited articles); or (c) the specification does not conform to required stipulations or fails to state true methods completely and truthfully.
guidance: Invalidity may relate to all or some claims; certificates for improvements not connected with the utility model shall likewise be declared invalid.

name: Right to the mark determined by first filing
description: Ownership of a mark belongs to the person who first deposited it; joint ownership allowed; exclusive ownership cannot be claimed by performing acts unless filed for registration as prescribed.

name: Ascertaining the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art
description: Office personnel must interpret the claim language and consider both the invention and the prior art as a whole to ascertain differences between the claimed invention and the prior art.
guidance: Interpreting claim language should follow MPEP § 2111 and the analysis in MPEP § 2141.02. The examiner must consider the entire prior art and claimed invention when identifying the distinctions relied upon in an obviousness rejection.
