name: Articulation of factual findings and reasoned explanation supporting an obviousness rejection
description: The key to supporting any rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 is the clear articulation of the reason(s) why the claimed invention would have been obvious; rejections cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements.
guidance: Office personnel must ensure the written record includes findings of fact concerning state of the art and teachings of applied references and must provide an explanation (rationale) linking those facts to the legal conclusion (Kahn/KSR). Examiners should explicitly state findings and rationale so applicant can respond (35 U.S.C. 132). Failure to articulate reasoning is an error; simply asserting lack of documentation is insufficient as a traverse by applicant.

name: Claim construction: give claims the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification
description: The scope of the claimed invention must be clearly determined by giving the claims the 'broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.'
guidance: Claim scope determination guides what to search and what prior art to apply; see Phillips v. AWH and MPEP § 2111. Accurate claim interpretation is foundational to identifying differences from prior art and to articulating factual findings.

name: Applicant reply requirements under 37 CFR 1.111(b)
description: An applicant must distinctly and specifically point out the supposed errors in the Office’s action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the Office action.
guidance: A proper reply must present reasoned arguments pointing out specific distinctions believed to render the claims patentable over applied references. Mere statements that the Office hasn't established a prima facie case or that common knowledge is unsupported by documentary evidence are inadequate (and may permit the examiner to repeat the rejection or make it final). See MPEP § 706.07(a).

name: State Street 'useful, concrete, and tangible result' test (criticized)
description: The Federal Circuit's prior State Street test allowed patentability for anything producing a 'useful, concrete, and tangible result,' a standard which the Supreme Court disapproved of as too expansive.
guidance: Avoid relying on State Street's broad formulation for eligibility; courts and examiners have been warned not to read §101 to embrace that standard. This is relevant for business-method-like diagnostic claim forms.

name: Subject matter eligibility as a threshold test
description: Courts often describe §101 as 'only a threshold test' before examining other statutory requirements (novelty, nonobviousness, utility, disclosure), but current doctrine provides minimal clarity for functioning as a practical initial screen.
guidance: Although framed as preliminary, §101 should be applied thoughtfully because it may directly exclude claims that otherwise meet §102/§103/§112; do not treat it as a perfunctory step.

name: Claiming 'basic scientific relationships' (determine-and-infer claims)
description: Claims that monopolize a basic scientific relationship (e.g., correlating a biomarker with disease) risk invalidation as claiming a basic scientific relationship or natural phenomenon (Metabolite/Prometheus discussion).
guidance: Scrutinize claims framed as 'assaying and correlating' — mere recitation of a correlation without novel, concrete application or inventive steps may be excluded under §101; drafting should tie correlations to inventive laboratory steps, specific transformations, or applications.

name: Function of subject matter doctrine: limiting claim scope to preserve public domain
description: Patentable subject matter doctrine can function to leave some aspects of discoveries in the public domain and to limit the allowable scope of claims in ways that differ from prior art and disclosure constraints.
guidance: Use §101 to consider whether granting broad claims would unduly impede future research by excluding 'basic tools' from public use; analyze whether claimed subject matter should remain free for subsequent innovators even if novel or inventive.

name: Basic tools of scientific and technological work principle
description: Courts frequently invoke the idea that excluded subject matter constitutes 'basic tools' of scientific or technological work; the justification is to avoid granting patents that impede future innovation by monopolizing foundational knowledge.
guidance: Evaluate whether the claimed matter is a foundational building block likely to be widely used; if so, consider whether exclusion from patentability or narrowing of claim scope is appropriate to protect downstream innovation.

name: Written description requirement as a distinct constraint on claim scope
description: The written description requirement under §112 has been fortified by the Federal Circuit and operates separately from enablement to limit claim scope, especially in biotech (Ariad en banc and related cases).
guidance: Ensure the specification provides adequate written description for the claimed invention's full scope (e.g., later-developed embodiments may require explicit description); written description often controls claim breadth in biotech patents.

name: Enablement doctrine and undue experimentation
description: Enablement requires disclosure sufficient for a person skilled in the art to make and use the full scope of the claims without undue experimentation; inconsistent case law exists about whether a single embodiment can enable broad claims and how to treat future technologies.
guidance: Assess whether the patent disclosure enables the entire claimed genus, particularly where claims cover future or after-arising technologies. Be cautious: courts differ on whether a single embodiment suffices to enable broad claims.

name: Claims covering future/after-arising technologies
description: Claims that encompass future embodiments using technologies not available at filing raise special enablement/written-description problems; precedent is mixed on whether such claims are enabled.
guidance: When drafting or evaluating claims that anticipate future technological developments, provide robust disclosure of principles, exemplars, and guidance to reduce risk of invalidation for lack of enablement or written description.

name: Use of §101 as a backstop to limit overly broad claims on fundamental principles
description: Subject matter doctrine can act as an additional check to prevent claims that would monopolize fundamental principles or natural phenomena, protecting downstream innovators where prior art constraints are weak.
guidance: If novelty/nonobviousness cannot adequately contain claim breadth (e.g., few prior art constraints), consider §101 analysis to determine whether aspects of the claim must remain in the public domain.

name: PHOSITA-perspective for defining 'basic tools' or eligibility
description: One proposed approach is to assess whether something is a 'basic tool of scientific and technological work' from the perspective of a person having ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA), which would focus the analysis on the costs and effects for practitioners in the field.
guidance: Consider deploying a PHOSITA-centered inquiry when arguing whether a claimed subject matter is foundational and should remain public; this reframes the test in pragmatic, field-specific terms but does not eliminate line-drawing difficulty.

name: Avoid treating §101 as a vehicle for broader policy preferences without principled analysis
description: Courts and commentators sometimes use §101 to achieve policy results better addressed by other doctrines or legislative action; this risks doctrinal confusion and unpredictability (critique that §101 rejections act as proxies for other standards).
guidance: Advocate for using the most appropriate doctrinal tool (novelty, nonobviousness, disclosure, claim construction, or statutory reform) rather than shoehorning policy objections into §101; where §101 is used, provide principled reasoning linking exclusion to concrete harms (e.g., blocking downstream research).

name: Claims that impermissibly 'claim a monopoly' over basic relationships
description: Claims that effectively grant a monopoly over a basic scientific relationship (e.g., correlation between a biomarker and disease) may be invalid under §101 because they would require every practitioner to seek a license to think about or use that relationship.
guidance: Draft and evaluate claims to avoid language that reads as claiming the relationship per se; incorporate concrete, inventive, and application-specific limitations (transformations, particular assay steps, or treatment decision rules tied to technology) to reduce §101 risk.

name: Figure descriptions and permissible specification statements
description: Figure descriptions should indicate what each view represents (front elevational, top plan, perspective, etc.). Aside from a brief description of the drawing, additional descriptions are generally unnecessary but permissible. Permissible statements include: (1) description of portions not illustrated (e.g., 'right side is mirror image of left side'); (2) disclaiming portions not shown that form no part of the claimed design; (3) statement that broken line illustration of environmental structure is not part of the design; (4) description denoting the nature and environmental use if not in the preamble.
guidance: Keep figure descriptions precise. Use allowed special descriptions when omitting views or using broken lines.

name: Single claim form and wording
description: A design patent application may include only a single claim. The claim must be in formal terms: 'The ornamental design for (the article which embodies the design or to which it is applied) as shown.' If the specification properly includes a special description or modified forms, add the words 'and described' after 'shown.' The terminology in the claim's description of the article should be consistent with the title.
guidance: Follow the exact formal language and ensure consistency with title and figure descriptions. Examples of claim wordings are provided in the Sample Specification and Disclosure Examples.

name: Drawings or black & white photographs as the primary visual disclosure
description: Every design patent application must include either drawings or a black and white photograph as the entire visual disclosure of the claim. The drawing or photograph must be clear and complete so nothing regarding the design is left to conjecture and must comply with 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, by including a sufficient number of views.
guidance: Drawings normally in black ink on white paper. Photographs allowed subject to 37 CFR §1.84(b)(1) and §1.152. Do not combine photographs and ink drawings in a formal submission. Photographs must not disclose environmental structure and must be limited to the claimed design.

name: Color drawings or photographs rules
description: Color drawings or photographs are accepted only after granting of a petition under 37 CFR §1.84(a)(2) explaining necessity, including the fee (37 CFR § 1.17(h)), three sets of color drawings/photographs, a black & white photocopy that accurately depicts the subject matter, and a required statement in the specification indicating the file contains color drawings.
guidance: If color photographs are submitted informally and color is not part of the claimed design, add the disclaimer: 'The color shown on the claimed design forms no part thereof.' Absent such disclaimer, color will be considered an integral part of the claimed design.

name: Views: sufficiency, perspective, and omissions
description: Drawings/photographs must contain a sufficient number of views to completely disclose the appearance of the claimed design (front, rear, right, left, top, bottom). Perspective views are suggested to show 3D appearance. Duplicate or flat views with no ornamentality may be omitted if the specification explicitly states mirror images/identities. 'Unornamented' should not describe visible surfaces that are clearly not flat.
guidance: If surfaces shown in perspective are fully disclosed, those surfaces normally need not be illustrated in other views. Sectional views are permissible to bring out elements of the design but not to show functional interior structure. For surface ornamentation claims, the article must be shown in broken lines.

name: Broken line usage and conventions
description: Broken lines are understood to be illustrative only and form no part of the claimed design. When used, broken lines should not intrude upon or cross the showing of the claimed design and should not be heavier than the lines used to depict the claimed design.
guidance: If a broken line environmental structure necessarily intrudes on the claimed design and obscures understanding, include a separate figure that discloses the claimed design without such intrusion. For surface ornamentation, the environment/article must be in broken lines to indicate it is not claimed.

name: Examination standards and reasons for rejection
description: Examination entails checking for compliance with formalities, ensuring completeness of the drawing disclosure, and comparing claimed subject matter with the prior art (issued patents and published materials). Rejection may occur if disclosure is incomplete/unclear or if prior art shows the design to be unpatentable.
guidance: An Office action will detail rejections and may suggest amendments. Keep all Office actions for your files; do not send them back to the Office. Address each rejection specifically in any reply.

name: Responding to Office actions: specificity and procedural items
description: Replies must be timely and in writing, must distinctly and specifically point out supposed errors in the Office action, and must address every objection/rejection. A general statement that the claim is patentable without addressing how it is patentable over prior art does not comply.
guidance: Include identifying information in all communications: application number, group art unit number, filing date, name of examiner, title of invention. Attach a Certificate of Mailing as evidence of timely mailing. If a receipt is desired, include a stamped, self-addressed postcard listing papers submitted to be date-stamped and returned.

name: Amendments and prohibition on new matter
description: Amendments to the application (specification, claims, drawings) must follow 37 CFR 1.121 and related rules. No amendment may introduce new matter into the disclosure. Changes to drawings must be submitted on a separate paper showing proposed changes (in red) for examiner approval; upon approval, new compliant drawings must be filed.
guidance: Amendments to specification paragraphs or sections must include clean replacement text and, when required, a marked-up version showing changes. Reinstating deleted matter requires a subsequent amendment presenting the previously deleted matter. Claim amendments must be presented in clean form and accompanied by marked-up versions showing changes.

name: Arrangement of application elements and specification section headings (37 CFR §1.154)
description: Where applicable, application elements should appear in the following order: (1) design application transmittal form; (2) fee transmittal form; (3) application data sheet; (4) specification; (5) drawings or photographs; (6) executed oath/declaration. The specification should include sections in order: preamble; cross-reference to related applications; statement regarding federally sponsored research; description of figures; feature description; a single claim. Section headings should be uppercase letters without underlining or bold.
guidance: Follow the enumerated order and heading conventions to facilitate processing and examination.

name: Double patenting prohibition applies to divisional inventions
description: Only inventions claimed in a divisional application may potentially be subject to the prohibition against double patenting rejections under 35 U.S.C. 121.
guidance: Text revised to replace 'continuing' with 'divisional' to clarify scope; applies in context of restriction/election and rejoinder analysis.

name: Procedure when elected claims all found allowable after amendment
description: Added a new paragraph explaining the procedure when the examiner finds all elected claims allowable following the amendment that added claims drawn to a new invention.
guidance: Specifies steps to follow when amendment introduces new-invention claims and subsequently the elected claims are determined allowable; ensures proper treatment of nonelected claims and rejoin/withdrawal issues.

name: Restriction withdrawal when all nonelected claims are rejoined 'in its entirety'
description: Added 'in its entirety' to clarify that the restriction is entirely withdrawn when all claims to the nonelected invention are rejoined.
guidance: When full rejoinder occurs, the prior restriction should be considered fully withdrawn; examiners should use the clarified language when documenting withdrawal.

name: Clarify 'still withdrawn' wording for nonelected claims
description: Inserted 'still' before 'withdrawn' to clarify that the nonelected claims were previously withdrawn and are not being rejoined.
guidance: Use precise wording to avoid confusion about the status of nonelected claims in the file history.

name: Consideration of variant embodiments not disclosed
description: Variant embodiments which are included in the breadth or scope of a claim but not disclosed in the application may anticipate or render obvious a claim and should be considered during search.
guidance: Search and obviousness analyses should account for claim scope that covers variants not explicitly disclosed; such variants can be relevant prior art considerations.

name: Elements of a thorough and complete search
description: A thorough and complete search will include the identification and review of the areas with the highest probability of including prior art and the search should cover disclosed features related to the inventive concept of the claims.
guidance: Searchers must identify high-probability areas, review disclosed features tied to the inventive concept, and ensure the search covers both claimed subject matter and reasonably expected claimable features.

name: Search should cover claimed subject matter and disclosed inventive features
description: The search should cover the claimed subject matter and should also cover the disclosed features related to the inventive concept of the claims which might reasonably be expected to be claimed.
guidance: Do not limit searches only to literal claim language — include disclosed embodiments and features tied to the inventive concept that could reasonably be claimed later.

name: RCE filing and continuation timing after Federal Circuit decision
description: Applicants wanting to continue prosecution where all claims are rejected after a Federal Circuit decision must file a continuation application prior to the court mandate because RCE under 37 CFR 1.114 is not available in that situation.
guidance: This is a procedural limitation affecting how to continue prosecution post-appellate decisions; examiners and applicants must follow the timing rules described.

name: Reissue oath/declaration and 'at least one error' requirement
description: Clarified that the reissue oath or declaration must specifically identify the claim and the error to support a broadening reissue and that examiners should not object if more than one error is stated; 'at least one error' is pursuant to 35 U.S.C. 251 and required by 37 CFR 1.175(a).
guidance: Examiner review of reissue filings should focus on compliance with statutory/regulatory specificity requirements and updated case law citations; do not improperly restrict the number of errors stated.

name: Design protection and segregable parts
description: Design protection does not extend to patentably distinct segregable parts of a design; a design patent covers only the design disclosed as an entirety.
guidance: If parts are patentably distinct segregable parts, the only way to protect them is separate patents (Ex parte Sanford; Blumcraft v. Ladd). Combination/subcombination subject matter, if patentably distinct, must be supported by separate claims; only a single claim is permissible in a design patent application (In re Rubinfield).

name: Same-invention double patenting (35 U.S.C. 171) criteria
description: A statutory design-design double patenting rejection under 35 U.S.C. 171 prevents issuance of a second patent for a design already patented; requires identical designs with identical scope to be twice claimed.
guidance: For this type of rejection to be proper, identical designs with identical scope must be twice claimed (In re Goodman). A terminal disclaimer may not be used to overcome a 'same invention' type double patenting rejection (In re Thorington; In re Swett). Use form paragraph 15.23.02 following such rejections.

name: Design-utility and design-design 'same invention' considerations
description: A design-utility 'same invention' double patenting rejection is based on judicial doctrine since certain statutory sections cannot be applied against both claims.
guidance: The 'same invention' type, whether statutory or nonstatutory, cannot be overcome by terminal disclaimer. Use the designated form paragraph sequence.

name: Nonstatutory double patenting — obviousness-type criteria
description: An obviousness-type nonstatutory double patenting rejection applies to claims directed to the same inventive concept with different appearances which are obvious variations of each other; differences are not patentably distinct.
guidance: The obviousness standard of 35 U.S.C. 103(a) applies: differences must be de minimis/unrelated to overall aesthetic or obvious to a designer of ordinary skill in the art in view of prior art or case law. This type of rejection may be overcome by submission of a terminal disclaimer if conditions are met (common ownership).

name: Nonstatutory double patenting — differing scope criteria (A/B/C test)
description: A nonstatutory differing-scope double patenting rejection is appropriate if: (A) the difference in scope is de minimis and unrelated to overall aesthetic appearance; (B) patent protection for the design, fully disclosed in and covered by the claim of the reference, would be extended by allowance of the later claim; and (C) no terminal disclaimer has been filed.
guidance: This situation often involves a combination (narrow claim) vs a subcombination/element (broad claim). Examiner must determine whether the narrower claim is fully disclosed in and covered by the broader claim reference (including title, description, or broken-line drawings). If not fully disclosed, the double patenting rejection is inappropriate.

name: Form paragraph procedures for obviousness-type double patenting (single reference)
description: Standard form paragraph language to reject a claim under the obviousness-type double patenting doctrine based on a single prior patent.
guidance: Insert conflicting prior U.S. patent number and an explanation why claims are not patentably distinct. Precede with paragraph 15.24.06 and follow with form paragraph 15.67 (rationale for 103(a) rejection).

name: Form paragraph procedures for obviousness-type double patenting (multiple references)
description: Standard form paragraph language to reject a claim under the obviousness-type double patenting doctrine based on multiple references.
guidance: Insert conflicting patent number and secondary reference(s), and explain basis for rejection including how a designer of ordinary skill would have been led to combine references. Precede with paragraph 15.24.06 and follow with form paragraph 15.68 (rationale for 103(a) with multiple references).

name: Rationale for 35 U.S.C. 103(a) rejections — overall appearance test
description: Unobviousness in design patents is determined by the overall appearance of the claimed design compared with the prior art, not by minute details or small variations.
guidance: Cite In re Frick and In re Lamb. Examiner should articulate why overall appearance is unobvious when making a 103(a) rejection; use form paragraphs 15.67 (single reference) and 15.68 (multiple references) as applicable.

name: Identical claim with common assignee — priority resolution requirement
description: When a claim is directed to the same invention as a claim of a commonly assigned copending application, the issue of priority under 35 U.S.C. 102(f)/(g) must be resolved.
guidance: Since PTO normally will not institute interferences between commonly owned applications, the assignee is required to state which entity is the prior inventor of the conflicting subject matter. A terminal disclaimer has no effect here because the basis is priority of invention; failure to comply will result in abandonment of the application.

name: Nonstatutory double patenting based solely on improper timewise extension
description: A claim may be rejected under the nonstatutory double patenting doctrine if allowance of the later claim would improperly extend the right to exclude granted in an earlier patent (differing scope based solely on timewise extension).
guidance: Use when subject matter of the later claim is fully disclosed in issued patent commonly owned or with common inventorship and the claims are not patentably distinct (Blumcraft v. Ladd; In re Schneller). Precede with form paragraph 15.24.06.

name: Provisional nonstatutory double patenting with another application (differing scope)
description: A provisional rejection may be made under the nonstatutory differing-scope doctrine over a copending application if allowance of the claim would improperly extend the right to exclude granted in any patent that may issue on the copending application.
guidance: Use only when the subject matter of the claim is fully disclosed in the copending application which is commonly owned or has common inventorship and the claims are not patentably distinct. Precede with form paragraph 15.24.06.

name: Right of priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(b) — certification and timing
description: No design application is entitled to right of priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(b) unless a claim and a certified copy of the original foreign application, specification and drawings are filed in the USPTO before the issue fee is paid or at such time during pendency as required by the Commissioner (not earlier than six months).
guidance: Certification shall be made by the foreign Patent Office or other proper authority and show the date of the application and filing of specification and papers. Commissioner may require translation and other information. The notation requirement on application file wrappers when foreign priority is claimed is in MPEP § 202.03.

name: Examination of priority papers for design patents
description: Unlike some practice, in design patent applications the priority papers will normally be inspected to determine that the foreign application is for the same invention as the U.S. application (35 U.S.C. 119).
guidance: If inspection indicates the prior foreign application was not for the same invention as claimed, the priority claim is improper and the papers are returned. Attention is directed to handling cases where an actual model was originally filed in Germany (MPEP § 201.14(b)).

name: Determination of volunteer versus militia status depends on statutory authority
description: If volunteers actually performed service at a time when an act of Congress authorized them to be raised, maintained, and employed, their status is determined to be that of Volunteers; absent such statutory authorization, their claim to volunteer status must fail even if paid or recognized administratively.
guidance: Executive recognition or payment alone cannot substitute for statutory authorization.

name: Content of the prior art must be determined as of the time the invention was made (avoid hindsight)
description: The content of the prior art is determined at the time the invention was made to avoid impermissible hindsight. Decisionmakers must 'cast the mind back to the time the invention was made... to occupy the mind of one skilled in the art.'
guidance: This requirement helps avoid hindsight bias when comparing prior art to claimed inventions. See MPEP § 2145 subsection X.A. and W.L. Gore & Associates v. Garlock. Examiners should not rely on later-acquired understanding to judge what would have been obvious at the relevant time.

name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) — applicant burden to show conditions apply
description: An applicant subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 who wants to avail of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) benefits has the burden of establishing that subject matter which only qualifies as prior art under subsection (e), (f) or (g) of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 used in a rejection under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.
guidance: To establish joint research provisions of pre-AIA 103(c) (for applications pending on or after Dec 10, 2004), the applicant must establish: (A) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the invention date; (B) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities within the scope of that agreement; and (C) the patent application discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the agreement. See MPEP § 706.02(l)(1)-(2) and case law (e.g., In re Bartfeld).

name: Reference must be analogous prior art to be relied on under 35 U.S.C. 103
description: In order for a reference to be proper for use in an obviousness rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103, the reference must be analogous art to the claimed invention. A reference is analogous art if: (1) the reference is from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention (even if it addresses a different problem); or (2) the reference is reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor (even if it is not in the same field).
guidance: Examiner must determine what is 'analogous prior art' for obviousness analysis (In re Bigio; KSR v. Teleflex). The examiner may include a statement of the examiner's understanding of the problem to support that a reference is reasonably pertinent. The question often turns on how the problem to be solved is perceived; if an overly narrow view inconsistent with the specification is used, art may be inappropriately limited. Any applicant argument that the examiner misconstrued the problem should be fully considered in light of the specification.

name: Analogy in the mechanical arts (broad exploration of prior art is reasonable)
description: In simple mechanical inventions a broad spectrum of prior art must be explored and it is reasonable to permit inquiry into other areas where one of ordinary skill would be aware similar problems exist.
guidance: Court decisions (e.g., Stevenson v. ITC; In re Bigio; In re Deminski) support looking to structurally/functionally similar devices (e.g., toothbrushes for hair brush claims, pumps vs compressors) when the problems and functions overlap. Examiner should consider whether cited prior art shares function/structure with claimed device.

name: Analogy in the design arts (consider designer's knowledge scope and general use)
description: Design references are analogous if they reasonably fall within the scope of knowledge of a designer of ordinary skill and if a prior design has the same general use as that claimed in the design patent application.
guidance: See MPEP § 1504.03 and examples (In re Rosen; Ex parte Pappas; In re Butera) — design references from related product categories may be analogous when designers would be aware of those references; but a design for a metal ball anode was nonanalogous to a combined insect repellent and air freshener because designers would not look to an anode design for that combined use.

name: Differences between prior art and claimed invention — consider claimed invention 'as a whole'
description: Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims requires interpreting the claim language and considering both the invention and the prior art references as a whole. The question under 35 U.S.C. 103 is not whether the differences themselves would have been obvious, but whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious.
guidance: Interpret claims per MPEP §§ 2111-2116.01 and consider all claim limitations. Case examples: Stratoflex v. Aeroquip; Schenck v. Nortron; In re Hirao — admitted unobvious aspects of some claim elements can make the subject matter as a whole nonobvious. Do not improperly focus on a single structural difference to the exclusion of other claim elements.

name: Do not distill invention to a 'gist' or 'thrust'—avoid disregarding 'as a whole' requirement
description: Distilling an invention down to the 'gist' or 'thrust' disregards the requirement of analyzing the subject matter 'as a whole.'
guidance: Restricting consideration to one perceived advantage or a subset of claim limitations can lead to improper obviousness conclusions. Examples: W.L. Gore; Bausch & Lomb v. Barnes-Hind/Hydrocurve; Jones v. Hardy; Panduit — courts reversed analyses that treated claims as though they read differently than allowed or that treated the advantage as the invention.

name: Discovery of source/cause of problem can be part of 'as a whole' inquiry (may support patentability)
description: A patentable invention may lie in the discovery of the source of a problem even though the remedy may be obvious once the source is identified; discovery of the source is part of the 'subject matter as a whole' inquiry.
guidance: Determination is fact-specific: discovering the cause of a problem can render the claimed subject matter nonobvious if prior art did not teach that cause or suggest the selection of claim elements (In re Sponnoble). But if prior art contains the same solution for a similar problem, discovery of cause may not result in patentability (In re Wiseman). Use examples (Sponnoble; Wiseman) to support examiner reasoning.

name: Search scope in examination
description: The search is carried out to identify the relevant state of the art to assess whether the filed invention is patentable; the subject matter of a search is the invention given in the patent claims; the description and drawings are used to interpret the claims; the search covers all independent and dependent claims.
guidance: The examining section in charge of the main class is responsible for the search. Ensure claims are properly interpreted using description/drawings and search all claim scope including dependent claims.

name: Search methods, tools and termination
description: The examining section must carry out the search utilising the technical tools and information sources made available to the extent that seems promising and justified, considering effort and time requirements; the search is concluded where disproportionate effort would be required to only slightly improve results.
guidance: Apply the Guidelines for the Search under Section 43 (use of external electronic sources). To avoid unnecessary procedural delay, carry out and finalise the search in one working step for all claims before the first communication. Beware searches done before six months after filing may be erroneous due to incomplete availability in systems.

name: Amendments and prohibition of extension (no added subject‑matter)
description: Original application documents may be amended up to the decision on grant provided that the scope of the subject matter is not extended; only corrections of obvious mistakes, remedying deficiencies pointed out by the examining section, or amendments to the patent claims are admissible before filing a request for examination. Section 38 prohibits amendments that extend scope.
guidance: If unallowable extensions are not removed, the application must be refused. Carefully check that amendments are directly and unambiguously derivable from the original documents.

name: Patent claims form and drafting (one‑part and two‑part form)
description: An application must contain one or more patent claims defining the subject matter sought; claims may be drafted in one-part form or divided into a generic part and a characterising part (two-part form). The characterising part must include the features of the invention for which protection is sought in connection with the generic part and be preceded by wording such as 'characterised in that'.
guidance: In two-part form the generic term is usually formed from one document or subject matter made available to the public. The entire claim (generic + characterising parts) must be examined; there is no substantive difference between one-part and two-part forms for examination.

name: Claims determine scope of protection and drafting balance
description: Under section 14 the content of the patent claims determines the scope of protection; matter merely presented in the description and not clearly claimed is not protected. The inventive idea should be described abstractly to comprise all embodiments desired by applicant, subject to original disclosure and state of the art.
guidance: When drafting, weigh applicant's interest in broad protection against public interest in clarity. Use the description to interpret the claim, but avoid unnecessary features in the main claim; define the subject matter with as few characteristics as possible to avoid undue narrowing.

name: Main claim essentials and dependent claims
description: The main claim must contain the essential features of the invention. The main claim may be followed by subsidiary (dependent) claims relating to particular embodiments, admissible provided the principle of unity is complied with. Sub‑claims involving a change of category must be examined separately.
guidance: Ensure the main claim captures the core inventive concept; dependent claims may cover specific embodiments but must remain within unity and proper claim category treatment.

name: Product‑by‑process and purpose/function indications
description: Product-by-process claims are admissible (especially for chemical compounds not identifiable structurally). Indications concerning purpose, effect or function used to designate a device are not inadmissible and often necessary to establish clear connection of structural characteristics.
guidance: Purpose/function language usually does not limit subject matter to the stated purpose but indicates the device must be objectively fit for that purpose. Such indications help the skilled person determine how to design features spatially and geometrically.

name: Optional/embellishing claim language
description: Optional features such as 'in particular', 'preferably' or 'for example' are permissible in claims; they do not limit the claimed subject matter and are not relevant for substantive patent examination.
guidance: Treat such phrasing as non-limiting; examination focuses on the features that define the claimed subject matter.

name: Claim category classification and content
description: Patents may concern products (devices, apparatus, substances) or processes; the objectively evaluated subject matter determines the patent category and thus limits free choice of claimed category by applicant.
guidance: Avoid including features of different categories in a single claim to maintain unambiguous IP rights. For manufacturing processes, claims must contain the original material and chronological sequence of actions; use claims are classified as process claims.

name: Passage Retrieval — feature-level
description: For each claim feature f_i (in the model's segmentation ˆS(C)), retrieve passages p_j from the prior art document D that disclose f_i. The gold set is P(f_i, C, D) = {p_j ∈ D | p_j discloses f_i} and the model's set is ˆP(f_i, C, D).
guidance: Evaluate by computing precision (P), recall (R), F1, and nDCG between P(f_i, C, D) and ˆP(f_i, C, D) after mapping features in ˆS(C) to gold features via minimal edit distance. Retrieval metrics at the feature level are considered a core sub-task and are computed only for rejected (not-novel) claims.

name: Passage Retrieval — claim-level
description: Aggregate passages across all features P(C, D) = ⋃_{f_i ∈ S(C)} P(f_i, C, D) and evaluate retrieval of passages that disclose at least one feature of the claim.
guidance: Compute precision, recall, F1, and nDCG between aggregated gold passages and predicted aggregated passages. This provides a claim-level retrieval signal complementary to the feature-level evaluation.

name: Novel Feature Identification
description: Identify which features of a claim are novel (binary ˆN(f_i, C, D) ∈ {0,1}). Extract character ranges of features predicted as novel and compare them to the character ranges actually added during prosecution (between A1 and B1).
guidance: Report precision, recall, and F1. Since added-feature ground truth is only available for granted claims, compute these scores only for claims labelled as novel.

name: LLM structured output and label schema
description: Models (especially LLM workflows) should output (i) relevant prior-art passage identifiers for each claim feature, (ii) a novelty prediction per feature with labels like "Fully Disclosed", "Partially Disclosed", "Not Disclosed", and (iii) an overall claim-level novelty label "Novel" or "Not Novel".
guidance: Workflows can be single-step (one call producing segmentation, passage references, and claim prediction) or hierarchical (segment claim, analyze each feature separately against full prior-art doc, then aggregate). Hierarchical examination may improve feature-level reasoning at higher token cost.

name: Dataset inclusion and seed selection criteria
description: Seed patent applications are retrieved from the EPO in CPC classes G06, G10L, H04L, and H04N from 2012 onwards; focus is on first claims because they are broad and frequently examined in ESOPs.
guidance: Filter to applications that were finally granted, require availability of ESOP documents with feature-level prior-art references, and only include samples where prior-art documents are retrievable (EPO/USPTO).

name: Newly added character spans as proxy for novel features
description: Use character spans added between the initial (A1) and granted (B1) claim versions (computed via character-level Levenshtein diff) as a proxy for novel features added during prosecution.
guidance: Compare model-predicted novel-feature character ranges to these added spans to compute precision/recall/F1 for novel feature identification (only for granted claims).

name: Length stratification to mitigate spurious correlations
description: Claim length provides a strong shortcut for novelty (applicants add limitations). To mitigate this, stratify the dataset into 100 bins by claim length and sub-sample the majority class so that each bin contains equal numbers of novel and not-novel samples.
guidance: This stratification balances length distributions across classes and reduces the model's ability to exploit claim-length shortcuts.

name: Qualifying patent (general definition)
description: A qualifying patent is defined as: '(a) a patent granted following substantive examination for novelty and inventive step, or (b) a patent, other than a short term patent within the meaning of section 63 of the Patents Act 1992, or an equivalent provision in another jurisdiction, where - (i) the Intellectual Property Office in the State, or equivalent Office elsewhere, has caused a search to be undertaken in relation to the invention and a search report (within the meaning of section 29 of the Patents Act 1992) prepared,……'
guidance: Short term patents are explicitly excluded. The majority of KDB claims are expected to relate to income from inventions protected by patents 'granted following substantive examination for novelty and inventive step.' Irish law (Patents Act 1992) has been amended to facilitate granting of long-term patents following substantive examination; Patents Rules were also amended (Patents (Amendment) Rules, 2017 S.I. No. 206 of 2017).

name: Small company size and group thresholds for secret-invention route
description: A small company is defined for KDB purposes as a company which has income arising from intellectual property of less than €7,500,000 in a 12 month accounting period, is a member of a group with group turnover of less than €50,000,000 and the company is a micro, small or medium sized company within the meaning of the Annex to Commission Recommendation 2003/361/EC of 6 May 2003.
guidance: Only companies meeting all these numerical and SME-status criteria are eligible to use the 'patentable but kept secret' certification route; documentation and evidence supporting these thresholds will be required for certification and any KDB claim.

name: Formality examination required elements
description: Formality requirements that must be satisfied during formality examination (S.3(1); S.3ter(3); S.4(1); R.5-8, R.10, R11; Rule 15).
guidance: Required items: request Form (Form 3); description; one or more claims; drawing(s)/sequence listing when necessary; abstract; designation of at least one state; English translation if filed in another language; payment of application and designation fees or an undertaking to pay within 21 days; acceptable physical document requirements.

name: Clarity and full support of claims
description: Claims must define the matter for which protection is sought and be clear, concise and supported by the description (Sec. 2bis(2)).
guidance: Claims lacking clarity or adequate support in the description can be objected to during substantive examination.

name: Novelty (newness) standard
description: When a claimed invention lacks novelty.
guidance: An invention lacks novelty if every feature or step in the claim is explicitly or implicitly disclosed within the relevant prior art, including inherent features known to a person skilled in the art. A single prior-art document defeats novelty if it contains all limitations of the claimed invention.

name: Post-grant amendment (Sec. 5ter)
description: Requirements for amending patents after grant/registration.
guidance: Request must be filed with the ARIPO Office in writing; not deemed filed until the limitation fee is paid. Any amendment to the claims must fall within the scope of the claims before the amendment.

name: Clear and comprehensive office actions
description: Office actions should be clear and comprehensive, identifying how the claim is being interpreted and the passages of the reference(s) being relied upon.
guidance: Clear identification of claim interpretation and specific reference passages aids applicants and improves prosecution efficiency and quality.

name: Claim construction: ordinary meaning and intrinsic evidence
description: Claim terms are generally given their ordinary meaning to a person of ordinary skill in the art in question at the time of the invention; claim construction begins with the claim language and relies on intrinsic evidence.
guidance: When claim construction is decided solely on intrinsic evidence, review is de novo. Courts must avoid importing limitations from the specification into the claim (Phillips, Comput. Docking Station).

name: Do not import limitations from embodiments/figures
description: Courts will not countenance importing claim limitations from a few specification statements or figures into the claims, particularly if those extracts describe only embodiments of a broader claimed invention.
guidance: A single embodiment (e.g., an I‑beam shown in figures) does not limit a broader claim that does not recite that embodiment; avoid confining claims to disclosed embodiments.

name: Meaning and effect of 'comprising'
description: The transition 'comprising' creates a presumption that the recited elements are only part of the device and does not exclude additional, unrecited elements.
guidance: Claims using 'comprising' should be read to allow additional elements (e.g., an intervening shuttle) and not to require direct contact or exclude additional structure (Crystal Semiconductor, AFG Indus.).

name: Direct infringement is strict liability (no intent required)
description: Direct infringement does not require intent to infringe; it is a strict‑liability offense.
guidance: Whether the accused designer intended the accused function is immaterial to liability; focus is on whether accused product meets claim limitations (Trim‑Lok).

name: Written description requirement (35 U.S.C. § 112(a))
description: The specification must contain a written description that reasonably conveys to those skilled in the art that the inventor had possession of the claimed subject matter as of the filing date.
guidance: The inquiry asks whether the disclosure reasonably conveys possession of the claimed invention; applicants are not required to describe every conceivable future embodiment. Written description is a question of fact (ScriptPro, Ariad, Rexnord, Moba).

name: Examiner procedure to determine whether a claim recites an abstract idea (Step 2A Prong One)
description: Examiners should (1) identify the specific limitation(s) in the claim that the examiner believes recites an abstract idea, and (2) determine whether the identified limitation(s) fall within at least one of the enumerated groupings of abstract ideas.
guidance: If the identified limitation(s) falls within at least one grouping, conclude the claim recites an abstract idea in Step 2A Prong One and proceed to Step 2A Prong Two to determine whether additional elements integrate the abstract idea into a practical application (see MPEP §2106.04(d)). If the identified limitation(s) do not fall within any grouping, conclude the claim does not recite an abstract idea (eligible at Step 2A Prong One, Pathway B), except in the rare circumstances discussed in MPEP §2106.04(a)(3). If the claim recites another judicial exception (e.g., law of nature or natural phenomenon), follow the guidance in MPEP §§2106.04(b) and 2106.04(c).

name: Enumerated abstract idea groupings (general)
description: The Office groups abstract ideas into enumerated categories to guide examiners: (1) Mathematical concepts; (2) Certain methods of organizing human activity; and (3) Mental processes.
guidance: This grouping-based approach shifts examiners from relying on individual cases to applying a broad body of precedent across technologies and claim types. Groupings are rooted in Supreme Court and Federal Circuit precedent. Groupings are not mutually exclusive; a limitation may fall within multiple groupings and examiners should identify at least one, preferably all applicable groupings.

name: Commercial or legal interactions (subgroup)
description: Includes agreements in the form of contracts, legal obligations, advertising, marketing or sales activities or behaviors, and business relations.
guidance: Claims reciting contractual relationships or transaction guarantees (e.g., transaction performance guaranty in buySAFE v. Google) are examples of this subgroup. Such commercial/legal interactions may be treated as abstract ideas when they recite those types of interactions.

name: Groupings not mutually exclusive; identify multiple groupings when applicable
description: Some claims recite limitations that fall within more than one grouping or sub-grouping (e.g., a claim performing mathematical calculations using a formula that could be performed in the human mind).
guidance: Examiners should identify at least one abstract-idea grouping, but preferably identify all groupings to the extent possible if a limitation falls within multiple groupings, and then proceed with Step 2A Prong Two analysis.

name: Avoid claims that can be performed in the human mind
description: Claims directed towards a process that can be performed in the human mind will likely not be found patent eligible by PTAB (as well as Federal Circuit) unless Applicant adds specific elements directed to an improvement in computer technology or the particular technology field or process.
guidance: Under the Guidance, 'determining' steps that can be practically performed mentally (or with pen and paper/lookups) fall into the 'mental process' grouping; see MPEP 2106.05(a) for related USPTO guidance.

name: Make data-analysis/determining steps non-manual
description: Claims focused on 'determining' or other data-analysis steps should emphasize and claim specific elements that support the inability to perform those steps manually or in the human mind.
guidance: Such specific elements should be supported in the Specification to emphasize the unique advantages of performing the steps through software for the particular technology field or technological process (e.g., golf club fitting technology).

name: Highlight technical innovations in specification and claims
description: Applicants should emphasize and highlight any technical innovations in the invention, both in the specification and the claims.
guidance: Prepare the Specification and claims to support a technical solution to a technical problem; tie algorithmic or analytic steps to particular technological benefits and uses.

name: Additional elements must be more than well-understood, routine, conventional
description: Additional elements must provide more than well-understood, routine, and conventional functionality; otherwise they do not provide an inventive concept.
guidance: Claims that are an 'abstract-idea-based solution implemented with generic technical components in a conventional way' will be held ineligible under the Guidance's inventive-concept analysis (Step 2B).

name: Recite concrete device interactions and machine steps when possible
description: Claims that include specific device interactions (e.g., scanning by a second device, identifying via machine-readable code, delivering formatted results between devices) can support a finding that the claims are not directed to an abstract idea.
guidance: The Board found claims that recited concrete steps performed by multiple devices and automated processing to identify lab tests were not directed to an abstract idea, even where underlying technologies were generic.

name: Integrate mathematical concepts into a practical application
description: Claims that recite mathematical concepts should recite additional elements that integrate the mathematical concepts into a practical application (e.g., specific physical steps or particular machine use).
guidance: Example: reciting steps of placing a tool on an organ surface, associating positions with a 3D image, and generating mapping functions using thin plate splines to improve catheter navigation demonstrated integration (improving registration and reducing localization errors).

name: Recite implementation details of algorithms and surrounding technology
description: Claims should recite surrounding technology and implementation details of the algorithm to ensure it is viewed as a 'practical application' of those concepts.
guidance: Specifications should likewise highlight the benefits to the technology and specific uses of any mathematical concepts within the technology so that the algorithm is shown as applied to a technological problem.

name: Use 'configured to' and structural limitations to claim special-purpose machines
description: Use 'configured to' device language and add structural limitations to claim special-purpose improved machines rather than generic processors.
guidance: PTAB found device claims 'configured to' perform steps were persuasive as 'special-purpose improved machines'; adding structural and specific method limitations post-appeal led to allowance in an example case.

name: Amend claims post-appeal to add structural/specific method limitations
description: Post-appeal claim amendments adding structural limitations and specific method limitations directed towards an improvement to the technology can lead to allowance.
guidance: Example: after adding such limitations directed to improvement in golf fitting technology, the Examiner allowed the application, noting the amendments integrated the abstract idea into a practical application.

name: Processor limitations must show technical solution to technical problem
description: Processor limitations that only perform mental/calculational tasks are insufficient; claims should show how the processor contributes to a technical solution to a technical problem.
guidance: PTAB criticized processors 'merely used to perform calculations' when those calculations could be done mentally; claims should instead recite how the processor improves measurement, manufacturing, or other technical operations.

name: Written description must be complete in itself; drawings/models are auxiliary
description: The written Description must be complete in itself, although its language may be illustrated and applied by a model or drawings which accompany it.
guidance: Drawings or models may illustrate form or position of parts but cannot supply the place of a written description to the extent that a claim would cover matter indicated only by the drawings. A model cannot replace a written Description.

name: Multiple inventions in one application require particularity for each
description: When several inventions are joined in one application, the same particularity of description is necessary in regard to each.
guidance: Each distinct invention claimed must be described with sufficient specificity to enable practice; failure to do so for any joined invention risks invalidity for that invention.

name: Education and schools (attendance, facilities, outcomes)
description: Quality and reach of education: day and boarding schools, attendance rates, boarding accommodations, and measurable student progress.
guidance: Measure average attendance (examples: day school average 20; multiple boarding/day-school enrollments listed), success indicators (monthly reports, letters from students, comparison to white schools), infrastructure needs (erect boarding-school buildings, room to accommodate target enrollments — e.g., target of 250 average attendance claimed), staffing/outsourcing (students sent to Carlisle Barracks), and special emphasis on educating girls/mothers as leverage for civilizing future generations. Note difficulties motivating children to attend when living far away.

name: Commonly Sought Additional Discovery Topics and Tailoring
description: Two frequently sought discovery areas are identifying real parties-in-interest (RPI) and secondary evidence of non-obviousness.
guidance: Narrowly focused, appropriately tailored requests on these issues may be permitted (examples of both grants and denials are provided). Overbroad, unfocused, or unduly burdensome requests (e.g., broad copying allegations without showing how feature is embodied in claims) are likely to be denied.

name: Petition Claim Construction Requirement
description: A petitioner who believes a claim term requires express construction must include a statement identifying a proposed construction and where intrinsic and/or extrinsic evidence supports that meaning; a petitioner may instead state that no express construction is required.
guidance: The patent owner may respond and propose additional terms; the petitioner may reply to new constructions but cannot raise new claim construction issues that were not raised in its petition. If the Board raises a claim construction issue, both parties get an opportunity to respond prior to the final written decision.

name: § 112(f) (Means-Plus-Function) Construction Requirement
description: Where claim language may be construed under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f), a petitioner must provide a construction that includes both the claimed function and the specific portions of the specification that describe the structure, material, or acts corresponding to each claimed function. 37 C.F.R. § 42.104(b)(3).
guidance: A party may explain why § 112(f) should or should not apply. Failure to address § 112(f) risks not satisfying 37 C.F.R. § 42.104(b)(3).

name: Claim Construction Standard — District Court (Phillips) Standard Applies
description: The Board applies the same claim construction standard that would be used in a civil action under 35 U.S.C. § 282(b) (Phillips v. AWH), per final rule changes; this applies to IPR, PGR, and CBM petitions filed on or after Nov. 13, 2018.
guidance: The Board will construe claims and proposed substitute claims based on the record of the proceeding — claim language, specification, prosecution history, and relevant extrinsic evidence. Parties should point to specific portions of specification, prosecution history, and extrinsic evidence and explain relevancy. Each party bears the burden of providing sufficient support for constructions.

name: Consideration and Weight of Prior Claim Constructions
description: Any prior claim construction determination in a civil action or ITC proceeding, if timely made of record in the PTAB proceeding, will be considered and given appropriate weight.
guidance: Non-exclusive factors for weight include similarity between district/ITC record and the PTAB record, and whether the prior construction is final or interlocutory. Parties should submit prior constructions as soon as available (preferably with petition, preliminary response, or response). After institution, supplemental information rules (37 C.F.R. §§ 42.123, 42.223) require authorization to submit new material, and if >1 month after institution the movant must show why it could not have been obtained earlier.

name: Consideration of Parties' Statements from Other Proceedings
description: The Board may consider statements regarding claim scope or claim construction made by patent owners or petitioners in other proceedings (including statements submitted under 35 U.S.C. § 301(a)) if timely made of record.
guidance: To ensure consideration, a party should specifically point out such statements and explain how they support or contradict a proposed construction. Each party bears the burden of providing sufficient support.

name: Patent Owner Preliminary Response — Permissible Arguments
description: A patent owner may file a preliminary response (within three months after the Notice of Filing Date Accorded to Petition) presenting arguments and supporting evidence to demonstrate that no review should be instituted. 37 C.F.R. §§ 42.107(a),(b), 42.207(a),(b).
guidance: Examples of arguments include: (1) petitioner is statutorily barred; (2) asserted references are not printed publications; (3) prior art lacks a material limitation; (4) prior art does not teach/suggest the petitioner's combination; (5) petitioner's claim interpretation is unreasonable; (6) for § 101 grounds in PGR/CBM, explanation why claims are patent-eligible; (7) reasons to exercise Director’s discretion to deny institution under 35 U.S.C. § 314 and/or § 325(b).

name: Patent Owner Election to Waive Preliminary Response or Statutory Disclaimer
description: A patent owner may elect to waive the preliminary response (no adverse inference will be drawn) or file a statutory disclaimer of challenged claims to streamline proceedings.
guidance: If all challenged claims are disclaimed, Board will terminate the proceeding. If some claims remain, the institution decision will be based on the remaining claims. Once trial is instituted, the Board may decline to consider preliminary-response arguments not renewed in the patent owner response (waiver).

name: General Plastic Factors for Follow-On Petitions and Discretion in Institution
description: In exercising discretion to institute (especially for 'follow-on' petitions challenging the same patent), the Board considers the non-exclusive General Plastic factors to assess impacts on efficiency and fairness.
guidance: General Plastic factors include: (1) whether same petitioner previously filed a petition directed to the same claims; (2) whether petitioner knew or should have known of the prior art asserted in the second petition when filing the first; (3) whether petitioner had received the patent owner’s preliminary response or Board decision on institution in the first petition when filing the second; (4) length of time between learning of the prior art and filing the second petition; (5) adequacy of petitioner’s explanation for elapsed time between filings; (6) finite resources of the Board; (7) requirement to issue a final determination within one year after institution (35 U.S.C. § 316(a)(11)). The factors are not dispositive or exclusive; they form a balanced assessment along with merits. The Board also considers relationships between different petitioners when different entities file follow-on petitions.

name: Public use statutory bar criteria
description: Two primary factors determine public use: (1) whether the use was public (not kept secret or under confidentiality), and (2) whether the invention existed in a sufficiently definable form at the time of use (e.g., prototype or description enabling practice).
guidance: An invention is 'ready for patenting' when reduced to practice or when drawings/descriptions are specific enough to enable a person skilled in the art (Pfaff v. Wells). Experimental testing arguments can be scrutinized; courts evaluate whether the testing was necessary to define the claimed invention or merely to establish efficacy/safety.

name: Inventorship is a question of law (conception + reduction to practice)
description: Inventorship requires legal determination of who contributed to the claimed invention based on conception and reduction to practice (conception is primary; reduction to practice can also contribute).
guidance: Inventorship is distinct from authorship. Incorrect inventorship can invalidate a patent (and cannot be corrected if the error involved deceptive intent). The determination should be made by the registered patent attorney/agent drafting the application to provide an objective, legally sound analysis.

name: Policy to merge or stay concurrent reissue and ex parte reexamination proceedings
description: If a reissue application and an ex parte reexamination proceeding on which an order pursuant to § 1.525 has been mailed are pending concurrently on a patent, a decision will normally be made to merge the two proceedings or to suspend one of the two proceedings.
guidance: Where merger is ordered, merged examination will be conducted in accordance with §§ 1.171 through 1.179 and the patent owner will be required to place and maintain the same claims in the reissue application and the ex parte reexamination during the pendency of the merged proceeding. Examiner actions and patent owner responses in a merged proceeding will apply to both files and be physically entered into both files. Any ex parte reexamination proceeding merged with a reissue application shall be terminated by the grant of the reissued patent.

name: Requirement for identical claims when merger ordered
description: If a merger order requires that the patent owner place the same claims in the reissue application and the reexamination proceeding, an amendment may be required to be filed within a specified time set in the order merging the proceedings.
guidance: If an amendment to make the claims the same in each file is required but not timely submitted, any claim that does not contain identical text in all merged proceedings should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, paragraph 2, as being indefinite and failing to particularly point out the invention.

name: Effect of Federal court decisions known at time of reexamination determination
description: If a Federal Court decision on the merits of a patent is known to the examiner at the time the determination on the request for ex parte reexamination is made, the existence of a final court decision of claim validity does not necessarily mean that no new question is present because the Office uses different standards of proof and claim interpretation.
guidance: Office may accord deference to factual findings of the court where evidence is the same, but determination of whether a substantial new question of patentability exists will be made independently of the court’s decision. A non-final holding of claim invalidity or unenforceability will not be controlling. A final holding of claim invalidity or unenforceability (after all appeals) is controlling on the Office and a substantial new question would not be present as to those claims.

name: Patentable subject matter under 35 U.S.C. §101
description: The scope of patentable subject matter is confined to any 'new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof.' This provision excludes from patent eligibility those claims that pertain to abstract concepts (such as mathematical formulas), naturally occurring phenomena, or fundamental scientific principles.
guidance: Supreme Court justification: such ideas are building blocks of scientific and technological progress and granting exclusivity could obstruct innovation (citing Mayo). Use §101 analysis to screen out abstract ideas before substantive patentability inquiries.

name: Liability allocation for AI-caused patent infringement
description: Patent infringement analysis currently involves claim construction and proving that accused technology fulfills each claim element (or equivalents); induced infringement holds liable those who knowingly aid direct infringement. U.S. statutes do not contemplate autonomous AI committing infringement without human oversight.
guidance: Unclear how to assign accountability when AI independently infringes. Options include holding users, developers/manufacturers, owners, or AI itself liable. Any regime should consider deterrence, fairness, foreseeability, and effects on innovation.

name: Technology-specific indicator weights
description: Weights in the composite index differ by technology field reflecting differing factor loadings and covariance structure (Table 3 gives percent weights on log indicators by field).
guidance: For drugs the weights place ~48% on forward citations and ~29% on claims; in biotech and many other fields claims receive >50% weight. Use field-specific weights rather than a single pooled weight when feasible. If family size unavailable, re-normalise weights among remaining indicators (authors provide renormalised weights when family size omitted).

name: Three exceptions to §101
description: Courts recognize three specific exceptions to §101's broad terms: 'laws of nature, physical phenomena, and abstract ideas.'
guidance: These exceptions protect basic tools of science/technology that must remain free for public use. A claim that expressly claims such subjects or in practical effect wholly preempts them is invalid. Apply these exceptions sparingly and with their animating purposes in mind.

name: Process as transformative series of acts
description: A 'process' is a mode of treatment of certain materials to produce a given result — an act, or series of acts, performed upon the subject-matter to be transformed and reduced to a different state or thing.
guidance: The transformative nature of a claimed method (e.g., administration of a drug that alters body chemistry, and testing bodily samples) is a classic indicium of §101 eligibility. Consider the claim 'as a whole' rather than dissecting into old and new elements.

name: Transformations occurring inside the human body are patent-eligible
description: The fact that a claimed transformation occurs within the human body does not render the claimed process ineligible; methods of treating patients have long been considered within the field of patentable subject matter.
guidance: Historical and administrative practice (e.g., many patents with treatment claims, Board decisions like Ex parte Scherer, and precedents such as Diehr and International Tooth Crown) support eligibility for medical treatment methods, subject to other statutory limitations (e.g., 35 U.S.C. 287(c)).

name: Do not conflate §101 eligibility with novelty or inventive contribution
description: Whether an invention is novel (§102) or nonobvious (§103) is distinct from whether it falls into a statutory category under §101.
guidance: The §101 inquiry should not dissect the claim into old and new elements to test eligibility; novelty and nonobviousness are evaluated under §§102 and 103. A process can be §101-eligible yet invalid under §§102/103.

name: When mental steps may be acceptable (decision-tree style)
description: Claims that include mental steps which functionally affect subsequent physical steps (e.g., 'perform A and B, then do either C or D depending on results') can be acceptable.
guidance: The critical distinction is whether the mental step changes what physical acts are to be performed; a mental inference that modifies subsequent physical treatment can be part of a patentable process, whereas a terminal mental 'interpretation' that leaves no further physical action recited generally will not.

name: Printed numeric ranges and claim scope in preemption analysis
description: Claims that specify particular numeric ranges (e.g., metabolite concentrations) may exclude other uses and therefore may not preempt all practical applications of a general correlation.
guidance: Specific numeric limits or explicit exclusions (e.g., excluding transplant patients) narrow claim scope and reduce preemption concerns; whether those limits avoid preemption may depend on whether other practitioners can reasonably rely on substantially different numbers without infringing.

name: Role of §§102 and 103 in policing claims that append interpretive steps
description: Claims that append interpretive/mental steps to pre-existing physical processes are properly analyzed under §§102 and 103 for novelty and obviousness rather than rejected under §101.
guidance: If administering and assaying steps were known in the prior art, merely adding an interpretive 'wherein' clause identifying a correlation likely fails §§102/103 because it does not recite new physical steps or a new series of acts that differ from prior art.

name: Claim drafting strategy implication
description: Including concrete downstream treatment steps in claim drafting can help distinguish a claimed process from the prior art.
guidance: Applicants who draft claims to include actionable treatment adjustments (rather than ending with an interpretive mental step) may create more robust novelty/nonobviousness arguments, though doing so may complicate enforcement (proof of attributable steps) and narrow claim scope.

name: Preemption assessment sensitive to level of generality
description: The degree to which a claim preempts a natural relationship depends on how the relationship is characterized—very fine particularity vs. high-level generality.
guidance: If a correlation is described at a very fine degree of particularity (e.g., specific metabolite thresholds), preemption arguments may be stronger; if described at higher generality, many practical uses may remain available. Courts should beware of describing inventions at such a general level that every invention would appear to 'claim' a correlation.

name: Authoritative precedents to apply in §101 analysis
description: Key Supreme Court precedents shaping §101 include Diamond v. Chakrabarty, Gottschalk v. Benson, Diamond v. Diehr, Funk Bros., Parker v. Flook, Bilski v. Kappos, LabCorp (Breyer opinion), and related Federal Circuit decisions.
guidance: Use these precedents to distinguish (a) claims that expressly claim laws of nature or abstract ideas, (b) claims that merely append mental steps to known processes, and (c) claims that recite transformative, concrete processes. Apply precedents consistently and recall that some tests (e.g., machine-or-transformation) are helpful clues but not exclusive rules.

name: Box VIII — Specific remarks on the international application
description: Box No. VIII is used for special remarks regarding the international application, such as unclear claims, description or drawings or claims insufficiently supported by the description.
guidance: Such remarks must be substantiated/reasoned in the WO.

name: Article 19 amendments to claims after ISA stage
description: Under Article 19 the applicant has one opportunity to amend claims in the international phase; amended claims must be sent to the IB in the publication language and are published with the PCT application.
guidance: Timing: amendments available until 16 months from priority or until 2 months from the date of sending the ISA results, whichever is later. If some claims were not examined, Article 19 amendments can only be made to claims that were examined. Applicant must submit all claim pages replacing earlier pages and a letter indicating differences and grounds for the changes; amendments are free of charge. If Demand is filed, Article 19 amendments are forwarded to IPEA; applicant may also amend under Article 34 during the IPEA phase.

name: SISR content requirements
description: SISR (form PCT/SISA/501) comprises first and second sheets and optional annexes; the first sheet indicates documents on which the report is based and whether the ISA ISR/WO were available; the second sheet is similar to PCT/ISA/210 but without classification data.
guidance: First sheet notes if some claims were not examined and whether the invention is non-unitary; a 'Scope Annex' can describe the search scope and is useful if earlier ISA report not available to SISA.

name: IPER purpose and scope
description: IPEA's purpose is to prepare a preliminary, non-binding opinion (IPER) on whether the invention(s) are new, involve an inventive step and are industrially applicable.
guidance: IPEA will take positions only on claims that were the subject of an ISA search. Nevertheless, the IPEA must consider all relevant material whether or not it was mentioned in the ISR (Article 33(6); Rule 70.7). IPEA may carry out a top-up search for publications after the ISR date unless such top-up is unnecessary (e.g. where Rule 67.1 excludes consideration or application is too unclear to allow meaningful search). IPEA also considers timely third-party observations provided supporting documents are available.

name: IPEA written opinion content and form
description: IPEA's written opinion (form PCT/IPEA/408, English) should address matters specified in Rule 66.2 and Article 34(4), including missing matters defined in Article 34(4), lack of novelty, inventive step or industrial applicability, formal/content deficiencies that IPEA examines, changes introducing matter not present in the original, claims not sufficiently supported by the description, claims not searched because ISA did not search them, and sequence listing format issues.
guidance: The form includes a cover sheet and Box No. I–VIII plus sequence listing annexes; include only the sheets needed. Box descriptions correspond to the ISA boxes (see ISA WO box guidance). The response deadline for the applicant to the written opinion is generally two months from the mailing date (min 1 month, max 3 months) and can be extended if applicant requests before expiry.

name: IPEA top-up search policy
