description: IPEA may perform an additional (top-up) search for documents published or made known after ISR preparation unless IPEA considers such top-up unnecessary (e.g., if Rule 67.1 indicates no substantive opinion is to be given, if the application is too unclear to permit meaningful search, or if no claims were searched in ISA).
guidance: Top-up search is unnecessary if the entire claim set is not to be considered on novelty/inventive step/industrial applicability, or if the claims cannot be meaningfully researched because of lack of clarity or lack of support. If top-up finds new relevant publications, a written opinion should be given.

name: Bill of particulars: scope and function
description: A further and better statement of the nature of the claim or defence, or further and better particulars of any matter stated in any pleading may be ordered upon such terms as to costs and otherwise as may be just.
guidance: The bill of particulars amplifies general allegations to inform the adversary of the precise nature and character of the claim/defence to prevent surprise at trial. It is intended to remedy ignorance of the nature of the claim, not mere ignorance of facts. Courts (e.g., SDNY) have used bills of particulars to require descriptions of inventions/uses and the patents/publications relied upon.

name: Burden and standard of proof for defeating reciprocal discipline
description: The respondent must 'clearly and convincingly demonstrate' a genuine issue of material fact as to one of the defenses in § 11.24(d)(1).
guidance: Federal courts (and the USPTO) treat this as a narrow standard; the respondent carries the burden of proof. Precedent (In re Kramer; In re Friedman) recognizes the difficulty of overturning state disciplinary findings in reciprocal proceedings. Evidence must be persuasive and go beyond mere assertions or speculative claims.

name: Ignorance of the rule is not a defense
description: A practitioner's claimed lack of knowledge of PTO rules (e.g., duty to withdraw immediately upon suspension) does not excuse unauthorized practice.
guidance: The decision stresses that the rule is not 'arcane' for a practitioner with longstanding practice before the PTO, and mere ignorance would not negate clear evidence of drafting and participating in filings while suspended.

name: Selective prosecution defense requirements
description: To succeed on a selective prosecution claim, a respondent must show both a discriminatory effect and a discriminatory intent in the federal prosecutorial policy.
guidance: The Tribunal cited precedent stating the burden for selective prosecution is high; unsupported assertions or internet opinions do not constitute sufficient evidence of discriminatory intent or effect.

name: Numerical definitions connote modes of formation; arithmetical propositions state modes of formation
description: Number words denote physical aggregates and connote the characteristic manner in which an aggregate is formed and may be separated into parts; arithmetical propositions assert that certain aggregates can be formed from others in particular ways.
guidance: Example: Saying '12' denotes dozens of things and implies specific modes of forming 12 (e.g., 12 = 10 + 2 or 6 + 6); the cube of 12 = 1728 is a claim about forming aggregates of aggregates. This grounds arithmetic in observable composition and decomposition of collections.

name: Requirement for biological deposit when words alone are insufficient
description: When the invention involves a biological material and words alone cannot sufficiently describe how to make and use the invention in a reproducible manner, access to the biological material may be necessary for satisfaction of the statutory requirements for patentability under 35 U.S.C. 112.
guidance: The examiner shall determine in each application if a deposit is needed. If a deposit is needed and has not been made or replaced, the examiner shall reject the affected claims under the appropriate provision of 35 U.S.C. 112.

name: Functional claim limitations under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre-AIA sixth paragraph)
description: Language 'shall be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.' 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph.
guidance: If the specification fails to disclose sufficient corresponding structure, materials, or acts that perform the entire claimed function, then the claim limitation is indefinite (35 U.S.C. 112(b)) and also lacks adequate written description (35 U.S.C. 112(a)) because an unbounded functional limitation would cover all ways of performing the function and indicate lack of possession. See In re Donaldson Co.

name: Burden on the examiner regarding written description
description: The inquiry is case-by-case and a question of fact; description as filed is presumed adequate unless examiner rebuts presumption. Examiner has initial burden to present by a preponderance of evidence why a person skilled in the art would not recognize the disclosure as describing the claimed invention.
guidance: When rejecting, examiner must set forth express findings of fact supporting lack of written description. Findings should (A) identify the claim limitation(s) at issue; and (B) establish a prima facie case with reasons why a skilled person would not recognize possession of the claimed invention from the disclosure. A general allegation of 'unpredictability in the art' is insufficient. A simple statement pointing out lack of apparent support may be sufficient for new or amended claims where support is not apparent and applicant has not pointed it out. Suggest amendments when appropriate but avoid adding new matter. After applicant's reply, review the whole record (amendments, arguments, evidence); if record shows requirement satisfied, do not repeat the rejection. If rejection is maintained, thoroughly analyze affidavits and reply evidence. See In re Wertheim; In re Marzocchi; Hyatt v. Dudas; Rasmussen; In re Alton.

name: Support for claim scope in original disclosure (general rule)
description: To comply with the written description requirement and to be entitled to an earlier priority or filing date, each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure.
guidance: This principle applies when claims are changed after filing (broadened, narrowed, numerical ranges altered, or terms changed). See MPEP § 2163 for examination guidelines.

name: Broadening by omission of a limitation (omission of essential feature)
description: Omission of a limitation can raise an issue whether inventor had possession of a broader, more generic invention; a claim that omits an element described as essential or critical in the original disclosure does not comply with the written description requirement.
guidance: If the specification contains statements making a particular element the 'only possible location' or 'essential' or 'outside the purpose' to vary it, omission likely invalid (e.g., Gentry Gallery). If the specification does not describe a feature as essential, omission may be acceptable (e.g., In re Peters). A claim omitting matter disclosed to be essential may also be subject to enablement or indefiniteness rejections. See cases: Gentry Gallery; Tronzo; In re Wilder; In re Sus; In re Peters; In re Mayhew; In re Venezia; In re Collier; see also MPEP § 2172.01.

name: Narrowing or subgeneric claim changes (unsupported narrowing)
description: Introducing claim changes that narrow claims by adding elements or limitations not supported by the as-filed disclosure violates the written description requirement.
guidance: A mere 'laundry list' of moieties does not constitute written description support for every species. Adding a recited species not specifically disclosed can be improper (cases: Wattanasin; In re Ruschig; Rozbicki v. Chiang; Ex parte Ohshiro). Subgeneric terminology may be acceptable or not depending on whether reasonably communicated to skilled artisans; decide each case on facts (In re Lukach; Ex parte Sorenson; In re Smith; In re Wilder).

name: Changes to numerical range limitations
description: When changing numerical ranges, determine which ranges would be inherently supported by the original disclosure as understood by one skilled in the art.
guidance: Example: original range 25%-60% with examples 36% and 50%—a new claim 'at least 35%' failed because 'at least' had no upper limit and would cover embodiments outside 25%-60' (In re Wertheim); but 'between 35% and 60%' met description. Consider whether the specification indicates inventors considered particular ranges part of their invention (Purdue Pharma; Union Oil). Evaluate ranges in context.

name: Relationship of written description to new matter
description: Lack of written description generally arises with respect to claim subject matter; amending abstract, specification, or drawings may introduce new matter if not described in the application as filed.
guidance: Two statutory prohibitions on introducing new matter: 35 U.S.C. 132 (no amendment introducing new matter into disclosure) and 35 U.S.C. 251 (no new matter in reissue). Information from one part of the application may be added to another part without introducing new matter, but additions beyond the original disclosure should be objected to or rejected.

name: Treatment of new matter by examiner
description: If new subject matter is added to the disclosure, the examiner should object under 35 U.S.C. 132 or 251 and require applicant to cancel the new matter; if new matter is added to claims, the examiner should reject claims under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (written description).
guidance: If the specification is amended to add new matter affecting claim limitations, a 112(a) rejection should be made. When amendments are filed in reply to objections/rejections, examine the entire application to determine whether new matter is involved; applicants should specifically point out support for amendments. The examiner should still consider the added subject matter for prior art rejections since new matter rejections may be overcome by applicant.

name: Review and appealability of new matter objections/rejections
description: Rejection of claims is reviewable by the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB); an objection/requirement to delete new matter is subject to supervisory review by petition under 37 CFR 1.181.
guidance: If both claims and specification contain new matter and there is both a rejection and objection, the issue becomes appealable and should not be decided by petition.

name: Claimed subject matter present only in claims (antecedent and disclosure issues)
description: Claims as filed are part of the disclosure; if the originally filed claims disclose material not elsewhere in the specification, the applicant may amend the specification to include the claimed subject matter.
guidance: If originally claimed subject matter lacks proper antecedent basis in the specification, use form paragraph 7.44. See In re Benno and MPEP § 608.01(o).

name: Enablement requirement (35 U.S.C. 112(a) / pre-AIA first paragraph)
description: The specification must describe how to make and how to use the invention defined by the claims so that one skilled in the art can make and use it; the invention to be enabled is that defined by the claim(s).
guidance: Purpose: ensure invention is communicated to the public meaningfully. It is not necessary to enable a perfected or commercially viable embodiment unless the claim requires it. Enablement is separate and distinct from written description; a limitation not described may nonetheless be enabling if one skilled in the art could make and use the claimed invention with that limitation. If claimed subject matter appears only in claims and not specification, object under form paragraph 7.44 for lacking support; treat enablement separately.

name: Factors for undue experimentation (Wands factors)
description: Factors to consider when determining whether necessary experimentation is 'undue' include (but are not limited to): (A) breadth of the claims; (B) nature of the invention; (C) state of the prior art; (D) level of one of ordinary skill; (E) level of predictability in the art; (F) amount of direction provided by the inventor; (G) existence of working examples; and (H) quantity of experimentation needed.
guidance: These factors are non-exclusive and must be considered together; it is improper to conclude non-enablement by analyzing only one factor while ignoring others. The examiner's analysis must consider all evidence related to each factor and base a conclusion on the evidence as a whole. See In re Wands; In re Wright; In re Certain Limited-Charge Cell Culture Microcarriers; cases illustrating application (Wands decision where specification provided considerable direction and art had high skill level).

name: Proper basis for a conclusion of lack of enablement
description: A conclusion of lack of enablement means that, based on the evidence regarding the undue experimentation factors, the specification at filing would not have taught one skilled in the art how to make and/or use the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
guidance: Examiner must tie factual findings to legal conclusion; consider the totality of the evidence and not rely on speculation. See In re Wright; In re Wands; United States v. Telectronics.

name: Use of reservation annuity funds to clear title clouds and enable partition
description: Consider using a portion of Indian annuity funds to extinguish external claims (e.g., pre-emption claims) that cloud titles and prevent partitioning lands in severalty, since partition has proved to promote industry and prosperity.
guidance: Report cites Ogden Land Company pre-emption claim impeding Allegany and Cattaraugus partitions; examples (Oneidas, Cornplanter, Tuscaroras) show partitioning lands in severalty fosters farming, industry, and prosperity. Department should protect tribal titles to encourage improvement.

name: Balance claim scope (not too broad or too narrow)
description: A Claim must not be too broad to embrace more than what the applicant has in fact invented (may encroach on public domain or others' subject matter). A claim must not be too narrow because such a Claim would not be sufficiently effective against potential infringement.
guidance: A Claim which is too broad may encroach upon the subject matter which is in public domain or belongs to others. If claims were too narrow an infringer would go scot-free and the full benefit of the invention may not accrue to the inventor.

name: Use multiple claims to cover different scopes/aspects
description: Having many claims, where each claim has a different scope, allows the applicant to have a legal title to different aspects of the invention.
guidance: A good drafting may begin with broad claims and develop towards claims that are narrower in scope.

name: Avoid terms that confuse scope or are non‑specific
description: Terms of the claim which confuse the scope of the invention, or claims that are not specific (e.g. 'Any novel matter') should be avoided.
guidance: Avoid words that cause subjective judgment (e.g. 'thin', 'strong', 'a major part', 'such as', 'when required', 'any') unless such expression follows some definite value.

name: Claims must be for a product or process and be one sentence
description: A claim shall be for the protection of either a product or process, as the case may be, and shall be in one sentence according to the standard practice.
guidance: Each claim should be in a single sentence and should be clearly worded.

name: Claims formatting and preamble requirement
description: The description of invention in the complete specification is to be followed by a 'statement of Claims' preceded by the prescribed preamble, 'I / We claim' as the case may be.
guidance: Claims should start from a fresh page, after detailed description of the invention and should be serially numbered.

name: Claims should not be verbose
description: A claim should not be verbose.
guidance: Be concise; clarity is preferred and verbosity to be avoided.

name: No restriction on number of claims (fees apply after ten)
description: There is no restriction as to the number of claims that can be incorporated in the specification.
guidance: Applicant has to pay additional fee, if total number of claims are more than ten.

name: Claims must be fairly based on matter disclosed in the specification
description: Each claim should be fairly based on matter disclosed in the specification. All the characteristics of the invention that form part of the Claims must be fully explained in the description.
guidance: Each claim should be complete so that it covers the inventive feature and enough elements around it to put the invention in the proper context.

name: Terms in claims must appear in or be clearly inferred from description
description: Any term which is used in the claim must be either found in the description or clearly inferred from the description.

name: Trade marks generally not to be used in claims
description: Trade Marks are an indication of the origin rather than the composition or content of goods, and should not be used in Patent Applications where a generic term can be used instead.
guidance: Trade Marks are only permitted in Claims where it can be shown that their use is unavoidable and does not introduce ambiguity. Where registered marks are mentioned, they should be acknowledged as such. If a Trade Mark is not registered, its owner should be indicated.

name: Independent (principal) claim requirements
description: The first claim is always an independent claim (Principal Claim). It should clearly define the essential novel features of the most preferred embodiment of the process/product that constitutes the invention.
guidance: The claim may be properly characterized with respect to the prior art, defining all the technical features essential to the invention or inventive concept. The claim should bring out sufficient details of interrelationship, operation or utility to establish that the invention achieves the intended objectives.

name: Dependent claims must be fully limited by preceding independent claim
description: Dependent Claims that are not fully limited by the terms of the preceding independent claim (e.g. dependent claims which omit, modify or substitute a feature of an independent claim) are not acceptable.

name: Omnibus claim is not allowed
description: The practice of including an omnibus claim does not have any legal basis under the Patent Act and such a claim cannot be allowed (Section 10(4)(c)).
guidance: Omnibus claims are unclear, vague and unsearchable and are desirable to avoid.

name: Each claim must have a priority date
description: Each claim of a complete specification shall have a priority date. If the complete specification is filed along with the application, the date of filing of the application is the date of the priority of the claim(s) of the specification if the claim(s) are fairly based on the matter disclosed in the specification.
guidance: General rule establishing that priority attaches at the claim level; dependent on fair basis in the specification.

name: Priority for complete specification based on multiple cognate provisionals
description: When a complete specification is filed based on two or more provisional specifications which are cognate, the priority dates for claims arising from each of the provisional specifications will be the date of the respective provisional specification.

name: Priority on conversion between complete and provisional
description: When a complete specification is converted into a provisional specification and a fresh complete specification is filed thereafter, the priority date of claims shall be the date of disclosure.
guidance: Section 11(3) addressed.

name: Priority when claim is based partly on different previous applications
description: If the Claim is fairly based on the matter disclosed partly in one and partly in another such previous application accompanying provisional specification, the priority date of the claim shall be the date of the later filed Specification.

name: Priority from earlier Indian application filed within 12 months
description: Where a complete specification based on a previously filed application in India has been filed within twelve months from the date of that application and the claim is fairly based on the matter disclosed in the previously filed application, the priority date of that claim shall be the date of the previously filed application in which the matter was first disclosed.
guidance: Section 11(2).

name: Protection against invalidation by publication/use or later patent (Section 11(3A))
description: A claim in a complete specification of a patent shall not be invalidated by reason only of: (a) the publication or use of the invention so far as claimed in that claim on or after the priority date of such claim; or (b) the grant of another patent which claims the invention, so far as claimed in the first mentioned claim, in a claim of the same or a later priority date.
guidance: Section 11(3A) provides protection in specified circumstances.

name: Divisional application contents and claims
description: The Divisional Application should be filed along with a Complete Specification. The Claims of the Divisional Application shall not conflict with those of main application.
guidance: Section 16(3).

name: Patent of Addition: reference requirement in specification
description: The complete specification of application for patent of addition shall include specific reference to the number of main patent or the application for main patent, and a definite statement that the invention comprises an improvement in, or a modification of the invention claimed in the specification of the main patent.
guidance: Rule 13(3).

name: Convention application: right of priority (Paris Convention)
description: Where a person has made an Application in a Convention country (basic application), and makes an application in India within twelve months, the priority date of a claim of the complete specification based on matter disclosed in the basic application is the date of making of the basic application.
guidance: If several convention applications were filed, the twelve month period is reckoned from the earliest of those applications.

name: PCT international application required contents
description: The International Application should contain a request, a description, one or more claims, one or more drawings (where required) and an abstract. It should comply with the prescribed physical requirements, be in a prescribed language, and required fee should be paid.
guidance: Request may be computer printout; request should contain petition, title, applicant/inventor/agent details, declaration of inventorship signed appropriately, details of priority and indication of competent International Searching Authority, optional indications such as priority claim.

name: PCT language, abstract, claims and drawings standards
description: Language of International Application must be one the Receiving Office accepts. Abstract is intended for technical information and cannot be used to interpret scope; should be 50–150 words summarizing technical problem, gist of solution and principal use. Claims must define subject matter and be clear, concise and fully supported by the description. Drawings required only when necessary for understanding.
guidance: If Application is filed in India it has to be in English or Hindi (Hindi must have verified English translation). The request must be in a language accepted by the Receiving Office and one of the publication languages. Sequence listings and electronic filing rules apply as per PCT provisions and Applicant’s Guide.

name: Receiving Office checks and international filing date conditions
description: The Receiving Office accords the date of receipt as international filing date provided at time of receipt: (i) applicant has right to file with that Office; (ii) application is in prescribed language; (iii) application contains an indication it is intended as international application, designation of at least one contracting state, name of applicant, a part appearing to be a description, a part that appears to be claim(s).
guidance: If missing, Office invites correction; correction within time can preserve filing date. The Office also checks other defects (signature, applicant indications, title, abstract, physical requirements) and may invite correction within time limits or declare application withdrawn. Typical correctable defects listed.

name: Scope of ARP review (focus of rehearing)
description: The ARP review will focus on the Board’s new ground of rejection of claims 1–6 and 8–20 under 35 U.S.C. § 101.
guidance: The rehearing is limited in scope to the identified new ground(s) of rejection (here, § 101 for specified claims); other issues outside that identified scope are not the focus of this ARP action.

name: Reduction of applicant-attributable periods where objective ground not attributable to applicant exists
description: Where there exists an objective ground which is not attributable to an applicant, among grounds for delaying registration under Article 92-2(1) of the Act, the relevant period shall be reduced from a period under paragraph (1), notwithstanding the provisions of paragraph (1).
guidance: If part of the overall delay was due to objective reasons (e.g., administrative error, force majeure), those periods may be removed from the applicant-attributable deduction. Provide evidence to support such claims.

name: EPO two‑hurdle approach to mathematical methods/AI
description: The EPO uses a two‑hurdle approach: (1) determine whether the claimed subject matter is excluded (e.g., a mathematical method per se), and (2) substantive examination to assess enablement, clarity, novelty, and inventive step.
guidance: Presence of any technical means (computer, network, internet) is often sufficient to overcome the first hurdle. The second hurdle addresses whether the disclosure is enabling and whether claims are clear, unitary, novel, and inventive.

name: Specificity of application to a field of technology (EPO)
description: The application to a field of technology must be specific; a generic purpose (e.g., 'controlling a technical system') is insufficient. Claims should be functionally limited to the technical application and not encompass further non‑technical applications.
guidance: Examples of technical contributions: controlling specific technical systems/processes (X‑ray, steel cooling), digital audio/image/video enhancement or analysis (de‑noising, feature detection), classifying digital images based on low‑level features, using a neural network in heart monitoring to identify irregular heartbeats. Examples of non‑technical purposes: classifying text documents by textual content or abstract data records without technical use indication.

name: Claim drafting best practices for AI‑related European patent applications
description: Craft separate claims for training and inference phases; make technical features in each phase the core of the claim so that the technical purpose and technical effect are evident.
guidance: Provide sufficient specific technical detail in the description (training data, training parameters, input data for inference, inference parameters) to enable the claimed invention. Disclose fallback positions in claim‑ready language (e.g., in summary) given restrictive EPO added‑matter rules. Even if not included in claims, disclose technical features that could serve as fallbacks.

name: Avoid non‑technical terminology and show causal chain to technical effect in claims
description: Avoid non‑technical terms (that may be associated with mathematical/business methods) in claims; ensure claim features form a causal chain leading to the asserted technical effect.
guidance: Support the causal chain by ensuring interconnections/interactions between claim features are present and highlighted so the technical effect is clear to the examiner.

name: CNIPA claim evaluation as a whole and inventive step via algorithm adjustments
description: China's CNIPA requires considering the claim as a whole; technical features, algorithms, business rules, and process steps should not be evaluated separately. Algorithm adjustments that differ from existing technology may support inventive step.
guidance: Examples: a claimed solution that enables a CNN to process images of various sizes (solving a technical problem) can be patentable. Section 9.6 clarifies examination of algorithmic/business rule features together with practical application.

name: UK exclusions and positive treatment for specific technical AI applications
description: UK Patents Act exclusions (discovery, mathematical method, computer program, presentation of information, schemes/rules) apply 'to the extent' the application relates to that thing as such; UK practice interprets exclusions narrowly since 2012.
guidance: Claims functionally limited to a specific technical application of AI/ML can be patentable; abstract mathematical methods and non‑technical business method applications will be refused. Include within the application inputs, training, outputs, technical applications, interactions with physical systems outside the computer, and detailed system/software architecture for sufficiency. Recent case law (Emotional Perception AI v Comptroller‑General) found an ANN/training could produce a technical effect (external technical effect) that contributes to patentability; UKIPO updated practice to reflect that ANNs should not be objected under the 'program for a computer' exclusion.

name: Statutory patentability requirements (Title 35)
description: Patents must satisfy the four statutory requirements codified in Title 35 of the U.S. Code: Section 101 (subject matter eligibility), Section 102 (novelty), Section 103 (non-obviousness), and Section 112 (clear and sufficient claims and description).
guidance: The report aligns its definition of patent quality with these statutory and judicial standards and treats compliance with them as the central criterion for a 'quality' patent.

name: Claim-level analysis vs patent-level analysis
description: Claims are the main subject of examination; claim-by-claim analysis is the most effective method to measure compliance with each statutory provision. Independent claims are primary; dependent claims clarify scope.
guidance: Patent-level aggregation can bias assessments (e.g., a patent with 9 valid claims and 1 invalid claim could be characterized very differently). The report prefers claim-level (intensive) measures for precision and policy relevance.

name: Extensive vs intensive error margins
description: Extensive margin measures the proportion of patents with at least one estimated invalid (or valid) claim. Intensive margin measures the proportion of claims (granted or abandoned) that are estimated invalid (or valid).
guidance: The report focuses on intensive (claim-level) errors because they provide a more precise and accurate estimation of invalidity; extensive margins can overstate the prevalence of low-quality patents when most invalidity is concentrated in few claims.

name: Independent claim distance (NLP similarity measure) and threshold for patentability
description: Use of NLP to compute similarity/distance between a patent application claim and prior independent claims (an 'independent claim distance'), allowing synonyms/technical terminology, with a threshold distance used to infer patentability.
guidance: Machine learning and modern NLP (e.g., distributed representations) can scale assessment across millions of claims; an economic model is calibrated to observed prosecution outcomes to identify the patentability threshold and estimate Type 1/Type 2 errors.

name: Need for disaggregated claim-level public data
description: USPTO currently releases aggregate compliance metrics; the report recommends publishing more granular, claim-level data on compliance metrics, including segmentation by technological areas and on Type 1/Type 2 errors.
guidance: Disaggregated data (claims denominators, claim-level findings) are required to disentangle errors within Rejections, enable precise estimations of Type 2 error, and improve transparency for researchers and policymakers.

name: Interpretive caveats for modeling and measurement
description: Models and measurement approaches simplify reality (e.g., focusing on §§102/103, independent claims, or particular years); simplifications are necessary for tractability but introduce limitations.
guidance: Analysts should be explicit about assumptions (choice of claims, statutes included, time periods), validate new AI/NLP methods, and interpret estimates (e.g., threshold distance, estimated error rates) cautiously, acknowledging sampling and model uncertainties.

name: Streamline the discovery process
description: Conduct a detailed substantive assessment of risks and tailor discovery to what is necessary rather than permit broad, fishing expeditions.
guidance: Implement focused discovery (not fishing); provide initial document disclosures on conception of the invention, operation of the accused product, and damages; streamline the scope of discovery to core areas (patent claims, relevant prior art, invalidity grounds, specific discovery requests, and 30(b)(6) topics); rely on summary judgment where appropriate; follow existing guidance (Sedona Conference, Federal Circuit Advisory Council) to limit disputes.

name: Focus claim construction on disputes that matter
description: Limit claim construction disputes to terms and issues that have a legitimate chance of affecting the outcome.
guidance: Assess which claim construction disputes are central to liability or damages and concentrate resources on those; avoid expansive claim-construction battles over peripheral terms.

name: Factors considered when denying entry for undue interference
description: When denying entry of a preliminary amendment for unduly interfering with preparation of an Office action, consider the state of preparation of the first Office action and the nature of any changes resulting from entry.
guidance: Specifically consider (A) the state of preparation of a first Office action as of the date of receipt (37 CFR 1.6) of the preliminary amendment, and (B) the nature of any changes to the specification or claims that would result from entry of the preliminary amendment. If these show undue interference, entry may be denied (requires SPE approval).

name: Examples of amendment contents that may cause significant additional examiner time
description: Types of amendment changes that, if inserted, would likely require significant additional examiner time and thus may support denial of entry.
guidance: Includes: amends the claims; adds numerous new claims; amends the specification to change the scope of the claims; amends the specification so that a new matter issue would be raised; includes arguments; includes an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 or 1.132; includes evidence traversing rejections from a prior Office action in the parent application. This list is not exhaustive.

name: Form paragraph 7.46 for denial due to undue interference
description: Use form paragraph 7.46 to notify applicant that entry of a preliminary amendment is denied because it unduly interferes with preparation of the Office action (37 CFR 1.115(b)(2)).
guidance: Form should state the date received, what the examiner had completed when the amendment was received, and how entry would require significant additional time. Examiner notes: use 37 CFR 1.6 receipt date; describe state of preparation (e.g., claim analysis, prior art search, drafting awaiting SPE approval); explain additional time (e.g., need to search another classification area or extensively revise the Office action). Suggest resubmission with a responsive reply to ensure proper entry.

name: Requirement for replies to be fully responsive (37 CFR 1.111(b))
description: To be entitled to reconsideration or further examination, the reply must be in writing and distinctly and specifically point out supposed errors and reply to every ground of objection and rejection.
guidance: The reply must present arguments pointing out specific distinctions believed to render the claims patentable over applied references. A general allegation that the claims define a patentable invention without specific distinctions does not comply. The reply must appear to be a bona fide attempt to advance the application or reexamination to final action.

name: Amendments in reply must point out patentable novelty
description: When amending in reply to a rejection, the applicant must clearly point out the patentable novelty believed to be present and show how amendments avoid cited references or objections.
guidance: This requirement applies to new or rewritten claims presented in reply. Failure to point out patentable novelty may lead to the amendment being held not fully responsive and a time period set to furnish a proper reply; if claims remain clearly open to rejection, a final rejection should generally be made.

name: Supplemental replies entry limitations
description: A supplemental reply that is supplemental to a § 1.111(b)-compliant reply will not be entered as a matter of right except when it is clearly limited to specified categories or filed during a suspended period.
guidance: Office may enter a supplemental reply if clearly limited to: cancellation of claim(s); adoption of examiner suggestions; placement of the application in condition for allowance; reply to an Office requirement made after the first reply; correction of informalities; or simplification of issues for appeal. A supplemental reply filed during a suspension under 37 CFR 1.103(a) or (c) must be entered. Examiner should annotate 'OK TO ENTER' if entered; 'DO NOT ENTER' and notify applicant if not entered. Supplemental replies reduce any accumulated patent term adjustment under 37 CFR 1.704(c)(8).

name: Claims presented without attempt to point out patentable novelty
description: If claims presented in an amendment make no attempt to point out patentable novelty, the claims should not be allowed.
guidance: An amendment failing to point out the patentable novelty believed to be present may be held not fully responsive and a time period set to furnish a proper reply (MPEP § 714.03). If claims are clearly open to rejection on the record, a final rejection should generally be made.

name: Immediate review of applicant actions near end of reply period
description: Actions filed near the end of the reply period should be reviewed as soon as possible upon availability to determine complete responsiveness and prevent abandonment.
guidance: Examiners should check (A) proper signature, (B) filing within statutory or shortened time period, (C) full responsiveness and compliance with 37 CFR 1.121, (D) whether changes warrant transfer, (E) whether application is special, (F) if claims suggested for interference have been copied, (G) traversal of a restriction requirement, (H) whether applicant cited references, (I) whether a terminal disclaimer has been filed, and (J) whether security-related matter was added. If inadequate and sufficient time remains, notify applicant to complete the reply within the period.

name: Excess claims fees when adding claims beyond previously paid-for counts
description: Applicant must pay excess claims fees for each claim in excess of the previously paid number of independent and total claims before the examiner considers the new claim.
guidance: Fees: required for claims in excess of 3 independent claims or in excess of 20 total claims (dependent or independent). Multiple dependent claim fees are calculated based on the number of claims referred to. Nonelected claims withdrawn after restriction are included in determining fees for subsequent amendments unless canceled. Example provided illustrating how cancellations and additions affect the need for additional excess claim fees.

name: What constitutes abandonment (general)
description: No abandonment can take place unless the invention is complete and operative and available for immediate public use.
guidance: Abandonment is shown by acts or declarations manifesting an intention to abandon, by public use or sale with the inventor's acquiescence (see two-year rule), or by specific disclaimers or omissions in applications/claims. Mere omission to practice or to make application is not sufficient.

name: Abandonment by application: disclaimers and omissions
description: An abandonment by application may consist in a specific disclaimer of the invention, or in describing but omitting to insert it in the claim.
guidance: A certified copy of the application containing the disclaimer is usually conclusive. Omission to claim a fully disclosed invention is regarded as conclusive dedication to the public unless the omitted invention is embraced in a new application or an amendment within a reasonable time. If suit is on a re-issue that supplies the defect, the issue is validity of the reissue, not abandonment.

name: Unreasonable delay in seeking new patent may show abandonment
description: Delay in securing a new patent, after knowledge of a discrepancy between description and claim, may indicate unreasonable delay and support abandonment.
guidance: Evidence must show inventor could have applied earlier and acquiesced in the disclosure of his unprotected invention for a period inconsistent with an original intention to claim it. Plaintiff may rebut only on the question of unreasonable delay except where his knowledge of insufficiency is derived from extraneous sources.

name: Multiple inclusion (double inclusion) of elements
description: Evaluate the facts in each case to determine whether the multiple inclusion of one or more elements in a claim gives rise to indefiniteness in that claim.
guidance: Do not apply automatic rules for or against 'double inclusion'; the governing consideration is what is a reasonable construction of the claim language (In re Kelly). A compound embraced by more than one member of a Markush group does not by itself create uncertainty as to claim scope, but a device claim that can be read to include the same element twice may be indefinite (Ex parte Kristensen). Apply older cases (Ex parte White, Ex parte Clark) with care according to case facts.

name: Product and process in the same claim (mixed apparatus/method)
description: A single claim that claims both an apparatus and the method steps of using the apparatus is indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b).
guidance: If a system claim contains limitations that are actions of users (i.e., not directed to the system), it creates confusion as to when infringement occurs and is indefinite (In re Katz Interactive Call Processing Patent Litigation; IPXL Holdings v. Amazon.com). Ex parte Lyell held a claim that combined an automatic transmission workstand and the method of using it ambiguous and properly rejected. By contrast, if additional limitations focus on the capabilities of the system (not specific user actions), the claim may be definite (Mastermine Software, Inc. v. Microsoft Corp.).

name: "Use" claims (claims reciting mere use without steps)
description: Attempts to claim a process without setting forth any steps (mere 'use') generally raise an indefiniteness issue under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) and may fail to claim statutory subject matter under 35 U.S.C. 101.
guidance: Claims that simply recite a use without active, positive steps delimiting how the use is practiced can be held indefinite (Ex parte Erlich). Claims that do not purport to claim a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter fail to comply with 35 U.S.C. 101 (In re Moreton). Examples of improper 'use' claim wording and case outcomes are provided (Ex parte Dunki; Clinical Products Ltd. v. Brenner). Procedurally, a claim reciting a use but failing to recite steps may be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 (form paragraph 7.05.01) and/or as indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (form paragraph 7.34.01). Note: in some instances a recited step such as 'utilizing' was held not indefinite (Ex parte Porter).

name: Do not import specification limitations into claims
description: Although a claim should be interpreted in light of the specification disclosure, it is generally improper to read limitations contained in the specification into the claims.
guidance: Examiners and courts should not rely on the specification to impart limitations to the claim that are not recited in the claim (In re Prater; In re Winkhaus). Interpretation must respect the claim language as written.

name: Chemical formula/structure claims and definiteness
description: Claims to chemical compounds or compositions using formulas or partial structures are not necessarily indefinite in the absence of evidence that the assigned formula is in error.
guidance: Do not find chemical structure claims indefinite merely because a structure is not fully presented or corroborating spectroscopic data is absent (Ex parte Morton; Ex parte Sobin). A claim to a chemical compound with partial structure or with wording like 'polypeptide of at least 24 amino acids having the following sequence' may be broad but not indefinite (In re Fisher). Compounds may be claimed by a name that adequately describes the material to one skilled in the art (Martin v. Johnson). Unknown structures may be claimed by a combination of physical and chemical characteristics (Ex parte Brian). A compound may also be claimed in product-by-process terms without raising indefiniteness.

name: Trademarks or trade names in claims
description: The presence of a trademark or trade name in a claim is not per se improper, but the claim must be analyzed to determine how the mark or name is used and whether it renders the claim indefinite.
guidance: A trademark identifies a source of goods and does not define the goods themselves (see MPEP § 608.01(v)). If a trademark/trade name is used as a limitation to identify or describe a particular material or product, the claim does not comply with 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (Ex parte Simpson). If present but not intended as a limitation, the reason for its inclusion should be addressed; if it causes confusion as to scope, the claim should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b). If an applicant replaces a trade name with a generic term, the examiner should determine whether there is sufficient support in the application for the generic term (see MPEP § 2163). Example: Examiner rejection of 'ALIMTA' as indefinite (Eli Lilly & Co. v. Apotex, Inc.).

name: Mere function of a machine is not sole ground for rejection of process claims
description: Process or method claims should not be rejected solely because they define an inherent function of a disclosed machine or apparatus.
guidance: A process claim that is otherwise patentable should not be rejected merely because the application discloses an apparatus that will inherently carry out the recited steps (In re Tarczy-Hornoch). Examiners should not use the mere fact of inherent machine function as the sole basis for a 35 U.S.C. 112(b) rejection of process claims.

name: Compact prosecution: interpret claims and state indefiniteness interpretation early
description: Under compact prosecution, the examiner should review claims for all statutory requirements early and clearly articulate any rejection and the interpretation of indefinite terms in the first Office action.
guidance: The goal is to articulate rejections early so applicant can timely respond with evidence of patentability (see MPEP § 706; 37 CFR 1.104(a)(1)). When a claim term renders the claim indefinite, the examiner should make a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) and also make any rejection(s) under 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103 that apply based on the examiner's interpretation of the claim. The examiner must state on the record how a claim term or phrase is being interpreted with respect to the prior art applied, thereby avoiding piecemeal examination (see In re Packard; MPEP § 707.07(g)).

name: Prior art rejection practice when claim is indefinite (two-approach guidance)
description: When terms of a claim are considered indefinite, determine whether to also reject over prior art depending on the degree of uncertainty.
guidance: Approach 1 (recommended when uncertainty is not great): Enter two rejections — (A) indefiniteness under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) and (B) a rejection over the prior art based on the interpretation that renders the claim unpatentable; when making the prior art rejection, point out how the claim is being interpreted (Ex parte Ionescu). Approach 2 (when there is great confusion/uncertainty): Do not base a 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection on considerable speculation about claim meaning or assumptions about scope (In re Steele). The first approach avoids piecemeal examination and may give applicants better appreciation of relevant prior art if claims are redrafted.

name: Two different reply periods running — general rule
description: When two different periods for reply are running against an application (the regular statutory period and a limited period set in a subsequent Office action), the running of the first period is not suspended nor affected by an ex parte limited time action or by an appeal therefrom.
guidance: There are exceptions (e.g., suggested claims — see MPEP Chapter 2300). The controlling period depends on the specific actions and dates in the file; examiners should follow applicable precedent and MPEP guidance.

name: Refund of search fee and excess claims fee via express abandonment (37 CFR 1.138(d)) — timing requirements
description: To obtain a refund of the search fee and excess claims fee paid in an application filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a) and § 1.53(b) on or after December 8, 2004, an applicant must submit a declaration of express abandonment by way of a petition under 37 CFR 1.138(d) before an examination has been made of the application.
guidance: The date on any certificate of mailing or transmission under § 1.8 is not taken into account in determining whether petition was filed before an examination. If the request for refund is not filed with the declaration or within two months from the date the declaration was filed, the Office may retain the entire search fee and excess claims fee; the two‑month period is not extendable. A petition under 1.138(d) will be granted only if filed before an examination has been made; an examination is counted when an action is shown in the One Patent Data Portal (PDP) as having been counted (status higher than 031). If PDP status is higher than 031 before or on the day the petition was filed, the petition will be denied.

name: National fast-track/acceleration programmes
description: Some AMS (Malaysia, Thailand, Singapore) provide domestic fast track programmes to expedite examination and grant of patents, with country-specific conditions, caps and expected grant timelines.
guidance: Examples: Singapore launched a program (from 4 May 2020) allowing 10 applications/month with per-entity caps; Thailand pilot requires applicant reasons and limits claims and monthly acceptances; Malaysia has tech-field based provision. Conditions commonly require applicants to state reasons for expedited examination and may impose claim limits, caps per month, applicant residency/filing conditions and response deadlines. Expected grant timelines (where specified) may be under 12 months or as short as 1 week after clear S&E report for some cases.

name: Grounds for opposition (enumerated)
description: Permissible grounds for pre- and post-grant opposition include: (1) claimed invention is not patentable; (2) lacks novelty; (3) lacks inventive step; (4) lacks industrial applicability; additionally, lack of disclosure/support, incorrect amendments and applicant eligibility are grounds in some countries (Indonesia, Lao PDR, Singapore, Viet Nam).
guidance: Opponents must state grounds and provide supporting evidence (e.g., prior art documents) within prescribed times and fees.

name: Computer programs excluded 'as such' but patentable if producing technical effect
description: Computer programs as sequences of executable instructions are abstract and excluded 'as such'. However, inventions implemented by a computer program that produce a technical effect beyond normal physical interactions of software and hardware are not excluded.
guidance: Normal electricity flow in execution is insufficient. Examples of technical effects: controlling anti-lock brakes, emissions determination by X-ray device, video compression, image restoration, encryption, security measures protecting boot integrity. Claims must include essential technical features; product, process and use claims may be allowable once technical character established.

name: Four-step approach for assessing computer program patentability
description: One approach to determine whether a claimed contribution from a computer program is patentable: (1) properly construe the claim; (2) identify the actual contribution made by the invention; (3) determine whether the actual contribution falls solely within excluded subject matter 'as such'; (4) determine whether the contribution is technical in nature.
guidance: Examiners should objectively investigate actual contribution (not be bound by applicant's assertion). If technical character is found, proceed to examine novelty and inventive step.

name: Refund when nonelected species embraced by allowable generic claim
description: Whenever claims drawn to an additional species in a transitional application for which applicant paid the fee in 37 CFR 1.17(s) are no longer withdrawn from consideration because they are fully embraced by an allowable generic claim, applicant should be notified that he or she may request a refund of the fee paid for that additional species.
guidance: Determination of when claims to a nonelected species would no longer be withdrawn should be made as indicated in MPEP §§ 806.04(d), 821.04, and 821.04(a).

name: Partial waiver: reasonable number of nucleotide sequences (ten)
description: The Director has sua sponte partially waived the requirements of 37 CFR 1.141 et seq. and permitted a reasonable number of nucleotide sequences to be claimed in a single application; it has been determined that normally ten sequences constitute a reasonable number for examination purposes.
guidance: Accordingly, in most cases, up to ten independent and distinct nucleotide sequences will be examined in a single application without restriction. Exceptional cases (complex claims) may require fewer than ten. Applicants may petition under 37 CFR 1.181 for examination of additional sequences by providing evidence that the different nucleotide sequences do not cover independent and distinct inventions. See MPEP §1850 for PCT/national stage treatment.

name: Patentably indistinct sequences examined with selected sequences
description: In addition to the specifically selected sequences, those sequences which are patentably indistinct from the selected sequences will also be examined.
guidance: When applicant selects sequences for examination, any claim elements patentably indistinct from those sequences are also to be examined and may be rejoined/allowed as appropriate.

name: Definition and public-policy basis of double patenting
description: The doctrine of double patenting seeks to prevent the unjustified extension of patent exclusivity beyond the term of a patent; double patenting results when the right to exclude granted by a first patent is unjustly extended by the grant of a later issued patent or patents.
guidance: The focus of any double patenting analysis is on the claims in the multiple patents or patent applications involved. For double patenting to be considered, two or more patents or applications must have at least one common inventor and/or be commonly assigned/owned or be subject to a proper joint research agreement (35 U.S.C. 103(c)(2) and (3)).

name: Two types of double patenting rejections (statutory vs nonstatutory)
description: There are generally two types of double patenting rejections: (1) 'same invention' statutory type based on 35 U.S.C. 101, and (2) 'nonstatutory-type' double patenting rejection (judicially created) grounded in public policy, primarily to prevent prolongation of patent term when later claims are not patentably distinguishable from earlier claims.
guidance: Nonstatutory double patenting includes rejections based on one-way or two-way obviousness determinations (obviousness-type double patenting). Nonstatutory rejections cannot be based on mere 'domination' absent statutory or nonstatutory grounds.

name: Statutory double patenting test (35 U.S.C. 101 — 'same invention')
description: Statutory double patenting asks: Is the same invention being claimed twice? 'Same invention' means identical subject matter. A reliable test is whether a claim in the application could be literally infringed without literally infringing a corresponding claim in the patent (In re Vogel).
guidance: If there exists an embodiment that falls within the scope of one claim but not the other, then identical subject matter is not defined by both claims and statutory double patenting does not exist. Example: 'halogen' vs 'chlorine' — not identical; '36 inches' vs '3 feet' — same invention. Statutory double patenting cannot be overcome by a terminal disclaimer; it can be overcome by canceling or amending conflicting claims so they are no longer coextensive.

name: Provisional double patenting rejections practice
description: A 'provisional' double patenting rejection may be made where conflicting claims exist between copending applications or between an application and a published application, provided confidentiality is not violated. Provisional rejections alert applicant to potential double patenting if one application issues as a patent.
guidance: Make provisional rejection in each application as long as conflicting claims exist in more than one application unless that provisional rejection is the only rejection remaining in at least one application. Procedures vary depending on which application has other rejections remaining; see rules on withdrawing provisional ODP, requiring terminal disclaimers in later-filed applications, and special handling when applications filed same day or when three applications conflict (terminal disclaimers required in at least two). Use form paragraphs 8.32 for provisional rejections. Where provisional statutory double patenting is only rejection remaining, withdraw in earlier-filed app and permit issuance; maintain provisional rejection in other app to convert when that app issues.

name: Distinction between domination and double patenting
description: Domination exists when a first patent or application has a broad/generic claim that fully encompasses an invention defined in a narrower claim in another patent/application; domination alone cannot support a double patenting rejection.
guidance: Although domination by itself is insufficient to support double patenting, its presence does not preclude double patenting if statutory or nonstatutory grounds otherwise exist. Cite In re Kaplan and In re Sarrett for guidance.

name: Use of form paragraphs for statutory double patenting (¶ 8.30, 8.31, 8.32)
description: Form paragraph 8.30 is the heading for statutory (same invention) double patenting rejections; ¶8.31 is used to reject claim as claiming same invention as claim of prior U.S. patent; ¶8.32 is used for provisional 35 U.S.C. 101 double patenting rejections against copending applications.
guidance: ¶8.30 must be used as a heading preceding statutory double patenting rejections. ¶8.31 is used only for earlier patents (not copending apps); ¶8.32 is used only for conflicting claims in copending applications. Refer to examiner notes for bracket insertions, when to use additional form paragraphs (e.g., 7.15, 7.19, 8.27), and other procedural specifics.

name: PATENT CLAIMS (Claim Construction)
description: Describe what patent claims are (concise, formal definitions that set the boundaries of the invention) and how they should be read for infringement/validity analysis.
guidance: Explains that each claim is a numbered paragraph, may be independent or dependent, and that infringement requires that an accused device or method contain every claim limitation.

name: SECTION 112, PARAGRAPH 6 / 35 U.S.C. § 112(f) (means-plus-function)
description: Instruction on claims that use means-plus-function language and how such claim elements are construed and infringed.
guidance: Explains that certain claim language may be interpreted to cover the corresponding structure, materials, or acts described in the specification and equivalents; sets standard for reading such limitations.

name: INFRINGEMENT GENERALLY
description: Legal standard for what constitutes infringement (making, using, selling, offering to sell, or importing a patented invention within the United States during the patent term without permission).
guidance: Explains direct, indirect (inducement and contributory), and other forms of infringement; jury must determine whether the accused product or action meets each claim limitation.

name: DIRECT INFRINGEMENT — LITERAL INFRINGEMENT OF §112(f) (means-plus-function) LIMITATIONS
description: How literal infringement analysis applies when claim limitations are expressed in means-plus-function form under §112(f).
guidance: Requires comparing accused structure/acts to the corresponding structure/materials/acts disclosed in the specification (and equivalents) that perform the claimed function.

name: ENABLEMENT (§112)
description: The patent specification must enable persons skilled in the art to make and use the invention without undue experimentation.
guidance: Jurors should consider whether the disclosure provides sufficient detail and guidance for a skilled person to practice the invention across the full scope of the claims.

name: ANTICIPATION
description: A claim is invalid as anticipated if a single prior-art reference discloses each and every claim limitation (i.e., the claimed invention is not new).
guidance: Jurors must determine whether a single prior reference reads on all claim elements; requires clear and convincing proof if challenging validity.

name: OBVIOUSNESS
description: Claim invalidity for obviousness requires showing that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art at the relevant time.
guidance: Includes subfactors jurors should consider (level of ordinary skill, scope and content of prior art, differences between prior art and claims, objective indicia of nonobviousness). References Graham factors and controlling precedent (e.g., KSR).

name: GLOSSARY — KEY TERMS (Abstract, Claim, Enablement, Anticipation, Prior Art, etc.)
description: Definitions of patent-law terms jurors will encounter (e.g., abstract, claim, limitation, enablement, anticipation, prior art, prosecution history, reads on).
guidance: These definitions control deliberations where the instructions define terms; judges should add technical terms from the case’s art and delete inapplicable terms.

name: Rectification — Evidence to be Considered and Applicable Date
description: For mistakes in description/claims/drawings the competent authority shall, for purposes of determining obviousness, take into account only the contents of the description, claims and drawings and any applicable correction/amendment. For mistakes in the request part or other documents, the authority shall take into account the contents of the international application itself and any submitted corrections, accompanying documents, any available priority document, and any other document in the authority’s international application file at the applicable date.
guidance: The applicable date is: (i) the international filing date for a mistake in a part of the international application as filed; (ii) the date on which the document was submitted for mistakes in a document other than the international application as filed (including corrections/amendments).

name: Non-rectifiable Mistakes and Invitation to Request Rectification
description: A mistake shall not be rectifiable if: (i) the mistake lies in the omission of one or more entire elements of the international application referred to in Article 3(2) or one or more entire sheets; (ii) the mistake is in the abstract; (iii) the mistake is in an amendment under Article 19, unless the IPEA is competent; or (iv) the mistake is in a priority claim or in a notice correcting/adding a priority claim under Rule 26 bis.1(a) where rectification would cause a change in the priority date (subject to operation of other Rules).
guidance: Where an Office/Authority/IB discovers what appears to be a rectifiable obvious mistake, it may invite the applicant to request rectification under this Rule.

name: Level of Ordinary Skill in the Art
description: Obviousness must be evaluated from the perspective of a 'designer of . . . articles of the types presented' — i.e., a designer of ordinary skill in the art to which the subject matter pertains.
guidance: Cite In re Nalbandian and In re Carter. Examiners must determine whether the design would have been obvious to a designer of ordinary skill with the claimed type of article.

name: Prima Facie Obviousness — Overall Appearance Standard
description: In determining patentability under 35 U.S.C. 103, it is the overall appearance of the design that must be considered.
guidance: After factual inquiries (Graham v. John Deere), examiner must determine whether they establish a prima facie case. To establish prima facie obviousness, all claim limitations must be taught or suggested by the prior art. The proper standard is whether the design would have been obvious to a designer of ordinary skill with the claimed type of article (see In re Nalbandian).

name: Functional or Hidden Features Cannot Support Patentability
description: Features of the design which are functional and/or hidden during end use may not be relied upon to support patentability; a design claim must be ornamental.
guidance: Examiners must provide evidence to support the prima facie functionality of such features. Hidden portions or functional features cannot be relied upon as a basis for patentability. If applicant wishes to rely on functional/hidden features, the standard for establishing ornamentality under 35 U.S.C. 171 must be applied (see Jones v. Progress Ind., In re Cornwall, In re Garbo).

name: Procedural Form Paragraphs and Remedies to Overcome 103 Rejections
description: Form paragraphs provide language for rejections and list procedural showings that may overcome a 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection (single or multiple references; AIA/pre-AIA differences; common ownership; provisional rejections).
guidance: Possible ways to overcome a rejection include: (1) showing under 37 CFR 1.130(a) that the design in the reference was obtained from the inventor (not prior art); (2) perfecting a claim to priority under 35 U.S.C. 119 by filing certified priority documents satisfying 35 U.S.C. 112(a); (3) perfecting benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 120 with an application data sheet under 37 CFR 1.76 and establishing enablement/description under 35 U.S.C. 112(a); (4) showing prior public disclosure under 37 CFR 1.130(b); (5) providing a statement under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) of common ownership/assignment; (6) merging applications or showing common ownership to overcome provisional rejections. Examiner Notes describe bracket insertion and sequencing requirements (e.g., preceding form paragraphs for certain priority situations).

name: Analogous Art for Simulative Portions of a Design
description: Analogous art can be more broadly interpreted when a claim is directed to a design with a portion simulating a well-known or naturally occurring object or person.
guidance: The simulative nature of that portion of the design is prima facie evidence that art which simulates that portion would be within the level of ordinary skill under 35 U.S.C. 103.

name: Statement of Claim — Infringement of Copyright in a Design
description: Form elements for a plaintiff's statement of claim in an action for infringement of copyright in a registered design.
guidance: As framed: (1) Allegation that the defendant has infringed the plaintiff's copyright in a registered design, specifying the registered design number, class and date of registration; (2) A description of the registered design ("The said registered design is [describe the design]"); (3) Allegation that the plaintiff duly caused the prescribed mark to be duly marked on all articles to which the design was applied, before delivery on sale; (4) Set out the acts complained of with reference to s.59. Relief claimed: injunction (state particular injunction sought) and a sum for damages. (Use the model on action for infringing Trade Mark, R.S.C. 1883, App. C.)

name: Injunction restraining infringement of Copyright in a Design (form and scope)
description: Form and operative terms for an injunction restraining infringement of copyright in a design.
guidance: Usual undertaking required. Example operative language: restrain the defendant, his servants and agents from selling the design in the statement of claim and from applying the same or any colourable imitation thereof to any substance or article of manufacture; in particular prohibit manufacturing and selling articles (example: ornamental sweetmeats) made so as to resemble the plaintiff's. Specify prohibited acts (manufacture, apply, sell, offer for sale, expose for sale) and identify particular articles by reference to the statement of claim.

name: Statement of Claim — Infringing a Trade Mark
description: Form elements for plaintiff's claim in a trade mark infringement action.
guidance: Allege (1) the defendant has infringed the plaintiff's trade mark; (2) describe the trade mark; (3) if plaintiff is not original proprietor, show briefly how title is derived; (4) set out the acts complained of. Relief claimed: injunction (state particular injunction sought) and an account or damages. Use R.S.C. 1883 App. C s.6 No.8 as model.

name: Assessment of consistency across filings when evaluating truthfulness
description: Consistency (or inconsistency) of a party's characterizations across the petition, declarations, interrogatory responses, and other filings is material when assessing whether statements are misleading.
guidance: Inconsistent statements (e.g., claiming exclusivity in petition/declaration, later saying exclusivity was waivable, later saying they did not intend to waive) can indicate misleading argument or misrepresentation. The Office will examine the sequence and context of statements to determine sanctionability.

name: Prior invention (pre-AIA §102(g))
description: Claim is invalid if the invention defined in that claim was invented by another person in the United States before the patentee invented it.
guidance: Defendant must show by clear and convincing evidence that (1) before the patentee invented his invention, the third party reduced to practice a product or method that included all of the features of the claim, or (2) the third party was first to conceive and exercised reasonable diligence in later reducing the invention to practice. The prior invention must be sufficiently developed that one skilled in the art would have recognized it would work for its intended purpose. Practice Note: This defense may be negated if the invention was abandoned, suppressed, or concealed. Where priority of invention is a jury issue, further instructions about conception, reduction to practice, and diligence are required.

name: Earlier-filed patent application (pre-AIA §102(e))
description: A claim is invalid if the invention was described in a published U.S. or PCT patent application or U.S. patent filed by another person before the patentee invented the claimed invention.
guidance: If jury must resolve date of invention, instruct how to determine it; otherwise instruct as to the filing date. Use these instructions where filing date of application/patent is the relevant date.

name: Obviousness — general standard
description: A claimed invention is invalid as obvious if it would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art as of the Cutoff Date. Unlike anticipation, obviousness may be shown by one or more prior art items.
guidance: Avoid using hindsight — do not use the patent as a roadmap for selecting/combining prior art. Defendant must prove obviousness by clear and convincing evidence. Obviousness is a mixed question of fact and law; consider roles of court and jury and potential waiver of JMOL on appeal. Perform separate analysis for each claim alleged obvious.

name: Graham factors for obviousness — differences between claimed invention and prior art
description: Analyze relevant differences between the prior art and the claimed invention from the viewpoint of a person of ordinary skill as of the Cutoff Date.
guidance: Determine impact of differences on obviousness of the claimed invention as a whole. Consider inferences and creative steps a person of ordinary skill would have used; predictable results from combining known elements support obviousness; unexpected/unpredictable results or teachings away support nonobviousness. A claim is not proven obvious merely because each element was independently known. Consider whether a reason existed at the time to combine elements and whether there would have been a reasonable expectation of success. Consider 'teaching away' and, if inherency is alleged, instruct on inherency tailored to the evidence — inherency requires the element be the natural result of the explicit disclosure, not mere probabilities.

name: Graham factors for obviousness — secondary considerations (objective indicia)
description: Consider secondary considerations that may help determine whether the invention would have been obvious, as part of the obviousness inquiry.
guidance: Secondary considerations include: commercial success due to merits of the invention (not advertising or non-claimed features); long-felt but unsolved need satisfied by the invention; others tried and failed; copying by others; unexpectedly superior results over closest prior art; praise or surprise from others in the field or defendant; acceptance of licenses because of the merits. No single consideration is dispositive; relevancy requires a nexus between the consideration and the invention and admissibility is for the Court to decide. Patentee bears burden to show nexus. Consider these only if properly supported by evidence and analyze alongside other factors.

name: Enablement requirement (§112)
description: A patent must disclose sufficient information to enable a person of ordinary skill in the field as of the effective filing date to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
guidance: Enablement is a question of law for the Court; jury may be instructed on subsidiary fact issues only if specific factual disputes bearing on enablement are submitted. Defendant bears burden by clear and convincing evidence that the specification fails enablement. Patents are written for persons of ordinary skill and need not state information such a person would likely know. Factors (Wands) to consider for undue experimentation include: quantity of experimentation and whether it uses known techniques; amount of direction/guidance in the patent; presence/absence of working examples; nature of the invention; state of the prior art; relative skill of those in the art; predictability of the art; and breadth of the claims.

name: Written-description requirement (§112)
description: A patent must contain a written description of the product or method claimed to ensure the applicant actually invented the claimed subject matter.
guidance: Written-description is a question of fact (instruct jury only if specific claims are challenged and evidence supports it). Defendant bears burden by clear and convincing evidence. The specification must describe each limitation of a claim with clear, concise, and exact terms; view the claim as a whole. Exact words need not be used; specific examples are not required. The written-description requirement is satisfied if a person of ordinary skill would recognize from the specification that the inventor possessed the claimed subject matter as of the effective filing date. Consider factors including nature and scope of claims; complexity, predictability, and maturity of the technology; existing knowledge in the field; and scope/content of prior art. Sufficiency is decided claim-by-claim.

name: Damages — general rule and burden
description: If the accused device or method infringes and the claims are not invalid, the jury must determine the type and amount of damages to compensate the plaintiff.
guidance: Plaintiff must prove each element of damages, including amount, by a preponderance of the evidence (more likely than not). Damages must be adequate to compensate the plaintiff and cannot be punitive or include interest as an addition. If all asserted claims are invalid or not infringed, do not consider damages. Reasonable royalty is the minimum recoverable amount if infringement proven.

name: Date damages begin — marking and notice rules
description: The start date for damages depends on agreement or proof of when the defendant was put on notice of the claim.
guidance: Alternate A: parties may stipulate the start date. Alternate B: if disputed, the start date is when plaintiff first notified defendant of its patent claim. Plaintiff can give notice by marking substantially all products that practice the patent with the patent number (including virtual marking with internet address) or by direct specific notice to the defendant. Marking by licensees who use the patented invention also counts if they mark substantially all products. If plaintiff did not provide effective public marking and did not directly notify defendant, damages are recoverable only after the lawsuit filing date, except when plaintiff and licensees never made/offered/sold patented products (e.g., only method claims asserted)—then damages may be recovered up to six years before filing even without notice.

name: Public notice as primary function of patent claims
description: A primary function of a patent is to provide public notice about the claimed invention; patents must 'apprise the public of what is still open to them' and should not contain ambiguous language or vague descriptions.
guidance: Unclear claims harm the public by failing to mark what is in the public domain, encourage gaming, increase uncertainty, retard competition, and discourage use of unprotected ideas. The public-notice goal should guide interpretive rules and prosecution practices.

name: Broadest Reasonable Construction (BRC) rule during prosecution
description: During patent prosecution the USPTO examiner determines claim meaning by giving the proposed claims their 'broadest reasonable construction in light of the specification.'
guidance: The BRC is used to determine applicable prior art and to guide the examiner's search and rejections.
