It was intended to (1) force iterative clarifying amendments, (2) incentivize precise initial drafting, and (3) set an outer boundary to reduce risk of unexpected broader interpretations in litigation. In practice, BRC can fail to produce these benefits and can impose costs without corresponding benefits.

name: PHOSITA rule for litigation claim construction
description: In litigation, courts construe claim terms according to their 'ordinary and customary' meaning to a person having ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA) at the relevant time.
guidance: Ordinary meaning is informed primarily by the patent's intrinsic record (specification, claims, prosecution history). Specification definitions control if present (inventor-as-lexicographer). Extrinsic evidence (dictionaries, expert testimony) may be used if ambiguity remains, but intrinsic evidence takes precedence.

name: Three methods of enhancing public notice
description: A theoretical framework identifying three prosecution processes that could produce claim clarity: (1) iterative improvements (amendments and records), (2) ex ante incentives for precise claiming, and (3) definition of the outer limits of claims.
guidance: Interpretive rules and examiner practices should be evaluated by how well they foster these three methods.

name: Iterative improvements (use prosecution to create public record)
description: The idea that broad constructions during prosecution will make vague claims more likely to be rejected, forcing applicants to amend claims and thereby create a clarifying public record.
guidance: The prosecution process is interactive: examiner rejections push applicants to narrow or clarify claims, developing written record and notice. However, this depends on active examiner enforcement and applicant responses.

name: Ex ante incentives for more precise claiming (penalty-default effect)
description: The threat of a broad construction and rejection during prosecution should incentivize applicants ex ante to draft clearer initial claims to avoid costly amendments.
guidance: This functions like a penalty default—if applicants know vague claims will be broadly construed and likely rejected, they will draft more precisely. The effectiveness depends on applicants' expectations of examiner behavior and costs of prosecution.

name: Definition of the outer limits of claims (prevent ensnarement)
description: Interpretive approaches should set an outer boundary on claim meaning during prosecution to minimize the risk that potential infringers will be unfairly ensnared by broader litigation constructions.
guidance: BRC was supposed to create such outer limits, but courts often interpret issued claims more broadly than the USPTO, undermining that goal.

name: Examiners should require disclaimers and definitions (but not claim charts)
description: Examiners should require patentees to provide disclaimers or definitions in the specification to clarify vague claim terms; however, they should not require claim charts.
guidance: Requiring definitions/disclaimers helps fix term meaning contemporaneously; claim charts are discouraged. This change would increase clarity without excessive burden if done judiciously.

name: Require a description of the prior art in the specification
description: Patent applicants should be required to include a section explaining their understanding of known prior art and list preferred reference sources to reveal the applicant's view of the state of the art.
guidance: Benefits: reveals unwritten background, aids examiners, narrows claim construction in litigation by providing contemporaneous context, and helps identify what skills were ordinary at the filing date. Risks: could invite strategic misstatements, but duty of candor and inequitable conduct rules may limit abuse.

name: Relax obviousness standard to allow examiners to consider more prior art (KSR approach)
description: Relaxing the rigid 'teaching, suggestion, or motivation' test (per KSR) lets examiners consider predictable uses, market pressures, and 'obvious to try' considerations so more prior art can be invoked to reject obvious claims.
guidance: Expanding obviousness review can serve the same public-notice/outer-limits function as BRC by preventing overly broad claims from issuing; traditional secondary considerations remain available to rebut obviousness.

name: Examiners should reject claims not supported by the specification (written-description requirement enforcement)
description: Examiners should more vigilantly reject claims that lack support in the specification under 35 U.S.C. § 112.
guidance: Enforcing support requirements pressures applicants to specify and limits vagueness; this complements definition/description requirements and helps delineate claim scope.

name: Intrinsic evidence controls claim meaning; extrinsic evidence disfavored
description: Claims are to be construed primarily from intrinsic evidence—the claims, the specification, and the prosecution history—while extrinsic evidence (dictionaries, expert testimony) is admissible but disfavored and subordinate.
guidance: Courts should rely on intrinsic record to avoid undermining public notice; extrinsic evidence only used when ambiguity persists despite intrinsic analysis.

name: Inventor-as-lexicographer: specification definitions govern where explicit
description: When a patent's specification provides specific definitions, those definitions control claim terms; the inventor may act as his own lexicographer.
guidance: Disclaimers and definitions in the specification will be applied; however, disclaimers of meaning and of prior art are excluded from claim construction rules that rely on definitions.

name: Construct claims to preserve validity if ambiguous
description: If a claim remains unclear after applying claim-construction tools, a court should construe the claim so as to be valid if possible.
guidance: This canon tends to produce more narrow constructions than BRC and serves as a tie-breaker favoring validity preservation.

name: Recognize and address examiner/applicant incentive problems (rational ignorance)
description: Applicants have incentives to keep claims vague (to allow ex post gaming); examiners have limited time and incentives focused on novelty/nonobviousness rather than claim clarity.
guidance: Policy and procedural reforms should account for these incentives—e.g., require better specs, require definitions, relax obviousness, or change the interpretive rule—to realign incentives toward public notice.

name: Limit weight of patentee/examiner testimony in construing claims
description: Patentee testimony about claim meaning is given little weight, and patent examiners rarely testify; courts prefer contemporaneous public records over later witness testimony.
guidance: Relying on public record and contemporaneous specification/prosecution history reduces hindsight bias and shifting witness positions; policies that produce richer contemporaneous records (definitions, prior art descriptions) will improve claim construction.

name: Real-world context of use / substantial utility (examples and non-examples)
description: A claimed assay or product that measures the presence of a material that has a stated correlation to a predisposition to a disease defines a 'real world' context of use and can establish a substantial utility. Conversely, certain situations do not define 'substantial utilities' and require further research or reasonable confirmation.
guidance: Non-examples that do NOT define substantial utility (require further research): (A) basic research studying properties or mechanisms of the claimed product; (B) a method of treating an unspecified disease or condition; (C) a method of assaying for or identifying a material that itself has no specific/substantial utility; (D) a method of making a material that itself has no specific, substantial, and credible utility; (E) a claim to an intermediate product for use in making a final product that has no specific, substantial and credible utility.

name: Wholly inoperative inventions / 'incredible' utility standard
description: An invention that is 'inoperative' (does not operate to produce the claimed results) is not useful, but to violate §101 the claimed device must be totally incapable of achieving a useful result.
guidance: A small degree or partial success is sufficient; rejections on inoperability are rare and fact-specific. Do not label asserted utility 'incredible' or 'speculative' unless it is clear the invention cannot and does not work as claimed. Examples of rejected 'inoperative' claims are fact-specific (e.g., perpetual motion, cold fusion, uncharacterized cures for many cancers) and should not be applied as per se rules.

name: Claim-level focus: evaluate each claim on its own merits
description: The claimed invention (each claim) is the focus of the utility assessment; each claim must be evaluated individually for compliance with statutory requirements.
guidance: Generally, a dependent claim has utility if its independent claim is in the same statutory class and defines an invention having utility. If a genus claim is supported by some species that have utility, treat the genus as sufficient unless it can be established that other species clearly lack utility; in such cases encourage narrowing amendments to exclude non-utility species.

name: Single credible assertion of utility suffices
description: An applicant need only make one credible assertion of specific utility for the claimed invention to satisfy §101 and §112(a); additional utility statements, even if not credible, do not negate utility.
guidance: Statements in the specification or prosecution history are not, standing alone, a basis for rejection. If a properly claimed invention meets at least one stated objective, utility under §101 is shown (citing Raytheon v. Roper and other cases).

name: ADS satisfies statutory/formal requirements for priority/benefit claims
description: Presentation of a priority or benefit claim in an ADS will satisfy the requirement in 37 CFR 1.55 or 1.78 and the underlying statutory requirements (e.g., 35 U.S.C. 119, 120, 121, 365), and presentation of the name of the applicant in an ADS will satisfy 37 CFR 1.46 when applicable.
guidance: Patent Law Treaty Model International Forms and the PCT Request Form can satisfy the ADS requirement for priority/benefit claims where indicated. However, a reference filing in an ADS under 37 CFR 1.57(a) that replaces the specification/drawings for purposes of a filing date is not by itself sufficient to establish a priority or benefit claim; applicants must still provide domestic or foreign priority/benefit information in the ADS as appropriate.

name: Advantages Disclosed or Inherent
description: The totality of the record must be considered when determining whether a claimed invention would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made. Therefore, evidence and arguments directed to advantages not disclosed in the specification cannot be disregarded.
guidance: Evidence and arguments rebutting a §103 rejection need not be contained within the specification; such evidence presented during ex parte prosecution is part of the totality of the record (In re Chu). Examples include inherent properties (In re Zenitz) and undisclosed relative toxicity (Ex parte Sasajima). The specification need not disclose proportions or values as critical for applicants to present evidence showing such proportions/values are critical (In re Saunders).

name: Burden of Production for Evidence of Commercial Success and Nexus
description: An applicant who is asserting commercial success to support its contention of nonobviousness bears the burden of proof in establishing commercial success.
guidance: The PTO relies on applicants to provide hard evidence of commercial success because the Office lacks resources to gather such evidence. The term 'nexus' denotes a factually and legally sufficient connection between the commercial success evidence and the claimed invention so the evidence is probative of nonobviousness (see In re Huang; Demaco Corp. v. F. Von Langsdorff Licensing Ltd.). See MPEP §§716.01(b) and 2145 for guidance on assessing nexus.

name: Commercial Success Commensurate in Scope With Claimed Invention
description: Objective evidence of nonobviousness including commercial success must be commensurate in scope with the claims.
guidance: Evidence of commercial success must be due to claimed features and not to unclaimed features (In re Tiffin; Joy Technologies Inc. v. Manbeck). Evidence limited to narrower embodiments or features recited only in dependent claims may not be commensurate with broader independent claims. See MPEP §§716.01(b) and 2145 for nexus guidance. A generic affidavit phrase saying a product was 'constructed according to the disclosure and claims' is insufficient to establish nexus (Ex parte Standish).

name: Requirements When Claimed Invention Is Not Coextensive With Commercial Product or Process
description: If a particular range is claimed, applicant does not need to show commercial success at every point in the range; evidence at typical points can be persuasive if affidavits indicate operation throughout the claimed ranges approximates that at the commercial point.
guidance: When the commercially successful product is not coextensive with the claimed invention, applicant must show a legally sufficient relationship between the claimed feature and the commercial product (In re Hollingsworth; Demaco). Affidavits indicating typical operation across ranges can support commensurateness.

name: Commercial Success Must Flow From Functions and Advantages Disclosed or Inherent in the Specification
description: To be pertinent to nonobviousness, the commercial success of devices within the claims must flow from the functions and advantages disclosed or inherent in the specification; success attributable to improvements/modifications by others is not pertinent.
guidance: Evidence must show the success results from the invention's disclosed/inherent advantages (In re Vamco Machine & Tool, Inc.; Merck & Cie v. Gnosis S.P.A.). If success results from a 'unique combination' or synergistic interaction not recited in the claims, nexus may be lacking.

name: Nexus Establishment in Design Cases
description: Establishing a nexus between commercial success and the claimed invention is especially difficult in design cases.
guidance: Evidence of commercial success in design patents must be clearly attributable to the design itself and not to brand recognition, improved performance, or other factors; lack of such attribution undermines probative value (Litton Systems, Inc. v. Whirlpool Corp.).

name: Sufficiency of Disclosure (Enablement under 35 U.S.C. 112(a))
description: Determining whether the specification provides an enabling disclosure in compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
guidance: Once examiner establishes a prima facie lack of enablement, the burden shifts to applicant to present persuasive arguments and suitable proofs that one skilled in the art could make and use the claimed invention from the disclosure (In re Brandstadter). Evidence supplementing a deficient specification must establish that the missing information would have been known to those skilled in the art (In re Howarth). Affidavits/declarations are not acceptable to establish facts the specification should recite (In re Buchner; In re Smyth). Opinion testimony that merely asserts disclosure is of limited weight, but expert testimony that explains the factual basis for an opinion may be helpful and is evaluated case‑by‑case (In re Oppenauer; Glaser v. Strickland).

name: Joint research agreement (JRA) safe-harbor requirements (35 U.S.C. 103(c)(2)/(3))
description: For purposes of 35 U.S.C. 103, subject matter developed by another person and a claimed invention shall be deemed to have been owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person if: (A) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement that was in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; (B) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (C) the application for patent for the claimed invention discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement.
guidance: The JRA must be a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement entered into by two or more persons or entities for the performance of experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention. The JRA must be in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made (it need not be in effect on or before the prior art date of the reference sought to be disqualified). To invoke this safe harbor, applicants must comply with statute and rules of practice (see 37 CFR 1.71(g) and 1.104(c)(4)).

name: Definition of "joint research agreement"
description: "Joint research agreement" means a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement entered into by two or more persons or entities for the performance of experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention.
guidance: This statutory definition (35 U.S.C. 103(c)(3)) is used for determining eligibility for the JRA safe harbor; the JRA must have been in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made.

name: Definition of "commonly owned" for 35 U.S.C. 103(c)
description: The term "commonly owned" is intended to mean that the subject matter which would otherwise be prior art to the claimed invention and the claimed invention are entirely or wholly owned by the same person(s) or organization(s)/business entity(ies). For purposes of 35 U.S.C. 103(c), common ownership must be at the time the claimed invention was made. If the person(s) or organization(s) owned less than 100 percent of the subject matter or less than 100 percent of the claimed invention, then common ownership would not exist.
guidance: Common ownership requires 100% ownership of both the reference subject matter and the claimed invention at the time the later invention was made. A license of the claimed invention to another by the owner where basic ownership rights are retained would not defeat ownership. The question is determined on the facts of the particular case; moral or unenforceable obligations do not evidence common ownership. Present statements of ownership are insufficient—ownership must be shown to have existed at the time the invention was made.

name: Required statement content, location, and signature (37 CFR 1.104(c)(4) and practice)
description: To overcome a 103(a) rejection based on subject matter qualifying under 102(e), (f), or (g) via 103(c)(2), the applicant must provide a statement to the effect that the prior art and the claimed invention were made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement that was in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made, and that the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the joint research agreement.
guidance: The statement should either be on or begin on a separate sheet and must not be directed to other matters (37 CFR 1.4(c)). The statement must be signed in accordance with 37 CFR 1.33(b). When an applicant disqualifies subject matter and follows the rules, the examiner will treat the application and the 102(e)/(f)/(g) prior art as if commonly owned for purposes of 103(a).

name: Recapture doctrine caution for reissue applications
description: For reissue applications, the doctrine of recapture may prevent the presentation of claims in the reissue application that were amended or cancelled from the application which matured into the patent, if the claims were amended or cancelled to overcome a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 based on prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) which was not able to be excluded under 35 U.S.C. 103(c) in the original application.
guidance: If an examiner determines this situation applies in the reissue application, consultation with the Office of Patent Legal Administration should be initiated via the Technology Center Special Program Examiner. The CREATE Act's effective date and prior prosecution history can affect recapture analyses.

name: Failure to submit deposit certificate after filing
description: Where the applicant filed an application by only disclosing the deposit number on the specification and failed to submit the deposit certificate through amendment even after filing the application, it shall be deemed that the deposit has never been made on the date of deposit.
guidance: Merely stating a deposit number in the spec without providing the certificate (and failing to supply it later) results in treating the deposit as not made at the claimed date.

name: Failure to disclose sequence list in specification (enablement rejection)
description: Where an invention disclosed in claims cannot be easily practiced because the sequence list is not disclosed in the specification, an examiner shall notify a ground for rejection under Article 42(3)(i) of the Patent Act.
guidance: Omission of required sequence data in the spec that renders claims non-enabled triggers a rejection under the specified Article.

name: Computer program per se non-statutory; computer-implemented inventions may be statutory
description: A computer program is a mere list of instructions and is not considered a statutory invention. However, inventions where data processing is specifically executed using hardware, a data processing unit operating with the program, operating methods, a computer-readable medium carrying the program, and the program stored in medium (applied to applications filed on/after July 1, 2014) are considered statutory.
guidance: Claims should emphasize technical implementation/hardware interaction to be patent-eligible; mere program listings are not patentable.

name: Utility model 'article' characteristics: shape, construction, combination
description: 'Shape' is external figuration (lines, surfaces); 'construction' is spatial/3D construction expressed in contour, plans, elevations; 'combination' is two or more spatially separate articles that functionally relate (e.g., bolt and nut).
guidance: Assess whether claimed subject matter is an article/quasi-article under utility model criteria.

name: Animal-limited methods may be industrially applicable
description: Even if a method could be used for human treatment, the method is considered industrially applicable if it is limited to be practiced on animal bodies excluded from humans.
guidance: Limiting claim scope to non-human animals can render otherwise-medical methods patentable.

name: ¶ 7.18.aia Rejection, Pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g)
description: Claim [1] rejected under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) as being [2] by [3].
guidance: Examiner Note: (1) Use only for an application/patent examined under AIA where the claims contain or contained an effective filing date before March 16, 2013 or a specific reference under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, or 365(c) to any patent/application that contains such a claim. (2) In bracket 1 insert claim numbers under rejection. (3) In bracket 2 insert either '--clearly anticipated--' or '--anticipated--' with explanation at end. (4) In bracket 3 insert the prior art relied upon. (5) Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.14.aia or 7.103.

name: ¶ 7.19.fti Rejection, pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f) Applicant Not the Inventor
description: Claim [1] is/are rejected under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f) because the applicant did not invent the claimed subject matter. [2]
guidance: Examiner Note: (1) This paragraph must be preceded either by paragraphs 7.07.fti and 7.13.fti or by paragraph 7.103. (2) In bracket 2 insert an explanation of the supporting evidence establishing that applicant was not the inventor. See MPEP § 2137.

name: ¶ 7.20.02.aia Joint Inventors, Common Ownership Presumed (AIA)
description: This application currently names joint inventors. In considering patentability of the claims the examiner presumes that the subject matter of the various claims was commonly owned at the time any inventions covered therein were effectively filed absent any evidence to the contrary.
guidance: Applicant is advised of the obligation under 37 CFR 1.56 to point out the inventor and effective filing dates of each claim that was not commonly owned at the time a later invention was effectively filed in order for the examiner to consider applicability of 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) for any potential 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) prior art against the later invention. Examiner Note: (1) Use only in applications filed on/after March 16, 2013 and must be preceded by 7.03.aia. (2) Must be used in all applications with joint inventors (unless claims are clearly restricted to only one claimed invention).

name: ¶ 7.21.fti Rejection, pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a)
description: Claim [1] is/are rejected under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over [2].
guidance: Examiner Note: (1) Must be preceded by either form paragraph 7.20.fti or 7.103. (2) An explanation of the rejection must follow; see MPEP § 2144. (3) If the rejection relies upon prior art under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e), use pre‑AIPA 102(e) as amended by AIPA to determine reference's prior art date unless reference is a U.S. patent issued from an international application with international filing date prior to Nov 29, 2000. See Examiner Notes for 7.12.fti and 7.12.01.fti. (4) If applicability prevents disqualification under pre‑AIA 103(c) then 7.20.01.fti must follow. (5) If provisional pre‑AIA 103(a) based on copending application use 7.21.01.fti instead. (6)-(7) Bracket instructions for claim numbers and prior art reference(s).

name: ¶ 7.21.01.fti Provisional Rejection, pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a), Common Assignee/Applicant/Joint Inventor
description: Claim [1] is/are provisionally rejected under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being obvious over copending Application No. [2] which has a common [3] with the instant application. Based upon the earlier effective U.S. filing date of the copending application, it would constitute prior art under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) if published or patented. This provisional rejection is based upon a presumption of future publication or patenting of the copending application. [4]
guidance: This provisional rejection might be overcome by: (a) showing under 37 CFR 1.132 that any invention disclosed but not claimed in the copending application was derived from the inventor/joint inventors of this application (not 'by another'); (b) showing a date of invention for the instant application prior to the copending application's effective U.S. filing date under 37 CFR 1.131(a); or (c) showing the copending application is disqualified under pre‑AIA 103(c) as prior art. Examiner Note: (1) Used to provisionally reject claims not patentably distinct from disclosure in copending application with earlier U.S. filing date and common assignee/applicant/joint inventor; (2) Use pre‑AIPA 102(e) rules for determining copending application's prior art date as applicable. (3) If claimed invention is fully disclosed use 7.15.01.fti. (4)-(6) Bracket instructions for claim numbers, application number, and type of common relationship. (8)-(9) Additional notes on follow‑on rejections and double patenting.

name: ¶ 7.21.02.fti Rejection, pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a), Common Assignee/Common Applicant/Joint Inventor
description: Claim [1] is/are rejected under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being obvious over [2]. The applied reference has a common [3] with the instant application. Based upon the earlier effective U.S. filing date of the reference, it constitutes prior art under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e).
guidance: This rejection might be overcome by: (1) showing under 37 CFR 1.132 that any invention disclosed but not claimed in the reference was derived from the inventor of this application (not 'by another'); (2) showing of a date of invention for the claimed subject matter prior to the effective U.S. filing date of the reference under 37 CFR 1.131(a); or (3) an oath/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(c) stating current common ownership and that the inventor named in the application is the prior inventor under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 104 together with a terminal disclaimer per 37 CFR 1.321(c). Also see notes on application of pre‑AIPA 102(e) and when to use other paragraphs (7.12.fti, 7.12.01.fti). (4) Bracket instructions for claim numbers and prior art references relied upon.

name: Format and content of the requirement (must state basis and form)
description: The requirement must clearly indicate that a requirement under 37 CFR 1.105 is being made, the basis for the requirement, and the specific information being required.
guidance: Requirements should specify the particular art area involved, the particular claimed subject matter within such art area, and the form the required information is expected to take (citations/copies of individual art references, identification of collections, answers to questions, or other specified form). Preferably prepare the requirement as a separate document to call attention and facilitate routing within applicant's organization. The requirement should state why it has been made and how the information is necessary to examination.

name: Form paragraph 7.106 (Domain of Search)
description: Use when the information is required to extend the domain of search for prior art: identify class and subclasses and describe why a broader range of art is needed to establish the level of knowledge of those of ordinary skill.
guidance: Must be preceded by 7.105 and followed by 7.122–7.126 as appropriate; insert description of art claimed but not fully represented in Office collections.

name: Form paragraph 7.117 (Art Relied Upon for Drafting Claimed Subject Matter)
description: Request title, citation and copy of each publication any applicant relied upon in drafting the claimed subject matter, with explanation of reliance in distinguishing claims from prior art.
guidance: Limited to documents actually relied on; must be preceded by 7.105 and followed by 7.122–7.126.

name: Form paragraph 7.119 & 7.120 (Names of Products or Services Incorporating Claimed/Disclosed Art)
description: Request names of any products or services that have incorporated the claimed subject matter (7.119) or the disclosed prior art (7.120).
guidance: Must be preceded by 7.105 and followed by 7.122–7.126; for prior art, specify attributes that most closely approximate the claimed subject matter to narrow focus.

name: Form paragraph 7.121 (Details of Improvement Over the Prior Art)
description: Request statement of specific improvements of claimed subject matter over disclosed prior art and indicate specific elements providing those improvements; for means/steps-plus-function claims provide page and line numbers describing the claimed structure and acts.
guidance: Must be preceded by 7.105 and followed by 7.122–7.126.

name: Appeals involving claims examinable in reporting TC
description: When an appeal is taken from rejection of claims all examinable in the TC preparing a P.R., and the application is otherwise allowable, formal transfer of the application to that TC should be made for appeal purposes; the receiving TC will take jurisdiction and prepare the examiner's answer; at allowance the application may be sent to issue by that TC with classification determined by controlling claims.
guidance: Use formal transfer to receive jurisdiction for appeal-only purposes.

name: Limitations on use of Patentability Report practice
description: P.R. practice is not obligatory and should be resorted to only where it will save total examiner time or result in improved quality due to specialized knowledge. Where claims are directed to the same character of invention but differ in scope only, P.R. is never proper.
guidance: Exemplary situations where P.R. ordinarily is not proper: (A) claims related as manufacturing process and a product defined by the process; (B) claims related as product and a process which merely makes the product having certain characteristics; (C) claims related as a combination distinguished solely by characteristics of a subcombination and such subcombination per se. Where P.R. will save total examiner time it is permitted with Director approval (stamp 'Approved' required).

name: Reasons sufficient to support non-entry (examples)
description: (A) an additional search is required; (B) more than a cursory review of the record is necessary; or (C) the amendment would involve materially added work on the part of the Office (e.g., checking excessive editorial changes in the specification or claims).
guidance: Any one of these reasons is considered sufficient to recommend non-entry of an amendment under 37 CFR 1.312 when appropriate.

name: Entry and approval authority signatures
description: Amendments under 37 CFR 1.312 that do not affect scope of claims may be signed by the primary examiner; those changing scope require supervisory patent examiner signature.
guidance: Use form paragraph 7.85 for entered amendments; if nonentry, use form paragraph 7.87 and specify reasons.

name: Handling formal-only amendments
description: Amendments which embody merely the correction of formal matters in the specification, formal changes in a claim without changing the scope thereof, or cancellation of claims may be indicated 'Enter Formal Matters Only.'
guidance: Such amendments do not require supervisory patent examiner submission prior to entry. If disapproved either in whole or in part, supervisory signature is required. IFW processing is substantially the same.

name: Amendments ordinarily denied entry — copied patent claims (conditional)
description: While copied patent claims are generally admitted even though application is under final rejection or on appeal, under certain conditions the claims may be refused entry.
guidance: See MPEP Chapter 2300 for the specific conditions under which copied claims may be refused entry.

name: Amendments ordinarily denied entry — drawings held to contain new matter
description: Amendments to the drawing held by the examiner to contain new matter are not entered until the question of new matter is settled.
guidance: This practice of nonentry because of alleged new matter does not apply to amendments to the specification and claims. See MPEP § 608.04 and § 706.03(o).

name: Amendments ordinarily denied entry — not in compliance with 37 CFR 1.121
description: An amendment including changes to the specification/claims which is not in compliance with 37 CFR 1.121 (e.g., not including replacement paragraphs or claim listings) is ordinarily denied entry.
guidance: See MPEP § 714 for examples and handling of non-compliant amendments.

name: Purpose of 37 CFR 1.131 affidavits/declarations
description: 37 CFR 1.131 permits an inventor/owner/qualified party to submit an affidavit or declaration to establish invention prior to the effective date of a reference or activity used to reject a claim (i.e., to 'swear back' a reference).
guidance: Prior invention may not be established under 1.131 in countries other than the U.S., certain NAFTA/WTO date limitations apply. Original exhibits (drawings/records) must accompany affidavit/declaration or their absence satisfactorily explained. The rejection is withdrawn (the reference is what is withdrawn), not the reference itself.

name: Inappropriate uses of 37 CFR 1.131 — statutory bars and other limits
description: An affidavit/declaration under 1.131 is inappropriate where: (A) reference publication date is more than 1 year prior to applicant's effective filing date (statutory bar under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)); (B) reference U.S. patent or application publication claims the same patentable invention; (C) reference is a foreign patent for the same invention to applicant issued prior to filing date where 35 U.S.C. 102(d) applies; (D) effective filing date of applicant's parent application makes affidavit unnecessary; (E) reference is prior U.S. patent to same entity claiming same invention (double patenting); (F) disclosure of prior U.S. patent to same party, not copending (dedication); (G) applicant has clearly admitted subject matter is prior art; (H) subject matter relied upon is prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(f); (I) subject matter is prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(g); (J) subject matter corresponding to a lost count in an interference where it constitutes prior art under 102(g) or is barred by interference estoppel.
guidance: Specific case law cited (In re Gibbs; In re Hellsund; In re Garfinkel; In re Blout; In re Lopresti; In re Bass; In re Bandel; In re Kroekel; In re Deckler; In re Zletz; In re McKellin) illustrates limits; 1.131 is designed to overcome references that are not statutory bars but have dates prior to effective filing date yet after applicant's date of invention. It cannot be used to overcome 102(f), 102(g), or clear admissions of prior art.

name: Priority / prior-filed application not basis for new-matter assessment
description: Since a first country application or a prior-filed application which forms the basis of the priority claim shall not correspond to the specification or drawing(s) as originally filed, such applications shall not be used as the basis of assessment in addition of new matter.
guidance: Do not rely on priority or earlier-filed documents as supplying original disclosure support when assessing whether an amendment introduces new matter into the current application.

name: Narrowing from genus to species requires original support or skilled-person recognition
description: Where an amendment is made to narrow a claim as from a genus to a species, unless the species is supported by the original specification and drawings, or unless one skilled in the art would readily recognize the species from the genus in light of ordinary skill in the art at the time the patent application was filed, it shall be viewed as introduction of new matter.
guidance: Examples: inserting a specific material (e.g., 'ABS') into a previously generic 'transparent plastic' may introduce new matter unless ABS was disclosed or would be obvious to skilled person. Conversely, if the skilled person would intuitively associate the generic term with the specific embodiment (e.g., 'sensor detecting rotation' -> 'proximity sensor'), amendment may be supported.

name: Broadening from species to genus and deletion of essential limitations
description: Where an amendment is made to broaden a claim as from a species to a genus, if the genus encompasses other species than the species disclosed in the original specification, and if the other species may have different function in addressing the problem to be solved or may accomplish different effects, the amendment shall constitute introduction of new matter. Where some limitations are deleted and the deleted limitations are described in the original disclosure as essential in solving a problem, it shall be viewed as introduction of new matter. However, deleting arbitrarily added limitations having nothing to do with solving problems may be supported.
guidance: Assess whether broadened claim covers embodiments with different effects/functions and whether deleted features were essential; examples include geometry changes affecting electrical contact, or deletion of an 'identifying code' limitation that was arbitrary.

name: Negative limitations (deleting elements) permitted only if no new technical matter
description: Amendment to delete some elements from the claims ('negative limitations') is permitted; provided, however, that such a negative limitation does not introduce any new technical matter which is not disclosed in the original specification. In particular, excluding particular subjects (e.g., humans) is acceptable if original specification did not restrict to particular animals.
guidance: Examples: amending 'treatment methods for mammals' to 'except humans' may be permitted where original disclosure did not limit to humans. Ensure deletion does not implicitly introduce an unsupported technical teaching.

name: Adding new effects generally adds new matter
description: The amendment to add new effects of the claimed invention shall be generally viewed as introduction of new matter; provided, however, that where one skilled in the art could easily recognize the effects from the configuration of the invention disclosed in the original specification or where it is commonly known in the relevant field that such effects can be accomplished from the configuration described in the original specification, it shall not be generally viewed as introduction of new matter.
guidance: Be cautious when adding statements of advantages/effects; allowed only if those effects are directly and unambiguously derivable from the original configuration or common general knowledge.

name: Adding titles/summaries of prior art vs. adding prior-art disclosure
description: The amendment to simply add the title of prior art documents and the amendment to add both the short summaries of the prior art documents and the title of the documents shall not be viewed as introduction of new matter. However, where the disclosure of a prior art document is added to address lack of written description or to complete an incomplete invention, or where comparisons suggesting advantages are added, it shall be generally viewed as introduction of new matter.
guidance: Permitted: inserting citation titles or brief summaries. Not permitted: inserting the substantive disclosure of prior art to fill original-specification gaps or to assert advantages of the claimed invention.

name: Permissible amendments under Article 47(3)
description: An amendment to claims among the amendments in response to the rejection necessitated by a previous amendment or upon a request for reexamination in accordance with Article 47(3) of the Patent Act shall be one of the followings: narrowing of claims by restricting claims, correction of clerical errors, clarification of ambiguous descriptions, or deletion of new matter.
guidance: Only these types of amendments are allowable under Article 47(3) when replying to such rejections; assess amended claims against the earlier (same-numbered) claim to determine correspondence.

name: Types of claim restriction (narrowing) permitted
description: Cases of narrowing of claims under Article 47(3) shall be limited to restricting a claim, deleting a claim and adding a technical element to a claim. Restricting includes reduction of numerical range, change from genus to species, deletion of alternatively recited elements, and reduction of referred claim from claims which refer to multiple claims.
guidance: Reduction of a numeric range is permitted only if it stays within the original claim's range; simultaneous reduction and extension (e.g., 10-20→15-30) is not reduction. Deleting alternative elements (A or B → A) is a valid restriction.

name: Adding described technical features to narrow claims
description: The scope of an invention is narrowed by adding new technical features described in the description of the invention or claims (e.g., changing 'B attached to A' to 'B attached to A and then C attached to B').
guidance: Adding features that are already described in the description/claims narrows and is permissible as a restriction, provided support exists in the original disclosure.

name: Amendments not falling under Article 47(3)(i)
description: Cases not falling under Article 47(3)(i) include: (i) where a claim is newly-added or an invention is added to claims by adding alternative elements or adding a referred claim (with some reorganization exceptions), and (ii) where a claim goes beyond the original scope due to certain amendments (change from species to genus, deletion of elements, addition & deletion of elements, broadening numerical range, replacement of element, change of numerical range).
guidance: Be alert to newly added matter or amendments that broaden scope—these are not permitted under Article 47(3) and may be refused.

name: Correction of clerical errors
description: Correcting clerical errors refers to the case where a description before an amendment and a description after an amendment are objectively deemed to be the same. Examples include incorrect description of claims explicitly recognized from matters in the description or where incorrectness is explicit based on features or empirical rules.
guidance: Only true objective/correctable clerical mistakes qualify; ambiguous edits that change substantive meaning are not clerical corrections.

name: Clarification of ambiguous descriptions
description: An ambiguous description is one whose meaning in the context is not clear (e.g., unclear claim language, elements that do not match other descriptions, or the claim is not technically specified). An amendment of redrafting the overall claim without any substantial changes shall be deemed to clarify an ambiguous description under Article 47(3)(iii), unless other specific conditions are present.
guidance: Redrafting for clarity is allowable provided no substantive change to scope; determine whether the redraft merely clarifies or actually changes the technical content.

name: Definition and assessment of 'new rejection necessitated by amendment'
description: A 'new rejection necessitated by the amendment' means a ground for rejection which did not exist prior to the amendment newly arises due to the submission of the amendment (e.g., amendment renders claim indefinite or creates new lack-of-novelty or lack-of-inventive-step grounds). Rejection grounds that were present before the amendment but not notified are not deemed new grounds.
guidance: When assessing refusal, determine whether the amendment itself created the new ground; pre-existing but unnotified grounds are not treated as 'new'.

name: Appeal brief core parts
description: An appeal brief consists of six parts: (1) Summary of claimed subject matter, (2) Real party in interest, (3) Related appeals, interferences, and trials, (4) Argument, (5) Conclusion (optional), and (6) Claims appendix.
guidance: Use the PTAB word template and PDF instructions available on the PTAB website to structure the brief.

name: Summary of claimed subject matter guidance
description: Provides a concise explanation of the subject matter defined in each of the rejected independent claims; not required for pro se applicants but may help the Board understand the arguments.
guidance: If included, should identify, for each claim element, supporting disclosure and figures.

name: Argument requirement in appeal brief
description: Argument section should explain why the examiner’s decision to reject the pending claims is improper and should be reversed.
guidance: Focus on legal and factual reasons demonstrating error in the examiner’s rejection and tie arguments to the claim elements and record.

name: COVID-19 Fast-Track Appeals pilot differences
description: Similar to Fast-Track Appeals Pilot but with no fee; technology limit: application must claim a product or process subject to an applicable FDA approval for COVID–19 use; no time limit for the pilot and 500 total granted petitions.
guidance: Certify the COVID-19 applicability when filing; eligibility narrower on technology but fee waived.

name: Preliminary Guidance (PG) content and timing
description: If PO requests PG, Board will provide PG within four weeks of due date for Opposition to MTA. PG is a preliminary, non-binding initial assessment of the MTA based on the record so far; typically short; focuses on limitations added in MTA; does not address patentability of original claims; does not provide dispositive conclusions; no rehearing from PG.
guidance: Use PG to shape a responsive revised MTA or reply; PG cannot be reheard directly.

name: MTA burdens of persuasion (final rule)
description: New subsection (d) to 37 C.F.R. § 42.121 and § 42.221 (effective Jan 20, 2021) assigns burdens: patent owner has the burden of showing that an MTA complies with statutory and regulatory requirements for such a motion; petitioner has the burden of showing the unpatentability of substitute claims.
guidance: For MTAs filed on/after Jan 20, 2021, craft filings knowing the allocation of burdens; evidence and argument should address the party’s specific burden.

name: Alice two-step test
description: Apply the Supreme Court's two-step Alice framework: (1) determine whether a claim is directed to a patent-ineligible concept like an abstract idea; (2) if so, determine whether the claim recites elements sufficient to transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application (i.e., contains an 'inventive concept').
guidance: Quoted formulation: 'Under step one of the Alice test, we review whether a claim is directed to a patent-ineligible concept like an abstract idea. ... At step two, we review whether the claim recites elements sufficient to transform it into a patent-eligible application.' (Alice, 573 U.S. 208). Use this two-step framework as the controlling inquiry.

name: Alice Step One — 'directed to' inquiry (character of the claims as a whole)
description: The 'directed to' inquiry looks to the character of the claims as a whole and does more than simply ask whether the claims involve a patent-ineligible concept.
guidance: Consider the claimed advance over the prior art (the focus of the claimed advance). Avoid characterizing claims at too high a level of generality untethered from claim language. See Enfish (look to character of the claims as a whole), Affinity Labs, and Free Stream Media guidance about examining limitations that describe the claimed advance.

name: Focus on the claimed advance over the prior art
description: In computer-related cases, determine whether the focus of the claimed advance is an improvement in computer technology (which can be non-abstract) rather than the mere use of computers to perform an abstract idea.
guidance: If the claims 'focus on a specific means or method that improves the relevant technology' they may be non-abstract (McRO). Otherwise, a claim that merely uses computers to obtain/manipulate/display data is likely directed to an abstract idea (Electric Power Group, Affinity Labs).

name: Avoid importing specification details into claims
description: Consider the specification but do not import unclaimed details from the specification into the claims when performing the Alice analysis.
guidance: ChargePoint and Phillips: specification evidence may inform the inquiry, but courts must avoid importing specification concepts into the claims themselves. Claimed limitations matter; unclaimed technical details in the spec do not save otherwise abstract claims.

name: High-level functional claiming is insufficient
description: Claiming a functionally-stated capability 'at a high level of generality' does not save a claim from abstraction.
guidance: Functional limitations that merely recite goals or outcomes without concrete means (e.g., 'achieving that stated goal' recited only functionally) fail to transform an abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter.

name: Specific example — converting information between formats is abstract
description: Converting information from one format to another is an abstract idea and does not, by itself, render a claim patent-eligible.
guidance: As stated in Hawk: 'converting information from one format to another . . . is an abstract idea.' Use such examples to assess whether claimed steps are merely abstract data transformations.

name: Alice Step Two — 'significantly more' / inventive concept requirement
description: At step two, the claim elements, individually and as an ordered combination, must supply 'significantly more' than the abstract idea — an 'inventive concept' that transforms the claim into a patent-eligible application.
guidance: Ask 'What else is there in the claims before us?' (Mayo). Mere recitation of the abstract idea plus conventional computer implementation is insufficient (Alice, Mayo, BSG Tech).

name: Routine, conventional, well-understood elements cannot supply the inventive concept
description: Claim elements or combinations that are routine, conventional, or well-known in the art do not transform an abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter.
guidance: If the intrinsic record (or properly pleaded facts) shows the technology is conventional (e.g., generic computer components), the claim fails at step two (BSG Tech, Int'l Bus. Machs. v. Zillow).

name: Real-time/on-demand operation alone is not a saving inventive concept
description: Claiming that an operation occurs 'on demand', 'in real time', or 'on the fly' does not by itself render the claim patent-eligible absent a concrete application or unconventional technique.
guidance: Affinity Labs and Electric Power Group illustrate that 'real time' or 'customized user interface' language without a concrete technological improvement is insufficient. The same logic applies to 'on-demand' virtual view creation.

name: Allegations of inventive concept may require factual support at pleading stage
description: Whether a limitation supplies an inventive concept can involve underlying factual questions; patentees who adequately allege factual bases for inventive concepts can survive a Rule 12(b)(6) motion.
guidance: Berkheimer and Aatrix: at the motion-to-dismiss stage, well-pleaded factual allegations that claim elements are unconventional may prevent dismissal. Conclusory allegations or allegations 'wholly divorced' from the claims/specification are insufficient (Cellspin, Simio).

name: Representative-claim treatment in § 101 analysis
description: Claims may be treated as representative for the § 101 inquiry if the patentee makes no meaningful argument for distinctive significance of limitations not present in the representative claim.
guidance: Berkheimer allows grouping claims and using representative claims where no meaningful differences are argued; parties may sort asserted claims into groups for analysis.

name: Evaluate claims in light of the intrinsic record
description: Review the claims in light of the specification and the intrinsic record to determine whether the claimed advance is indeed technical and unconventional.
guidance: Intrinsic evidence can show that an asserted 'innovation' was known in the art (undermining eligibility). But courts should not import unclaimed details from the spec into the claims; rather, use the spec to inform claim focus and conventionality.

name: Where to search / analogous art consideration
description: For 35 U.S.C. 103 purposes, prior art may be in the applicant's field or reasonably pertinent to the particular problem; examiners must determine what references are analogous art and where to search accordingly.
guidance: A reference may be analogous if (1) it is from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention (even if addressing a different problem), or (2) it is reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor (Bigio). Examiner may need to explain their understanding of the problem and factual reasons why a prior art reference would have commended itself to an inventor. Patent classification and cross-references provide some evidence but similarities/differences in structure and function carry greater weight.

name: Exemplary rationales to support 35 U.S.C. 103 rejections
description: List of illustrative rationales that may be used to support a conclusion of obviousness (not exclusive): (A) combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results; (B) simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results; (C) use of known technique to improve similar devices in the same way; (D) applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement to yield predictable results; (E) 'obvious to try' selecting from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions with reasonable expectation of success; (F) known work in one field may prompt predictable variations in same or different field; (G) some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art leading one of ordinary skill to modify or combine references.
guidance: TSM is a valid rationale among others; KSR cautioned against rigid application but recognized TSM as capturing a helpful insight. The list is exemplary, not exhaustive. Office personnel should consider these and any other valid rationales, and must clearly articulate why claimed invention would have been obvious under the chosen rationale(s). See MPEP §2143 and §2144 et seq. for examples and further guidance.

name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) — burden of proof to show disqualification of certain prior art
description: Applicants subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 who wish to avail themselves of 103(c) benefits bear the burden of establishing common ownership or joint research agreement conditions for disqualifying certain prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(e),(f),(g).
guidance: To establish joint research agreement benefits, applicant must show: (A) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on/before the date the claimed invention was made; (B) the invention was made as a result of activities within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (C) the application discloses or is amended to disclose names of parties to the joint research agreement. See MPEP §706.02(l)(2) for requirements and relevant case law.

name: Analogous art test and how to support an analogous-art determination
description: A reference is analogous art if (1) it is from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention (even if addressing a different problem), or (2) it is reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor (Bigio).
guidance: In applying the 'reasonably pertinent' prong, examiners should consider the problem faced by the inventor as reflected in the specification and may include a statement of the examiner's understanding of the problem to support that the prior art is pertinent. The question often turns on how the problem is perceived; examiners must explain why an inventor would have looked to the reference. Applicant arguments that the examiner misconstrued the problem should be evaluated against the specification's teachings. Similarities and differences in structure and function of inventions carry significant weight in analogy determinations.

name: Consider similarities/differences in structure and function for analogy
description: When determining whether a reference is reasonably pertinent (analogous), weigh similarities and differences in structure and function between the reference and the claimed invention.
guidance: Patent Office classification and search cross-references provide some evidence, but courts have found structural and functional comparisons to carry far greater weight (In re Ellis). Exemplar case law across chemical, mechanical, electrical, and design arts illustrates application of analogy tests.

name: License to a Federal agency (37 CFR 1.27(a)(4))
description: A license to a Federal agency resulting from a rights determination under Executive Order 10096 does not constitute a license that prohibits claiming small entity status for persons; and for small business concerns and nonprofits, a license to a Federal agency resulting from a funding agreement pursuant to 35 U.S.C. 202(c)(4) does not constitute a license for purposes of disqualification.
guidance: Licenses to the government under certain statutory/funding-agreement contexts are treated as not disqualifying; but other government-held rights or government organizations themselves do not qualify as nonprofits for fee reduction purposes.

name: Definition and scope of 'license' (includes implied and prototype orders)
description: The term 'license' includes non-exclusive as well as exclusive licenses and royalty-free as well as royalty-generating licenses. Implied licenses to use and resell patented articles purchased from a small entity do not preclude claiming small entity status. An order to a firm to build a prototype for the applicant’s own use is not considered a license for these purposes.
guidance: Not every transfer of rights or arrangement with a third party is treated as a disqualifying license; look to the substance (e.g., implied resale rights vs. actual transfer/licensing) and court precedent.

name: Title must be short and precise
description: Rule 5.1(a) stipulates that the description 'shall first state the title of the invention as appearing in the request'. The title must be short and precise.
guidance: The examiner should review the title in the light of the description and claims and any amendments thereto to ensure the title, as well as being concise, gives a clear and adequate indication of the subject of the invention. If amendments change categories of claims, the examiner should check whether a corresponding amendment in the title is needed, not going beyond the disclosure in the application as filed. See ISPE Guidelines 16.44-16.47 and GL/PCT-EPO B-X, 7.

name: Reference to drawings and reference signs in description
description: The description should include appropriate references to the drawings and use of reference signs as per ISPE Guidelines 4.08-4.09.
guidance: See GL/PCT-EPO F-II, 4.6-4.7 for details and for consistency with claims (reference signs in claims may create lack of clarity if used improperly).

name: Sufficiency of disclosure: general requirement (Art.5)
description: A detailed description of at least one way of carrying out the invention must be given so that a person skilled in the art can put the invention into practice; description must disclose any feature essential for carrying out the invention in sufficient detail.
guidance: A single example may suffice, but broad claim coverage normally requires multiple examples or alternative embodiments covering the claimed area. The skilled person must be able to perform the invention over the whole area claimed without undue burden and without needing inventive skill. For Art.5 objections, serious doubts must be substantiated by verifiable facts. See GL/ISPE 5.45-5.51 and GL/PCT-EPO F-III cross-references.

name: Relationship between sufficiency (Art.5) and clarity (Art.6)
description: An ambiguity in the claims may lead to an insufficiency objection only if the whole scope of the claim is affected so that it is impossible to carry out the invention; otherwise ambiguity is generally a clarity issue under Art.6.
guidance: Decisive is whether an ill-defined parameter prevents the skilled person from identifying technical measures necessary to solve the problem without undue burden. See GL/ISPE 4.12,5.58 and GL/PCT-EPO F-IV,4.

name: Claims: mandatory requirements
description: The international application must contain 'one or more claims.' The claims must (i) 'define the matter for which protection is sought;' (ii) 'be clear and concise;' and (iii) 'be fully supported by the description.'
guidance: Art.3(2), Art.6 and GL/ISPE 5.01-5.02 govern claims. This chapter sets out form/content and interpretation for novelty/inventive step assessment and prior art searching.

name: Form and content of claims: technical features and functional features
description: Claims' features should be technical; not every feature must be expressed structurally — functional features are acceptable where appropriate.
guidance: See F-IV,2.1 and GL/ISPE 5.04. Functional features are further dealt with in GL/PCT-EPO F-IV, 6.5; specific cases (e.g., functional definition of pathological condition) are addressed separately.

name: Two-part form of claim drafting
description: Where appropriate, use the two-part form for claims (see ISPE Guidelines 5.05 and 5.22); there are cases where two-part form is unsuitable.
guidance: Rule 6.3(b) and ISPE Guidelines 5.06-5.08 give guidance on when two-part form is required or unsuitable.

name: Kinds of claim and number/arrangement of claims
description: Claims may be of different categories; plural independent claims in one category complying with unity of invention may nonetheless be objected to under Art.6 if they result in lack of clarity or conciseness. Claims should be arranged logically (broadest first recommended).
guidance: See ISPE Guidelines 5.12-5.19, Rules 6.4 and 11.10, and GL/PCT-EPO F-IV,3.2 and 4 for examples. Multiple dependent claims are allowed provided they do not detract from clarity.

name: Clarity and interpretation of claims; invite informal clarification
description: If claims lack clarity, examiners may first invite the applicant to provide informal clarification before carrying out the search.
guidance: See ISPE Guidelines 5.31 and GL/PCT-EPO B-VIII, 3.3-3.6. Interpretation guidance follows ISPE Guidelines 5.20 and related appendix options.

name: Essential features and objections from missing essential features
description: Claims must include essential features of the invention; missing essential features give rise to objections under clarity/support provisions.
guidance: Definition, examples and treatment of essential features are given in F-IV,4.5.1-4.5.5 and Annex examples; implicit features are considered under ISPE Guidelines 5.33.

name: Relative terms, 'about'/'approximately', parameters and measurement methods
description: Use of relative terms, 'about'/'approximately', and parametric definitions require careful treatment; the method and means for measurement of parameters may need to be included in the claim or described.
guidance: See F-IV,4.6-4.7 and F-IV,4.11 and GL/PCT-EPO G-VI,6 for novelty assessment of parameter-containing claims; see GL/PCT-EPO F-IV,4.18 regarding methods of measurement.

name: Claims expressed as 'Apparatus for ...', 'Method for ...' and mixed-type claims
description: Guidance exists for claims directed to apparatus, methods, use and mixed/composite claims; combining incompatible claim types (e.g., combining a screening use with further production steps) may render a claim unclear under Art.6.
guidance: See F-IV,4.13 and examples regarding two-step claims that combine different types of process claims; Rule 6.2(a) guidance applies to such problematic combinations.

name: References to description/drawings in claims
description: References in claims to the description or drawings are governed by ISPE Guidelines 5.10 and Rule 6.2(b); reference signs may be used but bracketed added text or bracketed non-reference expressions can create lack of clarity.
guidance: If many embodiments exist, only reference signs of most important need be in independent claims. Bracketed features like 'securing means (screw 13)' are generally not permissible as it is unclear whether bracketed features are limiting. Acceptable forms include references to figure numbers where reference signs appear.

name: Comprising vs consisting
description: Distinctions between 'comprising' and 'consisting' and their effects on claim scope follow the EPO Guidelines and ISPE Appendix.
guidance: See F-IV,4.21 and GL/ISPE 5.24(a),(b) for application mutatis mutandis.

name: Trademarks, proper names and trade names in description and claims
description: Use of proper names, trademarks and trade names should comply with ISPE Guidelines 4.25; trademarks in claims raise clarity/support considerations under Art.6 and Art.5 if sufficiency is implicated.
guidance: For assessment of clarity of claims referring to a trademark see GL/PCT-EPO F-IV,4.8; acknowledge trademarks as such in description per GL/PCT-EPO F-II,4.13.

name: Optional features and definition in terms of result to be achieved
description: Optional features and claims defined as 'result to be achieved' have special tests; defining subject-matter by result differs from functional features and may pose problems if essential features are missing.
guidance: See F-IV,4.9-4.10 and GL/PCT-EPO F-IV,6.5 and GL/ISPE 5.36 for allowability and related issues.

name: Broad claims: potential objections and consequences
description: Although PCT Regulations do not explicitly mention 'overly broad' claims, objections may arise for lack of support, insufficiency, novelty or inventive step if claims are formulated so broadly they cover known subject-matter or embodiments for which the purported effect has not been achieved.
guidance: See GL/ISPE 5.42 and GL/PCT-EPO F-IV,6.1 and G-VII,5.2 for how to handle broad claims and when to raise objections under Art.5 and Art.6.

name: Order and arrangement of claims
description: Although there is no legal requirement that the first claim be the broadest, claims must be clear individually and as a whole; with many claims, they should be arranged with the broadest claim first or highlight the broadest claim in introductory parts.
guidance: If the broadest claim is not first, later broader claims must be independent. Objections under Rule 6 may arise if arrangement causes lack of clarity/conciseness. See Rule 6.1(a) and F-IV,4.24 guidance.

name: Support in the description for claims (Art.6)
description: Claims must be fully supported by the description; the extent of generalisation permitted depends on how groundbreaking the invention is and justification by the technical contribution.
guidance: Objection of lack of support is illustrated by examples in GL/EPO F-IV,6.3; once examiner sets out a reasoned case that a claim is not supported, the onus is on applicant to demonstrate support. See ISPE Guidelines 5.43-5.53.

name: Lack of support vs insufficient disclosure interaction
description: An objection under Art.6 for lack of support may also amount to an Art.5 insufficiency objection when the disclosure does not enable the skilled person to carry out the invention across the whole claimed breadth.
guidance: Both requirements reflect that claim terms should be commensurate with the invention's technical contribution. Examples include parametric claims lacking enabling information. See GL/PCT-EPO F-IV,6 and GL/ISPE 4.12,5.58.

name: Description and drawings must always be consulted when interpreting claims
description: “The description and any drawings are always referred to when interpreting the claims, and not just in the case of unclarity or ambiguity.”
guidance: This is a decisive EBA holding rejecting approaches that limit reference to specification only where claims are unclear. Practitioners and examiners should therefore treat the specification as an integral explanatory aid in every claim interpretation exercise (e.g., the Court endorsed consulting the patent’s explicit definition of “gathered” when interpreting that claim term).

name: There is no single clear EPC article that supplies the legal basis for claim interpretation in assessing patentability
description: The EBA considered that neither Article 69 EPC nor Article 84 EPC are entirely satisfactory as a basis for claim interpretation when assessing patentability and stated that there is no clear legal basis in the EPC articles for claim interpretation in this context (formal answer to Question 1: 'No').
guidance: Despite the absence of a single article, established principles (whether derived from Article 69 or 84) remain applicable; practitioners should not attempt to invent new principles but apply coherent interpretative principles informed by case law and harmonisation considerations.

name: Definitions in the description should not be disregarded when interpreting claims
description: Where a term is explicitly defined in the description, that definition is part of the specification context to be considered for claim interpretation and may not be lightly set aside.
guidance: Although Question 3 was held inadmissible as a separate question, amici curiae predominantly argued that explicit definitions in the description should not be disregarded and the EBA’s overall holding that the description is always referred to supports treating such definitions as relevant explanatory material when construing claims (consistent with UPC practice).

name: If a claim is unclear, the correct procedural response is amendment under Article 84 EPC
description: “The correct response to any unclarity in a claim is amendment.” The EBA highlighted the importance of examining divisions carrying out high-quality examinations of clarity under Article 84 EPC.
guidance: Where ambiguity or lack of clarity is identified, the appropriate remedy in prosecution is to require amendment of the claim rather than attempting to construe around the ambiguity. This reinforces examiners’ duty to scrutinise clarity during examination.

name: Specific requirements for petitions (claim charts and claim construction)
description: Petitions must identify all claims challenged and the grounds and supporting evidence on a claim‑by‑claim basis; may include claim charts and claim construction positions.
guidance: The petition should present grounds clearly and thoroughly; claim construction positions and properly prepared claim charts support the Board’s assessment at institution and guide trial scope.

name: Motions to amend practice and standards
description: Motions to amend are available in IPR and PGR subject to rules: content requirements, due dates, evidentiary standards, and claim construction considerations; Board evaluates amendments under applicable statutory and rule standards.
guidance: Appendix and guidance (including pilot programs) describe practice; motions to amend should disclose support for proposed substitute claims, show patentability, and follow timing constraints; opposition and reply practice is specified.

name: 112(f) Trigger Test
description: Absence of “means”: presumption against 112(f) applying. Test: does the element recite a function without particular structure, material, or acts (SMA) sufficient to perform the function?
guidance: Key points: an absence of the word “means” creates a presumption that §112(f) does not apply, but the dispositive inquiry is whether the claim element merely recites a function without reciting sufficient SMA to perform it. This is a question of law (claim construction). Examples in the slides ask: 'Does any part of this claim trigger construction under Sec. 112(f)? Why? Why not?'

name: Corresponding Structure/Material/Acts (SMA) Requirements
description: "… described in the specification …." (requirements for corresponding SMA).
guidance: Enumerated guidance from the slides: (1) Corresponding SMA must be described in the specification; (2) Saying the function is performed in a known or conventional way is insufficient; (3) The specification or prosecution history must clearly link the corresponding SMA to the claim‑recited function; (4) Corresponding SMA is limited to that necessary to perform the function; (5) SMA recited in a dependent claim can be included; (6) A generic computer or processor without an algorithm is normally insufficient SMA; (7) Determination is a question of law (claim construction).

name: Consequences of Inadequate SMA Disclosure
description: If the specification fails to disclose corresponding SMA necessary to perform a claimed function, the claim can be invalidated.
guidance: Concrete consequence: inadequate SMA disclosure can invalidate the claim under 35 U.S.C. §112(b) (indefiniteness / lack of particular and distinct claiming). The slides present this as a direct outcome of failing to identify adequate corresponding SMA.

name: Apply §112(f) to Method Claims — underlying function vs acts
description: If a method claim element recites only the underlying function without acts explaining how to accomplish it, §112(f) (step‑plus‑function) applies even absent express ‘step for’ language.
guidance: Seal‑Flex (Rader, J.) guidance: the 'underlying function' corresponds to what the element accomplishes; 'acts' correspond to how it is accomplished. If only the function is recited, §112(f) governs. The slides note non‑precedential Fed. Cir. decisions (Dionex, Intelligent Automation) showing method steps can trigger §112(f). A practical objection is difficulty identifying corresponding 'acts' in the spec; response: routinely treat algorithms as 'structure' and cite them as corresponding SMA.

name: Applying §112(f) in Life Sciences Claims
description: Life‑sciences/functionally‑worded claims can and have been treated under §112(f); drafters should not limit corresponding disclosure to 'structure' alone and should include 'acts' (or other non‑structure disclosures) that show how the function is performed.
guidance: Examples: Ex parte Gleave — the Board limited disclosure to specific antisense oligonucleotides and RNAi molecules and equivalents; recommended drafting techniques include describing 'acts' by which an antibody binds or blocks (e.g., 'one way the isolated monoclonal antibody binds ... is by doing the following acts: ...'). Also propose drafting claims that combine functional recitation with structure (variable and constant domains) or 'complementary determining means' to help tie function to structure/acts.

name: §112(f) as a Shield Against Alice/Mayo Eligibility Attacks
description: Invoking §112(f) can incorporate specification details into claim scope, satisfying the 'how' requirement and thereby help defend against subject‑matter eligibility (Alice/Mayo) attacks that target purely result‑oriented claims.
guidance: Rationale: courts have required claims to identify 'how' a functional result is achieved; §112(f) incorporates corresponding SMA from the specification into the claim, which can ground the 'how'. The slides cite American Axle, IBM (Zillow), Hawk Tech, and Internet Patents as examples of courts faulting claims for being result‑oriented without explaining how to accomplish tasks; the presenter argues §112(f) can be used to avoid that problem. Note: parties and courts have not uniformly used §112(f) this way, but Fed. Cir. has 'hinted' at the shield.

name: Genuine Ambiguity Over Whether §112(f) Is Triggered May Violate §112(b)
description: A genuine ambiguity about whether §112(f) applies can make a claim indefinite under §112(b).
guidance: Indicators/examples of genuine ambiguity include conflicting intrinsic evidence on: (a) whether the claim is to a 'combination'; (b) whether the claim recites structure/material/acts sufficient to perform the function; (c) whether the claim recites a 'means' or 'step for' performing a specified function; (d) whether the applicant or examiner treated the element as a §112(f) element. The slides cite MPEP 2181 II.A. and argue that such ambiguity can be a §112(b) violation. Also: all claim construction is a question of law, and the drafter could have made triggering clear.

name: Prosecution 'How' Inventory (Checklist)
description: A prosecution checklist for each claim‑recited function/result: identify how it is performed/achieved in the application; whether 'how' is recited in the claim; and whether 'how' is clearly linked to the function in the specification or prosecution history.
guidance: Matrix from slides: columns include 'Claim‑recited function or result', 'How performed or achieved in appln.?', 'How recited in claim?', 'How clearly linked to the function, in Spec. or PH?'. Use this during drafting and prosecution to ensure corresponding SMA is present and linked.

name: Prosecution: Expressly Associate 'Acts' with Method Steps and Functions in the Specification
