description: When drafting the specification, explicitly describe one or more ways (acts) of performing a claimed function so those acts can be relied on as corresponding SMA.
guidance: Sample drafting phrasing from slides: 'One way to adhere the mat to the foundation ... is to spread an adhesive tack coating. Another way ... is to do the following acts: ...' or 'One way the isolated monoclonal antibody binds ... is by doing the following acts: ...'. Use such explicit 'one way' language to tie acts to claimed functions.

name: Prosecution: Associate SMA with Functional Life Sciences Claim
description: For functional life‑sciences claims, include specification paragraphs that expressly describe 'structures, materials and acts by which' the disclosed molecule/antibody performs the recited function.
guidance: Suggested spec language: 'The following paragraphs describe embodiments of structures, materials and acts by which the disclosed antibody binds to at least two of the following residues ...' Use explicit embodiments and examples (e.g., specific sequences, examples, algorithms) to supply corresponding SMA and equivalents.

name: Benefits and Strategic Uses of §112(f)
description: Practical benefits for patent owners and challengers in asserting or contesting §112(f).
guidance: Benefits for patent owners: avoid invalidity for pure functional claiming (under §101, §112(a), or §112(b)), avoid invalidity over prior art while sometimes preserving an infringement fact question. Benefits for challengers/defendants: obtain narrowed constructions for non‑infringement and win §112(b) invalidity when the specification lacks support or when there is a genuine ambiguity over whether §112(f) triggered. Slides list these as strategic tradeoffs.

name: Generic Computer/Processor Without Algorithm Is Normally Insufficient SMA
description: A generic computer or processor recitation, standing alone and without an algorithm or instruction of how it performs the function, is normally insufficient to satisfy the SMA requirement.
guidance: Practical implication: when drafting computer‑implemented claims, include algorithmic detail, flowcharts, or specific acts/structure in the spec so that a computer recitation can be tied to corresponding SMA and not be treated as purely functional.

name: 1996 Guidelines: endorsement of Freeman-Walter-Abele test for algorithmic processes
description: The 1996 Examination Guidelines for Computer-Related Inventions explicitly endorse a particular test (the Freeman-Walter-Abele test) for analyzing claims directed 'solely' to a process for solving algorithms.
guidance: The guidance endorses that test as the Office's position on certain patentability standards for computer-related inventions. The final guidance was responsive to public comments, but it also explicitly rejected broad categorical presumptions (e.g., data structures per se or computer programs per se as statutory subject matter). It also sets forth a series of steps for examiners to follow when examining computer-related inventions.

name: 2005 Interim Guidelines: determine statutory category first; burden on USPTO
description: After reading the application and considering the breadth of § 101, examiners are instructed first to 'determine whether the claimed invention falls within an enumerated statutory category.' The guidance notes the 'burden is on the USPTO to set forth a prima facie case of unpatentability' and that an examiner must explain a rejection only if 'it is more likely than not that the claimed subject matter falls outside all of the statutory categories.'
guidance: Examiners need not obsess over precisely classifying ambiguous instances into one of the four statutory categories; the standard for the examiner to justify a rejection is a prima facie showing that the claim falls outside the statutory classes.

name: 2005 Interim Guidelines: judicial exceptions and practical application tests
description: Examiners must determine whether the claimed invention falls within judicial exceptions to § 101: 'abstract ideas, natural phenomena, and laws of nature.' To surmount a judicial exception by virtue of a practical application, an invention must either (i) 'transform[] an article or physical object to a different state or thing' or (ii) 'otherwise produce[] a useful, concrete and tangible result.'
guidance: The guidance emphasizes practical application as a path to eligibility and cites Diehr/Gottschalk support. It also explicitly rejects certain earlier tests (including the one earlier endorsed in 1996) as improper. The practical-application routes were presented as ways that inventions employing judicial-exception subject matter may nevertheless be eligible.

name: 2014 Interim Guidance / 2-part Mayo/Alice-based analysis (Step 2A & 2B)
description: The 2014 guidance sets forth a two-part analysis for judicial exceptions: Step 1 — determine whether the claim is in a statutory category; Step 2A — is the claim 'directed to' a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea; Step 2B — do additional elements amount to 'significantly more' than the judicial exception (the 'inventive concept').
guidance: The guidance includes a flowchart, nonlimiting lists of examples for Step 2A (with judicial citations), emphasizes that 'it is important to consider the claim as a whole' and 'every claim must be examined individually,' and provides examples of language found sufficient or insufficient for Step 2B. It also permits streamlined analyses for claims that 'clearly do not seek to tie up any judicial exception' (self-evident eligibility).

name: 2015 Update: abstract-idea examples and instructive positions on MDC and evidentiary practice
description: The July 2015 update listed specific abstract-idea categories (e.g., fundamental economic practices; certain methods of organizing human activity; an idea of itself; mathematical relationships/formulas) and synthesized public comments into themes. It also took a position on where markedly different characteristics (MDC) analysis belongs in the framework.
guidance: The update rejected moving the MDC analysis from Step 2A to Step 2B (observing that such reordering could change eligibility outcomes for some claims). It also instructed that findings that elements are 'well-understood, routine, or conventional' need not be supported by evidentiary submissions—judicial notice based on knowledge of those in the art or prior court cases is adequate.

name: 2018 Berkheimer Memorandum: factual findings and evidence requirement for Step 2B rejections
description: Following Berkheimer (which held that whether a claim element is 'well understood, routine, or conventional' is a question of fact), the USPTO instructed that examiners could not reject a claim under Step 2B without making a clear factual finding supported by evidence.
guidance: The memorandum specified four categories of evidence (the memo required at least one of these categories be used to support any rejection). This raised the evidentiary bar for examiners and made it more difficult to sustain ineligibility rejections absent factual support.

name: 2019 Revised Guidance: two-prong 'directed to' inquiry and practical-application carve-out
description: The revised Step 2A implements a two-pronged inquiry: (prong 1) does the claim recite a judicial exception (using the new groupings), and (prong 2) is the claim 'directed to' that judicial exception. A claim that integrates the judicial exception into a practical application is not 'directed to' the exception.
guidance: This approach creates a carve-out whereby claims that recite judicial-exception subject matter nonetheless are eligible if they integrate that matter into a practical application; it effectively shifts some 'practical application' considerations from Step 2B into Step 2A (a substantive change from earlier MPEP wording).

name: Claims/support must be supported by the description as filed
description: Any new claim or the addition of a new claim must be supported by the description of the invention in the application as filed; amendments to the specification (e.g., change in the definition of a term used both in the specification and claim) may indirectly affect a claim even though no actual amendment is made to the claim.
guidance: If a claim or claim amendment is not supported by the originally filed description, it may introduce new matter and be improper. Examiners should examine specification changes for indirect effects on claim scope.

name: Reliance on parent filing date under 35 U.S.C. 120 requires 112(a) support
description: Claims in a U.S. application are entitled to the benefit of the filing date of an earlier U.S. application only if the subject matter of the claim is disclosed in the manner provided by 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph) in the earlier-filed application.
guidance: When asserting priority to a parent U.S. application under 35 U.S.C. 120, ensure that each claimed subject matter is supported by the parent disclosure as required by written description law. See Tronzo v. Biomet, In re Scheiber.

name: Reliance on foreign/provisional priority under 35 U.S.C. 119 requires 112(a) support
description: Claims in a U.S. application can obtain benefit of a foreign priority date or provisional filing date only if the corresponding earlier application supports the claims in the manner required by 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre-AIA 112, first paragraph).
guidance: Do not grant priority based solely on filing dates; substantively compare claim subject matter to the earlier disclosure for written description support. See In re Ziegler, Kawai v. Metlesics, In re Gosteli.

name: Support for a claim corresponding to an interference count
description: A claim corresponding to a count in an interference must be supported by the specification in the manner provided by 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre-AIA 112, first paragraph).
guidance: When a party seeks benefit of an earlier-filed U.S. application for an interference count, the earlier application must meet 112(a) for the subject matter of the count. Broad generic disclosure to a class is insufficient for a specific compound. See Fields v. Conover, Hyatt v. Boone.

name: Original claim possibly lacking written description (functional claiming / genus-species gap)
description: An original claim may lack written description support when (1) the claim defines the invention in functional language specifying a desired result but the disclosure fails to sufficiently identify how the function is performed or the result is achieved; or (2) a broad genus claim is presented but the disclosure only describes a narrow species with no evidence that the genus is contemplated.
guidance: The mere presence of claim language in the specification is not dispositive; the specification must describe the claimed invention so one skilled in the art can recognize what is claimed. See Ariad Pharm. v. Eli Lilly and Enzo Biochem v. Gen-Probe.

name: Means-(or step-)plus-function limitations and indefiniteness under 35 U.S.C. 112(f)
description: A means- or step-plus-function limitation is construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents. If the specification fails to disclose sufficient corresponding structure/materials/acts that perform the entire claimed function, the limitation is indefinite (failure to particularly point out and distinctly claim under 35 U.S.C. 112(b)).
guidance: Lack of corresponding structure makes the claim indefinite and also can fail the written description requirement because an unbounded functional limitation covers all ways of performing a function, indicating lack of possession. See In re Donaldson Co.

name: Burden on the examiner regarding written description (presumption and rebuttal)
description: A specification as filed is presumed to provide an adequate written description unless and until the examiner presents sufficient evidence or reasoning to rebut the presumption; the inquiry is a question of fact.
guidance: The examiner has the initial burden of presenting by a preponderance of evidence why a person skilled in the art would not recognize in the disclosure a description of the claimed invention. See In re Wertheim, In re Marzocchi.

name: Statement-of-rejection requirements for lack of written description
description: When rejecting a claim for lack of written description, the examiner must set forth express findings of fact which support the conclusion: (A) identify the claim limitation(s) at issue; and (B) establish a prima facie case by providing reasons why a person skilled in the art would not have recognized that the inventor was in possession of the invention as claimed in view of the disclosure as filed.
guidance: A general allegation (e.g., 'unpredictability in the art') is insufficient. A simple statement pointing to absence of support for the limitation may be sufficient for new/amended claims. Where appropriate, suggest claim amendments supported by the original disclosure but avoid adding new matter. See MPEP §2163 and Hyatt v. Dudas.

name: Changes to claim scope after filing require original support (broadening/narrowing/range/terminology changes)
description: Failure to meet the written description requirement commonly arises when claims are changed after filing to broaden or narrow claim breadth, alter a numerical range limitation, or use claim language not synonymous with terminology used in the original disclosure. Each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure to comply with 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or to be entitled to earlier priority dates.
guidance: When assessing amended claims or claims in a child application seeking priority, check whether each limitation has clear support in the original disclosure. See MPEP §2163.

name: Broadening by omission of a limitation (omitting an essential/critical element)
description: Omission of a limitation can raise whether the inventor had possession of a broader, more generic invention. A claim that omits an element which the applicant describes as an essential or critical feature of the original disclosure does not comply with the written description requirement.
guidance: Look for express statements in the specification that a feature is 'the only possible location' or 'essential' to the invention; omitting such features can cause rejection. Compare cases such as Gentry Gallery, Tronzo, In re Wilder, In re Sus, In re Peters.

name: Addition of a generic (genus) claim requires sufficient species disclosure
description: A claimed genus may be supported through sufficient description of a representative number of species; when there is substantial variation within the genus, a sufficient variety of species must be described to reflect that variation. A single species may support a genus only if the disclosure indicates the patentee has invented species sufficient to constitute the genus.
guidance: Assess whether disclosed species are representative of the claimed genus; courts have found genus unsupported where only one structurally similar species is described and not representative (see AbbVie v. Janssen, Enzo Biochem, In re Curtis). There are exceptions when one species would reasonably signal a broader genus to skilled artisans (see In re Rasmussen, In re Herschler).

name: Narrowing or subgeneric claim changes must be supported
description: Introducing claim changes that narrow the claims by adding elements or limitations not supported by the as-filed disclosure violates the written description requirement; subgeneric terminology may or may not be acceptable depending on whether species within the subgenus are disclosed.
guidance: A 'laundry list' of possible moieties does not necessarily support each species. Whether a subgenus is described by a genus plus a species depends on whether the skilled artisan would be reasonably led to that subgenus. Each case is fact-specific. See Fujikawa, In re Ruschig, Rozbicki v. Chiang, In re Lukach, Ex parte Sorenson, In re Smith.

name: Relationship of written description to new matter (statutory prohibitions)
description: Lack of written description generally concerns claim subject matter. If an applicant amends abstract, specification, or drawings to add matter not described in the application as filed, new matter issues arise. Two statutory provisions prohibit introducing new matter: 35 U.S.C. 132 (no amendment shall introduce new matter) and 35 U.S.C. 251 (no new matter in reissue).
guidance: Information present in any one part of the application as filed may be added to another part without introducing new matter, but adding content not present in the filed disclosure is impermissible.

name: Review procedures for new matter objections and rejections
description: A rejection of claims is reviewable by the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB), whereas an objection and requirement to delete new matter is subject to supervisory review by petition under 37 CFR 1.181. If both claims and specification contain new matter and there has been both a rejection and an objection, the issue becomes appealable and should not be decided by petition.
guidance: Follow proper administrative routes: appeals for rejections, petitions for objections; do not conflate procedures when both rejection and objection exist.

name: Claims as filed are part of the disclosure; remedy for claimed subject matter not in remainder of specification
description: Claims filed in the original specification are part of the disclosure. If the original specification contains a claim disclosing material not disclosed in the remainder of the specification, the applicant may amend the specification to include the claimed subject matter.
guidance: Use Form paragraph 7.44 where originally claimed subject matter lacks proper antecedent basis in the specification. See In re Benno.

name: Field of use / technological environment limitations do not add an inventive concept
description: Limitations that merely indicate a field of use or technological environment (e.g., limiting use to a particular industry, to the Internet, to a telephone network, or to a particular patient population) typically do no more than describe the environment in which a judicial exception is applied and therefore do not meaningfully limit the claim.
guidance: Courts have characterized many such limitations as token or incidental additions that fail to integrate the judicial exception into the claim as a whole. Examples cited include limiting drug administration to certain patients (Mayo/Prometheus), identifying commodity providers/consumers (Bilski), limiting a formula to wheel circumference (Flook), specifying execution on a generic computer or Internet (FairWarning, Intellectual Ventures, buySAFE, Ultramercial), and limiting information collection/analysis to power grid data (Electric Power Group). Examiners should treat 'technological environment' and 'field of use' interchangeably for eligibility analysis and consider overlap with insignificant extra-solution activity (see MPEP § 2106.05(g)). When a limitation generally links a judicial exception to a particular environment, the examiner should explain why it does not meaningfully limit the claim (e.g., merely employing well-known computer functions to execute an abstract idea).

name: Integration of additional elements into the claim as a whole
description: Determine whether additional claim elements are integrated into the claim as a whole (i.e., act in concert with other limitations) or are merely incidental/token additions that do not alter how the claimed invention operates.
guidance: Use the Diehr/Flook contrast: Diehr's specific, interrelated limitations (monitoring elapsed time, measuring temperature, repetitively calculating cure time, opening press automatically) were integrated and transformed a process, while Flook's catalytic chemical conversion limitation was incidental and not integrated. Integration that meaningfully transforms the claimed process can support eligibility; lack of integration suggests the limitation is a non-meaningful field-of-use or extra-solution activity.

name: Streamlined eligibility analysis (Pathway A) may be used when eligibility is self-evident
description: Examiners may use a streamlined analysis when, viewed as a whole, the claim's eligibility is self-evident (for example, because the claim clearly improves a technology or computer functionality).
guidance: The streamlined analysis (Pathway A) is for efficiency and yields the same result as the full Alice/Mayo analysis; it must not be used to avoid a finding of ineligibility that would occur under the full analysis. If there is doubt whether the applicant seeks coverage of a judicial exception, the full analysis should be conducted. The record may show eligibility simply by absence of an eligibility rejection or include clarifying remarks. Examples where streamlined analysis is appropriate: a robotic arm assembly with a control system operating using certain mathematical relationships, artificial hip prosthesis with a coating that does not tie up a nature-based product, or manufactured products with meaningful limitations that prevent tying up an exception.

name: Clear improvement to technology or computer functionality avoids full Alice/Mayo analysis
description: Claims directed to clear improvements in technology or computer functionality are not abstract when appropriately claimed and therefore may avoid full eligibility analysis.
guidance: Court decisions (e.g., Enfish, McRO) support that claims demonstrating a tangible improvement to computer-related technology or other technological processes can be eligible at Step 2A (or allow Pathway A). If the improvement is clear, no further analysis may be needed. If it's a close call, perform the full analysis.

name: Formulate eligibility rejections based on substantive law and establish a prima facie case
description: Eligibility rejections must be grounded in substantive law under 35 U.S.C. §101 as interpreted by judicial precedent and must set forth a prima facie case of ineligibility with sufficient clarity and specificity to notify the applicant and allow effective response.
guidance: Examiners should review the entire record (specification, claims, prosecution history, relevant case law, prior art) and evaluate eligibility claim-by-claim. The initial burden is on the examiner to explain why a claim is ineligible. Training materials and examples do not themselves form the basis for rejection, though applicants may cite them in responses.

name: When rejecting under Step 1, explain why claim is outside statutory categories
description: If a claim is determined not to fall within a statutory category (Step 1: NO), the rejection must explain why the claim is not directed to one of the four statutory categories of invention.
guidance: See MPEP § 706.03(a) for making such a rejection. Provide sufficiently clear and specific reasoning in the Office action to enable applicant to respond.

name: When rejecting under Step 2A, identify and explain the judicial exception recited in the claim
description: The rejection must point to specific claim limitation(s) that recite or describe the judicial exception and explain why those limitations constitute an exception (e.g., an abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon, or product of nature).
guidance: For abstract ideas, identify the idea as recited and explain why it corresponds to concepts courts have identified as abstract (see MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2)). Citing appropriate precedent that supports the identification is best practice; ensure cited decisions are factually applicable and avoid overreaching or relying on non-precedential decisions unless fact patterns match. For laws of nature/natural phenomena/product of nature, identify the recited subject matter and provide a reasoned rationale why it is such an exception (see MPEP § 2106.04(b) and § 2106.04(c)). Sample explanations are provided (e.g., claim recites sorting information by X similar to Digitech/Content Extraction; claim recites a correlation of X that is a law of nature).

name: When rejecting under Step 2B, identify additional claim elements and explain why they do not amount to significantly more
description: After identifying the judicial exception, the rejection must: (1) point to any additional elements beyond the exception, and (2) explain why these additional elements, individually and in combination, fail to add significantly more than the judicial exception.
guidance: Address the combination of elements as well as individual elements because a new combination may be patent eligible even if individual steps were known (Diamond v. Diehr). Where examiner concludes elements are well-understood, routine, conventional, explain why courts or skilled persons would so recognize them. Provide a reasoned explanation (not conclusory statements) supporting the conclusion that additional elements are conventional or fail to meaningfully limit the exception. Conversely, when appropriate, explain why additional elements do provide an inventive concept by adding meaningful limitations (see MPEP § 2106.05 and § 2106.07(c)).

name: Provide reasoned rationale and factual tying when asserting abstract idea or conventionality
description: Do not merely assert that claim language recites an abstract idea or conventional activity; explain with reasoned rationale and, where applicable, factual support how the claim language maps to the judicial exception or to well-understood, routine, conventional activities.
guidance: Cite applicable case law and tether the legal conclusion to the specific claim language and relevant facts in the record. Avoid reliance on language taken out of context and be cautious about citing non-precedential decisions unless the facts closely match the application under examination.

name: Evaluate claims individually and consider dependent claims separately
description: Eligibility should be evaluated claim-by-claim; dependent claims may add limitations that render them eligible even if the independent claim is ineligible.
guidance: Do not assume all claims with similar language stand or fall together. Each claim must be analyzed on the particular elements it recites, and dependent claims that add limitations may provide significantly more than the judicial exception.

name: Under compact prosecution, state all non-cumulative reasons for rejection in the first Office action
description: Regardless of whether a §101 rejection is made, examiners should perform a complete examination for every claim under other patentability requirements (35 U.S.C. 102, 103, 112, utility, inventorship, double patenting) and state all non-cumulative reasons and bases for rejecting claims in the first Office action.
guidance: This ensures that applicants receive a complete, efficient initial examination and supports prosecution procedure.

name: Stoichiometric inference from measured masses and correction for minor effects
description: Ainsi dans cette expérience, 85 grains 7/10 d'eau, plus 28 grains de charbon ont formé 100 grains d'acide carbonique ... Mais j'ai fait voir plus haut, que pour former 100 grains de gaz acide carbonique, il falloit unir 72 grains d'oxygène à 28 grains de charbon; donc les 28 grains de charbon ... ont enlevé à l'eau 72 grains d'oxygène; donc 85 grains 7/10 d'eau sont composés de 72 grains d'oxygène & de 13 grains 7/10 ...
guidance: Perform arithmetic stoichiometric deductions from mass measurements to determine elemental composition (e.g., deduce the oxygen and hydrogen portions of water by comparing masses of gases and residues). Account for small perturbations (gas dissolving a little charcoal, etc.) and correct by calculation; present results with indicated precision (author claims accuracy to ~1/200 in some experiments).

name: Preamble limiting effect
description: Whether preamble language limits the claim depends on whether the preamble is necessary to give life, meaning or vitality to the claim or whether there was clear reliance on the preamble during prosecution to distinguish the claimed invention from the prior art.
guidance: A preamble generally is not limiting when the claim body describes a structurally complete invention such that deletion of the preamble does not affect the structure or steps of the claimed invention. However, clear reliance on the preamble during prosecution to distinguish the claimed invention from the prior art transforms the preamble into a claim limitation. Preamble language that merely extolls benefits or features does not limit claim scope without clear reliance. Conversely, where the preamble discloses a fundamental characteristic of the claimed invention (e.g., 'blown-film'), it may properly be construed as a limitation. Case examples: Catalina Marketing, Poly‑America, Intirtool.

name: Meaning of 'comprising' (open-ended transition)
description: The transitional term 'comprising' is inclusive or open-ended and does not exclude additional, unrecited elements or method steps.
guidance: 'Comprising' is synonymous with 'including,' 'containing,' or 'characterized by.' It indicates the claim is open-ended and allows additional steps or elements. Case examples: Mars v. H.J. Heinz; Invitrogen v. Biocrest; Genentech v. Chiron. Use 'comprising' to keep claims presumptively open-ended (e.g., a razor 'comprising' blades can encompass razors with more blades).

name: Meaning of 'consisting of' (closed transition)
description: 'Consisting of' excludes any element, step, or ingredient not specified in the claim.
guidance: A claim depending from a 'consists of' claim cannot add an element or step. When 'consists of' appears in a clause in the body, it limits only that clause's element set. Although generally closed, courts have found factual exceptions (e.g., Norian v. Stryker where an unrelated spatula did not avoid infringement). Case examples: In re Gray; Ex parte Davis; Mannesmann Demag.

name: Meaning of 'consisting essentially of' (middle-ground transition)
description: 'Consisting essentially of' limits the scope to the specified materials or steps 'and those that do not materially affect the basic and novel characteristic(s)' of the claimed invention.
guidance: This transitional phrase occupies middle ground between 'consisting of' and 'comprising.' The applicant bears the burden of showing that introduction of additional steps/components would materially change the invention's characteristics. Absent clear specification guidance as to what constitutes a material change, courts may construe 'consisting essentially of' as equivalent to 'comprising' for prior art searching. Case examples: In re Herz; PPG Industries v. Guardian; AK Steel v. Sollac; In re Janakirama‑Rao. Applicants should define 'basic and novel characteristics' in the specification if they intend a narrow meaning.

name: Interpretation of other transitional phrases ('having','composed of')
description: Transitional phrases such as 'having' and 'composed of' must be interpreted in light of the specification to determine whether open or closed claim language is intended.
guidance: 'Having' has been interpreted as open terminology in some contexts but does not create a universal presumption of openness—context controls. 'Composed of' has been interpreted either like 'consisting of' or 'consisting essentially of' depending on facts and specification. Case examples: Lampi Corp.; Crystal Semiconductor; AFG Industries; In re Bertsch.

name: Effect of 'adapted to/for', 'wherein', and 'whereby' clauses
description: Clauses that suggest optional or result-oriented features ('adapted to', 'adapted for', 'wherein', 'whereby') may or may not limit claim scope depending on the specific facts of the case.
guidance: Determination whether such clauses are limitations depends on whether they impose a requirement or merely state an intended result. A 'wherein' clause that gives meaning and purpose to manipulative steps may be limiting. A 'whereby' clause that states a condition material to patentability cannot be ignored. Conversely, a 'whereby' clause that simply expresses an intended result of a positively recited step is often not given weight. Case examples: Griffin v. Bertina; Hoffer v. Microsoft; Minton v. NASD.

name: Printed matter: requirement of a functional relationship for patentable weight
description: Printed matter (descriptive material) added to a known product is not given patentable weight unless there is a new and unobvious functional relationship between the printed matter and the substrate (product).
guidance: USPTO personnel must consider all claim limitations when determining patentability, but printed matter lacks patentable weight absent a functional relationship. The inquiry for printed matter parallels method claims with instructional limitations: is there a functional relationship that is new and unobvious? Case law: Gulack; Lowry; Ngai; Diamond v. Diehr.

name: Functional relationship must be new and unobvious
description: Even when a functional relationship exists between printed matter and substrate, to be given patentable weight it must be new and unobvious over the prior art.
guidance: A color-coded indicia that indicates expiration date may be functional, but if the same teaching exists in prior art (or is obvious), the claim may be anticipated or obvious. Examiner should assess novelty and obviousness of the functional relationship itself.

name: Machine‑readable media claims: relationship of program to intended computer system
description: For claims to a computer-readable medium containing programming, the examiner should evaluate the relationship between the programming and the intended computer system to determine whether a functional relationship exists.
guidance: If the programming performs some function with respect to the intended computer (e.g., attribute data objects facilitating retrieval/addition/removal), a functional relationship is present and the claim elements may be given patentable weight. If the medium merely serves as a support for information intended for a human (e.g., tables of batting averages, music tracks), no functional relationship exists and the claim is directed to conveying meaning to humans rather than a function with the computer. Case examples: Lowry; Ngai.

name: Inherency may support rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102/103
description: Express, implicit, and inherent disclosures of a prior art reference may be relied upon for rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103; inherency is a question of fact that can arise in anticipation and obviousness contexts.
guidance: Inherency can justify anticipation or obviousness rejections where a prior art reference necessarily possesses the claimed characteristic even if not explicitly disclosed. Case examples: In re Napier; In re Grasselli; In re Crish (promoter sequence inherent in prior plasmid). See MPEP § 2112.01 and § 2141.02 for related guidance.

name: 35 U.S.C. 102/103 rejection may be appropriate even if prior art is silent as to an inherent characteristic
description: Where the composition of the prior art is the same as the claimed composition but the function/property is not explicitly disclosed, the examiner may make a 102/103 rejection (expressing both anticipation and obviousness).
guidance: Concurrent rejections under 102 and 103 are appropriate for function/property claims where the prior art product appears identical but is silent as to the function; the rationale that identical compositions necessarily possess the same properties supports such rejections. Case example: In re Best (and related discussion).

name: Applicant's burden after prima facie inherency showing
description: Once an examiner shows a prior art product appearing substantially identical and presents evidence or reasoning tending to show inherency, the burden shifts to the applicant to show an unobvious difference.
guidance: Applicant must rebut the prima facie case with objective evidence demonstrating that the prior art product does not necessarily or inherently possess the claimed characteristics. Declarations lacking required specifics (dimensions, materials, etc.) may fail (In re Schreiber; In re Fitzgerald). See MPEP § 2113 for product-by-process analogies.

name: Product and apparatus claims: identity of structure/composition presumes inherent properties/functions
description: Where claimed and prior art products are identical or substantially identical in structure/composition or produced by substantially identical processes, a prima facie case of anticipation or obviousness is established and claimed properties/functions are presumed to be inherent.
guidance: If the PTO shows a sound basis for believing products are the same, applicant must show they are not. The prima facie case can be rebutted by evidence that the prior art product lacks the claimed characteristics. Case examples: In re Best; Titanium Metals v. Banner; In re Ludtke.

name: Composition claims: identical chemical composition implies same properties
description: Products of identical chemical composition cannot have mutually exclusive properties; if prior art teaches the identical chemical structure, the properties claimed are necessarily present.
guidance: A prior art composition with the same monomers and procedures can support a prima facie lack of novelty for claimed properties (In re Spada). Examiner should treat identical compositions as presumptively possessing the same properties unless applicant rebuts with evidence.

name: Nonfunctional printed matter does not distinguish otherwise identical product claims
description: Nonfunctional printed matter on a product does not distinguish a claimed product from an otherwise identical prior art product for purposes of novelty/patentability.
guidance: If printed matter merely conveys a message or aesthetic and does not have a functional relationship with the product, it cannot supply patentable novelty to overcome otherwise identical prior art. See related printed matter sections and In re Ngai, Ex parte Gwinn.

name: Means-plus-function claiming under 35 U.S.C. §112(f)
description: An element may be expressed as a means or step for performing a specified function without reciting structure, and such a claim is construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof (35 U.S.C. §112(f)).
guidance: Recognize when a claim element invokes §112(f); doing so requires looking to the specification for corresponding structure. The doctrine allows claiming function without reciting particular structure in the claim, but displaces the requirement by importing structure from the specification.

name: Corresponding structure must be disclosed in the specification; absence renders claim indefinite
description: Identifying the structure corresponding to a means-plus-function element is necessary for understanding the claim; if the specification does not disclose adequate corresponding structure, the claim is indefinite.
guidance: A generic or purely functional recital (e.g., a generic 'control' box with no indication of structure) is inadequate. If no corresponding structure can be identified in the specification, the proper result is indefiniteness (see Fiber decision affirming district court).

name: Permitted incorporation per 37 C.F.R. 1.57(d) applies only to essential material
description: Generally, 'essential material' may be incorporated by reference where it is necessary to describe the structure, material, or acts that correspond to a claimed means or step for performing a specified function as required by 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (37 C.F.R. 1.57(d)).
guidance: Although the regulation allows incorporation of essential material, courts remain reluctant to treat incorporated documents as supplying corresponding structure unless incorporation is explicit and targeted. If incorporation is intended to supply structure, do so expressly and clearly in the specification.

name: Specification must expressly point to a specific reference if relying on incorporated material for structure
description: To rely on a structure in material incorporated by reference, the specification must expressly state in which specific reference the structure corresponding to the claimed functionality is found.
guidance: Best practice (and judicial requirement) is to make a clear, express statement in the specification naming the external reference and indicating that the structure therein is being imported to supply the corresponding structure for the means-plus-function element (see Otto Bock and Fiber guidance).

name: Anti-pattern: merely mentioning prior art or citing references does not import their structures
description: Simply mentioning prior art references in a patent does not suffice as a specification description to give the patentee claim to all of the structures disclosed in those references.
guidance: Avoid assuming that citations or general references in the specification will permit importing detailed structure from external documents. Cases like Pressure Prods. reject claim-scope importation based on mere mention; explicit incorporation for the purpose of importing structure is required.

name: Non-Statutory Subject Matter (examples)
description: Categories expressly identified as non-statutory: intangible information or data lacking physical form; software per se without structural limitations; transitory signal transmissions.
guidance: Use these examples to screen claims that appear to be merely information or ephemeral signals rather than statutory subject matter. Structural/technical limitations that tie software to a concrete implementation may change the analysis.

name: Abstract Idea Grouping — Mathematical Concepts
description: Abstract ideas include mathematical relationships, formulas/equations, and calculations.
guidance: Examples: conversion algorithms (e.g., binary-coded decimal to binary), numerical formulas and their textual equivalents, statistical calculations and computational operations. These are paradigmatic abstract ideas and warrant careful Step 2A analysis when recited in claims.

name: Abstract Idea Grouping — Mental Processes
description: Abstract ideas include concepts performable in the human mind without technological aid, such as observations, evaluations, judgments, and opinions.
guidance: If a claim's steps can be carried out mentally or with minimal mental effort, it may be directed to a mental process exception unless additional elements meaningfully limit or integrate it into a practical application.

name: Step 2B — Inventive Concept ('Significantly More') Analysis
description: When claims are directed to judicial exceptions (Step 2A: YES), Step 2B determines whether additional elements provide 'significantly more' than the exception itself.
guidance: This is the locus for determining whether the claim contains an 'inventive concept' that transforms the exception into a patent-eligible application. The analysis weighs whether claim elements meaningfully limit or add unconventional steps/structure beyond the judicial exception.

name: Sufficient Factors Under Step 2B
description: Factors that can supply 'significantly more' include unconventional technical solutions to technological problems, meaningful integration improving existing technology, and non-conventional application of the exception.
guidance: Examples: claim elements that recite specific technical improvements (not routine or conventional) to a computer or other technology; meaningful integration of the exception into a technical environment; or an application that departs from how the exception is conventionally used, thereby solving a technological problem.

name: Eligibility Pathways (A, B, C)
description: Three outcome pathways: Pathway A = self-evident eligibility for claims clearly within statutory categories without exception concerns; Pathway B = claims within statutory categories that do not recite judicial exceptions (Step 2A: NO); Pathway C = claims within statutory categories, directed to exceptions (Step 2A: YES), but containing additional elements amounting to significantly more (Step 2B: YES).
guidance: Use these pathways to categorize the result of the analysis: A and B lead to eligibility without needing Step 2B; C leads to eligibility because the claim supplies significantly more despite reciting an exception.

name: Examine cited documents relevant to invention understanding
description: Documents cited in the international application should be examined if cited as the starting point of the invention, as showing the state of the art, as alternative solutions, or when necessary for correct understanding.
guidance: Citations that clearly relate only to details not directly relevant to the claimed invention may be disregarded.

name: Search statement defining subject of search
description: It may be desirable for the examiner to prepare a written search statement defining the subject of the search as precisely as possible.
guidance: Claims may serve but may need generalization to cover all aspects/embodiments. Consider exclusions from international search and lack of unity; any restrictions should be indicated in the international search report; if no search is made, issue a declaration under Article 17(2)(a).

name: Analogous fields — basis for inclusion
description: Fields to be regarded as analogous are considered in light of the necessary function or use of the claimed invention, not only specific functions in the application.
guidance: Consider (i) fields where same/similar structure is expected to be used in different work/use; (ii) fields to which a generic concept of claimed features pertains; (iii) art within the inventor’s endeavor reasonably pertinent to the problem involved; (iv) fields relevant to the function or utility inherent in claimed subject matter.

name: Focus of search — novelty, inventive step and sufficiency
description: The examiner carries out the search directing attention to prior art likely to have bearing on novelty or inventive step, and is encouraged to cite prior art useful for determining sufficiency of description across the whole field claimed.
guidance: Also note documents that may put doubt on validity of priority, aid understanding, or illustrate background, but do not spend time searching for these unless special reason exists.

name: Stopping the search — when to end
description: Use judgment to end the search when the probability of discovering further relevant prior art becomes very low in relation to the effort needed.
guidance: Stop also when documents found clearly demonstrate lack of novelty in the entire subject matter to which the claims are directed (with exceptions for well-known features). Do not stop if lack of novelty is demonstrated for only a limited number of claimed embodiments. Continue searching if outstanding issues about sufficiency, support, or industrial applicability could be clarified by additional prior art.

name: Apply PCT standards for novelty and inventive step
description: Evaluate prior art against the standards for novelty and inventive step as set out in Chapters 12 and 13 of the Guidelines.
guidance: Determine whether the claimed invention meets those substantive requirements when selecting citations and forming conclusions.

name: Scope and limitations of supplementary search
description: Details and scope of the service offered are decided by the Authority providing it and may be subject to limitations (e.g., subject matter, number of searches, number of claims searched).
guidance: The scope is defined in an annex to the agreement between the International Bureau and the Authority; details published in the PCT Applicant’s Guide Annex SISA.

name: What Is a Method Claim?
description: A method (or process) claim recites a series of steps.
guidance: Method claims are useful for inventions that are sequences of operations: software algorithms, manufacturing processes, treatment regimens, communication protocols, control sequences.

name: Order of Steps
description: By default, the order in which steps are recited in a method claim does not require a specific order of performance.
guidance: To require an order, use language like "after the receiving step" or "in response to the determining step."

name: Step Granularity
description: Each step should be granular enough to be a meaningful technical operation, but not so granular that the claim becomes a rigid recitation of one specific implementation.
guidance: "Applying a hash function to the input" is good; "computing 256 SHA-256 rounds" is too narrow.

name: Beauregard Claims (Computer-Readable Medium)
description: For software inventions, file a parallel CRM claim: "A non-transitory computer-readable medium storing instructions that, when executed by a processor, cause the processor to: [recite the same method steps]."
guidance: This reaches different infringers.

name: Classification should represent invention information primarily
description: Invention information comprises all novel and unobvious subject matter in a patent document's total disclosure and is the primary matter to be represented by classification (usually determined using the claims for guidance).
guidance: Classify invention information first. 'Inventive thing' and 'invention information' are the core focus—classification should aim to represent these novel aspects completely; additional (non-inventive) information may be classified as secondary if needed.

name: Reexamination statutory framework and scope
description: Administrative reexamination procedures (since 1980) allow any person at any time to request reexamination of any patent claim on the basis of published prior art (35 U.S.C. §302), and the PTO may confirm or cancel claims upon reexamination.
guidance: Reexamination provides the PTO an opportunity to review and correct its work based on fuller information; the 2011 Act's sections 6 and 18 expand grounds for such administrative review but do not alter substantive patentability standards.

name: 2152.01 Effective Filing Date of the Claimed Invention
description: Guidance on how to determine the effective filing date of a claimed invention for purposes of applying AIA prior art rules.
guidance: Explains rules for priority/benefit claiming, how earlier filings affect effective date, and how effective filing date controls whether a reference is prior art under AIA.

name: 2159 Applicability Date Provisions and Determining Whether an Application Is Subject to the First Inventor To File Provisions of the AIA
description: Explains how to determine whether an application is governed by the AIA FITF provisions based on filing dates and claimed effective filing dates.
guidance: Includes rules for applications filed before/after March 16, 2013 and transition applications containing claimed inventions with mixed effective filing dates; includes required applicant statements for transition applications.

name: 2141 Examination Guidelines for Determining Obviousness Under 35 U.S.C. 103
description: Detailed guidance on making and supporting obviousness rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103 (principles, prima facie case, and factors).
guidance: Covers scope/content of prior art, analogous art, differences between prior art and claimed invention, level of ordinary skill, suggestion/motivation to combine references, reasonable expectation of success, and considering all claim limitations and applicant rebuttal.

name: 2131 Anticipation — Application of 35 U.S.C. 102
description: Guidance on applying anticipation (novelty) principles under 35 U.S.C. 102 to determine whether claims are anticipated by prior art.
guidance: Includes treatment of multiple-reference 102 rejections, genus-species issues, anticipation of ranges, and secondary considerations.

name: 2111 Claim Interpretation; Broadest Reasonable Interpretation
description: Standards for interpreting claim language during examination using the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.
guidance: Discusses plain meaning, effect of preamble, transitional phrases, functional and nonfunctional descriptive material, and related claim construction considerations.

name: 2163 Guidelines for the Examination of Patent Applications Under the 35 U.S.C. 112(a) 'Written Description' Requirement
description: Standards and procedures for determining whether the specification provides adequate written description support for the claimed subject matter.
guidance: Covers support for claimed subject matter, standard for compliance, typical circumstances where issues arise, examiner burden, changes to claim scope, relationship to new matter, and amendments supported by original description.

name: 2164 The Enablement Requirement
description: Guidance on the enablement requirement under 35 U.S.C. 112(a): whether the specification enables a person skilled in the art to make and use the claimed invention as of the filing date without undue experimentation.
guidance: Includes tests of enablement, undue experimentation factors, how to make/use the invention, working and prophetic examples, predictability, burden on the examiner, and enablement commensurate in scope with the claims.

name: 2171 Two Separate Requirements for Claims Under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, Second Paragraph
description: Explains the distinct requirements for claims under 112(b): that claims must particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention, and related claim-drafting standards.
guidance: Cross-references MPEP §2173 for interpreting claims, definiteness, correspondence to the specification, and addressing specific claim-language issues.

name: 2173 Claims Must Particularly Point Out and Distinctly Claim the Invention
description: Standards and procedures for assessing whether claim language meets the statutory definiteness requirement and particularly points out the invention.
guidance: Includes interpreting claims, determining whether claim language is definite, correspondence between specification and claims, breadth vs indefiniteness, and many specific claim-language topics (antecedent basis, functional limitations, negative limitations, ranges, multiplicity, etc.).

name: 2181 Identifying and Interpreting a 35 U.S.C. 112(f) Limitation
description: Guidance on when claim language invokes 112(f) (means-plus-function) treatment and how to interpret such limitations.
guidance: Explains how to identify 112(f) claim elements, required structural support in the specification, and claim construction rules for means-plus-function claims.

name: Material/composition limitations affect scope — claiming material can limit infringement
description: When a patentee specifies a particular material (e.g., patent covers a superior material), use of a different or inferior material by a defendant may or may not constitute infringement; if the patentee covered material specifically, employing a different material may avoid liability, especially if patentee had rejected the alternative as valueless.
guidance: Aiken v. Bemis: whether difference is immaterial or a deliberate limiting choice by patentee affects infringement analysis.

name: Step 2A Prong One — Identify Abstract Idea & Map to PEG Groupings
description: Identify the specific limitation(s) in the claim that you believe recite an abstract idea, and determine whether the identified limitation(s) fall within at least one of the groupings of abstract ideas enumerated in the 2019 PEG.
guidance: Two-part instruction: (a) point to the particular claimed limitations that embody the purported abstract idea; (b) decide whether that concept fits one or more PEG groupings (mathematical concepts; mental processes; certain methods of organizing human activity).

name: Step 2A Prong Two — Meaningful Limit / Integration into Practical Application
description: Are there additional element(s) or a combination of elements in the claim that apply, rely on, or use the judicial exception in a manner that imposes a meaningful limit on the judicial exception, such that the claim is more than a drafting effort designed to monopolize the judicial exception?
guidance: Assess whether the additional elements (alone or in combination) integrate the exception into a practical application (i.e., meaningfully limit the abstract idea). Examples: cryptography claim — mathematical concepts used in a specific manner to secure communications (integration -> eligible); medical-records claim 1 — combination provides a specific improvement over prior art (integration -> eligible). By contrast, a claim that merely invokes generic computer components to implement the abstract idea at a high level (e.g., 'content server', 'generic network-based storage devices') and merely describes applying the idea on a computer does not impose meaningful limits and fails Prong Two.

name: Generic computer implementation does not by itself make a claim eligible
description: The performance of claim limitations using generic computer components (e.g., content server, generic network-based storage devices) does not preclude classification as an abstract idea, nor does it, by itself, integrate the idea into a practical application.
guidance: Claims that simply implement an abstract idea on a generic computer, without meaningful technological improvement or specific limitations, fail to satisfy Prong Two/Step 2B. Conversely, claims that show how the computer components are used in a specific, limiting, and practical way (e.g., solving a technical problem, securing communications via specific cryptographic use of math) can succeed.

name: Practical-application evidence — specific improvements and limits
description: A showing that claimed elements use the judicial exception in a specific manner that sufficiently limits its use to a practical application supports eligibility.
guidance: Look for claim language and reasoning that ties abstract concepts to technical details or improvements (e.g., limiting use to transmitting ciphertext over a communication channel; relying on hardness of factoring to secure communications; providing real-time standardized updating across heterogeneous systems). Such concrete ties indicate integration into a practical application rather than mere drafting to monopolize an idea.

name: Focus on claim sentences
description: The dataset and experiments focus specifically on the claim sentences of the draft, cited, and final patents.
guidance: Claims are the critical legal section and primary focus during USPTO review; all edit labeling and prediction in PatentEdits operates at the sentence-level for claims.

name: Limitations & need for expert validation
description: Limitations: edit actions are determined by automatic rules and metrics validated with non-expert human annotators; expert (patent agent / USPTO examiner) evaluation could further improve quality. The dataset does not predict 'Added' claims and does not exploit claim dependency (independent-dependent claim relations).
guidance: Be explicit about these limitations when using PatentEdits for downstream tasks; consider expert review or extended labels to capture added claims and claim-dependency structure when necessary.

name: Reply for abandonment for failure to reply to a final action
description: A reply under 37 CFR 1.113 to a final action must include a request for continued examination (RCE) under 37 CFR 1.114 or cancellation of, or appeal from, the rejection of each rejected claim. Thus, the required reply must be one of: (A) a Notice of Appeal and appeal fee; (B) an amendment under 37 CFR 1.116 that cancels all rejected claims or otherwise places the application in condition for allowance; (C) filing an RCE accompanied by a submission meeting 37 CFR 1.111 and the requisite fee (for certain utility/plant apps); or (D) filing a continuing application (or CPA for design).
guidance: If a Notice of Appeal is filed as the reply, the Director will set the time period under 37 CFR 41.37 for the appeal brief in the decision granting the petition. The Office of Petitions normally routes proposed amendments under 1.116 to the Technology Center to determine whether the amendment places the application in condition for allowance before granting revival. Examiners should annotate replies that are 'OK to enter upon revival'; otherwise they complete form PTOL-303 to advise denial.

name: Petition fee requirement and refund policy (35 U.S.C. 41(a)(7) / 37 CFR 1.17(m))
description: The Office shall charge $1,700.00 on filing each petition for revival of an abandoned application (and for related delayed fees/claims/extensions) (35 U.S.C. 41(a)(7)). The Director may refund any part of the fee in exceptional circumstances as determined by the Director.
guidance: The phrase 'on filing' means the petition fee is due on filing (not merely grant). The Office will not refund the petition fee regardless of whether the petition is dismissed or denied (unless exceptional circumstances). The Office will not reach the merits of any petition lacking the requisite petition fee.

name: Authority for restriction (35 U.S.C. 121)
description: If two or more independent and distinct inventions are claimed in one application, the Director may require the application to be restricted to one of the inventions.
guidance: Restriction is the practice of requiring an applicant to elect a single, claimed invention for examination when two or more independent inventions and/or two or more distinct inventions are claimed. The terms 'independent' and 'distinct' are mutually exclusive alternative requirements; only one must be met to support restriction. (MPEP 802, 802.02)

name: Interaction with non-statutory double patenting
description: If the examiner indicates via restriction that inventions A and B are independent or patentably distinct, the examiner is generally prohibited from later asserting non-statutory double patenting between claims to A and B (with limited exceptions).
guidance: Exceptions: a nonstatutory double patenting rejection may be proper if the restriction was withdrawn before the rejection, or if the examiner later determines the inventions are patentably indistinct and the later application is not a divisional maintaining consonance with the restriction. Improper restriction of patentably indistinct sets can result in multiple patents on indistinct variations. If unclear whether to restrict, ask whether you would apply a nonstatutory double patenting rejection if claims were in different applications: if yes, do not require restriction; if no, restriction may be appropriate but still requires showing serious burden. (MPEP 804.01, 804.01A-H)

name: Breadth vs patentable distinctness
description: Do not mistake variations in claim breadth for patentable distinctness. Claims should not be restricted if they define the same essential characteristics of a single disclosed embodiment.
guidance: Claims define the same essential characteristics when they provide different definitions of the same invention or vary only in breadth/scope (e.g., a broad claim and narrower dependent claims to the same structure). Such claims are not restrictable because they could serve as a basis for non-statutory double patenting if prosecuted separately. (MPEP 806.03)

name: Combination-subcombination two-way distinctness test
description: To support a restriction between a combination and a subcombination, both (i) and (ii) must be met: (i) the combination as claimed does not require the particulars of the subcombination as claimed for patentability; AND (ii) the subcombination has utility either by itself or in another materially different combination.
guidance: If these factors cannot both be shown, the inventions are not distinct. (MPEP 806.05(c); FP 8.15) Examples throughout the guidance illustrate ABsp–Bsp, ABbr–Bsp, etc.

name: Subcombinations usable together criteria
description: Two or more claimed subcombinations disclosed as usable together are usually restrictable when: at least one subcombination can be shown to be separately usable or have utility other than in the disclosed combination; the subcombinations do not overlap in scope; and they are not obvious variants of one another.
guidance: 'Not overlapping in scope' means mutually exclusive limitations or limitations that would not read on each other. Serious burden must also be shown. When plural subcombinations usable together are present and a combination requires particulars of at least one subcombination, a two-way distinctness and serious burden must be shown. (MPEP 806.05(d); FP 8.16)

name: Process of making and product made one-way test
description: Restriction between a process of making and a product made is based on a one-way test: (i) the process is not an obvious process of making the product and can be used to make another materially different product; OR (ii) the product can be made by another materially different process.
guidance: Apply this test to determine distinctness between process-of-making claims and product claims. (MPEP 806.05(f); FP 8.18)

name: Related products or related processes two-way distinctness test
description: Restriction between related products or related processes is based on a two-way test: (i) the inventions as claimed do not overlap in scope, AND (ii) the inventions are not obvious variants, AND (iii) the inventions are not capable of use together or can have a materially different design, mode of operation, function, or effect.
guidance: All (or more than two, if applicable) claim groups in question must meet these criteria. (MPEP 806.05(j))

name: Election of species two-prong test
description: Each species, as claimed, must (i) require a mutually exclusive limitation, AND (ii) the species must not be obvious variants of each other.
guidance: Election of species cannot be required when species are obvious variants, when examining together would not present a serious burden, or when claims are only directed to a single species with no generic claim. (MPEP 806.04(f); MPEP 803, 806.04, 809.02(a), 808.01(a), FP 8.01)

name: Markush group guidance for election of species
description: A Markush group (closed list of alternatives) may require election of species only between patentably distinct alternatives; patentably indistinct alternatives should be grouped together.
guidance: Specific 'selected from the group consisting of …' wording is not required for Markush treatment. When an elected species in a proper Markush claim is found allowable, another species must be examined until one species is found in the prior art or until the entire Markush group is allowable. (MPEP 803.02 III(A); 2117)

name: Limits on election by original presentation
description: Election by original presentation is NOT applicable when: a provisional election of a single species in a Markush claim was made and the applicant later cancels the elected species; OR the applicant presents claims that could not have been restricted from the claims drawn to the elected invention had they been presented earlier.
guidance: See MPEP for specific procedural references. (MPEP 803.02, 809.02(a), 808.01(a))

name: Rejoinder eligibility and requirements
description: Rejoinder is withdrawal of a restriction between an allowable elected invention and a non-elected invention and examination of the formerly non-elected invention on the merits; to be eligible, a claim to a non-elected invention must depend from or otherwise require all the limitations of an allowable claim.
guidance: Rejoined claims must be fully examined for patentability under 35 U.S.C. 101, 102, 103, and 112 and any rejoinder must be clearly explained on the record. (MPEP 821.04)

name: Rejoinder of allowable linking claims
description: When a linking claim is allowable, any restriction between the inventions it links cannot be maintained; rejoin pending claims that depend from or require all limitations of the allowable linking claim.
guidance: The record must state the restriction withdrawal. Rejoined claims must be re-examined and the applicant may reintroduce canceled subject matter by amendment. Applicant need not request rejoinder. (MPEP 809, FP 8.01, FP 8.02, FP 8.12)

name: Rejoinder relating to combinations
description: If all claims directed to an elected combination invention are allowable, the examiner must reconsider any restriction between the combination and subcombinations and withdraw restriction where a subcombination is allowable.
guidance: Rejoin any subcombinations that were searched and found allowable, and rejoin any non-elected claims that require all limitations of the allowable claim. (MPEP 806.05(d))

name: Rejoinder of process when product claim is allowable
description: If elected product claim(s) are subsequently found allowable, consider withdrawing process claims which depend from or otherwise require all the limitations of an allowable product claim so they may be rejoined and examined.
guidance: All claims directed to a non-elected process invention must depend from or otherwise require all the limitations of an allowable product claim to be rejoined. If applicant cancelled all claims to a non-elected process before rejoinder occurs, the examiner should not withdraw the restriction requirement to preserve rights under 35 U.S.C. 121. (MPEP 821.04(b))

name: Filing date of a provisional application
description: The filing date of a provisional application is the date on which a specification as prescribed by 35 U.S.C. 112(a), and any drawing required by 37 CFR 1.81(a), are filed in the Patent and Trademark Office.
guidance: For provisional applications filed on or after December 18, 2013, the filing date is the date on which a specification as prescribed by 35 U.S.C. 112(a), with or without claims, is filed. The filing date is accorded regardless of whether drawings are submitted, but applicants are advised to submit required drawings.

name: Conversion of a nonprovisional to a provisional (and vice versa) — timing and fees
description: An application filed under 37 CFR 1.53(b) may be converted to a provisional application if a request and fee (37 CFR 1.17(q)) are submitted prior to the earlier of abandonment, payment of issue fee, or expiration of 12 months after the filing date. Likewise, a provisional application may be converted to a nonprovisional application if a request (with fee 37 CFR 1.17(i)) and required amendment(s) are filed prior to the earlier of abandonment or expiration of 12 months after the provisional filing date.
guidance: The grant of such a conversion request will not entitle applicant to a refund of fees properly paid. Conversion of a provisional to a nonprovisional will result in the term of any patent issuing from the application being measured from at least the filing date of the provisional application (adverse patent term impact). Applicants are advised to consider claiming the benefit under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) rather than converting to avoid this impact. The nonprovisional resulting from conversion must include the filing, search, and examination fees, the inventor's oath or declaration, and any surcharge under 1.16(f) if appropriate; an amendment including at least one claim as prescribed by 35 U.S.C. 112(b) is required unless the provisional already contained at least one such claim.

name: Filing date rules for nonprovisional applications (post‑Dec 18, 2013)
description: For applications filed on or after December 18, 2013, the filing date of a nonprovisional application (other than a design patent application) is the date on which a specification, with or without claims, is received in the Office. Utility and plant patent applications filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a) are no longer required to include at least one claim or any drawings to receive a filing date. The filing date of a design patent application is the date on which the specification including at least one claim and any required drawings are received.
guidance: Effective December 18, 2013, a nonprovisional application may be filed by a reference to a previously filed application indicating that the specification and any drawings of the application are replaced by the reference to the previously filed application (per 35 U.S.C. 111(c)).

name: Answering each interrogatory and option to produce business records (Rule 33(d))
description: Each interrogatory must, to the extent not objected to, be answered separately and fully in writing under oath. Alternatively, if the answer may be determined by examining business records and the burden of deriving the answer is substantially the same for either party, the responding party may (1) specify the records in sufficient detail to enable the interrogating party to locate and identify them as readily as the responding party could, and (2) give a reasonable opportunity to examine, audit, or copy the records.
guidance: If the responding party elects to answer by specifying business records, the specification must be sufficiently detailed. A party invoking Rule 33(d) with regard to electronic information may be required to provide technical support or information on application software. If direct access to an electronic system is necessary, privacy/confidentiality concerns may justify deriving the answer without granting access. A responding party cannot simultaneously invoke Rule 33(d) and claim privilege as to the same documents. Case law sets out prerequisites for invoking this option (e.g., Johnson & Johnson v. WDS; Jain v. Ramparts).

name: Scope of requests for production (what may be requested)
description: A party may request production of any designated documents or ESI (writings, drawings, graphs, charts, photographs, sound recordings, images, and other data or data compilations) stored in any medium from which information can be obtained, or designated tangible things, or entry onto designated property for inspection — subject to Rule 26(b) scope limits.
guidance: Generally, a party is not obligated to locate documents not in its possession, custody, or control, nor to create documents that do not exist; but a party may not mislead its adversary by promising production and then claiming no possession or control. Because TTAB proceedings concern registration rights, entry onto land is rarely used.

name: Types of patents
description: Three types of patents exist: (1) Utility patents for new and useful processes, machines, manufactures, compositions of matter, or improvements; (2) Design patents for new, original, and ornamental designs for articles of manufacture; (3) Plant patents for distinct and new varieties of asexually reproduced plants.
guidance: Each patent type has specific subject-matter scope and some procedural differences (e.g., design/plant have single-claim conventions, plant patents require botanical description and certain drawing/color rules).

name: Effective filing date / priority basics
description: The 'effective filing date' for a U.S. nonprovisional application is the actual filing date of the nonprovisional; it can be the filing date of an earlier U.S. provisional (if the provisional sufficiently describes the claimed invention), an earlier-filed U.S. nonprovisional (continuation/division), or an earlier foreign application to which priority is claimed (if that foreign application sufficiently describes the claimed invention).
guidance: Properly supported priority claims can provide earlier effective dates for novelty and obviousness determinations; adequacy of the earlier application's description is critical.

name: Non-obviousness (inventive step) requirement
description: Even if differences exist over known art, an invention may be refused if those differences would be obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the relevant technology; routine substitutions (e.g., color changes, size changes) are ordinarily not patentable.
guidance: Assessment is factual and depends on the knowledge of a PHOSITA; the specification and claim drafting should emphasize non-routine advantages and inventive features.

name: Application components for a nonprovisional patent application
description: A nonprovisional application includes: (1) A written document comprising a specification (description and claims); (2) Drawings (when necessary); (3) An oath or declaration; and (4) Filing, search, and examination fees.
guidance: All required parts must comply with rules to obtain a filing date; missing parts may generate a Notice of Incomplete Application and possibly a surcharge; filing fee and declaration need not be submitted to get a filing date but omitting them may trigger notices and deadlines.

name: Specification and claims: required content and role
description: The specification (description and claims) must particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter the applicant regards as the invention; the claims define the scope of protection. The specification must conclude with a claim or claims.
guidance: Claims must commence on a separate sheet; multiple claims are permitted provided they differ; dependent claims may refer back and further limit other claims; multiple dependent claims are allowed and have special treatment.

name: Claims drafting conventions (independent/dependent/multiple dependent)
description: Claims may be independent (stand alone) or dependent (referring back to and further limiting another claim). A dependent claim that refers back to more than one other claim is a 'multiple dependent claim.'
guidance: Claims define protection scope; dependent and multiple dependent claims have specific formal and substantive rules — claims must commence on a separate sheet and differ from one another.

name: Design patent substantive and formal requirements
description: Design patents protect only the ornamental appearance of an article of manufacture; the specification is short and follows a set form; only one claim is permitted; drawings define the scope of protection; no reference characters allowed in drawings.
guidance: Design patent term: design patents issuing on/after May 13, 2015 have a 15-year term from grant (previously 14 years). On examination, a notice of allowance triggers payment of an issue fee. See current fee schedule for filing fees.

name: Plant patent substantive and formal requirements
description: Plant patents cover distinct and new varieties of plants that are asexually reproduced (not tuber-propagated or found in uncultivated state); an application must include a complete detailed botanical description, origin/parentage, how it was asexually reproduced, and the Latin genus/species name. Only one claim is permitted.
guidance: If color is distinctive, identify color by a recognized color dictionary and submit color drawings (two duplicate copies). Plant patent drawings must disclose distinctive characteristics; specimens generally should not be submitted unless requested. Plant patents have a 20-year term from filing and cannot be filed via EFS-Web.

name: Filing abroad for foreign applicants and claiming foreign priority
description: Foreign applicants may apply for U.S. patents on the same basis as U.S. citizens, but special points apply: an oath/declaration signature is required; to claim priority to a foreign application, the U.S. application must be filed within 12 months (6 months for designs) of the earlier foreign filing and a certified copy of the foreign application may be required.
