guidance: The oath/declaration must identify foreign applications filed more than a year before the U.S. filing that disclose similar inventions; procedures exist for taking oaths before foreign officials and for using declarations instead of oaths.

name: Infringement enforcement and USPTO jurisdiction limits
description: The USPTO has no jurisdiction over patent infringement questions; infringement suits are federal court matters; infringement is primarily determined by the language of the claims; defendants may challenge patent validity in litigation.
guidance: From district court decisions there is appeal to the Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit and potentially to the Supreme Court. For U.S. government infringement, remedies lie in the Court of Federal Claims; the USPTO does not advise on infringement or whether an invention infringes existing patents.

name: Exceptions to § 314(d) review bar — colorable constitutional or certain statutory claims
description: Possible exceptions to the § 314(d) nonreviewability bar include colorable constitutional claims and certain statutory challenges, which may permit judicial review despite § 314(d).
guidance: Such exceptions are narrow: the constitutional claim must be 'colorable' and substantial (see Mylan, Apple, Motorola). Absent a colorable constitutional or specified statutory claim, mandamus is not available to review institution decisions.

name: What a 'colorable constitutional claim' requires
description: A colorable constitutional due-process claim must identify the kind of constitutionally protected interest (e.g., property rights or retroactivity concerns) that might support relief; mere expectation that a petition would be evaluated under certain criteria is insufficient.
guidance: There is no constitutional right to an IPR; petitioners must show more than disagreement with the Director's criteria to make out a colorable constitutional claim (citing Motorola, Mylan, United States v. Carlton).

name: Director's discretion to consider 'settled expectations' (patent age) among factors for discretionary denial
description: The Director may consider 'settled expectations of the parties, such as the length of time the claims have been in force,' as one factor in deciding whether to exercise discretion to deny institution.
guidance: The PTO applied this factor to deny institution where patents had 'been in force for nine and seven years, respectively,' finding 'settled expectations' favored discretionary denial; by contrast, patents issued in 2019–2020 were considered 'not... in force for a significant period' and did not support settled-expectations denial. The court does not decide whether use of the factor is correct, only that review is limited.

name: Examination procedures regarding deposits (§ 1.809)
description: Examiners must determine under §1.104 if a deposit is needed, and if needed, whether a deposit made is acceptable; if needed and not made/replaced/supplemented per regulations, examiner shall reject affected claims under 35 U.S.C.112 explaining need for deposit or why deposit is unacceptable.
guidance: Applicant/patent owner must reply by (1) making acceptable original/replacement/supplemental deposit or assuring Office in writing that acceptable deposit will be made (or patent owner requesting certificate of correction meeting §1.805(b),(c)); or (2) arguing why deposit is not needed and/or why deposit made should be accepted. Other replies are nonresponsive. Rejection will repeat until cured or examiner convinced deposit not needed. If application otherwise allowable except for needed deposit and Office has written assurance that acceptable deposit will be made, Office may issue notice of allowability and set a three-month non-extendable period to make the deposit to avoid abandonment. For each deposit, the specification must contain accession number, deposit date, description sufficient to identify the material and permit examination, and depository name/address. Amendments to add accession number, deposit date, or depository name/address must be filed before or with payment of the issue fee.

name: Showing Possession of the Claimed Invention
description: Possession is shown by describing the claimed invention with all of its limitations using descriptive means such as words, structures, figures, diagrams, and formulas that fully set forth the claimed invention.
guidance: Possession may be shown by reduction to practice, showing the invention was 'ready for patenting' (e.g., drawings, structural chemical formulas), or by describing distinguishing identifying characteristics sufficient to show possession. See Lockwood, Pfaff, Regents v. Eli Lilly, Amgen v. Chugai.

name: Nonliteral Description Permitted but Amendments Must Be Supported
description: The subject matter of the claim need not be described literally (in haec verba) to satisfy the description requirement; however, if a claim is amended to include subject matter, limitations, or terminology not present in the application as filed (a departure, addition, or deletion) the claimed subject matter is not described in that application.
guidance: Such amendments will result in rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph (written description) or denial of the benefit of an earlier filing date. See MPEP § 2163.

name: Typical Circumstances Raising Written Description Issues
description: Written description issues commonly arise when: (I) claims are amended or new claims are added; (II) reliance on the filing date of a parent application (35 U.S.C. 120); (III) reliance on foreign/provisional priority (35 U.S.C. 119); and (IV) support for a claim corresponding to a count in an interference.
guidance: Most often the issue arises upon claim amendments; an original claim rejection for lack of written description should be rare because of the strong presumption that the originally filed specification is adequate (see In re Wertheim).

name: Burden on the Examiner and Presumption of Adequacy
description: A description as filed is presumed adequate unless and until sufficient evidence or reasoning to the contrary is presented by the examiner; the examiner must have a reasonable basis to challenge adequacy and bears the initial burden of presenting by a preponderance of evidence why a person skilled in the art would not recognize a description of the invention defined by the claims.
guidance: See In re Marzocchi and In re Wertheim. The examiner must set forth express factual findings supporting a lack of written description conclusion (see MPEP § 2163).

name: Statement of Rejection Requirements (Identify Limitations and Prima Facie Case)
description: When rejecting for lack of written description the examiner must (A) identify the claim limitation(s) at issue; and (B) establish a prima facie case by providing reasons why a person skilled in the art at the filing time would not have recognized that the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention in view of the application disclosure.
guidance: A general allegation such as 'unpredictability in the art' is insufficient. In some cases a simple statement pointing out lack of apparent support may be sufficient for new or amended claims where applicant has not pointed out support. See MPEP § 2163.04(I)(A)-(B) and Hyatt v. Dudas.

name: Requirement That Each Claim Limitation Be Supported
description: To comply with the written description requirement or to be entitled to an earlier priority/filing date, each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure.
guidance: This applies to broadenings or narrowings, numerical ranges, and use of different terminology. See MPEP § 2163 and related case law.

name: Broadening Claims — Omission of an Essential Limitation
description: Omission of a limitation can raise written description issues regarding whether the inventor possessed a broader, more generic invention. A claim that omits an element described as essential or critical in the original disclosure does not comply with the written description requirement.
guidance: Court examples include Gentry Gallery and Tronzo. If the specification makes clear that a particular narrow understanding is essential, removing that limitation can invalidate broader claims. Consider whether the original disclosure describes a feature as 'the only possible location' or 'outside the stated purpose' as indicating essentiality.

name: Narrowing or Subgeneric Claim Changes
description: Introducing narrowing changes (subgeneric terminology or specific species) not supported by the as-filed disclosure can violate the written description requirement; a 'laundry list' disclosure of many possible moieties does not necessarily describe every species.
guidance: Each case decided on its facts; examples include Fujikawa, In re Ruschig, Ex parte Ohshiro. A subgenus may or may not be acceptable depending on whether species within it were disclosed.

name: Range Limitations Must Be Supported
description: When changing numerical range limitations, the analysis must account for which ranges would be inherently supported by the original disclosure; claims that read literally on embodiments outside disclosed ranges may fail the description requirement.
guidance: Example: original '25%-60%' with examples '36%' and '50%' — a new limitation 'at least 35%' failed because it had no upper limit, whereas 'between 35% and 60%' met the requirement (In re Wertheim). Consider whether a skilled artisan would consider the broader range inherently supported.

name: Treatment of New Matter — Examiner Actions
description: If new subject matter is added, the examiner should object to the introduction of new matter under 35 U.S.C. 132 or 251 as appropriate and require applicant to cancel the new matter; if new matter is added to claims, reject the claims under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
guidance: If claims are unaffected per se but the specification is amended to add new matter that affects claim limitations, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, para. 1 should be made. Applicant should specifically point out support for any amendments. Rejections are reviewable by the Board; objections to delete new matter are subject to petition (37 CFR 1.181). If both claims and specification contain new matter with both rejection and objection, the issue is appealable.

name: Claims Filed But Not Disclosed Elsewhere in Specification
description: If originally filed claims disclose material not disclosed in the remainder of the specification, the applicant may amend the specification to include the claimed subject matter (providing proper antecedent basis).
guidance: Form Paragraph 7.44 may be used where originally claimed subject matter lacks proper antecedent basis. See MPEP § 608.01(o) and In re Benno.

name: Inherent Function, Theory, or Advantage May Be Later Claimed
description: If a patent application discloses a device that inherently performs a function or has a property, operates according to a theory, or has an advantage, the application necessarily discloses that function/theory/advantage even if nothing explicit is said; the application may later be amended to recite it without introducing new matter.
guidance: To establish inherency, extrinsic evidence must make clear that the missing descriptive matter is necessarily present in the thing described and would be recognized by persons of ordinary skill. Inherency cannot be established by probabilities or possibilities. See In re Reynolds, In re Smythe, In re Robertson.

name: Test of Enablement — Undue Experimentation
description: The enablement inquiry asks whether the amount of experimentation required to practice the invention would be undue or unreasonable (the Mineral Separation undue experimentation standard).
guidance: Assess whether the disclosure, when filed, contained sufficient information that one skilled in the art could make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation. Consider the nature of the invention, state of the art, availability of routine optimization, quantity of guidance provided, and predictability of the art.

name: Determine whether the function includes dependent/result clauses (Lockheed analysis)
description: Assess whether language following the basic 'means for' phrase (e.g., a 'so that', 'into a single data [set]', or similar clauses) limits or describes the claimed function rather than merely stating a result.
guidance: Use Lockheed: do not incorrectly omit limitations that disclose a manner of performing the function. If the clause describes a manner (analogous to Lockheed's 'predetermined rate schedule') it should be treated as part of the function; if it merely recites a result (a 'whereby' clause that adds nothing substantive) it may be excluded. Examine the claim grammar and context; parties' concession on typographical errors (e.g., 'data' -> 'data set') may be adopted for clarity.

name: Katz exception (when no algorithmic disclosure is required)
description: A specification need not disclose an algorithm for a claimed function if a general-purpose computer can perform the function without 'special programming.'
guidance: Apply Katz: functions coextensive with the structure of a general-purpose processor (e.g., 'processing,' 'receiving,' 'storing' in Katz) may avoid algorithm disclosure. But evaluate whether the claimed function truly is coextensive with general purpose computing; mere assertion that a PHOSITA could perform it is insufficient without showing lack of special programming.

name: Sufficiency of algorithmic structure (what counts as an algorithmic disclosure)
description: An adequate algorithm may be disclosed in mathematical formula, prose, flow charts, or other understandable terms, and must provide sufficient detail about how the claimed function is accomplished.
guidance: Cite Finisar/Net MoneyIN/Noah: mere mention of software or general statements at the same level of generality as the claim term is not enough. The specification must disclose concrete steps or other descriptive detail enabling a PHOSITA to associate structure with the claimed function. Partial algorithms that fail to disclose all aspects of the claimed function are treated as non-disclosure.

name: Consequences of lacking algorithmic disclosure
description: If no adequate algorithmic structure is disclosed and Katz does not apply, the means-plus-function claim element is indefinite under § 112(f).
guidance: If a PHOSITA 'would be unable to recognize the structure in the specification and associate it with the corresponding function in the claim,' the claim is indefinite (Noah, AllVoice). The inquiry is complete once no disclosed algorithm is identified.

name: PHOSITA association requirement
description: A means-plus-function limitation is valid only if a person of ordinary skill in the art can recognize the structure disclosed in the specification and associate it with the claimed function.
guidance: Evaluate whether the specification's identified structures (figures, boxes, described components) are linked clearly enough to the claimed function so that a PHOSITA would see them as the corresponding structure. Vague pointers or mere naming of components without procedural detail may fail this test.

name: Assessing examples and embodiments for algorithmic support
description: Figures, flowchart steps, and descriptive embodiments may supply algorithmic detail, but only if they disclose concrete steps or procedures rather than restating the function at the same level of generality.
guidance: Compare the specificity of figure steps and textual descriptions to the claimed function. If figures (e.g., step labeled 'display transformed document') or prose merely restate outcomes or high-level actions ('determine adjustments and then accomplish them') without algorithms for the how, they are insufficient. Do not treat UI snapshots or result displays as algorithmic disclosure absent procedural detail.

name: Treatment of combining/processing/identifying functions where multiple ways exist
description: When the specification and claim disclose that there are 'many different ways' to perform a function (e.g., combining documents), that plurality suggests specialized programming may be required and the Katz exception may not apply.
guidance: If multiple manners to perform the function are possible, the patent must disclose which manner(s) and the algorithms for them; otherwise, the function likely requires algorithmic support and may be indefinite if none is provided.

name: First Schedule (Table I) substituted — comprehensive fee schedule
description: “In the said rules, for Table I of THE FIRST SCHEDULE, the following table shall be substituted, namely, - TABLE I …” (substituted table contains itemised fees for filing forms/actions: application fees, per-sheet/per-claim fees, sequence listing page fees, reductions for section 54 applications, fees for filing complete specification after provisional, fees for statement and undertaking under section 8, fees for requests for extension of time/condonation (per month), declaration as to inventorship, postdating, deletion of reference, claims under section 20, notices of opposition, requests for hearing, renewal fees by year, fees for amendments, certified copies, inspection, information requests, patent agent registration, transmittal fees for international applications, fees for preparation/transmission of certified priority documents, Form 27 (statement of working) — and many other entries with amounts specified for natural person/startup/small entity/educational institution and for other applicants).
guidance: The First Schedule replaces the entire fee matrix for a very large number of patent office transactions. Practitioners must consult the substituted Table I for the exact fee amounts applicable to each form/entry/action (the Gazette reproduces the detailed numeric amounts and caps for multiple-priority cases and per-page charges). Key features include per-sheet and per-claim extra fees, a 50% reduction for section 54 applications in some items, and differentiated fees for 'natural person/startup/small entity/educational institution' versus 'other(s)'.

name: Fees-related specific rules: per-sheet, per-claim, sequence-listing charges and section 54 reductions
description: Table I entries: On application for a patent under sections 7, 54* or 135 and rule 20(1) accompanied by provisional or complete specification— (i) for each sheet of specification in addition to 30, excluding sequence listing of nucleotides and/or amino acid sequences under sub-rule (3) of rule (9); (ii) for each claim in addition to 10; (iii) for each page of sequence listing of nucleotides and/or amino acid sequences under sub-rule (3) of rule (9). *An application for a patent made under section 54 shall be eligible for a reduction of 50 per cent in fee as compared to other applications.
guidance: When preparing and filing specifications, applicants must account for extra fees for sheets beyond 30, extra claims beyond 10, and sequence listing pages; section 54 applications may receive a 50% fee reduction where indicated.

name: ¶ 2.10 Disclosure of Prior-Filed Application Does Not Provide Support for Claimed Subject Matter
description: The disclosure of the prior-filed application fails to provide adequate support or enablement under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre-AIA 112) for one or more claims of this application; therefore those claims are not entitled to the benefit of the prior filing date.
guidance: Must be preceded by heading form paragraph 2.09. Can be used when lack of support/enablement in prior-filed application for claims in the later-filed application claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, 365(c), 386(c) or 119(e). In bracket 1 insert prior application number; in bracket 2 provide explanation and list of claims not entitled to benefit if only some claims affected.

name: ¶ 2.11.01 Application Must Be Filed Within 12 Months From the Provisional Application Unless Petition Granted
description: To claim benefit of a provisional under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) the later application must be filed within twelve months of the provisional filing date, unless a petition to restore benefit under 37 CFR 1.78(b) or PCT Rule 26bis.3 has been granted.
guidance: Use when an application claims benefit of a provisional but was not filed within twelve months and no intermediate application exists and no petition was granted. Explains contents of a 37 CFR 1.78(b) petition: reference to provisional, petition fee (37 CFR 1.17(m)), and statement that delay was unintentional; address for petition provided. Must be preceded by heading 2.09 and insert prior provisional application number in bracket 1.

name: ¶ 2.13.01 Correction of Inventorship Under 37 CFR 1.48(b), Insufficient
description: The request for deletion of an inventor under 37 CFR 1.48(b) is deficient because it lacks required elements (e.g., written consent of assignee) or other defects.
guidance: Use when inventorship was previously correct but an inventor is being deleted because claims were amended/canceled. Follow with form paragraphs 2.13c and/or 2.13g as applicable. See note 1 of 2.13 regarding potential rejections.

name: ¶ 2.13.02 Correction of Inventorship Under 37 CFR 1.48(c), Insufficient
description: The request to correct inventorship under 37 CFR 1.48(c) requesting addition of an inventor(s) is deficient because required elements are missing.
guidance: Use when inventorship was previously correct but now needs change due to subsequent addition of subject matter from specification to claims contributed by a party not originally named. Follow with any of 2.13b–2.13e or 2.13h. Consider notes 2 and 4–7 of 2.13.

name: ¶ 2.13h Statement of Facts, Added Inventor (for Use Following FP 2.13.02, If Applicable)
description: The statement of facts by the inventor(s) to be added does not explicitly state that the amendment of inventorship is necessitated by amendment of the claims and that the inventorship error occurred without deceptive intent.
guidance: Use after 2.13.02 when the added-inventor statement of facts fails to state required elements.

name: ¶ 2.15 Reference to Prior Application, 35 U.S.C. 119(e), 120, 121, 365(c), or 386(c) Benefit
description: If applicant desires to claim benefit of a prior-filed application under the cited statutes, the instant application must contain a specific reference to the prior-filed application in compliance with 37 CFR 1.78, located as required depending on filing date and application type; failure to timely submit specific reference results in waiver of benefit unless accompanied by a grantable petition.
guidance: Details timing: for 35 U.S.C. 111(a) utility/plant apps: submit during pendency and within the later of 4 months from actual filing date or 16 months from prior filing date; for national stage under 371, timing differs as set forth. Requirement location changed for filings on/after Sept. 16, 2012 (ADS). Time period is not extendable but a petition under 37 CFR 1.78(c)/(e) may be accepted with required reference, petition fee (37 CFR 1.17(m)), and statement of unintentional delay. If reference was previously submitted but not in required location and recognized by Office (e.g., included on first filing receipt), petition/fee may not be required but applicant still must file ADS or amendment. Use when application references but does not claim benefit; insert prior app number/date in brackets and note CPA exception under 1.53(d). See MPEP § 211.02.

name: ¶ 29.11 Reproductions Objected to, Design Not Fully Disclosed in Reproductions
description: The reproductions are objected to for failing to fully disclose the industrial design because [1]; use where failure does not render the claimed invention non-enabled and/or indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112 (e.g., minor inconsistencies among views).
guidance: If failure renders design non-enabled/indefinite use form paragraph 15.21 or 15.22 instead. Insert explanation in bracket 1 and follow with 15.05.04.

name: ¶ 29.21 Rejection, 35 U.S.C. 112(b) - Undescribed Broken Lines (International Design Application)
description: The claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention because reproductions include broken lines not described in the specification, making scope of claimed design indeterminate.
guidance: If broken lines represent matter for which protection is not sought, applicant may overcome rejection by inserting statement immediately preceding the claim (provided it does not introduce new matter): e.g., 'The broken line showing of [2] is for the purpose of illustrating [3] and forms no part of the claimed design.' Insert figure numbers and structure/type in brackets as directed. Use in international design applications when reproductions include undescribed broken lines.

name: ¶ 29.22 Description of Broken Lines Added by Examiner's Amendment (International Design Application)
description: Examiner's amendment has added a sentence to the specification immediately preceding the claim clarifying the meaning of broken lines: 'The broken line showing of [1] is for the purpose of illustrating [2] and forms no part of the claimed design.'
guidance: Use only in an Examiner's Amendment for international design applications to explain broken lines. Insert name of structure and whether broken lines indicate portions of the 'article' or environmental structure.

name: ¶ 29.24 Description of Broken Lines as Boundary of Design Added by Examiner's Amendment (International Design Application)
description: Examiner's amendment has added a sentence to the specification: 'The [1] broken line(s) define the bounds of the claimed design and form no part thereof.'
guidance: Use when broken lines define boundary and were added by Examiner's Amendment. Insert appropriate descriptor (e.g., portions of the 'article' or environmental structure).

name: ¶ 29.23 Rejection, 35 U.S.C. 112(b) - Undescribed Broken Lines as Boundary of Design (International Design Application)
description: Claim rejected for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention because reproductions include broken lines not described in the specification and the broken lines are presented as boundary lines, making scope indeterminate.
guidance: If broken lines represent a boundary for which protection is not sought, applicant may insert statement like: 'The [2] broken line(s) define the bounds of the claimed design and form no part of the claimed design.' Insert type of broken line and other specifics in brackets. Use in international design applications; explain in Examiner's Amendment if applicable.

name: ¶ 29.25 Rejection, 35 U.S.C. 112(b) - Unclear Use of Coloring (International Design Application)
description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) because reproductions include coloring not described in the specification, making the scope of the claimed design indeterminate.
guidance: If coloring identifies matter for which protection is not sought, applicant may overcome rejection by inserting a statement immediately preceding the claim (provided no new matter): e.g., 'The portion of the design shown in the color [2] is for the purpose of illustrating [3] and forms no part of the claimed design.' Insert figure numbers, color identification, and whether portions are 'article' or environmental structure.

name: ¶ 29.26 Description of Coloring Added by Examiner's Amendment (International Design Application)
description: Examiner's amendment has added the sentence to the specification: 'The portion of the design shown in the color [1] is for the purpose of illustrating [2] and forms no part of the claimed design.'
guidance: Use only in an Examiner's Amendment for international design applications to explain meaning of coloring in reproductions. Insert color and whether portions are 'article' or environmental structure.

name: ¶ 29.27 Suggestion To Overcome Rejection Under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b) (International Design Application)
description: Applicant may indicate that protection is not sought for reproductions considered indefinite or nonenabling by amending reproductions to color those portions or convert them to broken lines and by amending the specification to state that those portions form no part of the claimed design, provided such amendments do not introduce new matter.
guidance: Use only in international design applications; insert title of the article in bracket 1. Advises conversion of problematic portions to broken lines or coloring and adding appropriate specification statements consistent with 35 U.S.C. 132 and 37 CFR 1.121.

name: Elements of prosecution laches defense
description: Prosecution laches requires proving two elements: (a) the patentee’s delay in prosecution was unreasonable and inexcusable under the totality of the circumstances, and (b) the accused infringer suffered prejudice attributable to the delay.
guidance: To establish prejudice, an accused infringer must show evidence of intervening rights — that the accused infringer or others "invested in, worked on, or used the claimed technology during the period of delay." (Cancer Research). Both elements must be considered under a totality-of-the-circumstances inquiry.

name: Totality of the circumstances inquiry
description: "An examination of the totality of the circumstances, including the prosecution history of all of a series of related patents and overall delay in issuing claims, may trigger laches."
guidance: The analysis is not limited to the prosecution history of the particular application at issue; courts should consider a series of related applications (e.g., continuations, families) and overall patterns of delay. Focusing narrowly on only the specific applications can be error.

name: Reasonable examples of delay (non-exhaustive)
description: Examples of reasonable delay include: (i) filing a divisional application in response to a restriction requirement, even if filed immediately before issuance of the parent; (ii) refiling an application to present new evidence of an invention’s unexpected advantages; and (iii) refiling to add subject matter to support broader claims as development progresses.
guidance: These examples are not exhaustive; an applicant could reasonably refile where the refiling "is not unduly successive or repetitive." Courts should consider the context and purpose of refilings.

name: Prosecution conduct characteristics that indicate undue delay
description: Certain prosecution features can make examination effectively impossible and support a laches finding: claiming many priority dates, long/complex specifications, extremely large claim counts across applications, repeatedly adding hundreds of claims that restart examination, filing identical or patentably indistinct claims across different applications, and rewriting claims mid-prosecution.
guidance: These combined characteristics create a 'perfect storm' that overwhelms examiners' ability to determine priority, perform double-patenting analyses, or identify written description support. Evidence that prosecution "all but guaranteed indefinite prosecution delay" supports unreasonable delay.

name: Citing prior patents does not by itself demonstrate integration or enablement
description: Merely citing prior art patents to show that challenged components are old may not suffice to show how those components would be interconnected to function in the claimed complex combination.
guidance: The specification must set forth the integration of the prior art; otherwise undue experimentation or more than routine experimentation may be required to implement the claimed invention (In re Scarbrough). Any cited patents used to show components are old must be analyzed for germane relevance and whether they provide better disclosure than applicant's own disclosure.

name: When utility is not satisfied (nonuseful or inoperative claims)
description: If a claim fails the utility requirement of 35 U.S.C. 101 because it is nonuseful or inoperative, it necessarily fails the how-to-use aspect of enablement under 35 U.S.C. 112(a).
guidance: The examiner should make both rejections (35 U.S.C. 112(a) and 35 U.S.C. 101) where subject matter has been shown to be nonuseful or inoperative (In re Fouche). Do not impose or maintain a 112(a) rejection grounded on 'lack of utility' unless a proper 101 rejection exists.

name: Examiner burden to show lack of utility
description: When the examiner concludes an application claims an invention that is nonuseful, inoperative, or contradicts known scientific principles, the burden is on the examiner to provide a reasonable basis to support this conclusion.
guidance: The examiner has the initial burden of challenging an asserted utility: they must provide evidence showing that one of ordinary skill would reasonably doubt the asserted utility. Only then does the burden shift to the applicant to rebut (In re Fisher; In re Swartz; In re Brana; In re Bundy).

name: Enablement can fail even when utility is satisfied
description: An invention may have a specific and substantial utility and a credible basis for that utility, yet still fail the enablement requirement if a person skilled in the art would need to engage in undue experimentation to practice the claimed invention.
guidance: In such cases, no 101 rejection is appropriate but a 112(a) rejection should be made (Mowry v. Whitney). Examiners must separately consider enablement even when utility is present.

name: Enablement evaluated against the full scope of the claims (commensurate in scope)
description: All questions of enablement are evaluated against the claimed subject matter. The focus is whether everything within the scope of the claim is enabled; the examiner must determine exactly what is encompassed by the claims.
guidance: Examination looks to the claim as a whole (including dependent claims under 35 U.S.C. 112(d)/pre-AIA 112, fourth paragraph). If a range is claimed, there must be reasonable enablement across that range (AK Steel v. Sollac). The examiner should identify the subject matter considered enabled if making a lack-of-enablement rejection.

name: Specification must teach how to make and use the full scope without undue experimentation
description: The specification must teach those skilled in the art how to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention without 'undue experimentation.'
guidance: Not everything necessary need be disclosed — well-known information may be omitted. The required scope of enablement must have a reasonable correlation to the scope of the claims (In re Wright; In re Buchner; In re Fisher). Examiners should consider the level of ordinary skill in the art and what is routine knowledge.

name: Rejection under 112(a) for breadth not 112(b) definiteness
description: A rejection that the claim is broader than the enabling disclosure is an enablement rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and not a definiteness rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b).
guidance: Claims are not rejected as broader than the enabling disclosure simply for omitting limitations that are presumed within ordinary skill. One looks to the specification to find out how to practice the claimed invention (W.L. Gore; In re Johnson).

name: Claim interpretation in light of the specification
description: Claims are to be given their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification; the teachings of the specification must not be ignored when analyzing enabled scope.
guidance: Interpretation in light of the specification does not mean everything in the specification is read into the claims (Raytheon v. Roper). If a reasonable interpretation of a claim is broader than the description in the specification, the examiner must ensure the full claim scope is enabled. Limitations and examples in the specification do not generally limit what is covered by the claims.

name: Inoperative subject matter standard
description: The presence of inoperative embodiments within the scope of a claim does not necessarily render a claim nonenabled; the standard is whether a skilled person could determine which conceived-but-not-yet-made embodiments would be inoperative or operative with expenditure of no more effort than is normally required in the art.
guidance: Prophetic examples do not make a disclosure nonenabling (Atlas Powder). A single inoperative embodiment among many operable ones may not render the claim nonenabled (In re Angstadt). However, claims that read on significant numbers of inoperative embodiments may be nonenabled where the specification fails to clearly identify operative embodiments and undue experimentation is required (Atlas Powder; In re Cook).

name: Critical feature taught in specification must be claimed
description: A feature that the specification teaches as 'critical' and is not recited in the claims should result in a rejection of such claim under the enablement provision of 35 U.S.C. 112.
guidance: Determination of criticality considers the entire disclosure; features merely described as preferred are not 'critical' (In re Mayhew; In re Goffe). An enablement rejection based on omission of a disclosed critical limitation should be made only when the specification language makes clear that the limitation is critical for the invention to function as intended. Broad language in the disclosure tends to rebut arguments of criticality.

name: Best mode requirement (statutory obligation and scope)
description: The specification shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor of carrying out the invention (pre-AIA language preserved in 35 U.S.C. 112(a) for examination purposes). Determining compliance requires a two-prong inquiry: (1) whether the inventor possessed a best mode at filing (subjective), and (2) whether the written description disclosed the best mode sufficiently to enable one skilled in the art to practice it (objective).
guidance: The best mode requirement prevents applicants from retaining their best-known way while disclosing only second-best embodiments (In re Nelson). Failure to disclose the best mode can be found even absent active concealment if the inventor knew of a specific material or method that would make reproduction possible but did not disclose it (Union Carbide v. Borg-Warner). The best mode requirement is distinct from enablement: best mode imposes an obligation to disclose the inventor's recognized best practice; enablement looks to whether the public can practice the claimed subject matter generally.

name: Best mode — considerations and limitations (examples and practical rules)
description: Practical considerations: determine what the invention is (defined by the claims); a specific example is not required; designation of an embodiment as 'best' is not required; updating best mode is not required in priority filings; best mode defects cannot be cured by adding new matter after filing.
guidance: The specification need not set forth details unrelated to the essence of the invention (In re Bosy). Presence or absence of a working example is not dispositive (In re Gay; In re Honn). There is no statutory duty to label an embodiment as 'best.' Do not add best mode by amendment (new matter) — such amendments should be objected to and treated as new matter (In re Hay).

name: Form Paragraph 7.12 — 102(e) Patent/Application Publication to Another with Earlier Filing Date (AIPA & 2002 Amendments)
description: (e) the invention was described in (1) an application for patent, published under section 122(b), by another filed in the United States before the invention by the applicant... or (2) a patent granted on an application for patent by another filed in the United States before the invention by the applicant for patent.
guidance: This form paragraph should only be used if the reference is (a) filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a); or (b) a U.S. patent issued directly or indirectly from, or a U.S. or WIPO publication of, an international application if the international application has an international filing date on or after November 29, 2000. In determining the 102(e) date, consider priority/benefit claims to earlier-filed U.S. provisionals (119(e)), nonprovisionals (120/121), and internationals (120/121/365(c)) only if the subject matter used is appropriately supported in the relied upon earlier-filed application's disclosure. Do NOT consider foreign priority claims under 119(a)-(d) and 365(a). Detailed examiner notes (1–8) explain international filing date, language, designation, and pre-/post-AIPA considerations.

name: Form Paragraph 7.12.01 — Pre-AIPA 102(e) (Refs from International Applications Filed Prior to Nov 29, 2000)
description: (e) the invention was described in a patent granted on an application for patent by another filed in the United States before the invention... (pre-AIPA 35 U.S.C. 102(e)).
guidance: Use this paragraph when the reference is a U.S. patent issued directly or indirectly from a national stage of, or a continuing application claiming benefit under 365(c) to, an international application having an international filing date prior to November 29, 2000. Examiner notes explain determination of the reference's 102(e) date and caution that WIPO publication may give earlier prior art date under 102(a) or (b). Consider benefit claims to earlier-filed U.S. provisionals/nonprovisionals and internationals only if supported in the earlier disclosure.

name: Form Paragraph 7.15 and Variants — Generic 102 Rejection Language and Follow-ups
description: ¶ 7.15 Rejection, 35 U.S.C. 102(a), (b) Patent or Publication, and (g): 'Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102[2] as being [3] by [4].' (Instructions for bracket insertions provided.)
guidance: This rejection must be preceded by form paragraph 7.07 and form paragraphs 7.08, 7.09, and 7.14 as appropriate, or by form paragraph 7.103, and must be followed by either form paragraph 7.15.02 or 7.15.03. Use bracket instructions to indicate anticipation vs. clear anticipation and to identify prior art relied upon.

name: Form Paragraph 7.15.01 — Provisional Rejection, 35 U.S.C. 102(e) (Common Assignee or Common Inventor)
description: Claim [1] provisionally rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as being anticipated by copending Application No. [2] which has a common [3] with the instant application.
guidance: Used to provisionally reject over an earlier-filed copending application that discloses the claimed invention and has either a common assignee or at least one common inventor. Based upon the earlier effective U.S. filing date, it would constitute prior art under 102(e) if published or patented. This provisional rejection might be overcome by a showing under 37 CFR 1.132 (derivation), 37 CFR 1.131 (date of invention), or other appropriate actions. This rejection may not be overcome by filing a terminal disclaimer.

name: Form Paragraph 7.15.02 — 102(e) Rejection (Common Assignee or Inventor(s))
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as being anticipated by [2]. The applied reference has a common [3] with the instant application.
guidance: Based upon the earlier effective U.S. filing date of the reference, it constitutes prior art under 102(e). The rejection might be overcome by a showing under 37 CFR 1.132 that any invention disclosed but not claimed was derived from the inventor of this application or by a showing under 37 CFR 1.131. Apply AIPA and 2002 amendments to determine 102(e) dates when appropriate; use pre-AIPA 7.12.01 when required.

name: Form Paragraph 7.15.03 — 102(e) Rejection (No Common Assignee or Inventor)
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as being [2] by [3].
guidance: Used to reject over a patent or patent application publication with an earlier filing date that discloses but does not claim the same invention; the patent or publication is not required to have a common assignee or inventor. Apply AIPA/2002 rules or pre-AIPA 7.12.01 as appropriate when determining the reference's 102(e) date.

name: Form Paragraph 7.19 — 102(f) Applicant Not the Inventor (usage)
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(f) because the applicant did not invent the claimed subject matter.
guidance: This paragraph must be preceded either by paragraphs 7.07 and 7.13 or by paragraph 7.103. In bracket 2 insert an explanation of the supporting evidence establishing that applicant was not the inventor. See MPEP § 2137.

name: 35 U.S.C. 103(c) / CREATE Act Disqualification — Commonly Assigned or Joint Research Agreement
description: Subject matter which was prior art under former 103 via 102(e) may be disqualified as prior art if it was, at the time the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person. The CREATE Act further provides joint research agreement disqualification if three conditions are met.
guidance: The three CREATE Act conditions: (A) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; (B) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (C) the application for patent discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement. These rules affect whether provisional 103 rejections should be made and apply to patents granted on or after Dec 10, 2004 (with transitional rules for earlier grants/applications). See MPEP § 706.02(l)(1).

name: Provisional Double Patenting and Terminal Disclaimer Guidance
description: If the claims of copending applications conflict, a provisional double patenting rejection should also be given; where the applications claim the same patentable invention, a terminal disclaimer and a 37 CFR 1.130 affidavit may be used to overcome a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 in a common ownership situation if the earlier application has been published or matured into a patent.
guidance: Combining copending applications into a single application may avoid a provisional rejection; however, combining into a continuation-in-part has implications for 35 U.S.C. 120 benefit and entitlement. See MPEP § 718 and examples provided.

name: Separate sheet and placement
description: The abstract must be included in the application on its own sheet of paper proceeding the claim section and must be clearly labeled.
guidance: Follow the USPTO outline for patent abstracts; failure to put the abstract on a separate sheet can trigger USPTO objections or require correction.

name: Avoid claims and legal scope language
description: Abstracts do not need to mention claims or their scope. This isn't the legal part of the application, so leave that topic out.
guidance: Do not include claim language or attempt to define legal scope in the abstract — claims belong in the claims section and including them can be improper or misleading.

name: Avoid promotional/comparative language
description: Abstracts should avoid claims, legal jargon, comparisons, or marketing language.
guidance: Avoid words like “revolutionary” or “novel” and do not compare the invention to prior inventions or marketability — those belong elsewhere in the application or prosecution history.

name: Avoid overly technical or legal jargon; use plain language
description: Use plain language. Patent abstracts shouldn't use too much legal jargon. Leave the legal language for the claims section.
guidance: Write so that someone with a basic understanding of patents can grasp the invention; clear non‑expert language improves searchability and usefulness.

name: Avoid redundancy and repetition
description: Avoid redundancy. Do not repeat the title or claim language.
guidance: Do not restate the title or duplicate claim wording in the abstract; redundant text wastes words and may reduce clarity.

name: Written description requirement (35 U.S.C. 112(a) / pre-AIA 112, para. 1)
description: Each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure; the written description requirement ensures the inventor had possession of the claimed invention as of the filing date.
guidance: If the whole record (including amendments, arguments, and evidence) shows written description satisfied, do not repeat a rejection. If not satisfied, repeat the rejection, fully address rebuttal arguments, and analyze any affidavits. Suggest amendments supported by the original description when appropriate, but avoid adding new matter (see Rasmussen; Hyatt v. Dudas).

name: Changes to claim scope require original support
description: Failure of written description commonly arises when claims are changed after filing to broaden or narrow limitations, alter numerical ranges, or use non‑synonymous language relative to the original disclosure.
guidance: To comply with written description or to obtain benefit of earlier priority/filing date under 35 U.S.C. 119/120/365(c), each claim limitation must be supported in the originally filed disclosure. See MPEP § 2163.

name: Omission of a limitation (broadening by omission)
description: Omitting an element that was described as essential or critical in the original disclosure can raise written description problems because the inventor may not have possessed the broader invention.
guidance: Claims omitting matter disclosed as essential/critical violate the requirement (examples: Gentry Gallery, Tronzo, In re Wilder). Such omissions can also give rise to enablement or 112(b) problems. Compare cases where a shape or feature was not described as essential (In re Peters) and was acceptable.

name: Support for genus claims (addition of generic claim)
description: A claimed genus may be supported by disclosure of a representative number of species or other indicia that the patentee invented species sufficient to constitute the genus; a single species may suffice only in certain circumstances.
guidance: If there is substantial variation within a genus, describe a sufficient variety of species. Cases: AbbVie (functionally defined antibody genus not supported by one structurally similar species), Enzo (single species may suffice when disclosure indicates inventor invented species sufficient to constitute genus), Rasmussen, Herschler, Smythe, Curtis, Gosteli. Examiner must evaluate whether the disclosed species are representative of the claimed genus; inability of ordinary artisans to predict operability of other species weighs against support.

name: Narrowing or subgeneric claim additions
description: Introducing new elements or limitations (narrowing) not supported by the as‑filed disclosure violates the written description requirement.
guidance: A 'laundry list' of possible moieties does not constitute support for every species. Subgeneric terminology may or may not be acceptable; each case decided on facts and what is reasonably communicated to those skilled in the art (see Fujikawa, In re Ruschig, Rozbicki, Ex parte Ohshiro, In re Lukach, Ex parte Sorenson, In re Smith).

name: Treatment of numerical range limitations
description: New or altered numerical ranges must be supported by the original disclosure; the analysis considers which ranges a skilled artisan would consider inherently supported.
guidance: Example: Original ranges 25%-60% and examples 36%, 50% — a claim to 'at least 35%' lacked support (no upper limit), while 'between 35% and 60%' met the requirement (In re Wertheim). Consider whether disclosure indicates inventors considered the ratio/ range part of their invention (Purdue, Union Oil comparisons).

name: Prohibition on new matter (35 U.S.C. 132 and 251)
description: No amendment may introduce new matter into the disclosure of the invention; adding new subject matter to abstract, specification, or drawings raises a new matter objection under 35 U.S.C. 132 or 251 as appropriate.
guidance: If new subject matter is added to claims, reject claims under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (written description). If specification amended to add new matter that affects claim limitations, reject claims under 112(a). Examiner should require cancellation of new matter; consider added subject matter in making prior art rejections as applicable (In re Rasmussen).

name: Review and procedural handling of new matter objections/rejections
description: Objections to new matter in the specification (requirement to delete) are subject to supervisory petition (37 CFR 1.181); rejections of claims are appealable to the PTAB.
guidance: If both claims and specification contain new matter and examiner has both objection and rejection, the issue becomes appealable and should not be decided by petition.

name: Claimed subject matter present only in claims (not elsewhere in spec)
description: Claims filed as part of the original specification are part of the disclosure; if originally filed claims disclose matter not in remainder of specification, that claimed subject matter may be problematic for antecedent basis/support.
guidance: Applicant may need to amend the specification to include claimed subject matter; Form paragraph 7.44 may be used where originally claimed subject matter lacks proper antecedent basis (In re Benno; MPEP § 608.01(o)).

name: Enablement requirement (35 U.S.C. 112(a) / pre-AIA 112, first paragraph)
description: The specification must describe how to make and how to use the invention defined by the claims so that one skilled in the art can make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
guidance: The invention to be enabled is that defined by the claims. The purpose is to meaningfully communicate how to make and use the invention to the public. Not required to enable a perfected or commercially viable embodiment. Enablement is separate and distinct from written description; a limitation may lack descriptive support but still be enabled if one skilled could make and use the claimed invention with that limitation.

name: How to make the claimed invention (enablement: method of making)
description: Specification must disclose at least one method for making the claimed invention that reasonably correlates to the full scope of the claim; disclosure of other methods is not required.
guidance: Failure to disclose alternative methods does not render a claim invalid if at least one method is disclosed (In re Fisher, Spectra‑Physics v. Coherent). For unstable/transitory intermediates, need not teach how to make in stable/isolatable form (In re Breslow). If practicing the method requires particular apparatus or starting materials not readily available, the application must sufficiently disclose them (In re Ghiron, In re Howarth).

name: How to use the claimed invention (enablement: use / utility)
description: A statement of utility that connotes how to use the invention, plus recognition by the art that standard modes of administration are known, can satisfy the enablement/use requirement.
guidance: Dosage or method of use need not be specified if one skilled in the art could obtain such information without undue experimentation. The applicant need not prove the invention is completely safe. See In re Johnson, In re Hitchings, In re Brana; refer also to MPEP §§ 2107.01 and 2107.03.

name: Admissible grounds for revocation (grounds of opposition)
description: A European patent may only be opposed on the grounds that: (1) the subject-matter of one or more claims is not patentable (in particular not new or not inventive); (2) the patent does not disclose the invention sufficiently clearly and completely for it to be carried out by a person skilled in the art; (3) the subject-matter of the patent extends beyond the content of the application as filed.
guidance: Other grounds of opposition are not admissible.

name: Inadmissible grounds of opposition
description: Opposition may not be based on the grounds that the wording of the claims lacks clarity, or that the claimed invention was 'stolen' from the opponent or a third party by the patent proprietor.

name: Scope of examination by the Opposition Division
description: The Opposition Division considers legal questions and evaluates the facts on its own motion (ex officio) but is bound to the extent to which the patent has been opposed.
guidance: If the opposition attacks only certain independent claims, other independent claims of the granted patent are not to be examined.

name: Amendment rules for the patent proprietor
description: The patent proprietor may defend the opposed patent as granted or in a limited version; amendments may be chosen from the whole content of the original patent application's disclosure as long as the scope of protection is not extended beyond the granted patent's scope of protection; amendments need to be occasioned by a ground of opposition.
guidance: Opposition proceedings must not be used to reformulate claims or description for clarity/cosmetic reasons or to adapt to competitors' embodiments. Amendments must be supported by the original disclosure.

name: Substitute specification required when preliminary amendment modifies specification (other than benefit claim)
description: If a notice requires filing a substitute specification because a preliminary amendment adds or amends the specification (other than only adding/amending a benefit claim), the applicant must file the substitute specification or explain why it is not necessary to avoid abandonment.
guidance: If preliminary amendment only amends a benefit claim, applicant may reply explaining a substitute specification should not have been required. If the preliminary amendment contains other amendments to the specification (other than the claims), a substitute specification will be required; a reply without the substitute specification will be treated as incomplete with no new time period for reply. Requiring a substitute specification ensures compliance with redacted-publication limitations (35 U.S.C. 122(b)(2)(B)(v)) and allows the Office to publish any new matter included on the filing date.

name: Preliminary amendments to claims/abstract may be published without substitute specification
description: A preliminary amendment to the claims or abstract in compliance with 37 CFR 1.121(c) or 1.121(b)(2) that includes a complete claim listing or replacement abstract can be published as submitted without a substitute specification.
guidance: There is no need to file a preliminary amendment to the claims on filing; making the new claim set part of the originally filed specification may avoid application size fees because both the specification (including claims) and any preliminary amendment are used in counting pages per 37 CFR 1.16(s). Claims submitted on filing should be the set intended for examination and, if part of the specification on sequentially numbered pages (37 CFR 1.52(b)(5)), need no status identifiers or change markings.

name: Avoid filing preliminary amendments when possible (publication/timing concern)
description: Filing a preliminary amendment is not recommended because changes made by it may not be reflected in the patent application publication if technical preparations for publication have begun.
guidance: Technical preparations generally begin four months before publication. Applicants may avoid preliminary amendments by incorporating desired amendments into the specification text (including a new claim set) when filing, even in continuations/divisionals; a clean copy reflecting parent amendments and a copy of the prior oath/declaration may be submitted so long as no new matter is included. See 37 CFR 1.63(d)(1)(iii) and MPEP §201.06(c).

name: Undue interference denial: two-condition test
description: Entry of a preliminary amendment may be denied as unduly interfering only when (A) the examiner has devoted a significant amount of time preparing a first Office action before receipt of the amendment, and (B) entry of the amendment would require significant additional time in preparing the Office action.
guidance: If both conditions are met, the examiner must obtain SPE approval before denying entry. Factors satisfying the first condition include substantial time spent on prior art search or drafting. Examples of changes that may satisfy the second condition: amending claims, adding numerous new claims, changing scope of claims via spec amendments, raising new matter issues, including arguments, submitting affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.131/1.132, or including evidence traversing rejections from a parent application. This list is not exhaustive.

name: Replies to non-final Office actions must be fully responsive (37 CFR 1.111)
description: To be entitled to reconsideration or further examination, the applicant or patent owner must file a written reply that distinctly and specifically points out supposed errors and replies to every ground of objection and rejection in the prior Office action.
guidance: The reply must present arguments showing specific distinctions believed to render the claims patentable over applied references. A general allegation that claims define a patentable invention without specific explanation does not comply. If replying with amendments, the applicant must clearly point out the patentable novelty and show how amendments avoid the references or objections. See 37 CFR 1.111(b)–(c).

name: Limits on supplemental replies
description: A reply that is supplemental to a §1.111(b)-compliant reply will not be entered as a matter of right except as provided in §1.111(a)(2)(ii); the Office may enter a supplemental reply only if it is clearly limited to specific categories.
guidance: Permitted supplemental-reply topics include cancellation of claims, adoption of examiner suggestions, placement in condition for allowance, reply to a requirement made after the first reply, correction of informalities (e.g., typographical errors), or simplification of issues for appeal. A supplemental reply filed during a period when Office action is suspended under §1.103(a) or (c) will be entered. See 37 CFR 1.111(a)(2).

name: Complete reply: formal compliance or specific traversal
description: Where reply to a requirement is necessary for further consideration of claims or allowable subject matter has been indicated, a complete reply must either comply with formal requirements or specifically traverse each formal requirement not complied with.
guidance: Drawing and specification corrections, presentation of a new oath, etc., are generally formal matters; however, when merits require, such formal corrections may be insisted upon prior to indication of allowable subject matter. The line between formal and merit matters is not sharp.

name: Form paragraph 7.95 for bona fide but non-fully responsive amendments
description: Form paragraph 7.95 (and optionally 7.95.01) should be used where a bona fide reply to a non-final Office action is not fully responsive; it notifies applicant of omissions and gives a one-month (30-day) time period to supply omissions to avoid abandonment (extensions possible under 1.136(a)).
guidance: Examiner Note: This practice does not apply where there has been a deliberate omission or where the application is subject to a final Office action. Paragraph 7.95.01 specifically requests that applicant submit argument under the heading 'Remarks' explaining disagreements and discussing the references applied against the claims.

name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) general prior art rule
description: A person shall be entitled to a patent unless the claimed invention was patented, described in a printed publication, or in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public before the effective filing date of the claimed invention; or described in an issued patent or published application naming another inventor and effectively filed before the claimed invention's effective filing date (102(a)(1) and 102(a)(2)).
guidance: Office bears the initial burden of explaining why statutory/regulatory requirements are not met when rejecting a claim. The categories set forth in 102(a)(1) and (a)(2) are used to determine novelty/nonobviousness; (a)(1) references include patents, published applications, and printed publications and public uses/sales/availability; (a)(2) references are U.S. patent documents only.

name: Effective filing date of the claimed invention (35 U.S.C. 100(i))
description: The effective filing date is the earliest of: (1) the actual filing date of the patent/application containing the claimed invention; or (2) the filing date of the earliest application for which the patent/application is entitled to priority/benefit under 35 U.S.C. 119, 120, 121, 365, or 386.
guidance: Determine effective filing date claim-by-claim. Special situations: (A) continuation/divisional with proper 120/365/386(c) benefit — earliest date in line; (B) continuation-in-part — claims unsupported by parent have filing date of new app, those fully supported take parent's date; (C) provisional benefit under 119(e) — claims fully supported by provisional have provisional date; (D) foreign priority — claims supported by foreign priority doc get foreign filing date. Reissued patents are deemed to have the claim contained in the original patent for effective date purposes. The actual filing date of a national-stage 371 application is the international filing date; international design applications use International Bureau date per Hague rules.

name: Claim-by-claim determination of effective filing date
description: Effective filing date is determined on a claim-by-claim basis rather than an application-by-application basis.
guidance: Different claims in the same application may be entitled to different effective filing dates. However, whether to apply pre-AIA or AIA 102/103 is determined application-by-application (see MPEP guidance on applicability).

name: Described in a printed publication (102(a)(1)) — anticipation requirements
description: A patent, published patent application, or printed publication may be prior art if it 'describes' the claimed invention — meaning it discloses each and every element of the claimed invention, explicitly or inherently, arranged or combined as in the claim, and provides sufficient guidance to enable a person of ordinary skill in the art to make the invention without undue experimentation.
guidance: The 'described' standard under 102 is the same as pre-AIA. Unlike 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (written description/enablement for claims), 102 anticipation need only enable a single species or embodiment to anticipate a broader claim. A prior art document need not disclose 'how to use' the invention for anticipation. A document inadequate for anticipation may still be relied upon under 35 U.S.C. 103 for obviousness for what it reasonably would have made known to a skilled artisan.

name: Public use (102(a)(1))
description: Public use rejections may be based on uses anywhere in the world that made the invention available to the public before the effective filing date.
guidance: No geographic limitation (contrast pre-AIA 'in this country'). Pre-AIA public use bars required the invention to be ready for patenting and either accessible to the public or commercially exploited; those concepts remain relevant. Uses by the inventor or those who obtained the invention from the inventor may be subject to 102(b)(1) grace period exceptions. When aware of a potential public use, examiners should require applicant info showing it did not make the claimed process accessible to the public.

name: Anticipation vs obviousness application of prior art
description: A prior art disclosure must satisfy the stricter 'each and every element arranged as in the claim' and enablement for anticipation under 102, but may still be used in an obviousness rejection under 103 for what it would have reasonably taught a skilled artisan even if not anticipatory.
guidance: An examiner may cite a disclosure under 103 for all that it would reasonably have made known; lack of anticipatory detail does not preclude reliance in obviousness analyses.

name: Determining whether to apply 102(a)(1) or 102(a)(2)
description: Choose the appropriate 102(a) subsection based on the nature of the reference: (a)(1) covers patents, published applications, printed publications, public uses, on sale, otherwise available; (a)(2) covers U.S. patent documents and related published applications where the patent/application names another inventor and was effectively filed earlier.
guidance: Consider the type of reference (U.S. patent/published application vs non-patent literature or public activity), effective filing dates for both the reference and the claimed invention, and whether the reference names another inventor. See MPEP §2154 and related sections for details on U.S. patent documents as references.

name: Overcoming a 102(a)(1) or 102(a)(2) rejection
description: Procedures and substantive grounds an applicant may use to overcome a prior art rejection under AIA 102(a)(1) or (a)(2).
guidance: Possibilities include showing that the reference does not disclose each and every claim element arranged as claimed, that the prior art is not enabling, asserting applicable 102(b) exceptions with supportive declarations/affidavits under 37 CFR 1.130, demonstrating claim support in earlier priority documents so the effective filing date predates the reference, or showing common ownership/assignment in 102(b)(2)(C). See MPEP §2152.06 and §2155 for detailed affidavit/declaration guidance.

name: Common ownership/obligation of assignment (102(b)(2)(C))
description: A disclosure shall not be prior art under 102(a)(2) if the subject matter disclosed and the claimed invention were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person by the effective filing date.
guidance: This prong is aimed at U.S. patent document references; examiners should assess ownership/assignment relationships and dates to determine whether the common ownership exception applies.

name: Applicability dates and determining FITF coverage
description: Guidance on which applications are subject to First-Inventor-to-File (FITF) AIA provisions versus pre-AIA rules, and how to determine which set of rules (pre-AIA or AIA) applies to particular claimed inventions.
guidance: See MPEP §2159 and related subsections for detailed rules about applications filed before/after March 16, 2013, transition applications, and how to treat claimed inventions with effective filing dates on either side of the cutoff.

name: Patent classification: multi-label hierarchical formulation
description: Patent classification is a multi-label classification where the classification scheme is hierarchical (IPC/CPC) and a single patent can be assigned multiple labels across levels (section, class, subclass, group, subgroup). The paper gives the formal formulation: patents (xi, yi) with yi a binary multi-label vector over classes C.
guidance: Methods must capture dependencies between broad and fine-grained categories and handle hierarchical structure. Inputs may come from different patent sections (title, abstract, description, claims); due to long full-text documents, models should identify the most relevant sections for classification. See Appendix A.3.1 for formal notation.

name: Patent quality analysis indicators (features used to estimate value/quality)
description: Commonly used indicators for patent quality/value include forward and backward citations, number of claims, grant lag, patent family size, remaining lifetime (maintenance period), investor reaction, and various composite patent indices (e.g., OECD indices).
guidance: Because the weight of each indicator is ambiguous, studies apply regression/classification models (linear, ridge, RF, XGBoost, MLP, CNN, LSTM). Explicitly list indicators used and justify selection; consider feature engineering from text, metadata, citations and metadata integration (knowledge graphs).

name: Patent generation task formulation
description: Patent generation is formulated as producing one part of a patent yi from input xi (e.g., generate abstract/first claim from title/description), modeled as yi = G(xi; θ) where G is the generation model.
guidance: Specify which patent parts are input vs. output (claim-to-specification, claim+drawing-to-specification, etc.), training data sources, and any multimodal inputs (drawings). Provide exact generation prompts/instruction formats used for LLMs.

name: Desired qualities of generated patent text (factual, legal, novelty, clarity)
description: Generated patent text should be factually accurate, legally correct/robust, novel (non-infringing), clear, and include desirable drafting features (e.g., appropriate claim length and limiting terms). The survey states PLMs/LLMs can hallucinate and produce repetitive or legally weak text.
guidance: Automatic n-gram metrics (BLEU, ROUGE) are insufficient. Use retrieval-based evaluation to check consistency with prior art, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for grounding, RLHF to align outputs with expert preferences, and involve patent attorneys/examiners for human evaluation on novelty, clarity, and legal robustness. When using RLHF, incorporate reward components for claim length and inclusion of limiting terms as appropriate.

name: Definiteness judged in context of the specification
description: A claim phrase is not necessarily indefinite if, when viewed in the context of the specification and figures, a person skilled in the art would understand the claim (e.g., clause 'welded to said wire legs at the separation' was held definite when read in context; reciting 'at a separation' would also cure indefiniteness).
guidance: Evaluate claim terms in light of the intrinsic record (specification and figures). Antecedent basis or additional wording may not be required if the specification makes the meaning clear to one of ordinary skill. If ambiguity remains, consider whether a simple amendment (e.g., changing 'the separation' to 'a separation') would resolve indefiniteness.

name: Terms of art may be definite if intrinsic evidence supports meaning
description: A specialized term (term of art) that is a well-known device or concept (e.g., 'POL regulator') is not necessarily indefinite if the intrinsic evidence supports the district court's construction and one of ordinary skill in the art would understand where and how to use it.
guidance: When a claim term is a known device or term of art, rely on the intrinsic record to confirm that PHOSITA would understand its location/function; if so, do not treat it as indefinite under § 112, ¶ 2.

name: Breadth alone does not make a claim indefinite
description: A broad claim reciting many possible combinations (e.g., a formula yielding over 5,000 combinations) is not necessarily insolubly ambiguous if it sufficiently notifies the public of the scope of the claims.
guidance: Do not equate claim breadth with indefiniteness. Analyze whether the claim language gives the public notice of scope such that a PHOSITA can determine whether a given embodiment falls within the claim.

name: Claims must correspond to the specification (consistency requirement)
description: No claim may be read apart from and independent of the supporting disclosure on which it is based; claim language that is inherently inconsistent with the specification (e.g., defining an 'opaque finish' in the spec but claiming a process that produces glaze-like finish) renders the claim indefinite under § 112, ¶ 2.
guidance: Check claims for internal inconsistency with the specification, definitions, or examples. If the claim language conflicts with the specification's disclosed meaning, sustain an indefiniteness rejection.

name: Non-'means' terms can invoke § 112, sixth paragraph (general evaluation)
description: The analysis of whether a limitation invokes § 112, ¶ 6 includes evaluation of limitations using other non-structural terms (e.g., 'mechanism,' 'member,' 'element,' 'device,' 'assembly') in context of the claim and specification to determine whether the term recites sufficient structure or is purely functional.
guidance: Do not rely solely on the absence of 'means for' language. Examine the term, its modifiers, surrounding claim language, and the specification to determine whether the term conveys sufficiently definite structure or instead invokes means-plus-function treatment.

name: Structural modifier can prevent means-plus-function treatment ('detent mechanism' example)
description: A non-structural term (e.g., 'mechanism') when modified by a word that has structural meaning (e.g., 'detent mechanism') may be indicative of a structural recitation and avoid § 112, ¶ 6.
guidance: If the modifier is itself a recognized structural term and the claim further defines structure, treat the limitation as structural rather than a means-plus-function limitation.

name: Generic 'mechanism' without structural context likely invokes § 112, ¶ 6
description: The use of a generic term like 'mechanism' followed by functional language (e.g., 'mechanism for moving') and lacking structural modifiers or context typically invokes § 112, ¶ 6 because it connotes little structure.
guidance: Absent structural modifiers or supporting structure in the claim/specification, treat generic 'mechanism' recitations as means-plus-function and require corresponding structure disclosure.

name: Generic terms 'member'/'element' invoke § 112, ¶ 6 unless claim recites structure
description: Terms like 'member' or 'element' are generic; whether they invoke § 112, ¶ 6 depends on whether the term is given structural context in the claim (e.g., claimed ends, connections, or other structure) or remains only functionally described.
guidance: If the claim recites specific structural features (e.g., ends, attachments, connections) that impart structure to 'member'/'element', then § 112, ¶ 6 is not invoked. If the term is only functionally described with no structural details, treat it as means-plus-function.

name: If § 112, ¶ 6 is invoked, the specification must disclose corresponding structure/material/acts
description: Once a limitation is determined to be a means-plus-function limitation under § 112, ¶ 6, the examiner must review the written description from the perspective of one of ordinary skill in the art to determine whether the corresponding structure, material, or acts that perform the claimed function are disclosed.
guidance: Perform a detailed search of the specification for structures, algorithms, materials, or acts explicitly linked to the claimed function. If no corresponding disclosure exists, an indefiniteness rejection under § 112, ¶ 2 is appropriate.

name: Bare statements that 'known techniques' may be used are insufficient as corresponding structure
description: A disclosure that the claimed function 'may be controlled automatically by known differential pressure, valving and control equipment' or a figure showing a box labelled 'Control' does not disclose corresponding structure sufficient to avoid indefiniteness.
guidance: Do not accept generic references to 'known' equipment or unlabeled boxes as disclosure of corresponding structure. The specification must identify or describe the structure that performs the function.

name: For computer-implemented functions, disclosure of a general-purpose processor plus 'appropriate programming' is insufficient
