description: Stating that a function can be performed by a 'standard microprocessor' with 'appropriate programming' does not satisfy § 112, ¶ 6; the patentee must disclose an algorithm, specific software, or a special-purpose computer transforming the general-purpose processor.
guidance: Require disclosure of the algorithm or sufficient structure (e.g., flowcharts, pseudo-code, specific module descriptions) that links the claimed function to corresponding structure. Mere invocation that a programmer could implement the function is not enough.

name: Concrete disclosure of modules/components can satisfy corresponding structure requirement
description: When the specification discloses concrete structures or modules (e.g., an 'Access control manager' that 'creates an access control list (ACM)') and explains how they operate, that disclosure can satisfy the corresponding structure requirement for means-plus-function limitations.
guidance: Look for explicit descriptions of system components, data structures, or processes in the specification that perform the claimed functions; such concrete disclosures can avoid indefiniteness under § 112, ¶ 2 even if the claim uses functional language.

name: Patent valuation (real property metaphor)
description: Patent valuation can be usefully understood by analogy to real property: prior art is like public lands or lands claimed by others; 'location, location, location' applies — claims that map onto valuable inventions are worth more.
guidance: A patent's worth depends on where its claims sit relative to valuable inventions (location) and on the quality of the patent's construction (how well it was drafted). Legal remedies are analogous to remedies for encroachment in real estate. Full valuation discussion is out of scope but the metaphor helps frame strategic choices.

name: Design-around techniques
description: Designing around patents involves determining the scope of claim coverage by detailed review of the patent, its cited prior art, and its prosecution history to identify limiting admissions or claim constructions.
guidance: Apply jurisdiction-specific claim construction rules; consider ordinary/plain meaning, specification context, prosecution history, and means-plus-function consequences. Prepare detailed opinions when needed. Close analysis can reveal admissions that limit claim scope; the drafter should assist with interpretation but be cautious about creating potentially limiting client communications.

name: Claim interpretation considerations (including means-plus-function)
description: Claim construction rules vary by jurisdiction; initial interpretation often gives plain/ordinary meaning but may be informed by the specification and prosecution history; means-plus-function language requires special consideration.
guidance: When performing design-around or infringement analyses, determine precise meanings of claim terms per applicable judicial and patent-office rules. Consider how courts in the jurisdiction treat prosecution history, specification reliance, and functional claim language.

name: Photograph usage and limits
description: Photographs (including photocopies and computer renderings treated as photographs) may be used where they are the only practicable medium for illustrating the claimed subject matter (37 CFR 1.84(b)).
guidance: Photographs are accepted in utility and design applications in limited circumstances; if photographs are not of sufficient quality so that all details are reproducible, examiners should object and no application will be issued until acceptable photographs are submitted. Photographs submitted in lieu of ink drawings in design patent applications must be limited to the design claimed and must not disclose environmental structure (37 CFR 1.152; MPEP 1503.02(V)).

name: Shading conventions and limitations
description: Shading is encouraged if it aids understanding; spaced thin oblique lines preferred; shade lines must be thin, few, and contrast with the rest of the drawing; solid black shading is not permitted except to represent the color black (37 CFR 1.84(m)).
guidance: Use oblique line shading for contours and to show transparent/translucent/highly polished surfaces. Avoid solid black areas except to denote black color or color contrast. Improper shading may lead to objections or limitations in claim scope.

name: Design drawings must comply with §1.84 and be complete
description: The design must be represented by a drawing that complies with the requirements of §1.84 and must contain a sufficient number of views to constitute a complete disclosure of the appearance of the design (37 CFR 1.152 / MPEP 1503.02).
guidance: Because the drawing/photograph is the entire visual disclosure of the claim, it must be clear and complete; nothing regarding the design should be left to conjecture. Ensure all required views are present or that statements in the specification explicitly allow omission (e.g., 'other side is identical').

name: Contrast in materials by shading/stippling to avoid color limitation
description: Contrast in materials may be shown by using line shading in one area and stippling in another so the claim covers contrasting surfaces without being limited to colors (MPEP 1503.02(II)).
guidance: Use different shading techniques (lines vs stippling) to indicate material/texture contrast; this helps keep the claim from being limited to specific colors or materials unless color is intended to be claimed.

name: Color drawings and ‘lined for color’ statement
description: Color drawings are permitted in design applications when filed in accordance with 37 CFR 1.84(a)(2); color may also be shown by lining the surfaces for color per MPEP 608.02 and, if so, the specification should state: 'The drawings are lined for color.' (MPEP 1503.02(V)).
guidance: If color drawings or color photographs are filed with the original application, color is considered an integral part of the disclosed and claimed design. Omission of color later may be permitted only if the application shows possession of the underlying configuration without color at filing (see In re Daniels). Lining entire surfaces to show color may interfere with surface shading used to define contours and can create 35 U.S.C. 112(a) issues.

name: Effect of filing color on claim scope and later amendments
description: If color photographs or color drawings are filed with the original application, color will be considered an integral part of the disclosed and claimed design; omission of color later is permitted only under limited circumstances (MPEP 1503.02(V)).
guidance: Determine whether the original disclosure demonstrates possession of the design without color. If not, treating color as integral can limit the claim and prevent later omission of color without risking new matter or lack of possession.

name: Inconsistencies among views: objection vs rejection
description: When inconsistencies are found among the views, the examiner should object to the drawings and request that the views be made consistent. When inconsistencies are of such magnitude that the overall appearance of the design is unclear, the claim should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b) (MPEP 1503.02).
guidance: Assess severity: minor drafting mistakes or inconsequential inconsistencies warrant an objection and request for corrected drawings; inconsistencies that preclude an overall understanding of the design require rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112. Use examples (toy construction vehicle, building model) to gauge threshold between objection and rejection.

name: Multiple parts in a single article — bracket and broken-line rules
description: If separate parts are shown in a single view, the parts must be shown embraced by a bracket '}'. If the claim involves multiple parts of a single article where the article is shown in broken lines and various parts are shown in solid lines, no bracket is needed (MPEP 1504.01(b)).
guidance: Use the bracket to indicate separate parts clearly when depicted together. When depicting the overall article in broken lines with solid-line parts, the bracket is unnecessary; ensure the representation matches claim drafting strategy for claiming multiple parts.

name: Textual features extracted from claim section
description: Construct a document-term matrix from the claim section using unigram, bigram, and trigram features with tf-idf weighting; select the top textual features by information gain.
guidance: Use tf-idf so common words that appear across many documents are down-weighted. Generate a large matrix then select 30 textual features with highest information gain for modeling. Report the top textual features (e.g., 'device', 'system', 'network' for Wireless Network).

name: Account for case complexity and assignment bias (lower stats ≠ poor performance)
description: Lower allowance rates or longer times may reflect attorneys taking harder cases, contested claims, or difficult examiners rather than poor skill.
guidance: Why it matters: Use qualitative follow-up (type of technology, claim scope, examiner difficulty) when interpreting lower-performance metrics. Don’t automatically penalize attorneys working on high-complexity matters.

name: Claims must be directed to an improvement in computer/technology functioning to be eligible
description: Claims that are 'directed to an improvement in computer technology' (or solve a technological problem in computers/networks) can be eligible, whereas claims that simply apply abstract ideas using computers are not.
guidance: The chart contrasts eligible and ineligible decisions, noting that claims unlike those in DDR Holdings, Enfish, or McRO — i.e., claims not 'rooted in computer technology' and not showing an 'improvement in computer or network functionality' — are ineligible. Assess whether the claim recites a technical solution or an improvement in how computers operate, not merely an application of a business/abstract idea.

name: Novelty/nonobviousness under §§102/103 are not substitutes for §101 eligibility
description: It 'is not enough for subject-matter eligibility that claimed techniques be novel and nonobvious in light of prior art' — an advance that lies entirely in the realm of abstract ideas remains ineligible.
guidance: SAP Am. v. InvestPic and other summaries emphasize that passing §§102/103 does not cure §101 problems. When advising clients, separate the §101 analysis from novelty/nonobviousness arguments; technical improvements matter for §101, not merely field-specific advances.

name: Preemption concerns inform eligibility analysis
description: Courts treat preemption as related to §101 — claims that risk preempting use of an abstract idea across its practical applications support ineligibility findings ('preemption concerns are fully addressed and made moot' when claims are ineligible).
guidance: Use preemption as an indicator: broad claims that would monopolize an abstract idea (e.g., all ways of conducting a basic economic practice) are especially likely to be held ineligible. However, courts analyze substance (directed-to/inventive-concept) rather than preemption alone.

name: Factual disputes about conventionality can affect the §101 inquiry
description: Following Berkheimer, whether claim elements are 'well-understood, routine, and conventional' can be a factual question that may preclude resolution at the pleading or summary-judgment stage.
guidance: The chart records cases remanded or reversed where factual evidence (e.g., specification disclosures, extrinsic evidence) raised disputes about conventionality. Note, however, that some judges (e.g., Judge Mayer) dissent and dispute that §101 should involve fact questions. Treat conventionality evidence carefully: it can create triable issues.

name: Claims that merely state resulting systems/functionality without specific programming/design are insufficient
description: Claims that 'merely claim the resulting systems' or 'functionality' and fail to 'claim a particular way of programming or designing the software' are directed to an abstract idea and lack inventive concept.
guidance: Assess whether claims specify how the software/hardware achieves the result (specific architecture, unconventional steps) rather than simply claiming the end result or function. Many cases reject claims that restate functions at a high level of generality.

name: Inclusion of conventional hardware or identifiers does not render claim eligible
description: Adding known hardware components or identifiers (e.g., tags, basic hardware identifiers) without more does not create an inventive concept; courts have held there was 'no indication that their inclusion produce[d] a result that overrides the routine and conventional use' of the hardware.
guidance: Examine whether hardware elements are novel or used in a non-conventional way producing a technical improvement. Mere presence of generic hardware (interfaces, servers, databases, cellular phone features) is usually insufficient.

name: Claims must recite how data is transformed to show a technical contribution
description: Claims that gather and output data but 'did not recite how data was transformed in any way' were held ineligible because they fail to show a technical manner of transformation.
guidance: When claims process data, identify concrete transformational steps (e.g., changing data representation in a way that improves technology) rather than mere collection/printing/displaying. Lack of transformation detail often supports finding of abstractness.

name: Claims directed to fundamental economic practices are abstract
description: Claims involving fundamental economic concepts — e.g., loan-application clearinghouses, financial instruments, auction payment mechanics, conditioning access on payment, pricing/advertising strategies — are routinely characterized as abstract ideas.
guidance: Financial/business-method claims must show a technical solution or improvement beyond the mere economic practice implemented on conventional systems to survive §101 scrutiny.

name: Patent eligibility can be decided at Rule 12(b)(6) or Rule 12(c) when facts undisputedly show ineligibility
description: Courts have repeatedly stated that, 'like other legal questions based on underlying facts,' subject-matter eligibility 'may be, and frequently has been, resolved on a Rule 12(b)(6) or (c) motion where the undisputed facts ... require a holding of ineligibility under the substantive standards of law.'
guidance: If the claim language and acceptably pleaded facts establish that the claims are directed to an abstract idea and lack inventive concept (and no factual disputes over conventionality exist), dismissal on the pleadings or summary judgment is appropriate. If factual disputes exist (see Berkheimer), proceed to fact development.

name: Claims that provide only high-level steps of conventional processes are ineligible
description: Claims reciting 'conventional steps, specified at a high level of generality' are inadequate to supply an inventive concept.
guidance: Look for specificity in how steps are performed and whether their ordering or combination produces a non-conventional technical result; blanket recitation of 'interfaces,' 'networks,' 'databases,' or 'generic steps' is usually insufficient.

name: Presumption that distinct nucleotide sequences are independent inventions
description: Polynucleotide molecules defined by their nucleic acid ("nucleotide sequences") that encode different proteins are structurally distinct chemical compounds. These sequences are thus deemed to normally constitute independent and distinct inventions within the meaning of 35 U.S.C. 121. Absent evidence to the contrary, each such nucleotide sequence is presumed to represent an independent and distinct invention, subject to a restriction requirement pursuant to 35 U.S.C. 121 and 37 CFR 1.141 et seq.
guidance: Director has partially waived certain restriction rules to permit a reasonable number of nucleotide sequences to be claimed in one application (see Examination of Patent Applications Containing Nucleotide Sequences).

name: Definition and policy purpose of double patenting doctrine
description: The doctrine of double patenting seeks to prevent the unjustified extension of patent exclusivity beyond the term of a patent. Double patenting results when the right to exclude granted by a first patent is unjustly extended by the grant of a later issued patent or patents.
guidance: Focus of double patenting analysis is on the claims; requires at least one common inventor and/or common ownership or applicability of joint research agreement exclusions under 35 U.S.C.103(c)(2) and (3).

name: Statutory double patenting (35 U.S.C. 101) test
description: Statutory double patenting asks: is the same invention being claimed twice? 'Same invention' means identical subject matter. A reliable test is whether a claim in the application could be literally infringed without literally infringing a corresponding claim in the patent; if such an embodiment exists, statutory double patenting does not exist.
guidance: Claims may be worded differently yet be identical in scope (e.g., '36 inches' vs '3 feet'). Statutory double patenting cannot be overcome by a terminal disclaimer; it can be overcome by canceling or amending conflicting claims so they are no longer coextensive in scope.

name: Double patenting in reexamination proceedings
description: A double patenting issue may raise a substantial new question of patentability of a claim of a patent, and thus be addressed in a reexamination proceeding. Double patenting may exist where the reference patent/application and the patent under reexamination are filed by inventive entities with at least one common inventor and/or common owner/assignee.
guidance: If the patent under reexamination was granted on or after Dec 10, 2004, double patenting may also exist where inventions resulted from activities undertaken within scope of a joint research agreement pursuant to 35 U.S.C. 103(c)(2) and (3), provided evidence is of record. A DP rejection may NOT be made on this basis if the patent under reexamination issued before Dec 10, 2004. The prior art exclusion under 35 U.S.C. 103(c) cannot be used to overcome an obviousness-type double patenting rejection. See MPEP §2258 and §706.02(l).

name: Examiners reporting improved decision-making
description: 45% of patent examiners believe that AI tools have improved their decision-making capabilities.
guidance: AI provides comprehensive analyses of prior art, claims, and documents, supporting more informed human judgments.

name: Percentage of patent attorneys using AI for drafting
description: 80% of patent attorneys use AI tools to assist with patent drafting and prosecution.
guidance: AI helps draft clearer, more precise claims and navigate prosecution — broad attorney adoption underscores practical utility.

name: Affirmative Recitation Requirement for Treatment/Prophylaxis
description: To qualify as a 'treatment' or 'prophylaxis' limitation, the claim limitation must affirmatively recite an action that effects a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition.
guidance: Examples of affirmative limitations: 'administering amazonic acid to a patient', 'administering a course of plasmapheresis to a patient'. Non-qualifying language includes mere intended use, field-of-use, or prescriptions that do not require actual use (e.g., 'prescribing a topical steroid to a patient' is not positive because it does not require that the steroid actually be used; 'pharmaceutical composition' or 'feed dispenser operable to dispense' are not affirmative).

name: More-Than-Nominal Relationship to the Judicial Exception
description: The treatment or prophylaxis limitation must have more than a nominal or insignificant relationship to the recited judicial exception(s).
guidance: Evaluate whether the claimed treatment meaningfully addresses the recited law/correlation (e.g., treating blood glucose >250 mg/dl with insulin meaningfully relates to the correlation and integrates the law of nature; treating with aspirin, not known to treat ketoacidosis, has at best a nominal connection and does not integrate the law of nature). See guidance to consider insignificant extra-solution activity and field-of-use considerations (MPEP § 2106.05(g),(h)).

name: Search for an Inventive Concept (Step 2B) — Overarching Principle
description: An 'inventive concept' is an element or combination of elements recited in the claim in addition to the judicial exception that is sufficient to ensure the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception itself; it cannot be furnished by the judicial exception alone.
guidance: Evaluate additional elements to determine whether they amount to an inventive concept by considering them both individually and in combination. The analysis is consistent with the rule that claims must be considered as a whole; combinations of conventional elements can, in some cases, amount to significantly more.

name: Consider Elements Individually And In Combination
description: When evaluating additional elements for an inventive concept, consider each additional element on its own and also consider the elements as an ordered combination.
guidance: Even if an element does not amount to significantly more by itself, it can when combined with other elements (e.g., BASCOM: location of filtering tool remote from end-users with customizable features produced an inventive concept when considered in combination). Courts identify additional elements, assess conventionality, and then assess whether the claimed combination is non-conventional and non-generic.

name: Improvement To The Functioning Of A Computer Can Be 'Significantly More'
description: Limitations that improve the functioning of a computer (e.g., modification of conventional internet hyperlink protocol to dynamically produce a dual-source hybrid webpage) can qualify as an inventive concept.
guidance: See DDR Holdings example; improvements to computer operation or behavior may establish significantly more when the claim is not merely applying an abstract idea on a generic computer.

name: Effecting A Transformation Or Reduction Of A Particular Article
description: Limitations that effect a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing can qualify as significantly more.
guidance: Example: transforming raw uncured synthetic rubber into precision-molded products (Diehr). The claimed process must effect a concrete transformation, not merely apply an abstract idea.

name: Adding Specific Limitations Or Unconventional Steps That Confine The Claim
description: Adding a specific limitation other than well-understood, routine, conventional activity in the field, or adding unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application, can supply an inventive concept.
guidance: Example: non-conventional and non-generic arrangement of computer components for filtering Internet content (BASCOM). The presence of unconventional arrangement or confinement to a useful application supports eligibility.

name: Appending Well-Understood, Routine, Conventional Activities Is Insufficient
description: Merely appending well-understood, routine, conventional activities previously known to the industry, specified at a high level of generality, will not make a claim significantly more.
guidance: Generic computer functions performed by a generic computer are inadequate. The inventive-concept inquiry looks for more than recognition that each claim element was known in the art.

name: Physicality/Tangibility Is Not A Determinative Factor
description: Mere physicality or tangibility of an additional element is not a relevant consideration in Step 2B; a computer being physical does not by itself supply an inventive concept.
guidance: The presence of a tangible element does not guarantee eligibility (Alice). Conversely, non-physical or intangible additional elements do not necessarily doom eligibility (Enfish, McRO). Focus on what the claim adds conceptually and functionally, not mere physical presence.

name: How Courts Conduct The Significantly-More Analysis (Alice and BASCOM Examples)
description: Courts identify additional elements, consider those elements individually (including conventionality), and then consider the elements as an ordered combination to determine whether the claim amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception.
guidance: Alice: Court identified additional computer/hardware elements, found each to be generic and routine, then concluded the ordered combination added nothing (claims ineligible). BASCOM: district court identified elements as generic, but Federal Circuit held the combination (installation location + customizable features) could be non-conventional and thus supply an inventive concept. Consult the specification to determine whether elements are well-understood, routine, conventional.

name: Patent quality definition
description: Actions which increase the likelihood that claims granted by the USPTO are legally valid plus actions which reduce the likelihood that valid claims are not improperly rejected by the USPTO. Divided by timeliness (actions which increase process efficiency and reduce overall application pendency).
guidance: Patent quality does not include a legal determination of eligibility of any particular technology, economic contribution of an invention, or patent procurement cost; applies to all statutory eligible inventions equally. Cost impacts of proposed procedural changes must be factored into fee/implementation decisions.

name: Applicant responsibility to improve quality
description: Applicants have responsibility to improve patent quality by filing well-prepared specifications and claims; the PTO cannot produce high-quality patents from poor-quality applications.
guidance: Incentivize applicant pre-filing search and clarity; consider mechanisms (preliminary searches, advisory actions) to improve application quality before full examination.

name: Search: identify closest prior art promptly and comprehensively
description: Quality requires that the closest prior art relevant to determining patentability, clarity and scope of claims is identified and properly evaluated as soon as possible; the search must be comprehensive and done preferably only once per application.
guidance: Examiners must have ample time and credit for the search; time studies by technology area may be needed to determine adequate search time.

name: Examiner responsibility to identify, apply and explain prior art findings
description: Examiners have primary responsibility to identify, apply and clearly explain either why a claim is valid/allowable or should be rejected in view of the closest prior art.
guidance: Office Actions should clearly articulate pertinence of cited portions and provide guidance for applicants where possible.

name: 35 U.S.C. §112 review to aid search
description: Clarity of claimed invention and adequacy of written description and antecedent basis aid the search; pre-search review for §112 compliance (original or provisional) could identify undefined/inconsistent terms and deficiencies.
guidance: An advisory action on provisional could notify applicant of deficiencies within ~8 months to permit corrective action in the original application.

name: Third-party search assistance and specialist search examiners
description: Consider third-party assistance (e.g., Peer-to-Patent/wiki), incentive mechanisms/bounties for prior art submission, use of search-specialist examiners with advanced search/software expertise, and partnerships with private search firms.
guidance: Peer-to-patent feedback may help guide examiners but scaling is uncertain; third-party submissions could be allowed with strict format (identify claim elements and specific wording/figures relevant) and limited/no arguments to avoid examiner burden.

name: Application quality: defining terms and format
description: Clear definition of terms in the specification and consistent application formatting improve examination quality and search/classification.
guidance: Encourage applicants to define terms, use consistent terminology and follow standardized formats; consider guidance on standard algorithms and support for claim language.

name: Tools to assist examiners and improve data collection
description: Develop and evaluate tools (commercial and in-house) to assist examiners: concept/semantic search algorithms, context-aware navigation linking claims/spec/figures, URL naming schemes, harmonized filing forms, checklists, and text-to-speech functionality.
guidance: Tools can reduce examiner burden and improve understanding of scope; modify office action forms and PAIR portals to enhance structured data collection (e.g., standardized checkboxes).

name: Sample survey evaluation questions (MPEP/legal compliance focus)
description: Survey questions should probe whether examiners consistently follow required legal frameworks and MPEP guidance for rejections under 35 U.S.C. §§ 101, 102, 103, and 112 (e.g., follow flowcharts, consider all claim language, show technical reasoning for inherency, follow rationales for obviousness, make enablement/showings).
guidance: Use such targeted questions to evaluate corps-wide consistency without focusing on individual examiners when respondents may be reluctant to identify specific examiners.

name: Patent Quality Index (PQI) and correlates of validity
description: Develop metrics (e.g., Patent Quality Index) that evaluate characteristics associated with validity; examples include closeness of claims to specification and the quality of applicant/examiner prior art identification and use.
guidance: Use PQI to identify problematic aspects of the process, automate evaluation, identify critical steps in examination, and guide targeted improvements.

name: Governing Standard — 'Substantial New Question of Patentability' (SNQ)
description: The presence or absence of 'a substantial new question of patentability' determines whether or not reexamination is ordered. The meaning and scope is developed case-by-case using case law.
guidance: If prior art patents and printed publications raise an SNQ of at least one claim, then an SNQ is present unless the same question has already been decided in a final federal court holding, decided in an earlier concluded Office examination or review, or raised in a pending reexamination or supplemental examination. Issues involving 35 U.S.C. 325(d) must be brought to appropriate SPRS or CRU Director attention.

name: Second or Subsequent Request Must Stand on Own Merits
description: A second or subsequent request should be determined on its own merits without reference to the pending reexamination. The second/subsequent requester must independently provide an SNQ which is different from that raised in the pending reexamination for the claims in effect at the time of the determination.
guidance: Decision on second/subsequent request is based on the claims in effect at the time of determination (37 CFR 1.515(a)). If a different SNQ is not provided for the claims in effect, the second/subsequent request must be denied because statute authorizes reexamination only based on an SNQ affecting any claim of the patent.

name: Old Art Can Be Sole Basis for SNQ (post-Nov 2, 2002)
description: Reliance on previously cited/considered art ('old art') does not necessarily preclude existence of an SNQ for reexamination ordered on or after November 2, 2002; determinations are fact-specific.
guidance: Old art may constitute sole basis for SNQ where it is presented/viewed in a new light or different way, e.g., in view of a material new argument or interpretation (including claim scope). Use form paragraph 22.01.01 when SNQ is based solely on old art and explain how the old art is applied and why it raises an SNQ. This form paragraph is used only the first time that 'already cited/considered' art is applied.

name: Effect of Final Federal Court Decision That Patent Not Proven Invalid
description: A final court decision that a claim has not been proven invalid in view of the same or different prior art does not necessarily mean that no SNQ is present because Office and courts use different standards of proof.
guidance: Office may accord deference to district court factual findings, but the SNQ determination is made independently of the court's decision. See In re Swanson and In re Baxter for precedent.

name: Claims Considered — Claims in Effect at Time of Determination
description: The claims of the patent in effect at the time of the determination will be the basis for deciding whether an SNQ is present. 37 CFR 1.515(a).
guidance: Office determination will generally be limited to review of the claim(s) for which reexamination was requested. Requester must set forth the pertinency and manner of applying cited prior art to every claim requested (37 CFR 1.510(b)); failure to do so generally precludes reexamination of that claim. The Office may, at its discretion, reexamine other claims or initiate reexamination on non-requested claims (35 U.S.C. 303(a)). Examiner should discuss all patent claims requested in the decision letter and limit discussion to whether an SNQ has been raised.

name: Decision Content When Granting Reexamination
description: If a request is granted, the examiner’s decision will: (A) identify all claims and issues, (B) identify the patents and/or printed publications relied on, and (C) provide a brief statement of the rationale supporting each new question.
guidance: Examiner must identify at least one SNQ and explain how the prior art raises such. Examiner should indicate, insofar as possible, initial positions on all issues identified so patent owner and requester can comment. Prior art relied on should be listed on PTO form (e.g., PTO-892) if not already listed; supply copies only where not previously supplied to patent owner and requester.

name: Specific Points the Decision Should Address (A–F)
description: As to each SNQ identified, the decision should point out: (A) the prior art which adds some new teaching as to at least one claim; (B) what that new teaching is; (C) the claims that the new teaching is directed to; (D) that the new teaching was not previously considered/addressed or raised in pending proceedings; (E) that the new teaching is such that a reasonable examiner would consider it important; and (F) where relevant, why the patent or printed publication is deemed available against the patent claims.
guidance: Use MPEP § 2247.01 for examples. In simple cases examiner may adopt requester’s reasons for SNQ; if request does not indicate claims to be unpatentable, decision should phrase that SNQ is raised as to listed claims rather than saying requester considers claims unpatentable.

name: Decision Is Not a Determination of Patentability
description: In the decision on the request, the examiner will not decide, and no statement should be made as to, whether the claims are rejected over the patents and printed publications; the examiner only decides whether there is an SNQ to order reexamination.
guidance: The actual patentability issues are addressed during the reexamination examination stage; the decision letter should avoid making patentability rejections at the request-decision stage.

name: Claims-related fees (independent claims >3, claims >20, multiple dependent claims)
description: Fees apply for independent claims in excess of three, claims in excess of 20, multiple dependent claim fees, and parallel reissue-claim excess fees (reissue independent claims in excess of three; reissue claims in excess of 20).
guidance: Count claims and apply the excess-claim fees when thresholds are exceeded. Multiple dependent claim surcharges apply where applicable. Reissue-specific claim excess rules mirror the application claim excess rules.

name: Patent trial and appeal fees (PTAB and appeals)
description: Fees in this category include Notice of Appeal, Request for oral hearing, filing a brief in support of an appeal in inter partes reexamination, petitions under 37 CFR 41.3, Inter Partes Review (IPR) request fee (up to 20 claims), IPR per-claim fees in excess of 20, Post‑Grant Review (PGR) request fees, post-institution fees (IPR/PGR) up to 20 claims and per-claim excess; petitions for derivation, forwarding appeals to the Board, Pro Hac Vice admission fee, and other PTAB-related fees.
guidance: Different fees apply depending on the proceeding (IPR, PGR, covered business method review, appeal). There are distinct initial-institution fees (up to 20 claims) and per-claim fees for claims in excess of 20; post‑institution fees are separate. Consult the fee table to determine the correct fee code for the specific PTAB filing.

name: Expedited/accelerated examination of utility-model applications (Rule 18ter(3)(a))
description: An applicant may request expedited/accelerated examination so a decision on suitability for registration is made within a period specified in the Administrative Instructions.
guidance: Expedition is subject to conditions: (i) application is for a single invention and/or applicant agrees examination division will consider only the first identified invention; (ii) applicant undertakes to respond immediately to clarifications; (iii) application is not withdrawn and then reinstated before conclusion of examination; (iv) a search report based on acceptable minimum documentation on claims of same or narrower scope than the ARIPO claims is provided. Timeframe for decision is set in Administrative Instructions.

name: Third‑party observations after publication (Rule 19ter)
description: Following publication, any person may submit observations concerning the patentability of the invention; observations may be considered if they concern novelty, inventive step, claim clarity, sufficiency of disclosure, patentability of subject matter and unallowable amendments.
guidance: Observations must be filed in writing in English and include a statement of the grounds. Documentary evidence may be filed in any language but Office may request translation into English within a specified period or evidence will be disregarded. The person filing may not become a party to proceedings. Observations should preferably be filed electronically. The Office acknowledges receipt if not anonymous but does not inform further action beyond subsequent published office actions. The Office will endeavour to issue the next office action to communicate substantiated observations to the applicant. If observations call patentability into question they must be taken into account in any proceedings until terminated. Observations alleging prior art from use are taken into account only if facts are not disputed by the applicant/proprietor or are established beyond reasonable doubt. Observations received after decision to grant/refuse are included in the file without noting content. Observations filed during international phase will be considered on entry into the Regional phase.

name: Requirements for request for limitation (post‑grant amendment) (Rule 21bis)
description: Request for limitation of an ARIPO patent or utility model shall be filed in writing and contain specified particulars.
guidance: Request must contain: (a) particulars of the proprietor (as in Rule 5(5)(c)) and an indication of the Contracting States for which requester is proprietor; (b) patent number; (c) complete version of amended claims and, if applicable, amended description and drawings; (d) particulars of representative if appointed (as in Rule 5(5)(d)).

name: Status of claims: acceptance or dispute with particularity
description: Status of claims. A statement accepting or disputing appellant’s statement of the status of claims. If appellant’s statement of the status of claims is disputed, the errors in appellant’s statement must be specified with particularity.
guidance: Simply denying appellant's status is insufficient—must specify precise errors (with record citations as appropriate).

name: Summary of claimed subject matter: acceptance or dispute
description: Summary of claimed subject matter. A statement accepting or disputing appellant’s summary of the subject matter defined in each of the independent claims involved in the appeal. If appellant’s summary of the subject matter is disputed, the errors in appellant’s summary must be specified.
guidance: Disputes to appellant's claim summaries must be particularized; include precise points of contention.

name: Examiner cannot make new determination to not adopt proposed rejection in answer
description: An examiner’s answer may not include a new determination not to make a proposed rejection of a claim.
guidance: Such determinations must be made in an Office action reopening prosecution, not in the examiner’s answer.

name: Board decisions: affirm, reverse, remand and new ground rules
description: The Board may affirm or reverse each decision of the examiner on all issues raised on each appealed claim, or remand the reexamination proceeding. The reversal of the examiner’s determination not to make a rejection proposed by a third party requester constitutes a decision adverse to patentability and will be set forth as a new ground of rejection. The Board may include new grounds of rejection; such decisions are not final for judicial review.
guidance: When Board states a new ground of rejection, special procedural options (reopen prosecution or rehearing) become available to the owner and the decision is not final for judicial review.

name: Owner options after new ground of rejection
description: When the Board makes a new ground of rejection, the owner, within one month from the date of the decision, must either (1) reopen prosecution by filing an amendment or new evidence relating to the claims so rejected, or (2) request rehearing addressing the new ground and stating with particularity points believed to have been misapprehended or overlooked.
guidance: Owner must act within one month to avoid termination of appeal as to the rejected claim; reopening requires amendment and/or new evidence.

name: Filing clean and annotated copies of claims
description: Within 14 days of the initiation of the proceeding, each party must file a clean copy of its involved claims. Within 28 days, each party must file annotated copies where limitations are illustrated in drawings or biotechnology sequences, indicating in bold face between braces where each limitation is shown; for 35 U.S.C. 112(f) limitations, indicate spec portions describing structure/material/acts corresponding to each claimed function.
guidance: Timely submit both clean and, when applicable, annotated claim copies; required annotations aid claim construction and comparison.

name: Motions: types, burden, and content requirements
description: Motions may be substantive (e.g., to redefine scope, change benefit, or for judgment), responsive (e.g., to amend/add claim), or miscellaneous. The party filing the motion has the burden of proof. Each motion must be filed as a separate paper and include: (i) a statement of the precise relief requested, (ii) a statement of material facts, and (iii) a full statement of the reasons for the relief requested, including detailed explanation of the significance of the evidence and the governing law, rules, and precedent.
guidance: Motions must be separately captioned, factually precise, and legally detailed; include claim charts when comparing claims; Board may require additional showings.

name: Claim chart requirement
description: Claim charts must be used in support of any paper requiring the comparison of a claim to something else, such as another claim, prior art, or a specification. Claim charts must accompany the paper as an appendix. Claim charts are not a substitute for appropriate argument and explanation in the paper.
guidance: Always include claim charts where comparisons are required, and provide concomitant legal argument in the motion/paper itself.

name: Filing languages and translation requirements
description: Application documents may first be filed in any language; the language of proceedings is Russian and a Russian translation must be filed within two months from the filing date (extendible by two months on payment of a fee).
guidance: If filed in another language the translation must contain the description, claims, text matter of drawings and abstract; failure to file translation within the required period (including paid extension) results in withdrawal. For PCT regional phase the time limits differ (see PCT section: 33 months for Russian translation).

name: Claims requirements (structure, clarity, support)
description: Claims must define the subject matter for which protection is sought. Claims must be clear and concise and must be fully supported by the specification. Number of claims must be reasonable.
guidance: Each claim must be one sentence, generally with an introductory (pre-characterizing) part and a characterizing part preceded by words such as 'characterized in that' or 'wherein the improvement comprises'. Claims should not refer to the specification or drawings except if absolutely necessary. Claims may be independent or dependent; dependent claims must specify development or precise features of the independent claim and should be grouped together. Multiple dependency of claims is allowed. Additional claims fees apply for claims exceeding five (and further thresholds). Unity requirement: group of inventions forming single inventive concept defined by common technical features; multiple inventions allowed only if unity satisfied.

name: Fees: payment, currency, evidence and reductions
description: Official fees due to EAPO are fixed in Russian Roubles. A document evidencing payment must be submitted, indicating application title/serial number or patent number and action for which fee is paid.
guidance: Reductions: natural persons from certain states pay 50% of prescribed fee; natural persons from Contracting States pay 10%; scientific/educational organizations from Contracting States pay 30%; other entities from Contracting States pay 90%. Reductions apply to fees for filing, appeals, substantive exam, grant, amendments, restoration and assignment. Specific fee amounts and surcharges listed in the fee table (single procedural fee, additional claims fees, examination fee, accelerated processing fees, late-payment surcharges, restoration fees, etc.).

name: Specific treatment for chemical compositions and pharmaceuticals
description: Chemical products and pharmaceutical products may be patented.
guidance: Pharmaceuticals may also be eligible for term extension/SPC in most Contracting States (see national chapters); disclosure and claim drafting guidance (e.g., for second medical use) provided elsewhere in the manual.

name: Second medical use / 'use' claims
description: Both first and second use may be patentable. If invention is use of a known device/method/substance/product for a previously unknown purpose, claims should identify the known item and indicate that the subject matter is the use for the new purpose.
guidance: Suggested claim structure: 'Use of device/method/substance/product X as…/for…/in the manufacture of [the purpose]'. Ensure claims contain features necessary to identify the known item and the new purpose.

name: Treatment methods and medical procedures
description: The Eurasian Patent System allows obtaining patents for methods for treatment of the human or animal body by surgery or therapy and methods for medical diagnosis.
guidance: Earlier wording indicated methods for treatment/diagnosis were not designated unpatentable; the manual clarifies that such methods can be patented under the system. Drafting and claim strategy should follow guidelines on claims and second medical use where relevant.

name: Software-related inventions (nuanced treatment)
description: The manual contains apparently differing statements: summary initially states 'computer programs are not patentable' while a later section states 'computer-related inventions (inventions involving the use of a computer program) may be patented.'
guidance: Practical implication: pure computer programs as such are excluded, but computer-related inventions with technical character or involving a technical contribution may be patentable. Claim drafting should emphasize technical features and practical application to satisfy patentability requirements.

name: Additional procedural points for PCT entering regional phase
description: When designating the Eurasian Patent Office in a PCT application it is valid for all Contracting States. Receiving Office and ISA/IPEA particulars provided: EAPO may act as Receiving Office; ISR by Rospatent or EPO depending on language; timelines for fees, translation, examination and processing explained.
guidance: Fees: within 31 months a single procedural fee (filing, novelty search, publication) and special claims fee for claims over the fifth must be paid; fee reductions available if ISR prepared by an ISA; average processing time from entry to grant ~2 years. Specific deadlines and fees enumerated in the PCT section.

name: Assignor estoppel and privity
description: An inventor who assigns patent rights is estopped from asserting invalidity as a defense or as the basis of a declaratory-judgment claim; those in privity with the assignor may also be estopped.
guidance: Doctrine sources: Pandrol USA, LP v. Airboss Ry. Prods., Inc., 424 F.3d 1161 (Fed. Cir. 2005); Diamond Sci. Co. v. Ambico, Inc., 848 F.2d 1220 (Fed. Cir. 1988). Assignor estoppel is an equitable doctrine concerned with balancing equities and functions as an affirmative defense, not a separate federal cause of action. Privity is determined by balance-of-equities factors and may consider (1) extent and nature of business relationships, (2) financial dealings such as indemnification agreements, and (3) whether the alleged infringer availed itself of the inventor’s knowledge and assistance (Intel Corp. v. U.S. Int’l Trade Comm’n, 946 F.2d 821 (Fed. Cir. 1991); Checkpoint Sys. v. All-Tag Sec. S.A., 412 F.3d 1331 (Fed. Cir. 2005)).

name: Joinder standards after In re EMC and the AIA §299
description: Joinder of multiple accused infringers requires an 'actual link'—shared, overlapping facts that give rise to each cause of action; mere common infringement of the same patent is insufficient. The AIA §299 narrows joinder in patent cases.
guidance: In re EMC Corp., 677 F.3d 1351 (Fed. Cir. 2012) requires a link between facts underlying each claim of infringement. AIA §299(a)(1) permits joinder only where (1) any right to relief is asserted against the parties jointly, severally, or in the alternative with respect to or arising out of the same transaction, occurrence, or series of transactions relating to the making, using, importing into the U.S., offering for sale, or selling of the same accused product or processes; and (2) common questions of fact will arise. §299(b) expressly states that common infringement of the same patent alone is not enough. §299(c) allows consent to joinder. District courts retain discretion to refuse joinder to avoid prejudice, delay, or unfairness; courts have severed defendants under §299 and have also consolidated pretrial proceedings (e.g., for claim construction) while preserving separate trials. Be alert to serially filed cases and potential abuse (e.g., filing to avoid deadlines).

name: Infringement pleading requirements and specificity (Form 18 vs Twombly/Iqbal)
description: Complaints should identify the asserted patents, state ownership of the patents, identify the accused infringers, provide a brief statement of alleged infringing acts, and, if applicable, state marking under §287. There is tension between historical Form 18 practice and the heightened pleading standards of Twombly/Iqbal.
guidance: Historically notice pleading (Rule 8(a) and Form 18) produced sparse, conclusory patent complaints, sometimes omitting which claims or products were accused. Supreme Court decisions (Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007); Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)) require pleadings to state plausible claims with sufficient factual matter. The Federal Circuit has held Form 18 controlling for direct infringement in some cases (In re Bill of Lading, 681 F.3d 1323; McZeal v. Sprint Nextel Corp., 501 F.3d 1354), and held a complaint conforming to Form 18 may not need to identify a specific accused product (K-Tech, 714 F.3d 1277). District courts are split: some apply Twombly/Iqbal to patent complaints (Macronix Int’l Co. v. Spansion Inc., 4 F. Supp. 3d 797), others follow the Federal Circuit. On Dec 1, 2015, Rule 84 and the Appendix of Forms (including Form 18) were abolished; Twombly/Iqbal pleading standards now govern patent complaints. For indirect infringement, courts generally require more detailed allegations (identity of underlying direct infringer and facts supporting specific-intent knowledge), and courts disagree on whether the filing of the complaint alone suffices to establish postsuit knowledge (compare Bascom Research LLC v. Facebook, Inc. and Mallinckrodt Inc. v. E-Z-EM Inc.). Some courts require identification of specific accused products; Rule 11(b)(3) permits allegations likely to have evidentiary support after discovery, but some courts hold Rule 11(b)(3) does not lower Rule 8(a) standards. Local rules (e.g., N.D. Cal. Patent L.R. 3-1) may require early disclosure of asserted claims and accused products, and amendment of those disclosures typically requires leave for good cause (see O2 Micro, Abbott Diabetes Care Inc. v. Roche Diagnostics Corp.).

name: Use the eligibility flowchart and three pathways (A, B, C)
description: Examiners should determine whether a claim satisfies subject matter eligibility criteria by evaluating the claim in accordance with the MPEP flowchart which illustrates steps for products and processes during examination.
guidance: The flowchart shows Step 1 (statutory categories), Step 2 (Alice/Mayo two-part test, implemented as Steps 2A and 2B), and three eligibility pathways: Pathway A (streamlined/self-evident eligibility), Pathway B (Step 1 YES and not directed to a judicial exception — Step 2A NO), and Pathway C (Step 1 YES, Step 2A YES, but additional elements amount to significantly more — Step 2B YES). If a claim is not eligible under any pathway, it is patent ineligible and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101. If uncertain about streamlined analysis, conduct full analysis. Regardless of 101 outcome, examine other requirements (35 U.S.C. 102, 103, 112, utility, inventorship, double patenting). See MPEP §§ 2106.04–2106.06 for details.

name: Step 1: Claim must fall within one of the four statutory categories
description: Determine whether the claim as a whole is to a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter (the four statutory categories of invention under 35 U.S.C. 101).
guidance: If the claim as a whole does not fall within any category (Step 1: NO), it is non-statutory and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 (use form paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01). It is not necessary to identify a single correct category so long as the claim clearly falls within at least one. If the BRI of the claim covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments, the claim fails Step 1 and should be rejected; best practice is to point out the BRI and recommend an amendment narrowing the claim to statutory embodiments. See MPEP § 2106.03.

name: Non-statutory product examples (Step 1 guidance on intangible products)
description: Products that do not have a physical or tangible form do not fall within the machine/manufacture/composition categories (e.g., information/data per se, computer program per se, transitory signals per se).
guidance: A claim to software 'detached from any medium' or an intangible collection of information lacks physical/tangible form and is non-statutory (e.g., Digitech, Microsoft v. AT&T, Benson). Transitory propagating signals are physical but lack concrete structure and are non-statutory (Nuijten, Mentor Graphics). If BRI encompasses such non-statutory embodiments (e.g., computer-readable medium that can be a carrier wave), rejection is appropriate. See MPEP § 2106.03.

name: Construct claims under the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) for eligibility
description: Evaluate Step 1 and later steps after determining what applicant has invented by reviewing the entire disclosure and construing claims according to their BRI.
guidance: If BRI of the claim covers statutory and non-statutory embodiments, claim fails Step 1. Examiners should point out BRI and recommend narrowing amendments when appropriate. See MPEP § 2111 and § 2106 subsections II–III for BRI importance.

name: Step 2A overall: Determine if claim is directed to a judicial exception
description: Step 2A (first part of Alice/Mayo test) asks whether the claim is directed to a law of nature, a natural phenomenon (product of nature), or an abstract idea; if so, further analysis at Step 2B is required.
guidance: Evaluate Step 2A after claim construction/BRI. If claim as a whole is not directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: NO), it is eligible at Pathway B. If it is directed to an exception (Step 2A: YES), proceed to Step 2B to determine if additional elements amount to 'significantly more.' See MPEP § 2106.04.

name: Step 2A Prong One: Does the claim recite a judicial exception?
description: Prong One asks whether the claim 'recites' (sets forth or describes) an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon — i.e., whether a judicial exception is explicitly stated or described in the claim limitations.
guidance: Distinguish 'recites' (sets forth/ describes) from merely 'involves' — claims that merely involve an exception may still be eligible. Examples: Diehr/Mayo claims that 'set forth' exceptions vs Alice claims that 'describe' the concept. If Prong One is met, evaluate Prong Two; if not, claim is not directed to an exception (Step 2A: NO). See MPEP § 2106.04(a).

name: Step 2A Prong Two: Does the claim integrate the judicial exception into a practical application?
description: Prong Two asks whether additional claim elements integrate the recited judicial exception into a practical application; if so, the claim is not directed to the exception (Step 2A: NO) and is eligible at Pathway B.
guidance: If additional elements transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application of the exception, then claim avoids being 'directed to' the exception. Mere recitation of an exception or adding only another judicial exception is insufficient to integrate. See MPEP § 2106.04(d)(2) and Alice Corp. guidance. If Prong Two fails, proceed to Step 2B to assess whether elements amount to 'significantly more.'

name: Multiple judicial exceptions: how to analyze
description: Claims may recite multiple judicial exceptions; examiners should apply the same eligibility analysis regardless of the number of exceptions and should avoid unnecessarily parsing claims into multiple exceptions.
guidance: If possible, treat multiple abstract ideas together as a single abstract idea for Prong Two and Step 2B. If exceptions are distinct (e.g., a law of nature and an abstract idea), examiners may select one exception and conduct the analysis on that selected exception for examination efficiency — if selected-exception analysis shows integration or significantly more, claim should be considered eligible. If not, and no other elements amount to significantly more, the claim is ineligible. See MPEP § 2106.04.

name: Insufficiency of mere additional judicial-exception elements
description: If the claim contains no additional elements beyond the judicial exception, or if the additional elements merely recite another judicial exception, that is insufficient to integrate the exception into a practical application or to show significantly more.
guidance: Adding one abstract idea to another does not render the claim non-abstract (RecogniCorp v. Nintendo). For eligibility, additional elements must transform the claim into a patent-eligible application (Alice Corp.). If no sufficient additional elements, make appropriate rejection and recommend amendment if possible. See MPEP § 2106.04.

name: Examiner best practices when claim fails Steps
description: When a claim fails Step 1 or is directed to a judicial exception without integration, examiners should make the appropriate 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection and recommend claim amendments where possible.
guidance: If claim fails Step 1 (non-statutory), use form paragraphs 7.05/7.05.01 and recommend an amendment to resolve eligibility. If claim recites an exception and has insufficient additional elements, indicate deficiency and recommend amendments. If uncertain about streamlined Pathway A, perform full analysis to ensure consistency. See MPEP §§ 2106.03–2106.07.

name: Re-issue may enlarge claims (with limits)
description: Re-issue may enlarge claims.
guidance: Although reissue can in some circumstances broaden the scope of claims (see multiple citations, e.g., 656), enlargement is constrained by prohibitions on introducing new matter, by delay, and by requirements that the enlargement be due to inadvertence, mistake, or accident without fraud.

name: Re-issue of combination patent may cover subcombinations and elements
description: Re-issue of a combination patent may cover subcombinations and elements.
guidance: Reissue of combination patents may properly claim subcombinations or individual elements in certain circumstances (see 671–672), but such claims are limited by what was originally described and by the prohibition on adding new matter.

name: Reduction to practice necessary (principle & instruments)
description: Reduction to practical art or instrument is necessary; reduction to practice is generally required.
guidance: For patents on many inventions, especially machinery and processes, actual reduction to practice (or constructive reduction via an adequate specification and claims) is required to establish rights; principle reduced to practice may be patentable.

name: Description construed with other parts of the specification; ambiguity in description
description: The description is construed with other parts of the specification; ambiguity in the description is relevant.
guidance: The specification is read as a whole; ambiguities may make sufficiency a question of fact, may render a claim void, or otherwise affect claim scope and validity.

name: Abandonment by describing and not claiming
description: Abandonment may occur by describing and not claiming an invention.
guidance: If matter is described in the specification but not claimed, that omission may be treated as abandonment to the public in some circumstances; whether omission equals abandonment depends on context.

name: Claims: purpose, requisites, and essential relation to specification
description: Claims serve a particular purpose and have requisites; they are essential to the specification and define the monopoly.
guidance: Claims are the legal definition of the patentee’s monopoly; they must satisfy statutory and doctrinal requisites (clarity, support in the specification, definiteness) and must correspond to what is described so skilled artisans can practice the invention.

name: Claim must be precise, complete within itself, and define the invention; ambiguity is fatal
description: A claim must precisely define the invention, be complete within itself, and ambiguity in a claim is fatal.
guidance: Claims must 'precisely define' the invention, show the class it belongs to, be capable of standing or falling alone, and contain no useless or equivocal language; courts construe claims as a matter of law.

name: Claims must include all essential features and exclude non-essential features
description: Claims must include all essential features of the invention and exclude non-essential features.
guidance: A valid claim embraces the essential elements necessary to produce the claimed result; it must not include irrelevant matter and should exclude non-essential features.

name: Claims must be limited to the actual patentable character of the invention; cannot claim principles, effects, or mere functions
description: Claims must be limited to the patentable character of the invention and must not claim a principle, mode of action, idea, or mere result/effect.
guidance: Functional claims that are merely statements of effect or result are void; where possible, functional language should be construed to cover the means disclosed, but a claim cannot claim all modes of achieving a result.

name: Functional language and 'means' claims — how construed and limited
description: Claims using functional language ('means', 'mechanism', 'for doing X') are treated specially: they may be construed to cover disclosed means but can be improper if they attempt to claim mere function without structure.
guidance: Functional claims should, if possible, be read to cover the corresponding disclosed means; purely functional claiming of a result or all modes of performing a function is generally improper.

name: Claims must correspond with the description and be based on sufficient description
description: Claims must correspond to the description and be for matter properly and sufficiently described so that skilled artisans could practice it.
guidance: Claims that attempt to cover matter not supported by the specification or that rely on insufficient disclosure are invalid; the description may aid construction but cannot enlarge an inadequate claim.

name: Claims control when inconsistent with the description; description cannot enlarge claims
description: When claims and description conflict, claims control; description does not enlarge claims.
guidance: While the description construes the claims, claims define the scope. A specification cannot be used to expand the claim beyond its proper meaning; contradictions may render both invalid in extreme cases.

name: Claims for combinations: requisites and limits
description: Claims for combinations must separate new and old, be confined to essential elements, and sufficiently describe the union that produces a given effect.
guidance: A combination claim should explicitly distinguish the novel combination from prior elements, embrace enough elements to produce the claimed result, and cannot be used to claim individual elements unless properly disclosed and claimed.

name: Claims for an art (process): requisites and coverage
description: Claims for an art (process) must meet requisites; they cover all ways of practicing the art but cannot simultaneously claim the product in certain circumstances.
guidance: A process claim is proper when the effect results from a new use of natural forces or chemical action, but the claim must be supported by a generic description and cannot improperly claim the product unless supported.

name: Multiplication and needless repetition of claims improper; disclaimers and amendments governed by delay/fraud rules
description: Needless multiplication or repetition of claims creates ambiguity and is improper. Claims may be disclaimed or amended, but disclaimers/amendments are subject to timing (delay) and fraud constraints.
guidance: Patent Office and courts discourage superfluous claims and will police multiplicity; disclaimers can cure defects but may be barred by unreasonable delay or evidence of fraud.

name: Subcombinations and relation to principal combination
description: Subcombinations and elements relate to the principal combination and have special treatment in claims and reissue.
guidance: Claims to subcombinations may be permissible, but whether a subcombination is covered depends on the original disclosure and claim language; reissue can sometimes claim subcombinations consistent with original description.

name: Patent construed in view of the actual invention
description: Patents are construed in view of the actual invention and the nature of the invention.
guidance: Claim construction considers the real nature of the patented subject matter; courts interpret patents in light of the invention's specifics and purpose.

name: Result or effect is not patentable; invention is a means not an end
description: A result or effect as such is not patentable; an invention is a means, not an end.
guidance: Patents must claim concrete means or methods; claiming only an intended result without structure or steps is improper.

name: Proposed terminal-disclaimer enforceability clause
description: The USPTO proposes requiring any terminal disclaimer to include a clause stipulating that a terminally disclaimed patent will be enforceable only if the patent is not and has never been tied directly or indirectly to a patent in which any claim has been finally held invalid as anticipated or obvious in a civil litigation or a USPTO proceeding.
guidance: This proposed clause would be in addition to the current requirements that a terminal disclaimer tie the expiration and ownership of patents. The rule would apply across industries and at all stages of product development; it is not limited to Hatch-Waxman or BPCIA contexts.

name: Definition of 'directly' tied via terminal disclaimer
description: A patent is 'directly' tied by a terminal disclaimer to 'another patent' when: (1) the terminal disclaimer is filed in the subject patent or application; and (2) the other patent, or the application that issued as the other patent, is the reference patent or application identified in the terminal disclaimer.
guidance: When two patents are directly tied, only one terminal disclaimer is at issue. Under the proposed rule, a direct tie can render the subject patent unenforceable if a claim of the reference patent is finally held unpatentable or invalid and the terminal disclaimer contains the proposed agreement.

name: Enforceability consequence when a tied patent has a claim finally held invalid
description: If a claim of a referenced patent is finally held unpatentable or invalid over prior art, patents tied (directly or indirectly, as defined) to that referenced patent may not be enforceable if their terminal disclaimers contain the proposed agreement.
guidance: The Federal Register examples demonstrate specific chain outcomes: e.g., in W ← X ← Y ← Z, if a claim of W is held invalid and the terminal disclaimer in Z contains the proposed agreement, Z may not be enforced. These consequences depend on the presence of the proposed enforceability clause in the terminal disclaimers in the chain.

name: Statutory presumption of validity (35 U.S.C. § 282) and terminal disclaimer effects
description: Under 35 U.S.C. § 282, 'Each claim of a patent ... shall be presumed valid independently of the validity of other claims; dependent or multiple dependent claims shall be presumed valid even though dependent upon an invalid claim.' Historically, filing a terminal disclaimer is not an admission of obviousness.
guidance: The proposed rule would require a patent owner filing a terminal disclaimer to abandon part of that statutory presumption of validity and to give up the current legal presumption that filing a terminal disclaimer is not an admission of obviousness (citing Motionless Keyboard Co. v. Microsoft Corp. and Quad Environmental Techs. Corp. v. Union Sanitary Dist.).

name: Risk that valid, nonobvious claims become unenforceable due to ties
description: A patent containing nonobvious (patentable distinct) claims may become unenforceable simply because it is directly or indirectly tied via terminal disclaimers to a patent that contains a single claim found anticipated or obvious.
guidance: Illustrative prosecution scenarios: (a) A genus claim directly tied to a species claim can make the species claim unenforceable if the genus has a claim later held invalid. (b) Chains of continuation/species filings can lead to an indirectly tied species becoming unenforceable even if its claims are patentably distinct from upstream claims.

name: Practical prosecution strategy impacts
description: If the proposed rule is implemented, applicants will need to change prosecution strategies to avoid unintentionally creating unenforceable patents via terminal disclaimers.
guidance: Potential adaptations include: prosecuting broader claim sets early to provoke a restriction requirement (which may be uneconomic due to excess claim fees); spending time and resources to traverse obviousness-type double patenting rejections rather than filing terminal disclaimers; expecting additional rounds of arguments and appeals, higher prosecution costs, and delays in grant.

name: USPTO policy rationale for the proposed rule
description: The USPTO states the rule 'is intended to promote competition by lowering the cost of challenging groups of patents tied by terminal disclaimers, resulting in reduced barriers to market entry and lower costs for consumers.'
guidance: The USPTO also asserts that narrowing validity disputes to only one patent tied by terminal disclaimers could lead to more focused claim construction hearings, lower litigation costs, and faster resolution, and allow only one patent to be challenged via post-grant challenge. The article notes the USPTO provided no empirical evidence in the Federal Register notice to support the proposition that the rule will reduce prices for consumers.

name: Description: sufficiency and structure
description: The description discloses the invention sufficiently clearly and completely so that a person skilled in the art will be able to carry out the claimed invention.
guidance: To improve readability the description usually contains: title; technical field; background art; summary of the invention outlining scope and how it solves background problems; brief explanation of the drawings; detailed examples (embodiments) referencing the drawings. Examples often play an important role in meeting support and enablement requirements.

name: Claims define scope and legal operativity
description: The claims define the scope of exclusive patent protection in terms of the technical features of the invention; they are the legally operative part of a patent application and patentability is determined on the basis of the claims.
guidance: Claims must be clear and concise, and fully supported by the description. Choice of terminology should track through the description consistently; unsupported claims can be thrown out for lack of support.

name: Drawings as visual support
description: The drawings provide visual support in describing the invention and often facilitate better understanding of the claimed invention.
guidance: Drawings may include figures, tables, flow charts and diagrams. A representative drawing is usually positioned on the front page of a published patent document.

name: Abstract: concise summary for search/readers
description: The abstract is a summary (a digest) of the invention limited to a certain number of words and typically includes key features recited in the claims.
guidance: The abstract is primarily an aid for those conducting patent searches and readers of patent documents.

name: Initial patent drafter questions
description: When an inventor instructs to file, the patent drafter must ask: What has been invented? What is the essential inventive concept? Does the inventor know what they want to protect? How should we claim the invention?
guidance: Understanding these points informs claiming strategy and ensures drafting aligns with client's protection goals.

name: Support requirement between description and claims
description: The description must support the patent claims; after drafting claims and description, the drafter must ensure every claim is adequately supported in the description.
guidance: In strictly evaluated jurisdictions (e.g., EPO) the description must specifically include at least one embodiment that demonstrates claimed combinations (e.g., glass table with four legs) to meet support.

name: Aim for a mix of broad and narrow claims
description: Patent drafters should aim at a broad set of claims covering various aspects at different levels of detail, while including narrower claims as fallbacks.
guidance: Broader claims increase protection but risk invalidity; narrower claims may survive litigation. Prior art unpredictability and unpublished applications may affect scope; claiming strategy is complex and may be adjusted during prosecution.

name: All-elements rule for infringement
description: To assert patent infringement, all of the elements of a claim must be reproduced in the third party's accused embodiment; comparison is done element-by-element.
guidance: If an accused product lacks even one claimed element (or has elements in different relationships), there is no infringement under the all-elements rule. Use this to assess claim coverage and potential circumvention by competitors.

name: Types of claim elements
description: Elements may be structural (what they are), functional (what they do), relational (relationships between elements), activity (steps in process claims), intentional (purpose), or parametric (measurable properties).
guidance: Choose element types appropriate to the subject matter; e.g., activity elements often use gerunds for process claims; parametric elements specify values like melting point or resistance.

name: General claim format conventions
description: A patent claim is traditionally written as a single sentence in the present tense, beginning with a capital letter and ending with a period; semicolons separate clauses and phrases; claims are numbered consecutively and appear in a separate 'Claims' section.
guidance: Although formats vary, many patent offices expect heavy punctuation, specific indentation, and separation from the description. In some offices (CNIPA, JPO, KIPO) claims appear before the description; in the US the distinction is by phrases like 'I/we claim'.

name: Three parts of a claim: preamble, transitional phrase, body
description: A claim generally has a preamble (identifies category of the invention), a transitional phrase, and a body (elements and limitations).
guidance: Preamble should be chosen at the right level of breadth; it may be accorded differing weight in litigation depending on jurisdiction. The body must recite elements and their relationships, not just a list of parts.

name: Preamble: choose level of breadth carefully
description: The preamble is an introductory noun phrase identifying the category (e.g., apparatus, method) and may include modifiers that narrow scope.
guidance: Broader preambles increase scope but risk unity objections (multiple inventions) and divisional requirements. Keep preamble consistent with title where appropriate; avoid accidental narrowing (e.g., claiming 'telephone' when the invention is the mounting).

name: Transitional phrases: open-ended vs closed
description: Open-ended phrases (comprising, including, containing, characterized by) are inclusive and do not exclude additional elements; closed phrases (consisting of) limit the claim to only the recited elements.
guidance: Using 'comprising' leaves room for additional elements (e.g., a cap); 'consisting of' excludes unrecited elements and is rarely used because infringers can avoid infringement by adding an extra element. Jurisdictions interpret phrases differently (e.g., 'comprising' in Australia may be narrow). Check jurisdictional interpretations before choosing.

name: Body of the claim must interrelate elements
