description: The body recites elements and explains how they exist in relationship to one another; claims cannot merely be a list of parts.
guidance: Patent offices often reject mere lists. Use proper connectors and relationships (e.g., 'a top configured to be supported by at least one leg'). Open/closed phrasing can also be used within the body to define element groups.

name: Punctuation and layout of claims
description: Claims are frequently more extensively punctuated than grammatically required: comma separates preamble from transitional phrase; colon separates transition from body; elements typically separated by semicolons with '; and' before the last; many offices require line indentation for each element.
guidance: Follow expected punctuation and indentation to ensure claims are interpreted as intended and to avoid formal objections or rejections by patent offices.

name: Patentability of an intermediate via contributing cause and nexus
description: The patentability of an intermediate may be established by unexpected properties of an end product 'when one of ordinary skill in the art would reasonably ascribe to a claimed intermediate the 'contributing cause' for such an unexpectedly superior activity or property.' In re Magerlein, 602 F.2d 366, 373.
guidance: Applicant must identify the cause of the unexpectedly superior activity in the end product and establish a nexus between that cause and the claimed intermediate; mere correlation is insufficient.

name: Nonobviousness of a genus or claimed range may be supported by species/narrow-range data where trend permits
description: The nonobviousness of a broader claimed range can be supported by evidence based on unexpected results from testing a narrower range if one of ordinary skill would be able to determine a trend in the exemplified data allowing reasonable extension of probative value. In re Kollman, 595 F.2d 48.
guidance: Provide sufficient exemplified species/range data showing trends that justify extrapolation to the broader claimed range; isolated or inconsistent species data may fail (In re Lindner, Kollman examples).

name: Affidavit/declaration must compare claimed subject matter with the closest prior art
description: An affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 must compare the claimed subject matter with the closest prior art to be effective to rebut a prima facie case of obviousness. In re Burckel, 592 F.2d 1175.
guidance: Identify the closest single prior art reference (compare claim limitations and relative importance), explain deviations from references, and provide evaluative comparisons; unexplained deviations should be noted and evaluated (In re Merchant, Finley, Armstrong).

name: Claimed invention may only be compared to subject matter existing in the prior art
description: Although evidence must compare the claimed invention with the closest prior art, applicant is not required to compare with subject matter that does not exist in the prior art.
guidance: Do not require hypothetical or post-combination polymers/structures that are not actually disclosed in the prior art (In re Geiger; In re Chapman).

name: Commercial success requires nexus to claimed invention; applicant bears burden
description: An applicant asserting commercial success to support nonobviousness bears the burden of proof of establishing a nexus between the claimed invention and evidence of commercial success. In re Huang, 100 F.3d 135.
guidance: Provide hard evidence linking sales/market performance to claimed features; the PTO will rely on applicant to supply such evidence in ex parte prosecution.

name: In design cases, establishing nexus for commercial success is especially difficult
description: Evidence of commercial success must be clearly attributable to the design to be of probative value, and not to brand name recognition, improved performance, or some other factor. Litton Systems, Inc. v. Whirlpool Corp.
guidance: Provide direct evidence attributing sales or market acceptance specifically to the claimed design features, not to brand or unrelated attributes.

name: Sufficiency of disclosure / enablement (reference to MPEP §2164 guidance)
description: See MPEP § 2164 - § 2164.08(c) for guidance in determining whether the specification provides an enabling disclosure in compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
guidance: Apply the enablement guidance in MPEP §2164 when assessing whether the specification teaches how to make and use the claimed invention over the full scope claimed.

name: Identify invention and establish broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI)
description: Review the disclosure to identify what applicant considers as the invention. (MPEP 2103(I)). This can be a brief description and should not merely reproduce the claim. The take away is the focus of the invention (example: diagnosing julitis based on presence of JUL-1 in plasma).
guidance: Use the disclosure to state briefly what applicant invented; do not just copy claim language. Establish the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim before proceeding with Steps 1 and 2. Use a separate worksheet for each claim.

name: Product-of-nature — markedly different characteristics analysis
description: A claim is 'directed' to a product of nature exception when the claim recites a nature-based product limitation that does not exhibit markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state.
guidance: Apply the markedly different characteristics analysis only to the nature-based product limitations in the claim. Non-limiting examples of characteristics considered include: biological or pharmacological functions or activities; chemical and physical properties; phenotype (functional and structural characteristics); and structure and form (chemical, genetic or physical). Document the claimed limitation(s), the closest naturally occurring counterpart, and whether the claimed product exhibits markedly different characteristics.

name: Process claims and the markedly different analysis exception
description: Note that a process claim is not subject to the markedly different characteristics analysis for nature-based products used in the process, except where the process claim has no substantive difference from a product claim (e.g., 'a method of providing an apple').
guidance: Do not perform the product-of-nature markedly-different analysis on nature-based materials merely recited as part of a process claim unless the process claim is substantively equivalent to a product claim.

name: Identify other judicial exceptions (law of nature, natural phenomenon, abstract idea)
description: Even if not product-of-nature, a claim may recite a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea; identify the limitation(s) that align with judicial exceptions.
guidance: Abstract ideas include fundamental economic practices, certain methods of organizing human activity, ideas themselves, or mathematical relationships/formulae. Laws of nature and natural phenomena include naturally occurring principles or substances. For life-science examples, identify correlations/relationships (e.g., correlation between a biomarker and disease) and mental steps as potential exceptions (cases: Mayo, Ambry Genetics, Grams).

name: Streamlined analysis when eligibility is self-evident
description: When eligibility is self-evident and the claim clearly does not attempt to tie up an exception, a streamlined analysis is appropriate and a full eligibility analysis is not needed.
guidance: Refer to training slides for examples. If using the streamlined approach, conclude SME analysis and continue with other patentability requirements; document the rationale if necessary.

name: If claim directed to a nature-based product: identify limitation(s), closest natural counterpart, and compare
description: For nature-based product limitations, (a) identify the limitation(s) in the claim that set forth or describe a nature-based product; (b) identify the closest naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state; (c) compare the claimed product to its counterpart to determine whether it exhibits markedly different characteristics.
guidance: Complete all of (a), (b) and (c). Based on the comparison, choose (i) the product exhibits markedly different characteristics (not a product-of-nature exception) or (ii) it lacks markedly different characteristics (is a product-of-nature exception). Provide factual support for the comparison.

name: If claim recites abstract idea/law of nature: identify limitation(s) and explain why they are exceptions
description: Identify the claim limitations that recite the exception and explain why those recited subject matters are judicial exceptions (for example, correlations or mental steps).
guidance: Explain how the limitation maps to case law examples (e.g., correlation = law of nature as in Mayo; mental comparison/diagnosis = abstract idea as in Ambry/Grams). Note that judicial exceptions need not be old or long-prevalent.

name: Are there additional elements beyond the exception (Step 2B — presence of additional elements)?
description: Determine whether the claim includes any features/limitations/steps beyond the identified exception(s). If the claim is a product composed of components not occurring together in nature, treat each component as an additional element relative to the others.
guidance: Choose 1 (no additional elements — make §101 rejection and consider suggesting elements to applicant) or 2 (yes — list the additional elements and continue to evaluate their significance). If suggesting claim amendments, identify elements in the disclosure that could be added.

name: Evaluate significance of additional elements — search for an 'inventive concept' (Step 2B)
description: Identify whether additional elements, individually or in combination, result in the claim amounting to significantly more than the judicial exception (i.e., whether they show an 'inventive concept').
guidance: Consider the additional elements individually and in combination, and evaluate relative to what applicant invented. Reasons supporting significance can include one or more of the following: improves another technology or technical field; improves the functioning of a computer itself; applies the exception with or by use of a particular machine (not a generic computer performing generic functions); effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing; adds a specific limitation other than what is well-understood, routine and conventional; adds unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application (not insignificant extrasolution activity such as mere data gathering); adds meaningful limitations more than generally linking use of the exception to a particular technological environment. Avoid counting as significant: generic computer functions, mere instructions to 'apply' the exception, or mere data gathering.

name: Presence of well-understood, routine and conventional elements is not dispositive
description: The presence of one or some well-understood, routine and conventional elements in a claim does not alone confer or preclude eligibility.
guidance: Note that such elements, especially when recited at a high level of generality (e.g., 'obtaining a sample'), may amount to insignificant pre-solution activity; however, they must be weighed in the context of the entire claim and in view of the invention.

name: Form paragraphs and sample Office Action wording for §101 rejections and eligible findings
description: Use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015 (and 7.05.01 where noted) for making §101 rejections or sample eligible findings. The worksheet gives example language for a §101 rejection explaining why a claim is directed to a judicial exception and lacks significantly more.
guidance: When making a rejection, include: identification of the exception (e.g., diagnosing when presence of JUL-1 is detected), explanation linking to case law (Mayo, Ambry, Grams), why additional elements are routine or mere data gathering, and why combination adds no meaningful limitations. When concluding eligibility, explicit explanation is not required in Office action unless clarification would benefit the record, but notes/examples of eligible claim reasoning are provided in the worksheet.

name: Suggest claim amendments from disclosure to attempt to confer eligibility
description: Identify elements in the disclosure that could be added to claims to make them eligible (e.g., a specific anti-JUL-1 antibody 'mAb-D33' or a type of antibody not routinely used to detect human proteins).
guidance: Consider adding unconventional or non-routine features (specific antibodies, particular machines, transformations, specific treatment steps) and document examples. Note that multiple other limitations might also render the claim eligible; list candidate limitations for applicant to consider.

name: Step one — directed to an abstract idea?
description: Assess whether the claim is 'directed to' an abstract idea (historically this has encompassed business methods and mathematical algorithms) or to an improvement in computer/technical functionality.
guidance: If the claim is properly characterized as a 'basic concept' (e.g., collecting, storing, transmitting data; business practices; mental steps; purely mathematical operations), it will often trigger step one. Courts have tended to list many computing activities as 'abstract' absent a showing of a technical improvement.

name: Step two — inventive concept / 'significantly more'
description: If a claim is directed to an abstract idea, assess whether claim elements, individually and in combination, provide an 'inventive concept' that transforms the abstract idea into a patent-eligible application.
guidance: The inventive concept requires more than the performance of well-understood, routine, and conventional activities previously known in the industry. Generic computer implementation, or use of standard hardware components, normally does not supply 'significantly more.'

name: Consider claims as a whole; avoid improper dissection
description: Claims must be considered 'as a whole' rather than dissected into old and new elements and ignoring the old (Diehr). Courts should not import novelty into the § 101 analysis by dissecting the claim.
guidance: Diehr holds that dissecting claims into old/new and treating the mathematical part as if it were in the prior art is improper. Alice states its approach is consistent with considering all elements both individually and in combination.

name: Improvement to computer functionality or other technical field is eligible
description: Inventions that 'improv[e] the functioning of the computer itself' or 'effect[] an improvement in any other technology or technical field' remain patent-eligible under Alice.
guidance: When claims are directed to a specific technical improvement in computers (e.g., new data structure, new way to organize memory, faster/simpler processing) courts have found eligibility (Enfish, DDR Holdings, Finjan). Drafting to articulate a concrete technological improvement supports eligibility.

name: Generic computer components alone do not confer eligibility
description: Reciting conventional computer components (e.g., 'data processing system,' 'communications controller,' 'memory,' 'processor,' 'network') is insufficient to render an abstract idea patent-eligible.
guidance: Functional recitation of generic hardware that performs conventional functions is treated as 'purely functional and generic.' Cases: Alice; Mortg. Grader; buySAFE; TLI. Claims should not rely on boilerplate computer hardware language as the inventive concept.

name: Question of fact whether elements are 'well-understood, routine, conventional' (Berkheimer)
description: Whether claim elements (or their combination) are well-understood, routine, and conventional is a question of fact; factual findings relevant to eligibility must be proven by clear and convincing evidence.
guidance: Berkheimer means courts cannot resolve some § 101 challenges on the pleadings or purely as a matter of law when there are factual disputes about conventionality. However, disclosure of a feature in a prior art reference does not automatically mean it was 'well-understood, routine, and conventional.'

name: Limiting to a specific field or adding post-solution activity does not save an abstract idea
description: Limiting an abstract idea to a particular field of use or adding token post-solution steps (e.g., performing on a computer, applying to a specific industry) does not make the concept patentable (Flook; Bilski).
guidance: Claims that merely restrict an abstract idea to a technological environment or append conventional post-solution activity are insufficient under Alice step two; courts view such limitations as immaterial unless they supply a technical improvement.

name: Claims directed to data-management or other high-level functional concepts are vulnerable
description: Claims that broadly claim concepts like 'receiving, storing, transmitting, comparing, deleting, and restricting access to data' without a concrete technical improvement are often characterized as abstract.
guidance: Courts have repeatedly found that high-level data-management functions, even when implemented with hashing or identifiers, are abstract when the claim merely applies known techniques to generalized data-management goals (TLI; Bridge & Post; decisions invalidating 'content-based identifier' applications).

name: Federal Circuit inconsistency and need for clarifying principles
description: Post-Alice, lower courts—especially the Federal Circuit—have applied the Alice/Mayo framework inconsistently, expanding the list of technologies considered 'abstract' and varying panel-to-panel.
guidance: Document emphasizes that clear guiding principles from the Supreme Court are needed to restore predictability. This affects how practitioners evaluate and draft claims and how courts review eligibility questions.

name: Utility requirement (35 U.S.C. 101) and utility-based rejections
description: A claimed invention must have patentable utility; lack of utility includes inoperativeness, perpetual motion, frivolous, fraudulent, or against public policy uses.
guidance: Use form paragraphs 7.05.02 (utility lacking), 7.05.03 (inoperative) and 7.05.04 (utility + 35 U.S.C. 112 first paragraph combinations). For 7.05.04 formats, insert whether utility is 'specific and substantial' or 'credible' depending on the factual situation; treat inoperative utilities as not credible. If utility is lacking, also consider enablement (35 U.S.C. 112) and apply In re Wands undue-experimentation analysis per MPEP §§2164-2164.08(c).

name: Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) and determination of prior art date
description: Use form paragraph to reject over a reference (patent or published application) with an earlier filing date that qualifies as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(e); reference must have common assignee or at least one common inventor when appropriate.
guidance: For applications filed on/after Nov 29, 1999, a 102(e) rejection might be overcome by showing the subject matter of the reference and the claimed invention were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment at the time the invention was made (see MPEP §706.02(l)(1) and (2)). Apply AIPA-amended 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rules for U.S. patents and U.S. published applications filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a), and for international applications with international filing date on/after Nov 29, 2000. Use pre-AIPA 102(e) only for U.S. patents issued directly/indirectly from international applications filed prior to Nov 29, 2000; consult form paragraph Examiner Notes (e.g., 7.12, 7.12.01) to determine the 102(e) date. Overcoming techniques include showing effective U.S. filing date of the reference under 37 CFR 1.131, submitting an oath/declaration under 37 CFR 1.130 that inventor is prior inventor together with a terminal disclaimer per 37 CFR 1.321(c), or proof of common ownership/assignment.

name: Graham v. Deere factual inquiries for obviousness (35 U.S.C. 103(a))
description: Obviousness analysis requires (1) determining the scope and contents of the prior art; (2) ascertaining differences between the prior art and the claims; (3) resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; and (4) considering objective evidence (secondary considerations) indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
guidance: An explanation of the rejection applying the Graham v. Deere test must follow the form paragraph for an obviousness rejection. Use these four inquiries to structure the factual and legal rationale for a 103 rejection and address any applicant arguments invoking Graham.

name: Use of combined 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103(a) rejection (form paragraph 7.27)
description: Form paragraph 7.27 may state a claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102 (anticipation) or alternatively under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) (obviousness) when appropriate.
guidance: This paragraph is NOT intended as a common substitute for making a single, specific 102 or 103 rejection; use only in limited circumstances such as: (a) disputed claim interpretation where one interpretation yields 102 and another yields 103; (b) when reference discloses all limitations except a property/function whose inherent presence is uncertain; (c) when a reference teaches a small genus placing a claimed species in public possession; (d) product-by-process situations where product appears same though made by different process; (e) where means-plus-function equivalence is uncertain; (f) overlapping but non-identical ranges where reference lacks specific example within claimed range. Always follow with a full explanation; if relying on 102(e) prior art, determine 102(e) date per AIPA rules as explained in Examiner Notes.

name: 35 U.S.C. 103(b) applicability for biotechnological processes
description: A biotechnological process using or resulting in a composition of matter that is novel and nonobvious under 103(a) shall be considered nonobvious under 103(a) if specified conditions are met.
guidance: Requirements (per statute and MPEP summary): (A) process and composition claims are in the same application or in separate applications having the same effective filing date; (B) composition and process were owned by the same person or subject to obligation of assignment at the time invented; (C) a patent on the process must also contain the claims to the composition used or made by the process, or if composition is claimed in another patent, the patents must expire on the same date; (D) the process falls within the statutory definition of 'biotechnological process'; and (E) a timely election to proceed under 103(b) is made via petition under 37 CFR 1.182 that establishes all requirements are satisfied. Definition of biotechnological process includes genetic alteration to express/inhibit nucleotide sequences, cell fusion producing a cell line expressing a specific protein (e.g., monoclonal antibody), and methods of using products produced by such processes. Timeliness: election normally by earlier of issue fee payment or filing an appeal brief; certain historical timing exceptions noted (e.g., issue fee paid before Mar 26, 1996).

name: Scope of enablement (commensurability) — 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph (7.31.03)
description: A rejection where the specification is enabling for some aspects but does not reasonably provide enablement commensurate in scope with the claims.
guidance: Use form paragraph 7.31.03 preceded by 7.30.01. Identify which subject matter is enabled and which aspects the specification does not enable; explain whether the specification enables 'make'/'use'/'make and use' for the scope commensurate with the claims and apply In re Wands factors as appropriate.

name: Essential subject matter missing from claims (enablement/critical feature omitted) — 7.33.01
description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, where disclosure is not enabling and a feature considered critical or essential by applicant to practice the invention is omitted from the claims.
guidance: Precede with form paragraph 7.30.01. In bracket 2 recite the subject matter omitted from the claims. Examiner must cite applicant statement/argument/drawings or other evidence demonstrating the feature was considered essential by applicant and explain why omission renders the claims non-enabling (see In re Mayhew).

name: Definiteness requirement (35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph) — failure to particularly point out and distinctly claim
description: Claims must particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which applicant regards as the invention; otherwise they are indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph.
guidance: Use form paragraph 7.34.01 preceded by form paragraph 7.30.02. Follow with one or more specific form paragraphs 7.34.02–7.34.11 as applicable, or supply a full explanation identifying the particular terms/limitations making claims indefinite and why. If the claim scope can be determined by one of ordinary skill in the art, a 7.34.01 rejection is inappropriate. See §§2171-2174 for guidance.

name: Terminology inconsistent with accepted meaning (applicant as lexicographer) — 7.34.02
description: When applicant acts as own lexicographer redefining a claim term contrary to its ordinary meaning, the written description must clearly redefine the term to put one skilled in the art on notice of the uncommon definition.
guidance: Use form paragraph 7.34.02 (preceded by 7.34.01). Identify the term, the meaning assigned by applicant in claim, and the accepted meaning; supply support for examiner's stated accepted meaning (textbook/dictionary). The specification must clearly redefine the term or the term renders the claim indefinite.

name: Relative term / term of degree rendering claim indefinite — 7.34.03
description: Use of a relative term (term of degree) without a standard for ascertaining the requisite degree renders the claim indefinite if one skilled in the art would not be reasonably apprised of scope.
guidance: Precede with form paragraph 7.34.01. In bracketed explanation specify which parameter/quantity/limitation is rendered indefinite by the relative term and why; provide analysis showing absence of a standard in the claim or specification.

name: Broad range and narrow range/limitation in same claim rendering indefiniteness — 7.34.04
description: A claim that recites a broad range or limitation together with a narrower range/limitation that falls within the broad range may be indefinite because it raises doubt whether the narrow language is exemplary or required.
guidance: Use form paragraph 7.34.04 (preceded by 7.34.01). Identify the broader range/limitation and the narrower one (insert in brackets) and explain how the inclusion creates indefiniteness. See cited Board of Patent Appeals decisions (Ex parte Wu, etc.) for examples. Modify the paragraph to fit other instances of indefiniteness arising from similar language patterns.

name: Lack of antecedent basis in the claims — 7.34.05
description: A claim reciting a limitation without proper antecedent basis (e.g., introducing an element without previously identifying it) is indefinite.
guidance: Use form paragraph 7.34.05 (preceded by 7.34.01). In bracketed text insert the limitation lacking antecedent basis and indicate where in the claim it appears; explain why antecedent basis is insufficient to inform one of ordinary skill in the art of the scope and meaning of the limitation.

name: Patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101 (Alice/Mayo two-step framework)
description: Evaluate (1) whether the claims are directed to a patent-ineligible concept (e.g., an abstract idea), and if so (2) whether the claim elements, individually or as an ordered combination, amount to 'significantly more' — an inventive concept that transforms the abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter.
guidance: Practical application: courts may treat claims directed to 'collecting, analyzing, manipulating, and displaying data' or 'filtering patient [physical] signals to increase accuracy' as abstract ideas; to survive, a pleading must allege specific, plausible factual allegations showing the claim amounts to significantly more than the abstract idea (citing Alice; Aatrix Software, Inc. v. Green Shades Software, Inc., 882 F.3d 1121 (Fed. Cir. 2018)).

name: Pleadings standard for §101 challenges (sufficiency of allegations)
description: When faced with a motion to dismiss under RCFC 12(b)(6), a plaintiff must plead specific, plausible factual allegations sufficient to show that the patent in practice amounts to 'significantly more' than an abstract idea and/or that its techniques were implemented in a specific combination or in an uncommon manner.
guidance: If the complaint fails to recite such specific factual allegations, dismissal for failure to state a claim is appropriate. The court in this case held plaintiff did not plead facts demonstrating an inventive concept and therefore the patents were directed to ineligible subject matter.

name: When evaluating patent claims, courts consider the patents 'as a whole' and may dismiss claims directed to abstract ideas even where the specification describes advantages
description: Courts look to the character of the claimed invention as a whole. Even if the specification describes purposes like facilitating diagnosis or eliminating background noise, the claims may still be directed to an abstract idea absent an inventive concept.
guidance: Example from opinion: despite descriptions of a 'simple interface' or noise-reduction objectives in the specification, the court found the claims directed to abstract ideas (collecting/processing/displaying data) and lacking the required inventive concept; thus, factual allegations about purported improvements must connect to claim elements that amount to 'significantly more.'

name: Fed. Cir. R. 28: Addendum organization, standard of review heading, patent claim language, and informal brief form clarifications
description: Moving the principal brief addendum requirements to their own subsection and addressing multi-volume addenda; requiring a separate heading for the standard of review and clarifying location expectations; clarifying patent claim language on inside front cover of principal briefs and relocating requirement to FCR 32; clarifying informal brief form requirement; requiring separate heading for the jurisdictional statement in informal response briefs; adding Practice Note to address inclusion of patents in the addendum.

name: Fed. Cir. R. 32: Relocate patent claim language, spacing, and word-count exclusions
description: Relocating patent claim language on inside front brief cover requirement to this rule from FCR 28 and permitting single-spacing of this language; excluding inside front cover contents and contents required on the first page of a filing in lieu of a cover from word counts; clarifying informal brief form and type-volume requirements.

name: Scope and Purpose of IPRs and PGRs
description: An inter partes review (IPR) or post-grant review (PGR) is a proceeding designed to allow a Petitioner to attack the validity of one or more claims of an issued patent. These proceedings are designed to provide a faster, cheaper alternative to district court litigation. IPRs and PGRs only examine validity and do not adjudicate infringement or award damages, injunctions, or other remedies.
guidance: Use IPR/PGRs when the goal is to challenge patent validity quickly and cost-effectively; they do not resolve infringement or award relief beyond patentability determinations.

name: Differences: Eligibility and Window of Opportunity (IPR vs PGR)
description: For PGRs, only patents with at least one AIA claim (priority date on or after March 16, 2013) are eligible, and a PGR must be brought within nine months of issuance (or re-issuance). For IPRs, all patents are eligible and there is no general deadline to file, but if the patent has at least one AIA claim, one must wait to file a Petition until the later of nine months after issuance (or re-issuance) or termination of any PGR on the patent.
guidance: Check patent priority dates and issuance/re-issuance dates to determine whether to pursue PGR or IPR and to avoid premature filing.

name: Permissible Grounds of Attack (IPR vs PGR)
description: For IPRs, the only attacks allowed are anticipation (35 U.S.C. § 102) and obviousness (35 U.S.C. § 103) based upon patents and printed publications. For PGRs, in addition to anticipation and obviousness, one can also attack based on lack of written description (§ 112), indefiniteness (§ 112), lack of enablement (§ 112), and eligibility (§ 101).
guidance: Select the proceeding that permits the substantive grounds you intend to assert. Note eligibility challenges (§ 101) cannot be initially raised in IPR but may arise for proposed amended claims.

name: Required Contents of a Petition
description: The Petition must set forth: the grounds for standing, the claim(s) attacked, the statutory grounds for the attack, how the claims are to be construed, and how/why the construed claim is unpatentable. The Petition must also identify the real parties-in-interest, related matters, lead and back-up counsel, and service information. The Petition is typically supported by one or more declarations of technical experts and supporting exhibits.
guidance: Ensure petitions include complete procedural and substantive components; include clear claim charts, claim constructions, and supporting expert declarations/exhibits.

name: Cost and Fee Structure
description: PTO filing fee for an IPR is currently $19,000 (for up to 20 claims) and $22,500 for the post-institution fee (for up to 20 claims), which must be paid at filing. PTO filing fee for a PGR is currently $20,000 (for up to 20 claims) and $27,500 for the post-institution fee (for up to 20 claims), which must be paid at filing. Filing fees alone are at least $41,500 for IPRs and $47,500 for PGRs. Additional claims can be challenged with payment of additional fees. If the petition is not instituted, the post-institution fee will be refunded upon request. Significant additional attorney and expert fees are typical.
guidance: Budget for both PTO fees and substantial outside counsel/expert costs; account for additional-claim fees and possible refunds if not instituted.

name: Use and Importance of Technical Experts
description: Likely yes. Petitions are typically supported by at least one detailed declaration of a technical expert. The expert should have extensive experience in the subject matter of the challenged claims, be technically proficient, able to set forth opinions and bases, and able to withstand deposition. Commonly the same expert is used for the Petition and the Reply, though additional experts (e.g., economists) may be warranted to rebut Patent Owner evidence on objective indicia of non-obviousness.
guidance: Retain qualified experts early; ensure declarations are detailed and defensible under cross-examination.

name: Motions to Amend — Availability and Burdens
description: Patent Owner may propose substitute claims (generally claim-for-claim). Motions to Amend are granted very rarely. Rules (as of Jan. 2021) state that the Patent Owner 'bears the burden of persuasion to show, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the motion to amend complies' with statutory/regulatory requirements; the Petitioner 'bears the burden of persuasion to show, by a preponderance of the evidence, that any proposed substitute claims are unpatentable.' The Board may, in the interests of justice, exercise discretion to grant or deny a motion to amend only for reasons supported by readily identifiable and persuasive evidence of record.
guidance: Anticipate high bar for successful motions to amend; litigate amendment issues aggressively and develop record-based reasons for/against amendment.

name: Final Written Decision Content and Timing
description: Within three months of the Oral Hearing the panel issues its Final Written Decision, which addresses all bases and all claims raised in the Petition as well as patentability of any proposed amended claims. Final Written Decisions typically address claim construction (when necessary), weight given to experts' opinions, fact-findings regarding scope and content of the prior art, the Panel’s judgment on disputed evidence, and reasoning behind the Board’s conclusion as to patentability.
guidance: Develop record evidence and expert testimony to support favorable fact-findings and to counter opposing expert weight arguments.

name: Estoppel Effects — Impact on District Court and PTO Proceedings
description: Estoppel attaches once a Final Written Decision issues. A Petitioner cannot assert in district court any ground (invalidity argument) that was raised or reasonably could have been raised in the IPR or PGR. Similarly, the outcome may impact other proceedings at the PTO: a Petitioner (and any RPI and privy) is estopped from requesting or maintaining a proceeding in the PTO with respect to a claim for which a Final Written Decision has issued on any ground that was raised or reasonably could have been raised in the IPR or PGR. See 35 U.S.C §§ 315(e), 325(e); 37 C.F.R. § 42.73(d)(1).
guidance: Analyze long-term litigation strategy and collateral estoppel consequences before filing or settling; preserve issues you want to keep available for other forums.

name: Statistics and Strategic Considerations (why file)
description: Patents attacks before the PTAB have a high rate of success — approximately 60% of claims for which a trial has been instituted have been found unpatentable. Considering the high 'kill rate,' the speed, and the cost savings relative to district court proceedings, many find IPRs and PGRs attractive tools for removing patent obstacles.
guidance: Factor institution/outcome statistics into forum selection and client counseling, but assess the merits of the specific claims and prior art before filing.

name: Claim language defines scope
description: By understanding the meaning of the words in a claim and by understanding that the words in a claim set forth the requirements that a product or process must meet in order to be covered by that claim, you will be able to understand the scope of coverage for each claim.
guidance: Once you understand what each claim covers, you are prepared to decide issues such as infringement and invalidity. (Implied: compare accused product/process to claim requirements to determine coverage.)

name: Transitional phrase meanings (comprising/consisting of/consisting essentially of)
description: The document explains the different transition phrases used in claims: 'comprising' is open-ended and allows additional steps; 'consisting of' is closed-ended meaning 'I claim what follows and nothing else'; 'consisting essentially of' is a middle ground between 'comprising' and 'consisting of'.
guidance: Authorities and case citations illustrate how these transitions affect claim scope (e.g., Cook Biotech, Invitrogen, Conoco, Vehicular Techs., CIAS, AK Steel). Apply the appropriate transition meaning when comparing accused product/process to the claim.

name: Independent vs. dependent claims
description: An 'independent claim' sets forth all of the requirements that must be met in order to be covered by that claim. A 'dependent claim' does not recite all requirements itself but refers to another claim, incorporating that claim's requirements and adding its own.
guidance: To determine what a dependent claim covers, it is necessary to look at both the dependent claim and any other claim(s) to which it refers. A dependent claim includes all requirements of the claim(s) to which it refers plus additional requirements. (Note: It may be helpful to submit to the jury a chart setting forth all dependencies.)

name: Means-plus-function / Step-plus-function (§112, ¶6) — scope
description: A 'means for [function]' or 'step for [function]' phrase has a special meaning: it does not cover all structures/acts that could perform the function, but instead covers a structure (or set of structures) or acts that perform that function and that are identical or 'equivalent' to the structure(s)/act(s) described in the patent for performing that function.
guidance: The court will identify the structures/acts described in the patent that perform the function; those identifications should be applied like any other claim-term definition. The issue of whether two structures/acts are identical or equivalent is for the jury to decide; the judge will later explain how to determine 'equivalence.'

name: Means/step-plus-function literal infringement test
description: A product/process meets a means/step-plus-function claim requirement if (1) it has a structure/set of structures or action/set of actions that perform the identical function recited in the claim, and (2) that structure/set of structures or action/set of actions is identical or 'equivalent' to one or more of the described structure(s)/action(s) from the specification.
guidance: If the product does not perform the specific function, it does not literally infringe. If it performs the function but the structure/action is not identical or equivalent to the disclosed structure/act, it does not literally infringe. Equivalence requires that differences were insubstantial or that they perform substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result, and that interchangeability was known to persons of ordinary skill at the time the patent issued. Equivalence cannot embrace technology developed after issuance.

name: Infringement assessed claim-by-claim
description: Infringement is assessed on a claim-by-claim basis; there may be infringement as to one claim but not another.
guidance: The patentee must prove infringement of one or more claims by a preponderance of the evidence (more likely than not). Compare the accused product/process to each and every claim requirement to determine whether all requirements of that claim are met.

name: Five types of infringement to consider
description: There are five possible ways that a claim may be infringed: (1) direct infringement; (2) active inducement; (3) contributory infringement; (4) infringement through the supply of components from the United States to another country; and (5) infringement through importation of a product made abroad by a patented process.
guidance: Active inducement and contributory infringement are indirect infringement and cannot exist without someone else engaging in direct infringement. The jury will be instructed on each type in detail.

name: Literal direct infringement — element-by-element rule
description: To prove direct literal infringement, the patentee must show by a preponderance of the evidence that the accused made, used, sold, offered for sale within, or imported into the U.S. a product or process that meets all of the requirements of a claim without permission during the patent term.
guidance: You must compare the accused product/process with each and every one of the claim's requirements. If any claim element is missing, there is no literal infringement. Dependent-claim logic: if an independent claim is not infringed, dependent claims that refer to it cannot be infringed; if an independent claim is infringed, you still must decide separately whether dependent claims are also infringed.

name: Doctrine of equivalents — general test
description: Even if the accused product/process does not literally meet all claim requirements, it can infringe under the doctrine of equivalents if it contains elements or performs steps corresponding to each and every claim requirement that are equivalent to the claimed requirement.
guidance: An element or step is equivalent if a person of ordinary skill would have considered the differences insubstantial, or would have found that the structure/action: (1) performs substantially the same function, (2) in substantially the same way, (3) to achieve substantially the same result. Interchangeability must have been known to a person of ordinary skill at the relevant time; present-day interchangeability alone is insufficient. Equivalence must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence.

name: Limits on doctrine of equivalents — prior art / obviousness
description: Prior art may preclude a finding of infringement under the doctrine of equivalents. The jury must determine what products/processes are in the prior art and what would have been obvious from the prior art to a person of ordinary skill at the time of the invention.
guidance: If the alleged equivalent feature was in the prior art or would have been obvious, you must find no infringement under the doctrine of equivalents. The patentee of the hypothetical equivalent claim must be shown by the alleged infringer by a preponderance of the evidence.

name: Prosecution history estoppel (argument- and amendment-based) constraints
description: A patentee may be estopped from asserting equivalence where, during prosecution, the applicant distinguished the unmet requirement from the allegedly equivalent alternative or amended claims in a way that surrendered scope.
guidance: For amendment-based estoppel, to find equivalents despite an amendment you must find one or more factors such as: (1) the amendment substituted a broader requirement for a narrower one or replaced equal scope; (2) the reason for the amendment was unrelated to patentability; (3) a person of ordinary skill at the time of amendment would not have foreseen substitution of the allegedly equivalent alternative; (4) the amendment was tangential; or (5) other reasons (e.g., shortcomings of language) prevented claiming the alternative. If none apply, equivalence may be precluded.

name: Vitiation limitation on equivalents
description: You may not determine that an alternative aspect of a product/process is equivalent to an unmet requirement if a finding of equivalence would effectively eliminate that requirement.
guidance: The alleged equivalent cannot eliminate or ignore an element or requirement of the claim (i.e., cannot 'vitiate' the claim element).

name: Indirect infringement — contributory infringement elements
description: Contributory infringement exists if the patentee proves by a preponderance of the evidence that: (1) the alleged infringer sells/offers/imports a component of a product or apparatus for use in a process during the patent term; (2) the component has no substantial noninfringing use; (3) the component constitutes a material part of the invention; (4) the alleged infringer is aware of the patent and knows that the component's only substantial use may be covered by a claim or satisfy a claim under the doctrine of equivalents; and (5) that use directly infringes the claim.
guidance: Each of the above requirements must be proved by a preponderance of the evidence. Case law (35 U.S.C. §271(c), Aro, Ricoh, etc.) provides context such as 'not a staple article' concept and knowledge requirements.

name: §271(f)(1) — supply-from-U.S. for foreign combination (active inducement) elements
description: Under §271(f)(1), the patentee must prove by a preponderance that: (1) the alleged infringer supplies (or causes to be supplied) components from the United States to a place outside the U.S. that make up all or a substantial portion of the invention claimed; (2) the alleged infringer intentionally took action to cause another outside the U.S. to assemble the components; (3) the alleged infringer knew of the patent and knew the encouraged acts constitute infringement; and (4) the encouraged acts would constitute direct infringement if carried out in the United States.
guidance: If the alleged infringer believed the acts it encouraged would not constitute infringement if carried out in the U.S., it cannot be liable under §271(f)(1). Specific intent to cause assembly abroad and knowledge of the patent are required; proof is by preponderance of the evidence.

name: Purposive construction (Catnic / Lord Diplock)
description: A patent specification should be given a purposive construction rather than a purely literal one; the question is whether persons with practical knowledge would understand that strict compliance with a particular descriptive word or phrase was intended by the patentee to be an essential requirement of the invention.
guidance: Avoid meticulous verbal analysis; interpret claims in light of practical knowledge of the relevant art. Use Lord Diplock's Catnic formulation as the baseline for construing specifications under the Patents Act/EPC Protocol.

name: Hoffmann's three-question test (overview)
description: When deciding whether a variant embodied in an alleged infringing product falls within the claim as properly interpreted, the court should ask: (1) does the variant have a material effect on the way the invention works; (2) would it have been obvious at the publication date to a skilled reader that the variant has no material effect; and (3) would a skilled reader nonetheless have understood from the claim language that the patentee intended strict compliance with the primary meaning?
guidance: Apply the three questions sequentially: materiality (fact), obviousness (fact), and patentee intent/construction (construction). A negative at any stage generally leads to no infringement, but the third question is one of construction and can override the first two.

name: Question (1): Material effect on the way the invention works
description: If the variant has a material effect upon the way the invention works, the variant is outside the claim and there is no infringement.
guidance: Two key guidelines: (a) a 'variant' is a feature in the alleged infringing product not within the literal or contextual meaning of a claim term; (b) whether the variant makes a material difference is a question of fact (not construction) and must be sensibly answered with reference to the patent. Describe the invention's working at the same level of generality as the claim.

name: Question (3): Whether the skilled reader would construe the claim as excluding the variant
description: Would the reader skilled in the art have nevertheless understood from the language of the claim that the patentee intended strict compliance with the primary (literal) meaning as an essential requirement of the invention? If yes, the variant is outside the claim and there is no infringement.
guidance: This is a question of construction (not fact); answers to the first two questions are not conclusive. Consider the claim language, specification (including any 'equivalents clause'), drawings, and expert views about how a skilled reader would understand the patentee's intention.

name: Use and interpretation of an 'equivalents clause' in the specification
description: A general statement in the description that embodiments are 'illustrative and not restrictive' and that 'all variations which come within the meaning and range of equivalency of the claims are intended to be embraced' can be evidence regarding patentee intent to include equivalents.
guidance: Courts may read such a clause as directing that claims be construed purposively under Catnic/Protocol, but the clause does not automatically broaden claims to include variants if a skilled reader would construe the claim literally. How the clause is interpreted depends on context and expert evidence.

name: Statutory/Protocol interpretive rule (Section 125 / Protocol on Article 69 EPC)
description: For purposes of the Patents Act (and corresponding EPC Article 69), an invention is taken to be that specified in the claim as interpreted by the description and any drawings; the Protocol on the Interpretation of Article 69 applies.
guidance: Claims are to be interpreted by reference to the specification and drawings, with the Protocol guiding balance between literal scope and scope indicated by description. This statutory framework governs purposive construction analyses.

name: German two-question test for equivalence
description: The German District Court applied a two-question test: (1) does the alleged equivalent have the identical effect as the claimed element (i.e., is it an equivalent); and (2) would the alleged equivalent have been an obvious equivalent to a person skilled in the art from the prospective viewpoint at the time the patent was issued.
guidance: The court begins by using the claim to determine the patent's 'teaching.' Both questions involve factual inquiry (identical effect) and an obviousness assessment at the patent issue date; if both are satisfied, infringement can be found under equivalence.

name: Role of expert testimony in equivalence and construction inquiries
description: Expert witnesses are used to address factual questions (material effect; obviousness) and to inform how a person skilled in the art would understand claims, specification, and any equivalents clause.
guidance: Experts may present competing views on whether a variant makes a material difference, whether it would have been obvious to substitute, and whether the specification indicates an intent to cover alternatives. Courts weigh expert evidence in applying factual and construction questions.

name: Disclosed inherent properties part of 'invention as a whole' inquiry
description: In delineating the invention as a whole, look not only to subject matter literally recited in the claim but also to those properties of the subject matter which are inherent in the subject matter and are disclosed in the specification.
guidance: Examples: In re Antonie — consider inherent parameters (tank volume to contactor area) disclosed in specification as part of invention; In re Papesch — a compound and all its properties are inseparable. However, 'Obviousness cannot be predicated on what is not known at the time an invention is made,' (In re Rijckaert). See MPEP § 2112 for inherency rejection requirements.

name: Examiner's required articulation in a 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection (A–D)
description: When indicating a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103, the examiner should set forth: (A) relevant teachings of prior art relied upon (with citations); (B) differences between the claim and applied references; (C) proposed modification(s) of the applied references necessary to arrive at the claimed subject matter; (D) explanation why the claimed invention would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill at the time the invention was made.
guidance: Cite relevant column/page/line where appropriate. Positive inclusion of every reference relied upon is required (In re Hoch). Clear communication of rationale helps applicants respond and supports later interpretation of issued patents.

name: Rationale G — Teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art to modify or combine references
description: Obviousness may be supported where some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art would have led one of ordinary skill to modify a reference or to combine reference teachings to arrive at the claimed invention.
guidance: The teaching/suggestion/motivation can be explicit or implicit; examiners must articulate the factual basis for why the prior art would prompt the modification or combination (link to Graham findings).

name: Drawings constitute the entire legal disclosure (the claim)
description: Under MPEP § 1503.02 and 35 U.S.C. § 171, the drawing disclosure is 'the most important element of the application' and 'the drawing is the claim.' There is no written description of the design — only the illustration defines what is protected.
guidance: Every line, surface, view, and broken line directly determines the scope of protection. Nothing should be left to conjecture; the drawings must provide a complete disclosure of the appearance of the design.

name: Broken lines — disclaims environmental structure and affects claim scope
description: Broken lines show environmental structure or context that forms no part of the claimed design; solid lines show claimed elements. Every use of broken lines must be explained in the specification.
guidance: Broken lines may NOT be used to show hidden planes or internal surfaces; alternate positions shown by full and broken lines in the same view are NOT permitted. Strategic choices about broken vs. solid lines directly impact claim breadth (more broken lines = potentially broader scope) and must be coordinated with counsel.

name: Color drawings and photographs rules
description: Color drawings are permitted without a petition, but if color is included it becomes an integral part of the claimed design. Photographs may be used in lieu of ink drawings but cannot be combined with black-and-white line drawings in the same application.
guidance: Practitioners generally recommend black-and-white line drawings unless color is essential. Photographs must not show environmental structure and have limitations for strategic shading/broken-line use.

name: Reference numerals not required for design drawings
description: Unlike utility patent drawings, reference numerals are not required for design patent drawings because there are no written claims needing reference support.
guidance: Do not include unnecessary reference numerals in design drawings; if preparing coordinated utility drawings, include numerals where required for utility claims.

name: Strategic broken-line usage affects claim breadth
description: Choosing what to show in broken lines versus solid lines is a strategic decision: more broken lines can yield broader claim scope but requires careful drafting and specification language.
guidance: Work with patent counsel to balance claiming scope and enforceability; deliberate broken-line strategy should be determined before preparing the drawing set.

name: Claims not requested are not reexamined
description: Claims for which reexamination has not been requested will not be reexamined.
guidance: Explicitly identify which claims are part of the reexamination order. Example language: 'reexamination has not been requested for claims 5–20 ... will not be reexamined.'

name: Content required in patent owner statement (37 CFR 1.530(c))
description: Any statement filed by the patent owner shall clearly point out why the subject matter as claimed is not anticipated or rendered obvious by the prior art patents or printed publications, either alone or in any reasonable combinations.
guidance: Statements must specifically address anticipation/obviousness over each cited reference and combinations; where a third-party requester filed the request, the owner’s statement must be served on the requester per §1.248.

name: General manner of making amendments in reexamination (37 CFR 1.530(d))
description: A proposed amendment is made by filing a paper directing specified changes to the patent specification (including claims) or drawings. Amendments may accompany an owner request under §1.510(e), be part of a patent owner statement under paragraph (b), or be submitted during prosecution under §1.550(a) or §1.937.
guidance: Follow §1.530(d) pathways for timing of when amendments may be submitted; adhere to formal presentation rules in §1.52.

name: Amendment of disclosure to secure correspondence
description: The disclosure must be amended, when required by the Office, to correct inaccuracies of description and definition, and to secure substantial correspondence between the claims, the remainder of the specification, and the drawings.
guidance: Office may require specification amendments to ensure support for claim changes and internal consistency.

name: No enlargement of claim scope or new matter (37 CFR 1.530(j))
description: No amendment may enlarge the scope of the claims of the patent or introduce new matter. No amendment may be proposed for entry in an expired patent. Amendments will not be effective until the reexamination certificate is issued and published.
guidance: Reject amendments that broaden claims or introduce new matter (see 35 U.S.C. 305 and MPEP §2258). Even accepted amendments are not effective until certificate issuance; expired patents cannot be broadened.

name: Formal requirements for papers (37 CFR 1.52)
description: Papers to become part of USPTO records must be on uniform-size sheets (A4 or 8.5x11), unbound, flexible, white, single-sided, with specified margins (top ≥2.0 cm, left ≥2.5 cm, right ≥2.0 cm, bottom ≥2.0 cm), typed or machine-printed in permanent dark ink, with sufficient clarity/contrast. Specifications must be 1.5 or double spaced, nonscript font (e.g., Arial, Times Roman, Courier) preferably size 12 (but not smaller than 0.08 inch), single column; claims and abstract must begin on separate physical/electronic pages. Electronic filings must comply with Office electronic filing requirements.
guidance: Follow all 1.52(a)/(b) formalities strictly. See §§1.58 and 1.84 for formulas/tables and drawings formatting. Avoid holes in sheets; pre-printed Office forms exceptions noted.

name: Status of claims and support for claim changes (37 CFR 1.530(e))
description: Whenever there is an amendment to the claims, there must be supplied, on separate pages from the changes, the status (i.e., pending or canceled) as of the date of the amendment for all patent claims and added claims, and an explanation of the support in the disclosure of the patent for the changes to the claims made by the amendment paper.
guidance: Failure to submit claim status generally results in an informal response (see MPEP §2266.02) and may lead to non-entry if submitted after final rejection. The support explanation is critical to meritorious consideration (see MPEP §2266.01).

name: Amendment entry policy
description: Amendments which comply with 37 CFR 1.530(d)-(j) and are formally presented pursuant to 37 CFR 1.52(a) and (b), and contain all fees required, will be entered in the reexamination file pursuant to guidelines in MPEP §2234.
guidance: Ensure full compliance with procedural, formatting, marking, support, claim-status, and fee requirements to have amendments entered; otherwise, expect informal responses or non-entry.

name: Who may sign the reissue declaration
description: The inventor’s oath or declaration must be executed by or with respect to each inventor before the case can be released for examination. The assignee of 100% of the entire right, title and interest (who must be named as the reissue applicant) may sign the declaration if the application does not seek to enlarge the scope of the claims in the original patent, or the original application was filed under 37 CFR 1.46 by the assignee of the entire interest.
guidance: If the reissue applicant is a juristic entity, the declaration must be signed by an official who has a title that carries apparent authority or by someone who makes a statement of authorization to act (e.g., employee authorized by corporate resolution). A patent practitioner may sign the reissue declaration as an official of a juristic entity only if given authority as explained above and may not sign a substitute statement merely on the basis of having power of attorney. See MPEP § 605.01 and 37 CFR 1.175(e).

name: Substitute statement for unavailable inventor
description: The patentee, or current patent owner if there has been an assignment, may sign a substitute statement in accordance with 37 CFR 1.64 on behalf of an inventor who is deceased, legally incapacitated, cannot be found or reached after diligent effort, or refused to execute the oath or declaration under 37 CFR 1.175.
guidance: This substitute-statement procedure is available even if the reissue application was filed to enlarge claim scope (e.g., a broadening reissue), pursuant to 37 CFR 1.175(c) and § 1.64. Forms such as PTO/AIA/07 may be used where appropriate.

name: Pre-AIA 37 CFR 1.175 substantive requirements for reissue oath/declaration
description: For reissue applications filed before September 16, 2012 the reissue oath/declaration, in addition to complying with § 1.63, must state: (1) the applicant believes the original patent to be wholly or partly inoperative or invalid by reason of a defective specification or drawing, or by reason of claiming more or less than the patentee had the right to claim, stating at least one error being relied upon as the basis for reissue; and (2) all errors being corrected in the reissue application up to the time of filing arose without any deceptive intention on the part of the applicant.
guidance: Any error corrected that is not covered by the original oath/declaration requires a supplemental oath/declaration. The examiner checks for presence of the averment, not the truth of absence of deceptive intent. See pre-AIA 37 CFR 1.175 and MPEP § 1414.02.

name: Content required by 37 CFR 1.63 in reissue oath/declaration
description: The reissue oath/declaration must comply with pre-AIA 37 CFR 1.63 and include the averments required by 1.63(a) and (b): (A) that applicants have reviewed and understand the contents of the specification, including claims as amended; (B) believe the named inventor(s) to be the original and first inventor(s) of the claimed subject matter; and (C) acknowledge the duty to disclose to the Office all information known to be material to patentability as defined in 37 CFR 1.56.
guidance: OPAP should review reissue oaths/declarations for compliance with 1.63; the examiner is not required to do so. See MPEP § 602 and MPEP § 1414.02.

name: Excess claims fees for reissue applications
description: Excess claims fees apply per 37 CFR 1.16(h) for each independent claim in excess of three and per 37 CFR 1.16(i) for each claim (independent or dependent) in excess of twenty.
guidance: For reissue applications filed on/after Dec 8, 2004, where a petition under 37 CFR 1.138(d) to expressly abandon was filed on/after Mar 10, 2006, applicant may request refund of search and excess claims fees paid in the application (see MPEP § 711.01). The number of claims in the original patent is not relevant in determining excess claims fees for a reissue. Excess claims fees due with an amendment are required before any consideration of the amendment by the examiner; additions of claims require payment. Amendments filed before first Office action presenting additional claims without full fees will not be entered and will be non-responsive (see MPEP § 714.03).

name: Breadth of claim — claiming every shape equals claiming a principle
description: If you claim every shape (or every form of achieving a result), you claim a principle; you must claim some specific mode of doing it.
guidance: Walton's case (claiming elasticity to card backs 'from whatever source derived') was said to amount to a claim for a principle. The courts will reject or construe overly general claims that effectively monopolize a principle rather than a particular mode.

name: No patent vitiation solely for generality of claim — fact-specific adjudication
description: Letters-patent have not been held vitiated merely because of generality of the claim; questions of claim generality must be decided on the special facts of each case.
guidance: Although courts guard against monopolization of principles, they have not adopted a blanket rule invalidating broadly worded claims in every instance; context, disclosure, and circumstances determine outcome.

name: Declaration should set forth substance of the grant
description: The substance of the grant should be set forth — that the letters-patent secured to the plaintiff for a term (e.g., fourteen years) the full and exclusive right of practising the invention — and the invention should be described briefly as set forth in the letters-patent, with profert.
guidance: When describing the invention, using the words of the patent is common; the declaration must connect the grant to the claimed subject-matter and make profert of the patent.

name: Two-step judicial test (Mayo/Alice framework)
description: Courts use a two-step test: (1) Is the claim directed to a law of nature or abstract idea? (2) If so, does it add 'something more' (an inventive concept) to make it patentable?
guidance: The test is described as vague—what counts as 'something more' is unclear. Practical drafting should therefore emphasize concrete steps, human intervention, and real-world application to satisfy the second step.

name: Diagnostics: avoid natural-law rejections
description: Diagnostic tests and biomarker correlations are vulnerable because they can be characterized as natural correlations or laws of nature.
guidance: To protect diagnostics, focus on 'how the result is obtained' (sample preparation, lab techniques), include actionable steps that change care, or tie the test to a treatment decision. Avoid claims that merely recite a correlation between biomarker and disease.

name: Methods of treatment: require concrete steps
description: Method-of-treatment claims are generally safer if they describe clear, concrete steps (e.g., administering a specific dose to achieve a result).
guidance: Careful drafting is required when the method relies on a diagnostic step—if that diagnostic is seen as a natural law, the whole claim can be vulnerable. Emphasize the treatment action and its practical implementation.

name: CRISPR and gene-editing claims: draft around application/details
description: Claims centered solely on CRISPR components may be seen as too close to natural bacterial proteins; claims emphasizing novel uses, guide sequences, or delivery methods are more likely to be approved.
guidance: Structure claims to focus on specific applications (e.g., novel guide sequences, novel delivery systems, specific gene modification methods) and measurable improvements. Broad claims like 'we used CRISPR to cut this gene' are vulnerable.

name: Patenting natural products and derivatives: require transformation
description: Things that exist in nature 'exactly as claimed' are not patentable; derivatives or modifications that confer new properties can be patentable.
guidance: Emphasize the chemical/structural modification, improved delivery, or binding to other compounds that create new function. Highlight the transformation from natural to engineered and why it is inventive and non-obvious.

name: Claim specificity vs. breadth (scope management)
description: Specific, detailed claims linking biology to industrial use tend to withstand challenges better than broad, vague claims.
guidance: Draft a mix of claim types but favor specificity (sequences, structures, manufacturing steps) for enforceability. Broad claims are easier to attack in litigation or eligibility analyses.

name: Software-biology combinations: demonstrate technical effect in biotech
description: Combining software with biological processes demands clarity that the invention has a technical, biological effect rather than mere data handling.
guidance: For platforms, pipelines, or predictive models, show how the software produces a biological result (identifies a target that leads to compound production, improves experimental outcome). Avoid claims that merely visualize or organize data.

name: Litigation-readiness: drafting for enforcement and defense
description: Patents are often litigated; how claims are worded influences their strength in court.
guidance: Anticipate disputes by using precise language, emphasizing practical implementation, and documenting development milestones. Specific sequences, structures, and manufacturing steps make patents harder to invalidate or design around.

name: Avoid abstract, vague claim language; focus on application and impact
description: Abstract, high-level claims invite rejection under eligibility doctrines; claims should instead emphasize tangible impact and application.
guidance: Frame inventions in terms of use, application, and human intervention. 'Avoid abstract claims — focus on tangible impact' is repeated as practical advice: concrete steps, engineered systems, and measurable benefits strengthen applications.

name: Draft for global flexibility and future legal changes
description: Because law and policy are changing (including possible legislative reform), filings should be resilient and adaptable across regimes and over time.
guidance: Include a mix of claim categories (method, composition, system), document development milestones, and draft descriptions that can support alternative claim scopes if legal standards shift. Work with counsel to balance immediate defensibility with long-term optionality.

name: Court-recognized well-understood computer functions
description: Certain computer functions have been recognized by courts as well-understood, routine, and conventional when claimed at a high level of generality or as insignificant extra-solution activity.
guidance: Examples the courts have treated as well-understood when recited generically: (i) receiving or transmitting data over a network (e.g., using the Internet to gather data, forwarding information via intermediary computer); (ii) performing repetitive calculations; (iii) electronic recordkeeping (creating/maintaining shadow accounts, updating activity logs); (iv) storing and retrieving information in memory; (v) electronically scanning or extracting data from a physical document (OCR); (vi) web browser back/forward functionality. Caveats: this listing is not exhaustive and does not mean all computer functions are conventional. Claims reciting only generic computer components performing generic computer functions may be ineligible if they amount to nothing more than implementation of an abstract idea, but generic components in combination can perform non-generic functions and be eligible (see DDR Holdings, BASCOM, Amdocs). Case citations: Symantec, TLI Communications, OIP Techs., buySAFE, DDR Holdings, Flook, Bancorp, Alice, Ultramercial, Versata, Content Extraction, Internet Patent Corp.

name: Court-recognized well-understood laboratory techniques (life sciences)
description: Certain laboratory techniques in the life sciences have been treated by courts as well-understood, routine, and conventional when claimed at a high level of generality or as insignificant extra-solution activity.
guidance: Examples the courts have recognized as conventional when claimed generically: (i) determining the level of a biomarker in blood by any means; (ii) using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) to amplify and detect DNA; (iii) detecting DNA or enzymes in a sample; (iv) immunizing a patient against a disease; (v) analyzing DNA for sequence information or allelic variants; (vi) freezing and thawing cells; (vii) amplifying and sequencing nucleic acid sequences; (viii) hybridizing a gene probe. Citations include Mayo, Cleveland Clinic Foundation v. True Health Diagnostics, Genetic Techs. v. Merial, Ariosa v. Sequenom, Classen, Rapid Litigation Mgmt., Ambry Genetics, University of Utah Research Foundation. As with computers, claiming these techniques at a high level of generality or as mere extra-solution activity can weigh against eligibility; context and how the technique is integrated into the claim matter.

name: Other activities courts have found well-understood, routine, conventional
description: Courts have identified other non-technical activities as well-understood, routine, and conventional when claimed generically or as insignificant extra-solution activity.
guidance: Examples include: (i) recording a customer's order; (ii) shuffling and dealing a standard deck of cards; (iii) restricting public access to media by requiring viewing an advertisement; (iv) presenting offers and gathering statistics; (v) determining an estimated outcome and setting a price; (vi) arranging a hierarchy of groups, sorting information, eliminating less restrictive pricing information and determining the price. Case citations include Apple v. Ameranth, In re Smith, Ultramercial, OIP Techs., Versata. Examiners should consider these activities' level of generality and whether they are merely additional generic steps.

name: Mayo/Alice two-step framework (U.S.)
description: Analyze claims under the two-step Mayo/Alice test: (1) determine whether the claim is 'directed to' a patent-ineligible concept (law of nature, natural phenomenon, abstract idea); (2) if so, determine whether the claim recites an 'inventive concept' sufficient to transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application.
guidance: Courts must ask whether the patent-ineligible concept is what the claim is 'directed to' (step one) and, at step two, whether the claim's limitations (individually and as an ordered combination) supply an inventive concept. Cases: Mayo, Alice, DDR Holdings, Enfish, Bascom, Amdocs, CellzDirect/Rapid Litigation. Criticisms noted: some judges viewed Mayo's second-part breadth as unnecessary and worried it discounts post-solution conventional activity.

name: Directed-to inquiry (what the claim is 'directed to')
description: Under step one, identify whether the claim is directed to an ineligible concept or instead to a specific application or improvement.
guidance: It is 'not enough to merely identify a patent-ineligible concept underlying the claim' — the court must determine whether that concept is what the claim is directed to. Examples: CellzDirect (claims directed to new laboratory technique); Enfish (claims directed to specific improvement in computer memory).

name: Inventive concept as ordered combination
description: At step two, consider whether the claim limitations, individually and as an ordered combination, provide an 'inventive concept' beyond generic computer/known components.
guidance: Courts have found eligibility where the ordered combination recites something more than generic components (e.g., Bascom's remote installation with customizable features; Amdocs' distributed architecture and specific computer code enhancing records). The ordered-combination analysis can rescue claims that are otherwise abstract when taken element-by-element.

name: Presence of a technological solution to a technological problem (computer-related inventions)
description: Claims that provide a technological solution to a problem specifically arising in the realm of computer networks/technology are more likely to be patent eligible.
guidance: DDR Holdings found eligibility where the claimed webpage-generation system was 'necessarily rooted in computer technology' to overcome a computer-network-specific problem. Enfish found claims eligible as a specific improvement to how computers operate. The 'technological solution' framing distinguishes improvements in computer technology from abstract business practices merely implemented on a computer.

name: Specific, tangible application moves through §101 filter
description: Claims that are directed to a specific, tangible application (not merely an abstract idea) are more likely to pass the §101 coarse eligibility filter.
guidance: Classen held that claims to administering vaccines according to a determined schedule were directed to a specific, tangible application (administering a vaccine) and thus traversed the §101 filter; by contrast, claims that merely collect and compare known information (abstract principle) failed.

name: Avoiding preemption concerns
description: Eligibility analysis considers whether the claim preempts all applications of an idea or is narrowly drawn to a specific implementation.
