guidance: Courts emphasize that claims should not 'attempt to preempt every application' of an idea. Bascom and Amdocs stressed that claims limited to particular architectures or ordered combinations that do not preempt all approaches can be eligible.

name: Claims directed to natural laws or natural phenomena
description: Claims that merely claim a natural law, natural phenomenon, or newly discovered natural relationship can be treated as patent-ineligible unless recited application adds significantly more.
guidance: Judges criticized Mayo for discounting 'post-solution activity that is purely conventional or obvious.' Some judges argue inventive concept can arise from application of a natural discovery, while others find overbreadth or lack of inventive concept renders such claims ineligible. Example: Ariosa/Sequenom disputes over claims claiming natural correlations vs. application.

name: Overbreadth and §112 as alternative filter
description: Overbroad claims may be problematic under §101, but some judges propose resolving such problems under §112 (indefiniteness/written description) rather than by deeming them ineligible under §101.
guidance: Judge Lourie suggested the 'fine filter of §112' may be better suited to treating claims that 'may be indefinite or too broad' rather than exclusion under poorly-defined eligibility rules (Ariosa concurrence).

name: EPO diagnostic-methods test (clinical-diagnosis step requirement)
description: A claim is a diagnostic method under Article 53(c) only if it includes all steps necessary for a medical (clinical) diagnosis; methods that merely acquire data or perform in vitro processing without yielding a clinical diagnosis may be patent-eligible.
guidance: EPO Enlarged Board (G 0001/04) and Technical Boards applied this test; examples of eligible claims include methods determining ear temperature or imaging an artery, and in vitro diagnostic steps or software-only processing that do not lead to a clinical conclusion.

name: Jurisdictional approach to diagnostics (Japan/Korea/China)
description: Japan, Korea, and China generally exclude certain diagnostic/therapeutic methods when they are medical in nature, but recognize method claims that do not lead to a medical or clinical diagnosis (e.g., data acquisition or in vitro steps) as potentially patent-eligible.
guidance: JPO, KIPO, and SIPO guidelines treat preparatory or separable analytical steps performed outside the body as industrially applicable; China permits methods that obtain intermediate treatment information rather than final diagnostic results to be eligible.

name: China's patent exclusions (statutory)
description: China's Patent Act defines invention as new technical solutions for a product/process; it precludes inventions that violate law or social ethics or harm public interests, and specifically excludes scientific discoveries, rules/methods for intellectual activities, methods for diagnosis or treatment of diseases, and animal/plant varieties.
guidance: SIPO Guidelines elaborate practice (e.g., allowing intermediate, non-final diagnostic-step claims and conditions for biological material patenting).

name: Case-specific examples emphasizing technical character
description: Courts rely on claim-specific factual findings about whether the claim embodies a technical improvement or specific laboratory/technical steps to find eligibility.
guidance: Examples from Federal Circuit: Rapid Litigation/CellzDirect (cryopreserving hepatocytes = new laboratory technique; eligible), McRO (automatic lip-sync animation = improvement rendering information into specific format), Research Corp. (halftone image rendering = 'functional and palpable' application). These illustrate how factual technical features can carry claims through §101 analysis.

name: Three-prong analysis for invoking § 112(f)
description: Use the three-prong analysis in MPEP 2181 to determine whether the claim limitation invokes § 112(f).
guidance: Prong A: does the limitation recite 'means' or a generic placeholder for 'means'? Prong B: is the generic placeholder modified by functional language? Prong C: is the limitation further modified by sufficient structure, material or acts for performing the claimed function? (If Prong A/B/C as applicable are met, § 112(f) may be invoked.) See MPEP 2181 and related training modules.

name: BRI of functional language when § 112(f) is invoked
description: When § 112(f) is invoked, the BRI of the 'means-plus-function' limitation is restricted to the corresponding structure in the supporting disclosure, and its equivalents.
guidance: The corresponding specification that identifies and links the structure, material or act to the function recited in the claim is considered to be part of the claim limitation. Example (Claim 5): corresponding structure may be aesthetic correction circuitry, or software and microprocessor with the disclosed algorithm (VMA = VA+VADA), and equivalents thereof.

name: BRI of functional language when § 112(f) is not invoked
description: When § 112(f) is not invoked and an element is recited along with a function, that element is construed as being capable of performing the function — i.e., the BRI of that element is limited by the function.
guidance: Example (Claim 3): the recited elements of the system as a whole (scanner, aesthetic correction circuitry, display, disk memory) work together to perform the function; the BRI may be an intended use of the system. Example (Claim 4): the structure is the 'circuitry' and the BRI is that the circuitry has a structure that produces modified appearance signals based on user input.

name: Distinguish recited function from intended use/result
description: There is a distinction between reciting a function compared to reciting an intended use or result.
guidance: A functional limitation can provide a patentable distinction (limit claim scope) by imposing limits on the function of a structure, material or action. Typically no patentable distinction (no limit on claim scope) is made by an intended use or result unless some structural difference is imposed by the use or result on the structure or material recited in the claim, or some manipulative difference is imposed by the use or result on the action recited in the claim.

name: Does the functional language limit claim scope (anticipation relevance)?
description: Determine whether the functional language limits the claim scope such that a prior art reference must disclose the functional limitation to anticipate the claim.
guidance: If functional language modifies the structure recited in the claim (e.g., describes what the circuitry does and how), it can impose limits on the structure and thus must be shown by prior art to anticipate. If the functional language is merely an intended use that does not recite structure or provide context, it may not limit claim scope (prior art meeting structural limitations may anticipate regardless of explicit disclosure of the function).

name: Definiteness under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) for functional limitations
description: Functional limitations must have clearly defined boundaries to be definite under § 112(b); language that merely states a result without specifying ways to achieve it is unclear.
guidance: Consider whether one of ordinary skill in the art can determine what structure, material or act in the claim performs this function; whether the limitation has well defined boundaries or only expresses a problem solved or intended result; and what an anticipatory reference would need to disclose to satisfy this claim limitation. These considerations are not all-inclusive.

name: Requirements for corresponding structure in 'means'-type § 112(f) claims
description: For 'means'-type claims, the specification must adequately disclose a corresponding structure or material that performs the recited function.
guidance: Adequate disclosure requires that the corresponding structure or material: (a) is disclosed so one of ordinary skill will understand what specific structure/material the inventor identified to perform the function; (b) is sufficient to perform the entire function recited in the claim limitation; and (c) is clearly linked to the function in the written description. See MPEP references.

name: Examiner action when claim boundaries are not reasonably clear
description: When the examiner determines that the boundaries of a claim are not reasonably clear, a rejection under § 112(b) should be made.
guidance: Such a rejection puts the applicant on notice to fulfill their statutory duty under § 112(b). In making a rejection, the examiner must identify the specific claim language that is indefinite and explain why it renders the boundaries unclear. When possible, the examiner should suggest how the indefiniteness issues may be resolved. Consider also other applicable rejections (e.g., §§ 101, 102, 103, and/or 112).

name: Part IV §112(f) factual checklist (disclosed structure / sufficiency / linkage)
description: If the functional language is part of a 'means'-type § 112(f) limitation, answer whether (A) specification discloses a structure/material performing the claimed function, (B) the disclosed structure/material is sufficient to perform the entire claimed function, and (C) the specification clearly links the structure/material to the claimed function.
guidance: For each question, state Yes/No and provide the corresponding structure/material and explanatory notes. If any are negative, that supports indefiniteness or §112 rejections.

name: Consequences of indefinite functional language (§ 112(a) and prior art implications)
description: Indefinite, unbounded functional limitations typically lack an adequate written description under § 112(a) and may cover all ways of performing a function, indicating insufficient disclosure of possession.
guidance: Thus, a § 112(b) rejection based on unclear functional boundaries should often be accompanied by a § 112(a) written description rejection. Additionally, because functional claim language not limited to specific structure can cover all devices/materials capable of performing the function, §§ 102 or 103 rejections may be appropriate if prior art discloses a device/material that can inherently perform the claimed function. When making prior art rejections, the examiner must state how the functional term is being interpreted with respect to the prior art applied.

name: Compact prosecution principle — examine all statutory requirements initially
description: Examiners should, under compact prosecution principles, examine each claim for compliance with every statutory requirement for patentability in the initial review.
guidance: When the examiner determines that a claim term or phrase renders the claim indefinite, the examiner should make a § 112(b) rejection as well as any other applicable rejections (e.g., §§ 101, 102, 103, and/or 112).

name: Prior art rejection considerations for functional/structural scenarios
description: When prior art X meets the structural elements recited in the claim, consider whether X explicitly discloses the recited function, or whether the structure in X performs the function with the same means, an equivalent means, or a different means.
guidance: If functional language does not further limit the claim (structure recited does the work), then prior art meeting the structural limitations anticipates regardless of explicit disclosure of the function. If X is silent as to function, it cannot anticipate unless the function is inherent in X's disclosed structure (e.g., a commercial circuit whose manual indicates programming to perform the claimed function). If §112(f) limits the claim, a reference must disclose the corresponding structure or equivalent to anticipate.

name: Use a separate worksheet per claim
description: Every claim must be examined individually based on the particular elements recited therein; use a separate worksheet to analyze each claim.
guidance: This worksheet is optional during examination but aids analysis and record clarity. The answer key includes example analyses and references to MPEP and training modules so examiners can obtain more information if needed.

name: Institution threshold under 35 U.S.C. § 314(a)
description: An inter partes review may not be instituted unless the information presented in the petition “shows that there is a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail with respect to at least [one] of the claims challenged in the petition.”
guidance: Findings of fact and conclusions made at institution are preliminary (not final) and are for the sole purpose of determining the institution threshold; any final decision will be based on the full trial record, including any timely Patent Owner response.

name: Anticipation standard under 35 U.S.C. § 102
description: A claim is unpatentable as anticipated if each and every limitation is found either expressly or inherently in a single prior art reference.
guidance: Anticipation requires that all claim elements be disclosed within the four corners of the reference, in a manner enabling one skilled in the art to practice an embodiment of the claimed invention without undue experimentation (Sanofi–Synthelabo; ClearValue).

name: Obviousness standard under 35 U.S.C. § 103 (Graham factors / KSR)
description: A claim is unpatentable under § 103 if the differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention.
guidance: Resolve obviousness by considering: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art; (3) the level of ordinary skill in the art; and (4) objective evidence of nonobviousness (Graham). KSR governs motivation to combine and predictable results; Board assesses whether a person of ordinary skill would have been motivated to combine teachings and whether the combination yields predictable results.

name: Claim construction standard (district-court-type / Phillips)
description: In IPRs, claim language is interpreted using the district-court-type standard: give claim terms their ordinary and customary meaning as understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art in light of the claim language, specification, and prosecution history.
guidance: Extrinsic evidence may be useful but must be considered in the context of intrinsic evidence (Phillips). The Board construes only terms in controversy and only to the extent necessary to resolve the controversy (37 C.F.R. § 42.100(b); Realtime Data).

name: Evidentiary assessment and burden at institution
description: At the institution stage, the Board determines whether the information in the petition and supporting evidence is sufficient to meet the statutory institution threshold (reasonable likelihood to prevail on at least one claim).
guidance: The Board reviews petitioner’s contentions, declarations, cited references, and any Patent Owner preliminary response; institution findings are preliminary and focused on threshold sufficiency rather than final adjudication. Examples in this decision: sufficiency findings regarding printed publications and the asserted obviousness/anticipation showings.

name: Claim construction — basic principle
description: Claim construction issues recurring across opinions
guidance: Courts emphasize construing claims according to intrinsic evidence and avoid importing embodiment aspects as requirements (Promptu v Comcast). Functional constructions may be appropriate where warranted.

name: Written description requirement and numeric ranges
description: Satisfaction of written description for claims reciting numerical ranges
guidance: Court may find WDR satisfied where the specification discloses overlapping ranges and both endpoints are disclosed; analysis is fact-specific (RAI v Philip Morris).

name: Administrative Procedure Act (APA) and implicit claim construction
description: Whether PTAB's implicit claim construction violated the APA and whether parties had notice
guidance: Board may implicitly construe claims when its assessment of a limitation establishes its scope; notice to parties is relevant but not always fatal (Google v EcoFactor).

name: Section 101 patent-eligibility (Alice two-step)
description: §101 analysis for abstract ideas and inventive concept under Alice
guidance: Claims directed to abstract ideas without an inventive concept or technological improvement are ineligible; courts apply familiar indicators of abstractness and analyze whether claims recite well-understood, routine, conventional elements (Chewy v IBM; AI Visualize v Nuance; Beteiro v DraftKings; BroadbandTV v Amazon).

name: Result-effective variable / optimization analysis in obviousness
description: Treatment of molecular weight ranges or other 'result-effective' variables as motivations to optimize
guidance: If a claim recites a result-effective variable, PHOSITA may be motivated to optimize and obviousness may follow even without exact overlapping ranges (Pfizer v Sanofi).

name: Claim definiteness and apparently contradictory limitations
description: How courts assess claims with multiple limitations that may seem contradictory
guidance: Courts reject indefiniteness where claim limitations can be satisfied together even if drafting could be clearer (Maxell v Amperex).

name: Narrowing limitations are not mere 'options'
description: Limitations added to overcome prior art that narrow claim scope should be treated as requirements
guidance: Added narrowing limitations cannot be treated as optional; they must be given effect (Maxell v Amperex).

name: Printed matter doctrine
description: Whether claim limitations concerning communicated content are 'printed matter' lacking patentable weight
guidance: If limitations are not claimed for the content they communicate but for functional aspects, they may not be printed matter (IOEngine v Ingenico).

name: IPR estoppel and meaning of 'obtaining a claim'
description: Scope of estoppel under 35 U.S.C. 316(a)(4) and 37 C.F.R. 42.73(d)(3)(i) regarding amended claims
guidance: PTO may lawfully promulgate rules estopping a patentee from obtaining claims in reexaminations that are not patentably distinct from claims cancelled in an adverse IPR, but such estoppel has limits and does not automatically apply to 'issued' claims (SoftView v Apple).

name: Interference/priority and §135 time bar (pre-AIA)
description: Priority contests and application of the pre-AIA §135 time bar in interference proceedings
guidance: Apply a two-way test to see if pre- and post-critical date claims are materially different; added limitations may be material and trigger time bars (Speck v Bates).

name: Trade secret definition and DTSA enforcement
description: Definition of trade secret under DTSA and related preliminary injunction/statute of limitations analysis
guidance: Courts require clear definition of 'trade secret' and analysis of the three-year statute of limitations for DTSA claims; broad labels like 'confidential information' may be insufficient (Insulet v EOFlow).

name: Indicators of abstractness for patent eligibility
description: Well-settled indicators that claims are abstract (result-focused, functional language, use of generic computer components)
guidance: Claims framed as result-oriented functional language without technological improvement indicate abstractness; courts compare claims to Enfish and other examples (Beteiro v DraftKings; MillerMendel v City of Anna).

name: Well-Understood, Routine, and Conventional (WUR&C) elements in §101 analysis
description: Role of WUR&C in deciding patent-eligibility
guidance: Claims that merely invoke WUR&C computer elements without improving computer technology are ineligible (MillerMendel; Mobile Acuity v Blippar).

name: Board's use of reply briefs and MTA Pilot Program
description: Permissibility of using reply briefs to supplement written-description support for substitute claims under PTAB pilot programs
guidance: PTAB may permit reply briefing to address deficiencies and the MTA Pilot Program aims to let reply briefs correct errors (ZyXel v UNMRI).

name: Design patent obviousness framework
description: New framework: apply Graham factors to design patents — analogous art, visual comparison, ordinary designer skill, combining references, and secondary considerations
guidance: Focus on the visual impression of the claimed design as a whole and identify a primary reference; require record-supported reason to combine references without hindsight (LKQ v GM en banc).

name: False advertising via asserting 'patented' product (Lanham Act §43)
description: When falsely claiming a product feature is patented supports a Lanham Act false-advertising claim
guidance: False statements that a material is patented linked to a product's characteristics can mislead consumers and give rise to §43(a) liability (Crocs v Effervescent).

name: Claim construction — Phillips vs PTAB BRC
description: Differences between the PTAB’s Broadest Reasonable Construction (BRC) and the Phillips standard used by courts
guidance: Federal Circuit recognizes differences; BRC is not binding on courts, and incorporation by reference and provisional claims must be read in light of the specification (DDR Holdings v Priceline).

name: Substantial new question of patentability standard (35 U.S.C. 304 / MPEP § 2216)
description: Under 35 U.S.C. 304 the Office must determine whether “a substantial new question of patentability” affecting any claim of the patent has been raised. The request must demonstrate an SNQ based on patents and printed publications.
guidance: It is not sufficient merely to propose rejections; the cited patent or publication must present a new, non-cumulative technological teaching that was not previously considered and discussed during prosecution or prior proceedings. Old art may raise an SNQ only if presented/viewed in a new light or different way with a material new argument or interpretation (e.g., new analysis under KSR rationales). KSR did not alter the SNQ legal standard. Questions based on matters other than patents/printed publications (public use, on sale, inventorship, 35 U.S.C. 101/112, conduct) should not be included and will not be considered.

name: Explanation must be complete and specific (I. EXPLANATION MUST BE COMPLETE)
description: The mere citation of patents or printed publications without an explanation does not comply with 37 CFR 1.510(b)(2). The requester must present an explanation of how the cited documents are applied to all claims which the requester considers to merit reexamination.
guidance: Do not include citations to background references not used to support an SNQ or proposed rejection. For each proposed combination, explain how each reference is used and applied to each claim (e.g., claims 1-10: explain application to claim 1, claim 2, etc.). Preferred format is a detailed claim chart. For obviousness proposals, provide at least one basis to combine references and explain why the claim would have been obvious over the combination. Avoid language that lumps alternative references or combinations together; the MPEP provides specific 'inappropriate' and 'appropriate' language examples. If a Notice of Failure to Comply identifies missing explanations, the requester may either (A) provide separate explanations for each identified combination/document/claim, or (B) explicitly withdraw any document/combination/claim lacking explanation.

name: Examples of inappropriate vs appropriate claim-language and combination statements
description: MPEP gives explicit examples of inappropriate language (e.g., lumping alternatives or multiple combinations together) and appropriate language (e.g., specifying claim-by-claim rejections and explicit combinations).
guidance: Use clear, claim-specific rejection statements such as 'Claim 1 is unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being obvious over Smith in view of Jones.' Avoid alternatives like 'Smith and/or Charles' or grouping claims and many alternative combinations in a single sentence unless each alternative is separately articulated and justified.

name: Restrictions on claim types of questions presented
description: Substantial new questions of patentability in reexamination under 35 U.S.C. 302 must be based on patents or printed publications; other matters (public use, on sale, conduct, inventorship, 35 U.S.C. 101, 35 U.S.C. 112, etc.) will not be considered in determining whether to order reexamination.
guidance: A prior art patent or printed publication cannot be used merely to evidence alleged public use or on sale or insufficiency of disclosure; it must be applied directly to claims under 35 U.S.C. 103 and/or appropriate portions of 35 U.S.C. 102.

name: No amendment to broaden patent protection after PatL 19 notice
description: Patent claims may not be amended so that the patent protection is extended after a PatL 19 § notification has been given.
guidance: Also: after the PatL 19 § notification new divisional applications cannot be filed by splitting (PatA 22 and 23 §). The purpose is to prevent changes that unnecessarily prolong grant proceedings.

name: Permissible grounds for opposition (PatL 25 § 1)
description: Grounds for an opposition are: (1) the patent was granted despite failure to meet PatL §§ 1, 1a, 1b, or 2; (2) the patent does not disclose the invention sufficiently for a skilled person to use it; (3) the patent contains subject‑matter that did not emerge from the application as filed (added matter); (4) the patent protection was extended after the PatL 19 § notification.
guidance: The grounds differ from grant‑phase requirements: vague claim wording in granted claims is not per se a ground if the description enables the skilled person (cf. PatL 8 § 2 mom.). Lack of unity (PatL 10 §) is also not a ground.

name: Amendments to claims during opposition: no new matter, no broadening
description: Changes made to a granted patent during opposition must not introduce subject matter that did not appear in the application as filed, nor may the patent protection be broadened as compared to the state after the PatL 19 § notification.
guidance: Protection broadens if a feature is removed entirely from a claim; it is allowed to replace the removed feature with a narrower feature taken from the description (permitted). Removing alternative features is allowed without broadening. Category changes (e.g., from method to product) can risk broadening; converting a product claim to a use claim for achieving a particular effect is generally acceptable.

name: Added subject‑matter / new matter evaluation scope
description: The opposition phase evaluates added subject‑matter only with respect to whether features introduced in amended claims arise from the description or drawings; imprecision of granted independent claims is not itself a ground unless new features are imported from the description or figures.
guidance: If independent claims are amended based on dependent claims, the clarity of the amended claims is not re‑examined in certain MAO precedents (examples referenced).

name: Language and translation provisions in opposition
description: Opposition and its reasoning must be submitted in Finnish or Swedish (PatM 52 §). Annexes may be in other languages. If supporting publications are in a language outside the listed set (fi/sv/no/da/en/de/fr), PRH may require translations of those publications if relevant to decision‑making.
guidance: PRH sends procedural communications in Finnish or Swedish depending on the language used during examination. When the application was processed in English, claim language translations rules apply (see handling of English specification translations).

name: Abstract (tiivistelmä) checking rules for publication
description: When the application becomes public, PRH prepares the application publication whose front page includes an abstract in two languages. PRH checks the substantive content and translation of the abstract; if noncompliant the applicant is asked to correct defects. PRH may itself make small necessary changes to the abstract without hearing the applicant (PatL 15 § 1 mom.).
guidance: PRH also decides which drawings to publish with the abstract (PatM 27 §). The final abstract should, if possible, be confirmed before publication and must describe the invention as in the main application document; the abstract is not re‑examined/rewritten later due to claim changes or prosecution developments.

name: Specification: Its Importance and Twofold Object
description: The specification sets forth the contract between the public and the patentee and has a twofold object (description and claim).
guidance: Specification both discloses the invention to satisfy public notice/enablement and defines the monopoly by claims; it is central to validity and scope.

name: Specification Divisions: Description and Claim
description: The specification has two divisions: the description (the narrative disclosure) and the claim(s) (the definition of the monopoly).
guidance: Both parts are read together; claims are interpreted with reference to the description, drawings, and other parts of the application.

name: Description Must Disclose the Mode of Use of the Invention
description: The description must disclose the mode of use of the invention.
guidance: When relevant, describing how to use the invention is part of the enabling disclosure and may affect claim scope/interpretation.

name: The Claim: Its Objects and General Requisites
description: Claims state the objects and general requisites: they are the life of the patent and the measure of the patent privilege.
guidance: Claims define what the patentee regards as his invention; strict rules govern form and content; claims determine infringement and validity.

name: The Claim Must Claim a Single and Distinct Invention
description: Each claim must claim a single and distinct invention.
guidance: Joinder of multiple distinct inventions in one claim or in a single application is restricted; claims must be definite and focused.

name: The Claim Must Precisely Define and Distinguish the Invention from Known Inventions
description: The claim must precisely define the invention and must distinguish it from all known inventions (the prior art).
guidance: Claims that fail to distinguish over prior art are invalid; precision in claim language is essential for both validity and enforcement.

name: The Claim Must Set Forth the Invention in its Most Perfect Concrete Form
description: The claim should set forth the invention in its most perfect concrete form.
guidance: Draft claims to capture a clear, practicable embodiment and to avoid vague, overly broad or speculative language.

name: The Claim Must Correspond with the Description
description: The claim must correspond with the description (claims should be supported by and consistent with the specification).
guidance: Claims inconsistent with the description may be defective; claims are interpreted in light of the specification.

name: No Particular Form Required for a Claim; Technical Phrases Allowed
description: No particular form is required for claims; technical phrases may be used when appropriate.
guidance: While form flexibility exists, strict substance rules apply (definiteness, support, operability). Technical language must be clear to skilled persons.

name: Claim Must Not Claim a Mere Function or Mere Effect
description: The claim must not claim a mere function or a mere effect without claiming means/structure to accomplish it.
guidance: Claims that only recite results or effects without structural or operative limitation are improper and often invalid.

name: Claim Must Not Claim a Mere Effect and Must Not Be Alternative
description: Claims must not be framed as mere effects, nor be stated in alternative (indefinite, multiple incompatible alternatives) form.
guidance: Alternatives and functional claiming that obscure boundaries of the invention risk indefiniteness or invalidity.

name: Joinder Rules for Claims (Combinations, Elements, Sub-Combinations)
description: Rules govern joinder of claims for different inventions, combinations, sub-combinations and elements; combinations are treated specially.
guidance: A claim for a combination covers only the precise combination claimed; claims may be joined for combinations and for elements when appropriate under rules.

name: Claims for Specific Classes (Art, Machine, Manufacture, Composition, Design, Improvement)
description: There are general requisites tailored to claims for an art, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, design, and improvement.
guidance: Each class has distinctive drafting/interpretation rules (e.g., process claims vs. apparatus claims vs. composition claims).

name: Amendment of Letters-Patent: Clerical Errors, Disclaimers, and Re-issue
description: Letters-patent may be amended to correct clerical errors, by disclaimer (to remove excess), or by re-issue to amend defective language under strict conditions.
guidance: Clerical errors may be corrected without affecting intervening rights; disclaimers are limited (e.g., to excess arising without fraud); re-issue may not change the nature of the invention or expand claims beyond what the original attempted to describe and claim; re-issue requires inadvertence/ mistake (no fraud) and other procedural conditions.

name: Construction: Special Rules (pioneer patents, re-issued patents, claims for principles/functions/effects)
description: Special rules apply to pioneer patents, re-issued patents, claims for combinations, improvements, joint inventions, and claims that attempt to cover principles, functions, or effects.
guidance: Terms like 'substantially as described' and 'generic' admit nuances; claims for an entirety not divisible and terms admitting degrees require careful treatment.

name: Notice and exact statement of conflicting claims
description: The examiner must secure from adverse parties an exact statement of their conflicting claims and give notice thereof to the applicants or patentee, directing the primary examiner to proceed to determine the question of priority.
guidance: Whenever an examiner discovers conflicting claims the duty is to notify such applicants/patentees/caveators and, if necessary, require them to state their claims so that the nature and extent of antagonism are distinct and unmistakable. Parties must put claims in such condition that no further change will be required to precisely cover their respective rights; want of exactness is sufficient reason to require further amendment. Parties who fail to comply with the notice will be excluded from the interference (but without prejudice to other rights).

name: Content and form of notices of interference
description: Notices of the interference must disclose the name and residence of each contestant and attorney, the date of filing of the contestant's application (or date/number if a patentee), the ordinals of conflicting claims, and the invention claimed — clearly and concisely defining them in as many counts as necessary.
guidance: Notices and accompanying files are transmitted to the examiner of interferences, who reviews them for defects; defective notices are returned for amendment and, upon perfection, the interference is formally declared and notices sent to parties with an order to file preliminary statements.

name: Examiner duty to define subject-matter and issues
description: The examiner must see that the subject-matter put in issue by the interference is properly defined and must direct that the issues represent what the parties actually claim, not what they might claim.
guidance: Issues must point out the conflicting claims and contain a summary of the contested matter; hypothetical issues are not permitted. The primary examiner must decide whether claims interfere, looking to the language of the application alone in declaring an interference.

name: Issues must have the same meaning to all parties; construction conclusive
description: An issue must have the same meaning as to all claimants; if susceptible of various meanings, adopt the one which sustains the interference and best agrees with the specifications; the Patent Office's construction of an issue is conclusive.
guidance: When multiple constructions exist, the one that sustains the interference and aligns best with claimants' specifications will be adopted. The construction placed upon an issue by the Patent Office is final for the interference.

name: Rules of evidence and burden/standard of proof for priority
description: General rules of evidence apply; priority consists of prior conception plus reduction to practice or reasonable diligence in reducing to practice; successful claimant must establish priority by a clear preponderance of the evidence (not necessarily beyond reasonable doubt) and must overcome presumptions arising from earlier applications and patents.
guidance: A claimant must establish his conception and reduction to practice and must affirmatively demonstrate right to priority as against adversaries (sufficient to defeat their patents in the courts). In an interference with a patent, the applicant must offer such evidence of priority as would defeat the patent in court. The examiner has exclusive authority to decide competency, construction, scope and legal meaning of foreign patents/other evidence when determining whether they cover the same invention.

name: Access to interference materials and confidentiality
description: Adverse parties in an interference are allowed to see copies of interfering claims and specifications, but other persons cannot have access to interference files.
guidance: Interference files are not public; only the contestants (and their attorneys) may inspect the specific materials necessary for the contest.

name: When a three-judge court is required
description: Coverage questions under Section 5 are generally to be determined by a three-judge court pursuant to 28 U.S.C. §2284.
guidance: The single-judge district court to whom the request is made has authority to determine if a three-judge court is required. A three-judge court is not required if the claim is wholly insubstantial or completely without merit (United States v. Saint Landry Parish School Bd.).

name: Pleading must be construed favorably but contain factual allegations
description: To test the sufficiency of a complaint, a court must construe the complaint favorably to the pleader (Scherer v. Rhodes; Conley v. Gibson).
guidance: Nevertheless, pleadings that do nothing more than 'track the statute' and constitute unsupported legal conclusions cast as factual allegations fail to state a cause of action (Webber v. White). Complaints must contain allegations which, if proved, would constitute a violation of the statute claimed.

name: Rule 12(b)(6)/failure-to-state-a-claim standard in Section 5 context
description: A complaint may be dismissed under Rule 12(b)(6) for failure to state a claim upon which relief can be granted if the pleadings do not allege facts that, if proved, would constitute a violation of Section 5 (or other invoked federal provisions).
guidance: Courts look beyond labels and statutory recitals to whether factual allegations support the claimed violation; if the Section 5 claims are 'completely without merit' dismissal is appropriate and convening a three-judge court unnecessary.

name: Pendent (supplemental) jurisdiction power and discretion (Gibbs)
description: If the pleadings disclose a substantial federal claim, there is power to hear pendent claims that 'derive from a common nucleus of operative fact.' Pendent jurisdiction is a doctrine of discretion, not of right.
guidance: Even where power exists, courts consider factors of judicial economy, convenience, and fairness in deciding whether to exercise pendent jurisdiction. If the federal claim is too insubstantial to support federal-question jurisdiction, there can be no pendent jurisdiction of other claims.

name: Anti-injunction statute limits (28 U.S.C. §2283)
description: 28 U.S.C. §2283 prohibits a court of the United States from enjoining proceedings in a State court except where necessary in aid of its jurisdiction or to protect or effectuate its judgments.
guidance: State-law claims that are the subject of pending state proceedings ordinarily cannot be enjoined by a federal court unless they fall within the narrow exceptions in §2283; courts will deny federal injunctive relief where the exceptions do not apply.

name: Attorney General 'no objection' letters as evidence of preclearance
description: A Justice Department/Attorney General letter stating 'The Attorney General does not interpose any objections to the changes in question' demonstrates that the submission has been reviewed and that the AG interposes no objections.
guidance: Such letters can establish that elections and procedures have been submitted for approval and that there is no basis for Section 5 relief; courts may find Section 5 claims 'completely without merit' on that basis.

name: Subjectivity/arbitrariness of the 'abstract' determination
description: Determinations of whether a claim is 'directed to' an abstract idea (or other judicial exception) are subjective and can be arbitrary without clearer guideposts.
guidance: Page notes that courts have not adequately defined 'abstract,' so determining if a claim is 'something more' than the undefined abstract is difficult and often arbitrary. Commenters observed that this subjective judgment relies heavily on fact-specific prior decisions, producing inconsistent application.

name: Current jurisprudence improves patent quality and public disclosure
description: The idea that eligibility jurisprudence forces applicants to better define inventions, improving patent quality and useful public disclosure.
guidance: Commenters (e.g., CCIA, Google) stated the eligibility test acts as a 'forcing function' leading to greater detail and clarity in patent applications, thereby providing more useful information to the public and clearer claim boundaries.

name: Impact on innovation — jurisprudence is beneficial
description: The view that exclusions from patentability (laws/products/abstract ideas) play a crucial role in fostering technological invention and public-benefiting research by keeping basic tools free for follow-on work.
guidance: Civil liberties and public-interest commenters argued expanding eligibility to basic tools would impede innovation; examples include free access to genomic information during COVID-19. Some claimed the current regime prevents overbroad patents by NPEs, preserving resources for productive innovation.

name: Markedly Different Characteristics (products of nature)
description: To be 'markedly different' from its naturally occurring counterpart, a claimed product must possess at least one characteristic that is changed as compared to the counterpart; the characteristic cannot be an inherent or innate characteristic of the naturally occurring counterpart or an incidental change.
guidance: Courts require that the inventor caused the change. Examples of markedly different products: Chakrabarty (genetically modified bacterium with additional plasmids and expanded hydrocarbon degradation capability); Myriad (full-length cDNA with a different nucleotide sequence containing only exons). Anti-examples: mere isolation or incidental structural differences that leave the molecule otherwise identical (Myriad's isolated BRCA genes), single-stranded primers whose sequences are identical to natural strands (Ambry), clones that are genetic replicas (Roslin). Cite Myriad, Chakrabarty, Ambry Genetics, In re Roslin, and In re Marden.

name: Product-of-nature exception applies when no marked difference
description: If there is no change in any characteristic between the claimed product and its natural counterpart, the claimed product lacks markedly different characteristics and is a product of nature exception.
guidance: Isolation that only removes covalent bonds but leaves genetic structure and nucleotide sequence identical is insufficient (Myriad). Changes that are incidental or innate to the natural material do not avoid the exception. Courts consider whether patented claims would improperly tie up future use and study of the natural material.

name: Considerations indicative that additional elements may integrate the exception
description: Limitations the courts have found indicative that an additional element (or combination of elements) may have integrated the exception into a practical application include: improvements in functioning of a computer or other technology; applying/using the exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis; implementing/using the exception with a particular machine or manufacture integral to the claim; effecting a transformation or reduction of an article to a different state or thing; applying/using the exception in some other meaningful way beyond generally linking it to a technological environment.
guidance: This list is not exclusive or limiting; additional elements can be analyzed based on more than one consideration. See MPEP §§ 2106.04(d)(1), 2106.04(d)(2), and 2106.05(a)-(h) for detailed treatment and examples (Enfish, McRO, Visual Memory, Finjan, SRI, BASCOM).

name: Limitations that did not integrate a judicial exception
description: Limitations the courts have found did not integrate the judicial exception include: merely reciting 'apply it' (or equivalent) with the judicial exception, merely including instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer, or merely using a computer as a tool; adding insignificant extra-solution activity to the exception; generally linking the use of the exception to a particular technological environment or field of use.
guidance: Such limitations are insufficient to impose a meaningful limit and often result in the claim being directed to the judicial exception. See MPEP §§ 2106.05(f)-(h) and cases like Alice and Bilski for context.

name: Specificity of a method of achieving a result is not a stand-alone consideration
description: A specific way of achieving a result is not itself a stand-alone consideration in Step 2A Prong Two.
guidance: However, specificity of limitations is relevant to evaluation of other considerations such as use of a particular machine, particular transformation, or whether limitations are mere instructions to apply an exception. Example: Parker v. Flook—failure to explain specifics of how to use a claimed formula informed the court that additional elements were insignificant post-solution activity.

name: Procedure for evaluating integration (how to evaluate additional elements)
description: Evaluate integration into a practical application by: (1) identifying whether there are additional elements recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception(s); and (2) evaluating those additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether they integrate the exception into a practical application using one or more of the relevant considerations.
guidance: Not all considerations will be relevant to every claim. The evaluation is not a weighing test; it is important to evaluate the significance of the additional elements relative to the invention and whether the exception is integrated. If the claim as a whole integrates the exception based on these considerations, the additional limitations impose a meaningful limit and the claim is eligible at Step 2A. For multi-exception claims, see MPEP § 2106 subsection II.B.

name: Evaluating improvements in computer functioning or other technology (Step 2A)
description: A claim reciting a judicial exception is not directed to the exception if it recites additional elements demonstrating the claimed invention improves the functioning of a computer or another technology or technical field; using the exception in this manner meaningfully limits the claim and transforms it into patent-eligible subject matter.
guidance: To evaluate, first review the specification to determine if the disclosure provides sufficient details such that one of ordinary skill in the art would recognize the claimed invention as providing an improvement. The specification need not explicitly assert the improvement, but the improvement must be apparent to a POSITA. Second, ensure the claim includes the components or steps that provide the improvement; the claim need not explicitly recite the improvement. This Step 2A improvements analysis differs from Step 2B analysis because it does not reference whether elements are well-understood, routine, conventional. Examples of eligible improvements include Enfish (self-referential table), McRO (automatic lip-sync), Visual Memory (enhanced memory system), Finjan (virus scanning that improves functionality). See MPEP § 2106.05(a).

name: Particular treatment or prophylaxis as an integrating consideration
description: Applying or using a judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition can integrate the exception into a practical application and render the claim not directed to the judicial exception (eligible at Step 2A).
guidance: Originated from 'other meaningful limitations' consideration and elevated due to cases like Vanda. Examples include administration of medication, surgery, dialysis, phototherapy, immunization steps that lower risk. The limitation must affirmatively recite an action of treatment or prophylaxis (e.g., 'administering amazonic acid to a patient'); mere statements of intended use, field-of-use, or non-affirmative recitations (e.g., 'prescribing' or 'a pharmaceutical composition') do not qualify.

name: Whether limitation(s) have more than a nominal or insignificant relationship to the exception
description: When determining whether a claim uses a recited judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis, assess whether the treatment/prophylaxis limitation has more than a nominal or insignificant relationship to the exception(s).
guidance: Vanda contrasted with Mayo: Vanda's administration steps used the law of nature to safely treat patients (reducing risk), whereas Mayo's administration step was ancillary and performed to gather data about the law of nature. Thus, the relationship must be substantive (not ancillary or merely for data gathering) so the limitation meaningfully applies the exception rather than being ancillary to a diagnostic focus. Consider particularity and the role the limitation plays relative to the exception when making this determination.

name: Novelty of numerical ranges / sub-ranges
description: A claimed invention that selects a narrower sub-range of numerical values within a broader known range may be novel if the selected sub-range has not been explicitly mentioned in the prior art.
guidance: To establish the novelty of the sub-range, the selected sub-range should be narrow and sufficiently specific from the known broader range, illustrated by means of examples. The interpretation of 'sufficient specificity' is key and may vary on the facts of the case; novelty must be decided on a case-by-case basis. If the claimed range merely falls within the broader range without sufficient specificity, anticipation may occur.

name: Prior-art teaching very close to claimed range does not anticipate
description: Prior art which teaches a value or range very close to, but not overlapping or touching, the claimed range does not anticipate the claimed range; the claimed subject matter is novel in that situation.
guidance: Inventive step still needs to be determined. Some AMS (e.g., Viet Nam) provide specific criteria when a claimed numerical range is 'close' to a specific prior-art number: (a) the claimed range is sufficiently far removed from any specific number disclosed; (b) the claimed range is narrow compared to the specific number; (c) the claimed range provides an effect that makes the claimed subject matter 'special' (e.g., particular technical effect).

name: Selection invention / narrow-range unexpected results
description: If the claim is directed to a narrow range and the prior art discloses a broad range, the narrow range may be novel if it is not merely one way of carrying out the prior-art teaching and there is evidence (e.g., unexpected results) that the advantageous effect occurs only within the claimed narrow range.
guidance: Unexpected results that occur with high probability only within the claimed range may render the claims unobvious as well as novel (selection invention). Consider all relevant facts of the case.

name: Anticipation requires sufficient specificity in prior art
description: To anticipate a claim, the claimed subject matter should be disclosed with sufficient specificity in the item of prior art.
guidance: Sufficient specificity is interpreted case-by-case; mere proximity or closeness of numbers is not necessarily anticipation. The examiner must evaluate whether prior art discloses the claimed subject matter with the necessary detail.

name: Novelty/inventive-step assessment difference for second medical uses
description: Second medical use claims can derive novelty from the specified medical use if that use is new and inventive, even where the substance itself is known.
guidance: Some AMS exclude claims that apply the product into a subject's body or involve dosage/efficacy in the claim; acceptable formats avoid direct method-of-treatment language. National laws may further limit second use claims (e.g., Indonesia's Article 4(f) excluding new uses that do not show significant efficiency increase).

name: Problem-solution approach (method for determining inventive step)
description: A three-step test: (i) determine the closest prior art; (ii) establish the objective technical problem to be solved; (iii) consider whether the claimed invention starting from the closest prior art and the objective technical problem would have been obvious to the PSIA.
guidance: Closest prior art is the single reference that is the most promising starting point (same field or problem, most features in common, similar use, fewest modifications). The objective technical problem is derived objectively from differences between the claimed invention and closest prior art and may be reformulated based on facts found in examination; it can be an aggregation of partial problems if multiple technical effects exist. In stage three, the examiner asks whether prior art teachings would have 'prompted' the PSIA to reach the claimed invention (not merely that they 'could' have).

name: Joint authorship standard
description: A joint work is prepared by two or more authors with the intention that contributions be merged into inseparable or interdependent parts of a unitary whole; each joint author is a co-owner.
guidance: Under Goldstein’s test, a contribution must be original expression that could stand on its own; courts consider creative control, objective manifestations of intent to be co-authors, and audience appeal. Co-ownership claims have a three-year statute of limitations; each joint author may exploit the work but may owe accounting for profits.

name: Claims must be clear, definite, and not use ambiguous/useless words
description: The Claim should clearly, definitely, and correctly comprehend the alleged subject-matter of the invention and nothing more; no ambiguous or useless word or phrase ought ever to be allowed in a Claim.
guidance: Although courts will sometimes sustain a claim inaccurately expressed if the court can see what the invention really is, applicants should draft claims to be self-sufficient and definite. Ambiguity may sometimes be cured by examining the Description, but claims ought not to rely on vague wording. (Cases cited: Stover v. Halsted; Ex parte Demming.)

name: Avoid indefinite expressions such as 'means' or 'mechanism' for essential elements
description: A Claim cannot use such indefinite expressions as 'means,' 'mechanism,' etc., when referring to essential elements of the patentable subject-matter.
guidance: While the words 'means', 'mechanism', 'connections' may be proper when used to denote appliances which are not part of the invention, they must not be used with reference to essential elements. An apparatus should be claimed as a specific device rather than as a vague 'means of doing'. (See Ex parte Demming; Ex parte Bates.)

name: Do not expressly claim 'equivalents' or use equivocal/repetitive synonymous words
description: The repetition of synonymous words is improper and equivocal words (such as 'equivalent') must not be used; the insertion of 'equivalent' in a Claim implies matter outside its ordinary meaning and may widen the scope while leaving limits undefined.
guidance: Equivalents are generally regarded as covered even if not mentioned, so stating 'equivalents' adds nothing and can be harmful. Equivalents should not be expressly claimed unless the equivalents are described in the specification or special circumstances (e.g., mutual blocking patents) make it necessary. Examiners may require deletion of 'or equivalents', and applicants can then insert particular claims for alleged equivalents. (Cases: Burden v. Coming; Ex parte Reid; Ex parte Dolph; Ex parte Johnson.)

name: Be cautious with technical phrases like 'as described' and 'substantially as described'
description: Phrases such as 'as described', 'substantially as described', or 'substantially as and for the purposes set forth' refer to the Description and are neither necessary nor inherently limiting; their legal effect depends on the clarity of the Description and the intended limitation.
guidance: These phrases add nothing to the certainty of a properly drawn claim and may be dangerous if used as substitutes for clear language. 'Substantially as described' has no efficacy unless the Description is clear; 'substantially as and for the purposes set forth' is a words-of-limitation and should be used only when that special signification is intended. 'Mechanism substantially as described' can be too vague. (See Mitchell v. Tilghman; Ex parte Skinner; Ex parte Wilkin; Ex parte Ewart.)

name: Claim must set out the invention, not merely refer to the Description
description: A Claim must set out the invention itself rather than merely refer to or restate the Description; a claim that merely refers to the specification without stating the invention is too vague.
guidance: The Claim should be sufficient in its own terms to the specific features set out in the Description. However, in construing the Claim the courts will consider the whole specification and drawings; where consistent, the Description may amplify and explain concise claim language. Drawings cannot replace a written Description such that a claim covers matter shown only in drawings. (See Ex parte Demming; Westinghouse v. Gardner & Ransom; Gunn v. Savage.)

name: Do not claim a mere function (functional claims are void)
description: A Claim for the function of the invention—claiming the producing of an effect rather than the means by which it is produced—is void, since it neither covers a patentable invention nor corresponds with the given Description.
guidance: Courts will, if possible, construe participial or functional claims as claims for the means by which the function is performed; apparatus must be claimed as specific devices, not as 'means of doing'. Participial forms like 'producing', 'operating', 'determining' are suspect. Functional language may be acceptable where the invention is itself an art or process and the function is the true invention. (See Ex parte Ives; Matthews v. Schoneberger; Royer v. Schultz; Ex parte Cox.)

name: Avoid alternative (disjunctive) claiming that creates uncertainty
description: A Claim stated in the alternative is invalid when its language either covers nothing positively or leaves uncertain which of several things the inventor intends to claim.
guidance: Use of disjunctive conjunctions does not automatically render a claim uncertain if the essential characteristics are properly set forth. Alternatives that merely describe modes or connections may be acceptable; but alternative claims are disfavored by the Patent Office and it is preferable to state separate claims for separate alternatives when practicable. Courts may sustain alternative claims where intelligible. (See Union Paper Bag Mach. Co. v. Nixon; Ex parte Holt.)

name: Do not unnecessarily multiply claims (avoid redundant or fictitious claims)
description: Repetition of the same Claim or multiplication of claims for the same invention is not allowed except where necessary to describe the invention in different methods to make it clear or to state all that can rightfully be claimed.
guidance: Unnecessary multiplication tends to mislead by implying substantive differences where none exist and may, if carried too far, create ambiguity that renders the patent void. Where one claim will suffice, no others should be made. Some repetition in different language to prevent misunderstanding may be tolerated, but divided or multiplied claims that appear fictitious or redundant are disapproved. (See Dederick v. Cassell; Carlton v. Bokee.)

name: Proper joinder of claims for different inventions
description: Claims for different inventions may be joined in the same specification only insofar as the nature and dependence of those inventions permit their joinder; each claim must possess all characteristics and fulfil all requirements necessary to its validity as if it were the sole invention claimed.
guidance: Claims are the 'life' of the patent and may embrace every invention for whose protection the applicant may lawfully apply; but a claim for a separate invention must stand on its own merits. A second claim for an inseparable feature of an already claimed invention is improper. (See Ex parte Smith; Combined Patents Can Co. v. Lloyd.)

name: Claims are interpreted and limited by the specification and drawings (but claims control where conflict exists)
description: In construing a Claim the whole specification is taken together; if the Claim's language is consistent with the Description and drawings, the latter are treated as amplification and explanation, and features declared essential in the Description are covered by the Claim even if not expressly mentioned.
guidance: The Claim must still be complete in itself and cannot be enlarged by the Description. Drawings may limit a claim where they describe the device by reference letters, but drawings cannot wholly supplant a written Description. When Claims and Description disagree, the Claims control. Courts construe claims in view of the state of the art to render the claimed invention evident to those skilled in the art. (See Snow v. Lake Shore & Mich. S.R. Co.; McKesson v. Camdick; Gunn v. Savage.)

name: Combination claims must be claimed as combinations and include all essential cooperating elements
description: A combination is an invention distinct from its elements and from the law of their co-operation; a claim for a combination must include all its essential characteristics and embrace enough to produce a distinct and useful result, and must be confined to the union of elements the inventor has created and described.
guidance: Claims for individual elements do not cover the combination; nor does a claim for all elements collectively under a different co-operative law. A claim that includes an element not co-acting as part of the combination is invalid. Combination claims must distinguish clearly between elements and the manner of their co-operation. (See Delaware Coal & Ice Co. v. Packer; Van Camp v. Maryland Pavement Co.)

name: Problem-solution approach (practical prosecution steps)
description: The Australian Patent Office favours a problem-solution approach that involves: (i) construing the specification to determine the problem the invention solves; (ii) identifying the relevant PSA; (iii) determining whether, in the context of the problem, any pieces of prior art could reasonably be expected to have been combined by the PSA; (iv) determining the CGK; and (v) determining whether, in the context of the problem, the claimed invention would have been obvious to the PSA.
guidance: Step (v) typically involves applying one or more of the judicial tests for inventive step; other factors (secondary indicia) may also be considered for/against obviousness.

name: Innovative step standard (innovation patents)
description: Innovation patents require only an 'innovative step' — i.e., that the claims make a substantial contribution over the prior art — a lower threshold than inventive step.
guidance: Innovation patents: max term 8 years, up to five claims, quick grant but substantive examination and certification required for enforcement; phasing out began 26 Aug 2021 (divisional innovation patents allowed from standard applications with effective filing date before that); innovative step is easier to meet and hence often harder to invalidate.

name: Timeline audits (practitioner action point)
description: Map pending/appealed cases against the 1 April 2027 sunset clause for Standard 1 and consider timing effects on applicable inventive-step standards.
guidance: Assess whether divisional claims subject to a higher inventive step standard can be incorporated into a parent patent subject to a lower standard (e.g., by narrowing post‑grant amendments); consider filing divisional innovation patent applications where permitted to strengthen position.

name: 37 CFR 1.131 does not apply in interference proceedings
description: Interference practice operates to the exclusion of ex parte practice under 37 CFR 1.131; subject matter that is prior art under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) and is subject to an interference is not open to further inquiry under 37 CFR 1.131 during the interference proceeding.
guidance: If an application claim is the “same patentable invention” as a domestic patent, interference practice (not 1.131 affidavits) governs antedating. The term 'same patentable invention' includes anticipation or obviousness relative to the patent claim.

name: Utility: known utility required at time of reduction to practice
description: A claimed invention is not actually reduced to practice unless there is a known practical utility for the invention at the time of reduction to practice (except for plant and design inventions).
guidance: Utility may be shown by successful tests (human or appropriately correlated animal tests) or other evidence establishing substantial utility. Demonstrated substantial utility for any purpose can suffice if the count does not recite a particular utility.

name: Patent quality — correctness and clarity
description: Patent quality is central ... it is critically important that the USPTO issue patents that are both correct and clear. Historically the USPTO’s primary focus has been on correctness, but the evolving patent landscape has challenged the agency to increase its focus on clarity.
guidance: The agency assesses both correctness (legal/technical correctness of decisions) and clarity (clear reasoning, claim interpretation, and record) as dual pillars of patent quality; programs and trainings are oriented to improving both dimensions.

name: Clarity of the Record — best practices for prosecution record clarity
description: The Clarity of the Record Pilot is identifying best practices for enhancing the clarity of particular aspects of the prosecution record, namely claim interpretation, reasons for allowance, and interview summaries, and is exploring the impact of implementing these best practices during examination.
guidance: Pilot identifies concrete practices (e.g., clearer reasons for allowance, better interview summaries) and evaluates effects on examination outcomes and record usefulness.

name: Claims define scope of the patented invention
description: “claims of a patent define the scope of a patented invention and the patentee’s right to exclude.” Claims are 'the life of the patent,' defining the limits of the patent’s scope.
guidance: Use claims to determine the patent’s scope because that scope must be known for protection of the patentee and encouragement of others; treat claim language as central in any scope analysis (citing Teva, Markman, Philips, Gen. Elec.).

name: Claim construction serves to define scope and is a judicial statement
description: “Claim construction serves to define the scope of the patented invention and the patentee’s right to exclude.” A claim construction is the judicial statement of what is and is not covered by the technical terms and other words of the claims.
guidance: Recognize when an analysis is determining the meaning/boundaries of claim terms — that is claim construction — regardless of label the tribunal uses.

name: Standard of review: de novo for construction; substantial-evidence for underlying facts
description: “We review the issue of claim construction of a patent claim de novo with any underlying fact findings reviewed for substantial evidence.”
guidance: On appeal, claim construction is reviewed de novo (cases cited). Factual findings supporting construction or application to facts are reviewed for substantial evidence; properly distinguish which standard applies to each aspect of the tribunal’s decision.

name: Determine whether a tribunal has construed a claim by whether its analysis established scope/boundaries
description: “To determine whether a court, or the Board, has construed a claim, it is helpful to look to the outcome of the tribunal’s analysis. If the outcome ... establishes the scope (e.g., boundaries) and meaning of the patented subject matter, the court (or the Board) has most likely construed the claim.”
guidance: Even if the tribunal says it did not construe a claim, examine whether its findings effectively established claim scope (citing Netword, HTC, Trading Techs.). If so, treat it as claim construction for purposes of review.

name: Separately listed claim elements create a presumption of distinctness
description: “Where a claim lists elements separately, the clear implication of the claim language is that those elements are distinct components of the patented invention.”
guidance: Apply the presumption that separately recited elements denote distinct components (citing Becton, Engel), but do not treat this presumption as absolute.

name: Presumption of distinctness is rebuttable by the intrinsic record/specification
description: “There is a ‘presumption’ that separately listed claim limitations may indicate separate and distinct physical structure, but that presumption may always be rebutted in the context of a particular patent.”
guidance: If claim language or the specification contemplates embodiments where one claimed input is calculated from another (or otherwise intertwines elements), that intrinsic evidence can rebut the presumption of distinctness (examples and citations: Powell, specification §§).

name: Do not interpret claims to exclude embodiments disclosed in the specification
description: “We normally do not interpret claim terms in a way that excludes embodiments disclosed in the specification.”
guidance: Ensure claim construction reads claims to encompass embodiments expressly disclosed in the specification unless the patentee clearly disavowed that scope; a construction that excludes such embodiments is likely erroneous (citing Oatey).

name: Claim differentiation is a guide, not a rigid rule
description: The doctrine of claim differentiation only creates a rebuttable presumption that each claim in a patent has a different scope; it is a guide, not a rigid rule of claim construction.
guidance: Do not mechanically apply claim-differentiation to restrict scope; evaluate whether intrinsic evidence rebuts the presumption (citing Curtiss‑Wright).

name: Tribunal may adopt a construction neither party proposed but must afford APA notice and opportunity to respond
description: “The Board may adopt a claim construction of a disputed term that neither party proposes without running afoul of the APA.” However, the Board cannot, without notice and opportunity for the parties to respond, change theories midstream by adopting a claim construction in its final written decision that neither party requested nor anticipated.
guidance: If the Board’s construction was not proposed by the parties, ensure the record shows the parties had notice of the contested construction issue and an opportunity to address it; otherwise APA violation may require reversal (citing Qualcomm, SAS, Hamilton Beach).

name: Language like 'based at least in part on' places no constraint on manner inputs are used
description: In the ’753 claim the phrase that a time is determined 'based at least in part on' each of five inputs 'places no constraint on the manner in which the inputs are used.'
guidance: When claim language uses broad linking phrasing (e.g., 'based at least in part on'), prefer a construction that permits interdependence among inputs unless the specification or prosecution history indicates otherwise.

name: Implicit constructions and the necessity to examine whether parties litigated the issue
description: A tribunal can implicitly construe a claim even if it states it did not, and an implicit construction does not violate the APA if the parties had notice of the contested claim construction issues and an opportunity to be heard.
guidance: Examine the record for whether the parties disputed the scope/meaning of the claim term during proceedings; if the issue was squarely presented, the tribunal's implicit construction is less likely to be an APA problem (examples in the record).

name: Written description requirement (Federal Circuit formulation)
description: The specification must describe an invention 'understandable to that skilled artisan and show that the inventor actually invented the invention claimed.'
guidance: This is a separate requirement from enablement; courts ask whether the specification puts the PHOSITA in possession of the claimed invention. Applied via tests like the representative species test and structural-features analysis; failure occurs when disclosure only describes a portion of a genus or amounts to a research plan.

name: Enablement requirement (statutory phrasing)
description: A written description of how to make and use the invention 'in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art . . . to make and use the same.'
guidance: Enablement is judged by whether the specification enables a PHOSITA to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention. The enablement prepositional phrase was construed to modify the manner-and-process description (how to make and use) and not the separate written-description component.

name: Full-scope enablement (Supreme Court rule)
description: A patent must enable the full scope of the claimed monopoly; 'the more a party claims, the broader the monopoly it demands, the more it must enable.'
guidance: The Supreme Court emphasized that reasonable experimentation may be permitted, but broad claims that demand a large monopoly require proportionally greater disclosure. Whether experimentation is reasonable depends on the nature of the invention and the underlying art.

name: Undue experimentation / In re Wands analysis
description: Enablement is defeated if practicing the full scope of the claim would require 'undue experimentation.'
guidance: Courts apply Wands factors (e.g., breadth of functional limitations, the presence/absence of detailed guidance or examples, predictability of the art) to assess whether undue experimentation is required. Applied to antibody genus claims: broad functional limitations + narrow examples + unpredictable effects of sequence changes => undue experimentation and lack of enablement.

name: Representative species test / structural-features test for written description
description: A written-description inquiry can ask whether the specification provides representative species or structural features sufficient to show possession of the claimed genus.
guidance: If disclosed species only occupy a 'corner' of the genus and are not representative of its diversity, the disclosure shows possession only of that portion (a 'research plan') and not the whole genus (see AbbVie analogies: plot of land).

name: Antibody exception / newly characterized antigen test
description: Historical doctrine (and USPTO Training Materials) sometimes held that disclosing a well-characterized (newly characterized) antigen could satisfy written description for antibodies that bind it, i.e., disclosure of the antigen put the applicant in possession of antibodies which bind to that antigen where generation of antibodies was routine.
guidance: This 'antibody exception' allowed sparse disclosure (e.g., in USPTO 1999 and 2008 Training Materials an example where the specification states 'antigen X has been isolated' and the claim 'an isolated antibody capable of binding to antigen X' was treated as adequate). Courts have limited or retreated from this exception where generating antibodies was not routine or would require substantial experimentation.

name: Product-by-process claiming as an enablement path
description: Product-by-process claims can satisfy enablement by describing a process and the resulting product where the inventor cannot otherwise describe the structure of the product.
guidance: The Federal Circuit has allowed such claims (e.g., Hybritech), especially early in antibody technology when structure was not well understood. But functional/product-by-process claims still require sufficient disclosure and can be vulnerable if they attempt to claim more than the specification enables.

name: Functional/genus claiming requires a 'quality common to' the genus or sufficient correlation between structure and function
description: Broad functional claims that attempt to cover a genus of molecules must show a quality common to the entire genus (or otherwise provide a correlation between structure and function) in order to be sustained.
guidance: Because many antibodies with widely varying sequences can fulfill the same function, claimants must identify a unifying quality (e.g., epitope, binding affinity, representative structural features) or provide representative species; otherwise claims risk invalidity for lack of written description or enablement.

name: Centocor standard limiting the antibody exception
description: The antibody exception applies only where creation of the claimed antibodies is 'routine' — if generating the antibodies is not straightforward using conventional methods, disclosure of an antigen alone is insufficient.
guidance: Centocor held that disclosure of a well-characterized antigen supports written description only where generating the claimed antibodies from that antigen would be routine for a PHOSITA. If generating antibodies with the claimed properties was not straightforward, the written description fails.

name: AbbVie precedent on representativeness and research plans
description: Functional genus claims are 'inherently vulnerable' where it is difficult to establish a correlation between structure and function for the whole genus; describing only one type of structurally similar antibodies that are not representative of the full genus is insufficient.
