guidance: The court warned that outlining limited examples without enough representative species is tantamount to a research plan and not a sufficient written description for a broad genus claim (AbbVie: genus invalid for lack of written description where disclosed species were not representative).

name: Supreme Court practical guidance: 'research assignments' vs. adequate disclosure
description: The Supreme Court criticized disclosures that ask scientists to create and screen a wide range of candidates (i.e., tasks amounting to 'randomly try[ing] a large set of combinations') and held that disclosures which amount to research projects are not enabling of all claimed embodiments.
guidance: Court analogies (e.g., lock with many combinations) show that providing a few successful examples and instructions that effectively tell practitioners to 'try many combinations and record the successful ones' does not enable the full scope. 'Roadmap' and 'conservative substitution' methods that only yield research assignments are insufficient to enable a broad genus.

name: USPTO examiner guidance (1999 and 2008 Written Description Training Materials)
description: USPTO training materials historically instructed examiners that certain sparse disclosures (e.g., identifying and characterizing an antigen and contemplating antibodies to it) could suffice for written description of antibody function claims.
guidance: The Training Materials included hypothetical specifications and concluded that statements like 'antigen X has been isolated' plus molecular weight and isolation protocol — even without teaching antibodies that specifically bind X — could 'meet the requirement' under 35 U.S.C. §112 according to the 1999 guidance. Later case law has curtailed reliance on these lower-expectation examiner practices.

name: Claim interpretation in reexamination
description: Original patent claims in reexamination are given the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification; limitations in the specification are not read into the claims.
guidance: Exception: for reexamination of expired patents whose claims cannot be amended, apply a policy of narrow construction favoring validity (see In re Papst-Motoren). The statutory presumption of validity (35 U.S.C. 282) does not apply in reexamination (In re Etter).

name: 35 U.S.C. 112 compliance limited to amendatory/new matter
description: When new claims are presented or any part of the disclosure is amended, compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112 (enablement/ written description and claim definiteness) is to be examined only as to the amendatory (new) matter.
guidance: Do not raise 112 issues as to matter that is identical to the original patent disclosure. If an amendment adds a limitation not found in the original claim/disclosure, the examiner should consider 112 only with respect to that limitation. See MPEP §§ 2163 - 2173.05(v).

name: Prohibition on new matter (35 U.S.C. 132) in reexamination
description: 35 U.S.C. 305 authorizes examination under 35 U.S.C. 132 which prohibits introduction of new matter into the disclosure during reexamination; new matter added to claims or affecting claim limitations should lead to rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112 (written description).
guidance: Consider the relationship between the written description requirement and the new matter prohibition (see MPEP § 2163.06).

name: Amendment of the specification must comply with 35 U.S.C. 112
description: If the specification is amended in reexamination, the examiner must ensure the amendment meets 35 U.S.C. 112 requirements because an amendment can redefine claim terms and render claims unsupported or unclear.
guidance: An amendment to the specification can cause claims to fail 112 even if claims themselves were not amended.

name: No enlargement of claim scope (35 U.S.C. 305)
description: No proposed amended or new claim enlarging the scope of the claims of the patent will be permitted in a reexamination proceeding.
guidance: Examine new/amended claims under 35 U.S.C. 305 to determine enlargement. If a claim enlarges scope it must be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 305 using form paragraph 22.11.

name: Criteria for determining enlargement of scope
description: A presented claim 'enlarges the scope' where it is broader than each and every claim of the patent; a claim is broadened if it contains any conceivable product or process that would not have infringed the original patent, and it is broadened if broader in any one respect even if narrower in others.
guidance: See MPEP § 1412.03 for guidance on what is broadening. Examiner should identify and explain the claim limitations that broaden the scope.

name: Form paragraph 22.11 for 35 U.S.C. 305 rejections
description: Use form paragraph 22.11 to reject claims under 35 U.S.C. 305 as enlarging the scope of the patent in ex parte reexamination.
guidance: In bracket 2 identify the claim limitations considered to broaden the claim and explain in the Office action why those limitations broaden the scope (see MPEP § 2258 guidance).

name: Claiming foreign and domestic priority in reexamination
description: Patent owner may perfect previously made foreign priority claims under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) by submitting certified copies; in some circumstances patent owner may submit both the priority claim and certified copy for the first time in reexamination but certain limitations apply for patents matured from applications filed on/after November 29, 2000.
guidance: If correcting or adding a priority claim for a patent matured from a utility/plant application filed on/after Nov 29, 2000, the patent owner must file a grantable petition for an unintentionally delayed priority claim under 37 CFR 1.55(c) or 1.78(a)(3) as appropriate. Reexamination cannot be used to add or correct benefit claims under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) after a patent has issued for patents matured from applications filed on/after Nov 29, 2000 (AIPA amendment). See MPEP §§ 201.11, 201.14(a).

name: Requests for reexamination filed on a patent after it has been reissued
description: Reexamination requests filed on a patent after it has been reissued will be denied because the prior patent has been surrendered; to reexamine the reissued patent, a new request based on the reissue specification and claims must be filed.
guidance: Any patent-owner amendments accompanying the initial reexamination request should treat the granted reissue text as the patent text; bracketing/underlining should reflect the reissue changes. See MPEP § 2285 for post-issuance reissue timing.

name: Examples and exceptions where old art may be relied upon despite prior citation
description: Illustrative unusual fact patterns where previously cited art may nonetheless support reexamination include: (a) the old art is presented in a new light or different way due to a material new argument; (b) only part of a cited reference (e.g., portion of a textbook) was previously considered and other portions now relied upon teach the claims; (c) prior examiner misappreciated the reference (wrong date, inadequate antedating declaration, incorrect filing date); (d) a foreign-language reference was not previously fully/accurately translated; (e) cumulative references that merely reiterate verbatim teachings of previously applied references are generally not grounds alone.
guidance: These examples are illustrative, not exhaustive. Where a foreign language reference is now fully translated and the translation shows teachings that were not previously considered, reexamination may proceed. Cumulative references that substantially reiterate prior teachings will rarely preclude reliance on new art because most references add new information or present it differently.

name: Statutory categories (Step 1): process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter
description: 35 U.S.C. 101 defines four categories of invention: processes (actions or series of steps) and three categories of 'things'—machines, manufactures and compositions of matter.
guidance: For non-process categories, the eligible subject matter must exist in some physical or tangible form. A claim need only fall within at least one category. When in doubt, examine the entire disclosure and construe claims under the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI). See MPEP § 2106.03 for definitions and examples (e.g., microprocessor as manufacture; bicycle as both machine and manufacture).

name: Product must have physical/tangible form for machine/manufacture/composition
description: For machines, manufactures, and compositions of matter, the claimed product must have a physical or tangible form to fall within a statutory category.
guidance: Intangible collections of information or software expressed as code detached from any medium are not statutory products. If a product claim lacks physical structure or tangible form, it may fail Step 1 even if otherwise new and useful. See Digitech and Microsoft v. AT&T examples in MPEP § 2106.03.

name: Step 1 evaluation procedure
description: Step 1 asks whether the claim is to a process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter (i.e., whether it falls within one or more statutory categories).
guidance: If the claim as a whole does not fall within any statutory category (Step 1: NO), make a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 (use form paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01 as appropriate). If the BRI covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments, the claim may fail Step 1 and examiner should point out the BRI and recommend narrowing amendment if possible. If claim falls within a statutory category (Step 1: YES), proceed to Step 2A (Alice/Mayo). See MPEP § 2106.03 and § 2106.04.

name: Alice/Mayo two-part test (Step 2 overall)
description: Step 2 is the Alice/Mayo test: Step 2A — determine whether the claims are directed to a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon). If yes, Step 2B — determine whether the claim recites additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception.
guidance: Only the Alice/Mayo framework should be used for 35 U.S.C. 101 eligibility determinations. If Step 2A is NO, the claim is eligible without reaching Step 2B. See MPEP § 2106.04 and § 2106.05.

name: Judicial exceptions identification (Step 2A)
description: Judicial exceptions are abstract ideas, laws of nature, and natural phenomena; these concepts have also been described as physical phenomena, products of nature, scientific principles, mental processes, disembodied concepts, mathematical algorithms, etc.
guidance: There are no bright lines among the exceptions; it is sufficient that the claimed concept aligns with at least one judicial exception. The examiner should identify the specific claim limitation(s) believed to recite an exception. The Supreme Court's preemption concern guides this inquiry. See MPEP § 2106.04.

name: Markedly different characteristics analysis for natural products (2106.04(c))
description: When assessing product claims that implicate nature-based subject matter, determine whether the claimed product has markedly different characteristics from any natural product (i.e., whether the claimed product exhibits characteristics that are markedly different in kind and not merely in degree).
guidance: Compare the claimed product as a whole with the naturally occurring counterpart. The analysis looks to whether the claim recites features that give rise to new or enhanced properties or functionalities. See MPEP § 2106.04(c) and cases distinguishing products of nature.

name: Step 2B: 'Significantly more' / inventive concept (overview)
description: If a claim is directed to a judicial exception under Step 2A, Step 2B asks whether the claim as a whole recites additional elements, individually or in combination, that amount to significantly more than the exception (i.e., provide an 'inventive concept' or practical application).
guidance: Consider whether additional claim limitations integrate the exception into a practical application or provide an unconventional technical solution. The machine-or-transformation test is a useful clue to this inquiry but not a standalone test. See MPEP § 2106.05 for specific considerations and examples.

name: 2106.05(a) — Improvements to computer functioning or other technology
description: A claim that improves the functioning of a computer or another technology or technical field can demonstrate 'significantly more.'
guidance: If the claim limitations provide an improvement in computer technology (e.g., improved data structure, enhanced processing) or solve a technological problem, this supports eligibility. Enfish and McRO are cited as examples where improvements supported eligibility. See MPEP § 2106.05(a).

name: 2106.05(c) — Particular transformation
description: A claimed transformation of an article to a different state or thing (a particular transformation) can support a 'significantly more' finding.
guidance: Transformations that meaningfully change the nature of an article (physical transformations) are relevant under Step 2B and are related to the machine-or-transformation analysis. See MPEP § 2106.05(c).

name: 2106.05(e) — Other meaningful limitations / unconventional ordered combination
description: Other limitations that meaningfully limit the judicial exception or that recite an unconventional ordered combination of elements may supply 'significantly more.'
guidance: Assess whether the claim recites limitations that integrate the exception into a practical application or produce an improvement. An unconventional combination that offers a technical solution supports eligibility. See MPEP § 2106.05(e) and cited Federal Circuit examples.

name: Preemption concern underlying the Alice/Mayo framework
description: The underlying concern driving the two-part framework is preemption — whether the claim effectively monopolizes a judicial exception and would prevent others from using basic tools of scientific and technological work.
guidance: Although preemption is not a standalone statutory test, examiners should consider whether a claim's breadth would preempt use of the exception when analyzing Steps 2A and 2B. Cite relevant case law and factor preemption into eligibility rationale. See MPEP § 2106.05.

name: Streamlined analysis and Pathways A/B/C (2106.06)
description: The flowchart shows three pathways to eligibility: Pathway A (self-evident eligibility; streamlined analysis), Pathway B (claim falls within a statutory category and is not directed to an exception — Step 2A: NO), and Pathway C (claim falls within a statutory category, is directed to an exception, but recites significantly more — Step 2A: YES; Step 2B: YES).
guidance: If eligibility is self-evident, use streamlined analysis (Pathway A). If uncertain whether a streamlined analysis applies, conduct a full Alice/Mayo analysis. Claims found eligible at A but analyzed further will be found eligible at B or C. See MPEP § 2106.06 for examples of self-evident eligibility and clear improvements to technology.

name: Formulating and supporting rejections for lack of subject matter eligibility (2106.07(a))
description: When making a 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection, the examiner must identify the judicial exception at issue, explain why the claim is directed to that exception (identify specific claim limitations), set forth the BRI, and explain why the additional limitations do not amount to significantly more — supporting factual findings with evidence.
guidance: Use appropriate form paragraphs where applicable, cite the specification and prior art/evidence for conventionality, and explain the reasoning clearly to assist applicant's response. See MPEP § 2106.07(a) for required content and examples of acceptable explanations.

name: Evaluating applicant's response to 101 rejection (2106.07(b))
description: On receiving applicant's arguments or evidence in response to a 101 rejection, the examiner must evaluate whether the applicant has rebutted the factual bases of the rejection or shown error, and determine whether to maintain, withdraw, or reopen the rejection.
guidance: Consider claim amendments, factual evidence submitted (e.g., declarations, references), and whether the examiner's characterization of the claim and the BRI were correct. Provide further explanation if maintaining the rejection. See MPEP § 2106.07(b).

name: Clarifying the record when claims are found eligible or in rejections (2106.07(c))
description: When claims are deemed patent eligible, examiners may make clarifying remarks on the record (e.g., reference portions of the specification that describe claimed improvements and note claim elements producing that improvement). Similarly, clarifying remarks may assist in explaining the rationale for a rejection (e.g., explaining the BRI).
guidance: Clarifying remarks may be made at any point during prosecution, including with a notice of allowance. They help applicants understand the examiner's rationale and suggested amendments. See MPEP § 2106.07(c).

name: Use other statutory provisions (35 U.S.C. 112/102/103) in conjunction with 101
description: Examiners are reminded that 35 U.S.C. 101 is not the sole tool for determining patentability; 35 U.S.C. 112, 102, and 103 provide additional requirements and tools to ensure claims meet patentability conditions.
guidance: Even if a claim meets 101, it still must satisfy novelty, non-obviousness, enablement/written description, and other statutory requirements. Cite and apply these provisions as needed (see MPEP § 2103 and related sections).

name: Claim interpretation examples as guidance for eligibility determinations
description: Recent case law examples (e.g., Mentor Graphics, Synopsys, Enfish, McRO, Amdocs) illustrate that claim interpretation — in light of the specification and BRI — can determine whether claims are mental processes/abstract ideas or improvements in technology.
guidance: Interpret claim terms in light of the specification and record; whether limitations require implementation (e.g., specific algorithms, specific machine limitations) can be determinative. Use these cases as analogies but analyze each claim on its facts. See MPEP § 2106 II and examples throughout § 2106.04–2106.05.

name: Documenting conventionality and factual findings
description: When concluding that claim elements are well-understood, routine, or conventional, examiners should support such findings with evidence from the specification, prior art, or other factual sources.
guidance: Conclusions that elements are conventional must be supported; unsupported conclusory statements are improper. When relying on common sense or routine-ness, document the rationale and any supporting citations. See MPEP § 2106.05(d) and 2106.07(a).

name: Best practice to suggest amendments when BRI covers non-statutory embodiments
description: When the BRI of a claim covers non-statutory embodiments, the examiner should, as a best practice, point out the BRI and recommend an amendment to narrow the claim to those embodiments that fall within a statutory category.
guidance: This practice helps the applicant resolve eligibility issues and facilitates prosecution. Examples include narrowing machine-readable media claims to exclude carrier waves. See MPEP § 2106.03 and § 2106.07(c).

name: IDS filed after payment of the issue fee generally not considered
description: After the issue fee has been paid, information disclosure statements filed in the application will not be considered and will merely be placed in the application file.
guidance: Applicants may pursue alternatives to have information considered: file a petition under 37 CFR 1.313(c) to withdraw application from issue (with stringent requirements and timing uncertainties), file an RCE under 37 CFR 1.114, or file a continuing application under 37 CFR 1.53(b)/(d). The Quick Path IDS (QPIDS) pilot program (under specific circumstances) may allow submission after issue-fee-but-prior-to-grant — see USPTO QPIDS materials. Petitions under 1.313(c)(1) to withdraw from issue require an unequivocal statement that one or more claims are unpatentable over the information (a statement that only a 'serious question' exists is insufficient).

name: Effect of IDS submission on finality of next Office action when IDS used in new ground of rejection
description: If information submitted during the period governed by 37 CFR 1.97(c) with a 1.97(e) statement is used in a new ground of rejection on unamended claims, the next Office action will not be made final because it is clear applicant submitted the information promptly.
guidance: Conversely, the information submitted with a 1.97(e) statement may be used and the next Office action made final if the new ground of rejection was necessitated by an amendment of the application by applicant. If the IDS was filed with the fee under 1.17(p) in this period, the examiner may use the information and make the next Office action final provided no other new ground not necessitated by amendment is introduced.

name: Public-domain works: references to Project Gutenberg may be removed but license advised
description: If an individual Project Gutenberg electronic work is unprotected by U.S. copyright law and you are located in the United States, we do not claim a right to prevent you from copying, distributing, performing, displaying or creating derivative works based on the work as long as all references to Project Gutenberg are removed.
guidance: Although removal is allowed for public-domain works, Project Gutenberg asks users to keep the license and references to support the Project Gutenberg mission; removal is permitted but then Project Gutenberg trademark rules no longer apply.

name: Provisional nonstatutory double patenting rejection (no secondary references)
description: Claim [1] provisionally rejected on the ground of nonstatutory double patenting as being unpatentable over claim [2] of copending Application No. [3] (reference application). Although the claims at issue are not identical, they are not patentably distinct from each other because [4]. This is a provisional nonstatutory double patenting rejection because the patentably indistinct claims have not in fact been patented.
guidance: Use when the patentably indistinct claims are in another copending application. Form paragraph 8.33 must precede this form paragraph and be used only once in an Office action. Do not use this paragraph if the patentably indistinct claims are in a patent (use 8.33 + 8.34 instead). May be used where reference application and application under examination: (a) name same inventive entity; (b) name different inventive entities but are commonly assigned; (c) are not commonly assigned but have at least one common (joint) inventor (unless confidentiality under 35 U.S.C. 122 prevents disclosure); (d) are filed by a common applicant (35 U.S.C. 118); (e) claim patentably indistinct inventions made within a joint research agreement scope under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) (for pre‑AIA filings); or (f) claim patentably indistinct inventions and were commonly owned or deemed commonly owned under certain 35 U.S.C. provisions (for FITF/AIA). If the reference application is currently commonly assigned but file does not establish common ownership at time of invention, form paragraph 8.28.fti may be used additionally to resolve priority issues under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f)/(g). In bracket 4 provide appropriate explanation for anticipation or rationale for obviousness of the claims being rejected over the claims of the cited application. For pre‑AIA first‑to‑invent law, if the reference application is prior art under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e), also consider making a provisional 102(e)/103(a) rejection using form paragraph 7.21.01.fti; do not make/maintain such rejections if the reference application is disqualified as prior art under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c). For FITF/AIA examinations, also make rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) or 35 U.S.C. 103 where appropriate.

name: Provisional nonstatutory double patenting rejection with secondary references (primary reference = copending application)
description: Claim [1] provisionally rejected on the ground of nonstatutory double patenting as being unpatentable over claim [2] of copending Application No. [3] in view of [4]. [5] This is a provisional nonstatutory double patenting rejection.
guidance: Use where the primary reference is a copending application and an obviousness analysis is required (form paragraph 8.37). Form paragraph 8.33 must precede. Do not use if patentably indistinct claims are in a patent (use 8.36 instead). May be used where copending application and application under examination: (a) name same inventive entity; (b) are commonly assigned; (c) not commonly assigned but have at least one common (joint) inventor (unless disclosure would violate 35 U.S.C. 122 confidentiality); (d) filed by common applicant (35 U.S.C. 118); (e) claim indistinct inventions under joint research agreement scope (pre‑AIA 103(c)); or (f) claim indistinct inventions and were commonly owned or deemed commonly owned under applicable provisions for FITF/AIA. If currently commonly assigned but file does not establish common ownership at time of later invention, use form paragraph 8.28.fti in addition to resolve priority issues under pre‑AIA 102(f)/(g). For FITF/AIA, if primary reference application is to a different inventive entity and is commonly assigned, also use form paragraph 8.28.aia if no evidence of common ownership not later than the effective filing date; make 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) or 103 rejections where appropriate. In bracket 3 insert number of primary reference application; bracket 4 insert secondary reference (must be prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102); bracket 5 insert explanation of obviousness analysis. Provisional nonstatutory double patenting rejection should also be made in the primary reference application.

name: Two‑way test for distinctness (when required and how to apply)
description: A two‑way test is to be applied only when the applicant could not have filed the claims in a single application and the Office is solely responsible for any delays. When making a two‑way distinctness determination, apply the obviousness analysis twice: (1) analyze obviousness of the application claims in view of the patent claims; and (2) analyze obviousness of the patent claims in view of the application claims.
guidance: If both analyses lead to a conclusion that the claimed invention is an obvious variation of the invention claimed in the other application/patent, an obviousness‑type nonstatutory double patenting rejection is appropriate. If either analysis does not lead to a conclusion of obviousness, no obviousness‑type double patenting rejection is made (though equitable double patenting may still be possible). Unless the record clearly shows administrative delay solely caused by the Office and that the applicant could not have avoided separate filings, the examiner may use the one‑way distinctness determination and shift the burden to the applicant to show why a two‑way determination is required. The MPEP cites case law (In re Berg; In re Hubbell; In re Goodman; Pierce v. DuMont; In re Emert; In re Braat) illustrating factors: applicant control of prosecution, applicant delay (e.g., repeated extensions, abandonments and continuations), or Office delay. Document reasons for adopting one‑way vs two‑way approach and apply both directions only when warranted by facts.

name: Bracket/fill‑in guidance for form paragraphs
description: Insert appropriate information into numbered brackets in form paragraphs: e.g., bracket 1 = claim number(s) being rejected; bracket 2 = claim number(s) of reference; bracket 3 = number of the reference patent or application; bracket 4 = explanation of subject matter or secondary reference; bracket 5 = explanation of obviousness analysis.
guidance: Follow the specific bracket guidance in each form paragraph: • For form paragraph 8.35/8.37 bracket 3 = number of reference application; bracket 4 = secondary reference (must be prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102); bracket 5 = explanation of obviousness analysis. • For form paragraph 8.36 bracket 3 = number of primary reference patent; bracket 4 = secondary reference; bracket 5 = explanation of obviousness analysis. • For Schneller‑type paragraphs 8.38/8.39 bracket 4 = description of subject matter covered in the earlier patent/application. Ensure clarity in bracketed explanations to support anticipation or obviousness rationale.

name: Double patenting in design/plant vs utility situations
description: Double patenting issues may be raised where an applicant has filed both a utility patent application (35 U.S.C. 111) and either an application for a plant patent (35 U.S.C. 161) or a design patent (35 U.S.C. 171). In general, the same double patenting principles and criteria that are applied in utility‑utility situations are applied to utility‑plant or utility‑design situations.
guidance: Double patenting rejections in utility‑plant situations may be made in appropriate circumstances. Double patenting is rare in design‑utility contexts; courts have found in some cases no double patenting where the utility claims are directed to internal construction and design claims to external appearance (Carman Indus. v. Wahl). Two‑way distinctness determinations may be necessary in design‑utility cases depending on facts. Apply case law and policy consistently and evaluate whether claims are directed to the same invention or obvious variations.

name: Factors to lift a stay during appeal
description: Court may lift a stay during appeal where further delay would create undue prejudice (e.g., due to age of owner/primary witness), the appeal involves only a single claim (especially one affirmed previously), and substantial district-court progress (discovery begun, Markman hearing held) has occurred.
guidance: Taken together these factors can warrant lifting a stay even while an appeal is pending; courts weigh undue prejudice, scope of the appeal, and case progress.

name: Stay when some patents have instituted IPRs and others denied
description: Courts may stay litigation only as to patents that are subject to instituted IPRs and decline to stay patents where IPR was denied.
guidance: Court considers simplification of issues, whether PTAB claim constructions bind the court, stage of the case, plaintiff's willingness to proceed on specific patents, and undue prejudice (e.g., small plaintiff vs large defendant, independence of infringement claims).

name: Use of PTAB expert application to assess claim definiteness
description: An expert’s prior application of a reference using a disputed claim term 'without any uncertainty' can support the conclusion that a skilled artisan would understand the claim term with reasonable certainty.
guidance: Prior expert usage in IPRs can be persuasive in district court indefiniteness disputes; courts may rely on how experts applied terms in related PTAB proceedings.

name: Collateral estoppel dismissal based on PTAB IPR decisions
description: A court may dismiss an infringement complaint due to collateral estoppel when PTAB final written decisions held claims unpatentable and differences between asserted claims do not materially alter the invalidity question, and the other elements of collateral estoppel are met.
guidance: Material similarity of the invalidity question is key; slight rewording of claims will not avoid collateral estoppel if the invalidity analysis is unchanged.

name: Genus vs species identity rule
description: A genus invention of a later-filed application is deemed to be identical with a species invention of a prior-filed application.
guidance: This addresses identity when claim scope overlaps across genus/species between filings of different dates.

name: Permissible claim amendment cases (Article 47(3))
description: Claims may be amended only in the following cases: 1) claims are narrowed by restricting or deleting claims, or adding limitations; 2) clerical errors corrected; 3) ambiguous description clarified; 4) amendment to reinstate previously presented claims under specified conditions.
guidance: Claim amendments that broaden scope are generally disallowed except in tightly-defined reinstatement scenarios.

name: Substantive restriction: prohibition of addition of new matter depending on amendment period
description: The addition of new matter shall be prohibited when an amendment is made within the voluntary amendment period before the start of examination or within the period designated for submitting arguments on a non-final rejection. During certain later periods only narrowing of claims and similar limited amendments are permitted; addition of new matter remains prohibited.
guidance: Scope of permissible amendment differs by period; later periods impose further restrictions (e.g., only narrowing allowed).

name: Assessment rules: sources not usable as basis for original disclosure
description: A first country application or a prior-filed application forming the basis of a priority claim shall not correspond to the specification or drawing(s) as originally filed and shall not be used as the basis of assessment in addition of new matter. An abstract shall also not be included in the specification/drawings which form the basis of assessment.
guidance: Comparisons must use the specification/drawings filed on the filing date; abstracts and priority documents are not substitutes.

name: Narrowing genus to species: when it constitutes new matter
description: Where an amendment is made to narrow a claim as from a genus to a species, unless the species is supported by the original specification and drawings, or unless one skilled in the art would readily recognize the species from the genus in light of ordinary skill at filing time, it shall be viewed as introduction of new matter.
guidance: Examples: inserting specific material (e.g., 'ABS') is new matter unless originally disclosed or obvious; specifying 'proximity sensor' for 'sensor detecting rotation' is acceptable if skilled person would intuitively associate them.

name: Broadening species to genus and deletion of essential limitations
description: Where an amendment broadens a claim as from a species to a genus, if the genus encompasses other species than the species disclosed and the other species may have different function or effects, the amendment shall constitute introduction of new matter. Deleting limitations described as essential for solving a problem is introduction of new matter; deleting arbitrary limitations unrelated to solving the problem may be allowed.
guidance: Examples: changing a detailed structural limitation to a broader term may alter expected effects and be new matter; deleting purely arbitrary limitations may be acceptable.

name: Statutory obviousness standard (35 U.S.C. §103)
description: Obviousness under §103: patentability is precluded when the differences between the subject matter sought to be patented and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: This statutory definition is the starting point for analysis. Interpretations and applications are shaped by Graham and later cases; treat it as the legal standard to be applied through subsidiary factual inquiries (scope/content of prior art; differences with claims; level of ordinary skill).

name: Graham factual framework
description: Under Graham, determine (1) the scope and content of the prior art, (2) the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue, and (3) the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; then weigh secondary considerations.
guidance: Use this roadmap to structure the obviousness inquiry. Secondary considerations (commercial success, long-felt need, failure of others, etc.) may be used to illuminate the circumstances surrounding invention and to rebut a prima facie case of obviousness.

name: Differences between claims and prior art (claim scope)
description: Ascertain claim scope and what features differ from the prior art; claim scope is a question of law informed by claim construction.
guidance: Broad claim scope may make combining prior art more likely to render claims obvious; avoid reading unclaimed limitations into claims to escape relevant prior art (district court guidance).

name: Motivation to combine prior art (TSM as a factor, not rigid rule)
description: Identify a reason that would have prompted a person of ordinary skill to combine elements of the prior art in the way claimed; KSR rejected TSM as a rigid test but acknowledged motive can inform analysis.
guidance: Motivation may be explicit in prior art or implicit in market forces, design incentives, known benefits, or common sense; courts require some articulated reasoning but not necessarily precise teachings directed to the specific subject matter (Translogic; Aventis).

name: Operability and inoperability evidence
description: Evidence that the claimed combination would be inoperable or uniquely difficult to make may weigh against a finding of obviousness.
guidance: Courts will consider whether PHOSITA would have known how to make the combination operable; claim breadth can affect this analysis. Lack of evidence of difficulty may support obviousness (Icon; Leapfrog observation about reduction-to-practice difficulty).

name: Standard for summary judgment on obviousness
description: Obviousness is ultimately a legal determination; summary judgment is appropriate when the prior art, claim scope, and level of ordinary skill are not in material dispute and obviousness is apparent from those factors.
guidance: If the key factual predicates are undisputed and the obviousness conclusion follows as a matter of law, courts may grant summary judgment (KSR). However, genuine disputes of material fact (e.g., analogous art, motive to combine, secondary considerations) preclude summary judgment.

name: Determination of novelty (general procedure)
description: The examiner determines novelty by judging whether the claimed invention falls under the inventions categorized in Article 29(1)(1) to (2). If it does, it is not novel; if it does not, it is novel.
guidance: Claims must describe the subject matter sought for protection (Article 42(4)). Determination of identicalness is based on matters described in the claims. When multiple claims exist, novelty must be determined for each claim separately.

name: Defining inventions disclosed in claims — clear claim language
description: When claim language is clear, the claimed invention should be defined as recited in the claim. Terminology in claims is interpreted with the general meaning accepted in the technical field, except where a specific meaning is explicitly defined in the description.
guidance: Interpretation should be objective and reasonable, considering technical meaning and a person skilled in the art at filing time. Example: 'cream' in claims should not be limited to a specific embodiment described in the description if 'cream' has its general meaning in the art.

name: Avoid limiting claims by referencing description or drawings
description: Where the claim description is clearly understood, an examiner should avoid limiting interpretation merely by referencing the description or drawings.
guidance: Matters described only in the description or drawings and not in the claims should be considered not recited in the claims. Conversely, matters recited in the claims should be considered even if not in the description. Examples: do not limit 'thin film type probe' to patterns shown only in the drawings; do not import rotation direction from drawings if not recited in claims.

name: Estoppel under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 317(b)
description: The phrase 'raised or could have raised' applies only to patent claims that were in suit and for which a final decision on non-invalidity has been entered. Once the claims that were actually before the court at the time of the court's decision are determined, the statute prohibits the Office from maintaining an inter partes reexamination of any such patent claim on the basis of issues which the requester raised or could have raised in the litigation.
guidance: Evidence showing which claims were before the court may include a copy of the jury verdict form, other court documents, and docket entries. The petitioner must show that the issue(s) raised in the reexamination proceeding are the same issue(s) that were raised or could have been raised by the requester in the civil action. The requester may still assert invalidity based on newly discovered prior art unavailable to the requester at the time of the civil action; the patent owner bears the burden of showing a reference was 'available' (i.e., known to the requester) at a time it could have been raised (e.g., prior to trial).

name: Factors to consider when determining 'good cause' to suspend
description: When determining whether there is 'good cause' to suspend action in the reexamination based on pending litigation, the Office may consider the following elements: (1) requester is a party to the litigation; (2) claims at issue in litigation are identical to the claims under reexamination; (3) issues raised in reexamination are the same issues that were raised or could have been raised in the litigation; (4) litigation has advanced to a late enough stage with sufficient probability of a final adverse decision to the requester; (5) there is a concurrent ex parte reexamination for the patent.
guidance: Element (2) emphasizes estoppel applies only to patent claims litigated in the suit. For element (3), new art that could not have been raised in litigation does not trigger estoppel. For element (5), concurrent ex parte reexamination may allow the Office to proceed (Ethicon v. Quigg), and consultation with OPLA is recommended. Each factor is fact-specific and should be weighed together.

name: Preparation of NIRC when no allowed claims exist
description: Where all claims are rejected or objected to in the prior Office action, the examiner will issue a NIRC indicating that all claims have been canceled and terminating the prosecution. The examiner will draft an examiner's amendment canceling all live claims and check the appropriate box on PTOL-2068.
guidance: In the remarks of the examiner’s amendment, point out why the claims have been canceled. No reasons for patentability are attached. No panel review conference is needed in this ministerial instance.

name: Reasons for patentability and/or confirmation requirements
description: Reasons for patentability must be provided for every claim identified as patentable in the NIRC, unless all claims are canceled in the proceeding.
guidance: Indicate why the claims found patentable are clearly patentable over the cited patents or printed publications, similar to reasons for allowance in an application (see MPEP §1302.14). Examiner may refer to portions of the record that establish patentability. Reasons may be set forth on Form PTOL-476 or by using form paragraph 26.70. Patent owner must be notified in the NIRC that it may provide comments on the statement of reasons for patentability/confirmation; comments will be placed in the reexamination file without comment.

name: Reexamination reminders — substantive checklist items
description: Before forwarding for processing of the NIRC, the examiner should ensure certain items have been correctly completed or followed.
guidance: Items to ensure: (A) All patent claims for which a substantial new question of patentability or reasonable likelihood of prevailing had been found must have been examined (see MPEP §2643). (B) No renumbering of patent claims is permitted (new claims may require renumbering; see MPEP §§2666.01 and 2250). (C) Amendments to description and claims must conform to 37 CFR 1.530(d)-(k). (D) Prior art must be listed on approved forms (PTO-892, PTO-1449, PTO/SB/08A/08B, PTO/SB/42 or equivalent) (see MPEP §2657). (E) Examiner and clerk checklists PTOL-1516 and PTOL-1517 must be entirely and properly completed and cross-checked. (F) Multiple copending reexamination proceedings are often merged (see MPEP §2686.01). (G) If copending with a reissue application, files must be forwarded to OPLA for potential merger with decision in file (see MPEP §2686.03). (H) Reasons for patentability/confirmation are required for each claim found patentable. (I) There is no issue fee in reexamination (see MPEP §2634). (J) Patent claims may not be amended nor new claims added after expiration of the patent (see MPEP §§2666.01 and 2250). (K) Original drawings cannot be physically changed; amended or new figures must be labeled and on new sheets in compliance with 37 CFR 1.84 (see 37 CFR 1.530(d)(3) and MPEP §2666.02). (L) An amended or new claim may not enlarge the scope of the patent claims (see MPEP §§2658, 2666.01, and 2250). (M) If the patent has expired, all amendments made during the proceeding must be withdrawn and presently rejected and objected claims canceled (see MPEP §2250).

name: Handling of multiple dependent claims for publication
description: Treatment of multiple dependent claims when preparing a reexamination proceeding for publication is addressed and should follow the discussion in MPEP §2287.
guidance: Follow MPEP §2287 for specifics on how multiple dependent claims are to be presented in preparation for issuing the reexamination certificate and publication.

name: Procedure when all claims are canceled
description: When all claims in the reexamination proceeding are to be canceled (e.g., patent owner fails to timely respond, or Board decision affirms rejections and appeals time has expired), examiner will issue a NIRC indicating all claims canceled and terminating prosecution. Examiner will draft an examiner's amendment canceling all live claims and explain why in the remarks.
guidance: Provide a scanned copy of claims with brackets and place in file history. Panel review is not held. Examiner will designate a canceled original patent claim to be printed in Official Gazette on the Issue Classification IFW form.

name: Issuance and content requirements for inter partes reexamination certificate (35 U.S.C. 316; 37 CFR 1.997)
description: At conclusion of inter partes reexamination, Director shall issue and publish a certificate canceling any claim finally determined unpatentable, confirming claims determined patentable, and incorporating in the patent any proposed amended or new claim determined patentable. The certificate concludes the proceeding and must be issued/published for each patent where a reexamination proceeding was ordered, except where proceeding vacated or replaced by reissue patent.
guidance: Certificate will be sent to patent owner (per §1.33(c)) and third party requester; notice of issuance published in Official Gazette. If certificate cancels all claims, no further Office proceedings will be conducted with that patent or related reissue/reexamination requests. A reissued patent may serve as the reexamination certificate where applicable.

name: Software patents: requirement of hardware/system element in many jurisdictions
description: In most of the countries, software cannot be patented unless it forms an element within a hardware or a system.
guidance: Practical implication: pure-software claims that do not tie the software to a particular machine or system are at higher risk of ineligibility. The article notes national differences and that Alice significantly curtailed software patentability in the US.

name: Mayo two-step framework — Step 1: determine whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea
description: In the first Mayo step, the court must determine if the patent claim at hand contains an abstract idea. If not, the claim is potentially patentable subject to other requirements.
guidance: This is a threshold inquiry; if the claim is not directed to an abstract idea, no further Mayo-step-2 inventive-concept analysis is required for §101 eligibility (though other patentability requirements still apply). The article emphasizes correctly identifying ‘directed to’ versus merely involving an idea.

name: Mayo two-step framework — Step 2: determine whether the claim embodies an 'inventive concept'
description: In the second step analysis, the Court must determine whether the patent embodies the inventive concept — i.e., the implementation of the idea must not be generic, conventional or obvious and must add something that transforms the idea into patent-eligible subject matter.
guidance: Look for elements or combinations that integrate the building blocks into something more; trivial token implementation (e.g., conventional computer hardware) will not qualify. The inventive concept must be sufficient to ensure the patent amounts to significantly more than the abstract idea itself.

name: Generic computer implementation fails to transform an abstract idea
description: "Merely requiring generic computer implementation fails to transform [an] abstract idea into a patent eligible invention; mere recitation of a generic computer cannot transform a patent-ineligible abstract idea into a patent-eligible matter."
guidance: Claims that simply recite using a generic computer to perform well-known steps should be treated as ineligible. Drafting should avoid claiming only standard computer components or generic automation as the novel feature.

name: 'Apply it' language is insufficient to confer eligibility
description: Stating an abstract idea by adding the words 'apply it' is not enough for patent eligibility.
guidance: Simply phrasing a claim as 'apply the idea using a computer' or similar boilerplate will not meet §101 requirements after Alice; claims must show a non-generic, inventive implementation rather than mere application language.

name: High-level/generalized claiming of routine features will not establish an inventive concept
description: Claiming a well understood, routine and conventional feature at a higher level of generality does not suffice for an 'inventive concept'.
guidance: Drafters should avoid broad functional claiming that abstracts routine practice to a high level; instead, emphasize specific technical improvements, non-conventional architecture, or particular machine-oriented implementations that demonstrate a concrete inventive contribution.

name: Practical recommendation: scrutinize pre-Alice software patents before asserting infringement
description: Before filing a lawsuit for infringement of a software patent it is pertinent to scrutinize the claims in the light of the Alice case.
guidance: Because many patents issued pre-Alice may be vulnerable under the Alice/Mayo framework, defendants-in-suit or patentees bringing suits should analyze whether claims are directed to abstract ideas and whether they include sufficient inventive concept; consider re-drafting, reexamination, or other risk mitigation steps.

name: Complete application content (nonprovisional)
description: A complete application filed under § 1.53(b) or § 1.53(d) comprises: (1) A specification as prescribed by 35 U.S.C. 112, including a claim or claims (see §§ 1.71 to 1.77); (2) An oath or declaration (see §§ 1.63 and 1.68); (3) Drawings, when necessary (see §§ 1.81 to 1.85); and (4) The prescribed filing fee, search fee, examination fee, and application size fee (see § 1.16).
guidance: Failure to meet these requirements will result in the application being denied a filing date; the filing date is the date on which all of these requirements are met. No new matter may be introduced after the filing date.

name: Complete provisional application content
description: A complete provisional application filed under § 1.53(c) comprises: (1) A cover sheet identifying (i) that it is a provisional application, (ii) name(s) and residence(s) of inventor(s), (iii) title of the invention, (iv) attorney/agent name and registration number (if applicable), (v) docket number (if applicable), (vi) correspondence address, (vii) name of U.S. Government agency and contract number if federally funded; (2) A specification as prescribed by the first paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112; (3) Drawings, when necessary; and (4) The prescribed filing fee and application size fee.
guidance: A provisional application does not require claims or an oath/declaration, and an information disclosure statement (IDS) may not be filed in a provisional application. See MPEP § 201.04(b) for a sample cover sheet.

name: Filing date requirements for nonprovisional applications
description: The filing date of a nonprovisional application under § 1.53(b) is the date on which a specification containing a description pursuant to § 1.71 and at least one claim pursuant to § 1.75, and any drawing required by § 1.81(a), are filed in the USPTO.
guidance: If the application does not meet these requirements it will be denied a filing date; no amendment may introduce new matter after the filing date. Certain required parts (fees, oath) may be submitted later within permitted periods (see completion subsequent to filing).

name: Continued prosecution application (CPA) and continuation/divisional filing rules
description: Under § 1.53(d) a continuation or divisional (but not CIP) of a prior nonprovisional application may be filed as a continued prosecution application for design applications only; the CPA must disclose and claim only subject matter disclosed in the prior application and name the same or fewer inventors. The filing date for a CPA is the date a request on a separate paper is filed.
guidance: CPAs are limited in scope (design-only after certain dates). Applications under this paragraph utilize the file jacket and contents of the prior application and are assigned the prior application number for identification.

name: Arrangement and required sections of the specification
description: Preferred order of arrangement (each lettered item should appear in uppercase): (A) Title of the invention; (B) Cross-reference to related applications; (C) Statement regarding federally sponsored research or development; (D) Names of parties to joint research agreement; (E) Reference to sequence listing/table/computer program listing appendix; (F) Background of the invention (field and description of related art); (G) Brief summary of the invention; (H) Brief description of the several views of the drawing; (I) Detailed description of the invention; (J) Claims (commencing on a separate sheet); (K) Abstract of the Disclosure (commencing on a separate sheet); (L) Sequence listing, if on paper.
guidance: This order is preferable but suggested for applicant’s use; headings should be upper case without underlining or bold type. See MPEP § 608.01(a) for paper requirements.

name: Brief required item (3): Status of claims (37 CFR 1.192(c)(3))
description: A statement of the status of all claims in the application (pending, cancelled, allowed, rejected, etc.) and identification of each claim on appeal.
guidance: Purpose is to avoid confusion about which claims are on appeal and their precise wording; appellant's understanding of claim status assists examiner and Board in resolving disagreements before decision.

name: Brief required item (5): Summary of the invention (37 CFR 1.192(c)(5))
description: A concise explanation of the invention defined in the appealed claims, referring to the specification by page and line number and to drawings by reference characters, if applicable.
guidance: Preferable to read the appealed claims on the specification and drawings; specificity (page/line) helps the Board quickly locate where claimed subject matter is described.

name: Brief required item (7): Grouping of claims (37 CFR 1.192(c)(7))
description: For each ground of rejection contested that applies to a group of two or more claims, appellant must indicate whether the claims 'stand or fall together' or explicitly state they do not and provide arguments explaining separate patentability.
guidance: If appellant omits the statement and argument, it is a concession that the ground applies equally to all claims; the Board will select a single claim (generally the broadest) to decide the rejection unless appellant states otherwise and provides reasons. Mere pointing out differences is not sufficient—reasons for separate patentability must be argued in the Argument section.

name: Argument requirements for 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph (37 CFR 1.192(c)(8)(i))
description: For rejections under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, the argument must specify the errors in the rejection and how the first paragraph of 112 is complied with, including (as appropriate) how the specification and drawings (A) describe the subject matter defined by each rejected claim, (B) enable one skilled in the art to make and use the subject matter, and (C) set forth the best mode contemplated.
guidance: Be specific as to how the specification/drawings satisfy description/enablement/best mode for each rejected claim; a general statement is insufficient.

name: Argument requirements for 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph (37 CFR 1.192(c)(8)(ii))
description: For rejections under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, the argument must specify the errors in the rejection and how the claims particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter applicant regards as the invention.
guidance: Explain why claim language satisfies the definiteness requirement; point to claim language and record to rebut examiner's position.

name: Argument requirements for 35 U.S.C. 102 rejections (37 CFR 1.192(c)(8)(iii))
description: For rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102, the argument must specify the errors and why the rejected claims are patentable under 102, including specific claim limitations not described in the prior art relied upon.
guidance: Identify the particular claim limitations absent from the asserted reference(s) and explain why those differences render the claims novel.

name: Argument requirements for 35 U.S.C. 103 rejections (37 CFR 1.192(c)(8)(iv))
description: For rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103, the argument must specify the errors and, where appropriate, identify specific claim limitations not described in the prior art and explain how such limitations render the claimed subject matter unobvious; if rejection is based on a combination of references, explain why the references, taken as a whole, do not suggest the claimed subject matter and why features from different references should not be combined.
guidance: A general argument that limitations are not all disclosed in a single reference is insufficient; explain non-obviousness and the inappropriateness of combining references when relevant.

name: Argument for other rejections (37 CFR 1.192(c)(8)(v))
description: For any rejection other than those specifically covered by (i)-(iv), the argument must specify the errors in the rejection and the specific limitations in the rejected claims (if appropriate) or other reasons which cause the rejection to be in error.
guidance: Tailor the argument to the statutory/ground basis of the rejection (e.g., 101 subject-matter issues may not require pinpointing claim limitations but should explain why the rejection is erroneous).

name: Notices of Appeal unacceptable — common defects (form ¶¶ 12.01–12.04)
description: Common reasons a Notice of Appeal is unacceptable include unpaid appeal fee, absence of a second or final rejection, untimely filing, or the claims already being allowed.
guidance: If fee unpaid, applicant may obtain extension under 37 CFR 1.136(a). For untimely filings, the date of filing the notice, fee, and petition determine extension period. If a notice is unacceptable because claims are allowed, it will be rejected as such.

name: Board selection of single claim from a group when claims stand or fall together
description: Where appellant does not state that claims in a rejected group do not stand or fall together and does not argue separate patentability, the Board will normally select a single claim (often the broadest) from the group and decide the rejection on that claim alone.
guidance: If separate patentability is asserted, appellant must state so and present reasons in the Argument section. Examples and case law cited (In re Young; In re Nielson; In re King; In re Sernaker) illustrate the practice and rationale to promote efficiency.

name: Objective Indicia of Nonobviousness
description: Objective indicia (secondary considerations) should be presented where relevant to nonobviousness analyses.
guidance: Provide evidence (e.g., commercial success, long-felt need, copying, unexpected results) with supporting data and linkages to claimed features.

name: Petition Filing Date and Minimum Procedural Compliance
description: Petition must be filed consistent with statutory time periods and be accompanied by the evidence the petitioner relies upon; minimum procedural compliance determines filing date. 35 U.S.C. §§ 135(a), 311(c); 37 C.F.R. § 42.3.
guidance: Ensure all required parts (claims challenged, grounds, evidence, notices) are included to secure a proper filing date; failure may cause filing date vacatur or rejection.

name: Specific Requirements for a Petition
description: A petition must identify all challenged claims and the grounds and supporting evidence on a claim-by-claim basis.
guidance: Include claim charts, reference to prior art, declarations, and exhibits; ensure claim-by-claim analysis to satisfy rule requirements and to assist Board evaluation.

name: Claim Charts
description: Claim charts should present a claim-by-claim mapping of prior art to claim limitations to support unpatentability grounds.
guidance: Provide clear, specific mappings with citations and supporting evidence; vague or conclusory charts can undermine the petition.

name: Motions to Amend — General Practice
description: Motions to amend are governed by specific practice rules for IPR, PGR, and CBM; parties should follow motion timing, content, and evidentiary standards.
guidance: Board expects motions to amend to comply with contents requirements, include proposed claims and show patentability, and be filed by scheduled dates. The Guide provides practice tips and a sample framework for motions to amend.

name: Motion to Amend — Evidentiary Standards
description: Motions to amend are subject to evidentiary standards requiring sufficient supporting evidence to show proposed amended claims are patentable over the prior art of record.
guidance: Provide declarations, tests, and factual support tying proposed claim features to patentability; be prepared for oppositions and cross-examination of declarants.

name: Contents of Motion to Amend
description: A motion to amend should include the proposed substitute claims, claim support in the specification, arguments and evidence of patentability, and any necessary claim construction positions.
guidance: Demonstrate written support in the patent specification and explain how substituted claims differ from prior art; follow the procedural content requirements closely.

name: Claim Construction in Motion to Amend
description: Claim construction principles apply to motions to amend and the Board may apply constructions consistent with trial practice.
guidance: Argue constructions as needed to support patentability of amended claims, using intrinsic and extrinsic evidence; be aware of how constructions affect novelty and obviousness assessments.

name: Opposition to a Motion to Amend
description: Petitioner may oppose motions to amend by filing oppositions addressing adequacy of support and patentability over prior art.
guidance: Oppositions should point to prior art, claim construction, and record deficiencies; include declarations where needed to rebut patent owner evidence.

name: Managing personal behavior, relationships, or interpersonal interactions
description: Claims directed to managing human activity, social activities, teaching, following rules or instructions, or interactions between people (e.g., budgeting/setting spending limits; filtering content; voting; providing information without disrupting primary activity; rules for games) are classed as abstract ideas.
guidance: Examples include Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One (budgeting/spending limits), BASCOM (content filtering - abstract at step 2A though step 2B analysis may differ), Voter Verified (voting/verification), Interval Licensing (attention manager), In re Marco Guldenaar (rules for playing games). Examiner should consider these as 'organizing human activity' type abstract ideas and consult cases cited for specific fact patterns.

name: Mental processes (definition)
description: A 'mental process' is a concept that can be performed in the human mind, or by a human using a pen and paper (observations, evaluations, judgments, opinions), and is considered an abstract idea.
guidance: Courts treat methods that can be performed mentally or with pen-and-paper as unpatentable abstract ideas (citing CyberSource, Benson, Mayo, Parker v. Flook). The phrase 'mental processes' refers to a type of abstract idea and applies to both product and process claims. Examiners should apply the subsequent sub-points A–D when evaluating whether a claim recites a mental process.

name: A: Limitations that cannot practically be performed in the human mind do NOT recite a mental process
description: If a claim contains limitations that cannot practically be performed in the human mind (the human mind is not equipped to perform them), the claim does not recite a mental process.
guidance: Examples where claims were not mental processes: GPS pseudorange/time calculations (SiRF Tech.), detecting suspicious activity via network monitors/analyzing network packets (SRI Int'l), specific multi-step data encryption methods (Synopsys), halftone image rendering requiring manipulation of computer data structures (Research Corp.). Examiner should assess whether the claimed steps are practically performable mentally; if not, treat as not a mental-process-type abstract idea.

name: B: Claims that encompass a human performing the steps mentally (with or without a physical aid) recite a mental process
description: If a claim limitation can practically be performed in the human mind, with or without a physical aid (e.g., pen and paper, slide rule), the limitation is within the mental processes grouping and the claim recites an abstract idea.
guidance: Use of physical aids to extend memory/capacity does not negate mental nature (cases: Benson; CyberSource; Synopsys; University of Florida; Symantec). Examiners should consult the specification (e.g., whether the claimed map is merely a listing) to determine if the limitation reads on someone performing the steps mentally or with simple aids.

name: C: Claims that require a computer may nevertheless recite a mental process
description: A claim may still be an abstract mental process even if claimed as performed on a computer; requiring a computer does not necessarily take a claim out of the mental-process grouping.
guidance: Examiners must carefully consider the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim in light of the specification to determine whether the applicant merely claims a concept performed: (1) on a generic computer, (2) in a computer environment, or (3) using a computer as a tool. If so, the claim is considered to recite a mental process (examples: Benson; Mortgage Grader; Voter Verified; Versata). Subpoint: performing a mental process on a generic computer has been treated as an abstract idea when the underlying steps remain human cognitive actions described at high level.

name: Submission content required by 37 CFR 1.114(c)
description: The submission may include an information disclosure statement (IDS), an amendment to the written description, claims, or drawings, new arguments, or new evidence in support of patentability. If a reply to an Office action is outstanding, the submission must meet the reply requirements of 37 CFR 1.111.
guidance: Arguments previously filed (e.g., in an after-final reply) that were entered but not found persuasive may satisfy the submission requirement if they are responsive within the meaning of 37 CFR 1.111 to the outstanding Office action. A statement that incorporates by reference the arguments in a previously filed appeal brief or reply brief may be acceptable. See form paragraphs 7.42.04 and 7.42.08 for examiner use.

name: Filing supplemental oaths after allowance
description: Supplemental oaths and declarations covering the claims in the application may be filed after allowance as a matter of right.
guidance: When received they are placed in the file by the Office of Data Management, but receipt will not be acknowledged. They should not be filed or considered as amendments under 37 CFR 1.312, since they make no change in the wording of the papers on file (see MPEP § 714.16).

name: Sufficiency of disclosure / enablement (Article 25(3))
description: The description of an Invention must clearly and completely describe how an Invention may be implemented by a person skilled in the art.
guidance: Core enablement requirement: supports implementation by skilled person; tied to claims support (Article 25(4)).

name: Claims support and clarity (Article 25(4))
description: The claim(s) of Invention must disclose clearly and consistently the field of technical Invention and be supported by the description.
guidance: Claims must be supported by the written description; clarity and consistency required.

name: Amendments to application / scope narrowing (Articles 38–40)
description: Application may be amended or divided before grant; amendments to description/claims may be carried out provided the amendment does not extend the scope of Invention of the original Application; adding more than 10 claims incurs fees for excess claims; application may be changed between Patent and Simple Patent without losing original filing date.
guidance: Amendments allowed but cannot introduce new matter / broaden scope; fees apply for excess claims; conversion between types keeps original date.

name: Grant procedures and certificate (Article 58)
description: Minister grants if substantive examination shows compliance with provisions; Minister notifies Applicant in writing; within 2 months from notification, Minister issues a Patent certificate; Applicant may not withdraw or modify description/claims during that 2-month period; granted patent is recorded and published except for defense/security cases.
guidance: Issuance of patent certificate follows formal grant notice; prevents last-minute withdrawals or broadening post-grant.

name: Re-issue cannot embrace new matter not disclosed in the original specification
description: A re-issue cannot embrace new matter under any circumstances; matter not described in the original specification cannot be inserted in the re-issue.
guidance: Courts repeatedly hold that new matter may never be claimed in a re-issue. The re-issue is limited to correcting errors in the original disclosure/claims and cannot add subject-matter that was not originally described.

name: Omission of matter clearly described but not claimed indicates intentional abandonment unless promptly remedied
description: The omission from the claims of matter that was clearly described in the original patent indicates, prima facie, an intention to abandon that matter unless the claims are amended by re-issue without unreasonable delay.
guidance: When the specification discloses but the claims omit subject-matter, that omission is strong evidence of deliberate exclusion; delay in seeking re-issue after gaining knowledge of the omission supports an inference of abandonment and may bar reclamation in equity or by re-issue.

name: Knowledge or constructive notice imputed by reasonable inspection
description: If a reasonable inspection of the issued patent would have informed the patentee of the omission or narrowness of the claims, the law imputes knowledge and the patentee is chargeable from issuance.
guidance: Decisions (e.g., Wollensak v. Reiher; cases cited) hold that the patentee must promptly examine his patent and that failure to act after notice (actual or imputable) amounts to laches. The standard is what a person reasonably diligent in management of their own interests would discover.

name: Distinguish between adding new matter and correcting a misstatement
description: It is one thing to enlarge a claim by inserting matter never before contained in it; it is quite another to amend a misstatement to reflect what the original disclosure already supported.
guidance: Courts maintain a strict distinction: correction of a misstatement supported by the original disclosure may be permitted (subject to delay rules), whereas inserting genuinely new matter is forbidden. Judicial construction determines whether a proposed amendment is corrective or adds new matter.

name: Re-issue cannot be used to claim new uses or new modes of use after unreasonable delay
description: A re-issue obtained after unreasonable delay cannot validly claim a new use or a claim whose novelty rests on a new mode of use.
guidance: Cases (e.g., Gardner v. Herz) hold that attempts to claim a new mode or use in a re-issue after delay are invalid. The law distinguishes between broadening to cover originally intended subject-matter and expanding to capture new uses discovered later.

name: Judicial construction required where misstatement permits multiple interpretations
description: When a claim is misstated in a way that allows several constructions—some of which would include the omitted matter and some which would exclude it—judicial interpretation is required to determine whether correction is permissible.
guidance: Because ordinary claim interpretation may be ambiguous, courts determine whether the misstatement is correctable without introducing new matter; the outcome affects whether the re-issue is an enlargement or a corrective amendment.

name: Matters described but not claimed may be dedicated to the public and strengthen public reliance over time
description: When the patentee receives his patent and fails to claim parts of the disclosed invention, those unclaimed parts may be treated in law as dedicated to the public; every day that passes increases the strength of public reliance and the barrier to later expansion by re-issue.
guidance: The issued patent is a public instrument; if the patentee holds back claiming certain disclosed elements, the public acquires the undoubted right to use them and courts are reluctant to permit later re-issues that would upset reliance and vested interests.

name: Specific fact-pattern exceptions and time thresholds are case-dependent (examples cited)
description: A number of cases articulate specific limits (e.g., no allowance after 8-9 years unless original claimed the matter; inability to re-issue after 14 years to claim an improvement; re-issue to cover machine part without claimed use invalid after ~3 years).
guidance: These temporal rules are illustrative of how courts have applied the general principles; they demonstrate that long delays (multi-year periods) often give rise to invalidation of re-issues, but exact thresholds vary by facts and case law cited (e.g., Clements v. Odorless Excavating Apparatus Co.; Sickels v. Falls Co.; Reay v. Raynor).

name: Determine what the invention is
description: The invention is defined in the claims. The specification need not set forth details not relating to the essence of the invention.
guidance: Examiners should identify the invention by the claims. Unclaimed matter unrelated to the operation of the claimed invention does not trigger requirements (cites: In re Bosy; Northern Telecom v. Samsung; Eli Lilly & Co. v. Barr Labs). Focus examination on claim-defined invention; do not require disclosure of irrelevant details.

name: Best mode requirement distinct from enablement
description: The best mode requirement is a separate and distinct requirement from the enablement requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre-AIA first paragraph).
guidance: Do not conflate lack of any mode (nonenablement) with best mode. Best mode addresses whether inventor knew of a preferred mode and failed to disclose it, while enablement addresses whether the disclosure places the claimed subject matter generally in the public's possession (cites: In re Newton; In re Glass).

name: Enablement requirement under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (form paragraph 7.31.02)
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) as failing to comply with the enablement requirement because the claim contains subject matter not described in a way to enable one skilled in the art to make and/or use the invention.
guidance: Precede with 7.30.01 or 7.103. If problem is scope (breadth vs disclosure), consider form paragraph 7.31.03. In explanations, identify claimed subject matter for which the specification is not enabling and explain why using the In re Wands factors as appropriate (see MPEP §§ 2164.01(a), 2164.04). Include examiner questions not resolved that raise doubt.

name: Scope of enablement must be commensurate with claim scope (form paragraph 7.31.03)
description: Reject when the specification, while enabling for some subject matter, does not reasonably provide enablement commensurate in scope with the claims.
guidance: Use 7.31.03 when some embodiments are enabled but the claims are broader than the enabling disclosure. Identify what is enabling (bracket 2), aspects of claims not enabled (bracket 3), and whether the claim fails to enable to 'make,' 'use,' or 'make and use' (bracket 4). Explain with In re Wands factors and cite specific portions of the specification.

name: Enablement of 'single means' / means-plus-function claims (form paragraph 7.31.05)
description: Claim [1] rejected because it purports to invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre-AIA sixth paragraph) but fails to recite a combination of elements as required, reciting instead a function with no limits while the specification discloses at most the means known to the inventor.
guidance: This paragraph is to be used only when a claim recites a single element in means-plus-function format. Such rejection is rare. Precede with 7.30.01 or 7.103. Explain how the claim recites a function without limits and why the disclosure is not commensurate with the broad functional claim.

name: Essential subject matter missing from claims (form paragraph 7.33.01)
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre-AIA) first paragraph as based on a disclosure which is not enabling because the disclosure does not enable one of ordinary skill in the art to practice the invention without [2], which is critical or essential but not included in the claim(s).
guidance: Precede with 7.30.01 or 7.103. In bracket 2, recite the omitted subject matter. Provide the rationale for considering it critical or essential (bracket 3) and cite statements, arguments, dates, drawings, or other evidence demonstrating the applicant considered the feature essential.

name: Two separate requirements under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre-AIA second paragraph)
description: (A) Claims must set forth the subject matter the inventor regards as the invention (subjective). (B) Claims must particularly point out and distinctly define the metes and bounds of the subject matter to be protected (objective).
