guidance: Treat these as separate inquiries: (A) depends on inventor's perspective (evidence outside the specification may show divergence); (B) is an objective definiteness requirement evaluated against a hypothetical person of ordinary skill. Rejections under 112(b) should identify whether the basis is indefiniteness or failure to claim what inventor regards as invention.

name: Rejection for failure to claim subject matter inventor regards as invention
description: A rejection based on failure of the claims to set forth subject matter inventor regards as the invention is appropriate only where inventor has stated elsewhere (outside the application as filed) that the invention is different from what is defined by the claims.
guidance: Evidence 'to the contrary' may come from applicant remarks, briefs, or 37 CFR 1.132 affidavits (cites: Solomon v. Kimberly-Clark; In re Prater; In re Cormany). Do not use the specification content as evidence for this inquiry; see MPEP § 2172 for guidance and examples.

name: Unclaimed essential subject matter: multiple possible rejections
description: Omitted matter that appears necessary to describe or make the invention may justify rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (enablement or written description) or under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (indefiniteness or failure to claim what inventor regards as invention), depending on facts.
guidance: Follow MPEP § 2163 and § 2164 guidance to determine whether to make a written description/enablement rejection. If claim fails to interrelate essential elements, consider indefiniteness under 112(b). Provide reasons and cite appropriate case law (e.g., In re Mayhew; Gentry Gallery; In re Venezia) and explain why omitted matter is critical or essential.

name: Claims must particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention (definiteness requirement)
description: Claims must be definite so the scope is clear to persons skilled in the art; if not, reject under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre-AIA second paragraph) as indefinite.
guidance: Indefiniteness rejections must clearly identify the language causing indefiniteness and thoroughly explain the reasoning. The primary purpose is clear public notice of claim boundaries; secondary purpose is to permit assessment of compliance with other patentability criteria. Require applicant response to explain or amend.

name: Interpreting claims — applicants are their own lexicographers
description: Applicants may define terms in their specification; claim language may be functional, use alternative expressions, negative limitations, or any style so long as any special meaning assigned is clearly set forth in the specification.
guidance: Do not reject a claim solely because of the type of language used. Allow applicant-defined meanings if clear in the specification (see MPEP § 2111.01, In re Swinehart). Apply the claim interpretation principles (e.g., broadest reasonable interpretation for FITF applications) when evaluating definiteness and claim scope.

name: Scope of protection: plant patent vs PVPA
description: A US plant patent prevents asexual reproduction (cloning) of the particular variety identified in the patent; a PVPA certificate protects not only the particular variety but also certain varieties derived from the protected variety if they meet statutory requirements.
guidance: PVPA protection can therefore be broader than a plant patent because it can reach derived varieties, not just exact clones of the claimed variety.

name: Simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results
description: Simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results is an exemplary rationale supporting obviousness.
guidance: When a claimed change is merely the substitution of a known element with predictable results, the combination may be obvious (see United States v. Adams discussion in KSR).

name: Prima facie case of nonuse to institute proceedings
description: An expungement or reexamination proceeding will be instituted only for goods/services for which a prima facie case of nonuse for the relevant time frame has been established. A prima facie case requires only that a reasonable predicate concerning such nonuse be established. See 37 C.F.R. §2.92.
guidance: Prima facie includes sufficient notice of the claimed nonuse to allow the registrant to respond with competent evidence. For petition-based proceedings, the determination is based on petition evidence collected via the reasonable investigation plus the USPTO registration record. For Director-initiated proceedings, the USPTO’s available information must establish a prima facie case; sources may be essentially the same as for petition-based proceedings.

name: Separate worksheet / analyze each claim individually
description: As every claim must be examined individually based on the particular elements recited therein, a separate worksheet should be used to analyze each claim.
guidance: Use one worksheet per claim in the SME analysis; do not lump multiple claims together.

name: Identify what applicant invented (Section I)
description: Review the disclosure to identify what applicant considers as the invention (MPEP 2103(I)).
guidance: Provide a brief description that does not merely reproduce the claim. The take away should capture the focus of the invention (example: 'invention focuses on scanning and cleaning electronic communications'). This informs later evaluation of additional elements relative to the invention.

name: Construe the claim using broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI)
description: Establish the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim.
guidance: BRI can be a brief description; avoid merely restating the claim. Use BRI to determine what the claim is 'directed to' in later steps.

name: Step 2A outcome — No (claim not directed to abstract idea) => eligible
description: If the claim does not recite a concept similar to those found by the courts to be abstract, conclude SME analysis and continue with examination under other patentability requirements.
guidance: An explanation of why the claim is eligible is not necessary in the Office action unless the record would benefit from clarification (for example, to explain interpretation of the claim).

name: If directed to an abstract idea, identify the limitation(s) and explain why
description: When Step 2A shows the claim is directed to an abstract idea, identify the limitation(s) in the claim that recite the abstract idea and explain why the recited subject matter is an abstract idea.
guidance: Fill-in the claim limitations that set forth or describe the abstract idea and provide reasons those limitations are considered abstract (worksheet provides blanks for these).

name: Step 2B — Identify additional elements beyond the abstract idea
description: Determine whether there are additional elements (features/limitations/steps) recited in the claim beyond the identified abstract idea.
guidance: Choose 1: No additional elements => make §101 rejection (use FP 7.05 and 7.05.015) and consider whether disclosure contains elements that could be added to make claim eligible. Choose 2: Yes => list the additional claim elements and continue to evaluate their significance.

name: If no additional elements => §101 rejection and suggest possible amendments
description: If there are no elements in the claim in addition to the abstract idea, conclude SME analysis by making a §101 rejection.
guidance: Use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015. Also search the disclosure for elements that could be added to the claim to make it eligible and consider suggesting them to applicant.

name: Search for an 'inventive concept' when evaluating additional elements
description: Identifying additional elements and evaluating their significance involves the search for an 'inventive concept' in the claim.
guidance: Keep in mind what applicant invented (Section I) and how that relates to the additional elements. Consider all identified additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the abstract idea.

name: Significance consideration: improves another technology or technical field
description: One reason supporting the significance of additional elements is that they improve another technology or technical field.
guidance: Use this consideration when the claim limitations produce a technological improvement beyond the abstract idea itself.

name: Significance consideration: improves the functioning of a computer itself
description: Additional elements that improve the functioning of the computer itself can support finding significantly more.
guidance: Evaluate whether claim limitations change how the computer operates or improve its performance (e.g., faster computation, less memory usage) rather than merely using a computer as a tool to implement the idea.

name: Significance consideration: effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing
description: Elements that effect a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing can support that the claim amounts to significantly more.
guidance: Look for concrete transformations tying the abstract idea to a real-world change of state or thing.

name: Evaluate additional elements both individually and as an ordered combination
description: Consider all identified additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether, taken together, they result in the claim amounting to significantly more than the abstract idea.
guidance: Document reasons supporting significance; if any elements or combination amount to significantly more, conclude SME analysis as eligible. If not, make a §101 rejection.

name: Improvement to technology need not be explicit in the claim
description: Note that the improvement does not need to be explicitly recited in the claim to support eligibility.
guidance: An improvement may be shown by how the additional elements integrate the abstract idea into a practical application (e.g., improved performance, reduced memory). Explanations can be included in Office action remarks if helpful to the record.

name: If elements amount to significantly more => conclude eligible and document reasoning if needed
description: If any elements, individually or as a combination, amount to the claim reciting significantly more than the abstract idea, conclude SME analysis and continue with examination under other patentability requirements.
guidance: Record can be clarified by providing remarks in the Office action explaining why the claim amounts to significantly more (for example: claim recites abstract idea 'x' but amounts to significantly more with additional element 'y' because 'abc'). An explicit eligibility explanation is not necessary unless the record benefits from clarification.

name: If elements do not amount to significantly more => §101 rejection and suggest claim changes
description: If no elements, taken individually and as a combination, amount to significantly more than the abstract idea, conclude SME analysis by making a §101 rejection and continue with other patentability requirements.
guidance: Use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015 for the rejection. Identify any disclosure elements that might be added to the claim to make it eligible and consider suggesting such amendments to applicant.

name: Sample rejection wording / Form Paragraph guidance
description: Provide suggested template language for a §101 rejection and reasons why the claim is directed to a judicial exception without significantly more.
guidance: Example: 'Claim __ is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 because the claimed invention is directed to a judicial exception (i.e., a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea) without significantly more. Claim __ is directed to ____. The claim does not include additional elements that are sufficient to amount to significantly more than the judicial exception because ____.' Use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015 as appropriate.

name: Novelty assessment test — inevitability / clear and unmistakeable directions
description: To determine anticipation, compare the earlier disclosure with the patent claim as at its publication date; if the prior art so construed discloses the same product/process or contains 'clear and unmistakeable directions' to the invention, the claim is anticipated.
guidance: Singapore cites General Tire & Rubber Co v Firestone: both prior art and claim must be interpreted at date of publication without hindsight. The practical question: does following the teachings in that disclosure inevitably lead to the invention?

name: Applicant procedural obligations — citing closest prior art and priority allocation
description: Applicants may be required to present known prior art useful for understanding the invention, cite documents, and show at least one closest solution; when claiming priority an applicant may be obliged to allocate one and only one priority date per claim.
guidance: Romania: Rule 13 requires presentation of prior art known to applicant and identification of the closest solution; Poland: 'claiming priority, the Applicant is obliged to point out (allocate) one and only one priority date for each claim.' These are procedural duties that affect examination clarity.

name: Correction and Addition of Inventor During Examination
description: An applicant may add or correct omitted/misspelled inventor names until an examiner determines the patentability of the claimed invention; after an examiner's determination, addition of a new inventor is generally not accepted except for corrections of errors.
guidance: If an amendment changing inventor name is submitted during examination, the examiner need only determine if omission/misspelling was by mistake and need not request evidential documents unless there are 'special reasons' (e.g., suspected intentional omission to address a ground of rejection). Where examiner reasonably suspects the listed inventor is not genuine (e.g., inventor not natural person, a minor not capable of creating the invention), the examiner may order amendment.

name: Scope Requirement for Retroactivity of Filing Date
description: The invention disclosed in the description/drawings and the claimed invention of the legitimate-holder's application must be included within the scope of invention of the unentitled person's application for retroactive filing date to apply; if the legitimate-holder's application contains inventions outside the scope of the unentitled person's disclosure, retroactivity does not apply to those out-of-scope inventions.
guidance: If multiple inventions are included in the legitimate-holder's application but only some were disclosed in the unentitled person's application, the out-of-scope inventions will not benefit from the earlier filing date.

name: Required Patent Application Documents (Article 42)
description: A patent application must include a cover sheet stating applicant and agent information, title of invention, and inventor name(s); it must be accompanied by a specification containing description and claims, necessary drawings, and an abstract.
guidance: The cover sheet is the essential information sheet. The specification must include the description of the invention and the claims; drawings where necessary should be provided. The abstract is for technical information only and must not be used to define the scope of the invention (Article 43).

name: Application Cover Sheet Content and Title Requirements
description: The cover sheet must include: (1) name and domicile (or if corporation, name and place of business) of applicant; (2) name and domicile/place of business of agent (and patent firm info and designated attorney if applicable); (3) title of the invention; (4) name and domicile of inventor. The title should be brief and concise and identical to the title in the specification.
guidance: The cover sheet also should indicate applicant code, priority claims, claims on grace-period disclosure exceptions, and request for examination. The title must reflect the subject matter and match the specification exactly.

name: Substitute specification entry under 37 CFR 1.125
description: A substitute specification which complies with 37 CFR 1.125 should normally be entered; a substitute specification is not permitted in a reissue application or in a reexamination proceeding (37 CFR 1.125(d)).
guidance: If a substitute specification filed under 37 CFR 1.125(b) and (c) is denied entry, it should be so marked and applicant notified (use form paragraph 6.28.02). Typical examiner reasons to insert: missing statement as to lack of new matter under 37 CFR 1.125(b); missing marked-up copy in addition to clean copy; missing clean copy in addition to marked-up copy; filed in a reissue or reexamination proceeding; filed after payment of the issue fee; or contains claims. Substitute specifications filed after final action or appeal are governed by 37 CFR 1.116; those filed after mailing of a notice of allowance are governed by 37 CFR 1.312. See MPEP § 714.20 for entry of amendments which substitute specification and MPEP § 608.04 for new matter in amendments.

name: Restoration of canceled matter (37 CFR 1.121)
description: Canceled text in the specification can be reinstated only by a subsequent amendment presenting the previously canceled matter as a new insertion (37 CFR 1.121(b)(4)). A claim canceled by amendment (deleted in its entirety) may be reinstated only by a subsequent amendment presenting the claim as a new claim with a new claim number (37 CFR 1.121(c)(5)).
guidance: Reinstatement is not by simple reactivation of prior-canceled material; it must be introduced as new matter in a later amendment (subject to new-matter rules). See MPEP § 714 for handling canceled matter.

name: Use of marks/trade names in specification — identification requirement
description: A mark or trade name may be used in a patent application to identify an article, product, service, or organization only if (A) its meaning is established by an accompanying definition in the specification which is sufficiently descriptive, enabling, precise and definite such that a claim including the mark or trade name complies with 35 U.S.C. 112, or (B) its meaning is well‑known to one skilled in the relevant art and is satisfactorily defined in the literature.
guidance: Condition (A) or (B) must be met at the time of filing of the complete application (see examples such as United States Gypsum Co. v. National Gypsum Co.). If the identification is omitted and deemed necessary, the examiner should hold the disclosure insufficient and reject claims based solely on the mark/trade name. If the product/service identity requires further description (e.g., process of manufacture), such an amendment may be permitted only if it does not introduce new matter and is supported by satisfactory showings that the characteristic was known at filing.

name: Drawing requirement where necessary for understanding (35 U.S.C. 113 & 37 CFR 1.81)
description: The applicant shall furnish a drawing of the invention where necessary for the understanding of the subject matter to be patented (35 U.S.C. 113). For design applications, a drawing is required to be entitled to a filing date (35 U.S.C. 171). For applications filed on or after December 18, 2013 (except design), 35 U.S.C. 111 no longer requires a drawing for a filing date, but 35 U.S.C. 113 still requires a drawing where necessary for understanding.
guidance: Absence of a drawing where necessary may prevent obtaining a patent for claimed invention if drawings later cannot cure insufficiency. Applicants should be prudent and include drawings where necessary. Examiners should require drawings where needed under 37 CFR 1.81 and follow OPAP determinations regarding whether drawings are 'necessary' for filing-date purposes for applications filed before Dec 18, 2013.

name: Effect of drawings submitted after filing date
description: Drawings submitted after the filing date may not be used (i) to overcome any insufficiency of the specification due to lack of an enabling disclosure or otherwise inadequate disclosure therein, or (ii) to supplement the original disclosure for the purpose of interpretation of the scope of any claim.
guidance: Drawings submitted post-filing that introduce new matter should not be entered; if entered, they cannot be used to expand or supply missing enabling disclosure. Examiners must describe new matter found in substitute or additional drawings in the next Office action and may refuse entry.

name: Claim types where drawings are not required for filing date (pre-PLT exceptions)
description: For applications filed before December 18, 2013, a drawing is not required for a filing date under pre-PLT 35 U.S.C. 111 if the application contains: (A) at least one process claim including the term 'process' or 'method' in its introductory phrase; (B) at least one composition claim including 'composition,' 'compound,' 'mixture' or 'pharmaceutical' in its introductory phrase; (C) at least one claim directed to a coated article or product or an article made from a particular material; (D) at least one claim directed to a laminated article or product; or (E) at least one claim where the sole distinguishing feature is the presence of a particular material.
guidance: See MPEP § 601.01(f) for more complete explanation. These exceptions affect whether OPAP treats an application without drawings as incomplete for filing-date purposes under pre-PLT rules.

name: Requirement procedure when subject matter admits of illustration by a drawing (form paragraphs 6.23 / 6.23.01)
description: If the subject matter admits of illustration by a drawing and none was furnished, the examiner should require submission of a drawing under 37 CFR 1.81(c). Use form paragraph 6.23 (or 6.23.01 when no examination of claims yet) to require a drawing.
guidance: When requiring drawings before examination use form paragraph 6.23.01 with a PTOL-90 or PTO-90C cover sheet. No new matter may be introduced in the required drawing. Applicant is given a shortened statutory period of TWO (2) MONTHS to submit a drawing in compliance with 37 CFR 1.81; extensions under 37 CFR 1.136(a) are possible but cannot extend reply beyond SIX MONTHS statutory maximum (35 U.S.C. 133). Failure to timely submit results in ABANDONMENT of the application. Examiners should specifically request at least an ink sketch or permanent print as part of the reply to facilitate early sufficiency determination and absence of new matter (see 37 CFR 1.121 and 1.81(d)).

name: Views — include as many views as necessary
description: The drawing must contain as many views as [necessary to] ... (i.e., include as many views as are necessary to show the invention).
guidance: Ensure the drawings present sufficient views to understand the claimed subject matter and to avoid ambiguity or insufficiency. (Text truncated in source, but principle is to include all necessary views.)

name: Reasonable expectation of success (obviousness)
description: A finding of obviousness does not require a guarantee of success—only a reasonable expectation of success is needed.
guidance: Certainty and absolute predictability are not required. Prior art that demonstrates successes (not only failures) across relevant embodiments can support a reasonable expectation of success. Courts should assess whether a skilled artisan would have had a reasonable expectation of achieving the claimed result (e.g., a 2-log increase across serotypes, or achieving a claimed dosage/form).

name: Secondary considerations (objective indicia) analysis
description: Secondary considerations — unexpected results, industry praise, long-felt need (and the effect of blocking patents), and commercial success — must be properly analyzed in the obviousness inquiry.
guidance: District courts should evaluate and weigh secondary considerations appropriately; failure or misanalysis can require remand. Guidance includes examining unexpected results relative to claim scope, how blocking patents affect long-felt need, and whether commercial success is causally tied to the claimed invention.

name: Indefiniteness: reasonable certainty
description: Claims are definite if they inform, with reasonable certainty, those skilled in the art about the scope of the invention.
guidance: Apparent contradictions across limitations do not automatically render a claim indefinite if it is possible to meet both limitations. Measurement technique disputes (e.g., particle-size techniques) require more than an outlier discrepancy to show indefiniteness; an isolated outlier measurement is not evidence that different techniques would typically yield materially different results.

name: Written description requirement (possession)
description: The written description is met when the disclosure reasonably conveys to those skilled in the art that the inventor had possession of the claimed subject matter as of the filing date.
guidance: A specification need not expressly recite a claimed subrange if the disclosure (including explicit disclosure of endpoints) reasonably conveys possession. The amount of detail required depends on the predictability of the art (less detail required for more predictable/electromechanical arts). Compare to prior precedent (Wertheim, Blaser, Kolmes) when analyzing subrange support.

name: Analysis of claimed ranges and subranges
description: A claimed narrower subrange can be supported by broader disclosed ranges when the disclosure reasonably conveys possession of the subrange.
guidance: Courts should assess whether the specification's disclosed ranges and endpoints reasonably convey the narrower claimed range; predictability of the technology and whether both endpoints are disclosed are relevant factors.

name: Unclean hands doctrine in patent litigation
description: Unclean hands can bar a party from obtaining relief when the party engaged in deceitful or reprehensible conduct that has an immediate and necessary connection to the claims for relief.
guidance: Examples of conduct supporting unclean hands include failure to disclose related patent applications, obstructing discovery, evasive testimony, and false testimony contradicted by contemporaneous evidence. The misconduct must be directly relevant to the litigation and affect the opposing party's ability to litigate the issues.

name: Personal jurisdiction (specific jurisdiction)
description: Specific personal jurisdiction requires that the defendant purposefully directed activities at the forum and that the action arises out of or relates to the defendant's forum activities.
guidance: Insufficient contacts with the forum (e.g., mere online listings or generalized contacts) can preclude specific jurisdiction; courts examine purposeful direction and the causal nexus between the forum contacts and the asserted claims.

name: Claim drafting and functional limitations (mutually exclusive concern)
description: Claims in the same patent may recite different ordered combinations of limitations and need not be totally consistent; functional limitations (e.g., 'substantially rigid portion') need not have identical boundaries across independent claims.
guidance: Labeling claims as 'mutually exclusive' is not a basis for indefiniteness if each claim, construed in context, informs a POSA of its scope with reasonable certainty. Functional claim terms are construed by their function and need not specify exact boundaries so long as the construction is consistent across claims.

name: Reasonable expectation in polymorph/form claims
description: Whether a skilled artisan would have a reasonable expectation of obtaining a claimed polymorphic form depends on whether prior art provides processes, characterizations, or routine assays that would lead to detection or production of that form.
guidance: If prior art discloses a process producing a crystalline form and characterization would routinely reveal the claimed polymorph (with expert support), a reasonable expectation may be found. Contrast with cases where prior art consistently produced a different form and lacked guidance on conditions to obtain the claimed form (e.g., Grunenthal).

name: Different inventive entity with at least one common inventor
description: When subject matter disclosed in a patent or patent application publication (reference) naming an inventive entity including joint inventor S and another joint inventor is claimed in a later application naming sole inventor S without the joint inventor, the reference may be properly applied under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a), (e), or (f) until overcome by an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(a) showing prior invention or by an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 traversing the rejection.
guidance: An unequivocal declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 by S that S conceived or invented the subject matter that was disclosed but not claimed in the patent or application publication and relied on in the rejection has been sufficient to overcome the rejection. However, an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 that is only a naked assertion of inventorship by an (joint) inventor who has an interest at stake and that fails to provide any context, explanation or evidence to support that assertion is insufficient. Where the reference is a U.S. patent or patent application publication which includes a claim reciting the subject matter relied upon, a declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 must also explain the presence of the additional joint inventor in the reference (e.g., explain which claims each inventor contributed to). Testimony or disclaimer from the other joint inventor(s) is usually not required but, if submitted, should be considered by the examiner.

name: Activities applied against the claims (prior use/knowledge)
description: Unless it is a statutory bar, a rejection under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103 based on an activity showing that the claimed invention was used or known prior to the filing date may be overcome by an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(a) establishing a date of invention prior to the activity or by a specific affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 showing that the activity was performed by the inventor or at least one joint inventor.
guidance: Affidavits under 1.131(a) are used to antedate activities by establishing an inventor's earlier date of invention; 1.132 is used to attribute the activity to the inventor or joint inventor. Statutory bars cannot be removed by these showings.

name: Genus‑Species: Species claim (overcoming reference that discloses a species)
description: Where the claim under rejection recites a species and the reference or activity discloses the claimed species, the rejection can be overcome under 37 CFR 1.131(a) directly by showing prior completion of the claimed species or indirectly by showing prior completion of a different species coupled with a showing that the claimed species would have been an obvious modification of the species completed by the inventor.
guidance: Case law (In re Spiller, In re Clarke, In re Plumb, In re Hostettler) illustrates that proof of prior completion of a different species can suffice if the claimed species would have been obvious from what the inventor had made.

name: Inquiry for applying 102(b)(2)(B) does not compare claimed invention
description: A determination of whether the 102(b)(2)(B) exception applies does not involve comparing the subject matter of the claimed invention to the inventor's disclosure or the intervening U.S. patent document.
guidance: The only inquiry with respect to the claimed invention is whether the prior art disclosure being relied upon anticipates or renders obvious the claimed invention. Applicability of the exception to subject matter in an intervening reference is determined without comparing those disclosures to the claimed invention.

name: Scope and limits of AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) (common ownership/obligation to assign)
description: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) excepts subject matter disclosed in a U.S. patent document from constituting prior art under 102(a)(2) if the subject matter disclosed and the claimed invention were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person not later than the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
guidance: This exception may apply to any U.S. patent document regardless of its potential prior art date (no grace-period limitation). It differs from pre-AIA 103(c) because, if 102(b)(2)(C) is met, the document cannot be applied as prior art under either 102 or 103 (so it cannot be used in anticipation or obviousness rejections). However, the exception does not apply to disclosures that qualify as prior art under 102(a)(1) (disclosures made before the effective filing date). Even if the exception applies, a double patenting rejection (statutory or nonstatutory) may still be made based on the document's claims, and the document may be cited for lack of enablement under 35 U.S.C. 112(a). A document that is excepted by 102(b)(2)(C) cannot serve as a secondary reference in a nonstatutory double patenting rejection because a secondary reference must be prior art.

name: Establishing common ownership by statement
description: A clear and conspicuous statement by the applicant (or representative) that the claimed invention and the subject matter disclosed in the cited U.S. patent document were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person not later than the effective filing date will be sufficient to establish that the 102(b)(2)(C) exception applies.
guidance: Applicants may present supporting evidence such as assignment documents, but are not required to do so. The Office will not request corroborating evidence absent independent evidence raising doubt as to the statement's veracity. A statement is required regardless of any assignment information recorded in the Office's assignment database. The Office treats such statements analogously to statements under pre-AIA 103(c).

name: Limitations on availability of 37 CFR 1.130(a)/(b)
description: The provisions of 37 CFR 1.130 are not available in all circumstances.
guidance: Affidavits/declarations under 1.130 are not available if the rejection is based upon a disclosure made more than one year before the effective filing date of the claimed invention. 1.130 may not be available if the rejection is based on a U.S. patent or published application naming another inventor that claims the same or substantially the same invention and the affidavit/declaration contends derivation by that named inventor; in such cases the applicant may need to file a petition for a derivation proceeding under § 42.401 et seq.

name: Effect of 102(b) exceptions on double patenting and enablement rejections
description: Even when a U.S. patent document is not available as prior art under 102 or 103 because a 102(b) exception applies, that document may still be relevant for other rejections.
guidance: A document excepted by 102(b)(2)(C) may still be the basis for a statutory or nonstatutory double patenting rejection (its claims can support double patenting), and it may be cited to show the state of the art for a lack of enablement rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a). However, a secondary reference used in a nonstatutory double patenting rejection must itself be prior art; thus, if the 102(b) exception applies, the document cannot be used as that secondary reference.

name: Likelihood of Prevailing on the Merits
description: Whether a litigant has a reasonable chance of prevailing on the merits in the venue.
guidance: Factor in the intrinsic quality of the patent (novelty, inventive step, specification quality, claim quality), fairness and impartiality of the forum (judicial independence, avoidance of extrajudicial influence), quality/specialization of the judiciary, and practical evidentiary considerations (e.g., can infringement be proved without broad discovery?). Also consider whether the venue provides meaningful protection for the specific technology at issue.

name: Prior Public Use
description: The patent claim is invalid if the claimed invention was in public use anywhere in the world before the effective filing date. An invention was in public use if the claimed invention was accessible to the public or commercially exploited anywhere in the world. An invention is publicly used if it is used by the inventor or by a person who is not under any limitation, restriction, or obligation of secrecy to the inventor. The absence of affirmative steps to conceal the use of the invention is evidence of a public use. Secret use by a third party is not public unless members of the public or employees of the third party have access to the invention.
guidance: Factors relevant to determining whether a use was public include: the nature of the activity that occurred in public; public access to the use; confidentiality obligations imposed upon observers; commercial exploitation; and the circumstances surrounding any testing and experimentation. If pre-AIA §102(b) is at issue, give additional instruction about exceptions under §102(b) and (c) when relevant. Cases cited: Pfaff; Barry v. Medtronic; Clock Spring; others.

name: Printed Publication
description: A patent claim is invalid if the invention was described in a printed publication before the applicable cutoff date. A printed publication is maintained in tangible form (e.g., printed pages, electronic files, microfilm, photographs, Internet publication, photocopies) and must have been sufficiently accessible to persons interested in the subject matter.
guidance: In determining accessibility, consider whether persons interested and ordinarily skilled in the subject matter, exercising reasonable diligence, could locate it; it need not be available to every member of the public. Issued patents and published patent applications are printed publications as of their publication date. The disclosure must be enabling—complete enough to enable a POSITA to use the invention without undue experimentation, judged by what a POSITA would have known as of the cutoff date. Practice note: when accessibility is disputed, give supplemental instruction on public accessibility. Cases: Blue Calypso; Orion IP; In re Lister; others.

name: Prior Invention (Pre-AIA)
description: A patent claim is invalid if the invention was invented by another person in the United States before the patentee invented it (pre-AIA §102(a),(g)). The defendant must show by clear and convincing evidence that (1) the other person reduced to practice a product or method including all the claim features before the patentee, or (2) the other person was first to conceive and exercised reasonable diligence in later reducing the invention to practice.
guidance: The prior invention must have been sufficiently developed that one skilled in the art would have recognized it would work for its intended purpose. This defense may be negated if the prior invention was abandoned, suppressed, or concealed. If abandonment/suppression/concealment is alleged, instruct jury on those terms: active concealment or unreasonable delay in making the invention publicly known supports a finding of abandonment/suppression/concealment; reasonable efforts to bring to market during a delay weigh against that finding. Cases: Teva v. AstraZeneca; Rosco; Dow Chem.; Apotex; others.

name: Prior U.S. / Earlier-Filed Patent Application
description: A claim may be invalid if the invention was described in a published U.S. patent application or published international (PCT) patent application that designates the U.S. (pre-AIA or AIA provisions vary) that was effectively filed before the patentee's invention or before the effective filing date.
guidance: Pre-AIA: prior published U.S. patent applications/patents filed by another before the invention date can anticipate. AIA: prior published patent documents/published PCT documents effectively filed before the effective filing date can be prior art. If questions exist whether the disclosure was obtained from the inventor or whether subject matter was commonly owned or under obligation to assign, instruct on §§102(b)(2) and (c) (AIA) and related exceptions. Provide effective filing date as determined under 35 U.S.C. §102(d) when applicable.

name: Obviousness — General (Graham Framework)
description: A claimed invention is invalid as 'obvious' if it would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art as of the Cutoff Date. Obviousness may be shown by one or more items of prior art. The analysis must avoid hindsight and not use the patent as a road map. The defendant must prove obviousness by clear and convincing evidence.
guidance: Obviousness is a mixed question of fact and law. The following four Graham factors must be evaluated (scope and content of prior art; differences between claimed invention and prior art; level of ordinary skill in the art; and secondary considerations/other considerations). Each factor must be evaluated for each claim alleged obvious, and may be analyzed in any order. Practice note on jury vs court roles and effect of PTO having had (or not had) material facts (Microsoft v. i4i guidance).

name: Obviousness Factor 2: Differences Between Claimed Invention and Prior Art
description: Analyze any relevant differences between the prior art and the claimed invention from the viewpoint of a POSITA as of the Cutoff Date. Determine the impact of differences on obviousness of the claimed invention as a whole, not just a portion.
guidance: Consider inferences and creative steps a POSITA would have used. If combining known elements yields predictable results, that supports obviousness; unexpected/unpredictable results or teaching away favor nonobviousness. A claim is not proven obvious merely by showing each element was independently known. Consider whether a reason existed at the time to combine elements and whether there would have been a reasonable expectation of success. If inherency is asserted, tailor instructions on inherency to the admissible evidence (see separate inherency entry). Analyze separately for each claim. Cases: KSR; Graham; ParPharm; others.

name: Inherency in Obviousness Analysis
description: Inherency may supply a claim element missing from explicit disclosure of a prior art reference only if that element is present in or is the natural result of the combination of elements explicitly disclosed by the prior art; inherency cannot be established by probabilities or possibilities.
guidance: The inherent element must be the natural result flowing from the explicit disclosure. Unexpected properties may be nonobvious even if inherent. Use inherency in obviousness analysis only when properly raised and supported by evidence; tailor instructions accordingly.

name: Obviousness Factor 4: Secondary Considerations / Other Considerations
description: Consider other factors that may indicate obviousness or nonobviousness (secondary considerations), which should be considered before deciding obviousness. No single factor is dispositive; evaluate the invention as a whole.
guidance: Potential secondary considerations include: commercial success due to the merits of the claimed invention (not advertising or non-claimed features); long-felt but unsolved need addressed by the invention; failed attempts by others to solve the problem; copying of the claimed invention; unexpectedly superior results; praise or surprise expressed by others in the field (including defendant); acceptance of licenses because of the invention’s merits. Carefully assess admissibility and nexus between secondary consideration and the claimed invention; the patentee bears the burden of proving a sufficient nexus. Only include instructions on particular considerations that are supported by the admitted evidence.

name: Determination of identicalness of compositions between patented substance and approved substance
description: The approved substance shall have the same composition as the substance recited in claims in an application to register patent term extension (where the claimed invention is a substance) or as the matter manufactured by the method described in claims (where the claimed invention is a use of a substance).
guidance: (i) For a substance invention, an examiner shall compare the concerned substance and the approved substance. (ii) For a manufacturing-method invention, an examiner shall compare the substance manufactured by the disclosed method with the approved substance; the manufacturing methods need not be compared. Where compositions are not identical, deem it a ground for rejection under Article 91(1) of the Patent Act and notify applicant of the ground for rejection.

name: Determination of identicalness of use for use inventions
description: Where the patented subject matter is a use invention, the use of the approved substance must be the same as the use disclosed in the patented invention.
guidance: If the use of the approved substance is not the same as the claimed use, the patent term shall not be extended even if compositions are identical. However, when the use of the patented substance includes the use of the approved substance, it shall be deemed that the uses are the same.

name: Treatment of written arguments
description: An applicant can submit written arguments in response to a notice of grounds for rejection.
guidance: A written argument shall be submitted within the designated period. Where an argument is submitted, the examiner shall determine whether the ground for rejection really exists while considering the applicant’s claims in the written argument. Even if an argument is submitted after the period has elapsed or before notification, examiner shall take the argument into consideration rather than returning it.

name: Matters eligible for amendment under Article 90(6)
description: Matters eligible for amendment in an application for registration of extension under Article 90(6) include specific items.
guidance: Eligible items include: ① an indication of claims for registration of extension, ② the period for extension request, ③ the content of approval, etc. under Article 89 of the Patent Act, ④ the ground for extension specified in Ordinance of the Ministry of Knowledge Economy. Amendment cannot be allowed except for amending clerical errors such as changing the applicant for registration of extension and changing the patent number of the patent right eligible for registration of extension (see notes on wrongly-indicated patent numbers being correctable as clerical errors). Examiner shall determine legitimacy of subject for amendment; if amendment not eligible, deliver preliminary notice for inadmissible amendment and re-examine pre-amendment application.

name: Transmittal and publication after decision to register extension
description: When a decision to register patent term extension is made, specific transmittal and publication steps are required.
guidance: Commissioner shall deliver a copy of the decision to the applicant. Examiner shall ask registration division to include in the patent gazette: ① name and address of patent right holder (or entity title and business address), ② patent number, ③ date of registration of extension, ④ period for extension, ⑤ content of approval under Article 89 (indications such as claims for registration of extension, contents of approval or registration, ground for extension, etc.). See provisions regarding service of a copy of a decision to grant a patent for detailed transmittal rules.

name: Definition and scope of 'period delayed due to an applicant' (Enforcement Decree Article 7(2))
description: The 'period delayed due to an applicant' includes numerous specific procedural periods in which applicant actions or requests cause delay, spanning patent-office proceedings, litigation, and administrative appeal/litigation procedures.
guidance: The Enforcement Decree enumerates detailed subcases, including (but not limited to): (1)(a)-(t) delays in patent-related proceedings before KIPO or the Trial and Appeal Board (e.g., time to appoint/replace agent, periods extended at applicant request, postponed dates at applicant request, suspensions/interruptions, applicant-requested consultations, specification amendments, claim withdrawal, delayed expedited examination determinations, applicant delays in submission of arguments, fee payments after grant steps, reexamination requests, requests for examination after a cause ceases, motions for disqualification not accepted, delayed evidence preservation conclusions, resumed reviews after closing, requests for retrials and related periods, service delays due to applicant); (2)(a)-(m) periods in litigation proceedings (e.g., stays, motions for disqualification of judges, court-ordered corrections, appointment of special representatives, resumed trials due to applicant, extensions/grants of additional periods, service delays); (3)(a)-(g) periods in administrative appeal or administrative litigation (e.g., rejections of disqualification requests, appeals after force majeure, Commission-ordered corrections, deadlines for supplemental briefs, postponed hearing dates, service provisions applied mutatis mutandis). Examiners must apply this comprehensive list to determine applicant-caused delay for deduction from extension.

name: Withdrawal of previous rejection and reasons for allowance
description: If the withdrawal of the previous rejection results in the allowance of the claims, the reasons, which form the basis for the withdrawal of the previous rejection, may be included in a reasons for allowance.
guidance: Form paragraph 7.38.01 may be used. See MPEP §1302.14. If applicant’s arguments are persuasive and the examiner determines that the previous rejection should be withdrawn but that, upon further consideration, a new ground of rejection should be made, form paragraph 7.38.02 may be used. See MPEP §706.07(a) to determine whether the Office action may be made final.

name: Identification of ground of rejection applied to new/amended claim
description: If a rejection of record is to be applied to a new or amended claim, specific identification of that ground of rejection should be given.
guidance: Provide identification as by citation of the paragraph in the former Office letter in which the rejection was originally stated so the basis for the rejection applied to the new/amended claim is clear and traceable.

name: ¶ 7.38 — Arguments are moot because of new ground of rejection
description: Use form paragraph 7.38 when applicant’s arguments have been considered but are moot because a new ground of rejection does not rely on any reference applied in the prior rejection for any teaching specifically challenged.
guidance: Examiner must still address any arguments presented by the applicant which are still relevant to any references being applied. In bracket insert claim numbers, etc., as directed by the form paragraph.

name: ¶ 7.38.01 — Arguments persuasive; previous rejection/objection withdrawn
description: When applicant’s arguments have been fully considered and are persuasive, the prior rejection/objection may be withdrawn.
guidance: Form paragraph 7.38.01 should identify the applicant remarks (page/line numbers) forming the basis for withdrawal, identify the subject matter (claim, figure, specification, abstract, etc.), and insert the rejection or objection withdrawn. Follow bracket instructions in the form paragraph.

name: Unpersuasive argument: Arguing limitations not claimed (¶ 7.37.08)
description: Applicant cannot rely on features not recited in the rejected claim(s); limitations from the specification are not read into the claims.
guidance: Cite In re Van Geuns. Recite the features relied upon by applicant that are not in the claims. Precede with 7.37.

name: Unpersuasive argument: Intended use (¶ 7.37.09)
description: A recitation of intended use must result in a structural difference between the claimed invention and the prior art to patentably distinguish; if prior art structure can perform the intended use, it meets the claim.
guidance: Identify the claim(s) and restate the recitation. Precede with 7.37.

name: Unpersuasive argument: Limitation(s) in preamble (¶ 7.37.10)
description: Preamble language that does not provide distinct definition is not considered a limitation when the body of the claim describes a complete invention.
guidance: Cite Pitney Bowes v. Hewlett-Packard and MPEP §2111.02. Precede with 7.37.

name: Unpersuasive argument: General allegation of patentability (¶ 7.37.11)
description: Arguments that amount to a general allegation that the claims define a patentable invention fail to comply with 37 CFR 1.111(b) because they do not point out how the claim language patentably distinguishes from references.
guidance: Use form paragraph 7.37 as a precursor; explain non-compliance with 1.111(b).

name: State when claims are allowable; assist pro se applicants
description: When patentable subject matter is apparent, examiners should draft one or more claims for pro se applicants and indicate such claims would be allowed if incorporated, and otherwise indicate allowable subject matter and suggest definite corrections.
guidance: This expedites prosecution for pro se inventors. If claims are allowable except for form defects or omission of a limitation, offer constructive suggestions and consider suggesting an interview. Use form paragraphs 7.43, 7.43.01, 7.43.02, and 7.97. If a claim is allowable but dependent on a canceled or rejected claim, state it would be allowable if rewritten in independent form.

name: Comment on examples, tests, and results
description: Results of tests and examples should not normally be questioned by the examiner unless there is a reasonable basis for questioning the results.
guidance: If examiner questions results, appropriate claims may be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) for insufficient disclosure (see In re Borkowski). Applicant must reply with actual test results or arguments showing reason to believe predicted results; avoid entering new matter. If operability or utility is in question, consider a 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection. See MPEP §§2161–2164.08(c) for written description and enablement discussion.

name: Use sufficiently large and appropriate datasets with clear train/validation/test splits
description: Experiment on large-scale patent datasets (examples: AI-Growth-Lab dataset of 1.5M claims annotated with classes; BigPatent with ~35k labelled texts and pre-split training/validation/testing).
guidance: Be explicit about dataset preprocessing (claims vs human-generated abstracts), splits (BigPatent example: 25k train, 5k val, 5k test), and how dataset characteristics (e.g., abstracts vs claims) affect semantic representation and performance.

name: Legal effect of listing a reference in an IDS
description: Art listed on an IDS, on its own, is not automatically considered prior art; mere listing of a reference in an IDS is not taken as an admission that the reference is prior art against the claims.
guidance: Listing does not equate to conceding that a reference is prior art; the examiner must still determine relevance and patentability effect.

name: Obligation to consider and address Patent Owner's arguments
description: The Board must consider and address arguments a Patent Owner actually raised regarding patentability (e.g., Patent Owner presented multiple arguments disputing Petitioner's unpatentability contentions for claim 17).
guidance: If the record shows the Patent Owner raised specific arguments (for example, that a reference discloses time division multiplexing rather than the claimed time division duplex and is silent on claimed beacon messages), the Board must consider those arguments; failure to do so can warrant Director Review and vacatur/in part remand.

name: Accuracy in stating the record
description: The Board should not state that a Patent Owner 'does not present any arguments' when the record demonstrates otherwise (the Decision's statement that Patent Owner 'does not present any arguments specific to claims 2, 9, and 17' was found erroneous).
guidance: Before relying on such statements as a basis for a decision, the Board must ensure its characterization of the record is correct; erroneous characterizations may require vacatur and remand.

name: Burden of proof in IPR — preponderance of the evidence
description: The petitioner must show unpatentability by a preponderance of the evidence (the Board shall determine whether Petitioner has shown by a preponderance of the evidence that claims 2 and 9 are unpatentable).
guidance: Even when claims are addressed together because they share limitations, the Board must determine whether the petitioner has met the preponderance‑of‑the‑evidence burden for each asserted claim.

name: Remand instruction to evaluate specific claim limitations against asserted grounds
description: Where Director Review is granted because the Board omitted addressing arguments, the Board is instructed to consider the Patent Owner's arguments as to the specific claim (here, claim 17) under the identified grounds (here, Grounds 3 and 4).
guidance: On remand the Board must evaluate whether the asserted references actually teach the claimed limitations (e.g., whether Amit teaches TDD or only time division multiplexing, and whether DSL‑Book's pilot tones suggest claimed beacon messages) and explain its conclusions.

name: Treatment of claims that share limitations
description: When claims recite the same limitations (claims 2 and 9 recite the same limitations as claim 17), the Board may address them together but still must determine whether petitioner has proven unpatentability for each claim.
guidance: Addressing claims together is permissible for efficiency, but the Board should still make clear, claim‑by‑claim findings or otherwise ensure the record supports a determination for each claim under the required burden.

name: Identification and articulation of obviousness grounds
description: Ground 3 challenges certain claims as obvious over Amit and Jacobsen; Ground 4 challenges certain claims as obvious over Amit, Jacobsen, and DSL‑Book.
guidance: Obviousness grounds must identify the references and combinations relied upon and be evaluated with respect to the specific claim limitations at issue (e.g., TDD protocol, beacon messages). The Board should explain how the combination teaches or renders obvious the claimed limitations or why it does not.

name: PPH basic principle
description: Allows applicants who received a determination of allowable claims in an application from one Intellectual Property (IP) Office to obtain fast track processing of corresponding claims in an application pending in other IP Offices.
guidance: Effective strategy for U.S. applicants to get IP rights faster in global markets; participating Offices leverage each other's work to expedite examination when corresponding claims exist.

name: Types of PPH agreements / participating regimes
description: PPH operates under different agreement types: Global PPH, IP5 PPH, and bilateral agreements.
guidance: Global PPH (began 2014) includes a broad set of participating Offices; IP5 PPH involves the five largest offices (EPO, JPO, KIPO, CNIPA, USPTO); USPTO also maintains multiple bilateral PPH agreements. Eligibility and specific document/claim correspondence rules may vary by agreement and Office—confirm Office-specific requirements.

name: Identify judicial exception(s)
description: Determine whether the claim is directed to any judicial exception: laws of nature, natural phenomena/product of nature, or abstract ideas.
guidance: Examples: a claimed correlation between a biomarker and disease can be a law of nature; mental comparison/critical thinking steps can be an abstract idea; isolated or unmodified natural products can be a 'product of nature' exception.

name: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) of claim terms
description: Interpret claim language under the broadest reasonable interpretation when evaluating eligibility (e.g., 'cream', 'vaccine', 'immuno-effective amount', 'microneedle array').
guidance: Use the plain meaning in the relevant art to identify embodiments encompassed by the claim (e.g., 'cream' = semi-solid homogeneous emulsion comprising water and oil; 'vaccine' = mixture of peptide and adjuvant sufficient to produce immunogenic response). BRI informs which embodiments/counterparts to compare in the exception analysis.

name: Product-of-nature: compare to closest naturally occurring counterpart
description: For nature-based products, compare the claimed subject matter to its closest naturally occurring counterpart to determine if it has 'markedly different characteristics.'
guidance: If components do not occur together in nature, compare the claimed mixture to its individual natural components. If a component occurs naturally in combination with others, use that combination as the closest counterpart. The analysis asks whether the claimed item exhibits marked differences relative to that counterpart.

name: Markedly different characteristics — structural/physical/functional
description: Marked differences can be in structural, physical, functional, or other characteristics; such differences can show the claim is not a 'product of nature.'
guidance: Concrete examples: structural/physical — emulsification producing small uniform oil droplets homogeneously dispersed in water causing a semi-solid, non-flowable cream that adheres to skin; functional — a mixture exhibiting greatly enhanced immunogenicity (e.g., 30% + 0% -> 80% seroprotection). Even functional changes (increased immunogenicity) can constitute 'marked differences.'

name: Process claims focused on action vs. product limitations
description: If a claim as a whole is focused on a process (e.g., detecting a protein), the existence of nature-based product limitations in the claim does not always require performing the 'markedly different characteristics' analysis on those product limitations.
guidance: Example: a detection method that recites a plasma sample and JUL-1 may be analyzed as a process, and the eligibility inquiry can end at Step 2A when the claim is not directed to an exception as a whole.

name: Step 2A / Step 2B: 'significantly more' / additional elements analysis
description: If the claim is directed to a judicial exception, determine whether elements beyond the exception — individually or in combination — amount to 'significantly more' such that the claim is a patent-eligible application of the exception.
guidance: Evaluate whether additional elements are meaningful limitations that confine the exception to a particular useful application (not merely instructions to 'apply' the exception). Consider whether the limitation is unconventional and whether the combination yields an improvement in a technical field (analogous to Diehr).

name: Unconventional, specific limitations can provide 'significantly more'
description: Recitation of specific, unconventional reagents, treatments, or devices that were not routine or conventional at the time of filing can render a claim eligible by supplying 'significantly more.'
guidance: Examples cited: detecting JUL-1 using a porcine anti-JUL-1 antibody (not conventionally used for human proteins), detecting using a specific monoclonal antibody mAb-D33, administering topical vitamin D (not previously routine for julitis), and a coated microneedle array as an unconventional delivery device. Such limitations can confine the claim to a particular useful application and thereby amount to 'significantly more' (Step 2B yes).

name: Identify and explain exception and insufficiency in Office actions (practice note)
description: When issuing rejections or reasons for allowance, the examiner should identify the claim limitation that is an exception and explain why it is an exception and why additional elements do or do not amount to 'significantly more.'
guidance: A rejection should point to the claim element (e.g., a correlation step) and explain that it is a law of nature/abstract idea/product of nature, and then explain why the other claim limitations are merely data-gathering or well-understood, routine and conventional activities (or why they are unconventional and therefore sufficient). Remarks may also be added when a claim is allowed to clarify that it 'is not directed to any judicial exception.'

name: Undue Experimentation Factors (Wands test)
description: When determining whether undue experimentation is required (i.e., enablement), weigh the Wands factors.
guidance: The Wands factors: (1) breadth of the claims; (2) nature of the invention; (3) state of the prior art; (4) level of one of ordinary skill; (5) level of predictability in the art; (6) amount of direction provided by the inventor; (7) existence of working examples; (8) quantity of experimentation needed to make or use the invention. The undue experimentation determination is reached by weighing all these considerations together (In re Wands).

name: Examiner's Burden to Establish a Reasonable Basis for Enablement Rejection
description: Before making an enablement rejection, USPTO personnel must establish on the record a reasonable basis for questioning whether the disclosure enables a person of ordinary skill in the art to make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
guidance: Once the examiner advances a reasonable basis for questioning enablement, the applicant must rebut and factually demonstrate that the disclosure is sufficient. Cases: In re Brown; In re Ghiron; In re Doyle; In re Scarbrough. Examiners should analyze what the claim recites and what subject matter it encompasses as a whole.

name: Written Description for Computer‑Implemented Functional Claims (algorithm/structure disclosure)
description: For computer‑implemented functional claim limitations, the specification must disclose sufficient corresponding computer and algorithmic structure (the necessary steps and/or flowcharts) so that one skilled in the art can reasonably conclude the inventor possessed the claimed subject matter at filing.
guidance: Algorithm may be expressed as mathematical formula, prose, flow chart, or other understandable terms that provide sufficient structure. It is not enough that one skilled in the art could write a program to achieve the function; the specification must explain how the inventor intended the function to be performed. If the specification fails to disclose the computer and algorithm in sufficient detail, a written description rejection must be made. See Finisar; Vasudevan; Ariad; MPEP §§2163, 2181.

name: Means‑(or Step‑)‑Plus‑Function (35 U.S.C. 112(f)) Corresponding Structure Requirement
description: For claims invoking 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (or pre‑AIA sixth paragraph), the specification must provide corresponding structure, material, or acts that perform the entire claimed function; absent such disclosure, the applicant has failed to particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention.
guidance: If a means/step‑plus‑function limitation lacks sufficient corresponding structure in the specification, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (second paragraph) must be made in addition to any written description rejection. See In re Donaldson; MPEP §2181. Examiner should check for adequate disclosure of structure/materials/acts that perform the claimed function.

name: Genus‑Species Support for Broad (Genus) Claims
description: A disclosure of a species does not automatically support a claim to a broader genus; whether a genus is supported depends on the state of the art and the nature and breadth of the genus. Adequate written description of a genus requires more than a generic statement of boundaries.
guidance: The specification must convey to one skilled in the art that the inventor possessed the genus (Hynix). Disclosure of some species can support a genus if it reasonably conveys possession of the broader subject matter, but disclosure of only a single embodiment often does not (LizardTech). Anti‑patterns include claiming a broad genus based on one method/embodiment without evidence the inventor conceived other species achieving the genus result.

name: Risks of Functional or Generic Claim Language
description: Claims defined solely by desired results or by functional language, without describing how the function is performed, often fail the written description (and/or enablement) requirement.
guidance: Particularly acute for genus claims that use functional language to define boundaries: the functional claim may claim a desired result without describing species that achieve it. For software, simply restating a function in the claim without explaining the algorithm/steps/procedure is insufficient. Examiner should look for disclosure of how the function is achieved, not merely the statement of the goal (Ariad; LizardTech; MPEP §§2163.02, 2181).

name: Reliance on Knowledge of One Skilled in the Art Is Limited
description: While the specification need not disclose what is well known in the art, the applicant cannot rely on the knowledge of one skilled in the art to supply information necessary to enable the novel aspects of the claimed invention when that information is not known in the art.
guidance: Rule of supplementation: well known information may be omitted, but omission is not a substitute for a basic enabling disclosure of novel aspects. Cases: Genentech; ALZA; Auto. Technologies. Omission of only minor details may be acceptable, but lack of disclosure of any specific starting materials or conditions when needed can render the specification non‑enabled.

name: Motion to terminate and settlements (37 C.F.R. §§ 42.72–42.74; 35 U.S.C. §§ 317, 327)
description: Termination: § 42.72 covers termination of a party (Board may proceed to final written decision even if no petitioner remains) and termination of the proceeding (Board enters judgment). A party may request adverse judgment: § 42.73(b). Disclaimer of patent, claim cancellation, concession of unpatentability, and abandonment of contest may be construed as such a request. Parties can settle any issue via joint request: 35 U.S.C. § 317(a), § 327(a). All agreements/understandings must be in writing & filed with the Board; no side agreements (panel may require parties to represent that no side agreements exist in the motion). Settlement materials may be treated as business confidential — request to keep separate. The Board is not a party to the settlement.
guidance: File joint requests for settlement with full disclosure and required filings; do not rely on side agreements; consider business confidential handling and possible expungement or special treatment.

name: Estoppel under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(1)
description: (e) Estoppel. — (1) Proceedings before the office.—The petitioner in an inter partes review of a claim . . . that results in a final written decision . . . may not request or maintain a proceeding before the Office with respect to that claim on any ground that the petitioner raised or reasonably could have raised during that inter partes review. 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(1); see 37 C.F.R. § 42.73(d). Termination: Of a second proceeding – Board enters judgment in a first proceeding and terminates a second proceeding (no joinder) having a ground that reasonably could have been raised in first proceeding.
guidance: Be mindful that claims and grounds litigated (or reasonably raisable) in a prior final IPR can estop later PTO proceedings; consider estoppel implications when deciding whether to assert grounds or join proceedings.

name: Use of foreign patent office search results
description: If foreign patent offices or search organizations already conducted a search regarding the claimed invention, the examiner shall review those search outcomes to determine whether they can be used as relevant prior art.
guidance: Assess appropriateness and applicability of such external search reports.

name: Circumstances where search is not required or may be limited
description: No special search effort is necessary or search may be limited if the claimed invention falls under certain cases where meaningful search is impossible for some/all claims.
guidance: Enumerated cases: ① amendment beyond scope under Article 47, ② claimed invention not patentable under Article 32, ③ claimed invention incomplete or not industrially applicable under Article 29, ④ lack of unity of invention under Article 45 (claims do not relate to one invention or linked group), ⑤ inability to interpret claims due to lack of clarity/conciseness. In such cases notify applicant and may wait for response; if claims can be understood despite deficiencies, proceed within defined scope.

name: Suspension of search when lack of novelty/inventive step is clear
description: Examiner may suspend search when prior art clearly demonstrates lack of novelty or inventive step for the entire claimed subject-matter.
guidance: Suspend to conserve resources once a clear ground of rejection is found.

name: When claims of different categories exist, include categories as appropriate
description: When application contains claims of different categories (product, process, use), all must be included in the search; however, if a product claim is clearly new/non-obvious, no special effort required to search process or use claims that inevitably result in that product.
guidance: If only one claim category present, may consider including other categories desirably.

name: Examiners to check publication date and content without over-interpretation
description: Examiner shall determine whether retrieved prior art provides grounds for rejection regarding novelty, inventive step, enlarged concept of novelty or earlier application; check bibliography to ensure publication date precedes filing date (or priority date); check inventors/applicants for enlarged-concept issues.
guidance: Have clear understanding of technical issues disclosed in prior art; avoid acknowledging matters not disclosed in those documents and be cautious not to over-interpret claims without logical grounds.

name: Priority claim under treaty: eligibility and declaration timing
description: A person who can claim treaty priority is the applicant who filed in a State party or his/her legitimate successor; priority claim must be declared within 12 months from first filing date of the first application on which priority is based.
guidance: If applicants differ between original and subsequent applications, examiner may request evidential documents proving succession; late declaration leads to amendment request and possible invalidation of the priority procedure; procedural amendment scope is limited to correcting self-evident errors.

name: Priority claim reference date determined claim-by-claim and identity rules
description: If claimed invention in priority claim is identical (including de facto identical) to invention in original application, reference date is filing date of original application; for multiple priority claims, use earliest filing date; where invention is a combination of matter from multiple originals, treat as not stated in original application and use appropriate reference date.
guidance: Effects of priority in setting reference date are determined on a claim-by-claim basis; where original application claims priority to an earlier application, the original may not be the 'earliest application' under Paris Convention and retroactive effect may not apply—examiner must state reasons for non-retroactive application.

name: Domestic priority claim rules and limitations
description: Domestic priority claim eligibility is limited to the applicant of the earlier application; domestic priority must be claimed within one year of earlier filing; divisional/converted applications cannot serve as basis for domestic priority; earlier applications invalidated/withdrawn/abandoned cannot serve as basis.
guidance: When inventions are identical between earlier application and domestic priority claim, reference date is earlier application's filing date; complex domestic priority uses earliest filing date; earlier application is regarded withdrawn after one year and three months; examiner defers further examination until earlier application is considered withdrawn and may defer grant decisions accordingly.

name: Separate oral hearings by issue
description: If necessary, the Court may hold separate oral hearings according to specific issues when several issues are in dispute (examples: claim construction or whether prior art was published must be resolved first; multiple grounds for invalidation asserted; whether an invention subject to confirmation is specified and implemented).
guidance: Scope of each hearing is limited to the designated disputed issue. After a hearing, the Court may disclose opinions (oral/written) on examined issues and order preparation for remaining issues.

name: Instructive note: amendments/corrections to claims or descriptions
description: If any claims or descriptions in the specification of a patent or utility model are changed due to a petition for amendment or correction, such changes shall be stated in detail, and claims or descriptions in the specification subject to litigation shall be specified.
guidance: Clearly identify amended text and the precise scope of what is litigated after amendment/correction.

name: Written description deficiency arguments and legal citations
description: An argument regarding a lack of written description in the specification shall specify an applicable legal provision on which the argument is based (e.g., whether the patent can be readily practiced by the explanation therein — Article 42(3)1 of the Patent Act; whether a claim is supported by the explanation — Article 42(4)1; whether the scope of a claim is clearly specified — Article 42(4)2).
guidance: Cite the specific legal provision and explain how the specification fails that statutory requirement.

name: Grounds for requesting a claim construction hearing
description: If it is necessary to conduct a hearing for claim construction first, the grounds shall be specified, and the terms for which claim construction is necessary, the descriptions relating to such terms in the specification, the parties’ proposed claim constructions, and specific grounds for such constructions shall be stated.
guidance: Provide precise claim terms, textual support in the specification, and reasons why construction affects remaining issues.

name: Background art disclosure
description: The description should mention any background art of which the applicant is aware and which is useful for understanding the invention and its relationship to the prior art; identification of documents, especially patent specifications, should preferably be included.
guidance: Particularly apply to background art corresponding to technical features necessary for definition of the claimed subject matter but which, in combination, are part of the prior art.

name: Disclosure of the invention (problem and solution)
description: The invention as claimed should be disclosed so that the technical problem(s) can be appreciated and the solution understood; include only details necessary for elucidating the invention.
