guidance: Not necessary to present explicitly in problem-and-solution form. State advantageous effects but do not disparage prior art or present ambiguous comparisons that mislead about prior art accomplishments.

name: Brief description of drawings
description: If drawings are included they should first be briefly described (e.g., 'Figure 1 is a plan view...'); when referring to elements, name the element as well as its number (e.g., 'resistor 3 is connected to capacitor 5 via switch 4').
guidance: Description and drawings should be consistent in reference numbers and signs. Examiner need not rigorously require deletion of superfluous drawing references after certain amendments, but references used in description or claims should also appear on drawings.

name: Sufficiency of disclosure and irreparable insufficiencies
description: Applicant must supply sufficient disclosure to meet Rule 6 for all claims; where disclosure is insufficient to enable a skilled person to carry out the claimed invention, claims may be too broad and unsupported.
guidance: Two special instances of fundamental insufficiency: (a) success dependent on chance (results not reproducible, e.g., certain microbiological mutation processes); (b) inherently impossible performance contrary to established physical laws (e.g., perpetual motion machine). Distinguish from processes with some failure rate that can be sorted by nondestructive testing.

name: Deposit of biological material for sufficiency
description: Where the application refers to biological material that cannot otherwise be described to meet Rule 6, a deposit of such material is taken into consideration when determining whether sufficiency requirements are met; deposit is considered part of the description to that extent.
guidance: Mere reference to deposited material may not replace explicit disclosure. In some Authorities deposit is also considered for the support requirement of claims (Rule 7).

name: Treatment of irrelevant matter
description: Irrelevant matter that is 'obviously irrelevant or unnecessary' (having no bearing on the subject matter or its background) is prohibited and may need removal; matter may become irrelevant during examination due to claim limitations.
guidance: Examiner's attention is drawn to PCT Rule 9 for application of these provisions.

name: Claims: general requirements
description: The claims must: (i) define the matter for which protection is sought; (ii) be clear and concise; and (iii) be fully supported by the description.
guidance: This chapter sets out appropriate form and content of claims and how they should be interpreted for assessing novelty, inventive step, and for searching relevant prior art.

name: Claims drafted in terms of technical features
description: Claims must be drafted in terms of the 'technical features of the invention' and should not contain statements relating to commercial advantages or non-technical matters; statements of purpose are allowed if they assist in defining the invention.
guidance: Functional limitations are permissible provided a skilled person would have no difficulty in providing means to perform the function without inventive skill or such means are fully disclosed. Evaluate functional limitations in context for what they fairly convey to a skilled person. Claims to the use of the invention (technical application) are permissible.

name: Two-part claim (Rules 7(1)(a) and (b))
description: Where appropriate, a claim should take a two-part form: first part indicating designation of subject matter and prior-art features necessary for definition; second 'characterizing portion' stating the technical features which, in combination with first-part features, it is desired to protect (the features the invention adds to the prior art).
guidance: Invite applicant to use two-part form when invention is a distinct improvement on known combination. Two-part form need only be used when appropriate; inappropriate in cases like (i) combination of known elements of equal status where inventive step is in the combination, (ii) modification of a known chemical process (omitting or substituting substance), (iii) complex systems with interrelated parts. Purpose is to show which features are part of the prior art; if prior-art indication in description makes this clear, alternative claim forms may be appropriate.

name: Use of reference signs in claims
description: If drawings are present and technical features of the claims would be rendered more intelligible by relating them to corresponding features of the drawings, appropriate reference signs may be placed in parentheses after features in the claims.
guidance: Reference signs are aids to understanding and are not to be construed as limiting the scope of a claim.

name: Claim construction standard (broadest reasonable interpretation)
description: The Office adopts the 'broadest reasonable interpretation' standard for claim construction in inter partes review, post-grant review, and covered business method patent review proceedings.
guidance: This standard is consistent with AIA legislative history and long-standing USPTO and Federal Circuit practice; it applies to patentability determination proceedings and is the proper method for construing claims in those contexts (citations: NTP, Yamamoto, Phillips, etc.).

name: Apply claim construction standard throughout proceeding
description: The 'broadest reasonable interpretation' standard must be applied throughout a proceeding when the Board determines whether to institute the review and when the Board determines patentability of any challenged patent claim and any new claims.
guidance: Applies to challenged claims, new claims added under 35 U.S.C. 316(d)/326(d), claims from merged derivation proceedings, original/new/amended claims from merged reissue applications, and merged reexaminations; a single claim construction standard must be used to prevent inconsistencies and inefficiencies.

name: Consideration of patent owner statements under 35 U.S.C. 301(d)
description: The Office may consider written statements of the patent owner filed in court or the Office regarding claim scope, but such statements are limited under 35 U.S.C. 301(d) 'to determine the proper meaning of a patent claim' and do not mandate adoption of the district court standard.
guidance: Statutory language does not set a claim construction standard nor require the Office to adopt district court claim construction; Office has discretion whether to consider such statements in an instituted review.

name: Petitioner must set forth claim construction in petition
description: Petitioners must identify how the challenged claim is to be construed in the petition (see § 42.104(b)(3)).
guidance: This requirement is intended to provide sufficient notice to the patent owner and assist the Board in analyzing how cited prior art meets claim limitations. Petitioners are not required to define every claim term but must state that terms take their ordinary and customary meaning and point out any claim term with a special meaning and its specification definition.

name: Presumption of ordinary and customary meaning for claim terms
description: A claim term is presumed to take on its ordinary and customary meaning — the meaning it would have to a person of ordinary skill in the art — unless the specification provides a special definition.
guidance: Words of the claim are given their plain meaning unless that plain meaning is inconsistent with the specification (citing In re Zletz, In re Am. Acad. of Sci. Tech Ctr.). Petitioners need not define every term, only identify special definitions where present.

name: Filing date — acceptance of minor deficiencies
description: The Board generally will accord a filing date and accept minor deficiencies that do not impact the Board’s ability to determine whether to institute the review or the patent owner’s ability to file a preliminary response.
guidance: Petitioners should still make every effort to complete petitions accurately. Some omissions/mistakes can affect institution (e.g., citing incorrect portion of a reference or omission of a challenged claim). The Board plans to process petitions and accord a filing date as soon as practical.

name: Certain omissions are not minor (failure to state precise relief requested)
description: Failure to include the specific relief requested for each claim challenged is not considered a minor deficiency and cannot be cured without consequence.
guidance: The Office refused to adopt a rule expressly allowing cure of such an omission without impact.

name: Scope of institution decisions (claim-by-claim and ground-by-ground)
description: The Board may authorize review to proceed on all or some of the challenged claims and on all or some of the grounds of unpatentability asserted for each claim (§§ 42.108(a), 42.208(a)).
guidance: Institution is a threshold decision and can be limited to particular claims/grounds for which the required statutory threshold is met.

name: Institution thresholds: 'reasonable likelihood' and 'more likely than not'
description: Review will not be instituted unless the Board decides that the petition would demonstrate a 'reasonable likelihood' (inter partes review) or 'more likely than not' (post-grant review) that at least one of the claims is unpatentable (35 U.S.C. 314(a)/324(a)).
guidance: Whether a petitioner meets the threshold is evaluated case-by-case. 'Reasonable likelihood' is a lower threshold than 'more likely than not'. The Office declines to further define beyond following statutory language.

name: Declining institution for inability to complete timely or for extreme complexity
description: The Office may decline to institute a proceeding where it determines it could not complete the proceeding timely or where the petition seeks review that is unmanageably large or complex (e.g., several hundred claims, a thousand references, or need for many foreign depositions).
guidance: The Board may take into account the Office's ability to timely complete the review as part of the considerations under 35 U.S.C. 316(b) and 326(b).

name: Consistency of reference signs between drawings, description and claims
description: Reference signs not mentioned in the description and claims shall not appear in the drawings, and vice versa. Reference signs to features shall be consistent throughout the application.
guidance: Use the same reference numerals/letters in drawings, description and claims; do not introduce signs in the drawings that are not referenced in the specification or claims.

name: When to set forth reasons for allowance (37 CFR 1.104(e))
description: If the examiner believes that the record of the prosecution as a whole does not make clear his or her reasons for allowing a claim or claims, the examiner may set forth such reasoning.
guidance: Reasons may be in an Office action rejecting other claims or a separate communication; applicant may comment and the examiner’s failure to respond to comments does not imply anything. The purpose is to improve the quality and reliability of issued patents by providing a clear file history.

name: Required content when reasons are recorded (minimum content)
description: Each statement should include at least (1) the major difference in the claims not found in the prior art of record, and (2) the reasons why that difference is considered to define patentability over the prior art if either of these reasons for allowance is not clear in the record.
guidance: Statements should be accurate, precise, and avoid placing unwarranted interpretations upon claims; avoid stock paragraphs or meaningless boilerplate.

name: Avoid using statements to create unsupported claim narrowing or special definitions
description: It is improper to use a statement of reasons for allowance to attempt to narrow a claim by providing a special definition to a claim limitation which is argued by applicant, but not supported by a special definition in the description.
guidance: Do not provide or imply special definitions or limitations in the statement that are unsupported by the specification; be mindful of possible misinterpretations and legal effects (e.g., Festo implications).

name: Situation B: First-action allowance where reasons are not discussed
description: First action allowance: (1) of a noncontinuing application wherein claims are very close to cited prior art and differences not discussed elsewhere; (2) of a continuing application where reasons for allowance are not apparent from the parent case or preliminary filed matters.
guidance: When allowance occurs at first action or in a continuing app lacking clear parent-record reasons, include a clear statement of reasons of allowance.

name: Situation G: Allowance based on non-obvious claim interpretation
description: Allowance based on a claim interpretation which might not be readily apparent, for example: (1) article claims in which method limitations impart patentability; (2) method claims in which article limitations impart patentability; (3) claim drafted so that 'nonanalogous' art is not applicable; (4) preamble or functional language 'breathes life' into claim.
guidance: Explain the interpretive basis (e.g., interplay of claim types, functional language, nonanalogous art) underlying allowance so the rationale is evident.

name: Situation I: Allowance based on PCT search report references
description: Where the claims are considered patentable over the X and/or Y references cited in a search report of a corresponding PCT application and the reasons for allowance are not apparent from the record.
guidance: If relying on PCT search report references, state why the claims are patentable over those cited X/Y references when the record does not already make this clear.

name: Examples of suitable statement content
description: Illustrative acceptable statements (examples A–G) show the form suitable for reasons for allowance: identify specific claim limitations (e.g., 'inclusion of .03 to .05 percent nickel'), reference applicant affidavits showing unexpected results, reference telephonic interview substance and agreed amendments, compare to specific prior patents, incorporate court decisions, identify agreed claim limitations from interviews or amendments, explain non-obviousness reasoning.
guidance: Use concrete, specific factual and legal bases (limitations, dates, interviews, affidavits, court decisions) rather than vague assertions; provide enough detail to show why the claims are patentable without overclaiming completeness.

name: Examples of unsuitable statement content
description: Statements not suitable include vague technical descriptions without explanation of significance, statements that merely recite that applicant’s remarks or agreements occurred without explaining why persuasive, broad assertions that no prior art corresponds without support, or generic statements 'Claims 1-6 have been allowed because they are believed to be both novel and nonobvious.'
guidance: Do not include matter that does not relate directly to reasons for allowance; avoid statements that fail to make clear the examiner’s substantive basis for allowance.

name: Refer when claimed inventions fall in other technology areas
description: If some of the claimed inventions are classifiable in a technology that the examiner does not examine and the examiner has any doubt as to the proper restriction among the claimed inventions, the application should be referred to an examiner who regularly examines that technology.
guidance: Where an examiner lacks subject-matter jurisdiction or expertise for portions of the claimed inventions and is uncertain about proper restriction, the application must be referred to an examiner in the appropriate technology area for determination.

name: Required bibliographic particulars for register entries (Form P2 / register fields)
description: Register entries require specific bibliographic items: official application no., international classification, full names of applicants/patentees, assignees, inventors, priority claimed, title, addresses, patent of addition number, dates of lodging/acceptance/grant/registration, amendments/rectifications, proceedings and related dates, licences, renewals, restorations and remarks.
guidance: Form P2 / Register fields list numerous numbered items (e.g., 01, 21, 31–33, 43–47, 51, 54, 71–76 etc.) and spaces for recording events, dates, proceedings, appeals and outcomes. Use the provided fields for official records.

name: Minimum bibliographic and technical data elements for patent documentation (Schedule 3)
description: Patent documentation must use specified numerical references and include minimum data elements: document id (10), document number (11), country code (19), domestic filing date (20), application numbers/dates (21–23), convention priority data (30–33), dates of making available/publication (40–47), technical information (50–58) including IPC (51), title (54), keywords (55), list of prior art (56), abstract/claim (57), field of search (58), references to related domestic documents (60–64), and identification of parties (70–76 such as applicant, inventor, grantee, attorney, etc.).
guidance: Schedule 3 provides definitions and notes which indicate which items are minimum data elements for documents and for journal entries. Items marked with * indicate minimum elements for documents; the minimum data requirement may be met by indicating the date of making available to the public for the concerned document.

name: Multiple independent claim sets / alternative claim sets
description: Draft alternative independent claim sets (e.g., apparatus for the whole device, a claim focused on a key component such as the lead–gold zapper, method claims for the component, and a process claim for the overall invention).
guidance: Include claim sets that focus on alternative points of novelty or different categories (apparatus, component, method, process). Pursue such alternatives only when each truly represents independent novelty of commercial significance or when the prior art is unclear or ambiguous. Be mindful of jurisdictional limits on claim numbers; avoid multiple trivial claims. If an examiner objects, push for appropriate scope for the client but recognize there is a point beyond which additional claims are not in the client’s interest.

name: Align claim breadth with inventor’s envisioned scope
description: Before drafting the broadest possible claims, check whether the inventor envisioned a viable scope significantly narrower than the proposed claims.
guidance: If the inventor sees the invention as narrow (e.g., a car with three wheels only), draft claims narrowly to match; if the invention is adaptable, draft broader claims to cover likely adaptations. Help clients recognize potential broader applications they may not foresee.

name: Maximize protection while building fallback positions
description: Be creative to obtain the maximum possible protection, while also building in fallback positions within the claim set.
guidance: Draft broad claims supported by narrower dependent claims or alternative independent claims to provide fallback options during prosecution or litigation.

name: Conciseness of claims and avoidance of undue repetition
description: Claims (and the claim set as a whole) should be concise; avoid unnecessary repetition of wording between claims.
guidance: Some jurisdictions require claims to be 'concise.' Use dependent form to avoid repetition. Avoid verbose phraseology (e.g., unnecessary 'characterized in that ...') and redundant statements when labels and reference numerals already show distinction.

name: Clarity and careful claim word choice
description: Words chosen to describe the invention must capture the invention in its specific form and relevant variants and must convey the intended meaning and scope.
guidance: Claims must be self-contained and their terms should be clear to a person skilled in the art; define unfamiliar or nonstandard uses of terms in the description and ensure the meaning is clear in the claims. Read through each claim for both technical sense and likely interpretation by examiners or courts to avoid ambiguity.

name: Defining terms in the description
description: If terms may be unfamiliar or used in an unfamiliar way, define them in the description so that any new or alternative meaning is clear in the claims.
guidance: Definitions may depart from literal meaning but should not depart from established meaning in the relevant art. Ensure definitions are appropriate to the circumstances and have basis in the disclosure.

name: Same element — same term — same numeral
description: Use consistent terminology and numbering: a single particular element should be named and numbered consistently throughout the application.
guidance: If several synonymous terms exist in practice, cite them on first mention and confirm which will be used. Define abbreviations in full on first instance and use the same abbreviation thereafter. This consistency supports claim self-containment.

name: Avoid relative/adjectival terms without reference
description: Avoid relative adjectives such as 'long', 'short', 'tall', 'wide', 'fast', 'slow', 'perfect' unless framed with reference to another claim element.
guidance: Relative terms are subjective and provide unclear limitations unless defined relative to another element (e.g., 'a first piece of wood; a second piece of wood, wherein the first piece is longer than the second'). If a term has a well-recognized meaning in the art (e.g., 'high-frequency'), it may be acceptable. If no basis exists to define it, consider deleting the term.

name: Careful use of prepositions (especially 'in')
description: Claims employing 'in' (and other prepositions) to define relationships can be unclear whether protection is for a subunit or the whole unit.
guidance: Consider directing claims to 'a unit with (or comprising) a subunit' or to the 'subunit as such' specifying its purpose (e.g., 'cylinder head for a four-stroke engine'). Beware that 'in' claims may unnecessarily limit scope or create ambiguity about whether the improvement or the whole is claimed.

name: Avoid inconsistencies between description and claims
description: Any inconsistency may throw doubt on the extent of protection, rendering claims unclear or unsupported and objectionable.
guidance: Examples include verbal inconsistencies (description limits an element not reflected in claims), omission of apparently essential features from claims, and parts of the description/drawings not covered by claims. Remedies include broadening claims (if supported), limiting claims, or removing excess description (subject to filing-date constraints). Note that in some jurisdictions unclaimed subject matter may be considered dedicated to the public.

name: Jurisdictional differences in clarity practice
description: Practice in enforcing clarity varies across jurisdictions (e.g., US, EPO, Japan).
guidance: US: common indefinite objections for lack of antecedent basis. EPO: independent claims must recite essential technical features; description must disclose technical problem, solution, and advantageous effect. Japan: product-by-process claims are typically unclear unless unavoidable. For functional therapeutic claims, ensure testable criteria or guidance to identify covered conditions where required (e.g., EPO).

name: KISS — keep it short and simple
description: Draft claims and descriptions with clarity and brevity: use plain language, short sentences, and avoid redundant expressions.
guidance: Prefer simpler constructions (example shows removing 'characterized in that ...' and shortening long repetitive clauses). Review whether verbose phrasing is necessary; eliminate needless words to improve clarity.

name: Consider and claim variations / alternative embodiments
description: Constantly think about variations (embodiments) and how competitors might work around the claims; include alternative embodiments in description and claims.
guidance: Draft claims directed to preferred and alternative embodiments (e.g., pencil, crayon, broader 'writing implement'). Include claims to perform same function by alternative means. Be mindful of client budget and the inventor’s actual scope.

name: Avoid unnecessary limitations; delete inessential elements
description: Continuously review claims to delete unnecessary elements and arrive at the essence of the invention.
guidance: One technique: draft a single extended claim including all reasonable elements, then remove inessential elements. Supplement with dependent claims that reintroduce elements. Do not rely on references to the description or drawings (avoid omnibus claims) except where absolutely necessary (rare cases such as peculiar shape or chemical features defined by graphs).

name: Negative limitations and disclaimers rules
description: Negative elements or disclaimers may be used to exclude features (e.g., 'nonwooden') or to exclude prior-art disclosures in some jurisdictions.
guidance: Disclaimers with no basis in the application as filed can only re-establish novelty (not inventive step) and must not extend beyond the content of the application as filed. Negative elements should be used only when adding positive features would not define the protectable subject matter more clearly or would unduly limit the claim. Avoid negative elements when possible for elegance and clarity.

name: Claims must overcome prior art; duty to disclose
description: Prepare claims that overcome any known prior art; otherwise the patent will be invalid.
guidance: Draft claims narrower than known prior art but broader than competing products. In some jurisdictions (e.g., U.S.) there is a duty for inventors and drafters to disclose pertinent prior art; failure to disclose can invalidate the patent and implicate the drafter.

name: Use multiple claim types for the same invention
description: If an invention can be claimed in different forms (e.g., apparatus/system and method), claim it in each appropriate form to obtain broader protection.
guidance: Examples: system claim enumerating components and their functions; method claim enumerating steps. Claims in different categories capture both components and the steps performed by them.

name: Ensure the description supports the claims (support requirement)
description: The description and drawings must provide a basis in the disclosure for the subject matter of every claim.
guidance: Scope of claims will typically not be interpreted broader than the description/drawings. Do not claim what is not supported; you cannot add wholly new material after filing. For broader claims, provide more extensive disclosure; for narrow claims, less may suffice. Examples show claims that must be restricted when the description supports only a specific embodiment. Anticipate narrower claim elements you may later need and embed support in the description from the outset.

name: Unity of invention / restriction requirement
description: A patent application must relate to one invention only or to a group of inventions so linked as to form a single general inventive concept.
guidance: Where multiple inventions are present, they may give rise to multiple independent claims in the same or different categories; be aware of restriction/Unity objections (e.g., U.S. restriction requirement) and structure applications accordingly.

name: CBM eligibility statutory two-prong
description: The patent must: (1) claim a method or apparatus for performing data processing or other operations used in the practice, administration, or management of a financial product or service; and (2) not claim a technological invention. (AIA § 18; 37 C.F.R. § 42.301(a)).
guidance: CBM review differs from IPR/PGR in that non-prior-art challenges (e.g., § 101 and § 112) are available in CBM and estoppel is narrower. Both prongs must be satisfied for CBM institution.

name: Financial product or service prong — focus on claims
description: PTAB increasingly requires that the financial aspect be shown in the claims rather than relying on the specification alone; claim language must demonstrate a link to financial activity.
guidance: Recent denials (e.g., CoreLogic, AT&T Mobility) found that specification examples of billing or revenue models were insufficient absent claim language. Conversely, dependent claim recitations tied to revenue (e.g., 'advertising data') have supported eligibility (iBiquity). When drafting or petitioning, emphasize claim elements that manifest financial activity.

name: Specification vs. claim evidence — when the specification can suffice
description: Although the PTAB has trended toward requiring claim language, there are cases where the specification's teaching that an element is used to generate revenue can establish CBM-eligibility (e.g., iBiquity relied on specification teaching that 'advertising data is used to generate revenue').
guidance: Because panels are inconsistent, cite both claims and specification where possible; dependent claims that tie generic elements to financial uses strengthen CBM eligibility arguments.

name: Could be used for a financial service vs specifically intended for such use
description: The PTAB distinguishes inventions that merely could be used for financial products/services from inventions specifically intended for financial use.
guidance: Decisions (e.g., ServiceNow, Par Pharmaceutical) show that mere potential for financial use (e.g., ATM example) is insufficient absent claim-specific limitation or specification support establishing financial purpose or monetary consideration.

name: No one-size-fits-all; panel inconsistency
description: PTAB panels have reached divergent outcomes on similar facts; some panels infer financial status from specification where unequivocal, others require claims to show financial nature.
guidance: Prepare for inconsistent panel treatment (see Motorola Mobility split panel outcomes); build multiple lines of support (claim language, dependent claims, specification, prosecution history) when arguing CBM eligibility.

name: CBM practical recommendation — heightened scrutiny requires careful consideration
description: Because the PTAB has increased reliance on the financial prong as a basis to deny CBM petitions, the financial aspect must be given careful consideration when evaluating a patent’s eligibility for CBM review.
guidance: When assessing petitions or preparing patents, evaluate whether claim language, dependent claims, or specification examples unmistakably connect the invention to a financial product/service; absent that, institution risk is elevated.

name: §101 Alice framework — look at the claim as a whole
description: Apply the two-step Alice test: (1) whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception (e.g., abstract idea, natural phenomenon), and (2) if so, whether the claim as a whole is significantly more than that exception. The Federal Circuit emphasizes examining the claim as a whole and its purpose.
guidance: Rapid Litigation, Enfish, and BASCOM emphasize that simply identifying a judicial exception is insufficient; consider whether the claim uses a phenomenon to attain a distinct end or transforms it into an inventive application. Arguments should treat the claim holistically, including purpose and ordered combination of elements.

name: Enfish guidance for computer-related claims
description: For computer-related patents, ask whether claims are directed to an improvement to computer functionality rather than an abstract idea.
guidance: Enfish supports finding eligibility where claims improve computer functionality (example: self-referential table). The PTAB has cited Enfish but its impact has been limited and fact-dependent; compare claim features to Enfish's improvement characteristics when making or opposing §101 arguments.

name: BASCOM guidance — ordered combination can confer eligibility
description: Even if individual elements are conventional, an inventive ordered combination of elements may render the claim 'significantly more' than an abstract idea.
guidance: BASCOM remanded where the lower tribunal failed to explain why the ordered combination was conventional. In briefing, address whether the combination of conventional components yields a non-conventional whole.

name: Burden and completeness of petitioner’s §101 analysis at PTAB
description: The petitioner must analyze claims as a whole and provide sufficient proof; incomplete analyses or failure of proof can lead to denial of institution under §101 (e.g., Walgreen denial where petitioner’s analysis was incomplete).
guidance: Ensure petitioners fully address each claim element, the 'select code' or other specifics, and do not rely on selective snippets of the specification. Anticipate PTAB scrutiny on completeness.

name: Statement of rejection requirements (written description)
description: When rejecting a claim for lack of written description, the examiner must set forth express findings of fact which support the conclusion.
guidance: Findings should (A) identify the claim limitation(s) at issue; and (B) establish a prima facie case by providing reasons why a person skilled in the art at the time of filing would not have recognized that the inventor was in possession of the invention as claimed in view of the disclosure. A general allegation of 'unpredictability in the art' is not sufficient. A simple statement pointing out where support is not apparent may suffice for new or amended claims where support is not obvious. When appropriate, suggest claim amendments that can be supported, mindful of the prohibition against adding new matter. See MPEP § 2163.04 and Hyatt v. Dudas.

name: Addition of a generic claim (genus/species support)
description: A claimed genus may be supported by a sufficient description of a representative number of species; one species may suffice only when the disclosure indicates the patentee has invented species sufficient to constitute the genus or where the species is representative and would lead skilled artisans to the genus.
guidance: Assess variation within the genus and whether a sufficient variety of species are described to reflect that variation. A single species is inadequate when ordinary artisans could not predict operability of other species. Conversely, in some situations (e.g., In re Rasmussen, In re Herschler, In re Smythe) disclosure of one species or functional recitation may sufficiently support a genus. Use case law (Enzo Biochem, In re Curtis, Tronzo v. Biomet, In re Gosteli) to guide the analysis.

name: Narrowing or subgeneric claim
description: Introducing claim changes that narrow claims by adding elements or limitations not supported by the as-filed disclosure violates the written description requirement.
guidance: A 'laundry list' of possibilities does not constitute written description of every species (Fujikawa v. Wattanasin). It may be improper to claim a subgenus that was not reasonably communicated by the original disclosure (In re Lukach). Each case depends on whether the original disclosure would reasonably convey the subgenus to those skilled in the art (In re Wilder).

name: Range limitations
description: When changing numerical range limitations, the analysis must consider which ranges one skilled in the art would consider inherently supported by the original disclosure.
guidance: Example: original ranges of 25%-60% with specific examples of 36% and 50% did not support a new claim to 'at least 35%' because it read on embodiments outside the disclosed 25%-60% range, but 'between 35% and 60%' did meet the requirement (In re Wertheim). Consider whether the specification clearly discloses that a claimant considered a numeric ratio to be part of the invention (Purdue Pharma v. Faulding) and whether combinations of ranges are adequately described (Union Oil v. Atlantic Richfield).

name: Relationship of written description requirement to new matter (statutory prohibitions)
description: If an applicant amends or attempts to amend the abstract, specification or drawings to add content not described in the application as filed, an issue of new matter arises. Two statutory provisions prohibit introduction of new matter: 35 U.S.C. 132 (No amendment shall introduce new matter) and 35 U.S.C. 251 (No new matter in reissue).
guidance: Treat added subject matter in any part of the application consistently: information in specification, claims, or drawings as filed can be added to other parts without introducing new matter, but adding new content where none existed is prohibited. See MPEP § 2163.06.

name: Treatment of new matter (examiners' actions)
description: If new subject matter is added to the disclosure, the examiner should object to the introduction of new matter under 35 U.S.C. 132 or 251 as appropriate, and require applicant to cancel the new matter. If new matter is added to the claims, the examiner should reject the claims under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph - written description requirement.
guidance: Even if claims are not directly amended, an amendment to the specification that adds material affecting claim limitations should trigger a 112, first paragraph rejection. The examiner should still consider added claim matter in prior art rejections because a new matter rejection may be overcome by the applicant.

name: Opinions must be supported by underlying facts and data; patent-law opinions not admissible
description: Expert opinions must be supported by sufficient facts and data and must be the product of reliable principles and methods; testimony on U.S. patent law itself is not admissible from experts.
guidance: Declarations should tie opinions explicitly to factual bases and technical data. Parties should avoid submitting expert opinions that purport to interpret or state conclusions of law about claim construction or patentability; legal conclusions are for the Board, not the expert.

name: Relevance / scope of expert’s experience must be commensurate with testimony
description: An expert’s qualifications must be commensurate with the scope of the testimony offered; experience in a different field may be challenged as not qualifying the witness for the subject matter.
guidance: If an expert's background is in a different but arguably related field, parties should submit supplemental information establishing relevance (and be prepared for the Board to allow discovery so the opponent can challenge it). Consider tailoring testimony to the expert's demonstrable areas of competence and clearly explain how experience transfers to the claimed technology.

name: Enabling disclosure requirement
description: The information made available must be such that if the person skilled in the art were to write down that information, they would have drafted a clear and unambiguous description of the claimed invention.
guidance: An enabling disclosure makes available the necessary information to practise the invention. The disclosure must permit the skilled person to operate the invention; merely mentioning an idea without enabling details may not anticipate. See also requirements for implicit/inherent disclosure and reverse engineering analysis.

name: Identifying the inventive concept (step 2)
description: The inventive concept comprises the features of the claim that appear to be inventive over the common general knowledge and/or which the applicant appears to consider inventive; it is a separate exercise from claim construction.
guidance: Purposive construction determines essential elements; inventive concept may include a combination of essential elements but need not include all. Identification should be based on reading the specification as a whole from the POSITA perspective in light of CGK.

name: Identifying differences between inventive concept and state of the art (step 3)
description: Compare the inventive concept to the state of the art to determine whether an equivalent or similar solution was known at the claim date; the state of the art is information available to the POSITA, generally identified by specific prior art documents found in a reasonable and diligent search.
guidance: If there is no difference, the claim is likely anticipated or obvious. If the prior art is not enabling, the claim may not be anticipated but could still be obvious. Multiple documents may need to be combined to arrive at the inventive concept; differences must be assessed for obviousness.

name: Use of live demonstrations and expert deputations
description: Support claims with deputations and live observations of locomotives in operation to give committees direct evidence of capability.
guidance: Promoters repeatedly 'proceeded to Killingworth' to 'witness the performances of his locomotive engines,' reporting speeds and loads (e.g., 'a train... 54 tons... average rate about 7 miles an hour'). Demonstrations and eyewitness reports helped persuade skeptical committees.

name: Statutory double patenting (35 U.S.C. § 101) — same invention
description: Based on 35 U.S.C. § 101 — an applicant (or assignee) is prohibited from obtaining two patents for the same invention.
guidance: Reliable test: Is there an embodiment that falls within the scope of one claim, but not the other? Could one claim be literally infringed without literally infringing the other claim? If the answer is 'yes' to either question, then there is no basis for a statutory double patenting rejection. Statutory (35 U.S.C. 101) double patenting requires that the examined claim and the claim of the potentially conflicting patent/application exactly match in scope. Note: A terminal disclaimer (TD) will NOT overcome a 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection.

name: Nonstatutory double patenting (obviousness-type, ODP)
description: A judicially created doctrine prohibiting issuance of a patent on an invention that is an obvious variation of an invention for which the applicant (or assignee) already has a patent (unless conditions such as a terminal disclaimer are met).
guidance: Treat ODP analogously to a 35 U.S.C. § 103 analysis: determine the scope and content of the 'Prior Art', ascertain the differences between the 'Prior Art' and the claim at issue, resolve the level of ordinary skill in the art, and evaluate evidence of secondary considerations. Nonstatutory DP is NOT a prior art rejection — the patent or co-pending application used in the analysis does not need to qualify as prior art, but any secondary references used in the obviousness analysis should qualify as prior art within the meaning of 35 U.S.C. § 102.

name: Focus on the claims — claims are primary for DP analysis
description: The claims of the potentially conflicting patent or application versus the examined claims are the basis for consideration in double patenting analysis.
guidance: Use of the specification of the potentially conflicting patent or application is generally prohibited except for limited exceptions (e.g., claim term definitions, support). The examiner should compare claim scopes first and resort to specification only where permitted.

name: Proper/limited uses of specification (MPEP § 804 II(b)(1))
description: Specification can be used in certain circumstances to aid DP analysis.
guidance: Permitted uses include: using the specification as a dictionary for claim terminology; using portions of the disclosure which provide support for the claims in the potentially conflicting patent or application to determine whether claim sets represent an obvious variation. See MPEP 804 II(b)(1) for scope of allowable uses.

name: Withdrawn claims in copending cases — when to consider
description: Withdrawn claims in copending applications have specific treatment in provisional NSDP analyses.
guidance: Withdrawn claims in a reference (copending) application must be considered in a provisional nonstatutory double patenting (NSDP) analysis of elected claims in an application under examination. However, withdrawn claims in the case under examination should never be considered in a NSDP rejection of that case.

name: A 35 U.S.C. § 101 DP rejection requires exact same scope
description: For a statutory double patenting rejection under 35 U.S.C. § 101, the two claims must exactly match in scope.
guidance: If the examined claim and the claim of the potentially conflicting patent/application do not exactly match in scope, do not make a statutory (35 U.S.C. 101) double patenting rejection; perform further analysis for possible nonstatutory double patenting instead.

name: Typical ways to overcome nonstatutory DP rejections
description: Available applicant responses to a provisional/proper NSDP rejection.
guidance: Options include: amend claims to encompass non-obvious subject matter; provide persuasive arguments why the current claims are not obvious variants over the co-pending application/patent claims; file an appropriate terminal disclaimer pursuant to 35 U.S.C. § 253 (to disclaim the terminal portion of a patent term); or abandon one of the cases.

name: Two terminal disclaimers needed for same-day filings
description: When two or more applications are filed on the same day and claim obvious variations of each other, TD treatment differs from ordinary earlier/later rules.
guidance: To overcome provisional NSDP rejections when both applications are filed on the same day, the provisional NSDP rejection made in each application should be maintained until a showing is made that the claims are patentably distinct or a terminal disclaimer is filed in both applications. See MPEP 1490 and the 'n-1' rule discussion; earlier-filed determination takes into account certain benefit claims (35 U.S.C. 120, 121, 365(c)) but not provisional or foreign priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) / 119(a).

name: MPEP/Basell: use of specifications to interpret claims and determine obvious variants
description: The specification of the earlier (or later) patent/application may be used to learn the meaning of terms, interpret the coverage of a claim, and determine whether claims are obvious variants (In re Basell; MPEP § 804 II(B)(1)).
guidance: Even if later claims are narrower species of earlier claims, if the species were disclosed in the earlier specification such that the species fall within the meaning of the earlier claims, a nonstatutory DP rejection can be proper. Use specifications only for permitted purposes (term meaning, claim coverage, support for obvious_variation analysis).

name: Specification disclosure of utility can create ODP (Sun Pharmaceutical v. Eli Lilly)
description: A specification that discloses an unclaimed use of a compound can render later claims to that use invalid for obviousness-type double patenting.
guidance: Example: Earlier patent disclosed using gemcitabine to fight cancer (but did not claim it); later patent claimed methods of using gemcitabine to treat cancer — later claims were held invalid for ODP because the later claims simply claimed a use disclosed in the earlier specification.

name: ODP-Anticipation: examined claim fully encompassed by potentially conflicting claim
description: A category of nonstatutory double patenting where the examined claim is generic to (fully encompassed by) a claim in the potentially conflicting patent or application.
guidance: When the examined claims are fully encompassed by a claim in the potentially conflicting patent/application, an ODP-anticipation rejection is appropriate and no Graham v. Deere (full obviousness) analysis is needed. Visualize via claim-inclusion Venn diagram: if the examined claim lies entirely within the scope of the conflicting claim, treat as anticipation for ODP purposes.

name: Field-of-use / technological environment limitations often non-meaningful
description: Many field of use limitations (and other non-meaningful claim limitations) are identifiable by an absence of integration into the claim as a whole and therefore do not add an inventive concept to the claims.
guidance: Examples the courts have described as mere field-of-use/technological-environment limitations: limiting drug administration to a particular patient population (Mayo v. Prometheus); identifying participants as commodity providers/consumers (Bilski); narrowing a formula to a particular object (Flook); requiring execution in a computer environment or over the Internet (FairWarning; Intellectual Ventures; Ultramercial; buySAFE); limiting abstract ideas to power-grid data (Electric Power). Examiners should consider these limitations interchangeable with “technological environment” and consider overlap with insignificant extra-solution activity (see MPEP § 2106.05(g)). When a limitation merely links use of a judicial exception to a technology/field, explain why it does not meaningfully limit the claim (e.g., employing well-known computer functions in a particular environment does not add significantly more).

name: Consider overlap with insignificant extra-solution activity
description: A data-gathering step limited to a particular data source or type may be both insignificant extra-solution activity and a field-of-use limitation and thus not meaningfully limit a judicial exception.
guidance: Examples include limiting an abstract idea to the Internet or to power-grid data. Examiners should carefully consider each claim on its own merits and evaluate all relevant Step 2B considerations before making a determination on this consideration.

name: Eligibility is self-evident when claim does not tie up judicial exceptions
description: A claim may bypass the full analysis if, viewed as a whole, it clearly does not seek to tie up any judicial exception such that others cannot practice it.
guidance: Claims that clearly improve technology or computer functionality (Enfish, McRO) or that clearly do not attempt to tie up a nature-based product may qualify. Only use streamlined analysis when eligibility is clear; otherwise use full Alice/Mayo analysis.

name: Clear improvement to technology or computer functionality means not abstract
description: Claims directed to clear improvements in technology or to computer functionality may not be abstract and thus may not require full eligibility analysis.
guidance: Court examples: Enfish (self-referential table) and McRO (automatic lip synchronization). If the claim clearly improves computer-related technology or other technologies/technological processes, its eligibility may be self-evident. But if it’s a close call (e.g., claims describing filtering content in BASCOM), perform the full Step 2B analysis to determine whether claims amount to significantly more.

name: Prima facie case requirement when making an eligibility rejection
description: If more likely than not that a claim fails both criteria for eligibility (Step 1: NO and/or Step 2B: NO), examiners should formulate an appropriate rejection and set forth a prima facie case of ineligibility under substantive law.
guidance: Prima facie is a procedural tool allocating burdens between examiner and applicant: initial burden on examiner to clearly and specifically explain why a claim is ineligible so applicant has sufficient notice to respond effectively.

name: When making a §101 rejection, identify and explain why claim is not within a statutory category (Step 1)
description: If claim is determined not to fall within a statutory category, the rejection should explain why the claim is not directed to one of the four statutory categories of invention.
guidance: See MPEP § 706.03(a) for making such rejections and MPEP § 2106.03 for Step 1 discussion. The Office action must provide a sufficiently clear and specific explanation to enable effective applicant response.

name: When making a Step 2A rejection, identify and explain the judicial exception recited in the claim
description: A subject matter eligibility rejection should point to the specific claim limitations that recite or describe the judicial exception and explain why those limitations set forth an exception (e.g., an abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon, or product of nature).
guidance: If claim describes but does not expressly set forth the exception, explain what subject matter is described and why it is an exception. When identifying an abstract idea, link it to concepts courts have identified as abstract (see MPEP §2106.04(a)(2)). Citing appropriate case law is a best practice. Avoid going beyond concepts similar to those courts identified and avoid non-precedential decisions unless facts match. Sample explanations provided: "The claim recites the steps of sorting information by X, which is an abstract idea similar to..." For laws of nature/natural phenomena: explain with reasoned rationale why the recited correlation or phenomenon is a law of nature or natural phenomenon. For products of nature: explain why the claimed product lacks markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart and use the markedly-different-characteristics analysis (MPEP §2106.04(b)/(c)).

name: When making a Step 2B rejection, identify additional claim elements and explain why they do not add significantly more
description: After identifying the judicial exception, point out additional elements beyond the exception and explain why those elements, individually and as a combination, do not result in the claim as a whole amounting to significantly more than the judicial exception.
guidance: Address the combination of additional elements because a new combination of known steps may be patent eligible (Diamond v. Diehr). Explain why particular claim elements are well-understood, routine, conventional activities in the relevant art; provide a reasoned explanation supporting that conclusion. See MPEP §2106.05 for considerations courts have found to qualify or not qualify as significantly more. If additional elements provide an inventive concept, explain why they add a meaningful limitation.

name: Apply analysis on a claim-by-claim basis
description: Evaluate eligibility on each claim separately because dependent claims may add limitations that render them eligible even if the independent claim is ineligible.
guidance: Claims do not automatically rise or fall with similar claims in an application; consider the particular elements recited in each claim when evaluating eligibility.

name: Explain why additional elements are well-understood, routine, conventional when asserted
description: When concluding that particular claim limitations are well understood, routine, conventional activities, the rejection should explain why the courts or those in the relevant field would recognize those elements as such.
guidance: Provide a reasoned explanation that supports the conclusion; do not merely assert routine/conventional status without evidentiary or reasoned support. This explanation applies both to individual elements and to their combination when assessing whether claims amount to significantly more.

name: Patent Infringement (general definition and role of claims)
description: A patent is infringed if someone makes, uses, offers to sell, sells, or imports what is covered by the patent, without permission. To figure out whether or not this patent has been infringed, you must rely on the patent claims. The claims define what the invention is.
guidance: ‘‘Without permission’’ means without the patent owner’s permission or without other legal authority. The claims are the numbered paragraphs at the end of the patent and often are highly technical; the judge will tell you the proper meaning of the claim language, and it is your duty as jurors to accept that meaning. Claims are like a deed (they define the boundaries of property) or a recipe (apparatus claims = ingredients; method claims = instructions). According to the law, only the claims can be infringed; other parts of the patent application, such as the written description or drawings, are not bases for judging infringement. Each numbered claim must be considered one at a time; if even one claim is infringed, you must find in favor of the plaintiff.

name: Novelty (Newness / Prior Art)
description: Newness means that the invention, as it is, with all of its parts, cannot be found in any single piece of prior art. Prior art includes things, prior to the invention, that were publicly known, used in a publicly accessible way in this country, or patented or described in a publication in any country.
guidance: If a specific device already exists with all of the same parts as the patented invention, then the patent is not valid. Prior art is, by definition, publicly available; an inventor's ignorance of the prior art is not an excuse. For each numbered claim you must decide: Is the patent claim invalid because the invention was not new? If the claim's invention existed with all features in a single piece of prior art, find the claim invalid; otherwise it passes the newness test.

name: Obviousness (Non-obviousness standard and factors)
description: An invention is unpatentable if it would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made. A person of ordinary skill in the art is a hypothetical person who knows the prior art, has the relevant training in the field, and is not a genius.
guidance: To decide obviousness, jurors should: (1) consider the prior art and what was done before the invention; (2) identify similarities and differences between each claim and the prior art; and (3) describe the level of ordinary skill in the art at the time. Additional secondary considerations that tend to show non-obviousness include: commercial success of the invention; meeting a long-felt need; others' failed attempts to solve the problem; evidence that others took licenses and paid royalties; whereas contemporaneous independent inventions by others tend to support obviousness.

name: Principle No. 3 – Parties should actively and cooperatively work to narrow asserted claims, representative products, and prior art references in good faith and efficiently.
description: Early narrowing conserves resources and allows the court and parties to focus on the most significant disputes.

name: Best Practice 6 – The court should encourage the patent holder to identify an initial set of representative claims for discovery and claim construction purposes no later than the case management conference.
description: Parties should propose limits on number of representative claims, and the court and parties should decide on a process and timeframe to reach a final limit. Parties should narrow asserted claims during discovery and select final claims for trial at least 30 days prior to service of any expert report.

name: Best Practice 26 – Parties should advise the court, no later than the case management conference, whether a focused claim construction proceeding followed by a limited summary judgment motion is appropriate.
description: Consider staging claim construction with narrow issues followed by targeted summary judgment to resolve dispositive matters early.

name: Best Practice 37 – The parties should prioritize by their relative importance the claim terms to be construed.
description: Prioritizing terms helps the court and parties focus resources on the most significant claim construction disputes.

name: Best Practice 39 – If there are a large number of terms to be construed, the court should organize Markman presentations by term, not by parties.
description: Organizing by term reduces redundancy and improves clarity in claim construction proceedings.

name: Best Practice 63 – The jury instructions should identify the burden of proof required to make a showing of obviousness.
description: Where the court submits obviousness to the jury, the instructions may state that the alleged infringer must prove by clear and convincing evidence that the claimed invention was obvious.

name: Best Practice 64 – The jury instructions should describe the relevant factors involved in the obviousness determination in some detail depending upon nature and scope of disputes between parties.
description: Only disputed factual issues need instruction; describe relevant factors (e.g., level of ordinary skill, differences between claimed invention and prior art) in adequate detail to allow jurors to appreciate their import.

name: Best Practice 65 – Jury instructions should specifically identify each prior art reference or combination being asserted to invalidate each claim under obviousness and the details of the dispute.
description: To the extent possible, submit only a limited number of asserted combinations to the jury and provide guidance on what constitutes pertinent or analogous art; highlight preliminary factual disputes (e.g., availability dates) that must be resolved first.

name: Rule 1.6 Confidentiality of Information
description: A practitioner shall not reveal information relating to the representation of a client unless the client gives informed consent, disclosure is impliedly authorized to carry out the representation, or the disclosure is permitted by specified exceptions. A practitioner may reveal information to the extent reasonably necessary to: (1) prevent reasonably certain death or substantial bodily harm; (2) prevent the client from committing a crime/fraud reasonably certain to result in substantial injury to another and in furtherance of which client used practitioner’s services; (3) prevent, mitigate or rectify substantial injury to another caused by client’s crime/fraud or inequitable conduct before the Office; (4) secure legal advice about compliance with the Rules; (5) establish a claim or defense on behalf of the practitioner in a controversy with the client or respond to allegations concerning the practitioner’s representation; or (6) comply with law or court order. A practitioner shall disclose to the Office information necessary to comply with applicable duty of disclosure provisions.
guidance: Balances client confidentiality with narrow exceptions for preventing serious harm, fraud/inequitable conduct (including before the Office), compliance advice, self-defense, and legal compulsion; includes specific duty-to-Office disclosure in patent prosecution contexts.

name: Rule 1.7 Conflict of Interest: Current Clients
description: A practitioner shall not represent a client if the representation involves a concurrent conflict of interest, which exists if (1) representation of one client will be directly adverse to another, or (2) there is a significant risk that representation will be materially limited by responsibilities to another client, former client, third person, or by a personal interest. Notwithstanding this, representation is permitted if the practitioner reasonably believes they can provide competent/diligent representation to each affected client; the representation is not prohibited by law; it does not involve asserting claims by one client against another in the same litigation or proceeding before a tribunal; and each affected client gives informed consent, confirmed in writing.
guidance: Requires objective assessment of significant risk of material limitation and written informed consent when waiving conflicts; prohibits certain adverse-claim scenarios even with consent.

name: Rule 1.8 Conflict of Interest: Specific Rules
description: Specific prohibitions and requirements when practitioners interact with clients in transactional contexts: (a) business transactions with clients or acquiring adverse pecuniary interests require fairness, full written disclosure, advising client in writing of seeking independent counsel, and client’s informed written consent; (b) cannot use information relating to representation to client’s disadvantage without informed consent except as permitted; (c) cannot solicit substantial gifts from clients except to related persons; (d) cannot make literary or media-rights agreements prior to conclusion of representation; (e) limitations on providing financial assistance to clients with exceptions (advancing costs, representing indigent clients, advancing costs for Office proceedings with client ultimately liable, advancing fees to prevent abandonment due to practitioner error); (f) accepting compensation from third parties requires client informed consent, no interference with independence, and protection of client information; (g) aggregate settlements require each client’s informed written consent and disclosure of claims/participation; (h)-(k) other prohibitions apply (e.g., prospective limitation of malpractice liability requires independent representation).
guidance: Detailed requirements protect clients from unfair transactions, preserve independence of judgment, regulate financial assistance and fee arrangements, and require written informed consents and disclosures in many contexts; includes patent-specific allowances (e.g., taking interest in patent/application as part of fee).

name: Rule 8.4 Misconduct
description: It is professional misconduct for a practitioner to: (a) violate or attempt to violate the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct or knowingly assist/induce another to do so; (b) commit a criminal act that reflects adversely on honesty, trustworthiness or fitness; (c) engage in dishonesty, fraud, deceit or misrepresentation; (d) engage in conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice; (e) state or imply an ability to improperly influence a government agency or official or to achieve results by means that violate the Rules or law; (f) knowingly assist a judge or judicial officer in conduct violating rules or law; (g) knowingly assist an officer or employee of the Office in conduct violating rules or law; (h) be publicly disciplined on ethical/professional misconduct grounds by a duly constituted authority; or (i) engage in other conduct that adversely reflects on fitness to practice before the Office.
guidance: Broadly enumerates types of misconduct that can trigger discipline, including conviction, fraud, deceit, improper influence claims, assisting officials to violate rules, public discipline elsewhere, and other adverse conduct.

name: Rationale A: Combining Prior Art Elements According to Known Methods
description: Applies when the examiner identifies separate elements of the claim across different prior art references and argues that combining them would yield predictable results.
guidance: The examiner must show each claimed element existed in the prior art, that the combination would have been recognized by a skilled artisan as likely to succeed, and that the result is no more than the sum of individual parts. Vulnerability: if the combination produces a synergistic or unexpected effect beyond the individual components, Rationale A weakens. Challenge whether the examiner explained why a PHOSITA would assemble these specific parts rather than merely locating them in the prior art.

name: Rationale G: Teaching, Suggestion, or Motivation in the Prior Art (TSM)
description: Preserves the classic TSM approach as one valid rationale: examiner relies on an explicit teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art to combine references.
guidance: Verify the cited teaching supports the specific combination, not just generally invites exploration. A generic ‘alternative approaches include…’ is insufficient unless it reasonably leads a PHOSITA toward the claimed invention with a reasonable expectation of success.

name: Examiner’s Burden / Evidentiary Standards for a Prima Facie Case
description: MPEP 2143 requires four elements: (1) factual finding mapping each claim element to prior art; (2) identification of the specific MPEP 2143 rationale (A–G); (3) explanation of why a PHOSITA would be motivated to arrive at the claimed combination; and (4) articulation of why the result would have been predictable.
guidance: The examiner need only show a PHOSITA could have made the combination with a reasonable expectation of success, not that they would have—but ‘could have’ still requires evidence and reasoning. Conclusory 'it would have been obvious' statements are legally deficient. Look to Federal Circuit decisions (e.g., In re Van Os) vacating findings lacking rational underpinning.

name: Avoiding Hindsight Bias (Examiner Obligation)
description: The MPEP warns against hindsight reconstruction; examiners must not use the applicant’s disclosure as a roadmap or selectively read prior art to map exactly to the claim.
guidance: Signs of hindsight include combining disparate fields without justification, relying on the applicant’s specification to establish motivation, or selectively picking narrow passages that only make sense given knowledge of the invention. Challenge rejections by reframing what a PHOSITA would have known and done at the time of invention.

name: Claim Drafting Strategies to Resist §103 Challenges
description: Claim-drafting techniques that make prior-art mapping harder: include limitations reflecting non‑obvious structural/functional relationships, use dependent claims to capture unexpected synergies, and consider means‑plus‑function (§112(f)) to tie claim scope to disclosed structure.
guidance: Claims that assert specific interactions (not mere A combined with B) force examiners to find both the elements and their claimed interaction. Dependent claims preserve fallback positions that are progressively harder to reject. Means‑plus‑function can narrow the prior-art comparison by interpretation tied to the specification’s disclosed structure.

name: Use of Case Law to Shape Arguments Against Specific Rationales
description: Leverage controlling and persuasive Federal Circuit decisions (e.g., KSR, Ortho‑McNeil, Perfect Web, Arendi, Wyers, In re Kubin, In re Van Os) to show limits of particular rationales or to emphasize predictability requirements in certain arts.
guidance: Cite Ortho‑McNeil to argue higher bars for 'obvious to try' in unpredictable arts; cite Arendi when an examiner relies on common sense to supply missing claim elements; cite In re Kubin to rebut or contextualize biotech obviousness; use KSR to insist on articulated reasoning with rational underpinning. Tailor case law to the rationale invoked.

name: Strategic Positioning Across Multiple Patent Families / Portfolio-Level Considerations
description: Align prosecution tactics with business objectives across patent families: use portfolio analysis to prioritize where to invest in declarations, interviews, or appeals versus where to maintain broader claims and pursue continuation practice.
guidance: Use limited resources selectively: complex §103 defenses (expensive declarations, experiments) may be warranted for high-value assets, while lower-value families might accept narrower claims or quicker compromises. Portfolio alignment helps determine when to fight a difficult rationale and when to negotiate scope.

name: Divisional application properness
description: Where an application (the “original application”) describes more than one invention, an applicant may file a divisional application to protect described inventions other than the one invention only to which the original application’s claims were directed or, as the case may be, to which the original application’s claims were limited.
guidance: Compare the content of the specification and drawings of the purported divisional to the parent to determine if the divisional's claims are directed to a different invention and whether the divisional was filed with new matter. If claims are not directed to a different invention than the parent, the later-filed application is not a proper divisional under section 36. If a divisional has a presentation date after Oct 30, 2019 and contains new matter relative to its parent, it is defective under sections 91 or 155.7 of the Patent Rules. If a divisional was 'directed by the Patent Office', double-patenting does not apply between the divisional and parent/siblings. Amendments introducing new matter are governed by subsection 38.2(3.1) of the Patent Act or 155.6 of the Patent Rules.

name: Subject-matter must fall within statutory categories
description: The claimed subject-matter of a computer-implemented invention must fall within one of the five categories in the section 2 definition of 'invention': art, process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter.
guidance: Guidance refines how those five categories apply to computer-implemented inventions (e.g., methods as art; devices as machines; physical memory storing instructions as manufacture). Certain items (computer programs per se, data structures, computer-generated signals) may not be statutory. See related chapters for finer distinctions.

name: Machine/device criterion: must provide a technological solution (contributed practical form)
description: For a claim to a device to be patentable it must define at least one statutory element that forms part of the contribution. The device itself must be a contributed practical form providing a novel and unobvious technological solution to a technological problem.
guidance: Determination can be by assessing the device itself or indirectly by reference to the method implemented. A machine adapted to implement a patentable method is necessarily a solution to a practical problem. The technological solution need not be an improvement to the computer as a general purpose device; adapting a general purpose device to act as a special purpose device suffices. Examples include known hardware controlled by new software or new arrangements of known hardware.

name: Objecting to claims defined by discrete non-statutory features
description: Where a device does not provide a solution to a technological problem, and is further defined in terms of discrete non-statutory features, the claim would be objected to on the ground that it does not define a statutory 'invention' within section 2 of the Patent Act.
guidance: A computer cannot be patentably distinguished from other computers simply on the basis of stored information; stored information does not cause the computer to become a new and unobvious solution to a practical problem.

name: Claims must include a statutory contribution
description: A patentable claim must include a statutory contribution. For a claim directed to a computer, it must be determined whether the device itself is part of the contribution — i.e., whether the computer itself may be considered novel and inventive.
guidance: Identify the essential elements of the device that, as a set, provide a technological solution to a technological problem. That set must be novel and inventive. If a machine implements a non-statutory method, inventive ingenuity associated with the method does not provide the inventive step necessary for the machine; the inventive effort must relate to adapting the machine to implement the method.

name: Computer program per se and when it bestows patentability
description: A computer program is not, by itself, statutory subject-matter. However, if the result of running the program on a computer provides a novel and inventive technological solution to a technological problem, then the program is viewed as modifying the technological nature of the computer as a whole.
guidance: If the program expresses a statutory method that is novel and inventive, the programmed computer would be patentable. If the program expresses a non-statutory method, the non-statutory method itself is not a patentable contribution, regardless of novelty. Patentability of computer claims in such cases will depend on additional elements defining how the computer is adapted to implement the method.

name: Utility: usefulness, demonstrable or by sound prediction, operable and reproducible
description: An invention must be useful in the sense of doing whatever was promised by the inventors. The utility of the claimed subject-matter must be established by demonstration or sound prediction, and must be operable to produce the promised result in a manner that is controllable and reproducible.
guidance: Computers are generally capable of reproducibly performing operations, but the invention as a whole may require other elements for proper operation. If operator judgement/interpretative reasoning is implicated in proper operation, reproducibility may not be satisfied. Where an operator's input is required but involves no judgement, reproducibility is not affected. When claiming computer-implemented methods, it must be unambiguously clear which steps are carried out on/by a computer.

name: Sufficiency: written description and enablement standards
description: The specification must correctly and fully describe the invention (written description) and provide any teachings necessary to allow a person skilled in the art to operate the claimed invention (enablement).
guidance: A skilled person must understand, from the specification alone and common general knowledge, what the invention is, what it does, and how to make it work. Level of description depends on facts: known elements can be merely identified; novel applications of hardware/software require greater detail. Where claimed as means-plus-function, the nature and arrangement of the means must be clear. Limited description may indicate the applicant believes suitable means are readily apparent.

name: Examples as guidance for contribution/novelty assessment
description: Worked examples illustrate application of contribution analysis, showing how to treat information-only claims, storage-media claims, computer-implemented methods, systems, and claims that amount to mental methods.
guidance: Examples demonstrate: (a) information (atomic coordinates) as non-statutory by form; (b) storage medium statutory in form but lacking contribution if medium known; (c) methods that implement technological steps may be statutory but require inventive step over prior art; (d) systems/machines specifically adapted to perform patentable methods inherit patentability if adapted; (e) claims that merely define intellectual content or mental steps executed on a computer may be defective under section 2. Use examples to guide whether features are mere information, mental methods, or technological contributions.

name: Rule 44. CONTENT OF THE EUROPEAN SEARCH REPORT
description: The search report must mention documents available to the EPO at the time of drawing up the report which may be relevant to novelty and inventive step.
guidance: Each citation shall be referred to the claims to which it relates; identify relevant parts of cited documents where necessary (e.g., page/column/lines or diagrams). The report shall distinguish between documents published before the priority date, between the priority date and filing date, and on or after filing. Any document referring to an oral disclosure, use or other non-written disclosure prior to filing must be mentioned together with the date of publication, if any, and the date of the non-written disclosure. The report shall be drawn up in the language of the proceedings and shall contain the IPC classification of the subject-matter.

name: Rule 49. FORM OF THE PUBLICATION OF EUROPEAN PATENT APPLICATIONS AND EUROPEAN SEARCH REPORTS
description: The President prescribes the form of the publication of the application and the data to be included; same applies when search report and abstract are published separately.
guidance: Designated Contracting States shall be specified in the published application. If claims are amended under Rule 86(2) before termination of technical preparations, the new or amended claims shall be included in publication in addition to original claims. Special conditions for abstract publication may be laid down.

name: Rule 51. EXAMINATION PROCEDURE
