description: In invitations under Article 96 the EPO invites the applicant to comment on the search report and to amend description, claims and drawings; in communications under Article 96(2) the Examining Division invites correction of disclosed deficiencies and may request amended filing of description, claims and drawings.
guidance: Any communication under Article 96(2) shall contain a reasoned statement covering grounds against grant. Before grant the Examining Division shall inform the applicant of the text intended for grant and request payment of grant/printing fees and translations of claims into the two EPO official languages other than the language of proceedings within three months. If the applicant communicates disapproval within that period, the communication shall be deemed not to have been made and examination resumes. The communication shall indicate designated Contracting States requiring translations. The decision to grant shall state which text forms the basis for grant.

name: Exclude §§102/103/112 issues from §101 analysis
description: The subject-matter eligibility analysis should not consider inventiveness/patentability issues that are addressed by other statutory sections (novelty, nonobviousness, enablement/definiteness).
guidance: The proposal expressly prohibits consideration of 'inventiveness' and issues under §§102, 103, and 112 during the §101 inquiry, arguing that other parts of the statute are sufficient to address preemption and claim breadth concerns.

name: Eligibility based on claimed invention (claimed-invention-centric analysis)
description: Eligibility should be determined with reference to the 'claimed invention' (the claim as a whole), aligning §101 with §§102/103/112 which are claim-directed.
guidance: The draft statute emphasizes that eligibility is based on what is claimed (not a 'gist' or purpose), and that claim construction principles should apply to §101 as they do to other sections.

name: Historical scope of the mental-steps doctrine
description: Originally used to exclude methods that could only be performed in the human mind when no apparatus was disclosed; disclosure of apparatus for performing the process without human intervention historically made a process statutory.
guidance: This historical distinction suggests courts should consider whether claims actually require human mental performance or instead disclose machinery/apparatus that performs the steps.

name: Generic physical elements insufficient to confer eligibility
description: Courts have characterized routine physical components (e.g., inertial sensors, radiation detectors, computers) as 'generic' and insufficient to impart eligibility under Alice.
guidance: The report criticizes treating common physical parts as mere 'generic' add-ons; if standard mechanical or electronic elements are deemed generic, that undermines claims that rely on new uses of known machines (contrary to §100(b)). Examples: Thales (inertial sensors), Exergen (radiation detector/thermometer).

name: Specification and claims compliance
description: (4) A specification (in compliance with 37 CFR 1.52) containing a description (37 CFR 1.71) and claims in compliance with 37 CFR 1.75
guidance: Specification must conform to formal requirements; claims must meet 37 CFR 1.75 formatting and content rules.

name: Domestic benefit claim compliance
description: (9) Domestic benefit claims under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), 120, 121, or 365(c) in compliance with 37 CFR 1.78 (e.g., the specific reference to the prior application must be submitted in the first sentence(s) of the specification or in an application data sheet, and for any benefit claim to a non-English language provisional application, the application must include a statement that (a) an English language translation, and (b) a statement that the translation is accurate, have been filed in the provisional application) (if applicable)
guidance: Benefit claims must follow 37 CFR 1.78: cite the prior application in the first sentence(s) of the spec or ADS; if claiming benefit to a non-English provisional, include explicit translation and accuracy statements as required.

name: Election by originally presented claims (818.02(a))
description: Claims originally presented and acted upon by the Office on their merits determine the invention elected by an applicant in the application.
guidance: Where claims to another invention are properly added and entered before an action, they are treated as original claims for restriction purposes; but generally original acted-upon claims fix the elected invention.

name: Form paragraph 8.22: required content for replies
description: Replies must include (i) an election of a species or invention to be examined and (ii) identification of the claims encompassing the elected invention. To reserve a right to petition, the election must be made with traverse.
guidance: If reply does not distinctly and specifically point out supposed errors, the election is treated as without traverse. If traversing on non-patentable-distinctness grounds, applicant should submit evidence or admit obvious-variant status now on the record; that evidence/admission may be used against the other invention under 35 U.S.C. 103(a).

name: Incomplete or non-specific traverse results in election without traverse
description: If applicant does not distinctly and specifically point out supposed errors in the restriction requirement, the election will be treated as an election without traverse (MPEP § 818.03(a)).
guidance: Form paragraph 8.25.02 is used to notify applicant that their election is treated as without traverse; this affects petition rights and treatment of nonelected claims.

name: Treatment and notification for claims held to be drawn to nonelected inventions (37 CFR 1.142(b))
description: All claims that the examiner holds as not being directed to the elected subject matter are withdrawn from further consideration; the examiner should clearly set forth reasons why the claims withdrawn are not readable on the elected invention.
guidance: Applicant may traverse the requirement pursuant to 37 CFR 1.143; if a final requirement for restriction is made, applicant may petition under 37 CFR 1.144.

name: Rejoinder eligibility and requirements (821.04)
description: To be eligible for rejoinder, a claim to a nonelected invention must depend from or otherwise require all the limitations of an allowable claim. Rejoined claims must be fully examined for patentability in accordance with 37 CFR 1.104 and must meet 35 U.S.C. 101, 102, 103 and 112.
guidance: Rejoinder withdraws the restriction between the inventions and allows examination on merits of previously nonelected inventions. Applicant should amend nonelected claims during prosecution to require limitations of the elected invention to retain right to rejoinder. Double patenting and 35 U.S.C. 121 considerations apply as explained (e.g., withdrawals may eliminate 35 U.S.C. 121 protection). Consult relevant MPEP sections for biotechnological processes and special process-claim treatments.

name: Rejoinder between product and process (and product/process-specific rules) (821.04(a))
description: Where restriction was required between independent or distinct products or processes and all claims to an elected invention are allowable, any restriction between the elected invention and a nonelected invention that depends from or otherwise requires all limitations of an allowable claim should be withdrawn and the previously withdrawn claims rejoined and fully examined.
guidance: Claims that do not require all limitations remain withdrawn. Amendments presenting additional claims that depend from or require all limitations of an allowable claim will be entered as a matter of right if presented prior to final rejection or allowance. Amendments after final are governed by 37 CFR 1.116; after allowance by 37 CFR 1.312. Use form paragraphs 8.45, 8.49, 8.50, etc., as applicable to notify applicant of rejoin/withdrawal status and double-patenting cautions.

name: Types of prior art searches — Novelty search
description: A novelty search determines if your invention is new before you file a patent.
guidance: Use to assess whether any single prior art reference discloses all features of a claim; start here if primary goal is getting a patent.

name: Types of prior art searches — State-of-the-art search
description: A state-of-the-art search reviews existing technologies in a field for R&D or competitive intelligence.
guidance: Broad landscape review to identify trends, white spaces, and competitor activity rather than testing a single claim for novelty or infringement.

name: Define the invention clearly
description: Break your invention into its essential technical features: purpose, components, and unique aspects.
guidance: Start by explicitly listing the invention’s core elements so you can target searches to each element and combinations of elements (claims-level thinking).

name: Build effective search queries (Boolean and field tags)
description: Use Boolean operators (AND, OR, NOT) and field tags (title, abstract, claims) to construct precise queries.
guidance: Use AND to combine keywords and narrow results, OR to include synonyms, NOT to exclude irrelevant topics, and field tags to search within specific parts of documents. Combine keyword searches with classification filters for best results.

name: Analyze and document findings
description: Review abstracts and claims first; note publication numbers, filing dates, and applicants, and keep a record of search terms and databases used.
guidance: Documenting search queries, dates, and results supports reproducibility, prosecution strategy, and later defenses. Prioritize reading claims and filing/publication dates to assess relevance.

name: What patent examiners check — Inventive step / Obviousness
description: Examiners ask whether combining known elements would have been obvious to a person skilled in the art.
guidance: Consider plausible combinations of references and whether those combinations render the claim obvious; anticipate obviousness-type rejections when evaluating patentability.

name: When to seek professional help
description: Patent attorneys and professional searchers use advanced commercial tools and provide legal opinions; consider hiring them for core inventions or international filings.
guidance: Professional tools (Derwent Innovation, Orbit, PatBase) can interpret claims and equivalents more accurately, access non-English full-text, and deliver structured reports. Use professionals when the invention is commercially important or when an FTO/validity opinion is required.

name: Who qualifies as a licensee by operation of law / scope of prior-user protection
description: To claim benefit as a licensee by operation of law, the person must be a purchaser or have used the invention before the patent was issued by license/grant/consent of the inventor (not a mere wrong-doer).
guidance: Examples: an employee who made experiments in the employer's manufactory, permitted employer's use without compensation being demanded, and then obtained a patent — such unmolested and notorious prior use may bring the case within the statute and protect the prior user.

name: False suggestion or misleading specification as ground for invalidity
description: If part of a specification is useless or the patent contains a false suggestion calculated to mislead the public, that may render the patent void (i.e., the inquiry whether a claimed part is useless relates to false suggestion/misleading).
guidance: Distinguish statutory 'useful' requirement from questions about whether particular claimed elements are essential or are misleadingly presented in the specification.

name: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) requirement
description: During patent examination, the pending claims must be 'given their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.'
guidance: BRI is the standard the USPTO applies in prosecution (citing Phillips, In re Am. Acad. of Sci. Tech. Ctr., etc.). It is applied to the words of the proposed claims as they would be understood by one of ordinary skill in the art, taking into account definitions or other enlightenment in the written description. BRI is used because applicants can amend claims during prosecution; giving claims their BRI reduces the possibility that an issued claim will be later interpreted more broadly than justified. The Office does not interpret claims during prosecution the same way courts do in infringement or validity proceedings.

name: BRI is not the broadest possible interpretation
description: The broadest reasonable interpretation does not mean the broadest possible interpretation.
guidance: The meaning given to a claim term must be consistent with the ordinary and customary meaning of the term (unless specially defined), and consistent with the use of the term in the specification and drawings. The BRI must also be consistent with the interpretation those skilled in the art would reach (citing In re Cortright, Buszard examples). Examiners should avoid unreasonable constructions that are inconsistent with the disclosure or ordinary meaning.

name: Plain meaning rule
description: Words of a claim must be given their 'plain meaning' unless such meaning is inconsistent with the specification.
guidance: ‘Plain meaning’ = the ordinary and customary meaning given by those of ordinary skill in the art at the relevant time (effective filing date). The best source is the specification (serves as a glossary when clear). Other intrinsic sources include the claims themselves, drawings, and prosecution history. Ordinary words whose meaning is clear are construed to mean exactly what they say unless context indicates otherwise (examples: heating dough vs oven air).

name: Do not import limitations from the specification
description: It is improper to import into a claim limitations that are not part of the claim simply because they appear in the written description or preferred embodiments.
guidance: A particular embodiment in the specification should not be read into a claim when the claim language is broader than the embodiment (citing Superguide, Liebel‑Flarsheim, E‑Pass). Examiners should refrain from narrowing claims by reading disclosed embodiments or exemplary sequences into the claim unless the claim language itself demands it or a statutory provision (e.g., 35 U.S.C. 112(f)) requires reference to the specification.

name: Prefer intrinsic evidence; use extrinsic evidence only when intrinsic is insufficient
description: The ordinary and customary meaning should be derived from intrinsic evidence (claims, specification, drawings); extrinsic evidence (dictionaries, treatises, expert testimony) is secondary and used only if intrinsic evidence fails to provide sufficient clarity.
guidance: When the specification is clear about scope and content, there's no need to consult extrinsic evidence (citing 3M v. Tredegar). In some cases where claims, specification, and prosecution history do not offer sufficient clarity, extrinsic evidence may be necessary (Actelion example). Any meaning taken from prior art or dictionaries must be consistent with the specification and drawings.

name: Applicant-as-lexicographer (special definitions)
description: An applicant may rebut the presumption of ordinary meaning by clearly setting forth a special definition of a term in the specification.
guidance: To act as their own lexicographer the applicant must define the term with reasonable clarity, deliberateness, and precision in the specification so that one of ordinary skill in the art would understand the departure from common usage (citing In re Paulsen, Intellicall). When an explicit definition is provided, that definition controls claim interpretation (Toro Co. v. White). Any special meaning must be sufficiently clear in the specification.

name: Disavowal (clear and unmistakable disclaimer of claim scope)
description: Applicant may rebut ordinary meaning by clearly disavowing or disclaiming the full scope of a claim term in the specification; disavowal must be clear and unmistakable.
guidance: If the specification makes clear the invention does not include a particular feature, that feature is outside the reach of the claims even if the claim language appears broad (SciMed example). Disavowal can be explicit or, in some cases, implicit (e.g., specification repeatedly disparages a feature and all embodiments exclude it — In re Abbott Diabetes Care). If examiner believes implicit disavowal narrows BRI, the examiner should make that interpretation clear on the record and cite MPEP § 2173.05(a) as relevant.

name: Means-plus-function (35 U.S.C. 112(f)) construction
description: When an element is claimed using means- or step-plus-function language (112(f)/pre‑AIA 112 sixth paragraph), the specification must be consulted to determine the corresponding structure, material, or acts and the claimed element is limited to those structures/materials/acts and equivalents.
guidance: Means-plus-function limitations are construed by reference to the specification (citing In re Donaldson and MPEP §§2181–2186). Examiners must identify the corresponding structure in the written description and construe the claim limitation accordingly; the limitation is not indefinite merely because the specification discloses only a single embodiment, but the corresponding structure must be present.

name: Flow-chart process for determining claim term meaning (when 112(f) not invoked)
description: If a claim term has an ordinary and customary meaning, check the specification for a special definition; if none, apply the ordinary meaning. If no ordinary meaning exists, follow the alternative flow to seek a special definition or other guidance.
guidance: The MPEP flowchart directs examiners to: (1) determine whether the term has an ordinary and customary meaning to a person of ordinary skill in the art; (2) if so, check specification for a special definition — if present, use it (and acknowledge it in the Office action); (3) if not present, apply the ordinary meaning. If the term lacks ordinary meaning, consult the specification for an implied definition and, if necessary, other evidence. Office actions should acknowledge and identify any special definitions used.

name: Grammar, syntax, and ordinary reading of claim language control scope
description: Grammatical and syntactic features of claim language (e.g., singular vs plural, antecedent basis) affect interpretation and may limit claim scope based on ordinary reading.
guidance: Claims should be read according to their grammar and ordinary usage: e.g., use of 'said microprocessor' can require a singular element capable of performing recited functions (Salazar example). Examiners should ensure antecedent basis and claim grammar are properly considered and addressed (see MPEP § 2173.05(e) and related examples).

name: Machine (statutory category)
description: Machine – a concrete thing, consisting of parts, or of certain devices and combination of devices. Includes mechanical devices or combinations of devices to perform functions and produce effects or results. (Cites: Burr v. Duryee; Corning v. Burden.)
guidance: For product/machine claims, tangible structural elements that evidence a particular practical application favor eligibility. Claims that recite a machine but include no tangible structural elements under BRI may be construed to embrace the underlying concept and be ineligible.

name: Manufacture (statutory category)
description: Manufacture – an article produced from raw or prepared materials by giving to these materials new forms, qualities, properties, or combinations, whether by handlabor or by machinery. (Cites: Diamond v. Chakrabarty.)
guidance: Manufacture claims are typically tangible and their claim limitations often make practical application self-evident; evaluate whether claimed limitations are tangible and limit the claim to a particular application.

name: Composition of matter (statutory category)
description: Composition of matter – all compositions of two or more substances and all composite articles, whether result of chemical union or mechanical mixture, or gases, fluids, powders or solids. (Cites: Chakrabarty.)
guidance: Composition claims are product-oriented and eligibility often follows if the claim does not recite a judicial exception or if any recited exception is practically applied in the tangible composition.

name: Examples of non-statutory subject matter
description: Non-limiting examples of claims that are not directed to one of the statutory categories: transitory forms of signal transmission (e.g., a propagating electrical or electromagnetic signal per se), a naturally occurring organism, a human per se, a legal contractual agreement, a game defined as a set of rules, a computer program per se, a company, and a mere arrangement of printed matter.
guidance: Use these examples when assessing whether a claim is within the four categories. If the broadest reasonable interpretation in view of the specification encompasses such non-statutory embodiments, reject under 35 U.S.C. 101.

name: Claim breadth across statutory and non-statutory embodiments
description: A claim that covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments (under the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim when read in light of the specification and in view of one skilled in the art) embraces subject matter that is not eligible for patent protection and therefore is directed to non-statutory subject matter.
guidance: If claim language, when broadly read, includes non-statutory embodiments (e.g., a computer-readable medium that can be a carrier wave), a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 is appropriate. Consider whether amendment could restrict the claim to statutory embodiments; still perform Step 2 if amendment might cure.

name: Judicial exceptions and 'practical application' concept
description: Judicially recognized exceptions include laws of nature, physical phenomena, and abstract ideas. While these exceptions are not patentable, methods and products employing them to perform a real-world function may be eligible if the claim as a whole is a particular practical application of the exception.
guidance: Evaluate the claim as a whole to determine whether it is merely the exception itself (ineligible) or a particular practical application (eligible). Practical application relates to how the exception is applied in a real-world product or process, not merely to the result. Practical application evidence can show the subject matter is not abstract and does not preempt substantially all uses.

name: Practical application for product claims (machines/manufactures/compositions)
description: If a claimed product falls within one of the product categories and does not recite judicially excepted subject matter, it qualifies. If a judicial exception is recited, determine if it has been practically applied in the product. Eligible products are non-naturally occurring, tangible embodiments formed of elements/parts that embody a specific, tangible practical application.
guidance: Tangible structural claim limitations provide evidence of a practical application (e.g., a cup as application of containing liquid; magnetic door latch as application of magnetism). Claims that recite a product but lack tangible limitations under the broadest reasonable interpretation may be viewed as embracing the abstract concept and be ineligible. Evaluate whether the claimed structure limits the claim so it does not cover substantially all practical uses of the underlying concept.

name: Preemption / coverage of substantially all practical applications
description: Once a practical application has been established, the limited occurrence of preemption must be evaluated to determine whether the claim impermissibly covers substantially all practical applications of the judicially excepted subject matter.
guidance: If the claim covers substantially all practical applications of the exception, it is not patent-eligible; if it covers only a particular practical application, it may be eligible. Assess claim scope carefully in view of the specification and possible embodiments.

name: Practical application for process claims and machine-or-transformation considerations
description: A process claim must be limited to a particular practical application to be statutory. The machine-or-transformation test remains a useful investigative tool: a claimed process is surely patent-eligible if (1) it is tied to a particular machine or apparatus, or (2) it transforms a particular article into a different state or thing. The test is not sole determinant but provides important factors.
guidance: Not every method is statutory; consider whether recited structure or a transformative component meaningfully limits the claim. Field-of-use limitations and mere post-solution activity generally do not make an abstract idea patentable (Flook). Use the listed factors (below) to weigh evidence for or against abstractness; consider multiple factors together rather than relying on one.

name: Factor: whether the method involves or is executed by a particular machine or apparatus
description: Consider whether the method involves or is executed by a particular machine or apparatus; the machine-or-transformation test is a useful investigative tool for determining whether some claimed inventions are processes under §101.
guidance: Relevant subfactors: (a) the particularity or generality of the machine elements (specific identification of the machine weighs toward eligibility); (b) whether the machine implements the steps of the method (integral use weighs toward eligibility; mere object on which method operates weighs against); (c) whether the machine's involvement is extrasolution activity or a field-of-use (nominal contribution or mere data-gathering/field-of-use weighs against). For computer-implemented processes, programming that causes a general purpose computer to perform the claimed steps may be sufficient to render it a particular machine.

name: Computer-implemented processes: programming and 'computer-aided' limitations
description: For computer implemented processes, a general purpose computer may be sufficiently particular when programmed to perform the process steps; such programming creates a new machine because a general purpose computer becomes a special purpose computer once programmed. However, adding a 'computer-aided' limitation without explaining how the computer aids the method is insufficient to render an abstract concept eligible (DealerTrack v. Huber).
guidance: Claims must clearly convey that the computer is programmed to perform the steps (i.e., describe how/extent/significance of computer involvement). Mere recitation of a computer or the Internet, or generic 'computer-aided' language, can be insufficient if the claim is otherwise abstract and would preempt substantially all practical applications.

name: Field-of-use and 'insignificant extra-solution activity' are not meaningful limits
description: A 'field-of-use' limitation does not impose actual boundaries on the scope of the claimed invention. Insignificant 'extra-solution' activity means activity that is not central to the purpose of the method invented by the applicant (e.g., gathering data when all applications of the method would require data gathering).
guidance: Do not rely on mere field-of-use or token extra steps to render an abstract idea patentable. Such limitations are often insufficient to overcome a §101 rejection.

name: Responding to a §101 rejection — amendments and persuasive arguments
description: A proper response to a rejection based on failure to claim patent-eligible subject matter would be an amendment adding additional steps/features or amending existing steps/features that integrate the natural principle into the process (by practically applying or making use of the principle) and are sufficient to limit the application of the natural principle to more than the principle itself + steps that do more than simply 'apply it' at a high level of generality.
guidance: Amend by adding meaningful limitations that confine the use to particular applications; present persuasive arguments that additional steps add 'something significantly more' than merely describing the natural principle. Showing that steps are not routine, well-known, or conventional can help. Examples: constructing a sanitizing device that integrates UV light rather than merely exposing to sunlight; adding nonconventional testing or treatment steps beyond routine blood sampling when claiming a blood glucose–disease correlation.

name: Actions on Petitions to the Director — Patent Matters (Table 24, FY2017–FY2021)
description: Annual counts of actions on patent-related petitions to the Director, by petition nature: Actions on Patent Petitions (total), Acceptance of Late Assignments, Late Issue Fees, Late Priority Papers, Access, Certificates of Correction, Deferment of Issue, Entity Status Change, Filing Date matters, Maintenance Fees, Revivals, Rule 47 (37 CFR 1.47), Supervisory Authority, Suspend Rules, Withdrawal from Issue, Withdraw Holding of Abandonment, Late Benefit or Priority Claim, Withdraw as Attorney, Matters Not Provided For (37 CFR 1.182), To Make Special, Patent Term Adjustment/Extension, and other categories.
guidance: Footnotes: Annual totals and category breakdowns are shown; table notes changes and provides totals. The table shows both counts and trend changes; '-   Represents zero.'

name: Liability of Contracting Member States for infringements of Union law by the Court
description: Contracting Member States are jointly and severally liable for damage resulting from an infringement of Union law by the Court of Appeal; action for damages may be brought against the Contracting Member State where the claimant has residence or place of business, or where the Court of Appeal has its seat.
guidance: Rules on contribution among Member States and procedural detail to be determined by the Administrative Committee.

name: Use of patent claims as primary textual input
description: Claims are preferred because they contain more comprehensive and accurate information; the first claim is considered the backbone of the claim hierarchy and was used as input in this study.
guidance: The paper uses only the first claim to create embeddings, noting claims are more informative than title/abstract. It suggests future work combining all claims based on their tree structure. Mean claim length reported (~162 tokens) motivated sequence length choices.

name: Model limitations & reporting
description: Explicitly report dataset and methodological limitations (sample size, truncation, class imbalance) and propose follow-up experiments to address them.
guidance: Authors report sample-size limitation (1.5M claims) and plan larger-sample tests with ANN; note truncation due to token limits and propose exploring longer-input approaches; explicitly list how limitations might affect generalization.

name: Derivation proceeding requirements
description: An applicant requesting a derivation proceeding must set forth the basis for finding that an earlier applicant derived the claimed invention and without authorization filed an application claiming such invention.
guidance: The request must be filed within 1 year of the date of first publication of an application for a claim that is substantially the same as the claimed invention. The Patent Trial and Appeal Board determines the right to patent and issues a final decision; decisions may be appealed to the Federal Circuit or to district court under Sec. 146.

name: Post-grant review availability and scope
description: Post-grant review may be sought on any invalidity ground during the first 12 months after a patent is issued or reissued.
guidance: Post-grant review is a court-like proceeding in which both challenger and patent owner present information. The proceeding may be used to challenge any invalidity ground and may be instituted only if the petition, if not rebutted, shows it is more likely than not that a claim would be found invalid, or if the petition raises a novel or unsettled legal question important to other patents or applications. Post-grant petitioners are estopped only for issues they actually raised in the post-grant review.

name: Inter partes review availability and scope
description: Inter partes review may be sought on the basis of patents and printed publications any time after a post-grant review is concluded or, if no such review is instituted, after the time for seeking such review has expired.
guidance: Inter partes is limited to prior-art patents and printed publications and may not be instituted unless the petition and response show there is a reasonable likelihood that a claim would be found invalid. Inter partes petitioners are estopped from raising in subsequent Office proceedings any issue they raised or reasonably could have raised, and are also estopped from raising such issues in civil litigation or ITC proceedings.

name: Generic prior art does not necessarily destroy novelty of a selection
description: A novidade para tal seleção poderá ser atribuída se a descrição em um documento anterior for apenas genérica, sem que o item específico que está sendo selecionado tenha sido mencionado de maneira explícita, isto é, textualmente e concretizado na forma de exemplos, testes, resultados, listas e tabelas.
guidance: A prior generic disclosure alone does not necessarily take away novelty of a specifically claimed selection unless the specific item was explicitly and concretely disclosed (e.g., in examples/tests).

name: Prior explicit disclosure of a product removes selection patentability
description: Se um produto foi revelado em um documento do estado da técnica, por exemplo, um composto, através de sua nomenclatura, ou pela sua fórmula estrutural, dentre os compostos ditos referenciais e concretizados nos exemplos de preparação/utilização, esse não pode ser a matéria objeto de uma patente de seleção, pois o composto é considerado como especificamente revelado e não preenche o requisito de novidade.
guidance: If the prior art explicitly identifies the specific product (by name, formula, or concrete example), selection claims to that product lack novelty and cannot be patented as a selection.

name: Selected sub-range must not be specifically disclosed in prior art
description: No caso de pedidos de seleção de processo em que é selecionada uma subfaixa de uma faixa mais ampla compreendida no documento do estado da técnica, para o preenchimento do requisito de novidade é necessário que a subfaixa selecionada não tenha sido especificamente revelada e concretizada no estado da técnica.
guidance: When claiming a sub-range from a broader known range, ensure the sub-range was not specifically disclosed or exemplified in prior art; examples are given comparing temperature ranges to decide novelty.

name: Numeric values subject to measurement error and rounding conventions
description: O examinador deve levar em conta que os valores numéricos relacionados a medidas estão sujeitos a erros, que apresentam limites em sua precisão. A convenção geral ... é aplicável, na qual última casa decimal de um valor numérico indica o seu grau de precisão. Em casos onde não existe nenhuma outra margem de erro, a margem máxima deve ser determinada por meio do arredondamento da última casa decimal.
guidance: When comparing claimed numeric values to prior art, consider measurement error and rounding: e.g., a claim of 3.5 cm vs prior disclosure of 3.45 cm may be within expected measurement tolerance and therefore not novel. Use usual technical/scientific rounding conventions to set margins.

name: Invention must be considered as a whole when assessing obviousness
description: A invenção reivindicada deverá ser considerada como um todo, levando-se em conta os elementos constantes no preâmbulo e na parte caracterizante. Na determinação das diferenças entre as reivindicações e o estado da técnica, a questão não é se as diferenças seriam óbvias individualmente, mas se a invenção reivindicada seria óbvia como um todo.
guidance: Do not dissect combinations into isolated known features to declare obviousness; consider whether the claimed combination as a whole would have been obvious. However, if the claim is a mere aggregation/juxtaposition with no synergistic effect, it lacks inventive step.

name: Treatment of independent vs dependent claims in inventive step analysis
description: Em geral, se uma reivindicação independente apresenta atividade inventiva, não é necessário examinar a atividade inventiva de suas reivindicações dependentes. Ao contrário, se uma reivindicação independente não apresenta atividade inventiva, suas reivindicações dependentes devem ser examinadas, pois podem conter elementos específicos que tornem a matéria inventiva.
guidance: Prioritize independent claims: if independent claim lacks inventive step, check dependents individually for possible inventive features.

name: Judgement of obviousness: need for motivation to apply distinguishing features
description: O examinador deve julgar, a partir do estado da técnica mais próximo e da solução proposta para o problema técnico, se a invenção é ou não óbvia para um técnico no assunto. Deve ser determinado se existe uma motivação para aplicar as características distintivas da invenção ao estado da técnica mais próximo visando solucionar o problema técnico existente. Tal motivação não precisa estar explicitada nos documentos do estado da técnica.
guidance: Look for whether a person skilled in the art would have been motivated (explicitly or implicitly) to combine teachings or modify the prior art to arrive at the claimed invention; absent any reasonable motivation, inventive step may be present.

name: Multiple intermediates for different structural parts — lack of unity between intermediates
description: If the same international application claims different intermediates for different structural parts of the final product, unity is not regarded as being present between the intermediates.
guidance: Claiming different intermediates each corresponding to distinct structural parts of the final product breaks unity among those intermediate claims.

name: Families mapping requirement for intermediate/final compound families
description: If the intermediate and final products are families of compounds, each intermediate compound must correspond to a compound claimed in the family of the final products; some final products may have no corresponding intermediate compound so families need not be absolutely congruent.
guidance: One-to-one correspondence is expected for claimed family members, but exact congruence of families is not required; see AI Annex B, paragraph (h).

name: Process/product correspondence (inherent product feature)
description: A process claim can correspond to a product claim if the process steps inherently produce the product feature that is the special technical feature of the product claim.
guidance: Even if the product feature is not explicit in the wording of the process claim, disclosure in the description showing the process inherently yields the product characteristic can establish unity (Example 3).

name: Markush/grouping test for alternatives
description: A Markush grouping (one claim listing alternatives) is acceptable where the alternatives share a significant structural element that is essential to the common property or activity; this shared core provides unity a priori.
guidance: The indolyl moiety, thiazole ring, or other shared cores can be the significant structural element. Prior art showing the shared core with the claimed function can destroy unity a posteriori (see Examples 25–29).

name: Partial novelty within family members does not necessarily destroy unity
description: If not all members of a claimed family are novel (e.g., some are known), there may nevertheless be unity between a family claim and a specific member claim provided the specific member has the claimed activity that is the special technical feature.
guidance: Example 7: even if not all compounds in a family are novel, unity can exist if the particular member has the shared activity.

name: Selecting first invention to be searched in Markush/non-unity a posteriori cases
description: If unity is lacking a posteriori for a Markush-style claim, Authorities may determine the first named invention searched as the embodiment comprising the first-listed options for each variable (but discretion exists to include sub-genuses depending on circumstances).
guidance: Examiners consider interdependence of groups, examples, and prior art. Practices differ; sometimes the first embodiment listed is used, other times different groupings are chosen (see Example 25 discussion).

name: Overlapping numerical ranges — fact-specific approach
description: Determination of unity for claims containing overlapping ranges requires careful factual consideration; avoid narrow, literal or academic approaches when raising lack of unity objections.
guidance: Example 20 (manganese ranges) shows that unity between overlapping ranges depends on whether the shared portion is associated with the same technical effect and prior art teachings; prior art can change a priori unity to lack of unity a posteriori.

name: Method-of-screening vs compounds — lack of unity without structural/activity link
description: A screening method claim and claims to compounds identified by that method may lack unity a priori if there is no teaching of a structural element shared by the compounds or a disclosed relationship between structure and activity linking the method to the compounds.
guidance: Example 23: method for identifying antagonists vs diverse compounds X, Y, Z—without structural commonality or explanation of structure–activity relation, there is no single general concept linking the method and compounds, so separate inventions are appropriate.

name: Permitted copying/displaying of public-domain works (without Project Gutenberg references)
description: If an individual work is unprotected by copyright law in the United States and you are located in the United States, the Foundation does not claim a right to prevent you from copying, distributing, performing, displaying or creating derivative works based on the work as long as all references to Project Gutenberg are removed.
guidance: This means you may copy and distribute such works freely within the U.S. provided you remove references to Project Gutenberg when you choose not to comply with the full license terms.

name: Prerequisites for accelerated examination (special status for new applications)
description: A new application may be granted special status (accelerated examination) provided applicant complies with each of the following items: (A) submits a petition to make special accompanied by the fee in 37 CFR 1.17(h); (B) presents all claims directed to a single invention or will make an election without traverse; (C) submits a statement that a pre-examination search was made, listing field of search by class/subclass and other sources; (D) submits one copy each of the references deemed most closely related; and (E) submits a detailed discussion of the references pointing out, with the particularity required by 37 CFR 1.111(b) and (c), how the claimed subject matter is patentable over the references.
guidance: If the Office determines claims are not obviously directed to a single invention and no election without traverse is made, the petition will be denied and application awaits regular turn. A foreign patent office search satisfies (C) if corresponding foreign claims are of same/similar scope. References in (D) are required only if not already of record. The discussion in (E) must meet the particularity of 37 CFR 1.111(b),(c).

name: Election to a single invention requirement for accelerated examination
description: Applicant must present all claims directed to a single invention, or if Office determines claims are not directed to a single invention, applicant must make an election without traverse as prerequisite to grant of special status.
guidance: Election may be made at time of filing petition. If applicant fails to include election and Office determines requirement should be made, telephone restriction practice will be followed. If applicant refuses to make an election without traverse, application will not be further examined at that time and petition denied.

name: Pre-examination search statement requirement
description: Submit a statement(s) that a pre-examination search was made, listing the field of search by class and subclass, publication, Chemical Abstracts, foreign patents, etc.
guidance: The pre-examination search must be directed to the invention as claimed in the application for which special status is requested. A search made by a foreign patent office satisfies this requirement if the claims in the corresponding foreign application are of the same or similar scope to the U.S. claims for which special status is requested.

name: Detailed discussion of references (37 CFR 1.111(b) and (c) particularity)
description: Submit a detailed discussion of the references which points out, with the particularity required by 37 CFR 1.111(b) and (c), how the claimed subject matter is patentable over the references.
guidance: The discussion must be specific and address how each reference does or does not teach or render obvious the claimed subject matter—meeting the same particularity as required for replies under 37 CFR 1.111(b) and (c).

name: Accelerated examination first action, search scope, and shortened reply period
description: The examiner will take up the application before other categories (except those clearly in condition for allowance and those with set time limits) and will give a complete first action including all essential matters as to all claims. The examiner’s search will be restricted to the subject matter encompassed by the claims. A first action rejection will set a 3-month shortened period for reply.
guidance: The restricted search and requirement for a complete first action speed resolution. Applicants must be prepared to respond within shortened time frames (3 months) or arrange appropriate interviews.

name: Special status for inventions materially contributing to countering terrorism
description: Applicants should petition that their applications be accorded special status; the petition under 37 CFR 1.102 must state that special status is sought because the invention materially contributes to countering terrorism.
guidance: No fee is required (see 37 CFR 1.102(c)). If disclosure is not clear that the claimed invention is materially directed to countering terrorism, petition must be accompanied by a statement under 37 CFR 1.102 explaining how the invention materially contributes. The materiality standard does not permit speculation about hypothetical end-user application nor a benefit merely because some minor aspect may be directed to countering terrorism. Examples of counter-terrorism technologies include detection/identification of explosives, aircraft sensors/security systems, vehicular barricades/disabling systems.

name: Licensee's right to contest validity when sued for infringement
description: Whether a licensee can contest the validity of the patent when sued for infringement depends on the license's terms: absent admissions or estoppel the licensee may challenge validity; if the license contains admissions or the licensee seeks to repudiate the license and assert invalidity, he forfeits benefits of the license and may still be estopped by contractual admissions unless deceived.
guidance: A licensee who stops paying or repudiates the license to claim the patent is invalid gives up the license's protections; courts will permit contesting validity where there are no estoppel-producing recitals, but admissions or covenants in the deed may bar such defenses unless fraud or deception is shown.

name: New matter and claim-enlarging amendments (legal effect and treatment)
description: A 'new matter' amendment to the disclosure (35 U.S.C. 132) will be required to be canceled, and claims containing new matter will be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112. A 'new matter' amendment to the drawing is ordinarily not entered. Where an amendment enlarges the scope of the claims of the patent, the amendment will be entered; however the appropriate claims will be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 305.
guidance: Clerical entry does not equate to legal effect; beware of introducing new matter or enlarging claim scope—such changes trigger statutory rejections.

name: Consequences of failure to file timely notice of appeal or fee
description: If the patent owner does not timely file a notice of appeal and/or the appropriate appeal fee, the appeal is dismissed, the reexamination prosecution is terminated, and a Notice of Intent to Issue Ex Parte Reexamination Certificate (NIRC) will be issued indicating claim status at time of final rejection.
guidance: Meeting appeal filing and fee deadlines is critical—failure terminates the reexamination and leads toward certificate issuance reflecting current claim status.

name: Grounds for patent nullity/challenge
description: The validity of a patent can be challenged through a nullity action before the IMPI on grounds including: subject matter excluded from patent protection; disclosure not clear and sufficient to enable the invention to be performed; claims exceed those originally disclosed; invention disclosed in a divisional application and includes illegal claims; patent has been subject to rectification or limitation; patent was granted in error or due to serious oversight, or was granted to a person not entitled; patent was granted in violation of the law in force at the time it was granted.
guidance: Invalidation actions can be brought at any time. IMPI can partially invalidate a patent and will explain changes in its final resolution.

name: Remedies and preliminary measures in patent infringement actions
description: Patent holders can request preliminary measures if they show ownership of the patent, imminent violation and possibility of irreparable damage; provide security or an economic guarantee; and provide necessary information to determine specific goods that are object of the infringement.
guidance: IMPI can order removal of infringing goods from circulation; forbid distribution or use; order seizure of infringing goods; order cease and desist; order suspension of services or closure of commercial establishment. Administrative infringements punishable with fines up to MXN21.72 million, additional fine up to MXN86,000 per day, temporary closure up to 90 days, or permanent closure. Once IMPI decision is enforceable, patent owner can bring claim for damages before the courts; courts will consider date of proven infringement and evidence of patent's value.

name: Interim extension application content under 35 U.S.C.156(d)(5)
description: An application for interim extension shall contain the identity of the product subject to regulatory review and the Federal statute under which such review is occurring; identity of the patent and each claim which claims the product or a method of using or manufacturing the product; information to enable the Director to determine eligibility under subsection (a)(1)-(3); a brief description of activities undertaken during the regulatory review period to date and significant dates; and such patent or other information as the Director may require.
guidance: These enumerated items are mandatory content for an interim-extension application under subsection (d)(5)(A)(i)-(v).

name: Scope of patent rights during interim extension
description: The rights derived from any patent the term of which is extended under this paragraph shall, during the period of interim extension, be limited to the use then under regulatory review (if patent claims a product), to the use claimed then under regulatory review (if claims method of use), or to the method of manufacturing as used to make the product then under regulatory review (if claims manufacturing).
guidance: Interim extension confers narrower rights limited to the subject matter being reviewed; do not assume full patent scope during interim period.

name: Copies requirement for cited documents (37 CFR 1.98(a)(2))
description: Copies must be provided for: (a) each cited foreign patent document; (b) each cited non-patent literature publication or the portion which caused it to be listed; (c) each cited U.S. pending application that is not stored in IFW; (d) all information cited (e.g., an affidavit or Office action), other than the specification, including claims and drawings of a pending U.S. application; and (e) all other cited information or the portion which caused it to be listed.
guidance: When listing a document you must attach a legible copy of the required portion; failure to provide required copies causes the IDS to be non-compliant and the items not to be considered.

name: Distance from the closest prior art (inventive step)
description: The bigger the inventive step / the further the claimed invention is from the closest prior art, the harder it is to attack under 35 U.S.C. §102/103.
guidance: When drafting and prosecuting, emphasize novel features and how they differ from prior art; document why the invention is non-obvious. Large factual/technical gaps from prior art increase validity strength.

name: Clean prosecution history
description: A prosecution history with few amendments and no inconsistent or broad disparaging statements increases validity; messy prosecution can create estoppel and weaken enforceability.
guidance: Avoid contradictory arguments (e.g., arguing prior art doesn't teach X and later saying it does). Minimize unnecessary claim amendments and explain which amendment overcame which rejection to reduce estoppel/Festo risk.

name: Strong written description with multiple embodiments and ranges
description: A robust written description that includes multiple embodiments, explicit ranges, and defined terms supports claim scope and resilience in litigation.
guidance: Include examples, variations, alternatives, and explicit 'in some embodiments' language. Define key terms and disclose multiple ways to implement the inventive concept so courts cannot later read in limitations absent from the spec.

name: Detailed enablement
description: The specification should enable a POSITA to make and use the invention; detailed disclosure reduces successful enablement challenges.
guidance: Provide sufficient technical detail, algorithms where needed (avoid means-plus-function without algorithmic disclosure), and practical instructions so an expert cannot credibly claim insufficiency.

name: Elements performed by a single actor
description: Claims whose elements are all performed by a single actor are easier to assert and enforce (reduced divided-infringement risk).
guidance: Where possible, draft claims that avoid multi-party performance requirements or include appropriate joint/infringement language. Ensure claim drafting contemplates single-actor performance if that matches commercial practice.

name: Commercial relevance of claimed subject matter
description: Claims should cover what people actually do or want to do commercially, not a niche variant, to maximize enforcement leverage and licensing value.
guidance: Align claim scope with real-world product features and market practices; overly narrow or eccentric claim targets reduce commercial enforcement options and damages.

name: Damages base — claimed feature drives demand
description: A strong damages base exists when the claimed feature materially drives customer demand or product value.
guidance: Draft claims around commercially significant features and document their contribution to value. Claims that capture a demand-driving element support larger damages and settlement leverage.

name: Common markers of a weak patent
description: Characteristics commonly seen in weak patents include a single-page spec; one independent claim of moderate scope without a ladder of dependent claims; means-plus-function language without algorithmic disclosure; over-the-top characterizations of 'the invention'; marketing-style preambles; and no clear description of the inventive concept.
guidance: Avoid minimal specs, insufficient claim drafting, and vague marketing language. Provide claim ladders, technical detail for means-plus-function claims, and a clear statement of the inventive concept.

name: Patentometrics heuristics (correlation vs. individual prediction)
description: Metrics like Allison-Lemley validity rates, USPTO art unit allowance rates, and forward citation counts correlate with patent quality but are not predictive at the individual-patent level.
guidance: Use metrics as broad signals or portfolio-level heuristics, but rely on substance — spec quality and the clarity of the claim ladder — when assessing individual patent strength.

name: Length and richness of the specification
description: A strong spec is almost always long: Federal Circuit decisions often hinge on what the spec says or does not say; a 50–100 page spec with multiple embodiments, defined terms, ranges, and explicit 'in some embodiments' framings is more litigation-resilient than a short spec.
guidance: Favor comprehensive disclosure over brevity. Include multiple examples, permutations, and explicit fallback language to support claim scope during litigation or prosecution.

name: Continuation pendency and family prosecution
description: A patent in a family with pending continuations is worth more: the ability to file continuation claims (or threaten new claims) deters competitors and adds tactical value.
guidance: Maintain continuation options where strategically useful to prosecute further claim scope or to respond to competitor behavior. Portfolio-level prosecution strategy (continuations, claims amendments) increases enforcement leverage.

name: 0600 - Parts, Form, and Content of Application
description: MPEP chapter 600: required parts, formal requirements, and content standards for patent applications.
guidance: Details formal form and content requirements (specification, claims, drawings, oath/declaration), including statutory compliance and filing checklist items.

name: 1500 - Design Patents
description: MPEP chapter 1500: rules specific to design patent applications and prosecution.
guidance: Covers statutory requirements, claim/drawing standards, examination, and issuance procedures unique to design patents.

name: Moral claims cannot be asserted as facts of consciousness without empirical grounding
description: The moral law should not be presented as an empirically unexamined 'fact of consciousness' unless supported by evidence; to treat Autonomy or the Categorical Imperative as directly given in consciousness makes the claim anthropological/empirical and conflicts with Kant's repeated rejection of such grounding.
guidance: If one treats autonomy or moral duty as a fact of consciousness, this implies an empirical foundation and must be coherently defended; otherwise the move either commits petitio principii or contradicts one's stated methodological commitments.

name: Sufficiency of disclosure (sufficient description)
description: The description must disclose the claimed invention in a sufficiently clear and complete manner to enable a person of ordinary skill in the art to carry it out, including the best method known to the applicant and information supporting industrial applicability.
guidance: (Article 94(IV), LFPPI). Sufficiency is assessed as of the effective filing date and failure can render claims invalid (Article 154(II), LFPPI). Sufficiency generally depends on the specification’s contents, not on external references; referenced but undisclosed information usually cannot satisfy sufficiency.

name: Claims: clarity, conciseness, and support
description: Claims must be clear and concise, precisely define the subject matter for which protection is sought based on essential technical features, be supported by the description, and not exceed the description’s scope.
guidance: (Article 94(V), LFPPI; Article 29, RIPL). Claims are interpreted as of the effective filing date using the description, drawings, sequence listings, and deposit information. Use standard technical terminology of the field to satisfy clarity (analogous to definiteness).

name: Claims format and drafting preferences
description: Claims should be numbered consecutively using Arabic numerals; the first claim must be independent and refer to essential features; claims must be drafted based on the invention’s technical features; claims must not reference the description or drawings unless necessary; claims may include reference signs in parentheses for clarity.
guidance: Article 29, RIPL. The number of claims should correspond to the nature of the claimed invention. Chemical formulas, equations, and tables may be included when appropriate (Article 27, RIPL).

name: Dependent claim rules and limitations
description: Dependent claims must reproduce and include features of the claim to which they refer and specify additional features consistent with the related claim; multiple dependent claims cannot depend on another multiple dependent claim and cannot be the basis for a claim that depends on two or more claims.
guidance: Article 97, LFPPI; Article 29, RIPL. Draft dependent claims carefully to avoid prohibited dependency structures.

name: Preamble/characteristic-part structure (Agreement rules)
description: When applicable, a claim must contain a preamble indicating technical features necessary for understanding the claimed object and a characteristic part introduced by phrases like 'characterized in that' which concisely set forth the technical features to be protected.
guidance: Under Article 12 of the Agreement that Establishes the Rules for Filing Applications before IMPI. A preamble is unnecessary for self-explanatory novel products (e.g., new chemical compound). Preambles are typically helpful for mechanical inventions.

name: Description must support claims and align with claims
description: The description must provide adequate support for the claims and be drafted according to the submitted claims; claims must not exceed the description’s scope and the description should be used to interpret claims.
guidance: (Articles 94, 96, LFPPI; Article 28, RIPL). Failure to support claims may lead to limitation or revocation of claim scope; amendments cannot introduce new subject matter not in the original filing.

name: Experimental data and exemplification
description: Applicants need not provide experimental evidence for every embodiment claimed, but descriptions lacking exemplification or experimental demonstration commonly are considered unclear or insufficient; comparative examples are advisable for selection patents and where technical advantage must be shown.
guidance: Post-filing experimental evidence is commonly accepted when submitted in response to substantive objections, provided it is consistent with the original application and supports the technical effect claimed.

name: Avoiding vague, subjective or comparative claim language
description: Claims and descriptions should avoid vague terms (e.g., 'approximately', 'around') and subjective or comparative expressions (e.g., 'greater', 'thin', 'strong') that introduce ambiguity; use specific values, ranges, and clearly defined technical terms.
guidance: Using standard terminology of the technical field increases likelihood of satisfying clarity/definiteness. Define terms in the description where ambiguity may arise.

name: Practical prosecution and examination remedies
description: If IMPI raises objections (clarity, enablement, support), patentees can submit additional examples, experimental data, or clarifications provided the new information is consistent with the original application; amendments may be necessary but must avoid new matter.
guidance: Prepare to define ambiguous terms, provide technical examples and the best-known method, and be ready to narrow claims or file divisional applications when unity objections arise. IMPI may request samples or models in unusual cases (Article 26, RIPL).

name: Restrictions on patentability related to subject matter
description: Claims directed to purely abstract ideas (mathematical methods or general principles) are not allowed; the specification should demonstrate technical application and contribution.
guidance: For computer-implemented inventions, focus on technical solution and implementation details rather than abstract functional descriptions. See Practice Note on Patent-Eligible Subject Matter (Mexico).

name: Support requirement preventing overbroad/genus claims
description: The description must adequately support any claimed ranges, genera or species; disclosing specific ranges or species may limit claim breadth and claims cannot generally claim a genus unless the description provides adequate support for it.
guidance: When claiming broad subject matter, ensure the description contains sufficient examples, embodiments, or reasoning to support the breadth; otherwise expect examiner objections or validity challenges.

name: Limitations on using international applications to 'reach back'
description: International applications which (1) were filed prior to November 29, 2000, or (2) did not designate the U.S., or (3) were not published in English under PCT Article 21(2) by WIPO, may not be used to reach back (bridge) to an earlier filing date through a priority or benefit claim for prior art purposes under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e).
guidance: Examiners and practitioners must check filing dates, designations, and publication status/language before treating an international application as antedating prior art under pre-AIA 102(e).

name: Benefit of U.S. parent filing date under 35 U.S.C. 120
description: A U.S. patent or patent application publication that claims the benefit of an earlier filing date under 35 U.S.C. 120 will be accorded the earlier filing date as its prior art date under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e), provided the earlier-filed application properly supports the subject matter relied upon in any rejection in compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
guidance: In other words, subject matter used in a rejection must be disclosed in the earlier-filed application in compliance with written description/enablement requirements in order to be entitled to the earlier filing date. See MPEP § 2136 and examples referenced in the text.

name: Methods to overcome a pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection
description: An applicant may overcome a pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection by: (A) persuasively arguing claims are patentably distinguishable; (B) amending the claims to patentably distinguish; (C) filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 showing the reference invention is not by 'another'; (D) filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(a) showing prior invention (in limited circumstances); (E) submitting and perfecting a claim to priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d); and/or (F) submitting a benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or 120 and establishing the prior application satisfies 35 U.S.C. 112 enablement/written description.
guidance: Choose the appropriate method depending on the nature of the reference and available evidence. See MPEP §§ 2132.01, 2133.02(a), 715, 716.10, and the specific subsections referenced for details on timing, content, and limits (e.g., when 1.131 is or is not permitted, and written description/enablement requirements).

name: Requirements for claiming foreign priority (35 U.S.C. 119) and benefit claims (35 U.S.C. 119(e)/120)
description: To antedate a reference, an applicant can: (A) submit a claim to priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) within the time in 37 CFR 1.55 and establish that the prior foreign application satisfies enablement and written description of 35 U.S.C. 112(a)/pre-AIA 112 first paragraph; or (B) submit a benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or 120 within 37 CFR 1.78 and establish the prior application satisfies 35 U.S.C. 112(a)/pre-AIA 112 first paragraph.
guidance: For applications filed on/after Sept 16, 2012, a corrected application data sheet under 37 CFR 1.76 identifying the prior application is often required; for earlier applications, specification amendments or oath/declaration techniques may be needed. Certified priority documents (and English translations when necessary) must be filed to perfect the priority date. Failure to perfect the priority/benefit claim prevents using that earlier date to antedate a reference.

name: Affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 to show reference is inventor's own work
description: An affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 can overcome a pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection by showing the relied-on reference describes an inventor's or at least one joint inventor's own work (i.e., the reference is not 'by another').
guidance: A 1.132 declaration cannot be a naked assertion of inventorship — it must provide context, explanation, or evidence to support the claim (see EmeraChem Holdings v. Volkswagen example of insufficiency). Proof may include showing association (same assignee) and that the inventor learned of the inventor's work from the inventor directly/indirectly. See MPEP §§ 715.01(a), 715.01(c), 716.10 and § 2136.05(b) for required contents and uses of 1.132 affidavits.

name: Combination claims in reference do not prove inventorship of individual elements
description: The existence of combination claims in a reference is not evidence that the inventor or at least one joint inventor invented individual elements or subcombinations included in that combination if those elements/subcombinations are not separately claimed.
guidance: Use case law (In re DeBaun, In re Facius, In re Mathews) when evaluating whether a reference inventor actually invented an unclaimed subcomponent; a declaration of non-inventorship that is vague or addresses only a generic concept may be insufficient.

name: Derivation requires complete conception by another and communication to the deriver
description: Derivation requires that another party completely conceive the invention and communicate that conception to the alleged deriver prior to any date on which the deriver possessed knowledge of the invention.
guidance: The communication must be sufficient to enable one of ordinary skill in the art to construct and successfully operate the invention (Kilbey v. Thiele; Hedgewick v. Akers; Gambro Lundia AB v. Baxter). Examiners look for evidence of enabling communication when assessing derivation claims.

name: Order of specification sections (37 C.F.R. 1.77(b))
description: The specification should include the following sections in order: (1) Title of the invention; (2) Cross-reference to related applications; (3) Statement regarding federally sponsored research or development; (4) The names of the parties to a joint research agreement; (5) Incorporation by reference statement for certain electronic file types; (6) Statement regarding prior disclosures by the inventor(s); (7) Background of the invention; (8) Brief summary of the invention; (9) Brief description of the several views of the drawing; (10) Detailed description of the invention; (11) A claim or claims; (12) Abstract of the disclosure; (13) Sequence Listing (where applicable).
guidance: This ordering is the preferred arrangement for a nonprovisional specification. Each item should be present as applicable; sequence listing requirements (item 13) are addressed in 37 C.F.R. 1.821–1.825 and MPEP §§ 2421–2431.

name: CLAIM OR CLAIMS formatting and placement
description: The claim or claims must commence on a separate sheet or electronic page (37 CFR 1.52(b)(3)). Where a claim sets forth a plurality of elements or steps, each element or step of the claim should be separated by a line indentation. There may be plural indentations to further segregate subcombinations or related steps.
guidance: Place claims on a separate sheet/page and format with line indentations between elements or steps to clearly delineate claim structure. See 37 CFR 1.75 and MPEP 608.01(i)-(p) for further claim formatting rules.

name: Recommendation for provisional applications
description: It is recommended that provisional applications follow the same general format as the nonprovisional specification, although claims are not required.
guidance: Although provisional filings do not require claims, adopting the recommended arrangement increases clarity and may ease conversion or continuity filings.

name: Claim indentation and subcombination formatting
description: Where a claim sets forth a plurality of elements or steps, each element or step should be separated by a line indentation; there may be plural indentations to further segregate subcombinations or related steps (see 37 CFR 1.75).
guidance: Use indentation consistently to show claim element hierarchy and subcombinations for readability and correct claim interpretation.

name: Use of the public record to determine claim meaning
description: Courts should rely on the public record (claims, specification, prosecution history) to determine what the patent does and does not claim and to resolve vague terms, rather than extrinsic evidence.
guidance: The Article explains that testimony (including patentee testimony) is given little weight and that extrinsic evidence is disfavored because it risks changing claim meaning 'in derogation of the indisputable public records consisting of the claims, the specification and the prosecution history.' Example citations: Phillips v. AWH Corp.; courts prefer using the public record to aid public notice.

name: Interpret claims to incentivize precise initial claim drafting
description: Claims should be interpreted in a manner that creates incentives for applicants to draft precise claims in their initial applications to reduce uncertainty in claim scope.
guidance: This interpretive approach aims to motivate ex ante clarity by imposing costs (e.g., rejections) on vague claims so applicants choose clearer language up front. The Article links this to the idea of a 'penalty default' that increases the cost ex post if clarity is absent, but notes practical limits to the incentive (applicants may lack resources or information).

name: Presumption against broad constructions that ensnare unwary infringers
description: Ambiguous claims should presumptively not be construed broadly if such a construction would 'ensnare unwary infringers' or improperly expand claim scope leading to invalidity.
guidance: Courts apply a presumption favoring narrower readings of ambiguous claims in litigation to protect potential infringers and avoid granting unjustifiably broad post-issuance scope. The Article cites Athletic Alternatives v. Prince Mfg. and discusses this presumption as one of three claim-interpretation approaches supporting public notice.

name: Broadest Reasonable Construction (BRC) during prosecution to promote iterative clarification
description: During prosecution, claims should be given the broadest reasonable construction to encourage rejection of imprecise claims, prompting applicants to amend and thereby create a clearer public record.
guidance: The Article states the BRC was created to (1) generate clarifying amendments and a developed prosecution record through iterative rejections, (2) induce more precise initial drafting, and (3) fix an outer limit for claims. Example: In re Bigio — BRC led to rejection based on toothbrush prior art and forced Bigio to amend a claim to 'hair brush for a person’s head or scalp.' The Article also notes limits: examiners may still allow broad claims due to inadequate prior art or differing understandings.

name: BRC as an ex ante 'penalty default' to create drafting incentives
description: The BRC should function like a penalty default: by imposing a costly consequence (broad construction leading to rejection) on vague claims, applicants are incentivized ex ante to draft narrower, clearer claims.
guidance: The Article explains the theoretical similarity to economic penalty defaults but notes empirical failures: the cost of iterative prosecution does not reliably induce precise initial drafting, applicants may gamble, and the rule’s effect depends on examiner practice and search quality.

name: BRC to fix outer limits of claim scope (prevent later expansion)
description: If the USPTO applies the broadest reasonable construction at prosecution and states its understanding clearly, that construction can serve as a fixed outer boundary so courts will not later construe claims more broadly in litigation.
guidance: In theory this prevents unwary infringers from being later caught by broader litigation interpretations. In practice, the Article finds this effect limited because courts sometimes construe claims more broadly than the USPTO, and appellate reversal/modification rates for claim constructions are high (cited empirical statistics).

name: Iterative improvements via rejection-and-amendment process
description: A healthy prosecution process should produce iterative improvements: broad constructions cause rejections, applicants amend to clarify, and the resulting prosecution history clarifies claim scope for the public.
guidance: The Article describes how iterative rejection/amendment builds a written record showing what the applicant/examiner believe the claims mean (and do not mean). However, it notes practical barriers: examiners often exercise broad discretion, may not suggest corrective language, and applicants alone determine amendments—so iterative improvements can be incomplete or produce new ambiguities (Bigio example where some claims were clarified while others issued broadly).

name: Examiners must conduct adequate prior art searches (limitations noted)
description: Effective application of BRC presumes examiners perform adequate prior-art searches so that broad constructions will surface relevant art to prompt rejections of overbroad claims.
guidance: The Article documents limits on examiners' searches: resource/time constraints; statutory/search-method mismatch (statute covers prior use but examiners focus on printed publications); prohibition on using 'common knowledge and common sense'; limits on Internet searches pre-publication. Inadequate searches can allow vague, broad claims to issue as 'valid' and undermine public notice.

name: Complete review of specification, dependent claims, and prosecution history
description: Examiners should thoroughly review the specification, dependent claims, and prosecution history because these materials bear on claim scope and can disclose disclaimers limiting claim meaning.
guidance: Under BRC, examiners often fail to identify disclaimers or nuances in dependent claims; dependent claims receive less scrutiny because they are assumed narrower than independent claims. The Article gives Inpro II as an example where failure to address ambiguity (parallel vs. serial interface) at prosecution led to expensive litigation.

name: Scrutinize dependent claims and new claim language
description: Examiners should not assume dependent claims are automatically acceptable whenever the independent claim is allowable; new language in dependent claims may affect search scope and requires independent scrutiny.
