guidance: The text warns that the presumption that dependent claims are patentable if the parent is patentable can leave ambiguities untested until litigation, because added dependent limitations could change the relevant prior-art search or claim meaning.

name: Account for applicant-side limits on producing clarity (incentives and abilities)
description: Assess whether applicants have incentives, drafting skill, and resources to produce clear claims—lack of these can prevent the BRC from causing ex ante clarity.
guidance: The Article notes patentees may not write well, may lack funds, or may not think the patent justifies investment in specificity. Applicants are not required to search for prior art before filing; the initial claim language reflects their beliefs, and they often await examiner search results before amending. Duty of candor (37 C.F.R. §1.56) exists, but applicants control amendments.

name: Courts in litigation will often construe claims more narrowly to preserve validity
description: Because courts cannot amend claims post-issuance, in litigation they may construe claims narrowly (to save validity), and thus cannot rely on the prosecution-stage iterative or penalty-default mechanisms.
guidance: The Article explains courts' limited ability to clarify claims after issuance justifies using different interpretive rules in litigation than during prosecution; cites cases (In re Etter, Athletic Alternatives, Phillips) and explains that reliance on post-issuance narrowing can protect alleged infringers but reduces the BRC's effectiveness in fixing outer claim limits.

name: No fixed temporal standard for 'long possession' — practical commercial test
description: No specific lapse of time is adopted as a universal standard; the general principle is that the time elapsed must have been sufficient to permit articles or machines to be constructed by the patentee in conformity with his claim, and to be sold publicly and repeatedly.
guidance: Court looks to practical evidence: construction, public sales, repeated use — not to an arbitrary number of years. Short periods have sufficed where actual use and sales occurred; in some cases a few years (even 3–6) have been enough if accompanied by public use and sales.

name: How to complete the statement concerning amendments (specific check‑boxes)
description: If amendments to the claims were made under Article 19 prior to filing the demand, the statement must indicate whether those amendments should be taken into account or considered reversed by an Article 34 amendment. If no Article 19 amendments have been made but the time to file them has not expired, the statement may indicate that the applicant wishes the start of IPE to be postponed. If Article 34 amendments are submitted with the demand, the statement must so indicate.
guidance: A detailed explanation is given for each check‑box in Box IV; marking the appropriate box affects whether and when the IPEA starts examination and whether particular amendments will be considered as the basis for examination.

name: Consequences of failure to timely reply to a new ground of rejection
description: If appellant fails to timely file a reply under 37 CFR 1.111 or a reply brief in response to an examiner's answer that contains a new ground of rejection, the appeal will be sua sponte dismissed as to the claims subject to the new ground of rejection. If all claims under appeal are subject, the entire appeal will be dismissed.
guidance: Examiners will not normally determine sufficiency of such replies once jurisdiction passes to the Board. If some claims remain, dismissal authorizes cancellation of the affected claims and the appeal continues as to the remaining claims.

name: 37 CFR 1.113(b) — examiner must state all grounds and reasons
description: In making such final rejection, the examiner shall repeat or state all grounds of rejection then considered applicable to the claims in the application, clearly stating the reasons in support thereof.
guidance: A final action must identify and explain each ground of rejection so applicant understands the basis for the final rejection.

name: MPEP § 706.07(a) — limitation on introducing new grounds in subsequent final action
description: Second or any subsequent actions on the merits shall be final, except where the examiner introduces a new ground of rejection that is neither necessitated by applicant's amendment of the claims, nor based on information submitted in an IDS filed during the period set forth in 37 CFR 1.97(c) with the fee.
guidance: An examiner generally may not introduce a new ground of rejection in a final action unless it was necessitated by a claim amendment or arises from an IDS timely filed with required fee; use of IDS-submitted info may allow finality but introduction of other new grounds is improper.

name: Claims limited to the actual invention — whole machine vs improvement
description: If a specific machine already exists producing certain effects, merely adding an improvement does not entitle the patentee to a patent for the whole machine — only for the actual improvement.
guidance: A patent cannot be broader than the inventor's contribution. Combining previously separate operations into one machine does not make the whole machine new unless the principles of operation themselves are new. Examples: lever in a watch or Watt's improvements do not permit patents covering the whole machine beyond the actual improvement.

name: Include all relevant groups/subgroups and secondary classification areas
description: Every group/subgroup of CPC and/or class/subclass of the U.S. Patent Classification and other organized systems pertinent to the claimed subject matter should be included, from largest subcombinations to the most elementary part.
guidance: Field of search should extend to all probable areas relevant to claimed subject matter and cover disclosed features likely to be claimed; consult other examiners or supervisors for unfamiliar subject matter.

name: Internet searching for published applications allows applicant terminology
description: For published applications, reissue, or reexamination proceedings (not confidential), restrictions on search queries applicable to unpublished apps do not apply and queries may include terminology from applicant’s disclosure and claims.
guidance: See MPEP § 707.05(e) for citation of electronic documents and § 719.05 for documenting Internet searches.

name: Thorough and complete search commensurate with most detailed claims
description: A prerequisite to speedy and just examination is that a thorough and complete search, commensurate with the limitations appearing in the most detailed claims, be made in preparing the first action on the merits.
guidance: The first action should be prepared so the second action can be made final or the application allowed with no further searching other than updating the original search.

name: Search should anticipate likely claim amendments
description: Search should, insofar as possible, cover all subject matter examiner anticipates might be incorporated into applicant’s amendment.
guidance: Applicants can facilitate this by including claims ranging from the broadest to the most detailed they would accept.

name: Study full specification of references
description: For all references considered (NPL, foreign, domestic patents), examiner should study the specification/description sufficiently to determine the full value of the reference disclosure relative to claimed or claimable subject matter.
guidance: Examine the full disclosure to evaluate relevance and applicability to claims.

name: Search related post‑grant proceedings when specified conditions met
description: An application under examination is sufficiently related to another proceeding such that a complete search requires review of a post-grant proceeding if any one of enumerated conditions are met (e.g., reissue of a patent previously/currently subject to a post-grant proceeding; benefit claim to a prior US application that issued as a patent previously/currently subject to a post-grant proceeding).
guidance: If any such condition is met, examiner is required to review specific PTAB papers of related post-grant proceedings.

name: When related PTAB proceeding identified, compare claims and consider listed documents
description: When a PTAB post-grant proceeding is identified as related, examiner must compare the claims of the examined application with challenged patent claims to determine if they have similar scope or similar claim elements.
guidance: If similar, examiner must consider: Petition; Patent Owner’s Preliminary Response; PTAB’s Decision on Institution (and subsequent Patent Owner responses and Final Written Decision if instituted); any court decisions and subsequent PTAB proceedings; and any parties’ supporting evidence including expert declarations. Document review per MPEP § 719.05 II.A., element L.

name: C-STAR (C*) designations for claimed concepts
description: A C* is applied to an allocated symbol when that symbol represents at least one claimed concept; C* designations should be applied regardless of type or position and at least one CPC symbol must be designated C*.
guidance: Do not allocate new CPC symbols merely to address C*s; designate narrow/specific symbols falling within claimed subject matter as C*.

name: Standard for motions to disqualify or strike (need authority and evidence)
description: Motions seeking disqualification or striking of opposing counsel must be supported by binding authority and evidence of the alleged conflict or misconduct; unsupported assertions or a jumble of allegations are insufficient.
guidance: The Order denied a motion to disqualify where the movant provided no proof or controlling authority and only advanced unsupported claims.

name: Minimum content for international filing date (name, description, claims)
description: The application must contain the name of the applicant, a description, and a claim or claims pursuant to PCT Article 11(1)(iii)(c)-(e).
guidance: To secure an international filing date, include at least these elements in the initial filing; missing items may lead to defects and invitations to correct.

name: Effect of a markedly different characteristic on eligibility
description: If the claim includes a nature-based product that has markedly different characteristics, then the claim does not recite a product of nature exception and is eligible (Step 2A: NO) at Pathway B unless the claim recites another exception (such as a law of nature or abstract idea, or a different natural phenomenon).
guidance: For claims where the entire claim is a single nature-based product (e.g., a claim to “a Lactobacillus bacterium”), once a markedly different characteristic in that product is shown, no further analysis would be necessary for eligibility because no product of nature exception is recited (i.e., Step 2B is not necessary because the answer to Step 2A is NO). For claims including limitations in addition to the nature-based product, examiners should consider whether the claim recites another exception and thus requires further eligibility analysis.

name: Evaluating whether a characteristic is 'markedly different'
description: Compare the claimed product's characteristics to the counterpart to determine whether they are 'markedly different.'
guidance: To show a marked difference, a characteristic must be changed as compared to nature and cannot be an inherent or innate characteristic of the naturally occurring counterpart or an incidental change. The inventor must have caused the claimed product to possess at least one characteristic that is different from that of the counterpart. If there is no change in any characteristic, the claimed product lacks markedly different characteristics and is a product of nature exception. If there is a change in at least one characteristic and that change came about or was produced by the inventor’s efforts or influences, then the change will generally be considered a markedly different characteristic so the claimed product is not a product of nature exception.

name: Examples of products lacking markedly different characteristics
description: Court examples illustrating products found to be products of nature because they lacked markedly different characteristics.
guidance: Myriad: isolated gene sequences that differ only by isolation (loss of chromosomal covalent bonds) but are otherwise identical to natural genes were not markedly different. Ambry Genetics: synthetic primers corresponding to natural nucleotide sequences lacked markedly different structure and function (primer binding is innate), thus they were products of nature. In re Marden: ductility of vanadium is inherent and not conferred by a new combination. Roslin: cloned animals that are genetic copies lacked markedly different characteristics; alleged phenotypic differences not claimed could not make them markedly different. These examples underscore that incidental differences, innate functions, or unclaimed phenotypic variations do not establish marked difference.

name: No new matter may be introduced in amendments (37 CFR 1.121(f))
description: No amendment may introduce new matter into the disclosure of an application.
guidance: When new matter is introduced into the specification, the amendment should be objected to under 35 U.S.C. 132 (35 U.S.C. 251 for reissue) and a requirement made to cancel the new matter. The subject matter considered to be new matter must be clearly identified by the examiner. If new matter has been entered into the claims or affects claim scope, the affected claims should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, because the new matter is not described in the application as originally filed. While amendments involving new matter are ordinarily entered, such matter is required to be canceled from the descriptive portion and affected claims rejected.

name: Condition for examination defined (37 CFR 1.704(f))
description: An application filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a) is in condition for examination when it includes a specification with at least one claim and an abstract (§ 1.72(b)), papers in compliance with § 1.52, drawings if any (§ 1.84), any required English translations, Sequence Listing/Sequence Listing XML (if applicable), an inventor’s oath/declaration or ADS with § 1.63(b) info, basic filing/search/examination fees, any certified copy required by § 1.57(a), and any application size fee required under § 1.16(s). International applications must have entered the national stage and include analogous items and fees.
guidance: This list is used for applying the eight-month condition-for-examination rule and other timing rules; missing elements mean the application is not ready and applicant delay may be charged.

name: Fallback: reasonable royalty must be attributable to specific contribution over prior art
description: If neither the entire market value rule nor marketplace licensing is applicable, the trier of fact must ensure the damages award accurately reflects the harm caused by the infringement; the jury is admonished to apply the reasonable royalty calculation only to the portion of the economic value of the infringing product or process properly attributable to the claimed invention’s specific contribution over the prior art.
guidance: The Committee intends “specific contribution over the prior art” to capture the ‘actual invention’ or the reason the patent was allowed. For combination inventions whose elements are individually in the prior art, contribution may include added function or enhanced value from the combination, if demonstrated. Language mandating a specific methodology (e.g., apportionment) was removed; instead the court shall exclude economic value properly attributable to prior art and other features or improvements (whether patented or not). The provision is aimed at ensuring damages reflect harm from the claimed invention, not unrelated features.

name: Willfulness pleading and notice requirements
description: Conclusive or boilerplate allegations no longer suffice for notice of infringement; the patent holder must allege acts of infringement sufficient to give the alleged infringer an objectively reasonable apprehension of suit, and must plead with particularity which products or processes allegedly infringe which claims of the patent, as well as the basis for such a belief.
guidance: Aims to prevent pleading of willfulness based on conclusory letters or vague accusations; intended to curb abusive pleadings that impose discovery burdens.

name: Evidentiary standard for certain allegations (clear and convincing)
description: Some allegations of lying or misrepresentation to the Board require proof by clear and convincing evidence.
guidance: The Director observed that OED had not established by clear and convincing evidence that Respondent lied or was dishonest to the Board; therefore, the level of proof required is a material consideration when evaluating such claims.

name: Utility: when it is fact versus law
description: The question of utility is sometimes a question of fact and sometimes one of law; a 'useful invention' is one not injurious to society, not frivolous or insignificant, and capable of use to derive some advantage.
guidance: If the invention is clearly injurious or not a patentable subject, utility is a legal question for the court; if the means' practical success is in doubt, utility depends on evidence and is a question of fact for the jury. Degree of usefulness is unimportant, but total failure of an essential claimed part renders the patent invalid.

name: Construction of the specification and claim extent belongs to the court
description: The construction of the specification as to the extent of the claim is for the court: the court must determine what the claim actually covers and whether the patent is valid in law.
guidance: The jury takes the court's construction when assessing novelty/validity; if terms of art require explanation by evidence, the jury may be called to find meanings of those terms.

name: Sources for construing a claim: descriptive parts and claim language
description: The court may resort to the descriptive parts of the specification to ascertain what the patentee has said he had invented; if the description is clear, claim language should be construed to include the actual invention previously set forth (ut res magis valeat quam pereat).
guidance: The whole specification, including preamble/body/summing-up, should be examined together unless a part explicitly excludes the rest.

name: Presumption against claiming known in-use items
description: A patentee is to be presumed not to intend to claim things which he must know to be in use; specifications should be read, consistently with fair import, to make the claim coextensive with the actual discovery or invention.
guidance: The degree to which a thing was known and its familiarity will influence whether the patentee is understood to have claimed it.

name: Construction based on factual statements incorporated into the description
description: Sometimes construction rests on facts that are referred to as part of the description and govern it; if such facts are controverted they are left to the jury, but if proved or admitted, the court will take notice of them in giving legal construction.
guidance: Example: where specification described a 'flyer in one continuous piece' and claims summed up combination language, the court considered the admitted facts to determine the kind of flyer intended.

name: Conditional versus absolute constructions depending on evidence
description: If facts material to claim construction are not left in doubt by the evidence, the court will give the construction absolutely; if the evidence requires factual findings by the jury, the court will give the construction conditionally.
guidance: The judge must observe what facts are controverted and what are not, and inform himself by the evidence while determining the legal meaning of the claim.

name: Lead compound obviousness (structural similarity)
description: Obviousness based on structural similarity can be proved by identification of some motivation that would have led one of ordinary skill in the art to select and then modify a known compound (i.e. a lead compound) in a particular way to achieve the claimed compound. ... it is sufficient to show that the claimed and prior art compounds possess a ‘sufficiently close relationship ... to create an expectation,' in light of the totality of the prior art, that the new compound will have ‘similar properties’ to the old.
guidance: The requisite motivation may come from any number of sources and need not necessarily be explicit in the art. Office personnel should consider whether the prior art taught modifying the lead compound in the claimed way and whether that modification would have been expected to yield similar properties. Structural similarity alone is insufficient without a reason to select and modify the prior art compound and a reasonable expectation of success. Example: Eisai (lead compound characterized) and Altana/Procter & Gamble discussions illustrate need for both a reason to modify and reasonable expectation.

name: Requirement to articulate reason to select and modify a lead compound
description: There must be some reason 'to select and modify a known compound' to support an obviousness rejection based on a lead compound rationale.
guidance: When asserting obviousness from a lead compound, examiners must identify the motivating factors (explicit or implicit in the prior art) that would have led one of ordinary skill to choose that starting compound and to make the claimed modification. Reasons may derive from the totality of the prior art, expert opinion, or other sources; mere existence of the prior compound is insufficient. See Altana Pharma AG v. Teva, and related Federal Circuit precedent.

name: Identification of a single lead compound not always required
description: The lead compound cases do not stand for the proposition that identification of a single lead compound is necessary in every obviousness rejection of a chemical compound.
guidance: Alternate bases for obviousness may include prior art suggestions to formulate compounds having certain structurally defined moieties or viewing a claimed compound as two known compounds linked by a chemical linker. If one of ordinary skill would have known how to synthesize such a compound and the structural/functional result would have been reasonably predictable, a prima facie case of obviousness might exist without a single identified lead compound.

name: Use of Known Technique To Improve Similar Devices (methods or products)
description: To reject a claim based on applying a known technique to improve similar devices, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries and articulate: (1) a finding that the prior art contained a 'base' device; (2) a finding that the prior art contained a 'comparable' device that has been improved in the same way as the claimed invention; (3) a finding that one of ordinary skill could have applied the known 'improvement' technique in the same way to the 'base' device and the results would have been predictable; and (4) any additional Graham-based findings necessary to explain obviousness.
guidance: Rationale: a method of enhancing a class of devices has become part of ordinary capabilities, so applying it to a base device would have been predictable. Cite KSR: if actual application would have been beyond skill, then not obvious. Example support: Intel Corp. v. PACT XPP Schweiz AG (both references address same problem; motivation to combine under KSR). If any of the four findings cannot be made, this rationale cannot support obviousness.

name: "Obvious to Try"—finite identified predictable solutions with reasonable expectation
description: To reject a claim based on an 'obvious to try' rationale, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries and articulate: (1) that a recognized problem or need existed at the relevant time; (2) that a finite number of identified, predictable potential solutions to the problem existed; (3) that one of ordinary skill could have pursued the known potential solutions with a reasonable expectation of success; and (4) any additional Graham findings necessary to explain obviousness.
guidance: Rationale: a skilled person has reason to pursue known options and, if success was expected, the result may reflect ordinary skill. Courts emphasize predictability and reasonable expectation of success; mere 'obvious to try' without predictability is insufficient. Consider characteristics of the science/technology, state of advance, specificity of prior art, and predictability of results (Abbott Labs. v. Sandoz caution). Examples: Pfizer v. Apotex (finite set of pharmaceutically acceptable salts gave reasonable expectation); courts have applied this especially in chemical arts but require careful, context-specific analysis. If any required finding cannot be made, do not use this rationale.

name: Resolve Graham factual inquiries before applying any rationale
description: Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries (scope and content of prior art; differences between prior art and claims; level of ordinary skill; and objective evidence) before applying lead compound, known technique, or obvious-to-try rationales.
guidance: All of the specific rationales (lead compound, known technique, obvious to try) are contingent upon first addressing the Graham factors. Additional findings based on those inquiries may be necessary for a proper explanation of obviousness in view of the facts of the case.

name: Statement of claims / what is claimed as novel
description: The inventor must state what he claims as novel.
guidance: Patents are granted on the points specified in the claims (Spain). Claim drafting determines scope of protection; claims must be consistent with specification.

name: Specifications, claims, and measurement/drawing formalities (Spain example)
description: Documents needed: (1) power of attorney in Spanish; (2) a complete specification explaining the invention and the points claimed — the patent will be granted on the points specified in the claims; references to weights or measures must be in the French metrical system; (3) drawings must be on tracing cloth, in black ink, without colours, on the French metrical scale, and in duplicate.
guidance: Follow strict formal drafting and drawing requirements (language, units, medium, duplication). Incomplete filings may be given time to correct depending on applicant residence.

name: Nullity for insufficient specification or non-enablement relative to model
description: Patents will be declared null if the specification is not sufficient or does not accord with the model; also if the invention cannot be carried into effect or is not new.
guidance: Enablement/adequacy to practice is essential; mismatch between claims/specification and model/figures can be fatal.

name: Rights of heirs and transmission on death
description: The lawful representatives of a deceased inventor may obtain a patent right for the invention on making application within six months of the death (Transvaal); proprietorship is hereditary in some jurisdictions (Spain).
guidance: Death of inventor triggers specific timing and procedural steps for heirs to claim or continue patent rights.

name: Obviousness-type double patenting (ODP)
description: A judicial doctrine intended to prevent an inventor or assignee from obtaining or owning a second, later-expiring patent that claims only an obvious variant of a first patent. ODP often arises when a continuation application claims an obvious variant of subject matter claimed in an earlier application.
guidance: ODP analysis compares a challenged patent to a reference patent (commonly owned or sharing at least one inventor). ODP's key purposes include preventing unjustified timewise extension of exclusionary rights and avoiding harassment by multiple assignees; ODP can be overcome by filing a terminal disclaimer (subject to requirements). See Practice Note, Double Patenting: Obviousness-Type Double Patenting.

name: Justifications and public-policy purposes of ODP
description: Courts justify ODP based on (i) the public's right to use an invention and its obvious variants after patent expiration and (ii) avoidance of multiple suits from multiple patent owners.
guidance: A 'key purpose' of ODP is to prevent a patent owner from extending exclusivity rights beyond a full patent term, e.g., by obtaining multiple patents with different expiration dates that claim obvious variants of each other (cases cited: In re Van Ornum; In re Fallaux; Novartis decisions).

name: Terminal disclaimer as the primary defense to ODP
description: A patent applicant or owner can overcome ODP by filing a terminal disclaimer (35 U.S.C. § 253; 37 C.F.R. § 1.321(c)) that disclaims any patent term extending beyond the expiration of the reference patent and obligates common ownership of the patents.
guidance: Requirements and practical notes: (i) a terminal disclaimer must be filed before the reference patent expires to be effective; (ii) it includes an obligation that the two patents will only be enforceable while commonly owned; (iii) terminal disclaimers cannot be withdrawn after issuance; (iv) the USPTO has refused contingent terminal disclaimers (see Acadia); (v) a proposed USPTO rule would tie patents connected by a terminal disclaimer together so that invalidity of one claim could render connected patents unenforceable (monitor rulemaking). See Practice Note, Patent Correction: Statutory and Terminal Disclaimers.

name: Federal Circuit Allergan decision narrowing Cellect's reach
description: The Federal Circuit held that 'a first-filed, first-issued, later-expiring claim cannot be invalidated by a later-filed, later-issued, earlier-expiring reference claim having a common priority date.'
guidance: Allergan clarifies that Cellect addressed when a claim may serve as an ODP reference but did not hold that first-filed, first-issued patents are vulnerable to ODP based on later-filed child patents; Allergan thus provides some protection for first-filed, first-issued claims that later receive PTA. The Allergan opinion also emphasized the principle of party presentation where Cellect did not address whether the reference claims were proper ODP references.

name: Practical prosecution and portfolio-management strategies to mitigate ODP/PTA risk
description: Actions patent applicants and owners may take when family members receive differing amounts of PTA that cause different expiration dates, potentially exposing patents to ODP challenges.
guidance: Strategies discussed include: (i) conduct a detailed audit of patent portfolios to identify patents at ODP risk; (ii) preserve PTA by not disclaiming it while the potential reference patent is not near expiration; (iii) prosecute all important claims in a first-filed application to minimize differing expiration dates; (iv) consolidate claims in co-pending applications to avoid one application receiving more PTA than another; (v) seek a restriction requirement to secure § 121 safe harbor; (vi) withdraw a terminal disclaimer before a patent issues to preserve a challenge and maintain PTA (because terminal disclaimers cannot be withdrawn after issuance); (vii) file a reissue application (subject to a two-year limitation for broader claims and full re-examination) rather than pursue claims in a continuation; (viii) appeal ill-founded ODP rejections rather than immediately filing terminal disclaimers (recognizing USPTO appeals are lengthy). This list is non-exhaustive and should inform bespoke practitioner strategies.

name: Written application and specification content (enablement / best mode / distinct claims)
description: Before any inventor shall receive a patent he shall make application ... and shall file in the Patent Office a written description of the same, and of the manner and process of making, constructing, compounding, and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art ... to make, construct, compound, and use the same; and in case of a machine, he shall explain the principle thereof, and the best mode in which he has contemplated applying that principle ... and he shall particularly point out and distinctly claim the part, improvement, or combination which he claims as his invention or discovery; and said specification and claim shall be signed by the inventor and attested by two witnesses.
guidance: Contains classic enablement, best mode, and distinct-claim requirements; specification and claims must be signed and witnessed.

name: Rejection notice and information to applicant
description: Whenever, on examination, any claim for a patent is rejected for any reason whatever, the commissioner shall notify the applicant thereof, giving him briefly the reasons for such rejection, together with such information and references as may be useful in judging of the propriety of renewing his application or of altering his specification; and if ... the applicant shall persist in his claim ... the commissioner shall order a re-examination of the case.
guidance: Commissioner must provide brief reasons and useful references when rejecting claims; applicant can prompt re-examination by persisting.

name: Examiners-in-chief qualifications and duties
description: The examiners-in-chief shall be persons of competent legal knowledge and scientific ability, whose duty it shall be, on the written petition of the appellant, to revise and determine upon the validity of the adverse decisions of examiners upon applications for patents, and for reissues of patents, and in interference cases; and when required by the commissioner, they shall hear and report upon claims for extensions, and perform such other like duties as he may assign them.
guidance: Specifies required mix of legal and scientific competence and enumerates appellate and interference responsibilities.

name: Commissioner powers over office practice and filings
description: The commissioner may ... require all papers filed in the Patent Office, if not correctly, legibly and clearly written, to be printed at the cost of the party filing them. The commissioner, subject to approval of the Secretary, may from time to time establish rules and regulations, not inconsistent with law, for the conduct of proceedings in the Patent Office. The commissioner may print copies of specifications and drawings and copies of claims of current issues and necessary laws/decisions/rules/circulars for public information.
guidance: Commissioner has broad administrative authority to order printing, promulgate rules, and publish official materials; subject to Secretary approval where specified.

name: Printing/certified copies and their evidentiary value
description: Printed copies of the letters-patent of the United States, with the seal of the Patent Office affixed thereto and certified and signed by the Commissioner of Patents, shall be legal evidence of the contents of said letters-patent in all cases.
guidance: Certified printed copies serve as legal evidence; commissioner authorized to print copies of specifications, claims, drawings and related laws/decisions for public information, with specified cost limits in earlier provision.

name: Isolated DNA is not patent eligible
description: Isolated naturally occurring genes are not patent eligible subject matter.
guidance: The Supreme Court found that Myriad did not 'create anything new' by isolating BRCA1/BRCA2 and concluded isolated DNA is a product of nature and therefore generally patent ineligible. The Court relied on earlier precedent (e.g., Funk Brothers) to hold that mere isolation does not create a new composition of matter. This principle means claims that merely recite 'isolated' natural gene sequences will face §101 invalidity.

name: Short cDNA / indistinguishability exception
description: cDNA may be ineligible where it consists of a very short series of DNA without intervening introns and thus is indistinguishable from natural DNA.
guidance: Even if cDNA is generally patent eligible, examiners and drafters should evaluate the length and structure of the claimed cDNA; very short exon-only sequences that are effectively identical to natural sequences may be treated as products of nature.

name: Claims must define sequences more precisely than by saying 'isolated'
description: Claims concerning genes may still be patentable if they define the concerned DNA sequences more precisely, or differently, than simply with the word 'isolated'.
guidance: The Court's ruling suggests claim drafting should avoid relying solely on 'isolated' language and instead claim novel aspects (e.g., engineered changes, specific, novel sequence features, functional or structural modifications) to survive §101 scrutiny.

name: Identity of inventors requirement
description: The inventors of the U.S. nonprovisional application and the foreign application must be the same; right of priority does not exist if inventor A filed abroad and inventor B filed in the U.S., even if ownership is the same. The foreign application may, however, have been filed by the assignee, legal representative, or agent instead of the inventor, provided the inventor is identified in the foreign file.
guidance: An indication of inventor identity in the U.S. oath/declaration identifying the foreign application and stating it was filed by the assignee/representative/agent is acceptable. Joint inventors can each claim benefit of their respective foreign applications for their common U.S. application (see MPEP §605.07).

name: Grounds of Rejection To Be Reviewed (37 CFR 41.37(c)(1)(vi))
description: A concise statement of each ground of rejection presented for review (e.g., 'Whether claims 1 and 2 are unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. 103 over Smith in view of Jones').
guidance: Statements must be specific as to statutory basis and references; general statements like 'Whether claims 1 and 2 are unpatentable' do not comply. The statement must not include argument — arguments belong in the Argument section.

name: Claims Appendix (37 CFR 41.37(c)(1)(viii))
description: An appendix containing a copy of the claims involved in the appeal.
guidance: The copy should be a clean copy without markings (except in reissue applications or specific reexamination rules), double-spaced, and the appendix should start on a new page. See MPEP §1454 for reissue claim presentation and 37 CFR 1.530(d)/(f) for reexamination proceedings.

name: Amendments Filed After Notice of Appeal But Before Filing Brief (37 CFR 41.33(a))
description: Amendments filed after notice of appeal but prior to filing a brief may be admitted as provided in 37 CFR 1.116; specifically, such amendments may be admitted to cancel claims, to comply with form requirements set in a previous action, to present rejected claims in better form for consideration on appeal, or to amend specification/claims upon a showing of good and sufficient reasons why necessary and not earlier presented.
guidance: Entry of a new amendment is not a matter of right and is governed by 37 CFR 41.33 (not 1.116). If the examiner denies entry, use PTOL-303 to notify applicant of non-entry and reasons. Examiners must respond to all amendments filed after appeal and prior to termination; if an amendment clearly places the application in condition for allowance, the examiner may enter and allow it. Otherwise, entry is limited to the situations permitted by the rules.

name: Amendments Filed On or After Filing Brief (37 CFR 41.33(b))
description: Amendments filed on or after the filing date of the brief may be admitted only to cancel claims (without affecting scope of other pending claims) or to rewrite dependent claims into independent form.
guidance: Rewriting dependent claims into independent form includes (A) rewriting a dependent claim into independent form by adding parent claim limitations, and (B) rewriting an independent claim to incorporate subject matter of a dependent claim, canceling the dependent claim, and adjusting dependencies of other claims accordingly. If examiner denies entry of such an amendment after the brief, use PTOL-304 to notify applicant of non-entry and reason.

name: Examiner's Responsibilities Regarding Post-Appeal Amendments and Advisory Actions
description: Examiners must respond to all amendments filed after appeal and prior to termination. If an advisory action indicates an amendment would be entered, the examiner must state how individual rejections would be impacted, except where the amendment merely cancels claims.
guidance: If the examiner determines an amendment places the application clearly in condition for allowance, the examiner may enter the amendment and allow the application. For denials of entry, examiners should use PTOL-303 (before filing brief) or PTOL-304 (after filing brief) to notify the applicant and state reasons for non-entry. Entry of amendment on appeal is governed by 37 CFR 41.33.

name: Partial uselessness and essentiality
description: The uselessness of part of an invention will not vitiate the whole patent unless that part is described as something essential to the invention (or unless its inclusion misleads the public).
guidance: Lewis v. Marling: where a brush claimed was later found unnecessary but not described as essential, the patent was not held void; if patentee knowingly includes a useless 'essential' element to mislead, the patent may be invalid.

name: Patent application contents (required documents)
description: A patent application must contain: a request on the prescribed form; a description; one or more claims; drawings, if any; an abstract; the applicant’s details (name, nationality, legal status, physical address); designation of one or more Member States; Deed of Assignment if applicant is not the inventor; certified copy of the priority document if priority claimed; prescribed application fees; sequence listing if nucleotide/amino acid sequences disclosed.
guidance: Ensure inclusion of sequence listings where applicable. Indicate designated states clearly when filing through national offices to show the application is regional via ARIPO.

name: Combination patents do not grant exclusive rights in old constituent elements singly
description: The patent is for an entire process, made up of several constituents. The patentee does not claim to have been the inventor of the constituents. The exclusive use of them singly is not secured to him. What is secured is their use when arranged in the process.
guidance: Where a patent claims a combination or entire process composed of known elements, others remain free to use individual known elements unless the patentee separately claims them. The patentee cannot appropriate each old device singly by virtue of the combination claim.

name: Recoverable profits only when patented element used substantially as claimed
description: He was liable to account for such profits only when he used slow cooling in connection with reheating in the manner described in Whitney's claim substantially, or when extraneous heat was employed to retard the progress of cooling.
guidance: Liability to account for profits requires that the defendant employ the patented process or element substantially as claimed, not merely use a similar or incidental technique that exists in other processes.

name: Determining FRAND terms (factors considered)
description: FRAND terms are typically determined via negotiation and depend on multiple factors.
guidance: Relevant factors include the value of the technology, the scope of the patent claims, the market demand, and the competitive landscape. There is no single enforcing entity that sets FRAND — courts and regulatory bodies may play a role in settling disputes. Note also that patents not declared to an SSO (e.g., owner did not participate in standard setting) may not be contractually obligated to license on FRAND terms.

name: How to determine if a patent is essential to a standard (six-step process)
description: A recommended process to assess essentiality: (1) Identify relevant standards, (2) Access standard documentation, (3) Search for declarations, (4) Review patent declarations, (5) Verify claims coverage, (6) Seek legal advice if necessary.
guidance: Step details: 1) Identify relevant SSOs (e.g., IEEE, ITU, ETSI). 2) Obtain official standard specifications and technical documentation. 3) Consult declarations (e.g., ETSI IPR Online Database for ICT/3GPP). 4) Examine declarations for patent info, claims and relevance. 5) Analyze patent claims to determine if they cover technology necessary for implementing standard functionalities — perform a patent-to-standard claim mapping (SEP Essentiality Check) to match claim elements to the standard. This mapping can reveal potential patent infringements and establish essentiality. 6) When uncertain, seek a patent attorney or SEP expert to interpret technical specs and assess relevance.

name: Novelty in machinery assessed by mode of operation
description: In machinery, the test of novelty is what is new in the mode of operation: if the principles or peculiar device or manner of producing the given effect are new a patent may be claimed.
guidance: It is not necessary that a prior machine be identical in every respect to defeat a patent; mere change of proportions will not support a patent. In complicated machinery composed largely of long-known elements, focus on the new mode, method, or application of mechanism to produce a new effect or an old effect in a new way.

name: Patents should be construed as contracts between patentee and the public
description: A patent is in substance a contract or bargain between the patentee and the public on points affecting the rights and interests of either party, particularly the extent of the claim and the intelligibility of the description for practice.
guidance: Extent of the claim is primarily a question for the court; intelligibility of the description is generally for the jury under court direction. Construction should be fair: if doubt remains whether the claim is broader than the invention, presume the patentee intended to claim no more than actually invented. Fraud (claiming more than invented) is not to be presumed and must be proved.

name: Two-part inquiry where claim may include pre-existing matter
description: To determine whether a patentee has included in his claim anything that existed before, ascertain (1) whether he makes use of anything not new, and (2) whether that thing, according to the fair import of his language, is represented to be part of the invention he claims.
guidance: Whether he makes use of anything not new is a question of evidence (unless manifest on the face). The second branch involves applying true principles of construction to the claim language. If doubt persists, construe in favor of the patentee so as to make the claim coextensive with the actual invention where consistent with principle.

name: Rule of construction in doubtful cases: favor the patentee (ut res magis valeat quam pereat)
description: Where, after fair construction, doubt remains whether the claim is broader than the invention, the claim should be presumed to claim no more than actually invented; courts have applied maxims like ut res magis valeat quam pereat to support a patentee where consistent with principle.
guidance: This does not protect plainly overbroad claims; where a claim is manifestly too comprehensive the presumption does not apply. The practical effect is to support the patent for the real invention rather than to destroy it lightly for uncertain overbreadth.

name: Decision point: Second Examination — post-response decision and office action procedure
description: If a compliant response is filed, then: An examiner with signatory authority decides to reject or allow claims. An examiner without signatory authority prepares an Office action in which claims are rejected or allowed, and an examiner with signatory authority or SPE reviews, approves, and signs Office action.
guidance: The same decision/signing authority structure applies on second examination after a compliant response. The trigger for this stage is the filing of a compliant response by the applicant.

name: Contemporaneous generic vs specific applications rule
description: When two applications by the same inventor are filed contemporaneously, one with generic claims and the other with specific claims, the inventor does not lose his right to the generic patent because it happens to issue after the issuance of the specific patent.
guidance: Same rule applies where patentee files an improvement after filing for a generic invention and the improvement issues first; no express disclaimer of the first invention is necessary. (Cases cited.)

name: Concurrent applications/patents that do not claim the same invention do not anticipate one another
description: Where several applications describe the same structure or process, but no one of the issued patents claims any invention claimed in any of the others and they are all pending at the same time, the applications and patents cannot be used to anticipate each other.
guidance: Rule applies where none of the issued patents contains claims covering the others; explanation and authorities provided in text.

name: Awareness of differing claim construction standards (USPTO examination vs. PTAB/courts)
description: The USPTO examination standard is the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim; post-grant proceedings before the PTAB and federal courts use the ordinary and customary meaning (the 'Phillips' standard). Both standards are viewed in the context of the person of skill in the art (POSITA) at the time of filing.
guidance: Know which forum will apply which standard (BRI during examination, Phillips for PTAB/courts since Nov. 13, 2018). Strategically, drafting should account for both because both rely on POSITA and the specification; MPEP 2111 constrains BRI to be consistent with ordinary meaning and the specification. See Cuozzo, Phillips, and Federal Register notice changing PTAB standard.

name: Drafting claim-term definitions in the specification (be your own lexicographer)
description: Consider providing detailed definitions of claim terms in the specification; practitioners may act as their own lexicographers to define terms for claim construction.
guidance: There is a tradeoff: specifying definitions can lead courts to adopt narrower constructions than plain meaning, but current trends often favor detailed definitions. When defining terms, consider whether definitions differ from plain and ordinary meaning and whether to include a fallback definition that preserves broader plain-meaning coverage.

name: Consider the Person of Skill in the Art (POSITA) when construing and drafting claims
description: Both BRI and Phillips standards interpret claims in the context of the POSITA at the time of filing.
guidance: Frame claim language and specification examples with the knowledge level and expectations of POSITA in mind; use specification disclosure to clarify ambiguous terms for that hypothetical skilled worker.

name: Markush group membership requirement (recognized class)
description: Members of a Markush group ordinarily must belong to a recognized physical or chemical class or to an art-recognized class (MPEP 803.02; Ex parte Markush).
guidance: When drafting Markush groups, ensure listed members form an art-recognized class (chemical/physical grouping) to avoid challenges to claim correctness or interpretation.

name: Language determines Markush openness/closedness ('consisting of' presumption)
description: Use of 'consisting of' creates a very strong presumption that a Markush group is closed (excludes unrecited elements); 'comprising' and certain phrases (e.g., 'at least one') can support an open interpretation.
guidance: Assume 'consisting of' will be construed as closed unless the specification or prosecution history unmistakably manifests otherwise (Shire). Use claim language carefully to secure desired openness or closedness; case examples: Abbott (presumed exclusion of mixtures), Shire (closed), Amgen (open due to 'at least one').

name: Practice points for Markush drafting (include desired compounds; align dependent claims)
description: Take care to include all desired compounds in a Markush group and ensure any compound recited in a dependent claim also appears in the independent claim's Markush group.
guidance: Omitting a compound from the independent claim's Markush list can render dependent claims improper or invalid. Use claim drafting checklists to confirm that dependent claim species are encompassed by their base claim's Markush group.

name: Dependent claim proper form under 35 U.S.C. §112(d)
description: A claim in dependent form must contain a reference to a previous claim and 'specify a further limitation' of the claimed subject matter; it is construed to incorporate all limitations of the claim to which it refers (35 U.S.C. §112(d); MPEP 608.01(N)).
guidance: Ensure dependent claims truly further limit the base claim and do not introduce subject matter that the base claim did not permit (e.g., salts when the base claim was not open to salts). Failure to further limit can be an independent ground for invalidation (see Multilayer; Pfizer v. Ranbaxy).

name: Avoid improper dependent claims that introduce unrecited categories (examples: salts, homopolymers)
description: Dependent claims that add elements or categories not open in the base claim risk invalidation (e.g., dependent claim reciting 'low density polyethylene homopolymers' when the Markush group did not include that species).
guidance: Cross-check dependent claim limitations against the language and scope of the base claim; if the base claim is closed to certain categories, do not attempt to add them in a dependent claim without ensuring the base claim permits them.

name: Use MPEP and controlling case law to guide drafting choices
description: MPEP sections (e.g., 2111, 803.02, 608.01(N)) and Federal Circuit/Supreme Court cases (Phillips, Cuozzo, Multilayer, Abbott, Shire, Amgen, Pfizer, etc.) provide binding or persuasive guidance on claim construction, Markush interpretation, and dependent-claim form.
guidance: Consult and cite relevant MPEP sections and case law when drafting/specifying claim language. Use prosecution history and specification drafting to support desired claim interpretations in view of precedent.

name: Obligation to pay official/patent fees (who pays)
description: A person who performs a patent-related proceeding shall pay official fees. If the number of claims is increased by amending the specification after a person other than the applicant files a request for examination, the applicant shall pay the fees for examination of the increased claims.
guidance: Payment methods, deadlines and other necessary matters are prescribed by Ordinance of the Ministry; Fee Collection Rules specify amounts and payment methods. Fees are fees for services provided by the State and differ from ordinary taxes.

name: Refunds of patent fees and official fees — qualifying cases
description: Patent/official fees paid shall be refunded only upon payer’s request in specific cases, including: erroneous payments; portions for years after a patent revocation becomes final; portions after invalidation of patent term extension; official fees for filing/priority where application voluntarily withdrawn/abandoned within one month (with exceptions); certain request-for-examination refunds where withdrawal occurs before certain events; refunds for various trial-related withdrawals or dismissals (often half refunds).
guidance: A detailed enumerated list (Article 84) specifies many refund-triggering events and related conditions (including which portions may be refunded). No refund claim may be filed after three years from notice to payer (see timeline rubric).

name: Deadline for refund claims
description: No claim for refund of a patent fee or official fee may be filed after three years from the date when a person receives notice that the refund-triggering event applies.
guidance: If paragraph (1) of Article 84 applies, Commissioner or president of IP Trial and Appeal Board shall notify the payer; the 3-year limitation runs from that notification.

name: Flexibility in recognizing joint inventorship
description: Inventors may apply for a patent jointly even though they did not physically work together or at the same time; each did not make the same type or amount of contribution; or each did not make a contribution to the subject matter of every claim of the patent.
guidance: Joint inventorship is not limited by contemporaneous collaboration, equal contribution, or contribution to every claim — disparate, asynchronous, or partial contributions can still support joint inventorship.

name: Search based on actual U.S. filing date, not parent's filing date when benefit claimed
description: Examiners should search all applications based on the actual U.S. filing date of the application rather than on the filing date of any parent U.S. application for which benefit is claimed, due to 20-year patent term rules (Public Law 103-465).
guidance: Be aware applicants may cancel benefit/priority claims by amending specification; ensure search uses correct effective filing date.

name: Format and citation requirements for electronic documents (WIPO ST.14 alignment)
description: Follow WIPO ST.14 recommended format for electronic documents: make format analogous to paper citation and add (A) type of electronic medium in square brackets (e.g., [online], [CD-ROM]); (B) date retrieved in square brackets (YYYY); (C) 'Retrieved from' and address; (D) DOI or other unique identifier if known; (E) standard identifier like ISBN/ISSN if known; (F) indicate format when multiple renderings exist (e.g., PDF, HTML); (G) use paragraph/sentence/line numbers to describe specific location; (H) include claim/figure/formula/sequence numbers where available; (I) indicate specific headings if pagination not available; (J) indicate specific passages when pagination or internal referencing exists.
guidance: Examples are provided (documents from online databases, Internet, electronic serials). Retain office copies where electronic sources may not be available later. If also available in paper form, it need not be identified as electronic.

name: Restriction for segregable parts / combination-subcombination
description: Designs which involve a change in scope or patentably distinct segregable parts may not be included in the same design application; design protection does not extend to patentably distinct segregable parts of a design.
guidance: Combination/subcombination subject matter, if patentably distinct, must be supported by separate claims, whereas only a single claim is permissible in a design patent application. The only way to protect patentably distinct segregable parts is to apply for separate patents. Restriction to one of the inventions is required under 35 U.S.C. 121 in such situations.

name: Characteristic feature statement — permissibility and caution
description: A 'characteristic features' statement describing a particular feature of novelty or nonobviousness in the claimed design may be permissible in the specification (e.g., 'The characteristic feature of the design resides in [1]').
guidance: While permissible, the patentability of the claimed design is not based on the specified feature but rather on a comparison of the overall appearance of the design with the prior art. Use of a characteristic feature statement may later serve to limit the claim. Examiner notes should ask for brief but accurate descriptions of the feature of novelty or nonobviousness.

name: Necessity for good drawings — drawings as whole disclosure
description: The necessity for good drawings in a design patent application cannot be overemphasized. As the drawing constitutes the whole disclosure of the design, it is of utmost importance that it be so well executed both as to clarity of showing and completeness, that nothing regarding the design sought to be patented is left to conjecture.
guidance: An insufficient drawing may be fatal to validity (35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph) and may negatively affect the effective filing date of a continuing application. Examiner should ensure drawings fully disclose claimed design.

name: Use of broken lines for indicating unimportant features not permitted
description: The ornamental design which is being claimed must be shown in solid lines in the drawing. Broken lines for the purpose of indicating unimportant or immaterial features of the design are not permitted.
guidance: There are no portions of a claimed design which are immaterial or unimportant. See In re Blum and In re Zahn. Where environmental structure is illustrated, broken lines may be used only if clearly designated as environment in the specification (see 37 CFR 1.152 and MPEP § 1503.02, subsection III), and a statement describing the broken lines must be inserted in the specification. Do not use environmental-broken-line paragraphs in international design applications. If superimposed broken lines obscure full-line disclosure, a separate figure showing the broken lines must be included in addition to figures showing only claimed subject matter.

name: Description of broken lines — required statement
description: A statement similar to: 'The broken line showing of [1] is for the purpose of illustrating [2] and forms no part of the claimed design.' should be used to describe the broken lines on the drawing.
guidance: Insert such a statement in the specification preceding the claim. In bracketed form paragraphs, specify the name of the structure and whether the broken lines illustrate 'portions of the "article"' or 'environmental structure', and whether the statement 'must be' or 'has been' inserted.

name: Types of changes considered 'amendments' under 37 CFR 1.312
description: The amendment of an application by applicant after allowance broadly encompasses any change in the file record of the application.
guidance: Examples include: (A) an amendment to the specification, (B) a change in the drawings, (C) an amendment to the claims, (D) a change in the inventorship, (E) the submission of prior art, etc. (text explicitly lists these examples).

name: Primary examiner authority to enter formal corrections after Notice of Allowance
description: After the Notice of Allowance has been mailed, the application is technically no longer under the jurisdiction of the primary examiner. He or she can, however, make examiner’s amendments and has authority to enter amendments submitted after Notice of Allowance which embody merely the correction of formal matters in the specification or drawing, or formal matters in a claim without changing the scope thereof, or the cancellation of claims, without forwarding to the supervisory patent examiner for approval.
guidance: See MPEP § 1302.04 for examiner’s amendments. Such formal corrections may be entered by the primary examiner; other types require supervisory approval.

name: Amendments requiring supervisory patent examiner approval
description: Amendments other than those which merely embody the correction of formal matters without changing the scope of the claims require approval by the supervisory patent examiner.
guidance: TC Director establishes policy for trivial informalities. Amendments that (A) are needed for proper disclosure/protection and (B) require no substantial additional work by the Office may be considered and recommended by the primary examiner for entry. Consider whether amendment reopens prosecution or requires extra work.

name: Required remarks accompanying amendments that affect disclosure/scope/add claims
description: As to amendments affecting the disclosure, the scope of any claim, or that add a claim, the remarks accompanying the amendment must fully and clearly state the reasons on which reliance is placed to show specified points.
guidance: The remarks must state: (A) why the amendment is needed; (B) why the proposed amended or new claims require no additional search or examination; (C) why the claims are patentable; and (D) why they were not presented earlier.

name: Amendments concerning merely formal matters
description: Amendments which embody merely the correction of formal matters in the specification, formal changes in a claim without changing scope, or cancellation of claims may be approved by the primary examiner without supervisory approval.
guidance: Examiner indicates approval by writing 'Enter Formal Matters Only' and initialing. Such amendments do not require submission to supervisory examiner prior to entry. If disapproved in whole or part, supervisory signature is required. Response to Rule 312 Communication (PTO-271) is date stamped and mailed by the TC.

name: Types of amendments ordinarily denied entry (list A–Q)
description: A catalog of amendment categories that are ordinarily denied entry after final prosecution is closed or where other defects exist.
guidance: The MPEP lists: (A) amendments presenting an unpatentable claim or requiring a new search or raising new issues where prosecution is closed; (B) substitute specifications not complying with 37 CFR 1.125; (C) a patent claim suggested by examiner but not timely presented (absent Commissioner authorization); (D) certain copied patent claims (see MPEP § 2307.03); (E) unsigned/improperly signed amendments or signed by suspended/excluded practitioner; (F) amendments filed after statutory/set period for reply; (G) amendments so worded they cannot be entered with accuracy; (H) amendment canceling all claims and presenting no substitute; (I) amendment in application no longer within examiner’s jurisdiction except exceptions; (J) drawing amendments held to contain new matter until settled; (K) amendatory papers with objectionable remarks (37 CFR 1.3) referred to TC Director; (L) amendments not in permanent ink or on easily erasable paper; (M) amendments presenting claims in excess of number paid for without fee; (N) amendments canceling elected invention claims and presenting only nonelected invention claims (nonresponsive); (O) amendments including changes not in compliance with 37 CFR 1.121 (no replacement paragraphs/claims); (P) preliminary amendments unduly interfering with first Office action (37 CFR 1.115(b)); (Q) second/subsequent supplemental replies unduly interfering with an Office action (37 CFR 1.111(a)(2)). While ordinarily denied, a subsequent showing by applicant may lead to entry.

name: Situations where amendments are entered in part (examples A–E)
description: Circumstances in which a partial entry of an amendment is appropriate to avoid record confusion or to accept non-problematic portions.
guidance: Examples: (A) substitute specification unacceptable but other amendatory matter (claims/new claims) acceptable — enter acceptable parts and deny substitute spec entry; (B) 1.312 amendment partly approved and partly disapproved — enter approved parts only; (C) where prosecution on the merits is closed (Ex parte Quayle) and amendment cures only formal defect but adds claims some of which are unpatentable or require further search — enter only formal matter; (D) amendment accompanying motion granted only in part — enter to extent motion was granted; (E) after March 1, 2001, an amendment that amends specification not in compliance with 37 CFR 1.121 but presents rewritten/new claims should be entered in part (deny spec changes, enter compliant claim changes). Examiner writes 'Enter' in red ink and initials left margin opposite enterable portions.

name: Manner of making amendments — 37 CFR 1.121 formatting rules (specification, claims, drawings, no new matter)
description: Amendments in applications are made by filing a paper directing specified amendments and must comply with 37 CFR 1.121 (and §1.52). Rules cover how to present amendments to the specification, replacement sections, substitute specifications, claims, drawings, and limitations such as no new matter.
guidance: Key rules include: (b)(1) instruction unambiguously identifying location to delete/replace/add paragraphs; supply replacement paragraph(s) in clean form and a marked-up version showing changes (brackets for deletions, underlining for additions) except added/deleted paragraphs where marked-up not required; (b)(2) replacement section procedure; (b)(3) substitute specification requires instruction, substitute spec (complying with §1.125(b)), and a marked-up version; (b)(4) deleted matter may be reinstated only by a subsequent amendment presenting the previously deleted matter; (c)(1) claims amended by rewriting must be in clean form and accompanied by a marked-up version on separate pages showing changes; parenthetical status (e.g., 'amended', 'new') must follow claim number and be consistent between clean and marked-up versions; (c)(2) canceled claim may be reinstated only as a new claim with new number; (c)(3) a clean version of entire claim set may be submitted but will be construed as cancellation of prior versions, and a marked-up version is required only for claims being changed; (d) drawings: changes must be submitted on separate paper showing proposed changes in red for approval, and upon approval new compliant drawings (§1.84) must be filed; (e) disclosure consistency: amendment must secure substantial correspondence among claims, specification, and drawings; (f) no amendment may introduce new matter into the disclosure; (g) exception for examiner’s amendments: Office-made changes may be made by specific instructions to insert/delete set forth in examiner’s amendment (compliance with certain paragraphs not required); (h)-(j) special rules for reissue, reexamination, and provisional applications respectively (e.g., reissue amendments follow §1.173; reexamination amendments follow §1.530(d)-(j); provisional amendments not normally made but if made must comply and be placed in provisional file but may not be entered). The term 'brackets' means square brackets [ ].

name: USPTO updates to examination time and routing
description: USPTO is engaged in ongoing updates to examination time, application routing, and examiner performance appraisals, and considers application-specific factors (claim number, IDS volume) when refining times.
guidance: Applicants should be aware that baseline hours per PU and routing practices may change over time and that claim drafting and IDS management can influence the examiner's assigned time.

name: Strategy: minimize examiner time per action (make examination efficient)
description: Design prosecution materials and responses to minimize the time an examiner needs to fully examine and allow an application.
guidance: Tactics include clear claim drafting aligned with commercial embodiments and U.S. law, concise yet complete responses, targeted prior-art explanations, and efficient use of interviews so the examiner can review and decide more quickly.

name: Strategy: consider preliminary amendments before examination
description: Consider submitting preliminary amendments to claims prior to examination to define invention scope in view of preferred commercial embodiments and U.S. law.
guidance: This is particularly useful when pendency before a first office action is long or when the application was drafted initially for another jurisdiction; it may reduce examiner time needed to understand and examine the claims.

name: Rely on case-identified concepts, not judicial descriptors
description: Examiners should rely on the substantive concepts identified in court decisions (the underlying concepts), not merely the shorthand judicial descriptors/labels when determining whether a claimed concept is similar to a court-identified abstract idea.
guidance: Do not mechanically match a claim to a judicial label (e.g., 'fundamental economic practice'); instead analyze whether the claim recites a concept similar to the concepts courts found abstract. Use the cases cited as conceptual guides rather than fixed labels.

name: Claim is directed to an abstract idea only if the claim recites the abstract idea (MPEP Step 2A requirement)
description: Under Step 2A, a claim must recite (set forth or describe) an abstract idea in order to be 'directed to' that abstract idea. Not all inventions that embody or use abstract ideas are necessarily 'directed to' them.
guidance: Keep in mind Alice/Mayo: while all inventions may use laws of nature, natural phenomena, or abstract ideas at some level, Step 2A separates claims that explicitly recite abstract ideas from those that merely may be based on them. Evaluate the claim language for whether it sets forth or describes an abstract concept.

name: If a claim is based on or involves an abstract idea but does not recite it, it is not directed to the abstract idea
description: Claims that are based on or involve an abstract idea but do not actually recite anything similar to a judicially-identified abstract idea are not 'directed to' an abstract idea.
guidance: Examples and relevant cases: Enfish (self-referential table — based on but not directed to organizing information), DDR Holdings (modifying hyperlink protocol to produce hybrid webpages — not directed to previously identified abstract ideas), Trading Technologies (graphical UI improving trader accuracy — not directed). Non-limiting hypotheticals include purely structural or physical device claims (printer, washing machine, earring with sensor), a BRCA1 sequencing method, BIOS loading into volatile memory — these may be based on abstract concepts in the broadest sense but do not recite judicially-identified abstract ideas and thus are not 'directed to' them.

name: If a claim recites an abstract idea but the claim as a whole is directed to an improvement (or otherwise does not seek to tie up the abstract idea), it is not directed to an abstract idea
description: Claims that recite an abstract idea can nevertheless not be 'directed to' that idea when, as a whole, they recite additional elements (such as a technological improvement) showing the claim does not tie up the abstract idea.
guidance: Identify whether the additional elements represent a specific improvement to computer-related technology or other concrete technological improvement (see MPEP §§2106.05(a) and 2106.06(b)). Cases: McRO (automated lip-synchronization and facial animation — improvement in computer-related technology), Enfish (self-referential table — specific improvement in computer operation), Research Corp. (blue-noise mask plus additional steps improving computer functioning). Non-limiting hypotheticals: surgical shears with pressure regulator, robotic arm assembly with sensor/control for smooth motion, autofocus camera system with processor/algorithm/drive mechanism, internal combustion engine with EGR control system — these examples illustrate improvements that render eligibility self-evident.

name: Categories of concepts courts have identified as abstract ideas
description: Courts have repeatedly identified several broad categories of concepts that are commonly treated as abstract ideas: (I) fundamental economic practices; (II) certain methods of organizing human activity; and (III) an idea 'of itself' (mental processes, concepts performable in the human mind or by pen-and-paper, or ideas with no particular concrete form).
guidance:
Use these categories as signposts when comparing claim concepts to judicially-identified abstractions. The MPEP enumerates subtypes and many cases as examples:
- I. Fundamental economic practices: concepts relating to economy/commerce such as agreements/contracts, performance of financial transactions (buySAFE), offer-based price optimization (OIP Techs.), hedging (Bilski), processing financing applications, rules for wagering games (In re Smith), etc. Also includes mitigating financial risk/intermediated settlement (Alice).
- II. Certain methods of organizing human activity: concepts relating to managing relationships/transactions or legal obligations (buySAFE, Dealertrack, Bancorp), advertising/marketing/sales activities (Ameranth, Ultramercial), managing human behavior (budgeting/tracking spending — Intellectual Ventures v. Capital One), and tracking/organizing information (BASCOM, TLI Communications, Electric Power Group).
- III. An idea 'of itself': mental processes and information manipulation that can be performed mentally or with pen-and-paper (CyberSource, Ambry Genetics, Synopsys), collecting/analyzing/displaying information (Content Extraction, FairWarning, Electric Power Group), data comparisons analogous to human mental work (CyberSource, Mortgage Grader), and concepts described as having no particular concrete or tangible form (Ultramercial — using advertising as exchange).
Examples in guidance: collecting, comparing, classifying, encoding/decoding, organizing via mathematical correlations, creating indices, relaying mailing address data, retaining navigation info in online forms. Courts have treated mere presentation of results of abstract processes without more as abstract (Content Extraction, Ultramercial, Content Extraction & Transmission).

name: Semi-autocompletion / workflow support
description: System must extract bibliographic and technical keywords (claim numbers, cited cases, inventor names, drawings), autofill template blanks, import previous claims, and leave argument sections for manual attorney completion.
guidance: Use an NLP parser, part-of-speech tagging, patent-specific regex adjustments, and an autofill UI that preserves manual editability; prioritize preserving attorney control over argumentative content.

name: Avoiding hallucination / proper use of LLMs (scope of generation)
description: LLM generation should focus on arguing technical differences and drafting response drafts rather than generating patent claims (claims are prone to hallucination); ensure alignment with factual and legal sources.
guidance: Use external relevant resources (Re-examination, MPEP-2100) for references, weight Response Draft highest among inputs, and design prompts to reduce hallucination; consider RLHF/fine-tuning on OA-response data for alignment.

name: Identification when referencing dependent claims (A/B/C)
description: When making reference to a dependent claim either singular or multiple: (A) For a singular dependent claim which does not include a reference to a multiple dependent claim, reference only to the number of the dependent claim. (B) When identifying the embodiments included within a multiple dependent claim, or a singular dependent claim which includes a reference to a multiple dependent claim, each embodiment should be identified by using the number of the claims involved, starting with the highest, to the extent necessary to specifically identify each embodiment. (C) When all embodiments included within a multiple dependent claim or a singular dependent claim which includes a reference to a multiple dependent claim are subject to a common rejection, objection, or requirement, reference may be made only to the number of the dependent claim.
