guidance: Includes table/example showing allowed 'approved practice' identifications versus 'all claims' lists; if multiple dependent claim embodiments share a common ground of rejection, refer only to the dependent claim number (e.g., if 4/2 and 4/3 have common rejection, refer only to claim 4).

name: Office actions must identify treatment for each claim embodiment (35 U.S.C. 132)
description: The provisions of 35 U.S.C. 132 require that each Office action make it explicitly clear what rejection, objection and/or requirement is applied to each claim embodiment.
guidance: When multiple embodiments arise from multiple dependent claims, the examiner must explicitly state which rejection/objection applies to each embodiment; may use condensed references only when all embodiments share the same ground (see Identification rules).

name: Use of form PTO/SB/07 for multiple dependent claim fee computation
description: A separate 'Multiple Dependent Claim Fee Calculation Sheet,' form PTO/SB/07 is used with form PTO/SB/06 to assist in computation of fees for multiple dependent claims; OPAP places the form in the file when multiple dependent claims are present as filed or later added.
guidance: If multiple dependent claims are added later, TC technical support places form in file; totals from PTO/SB/07 are transferred to PTO/SB/06 for final fee calculation. This is an administrative requirement to compute fees correctly.

name: Initial administrative acceptance of dependent claims for fee purposes
description: The initial determination for fee purposes as to whether a claim is dependent must be made by persons other than examiners; at that time, virtually every claim which refers to another claim is accepted as dependent without determining whether a true dependent relationship exists.
guidance: Initial acceptance as dependent for administrative fee counting does not preclude a later examiner determination that the claim is not a proper dependent claim for substantive examination; the examiner may subsequently hold a claim improper.

name: Test for proper dependency under 35 U.S.C. 112(d)
description: In accordance with 35 U.S.C. 112(d), a claim in dependent form shall contain: (i) a reference to a claim previously set forth, and (ii) then specify a further limitation of the subject matter claimed. A dependent claim is construed to incorporate by reference all the limitations of the claim to which it refers.
guidance: The dependent claim must include every limitation of the claim from which it depends and specify an additional limitation; omitting an element from the base claim (or replacing it) renders a dependent claim improper even if other limitations are added. The significance of the added limitation is not determinative; the requirement is formal: include all base limitations and add a further limitation.

name: Dependent claims across statutory classes and separate inventions
description: A dependent claim that relates to a separate invention that would require a separate search or separate classification from the base claim is not necessarily improper. The fact that independent and dependent claims are in different statutory classes does not, in itself, render the dependent claim improper.
guidance: Examples: a product claim may properly have a dependent method-of-making claim that further specifies limitations; conversely, a product claim would be improper as dependent on a method claim if the product can be made by methods other than that recited in the base method claim. Examiners must treat dependent claims as combinations (base limitations + dependent limitations) when comparing to prior art.

name: Examination treatment for dependent claims that fail 35 U.S.C. 112(d)
description: If a dependent claim does not comply with 35 U.S.C. 112(d), the examiner should reject the dependent claim under 35 U.S.C. 112(d) as unpatentable rather than merely objecting to the claim.
guidance: Use form paragraphs 7.36 (statutory basis) and then 7.36.01 (rejection wording). Form paragraph 7.36 should be used only once per Office action and must precede 7.36.01. Examiner notes instruct insertion of an explanation of why the dependent claim fails to constitute a further limitation and remind that non-compliance renders the claim unpatentable (citing Pfizer v. Ranbaxy).

name: Rejection/objection handling when base claim canceled or rejected
description: If the base claim has been canceled, a claim which is directly or indirectly dependent thereon should be rejected as incomplete. If the base claim is rejected, the dependent claim should be objected to rather than rejected if it is otherwise allowable.
guidance: Form paragraph 7.43 can be used to state the objection: 'Claim [1] objected to as being dependent upon a rejected base claim, but would be allowable if rewritten in independent form including all of the limitations of the base claim and any intervening claims.'

name: Claim terminology must have antecedent basis in description
description: The meaning of every term used in the claims should be apparent from the descriptive portion of the specification with clear disclosure as to its import; in mechanical cases, refer to drawings/parts. New terminology introduced in claims (especially late in prosecution) should have clear support or antecedent basis in the specification so the meaning may be ascertained.
guidance: Avoid a confusing variety of terms for the same thing. When claims are amended or new claims added that introduce new terms, appropriate amendment of the specification is necessary (without introducing new matter) to provide clear support per 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1). If the specification fails to provide proper antecedent basis, use form paragraph 7.44 to object to the specification.

name: Completeness of specification: written description, enablement, and utility requirements (35 U.S.C. 112)
description: An application must include a specification containing a written description of the invention that enables a person skilled in the art to make and use the invention as of its filing date (35 U.S.C. 112). At least one specific operative embodiment or example must be set forth; examples and description should be of sufficient scope to justify the scope of the claims. The specification must reasonably convey possession of the claimed invention and enable it without undue experimentation.
guidance: Complex experimentation is permitted if typical for the art; see additional MPEP sections for detailed guidance (e.g., enablement, written description, utility, computer-related claims, functional claims). For lack of utility or other specialized issues, consult referenced MPEP sections.

name: Essential vs nonessential material for incorporation by reference (37 CFR 1.57(d)/(e))
description: Essential material (material necessary to provide written description/enablement, to particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention, or to describe structure/material/acts corresponding to a claimed means/step) may be incorporated by reference only to a U.S. patent or U.S. patent application publication that does not itself incorporate that essential material. Nonessential material may be incorporated by reference to U.S. or foreign patents or published applications, commonly owned U.S. applications, or non-patent publications.
guidance: Essential material is narrowly defined and cannot be incorporated by reference to foreign or non-patent sources for applications to issue as U.S. patents. An incorporation by hyperlink is not permitted. If incorporation is defective, the examiner may require applicant to supply a copy; insertion of incorporated material into the specification must be by amendment with a statement that no new matter is introduced. Corrections to incorporations must be made within Office-set time periods (no later than close of prosecution).

name: Procedures and limitations when material is inadvertently omitted or added by reference
description: If all or a portion of the specification or drawings is inadvertently omitted but is completely contained in a prior-filed application (priority or benefit claim present), the omission may be treated as incorporation by reference provided the omitted portion is later added within any office-set time (no later than close of prosecution) and certain documents/copies/translations and fees are supplied.
guidance: Requirements include supplying a copy of the prior-filed application, translations if needed, identifying where omitted portion is found, possible petition/fees if not entitled to filing date, and time limits for certified copies (e.g., within later of four months from filing date or sixteen months from previous filing date) unless petitioned. For international applications, special rules apply and additions may be effective only for the U.S. national stage.

name: Wands undue experimentation factors
description: Application of the Wands test involves weighing eight factual considerations, including: the quantity of experimentation necessary; the amount of guidance presented in the patent; the nature of the disclosed working examples; the unpredictability of the art; and the breadth of the claims.
guidance: The court evaluates these factors together to decide whether practicing the full scope would require 'undue experimentation.' The piece notes that arguments about failure to identify a single unreproducible antibody or reliance on precedent (Wands) were considered but rejected on the facts.

name: Representative embodiments / written description vs enablement
description: Disclosed embodiments may be representative enough to satisfy the written description requirement, but that does not automatically satisfy enablement across a broad genus.
guidance: Amgen argued its 26 disclosed antibody sequences were representative and established structure/function correlation. The Federal Circuit found representative examples insufficient where the functional diversity of the claimed genus far exceeded the examples and where unpredictability suggested substantial additional experimentation would be required.

name: Structure–function predictability
description: Functional claiming is permissible only when there is a predictable relationship between structure and function; if there isn't, functional claims are difficult to sustain.
guidance: The article highlights that predictability of how structural changes affect function is key—chemicals are easier in this respect than antibodies. For antibodies, structural changes often affect function unpredictably, raising the enablement bar.

name: Claim breadth / size of genus
description: The broader the claim (e.g., covering tens of thousands or millions of potential compounds), the harder it is to show enablement, particularly in unpredictable arts.
guidance: Quotes from practitioners in the article make clear that when a claim covers large numbers of potential embodiments, courts scrutinize whether the specification provides sufficient guidance to make the full scope without undue experimentation.

name: Exhaustive enumeration not required, but enablement across breadth still required
description: The enablement requirement does not require a skilled artisan to find every member of a genus, but the specification still must enable practice across the claimed scope without undue experimentation.
guidance: The court stated that effort required to 'exhaust' a genus is not dispositive; however, lack of a predictable path to make a meaningful portion of the genus can still render claims invalid for lack of enablement.

name: Need for structural limitations when structure–function correlation is unpredictable
description: Where structure–function correlation is unpredictable (as with many antibodies), patents should include structural limitations to the claimed genus rather than relying solely on functional language.
guidance: Practitioners quoted in the article advise that it is difficult to 'own an antibody target' by purely functional claiming; drafting should aim to provide structural definitions or other enabling disclosures to meet the higher enablement bar.

name: Judicial trend: enablement increasingly decisive in life‑science genus challenges
description: Recent Federal Circuit decisions have increasingly invalidated broad genus claims under enablement (Section 112(a)), elevating enablement's role relative to written description in life sciences.
guidance: The article cites a line of cases (ALZA v Andrx, Wyeth & Cordis v Abbott, Enzo v Roche, Idenix v Gilead) culminating in Amgen v Sanofi, indicating that enablement challenges are now a primary pathway to attack broad genus claims in biotech.

name: Graham v. John Deere factors
description: To make out a case of obviousness, one must: (A) determine the scope and contents of the prior art; (B) ascertain the differences between the prior art and the claims in issue; (C) determine the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; and (D) evaluate any evidence of secondary considerations.
guidance: If a prima facie case is established, the burden shifts to applicant to come forward with rebuttal evidence or argument. Office personnel should evaluate the totality of the facts and all of the evidence to determine whether they support a conclusion that the claimed invention would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made.

name: Findings for prior art genus — structure
description: When a prior art reference discloses a genus, make findings as to the structure of the disclosed prior art genus and that of any expressly described species or subgenus within the genus.
guidance: Explicitly identify the genus structure and any species/subgenus described; use these structural findings when comparing to the claimed species or subgenus.

name: Ascertain differences between closest disclosed prior art species and claimed species
description: Identify and compare the closest disclosed prior art species or subgenus of record to the claimed species or subgenus to determine the differences.
guidance: Make explicit findings on similarities and differences including findings relating to similarity of structure, properties, and utilities; the question is whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious.

name: Determine the level of ordinary skill in the art
description: Evaluate the prior art from the standpoint of the hypothetical person having ordinary skill in the art at the time the claimed invention was made.
guidance: The level of skill is important for objectivity in the obviousness inquiry; facts of record pertaining to level of skill often are found within the prior art reference but additional applicant evidence should be evaluated.

name: Determine whether a person of ordinary skill would be motivated to select the claimed species (motivation/suggestion)
description: In light of findings relating to the Graham factors, determine whether it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill to make the claimed invention as a whole, i.e., to select the claimed species or subgenus from the disclosed prior art genus.
guidance: Consider all relevant prior art teachings, focusing on categories such as size of genus, express teachings, structural similarity, similar properties/uses, predictability of technology, and any other teachings; make explicit why the prior art would have motivated selection.

name: Consider the size of the genus
description: Consider the size of the prior art genus when assessing motivation to select a claimed species from it.
guidance: Size alone cannot support an obviousness rejection; however, a genus may be so small that, in light of total circumstances (limited variations, unchanging nucleus, etc.), it would effectively anticipate or render obvious a claimed species (see In re Petering and related cases).

name: Consider teachings of similar properties or uses
description: Consider the properties and utilities of structurally similar prior art species or subgenus, because properties/utilities provide real world motivation to make related species.
guidance: If claimed and prior art species share any useful property, that generally motivates selection; conversely, lack of a disclosed useful property weighs against motivation. Very close structural similarity plus similar utilities can create a prima facie case.

name: Consider predictability of the technology
description: Consider how predictable the technology is when assessing whether structural similarity provides a reasonable expectation of similar properties.
guidance: If the technology is unpredictable, structurally similar species are less likely to render a claimed species obvious; obviousness requires only a reasonable expectation of success, not absolute predictability.

name: Make express fact-findings supporting or refuting a prima facie case
description: Based on the evidence as a whole, make express fact-findings relating to the Graham factors and articulate what teachings or suggestions in the prior art would have motivated one of ordinary skill to select the claimed species or subgenus.
guidance: After articulating fact-findings, determine whether these findings, considered as a whole, support a prima facie case of obviousness; cite appropriate case law where relevant.

name: Prima facie obviousness from close structural similarity (chemical compounds)
description: A prima facie case of obviousness may be made when chemical compounds have very close structural similarities and similar utilities; the motivation is the expectation that compounds similar in structure will have similar properties.
guidance: Analyze structural and functional similarity together; use precedent (e.g., In re Payne, In re Dillon, In re Papesch) to assess whether similarity and shared utilities create motivation to make the claimed compound.

name: Treat homology and isomerism as facts to be weighed with other evidence
description: Homologs, isomers, stereoisomers, and adjacent homologs are generally of sufficiently close structural similarity to create a presumed expectation of similar properties, but these facts must be considered with all other relevant facts.
guidance: Do not equate homology/isomerism automatically with prima facie obviousness; view claimed invention and prior art as a whole (see cases where homologs were and were not held prima facie obvious).

name: Presence or absence of prior art method of making the claimed compound
description: The presence—or absence—of a suitably operative, obvious process for making a composition of matter may have an ultimate bearing on whether that composition is obvious.
guidance: If the prior art fails to disclose or render obvious a method for making the claimed compound at the relevant time, it may preclude concluding the compound is in the possession of the public and may overcome a presumption of obviousness based on structural similarity.

name: If prior art compounds have no utility or only utility as intermediates, may not be prima facie obvious
description: If the prior art does not teach any specific or significant utility for disclosed compounds, or teaches them only as intermediates, the prior art is unlikely to render structurally similar claims prima facie obvious absent a reason to make such compounds.
guidance: Consider whether the reference teaches usefulness of the compounds; intermediates not known to have relevant utility weigh against motivation to select related compounds.

name: Prima facie case rebuttable by evidence of superior or unexpected results
description: A prima facie case of obviousness based on structural similarity is rebuttable by proof that the claimed compounds possess unexpectedly advantageous or superior properties.
guidance: Rebuttal must be based on evidence (comparative data, affidavits); mere recognition of a benefit by the patentee is not sufficient if the prior art compound actually possessed the benefit. See MPEP § 716.02 and cases (Papesch, Wiechert, Dillon).

name: Photographs ordinarily not permitted — exceptions
description: Photographs, including photocopies, are not ordinarily permitted in utility and design patent applications but will be accepted if photographs are the only practicable medium for illustrating the claimed invention.
guidance: Examples where photographs/photomicrographs are acceptable: electrophoresis gels, blots, autoradiographs, cell cultures, histological tissue cross sections, animals, plants, in vivo imaging, thin layer chromatography plates, crystalline/metallurgical microstructures, textile fabrics, grain structures, and ornamental effects in design patents. If subject matter admits illustration by drawing, examiner may require a drawing in place of the photograph. Photographs must be of sufficient quality so all details are reproducible in the printed patent.

name: Views required and placement
description: Drawings must contain as many views as necessary to show the invention (plan, elevation, section, perspective, detail views). All views must be grouped together and arranged on the sheet(s) without wasting space, preferably upright, clearly separated, and not included on specification/claims/abstract sheets.
guidance: Views must not be connected by projection lines and must not contain center lines. Waveforms may be connected by dashed lines to show relative timing.

name: Starting examination on later-filed application after prior-filed processed
description: When the prior-filed application is examined or laid open or registered after examination on later-filed applications is deferred, the examiner may conduct examination on the later-filed application.
guidance: Even though examination on later-filed application is conducted, the examiner shall make the final decision on examination in applying Article 36(1) of the Patent Act once the scope of claim of the prior-filed application is determined.

name: Refusal to enter amendment when amendment generates new ground
description: Where the amendment in response to final rejection fails to meet amendment scope prescribed in Article 47(2) and (3), or where new grounds for rejection occur from the amendment (excluding certain deletions), the amendment shall be refused to be entered.
guidance: If a new ground of rejection can be cured by ex-officio amendment, the examiner shall approve the amendment and carry out subsequent procedures. New ground does not include grounds that were previously notified or existed without notification. Several concrete examples (adding/deleting elements or claims) illustrate how to decide admission vs refusal.

name: Contents and confirmation of decision to grant a patent
description: Where no ground for rejection is discovered, an examiner shall make a decision to grant a patent in writing with rationale attached. The written decision shall include application number, title, name and address of applicant and agent, text of decision and its rationale, number of claims to be patented, date of decision, matters amended ex officio, along with examiner's sign and seal.
guidance: The Commissioner shall deliver a certified copy to the applicant; the decision is confirmed upon delivery. For certain applications (filed by KIPO examiners, recent retirees, or KIPO-supervised prior art searchers), the examiner shall determine consequences in consultation with three persons including a director or head.

name: Contents and confirmation of decision to reject an application
description: Where an applicant fails to overcome grounds for rejection, an examiner shall make a decision to reject in writing with rationale attached. The written decision shall include application number, title, name and address of applicant and agent, date of notice of grounds, text and rationale of decision, and date of decision, with examiner's sign and seal.
guidance: Commissioner delivers certified copy; decision is confirmed when it cannot be revoked (e.g., no appeal). If a ground may be cured by ex-officio amendment, examiner shall make ex-officio amendment and allow grant. Examiner shall indicate determination on applicant's amendment and issuable items in the written argument. For applications with multiple claims, if any claim contains grounds for rejection, make decision to reject.

name: Subcombinations usable together distinctness
description: Subcombinations disclosed as usable together in a single combination are distinct if they do not overlap in scope, are not obvious variants, and at least one subcombination is separately usable (MPEP § 806.05(d)).
guidance: Use when claims are presented to subcombinations usable together. In bracket 3 identify the subcombination (group number or identifier); in bracket 4 suggest a separate utility other than use with the other subcombination. Conclude with form paragraph 8.21. If applicant elects and claims to the elected subcombination become allowable, dependent claims requiring all limitations will be examined per 37 CFR 1.104.

name: Apparatus and product-made distinctness
description: Apparatus and product-made inventions are distinct if either: (1) the apparatus as claimed is not an obvious apparatus for making the product and the apparatus can be used to make a materially different product, or (2) the product as claimed can be made by another materially different apparatus (MPEP § 806.05(g)).
guidance: In bracket 3 insert one or more supporting reasons (e.g., apparatus can be used to make a different product, product can be made by a materially different apparatus, or process can be practiced by hand). A process is 'by hand' if performable without any apparatus. Conclude the restriction requirement with form paragraph 8.21. Follow with form paragraph 8.21.04 to notify of potential rejoinder of process claims. See MPEP § 806.05(g).

name: Product and process-of-using distinctness
description: Product and process-of-using the product can be shown distinct if either: (1) the process for using the product can be practiced with another materially different product, or (2) the product as claimed can be used in a materially different process of using that product (MPEP § 806.05(h)).
guidance: Use when claims are presented to both the product and a process of using the product. If process-of-making claims that are specially adapted for making the product are present, those should be grouped with the product invention (MPEP § 806.05(i)). In bracket 3 insert specific reasons (examples provided). Conclude with form paragraph 8.21 and, where applicable, follow with 8.21.04 for rejoinder notice.

name: Burden and requirement for election / traversal
description: Restriction is proper because the listed inventions are independent or distinct and there would be a serious search and/or examination burden if restriction were not required; the reply must include (i) an election of an invention to be examined even if traversed and (ii) identification of the claims encompassing the elected invention (37 CFR 1.143).
guidance: In bracket 1 insert the specific reason(s) why a search/examination burden exists (examples: separate classification; recognized divergent subject matter; different field of search such as different classes/subclasses, electronic resources, or search strategies). Election may be made with or without traverse; to reserve petition rights, election must be with traverse. A traverse must distinctly and specifically point out alleged errors to be timely; failure to timely traverse results in loss of petition right under 37 CFR 1.144. If claims are added after election, applicant must indicate which are readable on the elected invention. If applicant traverses on ground that inventions are not patentably distinct, applicant should submit evidence or identify such evidence now, or clearly admit they are obvious variants; examiner may use evidence/admission in a 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection.

name: Notice of potential rejoinder of process claims
description: When restriction is between product/apparatus and process claims, withdrawn process claims that include all limitations of an allowable product/apparatus claim should be considered for rejoinder; rejoined claims will be fully examined per 37 CFR 1.104.
guidance: To be rejoined, withdrawn process claims must include all limitations of the allowable product/apparatus claim; rejoined claims must meet 35 U.S.C. 101, 102, 103 and 112. Withdrawn process claims not commensurate in scope with an allowable product/apparatus claim will not be rejoined. Applicant is advised to amend process claims during prosecution to require limitations of product/apparatus claims; failure to do so may prevent rejoinder. Note that 35 U.S.C. 121 double-patenting prohibition does not apply where restriction is withdrawn before issue. Use form paragraph 8.21.04 at the end of relevant restriction requirements (process vs product/apparatus/making/using). See MPEP § 821.04 for rejoinder practice.

name: Different inventors, common assignee, same invention — pre-AIA (FTI) handling
description: If a claim is directed to the same invention as that of a commonly assigned patent/application under pre-AIA (first to invent) law, priority issues under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f)/(g) must be resolved.
guidance: The applicant must amend/cancel claims or the assignee must identify the prior inventor. The USPTO normally will not institute an interference between commonly owned applications/patents. A terminal disclaimer has no effect in this situation because the issue is priority, not extension of monopoly. Failure to comply may result in abandonment. Use form paragraph 7.03.fti and appropriate 7.15/7.19 paragraphs where applicable.

name: Patentably indistinct claims in copending applications
description: When claim(s) of this application are patentably indistinct from claim(s) in a copending application, elimination from all but one application may be required absent good and sufficient reason (37 CFR 1.78(f)).
guidance: Applicant is required to cancel patentably indistinct claims from all but one application or maintain a clear line of demarcation between applications. See MPEP § 822. Use form paragraph 8.29 and insert reference application number where indicated.

name: Statutory double patenting — 35 U.S.C. 101 (same-invention) heading and remedy
description: A statutory double patenting rejection (same invention type) is founded on the principle that one inventor may obtain a patent for a single invention only (35 U.S.C. 101); 'same invention' means identical subject matter.
guidance: This heading (form paragraph 8.30) must precede statutory-type double patenting rejections (8.31/8.32). A statutory double patenting rejection can be overcome by canceling or amending claims so they are no longer coextensive in scope. Filing of a terminal disclaimer cannot overcome a 35 U.S.C. 101 double patenting rejection.

name: Preamble patentable weight
description: A preamble is generally not accorded any patentable weight where it merely recites the purpose of a process or the intended use of a structure, and where the body of the claim does not depend on the preamble for completeness but, instead, the process steps or structural limitations are able to stand alone.
guidance: Cite In re Hirao and Kropa v. Robie. Evaluate whether the claim body stands alone; if so, do not import patentable weight from the preamble.

name: Treatment of claims retained under specific CFR sections
description: Claims retained under 37 CFR 1.142 and 37 CFR 1.146 should be treated as set out in MPEP §§ 821 - 821.03 and § 809.02(c).
guidance: See MPEP § 2363.03 for claims in losing party application in interference; keep Index of Claims up to date per MPEP § 719.04.

name: Allowable except as to form — offer definite correction suggestions
description: When an application discloses patentable subject matter but claims cannot be allowed due to form defects or omission of a limitation, the examiner should not merely object or reject; the action should offer a definite suggestion for correction.
guidance: Constructive suggestions and indication of possible interview may accelerate agreement on allowable claims.

name: If dependent claim depends on rejected/cancelled claim, state rewrite for allowance
description: If a claim is otherwise allowable but dependent on a canceled claim or on a rejected claim, the Office action should state that the claim would be allowable if rewritten in independent form.
guidance: Use form paragraph language (e.g., ¶ 7.43) to indicate dependence issues and rewrite guidance.

name: Early allowance of clearly allowable claims
description: Where the examiner is satisfied the prior art has been fully developed and some claims are clearly allowable, allowance of such claims should not be delayed.
guidance: Prompt allowance avoids unnecessary delay; do not withhold allowance pending other matters.

name: Petition grounds and requirements to make application special
description: Applications may be made special by petition under 37 CFR 1.102 for specific grounds such as manufacture, actual infringement, applicant's health, applicant's age, environmental quality, energy contribution, or recombinant DNA safety.
guidance: Each ground has specific documentary or statement requirements: e.g., Manufacture requires fee, statement of capital/facilities, obligation to manufacture in U.S., and prior-art search; Infringement requires showing of an infringing device/method on market and a rigid comparison showing some claims unquestionably infringed; Health/Age petitions require evidence (doctor's certificate, birth certificate) and have no fee; Environmental/Energy/Recombinant DNA petitions require statements explaining contribution and may be fee-free or require fee per 37 CFR 1.17(h). Applicants must provide copies of closest references if not of record.

name: Accelerated examination special-status prerequisites
description: To obtain special (accelerated) status for a new application, applicant must comply with specific prerequisites.
guidance: Requirements: (A) submit petition to make special with fee (37 CFR 1.17(h)); (B) present all claims directed to a single invention or elect without traverse; (C) submit a statement that a pre-examination search was made, listing field by class/subclass and publications; (D) submit one copy of each reference deemed most closely related if not of record; (E) submit a detailed discussion of the references pointing out with particularity (per 37 CFR 1.111(b) and (c)) how claims are patentable over references. Divisional applications must independently meet requirements.

name: Protection of unfair competition
description: Article 168.2 IP Code provides a cause of action for unfair competition when a person employs deception or other means contrary to good faith in passing off goods or services; Article 28 New Civil Code gives broader relief against unjust or oppressive methods causing unfair competition.
guidance: Proof of fraud is essential under Article 168.2; unfair competition claims may be broader under civil code.

name: Fee structures and payment requirements (patents, utility models, industrial designs, trademarks)
description: Detailed official fees apply for filings and annuities: examples include patent filing fees (small entity ₱2,020.00 for up to 5 claims inclusive of 1% legal research fee), additional claim fees, priority claim fees; annuity ranges (small entity ₱1,565.50 to ₱31,534.22 for 5th to 20th year). Utility model and industrial design application and renewal fees specified; trademark basic fees per class and publication fees differ for big/small entities.
guidance: An application is subject to full payment of filing fee and first publication fee upon filing (Memorandum Circular No. 2022-016). Late renewals typically incur a surcharge (e.g., 50% for industrial designs). Monitor fee schedules closely.

name: Available defenses to infringement
description: Defenses include proof confusion is unlikely (trademark), prior use in good faith, innocent infringer (printing businesses), publisher/distributor protections, laches/acquiescence, fair use (copyright), patent invalidity, failure of doctrine of equivalents (function-means-result), surrender/lapse/expiration of patent, and plant variety specific defenses (non-infringement, not distinct/novel, prior adverse right).
guidance: Good faith alone is not a defense in many infringement actions; defendants often raise invalidity to counter patent/utility model claims.

name: 112(a) Written Description - compliance determination
description: Were all the 35 U.S.C. 112(a) Written Description rejection(s) in compliance? (Yes/No). Determination based on the rejection properly identifying the claim(s), the statute (including subparagraphs), and being supported by sufficient evidence to support the conclusion of lack of sufficient written description of the claim(s).
guidance: If a 112(a) rejection was made, answer Yes or No. Consult the statutory compliance standard and scenarios for assistance. If Yes, proceed to question for accolades; if No, proceed to identify noncompliant claims and explain.

name: Identify claims with non-compliant 112(a) rejections
description: List each claim discussed individually as a basis for the noncompliance and include dependent claims which inherit the noncompliance.
guidance: Each claim must be discussed individually in an 'Explanation of Noncompliance' section. Include dependent claims that inherit noncompliance. Use claim numbering and tie explanations to specific claim limitations.

name: 112(a) Noncompliance root - limitation origin (independent/dependent/both)
description: Indicate whether the noncompliance is directed to limitations introduced in: (a) Only the independent claim(s); (b) Only the dependent claim(s); or (c) Both the independent and dependent claim(s).
guidance: Check only one box based on where the limitation that is the basis for the noncompliance first appears in the claim tree. Examples provided illustrate independent-only, dependent-only, and mixed-origin situations.

name: 112(a) Noncompliance reason: insufficient evidence inventor lacked possession (4b)
description: The rejection(s) does not provide sufficient evidence as to why applicant did not have possession of the claimed invention.
guidance: Consult statutory compliance scenarios to determine sufficiency of evidence. If 4(b) is checked, at least one of 4(b)(i)-4(b)(iii) must be checked. Explanation should be focused, avoid rhetorical questions and personalization, and be consistent with boxes checked under 4(b).

name: 112(a) 4(b)(i) - insufficient evidence that amended/new limitations lack support (new matter)
description: The rejection does not provide sufficient evidence to support the conclusion that the amended or newly added claim limitations lack support in the original disclosure (i.e., new matter).
guidance: If asserted new matter actually has support in the original disclosure, indicate which source(s) of support apply: A. Original claim(s); B. Original drawing(s); C. Original specification through express, implicit or inherent disclosure. Use these boxes to identify the nature of the incorrect new-matter finding.

name: 112(a) 4(b)(ii) - new matter only in specification that doesn't change claim scope
description: The new matter was added only to the specification and does not change the scope of the claimed invention and therefore does not necessitate a rejection.
guidance: Check when the alleged new matter appears solely in the specification and does not alter claim scope; explain why the added specification content does not create new matter for the claims.

name: 112(a) 4(b)(iii) - insufficient evidence inventor lacks possession of originally claimed invention
description: The rejection does not provide sufficient evidence to support the conclusion that the inventor lacks possession of the originally claimed invention.
guidance: Explain why the examiner's evidence does not reasonably establish lack of possession of the originally-claimed invention; tie explanation to the record and disclosure.

name: 112(a) Additional information/feedback categories (5a-5g)
description: Optional feedback boxes to indicate additional characteristics or root causes related to the noncompliance (check all that apply).
guidance: Boxes include: 5a analysis more appropriate for lack of enablement; 5b analysis primarily questions to applicant rather than analysis of written description; 5c noncompliance due to unreasonable claim interpretation (only if rejection indicates how limitation is construed); 5d 112(f)-related; 5e lack of sufficient algorithm for CII; 5f related to deposit of biological material; 5g None of the above. Comments must support reasoning for boxes checked; do not guess root cause.

name: Characteristics of 112(a) Written Description rejection(s) (Q7)
description: Checklist of characteristics that may be exemplified in 112(a) rejections; reviewer checks all that apply.
guidance: Options include: addresses substantially all claims individually (limited claim lumping); provides citations to relevant portions of the specification and thorough explanation of lack of possession; sets forth a claim interpretation that indicates how the examiner is construing the claim/term/phrase; included detailed legal analysis referencing case law/policy; included appropriate suggestions to overcome the rejection (not generic FP language); None of the above. Checking indicates presence of a characteristic — it does not assess accuracy or accolade-worthiness.

name: 112(b) Indefiniteness - compliance determination
description: Were all the 35 U.S.C. 112(b) rejection(s) in compliance? (Yes/No). Determination based on proper identification of claim(s), statute (including subparagraphs), and sufficient evidence to support conclusion of indefiniteness.
guidance: If a 112(b) rejection was made, update the answer to Yes or No. Consult statutory compliance standard and scenarios. If Yes, proceed to accolade question; if No, go to identify noncompliant claims.

name: Identify claims with non-compliant 112(b) rejections
description: List each claim discussed individually as a basis for the noncompliance and include dependent claims which inherit the noncompliance.
guidance: Each claim discussed must be tied to the 'Explanation of Noncompliance' and dependent claims inheriting the defect must be listed. Use the claim-tree approach to determine origin of limitations.

name: 112(b) Noncompliance root - limitation origin (independent/dependent/both)
description: Indicate whether the noncompliance is directed to limitations introduced in independent claims, dependent claims, or both (check only one).
guidance: Selection is based on where the limitation that is the basis for the noncompliance first appears in the claim tree. Examples provided to illustrate proper selection.

name: Presence of another compliant 112(b) basis
description: For claims with noncompliant 112(b) bases, determine whether another compliant 112(b) rejection basis was applied to the same claim(s). (Yes/No).
guidance: If every claim with a noncompliant basis also has another compliant basis, answer Yes. If even one claim lacks any compliant basis, answer No. Examples illustrate mixed-basis scenarios.

name: 112(b) Noncompliance reason: insufficient evidence of indefiniteness (4b)
description: The rejection(s) does not provide sufficient evidence that the claim(s) does not particularly point out and distinctly claim that which the inventor regards as the invention.
guidance: If 4(b) is checked, identify at least one of 4(b)(i)-4(b)(iii): i) rejection did not point out the specific term/phrase that is indefinite; ii) rejection did not provide sufficient reasoning to support the conclusion of indefiniteness; iii) rejection did not provide sufficient reasoning that the claims are not drawn to that which the inventor regards as the invention. Note that 112(b) has two separate requirements (MPEP 2171) and there is a presumption the claims are directed to what the inventor regards as the invention (MPEP 2172).

name: 112(b) Noncompliance issues list (5a-5k)
description: Specific issue categories that may relate to noncompliance under 112(b); reviewer must check at least one.
guidance: Options include: a. Breadth versus indefiniteness; b. Relative terminology; c. Ranges and amounts limitations; d. Exemplary language (e.g., 'for example'); e. Lack of antecedent basis; f. Functional language; g. Alternative limitations (e.g., Markush group); h. Unclaimed/omitted essential subject matter; i. 112(b) is related to 112(f); j. Unbound functional claiming; k. Other (specify). Check all that apply and support with explanations.

name: 112(b) Additional information/feedback (6a-6c)
description: Boxes to capture additional feedback reasons for noncompliance under 112(b).
guidance: Options: 6a rejection only based on specification without basis in claim terminology; 6b noncompliance result of unreasonable claim interpretation (only when rejection indicates how claim is being construed); 6c none of the above. Comments must support checked boxes.

name: Characteristics of 112(b) Rejection(s) (Q8)
description: Checklist of characteristics that may be exemplified in 112(b) rejections; check all that apply.
guidance: Options mirror 112(a): addresses substantially all claims individually (limited claim lumping); provides citations to the specification and explains why claim does not particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention; sets forth claim interpretation (e.g., BRI, special definitions); included detailed legal analysis and case law/policy; included appropriate suggestions to overcome rejection(s); none of the above. Checking indicates presence of a characteristic, not an endorsement of accuracy.

name: 112(d) Improper dependent claim - compliance determination
description: Were all the 35 U.S.C. 112(d) rejection(s) in compliance? (Yes/No). Determination based on proper identification of claim(s), statute (including subparagraphs), and sufficient evidence to support the rejection.
guidance: If a 112(d) rejection was made, update Yes or No. Consult statutory compliance standard and scenarios. If No, identify noncompliant claims and proceed to explanations.

name: Identify claims with non-compliant 112(d) rejections
description: List each claim discussed individually as a basis for the noncompliance and include dependent claims which inherit the noncompliance.
guidance: Each claim discussion must be tied to the 'Explanation of Noncompliance.' Use claim-tree logic to determine where the problematic limitation originates.

name: 112(d) Noncompliance root - limitation origin (independent/dependent/both)
description: Indicate whether the noncompliance is directed to limitations introduced in independent claims, dependent claims, or both (check only one).
guidance: Select based on where the limitation forming the basis for noncompliance first appears in the claim tree; examples illustrate selection.

name: 112(d) Noncompliance reason: insufficient evidence to support the 112(d) rejection (4b)
description: The rejection(s) does not provide sufficient evidence to support the rejection.
guidance: If 4(b) is checked, identify at least one: 4(b)(i) the rejection does not provide sufficient evidence that the claim(s) does not specify a further limitation of the subject matter of the claim from which it depends; 4(b)(ii) the rejection does not provide sufficient evidence that the claim(s) does not include all of the limitations of the claim from which it depends. Provide reasoned explanation consistent with boxes checked.

name: 112(d) Additional information/feedback (5a-5d)
description: Feedback boxes for root causes related to 112(d) noncompliance (check all that apply).
guidance: Options: 5a rejection should have been made under 112(b); 5b noncompliance is result of unreasonable claim interpretation (check only when rejection shows how a limitation is construed); 5c rejection improperly based on the patentable significance of the further limitation; 5d none of the above. Support choices with explanation.

name: Improvement to computer-functionality or other technology
description: The application should disclose sufficient details such that one of ordinary skill in the art would recognize the claimed invention as providing an improvement, and the claim itself must reflect the improvement in technology.
guidance: Consider whether the claim covers a particular solution or way to achieve a desired outcome rather than merely claiming the idea of a solution or outcome, and whether the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) is limited to computer implementation. See MPEP § 2106.05(a). Mere automation of manual processes or increasing speed when those improvements arise solely from a general-purpose computer is not sufficient to show an improvement in computer-functionality (see FairWarning, Credit Acceptance). A claim must include more than conventional implementation on generic components or machinery to qualify as an improvement (see Affinity Labs, TLI).

name: Resolve improvement question early in eligibility analysis
description: Although the question of whether a claim improves computer-functionality or other technology may be considered in either step of the Alice/Mayo test (Step 2A or 2B), examiners are encouraged to resolve this question as early as possible in the eligibility analysis.
guidance: A claim directed to a clear improvement in computer-related technology (e.g., Enfish) could be found eligible at Pathway A under the streamlined analysis (MPEP § 2106.06(b)) or at Pathway B as not being directed to an abstract idea. If an improvement is not clear enough for Step 2A, it may still contribute to eligibility in the Step 2B analysis (see Amdocs v. Openet example).

name: Claim must recite an abstract idea to be directed to it
description: The Step 2A analysis requires a claim to recite (i.e., set forth or describe) an abstract idea in order to be directed to that idea, thereby separating claims that merely involve or are based on abstract ideas from those that recite them.
guidance: Keep in mind that 'all inventions at some level embody, use, reflect, rest upon, or apply laws of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract ideas' (Alice), but only claims that recite an abstract idea are 'directed to' one for Step 2A purposes. Examine claims for whether they actually set forth a concept similar to judicially-identified abstract ideas before concluding they are directed to an abstract idea.

name: Claims based on or involving an abstract idea but not reciting it are not directed to an abstract idea
description: Some claims are not directed to an abstract idea because they do not recite anything similar to a judicially-identified abstract idea, although at some level they may be based on or involve an abstract idea.
guidance: Judicial decisions (e.g., Enfish; DDR Holdings; Trading Techs.) illustrate that claims improving database structures, modifying conventional Internet hyperlink protocols, or improving GUIs to prevent incorrect order entry can be not directed to an abstract idea when they don't recite a concept similar to those identified as abstract. Non-limiting hypothetical examples (printer, washing machine, earring sensor, BRCA1 sequencing method, BIOS loading method) illustrate claims that do not set forth an abstract idea.

name: If a claim recites an abstract idea, the claim-as-a-whole may still be not directed to it if it recites an improvement or additional elements that shift the focus
description: Some claims that recite an abstract idea are not directed to it because they also recite additional elements (such as an improvement) demonstrating that the claims as a whole clearly do not seek to tie up the abstract idea.
guidance: The improvement or additional elements must shift the focus of the claimed invention from the abstract idea that is incidentally recited. Courts have identified such improvements as indicative of eligibility in Step 2A (see McRO, Enfish, Research Corp.). Non-limiting hypothetical examples include surgical shears with a pressure regulator, a robotic arm assembly with sensor-based control for smooth motion, an autofocus camera system with a particular autofocus algorithm and drive mechanism, and an internal combustion engine with exhaust gas recirculation controlled by a processor—each recites specific improvements to how technology operates.

name: Rely on concepts identified in case law, not judicial descriptors
description: Examiners should rely on the concepts identified in the cases, not the judicial descriptors themselves, when determining whether a claimed concept is similar to a concept that the courts have identified as an abstract idea.
guidance: Associations of concepts with descriptors (e.g., 'fundamental economic practices') are not mutually exclusive and some concepts may map to multiple descriptors (e.g., hedging was described as both organizing human activity and a fundamental economic practice). Use the factual concept in precedent rather than only the label.

name: Certain methods of organizing human activity — managing relationships/transactions/legal obligations
description: Concepts relating to managing relationships or transactions between people, or satisfying or avoiding a legal obligation, are a category the courts have identified as often being abstract ideas.
guidance: Cases include buySAFE (transaction guarantees), Dealertrack (managing credit applications/clearing-house processing), and Bancorp (managing life insurance policy values). Such claims can be 'squarely about' contracting or processing information between parties and may be abstract absent a technological improvement.

name: Certain methods of organizing human activity — tracking or organizing information
description: Concepts involving tracking or organizing information (e.g., filtering content retrieved from a network) have been identified as abstract ideas.
guidance: BASCOM described content filtering as an abstract idea and a method of organizing human behavior. Claims that merely organize or filter information using conventional components may be treated as abstract absent an inventive concept or technology-specific improvement.

name: Non-limiting hypothetical examples of claims that do not set forth an abstract idea
description: Examples of claims that do not recite an abstract idea include a printer with belt/roller/printhead/ink cartridge; a washing machine with tub/motor/controller; an earring with a sensor for blood glucose measurement and memory; a method for sequencing BRCA1 gene sequences via PCR and sequencing; a BIOS loading method for a local computer requesting BIOS from remote memory.
guidance: These examples illustrate claims reciting concrete physical structures or technical processes that do not set forth judicially-identified abstract ideas and therefore are not 'directed to' abstract ideas for Step 2A purposes.

name: Statutory categories under 35 U.S.C. §101
description: Whoever invents or discovers any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof, may obtain a patent therefor, subject to the conditions and requirements of this title.
guidance: Step 1 of the USPTO analysis addresses whether the claimed invention falls into one of the four categories recited in 35 U.S.C. §101 (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter). This is the threshold inquiry and distinct from other patentability requirements (utility, novelty, non-obviousness, written description, enablement).

name: Alice/Mayo two-step framework (general)
description: A two-step framework: (1) determine whether the claim is 'directed to' a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon); (2) if so, determine whether the claim recites additional elements that amount to 'significantly more' than the judicial exception (an 'inventive concept').
guidance: The USPTO implements this framework within its own procedures (see steps 2A and 2B). Under step two the court’s search for an 'inventive concept' helps decide whether the claim transforms an ineligible concept into a patent-eligible application.

name: USPTO unified eligibility analysis (Step 1 / Step 2A / Step 2B)
description: The USPTO combines criteria into a single analysis: Step 1 (statutory category), Step 2A (determine if claim is directed to a judicial exception and second prong whether it integrates the exception into a practical application), Step 2B (determine whether additional elements amount to significantly more).
guidance: Examiners use step 2A to evaluate 'directed to' and, if a judicial exception is present, proceed to step 2B to evaluate whether additional elements provide an inventive concept. If a claim is found eligible at any point, the eligibility analysis stops.

name: Step 2A — first prong: determine whether claim recites a judicial exception
description: Evaluate whether the claim limitations recite an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon by analyzing the claim limitations in connection with scientific principles, natural laws, or known categories of abstract ideas.
guidance: For laws of nature or natural phenomena, evaluate limitations in connection with scientific principles (e.g., laws of thermodynamics, Newton's laws). For products of nature, determine whether a nature-based product has characteristics markedly different from its naturally occurring counterpart (Myriad considerations).

name: Step 2A — second prong: integration into a practical application
description: If the claim recites a judicial exception, determine whether the claim integrates the exception into a practical application (in which case the claim is eligible) rather than being directed to the exception itself.
guidance: Considerations include whether additional claim elements improve the functioning of a computer or other technology, whether the claim merely applies the exception in a particular environment or field of use, or whether a claim step applies or uses the exception to effect a specific treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition. If the claim passes this prong, the eligibility analysis stops and the claim is eligible.

name: Identification of abstract ideas by groupings
description: Abstract ideas are identified by whether a claim limitation falls into one or more groupings derived from judicial precedent: mathematical concepts, mental processes, and certain methods of organizing human activity.
guidance: The USPTO revised its approach (January 2019) to require examiners to identify abstract ideas by these groupings (rather than attempting to compare each claim to every court-identified abstract idea) to promote consistency and predictability.

name: Products of nature / 'markedly different' characteristics test (Myriad)
description: A claim to a nature-based product (product of nature) is evaluated to determine whether it has 'markedly different characteristics' from its naturally occurring counterpart.
guidance: If the nature-based product does not exhibit markedly different characteristics (e.g., Myriad's isolated DNA claims lacked such characteristics), the claim may be directed to a product of nature and thus be a judicial exception.

name: Step 2B — 'significantly more' / inventive concept analysis
description: Evaluate whether additional claim elements, individually or as an ordered combination, amount to significantly more than the judicial exception (i.e., supply an inventive concept sufficient to render the claim patent eligible).
guidance: USPTO personnel use similar considerations as in step 2A. If additional elements are merely conventional or generic, they typically do not supply the needed inventive concept and the claim can be rejected for lack of eligibility.

name: Claim construction principle — broadest reasonable interpretation
description: Establish the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim as a whole when performing eligibility analysis.
guidance: The USPTO flowchart and guidance instruct examiners to interpret claims under the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim language as part of determining eligibility and whether amendments could place the claim within a statutory category.

name: Amendment pathway and procedural handling
description: If a claim is not eligible as written, consider whether the claim can be amended to fall within a statutory category or otherwise be framed to integrate the exception into a practical application.
guidance: If the examiner makes an eligibility rejection, the applicant is given an opportunity to respond (e.g., amend the claim or argue why the claim is eligible). The examiner will also evaluate other patentability requirements (novelty, non-obviousness, written description, enablement) regardless of the eligibility determination.

name: Consideration of 'improvement to the functioning of a computer or other technology'
description: An additional element that 'improves the functioning of a computer or any other technology or technical field' is a relevant consideration that may indicate the claim integrates a judicial exception into a practical application.
guidance: This consideration has been applied in multiple decisions and USPTO memoranda; if a claim limitation meaningfully improves computer functionality or another technical field, it supports eligibility under the second prong of step 2A or in step 2B.

name: Procedural stop/start rules in eligibility flow (stop analysis when eligible)
description: If a claim is determined not to recite a judicial exception or is found to integrate the exception into a practical application (passes step 2A prong two), the eligibility analysis stops and the claim is eligible.
guidance: Only when a claim is directed to a judicial exception and fails the practical application prong does the examination proceed to step 2B. This procedural flow is reflected in the USPTO flowchart in MPEP §2106 and accompanying guidance.

name: Amendment of specification — process, advertisement, opposition, limits
description: An applicant or patentee may from time to time by request in writing seek leave to amend his specification, including drawings, by way of disclaimer, correction, connection, or explanation, stating nature and reasons. The request and proposed amendment shall be advertised; any person may give notice of opposition within one month; the comptroller shall hear and decide subject to appeal to the law officer.
guidance: If the law officer is required he shall hear the person making the request and any opposer and may determine whether and subject to what conditions the amendment shall be allowed. When no opposition is given the comptroller determines. If leave is refused the requester may appeal. No amendment shall be allowed that would make the specification claim an invention substantially larger than or substantially different from that claimed before amendment. Leave, when given, is conclusive except in case of fraud and the amendment is deemed to form part of the specification in all courts. Provisions do not apply while any action for infringement or legal proceeding relating to the patent is pending. Forms, fees and hearing procedures are set out in Patents Forms and Patents Rules.

name: Test of invention — novelty / substantial novelty
description: Historically in the American system (until late 19th/early 20th century) the principal test of invention was that the claimed subject matter be new; courts held that mere change in color or shape did not suffice—'substantially new' was required.
guidance: Administration of a substantial novelty test has problems but at least poses a clear question: is the subject matter substantially new?

name: Test of invention — non-obviousness (35 U.S.C. §103)
description: Since the Patent Act of 1952, the statutory standard is 'non-obviousness': the claimed subject matter must not have been obvious to a person skilled in the relevant prior art at the time the invention was made.
guidance: The standard is ambiguous in practice (e.g., courts have invalidated inventions that were not 'immediately obvious'), and judicial formulations have varied (e.g., 'flash of creative genius' criticisms).

name: Commercial success as evidentiary factor for validity
description: Subsequent commercial success of a product claimed by a patent can be relevant evidence supporting validity because commercial success shows the patent serves as foundation for valuable contract rights and increases security of the investment process.
guidance: Critics argue commercial success says little about the cost conditions of producing the invention; author explains how prospect function clarifies why commercial success affects patentability inquiries.

name: Prior user/purchase exemption for tangible specimens (Revised Statutes §4899)
description: No patent covers any use or sale of any specimen of the patented thing which was purchased of the inventor, or made by another with his knowledge and consent, before his application for a patent.
guidance: Applies to tangible machines/articles (not processes). The word 'person' is interpreted broadly (not restricted to privity by purchase). If applicant submitted device plans to federal government to obtain bids and the successful bidder had consent, no injunction will issue even after patent issuance. Willful obstructive interference delaying issuance may defeat damages claims. Case examples: Sub-Target Gun Co. v. Hollifield Target Practice Rod Co.; Federal Construction Co. v. Park Improvement Co.; Wade v. Metcalf.

name: Effect of prior foreign patents on U.S. patent term (limitation to foreign term in some cases)
description: Statutory rule (historical): 'Every patent granted for an invention which has previously been patented in a foreign country shall be so limited as to expire at the same time with the foreign patent...' (applies to certain patents granted after July 8, 1870, on applications filed before Jan. 1, 1898). The rule applies only where the foreign patent was taken out by the U.S. patentee or with his knowledge/consent or by someone in privity.
guidance: Treat applicability carefully: subsequent treaty provisions (e.g., Brussels treaty Art. 4 bis) were held not self-executing in some domestic cases (Cameron Septic Tank Co. v. Knoxville), and amendments to statutes changed coverage. Does not apply where the invention was only described (not claimed) in the foreign patent, or where the foreign patent never became operative; may apply where foreign patent granted exclusive right to make but not to use or sell. There is complex case law on whether extensions of foreign patents affect U.S. patent term—depends on whether extensions were possible/absolute under foreign law at relevant times.

name: Establishing and correcting bid errors
description: Where a bidder seeks to amend a bid for a claimed mistake, the bidder must clearly establish the error by evidence under oath and show that the lead-pencil memorandum (or original estimate) was the basis of the bid; if the error is shown to be fundamental and the bid did not express the real intention of the bidder, reformation may be proper but the corrected bid should include the same percentage of profit on the amount of the error as was calculated in the bid, and nothing more. A bidder may not amend to add items already covered by the original estimate if the original estimate was not shown to be the result of a fundamental error.
guidance: Example: bidder submitted $40,000 with ~13% profit; correction permitted limited to restoring same profit percentage; could not add a separate item for piles that were already in the original estimate. (C. 165U, July 6, 1904.)

name: Standard for institution
description: Different evidentiary thresholds to institute proceedings: PGR requires showing 'more likely than not' that at least one challenged claim is unpatentable; IPR requires a 'reasonable likelihood' of prevailing on at least one claim; EPR requires raising a 'substantial new question of patentability.'
guidance: These differing standards affect petition drafting and evidentiary burdens (35 U.S.C. §§324(a), 314(a), 303). PGR's 'more likely than not' is stricter than IPR's 'reasonable likelihood.' All administrative standards are easier to meet than district court 'clear and convincing' standard (Microsoft v. i4i). Choose the forum with the institution standard most aligned to your available evidence.

name: Offensive vs defensive use cases
description: Typical strategic uses: IPR/PGR commonly used offensively to challenge asserted patents; EPR can be used offensively but also defensively by patent owners to strengthen claims against newly discovered prior art or as a faster alternative to reissue.
guidance: Patent owners may proactively request EPRs for high‑value patents to correct or strengthen claims (faster than reissue). Petitioners use IPR/PGR to cancel or narrow claims when facing assertion; use the proceeding that matches tactical goals (eliminate claims, amend claims, clarify validity) and timeframes.

name: Practical strategic considerations (monitoring and forum choice)
description: Operational strategy guidance: monitor prosecution/grants of competitors, evaluate infringement risk and patent value, review prosecution history and family patents, identify positions to challenge, and strategically choose forum (PGR vs IPR vs EPR vs district court) considering timing, estoppel, scope, and claim construction.
guidance: Decision factors include timing windows, estoppel risk, ability to raise §101/§112 issues (favor PGR), participation and discovery needs, likelihood of amendment vs cancellation, and empirical institution/outcome rates. Proactive measures (e.g., EPR for high‑value patents when new art appears) and preserving options in parallel litigation are emphasized.

name: Claim construction and preservation of issues
description: Considerations about claim construction differences and preserving issues for district court (e.g., whether to preserve §112 or other issues by foregoing PGR).
guidance: Strategically decide whether to raise all potential invalidity grounds before the PTAB (risking estoppel) or to preserve certain defenses or arguments for district court by choosing a proceeding with narrower scope (e.g., IPR) or forgoing PTAB altogether. The article highlights preserving §112 and related issues by filing an IPR instead of PGR when appropriate.

name: Prepare for Analysis – What Has Applicant Invented?
description: Before analyzing for eligibility or any other patentability requirement: review the detailed disclosure and specific embodiments to understand what the applicant has invented; determine the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claims; identify the boundaries of protection sought by applicant; understand how the claims relate to and define what applicant has indicated as the invention.
guidance: See MPEP 2103 for more information. Understanding the disclosure and BRI is a prerequisite to proper §101 analysis.

name: Use the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim
description: Use the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim when performing the eligibility analysis.
guidance: BRI governs claim scope for examination; interpret claim language in light of the specification to identify what is recited.

name: Analyze the claim as a whole
description: Analyze the claim as a whole when performing the §101 judicial-exception analysis.
guidance: Consider all claim elements individually and in combination; do not isolate a single element absent context.

name: Step 2: Two‑part judicial‑exceptions analysis
description: Step 2: A two‑part analysis to determine whether a claim that is directed to a judicial exception recites additional elements that amount to significantly more than the exception (used for all claims).
guidance: This replaces prior guidance and should be applied to identify laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas, and then determine whether the claim adds significantly more.

name: Step 2A: 'Directed to' a judicial exception
description: Step 2A: Is the claim directed to a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea? 'Directed to' means the exception is recited in the claim, i.e., the claim sets forth or describes the exception.
guidance: If no, the claim is eligible and examination continues. If yes, proceed to Step 2B. Example: a claim reciting F=ma is directed to an exception. If the claim recites an exception but clearly does not seek to 'tie up' the exception, a streamlined analysis may be used.

name: Definition of judicial exceptions; no bright line
description: Law of Nature, Natural Phenomenon, Abstract Idea — these are labels courts commonly use but there is no bright line between the exceptions.
guidance: Identify the exception recited in the claim; the analysis is the same regardless of which label is used. Even narrowly defined exceptions (e.g., highly detailed mathematical formula) will trigger eligibility analysis.

name: Abstract ideas — types and instruction to identify
description: Abstract ideas include: fundamental economic practices; certain methods of organizing human activities; ideas themselves; mathematical relationships/formulas. When making a rejection, specifically identify the abstract idea (e.g., the claim recites the steps of creating a contractual relationship) rather than merely labeling its type.
guidance: Software or business methods are not automatically abstract ideas; identify the specific concept recited in the claim.

name: Step 2B: Does the claim as a whole amount to 'significantly more'?
description: Determine whether any element, or combination of elements, in the claim is sufficient to ensure that the claim amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception; analyze each claim as a whole and consider additional elements individually and as an ordered combination to ensure the claim applies the exception in a meaningful way.
guidance: While this analysis no longer weighs factors, considerations are similar to prior Bilski and Mayo/Myriad guidance. Consider each claim separately; similar claims do not automatically rise or fall together.

name: Identify the additional limitations in the claim
description: Considering the claim as a whole, determine whether the additional elements in the claim establish meaningful limitations on the exception and are more than a drafting effort designed to monopolize an exception.
guidance: Individual elements may not add significantly more alone but may do so in combination. Evaluate specific elements recited in the claim.

name: Limitations that may qualify as 'significantly more'
description: Limitations that may be enough to qualify as significantly more include: improvements to another technology or technical field; improvements to the functioning of the computer itself; applying the judicial exception with, or by use of, a particular machine; effecting a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing; adding a specific limitation other than what is well‑understood, routine and conventional in the field, or adding unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application; other meaningful limitations beyond generally linking the use of the exception to a technological environment.
guidance: These are considerations that support finding 'significantly more' when appropriately recited in claim elements or combinations.

name: Limitations that are not enough to qualify as 'significantly more'
description: Limitations found not sufficient include: merely adding the words 'apply it' or equivalent instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer; simply appending well‑understood, routine and conventional activities known to the industry at a high level of generality; adding insignificant extrasolution activity (e.g., mere data gathering); generally linking the use of the exception to a particular technological environment or field of use; using a generic computer to perform generic computer functions.
guidance: Examples: a claim requiring only a generic computer to perform generic functions; data gathering steps that are routine; mere recitation of computer implementation does not render an abstract idea patent‑eligible.

name: Outcome when Step 2B is Yes
description: If the claim as a whole recites additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception, the claim qualifies as eligible subject matter.
guidance: Eligibility analysis is complete; examiners should continue to examine under other statutory provisions (35 U.S.C. §§ 101 (utility, inventorship, double patenting), 102, 103, 112).

name: Outcome when Step 2B is No
description: If the claim as a whole does not recite additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception, the claim is not eligible and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 101.
guidance: Use form paragraphs 7.05 [revised] and 7.05.015 [new]; examiners should continue examination under other statutory provisions (35 U.S.C. §§ 101 (utility, inventorship, double patenting), 102, 103, 112).

name: Claims reciting a plurality of judicial exceptions
description: When a claim recites multiple judicial exceptions, conduct the eligibility analysis for one of the exceptions; if the claim recites elements that amount to significantly more than that exception, consider whether those elements ensure the claim does not have a preemptive effect for other claimed exceptions.
guidance: If Step 2B: YES for one exception, Step 2B is likely satisfied for all exceptions in the claim; if Step 2B: NO for one exception, then the claim is ineligible.

name: Making the §101 rejection — required content
description: The rejection should include identification of the judicial exception by explaining how it is recited in the claim and an explanation of why it is considered an exception; identification of the additional elements in the claim, if any, and an explanation of why they do not add significantly more to the exception.
guidance: Provide a clear, claim‑specific explanation tying claim language to the exception and showing why additional elements are insufficient.

name: New §101 rejections should not be final (when new grounds)
description: If the examiner determines that new grounds of rejection should be made under §101 that are not necessitated by applicant’s amendment of the claims, the Office action should be non‑final so applicant can respond to new grounds.
guidance: See MPEP 706.07(a) regarding appropriate circumstances for making a rejection final.

name: Use of new form paragraph 7.05.015
description: Use new form paragraph 7.05.015 when rejecting a claim directed to a judicial exception without significantly more. (Provides template rejection language identifying the exception and explaining why additional elements do not amount to significantly more.)
guidance: Form ¶ 7.05.015 text should be used in Office actions; older form paragraphs 7.05.011–7.05.014 should no longer be used and will be deleted.

name: Applicant response to a §101 rejection — acceptable approaches
description: A proper response: persuasive arguments/evidence that the claim is not directed to a judicial exception; persuasive arguments/evidence that additional elements amount to significantly more; or claim amendments (removing/adding/changing elements) that cause the claim to not be directed to the exception or to amount to significantly more.
