guidance: Applicants should be given opportunity to present evidence and amendments; examiners should consider such responses in further prosecution.

name: Streamlined eligibility analysis for claims that do not seek to 'tie up' an exception
description: For efficient examination, a streamlined analysis can be used for claims that clearly do not seek to tie up any judicial exception — such claims may recite an exception, but eligibility will be self‑evident, so no detailed analysis is needed.
guidance: If there is doubt whether the claim seeks coverage for a judicial exception, perform a full analysis. See provided streamlined examples (hip prosthesis, robotic arm) illustrating when full analysis is unnecessary.

name: Use case law examples to apply the framework (e.g., Mayo, Alice)
description: Apply the framework to prior case law facts to illustrate how claims were analyzed under Step 1/Step 2A/Step 2B (e.g., Mayo — law of nature; Alice — abstract idea) and the reasons for eligibility/ineligibility.
guidance: Examples show identifying the exception, assessing additional elements, and concluding whether elements add significantly more (e.g., Mayo: 'administering' and 'determining' were routine data gathering; Alice: recited hardware was generic).

name: Now for the legalese—the claims
description: Draft clear, properly‑structured patent claims that define the legal scope of the invention.
guidance: Chapter dedicated to claims drafting; implies guidance on claim scope, dependent/independent claims, and claim language.

name: Going abroad (foreign filing strategy)
description: Considerations and procedures for filing patent applications outside the United States (foreign filing, PCT, priority claims).
guidance: Chapter 'Going abroad' implies coverage of international filing routes and timing but details are not visible on this listing page.

name: Conceptual Clarity
description: The clarity and unambiguity of the language used in the claims.
guidance: Human rating scale 0–10 with anchors: 0–2 Very unclear/ambiguous; 3–4 Significant clarity issues; 5–6 Mostly clear but some ambiguous language; 7–8 Clear with minimal ambiguity; 9–10 Exceptionally clear and unambiguous. Guidance highlights avoiding ambiguous pronouns (e.g., 'it') and that clarity/precision are paramount for legal enforceability. Multi-task fine-tuning was observed to reduce conceptual clarity in some models.

name: Consistency in Terminology
description: Uniformity in the use of terms throughout the claims.
guidance: Human rating scale 0–10 with anchors: 0–2 Highly inconsistent; 3–4 Significant inconsistencies; 5–6 Some inconsistencies but mostly uniform; 7–8 Largely consistent with minor inconsistencies; 9–10 Completely consistent. Paper notes that even minor inconsistencies can cause rejection or loss of patent value; current LLMs achieve mostly consistent terminology but require perfection.

name: Claims must be crafted with high-level precision and clarity
description: Patent claims require strict writing standards, precise and unambiguous wording, and must define the legal protection scope of the invention.
guidance: Claims are legally significant and must be precise enough to withstand legal scrutiny. Guidance includes: prefer avoiding pronouns, ensure unambiguous references, and craft claims to be specific enough to distinguish from prior art while broad enough to cover reasonable implementations.

name: Independent vs Dependent claim structure and purpose
description: Independent claims outline essential features broadly; dependent claims incorporate additional features or limitations to refine embodiments and enhance protection scope.
guidance: Independent claims should aim to encompass the invention broadly while distinguishing from existing technologies. Dependent claims should add meaningful limitations (not mere references) and avoid redundancy. Dependent claims should refine or specify embodiments logically tied to the independent claim.

name: Avoid pronouns and ambiguous referents
description: References such as 'it' must not introduce ambiguity; preferable to avoid pronouns entirely in claims.
guidance: Ambiguous pronouns reduce conceptual clarity and can undermine enforceability. Ensure every referent is explicit and unambiguous.

name: Avoid repetitive or redundant claims
description: Generated claim sets should not repeatedly restate identical claims or produce multiple claims with no added limitations.
guidance: Repetition signals poor claim drafting and reduces claim set value. Fine-tuning can help reduce repetitions, but models still often generate redundant claims; ensure dependent claims add distinct, substantive limitations.

name: Avoid null features and non-contributory limitations
description: Dependent claim restrictions should meaningfully contribute to differentiation and protection; features that do not contribute (null features) should be avoided.
guidance: Some generated restrictions may not improve protection or differentiation; these should be identified and removed/replaced during revision to improve legal robustness.

name: Terminology must be completely consistent throughout claim set
description: Domain-specific terminology should be used uniformly across claims to prevent inconsistency-based rejections or loss of clarity.
guidance: Minor inconsistencies can have large legal consequences; human reviewers should enforce absolute consistency of key terms and definitions.

name: Dataset and input selection constraints for evaluation
description: Use description-based inputs (rather than abstracts) for claim generation because descriptions contain more detailed technical/legal specifics required for claims.
guidance: Paper filters documents (e.g., granted patents filed in 2017, descriptions < 8,000 tokens) to construct the HUPD-DCG dataset. Guidance: description-based generation yields higher feature completeness and better claim outputs than abstract-based generation.

name: Economic/public-goods justification for subject matter eligibility
description: Subject matter should be patentable only if a public goods problem exists—i.e., patent protection is needed to provide incentives for production of the public good; if no such problem exists, subject matter patentability should be denied and the patentability inquiry should end.
guidance: (Original wording) “If no public goods problem exists, either because of the nature of the subject matter, or because other factors exist that adequately incentive production of the public good, then subject matter patentability should be denied and the patentability inquiry should end.” Use economic analysis to justify inclusion/exclusion of categories of subject matter rather than relying on intuition or historical attributions of economic reasoning by courts. Consider whether claimed subject matter genuinely requires patent incentives to be produced.

name: Appropriate functional role: threshold exclusion vs limitation on claim scope
description: Determine whether subject matter doctrine should function as a threshold gatekeeper excluding categories from entry (front‑door exclusion) or as a tool to limit the permissible scope of claims (scalpel to sever overly-broad claims).
guidance: Current doctrine often operates to limit claim scope (e.g., abstract ideas and natural phenomena are used to avoid unduly broad claims) rather than to exclude whole fields at the threshold. Practical implication: exclusions that mainly require careful claim-drafting do not economize on administrative costs because examiners must evaluate claim breadth in detail.

name: Concern for unduly broad claims and preemption
description: A key concern in §101 jurisprudence is whether claims are so broad that they would preempt use of an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon — effectively granting a monopoly over the underlying principle rather than a particular application.
guidance: Examples: Morse (invalidating an eighth claim because it would give control over future inventions), Benson, Bilski, Grams. Breadth and preemption risk indicate that a claim is improperly directed to the principle/algorithm itself rather than a patent-eligible application. Evaluate whether the claim would 'wholly pre-empt' future uses or applications.

name: Claim breadth should be tested against enablement and disclosure (§112) as well as §101
description: When claims appear overly broad, the statutory grounds of enablement and adequate disclosure (§112) may be the appropriate vehicle to invalidate them rather than treating breadth as a §101 ineligibility problem.
guidance: The text argues that if the problem with a claim is that it is too broad, statutory grounds such as failure of enablement under §112 should arguably be the basis for invalidity. Anti-pattern: resolving what are effectively enablement/disclosure problems solely through §101.

name: Prefer tailored remedies over categorical exclusions where possible (use subject-matter limits to avoid unduly broad claims)
description: Subject matter doctrine can be used as a tool to deny or invalidate particular claims that threaten to impose costs that exceed their benefits even if it cannot serve efficiently as a categorical threshold exclusion.
guidance: While categorical exclusions may be ill-suited to the current doctrinal form, §101 limitations remain useful as a 'scalpel' to carve out unduly broad claims. Consider whether other doctrines fail and whether §101 should operate as a backstop. Recognize doctrinal redundancy is common and may be justified when the interest at stake is important.

name: Temporal limitation — one-year grace period
description: 37 CFR 1.130 is not available to except disclosures that were made more than one year before the effective filing date of the claimed invention; such disclosures are prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1).
guidance: Check effective filing date per MPEP §2152.01. There are nuanced availability rules for 102(a)(2) references that were effectively filed earlier but published later; consult MPEP §2155.06 and §2154.01 et seq. as applicable.

name: Form paragraph content and use (7.67.aia and 7.68.aia)
description: Use the MPEP form paragraphs when indicating an affidavit/declaration is effective (7.67.aia) or ineffective (7.68.aia). Required bracketed insertions include: type (affidavit/declaration), subsection (a)/(b), filing date of the affidavit/declaration, affected claim(s), specific reference, and explanation of how the affidavit/declaration does or does not satisfy 35 U.S.C. 102(b) exception elements.
guidance: Form paragraph 7.67.aia must be preceded by 7.03.aia. When using 7.68.aia, include the statutory grounds and explanation of insufficiency. Populate brackets carefully (see list of bracket meanings in MPEP).

name: Transform abstract idea into a practical technological application
description: The Guidance assumes many AI-based method claims are abstract ideas; the central inquiry is whether the claim transforms that abstract idea into a practical technological application (i.e., a patent-eligible technological improvement).
guidance: Focus examination on whether claimed elements integrate the abstract idea into a specific, practical technological solution rather than merely reciting the abstract idea itself. Examples 47–49 illustrate claims that fail or succeed on this point.

name: Claims that generically recite training/using AI models are likely abstract
description: Claims that generally refer to training an AI model and using the model to detect patterns or analyze data are less likely to survive subject-matter eligibility review because they are treated as abstract ideas.
guidance: Avoid high-level recitations like 'train a model' and 'use the model to detect patterns' without further technical integration or specific applications; include additional claim elements showing how the model is applied to a concrete technological problem.

name: Reciting specific, practical uses of AI analysis results supports eligibility
description: Claims that explicitly recite practical uses of the results of AI analysis—i.e., how detected information is used to effect a technological outcome—are more likely to be found eligible.
guidance: Example 47 Claim 3 was found eligible because it required using detected anomaly information to detect source addresses, drop potentially malicious packets, and block future traffic—concrete actions that convert abstract detection into a technological response.

name: Specially customized physical structure (hardware) can render claim eligible
description: Claims that require a specially customized physical structure (e.g., an ASIC with particular neuron/register/microprocessor organization) are more likely to be eligible because they recite a non-abstract physical device.
guidance: Example 47 Claim 1 (an ANN implemented as an ASIC with specified components) was found eligible under this principle; drafting that includes physical/hardware limitations or specially configured circuitry can strengthen eligibility.

name: Using detected information to effect concrete actions adds an inventive concept
description: Claims that use detected or classified information to trigger specific corrective or control actions (e.g., dropping packets, blocking addresses) add an inventive concept beyond mere abstract classification/detection.
guidance: Draft claims to show downstream application of the AI output in specific operational steps that change system behavior or accomplish a technical control function; Example 47 Claim 3 illustrates this.

name: Claim must reflect a technical improvement, not merely a mathematical operation
description: A claim that performs mathematical operations or data transformations (e.g., feature determination) but does not sufficiently integrate those operations into a technical improvement is likely abstract and ineligible.
guidance: Example 48 Claim 1 (speech separation DNN determining features) was ineligible because it was treated as a mathematical operation not integrated into a technical improvement; ensure claims tie algorithmic steps to improvements in system performance, signal processing, or other technology.

name: Reciting particular processing steps or outputs that give a concrete improvement supports eligibility
description: Claims that recite particular processing steps (e.g., synthesizing speech waveforms from masked clusters, combining waveforms to generate a mixed signal, transmitting for remote storage) can show a 'particular' improvement over prior methods and be eligible.
guidance: Example 48 Claim 2 was eligible because the claimed steps (synthesizing and combining waveforms, remote storage) were specific technical operations tied to an improvement. Include specific processing actions and concrete outputs in claims.

name: Ordering of steps and specifying how training aids downstream processing can add inventive concept
description: Claims that detail the ordering of steps and how a trained model specifically aids subsequent assignments or processing can direct the claim to a technical improvement despite some abstract elements.
guidance: Example 48 Claim 3 was eligible because it recited details of how DNN training aids cluster assignments and the ordering of steps; draft claims to show interdependence and particular roles of processing stages.

name: Vague treatment steps that do not meaningfully limit claims are ineligible
description: Broad or vague steps like administering 'an appropriate treatment' that do not require any particular application of the abstract idea generally fail eligibility.
guidance: Example 49 Claim 1 was ineligible because step (c) 'administering an appropriate treatment' did not meaningfully limit the claim. Replace vague, catch‑all functional language with specific treatments or concrete therapeutic actions.

name: Reciting a specific, particular treatment can convert an abstract idea into a patent-eligible application
description: Adding a short, specific limitation identifying a particular treatment (e.g., 'wherein the appropriate treatment is Compound X eye drops') can transform a claim from abstract to a particular, patent-eligible medical treatment.
guidance: Example 49 Claim 2 became eligible by naming a specific treatment; consider claiming particular compounds, dosages, or concrete medical interventions when appropriate to ground a claim in a concrete application.

name: Completeness may be limited in certain circumstances
description: The examiner’s action will be complete as to all matters, except that in appropriate circumstances, such as misjoinder of invention, fundamental defects in the application, and the like, the action of the examiner may be limited to such matters before further action is made. However, matters of form need not be raised by the examiner until a claim is found allowable.
guidance: If fundamental problems exist, examiner can limit scope of action; form objections can be deferred until allowance.

name: Rejections must cite best references and explain pertinence
description: In rejecting claims for want of novelty or for obviousness, the examiner must cite the best references at his or her command. When a reference is complex or shows or describes inventions other than that claimed by the applicant, the particular part relied on must be designated as nearly as practicable. The pertinence of each reference, if not apparent, must be clearly explained and each rejected claim specified.
guidance: Cite the best prior art; identify the exact parts relied upon; explain why each reference is pertinent; specify which claims are rejected. For 35 U.S.C. 103 rejections, set out how references are modified or combined.

name: Permissible reliance on admissions and personal-knowledge facts
description: In rejecting claims the examiner may rely upon admissions by the applicant ... and, insofar as rejections in applications are concerned, may also rely upon facts within his or her knowledge pursuant to paragraph (d)(2) of this section.
guidance: Examiners can use applicant admissions and personal-knowledge facts; when relying on facts within personal knowledge, the data shall be as specific as possible and must be supported, when called for by the applicant, by the affidavit of such employee (subject to contradiction).

name: Restriction Requirement Rate (Restrictions)
description: The total number of restriction requirements issued by an Examiner or art unit divided by the total number of applications processed by that Examiner/art unit.
guidance: Equivalent to the probability of receiving a restriction requirement; helps with claim drafting and divisional strategy.

name: Amendments before designated/elected Offices (Articles 28 & 41)
description: The applicant shall be given the opportunity to amend the claims, the description, and the drawings, before each designated (Article 28) and each elected Office (Article 41) within the prescribed time limit. No designated/elected Office shall grant or refuse a patent before such time limit has expired except with the express consent of the applicant.
guidance: Amendments shall not go beyond the disclosure in the international application as filed, unless the national law of the designated/elected State permits. Amendments must conform to national law for matters not covered by the Treaty/Regulations. Where a translation is required, amendments shall be in the language of the translation.

name: Objective and criteria of the International Preliminary Examination (Article 33)
description: The objective is to formulate a preliminary and non‑binding opinion on whether the claimed invention appears to be novel, to involve an inventive step (to be non‑obvious), and to be industrially applicable.
guidance: For international preliminary examination purposes: novelty = not anticipated by prior art as defined in the Regulations; inventive step = not obvious to a person skilled in the art at the prescribed relevant date; industrial applicability = can be made or used in any kind of industry (industry in broad sense). These criteria serve only for international preliminary examination; Contracting States may apply additional or different criteria nationally. Examination shall consider all documents cited in the international search report and may consider additional relevant documents.

name: Scope limitations for IPEA (Article 34(4) & 35(3))
description: If the IPEA considers the application relates to subject matter on which it is not required to carry out an international preliminary examination, or that description/claims/drawings are so unclear or inadequately supported that no meaningful opinion can be formed on novelty, inventive step, or industrial applicability, the Authority shall not go into those questions and shall inform the applicant with reasons.
guidance: If these situations exist only for certain claims, the Authority's limitation applies to those claims only. The IPEA's report in such cases shall state this opinion and reasons, and shall not contain the usual claim-by-claim statements under Article 35(2).

name: Content and limits of the International Preliminary Examination Report (Article 35)
description: The report shall be established within prescribed time and form and shall not state whether the invention is or seems patentable under any national law. It shall state, for each claim, whether the claim appears to satisfy the criteria of novelty, inventive step, and industrial applicability as defined for international preliminary examination, accompanied by citation of supporting documents and explanations and other observations as provided in the Regulations.
guidance: If Article 34(4)(a) situation exists, the report shall state that opinion and reasons and shall not contain the Article 35(2) statements. If only some claims are affected, the report should mix the appropriate statements for affected and unaffected claims.

name: Subject-matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101
description: The Supreme Court in Diamond v. Chakrabarty held that a live, man-made microorganism is patentable subject matter under Section 101; the principle articulated was that “anything under the sun that is made by man” is eligible for patenting.
guidance: Use Chakrabarty as controlling U.S. precedent for patenting genetically engineered microorganisms and similar biotechnological inventions. The article recounts the Court’s focus on whether the claimed microorganism constituted a “manufacture” or “composition of matter.” Quote and rely on the broad congressional mandate regarding patentable subject matter embodied in §101 when evaluating biotech inventions.

name: Non-naturally occurring non-human multicellular organisms are patentable (PTO position)
description: The PTO stated (April 7, 1988) that it “now considers non-naturally occurring non-human multicellular living organisms, including animals, to be patentable subject matter within the scope of 35 U.S.C. 101.”
guidance: Rely on the PTO’s policy and subsequent allowance history (e.g., Harvard Mouse) when prosecuting claims to transgenic animals and other non-natural higher life forms in the U.S. Cite Ex Parte Allen and PTO notices to show consistency with agency precedent.

name: Jurisdictional variance in eligibility (national differences)
description: Not all countries follow the U.S. approach to patenting higher life forms; for example, Canada refused to patent the Harvard Mouse—the Supreme Court of Canada ruled it was not patentable subject matter under the Canadian Patent Act.
guidance: Assess patent strategy globally: evaluate domestic eligibility rules and relevant case law in each jurisdiction before filing. Don’t assume U.S. precedent will be accepted abroad; tailor claims and arguments to national statutes and precedent (and consider parallel filings, defensive strategies, or trade‑secret options where foreign eligibility is doubtful).

name: Examples of patentable biotechnology subject matter (processes, organisms, engineered crops, cell-line methods)
description: The article catalogs successful patents: PCR process patents (amplifying DNA), genetically engineered crops (herbicide-resistant seeds), transgenic animals (Harvard Mouse), and methods for isolating embryonic stem cells (Thomson).
guidance: Use these categories as precedent that processes, compositions, genetically modified organisms, and methods for deriving and sustaining cell lines can be claimed and obtained in the U.S. Provide detailed enabling disclosure for these categories and anticipate prior art challenges specific to each technology (e.g., molecular process prior art for PCR; sequence/construct prior art for transgenics).

name: Importance of claim drafting skill in defining patent scope
description: The authors note that “The patents for these innovations are limited only by the skill of the individuals drafting the claims,” implying that claim drafting determines the effective breadth and enforceability of biotech patents.
guidance: Invest in precise, thoughtful claim drafting: define scope to cover commercially important embodiments while providing adequate support and enablement in the specification. Anticipate infringement/invalidity arguments and craft dependent claims and claim charts to tie claims to technical evidence.

name: Determine whether claim is directed to a judicial exception
description: Analyze whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon, or product of nature.
guidance: If the claim is directed to an exception, continue through the 2A/2B evaluation. If not directed to any exception, the claim is eligible and further 2A/2B analysis is unnecessary. Examples: comparing sequences can be an abstract idea; using gravity per se is a law of nature but a machine that meaningfully limits its use may not be 'directed to' the exception.

name: Product-of-nature / nature-based product: compare to closest naturally occurring counterpart
description: For nature-based product claims, compare the claimed nature-based product to its closest naturally occurring counterpart to determine if it has markedly different characteristics.
guidance: Evaluate disclosed altered properties (e.g., specific particle size distribution -> increased/consistent dissolution) to see if they yield a marked difference relevant to the invention. If the claimed product has markedly different characteristics from its natural counterpart (and those differences are relevant to the claimed invention), it is not a ‘product of nature’ exception and may be eligible.

name: Step 2A — is the claim 'directed to' the judicial exception?
description: Analyze whether the claim, as a whole, is directed to the exception (for example, an abstract idea) or whether the additional elements remove it from being 'directed to' the exception.
guidance: If the claim as a whole is not directed to an exception, conclude eligibility at Step 2A and do not perform Step 2B. If it is directed to an exception, proceed to Step 2B (significantly more). Examples: certain hybridizing/detecting process claims are not directed to an exception and so are eligible at Step 2A.

name: Step 2B — do additional elements amount to 'significantly more'?
description: If the claim is directed to an exception, determine whether any additional element or combination of elements ensures the claim amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception.
guidance: Additional elements that are merely instructions to apply the abstract idea using well-understood, routine, conventional techniques do not confer eligibility (Alice). However, recitation of unconventional, non-routine, specific techniques (or a meaningful combination of elements that together improve technology) can provide 'significantly more' (BASCOM, examples like SNOM or Cool-Melt PCR).

name: When claim focuses on a process, no need for product marked-difference analysis
description: If analysis of the claim as a whole shows the claim is focused on a process rather than on recited nature-based products, examiners need not perform the markedly different characteristics analysis on the recited product limitations.
guidance: Example: a claim directed to comparing sequences (a process) does not require performing the product-of-nature marked-differences test on recited genes/probes because the claim focus is the comparison process.

name: Mental steps / human-performable steps indicate abstract idea
description: If claimed steps could be performed by a human using mental steps or basic critical thinking, courts have treated such claims as abstract ideas.
guidance: Identify whether steps like 'comparing information' are recited at high-level generality with no limits on how the comparison is performed. If so, they likely reflect an abstract idea (Classen, Myriad, Ambry examples).

name: Combination of elements may yield significantly more
description: Even if individual additional elements do not amount to significantly more, a specific combination of elements together may provide significantly more than the judicial exception.
guidance: Assess the claim as a whole — e.g., hybridizing + detecting by non-routine technique (SNOM) or comparing + Cool-Melt PCR amplification + sequencing can together be 'significantly more.'

name: Rejection drafting: identify the exception and explain insufficiency of claim elements
description: When issuing a rejection, identify the judicial exception the claim is directed to and explain why the claim elements amount to that exception and why additional elements/wherein clauses do not impose meaningful limitations.
guidance: Specifically point to the claimed comparison/abstract idea and explain why limiting language (e.g., a wherein clause) merely states a result and does not impose additional limiting steps. Explain absence of additional meaningful limitations in the claim as a whole.

name: Allowance/remarks drafting for eligible claims
description: If claim is eligible (either not directed to an exception or amounts to significantly more), examiners may add remarks to an Office action or reasons for allowance indicating that the claim is not directed to any judicial exception.
guidance: Use remarks to clarify that the claim recites additional limitations that, alone or in combination, are more than a mere instruction to apply the exception using well-understood, routine, conventional techniques, or that the claim adds meaningful limitations/improvements to technology.

name: Claims reciting laws of nature may still be eligible if they add specific unconventional steps that effect transformation
description: A claim founded on a scientific/chemical principle or law of nature can be eligible if the claim does not recite the law and instead recites specific, unconventional steps that effect a transformation (e.g., hydrolysis process mixing/heating under specific conditions).
guidance: Assess whether the claim's specific steps effect a transformation (e.g., fat + water heated under pressure to produce free fatty acids and glycerol) and add meaningful limitations beyond the law itself; eligibility can be self-evident without full 2A/2B analysis.

name: Use of case law as analytical touchstones
description: Apply relevant judicial decisions (e.g., Myriad, Mayo, Alice, Roslin, Diamond v. Diehr, Eibel Process Co., Tilghman) as precedential or illustrative guidance when identifying exceptions and evaluating whether additional elements are conventional or sufficient to confer eligibility.
guidance: Cite cases where applicable to explain why an activity is an abstract idea or why particular limitations do/don't amount to significantly more. Use examples from those cases to illustrate outcomes (e.g., Myriad: comparison/sequence claims; Diehr/Eibel: processes/machines that improve technology).

name: Comparable agreements (Factor Three)
description: Jury should consider prior agreements by the patent holder to license the patent(s)-in-suit or other agreements if they were negotiated in circumstances, and concerned subjects, sufficiently comparable to those that would be involved in the parties' negotiation regarding the patent(s)-in-suit.
guidance: The offering party bears the burden to show technological and economic comparability by comparing technology, scope, context, and value of the prior license to the pre-investment hypothetical license; licenses need not be identical but must be more than loosely or vaguely comparable. Examples/citations show courts rejecting licenses that bear no discernible link to the claimed technology.

name: Customize instructions to the facts; define non-infringing alternatives concretely
description: Generic recitation of factors is often too abstract; instructions should be tailored to the facts, e.g., explicitly telling the jury what a ‘non-infringing alternative’ is in the case and how the defendant alleges a particular alternative affects the royalty.
guidance: Provide specific, case-tied wording: identify the alleged non-infringing alternative, state whether it was available at the relevant negotiation date, and instruct that any royalty must be based on the incremental value of the claimed invention over that commercially acceptable alternative.

name: Step 1 — Statutory Category Determination
description: Step 1 determines whether the claim is directed to a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter.
guidance: If the claim is not directed to one of these statutory categories, reject the claim under 35 U.S.C. § 101 as being drawn to non-statutory subject matter, using revised form paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01, and continue examination for patentability. This step has not changed and is explained in MPEP 2106(I).

name: Step 2 — Two-part Alice/Mayo Analysis
description: Step 2 is the two-part analysis from Alice Corp. (also called the Mayo test) for claims directed to laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas (the judicially recognized exceptions).
guidance: This two-part test is represented in diamonds (2A) and (2B) in the flowchart and is the subject of the Interim Eligibility Guidance. Use Step 2A to determine whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception and Step 2B to determine whether the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the exception.

name: Step 2A — 'Directed to' a Judicial Exception
description: In Step 2A, determine whether the claim is directed to a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea (judicial exceptions).
guidance: 'Directed to' means the exception is recited in the claim, i.e., the claim sets forth or describes the exception. If no, the claim is eligible and examination should continue for patentability. If yes, proceed to Step 2B. Examples of concepts courts have found to be laws of nature, natural phenomena, or abstract ideas are provided in Parts I.A.2 and IV of the Interim Eligibility Guidance.

name: Streamlined analysis when claim does not 'tie up' exception
description: If the claim, when viewed as a whole, clearly does not seek to 'tie up' any judicial exception, use the streamlined analysis.
guidance: Use the 'streamlined analysis' discussed in Part I.B.3 of the Interim Eligibility Guidance when it is clear that a claim does not attempt to preempt all practical applications of an exception. (See referenced part for application guidance and examples.)

name: Step 2B — 'Significantly More' / Inventive Concept Inquiry
description: In Step 2B, determine whether any element, or combination of elements, in the claim is sufficient to ensure that the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception.
guidance: If no, the claim is ineligible and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 101 using form paragraphs 7.05 [revised] and 7.05.015 [new]. If yes, the claim is eligible. The additional elements should be considered both individually and as an ordered combination. Individual elements when viewed on their own may not appear to add significantly more, but when viewed in combination may amount to significantly more than the exception. The Supreme Court has identified a number of considerations for determining whether a claim with additional elements amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception itself; examples and applications are in Parts I.B.1 and III of the Interim Eligibility Guidance. Consider each claim separately based on the particular elements recited therein — claims do not automatically rise or fall with similar claims in an application.

name: Handling of claims directed to multiple exceptions
description: If a claim is directed to a plurality of exceptions, conduct the eligibility analysis for one of the exceptions.
guidance: Additional elements that satisfy Step 2B for one exception will likely satisfy Step 2B for all exceptions in a claim. Conversely, if the claim fails under Step 2B for one exception, the claim is ineligible and no further eligibility analysis is needed.

name: Form Paragraph 7.05.015 — Non-Statutory (Directed to Judicial Exception without Significantly More)
description: Form paragraph 7.05.015 is used when the claimed invention is directed to a judicial exception (law of nature, natural phenomenon, abstract idea) without significantly more.
guidance: Text template: 'the claimed invention is directed to a judicial exception (i.e., a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea) without significantly more. Claim(s) [1] is/are directed to [2]. The claim(s) does/do not include additional elements that are sufficient to amount to significantly more than the judicial exception because [3].' Examiner Note guidance: (1) This form paragraph should be preceded by form paragraph 7.05. (2) This form paragraph is for use with all claims, including product (machine, manufacture, and composition of matter) and process claims, and for any type of judicial exception. (3) In bracket 1, identify the claim or claims that recite the judicial exception. (4) In bracket 2, identify the exception by referring to how it is recited (set forth or described) in the claim and explain why it is considered an exception (examples: 'the Arrhenius equation, which is a law of nature in the form of a mathematical algorithm' or 'the series of steps instructing how to hedge risk, which is a fundamental economic practice and thus an abstract idea'). For products of nature, explain how the characteristics are not markedly different from the product’s naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state (example wording provided). (5) In bracket 3, identify the additional elements and explain why, when considered separately and in combination, they do not add significantly more to the exception (examples: generically recited computer elements do not add a meaningful limitation because they would be routine in any computer implementation; routine data-gathering steps do not add a meaningful limitation because they would be routinely used by those of ordinary skill in the art).

name: National phase deadline
description: The national phase deadline with the Brazilian Patent Office (INPI) is 30 months from the priority date.
guidance: Translation of the title, claims, and abstract must be submitted at the 30-month deadline in Brazil. Applicants may file an extension for the Portuguese specification.

name: Translation requirements and extension
description: Translation of the title, claims, and abstract must be submitted at the 30-month deadline; extension for the Portuguese specification is possible.
guidance: Submit translated title, claims and abstract at 30 months. If additional time is needed for the full Portuguese specification, an extension may be filed (the page explicitly notes applicants may file an extension for the Portuguese specification).

name: PPH (Patent Prosecution Highway) eligibility and procedural requirements
description: Requirements and procedural conditions for requesting participation in the PPH in Brazil.
guidance: Key points listed on the page: - No fixed deadline to request PPH in Brazil, but the application must have been published (or an anticipated publication requested). - The technical examination must have been requested (but not yet initiated by the BRPTO for PPH purposes — initiation occurs when an office action, unfavorable opinion, or grant publication happens). - Application must have been filed for at least 18 months or have a request for anticipated publication, or (for international applications) been published by WIPO. - No divisional or voluntary amendments may be made between PPH request submission and its decision (divisional filings must be done before the PPH request; the PPH request is possible for either parent or divisional individually). - The application must belong to a patent family with at least an older patent application filed with INPI or an Office of Earlier Examination. - The family must include an Office of Earlier Examination that has examined the family and considered subject matter patentable in a substantive examination, or that has issued a decision of approval/grant. - Claims submitted must be equal to or more restricted than the subject matter considered patentable by the Office of Earlier Examination; inclusion of matter not searched/examined by the Office of Earlier Examination is prohibited even if the claim is restricted. - Provide the required supportive documents.

name: Divisional filing timing and content limitations
description: Scope and timing constraints for filing divisional patent applications in Brazil.
guidance: In Brazil, divisionals are limited to what is presented in the claims filed when the application starts examination. Best practice: retain the entire claim chapter (do not delete claims) until the Brazilian Office decides on patentability and any lack-of-unity objections.

name: Known‑in‑the‑art elements can still be unconventional (novelty/obviousness distinct from eligibility)
description: An additional element (or combination of elements) that is known in the art can nonetheless be unconventional or non‑routine for purposes of eligibility; novelty/obviousness inquiries are separate from eligibility.
guidance: Claims may improve conventional computer functionality even if anticipated by prior art (e.g., Enfish). Examiners should consider whether features provide technical benefits (faster searches, reduced memory, etc.) that reflect an improvement rather than treating mere prior‑art teaching as dispositive against eligibility.

name: Computer functions commonly recognized as well‑understood/routine when claimed generically
description: Courts have identified certain computer functions as well‑understood, routine, conventional activities when recited at a high level of generality or as insignificant extra‑solution activity.
guidance: Examples include: receiving/transmitting data over a network (using Internet to gather data; forwarding information), performing repetitive calculations, electronic recordkeeping (creating/maintaining accounts or logs), storing and retrieving information in memory, scanning/extracting data from documents (OCR), and standard web‑browser navigation (back/forward). However, not all computer functions are conventional — claims specifying how interactions are manipulated to yield a desired result or providing technical details may be eligible (see DDR Holdings, Amdocs, BASCOM).

name: Life‑science laboratory techniques commonly recognized as well‑understood/routine when claimed generically
description: In the life sciences, courts have recognized various laboratory techniques as well‑understood, routine, conventional activities when claimed at a high level of generality.
guidance: Examples include: determining biomarker levels in blood by any means, using PCR to amplify/detect DNA, detecting DNA or enzymes in a sample, immunizing a patient, analyzing DNA for sequence/variants, freezing and thawing cells, amplifying/sequencing nucleic acids, and hybridizing a gene probe. When recited generically these techniques may not provide 'significantly more' unless tied to specific, unconventional applications or integration into treatment/prophylaxis.

name: Other non‑technical activities recognized as conventional when claimed generically
description: Courts have found commonplace non‑technical activities to be well‑understood/routine when claimed at a high level of generality.
guidance: Examples include: recording a customer's order, shuffling/dealing a deck of cards, restricting public access by requiring viewing of an ad, presenting offers and gathering statistics, determining estimated outcomes and setting prices, and arranging/sorting information or pricing hierarchies. Generic recitation of these activities often will not supply 'significantly more.'

name: Other Meaningful Limitations — claim must add meaningful limitations beyond mere linkage to a technological environment
description: A claim should add meaningful limitations beyond generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment to transform the judicial exception into patent‑eligible subject matter.
guidance: Considerations in MPEP §2106.05(a)‑(d) (improvement, integration into practical application, etc.) qualify as meaningful limitations when they amount to significantly more. Examples: Diehr (arrhenius equation applied in automated rubber‑molding process — steps that limited application to a practical molding process were meaningful) and Classen (immunization integrated into a specific, tangible method). Examiners should explain on the record why additional elements meaningfully limit the exception and assess both individual elements and their combination.

name: Provide 'problem/solution' in the specification
description: When drafting your patent application, consider providing 'problem/solution' in the specification to highlight the various inventive concepts of your software related invention as an improvement over known prior art.
guidance: Explicitly stating advantages of your inventive concept may help support the inventive concept captured in your claims as not routine or conventional (example: Aatrix’s claimed 'data file contains an inventive concept directed to improved importation of data and interoperability with third-party software').

name: Support asserted claims in pleadings with specification evidence
description: When filing a complaint, consider providing support from your patent specification that your asserted claims include inventive concepts that are not routine and conventional.
guidance: Include citations and excerpts from the specification and any declarations that tie claimed limitations to described inventive concepts to avoid early dismissal under §101.

name: Use factual allegations/evidence to oppose §101 dismissal
description: Plausible factual allegations may preclude dismissing a case under §101 where 'nothing on th[e] record...refutes those allegations as a matter of law or justifies dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6).' (Aatrix)
guidance: Submit declarations or factual pleadings that, taken as true, would directly affect the court’s Alice patent-eligibility analysis (e.g., evidence that claimed elements are unconventional).

name: Courts must state reasoning/evidence before deeming components 'well understood' or 'routine'
description: A district court should provide reasoning or evidence when finding that a claimed component 'describes a well understood and routine component and function of a computer' rather than asserting that conclusion without support.
guidance: Anticipate and rebut blanket characterizations of claim elements as 'routine' by documenting why elements are unconventional or how they operate differently from prior art.

name: Be specific in the specification about how the invention operates to provide an improvement
description: When drafting specifications, consider being specific with respect to how the invention operates to provide an improvement over the state of the art.
guidance: Describe the concrete technical benefits, the mechanism by which the benefits are achieved, and how the claimed arrangement departs from earlier approaches (examples: distributed enhancement for data flows, storing verification structure in BIOS memory, parser transforming data to improve functionality).

name: Claim specific ways/means of achieving results (not only results)
description: Carefully review the claims to determine if the claims are directed to the result rather than how to solve the problem at hand; the distinction between results and means is fundamental to eligibility analysis.
guidance: Draft claims to recite how the desired result is achieved (concrete steps, structures, configuration), not merely the desired outcome; ensure claimed features that effect the solution are actually claimed, not only described in the specification.

name: Avoid leaving implementation to unbounded trial-and-error
description: A direction to engage in a conventional, unbounded trial-and-error process (e.g., perform a plurality of experiments) does not make a patent-eligible invention, even if the desired result would be new and unconventional.
guidance: Provide specific guidance, parameters, tuning instructions, or concrete techniques in the specification and claims rather than instructions that require open-ended experimentation.

name: Include sufficient detail in application and claims (extend detail to dependent claims)
description: Sufficient detail should be included in the application draft describing the solution to the problem rather than simply applying a natural law or mathematical formula; this should be extended to the claim scope where, at the very least, dependent claims should include limitations with sufficient detail to describe the solution to the problem.
guidance: Use dependent claims to narrow and define how the invention achieves its effects and to preserve claim scope that may bear on eligibility and enablement.

name: Dependent claims may affect §101 — do not concede one claim is representative
description: Dependent claims can bear on patent eligibility; plaintiffs should not concede that a single representative independent claim covers all claims for §101 analysis.
guidance: Identify and preserve arguments based on dependent-claim limitations that may supply an inventive concept or technical improvement; analyze multiple claims rather than relying on a single representative claim.

name: Whether elements are 'well-understood, routine and conventional' is a question of fact
description: In assessing Alice step two, the question of whether a claim element or combination of elements is well-understood, routine and conventional to a skilled artisan in the relevant field is a question of fact.
guidance: Build factual record (expert declarations, technical evidence, specification support) to create genuine issues of material fact where appropriate; absent factual disputes, courts may decide the issue as a matter of law.

name: Show inventive concept in ordered combination or unconventional arrangement
description: An inventive concept can be found in the non-conventional and non-generic arrangement of known, conventional pieces; claims may be eligible because they recite a specific discrete implementation that provides a technical improvement.
guidance: Draft claims that carve out a specific implementation (location, arrangement, customization) and explain how that arrangement improves computer functionality or solves a technical problem (e.g., remote ISP server with per-user filtering).

name: Avoid describing elements as 'conventional' or relying on well-known business practices
description: Make sure your specification contains details of how claimed functionality is performed and avoids characterization of elements that are claimed as conventional or typical or commonly known; also avoid referencing well-known business practices.
guidance: When there is a technical problem, describe specifics of how the technical problem is solved rather than labeling components as generic or invoking business-practice rationales that the court may treat as abstract.

name: Provide implementation details when dependent claims must demonstrate inventive concept
description: The specification should provide details of how claimed functions are implemented, especially if dependent claims are relied on to show inventive concept; for at least some dependent claims the specification should describe how to implement claimed functions (e.g., linking an order to a table).
guidance: Ensure the specification contains examples, flow, structures, or algorithms that concretely implement claimed functions to avoid claims being treated as merely aspirational or result-oriented.

name: Clear articulation / explicit analysis for 35 U.S.C. 103 rejections
description: The key to supporting any rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 is the clear articulation of the reason(s) why the claimed invention would have been obvious. The analysis supporting a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 should be made explicit.
guidance: Office personnel must provide a reasoned explanation for every obviousness rejection; rejections cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements. Courts (KSR; Ball Aerosol; In re Van Os) require that the examiner articulate the factual findings and explain how those findings support the legal conclusion of obviousness. Even when relying on common sense, Office personnel must articulate an appropriate rationale and factual basis (see MPEP §2141 and §2143).

name: Rationale A: Combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results
description: Combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results.
guidance: To reject a claim based on this rationale, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries and articulate the following findings: (1) that the prior art included each element claimed (not necessarily in a single reference); (2) that one of ordinary skill could have combined the elements as claimed by known methods and that in combination each element merely performs the same function as it does separately; (3) that one of ordinary skill would have recognized that the results of the combination were predictable; and (4) whatever additional findings based on the Graham factual inquiries are necessary. If any of these findings cannot be made, the combining-elements rationale cannot be used. Examples: Anderson’s-Black Rock, Sundance, Crocs (illustrating predictable results vs. unpredictability).

name: Any rationale must link factual findings to the legal conclusion of obviousness
description: Any rationale employed must provide a link between the factual findings and the legal conclusion of obviousness.
guidance: Examiner must show how the resolved Graham inquiries (scope/content of prior art, differences between prior art and claims, level of ordinary skill, secondary considerations) support the chosen rationale and the ultimate legal conclusion. Mere conclusory statements that a combination would have been 'obvious' are insufficient; the examiner must articulate the inferences, reasoning, and factual underpinning (Ball Aerosol; KSR).

name: Required contents of the international application
description: An international application shall contain a request, a description, one or more claims, one or more drawings (where required), and an abstract (Art.3(2)).
guidance: These elements are specified by the Treaty and Regulations and are prerequisites for processing and for being accorded an international filing date. Missing required parts may trigger invitations to correct or lead to the application being considered withdrawn.

name: Description (sufficiency / enablement)
description: The description shall disclose the invention in a manner sufficiently clear and complete for the invention to be carried out by a person skilled in the art (Art.5).
guidance: This is an enablement requirement: the description must support the claims and provide technical teaching enabling practice of the invention without undue experimentation.

name: Claims: definition, clarity, and support
description: The claim or claims shall define the matter for which protection is sought. Claims shall be clear and concise and shall be fully supported by the description (Art.6).
guidance: Claims draftsmanship must ensure clarity, concision, and basis in the description; lack of support or unclear claims can trigger objections, affect search/examination, and limit enforceable scope.

name: Criteria for accorded international filing date
description: The receiving Office shall accord as the international filing date the date of receipt provided that, at time of receipt, the applicant does not obviously lack the right to file there, the application is in the prescribed language, and the application contains at least: an indication it is intended as an international application; designation of at least one Contracting State; name of the applicant; a part appearing to be a description; and a part appearing to be a claim or claims (Art.11(1)).
guidance: These minimal elements determine whether the filing date is credited; if elements are missing the RO will invite correction per Regulations and a corrected date may be accorded if corrected in time (Art.11(2)).

name: Basis and scope of the international search
description: International search shall be made on the basis of the claims, with due regard to the description and the drawings (Art.15(3)); the ISA shall endeavor to discover as much relevant prior art as its facilities permit and shall consult documentation specified in the Regulations (Art.15(4)).
guidance: Claim clarity and support affect search scope; the ISA's documentation holdings and capacities limit the extent of prior art retrieved; applicants may request international-type searches for certain national filings where permitted.

name: ISA procedure: refusal to search where meaningful search cannot be carried out
description: If the ISA considers the subject matter is not required to be searched or that the description, claims, or drawings fail to comply with requirements to such an extent that a meaningful search could not be carried out, the ISA shall declare that no international search report will be established (Art.17(2)(a)). If only certain claims are affected, the ISA will indicate which claims were not searched (Art.17(2)(b)).
guidance: Applicants must ensure clarity and formal compliance; a declaration of no ISR affects communication to DOs and may trigger other procedural consequences and time limits under the Regulations.

name: Amendment of claims before the International Bureau
description: After receiving the ISR the applicant is entitled to one opportunity to amend the claims by filing amendments with the International Bureau within the prescribed time limit and may file a brief statement explaining amendments and impacts; amendments shall not go beyond the disclosure in the international application as filed (Art.21(1)-(2)).
guidance: Amendments must remain within original disclosure (no added matter) for PCT purposes; some designated States' national law may permit broader amendments with differing effects in those States (Art.21(3)).

name: Communication to designated Offices (content and translations)
description: The international application together with the ISR (or declaration) shall be communicated to each designated Office per the Regulations and shall include prescribed translations; if claims were amended under Art.19(1), the communication shall contain full texts of claims both as filed and as amended, specify amendments, and include the Art.19(1) statement if any (Art.20(1)-(2)).
guidance: DOs receive both original and ISR to conduct national processing; accurate translations and clear indication of amended claims are crucial for consistent national examination.

name: Availability of unpublished pending applications whose benefit is claimed (37 CFR 1.14(a)(1)(v))
description: A copy of the file contents of an unpublished pending application may be provided to any person, upon written request and payment of the appropriate fee (§ 1.19(b)), if the benefit of the application is claimed under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), 120, 121, 365(c), or 386(c) in an application that has issued as a U.S. patent or has published (patent application publication, statutory invention registration, international publication, or Hague publication).
guidance: The Office will not provide access to the paper file of a pending application except as provided in paragraph (c) (power to inspect) or (i) (petitions) of 37 CFR 1.14. Copies provided may be the application-as-filed or specific documents from the file.

name: Examiner's prior art search proficiency
description: In the reviewers' opinion, the examiner’s search was deficient in more than half (37 prosecution histories or 61 percent) of the cases for which the PTAB determined that at least one claim was unpatentable over prior art not found by the examiner’s search.
guidance: Caveats: the sample is self-selected (IPR-petitioned patents), reviewers may be subject to hindsight or confirmation bias, and reviewers did not perform independent prior-art searches. Recommendation: expand the study with reviewer-blind reviews and have reviewers conduct their own prior art searches as in general compliance review to better assess adequacy of examiner searches.

name: Examiner's handling of prior art rejections
description: When examiners rely on a reference as the basis of a prior art rejection, they most often do so properly; examiners usually make appropriate decisions regarding withdrawal of rejections.
guidance: Data: out of 78 IPR proceedings, only four (5%) had a claim found unpatentable by PTAB based on a prior-art rejection previously made by the examiner but later withdrawn. Examiners generally do not limit a reference to anticipation-only when it could support obviousness. These findings suggest competent application of recognized references once examiners identify them.

name: Claim interpretation consistency and clarity
description: Compare examiner and PTAB claim interpretations; disagreements may affect patentability. In the study, examiner and PTAB disagreed in 18% (14 cases) and the difference impacted patentability in 9 cases (12% of total).
guidance: Initiatives like the Glossary Pilot Program (launched to promote claim clarity) may reduce disagreements about claim construction by encouraging clear explanations of claim terminology.

name: Words per independent claim (claim breadth/clarity) as predictor
description: Patents with fewer words per independent claim are more likely to be involved in subsequent litigation and IPR.
guidance: This may reflect narrower, less detailed claim drafting or technology lexicon issues; more study is needed to determine whether this arises from examination quality or inherent invention characteristics.

name: GS-level of the allowing examiner
description: The GS-level of the allowing examiner is correlated with litigation/IPR outcomes: patents allowed by lower GS-level examiners are generally less likely to be asserted or petitioned for IPR; GS-level was also the most significant variable in comparing instituted vs. non-instituted IPR-petitioned patents.
guidance: Ambiguity remains (e.g., GS-13 examiners in Signatory Review Program may allow only clear/narrow claims). Interpretation requires caution and further research.

name: Allowance without previous rejection (first-action allowance)
description: Patents allowed on first action are correlated with litigation outcomes: allowed-on-first-action patents are likely to contain clearer and more narrowly drafted claims, which may reduce challenges.
guidance: This variable had measurable but smaller impact than non-examination variables; consider claim clarity as a mediating factor in downstream dispute risk.

name: Alice Step One — focus of the claimed advance
description: Consider 'the focus of the claimed advance over the prior art' to determine whether the claims are directed to an abstract idea.
guidance: If the focus is on receipt and display of information (even of a particular type) and use of that information to engage in a fundamental economic practice, that focus can be an abstract idea (e.g., receipt/display of bids and offers to assist trading). Compare whether the claim improves computers or merely arranges information. See IBG II and related precedents.

name: Alice Step Two — inventive concept requirement
description: An inventive concept is required to transform a claim directed to an abstract idea into eligible subject matter; the abstract idea itself cannot supply the inventive concept.
guidance: Claim elements, individually and as an ordered combination, must add something significantly more than the abstract idea. Mere use of preexisting computers or routine programming does not supply an inventive concept. Courts treat routine data gathering and conventional display techniques as not adding an inventive concept (e.g., receiving market information and displaying indicators along a scaled price axis).

name: Improvement in computer functionality required (negative test)
description: A claim must show an improvement in computer functionality to avoid being merely an automation of a manual process using generic computers.
guidance: Mere automation of manual processes using generic computers is not an improvement; arranging information along an axis does not improve computer functioning or solve a technological problem. Look for language in the specification that calls for more than preexisting computers and known programming techniques.

name: Assess claim elements both individually and as an ordered combination
description: When evaluating inventive concept, consider whether the specific claim elements, individually and as an ordered combination, add the necessary inventive concept.
guidance: Even if claim elements make particular choices among abstract ideas involving information and ordering, those choices alone do not suffice unless they amount to something significantly more that transforms the abstract idea into eligible subject matter.

name: Use of precedent and precedential weight
description: Non-precedential decisions are not binding and cannot be treated as controlling authority for eligibility or other issues.
guidance: Do not rely on non-precedential decisions as binding law; differences in claims, specifications, or patents can be a sufficient basis to distinguish them. Precedential decisions and a body of case law applying Alice should be followed where applicable.

name: Hypothetical negotiation for reasonable-royalty calculation
description: Use the common hypothetical-negotiation approach to calculate a reasonable royalty: attempt to ascertain the royalty the parties would have agreed to just before infringement began.
guidance: The hypothetical negotiation should identify the incremental value of the claimed technology over noninfringing alternatives and determine how that gain would be shared. Courts and juries consider established authorities (Lucent, Asetek, VLSI, Carnegie Mellon, AstraZeneca) and jury instructions on the hypothetical negotiation.

name: Claim-as-a-whole analysis
description: “In determining the eligibility of respondents’ claimed process for patent protection under §101, their claims must be considered as a whole. It is inappropriate to dissect the claims into old and new elements and then to ignore the presence of the old elements in the analysis.” (Diamond v. Diehr cited)
guidance: Do not isolate a single step (e.g., an 'observed correlation') and evaluate only that piece for §101. Consider the combination of steps (including conventional or well-known steps) because a new combination of steps may be patentable even if constituents were known. The brief applies this to diagnostic claims: include 'administering' and 'determining' steps in the §101 inquiry even when those steps are well-known.

name: Transformation/reduction test (machine-or-transformation clue)
description: “Transformation and reduction of an article ‘to a different state or thing’ is the clue to the patentability of a process claim that does not include particular machines.” (Gottschalk v. Benson cited)
guidance: A process claim that effects a physical/chemical/electrical transformation of an article is an indicator of §101 eligibility. For diagnostic methods, transformations of body chemistry (through administering drugs or extracting/metabolite determination) may satisfy this clue. But the existence of a transformation is a clue, not an automatic rule of patentability.

name: Insignificant extra-solution / post-solution activity rule
description: “The notion that post-solution activity, no matter how conventional or obvious in itself, can transform an unpatentable principle into a patentable process is false.” (Parker v. Flook cited; Diehr discussion)
guidance: Adding conventional or token steps (e.g., 'apply to surveying techniques' or routine data-gathering) to an abstract idea, law of nature, or mathematical formula does not make the claim patentable. Courts should identify and disregard insignificant post-solution activity when it is merely a drafting device to claim an unpatentable principle.

name: Centrality of transformative steps (not token extra-solution activity)
description: Transformative steps that are central/essential to the claim (i.e., not 'token extra-solution activity') must be considered and can support patent eligibility.
guidance: Evaluate whether recited transformative steps (e.g., 'administering' a drug, 'determining' metabolite levels) actually contribute meaningful limitations and practical application, rather than merely gather information. Central transformative steps that generate data applied to enable a practical adjustment (e.g., drug dosage change) weigh in favor of §101 eligibility.

name: Physical link to a specific physical/tangible object
description: A clue to patentability is whether claim steps have a 'physical' link to (i.e., manipulate) a specific physical or tangible object (e.g., manipulating blood chemistry, loading a mold, opening a press). (Diehr, Corning, Tilghman examples)
guidance: If the claimed steps physically manipulate or transform a real-world thing (including physical phenomena like electrical signals or chemical properties), that connection supports patent eligibility. For diagnostics, 'administering' and 'determining' that manipulate blood chemistry provide such a physical link.

name: Virtual link: manipulation of data representing physical objects
description: Manipulating data that represent a specific physical or tangible object (a 'virtual link') can be sufficient for patent-eligibility. (O’Reilly v. Morse; In re Abele cited)
guidance: Claims that transform or manipulate data tied to real-world physical objects (e.g., CT X‑ray attenuation data representing bones; data tagged with dosage indicators) create a virtual link to those objects and may be patentable. The claim must tie the data to the particular physical object or representation, not to abstract or generic data.

name: Avoiding preemption of laws of nature, natural phenomena, or abstract ideas
description: A claim must be tailored so it does not preempt the fundamental principle itself; it must encompass only a particular application rather than all uses of the principle. ('Claims that are close to ‘laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas’ ... do not count as ‘processes’ under §101.') (Diehr, Bilski discussions)
guidance: Assess whether the claim, considered as a whole and excluding insignificant extra-solution activity, would preempt all practical uses of a natural law/phenomenon or abstract idea. If it would, the claim likely fails §101. Narrowly tie claims to specific applications or transformations to avoid preemption.

name: Subject-matter patentability filter (Classen): practical application vs mere data-gathering
description: Not all transformative steps suffice; courts should apply a 'subject matter patentability filter' to distinguish transformations that merely gather data for a body of knowledge from those that put knowledge to a practical use.
guidance: Under Classen, transforming steps that only collect data (for later comparison or to build knowledge) may be insufficient, whereas transformations that enable a practical application (e.g., generating a subject-specific regimen used in a subsequent implementation step) are likely patent-eligible. Evaluate claim order and how the transformative step is used (before/after comparison, whether it enables later action).

name: Diehr principle for formulas implemented in structure/process
description: When a mathematical formula is implemented or applied in a structure or process that, considered as a whole, performs a function the patent laws protect (e.g., transforming or reducing an article to a different state or thing), the claim satisfies §101.
guidance: If an otherwise abstract formula is integrated into a practical process that effects a tangible transformation or control of physical apparatus (e.g., software that signals a device to open a press), the claim can be patent-eligible. Mere limitation to a technological environment without meaningful integration is insufficient.

name: Distinguish §101 from §§102/103 (novelty/obviousness)
description: Whether individual steps of a claim are 'well-known' may be relevant to novelty (§102) or obviousness (§103), but does not by itself determine whether §101 is satisfied.
guidance: In a §101 inquiry, do not conflate knownness of claim elements with subject-matter eligibility; assess eligibility under §101 first via claim-as-a-whole, transformation/links, and preemption analysis, and leave novelty/obviousness defenses to §§102/103 analysis.

name: Functions (as related to equivalents and claims)
description: Functionality considered in determining equivalents and identity of an invention; functions may be stated in claims and performed substantially the same way.
guidance: Subpoints: functions considered in respect of equivalents (352); difference of function consistent with identity (180a); performed in substantially the same way (353); stated in claims (117a, 176, 183, 220).

name: "For the Purpose Set Forth" (claim language)
description: Nature and interpretation of the phrase 'for the purpose set forth' within a claim.
guidance: Indexed under the nature of the phrase in claims (182); used in claim construction analysis.

name: Means (claim drafting / claim language)
description: Use and interpretation of the word 'means' in claims.
guidance: Indexed reference to use of the word in claims (117a); relevant to claim construction and means-plus-function analysis.

name: Non-Use (of patent) and its consequences
description: Non-use of a patent as a ground for narrow construction of claims and its (limited) effect as a defense in equity.
guidance: Non-use grounds narrow construction of claims (185); non-use is not a defense in equity generally (701a).

name: Formal presentation requirements for amendment papers
description: All amendment papers to be part of the permanent USPTO file must comply with the formal requirements of 37 CFR 1.52(a) and (b); 37 CFR 1.530(d)-(k) uniquely apply to amendments in reexamination proceedings.
guidance: If adding claims, excess claim fees per 37 CFR 1.20(c)(3) and (4) may apply. Submissions must comply regardless of medium (paper or compact disc under 1.96 or 1.825). Failure to comply may lead to informal response, non-entry of the amendment, or termination of prosecution (see PTOL forms guidance).

name: Claim status and explanation requirement (37 CFR 1.530(e))
description: Each amendment submitted must set forth the status of all patent claims and all added claims as of the date of submission (whether pending or canceled) and must be accompanied by an explanation of the support in the disclosure of the patent for the amendment.
guidance: Failure to submit claim status will generally result in a notification to patent owner of an informal response (see MPEP § 2266.02) prior to final rejection. Failure to submit the explanation of support will generally result in a notification that the amendment prior to final rejection is not completely responsive because omission goes to the merits (see MPEP § 2266.01). Amendments submitted after final rejection will not be entered. Patent owners must point out what is changed in the “Remarks” portion of the amendment when amending previously added claims.

name: Presentation and amendment of new claims (claims not in patent)
description: Each proposed new claim must be presented with underlining throughout; an amendment of a new claim must present the entire text of the new claim containing the amendatory material, underlined throughout, and cannot contain any bracketing or other indication of what was in the previous version of the claim.
guidance: Because changes are made vis-à-vis the original patent, the presentation of an amended new claim does not indicate what changed from a previous version; patent owner must point out what is changed in the “Remarks” portion. Each change must be accompanied by explanation of support in the disclosure (37 CFR 1.530(e)). Examples are given of proper presentation. The presentation cannot show prior-version bracketing.

name: Prohibition on proposing amendments to expired patents (37 CFR 1.530(j))
description: No amendment may be proposed for entry in an expired patent; if a patent expires during the pendency of a reexamination, all amendments to the patent claims and all claims added during the proceeding are withdrawn.
guidance: Withdrawn amendments are carried out by placing a diagonal line across all amended and new claims (and added specification text) residing in amendment papers. Patent owner should be notified in next Office action. Office action will hold amendments to be improper and state subsequent reexamination will be on basis of unamended patent claims. Only cancellation of original patent claims is permitted after expiration. Examiner should ensure all rejected and objected-to claims are canceled at time NIRC is to be issued; examiner may issue examiner’s amendment canceling such claims not already canceled.

name: Procedures and examples for common amendment actions (presentation, cancellation, multiple amendments)
description: MPEP provides detailed examples showing proper formats: replacing a specification paragraph with underlining/bracketing; amending claims (showing bracketed deletions and underlined additions); canceling original patent claims by written direction; presenting new claims underlined; amending original patent claims more than once must include previous changes and new changes in the full-text presentation.
guidance: Examples include: how to present a replaced paragraph; how to amend claim 6 with bracketed deletions and underlined additions; canceling claim(s) by 'Cancel claim X.'; adding claim 7 underlined; handling sequential amendments where earlier-added word (e.g., 'bone') is later deleted and thus not bracketed in second amendment; show that all amendments are compared to original patent text only. These examples illustrate anti-patterns (e.g., showing changes relative to prior amendment rather than original) and proper formatting.

name: Fees for filing reexamination requests and excess-claims fees (37 CFR 1.20(c) and 35 U.S.C. 41(a)(2))
description: Fees: filing a request for ex parte reexamination (§1.510(a)) — $2,520.00; filing a request for inter partes reexamination (§1.915(a)) — $8,800.00.
