Excess claims fees apply for claims added in reexamination per 37 CFR 1.20(c): independent-claims fee for each independent claim in excess of three and in excess of number of independents in patent (small entity $100; other than small $200); total-claims fee for each claim in excess of twenty and of the number in patent (small entity $25; other than small $50).
guidance: Excess claims fees became applicable to reexamination amendments filed on or after December 8, 2004 (per amendment implementing 35 U.S.C. 41(a)(2)). Excess claims fees apply only to new (excess) claims. A claim disclaimed under 35 U.S.C. 253 or canceled via prior reexamination certificate, reissue, or certificate of correction as of the request filing date is not considered part of the patent for fee calculations. Examples illustrate various cancellation/addition scenarios to determine fees due. If excess claims fees are not paid when due, a Notice of Defective Paper (PTOL-475) will issue with a one-month time period (extensions per 37 CFR 1.550(c) may be requested); failure to pay results in termination/abandonment of prosecution under 37 CFR 1.550(e).

name: Fee-deficiency and procedural consequences (PTOL-475, PTOL-473, PTOL-467)
description: If excess-claims fees required by 37 CFR 1.20(c) are not paid with presentation of excess claims, the Office issues a Notice of Defective Paper (PTOL-475) with a one-month time period to correct; failure to timely correct will lead to termination of the reexamination proceeding under 37 CFR 1.550(e).
guidance: PTOL-475 is a Notice of Defective Paper in Ex Parte Reexamination used for fee deficiencies; a cover sheet PTOL-473 is used for mailing notification to patent owner. If an informal amendment is submitted after final rejection, PTOL-475 and form paragraph 22.13 should not be used; instead issue advisory Office action using PTOL-467 indicating the amendment was not entered. Extensions of time to correct fee deficiencies may be requested under 37 CFR 1.550(c). Termination results in issuance of a reexamination certificate or abandonment as appropriate.

name: Jepson claims / improvement patent identification
description: A Jepson claim is a special claim format used to draft an improvement patent; 'strictly speaking only a patent drafted in Jepson format is an improvement patent.' A Jepson claim has the same effect as a judicial finding that a patented invention is 'dominated' by another invention.
guidance: Use of Jepson format signals that the claim is an improvement and affects claim construction and scope (see Pentec, Inc. v. Graphic Controls Corp.; R. Ellis, Patent Claims §197). The article also notes that the term 'improvement patent' is used more loosely to cover patents later found to be dominated by earlier patents. See 35 U.S.C. §101 for statutory provision relating to improvement patents.

name: Reverse doctrine of equivalents — applicability
description: The reverse doctrine of equivalents can provide immunity from infringement even where there is literal infringement, but applies only when the accused device, though literally within claim language, is sufficiently different so that it does not perform in the same way as the claimed invention.
guidance: Doctrine applies only where there is literal infringement; it is invoked when 'claims are written more broadly than the disclosure warrants.' Courts treat reverse equivalents as fact-intensive (sometimes a matter of fact, not law) and it has been 'rarely successfully asserted' by infringers. See Westinghouse v. Boyden Power Brake Co.; Texas Instruments v. USITC; SRI Int'l v. Matsushita (en banc) and commentary in the text.

name: Literal claim scope vs. functional/operational principle (infringement analysis)
description: Even if an accused device falls within the literal language of a claim, there may be no infringement if the device operates on a substantially different principle or way.
guidance: Courts have held no infringement where defendant's machines 'do not operate on the same principle as plaintiff's' even though the devices fall within literal claim language (cases: Leesona Corp. v. United States; Precision Metal Fabricators v. Jetstream Sys.; Mechanical Plastics Corp. v. Unifast Indus.). This supports narrowing claim scope by reference to function/principle in some contexts (related to the 'reverse equivalents' and claim-saving-by-specification doctrines).

name: Claim breadth tradeoffs — breadth vs. deadweight loss and length
description: Increasing the breadth of a patent typically increases deadweight loss (especially as the patentee's market power grows); there is a tradeoff between breadth and length when designing patent rewards.
guidance: Economic models suggest social-cost effective policy may adjust both breadth and length to attain desired rewards (citations to Gilbert & Shapiro; Klemperer). Broad claims have greater preclusive effects than longer duration; in some models infinitely-lived patents with adjusted scope could be considered, but there are cautions that excessive breadth can retard subsequent innovation.

name: Claims must be commensurate with specification / not broader than disclosure warrants
description: Claims written broader than the disclosure warrants invite invocation of doctrines like reverse equivalents and may be vulnerable; claims should be commensurate with the written disclosure.
guidance: Judge Newman observed reverse equivalents 'is invoked when claims are written more broadly than the disclosure warrants.' Drafting should avoid overbroad claims relative to the specification to reduce risk of equitable defenses or invalidation.

name: Species vs genus patent scope
description: A defendant's machine may be of a different species and of course cannot infringe a patent of a different species than itself although it might infringe the genus patent of which both are species.
guidance: Assess whether the accused device falls within the claims (genus) or is a different species; species-patent vs genus-patent distinctions determine possible infringement relationships.

name: Court of Claims has jurisdiction for suits against U.S. for government use of patents
description: The Court of Claims is the tribunal with jurisdiction of actions brought by owners of patent rights against the government of the United States for compensation for the use by the Government of patents and patent rights owned by individuals.
guidance: Such suits are subject to a six-year statute of limitations; absent an established royalty the claimant may recover what a reasonable royalty for an express license would have been (Act of June 25, 1910, 36 Stat. 851).

name: Requirement of specific, substantial and credible utility in description (biotechnological inventions)
description: In regard to an invention of a gene or a protein encoded by the gene, a specific, substantial and credible utility should be stated in the description of the invention.
guidance: For chemical substances such as genes, the requirements for description involve a well-established utility; a person skilled in the art must be able to make and use the claimed invention in view of the level of skill as of the filing date, and utility should be clearly and sufficiently stated in the description.

name: Enablement and sufficiency for chemical/biotech substances
description: To carry out the invention of chemical substances a skilled person must be able to make and use the claimed invention; utility should be clearly and sufficiently stated because the substance of the claimed invention cannot be used without clear and sufficient description.
guidance: References to court verdicts emphasize requirement of concrete disclosure to meet Article 42(3) of the Patent Act.

name: Claims for genes and DNA fragments — sequence specification
description: A gene and a DNA fragment should be described by specifying the sequence thereof.
guidance: The expression 'a sequence having ~% homology with a specific reference sequence' in the claim is not permitted in principle, unless the description provides solid evidence that variants with certain homology contain the same activity.

name: Disclosure requirements for genetic variants (deletions/substitutions/additions)
description: When the expressions 'deletion', 'substitution' or 'addition' are used along with the disclosure of a sequence, the position and the content thereof should be specifically disclosed.
guidance: If examples of genetic variants are provided in the description, it is permitted to define the invention in the claim by limiting the function of the gene and the scope of the variant; merely describing actual hybridization conditions is not considered sufficient to specify scope of genetic variants.

name: Category and claim drafting for pharmaceutical inventions
description: A medicinal use invention should be recited as a product invention.

name: Scope and examples for determining unity in biotech (illustrative examples)
description: Unity determinations hinge on whether claimed items share a special technical feature that contributes over prior art; examples (multiple claims of different DNA sequences or SNPs or peptide lists) illustrate when unity is or is not present.
guidance: If claimed items share a common structural feature shown to underlie a shared function and that feature contributes over prior art, unity met; if only shared function is already known or no common technical feature exists, unity not met.

name: Definition of means-plus-function claim language and statutory scope
description: Means-plus-function claim language employs generic terms (such as 'means' or 'device') in a patent claim to describe a structural claim element by its function. The statute, 35 U.S.C. § 112(f), specifies that such generic claim terms are construed to cover 'the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.'
guidance: The specification’s description for the generic claim term helps to define the term’s scope. Drafting examples: 'means for fastening' can cover staples, clips, screws, bolts, rivets; in software, 'a processor for performing' may be supported by algorithms/flow charts. Using means-plus-function allows functional claiming but ties claim scope to the specification's disclosed corresponding structure and equivalents.

name: Examiner interpretation standard when §112(f) applies
description: The Memorandum tells examiners that their 'broadest reasonable interpretation' of a claim term in means-plus-function format is tied to the patent specification, whereas a claim recitation of structure does not have to be.
guidance: When §112(f) applies, the means-plus-function term should receive a narrower interpretation than a non-means-plus-function term. A narrower interpretation requires applying a narrower range of prior art; if an examiner applies an exceedingly broad scope of prior art, the applicant may argue against the rejection on that basis.

name: Sufficiency of specification to support functional claim terms (§112(a) and (b) evaluation)
description: A patent applicant who wishes to use means-plus-function language must ensure that the patent specification contains sufficient detail to show how a claimed function is to be performed.
guidance: Examiners will evaluate the disclosure under 35 U.S.C. §§ 112(a) and (b) to determine whether the functional claim terms are clearly defined and adequately supported in the written description. If the examiner does not find clear definition and adequate support, the examiner may reject the claim for inadequate written description (§112(a)) and/or indefiniteness (§112(b)). Applicants should identify and describe all contemplated means for performing a recited function in the specification to avoid such rejections.

name: Presumption that 'means' or 'step' + functional language invokes §112(f)
description: A claim element is presumed to be a means-plus-function term if the limitation explicitly uses the term 'means' or 'step' and includes functional language.
guidance: Transitional/functional phrases such as 'means for,' 'configured to,' and 'so that' may signal functional claiming. This presumption can be rebutted by the claim itself if the applicant couples the 'means' or 'step' with the structure, material, or acts for performing the function within the claim language.

name: How to rebut the 'means' presumption in the claim
description: An applicant can overcome the presumption that a 'means' or 'step' term invokes §112(f) by coupling, in the claim itself, the 'means' or 'step' with the structure, material, or acts for performing the function.
guidance: Example: 'means for cutting' could be written as 'blade means for cutting,' which implies structure (scissors, razors, knives). If the specification mentions only a knife, 'means for cutting' may receive a narrower interpretation than 'blade means for cutting.' Draft claims that explicitly identify structure/material/acts to avoid unintended means-plus-function treatment.

name: Presumption against §112(f) for non-'means' terms, but generic placeholders can trigger §112(f)
description: A claim element that does not use the term 'means' or 'step' is presumed not to invoke 35 U.S.C. §112(f). However, when the claim includes a generic placeholder term such as 'device' or 'apparatus' instead of 'means' or 'step' but does not implicate specific structure that performs the function, then the examiner may interpret the element under §112(f).
guidance: Applicants should avoid bare generic placeholders without structural recitation. An examiner may treat generic placeholders as means-plus-function if no structure is recited; applicants can argue structure is implied when appropriate.

name: Software-related terms may connote structure and not be generic placeholders
description: Software-related terms such as 'code,' 'application,' 'program,' and 'user interface' have been found not to be generic placeholders, as the terms connote structure when used in combination with the function performed by the code or application.
guidance: If an examiner construes one of these software terms as means-plus-function, an applicant can argue that the term implies structure and therefore should not be interpreted under §112(f). Drafting claims to emphasize the structural aspects of software elements (e.g., modules, data structures, algorithms) can help avoid means-plus-function treatment.

name: Practical takeaways for practitioners
description: Be mindful of the use of nonce terms (i.e., terms the USPTO says have no structural meaning), and be prepared to argue with the examiner if the examiner misses structure in a claim term the examiner construes as means-plus-function.
guidance: If/when an examiner applies prior art with embodiments not corresponding to means-plus-function terms in the claims, practitioners may be well-advised to argue against the application of that prior art. Proactively identify structure in claims and in the specification and be ready to rebut examiner characterizations and overbroad prior-art application.

name: Matters to be determined during examination (Rule 2A(1) / Section 29)
description: When conducting examination the Examiner must determine, inter alia, whether, taking into account all relevant prior art, each claim satisfies each condition or requirement for patentability under section 13; whether the conditions in section 25(4) and (5) have been complied with; whether the application discloses any additional matter referred to in section 84(1) or (2) or any matter in section 84(3); and whether there is any other application or earlier grant for the same invention with the same priority date to the same applicant or successor in title.
guidance: Examiners must consider all relevant prior art discovered by search or otherwise. This is the primary statutory checklist framing examination work.

name: Purposive construction of claims
description: Claims must be interpreted purposively: what would the person skilled in the art have understood the patentee to mean by the language of the claims, read in light of the description and drawings.
guidance: Construction is objective and not concerned with the patentee's subjective intentions. Use purposive approach consistently for examination (validity, novelty, infringement).

name: Consistency of claim construction
description: Claims should be construed consistently regardless of subject matter; avoid construing broadly for novelty and narrowly for support (or vice versa).
guidance: Interpret claims in the same way for both infringement and validity considerations to provide certainty to public and patentees.

name: Section 113(1) scope principle
description: Extent of protection conferred is that specified in a claim as interpreted by the description and drawings (Section 113(1)): codifies purposive approach.
guidance: Claims are interpreted in light of the whole specification and drawings; not purely literal.

name: Treatment of variants and unessential features
description: A purposive construction may treat variants that have no material effect on how the invention works as within the claim; exclude variants that would have a material effect.
guidance: Examine whether a variant would have a material effect from the viewpoint of the skilled person. Examples: small angular deviations that have negligible functional effect may fall within claim scope.

name: No doctrine of equivalents beyond the claims
description: Protection cannot extend beyond the claims — purposive construction does not create a separate doctrine of equivalents that expands claim scope beyond claim language.
guidance: Doctrinal limits set by Kirin-Amgen and subsequent cases: ensure claim scope remains within claim language as purposively construed.

name: Use of Improver/Protocol questions
description: Use the Improver (Protocol) questions to determine whether a variant falls within the claim (guidance for equivalents analysis under purposive construction).
guidance: Apply these established questions when assessing whether a variant is covered by the claim under purposive construction (case law guidance).

name: Person skilled in the art — role and assessment
description: Claims are construed from the viewpoint of the person skilled in the art; that person's common general knowledge informs interpretation and enablement assessments.
guidance: Avoid making findings about what the skilled person knows without evidence; where common general knowledge is unclear, expert evidence may materially affect outcomes.

name: Avoiding importing gloss or re-drafting claims
description: Examiners should avoid reading limitations from the description/drawings into the claims that are not expressed by the language of the claims.
guidance: Construction should not become claim re-drafting; preserve claim boundaries as written unless clearly supported by the specification.

name: Special meanings and claim language
description: Where the specification assigns a special meaning to a term, that special meaning governs construction; otherwise ordinary meaning in context applies.
guidance: Identify and apply special definitions from the description; otherwise interpret terms as the skilled person would.

name: Independent and dependent claims interpretation
description: Independent claims define the invention; dependent claims incorporate features of claims they depend on and may limit scope accordingly.
guidance: Consider dependencies in assessing novelty, inventive step, support and sufficiency.

name: Open- and closed-ended terms
description: Recognise and treat open-ended (e.g., 'comprising') and closed-ended (e.g., 'consisting of') claim language appropriately in scope assessment.
guidance: Open-ended language generally allows additional unspecified features; closed-ended limits to stated features.

name: Treatment of reference numbers in claims
description: Reference numbers in drawings are generally not limiting unless the claim language makes them so or the specification indicates otherwise.
guidance: Do not import unnecessary limitations from reference numerals into claim scope.

name: Product-for / Method-for / Use claims
description: Specific guidance applies to 'product for …', 'method for …', and 'use of … in …' claim formats regarding what is claimed and how to assess novelty/inventive step.
guidance: Assess such claim forms with attention to their functional language and possible requirement to link to a new technical effect or use.

name: Alternatives / Markush claims
description: Markush or alternative claim groupings must be clear and properly structured so that each alternative is supported and enabled.
guidance: Ensure alternatives are not so numerous or unrelated as to cause unity/support/clarity problems.

name: Novelty — each and every feature disclosure
description: A document anticipates (destroys novelty of) a claim only if it discloses each and every feature of the claim (explicitly or implicitly/inherently), with enablement where required.
guidance: Assess explicit disclosure, implicit disclosure and inheritability; distinguish between novelty and inventive step issues if differences exist.

name: Publication and enabling disclosure
description: For a prior publication to be novelty-destroying, it must have been made available to the public and must enable the relevant subject matter to the skilled person (as required).
guidance: Establish date of availability and whether the disclosure is enabling for the claimed subject-matter.

name: Obvious to try and selection inventions
description: Consider 'obvious to try' tests (was it obvious to try a route with a reasonable expectation of success) and special rules for selection inventions where a subset is claimed from a broader class.
guidance: Evaluate whether routine trials would have been undertaken by the skilled person and whether success would have been reasonably expected.

name: Statutory application formalities and requirements
description: Applications must comply with statutory requirements (e.g., claims numbering, number of claims per Rule 19(6), claims drafted in technical terms per Rule 19(7), two-part form per Rule 19(8), omnibus claims Rule 19(9)).
guidance: Check formal compliance: numbering, claim count, claim form and technical wording per the Rules.

name: Sufficiency of disclosure (Section 25(4) and 25(5)(c))
description: The specification must disclose the invention sufficiently for the skilled person to perform it; description must enable the invention across the breadth of the claim.
guidance: Assess enabling disclosure, role of skilled person, clarity of description, and whether undue burden is required to practice the invention.

name: Claims define the matter for which protection is sought (Section 25(5)(a))
description: Claims must define the subject-matter for which protection is sought; they must be clear and adequately set out the boundaries of protection.
guidance: Ensure claims correspond to the technical contribution and are not mere statements of intent.

name: Clarity and conciseness of claims (Section 25(5)(b))
description: Claims must be clear and concise; avoid indefinite terms, unexplained relative terms, lack of antecedent, inconsistent language, overly broad multiple alternatives and unnecessarily verbose claims.
guidance: Assess each of the enumerated clarity issues (indefinite terms, relative terms, preferred/optional definitions, ranges, single-ingredient compositions, multiple alternatives, inconsistencies between claims and description, conciseness).

name: Claims to be supported by the description (Section 25(5)(c))
description: Claims must be supported by the description — mere coincidence of language is insufficient; claims must reflect the technical contribution and be enabled by the description.
guidance: Evaluate support in terms of essential features, features defined by function, parametric claims, reach-through claims and whether the description provides clear basis for the claimed scope.

name: Disclosure and enabling requirements for the specification
description: The description must provide enabling disclosure, the role of the skilled person must be clear, the description must be comprehensible, and references to prior art, trademarks and standards should be used carefully.
guidance: Check that the specification allows the skilled person to carry out the invention across its claimed scope without undue experimentation.

name: Unity of invention (Section 26 and related rules)
description: An application must meet unity of invention requirements: claims should relate to a single inventive concept or be linked such that a single general inventive concept is present; lack of unity can be a priori or a posteriori.
guidance: Assess unity objectively; avoid literal or over-technical approaches; flag unduly complex claims, mixed categories, Markush/group claims issues; follow approach for determining lack of unity in Singapore.

name: Biotechnological subject matter (devices, antibodies, microorganisms)
description: Specific guidance applies to biotech inventions, including deposit of micro-organisms, claims to antibodies and device claims; special support, enablement and patentable subject matter considerations apply.
guidance: Check compliance with deposit requirements, sufficiency for biological materials, and particular case law on antibodies and biotech claims.

name: Supplementary examination (requirements and process)
description: Supplementary examination for certain national/regional/PCT situations requires prescribed documents (e.g., corresponding applications, certified copies, translations) and follows defined process and grounds (including claim relatedness and medical use claims).
guidance: Ensure required documents are provided within prescribed time limits and that supporting documents are verified and correctly identified.

name: Contents and form of re-examination requests
description: Requests must clearly identify each ground for re-examination, explain how each ground is established, identify claims affected, and where prior art is relied upon, point to relevant portions and map claim features to prior art.
guidance: Provide constructions and new arguments if relying on previously considered documents; file supporting documents/English translations and verifications together with the request.

name: Scope of Examiner's consideration in re-examination (Section 38A(8))
description: During re-examination, Examiner determines whether grounds specified are made out and may report on any other grounds in Section 38A(1) based on submitted documents; Examiner may examine claims not identified in the request if relevant documents support doing so.
guidance: Examiners primarily rely on documents submitted by requester but may cite additional documents to establish common general knowledge.

name: Documenting claim scope during prosecution
description: More thoroughly document key issues of claim scope during prosecution; explicitly inform patent owner and public of the decision making during prosecution; clearly record the examiner’s reasoning.
guidance: Record on the file why claims are interpreted as they are so applicants and the public understand examiner reasoning and to avoid prosecution delays due to misunderstandings.

name: Apply Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI)
description: During patent examination, claims are given their broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) in light of the specification as it would be interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art; the BRI of the claim is then used to evaluate patentability under each of the statutes.
guidance: Establish the BRI clearly on the record and use that BRI when examining claims for patentability (e.g., in anticipation/obviousness rejections). The Pilot addresses putting the BRI and the examiner’s understanding on the record for certain claim language.

name: Acknowledge and identify special definitions of claim terms
description: Under BRI, words of a claim are given their plain meaning unless inconsistent with the specification. Applicants can rebut the plain meaning by clearly setting forth a special definition of the term in the specification.
guidance: When a special definition is used, identify the claim term and the special definition and note where it appears in the specification so the record shows the claim was interpreted using the special definition.

name: Identify language that suggests optional limitations and explain whether limiting
description: Language that suggests or makes optional, but does not require, a particular structure or particular steps to be performed does not limit the claim scope. Examples include “adapted to/for” clauses, “for example” phrases, “such as” phrases, “wherein” clauses, and “whereby” clauses.
guidance: Identify such optional language on the record and explain whether it has a limiting effect on claim scope; determination depends on particular facts, so explain the factual basis for whether it limits BRI.

name: Evaluate functional language and note §112(f) implications
description: A limitation is functional when it recites a feature by what it does rather than by what it is. The BRI will depend on whether §112(f) (means-plus-function) is invoked or not. When §112(f) is not invoked, whether the BRI is limited by the function turns on the existence of a connection between the functional language and structure, material, or acts recited in the claim.
guidance: State whether functional language limits the BRI of the claim and explain why. In the Pilot, when functional language is present without invoking §112(f), add a statement whether it has been given patentable weight along with explanation and examples (e.g., 'function Y limits the operation of widget A' vs 'function Y is unconnected to any structure... and therefore imposes no limits').

name: Identify statements of intended use, purpose, or result and indicate limits
description: A statement of intended use or result typically does not provide a patentable distinction unless some structural or manipulative difference is imposed on the claimed structure or action; intended use/result can appear in a preamble or claim body and is evaluated case-by-case.
guidance: Identify statements of intended use/purpose/result and indicate whether they impose any limits on the BRI. Pay particular attention to preambles and whether they limit claim scope; record the rationale.

name: Determine whether non-functional descriptive material (printed matter) is given patentable weight
description: Non-functional descriptive material (printed matter) refers to content of information recited in a claim (e.g., dosage instructions on a label). As claims are read as a whole, printed matter may not be disregarded, but absent a new and unobvious functional relationship between the material and the substrate patentable weight need not be given.
guidance: Identify descriptive material in the claim, explain whether a functional relationship is found between the material and the product or step claimed, and state whether the material is being given patentable weight.

name: Apply §112(f) (means-plus-function) presumptions and explain when overcome
description: When functional language is used in a claim, determine whether §112(f) is being invoked. Use of the word “means” raises a rebuttable presumption that §112(f) applies; absence of the word “means” raises a rebuttable presumption that §112(f) does not apply.
guidance: Note the §112(f) presumptions on the record and explain when they have been overcome. Specifically identify language using 'means' or generic placeholders and explain why §112(f) is or is not invoked, using FP 7.30.04 when appropriate.

name: When §112(f) is invoked, identify corresponding structure/material/acts in the specification
description: If a claim limitation is to be treated under §112(f), corresponding structure, material, or acts in the specification must be identified as performing the claimed function.
guidance: As a best practice, identify the corresponding structure/material/acts in the specification on the record to clearly establish the BRI for that claim limitation.

name: Use the established claim interpretation in rejections and explain how it affects patentability analysis
description: Once the BRI is clearly established and explanations for the types of language focused on in this Pilot are on the record, use that BRI and explanation when examining the claims for patentability under the statutes.
guidance: When making rejections (e.g., anticipation), explicitly tie the rejection to the claim interpretation on the record—for example, noting that an intended use is not given weight because it does not impose a limit on claim scope as explained in the claim construction portion of the Office action.

name: Provide a clear record to enable applicant response and downstream use by courts/PTAB and public
description: By providing enhanced claim interpretation on the record, the Pilot aims to provide an opportunity for applicants to agree or respond to the examiner’s claim interpretation, provide information for courts and the PTAB, provide certainty as to the boundaries of the claims, and enable potential users to make informed decisions concerning scope of issued patents.
guidance: Ensure the record includes sufficient explanation of interpretation choices (special definitions, non-weighted terms, §112(f) invocation, algorithm/hardware identification) so applicants, courts, PTAB, and public can understand and act on the examiner’s interpretation.

name: PCT Filing — preservation of options and overview of Chapter I/II processes
description: PCT filing provides a single international application convertible into multiple national applications up to 30 (and sometimes 31) months from filing or priority date and includes international search (ISR) and written opinion (ISA‑WO), publication at ~18 months, and optional Chapter II international preliminary examination.
guidance: ISA prepares ISR and ISA‑WO about 16 months from earliest priority date addressing novelty, inventive step, and industrial applicability and may point out form/clarity objections. Article 19 claim amendments may be filed but are not substantively considered during international examination. IPRP (Ch I) issued if no Chapter II; Chapter II (demand filed at later of 22 months or 3 months after ISR) allows dialogue and may produce IPRP (Ch II) ~28 months. National conversion deadlines typically at 30/31 months (extended from 19 months for many states). Many national offices use the international examiner’s decision as a starting point—resolving issues during PCT can reduce national prosecution costs. Confidentiality considerations: selecting EPO vs USPTO as ISA/IPEA can affect public availability of prosecution file.

name: Terms for completing payment for Kansas trust and diminished-reserve lands
description: Persons included under prior acts may complete payment for lands at newly appraised value with credit for sums already paid; the balance shall be paid in three equal installments, first due Jan 1, 1881, remaining annually; installments draw interest at 6% per annum from date of last payment received; those in possession who failed prior payments must make entry and pay in three installments; bond required for timbered lands to prevent waste.
guidance: Statute prescribes how existing claimants and entrants may complete purchases: appraisal, credits, installment schedule, interest rate, bonds for timbered lands, and consequences for noncompliance.

name: Improvement consideration (claim/specification must show improvement)
description: The specification need not explicitly set forth the improvement, but it must describe the invention such that the improvement would be apparent to one of ordinary skill in the art. A conclusory assertion of improvement without necessary detail is insufficient. The claim must be evaluated to ensure the claim itself reflects the disclosed improvement; the claim must include the components or steps of the invention that provide the improvement, though it need not recite the improvement in boilerplate language.
guidance: Examiners should consult the specification and determine whether a technical explanation of the asserted improvement is present and whether the claim reflects that improvement (consider the claim as a whole under the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI)). Avoid oversimplifying claims or ignoring specific claim requirements. The judicial exception alone cannot provide the improvement; the improvement can be provided by additional element(s) or by additional elements in combination with the recited exception. Generally examiners are not expected to make a qualitative judgment on the merits of the asserted improvement — if the examiner concludes no improvement, the burden shifts to applicant to provide persuasive arguments and supporting evidence (e.g., a § 1.132 declaration) showing what the specification would convey to one of ordinary skill in the art (evidence cannot be used to supplement the specification). Examples (illustrative): McRO (specification explained how claimed rules automated specific animation tasks and demonstrated improvement); Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec (claims did not include limitations addressing asserted improvement).

name: Improvements to computer functionality
description: For computer-related technologies, determine whether the claim purports to improve computer capabilities (an improvement to computer functionality) or merely invokes computers as a tool to implement an abstract idea.
guidance: Positive indicators: specification discussion of prior art and how invention improved computer storage/retrieval or other computer capabilities; specific implementations or data structures recited in claims. Examples courts have indicated may show improvement include: modification of Internet hyperlink protocol to produce hybrid webpages (DDR Holdings); inventive distribution of functionality within a network to filter Internet content (BASCOM); methods of rendering halftone digital images (Research Corp. Techs. v. Microsoft); distributed network architectures to reduce congestion (Amdocs); memory systems with programmable operational characteristics (Visual Memory); technical details for transmitting images over cellular networks (TLI) (note: lack of requisite technical details can make claims ineligible); particular server structures for organized digital images (TLI); specific programming/design techniques to create menus (Apple v. Ameranth); security-profile generation improving virus scanning (Finjan); improved user interfaces with particular data selection (Core Wireless); specific interface/implementation for 3D spreadsheets (Data Engine); methods restricting software by license (Ancora). Negative indicators: claim scope that can be performed mentally or entirely without a computer; mere addition of a generic computer or general-purpose computer functions; mere automation of manual processes or mere speed improvements due to generic computer capabilities. Case examples: Synopsys v. Mentor Graphics (method wholly performable mentally); FairWarning (speed increase solely from general-purpose computer); Credit Acceptance (mere automation of manual processes); RecogniCorp (process could be practiced verbally or by telephone). In determining improvement, consider overlap with other considerations (particular machine, mere instructions to apply an exception).

name: Improvements to other technology or technical fields
description: Consideration of improvements to technology applies across technologies (not limited to computers); an improvement to technology in life sciences or other fields may demonstrate patent eligibility when the claim reflects a new and improved technical way of achieving an outcome.
guidance: An improvement in the abstract idea itself (e.g., an improved economic concept) is not an improvement in technology. Courts have found eligibility where claims improved existing technological processes (e.g., McRO: improved computer animation via particular rules; Rapid Litigation Mgmt. v. CellzDirect: improved method for preserving hepatocytes). Examples that may show improvement include: particular computerized method of operating a rubber molding press (Diehr); new telephone/server combinations (TLI Communications); advances in content downloading for streaming (Affinity Labs v. DirecTV); improved digital data compression (DDR Holdings, Intellectual Ventures I); particular methods incorporating virus screening into the Internet (Symantec); components or techniques that generate new data (Electric Power Group); particular configurations of sensors and methods of using raw data (Thales Visionix); specific structured GUIs that improve transaction accuracy (Trading Techs. Int’l v. CQG); improved processes for preserving hepatocytes (Rapid Litig. Mgmt.). Examples that may not be sufficient include commonplace business methods on general-purpose computers (Alice, Versata), use of well-known lab techniques (Cleveland Clinic v. True Health Diagnostics), gathering/analyzing information by conventional techniques then displaying results (TLI), high-level delivery of broadcast content to devices (Affinity Labs), general email screening on a generic computer (Symantec), advances only to informational content (Affinity Labs), or selecting one type of content from existing types or using generic hardware functions (Affinity Labs). Claims must recite details about how a computer aids the method or the significance of computer involvement; merely adding generic computer components is insufficient. See MPEP § 2106.05(f) for 'mere instructions to apply an exception.'

name: Particular machine consideration (machine-or-transformation clue)
description: When determining whether a claim integrates a judicial exception into a practical application (Step 2A Prong Two) or recites significantly more (Step 2B), consider whether the judicial exception is applied with or by use of a particular machine; the machine-or-transformation test is a useful investigative clue but is not a stand-alone test for eligibility.
guidance: Examiners must still apply Alice/Mayo two-part test; a claim that passes Alice/Mayo is eligible even if it fails the M-or-T test, and a claim failing Alice/Mayo is ineligible even if it passes M-or-T. Relevant factors include: the particularity or generality of the machine elements (degree to which the machine can be specifically identified rather than 'any and all machines'); whether the machine implements the steps of the method (integral use vs. merely an object on which the method operates); whether the machine's involvement is extra-solution activity or only a field-of-use limitation (nominal contribution does not integrate the exception). Examples where machine particulars mattered: Mackay Radio (particular antenna structure), Eibel Process (Fourdrinier machine structure). A general-purpose computer performing conventional functions does not qualify as a 'particular machine' (Ultramercial v. Hulu, Eon v. AT&T); mere recitation of tangible components or adding a generic computer or 'specially programmed' generic computer does not automatically provide significantly more. Examiners should evaluate interplay with other considerations (mere instructions to apply an exception, insignificant extra-solution activity, field-of-use/technological environment). See MPEP § 2106.03 for definition of 'machine.'

name: Particular transformation consideration
description: Consider whether the claim effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing — a transformation is a clue that the claim integrates the exception into a practical application or recites significantly more.
guidance: An 'article' includes a physical object or substance that must be particular; 'transformation' means the article has changed to a different state or thing (more than mere use or change in location). New/different function or use can be evidence of transformation. Purely mental processes or mere manipulation of basic mathematical constructs are not eligible transformations. Relevant factors when a transformation is recited: (1) particularity or generality of the transformation (more particular transformations likely provide significantly more); (2) degree to which the recited article is particular (generic recitation or 'any and all articles' is less likely to provide significantly more); (3) nature/extent of change in state or thing (change in function/use > mere change in location); (4) nature of the article transformed (physical/tangible transformations weigh more than intangible concepts); (5) whether the transformation is extra-solution activity or a field-of-use limitation (a transformation that contributes only nominally to execution likely does not provide significantly more). Examples: Tilghman v. Proctor (transformation of fatty bodies into fat acids and glycerine); Diamond v. Diehr (transforming raw uncured rubber into molded products). Examiners should still apply Alice/Mayo test; M-or-T is a clue but not dispositive.

name: Sufficiency of disclosure (general requirement)
description: On filing their application, applicants must supply a sufficient disclosure in respect of the invention as claimed with regard to all of the claims.
guidance: The disclosure must enable a person skilled in the art (PSIA) to carry out the invention; insufficient disclosure cannot be cured after filing by adding new examples or features that introduce added subject-matter.

name: Parameter-defined claims — methods to determine parameter values
description: If the claims define the invention, or a feature thereof, in terms of parameters, the application as filed must include a clear description of the methods used to determine the parameter values, unless a PSIA would know which method to use or unless all methods would yield the same result.
guidance: Provide clear methods/measurements for parameter features in the specification; otherwise objection for insufficiency may arise.

name: Remedy for insufficient disclosure via claim restriction
description: Insufficient disclosure could be remedied by restricting the claims to correspond to those embodiments which have been sufficiently described, and by deleting the description of the remaining embodiments.
guidance: Where disclosure is deficient, applicants should consider limiting claim scope to what was actually described at filing.

name: Factors for determining undue experimentation
description: Factors to be considered in determining whether undue experimentation is needed to carry out the claimed invention include: (i) the breadth of the claims; (ii) the nature of the invention; (iii) the general knowledge of a person skilled in the art; (iv) the level of predictability in the art; (v) the amount of direction provided in the application, including references to prior art; and (vi) the amount of experimentation required to carry out the claimed invention on the basis of the disclosure.
guidance: Assess enablement by weighing these six factors (from narrow to broad) to decide if the disclosure suffices or if undue burden is required.

name: Insufficient disclosure can undermine claim support
description: Where the disclosure is insufficient to enable a PSIA to carry out the claimed invention, the claims may also be too broad to be supported by the description.
guidance: Non-compliance with sufficiency often coincides with lack of support for claims; consider both grounds.

name: Disclosure vs clarity balance
description: There is a delicate balance between lack of clarity and lack of disclosure. An ambiguity in the claims may lead to an objection for lack of disclosure if the whole scope of the claim is affected (impossible to carry out); otherwise an objection under lack of clarity is more appropriate.
guidance: Choose objection type depending on whether ambiguity prevents implementation across the claim scope.

name: Search objective — discover relevant prior art
description: The objective of search is to discover relevant prior art(s): everything capable of being of assistance in determining whether the claimed invention is new and involves an inventive step.
guidance: Searching authority must attempt to discover as much relevant prior art as its facilities permit, including material that assists on sufficiency, support and industrial applicability.

name: Internet search confidentiality caution
description: The examiner may use the internet as necessary when searching unpublished applications but must take great care not to disclose confidential information through the inadvertent use of search terms.
guidance: Select limited, non-disclosing keywords rather than long claim text when searching public internet resources.

name: Analogous fields — when to include
description: The field of search should, where appropriate, include analogous fields to the extent that they are consistent with the description and drawings. Fields regarded as analogous are considered in light of necessary function or use, not only specific functions indicated in the application.
guidance: Consider (i) fields where same/similar structure would be used for different activities, (ii) fields to which a generic concept pertains, (iii) art within inventor's activity relevant to the problem, (iv) fields relevant to function/utility inherent in the claims; extend only when a reasonable objection of lack of inventive step could be established.

name: Analysis of the claims for search subject
description: When beginning to search an application, the examiner first considers the application in order to determine the subject of the claimed invention and makes a critical analysis of the claims in light of the description and drawings.
guidance: Search is directed to invention as interpreted with due regard to description/drawings, with particular emphasis on the inventive concept towards which the claims are directed.

name: Speculative/unduly wide claims handling
description: No special search effort needs to be made when searching unduly wide or speculative claims, beyond the extent to which they are supported by the description.
guidance: Do not expand search into remote areas merely because of broad claim wording, unless it is probable that relevant documents could establish lack of novelty/inventive step.

name: Search of particular claim types and parts (two‑part, preamble, etc.)
description: The words of a claim must be read as they would be understood by a PSIA. In two-part claims, the preamble is regarded as a limitation on the scope of the claim; in some circumstances it may be desirable to extend the search to include the technological background, preamble, or general state of the art.
guidance: Include preamble/intro/background where relevant to find closest prior art or context; interpret claim terms as understood in the art.

name: Combination claims — search combinations and sub‑combinations
description: For claims characterised by a combination of elements (e.g., A, B and C), the search should be directed towards the combination; however, sub-combinations (AB, AC, BC) and individual elements should be searched in those units at the same time.
guidance: Search additional classification units for sub-combinations only if necessary to establish novelty of an element or to assess inventive step of the combination.

name: Encouragement to cite prior art aiding sufficiency/support
description: The examiner is encouraged to cite any prior art likely to be of assistance in determining sufficiency of description throughout the whole of the field claimed and the requirement that the claimed invention be fully supported by the description.
guidance: Cite documents that illuminate whether the disclosure enables the claimed scope or supports claim features.

name: Requirement to maintain identical claims in merged proceedings; consequences of failure
description: Where merger is ordered, the patent owner is required to maintain identical amendments/claims in the reissue application and the reexamination file for purposes of the merged proceeding.
guidance: If identical amendments are not present at time of merger, the patent owner will be required to submit appropriate amendments to make claims identical in both proceedings. The patent owner must not address patentability in the amendment. If required identical text is not timely submitted, any claim lacking identical text in all merged proceedings may be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, paragraph 2, as indefinite.

name: Reexamination certificate/reissued patent effects (37 CFR 1.997 / 1.991)
description: To conclude an inter partes reexamination proceeding, the Director will issue and publish an inter partes reexamination certificate setting forth results. If the reexamination is terminated by the grant of a reissued patent as provided in §1.991, the reissued patent will constitute the reexamination certificate.
guidance: If a certificate cancels all claims of the patent, no further Office proceedings will be conducted with that patent or any reissue applications or reexamination requests relating thereto.

name: Effect of prior adjudication on reissued patents
description: An adjudication on an original patent is not a ground for an injunction on a reissue where the reissue claims are different, or where the reissue is broader than the original patent.
guidance: If the reissue attempts to broaden coverage beyond the original patent, prior adjudication of the original does not automatically support an injunction on the reissue. Also, if the Supreme Court has held the original patent invalid, an injunction on the reissue will generally not be granted as if it were a new valid patent. Cases: Poppenhusen v. Falke; Wells v. Jacquet; Jones v. McMurray.

name: Identification of the challenge and precise relief requested
description: The petition must state the precise relief requested and identify the challenge being made to the patent.
guidance: Clearly state which claims are challenged and what specific relief (e.g., cancellation of specified claims) the petitioner seeks.

name: Identify the challenged claims (37 CFR 42.104(b)(1))
description: The petition must identify the challenged claims of the patent.
guidance: List claim numbers clearly and unambiguously; treat each claim addressed as a discrete item of analysis elsewhere in the petition.

name: Specify statutory grounds and relied-upon patents/printed publications (37 CFR 42.104(b)(2))
description: For each claim challenged, the petition must state the specific statutory grounds under 35 U.S.C. §§ 102 or 103 and the patents or printed publications relied upon for each ground.
guidance: Tie each ground to the supporting reference(s); be precise about which reference supports which ground for which claim.

name: State claim construction and, for 112(f) terms, identify corresponding structure (37 CFR 42.104(b)(3))
description: The petition must state how the challenged claim is to be construed; where a claim contains a means-plus-function or step-plus-function limitation under 35 U.S.C. 112(f), the construction must identify the specific portions of the specification that describe the structure, material, or acts corresponding to each claimed function.
guidance: Include a discrete claim construction section for disputed/important terms and provide support (specification citations). For 112(f) claims, map functions to specification disclosure explicitly.

name: Explain how the construed claim is unpatentable and map claim elements to prior art (37 CFR 42.104(b)(4))
description: The petition must explain how the construed claim is unpatentable under the identified statutory grounds and must specify where each element of the claim is found in the relied-upon prior art patents or printed publications.
guidance: Provide element-by-element analysis with clear citations to the prior art; failure to map elements will weaken the petition and may lead to exclusion or no weight.

name: Avoid improper usage of claim charts
description: A claim chart is a common way to specify where each element of a claim is found in prior art (per 37 C.F.R. § 42.104(b)(4)), and claim charts may use single spacing (42.6(a)(2)(iii)), but petitioners must not misuse the chart format to hide necessary argumentation or insert claim constructions and unpatentability arguments improperly.
guidance: Use claim charts for element-to-reference mapping only; do not bury substantive construction or legal reasoning inside chart formatting to game page limits. Follow USPTO guidance and FAQs on acceptable chart use.

name: Explicitly set forth any claim constructions and identify parallel constructions
description: Failure to expressly set forth claim construction of disputed or important claim terms in a claim construction section is a common error; petitioner must include a statement identifying how a claim term is to be construed and support for that construction. If a parallel proceeding has a specific construction, identify it for the Board’s consideration (CTPG, 47; 37 CFR 42.100(b)).
guidance: Provide a dedicated claim construction section, cite support, and flag any relevant constructions from parallel proceedings. After filing, respond to new constructions raised by the Patent Owner, but do not raise new claim construction issues in the reply that were not previously presented.

name: Deserter_release_not_equivalent_to_discharge_certificate
description: The deserter's release relieves from liability to arrest and trial but does not serve as a discharge from the Army, is not evidence of discharge, and should be prepared so as to preclude any claim that it operates as an actual discharge certificate.
guidance: P. 52, 61, 62, 63; Circular No. 5, A. G. O., 1894; C. 13896; C. 21367. Language in General Orders describing it as 'Release from the Army' is faulty.

name: Possible interview topics
description: Common substantive topics appropriate for interview discussion.
guidance: Nature of the invention and state of the art (what problem was solved/what improvement is provided); claim interpretation and scope (e.g., preamble, functional language, means-plus-function, intended use language, non-positive claim language, clarity); meaning of particular limitations and how supported by the specification; broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim; statutory subject matter; prior art; rejections and objections; proposed amendments.

name: Documenting an interview (use PTOL-413)
description: Requirements for documenting interviews and what must be included in the Interview Summary form (PTOL-413).
guidance: Use the Examiner’s Interview Summary form (PTOL-413). An interview summary should include attendees and date; prior art, claims and exhibits discussed; details of the discussion (specifics about issues discussed, claim limitations, any proposed claim amendments, and any agreement as to allowability of claims or next steps). Document agreements reached or not reached (e.g., allowability, interpretation of claim language, priority dates, application of case law, next steps such as filing a proposed amendment or withdrawing a rejection). If a proposed amendment is agreed to, attach a copy or otherwise make the record clear as to what was agreed to. If electronic communication (e-mail) has been authorized by applicant, attach copies of all e-mail correspondence. Do not include comments of a personal nature. Any discussion that touches on merits of the invention or application is to be considered an interview and should be documented. The purpose of the interview summary is to complete and clarify the record; do not prosecute “off the record.” Further guidance in MPEP 713.04, 502.01, 502.02, and 502.03.

name: Patentability requirements (§101–§103, utility/novelty/nonobviousness)
description: A patent must be novel, nonobvious, useful, and meet subject-matter eligibility. The claims (defined by the specification) are examined against these statutory requirements (35 U.S.C. §§ 101–103, 112).
guidance: Novelty (§102): no single prior art reference discloses all claim elements. Nonobviousness (§103): invention not an obvious combination to a person of ordinary skill. Utility (§101 as use): must have a beneficial use. Subject-matter eligibility (§101) is a separate gate often dispositive for AI inventions.

name: Alice two-step test (Alice/Mayo framework)
description: Step 1: Determine whether the claims are directed to a patent-ineligible concept (e.g., an abstract idea). Step 2: If so, determine whether additional claim elements contain an 'inventive concept' sufficient to transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application.
guidance: Token recitation of 'apply it' or generic computer components will not satisfy step two. Technical improvements that achieve something 'industry has not been able to obtain' can supply an inventive concept (Diehr example). Preemption risk is the driving concern of the test.

name: Step-one inquiry — 'directed to' an abstract idea (centrality test)
description: At step one, assess whether the claim is 'directed to' an abstract idea, which is more than merely 'contains' an idea; it asks how central the abstract idea is to the claim.
guidance: Lower courts must resolve how central a concept must be to be 'directed to' it. For software/AI, many claims are treated as directed to abstract ideas unless they are tied to an improvement in computer functioning or otherwise claim a specific technological solution.

name: Step-two inquiry — 'inventive concept' requirement
description: Determine whether the claim's additional elements transform the ineligible concept into a patent-eligible application by providing an inventive concept beyond well-understood, routine, conventional activity.
guidance: An inventive concept often requires a technical solution to a technical problem (not merely automation or implementation on generic hardware). Mere use of conventional computer components or generic data operations fails; improvements in computer performance or new computer capabilities favor eligibility.

name: Bandai (McRO) framework for software/AI eligibility
description: Federal Circuit in McRO, Inc. v. Bandai Namco identified factors supporting eligibility for computer-implemented inventions: (1) an improvement to computer capabilities; (2) automation carried out in a way different from the human-performed prior art; and (3) absence of total preemption.
guidance: Apply Bandai to AI: claims that give machines new capabilities (not mere automation of human thought processes), that operate in a qualitatively different manner than manual methods, and that avoid preempting all such automation, are more likely eligible. Bandai is proposed as a preferable rubric for AI eligibility.

name: Technical-solution-to-technical-problem criterion
description: Claims are more likely to supply an inventive concept if they represent a technical solution to a technical problem (i.e., they improve the functioning of the computer or solve a computer-specific problem).
guidance: Diehr-like examples (improving a physical or computational process) show eligibility; courts should favor technological improvements over abstract results or mere data manipulation.

name: Conventional or routine data operations do not supply eligibility
description: Adding conventional data-collection, storage, or generic algorithmic steps to an abstract idea is insufficient to transform the claim into an eligible invention.
guidance: Anti-pattern: claiming 'using machine learning' broadly or reciting common ML techniques (regression, decision trees) without claiming a specific technical improvement will likely fail Alice step two.

name: Claim breadth and specificity (avoid overbroad claims)
description: Excessively broad claims that preempt a wide swath of techniques (e.g., all machine learning methods for a purpose) are more likely to be ineligible.
guidance: Draft claims to describe particular AI processes, architectures, training steps, or technical improvements to avoid preemption; narrow, particularized claim language reduces risk of being categorized as an abstract idea or an 'application' that preempts the field.

name: Datasets vs models vs applications — policy distinctions
description: Normative recommendations: datasets should be patent ineligible because they stymie follow-on innovation; applications of AI (application-in-context claims) should generally be ineligible; AI methods and models should usually be patent eligible.
guidance: Policy-based rubric: allow patents that incentivize development of AI methods/models without chilling follow-on research; exclude patents whose primary effect is to preempt raw data or broad applications that block others from using AI in particular contexts.

name: Avoid claiming generic 'machine learning' without inventive detail
description: Claims that recite machine learning generically (e.g., 'using machine learning to optimize X') are likely to be treated as abstract ideas or routine data operations and thus ineligible.
guidance: Better practice: claim particular training regimens, model architectures, data transformations, loss functions, iterative steps, or computational resource improvements that show a concrete technical innovation.

name: Distinguish human-performed prior art from claimed automated process
description: Eligibility is supported when the claimed automation carries out tasks differently from how humans perform them (qualitatively different process), not merely by automating the same mental steps.
guidance: Demonstrate in the specification how the AI method changes the order, type, or nature of steps compared to the human technique and how this yields a new computer capability or technical benefit.

name: Be mindful of litigation risk and examiner inconsistency
description: Because guidance has changed and courts remain the ultimate arbiter, many patents granted under permissive MPEP guidance may face invalidation. Examiners may apply guidance inconsistently.
guidance: Applicants should prepare for potential litigation by grounding claims in technical detail, evidencing technological improvements, and anticipating Alice/Mayo challenges in prosecution and claim drafting.

name: Examining Computer-Implemented Functional Claim Limitations for Compliance with 35 U.S.C. § 112
description: Topic: Examining Computer-Implemented Functional Claim Limitations for Compliance with 35 U.S.C. § 112 (June 11, 2019).
guidance: Presentation slides available; addresses substantive examination standards under §112 for functional claim language.

name: Substantive 112 Issues Addressed
description: Substantive 112 rejections and their resolution are a marker of thorough review.
guidance: Presence of meaningful 112 engagement (written-description/enablement) in prosecution suggests careful scrutiny of claim support and scope; absence reduces confidence in quality.

name: Restriction Requirement Applied Where Appropriate
description: Application of restriction requirements where appropriate indicates careful claim-scope management during examination.
guidance: Use appropriate restriction practice as a positive quality indicator — it reflects examiner attention to claim clarity and proper prosecution procedures.

name: Examiner Amendments Narrowing Claims
description: Examiner amendments that narrow claims during prosecution are a sign of substantive examination and quality-focused resolution.
guidance: Identify examiner-originated claim narrowings as evidence that examination constrained overbroad claims, improving expected patent quality.

name: Representative-claim treatment at pleading stage
description: A claim may be treated as 'representative' for purposes of a § 101 eligibility analysis when briefing does not present any meaningful argument for the distinctive significance of any claim limitations other than those in the representative claim.
guidance: Use representative-claim treatment where the plaintiff's briefing refers generally to the 'Asserted Patents' and does not make arguments relying on limitations found only in other claims (Elec. Power Grp. v. Alstom).

name: §101 / Alice two-step framework
description: First determine whether the claims are drawn to a patent-ineligible concept (laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract ideas). If yes, then look to the elements of the claim individually and as an ordered combination to determine whether there is an 'inventive concept' sufficient to ensure the patent amounts to 'significantly more' than the ineligible concept itself.
guidance: A claim that recites an abstract idea must include additional features that ensure it is more than a drafting effort to monopolize the idea. The mere recitation of a generic computer cannot transform an abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter (Alice; Mayo).

name: Evaluate claims in light of specification and identified technical problem
description: Claims should be considered as a whole in light of the specification; where the specification identifies a specific problem in the prior art and the claims recite a specific solution (an improvement to computer functionality), the claims may be patent-eligible.
guidance: Precedent recognizes that specific technological modifications to solve a problem or improve the functioning of a known system generally produce patent-eligible subject matter (Core Wireless, Trading Techs, Data Engine). Look for specification language describing prior-art problems and specific structural/functional improvements (e.g., interactive links/reference indicators improving messaging GUI).

name: Real-world analogy not dispositive
description: Tracing the invention to some real-world analogy (e.g., characteristics of human conversation) is not, by itself, sufficient to render a claim abstract.
guidance: Even if the claimed concept has an analog in human behavior, the court must assess whether the claim as a whole provides a concrete technological solution or merely recites an abstract idea implemented on generic technology (Data Engine).

name: Functional/results-only claim language signals ineligibility
description: Claims that contain only results-based and functional language and lack any explanation of how to achieve the desired result are hallmarks of ineligible claims.
guidance: Compare such claims to those that recite a specific structure performing a function (e.g., 'notebook tabs' or specific GUI elements); reciting a specific structure within a particular display that performs a specific function can support eligibility (Data Engine).

name: Pre-suit knowledge requirement for induced and willful infringement
description: Allegations of pre-suit knowledge are necessary to support claims of willful and induced infringement based on pre-suit conduct.
guidance: Specific factual allegations (e.g., an inventor emailed a company VP with a link to a presentation that included the patent number and the VP acknowledged receipt) can plausibly allege pre-suit knowledge. General allegations (e.g., defendant is a 'sophisticated corporate entity' or that prosecution was 'public record') are insufficient without more specific facts.

name: Treatment of post-suit knowledge and amendment rules
description: A complaint generally does not operate going forward to establish knowledge for post-suit willfulness/inducement; plaintiffs should be allowed to amend to allege knowledge acquired since filing for indirect infringement but post-suit willfulness allegations are usually implausible alone.
guidance: For indirect infringement, courts may permit amendment to allege knowledge since filing because otherwise indirect infringement claims could be foreclosed. For willfulness, post-suit allegations typically fail absent pre-suit knowledge or other specific facts showing a culpable mind; evidence of post-suit bad conduct is often privileged (advice of counsel), making such allegations difficult to plead plausibly. The court here granted leave to amend limitedly (two weeks).

name: Resolve Graham factual inquiries
description: Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries (scope and content of the prior art, differences between the prior art and the claims, level of ordinary skill in the art, and secondary considerations) before applying any obviousness rationale.
guidance: This requirement appears at the start of each rationale: examiners must identify the relevant Graham findings and then—based on those facts—make additional findings specific to the chosen KSR rationale. Additional factual findings beyond the numbered rationale items may be necessary to explain a conclusion of obviousness.

name: Rationale B — Simple Substitution of One Known Element for Another to Obtain Predictable Results
description: To reject a claim based on this rationale, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries. Office personnel must then articulate the following: (1) a finding that the prior art contained a device (method, product, etc.) which differed from the claimed device by the substitution of some components (steps, elements, etc.) with other components; (2) a finding that the substituted components and their functions were known in the art; (3) a finding that one of ordinary skill in the art could have substituted one known element for another, and the results of the substitution would have been predictable; and (4) whatever additional findings based on the Graham factual inquiries may be necessary, in view of the facts of the case under consideration, to explain a conclusion of obviousness.
guidance: Guidance/example: Obviousness can be shown by replacing a known component with another known component that performs the same function predictably. Example: substituting bioauthentication (fingerprint sensor) for a PIN in a consumer electronics device—primary reference showed sub-credit/PIN structure, secondary references showed bioauthentication; substitution was predictable and rendered the claim obvious (ex parte Catan example). Examiners should identify each element and confirm the substituted element and its known function in the prior art.

name: Rationale C — Use of Known Techniques to Improve Similar Devices (Methods, or Products) in the Same Way
description: To reject a claim based on this rationale, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries. Office personnel must then articulate the following: (1) a finding that the prior art contained a 'base' device (method, or product) upon which the claimed invention can be seen as an 'improvement'; (2) a finding that the prior art contained a 'comparable' device (method, or product that are not the same as the base device) that was improved in the same way as the claimed invention; (3) a finding that one of ordinary skill in the art could have applied the known 'improvement' technique in the same way to the 'base' device (method, or product) and the results would have been predictable to one of ordinary skill in the art; and (4) whatever additional findings based on the Graham factual inquiries may be necessary, in view of the facts of the case under consideration, to explain a conclusion of obviousness.
guidance: Guidance/example: This rationale applies when a known improvement technique taught in one context would predictably improve a base device in a similar way. The Supreme Court in KSR warns that if the application would have been beyond ordinary skill, the rationale is inappropriate. Example: adding biometric+smart-card authentication and validation form (Wells) to a base remote-transfer system (Barnes) to achieve improved security—predictable adaptation supports a 103 rejection (Barnes in view of Wells). Examiners should identify base and comparable devices and show predictable application of the improvement.

name: Rationale D — Applying a Known Technique to a Known Device Ready for Improvement to Yield Predictable Results
description: To reject a claim based on this rationale, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries. Office personnel must then articulate the following: (1) a finding that the prior art contained a 'base' device (method, or product) upon which the claimed invention can be seen as an 'improvement'; (2) a finding that the prior art contained a known technique that is applicable to the base device (method, or product); (3) a finding that one of ordinary skill in the art would have recognized that applying the known technique would have yielded predictable results and resulted in an improved system; and (4) whatever additional findings based on the Graham factual inquiries may be necessary, in view of the facts of the case under consideration, to explain a conclusion of obviousness.
guidance: Guidance/example: Similar to C but emphasizes that the base device was 'ready for improvement' and a known technique could be directly applied with predictable results. Example provided: record-keeping system (Reference A) and data-processing breakdown technique (Reference B) — applying sub-files/category codes to banking records would be a predictable improvement (Reference A in view of Reference B). Examiners should explain readiness for improvement and predictable results, and may cite benefits/advantages to support the motivation to adapt.

name: Rationale E — Obvious To Try: Choosing From a Finite Number of Identified, Predictable Solutions, With a Reasonable Expectation of Success
description: To reject a claim based on this rationale, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries. Office personnel must then articulate the following: (1) a finding that at the time of the invention, there had been a recognized problem or need in the art, which may include a design need or market pressure to solve a problem; (2) a finding that there had been a finite number of identified, predictable potential solutions to the recognized need or problem; (3) a finding that one of ordinary skill in the art could have pursued the known potential solutions with a reasonable expectation of success; and (4) whatever additional findings based on the Graham factual inquiries may be necessary, in view of the facts of the case under consideration, to explain a conclusion of obviousness.
guidance: Guidance/example: 'Obvious to try' supports obviousness where there were a limited set of predictable options and a person of ordinary skill would have pursued them expecting success. Example: online bookstore with e-mail customer surveys—survey methods were a finite set and e-mail was an obvious, predictable choice (Smith in view of John). Examiners should identify the recognized problem, the finite predictable solutions, and the reasonable expectation of success for the selected option.

name: Rationale F — Known Work In One Field May Prompt Predictable Variations for Use In Same or Different Field Based On Design Incentives or Market Forces
description: To reject a claim based on this rationale, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries.
