Office personnel must then articulate the following: (1) a finding that the scope and content of the prior art, whether in the same field of the endeavor as that of the applicant's invention or a different field of endeavor, included a similar or analogous device (method, or product); (2) a finding that there were design incentives or market forces which would have prompted adaptation of the known device (method or product); (3) a finding that the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art were encompassed in known variations or in a principle known in the prior art; (4) a finding that one of ordinary skill in the art, in view of the design incentives or other market forces, could have implemented the claim variation of the prior art, and the claimed variation would have been predictable to one of ordinary skill in the art; and (5) whatever additional findings based on the Graham factual inquiries may be necessary, in view of the facts of the case under consideration, to explain a conclusion of obviousness.
guidance: Guidance/example: Applies when adaptation from one field to another (or within the same field) would be predictable in view of market/design incentives. Example: modernizing an electro-mechanical child's toy to electronics (Leapfrog v. Fisher-Price)—applying known electronics to achieve smaller size, reliability, and lower cost was predictable and obvious. Examiners should identify analogous prior art, design incentives, known variations, and predictability of the adaptation; list advantages and show no unpredictable results.

name: Step 1 — statutory categories
description: Determine whether the claim falls within a statutory category (process, machine, manufacture, composition, etc.).
guidance: No change in 2019 PEG. Example: a claim reciting a series of steps is a process (Step 1 = Yes).

name: Revised Step 2A — two-prong inquiry
description: Under revised Step 2A, a claim is eligible at Step 2A unless it (1) recites a judicial exception and (2) the exception is not integrated into a practical application of the exception.
guidance: If no judicial exception is recited (Prong One), claim is eligible and analysis ends. If exception recited but integrated into a practical application (Prong Two), claim is eligible and analysis ends. If recited and not integrated, the claim is 'directed to' the exception and proceed to Step 2B.

name: Step 2A Prong One — identify recitation of a judicial exception
description: Evaluate whether the claim recites a judicial exception (an abstract idea, a law of nature, or a natural phenomenon).
guidance: Procedure: identify the specific claim limitation(s) that the examiner believes recite an exception and determine whether those limitation(s) fall within the enumerated groupings of abstract ideas in the 2019 PEG. For laws of nature/natural phenomena, continue to use the MPEP 'recite' standard (including markedly different characteristics). For abstract ideas, do not use the prior 'Eligibility Quick Reference Sheet'; use the 2019 PEG groupings. Limitations not in the enumerated groupings generally should not be treated as abstract ideas except in rare 'tentative abstract idea' circumstances.

name: Consideration: improvements to functioning of a computer or other technology
description: An additional element that reflects an improvement to how a computer functions or to any other technology or technical field can indicate integration (Prong Two) or an inventive concept (Step 2B).
guidance: In Step 2A focus on whether the claim pertains to an improvement to technology (a 'technological solution to a technological problem') without considering whether limitations are WURC. Evaluate whether the specification provides a technical explanation of how to implement the invention and whether the claim itself reflects the improvement. In the streamlined analysis and Step 2B, continue evaluating improvements with reference to whether elements are conventional (MPEP 2106.05(a)). Examples: Enfish (specific data structure that improved computer functionality) vs. Intellectual Ventures v. Symantec (claims did not contain limitations addressing the alleged improvement).

name: Consideration: applying the exception with/by a particular machine or manufacture
description: Implementing or using a judicial exception with a particular machine or manufacture that is integral to the claim can integrate the exception or provide an inventive concept.
guidance: Discussed in MPEP 2106.05(b). The machine must be integral and enable a practical application (example: a body temperature detector that takes multiple readings in a particular way to output an accurate core temperature integrates a law of nature into a specific manufacture). Generic invocation of a computer is not sufficient.

name: Consideration: effecting a particular transformation
description: A claim limitation that effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing can integrate a judicial exception or supply an inventive concept.
guidance: Discussed in MPEP 2106.05(c). Example: process steps that change fat and water into free fatty acids and glycerol with specific parameters effect a transformation and practically apply the law of nature.

name: Prong Two excludes WURC consideration
description: Well-understood, routine, conventional (WURC) activity is not considered in Step 2A Prong Two.
guidance: Examiners should give weight to all claimed additional elements in Prong Two even if those elements represent WURC activity. WURC is evaluated only at Step 2B. As a result, a claim that includes WURC elements may still integrate an exception into a practical application at Step 2A.

name: Improvements: specification must show technical explanation
description: The specification must provide sufficient details so that one of ordinary skill would recognize the claimed invention as pertaining to an improvement in technology.
guidance: The specification could identify a technical problem and explain how the specification provides a technical solution. Case examples: McRO v. Bandai (spec explained automation rules for animation tasks), Affinity Labs v. DirecTV (failure to provide details led to ineligibility). After confirming the specification shows an improvement, the claim must reflect that improvement (e.g., claims covering a particular solution rather than merely the idea of a solution).

name: Step 2B — inventive concept ('significantly more') evaluation
description: If claim is directed to an exception at Step 2A (not integrated), evaluate at Step 2B whether the claim recites additional elements that amount to an inventive concept—i.e., significantly more than the judicial exception.
guidance: Procedure: identify additional elements beyond the exception and evaluate them individually and in combination using considerations (improvements, particular machine, transformation, other meaningful limitations, unconventional combination or specific limitations beyond WURC). If claim as a whole amounts to significantly more, claim is eligible; otherwise ineligible. Step 2B continues to consider whether elements are well-understood, routine, conventional (WURC).

name: Indicators of an inventive concept (Step 2B positives)
description: Types of claim features indicative of an inventive concept (i.e., 'significantly more').
guidance: Includes: improvements to computer functioning or other technology (MPEP 2106.05(a)); applying the exception with/by a particular machine (MPEP 2106.05(b)); effecting a transformation (MPEP 2106.05(c)); applying the exception in some other meaningful way beyond a mere link to technology (MPEP 2106.05(e) and Vanda); and adding a specific limitation other than what is WURC in the field (MPEP 2106.05(d)).

name: Procedure for tentative abstract ideas (non-enumerated)
description: When an examiner believes a claim limitation should be treated as an abstract idea even though it does not fall within the enumerated groupings (a 'tentative abstract idea'), follow 2019 PEG-specific steps.
guidance: Evaluate under 2019 PEG: if the claim integrates the tentative abstract idea into a practical application, claim is eligible. Otherwise proceed to Step 2B. If claim fails Step 2B, bring the application to the Technology Center (TC) director. Any rejection treating a non-enumerated limitation as an abstract idea must be approved by the TC director (approval recorded in the file) and must provide justification for treating the limitation as an abstract idea.

name: Drafting a rejection under 2019 PEG
description: Required content and approach when issuing a 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection under the 2019 PEG.
guidance: A rejection should: identify the abstract idea recited in the claim and include a reference to the appropriate enumerated grouping of abstract ideas; identify the additional elements and explain why they do not integrate the abstract idea into a practical application; and explain why the additional elements do not provide an inventive concept. Use the new form paragraphs where applicable (see form paragraph guidance).

name: Reminders & substantive practice takeaways
description: High-level examiner guidance to ensure consistent, accurate application of 2019 PEG.
guidance: Treat the claim as a whole — consider all recited limitations when determining eligibility. Do not use the old 'Eligibility Quick Reference Sheet Identifying Abstract Ideas' for determining whether a claim recites an abstract idea. WURC is considered at Step 2B, not Step 2A. The key inquiry in revised Step 2A is whether a claim reciting a judicial exception is directed to the exception itself or to a practical application of the exception. Practice compact prosecution by addressing all statutory requirements (not just eligibility) and, when possible, point applicants to eligible subject matter in the specification.

name: Use of examples and reliance on fact patterns
description: How to use USPTO examples (including new examples 37–42) when applying the 2019 PEG.
guidance: New examples 37–42 illustrate 2019 PEG application and should be interpreted based on their specific fact patterns; a claim under examination need not mirror an example claim to be eligible. Existing examples 1–36 were issued prior to the 2019 PEG and may contain analyses not entirely consistent with the 2019 PEG; claims indicated as eligible in prior examples remain eligible but use prior examples with caution. Example analyses highlight application of the groupings, Prong Two considerations, and Step 2B evaluations.

name: Handling applications in process and re-evaluation guidance
description: How to proceed when applicants respond or when claims were previously rejected under pre-2019 guidance.
guidance: If applicant argues claims are eligible, examiners should re-evaluate eligibility of previously rejected claims under the 2019 PEG. If claim is now eligible, withdraw the 101 rejection. If still ineligible, update form paragraphs used and ensure the rejection explains why the claim recites a judicial exception, fails to integrate into a practical application, and fails to provide an inventive concept. Also consider patentability under 102, 103, and 112.

name: Contractual obligations of depositor (NCIMB example)
description: The NCIMB application form constitutes a contract binding the depositor to provide all necessary information requested, to pay all necessary fees, to indemnify NCIMB against claims arising from release of samples (unless due to NCIMB negligence), not to withdraw the deposit during required storage, and to authorize NCIMB to furnish samples according to applicable patent requirements.
guidance: Similar contractual terms appear at other collections (NIBSC: provide biohazard statement, material in required form/quantity, pay transportation charges, observe Budapest Treaty terms, indemnify).

name: Reissue oath/declaration substantive requirements (37 CFR 1.175)
description: The reissue oath/declaration must include: (A) a statement that the applicant believes the original patent to be wholly or partly inoperative or invalid (by defective specification/drawing or by claiming more or less than right to claim); (B) a statement of at least one error relied upon to support the reissue application; (C) a statement that all errors being corrected arose without deceptive intention; and (D) the information required by 37 CFR 1.63.
guidance: MPEP §1414 discusses each element and examiners should carefully review the oath/declaration for compliance. If the oath/declaration is insufficient, the examiner should reject all claims under 35 U.S.C. 251 and use form paragraphs (e.g., 14.01–14.01.04) to state defects, followed by paragraph 14.14 to reject claims under 35 U.S.C. 251.

name: Utility requirement (usefulness)
description: An invention must serve some specific, presently known purpose (utility).
guidance: Cites Brenner v. Manson: utility requires a specific, presently known use; applied here to require that claimed genetic inventions demonstrate practical utility (e.g., diagnostic relevance).

name: Disclosure / written description and enablement (§112)
description: Applicants must disclose the invention so others skilled in the art can replicate it and must precisely stake out what is claimed.
guidance: Adequate disclosure is a statutory requirement and guards against overbroad claims that would stifle follow-on research.

name: European approach: DNA sequences patentable with industrial application (Directive 98/44/EC)
description: In the EU, DNA sequences are inventions (not mere discoveries) so long as the claimed sequence has an industrial application such as use in diagnosis.
guidance: The Note cites the EPO/EPC and Directive 98/44/EC as a narrowly tailored model allowing gene patents conditioned on industrial application.

name: Requirement that patented mutations be clinically relevant / tied to a disease (specific-mutation utility)
description: Patents on gene variants should be limited to specific mutations that the applicant has shown to be associated with a disease (demonstrable utility).
guidance: This mirrors pre-Myriad practice and prevents granting broad claims absent clinical relevance; does not impose extra burdens beyond pre-Myriad requirements.

name: Prevent overbroad claims: disallow claiming entire genes from single mutation discoveries
description: Patent claims should not permit an inventor to claim an entire gene based on discovering a single mutation; claims must be mutation-specific.
guidance: Limiting claims to specific mutations addresses concerns that a single discovery could foreclose further research on the overall gene.

name: Recites only idea or outcome (no details of how solution is accomplished)
description: Whether the claim recites only the idea of a solution or outcome i.e., fails to recite details of how a solution to a problem is accomplished. Recitation of claim limitations that attempt to cover any solution to an identified problem with no restriction on how the result is accomplished and no description of the mechanism for accomplishing the result does not integrate a judicial exception into a practical application or provide significantly more.
guidance: Result-oriented or highly functional claims that merely state a desired outcome are equivalent to saying 'apply it.' Cases: Electric Power Group; Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec; Internet Patents v. Active Network. In contrast, claiming a particular solution or a particular way to achieve an outcome may integrate the exception into a practical application or provide significantly more. Example: IV v Capital One (dynamic XML modifications lacked specific steps and were ineligible).

name: Particularity vs generality of application (breadth of claim)
description: The particularity or generality of the application of the judicial exception: a claim having broad applicability across many fields of endeavor may not provide meaningful limitations that integrate the judicial exception into a practical application or amount to significantly more.
guidance: Claims that generically recite an effect or claim every mode of accomplishing that effect are effectively adding 'apply it.' Cases: Internet Patents v. Active Network (maintaining state of data in online form without mechanism), O'Reilly v. Morse, The Telephone Cases. Limitations that confine the exception to a particular, practical application may amount to significantly more (see BASCOM example where filtering at a specific ISP location with customizable features was meaningful).

name: Extra-solution consideration: whether the limitation is significant
description: Whether the limitation is significant (i.e., it imposes meaningful limits on the claim such that it is not nominally or tangentially related to the invention).
guidance: If a limitation meaningfully confines the claim it may not be 'insignificant extra-solution activity.' Cases: Ultramercial (restricting public access to media found insignificant), Apple v. Ameranth (certain electronic menu features found significant/insignificant in context). This factor is considered in Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B.

name: Examples: insignificant application (post-solution activity)
description: Post-solution activities that do not integrate the exception (e.g., cutting hair after selecting a hairstyle; printing/downloading generated menus) are examples of insignificant application.
guidance: Cases/examples: In re Brown (cutting hair after hairstyle determination); Ameranth (printing/downloading menus). These are treated as nominal additions that do not make the claim patentable.

name: Field of use / technological environment limitation
description: Whether the additional elements amount to more than generally linking the use of a judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use. Merely indicating a field of use or technological environment does not make a claim eligible.
guidance: Supreme Court example: Parker v. Flook (limiting formula to petrochemical/oil-refining fields was insufficient). Diamond v. Diehr shows contrast when specific limitations act in concert to transform a process. Affinity Labs v. DirecTV is an example where limiting to cellular telephones was insufficient. Examiners should consider that 'technological environment' and 'field of use' are interchangeable for eligibility analysis. This consideration overlaps with extra-solution activity; examiners must explain why such a limitation does not meaningfully limit a claim in a rejection. See list of field-of-use examples in MPEP §2106.05(h).

name: Technological solution to a technological problem may integrate a judicial exception
description: When the claim recites a technological solution to a technological problem (specific configuration, manipulation, or methods that override conventional behavior), the additional elements can be more than mere instructions to apply an exception and thus integrate into a practical application.
guidance: Cases: DDR Holdings (manipulating Internet interactions to yield a desired result that overrode routine/conventional sequences), BASCOM (filtering tool at a specific ISP location with customizable features), Thales Visionix (particular inertial sensor configuration and raw-data usage). Examiners should look for specificity that describes how the technological result is achieved rather than a mere result-oriented limitation.

name: Examiner explanation requirement for eligibility rejections
description: When claim limitations do not meaningfully limit the claim (mere 'apply it', insignificant extra-solution activity, merely linking to a field of use), examiners should explain in an eligibility rejection why those limitations do not integrate the judicial exception into a practical application or provide significantly more.
guidance: Example explanatory approach: explain that implementing an abstract idea on a generic computer does not integrate the idea (as in Alice). Provide reasoning showing why added steps are nominal/tangential, well-known, or merely link to a field of use. See MPEP §2106.07(a) for additional guidance on formulating subject matter eligibility rejections.

name: Whether the court of appeals erred in upholding a method claim inconsistent with Mayo v. Prometheus
description: Petitioners assert that the court of appeals upheld a Myriad method claim that is irreconcilable with this Court's ruling in Mayo Collaborative Servs. v. Prometheus Labs., Inc., 132 S. Ct. 1289 (2012).
guidance: This criterion evaluates method-claim eligibility in light of the Mayo decision, which addresses patent claims that effectively cover natural laws, natural phenomena, or abstract ideas when implemented using well-understood, routine, conventional activity. Apply Mayo's framework: determine whether the claim is directed to a natural law or phenomenon and, if so, whether it recites an inventive concept sufficient to transform the nature of the claim into patent-eligible subject matter. Assess compatibility of the appealed method claim with Mayo's standards.

name: Do not conflate the patentee's invention with the linguistic meaning of claim text
description: Courts often (incorrectly) treat 'the understanding of claim text by a person of skill in the art' and 'the patentee’s invention' as interchangeable; they are distinct concepts.
guidance: Recognize that the 'invention' is the new, useful, non-obvious idea disclosed in the specification and that the linguistic meaning is how a POSITA would understand the claim language. Equating the two obscures whether courts are making a linguistic determination or a policy decision about patent scope. Examples: Phillips, Retractable Technologies, Marine Polymer.

name: Use specification as a source of linguistic context—but beware of using it as a proxy for 'the true invention' without acknowledging policy choices
description: The specification is an essential source of linguistic context for interpreting claim language, but using it to define the patentee’s 'true invention' is a policy move, not a purely linguistic one.
guidance: Leverage internal semantic clues in the specification (e.g., modifiers, usage) to determine ordinary meaning, but do not treat the specification’s description of embodiments as automatically equating to the objective 'invention' absent explicit construction. Example: in Kinetic Concepts the specification's repeated references to skin wounds supply linguistic context for the meaning of 'wound.'

name: Recognize that invoking the patentee’s 'true invention' is a normative, judge-dependent construct
description: There is no objective single 'true invention' in most patents; choosing one level of abstraction as the inventive idea is a legal construct shaped by judicial normative preferences.
guidance: Be explicit that using the 'true invention' to limit claim scope imports policy judgments (e.g., what is 'useful' or socially valuable) and can vary by judge. Example: Wright brothers illustration shows multiple plausible abstraction levels of the 'invention.'

name: Prefer transparency: when narrowing claims for policy reasons, use explicit doctrines rather than covert re-interpretation
description: If a court believes a claim's linguistic meaning is overbroad relative to a conception of the invention, it should either invalidate the claim or explicitly invoke doctrines (e.g., construction-to-save-validity, reverse doctrine of equivalents) instead of covertly saying the claim 'meant' the narrower scope all along.
guidance: Explicit invocation makes judicial policy choices visible and accountable, though the article recognizes political incentives make courts reluctant to do so. This is a recommended normative practice to avoid obfuscation.

name: Acknowledge that PTO examiners engage in construction as well as interpretation
description: Historically the PTO claimed examiners only 'interpret' claims while courts 'construe' them; this view is defective because examiners assess the legal effect of claims when deciding entitlement to issue.
guidance: Treat PTO examination decisions as involving constructional judgments (legal scope) as much as courts do; do not assume examiners are merely applying different, purely linguistic rules.

name: Consistency throughout the patent application
description: Maintain consistency throughout the patent application, both at the general and specific levels (e.g., if the claims use the term “warning device” for an automobile horn, the description of embodiments should use consistent phrasing).
guidance: Provide alternative examples (e.g., siren, buzzer) to support broader interpretation. Ensure terms used in claims, description and drawings match; inconsistent terminology can narrow interpretation or create ambiguity.

name: Balance disclosure of unclaimed subject matter
description: Balance the risks of too bare a description of embodiments against disclosing too much unclaimed subject matter.
guidance: Unclaimed subject matter is considered dedicated to the public unless claimed later. Drafting the claims before the description can help tailor the description to claim content. Err on the side of inclusion to avoid inability to narrow claims later to address novelty/inventive step objections.

name: Avoid wording that narrows scope ('the invention is...')
description: Avoid using phrases such as 'the invention is …' in the description; prefer 'an embodiment of the invention' or 'an exemplification of the invention.'
guidance: Calling something 'the invention' can foreclose a broader reading and unnecessarily narrow claim scope; descriptions are generally presumed to disclose 'an embodiment' unless limiting language is used.

name: Condition contextual/discussion language to avoid limiting claims
description: When adding drawings or discussions that provide context or operation, condition those discussions so they do not become limiting parts of the invention.
guidance: Be careful with context and examples so they do not inadvertently narrow claim interpretation.

name: Preferred and optional features should be labeled as such
description: Describe subject matter or features in dependent claims as preferred or optional embodiments or features; recite their advantages.
guidance: If not labeled optional/preferred, features may be regarded as essential. Also useful to set out further characteristics or narrower preferred ranges when a claim sets a preferred feature/range. (Note: in the United States practitioners often avoid discussing 'preferred' embodiments because of case law concerns.)

name: Tailor number of embodiments/examples to claim scope
description: Decide the number of embodiments or examples based on the scope of the claims; one embodiment can suffice for many mechanical/engineering inventions, whereas chemical/biological inventions may require many examples.
guidance: Chemical/biological fields often need multiple examples to support broad claims; match examples to the breadth you seek to claim.

name: Prepare clear visual supporting materials (drawings)
description: Prepare good visual supporting materials that describe the claimed invention; drawings are often the most important part of the application after the claims in mechanical, electrical and electronic fields.
guidance: Drawings should explain the invention and, where appropriate, be sufficient that the description confirms the drawings. They can illustrate principles, embodiments, or experimental results (e.g., graphs).

name: Show every claimed element in drawings where required
description: In jurisdictions such as the United States, laws require every claimed element to be shown in the drawings where appropriate.
guidance: Ensure drawings include claimed elements when the local law demands; otherwise the drawings should at least illustrate the invention sufficiently for the written description to confirm.

name: Appropriate level of detail in drawings
description: Provide sufficient detail in drawings to deliver supportive and enabling disclosure, but avoid unnecessary detail that could be interpreted as essential.
guidance: A 'black box' with no subcomponents may be insufficient; conversely, excessive detail risks narrowing the invention (especially with means-plus-function claims). Drawings should tell the story and include necessary detail without over-specifying.

name: Do not rely on the abstract to interpret claims (jurisdictional caveat)
description: In most countries the abstract delivers technical information only and is not used to interpret claim scope or determine patentability; the United States is an exception.
guidance: Draft abstracts broadly for U.S. filings to avoid unintended limitation; in many offices, abstracts are mainly checked only for adherence to word/character limits.

name: Avoid reference signs in the abstract (U.S. caution)
description: Adding reference indicators to the abstract can help understanding but in the United States such reference signs have been found to narrow claim interpretation.
guidance: In U.S. applications, omit or delete reference signs from the abstract to avoid narrowing effect.

name: Prepare the abstract at the end and verify disclosure consistency
description: Prefer preparing the abstract at the end of the drafting process and verify that all elements in the abstract are disclosed in the description/claims.
guidance: If elements in the abstract are not disclosed elsewhere, add them to the description or claims or modify the abstract to avoid introducing undisclosed subject matter.

name: Paris Convention priority (12‑month rule)
description: Under the Paris Convention, a subsequent application claiming priority must be filed within 12 months of the first filing to enjoy the priority date.
guidance: Right of priority protects subsequent filings from intervening acts; verify dates and obtain certified copies if required. Counsel clients on grace-period issues in specific national laws.

name: PTOL‑413 required information items
description: The PTOL‑413 form provides for recordation of: (A) application number; (B) name of applicant; (C) name of examiner; (D) date of interview; (E) type of interview (personal, telephonic, electronic mail or video conference); (F) name of participant(s); (G) indication whether an exhibit was shown or demonstration conducted; (H) identification of claims discussed; (I) identification of specific prior art discussed; (J) indication whether an agreement was reached and description of general nature of agreement; (K) signature of examiner who conducted the interview; (L) names of other USPTO personnel present.
guidance: PTOL‑413 also contains a statement reminding the applicant of his/her responsibility to record the substance of the interview. The form must be given an appropriate paper number, placed in the right hand portion of the file, and listed on the file wrapper contents list.

name: Minimum contents required for a complete interview record
description: A complete and proper recordation of the substance of any interview should include at least the applicable items: (A) brief description of any exhibit shown or demonstration; (B) identification of claims discussed; (C) identification of specific prior art discussed; (D) identification of principal proposed substantive amendments discussed (unless already described on PTOL‑413); (E) general thrust of principal arguments of applicant and examiner (need not be verbatim or highly detailed); (F) general indication of any other pertinent matters discussed; (G) if appropriate, general results or outcome of the interview; (H) for e‑mail interviews, a paper copy of the e‑mail MUST be made and placed in the patent application file as required by the Federal Records Act.
guidance: Identification of arguments is sufficient if the general nature or thrust can be understood in file context; applicants may provide fuller descriptions of arguments they believe persuasive. An Interview Summary alone will not be a complete record unless it includes or is supplemented to include all applicable items above.

name: Interviews after application sent to issue or after notice of allowance
description: After an application is sent to issue (37 CFR 1.312) it is technically no longer under the primary examiner's jurisdiction; interviews involving detailed consideration of claims sought to be entered and prior art discussion for allowability should not be given. Requests for interviews on cases where a notice of allowance has been mailed should be granted only with specific approval of the Technology Center Director upon a showing in writing of extraordinary circumstances.
guidance: An applicant is not entitled to greater consideration for informally presented amendments than for formally presented amendments; consideration of an amendment under 1.312 cannot be demanded as a matter of right.

name: Amendments to specification — replacement paragraphs/sections and substitute specification
description: Amendments to the specification (other than claims/listings) may be made by instruction to delete/replace/add a paragraph, by replacement section, or by submitting a substitute specification, subject to requirements: replacement/added paragraphs/sections/substitute specification must be provided in clean form and accompanied by a marked‑up version showing changes relative to the previous version (37 CFR 1.121(b)).
guidance: Clean form = no markings to indicate changes. The marked‑up version is required as an aid to the examiner and must be based on the immediate previous version of record. Paragraphs should be unambiguously identified (paragraph number, page/line, or other method). Deleted matter can only be reinstated by a subsequent amendment presenting the previously deleted matter.

name: Format recommendation for amendment paper
description: Recommended format for amendment paper: (A) a clean version of the amended (replacement) paragraph(s)/claim(s); (B) a remarks section beginning on a separate sheet; and (C) a marked‑up version (also on a separate sheet) showing changes and clearly identified as 'Version with markings to show changes made.'
guidance: Following this order aids examiner review and complies with the revised amendment practice requirements effective after March 1, 2001.

name: Special rules for reissue, reexamination, and provisional amendments
description: Amendments in reissue applications must be made in accordance with §1.173. Proposed amendments to description and claims in patents involved in reexamination (ex parte §1.510 and inter partes §1.913) must comply with §1.530(d)‑(j). Amendments in provisional applications are not normally made; if made, they must comply with §1.121 and will be placed in the provisional application file but may not be entered.
guidance: Follow the cited specific regulatory provisions for these special proceedings; provisional amendments are treated differently and may not be entered.

name: Catchall misconduct provision (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(i))
description: Prohibits 'other conduct that adversely reflects on the practitioner's fitness to practice before the Office.'
guidance: Must be alleged and supported by evidence; claims not supported may be deemed waived. This is a broad backstop for conduct that does not fit other enumerated subsections.

name: Positioning and print requirements for listings >60 lines and ≤300 lines
description: Any listing having more than 60 lines that is submitted as part of the specification must be positioned at the end of the description but before the claims.
guidance: Amendments to such listings must be made by substitute sheet. Alternatively, applicant may cancel and move the listing to a compact disc. If retained on paper as printouts, use direct printouts with dark solid black letters not less than 0.21 cm high, on white, unshaded, unlined paper.

name: IDS required documentary attachments (37 CFR 1.98(a)(2))
description: The IDS must include a legible copy of: each foreign patent; each publication or the portion causing it to be listed (other than U.S. patents and U.S. patent application publications unless required); for each cited pending unpublished U.S. application, the application specification including the claims and any drawing or the portion that caused it to be listed; and all other information or portions that caused the listing.
guidance: Provide the specific portions that caused the citation to be listed to assist examiner review.

name: Form and filing requirements for patent applications
description: An application shall be made in the prescribed manner, on payment of the prescribed fee, accompanied by a provisional or complete specification, contain an address for service in the Republic, and be accompanied by a prescribed declaration before acceptance; persons other than inventors must furnish prescribed proof of title/authority.
guidance: Applications date from lodging; a lodging date shall not be denied on formal grounds only if accompanied by prescribed fee, prescribed signed application form, one copy of the specification in an official language or official language of a convention country, and one copy of drawings (if any), even if drawings not in prescribed form. Translations of specs not in an official language must be furnished within three months, certified to registrar's satisfaction. An application may be amended within two months to claim priority.

name: Claiming priority (conditions and time limits)
description: A complete-specification application may claim priority from prior applications (provisional, complete, or convention-country application) provided specified time limits are met (generally within one year, or with prescribed fee within 15 months for certain cases) and other conditions such as being the first application in a convention country and applicant being owner or having acquired right to claim priority.
guidance: Detailed timing and documentary requirements apply; where a subsequent application in a convention country can be deemed the first in limited circumstances (withdrawn/abandoned/refused without public inspection, no priority claimed off it, no rights outstanding). Failure to claim priority within prescribed periods causes lapse.

name: Contents of specification (provisional and complete)
description: Every specification must indicate whether provisional or complete and commence with a title sufficiently indicating subject-matter. A provisional specification shall fairly describe the invention. A complete specification shall have an abstract as prescribed; sufficiently describe, ascertain and, where necessary, illustrate or exemplify the invention and the manner in which it is to be performed to enable a person skilled in the art to perform it; and end with a claim or claims defining the invention for which protection is claimed.
guidance: Claims of complete specification must relate to a single invention, be clear, and be fairly based on matter disclosed in the specification. Drawings/illustrations must follow prescribed form. For micro-biological inventions requiring a microorganism not publicly available and not obtainable from the specification, the microorganism must be dealt with in the prescribed manner (deposit rules).

name: Priority dates rules
description: Priority date for an invention or any matter in an application is, except as otherwise provided, the date of lodging of the application; where priority is claimed from earlier applications, priority date is the earliest lodging date in which the invention is fairly based on matter disclosed there; an invention may have one or more priority dates; until contrary proven, priority date is the earliest claimed.
guidance: Determination of 'fairly based' involves considering disclosures in all documents lodged with that prior application; new matter introduced by supplementary disclosure has priority equal to lodging date of supplementary disclosure.

name: Power to refuse applications in particular cases (frivolous/illegal/immoral)
description: Registrar shall refuse an application if it appears frivolous (claims anything obviously contrary to well-established natural laws) or if use of the invention would be generally expected to encourage offensive or immoral behaviour. If the invention might be used contrary to law, the registrar may refuse unless the specification is amended by adding a disclaimer or other reference to the illegality as the registrar thinks fit.
guidance: Grounds for refusal include scientific impossibility, public morality, and illegality; amendment/disclaimer may salvage otherwise problematic applications.

name: Amendment of application, lodging of fresh application, and post-dating
description: Where a fresh application is made by the same applicant in respect of part of matter disclosed in an earlier application and before acceptance, the registrar may direct that the fresh application be ante-dated to a date not earlier than the date of the first application. A patent on such fresh application shall not be revoked/invalidated solely because the invention is not new having regard to matter disclosed in the first application. A complete specification may be treated as provisional on applicant's request within 12 months of lodging; applications may be post-dated on request subject to limits (no later than six months from actual lodging or to avoid conflicting priority rights).
guidance: Registrar discretion and strict time limits govern ante-dating, conversion to provisional, and post-dating; priority claim rules constrain post-dating.

name: Disposal of specifications in lapsed applications
description: Where no priority was claimed from an application accompanied by a provisional specification and the application has lapsed (or an application and every application claiming priority from it has lapsed/abandoned/finally refused), the registrar shall, at applicant's request in prescribed manner, return any specification lodged in connection with the application, except documents showing proof of payment.
guidance: Practical rule for applicants to recover specification documents after lapse; financial proof documents retained.

name: Inspection by public and access to documents
description: After publication or after being open for public inspection, the patent and the application and all documents lodged in support shall, on payment of prescribed fee, be open to public inspection in the patent office. When an application claiming priority is open to public inspection, any other application from which it claims priority and supporting documents shall simultaneously be open to inspection.
guidance: After five years from date of application, any person may apply for patentee to supply particulars of any search report issued in another country for an application on same subject-matter; registrar forwards copy to patentee and commissioner can order compliance/enforce orders if patentee fails to comply.

name: Patented invention — nature determined by construction
description: Is the invention claimed in the patent; its nature is determined by construction given to the patent.
guidance: Presumed to differ from all prior inventions; not to infringe prior patents; enjoyment by owner unrestricted by law except as its nature restricts; the patented invention is twofold (the invention and the monopoly). Property in the invention originates in the inventive act and is the right to practise the invention; property in the monopoly is created by the patent and is the right to prevent others from practising the invention. Transferability and limits (e.g., federal statutes) and remedies for injuries noted.

name: Patentees — who may be patentee and scope of rights
description: Classes of patentees; who may be patentee and how title vests at grant.
guidance: May be earliest conceiver if diligent in reduction; may be alien, infant, married woman; Patent Office employee may not be; legal title vests at grant; rights depend on legal construction of patent; patentee is chargeable with notice of what patent contains; bound by actual invention and by claims; may discard unclaimed matter; estopped to claim matter covered by prior patent; must amend faulty description/claim without unreasonable delay; presumptions about ownership until transfer proved.

name: Principle — misuse and patentability
description: Meaning and misuse of the word 'principle' and its relation to patentability.
guidance: Principle misused in various instances; not an invention and not patentable; cannot be claimed; must be fully described in specification when used; distinctions between principle as force vs idea of means; essential to invention but not itself monopolizable; see long explanatory citations.

name: Property in a patent — twofold nature
description: Property in a patent is twofold (invention and monopoly) and related ownership issues.
guidance: Property distinctions explained; transferability rules and limitations, personal property aspects, effect of assignments and creditors' claims covered in cross-references.

name: Re-issue — scope, conditions, and limitations
description: Re-issue as a statutory mode to amend letters-patent; conditions when permitted and limits on new matter.
guidance: Origin and statutory background; re-issue available only under statutory conditions for imperfect patents; not allowed to add new matter beyond what original described and attempted to claim; cannot expand invention or include improvements/new matter; identity with original presumed until contrary shown; re-issue cannot cure a void ab initio patent; re-issue may amend defective description or excessive claim but limited to subject-matter attempted to be described and claimed in original; identity determined by comparing specifications, drawings, and models; courts/Patent Office follow same rules; many specific limits and presumptions detailed (citations).

name: Requirement to provide articulated reasoning (avoid conclusory statements)
description: Rejections on obviousness cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements; there must be articulated reasoning with some rational underpinning to support the legal conclusion of obviousness.
guidance: KSR and In re Kahn require explicit analysis explaining why differences between prior art and claims would have been obvious. Use reasoned explanation that avoids conclusory generalizations; employ common sense but support it with factual findings and rationale.

name: Consideration of applicant's rebuttal evidence (secondary considerations)
description: Office personnel should consider all timely rebuttal evidence submitted by applicants when reevaluating obviousness determinations; rebuttal evidence may include secondary considerations (commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others) and evidence of unexpected results.
guidance: After presentation of rebuttal evidence, reconsider initial obviousness determination in view of the entire record (see In re Piasecki, In re Eli Lilly). Examples of evidence applicants may submit for combination claims: (A) one of ordinary skill could not have combined the claimed elements by known methods (due to technical difficulties); (B) the elements in combination do not merely perform the function each performs separately; (C) the results were unexpected. Review all rejections and proposed rejections to confirm viability; follow MPEP § 706.07(a) when determining finality.

name: Quality patent (USPTO definition)
description: A quality patent is one that is correctly issued in compliance with all the requirements of Title 35 as well as the relevant case law at the time of issuance.
guidance: Quality work product includes appropriate and clear patentability determinations for every pending claim throughout prosecution; USPTO focuses on continuous quality improvement and efficiency to support issuance of quality patents.

name: Statutory compliance standard (overall)
description: OPQA reviews Office actions for statutory compliance by evaluating whether the Office action includes appropriate and clear determinations for every pending claim based on the patentability statutes.
guidance: Review evaluates each claim under each relevant statute; a single improper or omitted determination for any claim renders the entire Office action noncompliant. Rebuttal and reconsideration processes exist between OPQA and the TC.

name: 35 U.S.C. §102 — Novelty evaluation
description: Office actions are evaluated for correct determinations under 35 U.S.C. §102 (Novelty).
guidance: Part of the statutory compliance review: ensure rejections under §102 are correct, identify the claim and statute, and set forth sufficient evidence to put a person skilled in the art on notice why the claim is unpatentable.

name: Minimum content required in a rejection
description: To comply with the statutory compliance standard, rejections must be correct and must, at a minimum, appropriately (1) identify the claim and relevant statute and (2) set forth sufficient evidence to put a person skilled in the art on notice as to why the claim is considered unpatentable.
guidance: Insufficient explanation or omission of the claim/statute or supporting evidence leads to a finding of noncompliance.

name: Review flow principle: claim-by-claim, statute-by-statute evaluation
description: In evaluating work product under the statutory compliance standard, OPQA reviewers evaluate how an Office action addresses every claim under each statute to ensure proper rejections and that no proper rejections were omitted.
guidance: Because every claim is reviewed under each statute, many statutory compliance evaluations are performed per Office action. If any single claim has an improper determination under any statute, the entire Office action is identified as noncompliant regardless of other correct determinations.

name: Strategy — introduce new claims to reset prosecution (but avoid new matter)
description: Adding new claims can be a tactical way to reset prosecution if the new claims introduce significant limitations that require fresh examination and are fully supported by the original disclosure.
guidance: Requirements/cautions: the new claim scope must be fully supported by the specification to avoid a new matter rejection under 35 U.S.C. §112(a). This strategy works best when the added claims are substantively different (significant limitations) so the examiner is likely to raise a new ground of rejection; minor variations may not prevent a final Office Action. Not guaranteed — if changes are minor, examiner may still issue final rejection.

name: Use of inventor declarations under 37 CFR 1.132 to strengthen enablement (but not introduce new subject matter)
description: An inventor’s declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 can help establish that a person skilled in the art would understand how to implement a claimed feature, thereby strengthening the record on enablement.
guidance: Declarations can clarify how existing features are enabled but cannot introduce new subject matter. Use declarations to address perceived enablement deficiencies, but ensure the content stays within what the specification already discloses.

name: Practical takeaways: preferred tactical options to keep prosecution open
description: Summarized actionable tactics: (1) argue without amending if the examiner may introduce a new ground of rejection; (2) submit an IDS with relevant prior art before final rejection under 37 CFR 1.97(c) to trigger a non-final action; (3) introduce a new claim that is supported by the specification but forces new examination; (4) use declarations to clarify enablement but ensure they do not introduce new matter.
guidance: These are complementary tactics — choose based on case circumstances, timing, and risk tolerance. Always confirm procedural compliance (timing, fees, and support) and consider specialist advice for specific cases.

name: Claim construction is a question of law for the court
description: Claim construction is a question of law reserved for the court and not a question of fact left to the fact finder (Markman v. Westview Instruments Inc.).
guidance: On appeal, the Federal Circuit generally reviews district, ITC and USPTO claim determinations de novo; for district court constructions the Federal Circuit gives no deference to district court factual determinations.

name: Two-step process for infringement determinations
description: Patent infringement requires a two-step process: the court must construe the patent claims, then the fact finder must evaluate the construed claims against the allegedly infringing device or process.
guidance: Validity determinations likewise depend on the construed patent claims.

name: Intrinsic evidence components
description: Intrinsic evidence includes: the claims, the specification and the prosecution history (See Phillips, 415 F.3d at 1314).
guidance: Review disputed claim terms in light of the intrinsic evidence because a POSA reads claim terms in the context of the particular claim and the entire patent.

name: Ordinary and customary meaning to a POSA
description: Patent claim terms are generally given their ordinary and customary meaning as understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art (POSA), if possible (Vitronics).
guidance: A POSA is a fictional, objective person having the average knowledge, skill and expertise in the claimed invention's technical or scientific field (Phillips).

name: Context within the claim and claim differentiation
description: The context in which terms appear in the claim as a whole is important; different terms used to identify similar limitations should have different meanings (Bancorp).
guidance: Courts will attach different meanings to words/phrases used in separate claims (claim differentiation), but this presumption can be overcome by specification or prosecution history.

name: Consideration of claim parts (preamble, transitional phrases, limitations)
description: The court may consider the preamble, transitional phrase (e.g., 'comprising' vs 'consisting of'), and the claim limitations when construing terms.
guidance: Preamble may limit the claim where it recites essential structure or is necessary to give 'life, meaning and vitality' to the claim; 'comprising' is generally open-ended while 'consisting of' is limiting.

name: Specification is highly relevant and can be dispositive
description: The specification is always highly relevant to claim construction and is usually dispositive where the proposed construction aligns with the patent's description (Phillips).
guidance: Use specification where it describes preferred/sole embodiments, distinguishes prior art, or defines terms; but avoid improperly importing limitations from the specification into the claims.

name: Patentee can act as lexicographer but must do so clearly
description: A patentee is free to provide any definition for a claim term, often in the specification, but must clearly indicate the desired definition to overcome the presumption that ordinary meaning applies (Vitronics).
guidance: Clear indication can include explicit definitions or typographical cues (e.g., quotation marks).

name: Claim construction is case-specific
description: Interpretation of a claim term in one case may be completely different from that same term in another case, especially where fields of technology differ.
guidance: Always consider the particular intrinsic/extrinsic record and POSA context for the case at hand.

name: Preserve claim validity when possible
description: Courts should preserve the claims' validity, except where an invalidating construction is consistent with the claim language and specification (based on the presumption of validity under 35 U.S.C. §282).
guidance: Construction should not be unduly narrow or broad if that conflicts with patent text and specification (Marine Polymer; Rhine).

name: USPTO uses the broadest reasonable interpretation standard
description: Claim construction rule in USPTO proceedings applies the broadest reasonable interpretation to the claims, differing from district court approaches (In re Yamamoto).
guidance: Recognize divergent standards when litigating concurrently in district court and before the USPTO.

name: Markman brief contents and organization
description: Markman briefs are organized like typical briefs and usually contain: Introduction; Background (address technology of the patented invention); argument elements (discuss relevant claim construction law, describe a POSA, set out proposed constructions and supporting arguments); and Conclusion.
guidance: Include proposed constructions for each disputed term and arguments based on intrinsic and any extrinsic evidence; consider attaching expert declaration or prerecorded tutorial and conform to local/judge-specific rules.

name: Identify and limit claim terms for construction
description: Litigants should identify claim terms necessary for construction based on infringement and validity positions and the intrinsic/extrinsic evidence that supports their positions.
guidance: Local patent rules or judges' rules may limit the number of terms (e.g., N.D. Cal. Local Pat. R. 4-3(c) attempts to limit to the most significant terms, up to ten); minimize terms to avoid diluting key disputes.

name: Meet-and-confer on disputed claim terms
description: Courts often require parties to meet and confer regarding disputed claim terms before submitting claim construction briefs.
guidance: Use the meet-and-confer to narrow disputes and agree where possible on terms with no real impact on case outcome.

name: Strategic goals and appealability of Markman rulings
description: A successful claim construction ruling can support summary judgment motions and often determines outcomes (jury instructions, infringement/validity). A district court's Markman ruling is not final and therefore is not immediately appealable.
guidance: Parties may stipulate to resolve remaining issues to obtain a final decision more quickly and enable appeal to the Federal Circuit.

name: Deferral of examination under 37 CFR 1.103(d) requirements
description: A request for deferral of examination may be granted for up to three years from the earliest filing date for which benefit is claimed, provided: (1) the application is an original utility or plant application under 1.53(b) or a national-stage entry after compliance with 1.495; (2) applicant has not filed a nonpublication request under 1.213(a) (or has rescinded under 1.213(b)); (3) the application is in condition for publication as provided in 1.211(c); and (4) the Office has not issued an Office action under 35 U.S.C. 132 or a notice of allowance under 35 U.S.C. 151. The request must include the publication fee (1.18(d)) and processing fee (1.17(i)).
guidance: Applicants may consider deferral when they want to delay examination; requests that do not meet conditions will be denied. Deferral requests cause patent term adjustment reduction for the suspension period. The maximum deferral period is three years from the earliest claimed filing date.

name: Definition of "information material to patentability" in reexamination
description: Information is material to patentability in a reexamination proceeding when it is not cumulative to information of record or being made of record, and (1) it is a patent or printed publication that establishes, by itself or in combination with other patents/printed publications, a prima facie case of unpatentability of a claim; or (2) it refutes or is inconsistent with a position the patent owner takes in opposing an argument of unpatentability relied on by the Office or in asserting an argument of patentability.
guidance: A prima facie case of unpatentability is established when the information compels a conclusion that a claim is unpatentable under the preponderance of the evidence standard, giving each claim term its broadest reasonable construction consistent with the specification, and before considering evidence to establish a contrary conclusion of patentability. See 37 CFR 1.555(b).

name: IDS filing and required copies for reexamination (37 CFR 1.98 application)
description: Any information disclosure statement (IDS) must be filed with the items listed in §1.98(a) as applied to individuals associated with the patent owner in a reexamination proceeding, and should be filed within two months of the date of the order for reexamination, or as soon thereafter as possible.
guidance: 37 CFR 1.98(a)(2) requires a legible copy of: (1) each foreign patent; (2) each publication or that portion which caused it to be listed (other than U.S. patents and U.S. patent application publications unless required by the Office); (3) for each cited pending unpublished U.S. application, the application specification including the claims and any drawing or that portion causing it to be listed; (4) all other information or that portion which caused it to be listed. The exception to the copy requirement in 1.98(d) does not apply to ex parte and inter partes reexamination proceedings. Copies should be supplied to comply with 1.98(a).

name: Pre-interview submissions and interview duration limits
description: If the patent owner desires to initiate an interview, the owner should contact the examiner to indicate the issues and determine if an interview will be granted. If granted, the patent owner must file, at least three working days prior to the interview, an informal written statement of the issues to be discussed and an informal copy of any proposed claims to be discussed (unless examiner waives requirement). These materials should be faxed or hand-carried to the examiner to avoid delay.
guidance: The informal copies considered by the examiner will be made of record as an attachment to the Interview Summary form PTOL-474. The duration of the interview will not exceed one hour unless the patent owner files a petition under 37 CFR 1.182 showing sufficient cause for more time. Examiner may extend the interview at examiner’s discretion; only one interview may be requested after an Office action and prior to filing response absent showing of good cause.

name: Merger of copending reexamination proceedings and identical claims requirement
description: Where reexamination proceedings are merged, the CRU decision should require that the patent owner maintain identical claims in both files. Responses and other papers in the merged proceeding must consist of a single response, addressed to both files, filed in duplicate, each bearing a signature and identifying data for both files for entry in both files. If the claims are not the same, the merger decision will give the patent owner one month to provide an amendment to make the claims the same in each file; identical amendments are to be placed in all files.
guidance: If the patent owner fails to timely submit the amendment to make claims identical, any claim not identical in all merged proceedings should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as indefinite. Where claims already identical, prosecution continues at the most advanced point possible. A single certificate will be issued based on merged proceedings (37 CFR 1.565(c)).

name: Claiming benefit of provisional applications (37 CFR 1.78(a) timing and reference requirements)
description: A nonprovisional application (other than design) or an international application designating the United States may claim the benefit of one or more prior‑filed provisional applications under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) if: (i) the later application is filed not later than 12 months after the provisional (subject to paragraph (b)); (ii) each prior provisional names an inventor named in the later application and meets filing/date/fee requirements; and (iii) the later application contains or is amended to contain a reference to each such provisional application, identifying it by provisional application number.
guidance: If the later‑filed application is a nonprovisional application, the reference must be included in an application data sheet (§ 1.76(b)(5)). Failure to timely submit the reference during pendency (and the specific timing rules in (a)(4)) is considered a waiver of any benefit under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), except as provided in paragraph (c) for unintentional delays.

name: Requirements for claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120/121/365(c)/386(c) (37 CFR 1.78(d))
description: Each prior‑filed application must name the inventor or joint inventor named in the later application and must be either (i) an international application entitled to a filing date in accordance with PCT Article 11 and designating the U.S.; (ii) an international design application entitled to a filing date under § 1.1023 and designating the U.S.; or (iii) a nonprovisional application under 35 U.S.C. 111(a) entitled to a filing date as set forth in § 1.53(b) or (d) with the basic filing fee paid within pendency.
guidance: References to prior‑filed applications must be included (ADS for nonprovisionals) and must identify the relationship (continuation, divisional, continuation‑in‑part). Failure to timely submit required references is considered a waiver except as provided for unintentional delay; a request for a continued prosecution application under § 1.53(d) serves as the specific reference required by 35 U.S.C. 120.

name: Foreign-application-filed-more-than-12-months-before-US-effective-filing-date (102(d) requirement A)
description: The foreign application must be filed more than 12 months before the effective U.S. filing date of the claimed invention.
guidance: The examiner should search for an issued foreign patent only if there is a reasonable possibility that a foreign patent covering the same subject matter was granted to the same inventive entity before the U.S. effective filing date. The anniversary date falling on a weekend/holiday extends to the next business day (Ex parte Olah). See MPEP § 2139.01 for effective U.S. filing date determination when subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102.

name: Same-invention (foreign patent must involve same invention) (102(d) requirement D)
description: The same invention must be involved — the application claims in the U.S. could have been presented in the foreign patent; the foreign patent must support the subject matter of the U.S. claims.
guidance: Claims need not be identical or in same statutory class; if the foreign specification fully discloses the invention and would have supported the U.S. claims, the 102(d) bar applies (In re Kathawala). A foreign patent that discloses aspects of the invention can bar U.S. claims even if the foreign claims differ.

name: Determine-102(e)-date-for-references-not-resulting-from-international-application
description: If the potential reference did not result from, nor claimed the benefit of, an international application, its pre-AIA 102(e) date is its earliest effective U.S. filing date, taking into account any proper benefit claims under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or 120.
guidance: For benefit claims, prior application(s) must properly support the relied-upon subject matter in compliance with pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph (112(a)). For benefit claims under 119(e), at least one claim of the potential reference must be supported by the provisional's written description to be usable as prior art as of the provisional's filing date (see MPEP § 2136.03 subsection III).

name: International-application-conditions-for-using-international-filing-date-as-102(e)-date
description: If the potential reference resulted from, or claimed the benefit of, an international application (IA), the IA's international filing date is a U.S. pre-AIA 102(e) filing date only if three conditions are met: (a) IA filed on or after November 29, 2000; (b) IA designated the United States; and (c) IA was published by WIPO under PCT Article 21(2) in English.
guidance: If these three conditions are satisfied, the IA filing date (or an earlier effective U.S. filing date claimed properly) can be the 102(e) date, provided subject matter is supported under 112/120/119(e) as applicable. If an earlier application is an IA, it must also satisfy the three conditions for its date to be a U.S. filing date for 102(e).

name: Benefit-claims-and-written-description-support-requirements
description: For any benefit claim relied upon to establish an earlier 102(e) date (including 119(e), 120, 365(c), 386(c)), the subject matter used in the rejection must be disclosed in the earlier-filed application in compliance with pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph (112(a)).
guidance: Specifically for 119(e) provisional claims, at least one claim of the potential reference must be supported by the provisional application’s written description in compliance with 112 (see MPEP § 2136.03 subsection III). If benefit/priority is improperly claimed or lacks support, the earlier date cannot be used.

name: Examiners-follow-stepwise-guidelines-and-examples-to-determine-102(e)-date
description: Examiners must determine the appropriate pre-AIA 102(e) date for each potential reference by following the guidelines, examples, and flow charts in the section: (A) verify reference type; (B) check if reference resulted from/claimed benefit of IA; (C) if IA involved, evaluate the IA conditions and subrules; (D) be aware of exceptions where publication/issue dates may give earlier 102(a)/(b) dates.
guidance: MPEP provides nine illustrative examples covering common factual situations (Examples 1–9) to aid examiners in applying these rules. Examiners should consider international vs. U.S. filing/claim chains and applicable case law when assigning prior-art dates.

name: Repeals do not affect existing rights or liabilities; secrecy orders continuity
description: Section 5 ... repealed the sections or parts of sections of the Revised Statutes or Statutes at Large codified in this Act with the proviso that 'Any rights or liabilities now existing under such sections or parts thereof shall not be affected by this repeal.' An order of secrecy issued under or in effect under the repealed Act and in effect on the date of approval of this Act, shall be considered as issued under this Act, and any claims arising under the repealed Act or subject to presentation and determination pursuant thereto and unsettled as of the effective date of this Act, may be presented and determined pursuant to the provisions of this Act [this title].
guidance: Preserves substantive rights/liabilities from the repealed statutes and carries over secrecy orders into the new statutory regime; transitional procedures exist for claims under the prior law to be handled under Title 35.

name: Patents and What They Give (Background for Jury)
description: A patent gives the owner the right to exclude others from making, using, offering to sell, selling, or importing the patented invention in the United States; the specification should describe the invention and how to make and use it; claims define the invention's scope.
guidance: Provide jurors with a glossary and technical background; explain prosecution history/file wrapper and prior art concepts (publicly available before the invention or more than one year before filing).

name: Presumption of Validity and Burden for Invalidity
description: A patent is presumed valid; the accused infringer must overcome that presumption by clear and convincing evidence to establish invalidity (or unenforceability).
guidance: Clear and convincing evidence is defined as highly probable and is a higher standard than preponderance of the evidence but lower than beyond a reasonable doubt. Jury must apply same claim construction for infringement and invalidity.

name: Plaintiff's Burden to Prove Infringement
description: The patent owner (plaintiff) must prove infringement by a preponderance of the evidence — more likely than not.
guidance: The plaintiff must show that the accused product or method meets each element of at least one asserted claim (literal infringement) or, if arguing equivalents, that equivalents exist for missing claim elements.

name: Claim Construction — Judge's Role
description: It is the court's job to determine the meaning of claim language; jurors must accept and use the judge's constructions in assessing infringement and invalidity.
guidance: Only the claims define the boundaries of the invention; written description and drawings themselves are not infringed. Use the same claim meaning for both infringement and invalidity determinations. Follow governing authorities (e.g., Phillips, Markman).

name: Claim Construction for Means-Plus-Function (35 U.S.C. § 112 ¶ 6)
description: Means-plus-function (or step-plus-function) clauses cover only the structure (or step) described in the specification that performs the function or an equivalent.
guidance: Court must identify the structure in the specification that performs the recited function and instruct the jury accordingly. Instruction 2.2 is recommended to avoid jury confusion where §112 ¶6 limitations are present.

name: Direct Infringement — Elements Present (Literal Infringement)
description: A claim is literally infringed only if the accused product/method includes each and every element or step recited in that claim.
guidance: Determine literal infringement for each claim individually by comparing the accused product/method to the claim language using the court's claim constructions. The same accused feature may satisfy multiple claim elements.

name: Inducing Infringement — Elements
description: To prove inducement (35 U.S.C. §271(b)) the plaintiff must establish by a preponderance that: (1) the defendant aided, instructed, or otherwise acted with intent to cause acts by another that would constitute direct infringement; (2) the defendant knew of the patent or was willfully blind to its existence; (3) the defendant knew or should have known that its actions would result in infringement of at least one claim; and (4) another actually directly infringed at least one claim.
guidance: Willful blindness requires a subjective belief that there was a high probability that a patent existed and deliberate actions to avoid learning of it. Inducement requires an underlying direct infringement — without any direct infringement, inducement cannot be found.

name: Literal Infringement of Means-Plus-Function Claims (Proof Steps)
description: To show literal infringement of a means-plus-function or step-plus-function claim element, plaintiff must prove that the accused structure/step that performs the claimed function is identical to or equivalent to the structure/step disclosed in the specification.
guidance: Steps: (1) decide whether accused product/method has any structure/step performing the recited function; (2) identify that structure/step in the accused product; (3) determine whether it is identical to or equivalent of the structure/step in the specification; if so, the means-plus-function requirement is satisfied for that element.

name: Glossary Definitions to Guide Jury (Selected Terms)
description: Provide jurors with definitions of technical and legal terms used in the case (e.g., application, claims, prosecution history, ordinary skill in the art, prior art, specification, office action, license).
guidance: Parties may prepare a glossary of technical terms to distribute; terms to be agreed by parties where appropriate.

name: Substantial New Question (SNQ) of Patentability Required (35 U.S.C. 312(a))
description: A 'substantial new question of patentability' must be present for the Office to order inter partes reexamination.
guidance: The Office initially determines whether the request presents a substantial new question; if so, reexamination is ordered. The request must point out each SNQ and provide a detailed explanation of pertinency and application to each claim.

name: No Enlargement of Claim Scope by Amendment
description: The scope of the patent claims cannot be enlarged by amendment during inter partes reexamination.
guidance: Amendments that broaden claim scope are not permitted; only narrowing/amendments that do not enlarge the scope are acceptable consistent with statutory limits.

name: Content Requirements for Request (37 CFR 1.915(b))
description: A request for inter partes reexamination must include specified parts and meet defined content requirements.
guidance: Required parts (per 37 CFR 1.915(b)): (1) identification of the patent number and every claim for which reexamination is requested; (2) citation of patents/printed publications presented to provide an SNQ; (3) a statement pointing out each SNQ with a detailed explanation of pertinency and manner of applying the citations to every claim; (4) copy of every relied‑on patent/printed publication with English translations of pertinent parts of non‑English documents; (5) a copy of the entire patent (front page, drawings, specification/claims) and any disclaimers/certificates (single‑side pages); (6) certification that a copy of the request was served on the patent owner (name/address indicated) or, if service not possible, duplicate copy supplied to the Office; (7) certification that estoppel provisions of § 1.907 do not prohibit the inter partes reexamination; (8) a statement identifying the real party in interest to the extent necessary for subsequent filers to determine privy status. If filed by an attorney/agent identifying another party, a power of attorney or representative capacity under § 1.34 is required (see 1.915(c)).

name: Decision and Processing on Requests (CRU/TC handling; timing)
description: If a request is granted, reexamination is ordered and proceedings are processed with specified forms, panel review, and time reporting; decisions and workflows are subject to Office procedure requirements.
guidance: The manual details fee processing, assignment, transfer, time reporting, criteria for deciding requests, claims considered, prior art basis for determination, and examples of decisions. Panel review is conducted at each stage of examination (except non‑merits actions); appeal conferences are panel reviews prior to Examiner’s Answer.

name: Inter Partes Reexamination Certificate Content and Format
description: At conclusion, an inter partes reexamination certificate is issued and formatted similarly to a patent title page with specific additions: title 'INTER PARTES REEXAMINATION CERTIFICATE' with ordinal number; certificate number equals original patent number plus kind‑code suffix (C1, C2, ...); filing date/number of the request noted as 'Reexamination Request'; 'Reexamination Certificate for' identifies original patent; INID codes used similarly to patents; list of prior art documents limited to those in reexamination file.
guidance: Certificate will identify claims confirmed as patentable, canceled, disclaimed, and not examined; new claims printed in italics, amended claims printed with italics and bracketing; prior court decisions identified; example of kind code handling when prior B1 certificates exist is provided.

name: Intervening Rights for Amended/New Claims (35 U.S.C. 316)
description: Any proposed amended or new claim determined to be patentable and incorporated into a patent following inter partes reexamination has the same intervening rights effect as specified in 35 U.S.C. 252 for reissued patents.
guidance: This protects persons who made, purchased, used, or imported items, or made substantial preparations therefor, prior to issuance of the certificate. The manual cites cases and parallels to reissue/ex parte reexamination intervening rights doctrine.

name: Claim forms and formats in general
description: Claim forms and formats in general
