guidance: Likely covers acceptable claim structures, formatting conventions, dependency/independent claim relationships, and drafting form considerations; page contains only the section title.

name: Apparatus or machine claims
description: Apparatus or machine claims
guidance: Topic heading for drafting and evaluating apparatus/machine-type claims (structure, elements, functional language issues). No substantive text provided on the page.

name: Method or process claims
description: Method or process claims
guidance: Section heading addressing drafting of method/process claims (steps, order, statutory/process eligibility concerns). No further content on the page.

name: Article of manufacture claims
description: Article of manufacture claims
guidance: Heading indicating guidance for drafting claims to articles of manufacture (definition, claim scope considerations); page shows only the heading.

name: Composition of matter claims-chemical cases
description: Composition of matter claims-chemical cases
guidance: Focuses on chemical/composition claim drafting (claiming compounds, mixtures, formulations; written description and enablement issues implied). No detailed content present.

name: Claims of varying scope
description: Claims of varying scope
guidance: Addresses strategies for drafting claims with different breadths (narrow to broad claim drafting, dependent claims to capture fallback positions). Only the section title appears on the page.

name: Claiming biotechnology inventions
description: Claiming biotechnology inventions
guidance: Section heading for drafting claims in the biotech field (specific issues like patent-eligibility, sequence listing, functional claim language); no substantive text on the page.

name: Thoughts on writing a claim.
description: Thoughts on writing a claim.
guidance: Presumably a colloquial/practical chapter with drafting tips, common pitfalls, and stylistic guidance for claim writers; the page only lists the chapter title.

name: Whether prosecution involved any examiner rejections (proxy for narrowing)
description: Binary indicator from PAIR data whether the prosecution ever included an examiner rejection (non--final or final). Authors use this as a measure of whether the prosecution process compelled narrowing/amendments.
guidance: Used instead of raw claim-count changes because number-of-claims is an imperfect proxy for scope; rejections are a more direct signal that examiner compelled amendment or negotiation occurred.

name: Change in number of claims as a measure of scope (flagged as problematic)
description: The change in number of claims between the application and the issued patent is a candidate measure of narrowing of scope, but it is problematic because number-of-claims can increase for tactical reasons and does not consistently indicate scope narrowing.
guidance: Authors show many granted applications with rejections still exhibit no net decrease (and sometimes increases) in claim counts; therefore they caution against using claim-count change alone as evidence of narrowing.

name: Limitations on administrative review: claims outside the administrative record or frivolous
description: Allegations that are frivolous, unintelligible, or fall outside the purview of the proceeding or the record before the OED Director will not be further considered.
guidance: Petitioners must confine challenges to issues reflected in the administrative record and present intelligible, legally cognizable claims to obtain relief.

name: Explain principle and several modes for machines
description: In the case of any machine the inventor 'shall fully explain the principle, and the several modes, in which he has contemplated the application of that principle.'
guidance: Specification must not merely name parts but explain the principle and modes of application by which the invention is distinguished from others; this aids construction by skilled persons and delimiting the claim.

name: Claimed novelty must appear with reasonable certainty
description: It is sufficient if 'what is claimed as new appear with reasonable certainty on the face of the patent, either expressly or by necessary implication.'
guidance: Whether the claimed new matter appears with reasonable certainty is a question of law on the construction of the patent and specification.

name: Court discretion to award costs when claim is overbroad but some new part was truly infringed
description: When plaintiff fails because his specification or claim embraces more than that of which he was the first inventor, 'if it shall appear that the defendant had used or violated any part of the invention justly and truly specified and claimed as new, it shall be in the power of the court to adjudge and award, as to costs, as may appear to be just and equitable.'
guidance: Even if plaintiff's overall claim fails, courts may award costs or equitable relief where defendant has infringed genuinely new, truly specified parts.

name: Disclaimer for inadvertent over-claiming (§7, act of 1837)
description: A patentee who 'through inadvertence, accident, or mistake' has made his specification or claim too broad may make a written disclaimer of such parts, attested and recorded in the Patent Office on payment (e.g., $10), and such disclaimer shall thenceforth be taken as part of the original specification.
guidance: Disclaimer preserves the remainder of the patentee's rights (any material and substantial part truly his own) and must be recorded; it does not affect pending actions except as to questions of unreasonable neglect or delay in filing the disclaimer.

name: Retain and clarify other quality-enhancing statutory provisions
description: The bill includes changes such as adjustments to the best mode disclosure requirement, incentives for government labs to commercialize inventions, restrictions on false marking claims, clarification of tax strategy patents, small business assistance via a patent ombudsman, USPTO satellite offices, and a transitional postgrant proceeding for business method patents.
guidance: Legislative reform should bundle clarity and safeguards across multiple provisions to promote patent quality, commercialization, and administrative efficiency while preventing abuse (e.g., false marking) and supporting small entities.

name: State-granted rights and federal patent entitlement
description: Where any State before adoption of the present government 'shall have granted an exclusive right to any invention,' the claimant cannot obtain an exclusive right under this act except on relinquishing his right under such particular State; relinquishment and obtaining under the act is sufficient evidence.
guidance: Prior state-granted exclusivities must be relinquished to secure federal patent rights under the act; the statute requires clear relinquishment before federal grant will be recognized.

name: Specification content and arrangement requirements
description: Specification requirements (1.71–1.75): abstract (1.72(b)), amendments to specification (1.121, 1.125), arrangement of specification (1.77, 1.154, 1.163), best mode (1.71(b)), claims (1.75), commencement on separate sheet (1.71(f)), contents (1.71–1.75), copyright notice (1.71(d)), cross-references, description of the invention (1.71), must point out new improvements specifically (1.71(c)), must refer by figures to drawings (1.74), must set forth the precise invention (1.71(b)), object of the invention (1.73), order of arrangement in framing (1.77).
guidance: Specification must conclude with specific and distinct claim (1.75(a)), be separate from other parts of application (1.71(f)), and meet listed requirements; defective specifications may be corrected by reissue (1.171–1.178).

name: Claims — must conclude with specific and distinct claim; species of invention claimed; restriction practice
description: Claims must conclude with specific and distinct claim (1.75(a)); species of invention claimed addressed (1.141, 1.146); restriction practice and requirements for restriction (1.141–1.146, 1.176), withholding nonelected claims, constructive election, provisional election, petitions and reconsideration rules.
guidance: Includes rules for subsequent presentation of claims for different inventions and withdrawal of claims to nonelected inventions.

name: Statement under Article 19: format and content limits (PCT Rule 46.4 / Article 19(1))
description: A statement under Article 19(1) must be in the language of publication and shall not exceed 500 words if in English or if translated into English. The statement should be identified by a heading, preferably 'Statement under Article 19(1)'. It shall contain no disparaging comments on the international search report or relevance of citations; references to citations may be made only in connection with an amendment of that claim.
guidance: The statement is optional; it is published with the international application. It must be tied to specific amendments; general comments or disparaging remarks are prohibited. Statements not complying with requirements are not published nor communicated to designated Offices.

name: Requirement to indicate specific basis for amendments
description: The letter accompanying replacement sheets must indicate the basis for the amendments in the application as filed with specific references to particular parts of the application; non-specific indications such as 'see the description as filed' or 'see the claims as filed' are generally not considered sufficient.
guidance: Provide precise line/paragraph/drawing references so the examiner can assess whether amendments introduce subject-matter extending beyond the disclosure as filed. Examples illustrate acceptable phrasing (e.g., 'Basis for the amendment: Claim 1 ... basis found in original claims 2 and 4 as filed').

name: Supplementary search request timing and competent Authorities (PCT Rule 45 bis.1 & 45 bis.9)
description: An applicant may, at any time prior to the expiration of 22 months from the priority date, request a supplementary international search by an ISA competent under Rule 45 bis.9. Requests may be in respect of more than one such Authority. An Authority is competent if its preparedness to do so is stated in the applicable agreement under Article 16(3)(b), subject to limitations; the Authority that carried out the main international search under Article 16(1) shall not be competent to carry out the supplementary search for the same application.
guidance: Competence may have limitations (subject matter, total number of searches, claim limits). Verify applicable agreements and competence before requesting.

name: Start, basis and scope of the supplementary international search (PCT Rule 45 bis.5)
description: The Authority specified for supplementary search shall start the search promptly after receipt of the specified documents, but may delay until it receives the ISR/written opinion or until expiration of 22 months from priority date. The search is carried out on the basis of the international application as filed or an accepted translation, taking due account of the ISR and written opinion if available. The Authority may exclude claims not subject to the international search, may decide not to establish a supplementary search report if an Article 17(2)(a) declaration applies, and must cover at least the documentation indicated in the applicable agreement.
guidance: An Authority may restrict the search to certain claims; if exclusions or restrictions apply they must be indicated in the supplementary international search report.

name: Limitations and competence rules for Supplementary International Searching Authorities (PCT Rule 45 bis.9)
description: An Authority is competent to carry out supplementary searches if its preparedness is stated in the applicable agreement under Article 16(3)(b), subject to limitations and conditions in that agreement. The Authority that carried out the main international search under Article 16(1) shall not be competent to carry out supplementary searches for that application. Limitations may include subject-matter restrictions, caps on total supplementary searches, or maximum claims searched.
guidance: Applicants should select Authorities aware of these limitations and consistent with strategic national-phase plans; check agreements under Article 16(3)(b) for details.

name: Scope and limits of general authorizations to charge deposit accounts (37 CFR 1.25(b))
description: A general authorization to charge all fees, or only certain fees, set forth in 37 CFR §§ 1.16–1.18 to a deposit account may be filed in an individual application for the entire pendency or for a particular paper; such authorizations will be interpreted to cover fees set forth in 37 CFR 1.16 and 1.17 but will not apply to document supply fees (1.19), certain post-issuance fees (1.20), or most miscellaneous fees (1.21) except the processing fee under 1.21(m) for refused/charged-back checks or credit cards.
guidance: An authorization to charge the basic filing fee will be treated as authorization to charge the basic filing fee, search fee, examination fee, any excess claims fees, application size fee, and any non-electronic filing fee (37 CFR 1.16). An authorization to charge issue fees (37 CFR 1.18) may be filed only after mailing of the notice of allowance; a general authorization made prior to mailing of the notice does not apply to issue fees.

name: Small entity fee reductions: scope, amounts, and effective changes
description: Under 35 U.S.C. 41(h) and implementing regulations, many patent fees are reduced for qualifying small entities (persons, small business concerns, nonprofit organizations); as of December 29, 2022 most applicable fees were reduced by 60 percent (increased from 50%), and an 80 percent reduction applies to the filing fee for an electronically-filed nonprovisional original utility application by a small entity (per amendment to 35 U.S.C. 41(h)(3)).
guidance: Fees reduced by 60% include application filing fees (basic filing, search, examination, application size, excess claims), certain extension and petition fees, issue fees, maintenance fees, appeals fees, and others listed (see 37 CFR 1.16, 1.17, 1.18, 1.20, 41.20). Some fees remain ineligible for reduction (document supply fees under 1.19, certificate of correction fees 1.20(a), most miscellaneous fees 1.21), though some sequence-listing and other specific fees may be reduced. Effective dates for particular fee changes (e.g., PCT-related reductions) are specified in CFR references.

name: Federal Government use license exceptions to small entity disqualification
description: Certain government use licenses do not preclude claiming small entity status: e.g., use license resulting from rights determination under Executive Order 10096 in accordance with §501.60, use license resulting from 15 U.S.C. 3710d(a) when the Federal employee-inventor retains title as authorized, or use licenses arising under specified actions in funding agreements (35 U.S.C. 202 provisions) subject to enumerated conditions.
guidance: Detailed subconditions apply (e.g., inventions made solely by employees of the small entity, Federal agency actions assigning rights back to the small entity, CRADA-related waivers). Even if an exception applies, no refund under § 1.28(a) is available for any patent fee paid by the Government.

name: Rights in the invention and effect of transfers/licenses/security interests
description: The 'rights in the invention' refer to rights in the United States (exclude rights transferred abroad) and ownership or assignment/licensing of such rights to a non-small entity will disqualify an applicant from claiming small entity status; a security interest does not constitute an obligation to transfer unless defaulted upon, and default may cause loss of small entity status.
guidance: If rights are transferred to a non-small entity and later returned so all rights are again held by small entities, reduced fees may be reclaimed. A non-exclusive license to a non-small entity will disqualify small entity status (e.g., Ulead Systems v. Lex Computer & Management cited). Notification of loss of entitlement due to default on security interest must be filed under 37 CFR 1.27(g) prior to paying the earliest affected fee (issue or maintenance).

name: Reply requirements to non‑final Office actions (37 CFR 1.111(b))
description: To be entitled to reconsideration or further examination, the reply must be reduced to writing which 'distinctly and specifically points out the supposed errors in the examiner’s action' and must reply to every ground of objection and rejection.
guidance: The reply must present arguments pointing out specific distinctions believed to render the claims patentable over applied references. A general allegation that the claims define a patentable invention without specific explanation does not comply. A request may be made to hold form objections in abeyance until allowable subject matter is indicated. The reply must appear to be a bona fide attempt to advance the application or reexamination to final action.

name: Supplemental reply entry conditions (37 CFR 1.111(a)(2))
description: A supplemental reply to a reply in compliance with § 1.111(b) will not be entered as a matter of right except as provided; the Office may enter a supplemental reply only if clearly limited to certain topics or filed during suspension under § 1.103(a) or (c).
guidance: Permitted limited subjects: (A) cancellation of claim(s); (B) adoption of examiner suggestion(s); (C) placement of the application in condition for allowance; (D) reply to Office requirement made after first reply; (E) correction of informalities (e.g., typographical errors); (F) simplification of issues for appeal. A supplemental reply filed in sufficient time to be entered before examiner considers prior response may be approved after a cursory review for limitation to these conditions. If not approved for entry, contents should be included in a proper response to a subsequent Office action if the patent owner wishes them considered.

name: Amendments in reply must identify patentable novelty (37 CFR 1.111(c))
description: In amending in reply to a rejection the applicant/patent owner must clearly point out the patentable novelty believed present and show how the amendments avoid cited references or objections.
guidance: This requirement applies to applications and reexaminations; show specific claim language distinctions and how amendments overcome prior art or objections.

name: Prosecution bar
description: Absent written consent from the Producing Party, any individual who receives access to AEO or SOURCE CODE information shall not be involved in prosecution of patents or patent applications relating to the subject matter of this action before any foreign or domestic agency, including the Patent Office.
guidance: Prosecution includes drafting, amending, advising, or otherwise affecting scope or maintenance of patent claims (but does not include representing a party challenging a patent before an agency). The Prosecution Bar begins when access is first received and ends two (2) years after final termination of the action. Examples: original prosecution, reissue, and reexamination proceedings.

name: Specification of documents forming basis for European proceedings (Section 6 / Rule 159(1)(b))
description: When an application enters the European phase applicants must specify the application documents, as originally filed or as amended, on which the European grant procedure is to be based (Rule 159(1)(b) EPC).
guidance: Section 6 allows applicants to indicate whether they wish to proceed with (a) the published documents (where amended claims under Article 19 PCT replace the originally filed claims) — in proceedings before the EPO as designated Office without PCT Chapter II (section 6.1), or (b) the documents on which the international preliminary examination report is based — in proceedings before the EPO as elected Office under PCT Chapter II (section 6.2). Sections 6.1 and 6.2 also provide the possibility to indicate that amended documents filed on entry into the European phase are to form the basis for the grant procedure.

name: Translation of the international application (language and content)
description: If the international application was not published in an EPO official language, the applicant must furnish the EPO with a translation of that application in such a language within 31 months of the filing date or, where applicable, the (earliest) priority date.
guidance: Proceedings in the European phase will be conducted in the language of the translation. The translation must include the description, the claims as originally filed, any text in the drawings, and the abstract. It must also include any indications under Rule 13bis.3 and 13bis.4 PCT for inventions relating to biological material and any published request for rectification (Rule 91.3(d) PCT).

name: Basic eligibility requirements for PPH entry
description: Not every application is eligible; a number of requirements must be met.
guidance: Initial conditions: (1) the application must be an application claiming priority under the Paris Convention, a National Stage of a PCT application, or a bypass continuation application; (2) the application must have at least one claim allowed by the Office of First Filing (OFF); (3) claims provided to the Office of Second Filing (OSF) must correspond in scope to the claims found to be allowable in the OFF; (4) examination of the application must not have yet begun in the OSF. If these are met, an applicant can file a Request for participation in the PPH program.

name: USPTO-specific PPH filing requirements
description: When USPTO is the OSF, additional documentary and procedural submissions are required.
guidance: Required: Request for participation, petition to make special and required petition fee, copies of all office actions from the OFF relevant to patentability (with translations if in a foreign language), a table indicating correspondence between each claim in the OSF application and an allowed claim from the OFF, and an information disclosure statement listing all documents cited by the OFF. If OFF is EPO or JPO, applicant can request USPTO obtain documents electronically via Dossier Access System. USPTO will review submissions and give one chance to bring the application into compliance if found lacking. If granted, the application is examined in advance; any amendments must still correspond to one or more allowable claims from the OFF as shown in a new correspondence table filed with the amendment.

name: EPO-specific PPH rules and limits
description: EPO-USPTO PPH was a trial program with specific limitations and submission requirements.
guidance: Key points: EPO PPH not open to ex-PCT applications that have entered the European phase (excluding many U.S.-priority applications). For eligible EPO applications, applicant will be invited to amend claims to conform to corresponding U.S. patent claims; original or amended claims must sufficiently correspond in scope to patentable/allowable claims in the USPTO application and a claims correspondence chart must be filed. Applicant must submit copies of all USPTO office actions relevant to patentability and copies of all documents cited in the USPTO office action except European patents/published European applications (unless already filed in the U.S. application, in which case a reference is sufficient). When granted by EPO, application is advanced and processed under PACE.

name: Risk that OFF-allowed claims won't be allowable in OSF
description: Claims allowed by the OFF under their patent laws and rules might not be allowable under the patent laws/rules of the OSF.
guidance: Examples: an amendment to overcome a U.S. rejection under 35 U.S.C. §102(e) may not be required in the EPO; differing standards for obviousness (U.S.) and inventive step (other jurisdictions) may lead to no allowable corresponding claim in OSF. Also, amendments made during OFF prosecution could narrow claims more than necessary for OSF, and negative comments by an OSF examiner might be used against the OFF-granted patent in litigation. Applicants trade off claim breadth/admissions for earlier examination and potential earlier enforceable protection.

name: Strategic considerations for maximizing PPH benefits
description: Applicants should develop prosecution strategies to maximize advantages and mitigate disadvantages of PPH programs.
guidance: Consider subject matter, priority relationships, claim scope, and timing. Specific strategic actions: identify eligible pairs of OFF and OSF applications; identify potential future OFF/OSF pairs; choose preferred OFF or OSF; manage prosecution timelines to increase eligibility chances; identify subject matter, claims, and claim formats suitable for each PPH program; preserve ability to protect other inventions outside PPH programs.

name: Use of continuation/divisional practice to manage trade-offs
description: Continuation or divisional filings can be used so PPH examination applies to some claims while preserving broader claims elsewhere.
guidance: Examples: In an unexamined U.S. application with claims to multiple inventions, claims corresponding to allowable OFF claims can be examined under PPH while claims to other inventions are filed in divisional/continuation applications to be prosecuted separately. An applicant can file a continuation from the U.S. application and request that the continuation be examined under PPH, preserving broader claims in the first U.S. application for conventional prosecution while accelerating others.

name: Indicator table schema / variables
description: The indicator table contains per-patent variables such as Appln_id, Filing_year, WIPO_Tech and the indicators Patent_Scope, Fwd_Cits, Fwd_Cits_XY, Bwd_Cits, NPL, Claims, Claims_Bwd, Family_size, Grant_lag, Breakthrough, Breakthrough_XY and (in Normalised_table) Generality, Originality, Composite_index_4, Composite_index_6.
guidance: CREATE TABLE examples are provided showing the exact field names, datatypes and a primary key on Appln_id. Insert the list of patent documents (Appln_id) to be processed (example: SELECT distinct Appln_id from PATSTAT_APPLN WHERE Appln_auth='EP' AND Appln_kind='A' and IPR-Type='PI'). Note: Appln_id refers to PATSTAT surrogate keys.

name: Board remarks not authority to amend claims
description: A remark by the Board that a certain feature does not appear in a claim is not to be taken as a statement that the claim may be allowed if the feature is supplied by amendment; such remark shall not be construed by appellant to give authority to amend the claim.
guidance: Appellants should not treat Board comments as implicit permission to change claim scope; follow proper amendment procedures.

name: Two response options to a new ground of rejection
description: Upon a Board-designated new ground under 37 CFR 41.50(b), appellant must within two months either (1) reopen prosecution by appropriate amendment/new evidence (remand to examiner), or (2) request rehearing addressing the new ground and stating with particularity the points misapprehended or overlooked.
guidance: Failure to timely exercise one of these options will result in termination of the appeal as to the rejected claims. Arguments submitted without amendment/new evidence will be treated as a request for rehearing.

name: Scope and nature of appropriate amendment and new evidence
description: An amendment is 'appropriate' if it amends one or more of the claims rejected or substitutes new claims to avoid the art or reasons adduced by the Board, and must be directed to the same subject matter as the appealed claims; 'new evidence' may be a showing under 37 CFR 1.130, 1.131 or 1.132 as appropriate.
guidance: Adding new claims without amending or substituting for the rejected claims is not appropriate (new claims will not be entered and may be treated as a request for rehearing if they contain argument). Arguments submitted without amendment or new evidence will be treated as a rehearing request.

name: Board retains jurisdiction until specific events after new ground designation
description: When the Board designates a new ground under 41.50(b), the Board retains jurisdiction over the appeal until (a) the time for response expires and the Board enters an order of dismissal, or (b) the appellant reopens prosecution in response to the new grounds.
guidance: If appellant elects mixed responses (amend some claims, request rehearing on others), the examiner will not consider those claims for which rehearing is requested; rehearing will be considered after prosecution of the amended claims is terminated.

name: Handling when no claims stand allowed
description: If no claims stand allowed after Board action, examiner should consider the application abandoned and may either convert dependent claims to independent form by examiner's amendment and issue application or set a one-month (or two-month in certain draft paragraph) time for applicant to rewrite dependent claim(s) in independent form; if no timely reply, application is abandoned.
guidance: Form paragraph ¶12.291 (No Allowed Claim) may provide a TWO MONTH time period from mailing date to present dependent claims in independent form to avoid abandonment — extensions under 37 CFR 1.136(a) are stated as available in that paragraph. Use correct paragraph and time period depending on whether notice of appeal was filed on/after Jan 23, 2012 and the case specifics.

name: Consequences of inaction on 37 CFR 41.50(b) rejections
description: If the Board makes a new rejection under 37 CFR 41.50(b) and appellant takes no action within two months, the proceedings as to the rejected claims are considered terminated and examiner should proceed per MPEP guidance (e.g., issue form paragraph ¶12.297 indicating period for seeking court review has lapsed and identifying formal matters to correct).
guidance: Examiner should set shortened statutory periods for correction of formal matters (TWO MONTHS in sample ¶12.297) to avoid abandonment; identify allowed claims and outstanding formal matters in communications.

name: Hardware integration
description: Should be tied to specific hardware features.
guidance: Claims that meaningfully interact with or require particular hardware features are more likely to be treated as technical. Examiners look for specific hardware limitations or implementation details rather than purely abstract or generic computing steps.

name: Format-agnostic analysis (substance over form)
description: Substance of the invention is assessed regardless of claim/format wording.
guidance: Examiners must evaluate the underlying technical contribution and not be swayed by clever drafting or presenting an abstract idea as a computer-implemented process. The test is one of substance over form.

name: Assess technical contribution (over claim format)
description: Assessment should emphasize technical contribution rather than the way claims are drafted.
guidance: Examiners must look beyond the literal format of claims and determine whether there is a genuine technical contribution; claim drafting that disguises an abstract idea should not be sufficient.

name: Structured tests for traditionally complex exclusions
description: The 2025 guidelines introduce structured tests for algorithms, business methods, mathematical methods, and computer programs.
guidance: The guidelines aim to provide a systematic approach to evaluate these traditionally difficult areas; practitioners should apply these structured tests when drafting and prosecuting CRI-related claims.

name: Coverage for cutting-edge technologies (AI, blockchain, quantum)
description: Dedicated guidance and sections address AI/ML/DL, blockchain, and quantum computing within CRI examination.
guidance: The guidelines explicitly treat emerging technologies with tailored considerations; applicants working in these fields should align claims and specification to show technical contribution in those technical domains.

name: Strategic consideration — risk of pre-grant opposition
description: Pre-grant opposition can be triggered by competitors during examination, affecting prosecution strategy.
guidance: Because pre-grant opposition is permitted, applicants should plan prosecution and disclosure carefully (e.g., include supporting data early) and be ready to defend inventive step/technical contribution claims during examination.

name: Use of this record in future proceedings (aggravating/rebuttal factor)
description: The Office may consider the record of this disciplinary proceeding, including this Final Order, in any future complaint or evidence of the same or similar misconduct (i) as an aggravating factor in determining discipline and/or (ii) to rebut any statement or representation by Respondent.
guidance: Prior discipline and the written Final Order can be used to aggravate sanctions or to counter claims in subsequent disciplinary matters.

name: Two statutory criteria for a restriction requirement
description: Every restriction requirement has two criteria: the inventions, as claimed, must be independent or distinct; and there would be a serious burden on the examiner if restriction were not required. (MPEP 803, subsection I)
guidance: Both criteria must be satisfied to support a restriction requirement. Cite MPEP 803.

name: Restriction not proper when express admission of obviousness
description: If there is an express admission that the claimed inventions are obvious over each other within the meaning of 35 U.S.C. 103, restriction should not be required. (MPEP section 803)
guidance: Look for statements in the specification or prosecution history that concede obviousness among the claimed inventions.

name: Restriction not proper when claims are not distinct (overlap genus/subgenus/species)
description: When the inventions are not distinct as claimed, restriction is never proper. Example: Claim 1. A transgenic animal comprising SEQ ID No 1. Claim 2. A transgenic rodent comprising SEQ ID No 1. Claim 3. A transgenic mouse comprising SEQ ID No 1. Restriction among claims 1, 2 and 3 is not proper because claims 1, 2 and 3 overlap in scope as genus, subgenus and species claim. (MPEP 806)
guidance: Do not restrict claims that overlap in scope as genus/subgenus/species.

name: What is a genus claim
description: A claim that encompasses two or more disclosed embodiments (species) within its scope is considered to be a generic or genus claim. (MPEP 806.04(d) and 806.04(e))
guidance: Recognize genus claims whether written as a generic claim, a Markush, or as a series of single species claims.

name: Three ways to claim a genus
description: Three ways to claim a genus: (1) as a series of single species claims (e.g., Claim 1: An orange. Claim 2: A lemon); (2) as a Markush claim reading upon plural species (e.g., a citrus fruit selected from the group consisting of an orange or a lemon); (3) encompassed by a linking claim which reads upon but is not necessarily limited to plural species disclosed in the specification (e.g., Claim 4: A citrus fruit).
guidance: Identify which form the genus takes—series, Markush, or linking—because examination/restriction practice differs.

name: Allowable linking claims — consequences
description: When a linking claim is allowable, a restriction requirement between the inventions it links cannot be maintained. The restriction requirement should be withdrawn, even if claims to non-elected linked inventions have been canceled. Any claim(s) depending from or otherwise requiring all the limitations of the allowable linking claim(s) will be rejoined and fully examined for patentability. The Office must provide Applicant with an opportunity to reinstate canceled claims when a restriction requirement is withdrawn based on the allowability of the linking claim. (MPEP 809.03 and 821.04(a))
guidance: If linking claim becomes allowable, withdraw restriction, rejoin dependent claims, and offer opportunity to reinstate canceled claims.

name: Markush claim — definition/overview
description: A Markush claim recites a plurality of alternatively usable substances or members. Alternatives may be 'selected from the group consisting of A, B and C.' The group of alternatives A, B, and C is commonly referred to as a 'Markush group.' (MPEP 803.02)
guidance: Identify Markush groups and members when assessing possible restriction issues.

name: Markush examination sequence when species elected or found unallowable
description: Should the elected species be found allowable, the search/examination of the Markush type claim will be extended to determine the patentability of the claim, including the non-elected species. Should the elected species be found not allowable, the provisional election will be given effect and examination limited to the elected species. If examiner finds art on another species, the examiner does NOT extend search to cover ALL the non-elected species. (MPEP 803.02)
guidance: Understand when to extend examination to other members (if elected species allowable) versus when provisional election limits examination.

name: Markush election canceled species consequence
description: Should the examiner require election of a species recited in a Markush claim, and the elected species is canceled in response to a prior art rejection, such response is considered proper and the examination of the Markush type claim will be extended to the non-elected species to determine the patentability of the claim. The next Office action could be made final if appropriate. (MPEP 803.02 and 821.03)
guidance: If elected species is canceled due to prior art, extend to non-elected species and consider finality rules for the next action.

name: Examination practice contrasts: Markush vs Linking claims (rules and examples)
description: Detailed practice differences between Markush (MPEP 803.02) and Linking claims (MPEP 809) illustrated by examples: e.g., (1) If the species of claim 2 is elected, claim 3 would be withdrawn from consideration; (2) If prior art is found against claim 2, both claims 1 and 2 would be rejected; (3A) For Markush: If claim 2 is allowable, allow claim 2 and extend the search and examination for the species of claim 3; (3B) For Markush: Search/examination is limited to species of the Markush group of claim 1; (4) For Markush: If prior art is found against claim 3, bring claim 3 back into consideration and reject both claims 1 and 3; For Linking: (3) If claim 2 is allowable, allow claim 2 and examiner may extend search and examination for any species encompassed by claim 1; (4A) If prior art is found (a species other than elected), reject claim 1 and examiner is not required to extend search to claim 3; (4B) If prior art found is the species lime, bring claim 3 back into consideration and reject both claims 1 and 3; (5) For both sets: If claim 1 is allowable, then allow claims 1, 2 and 3.
guidance: Follow the specific Markush vs linking rules for withdrawing/withholding claims, extending searches, and effect of prior art; treat linking claims more broadly in allowing extension to other species when appropriate, but do not extend in some linking prior-art scenarios.

name: Claims as the heart and scope of the application
description: The Claims represent the heart of the patent application and define the scope of protection given to an invention; they are usually the first and sometimes the only parts of the patent application actually reviewed by the patent examiner.
guidance: Draft claims carefully because they legally determine protection; anticipate examiner focus and third‑party scrutiny.

name: Prepare draft claims first and iterate
description: Prepare draft claims for the invention as the first step. Write draft claims before preparing the description, drawings, etc., and discuss the draft claims with the inventor early in the drafting process. Review/revise the claims again once the specification has been completed.
guidance: Sketch draft claims during disclosure meetings for immediate inventor feedback; claims drafted early reveal which terms need clear description in the specification.

name: Use a "picture claim" in initial drafts
description: In the initial draft claims, the patent agent may wish to use a “picture” claim which essentially “draws a picture” of the invention in words.
guidance: A picture claim is not typically the broadest claim and does not use highly abstract language, but it is helpful in beginning the process of finding the broadest possible claim and useful in inventor meetings when inventors are unfamiliar with claim language.

name: Claims must be supported by the description and drawings
description: Claims must be supported by the description. The detailed description should breathe life into the claims and provide a sufficient disclosure so that a skilled person could make & understand the invention. If a highly abstract term is used in the claims, the same term should be used in the detailed description.
guidance: Ensure every claim has adequate support in the specification; verify drawings and description after finalizing claim set so claim terms are appropriately described and defined; provide sufficient depth to allow narrowing during prosecution.

name: Include claims of varying scope (broad and narrow)
description: Include both broad and narrow claims; consider claim sets of varying scope rather than only an independent claim followed by narrower dependents.
guidance: Broad claims catch a wider group of infringers, narrow claims are more likely to be valid over unknown prior art — provide the client with both options.

name: Create dependent claims from features removed to achieve breadth
description: Often the patent agent can prepare dependent claims from things removed from draft claims while writing broad claims.
guidance: Be creative when choosing which features to remove for broad independent claims so those features can be recaptured as dependent claims to maximize protection.

name: Claims must define the invention, be clear and concise, and be drafted in technical terms
description: Patent Claims must: define the invention for which protection is being sought, be clear and concise, be supported by the description and drawings, and be drafted in terms of technical features of the invention.
guidance: Avoid vague or non-technical language in claim elements; focus on technical features that will be used to assess novelty/inventive step and infringement.

name: Avoid ambiguous relative adjectives unless relationally defined
description: Watch out for “relative” words like fast, slow, long, short, tall, wide, perfect, complete, thin, strong, flat, etc., unless the relationship lies with another recited element in the claim (e.g., “wherein the first piece is shorter than the second piece”).
guidance: If using relative terms, explicitly define the relationship between claim elements or quantify where possible to avoid ambiguity.

name: Explain field-specific terms and define new terms
description: If you use a word established in a given technical field, make sure you understand what the word means and doesn’t mean. Explain the word’s meaning in the description if necessary. If you use a new word in the claims, then make sure that you clearly establish its meaning in the description.
guidance: Do not assume uniform understanding across jurisdictions; explicitly define novel terms to avoid indefiniteness or misinterpretation.

name: Avoid negative limitations; prefer positive phrasing
description: Avoid negative limitations in claims (e.g., “a tire that is not solid”); state limitations in positive terms (e.g., “a hollow tire”) unless the limitation cannot be phrased in any other manner (e.g., “a non-black color”).
guidance: Positive limitations are clearer and easier to enforce; use negatives only when unavoidable and supported by the description.

name: Ensure consistency and adequate support of claim language in the specification
description: Make sure every claim has adequate support in the specification; words and terminology should be consistent. You don’t need to define terms already known in the industry if using them consistent with industry practice.
guidance: Cross-check each claim element against the detailed description and drawings; inconsistent terminology can create vulnerabilities to invalidity or enablement objections.

name: Anticipate competitors and potential workarounds; draft alternative embodiments
description: Think about variations or other embodiments of the invention; think like a potential competitor trying to avoid the patent; assume the competitor has prior art that can knock out your broadest claim; incorporate alternative embodiments into the description and claim them to broaden protection.
guidance: Include fallback embodiments in the specification and claim a range of alternatives so competitors cannot easily design around the patent.

name: Avoid unnecessary limitations; file broadest patentable independent claim
description: Delete all unnecessary limitations before filing claims. File only the limitations or essential technical features necessary to recite the invention in its broadest patentable form in the broadest independent claim.
guidance: Trim superfluous detail from independent claims to preserve breadth; reserve non-essential features for dependent claims.

name: Balance claiming breadth with overcoming prior art and validity
description: Claims should, if possible, cover competing products but must overcome the prior art. Be aware of related prior art; do not file claims that you know to be invalid. Ideally draft a claim narrower than prior art but broader than competing (non‑prior‑art) products.
guidance: Search and analyze prior art before choosing claim scope; tailor claims to maximize enforceability while covering competitors.

name: Use multiple claim categories (device/method/uses) judiciously
description: Use multiple claim categories for the same invention to get the broadest possible protection — some competitors will infringe device claims but not method claims and vice versa. Don’t include every type of claim just for inclusiveness — use your judgment.
guidance: Draft claims in different statutory categories where appropriate (e.g., apparatus, method, use) but avoid unnecessary or unsupported claim types that complicate prosecution.

name: Consider who the infringer will be when drafting claims
description: Always think about who is the infringer — DON’T MAKE YOUR CUSTOMER THE ONLY POSSIBLE INFRINGER.
guidance: Draft claims to capture likely infringers (manufacturers, sellers, users) rather than only end customers, to improve enforceability.

name: Narrowing during prosecution must be supported by the original description and done with minimal harm
description: To narrow a patent claim during prosecution, add new elements to the claims and/or add new limitations to existing elements. All new additions must be supported by the description as filed. Consider all relevant options when amending a claim and do the least harm possible. The client should understand the implications of any claim amendments.
guidance: When planning possible amendments, ensure fallback language exists in the original filing; discuss prosecution strategy and tradeoffs with the client.

name: Include at least one claim that reads on the client’s actual activities/products
description: At least one claim in the application should read on what the client is actually doing. Defending the client’s products against infringement may be difficult otherwise; patent marking is also difficult.
guidance: Ensure practical enforceability by including claim language that covers the client’s real-world product(s) or methods so they can rely on the patent.

name: Draft claims early to identify specification requirements and define terms
description: When the claims are prepared before drafting the specification, the patent agent knows precisely which terms need to be described clearly in the description.
guidance: Use early claim drafts to guide the detailed description and drawings; this reduces the risk of missing support for claim terms and facilitates later amendments.

name: Treatment of Claims Retained under 37 CFR 1.142 and 1.146
description: Claims retained under 37 CFR 1.142 and claims retained under 37 CFR 1.146 should be treated as set out in MPEP § 821 to § 821.04(b).
guidance: Follow the MPEP sections referenced for handling retained claims; consult MPEP § 821 et seq. for specifics.

name: Drafting Claims for Pro Se (Inventor-Filed) Applications
description: When, during the examination of a pro se application it becomes apparent to the examiner that there is patentable subject matter disclosed in the application, the examiner should draft one or more claims for the applicant and indicate in his or her action that such claims would be allowed if incorporated in the application by amendment.
guidance: This practice expedites prosecution and aids individual inventors not represented by counsel; it should be applied when it is apparent the applicant is unfamiliar with proper preparation and prosecution of patent applications.

name: Constructive Office Actions — Allowable Except As To Form
description: When the application discloses patentable subject matter and it is apparent that the claims are intended to be directed to such subject matter, but claims in present form cannot be allowed because of defects in form or omission of a limitation, the examiner should not stop with a bare objection or rejection. The examiner’s action should be constructive in nature and, when possible, should offer a definite suggestion for correction.
guidance: Offer concrete suggestions for correction; note unclaimed aspects or features that if claimed may be favorably considered; suggest interviews when appropriate to accelerate agreement on allowable claims.

name: Dependent Claims Dependent on Cancelled or Rejected Claims
description: If a claim is otherwise allowable but is dependent on a canceled claim or on a rejected claim, the Office action should state that the claim would be allowable if rewritten in independent form.
guidance: Explicitly state the allowability contingent on rewriting dependent claims in independent form to include all necessary limitations.

name: Objection to Claims — Allowable Subject Matter (¶7.43)
description: Claim [1] objected to as being dependent upon a rejected base claim, but would be allowable if rewritten in independent form including all of the limitations of the base claim and any intervening claims.
guidance: Use this objection language to advise applicant how to rewrite dependent claims into allowable independent form.

name: Reconsideration on Allowance of Elected Combination
description: Upon determining that all claims directed to an elected combination invention are allowable, the examiner must reconsider the propriety of the restriction requirement and, where the combination is allowable in view of the patentability of at least one subcombination, withdraw the restriction requirement between the elected combination and patentable subcombination(s).
guidance: If withdrawn, any subcombinations that were searched and determined to be allowable must be rejoined. If a subcombination is elected and determined allowable, nonelected claims requiring all the limitations of the allowable claim will be rejoined in accordance with MPEP § 821.04. Use form paragraph 8.21 (and form paragraph 8.21.04 where applicable) to conclude restriction requirements and to notify applicant about potential rejoinder.

name: Distinctness of Subcombinations Usable Together
description: Subcombinations disclosed as usable together in a single combination are distinct if they do not overlap in scope, are not obvious variants, and at least one subcombination is separately usable.
guidance: Examiner must show, by way of example, that one of the subcombinations has utility other than in the disclosed combination. Use form paragraph 8.16 to make restriction requirements between subcombinations and conclude with form paragraph 8.21. Applicant is advised that claims in continuations/divisionals anticipated by or including all limitations of an allowable claim may be subject to double patenting rejections.

name: Process and Apparatus Distinctness Test
description: A claimed process and an apparatus for its practice are distinct if either (A) the process as claimed can be practiced by another materially different apparatus or by hand, or (B) the apparatus as claimed can be used to practice another materially different process.
guidance: Form paragraph 8.17 may be used for restriction between process and apparatus. Examiner should provide reasonable examples that recite material differences (example need not be documented). If applicant proves or convincingly argues there is no material difference or that the process cannot be performed by hand, the burden shifts to the examiner to document another materially different process or apparatus or withdraw the requirement. Conclude with form paragraph 8.21; follow with form paragraph 8.21.04 when applicable to notify about potential rejoinder.

name: Product and Process of Using Distinctness Test
description: A product and a process of using the product are distinct if (A) the process of using as claimed can be practiced with another materially different product; or (B) the product as claimed can be used in a materially different process.
guidance: Examiner must provide an example (not required to be documented). If applicant convincingly argues the suggested alternative use cannot be accomplished, the burden is on the examiner to support another viable alternative or withdraw the requirement. Use form paragraphs 8.20 and 8.21.04 in restriction requirements between product and method of using.

name: Related Products/Processes Distinctness Criteria
description: For related product or related process inventions, inventions are distinct only if (A) the inventions as claimed do not overlap in scope (mutually exclusive), (B) the inventions as claimed are not obvious variants, and (C) the inventions are either not capable of use together or can have a materially different design, mode of operation, function, or effect.
guidance: The burden is on the examiner to provide an example to support distinctness (example need not be documented). If applicant proves the examiner's example is not workable, the examiner must suggest another viable example or withdraw the restriction. See MPEP § 806.05(j) and form paragraph 8.14.01 for restriction between related products/processes.

name: Species Independence and Election Practice
description: Where there is no disclosure of a relationship between species, they are independent and restriction may be permissible if patentable differences exist and there would be a serious burden on the examiner. If a disclosed relationship exists, the disclosed relation must be discussed and reasons advanced that it does not prevent restriction.
guidance: Applicant must elect a single disclosed species under 35 U.S.C. 121 when restriction is required, even if applicant disagrees. Election should not be required between species that are clearly unpatentable over each other; examiner should group clearly unpatentable species together. Election may be required prior to a search in applications with multiple species and no generic claims, or with both species and generic/Markush claims. Use MPEP §§ 803, 809, 821.04 for further guidance.

name: Linking Claims and Their Effect on Restriction
description: Linking claims (e.g., genus claims linking species or subcombination claims linking plural combinations) if allowable, act to prevent restriction between otherwise divisible inventions by requiring rejoinder of the linked inventions.
guidance: Linking claims and inventions they link are usually all products or all processes. Linking claims must be examined with the elected invention and are considered part of the elected invention. When all claims directed to the elected invention are allowable and a linking claim is allowable, the restriction must be withdrawn and previously withdrawn nonelected claims that depend from or require all limitations of the allowable linking claim must be rejoined and fully examined. If previously withdrawn claims were canceled by applicant, they may be reinstated by amendment upon allowance of linking claim(s). See MPEP § 821.04 for rejoinder practice.

name: Notice of Potential Rejoinder of Process Claims (8.21.04)
description: When restriction is required between product/apparatus and process claims, the examiner must notify applicant that if product/apparatus claims are found allowable, withdrawn process claims that include all limitations of the allowable product/apparatus claim should be considered for rejoinder.
guidance: Rejoined process claims will be fully examined for patentability (35 U.S.C. 101, 102, 103, 112). Withdrawn process claims not commensurate in scope with an allowable product/apparatus claim will not be rejoined. Applicant is advised to amend process claims during prosecution to require the limitations of product/apparatus claims to facilitate rejoinder; failure to do so may result in no rejoinder. Note prohibition against double patenting rejections of 35 U.S.C. 121 does not apply where restriction is withdrawn before patent issues. Use form paragraph 8.21.04 at the end of restriction requirements between process and product/apparatus or product and process of using.

name: Election of Species Procedure and Required Contents of Reply
description: When election of species is required, the examiner should identify generic claims (or lack thereof), clearly identify disclosed species (preferably by figures/examples or distinguishing characteristics), provide reasons why species are independent or distinct, and require applicant to elect a single disclosed species under 35 U.S.C. 121.
guidance: A complete reply should include a proper election along with a listing of all claims readable on the elected species, including any claims subsequently added. In cases where restriction accompanies action on elected claims, that action will be considered an action on the merits and the next action may be made final where appropriate. For treatment of nonelected claims see MPEP § 821 et seq. Use form paragraph 8.01 (Election of Species; Species Claim(s) Present) with bracket fields for species and reasons.

name: Evidentiary burden for substitute claims (Aqua Products)
description: Allocation of burden of persuasion on patentability of substitute claims presented in a motion to amend.
guidance: Per Aqua Products (en banc), the PTO has not adopted a rule placing the burden of persuasion on the patent owner; absent such a rule, the burden ordinarily lies with the petitioner to show proposed substitute claims are unpatentable by a preponderance of the evidence. The Board may also justify findings by reference to the record; ultimately the Board determines patentability based on the entire record, including petitioner opposition and any cessation of participation.

name: Contents required in a motion to amend (37 C.F.R. §§ 42.121(b), 42.221(b))
description: Regulatory content requirements for any motion to amend.
guidance: Motion must include a claim listing (appendix allowed), clearly show changes being sought, and describe how the original disclosure (and any relied-upon application) supports each added/amended claim. Must identify proposed substitute claim(s) and the original claim they replace, with all changes clearly identified and discussed. Patent owners may not enlarge claim scope or add new matter (35 U.S.C. §§ 316(d)(3), 326(d)(3)).

name: Claim construction standard for substitute claims
description: Standard the Board will use to interpret claims, including substitute claims, for AIA petitions filed on/after Nov 13, 2018.
guidance: The Board will interpret claims using the same standard that would be used in a civil action under 35 U.S.C. § 282(b) (37 C.F.R. § 42.100(b); Final Rule). Patent owner may request a determination that an amended claim is 'substantially identical' to the original claim within the meaning of 35 U.S.C. § 252 and provide supporting arguments and evidence.

name: Identification of added features and constructions in substitute claims
description: Patent owners should identify features added to each substitute claim and any proposed constructions for new claim terms.
guidance: Although not required, patent owners may provide arguments regarding patentability of substitute claims and may support them with expert testimony explaining what would have been known to a person of ordinary skill and the significance of added features.

name: General practice tips on amendments (support, timeliness, clarity)
description: Practical expectations for motions to amend to increase the likelihood of grant.
guidance: File motions to amend by due dates set for patent owner response, though motions to cancel claims and correcting simple typographical errors may be permitted late. Amendments should clearly state where specification and drawings support all limitations in proposed substitute claims; if the Board cannot determine support, the motion may be denied. Motions must respond to a ground of unpatentability but may include other modifications (e.g., §101 or §112).

name: Independent versus dependent claims (definition and determination)
description: An independent claim is a claim that does not depend from any other previous claim; a dependent claim depends from another claim when it makes an explicit reference to that claim and its scope is a subset of the base claim.
guidance: Whether a claim is dependent from another depends on both the claimed subject matters and whether a reference is made from one claim to another. Examples: Claim 1 independent; Claim 2 dependent from Claim 1; Claim 3 dependent from Claim 2 (and, logically, also dependent from Claim 1 because its scope is a subset).

name: Dependency pyramid risk and fallback position planning
description: Avoid creating a dependency pyramid where many dependent claims all ultimately depend only from a single broad independent claim (the pyramid vertex), because this gives poor fallback positions if the independent claim is invalidated.
guidance: When EPO-style multiple dependencies are converted improperly (e.g., changed to all depend on Claim 1), a dependency pyramid may be created — not generally recommended. Plan dependent claims as fallback positions in case independent claim lacks novelty or inventive step.

name: Drafting independent claim to state essential elements
description: The independent claim should state the essential elements of the invention — the elements necessary to achieve the technical effect underlying the solution of the technical problem — and these elements should be explicitly described in the description.
guidance: Include all essential elements required for essential functionality. To achieve broad protection, stretch essential elements to their greatest reasonable extent, taking into account essential functionality and prior art. Do not draft as a 'mere desideratum' (state result without saying how achieved). For product claims, define the elements/technical features that give rise to an effect, not the effect itself.

name: Use dependent claims as fallback positions
description: Draft dependent claims to cover more particular embodiments and to act as fallback positions should the independent claim be found not novel or lack inventive step.
guidance: Identify order of importance of elements during brainstorming and draft dependent claims accordingly. In general, draft one dependent claim per selected/added element. Dependent claims can add selected values or further characterize elements. Consider business and enforcement strategy when ordering dependent claims.

name: Multiple dependent versus singular dependent forms (jurisdictional practice)
description: Multiple dependent claims (claims that depend from multiple preceding claims) are permitted in some jurisdictions (e.g., EPO) but are not allowed at the USPTO; choose appropriate dependency forms for the target office.
guidance: Write multiple dependent form for EPO when adding extra elements is desirable. Before entering the US national phase, deconstruct multiple dependencies into singular dependencies by preparing chains with broadest, narrowest and intermediate meanings. Consider claim count limits/fees (EPO allows fewer free claims than some offices; USPTO has limits and amendment/added-matter issues).

name: Converting EPO multiple dependencies to USPTO-style claims
description: When adapting claims drafted in EPO style (including multiple dependencies) to USPTO practice, prepare singular dependency chains representing broadest and narrowest meanings and possibly intermediate claims to stay within practical claim counts.
guidance: Prepare (i) dependency chains with broadest meanings of elements, (ii) chains with narrowest meanings, and (iii) intermediate claims if needed. Aim to keep total claims reasonably limited (ideally no more than ~20 to avoid extra fees). Provide clear instructions if drafting is transferred to another drafter to avoid accidental creation of a dependency pyramid.

name: Markush groups and alternative elements
description: Use Markush groups to claim an element as being selected from a group of alternatives (e.g., 'element D being D1, D2 or D3') to capture alternatives within claims.
guidance: Markush groups can broaden claim scope and allow later dependent claims to pick specific alternatives (e.g., Claims 4–6 selecting D1, D2, D3). A dependent claim that adds an element selected from a group can only depend on preceding claims that provide antecedent basis for that element.

name: Choosing claim format (standard format vs two-part format)
description: Decide whether to draft the independent claim in standard (single-part) or two-part format; EPO examiners may request two-part format where distinguishing from prior art is desirable.
guidance: Two-part format separates known features (preamble) from the characterizing portion. Example: where prior art discloses 'a writing device having A11 and B11', two-part format could read 'A writing device comprising: element A; and element B; characterized by further comprising element C...'. Choose format with awareness of prior art and office practice.

name: Preamble with purposive 'for' expression (functional limitation caution)
description: Claims that include a preamble with a purposive expression (e.g., 'An apparatus for carrying out the process ...') may be construed in many jurisdictions as covering an apparatus merely suitable for that purpose, which can affect novelty and infringement scope.
guidance: Be cautious using 'for' wording — it can imply suitability rather than a functional limitation. e.g., an apparatus claimed 'for molten steel' may exclude items unsuitable for molten steel. Distinguish cases where the purpose is a true functional feature of a method claim versus where it denotes mere suitability.

name: Novelty assessment using dependency analysis
description: Assess novelty by comparing claim scopes (starting with the independent claim) against prior art; novelty of an independent claim implies novelty of dependent claims in that chain with respect to that prior art reference.
guidance: If a prior art reference falls outside the independent claim, then by definition it falls outside all dependent claims in that chain (simplifying validity assessment). Be careful not to assume that invalidity of an independent claim necessarily implies invalidity of all dependent claims (a common nonexpert mistake). Also novel does not equal valid — inventive step must also be considered.

name: Literal infringement assessment using dependency analysis
description: Determine literal infringement by comparing the accused embodiment with claim scopes; if the accused embodiment falls inside the scope of a dependent claim, it may also fall within the scope of its base claims, but infringement conclusions must be drawn carefully by chain.
guidance: A finding that the accused embodiment falls outside an independent claim simplifies infringement assessment (none in that dependency chain will be infringed). Conversely, if it falls within a dependent claim, the dependent's base claim elements may also be present — but do not assume infringement of an independent claim implies infringement of all dependents nor vice versa.

name: Draft concisely: remove unnecessary words while preserving essence
description: Once the essence of the invention is captured, review claims to remove as many words as possible while still preserving the invention's essence, involving inventors as needed.
guidance: Professional tip: re-review claims for unnecessary adjectives/words (e.g., 'pivotal' in a mounting may be unnecessary). Concision can broaden scope and reduce inadvertent limitations.

name: Product (apparatus) claim drafting principles
description: When drafting a product/apparatus claim, prepare a preamble reciting what the apparatus is (and sometimes what it does) and list essential elements required for the invention to function in its basic form.
guidance: In general, infringement of a product claim occurs when third parties make, use, offer for sale, sell or import the product. Ensure essential components that confer novelty are captured in the claim body.

name: Process (method) claim drafting principles
description: A process claim should list the series of steps performed; in many jurisdictions steps are presumed to occur in any order unless the claim specifies order.
guidance: Be explicit about ordering when order matters. For infringement, unauthorized use of claimed process infringes; products directly obtained by a claimed process may also be encompassed (depending on jurisdiction). Consider whether steps like adding milk/sugar are essential to the claimed invention or removable to broaden scope.

name: Product-by-process claims: limits and evidentiary burden
description: Product-by-process claims (product defined by its process of manufacture) are allowable in some jurisdictions but the claimed product still must satisfy novelty and inventive step; the applicant bears the burden to show that the product so obtained is different if challenged.
guidance: Some offices (EPO) treat the claim as a claim to the product as such and extend protection to products directly obtained; in Japan product-by-process claims may be considered indefinite and used only in special circumstances. Provide evidence that process parameters produce a different product when relying on such claims.

name: Parameter claims (claims defined by measurable values)
description: Claims may define inventions by characteristic measurable parameters (e.g., melting point, viscosity) where the invention cannot otherwise be defined without undue restriction and where the result is directly verifiable by tests specified in the description.
guidance: Ensure the specification includes adequate directions to enable verification by routine tests. Parameter claims are useful when structural definition is impracticable but must be supported by the description so the skilled person can determine values without undue experimentation.

name: Antecedent basis for dependent claims
description: A dependent claim that adds an element selected from a group or further characterizes an element can depend only from preceding claims that provide an antecedent for that element; a dependent claim adding an extra element (not a selection) does not need antecedent and can depend from any preceding claim.
guidance: When drafting dependent claims, ensure antecedent basis is proper (the element referenced must have been introduced earlier). For selected elements (e.g., a value chosen from a Markush group), dependency must be to claims that provide that antecedent.

name: BitTorrent-related subject-matter eligibility
description: BitTorrent, if claimed as a standalone subject matter, shall fall under unpatentable rules and methods of intellectual activities.
guidance: However, in digital video-coding/decoding fields, if a specific method for generating BitTorrent is claimed as the technical solution, and the method for storing or transmitting and the computer-readable storage medium for storing the said BitTorrent achieve optimized configuration of storage or transmission resources, then such storage/transmission methods and computer-readable storage media are patentable. Key: tie BitTorrent-related claims to technical solutions that optimize resources.

name: Contextual Examination of Claim Amendments (no absolute bar)
description: Claim amendments must be examined in context of the prosecution history and do not necessarily bar assertions under the Doctrine of Equivalents due to prosecution history estoppel.
guidance: Do not apply an automatic/absolute bar to all amendments. Instead determine the extent to which the amendment surrendered coverage by looking at the reason for the change and the prosecution record.

name: Presumption of Surrender for Narrowing Amendments
description: When a patentee narrows claims through amendment in order to comply with the Patent Act, there is a presumption that the patentee surrendered the territory between the original claim and the amended claim (i.e., surrendered all equivalents for the narrowed limitation).
guidance: This presumption places the burden on the patentee/applicant to show which equivalents were not surrendered. In practice, once a narrowing amendment for statutory compliance is identified, courts presume surrender of equivalents for that limitation unless the patentee rebuts the presumption.

name: Reason for Amendment Controls Estoppel Effect
description: Whether an amendment surrenders equivalents depends on why the amendment was made (e.g., to clarify a translation versus to avoid overlapping another patent).
guidance: If the change was made to clarify a translation, the inventor should suffer no reduction in rights; if the change was made to keep the patent from overlapping with another patent, the applicant will be presumed to have given up the right to claim equivalents broader than the amended claim. Focus factual inquiry on the prosecution record and stated reasons for amendment.

name: Relation to 35 U.S.C. §112 and Other Statutory Compliance Amendments
description: Amendments made for compliance with statutory requirements (for example, claim structure under 35 U.S.C. §112) can give rise to estoppel depending on the nature and reason for the amendment.
guidance: Do not assume that amendments labeled as for §112 compliance are harmless; courts will examine the actual reason and effect of the amendment. Document and explain reasons for amendments during prosecution when possible to preserve arguments about equivalents.

name: Petition content and particularity (§311(a), §312(a)(3))
description: A petition to institute an inter partes review must identify each claim challenged and the grounds for challenge with particularity; the petition 'may request to cancel as unpatentable 1 or more claims of the patent' (grounds include lack of novelty or obviousness under §§102 and 103).
guidance: Petition is the centerpiece of the proceeding: it should enumerate each claim challenged, the specific grounds for each claim, and supporting evidence. The Court emphasizes that the petition, not the Director, defines the proceeding’s contours. (See §§311(a), 312(a)(3).)

name: Director’s institution threshold (§314(a))
description: Before instituting IPR, the Director must determine 'there is a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail with respect to at least 1 of the claims challenged in the petition.'
guidance: This is a threshold screening standard: a reasonable likelihood of prevailing on at least one challenged claim justifies institution. The Court reads this as consistent with allowing institution based on prospect of success on a single claim, not necessarily requiring assessment of every claim at the screening stage.

name: Scope of final written decision (§318(a))
description: If an inter partes review is instituted and not dismissed, the Board 'shall issue a final written decision with respect to the patentability of any patent claim challenged by the petitioner.'
guidance: The Court reads 'shall' as mandatory and 'any' as expansive (i.e., 'any' in this context means every claim challenged by the petitioner), concluding the Board must address the patentability of all claims the petitioner challenged when IPR is instituted.

name: No statutory basis for 'partial institution' power
description: The Patent Office's asserted power of 'partial institution' (per 37 C.F.R. §42.108(a) authorizing review 'on all or some of the challenged claims') is not found in the statutory text and cannot be inferred when §318(a) requires the Board to decide 'any patent claim challenged by the petitioner.'
guidance: Agency regulations claiming a power to institute review on only some challenged claims conflict with the Court's textual reading; policy or efficiency arguments for partial institution should be directed to Congress, not invoked to override clear statutory commands.

name: Petitioner, not Director, defines proceeding contours
description: Congress structured IPR so that the petitioner defines the proceeding’s contours: the petition identifies the claims and grounds; various provisions (e.g., §312(a)(3), §316(a)(8)) treat the petition as central.
guidance: Practically, filings, preliminary responses, and further proceedings should be aligned to the petitioned claims and grounds; departures from the petition’s scope are disfavored absent statutory text authorizing them.

name: Limitations on judicial review (§314(d) and Cuozzo) and APA remedies
description: Section 314(d) states that the Director’s determination whether to institute 'shall be final and nonappealable'; Cuozzo held §314(d) precludes review of the Director’s initial determination under §314(a) (reasonable likelihood), but it does not permit agency action 'outside its statutory limits'—judicial review under the Administrative Procedure Act remains available for actions 'not in accordance with law' or 'in excess of statutory jurisdiction, authority, or limitations' (5 U.S.C. §§706(2)(A),(C)).
guidance: Challenges that merely question the adequacy of the petition are typically precluded from review, but claims that the agency exceeded statutory bounds (e.g., instituting partial institution contrary to §318(a)) remain reviewable under APA standards.

name: Chevron deference threshold for agency interpretations
description: An agency’s interpretation (including a claimed power) is not owed deference under Chevron unless the statute is ambiguous after employing 'traditional tools of statutory construction'; if the statute is clear, there is no Chevron deference.
guidance: When evaluating agency rules or interpretations (e.g., partial institution regulation), first apply textual and contextual statutory interpretation; only if ambiguity remains consider deference and reasonableness of the agency’s interpretation.

name: Agency rulemaking authority may fill gaps but cannot override clear statutory text (§316(a)(2),(4))
