description: Congress authorized the agency to issue regulations 'setting forth the standards for the showing of sufficient grounds to institute a review' and 'establishing and governing inter partes review' (§316(a)(2),(4)), but regulations cannot create powers not supported by the statute’s text.
guidance: Regulatory gap-filling is appropriate where the statute is ambiguous and Congress granted rulemaking, but agency rules that conflict with clear statutory mandates (e.g., a regulation authorizing partial institution when §318(a) is read to require decisions on all challenged claims) are invalid.

name: Joint research agreement (JRA) definition and timing for CREATE Act disqualification
description: A joint research agreement for purposes of pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c)(3) is a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement entered into by two or more persons or entities for performance of experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention that was in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made.
guidance: The JRA must be shown to be in effect on or before the time the later invention was made; it need not be in effect on or before the prior art date of the reference to be disqualified. The JRA may be in effect prior to the CREATE Act effective date. Examples show JRAs that are effective (or not) for disqualification depending on timing and scope of activities.

name: Requirements to invoke CREATE Act / JRA‑based disqualification
description: To invoke disqualification under the CREATE Act (pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) as amended), the applicant/patent owner must provide a statement that the subject matter and the claimed invention were made by or on behalf of the parties to a JRA (within the meaning of 35 U.S.C. 100(h) and § 1.9(e)), that the JRA was in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made, and that the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the JRA.
guidance: Additionally, the application must disclose or be amended to disclose the names of the parties to the JRA. The statement should be on or begin on a separate sheet, must not address other matters (37 CFR 1.4(c)), and must be signed per 37 CFR 1.33(b). Applicants may submit supporting evidence but are not required to do so. See 37 CFR 1.71(g) and 1.104(c)(4) for form and processing requirements.

name: Provisional rejection (obviousness) using provisional prior art under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e)
description: When two copending applications of different inventive entities are unpublished under 35 U.S.C. 122(b) and have differing filing dates, a provisional rejection under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) based on provisional prior art under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) should be made in the later‑filed application unless the application has been excluded under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c).
guidance: Purpose: to alert the applicant that an actual rejection on the same ground may issue if one application issues, and to preserve confidentiality. Provisional rejections of obviousness type can be applied to copending applications having different effective filing dates with common assignee or common inventor. Ways to overcome include: (A) arguing patentability over the earlier filed application; (B) combining subject matter into a single application claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 and abandoning copending applications (with caution re: 35 U.S.C. 112/enablement/priority); (C) filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 showing derivation (not invention “by another”); (D) filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(a) showing an earlier date of invention prior to the effective U.S. filing date of the copending application.

name: Statute of limitations for trademark damages (Argentina)
description: If compensation of damages is claimed, there is a term of three (3) years to bring the case since the infringement or one (1) year from the day the owner had knowledge of the fact.

name: Markush claims and written description scrutiny (Brazil)
description: Markush claims are allowed but subject to scrutiny whether the application complies with written description/enablement and whether claims are fully supported by the description.

name: Claim clarity and drafting requirements (Brazil)
description: Claims must be based on the specification, characterize particularities, and define clearly and precisely the subject matter to be protected. Each claim must define technical characteristics in a clear, precise and positive manner, avoiding expressions that result in lack of definition.
guidance: Brazilian PTO guidelines: (i) claims should begin with the title or part of the title corresponding to its category, containing 'characterized by' only once; (ii) define characteristics clearly and positively; (iii) be fully grounded in the specification; (iv) avoid references to specification/drawings (e.g., 'as set forth in the specification'); (v) when drawings used, include reference indicators in brackets if necessary (but indicators impose no constraints on claims); (vi) no bullet point interruptions; (vii) have no segments explaining functioning, advantages or simple use of the object, as these will not be accepted.

name: Patent application formalities and required items (Brazil)
description: Application must include title, one or more claims, petition with applicant/inventor details, specification, abstract, drawings if necessary, power of attorney, payment of fees, certified copy of priority application, genetic resource access number if applicable, and number of biological deposit certificate if applicable (this information must be included in the specification).
guidance: Third parties may file documents/arguments to assist examination until end of examination; post-grant opposition available within six months from grant.

name: Provisos to exclude prior art
description: A proviso is an exclusionary limitation introduced to a claim to exclude some specified matter (e.g. 'provided said attachment means is not a rubber-based adhesive'). A proviso based on prior art may be introduced to establish novelty.
guidance: A proviso should not introduce new matter (must comply with subsection 38.2 of the Patent Act). When introduced as an amendment, a proviso excluding a feature not necessarily present in the original claim should be carefully considered because the excluded feature is presumably not required for proper operation. A proviso can render a claim patentable where a broad claim would be novel/inventive if not for an isolated earlier disclosure. Multiple provisos require greater scrutiny to ensure remaining subject-matter is a single invention and the nature of the original invention is not obscured (e.g., defining what the invention is not).

name: Utility requirement (section 2 of the Patent Act)
description: An invention must be useful: it must be capable of an actual relevant use and not be fanciful, speculative, or inoperable. The usefulness must be related to the nature of the subject-matter as identified by claim construction.
guidance: The Patent Act does not prescribe the degree of usefulness required; a single use related to the subject-matter suffices and the threshold is low ('a scintilla of utility will do'). Except where utility is the essence of the invention, the applicant need not expressly state the utility in the application, but if questioned, utility must have been demonstrated or soundly predicted as of the filing date. A claim must define the inventive element(s) necessary to enable proper operation; features understood by a person skilled in the art as implicit need not be explicit.

name: Three components of a sound prediction
description: A sound prediction analysis requires: (1) a factual basis for the prediction; (2) an articulable and 'sound' line of reasoning from which the desired result can be inferred from the factual basis; and (3) proper disclosure.
guidance: The factual basis generally comprises facts in the description and drawings, relevant scientific principles, and common general knowledge. The line of reasoning bridges the factual basis to the purported utility and must be understandable by a person skilled in the art. Proper disclosure requires that the description provide sufficient information such that a skilled person, in light of CGK, would understand the basis of the prediction and be able to predict the entire claimed scope would work when reduced to practice. The relevant date for soundness is the filing date; sound prediction is not a certainty but must be more than speculation.

name: Factual basis specifics for sound prediction
description: The factual basis may include experimental data but does not necessarily require it; it can be scientifically accepted laws/principles, data from the state of the art, or CGK.
guidance: Simple unsubstantiated statements or prophetic examples are not factual. Sufficiency of factual basis depends on claim scope, state of the art, nature of invention, predictability, and how extensively the applicant explored the claimed area.

name: Proper disclosure requirement for sound prediction
description: The description must disclose the factual basis and the sound line of reasoning sufficiently so that the skilled person could understand the basis of the prediction and predict that the entire scope of the claim would work.
guidance: Disclosure must be present in the original description; evidence generated after filing cannot be used to supply the disclosure for sound prediction. Elements of the factual basis or reasoning that are CGK need not be repeated, but if the prediction relies on non-public information it must be included in the original description. The disclosure requirement for sound prediction is distinct from the sufficiency requirement under subsection 27(3).

name: Examples illustrating demonstration vs sound prediction
description: Practical examples demonstrate application of the rules: (1) where a specific polymer (calcium alginate) was demonstrated to work, and common general knowledge supported extrapolation to other polymers with the same structural features, a sound prediction supported a broader claim; (2) where only one specific gene mutation was shown to confer herbicide resistance and no basis existed to predict all domain mutations would do so, the broader claim failed utility for lack of sound prediction.
guidance: Use examples to assess whether factual basis, line of reasoning and disclosure exist across full claim scope. These examples illustrate when demonstration suffices and when sound prediction is required (and when it fails).

name: Provisos affecting utility (reassessment required)
description: Where a proviso has been presented to avoid inoperative subject-matter, the basis upon which the utility of the remaining matter of the claim has been established must be reconsidered.
guidance: Since utility is often based on a sound prediction, excluding a known inoperative embodiment requires reassessing whether the line of reasoning that underpinned the utility still holds for the remaining claim scope.

name: Centrality of claim construction
description: Claim construction is the first step of the two-step process for proving patent infringement; the claims of a patent legally define the right to exclude others and proper interpretation is a fundamental stage of litigation.
guidance: Claim construction lays the groundwork for subsequent case development and controls case themes presented to the court and jury. Use claim construction to determine both infringement and validity issues.

name: Primacy of intrinsic evidence
description: Proper claim construction requires review of the intrinsic evidence – i.e., the claims, specification, and prosecution history – and, if appropriate, extrinsic evidence. (Phillips v. AWH Corp., 415 F.3d 1303.)
guidance: The analysis starts with the plain claim language and the specification 'is always highly relevant.' The court must ensure the claims cover what was actually invented and what the inventor intended to claim. If the inventor has acted as his own lexicographer or there is an intentional disclaimer, that dictates claim scope.

name: Role of prosecution history
description: The prosecution history 'can often inform the meaning of the claim language by demonstrating how the inventor understood the invention and whether the inventor limited the invention in the course of prosecution.'
guidance: Prosecution history can show that the inventor narrowed claim scope. It may lack the clarity of the specification but still be informative; include relevant prosecution history in briefing to demonstrate disclaimers or limitations.

name: Appellate review standards for claim construction
description: Different standards of review apply: when a district court relies only on intrinsic evidence, claim construction is reviewed de novo; when the court makes subsidiary factual findings based on extrinsic evidence, those findings are reviewed for clear error.
guidance: Cite Teva Pharms. USA, Inc. v. Sandoz, Inc., 135 S. Ct. 831 (2015) and subsequent cases. Structure your record accordingly if relying on extrinsic evidence to avoid reversible error on appeal.

name: Meaning according to a person of ordinary skill in the art
description: The court must determine the meaning the claims would have to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention; claims are generally given their 'ordinary and customary meaning' as understood by that person.
guidance: Define and support the definition of the person of ordinary skill in briefing. Declarations from technical experts are particularly useful to opine on the level of skill and how terms would be understood.

name: Timing and scheduling strategy for Markman
description: Claim construction procedures and scheduling are court- and judge-specific; a court may perform a Markman hearing at any time before charging the jury, construe claims piecemeal, or revisit earlier constructions.
guidance: Some jurisdictions require early Markman hearings while fact discovery is beginning (to streamline cases); others provide more flexibility. Consider pros and cons: early construction can focus issues and reduce costs or increase discovery if construction is broad; late construction allows fuller factual development but may raise costs and expert issues.

name: Venue/local rule considerations
description: Local patent rules vary (e.g., D. N.J., N.D. Cal., N.D. Ill., E.D. Tex., S.D.N.Y.) and may set regimented procedures, timing, term-identification requirements, and limits on claim terms and prior art references.
guidance: Evaluate the claim construction timing and procedures of potential venues when filing or opposing transfer. Be aware some courts require identification of most significant terms and reduction of asserted claims or prior art as part of the process.

name: Determine whether claim construction is necessary
description: Parties should determine if claim construction is even necessary; if claims are drafted in straightforward language, the parties may stipulate that claims have their plain and ordinary meaning.
guidance: In some cases (bench trial in a patent‑savvy court) a formal construction may not be necessary. Use a stipulation or letter to the court if appropriate, but if a claim term is disputed the court must construe it for the jury.

name: Markman briefing requirements and content
description: Briefing should include a background discussion of the technology, the patent-in-suit, the asserted claims, the disputed terms, relevant law on claim construction, and the definition of the ordinary person of skill in the art.
guidance: Each brief should expressly set forth the proposed construction for each disputed term, identify the relevant intrinsic and extrinsic evidence, apply that evidence to the proposed construction, and submit supporting evidence concurrently unless ordered otherwise. Expert declarations (similar to expert reports) are useful to introduce evidence about skill level and background.

name: Meet-and-confer process before briefing
description: Local rules or scheduling orders normally set forth a meet-and-confer process between the parties before briefing the proper construction of disputed claim terms.
guidance: Use the meet-and-confer to narrow disputed terms, discuss claim construction strategy, and identify which terms are most likely dispositive. Good-faith narrowing can preserve credibility and avoid sanction risk.

name: Prohibition on letting experts argue claim scope to the jury
description: It is error to allow experts to make arguments to the jury about claim scope when claim construction is a matter for the court.
guidance: Ensure the court provides jury instructions about claim meanings. Do not rely on expert argument to substitute for court's claim construction (NobelBiz; O2 Micro).

name: Claim indefiniteness as a construction argument
description: A party may assert that there can be no construction of a disputed term because the claim is indefinite (Nautilus standard).
guidance: Use indefiniteness arguments where appropriate; consider Federal Circuit precedent on when claims are properly held indefinite as part of claim construction.

name: Post-Markman strategic considerations
description: After a Markman ruling, parties should consider tactical and procedural decisions such as seeking reconsideration, construing additional terms, checking for new precedent, amending contentions, narrowing asserted claims, dropping prior art, filing summary judgment, revisiting settlement, or stipulating to allow earlier appeal.
guidance: Specific options include: motion for reconsideration of adverse term constructions; determining whether other terms become disputed; reducing asserted claims (patentee) or dropping prior art (defendant) in light of construction; amending infringement/invalidity contentions; filing summary judgment on clear issues; revisiting settlement leverage; stipulating issues for interlocutory appeal to reach the Federal Circuit sooner.

name: Preserving validity when construing claims
description: A court is charged with preserving the validity of an asserted claim unless the invalidating construction is dictated by the claim and specification.
guidance: If the only construction consistent with the claim language and written description renders the claim invalid, then the claim is invalid. Argue constructions that preserve validity where supported by intrinsic evidence (Phillips; Rhine).

name: Practice before the Office — patent matters (37 C.F.R. § 11.5(b)(1))
description: Specific patent-related activities that constitute practice.
guidance: Includes: preparing and prosecuting patent applications; consulting/advising clients in contemplation of filing patent applications or other documents with the Office; drafting specifications or claims; drafting amendments or replies that may require written argument to establish patentability; drafting replies to Office communications regarding patent applications; drafting communications for public use, interference, reexamination, petitions, appeals to or proceedings before the PTAB, or other proceedings.

name: Deceit and conduct prejudicial to administration of justice (case guidance and rule citations)
description: Examples of deceitful conduct and relevant disciplinary rules.
guidance: Case: In re Kroll (separate proceeding) — offered money-back guarantees, amended claims/specification without client authorization, paid clients not to file ethics grievances, and other deceitful conduct leading to exclusion. Rule highlights: giving false or misleading information to a client in connection with USPTO business (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(2)(i)); conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(5) & 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d)). Aggravating factors (e.g., prior history) increase severity of discipline.

name: Formats and placement for computer program listings
description: If the listing is submitted as drawings it must comply with drawing requirements (§ 1.84) and have at least one figure numeral per sheet. If submitted as part of the specification, it must comply with § 1.52. Any listing having more than 60 lines of code submitted as part of the specification must be positioned at the end of the description but before the claims; any amendment must be by substitute sheet.
guidance: Choose appropriate submission format: as drawings (follow § 1.84) or part of the spec (follow § 1.52), and place longer listings (>60 lines) at the end of description before claims to facilitate processing and amendments via substitute sheets.

name: IDS content: required legible copies (§1.98(a)(2))
description: Provide a legible copy of: each foreign patent; each publication or the portion that caused listing (other than U.S. patents and U.S. patent app publications unless required); for each cited pending unpublished U.S. application, the application specification including claims and any drawing or the portion that caused listing; and all other information or the portion that caused listing.
guidance: Include readable copies of cited documents or the specific portions relied upon to permit examiner review; do not assume the Office has the needed copy unless relying on properly identified earlier application per (d).

name: Prioritized examination filing specifics when filed with original application (§1.102(e)(1))
description: A request may be filed with an original utility or plant nonprovisional application. The application must include a specification as prescribed by 35 U.S.C. 112 including at least one claim, a drawing when necessary, and the inventor’s oath or declaration on filing (oath/declaration may be postponed if ADS conditions are met). Utility applications must be filed via EFS and include filing, search, and examination fees upon filing; plant applications include corresponding fees. Applicant may file an amendment to cancel any excess independent/total claims or multiple dependent claim not later than one month from a first decision on the prioritized-exam request; this one-month period is not extendable.
guidance: If requesting prioritized examination with the initial filing, ensure the application is complete per 112, pay fees, file via EFS for utility apps, and be ready to timely withdraw excess claims within the non-extendable one-month cure period after the PTO’s first decision on the request.

name: Design claimed is the design for an article, not the article itself
description: In a design patent application, the subject matter which is claimed is the design embodied in or applied to an article of manufacture (or portion thereof) and not the article itself.
guidance: Cites Ex parte Cady (1916) and In re Zahn (CCPA 1980). Emphasizes that 35 U.S.C. 171 refers to the design for an article, inclusive of surface ornamentation and configuration. Use this framing when identifying claim scope.

name: Design must be inseparable from the article and cannot exist as an abstract scheme
description: Design is inseparable from the article to which it is applied and cannot exist alone merely as a scheme of surface ornamentation; it must be a definite, preconceived thing, capable of reproduction and not merely the chance result of a method.
guidance: Cites In re SurgiSil (Fed. Cir. 2021) and Curver Luxembourg v. Home Expressions (Fed. Cir. 2019) for limits on 'design per se.' Ensure claimed design is tied to an identified article of manufacture and is reproducible; avoid claiming a design in the abstract.

name: Design claim is limited to the article of manufacture identified
description: A design claim is limited to the article of manufacture identified in the claim; it does not broadly cover a design in the abstract.
guidance: Court precedent and agency practice support that design patents are granted only for a design applied to an article of manufacture (i.e., include the article identification in the claim). Draft claims and identifications accordingly.

name: Purpose distinction: utility patents protect function; design patents protect appearance
description: Utility patents protect the way an article is used and works (35 U.S.C. 101), while design patents protect the way an article looks (35 U.S.C. 171).
guidance: Ornamental appearance includes shape/configuration or surface ornamentation, or both. Both types of patents may be obtained if invention resides in both utility and ornamentality—assess whether claimed subject matter is principally functional or ornamental.

name: Revised Step 2A two-prong inquiry
description: Under revised Step 2A, a claim is eligible at Step 2A unless it (1) recites a judicial exception and (2) the exception is not integrated into a practical application of the exception.
guidance: Prong One: determine whether the claim recites a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon). If no exception is recited, the claim is eligible and analysis ends. If an exception is recited, go to Prong Two. Prong Two: determine whether additional elements integrate the exception into a practical application; if so the claim is eligible, otherwise the claim is "directed to" the exception and proceed to Step 2B.

name: Prong One — recitation of judicial exceptions (laws/natural phenomena)
description: For laws of nature and natural phenomena, continue to use the 'recite' standard set forth in MPEP 2106.04(b) and (c), including markedely different characteristics analysis, to determine if a claim recites a law of nature or natural phenomenon.
guidance: If the claim recites a law of nature or natural phenomenon (including a product of nature), proceed to Prong Two.

name: Prong One — recitation of abstract ideas (use groupings)
description: For abstract ideas, Prong One requires identifying the specific limitation(s) that the examiner believes recite an abstract idea, and determining whether those limitation(s) fall within at least one of the groupings of abstract ideas enumerated in the 2019 PEG.
guidance: Do not use the prior "Eligibility Quick Reference Sheet Identifying Abstract Ideas." Claim limitations that do not fall within the enumerated groupings should not be treated as abstract ideas except in rare circumstances (see procedure for tentative abstract ideas). If a limitation falls within any grouping, proceed to Prong Two.

name: Grouping: Mathematical concepts
description: Abstract ideas that are mathematical concepts, including mathematical relationships, mathematical formulas or equations, and mathematical calculations.
guidance: Limitations that amount to mathematical relationships/formulas/calculations should be considered under this grouping when determining if a claim recites an abstract idea at Prong One.

name: Prong Two — integration into a practical application (general standard)
description: "Integration into a practical application" requires an additional element or combination of additional elements in the claim to apply, rely on, or use the judicial exception in a manner that imposes a meaningful limit on the judicial exception, such that the claim is more than a drafting effort designed to monopolize the exception.
guidance: Evaluate additional elements using considerations from Supreme Court and Federal Circuit decisions and MPEP 2106.05 subsections; most Prong Two considerations mirror those used in Step 2B, but do not include WURC analysis. If the exception is integrated into a practical application under these considerations, the claim is eligible at Prong Two.

name: Prong Two considerations — limitations indicative of integration into a practical application
description: Certain types of additional claim limitations are indicative that the judicial exception is integrated into a practical application.
guidance: Indicative limitations include: improvements to functioning of a computer or other technology/technical field (MPEP 2106.05(a)); applying/using an exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease/medical condition (per Vanda memo); applying/using the exception with/by a particular machine (MPEP 2106.05(b)); effecting a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing (MPEP 2106.05(c)); applying/using the exception in some other meaningful way beyond generally linking it to a technological environment or field of use (MPEP 2106.05(e) and Vanda memo).

name: Prong Two considerations — limitations not indicative of integration into a practical application
description: Certain claim recitations are not indicative that a judicial exception has been integrated into a practical application.
guidance: Not indicative: merely adding the words 'apply it' (or equivalent), mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer, or merely using a computer as a tool to perform an abstract idea (MPEP 2106.05(f)); adding insignificant extra-solution activity (MPEP 2106.05(g)); generally linking use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use (MPEP 2106.05(h)). Note: whether elements are well-understood, routine, conventional (WURC) is NOT evaluated at Prong Two.

name: Do not evaluate WURC at Prong Two (WURC exclusion)
description: Whether claim elements represent only well-understood, routine, conventional activity (WURC) is considered at Step 2B and is NOT a consideration at Step 2A Prong Two.
guidance: Examiners should give weight to all claimed additional elements in Prong Two, even if those elements represent WURC activity. Do not assess WURC unless the analysis proceeds to Step 2B.

name: Step 2B — inventive concept (aka 'significantly more')
description: At Step 2B, evaluate whether the claim recites additional elements that amount to an inventive concept — i.e., whether the claim as a whole amounts to 'significantly more' than the recited judicial exception.
guidance: Procedure: identify additional elements beyond the judicial exception, evaluate those elements individually and in combination to determine if they amount to significantly more, using considerations in MPEP 2106.05 and relevant case law. If inventive concept present, claim is eligible; if not, claim is ineligible. Step 2B uses WURC analysis (unlike Prong Two).

name: Examiners' procedure when applicants argue eligibility (applications in process)
description: If an applicant argues that previously rejected claims are eligible, examiners should re-evaluate each claim under the 2019 PEG.
guidance: If a claim is now eligible, withdraw the 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection. If the claim remains ineligible, update the form paragraph(s) used and ensure the rejection explanation addresses why the claim recites a judicial exception, fails to integrate the exception into a practical application, and fails to provide an inventive concept. Examiners should also consider other patentability statutes (35 U.S.C. 102, 103, 112) and consult the FAQ for guidance on final rejections.

name: General reminders and prosecutorial practice
description: Key takeaways about claim-level analysis and prosecution practice under the 2019 PEG.
guidance: Treat the claim as a whole and consider all recited limitations when determining eligibility. Do not use the old Eligibility Quick Reference Sheet for abstract idea identification. WURC is considered at Step 2B, not Step 2A. The key inquiry in revised Step 2A is whether a claim that recites a judicial exception is directed to the judicial exception itself or to a practical application of the judicial exception. Practice compact prosecution: address all statutory requirements (not just eligibility) and point applicants to eligible subject matter in the specification when possible.

name: Use of examples and supporting resources
description: The USPTO provides examples and resources to demonstrate application of the 2019 PEG.
guidance: New examples (37-42) analyze hypothetical claims under the 2019 PEG (including abstract ideas, computer-related inventions, and software). Examples 1-36 were issued prior to the 2019 PEG and may not be entirely consistent with it; claims previously indicated eligible remain eligible but use those earlier examples with caution. Additional resources: MPEP 2106 (except superseded portions), Berkheimer memo, subject matter eligibility webpage, sample rejections, and FAQ document.

name: Ready to file
description: Guidance on preparatory steps and checks applicants should complete before filing an application.
guidance: Covers preparedness items such as necessary disclosures, claim drafting, drawings, inventor declarations, and fee payment.

name: Schemes, Rules or Methods of Doing Business, Mental Acts, or Playing Games
description: Schemes, rules or methods of doing business, performing purely mental acts or playing games are examples of items of an abstract or intellectual character and may be excluded.
guidance: Determination focuses on whether the claimed invention is of an abstract character rather than on the art or classification. Where divergent practices exist between Authorities, specific guidance is set out in the appendix to the chapter.

name: Computer Programs (to the Extent Authority is not Equipped)
description: Computer programs are excluded subject-matter to the extent that the Authority is not equipped to carry out search or preliminary examination on such programs.
guidance: Normally, claims that merely recite program code are excluded. However, if a natural language description of a computer-executable program or self-documented code is included in the description and claims, the Authority may be considered equipped to carry out a search and preliminary examination based on such a description, subject to other exclusion conditions. Authorities have diverging practices; see appendix for guidance where practices differ.

name: Cases of Doubt — perform search to the extent possible
description: In cases of doubt as to whether claimed subject-matter constitutes excluded subject-matter, the Authority carries out the search or preliminary examination to the extent possible using the available documentation.
guidance: If doubt exists, proceed with whatever meaningful search/examination can be done; record limitations in reports/opinions.

name: Extent of Search When Application Fails to Comply with Prescribed Requirements
description: If description, claims or drawings fail to comply to such an extent that a meaningful search cannot be carried out for a particular claim, no search may be possible; if parts can be sufficiently understood, a search is performed taking non-compliance into account in determining extent of search.
guidance: The international search report and written opinion should indicate how the application fails to comply and specify to what degree that non-compliance has been taken into account in determining the extent of the search (as precisely as possible). In general, a search should be carried out to the maximum extent practical.

name: When Search Is Possible Despite Defects — indicate non-prior-art objections and scope
description: Where a search can be carried out despite defects (e.g., lack of support, claims defined solely by result, unusual parameters, Markush claims, multitudinous claims), the written opinion should include observations on non-prior-art grounds (sufficiency, support, clarity, conciseness) and explain extent of search.
guidance: Examples illustrate search strategy: search first for embodiments disclosed in description, then extend to broader relevant areas but need not search areas of low probability. Written opinion should identify non-prior-art objections (e.g., lack of support, lack of clarity, inability to determine parameters), and specify which parts were searched (e.g., disclosed examples, structural generalizations). For Markush-type or unclear/multitudinous claims, search may be limited to clearly disclosed or clearly prepared/tested embodiments and structural generalizations thereof; indicate precisely how objections were taken into account.

name: When No Search at All Is Possible — declaration under Article 17(2)(a)(ii)
description: When none of the claims can be meaningfully searched at all because no likely amendment can be determined to overcome the non-compliance, the International Searching Authority makes a declaration under Article 17(2)(a)(ii).
guidance: When only some claims cannot be meaningfully searched, indicate this in the international search report under Article 17(2)(b) and search other claims as usual. Written opinion should object on non-prior-art grounds (Article 6/Rule 6 etc.) and indicate to what degree the objection has been taken into account when determining that no search at all is possible. Examples: nonsensical or purely aspirational claims ('My invention is worth a million dollars'), undefined fictitious materials ('kryptonite'), or multitudinous overlapping claims with no reasonable basis.

name: Non-Prior-Art Issues to be Considered
description: Searches regarding non-prior-art issues include clarity of claims, conciseness and number of claims, support in the description, clear and complete disclosure, sufficiency commensurate with the claims, relationship of claims to disclosure, and new matter.
guidance: Detailed guidance and discussion of these non-prior-art concerns are contained in Chapter 5 (paragraphs 5.31 to 5.58) and paragraphs referenced for new matter (20.20, 20.21). If industrial applicability opinion is negative, cite prior art used and set out reasoning in the written opinion; indicate any implications for novelty/inventive step where appropriate.

name: Unclear Claims — search clear realizations; determine reasonable expected subject-matter
description: When claimed subject-matter includes alternatives, some clear and some unclear, the search examiner searches the clear realization(s) and determines the subject of search for unclear realizations based on what might reasonably be expected to be claimed by amendment.
guidance: The examiner takes into account description, drawings and common general knowledge to identify reasonable claimable subject-matter and conducts the search accordingly. If an alternative is totally unclear such that subject-matter cannot be determined, that alternative need not be searched. Examples provided with combinations of alternatives illustrate which combinations to search and which may be omitted.

name: Interference practice is based on 35 U.S.C. 102(g)
description: Subsection (g) is the basis of interference practice for determining priority of invention between parties; interference is an inter partes proceeding to determine first to invent among parties naming different inventors or combinations of pending applications and unexpired patents.
guidance: Interference practice (35 U.S.C. 135; 37 CFR Part 41 Subparts D & E; MPEP Chapter 2300) determines which party is first to invent; subject matter claimed by the losing party is rejected under 102(g) unless the acts showing prior invention were not in this country. First-to-invent rules detailed (conception + reduction + diligence).

name: 37 CFR 1.131 scope and its exclusion in interference proceedings
description: 37 CFR 1.131 permits an applicant to show an actual date of invention prior to the effective date of a patent or literature reference applied under 35 U.S.C. 102(a) or (e), except where interference practice applies.
guidance: 37 CFR 1.131 does not apply in interference proceedings; if a domestic patent claims the same patentable invention, interference rather than a 1.131 affidavit is required (Ex parte Standish). Subject matter available only under 102(g) is inherently made before the applicant and is not open to further inquiry under 1.131.

name: Knowledge may be inferred from circumstances (37 C.F.R. § 11.1)
description: The term 'knowingly' means actual knowledge of the fact in question, and a person's knowledge may be inferred from the circumstances. 37 C.F.R. § 11.1.
guidance: When a respondent had contact with OED or provided an e‑mail address that received RFIs, the court may infer actual knowledge even if the respondent claims otherwise; this inference supports findings of knowing failure to respond.

name: Exceptions where 37 CFR 1.136(a) extensions are not available
description: Extensions under 37 CFR 1.136(a) are not available for: (A) all extensions in a reexamination proceeding; (B) all extensions during an interference proceeding (but not preparatory to an interference where a claim is suggested); (C) situations where an Office action states that 1.136(a) is not applicable (e.g., reply to a notice of allowability, reissue applications associated with litigation, applications in allowable condition with nonelected claims set to cancel); and (D) limited instances where applicant is given a specified time limit to take certain actions.
guidance: See MPEP §§ 2265, 2665, Chapter 2300 and relevant CFR provisions for specifics.

name: Clean copy of claims
description: Within 14 days of the initiation of the proceeding, each party must file a clean copy of its involved claims and, if a biotechnology material sequence is a limitation, a clean copy of the sequence.
guidance: Strict 14-day deadline; applies to all involved claims and biotech sequences when applicable.

name: Annotated copy of claims
description: Within 28 days of the initiation of the proceeding, each party must file an annotated copy of each involved claim indicating (in bold face between braces {}) where each limitation is shown in the drawing or sequence, and for means-plus-function/step-plus-function limitations per 35 U.S.C. 112(6), indicate the specific portions of the specification that describe structure, material, or acts corresponding to each claimed function.
guidance: Annotation format required: bold face between braces. Applies both to drawing/sequence limitations and 112(6) limitations; 28-day deadline.

name: Claim charts required for comparisons
description: Claim charts must be used in support of any paper requiring the comparison of a claim to something else (another claim, prior art, or a specification) and must accompany the paper as an appendix.
guidance: Claim charts are not a substitute for appropriate argument and explanation in the paper.

name: Types of motions and classification
description: Motions are classified as substantive (e.g., to redefine scope, change benefit, or for judgment), responsive (e.g., to amend or add a claim, change inventorship), or miscellaneous (any request other than substantive or responsive).
guidance: The Board authorizes the filing of substantive motions consistent with any notice of requested relief.

name: Request for adverse judgment
description: A party may request judgment against itself at any time; actions construed to be such a request include abandonment of involved application, cancellation/disclaimer of a claim, concession of priority or unpatentability, or abandonment of the contest.
guidance: Parties may voluntarily obtain adverse judgment by clear actions that remove involvement.

name: Broadest reasonable claim construction in interferences
description: In patent interferences, a claim shall be given its broadest reasonable construction in light of the specification of the application or patent in which it appears.
guidance: Apply broadest reasonable interpretation standard when construing claims for interference proceedings.

name: Contents required to suggest an interference
description: An applicant suggesting an interference must: (1) identify the application/patent sought, (2) identify all claims believed to interfere and propose counts and show claim correspondence, (3) provide a claim chart comparing at least one claim of each party corresponding to the count and show why the claims interfere, (4) explain in detail why the applicant will prevail on priority, (5) if claim added/amended to provoke interference provide claim chart showing written description for each claim, and (6) for each constructive reduction to practice for which benefit is sought provide a chart showing where the disclosure provides a constructive reduction to practice within the scope of the interfering subject matter.
guidance: Comprehensive showing required; claim charts and priority explanations are central; providing constructive reduction-to-practice charts is necessary when seeking benefit.

name: Interference declaration criteria and notice contents
description: An interference exists if the subject matter of a claim of one party would, if prior art, have anticipated or rendered obvious the subject matter of a claim of the opposing party and vice versa. A notice declaring an interference must identify: (1) the interfering subject matter, (2) the involved applications, patents, and claims, (3) the accorded benefit for each count, and (4) the claims corresponding to each count.
guidance: Declaration lays out the formal scope and parties/claims/benefits; redeclaration may be used to change prior declaration details.

name: Solid lines define the claimed design
description: In a US design patent the claimed design comprises what is drawn in solid lines.
guidance: When preparing figures, only elements shown in solid lines are part of the claimed design. Use solid lines for features you intend to claim and dashed lines for elements you expressly do not claim.

name: Use dashed lines to show environmental/contextual elements (unclaimed)
description: Dashed lines enable an applicant to show the environment or context surrounding the claimed design by illustrating, but not claiming, what is external.
guidance: If the product can be attached to, clipped on, hung from or otherwise connected to something else, illustrate that something else in broken lines. Include a broken line statement regarding environmental structure in the specification (see MPEP 1503.02).

name: Strategic effect: how dashed lines can broaden protection
description: Dashed lines provide design patent owners with an argument that an accused product infringes even though certain parts of the product look different than what is shown in the design patent.
guidance: Ask whether the visual differences between the accused product and the patented design primarily consist of parts shown in broken lines, and whether the visual similarities are primarily captured by what is shown in solid lines. If so, a dashed-line drafting choice can support an infringement argument focused on the claimed (solid-line) features.

name: Checklist: factors to consider when deciding where to use broken lines
description: A set of practical questions to decide which components to show in broken lines rather than claim.
guidance: Consider these factors: Does the product have any functional features or structures that do not contribute to the unique design? Should any external or internal borders be shown in dashed lines? Are there any holes or openings that do not contribute to the unique design? Does the product hold, support, or attach to any external structures that should be shown in broken lines? Would it make sense to reduce the claimed design to a certain component of an overall product or assembly? Is the unique design a two-dimensional graphic artwork placed on a three-dimensional product or article (e.g., GUI)? Is the unique design combined with other features or structures that are not invented by the inventor(s)? Would it make sense to create a new fictional boundary (by using dashed-dot lines) that does not exist in the actual product? Can the product be attached, connected or coupled to something else?

name: Requirement to include a broken-line statement in the specification for environmental structures
description: If environmental structure is shown in broken lines, include a broken line statement in the specification.
guidance: Follow MPEP 1503.02 guidance for broken-line statements to explain that depicted environmental elements are not claimed. This supports consistent interpretation during examination and enforcement.

name: Visual example / appearance guidance
description: Broken lines can be used to indicate that the 3-dimensional structure of the product is not being claimed.
guidance: Refer to USPTO design patent application guide examples for how broken lines are depicted. Use clear dashed/broken-line conventions so examiners and courts can readily distinguish claimed (solid) from unclaimed (broken) elements. (Source link provided: USPTO design patent application guide.)

name: Interpretation of continuations vs. prosecution responses
description: Treat post-standard continuations as evidence of late claiming tailored to standards rather than merely responses to examiner rejections.
guidance: Provide supporting checks: (a) continuations are often filed after a notice of allowance rather than after rejections; (b) regressions of continuation indicators on measures of change in scope during examination show small and mixed effects; (c) timing of surge aligned with standard publication argues against rejection-synchronized continuation filings.

name: Statutory scope of 35 U.S.C. 156: what patents can be extended
description: The term of a patent which claims a product, a method of using a product, or a method of manufacturing a product shall be extended in accordance with this section from the original expiration date of the patent (including any PTA under 154(b)) if statutory conditions are met.
guidance: 35 U.S.C. 156 defines eligibility and extension rights (see subsections (a) and (b)).

name: 37 CFR 1.720 — conditions for extension (regulatory restatement)
description: The term of a patent may be extended if: (a) the patent claims a product as defined in §1.710; (b) the term has never been previously extended (with noted exceptions); (c) an application is submitted in compliance with §1.740; (d) the product has been subject to a regulatory review period as defined in 35 U.S.C. 156(g) before its commercial marketing or use; (e) the product has received permission for commercial marketing or use and meets the 'first permitted marketing' conditions (with exceptions); (f) the application is submitted within the sixty-day period beginning on the date the product first received permission; (g) the patent term has not expired before submission; and (h) no other patent has been extended for the same regulatory review period for the product.
guidance: This summarizes statutory and regulatory prerequisites; see MPEP narrative and statutory text for details and examples.

name: 37 CFR 1.710 — definition of product and drug product for PTE
description: A patent is eligible if it claims a 'product' as defined (drug product, medical device, food/color additive) either alone or in combination, or a method of using/manufacturing such product. 'Drug product' means the active ingredient of a new human/animal drug or biological product, excluding animal drugs primarily manufactured using recombinant DNA/RNA/hybridoma/site-specific genetic techniques, and includes salts/esters as single entities or in combination.
guidance: Also defines 'major health or environmental effects test' (test reasonably related to evaluation of health/environmental effects that requires at least six months to conduct).

name: 35 U.S.C. 156(d)(1) — required application contents
description: To obtain extension under this section, the owner of record or agent shall submit an application within the 60-day period; the application shall contain: (A) identity of the approved product and the Federal statute under which regulatory review occurred; (B) identity of the patent and identity of each claim which claims the approved product or method of using/manufacturing it; (C) information to enable Director to determine eligibility and rights and to enable Secretary of HHS or Agriculture to determine the period of extension; (D) a brief description of the activities undertaken by the applicant during the regulatory review period and significant dates; and (E) such patent or other information as the Director may require.
guidance: For purposes of determining the date a product receives permission, transmissions after 4:30 P.M. Eastern or transmissions on non-business days are deemed received the next business day. 'Business day' is defined as Mon–Fri excluding federal holidays under 5 U.S.C. 6103.

name: Consider the Teachings of Structural Similarity
description: Consider any teachings of a “typical,” “preferred,” or “optimum” species or subgenus within the disclosed genus. If such a prior art species or subgenus is structurally similar to that claimed, its disclosure may provide a reason for one of ordinary skill in the art to choose the claimed species or subgenus from the genus, based on the reasonable expectation that structurally similar species usually have similar properties.
guidance: Evaluate whether prior art expressly teaches related species/subgenera or art-recognized equivalences (e.g., Merck v. Biocraft). Consider conservative substitutions in proteins and how substitution location affects function. The closer the physical/chemical similarities, the greater the expectation of equivalent function. Conversely, dissimilar disclosed species may teach away (cf. Baird). Preferred/optimum species that are structurally very different may weigh against selecting the claimed species. Consider cited cases (Dillon, Deuel, Jones, Susi) and use them as factual analogies.

name: Consider the Number of Variables and Significance of Differences
description: In making an obviousness determination, consider the number of variables which must be selected or modified, and the nature and significance of the differences between the prior art and the claimed invention.
guidance: Assess how many independent choices an ordinary artisan would have to make to arrive at the claimed species and whether differences are minor or substantive. Large differences or many variables (e.g., structural features absent in prior art) weigh against a prima facie case (see In re Jones, In re Susi).

name: Consider the Teachings of Similar Properties or Uses
description: Consider the properties and utilities of the structurally similar prior art species or subgenus; properties and utilities provide real world motivation for selecting structurally similar species.
guidance: If the claimed invention and structurally similar prior art share any useful property, that generally motivates an artisan to make the claimed species. Lack of known useful properties weighs against motivation. Prior art need not disclose newly discovered properties to support a prima facie case. Very close structural similarity may allow presuming similar properties (see Dillon, Stemniski, Grabiak, Wilder, Lintner).

name: Consider the Predictability of the Technology
description: Consider the predictability of the technology: unpredictable fields make it less likely that structural similarity alone renders a claimed species obvious.
guidance: If the art is unpredictable, structural similarity is less persuasive because one cannot reasonably infer shared properties. Obviousness requires only a reasonable expectation of success, not certainty. Use relevant cases (May, Schechter, O’Farrell) to assess whether unpredictability in the field rebuts a prima facie case.

name: Make Express Fact-Findings and Determine Whether They Support a Prima Facie Case of Obviousness
description: Office personnel should make express fact-findings relating to the Graham factors, focusing primarily on the prior art teachings discussed above, and specifically articulate any teachings or suggestions that would have motivated one of ordinary skill to select the claimed species or subgenus.
guidance: State explicit fact-findings and a rationale (as required by KSR) that ties prior art teachings to a conclusion of obviousness. Thereafter determine whether, considered as a whole, these findings establish a prima facie case that the claimed invention would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill at the relevant time. Cite In re Bell, In re Kulling, Panduit for support.

name: Presence of a True Homologous or Isomeric Relationship Is Not Controlling
description: Prior art structures do not have to be true homologs or isomers to render structurally similar compounds prima facie obvious; non-homologous but structurally similar compounds can still motivate selection.
guidance: Look to overall structural and functional similarity and whether an ordinary artisan would be motivated to make the claimed compound even if it is not a strict homolog/isomer (see Payne, Mayne, Merck, Dillon). Conversely, also consider cases where substitution was not suggested (Grabiak, Bell, Deuel).

name: Presence or Absence of Prior Art Suggestion of a Method of Making the Claimed Compound May Be Relevant
description: The presence—or absence—of a suitably operative, obvious process for making a composition of matter may affect whether that composition is obvious under 35 U.S.C. 103.
guidance: If the prior art fails to disclose or render obvious a method for making the claimed compound at the relevant time, that may overcome a presumption of obviousness based on structural similarity (see Maloney, Hoeksema, Payne). Consider whether a prior-art synthesis would have led an artisan to the claimed compound.

name: If Prior Art Compounds Have No Utility, or Utility Only as Intermediates, They May Not Render Structurally Similar Compounds Prima Facie Obvious
description: If the prior art does not teach any specific or significant utility for disclosed compounds, the prior art is unlikely to render structurally similar claims prima facie obvious in the absence of reason to make the reference compounds or related compounds.
guidance: Assess whether prior art compounds were disclosed as useful or merely intermediates. Prior art teaching of no useful property or only intermediate use undermines motivation to make related compounds (see Stemniski, Albrecht, Lalu).

name: Prima Facie Case Rebuttable by Evidence of Unexpected Results
description: A prima facie case of obviousness based on structural similarity is rebuttable by proof that the claimed compounds possess unexpectedly advantageous or superior properties.
guidance: Affidavit or other evidence showing unexpectedly different utility/performance can overcome obviousness (see Papesch, Wiechert). However, mere recognition of a benefit by applicant is insufficient if the prior art compound actually possessed the benefit even if unrecognized (Dillon). Consult MPEP § 716.02–§ 716.02(g) for evidence types and handling.

name: Written description and enablement (patent validity)
description: Claims held invalid for "lack of adequate written description and enablement."
guidance: The companion Federal Circuit opinion held the same claims of the '039 patent invalid for lack of adequate written description and enablement (cited at slip op. 12, 18). A finding that a specification fails to provide an adequate written description or enable a claimed invention is a ground for invalidating the claims.

name: Mootness when invalidity determination issued in a companion case
description: An "invalidity determination renders moot 'all pending or co-pending actions'."
guidance: If a court invalidates the patent in a companion appeal, that invalidity determination typically renders related pending or co-pending actions moot. The opinion cites XY, LLC v. Trans Ova Genetics, 890 F.3d 1282, 1294 (Fed. Cir. 2018), and notes the court may decline to reach the merits of companion proceedings when claims are held invalid (see also Biogen Int’l GMBH v. Mylan Pharms. Inc., 18 F.4th 1333, 1346 (Fed. Cir. 2021)).

name: Ring substituent coding conventions
description: A ring substituent is any atom/group other than H bonded to a ring atom. Indexers attempt to index all specific substitution patterns disclosed for the most important ring system. Substituents generally do not change the ring code unless tautomerism changes ring hydrogenation state.
guidance: Substituent numbers in D0/F0/G0 refer to ring positions bearing substituents, not total substituent count. Use non-specific substitution codes (D010/D020/F010/G001–G003) when general patterns (e.g. 'optionally substituted benzene') are disclosed, while specifically exemplified/claimed patterns receive more specific substitution codes.

name: Electronic Priority Document Exchange (PDX) retrieval practice and limitations
description: A proper priority claim to an application filed in a participating foreign intellectual property office is treated as a request for the USPTO to obtain a copy from that office via PDX; the Office will attempt retrieval when the application is docketed to an examiner and after the Office of Patent Application Processing completes review.
guidance: Retrieval typically takes about one week. If an eligible foreign application is filed in a participating office, the USPTO will attempt retrieval; for certain receiving offices and if the WIPO DAS access code is provided, retrieval of international/PCT applications is automatic. If retrieval fails or the foreign application was not originally in a participating office, applicant may file Form PTO/SB/38 to request retrieval. Successful retrieval is not guaranteed; check Patent Center to confirm. Retrieval requires accurate citation format; incomplete claims prevent electronic retrieval.

name: Office acknowledgement and examiner communication (form paragraphs and when to use)
description: Examiners should use specific form paragraphs to notify applicants of priority claim status: e.g., ¶2.21.01 for untimely foreign priority claims, ¶2.26 (PTOL-326) to acknowledge timely certified copies, ¶2.27 to acknowledge a certified copy filed in a parent, ¶2.23 where foreign filing was more than 12 months earlier with no restoration, ¶2.22 where certified copy does not correspond to the identified priority claim or proper claim not made, and ¶2.25 when certified copy not filed.
guidance: Examiner Notes in the MPEP specify usage limitations (e.g., do not use certain paragraphs for design applications). Bracketed fields in the form paragraphs indicate insertion of dates, application numbers, or country names as appropriate. Examiners should follow the MPEP guidance for which paragraph to use in each situation.

name: General petition content and form requirements
description: A petition must meet the content and form requirements set by statute and regulation: pay the fee, identify real parties-in-interest, identify with particularity each claim challenged, state grounds for each challenge, and provide supporting evidence.
guidance: Specifically: include copies of relied-upon patents and printed publications; affidavits/declarations if relying on expert or factual opinions; any other information Director requires; and provide copies of required documents to the patent owner or designated representative. Petitions are made public as soon as practicable.

name: Timing limits for filing petitions
description: Statutory timing for filing petitions varies by proceeding: post-grant review must be filed not later than nine months after grant or reissue; inter partes petitions may be filed after the later of nine months after grant/reissue or termination of a post-grant review; CBM petitions may be filed any time except during the period in which a post-grant review would be timely.
guidance: Regulation elaborates reissue-claim nuances: petitions cannot request review for reissue-claims identical/narrower than original patent unless within nine months of original patent grant.

name: Standard for instituting inter partes review
description: Inter partes review will be instituted only if the Director determines the information in the petition and any preliminary response shows a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail with respect to at least one challenged claim.
guidance: This is the statutory 'reasonable likelihood' standard (35 U.S.C. 314(a)); the Director must make institution decision within three months after receiving a preliminary response or after the response deadline.

name: Standard for instituting post-grant review
description: Post-grant review will be instituted only if the Director determines the petition would, if unrebutted, demonstrate that it is more likely than not that at least one challenged claim is unpatentable, or that the petition raises a novel or unsettled legal question important to other patents/applications.
guidance: This is the 'more likely than not' institutional standard (35 U.S.C. 324(a)-(b)); Director's decision likewise must be timely (three-month rule).

name: Motion to amend — single initial motion and additional motions
description: A patent owner may file one motion to amend (cancel or propose substitute claims) only after conferring with the Board and normally no later than the patent owner response; additional motions require Board authorization and may be permitted for good cause or to materially advance settlement.
guidance: A reasonable number of substitute claims is presumed to be one substitute per challenged claim (rebuttable). Motions may be denied if they do not respond to a ground involved in the trial, enlarge scope, or introduce new matter. Board will consider supplemental information submitted by petitioner after the motion-to-amend filing period when deciding authorization for additional motions.

name: Content requirements for motions to amend
description: A motion to amend must include a claim listing, clearly show changes, and set forth support in the original disclosure for each added/amended claim and any earlier-filed disclosure relied upon for benefit of an earlier filing date.
guidance: Amendments must not introduce new matter or enlarge claim scope; support must be shown by citations to specification or earlier disclosures.

name: CBM petition content requirements
description: CBM petitions must request judgment against specific patent claims and (in addition to general petition requirements) identify the claim, statutory grounds (35 U.S.C. 282(b)(2) or (3) as modified by AIA §18(a)(1)(C)), claim construction (including 112(f) means/step-plus-function mappings), how the construed claim is unpatentable, and exhibit numbers with specific relevance.
guidance: Board may exclude or give no weight to evidence where relevance or supporting portions are not identified.

name: Claim construction standard in CBM and unexpired patents
description: A claim in an unexpired patent, including for CBM review, is given its broadest reasonable construction in light of the specification in which it appears.
guidance: This construction standard is applied for CBM proceedings under these rules (see § 42.300(b)).

name: Specific petition content requirements — mapping claims to prior art / statutory deficiencies
description: For prior-art-based grounds, the petition must specify where each element of the claim is found in the prior art; for other grounds, the petition must identify specific parts of the claim that fail to comply and state how they fail; the petition must supply exhibit numbers and identify specific portions that support the challenge.
guidance: The Board may exclude or give no weight to evidence when relevance or specific supporting portions are not stated.

name: Appropriate use of 'obvious to try' rationale
description: The 'obvious to try' rationale can properly support obviousness only when the claimed solution would have been selected from a finite number of potential solutions known to persons of ordinary skill and when the result would have been reasonably predictable.
guidance: Office personnel should not apply 'obvious to try' when, considering all evidence, the outcome would not have been reasonably predictable and the inventor would not have had a reasonable expectation of success. Cite Rolls-Royce and Sanders/Sanofi examples: where options were not known or the change would not have presented itself as an option, 'obvious to try' is inappropriate. Conversely, when a finite number of identified, predictable solutions exist (Perfect Web), 'obvious to try' may lead to obviousness.

name: Unexpected results can rebut prima facie obviousness
description: Evidence of unexpected results (e.g., unpredicted therapeutic advantages) can overcome a prima facie case of obviousness.
guidance: If applicants present credible evidence that the claimed invention produced unexpected properties (e.g., Sanofi D-isomer therapeutic advantage with low toxicity), examiners must consider that evidence; such evidence may prevent sustaining an obviousness rejection even where a prima facie case exists. The district court’s finding based on expert testimony may be dispositive if clear and convincing evidence of nonobviousness is shown.

name: Known work in one field prompting predictable variations in another
description: A known device/method/product in one field may prompt variations for use in the same or different field if the variations would have been predictable to one of ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: To reject based on this rationale, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries and explicitly articulate findings: (1) scope/content of prior art included a similar or analogous device; (2) design incentives or market forces would prompt adaptation; (3) differences between claimed invention and prior art were encompassed in known variations/principles; (4) a person of ordinary skill could have implemented the variation and it would have been predictable; and (5) any additional Graham-based findings necessary to explain obviousness. If any finding cannot be made, this rationale cannot support an obviousness conclusion.

name: Consideration of all claim limitations in obviousness analysis
description: All words in a claim must be considered in judging patentability against the prior art; dependent claims inherit patentability status from independent claims.
guidance: If an independent claim is nonobvious, dependent claims are nonobvious (In re Wilson; In re Fine). Do not ignore claim limitations; analyze each limitation in the context of the prior art combination.

name: Indefinite claim limitations must be considered and can mandate rejection
description: A limitation considered indefinite cannot be disregarded; if a claim term admits multiple interpretations and at least one renders the claim unpatentable over the prior art, examiner should reject the claim as indefinite and also reject over the prior art as applicable under that interpretation.
guidance: Where claim language lacks a reasonably definite meaning, issue a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112 (second paragraph) and address prior art under the interpretation that makes the claim unpatentable (Ex parte Ionescu). Compare to cases where no definite meaning can be ascribed (In re Wilson).

name: International application required contents for receiving an international filing date
description: An international application shall contain a Request, a description, one or more claims, an abstract, and one or more drawings (where required). An international filing date will be accorded by the United States Receiving Office provided that: (1) at least one applicant is a US resident or national and the papers show that; (2) the international application is in the English language; and (3) the international application contains at least the following elements: (i) an indication that it is intended as an international application (PCT Rule 4.2); (ii) the designation of at least one Contracting State; (iii) the name of the applicant; (iv) a part which on its face appears to be a description; and (v) a part which on its face appears to be a claim.
guidance: These are the minimum filing-date formalities under PCT Art. 11(1) and related provisions; additional documentary/fee steps follow (§ 1.431(b)-(c)).

name: Process patent — when both process and material are claimed
description: Where a process and its material both enter into an invention there is no infringement unless both are used.
guidance: If the invention is defined as the combination of a process plus a particular material, an accused product/process must appropriate both elements to infringe (text note: see Goodyear Dental Vulcanite Co. v. Davis).

name: Composition-of-matter — process-limited product claims
description: Where a product is patented as the result of a certain process, it is infringed only when made by that process.
guidance: If the patentee limited the claim to a product made by a specific process, an accused product made by a different process may avoid infringement (cases: Van Camp v. Maryland Pavement Co.; Cochrane v. Anilin).

name: Composition-of-matter — substitution-of-elements doctrine
description: A patent for a composition of matter is infringed if the new element does the same thing as the one for which it is substituted, though otherwise different.
guidance: Substituting an ingredient that performs the same cooperative function to produce the claimed properties can infringe (cases: Smith v. Murphy). Use of chemical equivalents can constitute infringement (Woodward v. Morrison).

name: Consultation to secure proper scope of patent via amendment
description: The examiner and the applicant shall make effort to consult possible amendment to resolve grounds for rejection discovered in the claimed invention and to secure proper scope of a patent based on advice on amendment and preliminary amendment proposed by each party.
guidance: Even if examiner suggests amendment, applicant is free to decide final amendment. Both parties should attempt to agree on suggested amendments or language; if no agreement is reached, statement of amendment discussed can be omitted.

name: Stating examiner's opinion on grounds for rejection
description: ‘Opinion on grounds for rejection’ is about results of review of the claimed invention conducted by examiner considering requirements for patentability and deficiencies in the specification, and applicant’s response to it.
guidance: Examiner is recommended to prepare the opinion in advance and use it during the interview; the minutes may simply state the purpose of each ground so it can be used as a reference.

name: Willingness to license
description: A patentee's willingness to license broadly is a factor that can rebut claims of irreparable harm and weigh against injunctive relief.
guidance: Mentioned in the concurrences in eBay and in the district court's post-remand opinion in MercExchange, willingness to license has been used by courts to deny injunctions (e.g., evidence of licensing behavior, lack of exclusivity). The Article examines correlations between licensing behavior and injunction outcomes (Part V.A.8 discussion).

name: Defining the Invention
description: Clearly defining the AI or ML invention is the first step in drafting robust patent claims. This involves describing the invention’s purpose, how it works, and what makes it unique compared to existing technologies.
guidance: Describe purpose, operation, and distinguishing features. Example: for a new neural network architecture, explain how it improves performance, reduces computational requirements, or enhances accuracy. Avoid vague or high-level descriptions that fail to identify the inventive contribution.

name: Identifying Key Components
description: AI and ML inventions often consist of multiple components, such as data preprocessing modules, learning algorithms, and output interfaces.
guidance: Identify and clearly describe each critical component to ensure comprehensive claim coverage. Example: an image recognition system’s components might include an image preprocessing unit, a convolutional neural network, and a classification module. Use these component descriptions to inform both system and method claims.

name: Crafting Clear and Precise Claims
description: The clarity and precision of patent claims are paramount. Clear claims help patent examiners understand the invention and ensure that the scope of protection is well-defined.
guidance: Strike a balance between comprehensiveness and specificity. Avoid ambiguity and overly broad language that can trigger rejections or legal challenges. Provide concrete limiting language where needed to define boundaries of the claimed invention.

name: Use Simple Language
description: While AI and ML technologies can be complex, using simple and clear language in patent claims is essential.
guidance: Avoid unnecessary technical jargon; ensure each term is understandable. Example: instead of 'gradient descent optimization,' use 'a method for adjusting model parameters to minimize prediction errors.' Simple phrasing helps examiners and can reduce misinterpretation.

name: Include Technical Advantages and Practical Benefits
description: Highlighting the technical advantages of the invention can strengthen the patent claims and demonstrate their practical benefits.
guidance: Explain how the invention solves specific problems, improves performance, or offers new capabilities. Provide concrete practical benefits (e.g., improved detection accuracy, reduced false positives, faster processing) to show utility and technical effect.

name: Support Claims with Data and Examples
description: Supporting the claims with data and examples provides tangible evidence of the invention’s effectiveness.
guidance: Include test results, performance metrics, case studies, and comparative data in the specification. Example: for a reinforcement learning algorithm, provide performance across scenarios to illustrate advantages and substantiate claimed improvements.

name: Draft Robust Independent and Dependent Claims
description: Drafting a combination of independent and dependent claims ensures comprehensive protection for AI and ML inventions.
guidance: Use independent claims to cover broad inventive concepts and dependent claims to add specific limitations and embodiments. Structure claims so dependent claims add fallback positions and narrower protection if independent claims are rejected.

name: Craft Broad but Supportable Independent Claims
description: Independent claims should cover the broadest aspects of the invention, focusing on the core innovation.
guidance: Draft broad independent claims that still have adequate support in the specification to avoid rejections for being overly broad or unsupported. Example template: 'A machine learning system for predictive analytics, comprising a model trained on historical data to generate future predictions.' Ensure embodiments and examples back up such breadth.

name: Add Specific Dependent Claims for Embodiments
description: Dependent claims add specific limitations and embodiments to the independent claims, providing additional layers of protection.
guidance: Use dependent claims to claim particular configurations, techniques, architectures, or applications (e.g., a neural network with a specific architecture for time-series analysis). Dependent claims serve as fallbacks and can capture commercially important variants.

name: Demonstrate Technological Improvement
description: Demonstrating how the invention provides a technological improvement over existing methods helps address patentability challenges.
guidance: Explain how the invention enhances performance, reduces costs, or solves a technical problem in a novel way. Provide comparative data and technical analyses to support the claim of improvement (e.g., faster convergence, lower resource usage).

name: Incorporate Implementation Details (Hardware/Software/Data Structures)
