description: Including implementation details in the patent application helps demonstrate the practical application of the AI or ML invention.
guidance: Describe hardware and software components, data structures, and implementation steps. Example: for autonomous vehicles, describe sensors, processors, and software algorithms. Provide diagrams and flowcharts to visualize processes and make claims more concrete and grounded.

name: Craft Clear and Comprehensive Specifications
description: The specifications section provides the detailed description and background information that supports the claims.
guidance: Provide a detailed description of purpose, structure, operation, advantages, and sufficient embodiments. Use simple language but include enough technical depth to support claim scope. Ensure the specification enables the claimed inventions.

name: Use Multiple, Diverse Examples and Embodiments
description: Examples are a powerful tool for illustrating the invention and demonstrating its practical applications.
guidance: Provide diverse examples across embodiments and industries to demonstrate versatility. Detail specific implementations, datasets, and results for each example to support broad claim coverage.

name: Respond Effectively to Examiner Rejections and Objections
description: Responding effectively to examiner rejections and objections is a critical aspect of the patent application process.
guidance: Understand the issues raised in office actions, analyze cited prior art, and craft persuasive responses. Amend claims where appropriate, supply technical explanations, and provide supporting data or arguments to distinguish over cited references.

name: Craft Persuasive Office-Action Responses
description: Crafting persuasive responses involves addressing each point raised by the examiner with clear and well-supported arguments.
guidance: Use claim amendments, provide technical data, and explain why the examiner’s interpretation may be incorrect. Highlight distinguishing features, technical advantages, or experimental results that demonstrate novelty and non-obviousness.

name: Avoid Overly Broad Claims
description: Overly broad claims can lead to rejections based on prior art or being deemed abstract ideas.
guidance: Tailor claim scope to what is supported by the specification and distinguishable from prior art. Example anti-pattern: claiming 'a method for data analysis using machine learning' without specifying a technical context or specific improvements.

name: Ensure Consistency Between Claims and Description
description: Inconsistencies between the claims and the detailed description can weaken the patent application and lead to rejections.
guidance: Make sure all claim features have corresponding support in the specification and that the specification does not introduce features unsupportable in the claims. If claims reference a preprocessing technique, the description should explain it in detail.

name: Leverage Claim Form Choices and Functional Language
description: Use appropriate claim formats (method, system) and functional language strategically to capture inventive concepts.
guidance: Craft method and system claims as complementary protections. Use functional language where supported by the specification, but ensure adequate structure and implementation detail are provided to avoid indefiniteness or abstractness rejections. Engage with examiners using these claim strategies during prosecution.

name: Double patenting (key term / 1504.06)
description: Double patenting refers to the prohibition against an inventor holding two patents for the same invention or for obvious variations of the same invention, to prevent unjustified extension of patent rights.
guidance: Discusses how double-patenting principles apply in the design patent context and the prohibition's effect on prosecution and claim scope.

name: Drawings or photographs requirement (37 CFR 1.152 / 1503.02)
description: 37 CFR 1.152 specifies that design patent applications must include drawings or photographs that clearly depict the design's appearance, showing all features of the claimed design.
guidance: Section 1503.02 (Drawings) explains acceptable drawing conventions, viewpoints, shading, broken lines, and photographic submissions for clearly showing the claimed ornamental features.

name: Simulation (1504.01(d))
description: 1504.01(d) — Issues relating to simulation (representations that simulate the appearance rather than the actual article).
guidance: Guidance on acceptability of simulated views (e.g., perspective vs. actual appearance) and limitations on representations that are not faithful to the claimed article.

name: Considerations under 35 U.S.C. 112 for design applications (1504.04)
description: Section 1504.04: Considerations under 35 U.S.C. 112 (written description, definiteness, etc.) as applied to design patent applications.
guidance: Addresses how written description/definiteness requirements are satisfied for design claims, the role of drawings vs. text, and permissible claim scope language.

name: Extent of legal protection determined by claims
description: The extent of the legal protection conferred by a Eurasian patent shall be determined by the claims; the description and drawings shall serve only to interpret the claims.
guidance: Article 10 — Interpretation guidance and claim-related rules are addressed in Patent Regulations (Article 14(vii)).

name: Patent Regulations: interpretation of claims
description: Patent Regulations shall provide for the interpretation of the claims.
guidance: Article 14(vii) — Rules for interpreting claim language, role of description/drawings to be set out.

name: Treat preamble and transitional phrases appropriately (comprising/consisting essentially of/consisting of)
description: Preamble language and the transitional term must be given proper import; 'comprising' is open-ended, 'consisting essentially of' signals limited openness, and 'consisting of' is closed.
guidance: ‘Comprising’ covers the recited subject matter alone or with unrecited subject matter. 'Consisting essentially of' occupies a middle ground; absent clear indication in spec/claims of what basic and novel characteristics are, 'consisting essentially of' will be construed as equivalent to 'comprising.' If applicant contends additional elements are excluded by 'consisting essentially of,' applicant bears the burden of showing additional elements would materially change the invention. (See Genentech v. Chiron; PPG Indus.; AK Steel.)

name: Review the entire application to find support for claimed elements
description: Prior to determining whether the disclosure provides adequate written description for the claimed subject matter, the examiner should review the claims and the entire specification, including specific embodiments, figures, and sequence listings, to understand how applicant provides support for the various features of the claimed invention.
guidance: Review should include summary, detailed description, claims, abstract, drawings, sequence listings. Determine the field of the invention and the level of skill and knowledge in the art; consider what a person of ordinary skill would understand from the disclosure at the filing date (see Wang Labs.). Information well known in the art need not be described in detail (Hybritech). Use patents and publications to assess maturity of the art.

name: Written description requires showing possession of the claimed invention as a whole
description: Determine whether there is sufficient written description to inform a skilled artisan that the applicant was in possession of the claimed invention as a whole at the time of filing.
guidance: Possession may be shown in many ways: reduction to practice, detailed drawings or structural chemical formulas, or any description of sufficient, relevant, identifying characteristics such that a skilled artisan recognizes applicant had possession. The inquiry is factual and case-by-case (Purdue Pharma; Pfaff v. Wells).

name: Actual reduction to practice can show possession
description: Possession may be shown by describing an actual reduction to practice of the claimed invention (constructing an embodiment or performing a process that met all claim limitations).
guidance: Reduction to practice requires a physical embodiment including all limitations and a determination that the invention will work for its intended purpose (Cooper v. Goldfarb; UMC Elecs.; Estee Lauder). For biological materials, description of a deposit in accordance with 37 CFR 1.801 et seq. may evidence reduction to practice.

name: Detailed drawings or structural chemical formulas can show possession
description: A clear depiction of the invention in detailed drawings or in structural chemical formulas can permit a person skilled in the art to recognize that applicant had possession.
guidance: Drawings alone may provide an adequate written description (Vas-Cath; Wolfensperger; Autogiro). Generic chemical formulae often indicate with specificity what a genus claim encompasses; one skilled in the art can identify many species from a formula (Eli Lilly). The description need only detail what is new or not conventional (Hybritech).

name: Functional disclosure vs structural disclosure — when function alone is insufficient
description: Describing a composition or gene by its function alone is typically insufficient to support claims to that composition; an inventor must provide structure, method of obtaining, or other distinguishing characteristics unless a well-established correlation allows prediction of structure from function.
guidance: Court examples: a gene cannot be claimed merely by describing its function (Eli Lilly); disclosure of an antigen does not by itself provide adequate written description of antibodies claimed by binding affinity (Amgen v. Sanofi; Centocor v. Abbott). If the art establishes strong correlation between structure and function, one skilled in the art may predict structure from function with reasonable confidence (Enzo Biochem). Without correlation, function-only disclosure is a 'wish' rather than possession (In re Wilder).

name: Means-plus-function (35 U.S.C. 112(f)/pre-AIA para 6) require corresponding structure/materials/acts in specification
description: If a claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (or pre-AIA sixth paragraph), it must be interpreted to cover the corresponding structure, materials, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.
guidance: The examiner must consider summary/detailed description, original claims, abstract, and drawings to find corresponding structure. Written description adequacy for means-plus-function requires either (1) the written description adequately links particular structure/materials/acts to perform the recited function, or (2) it is clear that one skilled in the art would know what structure in the specification performs the function. Failure to disclose sufficient corresponding structure makes the limitation indefinite under 112(b) and also fails 112(a). See Aristocrat; Atmel; Biomedino; In re Noll; MPEP §2181.

name: When a means-/step-plus-function limitation lacks corresponding structure, reject under both indefiniteness and written description
description: A rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (indefiniteness) for lack of corresponding structure for a means-plus-function limitation cannot stand where there is adequate description in the specification to satisfy 112(a); conversely, lack of corresponding structure supports rejection under both 112(b) and 112(a).
guidance: If a means-plus-function limitation is indefinite for lack of disclosed corresponding structure/materials/acts, then the claim limitation lacks an adequate written description as well and should be rejected accordingly. See In re Noll and cited guidance.

name: Analyze single-embodiment/species claims with a stepwise checklist
description: For claims drawn to a single embodiment or species, follow the specific checklist: (A) does the application describe an actual reduction to practice; (B) if not, does it include drawings or structural formulas sufficiently detailed; (C) if not, does it set forth distinguishing identifying characteristics sufficiently detailed to show possession.
guidance: If the application as filed describes the complete structure or acts of the claimed invention as a whole, the written description requirement is satisfied. If complete structure is not disclosed, determine whether other identifying characteristics (including function+structure correlation in biotech) allow a skilled artisan to recognize possession. Examples/case law and further sub-steps provided in the guideline (Fields v. Conover; Eli Lilly; In re Wilder).

name: Distinguish genus claims from species claims
description: A claim limited to a single disclosed embodiment or species is analyzed as a claim to that species; a claim encompassing two or more embodiments or species is analyzed as a genus.
guidance: See MPEP §806.04(e). The written description expectations differ: genus-level claims require adequate support across the breadth, while species claims are judged against the single disclosed embodiment/species.

name: Consider factors affecting sufficiency of written description (art maturity, skill level, method of making)
description: Whether the specification shows possession is a factual determination considering multiple factors: level of skill and knowledge in the art, partial structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics with correlation, and method of making the claimed invention.
guidance: Patents and printed publications in the art should be relied upon to determine whether an art is mature. In mature technologies where knowledge and skill are high, written description questions are less likely for claims present in the original filing, even when only a method of making is disclosed. In emerging or unpredictable technologies more evidence is required. Disclosure of a partial structure without additional characterization may be insufficient (Amgen).

name: Product-by-process vs product claims — process disclosure may not support product claim absent evidence product is produced
description: Disclosure of only a method of making the invention and the function may not be sufficient to support a product claim (other than a product-by-process claim). If the process has actually been used to produce the product, written description for a product-by-process claim is satisfied; otherwise the requirement may not be met.
guidance: See Fiers v. Revel; Amgen. Where it is not clear that the acts in the specification can be performed or that the product is produced by the process, written description may fail.

name: Necessity of determining inventive concept(s) (inC(s))
description: The MBA framework (as applied in Enfish & TLI) requires first determining an ETCI's 'inventive concept(s), inC(s)' as the foundational basis for enabling correct and complete description of the ETCI within SPL testing.
guidance: The paper treats inC(s) as indispensable: enabling refined claim interpretation and construction, enforcing 'levels of abstraction', and forming the proper semantic/pragmatic basis for all subsequent SPL tests. Enfish and TLI are cited as acknowledging this necessity; the author argues that testing should start with extracting inC(s) from the specification as understood by the person of pertinent ordinary skill and creativity (pposc).

name: Claim interpretation must depend on inC(s)
description: A correct claim interpretation for an ETCI should be founded on the invention's inC(s) rather than solely on a literal list of claim limitations.
guidance: The paper cites Enfish (page references) asserting the claim interpretation step must be grounded in the inC(s), enabling a refined (context-sensitive) interpretation that supports rational SPL testing rather than free‑style or purely limitations‑based interpretation (criticized as BRIPTO-style).

name: Claim construction must depend on inC(s)
description: Claim construction (the court/examiner's formal construing of claim scope) should follow from the inC(s) (and the resulting claim interpretation) to ensure determinate, MBA-consistent outcomes.
guidance: The author frames claim construction as the final step of a 2-step algorithm (inC(s) → claim interpretation → claim construction) required by the MBA framework and reflected in Enfish/TLI; proper construction may obviate certain speculative pitfalls and aligns with refined procedural testing (FSTP).

name: FSTP-Test (Facts Screening/Transforming/Presenting) — procedural, rational refinement of the TS test
description: FSTP is proposed as a procedural, exhaustive, and rational refinement of the Supreme Court's Two‑Step (TS) test for subject‑matter eligibility; it operates mainly at A-/E-levels (refined knowledge representations) and is intended to be (largely) automatable.
guidance: The paper states three claims about FSTP: (I) it is a rational refinement of the TS test; (II) an exhaustive refinement; (III) the only rational exhaustive refinement. FSTP moves from O-level descriptions (TS) to A-/E-level refined representations and enables deterministic/rational argumentation and potential automation. Passing the FSTP-Test (all component tests) indicates alignment with the MBA framework. The paper includes a formalized Figure 2 and claims executability even fully automatically where Rational (otherwise semi-automatic).

name: FSTP test 1 — Biosig-test (novelty/definiteness/completeness requirement)
description: Biosig-test is passed iff the examined COM(ETCI#) describes a new and useful invention and the COM(ETCI#) is definite and complete.
guidance: The paper links this test to ensuring the claimed invention (as represented by the COM construct) meets basic patentability prerequisites (new/useful) and that the communication/representation is definite and complete. Failing this test indicates absence of an inventive concept or insufficient disclosure for rational testing.

name: FSTP test 4 — Bilski-test (identifiability of unlimitedly preemptive E-crC)
description: Bilski-test is passed iff the set ULPE‑crC (the set of E‑crC elements that are unlimitedly preemptive) is identifiable.
guidance: This test seeks to identify any elements of the claimed invention that would afford unlimited preemption (which Bilski and related doctrine caution against). If such unlimitedly preemptive elements exist and cannot be identified/mitigated, patent-eligibility may fail.

name: FSTP test 5 — Mayo/Myriad/Alice-related test (statutory exceptions / abstractness / natural law checks)
description: The Mayo-/Myriad-test (and the Alice-test as incorporated) is passed iff the combined subtests (including Alice-related subtests 1–5 as used in the paper) hold and there is no E‑crC outside ULPE‑crC that is unlimitedly preemptive.
guidance: This composite test operationalizes the Supreme Court's Mayo/Alice/Myriad analytical concerns within the FSTP framework: determine whether claimed subject matter is directed to a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon), and if so, whether the claim applies that exception in a way that transforms it into patent‑eligible subject matter. The paper treats this as an explicit FSTP condition (see Figure 2 and associated text).

name: FSTP test 7 — KSR(RS)-test (obviousness / rationale test)
description: KSR(RS)-test (obviousness-related) is applied across enumerated element indices (formalized in the paper) as part of assessing inventive step (reasoned-synthesis or RS analysis).
guidance: Although only tersely formalized in the text, this test corresponds to KSR/Graham obviousness analysis performed at the refined knowledge levels (RS), integrated into the FSTP sequence to check whether claimed combinations are obvious in light of the relevant refined records.

name: Effect of similar but not identical prior devices
description: Prior use of articles less perfect but identical in principle invalidates the patent; prior use of similar but not identical devices cannot defeat the patent but may show the state of the art and limit the patent.
guidance: If prior devices embody the same principles and can produce the same result, the defence will prevail (Stitt v. Fastem R. B. Co.). Similar devices may restrict claim scope but not necessarily destroy novelty (Magin v. McKay; McFarland v. Spencer).

name: Acceptance of plans from party in possession or control
description: Plans for reconstruction, renewal, reconstruction, or repair of a bridge will be accepted from the person or corporation in actual possession or control of the property — presumption being that such possession or control is legal.
guidance: Applies where franchise passed with title after plans approved and bridge built; supports acting on plans from current occupant rather than remote claimants.

name: Failure to Claim Inventor’s Invention (35 U.S.C. 112(b), pre-AIA 112, 2nd para)
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as failing to set forth the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor, or for pre-AIA the applicant(s) regard as their invention. Evidence that claim [2] fail(s) to correspond in scope with that which the inventor or a joint inventor, or for pre-AIA the applicant(s) regard as the invention can be found in the reply filed [3]. In that paper, the inventor or a joint inventor, or for pre-AIA the applicant has stated [4], and this statement indicates that the invention is different from what is defined in the claim(s) because [5].
guidance: Examiner Note: This rejection must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.02 or 7.103. Use only where inventor/applicant has stated, somewhere other than in the application as filed, that the invention is different from what is defined in the claims. In bracket 3 identify the submission and date; in bracket 4 set forth what was stated; in bracket 5 explain how statement indicates a different invention.

name: Failure To Particularly Point Out and Distinctly Claim (Indefinite) (35 U.S.C.112(b), pre-AIA 112, 2nd para)
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor, or for pre-AIA the applicant regards as the invention.
guidance: Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.02 or 7.103. Follow with one or more of form paragraphs 7.34.02–7.34.11 as applicable; if none appropriate supply a full explanation of claim deficiency. Whenever possible, identify particular term(s)/limitation(s) rendering the claim indefinite and state why. If the scope can be determined by one of ordinary skill, this rejection is inappropriate. See MPEP §§2171–2174. For pro se applicants see 7.34.15.

name: Terminology Used Inconsistent with Accepted Meaning
description: Where applicant acts as his or her own lexicographer to specifically define a term of a claim contrary to its ordinary meaning, the written description must clearly redefine the claim term and set forth the uncommon definition so as to put one reasonably skilled in the art on notice that the applicant intended to so redefine that claim term. The term “[1]” in claim [2] is used by the claim to mean “[3],” while the accepted meaning is “[4].” The term is indefinite because the specification does not clearly redefine the claim term.
guidance: In bracket 3 point out the meaning assigned by applicant's claims (considering entire disclosure). In bracket 4 point out accepted meaning with support (textbook/dictionary). Must be preceded by 7.34.01. Use only where specification does not clearly redefine the term. See MPEP §2173.05(a).

name: Relative Term — Term of Degree Rendering Claim Indefinite
description: The term “[1]” in claim [2] is a relative term which renders the claim indefinite. The term “[1]” is not defined by the claim, the specification does not provide a standard for ascertaining the requisite degree, and one of ordinary skill in the art would not be reasonably apprised of the scope of the invention. [3]
guidance: In bracket 3 explain which parameter, quantity, or other limitation is rendered indefinite by the term in bracket 1. Must be preceded by 7.34.01.

name: Use Claims (claiming a use without steps)
description: Claim [1] provides for the use of [2], but, since the claim does not set forth any steps involved in the method/process, it is unclear what method/process applicant is intending to encompass. A claim is indefinite where it merely recites a use without any active, positive steps delimiting how this use is actually practiced. Claim [3] is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 because the claimed recitation of a use, without setting forth any steps involved in the process, results in an improper definition of a process.
guidance: See Ex parte Dunki and Clinical Products, Ltd. v. Brenner for examples. Use when a claim defines 'use' but lacks steps making it a proper process claim.

name: Modifier of 'Means' Lacks Function
description: (¶ 7.34.11) Examiner Note: In bracket 2, insert what is being used. For example: the monoclonal antibodies of claim 4, where the claim recites 'a method for using monoclonal antibodies of claim 4 to purify interferon.' See MPEP §2173.05(q).
guidance: This paragraph must be preceded by 7.34.01. Use when words preceding 'means' or substitute do not convey function vs. structure; see guidance on invoking 35 U.S.C. 112(f).

name: Claims Are a Literal Translation (narrative, indefinite, foreign-language translation)
description: Claim [1] uses 'means' or a generic placeholder and is preceded by the word(s) '[2]'. It is unclear whether these words convey function or structure. The claims are generally narrative and indefinite, failing to conform with current U.S. practice. They appear to be a literal translation into English from a foreign document and are replete with grammatical and idiomatic errors.
guidance: Use when it cannot be determined from the specification whether words convey function or structure; must be preceded by 7.34.01. If claim element recites structure for performing the function, 112(f) will not be invoked. See Ex parte Klumb and MPEP §2173.

name: Essential Steps Omitted (omitting essential process steps) (35 U.S.C.112(b))
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) as being incomplete for omitting essential steps, such omission amounting to a gap between the steps. The omitted steps are: [2].
guidance: Must be preceded by 7.30.02 or 7.103. In bracket 2 recite omitted steps and give rationale for considering them critical or essential. See MPEP §2172.01.

name: Essential Elements Omitted (omitting essential structural elements)
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) as being incomplete for omitting essential elements, such omission amounting to a gap between the elements. The omitted elements are: [2].
guidance: Must be preceded by 7.30.02 or 7.103. In bracket 2 recite omitted elements and explain why they are critical/essential. See MPEP §2172.01.

name: Essential Cooperative Relationships Omitted (omitting structural cooperative relationships)
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) as being incomplete for omitting essential structural cooperative relationships of elements, such omission amounting to a gap between the necessary structural connections. The omitted structural cooperative relationships are: [2].
guidance: Must be preceded by 7.30.02 or 7.103. In bracket 2 recite omitted structural cooperative relationships and give rationale for considering them critical/essential. See MPEP §2172.01.

name: Rejection Under 35 U.S.C.112, Pro Se (claims drafted by pro se applicant)
description: Claim [1] rejected as failing to define the invention in the manner required by 35 U.S.C. 112(b). The claim(s) are narrative in form and replete with indefinite language. The structure which goes to make up the device must be clearly and positively specified and organized to present a complete operative device. The claim(s) must be in one sentence form only.
guidance: Use for pro se applicants; note claim format examples in cited patents. This paragraph addresses common pro se drafting deficiencies.

name: Unclear Whether Recited Structure/Material/Acts Preclude Application of 35 U.S.C.112(f) (¶7.34.16)
description: The claim limitation '[1]' uses the phrase 'means for' or 'step for' or a generic placeholder coupled with functional language, but it is modified by some structure, material, or acts recited in the claim. It is unclear whether the recited structure, material, or acts are sufficient for performing the claimed function because [2].
guidance: Applicant may amend the claim to avoid invoking 112(f) or show that the phrase is functional without sufficient structure, or amend to add structure. In bracket 1 recite limitation; in bracket 2 explain why unclear. This form paragraph must be preceded by 7.30.02 and 7.34.01.

name: Applicant Asserts Claim Limitation Invokes 112(f) but 'Means for' Not Used (¶7.34.17)
description: Applicant asserts that the claim element '[1]' invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) even though the phrase 'means for' is not used. However, it is unclear whether the claim element invokes 112(f) because [2].
guidance: Applicant may (a) amend to include 'means for' modified by functional language and not by sufficient structure, (b) amend so it will not be interpreted under 112(f), or (c) amend the written description to expressly recite corresponding structure/material/acts without new matter. Alternatively applicant may present sufficient showing that the written description implicitly discloses the corresponding structure. In brackets: 1 recite limitation; 2 explain why unclear. Must be preceded by 7.30.02 and 7.34.01. See MPEP §707.07(a) and §2181.

name: No Disclosure or Insufficient Disclosure of Corresponding Structure/Material/Acts for Function (¶7.34.18)
description: Claim element '[1]' invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f). However, the written description fails to disclose the corresponding structure, material, or acts for the claimed function. [2]
guidance: In bracket 1 recite limitation invoking 112(f). In bracket 2 explain why disclosure is insufficient. Applicant may state on record what corresponding structure/material/acts implicitly set forth (see 37 CFR 1.75(d) and MPEP §§608.01(o), 2181). Must be preceded by 7.30.02 and 7.34.01.

name: Fails To Clearly Link/Associate Disclosed Structure/Material/Acts to Function (¶7.34.19)
description: Claim element '[1]' invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f). However, the written description fails to clearly link or associate the disclosed structure, material, or acts to the claimed function such that one of ordinary skill in the art would recognize what structure, material, or acts perform the claimed function. [2]
guidance: Applicant may (a) amend the claim to avoid 112(f), (b) amend the specification to clearly link structure/material/acts to the function without new matter, or (c) state on record where in the specification the corresponding structure/material/acts are set forth and linked to the function (see 37 CFR 1.175(d) and MPEP §§608.01(o), 2181). Must be preceded by 7.30.02 and 7.34.01.

name: Specification Objected; Written Description Only Implicitly/Inherently Discloses Structure (¶7.34.20)
description: Claim element '[1]' invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f). The written description only implicitly or inherently sets forth the corresponding structure, material, or acts that perform the claimed function.
guidance: Pursuant to 37 CFR 1.75(d) and MPEP §§608.01(o), 2181 applicant should (a) amend claim to avoid 112(f), (b) amend written description to expressly recite corresponding structure/material/acts and clearly link to function without new matter, or (c) state on record what corresponding structure/material/acts implicitly or inherently set forth in the specification perform the claimed function. In bracket 1 recite limitation.

name: Claim Limitation Interpreted under 35 U.S.C.112(f) (¶7.34.21)
description: Claim limitation(s) '[1]' has/have been interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) because it uses a generic placeholder '[2]' coupled with functional language '[3]' without reciting sufficient [structure/material/acts]. A review of the specification shows the following appears to be the corresponding structure described: [6].
guidance: If applicant disputes interpretation, they must identify corresponding structure with reference to specification page/line and drawing reference characters in response. If applicant does not intend invocation of 112(f), they may amend or present showing that claim recites sufficient structure. Use only when additional explanation regarding treatment under 112(f) is necessary. May be used for multiple claims. Provide bracketed items 1–6 as instructed. See MPEP §2173 and 2011 Supplementary Examination Guidelines.

name: Applicant Asserts Claim Limitation Does Not Invoke 112(f) but No Structure is Recited (¶7.34.22)
description: Applicant asserts that claim element '[1]' does not invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f). However, it is unclear whether the element invokes 112(f) because [2].
guidance: Applicant may (a) amend the claim to add sufficient structure/material/acts to perform the function, or (b) present sufficient showing that the claim limitation recites sufficient structure/material/acts to preclude application of 112(f). See MPEP §2181. Use when applicant replies asserting no invocation of 112(f) though no structure is provided. Must be preceded by 7.30.02 and 7.34.01.

name: Statement of Statutory Basis — 35 U.S.C.112(d) (pre-AIA 112, 4th paragraph)
description: Quotations of 35 U.S.C. 112(d)/pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, fourth paragraph: a claim in dependent form shall contain a reference to a claim previously set forth and then specify a further limitation of the subject matter claimed; a dependent claim shall be construed to incorporate by reference all limitations of the claim to which it refers.
guidance: Form paragraph 7.36 must be preceded by 7.30.02 and 7.34.01. Use paragraph 7.36 only once in a given Office action. The statute is required in first actions on merits and final rejections; otherwise use paragraph 7.103.

name: Improper Dependent Claim (35 U.S.C.112(d)/pre-AIA 112, 4th para)
description: Claim [1] rejected as being of improper dependent form for failing to further limit the subject matter of the claim upon which it depends, or for failing to include all the limitations of the claim upon which it depends. [2].
guidance: Applicant may cancel, amend to proper dependent form, rewrite in independent form, or present sufficient showing that the dependent claim complies. In bracket 2 insert explanation of what is in the claim and why it does not constitute a further limitation. Note Federal Circuit holdings that failure to comply renders dependent claim unpatentable; treat as unpatentable (not merely object to form). Must be preceded by 7.37.

name: Field of existing technology considered in inventiveness assessment
description: For invention patents, assess not only the technical field of the invention but also similar or related technical fields and technical problems that could prompt skilled persons to search other fields. For utility model patents, the general focus is on the technical field to which the utility model belongs; similar or related fields may be considered only if prior art gives clear inspiration prompting such a search.
guidance: This distinction affects the scope of prior art and analogous fields considered when determining whether a skilled person would be prompted to combine or adapt prior art to arrive at the claimed solution.

name: Form paragraph and notification when Certificate benefits denied (¶ 5.04)
description: When correspondence contains a Certificate of Mailing under 37 CFR 1.8 or requests Express Mail benefits under 37 CFR 1.10 but was not deposited with the U.S. Postal Service, a form paragraph (¶ 5.04) should be used to notify applicant that the paper is not entitled to the benefits and the Office receipt date is used to determine timeliness.
guidance: Misuse of a Certificate or improperly claiming Express Mail benefits that appears to be more than a one-time inadvertent error should be brought to the attention of the Office of Enrollment and Discipline.

name: Scope limitation: only searched subject-matter is examinable
description: If the search covered only some claims or part of claims, only the subject-matter which has been searched (as indicated in the ISR and/or WO-ISA) can be the object of the international preliminary examination; it should always be made clear which claims have been examined.
guidance: Any amended claims introducing unsearched matter will not be given an opinion in the IPER (indicate this under Section III with reasons on separate sheet). The IPEA has no responsibility for actions taken by the ISA and there is no PCT provision for an IPEA review/appeal of such ISA decisions.

name: Indication and handling of partial top-up searches
description: Where a top-up search is made for some claims or part of claims, there is no specific indication on the form of which claims are not covered by the top-up search or why only a partial top-up search was made.
guidance: Such information should be derivable from indications in Sections I and III of the WO/IPER; reasons for partial searches are not explicitly given on the form.

name: Right to telephone consultation (no personal interviews) and related effects
description: Art.34(2) gives applicant right to communicate orally with the IPEA; telephone consultations should be granted but personal interviews are not granted (applicants requesting personal interview are offered telephone consultation).
guidance: As a general rule applicant has right to one telephone consultation. After a telephone consultation applicant should generally be given a time limit (normally two months) to file amended claims/arguments. If applicant expresses intention not to file further observations and agrees to receive an IPER without further interaction, minutes are sent and directly followed up with a negative IPER (no time limit set). If consultation requested after issuance of further written opinion but before IPER establishment, request must be granted before a negative IPER is issued but applicant does not have right to file further amendments unless explicitly agreed. Matters for discussion should be clearly stated in advance; examiner records arrangement in file and sends a copy to applicant. If applicant wishes to discuss amended claims during consultation, a copy should be sent in advance. Result recorded and forwarded to applicant. If consultation replaces second written opinion and agreement on amendments reached, Form 428 includes warning that amendments cannot be made by IPEA and invitation to file amended sheets normally within one month but at least one month before IPER deadline. If no agreement reached, applicant informed arguments will be taken into account in IPER.

name: Content limitation of the IPER opinion
description: Art.35(2) specifies that the IPER shall not contain any statement on whether the claimed invention is or seems to be patentable or unpatentable according to any national law; the purpose is to give an opinion only and not to grant/refuse the application.
guidance: The report should not give the impression that any part of the application may or may not be allowable; it will only state whether or not the claims meet certain criteria. The IPER is drafted like the WO-ISA: a positive or negative opinion is given for all claims, taking into account arguments/amendments submitted by the applicant. The same criteria apply as to the WO-ISA with respect to examination issues.

name: Combining prior art elements to yield predictable results (rationale A)
description: To reject a claim based on this rationale, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries. Then, Office personnel must articulate: (1) a finding that the prior art included each element claimed, although not necessarily in a single prior art reference; (2) a finding that one of ordinary skill could have combined the elements as claimed by known methods, and each element merely performs the same function as it does separately; (3) a finding that one of ordinary skill would have recognized that the results of the combination were predictable; and (4) whatever additional findings based on the Graham factual inquiries may be necessary to explain a conclusion of obviousness.
guidance: All four findings must be made to support a combination-based obviousness rejection. Examiners must articulate why a person of ordinary skill would have combined the elements and why the combination would produce predictable results. Anti-patterns: pointing only to the presence of elements in prior art without finding predictability; failing to address teaching away or lack of motivation. Examples: Anderson’s-Black Rock (combination yielded no new function) vs. Adams (predictability absent because prior art taught away).

name: Simple substitution of one known element for another (rationale B)
description: To reject a claim based on this rationale, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries. Then, Office personnel must articulate: (1) a finding that the prior art contained a device differing from the claimed device by substitution of some components; (2) a finding that the substituted components and their functions were known in the art; (3) a finding that one of ordinary skill could have substituted one known element for another and the results would have been predictable; and (4) whatever additional Graham-based findings are necessary to explain obviousness.
guidance: Used when the claimed invention is a predictable result of replacing one known element with an equivalent known element. Must show the substitution would have been within the ordinary skill and predictable. Examples: In re Fout, In re O’Farrell, Ex parte Smith. Do not treat mere possibility to substitute as sufficient without predictability and supporting factual findings.

name: Resolve the Graham factual inquiries before applying rationales
description: Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries before applying any of the enumerated rationales for obviousness.
guidance: The Graham inquiries (scope and content of the prior art; differences between the prior art and the claims; level of ordinary skill in the art; and secondary considerations) are foundational. Every rationale applied (combination, substitution, obvious-to-try, etc.) requires that these factual inquiries be addressed and that additional relevant findings be articulated where appropriate.

name: Link factual findings to the legal conclusion; avoid conclusory rejections
description: Any rationale employed must provide a link between the factual findings and the legal conclusion of obviousness. Rejections on obviousness cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements; there must be some articulated reasoning with some rational underpinning to support the legal conclusion of obviousness.
guidance: Examiners must clearly explain the reasons why a claimed invention would have been obvious in view of the prior art. Cite In re Kahn and KSR: provide explicit reasoning, not bare conclusions. Where a rationale is invoked, map factual findings to the rationale and legal standard.

name: Teaching away reduces weight of obviousness
description: When the prior art teaches away from combining certain known elements or from the claimed modification, discovery of a successful combination may be nonobvious.
guidance: If references discourage the very combination or modification proposed, that can support nonobviousness (Adams, Crocs, DePuy Spine). Examiners must identify teachings that would have deterred a person of ordinary skill from combining the elements.

name: Articulated reason or motivation to combine (including common sense)
description: It can be important to identify a reason that would have prompted a person of ordinary skill in the relevant field to combine the elements in the way the claimed invention does; KSR allows recourse to logic, judgment, and common sense, but the analysis should explain why.
guidance: Motivation may derive from prior art teachings, market forces, or common sense, but examiners must explain the rationale. Common sense may support a motivation to combine in appropriate cases but must be accompanied by an explanation tied to the facts (see Wyers, Ecolab).

name: Meaning of 'substantially as described' in a claim
description: The phrase 'substantially as described' in the Claim signifies much or little, as the patentee evidently designed, and is always supposed to be incorporated in the Claim whether or not actually inserted.
guidance: This phrase relates only to the material features of the invention as shown by its purpose and the elements composing it; it allows the claim to be construed by reference to the specification for what the patentee intended to cover. (Cites Matthews v. Schonebeiger and others.)

name: Meaning of 'as herein described' and reference to specification
description: The similar phrase 'as herein described' likewise refers to the specification for a fuller and more exact statement of the subject-matter of the Claim.
guidance: When such phrases appear, interpret the claim in light of the specification; the specification may supply elements not explicitly mentioned in the claim. (Cites Seymour v. Osborne.)

name: Meaning of the word 'specification' depends on context
description: The word 'specification' is sometimes employed to denote both the Claim and the Description, and sometimes only the Description; when used without 'claim' it may mean the entire paper (Description and Claims), but when 'claim' is also used it often means the Description only.
guidance: Determine whether 'specification' denotes Description+Claims or Description alone by context and statutory references. (Cites Wilson v. Coon and statutory sections.)

name: Claims referring to the specification must be construed by it
description: Claims which refer to the specification must be construed by the specification.
guidance: If the claim points to the specification (e.g., via phrases like 'as described'), the specification governs construction and may make a claim valid even if it appears on its face to cover only a function or result. (Cites Gottfried v. Philip Best Brewing Co., Seymour v. Osborne.)

name: Limitation by words 'all as shown and described' in the claim
description: The words in the Claim 'all as shown and described' limit the Claim to the exact thing shown.
guidance: Such limiting language may confine the claim to the precise form depicted in the drawings and description. (Cites Osceola Mfg. Co. v. Pie.)

name: Separate claims cannot be construed together as one
description: Two apparently separate Claims cannot be construed together as one Claim and be supported by each other.
guidance: Do not merge separate claims to create a single claim scope; each claim must stand on its own. (Cites Seymour v. McCormick.)

name: Distinction between 'making/selling' and 'use' claims
description: The 'making' or 'selling' of a substance is essentially distinct from its 'use', and a patent for the latter does not confer upon the patentee any exclusive right to the former.
guidance: A patent claiming only the use of an item does not give rights to make or sell it; drafting and claim analysis must keep these distinctions clear. (Cites Keystone Bridge Co.)

name: Interpretive treatment of descriptive phrases such as 'in the manner and for the purposes herein specified'
description: In the Claim the words 'in the manner and for the purposes herein specified' should not be construed to cover every part shown in the drawings and Description, nor to confine the invention to the precise form therein shown.
guidance: These words should be read to avoid unduly narrow or overly broad interpretations: they do not automatically incorporate every drawing detail nor lock the patentee into a precise depicted form. (Cites Reed v. Chase.)

name: Use of specification to supply elements not in the claim
description: Phrases like 'as herein described' or references to the specification may embrace elements not mentioned in the Claim.
guidance: When the claim refers to the specification, courts may read in material features from the description to clarify the claim scope. (Cites Vance v. Campbell and others.)

name: Refusal to register pending determination of conflicting claims (special case)
description: Comptroller refuses to register any mark where there are conflicting claims until their rights have been determined according to law; the manner in which the rights of such claimants may be submitted to the Court by the Comptroller or, if the Comptroller so require, by the claimants, shall, unless the Court otherwise order, be by a special case; and such special case shall be filed and proceeded with in like manner as any other special case submitted to the Court, or in such other manner as the Court may direct.
guidance: Settlement of special cases: where the special case is to be submitted to the parties it may be agreed to by them, or if they differ, may be settled by the Comptroller on payment of the prescribed fees. The fees for settling the special case is 21. See First Schedule. Form of Request: Form 80.

name: Special particulars for certain goods and non-Roman characters
description: When a mark is used on metal goods other than cutlery/edge tools/raw steel, the Application Form should state of what metal(s) the goods are made. When the mark includes words printed in other than Roman characters, a translation of such words, signed by the Applicant or Agent, should be given at the back or foot of the Application Form and each additional representation. For marks claimed in Classes 23–25, the Applicant should state by what name the particular mark would be referred to in the invoices of his house.
guidance: See Rule 12, Rule 15 and class-specific notes (e.g., cotton goods).

name: Defense — Infirmity of proof (§ 11.24(d)(1)(ii))
description: The Office will not accept reciprocal discipline if there was such an infirmity of proof establishing the conduct as to give rise to a clear conviction that the Office could not, consistently with its duty, accept the state's conclusion.
guidance: This is a difficult collateral-attack standard. A voluntary resignation in lieu of discipline, especially where facts are largely uncontested, ordinarily does not constitute an infirmity of proof. Courts routinely reject claims that resignation before an adjudicatory hearing shows infirmity of proof.

name: Proper search / Search strategy
description: A proper search is the mainstay of the U.S. Patent system. The examiner must be trained in the art of analyzing the scope of the claims and searching.
guidance: Managers and Primary Examiners formulated standardized base search strategies for business technology aspects so that, once an examiner knows the technology and concepts in the application, the examiner can use the standardized search strategy to determine where to search in the U.S. patent system and which data files to search in Dialog and/or STN. An established search strategy advisory panel (managers and experienced examiners) is available to assist Class 705 examiners in developing a search strategy and to provide legal and procedural assistance.

name: Second-level review of allowed Class 705 applications
description: A new second-level review of all allowed applications in Class 705 is required to ensure compliance with the mandatory search requirements, clarity and completeness of reasons for allowance, and to determine whether the scope of the claims should be reconsidered.
guidance: This is a mandatory quality-control step applied to all allowed applications in the class to catch search/completeness issues and reconsider claim scope prior to allowance finalization.

name: Meaning of 'discovery' in patent law
description: In the Constitution and statute, the word 'discovery' means invention; it does not carry its broad dictionary meaning. The 'discoveries' of inventors are inventions; laws of nature or geographical discoveries are not patentable as 'discoveries.'
guidance: Patents reward inventions (created things) not findings of pre-existing natural facts. Examples: discovering an island or a law of nature is not patentable; a patent must claim invention (an art, machine, manufacture, or composition) or an improvement thereof.

name: Distinction between a process and a principle governs claim validity
description: Whether a particular patent is for a process or for a principle (law of nature) can determine its validity; claims that are for principles rather than concrete processes or apparatus may be invalid.
guidance: To decide validity, analyze if the claim is seeking to appropriate a principle/law of nature (impermissible) or is a claim to a concrete method/apparatus applying that principle. The text recommends examining controlling cases to derive the rule that underlies them all.

name: McClurg v. Kingsland (illustration of patentable process)
description: Harley's method of imparting rotary motion to molten metal by injecting it tangentially into a mould produced the desired result and was held by the Supreme Court to be a patent for a process.
guidance: This case illustrates that a practical method of applying known natural forces (centrifugal force) by a specific mechanical technique can be a patentable process, not merely a claim to the force or principle itself.

name: O'Reilly v. Morse (illustration of unpatentable principle)
description: Morse's eighth claim, construed as a claim for the use of an electric current for marking intelligible signs at any distance, was held void by the Supreme Court.
guidance: This decision exemplifies that claims which effectively claim the use of a broad natural principle (here, the electric current for conveying intelligence) without limiting to concrete means or methods are invalid.

name: Mowry v. Whitney (illustration of patentable process utilizing laws of nature)
description: Whitney's process for treating cast-iron wheels — chilling rims, then reheating in a furnace to equalize temperatures and cool slowly so as to achieve hardened rims and annealed hubs — was held to be a valid process patent.
guidance: Shows that exploiting knowledge of natural phenomena (thermal expansion/contraction) via a specific multi-stage process can be patentable; the claim was to a concrete sequence of operations, not to the natural law alone.

name: The Telephone Cases / Bell (process and apparatus claims can be patentable)
description: Bell's invention — mounting diaphragms on armatures and transmitting sounds by electrical undulations similar to air vibrations — was held to be a patent for a process as well as for an apparatus, and the process claim was valid.
guidance: Demonstrates that a novel apparatus with an associated process of application (transmitting speech by electrical undulations) can be protected; claims should tie the application of known physical laws to concrete structures and steps.

name: Step 2A — determine whether claim is directed to a judicial exception
description: Determine whether the claim is directed to a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea (judicial exceptions). If no, the claim is eligible and examination should continue for patentability. If yes, proceed to Step 2B to analyze whether the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the exception.
guidance: Examples of the types of concepts that the courts have found to be laws of nature, natural phenomena, or abstract ideas are provided in Parts I.A.2 and IV of the Interim Eligibility Guidance.

name: Definition of 'directed to'
description: "Directed to" means the exception is recited in the claim, i.e., the claim sets forth or describes the exception.
guidance: See Part I.A.1 of the Interim Eligibility Guidance for how to identify when an exception is 'recited' in the claim.

name: Streamlined analysis when claim does not 'tie up' an exception
description: If the claim when viewed as a whole clearly does not seek to 'tie up' any judicial exception, use the 'streamlined analysis' discussed in Part I.B.3 of the Interim Eligibility Guidance.
guidance: The streamlined analysis is an alternative path under Step 2A when the claim clearly does not risk preempting the exception.

name: Markedly different characteristics analysis for nature-based product limitations
description: If the claim recites a nature-based product limitation, the markedly different characteristics analysis is used to evaluate whether the claim is directed to a 'product of nature' that falls under the law of nature and natural phenomenon exceptions.
guidance: To determine whether the markedly different characteristics analysis is needed, and how to perform this analysis, see Part I.A.3 of the Interim Eligibility Guidance.

name: Supreme Court considerations for determining 'significantly more'
description: The Supreme Court has identified a number of considerations for determining whether a claim with additional elements amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception itself.
guidance: Examples of these considerations, and how they are applied, are provided in Parts I.B.1 and III of the Interim Eligibility Guidance.

name: Claim-by-claim evaluation
description: Consider each claim separately based on the particular elements recited therein – claims do not automatically rise or fall with similar claims in an application.
guidance: Do not assume a determination for one claim applies to other claims even if similar.

name: If claim recites multiple exceptions, analyze one exception
description: If a claim is directed to a plurality of exceptions, conduct the eligibility analysis for one of the exceptions. Additional elements that satisfy Step 2B for one exception will likely satisfy Step 2B for all exceptions in a claim. On the other hand, if the claim fails under Step 2B for one exception, the claim is ineligible, and no further eligibility analysis is needed.
guidance: Select an exception and apply Steps 2A/2B; a failure on one chosen exception is sufficient to deem the claim ineligible.

name: Form paragraph 7.05.01 — Rejection for non-statutory (not one of four categories)
description: Template: 'the claimed invention is directed to non-statutory subject matter. The claim(s) does not fall within at least one of the four categories of patent eligible subject matter because [1]'.
guidance: Examiner Note: (1) This form paragraph should be preceded by form paragraph 7.05. (2) In bracket 1, explain why the claimed invention is not patent eligible subject matter by identifying what the claim(s) is/are directed to and explain why it does not fall within at least one of the four categories recited in 35 U.S.C. 101 (process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter), e.g., the claim(s) is/are directed to a signal per se, mere information in the form of data, a contract between two parties, or a human being (see MPEP § 2106, subsection I). (3) For a claim that is directed to a judicial exception and is non-statutory, use form paragraph 7.05.015.

name: Form paragraph 7.05.015 — Rejection for judicial exception without significantly more
description: Template: 'the claimed invention is directed to a judicial exception (i.e., a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea) without significantly more. Claim(s) [1] is/are directed to [2]. The claim(s) does/do not include additional elements that are sufficient to amount to significantly more than the judicial exception because [3].'
guidance: Examiner Note guidance: (1) Precede with form paragraph 7.05. (2) For all claim types and any judicial exception. (3) In bracket 1, identify the claim(s) that recite the judicial exception. (4) In bracket 2, identify the exception by referring to how it is recited in the claim and explain why it is considered an exception (examples: 'the Arrhenius equation, which is a law of nature in the form of a mathematical algorithm' or 'the series of steps instructing how to hedge risk, which is a fundamental economic practice and thus an abstract idea'). For products of nature, explain how the characteristics are not markedly different from the naturally occurring counterpart (example: 'the naturally occurring DNA segment, which is not markedly different from its naturally occurring counterpart because it conveys the same genetic information'). Provide additional explanation when appropriate. (5) In bracket 3, identify the additional elements and explain why, when considered separately and in combination, they do not add significantly more — e.g., generically recited computer elements are routine in any computer implementation and do not add a meaningful limitation; steps for routine data gathering to test a correlation do not add a meaningful limitation.

name: Reasonable claim interpretation; no speculative interpretation
description: An examiner must not simply speculate about the meaning of claim language and then enter an obviousness rejection based on that speculative interpretation. A claim should not be rejected over prior art merely because it is indefinite; if a claim is susceptible to more than one interpretation, the examiner should not base a rejection on an interpretation that is not reasonable.
guidance: Cite In re Steele, In re Wilson, Ionescu; see MPEP § 2111 regarding proper claim interpretation. If claim language is considered indefinite, do not disregard the language or treat indefiniteness as a basis to reject unless a reasonable interpretation supports the rejection.

name: Consideration of all claim limitations (including negatives and new matter)
description: When evaluating obviousness, all limitations of the claims must be considered and given weight, including limitations that do not find support in the original specification (negative limitations or new matter).
guidance: All words in a claim must be considered when judging patentability against the prior art. See Ex parte Grasselli, In re Miller, and In re Wilson as authority that negative or unsupported claim limitations cannot be ignored in an obviousness analysis.

name: Do not take official notice of disputed or esoteric technical facts
description: It is inappropriate to take official notice of facts that are not beyond dispute or are esoteric; assertions of technical facts in specialized areas must be supported by reference to standard works or documentary evidence.
guidance: See In re Ahlert, In re Grose, In re Eynde: esoteric or specialized facts require documentary support; do not claim 'state of the art' by official notice where reasonable disagreement exists.

name: Omission of an element and its function is obvious if the function is not desired
description: Removing an element (and thereby omitting its function) from a prior art device is obvious if the omitted function is not desired or required in the claimed context.
guidance: Examples: Ex parte Wu, In re Larson, In re Kuhle. If the prior art feature serves a function not needed in the claimed use, omitting it may be an obvious expedient.

name: Omission of an element with retention of its function is an indicium of nonobviousness
description: If a claim omits an element of the prior art but nonetheless retains the function of that element (i.e., achieves the same function differently), this can indicate nonobviousness.
guidance: In re Edge: elimination of an element while retaining its function (via a different structure) supported nonobviousness because the function remained and the prior art approach was distinguishable.

name: Automating a manual activity is not sufficient to distinguish over prior art
description: Broadly providing an automatic or mechanical means to replace a manual activity that accomplishes the same result is generally not sufficient to render the claim nonobvious.
guidance: In re Venner: automating an old manual activity (e.g., adding timer/solenoid to known structures) is typically an obvious substitution unless unexpected results are shown.

name: Priority claims under the Paris Convention determined by national law
description: The international design application may rely for priority on prior-filed applications under the Paris Convention, but such priority is determined depending on the laws of each designated state.
guidance: When claiming priority, check how each designated contracting state interprets and applies priority rights to international design applications to avoid unintended loss of priority.

name: Intrinsic evidence (highest priority)
description: The patent itself (the claims); the patent specification; the patent prosecution history (file wrapper).
guidance: These three sources are the primary materials the court relies on when construing claim terms; the Federal Circuit (Phillips v. AWH) confirmed this hierarchy. Build constructions squarely on these sources and cite specific claim language, specification passages, and prosecution-history statements.

name: Specification as 'single best guide'
description: The specification is 'the single best guide to the meaning of a disputed term.'
guidance: Read claims in the context of the entire specification. Use statements in the specification to support or limit proposed constructions; the specification can override ordinary meaning when it clearly defines or limits a term.

name: Lexicography exception (patentee may act as lexicographer)
description: A patentee may act as their own lexicographer if they clearly redefine a term or disclaim claim scope, but this must be done with reasonable clarity.
guidance: When arguing a patentee-crafted definition, point to express definitional language or unmistakable disclaimers in the specification or prosecution history. Avoid creating ambiguous or subtle 'definitions' during prosecution that can be later used against you.

name: Prosecution history treated as intrinsic evidence
description: The patent prosecution history is intrinsic evidence and has the same authority as the specification for claim construction purposes.
guidance: Prosecution arguments, amendments, and disclaimers can narrow claim scope; look for statements that limit meaning. Defendants should search the file wrapper for narrowing statements; patentees should avoid prosecution statements that unintentionally limit claims (prosecution history estoppel).

name: Timing of Markman hearings
description: Most courts conduct Markman hearings before summary judgment, but district courts have discretion; some courts conduct early hearings while others include Markman in pretrial proceedings.
guidance: Decide when to push for an early Markman based on case posture (e.g., desire for early resolution via summary judgment or settlement). Prepare terms early—identify disputed terms during claim-charting and disclose constructions in the joint statement to preserve positions.

name: Standard of review on appeal (Federal Circuit)
description: Claim construction is a matter of law and is reviewed de novo by the Federal Circuit (often).
guidance: Because appellate review can be de novo, preserve and thoroughly develop intrinsic-record arguments and preserve issues for appeal. Recognize that factual subsidiary findings (e.g., extrinsic evidence reliance) may receive different review, but ultimate term meaning is legal.

name: Impact of claim construction on litigation outcome
description: Because claim construction defines the patent's scope, the Markman ruling often determines who wins—favorable interpretation can secure summary judgment or motivate settlement; unfavorable interpretation may eliminate key claims before trial.
guidance: Treat claim construction as a dispositive phase of litigation. Prioritize resources on persuading the court about critical claim terms and assess settlement posture in light of likely constructions.

name: Strategic considerations for patentees
description: Identify potentially disputed terms early; provide clear, supportable constructions; build constructions on intrinsic evidence; avoid creating prosecution history that limits scope.
guidance: Draft specification and prosecution arguments to support desired claim scope; produce claim charts linking claims to specification disclosures; avoid over-defensive or narrowing statements in prosecution that could be later used to limit claims.

name: Strategic considerations for defendants
description: Find narrowing constructions in prosecution history; identify lexicographic statements in specification; argue the specification limits scope; use prosecution history estoppel arguments.
guidance: Search the file wrapper and specification for admissions, definitions, or disclaimers that narrow claims. Emphasize intrinsic evidence that supports a narrow reading and challenge patentee attempts to expand plain meaning via extrinsic sources.

name: Phillips v. AWH (2005) holdings relevant to construction
description: Specification is the most important guide; prosecution history is intrinsic evidence with the same authority as the specification; extrinsic evidence (dictionaries) is less reliable; claims must be read in context of the entire specification; broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) applies during prosecution, ordinary meaning during litigation.
guidance: Frame arguments consistent with Phillips: anchor disputed-term meanings in the specification and prosecution history rather than in dictionaries or expert testimony. Distinguish prosecution-phase BRI from litigation-phase ordinary-meaning standards when arguing scope differences.

name: Implied license requires sale of the identical patented article
description: The sale from which the universal license is implied must be a sale of the precise article covered by the patent; purchasers of mere materials or parts do not thereby obtain right to make and use the patented article.
guidance: Exception: where an object can be used only in constructing a patented article, sale of that object by patentee implies license to use it for that purpose (see Roosevelt v. Western Electric). If article is broken up, purchaser of parts cannot reconstruct and claim right.

name: Patent strength, novelty, and breadth affect royalties
description: Stronger patents with broad claims and clear novelty/full protection typically secure better royalty agreements.
guidance: Assess claim breadth, enforceability, and novelty; the more the patent excludes alternatives and is enforceable, the more royalty leverage it provides. Prepare patent prosecution and validity evidence to support negotiations.

name: Licensing as post-infringement dispute resolution
description: A licensing agreement can be used to resolve a patent dispute after the invention has been manufactured and marketed.
guidance: Parties may settle infringement claims by negotiating a license rather than litigating; consider licensing as a pragmatic dispute-resolution tool but ensure terms reflect the infringement context.

name: Written description requirement — general rule
description: The subject matter of the claim must be described in the application as filed in a manner that shows the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention; the claim need not be described literally using the same terms as filed.
guidance: A claim amended to include subject matter, limitations, or terminology not present in the application as filed (a departure/addition/deletion) should be concluded by the examiner as not described in the application, resulting in a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph) or denial of benefit of an earlier filing date. See MPEP § 2163 for examination guidelines.

name: Typical situations raising written description issues
description: Written description issues commonly arise in specific procedural contexts where it must be determined whether the claim subject matter is supported in the application as filed.
guidance: Typical contexts include: (I) amendments affecting a claim (including specification amendments that indirectly affect claims); (II) claiming the benefit of an earlier U.S. filing date under 35 U.S.C. 120; (III) relying on foreign or provisional priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)/(e); and (IV) support for a claim corresponding to a count in an interference. Each circumstance requires assessing whether the earlier or original disclosure meets the 35 U.S.C. 112(a) written description standard.

name: Presumption and burden on examiner
description: A specification as filed is strongly presumed adequate to satisfy written description unless and until the examiner rebuts the presumption with sufficient evidence or reasoning.
guidance: The examiner has the initial burden of presenting by a preponderance of evidence why a person skilled in the art would not recognize in the disclosure a description of the invention defined by the claims. The inquiry is case-by-case and is a question of fact. See In re Wertheim, In re Marzocchi.

name: Statement of rejection requirements (what examiner must state)
description: When rejecting claims for lack of written description, the examiner must set forth express findings of fact supporting the conclusion.
guidance: Findings should (A) identify the claim limitation(s) at issue; and (B) establish a prima facie case by providing reasons why a person skilled in the art at the time of filing would not have recognized that the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention in view of the original disclosure. A general allegation of 'unpredictability in the art' is insufficient. In some cases a simple, specific statement pointing out the lack of apparent support may be sufficient, particularly for new or amended claims where applicant has not indicated support. When appropriate, suggest claim amendments that can be supported by the original disclosure but avoid adding new matter. See Hyatt v. Dudas; Rasmussen.

name: Changes to claim scope — general rule
description: To comply with the written description requirement or to be entitled to an earlier priority/filing date, each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure.
guidance: Common problematic changes include broadening or narrowing claim breadth, altering numerical range limitations, or using terminology not synonymous with the original disclosure. See MPEP § 2163 for guidelines and case examples.

name: Broadening claims — omission of a limitation
description: Omitting a limitation originally disclosed can raise written description issues when it causes the claim to cover a broader invention than what the inventor demonstrated possession of.
guidance: If the omitted element was described as essential or critical in the original disclosure, the broadened claim may fail the written description (and possibly enablement) requirement. Case examples: Gentry Gallery (control means location essential), Tronzo (generic cup vs conical cup), In re Wilder. Compare In re Peters where a removed shape limitation was not essential. If the specification describes an element as essential, omitting it from a claim typically does not comply.

name: Broadening claims — adding a generic (genus) claim
description: A claimed genus may be supported by sufficient description of a representative number of species; one species may suffice only in limited circumstances.
guidance: A 'representative number of species' means the adequately described species reflect the variation within the genus. Where there is substantial variation, one must describe enough species to reflect that variation. Disclosure of a single species supports a genus only if it indicates the patentee has invented species sufficient to constitute the genus. If the disclosure teaches against other species or artisans could not predict operability beyond the disclosed species, genus claims may lack support. Cases: Enzo Biochem, In re Curtis, In re Rasmussen, Tronzo, In re Gosteli. Functional recitations of known compounds may sometimes be sufficient (In re Herschler; In re Smythe).

name: Narrowing or subgeneric claims
description: Introducing narrower or subgenus limitations not supported by the original disclosure can violate written description; whether subgeneric language is acceptable is case-dependent.
guidance: A 'laundry list' of possible moieties does not necessarily provide written description of each species. Recitation of an undisclosed species may violate the requirement. Some subgeneric recitations are acceptable when species falling within the subgenus are disclosed; others are not. Each case must be decided on the facts as to what is reasonably communicated to those skilled in the art. Cases: Fujikawa, In re Ruschig, In re Lukach, Ex parte Sorenson, In re Smith, In re Wilder.

name: Range limitations (numerical ranges)
description: Changes to numerical range limitations require analysis of what ranges a skilled artisan would consider inherently supported by the original disclosure.
guidance: Examine whether the original description reasonably conveys possession of the new range. Example: In re Wertheim — original disclosure of 25%-60% and examples of 36% and 50% did not support a new 'at least 35%' claim (because it opened to embodiments outside 25%-60%), but a limitation to 'between 35% and 60%' did meet the description requirement. Other cases (Purdue Pharma, Union Oil) illustrate that sufficiency depends on whether the disclosure conveys that the inventor considered the claimed range part of the invention and whether sufficient description shows possession.

name: Treatment and review of new matter objections/rejections
description: Procedural handling differs: objections to added disclosure vs rejections of claims for new matter have different review routes and consequences.
guidance: An objection/requirement to delete new matter is subject to supervisory review by petition under 37 CFR 1.181; a rejection of claims for new matter is reviewable by the Patent Trial and Appeal Board. If both objection and rejection exist (claims and specification contain new matter), the combined issue is appealable rather than petitionable. When claims are not amended but the specification is amended to add new matter, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) should be made whenever any claim limitation is affected by the added material.

name: Claims as filed are part of the disclosure — remedying lack of antecedent support
description: Material originally claimed but not described in the remainder of the specification can be remedied by amending the specification to include the claimed subject matter.
guidance: Claims filed in the original specification are part of the disclosure; thus if the original specification contains a claim that discloses material not disclosed elsewhere in the specification, the applicant may amend the specification to include that claimed subject matter. Form paragraph 7.44 may be used where originally claimed subject matter lacks proper antecedent basis in the specification. See In re Benno.

name: Examiner should suggest amendments when appropriate
description: Where a rejection is based on lack of written description, examiners should suggest claim amendments that can be supported by the original disclosure, mindful not to introduce new matter.
