guidance: When appropriate, suggest amendments to the claims which can be supported by the application’s written description, being mindful of the prohibition against the addition of new matter in the claims or description. See Rasmussen.

name: Examination priority: focus on prior art rejections
description: The primary object of the examination of an application is to determine whether or not the claims are patentable over the prior art. This consideration should not be relegated to a secondary position while undue emphasis is given to nonprior art or 'technical' rejections.
guidance: Concentrate effort on truly essential matters; minimize or eliminate effort on technical rejections which are not really critical. Where a major technical rejection is proper (e.g., lack of proper disclosure, undue breadth, utility, etc.) such rejection should be stated with a full development of the reasons rather than a mere conclusion with stereotyped expression.

name: Double patenting prohibition
description: 35 U.S.C. 101 prevents two patents issuing on the same invention to the same applicant; the 'same invention' means identical subject matter is being claimed. If more than one patent is sought, a statutory double patenting rejection applies for claims included in more than one application that are directed to the same invention.
guidance: See MPEP Chapter 800 (specifically §804) for criteria relevant to double patenting. Use Form Paragraphs 8.30, 8.31, and 8.32 for statutory double patenting rejections.

name: ¶7.05.011 Rejection for method claims directed to abstract idea
description: This form paragraph should only be used when rejecting method claim(s) directed to an abstract idea: 'the claimed invention is not directed to patent eligible subject matter... claim(s) [1] is/are determined to be directed to an abstract idea. The rationale for this determination is explained below: [2]'
guidance: In the accompanying explanation, discuss relevant factors with respect to the claim as a whole and explain why the claim is interpreted to be an abstract idea.

name: ¶7.05.01 Rejection header requirements under 35 U.S.C. 101
description: ¶7.05: 'Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 because ...' (heading only)
guidance: This form paragraph must be followed by one or more specific form paragraphs (7.05.01, 7.05.011, 7.05.012, 7.05.013, 7.05.02, 7.05.03, or other). Explain the rejection following the statute recitation. Precede this header by ¶7.04 in first actions and final rejections.

name: ¶7.05.012 Dependent claim rejection when additional limitations insufficient
description: Dependent claim(s) when analyzed as a whole are held to be patent ineligible under 35 U.S.C. 101 because the additional recited limitation(s) fail(s) to establish that the claim(s) is/are not directed to an abstract idea.
guidance: Explain why the additional limitations are no more than a field of use or merely involve insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., data gathering). The explanation must be sufficient to establish a prima facie case of patent ineligibility under 35 U.S.C. 101.

name: ¶7.05.013 Rejection for law of nature / natural principle
description: Use when method claim(s) have a law of nature/natural principle as a claim limitation: 'claim(s) [1] is/are determined to be directed to a law of nature/natural principle. The rationale... is explained below: [2]'
guidance: Identify the natural principle limiting the claim and explain why additional elements/steps do not integrate the natural principle into the method and/or why they are not sufficient to amount to significantly more (e.g., are extra-solution activity or purely conventional). Must establish a prima facie case of ineligibility.

name: Utility-related rejections tied to 35 U.S.C. 112 (¶7.05.02, ¶7.05.03, formats)
description: Claims lacking specific and substantial asserted utility, lacking credible asserted utility, or being inoperative should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 and/or 112 as appropriate (¶7.05.02, ¶7.05.03).
guidance: Where specification would not enable one skilled in the art, make a separate rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph (enablement) using In re Wands factors. Use Formats A, B, or C as appropriate and provide bracketed explanations per the form paragraphs. Address multiple utilities individually (see ¶7.05.04).

name: ¶7.05.03 Inoperative rejection (lack of credible utility)
description: ¶7.05.03: 'the disclosed invention is inoperative and therefore lacks utility.'
guidance: Explain why the invention is inoperative and lacks credible asserted utility; insert claim numbers and specific explanatory text per the Format C instructions. Relate to enablement issues as needed.

name: ¶7.31.01 Written description rejection criteria (35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph)
description: Claim rejected as failing the written description requirement when 'the claim(s) contains subject matter which was not described in the specification in such a way as to reasonably convey to one skilled in the art that the inventor(s) ... had possession of the claimed invention.'
guidance: In bracketed explanation, identify by page/line and/or drawings the subject matter not properly described and explain the examiner’s position, including unresolved applicant responses that raise doubt as to possession. Must be preceded by ¶7.30.01 or ¶7.103.

name: ¶7.31.02 Enablement rejection criteria (35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph)
description: Claim rejected as failing to comply with the enablement requirement where the specification does not enable one skilled in the art to make and/or use the invention.
guidance: Identify the claimed subject matter not enabled and explain why not enabling, applying In re Wands factors and undue experimentation analysis. If problem is scope, consider ¶7.31.03. Precede by ¶7.30.01 or ¶7.103.

name: ¶7.31.03 Scope of enablement: commensurability requirement
description: Claim rejected because the specification, while enabling for certain aspects, 'does not reasonably provide enablement for' other claim aspects; 'the specification does not enable any person skilled in the art to [make/use] the invention commensurate in scope with these claims.'
guidance: Identify portions of the specification that are enabling and the specific claim aspects not enabled. Explain why the specification does not enable the claimed scope, applying In re Wands factors.

name: ¶7.33.01 Essential subject matter missing from claims (enablement)
description: Claim rejected where a feature considered critical or essential by applicant to the practice of the claimed invention is missing from the claim and the disclosure is not enabling for it.
guidance: Recite the omitted subject matter, give rationale for considering it essential, and cite statements/arguments/drawings showing the feature was considered essential by the applicant. Precede by ¶7.30.01 or ¶7.103.

name: ¶7.30.02 / ¶7.34.01 Indefiniteness under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph
description: Claim rejected as indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which applicant regards as the invention; 'Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as being indefinite...'
guidance: This rejection must be preceded by ¶7.30.02 or ¶7.103. Identify particular terms or limitations rendering the claim indefinite and explain why; follow MPEP §§2171-2174. Use ¶7.34.02 - ¶7.34.11 as applicable for more specific indefiniteness reasons.

name: ¶7.34.02 Inconsistent terminology / applicant-as-lexicographer
description: Where applicant acts as his or her own lexicographer to specifically define a term contrary to its ordinary meaning, the written description must clearly redefine the claim term and set forth the uncommon definition so as to put one reasonably skilled in the art on notice.
guidance: State the term usage in the claim, the meaning assigned by applicant, and the accepted meaning with supporting citation (textbook/dictionary). Precede by ¶7.34.01; use only where specification does not clearly redefine the term.

name: ¶7.34.03 Relative term/term of degree rendering claim indefinite
description: A relative term or term of degree (e.g., 'about', 'substantial') renders the claim indefinite if not defined by the claim and the specification does not provide a standard for ascertaining the requisite degree.
guidance: Explain which parameter or limitation is rendered indefinite and why one of ordinary skill in the art would not be reasonably apprised of scope. Precede by ¶7.34.01.

name: ¶7.34.04 Broad range and narrow range in same claim (indefiniteness)
description: A broad range or limitation together with a narrow range or limitation that falls within the broad range in the same claim is considered indefinite because the resulting claim does not clearly set forth the metes and bounds of the patent protection desired.
guidance: Insert the broader range and the narrower range and their locations in the claim. Precede by ¶7.34.01. May be modified to other indefiniteness instances where broad language is followed by 'such as' and then narrow language.

name: ¶7.34.05 Lack of antecedent basis
description: Claim recites a limitation without sufficient antecedent basis (e.g., 'said lever' without earlier 'a lever'), making scope indeterminate.
guidance: Use only in aggravated situations where lack of antecedent basis makes claim scope indeterminate. Precede by ¶7.34.01. Identify the limitation and where it appears in the claim.

name: ¶7.34.06 Use claims that recite use without steps (indefinite/improper process claim)
description: A claim providing for the use of something but not setting forth any steps delimiting how this use is actually practiced is indefinite and may be an improper process claim under 35 U.S.C. 101.
guidance: Explain that reciting a use without active positive steps fails to define a process. Cite examples and precedents (e.g., Ex parte Dunki, Clinical Products v. Brenner). Precede by ¶7.34.01.

name: ¶7.34.11 'Means' modifier lacking specified function (means-plus-function issue)
description: If the modifier of 'means' does not specify a function, it is impossible to determine equivalents as required by 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, rendering the claim indefinite.
guidance: Insert what is being used and demonstrate absence of a specified function. Cite relevant MPEP section (2173.05(q)) and precede by ¶7.34.01.

name: Pre‑AIPA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date for patent issued from continuing application
description: If the reference is a U.S. patent issued directly from a continuing application claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121 or 365(c) to such an international application (which had not entered the national stage prior to the continuing application’s filing date), the prior art reference’s pre‑AIPA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date is the actual U.S. filing date of the continuing application.
guidance: Caution: the international publication of the international application (PCT) by WIPO may have an earlier prior art date under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) or pre‑AIA 102(b). Apply proper statutes to determine which prior art date controls.

name: Consideration of benefit/priority claims and written‑description support
description: Consider benefit claims to earlier‑filed U.S. provisional applications under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), and to earlier‑filed U.S. nonprovisional applications and international applications under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, 365(c), or 386(c) only if the subject matter used to make the rejection is appropriately supported in the relied upon earlier‑filed application’s disclosure (and any intermediate application(s)).
guidance: A benefit claim to a U.S. patent of an earlier‑filed international application may only result in an effective U.S. filing date as of the date the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 371(c)(1), (2) and (4) were fulfilled. Do NOT consider benefit claims to U.S. applications which are filed before an international application. Do NOT consider foreign priority claims under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)‑(d), 365(a) or (b), or 386(a) or (b). In addition, a reference is entitled to the benefit of the filing date of a provisional application only if at least one of the claims in the reference is supported by the written description of the provisional application in compliance with pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph or 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (see Dynamic Drinkware; Amgen v. Sanofi).

name: Form and content of a pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)/(b)/(g) rejection (¶7.15.fti)
description: Template rejection: 'Claim(s) [1] is/are rejected under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 [2] as being [3] by [4].' Bracket fields specify which paragraph, whether 'clearly anticipated' or 'anticipated' with explanation, and identify the prior art relied upon.
guidance: This rejection must be preceded by required form paragraph(s) (7.07.fti and appropriate others) or by form paragraph 7.103. If pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) is also applied, follow with one of 7.15.01/02/03.fti. For applications with an actual filing date on or after March 16, 2013 claiming benefit to an application filed before that date, precede by form paragraph 7.06.

name: Provisional rejection over copending application (¶7.15.01.fti)
description: Claim(s) provisionally rejected under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as anticipated by a copending application which has a common assignee, common applicant, or at least one common (joint) inventor; the copending application would constitute prior art if published or patented, so the provisional rejection is based on a presumption of future publication/patenting.
guidance: This provisional rejection may be overcome either by a showing under 37 CFR 1.132 that any invention disclosed but not claimed in the copending application was derived from the inventor of this application (not 'by another'), or by an appropriate showing under 37 CFR 1.131(a). This rejection may NOT be overcome by filing a terminal disclaimer (In re Bartfeld). Examiner Notes: use only where copending app discloses claimed invention and has common assignee/applicant or at least one common inventor; apply AIPA/Technical Amendments rules to determine the reference’s 102(e) date; if claims would have been obvious over disclosures in the copending app use the obviousness form paragraphs; handle identical subject matter and nonstatutory double patenting per the cited form paragraphs (8.30–8.39, 8.27.fti, etc.).

name: Rejection over issued patent/publication with common assignee/applicant/inventor (¶7.15.02.fti)
description: Claim(s) rejected under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as being anticipated by an applied reference that has a common assignee, common applicant, or a common (joint) inventor with the instant application.
guidance: May be overcome by showing under 37 CFR 1.132 that any invention disclosed but not claimed in the reference was derived from the inventive entity of this application (not 'by another'), or by showing under 37 CFR 1.131(a). Apply amendments to pre‑AIA 102(e) (AIPA, Technical Amendments) to determine dates; consider benefit claims and provisional support requirements. If the reference is a PCT/unpublished international app with certain characteristics, do not apply 102(e) (see notes). Handle identical subject matter and nonstatutory double patenting per form paragraphs 8.30–8.39 and 8.27.fti. Patent application publications may be used only if preceded by form paragraph 7.12.fti.

name: Rejection over earlier‑filed patent/application with no common assignee/inventor (¶7.15.03.fti)
description: Claim(s) rejected under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as being [clearly anticipated/anticipated] by an earlier patent or patent application publication that is not required to have a common assignee or inventor.
guidance: Apply the AIPA/Technical Amendments rules (7.12.fti) where applicable to determine the reference’s 102(e) date; apply pre‑AIPA rules (7.12.01.fti) for international applications filed prior to Nov. 29, 2000. Consider benefit claims to earlier filings only if the subject matter is supported in the earlier disclosures. If the reference is a PCT publication that did not designate the U.S. or was not published in English, do not use this form paragraph; instead apply under pre‑AIA 102(a) or (b). Provide explanation of anticipation (insert 'clearly anticipated' or 'anticipated' with explanation) and identify the prior art relied upon.

name: Rejection for applicant not the inventor (pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f)) (¶7.19.fti)
description: Claim(s) rejected under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f) because the applicant did not invent the claimed subject matter.
guidance: This paragraph must be preceded either by paragraphs 7.07.fti and 7.13.fti or by paragraph 7.103. In bracket 2, insert an explanation of the supporting evidence establishing that applicant was not the inventor. See MPEP §2137 for further guidance.

name: Duties regarding communicating scope of representation, fees, and expenses (37 C.F.R. § 11.105(b))
description: A practitioner must communicate the scope of representation and terms of fees/expenses to the client.
guidance: Cited as a claimed violation; the Order notes failures related to client funds and lack of records that bear on fee handling and disclosure (e.g., collecting funds for fees but not remitting them and not maintaining records).

name: Matter not claimed not covered by patent
description: That matter not claimed is not covered by the patent.
guidance: Cited: Dickinson v. Parker (1889); Van Camp v. Maryland Pavement Co. (1888). Claim scope controls coverage.

name: Expressions adjacent to Claim can be part of Claim
description: That any perfectly clear expression of what the inventor intends to secure to himself in immediate connection with the Claim is virtually part of the Claim.
guidance: Cited: La Rue v. Western Electric Co. (1886). Surrounding language may inform claim scope.

name: Improvement-only inventor cannot claim entire means
description: That the inventor of an improvement only cannot claim the entire means.
guidance: Cited: Ex parte Miller (1888). Limitations on improvement inventors' scope.

name: 'As shown and described' implied in Claims
description: That 'as shown and described' will be implied by the courts in all Claims, but is usually required by the Patent Office, especially in design patents.
guidance: Cited: Ex parte Gerard (1888). Standard phrasing interpreting claim scope.

name: Certain generic words sometimes proper in claims
description: That the words 'means,' 'mechanism,' 'connections,' are sometimes proper.
guidance: Cited: Ex parte Stoughton (1888); Ex parte Stanbridge (1888). Functional language may be allowable.

name: All claimed elements are essential in a combination claim
description: That all claimed elements of a combination are thereby made essential.
guidance: Cited: Thompson v. Gildersleeve (1888). Claim drafting must account for essentiality of recited elements.

name: Construal to protect actual invention if language permits
description: That a patent is to be construed in view of the state of the art and so as to protect the actual invention, if its language will permit.
guidance: Cited: Consolidated Roller Mill Co. v. Coombs (1889). Give claims reasonable scope to cover the invention.

name: Narrow claim enlargement only by reissue
description: That a narrow Claim must be enlarged by re-issue, if at all, not by construction.
guidance: Cited: Becker v. Hastings (1884). Reissue procedure required to broaden claim scope.

name: Cannot retroactively give new construction not contemplated at drafting
description: That a construction not contemplated when the Claim was drawn cannot be afterwards given to it.
guidance: Cited: Ladd v. Mooney (1884). Limits on post-hoc reinterpretation.

name: Claim defines PTO-determined scope; cannot be enlarged by construction
description: That the claim of a patent defines what the Patent Office has determined to be the scope of the invention, and it cannot be enlarged by construction.
guidance: Cited: Day v. Fair Haven & Westville R.R. Co. (1889); U.S. Supreme Court references. Claim scope set by PTO determination.

name: Clear claim obviates need to consult drawings
description: That where the Claim is clear the drawings need not be considered in construing it.
guidance: Cited: Bidd v. Horry (1888). Primary weight to clear claim language.

name: Prior purchases by defendant create presumption of diversion
description: That where defendants, before infringing, bought of the plaintiff, as also during the infringement to some extent, it is a fair presumption that they would have bought of him all they made and used.
guidance: Cited: Creamer v. Bowers (1888). Past purchasing patterns support lost-sales claims.

name: Disclaimer affects Claims, not Description
description: That a disclaimer is not needed when the Description is excessive but not the Claim — the Claim controlling the Description and limiting the patent.
guidance: Cited: Brush Electric Co. v. Fort Wayne Electric Light Co. (1889). Claims control patent scope; disclaimers operate on claims.

name: Patentee bound by claim narrowed to meet PTO objection
description: That the patentee is bound by a Claim which has been narrowed to meet an unfounded objection in the Patent Office.
guidance: Cited: Lapham Dodge Co. v. Severin (1889). Prosecution concessions generally binding.

name: Instructions for written argument — admissibility and examiner duties
description: How examiners should treat written arguments and accompanying amendments submitted in response to grounds for rejection.
guidance: Where a written argument is submitted with an amendment, the examiner shall review both in depth and determine whether the notified grounds for rejection can be overcome. Where only a written argument is submitted without amendment, the examiner shall still sufficiently consider the argument. Written arguments and other documents (including experimental results) submitted in response to a notice of grounds for rejection are not part of the specification but may be referred to decide patentability. Amendments submitted after the designated period are returned, but written arguments may be admitted as reference. If an applicant claims amendments in a written argument but fails to submit them, examiner examines based on the existing description and claims; if there is discrepancy between insisted amendments and actual amendment, examiner bases examination on the actual amendment. If matters are disclosed only in the written argument and not in the amendment (indicating requirements are met), examiner may re-notify the same ground for rejection at his/her discretion (see re-notice procedures).

name: Requesting reference documents for examination — types and procedure
description: An examiner may ask an applicant to submit documents and other references required for examination to expedite proceedings; the request must state general information and which documents are required.
guidance: Examples of requested documents: (i) related documents and translations for international applications and examination outcomes from other offices; (ii) a written statement mapping each claim's technical subject matter to corresponding description paragraphs and explaining relations among claims for applications with voluminous description/claims; (iii) a written statement summarizing the gist of a claimed invention if too complex to comprehend within designated period; (iv) samples or experimental results where effects cannot be verified without them (submission should enable confirmation that the description was definite and sufficient upon filing); (v) written statement explaining process of inducing a formula and definitions/meanings of technical terminology or signs that are unclear; (vi) a written statement clarifying an applicant's claim in written arguments when hard to understand; (vii) documents relevant to examination results of the priority application and their Korean translations. Requests shall be made in the name of the examiner in charge, specifically clarify which document to submit, and designate the submission period within the period for written-argument submission. To expedite examination, examiner may include document requests in the notice of grounds for rejection. For international applications, IPSR/ISR copies may be requested in the Commissioner's name. If an applicant fails to respond, the application shall not be invalidated, but the examiner may instruct re-filing if documents are deficient.

name: Examination deferral or extension of processing period — grounds and procedures
description: When an examiner may defer examination or extend the processing period (within two months) and procedural requirements for such deferral/extension.
guidance: An examiner may defer/extend (within two months) when: (i) a prior-filed application or conflicting applications are not laid open or an examination request for conflicting applications is not made; (ii) the period during which a prior-filed application serving as a basis for domestic priority claim is deemed withdrawn has not elapsed; (iii) a patent trial or proceeding related to the application is pending (includes administrative trial/litigation); (iv) extension required because prior-art search is outsourced, expert opinions are inquired, or consultation examination is needed; (v) the period designated for submission of evidential documents for priority in treaty-claimed applications has not elapsed; (vi) other necessary occasions. Note: deferral/extension not allowed when the Commissioner or examiner designates the processing period. Deferrals/extensions must be reported to the head of the Examination Unit and notified to the applicant. Examiner shall review reasons more than once a month and conduct examination by the termination date if reasons are cleared. If further deferral/extension is needed, report to higher management and limit to two months; additional extension allowed in certain cases not imputable to examiner (e.g., prior-art search report not delivered). When deciding to defer/extend again, the examiner must notify the applicant of specific reasons.

name: Deferral rules for later-filed applications when identical inventions exist
description: How to handle examination start/deferral where multiple applications are filed on the identical invention (prior-filed vs later-filed).
guidance: If multiple applications on identical invention exist, the examiner shall defer examination for later-filed applications until the prior-filed application has been processed, laid-open, or registered. However, if the later-filed application can be rejected based on the same ground as the prior-filed application, the examiner can start examination on the later-filed application. Detailed handling depends on whether applicants are identical and whether the prior-filed application is laid-open, with different notification and determination procedures (including applying Article 36(1) or Article 29(3)(iv) where appropriate). If the prior-filed application is later examined/laidover/registered after deferral, the examiner may conduct examination on later-filed application but shall make final decision applying Article 36(1) once the scope of claim of the prior-filed application is determined.

name: Problem and solution approach — three main stages
description: In order to assess inventive step in an objective and predictable manner, apply the problem and solution approach which comprises three main stages: (1) determining the 'closest prior art', (2) establishing the 'objective technical problem' to be solved, and (3) considering whether the claimed invention, starting from the closest prior art and the objective technical problem, would have been obvious to the skilled person.
guidance: Deviation from this approach should be exceptional. The approach constructs a logical chain of arguments (a 'convincing chain of considerations') to demonstrate obviousness or inventive step (Art. 56 EPC).

name: Closest prior art — main selection criteria
description: A document qualifies as closest prior art if it: (a) should have the same or similar purpose or effect as the invention; or (b) should deal with a similar technical problem as the invention or at least belong to the same or a closely related technical field as the claimed invention; or (c) should have a similar use and require minimal structural modifications.
guidance: The number of features a claim has in common with prior art is not by itself a suitable criterion for selection. Consider purpose/type/use and minimal adaptations rather than simple feature-counting.

name: Appropriate/feasible starting point (document suitability)
description: Only documents that are an appropriate/feasible starting point for the assessment of inventive step should be used — i.e. those from which the skilled person had a reasonable chance to arrive at the subject-matter of the claim in an obvious manner.
guidance: Think in terms of a pre-selection (set) of documents rather than a single 'one and only' closest prior art. If one cannot arrive at the invention from these realistic starting points, one cannot reasonably argue it could be arrived at from other (inappropriate) starting points.

name: Avoid selecting closest prior art based on feature-counting
description: Selection of the closest prior art should not be based merely on the number of features common to the claim and a prior document.
guidance: Case law and Guidelines emphasize purpose/type/use and minimal structural changes over raw counts of common features. Relying on feature-counting is an anti-pattern (see T 870/96 example).

name: Applicant's subjective stated purpose cannot dictate closest prior art
description: The purpose of the invention when establishing the closest prior art is determined 'in the light of the application as a whole' and not by subjective statements of purpose in the description that are not achieved by the claims.
guidance: Applicants cannot influence selection of closest prior art by adding purposes to the description that are not actually realised by the claimed invention (see T 2255/10).

name: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI)
description: the Claim Construction standard which applies in PTAB Proceedings.
guidance: Claim terms are given their BRI in light of the specification to one having ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention. In contrast, in federal district court, claims are construed under the Ordinary and Customary Meaning Standard (Phillips Standard). 37 C.F.R. § 42.100(b). PTAB published a proposed rule change (Aug 20, 2015) to apply Ordinary and Customary Meaning for patents that will expire before issuance of a final decision, but otherwise to apply BRI to unexpired patents.

name: Burden of Proof
description: the evidentiary standard to legally establish a fact.
guidance: In PTAB Proceedings, the Petitioner must prove Invalidity of the challenged claims by a Preponderance of the Evidence. 37 C.F.R. § 42.1(d). In contrast, in federal district court the accused infringer must prove Invalidity by Clear and Convincing Evidence.

name: Certificate
description: after the PTAB issues a Final Written Decision and the time for appeal has ended, the PTO issues and publishes a Certificate
guidance: The Certificate (1) cancels any patent claim determined to be unpatentable, (2) confirms any patent claim determined to be patentable, and (3) incorporates any new or Amended Claim determined to be patentable. 35 U.S.C. § 318(b).

name: Claim Amendment(s)
description: after Institution of a PTAB Proceeding and conferring with the PTAB, a Patent Owner may file a Motion to Amend patent claims.
guidance: The Patent Owner may generally propose one Substitute Claim for each original claim it wishes to amend, which will only be considered if the original claim it replaces is canceled by the Patent Owner. A Claim Amendment will not be allowed if it does not respond to all Grounds of Invalidity asserted against the original claim, if it seeks to enlarge the scope of the claims, or if it introduces new subject matter. The Patent Owner must also show patentability of a Substitute Claim over the prior art generally, not just over references asserted against the original claims. 37 C.F.R. §§ 42.121, 42.221.

name: Claim Chart
description: typically a two-column chart providing an element-by-element breakdown of a patent’s claims.
guidance: Invalidity claim charts are useful for visualizing which claim elements exist in the prior art. Claim Charts may be single-spaced under Line Spacing requirements, but placing arguments and claim construction in a claim chart to circumvent double-spacing or Page Limits is prohibited. The PTAB will not consider such arguments and double-spaced Claim Constructions. 37 C.F.R. § 42.6(a)(2)(iii).

name: Covered Business Method (CBM)
description: CBM review is a PTAB Proceeding to challenge any patent that includes at least one claim directed to a method or apparatus used in the practice, administration or management of a Financial Product or Service.
guidance: CBM review is not available for patents for Technological Inventions. 37 C.F.R. § 42.301(a). CBM review may be requested on the basis of Novelty, Obviousness, Written Description, Enablement, Indefiniteness and Patentable Subject Matter. All prior art is available when challenging FTF patents; for FTI patents only patents and Printed Publications are considered. 37 C.F.R. § 42.304. Only a person who is sued or Charged with Infringement may Petition for CBM review. 37 C.F.R. § 42.302. Timing: may be requested at any time for FTI patents, but for FTF patents only nine months after issuance for petitions analogous to PGR window. 37 C.F.R. § 42.303.

name: Examination
description: the procedure by which the PTO reviews a patent application, interacts with applicants and their representatives and determines whether the claims are patentable over the prior art.

name: Financial Product or Service
description: to be eligible for CBM review, the patent at issue must have at least one claim related to a Financial Product or Service.
guidance: PTAB broadly construes Financial Product or Service to include activities financial in nature, incidental to a financial activity or complementary to a financial activity. 37 C.F.R. § 42.301(b). When a patent’s claims relate to money matters or can be performed by a financial institution, the patent likely relates to a Financial Product or Service even if not otherwise related to financial services. A single covered claim can make the entire patent eligible for CBM review. 77 Fed. Reg. at 48736. Examples and PTAB decisions cited.

name: Grounds of Invalidity
description: the grounds on which a Petitioner can challenge the Validity of patent claims in a PTAB Proceeding.
guidance: For IPR, Grounds limited to Novelty and Obviousness. For PGR and CBM, challenges may include Novelty, Obviousness, Written Description, Enablement, Indefiniteness and Patentable Subject Matter. 37 C.F.R. §§ 42.104, 42.204(b), 42.304(b).

name: Indefiniteness
description: Definiteness is a requirement for patentability; to satisfy Definiteness, a patent claim must particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter of the invention.
guidance: Indefiniteness is available as a Ground of Invalidity in PGR and CBM review, but not IPR. 35 U.S.C. § 112(b). 37 C.F.R. §§ 42.104(b), 42.204(b), 42.304(b).

name: Intervening Rights
description: an accused infringer’s rights to avoid infringement for previously lawful activity that later becomes unlawful when claims are substantively Amended during a PTAB Proceeding.
guidance: AIA explicitly provides Intervening Rights may exist for any amended or new claims determined to be patentable and incorporated into a patent during IPR, PGR or CBM. 35 U.S.C. § 318(c).

name: Line Spacing
description: PTAB imposes specific formatting requirements for filing documents.
guidance: Double spacing must always be used except for Claim Charts, headings, tables of contents, tables of authorities, indices, signature blocks and certificates of service. Block quotations may be 1.5 spaced, but must be indented from both left and right margins. 37 C.F.R. § 42.6(a)(2).

name: Primary Reference
description: prior art references can be combined to show that a claimed invention is Obvious.
guidance: A Primary Reference discloses many of the Claim Elements and may be combined with one or more Secondary Reference(s), which disclose other Claim Elements.

name: Secondary Reference
description: prior art references that can be combined with a Primary Reference to show Obviousness.
guidance: A Primary Reference discloses most Claim Elements. Secondary References disclose other Claim Elements combined with the Primary Reference.

name: Substitute Claim
description: a claim proposed by a Patent Owner to replace original claims through Claim Amendment in a Motion to Amend.
guidance: Patent Owner may propose one Substitute Claim per original claim it wishes to amend; each Substitute Claim must be traceable back to an original claim. A Substitute Claim will be considered only if the original claim it replaces is determined unpatentable or cancelled. Proposed Substitute Claim may only narrow the scope and not broaden the challenged claim. Patent Owner required to show proposed new claims are patentable at least over prior art it is aware of. 37 C.F.R. §§ 42.121, 42.221.

name: Technological Invention
description: a patent is not eligible for CBM review if it claims subject matter that as a whole recites a technological feature that is Novel and Unobvious over the prior art, and solves a technical problem using a technical solution.
guidance: 37 C.F.R. § 42.301; see Transitional Program for Covered Business Method Patents—Definitions of Covered Business Method Patent and Technological Invention, 77 Fed. Reg. 48734, 48753 (Aug. 14, 2012).

name: Vertical Redundancy
description: Petitioner’s assertion of multiple Grounds of Invalidity for a single claim based on different prior art references without explaining relative strengths and weaknesses of each Ground.
guidance: If a Ground is rejected for redundancy, Petitioner is statutorily estopped from pursuing the grounds in a later litigation or PTAB Proceeding. Petitioners should determine their strongest Grounds and proceed only with those.

name: Application-of-principle-to-specific-context (Le Roy)
description: A claim that applies an abstract principle to a specific context may be patent-eligible; historically the Court required only that abstract principles be applied to something specific.
guidance: Historically (19th century) courts accepted that carrying a principle into effect, even by simple means, could satisfy patent eligibility—i.e., application of the principle to a concrete context was sufficient.

name: Mayo/Alice two-step inventive-step test for excluded categories
description: For inventions directed to laws of nature, natural phenomena, or abstract ideas courts must determine whether the claimed invention transforms the ineligible concept into a patent-eligible application by adding an 'inventive concept.'
guidance: Mayo held that merely restating a natural law and saying 'apply it' is insufficient; Alice reiterated and formalized that mere application of an abstract idea without additional inventive features fails eligibility. Courts ask whether the claim adds something significantly more to the ineligible concept.

name: Not a general license — scope limited to specific subject matter (§273(e)(3))
description: The defense is not a general license under all claims of the patent at issue, but extends only to the specific subject matter for which it has been established that a qualifying commercial use occurred.
guidance: The statutory clause restates the "subject matter" limit and explains that "subject matter" has a relatively narrow meaning in patent law (does not include obvious variants). Legislative history and commentary emphasize that, except for the two enumerated exceptions (volume/quantity variations and certain improvements), the defense is limited to the embodiments/subject matter actually commercially used and established before the relevant date.

name: Exceptions to the subject-matter limit — variations in quantity/volume and permissible improvements (§273(e)(3) exceptions)
description: The defense shall extend to variations in the quantity or volume of use of the claimed subject matter, and to improvements in the claimed subject matter that do not infringe additional specifically claimed subject matter of the patent.
guidance: First exception ensures defendants may reasonably expand volume to meet market demand (unlike other jurisdictions that limit to prior activity levels). Second exception permits changes in the nature of use so long as the change would not infringe additional claims; illustrative example given (heating at different temperatures and claim scope). Committee report guidance: if alteration after filing would infringe claims other than those previously identified, liability follows for those additional claims.

name: Referencing of already-submitted evidential documents
description: Where a person conducts more than two patent-related proceedings simultaneously or consecutively and the contents of evidential documents are the same, the person can submit original copies for one proceeding and replace documents for the others by submitting copies or stating intention to reference the original documents in the attached-documents box. Referencing is allowed in specified cases (e.g., power of attorney, priority claim documents, successor-in-title, when permission/consent from third party is required, change of name/seal, representative acting for multiple parties).
guidance: When submitting copies instead of originals, the intention to reference must be stated in the attached documents box using the prescribed wording (example provided). This reduces repeated submission of identical evidence across multiple proceedings.

name: Provisional application filing date (post-December 18, 2013)
description: A provisional application filed on or after December 18, 2013 will be given a filing date as of the date a specification, with or without claims, is received in the Office.
guidance: For provisional applications filed prior to December 18, 2013, filing date is given per pre-PLT (AIA) 37 CFR 1.53(c) as of the date the written description and any necessary drawings are filed. Amendments, other than those required to make the provisional application comply with applicable regulations, are not permitted after the filing date of the provisional application.

name: Patent term consequences of converting provisional to nonprovisional
description: Conversion of a provisional application to a nonprovisional application will result in the term of any patent to issue from the application being measured from at least the filing date of the provisional application for which conversion is requested.
guidance: Applicants should consider avoiding adverse patent term impact by filing a nonprovisional claiming the benefit of the provisional under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), rather than converting the provisional to a nonprovisional. Claiming benefit is less expensive and will generally result in a longer patent term.

name: OPAP handling of applications filed without all pages of specification
description: The Office of Patent Application Processing (OPAP) reviews application papers to determine whether all of the pages of specification are present. If the application, though missing pages, contains something that can be construed as a written description, at least one drawing figure if necessary under 35 U.S.C. 113 (first sentence), and, in a nonprovisional application, at least one claim, OPAP will send a Notice of Omitted Items indicating that the application papers have been accorded a filing date but are lacking some pages of the specification.
guidance: If the application does not contain anything that can be construed as a written description, OPAP will mail a Notice of Incomplete Application indicating the application lacks the specification required by 35 U.S.C. 112 and no filing date is granted.

name: Applicant options after OPAP Notice of Omitted Items (entitled to filing date)
description: Under the revised procedure, the mailing of an OPAP notice regarding missing page(s) will permit the applicant to: (A) promptly establish prior receipt by filing a petition under 37 CFR 1.53(e) within two months with the petition fee and evidence; (B) promptly submit the omitted page(s) and accept the date of such submission as the application filing date by filing omitted pages and a petition under 37 CFR 1.182 within two months; or (C) accept the application as deposited by filing an appropriate amendment.
guidance: For option C, acceptable amendments include: (1) substitute specification (including claims) to renumber pages and cancel incomplete sentences without adding subject matter (37 CFR 1.121(b)(3), 1.125); or (2) substitute specification (excluding claims) relying on incorporation by reference under 37 CFR 1.57(b) to add subject matter in omitted pages without adding new matter. The two-month period is extendable under 37 CFR 1.136. For provisional applications, petition practice under 1.182 is generally not granted; the USPTO suggests filing a new provisional application instead.

name: If application is not entitled to a filing date (missing specification)
description: If the application lacks the specification required by 35 U.S.C. 112 and is not entitled to a filing date, the applicant may: (A) file a petition under 37 CFR 1.53(e) with the petition fee asserting missing specification was submitted or that papers contain an adequate written description and submit evidence; (B) submit the omitted specification (including at least one claim if required) and accept the date of such submission as the filing date; or (C) submit an amendment under 37 CFR 1.57(b) if the omitted material is completely contained in a prior-filed application (with petition under 1.53(e)).
guidance: For applications filed before September 16, 2012, omitted specification submissions should be accompanied by an oath or declaration in compliance with pre-AIA rules referring to the specification. The two-month period for some responses is extendable under 37 CFR 1.136.

name: Examiner duties when forwarded an application missing specification pages
description: If a forwarded application was filed without all of the pages of the specification and a Notice of Omitted Items has not been mailed by OPAP, the examiner should review the application to determine whether the application is entitled to a filing date.
guidance: Criteria: For an application filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a) prior to December 18, 2013 or a design application, it is entitled to a filing date if it contains something that can be construed as a written description, at least one drawing figure (if necessary under 35 U.S.C. 113), and at least one claim. For non-design applications filed on or after December 18, 2013 under 35 U.S.C. 111(a), the application is entitled to a filing date if filed with a specification, with or without claims (though claims must be filed before sent to the Technology Center). If entitled, the examiner should notify applicant in the next Office action and require applicant to take specified actions (accept as filed with amendment, submit omitted pages + petition, or file petition alleging prior deposit). If not entitled, forward to OPAP for Notice of Incomplete Application.

name: Applications filed without drawings (drawing necessity and filing date)
description: 35 U.S.C. 113 requires a drawing 'where necessary for the understanding of the subject matter sought to be patented.' For applications filed prior to December 18, 2013 and design applications, required drawings (where necessary) are needed to receive a filing date. For applications other than design filed on or after December 18, 2013, drawings are not required to receive a filing date though they should be submitted if necessary for understanding because no amendment may introduce new matter after filing date.
guidance: Applications filed without drawings are inspected to determine whether a drawing is referred to in the specification, and if not, whether a drawing is necessary. USPTO practice treats at least process/method claims and many composition applications as not requiring drawings. Specific situations usually not requiring drawings include: (A) coated articles or products where invention is solely coating; (B) articles made from a particular material where only material matters; (C) laminated structures unless significant structure details; (D) articles/apparatus/systems where sole distinguishing feature is presence of a particular material. If the Technology Center determines drawings are necessary under 35 U.S.C. 113, filing date will be reconsidered and application returned to OPAP for a Notice of Incomplete Application. If drawings are described in the specification but not filed, treated as filed without all drawing figures and handled per MPEP § 601.01(g).

name: Statutory categories under §101
description: Patentable subject matter is limited to inventions that fall within one of the four statutory categories: 'process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter.'
guidance: Claims must be directed to at least one of these categories; the scope of §101 is defined by these categories but analysis often focuses on the essential characteristics of the claimed subject matter rather than forcing it into a single pigeonhole. Citation: 35 U.S.C. § 101; State Street Bank v. Signature Financial Group discussed as focusing on essential characteristics.

name: Tangibility/permanence is not a prerequisite (concurrence view)
description: An invention need not be non-transitory or permanently tangible to be a 'manufacture' or composition of matter; transitory, unstable, or non-isolatable intermediates have been held patentable.
guidance: Do not automatically exclude transitory phenomena (e.g., propagating signals) from §101 on the basis of fleeting existence alone. Precedents cited: In re Breslow (transitory chemical intermediates patentable), In re Hruby (pattern over time patentable). Evaluate whether the claimed subject has 'some physical carrier of information' or an overall pattern/form created by human ingenuity.

name: §101 'useful' requirement (specific/substantial utility and attenuation)
description: Subject matter must be 'useful'—utility must be specific and substantial and not too attenuated from what is actually claimed.
guidance: Assess whether the claimed subject has practical specific benefits in its currently available form (Brenner; In re Fisher). The 'useful, concrete, and tangible result' language (Alappat/State Street) is an indicator but not dispositive. Consider whether the utility is merely an asserted end-use remote from the claimed abstraction.

name: Abstract ideas / mathematical algorithms exclusion
description: Laws of nature, physical phenomena, and abstract ideas (including pure mathematical algorithms) are not patentable subject matter under §101.
guidance: Cases such as Gottschalk v. Benson and Parker v. Flook show that an algorithm or mathematical relationship, even if novel, can be unpatentable if the claim would effectively monopolize the abstract idea. Determine whether the claim attempts to patent the algorithm/principle itself or an application of it to a new and useful end.

name: Focus on essential characteristics rather than form of claim
description: The inquiry should look to the essential character of the subject matter rather than merely which of the four categories a claim is drafted into.
guidance: Although a claim must be drafted to at least one statutory category, courts advise examining the invention's essential characteristics (State Street Bank). Avoid letting claim drafting form (e.g., drafting as a signal vs. a storage medium) determine patentability (Flook warning against 'draftman's art').

name: Application-of-principle vs. monopolization of principle
description: A claimant must show an application of a law of nature or abstract principle to a new and useful end rather than monopoly over the principle itself.
guidance: Funk Bros., Benson, and Flook articulate that inventions applying natural laws or algorithms may be patentable when tied to a specific, useful application. Evaluate whether the claim would preempt all uses of the underlying principle or merely claim a particular application with tangible benefits.

name: IPR scope — grounds and prior art limitations (35 U.S.C. 311(b))
description: A petitioner in an inter partes review may request to cancel as unpatentable 1 or more claims of a patent only on a ground that could be raised under section 102 or 103 and only on the basis of prior art consisting of patents or printed publications.

name: Petition requirements — fee, parties, claims, grounds, evidence (35 U.S.C. 312(a)(1)-(5))
description: A petition filed under section 311 may be considered only if: (1) accompanied by the fee; (2) identifies all real parties in interest; (3) identifies, in writing and with particularity, each claim challenged, the grounds for the challenge, and the evidence supporting the grounds, including copies of patents/printed publications and affidavits/declarations if relying on expert opinion; (4) provides other information as Director may require; and (5) provides copies of required documents to the patent owner or its representative.
guidance: Copies of cited patents/printed publications and supporting affidavits/declarations must be included; petitioner must serve required documents on patent owner.

name: Patent owner motion to amend — one motion, permitted remedies (35 U.S.C. 316(d)(1)-(3))
description: During an IPR, the patent owner may file one motion to amend the patent to (A) cancel any challenged claim; and/or (B) for each challenged claim, propose a reasonable number of substitute claims. Additional motions may be permitted jointly or by regulation. An amendment may not enlarge the scope of the claims or introduce new matter.
guidance: Regulations set standards and procedures for allowing amendment and require information submitted in support to be made part of prosecution history.

name: Final written decision and certificate (35 U.S.C. 318(a)-(b))
description: If an IPR is instituted and not dismissed, the PTAB shall issue a final written decision on patentability of challenged claims and any new claim added. If final and appeal time expired, the Director shall issue and publish a certificate canceling claims finally determined unpatentable, confirming patentable claims, and incorporating any new/amended claims determined patentable.

name: Intervening rights for amended/new claims (35 U.S.C. 318(c))
description: Any proposed amended or new claim determined patentable and incorporated after IPR shall have the same effect as specified in section 252 for reissued patents regarding rights of prior users/makers/importers or those who made substantial preparation before issuance of the certificate.

name: Transitional determination of reasonable likelihood within 3 months (35 U.S.C. 312(a) (transitional))
description: Not later than 3 months after filing of a request for inter partes reexamination, the Director shall determine whether the information shows a reasonable likelihood that the requester would prevail with respect to at least one challenged claim, with or without consideration of other patents/printed publications.
guidance: A showing of reasonable likelihood is not precluded because a patent/printed publication was previously cited or considered by the Office.

name: Order for inter partes reexamination if reasonable likelihood shown (35 U.S.C. 313 (transitional))
description: If the Director finds reasonable likelihood that the requester would prevail with respect to at least one claim, the determination shall include an order for inter partes reexamination of the patent to resolve the question; the order may be accompanied by the Office's initial action on the merits.

name: Conduct of pre‑AIA inter partes reexamination — procedures and responses (35 U.S.C. 314 (pre-AIA))
description: Reexamination shall be conducted according to procedures for initial examination (sections 132 and 133). Patent owner may propose amendments and new claims (not enlarging scope). Documents filed by either party (except the request) shall be served on the other. Third‑party requester gets copies of Office communications and one opportunity to file written comments within 30 days after service of patent owner's response.
guidance: Special dispatch required unless Director provides otherwise.

name: Pre‑AIA certificate of patentability/unpatentability (35 U.S.C. 316 (pre-AIA))
description: When appeal time has expired or appeals terminated, the Director shall issue and publish a certificate canceling any claim finally determined unpatentable, confirming any claim determined patentable, and incorporating into the patent any amended or new claim determined patentable. Such amended/new claims have effect like section 252 for reissued patents.

name: Post‑grant review scope — grounds (35 U.S.C. 321(2)(b))
description: A petitioner in a post-grant review may request to cancel as unpatentable one or more claims of a patent on any ground that could be raised under paragraph (2) or (3) of section 282(b) (relating to invalidity of the patent or any claim).

name: Thesis III: Not all actions performed in the state of mortal sin are necessarily sinful because of lack of grace
description: Thesis III (de fide): Not all actions performed by man in the state of mortal sin are sinful on account of his not being in the state of grace.
guidance: Proof and guidance: The Council of Trent anathematized the view that all pre-justification works are sins. Scriptural exhortations to sinners to repent, give alms, pray, etc., imply such acts can be salutary; patristic testimony (Origen, Augustine, Prosper) supports that some acts by sinners can be good. The thesis is defended against Jansenist/Baian extremes (which claimed universal sinfulness of sinners' acts) by showing misinterpretations of patristic texts and by logical consequences (God would not command sinners to commit new sins).

name: Limitation of fallen nature's moral power (necessity of grace for sustaining full observance)
description: Although man can perform some naturally good acts without grace, theologians hold that man cannot observe the natural law in its entirety for any considerable length of time without the aid of grace.
guidance: Guidance and evidence: Arguments include concupiscence and human frailty (shortness of life, limitations of intellect), Scripture (St. Paul describing the law in his members), and conciliar teaching (Council of Trent warns the justified must fear falling without grace). The claim is formulated also in terms of temptation: man cannot overcome all grievous temptations against the moral law without divine assistance; two formulations are offered (indefinite and more specific), and objections (Ripalda, Molina) are discussed and answered by appeal to Scripture and experience.

name: Consideration of judicial claim interpretations
description: Where there is related litigation and a federal court has made a judicial interpretation of a disputed claim term, the examiner in treating the disputed claim term should set forth his or her reasoning by, for example, acknowledging the judicial interpretation and assessing whether the judicial interpretation is consistent with the broadest reasonable construction of the term.
guidance: If adopting a different claim construction than the judicial interpretation, the examiner should supply reasoning to support the different interpretation.

name: Consideration of patent owner statements (35 U.S.C.301(a)(2) / 37 CFR 1.501(a)(2))
description: 35 U.S.C.301(a)(2) permits submission of written statements of the patent owner filed in a proceeding before a federal court or the Office in which the patent owner took a position on the scope of any claim of a particular patent.
guidance: Pursuant to 37 CFR 1.552, any such written statement of the patent owner of record in the patent (including reexamination files) should be considered (after reexamination ordered, but not at the order stage) to determine the proper meaning of a patent claim when applying patents or printed publications.

name: Claim construction standard in reexamination (35 U.S.C.304 and 257)
description: During reexamination ordered under 35 U.S.C. 304, and also under 35 U.S.C. 257, claims are given the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification and limitations in the specification are not read into the claims (In re Yamamoto).
guidance: In reexamination involving claims of an expired patent, apply Phillips ordinary-and-customary-meaning construction (words given their ordinary and customary meaning as understood by a person of ordinary skill at the time of the invention). The statutory presumption of validity (35 U.S.C. 282) has no application in reexamination.

name: Limit on 35 U.S.C.112 issues in reexamination under 304
description: In reexaminations ordered under 35 U.S.C. 304, consideration of 35 U.S.C. 112 issues should be limited to the amendatory (e.g., new language) matter.
guidance: A claim amended or newly presented containing a limitation not found in the original patent claim should be considered for compliance under 35 U.S.C.112 only with respect to that limitation. Terms/limitations present in the original patent claim generally should not be reexamined under 112 in a 304 proceeding unless the amendatory matter creates the issue (e.g., rewriting a dependent claim as independent that creates lack of antecedent). However, priority/benefit date determinations under 112 are permitted.

name: Examination of enablement/description and definiteness for new/amended claims
description: Compliance of new or amended claims with the enablement and/or description requirements of the first paragraph of 35 U.S.C.112 and with the second paragraph of 35 U.S.C.112 should be considered as to the amendatory and new text in the reexamination proceeding.
guidance: See MPEP § 2163 - § 2173.05(v) for extensive guidance on these matters; limit examination to the new/amended matter.

name: Prohibition on new matter (35 U.S.C.132/305) in reexamination
description: 35 U.S.C.305 provides for examination under 35 U.S.C.132, which prohibits the introduction of new matter into the disclosure.
guidance: Where new matter is added to the claims or affects claim limitations, the claims should be rejected under 35 U.S.C.112, first paragraph, for failing to meet the written description requirement. See MPEP § 2163.06 regarding the relationship between written description and the new matter prohibition.

name: Effect of amendment to the specification on 35 U.S.C.112 compliance
description: An amendment to the specification can redefine the scope of the terms in a claim such that the claim is no longer clear or is not supported by the specification.
guidance: Examiners should ensure that requirements of 35 U.S.C.112 are met when the specification is amended because such amendments can cause claims to fail compliance even if claims themselves are not amended.

name: Claims must not enlarge scope of patent (35 U.S.C.305)
description: Where new or amended claims are presented or any part of the disclosure is amended, the claims of the reexamination proceeding should be examined under 35 U.S.C.305 to determine whether they enlarge the scope of the original claims. 35 U.S.C.305 states that 'no proposed amended or new claim enlarging the scope of the claims of the patent will be permitted in a reexamination proceeding....'
guidance: A claim 'enlarges the scope' where it is broader than each and every claim of the patent. A claim is broadened if it contains any conceivable product/process that would not have infringed the original patent or if it is broader in any one respect.

name: Identification and explanation of broadening claim limitations
description: When making a rejection under 35 U.S.C.305, the claim limitations considered to broaden the scope should be identified and explained.
guidance: Use form paragraph 22.11 for rejections under 35 U.S.C.305; bracketed portions should identify the claim and explain why/which limitations broaden scope. Examiner Note: identify the claim limitations in bracket 2 and explain per MPEP § 2258.

name: Handling patents with prior Office or court decisions
description: Where some claims in a patent being reexamined have been the subject of a prior Office or court decision, those claims should be identified and handled per MPEP § 2242; copending proceedings addressed in MPEP §§2282-2286.
guidance: Patent claims not subject to reexamination because of prior adjudication should be identified. For claims dependent on a claim not subject to reexamination, see MPEP § 2260.01. If grounds in a prior Office/court decision are not based on patents/printed publications and clearly raise validity questions, the examiner’s Office action should state that the claims have not been examined as to those non-patent/non-printed-publication grounds (37 CFR 1.552(c)).

name: Scope limited to 'live' claims for which reexamination was requested
description: The Office’s determination will generally be limited solely to review of the 'live' claims (existing claims not held invalid by a final decision) for which reexamination has been requested. If requester did not request reexamination of certain claims, those claims generally will not be reexamined.
guidance: 35 U.S.C.302 requires the request must set forth the pertinency and manner of applying cited prior art to every claim for which reexamination is requested (37 CFR 1.510(b)). If the requester fails to apply the art to certain claims, requester is not statutorily entitled to reexamination of such claims. The Office, however, has discretion to reexamine non-requested claims under 35 U.S.C.303(a).

name: Restriction practice is improper in reexamination
description: Restriction requirements cannot be made in a reexamination proceeding since no statutory basis exists for restriction in reexamination.
guidance: Addition of claims to a 'separate and distinct' invention to the patent would be considered an enlargement of scope. See Ex parte Wikdahl and MPEP § 1412.03.

name: Check for previously cited/considered art ('old art') before making rejections
description: At the examining stage of a reexamination proceeding, the examiner will consider whether claims are subject to rejection based on art and should check the patent’s file history to ascertain whether the art that will provide the basis for the rejection was previously cited/considered in an earlier concluded Office examination (termed 'old art').
guidance: If the rejection will be based on a combination of old art and art newly cited during reexamination, the rejection is proper (In re Hiniker). Special rules apply when old art is the sole basis depending on the order date of reexamination (see following criteria).

name: Foreign language prior art previously cited — new translation may support reexamination
description: If a foreign language prior art reference was cited and discussed in any prior Office proceeding but was never completely and accurately translated into English during the original prosecution, a more complete and accurate translation may justify reexamination based on that reference.
guidance: A reexamination request should explain why the more complete and accurate translation actually teaches what is required by the claims.

name: Mental process determination
description: A claim limitation qualifies as a 'mental process' (a type of abstract idea) when the claimed steps can be performed mentally with pen and paper or by human cognition, as reflected in the specification and case law (e.g., CyberSource, Flook, Univ. of Florida Research, Symantec).
guidance: Examiners should look to the specification to determine whether the claimed map/analysis/steps are nothing more than a listing or mental procedures performable by humans. Cite cases indicating claimed computations or screening steps can be performed by pencil and paper or mentally. Use the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) in light of the specification.

name: Claim that requires a computer may still recite a mental process
description: Even if a claim is expressed as performed on or requiring a computer, it may nonetheless recite a mental process and thus an abstract idea (e.g., Benson; Mortgage Grader).
guidance: Examiners must carefully consider the claim's BRI in light of the specification to determine if the invention is described as a concept performed in the human mind and the applicant is merely claiming that concept: (1) performed on a generic computer, (2) performed in a computer environment, or (3) using a computer as a tool. If so, treat the claim as reciting a mental process.

name: Laws of nature and natural phenomena — definition and examples
description: Laws of nature and natural phenomena include naturally occurring principles/relations and nature-based products that are naturally occurring or lack markedly different characteristics from what occurs in nature. Courts have used terms such as 'physical phenomena', 'scientific principles', 'natural laws', and 'products of nature'.
guidance: Recognize examples identified by courts (isolated DNA; cloned farm animals; correlations between DNA regions and alleles; metabolic correlations; myeloperoxidase correlations; electromagnetism; bacterial qualities; primers; chemical principles; cell-free fetal DNA; genotype–drug reaction correlations). Use cited case law (e.g., Myriad, Roslin, Merial, Mayo, Cleveland Clinic, O’Reilly v. Morse, Funk Bros., Ambry Genetics, Ariosa, Vanda) when determining whether a claim recites such an exception.

name: Not every claim describing a natural ability/process recites a law of nature
description: Claims that describe natural abilities or responses (e.g., cells’ survival, body responses to aspirin) are not necessarily laws of nature; claims focused on process steps applying those natural properties may be eligible.
guidance: Evaluate whether the claim is focused on merely observing or detecting a natural ability, or whether it claims process steps that apply or use the natural property (example: Rapid Litigation Mgmt. v. CellzDirect — fractionating/recovering/cryopreserving hepatocytes held eligible). Such claims may be eligible at Prong One unless they recite another exception, in which case continue Prong Two (and Step 2B if needed). Manufacturing a new compound by combining components is likewise not per se directed to the components' natural tendencies.

name: Claims reciting laws/natural phenomena may still be eligible if integrated into a practical application
description: Even if a claim recites a law of nature or natural phenomenon, eligibility can be found if the claim as a whole integrates the exception into a practical application (example: Vanda — tailoring treatment dose to genotype).
guidance: Such integration is equivalent to finding eligibility at Step 2A Prong Two (Pathway B). Apply Prong Two analysis to determine if the claim applies the natural relationship in a manner that integrates it into a practical application.

name: Products of nature — scope and treatment
description: When a law of nature or natural phenomenon is claimed as a physical product, the exception is often referred to as a 'product of nature'. This includes naturally occurring products and non-naturally occurring products that lack markedly different characteristics from their natural counterparts (examples: isolated DNA, cloned animals).
guidance: Treat product-of-nature issues within Step 2A; recognize that synthetically replicated products that are structurally identical to natural counterparts are not patent eligible. Consider the markedly different characteristics analysis to determine whether a claimed nature-based product is a product of nature exception.

name: BRI considerations and examiner best practices for nature-based product claims
description: Under the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI), a nature-based product limitation may encompass both eligible and ineligible products; examiners should recognize this when rejecting claims.
guidance: If a claim is rejected at Step 2B for failing to provide an inventive concept and the BRI demonstrates the claim covers ineligible embodiments, it is best practice for the examiner to point out the BRI and recommend an amendment to narrow the claim to embodiments that are not directed to products of nature or that are otherwise eligible. Consider whether the streamlined eligibility analysis (MPEP § 2106.06) is appropriate for inventions that clearly do not seek to tie up judicial exceptions.

name: Approach to identifying abstract ideas
description: Examiners should determine whether a claim recites an abstract idea by (1) identifying the specific limitation(s) in the claim under examination that the examiner believes recites an abstract idea, and (2) determining whether the identified limitation(s) fall within at least one of the groupings of abstract ideas listed above.
guidance: If an identified limitation falls within at least one grouping, conclude the claim recites an abstract idea in Step 2A Prong One and proceed to Step 2A Prong Two to determine whether additional elements integrate the abstract idea into a practical application (see MPEP § 2106.04(d)). If the limitations do not fall within any grouping, find the claim does not recite an abstract idea and the analysis concludes (Pathway B), except in rare circumstances (see MPEP § 2106.04(a)(3)). The groupings are not mutually exclusive; examiners should identify at least one grouping, and preferably all groupings applicable, if claim limitations fall within multiple groupings.

name: Disclosure/enabling requirements for AI and mathematical-methods inventions
description: "Occasionally applications are filed in which there is a fundamental insufficiency ... another example can be found in the field of artificial intelligence if the mathematical methods and the training datasets are disclosed in insufficient detail to reproduce the technical effect over the whole range claimed. Such a lack of detail may result in a disclosure that is more like an invitation to a research programme." (Part F-III-3) and "If the technical effect is dependent on particular characteristics of the training dataset used, those characteristics that are required to reproduce the technical effect must be disclosed unless the skilled person can determine them without undue burden ... However, in general, there is no need to disclose the specific training dataset itself." (Part G-II-3.3.1)
guidance: AI-related applications require disclosure akin to biotech: mathematical methods and the essential characteristics of training data must be described sufficiently to reproduce the claimed technical effect across the claimed range; mere allegations of effect are insufficient though exhaustive proof is not required. Do not assume that omitting dataset characteristics will be acceptable where those characteristics are necessary to reproduce the effect. Also: the EPO checks that the designated inventor is a natural person (J 8/20/DABUS case law).

name: Antibody claims — permissible definitions and use of epitopes (G-II-6.1, 6.1.3)
description: Antibodies may be defined by their target antigen and other functional features (binding affinity, neutralising properties, induction of apoptosis, internalisation, inhibition/activation of receptors). Claims by reference to epitope are discussed: an antibody may be claimed by reference to its epitope, but some passages relating to epitope definitions have been reformulated/deleted in certain sections.
guidance: Claims that define antibodies only by competition with a reference antibody disclosed for the first time in the application will normally not sufficiently identify antibodies for search and may trigger an invitation under Rule 63(1) to indicate subject-matter for search. Where there is no indication to the contrary, assume a prior‑art antibody binding the same antigen will have the claimed functional properties (burden of proof on the applicant).

name: Antibody enablement and claim scope — requirement to enable production and verification
description: "The application must enable the person skilled in the art to produce further antibodies having the claimed functional property without undue burden ... the functional definition must allow the skilled person to easily and unambiguously verify whether they are working inside or outside the scope of the claim. The claim should therefore normally include the relevant characteristics of the method used to determine and define the functional property." (Part G-II, 6.1.3)
guidance: Functional antibody claims must include or enable the characteristics and methods needed to determine the functional property so that skilled persons can reproduce and verify the claimed property without undue burden; otherwise sufficiency objections (Article 83-like) and search/inventive-step problems may follow.

name: Antibody inventive-step standard — surprising technical effect or lack of reasonable expectation of success (G-II-6.2)
description: "The subject‑matter of a claim defining a novel antibody binding to a known antigen does not involve an inventive step unless a surprising technical effect is shown ... or unless there was no reasonable expectation of success of obtaining antibodies having the required properties ... Inventive step is not acknowledged solely on the basis that an antibody is structurally different from the prior‑art antibodies. ... Nevertheless, antibodies can be inventive if the application overcomes technical difficulties in generating or manufacturing the claimed antibodies. A novel type of functional antibody format may also be considered inventive." (Part G-II-6.2)
guidance: To establish inventive step for antibodies, show an unexpected improvement or property over prior art or demonstrate that obtaining antibodies with the required properties was not reasonably expected; structural unpredictability alone is insufficient. Evidence of overcoming technical difficulties or a novel functional format can support inventiveness.

name: Adaptation of the description / Article 84 examination (D-V-5)
description: "The description of the patent may be examined for compliance with the requirements of Art. 84 only when, and then only to the extent that, an amendment of the patent introduces non-compliance with Art. 84. In particular, inconsistencies between the description and the claims resulting from amendments during opposition proceedings and casting doubt on the subject-matter for which protection is sought must be avoided." (Part D-V-5)
guidance: EPO will not re-examine the description under Art.84 unless an amendment causes non-compliance. When amending claims, ensure the description is consistent with allowed claims to avoid objection and doubt on the scope of protection.

name: Establish Broadest Reasonable Interpretation Of Claim As A Whole
description: Interpret the claim as a whole under the broadest reasonable interpretation when conducting the eligibility analysis.
