guidance: Revise MPEP text so that the word 'application' is not confused with 'practical application' in prong two and include examples or discussion on how claim interpretation affects integration determinations in Step 2A Prong Two.

name: Eligibility Step 2: Whether a Claim Is Directed To A Judicial Exception (Step 2A)
description: Determine whether the claim 'recites' a judicial exception and whether any recited judicial exception is integrated into a practical application (two prongs of Step 2A).
guidance: Add discussion of Revised Step 2A: (1) whether the claim recites a judicial exception; and (2) whether a recited judicial exception is integrated into a practical application. Remove language equating 'recited' and 'directed to' and require examiners to 'slot' abstract ideas into a single abstract idea grouping per the proposed guidance.

name: Step 2A Prong One — Recitation of a Judicial Exception
description: Assess whether a claim recites (explicitly or inherently includes) a judicial exception.
guidance: Keep first and second paragraph discussions of 'recited' material; delete text superseded by new approach to identifying abstract ideas; remove any language that equates 'recited' with 'directed to.'

name: Abstract Ideas — groupings and terminology
description: Describe abstract ideas using the proposed guidance groupings: mathematical concepts, certain methods of organizing human activity, and mental processes.
guidance: Modify discussion to adopt these groupings, remove reliance on comparing claimed concepts to previously-identified court examples, and revise examples/hypotheticals to explain that abstract-idea exception includes these groupings.

name: Examples of Claims Not Directed To Abstract Ideas
description: Identify and document examples of claims that are not directed to abstract ideas, including claims that improve computer functionality or other technology.
guidance: Incorporate into the larger 'Integration' section; cite appropriate parts of 2106.05 for considerations; update case examples (including cases decided after Aug 2017) and explain how those examples integrate the abstract idea into a practical application.

name: Claims Directed To Improvements In Computer Functionality Or Other Technology
description: Recognize that claims which improve computer functionality or other technology are not abstract ideas.
guidance: Revise discussion to clarify difference between conventionality vis-à-vis prior art (used in improvements consideration) and WURC consideration; examiners should continue to give full weight to improvements in Step 2A while not treating WURC analysis as part of Step 2A.

name: Laws of Nature, Natural Phenomena & Products of Nature
description: Address claims that potentially recite laws of nature, natural phenomena, or products of nature and when such claims can be rendered eligible.
guidance: Add discussion (including from relevant memoranda) about how treatment steps can render a claim reciting a law of nature eligible in Step 2A (i.e., not directed to a law of nature) when appropriately integrated.

name: Eligibility Step 2B — Whether A Claim Amounts To Significantly More
description: Evaluate whether claimed additional elements, individually and in combination, add an 'inventive concept' (i.e., amount to 'significantly more' than a judicial exception).
guidance: Revise text to indicate how considerations are evaluated in both Step 2A Prong Two (integration) and Step 2B (significantly more), clarify overlap with WURC consideration (WURC evaluated only in 2B), and modify case exemplar discussions to address both integration and significantly more.

name: Search For An Inventive Concept
description: When performing Step 2B, search for an inventive concept in the additional claim elements beyond the judicial exception.
guidance: Explain when analysis from 2A may carry over to 2B and when it must be re-evaluated; clarify that WURC is an evidentiary, factual consideration to be evaluated only in 2B.

name: Well-Understood, Routine, Conventional Activity (WURC)
description: Evaluate whether additional claim elements are well-understood, routine, and conventional — a consideration relevant to Step 2B.
guidance: Add indication that WURC is evaluated only in 2B; remove language suggesting a WURC finding need not be supported. Add section addressing that WURC requires a factual determination and how examiners can support this determination (Berkheimer-related guidance).

name: Generic claim when species utility established
description: Where an applicant has established utility for a species that falls within an identified genus of compounds, a generic claim covering the genus should generally be treated as sufficient under 35 U.S.C. 101.
guidance: Only impose rejection on generic claim if it can be established that other species clearly encompassed by the claim do not have utility; encourage applicant to amend generic claim to exclude species that lack utility.

name: One credible assertion suffices
description: An applicant need only make one credible assertion of specific utility for the claimed invention to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 101 and 35 U.S.C. 112; additional statements of utility, even if not 'credible', do not render the claimed invention lacking in utility.
guidance: Cite case law (e.g., Raytheon v. Roper, In re Gottlieb). If at least one stated objective is met, utility under 35 U.S.C. 101 is shown.

name: Applicant statements alone not basis for rejection
description: Statements made by the applicant in the specification or incident to prosecution cannot, standing alone, be the basis for a lack of utility rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 or 35 U.S.C. 112.
guidance: Office should not require applicants to strike nonessential statements relating to utility; examiners should be careful not to read unclaimed results, limitations, or embodiments into claims.

name: Identify asserted or well-established utility on initial exam
description: Upon initial examination, the examiner should review the specification to determine if there are any statements asserting that the claimed invention is useful for any particular purpose and whether disclosure identifies a specific and substantial utility.
guidance: A complete disclosure should include a statement identifying a specific and substantial utility; examiner should locate and evaluate any such statements in the specification.

name: Specific and substantial utility requirement
description: A statement of utility must be 'specific and substantial': it should fully and clearly explain why the applicant asserts the invention is useful and enable one ordinarily skilled in the art to understand why the applicant asserts the claimed invention is useful.
guidance: Generic assertions (e.g., 'biological activity', 'pharmacological effects') without explaining why that activity is useful are insufficient (citing Brenner v. Manson, In re Ziegler, In re Kirk).

name: Failure to identify specific and substantial utility -> rejection
description: Except where an invention has a well-established utility, failure to specifically identify why an invention is believed useful renders the claimed invention deficient under 35 U.S.C. 101 and 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph).
guidance: Examples provided where general statements were insufficient; examiner should issue appropriate rejections and tie to enablement/best-mode concerns where applicable.

name: When examiner should reject for lack of recognized utility
description: If a person of ordinary skill would not immediately recognize a specific and substantial utility for the claimed invention based on its characteristics or applicant statements, the examiner should reject under 35 U.S.C. 101 and 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
guidance: Rejection should clearly indicate the basis (failure to identify specific and substantial utility) and specify that applicant must reply indicating why invention is believed useful and where support is in the specification as filed.

name: Form paragraph guidance for utility rejections
description: Use form paragraphs 7.05.02 (Utility Lacking), 7.05.03 (Inoperative), and 7.05.04 (Utility Rejections under 35 U.S.C. 101 and 112) to reject claims for failure to satisfy utility requirement, with bracketed inserts specifying explanations and wording (e.g., 'specific and substantial', 'credible').
guidance: Follow Format A/B/C instructions: which inserts to use, how to handle multiple utilities, and examiner notes regarding enablement overlap and use of Wands factors for enablement rejections.

name: Applicant rebuttal options and evidence standards
description: After a proper prima facie showing, the burden shifts to the applicant to rebut via claim amendments, arguments, new evidence in affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132, or printed publications. New evidence must be relevant to issues raised in the rejection.
guidance: Declarations that merely state conclusions without establishing nexus to supporting evidence or that are mere opinions may have limited probative value (citing In re Grunwell, In re Buchner).

name: Examiner evaluation of applicant reply
description: Office personnel must review the original disclosure, evidence relied upon for the prima facie showing, claim amendments, and any new reasoning/evidence provided; recognize, fully consider and respond to each substantive element of any response to a rejection based on lack of utility.
guidance: If totality of record would make asserted utility credible to a person of ordinary skill, the Office cannot maintain the rejection.

name: In vitro and animal testing generally sufficient for therapeutic utility
description: Data from in vitro or animal testing is generally sufficient to support an asserted therapeutic utility, provided there is a reasonable evidentiary correlation to the claimed human therapeutic use.
guidance: Such data should be considered along with other evidence and reasoning; courts recognize animal/in vitro data as relevant for predicting human therapeutic response when a reasonable correlation exists.

name: Same invention requirement
description: A re-issued patent must be for the same invention as the original patent; if the re-issued patent is for a different invention the re-issue is invalid.
guidance: Courts repeatedly hold the re-issued patent must cover the same invention as originally patented. The patentee may 'redescribe his invention, and include in the Description and Claims ... whatever else was suggested or substantially indicated in the old specification, drawings, or Patent-Office model which properly belonged to the invention.' The jury may look to the original drawings to determine whether the inventions are the same.

name: No enlargement of the invention (general prohibition)
description: A re-issue cannot enlarge or expand the Claims of the original patent; re-issue is not permitted to enlarge the original right.
guidance: Numerous cases (e.g., Dunbar v. White and others cited) assert that enlargement of the original claims by re-issue makes the re-issue void. However, courts differ in borderline situations; enlargement may be permitted only in narrow circumstances (see other metrics about inadvertence, promptness, and lack of intervening rights).

name: Correction for inadvertence, accident, or mistake
description: Re-issue is available when the Description or the Claim is inexact or incomplete, or when the Claim is broader than the actual invention, provided the error arose from 'inadvertence, accident, or mistake' and without fraudulent or deceptive intention.
guidance: This is the central statutory/ equitable ground for reissues: the error must be bona fide and inadvertent. The treatise summarizes: the act confers the privilege of a re-issue whenever the Description or the Claim is inexact or incomplete, or when the Claim is broader than the actual invention, provided the error stems from inadvertence/accident/mistake and not from fraud.

name: Actual bona fide mistake required (not mere error of judgment)
description: An 'actual mistake' (a bona fide inadvertent error) is required for an enlarging re-issue; mere error of judgment (which can be corrected on appeal) does not qualify.
guidance: Courts distinguish between mistakes of judgment (not grounds for re-issue) and inadvertent mistakes of fact in the specification/claim. The remedy is available where a court of chancery would have corrected the mistake — an actual inadvertence, not an after-the-fact change of mind or litigation strategy.

name: Claim as part of the specification — amendability
description: The Claim is an essential part of the specification and is amendable by re-issue to correct defects of undue restriction, excess, inexactness, or insufficiency.
guidance: Historically the claim (whether in grant language or petition language) has always been part of the specification and subject to the same kinds of defects as the descriptive part; therefore claims may be limited, clarified, or otherwise amended by re-issue to correct inadvertent defects. Courts recognize both undue restriction (claim too narrow) and undue excess (claim too broad) as correctable.

name: Drawings/models/drawings evidence may justify claim changes
description: Elements shown in original drawings or models, even if not expressly claimed, can support inclusion in a re-issue if they were part of the original invention.
guidance: Courts will look to drawings and models to determine if an element was part of the original invention; if so, the patentee (or assignee) may incorporate that element into the re-issued patent. The jury may examine drawings to determine identity of inventions covered.

name: Conflicting authorities on claiming described-but-unclaimed matter
description: There is tension in authority: some decisions assert a re-issue cannot claim what was described but not claimed in the original (e.g., Reed v. Chase), while many other courts have held re-issue is the proper mode to secure what was described but not claimed.
guidance: The treatise records this split in authority and indicates that later and numerous cases permit securing described-but-unclaimed elements by re-issue when they clearly belonged to the original invention, especially if the applicant acts promptly and no intervening rights exist. Practitioners must consider jurisdiction and precedent.

name: Drawing Must Be Clear and Complete
description: The drawing disclosure is the most important element of the application and must be clear and complete so that nothing regarding the design sought to be patented is left to conjecture.
guidance: Ensure all aspects of the claimed design are unambiguous and fully shown to permit proper examination and potential enforcement (MPEP 1503.02).

name: All views necessary to fully disclose the design must be provided
description: Provide every view necessary to fully disclose the claimed design so that the visual disclosure is complete.
guidance: Include enough orthogonal, sectional, perspective, or detail views to remove ambiguity about the claimed design's appearance.

name: Broken lines usage and limits
description: Broken lines may be used to show environmental structure or unclaimed subject matter, but must be clearly differentiated from solid lines; rules around broken lines include prohibitions against certain uses.
guidance: Use broken lines only to indicate non-claimed or environmental elements and ensure they are visually distinct from solid lines. The related MPEP entry 'Broken Lines Show Visible Structure Only' is listed as prohibited—follow MPEP guidance on permissible broken-line usage (MPEP 1503.02).

name: Color drawings/photographs: permitted and conditionally required
description: Color drawings or photographs are permitted for design applications and may be required when color is a feature of the claimed design or when submitted under certain circumstances.
guidance: If color is an element of the claimed design, submit color drawings or photographs as required and follow USPTO procedures for color submissions (MPEP 1503.02).

name: Claims and specification must follow design-patent-specific form
description: Claims must be in a specific form for design patents and design patent applications require certain elements (some elements similar to utility patents but with design-specific requirements).
guidance: Draft claims and the specification to conform to MPEP 1503 and design-patent practice (e.g., claim phrasing, reliance on drawings as the visual disclosure). Consult MPEP 1503 for details.

name: Principle of priority — conditions to claim priority
description: An applicant may claim priority from a first application if: (a) the first application was filed in Vietnam or a contracting party country; (b) the applicant is a citizen or resident/has establishment in Vietnam or the country of first filing; (c) the claim is clearly stated and a certified copy of the first application is enclosed; (d) the application is filed within the time limit provided in the relevant treaty. Applicants may claim priority from different earlier applications for corresponding contents; the priority date is the filing date of the first application.
guidance: Specifies documentary and substantive conditions for claiming priority under treaties and bilateral agreements (Article 91 clauses 1–3).

name: Documents evidencing priority right
description: Documents evidencing priority right include a copy of first application(s) certified by the receiving office and deed of assignment of priority right if acquired from another person.
guidance: Specify acceptable documentary proof to support priority claims (Article 100 clause 3).

name: Scope of protection of inventions — expression and compatibility
description: The scope of protection shall be expressed in the form of a combination of technical specifications which are necessary and sufficient to identify the scope of the rights, and compatible with the description and drawings.
guidance: Claims/scope must be technically precise, necessary & sufficient, and consistent with the disclosure (Article 102.3).

name: Industrial design scope of protection
description: The scope must clearly define features which need to be protected, including features new and different from similar known industrial designs.
guidance: Claims for design protection must identify protectable novel features (Article 103.3).

name: Court’s claim construction statements vs demonstratives/party arguments
description: The district court’s formal claim construction is what the court announces and reads to the jury; demonstratives or slides prepared by parties reflecting the court’s rulings or additional 'no disclaimer' language are party arguments and are not the court’s construction unless adopted by the court.
guidance: A demonstrative containing extra language (e.g., a 'no disclaimer' line) does not constitute a modification of the court’s construction. Parties may be permitted to argue the meaning of the construction (e.g., that it does not exclude gravity drop), but the court controls the formal construction given to the jury.

name: Claim term development: court need not sua sponte construe terms not requested
description: If a party never requests a construction of a particular claim term (here, 'capture'), the district court need not construe that term and the factual question of whether the accused device meets the term is for the jury to resolve.
guidance: Parties should request construction of disputed claim terms during claim construction; otherwise, the jury decides application of the existing construction. The absence of a requested construction means the party cannot later complain that the court failed to construe that term.

name: Permissible scope of trial argumentation when claim construction language is excluded from jury instructions
description: Even if the court declines to include certain explanatory or 'no disclaimer' language in the final jury instructions, parties may argue their interpretation of the court’s construction to the jury (so long as it does not contravene the court’s formal construction).
guidance: Courts may limit demonstratives or argument to avoid jury confusion, but they can allow parties to make arguments that the court’s construction permits (e.g., that the court’s construction does not exclude a gravity drop). Trial counsel should preserve arguments appropriately for appeal.

name: Patent owner burden on motions to amend (37 C.F.R. § 42.121(d)(1))
description: A patent owner bears the burden of persuasion to show, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the motion to amend complies with statutory and regulatory requirements (including paragraphs (1) and (3) of 35 U.S.C. 316(d) and paragraphs (a)(2) and (3) and (b)(1) and (2) of the section).
guidance: Specific statutory/regulatory components include showing a reasonable number of proposed substitute claims; that substitute claims respond to a ground of unpatentability; that proposed substitute claims do not enlarge the scope of the claims; and that the motion does not introduce new matter. These burden-allocation rules were unchanged from the 2021 revisions.

name: Petitioner burden on motions to amend (37 C.F.R. § 42.121(d)(2))
description: A petitioner bears the burden of persuasion to show, by a preponderance of the evidence, that any proposed substitute claims are unpatentable.
guidance: Petitioner must present prior art/arguments sufficient to satisfy preponderance for anticipation or obviousness (and may raise issues such as eligibility, indefiniteness, or enablement where appropriate).

name: MTA procedural structure retained (timing, listing support, additional MTA)
description: Prior rule structure retained in substance: (a) timing, scope, number of substitute claims; (b) listing of substitute claims and support in disclosures; (c) additional MTA; (d) parties' burden of persuasion and Board discretion (with changes reflected in final rule).
guidance: Section (b) and (c) are substantively unchanged in the final rule; practitioners should follow the established listing/support requirements when drafting MTAs.

name: Anticipation requires every claim element in a single reference
description: To reject a claim as anticipated under 35 U.S.C. 102, the reference must teach each and every element of the claim, either expressly or inherently, under the claim's broadest reasonable interpretation.
guidance: The identical invention must be shown in as complete detail as in the claim; elements must be arranged as required by the claim but exact phrasing is not required (ipsissimis verbis not necessary). See Verdegaal; Richardson; MPEP § 2114.

name: Different combinations/sub-combinations may be separately claimed if new and useful
description: If several combinations of elements are new and useful and will severally produce new and useful results, the inventor is entitled to a patent for the several combinations, provided he files written descriptions for each and complies with the Patent Act.
guidance: Such combinations can be claimed in one specification with separate claims, avoiding the need for separate applications (Stevens v. Pritchard; Banks v. Snediker).

name: Elements in general use cannot be joined with a combination
description: Elements already in general use in other connections cannot be joined with the combination.
guidance: If an element lacks novelty or utility in the relevant context (already known in the arts), the Patent Office may refuse joinder with a claimed combination (Ex parte LaBorde).

name: Generic and species claims — when genus + species can be joined
description: A discoverer of a genus may claim broadly; a generic invention and one species under the genus may be joined; but two distinct species under the same genus requiring different inventive acts cannot be joined.
guidance: When substitution of one form for another involves invention, the differences are patentable as distinct species; if substitution requires only mechanical skill (no inventive act), then differences are mere modifications of a single species (Ex parte Kook; Ex parte Howland).

name: Process vs apparatus: separability determines separate patentability
description: Where a process can be performed by different apparatus, it is separately patentable from the apparatus which performs it. Where an apparatus can be used for no other purpose than performing the process, the process may be the mere function of the apparatus and separability is affected.
guidance: If process can exist apart from one specific apparatus, claim process separately; if apparatus is inseparable (performs process exclusively), joinder may be proper but must be examined for dependence (Gage v. Kellogg; Ex parte Tyne).

name: Separate claims required when joinder covers multiple inventions
description: An application may include several inventions in one specification, but separate claims must be filed to secure exclusive rights to each separate combination or invention.
guidance: The inventor may describe multiple combinations in one specification and make separate claims referring to that description, avoiding multiple applications; omission of claims may jeopardize rights (Stevens v. Pritchard; Clifford discussion).

name: Alice two-step test (overview)
description: Apply the two-part Alice framework: (1) determine whether the claims are directed to a patent-ineligible concept (e.g., an abstract idea); (2) if so, consider the claim elements individually and as an ordered combination to determine whether additional elements transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application (i.e., whether an 'inventive concept' exists).
guidance: Quoting Alice/Mayo: Step One asks if claims are directed to an ineligible concept; Step Two searches for an 'inventive concept' that is 'sufficient to ensure that the patent in practice amounts to significantly more than a patent upon the ineligible concept itself.'

name: Focus on claim language but consider specification/prosecution history
description: The §101 inquiry must focus on the language of the asserted claims themselves, but courts may look to the written description and prosecution history to understand the problem facing the inventor and what the patent describes as the invention.
guidance: Precedents allow multiple analytical approaches: (1) consult the written description to understand inventor's problem and solution; (2) consider whether any technological improvement is 'embodied in the claims'; (3) analyze whether claims and specification 'describe how the improvement was accomplished.' (Cites: ChargePoint; Visual Memory; Recentive Analytics.)

name: Specific asserted improvement vs. abstract idea (software-specific guidance)
description: In software cases, the inquiry often turns on whether claims focus on specific asserted improvements in computer capabilities (patent-eligible) or instead on a process/system that qualifies as an abstract idea (patent-ineligible).
guidance: If the claim language and specification disclose concrete improvements to computer functionality, eligibility is more likely; if they merely implement desired results without technical detail, they are often directed to an abstract idea. (Cites: Int’l Bus. Machs. v. Zillow; Visual Memory.)

name: Anti-pattern — result-oriented functional claiming
description: Claims drafted using largely (if not entirely) result-focused functional language, containing no specificity about how the purported invention achieves those results, are almost always found to be ineligible under §101.
guidance: Result-oriented language such as 'able to' or 'arranged to allow' without describing how the results are achieved is a red flag. (Cites: Beteiro; examples in this opinion that claims merely state results for asynchronous review.)

name: Specification must show how improvement is achieved to support eligibility
description: A claimed technological improvement must be described in the specification (and, ideally, embodied in the claims) such that a skilled artisan can discern how the improvement is accomplished; mere statements of goals/benefits are insufficient.
guidance: Courts look for disclosure of specific means or technical solutions in the specification. Absence of such disclosure supports a finding that claims are directed to an abstract idea. (Cites: Recentive Analytics; Visual Memory; contrasted with Contour IP example.)

name: Comparative precedent analysis (distinguish patents that disclose specific means)
description: When analyzing eligibility, compare to precedent: patents that disclose specific means of achieving an improvement (e.g., generating high- and low-quality streams in parallel) are distinct from patents that merely claim the improvement without concrete implementation.
guidance: Use analogies to cases like Contour IP (eligible where specific technical means were claimed) vs. Hawk Technology (ineligible where claims recited goals without concrete solutions) to guide analyses.

name: When claim construction is required before §101 ruling
description: Claim construction is not necessary before deciding §101 unless the patentee proposes a specific claim construction and explains why that construction would change the patent-eligibility analysis.
guidance: To defeat a motion to dismiss based on the need for claim construction, the patentee must propose a specific construction and explain how resolving that dispute would affect the §101 outcome. (Cites: Mobile Acuity.)

name: Identification of each claim to be examined
description: The request must identify each claim of the patent for which supplemental examination is requested (37 CFR 1.610(b)(4)).
guidance: Because patentability issues pertain to claims, the patent owner must identify the specific claims to be examined so the Office can determine whether any item of information raises a SNQ affecting those claims. Patent owners are encouraged to specify which items of information apply to which claims; if not specified, the Office will assume all identified claims are to be considered in light of every listed item of information.

name: Separate, detailed explanation of relevance and manner of applying each item to each claim
description: For each item listed under 1.610(b)(2) the request must include a separate, detailed explanation of the relevance and manner of applying that item to each claim for which supplemental examination is requested (37 CFR 1.610(b)(5)).
guidance: The explanation must explain for each claim either (1) what the item teaches with respect to that claim, or (2) which teachings in the item an examiner may consider important in determining patentability. Citations to particular portions or figures should be included. Ideally provide a claim chart comparing each claim limitation with the teachings of each item. General statements not tied to claim limitations are insufficient. Provide separate explanations for dependent claims or expressly incorporate the independent claim explanation for dependent claims. Use headings and subheadings (identify each item and which claims are discussed); examples of acceptable headings are provided. Do not combine the required detailed explanation with optional patentability arguments (e.g., 1.610(c) discussions) because doing so can obscure the required explanation and risk a finding of noncompliance and loss of the filing date. Be comprehensive to frame potential issues and assist examiner review. The Office may accept imperfect explanations if the meaning is readily understood, but failure to provide required explanations will lead to a Notice of Noncompliant Supplemental Examination Request (37 CFR 1.610(d)).

name: Copy and formatting requirements for the patent copy
description: The request must include a copy of the patent (and any disclaimer or certificate) reproduced so specification and claims are in double-column format and drawing pages and front page are presented as in the printed patent; copies must be single-sided (each page plainly written on only one side).
guidance: Include any certificate of correction, extension, supplemental examination certificate, post-grant review certificate, ex parte/inter partes reexamination certificates, disclaimers, etc., because they generally become part of the patent. Use a full copy of the printed patent if desired; do not submit two-sided copies.

name: Markings for changes (deletions/additions)
description: All changes relative to the patent being reexamined which are made to the specification, including the claims, must include markings: matter to be omitted must be enclosed in brackets; matter to be added must be underlined.
guidance: Markings are made in comparison to the original patent (not to any prior amendment). Underlining for additions will be printed as italics in the reexamination certificate and brackets are printed as inserted in the proceeding. 37 CFR 1.530(f) identifies these marking types; added paragraphs must be submitted completely underlined.

name: Status of claims and explanation of support
description: Whenever there is an amendment to the claims, the status (pending or canceled) of all patent claims and added claims as of the date of the amendment must be supplied on pages separate from the changes, together with an explanation of the support in the disclosure of the patent for the changes.
guidance: Failure to submit claim status generally results in an informal response to the patent owner prior to final rejection; an amendment submitted after final rejection lacking this will not be entered. Explanations of support go to the merits and must cite where support exists in the specification (examples show column/line citations in Remarks).

name: No enlargement of claim scope / no new matter
description: No amendment may enlarge the scope of the claims of the patent or introduce new matter. No amendment may be proposed for entry in an expired patent; no amendment (other than cancellation) will be incorporated into the patent by a certificate issued after expiration.
guidance: Amended or new claims that broaden scope should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 305. Proposed amendments are treated as entered by Office actions for prosecution purposes but are not effective until the reexamination certificate is issued and published.

name: Formal paper requirements (37 CFR 1.52) for submissions
description: Papers to become part of permanent USPTO records must be on sheets of specified sizes (A4 or 8.5x11), single-sided, unbound, white, flexible, with specified margins (top ≥2.0 cm, left ≥2.5 cm, right ≥2.0 cm, bottom ≥2.0 cm), and plainly/legibly written by typewriter or machine printer in permanent dark ink.
guidance: Text must have sufficient clarity/contrast for reproduction and OCR. Preferably 12-point nonscript fonts (Arial, Times Roman, Courier); lines 1.5 or double spaced for specifications; single column text. Claims must commence on separate physical sheet/electronic page; abstract on separate sheet or first page in reissue/reexamination. See 37 CFR 1.52 for full specifics.

name: Specification amendment presentation
description: All amendments to the specification (other than claims/drawings) must be made by submission of the entire text of each added or rewritten paragraph with markings (single brackets for deletions, underlining for additions).
guidance: The only exception is deleting an entire paragraph by statement deleting it without presenting the paragraph text, although presenting the text aids proper entry. The precise point where any added/rewritten paragraph is located must be indicated; uncertainty may delay issuance of the reexamination certificate. Examiner amendments at NIRC also require the full text with markings; 1.121(g) exception does not apply in reexamination.

name: Accompanying explanation of support for claim changes (per 1.530(e))
description: Each claim amendment must be accompanied by an explanation of the support in the disclosure of the patent for the amendment (support for any insertions and deletions).
guidance: Failure to submit the explanation generally results in notification that the amendment prior to final rejection is not completely responsive; amendments submitted after final rejection without support explanation will not be entered. Examples show required 'Remarks' pages listing status and specific column/line support.

name: Amendment of new claims (no bracketing vs prior amendment)
description: An amendment of a new claim (previously presented in the reexamination) must present the entire text of the new claim containing the amendatory material and must be underlined throughout; the presentation cannot contain any bracketing or other indication of what was in the previous version of the claim.
guidance: Patent owner must point out what is changed in the 'Remarks' portion of the amendment and provide support citations. All changes in reexamination are made vis-à-vis the original patent, not in comparison with any prior amendment.

name: Dutch ex parte evidentiary seizure (saisie-contrefaçon) / Preliminary civil seizure
description: A preservatory ex parte procedure allowing a claimant to have evidence/products seized or described by a bailiff, subject to location/accessibility in the Netherlands and subsequent initiation of proceedings within a set term.
guidance: Procedure: request filed mentioning IP rights and reasons for suspected infringement; court decree typically in days; bailiff may enter premises, describe or seize products and store them; seizure is conservatory—claimant must initiate infringement proceedings within a set term or seizure becomes void and items returned; inter partes access to seized evidence requires subsequent proceedings. Seizures can assist litigants in other jurisdictions.

name: China – Preliminary injunction requirements (factors)
description: To obtain a preliminary injunction in China claimants must satisfy statutory/practical factors examining factual/legal basis, irreparable harm, balance of harms, public interest, and other relevant considerations.
guidance: Courts generally consider: (1) whether claimant’s request has factual ground and legal basis; (2) whether failure to take preservation measures will cause irreparable harm or enforcement difficulty; (3) whether harm from not taking measures exceeds harm to defendant from measures; (4) whether injunction would prejudice public interest; and (5) other factors. Preliminary injunctive relief historically difficult in some patent matters due to risk of later invalidity, though courts are more willing in design patent cases where infringement is easier to determine.

name: Improvement to existing technology consideration
description: Consideration of improvements is relevant to the eligibility analysis regardless of the technology of the claimed invention.
guidance: The invention may be eligible if the claim describes an improvement to technology (e.g., improved way of preserving cells or improved computer animation) rather than merely reciting an idea or outcome. An improvement in the abstract idea itself (e.g., a recited fundamental economic concept) is not an improvement in technology. See McRO and Rapid Litigation Management examples.

name: Claims must recite how a computer aids the method (not generic computer addition)
description: To show that involvement of a computer assists in improving the technology, the claims must recite the details regarding how a computer aids the method, the extent to which the computer aids the method, or the significance of a computer to the performance of the method.
guidance: Merely adding generic computer components or generic instructions to perform the method on conventional machinery is not sufficient. If applicant adds a generic computer or claims a 'specially programmed' computer, the examiner must assess whether the added elements integrate the exception into a practical application or provide significantly more than the judicial exception.

name: Machine-or-transformation test as investigatory clue (not stand-alone)
description: "The machine-or-transformation test is a useful and important clue, and investigative tool" for determining patent eligibility, but it is not a stand‑alone test.
guidance: All claims must be evaluated under the Alice/Mayo two-part test. A claim that passes Alice/Mayo is eligible even if it fails the M-or-T test; conversely a claim that fails Alice/Mayo is ineligible even if it passes the M-or-T test. Use M-or-T along with other considerations (mere instructions, insignificant extra-solution activity, field of use).

name: Whether the machine/apparatus implements the method steps
description: Determine if the machine plays an integral role in performing the claimed method steps rather than merely being an object on which the method operates.
guidance: Integral use of a machine to achieve performance of a method can integrate the judicial exception into a practical application; mere use of a machine as a tool to perform an existing process (or obvious speed-up) will generally not amount to significantly more. See CyberSource and Versata discussions.

name: Whether the machine's involvement is extra-solution activity or field-of-use
description: Assess the extent to which the machine or apparatus imposes meaningful limits on the claim versus contributing only nominally to execution of the method.
guidance: Use that contributes only nominally (e.g., data-gathering or identifying a data source) or field-of-use limitations generally do not integrate a judicial exception or provide significantly more. See Bilski, Parker v. Flook, and CyberSource examples; see MPEP §§2106.05(g) & (h) for more.

name: Transformation factor: nature and extent of change in state or thing
description: Evaluate the type/extent of change effected by the claimed transformation (different function/use vs. mere location change).
guidance: Transformations that result in the article having a different function or use are more likely to provide significantly more; mere relocation or insignificant change is less likely. Example: transforming uncured synthetic rubber into precision-molded products (Diehr) provides significantly more.

name: Transformation factor: whether the transformation is extra-solution activity or field-of-use
description: Assess whether the recited transformation merely imposes a field-of-use limitation or contributes only nominally to execution of the claimed method.
guidance: A transformation that is merely a field-of-use limitation or contributes only nominally (e.g., data gathering or routine administration steps) likely will not provide significantly more. Example: Supreme Court in Mayo found administering a drug was only a field-of-use limitation and did not supply significantly more.

name: Known-in-the-art elements can still be non-routine/unconventional
description: An additional element (or combination of additional elements) that is known in the art can nevertheless be unconventional or non-routine for eligibility purposes.
guidance: Patentability (novelty/obviousness) is distinct from eligibility. Features taught by prior art may still be considered unconventional in the eligibility analysis if they represent an improvement to conventional functionality (example: Enfish). Examiners should evaluate whether the claimed features are 'conventional' in the context of eligibility even if they are not novel.

name: Identify the subject-matter/claim before testing infringement
description: The first thing to be attended to is the subject-matter of the patent; a clear idea is to be formed of the object of the patent, and provided the specification properly points out what the claim of the patentee is, it is not material in what form his claim is presented.
guidance: Determine what the specification and claims actually cover (principle, application, process, manufacture). The form (labeled process or manufacture) is subordinate to the real subject covered; infringement analysis proceeds from that identification.

name: Proportions/degrees as part of the essence of some patents
description: Where proportions or degrees are specified as the mode in which a particular effect is to be produced, they make part of the essence of the invention, and departures in proportions may lead to a different subject-matter.
guidance: If the patent claims a combination that depends on particular proportions, use of the same ingredients in materially different proportions (even if producing a similar effect) can be a new invention and not an infringement. Courts will consider whether the specification treated those proportions as essential; slight departures intended only to evade are treated as fraud.

name: Slight departures for evasion are fraud
description: A slight departure from the specification for the purpose of evasion only would be a fraud upon the patent and will not avoid infringement.
guidance: When assessing differences, courts look for substantive, not cosmetic, departures. Evidence that changes were made purely to evade existing claims supports finding of infringement; the test is whether the defendant's operation is essentially or substantially different.

name: Superior utility / practical difference test
description: Two things are not the same under the patent law when one is practically, substantially better than the other, and this improvement is not gained by the use of known mechanical equivalents; superior utility may settle the question of identity.
guidance: If accused device achieves materially better practical results by means that are in fact different (not mere equivalents), it may be considered not the same under the law. Courts use this to limit overbroad claims to allow useful improvements to be separately patentable.

name: Combination patent rule (using parts of a combination)
description: Every patent stands upon its subject-matter; where the patent is for a combination, it is no infringement to use any of the parts or things which go to make up the combination if the combination itself is not used.
guidance: If claim is to an entire combination, merely practicing individual elements does not infringe unless the claimed combination (all essential elements) is practiced. Contrast with patents that claim several distinct improvements (below).

name: Distinct improvements rule (single-element infringement)
description: Where the patent is for several distinct improvements or things, and does not stand upon the combination of such things, then the use of any one of them will be an infringement.
guidance: When a patent claims multiple separate inventions rather than a unitary combination, defendants using any one claimed improvement may infringe. Historically, courts required novelty of all claimed improvements to sustain an action; practitioners should be aware of that rule's significance in claim drafting and litigation.

name: Structural difference as primary criterion
description: Structural differences between the claimed product and the natural counterpart are a primary (though not exclusive) factor favoring patent eligibility.
guidance: Words like 'isolated', 'recombinant', and 'synthetic' add no weight by themselves. A non-naturally-occurring structural derivative (e.g., a methylated derivative) is likely patent-eligible under USPTO examples; an isolated gene whose sequence is identical to a natural gene is not, because the structural difference was not deemed 'marked.'

name: Functional differences may support eligibility but are not mandatory
description: In the absence of a structural difference, a claimed natural product must exhibit new functions or characteristics that rise to the level of 'marked' differences to be eligible; functional differences are considered but are not necessarily decisive.
guidance: A product whose purification results in therapeutically different properties may be patentable; however, courts have also held that functional or commercial usefulness attributable to intrinsic natural qualities does not establish patentability. The USPTO guidance treats functional differences as secondary to structural differences for chemical products.

name: Myriad-specific rule for genetic material
description: Isolated DNA with an identical sequence to a natural gene is patent-ineligible; complementary DNA (cDNA) that removes introns may be patent-eligible, but short cDNA indistinguishable from natural DNA may not be.
guidance: The Supreme Court in Myriad held that mere severing/isolation of genetic material that leaves the genetic information unchanged does not create patentable subject matter; claims expressed primarily in terms of genetic information will be scrutinized for whether the patentee 'created' anything new.

name: Method-of-use claims must be practical, specific, and non-preemptive
description: Methods that use natural products must recite practical, specific, and significant applications so as not to merely recite natural principles or foreclose others from using the same natural product in other ways.
guidance: Claims should avoid: (i) general instructions to use the product; (ii) well-understood, purely conventional, or routine steps; or (iii) steps that everyone must use to apply the product. Good practice: include specific regimens, dosages, routes, and treatment schedules (e.g., administering amazonic acid 0.76–1.25 teaspoons daily for 10–20 days) to limit scope and survive eligibility scrutiny.

name: Product-by-process claim limitations and standards
description: Product-by-process claims are allowed when a product cannot be adequately defined by composition or structure, but in the U.S. patentability is determined by the product itself, not by the process used to make it.
guidance: If the claimed product is identical or obvious over a known product, a product-by-process claim will be unpatentable even if produced by a novel process. The process is relevant only when it 'imparts distinctive structural characteristics' to the product or the structure is otherwise implied by process steps. For infringement, courts often consider both product and process; some decisions hold product-by-process claims cover only products made by the recited process, so accused products made by different processes may not infringe. To broaden protection, draft both process claims and product-by-process claims and disclose as many characterizing features as possible.

name: Sufficient written description and enablement for broad claims
description: Claims reciting general formulas or broad genus scope must be supported by sufficient disclosure such that a person skilled in the art would recognize the full scope; mere disclosure of a few species may not enable a broad genus claim.
guidance: Example: listing only CH4 and C3H8 does not support a claim to CnH2n+2 generally. Provide detailed descriptions of embodiments, substitutions, and variations (including parameters like temperature, pH, reagents) to enable and support broader claim scope. Disclose as many foreseeable embodiments as possible to strengthen written description and enablement support.

name: Claim drafting strategy for natural-product inventions
description: Focus claim drafting on modifications (derivatives), optimized formulations/dosages, new uses/applications, and advanced preparation/manufacturing methods rather than mere isolation of natural products.
guidance: Draft claims with reasonable scope, include specific and significant limitations, identify and characterize individual embodiments and combinations to achieve broader coverage and enforceability. Frequent review of evolving case law and USPTO policy is recommended to adapt strategy.

name: Enforcement and scope considerations
description: Product-by-process and poorly characterized product claims may confer limited protection and be difficult to enforce; scope of claims should be carefully considered relative to how accused products are made and used.
guidance: Because product-by-process claims may not cover products made by different methods and lack explicit characteristics, enforcement can be challenging. To reduce risk, include both product and process claims, and provide as much structural/characterizing data as possible in the specification.

name: Respondent's duty to file a timely, fact-specific response
description: The Notice and Order pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.24 requires the respondent to file, within the time specified (40 days in this matter), a response containing all information the respondent believes sufficient to establish a genuine issue of material fact under § 11.24(d).
guidance: Responses must identify and support (with documents, affidavits, deposition excerpts, etc.) any claimed infirmity of proof, due process defect, or grave injustice. Vague disagreement or unsupported assertions will not meet the clear-and-convincing showing required.

name: Infirmity of proof — what will and will not suffice
description: An infirmity of proof claim must show such weakness in the evidence supporting the foreign adjudication that the USPTO could not accept the conclusion as final. Mere disagreement, differing investigative outcomes in other agencies, or later testimony do not automatically establish infirmity.
guidance: The Office gives weight to stipulated facts and hearing officer findings relied upon by the foreign tribunal. Evidence that other agencies declined action does not necessarily undercut the state court's later findings, especially when stipulations post-date those investigations.

name: Applicability of foreign criminal-statute definitions when assessing misconduct
description: When a foreign adjudication relies on criminal statutes (e.g., West Virginia Code definitions such as the statutory definition of 'custodian'), the Office will consider those statutory definitions and the foreign tribunal's application as part of the proof establishing misconduct.
guidance: A respondent claiming the foreign court misapplied a criminal statute must present clear and convincing evidence of that misapplication to create a genuine issue of material fact. Mere assertion of statutory ambiguity without supporting legal analysis or evidence is insufficient.

name: Interlocutory appeals for claim construction (Markman orders)
description: The bill 'provides the Federal Circuit jurisdiction over interlocutory decisions, known as Markman orders, in which the district court construes the claims of a patent as a matter of law.'
guidance: Permits early appellate review of claim construction to clarify issues earlier in litigation and potentially streamline or narrow disputed issues before trial.

name: Damages factor: Entire market value rule
description: If the claimant shows that the claimed invention is the predominant basis for market demand for a product or process that has a functional relationship with the claimed invention, damages may be based upon the entire market value of the products or processes involved that satisfy that demand.
guidance: Preserves the ability to award damages based on the entire market value only when the patented feature drives demand (i.e., a predominant basis), limiting blanket application of the entire-market-value rule.

name: Identify if claim is directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A)
description: Analyze whether the claim, viewed as a whole, is directed to a judicial exception (product of nature, law of nature, abstract idea).
guidance: For nature-based claims ask whether the claim as a whole is directed to a product of nature; for process claims ask whether the claimed steps (e.g., comparing sequences) recite an abstract idea. Use the claim's focus and high-level recitation to identify the exception. Example: a high-level comparing step was treated as an abstract idea in Myriad CAFC.

name: Product-of-nature analysis via closest naturally occurring counterpart and 'markedly different characteristics'
description: For nature-based products, compare the claimed subject matter to its closest naturally occurring counterpart to determine whether it has 'markedly different characteristics' from that counterpart.
guidance: Look for changes in structure, function, or other properties that are relevant to the invention (e.g., organoleptic properties, physical form, dissolution rate, time-release behavior). If the claimed product has such markedly different characteristics, it is not a product-of-nature exception. Examples: (eligible) gel with improved mouthfeel and spreadable solid form; formulation with altered time-release properties; granular texiol with specific particle-size distribution producing increased, consistent dissolution.

name: Use of Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) in identifying natural counterparts
description: Interpret the claim under the broadest reasonable interpretation to determine whether it covers a naturally occurring material or mixture and thus the relevant natural counterpart.
guidance: Apply BRI to claim language (e.g., % texiol + water) to see if it encompasses naturally occurring sap; the BRI affects which natural counterpart is the proper comparison for the marked-differences analysis.

name: Marked differences must be relevant to the nature of the invention
description: Any altered property relied upon to show 'markedly different characteristics' should be relevant to the invention's purpose or nature.
guidance: Evaluate whether the changed property (e.g., jelly-like spreadability, prolonged sweetness, improved dissolution) is meaningful to the invention (e.g., a dietary sweetener). If so, that supports eligibility (Claim 3, 4, 5, 6 examples).

name: Mixture analysis: consider components as additional elements to each other
description: When a claim recites a mixture of products of nature, consider each component as an additional element to the other(s) to assess whether the combination results in markedly different characteristics or significantly more than the components themselves.
guidance: Even if components are products of nature, their combination may produce new properties. Conversely, if mixing does not change structure/function and was routine/conventional, the mixture may remain an ineligible product of nature. Example: mixing texiol and water in routine ways did not produce marked differences (Claim 2), but adding Compound N that altered organoleptic profile did (Claim 3).

name: Abstract-idea identification for high-level information-processing steps
description: Claims that recite high-level steps of collecting, comparing, or analyzing information (e.g., comparing a patient sequence to wild-type) can be directed to an abstract idea.
guidance: If the recited comparison or mental steps impose no limits on how the comparison is performed, they are likely abstract. Narrowing the information compared (e.g., BRCA1 sequences) does not by itself make the claim non-abstract. Example: comparing BRCA1 sequences was treated as an abstract idea in the Myriad CAFC analysis.

name: Step 2B: Determine whether additional elements individually or as an ordered combination amount to 'significantly more'
description: If the claim is directed to a judicial exception at Step 2A, analyze whether the additional elements (or their combination) add significantly more to the exception, rendering the claim eligible.
guidance: Consider whether recited elements are unconventional or provide a specific, technical improvement beyond the exception. Example: reciting SNOM detection or Cool-Melt PCR (unconventional data-gathering or technique) can render a claim eligible at Step 2B because these elements are not routine or conventional in the field at the time of filing.

name: Specificity of amounts/ratios alone is insufficient without demonstrated marked differences
description: Reciting specific percentages, amounts, or ratios (e.g., 1–5% texiol, at least 90% water) does not by itself render a claim eligible unless those specifics produce or evidence marked differences from natural counterparts.
guidance: If claimed numeric ranges are routine or do not change structure/function, they won't save eligibility. Best practice: explain which characteristics are markedly different and why, rather than relying only on numerical specificity (Claim 2 discussion).

name: Rejection drafting guidance for examiners
description: When rejecting a claim under §101, clearly identify the exception(s) and explain why the claim is directed to that exception and why additional elements do not render it eligible.
guidance: Point to the nature-based product or abstract-idea limitation, explain lack of marked differences or why mixing is routine/conventional, and, if helpful, cite and explain analogous case law (e.g., Roslin, Funk Brothers, Myriad, Alice) showing how the claim is similar to precedent. Example language: identify nature-based product (texiol-water), explain it is a product of nature, and explain absence of additional elements that add significantly more.

name: Evaluate whether a claimed change is the result of a change in form/structure or mixing with other substances
description: Determine whether alterations asserted (e.g., controlled release behavior, encapsulation, crystallization to regular particle sizes) arise from a change in form/structure or from mixing with other substances and whether those alterations produce marked differences.
guidance: Examples: encapsulation in polymer-emulsifier mixtures that delay release (controlled release) or controlled crystallization/granulation producing regular particle-size distributions that increase dissolution are cited as changes in form/structure that support eligibility (Claims 5 and 6).

name: Focus-of-claim consideration: do not perform product-of-nature analysis when claim is focused on process/abstract idea
description: If the claim's focus is on an informational or process step (e.g., comparing sequences), there is no need to perform the marked-differences analysis on recited nature-based products in that claim.
guidance: Determine claim focus: if the claim is directed to an abstract idea/process, treat the exception analysis accordingly (see Claim 1 gene comparison example where the comparing step was the focus and treated as abstract).

name: Voluntary modifications before filing an examination request
description: Before filing an examination request, applicants may modify the patent application, including adding or cancelling claims, adjusting claim categories, adding or removing features, and re-writing entire portions of claims.
guidance: Use the pre-examination period to adjust scope and claim structure broadly; many substantive changes are permitted during this phase.

name: Voluntary modifications after filing an examination request (restrictions)
description: Once examination is requested, it is impossible to increase the claim's scope and several restrictions apply: applicants are prohibited from removing features from the claims, changing the category of a claim, or adding new independent claims.
guidance: Despite prohibitions on broadening, applicants may include dependent claims, include features in independent or dependent claims that are supported by the specification or other claims (drawings do not provide support), and remove features/words/phrases for the purpose of overcoming lack of clarity. Plan substantive claim-scope changes before the examination request is filed.

name: Support requirements for claim amendments
description: Features added after examination request must be supported by the specification and other claims; drawings do not provide support for claim amendments.
guidance: When drafting and amending claims, ensure added matter finds explicit support in the written description or existing claims; reliance on drawings for support is not accepted.

name: Divisional applications — scope and permitted content
description: Before requesting examination, applicants may file a divisional and amend claims in both original and divisional applications. Once examination is requested, applicants can only 'slice' the original to create a divisional: they must choose one or more existing claims from the parent to form the divisional and are prohibited from including new claims in the divisional or modifying existing claims.
guidance: After the divisional application is filed, voluntary modifications to the divisional's claims are permitted. Plan the parent application's claim set carefully prior to requesting examination if divisional flexibility is required.

name: Parent application definition and benefit (35 U.S.C. 120)
description: The term 'parent' is applied to an earlier application of an inventor disclosing a given invention; benefit of the filing date of a copending parent application may be claimed under 35 U.S.C. 120. The term 'parent' will not be used to describe a provisional application.
guidance: A parent application may or may not claim the invention; to receive benefit the applications must satisfy statutory/ regulatory conditions (see MPEP § 201.11).

name: Provisional conversion rules and consequences (conversion to/from nonprovisional)
description: An application filed under paragraph (b) (nonprovisional) may be converted to a provisional application and accorded the original filing date if a request for conversion and processing fee (37 CFR 1.17(q)) are filed prior to certain events. A provisional filed under paragraph (c) may be converted to a nonprovisional provided conversion request, fees, and an amendment including at least one claim (per 35 U.S.C. 112 second paragraph) are filed and other fees and an oath/declaration are supplied.
guidance: Conversion timing constraints: must be filed before the earliest of abandonment of the application, payment of issue fee, expiration of 12 months after the filing date, or filing of a request for a statutory invention registration. Conversion to nonprovisional does not entitle applicant to refund of earlier fees and may have adverse patent term impacts (term measured from at least filing date of the provisional). To avoid patent-term adverse effects, applicants should consider filing a nonprovisional that claims benefit under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) rather than converting.

name: Nonprovisional application filing requirements (37 CFR 1.53(b))
description: The filing date of a nonprovisional application is the date on which a specification as prescribed by 35 U.S.C.112 containing a description pursuant to §1.71 and at least one claim pursuant to §1.75, and any drawing required by §1.81(a) are filed in the PTO. No new matter may be introduced after the filing date.
guidance: Continuing applications (continuation, divisional, CIP) may be filed under conditions specified in 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, or 365(c) and §1.78(a). Ensure required claims and description are present to secure a filing date.

name: Divisional limitations regarding provisional applications and new matter
description: An application claiming the benefits of a provisional under 35 U.S.C.119(e) should not be called a 'division' of the provisional. A divisional may depart in phraseology from the parent but may not depart in substance or introduce matter that would be 'new matter' in the parent.
guidance: Divisional patent term and entitlement differ from provisional-derived filings—careful drafting and correct labeling are required to avoid loss of benefit or incorrect patent-term calculations.

name: Patentee cannot abandon or prove a part of a combination useless at trial
description: Where the patent is for a combination, the patentee is not permitted, on the trial, to abandon part of the combination as useless, nor to prove it useless.
guidance: A combination patent must stand or fall as claimed; patentee cannot drop elements opportunistically at trial. (Text: 'Where the patent is for a combination, the patentee is not permitted, on the trial, to abandon a part of the combination as useless, still less can he be suffered to prove it useless.')

name: When multiple inventions are claimed, each must be sufficiently specified
description: If a patent describes two or more inventions, each invention must be described with sufficient clearness and distinctness to enable a competent workman to carry it into effect; if any one is insufficiently specified, the patent fails as to that invention.
guidance: Patentee who puts multiple inventions in one patent cannot hold unless each can be supported as a separate patent; specification must be fair, open, and sufficient as a quid pro quo for monopoly. (Text: 'He has described two inventions, and if either of those inventions is not sufficiently specified, the patent fails.')

name: If a whole class of substances is claimed, plaintiff must show each will succeed
description: Where a patent claims a whole class of substances as suitable, plaintiff must show that each of them will succeed (i.e., the specification must enable across the claimed class).
guidance: Failure to show that members of the claimed class work will undermine sufficiency. (Text, footnote: 'And if a whole class of substances be stated as suitable, the plaintiff must show that each of them will succeed.')

name: Insufficiency of counter-affidavits alone when presumption strong
description: If long possession, use, sales, and prior judgments support the patentee, affidavits read by the respondent tending to cast doubt on originality are often insufficient to annul the patentee's claim to an interlocutory injunction.
guidance: Because preliminary affidavits are taken without cross-examination, courts require substantial opposing proof to overturn strong presumptions.

name: Duty not to invite futile experiments
description: A patentee, knowing that given materials will not answer the purpose, is bound so to word his specification as to prevent others from trying experiments on that which he knows will not answer.
guidance: If you know certain alternatives will not work, you must not suggest them as suitable. Avoid broad or permissive language ('any suitable material') when you know only specific materials are effective; otherwise you mislead and may render the specification bad (example: paper heated by cloth claimed 'any suitable material' though only linen-wool worked).

name: Combinations: do not claim old parts as new
description: When patenting a combination of well-known things, take care not to claim the old parts themselves as novel as well as the novel combination; if constituent parts are new and intended to be protected, they ought to be specially pointed out, fully described, and expressly claimed.
guidance: If only the combination is the invention, claims restricted to the combination suffice. If some constituent parts are themselves novel, describe and claim them separately if you wish protection for them. Avoid ambiguous drafting that might be read as claiming known parts as new.

name: When claiming a combination only, separation of new/old parts not required
description: If the only invention claimed is the combination and that is properly set forth, it is sufficiently described without separately distinguishing new parts from old; the combination itself constitutes the novelty.
guidance: A properly limited combination claim will be valid even if the specification does not segregate which parts are old, provided the manner of arriving at and working the combination and its utility are sufficiently described.

name: Point out small improvements within large known machines
description: When an inventor's improvement of a complicated machine is a small proportion of the whole, if he claims the entire improved machine he should distinctly point out the small addition or alteration which constitutes the improvement; otherwise the claim may be too wide or misleading.
guidance: If your improvement is minor relative to a known machine, expressly identify and describe that improvement even if you claim the whole machine, to avoid the claim being held vague or concealing the real invention.

name: Ambiguity is fatal; state invention and limits distinctly
description: A specification must state distinctly what the invention is and the limits within which the patentee is to enjoy the monopoly; equivocal or ambiguous claims/descriptions that leave doubt as to what is claimed render the specification bad.
guidance: Avoid ambiguous phrases ('of any size' etc.) and equivocal wording. Make the scope of the monopoly and the nature of the invention clear so third parties can know what is off-limits (Hastings v. Brown; Turnor v. Winter).

name: Do not materially misrepresent capabilities or objects
description: Misrepresentations as to the object or capabilities of the invention, or other important matters (e.g., claiming a machine will produce a wide range of outputs when it cannot), will deprive the inventor of his patent.
guidance: Be accurate about what the invention can do. Overstating capabilities or claiming broader functionality than demonstrated risks patent invalidation (paper-width machine example).

name: Permissible to suggest broader applications if not claiming them
description: Stating that an invention capable of application to other purposes beyond that for which protection is claimed, without describing how those purposes are to be effected, does not necessarily invalidate the patent.
guidance: It is acceptable to note potential applications beyond the principal embodiment, provided you do not claim exclusive rights over those un-described applications or mislead about them (Cole v. Saqui).

name: Complete specification must end with a distinct claim
description: By statute a complete specification must end with a distinct statement of the invention claimed; 'distinct' contemplates a summary of the main features to which the reader may readily refer.
guidance: Include a clear claim section at the end of the specification that summarizes the characteristic features of what is claimed. Although historically judicial opinions differ on the precise breadth of 'distinct', include an explicit, readable claim statement to satisfy the requirement.

name: Claims operate as disclaimers of unclaimed subject-matter
description: Everything described in the specification that is not expressly claimed is impliedly disclaimed; the claim defines the boundary of the patentee's monopoly and everything else falls open to the public.
guidance: Be deliberate about what you claim: do not inadvertently give away valuable embodiments by omitting them from the claims. Conversely, avoid claiming beyond what you have described.

name: Number and breadth of claims carry risk
description: Introducing a large number of claims is a dangerous practice: the more claims, the greater the risks (e.g., many of Edison's numerous claims were later struck out).
guidance: Balance breadth and number of claims strategically. Excessive or poorly drafted multiple claims increase exposure to objection, disclaimers, or invalidation.

name: Claims must show clearly what is intended to be claimed
description: Claims should be framed so that it can be seen without difficulty what the inventor wishes to secure; ambiguity as to whether a claim is for a combination or for constituent parts can invalidate the patent.
guidance: Draft claims that unambiguously state whether the protection sought is for a combination or for individual parts. If reliance is on a combination claim, ensure the specification enables a competent workman to make the combination without experiment.

name: Combination claims valid when specification enables construction
description: A claim for a combination will not be deemed too vague when there is proof that a competent workman can make the combination from the specification without experiment.
guidance: When claiming combinations, ensure the description enables straightforward construction by skilled artisans. Reference to drawings in conjunction with description can cure initial over-general descriptions (Daw v. Eley).

name: Claims are to ascertain scope, not to teach manufacture
description: The claim is not intended to aid the description (i.e., to teach how to make the device), but to ascertain the extent of what is claimed as new; if the description is precise, claims may use more general expressions without being fatal.
guidance: Make the specification itself sufficiently precise for enablement; the claims define legal scope. Avoid using the claim as a substitute for a clear technical disclosure, but do not fear using broader terminology in claims where the body furnishes the enabling details.

name: Specification must incorporate and support all features present in the claims
description: The generated specification must incorporate and support all the features present in the claims (formalized in the paper as: the generated specification must incorporate and support all the features present in the claims C).
guidance: This is a hard requirement: each claim element/feature should be described in the specification so that claims have explicit support. The system formalizes inputs as claims C, drawings B, and component pairs N and targets generating S that satisfies 'incorporate and support all the features present in the claims.' Mapping between claim features and drawing components is used to ensure coverage.

name: Conform to standard patent document structure and formal legal writing style
description: Patents are legal documents that adhere to a precise writing style and typically comprise organized sections (title, abstract, field, background, summary, independent/dependent claims, drawings, brief description of drawings, detailed description/specification).
guidance: Generated outputs are post-processed to conform to standard patent writing conventions. Fine-tuning on patent corpora (public USPTO data) is used to teach the stylistic and structural conventions of patent writing so that generated specifications follow the expected sections and legal style.

name: Mapping accuracy between claims and drawing components (matching strategy and precision@k)
description: Claims must be mapped to corresponding drawing features/components. Patentformer provides a Mapping Interface and an automatic matching strategy based on cosine similarity and BLEU-1 and BLEU-2 scores, using a threshold of 0.1 to select up to the top five matching components per claim feature.
guidance: Automatic mapping using the described strategy yielded precision@5 = 0.565 and precision@3 = 0.6 on ~6,000 samples. Manual correction via the GUI is supported; mapping accuracy directly affects whether the generated specification properly ties claims to figures and components.

name: 35 U.S.C. 101 Rejection (rejection_101)
description: Indicates whether a 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection is raised in the Office action.
guidance: Generally, an examiner rejects under 101 if any of four requirements is not met: (1) no statutory double patenting (one patent per inventor/discovery), (2) inventor identification requirements (pre/post Sept 16, 2012 rules), (3) claimed invention falls within patent‑eligible categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter) as interpreted by courts, and (4) claimed invention is useful (specific, substantial, credible). If a 101 rejection appears, it is further categorized into subtypes based on form paragraphs and triggering keywords.

name: Non‑statutory Double Patenting Rejection (rejection_dp)
description: Indicates whether a non‑statutory double patenting rejection is raised in the Office action.
