guidance: Non‑statutory double patenting generally occurs when similar (but not identical) scope is claimed by a common inventor and/or assignee. (See MPEP 804 for comprehensive discussion.)

name: Objection (objection)
description: Indicates whether an objection is raised in the Office action.
guidance: Objections are generally raised for minor informalities or violations of patent rules (e.g., claims not properly grouped, figure elements not properly referenced). Reference: 37 C.F.R. 1.75(g).

name: One Citation in 103 Rejection (cite103_eq1)
description: Indicates when only one reference is cited as the basis to reject certain claim(s) under 35 U.S.C. 103 in the Office action.
guidance: Note that examiners may rely on established knowledge or 'Examiner’s official notice' to support a 103 rejection based on a single citation.

name: Claims Rejected (claim_numbers)
description: The claim_numbers field lists the application claims in question for each action (action_type/action_subtype combination) raised.
guidance: Use claim_numbers to map document‑action pairs to specific claim identifiers for claim‑level analyses.

name: Dataset File Structure (office_actions, rejections, citations)
description: The release consists of three data files: office_actions (4.4M observations, each an Office action), rejections (10.1M document‑action pairs), and citations (58.9M unique application‑citation pairs).
guidance: office_actions contains indicators for action types and document metadata; rejections contains action_type/action_subtype and claim mapping; citations contains parsed citations plus flags indicating source and whether cited in an Office action. Use the ifw_number and action_type/action_subtype to link across files.

name: Known Data Limitations and Coverage Flags
description: Documented limitations such as typographical/input errors, missing Office actions for some applications, inability to parse many foreign patent document and non‑patent literature citations, and lag between filing and Office action mailing dates.
guidance: Users should merge this Dataset with other sources (e.g., PatEx, Public PAIR, Patent Claims Research Dataset) to obtain filing dates, continuation history, prosecution events, and claim text. Coverage varies by filing year and cohort; first‑action allowances are not captured (no Non‑Final/Final rejection issued).

name: Third party may comment on completed patent-owner responses
description: Where the patent owner did not file comments on a response that was determined by the Office to be incomplete, the third party requester may file comments on the response once it is completed (by patent owner’s submission of a supplemental response).
guidance: The response as completed is treated as a new response on-the-merits and the third party requester is entitled to 30 days to file comments. Exception: where only a fee (other than an excess claims fee) is needed to complete the response, the third party may not file comments after the fee is submitted; see MPEP § 2666.40.

name: Not fully responsive patent-owner submission (37 CFR 1.957)
description: A response by the patent owner will be considered not fully responsive to a non-final Office action where a bona fide response is filed before expiration but, through apparent oversight or inadvertence, some point necessary to a full response has been omitted.
guidance: In this situation the prosecution should not be terminated automatically; the examiner may (A) waive non-serious deficiencies and act on the submission, or (B) treat the amendment/response as incomplete and notify the patent owner to complete the response within a set period (37 CFR 1.957(d)) to avoid termination (1.957(b)) or limiting prosecution to patentable claims (1.957(c)).

name: Fee-only completion limitation on third party comments
description: If only a fee is needed for the patent owner to complete the response (other than a failure to pay excess claims fees), any third party requester comments must be filed within 30 days from the date of service of the patent owner’s original (incomplete) response; the third party is not permitted to file comments in response to the submission of the fee.
guidance: Submission of a fee alone adds nothing on the merits (example: terminal disclaimer filed but fee omitted). However, if the patent owner’s response also includes argument (not just a fee), the third party can comment since merits have been addressed.

name: Response too long — page limit enforcement (37 CFR 1.943)
description: Where the length of a patent owner or third party submission exceeds that permitted by 37 CFR 1.943, the submission is improper and a Notice will be mailed permitting the party to either (A) submit a redrafted response not exceeding page limit, or (B) file a copy with pages redacted to satisfy the page limit.
guidance: Notice sets a 15-day period to respond. If no response, the improper submission will not be considered and, if necessary to respond to an outstanding Office action, the reexamination prosecution may be terminated (1.957(b)) or limited (1.957(c)). Exceptions: table of contents, table of case law pages, and pages of the claims (but not claim charts) are excluded from the 30-page count. Affidavits/declarations containing arguments count toward the page limit; purely evidentiary exhibits generally do not unless they include argument.

name: Prior art submissions by third party requester must meet narrow criteria
description: For any third party requester comments containing a submission of prior art, the prior art must be limited solely to prior art which is necessary to (1) rebut a finding of fact by the examiner, (2) rebut a response of the patent owner, or (3) which for the first time became known or available to the third party requester after the filing of the request for inter partes reexamination.
guidance: Prior art submitted as newly known must be accompanied by a statement when it first became known/available to the third party and include discussion of pertinency of each reference to patentability of at least one claim. If these criteria are not met, the comments are improper and will be returned (see MPEP § 2666.05).

name: Disclaim prior matter and state improvement distinctly
description: he should then disclaim the invention of the thing thus referred to or described, and state distinctly his improvement as the thing which he claims to have invented.
guidance: When a specification refers to prior devices or matter, the patentee must disclaim the prior invention and clearly identify the improvement claimed as his invention. This prevents claiming old subject-matter as new.

name: Avoid vagueness/ambiguity in manner of description (distinct from term ambiguity)
description: Vagueness and ambiguity in the manner of describing the invention which makes it difficult or impossible to determine what the invention is.
guidance: Examples: ambiguous directions such as 'take any quantity of lead and calcine it, or minium, or red lead' (uncertain whether minium/red lead are to be calcined). Such vagueness as to what is intended misleads the public and may void the claim.

name: Generic claims permissible if inventor discloses what he actually uses
description: If the patentee states the substances which he makes use of himself, and there are still other substances which will produce the effect, and he claims them by a generic description, his claim will not be void for ambiguity, or too broad for his invention, provided the combination is new in respect to all the substances thus referred to.
guidance: It is acceptable to claim substitutes generically (e.g., 'chalk or other absorbent earths') so long as the inventor discloses the substances he actually uses and the combinations claimed are equally new. The patent acts permit claiming multiple modes/ingredients if they are part of the invention.

name: Give a liberal construction to protect real inventors where whole specification shows claim
description: If, taking the whole together, the court can perceive the exact nature and extent of the claim made by the inventor, it is bound to adopt that interpretation, and to give it full effect.
guidance: Courts favor construction 'ut res magis valeat quam pereat' (so that a thing may rather have effect than be destroyed). Minor ambiguities should not defeat a patent if the specification as a whole enables understanding of the claim.

name: When claiming an improvement, confine claim to the improvement (not the whole preexisting machine)
description: The description of an improvement, when an improvement is the real subject-matter of the patent, should be made in such a manner as will clearly show that the improvement only is claimed by the patentee.
guidance: If a machine substantially existed before, the patentee should not claim the whole machine in its improved state but should be confined to his improvement, even where the improvement is an addition producing the same effects better or new combinations producing new effects.

name: Recite prior use when claiming an improvement to avoid claiming an entire original discovery
description: If the invention be an improvement, and be claimed as such, but nothing is said of any previous use, of which the use proposed is averred to be an improvement, the patent may incur the risk of being construed as a claim of entire and original discovery.
guidance: To avoid being read as claiming an entire discovery, the specification should recite what had formerly been done and describe how the claimed mode differs and constitutes the improvement.

name: When describing improvement in a known machine, describe parts and effects (not entire machine)
description: In describing the improvement of a machine in use and well known, it is not necessary to state in detail the structure of the entire and improved machine. It is only necessary to describe the improvement by showing the parts of which it consists, and the effects which it produces.
guidance: Statutory requirements still require clarity: for machines, the patentee 'shall fully explain the principle, and the several modes in which he has contemplated the application of that principle... and shall particularly specify and point out the part, improvement, or combination, which he claims as his own invention or discovery.'

name: Explain the principle of a machine and all modes of its application that are claimed
description: By the principle of a machine is to be understood the peculiar structure and mode of operation... By explaining 'the several modes in which he has contemplated the application of that principle,' the statute is presumed to direct the patentee to point out all the modes of applying the principle which he claims to be his own invention.
guidance: State not only the peculiar device or construction you prefer, but also all other modes of producing the same effect which you intend to have covered by the patent — whether they are the best modes or mere formal variations.

name: Separable-claims rule (claims encompassing tax strategies vs. non-tax claims)
description: Any claim that encompasses a tax strategy will be subject to the provision and the novelty or nonobviousness of the tax strategy will be deemed insufficient to differentiate that claim from the prior art. However, any other claim that does not involve a tax strategy would not be subject to the provision.
guidance: If an application contains multiple claims, only those claims that 'encompass' the tax strategy are barred by the provision; separable, non-tax-related claims may still be evaluated and, if otherwise patentable, enforced. The assessment of separability determines which claims are affected.

name: Concepts relating to performing mathematical calculations are abstract ideas
description: Claims that recite generating/transforming data by mathematical computation or organizing information through mathematical correlations are directed to abstract ideas.
guidance: Cases: Bancorp (managing life insurance policy values by performing calculations is the abstract idea of performing calculations/manipulating results), Digitech (generating data by manipulating existing information with mathematical formulas = organizing information through mathematical correlations). Other examples include algorithms for optimizing visits (In re Maucorps), calculating abnormal-condition parameters (In re Grams), and calculating differences between local and average data values (In re Abele). Such recitations are treated as abstract ideas in Step 2A analysis.

name: Laws of nature and natural phenomena are judicial exceptions to §101
description: Laws of nature and natural phenomena include naturally occurring principles/relations and nature-based products that are naturally occurring or that do not have markedly different characteristics compared to what occurs in nature.
guidance: The basic tools of scientific and technological work (manifestations of laws of nature) are not patentable because they are part of the storehouse of knowledge (Funk Bros.). Examples identified by the courts include isolated DNA (Myriad), cloned farm animals (Roslin), correlations between non-coding and coding DNA regions (Genetic Techs.), correlations resulting from metabolism (Mayo), correlations of biomarkers to disease risk (Cleveland Clinic v. True Health), electromagnetism to transmit signals (O'Reilly v. Morse), bacterial qualities (Funk Bros.), primers (Ambry), chemical principles (Tilghman), and cffDNA existence (Ariosa). Not every claim describing a natural ability is directed to a law of nature; claims that recite concrete process steps (e.g., treating cancer with chemotherapy, cryopreserving hepatocytes) may be eligible if not focused on merely observing/detecting natural phenomena.

name: Products of nature exception (physical products that are natural or lack marked differences)
description: When a law of nature or natural phenomenon is claimed as a physical product, the courts often treat it as a 'product of nature' exception to eligibility.
guidance: Products of nature include both naturally occurring products and non-naturally occurring products that lack markedly different characteristics from their natural counterparts. Synthetically replicated gene sequences that are structurally identical to natural counterparts remain ineligible (Ambry). Examples: isolated gene and cDNA (Myriad), cloned animals (Roslin), bacteria (Chakrabarty). Examiners should apply the markedly different characteristics analysis (MPEP §2106.04(c)) to nature-based product limitations to determine Step 2A. A claim to a nature-based product may encompass both eligible and ineligible embodiments under the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI); examiners should point this out and, if appropriate, recommend narrowing amendments.

name: Markedly different characteristics analysis is used to identify product-of-nature exceptions
description: The markedly different characteristics analysis is part of Step 2A and compares the claimed nature-based product to its naturally occurring counterpart to determine whether the claimed product is a product of nature exception.
guidance: If the nature-based product has markedly different characteristics from its natural counterpart, the limitation is not a product-of-nature exception and the claim is eligible at Step 2A (Pathway B) unless another exception is present. If the product does not exhibit markedly different characteristics, it is a product-of-nature exception (Step 2A: YES) and requires further Step 2B analysis to determine whether additional claim elements add significantly more. Markedly different characteristics can be expressed as differences in structure, function, and/or other properties, and are evaluated on a case-by-case basis based on the claim recitation.

name: Apply the markedly different characteristics analysis only to nature-based product limitations
description: The markedly different characteristics analysis should be applied only to the nature-based product limitations in the claim, not to non-nature elements or entire claims that are not nature-based.
guidance: Care should be taken not to overextend the analysis to products that when viewed as a whole are not nature-based. Example distinctions: for a 'yogurt starter kit' claim, analyze only the Lactobacillus limitation for marked differences; container and instructions are not subject to this analysis but would be evaluated in Step 2B if the Lactobacillus is a product-of-nature exception.

name: Markedly different analysis for product-by-process claims: focus on product characteristics
description: For product-by-process claims, the analysis turns on whether the nature-based product in the claim has markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart.
guidance: See MPEP §2113 for more on product-by-process claims. The key inquiry remains whether the claimed product differs markedly from natural counterparts, regardless of the recited process.

name: How to perform the markedly different characteristics analysis — selecting appropriate counterpart(s)
description: Select the appropriate naturally occurring counterpart(s) to the claimed nature-based product; the comparison is to the counterpart in its natural state.
guidance: If the nature-based product is derived from a naturally occurring thing, the natural source is the counterpart (e.g., deoxyacid A derived from acid A → compare to acid A). Do not conflate the counterpart with adjacent natural material (e.g., compare a claimed gene to the gene, not to the whole chromosome). When multiple counterparts exist, compare to the closest naturally occurring counterpart based on examiner expertise (e.g., choose closest breed for a cloned sheep). For combinations without a natural counterpart, the closest counterparts may be the individual nature-based components (e.g., compare a claimed bacterial mixture to each species as it occurs in nature). If an examiner rejects on eligibility grounds, it is best practice to identify the selected counterpart in the Office action if not already clear.

name: How to perform the markedly different characteristics analysis — identifying and evaluating characteristics
description: Markedly different characteristics may be expressed as differences in structure, function, and/or other properties and are evaluated based on what is recited in the claim on a case-by-case basis.
guidance: If the claimed nature-based product is naturally occurring, no further marked-difference analysis is necessary (it falls under the product-of-nature exception). If it is not naturally occurring (e.g., created by human intervention), the examiner must identify appropriate characteristics for comparison and evaluate whether they are 'markedly different' from the natural counterpart. The evaluation depends on claim recitations and factual record.

name: Broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) and examiner best practices
description: Under BRI, a nature-based product limitation may encompass both eligible and ineligible products; examiners should consider BRI when determining eligibility and recommend claim amendments where appropriate.
guidance: Example: a claim to a 'cloned giraffe' may cover embodiments with and without markedly different characteristics. If a claim is directed to a product of nature and is rejected as failing to encompass an inventive concept (Step 2B:NO), it is a best practice for the examiner to point out the BRI and recommend narrowing amendments to limit the claim to embodiments that are not directed to products of nature or are otherwise eligible.

name: When to use the streamlined eligibility analysis (MPEP §2106.06)
description: Examiners should consider whether the streamlined eligibility analysis is appropriate for claims that recite a nature-based product limitation but do not seek to tie up any judicial exception.
guidance: If the claim clearly does not tie up a judicial exception despite reciting a nature-based product limitation, it may be appropriate to use the streamlined eligibility pathway and avoid performing the markedly different characteristics analysis.

name: Examiner must state and repeat all grounds and reasons
description: In making such final rejection, the examiner shall repeat or state all grounds of rejection then considered applicable to the claims in the application, clearly stating the reasons in support thereof.
guidance: All outstanding grounds of rejection of record should be carefully reviewed and any such grounds relied on in the final rejection should be reiterated and clearly developed so applicant may judge advisability of an appeal. If a single previous Office action contains a complete statement, the final rejection may refer to it but should include a rebuttal to applicant's arguments.

name: Do not make final when rejection relies on prior art not of record for amended claims
description: A second or any subsequent action on the merits should not be made final if it includes a rejection, on prior art not of record, of any claim amended to include limitations which should reasonably have been expected to be claimed.
guidance: Example: a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112 for incompleteness that would reasonably be replied to by an amendment supplying the omitted element should not be made final.

name: Limitations on withdrawing finality to apply new grounds
description: Withdrawal of finality to apply a new ground of rejection is permissible only in limited circumstances — normally where a new reference either fully meets at least one claim or meets it except for differences shown to be completely obvious.
guidance: The practice should not be used for application of subsidiary, cumulative, or merely 'better' references. When withdrawing finality for a new ground, withdrawal should normally be limited to the claims involved and amendments filed after final are ordinarily entered when finality is withdrawn.

name: Office action contents (definition)
description: An “Office action” is a written notification to the applicant of the examiner’s decision on patentability and generally discloses information, such as the grounds for a rejection, the claims affected, and the pertinent prior art.
guidance: Office actions are the primary unit of analysis: they should contain grounds for rejections/objections, the specific claims affected, and any cited prior art to be useful for dataset extraction and analysis.

name: Complete patent application components
description: A complete application includes a written description of the invention (called a “specification”), at least one claim, and any necessary drawings.
guidance: Only complete applications (with filing date assigned) proceed to examination; data users should be aware that dataset coverage is of such complete applications.

name: Examiner evaluation checklist (statutory and regulatory checks)
description: The examiner evaluates the claims for compliance with statutes and regulations: patent-eligible subject matter (35 U.S.C. 101), adequate written description/enablement/clarity (35 U.S.C. 112), novelty (35 U.S.C. 102), and nonobviousness (35 U.S.C. 103).
guidance: These statutory categories form the core action_type classification in the Dataset and drive the extraction and subtype mapping logic.

name: Office action structural segmentation
description: Office actions are segmented into three units: (1) heading, (2) form paragraph, and (3) action sentence.
guidance: The three-part segmentation is fundamental to extraction: headings and form paragraphs are matched to pre-labeled standardized text where possible; the action sentence is parsed for claim-level details.

name: Three-step examiner drafting process (for raising rejections/objections)
description: When an examiner raises an objection and/or rejection they typically: (1) enter an appropriate heading for the action, (2) insert an appropriate set of form paragraphs to specify the legal grounds for the action, and (3) apply a “standard” sentence structure to express the action taken on the claim(s).
guidance: Extraction methods exploit this typical structure; deviations are handled with additional NLP heuristics.

name: Standard action sentence structure
description: Typical action sentences contain: the claims to be addressed (subject), a verb phrase reflecting the action taken (e.g., 'are rejected'), a prepositional phrase stating the legal grounds (e.g., 'under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)'), and a prepositional phrase declaring prior art references.
guidance: Parsing expects these constituents and maps them to four main data elements (claims, action, legal ground, prior art). Nonconforming sentences require additional NER/entity-resolution logic.

name: Four main data elements to extract from action sentences
description: By analyzing action sentences the Dataset extracts: (1) Claim(s) in question, (2) Action taken on claim(s), (3) Legal ground for the action, and (4) Prior art(s) cited in the action.
guidance: These elements are encoded into the rejections and citations files and are central to downstream research uses.

name: Fallback NLP method for missing/nonstandard headings/form paragraphs
description: For documents without headings/form paragraphs or where similarity scores fall below thresholds, a second method uses NLP, domain knowledge, and heuristic logic to extract data from the action sentence(s).
guidance: This method involves syntactic parsing, named entity recognition, and heuristics to recover claims, actions, legal grounds, and prior art when structured markers are absent.

name: Constituency parsing with Stanford CoreNLP
description: Apply a sentence parser (Stanford CoreNLP) to generate a constituency-based parsing tree and part-of-speech labels, and then use the parsing tree to identify and map sentence constituents to the desired data elements.
guidance: Constituency parsing is used to identify NP/VP/PP constituents corresponding to claims, action verbs, legal grounds, and prior art mentions.

name: Action type taxonomy (document-level)
description: Action types encoded include: 35 U.S.C. 101 rejections, 102 rejections (lack of novelty), 103 rejections (obviousness), 112 rejections (written description/indefinite claims), non-statutory double patenting, objection, and allowable claim.
guidance: Action type categories are not mutually exclusive; a single Office action may include multiple action types (mean action types per Office Action = 2.1).

name: Data join keys and relational structure
description: The Dataset consists of three files: office_actions (document-level), rejections (document-action pair level), and citations (application-citation or document-citation level). Each Office action is identified by a unique ifw_number which serves as the key to join files; rejections are uniquely identified by ifw_number + action_type + action_subtype.
guidance: Users should join via ifw_number for document-level merges and use action_type/subtype for claim-level merges; citations include fields to link back to document-action pairs when referenced in action sentences.

name: Incorporation by reference of the Sequence Listing XML
description: When a Sequence Listing XML is submitted, the specification generally must include an incorporation by reference paragraph identifying the XML file.
guidance: Unless an exception applies (e.g., international applications during the international stage), when the Sequence Listing XML is submitted via e-filing or on read-only optical disc the specification must contain a separate paragraph (per §1.77(b)(5)) incorporating by reference the material in the XML file identifying: (i) the name of the file, (ii) the date of creation, and (iii) the size of the file in bytes. The incorporation by reference statement is required so the XML content is considered part of the disclosure capable of providing 35 U.S.C. 112(a) support for sequence-related claims. If the incorporation paragraph is omitted when required, pre-examination staff may issue a notice requiring a substitute specification or amendment to include the incorporation paragraph. Note: for international applications during the international phase, that incorporation paragraph is not required. (MPEP §2413.04 and discussion.)

name: Amendment requirements to add an initial Sequence Listing XML after filing (37 CFR 1.835(a))
description: An amendment adding an initial Sequence Listing XML after the application filing date must include the XML and supporting statements and requests.
guidance: When adding an initial Sequence Listing XML after the filing date, the amendment must include: (1) a Sequence Listing XML in accordance with §§1.831–1.834 submitted as an XML file via Patent Center or on a read-only optical disc; (2) a request to amend the specification to include an incorporation by reference paragraph identifying file name, date of creation, and file size (except for international applications filed to the U.S. International Preliminary Examining Authority); (3) a statement indicating the basis for the amendment with specific references to parts of the originally filed application (specification, claims, drawings) for all sequence data in the XML; and (4) a statement that the Sequence Listing XML includes no new matter. Applicant responses to notices requiring an initial Sequence Listing XML should provide these items. (MPEP §2414.02(a) and related text.)

name: Grantability as primary objective
description: Increase the likelihood for a language model to generate patent claims that have a higher chance of being granted.
guidance: Treat the probability of grant (or other prosecution success signals) as the principal optimization target when training and evaluating models; prefer outputs that historical data suggests are more likely to be examined and allowed.

name: Control claim length to influence scope
description: The experiments demonstrate the model's capability to learn from adjusting claim length ... for narrowing claim scope.
guidance: Use explicit length constraints or length-conditioned prompts/training to steer claim scope; evaluate how shorter vs longer claim formulations affect perceived breadth and grant likelihood.

name: Include limiting terms to narrow claim scope
description: Model can learn from inclusion of limiting terms for narrowing claim scope.
guidance: Encourage or enforce limiting language (e.g., "wherein", specific numerical/structural limits) when a narrower scope is desired; measure effect on downstream grantability signals.

name: Focus on claim ones (independent claims)
description: As proof of concept, the experiments focus on claim ones only.
guidance: Initial evaluation and model design may concentrate on independent claim 1 as a representative target; note limitations when generalizing to dependent claims or full specifications.

name: Circuitous mode can still infringe if it falls within the claim
description: A defendant's circuitous or different-seeming process may still infringe if it achieves the same result within the scope of the patentee's claims.
guidance: Walton v. Potter example: producing a cloth with rubber layers by a circuitous process was held to fall within the plaintiff's claim because it produced the same elasticity next to the teeth. Courts look to substance over form.

name: Proportions or degrees as part of the essence of the invention
description: When a specification specifies particular proportions or degrees as the mode of producing a particular effect, those proportions form part of the essence of the invention.
guidance: If another uses the same ingredients in materially different proportions (and thus an essentially different mode of working), that may not infringe. Where proportions are claimed as essential, differing proportions that still produce beneficial effects may constitute a different subject-matter (Hill v. Thompson).

name: Patent invalidity where patent claims include things not new or known to be useless
description: A patent may be void (or voidable) if it includes as part of the claimed invention one or more elements that were not new, or were known by the patentee to be useless when enrolled, thereby misleading the public.
guidance: Cases (and the statute of July 4, 1836 §15) recognize defence that patentee was not first inventor of a substantial part. Statutes later permit severing and upholding that portion truly invented by the patentee unless broad claims were made wilfully to defraud.

name: Specification must be sufficiently definite about quantities/degrees when they are part of the invention
description: When degrees or quantities (e.g., proportion, heat) are essential to producing the claimed effect, the specification should state them; insufficiency or uncertainty may vacate a patent.
guidance: Slight defects in specification can vacate a patent; courts have required the specification to show by what degree of heat or what proportions the effect is to be produced. Evidence that proportions are non-essential supports non-infringement when proportions were claimed as essential.

name: Prior art as contextual baseline
description: Prior art in the context of design patents includes designs and other published documents made publicly available prior to the filing date of a design patent.
guidance: Use prior art designs/publications to determine which aspects of the claimed design are novel or conspicuous; prior art can draw the observer's attention away from or toward certain features when comparing designs. Practical example: the Nailco and Falley buffers were considered as prior art in Egyptian Goddess.

name: Significance of small differences when close to prior art
description: When the claimed design is close to the prior art designs, small differences between the accused design and the claimed design are likely to be important to the eye of the hypothetical ordinary observer.
guidance: Where the patented design largely tracks prior art, even minor variations may be determinative and can lead to a finding of non-infringement if they distinguish the designs to the ordinary observer.

name: Substantial/deceptive similarity standard
description: The inquiry is whether the accused design is 'substantially the same' or 'deceptively similar' to the claimed design to the ordinary observer familiar with the prior art.
guidance: Frame infringement questions in terms of substantial or deceptive similarity rather than mechanical element-by-element matching; consider whether the accused design would deceive an ordinary observer into believing it is the patented design.

name: Patent agent privilege — scope and limits
description: Patent agent privilege can protect confidential communications between a client and a registered patent agent when intended to be confidential and made for the purpose of seeking or giving advice about a matter (applies to activities agent is authorized to perform, e.g., preparing/prosecuting patent applications, consulting about filings, drafting specs/claims, drafting amendments/replies).
guidance: Scope varies by state/federal case law. Cases discussed: Onyx Therapeutics v. Cipla (D. Del. 2019) (narrow application), In re Queen’s University (Fed. Cir. 2016) (privilege recognized only for activities agents are authorized to perform), In re Silver (Tex. 2018) (Texas Supreme Court ultimately recognized privilege). Application depends on whether communications were reasonably necessary and incident to prosecution; litigation contexts often parse these limits.

name: Patent owner allowed to amend but cannot enlarge claims
description: The patent owner will be permitted to propose any amendment and new claims to distinguish the invention from cited prior art or in response to an adverse decision, but no proposed amended or new claim enlarging the scope of a claim will be permitted in reexamination.
guidance: Responses to rejections may include further statements and/or proposed amendments/new claims to place patent in a condition where all claims, if amended as proposed, would be patentable. Examiners ensure amendments do not enlarge scope (35 U.S.C. 305).

name: Requirement to submit reference copies per 37 CFR 1.98
description: 37 CFR 1.98(a)(2) requires a legible copy of each foreign patent, each publication or that portion which caused it to be listed (other than U.S. patents and U.S. patent application publications unless required), for each cited pending unpublished U.S. application the specification including claims and drawings or the portion which caused listing, and all other information or that portion which caused listing.
guidance: The exception in 1.98(d)(1) does not apply to reexamination proceedings (they do not receive 35 U.S.C. 120 benefit). Submissions not complying may be returned/expunged/discarded.

name: Scope of reexamination per 37 CFR 1.552
description: Claims in ex parte reexamination will be examined on the basis of patents or printed publications and, with respect to subject matter added or deleted in the reexamination proceeding, on the basis of the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112. Claims will not be permitted to enlarge the scope of the claims of the patent. Issues other than those indicated will not be resolved in reexamination.
guidance: Reexamination provides complete reexamination of claims on prior art patents/printed publications; 35 U.S.C. 112 issues addressed only for new/amendatory subject matter. If other issues are raised, examiner notes them in next Office action and owner may consider reissue.

name: Intervening patents/printed publications as prior art when effective date limits apply
description: Rejections may be made based on intervening patents or printed publications where the patent claims under reexamination are entitled only to the filing date of the patent and are not supported by an earlier foreign or U.S. patent application whose filing date is claimed.
guidance: In re Ruscetta, In re van Langenhoven cited; see MPEP § 201.11 for details on effective dates.

name: Primary examiner must personally review sufficiency of reissue oath/declaration
description: The question of the sufficiency of the reissue oath/declaration filed under 37 CFR 1.175 must in each case be reviewed and decided personally by the primary examiner.
guidance: Much required content differs based on filing date, but all reissue oaths/declarations must contain (A) a statement that applicant believes original patent to be wholly or partly inoperative or invalid (by reason of defective specification/drawing or claiming more or less than right) and (B) a statement of at least one error relied upon to support the reissue. See MPEP § 1414 and subsections for details.

name: Corrections after allowance must follow 37 CFR 1.312 and justification requirements
description: Where applicant seeks to correct an error after allowance, any amendment of the patent correcting the error must be submitted in accordance with 37 CFR 1.312; no amendment may be made as a matter of right after mailing of the notice of allowance.
guidance: Amendments under 1.312 must be filed before or with payment of the issue fee and may be entered upon recommendation of the primary examiner and approval of the supervisory patent examiner. Remarks accompanying such amendments must fully and clearly state: (A) why the amendment is needed; (B) why the proposed amended or new claims require no additional search or examination; (C) why the claims are patentable; and (D) why they were not presented earlier. For pre‑2012 reissue applications, a supplemental reissue oath/declaration must accompany the amendment after allowance if correcting an error.

name: Lack of inventive concept — generic computer components
description: Claims lack an 'inventive concept' when they 'require only generic computer components' or merely implement the abstract idea on a generic computer.
guidance: Multiple holdings state that reciting generic hardware or conventional computer technology is insufficient to supply an inventive concept (e.g., claims that 'recited only generic hardware', 'provided no improvement over the existing art', or 'recited generic computer components functioning in a conventional manner').

name: Claims must recite specific ways, hardware, or software (not just functions)
description: Eligibility favors claims that recite specific ways to perform the invention, particular hardware, or software-based implementation details rather than high-level functional results.
guidance: Courts denied eligibility where the claims 'did not recite any “specific ways, hardware or software,” to carry out the claims' or 'failed to recite a means of achieving that result.' The absence of concrete implementation details tends to support a finding of abstraction.

name: Improvement to computer/technology required for eligibility
description: Claims are more likely eligible if they provide a specific improvement to computer functionality or to a technological process, rather than merely using computers as a tool to perform an abstract idea.
guidance: Examples on the page: claims that used 'engine frequency to measure run time' were considered 'innovative technology'; the tangible resumption of an interrupted file download was held to represent a 'specific improvement to a computer's capabilities'; claims improving data transmission over wireless networks were not abstract. Courts look for a specific, concrete contribution to the technology.

name: Whether the problem is 'rooted in computer technology'
description: If the problem the claim purports to solve is not 'necessarily rooted in computer technology,' courts may treat the claim as abstract and ineligible.
guidance: A holding noted ineligibility because the 'purportedly solved problem was not one “necessarily rooted in computer technology”.' Thus, showing that the claimed invention addresses a technical problem specific to computers supports eligibility.

name: Claims implementing conventional/longstanding business practices are abstract
description: Implementing a longstanding business practice, human activity, or conventional business process on a computer is treated as an abstract idea absent additional inventive concept.
guidance: Page holdings include many business/practice examples: 'account management', 'using a third-party intermediary to connect services', 'establishing a cross-reference resource', 'tailoring marketing communications', 'transmitting compressed images to facilitate buying/selling.' Courts repeatedly found such claims ineligible when they simply automated conventional practices.

name: Claims must recite new or improved physical components to show patentable invention
description: When claims involve physical devices (RFID readers, transponders, antennas, videophones, etc.), eligibility favors claims that describe a new or improved physical component; absence of such improvements weighed against eligibility.
guidance: The page notes holdings that claims failed because they did not 'describe a new or improved RFID transponder, a new or improved RFID reader, or a new or improved RFID antenna,' and where the specification did not disclose an improved videophone.

name: Failure to show improvement over the prior art undermines eligibility
description: Claims that do not demonstrate an improvement over existing technology or the prior art are likely to lack an inventive concept.
guidance: Several entries note ineligibility because the claims 'provided no improvement over the existing art' or there was 'no evidence that the claims improved computer functionality.' Demonstrating improvement over prior art is a common route to show inventive concept.

name: Claim limitations must correspond to physical or functional aspects of the described system
description: When claim limitations do not 'correspond to any physical or functional aspect of the described system,' courts have found no inventive concept.
guidance: A cited holding said the limitations did not 'correspond to any physical or functional aspect of the described system,' which supported ineligibility. Claims should tie limitations to tangible system aspects where possible.

name: Routine data collection/analysis/display is abstract absent a technical solution
description: Claims that are limited to collecting, organizing, analyzing, and displaying data are treated as abstract unless they recite a specific technical means or improvement for performing those tasks.
guidance: Many case holdings found ineligibility for claims described as 'collecting, organizing, comparing, and presenting data,' 'collecting information, analyzing it, and displaying results,' or 'collecting and reporting the missing power of a network device' when no specific technological contribution was present.

name: Specific, concrete contribution to the technology is required
description: Courts look for a 'specific, concrete contribution to the technology' (e.g., tangible improvements, specialized hardware/software) as evidence of eligibility.
guidance: A number of holdings reversed ineligibility when claims were found to involve 'a specific means of achieving' a technological goal or a 'specific improvement to a computer’s capabilities.' The guidance from cases is to craft claims and specifications that identify concrete technical advances.

name: Assignment of International Patent Classification (IPC)
description: The classification of a patent application is performed with taking into consideration the invention as claimed. It is necessary as an effective search tool for the retrieval of patent documents by intellectual property offices and other users.
guidance: KIPO adopts the IPC, a hierarchical patent classification under WIPO control. Classification decisions should reflect the scope of the claimed invention and may use detailed description if scope unclear.

name: Amendments/Arguments by Applicant
description: An applicant may submit arguments in response to an examiner's notice of grounds for rejection and may file amendments to the specification (including detailed description and claims) or drawing(s) within the period designated in Article 47.
guidance: Amendments are considered by examiner in subsequent examination; scope and timing of amendments are governed by statutory limits (Article 47) and further described in Parts dealing with amendment requirements.

name: Instructions of Amendment Ex Officio — Prohibitions and Cautions
description: The matters to be amended ex officio are limited to self-evident error. When an examiner amends ex officio, he/she should not alter the scope of the claim, and the amendment ex officio shall not be allowed if there arises any possibility of different interpretation.
guidance: If misstatement is a ground for rejection, no ex officio amendment allowed; when both ex officio matters and grounds for rejection exist, notify grounds for rejection and reference ex officio matters; examiner shall not add new matters; cannot amend errors referring to deleted claims; be careful with uses like 'the said' without clear specification.

name: IPC Assignment — General Principles
description: The technical subject-matter stated in the claimed invention of an application are classified into IPC symbols comprised of section, class, subclass, main group and sub-group. The classification shall be made on the basis of the scope of the claimed invention; when scope unclear, base on detailed description; some subject-matter not in claims but in description can form basis for classification.
guidance: Where multiple technical subject-matters exist, core subject-matter becomes 'main classification' and others 'sub-classification'; if unity lacking, claim 1 can be basis; indexing code and additional information rules; divisional/converted application classification should generally follow earlier application unless obviously different.

name: Search for Prior Art — Scope and Principles
description: Search procedure includes defining search scope, conditions under which search is not required or limited, time coverage of search, suspension, general principle of search, citation of prior art documents.
guidance: Search scope should be determined in light of claimed invention and IPC assignments; special provisions for when search may be limited or suspended; guidelines for citing prior art include patent, non-patent, and electronic documents.

name: Understanding of Invention
description: Examiners must understand the invention as claimed and as described to conduct substantive examination.
guidance: Understanding guides IPC assignment, search strategy, claim interpretation and determination of prior art relevance.

name: Review of Prior Art Documents
description: Examiners must review cited prior art documents in relation to the claimed invention to determine novelty, inventive step, and other statutory requirements.
guidance: Includes rules for disclosure of information on prior art documents (citation of patent/non-patent/electronic documents) and how to reflect such citations in notices.

name: Examination on a Claim-by-claim Basis
description: Examination may be carried out on a claim-by-claim basis with specific purpose and instructions for written notice of grounds for rejection and preparation of written decision of rejection.
guidance: Includes how to prepare notices per claim, when to select claim-by-claim examination and instructions for documenting the rationale.

name: Amendment Ex Officio — Specific Limitations and Examples of Prohibited Cases
description: Amendment ex officio is intended for obvious errors only and is subject to strict limits so it does not change claim scope or create new technical matter.
guidance: Prohibited: ex officio amendment if matter is ground for rejection; adding new matter in description or drawings; altering scope of claims; amending references to deleted claims; any amendment that could lead to different interpretations. Examiner should notify reasons and locations precisely; applicant's opposition means amended matters are treated as never having existed in published description.

name: Prior-art teaching of claim limitation via disclosure of inserted agents/bots
description: A prior-art disclosure that the advertisement management service 'may send bots or electronic agents into the game as advertising units or real characters' teaches inserting content beyond mere skins.
guidance: Where the prior art describes sending bots/agents into a game (not merely changing skins on preexisting geometry), that supports finding the prior art teaches insertion of updated content usable in the game (e.g., a bot offering a branded drink implies the player's character may interact/use it). Conflicting expert testimony that contradicts the disclosure may be disregarded.

name: Teaching 'checking what updated video-game content to send' based on factors including device type/service provider
description: Claim limitation [1b] requires 'checking what updated video-game content to send based on one of the factors including a type of the mobile communication device, a telecom service associated with the mobile communication device, and a service provider of the telecom service.'
guidance: A prior-art system that includes a client-type field (e.g., SKU indicating 'cellular or mobile phones') and an advertising matching/weighting system that derives weights from that client type teaches 'checking' based on device type. Demographic data like IP addresses, when tied to a cellular service provider, can correspond to 'service provider' factors. It is sufficient if the selection/weights are at least partly based on such factors even if additional internal weighting/comparisons between ads occur.

name: Claim-step ordering not presumed unless claim language requires it
description: Arguments that claim steps must occur in a specific order are forfeited if not raised earlier; and the claim language, not extrinsic assumptions, determines required order.
guidance: If the claim explicitly recites an order (e.g., 'receiving... then checking... then uploading'), that order may be given effect; however, a prior-art disclosure describing a request followed by matching/weighting and then sending content can satisfy ordered steps. New arguments about order raised for the first time late may be forfeited.

name: Claim term 'mobile communications device' scope is not limited to cellular phones
description: 'Mobile communications devices' can include consoles, PDAs, and other handheld devices capable of communication with a server; they are not limited to wireless-only devices.
guidance: If a device is capable of communicating with a server (regardless of transport), it can fall within 'mobile communications device.' Thus, prior-art disclosures of consoles or other devices capable of server communication can fall within the claimed scope.

name: Dependent-claim limitations analyzed individually against prior art (claims 2–9 examples)
description: Each dependent claim limitation (e.g., promotional content; technical media format checks; predetermined display period; location-based selection; demographic targeting) must be shown in the prior art to find that claim taught.
guidance: The decision evaluates dependent limitations separately: claim 2 (promotional content) is shown by branded in-game items; claim 3 (technical media formats/approval) by client-specific accepted media formats and approvals; claim 7 (display for predetermined period) by campaigns tied to seasons/dates/times; claim 8 (location-based selection) by GPS-based targeting; claim 9 (demographic targeting) by age/sex/location/purchasing-habit targeting. If the prior art includes examples or paragraphs disclosing these features, that supports teaching of the dependent claims.

name: Sending information that provides an in-game placement location as part of updated content (claim 4)
description: Claim 4 requires 'sending information to the mobile communication device as part of the updated content, the information providing an in-game placement location associated with the updated video-game content.'
guidance: A server that sends lists of advertisements 'for specific available ad units' or specifies which advertisements are for which ad units teaches sending placement-location information. Even if advertisers create standardized ads, when the server sends ad lists for specific ad units or insertion orders specify ad unit placement, the logical implication is that placement information is sent as part of the updated content.

name: Tracking what has been uploaded to the mobile communication device (claim 5)
description: Claim 5 recites 'the step of tracking what has been uploaded to the mobile communication device.'
guidance: Disclosure of an active session database that 'registers the game player... and is used to track and record all communications and data sent to and received from the advertisement recipient client' teaches tracking what has been uploaded. The claim language does not require tracking everything uploaded; tracking a portion of uploaded content (or all communications within sessions) can be sufficient if the specification describes such tracking.

name: Displaying updated video-game content at a location based on user interaction (claim 6)
description: Claim 6 requires that uploading comprises 'displaying the video-game content within the game at a location based on user interaction.'
guidance: Examples where a bot offers an item to a player, or ad units tied to particular storefronts/panels that appear when the player's character arrives at those locations, support that the displayed content's location is based on user interaction (e.g., player's character location or session continuity). Prior-art descriptions that the location of displayed adverts is determined by the player's character position or interaction support this limitation.

name: Interpretation of 'tracking' need not mean comprehensive coverage
description: A claim reciting 'tracking what has been uploaded' does not necessarily require tracking everything uploaded to the device in its entirety.
guidance: Where the claim language is broad or ambiguous, evidence that the prior art tracks at least a portion of uploaded content (e.g., all communications during a session) can meet the limitation. An opponent's argument that only partial tracking is disclosed may fail if the specification states tracking of 'all communications and data' for sessions.

name: Prima facie framework and burden-shifting
description: During patent examination and reexamination, the concept of prima facie obviousness establishes the framework for the obviousness determination and the burdens the parties face. The examiner must first set forth a prima facie case, supported by evidence, showing why the claims would have been obvious in light of the prior art; once set out, the burden shifts to the patentee to provide evidence or argument sufficient to rebut the examiner's evidence.
guidance: Quoted summary from ACCO Brands Corp. v. Fellowes, Inc.; the examiner must set forth a prima facie case supported by evidence; after that the applicant may submit rebuttal evidence or argument and the examiner weighs the totality of evidence in the final determination.

name: Required contents of an Office action asserting a 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection
description: After indicating that the rejection is under 35 U.S.C. 103, the examiner should set forth in the Office action: (A) the relevant teachings of the prior art relied upon, preferably with specific citations; (B) the differences in the claim over the applied reference(s); (C) the proposed modification of the applied reference(s) necessary to arrive at the claimed subject matter; and (D) an explanation as to why the claimed invention would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the relevant time.
guidance: Provide reference column/page/line numbers where appropriate; explicitly identify differences and proposed modifications; explain why the artisan would have been led to make the modification and why it would have rendered the claim obvious.

name: Consideration and weighing of applicant's rebuttal evidence; preponderance standard
description: When an applicant properly submits evidence (in the specification, prior to a rejection, or in reply), the examiner must consider the patentability of the claims in light of that evidence. The ultimate determination of patentability is based on the entire record, by a preponderance of evidence, with due consideration to the persuasiveness of any arguments and evidence made of record.
guidance: Cites In re Oetiker and In re Eli Lilly. Facts established by rebuttal evidence must be evaluated along with the facts on which the conclusion of obviousness was reached; the examiner's decision to make or maintain a rejection must show it was based on the totality of the evidence.

name: Requirement to evaluate the claimed invention 'as a whole' and consider differences
description: The examiner must make a determination whether the claimed invention 'as a whole' would have been obvious at the relevant time to a person of ordinary skill in the art, and must identify and evaluate the 'differences' between the claimed subject matter and the prior art.
guidance: Knowledge of the applicant's disclosure must be set aside in evaluating obviousness-as-a-whole, but used to determine differences and to conduct the search; consider Graham v. John Deere factors as discussed in MPEP § 2141 and related sections.

name: Importance of a clear written record and rationale for prosecution and later validity/interpretation
description: It is important for an examiner to properly communicate the basis for a rejection so that issues can be identified early, the applicant can reply, and the rationale may be important in interpreting the scope of any later-issued patent because issued patents are presumed valid.
guidance: Because examiners ordinarily cannot be compelled to testify regarding mental processes, the written record must clearly explain the rationale for decisions during prosecution (see MPEP §§ 2141-2144.09); clarity benefits later judicial/administrative proceedings and claim interpretation.

name: Must State 'Reviewed and Understands' the Application
description: The oath/declaration must state that the person making it has reviewed and understands the contents of the specification, including the claims, as amended by any amendment specifically referred to in the oath or declaration.
guidance: Omissions of this statement are defective and should be pointed out (form paragraph 6.05.05). The examiner must require remedy in the first Office action (see MPEP § 602.03).

name: Prohibition on false, misleading, fictitious, or fraudulent information
description: Submitting a document that includes false, misleading, fictitious, or fraudulent information or representations violates 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)(1). This includes false or misleading domicile information, attorney information, signatory information (e.g., where named signatory did not personally enter signature), applicant information, or claims of use (or intent to use).
guidance: Submitting without undertaking a reasonable inquiry into the factual basis, without evidentiary support, or coupled with other Terms of Use violations constitutes an improper purpose and violates 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)(2).

name: Ornamental-design requirement for design patents
description: Design-patent claims at issue were one-sentence claims about the ornamental design of an electronic device, accompanied by figures (e.g., a thin rectangular cuboid with rounded corners). Design patents therefore protect the ornamental (non-functional) appearance of an article.
guidance: When asserting a design patent, the focus is on ornamentation as shown in drawings; infringement and scope analyses look to the ornamental features rather than functional aspects. The particular drawings and what they disclose (including broken lines, figures) are central to claim scope.

name: Utility-patent functional-claim coverage
description: Utility patents at issue covered functional features such as the iPhone's 'bounce-back effect', 'on-screen navigation', and 'tap to zoom' functions.
guidance: Utility patents protect functional and technical innovations; infringement findings for utility patents depend on claim construction and comparison to accused products' functionality. Functional patents are subject to validity challenges (e.g., by PTO reexamination) and prior-art attacks.

name: Trade dress and dilution claims
description: The jury found that Samsung had diluted Apple's trade dress related to the iPhone.
guidance: Trade dress (distinctive non-functional product appearance or packaging) can be asserted alongside patents; dilution or trade-dress infringement findings may yield damages or injunctions but are evaluated under trademark/trade-dress law distinct from patent law.

name: Review for prior public use/on-sale and best mode
description: Any affidavits or declarations submitted under 37 CFR 1.131 and the accompanying evidence must be reviewed carefully to determine whether they show that the claimed invention was 'in public use' or 'on sale' in this country more than one year prior to the effective filing date (statutory bar under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)); where the 1.131 evidence relies on an embodiment not disclosed in the application, the best mode question must be considered.
guidance: Even if an affidavit overcomes a reference-based rejection, public use/on-sale activities may not be overcome under 37 CFR 1.131. A best mode rejection should be made only if the record, taken as a whole, establishes by a preponderance of the evidence that the specification has not set forth the best mode (see MPEP § 2133.03 and § 2165–2165.04).

name: Affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132: form and examiner responsibility
description: When any claim is rejected or objected to, any evidence submitted to traverse the rejection on a basis not otherwise provided for must be by oath or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132; it is the responsibility of the primary examiner to personally review and decide whether such affidavits or declarations are responsive to the rejection and present sufficient facts to overcome the rejection.
guidance: All affidavits/declarations not falling under specific other rules are to be treated under 1.132. Use form paragraphs (e.g., 7.65, 7.66, and 7.66.01–7.66.05) as appropriate to state whether the affidavit is sufficient or insufficient and to explain reasons for insufficiency (untimely, fails to set forth facts, not commensurate in scope, etc.).

name: Consideration of evidence and required explanation
description: Evidence traversing rejections, when timely presented, must be considered by the examiner whenever present; all entered affidavits, declarations, and other traversing evidence are acknowledged and commented upon in the next succeeding action.
guidance: If examiner holds evidence is sufficient to overcome the prima facie case, comments should follow guidance for reasons for allowance. If evidence is insufficient, the examiner must specifically explain why—mere general statements (e.g., 'lacks technical validity' or 'not commensurate with the scope of the claims') without supporting explanation are insufficient.

name: Consideration of objective evidence (secondary considerations)
description: Affidavits or declarations containing evidence of criticality or unexpected results, commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, skepticism of experts, etc., must be considered by the examiner in determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103.
guidance: Secondary considerations 'must always when present be considered en route to a determination of obviousness' (Stratoflex). Examiners must also consider comparative data in the specification intended to illustrate the claimed invention. Lack of objective evidence does not weigh in favor of obviousness, but failure to provide rebuttal evidence against an established prima facie case is dispositive.

name: Objective evidence must be supported by actual proof
description: Objective evidence (unexpected results, commercial success, solution of a long-felt need, inoperability of the prior art, invention before the date of the reference, derivation allegations, etc.) should be factually supported by an appropriate affidavit or declaration to be of probative value.
guidance: Mere assertions or untested claims are insufficient; experimental data or factual support are required (see In re De Blauwe). Examples show lack of tests/comparisons undermines claims of unexpected results.

name: Unexpected results: threshold and evaluation
description: Any differences between the claimed invention and the prior art may be expected to produce some differences; the issue is whether the properties differ to such an extent that the difference is really unexpected.
guidance: Cases assess whether differences are differences in kind vs degree; examiner must determine whether differences rise to the level of unexpectedness required to be probative (see In re Merck & Co., In re Waymouth, In re Wagner).

name: Superiority of a shared property as evidence
description: Evidence that a claimed invention is unexpectedly superior in a property shared with the prior art can rebut a prima facie case of obviousness.
guidance: No set number of examples is required; single-property unexpected superiority (with adequate support) may suffice (see In re Chupp and Ex parte A). Examiner should evaluate the significance and factual support.

name: Comparative tests (direct and indirect) are probative
description: Direct or indirect comparative tests of the claimed invention against the closest prior art, commensurate in scope with the claims, are probative of nonobviousness.
guidance: Comparative testing can rebut a prima facie case (see In re Boesch, In re Blondel, In re Fouche). For intermediates, applicant must identify the cause of unexpectedly superior activity in an end product and establish a nexus showing the intermediate is a 'contributing cause' (In re Magerlein).

name: Unexpected results must be commensurate in scope with the claimed invention
description: Objective evidence of nonobviousness must be commensurate in scope with the claims which the evidence is offered to support; results should occur over the entire claimed range.
guidance: Data limited to a narrow subrange or a single species may be insufficient to support a genus or broad claim unless circumstances justify extrapolation. Examples: In re Clemens (temperature ranges), In re Peterson (aluminum alloy range), In re Grasselli (catalyst alkali metal comparisons). Under some circumstances a genus may be supported by species data, but examiner must evaluate commensurability.

name: Federal Circuit Case Law Deep Dives
description: Within workgroups, trainers lead discussions of various Federal Circuit decisions (e.g., Electric Power Group v. Alstom, McRo v. Bandai, FairWarning v. Iatric, Amdocs v. Openet, Trading Technologies v. CQG, Ameranth v. Apple). These discussions comprise a deep dive look at the claims in question, a summarization and analysis of the decision rendered, and how these decisions can support an eligibility determination.
guidance: Perform claim-level analysis, summarize holdings, and explicitly connect case outcomes to eligibility reasoning used in examination practice.

name: Duty to Cooperate With Regard to Written Discovery and Disclosures / Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(g) Certification (408.01(c))
description: By signing, an attorney or party certifies that, to the best of the person's knowledge, information, and belief formed after a reasonable inquiry: (A) with respect to a disclosure, it is complete and correct as of the time it is made; and (B) with respect to a discovery request, response, or objection, it is (i) consistent with the rules and warranted by existing law or a nonfrivolous argument to change law, (ii) not interposed for an improper purpose (harass, delay, increase cost), and (iii) neither unreasonable nor unduly burdensome or expensive considering the needs of the case.
guidance: The signature constitutes a certification and violations may result in sanctions (per Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(g) and TBMP § 106.02). The duty requires a reasonable factual inquiry. Because a signature certifies that a request is warranted, a party ordinarily cannot claim propriety for its own requests but impropriety when propounded by an adversary absent persuasive reasons. Prior to filing a motion to compel disclosure or discovery, the moving party must make a good faith effort by conference or correspondence to resolve the dispute; a written statement showing such a good faith effort must support the motion (37 CFR § 2.120(e)). The Board may require parties to confer with the Board attorney before filing a motion to compel. See cases cited (Miss America Pageant v. Petite Productions; International Finance Corp. v. Bravo Co.).

name: Petition particularity requirement (initial petition)
description: In an inter partes review, the petitioner has the burden from the onset to show with particularity why the patent it challenges is unpatentable. 35 U.S.C. § 312(a)(3) requires petitions to identify 'with particularity . . . the evidence that supports the grounds for the challenge to each claim'.
guidance: Arguments or theories not identified in the initial petition may be considered waived (37 C.F.R. § 42.23(b); Intelligent Bio-Sys.). The initial petition must articulate the supporting evidence and reasoning sufficiently to put the Board and parties on notice.

name: Claim construction standard (Phillips / 37 C.F.R. § 42.100(b))
description: Claims are construed to have 'the ordinary and customary meaning of such claim as understood by one of ordinary skill in the art and the prosecution history pertaining to the patent.' The Board applies the same claim construction standard used in civil actions under 35 U.S.C. § 282(b) following Phillips v. AWH.
guidance: Only terms 'in controversy' need be construed and only to the extent necessary to resolve the controversy (Vivid Techs.). Use the specification and prosecution history to inform ordinary meaning. If the ultimate decision does not depend on a particular construction, the Board may decline to construe a term.

name: Antecedent basis and avoiding superfluity in claim interpretation
description: Claim terms with antecedent references must be interpreted consistently so that later occurrences refer back to earlier recitals; constructions that ignore antecedent basis or render claim language superfluous are improper (Process Control; Haemonetics).
guidance: Interpretations that read portions of a claim as separate, inconsistent definitions (thereby making parts superfluous) should be rejected. Give effect to all claim language, including 'wherein' clauses that refine previously introduced terms.

name: Obviousness requires more than generic desire to improve
description: A petitioner cannot satisfy the motivation-to-combine requirement by asserting only a generic desire to improve or replace a reference because it 'would be better'; specific rationale connecting features and a reasonable expectation of success are required (ActiveVideo and related authority).
guidance: Show how specific features in the prior art would be combined and why that combination would be expected to achieve the claimed result, not merely that one reference 'achieves better image quality' in general terms.

name: Double patenting rejections and how to overcome them
description: Commonly owned applications of different inventive entities may be rejected on the ground of double patenting, including statutory and nonstatutory double patenting, even if the later-filed application claims 35 U.S.C. 120 benefit.
guidance: Double patenting rejections prevent an organization from obtaining multiple patents with different expiration dates covering nearly identical subject matter. They can be overcome in certain circumstances by disclaiming, pursuant to 37 CFR 1.321, the terminal portion of the term of the later patent and including in the disclaimer a provision that the patent is enforceable only while commonly owned with the application/patent forming the basis for the rejection, thereby eliminating extension of patent life. See MPEP § 804 and § 804.02 for further guidance.

name: Form paragraphs addressing art disqualified by common ownership (7.20.01, 7.20.03) and joint inventors presumption (7.20.02)
description: Specific form paragraphs instruct examiners on language to use when applied art is disqualified due to common ownership and on presuming common ownership among joint inventors.
guidance: ¶7.20.01: For applications filed prior to Nov 29, 1999 — indicates the applied art is disqualified under 102(f)/(g) but may still qualify under another subsection of 102; advises how applicant may overcome (37 CFR 1.132 or 1.131). ¶7.20.03: For applications filed on/after Nov 29, 1999 — analogous wording for 102(e),(f),(g). ¶7.20.02: Joint inventors — presumes subject matter of various claims was commonly owned at the time inventions were made absent evidence to the contrary; instructs applicant of obligation under 37 CFR 1.56 to identify inventor and invention dates for claims not commonly owned to allow examiner to consider 103(c) and potential prior art under 102(e),(f),(g). Use notes specify mandatory usage conditions (e.g., must be used in all applications with joint inventors unless claims restricted to one invention).

name: Provisional rejection form paragraph 7.21.01 (copending application with common assignee or common inventor)
description: ¶7.21.01 is used to provisionally reject claims under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as obvious over a copending application that has a common assignee or at least one common inventor, based on the earlier effective U.S. filing date of the copending application.
guidance: The provisional rejection may be overcome by: (1) showing under 37 CFR 1.132 that disclosure in the copending application was derived from the inventor of the instant application (not an invention “by another”); (2) showing an earlier date of invention under 37 CFR 1.131; or (for applications filed on/after Nov 29, 1999) showing that the subject matter of reference and claimed invention were owned or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person at the time the invention was made. Examiner Notes explain proper use cases, limitations, and cross-references (e.g., use paragraph 7.15.01 if claimed invention is fully disclosed in copending application).

name: Graham v. Deere Test for Obviousness (¶7.23)
description: The factual inquiries from Graham v. John Deere Co. applied to establish background for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103(a): (1) determine scope and contents of prior art; (2) ascertain differences between prior art and the claims at issue; (3) resolve level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; (4) consider objective evidence (secondary considerations) present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
guidance: This paragraph may be used, if appropriate, in response to an argument invoking Graham v. Deere.

name: Combined 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103(a) rejection usage and examples (¶7.27)
description: ¶7.27 permits a combined rejection — claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102 as anticipated or, alternatively, under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as obvious — when appropriate.
guidance: This paragraph is NOT intended as a common substitute for distinct 102 or 103 rejections; examiners should make a single appropriate rejection when possible. Examples of when to use ¶7.27 include: (a) disputed claim interpretation where one interpretation supports 102 and another supports 103; (b) when a reference discloses all limitations except a property/function and the examiner cannot determine inherent possession vs obvious variant (In re Fitzgerald); (c) genus/species issues (In re Schaumann); (d) product-by-process claims produced by different processes (In re Marosi, In re Thorpe); (e) means-plus-function uncertainty; (f) overlapping ranges with no specific example in reference. When used, include a full explanation and precede with required paragraphs (e.g., 7.07 and others).

name: Biotechnological process treatment under 35 U.S.C. 103(b) (706.02(n))
description: 35 U.S.C. 103(b) provides a special rule for certain biotechnological processes: a biotechnological process using or resulting in a composition of matter that is novel and nonobvious shall be considered nonobvious if specific conditions are met.
guidance: Requirements of 103(b): (A) process and composition claims are in same application or in separate applications having same effective filing date; (B) both process and composition were owned or subject to assignment to same person at the time the process was invented; (C) a patent on the process must also contain composition claims or, if composition is in another patent, the patents must expire same date; (D) the process must fall within 103(b)'s definition of biotechnological process (e.g., genetic alteration to express exogenous nucleotide sequence, cell fusion yielding cell line expressing a protein, methods using products produced by such processes); and (E) a timely election to proceed under 103(b) must be made via petition under 37 CFR 1.182. Election timeliness: normally no later than earlier of payment of issue fee or filing of appeal brief where composition claim not rejected; special transitional rules for certain pending applications described.
