Generally, reliance on 103(b) should be rare in view of Federal Circuit decisions (In re Ochiai; In re Brouwer). See 35 U.S.C. 282 for effect on presumption of validity.

name: Priority of prior art rejections over non-prior-art ('technical') rejections (706.03)
description: The primary object of examination is to determine whether claims are patentable over the prior art; undue emphasis on non-prior-art or technical rejections should be avoided.
guidance: Examiner effort should concentrate on truly essential matters; minimize effort on technical rejections that are not critical. Where a major technical rejection is proper (e.g., insufficient disclosure, undue breadth, utility issues), the rejection should be fully developed with reasons rather than terse conclusions or stereotyped expressions.

name: Refine production standards for examiner time allotments
description: Revise time allotted for examiners to examine applications, including increased base/minimum time and additional time for applications exceeding thresholds (number of claims, specification length, IDS pages), and factor in an application's classification 'picture'.
guidance: Make allotments transparent and flexible; adjust as conditions change to maintain time needed for quality and to balance pendency, cost, and quality objectives.

name: Develop AI auto-classification with explainability and feedback integration
description: Auto-classification tool leverages ML to suggest CPC symbols, identify claimed subject matter for refinement, and link suggested CPC symbols to specific portions of the document to provide insight into AI reasoning.
guidance: Integrate enhanced feedback mechanisms with existing classification processes to train the AI; auto-classification implemented for internal operations to identify claimed subject matter with CPC and reduce expenditures on CPC data acquisition.

name: Estoppel following transitional proceeding
description: The petitioner in a transitional proceeding, or his real party in interest, may not assert either in a civil action arising in whole or in part under section 1338 of title 28, United States Code, or in a proceeding before the International Trade Commission that a claim in a patent is invalid on any ground that the petitioner raised during a transitional proceeding that resulted in a final written decision.
guidance: This is an affirmative bar: issues raised in the PTO transitional proceeding (if resulting in a final written decision) cannot later be re-asserted by that petitioner or its real party in interest in district court or ITC litigation. Applies to grounds raised during that specific transitional proceeding.

name: Definition of 'covered business-method patent'
description: For purposes of this section, the term 'covered business method patent' means a patent that claims a method or corresponding apparatus for performing data processing operations utilized in the practice, administration, or management of a financial product or service, except that the term shall not include patents for technological inventions. Solely for the purpose of implementing the transitional proceeding authorized by this subsection, the Director shall prescribe regulations for determining whether a patent is for a technological invention.
guidance: The statutory definition ties covered business-method patents to data processing operations for financial products/services, but explicitly excludes 'technological inventions' and delegates to the Director (PTO) the rulemaking authority to define and identify technological inventions for program implementation. This raises scope/interpretation issues and requires PTO regs.

name: Obviousness-type double patenting trigger conditions
description: Obviousness-type double patenting (nonstatutory double patenting) can be triggered when two patents or applications share patentably-indistinct claims and are commonly-owned, share at least one common inventor or are subject to a joint research agreement (JRA).
guidance: The doctrine is grounded in public policy to prevent unjust extension of the patent 'right to exclude' and harassment from multiple parties asserting essentially the same invention. A determination depends on an assessment of obviousness: if the Subject Patent's claims are not identical but are anticipated by or obvious over the claims of a qualifying Reference Patent (which need not be prior art), the challenged claims are invalid unless cured (e.g., by terminal disclaimer).

name: Terminal disclaimer content requirements (37 CFR § 1.321(b))
description: To overcome an OTDP rejection or finding by filing a terminal disclaimer, the terminal disclaimer must disclaim the terminal portion of the Subject Patent's term that extends past the Reference Patent's full statutory term, including any claims not rejected for OTDP.
guidance: The terminal disclaimer must also include a provision that the Subject Patent shall be unenforceable if it ceases to be commonly owned or, in JRA situations with different owners, commonly enforced with the Reference Patent. See 37 CFR § 1.321(b).

name: Effect of patent term adjustment (PTA) on OTDP (In re: Cellect ruling)
description: For a patent that has received patent term adjustment (PTA), OTDP must be based on the expiration date of the patent after PTA has been added.
guidance: A claim in a patent having a later expiration date solely because of PTA can be invalidated for OTDP over an earlier-expiring patent in the same family. A terminal disclaimer to overcome OTDP must disclaim any PTA beyond an earlier-expiring Reference Patent's expiration date, including any PTA granted to the Reference Patent. The Federal Circuit rejected treating PTA like patent term extension for OTDP purposes.

name: Consequences of a successful OTDP challenge
description: If a challenged claim is invalidated by OTDP, the entire term of that claim is invalidated, not just the portion that extends past the Reference Patent.
guidance: Invalidation of the full claim term precludes obtaining any infringement remedies, past or present, for OTDP-invalidated claims. This differs from a terminal disclaimer which leaves claims in force but shortens the patent term for all claims.

name: Tradeoff when using a terminal disclaimer vs. other options
description: A terminal disclaimer shortens the patent term for all claims in the Subject Patent, not just those with OTDP problems.
guidance: Because a terminal disclaimer limits term across the claim set, one should carefully consider whether filing it is worth shortening all claims; alternatives include canceling or amending only the OTDP-invalid claims, statutorily disclaiming claims under 35 U.S.C. § 253(a) (which does not require disclaiming the terminal portion of a granted patent), or arguing patentability with secondary considerations evidence.

name: Portfolio review timing best practice
description: Review patent-family claims sufficiently in advance (e.g., six months) of the expiration of the first-to-expire family member.
guidance: Proactive review allows filing terminal disclaimers while Reference Patents are still in force or otherwise taking action (cancellation/amendment, statutory disclaimer, prosecution) to avoid running into the situation Cellect faced where Reference Patents had already expired and terminal disclaimers were unavailable.

name: Reexamination SNQ and OTDP — prosecution record considerations
description: OTDP may be considered a substantial new question (SNQ) of patentability that justifies granting an ex parte reexamination even if OTDP was not raised during original prosecution.
guidance: An examiner's mere knowledge of related patents/applications (e.g., via an information disclosure statement) may not show that OTDP was considered during original examination. Patent owners should consider actively requesting on the USPTO record that OTDP over potential Reference Patents be considered, or preemptively filing terminal disclaimers if an OTDP challenge is likely (for example, where an application is a continuation with similar claims).

name: Inter Partes Review (IPR) — scope and grounds
description: Inter partes review is a new trial proceeding conducted at the Board to review the patentability of one or more claims in a patent only on a ground that could be raised under §§ 102 or 103, and only on the basis of prior art consisting of patents or printed publications.
guidance: The inter partes review process begins with a third party (a person who is not the owner of the patent) filing a petition after the later of either: (1) 9 months after the grant of the patent or issuance of a reissue patent; or (2) if a post grant review is instituted, the termination of the post grant review. The patent owner may file a preliminary response to the petition. An inter partes review may be instituted upon a showing that there is a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail with respect to at least one claim challenged. If the proceeding is instituted and not dismissed, a final determination by the Board will be issued within 1 year (extendable for good cause by 6 months). The procedure will take effect on September 16, 2012, and applies to any patent issued before, on, or after that date. See cited Final Rules and Trial Practice Guide (77 Fed. Reg. 48612; 48756; 48680).

name: Post Grant Review (PGR) — scope and grounds
description: Post grant review is a new trial proceeding conducted at the Board to review the patentability of one or more claims in a patent on any ground that could be raised under § 282(b)(2) or (3).
guidance: Post grant review process begins with a third party filing a petition on or prior to the date that is 9 months after the grant of the patent or issuance of a reissue patent. The patent owner may file a preliminary response to the petition. A post grant review may be instituted upon a showing that it is more likely than not that at least one claim challenged is unpatentable. If the proceeding is instituted and not dismissed, a final determination by the Board will be issued within 1 year (extendable for good cause by 6 months). The procedure takes effect on September 16, 2012, and generally applies to patents issuing from applications subject to first-inventor-to-file provisions of the AIA. See General Administrative Trial Final Rules and related Proposed Rules (77 Fed. Reg. entries).

name: Transitional Program for Covered Business Method Patents (TPCBM) — eligibility and special rules
description: The transitional program for covered business method patents (TPCBM) is a new trial proceeding conducted at the Board to review the patentability of one or more claims in a covered business method patent, employing the standards and procedures of a post grant review, with certain exceptions.
guidance: Exceptions include: for first-to-invent patents only a subset of prior art is available to support the petition. Further, a person may not file a petition for a TPCBM proceeding unless the person or the person's real party in interest or privy has been sued for infringement of the patent or charged with infringement under the patent. The procedure takes effect on September 16, 2012, but only applies to covered business method patents. The program will sunset for new TPCBM petitions on September 16, 2020. See Covered Business Method and Technological Invention Definitions Final Rules and related Proposed Rules.

name: Derivation proceeding — purpose, timing, and evidentiary requirement
description: A derivation proceeding is a new trial proceeding conducted at the Board to determine whether (i) an inventor named in an earlier application derived the claimed invention from an inventor named in the petitioner's application, and (ii) the earlier application claiming such invention was filed without authorization.
guidance: An applicant subject to the first-inventor-to-file provisions may file a petition to institute a derivation proceeding only within 1 year of the first publication of a claim to an invention that is the same or substantially the same as the earlier application's claim to the invention. The petition must be supported by substantial evidence that the claimed invention was derived from an inventor named in the petitioner's application. The procedure for derivation will take effect on March 16, 2013. See Proposed Rule for Derivation Proceedings (77 Fed. Reg. 7028) and related guidance.

name: Institution standards and final determination timeframes
description: Different proceedings have distinct institution standards and time-to-final decision rules.
guidance: Inter partes review may be instituted upon a showing that there is a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail with respect to at least one claim challenged. Post grant review may be instituted upon a showing that it is more likely than not that at least one claim challenged is unpatentable. If instituted and not dismissed, both IPR and PGR proceedings result in a final determination by the Board within 1 year (extendable for good cause by 6 months). The TPCBM generally follows PGR procedures (subject to its exceptions). Derivation proceedings require substantial evidence of derivation and are subject to a 1-year filing window measured from first publication of a claim.

name: Petitioner and filing-eligibility rules (who may file and timing windows)
description: Each proceeding has specific eligibility and timing rules for who may file a petition and when it must be filed.
guidance: IPR and PGR are initiated by a third party (a person who is not the owner of the patent). IPR petitions may be filed after the later of: (1) 9 months after patent grant/reissue or (2) termination of a post grant review. PGR petitions must be filed on or prior to the date that is 9 months after grant. TPCBM petitions are limited to persons (or their real parties in interest/privies) who have been sued or charged with infringement and the program sunsets for new petitions on Sept 16, 2020. Derivation petitions (for applicants under first-inventor-to-file) must be filed within 1 year of the first publication of a claim the same or substantially the same as the earlier application's claim. Patent owners in IPR and PGR may file preliminary responses to petitions.

name: Use of secondary evidence to show enabling disclosure for 35 U.S.C. 102 rejections
description: A 35 U.S.C. 102 rejection can be made even if the primary reference does not itself teach how to practice the invention, by citing secondary evidence (other patents/publications) to show public possession of methods of making/using.
guidance: If the reference teaches every claimed element, other patents/publications may be cited to demonstrate that the method of making/using was publicly available (In re Donohue). See MPEP § 2131.01 for procedures on using secondary references to show the primary contains an enabling disclosure.

name: Pictures/drawings can constitute enabling disclosure for apparatus/articles
description: Pictures and drawings may be sufficiently enabling to put the public in possession of the article pictured and therefore can anticipate claims to that article.
guidance: The picture must show all claimed structural features and how they are put together (Jockmus v. Leviton). Origin of drawing is immaterial. When the reference is a patent, unintended or unexplained features in drawings may still be relied upon. See MPEP § 2125 / § 2121.04.

name: Plant claims: ability to grow and reproduce the plant
description: For plant claims, the reference (combined with prior art knowledge) must enable one of ordinary skill to reproduce the plant (grow/cultivate) without undue experimentation.
guidance: Photographs alone may be insufficient if information like grafting/asexual reproduction is absent (In re LeGrice). Commercial availability (e.g., seeds) that permit reproduction can make the plant publicly possessed (Ex parte Thomson). Foreign sale plus publication and the ability to asexually reproduce without undue experimentation can create a 102(b) statutory bar (In re Elsner).

name: Later factual references may be used to show universal facts (limited exception to critical date rule)
description: Under certain circumstances, factual references that postdate the claimed invention may be used to show universal facts (e.g., characteristics of a material, that undue experimentation would have been required) even though they do not antedate the filing date.
guidance: Examples include showing that undue experimentation would have been required (In re Corneil), that a parameter was or was not critical (In re Rainer), or that the invention lacked utility (In re Langer). However, later references cannot be used to determine whether the application satisfied 35 U.S.C. 112 enablement or written description (In re Koller). See cited cases for limits.

name: Tax strategies treated as prior art (AIA §14)
description: For novelty/nonobviousness under 35 U.S.C. 102/103, any tax strategy (reducing/avoiding/deferring tax liability) shall be deemed insufficient to differentiate a claimed invention from the prior art; tax strategy limitations are treated as being within the prior art.
guidance: Two exclusions: (1) parts solely for preparing tax returns or filing-related software are not covered; (2) financial management inventions severable from tax strategy are not covered. Examiners should: (1) construe claim (MPEP §2111); (2) analyze 35 U.S.C. 100/112 compliance; (3) identify tax-strategy limitations and note exclusions; (4) evaluate claim under 102/103 treating tax strategy limits as prior art (form para 7.06 may indicate tax strategy limitation). Computer-implemented methods that are novel and non-obvious remain patentable unless the only novel aspect is the tax strategy.

name: Drawings as prior art: evaluate disclosure, not scale/proportions
description: Drawings and pictures can anticipate claims if they clearly show the structure claimed; proportions in drawings not to scale are not evidence of actual proportions.
guidance: When drawings are not stated to be to scale and dimensions are silent, measurements of drawings are of little value (Hockerson-Halberstadt v. Avia). Evaluate what the drawings and accompanying description would reasonably teach to one of ordinary skill. Examples (In re Mraz, In re Aslanian, In re Wright) show reliance on drawings plus description.

name: Scope of disclosure when using a document as a 'patent' (not a 'publication')
description: When a document is applied as a patent (rather than a printed publication), examiners may rely on unclaimed details in the patent specification that relate to the patented claims.
guidance: Even if certain matter was canceled from claims, the specification's disclosed details germane to the claimed subject matter can be used in a 102(a)/(b)/(d) rejection (Ex parte Ovist; In re Kathawala). However, matter canceled from the application file that did not issue cannot be relied on in a 102(e) rejection (see relevant cases).

name: Language requirement and translations for non-English filings
description: Applications filed in a language other than English must be accompanied by an English language translation of the application and a translation of any corrections or amendments into English together with a statement that the translation is accurate (with specific differences for nonprovisional vs provisional applications).
guidance: For nonprovisional applications under 35 U.S.C. 111(a), translation, an accuracy statement, and processing fee (§ 1.17(i)) are required; if not filed, applicant will be notified and given time to avoid abandonment. Provisional applications filed in non-English need not include an English translation at filing (see § 1.78 for claiming benefit later).

name: Specification formatting — line spacing, font, and single column
description: The specification (including abstract and claims) must have lines that are 1 1/2 or double spaced; text written in a nonscript type font (e.g., Arial, Times Roman, or Courier, preferably font size 12) with capital letters at least 0.3175 cm (0.125 inch) high but not smaller than 0.21 cm (0.08 inch); and only a single column of text.
guidance: Preferred examples given. Minimum character height and allowed font styles are specified; deviations risk requiring a substitute specification.

name: Page numbering requirements for specification (non-reissue/non-reexamination)
description: Other than in a reissue application or reexamination or supplemental examination proceeding, pages of the specification including claims and abstract must be numbered consecutively, starting with 1, the numbers being centrally located above or preferably below the text.

name: Paragraph numbering recommendations and format
description: Paragraphs of the specification (other than in claims or abstract) may be numbered at filing and should be individually and consecutively numbered using Arabic numerals, unambiguously identifying each paragraph. The number should consist of at least four numerals enclosed in square brackets including leading zeros (e.g., [0001]), appear to the right of the left margin as the first item in each paragraph before the first word, highlighted in bold, with a gap of approximately four spaces following the number. Nontext elements and lists are considered part of the numbered paragraph and should not be independently numbered. Paragraph or section headers are not paragraphs and should not be numbered.
guidance: Using the recommended format ([0001]) ensures unambiguous paragraph identification and is compatible with USPTO processing practices.

name: Filing date for nonprovisional applications
description: The filing date of an application for patent filed under this section (other than design patent or provisional) is the date on which a specification, with or without claims, is received in the Office. For a design patent (except continued prosecution application under paragraph (d)), the filing date is the date the specification as prescribed by 35 U.S.C. 112, including at least one claim, and any required drawings are received.
guidance: No new matter may be introduced into an application after its filing date. Continuing applications must meet conditions specified in 35 U.S.C. and § 1.78.

name: Continuation, divisional, and continuation-in-part filing rules
description: A continuation or divisional application that names as inventors the same or fewer than all of the inventors named in the prior application may be filed under paragraph (b) or (d). A continuation-in-part application (which may disclose and claim subject matter not disclosed in the prior application) or a continuation or divisional application naming an inventor not named in the prior application must be filed under paragraph (b).
guidance: Different types of continuing applications have specific filing paragraphs and limitations on inventorship and new matter; continuation-in-part may add new subject matter, but other categories are restricted.

name: Provisional application filing date and cover sheet requirement
description: The filing date of a provisional application is the date on which a specification, with or without claims, is received in the Office. A provisional application must include the cover sheet required by § 1.51(c)(1), which may be an application data sheet (§ 1.76), or a cover letter identifying the application as a provisional application; otherwise, the application will be treated as filed under paragraph (b) (nonprovisional).
guidance: Provisional applications lacking the cover sheet are recharacterized unless corrected; provisional applications cannot be amended except to comply with statute/regulations after filing.

name: Conversion between provisional and nonprovisional applications and patent-term impact
description: An application for patent under paragraph (b) may be converted to a provisional application and accorded the original filing date of the application filed under paragraph (b) (with fees), but conversion will not entitle applicant to refund of fees. A provisional application may be converted to a nonprovisional and accorded the provisional filing date if conversion is timely and accompanied by required fees and at least one claim, but conversion will not refund fees or apply them to nonprovisional fees. Conversion can affect patent term — conversion of a provisional to a nonprovisional will result in the patent term being measured from at least the filing date of the provisional application for which conversion is requested; applicants are advised to consider claiming the benefit under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) rather than converting to avoid adverse patent term impact.
guidance: Conversion requires payment of specified fees and possibly amendment to include claims; applicants should consider filing a nonprovisional claiming benefit instead of conversion to avoid patent-term loss.

name: Continued prosecution (nonprovisional) application — filing conditions
description: A continuation or divisional (but not a continuation-in-part) of a prior nonprovisional application may be filed as a continued prosecution application for design patents if: (i) the application is for a design patent; (ii) the prior nonprovisional is a design application complete as defined by § 1.51(b) (with conditions on oath/declaration and an application data sheet for filings on/after certain dates); and (iii) the continued prosecution application is filed before payment of issue fee, abandonment of the prior application, or termination of proceedings on the prior application. The filing date of a continued prosecution application is the date a request on separate paper for such application is filed. Such an application must identify the prior application, disclose and claim only subject matter disclosed in the prior application, name the same inventors (with some exceptions), include the request and will utilize the file jacket/contents of the prior application, and is a request to expressly abandon the prior application as of the filing date.
guidance: The continued prosecution application carries forward the prior application's file jacket and contents, may be filed by fewer inventors under stated conditions, and cannot introduce new matter. Fees for filing, search, and examination apply as specified.

name: Dataset inclusion criteria (timeframe, fields, and required fields)
description: The dataset includes approximately 270,000 published applications filed between 2013 and 2020 inclusive; each entry included the application number, the abstract, and the filing year. The dataset ultimately analyzed (after cleaning) contained 255,728 records with 37 columns.
guidance: Only entries for which an abstract could be identified were included. The study focused on utility patent applications (excluding design, plant, provisionals, reissues, etc.), restricted to filings that did not claim priority to an earlier filing (except priority claims to national stage entries or provisional applications), and used USPTO-assigned examination group to sort technological field. These scope choices were adopted to reduce noise and focus on direct links between inventor gender, patent attributes, and outcomes.

name: Incorporation by reference for PCT applications upon Chinese national entry
description: CNIPA accepts incorporation by reference as a tool to correct mistakes made to applications filed under the Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT). When anything is missing or mistaken in a PCT application, but the priority application has the missing or correct information, incorporation by reference is available to bring anything in the claims, specification, and drawings of the priority application to the PCT application.
guidance: In addition to requesting incorporation by reference during the international stage, a Chinese translation of the priority application must be provided and a reference to the corresponding disclosure in the priority application must be made upon Chinese national entrance. Use incorporation by reference to fix inconsistencies and align the PCT filing with priority disclosure.

name: Specific activities constituting practice in patent matters (37 C.F.R. § 11.5(b)(1))
description: Practice before the Office in patent matters includes, but is not limited to, preparing and prosecuting any patent application; consulting with or giving advice to a client in contemplation of filing a patent application or other document with the Office; drafting the specification or claims of a patent application; drafting an amendment or reply to a communication from the Office that may require written argument to establish the patentability of a claimed invention; drafting a reply to a communication from the Office regarding a patent application; and drafting a communication for a public use, interference, reexamination proceeding, petition, appeal to or any other proceeding before the Board, or other proceeding.
guidance: This non-exhaustive list is used to identify concrete acts (e.g., drafting claims, responding to office actions, advising on strategy) that amount to practice in patent matters; the Final Order lists multiple such acts as evidence of unauthorized practice.

name: Unauthorized practice of law (37 C.F.R. § 11.505)
description: A practitioner shall not practice law in a jurisdiction in violation of the regulation of the legal profession in that jurisdiction, or assist another in doing so. The USPTO is considered a jurisdiction for the purposes of this rule.
guidance: Applied to an unregistered attorney who provided patent legal services to clients (drafting responses, amended claims, advising strategy), holding such conduct to be the unauthorized practice of patent law before the Office.

name: Aggravating and mitigating factors (ABA Standards and examples)
description: Aggravating factors may include selfish motive, pattern of misconduct, multiple offenses, and substantial experience; mitigating factors may include absence of prior disciplinary record, good standing, and good intentions.
guidance: ALJ may reference ABA Standards when weighing sanction severity; the Final Order lists specific aggravating (paid fees for unauthorized work, repeated practice) and mitigating (no prior discipline, good standing, claimed good intentions) factors and balances them.

name: Setting the Context
description: Determine which aspects of the AI system comprise the inventive subject matter (e.g., data selection, data preparation, computing environment/constraints, training method, inference method, architecture, application).
guidance: Set the stage for the disclosure interview by identifying whether the invention relates to training, inference, architecture, preprocessing, post-processing, sensors/input, application of AI, or combinations; tailor follow-up questions and claim focus accordingly. Example: pruning or reward-function tuning -> focus on training and architecture; novel use of conventional NN -> focus on inference and supporting architecture.

name: Understanding the Training Process
description: Document the training algorithm type (supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement, diffusion, etc.), training data, labeling procedures, hyperparameters, loss functions, and any automated labeling.
guidance: Ask: What learning algorithm is used? What training data and how labeled? Which hyperparameters were set and why? Training details affect claim drafting (training claims vs inference claims), enablement, and enforcement/detectability considerations.

name: Understanding the Inference Process
description: Detail inference-time behavior: how the trained model processes new input, deployment constraints, runtimes, latency, and how inference integrates with other system components.
guidance: Document where inference executes (edge, cloud), timing/latency constraints, input handling at inference, and any architecture/hardware enabling inference. Inference details inform claim drafting and eligibility/practical-application arguments.

name: Three Levels of Description
description: Provide multiple levels of description in the specification (e.g., high-level overview, mid-level functional description, low-level implementation details).
guidance: Include conceptual descriptions, representative embodiments, and concrete implementation parameters (layer counts, parameter counts, sample datasets, training steps) to satisfy written description and enablement while supporting claim scope.

name: Problem/Solution Description
description: Explicitly present the problem solved and the solution implemented, linking the technical improvement to claim elements.
guidance: Use problem/solution language throughout the spec and claims to help show practical application under USPTO Step 2A Part 2 and to preempt eligibility rejections; include quantitative evidence of improvement where possible.

name: Drafting Claims for Subject Matter Eligibility (§101)
description: Draft claims to demonstrate integration of any alleged judicial exception into a practical application and to recite additional elements that show technological improvement.
guidance: Consider claim types (training, inference, architecture, problem/solution). Use system/apparatus limitations, technical constraints, specific structures, improvements to computer functioning, or specific post-processing to anchor claims. Include problem/solution wording and quantify improvements where feasible.

name: Drafting Definite Claims (§112(b))
description: Ensure claims provide clear, definite boundaries and are supported by specification to meet §112(b).
guidance: Avoid indefinite functional language without structure; support claim terms with examples and structure in the spec. Address representative-claim treatment (PTAB) by presenting claim-specific arguments where needed.

name: Inference Claims (advantages and drafting focus)
description: Draft inference-time claims to capture deployment improvements and practical applications of trained models.
guidance: Emphasize constrained inference behavior, device-specific implementations (edge/cloud), latency/resource improvements, or specific post-processing steps to strengthen §101/practical application positions and enforcement/detectability.

name: Architecture Claims
description: Claim structural aspects of AI models (layer arrangements, novel connections, encoder/decoder structures, compressed architectures, neuromorphic or hardware accelerators).
guidance: Capture architecture-level innovations and their functional benefits; provide detailed layer/connection descriptions, parameter relationships, or hardware arrangements in the spec to support these claims for §112 and non-obviousness.

name: Problem/Solution Claims
description: Include claims that explicitly tie a claimed technical solution to the technical problem and show how the solution improves a device or computer function.
guidance: Problem/solution language can assist in practical application analysis; ensure the claim recites how the claimed elements bring about the improvement (e.g., reduced memory, increased throughput).

name: Office Action Response Strategies for §101 Rejections
description: Respond to patent eligibility rejections by showing that the claim integrates the judicial exception into a practical application or recites significantly more than the exception.
guidance: Use problem/solution evidence, quantify improvements, claim specific structures, combine additional unconventional elements, and argue practical application per USPTO PEG. Prepare separate §101 arguments for representative claims when necessary.

name: Addressing Mental Process and Organizing Human Behavior Rejections
description: Anticipate and rebut rejections that characterize claims as mental processes or organizing human activity.
guidance: Emphasize concrete computer/technical implementation, sensors/data acquisition, device integration, or specific algorithmic steps performed by machines rather than purely human cognitive activities.

name: Addressing Mathematical Concept Rejections
description: Handle rejections that treat the claim as directed to mathematical formulas or abstract mental operations.
guidance: Show how the mathematical computation is applied to a technical problem in a particular machine or how it improves computer functioning; add physical or structured limitations and practical application language to claims/spec.

name: Using Specific Structures and Practical Applications
description: Include specific structures, hardware elements, or application-level details to demonstrate practical application and avoid abstract-idea characterizations.
guidance: Claim sensors, networks, edge devices, storage/processing constraints, or particular data flows; tie algorithmic elements to these structures in both claims and specification to strengthen §101 and enablement positions.

name: Combinations of Additional Elements and Unconventional Solutions
description: Show that claimed additional elements and their unconventional combinations provide more than well-understood routine activities.
guidance: Document why combinations are non-conventional and provide evidence of synergistic effects; use experimental/quantitative data where available to support inventive concept arguments.

name: Recent Changes Regarding Training Claims
description: Be aware of evolving practice and case law affecting the treatment, eligibility, and enforcement of training claims.
guidance: Monitor USPTO, PTAB, and court decisions on training-claim eligibility and enforcement/detectability issues; adjust drafting strategy accordingly (e.g., claim both training and inference/system embodiments).

name: Written Description and Definiteness Rejections (§112)
description: Avoid §112 rejections by ensuring sufficient disclosure, clear claim language, and support for terms, parameters, and scope.
guidance: Provide concrete examples (datasets, architectures, hyperparameters), define terms in the spec, and avoid overly broad claim terms unsupported by embodiments.

name: Detectability and Enforceability
description: Consider how claimed steps—especially training steps—can be detected and enforced in real-world infringement scenarios.
guidance: Claim system/apparatus elements or inference-time behaviors that are observable; include deployment constraints, data flows, or device-based steps to improve litigability. Recognize split-infringement risks where multiple actors perform different claim steps.

name: Ethics for AI Inventions — Safe and Effective
description: Ensure AI inventions are described and claimed with consideration for safety and effectiveness in their intended use.
guidance: Address safety measures, validation/testing results, failure modes, fallback mechanisms, and human-overrides in the specification to support practical application and regulatory/ethical considerations.

name: Ethics for AI Inventions — Human Alternatives and Fallback
description: Describe human oversight, alternatives, and fallback procedures when AI systems fail or are uncertain.
guidance: Specify thresholds for human intervention, fail-safe modes, and decision handoff processes in the specification to strengthen safety and practical implementation claims.

name: Considerations for Major Jurisdictions (EPO, Japan, China, Korea, UK)
description: Adapt drafting and prosecution strategies to jurisdiction-specific standards for patentability and inventorship.
guidance: EPO: emphasize 'technical character' and specific structural/technical effects; other jurisdictions have distinct approaches to AI and inventorship—review local case law and examiner guidance. Tailor claims/spec to meet regional eligibility, novelty, and inventive-step tests.

name: Responding to Proposed Legislation and Policy Changes
description: Anticipate and adjust to proposed statutory changes (e.g., Patent Eligibility Restoration Act) that could alter eligibility analysis and PTO practice.
guidance: Understand how elimination or modification of judicial exceptions might affect claim drafting strategies and the continued relevance of practical-application analysis. Maintain problem/solution claim drafting as USPTO/PTAB practice may persist despite legislative change.

name: Claim Drafting to Mitigate Representative Treatment Risk
description: When multiple claim types are filed, craft separate §101 and other arguments for different claim forms to avoid adverse representative-claim treatment.
guidance: Anticipate PTAB/Examiner selection of an exemplary claim; present distinct arguments for method, apparatus, and system claims to prevent method-claim treatment from dooming non-method claims.

name: Consideration of priority/benefit claims for determining 102(e) date
description: In determining the 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date, consider priority/benefit claims to earlier-filed U.S. provisional applications (35 U.S.C. 119(e)), U.S. nonprovisional applications (35 U.S.C. 120 or 121), and international applications (35 U.S.C. 120, 121 or 365(c)) only if the subject matter used to make the rejection is appropriately supported in the relied‑upon earlier‑filed application's disclosure (and any intermediate application(s)).
guidance: A benefit claim to a U.S. patent of an earlier-filed international application may only result in an effective U.S. filing date as of the date the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 371(c)(1),(2) and (4) were fulfilled. Do NOT consider benefit/priority to U.S. applications filed before an international application, nor foreign priority claims under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) and 365(a).

name: 35 U.S.C. 102(f) (applicant not the inventor) rejection criterion
description: A claim may be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(f) where the applicant 'did not himself invent the subject matter sought to be patented.'
guidance: Include an explanation of the supporting evidence establishing that applicant was not the inventor (see MPEP § 2137). This form paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.07 and may be preceded by 7.08–7.12.

name: Rejection wording for 35 U.S.C. 102(a)/(b)/(g)
description: Form paragraph 7.15 wording: 'Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102[2] as being [3] by [4].' In bracket 3 insert either '--clearly anticipated--' or '--anticipated--' with an explanation; in bracket 4 insert the prior art relied upon.
guidance: This rejection must be preceded by appropriate form paragraphs (7.07 and others) or form paragraph 7.103, and must be followed by either form paragraph 7.15.02 or 7.15.03 when 102(e) is also being applied. Provide explanatory material when using 'anticipated' vs 'clearly anticipated.'

name: Provisional rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) (common assignee or inventor)
description: Claim provisionally rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as being anticipated by a copending application with a common assignee or at least one common inventor; based on presumption of future publication or patenting of the copending application.
guidance: This provisional rejection may be overcome by (a) a showing under 37 CFR 1.132 that any invention disclosed but not claimed in the copending application was derived from the inventor of the instant application, or (b) an appropriate showing under 37 CFR 1.131. It may not be overcome by filing a terminal disclaimer. Use form paragraph 7.15.01 with explanatory text in bracket 4 as appropriate.

name: Contents required in a 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection
description: After indicating the rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103, the examiner should set forth: (A) relevant teachings of the prior art relied upon (with references to columns/pages/lines), (B) the differences in the claim over the applied reference(s), (C) the proposed modification of the applied reference(s) necessary to arrive at the claimed subject matter, and (D) an explanation why one of ordinary skill in the art at the time would have been motivated to make the proposed modification.
guidance: These elements are required to communicate the basis for the rejection and to establish a prima facie case of obviousness. Cite specific locations in references when appropriate. This form paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.07 and 7.10 or by 7.103.

name: Three basic criteria for prima facie obviousness
description: To establish a prima facie case of obviousness: (1) there must be some suggestion or motivation to modify the reference or to combine reference teachings; (2) there must be a reasonable expectation of success; (3) the prior art reference(s) must teach or suggest all the claim limitations.
guidance: The teaching/suggestion and the reasonable expectation of success must be found in the prior art and not based on applicant’s disclosure. See MPEP §§ 2143–2143.03 and decisions such as In re Vaeck for pertinent authorities.

name: Examiner's burden to present convincing line of reasoning
description: The initial burden is on the examiner to provide some suggestion of the desirability of doing what the inventor has done; either the references must expressly or impliedly suggest the claimed invention or the examiner must present a convincing line of reasoning why the artisan would have found the claimed invention obvious in light of the references.
guidance: See Ex parte Clapp and MPEP § 2144–2144.09 for examples of reasoning supporting obviousness rejections. Provide a clear, reasoned rationale rather than mere conclusory statements.

name: Provisional rejection (obviousness) disqualification under 35 U.S.C. 103(c)
description: Subject matter that was prior art under former 35 U.S.C. 103 via 102(e) is disqualified as prior art against the claimed invention if the prior art and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person; CREATE Act adds joint research agreement disqualification subject to three conditions.
guidance: CREATE Act conditions for joint research agreement disqualification: (A) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the date the invention was made; (B) the invention was made as a result of activities within the scope of the joint research agreement; (C) the patent application discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement. These changes apply to patents granted on or after Dec 10, 2004 (and to pending applications as specified). See MPEP § 706.02(k) and § 706.02(l)(1).

name: Ways to overcome a provisional 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/103 rejection
description: A provisional rejection of the obviousness type under 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/103 can be overcome by: (A) arguing patentability over the earlier filed application; (B) combining subject matter into a single application claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 and abandoning copending applications (subject to 35 U.S.C. 112 support requirements); (C) filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 showing derivation; (D) filing under 37 CFR 1.131 showing date of invention prior to the effective U.S. filing date of the copending application; (E) for applications pending on or after Dec 10, 2004, showing common ownership or disqualification under CREATE Act joint research agreement conditions.
guidance: Note that combining applications and obtaining 120 benefit requires earlier applications to provide adequate 35 U.S.C. 112 support for the claims in the later application. Terminal disclaimers and 1.130 affidavits/1.321(c) may be used in certain common ownership situations to overcome double patenting/103 rejections. See MPEP §§ 715, 718 and relevant form paragraphs.

name: Specification in reissue subject to revision/restriction; commissioner can require disclaimer/alteration
description: Whenever an application is made for addition of a newly discovered improvement to an existing patent or when a patent is returned for correction and reissue, the specification annexed is subject to revision and restriction as in original applications; the commissioner shall not add improvements or grant reissue until the applicant has entered a disclaimer or altered his specification of claim in accordance with the commissioner's decision.
guidance: The commissioner has authority to require disclaimers or claim amendments as a condition of granting reissue; omissions or restrictions may be imposed by the commissioner and sanctioned by law (act of 1836/1837 cited).

name: Patentee may narrow claims in reissue (omit parts of original invention)
description: On a reissue the patentee is at liberty to omit a part of his original invention if he deems it expedient, and to retain only that part of the original invention he deems fit to retain.
guidance: A renewed patent that claims less than the original may be equally valid. Public policy does not prohibit such restriction because giving up part of an invention allows the public to use it; omissions may also be made to avoid misleading or unnecessarily broad language that would render the specification invalid.

name: Reissue remedies defects in specification (omitted modes/claim scope)
description: A specification may be defective by omitting a full description of the mode of constructing a machine or by omitting to describe fully in the claim the nature, extent, and character of the invention; such defects are precisely what renewed patents are meant to remedy.
guidance: Renewed patents are commonly granted to cure defects of omission in the specification or claim; courts recognize reissue to correct defects that make original specification doubtful or defective rather than utterly void.

name: Disclaimers may amend specifications for inadvertent over-breadth; effect and joinder rules
description: Specifications may be amended by filing a disclaimer whenever, through inadvertency, accident, or mistake, the original claim was too broad, provided some material and substantial part of the thing patented is truly the patentee's own; such a disclaimer may be filed by the patentee, administrators, executors, and assigns, and thereafter is considered part of the original specification to the extent of the disclaimant's interest.
guidance: A disclaimer cannot operate in favor of an assignee without that assignee joining in it in any suit at law or in equity. Recordation of the disclaimer is important; consult statute references (acts cited) and case law on disclaimer effect.

name: Proper 37 CFR 1.501 submission content
description: A 37 CFR 1.501 submission must be limited to patents, printed publications, and/or patent owner written claim scope statements and additional information, and must include the requisite citation description and information (and proof of service).
guidance: If the submission lacks these elements it is not proper for entry. Use forms PTO/SB/08A, 08B, or PTO/SB/42 (or equivalent) to list cited prior art. Include translations of non-English pertinent parts. See MPEP § 2294 and § 2217.

name: Characteristics and policy goals of ex parte reexamination
description: Reexamination procedures provide for: reexamination of patents; essentially ex parte proceedings; minimized processing costs/complexities; maximized respect for the reexamined patent; and prompt, timely determinations under 'special dispatch' (35 U.S.C. 305).
guidance: Understand the listed basic characteristics (anyone can request; prior art limited to patents/printed publications; substantial new question required; ex parte proceedings if ordered; decision on request within 3 months; scope of claim cannot be enlarged; public access to files with electronic availability through PAIR). Parties must avoid litigation tactics and unauthorized submissions not provided for by regulations (see 37 CFR 11.18(b)).

name: 37 CFR 1.510(b) required parts of a reexamination request
description: A request for ex parte reexamination must include: (1) a statement pointing out each substantial new question of patentability; (2) identification of every claim for which reexamination is requested plus a detailed explanation of pertinency and manner of applying cited prior art to each claim; (3) copies of every relied-upon patent/printed publication (with English translations of necessary parts); (4) a copy of the entire patent (front face, drawings, specification/claims) and any disclaimers/certificates; (5) a certification that the request was served in its entirety on the patent owner (name/address indicated) or duplicate supplied; and (6) a certification that estoppel provisions do not prohibit filing.
guidance: Each element must be satisfied for the request to be complete; otherwise the requester will be notified and given an opportunity to complete the request within a specified time. Failure to comply results in no filing date and the request may instead be treated as a 1.501 citation if compliant with that rule.

name: Detailed explanation of pertinency to each claim
description: For each claim identified, the request must provide a detailed explanation of the pertinency and manner of applying the cited prior art to that claim, and if relying on patent owner statements submitted under § 1.501(a)(2), must explain how those statements are used to determine claim meaning and interpretation.
guidance: If appropriate, the requester may also point out how claims distinguish over cited prior art. The explanation must be sufficiently specific for each claim and proposed ground.

name: Copy and formatting requirements for submitted documents
description: Provide a copy of every cited patent or printed publication (with translations of necessary parts), and a copy of the entire patent including front face, drawings, and specification/claims in double-column format; all copies must have each page plainly written on only one side of a sheet.
guidance: Non-English documents require English translations of necessary parts. Include any disclaimers, certificates of correction, or reexamination certificates. Failure to provide proper copies/format may render the request incomplete.

name: Fee payment and filing date rule
description: The request must be accompanied by the reexamination fee set in 37 CFR 1.20(c)(1); the filing date of the request is the date on which the request satisfies all the requirements of 37 CFR 1.510.
guidance: If a request lacks the fee or required elements, the requester will be notified and usually given time to complete; failure to comply results in no filing date and possible treatment as a 1.501 citation. If the patent owner files and includes a proposed amendment under 1.530, excess claims fees under 1.20(c)(3)&(4) may apply.

name: No abandonment or withdrawal after fee-paid request
description: After the request and entire fee for requesting reexamination are received, no abandonment, withdrawal, or striking of the request is possible regardless of who requested it, except in limited circumstances (e.g., final court decision rendering claims finally invalid prior to order).
guidance: In limited cases (e.g., final court decisions) a reexamination order may be vacated or the proceeding terminated per MPEP § 2286.

name: Handling of inquiries from third parties
description: Examiners should not discuss or answer inquiries from third parties about specific reexamination proceedings; refer such inquiries to Technology Center Quality, Central Reexamination Unit (CRU), or Supervisory Patent Reexamination Specialist (SPRS).
guidance: Only strictly procedural questions (not directed to any specific proceeding) may be handled by CRU SPRS or TC QAS. Employees who conducted a concluded reexamination should not discuss whether a certain reference was considered or whether a claim would have been allowed over that reference. Improper inquiries by practitioners are prohibited (see 37 CFR 11.804).

name: Partial validity for bona fide claimed parts; disclaimer requirement
description: So much of the invention or discovery as shall be truly and bona fide his own ... shall be deemed good and valid for so much of the invention or discovery as shall be truly and bona fide his own: Provided, It shall be a material and substantial part of the thing patented, and be definitively distinguishable from the other parts so claimed without right.
guidance: If a specification embraces more than the applicant has a right to claim, the patent is valid for the material/substantial portion that is bona fide the patentee's. The patentee may sue for infringement of that part, but to recover costs he must have entered at the Patent Office, prior to suit commencement, a disclaimer of the part claimed without right. Unreasonable delay or neglect in entering the disclaimer may forfeit benefits of these provisions.

name: Applicant must be the inventor and provide a written description distinguishing the invention
description: The applicant must invent, contrive, or produce something that did not exist before; statutes require the applicant to swear or affirm that he is the true inventor or discoverer and to deliver a written description of his invention by which it may be distinguished from other inventions.
guidance: Constitutional/ statutory requirement that patents be granted to the inventor. Specifications must include a written description adequate to distinguish the claimed invention from prior art/other inventions—used to determine entitlement and scope.

name: Align prosecution with SSO participation and timelines
description: Successful SEP prosecution often points toward participatory contributions in SSO meetings and patent application filings aligned with the SSO’s development stages to maximize claim mapping to mandatory standard features.
guidance: Different SSOs have differing procedures and timelines (e.g., ETSI/3GPP structured release cycles, IEEE rapid Wi‑Fi amendments, video coding standards with distinct codec tools). Consider filing patent applications before submitting contributions and reference evolving SSO documents precisely. Tailor prosecution strategy to the specific standard and SSO.

name: Claim drafting to cover multiple standard features (mandatory and key optional)
description: Patent applicants should draft claims to cover multiple technical features specified in the standards, targeting both mandatory and key optional features.
guidance: To ensure claims read on applicable standards (to the extent predictable), internally maintain detailed and continuously updated claim charts during prosecution showing explicit references to relevant portions of the standards documents. Draft claims to target technically distinct tools in standards like video codecs and to encompass foreseeable standard permutations.

name: Synchronize prosecution across jurisdictions for overlapping claim scope
description: Because technical standards are global while patent rights are national, developing SEP portfolios with strong overlapping claims across jurisdictions requires careful coordination of prosecution in multiple countries.
guidance: Closely monitor office actions and legal developments in each jurisdiction to adapt claims while maintaining family claim scope overlap. Ensure consistent prosecution narratives and technical justifications across patent families to minimize invalidity risk and maximize retention of essentiality.

name: Post-issuance claim-chart mapping and portfolio hygiene
description: After a patent issues, create a detailed claim chart that maps patented claims to the relevant sections of the technical standard to determine whether claims read on the standard and identify deficiencies.
guidance: For large or growing portfolios, build systems to track which patents correspond to each standard. Claim charts help determine deficiencies that may be addressed via continuations, divisionals, or reissue applications. Tracking as the portfolio develops is easier than retroactive sifting.

name: Identify licensing targets and 'proud patents' through monitoring and diligence
description: Finding who is likely to require a license starts with monitoring industries and standards development and performing internal diligence to identify high-value patents.
guidance: Monitor SSO meetings, industry players, new entrants, and products that implement standards. Identify 'proud patents'—those with broad claims, strong essentiality reads, and low invalidity risk—as primary negotiation/leverage assets; proud SEPs can be charted before specific infringers are identified.

name: SEP licensing negotiation practices and FRAND compliance
description: SEP licensing negotiations should be conducted in good faith to comply with FRAND obligations, with the process typically centered on licensing terms and infringement/validity merits.
guidance: Negotiations often begin with a letter explaining that SEPs are essential and inviting discussion; initial letters generally avoid naming specific patents to prevent triggering IPRs (e.g., IPR petitions or declaratory judgment actions). Discussions involve claim charts and financial talks over months or years. Maintain repeated, continuous communications to demonstrate good-faith negotiation. Whether an offer is FRAND-compliant depends on variables like comparable industry licenses and parties’ conduct.

name: Specification must provide reasonable guidance/direction for experimentation
description: Enablement requires that the specification provide sufficient direction so that one skilled in the art can practice the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
guidance: If the specification provides working examples and considerable direction (techniques, methods, steps), enablement is more likely (e.g., In re Wands; Telectronics example of stainless steel electrodes). Conversely, mere 'plan' or 'invitation' to experiment is insufficient (e.g., Enzo Biochem).

name: Quantity of examples vs claim breadth (breadth commensurate with disclosure)
description: Quantity of examples is only one factor; broad claim language risks loss of any claim that cannot be enabled across its full scope.
guidance: Evaluate whether the number and nature of working examples and direction in the spec are commensurate with the breadth of the claims. Cases: Enzo Biochem (limited E. coli examples vs broad claims to many organisms), MagSil (claim breadth vs lack of teaching to achieve large resistive changes).

name: Examiner must identify missing information for enablement rejections
description: When doubt arises because information is missing about one or more essential claim elements or relationships, the examiner should specifically identify what information is missing and why the missing information is needed to provide enablement.
guidance: Be explicit in Office actions: point to specific claim elements and explain what disclosure is absent and how that absence prevents practice of the full claim scope.

name: Enablement prevents claims broader than the disclosed invention
description: Enablement serves the dual function of ensuring adequate disclosure of the claimed invention and of preventing claims broader than the disclosed invention.
guidance: Challenge claim scope when the specification lacks disclosure across the claimed scope (e.g., claim language covering mechanical and electronic sensors where only mechanical details are shown — Automotive Technologies).

name: Deposits and availability for microorganisms (biological enablement)
description: For inventions involving living biological products as critical elements, availability of the organism (e.g., via deposit) can satisfy written description and enablement where a sufficient description cannot be given to obtain the organism from nature.
guidance: Deposits must be made prior to issue (not necessarily prior to filing). Consider scope of claim (species vs strains): depositor must enable the claimed breadth (Ex parte Jackson, In re Argoudelis). See MPEP §§2402–2411.03 and §2411.01 for deposit issues.

name: Enablement in biological/chemical cases depends on unpredictability and breadth
description: In unpredictable arts (e.g., gene/antisense tech, vaccines, protein expression), broad claims require commensurately broad enablement; limited examples and narrow direction relative to claim breadth can render a disclosure nonenabling.
guidance: Consider (1) amount of direction and number of working examples, (2) unpredictability of the field, and (3) evidence of experimentation required to adapt techniques beyond examples (Enzo Biochem, In re Wright, In re Goodman, In re Vaeck).

name: Examiner must present factual analysis to support nonenablement
description: To establish a reasonable basis for questioning the adequacy of a disclosure, the examiner must present a factual analysis showing that a person skilled in the art would not be able to make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
guidance: Office actions should include factual evidence/analysis (time, skill, unpredictability, missing steps) rather than conclusory statements; absence of a reasonable factual basis may prevent sustaining a rejection on appeal.

name: Programmed steps, algorithms, or procedures should be disclosed in programming applications
description: A general guideline is to challenge sufficiency of disclosures that fail to include the programmed steps, algorithms or procedures the computer performs to produce the claimed function.
guidance: These can be described as program listings, detailed flowcharts, or other forms understandable to one of ordinary skill. Where an operative program and identified prior-art computer are present, enablement is more likely (Knowlton, Comstock).

name: False statements to a tribunal / failure to correct (37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a)(1))
description: 37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a)(1) proscribes making false statements of fact or law to a tribunal or failing to correct a false statement of material fact or law previously made to the tribunal by the practitioner.
guidance: Here, respondent claimed an incorrect priority date in related applications and put incorrect dates into application specifications; such misstatements to the Office violate § 11.303(a)(1). Practitioners must not make or leave uncorrected material misrepresentations to the Office.

name: Requirement a) Same earliest date (priority/filing date)
description: Both the DPMA application on which PPH is requested and the OEE application(s) forming the basis of the PPH request shall have the same earliest date (whether this be a priority date or a filing date).
guidance: Examples are given as Case I–IV: (Case I) DPMA application validly claims priority from the OEE (Paris route); (Case II) DPMA application provides the basis of a valid priority claim for the OEE application; (Case III) applications share a common priority (including various PCT/national-phase and domestic/divisional permutations); (Case IV) PCT national phase application where both DPMA and OEE apps are derived from a common PCT international application having no priority claim. See annex figures A–L for route-specific examples.

name: Requirement b) OEE determined one or more claims patentable/allowable
description: At least one corresponding OEE application has one or more claims that have been determined to be patentable by the OEE.
guidance: Claims are 'determined to be allowable/patentable' when the CNIPA examiner explicitly identified the claims to be allowable/patentable in the latest office action, even if a patent has not yet been granted. If an OEE office action does not explicitly state that a particular claim is allowable, those claims may be deemed implicitly allowable only if the applicant includes a declaration with the PPH request stating that 'no reason for rejection had been given in the CNIPA office action in relation to a claim and that this claim is therefore deemed to be allowable/patentable by the CNIPA.' Examples: claims not mentioned in the First Notice of the Opinion on Examination under the item concerning Claims, or in later Notices under the corresponding item, may be implicitly identified as allowable — in which case the declaration is required.

name: Requirement c) All DPMA claims must sufficiently correspond to OEE-allowable claims
description: All claims in the DPMA application, as originally filed or as amended, for examination under the PPH must sufficiently correspond to one or more of those claims indicated as allowable (patentable) by the OEE.
guidance: Sufficient correspondence is defined accounting for translation and claim format differences: claims are the same scope if they present the same technical features that made the OEE claims allowable; similar scope if differences are solely due to translation or claim format and do not deviate from original disclosure; narrower if the DPMA claim is further limited by an additional feature supported in the specification. A claim that introduces a new/different category of claims compared to those indicated as allowable by the OEE is not considered to sufficiently correspond (example: OEE only has process-of-manufacturing claims; DPMA adds product claims dependent on those process claims — not sufficient). 'Claim format' refers to the formal version of the claims.

name: Required document c) Completed claim correspondence table
description: A completed claim correspondence table showing the relationship between the claims of the DPMA application for accelerated examination under the PPH and the claims of the corresponding OEE application considered patentable by the OEE.
guidance: Sufficient correspondence of claims occurs where the claims are of such a scope as defined under requirement 3c. When claims are literally translated, the applicant can simply write 'they are the same' in the table. When claims are not just literally translated, the applicant is allowed to explain the sufficient correspondence of each claim based on the criteria under 3c. In all cases of doubt the examiner may request an explanation of each claim based on 3c; otherwise the claims are presumed to correspond.

name: Construction of Specifications — Purpose and Considerations
description: Purpose of construing a specification and factors relevant to construction: the addressee, common general knowledge, and the invention described.
guidance: Addresses initial considerations, role of common general knowledge, and how to approach differing aspects claimed.

name: Specification and Claims to Examine — Amendments and Unity
description: Consideration of amendments made prior to examination, assessment of unity (single invention), and treatment of provisional specifications and omnibus references.
guidance: Guidance on when to examine amended documents and how to handle lack of unity or complex claim sets.

name: Full Disclosure, Sufficiency, Clarity and Support (s40 considerations)
description: Requirements for clear and complete disclosure (s40(2)(a)), support for claims (s40(3)), claims to be clear and succinct, the best method, and specific rules for micro-organisms and sequence deposits.
guidance: Explains difference between 'clear and complete disclosure' and 'support' and includes annex examples.

name: Specification and claim must reflect an improvement
description: The specification should disclose sufficient details such that one of ordinary skill in the art would recognize the claimed invention as providing an improvement, and the claim itself must reflect the improvement in technology.
guidance: Examiners should assess whether the specification and claims show an improvement to computer-functionality or other technology (see MPEP § 2106.05(a)). If the disclosure and claim language do not reflect an improvement, eligibility is less likely. Examples and case law are cited to help determine whether claimed subject matter improves technology.

name: Claim scope must be a particular solution, not merely an idea/outcome
description: Consider the extent to which the claim covers a particular solution to a problem or a particular way to achieve a desired outcome, as opposed to merely claiming the idea of a solution or outcome.
guidance: Evaluate whether the claim ties the abstract idea to a specific technical implementation or merely preempts an idea. Also consider whether the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) limits the claim to computer implementation. See MPEP § 2106.05(a) for discussion and examples.

name: More than conventional implementation on generic components required
description: A claim must include more than conventional implementation on generic components or machinery to qualify as an improvement to an existing technology.
guidance: Claims that add only well-known computer components or conventional machinery likely fail to show improved computer-functionality (see Affinity Labs v. DirecTV; TLI Communications v. AV Auto.). Examiners should look for unconventional arrangement or operation that improves technology.

name: Resolve improvement question as early as possible (Step 2A or 2B)
description: Although the question of whether a claim improves computer-functionality or other technology may be considered in either step of the Alice/Mayo test (Step 2A or 2B), examiners are encouraged to resolve this question as early as possible in the eligibility analysis.
guidance: If an improvement is clear, eligibility may be resolved under a streamlined analysis (Pathway A) or found not directed to an abstract idea (Pathway B). If improvement is not clear, it still may contribute to eligibility under Step 2B. See discussion referencing Enfish and Amdocs.

name: Improvement can render claim eligible at Step 2A or contribute at Step 2B
description: A claim that is directed to a clear improvement in computer-related technology may be eligible at Pathway A under the streamlined analysis or at Pathway B as not being directed to an abstract idea; if improvement is less clear it may still contribute to eligibility in the Step 2B analysis.
guidance: Examples: Enfish claims (self-referential table) found eligible as improvement; Amdocs claims (distributed network architecture) were eligible under Step 2B because the unconventional architecture amounted to an inventive concept.

name: Claim must recite an abstract idea to be directed to it (Step 2A principle)
description: The Step 2A analysis requires a claim to recite (i.e., set forth or describe) an abstract idea in order to be directed to that idea. Claims that are based on or involve an abstract idea but do not recite it are not directed to an abstract idea.
guidance: This principle separates claims that merely use or involve abstract ideas from claims that are actually directed to those ideas. See Enfish, DDR Holdings, Trading Techs. examples and the non-limiting hypothetical examples (printer, washing machine, earring sensor, BRCA sequencing, BIOS loading) that illustrate claims not reciting an abstract idea.

name: If claim recites abstract idea but claim as whole is an improvement, it is not directed to abstract idea
description: Some claims reciting an abstract idea are not directed to the abstract idea because they also recite additional elements (such as an improvement) demonstrating that the claims as a whole clearly do not seek to tie up the abstract idea.
guidance: Courts have found that additional elements which improve computer functioning or other technology shift the focus from the abstract idea (see McRO; Enfish; Research Corporation Technologies). Non-limiting examples include surgical shears with a pressure regulator, robotic arm with sensor-based control, autofocus camera system, and an internal combustion engine with a control system.

name: Rely on concepts identified in cases, not the judicial descriptors
description: When determining whether a claimed concept is similar to a concept the courts have identified as an abstract idea, examiners should rely on the concepts identified in the cases, not the judicial descriptors themselves (e.g., 'fundamental economic practices').
guidance: Descriptors are not mutually exclusive and can overlap; use the factual and conceptual holdings of precedent to assess similarity (see MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2) discussion and examples).

name: Subcategory: Advertising, marketing, and sales activities as abstract ideas
description: Concepts relating to advertising, marketing, and sales activities (e.g., generating/transmitting menus, structuring a sales force, using advertising as exchange) can be abstract ideas.
guidance: See Apple v. Ameranth (menu generation), In re Ferguson (structuring sales force), Ultramercial (advertising as currency). Claims that simply add conventional computer components to these business practices are likely abstract.

name: Subcategory: Tracking or organizing information as abstract ideas
description: Claims directed to tracking, organizing, or manipulating information (e.g., data filtering, particular GUI arrangements to improve accuracy) may be abstract ideas depending on whether they provide a technical improvement.
guidance: BASCOM (content filtering) and Trading Techs. (GUI display improving trader accuracy) provide examples where the concept was considered; examine whether the claim recites a specific technical solution that improves computer operation.

name: Non-limiting examples of claims that do not recite an abstract idea
description: Examples include: a printer comprising a belt, roller, printhead, ink cartridge; a washing machine with drive motor and controller; an earring with a blood-glucose sensor and memory; method for sequencing BRCA1; method for loading BIOS into a local computer system.
guidance: These examples illustrate claims that do not set forth or describe an abstract idea. Use such concrete device or method examples to distinguish from claims that recite abstract concepts.

name: Non-limiting examples of claims not directed to an abstract idea because of an improvement
description: Examples include: surgical shears with a pressure regulator limiting applied force; a robotic arm assembly with sensor-based velocity adjustment for smooth motion; autofocus camera system combining autofocus algorithm and drive mechanism; an internal combustion engine with EGR valve controlled by processor based on throttle rate of change.
guidance: These show claims where additional elements clearly improved the functioning of the claimed technology and therefore were not directed to an abstract idea. Examiners should identify analogous technical improvements in examined claims.

name: Computer-generated icon: article-of-manufacture requirement
description: If the disclosure as a whole does not suggest or describe the claimed subject matter as a computer-generated icon embodied in a computer screen, monitor, other display panel, or portion thereof, reject the claimed design under 35 U.S.C. 171 for failing to comply with the article of manufacture requirement.
guidance: If disclosure does not support embodiment as an icon in a display, state that the claim is fatally defective under 35 U.S.C. 171; amendments attempting to overcome the rejection will ordinarily be entered but any new matter must be canceled (if new matter is added, reject under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph). If the disclosure as a whole does suggest such embodiment, indicate that drawings may be amended to overcome the rejection and suggest amendments to bring the claim into compliance. Upon applicant reply, enter amendments and review the record; if by a preponderance of the evidence (In re Oetiker) applicant establishes the icon is embodied in a display, withdraw the rejection.

name: Changeable (animated) computer-generated icons: claim requirements
