description: Computer-generated icons that change in appearance during viewing may be the subject of a design claim; such a claim may be shown in two or more views with images understood as viewed sequentially and no ornamental aspects attributed to the transitional process.
guidance: Include a descriptive statement in the specification describing the transitional nature and making clear the claim does not include anything not shown. Example statements are provided (e.g., 'The subject matter in this patent includes a process or period in which an image changes into another image. This process or period forms no part of the claimed design.'). The process/period of transition is not part of the claimed design.

name: Designs comprising multiple articles or multiple parts
description: A claimed design may encompass multiple articles or multiple parts within an article, but the title must identify a single entity of manufacture made up by the parts (e.g., set, pair, combination, unit, assembly).
guidance: Include a descriptive statement in the specification clarifying the claim is directed to the collective appearance. If separate parts are shown in a single view, show the parts embraced by a bracket '}'. For multiple parts of a single article: show the article in broken lines and various parts in solid lines (no bracket needed). See MPEP §1503.01 for further formal requirements.

name: Ornamentality standard (definition and overall test)
description: An ornamental feature/design is one 'created for the purpose of ornamenting' and is not merely a by-product of functional or mechanical considerations; to be patentable, a design must be 'primarily ornamental.'
guidance: Determine ornamentality by viewing the claimed design in its entirety—the ultimate question is whether the overall appearance is dictated by utilitarian purpose or created for ornament. Consider purposes of particular elements, but assess overall appearance. Distinguish functionality of the article from functionality of the specific design feature. Case law examples (In re Carletti; L.A. Gear; Norco) and tests are cited to guide the analysis.

name: Prima facie evidence requirements for lack of ornamentality
description: To properly reject a claimed design under 35 U.S.C. 171 for lack of ornamentality, the examiner must make a prima facie showing and provide a sufficient evidentiary basis for factual assumptions relied upon.
guidance: Proper evidentiary bases include evaluation of the appearance of the design itself, the examiner's knowledge of the art, a reply to a letter of inquiry, a brochure emphasizing functional/mechanical features, the specification of an analogous utility patent, or information in the application. Examiners must detail and support assertions, especially when an article has general use. Examples of acceptable evidence: (A) common knowledge in the art; (B) appearance of the design; (C) specification of a related utility patent; (D) information provided in the specification. Rejections should not be made absent such evidence.

name: Evaluation of evidence submitted to overcome rejection
description: The examiner must evaluate applicant-submitted evidence in light of the design as a whole to decide if the claim is primarily ornamental; mere display at trade shows or inclusion in catalogs is insufficient by itself.
guidance: Evidence must show the design was created for the 'purpose of ornamenting' (In re Carletti). Evidence must provide clear and specific indication of ornamentality to be probative (Berry Sterling). When visibility during end use is at issue, applicant must show the article's design is a 'matter of concern' during some period between manufacture/assembly and ultimate use (In re Webb). Declarations from customers/users attesting ornamentality during commercial life are appropriate. Applicants not directly involved in sales/users cannot generally provide factual evidence about purchase reasons.

name: Novelty standard for design patents (35 U.S.C. 102 and average observer test)
description: Novelty under 35 U.S.C. 102 requires that the claimed design not have been known or described in the prior art; the relevant test is the 'average observer' test — whether the average observer takes the new design for a different, not a modified, already-existing design. The reference must be identical in all material respects to anticipate.
guidance: The average observer test does not require analogous arts; the observer is not charged with knowledge of any art. Functional and/or hidden features may not be relied upon to support patentability in a 102 rejection. Differences in functional considerations alone do not negate anticipation. Case law: In re Barrlett/Barlett (quoting Shoemaker), Hupp v. Siroflex, In re Glavas, In re Cornwall, Black & Decker v. Pittway.

name: Foreign priority and 35 U.S.C. 102(d) for designs
description: Registration of a design abroad is treated as equivalent to patenting for 35 U.S.C. 102(d) purposes; a U.S. design application must be filed within six months of the foreign filing to claim priority (35 U.S.C. 172 modifies 102(d) for designs).
guidance: If the foreign protection vests (registration/grant) and the U.S. application is timely filed (within 6 months), priority will vest; otherwise a statutory bar arises. The MPEP provides a table of countries and the foreign dates usable for 35 U.S.C. 102(d) purposes (varies by country — e.g., date of registration, publication, filing date, etc.). See MPEP §1504.10 for details.

name: Argument content and structure requirements
description: Arguments must be presented for each ground of rejection and explain why the examiner erred, including citations to statutes, regulations, authorities, and parts of the Record relied on.
guidance: A statement that merely points out what a claim recites is not an argument for patentability. All arguments and authorities an appellant wishes the Board to consider for the present appeal should be included in the appeal brief (except limited exceptions under §§ 41.41, 41.47, 41.52). Arguments raised first at oral hearing are not normally entitled to consideration. Use separate headings for each ground of rejection; use subheadings to identify claims or claim subgroups being argued. Grouping claims without separate argument waives separate consideration of those grouped claims.

name: Headings and claim-subheading requirement
description: Each ground of rejection must be argued under a separate heading that clearly identifies the ground being contested; for claims argued separately or as subgroups, subheadings identifying claim numbers must be used.
guidance: Examples provided for various grouping strategies (e.g., 'Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) over U.S. Patent No. X' with subheadings 'Claims 1-3', 'Claim 4', etc.). To ensure separate consideration by the Board, the appellant must use subheadings for claims claimed to deserve separate consideration.

name: Claims appendix format and presentation
description: An appendix containing a copy of the claims involved in the appeal must be provided. The claims copy should be a clean copy and should not include markings such as brackets or underlining except for reissue/reexamination as permitted.
guidance: The claims copy should be double-spaced and the appendix should start on a new page. Specific MPEP and CFR references for reissue and reexamination claim presentation are noted.

name: Amendments filed on or after filing brief — limited admissibility
description: Amendments filed on or after the date of filing a brief may be admitted only to (1) cancel claims where cancellation does not affect the scope of other pending claims, or (2) rewrite dependent claims into independent form.
guidance: All other amendments filed after the date of filing an appeal brief will not be admitted except as permitted by specified CFR provisions (41.39(b)(1), 41.50(a)(2)(i), and 41.50(b)(1)). An amendment filed on the same date as a non-compliant brief is considered filed under 41.33(b).

name: Rules and examples for rewriting dependent claims into independent form
description: Rewriting dependent claims into independent form (permitted under 41.33(b)(2)) includes rewriting a dependent claim as independent by adding limitations of the parent claim(s), or rewriting an independent claim to incorporate a dependent claim and canceling the dependent claim while adjusting dependency of other claims.
guidance: Such amendments must be filed before the expiration of the time period set forth in 37 CFR 90.3 to avoid cancellation of objected-to claims. Recommended that appellants rewrite dependent claims which were objected to solely because of dependency before appeal is forwarded to the Board.

name: Examiner obligations when indicating entry of an amendment
description: If examiner indicates in an advisory action that an amendment will be entered, the examiner must state how the individual rejections in the final Office action will be impacted by entry of the amendment, except where the amendment merely cancels claims or rewrites dependent claims into independent form.
guidance: If an amendment clearly places the application in condition for allowance, the examiner may enter the amendment and allow the application. Examiners must respond to all amendments filed after an appeal has been taken and prior to transfer of jurisdiction to the Board.

name: Examiner’s answer — grounds of rejection content and new/withdrawn rejections
description: The examiner’s answer should state every ground of rejection set forth in the Office action from which the appeal is taken (as modified) that is being maintained, list any withdrawn rejections under 'WITHDRAWN REJECTIONS,' and list any new grounds under 'NEW GROUNDS OF REJECTION.'
guidance: A new ground of rejection must be clearly designated and, for each new ground, include a complete explanation with proper reference to statute, prior art relied upon, and claim numbers. An examiner’s answer including a new ground must be approved (signed) by the Director or delegated designee.

name: Presentation and parts of an application (transitional)
description: Category 3 applications may comply with former Patent Rules regarding page numbering of the specification (description and claims) rather than section 193 of the new Rules; pages of description may be numbered separately from pages of claims. Category 3 apps with filing date prior to June 2, 2007 may comply with former sequence listing requirements.
guidance: Transitional allowance to accommodate older-format filings and sequence listings that pre-date harmonization with PCT formatting (amendments on June 2, 2007).

name: Required attachments on filing (Specification tab)
description: Applicant must attach the abstract, description, claims, sequence listing (if any) and drawings (if any) in this part.
guidance: Claim(s) are not required to be furnished at the time of filing to obtain a date of filing; claims must be submitted to the Registry within the time period specified in Chapter 2.2.10.

name: Preliminary examination checklist (formalities examination)
description: During preliminary examination the Formalities officer will check numerous requirements including: (a) Patents Form 1 is filed; (b) Singapore address for service furnished; (c) address of each applicant furnished; (d) declaration of priority is within 12 months; (e) where date of filing accorded based on a description filed, no incorporation by reference to a priority application is made; (f) names and addresses complete; (g) title on Form 1 corresponds with title in specification; (h) number of sheets indicated matches actual number filed; (i) an abstract is filed; (j) the abstract indicates 1 or 2 figures for publication; (k) no drawing or part of description missing; (l) specification commences with an appropriate title; (m) the description, claims and abstract do not contain drawings; (n) drawings are executed in black, sufficiently dense and dark strokes; (o) documents are legible and suitable for direct reproduction; (p) documents commence on a new sheet, sheets are numbered consecutively, with drawings numbered as a separate series; (q) where inventor details are provided, the relevant section in Patents Form 1 should be indicated as 'No' if not all applicants listed are inventors and derivation of right should be filled.
guidance: If any requirements are not met, a Formalities Examination Adverse Report will be issued; applicant may amend using Patents Form 13 within 2 months from the date of the letter. Replacement sheets must be submitted for amended documents.

name: Limitations on drawings submitted after the filing date
description: Drawings submitted after the filing date of the application may not be used (i) to overcome any insufficiency of the specification due to lack of an enabling disclosure or otherwise inadequate disclosure therein, or (ii) to supplement the original disclosure thereof for the purpose of interpretation of the scope of any claim.
guidance: A substitute or additional drawing that introduces new matter should not be entered; the examiner should describe the new matter in the next Office action. Entry decisions are reviewable by petition (37 CFR 1.181).

name: Views — general requirements and placement (37 C.F.R. 1.84(h))
description: The drawing must contain as many views as necessary to show the invention. Views may be plan, elevation, section, or perspective; detail views may be used. All views must be grouped together and arranged on the sheet(s) without wasting space, preferably in an upright position, clearly separated from one another, and must not be included in the sheets containing the specifications, claims, or abstract.
guidance: Views must not be connected by projection lines and must not contain center lines. Waveforms may be connected by dashed lines to show timing. Views on multiple sheets that form a single complete view must be assemblable without concealing any part of the views on the various sheets.

name: Presumption of validity and burden of proof
description: A patent is presumed valid; each claim is presumed valid independent of other claims. The burden on the party challenging validity is to show, by clear and convincing evidence, that the patent is invalid.
guidance: This presumption is never destroyed; in an infringement suit, if the alleged infringer fails to prove invalidity, the court may conclude only that the patent has not been proven invalid. Courts give deference to prior PTO examination but are not bound by PTO decisions.

name: Process claims: limits on patentable processes
description: A process is a way to produce a result; the inventor need not know why it works, but not all processes are patentable.
guidance: Processes that require mental participation or the mechanical equivalent of mental participation are generally not patentable; processes requiring emotional reactions as an element are also not patentable. The patent is for the discovered and disclosed process, not for explanation of the scientific theory.

name: Section 102(a) prior art — patents and printed publications
description: Section 102(a) bars patents when the invention was patented or described in a printed publication in this or a foreign country before the applicant's invention.
guidance: A published patent or printed publication that adequately describes and enables the invention is part of the prior art; 'printed' is broadly interpreted to include tangible material accessible to the public (photographs, distributed conference papers unless recipients were asked to keep them secret). The date of publication is the date first available to the public; published patents place claims and disclosures into prior art, while unpublished foreign patents may place only claimed material into prior art.

name: Limits on reliance upon expert testimony for disclosure
description: Expert testimony cannot take the place of disclosure in a prior art reference when that disclosure is required (e.g., anticipation requires each claim element expressly or inherently described in a single prior art reference).
guidance: Examples/citations: Verdegaal Bros. v. Union Oil; K/S Himpp v. Hear-Wear. Conclusory third-party assertions without supporting evidence cannot supply a missing limitation. Expert testimony may explain patents/printed publications but cannot substitute for patents/printed publications (35 U.S.C. § 311(b)).

name: General Plastic non-exhaustive factors for follow-on petitions
description: When exercising discretion on instituting IPR for follow-on petitions, the Board considers non-exclusive factors including: (1) whether same petitioner previously filed on same claims; (2) whether petitioner knew or should have known of prior art asserted in second petition at time of first petition; (3) whether petitioner had preliminary response or institution decision on first petition when filing second; (4) elapsed time between learning of prior art and filing second petition; (5) whether petitioner provides adequate explanation for time elapsed; (6) finite resources of the Board; (7) requirement to issue final determination within one year of institution (35 U.S.C. § 316(a)(11)).
guidance: The factors are not dispositive, not exclusive, and are part of a balanced assessment including the merits. There is no per se rule precluding follow-on petitions; other circumstances (e.g., related proceedings in district court or ITC) may also inform discretion.

name: Rationale must be based on state of the art, not hindsight
description: In formulating a rejection under 35 U.S.C. § 103, the rationale should be based on the state of the art and not on impermissible hindsight, e.g., applicant’s disclosure.
guidance: Examiners should avoid relying on the applicant's disclosure to supply a motivation to combine or other hindsight-based inferences. Clear articulation of why the claimed invention would have been obvious, grounded in prior art and common knowledge, is required.

name: Account for all claim limitations
description: Examiners need to account for all claim limitations in their rejections.
guidance: Either indicate how each limitation is shown by the reference(s) applied, or provide an explanation. Each limitation must be addressed in the obviousness analysis rather than ignored or assumed.

name: Rationale A — Combining prior art elements by known methods (predictable results)
description: All the claimed elements were known in the prior art and one skilled in the art could have combined the elements as claimed by known methods with no change in their respective functions, and the combination would have yielded predictable results.
guidance: Examiners must articulate: (1) a finding that the prior art included each claimed element (not necessarily in a single reference); (2) a finding that one of ordinary skill could have combined the elements as claimed by known methods and each element would have performed the same function; (3) a finding that the results of the combination were predictable. Note caution: combining known prior art elements is not sufficient if the results would not have been predictable.

name: Rationale B — Simple substitution of known equivalent element
description: The claim would have been obvious because the substitution of one known element for another would have yielded predictable results to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention.
guidance: Examiners must articulate: (1) a finding that the prior art contained a device differing from the claimed device by substitution of components; (2) a finding that the substituted components and their functions were known in the art; (3) a finding that one of ordinary skill could have substituted one known element for another and the results would have been predictable.

name: Rationales list not exhaustive
description: The list of rationales provided (A–G) is not intended to be all-inclusive; other rationales may support a conclusion of obviousness.
guidance: Regardless of which rationale is used, the key is clear articulation of the reasons why the claimed invention would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art.

name: Permissible reliance on official notice and common sense
description: Examiners may rely on official notice, common sense, design choice, and ordinary ingenuity when appropriate to support obviousness findings.
guidance: Such reliance still requires articulation and should not be a substitute for evidentiary support when evidence is necessary. The rationale must show how such common-sense inferences make the claimed invention obvious.

name: Claim construction (general)
description: Claim construction — includes terms like 'comprising' and 'consisting of' and general claim-construction principles.
guidance: Rules and principles for interpreting claim language; construction affects infringement and validity analyses. (Index references: pages 11–12, 80.)

name: Claim types (independent/dependent/multiple-dependent)
description: Dependent and independent claims; multiple dependent claims.
guidance: Classification of claim forms and their drafting/interpretation consequences. (Index: dependent, independent, multiple dependent — pages 12, 11–12.)

name: Means-plus-function (35 U.S.C. §112) claims
description: Means-plus-function.
guidance: Claims drafted in means-plus-function format are governed by Section 112/112(f) rules constraining the scope to corresponding structure in the specification. (References: pages 80, 81–82.)

name: Basis for rejection of claims (prosecution grounds)
description: Claims — basis for rejection, generally.
guidance: Grounds on which examiners reject claims during prosecution (e.g., anticipation, obviousness, lack of enablement/written description, new matter). (Index: pages 15–16.)

name: Doctrine of equivalents (DOE)
description: Doctrine of equivalents.
guidance: Tests and limits for DOE including the function/way/result test, hypothetical claim analysis, range of equivalents, reverse doctrine of equivalents, and limitations such as prosecution history estoppel. (Index references: pages 80, 82–84; function/way/result test: 82; hypothetical claim analysis: 83; range of equivalents: 83; reverse doctrine: 84; prosecution history estoppel: 83–84.)

name: Infringement (elements and types)
description: Infringement — elements generally; direct, contributory, inducing, literal infringement; acts include making, using, offering to sell, selling, or importing.
guidance: Elements to prove infringement depend on claim scope and type (product vs process); statutory acts listed; distinctions among direct, literal, contributory, and induced infringement. (Index references: pages 75–79, 80–82, 76.)

name: Continuation practice (continuation, continuation-in-part, divisional)
description: Continuation, continuation-in-part, divisional applications; copending and serial relationships.
guidance: Different continuation filings, their purposes, and effects on priority/claim scope. (Index: continuation pages 19–21; copending 20; divisional 21; continuation-in-part 20–21.)

name: Enablement of algorithms/flowcharts
description: Where the algorithm or logic performed by the computer lie at the heart of the invention, a full description of the algorithm or logic tree should be provided.
guidance: If the algorithm is described by a flow chart (a drawing), a written explanation of the flow chart is necessary to provide support for any claims that refer to the algorithm or logic. To successfully practice the invention, the person skilled in the art must be able to put each step in the flow chart into operation without recourse to inventive ingenuity or undue experimentation; the flow chart and any accompanying description must therefore provide any information necessary to enable the algorithm to be so practised.

name: Flowcharts require accompanying textual description
description: Flow charts are diagrams with boxes and arrows representing states/steps; when they illustrate the algorithm of the invention, a written explanation is necessary.
guidance: Do not rely on a flowchart alone to enable claims referencing the algorithm; include textual detail sufficient for practice.

name: Novelty (no anticipation by prior art)
description: A computer-implemented invention must not be anticipated by prior art relevant under section 28.2 of the Patent Act.
guidance: To be anticipatory, a single prior written disclosure, understood in light of common general knowledge, must both provide a written description of the claimed invention and sufficient instructions to enable practice by the skilled person without inventive effort or undue burden.

name: Software commands as essential elements in device claims
description: When considering a computer device (machine) claim, the effect of any commands being implemented by software must be considered to determine if they lead to a technological effect relevant to the promised utility of the device; if so, those commands are essential elements of the device.
guidance: Commands that merely apply functionality the machine already had are not essential; commands that change technological behavior are essential and must be included in novelty analysis.

name: Anticipation by prior use/public availability (software)
description: Prior sale or use of an invention can amount to anticipation if it makes available information that describes the claimed invention and is enabling; publicly available software prior to the claim date can be prior art if it provides sufficient information to comprehend the invention.
guidance: The information made available must be such that the skilled person could write a clear and unambiguous description of the claimed invention; prior art software that achieves the same function could be anticipatory for broad functional claims, whereas for method-specific claims it must be shown the same method was used.

name: Automation of manual processes tends toward obviousness
description: It is considered obvious that computers can be used to automate many manual operations; the idea of automating a manual process is, absent reasons to the contrary, considered to be uninventive.
guidance: To support claims to computer-automated versions of known manual methods, the inventive step typically must be found in the solution to specific challenges attendant to enabling the automation.

name: Claims must fit a statutory category
description: The subject-matter of a claim must belong to a category of invention as defined in section 2 of the Patent Act; elements used to define the subject-matter must be of a type appropriate to that category.
guidance: Avoid mixing elements from different categories in a way that creates ambiguity about intended subject-matter.

name: Computer-implemented method claim clarity
description: Where a claim is directed to a method to be implemented in whole or in part by computer, it must be unambiguously clear which steps of the method are being carried out by the computer.
guidance: Specifying 'computer-implemented' implies some steps are by computer but does not force a presumption; avoid steps that could be performed by either a person or a computer without clarity.

name: Machine (computer) claim must define physical components
description: Where a claim is directed to a machine, it must be defined in terms of physical components.
guidance: Means statements are common but if interpreted as software they must be specified as stored on physical memory either in the claim or description; language should be clear, concise and unambiguous.

name: System claims require unambiguous meaning
description: The term 'system' may refer to a machine, a computer program or a method depending on context; care must be taken to ensure its intended meaning is unambiguous.
guidance: In computer arts, absent other indication it may be presumed to mean a machine; where not a machine, explicitly define category to comply with subsection 27(4).

name: Software product claim form and preamble wording
description: A computer program per se is considered an abstract scheme, plan or set of rules and not an invention; under certain circumstances software can be claimed by directing the claim to a physical memory storing the computer program.
guidance: The preamble 'a physical memory having stored thereon...' directs claim to statutory embodiment (manufacture), whereas 'a computer program stored on a physical memory' directs to a computer program (excluded). It must be explicitly defined that the computer program is present as machine-executable code; only machine-executable code can change the technological functionality of the physical memory. Non-executable code is mere descriptive matter.

name: Means statements support and specificity requirement
description: Means statements (defining a part of an invention by function rather than specific structure) are not objectionable per se, provided the claim meets all requirements of the Patent Act and Patent Rules.
guidance: The description must describe what types of means are contemplated unless this would be obvious to the skilled person; where it would not be obvious which means fall within the scope, the claim may be defective for lack of support or indefiniteness. Means statements may refer to hardware or software and context should clarify which.

name: Mixed claim types and category-appropriate elements
description: Where a claim in one category (e.g., a machine) defines its subject-matter in terms of elements from another category (e.g., method steps), there is a risk of ambiguity over the intended subject-matter.
guidance: A machine claim must define structural components that distinguish it from other machines. A method-of-using-device claim must include at least one step applying the device. Product-by-process claims define a product by its process of production and are not a format for defining a product in terms of the method for which it will be used.

name: Data structures treated as abstract
description: A data structure is a format for organizing related data items and is considered by the Office to be an abstract idea or plan; a data structure per se is disembodied and not an invention within section 2 of the Patent Act.
guidance: For a data structure to impact patentability it must in some way limit the technological nature of a statutory element in the claim (e.g., contribute to a technological solution).

name: Machine-or-transformation test (clue, not sole test)
description: The machine-or-transformation test is a useful and important clue, an investigative tool, for determining whether some claimed inventions are processes under § 101, but it is not the sole test for process eligibility.
guidance: Used by the Federal Circuit (In re Bilski) as a primary test; Supreme Court in Bilski held it is an important clue but rejected it as the exclusive test. Consider whether a claimed process is tied to a particular machine or transforms an article into a different state as one factor among others.

name: Is the claim directed to a judicial exception (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea)?
description: First-step inquiry: determine whether the claims are directed to a patent-ineligible concept such as a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea.
guidance: Supreme Court cases (Benson, Flook, Mayo, Alice) begin by identifying whether a claim is directed to an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon (e.g., Bilski: hedging; Myriad: genetic information). If so, proceed to the second-step inventive-concept inquiry.

name: Two-step Mayo/Alice framework
description: Step 1: Determine whether the claims are directed to a judicial exception (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea). Step 2: If so, ask whether the claim contains an ‘inventive concept’ sufficient to ensure the patent amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception itself.
guidance: Applied in Mayo and Alice and implemented by courts and USPTO guidance. Examples: Mayo (diagnostic thresholds held to be law of nature); Alice (intermediated settlement held to be abstract idea). Courts dissect claim elements and evaluate whether additional elements add 'significantly more.'

name: Inventive concept / 'significantly more' requirement
description: Claims that recite a judicial exception must contain additional elements (an 'inventive concept') that, individually or as an ordered combination, add significantly more than the ineligible concept itself.
guidance: Courts have examined whether additional steps are merely well-understood, routine, conventional activity (insufficient) or provide something qualitatively different. The opinion criticizes that this inquiry often imports novelty/obviousness-type reasoning (§§102/103) into §101 and can be arbitrary, depending on comparisons to prior §101 opinions.

name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity is insufficient
description: If the additional steps beyond the judicial exception are well-understood, routine, conventional activities previously engaged in by others in the field, they do not transform an ineligible law of nature or abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter.
guidance: Mayo dissected claim limitations and found that administering, informing, and determining steps amounted to routine activities that add nothing significant. Courts routinely apply this as part of the step-two inquiry.

name: Consider the claim 'as a whole' vs dissecting into old/new elements
description: Diehr requires that claims be considered as a whole and cautions against dissecting claims into old and new elements and ignoring old elements in the §101 inquiry; Mayo/Flook, by contrast, dissect claim elements.
guidance: Diehr: 'a new combination of steps in a process may be patentable even though all the constituents ... were well known' and novelty of elements 'is of no relevance' to §101. The page highlights the conflict between Diehr's whole-claim approach and Mayo/Flook dissection.

name: Preemption concern (avoid monopolizing basic tools)
description: A primary concern in judicial exceptions is preventing patents that would preempt broad use of laws of nature, natural phenomena, or abstract ideas—i.e., monopolization of basic tools of scientific and technological work.
guidance: Courts warn against upholding patents that claim processes that too broadly preempt the use of a natural law. This preemption rationale is central to Mayo and other opinions and is used to justify invalidation when claims would monopolize foundational principles.

name: Use of prior art/state-of-the-art evidence in §101 analysis
description: Courts have sometimes considered published texts and the state of the art to conclude that a claimed concept is an abstract idea or otherwise ineligible, effectively looking at prior-art-like materials in the §101 inquiry.
guidance: Bilski and Alice relied on existence/ubiquity of known techniques (e.g., hedging, intermediated settlement) and cited texts. The page notes courts did not apply §102 formality (anticipation) but nevertheless used state-of-the-art evidence—raising concerns about importing §§102/103 considerations.

name: Novelty/obviousness should not determine §101 eligibility
description: The novelty ('point of novelty') of claim elements and issues properly belonging to §§102 and 103 should not be decisive in determining whether subject matter falls within §101 categories of possibly patentable subject matter.
guidance: Diehr and earlier cases hold that novelty and obviousness are irrelevant to §101; the article criticizes Supreme Court decisions for regressing toward subjective inventiveness and effectively reintroducing these considerations into §101.

name: Ordered combination notion
description: Courts may consider claim limitations collectively as an 'ordered combination' when assessing whether the combination adds significantly more than the judicial exception alone.
guidance: Mayo asserted it was sufficient to consider claim limitations as an 'ordered combination' despite Diehr's whole-claim requirement; this has been used to argue that mere aggregation/order of conventional steps can still be insufficient to confer eligibility.

name: Specific filing and renewal fees (Schedule 1 items)
description: Schedule 1 lists applicable fees for many actions (e.g., application for a patent accompanied by a provisional specification R60; complete specification R590; various fees for late claiming of priority, inspection, extensions, corrections, restorations, renewals per year, recording transactions, agent registration, oppositions, revocation applications, PCT transmittal, international and search fees, and national PCT fees as enumerated).
guidance: Schedule provides year-by-year renewal fee schedule and itemised fees for many formal actions; specific values and items must be consulted in Schedule 1 (many entries and amounts given). Some items reference substitutions by later Government Notices.

name: Form P1 contents and attachments (Schedule 2 — Form P1)
description: Form P1 (Application for a patent and acknowledgement of receipt) must include applicant name/reference, title of invention, priority claim (country, number, date), whether patent of addition or fresh application, and be accompanied by specified documents (e.g., provisional or complete specification copies, drawings, publication particulars and abstract (Form P8), copy of priority documents, translations, assignments, declaration and power of attorney (Form P3), request for ante-dating Form P4, etc.). Applicants must have address for service in the Republic.
guidance: Duplicate returned as proof of lodging but not valid unless endorsed with official stamp. Attention drawn to regulations 34-37 and that fees are payable per Schedule 1.

name: Purpose of Prosecution History Estoppel
description: Prosecution history estoppel limits the doctrine of equivalents to preserve the definitional and public-notice functions of patent claiming; the public may rely on the prosecution record to understand claim scope (Warner-Jenkinson; Festo).
guidance: When evaluating non-literal infringement, weigh the public-notice function: estoppel prevents patentees from recapturing subject matter they surrendered during prosecution. Courts must balance incentives for innovation against the need for reasonable certainty about claim scope.

name: Festo Presumption from Narrowing Amendments
description: A narrowing claim amendment during prosecution gives rise to a presumption of prosecution history estoppel—a general disclaimer of the territory between the original claim and the amended claim (Festo).
guidance: When a claim was narrowed to secure allowance, begin with the presumption that the patentee surrendered the intervening territory. The inquiry then becomes what (if any) territory was actually surrendered by the amendment.

name: Limitation-by-Limitation Analysis / Presumption Applies Only to Amended Limitations
description: Prosecution history estoppel is determined on a limitation-by-limitation basis; a presumption of estoppel exists only for claim limitations that were actually amended or narrowed during prosecution (Honeywell; Ericsson; Abbott Labs).
guidance: Do not impose estoppel for claim elements that were never amended. First resolve whether the asserted limitation was amended; if not, there is no Festo presumption as to that limitation.

name: Scope of Surrender = Territory Between Original and Amended Claim
description: The central question is what subject matter the narrowing amendment surrendered—i.e., the territory between the original claim scope and the amended claim scope (Festo).
guidance: Analyze the precise change in claim scope effected by the amendment to identify what was relinquished. Only that surrendered territory is at risk of estoppel; equivalents outside that surrendered territory may remain.

name: Role of Public-Notice and Inherent Uncertainty
description: Patent claim language is inherently imperfect and some uncertainty about the scope of equivalents is unavoidable; reasonable certainty (not absolute precision) is the governing standard (Nautilus; Markman).
guidance: In balancing public notice against protection for patentees, recognize the inevitability of some uncertainty and that the doctrine of equivalents exists to prevent form-over-substance outcomes. Courts should aim for reasonable certainty while allowing room for appropriate equivalents.

name: Special Considerations When Claims Recite Multiple Alternative Limitations
description: When a claim defines an element in multiple alternative ways and only some alternatives were amended, estoppel analysis can be complicated and may raise a threshold question whether any presumption applies to the asserted alternative (as in this case where limitation (A) was never amended while (B)/(C) were) (Federal Circuit practice).
guidance: Resolve threshold issues first—determine which alternative(s) were amended, whether the asserted claim element is the amended alternative, and apply limitation-by-limitation analysis. Unusual factual configurations (multiple alternatives, partial amendments) can make the case a poor vehicle for broad doctrinal change.

name: Effective Filing Date of the Claimed Invention
description: The AIA defines the term "effective filing date" for a claimed invention as the earliest of: (1) the actual filing date of the patent or the application for the patent containing the claimed invention; or (2) the filing date of the earliest application for which the patent or application is entitled to a right of priority or the benefit of an earlier filing date under 35 U.S.C. 119, 120, 121, 365, or 386 (see 35 U.S.C. 100(i)(1)).
guidance: When examining applications subject to AIA 102, the effective filing date is the actual U.S. application filing date unless one of these situations applies: (A) continuation/divisional with 35 U.S.C. 120/365(c)/386(c) satisfied (effective date = earliest in line); (B) continuation-in-part — claims not supported in parent get new application's filing date while fully supported claims have parent's date; (C) proper claim to a provisional under 119(e) — claims fully supported by provisional have provisional filing date; (D) foreign priority under 119(a)-(d), 365(a)/(b), 386(a)/(b) — effective date = foreign priority date if adequately supported. Also: national-stage and international filing date rules (PCT/371, Hague design) apply as discussed in referenced MPEP sections. The one-year grace period in AIA 102(b)(1) is measured from the filing date of any U.S. or foreign patent application to which benefit/priority is claimed, differing from pre-AIA measurement.

name: Claim-by-claim determination of effective filing date and application-by-application determination of AIA applicability
description: The effective filing date of a claimed invention is determined on a claim-by-claim basis (different claims in the same application may have different effective filing dates). However, whether pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102/103 or AIA 35 U.S.C. 102/103 applies is determined on an application-by-application basis.
guidance: Examiners must evaluate effective filing dates for each claim separately (see MPEP § 2133.01 discussion of continuation-in-part issues). In contrast, applicability of pre-AIA or AIA law is decided for the whole application (see MPEP §§ 2151 and 2159). Note also that under AIA it is no longer possible to 'swear behind' certain prior art via 37 CFR 1.131 (antedating) because AIA 102 focuses on effective filing dates rather than invention date.

name: Described in a Printed Publication (anticipation under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1)/(a)(2))
description: To anticipate, a prior art printed publication (patent, published application, or other printed publication) must: (1) disclose 'each and every element of the invention' either explicitly or inherently, with the elements 'arranged or combined in the same way as in the claim'; and (2) enable a person of ordinary skill in the art to make the invention without undue experimentation.
guidance: The AIA does not change the extent required for a prior-art document to 'describe' a claimed invention for anticipation. There is no requirement that the prior art meet the 'how to use' aspect of 35 U.S.C. 112(a). For anticipation it is sufficient that one species or embodiment is described/enabled even if the claim is broader (see Vas-Cath v. Mahurkar and related cases). Prior art that does not meet anticipatory description may still be used in an obviousness rejection for what it would reasonably have made known to a person of ordinary skill. Case law examples: In re Gleave, Eli Lilly v. Zenith, Net MoneyIN v. VeriSign, In re Bond; enablement cases include Impax Labs., In re LeGrice; anticipatory-species cases include Vas-Cath, In re Lukach.

name: Determining Whether To Apply 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) or 102(a)(2)
description: Examiners should first consider whether a reference qualifies as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) and then determine if any exceptions in 102(b)(1) apply. Separately, they should consider whether the reference qualifies under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) and then determine if any exceptions in 102(b)(2) apply.
guidance: Under 102(a)(1) consider patents, printed publications, public use, on-sale, and otherwise-available disclosures that predate the claim's effective filing date; the activity need not occur in the U.S. If a reference is by the inventor or derived from the inventor and was made one year or less before the effective filing date, consider 102(b)(1)(A)/(B) exceptions (see MPEP §§ 2153.01(a), 2153.01(b), 2153.02). Under 102(a)(2), U.S. patents, U.S. patent application publications, and PCT published applications are prior art if their filing/effective filing date is before the claim's effective filing date; use 35 U.S.C. 102(d) to determine when subject matter was "effectively filed." Then consider 102(b)(2)(A)-(C) exceptions. See MPEP §§ 2152, 2154, 717.01, and cited sections for procedural application.

name: Anticipation vs Obviousness — differing description/enablement standards
description: For anticipation under 102(a)(1)/(a)(2), a prior art document must describe and enable all elements of the claim as arranged in the claim; for obviousness under 103, a disclosure may be cited for what it would reasonably have made known to a person of ordinary skill even if it does not anticipate.
guidance: The written-description/enablement needed to anticipate is less than that required to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112(a) for supporting a claim's entire scope: a single species disclosure can anticipate a broader claim. However, a reference lacking the requisite anticipatory description may still support an obviousness rejection for its teachings. See case law distinctions: Rasmussen v. SmithKline Beecham, Vas-Cath, Gleave, Schoenwald, Schering, Impax, and related MPEP discussion.

name: Full performance may permit recovery of agreed price despite void instrument (St. Louis Hay & Grain rule)
description: After actual performance, on the strength of the agreement, recovery may be had for the amount agreed upon, notwithstanding the instrument itself was void.
guidance: If the informal agreement was fully executed and the Government accepted/paid under its terms, the party cannot later claim more than the price agreed upon; a lawful transfer executed pursuant to the agreement fixes the parties' obligations (St. Louis Hay & Grain Co. v. U.S.).

name: Parol evidence rule against adding terms to an unambiguous written contract
description: Where a contract is not ambiguous or technically obscure, parol evidence is not admissible to establish a new term or add an understanding at variance with its written stipulations.
guidance: If the written contract expresses the final agreement, prior oral understandings (e.g., about deductions or additional obligations) cannot be enforced against the United States. Example: claimed oral agreement to permit deductions was estopped.

name: Enablement over the whole scope of the claim
description: The disclosure must be reproducible without undue burden, and this must be true over the whole scope of the claim.
guidance: Evaluate whether the skilled person can carry out the invention across the entire claimed range. If parts of the claim cannot be practiced without undue experimentation, those claim portions may be insufficiently disclosed.

name: Rule 42(1)(e) — describe at least one way and use examples/drawings
description: The description shall: describe in detail at least one way of carrying out the invention claimed; use examples where appropriate; refer to the drawings, if any.
guidance: Ensure the specification gives at least one concrete embodiment or working example and points to drawings where relevant. Lack of any concrete way of carrying out the invention is a key sufficiency weakness.

name: Plausibility of technical effect (G 2/21)
description: Technical effects relied upon for inventive step must be derivable from the application as filed; bald assertions are insufficient.
guidance: When an inventive-step argument depends on a technical effect, the specification must make that effect at least plausible (e.g., by data, examples, or a credible technical explanation). Mere unsubstantiated claims of effect risk insufficiency or loss of support for inventive-step arguments.

name: AI inventions — disclosure of training data and model details (T 1669/21)
description: For AI-related inventions, training data, model architecture, and hyperparameters may need to be disclosed if necessary to reproduce the technical effect.
guidance: Treat 'black-box' AI disclosures skeptically: if reproduction of the claimed technical effect depends on model internals or training data, the application should disclose those elements or sufficient alternatives so a skilled person can reproduce the effect without undue burden.

name: Distinction from Articles 84 (clarity) and 56 (inventive step)
description: Article 83: whole disclosure enables practice (sufficiency); Article 84: claims are clear and supported (clarity); Article 56: invention is non-obvious (inventive step).
guidance: Do not conflate lack of clarity or lack of inventive step with lack of sufficiency. Evaluate sufficiency on whether the invention can be performed as claimed, separately from clarity of claim wording or the inventive-step assessment.

name: Features of solely intellectual or aesthetic significance (non-statutory)
description: Features that have a purely intellectual or aesthetic significance are considered not to affect the functioning of the invention and cannot change how the practical form operates to solve the problem.
guidance: Where a claim is directed to subject-matter having solely intellectual or aesthetic significance, the claim is defective under section 2. However, if the practical form solves a practical problem and gives rise to new functionality, patentability is not impacted merely because the purpose is non-statutory (intellectual/aesthetic).

name: Printed matter (non-functional descriptive matter excluded)
description: Printed matter that has purely intellectual or aesthetic significance, such as a literary work, is excluded from patentability for the reasons outlined regarding features of solely intellectual/aesthetic significance.
guidance: Where printed matter provides a new functionality to the substrate on which it is printed (i.e., solves a practical problem related to use of the printed matter), a claim may be statutory. Examples: textile markings enabling precision in manufacturing; newspaper layout facilitating folding/reading; text layout facilitating bookbinding; ticket layout permitting division while retaining information. 'Printed matter' includes any means of displaying information, not just ink-on-paper. Example analysis (scratch-off lottery ticket maze) shows printed matter that provides no new functionality is non-statutory.

name: Novelty / Anticipation requirement
description: An invention must be novel; novelty requires that individual disclosures in the prior art do not anticipate the claimed invention.
guidance: Anticipation is assessed claim-by-claim by asking whether the prior disclosure, when understood by the person skilled in the art in light of their common general knowledge, provides both a description of the claimed invention (disclosure) and sufficient instructions to enable the invention to be practised (enablement). The comparison is based on the essential elements of the claim, properly construed, to the prior art.

name: Assessing anticipation (Apotex test: disclosure + enablement)
description: The test requires that a single prior disclosure both disclose and enable the claimed invention. The first part asks whether a single prior teaching discloses the same invention (or at least one operating embodiment) when read by a person skilled in the art in a purposive manner.
guidance: The prior disclosure need not be an exact description; if carrying out the directions in the prior disclosure would inevitably result in infringement of the examined claim, it discloses the same invention. The second part asks whether the prior disclosure enables operation without inventive effort or undue experimentation. For enablement, the skilled person is assumed willing to make trial-and-error experiments that are not inventive or an undue burden. If unclear, examiner must explain reasons for concluding disclosure is enabling. Reverse infringement principle ('what amounts to infringement, if posterior, should amount to anticipation, if anterior') can be used. Analyse essential elements of the claim; non-essential elements need not be disclosed. For claims covering multiple embodiments, anticipation of any one enabled embodiment suffices. Distinguish proper combinations vs aggregations; assess each collocated distinct invention individually.

name: Joinder: prohibition on claiming independent distinct inventions in one application
description: Two or more independent and distinct inventions may not be claimed in one national application, except that more than one species of an invention, not to exceed a reasonable number, may be claimed provided the application also includes an allowable generic claim and extra species claims are in dependent form or include all limitations of the generic claim.
guidance: Do not claim separate, patentably distinct inventions in one application; use divisional/continuing applications or proper dependent/species structure when a genus exists. (See § 1.141(a).)

name: Design patent title, claim and oath/declaration
description: The title of the design must designate the particular article. No description other than reference to the drawing is ordinarily required. The claim shall be in formal terms to the ornamental design for the article as shown, or as shown and described. More than one claim is neither required nor permitted. The inventor’s oath or declaration must comply with § 1.63 (or § 1.64 substitute statement where applicable).
guidance: Design applications are single-claim filings; ensure title names the article and the claim is strictly to the ornamental design as depicted. (See § 1.153.)

name: Arrangement and content order for design application elements
description: Elements of a design application should appear in order: transmittal form, fee transmittal, application data sheet, specification, drawings or photographs, and inventor’s oath or declaration. The specification should include preamble, cross‑reference to related apps, statement re: federally sponsored research, description of figures, feature description, and a single claim, each section headed in uppercase.
guidance: Follow prescribed element order and section headings to present a complete design application. (See § 1.154.)

name: Plant patent specification content and order
description: The specification must contain as full and complete a disclosure as possible of the plant and characteristics that distinguish it over related varieties, its antecedents, and must particularly point out where and how the variety has been asexually reproduced. The application elements should appear in an ordered list (transmittal, fees, ADS, specification, drawings, oath), and the specification should include title, cross‑references, federally sponsored research statement, Latin genus/species name, variety denomination, background, summary, drawing description, detailed botanical description, a single claim, and an abstract.
guidance: Provide a detailed botanical disclosure and follow the required element and section order; include variety denomination and Latin names where applicable. (See § 1.163.)

name: Plant patent claim and drawings
description: The claim shall be in formal terms to the new and distinct variety of the specified plant as described and illustrated and may recite principal distinguishing characteristics. More than one claim is not permitted. Plant drawings should be artistically and competently executed complying with § 1.84; drawings must disclose all distinctive characteristics capable of visual representation. Drawings may be in color and must be in color if color is a distinguishing characteristic; two copies of color drawings or photographs must be submitted.
guidance: Plant patents are single-claim filings; ensure drawings and description visually disclose distinguishing features and submit color copies when color distinguishes. (See §§ 1.164–1.165.)

name: Content of prior art determined at the time the invention was made
description: The content of the prior art is fixed 'at the time the invention was made' to avoid impermissible hindsight in obviousness determinations.
guidance: Examiner must avoid hindsight and, when necessary, consult MPEP § 2145 for rebutting applicant arguments that a rejection is based on hindsight. The decisionmaker should 'forget what he or she has been taught ... about the claimed invention and cast the mind back to the time the invention was made.'

name: 35 U.S.C. 103(c) — evidence required to show conditions apply
description: An applicant seeking the benefits of 35 U.S.C. 103(c) bears the burden of establishing that subject matter (which qualifies as prior art only under certain subsections of §102) and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.
guidance: For joint research provisions (for applications pending on or after Dec. 10, 2004), applicant must show: (A) claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the date the invention was made; (B) invention was made as a result of activities within the agreement's scope; and (C) the patent application discloses or is amended to disclose the parties' names. Note limits for applications filed before Nov. 29, 1999 and patents granted prior to Dec. 10, 2004; see MPEP § 706.02(l)(2) for requirements to establish common ownership or a joint research agreement.

name: Reference must be analogous prior art to be used in a 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection
description: A reference is proper for use in an obviousness rejection only if it is analogous prior art to the claimed invention.
guidance: A reference is analogous if (1) it is from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention (even if addressing a different problem), or (2) it is reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor (even if not in the same field). KSR and Bigio cited: 'any need or problem known in the field of endeavor ... can provide a reason for combining the elements in the manner claimed.' Examiner should determine 'analogous prior art' for obviousness analysis.

name: Do not distill the invention to its 'gist' or 'thrust'
description: Reducing an invention to a single 'gist' or advantage disregards the statutory 'as a whole' requirement.
guidance: Examples where focusing on a perceived advantage or a single concept led to erroneous obviousness determinations (W.L. Gore, Bausch & Lomb, Jones v. Hardy, Panduit). Examiner must respect express claim limitations and not ignore claim language by distillation.

name: Applicants alleging discovery must provide substantiating evidence
description: Applicants claiming they discovered the cause of a problem must substantiate that allegation with evidence.
guidance: Substantiate via affidavits/declarations or clear, persuasive assertions in the specification. Unsubstantiated statements of counsel are insufficient (In re Wiseman, In re Kaslow).

name: Disclosed inherent properties are part of the 'as a whole' inquiry
description: Properties inherent in the claimed subject matter and disclosed in the specification are considered in the 'as a whole' obviousness inquiry.
guidance: Look to the compound/device and its inherent properties disclosed in the specification when delineating the invention as a whole (In re Antonie, In re Papesch). However, obviousness cannot be predicated on properties not known at the time the invention was made even if later shown inherent (In re Rijckaert; see MPEP § 2112 for inherency requirements).

name: Establishing a prima facie case requires clear articulation of reasons with rational underpinning
description: A rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 must clearly articulate the reason(s) why the claimed invention would have been obvious; conclusory statements are insufficient.
guidance: KSR and In re Kahn require explicit analysis and 'some articulated reasoning with some rational underpinning.' The determination depends on the facts of each case (Sanofi-Synthelabo citing Graham). The examiner should make the analysis explicit, though record evidence need not show an explicit teaching of motivation to combine (Ball Aerosol; Federal Circuit guidance).

name: Software patents and limits
description: Software 'per se' is not patentable (protected by copyright). However, claims comprising embedded software in a system or in a specific step of a method are usually accepted; computer‑readable medium claims are not allowed. Means‑plus‑function claims are not allowable as main claims if there are no prior apparatus or method claims. Some examiners may be stricter.
guidance: Draft software‑related claims as apparatus or method claims tied to technical features; avoid computer‑readable medium main claims and be prepared to support means‑plus‑function with apparatus/method fallback.

name: Markush and chemical claim practice
description: Markush claims are accepted provided there is enough support in the specification for the claimed compounds; chemical compounds can be claimed by developed structural formulae.
guidance: Ensure adequate specification support for genus/Markush groups to withstand examination; include representative examples.

name: Novelty and inventive step definitions
description: Novelty: invention not included in the state of the art (all public technical knowledge before filing or priority date). Inventive step: invention not obvious or evidently deduced from the prior art to a person skilled in the art.
guidance: Perform clearance and inventive step analyses against the full state of the art (published descriptions, uses, disclosures worldwide) before filing or prosecuting claims.

name: Claim drafting: clarity, structure and support
description: Claims should define the invention; first claim should be independent and include relevant features; dependent claims subordinate. No limit on number of claims, but official fees apply for claims in excess of the 10th. Claims must have support in the specification as filed; new subject matter cannot be added at any stage.
guidance: Draft a clear independent first claim, well‑supported dependent claims, and manage claim count to control fees. Avoid introducing new matter in amendments.

name: Claim drafting: AR PTO 'Characterized' format
description: Claims should be characterized to adapt to AR PTO practice: a first part describing prior art features and a 'Characterized' part detailing the relevant novel features claimed.
guidance: Consider using the 'characterized in that' format when prosecuting in Argentina to align with Office preferences and improve examiner understanding.

name: Exclusions from patentability (examples)
description: Methods for intellectual activities, games, commercial activities; methods for presenting information; surgical, therapeutic or diagnostic methods applicable to humans and animals are not considered inventions and cannot be protected by patents in Argentina. Biological methods for reproduction and genetic processes may be considered inventions but are excluded from patentability under AR law.
guidance: Avoid drafting claims that would fall squarely into excluded categories when planning filings in Argentina; use alternative claim strategies where appropriate (e.g., device/apparatus or product claims).

name: Application formalities and required documents
description: Required at filing: applicant and inventor information; Power of Attorney (notarized and apostilled; can be filed within 40 working days if unavailable); title, specification, abstract, drawings (if available), one or more claims; priority information and priority documents (filed within 90 days with sworn Spanish translation); assignment of priority rights (if applicable) filed within 90 days.
guidance: Prepare translators and legalization (Apostille) processes in advance to meet 40‑ and 90‑day formal deadlines; include clear priority data at filing to avoid loss of rights.

name: Divisional application practice
description: Voluntary divisional applications are allowed before parent grant. Divisional applications are commonly filed when an examiner raises lack of unity; if requested by the examiner, divisional must be filed within 30 days.
guidance: Consider filing voluntary divisionals to preserve claim scope and manage unity objections; track deadlines when examiner requests divisional.

name: Statute of limitations on damages claims
description: Damage claims should be initiated within three (3) years from the time of the infringement. For trademarks some regimes allow one year from knowledge in certain circumstances.
guidance: Preserve evidence and act promptly to file damage claims within statutory limits; document discovery of infringement date to trigger limitation reckoning.

name: Claim construction in reexamination
description: During reexamination, claims are given the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification; limitations in the specification are not read into the claims (In re Yamamoto). For reexamination involving claims of an expired patent, claim construction pursuant to Phillips v. AWH Corp. (ordinary and customary meaning) should be applied.
guidance: Apply broadest reasonable interpretation during reexamination unless claims are expired (then use Phillips). Consider written statements of the patent owner of record (37 CFR 1.501(a)(2) and 1.552) after reexamination is ordered to determine proper claim meaning when applying patents/printed publications.

name: Scope of 35 U.S.C. 112 examination limited to amendatory matter
description: Where new claims are presented or any part of the disclosure is amended, examination under 35 U.S.C. 112 should be limited to the amendatory (new language) matter.
guidance: A limitation present in the original patent claim that is repeated in a newly presented or amended claim generally cannot be examined under 35 U.S.C. 112 unless the amendatory matter creates the issue. Rewriting a dependent claim as independent cannot be examined under §112 unless rewriting raises a new question (e.g., lack of antecedent). See MPEP §2163 - §2173.05(v).

name: 35 U.S.C. 112 issues to consider for new/amended claims
description: Compliance of new or amended claims with the enablement and/or written description requirements of the first paragraph, and compliance with the second paragraph of 35 U.S.C.112, should be considered as to the amendatory and new text.
guidance: Examiners should apply MPEP §2163 - §2173.05(v) for detailed guidance; focus only on the new/amendatory text for enablement/written description/definiteness issues.

name: Prohibition on new matter (35 U.S.C. 132/305)
description: 35 U.S.C. 305 provides for examination under 35 U.S.C. 132, which prohibits the introduction of new matter into the disclosure. New matter added to claims or affecting claim limitations should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, for failing to meet the written description requirement.
guidance: Check for new matter whenever claims or specification are amended in reexamination; rely on MPEP §2163.06 regarding relationship between written description and the new matter prohibition.

name: Amendments to the specification must comply with 35 U.S.C. 112
description: An amendment to the specification in a reexamination proceeding can redefine the scope of terms in a claim so that the claim is no longer clear or is not supported by the specification, causing failure to comply with 35 U.S.C. 112 even if claims are not amended.
guidance: Examiners should ensure specification amendments do not create written-description or enablement problems; a specification amendment may also enlarge claim scope (see related rubric).

name: Claims must not enlarge scope of original patent claims (35 U.S.C. 305)
description: Where new or amended claims are presented or any part of the disclosure is amended, the claims of the reexamination proceeding should be examined under 35 U.S.C. 305 to determine whether they enlarge the scope of the original claims. 'No proposed amended or new claim enlarging the scope of a claim of the patent will be permitted in a reexamination proceeding.'
guidance: Reject any claim that enlarges scope under 35 U.S.C. 305; employ form paragraph 22.11 when making such a rejection.

name: Rejection procedure for enlarged claims
description: Any claim in a reexamination proceeding which enlarges the scope of the claims of the patent should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 305.
guidance: Use form paragraph 22.11 (Rejection, 35 U.S.C. 305, Claim Enlarges Scope of Patent - Ex Parte Reexamination). In bracket 2 identify and explain the claim limitations considered to broaden the scope. Follow Examiner Note guidance in MPEP §2258.

name: Handling patents subject to prior Office or Court decisions
description: Where some patent claims have been the subject of a prior Office or court decision, those claims not subject to reexamination because of prior adjudication should be identified; see MPEP §2242. If other proceedings are copending, see MPEP §2282-§2286.
guidance: If prior Office/court decisions raise grounds not based on patents/printed publications, the examiner's Office action should clearly state that claims have not been examined as to those non-patent/printed publication grounds (37 CFR 1.552(c)).

name: Focus on 'live' claims in reexamination
description: The Office's determination in both the order and the examination stage is generally limited solely to review of the 'live' claims (existing claims not held invalid by a final decision) for which reexamination has been requested.
guidance: Requester must set forth pertinency and manner of applying cited prior art to every claim for which reexamination is requested (35 U.S.C. 302 and 37 CFR 1.510(b)). Failure to apply the art to certain claims generally precludes reexamination of those claims. The Office may nonetheless exercise discretion to reexamine non-requested claims or add claims if new art raises an SNQ (35 U.S.C. 303(a)).

name: Restriction requirements not proper in reexamination
description: Restriction requirements cannot be made in a reexamination proceeding since no statutory basis exists for restriction in reexamination.
guidance: Adding claims to a 'separate and distinct' invention would be considered an enlargement of scope (see Ex parte Wikdahl and MPEP §1412.03). Do not issue restriction requirements.

name: Ancillary matters permitted in reexamination
description: Matters ancillary to reexamination which are necessary and incident to patentability will be considered (e.g., amendments to the specification to correct inadvertent failures to claim foreign priority or continuing status if necessary to overcome a reference).
guidance: Use reexamination to make corrections that are incident to patentability, but observe other statutory limits (e.g., new matter prohibition).

name: Requests filed on patents after reissue are denied
description: Where a request for reexamination is filed on a patent after it has been reissued, reexamination will be denied because the patent on which the request is based has been surrendered.
guidance: To reexamine a reissued patent, a new request based on the specification and claims of the reissue patent must be filed. If a reissue issues after a reexamination request was filed, treat the reissue patent text as the patent text for any amendments filed subsequently.

name: Inventorship based on conception
description: The "'invention' in the Patent Act unquestionably refers to the inventor’s conception." Pfaff v. Wells Elecs., Inc., 525 U.S. 55, 60 (1988).
guidance: Inventorship determinations center on which individual(s) conceived the claimed invention (i.e., formed the definite and permanent idea of the invention), applying established conception-law principles rather than relying on the role of tools or assistance.

name: Statutory written-description and disclosure requirement
description: Before receiving a patent the inventor must deliver a written description of the invention and of the manner and process of making, constructing, using, and compounding the same 'in such full, clear, and exact terms, avoiding unnecessary prolixity, as to enable any person skilled in the art... to make, construct, compound, and use the same'; for machines the principle and several modes of application must be explained; the specification must particularly specify and point out the part, improvement, or combination claimed; and where the nature of the case admits, drawings or specimens and models must be filed.
guidance: This is the core statutory mandate (Act of July 4, 1836, §6, re‑enacted 1870). The text insists on sufficiency of description and drawings/models where applicable. The preparation must enable a skilled artisan to practice the invention; the claim must point out what is claimed as new. Failure to satisfy these statutory requirements can invalidate the patent.

name: Court role in claim construction; jury role for factual matters
description: It is the province of the court to determine what is intended to be patented and whether the invention is described with reasonable certainty (questions of law). Where terms of art or surrounding circumstances require factual determination, those matters go to the jury, which takes the court's conditional construction and applies it to found facts.
guidance: Where no technical terms or factual background are in dispute, construction is for the court. If expert evidence is needed to explain terms of art or surrounding circumstances, the jury resolves those facts and thereby conditions the ultimate construction.

name: Specification may limit patent generality but repugnancy voids patent
description: While a specification may control and restrict the generality of the patent terms, if there is a clear repugnancy between the description in the specification and the invention stated in the letters-patent, the patent will be void because the statute is not complied with.
guidance: The rule allowing the specification to control patent wording cannot save a patent where the patent claims an invention not described in the specification. Cases cited show patents void where the title/patent covered something the specification did not describe.

name: Liberal construction of patents (ut res magis valeat quam pereat)
description: Patents are to be construed liberally and not with over-nice or strict rules; the object is to ascertain, from the fair sense of the words, the nature and extent of the inventor's claim.
guidance: American courts favor a fair and liberal view in light of the constitutional purpose to promote science and useful arts. Formal or inartificial expression should not defeat a clearly ascertainable claim. Nevertheless statutory requisites must be met.

name: Specification must distinguish between old and new (point out what is claimed)
description: When the patentee uses prior (old) matter, the specification must distinguish what is old from what is new and must point out in what the invention or improvement consists; failing to do so may render the patent void or broader than the invention.
guidance: If a specification mixes old and new without clearly ascertaining what part is claimed as new, the patent may be void because it either covers too much (includes old matter) or is ambiguous as to what is claimed. Courts will not carve away portions to save an overbroad claim.

name: Claims' purpose: to ascertain the extent of the new invention (not a how-to)
description: The claim is introduced to ascertain and declare the extent of what the patentee claims as new; it is not intended as a description of the means to perform the invention or as an aid to the specification.
guidance: Claims identify the boundaries of the monopoly; they are not a substitute for the descriptive disclosure required to enable practice. The claim may, however, be construed in light of the specification.

name: Reasonable certainty requirement (avoidance of vagueness)
description: It must appear with reasonable certainty what the patentee intends to claim; inaccuracy or imperfect wording will not vitiate the specification if, by fair interpretation of the whole, the nature and extent of the claim are clear; but if wholly ambiguous and uncertain the patent is void.
guidance: Phrases should not be read in isolation; the entire specification and drawings should be taken together. Courts will uphold imperfect language where a reasonable construction identifies the invention, but will void patents that leave courts guessing or relying on conjecture.

name: Objectives of the specification: public enablement and public notice
description: The specification has two objects: (1) to make known the manner of constructing/using the invention so artisans can make and use it after patent expiration; (2) to put the public in possession of what the patentee claims as his own invention so the public can determine whether it is already known and to guard against prejudice or innocent infringement.
guidance: These twin objectives underlie the disclosure and claim rules: disclosure for enablement, and clear claims/description for public notice and to prevent overreaching by the patentee.

name: Comparing specifications for novelty: sufficiency and identity questions
description: When a defendant attacks novelty by producing a prior patent/specification, two questions arise: (a) whether the court alone can decide from mere comparison that the two inventions are identical; (b) whether the prior specification must itself be so clear and complete as to sustain a patent, or whether a mere hint may be enough to defeat a subsequent claim.
guidance: This raises evidentiary and legal issues; the text refers to detailed English discussions and to the chapter on actions at law. The sufficiency of a prior disclosure to anticipate is a substantive question to be examined.

name: Inaccuracy not fatal if fair interpretation reveals the claim
