description: While the specification must be reasonably certain, it is not necessary that the language be technical; inaccuracy or inartful expression will not vitiate the specification if the court can, by fair interpretation of the whole, ascertain clearly what is claimed.
guidance: Courts will construe drawings and text together and favor a reasonable interpretive approach rather than striking down patents on small drafting imperfections.

name: Claim construction in light of specification when claim immediately follows description
description: Where the claim immediately follows the description it may be construed in connection with the explanations contained in the specification and be restricted accordingly.
guidance: Claims are read in context; placement and proximity to descriptive matter affects how broadly claims will be interpreted. This supports limiting a claim by the specification where appropriate.

name: Read the rejection three times before doing anything
description: Read the Office Action three times: first for emotional reaction; second ignoring tone and identify which claims are rejected under which sections (101, 102, 103, 112); third with the cited references open to compare what they actually disclose.
guidance: First read: acknowledge your emotional reaction so it doesn't drive your drafting. Second read: objectively map which claims are rejected and under what statutory grounds (101, 102, 103, 112). Third read: open the cited references and verify whether the examiner's factual citations actually teach the claimed elements — many office actions that seem 'bad' are defensible once you check the references.

name: Map every claim element to every cited reference
description: For a 103 rejection, build a literal table: rows are claim elements, columns are references, and cells are the passages cited by the examiner.
guidance: Populate the table with the exact passages cited. This reveals (a) elements where the cited passage does not teach what the examiner asserts and (b) elements with no citation at all — both are valid bases for argument. Use the chart as an evidence-focused tool to identify weaknesses in the examiner's combination or factual assertions.

name: Weigh argument versus amendment strategically
description: Understand the trade-off: arguing without amending preserves claim scope but risks more file-history estoppel if you later amend; amending without argument concedes the rejection.
guidance: Prefer a combined approach when strong: make a narrow amendment to address the examiner's point and include a clear argument explaining why the amended language is not taught or suggested by the references. Be mindful that unnecessary amendment concedes patentably indistinct subject matter and that pure argument may fail to persuade and later limit you.

name: Include claim charts in the response
description: Although not required, include a one-page claim chart for the amended independent claim to make the examiner's job easier.
guidance: A concise claim chart clarifying where each claim element is located (or not) in the prior art dramatically increases odds of allowance. Keep it to one page for clarity and accessibility.

name: Know when to call the examiner (conduct an interview)
description: Schedule a 15-minute interview after a first office action — it's usually free, often results in agreed-upon language, and can save a round of correspondence.
guidance: If your amendment is non-trivial, call before filing the response to discuss and try to reach agreement on claim language. Short interviews can yield mutually acceptable solutions and prevent unnecessary amendment or appeals.

name: Date of first licensure determination
description: FDA must determine the date of first licensure for a biological product submitted under 351(a) to identify whether that product is eligible for a period of reference product exclusivity under 351(k)(7).
guidance: The date of first licensure generally is the initial date the product was licensed in the U.S., but exclusions in 351(k)(7)(C) mean not every 351(a) licensure gives rise to its own exclusivity period. Sponsors may submit information (and should include an exclusivity claim in eCTD Module 1.3.5.3) to assist FDA with the determination. Determinations may be deferred if issues are scientifically, legally, or factually complicated, information is submitted late, incomplete, or FDA requests more data.

name: Statutory and regulatory basis for restriction
description: The basis for restriction and double patenting practices is found in 35 U.S.C. 121 and 37 CFR 1.141–1.142, which provide that if two or more independent and distinct inventions are claimed in one application, the Director may require restriction to one invention and the examiner shall require the applicant to elect the invention to which the claims will be restricted.
guidance: Quotes of the statutes and rules are provided (35 U.S.C. 121; 37 CFR 1.141(a), 1.142(a)–(b)). The rule permits more than one species in one application only where a generic claim is allowable and excess species are in dependent form or include all limitations of the generic claim.

name: Two criteria for a proper requirement for restriction
description: There are two criteria for a proper requirement for restriction between patentably distinct inventions: (A) The inventions must be independent or distinct as claimed; and (B) There would be a serious burden on the examiner if restriction is not required.
guidance: Both criteria must be satisfied to support a restriction. Where plural inventions can be viewed as related in two ways, both applicable criteria must be demonstrated. Examiners must provide reasons and/or examples to support conclusions (though citation of documents is not required in most cases).

name: Unity test for Markush-type claims
description: Unity of invention exists where compounds included within a Markush group (1) share a common utility, and (2) share a substantial structural feature essential to that utility.
guidance: If Markush members meet unity, the claim should be examined as a whole; otherwise treatment as encompassing independent/distinct inventions (and provisional election) may be appropriate. See In re Weber, In re Haas, In re Harnisch, Ex parte Hozumi decisions cited.

name: Refunds when linking or generic claims become allowable (transitional)
description: Whenever divided inventions in a transitional application are rejoined because a linking claim is allowable, or whenever claims to an additional species for which the fee was paid are fully embraced by an allowable generic claim, applicant should be notified that they may request a refund of the fee paid for that additional invention/species.
guidance: Use form paragraphs and procedures referenced (MPEP § 803.03(a), § 803.03(b); MPEP § 821.04 and § 821.04(a)). Determination of when nonelected species are no longer withdrawn is made as indicated in MPEP § 806.04(d), § 821.04, and § 821.04(a).

name: Rejoinder of process claims upon allowance of product claim
description: When claims directed to a product and to a process of making and/or using the product are presented, if applicant elects the product and the product claim is subsequently found allowable, withdrawn process claims which depend from or otherwise require all the limitations of an allowable product claim will be considered for rejoinder and fully examined. All claims directed to a nonelected process invention must depend from or otherwise require all the limitations of an allowable product claim for rejoinder to occur.
guidance: If applicant cancels nonelected process claims before rejoinder, the examiner should not withdraw the restriction to preserve applicant’s rights under 35 U.S.C. 121. Applicants are encouraged to present process claims early and preferably as dependent claims to expedite rejoinder. Use appropriate form paragraphs (e.g., 8.42, 8.43). Amendments after allowance and after final rejection have different entry rules (37 CFR 1.312 and 1.116 respectively).

name: Treatment of conflicting claims in plural/copending applications (37 CFR 1.78)
description: Where two or more applications filed by the same applicant contain conflicting claims, elimination of such claims from all but one application may be required in the absence of good and sufficient reason for their retention during pendency. When claims are patentably indistinct across copending applications, applicant must cancel them from all but one or maintain clear demarcation.
guidance: A complete examination should be made of claims in each application and appropriate rejections (including provisional double patenting) should be entered in each application. The provisional double patenting rejection should continue in each application as long as conflicting claims exist unless it is the only remaining rejection in an application. Where appropriate, conflicting applications should be joined. Use form paragraphs (e.g., 8.29) where applicable.

name: Scope_of_§145_statutory_remedy_and_Article_III_limits
description: §145 provides that an 'applicant dissatisfied with the decision of the [Board]' may bring a civil action in district court and the court 'may adjudge that such applicant is entitled to receive a patent for his invention, as specified in any of his claims involved in the decision of the [Board]'.  But §145 does not override Article III: the applicant must still satisfy Article III's standing requirements as to each pending claim submitted to the district court.
guidance: The court rejects treating the Board's decision as an 'undivided whole' to bypass Article III. Congress can create statutory rights but cannot erase constitutional standing requirements (Spokeo). Thus §145 confers a statutory remedy but does not automatically confer Article III jurisdiction over claims where no injury is shown.

name: Special situations causing abandonment
description: Enumerated situations that often raise abandonment questions include: (A) copying claims from a patent (not a response), (B) withdrawal/failure to prosecute appeals, (C) dismissal of appeals/civil actions without filing responsive amendment, (D) interference claim suggestions near end of reply period, (E) FWC applications under former §1.62, (F) filing a continued prosecution application (CPA) under §1.53(d).
guidance: See MPEP cross-references. Examiners and practitioners should be aware of these circumstances when determining abandonment and appropriate remedial action or petitioning.

name: Terminal disclaimer requirement for revival (37 CFR 1.137(c))
description: For design applications, utility applications filed before June 8, 1995, or plant applications filed before June 8, 1995, petitions to revive must be accompanied by a terminal disclaimer dedicating to the public a terminal part of the patent term equivalent to the period of abandonment. Special terminal disclaimer rules also apply for untimely petitions to withdraw a holding of abandonment.
guidance: Terminal disclaimer must apply to any patent granted on continuing applications that claim priority under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, or 365(c). Terminal disclaimers are not required under §1.137(c) for relief under some other circumstances (see MPEP discussion), but may be required for treating untimely petitions on the merits per §1.183.

name: Examiner Reversed in Whole — immediate action
description: A complete reversal of the examiner’s rejection brings the case up for immediate action by the examiner. If the reversal does not place an application in condition for immediate allowance (e.g., Board entered a new ground of rejection under 37 CFR 41.50(b) or application contains withdrawn claims to a non-elected invention), the examiner should refer to MPEP § 1214.06 for guidance.
guidance: Do not treat reversal as routine reopening; determine whether application is in condition for allowance; consult §1214.06 when further action is required.

name: Authorization required to reopen prosecution for new references
description: If the examiner has specific knowledge of the existence of particular references indicating nonpatentability of appealed claims as to which the examiner was reversed, they should submit the matter to the Technology Center (TC) Director or Central Reexamination Unit (CRU) Director for authorization to reopen prosecution under 37 CFR 1.198 to enter the new rejection.
guidance: Do not unilaterally reopen prosecution to enter new rejections based on references discovered after reversal; obtain TC/CRU (and Director) authorization and place approval on the action reopening prosecution. See MPEP §§ 1002.02(c) and 1214.07.

name: Definition of termination of proceedings and appellate time limits
description: Proceedings are considered terminated by dismissal of an appeal or failure to timely file a court appeal/civil action, except where claims stand allowed or further action by examiner is required. The date of termination is the date the appeal is dismissed or the time for appeal expires; the time for seeking review to the Federal Circuit or ED Va is 63 days plus any additional time granted under 37 CFR 90.3(c).
guidance: Examiners must ensure applications that leave Board jurisdiction are not overlooked because every case is up for action if no court review is sought. See MPEP §§ 1216.01, 1216.02.

name: Handling provisional nonstatutory double patenting rejections after Board decision
description: If the Board did not opine on a provisional nonstatutory double patenting rejection but reversed other grounds as to the claim, and the applicant has not filed a proper terminal disclaimer, the examiner must act on the provisional rejection: determine if the reference application used in the provisional rejection has issued as a patent.
guidance: If the reference application has issued, re-issue the provisional rejection as a non-provisional rejection and require a terminal disclaimer (use form paragraphs 8.33–8.39). If the reference application has been abandoned or has not matured to a patent and the provisional rejection is the only remaining rejection, withdraw the provisional rejection. See MPEP § 804, subsection II.B and MPEP § 1214.06.

name: Dismissal for failure to file brief — timing and effect
description: If no brief is filed within the time prescribed by 37 CFR 41.37, the appeal stands dismissed by operation of the rule. Unless appellant specifically withdraws the appeal, do not dismiss until the extended period (up to 5 months extension under 37 CFR 1.136(a)) to file the brief has expired.
guidance: Applications with no allowed claims will be abandoned. Where allowed claims remain but formal matters exist, examiner may handle them by examiner’s amendment or set a shortened statutory period (commonly TWO (2) MONTHS) for correction; use form ¶12.209 to notify applicant. Extensions under 1.136 cannot extend reply beyond the six-month statutory maximum (35 U.S.C. 133).

name: Claim sections and their roles
description: A patent claim has three major sections, namely, a preamble, a transitional phrase, and a body. The body of the claim contains the elements which define the scope of patent protection as defined by that claim. The transitional phrase indicates whether incorporating other elements or components in an accused infringing device other than those elements recited in the body would avoid infringement of the claim. The preamble in general defines the environment (i.e., context) of the claimed invention but does not limit the claim unless the preamble breathes life into the claim.
guidance: Use this structure to reason about scope: the 'body' lists limitations that must be present; the 'transitional phrase' controls whether additional, unrecited elements exclude infringement; treat the preamble as non-limiting unless it supplies essential limitations ('breathes life').

name: Use of 'comprising' (open transitional phrase)
description: The transitional phrase 'comprising' is referred to as an open transitional phrase because even if the accused infringing device includes additional components and elements, the accused infringing device will not avoid infringement as long as the accused infringing device incorporates all of the elements recited in the body of the claims or the claim elements.
guidance: Prefer 'comprising' in most patent claims to retain an open-ended scope and avoid loss of infringement simply because an accused product has extra components. The article advises that 'in the vast majority of patent cases, the claims should utilize the open transitional phrase "comprising"' to avoid issues raised by closed forms.

name: Use of 'consisting of' (closed transitional phrase)
description: The transitional phrase 'consisting of' is referred to as a closed transitional phrase. When a claim's transitional phrase is 'consisting of,' adding an additional component or element to the accused infringing device may avoid infringement of the claim even if the accused infringing device incorporates all of the limitations and elements recited in the body of the claim.
guidance: For a claim with the 'consisting of' transitional phrase, if an added element is related to the invention then the accused infringing device does not infringe the claim. Case examples: Norian (spatula unrelated—court held accused product infringed despite additional element) and Shire Development (added lipophilic substance related—Federal Circuit held no infringement). Be cautious: using 'consisting of' can narrow scope and produce unexpected non-infringement depending on whether added elements are related to the invention.

name: Use of 'consisting essentially of' (partially closed transitional phrase)
description: The transitional phrase 'consisting essentially of' is referred to as a partially closed transitional phrase. If the accused infringing device includes an added component or element that materially affects the basic and novel characteristic of the invention, then the accused infringing device does not infringe the claimed invention. If the added component does not materially affect the basic and novel characteristic of the invention and affects it only in a minor way, then the accused infringing device would still infringe the patent claim.
guidance: Maintain the distinction between 'consisting of' and 'consisting essentially of': the latter permits additions that do not materially affect the invention's basic and novel characteristic, while excluding those that do. Courts guard this distinction and resist reading 'consisting of' as equivalent to the partially closed form.

name: Judicial precedent and MPEP govern interpretation
description: Judicial decisions (e.g., Shire Development LLC v. Watson Pharmaceuticals, Inc.; Norian) and the Manual of Patent Examining Procedure (MPEP § 2111.03) provide detailed explanations and govern how transitional phrases are interpreted for claim scope.
guidance: When evaluating or drafting claims, consult MPEP guidance and relevant case law because courts compare precedent (Norian vs. later cases like Shire) to determine whether added elements fall within or outside a closed/partially closed transitional phrase. Specific facts (e.g., whether an added element is related to the invention or materially affects a characteristic) drive outcomes.

name: Practical drafting/prosecution guidance: prefer open but consider closed forms strategically
description: For the layperson, in the vast majority of patent cases, the claims should utilize the open transitional phrase 'comprising' which is open-ended and avoids this issue altogether. However, during examination or patent prosecution, there may be times when utilizing the 'consisting essentially of' or 'consisting of' transitional phrases may be useful in overcoming a rejection made by the examiner.
guidance: Before using 'consisting of' or 'consisting essentially of' to overcome examiner rejections, explore the ramifications: closed or partially closed phrases can narrow claim scope and cause unintended non-infringement. Consider consulting counsel to weigh prosecution benefits versus future enforcement risks.

name: Anticipation — every claim element disclosed
description: In an anticipation analysis, the dispositive question is whether a skilled artisan would 'reasonably understand or infer' from a prior art reference that every claim limitation is disclosed in that single reference.
guidance: Extracted from Acoustic Tech., Inc. v. Itron Networked Sols., Inc. (quoting the standard). Use extrinsic evidence (declarations, depositions) to explain, but not to expand, the meaning of the reference. The petitioner must prove anticipation by a preponderance of the evidence in IPR.

name: Anticipation requires enabling disclosure, not reduction to practice
description: Anticipation does not require the actual creation or reduction to practice of the prior art subject matter; anticipation requires only an enabling disclosure.
guidance: Cites Schering: a public disclosure that enables the claimed steps can anticipate even if the prior art did not produce reported results. Therefore, a published study protocol that enables performance of the claimed steps can anticipate.

name: Claim construction — do not import unstated exclusions
description: Claims should not be construed to exclude treating other patients when the claim does not recite any steps or limitations regarding treatment of other patients.
guidance: Here, claim 1 recites testing a sample and treating the patient 'in response to' a determination; it does not forbid treating other patients. Therefore the presence of treatment of non-MSI-H patients in the prior art does not negate teaching of the recited steps.

name: "In response to" in treatment claims
description: A claim reciting 'in response to determining that the colorectal cancer is MSI-H... treating the patient' does not require that only MSI-H patients be treated or that treatment never occur absent the determination, unless expressly recited.
guidance: Court declined to require exclusivity or an express causal-bar to other treatment; focus remains on whether the two-step sequence (test, then treat if positive) is taught.

name: Use of contemporaneous publications to interpret scope of prior art
description: Publications contemporaneous with or referring to the prior art study may be used to show how the skilled artisan understood the study (e.g., described as involving metastatic disease).
guidance: Citing later papers that describe the trial as 'metastatic' supports that a skilled artisan would have understood the study to involve metastatic colorectal cancer, and thus supports anticipation of claims limited to metastatic disease.

name: Inference of clinical characteristics from eligibility language
description: Terms in a study record such as 'tumors' or 'measurable disease' can be interpreted in context by skilled artisans to imply clinical characteristics (e.g., metastatic or unresectable disease), which can bear on whether dependent claim limitations are taught.
guidance: Expert testimony explaining ordinary meaning in context can be credited; opposing general medical guidelines not directly addressing the specific study do not necessarily rebut such interpretations.

name: Obviousness analysis parallels anticipation when prior art fully discloses claim
description: 'Anticipation is the epitome of obviousness' — if a reference anticipates a claim (teaches every element), the claim is also obvious over that reference.
guidance: Applied in IPR Ground 2: if MSR anticipates, it is persuasive that the claims would also have been obvious over the MSR alone or with other references.

name: Patent term (20-year term) calculation
description: Subject to fee payment, patent term begins on the date the patent issues and ends 20 years from the date on which the application for the patent was filed in the United States or, if the application contains a specific reference to an earlier-filed application under sections 120, 121, 365(c), or 386(c), from the date on which the earliest such application was filed.
guidance: Design patents are treated differently (see MPEP §1505); amendments from the Hague Agreement and Patent Law Treaties Implementation Act affect cited sections (e.g., insertion of 386(c)). Continuations, internationals entering national stage, and continuing applications' term endpoints are governed by the earliest priority/benefit-claim as specified; foreign priority under 119/365/386 is not considered in determining the 20-year term.

name: Foreign priority and domestic provisional benefit not counted toward term
description: Foreign priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d), 365(a), 365(b), 386(a), or 386(b), and domestic benefit under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) to U.S. provisional applications are not considered in calculating the twenty-year term.
guidance: An application claiming such benefits ends twenty years from the U.S. filing date (or earliest effective U.S. benefit date under 120/121/365(c)/386(c)), not from the foreign/international filing or provisional filing date.

name: PTA grounds: failure to perform specified PTO actions within statutory timeframes
description: Under 35 U.S.C. 154(b) and 37 CFR 1.702, a patent term shall be adjusted if issuance was delayed due to the Office's failure to: (i) mail required notifications or a notice of allowance within specified months (14-month/14-month/earlier/4-month distinctions depend on effective dates), (ii) respond to a reply or appeal within 4 months, (iii) act within 4 months after certain Board or court decisions where allowable claims remain, or (iv) issue a patent within 4 months after issue fee paid and requirements satisfied.
guidance: Because of multiple regulatory effective dates (e.g., changes effective January 14, 2013 and April 1, 2013), the exact measurement (14-month vs 4-month accounting/when measured) depends on grant/filing and notice dates; examiners must determine which regulatory version applies for a given application/patent.

name: Processing of PTE applications when a reissue is filed
description: If the patent for which extension has been sought is reissued during PTE application processing, the original patent no longer exists; notice of the reissue should be provided and documents transferred to the reissue patent file rather than filing a new PTE application.
guidance: A petition under 37 CFR 1.182 should be filed in the original patent to request transfer of the PTE application and associated documents to the reissue patent file, including updated information reflecting claim scope changes. For calculating extension to which the reissued patent is entitled, the original patent grant date is used so long as the reissued patent claims the approved product.

name: Phillips methodology (order of consideration)
description: Look to the claims first, then to the specification (described as 'the single best guide to the meaning of a disputed term'), and then to the prosecution history to determine the meaning of a disputed claim.
guidance: Intrinsic evidence (claims, specification, prosecution history) controls claim meaning. Extrinsic evidence may be considered only after reviewing intrinsic evidence. The specification is the 'single best guide' to claim meaning.

name: Intrinsic evidence controls
description: The intrinsic record of the patent—the claims, written description and drawings (specification), and prosecution history—makes up the primary sources for claim construction and 'controls' over extrinsic sources.
guidance: Courts should rely on intrinsic sources before using extrinsic evidence; extrinsic sources cannot be used to contradict an unambiguous claim meaning derived from the intrinsic evidence.

name: Avoid importing limitations from the specification
description: District courts should be cautious not to import limitations into the claims from the specification, such as limiting a claim to a preferred embodiment.
guidance: Do not read preferred embodiments into the plain language of the claims. Example: Howmedica Osteonics Corp. v. Wright Medical Technology, where the district court improperly limited a claim to preferred embodiments.

name: Read claims in light of the specification to identify required limitations or specific definitions
description: Use the specification to determine if there is a specific definition or a required limitation that narrows the claim language.
guidance: If the specification indicates a necessary limitation or 'fundamental object of the invention,' the court must incorporate that limitation into claim construction. Example: Praxair v. ATMI—specification required the flow restriction be sufficient to prevent a hazardous release.

name: Use of extrinsic evidence (dictionaries) is permissible but subordinate
description: Dictionaries and other extrinsic evidence are 'among the many tools' that can assist the court, particularly to 'better understand the underlying technology and the way in which one of skill in the art might use the claim terms.'
guidance: Courts may rely on dictionary definitions when construing claim terms so long as the dictionary definition does not contradict any definition found in or ascertained from the patent documents. Consider extrinsic evidence only after intrinsic review and ensure consistency with intrinsic record.

name: No rigid 'magic formula' or required sequence for sources
description: There is 'no magic formula or catechism for conducting claim construction' and the court is not barred from considering sources in any particular order.
guidance: Flexibility in sequence is permitted, but any extrinsic source used must not contradict intrinsic evidence. The recommended practice remains claims → specification → prosecution history → extrinsic evidence to minimize error.

name: When claims are broad and specification discloses a narrow preferred embodiment, do not automatically narrow the claims
description: A common error is construing claim terms too narrowly by importing limitations from a narrow preferred embodiment disclosed in the specification even when the patent supports a broader interpretation.
guidance: Verify whether there is a basis in the intrinsic record for imposing a limitation; absence of such a basis means the plain language controls and broader reading may be appropriate.

name: Prefer broader construction when genuinely in doubt
description: When in doubt between two potential claim constructions, the district court should adopt the broader of the two potential constructions.
guidance: The Federal Circuit has tended to alter claims to make them broader rather than narrower; adopting the broader construction when uncertain may reduce likelihood of reversal.

name: Common appellate reasons for Federal Circuit review
description: Frequent reasons the Federal Circuit reviews district court claim constructions include: (1) patentees appealing a narrow construction for infringement reasons, (2) alleged infringers appealing a broad construction for infringement reasons, (3) patentees appealing a broad construction for validity reasons, and (4) alleged infringers appealing a narrow construction for validity reasons.
guidance: Be aware of these typical appeal drivers when framing and explaining claim constructions, since different parties will appeal depending on the perceived effect on infringement or validity.

name: Distinguish between failing to read claims in light of the specification and improperly reading in limitations
description: Two opposite errors exist: (a) improperly importing limitations from the specification into the claims (reading-in), and (b) failing to interpret the claims in light of the specification when a limitation is required.
guidance: Analyze whether the specification supplies a specific definition or required limitation; avoid both extremes by grounding the construction in the intrinsic record and explaining the rationale.

name: Complete district record can permit appellate resolution without remand
description: If the district court's record is complete, the Federal Circuit in some cases may decide the dispositive issue (e.g., infringement) without remanding to the district court.
guidance: Build a complete factual and claim-construction record at the district court level to enable appellate courts to resolve issues where appropriate and possibly avoid remand.

name: Dictionaries should be used to understand technology and POSITA usage
description: Dictionaries are useful 'to better understand the underlying technology and the way in which one of skill in the art might use the claim terms.'
guidance: Use dictionaries to illuminate technical meaning and POSITA usage, but corroborate dictionary meanings with intrinsic evidence and do not let dictionary definitions override the patent documents.

name: Circumstances requiring substitute specification (37 CFR 1.125(a))
description: If the number or nature of the amendments or the legibility of the application papers renders it difficult to consider the application, or to arrange the papers for printing or copying, the Office may require the entire specification, including the claims, or any part thereof, be rewritten.
guidance: Use when amendments or poor legibility impede consideration or printing/copying. A substitute specification required by the Office is governed by 37 CFR 1.125(a). Form paragraph references (e.g., 6.28) and examiner notes are available to explain and justify the requirement. A substitute required by the Office is not permitted in a reissue application or in a reexamination proceeding (37 CFR 1.125(d)).

name: Voluntary substitute specification filing limits and statement (37 CFR 1.125(b))
description: Subject to 37 CFR 1.312, a substitute specification, excluding the claims, may be filed voluntarily by the applicant at any point up to payment of the issue fee if it is accompanied by a statement that the substitute specification includes no new matter.
guidance: A substitute specification voluntarily filed under 1.125(b) must be accompanied by a statement indicating no new matter was included. The Office will accept such a filing only if requirements of 1.125(b) are satisfied. The examiner has no obligation to make a detailed comparison, but should object if aware of new matter. A substitute filed after final action or appeal is governed by 37 CFR 1.116; after mailing of a notice of allowance is governed by 37 CFR 1.312.

name: Form and marking requirements for substitute specifications (37 CFR 1.125(c))
description: A substitute specification submitted under 1.125 must be submitted with markings showing all the changes relative to the immediate prior version of the specification of record; added text shown by underlining; deleted matter shown by strike-through (or double brackets for five or fewer characters or if strike-through cannot be easily perceived); an accompanying clean version (without markings) must also be supplied. Numbering paragraphs of the specification of record is not considered a change that must be shown. Paragraphs of any substitute specification, other than the claims, should be individually numbered in Arabic numerals (for example [0001]).
guidance: 37 CFR 1.125(c) requires submission in clean form without markings and also a marked-up copy showing changes relative to the immediate prior version. Rules for showing additions/deletions (underlining, strike-through, double brackets) must be followed. Numbering substitute-spec paragraphs facilitates replacement-paragraph amendments per 37 CFR 1.121(b)(1).

name: Reasons for not entering a substitute specification (form ¶6.28.02)
description: A substitute specification filed has not been entered because it does not conform to 37 CFR 1.125(b) and (c) because: (examples:) the statement re: lack of new matter is missing; a marked-up copy was not supplied (in addition to the clean copy); a clean copy was not supplied (in addition to the marked-up copy); the substitute specification has been filed in a reissue application or reexamination proceeding; filed after payment of the issue fee; containing claims.
guidance: Insert specific statement(s) of why the substitute specification is improper. See MPEP § 714.20 and MPEP § 1302.02 for related procedures. For new matter in amendment, see MPEP § 608.04.

name: Restoration of canceled matter (608.01(s))
description: Canceled text in the specification can be reinstated only by a subsequent amendment presenting the previously canceled matter as a new insertion (37 CFR 1.121(b)(4)). A claim canceled by amendment (deleted in its entirety) may be reinstated only by a subsequent amendment presenting the claim as a new claim with a new claim number (37 CFR 1.121(c)(5)).
guidance: Reinstatement is treated as new insertion/new claim; follow 1.121 procedures and refer to MPEP § 714 for claim reinstatement handling.

name: Reservation for future application / transfer of specification parts not permitted (608.01(t))
description: A reservation for a future application of subject matter disclosed but not claimed in a pending application will not be permitted in the pending application (37 CFR 1.79). No part of a specification can normally be transferred to another application. Drawings may be transferred to another application only upon granting of a petition filed under 37 CFR 1.182.
guidance: Do not permit language reserving subject matter for future applications. For transfer of drawings, require petition under 1.182 and follow MPEP § 608.02(i).

name: Definitions and permissibility of trademarks and names used in trade (608.01(v) I)
description: Trademark: a word, letter, symbol, or device adopted by one manufacturer or merchant and used to identify and distinguish his or her product. Names Used in Trade: a nonproprietary name by which an article or product is known among traders or workers in the art. Names used in trade are permissible in patent applications if: (A) their meanings are established by an accompanying definition sufficiently precise and definite to be made part of a claim, or (B) their meanings are well-known and satisfactorily defined in the literature. Condition (A) or (B) must be met at the time of filing of the complete application.
guidance: Evaluate on a case-by-case basis whether a trademark or trade name supplies sufficient identification. If neither condition is met at filing, examiner should hold disclosure insufficient and reject any claims relying solely on the trademark/name. If product cannot be otherwise defined, an amendment defining the process of manufacture may be permitted, supported by showings that the process was known at filing.

name: Drawings required where necessary for understanding (35 U.S.C. 113; 37 CFR 1.81)
description: The applicant shall furnish a drawing where necessary for the understanding of the subject matter to be patented. When the nature of such subject matter admits of illustration by a drawing and the applicant has not furnished such a drawing, the Commissioner may require its submission within not less than two months from the sending of a notice. Drawings submitted after filing may not be used to overcome insufficiency of the specification due to lack of enabling disclosure or to supplement the original disclosure for claim interpretation.
guidance: If a drawing is necessary for understanding, lack of drawing renders application incomplete and no filing date may be given until drawing received. If drawings are merely illustrative (second sentence of 35 U.S.C. 113), the lack of drawing is an informality and may be required later; examiner should require sketch or permanent print as part of applicant's reply to permit early assessment and to detect new matter.

name: When drawings are not required for a filing date — claim-type exceptions (list A–E)
description: A drawing is not required for a filing date under 35 U.S.C. 111 and 113 if the application contains: (A) at least one process claim including 'process' or 'method' in its introductory phrase; (B) at least one composition claim including 'composition,' 'compound,' 'mixture' or 'pharmaceutical'; (C) at least one claim directed to a coated article or product or to an article or product made from a particular material or composition; (D) at least one claim directed to a laminated article or product; or (E) at least one claim directed to an article, apparatus, or system where the sole distinguishing feature is the presence of a particular material.
guidance: See MPEP §601.01(f) for further explanation. These categories indicate many non-structural claims do not require drawings for a filing date, but examiner should still consider whether a drawing is necessary for understanding during examination.

name: Photographs allowed only when only practicable medium (37 CFR 1.84(b))
description: Photographs, including photocopies, are not ordinarily permitted in utility and design patent applications but will be accepted if photographs are the only practicable medium for illustrating the claimed invention (examples: electrophoresis gels, blots, cell cultures, histological tissue cross sections, animals, plants, in vivo imaging, TLC plates, crystalline structures, and ornamental effects in design patents). Photographs must be of sufficient quality so that all details are reproducible in the printed patent. If the subject admits of illustration by a drawing, the examiner may require a drawing instead.
guidance: Color photographs allowed if conditions for color drawings and black-and-white photographs are satisfied. Use examiner discretion and require drawings if appropriate to avoid reliance on photographs when drawings suffice.

name: When an application is "in condition for examination" (37 CFR 1.704(f))
description: An application filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a) is in condition for examination when it includes: a specification with at least one claim and an abstract (§ 1.72(b)); papers in compliance with § 1.52; drawings (if any) in compliance with § 1.84; any required English translation (§ 1.52(d) or § 1.57(a)); a Sequence Listing in compliance with §§ 1.821–1.825 (if applicable) or Sequence Listing XML in compliance with §§ 1.831–1.835 (if applicable); an inventor’s oath or declaration or an application data sheet containing the information specified in § 1.63(b); the basic filing fee (§ 1.16(a) or (c)); the search fee (§ 1.16(k) or (m)); the examination fee (§ 1.16(o) or (q)); any certified copy required by § 1.57(a); and any application size fee required under § 1.16(s). For international applications entering the national stage, analogous items and fee citations (e.g., § 1.492 provisions) apply.
guidance: All listed items must be present for the application to be considered in condition for examination. For international applications, national-stage-specific fee citations apply. This definition is the basis for the 8-month 'in condition' rule and other PTA reductions.

name: 37 CFR 1.705(b) reconsideration request requirements and timing
description: Any request for reconsideration of the patent term adjustment indicated on the patent must be an application for patent term adjustment filed no later than two months from the date the patent was granted (extendable under § 1.136(a)). The application for PTA reconsideration must be accompanied by the fee set forth in § 1.18(e) and a statement specifying: the correct PTA and bases under § 1.702; the relevant dates per §§ 1.703(a)–(e) and adjustment per § 1.703(f); whether the patent is subject to a terminal disclaimer and any expiration date; and either (A) any circumstances during prosecution constituting a failure per § 1.704 or (B) that there were no such circumstances.
guidance: Reconsideration applications must include the indicated fee and a detailed factual statement establishing the claimed correct PTA and its statutory/regulatory bases. The two-month deadline is central but may be extended under § 1.136(a).

name: Improvement in functioning of a computer or other technology
description: An additional element (or combination of elements) may integrate the exception into a practical application when the claimed invention improves the functioning of a computer or improves another technology or technical field.
guidance: Examine the specification to see if disclosure provides sufficient detail so one of ordinary skill would recognize the improvement. The specification need not explicitly say 'improvement' but must make it apparent; conclusory assertions are insufficient. The claim must reflect the components/steps that provide the improvement (need not recite the improvement in explicit words). This consideration is evaluated without regard to whether elements are conventional in Step 2A Prong Two.

name: Applying or using a judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis
description: Claims that apply or use the judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition can integrate the exception into a practical application.
guidance: Examples include acupuncture, administration of medication, dialysis, organ transplants, phototherapy, physiotherapy, radiation therapy, surgery, etc. Vanda illustrates using a natural-law relationship (genotype-drug risk) to safely treat patients (dose adjustment) rather than merely gathering data, supporting eligibility at Step 2A.

name: Specificity of claim limitations as a relevant factor
description: Specificity of the claim limitations is relevant to evaluating considerations such as use of a particular machine, particular transformation, and whether the limitations are mere instructions to apply an exception.
guidance: Specificity is not a standalone consideration, but detailed claim limitations (or lack thereof) can inform whether the additional elements meaningfully integrate the exception. Parker v. Flook illustrates that failure to explain specifics can support a finding of insignificant post-solution activity.

name: Prong Two evaluation procedure
description: Evaluate integration into a practical application by: (1) identifying any additional elements recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception(s); and (2) evaluating those additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether they integrate the exception into a practical application using one or more of the listed considerations.
guidance: Not a weighing test—type or number of considerations applied is not decisive. Evaluate significance of additional elements relative to the invention and how limitations interact. If claim as a whole integrates the exception, the additional limitations impose a meaningful limit and claim is eligible at Step 2A. Examiners must analyze each claim separately; dependent claims may differ in eligibility.

name: Evaluate each claim on its own facts
description: Examiners should examine each claim for eligibility separately based on the particular elements recited; claims should not be judged to automatically stand or fall with similar claims in the application.
guidance: One claim may be ineligible while another dependent claim with additional elements may be eligible because it integrates the exception into a practical application or amounts to significantly more.

name: Examples and case-law guidance (use to inform considerations)
description: Case examples illustrate application of Prong Two considerations — e.g., Solutran (claims directed to abstract idea), Finjan (virus scanning improved computer functionality), Enfish, McRO, Visual Memory, SRI (improvements to computer/technology), Vanda (treatment/prophylaxis using genotype info).
guidance: Use these cases to analogize whether claimed additional elements show improvement, meaningful application, or are merely conventional/insignificant. Review MPEP §§ 2106.05(a)-(h) for additional case discussions and application of considerations.

name: Dedication by disclosure (disclosed but unclaimed subject matter)
description: A patentee who discloses subject matter in the specification but does not claim it cannot invoke the doctrine of equivalents to extend claim scope to encompass that disclosed-but-unclaimed subject matter.
guidance: The court holds that Johnston, having disclosed steel substrates but limited claims to aluminum, cannot assert the doctrine of equivalents to cover the disclosed but unclaimed steel. To the extent prior cases (e.g., YBM Magnex) conflict with this holding they are overruled. The opinion treats such disclosure-as-dedication as a bar to equivalence absent other saving principles (e.g., foreseeability exceptions).

name: Foreseeability bar to the doctrine of equivalents
description: The doctrine of equivalents does not capture subject matter that the patent drafter reasonably could have foreseen during the application process and included in the claims.
guidance: This principle enhances the notice function of claims by making them the sole definition of invention scope in all foreseeable circumstances. If a person of ordinary skill would reasonably anticipate ways to evade literal claim language, the applicant has an obligation to claim those foreseeable variants; DOE will not rescue a drafter who failed to provide such notice. The court cites Sage, Maxwell, and other precedent to support this bar.

name: Element-by-element requirement for applying DOE
description: Pennwalt and Warner–Jenkinson require an equivalent for each and every element of a claim; applying DOE to the claim as a whole gives too much room to expand claim scope beyond notice limits.
guidance: The court reiterates that DOE must be applied on an element-by-element basis rather than allowing a holistic expansion that would undermine the claim's public-notice role. Citation: Pennwalt Corp. v. Durand–Wayland and Warner–Jenkinson.

name: Festo/Warner–Jenkinson principle on surrendered subject matter
description: Festo and Warner–Jenkinson propose to bar patentees from expanding their claim scope to embrace subject matter surrendered during patent acquisition.
guidance: These precedents support the proposition that the public notice function requires limiting DOE when the patentee has given up claim scope during prosecution; the opinion cites Festo and Warner–Jenkinson as part of the doctrinal context limiting non-textual infringement.

name: Wilson Sporting Goods rule: DOE cannot embrace prior art
description: The doctrine of equivalents cannot be used to expand claim scope so as to encompass the prior art.
guidance: Wilson Sporting Goods prevents DOE from effectively re-claiming what is in the prior art; the opinion cites Wilson as another constraint protecting the public from overbroad equivalence that would eliminate prior-art boundaries.

name: Exceptions to foreseeability bar (after-arising technology; subtlety/complexity)
description: Subject matter arising from later-developed (after-arising) technology, or subject matter cloaked by subtlety of language or complexity of the technology, may not have been foreseeable and thus may remain eligible for DOE.
guidance: The court recognizes that foreseeability is not absolute: after-arising technologies (Al Site, Pennwalt, Hughes Aircraft examples) and cases where the specification is complicated or claims ambiguous may permit broader indulgence. Sage and other cases are discussed as acknowledging these exceptions.

name: Claim-drafting obligation and premium on adequate claim scope
description: Patent applicants have an obligation to draft claims that capture all reasonably foreseeable ways to practice the invention; failure to do so places the cost on the patentee rather than the public.
guidance: Foreseeability motivates a premium on careful claim drafting; if the patentee had a clear opportunity to seek broader claims but did not, courts may bar DOE relief and expect patentees to use statutory routes (reissue/continuation) to correct claiming errors. The Sage excerpt explicitly frames this allocation of cost.

name: Graver Tank distinction: claimed equivalents vs disclosed-only equivalents
description: If the patentee actually claimed the equivalent subject matter (even if those claims were later held invalid), the patentee may not be treated as having dedicated that subject matter to the public; dedication-by-disclosure is a distinct concept and was not decided by Graver Tank II.
guidance: The concurrence explains Graver Tank II may be distinguishable because the patentee there arguably claimed the equivalent subject matter; dedication by disclosure was not clearly decided by that Supreme Court case, so the distinction matters when assessing whether DOE is available.

name: Compelling merits standard
description: “Compelling, meritorious challenges are those in which the evidence, if unrebutted in trial, would plainly lead to a conclusion that one or more claims are unpatentable by a preponderance of the evidence.”
guidance: This standard is higher than the statutory "reasonable likelihood" standard. A challenge is "compelling" only if it is highly likely the petitioner would prevail on at least one claim. The Board follows OpenSky/CommScope precedent in applying this higher standard where Fintiv factors 1–5 favor denial.

name: Claim construction standard in IPRs (Phillips / 37 C.F.R. § 42.100(b))
description: In IPRs, the Board interprets claim language using the same claim construction standard as in a civil action under 35 U.S.C. § 282(b), as described in Phillips v. AWH Corp.
guidance: Per Nidec and Vivid, the Board construes only terms in controversy and only to the extent necessary to resolve the dispute. If claim construction is unnecessary to the disposition, explicit construction may be omitted.

name: Anticipation (35 U.S.C. § 102) — requirement for inherency / express disclosure
description: A claim is anticipated only if each and every element as set forth in the claim is found, either expressly or inherently described, in a single prior art reference.
guidance: Inherency cannot be established by probabilities or possibilities; the mere fact that a certain thing may result is insufficient (In re Robertson). The dispositive question: would one skilled in the art reasonably understand or infer that every claim element is disclosed in the reference.

name: Obviousness (35 U.S.C. § 103) — what must be shown
description: Obviousness analysis focuses on not just what references expressly teach, but what they would have suggested to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention.
guidance: References must fairly suggest or motivate the claimed combination/ modification (In re Lamberti, In re Burckel). The petitioner must provide reasoned explanation and, where relied upon, supporting expert testimony beyond bare conclusory assertions.

name: Special situations causing abandonment (enumerated examples A–I)
description: Certain specific circumstances often arise and should be specially noted as they may cause abandonment (A) copying claims from a patent not suggested by the Office, (B) withdrawal/failure to prosecute an appeal, (C) dismissal of appeals or civil action without appropriate amendment, (D) suggested claims for interference near end of reply period, (E) FWC application issues, (F) filing a CPA under former rules, (G) improperly filed RCE prior to Board decision, (H) RCE filed while reply outstanding to final action without required submission, (I) improper RCE prior to payment of issue fee.
guidance: See MPEP §2305, §706.07(h), §201.06, §1215–§1216 and related sections for detailed treatment; improper filings may not toll prior time periods and can result in abandonment.

name: Termination of proceedings (35 U.S.C. 120 context)
description: Proceedings are terminated for purposes of 35 U.S.C. 120 when (A) issue fee not paid and application abandoned (proceedings terminated as of date issue fee was due), (B) application loses an interference to all claims, (C) after decision by the Board, and (D) after decision by the court.
guidance: Termination means the earlier application is no longer copending for 35 U.S.C. 120 purposes; see MPEP §711.02(c) for further detail on dates and effects.

name: Examiner's amendment may change abstract when claims narrowed
description: An examiner’s amendment can be made to change the abstract, where the patent owner’s narrowing amendments during the prosecution of the reexamination have changed the focus of the invention.
guidance: Example: where a claim is made more specific during reexamination and the abstract does not focus on the specific limitation now required for all patent claims.

name: Select drawing figure and representative claim for Official Gazette
description: An appropriate drawing figure is to be indicated for printing on the certificate cover sheet and in the Official Gazette. In addition, a representative claim which has been reexamined is to be indicated for publication in the Official Gazette.
guidance: Selection instructions: (A) The broadest claim should be selected; (B) ordinarily designate but one claim on each invention (reexamination: examiner must select only one claim); (C) a dependent claim should not be selected unless the independent claim is also printed; in reexamination, a dependent patent claim may be selected where the independent original patent claim has been canceled; (D) in reissue applications, select the broadest claim with changes or the broadest additional reissue claim. When recording: write claim number clearly in black ink, separate multiple claim numbers with commas, and use renumbered patent claim numbers.

name: Telephone inquiry before canceling all claims
description: Prior to canceling the claims and issuing the NIRC, the examiner should telephone the patent owner to inquire if a timely response, timely appeal, etc., was filed with the Office to ensure a timely response has not been misdirected within the Office.
guidance: If patent owner indicates no such filing or cannot be reached, the examiner will proceed to issue a NIRC terminating prosecution. If reached and indicated no timely filing, the attachment to the NIRC will make the telephone interview of record.

name: Reasons for patentability and/or confirmation required for each patentable claim
description: Reasons for patentability are required for each claim found patentable unless all claims are canceled in the proceeding.
guidance: Box 2 of form PTOL-469 is checked and the reasons are provided as an attachment. Reasons should indicate why the claims found patentable are clearly patentable over the cited patents or printed publications, similar to reasons for allowance in an application (see MPEP § 1302.14). Examiner may use form PTOL-476 or preferred form paragraph 22.16. The examiner may refer to particular portions of the record that clearly establish patentability.

name: Statutory content and mailing requirements of ex parte reexamination certificate
description: An ex parte reexamination certificate will set forth the results of the ex parte reexamination proceeding and the content of the patent following the proceeding in accordance with 35 U.S.C. 307 and 37 CFR 1.570.
guidance: The certificate will: (A) cancel any patent claims determined unpatentable; (B) confirm any patent claims determined patentable; (C) incorporate into the patent any amended or new claims determined patentable; (D) make any approved changes in the description; (E) include any statutory or terminal disclaimer filed; (F) identify unamended claims held invalid on final holding by another forum on any grounds; (G) identify any patent claims not reexamined; (H) be mailed on its date to the patent owner (with a copy to the requester); and (I) identify patent claims dependent on amended claims determined patentable. If a certificate cancels all claims, no further Office proceedings will be conducted regarding that patent or related reissue/reexamination requests.

name: Statutory definiteness (35 U.S.C. § 112)
description: Claims must satisfy the statutory requirement that claims be definite (35 U.S.C. § 112).
guidance: The USPTO should not avoid the responsibility of ensuring definiteness by delegating it to another party; doing so is contrary to the original purpose of the broadest reasonable construction rule — to enhance public notice at the time of a patent grant.

name: Broadest reasonable construction (BRC) rule (as applied by USPTO)
description: Under the BRC rule, the USPTO applies the broadest reasonable construction of claim terms during prosecution.
guidance: Intended to enhance public notice at grant by construing claims broadly during examination; in practice, lack of consensus about how to apply BRC (e.g., whether examiners use dictionaries) produces examiner-dependent variability, reduces ex ante incentives for precise drafting, affects scope of prior art searches, and does not reliably define the outer limits of claim scope for later litigation.

name: PHOSITA rule for prosecution and reexamination
description: Claims should be interpreted as a person having ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA) would have understood them at the filing date in light of the specification and prosecution history.
guidance: Dictionary definitions implying broader interpretations should yield to meanings made clear by the specification. Adopting the PHOSITA rule in the USPTO aims to improve certainty in claim construction, reduce costs from conflicting rules used by courts vs. USPTO, and make the prosecution record more useful to later courts and litigants.

name: Enhancing public notice — iterative improvements
description: One method public notice is enhanced is through iterative improvements: prosecution (examiner prior-art searches and rejections) iteratively narrows and clarifies claim scope.
guidance: BRC and PHOSITA affect iterative improvements differently: BRC encourages broader prior-art searches (revealing more art), but its interpretive variability limits predictability; PHOSITA may cause examiners to scrutinize specification and issue more rejections for vagueness but may reduce the scope of prior-art considered (possibly lowering some obviousness rejections). The public record under PHOSITA is likely more useful to courts because it reflects ordinary-meaning discussions.

name: Enhancing public notice — ex ante incentives for precise claiming
description: A rule should encourage applicants, before filing, to draft claims precisely (ex ante incentives).
guidance: BRC does not necessarily create ex ante incentives because applicants do not know how examiners will apply the rule; applicants also face other barriers (drafting skill, funds, perceived patent value). PHOSITA may not materially change these incentives either; patentees who desire vagueness will still often draft broadly because of costs and strategic considerations.

name: Enhancing public notice — defining outer limits of claims
description: A rule should help define the outer bounds of claim scope so third parties can understand legal reach of a patent.
guidance: Neither BRC nor PHOSITA guarantees that the examiner can set the outer limits at prosecution because (1) examiners rarely disclose their constructions in the public record, and (2) courts do not give examiner interpretations binding deference and may construe claims differently at litigation. Thus, adoption of PHOSITA alone will not necessarily prevent unexpected broad constructions in litigation, though PHOSITA-based prosecution histories may be more relevant to courts.

name: Use of specification over dictionary definitions
description: The specification is a key interpretive guide and should take precedence over broad dictionary definitions when the specification indicates a narrower meaning.
guidance: Phillips supports reliance on the specification to inform claim meaning; dictionary definitions that imply broader interpretations should not be used if the specification makes a narrower meaning clear.

name: Prior art search scope tied to claim interpretation
description: The breadth of the examiner's prior art search should be determined by how the claims are interpreted.
guidance: Under BRC a broad claim construction leads to broader searches (beneficial for revealing art and shaping claims); PHOSITA would likely reduce the scope of prior art searched because claims are construed with ordinary meaning and specification context. The article notes that broad searches could be achieved by separate procedures rather than by interpretive rule alone.

name: Disclosure of examiner's claim interpretation in prosecution record
description: Examiners should disclose how they construe claim terms in the prosecution history to aid public notice.
guidance: In practice examiners often do not record their informal assumptions, and examiners almost never testify; absent disclosure, the prosecution history will not reveal the examiner's view and courts cannot rely on it. Enhancing disclosure would make the prosecution record more useful to courts and third parties.

name: Avoid delegation/blind reliance on others for claim definiteness
description: The USPTO should not avoid its responsibility to ensure definite claims by delegating that responsibility to other parties.
guidance: Delegation undermines the purpose of the BRC rule to enhance public notice at the time of patent grant; the agency must retain responsibility for claim definiteness.

name: Uniformity of claim meaning across prosecution and litigation
description: Claim meaning should not vary with time or audience; courts and the USPTO should use consistent interpretive standards to avoid a 'zone of uncertainty.'
guidance: Conflicting standards impose costs on patentees and third parties. A single rule (e.g., PHOSITA applied both in prosecution and litigation) would reduce costs and improve predictability of claim scope.

name: Court non-deference to USPTO interpretations
description: Federal courts do not give automatic deference to the USPTO's understanding of claim terms at any stage.
guidance: Even when the examiner discloses an interpretation, courts may construe claims differently (sometimes broader), so examiner interpretations cannot be presumed to define the outer bounds of claim scope.

name: Practical incentives and barriers affecting claim precision
description: Practical barriers (limited funds, drafting skill, perceived patent value, and applicants' practice of waiting for examiner prior-art search results) affect applicants' willingness and ability to draft precise initial claims.
guidance: These incentives are largely independent of the interpretive rule; applicants often await examiner searches and may rely on iterative amendment rather than investing in exhaustive initial drafting.

name: Description requirement — clarity (claim-identification)
description: One invention should be identified based on matters stated in one claim.
guidance: Mapped to Patent Law art.36(6)(ii) and GL part III chap.2 sec.3. The description must support identification of the invention corresponding to each claim.

name: Description requirement — support (scope-of-disclosure)
description: Whether or not the claimed invention exceeds 'the extent of disclosure in the description to which a person skilled in the art would recognize that a problem to be solved by the invention would be actually solved.'
guidance: Mapped to Patent Law art.36(6)(i). In AI cases, claims that go beyond the disclosed correlations, features, or training-data-supported relationships (e.g., claiming use of features not supported by description) fail the support requirement (Case 49 body weight estimation).

name: AI-specific disclosure: training-data correlation/support requirements
description: Correlation among data in training data should be presumable in view of common general technical knowledge, or supported by an explanation or statistic information in the description, or supported by a performance evaluation of the AI model.
guidance: Explicit AI-focused requirement: if claimed relationships between inputs and outputs (features and labels) cannot be presumed from common general technical knowledge, the description must contain explanations/statistics or actual model performance evaluations to satisfy support/enablement. Failure to disclose correlations or performance evaluation can lead to lack of enablement/support (Case 46, Case 49).

name: Inventive step for mixed-type (technical + non-technical) inventions
description: When claims mix technical and non-technical features, Japan does not distinguish between technical and non-technical features for inventive-step assessment, but features making no technical contribution cannot contribute to inventive step.
guidance: Contrast with EPO COMVIK approach; JPO will assess the whole claim but only technical contributions count toward inventive step. This affects AI/ software claims that include business or purely informational elements.

name: Inventive step: unexpected technical effect supports inventiveness
description: A claimed feature that produces a significant technical effect that a person skilled in the art cannot expect can support a finding of inventive step.
guidance: Example (Case 34 Claim 2): Addition of temperature data led to a significant, non-obvious improvement (accounting for meltwater) and was held inventive. Emphasizes evaluating technical effect and whether it would be expected by the skilled person.

name: Claim drafting/format expectations (case-example driven)
description: Claims should specify concrete means/methods and technical features rather than merely stating information content or abstract steps; one invention per claim and supported details are expected.
guidance: Derived from multiple case examples: claims that lack means for concrete processing or that claim broad data items without technical implementation risk ineligibility or failure under description requirements. Use case examples in HB Annex A/B to guide appropriate claim scope and supporting disclosure.

name: Core PPH eligibility (allowable claim in first office)
description: When an applicant receives a ruling from a first patent office that at least one claim is allowable, the applicant may request fast track examination of corresponding claim(s) in a corresponding patent application pending in a second participating patent office.
guidance: PPH "allows applicants who receive a determination of allowable claims in an application from one Intellectual Property (IP) office to obtain expedited examination of corresponding claims filed in an application pending in another participating IP Office." Use the work product of the first office (PCT or national) as the basis for requesting PPH status at the USPTO.

name: Orange Book Ineligible Patent Types
description: Certain patents are categorically ineligible for Orange Book listing: process patents, packaging patents, patents claiming metabolites or synthesis intermediates, and methods of use not approved by FDA. Polymorph patents are listable only with supporting analytical data proving presence and identical performance.
guidance: When screening Orange Book entries, filter out patents that are non‑listable by statute. For polymorph/salt/enantiomer patents, check whether the required supporting data was submitted; these are nuanced and require technical verification.

name: Assignment of contracts (Sections 3477 and 3737 R.S.)
description: Assignment statutes generally make certain assignments voidable but not void; statutory provisions define scope, instances void under section 3477, effect of assignment in bankruptcy/for creditors, and relationship to assignment of claims under a contract.
guidance: Distinguish assignment of contract from assignment of claim; money due under contract generally payable to the original contractor only unless statutory exception applies; review contract provisions and statute before allowing or recognizing assignments.

name: Entitlement and filing channel for Article 19 claim amendments
description: Under Article 19 the applicant is entitled to one opportunity to amend the claims in the international phase; any amendment under Article 19 must be filed with the International Bureau (not with the receiving Office or the ISA).
guidance: Further amendment opportunities (including description and drawings) are available only under Article 34 upon filing a demand for international preliminary examination. Article 19 amendments must be in the language in which the application is published.

name: Required contents of an Article 19 submission
description: Submission of Article 19 amendments must comprise: (i) a complete set of claims in replacement of the original claims; (ii) a letter indicating the differences between the claims as filed and as amended plus the basis for the amendments; and (iii) an optional statement under Article 19.
guidance: All three elements (replacement claims, explanatory letter, optional statement) should be considered when preparing an Article 19 amendment to avoid later problems in Chapter II or national phases.

name: Contents required in the accompanying letter
description: The letter must indicate (a) the differences between the claims as filed and those as amended and (b) the basis for the amendments in the application as filed. For each claim the letter should state whether it is unchanged, cancelled, new, replaces one or more claims as filed, is the result of division of a claim as filed, etc.
guidance: The basis for amendments must be given with specific references to parts of the original application (description, claims, drawings); non-specific indications such as “refer to the description as filed” are generally insufficient. Examples of suitable wording are provided in the Guide.

name: Statement under Article 19: content, form and limits
description: Any amendment may be accompanied by a brief statement explaining the amendment and indicating any impact on the description and drawings; the statement is published together with the application. Statements not referring to a specific amendment are not permitted. The statement must not exceed 500 words if in English or when translated into English, must not contain disparaging comments on the ISR or citations, and must be in the language of publication.
guidance: References to citations in the ISR may be made only in connection with a specific claim amendment. Failure to comply means the statement will not be published or communicated to designated Offices.

name: When to use Article 19 amendments (strategic considerations)
description: Because amendments under Article 19 are published with the international application, they may be useful to better define claim scope for provisional protection in designated States that provide such protection. However, if the applicant files a demand (Article 34) they can amend claims, description and drawings with the IPEA regardless of Article 19 amendments; therefore there is normally no need to use Article 19 when a demand is filed unless there is a specific reason, e.g., provisional protection.
guidance: Consider whether early public claim clarification (e.g., for provisional protection) outweighs possible disadvantages of publishing amendments.

name: Obtaining copies of priority documents
description: Third parties may apply to the Office with which the earlier application was filed, to certain designated Offices or to the IB for copies of priority documents. The IB makes copies of priority documents available after international publication on PATENTSCOPE or on paper upon request and reimbursement of cost, except where the international application was withdrawn prior to publication, or the priority claim was withdrawn or cancelled.
guidance: Check the status of the international application before requesting priority documents; withdrawn/cancelled priority claims may prevent IB from furnishing copies.

name: SME Step 2A Prong One — identifying claims that recite abstract ideas
description: Step 2A Prong One evaluates whether a claim is directed to a judicial exception (abstract idea), including mathematical concepts, certain methods of organizing human activity, and mental processes.
guidance: The 2024 update provides additional discussion on claims that do not recite abstract ideas and on those that do, informed by recent case law and USPTO-issued examples. Determination relies on claim language and how it maps to abstract-idea groupings.

name: SME Step 2A Prong Two — improvements analysis for AI inventions
description: Step 2A Prong Two examines whether limitations integrate an abstract idea into a practical application (e.g., provide an improvement to the functioning of a computer or another technology) or otherwise supply an inventive concept.
guidance: For AI inventions, specific steps showing how the output of an AI (e.g., using ANN output to solve a technological problem) amount to an improvement to computer functioning or a technical field can render the claim eligible. Distinguish improvements to the abstract idea vs improvements to computer/technical functioning. Particular treatment/prophylaxis limitations can render claims eligible; generic treatment steps may not.

name: Example-based eligibility teaching points (Examples 47–49)
description: Hypothetical examples illustrate SME analysis for AI inventions: Example 47 (anomaly detection) shows using ANN output to remediate network attacks in real time constitutes an improvement; Example 48 (speech separation) shows specific speech-separation techniques can improve technological functioning; Example 49 (fibrosis treatment) shows particular treatment steps and applying a weighted PRS model and ML model in a personalized medicine context can render claims eligible.
guidance: Examples are illustrative and fact-specific; a claim need not mirror an example to be eligible. Training and examiner guidance accompany the examples. Key teaching points: specific technical improvements, particular treatment steps, and explicit recitation of how AI outputs are used to improve technology or practice support eligibility.

name: Conduct a Patent / Prior Art Search
description: Inventors often search existing patents and publications to confirm that the invention is unique.
guidance: A thorough prior art search helps identify foreseeable rejections and refines claim drafting; applicable in every jurisdiction listed (US, Canada, China, India, PCT).

name: Prepare the Patent Application (required components)
description: A typical application includes: Specification (description of the invention); Claims defining the legal scope; Abstract; Patent drawings; Oath or declaration; Application Data Sheet.
guidance: Ensure the specification, claims, abstract and drawings meet the formal and substantive content requirements of the target patent office. These components form the core of the filing in the US, Canada, China, and India.

name: Prepare Design Drawings or Photographs with Multiple Views
description: Prepare design drawings showing multiple views of the article; or photographs where appropriate.
guidance: Design filings should include clear illustrations (multiple views) that disclose the claimed ornamental features; presentation requirements may vary by office.

name: Draft Short Specification / Title and Single Claim for Design Patent
description: Draft a short description and title of the article; for US design patents, draft a short specification and a single claim.
guidance: Design applications typically require concise descriptive text; U.S. design patents commonly have a single claim directed to the appearance as shown in the drawings.
