name: Infringement by use of a material part of a combination
description: Where a patent is for an invention consisting of several parts, the imitation or pirating of any part of the invention is an infringement of the patent.
guidance: If a patent claims a combination of parts, a user of the entire combination is clearly infringing; but even if only a material part of that combination is taken and used by another, that can be an actionable infringement. Example: a machine of three parts where one part is 'very useful' — copying that material part (even if substituting other modes for the less useful parts) may sustain an action for infringement.

name: Substantial-identity requirement for combination claims
description: A patent for a combination is for the union of all the parts arranged and combined as stated in the specification; the use of only some parts is not the same combination unless what is used is 'substantially the same thing.'
guidance: Whether use of less than the whole combination is infringement is a fact question for the jury: courts ask whether what the defendant used was 'substantially the same' as the patented combination. If the defendant's combination 'substantially differs' in any of its parts or arrangement, it is not the same combination. (Prouty v. Ruggles discussion.)

name: Statutory severability of overbroad patents (validity as to material and substantial parts)
description: A patent shall be deemed good and valid for so much of the invention as shall be truly and bona fide the invention of the patentee, if it is a material and substantial part of the thing patented and is definitely distinguishable from the other parts which the patentee had no right to claim.
guidance: This statutory rule salvages patents that were accidentally or mistakenly made too broad, allowing the valid, material, and distinguishable portions to remain enforceable — provided the overbreadth was not wilful or intended to defraud the public. The earlier doctrine that lack of novelty in any part vitiated the whole still applies where claims were knowingly made too broad to deceive.

name: Effect of lack of utility of one claimed part (false suggestion doctrine)
description: If a thing claimed as essential turns out to be useless and was known by the patentee to be useless when the specification was enrolled (a false suggestion of usefulness), the patent is voidable/void for misrepresentation.
guidance: If a part is subsequently discovered to be useless (but not known to be so at enrollment), that does not necessarily vitiate the patent. A patent for an entire machine that is useful on the whole will be valid even if parts are useless, so long as there was no false suggestion of utility at the time of grant. Courts distinguish between known-in-fact useless elements (which can void the patent) and those only later found impractical.

name: Chemical (composition) equivalents and claim scope
description: To substitute in place of some element in a composition a mere known equivalent is an infringement, because the patentee is understood in law to embrace known equivalents unless he expressly confines his claim.
guidance: In composition patents, a patentee may limit his claim to specific ingredients and thereby exclude equivalents; if he expressly disclaims or excludes an ingredient (e.g., 'without the addition of ... sulphuret of antimony'), he is estopped from later asserting that ingredient is covered. Courts examine the specification language and what a skilled person would understand the patentee to have intended to cover. Factual inquiry (e.g., whether the defendant's product contains the excluded substance) controls enforcement.

name: Express disclaimers/control public notice principle
description: A patentee who expressly excludes particular equivalents or ingredients in the claim is taken to have waived them, and cannot assert those excluded alternatives as covered by the patent.
guidance: One object of the patent specification is to inform the public what may be safely done without infringement during the patent term. If the patentee's claim language plainly excludes an equivalent, that exclusion governs even if it was based on mistake; patent law provides mechanisms to correct mistakes, but until corrected the record controls. (Byam v. Farr discussion.)

name: Product claims can be infringed irrespective of the process used
description: Where the specification amounts to a claim for the product (article) itself, the patent may be infringed by any one using the article regardless of the manner in which it was made.
guidance: Although sometimes obiter, courts have held that a product claim covers the article per se: if the patent covers the product, manufacture or use of that product by others infringes even if they used a different manufacturing process. This contrasts with situations where only a process is claimed.

name: Graham Inquiry: determine scope and content of the prior art
description: Determining the scope and content of the prior art.
guidance: The content of the prior art is determined at the time the invention was made to avoid hindsight. The examiner determines the most probable field of search for the invention as claimed and described in the specification. The most probable field of search includes the same field of applicant's endeavor as well as analogous areas.

name: Graham Inquiry: ascertain differences between prior art and claims
description: Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims in issue.
guidance: Ascertaining differences requires interpreting the claim language and considering both the claimed invention and the prior art reference as a whole. Examiner should identify which piece of art is closest, what differences exist with the closest prior art, and where the individual differences are shown in the prior art.

name: Graham Inquiry: evaluate objective evidence (secondary considerations)
description: Evaluating any objective evidence of nonobviousness (i.e., so-called 'secondary considerations').
guidance: Examples of objective evidence include commercial success; long-felt need; failure of others to solve the problem; skepticism of experts; copying. Such evidence must be commensurate in scope with the claims and there must be a nexus between the evidence and claimed features. Mere arguments are not evidence.

name: Determine what to search for (claim scope and breadth of search)
description: The scope of the claimed invention must be clearly determined prior to searching.
guidance: During examination, claims are given the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification. The search should not be limited to literal claim elements and should, insofar as possible, cover subject matter the examiner reasonably anticipates might be incorporated into applicant's amendment. The initial search should be sufficiently complete such that only an update search is needed in the second action, unless amendments require further searching.

name: Determine whether found art qualifies as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102
description: Art found during the search must qualify as 'prior art' as defined by 35 U.S.C. 102 before it can be used to reject a claimed invention.
guidance: Consider when the art became public, who was the source (inventor or another party), and whether the art satisfies the enablement provision of 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph. Subject matter that is prior art under 102 can support a 103 rejection.

name: Determine relevancy and closeness of prior art to the claimed subject matter
description: Evaluate which art is closest, whether the prior art shows all differences not shown by the closest prior art, and whether the art suggests combining individual teachings.
guidance: Continuously evaluate art found during the search to identify the closest reference and map claim differences to specific portions of prior references; determine where individual differences are shown in the art.

name: Prima facie obviousness — required factual/legal foundations
description: To establish a prima facie case of obviousness, three basic criteria must be met: (1) some suggestion or motivation to modify or combine references; (2) a reasonable expectation of success; and (3) the prior art must teach or suggest all claim limitations.
guidance: The initial burden is on the examiner to provide some suggestion of the desirability of doing what the applicant has done. Both the suggestion to combine and the reasonable expectation of success must be founded in the prior art and not in applicant's disclosure. The rationale for combining may be in the references themselves or presented as a convincing line of reasoning grounded in the prior art.

name: Avoidance of hindsight and improper motivation
description: Impermissible hindsight and application of per se rules must be avoided; do not rely on applicant's disclosure as the motivation to combine references.
guidance: The examiner must step backward in time into the shoes of the hypothetical person of ordinary skill and determine whether the claimed invention 'as a whole' would have been obvious. The tendency to resort to hindsight is often difficult to avoid but must be guarded against. Proposed motivations must be specific and directed to the claim differences, not general or hindsight-driven.

name: Examiner burden and required specificity in Office action
description: When rejecting a claim, administrative due process and 35 U.S.C. 132 require that applicant be adequately notified of the reasons for the rejection.
guidance: The Office action should designate the particular part of a reference being relied upon (37 CFR § 1.104(c)(2)); articulate the differences between the claim and the closest prior art; state where differences are found or suggested; explain how the teachings are combined; and explain why the combination would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill at the time of the invention. Do not cite applicant's disclosure as the motivation. After applicant rebuttal, reconsider the initial determination in view of the entire record before imposing any rejection.

name: Rebuttal evidence standards and types
description: Once a prima facie case is established, the burden shifts to the applicant to present evidence rebutting obviousness.
guidance: Evidence types: (1) evidence of unexpected or nonobvious properties/advantages (comparative examples, affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132), and (2) evidence of real world activities (commercial success, long-felt need, failure of others, skepticism, copying). Arguments are not evidence. Comparative tests must compare the claimed invention to the closest prior art, be commensurate in scope, not conducted under special conditions, and show truly significant differences. A nexus must be established between the objective evidence and the claimed features.

name: Written description applies beyond priority/new-matter contexts
description: The written description requirement extends beyond priority questions (new matter/parent application support) and must be satisfied by originally-filed claims as well as amended claims.
guidance: The court stated the requirement "extends beyond a priority context, such as in questions of new matter or whether claims are supported by a parent application, and is a requirement that even originally-filed claims must satisfy."

name: Genus claims require disclosure of representative species or common structural features
description: Claims that cover multiple embodiments or species (genus claims) can lack written description if the specification does not disclose representative species or structural features common to the genus.
guidance: Quoting prior case law, the court held "a sufficient description of a genus instead requires the disclosure of either a representative number of species falling within the scope of the genus or structural features common to the members of the genus so that one of skill in the art can 'visualize or recognize' the members of the genus." Without such disclosure, genus claims may be unsupported.

name: Functional claims require species support (cannot merely claim results)
description: Functional claims that simply claim a desired result without describing species that achieve that result are defective unless the applicant shows possession of species sufficient to support the claimed functional genus.
guidance: The court held an adequate description "must demonstrate that the applicant has made a generic invention that achieves the claimed result and do so by showing that the applicant has invented species sufficient to support a claim to the functionally-defined genus." Functional claiming is especially scrutinized in the biological arts.

name: Correlation between structure and function can satisfy written description
description: Functional claim language can satisfy the written description requirement when the art has established a correlation between structure and function.
guidance: The court cited Enzo Biochem, Inc. v. Gen-Probe Inc. to note that where a correlation between structure and function is established in the art, functional language may meet the written description requirement. In such cases, disclosing structural features that are known to cause a function can support functional claims.

name: Broad/outer-limits functional claiming is inadequate; obviousness is not enough
description: Merely 'drawing a fence around the outer limits of a purported genus' or providing a description that only renders the invention obvious does not satisfy the written description requirement.
guidance: The court declared that "merely drawing a fence around the outer limits of a purported genus is not an adequate substitute for describing a variety of materials constituting the genus," and that "a description that merely renders the invention obvious does not satisfy the requirement." Applicants must describe a sufficient variety or defining features, not just broad boundaries.

name: Functional claims must recite sufficient materials to accomplish the function (esp. in biological arts)
description: When a patent claims a genus by function or result, the specification must recite sufficient materials to accomplish that function; claims that merely recite the problem and claim all solutions are invalid.
guidance: The court warned that functional claims will fail when they "merely recite a description of the problem to be solved while claiming all solutions to it and … cover any compound later actually invented and determined to fall within the claim's functional boundaries — leaving it to the pharmaceutical industry to complete an unfinished invention." This is particularly acute in the biological arts.

name: Disclosing unclaimed/planned research without adequate description risks placing subject matter in the public domain
description: Material described in a patent application but not claimed — especially speculative or planned-research disclosures — may be placed in the public domain if not supported by adequate written description.
guidance: The article cautions applicants not to disclose planned research ideas insufficiently described to support claims, because such subject matter becomes public domain (citing Unique Concepts, Inc. v. Brown). This serves as a procedural warning when drafting disclosure.

name: Need for concrete examples and a descriptive link between disclosed species and claimed function (case-specific biotech lessons)
description: A specification must provide concrete examples or a descriptive link showing how disclosed molecules/structures achieve the claimed functional activity; mere suggestion or speculative teaching is inadequate.
guidance: The Ariad case facts illustrate this: the court found Ariad's specification lacked sufficient working examples showing inhibition of NF-κB or a descriptive link between disclosed molecules (e.g., tables of sequences) and claimed functional activity. The court discounted post-priority evidence and expert testimony about existence of molecules absent disclosure, and treated speculative plans (e.g., dominantly interfering molecules where key assumptions were unknown) as insufficient.

name: Machine claims require substantial novelty in structure or mode of operation
description: If it be a machine, it must be substantially new in its structure and mode of operation, and not merely changed in form or in the proportion of its parts.
guidance: Minor form or proportion changes do not support a patent; the new machine must embody a new mode, method, or application of mechanism that produces a new effect or an old effect in a new way. In complex machinery, focus on what is new in the mode of operation.

name: Preserve a 12-month grace period
description: Retain a real and substantial 12-month grace period so inventors and start-ups can disclose and still obtain patents if they file within 12 months.
guidance: Proposed S.23 102(b) contains a narrower grace period than current law; critics claiming 'no grace period' are mistaken. Concern that proposed language limits protection (does not extend to all third-party activities). Law should preserve broad, predictable protection currently enjoyed under 102(b).

name: Invention notebook standards — provable conception and diligence
description: Invention notebooks or records should identify conception and dates with sufficient detail that others skilled in the art understand what was invented and when, enabling proof of conception and diligence if needed.
guidance: Many inventor-supplied disclosures are inadequate (often one-paragraph). Reliable notebooks must be detailed enough to support a claim of conception; however, attorney-drafted provisionals are typically superior to cryptic notes. If relying on first-to-invent, maintain rigorous records.

name: Provisional drafting and prosecution workflow
description: Preferred drafting workflow: prepare thorough specification/description first (text), then translate into claim language; perform prior art search, patentability assessment, mapping, and identify base target and alternative embodiments to support multiple claims.
guidance: This approach (spec first, then claims) aids in creating a detailed specification supporting numerous claim sets. The 80-20 rule analogy: initial broad descriptive work takes less time, while final claim drafting and detailed linking consumes more time; use this to plan efficient provisional/nonprovisional preparation.

name: Types of evidence in patent causes
description: Evidence in patent litigation is usefully divided into evidence of title and evidence of infringement.
guidance: Evidence of title relates to the letters-patent, the plaintiff's interest, the novelty and utility of the invention, and the sufficiency of the specification. Evidence of infringement relates to the identity of what the defendant made, used, or practiced with the invention claimed by the patentee. Different proof rules and witnesses may apply to each category.

name: Multiple inventions in one patent must each be supported
description: If a single patent attempts to claim two or more inventions, each invention must be separately useful and sufficiently described in the specification to support it.
guidance: A patentee who 'runs the hazard of putting two inventions into one patent' cannot hold the patent unless each invention can be supported as a separate patent — each must be useful and described so people clearly know what the invention is and how to carry it into effect. Example: a patent claiming both a steam-engine and separate machinery for propelling vessels must sufficiently specify each invention.

name: Willfulness pleading particularity requirement
description: Conclusive allegations no longer suffice; under subparagraph (e)(2)(A), the patent holder must allege acts of infringement sufficient to give the alleged infringer an objectively reasonable apprehension of suit and must plead with particularity which products or processes allegedly infringe which claims, as well as the basis for such a belief.
guidance: Requires detailed factual pleading to support willfulness claims, reducing vague or boilerplate willfulness allegations.

name: Second-window PGR standards: standing, timing, and burdens of proof
description: In the second window, a PGR petition may be filed throughout the life of the patent only if (i) the continued existence of the challenged patent claim is likely to cause the petitioner significant economic harm, and (ii) the petitioner files the petition within 12 months after receiving notice of infringement. The presumption of validity applies; the petitioner may challenge a patent based on any defense available in district court, but the existence/authentication/availability/scope of evidence offered to establish invalidity must be established by clear and convincing evidence, and if such predicates are established, invalidity is proven only if the persuasive force of such facts demonstrates invalidity by a preponderance of the evidence.
guidance: Limits second-window challenges to parties with a stake and raises evidentiary predicates to deter frivolous or harassment filings while preserving broad substantive grounds available in court.

name: Claim amendment limits during PGR
description: After a PGR is initiated, the patent holder has one opportunity as a matter of right to amend the claims, and may only amend the claims subsequently on motion and a showing of good cause. No amendment during a PGR proceeding may enlarge the scope of a claim or add new matter.
guidance: Permits narrow claim corrections while preventing broadenings or new subject matter that could unfairly prejudice others.

name: Delay determination when reissue about to issue and reexamination requested
description: If a reissue patent will issue before the 3-month period for determination on the reexamination request has expired, the determination should normally be delayed until after granting of the reissue patent; any reexamination ordered would be on the reissue patent claims.
guidance: When reexamination is ordered after reissue issues, reexamination should proceed on reissue claims, and the reissue claims used must be presented as a "clean copy" (bracketed words removed; added words plain). Use form paragraph 22.05 to indicate proceedings are based on reissue claims.

name: Form paragraph for reexamination based on reissue claims (¶ 22.05)
description: Where the reissue patent has issued, the determination on the request for reexamination should specifically point out that the determination has been made on the claims of the reissue patent and not on the claims of the original patent.
guidance: Use ¶ 22.05 wording: e.g., note surrender of original patent and that subsequent proceedings are based on reissue patent claims; see MPEP for exact bracketed form paragraph.

name: Indefiniteness rejection if housekeeping amendment not timely submitted
description: If a housekeeping amendment to make the claims the same in each file is required by the merger decision but is not timely submitted, any claim that does not contain identical text in all of the merged proceedings should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as being indefinite.
guidance: Timely submission of identical claim text is mandatory to avoid indefiniteness rejections in merged files.

name: Withdrawal/addition of grounds upon dissolution based on abandonment
description: Where the merged proceeding is dissolved based on abandonment of the reissue application and the reexamination proceeding continues, any grounds of rejection not applicable under reexamination (e.g., based on public use or on sale) should be withdrawn and any new grounds applicable under reexamination (e.g., improper broadened claims) should be made by the examiner.
guidance: The examiner should note any questions remaining which cannot be considered under reexamination pursuant to 37 CFR 1.552(c).

name: Effect of known federal court decision at time of determination
description: If a federal court decision on the merits of a patent is known to the examiner at the time the determination on the ex parte reexamination request is made, the examiner must follow guidance: a court's decision does not necessarily mean no substantial new question (SNQ) exists because the Office uses different standards of proof and claim interpretation; non-final holdings are not controlling; a final holding of invalidity/unenforceability is controlling.
guidance: The examiner should accord deference to factual findings of the court where evidence is the same but determine independently whether an SNQ exists; examples and case citations (Trans Texas, Translogic, Swanson, Baxter) illustrate the principles.

name: Effect of federal court decisions issued after reexamination order
description: If a federal court decision issues while reexamination is pending, the order to reexamine is reviewed to determine whether an SNQ still exists; if no SNQ, the reexamination is terminated. Non-final court decisions have no binding effect on reexamination; a final holding that claims are not invalid also is not binding, but a final holding of invalidity or unenforceability (after all appeals) is binding and such claims are withdrawn from reexamination.
guidance: Use form paragraph 22.20 to note claims held invalid by court and not being reexamined; continue reexamination as to remaining claims if any.

name: Mayo two-step framework (Alice formulation)
description: Use the Mayo framework (as adopted in Alice) to decide §101 issues: first determine whether the claims are directed to a patent-ineligible concept (laws of nature, natural phenomena, or abstract ideas); if so, proceed to step two and determine whether the claim adds an 'inventive concept' sufficient to ensure the patent amounts to 'significantly more' than the ineligible concept itself.
guidance: From the page: 'In the first Mayo step, the court must determine whether the patent claim under examination contains an abstract idea... In the second step... determine whether the patent adds to the idea "something extra" that embodies an "inventive concept."' If no inventive concept exists (i.e., the addition is conventional, routine, or generic), the claim is invalid under §101.

name: Inventive concept requirement
description: A claim must include an 'inventive concept' — an element or combination of elements 'sufficient to ensure that the patent in practice amounts to significantly more than a patent upon the [ineligible concept] itself.'
guidance: The court explains that an inventive concept must be more than well-understood, routine, conventional activity and must contain 'additional substantive limitations that narrow, confine, or otherwise tie down the claim so that, in practical terms, it does not cover the full abstract idea itself.' Ordinary and customary use of a general-purpose computer is insufficient.

name: Identification of abstract idea
description: Step requires determining whether the claim is 'directed to' an abstract idea such as an algorithm, method of computation, or other general principle (e.g., intermediated settlement, risk hedging).
guidance: The opinion treats concepts like 'intermediated settlement' as abstract ideas. If the claim is directed to such an idea, proceed to inventive-concept analysis. The Court stated: 'First, we determine whether the claims at issue are directed to one of those patent-ineligible concepts.'

name: Preemption concern
description: Assess whether the claim would effectively preempt all uses of the fundamental concept (i.e., monopolize the abstract idea), since preemption of an abstract idea weighs strongly toward ineligibility.
guidance: Federal courts consider whether a claim 'poses a risk of preempting an abstract idea.' The Federal Circuit plurality and Alice emphasize that claims that preempt future innovation by covering the abstract idea itself are not patentable. Field-of-use limitations that still effectively preempt are insufficient.

name: Federal Circuit plurality four-step/preemption-focused test
description: Plurality (Lourie) articulated a test: (1) determine whether the claimed invention fits within one of the four statutory classes (process, machine, manufacture, composition); (2) determine whether the claim poses a risk of preempting an abstract idea; (3) identify the fundamental concept at risk of preemption; (4) perform an 'inventive concept' analysis to see whether there is a genuine human contribution that adds substantive limitations narrowing the claim.
guidance: The plurality framed the 'balance of the claim' concept: the human contribution must 'contain[] additional substantive limitations that narrow, confine, or otherwise tie down the claim so that, in practical terms, it does not cover the full abstract idea itself.' The court also asked whether steps combined with an abstract idea are 'insignificant, conventional, or routine.'

name: Federal Circuit's specific limiting-criteria (four questions)
description: Consider these specific questions when testing whether claim elements meaningfully limit an abstract idea: (a) is the limitation necessary to every practical use of the abstract idea and therefore not truly limiting; (b) does it 'amount to more than well-understood, routine, conventional activity previously engaged in by researchers in the field'; (c) is it a 'token or trivial limitation' (insignificant post-solution activity); (d) is it merely a field-of-use limitation where the claim still effectively preempts all uses within the stated field.
guidance: These questions (from the Federal Circuit plurality) are practical heuristics for assessing whether purported limitations add anything substantive beyond the abstract idea itself.

name: Statutory-class fit inquiry
description: Initial technical/formal check: determine whether the claimed invention fits within one of the four classes in the statute: process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter.
guidance: This is the plurality's first analytical step. Fitting into a statutory class does not decide eligibility; it is the starting point before analyzing abstractness and inventive concept.

name: Anti-pattern: functional-objective claim drafting
description: Claims that merely 'describe a problem, announce purely functional steps that purport to solve the problem, and recite standard computer operations' are deficient because they lack an inventive concept and preempt subsequent specific solutions.
guidance: Federal Circuit Judge Bryson's description: such patents 'represent little more than functional descriptions of objectives, rather than inventive solutions.' Courts treat those as claiming abstract ideas and thus ineligible under §101.

name: Equivalence of claim types under §101 (method/system/media)
description: Consider whether method, system (computer/system), and computer-readable-media claims should be treated equivalently for §101 analysis—i.e., whether a system or medium claim that merely recites an abstract idea implemented on a computer is subject to the same eligibility limits as method claims.
guidance: The Federal Circuit en banc asked whether these claim categories should be considered equivalent under §101; Alice treated system and media claims that merely required generic computer implementation as ineligible in similar fashion to method claims.

name: Analogous prior art
description: Whether a reference is 'analogous prior art' (and thus properly relied upon for an obviousness rejection) depends on whether it is from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention or is reasonably pertinent to the problem with which the inventor was involved.
guidance: The scope of analogous art should be construed broadly (KSR). A reference that addresses the same problem or is reasonably pertinent to solving the problem can be analogous even if outside the inventor's exact field (examples: sealed padlock reference applied to tow-hitch lock; Teague bed folding mechanism applied to treadmills because both address retaining a folding mechanism). Office personnel should consider the problem to be solved in determining analogous art.

name: Simple substitution of one known element for another (predictable results) — required findings
description: To reject a claim based on simple substitution of known elements yielding predictable results, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries and articulate specific findings.
guidance: Office personnel must articulate: (1) a finding that the prior art contained a device/method/product differing from the claimed device by substitution of components; (2) a finding that the substituted components and their functions were known in the art; (3) a finding that one of ordinary skill could have made the substitution and the results would have been predictable; and (4) whatever additional Graham-based factual findings are necessary for the case. If any of these findings cannot be made, the simple-substitution rationale cannot support obviousness. Examples: In re Fout; In re O'Farrell; Agrizap.

name: Predictable results includes functioning for intended purpose
description: The notion of a 'predictable result' covers not only that prior art elements can be physically combined, but also that the combination would have worked for its intended purpose.
guidance: Assess whether combining elements would have produced the claimed function or purpose (DePuy example). Even if elements are physically combinable, a prior art teaching that combining would destroy an advantageous property or render the device inoperative (i.e., teaches away) weighs against an obviousness finding.

name: Lead compound / structural similarity in chemical cases
description: In chemical/pharmaceutical cases, proving obviousness from structural similarity requires showing some motivation that would have led a person of ordinary skill to select and modify a known compound (a 'lead compound') and an expectation that the new compound would have similar properties.
guidance: Motivation to modify may come from various sources and need not be explicit in the art; structural similarity can create an expectation of similar properties in light of the totality of the prior art (Aventis, Eisai). However, if modification would destroy an advantageous property or no reason to isolate/modify exists, the claim may be nonobvious (Eisai: no reason to modify lead compound because modification would destroy useful property).

name: Graham obviousness factors
description: The question of obviousness is resolved on the basis of underlying factual determinations including: (1) the scope and content of the prior art; (2) any differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art; (3) the level of ordinary skill in the art; and (4) objective evidence of nonobviousness.
guidance: See Graham v. John Deere. These four factual inquiries frame the obviousness inquiry and guide whether a claimed invention would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art.

name: Motivation/suggestion to combine references
description: When all elements of a claim are found in various pieces of prior art, the factfinder must consider whether a person of ordinary skill in the art would be motivated to combine those references.
guidance: A suggested motivation or teaching to combine references must exist; courts look for some suggestion, teaching, or motivation in the prior art (or the knowledge of a skilled artisan) to combine the references. Citations: Dome Patent L.P. v. Lee; WMS Gaming; Concrete Pipe.

name: Obviousness need not seek precise teachings; can rely on inferences/creative steps
description: An obviousness analysis need not seek out precise teachings directed to the specific subject matter of the challenged claim, because a court can take account of the inferences and creative steps that a person of ordinary skill would employ.
guidance: KSR indicates that a skilled artisan's ability to combine, infer, or adapt teachings can support an obviousness determination even when the prior art does not spell out the exact claimed subject matter.

name: Inherency standard for anticipation
description: A reference may anticipate inherently if a claim limitation that is not expressly disclosed is necessarily present, or inherent, in the single anticipating reference.
guidance: The 'very essence of inherency' is that one of ordinary skill would recognize the reference unavoidably teaches the property. Possibility or likelihood is insufficient—there must be necessity (see Verizon; Agilent). The Board applied this when finding NCT ’653 did not inherently disclose a device that necessarily 'contains and delivers' a 162 mg fixed dose.

name: Limitations that require specific device disclosure cannot be supplied by mere implication
description: Claims that recite a specific functional device (e.g., 'a subcutaneous administration device, which contains and delivers to a patient a 162 mg fixed dose') require disclosure in the prior art that the device both exists and necessarily performs that function; mere mention of subcutaneous administration without device disclosure may be insufficient for anticipation.
guidance: Board analyzed whether NCT ’653's statement that patients receive drug subcutaneously inherently disclosed a device that contains and delivers the entire fixed dose; because multiple-injection possibilities were not excluded, inherency failed.

name: Avoid importing unclaimed limitations (no disease if not claimed)
description: One should not improperly import into claims limitations (such as a particular disease) that are not recited; claims that do not recite efficacy or a disease generally should not be limited by such unrecited features.
guidance: Petitioner argued it was improper to read a disease limitation into claims that do not recite a disease (citing Acceleration Bay), which affects whether efficacy is a required limitation for the obviousness analysis.

name: Specification amendment powers and limits
description: A patentee or applicant is empowered to amend the specification by disclaimer, correction, or explanation; amendments must not substantially enlarge or alter the invention claimed.
guidance: Amendments may be opposed; where litigation for infringement or revocation is pending, leave of the Court is required to apply for amendment and must generally be by disclaimer; the Court's discretion is absolute; amendments allowed by Comptroller or Law Officer may be questioned in court; amendments ought to be allowed at patentee's peril when doubtful; clerical corrections may be allowed; amendments when made must be advertised; conditions (e.g., restriction on recovery of damages for pre-amendment use) may apply.

name: Limits on amendment by disclaimer
description: A disclaimer may reject claim to parts where both combination and subordinate parts are claimed, but may not strike out a whole claim and insert a claim to a subordinate part; disclaimers should leave sufficient matter to support the patent.
guidance: Disclaimer practice: may cut down claims (e.g., limit methods to particular described methods); disclaimers must be applied carefully; historical case law guides the permissible scope of disclaimers.

name: Publication rules for specifications
description: Specifications are not published unless the applications are accepted; the acceptance of a complete specification is to be advertised.
guidance: If an application is abandoned or void then the specification is not to be published; publication in a colony within priority period will not necessarily invalidate a patent where priority claims are timely (e.g.,Tasmania rule on publication within seven months).

name: Priority claims from United Kingdom or foreign filings
description: Applicants who have applied for protection for an invention in the United Kingdom may be entitled to a patent in the colony with the same date as the UK protection provided the colonial application is made within specified priority periods (e.g., seven months in Tasmania; one year for foreign inventions in Victoria).
guidance: Publication in the colony within the priority period shall not invalidate the patent; forms for communication from abroad and priority procedures are prescribed.

name: Claims and construction of specification
description: Complete specifications must contain claims; specifications and claims are to be construed according to ordinary meaning and with reference to the state of knowledge when prepared; benevolent construction applied, with words and drawings considered together; prior specifications may show anticipation; technical terms may be explained by evidence but patentee's own evidence as to meaning is inadmissible.
guidance: Claims construction must consider whole context; when two meanings possible, rules for construction apply; claims may be appendant; case law cited for guidance (sections on interpretation and construction).

name: Permitted amendments after notice of appeal but before filing brief
description: Amendments filed after the filing of a notice of appeal, but prior to the date of filing a brief, may be admitted only to: (A) cancel claims; (B) comply with any requirement of form expressly set forth in a previous action; (C) present rejected claims in better form for consideration on appeal; or (D) amend the specification or claims upon a showing of good and sufficient reasons why the amendment is necessary and was not earlier presented. See 37 CFR 41.33(a).
guidance: If the examiner denies entry of such an amendment, use form PTOL-303 to notify applicant of the non-entry and the reason. If an amendment clearly places the application in condition for allowance, the examiner may enter the amendment and allow the application.

name: Permitted amendments after filing of an appeal brief
description: Amendments filed on or after the date of filing a brief pursuant to 37 CFR 41.37 may be admitted only to: (A) cancel claims, where such cancellation does not affect the scope of any other pending claim in the proceeding; or (B) rewrite dependent claims into independent form.
guidance: Rewriting dependent claims into independent form includes (A) rewriting a dependent claim in independent form by adding the limitations of the parent claim(s), and (B) rewriting an independent claim to incorporate all subject matter of a dependent claim, canceling the dependent claim, and modifying dependency of other claims as needed. If entry is denied after filing a brief, use PTOL-304 to notify applicant and state reason.

name: Advisory Action After the Filing of an Appeal Brief (PTOL-304) — required notice content
description: If an amendment is filed on or after the date of filing a brief, advisory action must explain why the proposed amendment(s) will not be entered (e.g., they raise new issues requiring further search, raise new matter, do not place the application in better form for appeal, or present additional claims without cancelling corresponding finally rejected claims), or cite non-compliance with 37 CFR 1.121.
guidance: Use PTOL-304 when denying entry post-brief and provide clear explanations of the specific reason(s) for non-entry.

name: Examiner duties when an amendment would be entered
description: If the examiner indicates in an advisory action that an amendment would be entered, it is imperative for the examiner to also state how the individual rejection(s) set forth in the final Office action will be impacted by the entry of the amendment except where an amendment merely cancels claims.
guidance: If the examiner determines that an amendment clearly places the application in condition for allowance, the examiner may enter and allow the application. Examiners must respond to all amendments filed after appeal has been taken and prior to termination of the appeal.

name: Examiner's obligation to restate prior Office action rejections fully
description: An examiner's answer should not refer, either directly or indirectly, to any prior Office action without fully restating the point relied on in the answer.
guidance: If further explanation of the rejection is necessary, include it in the grounds of rejection set forth in the answer. If a rejected claim were amended after the final rejection by adding limitations, the examiner should address the added limitations in the ground of rejection in the answer. The statement of the rejection in the answer must account for the claim as amended and include rebuttal of arguments presented in the appellant's brief.

name: Examiners treat all pending rejected claims as on appeal
description: Examiners are not required to make any determination whether fewer than all of the rejected claims are identified by the appellant as being appealed. If the notice of appeal or appeal brief identifies fewer than all of the rejected claims as being appealed, the issue will be addressed by the Board. Therefore, the examiner will treat all pending, rejected claims as being on appeal, and must maintain all of the rejections set forth in the Office action from which the appeal is taken, unless appellant has overcome the rejection.
guidance: In situations where appellant requests to hold a rejection in abeyance or did not present any argument on a rejection in the appeal brief, the examiner should maintain the rejection in the examiner's answer.

name: Grounds of rejection — 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph (written description/enablement/best mode)
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, the examiner's answer must explain how the first paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112 is not complied with, including, as appropriate, how the specification and drawings do not describe the subject matter defined by each rejected claim, would not enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the subject matter without undue experimentation (consider factors in MPEP § 2164.01(a)), or do not set forth the best mode contemplated by the appellant.
guidance: Provide specific explanation tied to the specification/drawings and discuss undue experimentation factors where relevant.

name: Grounds of rejection — 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph (definiteness)
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, the examiner's answer must explain how the claims do not particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which applicant regards as the invention.
guidance: Explain claim language problems and why the claim fails the definiteness requirement with specific references to claim language and, if necessary, specification support.

name: Grounds of rejection — 35 U.S.C. 102 (anticipation) requirements
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102, the examiner's answer must explain why the rejected claims are anticipated or not patentable under 35 U.S.C. 102, pointing out where all of the specific limitations recited in the rejected claims are found in the prior art relied upon in the rejection.
guidance: Point to specific places (page/line/drawing reference) in the prior art showing each limitation is present.

name: Grounds of rejection — 35 U.S.C. 103 (obviousness) requirements
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103, the examiner's answer must: (i) state the ground of rejection and point out where each specific limitation recited in the rejected claims is found in the prior art relied on in the rejection; (ii) identify the differences between the rejected claims and the prior art relied on (i.e., the primary reference); and (iii) explain why it would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person of ordinary skill in the art to have modified the primary reference to arrive at the claimed subject matter.
guidance: If questions remain as to how limitations correspond to features in the prior art, the examiner must compare at least one rejected claim feature-by-feature with the prior art, aligning claim language side-by-side with specific page/line/drawing references and quotations as appropriate.

name: Evidence relied upon — listing and citation specificity
description: The examiner must list the evidence relied on (e.g., patents, publications, admitted prior art) and, for nonpatent references, provide the relevant page(s).
guidance: When relying on prior art, include precise citations (page/line/drawing reference) so claim-to-reference comparisons can be evaluated.

name: Definition of Prior Art
description: Prior art constitutes those references or documents which may be used to determine novelty and/or non-obviousness of claimed subject matter in a patent application.
guidance: Includes anything that can be used as examiner evidence (prior publications, patents, admissions of prior art, on-sale items, etc.). Prior art is the evidentiary basis for establishing a prima facie case of non‑patentability.

name: Applicant’s Admissions of Prior Art (AAPA)
description: Statements made by applicant that certain information was 'prior art' (may appear in the background, drawings, or applicant remarks).
guidance: Admissions by an applicant can be used as prior art against claims. See MPEP 2129. Beware of language in your specification that concedes prior art.

name: Presumption of Patentability and Examiner's Prima Facie Burden
description: Claimed inventions are presumed patentable until the examiner establishes a prima facie case that a patentability requirement is not met.
guidance: A prima facie case requires sufficient initial evidence (typically prior art) to support non‑patentability. The examiner's evidence often consists of prior publications, patents, admissions, on‑sale items, etc.

name: Anticipation (Novelty) — Single Reference Requirement
description: Anticipation occurs when a single prior art reference describes, either expressly or inherently, each and every limitation of a claim.
guidance: If claim requires limitations A, B, C, and D, a single reference that discloses A, B, C, and D anticipates. Inherent disclosure counts. Examiner must show every claim element is present in the single reference.

name: Definition of 'Effectively Filed' — 35 U.S.C. 102(d)
description: For determining whether a patent or application is prior art under 102(a)(2), the patent/application is considered effectively filed as of its actual filing date unless it is entitled to claim priority/benefit of an earlier application, in which case the effective date is the earliest such application that describes the subject matter.
guidance: Effectively filed date can be the actual filing date or an earlier priority date under sections 119/365/120/121/ etc., but the prior application must describe the relied‑upon subject matter.

name: Effective Filing Date Rule (general)
description: The 'effective filing date' for a claimed invention in a patent or application is the earlier of the actual filing date of that patent/application or the filing date of the earliest priority application describing the subject matter.
guidance: Provisional, non‑provisional, international, or foreign applications can set the effective filing date for purposes of 102(a)(2) if properly claimed and supported.

name: AIA FITF Exception — Common Ownership / 102(b)(2)(C)
description: A disclosure appearing in applications and patents shall not be prior art under 102(a)(2) if the subject matter disclosed and the claimed invention were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person not later than the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
guidance: Common ownership/assignment can negate certain patent‑document prior art; ownership/assignment records and timing determine applicability.

name: Common Ownership Under Joint Research Agreements — 35 U.S.C. §102(c)
description: Subject matter disclosed and a claimed invention are deemed owned by the same person under subsection (b)(2)(C) if: (1) both were developed by parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the claimed invention's effective filing date; (2) the claimed invention resulted from activities within the scope of the agreement; and (3) the patent application discloses or is amended to disclose the parties' names.
guidance: Joint research agreement requirements are strict—ensure the agreement existed and scope/timing align and that parties are disclosed in the application to invoke this exception.

name: Additional Novelty Considerations — Analogous Art Not Required for 102
description: For 35 U.S.C. §102 rejections, prior art need not be analogous art to the claimed invention; if a reference discloses the claimed invention, it anticipates even if the reference disparages it.
guidance: MPEP 2131.05 indicates that a reference that discloses all claim elements anticipates regardless of field or disparagement. Also, a reference that makes an element optional can anticipate a claim that expressly excludes that element.

name: Additional Obviousness Considerations — Whole Claim and Every Element
description: To show obviousness, each and every element of the claim must be addressed and the rejection must consider the claimed invention as a whole.
guidance: Partial treatment of claim elements is insufficient. Examiner must explain how the combination of references addresses all limitations and why PHOSITA would combine them.

name: Analogous Art Requirement for Obviousness (MPEP 2141.01(a))
description: A reference relied upon under §103 must be analogous prior art: (1) from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention (even if addressing a different problem); or (2) reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor (even if from a different field).
guidance: If a reference is neither in the same field nor reasonably pertinent, it should not be used to support an obviousness rejection. The examiner must justify analogy/pertinence.

name: How Prior Art is Used for Obviousness — Teaching/Suggestion and PHOSITA Combination
description: To show obviousness, combined prior art references or a modified single reference must teach or suggest all claim limitations and it would have been obvious to a PHOSITA to combine or modify the art accordingly.
guidance: The question is whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious to PHOSITA at the relevant time. Rejections must show both the teachings and the rationale for combination/modification.

name: Graham v. John Deere — Four Factual Inquiries for Obviousness
description: To form a basis for an obviousness rejection, make four inquiries: (1) determine the scope and contents of the prior art; (2) determine the differences between the prior art and the claims; (3) determine the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; (4) evaluate evidence of secondary considerations (commercial success, long‑felt but unsolved needs, failure of others).
guidance: These Graham factors guide the legal analysis; secondary considerations can rebut a prima facie case of obviousness and must be considered when present.

name: Elements Required in a §103 Rejection Using Secondary Reference(s)
description: A §103 rejection using secondary references must include: (1) description of what the primary reference teaches relative to the claimed invention; (2) identification of differences between the claimed invention and the primary reference; (3) indication of what the secondary reference(s) teach relative to those differences; (4) explanation of how the primary reference is to be modified by each secondary reference to arrive at the claimed invention and the rationale for making each modification.
guidance: An examiner must explain why each modification or combination of prior art teachings would have been obvious to PHOSITA to support the legal conclusion—mere conclusory statements are insufficient.

name: Director's authority to accept unintentionally delayed foreign priority claims
description: The Director may consider failure to file a timely claim for priority as a waiver, but may establish procedures (including a surcharge) to accept an unintentionally delayed claim.
guidance: The Director may require a certified copy of the original foreign application, specification, and drawings upon which it is based, a translation if not in English, and any other information deemed necessary. Certification must be by the foreign intellectual property authority and show application and filing dates. Acceptance procedures may include payment of a surcharge.

name: General rule for incorporation by reference under 37 CFR 1.57(a)
description: If all or a portion of the specification or drawings is inadvertently omitted from an application, but the application contains a claim under 37 CFR 1.55 (foreign priority) or 37 CFR 1.78 (benefit of prior-filed provisional/nonprovisional/international application) that was present on the filing date, and the omitted portion is completely contained in the prior-filed application, the claim shall be considered an incorporation by reference of the prior-filed application as to the omitted portion.
guidance: This provides a safeguard for applicants when material was inadvertently omitted (e.g., clerical error) and allows that material to be added later by amendment if other requirements are met. See also explicit incorporation guidance in MPEP § 608.01(p).

name: Examiner responsibility to verify prior-application data (cross-noting)
description: Examiners should review the identifying data of all prior applications for which benefits are claimed to ensure accuracy and that the data is provided in the specification or application data sheet (see 37 CFR 1.78(a) and MPEP § 201.11).
guidance: Front page of printed patent identifies prior applications for which benefits are claimed. Where prior application data is preprinted on PALM bib-data sheet, the examiner should check that data for accuracy and initial the PALM bib-data sheet in the provided space when correct. Corrections to preprinted data can be made by Technology Center technical support staff, and a new sheet printed and scanned into the file. Inclusion of prior application information on the patent front page does not necessarily indicate claims are entitled to the earlier filing date.

name: Step-one focus: look to the claimed advance over the prior art
description: At Alice step one, the court looks at 'the focus of the claimed advance over the prior art' to determine whether the claim's character as a whole is directed to excluded subject matter and avoid overgeneralization.
guidance: Be careful not to overgeneralize claims into high-level abstractions (which would render nearly all inventions 'abstract'), nor to be misled by drafting that attempts to monopolize an abstract idea. (Affinity Labs, Diamond v. Diehr cited.)

name: Software-specific inquiry: specific asserted improvement vs generic computer implementation
description: In software cases, inquiry often turns on whether claims focus on 'the specific asserted improvement in computer capabilities' or instead on a process that invokes computers merely as a tool.
guidance: If the claims recite a software-specific improvement (e.g., a new data structure or new way of scanning/attaching security profiles), they are more likely to be non-abstract. Refer to Enfish, Finjan, McRO examples.

name: Requirement of specific means/method — improved result insufficient
description: Merely stating an 'improved result' is insufficient for eligibility; the patent must recite a 'specific means or method that solves a problem in an existing technological process.'
guidance: Claims that only promise an improved result without specifying how to achieve it are inadequate (Koninklijke KPN v. Gemalto cited).

name: Purely functional language and conventional technology indicates abstractness
description: Claims that recite only purely functional language and use conventional technology in a typical manner are likely directed to an abstract idea and not eligible.
guidance: Such claims risk covering an abstract combination of processes without adding 'any particular assertedly inventive technology.' (Electric Power Group cited.)

name: Claims that recite mental processes or mathematical algorithms are abstract
description: Claims that merely recite steps people go through in their minds, or mathematical algorithms, without more, are treated as abstract mental processes.
guidance: If claim elements can be performed mentally or are standard algorithms not tied to a technical improvement, they are likely ineligible. (TLI example cited.)

name: Fixed subject-matter with fixed parameters required
description: Eligibility favors claims that define some fixed subject-matter with fixed parameters—i.e., specific steps or structures with defined characteristics—rather than sweeping functional descriptions.
guidance: Patents like Finjan and Enfish were non-abstract because they claimed concrete, software-specific structures or steps that improved computer functionality.

name: A result alone is not patentable; must claim specific steps to achieve it
description: An innovative result standing alone does not render a claim patentable; the claims must recite the specific steps or means that accomplish that result.
guidance: Courts look for the particular steps that accomplish an improvement; bare recitation of the result is insufficient (Finjan cited).

name: Preemption is the central concern in Alice/Mayo
description: Preventing preemption of fundamental building blocks (abstract ideas, laws of nature) is central to the Alice/Mayo analysis; claims that would effectively monopolize an abstract idea weigh against eligibility.
guidance: The analysis should ensure claims do not foreclose future innovation by broadly preempting use of an abstract idea or basic tool.

name: Claim construction definitions (Judge Davis)
description: Court's claim constructions: (1) 'Data items' = 'sequence of bits'; (2) 'Data files' = 'a named data item(s)'; (3) 'Substantially unique identifier, Data identifier, True Name, Digital identifier, Data item identifier' = 'an identity for a data item generated by processing all of the data in the data item, and only the data in the data item, through an algorithm that makes the identifier substantially unique.'
guidance: These constructions guide how the asserted claims are interpreted in eligibility and validity analyses; precise construction can affect novelty and eligibility outcomes.

name: Hash vs. message digest equivalence (technical note)
description: The True Name patents use the terms 'hash' and 'message digest' interchangeably; 'message digest' functions (like MD5) are a type of hash function.
guidance: This equivalence matters when construing claims that refer to 'hash' or 'message digest' functions and when comparing to prior-art disclosures that may use differing terminology.

name: Novelty nuance: one-to-one comparison vs comparing to a plurality (PersonalWeb)
description: A prior-art system that inherently discloses only one-to-one comparisons of content-based identifiers does not necessarily anticipate a claim that requires comparing a content-based identifier with a plurality of identifiers; this distinction can support novelty.
guidance: Federal Circuit reversed PTAB where prior art did not inherently disclose comparing one identifier against multiple identifiers (PersonalWeb v. Apple). Careful parsing of prior-art capabilities vs claimed features is required.

name: Device reduced to practice must include every limitation of the count
description: The device reduced to practice must include every limitation of the count; every limitation in a count is material and must be proved to establish an actual reduction to practice.
guidance: Cite Fredkin v. Irasek; Meitzner v. Corte; Hull v. Bonis. There is no doctrine of equivalents for establishing an actual reduction to practice — remedy is a preliminary motion to amend the count to conform to proofs. Examiner/advocate must show each claim limitation is present in the reduction-to-practice example or test.

name: Utility must be known at time of reduction to practice
description: A claimed invention is not actually reduced to practice unless there is a known (practical) utility at the time of reduction to practice (except for plant and design inventions).
guidance: Cite Wiesner v. Weigert; Azar v. Burns; Ciric v. Flanigen; Engelhardt v. Judd; Rey-Bellet v. Engelhardt. For counts that do not recite a specific utility, evidence establishing a substantial utility for any purpose can suffice. Animal tests can be adequate in some circumstances where correlation to human utility exists or to show utility for animals.

name: Weigh the body of evidence for reasonable continuous diligence
description: Examiners should weigh the collection of evidence over the entire critical period to determine whether the invention was not abandoned or unreasonably delayed; absence of daily or frequent records is not alone dispositive.
guidance: Cite Perfect Surgical Techniques (841 F.3d). The point is to avoid scouring for gaps if the overall evidence shows lack of abandonment. In re Mulder does not mandate that any inactivity necessarily destroys a diligence claim — context and quantity of corroborating evidence matter.

name: Work relied upon to show diligence must be directly related to the reduction to practice
description: The work relied upon to show reasonable diligence must be directly related to the reduction to practice of the claimed invention; activity on related subject matter is insufficient unless it is closely related and directly advances reduction to practice.
guidance: Cite Naber v. Cricchi; Scott v. Koyama; In re Jolley; Gunn v. Bosch; Ginos v. Nedelec. Preparatory acts (e.g., building plant to practice a process) can be credited; work on closely related inventions may be credited in some circumstances. Fortuitous reductions while working on a different invention do not show diligence toward the invention in issue. Corroboration requirements and specifics of the inventor's circumstances should be considered.

name: Effective filing date under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102
description: For applications subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102, the effective filing date of the claimed invention is the actual U.S. filing date of the application unless special situations apply (A, B, C).
guidance: Situations: (A) continuation/divisional/priority under 35 U.S.C. 120/365(c) — effective date equals earliest in line if requirements met; (B) continuation-in-part — claims not supported by parent get new actual filing date; claims fully supported under 35 U.S.C. 112 get parent's effective date; (C) proper 35 U.S.C. 119(e) benefit to a provisional gives provisional filing date for fully supported claims. Note: national stage filing date and international filing date issues (MPEP cross-references).

name: Use of form paragraphs for pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 rejections
description: Office actions should use standardized form paragraphs for rejections under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 (e.g., ¶7.06, ¶7.07.fti, ¶7.08.fti, ¶7.09.fti, ¶7.10.fti, ¶7.11.fti, ¶7.12.fti), with specific ordering and usage rules.
guidance: ¶7.06 must be used in all Office Actions when a prior art rejection is made in an application with an actual filing date on or after March 16, 2013 that claims priority to an application filed before March 16, 2013; use it only once per Office action. ¶7.07.fti quotes the pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 statutory text and is required in first actions on the merits and final rejections (and used only once per action). Other ¶7.0x.fti paragraphs correspond to specific 102(a)-(e) grounds and must be preceded by ¶7.07.fti as indicated. Examiner notes in the MPEP explain precise sequencing and when each paragraph should or must be used.

name: Model: its General Requisites
description: A model must clearly exhibit every feature of the invention which forms the subject of a Claim, but should not include any other matter than that covered by the actual invention, unless it be necessary to the representation of the invention in a working model.
guidance: Working model often desirable to show precise operation. Model must be neatly and substantially made of durable material (metal preferred) unless material is an essential feature. Size, finish, and other minor requisites must conform to Patent Office regulations; sufficiency is conclusively determined by the Office. A model should not include unrelated matter except as necessary for representation.

name: Model: its Relation to other Parts of the Application
description: The filing of a model does not constitute the filing of an application, nor is it any evidence that the application is complete. Each portion of the application must be judged by itself. A sufficient model does not validate an imperfect Description nor an improper Claim, nor supply the place of an accurate drawing.
guidance: A model corresponds with the specification and drawings only so far as it adheres to established rules; it cannot cure defective written disclosure or improper claims. Filing a model alone will not start prosecution or substitute for required papers.

name: Examination of Application: Objections to Its Form
description: On the receipt of any application in the Office, and the payment of the fee, it is assigned to its proper class, and when its turn arrives is first subjected to an examination to determine whether it is in all respects in proper form. If found to be formally sufficient, an examination into the merits of the application, and the patentability of the invention therein claimed, is instituted. But if decided to be insufficient the applicant is notified of the defect, and such information is given to him as will enable him to judge of the propriety of the decision, and, if possible, to correct his error. Upon this notice he may either supply the alleged defect, or he may insist upon the sufficiency of the application and file a written request for a reconsideration, distinctly and specifically pointing out the errors in the finding of the examiner.
guidance: Examiners should state all formal objections and reasons (preferably in first letter); formal matters should be settled before rejecting claims on the merits. Applicant may request reconsideration or appeal. An examiner may consider merits despite form defects only if he gives the applicant sufficient information to remove the defects and states formal objections as required. The PTO must act as a friend to the applicant and aid in securing the actual invention when appropriate.

name: Examination on Merits: Questions to be Determined
description: This examination consists in an inquiry into the legal right of the applicant to a patent for the invention described and claimed in the application. It involves two questions: (1) Whether the subject-matter of the application is, in itself, a patentable invention; (2) Whether the applicant or his decedent was its true and first inventor. The former question is divisible into five subordinate ones: (1) Whether the subject-matter of the application is the result of a true and complete inventive act; (2) Whether it is embraced in either one of the six classes of inventions which are made patentable by the act of Congress; (3) Whether it is new; (4) Whether it is useful; (5) Whether it has been abandoned to the public.
guidance: In uncontested cases the oath is prima facie proof of priority; the examiner is not bound by strict rules of evidence but must ascertain as best he can from publications, patents, and general knowledge whether to allow or reject. The examiner must follow Commissioner's decisions and court rules. If patentable and inventor is true/first inventor, allowance; if not, rejection; if doubt, decision either way to permit reconsideration/appeal.

name: Rejection of Application: Notice and References
description: When an application, or one of the Claims in an application, is rejected upon any ground whatever the examiner is required to notify the applicant of such rejection, stating all his reasons therefor fully and precisely, and giving him such information and references as may assist him in judging of the advisability of prosecuting his application or of altering his specification. If the ground of the rejection be that the applicant is not the true and first inventor of the art or instrument described, the examiner must cite references establishing his assertion, or himself make oath to it, to overcome the presumption arising from the oath of the alleged inventor.
guidance: If rejection is for lack of novelty, the examiner must disclose all his information citing the best references: prior patents (date, number, patentee, class), prior publications (title, date, page/plate, place where copy may be procured), and any factual references supported by affidavit. Pertinence must be clearly explained and the anticipated Claim particularly specified. Devices cited need not have commercial value nor be identical in form, material, or mode of use—substantial correspondence suffices. An abandoned or rejected application is generally not a public document for prior knowledge, and the examiner is not obliged to suggest proper claims; all references and objections should be cited on or before final rejection (though late-discovered references may be urged promptly thereafter).

name: Patent subject‑matter eligibility (Mayo/Alice framework)
description: Patent claims must pass the Mayo/Alice two‑step test: (1) determine whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea (or other ineligible subject matter), and (2) determine whether the claim contains an inventive concept that transforms the abstract idea into a new and useful process.
guidance: The two‑step test renders patentability of algorithm- and AI-based innovations uncertain; evaluate whether an invention can be framed to survive the Mayo/Alice inquiry.

name: Nonobviousness (inventive step) standard and KSR impact
description: Claims must be nonobvious (involve an inventive step); KSR Int’l Co. v. Teleflex broadened the scope of the nonobviousness inquiry and criticized overly rigid tests.
guidance: KSR warns against limiting the analysis; the USPTO's nonobviousness guidelines reflect KSR's expansive inquiry. Increased nonobviousness scrutiny makes patents more vulnerable to invalidation; assess inventiveness in light of modern, flexible obviousness analysis.

name: Product-characterizable manufacturing-method claims
description: When a claimed invention (e.g., a product defined by a manufacturing method) can be characterized by certain properties, features, and composition based on the method description, the examiner can determine inventive step by comparing the product defined by the manufacturing method with the cited invention without considering the manufacturing method.
guidance: Example: a belt coupling apparatus described with a manufacturing method — if there is no difficulty characterizing the seat belt via its composition, inventive step may be determined by comparing the product with prior art, disregarding the manufacturing steps. Conversely, if the manufacturing method produces a measurable change in product properties (e.g., increased inorganic content in tea leaves by heating/IR), inventive step may be acknowledged because of the change in product properties.

name: Definition of combination invention
description: A combination invention comprises novel solutions by gathering technical features disclosed in the prior art as a whole in order to solve a technical problem. The invention described in a claim is to be considered as a whole.
guidance: Determination of inventive step for combination inventions relies on the technical idea of the claimed invention as a whole, not on whether each individual element is known. Examiner shall consider difficulty in forming structurally combined elements and the unique effect the invention has as a whole.

name: Combining multiple prior-art disclosures
description: Determining inventive step by combining more than two disclosures is allowed, but limited to situations where a person skilled in the art could easily combine the disclosures at the time of filing.
guidance: No strict limit on the number of prior-art disclosures to be combined, but when combining various prior arts, the examiner mainly considers whether the cited inventions contain a motivation or hint leading to the claimed invention by combining the disclosures, the state of the art, common general knowledge, technical trends and industry demands. If combination is deemed easily made by a skilled person, inventive step may be denied (citing relevant precedent).

name: Consideration of how many prior arts are combined
description: Care must be taken because the higher number of combined cited inventions, the more likely the claimed invention results from an ex post facto view or lacks a valid reason for rejection.
guidance: When determining whether it would have been obvious to combine two or more prior arts, examiner should consider: (①) whether there is a good possibility to combine them, ②) whether the prior arts come from similar or neighboring technical fields, and ③) whether there is a reasonable basis to associate them.

name: Caution against ex post facto reasoning from the specification
description: When determining inventive step in light of knowledge obtained from matters disclosed in the specification under examination, examiners should avoid concluding obviousness by using the specification (i.e., avoid ex post facto analysis).
guidance: Example: if cited invention merely mentions an objective like 'preventing others noticing a voice reception' but does not disclose the specific technical structure (e.g., tapping mode blocking reception while allowing emission), it is improper to conclude obviousness by retrofitting the claimed structure to the cited disclosure.

name: Dependent claims and inventive step
description: If an independent claim has an inventive step, a claim dependent on that independent claim is deemed to have an inventive step too. If the independent claim does not have an inventive step, determination should be made for each dependent claim individually.
guidance: When independent claim lacks inventive step, do not automatically dismiss dependents — examine their specific limitations.

name: Product inventions imply process/use inventive step
description: If a product invention explicitly has an inventive step, a process invention for making the product or a use invention for using the product also has an inventive step in principle.
guidance: This is a general presumption; specific process/use claims still need individual assessment when necessary.

name: Markush/multiple-selective alternatives caution
description: For claims in Markush form or comprising multiple selective technical features, if at least one Markush alternative is proven not to have an inventive step based on prior art, the applicant can be notified of refusal for the claim; the applicant may overcome refusal by deleting alternatives that lack inventive step.
guidance: Care must be taken not to expand the effect of one selective element to the whole claimed invention. All alternatives (e.g., chemical compounds) must show remarkable effect over cited prior inventions for grant based on that effect.

name: Legal prohibition irrelevant to inventive step
description: Implementation prohibited by law (domestic or foreign) is not taken into consideration in determining inventive step.
