guidance: Even if claimed method is illegal (e.g., certain lottery drawing methods), inventive step is assessed on technical difficulty and not on legal permissibility.

name: Article 29(3)/(4) — earlier application as prior art (enlarged novelty)
description: Where an invention claimed in a patent application is identical with an invention described in the specification or drawings originally attached to another application filed prior to the filing date of the concerned application and later laid open/published, the patent may not be granted — with exceptions where inventors/applicants are the same.
guidance: Purpose: prevent giving exclusive rights to later applicants for inventions already contributed to the public via earlier laid-open specifications/drawings. The proviso allows exceptions if inventor or applicant is the same person at time of filing.

name: Priority claim effects for determining filing date of another application
description: If another application is one with a priority claim under the Paris Convention, the filing date in the country of origin is deemed the filing date for inventions commonly disclosed in the original specification/drawings.
guidance: Only inventions actually disclosed in the priority-country filing count for the earlier filing date; inventions missing from that filing cannot be cited under Article 29(3).

name: Treatment of commonly disclosed matters between prior and subsequent applications
description: When an examiner cites an invention initially disclosed in the specification of a prior application that was a basis for a domestic priority claim or a subsequent application, matters commonly disclosed in initial specifications of both prior and subsequent applications are treated as having filing date of the prior application (or sometimes the subsequent application depending on domestic priority rules).
guidance: Rules distinguish inventions commonly disclosed in both, inventions solely in initial specification of subsequent (treated as filed on subsequent filing date), and inventions solely disclosed in initial specification of prior (not applied). Amended disclosures after filing are not treated as laid-open for Article 29(3)/(4).

name: Requirement that the claimed invention be identical to invention in initial specification of another application
description: An invention described in the claims of the present application should be completely or substantially identical to an invention or device described in the initial specification of another application to trigger Article 29(3)/(4).
guidance: Even if the matters were omitted by amendment after filing, Article 29(3) still applies. The 'identity' requirement is substantive (complete or substantial identity).

name: Two-step approach (origin-of-claim then application of §1.263(a)-4)
description: A two-step test (used by the Court of Federal Claims and described in the opinion) first applies the origin-of-the-claim doctrine to ascertain the character and nature of the expenditures, then applies the capitalization-of-intangibles regulations (C.F.R. § 1.263(a)-4) to that ascertained character to determine whether capitalization is required.
guidance: This hybrid approach focuses first on the nature of the litigation (what claim is being litigated) and then asks whether, given that nature, the expenses fall within regulatory categories requiring capitalization (e.g., amounts paid to facilitate creation of an intangible). The Federal Circuit noted it need not decide the correctness of the hybrid approach because the outcome was the same under either test.

name: Parity principle for patent litigation — defense costs generally deductible
description: Expenses incurred defending against ordinary patent infringement claims are generally deductible on the theory that the taxpayer is protecting or maintaining its income-generating business.
guidance: Because §271(e) Hatch-Waxman suits are litigated in essentially the same manner as ordinary patent infringement suits, the Court relied on the established deduction treatment in ordinary patent litigation to support deductibility for ANDA filers defending §271(e) claims; imposing different tax treatment on the opposing parties in the same litigation would be incongruous.

name: Application-specific criterion for Hatch-Waxman disputes — origin is patentee's §271(e) claim, not ANDA approval
description: For ANDA filers facing Hatch-Waxman suits, the origin of the litigation expense is the NDA holder's patent infringement claim (Section 271(e) Claim) rather than the ANDA filer's pursuit of FDA approval; thus such expenses are not incurred 'in the process of acquisition' of an FDA approval asset.
guidance: Court's applied reasoning: FDA review and patent litigation are distinct 'lanes,' resolved by different decisionmakers; the litigation may affect timing (e.g., 30-month stay) but does not control FDA's substantive approval decision, so the litigation does not constitute facilitation or acquisition of the FDA-approved intangible and therefore is deductible.

name: Classes are determined by characters, not solely by Type
description: Though groups are often suggested by types, a group when formed is determined by characters; it is inconsistent to claim classes are given by type and not by characters.
guidance: A class must possess characters enabling general assertions; reliance purely on resemblance to a type risks missing the true Kind.

name: Diagnostic methods exclusion (with in vitro exception)
description: Diagnostic methods are not eligible. “Method of extracting samples and data from the human body, or methods of analyzing, e.g., comparing such samples and data with standards, by utilizing samples and data extracted from the human body […] preparatory treatment for measuring structures or functions of various organs of the human body” are not such diagnostic methods so long as they are not claimed in conjunction with diagnosing a disease.
guidance: Some jurisdictions (e.g., JPO, KIPO, SIPO) carve out that methods consisting of steps separable from medical practice (e.g., treatment of samples extracted from the body or in vitro analysis) may be considered industrially applicable and not fall under the diagnostic-method exclusion. Example: EPO Technical Board found an in vitro method for diagnosing predisposition patent-eligible because technical steps were carried out in vitro and not directly on the subject.

name: China: exclusion of 'rules and methods for mental activities' and SIPO revision
description: China Patent Act excludes 'rules and methods for mental activities'; however, SIPO revised guidelines state a claimed invention having technical characteristics will not be excluded from patentability because it contains a business method or rule.
guidance: Post-revision, SIPO treats business-method-containing claims as potentially patentable when technical characteristics are present. Practitioners should emphasize technical character in specifications and claims when pursuing business-method-related inventions in China.

name: JPO hardware-implementation requirement for computer-related inventions
description: Under JPO guidelines, eligibility of computer-related technology turns on whether, when the invention is considered as a whole, its information-processing aspects are required to be 'specifically implemented by using hardware resources.'
guidance: JPO provides non-exhaustive examples of patent-eligible computer-related inventions (e.g., software to control appliances, software tied to physical/chemical relationships); focus claims on concrete hardware implementation or specific machine execution to satisfy eligibility.

name: KIPO software-plus-hardware / medium exception
description: KIPO guidelines state that a computer program per se is not a statutory invention, but software claimed in conjunction with hardware, the operating method of the combination, and a computer-readable medium containing the software that implicates the combination is patent eligible.
guidance: Draft claims that recite a specific machine, combination, or computer-readable medium with functional tie-ins to hardware to avoid 'program per se' rejections in Korea.

name: Mayo/Alice two-step patent-eligibility framework (as-applied standard)
description: Supreme Court's two-part eligibility test established in Mayo and developed in Alice (commonly applied in U.S. practice): (1) determine whether the claim is directed to a patent-ineligible concept (e.g., law of nature, natural phenomenon, abstract idea); (2) if so, determine whether claim elements, considered individually and as an ordered combination, contain an 'inventive concept' that transforms the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application.
guidance: This framework is the focal point of U.S. eligibility analysis and litigation; commentators debate its scope and application. Practical guidance: draft claims and specifications to recite concrete implementations, inventive concept details, and technical improvements to survive each step.

name: Requirement to claim a specific way, not just a result (anti-preemption principle)
description: Patents should be awarded for the particular way an inventor achieved a result rather than claiming only the result itself; claiming only the abstract result can preempt others from achieving the same utility by different means.
guidance: Emphasize specific algorithms, mechanisms, technical steps, or implementations in claims and disclosures; avoid claiming only the problem and its abstract solution. This principle is frequently invoked in software and business-method contexts.

name: Need for 'technical improvement' / 'technological solution' as entitlement to eligibility
description: A focus on whether the invention provides a technological improvement or technological solution can be central to eligibility determinations (emphasized in Federal Circuit precedent and many commentator submissions).
guidance: Draft and argue claims to show measurable technological benefits or specific technical effects (e.g., improved processing, reduced resource usage, improved device performance) rather than abstract advantages or business benefits.

name: Demand for objective, predictable, administrable eligibility criteria
description: Critics argue the Mayo/Alice two-step test is 'hopelessly subjective and unworkable' because key terms like 'abstract' and 'substantially more' lack objective definitions; calls exist for transparent, objective, predictable, and simple rules defining eligible subject matter.
guidance: When drafting or prosecuting, articulate clear factual support for why claims are concrete/technical and explain application of precedent; policymakers/examiners are urged to develop clearer bright-line or technology-specific guidance to improve predictability.

name: Identify and explain laws of nature or natural phenomena recited in the claim
description: If the claim recites a law of nature or natural phenomenon, the rejection should identify that law or phenomenon as recited in the claim and explain using a reasoned rationale why it is considered a law of nature or natural phenomenon.
guidance: See MPEP §2106.04(b) for more information. Sample explanations: (1) claim recites a correlation that is a law of nature because it describes a consequence of natural processes in the human body; (2) claim recites X which is a natural phenomenon because it occurs in nature and exists apart from human action.

name: Explain why additional elements do or do not add significantly more (Step 2B)
description: For Step 2B, the rejection should explain why the additional elements, taken individually and in combination, do not result in the claim, as a whole, amounting to significantly more than the identified judicial exception.
guidance: If the examiner has concluded particular limitations are well-understood, routine, conventional activities, the rejection must expressly support that conclusion in writing with one of the evidentiary options in Subsection III. Address whether a new combination meaningfully limits the judicial exception (Diamond v. Diehr); a combination of well-known elements may nevertheless amount to significantly more.

name: Rejection threshold: only when readily apparent based on examiner expertise
description: A rejection should be made only if it is readily apparent to an examiner relying on the examiner’s expertise in the art in the Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B inquiries that the additional elements do not integrate the exception into a practical application and do not amount to significantly more.
guidance: When making a rejection, explain the rationale underlying the conclusion so that applicant can effectively respond. If appropriate, explain why additional elements integrate an exception or provide an inventive concept. See MPEP §2106.07(c) for clarifying the record when a claim is found eligible.

name: Supporting assertion that elements are well-understood, routine, conventional (evidentiary requirement)
description: Examiners should not assert that an additional element (or combination of elements) is well-understood, routine, or conventional unless the examiner finds, and expressly supports the rejection in writing with one or more of the following options (A–D).
guidance: Option A: citation to express statement in the specification or applicant’s prosecution statement demonstrating routine/conventional nature (specification describing element as well-understood/routine/conventional or commercially available). Option B: citation to one or more court decisions that note the conventional nature of the element(s), ensuring the claim limitations match those in the decisions and are recited at the same high level of generality. Option C: citation to a publication (book/manual/review article) demonstrating the element is widely prevalent or in common use in the relevant field; the publication must show prevalence comparable to elements that need not be described in detail to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112(a). Option D: official notice by the examiner that the element is widely prevalent or in common use, used only when examiner is certain based on personal knowledge; procedures for taking official notice are in MPEP §2144.03. Avoid relying solely on specification silence to find an element conventional.

name: Evidentiary posture for Step 2A Prong One (no requirement for external evidence)
description: When performing the analysis at Step 2A Prong One, it is sufficient for the examiner to provide a reasoned rationale identifying the judicial exception recited in the claim and explaining why it is considered a judicial exception without relying on external evidence.
guidance: There is no requirement to rely on publications, affidavits, or declarations to find a claim recites a judicial exception. Courts have affirmed identification of abstract ideas without evidence. However, factual showings may be required when asserting elements are well-understood, routine, conventional in Step 2B (see Subsection III).

name: Generic computer functions and how to treat them
description: For claim limitations that recite a generic computer component performing generic computer functions at a high level of generality (e.g., using the Internet to gather data), examiners can explain why these generic computing functions do not meaningfully limit the claim.
guidance: Keep in mind that courts have found computer-implemented processes to be significantly more than an abstract idea where generic computer components in combination perform functions that are not merely generic (DDR Holdings). See MPEP §2106.05(f) for information about generic computing functions courts have found to be mere instructions to implement a judicial exception on a computer, and MPEP §2106.05(d) for information about well-understood, routine, conventional activities.

name: Address additional elements both individually and in combination
description: When analyzing whether a claim integrates an exception into a practical application or amounts to significantly more, the explanation should address additional elements both individually and as a combination.
guidance: A new combination of steps may be patent eligible even though all steps were individually known (Diamond v. Diehr). Therefore it is critical to consider whether the combination meaningfully limits the judicial exception (see MPEP §2106.05).

name: Consult the specification and suggest claim amendments when appropriate
description: When a rejection is made, it is a best practice for the examiner to consult the specification to determine if there are elements that could be added to the claim to make it eligible and, if so, identify those elements in the Office action as suggestions to overcome the rejection.
guidance: This helps compact prosecution and assists applicants in overcoming eligibility rejections.

name: Use of specified form paragraphs and required content for §101 rejections
description: Use the specified form paragraphs (e.g., 7.04.01, 7.05, 7.05.01, 7.05.016, 7.05.017) for §101 rejections and follow the ordering and bracketed-content instructions.
guidance: Examples: form paragraph 7.04.01 (Statement of Statutory Basis) must precede first use of 35 U.S.C. 101 in first actions/final rejections. Form paragraph 7.05 should be preceded by 7.04.01 and followed by detailed explanation using other form paragraphs. Form paragraph 7.05.016 (Nonstatutory directed to judicial exception without inventive concept) requires bracketed content: [1] identify whether claim directed to law of nature/natural phenomenon/abstract idea; [2] identify the exception by referring to how recited in claim and explain why considered an exception (e.g., identify abstract-idea grouping); [3] explain why combination of additional elements fails to integrate the judicial exception into a practical application; [4] explain why additional elements do not amount to significantly more. If the exception is a tentative abstract idea, include form paragraph 7.05.017 and the TC Director's signature.

name: Care in citing court decisions as evidence of conventionality
description: When relying on court decisions to support that an element is well-understood, routine, conventional, ensure the claim limitations under examination are the same as those found conventional by the courts and are recited at the same high level of generality.
guidance: It is not enough that the additional elements are similar to elements in those cases. Also, court decisions referenced are not meant to imply all computer functions are conventional or that claims reciting generic computer components are necessarily ineligible; DDR Holdings illustrates exceptions. See MPEP §2106.05(d) and §2106.05(f).

name: Adoptive sonship (filiatio adoptiva) as a formal effect
description: Sanctifying grace culminates in the adoption of the justified as children of God—an adopted sonship with claim to the paternal inheritance (the beatific vision); this is taught by Scripture and defined by Trent as inseparable from justification.
guidance: Scriptural proofs include Rom. viii; 1 John iii; Gal. iv. St. Thomas’ elements of adoption (the adopted is a stranger to the adopter, has no legal claim, gives consent, and is received with parental love) are applied analogically: adoption is gratuitous, confers a spiritual inheritance, presupposes the consent of the adult soul, and elevates the creature to participation in the Divine Nature. The text also distinguishes between the natural Son (Christ) and adopted sons (creatures): Christ cannot be adopted; adopted sonship is analogical and accidental. Debated issues include whether Old Testament just were adopted sons (Trent rejects denial) and whether adoptive sonship requires the personal indwelling of the Holy Ghost (see controversy between Scheeben and Granderath; Scheeben: sanctifying grace alone suffices though the indwelling perfects it).

name: Use inter partes review (IPR) at PTAB to challenge low‑quality patents
description: Filing IPR petitions at the PTAB is presented as an effective tactic to invalidate bad patents; Unified Patents has filed IPRs against patents asserted by NPEs (examples: U.S. Patent 5,966,658 and U.S. Patent 9,047,626).
guidance: Unified Patents' approach—bringing IPRs against prolific NPE-owned patents—is given as a practical model (similar in spirit to EFF). The post cites specific institution decisions (PTAB instituting trial on challenged claims) as evidence of IPRs' effectiveness.

name: Contents that qualify a 37 CFR 1.501 submission for entry
description: A 37 CFR 1.501 submission is proper (and should be entered) if it is limited to patents, printed publications, and/or patent owner written claim scope statements and additional information and includes the requisite citation description and proof of service.
guidance: If proper, the submission will be entered into the patent file; submissions received under 37 CFR 1.501 will be forwarded to the Technology Center that examines the class/subclass of the patent. See forms PTO/SB/08A/08B or PTO/SB/42 for citation listing (MPEP § 2217).

name: Non-qualifying 1.501 submissions (general)
description: If the 1.501 submission is not limited to patents/printed publications/patent-owner written claim scope statements and additional information, or it fails to include the requisite description/information or proof of service, it will not be entered into the patent file.
guidance: The handling varies by situation (see specific service scenarios); the third-party submitter (if known) and patent owner may be notified that the citation submission is improper and is not being entered.

name: Ex parte reexamination basic characteristics
description: Anyone can request ex parte reexamination at any time during the period of enforceability of the patent; for reexaminations ordered under 35 U.S.C. 304, prior art considered is limited to prior art patents or printed publications applied under 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103.
guidance: A substantial new question of patentability must be present for reexamination to be ordered. If ordered, the reexamination is ex parte in nature, decisions on requests must be made no later than 3 months, proceedings are to proceed with 'special dispatch', scope of a claim cannot be enlarged by amendment, and reexamination files are open to the public (with certain electronic access caveats). Parties must avoid 'litigation tactics' and multiple submissions such as replies/surreplies that are not provided for by the regulations; adherence to 37 CFR 11.18(b) is expected.

name: 37 CFR 1.510(b) required parts — identification and detailed explanation for every claim
description: The request must identify every claim for which reexamination is requested and provide a detailed explanation of the pertinency and manner of applying the cited prior art to each claim.
guidance: For each SNQ and proposed ground, the request must explain how the cited documents are applied to meet or teach the patent claim limitations to establish the SNQ or ground. If relying on any patent owner statement submitted under §1.501(a)(2), the request must explain how that statement is used to determine the proper meaning of the claim in connection with the prior art. The detailed explanation will be considered by the Office if reexamination is ordered; an owner's claim scope statements will not be considered at the order stage (35 U.S.C. 301(d)).

name: 37 CFR 1.510(b) required parts — copy of entire patent
description: The request must include a copy of the entire patent (front face, drawings, specification/claims in double column format) and copies of any disclaimer, certificate of correction, or reexamination certificate issued in the patent. All copies must have each page plainly written on only one side of a sheet.
guidance: Proper paper formatting and completeness of the patent copy are required for processing and acceptance.

name: Substantial new question (SNQ) assertion and explanation requirement
description: A request for reexamination must assert a substantial new question of patentability and for each identified SNQ and each proposed ground of rejection must explain how the cited documents raise that SNQ.
guidance: The cited prior art should be listed on appropriate PTO forms. The requester must not argue that the references do not raise an SNQ (i.e., do not negate the presence of an SNQ). Each SNQ and proposed ground must be identified separately and fully explained as applied to claim limitations (see MPEP § 2216 and § 2217).

name: Laws of nature, natural phenomena, and products of nature exceptions
description: Laws of nature and natural phenomena include naturally occurring principles/relations and nature-based products that are naturally occurring or that do not have markedly different characteristics compared to what occurs in nature; court decisions have called these exceptions by various names (e.g., physical phenomena, scientific principles, natural laws, products of nature).
guidance: These exceptions reflect that basic scientific and technological tools are not patentable (e.g., Funk Bros., Diamond v. Chakrabarty, Parker v. Flook). The Manual lists many court-identified examples (isolated DNA; cloned farm animals; correlations between genetic variations and alleles; metabolic correlations; naturally occurring biomarkers; electromagnetic phenomena; bacterial qualities; primers; chemical principles; cell-free fetal DNA; genotype–drug response relationships). Even if a claim describes a natural ability or quality, it might not recite an exception if it is focused on process steps or treatments (see Rapid Litig. Mgmt. v. CellzDirect and examples of treatment claims).

name: Claims reciting a law/natural phenomenon require Step 2A Prong Two analysis
description: A claim that recites a law of nature or natural phenomenon requires further analysis in Step 2A Prong Two to determine whether the claim integrates the exception into a practical application.
guidance: Even if a claim recites such an exception, it may still be eligible under Pathways A–C if it integrates the exception into a practical application (e.g., Vanda — genotype-tailored treatment step integrated the natural relationship). If a claim does not recite a law/phenomenon, it is eligible at Pathway B (Step 2A: NO) unless it recites another exception.

name: Scope of the markedly different characteristics analysis
description: The markedly different characteristics analysis is part of Step 2A Prong One and is used to identify product-of-nature exceptions by comparing the claimed nature-based product to its naturally occurring counterpart.
guidance: Apply this analysis only to nature-based product limitations in the claim (not to non-nature elements). Nature-based products include both eligible and ineligible products. If a product has markedly different characteristics, it is not a product of nature (Step 2A: NO) unless another exception is recited; if it lacks such characteristics, it is a product-of-nature exception and requires Prong Two analysis.

name: Application to combination and kit claims
description: When a claim is to a nature-based product produced by combining multiple components, analyze the resultant nature-based combination; when a nature-based product is claimed with non-nature elements, analyze only the nature-based limitation.
guidance: Example: For a probiotic composition comprising Lactobacillus and milk, analyze the mixture as the nature-based product. For a yogurt starter kit comprising Lactobacillus plus container and instructions, analyze the Lactobacillus for markedly different characteristics; evaluate container/instructions as additional elements in Prong Two/Step 2B if the Lactobacillus is a product-of-nature exception.

name: Process claims generally not subject to markedly different analysis
description: A process claim is generally not subject to the markedly different characteristics analysis for nature-based products used in the process because process analysis should focus on active steps.
guidance: Example: Rapid Litig. Mgmt. v. CellzDirect — process of creating a preparation of cryopreserved hepatocytes was analyzed as a process, not by comparing hepatocytes used in the steps. However, if a process claim is drafted so that it is substantively no different from a product claim (i.e., effectively focuses on the product), then the markedly different analysis applies to the recited nature-based product.

name: Broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) considerations and claim breadth issues
description: Under BRI, a nature-based product limitation may encompass both eligible and ineligible embodiments; examiners should consider BRI when determining whether the claim recites a product of nature.
guidance: Example: a claim to a 'cloned giraffe' could, under BRI, encompass cloned giraffes with and without markedly different characteristics. If claim breadth encompasses ineligible embodiments, the claim recites a product of nature and requires Prong Two/Step 2B analysis. If rejected, examiners should point out the BRI and recommend amendments to narrow the claim to eligible embodiments if possible.

name: Examiner best practices when rejecting on product-of-nature grounds
description: When rejecting claims as product-of-nature exceptions, the examiner should identify the selected natural counterpart and recommend claim amendments if possible to narrow claim scope to eligible embodiments.
guidance: Identifying the selected counterpart in the Office action assists applicant responses and clarifies how the examiner interpreted the claim. Pointing out the BRI and recommending amendments to narrow to embodiments not directed to products of nature is a best practice.

name: Standard for permitting additional briefing
description: In deciding whether to allow additional briefing, the panel will take into account whether the parties already have had an adequate opportunity to address the issues raised by the remand.
guidance: Examples: A new or revised claim construction not previously considered may justify additional briefing. A change in the law usually would justify additional briefing. Additional briefing, when permitted, will normally be limited to the specific issues raised by the remand. (See Microsoft v. Proxyconn; Dell v. Acceleron.)

name: Alice two-step framework (overall)
description: Apply the Supreme Court's two-step framework (Alice) to assess patent eligibility across all claim categories and judicial exceptions.
guidance: The unified USPTO guidance combines the criteria for eligibility into a single analysis. The two-step framework is applied as steps 2A and 2B after the initial §101 category inquiry. Examiners use the framework to determine whether claims are directed to judicial exceptions and whether additional claim elements supply 'significantly more' (an inventive concept).

name: Step 1 — §101 statutory category inquiry
description: Determine whether the claimed invention falls into one of the four statutory categories recited in 35 U.S.C. §101 (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter).
guidance: This is the initial threshold inquiry before applying the Alice two-step framework; if the claim does not fall within a §101 category it is not eligible. (See MPEP §2106.03 and USPTO unified guidance.)

name: Step 2A — Identify whether claim is directed to a judicial exception
description: Evaluate whether the claim is 'directed to' a judicial exception (abstract ideas, laws of nature, or natural phenomena).
guidance: Under USPTO practice this is step 2A of the analysis; guidance documents (2019 PEG and October 2019 Update) revised procedures for identifying abstract ideas and for determining directedness under step 2A. If a claim is not directed to a judicial exception, no further Alice analysis is required.

name: 'Well-understood, routine, conventional' is a factual determination
description: Whether a claim element or combination of elements is 'well understood, routine, and conventional' to a skilled artisan is a factual inquiry.
guidance: Following Berkheimer and related Federal Circuit guidance, USPTO memoranda instruct examiners that such determinations require factual support. The April 19, 2018 memorandum required examiners to support findings that claim elements (or their combination) are well understood, routine, and conventional with factual determinations in the record.

name: Procedures for identifying abstract ideas (2019 PEG and October 2019 Update)
description: Use the revised procedures in the 2019 Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance and the October 2019 Update to identify abstract ideas and determine whether a claim is directed to a judicial exception under step 2A.
guidance: The 2019 PEG and October 2019 Update revised USPTO procedures for identifying abstract ideas and for determining directedness under step 2A; these updates were incorporated into MPEP chapter 2100 (sections 2103–2106) in June 2020.

name: Claims should recite specific implementations rather than vague functional results
description: Claims framed as specific implementations of inventive solutions are more likely to pass eligibility scrutiny than broadly claimed functional results or abstract descriptions.
guidance: Supporters of the two-step framework observed that it encourages claims to be directed to specific implementations rather than vaguely claimed functional outcomes; the framework can serve as a 'forcing function' to bring greater detail and clarity to patent applications.

name: AI-specific eligibility sensitivity
description: AI-related inventions may be at risk of being characterized as methods of organizing human activity, mental processes, or mathematical concepts and therefore ineligible unless claims recite 'significantly more' than judicial exceptions.
guidance: Public Views on AI and IP Policy reported stakeholder concerns that many AI inventions could be treated as abstract ideas under Alice; USPTO analyses (Inventing AI; allowance-rate studies) tracked differential impacts on AI-containing applications and the effect of guidance in restoring allowance rates.

name: Two-step framework as a tool against overly broad patents and abusive litigation
description: The two-step framework can be used to challenge overly broad claims and to defend against abusive lawsuits by patent assertion entities (PAEs).
guidance: Some commenters viewed Alice and its subsequent application as beneficial for weeding out overly broad patents and reducing abusive litigation tactics, thereby improving the patent system's functioning.

name: Admission of new evidence on appeal requires remand
description: If evidence is admitted during an appeal to support the claims of the applicant against references and objections of the examiner, or to vary the issues of fact concerning patentability of the invention, the whole case must be remanded to the examiner.
guidance: An appellate forum will not decide newly-formed factual issues; introduction of evidence that changes factual issues requires remand so the examiner can reconsider in light of that evidence.

name: Consequences of abandoning an application: intervening public use/sale and advances in the art
description: By abandoning the application the date of the applicant's application is transferred to the day of the new application; publications, patents, inventions, or intermediate public use/sale occurring after abandonment may be cited against a later application and may defeat claims.
guidance: Abandoning an application risks that subject-matter which would have been safe under the original filing date becomes unpatentable because of intervening disclosures or uses.

name: Cancellation of all claims constitutes abandonment
description: Cancellation of all the claims is abandonment of the application; a power of attorney that gives full authority to amend does not authorize withdrawal of all claims so as to destroy the application.
guidance: Avoid broad cancellations without understanding abandonment consequences; ensure agent authority is carefully limited.

name: Single judge's authority to determine need for three-judge court and to dismiss insubstantial Section 5 claims
description: The single judge district court may make the determination regarding whether there is a Section 5 coverage question presented by the pleadings which would require a three-judge court and may also make the decision to dismiss a meritless claim.
guidance: 28 U.S.C. §2284(b)(3) and precedent (U.S. v. Saint Landry Parish School Board, Backus v. Spears, Webber v. White) allow a single judge to determine if a three-judge court is required; a three-judge court is not required if the claim is wholly insubstantial or completely without merit, and the single judge may dismiss such claims.

name: Single judge may enter dismissal orders under Rule 12(b)(6) even when Section 5 involved
description: A dismissal for failure to state a claim under Rule 12(b)(6) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure is not a judgment on the merits and is clearly an 'order permitted by the rules of civil procedure'. Therefore, such an order may be entered by a single judge even though the provisions of Section 5 are involved.
guidance: Authority to dismiss for failure to state a cause of action emanates from 28 U.S.C. §2284(3): 'A single judge may conduct all proceedings except the trial, and enter all orders permitted by the rules of civil procedure except as provided in this subsection.'

name: Effect of Justice Department preclearance/approval under Section 5
description: Once the State has successfully complied with the Section 5 submission and approval requirements, there is no further action or remedy provided for by Section 5.
guidance: If approval is obtained, the matter will be at an end (citing Allen v. State Board of Elections; Berry v. Doles). Letters from the Attorney General interposing no objections constitute evidence that the change was precleared and render §5 claims without merit.

name: Pleading requirements for statutory claims (general)
description: Merely alleging a violation of a statute is insufficient; all elements encompassing the offense must be adequately pled.
guidance: Pleadings that do nothing more than track the statutes on which they attempt to base a claim are not well pled. Such language constitutes unsupported legal conclusions cast in the form of factual allegations; pleadings that rely on such language fail to state a cause of action (Webber v. White).

name: Pleading requirements for Fifteenth Amendment and §2/§1971 claims
description: Claims under the Fifteenth Amendment and related statutory provisions must allege that plaintiffs were actually denied the right to register or to vote based on race, color, or previous condition of servitude and must allege discriminatory intent.
guidance: Absent invidious purpose there can be no Fifteenth Amendment claim (Gomillion v. Lightfoot; Arlington Heights; Washington v. Davis). Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is parallel to the Fifteenth Amendment and §1971 involves the same type of racial discrimination; mere recitation of minority status or statutory language is insufficient.

name: Use of administrative letters as conclusive evidence of preclearance
description: Letters from the Attorney General indicating 'The Attorney General does not interpose any objections to the changes in question' establish that the elections and procedures were submitted and interposed no objections.
guidance: Such letters 'clearly establish' preclearance and support dismissal of §5 claims as without merit where the record contains them (example: DOJ letters dated Feb 7 and Mar 3, 1986).

name: Claim construction is a matter of law for the court
description: ‘The construction of a patent, including terms of art within its claim, is exclusively within the province of the court.’ (Markman v. Westview, Justice Souter opinion.)
guidance: This is the controlling legal principle: interpretation of patent claims, including disputed technical and non-technical terms, is for judges, not juries, and thus is treated as a question of law. Use this as the baseline for allocating responsibility between judge and jury.

name: Local rules and local case law may mandate pretrial Markman hearings
description: Some district courts have required pretrial Markman hearings (example: C.D. Cal. held a pretrial hearing is required; N.D. Cal. adopted local rules providing procedures for such hearings).
guidance: Even though Markman itself does not mandate hearings, practitioners must check and follow district-specific local rules or controlling local precedents that may impose a requirement for a pretrial claim-construction hearing.

name: Practical neutrality: hearings neither inherently beneficial nor detrimental in short term
description: In the short term, the assumption that claim-construction hearings are necessary 'is probably not either beneficial or detrimental to the patent law, court efficiency, or specific litigants.'
guidance: Whether to press for or oppose a separate Markman hearing should be a tactical decision based on case specifics (complexity, technical issues, local practice), not a presumptive belief that hearings always help or harm.

name: Novelty determination per claim
description: When there are two or more claims in an application, the determination over novelty should be made by each claim.
guidance: Each claim is evaluated separately for novelty; identicalness of invention is determined by identicalness of the matters described in the claims.

name: Claim-language-first principle for defining invention
description: When the claim language is clear, defining the claimed invention should be made as recited in the claim.
guidance: Terminology in claims is interpreted according to its general meaning and scope in the technical field unless the description explicitly defines a specific meaning; interpretation should be objective and reasonable considering a person skilled in the art at the filing date.

name: Avoid limiting claims by embodiments/drawings
description: Where the description of claims is clearly understood, an examiner should avoid limited interpretation just by referencing the description of the invention or drawings in finding technical features of invention.
guidance: Matters described only in the description or drawings should be considered as not recited in the claims; conversely, matters recited in the claims must be considered when interpreting the invention. Example explanations show that broad claim terms should not be limited to specific embodiments.

name: Construction of functional/characteristic claim expressions
description: When a claim specifies a product by its work, function, property, or characteristic, such expression should, in principle, be construed as every product that has such function, characteristic, etc., except when specifically defined otherwise in the description.
guidance: Consider common general technical knowledge—sometimes products that technically cannot perform the function (e.g., magnets) are excluded from the scope. Examiner should not exclude the function/characteristic from claim features when interpreting the claims.

name: Limitation-by-use (use-limited claims) interpretation
description: Where a claim includes an expression specifying a product by its use (limitation of use), the examiner should interpret the claimed invention only as a product specially suitable for the use disclosed in the claim, taking into account description, drawings, and common general technical knowledge.
guidance: Even if a product includes all technical characteristics of the claim, it is not the claimed product if not appropriate for the relevant use or requires conversion. If a product with limitation of use is not suitable for that use, the limitation may have no impact on defining the claimed invention and thus not affect novelty (example: catalogue disclosure vs claimed agricultural use).

name: Product-by-process claim treatment
description: The manufacturing process recited in product-by-process claims is a means of defining the structure or properties of the final product; novelty and inventive step are determined by comparing the product having certain structure or properties defined by all claim limitations (including process).
guidance: If the manufacturing process does not affect structure/properties (only yield/efficiency), novelty is determined by the final product regardless of process; identical product obtainable by a different process is not novel. If it's difficult to determine process impact, examiner should issue a novelty rejection and consider applicant arguments or evidence.

name: Jepson-type claim construction
description: Even in Jepson type claims (preamble + body), an invention should be specified as a whole including the preamble because claim type does not change technical scope.
guidance: Elements in the preamble are not automatically considered publicly known merely because recited there; novelty/patentability is determined on the whole invention including preamble and body; preamble may be construed to limit field, applied product, or exclude scope if the preamble elements were publicly known.

name: General considerations on what counts as publication
description: Manuscripts kept secret by journals are not publications until contents are released; company catalogues produced to promote products are publications except in special unpublished circumstances; thesis publication time is when distributed to public/university libraries after final examination.
guidance: When filing date equals date of publication, claimed invention does not lose novelty except when filing clearly after publication time.

name: Method of novelty determination (basic comparison)
description: Novelty is conducted by comparing matters defining the claimed invention and matters disclosed in the prior art reference and extracting differences; if no difference, claimed invention is not novel.
guidance: A claimed invention is not novel when it is substantially or exactly identical to the prior art. 'Substantially identical' is further defined as differences caused by mere addition/conversion/deletion of well-known art that do not practically affect the technical idea.

name: Novelty with numerical limitations
description: When a claim includes numerical limitations, novelty is governed by specific rules depending on relation between claimed and prior-art ranges.
guidance: Rules: (1) New numerical limitation absent in prior art -> regarded novel unless the value can be chosen by skilled person or is hinted by prior art/common knowledge. (2) If claimed range is included in prior-art range, novelty is not negated if criticality of range is shown; to acknowledge criticality requires technical meaning described, embodiments or supplemental materials, and objective experimental proof. (3) If claimed range includes prior-art range, novelty can be denied at once. (4) If ranges differ, novelty generally acknowledged.

name: Novelty for parameter inventions
description: Parameter invention: applicant arbitrarily creates a parameter not standard or commonly used, parameterizes it arithmetically using correlations, and employs it as essential claim element; subject matter must be determined from description/drawings/common knowledge before assessing inventive step.
guidance: Novelty is determined by interpreting the parameter as part of the claim but novelty cannot be confirmed solely because the parameter is novel. Novelty is generally denied if the parameter just experimentally identifies nature/characteristics of a publicly known product or merely changes expression. If reasonable doubt exists about identity with prior art, examiner may wait for written arguments or experimental certificates; examiner must concretely describe grounds for doubt and may propose ways to overcome it. Criteria do not apply if parameter is standard/common/understandable by skilled person.

name: Generic vs specific expression rules
description: When claim/prior-art use generic or specific expressions, consider following: (i) If claim is generic and prior art specific -> claim not novel. (ii) If claim specific and prior art generic -> claim has novelty unless specific can be directly derived from generic by common general knowledge.
guidance: Examples provided: metal (generic) vs Cu (specific) negates novelty; specific superconducting silver cable may be negated if using silver was commonly known.

name: No combining multiple prior art references for novelty
description: Comparison for novelty shall not be conducted between a claim and a combination of two or more prior art references; combining references is for inventive step, not novelty.
guidance: Exceptions: when a prior art reference cites a separate publication, that separate publication is regarded as part of the cited reference and may be relied upon for novelty; dictionaries and references used to interpret a term in cited reference are regarded as cited references and can be cited.

name: Markush/multiple-embodiment claims novelty handling
description: If one or more inventions are described in a claim (e.g., Markush-type), the ground of rejection can be notified on lack of novelty and inventive step for each invention with one single prior art.
guidance: When prior art contains multiple embodiments, do not determine novelty by combining two embodiments; combining embodiments in a single reference concerns inventive step, except when one prior art reference is obviously drawn from more than two embodiments considering common general knowledge.

name: Judicial Exception — Abstract Idea
description: Identify whether the claim recites an abstract idea.
guidance: Abstract idea is one of the judicial exceptions listed in the index and is further subdivided into groupings (mathematical concepts; mental process; certain methods of organizing human activity). Examples are marked to show which recite abstract ideas.

name: Judicial Exception — Law of Nature
description: Identify whether the claim recites a law of nature (natural principle).
guidance: Listed as a distinct judicial exception used to categorize examples and determine applicable analysis steps.

name: Judicial Exception — Product of Nature
description: Identify whether the claim recites a product of nature limitation.
guidance: Used to flag examples and to trigger Markedly Different Characteristics (MDC) analysis where appropriate.

name: Judicial Exception — Multiple exceptions in same claim
description: Identify when a claim recites multiple judicial exceptions.
guidance: Examples are annotated to indicate when more than one exception is recited in the same claim for analysis purposes.

name: Judicial Exception — No recited exception
description: Identify claims that do not recite any judicial exception.
guidance: Such examples are indicated and typically do not proceed through exception-centered prong analyses.

name: Step 2A Prong One — Generally
description: Determine whether the claim limitation(s) recite a judicial exception under the general Step 2A Prong One analysis.
guidance: For examples issued after the June 2020 revision, the analysis references abstract-idea groupings in MPEP 2106(a)(2); for earlier examples (1–36) the rationale may rely on direct comparisons to judicial decisions.

name: Step 2A Prong One — Markedly Different Characteristics (MDC) analysis
description: For nature-based product (NBP) limitations, assess whether the claimed NBP has markedly different characteristics compared to its natural counterpart.
guidance: Index identifies which examples discuss MDC analysis. When to perform MDC analysis: (1) claim focused on NBP limitation(s) so MDC analysis is performed; (2) process claim not focused on NBP (general rule in MPEP 2106.04(c)(I)(c) applies) so no MDC analysis; (3) process claim focused on NBP because exception to general rule in MPEP 2106.04(c)(1)(c) applies so MDC analysis is performed. Characteristics evaluated in MDC analysis include chemical or physical property; function or activity; phenotype; structure or form. Also identifies whether claim recites a single NBP limitation, a combination/mixture of components, or multiple NBP limitations.

name: Step 2B — Generally
description: Evaluate whether the additional claim elements, individually or as an ordered combination, provide an inventive concept that transforms the exception into patent-eligible subject matter.
guidance: Index indicates which examples proceed to Step 2B and includes the particular reasoning when a claim is found eligible under Step 2B.

name: Step 2B — Claim is eligible because it provides an Inventive Concept
description: The conclusion that a claim is subject-matter-eligible at Step 2B because the claim provides an inventive concept beyond the judicial exception.
guidance: Examples are flagged where Step 2B supports eligibility; index distinguishes those conclusions in the 'Streamlined Analysis' column.

name: Consideration — Improvements to Functioning of a Computer or Other Technology
description: Determine whether claimed elements improve the functioning of a computer or other technology, supporting eligibility at Prong Two or Step 2B.
guidance: Listed among the 'Considerations Discussed in Step 2A Prong Two and/or Step 2B' and used as a positive indication of practical application/inventive concept.

name: Consideration — Particular Treatment or Prophylaxis (Prong Two only)
description: For medical/therapeutic claims, assess whether the claim recites a particular treatment or prophylaxis (relevant only at Prong Two).
guidance: Listed explicitly as a Prong Two-only consideration in the index.

name: Consideration — Particular Machine
description: Assess whether the claim is tied to a particular machine in a meaningful way (supporting eligibility).
guidance: Included in the index as a consideration for Prong Two/Step 2B analysis.

name: Consideration — Particular Transformation
description: Assess whether the claim effects a particular transformation of an article or material (supporting eligibility).
guidance: Listed among considerations used in Prong Two/Step 2B analyses.

name: Consideration — Other Meaningful Limitations
description: Identify other meaningful limitations beyond mere recitation of an exception that tie the claim to application (supporting eligibility).
guidance: Index flags when examples rely on limitations that meaningfully limit the exception in practice.

name: Consideration — Insignificant Extra-Solution Activity
description: Identify additional claim elements that are insignificant extra-solution activities (do not confer eligibility).
guidance: Included in the index as a factor weighing against eligibility in Prong Two/Step 2B.

name: Consideration — Field of Use and Technological Environment
description: Consider the claimed field of use and technological environment to determine practical application or lack thereof.
guidance: Listed as a contextual factor in Step 2A Prong Two/Step 2B analyses.

name: Consideration — No additional elements, so no Prong Two or Step 2B analysis
description: If a claim contains no additional elements beyond the exception, prong-two/Step 2B analysis does not proceed.
guidance: Explicitly listed in the index; such examples are flagged as having no additional elements.

name: Markedly Different Characteristics (MDC) — NBP Limitation Types
description: Identify whether the claim recites a single nature-based product (NBP) limitation, a combination/mixture of multiple components, or multiple NBP limitations (affects MDC analysis).
guidance: Index lists which examples involve single vs combination vs multiple NBP limitations and whether MDC analysis is performed.

name: When to Perform MDC Analysis (process vs product claims)
description: Rules for performing MDC analysis depending on whether the claim is process-focused or focused on NBP limitations and whether the MPEP exception to the general rule applies.
guidance: If claim is focused on NBP limitation(s), perform MDC analysis. If process claim is not focused on NBP (general rule MPEP 2106.04(c)(I)(c)), do not perform MDC analysis. If process claim is focused on NBP because the exception in MPEP 2106.04(c)(1)(c) applies, perform MDC analysis.

name: Applicability of June 2020 MPEP 2106 Revision to Examples
description: Guidance on how the June 2020 revision to MPEP 2106 affects the issued examples (1–36 issued prior to that revision).
guidance: For Examples 1–36, the Step 2A Prong One analysis in MPEP 2106 will differ from the analysis presented in the issued examples for abstract-idea identifications: post-revision, the rationale should point to abstract idea groupings in MPEP 2106(a)(2). For Examples 1–36, Step 2A Prong Two can be extrapolated from existing Step 2B analysis (minus WURC consideration); some of these examples would now be eligible at Step 2A Prong Two and a specific list of affected examples is provided (Examples now eligible at Step 2A Prong Two: 3, 4, 21(claim 2), 23(claim 4), 25, 29(claims 5 and 6)). Examples where the result is unchanged but that would require analysis under Step 2A Prong Two are also listed (e.g., 6, 7, 8, 21(claim 1), 22, 23(claims 2 and 3), etc.). Explanatory Notes also flag that WURC conclusions for pre-June 2020 examples may not meet the current MPEP 2106.07(a)(III) support options (1)-(4).

name: Methodology and Scope — inclusion/exclusion and counting rules
description: This year's study covers all patent cases decided by the Federal Circuit in 2024, whether by precedential opinion, nonprecedential opinion or summary affirmance. It includes merits decisions and rulings on writ petitions, but it excludes denials of leave to appeal, dismissals for lack of finality, stipulated dismissals and remands, and dismissals for mootness.
guidance: Includes appeals and writ petitions from district courts, the PTAB, the ITC and the Court of Federal Claims only when the Federal Circuit decided at least one patent law issue. If the court resolves companion cases separately, the decisions are counted separately. If the court decides multiple appeals in a single opinion, all are counted as one decision. Cross appeals count only when the Federal Circuit decides them. When the Federal Circuit grants rehearing and vacates an opinion, the study disregards the retracted opinion and counts only the replacement decision.

name: Broadest reasonable interpretation and analyze claim as a whole
description: Prior to evaluating a claim for patentability, establish the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim and analyze the claim as a whole when evaluating for patentability.
guidance: Determine what applicant has invented by reviewing the entire application disclosure and construing the claims in accordance with their broadest reasonable interpretation (MPEP 2103); analyze the claim as a whole for eligibility rather than dissecting only parts.

name: Step 1 — Statutory category requirement
description: The claimed invention (Step 1) must be directed to one of the four statutory categories: process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter.
guidance: If the claim is not directed to a statutory category (NO at Step 1), it is not eligible; if YES, proceed to Step 2 to determine whether it is wholly directed to a judicial exception.

name: Step 2A — Directed to a judicial exception
description: Determine whether the claim is directed to a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea (judicially recognized exceptions). A claim 'directed to' an exception is one in which the exception is recited (set forth or described) in the claim.
guidance: Claims reciting an exception require further scrutiny because of the risk of preempting basic tools of science and technology; courts tread carefully because inventions often embody or apply such concepts. If Step 2A is NO (not directed to an exception), the claim is eligible under 35 U.S.C. 101.

name: Identify the judicial exception recited in the claim
description: Identify whether the claimed concept aligns with at least one judicial exception (laws of nature/natural phenomena or abstract ideas).
guidance: There are no bright lines between exception types and many concepts may fall under multiple exceptions (e.g., mathematical formulas may be abstract ideas and laws of nature). It is sufficient to identify alignment with at least one exception. Examples: isolated DNA, metabolic correlations, electromagnetic transmission (laws/natural phenomena); fundamental economic practices, methods of organizing human activities, mathematical relationships (abstract ideas). See cited case examples.

name: Nature-based product: decide if markedly different characteristics analysis is needed
description: For claims reciting a nature-based product limitation, determine whether to apply the 'markedly different characteristics' analysis to evaluate whether the claim recites a 'product of nature' exception.
guidance: Nature-based products include naturally occurring products and some man-made products essentially no different from nature. Apply the marked-difference analysis to the nature-based product limitation (or the resultant combination if multiple components) to compare to the closest naturally occurring counterpart. Do not overextend this analysis to claims that as a whole are not nature-based. For product-by-process claims, the analysis turns on whether the nature-based product has markedly different characteristics. Process claims generally are not subject to this analysis except where substance is indistinguishable from a product claim.

name: Markedly different characteristics analysis (structure, function, and/or other properties)
description: Compare the nature-based product limitation to its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state to determine whether it exhibits markedly different characteristics.
guidance: Markedly different characteristics can be expressed as changes in structure, function, and/or other properties. Examples of characteristics considered: biological or pharmacological functions, chemical and physical properties, phenotype (functional and structural features), and structure/form (chemical, genetic, physical). Characteristics must be changes compared to nature and not inherent or independently arisen; even a small change can show a marked difference. Purification/isolation can be eligible if the resultant change shows marked difference. If no marked difference, the claim is directed to a 'product of nature' exception and proceed to Step 2B.

name: Step 2B — 'Significantly more' / inventive concept search
description: For claims directed to a judicial exception, determine whether any element, or combination of elements, in the claim is sufficient to ensure that the claim amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception (i.e., contains an 'inventive concept').
guidance: Analyze claim elements individually and as an ordered combination. A claim that merely drafts around an exception or adds conventional, routine steps likely fails. Every claim must be examined individually based on its particular elements; individual elements may be conventional but their combination could provide significantly more.

name: Considerations/examples of what qualifies as 'significantly more'
description: Limitations that may be enough to qualify as 'significantly more' when recited with a judicial exception include several types of features or results.
guidance: Non-exclusive examples from Supreme Court/Federal Circuit decisions: improvements to another technology or technical field; improvements to functioning of the computer itself; applying the exception with or by use of a particular machine; effecting a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing; adding a specific limitation other than what is well-understood, routine and conventional, or adding unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application; other meaningful limitations beyond merely linking the exception to a technological environment. Examiners should consider these factors but are not limited to them.

name: Streamlined analysis where claim does not seek to tie up the exception
description: If a claim recites a judicial exception but is directed to an invention that clearly does not seek to 'tie up' the exception, a streamlined eligibility analysis may be appropriate.
guidance: See Section I.B.3. for guidance on when full Step 2 analysis may not be necessary; the focus is on preemption risk and whether the claim meaningfully limits use of the exception.

name: Rejection drafting: identify exception and explain lack of marked difference
description: When issuing a 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection, the rejection should identify the exception as recited in the claim and explain why the claimed product does not have markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart (if applicable).
guidance: Examiners must provide reasons in the record explaining why the product is considered a 'product of nature' exception and why additional claim elements do or do not add significantly more beyond the exception.

name: Claims must be fully examined under other patentability requirements
description: Along with determining eligibility, all claims are to be fully examined under 35 U.S.C. §§ 102, 103, 112, and other applicable requirements (utility, inventorship, double patenting), and non-statutory double patenting.
guidance: Examination for eligibility is iterative and should be done in conjunction with other patentability examinations to support compact prosecution; MPEP sections (2103–2106, etc.) provide related instructions. Rejections continue to be based on substantive law and are appealable.

name: Use the two-part Mayo/Alice flowchart for products and processes
description: Follow the flowchart: Step 1 (statutory category), Step 2A (directed to judicial exception?), Step 2B (does claim recite additional elements that amount to significantly more than the exception?).
guidance: This two-part analysis implements the Mayo/Alice framework and promotes examination efficiency and consistency across technologies, while recognizing that variations in analysis contours may still achieve the same end result. The guidance supersedes prior MPEP sections to the extent indicated and will be iteratively updated based on case law and public feedback.

name: Determine what applicant has invented before performing eligibility analysis
description: Establish what the applicant has invented by reviewing the entire disclosure to properly interpret the claim and the exception recited.
guidance: Understanding the invention is critical because courts avoid claims that would preempt others from using the underlying basic tools; this step supports correct application of Steps 2A and 2B and may justify a streamlined analysis if the claim clearly does not tie up an exception.

name: Claim interpretation / broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI)
description: Under the broadest reasonable interpretation, terms of the claim are presumed to have their plain meaning consistent with the specification as it would be interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art. The same claim interpretation must be used when evaluating the claim for compliance with all requirements (eligibility, definiteness, novelty, non-obviousness, written description, etc.).
guidance: See MPEP 2111. Practice note: where a wherein clause or other clause provides a patentable distinction in the eligibility analysis, that same interpretation and distinction will apply across other patentability requirements (e.g., prior art applied to 112(f) elements).

name: Means-plus-function (35 U.S.C. 112(f)) interpretation
description: If a claim limitation satisfies the three-prong test set forth in MPEP 2181, it is interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (means-plus-function). When 112(f) is invoked, the BRI of the limitation is limited to the structure, material, or acts (and equivalents) disclosed and clearly linked in the specification to performance of the claimed function.
guidance: Examiners should establish the 112(f) interpretation and provide an explanation in the Office action using appropriate form paragraphs. See MPEP 2181 and related sections (2182, 2183) and training (e.g., USPTO CBT on addressing 35 U.S.C. 112(f)). Example: 'means for temperature measuring' limited to the disclosed thermocouple (ARCXY) and equivalents.

name: Step 2A Prong Two — integration into a practical application / 'other meaningful limitations'
description: Evaluate whether the claim as a whole integrates the recited judicial exception into a practical application. Perform this by (a) identifying any additional elements beyond the judicial exception and (b) evaluating those additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether they integrate the exception into a practical application.
guidance: See 2019 PEG Section III(A)(2). Additional elements that apply the exception in a particular, technical way (e.g., using comparison output to drive corrective control of machinery to solve a technical problem) can be 'other meaningful limitations' that integrate the exception. Example: a limitation that maintains mold temperature within two degrees and thereby prevents undercure/overcure is a meaningful limitation that integrates the exception and renders the claim eligible.

name: Improvements consideration (technical improvement requirement)
description: The 'improvements' consideration requires evaluation of the specification and the claim to ensure a technical explanation of the asserted improvement is present in the specification and that the claim reflects the asserted improvement.
guidance: Examiners are not expected to make a qualitative judgment on the merits of the asserted improvement except when a person of ordinary skill, consulting the claims and specification, would clearly understand the invention does not improve technology as applicant asserts. Under the 2019 PEG, examiners should perform the improvements analysis at Step 2A Prong Two without reference to what is well-understood, routine, or conventional. See FAQ G-2, MPEP 2106.05(a), and Advanced Module training.

name: Do not consider conventionality at Step 2A when evaluating 'insignificant extra-solution activity'
description: When determining whether an additional element is insignificant extra-solution activity at Step 2A (Prong Two), the analysis should not take into account whether the element is well-understood, routine, or conventional.
guidance: However, conventionality is considered at Step 2B when determining whether the claim amounts to significantly more. See 2019 PEG guidance and MPEP 2106.05(g).

name: Title of invention requirements (37 CFR 1.72)
description: The title of the invention may not exceed 500 characters in length and must be as short and specific as possible. The title should be brief but technically accurate and descriptive and should contain fewer than 500 characters. The title should be placed at the top of the first page of the specification unless supplied in an application data sheet.
guidance: Certain words (e.g., 'A', 'An', 'The', 'New', 'Improved', 'Design', 'Ornamental', etc.) are not considered part of the title and should not be included at the beginning. If the title is not descriptive of the claimed invention, the examiner should require substitution of a new title (form paragraphs 6.11/6.11.01). Examiner may change title at allowance by examiner’s amendment (see MPEP § 1302.04(a)).

name: Application size fee rules (37 CFR 1.16(s))
description: The application size fee applies when the specification (including claims) and drawings of an application, excluding certain sequence listings or computer program listings filed in compliance with rules, exceed 100 sheets of paper; the fee applies for each additional 50 sheets or fraction thereof over 100 sheets.
guidance: Preliminary amendments present on the filing date count toward the page total; the Office recommends against filing substitute specifications or multiple sets of drawings at initial filing. For applications submitted on electronic medium other than EFS-Web, each 3 kilobytes of content counts as a sheet. For applications submitted via EFS-Web, the paper-equivalent is considered 75% of the number of sheets when rendered by the Office. Sequence listings/computer program listings submitted as ASCII text via EFS-Web may be excluded; PDF/TIFF listings/drawings are not excluded.

name: Order for applying insufficient payments when applicant does not specify
description: When a payment submitted for the fees due on filing in a nonprovisional application is insufficient and applicant has not specified the fees to which payment should be applied, the Office will apply the payment in the following order until expended: (1) basic filing fee; (2) non-electronic filing fee; (3) application size fee; (4) late filing surcharge; (5) processing fee for application filed in a language other than English; (6) search fee; (7) examination fee; (8) excess claims fee.
guidance: For provisional applications, the Office will apply insufficient payment in this order: (1) basic filing fee; (2) application size fee; (3) late filing surcharge. See also MPEP § 509.

name: Deposit account authorization treatment for 'filing fee' charges
description: The Office will treat a deposit account authorization to charge 'the filing fee' as an authorization to charge the applicable fees under 37 CFR 1.16 (the basic filing fee, search fee, examination fee, any excess claims fee, and any application size fee) to the deposit account. A deposit account authorization to charge 'the basic filing fee' will be treated as authorization to charge the applicable basic filing, search, and examination fees.
guidance: Any deposit account authorization to charge the filing fee but not the search or examination fee must specifically limit the authorization by reference to the applicable paragraphs of 37 CFR 1.16. See MPEP § 509.01.

name: Drawings cannot be used to cure insufficiency or supplement original disclosure
description: Drawings submitted after the filing date of the application may not be used (i) to overcome any insufficiency of the specification due to lack of an enabling disclosure or otherwise inadequate disclosure therein, or (ii) to supplement the original disclosure thereof for the purpose of interpretation of the scope of any claim.
guidance: Do not rely on late drawings to fix specification defects or to broaden/clarify original claims' scope. See 35 U.S.C. 113 and 37 CFR 1.81(d).

name: Drawings must show every claimed feature (37 CFR 1.83(a))
description: The drawing in a nonprovisional application must show every feature of the invention specified in the claims. Conventional features not essential for understanding may be shown as graphical symbols or labeled representations.
guidance: If invention is improvement on old machine, show improved portion disconnected and also show sufficient old structure to show connection (37 CFR 1.83(b)). Examiner may require additional illustration within at least two months.

name: Photographs only when practicable (37 CFR 1.84(b))
description: Photographs, including photomicrographs, are not ordinarily permitted but will be accepted if photographs are the only practicable medium for illustrating the claimed invention (examples include gels, blots, histological sections, animals, plants, crystalline structures, ornamental effects for design patents).
guidance: Photographs must be of sufficient quality so all details are reproducible in the printed patent. Photographs cannot be removed from applications; keep originals. Mounted photographs are objectionable; glossy paper for photos is permitted. Color photos follow color-drawing conditions when applicable.

name: Filing date definition
description: The filing date of an application shall be the date on which a specification, with or without claims, is received in the United States Patent and Trademark Office.
guidance: This definition is critical for priority and statutorily defined filing-date rights.

name: Provisional application filing date
description: The filing date of a provisional application shall be the date on which a specification, with or without claims, is received in the United States Patent and Trademark Office.
guidance: Mirrors filing-date rule for non-provisional applications.

name: Claims must particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention (35 U.S.C. 112(b))
description: The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor regards as the invention.
guidance: Claims define the metes and bounds of the invention; claim drafting must satisfy the statutory 'particularly point out and distinctly claim' standard.

name: Claim forms: independent, dependent, and multiple dependent (35 U.S.C. 112(c)-(e))
description: A claim may be written in independent or, if the nature of the case admits, in dependent or multiple dependent form. A dependent claim shall contain a reference to a claim previously set forth and then specify a further limitation ... A multiple dependent claim shall contain a reference, in the alternative only, to more than one claim previously set forth ... A multiple dependent claim shall not serve as a basis for any other multiple dependent claim.
guidance: Dependent claims incorporate all limitations of the claim(s) to which they refer. Multiple dependent claims must reference in the alternative and cannot be bases for other multiple dependent claims.

name: Means-or-step plus-function claiming (35 U.S.C. 112(f))
description: An element in a claim for a combination may be expressed as a means or step for performing a specified function without the recital of structure, material, or acts in support thereof, and such claim shall be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.
guidance: Means-plus-function claim elements are construed to the corresponding structure/material/acts disclosed in the spec and equivalents—drafting/analysis must account for this limitation.

name: Joint inventions: filing and oath rules (35 U.S.C. 116(a))
description: When an invention is made by two or more persons jointly, they shall apply for patent jointly and each make the required oath, except as otherwise provided in this title. Inventors may apply for a patent jointly even though (1) they did not physically work together or at the same time, (2) each did not make the same type or amount of contribution, or (3) each did not make a contribution to the subject matter of every claim of the patent.
guidance: Joint inventorship has a broad scope; co-inventors can apply jointly despite differing contributions or timing of work.

name: IDS requirement when parent is an international application designating the U.S.
description: When a continuing application claims benefit to an international application that designated the U.S., applicant must submit an IDS complying with 37 CFR 1.97 and 1.98 listing documents cited in the international search report if applicant wishes to ensure that the information is considered by the examiner in the continuing application.
