guidance: See MPEP § 1895 and § 609.03 for PCT national stage specifics. If relying on ISR citations for consideration or printing on the patent, follow the separate listing and copy requirements of 37 CFR 1.98 and related MPEP guidance.

name: Reexamination procedural flow
description: Typical procedure: (1) Request filed by patent owner or third party; (2) Initial determination by the Central Reexamination Unit (CRU); (3) If granted, reexamination proceeds; (4) Patent owner statement allowed (optional); (5) Office actions issue similar to regular prosecution; (6) Patent owner response required; (7) Reexamination certificate issued (cancels, amends, or confirms claims).
guidance: The prosecution during reexamination resembles normal examiner–applicant interactions after institution, culminating in a reexamination certificate that resolves the claims' status.

name: Procedural and substantive limitations
description: Reexamination has several limitations: no discovery, no oral hearing, cannot challenge §101 or §112 issues, and grounds are limited to patents/printed publications (§102/§103).
guidance: Because of these limits, ex parte reexamination is less adversarial and narrower in scope than other post-grant proceedings; patent owners can also amend claims during prosecution (often used to escape narrow grounds).

name: Strategic considerations for filing
description: When to consider filing ex parte reexamination: limited budget for invalidation challenge; when a patent owner does not want claims broadened; to avoid a fully adversarial proceeding; after the IPR window has closed; when the available prior art consists of patents or printed publications.
guidance: Assess whether the goal is complete invalidation or merely narrowing scope, and consider timing relative to litigation and other post-grant options. The narrow scope and limited third-party role may favor ex parte reexamination in certain circumstances.

name: Possible outcomes of reexamination
description: A reexamination certificate is issued at the conclusion, which may cancel claims, amend claims, or confirm claims as patentable.
guidance: Understand that outcome can either eliminate claims, narrow them via amendment, or leave them intact; amendments during reexamination can affect subsequent enforceability and validity considerations.

name: Different Inventors, Common Assignee, Same Invention (8.27.fti)
description: Claim [1] directed to the same invention as claim [2] of commonly assigned [3]. The issue of priority under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) and possibly pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f) of this single invention must be resolved.
guidance: USPTO normally will not institute an interference between commonly owned cases. Applicant must amend or cancel claims so the reference and instant application do not claim the same invention, or the assignee must state which entity is the prior inventor. A terminal disclaimer has no effect for pre‑AIA priority issues. Failure to comply may result in abandonment. Examiner: include form paragraph 7.03.fti and follow bracket instructions (insert patent/application number in bracket 3; brackets 1 and 2 must be for the same invention).

name: Different Inventors, Common Assignee, Inventions Not Patentably Distinct (AIA) (8.28.aia)
description: Claim [1] directed to an invention not patentably distinct from claim [2] of commonly assigned [3]. Specifically, [4].
guidance: Use when commonly assigned case includes claims patentably indistinct but common ownership at or before effective filing date under 35 U.S.C. 100(i) is not established. Also make appropriate 35 U.S.C. 102/103 rejections (form paragraphs 7.21.aia family) as appropriate. Insert reference number in bracket 3 and explain why claims are patentably indistinct in bracket 4. Include form paragraph 8.28.01.aia immediately after. Also include a nonstatutory double patenting rejection using form paragraphs 8.34–8.37. Follow Examiner Notes about prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2)/103 and bracket instructions.

name: Different Inventors, Common Assignee, Inventions Not Patentably Distinct (pre‑AIA) (8.28.fti)
description: Claim [1] directed to an invention not patentably distinct from claim [2] of commonly assigned [3]. Specifically, [4].
guidance: Use when commonly assigned case includes claims patentably indistinct, but no indication they were commonly assigned at the time the invention was made (pre‑AIA priority issues). Make appropriate pre‑AIA 102(e)/103(a) rejections as needed (form paragraphs 7.21.fti family). Insert reference number in bracket 3 and explain patentable indistinctness in bracket 4. Form paragraph 8.28.01.fti must follow. Also include nonstatutory double patenting rejection using form paragraphs 8.34–8.37 as appropriate.

name: Rejection, 35 U.S.C. 102 (AIA) (7.15.aia)
description: Claim(s) [1] is/are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102 [2] as being [3] by [4].
guidance: Use for applications filed on or after March 16, 2013 (AIA). Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.03.aia. In bracket 1 insert claim numbers under rejection; bracket 2 insert '(a)(1)' or '(a)(2)' or both; if (a)(2) applicable, use 7.15.01.aia/7.15.02.aia/7.15.03.aia where appropriate. In bracket 3 insert either 'clearly anticipated' or 'anticipated' with explanation at end of paragraph; bracket 4 insert prior art relied upon. Precedence notes: must be preceded appropriately by 7.07/7.08/7.12.aia or 7.103. For claims claiming priority to pre‑AIA filings insert form paragraph 7.06 beforehand. If pre‑AIA 102(e) applied, follow with 7.15.01.aia/7.15.02.aia as applicable.

name: Rejection, Pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 (7.15.fti)
description: Claim(s) [1] is/are rejected under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 [2] as being [3] by [4].
guidance: Precede with appropriate paragraphs (7.07.fti etc.) or 7.103. In bracket 2 insert appropriate pre‑AIA paragraph letter(s). Bracket 3 insert 'clearly anticipated' or 'anticipated' with explanation; bracket 4 insert prior art. If pre‑AIA 102(e) applied, follow with 7.15.01.fti/7.15.02.fti/7.15.03.fti. For applications with actual filing date on/after March 16, 2013 claiming priority to pre‑AIA filings, precede with 7.06.

name: Rejection, pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f) — Applicant Not the Inventor (7.19.fti)
description: Claim [1] is/are rejected under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f) because the applicant did not invent the claimed subject matter. [2]
guidance: Must be preceded by 7.07.fti and 7.13.fti or by 7.103. In bracket 2, insert explanation of supporting evidence establishing applicant was not the inventor. See MPEP § 2137 for required evidence and procedures.

name: Rejection, pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) (7.21.fti)
description: Claim [1] is/are rejected under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over [2].
guidance: Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.20.fti or 7.103. An explanation must follow (see MPEP § 2144). If rejection relies on prior art under pre‑AIA 102(e), determine the reference's prior art date using pre‑AIPA rules as applicable (see 7.12.fti/7.12.01.fti notes). If a copending application has an earlier effectively filed date under 35 U.S.C. 102(d), consider making a provisional rejection based on the copending application using 7.15.01.aia or 7.21.01.aia (AIA) or the pre‑AIA counterparts. Note: a terminal disclaimer alone does not obviate 102 or 103 rejections.

name: Consideration of Copending Applications for Provisional Rejection
description: If a copending application has an earlier effectively filed date under 35 U.S.C. 102(d) than the claims under examination, the examiner should consider making a provisional rejection based on the copending application under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) (using 7.15.01.aia) or under 35 U.S.C. 103 (using 7.21.01.aia).
guidance: Similarly for pre‑AIA applications use the pre‑AIA form paragraphs (7.15.01.fti, 7.21.01.fti). Rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103 cannot be obviated solely by filing a terminal disclaimer. Where appropriate, include provisional rejection form paragraphs and explanatory paragraphs for anticipation or obviousness over copending applications.

name: Provisional Rejection, 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) — Common Assignee/Applicant/Inventor (7.15.01.aia)
description: Claim(s) [1] is/are provisionally rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) as being anticipated by copending Application No. [2] which has a common [3] with the instant application.
guidance: Used in AIA cases (filed on/after March 16, 2013) and must be preceded by 7.03.aia. The copending application would be prior art if published/patented. This provisional rejection may be overcome by: (1) a 37 C.F.R. 1.130(a) showing that subject matter was obtained directly/indirectly from the inventor/joint inventor (not prior art under 102(b)(2)(A)); (2) a 1.130(b) showing of prior public disclosure under 102(b)(2)(B); or (3) a 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) statement that subject matter and claimed invention were commonly owned or subject to assignment or a joint research agreement as of the effective filing date. Terminal disclaimers do not overcome this rejection (In re Bartfeld). Examiner notes: in bracket 3 insert 'assignee', 'applicant', or 'joint inventor'; bracket 4 provide explanation of anticipation; if claims would be obvious use 7.21.01.aia instead. Require applicant to amend/cancel identical claims (form paragraph 8.27.aia) and nonstatutory double patenting rejections where not patentably distinct (8.33 and 8.34–8.39).

name: Provisional Rejection, pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) — Common Assignee/Applicant/Inventor (7.15.01.fti)
description: Claim(s) [1] is/are provisionally rejected under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as being anticipated by copending Application No. [2] which has a common [3] with the instant application.
guidance: Copending application would constitute prior art if published/patented. May be overcome by showing under 37 C.F.R. 1.132 that disclosed‑but‑not‑claimed inventions were derived from this application's inventor (not 'by another'), or by a showing under 37 C.F.R. 1.131(a). Terminal disclaimers do not overcome. Examiner notes: use pre‑AIPA 102(e) rules to determine prior art date per 7.12.fti/7.12.01.fti; if claims obvious over copending application use 7.21.01.fti; insert 'assignee','applicant', or 'joint inventor' in bracket 3; provide explanation of anticipation in bracket 4 if needed. Require resolution of identical subject matter (8.30/8.32) and nonstatutory double patenting (8.33/8.34–8.39) as applicable.

name: Rejection, 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) — Common Assignee/Applicant/Joint Inventor (7.15.02.aia)
description: Claim(s) [1] is/are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) as being [2] by [3]. The applied reference has a common [4] with the instant application.
guidance: Used in AIA cases to reject over a U.S. patent, U.S. patent application publication, or WIPO publication with an earlier prior art date under 102(a)(2) where references have common assignee/applicant or at least one common inventor. May be overcome by: (1) 37 C.F.R. 1.130(a) showing derivation (not prior art under 102(b)(2)(A)); (2) 1.130(b) showing of prior public disclosure under 102(b)(2)(B) if same invention not being claimed; or (3) 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) statement of common ownership/assignment or joint research agreement. Examiner notes: precede with 7.03.aia and 7.12.aia; in bracket 1 insert claim numbers; in bracket 3 insert prior art relied upon; in bracket 4 insert 'assignee', 'applicant', or 'joint inventor'; terminal disclaimer issues and double patenting procedure notes apply.

name: Rejection, pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) — Common Assignee/Applicant/Inventor (7.15.02.fti)
description: Claim(s) [1] is/are rejected under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as being anticipated by [2]. The applied reference has a common [3] with the instant application.
guidance: Used to reject over a patent or patent application publication that is prior art under pre‑AIA 102(e). Apply pre‑AIPA/AIPA rules to determine 102(e) date per 7.12.fti/7.12.01.fti. The rejection might be overcome by 37 C.F.R. 1.132 showing of derivation or by 1.131(a) showing. Examiner notes: consider benefit claims to earlier-filed provisionals and other continuity rules in determining 102(e) date; ensure proper preceding paragraphs (7.12.fti or 7.12.01.fti); patent application publications only used if preceded by 7.12.fti; handle terminal disclaimer/nonstatutory double patenting issues and resolve priority issues under 102(g) as needed.

name: Provisional Rejection, pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) over Copending Application (7.21.01.fti)
description: Provisional pre‑AIA 103 rejection analogous to 7.21.01.aia for pre‑AIA cases (header present).
guidance: Use when copending application discloses invention and would be prior art under pre‑AIA provisions; may be overcome by derivation/showing of prior public disclosure or appropriate statutory statements under pre‑AIA rules. Follow corresponding pre‑AIA procedural and date‑determination rules. Insert required bracketed information and include supporting explanation of obviousness as per MPEP § 2144. If claimed invention fully disclosed in copending application, use the appropriate 102 provisional form paragraph instead.

name: Evidence: prior specifications must be produced where improvement claimed
description: When a patent claims 'improvements' upon an earlier patented machine, the earlier specification must be given in evidence to determine what was known before and what is truly new in the later patent.
guidance: Without knowing the prior specification, one cannot say what the improvements are; sometimes infringement may be presumed from acts (e.g., sales) where the defendant refuses to reveal manufacturing details or factory evidence.

name: Interpretive approach of US courts — liberal construction
description: The reports of decisions in the US Supreme Court indicate judges incline to put a liberal construction on letters patent.
guidance: When construing patent claims and specifications US courts historically favored a liberal interpretation, which may affect scope and enforcement.

name: Design patent statutory basis (35 U.S.C. § 171)
description: Patents for designs: Whoever invents any new, original and ornamental design for an article of manufacture may obtain a patent therefor, subject to the conditions and requirements of this title.
guidance: Establish that the claimed subject matter is a 'new, original and ornamental design' for an article of manufacture. This statutory language frames all patentability and drafting considerations for design patents.

name: Scope of protection — types of design subject matter
description: Scope of protection can cover: surface ornamentation applied to an article; configuration embodied in an article; or configuration and surface ornamentation for an article.
guidance: Decide whether the claimed design covers surface ornamentation, the overall configuration, or both, and depict drawings accordingly to capture the intended scope.

name: Design may be directed to less than an entire article
description: A design may be directed to less than an entire article.
guidance: You may claim a portion or feature of an article (e.g., a handle, a surface pattern). When doing so, depict the portion clearly, and use broken lines for unclaimed parts (see broken-line guidance).

name: Single claim requirement
description: Only one claim is permitted in a design patent application.
guidance: Draft a single claim that adequately defines the design as shown in the drawings; use drawings and specification to delineate what is claimed rather than multiple claims.

name: Drawings — show all parts of the design you claim
description: Drawings: Show all parts of the design you claim.
guidance: Ensure every feature you want protected is depicted in the drawings. Missing elements in drawings may limit the scope of protection.

name: Including alternative configurations
description: Alternative configurations can be included in the same design drawing set (example: coffee machine with alternative position).
guidance: Depict alternative positions or configurations within the same application when they represent the same overall design concept; clarity in drawings is required to show alternatives are part of the claimed design.

name: Portions shown separately do not get separate protection
description: Portions shown separately along with the whole do not get separate protection.
guidance: Showing a portion separately for clarity does not by itself create an independent claim to that portion; consider separate applications if separate protection is desired.

name: Application content and formal arrangement (37 C.F.R. 1.154)
description: A design patent application has essentially the elements required of an application for a utility patent. The arrangement of the elements of a design patent application and the sections of the specification are as specified in 37 CFR 1.154.
guidance: Follow 37 C.F.R. 1.154 in organizing the application. Include required parts such as drawings and a specification that describes each figure, broken lines, and the claim.

name: Specification — describe each figure
description: Specification: Describe each figure.
guidance: Provide a written description of every drawing figure to clarify what is depicted and to support claim interpretation.

name: Specification — include the claim
description: Specification: Include claim.
guidance: Include the single required design claim in the specification, tied to and supported by the drawings and figure descriptions.

name: Defendant’s Patent for an Improvement
description: A defendant who holds a patent for an improvement is not necessarily sheltered from injunction if the infringement of the plaintiff’s valid claims is clear; the improvement patent does not avail him beyond its proper scope.
guidance: An improvement patent may limit defendant’s exposure only to its scope; clear infringement of plaintiff’s claims can still justify injunction (examples: Morse Fountain Pen Co. v. Esterbrook Steel Pen Mfg. Co.).

name: Reissue Patents: Expanded Claims and Delay
description: Injunctions on re-issues are governed by whether the re-issue attempts to extend the original scope, whether the re-issue is broader, or whether the re-issue was delayed (e.g., ten years) with disputed validity; courts may refuse interim relief in such circumstances.
guidance: Where valid re-issue claims are infringed, injunctions can issue; but where breadth or timing of re-issue creates doubt, relief may be withheld (cases: Brewster v. Parry; Starrett v. Athol Mach. Co.).

name: When Plaintiff’s Title is Only Equitable and Being Litigated Elsewhere
description: If plaintiff claims only an equitable title which is being contested in local courts, a federal court may decline to issue an injunction in the patent suit pending resolution of local litigation.
guidance: Courts avoid interfering with state court determinations of equitable title (see Continental Store Service Co. v. New York Store Service Co.).

name: Analyze claim language using the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI)
description: During examination, a claim must be given its broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification as it would be interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: Start with the plain meaning of claim terms unless inconsistent with the specification. Because the applicant can amend claims during prosecution, apply BRI to reduce the chance the claim issues broader than justified. Sources of plain meaning include the words of the claims, the specification, drawings, and prior art. (See MPEP 2173.01(I); 2111.01(I) Plain Meaning.)

name: Determine if the metes and bounds of the claims are clear (threshold of clarity and precision)
description: After applying BRI, if the metes and bounds of the claimed invention are not clear, the claim is indefinite and should be rejected.
guidance: The examiner should apply the threshold requirement of clarity and precision: if a person of ordinary skill could not interpret the metes and bounds so as to understand how to avoid infringement, a 35 U.S.C. 112(b) rejection is appropriate. (See MPEP 2173.02(II).)

name: Provide a sufficient and clear explanation in the Office action (avoid conclusory rejections)
description: Only by providing a complete explanation in the Office action as to the basis for determining why a particular term or phrase is indefinite will the examiner enhance the clarity of the prosecution history record.
guidance: A complete rejection should include: (1) The analysis of the claim element in view of MPEP/Rule; (2) The conclusion of that analysis; and (3) If appropriate, a statement as to how to obviate the rejection. The examiner should avoid a conclusionary rejection which merely states the claim is indefinite without supporting analysis or guidance to applicant. Provide enough information to permit applicant to make a meaningful response. (Slides: 'The examiner should avoid a conclusionary rejection'; 'A complete rejection should include: ...')

name: Antecedent basis — lack of antecedent basis can render a claim indefinite (MPEP 2173.05(e))
description: A claim is indefinite when it contains words or phrases whose meaning is unclear, e.g., referring to 'said X' where no earlier recitation of X appears.
guidance: Identify whether a dependent claim term (e.g., 'said protein nanopores', 'said zinc anode') has clear antecedent basis in the dependency chain or specification. Under BRI, determine whether the ordinary meaning and the specification provide the necessary antecedent support. Note: failure to provide explicit antecedent basis does not always render a claim indefinite if the scope would be reasonably ascertainable by those skilled in the art (Ex parte Porter). Cite MPEP 2173.05(e) and analyze factually (examples in slides include protein nanopores lacking antecedent support and 'said zinc anode' which did have implied antecedent).

name: Dependent claims relying on cancelled base claims are incomplete (MPEP §608.01(n))
description: A claim which is directly or indirectly dependent on a canceled base claim should be rejected as incomplete; if the base claim is rejected the dependent claim should be objected to rather than rejected if otherwise allowable.
guidance: When a dependent claim depends on a canceled claim (e.g., 'Claim 61. The composition of claim 32...'), treat it as incomplete and, for purposes of 112(b), also analyze antecedent basis. The appropriate action is rejection as incomplete and/or rejection under 112(b) if lack of antecedent basis renders it indefinite. Suggest amendments (e.g., amend to refer to a claim that recites the subject matter or delete the claim) to obviate the rejection.

name: Breadth vs. indefiniteness — breadth alone does not make a claim indefinite (MPEP 2173.04)
description: A broad claim is not indefinite merely because it encompasses a wide scope, provided the scope is clearly defined; indefiniteness arises when claim boundaries are unclear.
guidance: Distinguish between a claim that is broad but clearly delimited (e.g., a genus that clearly defines which species are included) and a claim whose boundaries are ambiguous. Use BRI and the specification to determine whether the breadth leaves more than one reasonable interpretation of what is covered. Example in slides: a method 'providing an insect inhibitory amount' was broad but definite because BRI included generic application to an insect and the specification showed ways of providing the protein.

name: Unclaimed essential matter — claims must interrelate essential elements (MPEP 2172.01)
description: If a claim fails to interrelate essential elements of the invention as defined by the specification, it may be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) as indefinite.
guidance: Check whether the claim omits an essential element required to give life, meaning, and vitality to the claimed invention. If so, the claim may be indefinite even if other language is clear. Apply this when a preamble/purpose suggests essential steps or elements that are not recited in the body of the claim.

name: Relative and subjective terminology — acceptability depends on whether POSITA would understand the scope (MPEP 2173.05(b))
description: The use of relative terminology, including terms of degree or '...-like' expressions, does not automatically render a claim indefinite; acceptability depends on whether one of ordinary skill would understand what is claimed in light of the specification.
guidance: For subjective or relative terms (e.g., 'increased yield stability', 'Sumkinda-like') look to the specification for standards or comparisons that define the term. If the specification supplies a measuring standard or shows how to compare (e.g., transformed vs. untransformed cultivar), the term may be definite. If the specification and prior art leave the term's metes and bounds unclear, issue a 112(b) rejection. (See MPEP 2173.05(b) and 2173.05(b)(IV): Subjective Terms.)

name: Exemplary language in claims ('such as', 'for example') may render claim scope unclear (MPEP 2173.05(d))
description: Examples or preferences stated in the claims (e.g., 'R is halogen, for example, chlorine'; 'a pain reliever such as aspirin') may lead to confusion over intended scope and can render the claim indefinite.
guidance: Do not treat 'such as' or 'for example' as per se indefinite; perform fact-specific analysis. Look to the specification to determine whether the exemplification is intended to be limiting. If the specification does not establish that the example is limiting, the claim may be indefinite because it's unclear whether the example narrows the broader term or is merely illustrative. If appropriate, suggest deleting the exemplary phrase to obviate the rejection. (Slides provide multiple historical examples of problematic exemplary claim language and recommend amendment to delete such phrasing.)

name: Plain meaning rule and sources of meaning (2111.01(I))
description: Under BRI, words of a claim must be given their ordinary and customary meaning as understood by those of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention, unless the specification indicates otherwise.
guidance: To determine plain meaning, consult the claim language itself, the specification (including any special definitions), drawings, and the prior art. If the applicant acts as its own lexicographer, a clear special definition in the specification controls claim meaning; absent that, use ordinary meaning.

name: Preamble weight — determine whether preamble limits the claim (MPEP 2111.02)
description: Decide if the preamble gives 'life, meaning, and vitality' to the claim so that it should be construed as a limitation; if the body of the claim fully sets forth the limitations, the preamble may be non-limiting.
guidance: Analyze the preamble in the context of the entire claim. If the preamble merely states a purpose or intended use and the claim body includes all limitations, the preamble is not limiting; if it is necessary to make the claim definite, treat it as a limiting element.

name: Form and content when writing the rejection (form paragraph guidance)
description: When writing the rejection the examiner should explain their conclusion, include the detailed BRI analysis that provides a clear record of the systematic analysis, and, where appropriate, suggest how to overcome the rejection.
guidance: Use the recommended form paragraph(s) illustrated in the training: state the statutory basis (35 U.S.C. 112(b)), explain why the specific phrase lacks antecedent basis or otherwise renders the claim indefinite, cite the specification paragraphs relied upon, and, if possible, indicate an amendment that would obviate the rejection (e.g., amend 'said protein nanopores' to 'said nanopores' or delete 'such as aspirin'). If no helpful suggestion exists, do not invent one; still provide the full factual analysis and conclusion. The detailed BRI analysis should be on the record to enhance clarity of prosecution history.

name: Scope of 'laid open to public inspection' for international applications (pre/post Jan 1, 2015)
description: For international applications filed on or before Dec 31, 2014 and for those filed on or after Jan 1, 2015, specifies what 'laid open to public inspection' and 'a specification or drawings originally attached to a patent application' refer to when applying Article 29(3)-(6).
guidance: Where an application is filed on and before Dec 31, 2014, reference to a 'specification or drawings originally attached' refers to the translation of the specification, claims or drawings of the international application submitted at filing. For applications filed on and after Jan 1, 2015, 'laid open' includes international publication under Article 21 of the PCT and 'specification or drawings originally attached' refers to description, claims or drawings submitted until the date of filing the international application. Additionally, if an international application is deemed withdrawn because a Korean translation of the description and claims was not submitted within the period under Article 214(4), it cannot be relied upon under Article 29(3) and (4).

name: Application of Article 29 to international applications claiming domestic priority
description: When Article 29(3)-(6) is applied to an international patent application claiming domestic priority, inventions disclosed both in the international application's specification/claims/drawings and in its translation are relevant; an invention disclosed in the specification or drawings of a prior-filed domestic application on which priority is claimed shall be deemed laid open to public inspection when the international application is published under PCT Article 21 or published for registration.
guidance: If a later-filed application is identical to the invention disclosed in the prior-filed application's specification/claims/drawings submitted at the prior application's international filing date, the later application may be rejected based on that prior-filed disclosure.

name: Scope of enlarged novelty for international applications under Article 29(5)-(6)
description: When another application is an international application under Article 29 paragraphs 5 and 6, the extent of enlarged novelty applied is the invention(s) disclosed both in the specification, claims or drawings of the international application submitted at its international filing date and in its translation.
guidance: However, if another application claims domestic priority from a prior-filed international application and the invention of the present application is identical to that disclosed in the prior-filed application's specification/claims/drawings submitted at the prior-filed application's international filing date, the present application may be rejected over that prior-filed disclosure.

name: Method of Determination of Identicalness (overview/procedure)
description: Determination of whether Article 29(3) and (4) apply refers to whether a claimed invention is identical to an invention specified in the description or drawings in another application at its filing (a 'prior art reference').
guidance: Procedure: (1) Determine the claimed invention of the present application (method same as determining novelty). (2) Determine the disclosure of the prior art reference by the description of the specification of the other application; inherent disclosure obvious in light of common general knowledge may be considered. (3) Compare claimed invention with the prior art reference to find identicalness and differences (do not compare with a combination of more than two prior art references). (4) If no difference is found between the subject matters defining the claimed invention and the prior art reference, they are identical; identicalness includes substantial identicalness.

name: Substantial method for determining identicalness (principles)
description: Identicalness of invention is related to novelty, inventive step, disclosure exception, enlarged concept of novelty, protection of lawful holder, first-to-file, succession, divisional and converted applications, and priority claims; the same criteria apply across these cases.
guidance: Determination relies on comparison of subject matter defining the claimed invention and the prior art reference. If differences exist, inventions are not identical; if no difference or complete/substantial identicalness exists, they are identical.

name: Difference in expression (treated as non-substantial)
description: Differences in expression refer to cases where expressions used in patent claims differ but contents are substantially the same; such differences are treated as 'difference in expressions'.
guidance: Example: 'The method of desalination of sea water' vs 'the method of concentration of sea water' by separating water through insertion of an undissolved refrigerant — different wording but same content.

name: Reference date rules for determining earliest-filed application
description: The reference date used to determine earliest filing is recognized as: (i) actual filing date for applications without priority; (ii) filing date of the application which is the basis of the priority claim for treaty priority claims (for multiple priority claims, earliest filing date among each invention); (iii) filing date of the application serving as basis for domestic priority (similar multiple-priority rule); (iv) filing date of the original application for divisional and converted applications; (v) for applications filed by lawful holder of a right (misappropriation), the reference date is the filing date of the misappropriated application and the misappropriated application is deemed never filed.
guidance: Special rules apply for international applications: for those filed on/before Dec 31, 2014 the reference date is the filing date in which invention is disclosed in the translation; for those filed on/after Jan 1, 2015 the reference date is the date of filing the international application on invention disclosed in the specification or drawings.

name: Examination approach when conflicting applications filed on different dates
description: When more than two applications for the same invention are filed on different dates, the earliest filer is entitled; examiners must apply Article 29(3)-(4) or Article 36 depending on applicant/inventor identity and publication status of prior-filed applications.
guidance: If applicant and inventor are not the same and the prior-filed application is laid open/registered, Article 29(3)-(4) primarily apply to later-filed applications; proviso on enlarged novelty can be flexibly applied within specification/drawings if prior-filed is already laid open even before claims confirmed. If a prior-filed application is not laid open, examination on the later application is postponed until prior-filed is laid open or registered. If applicant of later-filed is same as prior or inventors are same, Article 36 applies and examiner should make rejection decision after claims in prior-filed are confirmed.

name: Priority/effective filing date under 35 U.S.C. §120 — sufficiency of support
description: To claim priority under § 120 to earlier filings (e.g., a PCT or provisional), the claims must be sufficiently supported by those earlier filings; otherwise the claim's effective filing date may be the later filed national application.
guidance: The effective filing date determination controls what constitutes prior art for the claims at issue; if the chain of priority 'could not reach back further under 35 U.S.C. § 120' because claims lacked sufficient support, earlier provisional/PCT filings cannot serve as the patent's effective date.

name: Practical consequence rule: incorporated provisional can be used in unpatentability arguments
description: If a provisional application becomes publicly available through incorporation in a PCT publication, it may be relied upon as prior art to support unpatentability arguments (anticipation or obviousness) against later-filed claims.
guidance: The Board may treat the provisional both as the source of disclosed limitations and as part of the published PCT itself when evaluating anticipation/obviousness; the effective-date/prior-art analysis follows from the public-availability and incorporation determinations.

name: Design patents protect ornamental appearance, not function
description: A design patent protects the ornamental appearance of an article of manufacture (35 USC 171). Functional features are not protectable through design patents - utility patents are the route for functional aspects. The line between ornamental and functional is sometimes contested.
guidance: Ensure the claimed subject matter is ornamental rather than functional. If features are primarily functional, consider a utility patent instead. Be aware the ornamental/functional distinction may be litigated; draft with an eye toward emphasizing aesthetic choices that have alternative functional implementations.

name: The Single Claim
description: A design patent has exactly one claim: "The ornamental design for [article], as shown and described." All scope is conveyed by the figures and the explanatory text.
guidance: Draft the single claim in the conventional form and rely on figures and description to define scope; do not attempt to add multiple independent design claims. Ensure the descriptive text aligns with and supports the figures.

name: Solid Lines vs. Broken Lines
description: Solid lines depict claimed design features. Broken lines depict unclaimed environmental features (the rest of the product, or context the design is used in).
guidance: Use broken lines strategically to exclude unclaimed/contextual elements and broaden claim scope; more broken lines generally yield broader scope. Deliberately choose which elements to render in solid vs. broken lines as a primary drafting decision.

name: Partial Designs
description: You can claim part of an article by drawing only that part in solid lines and the rest in broken lines.
guidance: Use partial claiming when only a specific feature is novel (e.g., the curve of a phone bezel, the shape of a car grille). This approach is powerful for isolating the novel ornamental feature while excluding the rest of the article.

name: Ordinary Observer Test
description: Infringement is determined by whether an ordinary observer would deem the accused design substantially the same as the claimed design (Egyptian Goddess v. Swisa, Fed. Cir. 2008, en banc).
guidance: When deciding which features to claim (solid vs broken lines), consider whether those features affect the overall visual impression to an ordinary observer. Draft with an eye toward the visual gestalt that will govern infringement analysis.

name: Functionality Defense
description: Accused infringers often argue the claimed design is dictated by function.
guidance: To defend against functionality arguments, focus on aspects that have alternative functional implementations and make clear the design choices are aesthetic rather than functionally necessary. Select claimed features and description to emphasize aesthetic motivation where possible.

name: Foreign Design Protection
description: The Hague Agreement allows international design filings through a single application. Many countries use registered design (not examined) systems with broader scope considerations than US design patents.
guidance: Consider international filing routes (Hague Agreement or national registered design systems) and be mindful that scope and examination practices differ by jurisdiction; coordinate drawing/claiming strategy accordingly for foreign protection.

name: Specification: six required parts
description: The specification properly consists of six parts: 1. The preamble. 2. A general statement of the nature and object of the invention. 3. A brief description of the drawings, if drawings are made. 4. A detailed description of the invention. 5. The claim or claims. 6. The signature of the applicant.
guidance: Prior witness requirement was dispensed with by the Act of March 3, 1915. Place claims in the part of the specification which immediately precedes the signatures.

name: General statement: avoid limiting particulars
description: The general statement of the nature and object of the invention is a convenient mode of introducing the detailed description and should be free from any particularity or limitation which, if imported into the claims by implication, might reduce the patent's coverage.
guidance: Do not include particulars in the general statement that could be read into claims and unintentionally narrow claim scope below what prior art requires.

name: Claims must particularly and distinctly claim
description: The applicant 'shall particularly point out and distinctly claim the part, improvement, or combination which he claims as his invention.' Claims should be made in that part of the specification which immediately precedes the signatures.
guidance: Ensure each claim clearly identifies the inventive subject matter and is placed properly in the specification.

name: Avoid vague, elastic claims and unnecessary multiplication
description: Writing claims in vague phraseology to gain 'elasticity' is improper; stretching claims to catch infringers often makes them vague and prone to invalidation. Multiplying claims unnecessarily is disapproved by the courts and can be dangerous to validity.
guidance: Prefer clear, precise claim language; don't add many slightly varied claims merely to 'cover' competitors.

name: Use of both generic and specific claims
description: It is proper to make a generic claim and also a specific claim in an application for a generic invention, even where only one species is described. If later prior art reduces scope, the specific claim may remain valid while the generic may fall.
guidance: Draft both levels of claim scope where appropriate to preserve fallback positions.

name: Claiming a whole machine vs. parts/combinations
description: If the description sets forth an entire machine that is novel, the applicant may claim the machine co-extensively with the description, but such a claim should seldom be the only one because it can often be readily evaded. Proper practice is to claim new parts and new combinations separately.
guidance: Include claims directed to the whole and to specific parts/combinations to improve enforceability.

name: To secure a particular part or combination, specify it
description: To secure a particular part of a machine, a claim must specify that part; to secure a particular combination of parts, a claim must specify all those parts, and the description must explain their joint mode of operation and joint function.
guidance: Claims should include the elements you seek to protect and the specification should explain how they work together.

name: Claim parts separately even if not independently useful
description: A part or combination may be claimed separately though it cannot do useful work separately from the remainder of the machine, because otherwise an infringer could take the important part and avoid infringement by altering how it is adapted.
guidance: Consider claims directed to subassemblies or key elements even if they require the machine context to function.

name: Claims need not list every connecting means
description: It is not necessary that a claim specify all the various means shown in the specification and drawings for connecting the various parts; the claim should be interpreted to include such connections of the several parts as are necessary to make them operative.
guidance: Do not overburden claims with every conceivable connector; ensure operative connections are encompassed by claim language or equivalents doctrine.

name: Use of names vs. reference numerals in claims
description: A part may be specified by name in a claim where no other part has a similar name; where a name alone is not sufficiently specific, mention the reference letter or numeral used in the description and drawings. Use of a reference letter or numeral does not necessarily confine the claim to the exact part shown.
guidance: Use reference numerals to clarify what a claim element refers to, but be aware amended claims with references can have limiting effects in prosecution history contexts.

name: Amendments by reference to drawings can limit claim breadth
description: Where the parts of a combination that differentiate from the prior art are specified in an amended claim by reference letters or numerals, the amended claim is limited to a combination of parts having those particular characteristics; the same is true if the parts are specified by names.
guidance: Amending claims with specific references to drawings or parts can narrow scope—amend carefully during prosecution.

name: Functional language ('means') and equivalents
description: Where some parts of a combination operate to give motion to others, it is proper to specify them by terms like 'means,' 'mechanism,' or 'devices' for giving that motion, except when such terms describe the essence of the invention. If used, the claim will be regarded as functional and will cover only those means shown in the patent and their equivalents.
guidance: Functional claiming is permissible but will be limited to disclosed structures and equivalents under established equivalence tests; avoid generic 'means' when structure-based claiming is appropriate.

name: Manufacture claims: one claim per patentable feature
description: In cases where the description sets forth a manufacture, there ought to be a separate claim for each of its patentable features or at least for the article without any dispensable feature; otherwise someone can remove a dispensable feature and avoid liability.
guidance: Draft claims to protect individual patentable features and fallback combinations without dispensable elements.

name: Composition claims: cover entirety and specify proportions
description: For compositions of matter the claim should cover the composition in its entirety and should either expressly or by reference to the description specify the respective proportions of the ingredients. If some ingredients may be dispensed with and that is stated, separate claims for the residue or a single claim for indispensable ingredients are available.
guidance: State proportions or ranges and optional/indispensable ingredients clearly in the specification so claims can be tailored appropriately.

name: Process claims: cover all necessary occurrences and no more
description: For processes, the claim should cover all necessary occurrences in that process and no more. If it covers less it will be void for want of utility; if it covers more it can be evaded by omitting an unnecessary occurrence.
guidance: List required steps clearly and avoid including superfluous steps that can be avoided by infringers.

name: Design claims: reference to drawings and 'substantially as shown'
description: In design cases the claim may identify its subject by reference to the drawing or photograph. Where a claim ends with 'substantially as shown' that claim refers to the description as well as the drawing. A design patent may contain a claim for the entire design and other claims for independently patentable parts, but several unconnected ornaments cannot lawfully be aggregated and claimed together.
guidance: Use clear drawings and consider separate claims for independently patentable ornamental parts; avoid combining unrelated ornaments.

name: Drawings: when required and required content
description: Drawings are required in all cases wherein the invention admits of representation by drawings. Statute requires drawings to be signed by the applicant or his attorney-in-fact; Patent Office rules require drawings to show every feature of the invention covered by the claims and, when the invention is an improvement, to exhibit the invention disconnected from the old structure and also to show so much of the old structure as will suffice to show the connection.
guidance: Follow Patent Office drawing rules (figures, letters/numerals, signatures). Drawings should show true positions and proportions as necessary to show the invention but need not be working drawings. Connect drawings to the specification by adjacent figure numbers and part letters/numerals incorporated into the descriptive text.

name: Prior Invention (Pre-AIA Only)
description: That patent claim is invalid if the invention defined in that claim was invented by [third party] before [the patentee] invented his invention, [and that other person did not abandon, suppress, or conceal the invention].
guidance: [The Defendant] must show by clear and convincing evidence that (1) before [the patentee] invented his invention, [third party] reduced to practice a [[product] [method]] that included all of the features of claim ___, or (2) [third party] was first to conceive the invention and exercised reasonable diligence in later reducing the invention to practice. In addition, [third party]'s [[product] [method]] must have been sufficiently developed that one skilled in the art would have recognized that it would work for its intended purpose. Practice Note: this defense may be negated if the invention was abandoned, suppressed, or concealed. If abandonment/suppression/concealment is asserted, the jury should be instructed that a prior invention does not anticipate if the prior inventor actively concealed the invention or unreasonably delayed public disclosure. Generally there is no abandonment/suppression/concealment if the invention was made public, sold, offered for sale, or otherwise used commercially; delay is not necessarily concealment if reasonable efforts to bring the invention to market occurred. Burden: clear and convincing evidence. (Cites: 35 U.S.C. §102(a),(g) (pre-AIA) and cases.)

name: Prior Patent (Pre-AIA)
description: [That] patent claim[s] [[is] [are]] invalid if the invention defined by [[that] [those]] claim[s] was disclosed in a patent in the United States or a foreign country [by [third party] before [§102(a) (pre-AIA) Cutoff Date]] [before [§102(b) (pre-AIA) Cutoff Date]].
guidance: If there is a factual issue for the jury about the date of invention of the patent claims in suit or the priority date, the jury should be instructed on how to determine that date; otherwise the Court should instruct the jury as to the Cutoff Date. (Cites: 35 U.S.C. §102(a),(b) (pre-AIA) and cases.)

name: Earlier-Filed Patent Application (Pre-AIA)
description: [That] patent claim[s] [[is] [are]] invalid if the invention defined by [[that] [those]] claim[s] was described in [[U.S.] [international PCT]] [[published patent application] [patent]] filed by another person before that invention was invented by [the patentee].
guidance: Used where the filing date of an application is the relevant date. If there is a factual issue as to the date of invention of the claims in suit, the jury should be instructed on how to determine that date; otherwise the Court should instruct as to the date of invention. (Cites: 35 U.S.C. §§102(e)(1) and (2) (pre-AIA) and cases.)

name: Obviousness—General (Graham Framework)
description: A claimed invention is invalid as 'obvious' if it would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art of the claimed invention as of the Cutoff Date. Unlike anticipation, which allows consideration of only one item of prior art, obviousness may be shown by considering one or more items of prior art.
guidance: Jury must avoid hindsight and not use the patent as a roadmap for selecting/combining prior art. The following four factors (Graham factors) must be evaluated separately for each claim: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between the claimed invention and the prior art; (3) level of ordinary skill in the art as of the Cutoff Date; (4) additional considerations (secondary considerations). [The Defendant] bears the burden of proving obviousness by clear and convincing evidence. (Cites: Microsoft v. i4i; KSR v. Teleflex; Graham v. John Deere; Apple v. Samsung.)

name: Fourth Graham Factor: Secondary Considerations (Other Considerations)
description: Consider secondary factors that may help determine whether the invention would have been obvious, recognizing no single factor is dispositive and the invention should be considered as a whole.
guidance: Examples include: (1) commercial success due to the merits of the claimed invention rather than advertising or other non-claimed features; (2) long-felt but unsolved need satisfied by the invention; (3) others tried but failed; (4) others copied the invention; (5) unexpectedly superior results; (6) praise or expressed surprise; (7) acceptance of licenses due to the merits. These factors are relevant only if there is a nexus between the consideration and the invention; the patentee bears the burden of showing a sufficient nexus. Court must consider admissibility of such evidence and only instruct the jury when supported by the evidence.

name: Damages—General Principles
description: If you find that the accused [[device] [method]] infringes any asserted claims and those claims are not invalid, you must determine the amount of damages to be awarded the Plaintiff for the infringement. The Plaintiff must prove each element of its damages, including amount, by a preponderance of the evidence.
guidance: Damages must be adequate to compensate the Plaintiff for the infringement and put the Plaintiff in about the same financial position it would have been in had the infringement not occurred. Damages cannot be punitive or include interest; reasonable royalty is the minimum amount recoverable. Do not consider damages if all asserted claims are invalid or not infringed. (Cites: 35 U.S.C. §284 and cases.)

name: Date Damages Begin / Notice and Marking
description: The start date for damages is either the date stipulated by the parties or, if disputed, the date the Plaintiff first notified the Defendant of its claim for patent infringement.
guidance: Two ways to give notice: (1) public notice by marking substantially all products practicing the invention with the patent number (or 'Patent'/'Pat' plus a freely accessible Internet address linking product to patent number); licensees who use the invention must also mark substantially all their products; marking is effective even if the Defendant did not see it. (2) Direct notice to the Defendant with a specific claim that the product infringed; notice starts on the date Defendant received it. If Plaintiff failed to provide effective marking or direct notice before suit, Plaintiff can only recover damages for infringement after filing suit, except that if no patented products were made/sold (e.g., only method claims asserted), Plaintiff may recover damages up to six years before filing suit. (Cites: 35 U.S.C. §§286, 287(a) and cases.)

name: Nonprovisional application definition
description: A nonprovisional patent application is an application examined by a patent examiner and may be issued as a patent if patentability requirements are met.
guidance: Nonprovisional applications must include a specification providing a detailed written description, drawings when necessary, claim(s), abstract of the disclosure, and title. See MPEP section 601 I for further details.

name: Purpose and content of claims
description: The claim defines the scope of the invention; it must particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter regarded as the invention.
guidance: One or more claims may be presented in dependent form, referring back to and further limiting another claim(s) in the same application. The claim(s) determine the limits of patent protection.

name: Claim drafting format requirements
description: Each claim should be a single sentence, and where a claim sets forth multiple elements or steps, each element or step should be separated by a line indentation.
guidance: For further details see Claim(s) at 37 C.F.R. 1.75. The USPTO provides Inventor Info Chat presentations on claim drafting including basic structure, examples, and questions to ask regarding your invention.

name: Claim drafting substance (questions and approach)
description: Use available claim-drafting guidance and a structured approach (e.g., ask questions about the invention when drafting a claim set).
guidance: The Office of Innovation Development holds presentations (Inventor Info Chat) that include examples, questions to ask, and one approach to claim drafting to help pro se applicants.

name: Notice of Missing Parts and Notice of Incomplete Application
description: A Notice of Missing Parts is sent when an essential filing requirement is missing; a Notice of Incomplete Application is sent when nonprovisional application papers are deemed incomplete.
guidance: Examples of essential filing requirements include appropriate filing fees, improper entity status, and improper priority claims. Essential filing papers include the specification, drawings, and claims. The filing date will be the date corrections are made. See MPEP section 506 and related guidance.

name: Application completeness and filing date implications
description: Application completeness affects filing date and processing; missing essential filing requirements can trigger Notices which must be corrected to establish the filing date.
guidance: Essential filing papers include specification, drawings, and claims. Correcting deficiencies affects the official filing date. See MPEP section 506 for more on completeness and section 509 for fee completeness.

name: Claim Count and Claim Type Limits
description: An application requesting prioritized examination must contain no more than four independent claims and no more than thirty total claims, and must not contain any multiple dependent claims.
guidance: If an amendment filed after prioritized examination is granted results in more than four independent claims, more than thirty total claims, or adds a multiple dependent claim, the prioritized examination status will be terminated. Applicants are encouraged to file without preliminary amendments but may file a preliminary amendment on filing to reduce claims to comply.

name: Applicant Practices to Maximize Benefit of Prioritized Examination
description: Applicants should (A) have a good knowledge of prior art and file with a clear specification and a complete schedule of claims from broad to narrow, (B) submit an application in condition for examination, (C) file replies that are completely responsive and within any shortened statutory reply period, and (D) be prepared to conduct interviews with the examiner.
guidance: The phrase “in condition for examination” aligns with the accelerated examination meaning discussed in MPEP § 708.02(a), subsection VIII.C. Following these practices helps the Office meet the 12‑month goal for final disposition.

name: Prosecution Time Periods and Termination Triggers
description: For applications under prioritized examination, time periods for reply in Office actions are the same as set forth in MPEP § 710.02(b) (i.e., standard periods), unlike accelerated examination which sets a one‑month no‑extension reply. Prioritized examination will be terminated if applicant files a petition for an extension of time, files a request for suspension of action, or files an amendment that results in exceeding claim limits or adding multiple dependent claims.
guidance: Upon termination, the application is removed from the examiner's special docket and placed on the regular docket according to its stage of prosecution. While amendment increasing claims is permitted, it simply terminates prioritized examination rather than being prohibited.

name: Definition of Final Disposition (12‑month goal)
description: For the 12‑month prioritized examination goal, final disposition means that within 12 months from the date prioritized status is granted one of the following occurs: (A) mailing of a notice of allowance; (B) mailing of a final Office action; (C) filing of a notice of appeal; (D) completion of examination as defined in 37 CFR 41.102; (E) filing of a request for continued examination (RCE); or (F) abandonment of the application.
guidance: Prioritized status is not accorded throughout appeals or interferences before the Board nor after filing of an RCE. Upon mailing of a final rejection (which terminates prioritized exam), applicants may amend claims under standard rules (see 37 CFR 1.116). Upon allowance, applicants may submit claim amendments subject to usual limitations (see 37 CFR 1.312).

name: Refund Policy for Fees Relating to Prioritized Examination
description: If a prioritized examination request is dismissed, the prioritized examination fee (37 CFR 1.17(c)) will be refunded automatically if paid. The processing fee (37 CFR 1.17(i)) will be retained. Application fees (basic filing, search, examination, application size, excess claims) are not refundable under 37 CFR 1.26, although some (search and excess claim fees) may be refunded via petition for express abandonment; publication fee refund possible per MPEP § 1126 if application is not published.
guidance: Termination of prioritized examination does not entitle the applicant to a refund of the prioritized examination fee because termination is not treated as payment made by mistake or in excess (see 35 U.S.C. 42(d) and 37 CFR 1.26(a)).

name: Generic vs Specific disclosure (novelty)
description: A generic disclosure does not take away the novelty of any specific example falling within the terms of that disclosure; a specific disclosure does take away the novelty of a generic claim embracing that disclosure.
guidance: Draft claims carefully: specific prior disclosures can anticipate broader generic claims; generic prior art may not anticipate specific embodiments.

name: Points to consider in drafting the specification
description: Verify: conduct patent search; enlist problems in prior art; what problem is sought to be solved; is it patentable subject matter; what is novel; is the solution obvious; has publication ensued; decide area and nature of protection (Domestic application, Paris Convention, PCT).
guidance: Use the search and problem analysis to define scope of claims and filing strategy (domestic vs foreign, priority routes).

name: Amendment of the disclosure (Rule 919) — new matter prohibition
description: No deletion or addition shall broaden the disclosure of an application to include new matter after the filing date of the application.
guidance: Any post-filing amendments cannot introduce subject matter extending beyond the original disclosure; limit claim amendments accordingly.

name: Contents of the description (Rule 407)
description: Description should include: Title; Technical Field; Background Art; Summary (Abstract of the Disclosure); Brief description of the several views of the drawings; Detailed Description; Claims; Abstracts; Drawings.
guidance: Organize the description to support claims and meet formal IRR requirements; include clear background and summary to contextualize inventive features.

name: Drawings requirements (Rules 413-414)
description: The drawing must be signed by the applicant or his attorney/agent; must show every feature of the invention; figures must be consecutively numbered; elements must be designated by reference numerals corresponding to the elements in the description.
guidance: Ensure drawings are clear, complete, signed, numbered and that reference numerals in drawings match the description for consistent claim support.

name: Claims — scope and quality requirements
description: Claims define the scope/boundary of protection. Claims must be: (a) Clear (clarity) — avoid vague terms such as 'thin', 'strong', 'a major part', 'such as', 'when required'; (b) Complete (enablement) — cover the inventive feature and sufficient surrounding elements; (c) Supported (support) — all claim characteristics must be fully explained in the description.
guidance: Draft clear, concise claims with adequate support in the description; avoid ambiguous wording and ensure claims are enabled.

name: Categories of claims
description: Physical Entity claims: apparatus/device/product claims. Activity claims: method claims covering operations comprising one or more steps (e.g., manufacturing process, chemical process, software operation).
guidance: Select claim category appropriate to the invention (product vs method) and draft elements accordingly.

name: Kinds of claims — Independent and Dependent
description: Independent claim: broadly describes the invention, typically written with broad terms, stands on its own (usually Claim 1). Dependent claim: describes the invention in a narrower aspect, clarifies independent claim language, expresses particular embodiments as fallback positions.
guidance: Use a broad independent claim plus dependent claims to provide fallback positions and to capture preferred embodiments.

name: Parts of a claim (preamble, body, transition)
description: Preamble: name of the subject matter or prior art environment. Body: recital of elements (structures, steps, parts or ingredients) and the manner in which elements cooperate. Transition: links preamble and body, often 'comprising' or 'which comprises' and typically followed by a colon.
guidance: Structure claims with a clear preamble, properly recited elements in the body, and an appropriate transitional phrase; use consistent punctuation and grammar.

name: Commercial success must flow from specification functions/advantages
description: Commercial success of devices within the claims must flow from the functions and advantages disclosed or inherent in the description in the specification; success may not be attributable to improvements or modifications made by others.
guidance: To be pertinent to nonobviousness, nexus is required between commercial success and the claimed invention (In re Vamco Machine & Tool, Inc., 752 F.2d 1564). If commercial success is due to features not disclosed or to later modifications, it is not probative. Examples and case citations illustrate limits.

name: Nexus especially difficult in design cases
description: In design cases, evidence of commercial success must be clearly attributable to the design and not to brand name recognition, improved performance, or other factors.
guidance: Establishing nexus is especially difficult in design patents; commercial success not accompanied by evidence attributing it to the design is not probative (Litton Systems, Inc. v. Whirlpool Corp.). Examiner should look for evidence directly tying sales to the claimed design rather than other causes.

name: Sufficiency of disclosure / enablement under 35 U.S.C. 112
description: If examiner establishes a prima facie case of lack of enablement, burden shifts to applicant to present persuasive arguments supported by proofs that one skilled in the art could make and use the claimed invention using the disclosure as a guide.
guidance: Evidence supplementing a specification that appears deficient must show that the missing information would have been known to those of ordinary skill (In re Brandstadter; In re Howarth). Affidavits/declarations are not acceptable to establish facts the specification should recite (In re Buchner). Opinion testimony merely asserting disclosure is insufficient, but opinion testimony that explains underlying factual basis may be admissible and weighed case‑by‑case (Glaser v. Strickland reexamining In re Oppenauer).

name: Corrections to file wrapper data must follow procedures
description: If an examiner notices an error in data on the file wrapper or PALM bib‑data sheet (inventorship, filing date, prior U.S. application numbers, priority claims), the application should be returned to OIPE for correction or routed to technical support staff for PALM correction.
guidance: Use Office of Initial Patent Examination Data Base Routing Slip with explanation. Examples of corrections: (A) inventorship changes under 37 CFR 1.48; (B) filing date corrections; (C) prior U.S. application number errors; (D) correction of priority claims. Other corrections performed in the TC; assignment name/address errors corrected by Assignment Division.

name: Anticipation / 'described' requirement under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102
description: The two basic requirements that must be met by a prior art document in order to describe a claimed invention such that it is anticipated under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 are: (1) 'each and every element of the claimed invention' must be disclosed either explicitly or inherently, and the elements must be 'arranged or combined in the same way as in the claim;' and (2) a person of ordinary skill in the art must have been enabled to make the invention without undue experimentation.
guidance: Cites In re Gleave; Eli Lilly; NetMoneyIN; In re Bond; enablement for anticipation judged from the viewpoint of a person of ordinary skill (In re Donohue). There is no requirement that a prior art document meet the 'how to use' requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) to anticipate (cases: Schoenwald; Schering; Impax Labs).

name: Anticipation may be shown by a single species/embodiment
description: For a prior art document to describe a claimed invention under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) or (a)(2), the prior art need only describe and enable one skilled in the art to make a single species or embodiment of the claimed invention.
guidance: Distinguishes the broader 35 U.S.C. 112(a) written description requirement (which must support the entire claimed scope) from anticipation (Vas-Cath; In re Lukach; In re Van Langenhoven; In re Ruscetta). A disclosure of a single embodiment can anticipate broadly claimed subject matter for anticipation purposes.

name: Public use as prior art under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1)
description: Public use rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) may be based on uses that are public anywhere in the world; a public use must occur before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to constitute prior art.
guidance: No geographic limitation under AIA (contrast pre-AIA §102(b) 'in this country'). Examiner should require the applicant to show that a potentially public use did not make the claimed process accessible to the public. Pre-AIA doctrines on readiness for patenting and whether use was 'accessible to the public' or 'commercially exploited' inform analysis (cases: Invitrogen; American Seating; Woodland Trust). Certain uses by the inventor or joint inventor within one year may fall under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1) exceptions (see MPEP §2154.02).

name: Procedure for determining whether to apply 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) or 102(a)(2)
description: Examiner should first consider whether the reference qualifies as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) and then whether any exceptions in 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1) apply; separately, the examiner should consider whether the reference qualifies under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) and whether any exceptions in 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2) apply.
guidance: Under 102(a)(1): patents, printed publications, public use, on sale, and otherwise making available qualify if reference predates effective filing date (sale/use need not occur in U.S.). Disclosures within one-year grace period may be excepted by 102(b)(1)(A) or (B) if made by inventor/joint inventor or derived from them. Under 102(a)(2): U.S. patents, U.S. patent application publications, and certain PCT publications are prior art if the disclosure's effectively filed date is before the claimed invention's effective filing date; see 35 U.S.C. 102(d) and MPEP §2154 for 'effectively filed' criteria.

name: 102(a)(2) 'effectively filed' requirement and related criteria
description: U.S. patents, U.S. patent application publications, and certain WIPO publications are prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) if the effectively filed date of the disclosure is before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
guidance: Even if issue/publication date is not before the claimed effective filing date (so it would not qualify as 102(a)(1)), the reference may still be applicable as 102(a)(2) if it was 'effectively filed' earlier. See 35 U.S.C. 102(d) and MPEP §2154 for criteria to determine when subject matter was effectively filed and when common ownership or derivation exceptions apply.

name: Ways to overcome a 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) or 102(a)(2) rejection
description: In addition to arguing patentable distinction or amending claims, a 102(a)(1) or 102(a)(2) rejection can be overcome by: (A) submitting a benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 120 within time and establishing the prior application satisfies 35 U.S.C. 112(a); (B) submitting a benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) (provisional) within time and establishing 112(a) support; (C) submitting a priority claim under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) with required documentation and establishing the foreign priority application satisfies 112(a); (D) filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.130 to show an applied disclosure is excepted under 35 U.S.C. 102(b); or (E) establishing common ownership or a Joint Research Agreement to obtain the 102(b)(2)(C) exception.
guidance: Each route has procedural requirements (corrected application data sheet under 37 CFR 1.76; time limits under 37 CFR 1.78/1.55; proof of enablement/written description under 35 U.S.C. 112(a); petitions for delayed benefit/priority where applicable). See MPEP §§211, 213-216, 717, 2155, 2154.02(c). Note these methods can also overcome 103 rejections based on 102(a)(1)/(a)(2) prior art.

name: Use of prescribed form paragraphs for rejections under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102
description: Office form paragraphs (e.g., ¶7.06; ¶7.07.aia; ¶7.08.aia; ¶7.12.aia; ¶7.14.aia; ¶7.15.01.aia) should be used when making appropriate rejections and certain instructions apply regarding their use and sequencing.
guidance: Examples of guidance: ¶7.06 must be used in all Office Actions when a prior art rejection is made in an application with actual filing date on/after March 16, 2013, that claims priority to an application filed before March 16, 2013 (use only once). ¶7.07.aia quotes 35 U.S.C. 102 and is required in first actions on the merits and final rejections; ¶7.08.aia for 102(a)(1) activity must be preceded by 7.03.aia and 7.07.aia; ¶7.12.aia for 102(a)(2) references must be preceded by 7.03.aia and 7.07.aia (and may also require 7.08.aia); ¶7.14.aia addresses pre-AIA 102(g) priority language and must be used with appropriate preceding paragraphs. Form paragraph instructions also include bracket insertions for claim numbers and prior art identification.

name: Representative-claim selection for eligibility analysis
description: Courts may select one or more claims as 'representative' of a broader group of claims for purposes of evaluating patent eligibility (e.g., district court analyzed claim 9 and the Federal Circuit also treated claims 11 and 16 as representative).
guidance: Representative-claim treatment permits resolving §101 issues without analyzing every claim, but the chosen representative must fairly represent the claim set; appellate courts will scrutinize whether the representative characterization improperly characterizes claims at an impermissibly high level of generality.

name: Alice Step One — directed to an abstract idea
description: Determine whether the representative claim is directed to an abstract idea (e.g., 'receiving information, associating information with images, comparing the images, and presenting information based on that comparison').
guidance: Claims that recite generalized steps of collecting, analyzing, and presenting information using nothing other than the conventional operations of generic computer components are typically directed to abstract ideas. How the court articulates the abstract idea (level of generality) can be outcome-determinative.

name: Functional/result-oriented claim language undermines eligibility
description: Claims characterized by result-oriented, functional language that omit specific requirements as to how steps are performed are more likely to be found directed to an abstract idea and ineligible under §101.
guidance: Courts look for specificity about how a claimed result is achieved; merely reciting high-level functions without technical detail or nonconventional implementation favors ineligibility.

name: Claims drawn to a specific technical solution may be eligible
description: Claims that recite a specific device or method that improves the relevant technology (e.g., an improved POV camera with dual recording configuration and wireless streaming of a low-quality stream to a remote device) can be treated as directed to a technical solution rather than an abstract idea.
guidance: Avoid characterizing such claims at an unduly high level of generality; emphasize the claimed technical improvements and concrete configuration/limitations that solve a technical problem.

name: Vague added limitations do not rescue eligibility
description: Adding limitations that are vague (e.g., 'extracting and matching interest points') but do not explain how the limitation is performed or how it improves technology typically do not affect the §101 analysis.
guidance: Limitations must provide specificity (how determined/used) and technical substance; mere labels for operations without implementation detail are insufficient to make claims 'significantly more' than an abstract idea.

name: Claim construction must follow claim language and specification
description: Claim terms should not be given restrictive meanings (e.g., requiring 'positioned above and in vertical and lateral alignment') unless the claim language or specification supports such a restriction.
guidance: Courts will reverse constructions that import limitations unsupported by the intrinsic record; claim construction should reflect ordinary meaning unless patentee acted as lexicographer or disavowed scope.

name: Pre-AIA on-sale invalidity elements
description: Under pre-AIA §102(b) an on-sale invalidity determination requires: (1) the subject of the offer embodies the claims; (2) the offer was 'in this country'; (3) the offer occurred before the critical date; (4) the offer was a commercial offer for sale; and (5) the invention was ready for patenting prior to the critical date.
guidance: Courts apply general contract principles to determine whether communications (e.g., a quotation letter) constitute a commercial offer; detailed, signed, and directed offers to a specific company can qualify even if no sale occurred.

name: Result-effective-variable and routine optimization analysis
description: The 'result-effective variable' doctrine is part of routine optimization analysis: an undisclosed parameter (e.g., molecular weight range) may be considered a result-effective variable that a POSA would optimize, and overlap in disclosed ranges is not strictly required.
guidance: Courts will consider whether parameters are typical/expected (supported by other prior-art data or expert testimony) and whether routine optimization would have led to the claimed value with a reasonable expectation of success.

name: Obviousness standard — reasonable expectation of success suffices
description: A finding of obviousness does not require a guarantee of success; it requires that a POSA would have had a reasonable expectation of success in bridging gaps in the prior art to arrive at the claimed invention.
guidance: Demonstrate that prior art provided specific reasons a POSA would be motivated and would have expected success; absence of 'only failures' in the prior art supports a reasonable-expectation finding.
