name: Written-description possession requirement and interpretation of 'optional'
description: For §112 written-description, the specification must show that the inventors possessed the claimed invention. Use of the term 'optional' in the specification indicates something may be present or absent; embodiments and originally filed claims are part of the specification for this analysis.
guidance: Courts will look for explicit disclosure or embodiments supporting absence/inclusion of elements. Expert testimony about POSITA practices may be weighed, but objective specification disclosures and original claim content are critical. Minority/dissenting views may give weight to unrebutted expert testimony but majority decisions will rely on textual disclosures and examples.

name: Effect of U.S. patent or application publication claiming same invention
description: For pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 applications: if a noncommonly owned U.S. patent or published application claims the same invention and its publication/issue date is less than 1 year prior to presentation of claims in the examined application, the applicant's remedy (if any) must be by interference under 37 CFR 41.202 rather than by a 37 CFR 1.131(a) affidavit. If a U.S. patent issues more than 1 year prior to presentation of claims, a rejection under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 135(b)(1) should be made. If a published application (35 U.S.C. 122(b) or certain WIPO PCT publications) published more than 1 year prior to presentation, a rejection under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 135(b)(2) may be appropriate if the examined application was filed after the publication date.
guidance: Note such facts in the Office action and use the appropriate form paragraphs (e.g., ¶¶23.14, 23.14.01). A 37 CFR 1.131(a) affidavit is ineffective to overcome a U.S. patent or publication not only when claims are verbatim but also when there is no patentable distinction; identical or non‑patentably distinct claims constitute 'interfering subject matter' (37 CFR 41.203(a)) and cannot be overcome by a Rule 131(a) affidavit. For commonly owned references where claims are not patentably distinct, a terminal disclaimer and an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(c) may be used to overcome a pre‑AIA 103 rejection (see MPEP §718).

name: Facts and documentary evidence required to establish priority
description: The essential showing under 37 CFR 1.131(a) is priority of invention by satisfactory evidence of FACTS, not mere conclusions. Exhibits may accompany the affidavit/declaration and each exhibit relied upon should be specifically referred to in terms of what it is relied upon to show.
guidance: Permissible supporting exhibits include attached sketches, blueprints, photographs, reproductions of notebook entries, models, supporting witness statements (for verbal disclosures), testimony from an interference (with specific parts pointed out), and documents from the Disclosure Document Program (where applicable historically). Exhibits and models must comply with 37 CFR 1.91 to be entered into the file. Each exhibit need not support all claimed limitations provided missing limitations are supported by the affidavit/declaration itself. General, vague allegations or conclusory statements describing exhibits without specifics are insufficient (see In re Borkowski, In re Harry). Cite specific parts of exhibits and explain exactly what facts they establish and when.

name: Definition / scope of PGR
description: Post-grant review (PGR) is an adversarial proceeding before the Patent Trial and Appeals Board (PTAB) of the USPTO, in which a petitioner challenges the patentability of one or more claims in a recently-issued US patent.
guidance: PGR was created by the America Invents Act (AIA) and became available in 2012; it is designed to challenge recently-issued patents and addresses patentability issues at the PTAB.

name: Exemplary Claim Language ("for example," "such as")
description: Description of examples or preferences is properly set forth in the specification rather than the claims. If stated in the claims, examples and preferences may lead to confusion over the intended scope of a claim. Note that the mere use of the phrase "such as" or "for example" in a claim does not by itself render the claim indefinite.
guidance: If it is not clear whether the claimed narrower range is a limitation, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph should be made. The examiner should analyze whether the metes and bounds of the claim are clearly set forth. Examples held indefinite (fact specific): (A) “R is halogen, for example, chlorine”; (B) “material such as rock wool or asbestos”; (C) “lighter hydrocarbons, such, for example, as the vapors or gas produced”; (D) “normal operating conditions such as while in the container of a proportioner”; (E) “coke, brick, or like material”. The above examples are fact specific and should not be applied as per se rules. See MPEP § 2173.02 for guidance regarding when it is appropriate to make a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b).

name: Markush Groups (Alternative Limitations)
description: A claim that recites a list of alternatives to define a limitation (Markush grouping) is an acceptable construction and should not necessarily be rejected as confusing under 35 U.S.C. 112(b). A Markush grouping is typically a closed group of alternatives (e.g., 'selected from the group consisting of A, B, and C').
guidance: Treatment is not governed by particular format (e.g., 'consisting of' vs 'A, B, or C'). If a Markush grouping uses an open list (e.g., 'comprising' or 'consisting essentially of'), the claim should generally be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) as indefinite because it is unclear what other alternatives are intended. If combinations/mixtures of alternatives are intended, include qualifying language (e.g., 'at least one member selected from the group' or 'or mixtures thereof'). A Markush group may be large and broad without being indefinite (breadth is not indefiniteness), but if so expansive that skilled artisans cannot determine metes and bounds, an indefiniteness rejection is appropriate. Use of Markush claims of diminishing scope is not by itself objectionable, but if it renders claims indefinite or causes undue multiplicity, reject appropriately. Double inclusion of an element in a Markush group is not per se a basis for rejection — evaluate facts to see if redundancy renders the claim indefinite (examples and case law cited, e.g., Eli Lilly v. Teva). See MPEP § 2117 and § 803.02 and Supplementary Guidelines.

name: Old Combination
description: A claim should not be rejected on the ground of 'old combination'.
guidance: Since the 1952 Patent Act, courts/Board have taken the view that an 'old combination' rejection is no longer valid. Claims should be considered proper so long as they comply with 35 U.S.C. 112(b). The old principle (Lincoln Engineering) required citation of a single reference broadly disclosing a combination functionally cooperating to produce substantially the same results; subsequent case law (Bernhart, Radio Steel) and Board decisions have effectively legislated that principle out. Accordingly, do not reject claims merely because they are an old combination if they meet statutory requirements.

name: Aggregation
description: A claim should not be rejected on the ground of 'aggregation'.
guidance: Case law (In re Gustafson, In re Collier) indicates 'aggregation' is a non‑statutory rejection and should not be used. If a claim omits essential matter or fails to interrelate essential elements of the invention as defined by the specification, see MPEP § 2172.01 for treatment. Assess whether the rejection is actually under a statutory ground (101/102/103/112) rather than a non‑statutory 'aggregation' label.

name: Prolix
description: Claims that are overly long or contain unimportant details should be rejected as prolix only when such recitations render the scope of the claimed invention indefinite.
guidance: Reject as prolix when long recitations prevent determination of the metes and bounds of the claimed subject matter. The basis for prolix rejection is that the long/irrelevant recitations cause indefiniteness — do not use prolix to penalize mere length if scope remains ascertainable.

name: Scope of inquiry for 102(b)(2)(B)
description: A determination of whether the exception in AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(B) is applicable to subject matter in an intervening U.S. patent document does not involve a comparison of the subject matter of the claimed invention to either the subject matter disclosed by the inventor or the subject matter of the subsequent intervening U.S. patent document.
guidance: The inquiry is limited to whether the subject matter of the intervening document was previously publicly disclosed by the inventor (or someone who obtained it from the inventor). Whether the prior art anticipates or renders obvious the claimed invention is a separate inquiry.

name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) common ownership/obligation-of-assignment exception
description: The exception disqualifies subject matter disclosed in a U.S. patent document from constituting prior art under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) if the subject matter disclosed and the claimed invention, not later than the effective filing date of the claimed invention, 'were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.'
guidance: If the conditions of 102(b)(2)(C) are met, the U.S. patent document may not be available as prior art under either AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103. This differs from pre-AIA 103(c). However, the exception does not apply to disclosures qualifying under 102(a)(1), and even if disqualified as prior art, such documents may still be used for double patenting, enablement, or to indicate state of the art where appropriate.

name: Limits on 102(b)(2)(C) — 102(a)(1), double patenting, enablement
description: The AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) exception does not apply to a disclosure that qualifies as prior art under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) (disclosures made before the effective filing date of the claimed invention). Also, a double patenting rejection may still be made on the basis of the U.S. patent or U.S. patent application publication, and such documents may be cited to indicate the state of the art for lack of enablement rejections under 35 U.S.C. 112(a).
guidance: Even when common-ownership/assignment conditions are asserted, examiners should check for 102(a)(1) status (publication/issue dates) and consider double-patenting and enablement contexts separately.

name: Statement by applicant to establish common-ownership exception
description: A clear and conspicuous statement by the applicant (or the applicant's representative of record) that the claimed invention and the subject matter disclosed in the U.S. patent document were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person not later than the effective filing date of the claimed invention will be sufficient to establish that the AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) exception applies.
guidance: Applicant may present supporting evidence such as assignment copies but is not required to do so. The Office will not request corroborating evidence in the absence of independent evidence raising doubt as to veracity. Statements under 102(b)(2)(C) are treated analogously to statements under pre-AIA 103(c).

name: 37 CFR 1.130(b) — affidavit/declaration of prior public disclosure
description: When any claim is rejected, the applicant or patent owner may submit an affidavit or declaration to disqualify a disclosure as prior art by establishing that the subject matter disclosed had, before such disclosure was made or before such subject matter was effectively filed, been publicly disclosed by the inventor or a joint inventor or another who obtained the subject matter disclosed directly or indirectly from the inventor or a joint inventor.
guidance: The affidavit/declaration must identify the subject matter publicly disclosed and provide the date such subject matter was publicly disclosed. If the earlier disclosure was a printed publication, a copy must accompany the affidavit (37 CFR 1.130(b)(1)). If not printed, describe the subject matter with sufficient detail and particularity to determine what was publicly disclosed (37 CFR 1.130(b)(2)).

name: Applicability scope for 37 CFR 1.130
description: The provisions of 37 CFR 1.130 apply to any application (and patents issuing thereon) that contains, or contained at any time, a claim to a claimed invention that has an effective filing date on or after March 16, 2013, or a specific reference under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, 365(c), or 386(c) to any patent or application that contains such a claim.
guidance: Check effective filing date and specific references to determine whether 1.130 relief is available in the case under examination.

name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(c) joint research agreement conditions
description: Subject matter disclosed and a claimed invention shall be deemed to have been owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person in applying subsection (b)(2)(C) if: (1) the subject matter disclosed was developed and the claimed invention was made by, or on behalf of, one or more parties to a joint research agreement that was in effect on or before the effective filing date; (2) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (3) the application for patent discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement.
guidance: A 'joint research agreement' is a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement by two or more persons/entities for experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention. If these three conditions are met, the joint research agreement prior art is not available as prior art under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2).

name: Invoking joint research agreement — procedural requirements
description: To invoke a joint research agreement to disqualify a disclosure as prior art, the applicant (or representative) must provide a statement that the disclosure and the claimed invention were made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement, that the agreement was in effect on or before the effective filing date, and that the claimed invention was made as a result of activities within the scope of the agreement.
guidance: If the names of the parties to the joint research agreement are not stated in the application, the application must be amended to include the names in accordance with 37 CFR 1.71(g). The applicant may but is not required to present supporting evidence; the Office will not request corroboration absent independent doubt.

name: Inventorship/naming requirement and corrective procedure
description: Patent laws require naming the actual inventor or joint inventors of the claimed subject matter (35 U.S.C. 115(a)). The Office presumes the named inventor(s) are correct.
guidance: If an application names incorrect inventorship, the applicant should submit a request to correct inventorship under 37 CFR 1.48. In rare situations where the application clearly does not name the correct inventorship and no correction is filed, Office personnel should reject the claims under 35 U.S.C. 101 and 115. Do not make a rejection under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f) if the application is subject to FITF provisions.

name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 103 — effective filing date and claim-focused differences
description: AIA 35 U.S.C. 103 continues to set forth the nonobviousness requirement, but AIA 35 U.S.C. 103 determines obviousness as of the effective filing date of the claimed invention (rather than as of the time the invention was made). AIA 35 U.S.C. 103 requires consideration of 'the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art.'
guidance: In practice during examination, this distinction only matters when the case is subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103 and evidence of an invention date prior to the effective filing date exists (often shown by affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131). The term 'claims' has been used historically to define the invention believed patentable; apply Graham factors and ascertain differences between the prior art and the claims at issue.

name: Prompt examination and duty to correct
description: When an inventor receives his patent, it is his duty to examine it promptly, see that his invention is properly described, and that his Claims are broad enough to embrace it in all its scope; failure to do this is a dedication to the public of so much of his invention as is not covered by his Claim.
guidance: Patentee must act with reasonable diligence and speed; unnecessary laches or delay affects right to alter or re-issue. Cases: Wollensak v. Reiher; Miller v. Brass Co.; Hahn v. Harwood. If upon mere reading it is obvious he is entitled to broader claims, he must apply speedily; failure may be treated as abandonment.

name: Re-issue available only for inadvertence, accident, or mistake
description: Re-issues for the enlargement of Claims should be the exception and not the rule; enlargement can only be done when an actual mistake has occurred — not from a mere error of judgment.
guidance: Courts will require clear proof of inadvertence/accident/mistake. Miller v. Brass Co. emphasizes re-issues are to correct real mistakes. If delay suggests the patentee simply exercised poor judgment, re-issue to enlarge is not permitted.

name: Effect of claims being too narrow vis-à-vis public notice
description: The patent (and specifically its Claim) operates in law as a disclaimer of what is not claimed; what is not claimed is public property and the public is notified by the patent of the patentee's claimed scope.
guidance: Where omitted matter is clearly described but not claimed, the law presumes the inventor intended to abandon it or withhold it for a future patent; the public may rely on that implied disclaimer.

name: No re-issue to claim matter clearly described but omitted after unreasonable delay
description: No re-issue can be allowed to claim matter clearly described in the original patent but omitted from its Claims, unless the re-issue is applied for within a reasonable time after the grant of the original.
guidance: Unreasonable delay converts the presumption of inadvertence into a presumption of intentional exclusion/abandonment. Authorities: Ives v. Sargent; Gage v. Kellogg; Reed v. Chase; Wooster v. Handy.

name: Reasonable time / no fixed limit
description: No invariable rule can be laid down as to what is reasonable time within which the patentee should seek correction of a claim considered too narrow; reasonable time depends on the particular facts and circumstances.
guidance: Courts weigh factors (commercial importance, knowledge of defect, intervening rights). Cases: Hahn v. Harwood, Stutz v. Armstrong, Odell v. Stout. Two years is a common benchmark but not definitive.

name: Intervening/adverse rights defeat re-issue
description: The question whether adverse rights have arisen since the original patent was granted is important to re-issue; intervening rights (public use/patent by another) can bar re-issue.
guidance: Courts consider whether third parties have begun using the omitted matter or another patent claims it; such rights support finding abandonment and prohibit re-issue. See Turrell v. Bradford; cases on sub-combinations.

name: Completing the international application form (DM/1) — Items 1–19
description: The Guide provides detailed instructions for each DM/1 item (Item 1: Applicant; Item 2: Entitlement to file; Item 3: Applicant’s Contracting Party; Item 4: Email for multiple applicants; Item 5: Appointment of representative; Item 6: Number of designs/reproductions/specimens; Item 7: Designated Contracting Parties; Item 8: Product indication; Item 9: Description; Item 10: Legends; Item 11: Identity of the creator; Item 12: Claim; Item 13: Priority claim; Item 14: International exhibition; Item 15: Exception to lack of novelty; Item 16: Related designs/variants; Item 17: Publication of the international registration; Item 18: Reduction of the individual designation fee; Item 19: Signature).
guidance: Follow the Guide's item-level instructions and the annexes (oath/declaration of creator, supporting documents). Use eHague assisted entry where possible to avoid errors.

name: Priority claims and supporting documents
description: Priority claims must be supported by a priority document; WIPO DAS and priority document procedures are available; annex lists supporting document requirements and how priority documents are handled.
guidance: Provide priority document or use WIPO DAS for electronic retrieval; Annex V and relevant A.I. sections explain required content and timing.

name: Competent representation; reasonable diligence and promptness (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.101, 11.103, 11.104)
description: Under 37 C.F.R. § 11.101, a practitioner shall provide competent representation to a client. Rules at 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.103 and 11.104 require a practitioner to provide competent representation and to act with “reasonable diligence and promptness” when representing clients.
guidance: Failures that support a violation include not promptly notifying a client of filing irregularities, failing to consult with the client about how to address irregularities, filing patent applications late, claiming wrong priority dates, allowing an application to be abandoned for failure to pay fees, failing to file required petitions (e.g., to restore priority), and failing to take steps to address errors or inform the client until much later. These factual examples (filing three applications late, loss of priority date due to late drawing, failing to respond to Notices to File Missing Parts, not filing petition to revive) are used as evidence of incompetence/lack of diligence.

name: False statements to tribunals and failure to correct misapprehension (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.303, 11.801(a) & (b))
description: 37 C.F.R. § 11.801 prohibits a practitioner from knowingly making a false statement of material fact, or knowingly failing to disclose a fact necessary to correct a known misapprehension, in connection with a disciplinary matter. 37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a)(1) and (3) prohibit knowingly making a false statement of fact or law to a tribunal and offering evidence known to be false.
guidance: Examples supporting violations: fabricating and presenting forged emails as evidence; making affirmative oral or written statements to the BBO or OED that the practitioner knows are false; failing to identify or produce facts showing that claimed oral notifications occurred. The ALJ’s credibility findings (rejecting unsupported testimony absent corroborating dates/facts) are relied on to support these violations.

name: Restriction of claim when goods indicated on mark face
description: Where there is an indication on the face of the mark of the goods to which the mark is applied, the claim for registration must be restricted to those goods only.
guidance: If the mark itself specifies goods, applicant cannot claim broader classes; Trade Mark Instructions require restriction in such cases.

name: Prohibited or specially restricted matter in representations
description: Certain representations should not appear in the representation forms and certain depicted elements will not be registered unless used before 13 August 1875.
guidance: Examples prohibited in representations: the Royal arms or similar, words like 'Registered', 'Registered Design', 'Copyright', 'Entered at Stationers' Hall', 'To counterfeit this is Forgery', 'Patent', 'Patented'. Elements not registerable (unless pre‑1875 use): portraits of Her Majesty or Royal Family, Royal Crown, national arms or flags, prize/exhibition medals. Ornamental or coloured groundworks (tartans/checks) cannot be claimed as part of a mark unless included by border or lines.

name: IPC assignment must be accurate and based on scope of claimed invention
description: IPC assignment must be made accurately based on the scope of the invention since it is necessary for effective search and retrieval.
guidance: Classification impacts search effectiveness for IP offices and users; ensure assignments reflect true scope of claimed subject-matter.

name: Primary basis for classification: claimed invention scope
description: Technical subject-matter in the claims should be classified into IPC symbols (section, class, subclass, main group, subgroup) and classification shall be made on the basis of the scope of the claimed invention.
guidance: If the scope of the invention is unclear, use the detailed description (and drawings if necessary); technical subject-matter only in the description can be an additional basis for classification.

name: Classification must reflect essential contents of claimed invention as a whole
description: Determine classification based on the essential contents of the claimed invention as a whole without regard to the category of invention.
guidance: Example: an electronic radio circuit with tuner/demodulator/amplifier/output is classified as the whole circuit unless core subject-matter concerns a specific part; then classify by that part.

name: Compounds classification (including when field of use is essential)
description: Chemical compounds (organic, inorganic, polymer) shall be classified in Section C according to intrinsic chemical-structure characteristics; if field of use is essential content, classify in place for field of use when pertinent place exists; if invention relates to use of compound, classify only the field of use if appropriate.
guidance: Classify by intrinsic chemical features first; use-of-compound claims may change classification.

name: Confirmation of IPC — examiner's verification of pre-classification
description: When pre-classification is assigned by an outsourcing agency, the examiner must check whether pre-classification was appropriate based on claim subject-matter with reference to description/drawings and reclassify if incorrect.
guidance: Reclassification by examiner is allowed; follow hierarchical IPC path from high to low level when determining classification.

name: Content scope and exceptions for laying open
description: In principle all patent applications shall be laid open after 1.5 years unless excluded: applications omitting statement of scope of claims (Article 42(5)), applications whose registration is published, or applications invalidated, withdrawn, abandoned, or rejected.
guidance: Follow Article 19(3) of Enforcement Decree for matters to be laid open and statutory exceptions.

name: Request for examination — general eligibility and single-request rule
description: Request for examination shall be filed only for an application pending in KIPO; request is allowed only once per application, cannot be withdrawn, and continues despite loss of legal capacity (e.g., death). For requests by applicant, description with scope of claims must be attached to written application (Article 59(2)).
guidance: Ensure attachments meet statutory requirements; a single, irrevocable request starts substantive examination.

name: Effects of filing request for examination
description: Applications with a valid examination request will be examined and can be terminated only by patent registration or rejection (unless invalidated/withdrawn/abandoned). When request is made before laying open, the purpose of the request is published upon publication; applicants must amend specifications omitting claim scope when notified by third-party request; Commissioner must notify applicant if request was filed by third party and notify third party of final decisions.
guidance: Understand procedural notifications and amendment obligations triggered by third-party requests.

name: Handling multiple applications claiming identical invention
description: When two or more applications claim identical invention, examination of later applications shall be deferred until the earlier application is processed/laidoff/registered in patent gazette. If both applications can be rejected by the same reason, examination may begin without deferral. Final decision for later application made after confirming claim scope in earlier application.
guidance: Coordinate examination to preserve priority and avoid conflicting grants.

name: General principle for law application to pending applications
description: When Patent Act revision occurs while an application is pending, transitional measures apply to prevent disadvantages; provisions of law are applied as of the filing date. Divisional/converted applications and those by lawful right holders are accorded the parent filing date so provisions are applied as of parent filing date.
guidance: For priority/domestic priority/claims of not-prejudicial disclosures, apply law as of original application filing date; use examples to determine applicable law when revisions occur.

name: Use of foreign patent office/search organization outcomes
description: If foreign patent offices or search organizations have conducted searches regarding the claimed invention, the examiner shall review those outcomes to determine whether they can be used as relevant prior art.
guidance: Leverage prior searching by other offices as appropriate but verify relevance.

name: Search may be limited or not required in certain cases
description: No special search effort is required or search may be limited if the claimed invention falls under certain cases (enumeration continues beyond this chunk).
guidance: Examiner should apply listed conditions to decide when exhaustive search is unnecessary; check the full guidelines for specific cases.

name: g_foreign_priority — Information about earlier foreign filings claiming priority
description: Table Description: Information about an earlier patent filing in a foreign country which gives the claim priority; Final Data Field List includes patent_id, priority_claim_sequence, priority_claim_kind, foreign_application_id, filing_date, foreign_country_filed. Note: Fields uuid and country were removed
guidance: Fields renamed for clarity (number->foreign_application_id, date->filing_date, country->foreign_country_filed).

name: Two-part form of claim (Rule 7(1))
description: The claim may be presented in a two-part form: the first part recites the known combination of features (prior art portion) and the second or "characterizing portion" states the technical features which, in combination with the first part, it is desired to protect (the invention's additions to the prior art).
guidance: Invite applicant to use the two-part form where invention is a distinct improvement in an old combination; do not force two-part form where inappropriate (e.g., combination of known elements of equal status, modification of known chemical process, complex systems with interrelated parts, new chemical compounds not falling within a known class). Purpose: allow reader to see clearly which features are part of prior art. Use other forms if two-part gives a distorted/misleading picture. Place reference signs in parentheses after features, if drawings make features more intelligible; such signs are aids and not limiting.

name: Reference signs to drawings are aids and not limiting
description: If drawings exist and relating claim features to drawing features renders claims more intelligible, place appropriate reference signs in parentheses after the features in the claims.
guidance: Reference signs should be used in both parts of two-part claims. They are not to be construed as limiting the claim scope but merely as aids to understanding the defined subject matter.

name: Unity of invention and proliferation of independent claims (Rule 7(6), 7(7))
description: Determination of unity: whether a group of inventions is so linked as to form a single general inventive concept shall be made without regard to whether inventions are claimed separately or as alternatives in a single claim. Examiner should take exception to unnecessary proliferation of independent claims but not to two or more independent claims in same category if there is a unifying inventive concept and claims as a whole are concise.
guidance: Consider remarks about claims of apparently similar scope. Situations where separate independent claims may be appropriate: improvements in two separate but interrelated articles sold separately (plug/socket), single-phase vs poly-phase electrical arrangements, group of new chemical compounds with several manufacture processes. Invite amendments if proliferation creates obscurity.

name: Independent and dependent claims (Rules 7(4)(b), 7(7))
description: All applications will contain one or more independent main claims directed to essential features. Dependent claims concern specific forms and must include reference to the claim they depend on and be construed as including all limitations of that claim. Multiple dependent claims include all limitations of the particular claim in relation to which considered.
guidance: Specific forms construed broadly as more specific definitions or different embodiments. Subject to Administrative Instruction allowances, reasonable number of dependent claims is permitted even where dependent claim features could constitute separate inventions. Group dependent claims together practically to enable association; invite amendment if arrangement creates obscurity. Claims may contain alternatives if similar and fairly substitutable and do not make the claim obscure. A claim may refer to another claim of a different category (e.g., "Apparatus for carrying out the process of Claim 1...")—this is not a dependent claim as defined but is permitted.

name: Interpretation of claims — ordinary meaning to person skilled in the art
description: Claims should be interpreted the same way for search and examination. Each claim should be read giving words the ordinary meaning and scope attributed by a person skilled in the relevant art, unless the description gives a special meaning by explicit definition or otherwise.
guidance: Apply ordinary meaning for both search and examination purposes; consider description if special meaning is provided.

name: Effect of the preamble on claim evaluation
description: The effect of the preamble on evaluation for search/examination should be determined case by case. Statements in the preamble reciting purpose or intended use must be evaluated to determine whether recited purpose results in a structural or process-step difference between the claimed invention and prior art. In two-part claims, the preamble is regarded as a limitation.
guidance: If a claim begins with "Apparatus for carrying out the process...", construe as apparatus suitable for the process. Apparatus that otherwise has all features but is unsuitable for stated purpose should not normally be within scope. Examples: "machine for cutting meat" construed as machine adapted to cut meat; "mold for molten steel" implies limitations like melting point, etc.

name: Open and closed claims — transition phrases
description: Examiners should consider which transition phrase is used (e.g., "consisting of", "comprising", "characterized by", "consisting essentially of") because the subject matter to be searched depends on it.
guidance: (a) "Closed" transition phrase: claim cannot include elements/steps beyond those set forth (e.g., "consisting of A, B and C"). Note that some Authorities may treat "consisting of" as equivalent to "consisting essentially of." (b) "Open" phrase: claim can be construed as including non-recited components (e.g., "comprising A, B and C" includes A,B,C and D). (c) "Consisting essentially of" occupies middle ground, limiting to specified materials/steps and those that do not materially affect basic and novel characteristics; absent clear indication, construed as open for search/examination.

name: Means-plus-function claim interpretation
description: Where a limitation defines a means or step in terms of function or characteristics without specifying structure/material/act, that limitation should be construed as defining any structure/material/act capable of performing the function or having the characteristics, unless further structure is specified.
guidance: If means are further specified, interpret to include those specifications. Example: "valve means for restricting flow" interpreted to include the further specified limitation if present; otherwise construed to any means capable of performing that function. Separately assess whether such claims are clear/concise and whether disclosure is sufficient for a skilled person.

name: Product and apparatus limitations appearing in process claims
description: Product and apparatus limitations that appear in process claims must be taken into account for search and examination purposes.
guidance: Do not ignore product/apparatus features when they appear within a process claim; include them in the subject of search and evaluation.

name: Clarity of claims (Rule 7(1))
description: Claims must be clear for individual claims and the claims as a whole. Clarity is essential for forming opinions on novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability; terms should, as far as possible, be clear for the person skilled in the art from the wording of the claim alone.
guidance: Claims must set forth the scope of the invention with a reasonable degree of clarity analyzed in light of the disclosure, prior art and interpretation by a skilled person. Breadth is not necessarily lack of clarity. Independent claim should specify essential features needed to define the invention except insofar as implied by generic terms (e.g., a "bicycle" need not list wheels). Process claims must necessarily produce the product when carried out reasonably; otherwise internal inconsistency and lack of clarity. For modified well-known products, specify what is modified and how.

name: Clarity of relative terms and terms of degree
description: Claims using vague or relative terms ("thin", "wide", "strong") should be objected to unless the term has a well recognized meaning in the art. Terms of degree require that a skilled person be apprised of meaning either by disclosure of a measuring standard or by prior art/state of the art.
guidance: Invite applicant to define or excise the term if they can do so without extending subject matter beyond the filing. An applicant cannot rely on an unclear term to distinguish over prior art. Claims defined by result to be achieved should generally be objected to as lacking clarity unless result is the only way to define the invention and achievable without undue experimentation (with tests/procedures specified). Defining product solely by parameters is acceptable if parameters can be clearly and reliably determined by description or objective procedures recognized in art; non-recognized parameters or inaccessible measurement apparatus may be objectionable. Pay attention when words like "about" or "approximately" are used; determine whether meaning is sufficiently clear in context. If such words prevent the invention from being unambiguously distinguished from prior art, raise objection to lack of novelty or inventive step.

name: Clarity of other terms (trademarks, "preferably", negative limitations)
description: Trademarks characterize commercial origin rather than properties relevant to the invention; expressions like "preferably", "for example" have no limiting effect and should be carefully considered so as not to introduce ambiguity. Negative limitations (disclaimers) are not per se ambiguous.
guidance: Invite removal of trademarks in claims unless unavoidable or generally recognized as precise. Treat features following "preferably" etc. as optional (non-limiting). Negative limitations are acceptable where clear; they render claim unclear if used to claim by excluding what was not invented rather than clearly reciting what was invented. Negative limitations are clear when each recited limitation is clear or when boundaries of protection are clear (examples provided). If alternative elements are positively recited in description they may be explicitly excluded in claims.

name: Clear and complete disclosure / sufficiency (Rule 7(1))
description: The subject matter of each claim must be supported by the description and drawings "in a manner sufficiently clear and complete for the invention to be carried out by a person skilled in the art." Disclosure is sufficient if it enables the skilled person, as of the international filing date, to carry out the invention without undue experimentation.
guidance: Skilled person may use general knowledge to supplement application. Reasonable trial and error is permissible; undue experimentation is not. Factors in assessing undue experimentation include: (i) breadth of the claims; (ii) nature of the invention; (iii) general knowledge of a person skilled in the art; (iv) level of predictability in the art; (v) amount of direction provided in the application, including references to prior art; and (vi) amount of experimentation required to carry out the invention on the basis of the disclosure. Breadth of claims is relevant because a skilled person must be able to carry out the entire scope. Representative examples and explanation of how to apply them across the claim scope may suffice, even in unpredictable arts, provided undue experimentation is avoided.

name: Document the invention thoroughly
description: Write a complete description of the invention before talking to attorneys. Include: what it does, how it works, what makes it different from existing solutions, alternative versions, and best results.
guidance: Date and witness the document. Provide enough detail to enable practice by a person skilled in the art and to support later claim scope and priority; disclose multiple embodiments and best modes where applicable.

name: Conduct a prior art search
description: Search the USPTO patent database, Google Patents, Espacenet, and academic literature. Look for patents and publications in the same technical field.
guidance: The goal is to find references that disclose anything similar (anticipation or relevant prior art for obviousness). Use these results to shape claim scope and specification disclosures; document search strategy and key references.

name: Decide provisional vs non-provisional filing
description: A provisional is cheaper and faster but does not get examined. A non-provisional starts the prosecution clock.
guidance: Most applicants file provisional first, then convert within 12 months. Remember a provisional establishes a filing date but does not mature into a patent without a later non‑provisional filing; plan conversion/timing and content to support desired claim scope.

name: Specification structure and required sections
description: Sections in order: Title, Cross-References, Field of Invention, Background, Summary, Brief Description of Drawings, Detailed Description, Claims, Abstract. Each section has a specific purpose.
guidance: Follow the conventional order and give each section its intended content (e.g., Background describes prior art/problems; Summary outlines invention; Detailed Description enables practice). Use the specification to support claim scope and alternatives; avoid over-limiting language.

name: Claim drafting fundamentals
description: Claims are the legal definition of the invention. Independent claims stand alone; dependent claims add limitations to a parent claim. Use specific transitional phrases ("comprising," "consisting of"). Each claim is a single sentence.
guidance: Draft independent claims to capture the broadest allowable invention, and dependent claims to add fallback limitations. Choose transitional language carefully (e.g., "comprising" is open-ended, "consisting of" is closed). Ensure each claim is written as one properly punctuated sentence and is supported by the specification.

name: Filing procedure and required documents
description: File electronically through Patent Center. Pay filing, search, and examination fees (reduced for small entity, micro entity). Include the specification, drawings, claims, abstract, oath/declaration, and assignment if applicable.
guidance: Use USPTO Patent Center for electronic filing; confirm entity status for fee reductions and include all required parts (oath/declaration, assignments). Check fee amounts and proper forms to avoid processing delays.

name: Practical drafting and disclosure tips for beginners
description: Avoid the words "essential" or "critical" in the spec. Disclose multiple ways to practice the invention. Use figures generously. Have a patent attorney review even if you are filing pro se.
guidance: Avoid language that may unduly limit claim scope (e.g., labeling features as essential). Broadly disclose alternative embodiments and implementation options to support claim breadth. Produce helpful figures. Even non-lawyers should seek attorney review before final filing to catch legal pitfalls.

name: Simultaneous survival of validity and infringement findings
description: A patent's enforcement success requires both validity and infringement findings to survive; quality requires the simultaneous survival of both.
guidance: Do not evaluate validity in isolation. A patent can be valid but not infringed (claims too narrow) or infringed but invalid (claims too broad). Best-quality patents survive both validity and infringement analysis.

name: Goldilocks scope (breadth-narrowness tradeoff)
description: Broad enough to read on competitor products, narrow enough to escape prior art.
guidance: Careful claim drafting should place asserted claims in this narrow band. Overly broad claims invite invalidity; overly narrow claims risk noninfringement. Assess where asserted claims sit on this tradeoff as a core quality metric.

name: Multiple asserted claim layers
description: Patentees typically assert several claims at varying breadth; quality patents have a defensible mid-tier claim that can survive validity while still reading on the accused product.
guidance: Draft and assert layered claims (broad, mid, narrow) so that if broad claims are invalidated, a defensible middle-ground claim remains to capture the accused product. Presence and defensibility of mid-tier claims is a positive quality indicator.

name: Clear construction anchors (reduce Markman risk)
description: Claim terms with unambiguous construction (defined in spec, prosecution-history-supported, or settled in art) reduce Markman risk.
guidance: Provide explicit definitions in the specification, consistent prosecution history, and citations to settled technical meaning where possible. Clear anchors reduce the chance of adverse claim construction and unpredictable scope shifts at Markman.

name: Prosecution-history cleanliness
description: A clean prosecution history (no estoppels, consistent claim interpretation) improves expected enforcement outcomes.
guidance: Evaluate file-wrapper for disclaimers, amendments, or arguments that could estop claim scope. Inconsistent statements or narrowing amendments increase invalidity/infringement risk and reduce expected enforceability.

name: Eligibility-safe drafting (Alice/Mayo/Bilski risks)
description: Claims must avoid the 'abstract idea / natural phenomenon plus conventional steps' pattern; survival of Alice/Mayo motions is a key quality threshold, especially in software, biotech, and diagnostics.
guidance: Draft claims emphasizing technical improvements, concrete implementations, or structural limitations rather than functional results. For life sciences, ensure claims do not recite mere natural phenomena without inventive application; for software, tie claims to technical solutions or hardware improvements.

name: Enablement and written-description sufficiency (biotech/genus risks)
description: Biotech genus claims often fail enablement; quality biotech patents must show enablement of the full genus and a written description demonstrating possession.
guidance: Support genus claims with representative examples, adequate experimental data, and disclosure of embodiments across the claimed scope. Ensure the specification shows possession of claimed inventions to survive enablement and written-description challenges (cf. Amgen v. Sanofi).

name: Structural specificity for chemical/pharmaceutical claims
description: Compound claims with structural specificity and scope tied to formulation or compound correlate with higher enforcement success.
guidance: Draft chemical/pharmaceutical claims to precise structural features and link claim scope to specific formulations or compounds. Robust ANDA defenses and surviving claim construction with a favorable (even broad) construction at Markman predict higher trial success in these industries.

name: Software-specific claim markers
description: Software patents perform poorly unless claims recite specific technical implementation or are tied to particular hardware/improvements rather than generic computer-implemented results.
guidance: Favor claims that describe how the software achieves a technical improvement, tie to particular hardware or architectural features, or otherwise avoid being framed as abstract ideas. Survival of Alice/Mayo dismissal motions is the critical early threshold.

name: Evidence that accused product literally falls within claim language
description: Is there evidence the accused product clearly falls within the literal claim language?
guidance: Assess factual and technical records showing literal infringement (claim elements present in the accused product). Strong, documentable evidence of literal infringement materially raises the chance of enforcement success, particularly when paired with defensible claim scope.

name: KIPO functionality guideline: Advertisements/promotions about distribution convenience and efficiency
description: Functionality is acknowledged if significant convenience in preservation, transport, handling (distribution) derives from the product or its packaging, or if advertisements promote significant efficiency of use due to its shape.
guidance: Consider marketing materials and promotional claims that tout distribution or usage efficiencies; such evidence supports a finding of functionality.

name: Classification of externally claimed apparatus (general rule)
description: Significantly claimed apparatus external to this class, claimed in combination with apparatus under the class definition, which perform data processing or calculation operations are classified in the class appropriate to the external device unless specifically excluded therefrom.
guidance: Apparatus that are external to Class 705 but claimed in combination with items under Class 705 are placed in the class appropriate to the external device unless that external class specifically excludes them. See Classification Definitions (Feb. 2011) for details.

name: Petition fee structure (claims-based)
description: Fees for filing petitions depend on the type of review and the number of claims challenged: for IPR, $27,200 to review 20 or fewer claims and $600 per claim in excess of 20; for PGR/CBM, $35,800 to review 20 or fewer claims and $800 per claim in excess of 20.
guidance: Fees are set to recover the aggregate cost of providing the review (judge time, support, indirect costs). An IT-component fee is included (see next rubric).

name: Enablement requirement (35 U.S.C. § 112(a))
description: When filing a patent application, an applicant is required to satisfy several requirements pertaining to the specification, including written description and enablement (35 U.S.C. § 112(a)).
guidance: The specification must contain enough information to enable one of ordinary skill in the art to make and use the claimed invention; enablement is a statutory requirement separate from written description.

name: Undue or unreasonable experimentation test (M.P.E.P. § 2164.01)
description: Examination guidance for enablement applies a test that asks whether experimentation needed to practice the invention is undue or unreasonable (M.P.E.P. § 2164.01).
guidance: If the amount of experimentation required to practice the invention is 'undue' or 'unreasonable,' the specification may fail to enable the claim; examiners apply this standard in prosecution.

name: Wands factor: breadth of the claims
description: One of the Wands factors is the breadth of the claims.
guidance: Broader claim scope can make enablement more difficult to satisfy because broader claims may cover embodiments not adequately supported by the disclosure.

name: Wands factor: amount of direction provided by the inventor
description: One of the Wands factors is the amount of direction provided by the inventor.
guidance: The more specific and directive the specification (e.g., protocols, parameters, selection criteria), the more likely claims will be found enabled.

name: Use of declarations and contemporaneous evidence to show enablement
description: USPTO appellate decisions show that declarations and other evidence submitted by applicants can be relied on to demonstrate what was known and an artisan's ability to select appropriate embodiments (e.g., PTAB decision in U.S. Application No. 17/321,012 relied on an Applicant Declaration about types of sensors).
guidance: Submit declarations and other contemporaneous evidence to show the knowledge base at filing and the ability of a skilled artisan to practice the claims; such evidence can rebut examiner enablement rejections.

name: Excessive or ambiguous claims and disclaimers
description: When claims are alleged excessive the court construes the claim and fixes the standard by which diligence in filing any necessary disclaimer is to be measured; the jury decide whether the claim exceeds the actual invention and whether delay in filing a disclaimer is unreasonable. For ambiguous claims, the court interprets the claim as far as capable of interpretation and the jury follow that interpretation.
guidance: What constitutes unreasonable delay in filing a disclaimer is a mixed question of law and fact for the jury under court instructions; under some circumstances it may be a question of law.

name: Re-issue patents and scope/fraud issues
description: When the defence alleges wrongful re-issue the court decides legal requisites of a legal patent, whether claims of a re-issue depart from the original invention, and whether re-issue was broader or obtained with fraudulent intent; the jury find whether legal requisites existed and whether the re-issue is identical or broader and whether intent was fraudulent.
guidance: Whether a re-issue departs from the original, or was obtained fraudulently, are jury questions under the court's instructions.

name: Identity of plaintiff's and defendant's inventions (infringement identity)
description: The court defines the patented invention as indicated by the language of the claims; the jury judge whether the invention so defined covers the art or article employed by the defendant.
guidance: The identity question, if the patent is in evidence and not excluded, may be submitted to the jury under court instruction; whether the defendant infringes is a jury question.

name: Estoppel defence
description: When the defence avers the plaintiff is estopped the court explains the doctrine of estoppel, interprets written instruments out of which an estoppel is said to have arisen, and defines any legal duty of the plaintiff by the neglect of which the defendant claims he was misled; the jury determine whether the estoppel exists.
guidance: Court provides legal framework; jury decides factual existence and effect of alleged estoppel.

name: Need for specialist tax advice
description: The tax implications of the Patent Box are complex, and specialist tax advice will be needed to determine the proportion of profits that qualify.
guidance: Engage specialist tax advisers (and patent advisers) to calculate qualifying income, residual profit, marketing asset adjustments and to prepare a compliant claim.

name: Permission to file overseas (conditions and procedures)
description: Where Korean government grants permission to file a patent application banned from filing overseas, an application may exceptionally file abroad subject to conditions. Korea has an agreement with the United States permitting filing in the US under confidentiality agreements; otherwise filing abroad is prohibited.
guidance: To obtain permission to file in the United States, applicant must submit a written request (Annex Form No.21). Conditions for permission include: 1) the specification must be clear and specific to examine the application in the US; 2) the right to claim damages caused by confidentiality in the US shall be waived (except for damages from US use/disclosure without permission). After filing in the US with permission, applicant must: attach two copies of application documents; attach copy of KIPO-issued permission; attach copy of representative's personal info and US security clearance documents; submit these to DAPA; designate a representative who has received US government security clearance; and immediately notify DAPA of the US application number and filing date.

name: Utility requirement (35 U.S.C. § 101)
description: The invention must be useful; § 101 requires that the inventor discovered something 'new and useful.' In many cases demonstrating utility is straightforward, but in life and chemical sciences utility is significant (e.g., a laboratory promise does not establish utility for human treatment claims).
guidance: Courts almost always identify utility as a question of fact, typically relying on expert testimony or skilled artisan evidence. Historical citations trace factual treatment of utility to policy considerations about evaluating case-specific scientific testimony. The factual framing influences whether juries decide utility and how appellate courts review those decisions.

name: Patent eligibility (§ 101) as a legal question with factual exceptions
description: Patent eligibility is generally treated as a question of law (e.g., whether claim is directed to a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter and meets judicial exceptions), but it can be treated as factual when the dispute centers on whether the patent involves well-understood, routine, or conventional activity.
guidance: The Federal Circuit often treats eligibility as legal, yet makes exceptions where factual showings (e.g., well-understood, routine, conventional) determine eligibility; this creates inconsistent practice and strategic uncertainty for litigants about whether eligibility will be decided by judge or jury.

name: Nonobviousness (35 U.S.C. § 103) — ultimate legal conclusion with factual underpinnings
description: Nonobviousness is ultimately a question of law, but it 'lends itself to several basic factual inquiries' per Graham: determining the scope and content of the prior art, ascertaining differences between prior art and the claims, resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art, and considering secondary considerations (objective indicia).
guidance: Although the Supreme Court in Graham and KSR frames obviousness as a legal determination built on specific factual findings, in practice courts (and juries) often decide obviousness via general verdicts and appellate review can be deferential. KSR rejected a rigid TSM test and urged courts to consider inferences and creativity of a POSITA, and emphasized that courts should make the analysis explicit; nevertheless, lower courts and the Federal Circuit have continued to apply fact-driven bright-line tests (e.g., TSM, analogous art, motivation to combine) that push obviousness toward jury resolution.

name: Graham framework / factual Graham factors
description: The factual inquiries required by Graham: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between the prior art and the claims at issue; (3) the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; and (4) consideration of secondary considerations such as commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, and failure of others.
guidance: These are treated as findings of fact that inform the legal determination of obviousness. Courts and model jury instructions may submit these factual questions to juries (preferably via special interrogatories) so that the judge can make an explicit legal ruling applying those facts; failure to obtain explicit findings (i.e., a black-box general verdict) impedes reasoned appellate review.

name: Analogous art requirement for relevance of prior art
description: For a prior art reference to be relevant to an obviousness inquiry, it must be from an analogous art—that is, sufficiently related to the problem addressed by the claimed invention.
guidance: The Federal Circuit treats analogous art as a question of fact. Determinations about whether a reference is analogous (and thus relevant) affect whether the reference can be used in an obviousness combination and often require factfinding amenable to jury resolution.

name: Claim construction / interpretation of patent instruments
description: The judge determines the scope of the patent by construing its claims in light of the specification, prosecution history, and sometimes extrinsic evidence, from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art; construction of written instruments is a judicial function.
guidance: Supreme Court precedent (Markman) treats claim construction as ultimately a question of law for the judge, even when factual inquiries are necessary. The Court emphasized that judges are trained in exegesis and are 'likely to do better than jurors' at construing written instruments. Claim construction informs other validity and infringement analyses and is reviewed de novo (subject to the Teva decision clarifying review of subsidiary facts).

name: Role of the person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA)
description: Many validity inquiries (written description, enablement, obviousness, claim construction to some extent) are conducted from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the relevant art.
guidance: Determinations about how a POSITA would understand disclosures, whether the POSITA could practice the invention without undue experimentation, or what a POSITA would find obvious are often informed by expert testimony and are central factual inputs that shape the legal conclusions. Jury instructions commonly ask jurors to assess issues from this viewpoint.

name: Application contents (Regulation 5)
description: An application for the grant of a patent shall contain a request for the grant of a patent; a description; a claim or claims; a drawing or drawings, where required; and an abstract.
guidance: The application shall be filed at the Patent Registration Office. All five elements are mandatory where applicable.

name: Claims — clarity, support and reasonableness (Regulation 13)
description: Claims shall be clear and concise and fully supported by the description; the number of claims shall be reasonable considering the nature of the invention; claims should be consecutively numbered; claims must not contain drawings and should not, unless necessary, rely on references to the description or drawings.
guidance: Claims must define the invention in terms of technical features; where drawings exist, reference signs may be used sparingly and consistently; claims should include, when appropriate, statements identifying features necessary but part of prior art and a characterising portion (e.g., 'characterised in that').

name: Dependent claims (Regulation 14)
description: A dependent claim (one including all features of another claim) shall, if possible at the beginning, reference the other claim(s) and then state the additional features; dependent claims are construed as including all limitations of the claims to which they refer; dependent claims referring back to a single or several previous claims should be grouped together.
guidance: Multiple dependent claims are to be interpreted as including limitations of the particular claim in relation to which they are considered.

name: Abstract content and length (Regulation 16)
description: Abstract shall commence with a title and contain a summary of the disclosure as contained in the description, claims and drawings and, where applicable, the chemical formula that best characterises the invention; it shall indicate the technical field, allow clear understanding of the technical problem, gist of solution and principal uses.
guidance: Abstract should be concise, preferably not more than 150 words, must not contain statements about merits or speculative applications; each main technical feature illustrated by a drawing should be followed by its reference sign in parentheses; abstract not to contain drawings but be accompanied by most illustrative drawing(s); it must be an efficient searching instrument to decide whether to consult full specification.

name: Physical presentation requirements (Regulation 18)
description: Documents should be filed in duplicate unless otherwise provided; documents must admit direct reproduction by photography/electrostatic/photo-offset/microfilming; sheets free from cracks/creases/folds and only one side used; documents on A4 paper (29.7 x 21 cm) durable, white, smooth; minimum margins 2 cm; sheets numbered at top centre in consecutive Arabic numerals; text typed/printed in dark indelible colour at least 1½ line spacing (certain formulae/graphics may be handwritten/drawn); every fifth line of description and claims shall be numbered in Arabic numerals placed to left of lines; drawings executed in durable black lines without colouring; application filed in national language or English.
guidance: Registrar may accept other sizes or require more copies; strict formatting required for reproduction and examination; deviation only as permitted by Registrar.

name: Unity of invention (Regulation 19)
description: For purposes of section 26, same patent application may include: (a) in addition to independent claim for product, an independent claim for process specially adapted for manufacture and independent claim for use of product; (b) in addition to independent claim for process, an independent claim for apparatus designed to carry out process; (c) combinations thereof; subject to section 26, application may contain two or more independent claims of same category not readily covered by a single generic claim; may contain reasonable number of dependent claims even if dependent features might be inventions by themselves.
guidance: Defines permissible claim groupings and acceptable number of independent and dependent claims based on unity; subject to statutory section 26 limitations.

name: Contents of patent document (Regulation 30)
description: The patent shall contain number, owner name/address, inventor name/address (unless opt-out), agent name/address (if any), filing date, priority date and country, date of grant, title, IPC symbol, abstract, description, claims and all drawings, if any.
guidance: Full specification and bibliographic data must be included in the granted patent.

name: Field-of-use or Internet limitation is insufficient
description: Limiting an abstract idea to a particular technological environment or field of use (e.g., 'over the Internet') does not by itself make the claim patent eligible.
guidance: Example: 'Internet limitations are simply a field of use that is an attempt to limit the abstract idea to a particular technological environment and, so do not add significantly more.' Use this when an asserted improvement is merely tying the idea to the Internet.

name: Broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of claims
description: Claims should be analyzed for eligibility according to their broadest reasonable interpretation.
guidance: Text: 'All of the claims are analyzed for eligibility in accordance with their broadest reasonable interpretation.' When construing claim scope, use BRI to determine whether recited elements are generic or limiting.

name: Preamble limitation rule (MPEP 2111.02): does the preamble limit?
description: Determine whether the claim preamble merely states purpose/field of use (non-limiting) or gives 'life, meaning and vitality' to the claim (limiting).
guidance: Guidance in examples: 'Where the preamble only states the purpose or the field of use of an invention, the preamble does not limit the scope of the claim... If the preamble gives “life, meaning and vitality” to the claim, it should be construed to limit the claim.' Apply MPEP 2111.02 when assessing whether preamble limitations can supply 'significantly more.'

name: Examiner Office-action/allowance drafting guidance
description: When issuing a rejection or allowance, examiners should explicitly identify the exception and explain why claim limitations do or do not amount to significantly more.
guidance: Example examiner guidance: 'A rejection of claim 1 should identify the exception by pointing to the filtering, generating and formatting steps and explain that the comparing and formatting of information is a mental process... The rejection should also identify the additional limitations regarding the transmission server and explain why those limitations comprise only a generic computer performing generic computer functions.' For allowances, add remarks explaining why the claim is not directed to any judicial exception.

name: Claims necessarily rooted in computer technology that solve computer-specific problems may be eligible
description: If the claimed invention is necessarily rooted in computer technology and addresses a problem specifically arising in that technological environment (and supplies meaningful limitations), the claim may not be directed to an abstract idea.
guidance: Example: the GUI relocating obscured textual information was found not to be directed to an abstract idea because it 'is necessarily rooted in computer technology to overcome a problem specifically arising in graphical user interfaces.' Use fact-based analysis showing the claim improves computer functionality or solves a technical problem.

name: Patentable Difference Requirement for Permissible Restriction
description: A requirement for restriction is permissible if there is a patentable difference between the species/inventions as claimed.
guidance: The presence of patentable differences between claimed species or inventions supports separate treatment; identical or patentably indistinct claims weigh against restriction.

name: Two-Step Test for Restriction
description: The examiner should apply a two-step test: (1) independent or distinct — are the inventions independent (no relation) or distinct (related but separately patentable)? and (2) burden — is there a serious examination/search burden?
guidance: Both prongs must be considered: first determine whether claims define independent or distinct inventions; then determine whether examining them together would create a substantial burden that warrants restriction.

name: Independent Versus Distinct Inventions
description: Independent = no relation between the inventions; distinct = related but separately patentable.
guidance: This distinction informs whether claims can be grouped for examination: independent inventions are clearly separate, while distinct inventions may be related yet still patentably separable and thus potentially restricted.

name: Required Reply to a Restriction Requirement
description: In the reply to the restriction requirement, applicant must elect one invention/species for examination.
guidance: The applicant's response must include a clear election; failure to elect may prevent examination progress. The election directs the examiner which claims to examine in the current file.

name: Provisional Election Practice
description: A provisional election allows examination to proceed while preserving the right to traverse.
guidance: Applicants may make a provisional election to enable prompt examination of chosen claims without waiving the right to contest the restriction; this can be used to delay deciding whether to traverse while keeping prosecution moving.

name: When proceedings are terminated (35 U.S.C. 120 context)
description: For purposes of copendency under 35 U.S.C. 120, a second application is copending with an earlier application only if filed before (i.e., not later than) the patenting, abandonment of, or termination of proceedings on the earlier application.
guidance: Proceedings are terminated in situations including (A) abandonment for failure to pay the issue fee (termination as of the date issue fee was due), (B) losing an interference as to all claims (termination as of the date appeal/review was due if none filed), (C) decision by the Patent Trial and Appeal Board, and (D) decision by the court. See MPEP § 711.02(c) and § 711.03(c).

name: Delgar v. Schuyler principle — nonreceipt allegation may justify withdrawal/remail
description: An allegation, supported by evidence, that an Office action was never received may be considered in a petition to withdraw the holding of abandonment; if adequately supported, the Office may grant withdrawal and remail the Office action. This applies to notices of abandonment and Notices of Allowance (and to abandonment for failure to prosecute or failure to pay issue fee).
guidance: Evidence must demonstrate nonreceipt (not merely poor recordkeeping), and historical patterns of nonreceipt by practitioner may undermine such a claim. See Delgar v. Schuyler and related case law cited in MPEP § 711.03.

name: Apply the Pannu Factors to Determine Inventorship
description: The USPTO will apply the Pannu factors to decide whether a potential joint inventor 'contribute[d] in some significant manner to conception or reduction to practice,' made 'a contribution to the claimed invention that is not insignificant in quality, when that contribution is measured against the dimension of the full invention,' and did more than merely explain well-known concepts or the current state of the art.
guidance: Use these three Pannu-factor questions as the threshold joint-inventorship inquiry for AI-assisted inventions.

name: Guiding Principle iv — Developing an Essential Building Block Can Be Sufficient
description: A natural person who develops an essential building block from which the claimed invention is derived may be considered to have provided significant contribution to conception even if not present for each activity that led to the invention; designing, constructing, or training an AI system for a specific issue could qualify.
guidance: Individuals who design/train an AI system specifically to generate a targeted solution may qualify as inventors when that work constitutes a significant part of the process that leads to the claimed invention.

name: Scenario 2 — Not Inventors If Only Reduction to Practice
description: Engineers who follow the AI system’s design exactly and only select a common manufacturing material (i.e., merely reduce the output to practice) are not proper inventors of dependent claim limitations reflecting those choices.
guidance: Selecting routine manufacturing choices does not create inventorship for AI-derived claim limitations.

name: Scenario 3 — Proper Inventors If They Substantially Modify the AI Output
description: Engineers who prompt the AI for alternatives and conduct experiments that allow them to substantially modify the AI output may be proper inventors of an independent claim covering the modified design because the Pannu factors are met.
guidance: Substantial modification and empirical work that produces a materially different, inventive result can support inventorship.

name: Scenario 4 — Proper Inventors of Dependent Claims When Contributions Remain Significant
description: Engineers who develop a modified design (as in Scenario 3) and then use AI suggestions for manufacturing may still be proper inventors of dependent claims covering the AI suggestions because their prior contributions remain significant when measured against the full invention.
guidance: A human's earlier significant contributions can support inventorship of later-related dependent claim limitations even if those limitations draw on AI suggestions.

name: Recordkeeping and Documentation Recommendation
description: Inventors using AI systems should keep detailed records and document their inventive process to help establish conception and significant contribution, including the natural person’s specific prompts to the AI system, the AI system’s specific output, and any changes made by the inventor to the output, on a claim-by-claim basis.
guidance: Detailed contemporaneous records will be important to establish inventorship, defend validity, and guard against inequitable conduct allegations; prosecution counsel should draft claims to preserve the natural person's significant contributions.

name: Directed-to-abstract-idea inquiry (step 1)
description: Determine whether the claim is 'drawn to' an abstract idea (a judicial exception such as an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon).
guidance: Examples the Court treated as abstract include 'intermediated settlement' and other fundamental economic practices 'long prevalent in our system of commerce.' If the claim's focus is the abstract idea itself rather than a particular application, it fails step 1.

name: Inventive-concept / 'significantly more' (step 2)
description: If a claim is directed to a judicial exception, determine whether the claim contains an 'inventive concept' sufficient to transform the claimed abstract idea into a patent-eligible application—i.e., whether it provides 'significantly more.'
guidance: The Court held that merely 'appending conventional steps, specified at high level of generality' is insufficient. The inventive concept must do more than implement the abstract idea on a generic computer; it must improve a technological process or otherwise add meaningful limitations that prevent pre-emption of the underlying idea.

name: System claims substantively treated like method claims
description: Labeling a claim as a 'system' or reciting 'specific hardware' does not by itself make a claim patent-eligible if its substance is the same as an abstract method claim.
guidance: The Court cautioned against interpreting §101 to depend on the 'draftsman's art.' Examiners and courts will examine the substance over form; drafting as system vs. method cannot be used to evade the Alice test.

name: Limitations that can qualify as 'significantly more' (examples from USPTO)
description: Certain claim limitations may transform a judicial exception into patent-eligible subject matter by supplying 'significantly more.'
guidance: The USPTO lists examples (not exclusive) of qualifying limitations: improvements to another technology or technical field; improvements to the functioning of the computer itself; applying the judicial exception with, or by the use of, a particular machine; effecting a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing. Claims exhibiting these features are more likely to survive §101 scrutiny.

name: Claims must be examined under other patentability requirements as well
description: §101 analysis does not replace examination for novelty, nonobviousness, written description, enablement, and other requirements.
