guidance: The USPTO instructed that all claims are to be fully examined under each of the other patentability requirements. §101 is an additional filter, not a substitute for other substantive examinations.

name: Burden to show 'substantially more' and rejection of 'creative writing'
description: Software developers and applicants bear the burden of showing their claims provide 'substantially more' than an abstract idea; creative drafting alone is insufficient.
guidance: The article concludes that the two-part Alice test has 'narrowed the scope' of software patent protection and places the burden on applicants to demonstrate that claims supply substantially more than abstract ideas rather than relying on creative claim language.

name: Courts will look to substantive essence over 'patent-ese' language
description: Courts will be 'careful to avoid allowing the typically convoluted claim language—"patent-ese"—to obfuscate the general purpose and real essence of software patent claims.'
guidance: When evaluating eligibility, focus on the real substance and purpose of the claimed invention rather than being misled by complex or jargon-heavy claim drafting. Claims that disguise an abstract idea with convoluted language remain at risk under Alice.

name: Enablement requirement (35 U.S.C. §112(a))
description: The specification must describe how to make and use the claimed invention in sufficient detail that someone skilled in the art can do so without undue experimentation.
guidance: Foundation for enablement rejections; assess whether the disclosure permits practicing the claimed invention across its full scope.

name: Wands Factor — Breadth of claims
description: Broader claims require more enabling disclosure.
guidance: A claim that covers a wide genus or multiple embodiments places a heavier enablement burden on the specification; 'the more one claims, the more one must enable.'

name: Wands Factor — Direction provided
description: The guidance and instructions present in the specification.
guidance: Evaluate whether the specification gives adequate direction (e.g., parameters, methods) so a skilled artisan can practice the claimed invention without undue experimentation.

name: Undue experimentation principle — scope matters (claim breadth effect)
description: The broader the claim scope claimed, the more enabling disclosure is required.
guidance: Broad genus or functional claims require disclosure commensurate with claim scope; this principle was emphasized in Amgen v. Sanofi.

name: Amgen impact — genus claims must enable full scope
description: Claims to an entire genus must enable the full scope, not merely a subset.
guidance: Applicants cannot rely on a few enabled species to claim a whole genus unless the specification shows enablement across the genus.

name: Amgen impact — functional claiming requires commensurate disclosure
description: Functional claiming of broad classes requires commensurate structural or enabling disclosure.
guidance: Purely functional language is insufficient to monopolize undisclosed embodiments; specification must supply structure, examples, or other teaching that enables the full claimed function.

name: Amgen impact — cannot monopolize undisclosed embodiments
description: Applicants cannot monopolize vast undisclosed embodiments through functional limitation alone.
guidance: Functional claiming cannot be used to claim more than what the specification enables; enablement must be commensurate with the monopoly sought.

name: Genus-claims representative examples rule
description: Representative examples plus a genus-wide statement can suffice if skilled artisans would reasonably expect the entire class to be operable without undue experimentation.
guidance: Assess whether the examples and descriptive language convey a 'general quality' that supports extrapolation to the full genus.

name: Predictable vs. unpredictable arts distinction
description: Mechanical and electrical arts (predictable) typically require less detailed disclosure; chemistry, biology, and other unpredictable arts demand more extensive teaching.
guidance: Tailor enablement expectations to the predictability of the art; single embodiments may enable broader claims in predictable arts but not in unpredictable ones.

name: Specification need not teach what's well-known
description: The specification is not required to teach subject matter that is already well-known in the relevant art.
guidance: Rely on common general knowledge when appropriate; however, if claimed subject matter depends on non-available components, those must be disclosed.

name: Specification must correlate to entire claim scope
description: The disclosure must enable practice of the entire claim scope, not just preferred embodiments or subsets.
guidance: Correlate the teaching to the claim limitations and ensure coverage across the claimed range or genus.

name: Specification may need to disclose apparatus/materials if not readily available
description: If required components, apparatus, or materials are not readily available to skilled artisans, the specification may need to provide them.
guidance: Failure to disclose necessary but unavailable components can render a claim non-enabling.

name: Block diagram sufficiency rule
description: Block diagrams alone are insufficient if the components lack sufficient detail to permit practice of the invention.
guidance: High-level diagrams without necessary implementation detail can fail the enablement requirement when they do not teach how to realize claimed functions.

name: Computer program disclosure rule
description: Computer programs must specify algorithms or procedures necessary to perform claimed functions.
guidance: Functional claim language for software must be supported by algorithms, flowcharts, pseudocode, or other disclosure that enables implementation; mere high-level functional descriptions may be inadequate.

name: Filing date requirements (pre- and post- Dec 18, 2013)
description: For applications filed before December 18, 2013 (under 37 CFR 1.53(b)), a specification as prescribed by 35 U.S.C. 112 containing a description pursuant to 37 CFR 1.71 and at least one claim pursuant to 37 CFR 1.75, and any drawing required by 37 CFR 1.81(a) were required for a filing date. For nonprovisional applications filed on or after December 18, 2013 (other than design patents), the filing date is the date on which a specification, with or without claims, is received; utility and plant applications no longer required at least one claim or drawings to receive a filing date. A design patent application’s filing date still requires a specification including at least one claim and any required drawings (35 U.S.C. 171(c)).
guidance: See MPEP § 601.01(a). Also, a nonprovisional filed under 35 U.S.C.111(a) on/after Dec 18, 2013 may be filed by reference to a previously filed application indicating the specification and any drawings are replaced by that reference (see MPEP § 601.01(a), subsection III).

name: Specification and drawings — no new matter allowed
description: A continuation or divisional application may be filed with a new specification and drawings or a new specification/drawings with a newly executed or copied oath/declaration provided the new specification and drawings do not contain any subject matter that would have been new matter in the prior application.
guidance: Applicant is responsible to review any new specification or drawings for a continuation/divisional application under 37 CFR 1.53(b) to determine they contain no new matter. If the examiner determines the continuing application contains new matter relative to the prior application, the examiner should notify applicant in the next Office action and indicate the application should be redesignated as a continuation-in-part. If new matter exists, applicant is required to delete the benefit claim or change the relationship to continuation-in-part (Form paragraph 2.10.01 may be used).

name: Claims submission practice in continuing applications
description: It is recommended that applicants file a new set of claims as the original claims of the continuing application rather than filing a copy of the claims from the prior application and a preliminary amendment to those claims.
guidance: Filing a continuing application under 37 CFR 1.53(b) with a preliminary amendment making desired changes to specification or claims is NOT recommended because for applications filed on/after Sept 21, 2004 a preliminary amendment present on the filing date is part of the original disclosure; problematic amendment formats may trigger notices from OPAP requiring resubmission in a publishable format (see 37 CFR 1.115(a)(1) and 1.215). To have a patent application publication contain only a desired set of claims, file a continuation/divisional under 37 CFR 1.53(b) with a new specification containing only the desired set of claims.

name: Publication and provisional rights consideration
description: Any utility or plant patent application that will be published pursuant to 35 U.S.C. 122(b) should be filed under 37 CFR 1.53(b) with a specification that includes any claim(s) and drawings that the applicant would like to have published, because under 35 U.S.C. 154(d) a patentee may obtain provisional rights if the invention claimed in the patent is substantially identical to the invention claimed in the application publication.
guidance: Be mindful that preliminary amendments present on filing may become part of the original disclosure for publication; ensure any amendment is in a format usable for publication (substitute specification per 37 CFR 1.121(b)(3) and 1.125).

name: Incorporation by reference — explicit statement requirement
description: An applicant may incorporate by reference the prior application by the continuing application-as-filed, by an explicit statement in the specification that such prior application(s) are 'hereby incorporated by reference.' The statement must appear in the specification (see 37 CFR 1.57(c) and MPEP § 608.01(p)).
guidance: Inclusion of this incorporation by reference permits applicant to amend the continuing application to include subject matter from the prior application(s) without the need for a petition provided the continuing application is entitled to a filing date notwithstanding the incorporation by reference. Mere reference to another application, patent, or publication is not an incorporation for purposes of the disclosure required by 35 U.S.C.112(a) (In re de Seversky). For apps filed on/after Sept 21, 2004 a claim for benefit under 37 CFR 1.78 present on the filing date is considered an incorporation by reference as to inadvertently omitted material subject to 37 CFR 1.57(b).

name: Incorporation by reference added after filing date is ineffective
description: An incorporation by reference statement added after an application’s filing date is not effective because no new matter can be added after the filing date.
guidance: If an incorporation by reference statement is included in an amendment to the specification to add a benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 120 after the filing date, the amendment would not be proper (Dart Indus. v. Banner). When a benefit claim is submitted after filing, the reference to the prior application cannot include an incorporation by reference statement of the prior application.

name: Substitute statement use (37 CFR 1.64)
description: A newly executed substitute statement under 37 CFR 1.64 is not required for an inventor in a continuing application that claims the benefit of an earlier-filed application provided a substitute statement under 1.64 was executed and filed in the earlier-filed application and a copy showing execution is submitted in the continuing application.
guidance: With respect to an application naming only one inventor, any reference to the inventor's oath/declaration includes a substitute statement executed under 37 CFR 1.64. For more than one inventor, references mean the collective oaths/declarations or substitute statements executed by or with respect to all joint inventors unless otherwise clear from context.

name: Scope of reexamination (§1.906)
description: Claims will be examined on the basis of patents or printed publications and, for subject matter added or deleted, on the basis of 35 U.S.C. 112; claims may not be permitted to enlarge the scope of the patent; other issues outside (a) and (b) will not be resolved in the proceeding.
guidance: If other issues are raised during reexamination, the examiner will note them and the patent owner may consider filing a reissue application to have such issues considered.

name: Content of request for inter partes reexamination (§1.915)
description: A request must be accompanied by the fee (§1.20(c)(2)) and include: (1) identification of patent and every claim challenged; (2) citation of patents/printed publications showing a reasonable likelihood the requester will prevail for at least one claim; (3) a statement explaining and pointing out each showing of reasonable likelihood and detailed explanation of pertinency and manner of applying the references to each claim; (4) copies of relied-upon patents/printed publications with English translations of necessary parts; (5) copy of the entire patent (front face, drawings, specification/claims in double column format) and any disclaimers/corrections/reexamination certificates; (6) certification that a copy of the request was served on the patent owner (name and address of party served) or duplicate supplied if service impossible; (7) certification that estoppel provisions of §1.907 do not prohibit the reexamination; (8) statement identifying the real party in interest sufficient to determine privy status.
guidance: If filed by an attorney/agent identifying another party, power of attorney or representative capacity per §1.34 is required. Failure to include fee or meet requirements will result in notice and opportunity to complete; failure to comply will result in no filing date and placement of the request in the patent file as a citation if it meets §1.501.

name: Examiner determination timeframe and standard (§1.923)
description: Within three months following the filing date, the examiner will determine whether the request and prior art establish a reasonable likelihood that the requester will prevail with respect to at least one challenged claim. The determination is based on the claims in effect at the time and will be mailed to the patent owner and requester. If the examiner finds no reasonable likelihood, the request is refused and no reexamination is ordered.
guidance: Three-month statutory consideration period; determination becomes part of official file.

name: Office action closing prosecution (§1.949)
description: Upon consideration of issues a second or subsequent time, or upon determination of patentability of all claims, the examiner shall issue an Office action treating all claims present in the reexamination, which may be an action closing prosecution. The action shall set forth all rejections and determinations not to make a proposed rejection and the grounds therefor. An action will not usually close prosecution if it includes a new ground of rejection not previously addressed unless necessitated by an amendment.
guidance: Office action must comprehensively state grounds; closing prosecution triggers limited response options.

name: Right of Appeal Notice and expedited stipulation (§1.953)
description: After considering post-closing comments or expiration of time, the examiner shall issue a Right of Appeal Notice unless prosecution is reopened. Parties may stipulate (patent owner + all third party requesters) that issues are appropriate for final action and request expedited Right of Appeal Notice identifying appealable issues and positions. The Right of Appeal Notice is a final action setting forth each ground of rejection and/or final decision favorable to patentability, identification of status of each claim, reasons for decisions, and sets a one-month period to appeal. If no appeal filed, prosecution terminates and a certificate is issued under §1.997.
guidance: Right of Appeal Notice is final and prohibits amendment in response; expedited notices require concurrence of all parties and clear identification of issues.

name: Failure to file timely/appropriate responses (§1.957)
description: If third party requester files untimely or inappropriate comment/notice/brief, it will be refused consideration. If no claims are found patentable and patent owner fails to file timely and appropriate response, prosecution will be terminated and a certificate issued under §1.997 per last Office action. If some claims are found patentable and patent owner fails to timely respond, further prosecution will be limited to claims found patentable at time of failure and to any claims added thereafter which do not expand the scope of those claims. Bona fide substantial attempts with inadvertent omissions may be given opportunity to explain and supply omissions.
guidance: Consequences range from refusal to termination or limitation of prosecution; some leeway for bona fide inadvertent omissions.

name: Conditions for not preparing a written opinion
description: If the same Authority is both International Searching Authority and International Preliminary Examining Authority and a demand has been filed before the ISA written opinion is prepared, no written opinion is required if criteria (i)–(vi) are satisfied.
guidance: (i) the claimed invention satisfies Article 33(1) (novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability); (ii) the application complies with PCT form and contents requirements; (iii) the application meets requirements on clarity of claims, description and drawings and claims are fully supported by the description as in Article 35(2) and Rule 70.12(ii) or the examiner does not wish to make observations (Rule 66.2(a)(v)); (iv) no amendment goes beyond the disclosure in the international application as filed; (v) all claims relate to an invention for which an ISR is being established and an IPEA report will be established for all claims; (vi) where applicable, a nucleotide/amino acid sequence listing is available in a form permitting meaningful IPE.  Also applies where the ISA written opinion is treated as the IPEA first written opinion; in that case the examiner takes into account applicant comments/amendments when establishing the IPEA report.

name: Scope limitation: claims without an international search report
description: International preliminary examination can be carried out only on inventions for which the International Searching Authority has established an international search report.
guidance: This follows from Article 33(6): the IPEA must take into consideration documents cited in the international search report. Claims for inventions without an ISR need not be subject to IPE. (See paragraph 10.73 for exceptions.)

name: Timeliness and content limits of the IPEA report
description: The IPEA report should be issued within the prescribed time limit; it follows written opinions and communications and must not contain any statement on national patentability.
guidance: All amendments, arguments and requests for rectification of obvious mistakes submitted before the examiner has begun to draw up the report must be taken into account. Amendments/arguments/requests received after drafting began need not be considered. The report is prepared on Form PCT/IPEA/409 and should avoid statements about whether the claimed invention is or seems to be patentable/unpatentable under national law. Chapter 17 provides detailed guidance on completing the form.

name: Determination and calculation of applicable time limits
description: When the Authority determines applicable time limits, the examiner must consult all relevant factors and PCT Regulations governing such time limits.
guidance: Factors include translations of priority documents, amendments, rectifications, response to first written opinion, restricting claims/payment of fees, furnishing priority documents, and establishment of the IPEA report. Time limits are usually specified in full months, calculated from the day after mailing of communication. Rules cover contingencies (office closed, official holidays), disruptions in postal service, excuse of delays for force majeure or unavailability of electronic means, and extension of time limits in case of general disruption affecting the Authority.

name: Effect of applicant's failure to respond within time limit
description: If the applicant does not respond within a prescribed time limit, the effect differs by circumstances; the IPEA may proceed in various ways.
guidance: The IPEA report may be established as if priority had not been claimed, established on the 'main invention', or established with a negative determination. Normally, amendments, arguments and rectifications received after the examiner has begun to draw up the opinion/report need not be taken into account.

name: Definition and formal requirements for amendments
description: Any change (other than rectification of obvious mistakes) to claims, description or drawings is an amendment; amendments must be submitted in the language of IPE and follow specified form requirements.
guidance: Amendments to description/drawings must be made by filing replacement sheets when they differ; amendments to claims must be filed as a complete set replacing all claims originally filed or previously amended (Articles 19/34). Replacement sheets must be accompanied by a letter drawing attention to differences, indicating basis in application as filed and preferably explaining reasons. Cancellation of entire sheets must be by letter. Replacement sheets/sets of claims must be in typed form, though handwritten amendments may be allowed at examiner's discretion. Minor corrections (e.g., ≤6 words) may be accepted as interlineations on a typescript if clean; examiners should invite resubmission in proper form when principles are not met.

name: Appraisal of amendments — examiner checks
description: The examiner ensures amendments do not add content beyond the application as filed and do not make the amended application objectionable under the PCT.
guidance: Acceptable amendments include restrictions of scope, improvements of clarity, or claim amendments desirable without changing subject matter. An amended application must satisfy all PCT requirements. When claims have been substantially limited, examiner should pay special attention to: (i) unity of invention (do amended claims satisfy Rule 13?), (ii) agreement of description and claims (do embodiments remain within claim scope; may require description amendment; check title appropriateness), (iii) support — are all amended claims supported by the description (see paragraphs 5.43–5.44).

name: Definiteness — Nautilus standard
description: Definiteness requires a claim to “inform those skilled in the art about the scope of the invention with reasonable certainty.” Nautilus, 572 U.S. at 910.
guidance: A broader scope alone does not render a claim indefinite. Ambiguities that a PHOSITA might see in the claim language can be resolved by the clarity of the specification. The court should assess whether, reading the claims in light of the specification, a PHOSITA would be reasonably certain of the term’s scope.

name: Use of specification / intrinsic evidence to resolve ambiguity
description: Claim terms are interpreted in light of the specification; a PHOSITA viewing claims “in light of the specification,” would recognize the specification teaches embodiments that clarify ambiguous claim language.
guidance: When a claim could plausibly be read multiple ways, the specification may supply antecedent basis or otherwise resolve ambiguity (Med. Co. v. Mylan, DeMarini Sports). Courts should examine specification disclosures (e.g., repeated recitation of RDML) to determine what a PHOSITA would understand the claim to require.

name: Antecedent basis requirement (including implied antecedent basis)
description: A claim term may have antecedent basis implied by earlier claim language (e.g., the use of “markup document” in claim 10 provides antecedent basis for 'the markup language' in claim 12).
guidance: Court may find antecedent basis based on claim phraseology combined with specification context; antecedent basis need not be explicit if a PHOSITA reading claims and spec would be reasonably certain of the reference.

name: Secondary characteristics do not necessarily create new claim scope
description: Compliance with secondary characteristics (e.g., XML 1.0 compliance) does not transform an underlying markup language into a different markup language such that claim scope becomes indefinite.
guidance: Distinguish between an underlying language (RDML) and optional compliance or secondary characteristics (XML compliance); differences in secondary traits do not alone create different ‘languages’ for claim-scope purposes.

name: Enablement and infringement are distinct from indefiniteness
description: The question of enablement is distinct from indefiniteness; likewise, infringement questions are separate from claim construction/indefiniteness findings.
guidance: Courts should avoid conflating enablement or infringement issues with the legal analysis of definiteness under §112(b) or (a); findings on indefiniteness at claim construction do not resolve enablement or infringement.

name: Means-plus-function construction: include claim limitations
description: The function of a means-plus-function claim must be construed to include the limitations contained in the claim language. Lockheed, 324 F.3d at 1319.
guidance: Courts may not improperly broaden a means-plus-function claim by ignoring clear limitations in the claim language; any limitation that materially restricts how the function is performed should be included in the recited function.

name: Treatment of 'so that' / 'whereby' clauses in function
description: Determine whether a 'so that' (or 'whereby') clause merely states a result or instead substantively limits the manner of performing the claimed function.
guidance: If the clause restricts how the function operates (i.e., requires transformation into a common format or unit), it is a substantive limitation that must be included in the function. If it only states the result of other limitations, it may be excluded (per Lockheed/Texas Instruments precedent).

name: Software means-plus-function: algorithmic disclosure requirement
description: For computer-implemented means-plus-function claims, the specification must disclose an algorithm for performing the claimed function such that a PHOSITA would recognize the structure and associate it with the function. (Noah Sys., Net MoneyIN, Aristocrat).
guidance: The disclosed algorithm may appear in figures and accompanying text describing stepwise procedures (examples: Figures 10 and 11 and associated col./line citations). The specification must disclose steps (not just high-level goals) that map to the claimed function.

name: If no algorithm is disclosed, claim is indefinite under §112(f)
description: If the specification discloses no algorithm for a computer-implemented means-plus-function claim, the inquiry is complete and the claims are indefinite. (CellCast, EON Corp.).
guidance: Courts should first ask whether any algorithm is disclosed; absence of any algorithmic disclosure mandates indefiniteness. If some algorithm is disclosed, adequacy may be litigated further.

name: Adequacy of disclosed algorithm — mapping and substeps
description: A disclosed algorithm must meaningfully map to the claim's recited function and include necessary substeps; an ad hoc list of special cases or a black-box 'determine desired transformation' is insufficient.
guidance: Assess whether the specification's algorithm describes how to determine what should be transformed, how to select transformation, and the concrete steps (e.g., accessing attributes, determining conversion factors, multiplying conversion factors, displaying transformed data). Missing substeps or opaque 'secret sauce' determinations support a contention of insufficiency.

name: Algorithm need not be source code
description: The algorithmic structure supporting a software-implemented claim need not be the operative source code itself.
guidance: High-level stepwise algorithms in the specification (flowcharts, descriptions of operations) can satisfy the requirement if they are sufficiently specific to associate structure with the claimed function.

name: Macros or alternate disclosed elements must show algorithmic detail to qualify as structure
description: Alleged alternate structures (e.g., macros) must themselves be disclosed with algorithmic steps corresponding to the claimed function; mere mentions that macros 'evaluate the transformation string' or update titles/legends do not suffice to show transformation of numerical values.
guidance: Courts should examine the actual specification passages cited for macros or alternative structures to confirm they disclose the algorithmic steps required by the claim function. If not, those elements cannot be included as structure.

name: Preliminary vs final construction and limits of claim-construction stage
description: Courts may issue a preliminary construction based on briefs, intrinsic evidence, and hearings, and later refine to a final construction; claims about algorithm adequacy (enablement) may be reserved for later proceedings.
guidance: At claim construction courts decide scope/definiteness based on intrinsic evidence and may rule the disclosed algorithm is sufficient to avoid indefiniteness without resolving whether the algorithm is enabling; adequacy disputes that depend on factual expert resolution may be left to summary judgment.

name: Applicant's burden after examiner raises reasonable basis of nonenablement
description: Once USPTO personnel have advanced a reasonable basis or presented evidence to question the adequacy of a disclosure, the applicant must show that the specification would enable one of ordinary skill in the art to make and use the claimed invention without resorting to undue experimentation.
guidance: Typical applicant responses include submitting affidavits, referencing prior art patents or technical publications, presenting arguments of counsel, or combinations of these approaches.

name: Integration/interconnection of prior art components
description: Even if enumerated devices or blocks are old, disclosure must make clear how they are interconnected to function in the claimed complex combination; otherwise undue experimentation is likely.
guidance: The specification must set forth the integration of the prior art; otherwise relying on old components does not demonstrate enablement for the combined system.

name: Distinction between utility (35 U.S.C. 101) and enablement (35 U.S.C. 112)
description: The 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph requirement as to how to use the invention is different from the utility requirement under 35 U.S.C. 101, which requires some specific, substantial, and credible use.
guidance: A claim may have credible utility yet still be defective under 35 U.S.C. 112 if one skilled in the art would have to engage in undue experimentation to practice the claimed invention.

name: Dependent claims incorporate limitations (35 U.S.C. 112, fourth paragraph)
description: When construing dependent claims, they shall be construed to incorporate by reference all limitations of the claim to which they refer and therefore further limit the subject matter claimed.
guidance: Examiners must follow the fourth paragraph when considering dependent claims in enablement analysis.

name: Rejection for claims broader than enabling disclosure (first paragraph enablement rejection)
description: A rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112 as broader than the enabling disclosure is an enablement (first paragraph) issue, not a definiteness (second paragraph) issue.
guidance: How teaching is set forth (specific example or broad terminology) is not determinative; the key is whether the disclosure enables the full claim scope.

name: Single means claim undue breadth
description: A single means claim (means recitation not in combination with other recited element of means) is subject to an undue breadth rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph if it covers every conceivable means for achieving the stated purpose while the specification discloses at most those means known to the inventor.
guidance: Such claims have been held nonenabling where specification does not limit or disclose the full range of means.

name: Inoperative embodiments and enablement
description: The presence of inoperative embodiments within the scope of a claim does not necessarily render a claim nonenabled; the standard is whether a skilled person could determine which conceived-but-not-yet-made embodiments are operative with no more effort than normally required in the art.
guidance: Claims reading on significant numbers of inoperative embodiments render claims nonenabled when the specification does not clearly identify operative embodiments and undue experimentation is involved in determining which embodiments are operative.

name: Critical feature taught but not claimed
description: A feature taught as critical in the specification and not recited in the claims should result in a rejection under the enablement provision of 35 U.S.C. 112.
guidance: In determining criticality, consider the entire disclosure; features that are merely preferred are not critical. Make an enablement rejection only when the specification language makes clear the limitation is critical for function.

name: Best mode — failure to disclose need not be extreme to be actionable
description: Failure to disclose the best mode need not rise to the level of active concealment or grossly inequitable conduct to support a rejection; omission of a specific material that would enable reproduction can violate the requirement.
guidance: If an inventor knows of a specific material that will make possible successful reproduction of claimed effects but only speaks in broad categories without disclosing that material, the best mode requirement may not be satisfied.

name: Considerations relevant to best mode (practical points)
description: When assessing best mode: determine what the invention is (claims define it); a specific working example is not required; designation as 'best mode' is not required; updating best mode is not required; a defect in best mode cannot be cured by adding new matter after filing.
guidance: The specification need not set forth details unrelated to the essence of the invention; best mode may be a preferred range or group of reactants; proposed amendments adding an undisclosed best mode are new matter and should be objected to.

name: Novelty Search — Semantic Search (precision metric)
description: Semantic Search finds the most similar technical solutions globally; Top 100 accuracy when identifying English X documents reaches 78%. Scope: search over >192M patents and 192M scientific articles using English or Chinese input.
guidance: Semantic search quality is measured by 'Top 100 accuracy' (probability of hitting X/affecting-novelty documents within top 100 results). Users can customize semantic inputs by adding/removing concept words to focus results. Platform claims a hybrid approach (traditional word-vector models + generative LLM semantic understanding) to reach higher precision.

name: Challenge awareness for search quality (anti-patterns)
description: Identified challenges include: semantic algorithms or incomplete data coverage leading to low relevance and time-consuming novelty checking; image searches suffering from incomplete global data coverage and low precision; missing search fields or use of common keywords causing high-recall noisy results; and manually reading many patents is time-consuming and prone to omissions.
guidance: These challenges serve as anti-patterns to check for in vendor claims; evaluate how a platform addresses each (algorithm sophistication, dataset completeness, deep fields, semantic filtering) rather than accepting claims at face value.

name: Exclusive deep-processed fields and AI transcription as a quality differentiator
description: Patsnap claims exclusive high-quality deep-processed patent fields and AI transcription capabilities (Patent DNA) to make it easier to find relevant comparison documents and improve novelty/invalidity search quality and efficiency.
guidance: When assessing platforms, verify the existence, scope, and accuracy of deep-processed fields and AI transcriptions and whether they materially improve precision over raw-text search and standard classification-based approaches.

name: Coverage and precision metrics presented as product KPIs
description: Product-level KPIs are provided as claims: Semantic Top100 Accuracy 78% (English X documents), Image Search TOP100 Accuracy 73.7%, multi-million to billion scale dataset counts, and jurisdictional coverage numbers (172 offices, 61 offices for citations).
guidance: These KPIs should be validated and benchmarked in procurement/evaluation: methodology for deriving 'Top100 accuracy', test corpora, and definitions (what counts as X documents, test cases) are necessary to accept claimed metrics.

name: Indicating relevant claims for 'A' citations
description: For “A” citations it is not necessary to indicate the relevant claims unless there is good reason to do so.
guidance: Examples of good reason include a clear lack of unity a priori where the citation is relevant only to a particular claim or group of claims, or when the claims meet criteria of novelty, inventive step, and industrial applicability and the A-category citations represent the most relevant prior art.

name: Purpose of a written opinion
description: The purpose of a written opinion is to give a primary indication to the applicant of the defects which the examiner considers to exist so the applicant can determine the most appropriate course of action (demand IPE, submit comments/amendments).
guidance: Its primary role is to identify whether the claimed invention appears to be novel, involve an inventive step (be non-obvious) and be industrially applicable. It will also include opinions on certain other substantive defects insofar as checked by the Authority and on certain form defects of the international application (see Rules referenced).

name: Matters a written opinion should cover (Rule 66.2 matters)
description: Any written opinion should usually cover matters such as (i) whether Article 34(4) situations apply; (ii) an apparent failure to meet novelty, inventive step or industrial applicability; (iii) defects in form or contents insofar as checked; (iv) amendments appearing to go beyond the disclosure; (v) apparent lack of clarity or support for claims; (vi) that a claim is directed to an invention on which no international search report has been established; (vii) nucleotide/amino acid sequence listing issues.
guidance: These are the principal substantive headings examiners should address in written opinions and international preliminary examination reports.

name: Indicating amendments resulting in gaps in numbering
description: Where amendments under Article 19 or 34 have been made which result in cancellation or gaps in numbering sequence of description pages, claim numbers, and/or drawing sheets, these are detailed in item 3 of Box No. I of the written opinion/report.
guidance: This records structural changes to the application numbering caused by amendments.

name: Additional observations in Box No. II limited to priority considerations
description: Additional observations in item 3 of Box No. II relate only to priority considerations and not to clarity, descriptive support, defects or any other consideration relevant to Box No. VIII.
guidance: Such observations might include reasons why a priority claim was considered invalid or an indication that it had been checked and considered valid.

name: Clarity or support issues causing non-establishment
description: Where the description, claims, or drawings are so unclear, or the claims are so inadequately supported by the description that no meaningful opinion can be formed on novelty, inventive step, or industrial applicability, the examination may be restricted to claims/parts sufficiently clear and supported.
guidance: Where an opinion cannot be established on a claim the examiner marks the appropriate check box in Box No. III and includes observations on lack of clarity and/or support. Issues of clarity and descriptive support should be raised separately from novelty/inventive step considerations in Box No. VIII (see Chapter 5 and paragraph 17.50).

name: No international search made for some or all claims (Article 33(6))
description: Where the ISA has not established an international search report and instead issued a declaration under Article 17 (relating to excluded subject matter, clarity, lack of unity, etc.), the questions of novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability cannot be addressed and this is noted using the sixth check box of Box No. III.
guidance: This applies even where Article 34 amendments may have overcome earlier considerations. See Article 33(6).

name: Patentable classes / subject-matter eligibility
description: Defence may be that the patented art or instrument is not within the patentable classes; theory, abstractions, and pure scientific theory are not patentable.
guidance: Determine whether claimed subject-matter fits statutory/recognized patentable classes (machine, manufacture, composition, process); exclude theories, laws of nature, principles unless reduced to practice in patentable form.

name: Sufficiency of specification / written disclosure
description: Ambiguity or defective disclosure in the specification can be a defence (Twelfth Defence; fraudulent concealment or misrepresentation in specification also a defence).
guidance: Specification must adequately describe invention and enable practice; fraudulent or misleading disclosures require notice; ambiguity may invalidate or limit claims; reissue can cure some errors in description.

name: Ambiguity and excessiveness in claims
description: Ambiguity in the claims (Fourteenth Defence) and excessive claims (Thirteenth Defence) are defensible defects; claims must be clear and limited to proper scope.
guidance: Claims are strictly construed; ambiguity may be raised as a defence and affect infringement analysis. Excessive claims (over-claiming) can render patent vulnerable to attack or reissue.

name: Temporal and territorial limits of infringement
description: No infringement can be committed before the issue of the patent; infringement can be committed only within the area of the United States (with special rules for Government use).
guidance: Consider date of issue and geographic scope when evaluating infringement claims; governmental use has distinct rules and potential compensation obligations.

name: Reissue and surrender to correct errors
description: Errors in stating the patent or claims may be cured by surrender and reissue; reissue and re-examination have defined effects and limitations.
guidance: Reissue procedures, grounds (e.g., claim excessiveness, error in description), time limits, and effects on rights and prior art are set out; undue delay and reissue doctrines discussed.

name: Examples of situations not defining "substantial utilities"
description: The following are examples of situations that require or constitute carrying out further research to identify or reasonably confirm a 'real world' context of use and, therefore, do not define 'substantial utilities': (A) Basic research such as studying the properties of the claimed product itself or the mechanisms in which the material is involved; (B) A method of treating an unspecified disease or condition; (C) A method of assaying for or identifying a material that itself has no specific and/or substantial utility; (D) A method of making a material that itself has no specific, substantial, and credible utility; and (E) A claim to an intermediate product for use in making a final product that has no specific, substantial and credible utility.
guidance: These situations are examples where further research is required and do not by themselves establish a substantial utility. Office personnel should treat such assertions as requiring additional support before accepting utility.

name: Inoperative inventions and 'incredible' utility threshold
description: An invention that is 'inoperative' (i.e., it does not operate to produce the results claimed) is not 'useful' under the patent law, but to violate 35 U.S.C. 101 the claimed device must be totally incapable of achieving a useful result.
guidance: A small degree of utility is sufficient; partial success is enough. Rejections as inoperative are rare and should be based on clear evidence of total incapacity. Do not label an asserted utility 'incredible' or 'speculative' unless the record supports that a rejection for lack of utility is proper. Examples of truly inoperative claims (perpetual motion, cold fusion, etc.) are fact-specific and not a per se rule.

name: Claim-focused evaluation and genus/species treatment
description: The claimed invention (each claim) is the focus of the utility requirement; each claim must be evaluated on its own merits. Generally a dependent claim will have utility if the independent claim to which it refers defines an invention having utility. Where an applicant has established utility for a species within a genus, a generic claim to the genus should generally be treated as sufficient under 35 U.S.C. 101 unless it can be established that other species encompassed by the claim lack utility.
guidance: If certain species clearly lack utility, encourage amendment of the generic claim to exclude those species. Ensure that when a dependent claim specifies a different utility than the independent claim, that difference is evaluated.

name: Procedure when no statement of utility appears in specification
description: If no statements asserting a specific and substantial utility are found in the specification, Office personnel should determine if the claimed invention has a well-established utility; if not, the examiner should reject under 35 U.S.C. 101 and 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
guidance: The rejection should clearly indicate failure to identify a specific and substantial utility and require the applicant to reply indicating why the invention is believed useful and where support for the asserted utility can be found in the specification as filed. See MPEP §2701 for further procedures.

name: Presumption of utility created by applicant's assertion and initial examiner approach
description: An applicant's assertion of utility creates a presumption of utility that will be sufficient in most cases to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 101; examiners must begin by asking if there is any reason to question the truth of the statement of utility rather than assuming it false.
guidance: Apply the Langer test: a disclosure teaching making/using the invention in terms corresponding in scope to the claim must be taken as in compliance with enablement unless there is reason to doubt the objective truth of statements relied upon. Examiners should evaluate the logic and any evidence provided by the applicant before challenging utility.

name: Scope limits on examiner reliance on applicant's prosecution statements
description: Statements made by the applicant in the specification or incident to prosecution cannot, standing alone, be the basis for a lack of utility rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 or 35 U.S.C. 112.
guidance: Office should not require an applicant to strike nonessential statements relating to utility from a disclosure if technical accuracy cannot be easily confirmed and those statements are not necessary to support patentability. Examiners should avoid reading unclaimed limitations or unclaimed embodiments into claims when evaluating utility.

name: 35 U.S.C. 112 (first paragraph) addresses more than utility
description: 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, addresses whether claims are fully supported by the disclosure, whether the disclosure is enabling, and whether the written description and best mode requirements are satisfied — matters separate from the question of utility.
guidance: A disclosure showing a specific and credible utility and credible basis does not necessarily satisfy all 112 requirements. For example, an invention may have utility but the specification may not enable one of ordinary skill to practice the full scope of claimed subject matter, in which case a 112 rejection (not based on utility) may be appropriate and should be imposed separately from utility-based rejections.

name: Enablement (35 U.S.C. § 112)
description: The specification must enable a person of ordinary skill in the art to practice the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
guidance: Enablement requires adequate disclosure, cogent explanation of mechanisms, and verifiable test data; bare, non-reproducible experimental reports or speculative assertions fail enablement. The examiner/Board may reasonably require experimental verification and sufficient detail of sources, detecting methods, and parameters to permit practice of the claims.

name: Written Description Requirement (35 U.S.C. § 112)
description: The specification must demonstrate possession of the claimed invention and support the full scope of the claims.
guidance: Claims will be rejected when the specification fails to describe the claimed subject matter with sufficient detail to show the inventor possessed it. The Board affirmed rejections where the specification did not provide a cogent explanation or sufficient examples to support broad claim scope (written description rejections in the ’739 and ’830 applications).

name: Indefiniteness / Particularity of Claim Limitations
description: Claims must have the requisite particularity and distinctness; limitations must be sufficiently definite to inform those skilled in the art of the claim scope.
guidance: Lack of particularity in structural or functional limitations (e.g., 'source' and 'container' described so generally that any known or unknown photon/magnetic pulse generator would suffice) supports indefiniteness or § 101 rejection for lack of a practical application (the Board found such limitations lacked the particularity necessary to qualify as a machine/transformation).

name: Preemption / Claim Scope Must Be Commensurate With Contribution
description: Claim scope must not preempt future developments beyond the applicant's demonstrated contribution to the art.
guidance: Even assuming some demonstrated embodiments, claims that 'far exceed' the applicant's contribution and would preempt future developments can be rejected (Board's concern that claim 5's scope 'would far exceed Appellants' contribution to the art—preempting the future before it has arrived').

name: Judicial Exceptions to Patentable Subject Matter (Natural Phenomena)
description: Claims directed to natural phenomena or natural laws are judicial exceptions to patentable subject matter and require additional elements to show a practical application.
guidance: An examiner may view phenomena (e.g., 'generating quantum entanglements' as a natural phenomenon) as unpatentable absent particularized machines, transformations, or useful applications. Lack of particularity or usefulness of the asserted application supports sustaining a § 101 rejection (as in the ’739 Board opinion adopting the Examiner's analysis).

name: Reexamination filing fees and formatting requirements (ex parte reexamination) (§ 1.20(c))
description: Fees for filing requests for ex parte reexamination and related reexamination fees, with explicit document formatting requirements for certain fee tiers.
guidance: For an ex parte reexamination request having 40 or fewer pages, double-spaced or 1.5 spaced lines, non-script font (e.g., Arial, Times New Roman, Courier), sufficient contrast and clarity to permit OCR, and otherwise complying with paragraph (c)(1): Table 1 to paragraph (c)(1)(i) — By a micro entity $1,355.00; by a small entity $2,710.00; by other than a small or micro entity $6,775.00. For requests meeting an alternate listed set of requirements (Table 2 to paragraph (c)(2)) the amounts shown include: micro $2,709.00; small $5,418.00; other $13,545.00. For filing a request with sufficient clarity (Table with smaller amounts): micro $120.00; small $240.00; other $600.00. For each claim in excess of 20 (and in excess of number of claims in the patent under reexamination): Table 4 to paragraph (c)(4): by a micro entity $40.00; by a small entity $80.00; (other-entity amount in table). Note: specified portions of ex parte reexamination requests are excluded from certain formatting provisions (e.g., copies of patents and printed publications relied upon, copy of entire patent, required certifications). Also font size, margins (§ 1.52(a)(1)(ii)), and clarity/contrast requirements are listed (e.g., font size no smaller than 12 point).

name: Application information specifics (title, entity status)
description: Application Information is displayed and editable; Title of the Invention is required; entity claims are handled here with limitations.
guidance: Do not use special characters in the Title field. You may claim small entity status by checking the box and properly signing the Corrected Web-ADS per 37 CFR 1.27. You cannot use a Corrected Web-ADS to notify the Office that you are no longer entitled to small entity status — a properly signed written notification per 37 CFR 1.27(g)(2) is required. Micro entity status requires a proper micro entity certification form (PTO/SB/15A or PTO/SB/15B).

name: Domestic benefit / national stage claim rules and ordering
description: Domestic benefit/National Stage data is displayed and editable; domestic benefit and national stage claims must comply with statutory/regulatory time limits and ordering requirements.
guidance: Adding domestic benefit claims in a utility or plant application after the time period in 37 CFR 1.78 requires a petition to accept an unintentionally delayed benefit claim (including petition fee). Deleting a domestic benefit claim may be considered an intentional waiver. When claiming benefit of more than one prior application, start with the most recent and go back chronologically for each chain; multiple chains must each be provided chronologically. The UI supports Add/Remove, Move Up/Move Down, and drag-and-drop to reorganize benefit claim order. Note: The Corrected ADS will display internal PALM codes for relationships (e.g., CON, DIV, CIP, NST, SUB, REI, PRO); these codes are accepted.

name: Foreign priority claim rules (35 U.S.C. 119(b) and 37 CFR 1.55)
description: Foreign Priority information entered in the ADS constitutes the claim for priority as required by statute and regulation.
guidance: Adding a foreign priority claim after the regulatory time limits (e.g., after the later of four months from filing date of the instant application or sixteen months from the filing date of the prior foreign application) requires a petition to accept an unintentionally delayed foreign priority claim (including petition fee). Deleting a foreign priority claim may be treated as an intentional waiver. The ADS supports adding/removing multiple foreign priority claims. There is a field for entering a WIPO DAS access code to identify a foreign priority document.

name: Post-appeal amendments and evidence admission rules
description: Amendments submitted on or after the date the proceeding has been appealed may be admitted as provided in § 1.116. Amendments filed on or after the date of filing a brief may be admitted only to cancel claims or to rewrite dependent claims into independent form (where cancellation does not affect scope of other pending claims), or otherwise only as permitted by §§ 41.39(b)(1), 41.50(a)(2)(i), 41.50(b)(1), and 41.50(c). Affidavits or other evidence submitted after appeal and prior to filing the brief may be admitted if the examiner determines they overcome all rejections under appeal and there is good and sufficient reason such evidence was not earlier presented; other affidavits/evidence after appeal will not be admitted except as permitted by specified provisions.
guidance: Amendments after final but prior to appeal, and amendments after appeal but prior to brief, are treated under § 1.116; stricter limitations apply after filing a brief. Good-and-sufficient-reason showings and examiner determinations are required for admission of certain affidavits/evidence.

name: Rewriting dependent claims into independent form (scope)
description: Rewriting dependent claims into independent form includes: (1) rewriting a dependent claim in independent form by adding thereto the limitations of the parent claim(s); and (2) rewriting an independent claim to incorporate therein all the subject matter of a dependent claim, canceling the dependent claim, and changing the dependency of claims that depended on the canceled dependent claim to the amended independent claim.
guidance: The MPEP will provide guidance; these situations are permitted under § 41.33 when rewriting dependent claims into independent form is allowed.

name: Statement of status of all claims and identification of appealed claims
description: Appeal brief must present a statement of the status of all the claims (e.g., rejected, allowed/confirmed, withdrawn, objected to, canceled) and identify which claims are being appealed.
guidance: This generally incorporates former § 1.192(c)(3) requirements; the Board uses this to determine scope of review and whether to make new grounds of rejection under § 41.50(b).

name: Concise explanation of subject matter of each independent claim
description: A concise explanation of the subject matter defined in each independent claim involved in the appeal must be provided, with reference to the specification by page and line number and to the drawing, if any, by reference characters; appellant may include any other information of record to aid the Board.
guidance: What is 'concise' is case-specific; the explanation need not show how each claim is different. The purpose is to aid claim construction and enable the Board to perform informed, claim-by-claim patentability determinations; appellant may decide whether to reference one representative drawing or multiple embodiments.

name: Identification of means-plus-function / step-plus-function elements (35 U.S.C. 112(6))
description: Every means-plus-function and step-plus-function limitation as permitted by 35 U.S.C. 112(6) used in the claims must be identified and the structure, material, or acts described in the specification as corresponding to each claimed function must be set forth with reference to the specification by page and line number and to the drawing, if any.
guidance: This requirement applies only to each independent claim involved in the appeal and to each dependent claim argued separately; concerns about estoppel are matters for proceedings outside the Office. Whether language invokes 112(6) is a merits issue discussed in MPEP 2181.

name: Claim-by-claim patentability and argumentation (waiver risk)
description: Patentability must be decided on a claim-by-claim basis; arguments in the Appeal Brief are preferably directed to individual claims. If appellant groups claims, the Board will pick a single claim to decide the appeal for that group. Failure to separately argue claims that are grouped may constitute waiver of arguments for dependent claims.
guidance: If rejections are 'jumbled' or unclear as to which grounds apply to which claims, appellant can seek relief via petition under § 1.181. The waiver provision reflects case law (e.g., In re McDaniel) that grouping claims can waive separate patentability arguments.

name: Addition of 'separate' before 'patentability' (clarification)
description: The rules were amended to add the word 'separate' prior to 'patentability' in § 41.37(c)(1)(vii) and § 41.67(c)(1)(vii) to clarify that pointing out what a claim recites will not be considered an argument for 'separate' patentability of a claim.
guidance: This clarifies that description of what a claim recites is not itself an argument that the claim is separately patentable; explicit argument is required for separate patentability positions.

name: Applying 35 U.S.C. 102(e) for references with earlier filing dates
description: This paragraph is used to reject over a reference (patent or published application) with an earlier filing date that discloses the claimed invention, and that only qualifies as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(e). The reference must have either a common assignee or at least one common inventor.
guidance: Do NOT use this form paragraph if the reference qualifies as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a) or (b) (use form paragraph 7.21 instead). Do not use when the reference is disqualified under 35 U.S.C. 103(c) as prior art in a 103(a) rejection. See Examiner Notes for form paragraph 7.12 to determine the 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date of the reference.

name: Graham v. Deere factual inquiries for obviousness
description: The factual inquiries set forth in Graham v. John Deere Co. that are applied for establishing a background for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103(a): 1. Determining the scope and contents of the prior art. 2. Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue. 3. Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art. 4. Considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
guidance: This form paragraph may be used, if appropriate, in response to an argument of the use of Graham v. Deere. An explanation of the Graham analysis must follow form paragraph 7.22 or similar rejections.

name: When to use combined 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103(a) rejection (form paragraph 7.27)
description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102([x]) as anticipated by or, in the alternative, under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as obvious over [reference].
guidance: This paragraph is NOT intended to be commonly used as a substitute for a single 102 or 103 rejection. Use only when appropriate, e.g.: (a) claim interpretation dispute where one interpretation yields 102 and another yields 103; (b) reference discloses all claim limitations except a property or function and examiner cannot determine whether the property is inherent; (c) genus/species disclosure issues; (d) product-by-process same product produced by different process; (e) means-plus-function uncertainties; (f) overlapping ranges where no specific example exists. Provide a full explanation following the form paragraph and precede with form paragraphs 7.07, 7.08-7.14 as appropriate, and 7.20 or 7.103.

name: Primary focus on prior art; limit undue emphasis on non-prior-art rejections
description: The primary object of examination is to determine whether claims are patentable over the prior art. This consideration should not be relegated while undue emphasis is given to nonprior art or 'technical' rejections.
guidance: Concentrate effort on truly essential matters and minimize effort on technical rejections which are not critical. Where a major technical (non-prior-art) rejection is proper (e.g., lack of proper disclosure, undue breadth, utility), state it with a full development of the reasons rather than a mere conclusion with stereotyped language. Use appropriate MPEP sections for nonstatutory subject matter, double patenting, new matter, foreign filing without license, disclaimers, reissue, etc. Incorporating form paragraph language reduces misunderstanding as to grounds of rejection.

name: Formatted utility/enablement rejection combining 35 U.S.C. 101 and 35 U.S.C. 112 (first paragraph)
description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 because the claimed invention is not supported by either a [asserted utility] or a well-established utility; and claim also rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph for lack of enablement if the specification would not enable one skilled in the art to make/use the claimed invention.
guidance: Use Format A, B, or C as appropriate: Format A inserts 'specific and substantial' where appropriate; Format B inserts 'credible'; Format C addresses multiple utilities that are not specific/substantial/credible. When specification is not enabling, make a separate enablement rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112 applying In re Wands factors and undue experimentation analysis (MPEP §§ 2164-2164.08(c)).

name: 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph — written description requirement
description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, as failing to comply with the written description requirement: the claim contains subject matter not described in the specification in such a way as to reasonably convey to one skilled in the art that the inventor had possession of the claimed invention.
guidance: This rejection must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.01 or 7.103. In the office action identify the subject matter not properly described by suitable reference to pages/lines/figures and explain your position, including any unresolved examiner questions that raise doubt as to possession at time of filing.

name: 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph — enablement requirement
description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, as failing to comply with the enablement requirement: the claim contains subject matter not described in the specification in such a way as to enable one skilled in the art to make and/or use the invention.
guidance: Precede this rejection with form paragraph 7.30.01 or 7.103. Identify claimed subject matter not enabled and explain why the specification is not enabling by applying the In re Wands factors (858 F.2d 731) and related MPEP sections. Explain any unresolved examiner questions that raise doubt as to enablement. If the problem concerns scope, use form paragraph 7.31.03 instead.

name: 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph — scope of enablement (commensurateness)
description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, because the specification, while being enabling for some embodiments, does not reasonably provide enablement for other claimed subject matter; i.e., the claims are not commensurate in scope with the enabling disclosure.
guidance: Precede with form paragraph 7.30.01 or 7.103. Identify what the specification does enable (by reference) and the aspects of the claims not enabled. State whether the specification fails to enable one to 'make', 'use', or 'make and use' the invention commensurate with claim scope. Apply In re Wands factors and include explanations of unresolved examiner questions where relevant.

name: 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph — essential subject matter missing from claims (enablement)
description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph when subject matter considered critical or essential to practice of the invention is missing from the claim(s) and therefore not enabled by the disclosure.
guidance: Precede with form paragraph 7.30.01 or 7.103. Recite omitted subject matter in the office action; cite statement/argument/date/drawing or other evidence showing applicant considered the feature essential. Give rationale for considering the omitted subject matter critical/essential. Use form paragraph 7.33.01 when an essential component or step is not recited in the claims.

name: 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph — claims must 'particularly point out and distinctly claim' (indefiniteness)
description: The specification must conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the applicant regards as his invention; failure to do so supports a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph.
guidance: Use form paragraph 7.30.02 (statutory quotation) in first actions and final rejections. Rejections under 112, second paragraph should be supported by one or more specific form paragraphs (7.34.02 - 7.34.11 etc.), and identify particular terms or limitations rendering the claim indefinite where possible. If none of the form paragraphs fit, provide a full explanation of the deficiency.

name: Terminology used inconsistent with accepted meaning (claim indefiniteness)
description: Where applicant acts as own lexicographer to redefine a term contrary to its ordinary meaning, the written description must clearly redefine the claim term and set forth the uncommon definition to put one reasonably skilled in the art on notice.
guidance: Use form paragraph 7.34.02 following 7.34.01. Identify the term, its meaning as used in the claim, and the accepted meaning. Provide support for the accepted meaning via references (textbook/dictionary). This paragraph should only be used where the specification does not clearly redefine the term.

name: Means‑plus‑function (§112, ¶6) requires disclosure of corresponding structure
description: When a claim limitation invokes §112, ¶6, the specification must disclose the corresponding structure, material, or acts that perform the recited function; merely stating known techniques or methods can be used is not a disclosure of structure.
guidance: The analysis begins by determining whether the specification discloses corresponding structure, material, or acts in accordance with §112, ¶6. Examples: failure to disclose structure for a ‘control means’ or ‘game control means’ renders the claim indefinite. Anti‑pattern: bare statements that a standard microprocessor with 'appropriate programming' or that 'known techniques can be used' are sufficient — they are not.

name: Computer‑implemented means need an algorithm to provide sufficient structure
description: For computer‑implemented means‑plus‑function claims, the patentee must disclose an algorithm that transforms a general purpose computer into a special purpose computer to perform the disclosed function.
guidance: Patentee may express the algorithm as a mathematical formula, in prose, a flow chart, or other understandable terms. Simply reciting 'software' or 'microprocessor with appropriate programming' without algorithmic detail is insufficient and constitutes impermissible pure functional claiming. (See Aristocrat, Finisar, Katz examples.)

name: Specification must 'clearly link or associate' disclosed structure to the claimed function
description: It is not enough that one of ordinary skill could implement a structure; the written description itself must disclose sufficient structure and clearly link/associate that structure to the claimed function so a skilled artisan understands the bounds of the claim.
guidance: If the specification links controllers/circuitry/ACM/software to the claimed function with descriptive detail, that can establish the necessary link (e.g., Telecordia shows controllers linked to monitoring). If the specification only restates outcomes or uses black‑box abstractions, the link is missing (e.g., Blackboard ACM as 'black box').

name: Pure functional claiming of a general purpose computer is indefinite unless algorithm disclosed
description: Claiming a general purpose computer programmed to perform a specialized function without disclosing the internal structure (algorithm) runs afoul of the prohibition on purely functional claiming and renders the claim indefinite under §112, ¶2.
guidance: The public notice function is implicated: without algorithmic disclosure, the public cannot tell the metes and bounds of the invention. Katz examples illustrate this risk when no algorithm for conditional coupling was disclosed.

name: Do not import unrecited functions from dependent claims into independent claims
description: The corresponding structure for a means‑plus‑function limitation should be limited to performing the recited function; one should not require disclosure of additional, unrecited functions (which may be recited in dependent claims) to support the independent claim.
guidance: Wenger example: 'circulating' is the recited function in claim 1; requiring structure for 'recirculating' (recited only in claim 3) would improperly import limitations. Examiner/practitioner must match structure to the specific recited function.

name: Specification must satisfy written description (§112, ¶1) by showing possession of claimed invention
description: To meet the written description requirement, the specification must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail that one skilled in the art would reasonably conclude the inventor had possession of the claimed invention.
guidance: The specification must describe the invention in a manner understandable to a person of ordinary skill and show the inventor actually invented the claimed subject matter. This is separate but related to §112, ¶6 analysis and impacts breadth of functional limitations.

name: Enablement (§112, ¶1) requires teaching how to make and use the full scope without undue experimentation
description: The specification must teach those skilled in the art how to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation to satisfy enablement.
guidance: Functional claim limitations that cover all means/methods of performing a function can render a claim broader than the enabling disclosure and thus unsupported. Examiner/practitioner should evaluate whether enabling disclosure commensurates with claimed breadth.

name: Assessment is fact‑specific — examples can support or defeat indefiniteness
description: Whether disclosure is sufficient is determined on facts: detailed embodiments, figures, controller circuitry, protocols (e.g., DDE) or equations can make a claim definite; generic or minimal disclosures can make it indefinite.
guidance: Use case law examples (Aristocrat, Finisar, Katz, Wenger, Dossel, All Voice, Telecordia) to analogize facts. Look for detailed description, links between structure and function, algorithms/protocols, or accepted domain techniques to determine sufficiency.

name: Determining priority: evidence must show conception of the same invention
description: In a priority contest the question is 'which, or whether either, of these applicants is entitled to receive the patent prayed for;' the inquiry is whether the earlier description/conception is 'substantially the same' as that for which a patent is now claimed.
guidance: To award priority, the court examines the evidence produced before the Commissioner to determine whether the earlier conception/description corresponds substantially to the claimed invention. The judge compares the specification/claims with the prior descriptions/drawings to see if they describe the same essential features.

name: Comparative/credibility weighing of conflicting testimony
description: When a witness gives a date contradicted by other circumstances, the court may find the witness erred and give less credence: 'the whole of the testimony shows that this machine was not put in operation until the month of July, 1845, subsequent to the time at which the witness testifies the said improvement was described to him ... [the Commissioner] erred in giving credence to the statement by a witness of a date, which all the circumstances ... clearly shows was the result of error.'
guidance: Evaluate witness credibility against the totality of circumstantial evidence; positive testimony that aligns with circumstances may outweigh inconsistent statements. The court may discount testimony where surrounding facts clearly show an error in claimed dates or recollection.

name: Claim status identifiers and usage
description: Each claim must be presented with a status identifier indicating its status (e.g., (Original), (Currently amended), (Canceled), (Withdrawn), (Previously presented), (New), (Not entered), (Withdrawn-currently amended)). Claims present on the international filing date or rectified pursuant to PCT Rule 91 must have the status identifier (original); claims amended or added under PCT Article 19 or 34 with effect in the U.S. national stage must have (previously presented); claims canceled pursuant to PCT Article 19 or 34 with effect in the U.S. national stage must have (canceled). If the amendment in the U.S. national stage application makes a change in a claim, use (currently amended) for that claim.
guidance: If the status identifiers used are incorrect but the amendment otherwise places the application in condition for allowance, the examiner may enter the non-compliant amendment and correct incorrect status identifiers via an examiner's amendment. The Office will accept certain alternative identifiers (see Acceptable Alternatives list) if the status is accurate and clear. When accepting alternatives, the examiner need not notify applicant or require corrective amendment; the examiner need not state on the record that alternatives were accepted.

name: Drawing amendment submission and identification
description: Any changes to application drawings must comply with 37 CFR 1.84 and be submitted on a replacement sheet (for changes) or a new sheet (for additions). The replacement sheet must be identified in the top margin as 'Replacement Sheet' and the new sheet as 'New Sheet.'
guidance: The replacement drawing sheet must include all figures appearing on the immediate prior version of the sheet, even if only one figure is amended. The figure(s) of the amended drawing(s) must not be labeled 'amended.' A marked-up copy of any amended drawing figure showing the changes may be included; it must be clearly labeled 'Annotated Sheet' and presented in the amendment or remarks section that explains the change. An explanation of changes must be presented in the 'Amendments to the Drawings' or remarks section. If changes are not approved, applicant will be notified in the next Office action and must amend the brief and detailed description sections of the specification to be consistent with drawing changes. The proposed drawing correction practice has been eliminated; do not submit changes in red ink. Replacement drawings without markings (in compliance with 37 CFR 1.84) are required. Drawing submissions without specification or claims amendments after allowance should be forwarded to the Office of Patent Publication.

name: Examiner's amendments: authority and limits
description: 37 CFR 1.121(g) permits the Office to make amendments to the specification, including claims, by examiner's amendments without paragraph/section/claim replacement to expedite prosecution and reduce cycle time. Examiner's amendments may add or delete subject matter by instructions to make changes at precise locations.
guidance: If a non-compliant amendment would otherwise place the application in condition for allowance, the examiner may enter it and provide an examiner's amendment to correct non-compliance (e.g., incorrect status identifier). The examiner may (A) provide a claim listing with proper identifiers in an examiner's amendment, (B) print the claim listing, cross out improper identifiers and write in correct ones as an attachment, or (C) correct improper identifiers by instructions in an examiner's amendment. The examiner's amendment should include why the amendment was non-compliant and indicate how it was corrected. Authorization from applicant or attorney/agent and extensions are not required if changes are non-substantive (formatting/typographical).
