Authorization and appropriate extensions are required if the examiner's amendment is substantive (e.g., cancellation of a claim or scope change); authorization must be given within the time period for reply set forth in the last Office action.

name: Preliminary amendment definition, effect on original disclosure, and publication format
description: A preliminary amendment is one received on or before the mail date of the first Office action (37 CFR 1.115). For applications filed on or after Sept 21, 2004, a preliminary amendment present on the filing date is part of the original disclosure; for earlier filings it is part of original disclosure only if referred to in the first executed oath/declaration.
guidance: A preliminary amendment filed after filing date is not part of original disclosure. If a preliminary amendment is in a format that cannot be included in the patent application publication, OIPE will issue a notice requiring a substitute specification in compliance with 37 CFR 1.121(b)(3) and 1.125. The only usable format for an amendment to the specification (other than claims) for publication is a substitute specification in compliance with those rules. Applicants should submit references to prior applications in an Application Data Sheet (ADS) under 37 CFR 1.76 rather than in a preliminary amendment. Preliminary amendments to claims or abstract compliant with 1.121(c) or 1.121(b)(2) include complete claim listings or replacement abstracts and can be published as submitted. There is no need to file a preliminary amendment to claims on filing; making the claim set part of the originally filed specification may avoid paying an application size fee, as both specification and preliminary amendment are used in counting pages for 37 CFR 1.16(s). A preliminary amendment filed with a national stage entry (35 U.S.C. 371) is not part of the original disclosure because it was not present on the international filing date.

name: Requirement that preliminary amendments comply with 37 CFR 1.121
description: Any preliminary amendment, regardless of filing time, must comply with 37 CFR 1.121 (e.g., include a complete listing of all claims and each section of the amendment must begin on a separate sheet). Preliminary amendments in a transmittal letter will not comply.
guidance: If a preliminary amendment filed after filing date fails to comply, applicant will be notified (e.g., Notice to File Corrected Application Papers) requiring a substitute specification if amendment amends the specification. Failure to file the required substitute specification will be treated as incomplete reply with no new time period for reply.

name: Essentiality assessment via claim-to-specification mapping
description: Determine whether any of the independent claims of the patent read onto normative parts of the 5G Technical Specifications.
guidance: Patents were assessed by mapping independent claims to the normative sections of 5G technical specs; a patent is scored as technically essential when at least one independent claim was found to be essential.

name: Peer review for scoring consistency and accuracy
description: Peer review processes were carried out to ensure consistency of scoring principles and accuracy of claims mapping.
guidance: Peer review helps validate that scoring and claim-to-specification mappings are consistent across reviewers and that essentiality determinations are robust.

name: Identify inventions disclosed to ETSI and evaluate for technical essentiality
description: The team identified inventions as disclosed to ETSI and evaluated them for technical essentiality by mining patents declared to 5G relevant specifications and projects.
guidance: This involves mining the declaration data, extracting the disclosed inventions/families, and assessing claim coverage against the relevant 5G specification elements.

name: Enablement evaluated against claimed subject matter as a whole
description: All questions of enablement under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) are evaluated against the claimed subject matter with the focus of the examination inquiry being whether everything within the scope of the claim is enabled.
guidance: Examiners should determine what each claim recites and what subject matter is encompassed by the claim when the claim is considered as a whole and not analyze the claim elements individually.

name: Examiner must establish reasonable basis before rejection for lack of enablement
description: When basing a rejection on the failure of the applicant’s disclosure to meet the enablement provisions of 35 U.S.C. 112(a), USPTO personnel must establish on the record a reasonable basis for questioning the adequacy of the disclosure to enable a person of ordinary skill in the art to make and use the claimed invention without resorting to undue experimentation.
guidance: Cite precedent (In re Brown; In re Ghiron). Once USPTO personnel have advanced a reasonable basis, it becomes incumbent on the applicant to rebut that challenge and factually demonstrate the disclosure is sufficient (In re Doyle; In re Scarbrough; see MPEP §§ 2164 - 2164.08(c)).

name: Broad functional claims raise enablement concerns
description: When a claim is not limited to any particular structure for performing a recited function and does not invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f), any claim language reciting the ability to perform a function per se would typically be construed broadly to cover any and all embodiments that perform the recited function.
guidance: Because such a claim encompasses all devices/structures that perform the function, examiners must be concerned whether the applicant's disclosure sufficiently enables the full scope of protection sought. Examples: In re Swinehart; AK Steel Corp. v. Sollac; In re Moore. Applicants presenting broad claim language must ensure the claims are fully enabled across their scope.

name: Claims scope must be commensurate with scope of enablement
description: The scope of the claims must be less than or equal to the scope of the enablement provided by the specification.
guidance: Court precedent (Sitrick v. Dreamworks; MagSil Corp. v. Hitachi) illustrates that claiming broader subject matter than the specification enables risks invalidity for lack of enablement; examiners should ensure claim scope does not exceed what the spec enables.

name: Specification need not teach what is well known in the art, but cannot rely on skill in the art to provide novel aspects
description: The specification need not teach what is well known in the art, but applicant cannot rely on the knowledge of one skilled in the art to supply information that is required to enable the novel aspect of the claimed invention when that enabling knowledge is not in fact known in the art.
guidance: Precedent: ALZA Corp., Auto. Techs. Int’l v. BMW, Genentech. Omitting minor details may be acceptable, but omission of any specific starting material or conditions under which a process can be carried out may render undue experimentation necessary.

name: Specification must teach how to make and use full scope without undue experimentation
description: The specification must teach those skilled in the art how to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
guidance: The 'scope of enablement' is that disclosed in the specification plus what would be known to one of ordinary skill without undue experimentation. Multiple Federal Circuit decisions reinforce this standard (e.g., Trs. of Bos. Univ.; Sitrick examples).

name: Rejection for lack of enablement must identify reasons and rely on substantive law
description: A rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) must be made when the specification does not enable the full scope of the claim; USPTO personnel should establish a reasonable basis to question the enablement provided and provide reasons for the uncertainty.
guidance: Examiners should cite MPEP §§ 2164.01(a) - 2164.08(c) (and § 2164.06(c) for computer programming examples) and provide concrete reasons why the specification does not enable the claimed scope.

name: Written description requirement is distinct from enablement
description: 35 U.S.C. 112(a) requires a written description of the invention; this requirement is separate and distinct from the enablement requirement and has the objective of clearly conveying the information that an applicant has invented the subject matter claimed.
guidance: Written description implements the principle that a patent must describe the technology sought to be patented and demonstrates that the patentee was in possession of the invention. See Ariad, Vas-Cath, Univ. of Rochester v. G.D. Searle, Capon v. Eshhar.

name: Written description: specification must show possession of the claimed invention
description: To satisfy the written description requirement, a patent specification must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail that one skilled in the art can reasonably conclude that the inventor had possession of the claimed invention.
guidance: Possession evidence may include description using words, structures, figures, diagrams, formulas, reduction to practice, drawings, or distinguishing identifying characteristics. Originally-filed claims or other portions of the original specification may sometimes provide satisfactory description (In re Koller; In re Gardner).

name: Written description issues arise in multiple procedural contexts
description: Questions about adequacy of written description may arise for original claims, new or amended claims, entitlement to priority dates, or to support claims corresponding to interference counts.
guidance: Examples include LizardTech, Enzo Biochem, Eli Lilly, In re Wright, New Railhead, Tronzo, Fiers, In re Ziegler, Martin v. Mayer, Fields v. Conover. Compliance is a fact-based inquiry resolved case-by-case.

name: Presumption of adequate written description at filing; examiner initial burden to make prima facie case
description: There is a presumption that an adequate written description of the claimed invention is present when the application is filed; the PTO (examiner) has the initial burden, after thorough review, of presenting evidence or reasons why persons skilled in the art would not recognize the disclosure as providing adequate support for the claimed invention.
guidance: To make a prima facie case, identify the claim limitations not adequately supported and explain why the claim is not fully supported by the disclosure. Example: Hyatt v. Dudas where examiner explained lack of adequate description of a combination even though individual elements were listed.

name: New or amended claims must be supported by original disclosure; new matter prohibited
description: The proscription against the introduction of new matter (35 U.S.C. 132 and 251) prevents an applicant from adding information beyond the originally filed subject matter; new or amended claims which introduce elements or limitations not supported by the as-filed disclosure violate the written description requirement.
guidance: If originally-filed claims disclose material not found elsewhere in the spec, applicant may amend the spec to include the claimed subject matter (In re Benno). Corrections of obvious errors may be permissible if the ordinary artisan would recognize the error and correction (In re Oda). Guidance on sequencing corrections and reliance on deposits (Cubist Pharm.) and 37 CFR 1.804 requirements apply.

name: Omission of an essential or critical feature undermines written description
description: Omission of a limitation can indicate the inventor lacked possession of a broader invention; a claim that omits matter described as an essential or critical feature in the specification does not comply with the written description requirement.
guidance: Examples: PIN/NIP, Gentry Gallery, Johnson Worldwide Assoc. v. Zebco, Tronzo. Such omissions may also give rise to enablement or 112(b) rejections. Examiner should consider statements in the spec that indicate a particular understanding was 'the only possible location' or 'outside the stated purpose.'

name: Methodology for examiners: read/analyze spec and identify deficiencies specifically
description: Office personnel should read and analyze the specification for compliance, and, because of the presumption of adequacy, the examiner must present evidence or reasons why the disclosure would not be recognized as adequate by a person skilled in the art.
guidance: The examiner must identify claim limitations lacking support and explain why; for newly added/amended claims, applicant should be required to point to original-support or amend. MPEP §§ 2163.04, 2163.06 and 714.02 provide further procedural guidance (e.g., a simple statement pointing out lack of support for an amendment may be sufficient when support is not apparent).

name: Support for amendments and added claims
description: Claims or the addition of a new claim must be supported by the description of the invention in the application as filed.
guidance: An amendment to the specification (e.g., a change in the definition of a term used both in the specification and claim) may indirectly affect a claim even though no actual amendment is made to the claim. See In re Wright, 866 F.2d 422, 9 USPQ2d 1649 (Fed. Cir. 1989).

name: Reliance on filing date of parent application (35 U.S.C. 120)
description: Claims in a U.S. application are entitled to the benefit of the filing date of an earlier filed U.S. application only if the subject matter of the claim is disclosed in the manner provided by 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph) in the earlier application.
guidance: Cites: Tronzo v. Biomet, Inc., 156 F.3d 1154; In re Scheiber, 587 F.2d 59. Examiner must determine whether the earlier application provides the written description support required for entitlement to parent filing date.

name: Reliance on foreign or provisional priority (35 U.S.C. 119)
description: Claims are entitled to the benefit of a foreign priority date or provisional filing date only if the corresponding earlier application supports the claims in the manner required by 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph).
guidance: Cites: In re Ziegler; Kawai v. Metlesics; In re Gosteli. The documentation and disclosure in the earlier-filed foreign or provisional application must provide the written description support for the claimed subject matter.

name: Support for claims corresponding to an interference count
description: In an interference, the claim corresponding to a count must be supported by the specification in the manner provided by 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph).
guidance: A broad generic disclosure to a class of compounds is not sufficient written description for a specific compound within the class (Fields v. Conover). When seeking benefit of an earlier U.S. application in an interference, the earlier application must meet 35 U.S.C. 112(a) for the subject matter of the count (Hyatt v. Boone).

name: Original claim may lack adequate written description
description: An original claim may lack written description support when (1) it defines the invention in functional language specifying a desired result but the disclosure fails to sufficiently identify how the function is performed or the result is achieved, or (2) a broad genus claim is presented but the disclosure only describes a narrow species with no evidence that the genus is contemplated.
guidance: Written description is not necessarily met even when claim language appears verbatim in the specification; mere indistinct words in a specification or claim do not satisfy the requirement. See Ariad Pharm. v. Eli Lilly; Enzo Biochem v. Gen‑Probe.

name: Indefiniteness of means‑/step‑plus‑function limitations (35 U.S.C. 112(f))
description: A means‑(or step‑)plus‑function limitation shall be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents. If the specification fails to disclose sufficient corresponding structure/materials/acts to perform the claimed function, the limitation is indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre‑AIA 112, second paragraph).
guidance: Such a limitation also may lack adequate written description under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) because an indefinite functional limitation could cover all ways of performing a function, indicating lack of possession. Authority: In re Donaldson Co.

name: Statement of rejection requirements (what examiner must include)
description: When rejecting a claim for lack of written description, the examiner must set forth express findings of fact supporting the conclusion (identify claim limitations at issue and establish a prima facie case with reasons).
guidance: Findings should: (A) Identify the claim limitation(s) at issue; and (B) Establish a prima facie case by providing reasons why one skilled in the art at the time of filing would not have recognized that the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention given the disclosure. A general allegation of unpredictability is insufficient. A concise statement identifying the unsupported limitation can sometimes be sufficient. See MPEP § 2163 and Hyatt v. Dudas.

name: Suggesting claim/specification amendments (examiner practice)
description: When appropriate, the examiner should suggest amendments to claims which can be supported by the application's written description, mindful of prohibition against adding new matter.
guidance: Suggested amendments should avoid introducing new matter into claims or description. See Rasmussen.

name: Changes to claim scope after filing require original support
description: Failure to meet written description commonly arises when claims are changed after filing to broaden or narrow breadth, alter a numerical range, or use terminology not synonymous with originally disclosed terminology; each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure to comply and to be entitled to earlier priority/filing date.
guidance: See MPEP § 2163 for detailed examination guidelines. This applies also for entitlement under 35 U.S.C. 119, 120, or 365(c).

name: Broadening claims by omission of a limitation
description: Omitting a limitation can raise whether the inventor had possession of a broader, more generic invention; if the omitted element was described as essential or critical to the invention, omission will fail the written description requirement.
guidance: Examples/cases: Gentry Gallery v. Berkline (omission of location of control means); Tronzo v. Biomet (parent disclosed conical cup, later generic cup claim not entitled to parent date); In re Wilder. A claim that omits matter disclosed as essential may also be subject to rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (not enabling) or 112(b) (indefinite). See related cases and MPEP § 2172.01.

name: Support for a genus via representative species (addition of generic claim)
description: A claimed genus may be supported by sufficient description of a representative number of species; where the genus exhibits substantial variation, a sufficient variety of species must be described to reflect that variation. Disclosure of only one species supports a genus only if it indicates the patentee invented species sufficient to constitute the genus.
guidance: If evidence indicates ordinary artisans could not predict operability of species other than the one disclosed, genus is not supported (AbbVie v. Janssen; In re Curtis). In some situations a single species may suffice (In re Rasmussen; In re Herschler; In re Smythe). Case‑by‑case analysis; see cited authorities.

name: Changing numerical range limitations
description: When changing numerical ranges, the analysis must consider which ranges one skilled in the art would consider inherently supported by the original disclosure; open‑ended changes may extend beyond the disclosed ranges and fail written description.
guidance: Example: original spec disclosed 25%–60% and examples of 36% and 50%; a claim to ‘at least 35%’ (no upper bound) was not supported, whereas ‘between 35% and 60%’ was supported. See In re Wertheim; compare Union Oil v. Atl. Richfield and Purdue Pharma v. Faulding for additional contexts.

name: Reviewability of new matter objections and rejections
description: A rejection of claims for new matter is reviewable by the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB); an objection and requirement to delete new matter is subject to supervisory review by petition under 37 CFR 1.181.
guidance: If both claims and specification contain new matter and there has been both a rejection and an objection, the issue is appealable and should not be decided by petition.

name: Claimed subject matter disclosed only in claims (antecedent/support issues)
description: Claims as filed are part of the disclosure; if the original specification lacks the remainder support for originally filed claim material, the applicant may amend the specification to include the claimed subject matter (use form paragraph 7.44 where originally claimed subject matter lacks proper antecedent basis).
guidance: See In re Benno. Examiner should consider that claims form part of the original disclosure and allow specification amendment to provide necessary support where appropriate.

name: Claim construction: ordinary and customary meaning; specification as guide
description: Patent claims are interpreted as they would be understood by 'one of ordinary skill in the art' — words are generally given their ordinary and customary meaning; the specification is 'the single best guide' to the meaning of a disputed claim term; a patentee may be his own lexicographer if a special definition is clearly stated in the specification or file history.
guidance: Courts first look at the words of the claims and the specification; review the specification to determine whether the inventor used terms inconsistently with ordinary meaning. If the intrinsic evidence resolves the meaning, it is improper to rely on extrinsic evidence to change that meaning.

name: Primacy of intrinsic evidence over extrinsic evidence
description: Intrinsic evidence (claims, specification, prosecution history) is 'the most significant source of the legally operative meaning of disputed claim language' and should be consulted first.
guidance: Extrinsic evidence (expert testimony, dictionaries, treatises, scientific articles) may be considered to help understand the technology but 'may not be used to vary or contradict claim language.' If intrinsic record is sufficient, extrinsic evidence should be excluded as contrary to precedent (citing Vitronics and Markman).

name: Prosecution history estoppel and Festo standards
description: Prosecution history is relevant to literal meaning and to the scope of equivalents; amendments made during prosecution may create a rebuttable presumption that narrower scope was surrendered (Festo).
guidance: A narrowing amendment triggers a presumption of surrender unless patentee shows at the time of amendment one skilled in the art could not reasonably have drafted a claim to encompass the equivalent. An amendment does not surrender an equivalent if (1) the equivalent was unforeseeable at application time; (2) the rationale for amendment is only tangential to the equivalent; or (3) other reasons suggest the patentee could not reasonably have been expected to describe the equivalent. The patentee bears the burden to rebut the presumption.

name: Use of an early combined Markman/Festo hearing with summary judgment
description: Where feasible, combine claim construction and equivalents (Markman/Festo) in a single early hearing together with summary judgment motions on infringement ('summary judgment trial') before extensive fact discovery.
guidance: Rationale: claim scope and infringement often decide the case and resolving them early can avoid millions in irrelevant discovery costs (damages, willfulness, broad invalidity searches). The combined hearing should permit targeted discovery limited to matters relevant to claim construction and infringement and may include live testimony, opening/closing, cross-examination, and dispositive summary judgment rulings.

name: Scope of document production for an early Markman/summary judgment phase
description: Document production for the initial round should be targeted and not open-ended, focusing on materials relevant to claim construction and infringement.
guidance: Suggested documents the patentee should produce: (1) all documents relating to patent prosecution from initial disclosure through issuance; (2) documents relating to inventors' conception and reduction to practice; (3) documents in the relevant technology area that use any claim term at issue; (4) documents discussing the patent or application (including marking); (5) documents adequate to show operation or design of any product the patentee contends is covered. Suggested documents the accused infringer should produce: (1) documents adequate to show operation or design of accused products; (2) documents reflecting accused infringer's knowledge of the patent-in-suit; (3) documents in the relevant technology area using any disputed claim term.

name: Depositions appropriate for the early phase
description: Limit depositions in the initial phase to fact witnesses whose testimony is relevant to claim construction and infringement rather than broad roving fact discovery.
guidance: Appropriate depositions include a Rule 30(b)(6) witness to discuss operation of accused products, inventor depositions, possibly the prosecuting attorney (where relevant), fact witnesses who produced responsive documents, and expert witness depositions. Avoid numerous marginal witnesses who have not read the patent and whose testimony invites 'legal conclusion' objections.

name: Pre-hearing procedures: simultaneous exchange, meet-and-confer, expert reports, and timetable
description: Use a structured pre-hearing process to narrow claim term disputes and prepare for the combined hearing: simultaneous exchange of proposed claim term definitions (without prejudice), meet-and-confer to narrow issues, exchange of briefs and expert reports, rebuttals, expert depositions, then the hearing.
guidance: Recommendations include: (1) exchange lists of claim terms with proposed definitions (inadmissible/without prejudice); (2) meet and confer and memorialize agreements; (3) exchange claim construction briefs and serve expert reports under Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a)(2) addressing claim construction and infringement; (4) serve rebuttal briefs and rebuttal expert reports; (5) take expert depositions; (6) hold Markman hearing combined with summary judgment motions. This simultaneous-exchange approach encourages narrowing and avoids tactical prejudice from interim concessions.

name: Markman/Festo hearing format and effect ('summary judgment trial')
description: A combined hearing can be conducted with features of a trial (opening, closing, live testimony, cross-examination) and may be dispositive via summary judgment, though technically the court's role is to construe claims as a matter of law.
guidance: While a Markman decision is a legal determination, in practice judges hearing live testimony may make credibility determinations and weight evidence — the proceeding may therefore have trial-like attributes. If the court grants summary judgment of non-infringement the case can end; if not, remaining issues (willfulness, damages, validity) proceed to discovery and jury trial as appropriate.

name: Evidentiary standards and expert evidence in claim construction hearings
description: Federal Rules of Evidence govern court proceedings generally, but courts often admit extrinsic evidence (expert testimony, tutorials, treatises) to educate the court; Daubert gatekeeping principles apply to expert testimony.
guidance: Daubert factors (testability, peer review, known error rates, general acceptance) guide admissibility and reliability of expert testimony; Kumho Tire extends Daubert to technical expertise. Courts frequently admit expert testimony as background to assist interpretation of claim language, and judges may consult treatises/dictionaries on their own. Parties should be prepared to raise evidentiary objections and to move to strike exhibits or seek in limine rulings where appropriate.

name: Counsel strategy and risks in early claim construction
description: Parties must clearly articulate their proposed claim scope early; patentees advocating broad constructions risk invalidity if the construction reads on prior art, while accused infringers benefit from early resolution to focus validity/design-around efforts.
guidance: Early construction reduces the problem of 'moving' claim constructions that change as new prior art or arguments appear. The proposal suggests that the patent owner bears the risk of pushing an expansive construction that later renders the patent invalid; defendants gain efficiency by knowing the claim scope early and concentrating subsequent discovery/trial strategy accordingly.

name: General amendment permission and timing
description: Once a filing date is established, the applicant can amend the application (specification, description, claims, drawings) before the patent is issued (subsection 38.2(1)). Amendments are made to the application on the day submitted.
guidance: Once a notice of allowance or conditional notice is issued, no amendments are permitted except obvious error under section 100, unless the allowance/conditional allowance is withdrawn or set aside or the amendments are those referred to in a conditional notice. Amendments may be submitted voluntarily or in response to requisitions; must comply with Patent Rules for written communications; amendments by unauthorized representatives will be placed on file but not entered into the visible application record.

name: Claim amendment deemed not included for final fee determination (eligibility criteria)
description: Under subsection 87(1.2), in some circumstances a claim amendment may be deemed not included for final fee determination.
guidance: Eligibility criteria: (1) date of the amendment intended to be 'deemed not included' must be on or after January 1, 2025; (2) applicant must file a statement confirming the error and must amend the application to remove the amendment made in error without undue delay after becoming aware of the error and before the examiner begins examination of the amended application; and (3) the Commissioner must be satisfied the circumstances justify that the claims not be included.

name: Statement of purpose and page replacement instructions on amendment cover letter
description: Each amendment must be submitted with a cover letter that includes a statement of purpose and instructions for entering the amendment (suitable to the amendment, may be simple or detailed with a blackline).
guidance: Amendments are performed by submission of new pages to replace those being modified. Covering page content is considered in context; instructions should clearly indicate how replacement should be made. Page numbering rules: pages of specification must be numbered consecutively (letters acceptable, e.g., 1,2,3,3A,3B,4). Deleted pages should be handled by renumbering or inserting a numbered blank page marked with a diagonal stroke or 'Z'. Claims must be numbered consecutively in Arabic numerals beginning with 1. If replacement instructions are unclear the Office may remove replacement pages.

name: Purpose of examination — thorough analysis and steps
description: The purpose of examination is to perform a thorough analysis of the patent application at each stage to determine whether it complies with the Patent Act and Patent Rules; as part of this analysis the examiner performs purposive construction of the claims and considers a search of the prior art.
guidance: If compliant, examiner will approve the application for allowance (notice of allowance). If not compliant, defects may be communicated via an examiner's report, examiner-initiated interview, or a conditional notice of allowance. An application may be examined prior to being laid open, but an examiner will not approve allowance or issue a conditional notice until it has been laid open.

name: Examination of claims by purposive construction
description: During examination the Commissioner’s identification of the actual invention must be grounded in a purposive construction of the patent claims consistent with Supreme Court jurisprudence.
guidance: Purposive construction requires consideration of what a person skilled in the art would, as of the date of publication of the patent application and on the basis of the particular words/phrases used in the claim, have understood the applicant to have intended as the scope of protection. The application of purposive construction must take into account the role of the examiner and the purpose and context of examination. Note: under subsections 15(3.2) and 155.5(4) text matter not in English or French in certain sequence listing or PCT fields should not be taken into account for interpreting scope of protection except where in free text or non-language dependent fields.

name: Examination of the claims using purposive construction
description: Use of purposive construction for claim interpretation, steps of purposive construction and considerations (fair, balanced informed approach; identify person skilled in the art; common general knowledge; identify problem/solution; determine elements solving problem).

name: Functional limitations and applicant as lexicographer
description: Guidance on functional claim limitations, applicants defining terms (lexicography), and description by reference to the claims or statements expanding scope.

name: Claims — basic requirements
description: Fundamental formal and substantive requirements for claims, including clarity, antecedents, ambiguity, negative limitations, completeness, support and dependence/formalities for dependent claims.

name: Principles of construction and clarity of claims
description: Rules for claim construction including antecedents, addressing ambiguities, and treatment of negative limitations.

name: Support and scope of claims in relation to description
description: Requirement that claims be supported by the description and drawings, and issues with ranges not specifically described.

name: Specific claim types (product, product-by-process, means, process/method/use, Markush, selection patents)
description: Guidance and requirements for various claim types and their particular formal/substantive considerations (including jurisprudence references).

name: Claim date and priority-based claim dating
description: Rules to determine claim date based on multiple previously filed applications and consequences for continuations/continuation-in-part matters.

name: Computer-Implemented Inventions — subject-matter and examination
description: Scope, subject-matter categories (art/process/machine/manufacture/composition), guidance on examining computer claims, adapting a computer to solve a problem, patentability and programming, examples, utility and sufficiency (written description, source code/pseudocode, common general knowledge), novelty and ingenuity considerations, and claim types specific to computers (method, computer claims, system claims, software product claims, means statements).

name: Biotechnology and Medicinal Inventions — disclosure and claim practice
description: Scope and special considerations for living matter, higher/lower life forms, organs/tissues, processes to produce life forms, bioinformatics, medical methods/uses, kits and packages, diagnostic methods (identifying problem, determining solution, purposive construction), sufficiency of description, nucleic acids/proteins (defining by structure/functional limitation/terminology), sequence listings, deposits of biological materials and Budapest Treaty practice.

name: Disclaimer practice
description: Filing a disclaimer, roles of the Patent Office and the Courts, and effect of a disclaimer on scope and enforcement of claims.

name: Claims must define the matter for which protection is sought
description: Article 84 EPC requires that claims shall define the matter for which protection is sought.
guidance: The claim wording should enable the scope of protection conferred by the patent to be determined; purpose is legal certainty so the public knows what is covered.

name: Claims must be clear
description: Claims shall be clear (the claim wording cannot be obscure).
guidance: Clarity is judged with regard to legal certainty and should be apparent to the person skilled in the art from the claim wording alone; avoid context-dependent or ambiguous expressions.

name: Define protection in terms of technical features
description: Claims must define the matter for which protection is sought in terms of the technical features of the invention.
guidance: Claim scope should be expressed by concrete technical features rather than purely non-technical or abstract language.

name: Clarity must be apparent from the claim wording alone to the skilled person
description: Clarity must be apparent to the person skilled in the art from the wording of the claim alone.
guidance: Do not rely on the description to cure an unclear claim; the skilled person should be able to understand claim meaning without resorting to other parts of the file.

name: Avoid relative or context-dependent terms (e.g., 'thin', 'wide', 'strong')
description: Relative or similar terms such as 'thin', 'wide' or 'strong' constitute potentially unclear elements due to context-dependent meanings.
guidance: If such terms are used, provide objective technical parameters or definitional context in the claim or ensure they are made clear in a way that the skilled person can interpret them reliably.

name: Avoid 'result-to-be-achieved' language without structure
description: Result-to-be-achieved language without structure is a common objection under Article 84.
guidance: Claims should not merely state a desired result; include structural or procedural elements that define how the result is achieved.

name: Avoid vague references and undefined terms
description: Vague references and undefined terms in claims give rise to clarity objections.
guidance: Define terms, use established technical terminology, or include measurable/qualitative limits so that the skilled person can apply the claim.

name: Ensure consistency between claims and description/drawings
description: Inconsistencies between claims and description/drawings could render the scope of claims unclear.
guidance: Adapt the description carefully when claims are amended; maintain internal consistency across claims, description and drawings to meet support and clarity requirements.

name: Respect the two-part form (Rule 43(1))
description: The two-part form must be respected: a portion indicating what is known from the prior art plus a characterising portion.
guidance: Claims in the two-part form should clearly separate the prior-art portion and the features that characterise the invention; failure to do so is a recognized clarity/formal objection.

name: Article 84 not a ground for opposition except when amendment introduces non‑compliance
description: Lack of compliance with Article 84 EPC may not be used as a ground of opposition, but compliance may be examined when, and to the extent that, an amendment introduces non‑compliance with Article 84 EPC.
guidance: During opposition proceedings Article 84 is generally not assessable unless an amendment creates a lack of clarity/support; practitioners should be aware of this timing when amending claims.

name: Claims to non-naturally-occurring nucleic acids may be eligible
description: Claims clearly limited to non-naturally-occurring nucleic acids, such as a cDNA or a nucleic acid in which the order of the naturally-occurring nucleotides has been altered (e.g., a man-made variant sequence), remain eligible.
guidance: The Supreme Court held that 'cDNA is not a 'product of nature' and is patent eligible under § 101.' Use this distinction when assessing composition claims.

name: Method and other claims involving naturally occurring nucleic acids require careful § 101 analysis
description: Other claims, including method claims, that involve naturally occurring nucleic acids may give rise to eligibility issues.
guidance: Such claims should be examined under the existing guidance in MPEP 2106, Patent Subject Matter Eligibility, to determine whether they present eligibility problems under § 101.

name: Supreme Court's factual holding on 'product of nature' for isolated DNA
description: In Myriad, the Supreme Court held that certain claims to isolated DNA are not patent-eligible, because they read on isolated naturally-occurring DNA that is a 'product of nature.'
guidance: Use the Court's analysis distinguishing natural products from man-made compositions when determining eligibility; claims that 'read on' a product of nature should be treated as ineligible.

name: Ways to overcome provisional 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection (A–E)
description: The provisional 103 rejection based on a copending earlier-filed application can be overcome by specific actions.
guidance: (A) Argue patentability over the earlier-filed application. (B) Combine the subject matter of the copending applications into a single application claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 and abandon the copending applications — note: claims in the later application relying on prior applications may not get 120 benefit unless each claim is supported by the earlier disclosure in compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph. (C) File an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 showing derivation (that the unclaimed invention was derived from the inventor of the other application) so it is not "invention by another." (D) File an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 showing a date of invention prior to the effective U.S. filing date of the copending application. (E) For applications pending on/after Dec. 10, 2004, show that (1) the prior art and the claimed invention were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person when the invention was made, or (2) the subject matter is disqualified under the CREATE Act amendment to 35 U.S.C. 103(c) (i.e., joint research agreement disqualification). Additionally, where the applications claim the same patentable invention, a terminal disclaimer and an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.130 may be used to overcome a 103 rejection in a common ownership situation if the earlier application has been published or matured into a patent.

name: 35 U.S.C. 103(c) prior-art disqualification for common ownership or joint research agreement
description: Subject matter developed by another person that qualifies as prior art only under subsections (e), (f), or (g) of 35 U.S.C. 102 shall not preclude patentability under 35 U.S.C. 103 where the subject matter and the claimed invention were, at the time the claimed invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.
guidance: For purposes of 103(c), subject matter and a claimed invention shall be deemed owned by the same person if: (A) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement that was in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; (B) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (C) the patent application discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement. The term "joint research agreement" means a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement between two or more persons/entities for experimental, developmental, or research work in the field. Important limits: 103(c) applies only to obviousness rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103 and does not affect anticipation under 35 U.S.C. 102 or double patenting rejections.

name: Requirements for claiming 35 U.S.C. 120 benefit in continuing applications
description: An application claiming the benefit of a prior filed copending national or international application under 35 U.S.C. 120 must name as an inventor at least one inventor named in the prior filed application, and the prior filed application must disclose the named inventor’s invention claimed in at least one claim of the later filed application in the manner provided by the first paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112.
guidance: So long as the applications have at least one inventor in common and the other requirements are met, the Office will permit a claim for 35 U.S.C. 120 benefit without additional submissions regarding inventorship differences. The examiner must examine the earlier filed application to determine common inventorship and that 120 and 37 CFR 1.78 requirements are met; the claim for 120 benefit may be permitted without full examination of the earlier application’s disclosure/support unless intervening references make examination necessary.

name: Definition and evidentiary elements of a joint research agreement for 103(c)
description: For 35 U.S.C. 103(c) purposes, a 'joint research agreement' means a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement entered into by two or more persons or entities for the performance of experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention.
guidance: To satisfy 103(c) via a joint research agreement, (1) the claimed invention must be made by or on behalf of parties to the agreement that was in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; (2) the invention must result from activities undertaken within the scope of the agreement; and (3) the patent application must disclose or be amended to disclose the names of the parties to the agreement. Example scenarios illustrate when joint-research disqualification prevents a provisional 103 rejection (e.g., two assignees I and J with compliant joint research agreement).

name: Practice regarding double patenting rejections and terminal disclaimers in commonly owned applications
description: In appropriate circumstances, double patenting rejections may be used in commonly owned applications of different inventive entities; such rejections can be overcome by filing terminal disclaimers.
guidance: The Director has reinstituted this practice in appropriate circumstances to prevent extensions of patent protection while permitting legitimate benefits. The use of terminal disclaimers and affidavits (e.g., under 37 CFR 1.130, 1.321) are described as means to obviate double patenting rejections when requirements are met. Examiners should consult the Office of Patent Legal Administration (via Technology Center Special Program Examiner) when reissue prosecution may implicate recapture issues for claims amended/cancelled to overcome 103 rejections based on 102(e) art not excluded under 103(c).

name: Meaning of Every Term Should Be Apparent (New Terminology)
description: The meaning of every term used in a claim should be apparent from the prior art or from the specification and drawings at the time the application is filed; claim language may not be 'ambiguous, vague, incoherent, opaque, or otherwise unclear.'
guidance: Applicants may use new terms but must make clear and precise the terms used to define the invention so the metes and bounds can be ascertained. During examination give claims the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification. If the specification states a term's meaning, use that meaning in examination. See cases (Packard; In re Morris; In re Zletz).

name: Balance Requirement for Clarity with Limitations of Language and Science
description: The requirement for clarity and precision must be balanced with the limitations of language and the science; the statute demands no more than the language permits in context.
guidance: New or evolving technologies may justify new terms. If claims, read in light of the specification, reasonably apprise skilled artisans of utilization and scope, and are as precise as the subject matter permits, no more is required. If language is less precise than the subject matter permits, the examiner should provide reasons for indefiniteness and suggest alternative claim language.

name: Use of Technical Dictionaries/Recognized Standards for Meaning
description: It is appropriate to consult technical dictionaries to ascertain the accepted meaning of a term in the art where the meaning is unclear.
guidance: Compare claim term meanings to technical dictionaries and recognized standards as guidance; see In re Barr and MPEP § 2111.01.

name: Relative Terminology: Terms of Degree
description: Terms of degree (relative terminology) do not automatically render a claim indefinite; acceptability depends on whether one of ordinary skill in the art would understand what is claimed in light of the specification.
guidance: If the specification provides a standard for measuring the degree (examples, figures, guidelines), the claim is likely definite. If not, determine whether POSITA could nonetheless ascertain the scope (e.g., via examples or declarations). Applicants may overcome an indefiniteness rejection with evidence (e.g., 37 CFR 1.132 declarations). Case examples: Interval Licensing v. AOL; Hearing Components v. Shure; Enzo Biochem; Seattle Box.

name: Approximations — 'About' (Contextual Determination)
description: The range encompassed by the term 'about' must be determined from context in the specification and claims; 'about' can be definite if the context allows clear infringement assessment.
guidance: Examples: W.L. Gore (stretch rate 'exceeding about 10% per second' definite because infringement assessable), Amgen (claims reciting 'at least about' invalid where nothing in spec/prosecution/prior art indicated the range). Consider related facts and prior art when deciding definiteness.

name: Approximations — Use of 'Type' (e.g., 'X-type')
description: Adding the word 'type' to an otherwise definite expression can extend scope and render it indefinite when it is unclear what 'type' is intended to convey.
guidance: Examples: Ex parte Copenhaver; Ex parte Attig ('ZSM-5-type' zeolites indefinite where dependent claims' zeolites were not within the genus). If 'type' is used, ensure the scope is made clear in the specification or claims.

name: Numerical Ranges and Amounts — General
description: Recitation of specific numerical ranges in a claim generally does not raise a definiteness issue.
guidance: Nevertheless, analyze the context and related claim language for clarity issues (e.g., overlapping ranges, inconsistent dependent claims).

name: Numerical Ranges — Narrow and Broader Ranges in the Same Claim
description: A single claim that includes both a broad range and a narrower (preferred) range may be indefinite when it is unclear whether the narrower range is intended as a limitation, leading to confusion over the intended scope.
guidance: Prefer placing narrower ranges in dependent claims or separate independent claims. If both appear in a single claim and the metes and bounds are unclear, reject under 35 U.S.C. 112(b). Examples of problematic language: 'temperature between 45 and 78°C, preferably between 50 and 60°C'; 'a predetermined quantity, for example, the maximum capacity.'

name: Numerical Ranges — Open-Ended Numerical Ranges
description: Open-ended numerical ranges (e.g., 'at least 20%') require careful analysis for definiteness in context, especially when dependent claims or compositions create apparent inconsistencies.
guidance: Watch for dependent claim percentages that add up to 100% seeming to exclude the 'at least' component. Cases: In re Kroekel (theoretical >100% not per se indefinite); In re Kirsch (maximum without minimum not necessarily indefinite).

name: Exemplary Claim Language ('for example', 'such as')
description: Description of examples or preferences belongs in the specification rather than the claims; if stated in claims, examples and preferences may lead to confusion over intended scope.
guidance: The mere use of 'such as' or 'for example' does not per se render a claim indefinite, but the examiner should analyze whether the metes and bounds are clearly set forth. Several fact-specific examples have been held indefinite (listed A–E in MPEP §2173.05(d)). Use caution and cite MPEP §2173.02 for context.

name: A Claim Term with No Antecedent Basis Is Not Necessarily Indefinite
description: The absence of an explicit antecedent basis in the specification for a term or phrase used in the claim does not automatically render it indefinite.
guidance: Applicants have latitude in terminology choices so long as the terms and phrases define the invention with reasonable clarity and precision; evaluate whether POSITA can reasonably ascertain the scope.

name: Preamble/Body Differences Do Not Per Se Render a Claim Indefinite
description: A claim is not per se indefinite if the body recites additional elements which do not appear in the preamble; consider the totality of claim limitations to determine whether the claim apprises POSITA of its scope.
guidance: Evaluate all limitations and their interactions. Example: In re Larsen — court reversed an examiner rejection where the claim in its entirety apprised POSITA of scope.

name: Timing for Decision on Request Filed under 35 U.S.C. 302
description: Within three months following the filing of a request for reexamination under section 302, the Director (or examiner under delegation) will determine whether a substantial new question of patentability affecting any claim is raised (35 U.S.C. 303(a); 37 CFR 1.515(a)).
guidance: If the 3-month period ends on a weekend or federal holiday in D.C., the determination must be mailed by the preceding business day. Determination may be made at any time during the patent's enforceability period.

name: Determination Basis — Claims in Effect and Exclusions from Consideration
description: The examiner's determination whether to order reexamination is based on the claims in effect at the time of the determination; certain submitted statements or amendments will not be considered when making the determination.
guidance: A statement and accompanying information submitted pursuant to § 1.501(a)(2) will not be considered when deciding the request. Amendments (1) presented with the request by the patent owner, (2) filed in a pending reexamination where certificate not issued, or (3) submitted in a reissue application on which no reissue patent has issued, will not be considered when deciding requests. The order for reexamination should discuss whether a substantial new question is raised but SHOULD NOT reject claims; any rejection is made in the first Office action on patentability after the patent owner statement/reply period.

name: Claim Construction Standard for Reexamination Determinations
description: In making the determination of whether to order reexamination (and during examination), the Office will determine the proper meaning of patent claims by giving the claims their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification (In re Yamamoto), except for expired patents where Phillips construction applies.
guidance: For expired patents in reexamination, claim construction follows Phillips v. AWH Corp. (ordinary and customary meaning as understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention). Statements submitted under 35 U.S.C. 301(a)(2) are limited to determining proper meaning only in proceedings ordered under 35 U.S.C. 304; they are not considered for ordering.

name: Scope Limitation to Requested Claims and Office Discretion
description: It is only necessary to establish a substantial new question of patentability as to one claim to grant reexamination, and the Office's review will generally be limited to the claims for which reexamination was requested.
guidance: If the requester wanted all claims reexamined, they had the opportunity to include them in the request. The Office may, however, choose to reexamine claims not requested at its discretion or may initiate reexamination on non-requested claims under 35 U.S.C. 303(a). Case law (e.g., Sony Computer Entertainment America Inc. v. Dudas) confirms that reexamination can be limited to requested claims.

name: Handling of Second or Subsequent Requests During Pending Reexamination
description: When a second or subsequent request for ex parte reexamination is filed while a first is pending, whether reexamination is ordered depends on whether the prior art cited raises a 'different' substantial new question of patentability for the claims in effect at the time of determination.
guidance: If the second request cites art that raises the same substantial new question as the pending reexamination, the second request should be denied. If it raises a different substantial new question for some claims but not others, grant in part. The later requester must independently provide a different substantial new question with respect to the claims in effect at the time. The second/subsequent request may include information directed to proposed new/amended claims in the pending reexamination, to permit examination of the entire patent package when appropriate. If a second/subsequent request appears filed for harassment and a petitioner shows this (e.g., by petition under 37 CFR 1.182), prosecution on the second/subsequent reexamination may be suspended.

name: AAPA can be used as evidence of the skilled artisan's general knowledge (limited purposes)
description: Although AAPA cannot be the § 311(b) basis of a ground, admissions in the specification of the challenged patent may be relied upon in IPR proceedings as evidence of what a person of ordinary skill in the art (POSA) would have known.
guidance: Permissible uses include furnishing a motivation to combine references, supplying a missing claim limitation, and establishing background knowledge. The court cites Koninklijke Philips, PharmaStem, Randal Manufacturing, McCoy, and other precedent describing these limited evidentiary uses. Such evidence is not a § 311(b) document-basis but may support an obviousness determination.

name: Initial petition must identify supporting evidence with particularity (timeliness and specificity requirement)
description: The initial IPR petition must identify with particularity the evidence that supports the grounds for the challenge to each claim; petitioners must adhere to this requirement.
guidance: The court quotes Intelligent Bio‑Sys.: 'It is of the utmost importance that petitioners in IPR proceedings adhere to the requirement that the initial petition identify with particularity the evidence...' New theories or motivations to combine raised for the first time on reply may be deemed untimely and disregarded (see Henny Penny; Apple’s hysteresis theory was untimely).

name: Mental process as an abstract idea
description: A claimed map/listing or other steps that can be performed mentally (e.g., with pen and paper) may qualify as a 'mental process' abstract idea.
guidance: Examiners should look to the specification to determine whether claimed steps are performable mentally (cases: CyberSource, Flook, University of Florida Research Foundation v. GE, Symantec). If the specification describes the claimed analysis/manipulation of data as being performed mentally or with pen and paper, the step may be an abstract mental process. Example anti-pattern: claiming high-level data-parsing or screening steps that humans could perform without a computer.

name: Claim requiring a computer may still recite a mental process
description: A claim that recites performance on a computer can nevertheless recite a mental process (abstract idea) if the underlying concept is one that humans can perform mentally.
guidance: When evaluating such claims, examiners should consider the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) in light of the specification to determine whether the invention is described as a concept performed in the human mind and applicant merely claims it: (1) on a generic computer, (2) in a computer environment, or (3) using a computer as a tool. If so, the claim is considered to recite a mental process. Case law: Benson, Mortgage Grader, Voter Verified, Versata.

name: Tentative abstract ideas procedure
description: When a limitation appears abstract but does not fall within the enumerated groupings (mathematical concepts, methods of organizing human activity, mental processes), it may be treated as a 'tentative abstract idea.'
guidance: Evaluate the claim under the subject matter eligibility framework: - If the claim as a whole integrates the tentative abstract idea into a practical application → not directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: NO) → eligible at Pathway B. - If not integrated → directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: YES) → requires Step 2B analysis: if the claim provides an inventive concept (Step 2B: YES) → eligible at Pathway C. - If no inventive concept (Step 2B: NO) → bring application to TC director; a Step 2B rejection of a claim reciting a tentative abstract idea must be approved by the TC director (approval indicated in file and Office action uses form paragraph 7.05.017 and TC Director’s signature). The TC Director will notify Patents Management for public notice (e.g., USPTO website). Interviews with the examiner may help; TC Director interview is not required for examiner to withdraw or maintain a rejection; examiner need not obtain approval to withdraw/maintain such a §101 rejection.

name: Laws of nature and natural phenomena (general rule)
description: Laws of nature and natural phenomena include naturally occurring principles/relations and nature-based products that are naturally occurring or that do not have markedly different characteristics compared to what occurs in nature; these are judicial exceptions to patent eligibility.
guidance: Courts describe them as 'physical phenomena', 'scientific principles', 'natural laws', and 'products of nature.' Examples provided by case law include isolated DNA (Myriad), cloned animals (Roslin), correlations between genetic variations and alleles, metabolic correlations (Mayo), myeloperoxidase correlation (Cleveland Clinic v. True Health), existence of cffDNA (Ariosa), CYP2D6 genotype correlation (Vanda), electromagnetism to transmit signals (Morse), qualities of bacteria (Funk Bros.). The basic tools of scientific/technological work are not patentable. Not every claim describing a natural ability or quality is an exception — process claims applying or integrating the natural ability (e.g., fractionating/recovering/cryopreserving hepatocytes) may be eligible. Even if a claim recites a law of nature/natural phenomenon, it may still be eligible under Pathways A–C (example: Vanda). If a claim recites a law of nature/natural phenomenon, further analysis in Step 2A Prong Two is required to determine whether the claim integrates the exception into a practical application.

name: Products of nature (nature-based products)
description: When a law of nature/natural phenomenon is claimed as a physical product, it may be a 'product of nature' exception; products include naturally occurring products and non-naturally occurring products that lack markedly different characteristics from natural counterparts.
guidance: Examples: isolated DNA (Myriad), primers (Ambry Genetics), bacterial mixtures (Funk Bros.), cloned animals (Roslin). Synthetically replicated sequences that are structurally identical to natural ones can still be products of nature. Use the markedly different characteristics analysis (MPEP §2106.04(c)) to evaluate nature-based product limitations. Under BRI, a nature-based product limitation may encompass both eligible and ineligible products; examiners should identify the BRI and, where appropriate, recommend narrowing amendments. For nature-based products that clearly do not seek to tie up any judicial exception, consider the streamlined analysis of MPEP §2106.06.

name: Disclaimer procedure and effect (remedy for over-broad claims)
description: A patentee who, through inadvertence/accident/mistake, claimed more than he was the original inventor of may file a disclaimer of such parts; the disclaimer must be in writing, attested by witnesses, recorded in the patent office upon payment, and thereafter considered part of the original specification to the extent stated.
guidance: Filing a disclaimer before suit may preserve the patent for the parts truly the patentee's and allows recovery of costs in some circumstances. If filed during pendency of suit, it will not afford benefit in that suit. Unreasonable neglect or delay in entering the disclaimer at the patent office can defeat its protective effect and may constitute a good defence to the suit.

name: Notice of appeal and cross appeal timing and content (inter partes)
description: Upon issuance of a Right of Appeal Notice under § 1.953, the owner or requester may appeal to the Board within the time provided in the Right of Appeal Notice and paying the fee set forth in § 41.20(b)(1). Cross appeals may be filed within fourteen days of service of the other party's notice upon payment of fee. The notice must identify the appealed claim(s) and be signed. An appeal or cross appeal must be taken from all the rejections or determinations which the appellant proposes to contest. The time periods for filing a notice of appeal or cross appeal may not be extended.
guidance: Timely file and sign the notice and pay fees; incomplete or untimely notices risk dismissal; identify all contested matters to avoid procedural issues.

name: Amendments and affidavits/evidence after filing an inter partes appeal
description: Amendments filed after the date of filing an appeal canceling claims may be admitted where such cancellation does not affect the scope of any other pending claim. All other amendments filed after the date of filing an appeal will not be admitted except as permitted by § 41.77(b)(1). Affidavits or other evidence filed after the date of filing an appeal will not be admitted except as permitted by reopening prosecution under § 41.77(b)(1).
guidance: Generally, post-appeal amendments/evidence are barred except narrow exceptions (e.g., claim cancellations or reopening per §41.77(b)(1)).

name: Appellant's brief required contents (inter partes)
description: The appellant’s brief shall contain the following items under appropriate headings and in the order indicated: (i) Real party in interest; (ii) Related appeals, interferences, and trials (identifying numbers and including copies of decisions in appendix); (iii) Status of claims; (iv) Status of amendments; (v) Summary of claimed subject matter (concise explanation of each independent claim with specification and drawing references, and identification of structure corresponding to any 35 U.S.C. 112(f) means-plus-function/step-plus-function elements with specification references); (vi) Issues to be reviewed on appeal; (vii) Argument with citations to statutes, regulations, authorities, and record; (viii) Claims appendix; (ix) Evidence appendix (copies of evidence submitted under §§1.130-1.132 or other evidence entered by the examiner and where entered in the record); (x) Related proceedings appendix (decisions); (xi) Certificate of service.
guidance: Each item must be included under proper headings and in order. For 112(f) elements identify corresponding structure/material/acts with exact specification citations. Failure to include these items or to comply may lead to dismissal after a non-extendable cure opportunity.

name: Respondent's brief scope and content requirements
description: Respondent(s) may file a respondent brief once within the time limit and must sign and pay the requisite fee. The respondent brief shall be limited to issues raised in the appellant brief to which the respondent brief is directed. The respondent brief shall contain items under headings similar to the appellant’s brief (real party in interest; related appeals; status of claims; status of amendments; summary of claimed subject matter; issues to be reviewed — accepting or disputing appellant's statements; argument with citations; evidence appendix; related proceedings appendix; certificate of service). If appellant’s statements are disputed, the errors must be specified with particularity.
guidance: Respondent briefs must mirror structure and specify particular errors when disputing appellant statements. A requester respondent may not address briefs of other requesters.

name: Grouping and separate argument rules for claims
description: If multiple claims subject to the same ground of rejection are argued as a group by appellant, the Board may select a single claim from the group to decide the appeal for the group on the basis of the selected claim alone. Failure to separately argue claims which appellant has grouped together shall constitute a waiver of any argument that the Board must consider the patentability of any grouped claim separately. Any claim argued separately should be placed under a subheading identifying the claim by number. A statement which merely points out what a claim recites will not be considered an argument for separate patentability of the claim.
guidance: If separate patentability is sought for specific claims, argue them separately under subheadings; mere recitation is insufficient and grouping can cause waiver.

name: Disclosure/Summary of Invention (Rule 5.1(a)(iii))
description: Disclose the invention, as claimed, in such terms that the technical problem (even if not expressly stated as such) and its solution can be understood, and state the advantageous effects, if any, of the invention with reference to the background art.
guidance: Preferably use heading 'Disclosure of Invention' or 'Summary of Invention'. Ensure the problem and solution are clear in relation to background art and claims.

name: Best mode / Modes for carrying out the invention (Rule 5.1(a)(v) and 37 CFR 1.435(b))
description: Set forth at least the best mode contemplated by the applicant for carrying out the invention claimed; this shall be done in terms of examples, where appropriate, and with reference to the drawings, if any. For international applications designating the United States the description must contain upon filing an indication of the best mode contemplated by the inventor.
guidance: Heading examples: 'Best Mode for Carrying out the Invention', 'Mode(s) for Carrying out the Invention', or 'Description of Embodiments'. Where national law of a designated State does not require best mode, failure to describe the best mode shall have no effect in that State. Draft descriptions to satisfy the strictest designated Office if practicable.

name: Support for long context lengths
description: patembed models support context lengths up to 4096 tokens.
guidance: Models and input pipelines should handle long patent documents/sections (thousands of tokens) to capture relevant information in claims/specifications; benchmarked models should demonstrate capability at extended context lengths.

name: Prior Art Search and Determination of Novelty
description: Prior Art Search and Determination of Novelty
guidance: Examination includes searching prior art and determining whether claimed subject matter is novel relative to the found prior art.

name: Comparison with the Most Similar Prior Art
description: Comparison with the most similar prior art
guidance: Determine the differences between the claimed invention and the closest/prior art reference(s) as a basis for assessing inventive step.

name: Common Technical Knowledge
description: Common technical knowledge in the relevant field
guidance: Take into account what is common general knowledge in the field when determining whether claimed features are inventive.

name: Written Amendment Procedures
description: Written Amendment procedures
guidance: Procedural rules and expectations for filing and evaluating written amendments to specifications and claims during prosecution before the JPO.

name: Statement of Claims (Clarity Requirements)
description: Statement of Claims (clarity requirements)
guidance: Claims must meet clarity/definiteness requirements; examination reviews whether claims clearly define the scope of the invention.

name: Use of AIPLA survey data for cost inputs and complexity cells
description: Draw attorney-fee and litigation-cost inputs from the AIPLA Annual Survey (median charges by technology and complexity). Define 'minimal complexity' (e.g., ten-page specification and ten claims) per AIPLA definitions when mapping costs to rounds of review.
guidance: Report the AIPLA source, relevant table rows (e.g., Table 5 median charges for 2008/2010/2012), and the technology/complexity cell used for per-round cost assumptions; discuss whether the chosen complexity cell is conservative/representative.

name: Grouping of Abstract Ideas (three categories)
description: Abstract ideas are categorized into three enumerated groupings: (1) mathematical concepts — relationships, formulas, calculations; (2) certain methods of organizing human activity — fundamental economic practices, commercial/legal interactions, managing personal behavior; (3) mental processes — observations, evaluations, judgments, opinions.
guidance: Claims that don't fall into one of these groupings should not typically be treated as reciting an abstract idea. Use these groupings to determine whether a claim recites a judicial exception under Step 2A Prong One.

name: Practical application indicators
description: Examples of how a claim may integrate a judicial exception into a practical application.
guidance: Indicators include: improvement to functioning of a computer or other technology; applied/used in conjunction with a particular machine; effecting a transformation of an article to a different state or thing; applies the judicial exception in some other meaningful way; beyond merely linking the use to a technological environment. These factors support a finding that Prong Two is satisfied.

name: "Mere instructions to apply" indicators (NOT practical application)
description: Examples of claim elements/limitations that do not show integration into a practical application and thus are NOT sufficient under Prong Two.
guidance: Indicators include: adding the words 'apply it' with the judicial exception; mere instructions to apply on a generic computer; field-of-use limitations; generic linking to a technological environment; adding insignificant extra-solution activity. Presence of these tends to weigh against finding a practical application.

name: Step 2B — Additional elements / inventive concept analysis
description: If Prong Two does not show integration into a practical application (i.e., claim is directed to an abstract idea), analyze whether additional elements, individually or as an ordered combination, add significantly more than the judicial exception (the 'inventive concept').
guidance: Look for elements that go BEYOND well-understood, routine, conventional activities. Berkheimer factors apply (i.e., courts may treat some aspects as factual questions). Generic computer components are not enough. The 'inventive concept' must be more than just the abstract idea itself.

name: Use of illustrative examples (Examples 37–46) to guide analysis
description: USPTO-provided examples (37–46) illustrate how the two-prong Step 2A and Step 2B analyses apply to different fact patterns (GUI icon relocation, audio-mixer simulation, neural-network training for facial detection, adaptive network monitoring, cryptographic communications, medical-record notifications, life-sciences diagnostics/treatment).
guidance: Review examples to see how specific features (e.g., particular machine/application, technical improvements, quantified thresholds) led to eligibility or ineligibility in practice (e.g., Example 40 shows two similar claims with different outcomes based on a specific traffic-monitoring threshold). Use examples to identify what made claims eligible (specific application, technical improvement) versus ineligible (generic implementation, mere instructions).

name: Strategic drafting implications to improve eligibility
description: Practical drafting strategies recommended to increase the likelihood that claims are found eligible under the PEG.
guidance: Recommendations include: state technical improvements explicitly in the specification; tie claims to specific technical environments; avoid pure mental-process steps; include hardware/structural elements where appropriate; quantify improvements where possible; consider adding technological problem statements. Avoid relying solely on generic computer implementation or field-of-use limitations.

name: Specification must set out at least one mode for carrying out the invention
description: The description should set out at least one mode for carrying out the invention claimed, using examples where appropriate and with reference to drawings, if any.
guidance: Practical examples and drawings help persons skilled in the art to make or use the invention. Omitting a mode or examples may lead to insufficiency findings because the specification fails to show how to implement the claimed invention.

name: When working an invention requires application of AI: sufficiency pitfalls
description: If practicing the claimed invention requires applying an AI technique, three problematic situations arise: (1) the AI technique is not disclosed (claims unsupported), (2) the invention is reproducible but the AI's workings are unexplainable, and (3) the AI-dependent invention cannot be reproduced.
guidance: Situation (1) implicates enablement (claims must be supported by the description). Situation (2) may raise explainability concerns but, per the article, patent law does not require inner workings explanation beyond enablement. Situation (3) triggers insufficiency because the invention cannot be carried out by a person skilled in the art without undue experimentation or access to undisclosed artifacts.

name: Claims: numbering and sentence structure
description: If there is more than one claim, the claims must be numbered consecutively by Arabic numerals. Each claim must consist of one sentence, generally comprising an introductory (pre-characterizing) part and a characterizing part.
guidance: Use one-sentence claims with an introductory part (features common with closest prior art) and a characterizing part (preceded by 'characterized in that', 'characterized by', 'wherein the improvement comprises' or the like).

name: Claims: two-part format and wording
description: In the introductory part, the technical features of the invention that are in common with the closest prior art shall be given including the generic concept reflecting the intended purpose of the invention. In the characterizing part ... the technical features distinguishing the claimed invention from the closest prior art shall be given.
guidance: Precede the characterising part with specified phrases ('characterized in that', etc.). Two-part form preferred except in certain cases (see exceptions).

name: Claims: avoid cross-reference to specification/drawings
description: Claims shall not (except if absolutely necessary) refer to the specification or drawings, e.g., in a manner like 'as described in part… of the specification', or 'as illustrated in figure…of the drawings'.
