guidance: Do not rely on references to the description or drawings to define claim scope; claims should be self-contained.

name: Claims: reference signs in claims
description: If the application contains drawings, the technical features mentioned in the claims must preferably be followed by reference signs in brackets relating to such features if that provides for better understanding of the invention.
guidance: Reference signs are optional but recommended when they improve clarity; ensure consistency with drawing numerals mentioned in the specification.

name: Independent claims: single invention requirement
description: An independent claim must relate to one invention only. An application may contain two or more independent claims of the same category ... if it cannot be readily covered by a single general claim.
guidance: Avoid drafting independent claims that claim multiple, unrelated inventions; multiple independent claims allowed when necessary.

name: Dependent claims: purpose and grouping
description: A dependent claim must specify the features which constitute development or precise the features of the invention of the corresponding independent claim thus defining the invention in particular implementations.
guidance: Group all dependent claims relating to the same preceding independent claim together. Dependent claims may disclose specific features that could themselves be independent inventions.

name: Abstract: length and content
description: The abstract must be as concise as the disclosure allows, and should not exceed 150 words. The abstract must contain a summary of the disclosure contained in the description, claims and drawings. This summary must specify the technical field ... and the gist of the invention mentioning the technical result obtained.
guidance: Abstract is for technical information only and is not to be used for interpreting scope of protection. Include the most representative chemical formula if applicable.

name: Formal examination: timing and scope
description: The Eurasian Patent Office examines the application for its correspondence to the formal requirements within two months from the filing date ... During the formal examination, it will be examined whether all required documents have been filed and are in compliance with the requirements, whether the invention is correctly classified according to the IPC, whether the priority claim(s) made (if any) is (are) statutory and whether or not the invention relates to subject matter which is unpatentable.
guidance: Office may invite applicant to correct/amend within a prescribed term; formal examination period extends correspondingly if invitations issued.

name: Search: automatic novelty search and basis
description: A novelty search is carried out automatically for each Eurasian patent application that has been accepted for further prosecution. The search is to be carried out on the basis of the claims, taking into consideration the specification and drawings (if any).
guidance: Ensure claims and specification clearly disclose the invention as search is claim-focused. Search performed by Rospatent under agreement with EAPO.

name: Search: handling lack of unity
description: If during the patent search it is revealed that the requirement of unity of invention is not met, the applicant may be invited within three months from sending of the notification to communicate a decision which invention(s) shall be searched. If the applicant has not replied in time ... the search is carried out in respect of the invention mentioned first in the claims.
guidance: Prioritize claims order or respond timely to unity notifications to control search scope.

name: PPH / PCT-PPH conditions for accelerated substantive examination
description: Applicant of a PCT application entering Eurasian regional phase can request accelerated substantive examination provided that in respect of the corresponding PCT application it was determined by one of certain ISAs/IPEAs that at least one independent claim meets patentability requirements, and the claims in the Eurasian application are sufficiently in conformity with one or more said claims determined as patentable.
guidance: Ensure conformity with claims found patentable by specified ISAs/IPEAs (EPO, JPO, KIPO, Rospatent, USPTO) to qualify for accelerated examination under PCT-PPH.

name: Scope of protection and claim interpretation
description: The scope of protection provided by a Eurasian patent is determined by the claims. The specification and drawings serve merely to interpret the claims. When interpreting the claims, due account is to be taken of every feature of the invention contained in an independent claim or a feature being equivalent thereto. The doctrine of equivalents can be used when the legislation of the Contracting State allows its applying. The interpretation of claims should serve not only to clarify the features thereof which are unclear or indefinite, but also to determine their complete and actual scope; when interpreting the claims the extremes of a strict, literal interpretation ... and a broad interpretation ... must be avoided.
guidance: Interpretation should balance literal wording and specification to determine actual scope; national courts may apply doctrine of equivalents subject to national law.

name: Limitation period for infringement claims
description: The ultimate term for infringement action is three years after the date on which plaintiff became aware or should have become aware of the infringement.
guidance: Monitor discovery/knowledge dates to preserve claims; national limitation rules may apply.

name: Effect of published application (provisional protection)
description: Provisional protection starts from the date of publication of the application. After publication of the Eurasian patent, the patent owner may claim ... a reasonable compensation ... from the persons who without the owner's consent used the invention ... during the period from the date of publication of the application until the date of publication of the Eurasian patent. The provisional protection is limited to the scope of the published claims of the application. For PCT applications designating EAPO provisional protection starts on the date of publication of the international application if the application is published in Russian; otherwise only after submitting a translation into Russian.
guidance: Provisional protection is limited and conditional; if grant is finally refused, provisional protection is considered never to have existed.

name: Focus of the claimed advance / 'character as a whole' inquiry
description: Identify the 'focus of the claimed advance over the prior art' to determine if the claim's 'character as a whole' is directed to excluded subject matter.
guidance: Look beyond isolated claim elements to the claim as a whole (Affinity Labs, Elec. Power). If the claimed advance is essentially an abstract idea (for example, collection/analysis/display of information), the claim is likely directed to an abstract idea.

name: Mental processes doctrine
description: Claim steps that can be performed in the human mind, or by a human using pen and paper, are mental processes and fall within the abstract-idea category.
guidance: If the core steps of the claim (e.g., selecting individuals, determining eligibility, making identifications) are things humans routinely do mentally, the claim is directed to an abstract idea (CyberSource, Elec. Power, Affinity Labs). Computer implementation alone does not avoid this if the steps remain essentially mental.

name: Information collection/analysis/display is an abstract idea absent inventive technology
description: Gathering and analyzing information of a specified content and then displaying the results is an abstract idea unless the claim recites a particular assertedly inventive technology for performing those functions.
guidance: Claims that merely collect information from sources, interpret its meaning, and indicate results (even if performed on a computer network) are typically abstract (Elec. Power, FairWarning). To survive § 101, the claim must do more than data gathering/analysis/display on generic computers.

name: Improvement to computer functionality vs. generic computer implementation
description: Claims that recite an improvement in the functioning of the computer itself (a specific technical solution) can supply an inventive concept; by contrast, claims that use generalized steps on a generic computer are not saved.
guidance: Distinguish claims that 'improve[] an existing technological process' or 'recite a specific, discrete implementation' (BASCOM, Enfish) from those that merely use generic computer components to perform conventional steps (TLI, buySAFE). Emphasize concrete technical improvement over invoking computer capabilities as a tool.

name: Well-understood, routine, conventional elements do not supply an inventive concept
description: Additional claim elements that are well-understood, routine, and conventional in the field do not provide the 'something more' required at Alice/Mayo step two.
guidance: Assess whether the specification or record admits the conventional nature of the computer elements; if so, those elements cannot supply an inventive concept (Alice; Berkheimer: where the specification admits conventionality, relying on the specification may be appropriate).

name: Claims directed to results without limiting means (preemption concern)
description: Claims that 'simply demand[] the production of a desired result . . . without any limitation on how to produce that result' are directed to an abstract idea and raise preemption concerns.
guidance: Evaluate whether the claim preempts all ways of achieving the result; absence of limitations about how the result is achieved points toward ineligibility (Interval Licensing).

name: Role of specification admissions and record evidence
description: Admissions in the specification that steps may be performed on any generic computer or that components are conventional can support a finding that claims lack an inventive concept.
guidance: Where the specification concedes that claimed computer components/operations are well-understood, routine, and conventional, that can supply substantial evidence for § 101 rejection without further proof (citing the application's own admission and Berkheimer commentary). Conversely, when non-conventional technical detail is present in the record, it may support eligibility.

name: Statutory (same invention) double patenting
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 as claiming the same invention as that of claim [2] of prior U.S. Patent No. [3]. This is a double patenting rejection.
guidance: Use form paragraph 8.31 (must be preceded by form paragraph 8.30/form paragraph 1). Used only where the "scope" of the inventions claimed is identical. Do not use this paragraph if conflicting claims are in another copending application (use provisional double patenting form paragraph 8.32 instead). In bracket 3 insert the number of the conflicting patent. If the patent is to a different inventive entity and is commonly assigned, also use form paragraph 8.27 to require the assignee to name the first inventor. If evidence indicates the patent is prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(f) or (g), also make rejections using form paragraphs 7.15 and/or 7.19; if the patent has an earlier effective U.S. filing date, also consider a 102(e) rejection using form paragraph 7.15.02.

name: Nonstatutory double patenting (obviousness-type)
description: A nonstatutory obviousness-type double patenting rejection is appropriate where the conflicting claims are not identical, but at least one examined application claim is not patentably distinct from the reference claim(s) because the examined application claim is either anticipated by, or would have been obvious over, the reference claim(s).
guidance: Based on a judicially created doctrine grounded in public policy to prevent unjustified timewise extension of the right to exclude. It is "analogous to [a failure to meet] the nonobviousness requirement of 35 U.S.C. 103" except that the patent principally underlying the double patenting rejection is not considered prior art. Use form paragraph 8.33 as a heading (once) before any of form paragraphs 8.34–8.39. A timely filed terminal disclaimer in compliance with 37 CFR 1.321(c) or (d) may be used to overcome an actual or provisional rejection based on a nonstatutory double patenting ground provided the conflicting application or patent either is shown to be commonly owned with this application, or claims an invention made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of a joint research agreement.

name: Obviousness-type rejection must state differences and reasons
description: Any obviousness-type double patenting rejection should make clear: (A) The differences between the inventions defined by the conflicting claims — a claim in the patent compared to a claim in the application; and (B) The reasons why a person of ordinary skill in the art would conclude that the invention defined in the claim at issue is anticipated by, or would have been an obvious variation of, the invention defined in a claim in the patent.
guidance: Provide explicit rationale in the action (e.g., in bracket [4] or [5] of the form paragraphs) explaining why claims are not patentably distinct; if using secondary references, explain the obviousness rationale. Do not treat the patent disclosure as prior art when making the obviousness determination.

name: Use of patent disclosure/specification in obviousness-type analysis
description: The disclosure of the patent may not be used as prior art, but the specification can be used as a dictionary to learn the meaning of a term and those portions which provide support for the patent claims may be examined when addressing whether an application claim defines an obvious variation of an invention claimed in the patent.
guidance: Cite cases: Toro Co. v. White Consol. Indus., Renishaw PLC v. Marposs. Use disclosure to determine proper meanings of claim terms and to identify portions of the specification that support the patent claims; do not use the patent as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 103.

name: One-way obviousness test (when appropriate)
description: If the application at issue is the later filed application or both are filed on the same day, only a one-way determination of obviousness is needed in resolving the issue of double patenting.
guidance: Assess whether the invention defined in a claim in the application would have been anticipated by, or an obvious variation of, the invention defined in a claim in the patent. Unless a claimed invention in the application would have been anticipated or obvious over a claimed invention in the patent, no obviousness-type double patenting rejection should be made. One-way test is appropriate absent administrative delay or inability to have filed claims in a single application.

name: Two-way obviousness test (when required)
description: A two-way test is to be applied only when the applicant could not have filed the claims in a single application and there is administrative delay; when the patent is the later filed application, the question whether timewise extension is justified must be addressed.
guidance: Apply the Graham analysis twice — once with application claims as the claims in issue and once with the patent claims as the claims in issue. An obvious-type double patenting rejection is appropriate only where each analysis compels a conclusion that the invention defined in the claims in issue is an obvious variation of the invention defined in a claim in the other application/patent. Burden may shift to applicant to show why a two-way determination is required. Consider factors indicating administrative delay (appeals, interferences, Office delay) versus applicant-caused delay (requests for extensions, strategic continuations).

name: Form-paragraph selection and sequencing for obviousness-type rejections
description: Form paragraph 8.33 is a 'Heading' only and must precede any one of form paragraphs 8.34 to 8.39; use specific form paragraphs depending on whether the primary reference is an issued patent or a copending application and whether secondary references are involved.
guidance: 8.34: Rejection, Obviousness Type Double Patenting - No Secondary Reference(s) (use when primary reference is a patent). 8.35: Provisional Rejection, Obviousness Type - No Secondary Reference(s) (use for copending application primary). 8.36: Rejection, Obviousness Type - With Secondary Reference(s) (primary reference is patent, insert secondary reference in bracket 4). 8.37: Provisional Rejection, Obviousness Type - With Secondary Reference(s) (primary reference is application). Always ensure 8.33 precedes the chosen paragraph and is used only once in an Office action. Insert appropriate bracketed information (claim numbers, patent/app numbers, secondary refs, and explanatory rationale).

name: Schneller-type (other) nonstatutory double patenting
description: There are unique circumstances (illustrated by In re Schneller) where another type of nonstatutory double patenting rejection is applicable even where the inventions claimed are nonobvious over each other.
guidance: Schneller situations are fact-specific and will be rare. The Technology Center (TC) Director must approve any nonstatutory double patenting rejections based on Schneller. Examiner should consult SPE and obtain TC Director approval before making such a rejection. Use form paragraphs 8.33 and the appropriate one of form paragraphs 8.38 (between an issued patent and one or more applications) and 8.39 (provisional rejections) for this type.

name: Focus on strong arguments; avoid weak or unsupported points
description: Do not waste brief and Board attention on weak arguments (e.g., claiming different channels of trade when the cited registration lacks trade restrictions).
guidance: Prioritize and concentrate on arguments supported by the evidentiary record to maximize persuasive impact.

name: Doctrine of inherency as basis for anticipation
description: Under the doctrine of inherency, if an element is not expressly disclosed in a prior art reference, the reference will still be deemed to anticipate a subsequent claim if the missing element is necessarily present in the thing described in the reference and it would be so recognized by persons of ordinary skill.
guidance: Applies to both published references and products sold to the public; once a product is sold, any invention inherent to that product becomes publicly available prior art (Rosco, Inc. v. Mirror Lite Co.).

name: Section 115: Director may require earlier inventor oaths/declarations when claiming benefit
description: New section 115(g) allows the Director to require an applicant claiming the benefit of an earlier-filed application to include copies of previous inventor's oaths used in those applications; the Office cannot begin examining an application until it knows who those inventors are.
guidance: Reason: inventor identity determines which prior art is counted; later-filed applications are not currently required to name inventors by statute, so requiring past oaths helps determine entitlement to benefit/priority.

name: Statutory basis for interferences (pre-AIA)
description: An interference is a contest under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 135(a) between an application and either another application or a patent to determine priority (who first invented) within the meaning of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g)(1).
guidance: Once suggested under 37 CFR 41.202, an administrative patent judge declares the interference and the Board adjudicates priority and patentability questions; final adverse decisions may constitute final refusal or claim cancellation under the statute.

name: Interfering subject matter test (37 CFR 41.203(a))
description: An interference exists if the subject matter of a claim of one party would, if prior art, have anticipated or rendered obvious the subject matter of a claim of the opposing party, and vice versa.
guidance: Claims must be construed in light of the application in which they appear for interference purposes. Identical claim language does not guarantee same invention; means-plus-function and differences in corresponding structure can change scope. Numerous examples illustrate species/genus, Markush groups, composition vs genus, and structural equivalence analyses.

name: Count and claim correspondence
description: A 'count' is the Board's description of the interfering subject matter that sets the scope of admissible proofs on priority. A claim corresponds to a count if the count, treated as prior art, would have anticipated or rendered obvious the claim.
guidance: Every count must have at least one corresponding claim for each party; a claim can correspond to more than one count. Examples explain when species/genus claims correspond and when a showing of obviousness is required for correspondence.

name: Non-interfering claims treatment
description: A claim that does not interfere is directed to a patentably distinct invention and should not be delayed; if an application contains both interfering and non-interfering claims, a restriction should be made between them.
guidance: Non-interfering claims should ordinarily be issued promptly unless term limited (terminal disclaimer, reissue). If applicant traverses restriction, traversal may be maintained or treated as concession that non-interfering claims correspond to the count; leaving non-interfering claims delays issuance unnecessarily.

name: Restriction of unpatentable claims to avoid delay
description: Restriction of unpatentable claims may be appropriate when prosecution of the unpatentable claims to completion would unduly delay initiation of an interference and that delay would prejudice another stakeholder (applicant, public).
guidance: Ordinarily restricting claims solely because they are not patentable is inappropriate; IPS approval is required before making such a restriction. Examples show broad vs narrow claims and prejudice to other parties.

name: Interference preparation tasks (headings)
description: When preparing an application for interference, tasks include: Interference Search; Obtaining Control Over Involved Files; Translation of Foreign Benefit Application; Sorting Claims; Applicant Suggestion; Identifying the Other Application or Patent; Counts and Corresponding Claims; Explaining Priority; Adequate Written Description.
guidance: These preparation steps require case-specific actions such as searches to identify potentially interfering subject matter, ensuring control/access to involved files, translating foreign priority documents, sorting and matching claims to counts, and documenting priority and written description support; consult IPS for details.

name: Derivation proceeding statutory basis (AIA)
description: A derivation proceeding under 35 U.S.C. 135 determines whether an inventor named in an earlier application derived the claimed invention from an inventor named in the petitioner's application and, without authorization, the earlier application was filed; derivation is applicable to AIA first-inventor-to-file applications and patents.
guidance: The petition must set forth with particularity the basis for finding derivation; where standards for instituting are met the Director may institute a derivation proceeding and the Board may correct inventorship where appropriate.

name: Derivation definitions and scope (37 CFR 42.2)
description: Key derivation definitions include: affidavit; Board; business day; confidential information; final; hearing; involved (application/patent/claim that is the subject of the proceeding); judgment; motion; party; petition; petitioner; preliminary proceeding; proceeding; trial; rehearing.
guidance: Understanding these definitions is necessary to determine applicable procedure under part 42 and to differentiate derivation trials from interferences (interferences are administered under part 41).

name: Action after a derivation proceeding is decided
description: Jurisdiction returns to the examiner once the derivation proceeding terminates. The examiner must reopen prosecution to consider Board recommendations, enter any recommended rejections, and maintain them unless the applicant overcomes them with amendment or new evidence.
guidance: A judgment against a claim in derivation finally disposes of the claim; if no claim remains allowable, issue a notice of abandonment. Extraordinary remedies (e.g., changes to inventorship or ownership) may require updating correspondence and should prompt consultation with a TCPS.

name: Insignificant extra-solution activity (definition and effect)
description: Whether additional elements add more than insignificant extra-solution activity to the judicial exception. 'Extra-solution activity' includes activities incidental to the primary process or product that are merely nominal or tangential additions to the claim, including pre-solution (e.g., gathering data) and post-solution activities (e.g., printing a report). The addition of insignificant extra-solution activity does not amount to an inventive concept.
guidance: Supreme Court and Federal Circuit guidance: Parker v. Flook (post-solution activity cannot transform an unpatentable principle into a patentable process); Mayo (measuring metabolites was insignificant extra-solution activity). Examiners should carefully consider each claim on its own merits and evaluate other Step 2B considerations (particular machine, particular transformation, well-understood/routine/conventional, field of use/technological environment). See MPEP §§2106.05(b),(c),(d),(h) for related considerations. When concluding an element is insignificant extra-solution activity, examiners should explain why it does not meaningfully limit the claim (see MPEP §2106.07(a)). Examples of extra-solution activity include mere data gathering and outputting, use of a printer to output results, or conventional pre- and post-processing steps.

name: Mere data gathering as an example of insignificant extra-solution activity
description: Activities courts have found to be insignificant extra-solution activity include mere data gathering steps that are incidental to the primary claimed process (e.g., performing clinical tests to obtain inputs, testing a system to obtain a response used to determine malfunction, presenting offers and gathering statistics).
guidance: Case examples include In re Grams (clinical tests), In re Meyers (system testing), OIP Technologies (presenting offers and gathering statistics), CyberSource v. Retail Decisions (obtaining transaction info via the Internet), Ultramercial (consulting/updating an activity log), Mayo (determining level of a biomarker). Examiners should treat mere data gathering as likely insignificant unless it is integrated and contributes a technological improvement or meaningful limitation.

name: Insignificant application (post-solution/ancillary steps) as an example
description: Post-solution or ancillary application steps that are incidental to the primary claimed process (e.g., cutting hair after deciding a hairstyle; printing/downloading generated menus) are examples of insignificant application that do not provide an inventive concept.
guidance: Case examples: In re Brown (cutting hair after determining the hairstyle), Ameranth (printing/downloading menus). Such steps are typically viewed as conventional or ancillary and do not meaningfully limit a claim unless integrated into a technological process in a non-conventional way.

name: Field of use and technological environment limitation: mere linking to environment does not make claim eligible
description: Whether additional elements amount to more than generally linking the use of a judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use. Merely indicating a field of use or technological environment in which to apply a judicial exception does not amount to significantly more and cannot make an ineligible concept patentable.
guidance: Supreme Court and Federal Circuit guidance: Diamond v. Diehr (limiting a formula to a particular technological use does not automatically make it eligible); Parker v. Flook and Bilski noted that limiting an abstract idea to one field of use or adding token postsolution components does not make the concept patentable. Examples: Flook (limiting a formula to petrochemical processes was insufficient); Affinity Labs v. DirecTV (limiting broadcast delivery to cellular telephones did not add an inventive concept). Distinguishing integration vs token addition: if the additional elements are integrated into the claim (as in Diehr), they may transform the claim; if they are incidental/not integrated, they likely do not. Examiners should evaluate integration of the technological environment into the claimed combination and explain findings.

name: Examiners must explain in eligibility rejections why limitations do not meaningfully limit the claim
description: For claim limitations that are mere instructions to apply an exception or that add insignificant extra-solution activity, examiners should explain why such limitations do not meaningfully limit the claim in an eligibility rejection.
guidance: Examples of how to explain: point out that implementing an abstract idea on a generic computer does not add significantly more (as in Alice) or that adding a final step of storing data to a mathematical computation does not meaningfully limit the process. Refer examiners and applicants to MPEP §2106.07(a) for guidance on formulating subject matter eligibility rejections and include citations to relevant case law when appropriate.

name: Enablement belongs to §112 and must be assessed under §112 using the specification, not shoehorned into §101
description: The Federal Circuit has 'imbued §101 with a new superpower—enablement on steroids,' demanding claim-level detail more appropriate to the §112 enablement inquiry.
guidance: Enablement should be assessed under 35 U.S.C. §112 based on the specification (not by imposing heightened enablement requirements in the §101 analysis). Courts must resist treating §101 as a substitute for §112.

name: Require appellate decisions to identify specific claims found unpatentable rather than invalidating entire patents wholesale
description: The Claims Court invalidated AED’s patents 'in their entirety' instead of identifying which specific claims failed §101, an approach described as contrary to law and meriting commentary.
guidance: Courts should invalidate only the particular claims that fail to satisfy §101 and should explain which claim limitations lead to ineligibility rather than sweeping invalidations that obscure the analysis.

name: Second embodiment drawings
description: FIG. 8 is a perspective view of a second embodiment; FIGs. 9–14 are front, right side, back, left side, top and bottom views of the second embodiment.
guidance: When multiple embodiments are claimed or shown, provide corresponding figures for each embodiment (full complementary views) and clearly label them as separate embodiments to illustrate variations of the design.

name: Broken lines excluded from claimed design
description: Broken lines shown in the figures described above are for illustrative purposes only and form no part of the claimed design.
guidance: Elements depicted in broken (dashed) lines are illustrative/environmental only and are not claimed as part of the patented design; use broken lines to indicate unclaimed subject matter or environment in which the claimed design is shown.

name: Claim scope formulation for design patents
description: The claim states: 'The package design with surface ornamentation, as shown and described.'
guidance: Design patent claims typically claim the appearance and are given scope by reference to the drawings and description. The singular, pictorial-focused claim formulation is standard: the claim covers the design as illustrated and described rather than functional features.

name: Bibliographic and priority/continuity information
description: The record lists publication number, application number, priority date, filing date, inventor, current/original assignee, related parent applications, applications claiming priority, and family applications.
guidance: Include full bibliographic data and continuity/priority relationships (e.g., earlier filed design applications, continuations) so the claim to priority and family history is clear. This information is important for assessing priority date, related filings, and potential prior art windows.

name: Figure legends and explicit labeling of embodiments
description: Each figure is captioned (e.g., 'FIG. 1 is a perspective view of a package design with surface ornamentation embodying the new design as shown, wherein the grayscale shaded regions are regions of color').
guidance: Figure legends should explicitly describe what each drawing depicts and may note special conventions (e.g., which shaded areas represent color). Clear captions help interpret the drawings and the scope of the claimed design.

name: 102(e) prior-art date for international applications published in English (filed on/after Nov 29, 2000)
description: All references (WIPO publication, U.S. patent application publication, or U.S. patent of, or claiming the benefit of, an international application (IA) filed on or after November 29, 2000, designated the U.S., and published in English under PCT Article 21(2)) have the 35 U.S.C. 102(e) prior art date of the international filing date or earlier effective U.S. filing date.
guidance: No benefit of the international filing date (nor any U.S. filing dates prior to the IA) is given for 35 U.S.C. 102(e) purposes if the IA was published under PCT Article 21(2) by WIPO in a language other than English. Use form paragraph 7.12 where applicable; consider priority/benefit claims to earlier-filed U.S. provisionals/nonprovisionals or internationals only if support exists (see 35 U.S.C. 119(e), 120).

name: Consideration of additional priority/benefit claims for 102(e) dates
description: If the IA properly claimed priority to an earlier-filed U.S. provisional (35 U.S.C. 119(e)) or an earlier-filed U.S. nonprovisional (35 U.S.C. 120) application, the 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date for references may be the filing date of the earlier-filed U.S. application, assuming proper support is present.
guidance: In determining the 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date, consider priority/benefit claims to earlier-filed U.S. provisional and nonprovisional applications and internationals under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), 120, 121 or 365(c) only if the subject matter used to make the rejection is appropriately supported in the relied-upon earlier-filed application's disclosure (and any intermediate application(s)). Do NOT consider foreign priority claims under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) and 365(a).

name: 102(e) date for U.S. publication/patent when IA not published in English (filed on/after Nov 29, 2000)
description: When an IA filed on or after November 29, 2000 was not published in English under PCT Article 21(2), the U.S. publication and U.S. patent of the 35 U.S.C. 111(a) continuation have the 35 U.S.C. 102(e) prior art date of the actual U.S. filing date of the 111(a) application; the IA publication by WIPO has no 102(e)(1) date.
guidance: The IA publication by WIPO can be applied under 35 U.S.C. 102(a) or (b) as of its publication date. If additional priority/benefit claims exist to earlier-filed U.S. apps, the 102(e) date for the U.S. publication/patent remains the actual filing date of the later-filed 111(a) application unless proper support yields an earlier effective date.

name: Provisional 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejections — when appropriate
description: If an earlier-filed, copending, and unpublished U.S. patent application discloses subject matter which would anticipate the claims in a later-filed pending U.S. application that has a different inventive entity, the examiner should determine whether a provisional 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection of the later-filed application can be made.
guidance: A provisional 102(e) rejection is appropriate where the earlier-filed application is not published at time of rejection; the rejection is based on a presumption of future publication or patenting of the copending application. Use form paragraph 7.15.01 when making a provisional rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(e).

name: ¶7.12 — 102(e) rejection rules under AIPA and 2002 amendments
description: ¶7.12 sets out the text of 102(e) as amended by AIPA and the 2002 Act and specifies that this paragraph should be used only if the reference is (a) filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a), or (b) a U.S. patent issued directly or indirectly from, or a U.S. or WIPO publication of, an international application with an international filing date on or after November 29, 2000.
guidance: In determining the 102(e) date, consider priority/benefit claims to earlier-filed U.S. provisionals, nonprovisionals, and internationals only if support exists; DO NOT consider foreign priority claims under 119(a)-(d) and 365(a). If conditions for relying on an international filing date are not met, apply the reference under 102(a) or (b) as of its publication date.

name: ¶7.12.01 — 102(e) rejection when reference derives from IA filed prior to Nov 29, 2000
description: ¶7.12.01 is to be used when the reference is a U.S. patent issued directly or indirectly from a national stage of, or a continuing application claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 365(c) to, an international application having an international filing date prior to November 29, 2000.
guidance: In this situation, pre-AIPA 102(e) is applicable. If the reference is a U.S. patent issued directly from a national stage, the reference's 102(e) date is the date the requirements of 371(c)(1), (2) and (4) were fulfilled. Consider priority/benefit claims only as permitted and only when supported by the relied-upon disclosures.

name: Sequence identifier reference requirement in descriptions, claims and drawings
description: Where the description or claims of a patent application discuss a sequence that is set forth in the Sequence Listing, reference must be made to the sequence by use of the sequence identifier (§ 1.823(a)(5)), preceded by 'SEQ ID NO:' or the like, in the text of the description or claims, even if the sequence is embedded in the text.
guidance: If a sequence appears in a drawing, the sequence must be referenced by the sequence identifier either in the drawing or in the Brief Description of the Drawings with a clear correlation.

name: Coverage of sequence rules to all sequences in the application
description: The sequence rules embrace all unbranched nucleotide sequences with ten or more nucleotide bases and all unbranched, non-D amino acid sequences with four or more amino acids ... The rules apply to all sequences in a given application, whether claimed or not.
guidance: All such sequences must be included to support building a comprehensive database and properly assessing prior art; omission may affect search/examination and database completeness.

name: Reissue application eligibility
description: A reissue application may be filed to correct an error made without any deceptive intent in the original patent. In order to qualify for reissue, the patent must be deemed wholly or partly inoperative or invalid as a result of the error.
guidance: Common reasons for filing a reissue include too narrow or too broad claims, inaccuracies in the disclosure, an incorrectly claimed foreign priority, or failure to make reference to or incorrectly making reference to prior copending applications. Reissues may not be filed for minor typing errors.

name: Broadening Reissue Claims
description: Broadening claims refer to amending a patent’s claims during reissue to expand their scope to cover more subject matter than originally claimed.
guidance: Broadening reissue claims are governed by specific rules (see MPEP 1412.03). Broadening is allowed only under statutory/regulatory constraints and may implicate intervening rights and time limits.

name: Recapture of Canceled Subject Matter
description: Recapture concerns attempting to reclaim subject matter that was canceled from original claims during reissue prosecution.
guidance: See MPEP 1412.02 for rules and limitations on recapturing canceled subject matter in a reissue.

name: Content of Reissue Application
description: A reissue application must include a reissue specification, drawings (if necessary), and any amendments necessary to correct the patent.
guidance: See 37 CFR 1.173 and MPEP 1410 and following (1410.01–1410.03). The application must include required oaths/declarations, revised specification and any claim amendments and must comply with form and content requirements.

name: 37 CFR 1.121 — Manner of making amendments in application
description: 37 CFR 1.121 details the specific procedures and formats required for making amendments to a patent application.
guidance: This regulation prescribes how to present amendments to claims, specifications, and drawings so they are acceptable to the Office; reissue filings/amendments must conform to these procedural rules.

name: 35 U.S.C. 253 — Disclaimer
description: 35 U.S.C. 253 allows a patent holder to formally disclaim or dedicate to the public any complete claim or terminal part of the term of a patent, effectively narrowing the scope or duration of the patent rights.
guidance: Disclaimers and their interaction with reissue/correction processes are addressed in MPEP 1490 and related sections.

name: Range of equivalents limited by prior art
description: Limitations in a claim cannot be given a range of equivalents so wide as to cause the claim to encompass anything in the prior art.
guidance: Courts will not enlarge claims by equivalents to encompass teachings of the prior art (cases cited: Senmed v. Richard-Allen; Tandon v. USITC). This principle constrains the permissible scope of equivalents so that patent protection does not cover what was already public.

name: Hypothetical-claim (patentability) test for limits on equivalents
description: A method for determining limits of claim coverage: write a hypothetical claim sufficient to literally cover the accused device and decide whether it would have been patentable over the prior art.
guidance: If the hypothetical claim could not have been allowed by the PTO over the prior art, it is improper to permit the patentee to obtain that coverage under the doctrine of equivalents; if the hypothetical claim could have been allowed, the prior art is not a bar. This test operationalizes the prior-art constraint on equivalents (discussed in Wilson Sporting Goods and related authority).

name: Effect of technological advances on equivalence
description: An 'embellishment' made possible by technological advances may not permit the accused device to escape the 'web of infringement,' but where extensive technological advances produce multiple departures from literal claim language, the totality of change may be too great to support infringement.
guidance: Courts recognize that technological progress can create unanticipated equivalents meriting protection, yet significant cumulative technical differences across claimed functions (see Texas Instruments) can defeat an equivalents finding. Evaluate both the nature and scope of departures caused by technological change.

name: Purpose of the doctrine — equity and prevention of piracy
description: The doctrine of equivalents was judicially devised to provide equity and to prevent 'pirating' of the patentee's invention where there is no literal infringement but liability is nevertheless appropriate.
guidance: As framed in Graver Tank and subsequent cases, the doctrine serves to protect substance over form and to prevent trivial changes from avoiding liability, while still respecting the public interest in clear claim boundaries.

name: Doctrine is an exception, not the default
description: Application of the doctrine of equivalents is the exception, not the rule; it should not be automatically considered in every case where literal infringement is absent.
guidance: Courts warn that routine reliance on equivalents would undermine the certainty of claim language and chill competitors' ability to design around patents. Use of the doctrine must be restrained to avoid eroding public notice of claim scope.

name: Broadening literal scope must be limited by public interest in certainty
description: Broadening the literal scope of a claim (i.e., redefining claims by equivalence) 'constitutes a deviation from the need of the public to know the precise legal limits of patent protection' and thus is admissible only to temper unsparing logic and serve justice.
guidance: Equivalents can be invoked to achieve equitable outcomes, but courts must weigh this against the public's need for reliable boundaries; expansion beyond permissible interpretation is justified only to serve the doctrine's real purpose.

name: EPC Article 69 and Protocol require an intermediate approach to claim interpretation
description: Under EPC Article 69, 'the extent of the protection conferred by a European patent shall be determined by the terms of the claims,' but the description and drawings shall be used to interpret the claims; the Protocol calls for an intermediate standard combining fair protection for the patentee with reasonable certainty for third parties.
guidance: In theory Article 69 and its Protocol permit use of the doctrine of equivalents (by avoiding a strict literal-only approach), but implementation is intended to strike a middle ground between literalism and open-ended protection.

name: Ascertaining differences between the claimed invention and prior art
description: Interpret claim language (see MPEP § 2111) and consider the invention and the prior art as a whole to identify differences between claim limitations and prior art disclosures.
guidance: All claim limitations must be considered; determine what differences remain once prior art is applied. Differences alone do not establish nonobviousness — examiner must explain why those differences would or would not have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in view of the record.

name: Permissible rationales for finding obviousness (including examples)
description: If Graham factual inquiries indicate obviousness, examiners may rely on several rationales — TSM is one but others are valid. Examples include (A) combining prior art elements by known methods to yield predictable results; (B) simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results; (C) using a known technique to improve similar devices in the same way; (D) applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement to yield predictable results; (E) 'obvious to try' when choosing from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions with a reasonable expectation of success; (F) recognizing that work in one field may prompt predictable variations for another field; (G) some teaching/suggestion/motivation in the prior art to modify or combine references.
guidance: This list is not exhaustive. The key is clear articulation of why the claimed invention would have been obvious. See MPEP § 2143 and § 2144 for examples and illustrations. Rationales must connect the facts to the legal conclusion and avoid conclusory generalizations.

name: Consideration of applicant’s rebuttal evidence and re-evaluation
description: Office personnel must consider all timely rebuttal evidence when reevaluating an obviousness determination and should reconsider initial findings in view of the entire record.
guidance: Rebuttal evidence may include secondary considerations or arguments demonstrating e.g. (A) that a POSITA could not combine elements due to technical difficulties; (B) the combination does more than the separate functions of elements; or (C) the claimed combination produced unexpected results. After rebuttal, examiners should review all rejections and proposed rejections for continued viability and clearly communicate findings and conclusions.

name: Specification requirement (written description of the invention)
description: The application includes what is called a “specification,” which contains a written description of the claimed invention telling what the invention is, how it works, how to make it, and how to use it.
guidance: The specification concludes with one or more numbered sentences (the claims). The specification must adequately describe the invention; later instructions address written description and enablement requirements in more detail.

name: Claims define the boundaries of protection
description: When the patent is eventually granted by the PTO, the claims define the boundaries of its protection and give notice to the public of those boundaries.
guidance: Figures and text in the rest of the patent provide description and context, but it is the claims that define the breadth of the patent’s coverage. Each claim is effectively treated as if it were a separate patent.

name: Prior art (general definition)
description: Prior art is information that demonstrates the state of technology that existed before the claimed invention was made or before the application was filed. The PTO searches for and reviews information that is publicly available or submitted by the applicant; this information is called 'prior art.'
guidance: A patent lists the prior art the Examiner considered (the 'cited references'). The instructions note that specific legal definitions of prior art will be provided later.

name: Anticipation (invalidity for not being new)
description: For a claim to be invalid because it is not new, [alleged infringer] must show, by clear and convincing evidence, that all of the elements of a claim are present in a single previous device or sufficiently described in a single previous printed publication or patent. We call these 'prior art.' If a claim is not new, it is said to be anticipated.
guidance: This sets the standard and burden for anticipation—clear and convincing evidence that a single prior-art reference discloses every claim element.

name: Obviousness (invalidity for being obvious)
description: A claim may be invalid if it would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the field of technology of the patent at the relevant time.
guidance: Even if every element is not shown in a single prior-art reference, a claim may be invalid as obvious in view of the state of the art; jurors will be provided a series of questions to decide obviousness in more detail later.

name: Written description requirement (Section 112)
description: To meet the written description requirement, the description of the invention in the specification portion of the patent must be detailed enough to demonstrate that the applicant actually possessed the invention as broadly as claimed in the claims of the issued patent.
guidance: This is a ground for invalidity where asserted; the instructions indicate that written description is a separate consideration under Section 112.

name: Role and meaning of claim language (claim elements/limitations)
description: A claim sets forth, in words, a set of requirements. Each claim sets forth its requirements in a single sentence. If a device or a method satisfies each of these requirements, then it is covered by the claim. The requirements of a claim are often referred to as 'claim elements' or 'claim limitations.'
guidance: Understanding the meaning of the words in a claim and that they set forth the requirements is necessary to decide infringement and invalidity issues; the court defines certain terms and the jury must apply those definitions.

name: Court's role in claim construction and jury's role in application
description: The law says that it is the court's role to define the terms of the claims and it is the jury's role to apply the court's definitions to the issues being decided. You must accept the court's definitions of claim terms as correct.
guidance: The court's definition of claim language should not be taken as an indication of the court's view regarding infringement or invalidity. For any claim words the court has not defined, the jury should apply the ordinary meaning (as understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art). Authorities such as Markman and Phillips are cited.

name: For claim terms without court definitions use ordinary meaning
description: For a claim term for which the court has not provided you with a definition, you should apply the ordinary meaning.
guidance: The 'ordinary and customary meaning' is based on the understanding of a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention; the jury must apply the court's provided constructions and otherwise use ordinary meaning.

name: Transition phrase meanings in claim drafting (comprising/consisting/consisting essentially of)
description: The instructions explain usage: 'comprising' is open-ended and allows additional elements; 'consisting of' is closed and means 'I claim what follows and nothing else'; 'consisting essentially of' is a middle ground between open-ended and closed-ended language.
guidance: Authoritative case law examples are provided to illustrate how courts interpret these transition phrases when construing claims.

name: Jury's ultimate tasks summarized
description: Your job will be to decide whether or not claims [ ] of the [ ] patent have been infringed and whether or not those claims are invalid. If you decide that any claim has been infringed and is not invalid, you will then need to decide any money damages to be awarded and whether any infringement was willful.
guidance: The summary frames the sequential determinations the jury must make (infringement by claim, invalidity defenses, damages, willfulness) and notes differing burdens/standards for different issues.

name: Section 112, paragraph 6 (means-plus-function / step-plus-function) applicability
description: Where the asserted claims include means-plus-function or step-plus-function requirements, Section 112, paragraph 6 applies (instruction provided only where such claims are at issue).
guidance: This instruction is flagged to be included only when means-plus-function claim elements are at issue; the full text of how to apply §112, ¶6 appears later in the instructions.

name: Claims as the primary source for scope, rest of patent as context
description: The figures and text in the rest of the patent provide a description and/or examples of the invention and provide a context for the claims, but it is the claims that define the breadth of the patent’s coverage.
guidance: Use the specification/drawings to understand claim terms where appropriate, but remember the claims set the legal boundaries.

name: Requirement to substantiate search/diligence with evidence
description: Petitioner should provide evidence (declarations, testimony, or factual record) describing the manner and timing of its prior-art searches and discovery of new references.
guidance: Attorney argument alone is insufficient; submissions should include factual support showing reasonable diligence. Failure to provide such evidence undermines claims that the reference could not have been found earlier and weighs against institution.

name: Sufficiency and scope of new-claim analysis in follow-on petitions
description: The extent and depth of a petitioner’s analysis for claims newly added in a subsequent petition (e.g., number of pages devoted to new dependent claims).
guidance: Minimal analysis (e.g., less than a page) for newly asserted claims suggests the petition is duplicative and may weigh against institution; petitioners should provide substantive claim-specific analysis for any new claims.

name: Signatures when adding an inventor
description: If an inventor is being added in a reissue application, the inventor being added must sign the reissue oath or declaration together with the inventors previously designated on the patent.
guidance: If the added inventor refuses to sign, the assignee of the entire interest may sign a substitute statement under 37 CFR 1.64. This applies even when the application both changes inventorship and enlarges claim scope.

name: Pre-September 16, 2012 inventorship/signature rules (pre-AIA)
description: For reissue applications filed before September 16, 2012 that change the claims to enlarge scope, the signature of all inventors is needed; if an inventor refuses to sign because they dispute the inventorship change, filing may still be possible with a petition under pre-AIA 37 CFR 1.47 together with written consent of all owners/assignees as required by pre-AIA 37 CFR 1.172(a).
guidance: If the consent requirement cannot be met (e.g., no assignee and an inventor refuses to consent), a pre-AIA 37 CFR 1.47 petition will not be appropriate and resort to the courts may be required (35 U.S.C. 256).

name: Reissue oath/declaration must state belief patent is inoperative or invalid
description: The reissue oath/declaration must contain a statement that the applicant believes the original patent to be wholly or partly inoperative or invalid—(1) by reason of a defective specification or drawing, or (2) by reason of the patentee claiming more or less than patentee had the right to claim in the patent.
guidance: MPEP provides example phrasings (e.g., 'Applicant believes the original patent to be partly inoperative or invalid by reason of a defective specification or drawing.'). If using PTO/SB/51 or PTO/SB/52 (or PTO/AIA/05/06), applicant must check appropriate box(es) identifying reasons; if not using a form, applicant must state each reason in the oath/declaration.

name: Reissue oath/declaration must identify at least one error (specificity)
description: The reissue applicant must acknowledge existence of an error in the specification, drawings, or claims which causes the original patent to be defective, and must specifically identify at least one such error being relied upon to support the reissue (35 U.S.C. 251).
guidance: Only one error need be specified; more than one may be specified; if some designated 'errors' are not errors under 35 U.S.C. 251, any remaining appropriate error still supports the reissue. It is not necessary to state how/when the error arose or was discovered; identification of 'at least one error' is required.

name: Additional specificity for broadening reissue (post-September 16, 2012)
description: For an application filed on or after September 16, 2012 that seeks to enlarge the scope of the claims, the reissue oath or declaration must identify a claim that the application seeks to broaden in the identification of the error relied upon to support the reissue; a general statement that all claims are broadened is insufficient.
guidance: It is sufficient to identify the claim being broadened and a single word, phrase, or expression in the specification or an original claim and how it renders the original patent wholly or partly inoperative or invalid. The corresponding corrective action need not be identified in the oath/declaration.

name: Insufficient/impermissible error-statements (anti-patterns)
description: Generic statements such as 'this application is being filed to correct errors in the patent which may be noted from the changes made in the disclosure' or merely reproducing claims with brackets/underlining without identifying specific errors are not sufficient; similarly, asserting 'failure to include a claim directed to …' by reciting new claim limitations without explaining what other claims lacked is insufficient.
guidance: Oath/declaration must point to specific claim(s) and specific claim language or explain, at least generally, what the remaining claims contain relative to the canceled or added claims. Simply canceling 'unduly broad' claims without identifying what they lacked is insufficient.

name: Continuation/divisional reissue oath reuse rules
description: A continuing reissue application may satisfy the oath requirement by copying the oath/declaration from the parent reissue application only if certain conditions are met (e.g., the inventor executed the oath for the earlier-filed reissue, the continuing reissue does not seek to enlarge claims, or the original patent application was filed under § 1.46 by the assignee).
guidance: If the parent oath does not identify an error that supports the continuation/divisional, the examiner should reject claims under 35 U.S.C. 251 and require a new oath/declaration. For continuations/divisionals filed before Sep 16, 2012, petitions under 37 CFR 1.183 may be needed to waive pre-AIA requirements when relying on a parent oath for a different corrective action. See MPEP § 1414.01 and 37 CFR 1.175(f)(2).

name: Manner of Making Amendments in Reexamination (§1.530 compliance)
description: Any proposed amendment to the description and claims in patents involved in reexamination proceedings must be made in accordance with §1.530; an amendment paper directs specified changes to the patent specification (including claims) or drawings and may accompany owner-request or be submitted during prosecution where permitted.
guidance: Amendment papers may be submitted with a request by patent owner under §1.510(e), as part of a patent owner statement under §1.530(b), or during prosecution per §1.550(a) or §1.937 where permitted.

name: Specification Amendments Must Present Entire Added/Rewritten Paragraphs
description: Changes to the specification other than to the claims must be made by submission of the entire text of any added or rewritten paragraph including markings pursuant to paragraph (f) of §1.530, except that an entire paragraph may be deleted by a statement deleting the paragraph without presentation of the text.
guidance: The precise point in the specification must be identified where any added or rewritten paragraph is located. This applies whether amendments are on paper or compact disc per §§1.96 and 1.825.

name: Changes Shown by Markings (brackets and underlining)
description: Any changes relative to the patent being reexamined which are made to the specification, including the claims, must show matter to be omitted enclosed in brackets and matter to be added underlined.
guidance: Markings pursuant to paragraph (f) of §1.530 govern presentation of additions and deletions.

name: Amendments Must Not Enlarge Claim Scope or Introduce New Matter
description: No amendment may enlarge the scope of the claims of the patent or introduce new matter. No amendment may be proposed for entry in an expired patent. No amendment, other than cancellation of claims, will be incorporated into the patent by a certificate issued after the expiration of the patent.
guidance: Absolute prohibition on enlarging claim scope or adding new matter; timing restrictions relative to patent expiration.

name: When combining prior art elements, show predictable results
description: A proper rejection based on the rationale that the claimed invention is a combination of prior art elements also includes a finding that results flowing from the combination would have been predictable to a person of ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: If results would not have been predictable, Office personnel should not enter an obviousness rejection using the combination-of-elements rationale and should withdraw such a rejection if it has been made (see Crocs example where combination yielded more than predictable results).

name: Simple substitution rationale (requirements for substitution rejection)
description: To reject a claim based on simple substitution of one known element for another, Office personnel must articulate specific findings resolving the Graham factual inquiries and the following four points.
guidance: The four findings to articulate are: (1) a finding that the prior art contained a device which differed from the claimed device by substitution of components; (2) a finding that the substituted components and their functions were known in the art; (3) a finding that one of ordinary skill could have substituted one known element for another and the results of the substitution would have been predictable; and (4) whatever additional Graham-based findings are necessary given the facts of the case. If any cannot be made, this rationale cannot support obviousness.

name: Consider capabilities of a person of ordinary skill (optimization)
description: When claimed differences are attainable by routine optimization, the knowing ability of a person of ordinary skill to adjust parameters can support an obviousness conclusion.
guidance: If optimization of application parameters was within the level of ordinary skill, an obviousness finding is more likely (Ecolab: expert admitted one skilled in the art would know how to adjust parameters and determine optimum values). Assess whether parameter tuning would have been routine.

name: Secondary considerations require a nexus and coextensiveness to claims
description: Objective evidence of nonobviousness (copying, praise, commercial success, skepticism) must have a nexus to the claimed invention and be coextensive with the claim scope to carry substantial weight.
guidance: If the proffered evidence is not coextensive with the claims or lacks nexus, it will be entitled to less weight (Muniauction: evidence lacked nexus and thus did not overcome the obviousness showing).

name: (iii) Grave injustice (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(iii))
description: "The imposition of the same public censure, public reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension or disciplinary disqualification by the Office would result in a grave injustice."
guidance: Claims of grave injustice can include arguments that the state proceeding was outside its authority (e.g., exclusive federal jurisdiction). Such jurisdictional preemption is narrowly construed: state disciplinary proceedings concerning ethical obligations typically are not preempted by federal patent law (see Christianson, Sperry, Kroll). To succeed requires a clear and convincing showing of a substantial, outcome-determinative injustice.

name: Due-process factual particulars accepted as satisfying (guidance from cases)
description: Specific elements constituting meaningful opportunity to be heard: notice of charges, participation in discovery, right to testify, present evidence, cross-examine witnesses, make objections, and present appellate challenges.
guidance: Case law (e.g., In re Squire, Mathews v. Eldridge, In re Zdravkovich) holds that attendance and active participation in hearings, ability to call/cross-examine witnesses, and the availability of counsel and appeal procedures satisfy due process. Tactical choices (e.g., not subpoenaing witnesses) preclude later claims of prejudice.

name: Recitation of specific technological solutions
description: Claims that recite specific technological solutions (as opposed to mere goals or results) are less likely to be directed to an abstract idea.
guidance: Example language: claims reciting ‘‘identifying and refining a conversational flow so that different connection flows can be associated with each other and ultimately an underlying application or protocol’’ were held not directed to an abstract idea because they recited a specific technological solution.

name: Specific technical solution to a specific technical problem
description: A claim directed to a specific technical solution to a specific technical problem (e.g., transparent data compression for telecommunications) supports patent-eligibility.
guidance: Courts look for an identifiable technical problem and a claimed technical solution that addresses it (e.g., ‘‘creating a method for compressing data in a transparent manner’’ was an eligible technical improvement).

name: Tangible, nonabstract device with unconventional component combination
description: Claims focusing on a tangible device whose components are combined in an unconventional way to provide new functionality are less likely to be abstract.
guidance: Haptic feedback claims were found eligible where they ‘‘focus[ed] on a tangible, nonabstract device . . . which, through the allegedly unconventional combination of components, contain[ed] the new and useful feature of notifying the device’s user of independent events through vibration.’’

name: Unconventional arrangement of claim elements (inventive concept)
description: An unconventional arrangement or ordered combination of claim elements can supply the requisite inventive concept under step two (Alice).
guidance: Courts treat the unconventionality of the claimed combination as a factual inquiry: if the ordered combination is ‘‘non-generic and non-conventional’’ in the industry, that supports eligibility.

name: Enhancement of conventional systems via specific mechanisms
description: Claims that enhance conventional systems by describing concrete mechanisms (e.g., converting various management data into a common format enabling remote monitoring) are more likely patent-eligible.
guidance: The presence of specific conversion/communication mechanisms that enable new functionality (remote monitoring/access) distinguishes claims from abstract ideas.

name: Claims not merely stating results but reciting how accomplished
description: Claims that do more than state a desired result (i.e., they also recite how that result is accomplished using specific structures or steps) weigh toward eligibility.
guidance: E.g., displaying location-relevant communications was eligible where the claims recited using location retrieved from a location server and functions stored in a datastore — i.e., how it was done, not only the result.

name: Claims tied to specific computer architectures or data structures
description: Limitations specifying particular architectures or data-structures (multi-layered data structures, semantic-to-nonsemantic routing) that improve scalability or flexibility indicate a technological improvement.
guidance: Courts have held that reciting ‘‘specific attributes’’ such as these can demonstrate the claimed invention is directed to a purported improvement to system flexibility/scalability rather than an abstract idea.

name: Sufficient factual development and claim construction required before eligibility determination
description: Courts may deny dismissal when the defendant’s analysis is inadequate or when factual development / claim construction are needed to determine whether claims are abstract or contain an inventive concept.
guidance: Example: a defendant provided ‘‘inadequate analysis and explanation of the substance of the claimed inventions, the prosecution history, and potential construction issues’’ so dismissal was denied without prejudice.

name: Claims that merely state conventional steps/methods without specific means are abstract
description: When claims describe known activities (e.g., sending/receiving/authenticating logon information) with no specific means for improving technology, they are often held abstract.
guidance: Court language: claims ‘‘directed to the abstract idea of ‘sending, receiving, and authenticating logon information, and not to a ‘specific means or method for improving technology.’’’

name: Claims that recite particular processing steps tethered to physical inputs/outputs
description: Where claimed processing steps are tied to physical inputs/outputs (e.g., camera images of user’s real physical space mapped into a virtual environment), the claims are less likely abstract.
guidance: Courts emphasize that mapping images from a user’s physical location into a virtual environment with specific instructions is not something humans can perform and thus may be patent-eligible.

name: Claims describing novel UI/interaction structures as structural improvements
description: Claims that define specific user-interface components or dialog structures that facilitate new presentation/sorting/selection behavior can be patent-eligible as structural improvements.
guidance: E.g., using a query dialog box designed to permit construction of filters and sort orders on the same screen was treated as a specific structural improvement over general methods of selecting/sorting data.

name: Claims producing tangible, physical results from sensor inputs
description: Claims that recite tangible physical results produced from sensor inputs (e.g., orientation status tracking with six-axis/nine-axis sensors and error correction) are less abstract.
guidance: Courts note such claims ‘‘entail more than simply performing a calculation or organizing information through mathematical correlations’’ when they yield tangible effects.

name: Claims directed to concrete physical tasks with specific tangible items in sequence
description: Claims that require performing specific physical tasks using specific tangible items in a specific order are not abstractions.
guidance: Example: pipe-pulling claims were held ‘‘not drawn to an abstraction, but to a concrete task’’ requiring specific physical tasks and tangible items in a specific order.

name: Claims that remove prior art dependencies or intermediaries via technical means
description: Claims that eliminate previously necessary third parties or intermediaries through a technical mechanism (e.g., transferring bar code data between mismatched systems) support eligibility.
guidance: Courts view solutions that remove dependency on ‘‘sophisticated software developed by third parties’’ through claimed mechanisms as technological improvements.

name: Claims addressing real-world operational problems in prior art
description: When the specification and claims identify concrete prior-art problems (e.g., failures to scan, detect theft) and claim elements address those problems, eligibility is supported.
guidance: Courts rely on allegations that the patented elements ‘‘allege to help resolve such problems’’ as evidence of technological improvement rather than abstract ideas.

name: Claims that are improvements in machine/device-read reliability
description: Claims that overcome technological limitations of machines (e.g., improving RFID tag readability) are treated as technological inventions.
guidance: The specification’s clear statement that the invention overcomes prior limitations (reader failures vs theft detection) supports eligibility.

name: Claims that improve industry-specific processes via technology
description: Claims that implement technology to improve narrow industry processes (e.g., turbine engine wash quality/safety) support eligibility when they are distinct from prior art methods.
guidance: Courts have found such industry-specific technological improvements ‘‘improve the narrow industry’’ and are not mere abstract ideas executed by a computer.

name: Claims that are tied to specific packet-level network mechanisms
description: Claims that classify at packet level and optimize data flow by assigning QoS characteristics are treated as technical solutions to technical problems in networking.
guidance: E.g., ‘‘classifying, on a packet level, what the ideal quality of services characteristics are for each type of data in order to optimize data flow’’ was held to present a technical solution.

name: Abstract idea + specific inventive solution (step two support)
description: Even if a claim is characterized as directed to an abstract idea, it can survive §101 under Alice step two if it contains a specific, inventive solution addressing recognized technical problems.
guidance: Example: deterministic mass messaging claims were held directed to communicating with groups quickly (abstract), but survive because they ‘‘present[ed] a specific, inventive solution to the problem . . . with messaging networks.’’

name: Whether an ordered combination is conventional is a factual question
description: Determining whether an ordered combination of claim elements is conventional/non-generic is typically a factual determination that can preclude dismissal at pleadings stage.
guidance: Courts often deny early dismissal where there is insufficient evidence to conclude the combination is conventional; factual development may be required.

name: Claims framed as improvements to device functioning rather than generic data handling
description: Courts distinguish claims that tie limitations to improved device functioning (e.g., portable device components configured to respond to specific events) from those that generically handle data or use vocabulary to convey information.
guidance: The presence of ‘‘specific components that are configured to perform specific functions in response to specific events’’ supports eligibility even if some abstract idea is present in part.

name: Specific limiting rules tied to digital image processing may confer eligibility
description: Claims that require extraction of structural and semantic saliency features and integrating them in particular ways tied to digital image processing can be viewed as technical and unconventional.
guidance: Courts consider whether such specific processing steps are ‘‘tied to digital image processing’’ and whether the specification plausibly alleges unconventionality.

name: Claim construction and further factual development can affect eligibility
description: Patent-eligibility analysis can depend on claim construction and factual development; courts may deny motions where claim construction could change the §101 outcome.
guidance: Example: video stream image modification claims where the specification characterized claims as unconventional and further factual development and claim construction could impact eligibility.

name: Claims relying on specification/expert testimony showing improvement
description: A claim supported by specification statements and expert testimony that the claimed method/framework ‘‘improves on previous data encoding methods’’ can meet the inventive concept requirement.
guidance: Courts give weight to specification characterization and expert testimony at motions stages when evaluating whether the claimed invention confers a technical improvement.

name: Claims directed to physical objects readily overcome Section 101 limits
description: Claims to tangible physical objects (e.g., bedframe, shoes) are generally patent-eligible subject matter under §101.
guidance: Courts state that claims ‘‘directed to a physical object [that] easily overcomes the Section 101 limit on patentability.’’ The specification’s description of manufacturing improvements may further support eligibility.

name: Claims measuring natural phenomena may be eligible if the measurement method is unconventional
description: Claims that measure a natural phenomenon can be patent-eligible if the claimed measurement method is not conventional, routine, or well-understood — i.e., the claim recites unconventional steps or coefficients discovered through development.
guidance: E.g., a forehead temperature detector claim was held not conventional because the inventor ‘‘determined for the first time the coefficient representing the relationship between temporal-temperature and core body temperature’’ and incorporated that into an unconventional measurement method.

name: Claims improving navigation/editing workflows can be eligible
description: Claims that recite specific methods improving user workflows (e.g., navigating and editing dictation transcripts without stopping playback) can be viewed as improvements in device functionality and thus patent-eligible.
