guidance: Court held transcription error recognition claims eligible because they ‘‘recite[d] specific methods for navigating and editing dictation transcripts more efficiently by eliminating the need to stop the acoustic playback each time a correction is made.’’

name: Claims that secure transactions via anonymous identification can be technological
description: Claims enabling anonymous identification that secures transactions without revealing merchant-identifying information can be considered improvements in computer functionality and thus eligible.
guidance: Court found such identity-authentication claims ‘‘directed to an improvement in computer functionality by enabling anonymous identification.’’

name: Claims to specific software architectures with defined inter-agent features
description: Claims that claim a concrete software architecture with facilitators for delegation/coordination, an inter-agent communication language, and a distributed process can be patent-eligible.
guidance: Court held cooperative software architecture claims not directed to an abstract idea because they recited a ‘‘specific software architecture’’ with enumerated technical features.

name: Claims to physical transmit/receive devices that improve prior art are eligible
description: Claims reciting physical devices (e.g., wireless transceivers that transmit authorization codes across protocols) that improve prior art device performance are treated as not abstract.
guidance: Court language: claims ‘‘not directed to an abstract idea, but rather to a physical device that improves the prior art.’’

name: Novelty under 35 U.S.C. 102
description: Begin by comparing the claimed subject matter to what is known in the prior art; if no differences are found between the claimed invention and the prior art, the claimed invention lacks novelty and is to be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102.
guidance: See MPEP §§ 2131-2146 for specific guidance on patentability determinations under 35 U.S.C. 102. Use applicable form paragraphs and confirm a prima facie case before imposing a rejection.

name: Nonobviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103
description: When differences are identified between the claimed invention and the prior art, assess whether those differences would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art; if not, the claimed invention satisfies 35 U.S.C. 103.
guidance: See MPEP §§ 2150-2159 for specific guidance on 35 U.S.C. 103. Ensure the analysis considers the knowledge possessed by a person of ordinary skill in the art and that a prima facie case is established before rejection.

name: Subject matter eligibility (two-criterion test under 35 U.S.C. 101)
description: Two criteria: (a) the claimed invention must fall within one of the four statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter); and (b) the claimed invention must be directed to patent-eligible subject matter and not to a judicial exception unless the claim as a whole includes additional limitations amounting to significantly more than the exception.
guidance: Judicial exceptions are abstract ideas, laws of nature, and natural phenomena (including products of nature). Use the Alice/Mayo two-part test for evaluating judicial exceptions (Step 2A/2B). See MPEP § 2106 and subsections for framework and detailed guidance.

name: Utility requirement (35 U.S.C. 101)
description: A claimed invention must be useful or have a utility that is specific, substantial and credible.
guidance: A rejection for lack of utility is appropriate when (1) it is not apparent why the invention is useful because applicant failed to identify any specific and substantial utility and there is no well established utility, or (2) an asserted specific and substantial utility is not credible. Such rejections can include inoperativeness (e.g., perpetual motion). Do not base a lack-of-utility rejection on grounds that the invention is frivolous, fraudulent, or against public policy. See MPEP § 2107 and subsections for guidance and form paragraphs.

name: Human organisms excluded from patenting (AIA sec. 33(a))
description: Notwithstanding any other provision of law, no patent may issue on a claim directed to or encompassing a human organism; if the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claimed invention encompasses a human organism, reject under 35 U.S.C. 101 and AIA sec. 33(a).
guidance: Use form paragraph 7.04.03 to reject a claim under 35 U.S.C. 101 and section 33(a). Explain in the Office action why the claim is interpreted to read on a human organism and follow the examiner notes for bracketed insertions and plurality.

name: Use Alice/Mayo two-part test for judicial exceptions
description: First determine whether the claims are directed to an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon (Step 2A). If so, determine whether the claim recites additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception (Step 2B), i.e., search for an 'inventive concept.'
guidance: The Alice/Mayo two-part test is the test that should be used to evaluate eligibility. The machine-or-transformation test and other older tests may be considered only as part of the 'integration' or 'significantly more' analysis, not as separate tests. Do not rely on superseded tests like 'useful, concrete, and tangible result' or the Alappat 'special purpose computer' rationale as standalone eligibility tests.

name: Establish the Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) before eligibility analysis
description: Claim construction under the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim as a whole must be established prior to examining a claim for eligibility because BRI sets the boundaries of coverage sought and influences whether the claim covers subject matter beyond the statutory categories or encompasses judicial exceptions.
guidance: Evaluating eligibility based on the BRI ensures eligibility does not depend on the draftsman's art. See MPEP § 2111. Claim interpretation examples (Mentor Graphics, Synopsys, Enfish, etc.) illustrate how BRI affects both Step 1 and the Alice/Mayo analysis.

name: Claim interpretation's effect on eligibility
description: Interpretation of claim terms can determine whether a claim falls within a statutory category or is directed to a judicial exception, and can affect whether additional elements amount to 'significantly more.'
guidance: Examples: Mentor Graphics (machine-readable medium construed to cover carrier waves -> non-statutory), Synopsys (claims interpreted as pure mental steps -> abstract idea), Enfish and McRO (constructions showing improvements in technology -> not directed to an abstract idea), Amdocs (term construction showing unconventional technical solution -> amounts to significantly more). Use specification and claim construction rules (including 35 U.S.C. 112(f) where applicable) in analysis.

name: Eligibility flowchart and three eligibility pathways (A/B/C)
description: Follow a two-step eligibility analysis (Step 1: statutory category; Step 2: Alice/Mayo test) and determine eligibility via one of three pathways: A (self-evident eligibility), B (Step1 YES and Step2A NO), or C (Step1 YES, Step2A YES, and Step2B YES). If none apply, reject under 35 U.S.C. 101.
guidance: Pathway A: streamlined analysis for self-evident eligibility (see MPEP § 2106.06). Pathway B: claims fall within a statutory category and are not directed to a judicial exception. Pathway C: claims fall within a statutory category, are directed to a judicial exception, but recite additional elements that amount to significantly more. If uncertain, examiners are encouraged to conduct the full eligibility analysis. Regardless of 101 outcome, complete examination under 35 U.S.C. 102, 103, 112 and utility/double patenting issues.

name: Eligibility Step 1: The four statutory categories
description: Confirm that the claim falls within one of the four statutory categories enumerated by 35 U.S.C. 101: processes, machines, manufactures, and compositions of matter.
guidance: If a claim covers material not found in any of the four statutory categories, it falls outside the scope of § 101 even if new and useful. See MPEP § 2106.03 for detailed information on the categories.

name: Title content conventions and prohibited leading words
description: The title should be brief but technically accurate and descriptive and should contain fewer than 500 characters. Words 'new,' 'improved,' 'improvement of,' 'improvement in' are not considered part of the title and should not be included at the beginning; the articles 'a,' 'an,' and 'the' should not be included as the first words and will be deleted when entered into Office computer records or when patent issues.
guidance: If title is not descriptive of the invention claimed, examiner should require substitution of a new title clearly indicative of the invention; if applicant does not supply satisfactory title, examiner may change title at allowance (examiner's amendment). Use form paragraphs 6.11 and 6.11.01 when requiring a title change.

name: Examiner may require change in title and suggested change practice
description: Where the title is not descriptive of the invention claimed, the examiner should require substitution of a new title that is clearly indicative of the invention to which the claims are directed.
guidance: Form paragraphs 6.11 (Title of Invention Is Not Descriptive) and 6.11.01 (Title of Invention, Suggested Change) may be used. If changing title, indicate change on file label or bib-data sheet and follow IFW/TC procedures for examiner's amendments.

name: Basic filing, search, and examination fees (37 CFR 1.16)
description: Patent application filing fees are set under 35 U.S.C. 41 and listed in 37 CFR 1.16. For nonprovisional applications filed on or after Dec 8, 2004, basic filing, search, and examination fees (and application size/excess claims fees if applicable) are required; for older filings different fee rules apply.
guidance: Fees are due on filing but may be paid later within time periods set by 37 CFR 1.53(f) (and surcharges may apply). Specific transitional rules apply for applications filed in particular date ranges; provisional and international national-stage applications have their own fee references (e.g., 37 CFR 1.492 for national stage).

name: Application size fee (37 CFR 1.16(s))
description: Application size fee applies when the specification (including claims) and drawings, excluding sequence listings or computer program listings in compliant electronic media, exceed 100 sheets of paper. The fee applies for each additional 50 sheets or fraction thereof over 100.
guidance: Sequence listings/computer program listings filed in electronic medium in compliance with rules are excluded. When submitted on electronic medium other than Office e-filing, each 3 kilobytes is counted as a sheet. For e-filed submissions, paper-size equivalent is 75% of the number of sheets when rendered by the Office e-filing system. Sequence listings in ASCII as associated file excluded; PDF/TIFF listings as part of specification/drawings are not excluded.

name: Excess claims fees (37 CFR 1.16(h),(i),(j))
description: Excess claims fee applies for each independent claim in excess of three (37 CFR 1.16(h)) and for each claim (independent or dependent) in excess of twenty (37 CFR 1.16(i)). A separate fee is required for an application containing a proper multiple dependent claim (37 CFR 1.16(j)).
guidance: Fees for multiple dependent claims are calculated based on the number of claims to which the multiple dependent claim refers (37 CFR 1.75(c)); improper multiple dependent claim charged as single dependent claim. Transitional rules apply for claims/fees across Dec 8, 2004. For reissue applications, original patent claims are not counted in determining excess claims fee for reissue.

name: Dependent claim treatment and improper dependent claims
description: For fee-determination purposes, a claim will be treated as dependent if it contains reference to one or more other claims. Any claim in dependent form that in fact is not a proper dependent claim (e.g., does not include every limitation of the claim on which it depends) must be canceled as not a proper dependent claim.
guidance: Cancellation of further claims depending on such improper dependent claim may be required. Applicant may amend the claims to place them in proper dependent form or redraft them as independent claims upon payment of any necessary additional fee.

name: Inclusion of nonelected claims after restriction for fee calculation
description: After a requirement for restriction, nonelected claims will be included in determining the fees due in connection with a subsequent amendment unless such claims are canceled.
guidance: Amendment canceling claims accompanying the papers constituting the application will be effective to diminish the number of claims to be considered in calculating filing fees. Preliminary amendments filed with response to Notice To File Missing Parts that cancel/add claims will be taken into account in determining appropriate fees due.

name: Order of applying insufficient payment for nonprovisional applications
description: If payment submitted for fees on filing is insufficient and applicant does not specify allocation, Office will apply payment in the following order until expended: (1) basic filing fee; (2) application size fee; (3) late filing surcharge; (4) processing fee for non-English application; (5) search fee; (6) examination fee; (7) excess claims fee.
guidance: This determines how partial payments are allocated when applicant is silent; separate order provided for provisional applications: (1) basic filing fee; (2) application size fee; (3) late filing surcharge.

name: Disclosure requirement and specification content (37 CFR 1.71)
description: The specification must include a written description of the invention and of the manner and process of making and using the same, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to make and use the invention. The specification must set forth the precise invention for which a patent is solicited, distinguish it from other inventions and from what is old, describe a specific embodiment, and explain mode of operation or principle when applicable. The best mode contemplated by the inventor must be set forth.
guidance: For improvements, specification must particularly point out parts of the process/machine/etc. to which improvement relates and be confined to the specific improvement and cooperating parts necessary for complete understanding. All amendments or claims must find descriptive basis in the original disclosure (no new matter).

name: Specification formatting and sheet separation (37 CFR 1.71(f))
description: The specification must commence on a separate sheet. Each sheet including part of the specification may not include other parts of the application or other information. The claim(s), abstract and sequence listing (if any) should not be included on a sheet including any other part of the application.
guidance: Director may require papers to be printed, typewritten, or on an electronic medium. Follow sheet-separation rules to avoid mixing parts on same sheet.

name: Claim-construction principle (ordinary meaning in context)
description: Claim terms must be construed in context; e.g., the Board construed 'defining' to mean 'setting' or 'establishing,' explaining that 'once the card information and fingerprint are received during enrollment, the card information provides data that establishes where, i.e., at what memory location or address, the system will store the fingerprint data.'
guidance: Adopt constructions grounded in the claim language, specification, and relevant intrinsic/extrinsic evidence. The Board may rely on dictionaries or technical references but must explain how the chosen meaning fits the claim context.

name: Prior-art disclosure must show controlling/establishing function when claim requires 'defining' a location
description: Mere 'association' of two pieces of data in a reference does not necessarily satisfy a claim limitation that requires 'defining,' 'setting,' or 'establishing' a memory location dependent upon received data; the prior art must disclose that the data element actually determines or establishes where the other data is stored.
guidance: When a claim requires that A (e.g., card information) defines the memory location for B (e.g., biometric data), the Board must point to disclosure or non-conclusory reasoning showing that A controls or determines the storage location rather than merely being associated with B. An inference that 'association' equals 'definition' requires evidentiary support.

name: Expert testimony must be non-conclusory to constitute substantial evidence
description: Conclusory expert testimony (mere assertions that a reference discloses a claim limitation or that a skilled artisan would do X) does not qualify as substantial evidence.
guidance: Experts must provide reasoning and evidentiary basis—explain mechanisms, cite relevant disclosure passages, or show common technical practice—rather than parroting claim language or labeling options as 'known' without support. See TQ Delta (conclusory testimony is insufficient).

name: Temporal sequencing evidence insufficient to prove functional control
description: Proof that one piece of information exists before storage of another (e.g., card information is received before biometric data is stored) does not by itself establish that the first piece of information 'sets' or 'establishes' the storage location of the second.
guidance: The Board must bridge the inferential gap with factual evidence or reasoned explanation that the temporal order implies the claimed functional relationship (control/definition), not leave the leap unaddressed.

name: Scope-of-review limitation when separate appeal resolved some claims
description: When a separate appeal has affirmed the unpatentability of certain claims, the reviewing court’s scope in the current appeal may be limited to the remaining claims not resolved by the other appeal.
guidance: Courts may decline to review arguments as to claims already finally resolved in another proceeding; cite XY, LLC v. Trans Ova Genetics for declining review because of a separate affirmance.

name: Use of dictionaries and technical references in construing claim terms
description: The Board may consult dictionaries (e.g., Merriam-Webster, Microsoft Computer Dictionary) or technical literature in construing claim terms, particularly to define ordinary meaning.
guidance: Extrinsic sources can support a claim construction, but the Board should tie dictionary meanings to the claim context and intrinsic evidence; relying on generic definitions without showing fit to the patent disclosure and claim language can be insufficient.

name: Representative-claim treatment in appeals
description: Parties may focus on a particular limitation of a representative claim and treat that claim as representative for appeal; the court may do likewise but must note limits (e.g., separate decisions may affect which claims remain for review).
guidance: When a claim is treated as representative, ensure the representativeness is appropriate for all challenged claims; otherwise, separately resolved appeals or different prior art may limit the scope of review.

name: Re-issue of generic patent cannot claim different species
description: Re-issue of generic patent cannot claim different species from original
guidance: From McClintock, Ex parte (1880) — limitation on scope of re-issue claims vis-à-vis original disclosure.

name: Duration of co-operation of combination elements
description: Duration of the co-operation of combination elements
guidance: Relevant to combination claims and their functioning over time (McKesson v. Carnrick).

name: Re-issue not to enlarge claims
description: Re-issue not to enlarge claims
guidance: Re-issue limitations (Miller v. Brass Co.; multiple entries on re-issue doctrine).

name: Combination-patent infringed by use of elements and subcombinations
description: Combination-patent infringed by use of elements and subcombinations
guidance: Infringement can occur by practicing portions that perform the claimed cooperation (Moody v. Fiske).

name: Claim for one form covers all forms (overbroad claims void)
description: Claim for one form of the invention covers all forms (void)
guidance: Claims that attempt to cover all modes of effecting a result may be invalid (O'Reilly v. Morse; other cites).

name: Patentee bound by the patent as accepted from Patent Office
description: Patentee bound by the patent as he accepts it from the Patent Office
guidance: Patentee cannot claim broader rights than the issued patent (New York Belting & Packing Co. v. Sibley).

name: Patent construed in view of nature of actual invention
description: Patent construed in view of the nature of the actual invention
guidance: Claims and specification are construed in light of what the inventor actually invented (Pidge v. Ferry).

name: Authorization of rejections under 37 CFR 1.193(a)(2) for amendments under 37 CFR 1.116
description: If an amendment under 37 CFR 1.116 proposes to combine limitations of previously rejected claims (e.g., combine claims 1 and 2 into a new claim), 37 CFR 1.193(a)(2) would authorize a rejection in the examiner's answer under 35 U.S.C. 103 on the basis of Reference A in view of Reference B, provided the applicant was advised that this rejection would be applied to the new/ amended claim.
guidance: Examples: combining claim 1 and 2 allows A in view of B rejection if that rejection was advised; combining claim 1 and 3 allows A in view of C rejection if advised. However, combining limitations of claims 1, 2, and 3 into a single new claim does NOT authorize a rejection of that new claim under A in view of B and C together even if the applicant was advised; such an amendment may raise a new issue and may be refused entry. Emphasizes that 1.193(a)(2) controls what rejections may be applied in an examiner's answer, but does not change 1.116 practice on whether an amendment is entitled to entry.

name: Expungement of information forming part of the original disclosure (MPEP § 724.05, IV)
description: A petition to expunge information that forms part of the original disclosure (specification, claims, drawings, prelim. amendments included in oath/declaration) must be filed under 37 CFR 1.183; such petitions ordinarily will not be favorably entertained.
guidance: Granting such a petition requires waiver of 37 CFR 1.59(a) and would require changing the USPTO record of the originally filed application (scanned into record), which may not be possible. Direct these petitions to the Office of Petitions and explain why justice requires waiver.

name: Information Disclosure Statement (IDS) content and timing requirements
description: Guidance on what constitutes compliant IDS content and the timing for filing IDSs (including handling omissions and timing when deadlines fall on weekends/holidays).
guidance: If a bona fide attempt is made to comply with IDS content requirements but part of the required content is inadvertently omitted, additional time may be given to enable full compliance. When no page numbers are supplied in an IDS, it is understood that all of the pages of the publication are the relevant pages. Clarified requirements for seeking consideration of documents other than the specification and drawings of a pending U.S. application cited in an IDS. The publisher of an Internet-obtained publication may be evident from the URL (see MPEP § 707.05(e)). There is no requirement for a copy of each U.S. patent or U.S. patent application publication listed in an IDS unless required by the Office. Circumstances under which electronic means/medium for filing IDSs is permitted are clarified. An IDS may be timely filed on the next succeeding business day if the last day of the three-month period set forth in 37 CFR 1.97(b)(1) and (b)(2) falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or a federal holiday in D.C. An IDS filed on the same day as or after the mailing date of an Ex parte Quayle action or notice of appeal must comply with 37 CFR 1.97(d). An IDS filed after the examiner has reached a final determination on patentability of the claims will be handled by the examiner as a “Printer Rush” per MPEP § 1309.02. A statement under 37 CFR 1.97(e) may be timely filed on the next succeeding business day if the last day falls on a weekend/holiday.

name: Handling IDSs filed after final/Printer Rush processing
description: How IDSs filed after an examiner’s final determination are handled.
guidance: An IDS filed after the examiner has reached a final determination on the patentability of the claims will be handled by the examiner as a “Printer Rush” per MPEP § 1309.02.

name: Entry of amendments under 37 CFR 1.312
description: Procedural rules on who must approve entry of amendments that affect specification disclosure, add claims, or change claim scope, and handling of formal amendments.
guidance: A recommendation must be forwarded to the supervisory patent examiner (SPE) for consideration and approval for an amendment under 37 CFR 1.312 which affects the disclosure of the specification, adds claims, or changes the scope of any claim. An examiner may approve the entry of an amendment under 37 CFR 1.312 concerning merely formal matters without the SPE signature. Form PTO-271 (Response to Rule 312 Communication) must be forwarded to the SPE for consideration, approval, and mailing when recommending to enter an amendment in part. Revised related form paragraphs (7.85, 7.86, 7.87).

name: Affidavits/declarations and other evidence traversing rejections (37 CFR 1.132)
description: Updated guidance on affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132 and treatment of other evidence (including publications) traversing rejections and nexus for objective evidence.
guidance: Section retitled to indicate it covers affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132 and other evidence; added discussion that publications may be evidence. Added two new paragraphs discussing requirements for affidavits and declarations and two new paragraphs regarding determining if there is a nexus between the merits of the claimed invention and the asserted objective evidence with citations to Federal Circuit precedent (Fox Factory, Demaco, In re Huang, In re Kao, WBIP v. Kohler, Campbell Soup, Teva v. Eli Lilly). Examiner should indicate an admitted affidavit or declaration on the Office Action Summary, Notice of Allowability, or Advisory Action cover sheet, as appropriate. Added cross references to MPEP §§ 716.01(b) and 2145 for nexus guidance.

name: Double patenting analysis and standards
description: Clarified rules and analyses for statutory and nonstatutory double patenting, including what constitutes serious burden and usage of reference patents/applications.
guidance: Changed 'common inventor' to 'common (joint) inventor' for consistency. Clarified that the serious burden requirement is a serious 'search and/or examination' burden and added explanation distinguishing serious examination burden from serious search burden and how to demonstrate serious examination burden. Election of species is a type of restriction requirement. Clarified explanations of scenarios in which double patenting may exist; updated basis for double patenting to remove emphasis on order of filing and updated citations (e.g., In re Van Ornum). Added explanation of when copending applications might raise double patenting issues and when an application can be utilized as a double patenting reference. Clarified that subject matter excepted under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) may not be used as a secondary teaching in a nonstatutory double patenting rejection; discussed applicability of benefit claims to patent term filing date; included changes resulting from Patent Law Treaties Implementation Act of 2012 and Uruguay Round Agreement Act. Updated many form paragraphs to align with statutory language.

name: Terminology and cross-reference updates (AIA definitions and CFR citations)
description: Replacements of terms and updated cross-references to reflect statutory/regulatory changes (e.g., AIA definition of 'inventor' vs 'applicant', updated CFR citations).
guidance: Replaced 'applicant derived' with 'inventor derived' and 'applicant’s invention' with 'the claimed invention' to reflect AIA definitions; replaced many references to older forms and rule citations (e.g., PTO/SB/08A and 08B to PTO/SB/08; eRed Folder to action folder; IFW to electronic file) and updated reproduced text of 37 CFR 1.102 and 37 CFR 1.121 to reflect ST.25/ST.26 rulemakings. Also deleted obsolete program references (e.g., Full First Action Interview Pilot Program).

name: Types of evidence to collect (physical, demonstrative, documentary, testimonial)
description: The main types of evidence collected are: Physical evidence: Physical objects or samples of infringing goods or material, usually collected through the making of a test purchase of the goods. Demonstrative evidence: photographs, diagrams, maps showing elements/locations. Documentary evidence: written or recorded documents or communications (IPR registration certificates, advertising or sales records, business documents and correspondence). Testimonial evidence: statements by persons about facts within their personal knowledge, under oath or by affidavit.
guidance: Use test purchases to obtain physical samples; take high-quality photographs and diagrams; collect business records showing sales/marketing; take sworn statements/affidavits from witnesses to support factual claims.

name: Comparative advertising limitations under the Code
description: The Code permits factual comparisons between products and services, but with clear limitations, including: adherence to all legal requirements, including compliance with the provisions of the Trade Marks Act; claims must be capable of substantiation; claims made must not be confusing or misleading and any claim must be material, relevant and objectively determinable; and there must also be no infringement of advertising goodwill.
guidance: Ensure comparative claims are provable, non-misleading, material and legally compliant; avoid using comparative material that infringes another's advertising goodwill.

name: Supplier responsibilities under the CPA
description: Suppliers must provide accurate and transparent information, honour warranties and guarantees, resolve consumer complaints, ensure product safety, and ensure fair pricing and advertising.
guidance: Suppliers should implement compliant terms, clear warranties and complaint-handling procedures to reduce risk of enforcement by the NCC or civil claims.

name: NDA substantive requirements & patent listing
description: An NDA must be supported by studies supporting the subject drug's safety and efficacy; drug efficacy studies must include adequate and well-controlled clinical investigations. NDA applicants must submit to FDA any patents that claim the drug itself or a method of using the drug for which approval is sought (for listing in the Orange Book).
guidance: Products approved through NDAs are often the reference listed drugs (RLDs) relied upon by ANDA applicants. NDA sponsors are required to list patents covering a drug substance, drug product, or an approved method of use; product-by-process patents where the product claimed is novel; and drug delivery system patents where the patent recites a drug substance or product.

name: Orange Book listing prohibitions and scope
description: FDA regulations prohibit the listing of patents claiming packaging, metabolites, intermediates, unapproved methods of use, or methods of manufacturing. The Orange Book lists drugs approved to be marketed in the United States and the patents sponsors submit for listing.
guidance: Orange Book listings should include patents covering drug substance, drug product, approved methods of use, product-by-process patents where product claimed is novel, and certain drug delivery system patents. FDA does not currently review the propriety of patents submitted for listing, which has led to disputes over improper listings.

name: Subject matter of the examination and required statutory compliance
description: The application must comply with the requirements of sections 34, 37 and 38 of the Patent Act, and the subject matter must be patentable under sections 1 to 5 of the Patent Act. Examination requires interpretation of the patent claim from the point of view of the competent skilled person, using the description and drawings.
guidance: The subject-matter must be searched based on this interpretation and examined for the explicit grounds for refusal under the Patent Act. Lack of 'clarity' should not be given as a single ground for refusal without interpretation of claims and carrying out a search.

name: Claim interpretation from skilled person's point of view
description: Claims must be interpreted from the viewpoint of the competent skilled person, using the description and drawings (see section 14 sentence 2), to determine the semantic content of the claim in its entirety and the contribution of individual features.
guidance: This interpretation defines the subject matter to be searched and assessed for patentability; description and drawings must be used where appropriate.

name: Novelty assessment (section 3)
description: During novelty examination it must be determined whether the subject matter differs in any respect from each individual prior publication or prior use. The subject matter is deemed new if each individual comparison shows at least one feature not comprised in the prior art; novelty is denied only if all claimed features can be inferred from a single citation.
guidance: The entire content of the prior teaching is relevant, and implicit disclosures may be 'read into' a document only if they are self-evident to the skilled person; one cannot add specialist knowledge beyond what the document discloses. Earlier applications’ content relevant for priority is to be considered; known substances may be patentable for a new therapeutic use (second medical indication) under section 3(3)/(4).

name: Inventive step assessment (section 4)
description: An invention involves an inventive step if, having regard to the state of the art, it is not obvious to a person skilled in the art. The assessment must be made on the basis of the state of the art available before the priority date, from the skilled person's perspective and avoiding a retrospective approach.
guidance: Define the competent skilled person (typically the developer, not the user). The skilled person must have had reason or a suggestion to choose the claimed solution. General expert knowledge may provide a reason in context, but its general suitability alone is not sufficient. Courts have not developed universally applicable specific criteria; case law can serve only as guidance. Auxiliary/post-hoc criteria may only in individual cases justify a critical review.

name: Role and definition of the person skilled in the art
description: For assessments of disclosure, novelty and inventive step, the relevant skilled person must be defined; the skilled person’s perspective is used to interpret claims, determine what is self-evident in prior art, and assess obviousness.
guidance: The skilled person is the one who would normally be assigned the technical task. If ascertained knowledge comes from another technical field it may be doubtful whether it belongs to that skilled person's knowledge. Teams of experts or consultations may be considered where appropriate.

name: Prior art search before filing
description: Search the USPTO patent database, Google Patents, foreign patent databases (Espacenet, J-PlatPat, KIPRIS), and academic literature.
guidance: The search informs what is novel and what claim scope is realistic.

name: Non-provisional application components
description: Required parts of a non-provisional application include: Title; Abstract; Background; Summary; Brief Description of Drawings; Detailed Description; Claims; Drawings; Oath/Declaration; Information Disclosure Statement.
guidance: Each component plays a role in disclosure and claim support (claims define the invention; the detailed description and drawings support the claims).

name: Types of formal training provided
description: Other than one-on-one mentorship, firms most often provide formal training on practice skills (e.g., claim drafting, case law review) 81.0% and business development 77.6%; personal growth 48.3%; team dynamics 44.8%; leadership 41.4%.
guidance: Guidance on common internal training priorities for IP practices and allocation of training resources.

name: Requirement of local agent and language for patent filings
description: Foreign applicants must file through a local agent; filings must be in Indonesian.
guidance: An application filed by an inventor or applicant who does not reside or have domicile in Indonesia must be filed through a local agent (art.28). Indonesian language required (art.24). If claims and description are in English they must be submitted with Indonesian translation no later than 30 days from filing date (art.34).

name: Rehearing where issues are narrowed by disclaimer
description: A disclaimer narrowing a claim does not change the issues such that a rehearing is required; it narrows but does not broaden the prior issues.
guidance: Case: Coburn v. Schroeder; disclaimer of part of a claim limits scope rather than expanding it.

name: Patent owner reply substance requirement (37 CFR 1.111)
description: To be entitled to reconsideration or further examination, the patent owner must reply in writing, distinctly and specifically pointing out supposed errors in the examiner’s action and must reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the prior Office action.
guidance: The reply must present arguments pointing out specific distinctions believed to render the claims patentable over applied references; a general allegation of patentability without specifics is inadequate. Show how amendments avoid references and why any 35 U.S.C. 112 rejections are incorrect or inapplicable.

name: Supplemental replies limited entry (37 CFR 1.111(a)(2)(i))
description: A supplemental reply will not be entered as a matter of right except where it is clearly limited to: (A) cancellation of claim(s); (B) adoption of examiner suggestion(s); (C) placement of the proceeding in condition for allowance/NIRC; (D) reply to an Office requirement made after the first reply was filed; (E) correction of informalities (e.g., typographical errors); or (F) simplification of issues for appeal.
guidance: A supplemental reply will be entered if filed within the period during which action by the Office is suspended under § 1.103(a) or (c).

name: Specification and drawing amendment format
description: Changes to the specification other than claims must be made by submission of the entire text of an added or rewritten paragraph including markings and must identify precise insertion points. Drawings changes must be submitted as a sketch on separate paper showing proposed changes in red for examiner approval.
guidance: Upon approval file new sheets of drawings complying with §1.84; amended figures identified as 'Amended', added figure as 'New', canceled figures bracketed and identified as 'Canceled.'

name: No enlargement of claim scope; no new matter
description: No amendment may enlarge the scope of the claims of the patent or introduce new matter; no amendment (other than cancellation) will be incorporated into an expired patent by certificate after expiration.
guidance: Amended or new claims which broaden or enlarge a claim should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 314(a). Apply same test as reissue enlarging claims (see In re Freeman and MPEP §2658). See MPEP §2670 for new matter handling.

name: Effect of patent expiration on amendments
description: If the patent expires during the reexamination procedure and the patent claims have been amended, the Office will hold the amendments as improper and subsequent reexamination will proceed on the basis of the unamended patent claims.
guidance: Once patent expires, a narrow claim construction is applied. See MPEP §2258 subsection I.G.

name: Title Requirements (37 CFR 1.1067)
description: The title of the design must designate the particular article in which the design is embodied; the title must correspond to the article named in the claim, and the title may not be directed to less than the claimed design.
guidance: Applicants may provide a title via an ADS (37 CFR 1.76) or by amending the specification (37 CFR 1.121). If applicant does not supply a title, the Office will establish one by retrieving the first listed product indication on the published international registration (INID code 54). When the article named in the title and the article named in the claim do not correspond, the examiner should object under 37 CFR 1.1067 and require correction (use Form Paragraph 29.59.02 or other form paragraphs as appropriate). When the applicant furnished the title, applicant approval is required for examiner's amendment to the title; when the Office established the title, applicant approval is not required.

name: Avoid 'Reference View' Terminology in Figure Descriptions
description: Applicants are cautioned against using 'reference view' as a figure description in international design applications designating the United States because that term has no special meaning in U.S. practice.
guidance: A 'reference view' will be treated as another view of the design and any inconsistencies between it and other figures may cause uncertainty as to claim scope, potentially leading to rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b) as nonenabling and indefinite. Describing a reference view as not included in the claimed design may still cause uncertainty if it includes features shown in other views.

name: Permissible and Prohibited Statements in Specification
description: Statements permissible in design applications under 35 U.S.C. chapter 16 (e.g., indicating nature & environmental use of design, purpose of broken lines) are permissible in nonprovisional international design applications; the specification may not include statements describing matters directed to function or unrelated to the design or suggest other embodiments not illustrated (except mirror images or obvious variants).
guidance: Statements that attempt to broaden the scope of the claimed design beyond what is shown are not permitted. Applicants may include statements explaining that protection is not sought for certain features; when excluding portions, applicants are strongly encouraged to indicate them by broken lines (or coloring) and include a statement explaining the meaning of broken lines/coloring (see MPEP §2920.05(c)).

name: Claim Form & Content — Single Claim Requirement (37 CFR 1.1025)
description: A design patent application may include only a single claim. The specific wording of the claim in an international design application designating the United States shall be in formal terms to the ornamental design for the article (specifying name of article) 'as shown' or 'as shown and described.'
guidance: If the specification includes a proper descriptive statement or showing of modified forms of the design, the words 'and described' must be added to the claim. Unless amended by applicant, the examiner should not object as to matters of form but should amend the claim by Examiner's Amendment to include 'and described' where appropriate. Use form paragraphs 15.62, 15.63, 15.64 to amend claim wording as needed.

name: Reproductions (Drawing Figures) — Must Be Complete and Clear (37 CFR 1.1026; Hague Rule 9)
description: Every design application must include a reproduction (drawing in black & white or color, or photograph) of the claimed design; because the drawing/photograph constitutes the entire visual disclosure of the claim, it must be a clear and complete depiction of the design applied to the article and nothing regarding the design sought to be patented should be left to conjecture.
guidance: Formal requirements for reproductions are set forth in Hague Agreement Rule 9 and Part Four of the Administrative Instructions. The USPTO may object to amended reproductions that fail to comply with these formal requirements (use Form ¶29.10). Drawing requirements in 37 CFR 1.84 generally do not apply, except as set forth in 37 CFR 1.84(c).

name: Restriction on Statements Describing Function or Other Embodiments
description: The specification of a nonprovisional international design application is not permitted to include statements describing matters that are directed to function or are unrelated to the design; the specification may also not include statements that describe or suggest other embodiments of the claimed design not illustrated in the drawing disclosure (except mirror images or shapes evident from the one shown).
guidance: Such prohibited statements may nevertheless be included in the original filing to provide antecedent basis for a future amendment, but applicants should not include statements that attempt to broaden the claimed design beyond what is shown.

name: Combining prior art elements — consider the problem known and the nature of modification
description: Even where a general method that could have been applied to make the claimed product was known and within the level of skill of the ordinary artisan, the claim may nevertheless be nonobvious if the problem which had suggested use of the method had been previously unknown. (In re Omeprazole Patent Litigation, 536 F.3d 1361 (Fed. Cir. 2008))
guidance: Modification that merely adds an extra process step or component that amounts to extra work and greater expense for no apparent reason is not the same as combining known prior art elements A and B where each would be expected to contribute known properties. Do not treat mere presence of elements in prior art as a complete statement of obviousness; analyze whether the prior art would have suggested making the combination for a reason and whether a problem motivating the change was known.

name: Combining prior art elements — predictability requirement (MPEP §2143 A(3))
description: A proper rejection based on the rationale that the claimed invention is a combination of prior art elements also includes a finding that results flowing from the combination would have been predictable to a person of ordinary skill in the art. MPEP § 2143 A(3).
guidance: ‘‘If results would not have been predictable, office personnel should not enter an obviousness rejection using the combination of prior art elements rationale, and should withdraw such a rejection if it has been made.’’ Include an explicit finding of predictability when relying on combination rationale; mere identification of elements is insufficient.

name: Specification must demonstrate 'possession' of the invention
description: The specification itself must demonstrate possession of the claimed invention; actual possession or reduction to practice outside the specification is not enough.
guidance: Possession language has been used historically although it may be 'not very enlightening'; nevertheless, the specification must show in a definite way that the inventor possessed the claimed invention.

name: Constructive reduction to practice can satisfy written description; actual examples not strictly required
description: The written description requirement does not demand either examples or an actual reduction to practice; a constructive reduction to practice that in a definite way identifies the claimed invention can satisfy the requirement.
guidance: Cites Falko-Gunter Falkner v. Inglis. However, the specification must still show possession — mere theoretical description without sufficient concrete disclosure may fail.

name: Written description does not require reciting claim terms verbatim, but mere obviousness is insufficient
description: The specification need not recite the claimed invention 'in haec verba', but a description that merely renders the invention obvious does not satisfy the requirement.
guidance: Cites Carnegie Mellon Univ. v. Hoffmann-La Roche and Lockwood v. American Airlines. Showing how to get to the invention by obvious steps is not the same as demonstrating possession.

name: No bright-line rule for number of species to support a genus claim; fact-specific inquiry
description: The Court will not set bright-line rules (e.g., a fixed number of species required to adequately describe a genus); satisfaction depends on the facts of each case.
guidance: Different facts lead to different outcomes; Wands factors and the state of the art (e.g., primitive/uncertain arts) will influence whether disclosure supports a genus claim.

name: Functional (result-oriented) genus claims require specification to recite sufficient materials to accomplish the claimed function
description: When a patent claims a genus by its function or result, the specification must recite sufficient materials to accomplish that function and demonstrate a generic invention that achieves the claimed result.
guidance: Particularly emphasized for biological arts: functional claim language that merely claims a desired result without describing species that achieve the result will fail written description.

name: Generic claim language in the original specification does not automatically satisfy written description
description: Generic claim language appearing in the original specification does not satisfy the written description requirement if it fails to support the scope of the genus claimed.
guidance: The Court uses the 'black box' analogy: defining boundaries without describing contents is insufficient. Cases cited include Fiers, Eli Lilly, and Enzo v. Genprobe as examples where generic language failed.

name: Written description applies to original and amended claims alike
description: There is no principled basis to distinguish original claims from amended claims for purposes of the written description requirement; even original claims can encompass subject matter not sufficiently described.
guidance: The requirement is not limited to policing priority; claims alone do not guarantee that the specification disclosed invention adequate to support claim scope.

name: Claims define boundaries/notice but are not a substitute for specification disclosure
description: Claims 'define the subject matter' and provide notice of the boundaries of the patentee's right to exclude, but their purpose is not to describe the invention — the specification must do that job.
guidance: Court emphasized that relying on claims to serve as the descriptive disclosure risks treating claim language as after-the-fact boundary-setting rather than description of what the inventor actually invented.

name: Written description serves to prevent overbroad claims that preempt future invention
description: The written description requirement helps curtail claims that do not require undue experimentation to make and use (and thus may satisfy enablement) but that have not been invented and thus cannot be described.
guidance: Cites policy concerns (e.g., Brenner v. Manson) that patents are compensation for a successful conclusion, not a reward for research; written description prevents preempting the future before it has arrived.

name: Particular importance of written description in chemical and biotechnological arts
description: A separate written description requirement plays a vital role in curtailing claims in chemical and biotech fields where enablement may be satisfied without the inventor having actually invented species within a broad genus.
guidance: Court stressed biotechnological examples where genus-by-function claims could claim a result without disclosing sufficient species; the doctrine is especially protective in unpredictable arts.

name: Description must provide sufficient species or a descriptive formula to identify others for broad genus claims
description: To support broad genus claims, the specification normally should identify a number of species and/or provide a descriptive formula or guidance enabling a PHOSITA to identify other species that fall within the genus.
guidance: There is 'no magic number' of species — what suffices depends on the technology and predictability; academic disclosures that stop at mechanism without describing useful compounds often fail.

name: Anti-pattern: avoiding recitation of species to skirt prior case law is disapproved
description: Strategies that attempt to avoid reciting specific molecules or species in claims to escape prior-case holdings (e.g., avoiding naming NF-kB inhibitors) are disfavored and may be rejected under written description analysis.
guidance: The Court specifically disapproved Ariad's approach of omitting molecule examples to circumvent prior decisions (e.g., University of Rochester v. G.D. Searle).

name: Alice/Mayo two-part test (primary framework)
description: All claims must be evaluated for eligibility using the two-part test from Alice/Mayo: (1) determine whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception (e.g., abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon) (Step 2A Prong One/Prong Two), and (2) if so, determine whether the claim recites significantly more than the exception (Step 2B).
guidance: Machine-or-transformation (M-or-T) is a useful investigative clue but is not a stand-alone test; a claim that passes Alice/Mayo is eligible even if it fails the M-or-T test, and a claim that fails Alice/Mayo is ineligible even if it passes the M-or-T test. See Bilski, McRO, DDR Holdings, and other cited cases for application.

name: Improvement to existing technology
description: Consider whether the claim demonstrates an improvement in an existing technological process or technology (as opposed to merely improving an abstract idea or business practice).
guidance: Improvement is relevant across technologies (computer-implemented, life sciences, etc.). The improvement must be to technology/computers themselves (e.g., improving how a computer performs a task), not merely an improvement in an abstract concept. Examples of sufficient improvements include particular computerized methods that solve technical problems (McRO, Diamond v. Diehr, Rapid Litig. Mgmt.), new or improved servers/telephone systems, improved data compression methods, specific GUIs improving transaction accuracy, and improved processes for preserving biological material. Non-examples include applying a commonplace business method on a general purpose computer, using standard lab techniques, or merely gathering/analyzing information using conventional techniques (see cited case law). See MPEP § 2106.05(a) and cited cases.

name: Detail of computer involvement / specific recitation of how computer aids method
description: To show that a computer's involvement improves technology, claims must recite details about how the computer aids the method, the extent of that aid, or the significance of the computer to performing the method.
guidance: Merely adding generic computer components or instructions to perform the method on generic machinery is not sufficient. If an applicant adds a 'generic computer' or claims it is 'specially programmed,' the examiner should assess whether those added elements integrate the exception into a practical application or provide significantly more than the judicial exception. See MPEP § 2106.05(f) and cases such as Ultramercial, TLI Communications, and Alice.

name: Whether the machine/apparatus implements the steps of the method (integral use)
description: Determine whether the machine plays an integral role in performing the claimed method steps (i.e., whether the machine implements the steps rather than merely serving as an object on which the method operates).
guidance: Integral use that enables the claimed method in a non-conventional way can integrate the exception into a practical application or provide significantly more. If the machine merely acts as an obvious mechanism or is only necessary for speed/automation, it likely does not add significantly more (see CyberSource; Versata discussion). Examiners should analyze whether the machine 'plays a significant part in permitting the claimed method to be performed.'

name: Whether machine involvement is extra-solution activity or mere field-of-use
description: Assess whether the machine's involvement imposes meaningful limits on the claim or is merely nominal/insignificant (e.g., data-gathering steps or field-of-use limitations).
guidance: Use of a machine that contributes only nominally to the execution of the claimed method will not integrate the exception into a practical application or provide significantly more. Data-gathering or stating the Internet as a data source without more are examples where machine recitation is insufficient. See Bilski, CyberSource, and MPEP §§ 2106.05(g),(h).

name: Whether the transformation is extra-solution activity or a field-of-use
description: Assess whether the transformation contributes meaningful limits to the claimed method or is merely an extra-solution activity/field-of-use that is nominal or insignificant.
guidance: A transformation that only amounts to a field-of-use limitation or nominal activity (e.g., administering a drug as merely a field-of-use in Mayo) will not provide significantly more. See Mayo and related discussion; see MPEP §§ 2106.05(g),(h) for more on insignificant extra-solution activity and field-of-use.

name: Known-in-art can still be unconventional (novelty separate from eligibility)
description: An additional element that is known in the art may nevertheless be unconventional or non-routine for purposes of eligibility; novelty/obviousness are distinct issues from Section 101 eligibility.
guidance: Claims may improve conventional computer functionality and be eligible even if the improvement lacks novelty over the prior art. See Enfish (eligible despite anticipation in prior art) contrasted with related cases; assess whether the known element in context is unconventional or confining in a way that provides significantly more.

name: Definition of practicing law (Massachusetts standard, In re Hrones)
description: "Directing and managing the enforcement of legal claims and the establishment of the legal rights of others, where it is necessary to form and to act upon opinions as to what those rights are and as to the legal methods which must be adopted to enforce them, the practice of giving or furnishing legal advice as to such rights and methods and the practice, as an occupation, of drafting documents by which such rights are created, modified, surrendered or secured."
guidance: Crafting and prosecuting a sophisticated civil rights lawsuit — drafting complex complaints and directing litigation strategy — falls squarely within the practice of law under this definition. The Tribunal used this to conclude that drafting and managing multi-count complaints constituted practice in Massachusetts.

name: Credibility expectations when claiming client notification of suspension
description: An attorney claiming to have notified a client of suspension should have corroborating evidence; 'Any nominally cautious and competent attorney would notify his client of his suspension in writing or at least create a written memorandum of the notice given for his own record purposes.'
guidance: Uncorroborated after-the-fact assertions that a client was verbally notified of suspension are treated as self-serving and may be disbelieved by the Tribunal absent supporting documentation or testimony.

name: Selective prosecution defense requires proof of both discriminatory effect and discriminatory intent
description: To succeed on selective prosecution, a defendant must show 'that the federal prosecutorial policy had both a discriminatory effect and a discriminatory intent.' (citing United States v. Darwich)
guidance: Generalized claims, internet postings, or conspiracy theories do not satisfy the burden; the tribunal rejected selective prosecution claims absent clear evidence of both effect and intent.

name: Two criteria for 35 U.S.C. 101 eligibility (two-step test)
description: There are two criteria for determining subject matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 101 and both must be satisfied. The claimed invention (1) must be directed to one of the four statutory categories, and (2) must not be wholly directed to subject matter encompassing a judicially recognized exception.
guidance: The following two step analysis is used to evaluate these criteria (Step 1: statutory category; Step 2: judicial exceptions). Both criteria must be satisfied for eligibility.

name: Step 1 — Directed to a statutory category
description: Step 1: Is the claim directed to one of the four patent-eligible subject matter categories: process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter? The subject matter of the claim must be directed to one of the four subject matter categories. If it is not, the claim is not eligible for patent protection and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101.
guidance: If the claimed invention is clearly not within one of the four categories, then a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 must be made. However, when the claim fails under Step 1 and it appears the claim could be amended to be directed to a statutory category, Step 2 should still be conducted.

name: Non-limiting examples of non-statutory subject matter
description: Non-limiting examples of claims that are not directed to one of the statutory categories include: transitory forms of signal transmission (e.g., a propagating electrical or electromagnetic signal per se); a human per se; a legal contractual agreement between two parties; a computer program per se; a company; a mere arrangement of printed matter; and data per se.
guidance: Each example is supported by case law citations (e.g., In re Nuijten; AIA; In re Ferguson; Gottschalk v. Benson; In re Miller; Digitech Image Tech.). Use these examples when assessing whether a claim falls outside the statutory categories.

name: Claim breadth that includes non-statutory embodiments (Step 1 failure)
description: A claim that covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments (under the broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the specification and a person skilled in the art) embraces subject matter that is not eligible for patent protection and therefore is directed to non-statutory subject matter.
guidance: If the broadest reasonable interpretation of a claim encompasses non-statutory embodiments (e.g., machine-readable media that can be a carrier wave), a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 as failing to claim statutory subject matter is appropriate.

name: Step 2 — Judicial exceptions (abstract ideas, laws of nature, natural phenomena)
description: Step 2: Does the claim wholly embrace a judicially recognized exception, which includes laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas? Determining that a claim falls within one of the four categories does not end the eligibility analysis because claims directed to nothing more than abstract ideas, natural phenomena, and laws of nature are not eligible.
guidance: Judicial exceptions have been described using various other terms, including 'physical phenomena,' 'scientific principles,' 'systems that depend on human intelligence alone,' 'disembodied concepts,' 'mental processes,' and 'disembodied mathematical algorithms and formulas.' See Alice, Myriad, Bilski and related cases for application.

name: Analysis for claims directed to judicial exceptions — 'significantly more' / inventive concept
description: If a claim is directed to a judicial exception, analyze whether the elements of the claim, considered both individually and as an ordered combination, are sufficient to ensure that the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the exception itself—this is a search for an inventive concept.
guidance: Consider whether the claim as a whole is for a particular application of an abstract idea, natural phenomenon, or law of nature, as opposed to the abstract idea, natural phenomenon, or law of nature itself. See Alice, Mayo, and Diehr for the courts' framework and examples.

name: Establish on the record a prima facie case (examiner burden)
description: USPTO personnel should review the totality of the evidence (e.g., the specification, claims, relevant prior art) before reaching a conclusion. USPTO personnel must reach a conclusion as to whether it is more likely than not that the claimed invention as a whole either falls outside of one of the enumerated statutory classes or within one of the exceptions to statutory subject matter. 'The examiner bears the initial burden … of presenting a prima facie case of unpatentability.'
guidance: If the record as a whole suggests it is more likely than not that the claimed invention would be considered significantly more than an exception, then USPTO personnel should not reject the claim. After USPTO personnel identify and explain why a claim is for an exception without significantly more, the burden shifts to the applicant to amend the claim or show eligibility (e.g., In re Brana).

name: Procedural action when claim fails Step 1
description: If the claimed invention is clearly not within one of the four categories, then a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 must be made indicating that the claimed invention is directed to non-statutory subject matter.
guidance: Form paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01 should be used; see MPEP § 706.03(a). Nonetheless, if the claim could be amended to be directed to a statutory category, Step 2 analysis should still be performed.

name: Patent formalities and specification of claims in the bill
description: A bill in equity ... must show compliance with Section 4886 ... that the invention had not been previously patented or described in a printed publication, that the patentee is the original inventor, and ... title in the complainant. Furthermore, it must allege that the patent was issued in the name of the United States and under the seal of the Patent Office and that it was signed by the Commissioner of Patents. ... The purport of the patent is properly embodied in a bill of complaint, by making profert therein, of the patent on which the bill is based. But the particular claims of the patent which the complainant intends to prosecute in the case, must be specified by their numbers in the stating part of the bill of complaint. If, however, the bill charges infringement of 'the claims' of the patent in suit, it will be construed to charge infringement of all the claims...
guidance: Plead statutory prerequisites (e.g., prior use, novelty, inventorship, title) and patent issuance formalities unless profert is used; specify claim numbers you will press (or be prepared that alleging 'the claims' will be deemed to allege all claims). Modern Rule 25 practice may permit shorter allegations (issuance and chain of title).

name: Scrutiny checklist for applications
description: Office checks jurisdiction, proof of right to file, prescribed formats and completeness of filings.
guidance: Specific checks include: correct jurisdiction; proof of right filed (or within six months or via petition); documents in prescribed forms (requests, petitions, assignment deeds, translations); correct paper size, font, spacing; signatures; abstract and drawings format; meaningful claims present; Power of Attorney or attested copy; Form-5 where applicable; Form-6 if invention assigned; if right assigned to legal entity, balance fees invited.

name: Required particulars in Official Patent Journal publication
description: The Official Journal is published weekly with specific particulars about each application.
guidance: Particulars include: application number; date of filing; title of invention; publication date; International Patent Classification; name and address of applicant; name of inventor(s); priority details; references to patent of addition/divisional and parent filing date; abstract; number of claims; drawings (if any).

name: Effects of publication
description: After publication the Specification and drawings are made available to the public; biological materials deposited become available; patentee can claim damages from date of publication but can sue only after grant.
guidance: Depository institution will make biological material available after publication; certain pre-2005 applications have rights accruing from date of grant with limited remedies; no patent shall be granted before expiry of six months from publication.

name: Provisional specification content requirements
description: A provisional specification must contain the title and description and start with the preamble 'The following Specification describes the invention.' Claims may not be included.
guidance: Description should include field of invention, background, object and statement of the invention; include as much information as available to adequately distinguish from prior art. Provisional specification cannot be filed for Divisional, Convention or PCT National Phase Applications.

name: Complete specification essential elements
description: Complete specification must (1) fully and particularly describe the invention and operation/use and method of performing it, (2) disclose the best method known, (3) end with claim(s) defining the scope of protection, and (4) reference deposit of biological material if applicable.
guidance: These are statutory requirements under Section 10; failure to meet them can affect patentability and validity.

name: Title drafting requirements
description: Title should be sufficiently indicative of inventive features, brief, precise, free from fancy expressions or ambiguity, normally consisting of around fifteen words.
guidance: Do not include inventor's name, the word 'Patent', words in other languages, abbreviations like 'etc' or fancy brand-like expressions. Title need not match preamble of main claim.

name: Claims as defining legal scope
description: Claims state technical facts in legal terms defining the scope of invention sought; no monopoly is obtained for matter not claimed.
guidance: Claims are critical and should be drafted carefully to cover aspects distinguishing from prior art; what is not claimed is open to public use; claims form the protective boundary and should be clear and precise.

name: Unity and clarity of claims
description: Claims must relate to a single invention or to a group of inventions linked as a single inventive concept; claims shall be clear, succinct and fairly based on matter disclosed.
guidance: Each claim must be fairly supported by the description; lack of unity or clarity can lead to objections.

name: Significance and independence of individual claims
description: Each claim is evaluated on its own merits; an objection to one claim does not invalidate others; applicants should claim all aspects to maximize protection.
guidance: Claims should be concise, precise and accurate so others can identify boundaries; draft multiple claims covering different aspects.

name: Appropriate breadth of claims
description: Claims must not be too broad (to avoid covering public domain/others' subject matter) nor too narrow (which would reduce enforceability).
guidance: Start with broad claims and progress to narrower dependent claims; avoid vague expressions like 'any novel matter' or subjective terms without definite values; many claims with differing scopes are useful.

name: Form and structure of claims
description: Claims must follow the prescribed format: start with 'I/We claim', be serially numbered, start on a fresh page after description, be single-sentence, clear and not verbose; there is no limit on number but fees apply beyond ten.
guidance: Each claim must be fairly based on disclosed matter and use terms found in or clearly inferred from the description. Avoid vague words ('thin', 'strong', 'any'). Trademarks should not be used unless unavoidable; if used, indicate registration status. A claim usually has preamble, transitional phrase (comprising, including, consisting of, consisting essentially of) and body. For improvements, use 'characterized by' or 'wherein' to separate prior art portion from novel features. The first claim is normally independent and should define essential novel features of preferred embodiment; multiple independent claims allowed if they fall under a single inventive concept.

name: Ordre public and morality exclusions (TRIPs Articles 27(2),(3))
description: Member states may exclude inventions from patentability to protect ordre public or morality, including exceptions 'to protect human, animal, or plant life or to avoid serious prejudice to the environment.'
guidance: When applying morality exclusions, consider factors like public health benefit, containment and environmental release risk, and reduction of animal suffering. Example: EPO’s handling of the Harvard Oncomouse — narrowing claim scope (to mouse) and lab-restricted use supported patentability because the object was to save human life and reduce overall animal testing.

name: Universities may establish copyright in scientific/technical articles without prior government approval
description: FAR 52.227-14(c) permits contractors to establish, without prior government approval, copyright in scientific and technical articles that contain 'data first produced in the performance of the contract' if published in academic, technical, or professional journals, symposia proceedings, or similar media.
guidance: Institutions can pursue scholarly publication and claim copyright in such articles; verify that contract alternates or agency-specific rules do not impose additional requirements.

name: FAR permission for universities/colleges to claim copyright in data for basic/applied research contracts
description: In contracts for basic or applied research performed solely by universities and colleges, FAR allows universities and colleges to claim copyright in any data (including computer software) produced under the contract.
guidance: This FAR provision protects academic dissemination and limits contractual restrictions on conduct/reporting of unclassified research, except as otherwise provided by U.S. statutes. Administrators should ensure contract language preserves publication rights.

name: DOE and NASA special rules for computer software where agency acquires contract rights
description: Where DOE (and similarly NASA) acquires contract rights to data, it requires DOE permission to claim copyright for any computer software produced under the contract; NASA has a similar restriction.
guidance: When negotiating DOE or NASA contracts, expect agency-specific limitations on asserting copyrights for software if the agency takes contract rights; plan negotiations and proposal-stage discussions accordingly.

name: Materiality standard under 37 CFR 1.56(b)
description: Information is material to patentability when it is not cumulative and (1) establishes, by itself or in combination with other information, a prima facie case of unpatentability of a claim; or (2) refutes, or is inconsistent with, a position the applicant takes in opposing an Office rejection or asserting patentability.
guidance: A prima facie case of unpatentability is established when the information compels a conclusion that a claim is unpatentable under the preponderance of the evidence standard, giving each claim term its broadest reasonable construction consistent with the specification, and before considering applicant's evidence to the contrary. In close cases, applicants should consider submitting the information; the Office may consider harmonizing materiality to a 'but-for' standard consistent with Therasense.

name: Prior art cited in related foreign applications is presumptively material
description: Applicants and associated individuals have a duty to bring to the Office any material prior art or other information cited or brought to their attention in any related foreign application; such references are especially likely material if used to reject similar claims abroad.
guidance: Foreign counsel and applicants must ensure adverse foreign-cited references are communicated to US prosecution counsel and to the USPTO; withholding such foreign-cited prior art can lead to inequitable conduct findings (Gemveto example).

name: Inherency in anticipating method claims
description: A prior art device or reference may inherently perform a claimed method when used in its 'normal and usual operation'; a prima facie case of anticipation can be made on that basis.
guidance: If a prior art structure inherently performs the claimed function (e.g., Donley inherently performs the function when used in ambient light), the examiner should explain that inherency. It is then up to the applicant to prove the prior art structure would not perform the claimed method when used normally. Examples: Donley/King (coated substrate inherent absorption/reflection), In re Best (cooling step inherent in handling Hansford's zeolite). Evidence comparing properties or showing a difference in operation could rebut the rejection; absence of such evidence supports anticipation under 35 U.S.C. 102.

name: Patentability of new uses of old structures
description: Discovery of a new use for an old structure based on previously unknown properties might be patentable as a process of using, but if the claim is directed to a result/property of an old composition/structure, it may be anticipated.
guidance: Case law: In re Hack supports patentability of new uses; In re May holds claims directed to a result/property of old compounds were anticipated where prior art disclosed same compounds and a method for effecting the same result (even if silent on another property like addiction). The mere finding of a new property in an old composition is 'tantamount only to finding a property in the old composition' and may not render a new patentable use. Applicants should claim/processes directed to new compounds or show unexpected properties to avoid anticipation/obviousness rejections (see Tomlinson, May, and Tomlinson examples).

name: Product-by-process claims judged by the product, not production steps
description: Product-by-process claims are defined by the process in the claim, but patentability is determined based on the product itself; if the product is the same as or obvious from a prior art product, the product-by-process claim is unpatentable even if made by a different process.
guidance: Authority: In re Thorpe, Amgen v. Roche, Biogen v. EMD Serono, United Therapeutics v. Liquidia, Purdue Pharma v. Epic. Examiners should compare the claimed product to prior art products; if identical or obvious from prior art products, reject under 35 U.S.C. 102/103. Note: for infringement analysis, a product-by-process claim is infringed only by a product made by the recited process. The examiner should consider both anticipation and obviousness aspects when relying on prior art products made by different processes.

name: Consideration of structure implied by process steps for product-by-process claims
description: Process steps in a product-by-process claim can imply structural characteristics of the product; those implied structures should be considered when assessing patentability over prior art.
