guidance: If the manufacturing process would be expected to impart structural characteristics to the final product, the implied structure can limit the claim (In re Garnero; In re Nordt Dev. Co.). Terms like 'interbonded by interfusion,' 'welded,' 'intermixed,' 'ground in place,' 'press fitted,' and 'etched' may be construed as structural limitations. Examiners should consider whether the process language conveys a structural limitation that distinguishes the product from prior art.

name: Manner of operating a device does not impart patentability to an apparatus claim
description: An apparatus claim covers what a device is, not how it is used; reciting the intended manner of use (preamble recitation) does not differentiate the claim from prior art if the prior art teaches all structural limitations.
guidance: Cases: Hewlett-Packard Co. v. Bausch & Lomb; Ex parte Masham. For example, a claim preamble stating 'for mixing flowing developer material' does not distinguish the apparatus if the prior art structure is the same despite differences in degree of submersion or intended use. Examiners should focus on structural elements rather than recited intended use.

name: Apparatus that performs claimed functions may still not anticipate if structural difference exists
description: Even if a prior art device can perform all the functions recited in the claim, anticipation requires disclosure (express or inherent) of the claimed structure; a structural difference can prevent anticipation.
guidance: Means-plus-function limitations are met only by structures equivalent to the corresponding structures in the specification (In re Donaldson). Example: a diaper reference disclosed two fastening elements that could perform the same function as three claimed elements, but the court required three separate elements (In re Robertson). Examiners must evaluate structural disclosure, not just functional capability.

name: Computer-implemented functional claim limitations — claim construction and patentability
description: Functional claim language not tied to specific structure covers all devices capable of performing the recited function; a prior art device that inherently performs the function may support a rejection, but claim construction can narrow a claim to hardware+software where appropriate.
guidance: Examples and guidance: In re Translogic ('coupled to receive' construed as 'capable of receiving'); Intel Corp. (programmable means can be programmed to perform claimed functionality); Nazomi Communications (claims construed to require hardware+software when hardware alone cannot meet limitations); Paulsen (broad 'computer' can encompass calculators). Automation of known functions on a general-purpose computer may be obvious (KSR) and applying routine computer/web technologies can be predictable. Examiners should consider specification support and claim construction to determine whether functional language requires specific structure (hardware, software) or is broad enough to read on prior art devices.

name: Effect of novel/nonobvious starting material or end product on obviousness
description: A process limited to making or using a novel and nonobvious product does not automatically make the process nonobvious; obviousness under §103 requires a fact-specific, whole-invention comparison to prior art.
guidance: Per In re Ochiai and In re Brouwer, per se rules are improper; a process yielding a novel and nonobvious product may nonetheless be obvious and vice versa. Applicants/Examiners must consider all claim limitations; cases illustrate outcomes both ways (Durden, Albertson, Kanter found obvious; Pleuddemann, Kuehl, Mancy found patentable). Treat language reciting making/using a nonobvious product as a material limitation for claim construction/analysis.

name: Definition and treatment of Markush claims
description: A Markush claim recites a list of alternatively useable members (a 'Markush group'); claims reciting alternatively usable members, regardless of format, should be treated as Markush claims.
guidance: Origins: Ex parte Markush; In re Harnisch. Markush groupings commonly appear in chemistry, biology, pharmacology, but can also be used in mechanical/process contexts. Terms like 'selected from the group consisting of' typically indicate a closed group, and 'consisting of' carries a strong presumption of being closed. See MPEP §2111.03 for 'consisting of' treatment and MPEP §803.02 for election/search/examination of claims with Markush groupings.

name: Substitutability and common use standards for Markush groupings
description: Where a Markush grouping describes part of a combination or process, alternatives must be substitutable with an expectation the same result will be achieved; for chemical compounds, the compound as a whole determines propriety even if individual members differ.
guidance: Example: in a combination/process context, alternatives must be functionally equivalent in the context of the claimed invention. For chemical compounds recited as part of a compound, the propriety of grouping is based on considering each alternative compound as a whole (In re Harnisch, In re Jones). Examiners should determine whether members are members of a recognized class or share an essential structural feature that supports a common use.

name: Single structural similarity standard for Markush groups
description: Members of a Markush group share a 'single structural similarity' when they belong to the same recognized physical/chemical/art-recognized class such that members are expected to behave similarly in the claimed context.
guidance: A recognized class is one where art knowledge gives an expectation members will behave the same in the claimed invention (e.g., diaper fasteners that are known to be substitutable). Where a Markush group includes only members from a recognized class, the existence of the group may itself evidence equivalence and, if one member is anticipated, the group may be rendered unpatentable absent convincing evidence of non-equivalency (In re Ruff). Examiners should assess whether the group members belong to such recognized classes.

name: Common use derived from substantial structural feature in Markush claims
description: When alternative compounds do not obviously belong to a recognized class, they may still be proper Markush members if they share a substantial structural feature essential to a common use.
guidance: If compounds share a substantial structural feature that is essential to achieving the claimed function, that structural commonality can support the propriety of the Markush grouping (Ex parte Hozumi). The examiner should look for disclosure in the specification or art evidence that the members are functionally equivalent or share the necessary structural feature for the claimed use.

name: Methods and use-claims generally excluded but narrow exceptions exist
description: Utility models cannot be used to protect method or use claims (§2 No. 3 Utility Model Act) in principle.
guidance: Case law (Federal Supreme Court) has allowed exceptions: (1) the use of a substance for treatment can be protectable if claims contain elements of a product claim (a drug); (2) product claims containing method features may be permitted if those method features indicate how structural features must be implemented (allowing product-by-process claims). Thus drafting to include product elements can preserve eligibility.

name: Branching off (filing from earlier patent applications) — timing and conditions
description: A utility model may be 'branched off' from an earlier German, European or PCT application (§5 Utility Model Act). Branching off is admissible up to the expiration of two months from the end of the month in which processing of the patent application or any opposition procedure is terminated, and the branched-off UM must be filed by the end of the tenth year from the date of filing of the earlier patent application.
guidance: Normally a pending patent application is required (cannot be branched off from a granted patent), except an exception exists if opposition proceedings are commenced; the branched-off UM can claim the priority and filing date of the parent to the extent claims are supported by the earlier application.

name: Claim drafting requirements and considerations
description: Claims for utility models "must be supported by the parent patent application" and "the subject matter of the utility model claims should be novel and inventive in view of the known prior art." Principles of claim construction must be taken into account.
guidance: Practical drafting tactics include tailoring claims to the infringing embodiment, branching off several UMs with different claim sets (claims must be somehow different from each other), claiming different aspects or perspectives of the same invention, and using UMs to adapt claim language to competitors' products. Expect GPTO and Federal Patent Court to be more flexible than EPO on support/formalities, but support remains necessary.

name: Earlier enforceability and scope of remedies
description: The utility model applicant obtains an enforceable right from the day of its registration and can sue an accused infringer on the basis of the utility model; damages can be claimed as soon as the utility model has been registered.
guidance: Because enforcement and full damages can commence at registration (2–3 months post-filing), UMs can stop infringing products earlier than a patent would. Compensation based on a registered UM may be higher than provisional remedies available from a published patent application.

name: Use in a portfolio: building a 'thicket' and simultaneous enforcement
description: A patentee can assert the granted patent and additionally one or more utility models against a competitor; UMs can help build a thicket of intellectual property rights to bolster enforcement strategy.
guidance: When drafting multiple UMs, ensure claims are 'somehow different' between applications; use UMs to adapt to market developments and to tailor claims closely to competitors' products for quicker enforcement.

name: Commercially-available prior art systems and enablement
description: The commercial availability of an identified prior art computer system is very pertinent to the issue of enablement, but in some cases this approach may not be sufficient to meet the applicant’s burden.
guidance: Merely citing excerpts from technical publications or a commercially-available system is insufficient unless it is made clear which parts/which circuits could be used and how they would be interconnected to construct the claimed device. Analysis is less critical where the circuits are essentially standard components of an identified prior art computer system and a standard device attached thereto (see In re Forman).

name: When utility requirement is not satisfied (operative/useful)
description: If a claim fails to meet the utility requirement of 35 U.S.C. 101 because it is shown to be nonuseful or inoperative, then it necessarily fails to meet the how-to-use aspect of the enablement requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a).
guidance: Examiner should make both rejections (under 35 U.S.C. 101 and 35 U.S.C. 112(a)) where subject matter is shown to be nonuseful/inoperative (see In re Fouche). The 112(a) rejection should indicate that because the invention lacks utility, a skilled person would not be able to use it as claimed. Office personnel should not impose a 112(a) rejection grounded on 'lack of utility' unless a proper 101 rejection is also made and factual showing for 101 is provided.

name: Examiner burden and applicant rebuttal on utility
description: When the examiner concludes an application claims an invention that is nonuseful, inoperative, or contradicts known scientific principles, the burden is on the examiner to provide a reasonable basis to support this conclusion; if a proper 101 rejection is imposed, the burden shifts to the applicant to rebut the prima facie showing.
guidance: No predetermined amount or character of evidence is required from the applicant; the character and amount vary depending on what is claimed and whether asserted utility appears to contravene established principles. Applicant's evidence must make the asserted utility more likely than not true; proof 'beyond a reasonable doubt' is not required (see In re Oetiker; Ex parte Ferguson; In re Irons; In re Fisher; In re Swartz; In re Brana).

name: When utility is shown but invention is not enabled
description: In some instances the utility of the claimed invention will be provided, but the skilled artisan will not know how to effect that use; in such a case no rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 will be made, but a rejection will be made under 35 U.S.C. 112(a).
guidance: An invention may have great utility yet the specification may fail to enable one skilled in the art to use it (Mowry v. Whitney). Examiners should evaluate enablement separately from utility.

name: Examiner identification of enabled subject matter when claiming broader than disclosure
description: If a rejection is made based on the view that the enablement is not commensurate in scope with the claim, the examiner should identify the subject matter that is considered to be enabled.
guidance: Limitations and examples in the specification do not generally limit the claims; however the record must be clear so the public has notice of the patentee's scope of protection. The examiner should articulate the specific unenabled portions of the claimed scope to justify a 112(a) rejection.

name: Single means claim enablement (single means recitation)
description: A single means claim, i.e., where a means recitation does not appear in combination with another recited element of means, is subject to an enablement rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) if the claim covers every conceivable means for achieving the stated purpose while the specification discloses at most only those means known to the inventor.
guidance: Such claims have been held nonenabling for scope of the claim (see In re Hyatt). When claims depend on a recited property, a comparable situation can arise (claim covers every conceivable structure for a stated property while spec discloses only those known to the inventor).

name: Inoperative subject matter within claim scope
description: The presence of inoperative embodiments within the scope of a claim does not necessarily render a claim nonenabled; the standard is whether a skilled person could determine which embodiments are operative with no more effort than is normally required in the art.
guidance: Prophetic examples do not make the disclosure nonenabling. Although inoperative embodiments are typically excluded by claim language, claims may still be nonenabled if undue experimentation is required to determine operable embodiments. A disclosure of many operable embodiments plus identification of a single inoperative one did not render claim nonenabled where undue experimentation was not involved. However, claims reading on significant numbers of inoperative embodiments may be nonenabled if the specification does not clearly identify operable embodiments (see Atlas Powder; In re Angstadt; In re Cook).

name: Best mode requirement — statutory statement
description: The specification shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor (pre-AIA language: 'The specification... shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor of carrying out his invention').
guidance: The best mode requirement prevents inventors from obtaining patent protection while withholding their preferred embodiment. Determining compliance requires (1) a subjective inquiry whether at filing the inventor possessed a best mode, and (2) an objective inquiry whether the written description disclosed the best mode such that a person skilled in the art could practice it (see Eli Lilly v. Barr). Failure to disclose the best mode need not rise to active concealment. Note: AIA amended enforcement (35 U.S.C. 282) so failure to disclose best mode is no longer a basis to cancel/invalid a claim in litigation, but the best mode requirement remains part of examination practice.

name: Best mode specifics — what is/ is not required
description: Considerations relevant to best mode include: determine what the invention is (claims define invention); a specific example is not required; designation as 'best mode' is not required; updating the best mode is not required in certain priority contexts; a defect in best mode cannot be cured by adding new matter after filing.
guidance: Unclaimed matter unrelated to operation of claimed invention does not trigger best mode. Absence of a working example is not determinative; best mode may be a preferred range or group. There is no statutory requirement that applicants point out which embodiment is best. Updating best mode is not required for foreign priority or certain benefit claims. Adding a specific mode after filing is treated as new matter and should be objected to (see In re Bosy; In re Gay; In re Honn; Ernsthausen; Standard Oil; In re Hay).

name: Best mode compared to enablement
description: The best mode requirement is separate and distinct from the enablement requirement. Best mode requires enabling one of ordinary skill to practice the best mode, whereas enablement aims to place the claimed subject matter generally in the public's possession.
guidance: Best mode is concerned with disclosure of applicant's recognized best way to practice the invention at time of filing; if applicant developed specific instrumentalities or techniques recognized as the best way, best mode requires disclosure of that information in addition to general enablement (see In re Newton; Spectra-Physics v. Coherent).

name: Claim scope analysis for enablement (claim-as-a-whole; dependent claims)
description: The examiner should determine what each claim recites and what the subject matter is when the claim is considered as a whole, not when its parts are analyzed individually. No claim should be overlooked; dependent claims incorporate limitations of the claims to which they refer.
guidance: When analyzing enabled scope, keep claims' broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with specification in mind. Do not read everything in the specification into the claims; but ensure the full scope of the claim is enabled. Examples from case law (AK Steel, Amgen, In re Wright, etc.) illustrate when broad generic claims were found not commensurate with limited enabling disclosure.

name: Filing deadline for substantive claim after precautionary order (20 days)
description: The owner must file a claim on the origin of the dispute within twenty days from issuance of the precautionary order or from notification of appeal rejection; otherwise the order will be cancelled at defendant's request.
guidance: Precautionary relief should be conditional on initiating substantive proceedings within a set period (20 days) to avoid indefinite interim measures.

name: Notification, inspection and challenge procedures for detained goods
description: If customs stops release it must notify importer and owner immediately, may provide owner on request with names/addresses of sender/importer/recipient and allow inspection per customs procedures; owner may file claim before the court within ten working days or decision void ab initio (subject to extension).
guidance: Ensure prompt notice, limited inspection rights and a short judicial challenge window (10 working days) with narrowly framed extensions to protect due process.

name: Select primary and secondary classifications for patent application publications based on claims and main inventive concept
description: A primary classification is based on the application's main inventive concept using the claims as a guide; there may be any number of secondary classifications for other inventive (mandatory) or valuable disclosure (discretionary) concepts. Applications are classified at least 9 weeks prior to projected publication date, and figure selection for publication occurs at classification.
guidance: Determine the primary classification from the controlling/main inventive concept (claims). Assign secondary classifications for other disclosed inventions or valuable disclosures; ensure timely classification before publication (≥9 weeks) and select figure(s) for publication during classification.

name: Determine original (OR) classification among mandatory classifications using stated criteria
description: If all mandatory classifications are in the same class, the original classification is the mandatory classification that, looking at the schedule top-down, is the most indented subclass array in which any classifications are assigned (subject to exceptions like genus-species). If mandatory classifications are in different classes, determine OR by, in turn: (A) selection based on the most comprehensive claim; (B) selection based on priority of statutory category of invention; (C) selection based on superiority of types of subject matter; (D) selection among classes in the 'related subject' listing in the front of the manual of classification.
guidance: Apply the listed tie-breaking criteria (A–D) in order to select the OR classification among multiple mandatory classifications, and consult the Examiner Handbook for genus-species and other special rules.

name: Include specific reasons on Application Transfer Request form
description: When effecting transfers, the Application Transfer Request form in PALM EXPO must include a full explanation and at least one of: (A) identification of the controlling claim examinable in another TC; (B) identification of any existing informal transfer agreement; (C) other reasons with full explanation.
guidance: Provide clear justification on the transfer request form—identify the controlling claim, cite informal agreements, or fully explain other reasons to support the transfer request.

name: Transfer on 'best examinable' basis when appropriate
description: Where an application’s claims include a combination of limitations across disciplines, an SPE or primary examiner may request transfer to another discipline on the ground that the application is 'best examinable' in the other discipline, even if controlling claims are properly classified in the original art unit. The requesting SPE/examiner should cite art showing limitations classifiable in the requesting discipline.
guidance: For multi-disciplinary applications, consider transfer to the 'best examinable' discipline; support the transfer with art that demonstrates the limitations relevant to the receiving discipline.

name: Contents of application for registration of patent term extension (Article 92-3(1))
description: An application shall state the following matters to the Commissioner: 1. The name and domicile of an applicant for registration of extension (if the applicant is a corporation, its name and the location of its business office); 2. The name and domicile of an agent, if any, or the location of his/her business office (if the agent is a patent firm or a limited-liability patent firm, its name, the location of its business office and the designated patent attorney’s name); 3. The number of a patent whose term is subject to extension; 4. The period of application for extension; 5. Grounds for extension prescribed by Ordinance of the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy (materials substantiating such grounds shall be attached thereto).
guidance: Applicant may amend matters falling under paragraph (1) 4 and 5 before an examiner decides whether patent term extension shall be registered; after receiving a notice of grounds for rejection, amendments to those matters are allowed only during the period for submission of arguments following the notice. Attach evidential documents substantiating claimed grounds.

name: Calculation of period allowed for requesting extension (detailed steps ①–⑤)
description: The period allowed is the number of days (E) from the date of establishment of a patent right (D) based on the reference date (C)—the later of (A) four years from filing date of the patent application, or (B) three years after the date of request for examination—minus the period of delay attributable to an applicant (F) under Article 7-2(1) of the Enforcement Decree.
guidance: Procedure: ① Determine filing date (includes divisional, converted, certain international request dates, etc.); ② Determine later reference date between four years from filing and three years after request for examination; ③ Calculate total period of delay (days between reference date and establishment date after fee payment); ④ Sum periods of delay attributable to applicant (include Article 7-2(1) paragraphs; overlapping applicant delays should not reduce more than actual delay); ⑤ Subtract attributable delay from total delay to get allowable extension. If applicant's written request claims a longer period than calculated, examiner issues ground for rejection and allows written argument/amendment to correct items ①–⑤. An illustrated example and table are provided.

name: Limits on amendable parts (under Article 92-3(4))
description: Amendable parts in an application for registration of extension include only: ① the period of request for extension and ② the ground for extension designated in Ordinance of the Ministry of Knowledge Economy. Amendment of applicant name and patent number shall not be allowed except for correcting clerical errors.
guidance: Amendments changing the patent number would change the subject of registration and are therefore generally not recognized, except for correcting clerical errors (where filing date, patent number and patent date support clerical error claim). Amendments to add co-owners after filing to cure a joint-owner defect are not recognized.

name: Practice before the Office in patent matters (37 C.F.R. § 11.5(b)(1))
description: Per 37 C.F.R. § 11.5(b)(1), practice of patent law before the USPTO includes, but is not limited to, preparing and prosecuting any patent application; consulting with or giving advice to a client in contemplation of filing a patent application or other document with the Office; drafting the specification or claims of a patent application.
guidance: This definition is used to determine whether a person who is not authorized to practice patent law before the Office has nevertheless engaged in patent practice. The Final Order cites examples (preparing provisional and non-provisional applications; providing patent legal advice; filing responses to Office correspondence) as activities falling within this definition.

name: Claim construction and review of the disclosure before eligibility analysis
description: Determine what applicant has invented by reviewing the entire application disclosure and construing the claims in accordance with their broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI).
guidance: See MPEP §2106 subsection II and MPEP §2111 for more information about the importance of understanding what the applicant has invented and the BRI. Eligibility evaluation should be made after this determination.

name: Claims whose BRI covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments fail Step 1
description: A claim whose BRI covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments embraces subject matter that is not eligible for patent protection and therefore is directed to non-statutory subject matter.
guidance: Such claims fail Step 1 (Step 1: NO) and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101. Best practice: examiner should point out the BRI and recommend an amendment, if possible, to narrow the claim to statutory embodiments.

name: Formulating Step 1 rejections and recommending amendments
description: If a claim is clearly not within one of the four categories (Step 1: NO), a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 must be made.
guidance: Use form paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01 for such rejections (see MPEP §2106.07(a)(1)). If the claim fails Step 1 but applicant’s disclosure suggests an amendable claim could fall within a statutory category, proceed to determine eligibility of a proposed amendment and recommend amendment as a best practice.

name: Step 2A two-prong inquiry: Prong One — does the claim recite a judicial exception
description: Prong One asks whether the claim recites (sets forth or describes) an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon.
guidance: ‘Set forth’ and ‘described’ are both equated with ‘recite’ but indicate two ways exceptions appear in claims (explicitly stated vs. described conceptually). Examiners must distinguish claims that recite an exception (require further analysis) from claims that merely involve an exception (eligible). Examples: 'A machine comprising elements that operate in accordance with F=ma' recites a law of nature; a teeter-totter claim that merely involves lever principles does not recite the exception.

name: Step 2A two-prong inquiry: Prong Two — integration of the exception into a practical application
description: Prong Two asks whether the claim recites additional elements that integrate the judicial exception into a practical application of that exception.
guidance: If the additional elements integrate the exception into a practical application, the claim is not directed to the judicial exception (Step 2A: NO) and is eligible at Pathway B. If the additional elements do not integrate the exception into a practical application, the claim is directed to the exception (Step 2A: YES) and requires Step 2B analysis. See MPEP §2106.04(d)(2) for details.

name: Insufficiency of mere additional elements that are also judicial exceptions
description: If there are no additional claim elements besides the judicial exception, or if the additional claim elements merely recite another judicial exception, that is insufficient to integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.
guidance: Adding one abstract idea to another does not render a claim non-abstract (RecogniCorp v. Nintendo). For eligibility, additional elements must 'transform the nature of the claim' into a patent-eligible application (Alice). If no sufficient additional elements exist, recommend amendment if possible and make appropriate §101 rejection (see MPEP §2106.07).

name: Evaluating claims reciting multiple judicial exceptions
description: A claim may recite multiple judicial exceptions; the eligibility analysis should be applied the same regardless of the number of exceptions.
guidance: Unless clear that exceptions are distinct (e.g., a law of nature and an abstract idea), avoid parsing the claim into multiple exceptions. If distinct, select one exception for efficiency and analyze it; if analysis shows additional elements integrate or amount to significantly more than the selected exception, consider the claim eligible. If multiple abstract ideas or laws of nature are recited together, treat them together for Prong Two and Step 2B where possible.

name: Procedure for identifying abstract idea limitations
description: Examiners should determine whether a claim recites an abstract idea by (1) identifying the specific limitation(s) in the claim that the examiner believes recites an abstract idea, and (2) determining whether those limitations fall within at least one enumerated grouping of abstract ideas.
guidance: If the identified limitation(s) falls within a grouping, conclude the claim recites an abstract idea and proceed to Prong Two. If not, conclude the claim does not recite an abstract idea and the abstract idea exception analysis concludes, except in rare circumstances (see MPEP §2106.04(a)(3)).

name: Preemption is a concern but not a standalone test
description: Although preemption is the policy concern underlying the judicial exceptions, the absence or presence of preemption itself is not the sole test for eligibility.
guidance: Questions of preemption are inherent in and resolved by applying the Alice/Mayo two-part framework (Steps 2A and 2B). A claim may be eligible despite not completely avoiding preemption in some narrow senses, and absence of complete preemption does not by itself demonstrate eligibility.

name: Investigate and process claims to tribal citizenship under department rules
description: There are 531 families ... who claim to be Cherokees and who have applied to the Cherokee citizenship court for confirmation of title and have been rejected. ... Under instructions from the Hon. Commissioner of Indian Affairs, I investigate the claims of these parties, and if I am satisfied they have prima facie a just claim to citizenship, I permit them to remain to await final action in these cases, which is to be determined by rules adopted by the department.
guidance: Follow departmental rules to investigate prima facie claims to tribal citizenship, allow claimants to remain pending final determination, and expedite rule-based resolution to avoid prolonged detriment to claimants and tribal administration.

name: Examiner role and public-interest duty
description: To serve as advocate and protector of the public interest with respect to intellectual property; to provide direct service and assistance to customers from inside and outside the USPTO; to evaluate patentability with respect to invention(s) claimed in a patent application under the conditions for patentability set forth in Title 35 of the United States Code.
guidance: Examiner responsibilities include reading and understanding the invention, checking application completeness and formal compliance, ensuring proper classification, determining whether the application adequately defines the metes and bounds of the claimed invention, determining the scope of the claims, searching existing technology, selecting relevant prior art references, writing office actions identifying and analyzing all issues pertinent to statutory compliance, responding completely to applicant replies, and issuing notices of allowance or abandonment.

name: Claims define the invention / claim interpretation
description: The claims define the invention and are analyzed by identifying and evaluating each claim limitation; for processes the limitations define steps or acts, and for products they define discrete physical structures or materials.
guidance: During examination, claims are given their broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) consistent with the specification as understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art. Examiner should identify and evaluate each claim limitation. See MPEP 2103(I), 2111. Example contrasts shown between method and product claim language.

name: 35 U.S.C. 112 — specification and claim requirements
description: Specification must meet written description, enablement, and best mode requirements. Claims must particularly point out (not be vague) and distinctly claim (not be indefinite); claim format must be appropriate (independent, dependent, multiple dependent).
guidance: Examiner determines whether there is an adequate written description of the claimed invention and whether the application is adequate to define the metes and bounds of the claimed invention. Claim content and format issues may be the basis for rejections or objections under 35 U.S.C. 112.

name: 35 U.S.C. 102 — novelty / anticipation
description: A claim is anticipated when a single prior art reference describes, either expressly or inherently, each and every limitation of a claim.
guidance: A single prior art reference anticipates if it describes every limitation, expressly or inherently. Prior art may be anything publicly available (papers, patents, theses, websites, videos, etc.) and in any language. Examples: Conestoga wagon anticipating a vehicle claim based on BRI of the claim consistent with the specification.

name: 35 U.S.C. 103 — Graham factors / factual inquiries
description: To determine obviousness, examiner must resolve: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) the differences between the prior art and the claims; (3) the relevant level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; (4) whether any objective evidence of non-obviousness exists.
guidance: See MPEP 2141. The examiner must consider all factual information and objective evidence of non-obviousness, including evidence in the specification and any evidence submitted by the applicant.

name: Alice two-part test for software patents (35 U.S.C. §101)
description: Under the two-part test a court must first consider whether the patent claims are directed to a patent ineligible concept such as an abstract idea, and if so, the court should consider whether the claim’s other elements transform the claim into a patent eligible concept.
guidance: Known ideas are abstract; reciting the use of a conventional computer in the claims to implement the known idea does not make the claim patentable subject matter. The two-step framework is the baseline legal standard for evaluating software patent eligibility under Alice.

name: Alice analysis relies on claim characterization and may not require evidentiary proof
description: Legal analysis of software patents under Alice differs from other legal analysis: while the Federal Rules of Evidence govern litigation, under Alice a court must first determine if the claim encompasses an abstract idea, and that first determination is a question of law that often does not require evidence.
guidance: Courts frequently rely on a characterization of the claims rather than the precise claim language; attorney argument is often sufficient, and courts commonly make Alice findings without supporting evidence. Terminology, claim length, or complexity often do not change the analysis. Anti-pattern: assuming that a voluminous evidentiary record or detailed claim wording will prevent an Alice dismissal.

name: Use Alice to seek quick resolution by avoiding complex invalidity inquiries
description: Alice allows defendants to seek invalidity of software patents by arguing abstractness instead of conducting fact-intensive novelty/obviousness/enablement inquiries.
guidance: Because proving obviousness/enablement/anticipation can require extensive discovery and technical evidence, Alice provides a faster path—show the claim is an abstract idea or combines only conventional elements (including a conventional computer). Combining conventional elements does not make a claim patentable. Strategic guidance: identify conventional methodologies and conventional computer implementation, and argue preemption/breadth to pursue early dispositive relief.

name: Claim breadth and preemption are indicators of abstractness
description: If a claim is broad enough to encompass (or preempt) all embodiments of an idea, that is an indicator that the claim is abstract (and thus unpatentable under Alice).
guidance: Broad claims that purport to monopolize an abstract idea also raise enablement concerns (doubtful that the specification enables every possible variation). Under Alice a defendant can emphasize overbreadth/preemption as evidence the claim is an abstract attempt to monopolize an idea rather than a patent-eligible invention.

name: Second-step factual inquiry can affect the viability of early Alice motions
description: The Federal Circuit has held that the second part of the Alice analysis may require a factual inquiry in some circumstances, which can limit the effectiveness of early dispositive Alice motions.
guidance: When a factual inquiry is required, courts may deny or defer early motions and permit discovery, making it harder for defendants to obtain early dismissal. Some courts still determine no factual inquiry is necessary for the particular case; assess whether the claimed invention's additional elements raise disputed factual issues before filing an early §101 motion.

name: Post-Alice trend: declining success of Alice challenges due to better claims and USPTO scrutiny
description: Since 2015 the percentage of successful Alice challenges has dropped each year; recent software patents are more likely to survive Alice because patentees draft better claims and the USPTO scrutinizes claims for patentability.
guidance: Patentees should improve claim drafting and consider Alice issues during prosecution; courts may defer to the USPTO's determination on Alice if the issue was considered during prosecution. For defendants, recognize that Alice motions may be less likely to succeed against recently issued, well-drafted software patents and weigh the economics of pursuing §101 challenges.

name: Graham factual inquiries as basis for determining obviousness
description: The factual inquiries in Graham are still the basis for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103.
guidance: Examiners should continue to apply the Graham factors (scope and content of the prior art; differences between the prior art and the claims; level of ordinary skill; and secondary considerations) as the foundational factual analysis when assessing obviousness.

name: Examiners must articulate a reason or rationale for obviousness rejections
description: In view of the guidance provided by the Supreme Court in KSR, an examiner must continue to articulate a reason or rationale to support an obviousness rejection.
guidance: A rejection under §103 must include a clear explanation of why the prior art would have led one of ordinary skill to the claimed invention—mere conclusory statements are insufficient.

name: Clear articulation of why the claimed invention would have been obvious
description: A key to supporting any rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 is the clear articulation of the reasons why the claimed invention would have been obvious.
guidance: Provide step-by-step reasoning linking prior art teachings to claim limitations and explain predictability or expectations of success; clarity is essential for defensible rejections.

name: Rationale B: Simple substitution of known elements to obtain predictable results
description: Simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results.
guidance: Replacing one known component with another known equivalent that performs the same function in a predictable way can render a claim obvious.

name: Include an article of manufacture (35 U.S.C. § 171 requirement)
description: A design patent must apply a shape, configuration, or surface ornamentation to a specific article of manufacture; a patent cannot claim a pattern 'in the abstract' without reference to an article of manufacture.
guidance: Reference Curver Luxembourg v. Home Expressions: drawings that depict only a pattern without a specific article led to the Federal Circuit construing the patent as limited to chairs (the referenced article) and rejecting attempts to cover every possible article. Ensure the drawings and title/claim link the design to a concrete article of manufacture to avoid being limited or invalidated.

name: Do not claim surface ornamentation in the abstract
description: Design patents should not be drafted so as to attempt to protect a surface ornamentation per se across every possible article of manufacture.
guidance: The court has stated it 'has never sanctioned granting a design patent for a surface ornamentation in the abstract such that the patent's scope encompasses every possible article of manufacture to which the surface ornamentation is applied.' Avoid claiming a pattern alone without tying it to particular article(s) or clear claim language.

name: Use wording/title and drawings together to define the invention
description: Describe the invention in the words and title as well as in the drawings; relying on 'abstracted' drawings without corresponding descriptive wording risks rejection or litigation defeat.
guidance: Curver demonstrates that disassociated drawings and indefinite wording can lead to a patent being construed narrowly or invalidated. Include clear title/claim language that identifies the article of manufacture and harmonizes with the figures.

name: Visual disclosure must not be internally inconsistent
description: A visual disclosure may be inadequate—and its associated claim indefinite—if it includes multiple, internally inconsistent drawings.
guidance: Federal Circuit in In re Maatita noted that inconsistencies in drawings can render a claim indefinite, but inconsistencies do not merit § 112 rejection if they 'do not preclude the overall understanding of the drawing as a whole.' Ensure multiple figures are consistent or collectively convey a clear, unified design.

name: Meet the definiteness standard: inform with reasonable certainty
description: The claim, read in light of the visual disclosure, must 'inform, with reasonable certainty, those skilled in the art about the scope of the invention.'
guidance: Quoting Nautilus and In re Maatita, the key test is whether the disclosure gives potential competitors notice of what design is claimed. Draft drawings and text so that an ordinary observer and those skilled in the art can reasonably ascertain claim scope.

name: Ordinary observer test allows multiple embodiments if scope is clear
description: A single design patent drawing may disclose multiple embodiments and still be definite if the scope is clear with reasonable certainty to an ordinary observer.
guidance: In re Maatita upheld that a two-dimensional drawing of a three-dimensional sole could be definite even if multiple 3D realizations are possible, provided an ordinary observer understands the claimed two-dimensional aspect. Use drawings that convey the aspect of the design that would be perceived by the ordinary observer.

name: Level of detail should match whether the design is definable by a planar illustration
description: The degree of drawing detail required depends on whether the claimed design for the article can be defined by a two-dimensional, plan- or planar-view illustration.
guidance: If the design is typically considered in a planar view (e.g., rug, shoe sole), a 2D drawing may suffice; for designs requiring depth/contour clarity, include additional views or detail to avoid indefiniteness or enablement objections. Evaluate whether additional perspectives are necessary to convey the claimed design unambiguously.

name: Avoid leaving design open to multiple patentably-distinct interpretations
description: If a drawing allows multiple plausible three-dimensional implementations that would be patentably distinct, an examiner may find the claim indefinite or not enabled.
guidance: In Maatita the examiner produced four different 3D renderings from a single 2D figure and concluded they were patentably distinct. Anticipate such alternate interpretations and either refine the drawings/text to narrow the intended scope or add figures/description to show the intended embodiment(s).

name: Strategically choose drawings and wording to control claim breadth
description: The right drawing and accompanying wording can broaden the scope of a design patent; the wrong drawing/wording can destroy or unduly limit it.
guidance: Use claims, title, and figures intentionally to capture desired scope. Consider whether to allow multiple interpretations (to broaden) or expressly limit embodiments (to avoid indefiniteness). Be mindful that overly abstract figures risk rejection or narrow construction in litigation, while well-chosen figures can cover multiple embodiments when appropriate.

name: Effect of Federal court decisions on reexamination
description: Non-final federal court decisions have no binding effect on reexamination; final decisions upholding validity are not binding but may be given deference; a final holding of invalidity or unenforceability (after all appeals) is binding on the Office.
guidance: Ethicon v. Quigg: Office uses a different standard (preponderance) than district courts (clear and convincing), so the Office is not bound by a court's validity holding; factual findings of a court will ordinarily be accorded deference when evidence is the same. If a claim is finally held invalid/unenforceable, it will be withdrawn from reexamination consideration; reexamination continues as to remaining claims. If all claims are finally held invalid/unenforceable, the TC Director will vacate the reexamination as no longer containing a substantial new question of patentability.

name: Changing the title or abstract during reexamination
description: Title changes generally not needed; if a title change is necessary the patent owner should be notified to provide an amendment early; if all claims are patentable and a NIRC is to be mailed, the examiner may change the title only by an examiner’s amendment (not by mere initialing).
guidance: An examiner’s amendment can change the abstract when the narrowing amendments during reexamination change the invention's focus (e.g., claim narrowed and abstract no longer focuses on required limitation).

name: Selection of representative claim(s) and drawing for publication
description: Select an appropriate drawing figure and a representative claim to be printed in the Official Gazette; reexamination instructions for claim selection: (A) select the broadest claim; (B) ordinarily designate only one claim per invention—reexamination: select only one claim; (C) do not select a dependent claim unless its independent claim is also printed (with reexamination exceptions); (D) in reissue, select the broadest claim with changes or broadest reissue claim.
guidance: When recording, write claim numbers in black ink, separate multiple claims by commas, and refer to renumbered patent claim numbers (not original application numbers). In reexamination a dependent patent claim may be selected where the independent original claim was canceled (dependent printed while independent not printed).

name: Reexamination reminders — reasons required for each claim found patentable
description: Reasons for patentability and/or confirmation are required for each claim found patentable (unless all claims canceled); the examiner should indicate why claims are clearly patentable over cited patents or printed publications.
guidance: Reasons may be set forth on form PTOL-476 or by using form paragraph 22.16 (preferred). Where the record clearly establishes patentability, the examiner may refer to specific record portions. Box 2 of PTOL-469 is checked and reasons attached. Patent owner comments on the reasons will be placed in the reexamination file without comment.

name: Reexamination reminders — original drawings and scope of amended/new claims
description: Original drawings cannot be physically changed; all drawing amendments must be presented on new sheets. An amended or new claim may not enlarge the scope of the patent claims.
guidance: A draftsperson’s approval stamp is no longer required. Examiner may have draftsperson review new sheets to identify errors. See MPEP § 2250.01 and § 2250.

name: Reasons for patentability and/or confirmation content and placement
description: Reasons for patentability must be provided (unless all claims canceled), typically as an attachment to Box 2 of PTOL-469, indicating why the claims found patentable are clearly patentable over cited patents/printed publications; examiner may use PTOL-476 or form paragraph 22.16.
guidance: The examiner may refer to record portions which establish patentability. The terms 'confirmed' and 'patentable' may be used flexibly; no need to separate categories in the reasons. Any comments from patent owner about the reasons will be placed in the reexamination file without comment.

name: Issuance and content of ex parte reexamination certificate (35 U.S.C. 307; 37 CFR 1.570)
description: Upon conclusion of ex parte reexamination and expiration/termination of appeals, the Director will issue and publish a certificate canceling any claim finally determined unpatentable, confirming any claim determined patentable, and incorporating proposed amended or new claims determined patentable.
guidance: An ex parte reexamination certificate will be issued for each patent where reexamination was ordered and not merged with an inter partes reexamination. Statutory disclaimers will be made part of the certificate. The certificate will be mailed to the patent owner and a copy to the requester on its date. If all claims are canceled, no further Office proceedings on that patent or related reissue/reexamination requests will be conducted. If terminated by grant of a reissued patent under § 1.565(d), the reissued patent constitutes the reexamination certificate.

name: Form and contents of a patent (formal requirements)
description: All patents issued from said office shall be issued in the name of the United States, under the seal of the office, signed by the Secretary of State and countersigned by the Commissioner, and recorded along with descriptions, specifications, and drawings. Every patent shall contain a short description or title correctly indicating its nature and design, and in its terms grant to the applicant (and heirs, administrators, executors, or assigns) for a term not exceeding fourteen years the full and exclusive right and liberty of making, using, and vending the said invention, referring to the specifications annexed, specifying what the patentee claims as his invention or discovery.
guidance: Patents must follow prescribed form (signatures, seal, recordation) and include a short descriptive title, annexed specification, and clear claim language; statutory maximum term is 14 years for the patents described.

name: Written description, enablement, and specificity of claims
description: Before receiving a patent the inventor shall deliver a written description of his invention and of the manner and process of making, constructing, using, and compounding same, in such full, clear, and exact terms, avoiding unnecessary prolixity, as to enable any person skilled in the art or science to make, construct, compound, and use the same; for machines he shall fully explain the principle and the several modes of application, and shall particularly specify and point out the part, improvement, or combination which he claims as his own invention or discovery.
guidance: This is the statutory written-description and enablement requirement: the specification must be sufficiently detailed to enable a skilled practitioner to practice the invention and must particularly point out the claimed subject matter (precise claiming).

name: Reissue and correction for inadvertent defects or overclaiming
description: Whenever any patent is inoperative or invalid by reason of a defective description or specification, or because the patentee claimed more than he had right to claim, if the error arose by inadvertence, accident, or mistake without fraudulent intent, the Commissioner, upon surrender of the patent and payment of $15, may issue a new patent to the inventor for the residue of the unexpired term in accordance with the corrected description and specification; similar right vests in executors/assignees. Patentee may also add description of a subsequent improvement and have it annexed for $15.
guidance: Provides a statutory reissue procedure to correct honest errors in description or overclaiming and to add subsequent improvements, preserving legal effect going forward as though originally filed in corrected form.

name: Inherent anticipation standard
description: Anticipation by inherent disclosure is appropriate only when the reference discloses prior art that must necessarily include the unstated limitation.
guidance: Quoting Transclean: inherent anticipation requires that the unstated limitation be necessarily present in the prior art reference. Example: King Pharms. — ordinary results of taking metaxalone with food (increased bioavailability) were inherent in prior art dosing, so claims were inherently anticipated. Courts will hold newly discovered benefits of old processes to be inherent in the prior art.

name: Preamble is non-limiting unless relied upon in prosecution
description: Preamble language that merely states the purpose or intended use of an invention is generally not treated as limiting the scope of the claim; a preamble becomes limiting only when the patentee clearly relies on it during prosecution to distinguish the prior art.
guidance: Marrin v. Griffin: district court and Federal Circuit found a 'for permitting' preamble to be a statement of intended use and not a limitation because patentees did not rely on it during prosecution; amendment history showed patentees expressly conceded the 'writing means' was not a limitation. Dissent (Judge Newman) warns against deleting limitations stated in the claim.

name: Informing/mental-step limitations do not cure lack of novelty
description: Adding an 'informing' limitation (or similar non-transformative step) to an anticipated claim does not cure lack of novelty; informational steps that do not transform the substantive process are not sufficient to create novelty.
guidance: King Pharms.: court held that informing a patient about a drug's benefit does not transform the process of taking the drug with food and therefore does not avoid inherent anticipation. District court's Bilski analysis aside, novelty cannot be saved by merely adding informational or advisory steps.

name: Single-reference rule: single reference must disclose every claim limitation (expressly or inherently)
description: To anticipate, a single prior art reference must disclose each and every limitation of the claimed invention, either explicitly or inherently.
guidance: Cited repeatedly (Finisar, Orion): anticipation requires one reference that contains all claim limitations. Incorporation by reference of other material is possible, but courts treat what is properly incorporated as part of the single reference (see incorporation-by-reference rule).

name: Anticipation is a question of fact and requires clear and convincing evidence
description: Whether a claim is anticipated is a question of fact for the finder; invalidity by anticipation must be proved by clear and convincing evidence, and appellate review of a jury trial on anticipation is for substantial evidence.
guidance: Orion v. Hyundai: Federal Circuit reversed a jury verdict where it found Hyundai showed by clear and convincing evidence that the printed brochure (with testimonial support) anticipated the claim. Cases cite Yoon Ja Kim for the clear-and-convincing standard and note substantial-evidence review on appeal.

name: Testimonial and documentary evidence can support that a printed reference anticipates
description: Testimony from experts and third-party fact witnesses, and documentary evidence, can establish that a printed publication or brochure anticipates a claim by showing the reference (as used) disclosed required limitations.
guidance: Orion and Verizon examples: expert/fact witnesses explained how an advertised system generated proposals; Cox's expert (author of the reference) provided detailed testimony that enabled a jury to find anticipation. The newsletter emphasizes the benefits of supporting anticipatory references with testimonial and fact evidence.

name: 35 U.S.C. §102(e) priority date can reach back to provisional applications (subject to §112 support)
description: A U.S. patent may qualify as prior art under §102(e) based on its earliest effective filing date; a provisional application can be treated as 'an application' under §102(e) such that the patent's effective date may reach back to the provisional, provided the earlier-filed specification provides written-description support under Section 112.
guidance: In re Giacomini: Federal Circuit affirmed that a provisional application is an 'application' for §102(e) purposes if it discloses the claimed invention (i.e., provides written description support). Practical effect: watch provisional content if relying on or defending against §102(e) rejections/anticipation.

name: Design patent anticipation: ordinary observer test is sole test; point-of-novelty abolished
description: For design patents, the Federal Circuit confirmed that the ordinary observer test — not the point-of-novelty test — is the sole test for determining anticipation (and infringement). The inquiry asks whether an ordinary observer would believe the designs are substantially the same.
guidance: Int'l Seaway Trading v. Walgreens (following Egyptian Goddess): abolishes point-of-novelty test to keep anticipation and infringement tests identical. The review must consider the state of the prior art: when the claimed design is close to the prior art, small differences will be important to the ordinary observer. Cites Peters maxim: 'That which infringes, if later, would anticipate, if earlier.'

name: Definition of a Patent Case
description: A case with one or more claims involving patent infringement, invalidity, or unenforceability brought under 35 USC § 271. False marking, inventorship, or contract cases are not included in the patent case type.
guidance: Used to determine which matters are included in the patent dataset; explicitly excludes false marking, inventorship, and contract cases. Applies across district courts, federal appeals, and PTAB-related analytics in this report.

name: Case Tagging System (Lex Machina case filter system)
description: Lex Machina uses machine learning and natural language processing to create case tags that identify certain claims in a case.
guidance: Tags (e.g., ANDA, High-Volume Plaintiff, design patent) enable filtering and comparison across cohorts. The platform supplements ML with human review and allows users to apply additional tags in their research.

name: Timing Metrics (time-to-event)
description: Timing analytics measure time from filing to key milestones (e.g., claim construction hearing, summary judgment decision, trial, termination).
guidance: Reported as medians and visualized with box plots. Example medians for non-ANDA terminated cases (2022–2024): claim construction hearing = 410 days; summary judgment = 848 days; trial = 1,040 days; termination = 208 days. ANDA medians differ (e.g., claim construction 482 days, trial 837 days). Timing ranges vary widely; additional factors (issues, venue, parties) should be considered.

name: Case Resolution Categories and Metrics
description: Classify terminated district-court patent cases into resolution types: claimant wins (default judgment, consent judgment, judgment on the pleadings, summary judgment, trial, judgment as a matter of law, etc.), claim defendant wins (same subtypes), likely settlement, procedural resolution (dismissal, consolidation, severance, transfer, stay, MDL, sealed), and open/no resolution.
guidance: Quantify proportions (e.g., ~90% of non-ANDA district cases resolved by settlements or procedural rulings in 2022–2024). Distinguish ANDA patterns (more consent judgments, fewer default judgments, defendants win trials more often in ANDA). Use granular categories to understand typical endgames in different case types.

name: Patent Invalidity Reasons (granular legal grounds)
description: Track specific legal grounds for invalidity findings: 101 Subject Matter, 102 Anticipation/Novelty, 102(f) Derivation (pre-AIA), 103 Obviousness, 112 Definiteness, 112 Enablement, 112 Written Description, defective correction statutes (132,251,255,305), obviousness-type double patenting, or No Invalidity Reason Specified.
guidance: Report highlights which grounds are most common (e.g., subject-matter ineligibility / §101 most frequent, often at judgment on the pleadings; indefiniteness often reached during claim construction). Break down findings by judgment event to see where specific grounds prevail.

name: PTAB Institution Rate and Trial Flow
description: Measure institution decisions and downstream trial outcomes: percent of petitions denied institution vs. instituted, and final trial outcomes (all claims unpatentable, all claims upheld, mixed findings, amended claims, patent owner disclaimed, settled, procedurally dismissed, joined to other trial).
guidance: Example flow for trials terminated 2022–2024 (out of 3,903 petitions): Denied institution 805 (21%); Instituted 2,278 (58%); Procedurally dismissed pre/post institution; Settled; Final outcomes include Petitioner Win 1,047 (27%), Patent Owner Win 2,447 (63%), Partial 219 (6%). Note policy influence (e.g., Fintiv doctrine changes) and that institution rates rose since 2022 but policy reversals (March 2025 director review) may shift future rates.

name: Drawings define the design claim
description: Unlike utility patents, a design patent’s scope is dictated almost entirely by its visual representation: 'the lines, shading, and perspectives are the claim.'
guidance: Because the drawings are the claim, every graphical choice (lines, shading, views) can expand or limit protection. Draft with both full disclosure and strategic flexibility in mind to avoid unintentional narrowing or indefiniteness.

name: Use of broken lines to exclude unclaimed subject matter
description: Broken lines (dashed or dotted lines) show parts of an article that are not part of the claimed design, allowing environment or non-claimed elements to be depicted without claiming them.
guidance: Three primary uses: (1) Unclaimed Subject Matter — show surrounding parts in broken lines (e.g., rest of phone around a novel charging port); (2) Environmental Context — indicate how the design is used (tractor attachment in solid lines, tractor in broken lines); (3) Boundary Lines — use 'phantom' lines to define boundaries where no physical edge exists. Strategic takeaway: using broken lines to exclude non-essential elements can broaden the scope of the claimed design and make 'design around' attempts harder.

name: Solid vs. broken lines: strategic toggling
description: Solid lines indicate claimed elements; broken lines indicate unclaimed elements or context.
guidance: Carefully choose which parts are in solid vs broken lines to define claim scope. Inconsistent or incorrect use can unintentionally claim or fail to claim elements. Use broken lines for background/context and phantom boundaries to avoid claiming environment or extraneous parts.

name: Strategic drafting to prevent design-arounds
description: Use drawing techniques (broken lines, boundary phantom lines, selective shading) to broaden claim scope and make it harder for competitors to design around the claimed appearance.
guidance: Balance full disclosure with deliberate exclusions via broken lines to preserve broad protection. Consider the competitive landscape when deciding which elements to show in solid vs broken lines and whether to include or omit ornamentation.

name: Use of automation to enforce compliance and consistency
description: Automated tools (e.g., AI trained on USPTO standards) can generate the seven required views with consistent line weights, compliant shading, and strategic broken/solid line toggles.
guidance: Automation reduces manual tracing errors and speeds drafting, but outputs should still be audited for strategic claim choices and office-specific requirements before filing.

name: Alice/Mayo two-step test for §101
description: This Court's two-step test: (1) determine whether the patent claims are directed to a patent-ineligible concept (e.g., an abstract idea); (2) if so, decide whether the claims contain an inventive concept sufficient to transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application.
guidance: Cite Alice, 573 U.S. at 217-18; if claims are directed to an ineligible concept at step one, the court proceeds to step two to look for an inventive concept. The brief emphasizes this framework as the controlling inquiry for patent eligibility.

name: Step 1 'directed to' inquiry — focus and permissible use of specification
description: Step one asks whether claims are 'directed to' an excluded concept and focuses on the character of the claims 'as a whole' — courts should focus on claim language itself but may use the specification to illuminate what the claims are directed to.
guidance: Specification may be useful to understand 'the problem facing the inventor' and 'what the patent describes as the invention.' Looking to the specification is consistent with Alice and prior Supreme Court decisions (Parker, Adams). However, courts must avoid oversimplifying claims and must not import improper Section 112 enablement considerations into the §101 directed-to analysis.

name: Preemption risk is central to step one
description: Step one is 'concerned with the risk that a claim will pre-empt others from using an abstract idea' regardless of its implementation.
guidance: Courts consider whether claim scope would preempt use of an abstract idea; step-one analysis is a stage-one filter to identify claims that essentially monopolize fundamental tools of science and technology.

name: Physical or machine implementation does not automatically make an abstract idea patent eligible
description: Implementing an abstract idea on a physical machine or computer does not necessarily render an otherwise ineligible claim eligible; focusing only on the physical aspects would 'make the determination of patent eligibility depend simply on the draftsman's art.'
guidance: Cite Alice, 573 U.S. at 222-24. Claims cannot be rescued solely by reciting generic hardware (e.g., receiver, display, processor) unless there is a particular inventive application or improvement in how the components operate.

name: Draftsman's art and Bilski limitation
description: The prohibition against patenting abstract ideas cannot be avoided by limiting the ineligible concept to a particular technological environment or by adding insignificant post-solution activity.
guidance: Cite Bilski v. Kappos, 561 U.S. 593, 610 (2010). Merely labeling components (e.g., 'wirelessly coupled') or adding generic physical descriptors (submersible, heat resistant) does not make a claim patentable.

name: Claims that state a goal without specifying a solution are patent-ineligible
description: Claims that identify a goal to be achieved but do not recite a particular way of achieving it (i.e., no solution) are ineligible.
guidance: Illustrative example: claims like 'illuminating dark rooms by any efficacious means' identify a goal but fail to recite a process for achieving it. The government brief in American Axle is cited for the proposition that claims stating only a goal are ineligible.

name: Enablement-style analysis should not be used to improperly disregard claim components
description: Courts should not engage in a quasi-enablement or §112-style analysis to disregard concrete claim components when determining what the claim is 'directed to' under §101.
guidance: Criticized practice: treating lack of specification detail as a basis to ignore recited structural components. The brief argues the district court did not do this, but recognizes the line must be observed: specification may illuminate claim focus, but not be used as an enablement substitute to rewrite claims.

name: Recitation of tangible components is immaterial if the claim is directed to an abstract idea
description: The mere fact that patent claims recite tangible components does not render a claim patent-eligible when the claim's focus is an abstract idea.
guidance: Cite Alice: allowing eligibility simply because claims recite physical components would permit claiming any principle via draftsman's art. Courts must look to whether the claimed combination yields a particular inventive manner of performing the abstract idea.

name: Statutory (same-invention) double patenting – identical scope required
description: Use form paragraph 8.31 where the ‘scope’ of the inventions claimed in the patent and the application is identical (i.e., same invention).
guidance: Form paragraph 8.31 must be preceded by form paragraph 8.30 and is used only where the conflicting claims are in an issued patent and the scope is identical. Do not use this paragraph if the conflicting claims are in a copending application (use provisional form paragraph 8.32). Do not use for nonstatutory-type double patenting (use 8.33–8.39). In bracket 3 insert the number of the conflicting patent. If the patent is to a different inventive entity and is commonly assigned, use form paragraph 8.27 to require the assignee to name the first inventor. If evidence shows the patent is prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(f) or (g), also make rejections using appropriate 102/103 form paragraphs (e.g., 7.15 and/or 7.19).

name: Provisional double patenting (copending application)
description: Use form paragraph 8.32 to provisionally reject claims under 35 U.S.C. 101 as claiming the same invention as claims of a copending application (conflicting claims not yet patented).
guidance: Form paragraph 8.32 must be preceded by form paragraph 8.30 and is used only where the conflicting claims are in another copending application and the scope is identical. Insert the number of the conflicting application in bracket 3. Do not use this paragraph if the conflicting claims are in an issued patent (see 8.31). Consider using form paragraph 8.28 as well to resolve priority issues under 102(f)/(g) when common assignment at present does not establish common ownership at the time the later invention was made. A corresponding provisional double patenting rejection should also be made in the conflicting application.

name: Obviousness-type nonstatutory double patenting (when appropriate)
description: Appropriate where conflicting claims are not identical but at least one application claim is not patentably distinct from the reference claim(s) because it is anticipated by, or would have been obvious over, the reference claim(s).
guidance: Obviousness-type double patenting parallels the analysis for 35 U.S.C. 103 obviousness determinations; the patent used as the reference is not treated as prior art. Use form paragraphs 8.34–8.37 depending on whether the primary reference is a patent or application and whether secondary references are used. If based on a patent, use 8.34 (no secondary) or 8.36 (with secondary). If based on a copending application, use provisional paragraphs 8.35 or 8.37. Ensure form paragraph 8.33 precedes the chosen paragraph and is used only once in an Office action. If evidence also shows 102/103 issues (e.g., 102(f)/(g) or 102(e)), add the appropriate 102/103 rejections as indicated in the MPEP (form paragraphs 7.15/7.19/7.21 etc.).

name: Apply Graham v. John Deere factual inquiries in obviousness-type double patenting
description: When making an obviousness-type double patenting analysis, apply the Graham factual inquiries: (A) determine scope and content of the patent claim relative to the application claim; (B) determine differences between the claims; (C) determine the level of ordinary skill in the art; (D) evaluate any objective indicia of nonobviousness.
guidance: The conclusion of obviousness-type double patenting is made in light of these factual determinations. Because the analysis parallels a 35 U.S.C. 103(a) obviousness determination, the examiner should follow the same inquiry steps and document findings accordingly.

name: Rejection must state differences and reasons (explanation requirement)
description: Any obviousness-type double patenting rejection should make clear: (A) the differences between the inventions defined by the conflicting claims, and (B) the reasons why a person of ordinary skill in the art would conclude that the claim at issue is anticipated by, or would have been an obvious variation of, the invention defined in the patent claim.
guidance: In bracketed explanatory text provide the specific rationale for why claims are not patentably distinct (e.g., supply factual comparisons, reasoning tying prior claim limitations to the application claim, and any secondary references used). For provisional rejections, provide appropriate rationale in bracket 4 or 5 as directed by the form paragraph templates.

name: Use of patent disclosure in obviousness-type analysis (limitations)
description: The disclosure of a patent may not be used as prior art, but the specification can be used as a dictionary to learn claim term meanings and portions of the specification that provide support for patent claims may be examined when addressing whether an application claim is an obvious variation of an invention claimed in the patent.
guidance: Do not treat the entire patent disclosure as a 103 reference; only use portions that define or support the patent claims. Cite relevant case law (e.g., Toro, Renishaw, Vogel) when using patent disclosure to construe terms or identify embodiments that support comparison. Be cautious not to improperly use the patent as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 103.

name: One-way vs two-way obviousness tests (when each applies)
description: A one-way determination of obviousness is normally sufficient (ask whether the application claim would have been anticipated by or an obvious variation of the patent claim). A two-way test is applied only when the applicant could not have filed the claims in a single application and there is administrative delay by the Office.
guidance: Use a one-way test in most cases, including when the application is later filed or both were filed the same day. Apply the two-way test only when administrative delay and inability to have claimed both inventions in one application are clearly shown; two-way requires applying the Graham analysis twice (with application claims as claims-in-issue and then with the patent claims as claims-in-issue), and both analyses must compel a conclusion of obviousness to support an obviousness-type double patenting rejection. Shift burden to applicant to show why two-way is required if record does not clearly show administrative delay or inability to file together.

name: Schneller-type (other) nonstatutory double patenting – rare circumstances
description: Certain unique fact patterns (illustrated by In re Schneller) justify another type of nonstatutory double patenting rejection even where inventions may be nonobvious over each other, e.g., when earlier patent claims effectively cover and would extend protection for later claimed subject matter.
guidance: Schneller-based double patenting rejections are rare and fact-specific. An examiner must consult with the SPE and obtain approval of the Technology Center Director before making such a nonstatutory double patenting rejection. Form paragraphs 8.33 and 8.38 (or 8.39 for provisional) may be used for this type.

name: Form paragraph usage and sequencing rules
description: Form paragraph 8.33 (heading for nonstatutory double patenting) must precede any one of form paragraphs 8.34–8.39 and must be used only once in an Office action.
guidance: Choose the appropriate specific form paragraph (8.34–8.39) depending on whether the reference is a patent or application, whether secondary references are used, and whether the rejection is provisional. Insert required bracketed information (claim numbers, patent/application numbers, rationale, secondary references). Use related form paragraphs (e.g., 8.27, 8.28) when required by ownership or priority issues.

name: National law may require translation of priority document under limited circumstances
description: The national law applicable may require the applicant to furnish a translation of the priority document, provided that such a translation may only be required: (i) where the validity of the priority claim is relevant to determining patentability; or (ii) where the international filing date was accorded on the basis of incorporation by reference of an element or part, and for determining under Rule 82 ter.1(b) whether that element or part is completely contained in the priority document.
