guidance: Where a part of the description, claims or drawings is involved, the Office may also require an indication of where that part is contained in the translation of the priority document. (Rule 51 bis.1(e) and 51 bis.1(e)(ii))

name: Allowing additional briefing on remand
description: In deciding whether to allow additional briefing, the panel will take into account whether the parties already have had an adequate opportunity to address the issues raised by the remand.
guidance: A new or revised claim construction not previously considered or a change in the law usually justifies additional briefing. Additional briefing, when permitted, will normally be limited to the specific issues raised by the remand.

name: Default appeals procedures for ex parte/reexamination remand scenarios
description: The SOP provides default outcomes for common ex parte/reexamination remand scenarios (non‑exhaustive): e.g., for Erroneous Claim Interpretation — 'No, unless alternative claim interpretation renders the present rejection(s) moot'; Failure to Consider the Evidence — 'No, unless the evidence of record is deemed entirely insufficient to support the present rejection(s)'; Inadequate Explanation — 'No — the Board provides additional explanation or reverses on the present record'; Erroneous Application of Law — 'No, unless correct application of law renders rejections moot'; Lack of Due Process — 'Yes – typically in the form of a new ground of rejection'; Improper Consideration — 'No – arguments not sufficiently briefed before the Board are deemed waived.'
guidance: These procedures are default and circumstances not contemplated may necessitate a different procedure.

name: Knowledge requirement for certain misconduct counts (e.g., 37 C.F.R. §§ 10.85(a)(2), 10.85(a)(3), 10.23(c)(10))
description: Some Disciplinary Rules proscribe 'knowingly' advancing unwarranted claims or 'knowingly' failing to disclose information required by law. Violations of these provisions require proof that the practitioner knew the conduct or information at issue.
guidance: For counts that include a 'knowing' element, the OED Director must prove the practitioner's knowledge (or intent). If the practitioner genuinely lacked awareness of the disqualifying facts (e.g., did not know § 102(b) applied), those particular counts are not proven. Distinguish these from rules like §10.77(c) where 'knowledge' is not required.

name: Affirmative defense pleading and proof requirements (37 C.F.R. § 11.36(c))
description: To raise an affirmative defense, a respondent must 'state affirmatively in the answer special matters of defense.' The statement must (1) specify the defense, (2) explain the defense's nexus to the alleged misconduct, and (3) explain why it provides a defense. Affirmative defenses must be proven by clear and convincing evidence.
guidance: A bare or generic assertion that the complaint fails to state a claim is insufficient. The defense must be pleaded with factual and legal specificity and supported at hearing with clear and convincing evidence.

name: Scope of Inter Partes Reexamination
description: The permissible scope—what issues and claims may be reexamined under inter partes reexamination.
guidance: Office does not accept requests filed on/after Sept 16, 2012; see prior MPEP revision for the former scope rules and limitations.

name: Amendment by Patent Owner
description: Procedure, timing, and requirements for patent owner amendments to claims or specification during reexamination.
guidance: Office does not accept requests filed on/after Sept 16, 2012; earlier MPEP revision outlines amendment practice, including fees and support requirements.

name: Doctrine of claim differentiation (presumption)
description: “The presence of a dependent claim that adds a particular limitation gives rise to a presumption that the limitation in question is not present in the independent claim.” (Phillips v. AWH Corp.)
guidance: Treat the existence of a dependent claim that adds a limitation as creating a presumption that the independent claim does not include that limitation. The article repeatedly treats this as a baseline canon of claim construction and a check against importing limitations from dependent claims into independent claims.

name: Strength of the claim-differentiation presumption
description: Chief Judge Rader: the presumption is a “strong presumption”; Judge Lourie: the implication “is not a strong one.”
guidance: The presumption is especially strong when the limitation in dispute is the only meaningful difference between an independent and dependent claim and one party is urging that the limitation be read into the independent claim (citing SunRace Roots). Whether the presumption is 'strong' can be dispositive in claim construction disputes.

name: Limits on importing limitations from dependent to independent claims
description: One should not read limitations recited in a dependent claim into the independent claim absent strong reason; importing such limitations is disfavored.
guidance: Anti-pattern: applying the dependent claim’s limitation to the independent claim without overcoming the claim-differentiation presumption. The article criticizes reading the dependent claim’s 'one-piece' limitation into the independent claim in Retractable Technologies.

name: Read claim language in view of the written description/specification
description: “The claim language must always be read in view of the written description” (Phillips).
guidance: A specification that repeatedly characterizes the invention in limiting terms (e.g., 'one piece hollow body', 'each syringe embodiment contains a one-piece') can be used to construe claim terms more narrowly. Courts will consider specification statements, prior-art discussion, and how embodiments are described when construing claim terms.

name: Claims themselves define the claimed invention; ordinary and customary meaning
description: The claims themselves, not the written description portion of the specification, define the claimed invention; claim language is to be given its ordinary and customary meaning.
guidance: If a term has no special technical meaning and parties do not contend otherwise, construction may require ‘little more than the application of the widely accepted meaning of commonly understood words.’ This supports resisting narrow constructions not supported by claim language.

name: When specification can rebut the claim-differentiation presumption
description: A specification that (1) disparages alternatives as prior art, (2) explicitly states the invention features a particular limited structure, and (3) describes each embodiment as containing the limitation, may rebut the presumption.
guidance: Judge Lourie relied on the 'Summary of the Invention' stating 'one piece hollow body', prior-art characterization, and that 'the specifications do not disclose a body that consists of multiple pieces' to justify limiting claim term 'body' to one-piece. Use of such specification language is a path for rebuttal, but must be weighed against the presumption.

name: Drafting guideline: exemplify alternative embodiments to avoid narrow constructions
description: Patent applicants should specifically exemplify alternative embodiments (e.g., multi-piece body) in the specification to avoid narrow constructions that import limitations.
guidance: Practical drafting tip from the article: explicitly describe embodiments that cover the alternative structures you want the claims to encompass. Failure to exemplify alternatives can create vulnerability to a narrow construction or enablement challenges.

name: Drafting guideline: avoid limiting statements in the Summary of the Invention
description: Avoid language in the Summary of the Invention that could be read as limiting, such as repeatedly stating the invention 'features a one piece hollow body.'
guidance: The article notes that limiting references in the Summary can create a faulty presumption in judges' minds that the claimed invention is limited by those descriptions—drafters should use careful, non-limiting phrasing in summaries.

name: Enablement risk under 35 U.S.C. § 112, first paragraph
description: Not specifically exemplifying certain embodiments (e.g., multi-piece bodies) may create enablement issues under 35 U.S.C. § 112, first paragraph.
guidance: Failure to disclose or exemplify claimed variations could give rise to a potential lack-of-enablement argument. The article flags enablement as a possible risk when alternative embodiments are not described.

name: Written-description and indefiniteness considerations (35 U.S.C. § 112)
description: Claim construction disputes may implicate written-description requirements and possibly indefiniteness under 35 U.S.C. § 112.
guidance: Judge Plager focused on concerns about 'indefinite and ambiguous claims, divorced from the written description' and suggested the need for stringent rules; drafters and courts should be mindful that ambiguous claim language divorced from specification support can trigger §112 issues.

name: Ordinary-meaning fallback where no special technical meaning exists
description: If no party contends that a claim term has a special technical meaning, construction should default to the ordinary and customary meaning of the word (e.g., 'body' not limited to 'one-piece' absent other indications).
guidance: This is a corollary to the 'claims define the invention' principle: courts should not construe ordinary words narrowly unless the specification or context clearly demands it.

name: Non-statutory examples (claims not within the four categories)
description: Non-limiting examples of claims that are not directed to one of the statutory categories include transitory forms of signal transmission (e.g., propagating electrical/electromagnetic signal per se), a naturally occurring organism, a human per se, a legal contractual agreement, a game defined as a set of rules, a computer program per se, a company, and a mere arrangement of printed matter.
guidance: If a claim is clearly not within one of the four categories, it is not patent eligible and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 for that reason. Provide examples and cite relevant case law (In re Nuijten, Chakrabarty, Gottschalk v. Benson, In re Miller, etc.).

name: Claims that encompass both statutory and non-statutory embodiments
description: A claim that covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments (under the broadest reasonable interpretation) embraces subject matter that is not eligible for patent protection and therefore is directed to non-statutory subject matter.
guidance: When a claim's broadest reasonable interpretation in view of the specification encompasses non-statutory embodiments (e.g., machine-readable media that includes a carrier wave), a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 is appropriate. If amendment could cure the defect, still conduct Step 2.

name: Judicial exceptions to statutory categories
description: Judicially recognized exceptions include laws of nature, physical phenomena, and abstract ideas. A claim wholly directed to such an exception is not eligible for patent protection.
guidance: Evaluate whether the claim is for a particular practical application of the exception (which may be eligible) or whether it claims the exception itself (which is ineligible). Consider other descriptive terms used in precedent (natural phenomena, scientific principles, mental processes, disembodied mathematical algorithms), and consult case law (Bilski, Diehr, Chakrabarty, Funk Bros., Le Roy).

name: Practical application for product claims (machines, manufactures, compositions)
description: For product categories, eligible items are non-naturally occurring products typically formed of tangible elements or parts that embody a particular or specific, tangible practical application of the invention.
guidance: Product claims that recite tangible structural limitations (e.g., 'a machine comprising...') are more likely to show a practical application. Claims that recite product categories but lack tangible limitations (i.e., cover every way of applying an abstract concept) are not limited to a practical application and are ineligible. Evaluate whether the claim's limitations limit the claim to a tangible embodiment and whether preemption of other applications occurs.

name: Practical application for process (method) claims
description: A process claim must be limited to a particular practical application to be statutory under 35 U.S.C. 101; not every claimed method qualifies as a statutory process.
guidance: Use inquiries and factors (including the machine-or-transformation test as a useful investigative tool) to determine whether the method claim is directed to an abstract idea or is a patent-eligible practical application. Consider whether recited steps are merely field-of-use or insignificant post-solution activity.

name: Machine-or-transformation test (investigative tool)
description: The machine-or-transformation test is a useful and important clue for determining whether a claimed invention is a process under § 101: (1) tied to a particular machine/apparatus, or (2) transforms a particular article into a different state or thing.
guidance: Although not the sole test, use it as part of the fact-specific analysis. Passing the test supports eligibility; failing it does not automatically render a claim ineligible, but it is relevant evidence.

name: Factor: particularity or generality of machine elements
description: When a machine or apparatus is recited, consider the degree to which the machine in the claim can be specifically identified (the particularity of the machine elements).
guidance: Incorporation of a particular, well-defined machine or apparatus into the claimed method weighs toward eligibility. Broad recitation of 'a computer' without particularized structure may be insufficient unless programming specifics make it a special-purpose computer.

name: Factor: whether the machine/apparatus implements the steps
description: Evaluate whether the recited machine/apparatus actually implements the steps of the method (integral to performance) or is merely an object on which the method operates.
guidance: Integral use of the machine to perform the method steps weighs toward eligibility. A machine that cannot perform the claimed steps (e.g., Internet merely as data source) or is only tangentially involved weighs against eligibility.

name: Factor: extrasolution activity and field-of-use limitations
description: Determine whether the machine's involvement or other recited activity is insignificant 'extra-solution' activity or merely a field-of-use limitation that does not meaningfully limit the claimed invention.
guidance: Field-of-use limitations and insignificant activities (e.g., mere data-gathering that all applications of the method would require) do not impose meaningful limits and weigh against eligibility. Cite examples (Bilski, Parker v. Flook, Cybersource).

name: Computer-implemented process requirements
description: For computer-implemented processes, a general purpose computer may be sufficiently particular when programmed to perform the claimed steps (programming creates a new, special-purpose machine).
guidance: Claims must clearly convey that the computer is programmed to perform the method steps; mere addition of 'computer-aided' or performing on a computer, without explanation of how the computer aids or the significance of the computer, is insufficient to render an abstract concept patentable.

name: Computer-readable medium (manufacture) guidance
description: A non-transitory, tangible computer-readable storage medium that possesses structural limitations qualifies as a manufacture and would be patent-eligible subject matter if the claim as a whole has a real-world use and does not cover substantially all practical uses of a judicial exception.
guidance: Adding executable instructions or stored data to such a statutory-eligible medium does not render it non-statutory so long as the claim as a whole remains a tangible embodiment and practical application. Evaluate whether claim still impermissibly preempts all uses of an abstract idea.

name: Preemption as a central concern
description: If the claim impermissibly covers substantially all practical applications of a judicial exception (preempts the exception), it is not patent-eligible.
guidance: Assess whether the claim's breadth would grant a monopoly over the basic tools of scientific and technological work. Use examples (e.g., hedging in Bilski) to illustrate preemption concerns.

name: Making a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 (what examiner must state)
description: When making a rejection for failure to claim patent-eligible subject matter, identify the natural principle/abstract idea, identify that the claim is effectively directed to that principle, and explain reasons the additional claim features or combination of features fail to integrate the principle into a practical application or fail to be sufficient to amount to significantly more than the principle.
guidance: Provide a clear analysis showing which inquiry the claim fails (e.g., passes Inquiries 1-2 but fails Inquiry 3) and why. Use sample rejections (e.g., insulin dosage example) as models for structure and required explanation.

name: Evaluating applicant responses and permissible amendments
description: A proper response to a subject-matter-eligibility rejection is an amendment adding features or amending existing features that integrate the judicial exception into the process (practically apply it) and are sufficient to limit the application to more than the principle itself, or persuasive argument that the additional steps add something significantly more.
guidance: Examples of persuasive amendments: add non-conventional, non-routine steps; claim a device that integrates the principle (e.g., a sanitizing device using UV light with specific structure) rather than merely instructing to 'apply' the principle. A showing that steps are not routine, well-known, or conventional can be persuasive. Refer to 2012 Interim Guidance for additional examples.

name: Insignificant post-solution activity and field-of-use limitations are insufficient
description: Limitations that are mere fields of use or insignificant post-solution activity do not render an otherwise abstract claim patent-eligible.
guidance: Adding steps that simply confine an abstract idea to a particular environment (e.g., 'for use with a machine') or adding data-gathering steps that are routine will not save a claim. Cite Parker v. Flook and Bilski decisions and relevant examples in the MPEP.

name: Status identifiers per 37 CFR 1.121(c)
description: Claims must use status identifiers as set forth in 37 CFR 1.121(c) (e.g., Original; Currently amended; Canceled; Withdrawn; Previously presented; New; Not entered).
guidance: The MPEP provides acceptable alternative phrasings (e.g., 'Original Claim'/'Originally Filed Claim', 'Presently amended'/'Currently amended claim', various forms of 'Canceled', 'Withdrawn from consideration', 'Previously amended', 'Newly added', 'Not entered claim'). The Office may accept additional variations if an Office personnel determines the status is accurate and clear. When accepting alternatives, the examiner is not required to correct them by examiner’s amendment, and applicant will not be notified or required to submit corrective compliant amendment; the examiner does not need to state on the record that the alternative identifiers have been accepted.

name: Notice and handling of non-compliant amendments (PTOL-324)
description: If an amendment fails to comply with 37 CFR 1.121, the Office will notify applicant by a Notice of Non-Compliant Amendment (Form PTOL-324) identifying the non-compliant sections, required items for compliance, and reasons for non-compliance.
guidance: The form identifies which section is non-compliant (e.g., amendments to the claims section), items required for compliance (e.g., a claim listing in compliance with 37 CFR 1.121(c)), and reasons why it fails to comply (e.g., missing status identifiers). The type of amendment determines whether a response period is provided and whether the applicant's reply must include only the corrected section (e.g., corrected claim listing) rather than the entire amendment. Various amendment types have specific processing rules and timeframes (see separate entries for amendment-type-specific handling).

name: Preliminary amendment present on the filing date (non-compliant procedure)
description: A preliminary amendment that is present on the filing date but fails to comply with 37 CFR 1.121 will prompt OPAP to send a 'Notice to File Corrected Application Papers' with a two-month reply period; extensions under 37 CFR 1.136(a) are available.
guidance: Failure to reply may result in abandonment of the application. Applicant's reply is required to include either a substitute specification under 37 CFR 1.125 if the amendment is to the specification, or a complete claim listing under 37 CFR 1.121(c) if the amendment is to the claims. For applications filed prior to certain dates, preliminary amendments present on filing date may or may not be part of original disclosure (see separate entry on original disclosure/timeliness).

name: Amendment of replacements (amendment of amendments)
description: When a replacement paragraph or section of the specification is to be amended, the replacement should be wholly rewritten and the original insertion canceled.
guidance: A marked-up version of the replacement paragraph/section should be presented using underlining to indicate added subject matter and strike-through to indicate deletions. Matter canceled by amendment can be reinstated only by a subsequent amendment presenting the canceled matter as a new insertion. A claim canceled in its entirety may be reinstated only by a subsequent amendment presenting the claim as a new claim with a new claim number.

name: Preliminary amendment content and publication compliance (37 CFR 1.121/1.115/1.215/1.125)
description: Any preliminary amendment, whenever filed, must comply with 37 CFR 1.121 (e.g., include a complete listing of all claims and each section must begin on a separate sheet) and must be in a format usable for publication if the Office is to publish it.
guidance: Preliminary amendments transmitted in a transmittal letter will not comply. If a preliminary amendment to the specification (other than claims) is filed in a format unusable for publication, OPAP will require the applicant to submit a substitute specification in compliance with 37 CFR 1.121(b)(3) and 1.125. Only a substitute specification is usable for publication as an amendment to the specification. Preliminary amendments to claims or the abstract in compliance with 37 CFR 1.121(c) and 1.121(b)(2) can be published without a substitute specification. Applicants should avoid preliminary amendments when possible, incorporating desired changes into the original specification and claim set at filing to avoid publication and processing issues; including a new claim set as part of the originally filed specification may avoid application size fees since both the specification and preliminary amendment count toward page limits per 37 CFR 1.16(s).

name: Differences Between Prior Art and Claims
description: Identifying what distinguishes the claimed invention from existing prior art disclosures.
guidance: Examiners must articulate the specific differences between the claimed subject matter and prior art teachings—conclusory statements are insufficient. Findings should address the whole claimed invention and be supported by reasoned explanation.

name: Whole Invention Analysis
description: The claimed invention must be evaluated as a complete system, not reduced to isolated 'gist' or 'thrust' elements; inherent properties disclosed in specifications count.
guidance: Avoid dissecting claims into over-simplified fragments. Consider the claimed invention in its entirety; include inherent properties and features disclosed in the specification when assessing obviousness.

name: Prior Art Considered in Its Entirety
description: References must be assessed in their entirety, including portions teaching away from the claimed invention.
guidance: Examiners should consider all teachings of a reference, both those that support and those that discourage the claimed approach. Mere disclosure of alternatives does not necessarily constitute teaching away—explain why portions teach away if asserting such.

name: If trial and error are required, it can’t be obvious
description: “Trial and error” suggests that research or experimentation has an unexpected, unsuccessful component. The “error” portion suggests that the skilled worker is going in the wrong direction, learning what didn’t work rather than going in the plain and 'obvious' direction of what would be expected to be a successful result. Thus anything that requires 'trial and error' cannot be obvious.
guidance: Trial and error indicates an unpredictable research path with intermediate failures and dead ends, not a route that leads 'directly and without difficulty' to the solution. Examples: unpredictable properties of separated isomers or unexpected beneficial properties of specific salts (e.g., bisulfate salt). If the skilled person would have to pursue such trial-and-error work, the claimed invention is not obvious.

name: Effective date for U.S. patents, U.S. patent application publications, and PCT/WIPO international publications
description: U.S. patents, U.S. patent application publications, and WIPO publications of international applications are available as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) and the effective date used to be overcome is their effective U.S. filing date, not any foreign filing date to which they may be entitled under 35 U.S.C. 119(a).
guidance: See MPEP §706.02(a), §706.02(f)(1), and §§2136–2136.03 for detailed discussion. In re Hilmer: effective date of a domestic patent as a reference is not the foreign filing date. When a U.S. patent/publication claims benefit of an earlier application, determine effective filing date under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) per MPEP guidance.

name: Activities applied against claims — remedies (antedate or show applicant performed activity)
description: A rejection based on an activity showing the claimed invention was used or known prior to the filing date may be overcome by an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 establishing a date of invention prior to the activity, or by a specific affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 showing that the activity was performed by the applicant(s).
guidance: See MPEP §715.01(d). Distinguish whether the activity constitutes a statutory bar and whether required acts occurred in a qualifying country under 37 CFR 1.131(a)(1) and 35 U.S.C. 104.

name: General rule regarding generic claims (species antedating genus)
description: In most cases, a reference or activity applied against generic claims may be antedated by an affidavit/declaration showing completion of only a single species within the genus prior to the effective date of the reference or activity (so long as the reference/activity is not a statutory bar or a patent/application publication claiming the same invention).
guidance: Cites Ex parte Biesecker, In re Fong, In re Defano. Exception: unpredictable arts — see MPEP §715.03 for practice in unpredictable arts where single species may not suffice; consider whether showing is commensurate with minimum patent specification support for a genus claim.

name: Genus-species and predictability (when species proof insufficient)
description: Where predictability is in question (unpredictable arts), an affidavit/declaration showing prior completion of one or a few species within a disclosed genus will generally not overcome a reference or activity that discloses a genus; the affidavit must show at least the minimum disclosure required by a patent specification to support a generic claim.
guidance: Apply tests from In re Shokal, Mantell, Rainer, DeFano, Clarke, Schaub. The number of species needed to infer genus possession depends on genus size (e.g., for small genus like halogens, reduction to practice of three species — perhaps two — might suffice; for large genera many more species may be required). The practical test is whether facts would persuade one skilled in the art that the applicant possessed as much of the invention as is shown in the reference or activity.

name: U.S. patent or application publication claiming same invention — remedies and limits of 1.131
description: When a noncommonly owned U.S. patent or application publication claims the same invention and its publication/issue date is within specified timeframes relative to presentation of claims, the remedy may be interference (37 CFR 41.202) rather than 37 CFR 1.131; 35 U.S.C. 135(b)(1) or (b)(2) may require ex parte rejection depending on dates. A 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit is ineffective to overcome a U.S. patent or application publication that claims the same invention or that is not patentably distinct from the application’s claims.
guidance: If the reference publication date is less than one year prior to presentation of claims, applicant’s remedy, if any, is via interference (37 CFR 41.202) rather than 1.131. If a U.S. patent issues more than one year before presentation of claims to that invention, reject under 35 U.S.C. 135(b)(1). For commonly owned references where claims are not identical but not patentably distinct, a terminal disclaimer and an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.130 may be used to overcome a 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection. Use form paragraphs 23.14/23.14.01 for 35 U.S.C. 135(b) rejections. Cites In re McGrew and a line of cases (In re Clark, In re Hidy, etc.) holding 1.131 ineffective where there is no patentable distinction.

name: Aggregation (mere combination) vs inventive step
description: If modification or substitution of elements does not lead to structural difficulties and the functional effect of new elements is not regarded as greater than the summed effects of the prior art references, the claimed invention falls within an aggregation and is denied inventive step.
guidance: Examples show combining known machine, vacuum chamber, and fastening system; if the combination causes no particular difficulties and yields no remarkable difference, it is obvious to a person skilled in the art. Examiner should ask whether combination yields more than the sum of parts (structural difficulty or remarkable effect).

name: When combining multiple prior arts — indicia to consider
description: In determining inventive step for a combination invention, the examiner should consider whether (①) there is good possibility that a person with ordinary skill would combine them, (②) the prior arts come from similar or neighboring technical fields, and (③) there is a reasonable basis to associate each other for the combination.
guidance: Also be cautious: reliance on a large number of prior-art references may indicate improper hindsight or that the rejection lacks a valid ground. Combining many references to reach the claim can be suspect.

name: Prior art that 'teaches away' supports inventive step
description: If a prior art reference teaches not to rely on that prior art (i.e., teaches away from the claimed invention), the inventive step is not denied by that prior art despite similarity.
guidance: Note: the mere description of a prior art as 'inferior' cannot necessarily be considered as teaching away. Examiner must identify explicit teach-away teaching in prior art.

name: Commercial success and market/favorable comment as secondary evidence
description: Commercial success or favorable industry comments, or that an invention was not implemented for a long time before filing, may be regarded as indicative of inventive step as secondary evidence, but these facts alone are not sufficient.
guidance: Commercial success must derive from the technical features of the invention (not e.g. sales technique or advertising). Examples illustrate that large sales or contracts do not prove inventive step if success is due to non-technical factors; if a claimed device shows a distinguished technical effect and had not been implemented before filing, that may support non-obviousness but objective evidence is required.

name: Overcoming otherwise irresolvable technical difficulties
description: If a claimed invention proposes means for overcoming technical difficulties not resolvable by other means, or solves a technical problem where other means fail, this is advantageous evidence for inventive step.
guidance: Examiner should treat such evidence as supportive of non-obviousness.

name: Dependent claims inherit inventive step when independent claim is inventive
description: If an independent claim involves an inventive step, a claim dependent on the independent claim is deemed to involve an inventive step too.
guidance: Conversely, if the independent claim lacks inventive step, the inventive step determination should be made for each dependent claim separately.

name: Case-by-case determination; foreign examination results are non-binding
description: Inventive step is determined case by case according to the concrete scope of the claimed invention; examination results in foreign countries are only references and the examiner does not need to follow them.
guidance: Different legal systems and customs abroad may lead to different results; use foreign outcomes only as non-binding guidance.

name: Legal prohibitions on implementation are irrelevant to inventive step
description: If implementation of a claimed invention is prohibited by law in Korea or abroad, such legal restriction is not taken into consideration in determining inventive step.
guidance: Example: a method of lottery drawing that is legally prohibited is still judged for inventive step on technical difficulty alone and may be considered obvious despite legal prohibition preventing implementation.

name: Examine whole disclosure of prior art rather than cherry-picked parts
description: When determining inventive step in view of prior art, the examiner should base findings on what a person skilled in the art can reasonably recognize from the whole disclosure of the prior art rather than from certain parts which could create a ground for lack of inventive step.
guidance: If the applicant presents other prior art that contradicts or makes parts of the disclosure unclear, the examiner should determine whether a skilled person can easily arrive at the claimed invention by taking the prior art comprehensively.

name: Scope of 'specification or drawings as originally filed' for international applications
description: When another application is an international application, 'specification or drawings as originally filed in another patent application' is construed as 'description of the invention, claims, or drawings submitted by the international application date' and 'laid open' includes international publication under PCT Article 21.
guidance: If the international application is in foreign language, the effect may be limited to the content in the translation. The extent of enlarged novelty applied to international applications depends on submission/translation rules and dates (special rules differ for applications filed before/after 2015).

name: Priority claim filing-date treatment for another application
description: Where another application claims priority under the Paris Convention, the filing date in the first country is deemed the filing date of the 'another application' for inventions commonly disclosed in both specifications/drawings.
guidance: Only the inventions disclosed in the first-country application count for the earlier filing date. Examples show which inventions of a multi-invention disclosure can be relied upon based on where they were disclosed and filed.

name: Requirement that the claimed invention be identical to what's described in the earlier application's original specification
description: The invention described in the claims of the present application must be completely or substantially identical to an invention or utility innovation described in the original specification of another application for Article 29(3)-(4) to apply.
guidance: Even if matters described in the original specification of the other application are omitted by amendment after filing, Article 29(3,4) is implemented; conversely, inventions newly added by amendment are not covered.

name: International application special rules and translation/withdrawal effect (post-2015 rules)
description: For international applications filed on/after Jan 1, 2015, 'laid open' includes PCT international publication, and the relevant 'specification or drawings' are those submitted by the international filing date; if a Korean translation is not submitted within the specified period (Article 201(4)), the international application may be deemed withdrawn and cannot be relied upon under Article 29(3)-(4).
guidance: When applying Article 29(3)-(6) to an international application claiming domestic priority, inventions disclosed in the international filing may be deemed laid open as of the international publication date for the purposes of domestic examination. The exact scope of what is relied upon may depend on whether translation was submitted and on priority relationships.

name: Limitation on use of Patentability Report practice
description: Patentability Report practice is discretionary and should be used only where it will save total examiner time or improve quality due to specialized knowledge. It is never proper where claims are directed to the same character of invention but differ in scope only.
guidance: Examples where P.R. is ordinarily not proper include (A) product/process manufacturing pairs, (B) product and process that merely makes the product, and (C) combinations distinguished solely by a subcombination. A P.R. may be used when it demonstrably saves examiner time with Director of Technology Center approval (mark 'Approved' on request).

name: Baseline claim examination goals
description: After reading the application, performing a prior art search, and analyzing application against the prior art, the examiner should determine whether the claims define a useful, novel, nonobvious, and enabled invention clearly described in the specification.
guidance: Goal of examination is to clearly articulate any rejection early so the applicant can respond; examiner should review all evidence, arguments, and responses before issuing the next Office action. Require information reasonably necessary under 37 CFR 1.105 generally prior to or with the first Office action on the merits.

name: Requirement to cite best references and explain pertinence
description: When rejecting claims for want of novelty or obviousness, the examiner must cite the best references at his or her command. For complex references or references showing multiple inventions, the particular part relied on must be designated as nearly as practicable.
guidance: If pertinence is not apparent, it must be clearly explained and each rejected claim specified.

name: Constructive handling of defects in form or omission of limitation
description: When patentable subject matter is disclosed but claims cannot be allowed due to defects in form or omission of a limitation, the examiner should not stop with a bare objection or rejection.
guidance: Examiner's action should be constructive and, when possible, offer a definite suggestion for correction.

name: Rejection on prior art (35 U.S.C. 102 and 103)
description: The most frequent grounds of rejection are lack of novelty under 35 U.S.C. 102 or obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103. Language used in rejecting claims should be unequivocal.
guidance: See MPEP §707.07(d) for guidance on phrasing rejections.

name: Choice of prior art; use the best available art
description: Prior art rejections should ordinarily be confined strictly to the best available art.
guidance: Exceptions permitted where (A) propriety of rejection depends on particular claim interpretation, (B) claim met only in terms by a reference that does not disclose inventive concept, or (C) most pertinent reference likely to be antedated by a 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit/declaration. Avoid merely cumulative rejections.

name: Distinction between 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 rejections
description: Under 35 U.S.C. 102, the reference must teach every aspect of the claimed invention explicitly or implicitly (anticipation). Under 35 U.S.C. 103, the reference teachings must be modified in a way that would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made.
guidance: See MPEP §§2131–2146 for detailed guidance on determinations under 102 and 103.

name: Determining whether to apply 35 U.S.C. 102(a), (b), or (e)
description: After finding a printed publication or patent disclosing the claimed invention, determine which subsection of 35 U.S.C. 102 applies by comparing the effective filing date of the application with the date of the reference.
guidance: Consider 102(b) first (statutory bar if reference >1 year before effective filing date). If 102(b) does not apply because reference is too recent, consider 102(e) and then 102(a) as appropriate.

name: Ways to overcome 35 U.S.C. 102(a) or 102(e) rejections
description: Rejections based on 35 U.S.C. 102(a) or 102(e) can be overcome by: (A) arguing patentable distinctness over the prior art; (B) amending the claims to patentably distinguish over the prior art; (C) filing affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.131 (for (e)) or 1.132/1.131 (for (a)) where appropriate to show prior invention or that the reference invention is not by 'another'; (D) perfecting priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d), 119(e) or 120 where applicable.
guidance: For 102(e) specifically, a 1.132 declaration may show the reference invention is not by 'another'; see MPEP §§715, 715.01(a), 715.01(c), and 716.10 for affidavit/declaration requirements.

name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) — Patent Application Publication or Patent to Another with Earlier Filing Date (7.12.fti)
description: Use when the invention was described in (1) an application published under 122(b) by another filed in the U.S. before the applicant's invention, or (2) a patent granted on an application by another filed in the U.S. before the applicant's invention; international applications under section 351(a) have the effects of a U.S. application only if they designated the U.S. and were published under PCT Article 21(2) in English.
guidance: Only use if reference is (a) a U.S. patent or U.S. application publication filed under 111(a), (b) a U.S. patent issued from, or a U.S./WIPO publication of, an international application with an international filing date on/after Nov 29, 2000, or (c) a U.S. patent from, or WIPO publication of, an international design application that designates the U.S. Consider benefit claims under 119(e), 120, 121, 365(c), 386(c) if subject matter is supported in the earlier application. To rely on an international filing date under pre-AIA 102(e), the PCT must be filed on/after Nov 29, 2000, designate the U.S., and be published in English by WIPO; if not met, treat the reference under 102(a) or (b) as of publication date (see form paragraphs 7.08.fti and 7.09.fti). Precede this paragraph with 7.07.fti (and as appropriate 7.08.fti–7.11.fti).

name: Pre‑AIPA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) — U.S. Patent Issued From International Application Filed Before Nov 29, 2000 (7.12.01.fti)
description: When the reference is a U.S. patent issued (directly or indirectly) from an international application having an international filing date prior to Nov 29, 2000, the changes made by AIPA/2002 do not apply and the prior art date is determined under pre‑AIPA 35 U.S.C. 102(e).
guidance: Use only if reference is a U.S. patent issued from a national stage or continuing application claiming benefit to an international application with an international filing date prior to Nov 29, 2000. If the reference issued from a national stage, the pre‑AIPA 102(e) date is when requirements of 371(c)(1),(2),(4) were fulfilled. Consider benefit claims under 119(e), 120, 121, 365(c), 386(c) only if the relied‑upon subject matter is appropriately supported. Do NOT consider foreign priority claims under 119(a)–(d), 365(a)/(b), or 386(a)/(b). Precede with 7.07.fti and optionally 7.08.fti–7.11.fti.

name: Pre-AIA/AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) — Priority of Invention (7.14.aia / 7.14.fti)
description: Rejection based on another inventor establishing in an interference (or prior invention in this country) that the other inventor made the invention earlier and did not abandon, suppress, or conceal it; priority determination considers conception dates, reductions to practice, and reasonable diligence.
guidance: For AIA situations, use 7.14.aia (must be preceded by 7.07.aia). For pre‑AIA use 7.14.fti (precede with 7.07.fti and optionally 7.08.fti–7.13.fti). Note: A 102(g) rejection is appropriate in applications/patents examined under first‑to‑file if they contain claims with effective filing dates before March 16, 2013 or specific 120/121/365(c) references to patents/applications that contain such claims.

name: Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1)/102(a)(2) (7.15.aia)
description: Form paragraph for rejecting claim(s) under 35 U.S.C. 102 (a)(1) or (a)(2) as being anticipated by prior art.
guidance: Use only for applications filed on/after March 16, 2013 examined under AIA; must be preceded by 7.03.aia. Insert claim numbers in bracket 1; insert '(a)(1)' or '(a)(2)' in bracket 2 (or both); bracket 3 indicates 'clearly anticipated' or 'anticipated' with explanation; bracket 4 lists prior art relied upon. If (a)(2) applies, use the more specific subparagraph form paragraphs (7.15.01.aia, 7.15.02.aia, or 7.15.03.aia) as applicable. Precede with 7.07.aia and as appropriate 7.08.aia and 7.12.aia, or use form paragraph 7.103. For claims claiming priority/benefit to pre‑March 16, 2013 applications, precede with 7.06.

name: Rejection under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)/(b) and (g) (7.15.fti)
description: Form paragraph template for rejecting claims under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a), 102(b) (patent or publication), and 102(g).
guidance: Insert appropriate paragraph letter(s) of pre‑AIA 102 in bracket 2; indicate 'clearly anticipated' or 'anticipated' in bracket 3 and cite prior art in bracket 4. Precede by 7.07.fti and 7.08.fti/7.09.fti/7.14.fti as appropriate, or by 7.103. If pre‑AIA 102(e) is also applied, follow with one of 7.15.01.fti–7.15.03.fti. For applications with actual filing dates on/after March 16, 2013 that claim priority to pre‑March 16, 2013 filings, precede with 7.06.

name: Provisional Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) — common assignee/applicant/joint inventor (7.15.01.aia)
description: Provisional rejection of claims under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) as anticipated by a copending application that has a common assignee/applicant or at least one joint inventor and an earlier effective filing date.
guidance: Used in applications filed on/after March 16, 2013 (precede with 7.03.aia). The provisional rejection is based on presumption of future publication/patenting of the copending app. May be overcome by (1) showing under 37 CFR 1.130(a) that the disclosure was obtained from the inventor/joint inventor (not prior art), (2) showing under 37 CFR 1.130(b) of prior public disclosure under 102(b)(2)(B), or (3) statement under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) establishing ownership/assignment/joint research agreement as of the effective filing date. Terminal disclaimer does not overcome this rejection (In re Bartfeld). If claims would be obvious over the copending app, use obviousness form paragraph 7.21.01.aia. Insert required bracket items for claim numbers and application number and explanations of anticipation.

name: Provisional Rejection under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) — common assignee/applicant/joint inventor (7.15.01.fti)
description: Provisional rejection under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) when a copending application with earlier effective U.S. filing date (common assignee/applicant/joint inventor) discloses the claimed invention but has not yet been published under 122.
guidance: Based on presumption of future publication/patenting of the copending application. May be overcome by showing under 37 CFR 1.132 that any invention disclosed but not claimed in the copending app was derived from the inventor of this application (not 'by another'), or by appropriate showing under 37 CFR 1.131(a). Terminal disclaimer does not overcome this rejection. Use form paragraph 7.12.fti to determine copending application's pre‑AIA 102(e) date unless the copending app stems from an international application filed before Nov 29, 2000 (then use 7.12.01.fti). If claims are directed to same invention, make provisional double patenting rejection using form paragraphs 8.30 and 8.32.

name: Rejection under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) — common assignee/applicant/joint inventor (7.15.02.fti)
description: Reject claims under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as anticipated by a patent or patent application publication with an earlier effective filing date that has common assignee/applicant or a common joint inventor.
guidance: Use pre‑AIA 102(e) as amended by AIPA/2002 (form paragraph 7.12.fti) to determine the reference's 102(e) date unless the reference stems from an international application filed before Nov 29, 2000 (then use 7.12.01.fti). May be overcome by a showing under 37 CFR 1.132 that any disclosed-but-unclaimed invention was derived from the same inventive entity, or by 37 CFR 1.131(a) if the same invention is not being claimed. Consider benefit claims under 119(e), 120, 121, 365(c), 386(c) only if supported. Do not consider foreign priority claims under 119(a)–(d), etc. Patent application publications may be used only if preceded by 7.12.fti.

name: Rejection under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) — no common assignee or inventor(s) (7.15.03.fti)
description: Reject claims under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as anticipated by a patent or patent application publication with an earlier filing date where the reference need not have a common assignee or inventor.
guidance: Use when reference is a patent or patent application publication with earlier filing date; apply 7.12.fti or 7.12.01.fti as appropriate to determine 102(e) date. If a PCT publication has international filing date prior to Nov 29, 2000 and did not designate the U.S. or was not published in English by WIPO, do not use this paragraph and treat the reference as prior art under 102(a) or (b) as of publication date (see 7.08.fti/7.09.fti). Insert 'clearly anticipated' or 'anticipated' with explanation and cite prior art; patent application publications may be used only if 7.12.fti preceded this paragraph.

name: Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) — no common assignee or inventor(s) (7.15.03.aia)
description: Reject claims under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) as anticipated by a U.S. patent, U.S. patent application publication, or WIPO publication with an earlier effective filing date; the reference need not have a common assignee or inventor.
guidance: Used for applications filed on/after March 16, 2013 (precede with 7.03.aia). 102(a)(2) may be applied if the reference is (a) U.S. patent under 151 with earlier effective filing date, (b) U.S. patent application publication under 122(b) with earlier effective filing date, or (c) WIPO PCT publication/designating international design application with earlier effective filing date. If any of the three types was published before the claimed effective filing date, it is also applicable under 102(a)(1). Insert claim numbers, indicate 'clearly anticipated' or 'anticipated' and provide explanation and prior art. Precede by 7.12.aia.

name: 37 CFR 1.22(b) — fees must be itemized
description: All fees paid to the USPTO must be itemized in each individual application, patent, or other proceeding so that it is clear for which purpose the fees are paid; the Office may return fees that are not itemized as required.
guidance: A reference to 'filing fee(s)' is generally sufficient to cover filing/search/examination fees; references to 'any corresponding fee under 37 CFR 1.16' will cover surcharges, application size fee, excess claims fees, etc. Itemization is intended to help Office accounting and avoid returns.

name: Application of insufficient payment — nonprovisional filing order
description: If a payment submitted on filing of a nonprovisional application is insufficient and the applicant has not specified application of payment, the Office will apply the payment in this order until expended: (1) basic filing fee; (2) application size fee; (3) late filing surcharge; (4) processing fee for non-English application; (5) search fee; (6) examination fee; (7) excess claims fee.
guidance: Applicants should specify allocation to ensure intended fees are covered; otherwise Office follows this prescribed priority to determine which fees are satisfied.

name: Interpretation of 'filing fee' and 'basic filing fee' in deposit-account authorizations
description: The Office will treat an authorization to charge 'the filing fee' as authorization to charge applicable fees under 37 CFR 1.16: basic filing, search, examination, excess claims, and application size fees. An authorization to charge 'the basic filing fee' will be treated as authorization to charge basic filing, search, and examination fees. Authorizations that exclude search/examination must specifically limit the authorization by reference to paragraphs of 1.16.
guidance: Draft authorizations precisely. Broad language will be interpreted to include 1.16 and 1.17 fees but not 1.19/1.20/1.21 unless explicitly stated as noted above.

name: Known utility at time of reduction to practice
description: The claimed invention is not actually reduced to practice unless there is a known/practical utility at the time of reduction to practice (except for plant and design inventions).
guidance: Utility must be demonstrated by testing or other accepted evidence; for compounds, animal tests that reasonably correlate to human utility may suffice; a demonstrated substantial utility for any purpose (when no specific utility recited) can be sufficient (Wiesner v. Weigert; Ciric v. Flanigen; Rey-Bellet v. Engelhardt).

name: Consider claims as a whole (Diehr holistic principle)
description: Claims must be considered as a whole; it is inappropriate to dissect the claims into old and new elements and then ignore the presence of the old elements in the analysis.
guidance: Diamond v. Diehr directs holistic consideration of claims. The draft legislative text and some USPTO guidance emphasize holistic eligibility determinations, which tend to favor patentability because otherwise-ineligible elements may be rendered eligible when considered alongside other claim limitations.

name: Draft legislative reform features affecting eligibility
description: Draft bill provisions include deleting 'new' before 'useful', codifying holistic eligibility, creating a presumption in favor of eligibility, abrogating judicial exceptions, and removing Berkheimer-type factual elements from § 101 analysis.
guidance: Collectively these changes would skew toward expanding eligibility (making more subject matter patentable) but also include adjustments (e.g., § 112 changes) that could constrain claim breadth. Use these features to assess proposed statutory impacts on eligibility determinations.

name: Complete specification — content and claims requirement
description: The complete specification must contain a full description of the invention and in what manner the same is to be performed, and must end with a distinct statement of claims in the form: 'Having now particularly described and ascertained the nature of my said invention, and in what manner the same is to be performed, I declare that what I claim is, ...' followed by distinct statement of the features of novelty claimed.
guidance: The Complete Specification and its duplicate must be signed by the applicant or his agent on the last sheet with the date inserted ('Dated this day of 18__').

name: Compulsory licence petition requirements
description: A petition for compulsory grant of licences must clearly set forth the facts of the case and show that the petitioner's interest arises by reason of the default of the patentee to grant licences on reasonable terms; the statement of the case should show as far as possible that the terms of the proposed order are just and reasonable. Paragraphs should be numbered consecutively and the petition should specify the relief claimed.
guidance: The petition must be accompanied by an examined copy where required and the petition should state grounds under section 22 of the Act.

name: Complete breakdown of each claim into elements/limitations
description: The main purpose of Patent claim chart is to show the complete breakdown of each constituent into its elements or limitations.
guidance: Reviewing a claim and breaking it down into several limiting components is the first step in creating a claim chart. The claim chart presents all the data analyzed in a patent claim and is used to prove or analyze usage of the claimed invention in products, services, or standards.

name: Accurate interpretation of each claim element (not just keywords)
description: It is important to understand the interpretation of each element rather than just limiting to synonyms or keywords comprehensively.
guidance: Avoid superficial keyword/synonym matching. Determine the correct legal and technical scope of each limitation and use that interpretation when mapping evidence or prior art.

name: Evidence mapping for infringement (Evidence of Use / EOU) — satisfy the 'all elements test/rule'
description: An Evidence of Use (EOU) or Infringement Claim Chart shows how a product or technique is accused of infringement, including each claim element to fulfill the 'all elements test/rule' for infringement.
guidance: For infringement charts, demonstrate with specific evidence how each and every claim limitation is present in the accused product/service/standard. Use the chart to support Initial or preliminary infringement contentions (PICs), licensing presentations, or expert reports.

name: Invalidity charting to show anticipation or obviousness (Chart of References)
description: An Invalidity Chart, also known as a 'Chart of References', depicts the patent’s invalidity owing to anticipation or obviousness and is typically prepared by a defendant.
guidance: Map prior art references to claim limitations to show anticipation (exact limitation present) or obviousness (combination of references or reasoning). Use these charts in invalidity analysis during litigation, reexamination, or PTAB proceedings.

name: Claim construction/interpretation charts tying claim language to specification and literature
description: Plaintiffs and defendants construct a Claim Construction or Claim Interpretation Chart, which shows patent specifications or technical literature citations with accurate claim language interpretations.
guidance: Use cited portions of the specification and relevant technical literature to support the proposed meaning of claim terms. These charts assist in claim construction disputes and ensure claimed terms are grounded in the intrinsic/extrinsic record.

name: Use claim charts to analyze novelty and prior art relationships
description: For the purpose of invalidity analysis in litigation, Claim charts assist in confirming or refuting the novelty of a claim in relation to the prior art.
guidance: Explicitly show where prior art anticipates each limitation or how combinations render claims obvious. Use clear citations and side-by-side mappings to support novelty conclusions.

name: Use claim charts to verify presence of every limitation for infringement analysis
description: During infringement investigation and litigation, Claim charts aid in confirming or disputing whether each and every limitation of the claim is included in a good, service, or standard.
guidance: Document factual evidence (e.g., product specs, screenshots, standards text, reverse-engineering results) that corresponds to each limitation. Be explicit about gaps or elements not found.

name: Format choice: graphical or tabular representation as evidence
description: A patent claim chart can be a graphical or tabular (for use as evidence of use) representation of claims.
guidance: Use tabular layouts for clear side-by-side mapping of claim language to evidence/references; graphical depictions can aid visual understanding for presentations or expert exhibits. Ensure the chosen format is admissible and fits the target audience's needs.

name: Presumption of surrender from narrowing or unexplained amendments
description: A narrowing amendment (including an 'unexplained' amendment) made during prosecution triggers a rebuttable presumption that the patentee surrendered the entire territory between the original and the amended limitations.
guidance: See Festo VIII, 535 U.S. at 740–41. The presumption arises when the original claim as presented covered the alleged equivalent and the claim was subsequently narrowed; it applies whether the amendment was made for patentability or left unexplained. The party seeking to rely on the doctrine of equivalents must attempt to rebut this presumption under the Court's rebuttal criteria.

name: Scope of surrendered territory — 'entire territory between original and amended limitations'
description: When the presumption applies, the surrendered territory presumptively includes the entire intervening territory between the scope of the originally presented claim and the narrowed claim.
guidance: Courts must determine 'what territory the amendments surrendered' (Festo, 535 U.S. at 741). This requires attention to what was actually claimed and disclosed during prosecution; hindsight speculation about hypothetical claim language is improper. Disputes can arise over whether the original claim in fact encompassed the accused equivalent (e.g., whether a broader literal claim could have been presented consistent with the specification).

name: Rebuttal criterion — tangentiality of the amendment
description: A patentee can rebut the presumption by showing that the reason for the narrowing amendment was only tangentially related to the particular equivalent in question (i.e., the amendment was peripheral to the accused equivalent).
guidance: The patentee must explain how the rationale for adding or changing claim language was peripheral to the accused equivalent. Tangentiality is meant to permit courts to honor the objective intent of amendments where the surrendered subject matter bears only a peripheral relation to an alleged equivalent (example: amendment to adjust the top end of a claimed range may be tangential to equivalents beneath the range). Whether tangentiality is satisfied depends on the prosecution history and the patentee's stated rationale; courts should examine the record rather than rely on hindsight.

name: Rebuttal criterion — 'some other reason' the patentee could not reasonably have been expected to describe the equivalent
description: A patentee can rebut the presumption by showing there was some other reason (linguistic or practical) that the patentee could not reasonably have been expected to describe the insubstantial substitute in question.
guidance: Examples include shortcomings of language or other constraints that would have prevented the drafter from describing the equivalent. Arguments that an equivalent was merely 'inferior' or 'unacceptable' do not typically satisfy this criterion if the patentee could reasonably have described the equivalent (e.g., by using broader descriptive terms such as 'aluminum', 'metal', or claim phrasing like 'at least one sealing ring'). Courts should avoid using hindsight to rewrite the prosecution record; the inquiry focuses on what a careful drafter could reasonably have been expected to claim at the time.

name: Foreseeability principle limiting doctrine of equivalents
description: The doctrine of equivalents does not encompass subject matter that the patent drafter could have foreseen during prosecution and thus could have included in the claims; it protects only against insubstantial and unforeseeable substitutions.
guidance: Foreseeability reconciles the notice function of claims with the protective function of the doctrine of equivalents and can be applied both to rebut estoppel presumptions and more broadly to bar foreseeable equivalents outside the estoppel context. Application of foreseeability requires factual assessment of the state of the art at the time of drafting and amendment, and judges should consult expert evidence to approximate what a careful drafter would have foreseen and claimed.

name: Means-plus-function (§112, ¶6) and literal scope including structural equivalents
description: A 'sealing means' or similar means-plus-function limitation under §112, ¶6 can literally encompass structural equivalents disclosed in the specification.
guidance: Where the original claim used means-plus-function language, the literal scope of the original claim may have included structural equivalents; this affects whether an amendment actually narrowed coverage of an accused equivalent. Courts should analyze whether the original 'means' limitation literally encompassed the accused structure before concluding that the amendment surrendered that territory.

name: Who decides presumption and rebuttal issues — court role and procedural posture
description: Determination of the presumption of surrender and whether it has been rebutted is for the court (analogous to Markman for claim construction), but many aspects involve factual findings appropriate for the trial court.
guidance: The appellate court emphasized that while the legal determination of whether estoppel applies is for the court, the factual elements (particularly unforeseeability) require a trial record and evidentiary presentation. Some judges warned against converting tangentialness and 'other reason' inquiries into pure questions of law without permitting trial evidence. Remand to the district court is appropriate to receive evidence and make factual findings on unforeseeability (and, where contested, on other factual matters).

name: Disclosure / Enabling Disclosure (Enablement)
description: A disclosure must be sufficient for one skilled in the art to (1) understand what is being claimed (description requirement) and (2) to enable the person to make and use the invention (enablement requirement).
guidance: Also, in the U.S., the best mode of the invention must be disclosed in the application. See MPEP 608, 2161-2164.

name: Definiteness (Claim Clarity)
description: A characteristic of a patent claim in which claim language makes the scope of the claim clear to a person skilled in the art to which the invention pertains.
guidance: Claims must be definite to satisfy 35 U.S.C. §112 requirements; see MPEP 2173 series.

name: Claims Define the Monopoly (Claim Drafting)
description: Claims are what the inventor states to be unique about the invention and become the actual monopoly granted; claims define the scope of protection.
guidance: The specification should support the claims; careful claim drafting (independent and dependent claims) controls protection. See MPEP 608.01(i),(k),(m).

name: Transitional Phrases: 'Comprising' vs 'Consisting of'
description: 'Comprising' is inclusive and open-ended (does not exclude additional unrecited elements); 'Consisting of' is exclusive and excludes elements not specified.
guidance: Choose transitional language deliberately to control claim scope. 'Consisting essentially of' is a middle ground allowing inconsequential additional elements. See MPEP 2111.03.

name: Claim Types and Forms (e.g., Apparatus/Process/Product, Jepson, Markush)
description: Various statutory and stylistic claim forms exist (process/machine/article of manufacture/composition of matter); specialized forms include Jepson claims or Markush groups for claiming alternatives.
guidance: Select appropriate claim form for subject matter; Markush requires members to share a defining property (MPEP 803.02). Jepson claims recite known art then the improvement.

name: Teaching Away / Teaching Toward (Evidence for Obviousness)
description: 'Teaching Away' describes prior art that suggests a claimed invention is not possible (supports non-obviousness); 'Teaching Toward' describes prior art that points in the direction of the invention (supports obviousness).
guidance: These concepts are used when evaluating whether a combination of references would have been obvious to one skilled in the art. See MPEP 2145.

name: 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2)/103 rejection - design disclosed, no common inventors or common assignees
description: The claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being obvious over [1]. Because the reference names another inventor and has an earlier effectively filed date, it constitutes prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2).
guidance: Although the invention is not identically disclosed, if differences would have made the claimed invention obvious to a person of ordinary skill before the claimed effective filing date, it is unpatentable. This rejection might be overcome by: (1) a showing under 37 CFR 1.130(a) that the subject matter disclosed in the copending application was obtained directly or indirectly from the inventor or a joint inventor of this application (not prior art under 102(b)(2)(A)); (2) perfecting a claim to priority under 35 U.S.C. 119 by filing a certified priority document that satisfies enablement and description under 112(a); (3) perfecting the benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 120 by filing an application data sheet under 37 CFR 1.76 with a specific reference under 1.78 and establishing the prior application satisfies 112(a); or (4) a showing under 37 CFR 1.130(b) of a prior public disclosure under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(B). Provide explanation of obviousness including differences. For certain priority claims, precede with form paragraphs 15.10.aia and 15.10.15.

name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/103(a) rejection - design claimed in design patent with earlier prior art date and common assignee
description: The claim is rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being obvious over the claim in design patent [1]. Based upon the different inventive entity and the pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date of the reference, it constitutes prior art.
guidance: If the design claimed in the present application is not patentably distinct from the design claimed in the [3] patent, this rejection may be overcome by submitting an oath or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(c) stating that this application and the reference are currently owned by the same party and that the inventor named in this application is the prior inventor of the subject matter in the reference under 35 U.S.C. 104 (as in effect on March 15, 2013). In addition, a terminal disclaimer under 37 CFR 1.321(c) is required. A nonstatutory double patenting rejection must also be included in the action. Provide explanation of obviousness including differences and follow with form paragraphs 15.70.fti and 15.67 or 15.68. Precede by form paragraph 15.19.02.fti and, where applicable, 15.10.15.

name: Final rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 (single reference) (15.39.02)
description: The claim is FINALLY REJECTED under 35 U.S.C. 103 over [1].
guidance: In bracket 1, insert reference citation. See related form paragraphs in MPEP Chapter 700 for 'Action is Final' and 'Advisory after Final' paragraphs. Use appropriate wording where pre-AIA distinctions apply.

name: Final rejection under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) (single reference) (15.39.02.fti)
description: The claim is FINALLY REJECTED under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) over [1].
guidance: This description is incorporated into the claim by use of the language 'as shown and described.' See MPEP § 1503.01, subsection III. See form paragraphs in Chapter 700 for final action/advisory language.

name: Specification requirements under 35 U.S.C. 112 (general)
description: The specification shall contain a written description of the invention, and of the manner and process of making and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to make and use the same, and shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor or joint inventor. The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the inventor regards as the invention.
guidance: Begin compliance analysis with determination of scope of protection sought by the claims (see In re Moore). For design applications, the drawing is incorporated into the claim by use of 'as shown' and 'and described.' If appearance/shape cannot be determined due to inadequate visual disclosure, rejection under 112(a) and (b) is warranted.

name: Drawing incorporated into the claim; drawing adequacy
description: The drawing in a design application is incorporated into the claim by use of the claim language 'as shown.' Any determination of the scope of protection sought by the claim is also a determination of the subject matter that must be enabled by the disclosure.
guidance: If the appearance and shape/configuration of the design cannot be determined or understood due to an inadequate visual disclosure, the claim violates 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (definiteness) and 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (enablement). The drawing disclosure can be supplemented by narrative description (see MPEP § 1503.01, subsection II).

name: Level of drawing detail depends on whether design is inherently 2D or 3D (Maatita principle)
description: Some claimed designs are capable of being enabled and definite despite being disclosed using only a single plan- or planar-view. The level of detail required should be a function of whether the claimed design for the article is inherently two-dimensional (planar) or three-dimensional.
guidance: Example: In re Maatita permitted a single plan-view for a shoe bottom because the scope could be understood from that view. Conversely, inherently three-dimensional articles (e.g., entire shoe, teapot) could not be adequately disclosed with a single plan view.

name: Claim scope limited to surfaces shown in full lines and written description
description: The scope of a claimed design is understood to be limited to those surfaces or portions of the article shown in the drawing in full lines in combination with any additional written description in the specification.
guidance: The title of the design identifies the article and may contribute to scope. It is assumed the claim was crafted to protect what the inventor regards as the invention. In absence of additional written disclosure, visible portions not shown are prima facie not part of the claim (see In re Zahn).

name: Only surfaces visible at point of sale or during use must be disclosed
description: Only those surfaces of the article that are visible at the point of sale or during use must be disclosed to meet 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b). The undisclosed surfaces not seen during sale or use are not required to be described.
guidance: The drawing should illustrate the design as it will appear to purchasers and users since appearance is the basis for design patentability. The functionality need not be reproduced. If visible surfaces are flat and devoid of ornamentation, they need not be shown but should be described in the specification if they are considered part of the claimed design.

name: When title defines entire article but drawings omit visible portions
description: Applications whose title defines an entire article but whose drawings/specification fail to disclose portions or surfaces of the article that would be visible either during use or on sale will not be considered to violate 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b).
guidance: Amendment to the title will not be required. Examiners should include a statement in the first Office action indicating that the surface(s) or portion(s) of the article that would be normally visible but are not shown in the drawing or described in the specification are understood to form no part of the claimed design; form paragraph 15.85 may be used.

name: Examiners must specifically identify drawing deficiencies for 35 U.S.C. 112 rejections
description: When a claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b) as nonenabling and indefinite due to an insufficient drawing disclosure, examiners must specifically identify in the Office action what the deficiencies are in the drawing.
guidance: A mere statement that the claim is nonenabling and indefinite due to poor drawing quality is insufficient. Examiners must specifically point out portions of the drawing that are insufficient to permit understanding of the shape and appearance and, if possible, suggest how the rejection may be overcome. Form paragraphs 15.21 and 15.20.02 may be used.

name: Inconsistencies between drawing views
description: When inconsistencies between the views of the drawings are so great that the overall appearance of the design is unclear, the claim should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b) as nonenabling and indefinite.
guidance: Otherwise, inconsistencies between drawing views will be objected to by the examiner and correction required by the applicant. See MPEP § 1503.02. The Office action should specifically identify all inconsistencies when rejection is made.

name: Narrative description limitations (no unsupportable broad language)
description: A narrative description in the specification can supplement the drawing, but if the description refers to embodiments or modified forms not shown in the drawing, or includes vague words such as 'variations' and 'equivalents,' or states the claimed design is not limited to the exact shape and appearance shown, the claim should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b) as nonenabling and indefinite.
guidance: Such descriptive statements fail to enable a designer to make the other embodiments absent additional drawing views, and fail to particularly point out and distinctly claim the shape and appearance of those other embodiments. Form paragraph 15.21 may be used to reject on these grounds.

name: Undisclosed visible surface(s)/portion(s) do not form part of claimed design (15.85)
description: The [1] of the article [2] not shown in the drawing or described in the specification. It is understood that the appearance of any part of the article not shown or described forms no part of the claimed design. Determination of patentability is based on the design shown and described.
guidance: Use form paragraph 15.85 to indicate which visible surfaces/portions are not shown and thus not part of the claim; cite In re Zahn.

name: Amendment may not be possible (15.65)
description: The application might be fatally defective because [1]. It might not be possible to identify any definite and enabled design claim without introducing new matter (35 U.S.C. 132, 37 CFR 1.121).
guidance: In bracket 1, identify the subject matter which is insufficiently disclosed. Use when drawing disclosure cannot be cured without adding new matter.

name: New matter objection under 35 U.S.C. 132 (general)
