description: New matter is subject matter which has no support in the original specification, drawings or claim. An amendment to the claim must have support in the original disclosure. Amendments introducing new matter must be objected to under 35 U.S.C. 132 and 37 CFR 1.121.
guidance: Prior to final action, all amendments are entered and considered. To overcome objection, applicant may demonstrate by argument or evidence that original disclosure establishes possession of the amended subject matter. Form paragraph 15.51.01 may be used to object to new drawing/specification matter that lacks support.

name: Amendments affecting the claim must comply with written description (35 U.S.C. 112(a))
description: A design claim may be amended by broadening or narrowing its scope within the bounds of the disclosure as originally filed provided it complies with the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a). An amendment with no support introduces new matter and the claim must be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a).
guidance: Evaluate any amendment that affects the claimed design for compliance with the written description requirement (see MPEP § 1504.04, subsection I.C).

name: Amendment converting solid/broken line structure
description: Converting originally-disclosed solid lines to broken lines, or broken lines to solid lines, does not introduce new matter if such conversion does not introduce subject matter not originally disclosed; however, if such an amendment affects the claimed design the resulting design must be evaluated for written description compliance.
guidance: Additional examples of amendments that would not introduce new matter include: (A) a preliminary amendment filed simultaneously with the application papers; and (B) inclusion of a disclaimer in the original specification or on the drawings/photographs as filed.

name: ¶15.21 Rejection template for 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b)
description: The claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b), or pre-AIA equivalents, as the claimed invention is not described in such full, clear, concise and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to make and use the same, and fails to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor regards as the invention. The claim is indefinite and nonenabling [1].
guidance: This form paragraph should not be used when separate rejections under 112(a) and/or (b) are appropriate. In bracket 1, provide a complete explanation of the basis for the rejection.

name: ¶15.20.02 Suggestion: disclaiming indefinite/nonenabling areas via broken lines
description: Applicant may disclaim the areas or portions of the design which are considered indefinite and nonenabling in the rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112 above by converting them to broken lines and amending the specification to include a statement that the portions of the [1] shown in broken lines form no part of the claimed design.
guidance: For international design applications, use form paragraph 29.27 instead. In bracket 1, insert title of the article. Use when conversion to broken lines can cure the deficiency without introducing new matter.

name: ¶15.51.01 Amendment to disclosure (not affecting claim) - 35 U.S.C. 132 objection
description: The [1] is objected to under 35 U.S.C. 132 and 37 CFR 1.121 as introducing new matter. The original disclosure does not reasonably convey to a designer of ordinary skill that the inventor was in possession of the amended subject matter at the time the application was filed.
guidance: Specify whether new drawing or amendment to drawing, title or specification. Identify what is new matter so the basis for the objection is clear. To overcome, applicant may attempt to demonstrate (argument/evidence) that original disclosure establishes possession of amended subject matter, or provide specific corrective actions (e.g., omit broken-line environmental structure or amend title).

name: Petitioner’s initial burden and particularity requirement (§ 312(a)(3))
description: In an inter partes review, the petitioner has the burden from the onset to show with particularity why the patent it challenges is unpatentable. (Harmonic Inc. v. Avid Tech.; 35 U.S.C. § 312(a)(3)).
guidance: Petition must identify with particularity the evidence that supports the grounds for the challenge to each claim. This is a continuing burden on the petitioner at institution stage and throughout trial; failure to identify particularized evidence can defeat institution.

name: Obviousness analysis framework (Graham factors and KSR principles)
description: Obviousness is resolved based on underlying factual determinations: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art; (3) the level of ordinary skill in the art; and (4) objective evidence of nonobviousness (Graham). The inquiry typically requires articulation of a reason to combine known elements in the claimed fashion (KSR).
guidance: A reason to combine may be found in market forces, design incentives, interrelated teachings, need or problem known in the field, and the background knowledge/creativity/common sense of a POSITA. The petitioner cannot rely on mere conclusory statements to show obviousness (In re Magnum Oil Tools); must articulate reasoning with some rational underpinning. When in evidence, objective indicia of nonobviousness are considered and may overcome apparent teachings of the prior art.

name: Claim construction standard in PTAB IPR proceedings
description: Claims are interpreted using the same claim construction standard that would be used in a civil action under 35 U.S.C. § 282(b) (37 C.F.R. § 42.100(b)). Claim terms are generally given their ordinary and customary meaning as understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention.
guidance: In determining meaning, the Board looks principally to intrinsic evidence (claim language, specification, prosecution history). Extrinsic evidence (dictionaries, expert testimony) is less significant than intrinsic evidence. Any special definition for a claim term must be set forth in the specification with reasonable clarity, deliberateness, and precision (In re Paulsen). The Board construes only those terms in controversy and only to the extent necessary to resolve the controversy (Realtime Data v. Iancu). Parties are expected to assert claim-construction arguments and evidence in the specified filings (Petition, Patent Owner’s Response, Petitioner’s Reply, Patent Owner’s Sur-reply) and a final determination will be made at the close of the proceeding after hearing and full record.

name: Consideration of extrinsic evidence and dictionaries
description: Extrinsic evidence such as dictionaries may be cited to support a proposed claim construction, but extrinsic evidence is less significant than the intrinsic record in determining legally operative meaning of claim language.
guidance: Petitioners and Patent Owners may cite extrinsic sources (e.g., American Heritage, Merriam-Webster) to support constructions, but the Board will prioritize specification and prosecution history; special definitions must be present in the specification to control over ordinary meaning.

name: Use of objective evidence of nonobviousness in the obviousness inquiry
description: When in evidence, the Board considers any relevant objective evidence of nonobviousness (secondary considerations) in determining obviousness (Graham).
guidance: Even if prior art teaching would have suggested the claimed invention, the totality of evidence, including objective indicia such as commercial success, long-felt need, failure of others, unexpected results, may lead to a conclusion that the claims would not have been obvious. At institution stage Patent Owner may present such evidence in its Preliminary Response; absence of such evidence is noted in institution analysis.

name: Board practice regarding scope of institution and scheduling
description: If the Board institutes trial, the trial will be authorized on all grounds set forth in the Petition and will be conducted according to a corresponding Scheduling Order.
guidance: The institution Order will state that trial is authorized on all grounds and commence on entry date; scheduling order will govern subsequent deadlines and proceedings. Parties should expect institution to open full trial on all challenged claims and grounds raised in the petition (37 C.F.R. § 42.108(a)).

name: Fielded/boolean structured search
description: Use Lens structured search controls to build boolean queries across a range of fields including full text, title, abstract or claims and to select jurisdictions.
guidance: Options include refining results to patent applications or grants, choosing full text or one doc per family to reduce result counts, and turning stemming on/off.

name: Use of national utility models (e.g., German) alongside Unitary Patent
description: Patentees choosing Unitary Patent (which gives UPC exclusive jurisdiction) who do not want to lose access to national courts may consider filing additional national patents or utility models (e.g., German utility models provide quick, cost‑efficient protection for products and uses but not for process claims and have a 10‑year term).
guidance: Utility models can supplement unitary protection where national remedies are desired; assess technical field, allowed claim types, and product life cycle before pursuing utility models.

name: Claim construction / UPC infringement test ('broadest meaningful interpretation')
description: The UPC applies a broad German‑style claim construction: claim features receive their 'broadest meaningful interpretation' focusing on technical function in the context of the technical problem. Claims are interpreted using the description and drawings as aids, not limited to preferred embodiments, and from the viewpoint of the person skilled in the art. The same test applies to Unitary and European bundle patents; a uniform standard for doctrine of equivalents remains to be established.
guidance: When drafting/arguing, rely on description/drawings to support broad interpretation or to limit scope; do not assume literal wording alone controls. Expect UPC to consider patentee's own lexicon if specification defines terms.

name: Damages under Art.68 UPCA and procedural timings for claims
description: Art.68 provides two options for damages: (a) consider all appropriate aspects including negative economic consequences (lost profits), unfair profits, and, where appropriate, non‑economic elements; or (b) set a lump sum on the basis of elements such as royalties. A damage claim may not be brought more than five years after awareness of last fact justifying the action (Art.72 UPCA). To pursue damages after a merits decision, the party must lodge the application no later than one year from service of the final decision (R.126 RoP).
guidance: There is limited UPC precedent on damage calculation; expect fact‑intensive assessments and possible separate proceedings to determine amount. Consider intervening EPO/national proceedings that might affect entitlement and quantum.

name: Cost rules: 'loser pays', ceilings, and cost security (R.152, R.158, R.370.6 RoP)
description: The UPC applies a 'loser pays' approach but the loser reimburses only 'reasonable fees up to a certain ceiling' (R.152.1-.2 RoP), with ceilings determined by the value of the proceedings (court sets value, reflecting plaintiff's objective interest; cf. R.370.6 RoP). Ceilings apply to representation costs; other expenses (prior art research, translations, experts) are additional. The court may order cost security under R.158 if a party's financial position raises legitimate concern about recoverability/enforceability of costs.
guidance: When calculating cost risk, account for potential six‑ or seven‑digit reimbursement claims under 'loser pays' and prepare to seek or oppose cost security early. Under R.158 the court examines facts and arguments; relative financial position alone is not dispositive, e.g., limited funding of enforcement vehicles is not per se a reason to order security.

name: Examiner initial burden: prima facie case and evidentiary support
description: To properly reject a claimed invention under 35 U.S.C. 101, the Office must (A) make a prima facie showing that the claimed invention lacks utility, and (B) provide a sufficient evidentiary basis for factual assumptions relied upon in establishing the prima facie showing.
guidance: The prima facie showing must be well-reasoned and specific; examiners should provide documentary evidence when possible (journals, treatises, patents) or explain the scientific basis for factual conclusions if documentary evidence is unavailable. Mere questioning of operability is insufficient—factual reasons that would lead one skilled in the art to question the objective truth must be set forth. (Cites In re Gaubert; In re Oetiker; Fregeau v. Mossinghoff.)

name: When examiners may request evidentiary support from applicant
description: In appropriate situations the Office may require an applicant to substantiate an asserted utility for a claimed invention.
guidance: Requests for additional evidence should be imposed rarely, and only if necessary to support the scientific credibility of the asserted utility (e.g., assertion inconsistent with record and current scientific knowledge). When requesting evidence, the examiner should indicate why the record is defective and, where appropriate, what type of evidentiary showing can remedy the problem. Examiners must not demand redundant test data or unduly burden applicants. (Cites In re Pottier; In re Citron; In re Isaacs.)

name: Burden shift and applicant's opportunities to rebut
description: If a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 has been properly imposed, the burden shifts to the applicant to rebut the prima facie showing.
guidance: Applicants may rebut by amendments to claims, arguments/reasoning, or new evidence (affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132, or printed publications). New evidence must be relevant to the issues raised; conclusory declarations lacking nexus to supporting evidence have limited probative value. Examiners must fully consider and respond to each substantive element of any response; if the totality of the record makes the asserted utility more likely than not credible, the rejection cannot be maintained. (Cites In re Oetiker; In re Grunwell; In re Buchner; In re Rinehart.)

name: Evaluation of sufficiency and character of applicant's evidence
description: There is no predetermined amount or character of evidence that must be provided by an applicant to support an asserted utility; the required character and amount vary with what is claimed and whether the asserted utility contravenes established scientific principles or beliefs.
guidance: Applicants need not prove utility beyond a reasonable doubt or with statistical certainty. Evidence is sufficient if, considered as a whole, it leads a person of ordinary skill to conclude the asserted utility is more likely than not true. Courts reversed 101 rejections where applicants supplied reasonable supporting evidence. (Cites Ex parte Ferguson; Nelson v. Bowler; Rey-Bellet v. Englehardt.)

name: Evaluation of claims directed to treatment of diseases with no prior cures
description: Claims directed to methods of treating or curing a disease for which there have been no previously successful treatments warrant careful review for compliance with 35 U.S.C. 101.
guidance: Prior lack of a cure is not a basis to conclude lack of utility. Examine the specification and evidence: claims to symptomatic treatments may require modest evidence; claims asserting a 'cure' may require significantly greater evidentiary support. Expert affidavit evidence with sound reasoning may suffice to establish credibility for use in previously untreatable conditions.

name: Claim interpretation: broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the specification
description: During patent examination, pending claims must be given their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.
guidance: The PTO construes claims based on claim language and the specification as interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art, applying the broadest reasonable construction allowed to establish a clear record of what applicant intends to claim. This standard differs from claim interpretation in court proceedings, where claims are not given the broadest reasonable interpretation. (Cites Phillips v. AWH; In re Am. Acad. of Sci. Tech. Ctr.; 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1).)

name: Domestic priority (benefit) information in ADS constitutes required specific reference
description: Domestic priority information includes the application number, filing date, status (including patent number if available), and relationship of each application for which a benefit is claimed under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), 120, 121, or 365(c). Providing this information in the ADS constitutes the specific reference required by 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or 120 and need not be made part of the specification.
guidance: If continuity data are included only in an ADS and not in the specification, the patent front page will take continuity data from the ADS. Pre-AIA 1.76(b)(5) does not apply to provisional applications.

name: Use of PLT Model International Forms and PCT Request Form can satisfy ADS requirements
description: The requirement in 37 CFR 1.55 or 1.78 for presentation of a priority or benefit claim in an ADS will be satisfied by presentation of such claim in the Patent Law Treaty Model International Request Form; similarly, the requirement in 37 CFR 1.57(a) for reference to previously filed application, and the requirement in 37 CFR 1.46 for presentation of the name of the applicant under 35 U.S.C. 118, will be satisfied by presentation in the appropriate PLT forms or the PCT Request Form.
guidance: For national stage applications under 35 U.S.C. 371, presentation of a benefit claim in the PCT Request Form or presence of the claim on the front page of the PCT publication under PCT Art. 21(2) will satisfy ADS requirements (37 CFR 1.76(f),(g)). However, ADS information will govern if inconsistent per 1.76(d)(2). Submission of PCT Request Form in an application under 35 U.S.C. 111 must be accompanied by a clear indication that treatment as an application under 35 U.S.C. 111 is desired.

name: Consideration of priority/benefit claims in determining 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date
description: In determining the 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date, consider priority/benefit claims to earlier-filed U.S. provisional applications under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), U.S. nonprovisional applications under 35 U.S.C. 120 or 121, and international applications under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121 or 365(c) if the subject matter used to make the rejection is appropriately supported in the relied upon earlier-filed application's disclosure (and any intermediate application(s)). A benefit claim to a U.S. patent of an earlier-filed international application, which has an international filing date prior to November 29, 2000, may only result in an effective U.S. filing date as of the date the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 371(c)(1), (2) and (4) were fulfilled. Do NOT consider any priority/benefit claims to U.S. applications which are filed before an international application that has an international filing date prior to November 29, 2000. Do NOT consider foreign priority claims under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) and 365(a).
guidance: Apply these rules when establishing the effective date of a reference relied upon for a 102(e) determination; see form paragraphs 7.12 and 7.12.01 and associated Examiner Notes for assistance in determining the 102(e) date.

name: Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(f) applicant not the inventor
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(f) because the applicant did not invent the claimed subject matter. [2]
guidance: This paragraph must be preceded either by paragraphs 7.07 and 7.13 or by paragraph 7.103. In bracket 2, insert an explanation of the supporting evidence establishing that applicant was not the inventor. See MPEP § 2137 for further guidance.

name: Contents required in a 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection (A-D)
description: After indicating that the rejection is under 35 U.S.C. 103, the examiner should set forth in the Office action: (A) the relevant teachings of the prior art relied upon, preferably with reference to the relevant column or page number(s) and line number(s) where appropriate, (B) the difference or differences in the claim over the applied reference(s), (C) the proposed modification of the applied reference(s) necessary to arrive at the claimed subject matter, and (D) an explanation as to why the claimed invention would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made.
guidance: When relying on references, include specific citations and explain modifications and reasoning to support the obviousness conclusion. Positively include any reference relied upon in the rejection (even if minor) in the statement of the rejection. See In re Hoch and Ex parte Clapp for precedent. Clear written rationale is essential for applicant reply and later judicial interpretation; issued patents are presumed valid, so the written record must be clear.

name: Importance of clear communication of the basis for a rejection
description: It is important for an examiner to properly communicate the basis for a rejection so that the issues can be identified early and the applicant can be given fair opportunity to reply. If an initially rejected application issues as a patent, the rationale behind an earlier rejection may be important in interpreting the scope of the patent claims.
guidance: Because examiners generally cannot be compelled to testify about their mental processes, ensure the written record clearly explains the rationale for decisions during prosecution. See MPEP §§2141–2144.09 and §2145 for patentability determinations and consideration of rebuttal arguments.

name: Ways to overcome a provisional 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection
description: A provisional 103 rejection can be overcome by: (A) Arguing patentability over the earlier filed application; (B) Combining the subject matter of the copending applications into a single application claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 of the prior applications and abandoning the copending applications (note the 35 U.S.C. 112 first paragraph support requirement); (C) Filing an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 showing derivation (unclaimed invention disclosed in the copending application was derived from the inventor of the other application); (D) Filing an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 showing a date of invention prior to the effective U.S. filing date of the copending application; or (E) For an application pending on or after December 10, 2004, showing that (1) the prior art and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person, or (2) the subject matter is disqualified under the CREATE Act (joint research agreement disqualification).
guidance: Additional remedies: where the earlier application has issued or been published, a terminal disclaimer and a 37 CFR 1.130 affidavit/declaration or a terminal disclaimer under 37 CFR 1.321(c) may be used in common ownership situations. Combining applications for 120 benefit requires that the earlier disclosure comply with 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, for each claim.

name: Provisional double patenting and terminal disclaimer interaction
description: Where the applications are claiming the same patentable invention, a terminal disclaimer and an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.130 may be used to overcome a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 in a common ownership situation if the earlier filed application has been published or matured into a patent. Provisional double patenting rejections may be made; they can be obviated if all requirements of 37 CFR 1.321 are met.
guidance: Provisional double patenting rejections arise in copending situations; filing terminal disclaimers or meeting the requirements of 1.321 can obviate them. Examples in the MPEP illustrate typical fact patterns and outcomes.

name: Scope and application of 35 U.S.C. 103(c) (AIPA and CREATE Act) — common ownership/joint research agreement disqualification
description: 35 U.S.C. 103(c) provides that subject matter developed by another person, which qualifies as prior art only under one or more of subsections (e), (f), and (g) of section 102, shall not preclude patentability under 103 where the subject matter and the claimed invention were, at the time the claimed invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person. For purposes of the subsection, subject matter and a claimed invention shall be deemed to have been owned by the same person if (A) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; (B) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (C) the application discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement. The term 'joint research agreement' means a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement for experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention.
guidance: 103(c) applies only to obviousness determinations under 103 and does not affect rejections under 102 or double patenting rejections. The CREATE Act widened applicability (effective to patents granted on or after Dec. 10, 2004) and the 1999 AIPA change affected applications filed on/after Nov. 29, 1999. In reexamination, applicability depends on grant date. See MPEP §706.02(l) for procedural details.

name: Definitions and interpretative guidance for 35 U.S.C. 103(c) terms
description: Terms are construed broadly: 'subject matter' is construed broadly as in the remainder of 35 U.S.C. 103; 'another' means any inventive entity other than the inventor and includes the inventor and any other persons; 'developed' is read broadly and is not limited by manner of development; 'commonly owned' means wholly owned by the same person(s) or organization(s) at the time the invention was made; 'joint research agreement' is a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement between two or more persons/entities for performance of experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention.
guidance: Use these broad constructions when determining whether subject matter is disqualified under 103(c).

name: Special rules for applications/patents with legacy filing/grant dates (pre-Nov. 29,1999 and pre-Dec. 10,2004)
description: For applications filed prior to November 29, 1999 and granted as patents prior to December 10, 2004, the subject matter disqualified under 35 U.S.C. 103(c) is strictly limited to subject matter that (A) qualifies as prior art only under 35 U.S.C. 102(f) or 102(g), and (B) was commonly owned with the claimed invention at the time the invention was made. For reexamination proceedings, applicability of the 1999 or 2004 changes depends on whether the patent being reexamined was granted on or after December 10, 2004.
guidance: If the subject matter that qualifies as prior art only under 102(f) or 102(g) was not commonly owned at the time of the invention, it is not disqualified under 103(c). Applicants combining subject matter into a single U.S. filing should still expect 103 rejections if common ownership at time of invention is lacking; applicants have duties under 37 CFR 1.56 to disclose inventorship and dates to enable examiner consideration.

name: Examiner duties when application claims 35 U.S.C. 120 benefit from earlier-filed application
description: An application claiming the benefit of a prior filed copending national or international application under 35 U.S.C. 120 must name as an inventor at least one inventor named in the prior filed application. The prior filed application must also disclose the named inventor’s invention claimed in at least one claim of the later filed application in the manner provided by the first paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112. So long as the applications have at least one inventor in common and the other requirements are met, the Office will permit a claim for 35 U.S.C. 120 benefit without any additional submissions or notifications regarding inventorship differences.
guidance: The examiner must examine the earlier filed applications as necessary to determine that the applications have at least one inventor in common and that 35 U.S.C. 120 and 37 CFR 1.78 requirements are met. The claim for 120 benefit will be permitted without examination of the earlier application for disclosure/support unless it becomes necessary, e.g., because of an intervening reference.

name: Timing requirement to claim disclosure exception
description: An application relying on Article 30 must be filed within twelve months (six months if filing date earlier than March 15, 2012) of the date on which the invention was disclosed.
guidance: Filing within the grace period is a strict formal requirement; for some filings (after July 29, 2015), supporting proof may be submitted within extended time windows (see procedural exceptions). The filing-time comparison is to the actual filing time (including hour/minute) for determining prior art.

name: Statement of intent and supporting documents (formal procedural requirement)
description: A person who intends to take advantage of Article 30(1)(1) must submit a written statement of that intention when filing and must submit documents proving the relevant facts within thirty days of the filing date.
guidance: Proving document may be submitted simultaneously with filing. For certain filings on/after July 29, 2015, the proving document can be submitted within 3 months from receipt of a certified copy of grant or within the period for amending specification/claims (but before registration publication). For international applications, the intention must be stated in the application and proof submitted within thirty days after the domestic reference date.

name: Substantive examination outcome for valid Article 30 claims
description: If no defects are found in application and supporting documents, disclosures falling under Article 30 are recognized as non-prior art for examination when Article 29(1) or (2) would otherwise apply.
guidance: If the claiming proceeding fails due to deficiencies, the submitted documents may instead be used as prior art against the application.

name: International (PCT) application procedure for claiming disclosure exception
description: For an international application, an applicant must state intention and submit proof within thirty days after the domestic reference date (Article 201(4)); declaration in PCT request form Box VIII(v) is treated as an application cover sheet declaration under Article 42(1).
guidance: If declaration is included in PCT request form and supporting evidence is legitimately submitted within 30 days from the reference date, the PCT filing meets Article 30(2) requirements and KIPO will examine it as a regular claim to exceptions to lack of novelty (see PCT Rule 4.17). For national phase entries, submit within specified national-phase periods.

name: Procedural relaxations for applications filed on/after July 29, 2015
description: For applications filed on/after July 29, 2015, proving documents for Article 30 may be submitted within 3 months from the date of receiving a certified copy of grant or within the period to amend specification, drawings, or claims (provided before registration publication). Examiner will issue all grounds for rejection at once.
guidance: Because applicant can invoke grace period within 3 months after grant or during amendment period, the examiner should issue all grounds for rejection together. If applicant remedies a rejection by claiming disclosure exception but new grounds arise from other documents, the examiner shall issue a first office action addressing the new grounds.

name: General principles for determining inventive step
description: Determine whether the invention as described in the claims could have been easily made by a person skilled in the art based on prior art references of Article 29(1); if so, the claim lacks inventive step. Assessment is done claim-by-claim.
guidance: Examiner may combine prior art references; determination of inventive step is separate from novelty but the office may notify grounds for rejection on both novelty and inventive step together when appropriate. Each claim must be assessed individually.

name: Definition of 'process' under §101
description: A 'process' is a mode of treatment of certain materials to produce a given result; if new and useful, it is just as patentable as a piece of machinery (Cochrane v. Deener).
guidance: Use the Cochrane/Deener formulation: processes are methods of treating materials to produce a result. The 1952 Act's use of 'process' was intended broadly ('include anything under the sun that is made by men'). When evaluating claims described as processes, treat them as methods of treatment producing a result rather than dismissing them because they are not a machine.

name: Transformation and reduction (machine-or-transformation) test
description: 'Transformation and reduction of an article "to a different state or thing" is the clue to the patentability of a process claim that does not include particular machines.'
guidance: Assess whether the claimed process effects a transformation or reduction of an article to a different state or thing (e.g., curing rubber to a new physical state). If the process performs such a transformative function, that supports §101 eligibility. Use transformation as a decisive indicator when a process claim lacks particular machines.

name: Whole-claim evaluation (no analytic dissection)
description: Claims must be considered 'as a whole' in judging whether they represent patentable subject matter rather than being dissected into their various elements.
guidance: Do not strip out or isolate an abstract element (e.g., a mathematical formula) and treat it alone; evaluate the claim's overall character and functionality. Old or known elements included in a claim do not necessarily render the claim unpatentable if the combination as a whole performs a function the patent laws were designed to protect.

name: Abstract formula / law of nature within a process does not automatically defeat eligibility
description: A process 'is not unpatentable because it contains a law of nature or a mathematical algorithm.' The presence of an abstract formula in a claim does not by itself make the claim ineligible under §101.
guidance: When a mathematical algorithm or law of nature is embedded in a process claim, determine whether the claim as a whole applies the algorithm to produce a practical application (e.g., transforms an article). Mere inclusion of the formula is permissible if the overall process falls within patentable subject matter.

name: Eligibility focus distinct from novelty/non-obviousness
description: Whether an invention falls under patentable subject matter (§101) is a separate inquiry from whether it meets the 'novelty' (§102) or 'non-obviousness' (§103) requirements; those criteria are considered later.
guidance: When determining subject-matter eligibility, do not resolve eligibility by reference to novelty or obviousness. First ask whether the claimed subject matter fits within §101 categories (as a whole); only after eligibility is established should novelty and inventive-step analyses be applied.

name: Avoid preemption of abstract ideas (limitation on software/business-method patents)
description: Software-related inventions or business models can be patentable when 'embedded in a proper claim' and do not preempt abstract ideas.
guidance: Draft and evaluate claims so they apply an idea to a specific practical application or transformative process rather than claiming the abstract idea itself. Ensure claims are limited to particular implementations or applications that avoid monopolizing the abstract idea across all uses.

name: Example of allowable claim structure: process applying a formula within an industrial curing operation
description: Diamond v. Diehr upheld a claim for a process of molding and curing synthetic rubber that constantly measured temperature inside a mold and fed data into a computer using an existing equation to calculate optimal cure time—i.e., a process applying a formula within an industrial transformation.
guidance: Use such factual patterns as a guide: claims that incorporate measurements, data processing, and application of equations to control a physical, transformative process (e.g., curing a material) illustrate how an abstract formula can be part of a patent-eligible process when the overall claim effects a physical transformation.

name: Examiners must explain discounting and assigned weights
description: If, after evaluating the evidence, the examiner is not convinced the claimed invention is patentable, the next Office action should state that and identify the reason(s) (e.g., commercial success not convincing or not related to the technology). Any conclusion about whether evidence of obviousness outweighs objective evidence, along with any individual weights assigned to different objective indicia, should be explained.
guidance: Provide clear reasoning for discounting or assigning weight to secondary considerations; vague or ambiguous assignments of weight are defective (see Volvo Penta example where assigning 'some weight' without explanation was rejected). See MPEP § 2145 for guidance on sufficiency of rebuttal evidence.

name: Greater‑than‑expected results support nonobviousness
description: A greater than expected result is an evidentiary factor pertinent to the legal conclusion of obviousness/nonobviousness of the claims at issue; synergistic (greater than additive) effects may be persuasive.
guidance: Such effects are not necessarily sufficient by themselves — applicants must show results were greater than would have been expected from the prior art to an unobvious extent and that the results are of significant, practical advantage. Prior art teachings that would have led to an expectation of such effects can defeat the showing (e.g., mixtures expected to be greater than additive).

name: Absence of an expected property is evidence of nonobviousness
description: Absence of a property which a claimed invention would have been expected to possess based on prior art teachings is evidence of unobviousness.
guidance: Example: claimed compounds expected to possess activity but do not, supporting nonobviousness. Consider whether prior art would have led one to expect the property.

name: Direct and indirect comparative tests are probative if commensurate
description: Evidence of unexpected properties may be in the form of a direct or indirect comparison of the claimed invention with the closest prior art which is commensurate in scope with the claims.
guidance: Both direct and indirect comparative testing can be sufficient; see cited cases for instances where indirect testing was upheld. Ensure comparisons are commensurate in scope with the claim limitations being tested.

name: Intermediate patentability by showing contributing cause in end product
description: The patentability of an intermediate may be established by unexpected properties of an end product when one of ordinary skill would reasonably ascribe to the claimed intermediate the 'contributing cause' for such unexpectedly superior activity or property.
guidance: Applicant must identify the cause of the unexpectedly superior activity/property in the end product and establish a nexus between the intermediate and the end product (i.e., show the intermediate is the contributing cause).

name: Weigh expected and unexpected properties together
description: Evidence of unexpected results must be weighed against evidence supporting a prima facie case of obviousness in making a final determination.
guidance: If unexpected properties are not shown to have significance equal or greater than expected properties, they may not rebut obviousness. Conversely, expected beneficial results are evidence of obviousness. Evaluate the relative significance of each property (e.g., which effect is most significant to the claimed invention).

name: Species data may support genus/range nonobviousness when trend is extendable
description: The nonobviousness of a genus or claimed range may be supported by data showing unexpected results of a species or narrower range if one of ordinary skill in the art would be able to determine a trend in the exemplified data which would allow reasonable extension of probative value.
guidance: If testing shows a trend that reasonably permits extrapolation to the broader claimed scope, species tests can be probative; isolated or unrepresentative species data without trend may be insufficient.

name: Affidavit/declaration must compare with the closest prior art
description: An affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 must compare the claimed subject matter with the closest prior art to be effective to rebut a prima facie case of obviousness.
guidance: Compare the claimed invention to disclosures of each cited reference to determine overlapping claim limitations and relative importance of limitations; deviations from references should be explained and evaluated; if unexplained and significant, require explanation.

name: Consider advantages disclosed in or inherent from the totality of the record
description: The totality of the record must be considered when determining whether a claimed invention would have been obvious; evidence and arguments directed to advantages not disclosed in the specification cannot be disregarded.
guidance: Undisclosed but argued advantages or inherently flowing properties should be considered during prosecution (specification need not disclose proportions or values as critical for applicants to present evidence showing criticality). Examiners must consider such proffered evidence and arguments even if not in the original specification.

name: Burden of production for commercial success and nexus on applicant
description: An applicant asserting commercial success to support nonobviousness bears the burden of production in establishing commercial success and establishing a factually and legally sufficient nexus between the commercial success and the claimed invention.
guidance: The PTO lacks means to gather evidence to support/refute assertions of commercial success and thus relies on the applicant to provide hard evidence. Evidence of commercial success for products not covered by the claims is not probative of nonobviousness.

name: Applicability of Form Paragraphs (FPs)
description: Do the FPs apply to the instant application? Yes, if the application is filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a), and plural inventions under 35 U.S.C. 121 are claimed. No, if the application is filed in the National stage under 35 U.S.C. 371. PCT unity of invention standards must be used for national stage entries. See MPEP 806.01.
guidance: FP changes published 1/21/10 apply to U.S. applications only; national stage (371) uses PCT unity standards and FPs do not apply. Compare claims to determine plural independent or distinct inventions.

name: Reasons must be concisely stated (MPEP 808)
description: "The particular reasons relied on by the examiner for holding that the inventions as claimed are either independent or distinct should be concisely stated. A mere statement of conclusion is inadequate. The reasons upon which the conclusion is based should be given."
guidance: Examiners should provide concise, specific factual bases for independence/distinctness rather than conclusory language. (MPEP 808)

name: Use FP 8.01 when single-species claims present; FP 8.02 when only generic claims present
description: "An examiner should set forth a requirement for election of a single disclosed species in a Markush-type claim — using form paragraph 8.01 when claims limited to species are present or — using form paragraph 8.02 when no species claims are present."
guidance: Examples provided: where individual claims recite Compound X/Y/Z (use FP 8.01); where only generic or Markush claims are present (use FP 8.02). When both species and generic claims are present and election is warranted, use FP 8.01. (MPEP § 808.01(a); MPEP 803.02)

name: Definition of mutually exclusive species (MPEP 806.04(f))
description: "Claims to different species are mutually exclusive if one claim recites limitations disclosed for a first species but not a second, while a second claim recites limitations disclosed only for the second species and not the first... to require restriction between claims limited to species, the claims must not overlap in scope."
guidance: Mutually exclusive = non-overlapping claim scope in practice; use this test when determining whether restriction to a single species is proper.

name: Examiner should group species considered unpatentable over each other
description: "Election of species should not be required between claimed species that are considered clearly unpatentable over each other ... the examiner should group together species considered clearly unpatentable over each other."
guidance: If species are obvious variants (clearly unpatentable over each other), group them rather than require election; see MPEP 808.01(a).

name: Practice tip: elect group of species and traverse when species are not distinct
description: If an examiner requires an election between species that are not distinct (identical scope, single disclosed embodiment, overlapping breadth), Applicant may wish to elect the 'group of species' and traverse such a requirement using MPEP 806.03, 806.04(f) and 806.04(h).
guidance: Examples provided in the memo show claim sets and suggested traversals; electing a group preserves positions and triggers examiner reconsideration protocols.

name: Provisional nonstatutory double patenting (NSDP) rejection — required responses
description: A complete response to a nonstatutory double patenting (NSDP) rejection is either a reply by applicant showing that the claims subject to the rejection are patentably distinct from the reference claims, or the filing of a terminal disclaimer in accordance with 37 CFR 1.321 in the pending application(s) with a reply to the Office action.
guidance: Such a response is required even when the NSDP rejection is provisional. Filing a terminal disclaimer or showing patentable distinctness is necessary for further consideration of the rejection, and the filing should not be held in abeyance. An application must not be allowed unless compliant terminal disclaimer(s) are filed and/or the withdrawal of the NSDP rejection(s) is made of record by the examiner. See MPEP § 1490 for terminal disclaimer discussion and MPEP § 714.03 for replies with omissions.

name: Patent term filing date for original utility or plant applications
description: The patent term filing date of an original utility or plant application filed on or after June 8, 1995 is the earliest of: (1) the actual filing date of the application; or (2) the filing date of the earliest application for which the application claims the benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, 365(c), or 386(c).
guidance: Benefit claims under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) and foreign priority claims under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d)/(f), 365(a)/(b), or 386(a)/(b) are NOT taken into account when determining patent term filing date. Determination of entitlement to the earlier filing's disclosure under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) is not required when calculating patent term filing date. Consult 37 CFR 1.78 and MPEP § 211 for proper benefit claim practice.

name: Provisional statutory double patenting rejections (35 U.S.C. 101)
description: Where the claims of an application are the same as those of a first patent they are barred under 35 U.S.C. 101 — the statutory basis for a double patenting rejection. A rejection based on double patenting of the 'same invention' finds support in 35 U.S.C. 101; 'same invention' means identical subject matter.
guidance: A statutory (35 U.S.C. 101) double patenting rejection can be overcome only by canceling or amending the conflicting claims so they are no longer coextensive in scope; filing a terminal disclaimer cannot overcome a statutory double patenting rejection. Use form paragraphs 8.30 (heading) and 8.31 (rejection against an issued patent) or 8.32 (provisional rejection against copending application) as appropriate.

name: Between one or more applications and a published application — provisional rejections
description: A published patent application and an application may give rise to double patenting where they share inventive entity/common applicant/common owner, or result from joint research agreement activities. If the published application has not yet issued as a patent, the examiner may make a provisional rejection on the ground of double patenting when the published application has not been abandoned and its pending claims conflict with the application being examined.
guidance: Provisional handling parallels other provisional double patenting guidance; statutory double patenting cannot be obviated by terminal disclaimer. See subsection B and other provisional rejection guidance.

name: Reexamination proceedings can address double patenting
description: A double patenting issue may raise a substantial new question of patentability of a claim and thus can be addressed in a reexamination proceeding. Double patenting may exist where the reference patent/application and the patent under reexamination share inventive entity/common applicant/owner, and (for patents granted on or after Dec 10, 2004) may arise from joint research agreement activity if evidence is made of record.
guidance: Prior art exceptions like 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) or disqualification under pre-AIA 103(c) generally cannot be used to overcome a double patenting rejection or NSDP, and an excepted reference cannot be used as a secondary reference in a NSDP obviousness-type rejection. See MPEP §§ 717.02, 2154.02(c), 2146, and 2258 for reexamination-specific guidance.

name: Requirements of a double patenting rejection (statutory vs nonstatutory and 35 U.S.C. 121 prohibition)
description: When a double patenting rejection is appropriate, it must be based on statutory grounds or nonstatutory grounds. The ground employed depends upon the relationship of the inventions being claimed. A double patenting rejection is generally not permitted where the claimed subject matter is presented in a divisional application as a result of a restriction requirement made in a parent application under 35 U.S.C. 121.
guidance: The examiner must determine: (A) whether a statutory basis exists; (B) whether a nonstatutory basis exists; and (C) whether a nonstatutory DP rejection is prohibited by the third sentence of 35 U.S.C. 121. Make these determinations on the basis of all facts in the application. Charts in MPEP § 804 illustrate the methodology.

name: Domination vs double patenting — distinction and treatment
description: Domination and double patenting are separate issues. One patent/application 'dominates' a second when the first has a broad claim that fully encompasses an invention defined in a narrower claim in another patent/application.
guidance: Domination by itself, absent statutory or nonstatutory double patenting grounds, cannot support a double patenting rejection (In re Kaplan; In re Sarett). However, domination does not preclude a double patenting rejection — it may be present alongside proper statutory/nonstatutory grounds (see In re Schneller, AbbVie v. Kennedy Institute). Evaluate domination as a factual circumstance but rely on statutory/nonstatutory legal bases for rejections.

name: Statutory double patenting test — 'same invention' (35 U.S.C. 101) and literal-infringement test
description: A reliable test for double patenting under 35 U.S.C. 101 is whether a claim in the application could be literally infringed without literally infringing a corresponding claim in the patent. 'Same invention' means identical subject matter.
guidance: If there exists an embodiment that falls within the scope of one claim but not the other, identical subject matter is not present and statutory double patenting does not exist. Examples: a claim reciting 'halogen' is broader than a claim reciting 'chlorine' (not identical); a claim reciting '36 inches' and one reciting '3 feet' define the same invention. If determined the same invention is being claimed twice, 35 U.S.C. 101 precludes the second patent regardless of terminal disclaimers. Use form paragraphs 8.30–8.32 as applicable; follow examiner notes regarding when to use each form paragraph.

name: 1205.02-Appeal Brief Content
description: Specific content requirements for the appeal brief (e.g., arguments, claims, references to the record).

name: Black and white photographs / grayscale drawings — limited acceptance
description: Photographs, including photocopies of photographs, are not ordinarily permitted in utility and design patent applications, but will be accepted if photographs are the only practicable medium for illustrating the claimed invention (e.g., electrophoresis gels, blots, autoradiographs, cell cultures, histological tissue cross sections, animals, plants, in vivo imaging, thin layer chromatography plates, crystalline structures, metallurgical microstructures, textile fabrics, grain structures).
guidance: If the subject matter admits illustration by a drawing, the examiner may require a drawing instead. Photographs must be of sufficient quality so that all details are reproducible in the printed patent. Black and white photographs submitted in lieu of ink drawings must comply with 37 CFR 1.84(b); no petition or fee required; only one set of photographs is required when via EFS-Web.

name: Applicant burden to rebut obviousness findings; 37 CFR 1.111(b)
description: When the Office finds that the claimed invention would have been obvious, the burden shifts to the applicant to (A) show that the Office erred in these findings or (B) provide other evidence to show that the claimed subject matter would have been nonobvious. 37 CFR 1.111(b) requires applicant to distinctly and specifically point out the supposed errors in the Office’s action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the Office action.
guidance: The reply must present arguments pointing out the specific distinction believed to render the claims patentable over any applied references. If an applicant disagrees with any factual findings, an effective traverse must include a reasoned statement explaining why the applicant believes the Office has erred substantively as to the factual findings. A mere statement or argument that the Office has not established a prima facie case of obviousness or that the Office’s reliance on common knowledge is unsupported by documentary evidence will not be considered substantively adequate. Office personnel may repeat the prior rejection and make the next Office action final (see MPEP §706.07(a)).

name: Substantive content of the prior art must be evaluated (enablement, inoperative devices, admissions, breadth)
description: Examiners must assess the substantive content of prior art with respect to issues such as availability of inoperative devices, whether prior art must be enabling, and whether a reference provides a broad disclosure versus only preferred embodiments or admissions.
guidance: See MPEP §2121–§2129 for case law and discussion on how these factors affect whether a reference can support anticipation or obviousness (examples: when a prior art device is inoperative, whether broad disclosures are sufficient, treatment of admissions). The evaluation concerns not just the existence of references but their substantive teaching and applicability to the claimed invention.

name: Pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) — evidence required to show conditions apply
description: An applicant subject to pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 who wants to avail themselves of pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) benefits bears the burden of establishing that subject matter used in a rejection and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.
guidance: To establish joint research agreement benefits (for applications pending on or after December 10, 2004), applicant must show: (A) claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the invention date; (B) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (C) the application discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement. This disqualification applies only to subject matter qualifying as prior art under subsections (e), (f), or (g) of pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102. See MPEP §2146.01 and §2146.02 and In re Bartfeld for limits and examples.

name: Analogous prior art requirement for 35 U.S.C. 103
description: To rely on a reference under 35 U.S.C. 103, the reference must be analogous art to the claimed invention.
guidance: A reference is analogous art if: (1) the reference is from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention (even if it addresses a different problem); or (2) the reference is reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor (even if not in the same field). Reasonably pertinent means it would 'logically have commended itself to an inventor's attention' in considering the problem. Examiners must determine analogous art and may include a statement of their understanding of the problem. Applicant arguments that the examiner misconstrued the problem (and thus improperly relied on nonanalogous art) should be fully considered and evaluated against the specification and inferences a person of ordinary skill would draw. See In re Bigio, In re ICON, In re Klein, In re Clay.

name: Analogy guidance in the chemical arts
description: In the chemical arts, references are analogous when their teachings would be pertinent to the problems addressed by the claimed invention, even if from different named arts.
guidance: Examples: Ex parte Bland – references concerning absorbing biologically active materials on carriers were pertinent across related problems; Stratoflex v. Aeroquip – solutions in PTFE vs rubber hose art were analogous because manufacturers and problems overlapped; In re Mlot-Fijalkowski – dye chemistry references were pertinent because the problem was one of dye chemistry. Examiners should consider the nature of the problem (e.g., chemistry) rather than narrow field labels.

name: Analogy guidance in the design arts
description: In design patent applications, analogous art determination follows specific case law; prior designs of contemporaneous furniture or related items may be analogous depending on general use and designer knowledge.
guidance: See MPEP §1504.03 and examples: In re Rosen (contemporary furniture designs analogous), Ex parte Pappas (architectural handbook analogous to feed bunk design), In re Butera (metal ball anode design was nonanalogous to insect repellent/air freshener design). Examiners should assess whether prior designs are of the 'type claimed' and whether a designer of ordinary skill would have reason to look to those references.

name: Do not distill an invention down to a 'gist' or 'thrust' (anti‑pattern)
description: Distilling an invention down to the 'gist' or 'thrust' disregards the requirement of analyzing the subject matter 'as a whole.'
guidance: Cases (W.L. Gore; Bausch & Lomb v. Barnes-Hind; Jones v. Hardy; Panduit) show that focusing on an advantage or single limitation while disregarding express claim limitations improperly treats claims as if they read differently than allowed. Examiners should analyze all claim limitations and contexts rather than abstracting the invention to a one-word or narrow gist.

name: Assignment of Patent Classification (CPC, IPC)
description: Assign classification taking into consideration the invention as claimed to enable effective prior-art search and retrieval.
guidance: KIPO adopts the IPC; CPC may be allocated (every application except PCT filed after Jan 2015 is allocated CPC and IPC automatically). Classification must be accurate and based on technical subject-matter.

name: Classification Assignment Must Reflect Essential Technical Subject-matter
description: Patent classification assignment must be made accurately based on the technical subject-matter of the invention, determined from claims in light of description and drawings.
guidance: Classification should be based on the essential contents of the claimed invention as a whole, not bound to formality such as category of invention; if claims unclear, use description/drawings; if claims and description differ, description matters are classified as additional information.

name: Secondary considerations as objective indicia of non-obviousness
description: Secondary considerations such as commercial success, long-felt need, and industry praise can weigh against a finding of obviousness.
guidance: Board may find claims non-obvious based on secondary considerations after otherwise finding prior-art grounds sufficient. Evidence must show nexus to the claimed invention (see 'coextensive' product or direct result of limitations). Petitioner must meaningfully rebut by, e.g., laying out timing of advertising/marketing and explaining how marketing—not claimed features—caused success. (Cases: Biotechnologies S.A. v. Novo Nordisk; Yita LLC v. MacNeil IP LLC; Ontel Prods. Corp. v. Guy A. Shaked Invs. Ltd.)

name: Presumption of nexus when commercial product is coextensive with claims
description: If the patent owner's commercial product is coextensive with the claims, a presumption of nexus to commercial success arises.
guidance: When coextensiveness is shown, nexus is presumed; Petitioner can attempt to rebut by showing success due to non-claimed factors (e.g., marketing), but must present timing/details. Board may decline to reach coextensiveness if nexus shown via direct causal link between praise/acceptance and claimed limitations.

name: Industry praise and acceptance as nexus evidence
description: Industry praise and acceptance may serve as objective indicia of non-obviousness if shown to be the direct result of claimed limitations.
guidance: Unrebutted testimony that industry praise is directly caused by claimed subject matter can satisfy nexus without requiring a coextensive product showing. Board found such evidence persuasive to defeat obviousness challenges. (Ontel Prods. case)

name: General Plastic factors for denying follow-on petitions/joinders
description: Under General Plastic, the Board may deny institution of follow-on petitions when multiple petitions present substantially similar grounds and a 'significant relationship' exists between petitioners or proceedings.
guidance: Factors include overlap of grounds and prior art, whether a later petitioner had a significant relationship with earlier petitioner(s), and whether later petitions raise unique challenges. The Board has denied institution where the later petition substantially duplicated an earlier one and significant relationship/overlap existed. Conversely, lack of significant relationship (no co-defendant status, different products, or additional claims) supports institution. (Home Depot v. Link Labs; Samsung v. Scramoge Tech.; Intel v. VLSI)

name: Indefiniteness prevents reaching merits on patentability
description: If claims are indefinite such that the Board cannot ascertain their scope with reasonable certainty, the Board will not make an unpatentability determination on the merits.
guidance: Applying district-court constructions may lead the Board to find claims indefinite; in that circumstance, PTAB cannot evaluate patentability of claims. (Micron Tech. v. Unification Techs.)

name: Discretionary denial when district court finds claims ineligible under §101
description: A district-court §101 invalidity finding can support discretionary denial based on efficiency, but the Board recognizes Fintiv is focused on §102/103 overlap and may analyze efficiency on other grounds.
guidance: Board may be reluctant to institute when efficiency strongly favors denial due to a district court's §101 decision, but it will explain that Fintiv specifically targets duplication of efforts for 102/103 issues. The Board evaluates whether institution would waste resources. (AviaGames v. Skillz Platform)

name: Grounds for revocation (permissible grounds)
description: A European patent may only be opposed on the grounds that: the subject-matter of one or more of the claims is not patentable (in particular not novel or not inventive); the patent does not disclose the invention in a manner sufficiently clear and complete for it to be carried out by a person skilled in the art; and the subject-matter of the patent extends beyond the content of the application as filed.
guidance: These are the exclusive substantive grounds on which an opposition can be based.

name: Other grounds not admissible
description: Other grounds of opposition are not admissible.
guidance: Examples of inadmissible grounds: lack of clarity of claim wording, or allegations that the invention was 'stolen' from the opponent or a third party.

name: Amendments to the patent (limits and requirements)
description: The patent proprietor may defend the opposed patent as granted or in a limited version. Amendments may be chosen from the whole content of the original patent application’s disclosure as long as the scope of protection is not extended beyond the granted patent’s scope of protection.
guidance: Amendments of the patent need to be occasioned by a ground of opposition; opposition proceedings must not be used to reformulate claims or description for clarity or cosmetic reasons or to adapt them to competitors' embodiments.

name: If claimed nature-based product has markedly different characteristics → not a product-of-nature exception (Step 2A: NO)
description: If the claim includes a nature-based product that has markedly different characteristics, then the claim does not recite a product of nature exception and is eligible (Step 2A: NO) at Pathway B unless the claim recites another exception (such as a law of nature or abstract idea, or a different natural phenomenon).
guidance: For claims where the entire claim is a single nature-based product (e.g., a claim to "a Lactobacillus bacterium"), once a markedly different characteristic in that product is shown, no further analysis would be necessary for eligibility because no product of nature exception is recited (i.e., Step 2B is not necessary because the answer to Step 2A is NO). For claims including additional limitations, examiners should still consider whether the claim recites another exception that requires further eligibility analysis.

name: If claimed nature-based product lacks markedly different characteristics → product-of-nature exception (requires further analysis)
description: If the claim includes a nature-based product that does not exhibit markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state, then the claim recites a 'product of nature' exception, and requires further analysis in Step 2A Prong Two to determine whether the claim as a whole integrates the exception into a practical application.
guidance: A finding that a limitation is a product-of-nature exception does not end analysis; examiners must proceed to Prong Two (and Step 2B if necessary) to determine whether additional claim elements integrate the exception into a patent-eligible application.

name: No analysis needed for limitations that are naturally occurring
description: If the nature-based product limitation is naturally occurring, there is no need to perform the markedly different characteristics analysis because the limitation is by definition directed to a naturally occurring product and thus falls under the product of nature exception.
guidance: If the nature-based product limitation is not naturally occurring (for example due to human intervention), then the markedly different characteristics analysis must be performed to determine whether the claimed product limitation is a product-of-nature exception.

name: Product claims: apply analysis to the entire claimed product or the resultant nature-based combination
description: Where the claim is to a nature-based product by itself (e.g., a claim to "a Lactobacillus bacterium"), the markedly different characteristics analysis should be applied to the entire product. Where the claim is to a nature-based product produced by combining multiple components (e.g., "a probiotic composition comprising a mixture of Lactobacillus and milk"), the analysis should be applied to the resultant nature-based combination rather than its component parts.
guidance: When the claim is to a nature-based product combined with non-nature elements (e.g., a 'yogurt starter kit' comprising Lactobacillus plus container and instructions), apply the markedly different analysis only to the nature-based product limitation (Lactobacillus). Non-nature elements are not subject to this analysis but may be evaluated in Prong Two/Step 2B if the nature-based product is found to be an exception. Case examples: Chakrabarty (entire bacterium), Funk Bros. (analyze bacterial mixture).

name: Process claims: generally focus on active steps; only apply MD analysis when claim is in substance a product claim
description: For a process claim, the general rule is that the claim is not subject to the markedly different characteristics analysis for nature-based products used in the process, because process analysis should focus on the active steps of the process rather than the products used in those steps.
guidance: Exception: where a process claim reciting a nature-based product is drafted such that there is no difference in substance from a product claim (e.g., 'a method of providing an apple'), then the claim is subject to the markedly different characteristics analysis for the recited nature-based product. Case examples: Rapid Litig. Mgmt. v. CellzDirect; Ariosa Diagnostics (detecting cffDNA).

name: Three-step framework for performing the markedly different characteristics analysis
description: The analysis involves (a) selecting the appropriate naturally occurring counterpart(s) to the nature-based product limitation, (b) identifying appropriate characteristics for analysis, and (c) evaluating characteristics to determine whether they are 'markedly different'.
guidance: Each step should be carried out on a case-by-case basis, using the claim language and the closest naturally occurring counterpart(s) in their natural state. The analysis looks at structure, function, and/or other properties as recited or encompassed by the claim.

name: Appropriate characteristics for comparison must be possessed by the claimed product
description: Appropriate characteristics must be possessed by the claimed product, because it is the claim that must define the invention to be patented. Unclaimed characteristics cannot contribute to eligibility.
guidance: Examiners identify characteristics from what is recited in the claim and what is encompassed within the broadest reasonable interpretation. Characteristics may be explicitly recited (e.g., chemical name indicating structural differences) or inferred from the BRI (e.g., 'isolated gene B' implies sequence and encoded protein). Case citation: Roslin (unclaimed characteristics cannot contribute).

name: Public requester entitlement when application is identified in published patent document
description: If the requester is not an authorized party but the application is (1) identified by application number (or serial number and filing date) in a published patent document, or (2) an application claiming the benefit of the filing date of an application identified by application number (or serial number and filing date) in a published patent document, then a written request including a copy of the published patent document which refers to the specific application must be provided when requesting status information.
guidance: If the published patent document is not in English, a translation of the pertinent part must be included. The published patent document may be presented in person to the FIU or by written correspondence (e.g., facsimile). Written correspondence must include a return address or facsimile number. PALM Intranet should be used to determine status and continuity data; limited status information for related child applications may be provided as per 37 CFR 1.14(a)(2)(iv).

name: Availability: unpublished abandoned applications identified or relied upon (37 CFR 1.14(a)(1)(iv))
description: The file contents of an unpublished, abandoned application may be made available to the public if the application is identified in a U.S. patent, statutory invention registration, a U.S. patent application publication, or an international patent application publication published in accordance with PCT Article 21(2). An application is considered identified when the application number or serial number and filing date, first named inventor, title and filing date or other application-specific information are provided in the text of the patent.
guidance: The file contents may also be made available if benefit of the abandoned application is claimed under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), 120, 121, or 365 in an application that has issued as a U.S. patent or published. A written request and payment of the appropriate fee (§1.19(b)) are required.

name: Confidentiality and private cause of action under §6103/§7431
description: Section 6103 provides that income tax returns and return information are confidential. Section 7431 provides a civil cause of action for damages for the intentional or negligent disclosure of confidential return information by officers or employees of the United States.
guidance: This is the substantive basis for a wrongful-disclosure claim; determine whether a disclosure falls within §6103 confidentiality and then whether an exception or authorization applies (e.g., §6103(k)(6)).

name: Appellate handling of preliminary injunctive hearing consolidation
description: A district court that consolidates a preliminary injunction hearing with the trial on the merits must still address all merits-based factual contentions (e.g., whether an assessment was ever made).
guidance: Entry of judgment following consolidation should be careful to resolve—on the merits—any disputed factual predicate that could support a wrongful-disclosure claim; failure to address a material factual gap (e.g., lack of evidence of assessment) can require remand.

name: General chemical formulae — classify fully identified compounds
description: For general chemical formulae (e.g., Markush claims) classification should be given to all 'fully identified' compounds that are novel and unobvious if they are specifically claimed, products of a claimed process, or derivatives of these.
guidance: A compound is 'fully identified' where (a) structure is given by exact chemical name/formula or deducible from specified reactants (not more than one from alternatives), and (b) the compound is characterised by a physical property (e.g., melting point) or its preparation is described in a worked example with practical details. Compounds identified only by empirical formula are not 'fully identified'.

name: Classification procedure for unsearched patent documents
description: For unsearched documents, all claimed subject matter that is potentially novel and unobvious in the opinion of the classifier (expert in the art) must be classified as invention information along with potentially novel/unobvious constituents or components.
guidance: Any unclaimed subject matter considered potentially novel/unobvious by the expert classifier must be classified. For classifiers who are not experts, use all claims to determine subject matter to be classified. Desirable to classify/index additional information if useful for search.

name: Unity not met when claims recite non-identical/non-corresponding special technical features
description: Where the special technical features are not identical or do not correspond, unity of inventions is not met between claims that recite different special technical features.
guidance: Example: Claim 1: DC motor control circuit A; Claim 2: DC motor control circuit B; Claim 3: apparatus using motor comprising control circuit A; Claim 4: apparatus using motor comprising control circuit B. Unity is met between claim 1 and claim 3, or claim 2 and claim 4, but not between claim 1 and claim 2 or claim 3 and claim 4, because control circuit A and B are different special technical features.

name: Unity with claims reciting multiple features (non-single features)
description: When claims recite distinct features (e.g., Feature A and Feature B), unity is met between claims that share one of those features and a claim combining them, but not between claims each having only different single features.
guidance: Example: Claim 1: conveyor belt comprising Feature A; Claim 2: conveyor belt comprising Feature B; Claim 3: conveyor belt comprising Features A and B. Unity is met between claim 1 and claim 3, and between claim 2 and claim 3, but not between claim 1 and claim 2.

name: Product and method of treating the product — definition and correspondence
description: 'Treating the product' means applying an external effect to maintain or exert the product's functions without changing the product's nature. Such treating methods correspond to the product invention for unity purposes.
guidance: Examples: Claim 1: prefabricated home with special structure; Claim 2: method of storing such home — storing intends to maintain/exert the function (easily-stored/transferred), so it corresponds. Another example: material A and method of storing material A by specific conditions — corresponds to treating the subject matter in claim 1.

name: Product and machinery/device for manufacturing the product — suitability and unity
description: Whether equipment used for manufacturing a product is suitable for manufacturing the product shall be crucial; if the equipment, when practiced, actually manufactures the product, unity is met between the product claim and the equipment claim.
guidance: 'Suitable' again means that practicing the equipment invention results in manufacture of the product, even if equipment can be used for other products. Example: Bolt A with special structure and Equipment B used for manufacturing Bolt A — unity met. The guidance reiterates suitability does not require exclusivity.

name: Markush-type claims — corresponding alternatives yield unity
description: Where alternative elements are recited in the Markush style in a single claim, if the alternative elements have corresponding qualities or functions, unity of inventions is met. The same criteria apply whether alternatives are in multiple independent claims or in a single Markush claim.
