guidance: If the Markush group includes alternative chemicals that meet other chapter requirements, the group is considered to have corresponding qualities/functions. Example: a formula where indole is the crucial structural element common among substituents; all claimed compounds deemed to have same use so unity is met. Another example: catalysts (X) and (X+a) share common element and activation and thus meet unity.

name: Groups of compounds correspondence rule (intermediate vs end product groups)
description: Where intermediate materials and end products are groups of chemical compounds, each intermediate compound shall correspond to one compound claimed in the group of end product compounds; but groups do not necessarily correspond one-to-one if parts of end materials lack corresponding intermediate compounds.
guidance: Examiner should analyze one-to-one correspondence between claimed compound groups; lack of correspondence may break unity.

name: Unity determination begins with independent claims; dependents inherit unity
description: Unity of invention shall be first determined on independent claims. Where independent claims are deemed to meet unity, dependent claims which refer to such independent claims shall be deemed to satisfy unity.
guidance: This is a primary procedural principle for examiners. Dependent claims are generally not separately assessed if the independent claim meets unity.

name: Generally no need to determine unity between independent and dependent claims, except when cited claim lacks novelty/inventive step
description: In principle, unity does not need to be determined between an independent claim and a dependent claim dependent upon it; however, where a cited claim lacks novelty or inventive step and thus lacks 'special technical features', unity cannot be met among claims citing the concerned claim and additional review is required.
guidance: Example shows independent claim A disclosed in prior art and dependent claims A+B, A+C, A+C+D, A+F: since independent claim lacks improvement, unity must be determined among dependent claims (claims 2-5) and examiner may split into groups (Group1: claims1-2; Group2: claims3-4; Group3: claim5) and notify accordingly. Examiner may also directly notify rejection on grounds of lack of novelty/inventive step for all claims if searching all groups is unnecessary.

name: Form paragraph and notice requirements for transitional after-final practice
description: Form paragraph 7.41.01.fti may be used to notify applicant that the application qualifies under 37 CFR 1.129(a). The submission under 37 CFR 1.129(a) may comprise, but is not limited to, an IDS, an amendment to the written description, claims or drawings, a new substantive argument and/or new evidence. No amendment considered as a result of payment of the fee set forth in 37 CFR 1.17(r) may introduce new matter into the disclosure of the application (35 U.S.C. 132).
guidance: If applicant has filed multiple proposed amendments which, when entered, would conflict with one another, provide specific instructions for entry or non-entry of each amendment upon payment of any fee under 37 CFR 1.17(r). Do not use this paragraph for design, reissue, or reexamination applications.

name: Dependent claim statutory requirements (35 U.S.C. 112(d))
description: A claim in dependent form shall contain a reference to a claim previously set forth and then specify a further limitation of the subject matter claimed. A claim in dependent form shall be construed to incorporate by reference all the limitations of the claim to which it refers.
guidance: The test is that the dependent claim must include every limitation of the claim from which it depends and specify a further limitation. Omitting or replacing an element of the base claim (e.g., omitting D or replacing D with E when base claim recites A,B,C,D) makes the dependent claim improper. A dependent claim does not lack compliance simply because there is a question as to the significance of the further limitation added.

name: Dependent claim may cross statutory classes and relate to separate inventions
description: The fact that a dependent claim relates to a separate invention requiring a separate search or is in a different statutory class from the claim on which it depends does not, in itself, render it an improper dependent claim.
guidance: Examples: a claim to a method of making the product of claim 1 may be a proper dependent claim; a product-by-process dependent claim may be proper only if it includes the limitations of the base claim. Examiner should still treat dependent claim as a combination of base + dependent limitations when comparing to prior art.

name: Comparison of dependent claim to prior art
description: A dependent claim is directed to a combination including everything recited in the base claim and what is recited in the dependent claim.
guidance: Examiners must compare the combined limitations (as if the dependent claim were presented as one independent claim) with the prior art.

name: Action when dependent claim fails 35 U.S.C. 112(d)
description: If the dependent claim does not comply with 35 U.S.C. 112(d), the examiner should reject the dependent claim under 35 U.S.C. 112(d) as unpatentable rather than objecting to the claim.
guidance: Use form paragraph 7.36 (statutory quotation) and form paragraph 7.36.01 (rejection wording). In form paragraph 7.36.01, insert explanation in bracket 2 explaining what in the claim fails to constitute a further limitation. Form paragraph 7.36 is to be used ONLY ONCE in a given Office action.

name: Claim terminology and antecedent basis (support in specification)
description: The meaning of every term used in any of the claims should be apparent from the descriptive portion of the specification with clear disclosure as to its import; in mechanical cases identify the part(s) in the drawings to which the term applies.
guidance: Avoid a confusing variety of terms for the same thing. New terms introduced after filing should be supported by appropriate amendment to the specification so there is clear support or antecedent basis (see 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1)). Examiners should ensure late-presented terms find clear support; object the specification using form paragraph 7.44 if it fails to provide proper antecedent basis.

name: Completeness of specification — written description, enablement, and utility (35 U.S.C. 112)
description: The specification must include a written description of the invention using such description and details as to enable any person skilled in the art to make and use the invention as of its filing date, and must include at least one specific operative embodiment or example sufficient in scope to justify the scope of the claims.
guidance: Written description must reasonably convey that the applicant was in possession of the claimed invention. Enablement requires disclosure without undue experimentation (complex experimentation that is typical in the art may be allowed). The specification should include a statement identifying a specific and substantial credible utility for the claimed invention. See cited MPEP sections for specialized contexts (e.g., biotech, functional claims, computer programs).

name: Definition of essential material and limits on incorporation
description: ‘Essential material’ is material necessary to (1) provide the written description/enablement/best mode (35 U.S.C. 112(a)); (2) describe the claimed invention in terms that particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention (35 U.S.C. 112(b)); or (3) describe structure/material/acts corresponding to a claimed means or step (35 U.S.C. 112(f)).
guidance: In an application to issue as a U.S. patent, essential material may only be incorporated by reference to a U.S. patent or U.S. patent application publication. Nonessential (background/state of the art) may be incorporated from a broader list of document types. Examiners should ensure incorporations comply with 37 CFR 1.57(c)-(e).

name: Examiner handling of dependent claims when base claim is canceled or rejected
description: If the base claim has been canceled, a claim directly or indirectly dependent thereon should be rejected as incomplete. If the base claim is rejected, the dependent claim should be objected to rather than rejected if it is otherwise allowable.
guidance: Use form paragraph 7.43 to state the objection: 'Claim [1] objected to as being dependent upon a rejected base claim, but would be allowable if rewritten in independent form including all of the limitations of the base claim and any intervening claims.'

name: Incorrect translation may limit or void patent scope
description: If, because of an incorrect translation of the international application, the scope of any patent granted exceeds the scope of the international application in its original language, competent authorities may retroactively limit the scope of the patent and declare it null and void to the extent it exceeded the original-language scope.
guidance: Translation errors that enlarge claimed scope relative to the original language allow competent authorities to restrict or invalidate the overbroad parts of the patent.

name: Priority exclusions in term calculation
description: Priority under section 119, 365(a), 365(b), 386(a), or 386(b) shall not be taken into account in determining the term of a patent.
guidance: Certain foreign or other priority claims do not alter the 20-year term calculation. (35 U.S.C. 154(a)(3))

name: Patent term adjustment for USPTO delays — general rule
description: If the issue of an original patent is delayed due to the failure of the Patent and Trademark Office to: (i) provide at least one of the notifications under section 132 or a notice of allowance under section 151 not later than 14 months after certain filing dates; (ii) respond to a reply under section 132 or to an appeal under section 134 within 4 months; (iii) act on an application within 4 months after certain Board or court decisions where allowable claims remain; or (iv) issue a patent within 4 months after payment of the issue fee and satisfaction of outstanding requirements, the term of the patent shall be extended 1 day for each day after the end of the specified period until the action is taken.
guidance: Separate guarantees address timely notifications, responses, actions after decisions, and issuing after fee payment; each day of PTO delay can result in a 1-day extension. (35 U.S.C. 154(b)(1)(A)-(iv))

name: Provisional rights — right to reasonable royalty from publication to issue
description: A patent shall include the right to obtain a reasonable royalty from any person who, during the period beginning on the date of publication of the application and ending on the date the patent is issued, (A)(i) makes, uses, offers for sale, or sells in the U.S. the invention as claimed in the published patent application or imports such an invention, or (ii) if the invention claimed in the published application is a process, uses/offers/sells/imports products made by that process; and (B) had actual notice of the published patent application (for foreign-language international publications, the person had a translation).
guidance: Provisional rights entitle the patentee to reasonable royalties for infringing acts during the pre‑grant publication window, but only with actual notice (and translation if necessary). (35 U.S.C. 154(d)(1))

name: Substantially identical claims requirement for provisional rights
description: The right to obtain a reasonable royalty shall not be available unless the invention as claimed in the patent is substantially identical to the invention as claimed in the published patent application.
guidance: Provisional rights require substantial identity between published claims and issued claims; protects against claim scope changes. (35 U.S.C. 154(d)(2))

name: Eligibility criteria for patent-term extension (PTE)
description: The term of a patent that claims a product, a method of using a product, or a method of manufacturing a product shall be extended if: (1) the term has not expired before an application for extension is submitted; (2) the term has never been extended under subsection (e)(1); (3) an application for extension is submitted by the owner of record or its agent and in accordance with subsection (d) requirements; (4) the product has been subject to a regulatory review period before its commercial marketing or use; and (5) except as provided, the permission for commercial marketing or use after such regulatory review period is the first permitted commercial marketing or use of the product under the law under which the regulatory review occurred (with specific exceptions for certain recombinant DNA and animal drug cases).
guidance: Establishes the basic statutory eligibility conditions for obtaining a regulatory-review-based patent-term extension. (35 U.S.C. 156(a)(1)-(5))

name: Scope of rights during patent-term extension
description: During the period the term of the patent is extended, the rights derived from the patent shall be limited: (1) for patents claiming a product, to any use approved for the product before expiration and on or after the expiration of the regulatory review period upon which the extension was based; (2) for patents claiming a method of using a product, to any use claimed by the patent and approved for the product as described; (3) for patents claiming a method of manufacturing, limited to the method of manufacturing as used to make the approved product.
guidance: Extension does not broaden claimed rights beyond approved uses and approved manufacturing methods; rights tied to regulatory approvals. (35 U.S.C. 156(b)(1)-(3))

name: Application contents for patent-term extension
description: To obtain an extension, the owner of record or agent shall submit an application within the 60-day period beginning on the date the product received permission for commercial marketing/use (with certain drug-specific timing exceptions). The application shall contain: (A) the identity of the approved product and the Federal statute under which regulatory review occurred; (B) the identity of the patent and each claim of such patent which claims the approved product or a method of using or manufacturing the approved product; (C) information to enable the Director to determine eligibility and the period of extension and to enable the Director and the Secretary of HHS or Agriculture to determine the period; (D) a brief description of activities undertaken by the applicant during the regulatory review period with significant dates; and (E) such patent or other information as the Director may require.
guidance: Specifies the documentary and factual content the PTO expects in a PTE application, including coordination with HHS/USDA for period determination. (35 U.S.C. 156(d)(1)(A)-(E))

name: Interim extensions when regulatory review may extend past patent expiry
description: If the owner reasonably expects that the applicable regulatory review period may extend beyond the expiration of the patent term, the owner or its agent may submit an application for an interim extension during the period beginning 6 months and ending 15 days before the term is due to expire. The application shall contain: (i) identity of product and statute under review; (ii) identity of the patent and claims; (iii) information to enable Director to determine eligibility; (iv) a brief description of activities undertaken during the review to date and significant dates; and (v) such patent or other information as the Director may require.
guidance: Allows seeking temporary protection when approval timelines risk rendering the patent expired before final extension determination. (35 U.S.C. 156(d)(5)(A))

name: Congruous Merit (meritum de congruo) gives only a quasi-claim and does not require state of grace
description: Congruous merit (meritum de congruo) differs from condign merit: it does not confer a real claim in strict justice but a quasi-claim based on equity (ex quadam aequitate, congruentia, decentia); it does not require the state of grace.
guidance: Although analogous to condign merit in many respects, congruous merit is distinct in that it lacks the same juridical force. Some scholastics rejected the term due to ambiguity, but the chapter defends its use and notes that requisites are identical to condign merit except for the requirement of state of grace.

name: A sinner cooperating with actual grace can merit de congruo to obtain dispositions for justification
description: A Christian in the state of mortal sin, from the moment he begins to cooperate with supernatural (actual) grace, can merit de congruo by good works and obtain by prayer the dispositions necessary for justification, and ultimately justification itself (as an equity-based claim).
guidance: The teaching is supported by Scripture and Augustine; prayer is contrasted with condign merit—'Prayer relies on mercy, condign merit on justice.' Conscientious preparation with actual grace probably merits an additional equitable claim to justification. Passages and patristic/supporting authorities are cited.

name: Markings for changes (brackets and underlining)
description: Any changes relative to the patent being reexamined which are made to the specification, including the claims, must include the following markings: (1) The matter to be omitted must be enclosed in brackets; and (2) The matter to be added must be underlined.
guidance: Markings must follow paragraph (f) requirements so that insertions and deletions are clear in relation to the current patent text.

name: Disclosure amendment when required
description: The disclosure must be amended, when required by the Office, to correct inaccuracies of description and definition, and to secure substantial correspondence between the claims, the remainder of the specification, and the drawings.
guidance: The Office may order amendment of the disclosure to ensure internal consistency among claims, specification, and drawings.

name: Amendments relative to patent status date
description: All amendments must be made relative to the patent specification, including the claims, and drawings, which are in effect as of the date of filing the request for reexamination.
guidance: Amendments are measured against the patent as it stood on the filing date of the reexamination request, not against subsequent changes.

name: Restriction on enlarging claim scope and introducing new matter
description: No amendment may enlarge the scope of the claims of the patent or introduce new matter. No amendment may be proposed for entry in an expired patent. Moreover, no amendment, other than the cancellation of claims, will be incorporated into the patent by a certificate issued after the expiration of the patent.
guidance: Amendments are strictly limited to narrowing/clarifying the claims and cannot add new subject matter or broaden claim coverage; expired patents cannot receive substantive amendments.

name: Director's decision timeline under 35 U.S.C. 303
description: Within three months following the filing of a request for reexamination under section 302, the Director will determine whether a substantial new question of patentability affecting any claim of the patent is raised by the request, with or without consideration of other patents or printed publications.
guidance: A record of the Director’s determination will be placed in the official file and a copy mailed to the owner and requester. A determination that no substantial new question has been raised is final and nonappealable; partial refunds may be made.

name: Examiner determination on ex parte requests (37 CFR 1.515)
description: Within three months following the filing date of an ex parte reexamination request, an examiner will consider the request and determine whether a substantial new question of patentability affecting any claim of the patent is raised by the request and the prior art cited therein.
guidance: The determination is based on the claims in effect at the time, becomes part of the official file, and is mailed to the patent owner and requester. A patent owner statement and accompanying information submitted pursuant to §1.501(a)(2) will not be considered when making the determination. If no SNQ is found, a portion of the fee will be refunded. The requester may petition under §1.181 within one month of mailing.

name: Standard for granting reexamination — substantial new question of patentability (SNQ) and scope
description: It is only necessary to establish that a substantial new question of patentability exists as to one of the patent claims in order to grant reexamination. The Office's determination in the order for reexamination and examination stage will generally be limited to a review of the claim(s) for which reexamination was requested.
guidance: 35 U.S.C. 302 requires the request to set forth the pertinency and manner of applying cited prior art to every claim for which reexamination is requested. If the requester fails to apply the art to certain claims, the requester is not statutorily entitled to reexamination of such claims; the Office may, at its discretion, reexamine non-requested claims or initiate reexamination of non-requested claims under 35 U.S.C. 303(a). No prima facie case of unpatentability need be found to grant an order for reexamination.

name: Content and limits of the decision on the request
description: The decision on the request for reexamination should discuss all of the patent claims requested for reexamination. The examiner should limit the discussion to whether a substantial new question of patentability has been raised and SHOULD NOT reject claims in the order for reexamination.
guidance: Any rejection of claims will be made in the first Office action on patentability issued after the time for submitting any patent owner statement and requester reply. Patent owner claim scope statements submitted under 37 CFR 1.501(a)(2) will not be considered when deciding whether to order ex parte reexamination under 35 U.S.C. 304.

name: Evaluate whether additional elements are well-understood, routine, conventional activity
description: When making a determination whether the additional elements in a claim amount to significantly more than a judicial exception, the examiner should evaluate whether the elements define only well-understood, routine, conventional activity; this consideration overlaps with improvement, mere instructions to apply an exception, and insignificant extra-solution activity.
guidance: Assess additional elements individually and in combination; use other Step 2B considerations (MPEP §2106.05(a), (f), (g)) to assist. If elements or functions are beyond those recognized in the art or courts as well-understood/routine/conventional, they will in most cases favor eligibility.

name: Known-in-the-art elements can still be unconventional/non-routine
description: An additional element (or combination of additional elements) that is known in the art can nonetheless be unconventional or non-routine such that it amounts to significantly more than a judicial exception.
guidance: Novelty/obviousness under §§102/103 is a separate inquiry; an improvement over conventional functionality can render a claim eligible even if not novel over the prior art (example: Enfish describing a self-referential database that provided technical improvements).

name: Court-recognized computer functions that can be well-understood/routine/conventional
description: The courts have recognized certain computer functions as well-understood, routine, and conventional when claimed in a generic manner or as insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., receiving/transmitting data over a network; performing repetitive calculations; electronic recordkeeping; storing and retrieving information in memory; scanning/extracting data; web browser navigation).
guidance: Specific cited cases: Symantec; TLI Communications; OIP Techs.; buySAFE; DDR Holdings (distinguishing cases where specific manipulation yields a technical result). Listing is illustrative, not exhaustive — a generic recitation of these functions may weigh against eligibility, but specific non-generic implementations can be eligible (see DDR, BASCOM, Amdocs).

name: Court-recognized life-science/laboratory techniques that can be well-understood/routine/conventional
description: In the life sciences, courts have recognized laboratory techniques as conventional when claimed at a high level of generality (e.g., determining biomarker levels in blood; using PCR to amplify/detect DNA; detecting DNA/enzymes; immunizing a patient; analyzing DNA sequences; freezing and thawing cells; amplifying/sequencing nucleic acids; hybridizing gene probes).
guidance: Cited cases include Mayo; Cleveland Clinic; Genetic Technologies; Ariosa/Sequenom; Rapid Litigation Management; Ambry Genetics. Generic recitation of such techniques may be insufficient to render claims eligible; specific unconventional applications may favor eligibility.

name: Other activities courts have found well-understood/routine/conventional
description: Courts have found other high-level activities to be conventional when recited generically (examples: recording a customer's order; shuffling/dealing a standard deck of cards; restricting public access by requiring ad viewing; presenting offers and gathering statistics; determining estimated outcomes and prices; arranging/sorting information for pricing).
guidance: These examples (from Apple v. Ameranth; In re Smith; Ultramercial; OIP Techs.; Versata) illustrate that routine business or clerical activities claimed at a high level typically do not add significantly more, absent specific technical integration or unconventional arrangement.

name: Other meaningful limitations — require limits beyond mere technological environment
description: The claim should add meaningful limitations beyond generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment to transform the exception into patent-eligible subject matter.
guidance: Meaningful limitations include considerations discussed in MPEP §2106.05(a)-(d) when they amount to significantly more or integrate the exception into a practical application. Examples: Diehr (Arrhenius equation applied within an automated rubber-molding process) and Classen (analysis plus a concrete immunization step). Avoid claims that only implement the exception via generic computer components (Alice). Consider treatment/prophylaxis overlap with Step 2A Prong Two (MPEP §2106.04(d)(2)). Examiners should analyze elements both individually and in combination and explain on the record where appropriate.

name: Consideration of breadth versus specificity — claim breadth does not determine eligibility alone
description: Requiring more than mere instructions to apply an exception does not mean a claim must be narrow to be eligible; courts have found both broad claims eligible and narrow claims ineligible depending on whether the claim adds significantly more.
guidance: Examples: McRO and Thales (broad claims held eligible); Ultramercial and Electric Power Group (narrow claims held ineligible). Focus analysis on whether the claim integrates the exception into a practical application or adds significantly more, not solely on claim breadth.

name: Eighteenth defence — prior patent of same inventor
description: Requires introduction in evidence of the prior patent granted on the application of the same inventor.
guidance: Seldom requires expert testimony because the prior claim must be so clearly co-extensive with the claim in suit that co-extensiveness is apparent on the faces of the two patents; however expert testimony may be necessary where one or both claims are in phraseology that cannot be understood without expert explanation.

name: Patent verdict rules — when plaintiff entitled to verdict
description: Plaintiff entitled to verdict if every defense except non-infringement fails and non-infringement fails as to any one claim; similar rules for combinations of partial defenses.
guidance: If some defenses succeed only against part of alleged infringement or part of claims, plaintiff may still be entitled to verdict as to the residue. Specific combinations (e.g., 16th–18th defences) described where plaintiff still entitled to verdict if those defences lack application to one or more claims shown violated.

name: Elements required by patent type
description: Required documents vary by patent type: Invention — request, claim(s) and description; Utility model — request, claim(s), description and drawing(s); Design — request, drawing(s) or photograph(s) and brief description.
guidance: Applicants must include the specified elements for the declared patent type at filing to avoid formal defects or non-acceptance.

name: Scope identified by specific claims
description: The ARP's review is specifically directed to claims 1-6 and 8-20 as to the new §101 ground of rejection.
guidance: The review and any resulting decision will pertain to the listed claims; other claims or issues not identified for review are not the focus of this rehearing order.

name: Mayo–Alice two-step framework
description: The Supreme Court’s two-step framework (commonly called Mayo/Alice) is the controlling test for patent-eligible subject matter: first determine whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea), then determine whether the claim elements contain an 'inventive concept' or are 'significantly more' than the exception.
guidance: Stakeholders widely criticized the framework as unworkable and unpredictable. The report notes the framework is applied unevenly by courts and examiners and is central to disputes over eligibility across technologies. Many comments describe the framework as causing uncertainty that harms innovation and investment.

name: Definition and clarity of 'abstract idea'
description: Whether a claimed invention is an 'abstract idea' is a threshold inquiry under step one of the Mayo/Alice framework.
guidance: Commenters observe there is no uniform definition of 'abstract idea,' creating subjectivity and unpredictability. Quoted criticisms: 'the “abstract idea” has created havoc' and courts/practitioners lack sufficient guidance to determine the scope of the exception.

name: 'Significantly more' / 'inventive concept' requirement
description: Under step two of the framework, the claim must recite elements that amount to 'significantly more' than the abstract idea or otherwise provide an 'inventive concept' to be eligible.
guidance: Stakeholders say the inquiry is ambiguous and often conflated with novelty/obviousness/enablement (35 U.S.C. §§102, 103, 112). Examples and commentary question how 'significant' is quantified; commenters give examples where substantial practical improvements were still found ineligible.

name: Treatment of computer-implemented inventions and software
description: Recognition that computing, algorithms, and software are inherently abstract and pose challenges under the Mayo/Alice framework.
guidance: Stakeholders argue the test biases against computer-related inventions and dissolves the boundary between claims to algorithms and legitimate system claims that use algorithms. Recommended drafting/claiming strategies include emphasizing improvements in computer technology or detailed technological solutions to problems.

name: Requirement that claims show an improvement in computer technology
description: To be eligible, computer-implemented inventions should claim an improvement in computer technology or recite a technical solution to a technical problem.
guidance: Several companies report success overcoming eligibility rejections by 'going into depth on the technological problem we are addressing and our technological solution.' This approach may also help define the 'abstract idea' and align U.S. practice internationally.

name: Consistency and clarity in USPTO and court application
description: Whether courts and USPTO examiners apply eligibility standards consistently and with adequate technical understanding.
guidance: Commenters reported inconsistent examiner treatment, over-generalization of components, and failure to appreciate complexity of computer or biotech inventions. Inconsistencies lead to narrow claim scope or added irrelevant limitations solely to satisfy eligibility tests.

name: Risk of divided infringement when drafting claims
description: Linking diagnostic claims to treatment can implicate divided infringement issues because different parties may perform separate claim steps.
guidance: Practitioners should be aware that adding affirmative treatment steps to satisfy eligibility can create enforcement difficulties. Commenters note that this dilutes the value of IP for companies that develop diagnostics but do not provide treatments.

name: If both parties do not claim same subject‑matter, interference dissolved
description: That if both parties do not claim the same subject‑matter the interference will be dissolved.
guidance: Interference requires a genuine conflict in claimed subject matter; divergence in claims that shows no overlapping subject matter leads to dissolution (cases: Sawyer v. Edison; Dod v. Cobb). Examiner examines claim scope to determine this.

name: Requirements and effect of a disclaimer during interference (§608b)
description: An applicant may file in the Patent Office a disclaimer in writing over his own signature and attested by two witnesses, averring that he does not claim to be the inventor of the particular matter in issue; the disclaimer must be accompanied by an amendment to the specification removing the contested matter from his claims.
guidance: The disclaimer must be timely (before the date fixed for preliminary statement presentation) and accompanied by amendment. The disclaimer is different from a patentee's disclaimer to amend an issued patent. If assignment exists, assignee's written consent is required. On disclaimer judgment will be rendered against him and his remaining application proceeds ex parte.

name: Time and attendance controls for patent examiners
description: Implement controls to prevent and detect time and attendance abuse among patent examiners, including ensuring a sufficient digital footprint for claimed work hours.
guidance: OIG analysis identified substantial unsupported hours across sampled examiners. USPTO actions include training, updated policies, added controls, tools for supervisors, and development of systems to improve workforce management and detection of unsupported time entries.

name: Initial overall visual impression (would an ordinary observer find designs substantially the same?)
description: Compare the patented design and the accused product 'in the eye[s] of an ordinary observer, giving such attention as a purchaser usually gives' and determine whether the 'two designs [were] substantially the same.'
guidance: Begin with the overall visual impression rather than immediately dissecting individual features. If the overall impressions are not substantially the same, the infringement claim is weak; if they appear substantially the same, move to finer-grained analysis and possibly prior-art comparison.

name: Application Must Identify Nature and Extent of Restriction Sought
description: In every concurrent use application the applicant shall (i) state exceptions to the claim of exclusive use and (ii) specify, to the extent of the verifier’s knowledge, any concurrent use by others, the goods and areas in which each concurrent use exists, the periods of each use, and the goods and area for which the applicant desires registration.
guidance: This requirement derives from Trademark Act § 1(a)(3)(D) and 37 C.F.R. § 2.42. The applicant’s statement of the area, goods/services, and (if applicable) mode of use for which registration is sought gives notice at publication and in any subsequent concurrent use proceeding of the scope of the registration sought; the statement setting forth concurrent lawful use by others gives notice of the applicant’s acknowledgement of others’ rights.

name: Publication, Notice, and Marking of Concurrent Use Proceedings
description: When an application is determined to be registrable subject to a concurrent use proceeding, the mark will be published for opposition and notification of institution of any concurrent use proceeding will be sent to the applicant and excepted users.
guidance: If no oppositions are filed (or all are dismissed/withdrawn), the Board will send notice of institution of the concurrent use proceeding and include a web link/address to access Office records related to the proceeding. When approved for publication, the application is marked by the examining attorney with a statement such as: 'SUBJECT TO CONCURRENT USE PROCEEDING WITH ________________. APPLICANT CLAIMS EXCLUSIVE RIGHT TO USE THE MARK IN THE AREA COMPRISING ________________.' See 37 C.F.R. §§ 2.80, 2.99(c), 2.99(d).

name: Predictability of results from combining prior art elements
description: A proper rejection based on combining known prior art elements includes a finding that results flowing from the combination would have been predictable to a person of ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: As explained (Crocs, Sundance, DePuy): merely pointing to presence of all claim elements in the prior art is not a complete obviousness rejection — Office personnel must find that the combination would have produced predictable results. If results would not have been predictable, do not use the combination rationale and withdraw such a rejection if entered.

name: Clear articulation of reason(s) to combine (no conclusory statements)
description: Rejections on obviousness cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements; there must be some articulated reasoning with a rational underpinning to support the legal conclusion of obviousness.
guidance: Cite KSR and In re Kahn: Office personnel should provide a reasoned explanation for every obviousness rejection, explicitly stating the rationale for why the claimed invention would have been obvious.

name: Simple substitution of one known element for another (requirements)
description: To reject based on simple substitution, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries and make specific findings about the substitution and predictability.
guidance: Required findings (verbatim structure provided): (1) a finding that the prior art contained a device (method, product, etc.) which differed from the claimed device by the substitution of some components (step, element, etc.) with other components; (2) a finding that the substituted components and their functions were known in the art; (3) a finding that one of ordinary skill in the art could have substituted one known element for another, and the results of the substitution would have been predictable; and (4) whatever additional findings based on the Graham factual inquiries may be necessary, in view of the facts of the case under consideration, to explain a conclusion of obviousness. If any of these findings cannot be made, the substitution rationale cannot be used.

name: Secondary considerations must have a nexus to the claimed invention
description: Objective indicia of nonobviousness (e.g., skepticism by experts, copying, praise, commercial success) require a nexus to the claimed invention and to the claim scope to be given substantial weight.
guidance: Muniauction/Leapfrog examples: where the proffered evidence is not coextensive with the claims or lacks a nexus to the claimed features, it is entitled to less weight in overcoming an obviousness case.

name: Unknown problems disclosed by patentee can alter obviousness analysis
description: If the patentee discovered a previously unknown problem that the prior art did not address or mention, there may have been no reason for a person of ordinary skill to make the claimed modification, supporting nonobviousness.
guidance: Omeprazole example: where prior art failed to mention a stability problem (even if a theoretical reason existed), discovery of that problem by the patentee can explain why a routine modification (e.g., adding a subcoating) would not have been made by those of ordinary skill.

name: Ex parte re-examination — USPTO threshold determination (substantial new question) and timing
description: The USPTO will determine within three months whether the request raises a 'substantial new question of patentability' affecting any claim, and if so, will initiate re-examination.
guidance: The USPTO's determination that no substantial new question has been raised is final and non-appealable by either party (i.e., no appeal from denial of re-exam institution).

name: Ex parte re-examination — conduct and scope of amendments
description: After initial time limits expire, the re-examination is conducted similarly to the initial examination. The patent owner may propose any amendment and may add a new claim to distinguish over cited prior art, but the scope of the claims may not be enlarged.
guidance: Procedure mirrors initial examination practice; amendments must not broaden the claim scope beyond the original disclosure.

name: Inter partes review — statutory scope of challenges
description: Inter partes review (IPR) reviews the patentability of one or more patent claims only on grounds that could be raised under 35 U.S.C. §§ 102 or 103 (novelty and non-obviousness), and only on the basis of prior art consisting of patents or printed publications (35 U.S.C. § 311).
guidance: Other grounds outside 102/103 are not available in IPR; testimonial evidence alone is insufficient — the basis must be patents/printed publications (though affidavits/declarations may support).

name: Inter partes review — timing limits to file a petition
description: A petition for IPR must be filed after the later of (1) nine months after grant of the patent or issuance of a reissue patent, or (2) if a post-grant review is instituted, the termination of the post-grant review.
guidance: Certain circumstances bar institution: if the petitioner filed a civil action challenging the validity of a claim before filing the petition, or if the petition is filed more than one year after the petitioner was served with a complaint alleging infringement.

name: Inter partes review — institution standard (reasonable likelihood)
description: To institute an IPR, it is necessary to show that there is a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail with respect to at least one claim.
guidance: The Director's threshold determination on institution is not appealable; this is analogous to the institution stage in other post-grant proceedings (see 35 U.S.C. § 314(a)).

name: Specification: two principal purposes
description: The specifications are required for two principal purposes: first to inform the public what the thing is of which the patentee claims to be the inventor; and, secondly, to enable the public, after the expiration of the patent, to practise the invention from the specification, as therein described.
guidance: Specification must both identify the invention and enable practice after expiration. (Forbes v. Barstow Stove Co. (1864) citation and related authorities cited.)

name: Specification must conclude with specific and distinct claims
description: Statute and Patent Office rules require that the specification shall conclude with a specific and distinct Claim or Claims of every separate subject-matter that the applicant desires to protect by the patent for which he has applied.
guidance: Where there is no Claim there is no application (Ex parte Lasscell, Ex parte Holt). The rules of the Patent Office prescribe the concluding claim(s).

name: Claim: function — defines limits of exclusive use
description: The office of the Claim is to define the limits of that exclusive use which is secured to the inventor by the patent, and thus to draw the line between those arts or instruments that are open to the public and those forbidden until patent expiration.
guidance: The Claim is an essential part of the specification; without it one of the two great purposes of the specification is unfulfilled.

name: Claim is the life of the patent and measure of privilege
description: The Claim is the life of the patent so far as the rights of the inventor are concerned, and by it the letters-patent, as a grant of an exclusive privilege, must stand or fall.
guidance: Claims determine the scope and identity of patents; a patent must be limited to the invention covered by its Claim. (Citations: Railroad Co. v. Mellon, etc.)

name: Claims must be particularly pointed out and distinctly claimed
description: The inventor shall 'particularly point out and distinctly claim the part, improvement, or combination which he claims as his invention or discovery.'
guidance: This statutory requirement relieves courts from reconstructing the invention from a laborious history-of-the-art inquiry; the Patent Office examines and scrutinizes the Claim. (Statutory language cited.)

name: Claims construed strictly; courts will not enlarge claim by description
description: When the terms of a Claim in the letters-patent are explicit, the courts cannot alter or enlarge it; the court will not go into the history of the art to expand a Claim beyond its language or allow it to be enlarged by the Description.
guidance: If patentees have not claimed the whole of their invention, they should correct by surrender and reissue; courts take patentees at their word. (Keystone Bridge Co. v. Phoenix Iron Co., James v. Campbell.)

name: Unclaimed matter: exclusion, abandonment, or postponement
description: All matters not claimed are considered as excluded from the particular invention. Failure to claim described matter may admit it to be old or may be an abandonment to the public, but these statements require qualification — omission does not automatically dedicate new matter unless intent or public use/sale indicates abandonment.
guidance: An inventor may describe but reserve other inventions for future patents (must expressly reserve). Claiming one specific device and omitting others apparent in the specification can be an abandonment of the latter unless inadvertence, reissue, etc. (cases cited: Swift v. Jenks, Miller v. Brass Co., Combined Patents Can Co. v. Lloyd, Ex parte Roberts, etc.).

name: Claim must set forth a practically operative means / usable invention
description: Every Claim must set forth and claim a practically operative means. The inventor must at least describe and claim some art or instrument capable of practical use; nothing less is a patentable invention.
guidance: A Claim may be narrow if it covers an operative means. Claims for devices that under some circumstances would not operate can still be proper. (Ex parte Cornell, American Pin Co., Wheeler v. Clipper Mower & Reaper Co., Ex parte Emerson.)

name: Claim must precisely define the exact limits of the invention
description: Every Claim must precisely define the exact limits of the invention claimed, either by enumeration of essential characteristics or by such delineation of the invention as identifies it with the one described.
guidance: When the invention is a complete art or instrument, it must be claimed as such without reference to purposes; when only parts are new, the Claim must state the new parts. Elements implied by the Claim may be read in where the device is useful only as part of a whole. (Ex parte Thompson, Seymour v. Osborne, Ex parte West.)

name: Claiming one specific arrangement excludes other arrangements
description: If new devices are claimed as specifically arranged, the Claim covers them only when thus arranged; a Claim that sets forth a certain arrangement as essential will not cover other arrangements.
guidance: Elements described as specifically arranged are limited to that arrangement (Tate v. Thomas, Carlton v. Bokee). Conversely, elements indispensable to the invention are not covered unless mentioned in the Claim. (McMillin v. Rees.)

name: Avoid claiming non-essential or auxiliary elements
description: Elements not essential to the invention should not be stated in the Claim; what is described as merely auxiliary should not be claimed as essential.
guidance: A Claim including useless things is not void unless they are claimed as essential. A Claim must not include parts/features not embraced in the intended invention. (Ex parte Skinner, Ex parte Wheat, Lewis v. — cited.)

name: Treat causes as controllable and recognize countervailing influences
description: Human actions are never (except in some cases of mania) ruled by any one motive with such absolute sway, that there is no room for the influence of any other. The causes, therefore, on which action depends, are never uncontrollable; and any given effect is only necessary provided that the causes tending to produce it are not controlled.
guidance: When assessing necessity or causation in human behavior, account for multiple interacting causes and possibilities of counteraction; avoid claiming absolute determinism where causes can be influenced.

name: Enforcement and infringement (scope and targets)
description: If you did it the way it's spelled out in detail in that patent application... you'd be an infringer. Typically, you don't go after an individual.
guidance: Infringement occurs when someone practices the claimed steps or makes the claimed product as detailed in the patent. Enforcement is often aimed at companies (commercial actors) rather than private individuals cooking at home, though technically anyone doing the patented method could infringe. The exact claim language matters for determining infringement.

name: Faith as the beginning and foundation of salvation
description: “Fides est humanae salutis initium, fundamentum et radix omnis iustificationis.” (Council of Trent, Sess. VI, cap. 8).
guidance: Faith is presented as the necessary initiating principle of human salvation; the text also explains that faith is received 'ex auditu' when awakened and aided by divine grace (Sess. VI, cap. 6) which moves the will freely to God. Several patristic and scholastic citations support this claim (Heb. XI, 6; St. Augustine, etc.).

name: Portuguese translation requirements at filing
description: Be sure to submit Portuguese translations of the claims and abstract at filing, and the full translation within 60 days.
guidance: Claims and abstract must be translated immediately at filing; complete specification translation must follow within 60 days to comply with INPI requirements.

name: Patent claims give notice of scope
description: Patent claims give notice of the scope of patent protection, giving notice both to the examiner at the Patent and Trademark Office (PTO) during prosecution, and to the public at large, including potential competitors, after the patent has issued.
guidance: Claims perform a notice function to PTO examiners and the public; this underpins many limitations on post-issuance expansion of scope (citations: Aro Mfg., Continental Paper Bag Co., Mahn).

name: Claims, not specification, measure patentee's right
description: The patent claims, not the specification, provide the measure of the patentee’s right to exclude.
guidance: While the specification teaches and may limit claim interpretation, it cannot be used to expand the scope of the claims; 'Specifications teach. Claims claim.' (citations and historical authorities included).

name: Compare accused product to claims as construed (not to preferred embodiments)
description: The law of patent infringement compares the accused product with the claims as construed by the court; infringement, either literally or under the doctrine of equivalents, does not arise by comparing the accused product with a preferred embodiment described in the specification, or with a commercialized embodiment of the patentee.
guidance: Do not base infringement findings on similarities to embodiments in the specification; focus on claim construction and element-by-element comparison (SRI Int’l cited).

name: Patentee's subjective intent irrelevant to dedication
description: The patentee’s subjective intent is irrelevant to determining whether unclaimed subject matter has been disclosed and therefore dedicated to the public.
guidance: Dedication is an objective legal determination based on the disclosure and claims, not on what the patentee intended or thought.

name: Disclosure without claiming dedicates subject matter to the public (Maxwell rule)
description: When a patent drafter discloses but declines to claim subject matter, this action dedicates that unclaimed subject matter to the public, and application of the doctrine of equivalents to recapture subject matter deliberately left unclaimed would conflict with the primacy of the claims in defining the scope of the patentee’s exclusive right.
guidance: If the specification describes an alternative and the patentee elects not to claim it, courts will treat that unclaimed alternative as dedicated to the public and unavailable to be recovered via the doctrine of equivalents; this avoids encouraging applicants to disclose broadly but file narrow claims to evade examination.

name: Patentee may not narrow claims to avoid PTO scrutiny then recapture via DOE
description: A patentee cannot narrowly claim an invention to avoid prosecution scrutiny by the Patent and Trademark Office (PTO), and then, after patent issuance, use the doctrine of equivalents to establish infringement because the specification discloses equivalents; such a result would encourage presenting a broad disclosure and filing narrow claims to avoid examination of broader claims.
guidance: Courts enforce Maxwell-type rules to prevent strategic narrowing during prosecution followed by post-issuance broadening through equivalents; prosecution history and disclosure are relevant to this determination.

name: Per se bar for disclosed-but-unclaimed subject matter (holding applied to facts)
description: A patent that specifically limits claims to 'a sheet of aluminum' but whose specification discloses that 'other metals, such as stainless steel ... may be used' cannot invoke the doctrine of equivalents to extend its aluminum limitation to encompass steel; disclosed-but-unclaimed subject matter is dedicated to the public (this decision overrules YBM Magnex to that extent).
guidance: On these facts the court held as a matter of law that equivalency was unavailable where the specification disclosed the unclaimed substitute; practitioners should not expect DOE to reach combinations explicitly disclosed but omitted from the claims.

name: Remedies for inadvertently unclaimed disclosed subject matter
description: A patentee who inadvertently fails to claim disclosed subject matter may, within two years from the grant of the original patent, file a reissue application and attempt to enlarge the scope of the original claims (35 U.S.C. § 251), or file a separate (continuation) application claiming the disclosed subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 120 if filed before all applications in the chain issue.
guidance: These statutory avenues (reissue and continuation/priority remedies) are the proper means to obtain coverage for disclosed-but-unclaimed subject matter rather than relying on the doctrine of equivalents.

name: Doctrine of equivalents: context-sensitive limitation (Graver Tank/Warner–Jenkinson)
description: The doctrine of equivalents extends the right to exclude beyond the literal scope of the claims, but 'equivalency must be determined against the context of the patent, the prior art, and the particular circumstances of the case.'
guidance: DOE remains available in appropriate cases, but its application must avoid significant conflict with the fundamental principle that claims define patent limits; consider prior art, degree of invention, and case-specific facts when applying DOE.

name: Prosecution history estoppel and amendments (Warner–Jenkinson guidance)
description: An amendment during prosecution (e.g., adding a lower limit) may make an element material to the claim, but that fact alone does not necessarily preclude the application of the doctrine of equivalents to that element; courts must inquire into the patentee’s reason for the amendment.
guidance: When claim language was narrowed during prosecution, evaluate why the amendment was made (e.g., to avoid prior art or for other reasons) before concluding that estoppel bars equivalents for that element.

name: Element-by-element requirement for DOE (Pennwalt principle)
description: To protect the notice function of claims, courts require an equivalent for each and every element of a claim rather than applying the doctrine of equivalents to the claim as a whole.
guidance: Apply DOE on a limitation-by-limitation basis; the absence of an equivalent for any required element weighs against a finding of non-literal infringement.

name: Festo / surrender during prosecution bars expansion for surrendered subject matter
description: To enhance notice, courts propose to bar patentees from expanding their claim to embrace subject matter surrendered during the patent acquisition process (prosecution history estoppel/surrender).
guidance: Consider whether claim amendments or arguments during prosecution amounted to surrender of claim scope; surrendered matter cannot later be reclaimed under DOE.

name: Device incapable of performing claimed functions cannot infringe
description: That an article incapable of performing the functions of a patented device cannot be an infringement.
guidance: If the accused article cannot perform the claimed functions, there is no infringement (Railway Register Mfg. Co. v. Broadway & Seventh Ave. R.R. Co. (1887)).

name: Use of an equivalent is not infringement when specification excludes it
description: That the use of an equivalent is not an infringement when the specification says it is not within the patent.
guidance: If the patent specification expressly disclaims equivalents or states certain equivalents are outside the claim scope, their use may not infringe (Curtia, 260 example).

name: Substitution of known device for another (even complex) can be infringement
description: That the substitution of one known device for another, though complex, is infringement.
guidance: Replacing claimed elements with known equivalents in order to practice the invention can infringe (Foster v. Moore (1852)).

name: Use/sale/manufacture must relate to the precise invention claimed
description: The acts of manufacture, use, and sale must relate to the precise invention claimed in the patent; using part of the patented invention is not an infringement of a patent covering the whole unless the act appropriates the complete expression of the invention (machine-patent exception).
guidance: Using only a portion of a claimed invention (especially when that part is covered by a different patent or disclaimed) is not infringement of the other patent; but machine patents may be infringed where the accused act appropriates the structural law or complete idea of the machine (discussion in § 900 and related notes).

name: Factual nature of conventionality determination (Berkheimer)
description: "Whether something is well-understood, routine, and conventional to a skilled artisan at the time of the patent is a factual determination." (Berkheimer v. HP Inc., 881 F.3d 1360 (Fed. Cir. 2018))
guidance: The Berkheimer decision makes clear that the question of whether claim limitations represent well-understood, routine, conventional activity raises disputed factual issues and cannot be resolved without appropriate factual support. Examiners must base such conclusions on factual findings supported as discussed in the Berkheimer memorandum and MPEP updates.

name: Prior-filed application claiming domestic priority (disqualification rule)
description: Where an application requested for expedited examination is a prior-filed application of an application claiming domestic priority, the application is not eligible for expedited examination because the ground for urgent processing under Article 61(2) is not recognized.
guidance: If confirmed before determination, examiner must order correction (complement the request) within designated period and then dismiss the request after that period. If the priority claim is withdrawn before dismissal, treat the request as valid and conduct expedited examination. If an application becomes a prior-filed application after determination, withhold examination until it is deemed withdrawn.

name: Definition of practicing (acts and territoriality)
description: “Practicing” refers to acts listed under Article 2(3) of the Patent Act / Utility Model Act: (a) product inventions — manufacturing, using, assigning, leasing, importing, offering for assignment/lease (including display for that purpose); (b) method inventions — using the method; (c) method-for-manufacturing inventions — manufacturing/using/assigning/leasing/importing/offering for the product manufactured by the method in addition to method use; (d) utility-model-related product acts.
guidance: ‘Practicing’ must occur in the Republic of Korea: practice only in a foreign country does not constitute practicing, but importing a claimed invention produced abroad into Korea does.

name: Determination of identicalness between practiced invention and claimed invention
description: A requester must clarify that the invention practiced by the third party is identical with the claimed invention and must prove the ground for identicalness of the two inventions.
guidance: Acceptable proof includes detailed descriptions of time/place/product name/sales numbers, photographs of the product with explanatory description (time/date of purchase, correlation to claimed invention), content-certified mail, other evidential documents or the product itself. Examiner compares submitted materials (products/pictures) to the claimed invention; if identicalness cannot be determined from submitted materials, examiner may order supplementation. If high possibility exists and requester cannot obtain cooperation from the practicing person, examiner may recognize the request without additional materials unless it is obvious the two are substantially not the same; if different, dismiss the request.

name: Handling requests in presence of warning from applicant
description: A person who received a warning letter about practicing the published invention without permission may request expedited examination by submitting the written warning or copy plus a detailed explanation (date, means, contents, relation to claimed invention).
guidance: Examiner shall recognize the request provided there is no special ground for the applicant’s rejection of the fact that a warning was delivered and the practiced invention is not clearly different from the claimed invention.

name: Examination guidelines for defense industry applications
description: A request for expedited examination on an application related to the defense industry does not require submission of additional evidential documents.
guidance: A requester may indicate the name of at least one of the items listed under the Directive (example given) in a written explanation and explain that the claimed invention constitutes the concerned item. If the examiner can determine the subject matter falls under the defense materials definitions even if the requester did not specify exactly, the examiner may recognize the request without making a correction order.

name: Eligibility: patent applications directly related to green technology / pollution prevention
description: To be eligible for expedited examination a claimed invention shall constitute green technology (including pollution prevention technologies); green technology broadly refers to technologies that minimize greenhouse gases and pollutants by saving/efficiently using energy across socioeconomic activities (examples listed).
guidance: When requesting expedited examination on green technology, requester must explain on what ground the claimed invention constitutes green technology in the written explanation. Determination is made based on the applicant’s argument. A long list of example initiatives and technologies (27 major initiatives and items from 17 new growth engines) are explicitly considered green technology. If no explanation is given or invention deemed irrelevant, examiner shall order correction of the request.

name: Green technology financed or certified by the State (eligible grounds)
description: Patent applications directly related to green technology financed or certified by the State (per Article 4(2)(b)) are eligible for expedited examination if they meet one of enumerated grounds (certified as green technology; filed by certified green business; subsidized by State/local governments; received investment from Green Technology Investment Co.; applicant stationed in Green Technology Industrial Cluster; financed/certified based on other national policies).
guidance: Examiner decides based on the requester’s explanation that the claimed invention constitutes green technology and is financed/certified by the State etc. Examiner must check submitted evidential documents by each ground and verify that the applicant and claimed invention correspond to the person/technology that got the support/certification. Refer to the Green Technology-related Evidential Documents table for required items.

name: Required evidential documents for green technology financing/certification
description: Specific evidential documents are required depending on the ground for request: green technology certification, green business, subsidization, investment from Green Technology Industry Co., being stationed in a Green Technology Industrial Cluster, or other financial support/certification.
guidance: Examples: certification of green technology under Article 32; explanation verifying claimed invention and business belong to same industry; evidential document of subsidization from State/local governments; evidential document of receiving investments (loan statement); evidence of being stationed in industrial cluster; documents such as R&D financing announcements, loan statements, environmental mark/carbon footprint/new technology certifications, GR certification, or other financial support/certification.

name: Non-eligibility example for pollution prevention (scope nuance)
description: Even if a claimed invention directly reduces emissions, it is not eligible if the facility is not one of the pollution prevention facilities designated under the environment-related acts.
guidance: Example: a car is not a designated air pollutant emitter under the Clean Air Conservation Act Annex; an exhaust gas converter installed within a car is therefore not eligible for expedited examination because it does not correspond to the designated air pollution prevention facilities.

name: Applications directly related to promotion of export (evidence and identicalness)
description: Applications directly related to promotion of export may be eligible; determination requires review of evidential documents such as statement of export result, arrival of letter of credit (L/C), purchaser's necessity documents, export contract, documents showing adoption to international standards, or other evidence that invention is directly related to trade promotion.
guidance: The invention to be exported and the claimed invention must be identical. The requester must prove identicalness; where identicalness normally cannot be determined solely from request documents, the examiner may recognize the request without requiring additional evidence if there is a high possibility they are the same and no grounds to doubt it.

name: 35 U.S.C. § 101 patent-eligibility framework (Alice/Mayo)
description: Patentable subject matter includes processes, machines, manufactures, and compositions of matter; judicial exceptions include laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas. The Alice two-step test applies: (1) determine whether the claims are directed to a patent-ineligible concept; (2) if so, consider the claim elements individually and as an ordered combination to determine whether additional elements transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application (an 'inventive concept').
guidance: Cites Mayo and Alice. Courts must identify whether claimed subject matter is an abstract idea (Alice step one) and whether the additional claim elements add something significantly more (Alice step two). The opinions emphasize the need to examine the claims, specification, and relevant factual context when applying the two-step test.

name: Alice step one may involve factual considerations (secondary evidence)
description: Under Alice step one, factual evidence such as commercial success and industry praise can be relevant to whether the claims are 'directed to' an abstract idea.
guidance: Cites Data Engine Techs. (considering contemporaneous articles and industry acclaim to find claims not directed to an abstract idea). The guidance is that objective evidence showing the invention improved computer functionality or was praised by industry can weigh against a finding that the claims are abstract at step one.

name: Alice step two factual inquiry (well-understood, routine, conventional)
description: Alice step two requires consideration of whether claim elements or their combination are 'well-understood, routine, [and] conventional'—a question of fact that may preclude resolution at the pleadings or summary judgment stages.
guidance: Cites Aatrix, Berkheimer, BASCOM, and Apple. Courts should treat determinations about whether elements are conventional as factual issues requiring evidence; exemplary guidance includes considering whether prior art taught away, whether elements behaved unexpectedly, and whether the record shows innovation beyond generic computer implementation. Anti-pattern: declaring elements 'generic' solely from claim language without factual record.

name: Claim construction / subsidiary factual findings (Teva)
description: Proper § 101 analysis often requires claim construction, and claim construction involves subsidiary factfinding; understanding claim scope requires consideration of relevant evidence, including the knowledge of a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of invention.
guidance: Cites Teva Pharm. USA v. Sandoz: ultimate claim construction is a question of law but may require subsidiary factual findings. Guidance: courts should not substitute their own unsourced factual beliefs about what a person of ordinary skill in the art would have known or considered routine when construing claims.

name: Step 2A: Is the claim directed to a judicial exception?
description: Analyze whether the claim is 'directed to' a judicial exception such as an abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon, or product of nature.
guidance: Look for recitations of mathematical operations, mental processes, organizing human activity, or nature-based subject matter. Examples cited: mathematical operations like calculating pseudo-ranges/absolute time (treated as abstract ideas); managing a Bingo game or creating contractual relationships (organizing human activity / fundamental economic practices). Note the example language: 'The claim recites mathematical operations ... which the courts have considered to fall within the judicial exceptions ... directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: YES).' Also: 'This describes the creation of a contractual relationship ... which is a commercial arrangement ... abstract idea (Step 2A: YES).'

name: Step 2B: Additional-elements / inventive-concept inquiry (significantly more)
description: Determine whether the claim's additional elements, individually or in combination, amount to significantly more than the judicial exception itself (i.e., supply an inventive concept).
guidance: Evaluate whether claimed extra features impose meaningful limitations on the exception or merely recite conventional/ generic implementation. Consider the claim elements both individually and in combination. Examples: reciting a general-purpose CPU, memory, display, or network at a high level does not transform an abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter; by contrast, meaningful limitations that apply the mathematical operations to improve existing technology may provide 'significantly more.' The guidance uses explicit Step 2B yes/no determinations in each example.

name: Generic computer/implementation recitations are insufficient
description: Reciting conventional computer components (CPU, memory, network, printer, input/output terminal, program) at a high level does not add significantly more to an abstract idea.
guidance: Multiple examples show that simply adding 'a computer with a CPU and memory' or 'a computer network' and asserting they perform basic functions is 'mere instructions to implement the abstract idea on a computer' and fails Step 2B. (Examples: Bingo, buySAFE, Ultramercial, Digitech explanations — 'these generic computer components are claimed to perform their basic functions ... do not amount to significantly more').

name: Mathematical operations / data manipulation as abstract ideas
description: Mathematical techniques, processing, and manipulation of data (e.g., generating data using Fourier analysis, computing pseudo-ranges, combining data into a profile) are treated as abstract ideas.
guidance: Claims that 'simply describe the concept of gathering and combining data by reciting steps of organizing information through mathematical relationships' are directed to abstract ideas (Digitech example; Benson analogy). Such claims require additional elements that add significantly more to be eligible.

name: Organizing human activity and fundamental economic practices as abstract ideas
description: Claims that recite schemes for organizing human activity (e.g., managing a game, underwriting/guaranteeing transactions, exchanging advertising for content) are likely abstract ideas.
guidance: The guidance equates concepts like managing Bingo, creating contractual relationships (underwriting/guaranty), and using advertising as currency with other abstract ideas (Bilski/Alice). Narrowing to particular types or parts of the transaction does not remove abstractness. (See Planet Bingo, buySAFE, Ultramercial analyses.)

name: Meaningful limitations that improve technology can provide 'significantly more'
description: Limitations that meaningfully limit application of the judicial exception and apply it to improve a technological process or device can render a claim eligible.
guidance: Assess whether the combination of elements imposes meaningful limits and effects a technological improvement (example: the GPS example — the programmed CPU 'acts in concert' with specific mobile-device features to improve signal-acquisition sensitivity and extend usefulness into weak-signal environments, and to provide location information for display). The guidance states that such features, especially in combination, 'amount to significantly more than the judicial exception (Step 2B: YES).' Use these factual showings when present.

name: Markedly different characteristics test for nature-based products
description: For claims to nature-based products (compositions derived from natural products or combinations of naturally occurring substances), determine whether the claimed product has 'markedly different characteristics' from any naturally occurring counterpart.
guidance: Compare the claimed product (as a whole) to naturally occurring counterpart(s). If no natural counterpart exists for the combination, compare to individual components as they occur in nature. If the claimed combination exhibits markedly different properties (e.g., explosive property of gunpowder, slowed spoilage of juice, improved bioavailability due to formulation), it is not a 'product of nature' exception and is not directed to a judicial exception (Gunpowder, Pomelo juice, Amazonic acid examples).

name: Claims are analyzed under their broadest reasonable interpretation
description: Eligibility analyses are performed according to the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim language.
guidance: The guidance repeatedly states that claims are analyzed for eligibility 'in accordance with their broadest reasonable interpretation,' and examples apply that interpretive standard when comparing claims to natural counterparts or determining whether a process claim is effectively a product claim.

name: Presence of at least one corresponding OEE application with patentable/allowable claim(s)
description: At least one corresponding application must exist in the OEE and have one or more claims that are determined to be patentable/allowable by the OEE.
guidance: Claims clearly identified to be patentable in the latest office action at examination stage can form the basis for a PPH request even if the OEE application has not yet been granted. Provide copies of the relevant office actions (see required documents).

name: All PRH claims must sufficiently correspond to OEE allowable claims
description: All claims in the PRH application (for which accelerated examination is requested) must sufficiently correspond to one or more of those claims determined to be patentable/allowable in the OEE application.
guidance: ‘Sufficiently correspond’ means, accounting for differences due to translations and claim format, the PRH claims are of the same or similar scope as the OEE claims, or are narrower in scope. A claim is narrower if an OEE claim is amended to be further limited by an additional feature supported in the specification. Introducing a new/different category of claim (e.g., adding product claims where the OEE only had process claims) is not sufficient correspondence. Claims amended or added after grant of the PPH request need not correspond.

name: PCT-PPH: PRH claims must sufficiently correspond to claims indicated patentable/allowable in international work product
description: All claims, as originally filed or amended, for examination under PCT-PPH must sufficiently correspond to one or more of those claims indicated to be patentable/allowable in the latest international work product of the corresponding international application.
guidance: Same 'sufficiently correspond' definition as national PPH: same/similar scope or narrower (narrower means further limited by an additional feature supported in the specification). Introducing a new/different category of claims is not sufficient. Claims amended or added after grant of the PCT-PPH request need not correspond.

name: PCT-PPH: copy of latest international work product and translations
description: Provide a copy of the latest international work product (WO/ISA, WO/IPEA or IPER) that indicated the claims to be patentable/allowable, with Finnish or English translations if not in English.
guidance: If the application is a national phase application satisfying certain relationships, the IPRP may already be in the file-wrapper and need not be submitted. If the documents are available via PATENTSCOPE, submission is not required unless PRH requests them. WO/ISA/W O/IPEA/IPER availability timing is noted (e.g., IPRP chapters usually available ~30 months after priority). Machine translations into Finnish or English are admissible but examiner can request resubmission if incomprehensible.

name: PCT-PPH: copy of set of claims indicated patentable/allowable and translations
