description: Provide a copy of the set of claims which the latest international work product indicated to be patentable/allowable, with Finnish or English translations if not in English.
guidance: If the claims are available via PATENTSCOPE or in the published international Patent Gazette, submission is not required unless requested by PRH. Machine translation guidance applies.

name: Statement under Article 19(1) — form and content limits
description: The statement referred to in Article 19(1) must be in the language of publication and shall not exceed 500 words if in English or translated into English; it shall be identified by a heading (e.g., “Statement under Article 19(1)”).
guidance: The statement shall contain no disparaging comments on the international search report or the relevance of citations in that report. Reference to citations in the ISR may be made only in connection with an amendment to the relevant claim.

name: Contents of the international publication
description: The publication shall contain a standardized front page, the description, the claims, the drawings (if any), subject to paragraph (g) the international search report or the declaration under Article 17(2)(a), any statement filed under Article 19(1) (unless non-compliant), and various additional items such as indications relating to deposited biological material, priority claim information, certain declarations and corrections, and information concerning restoration of priority requests.
guidance: Specific subitems listed include: standardized front page; description; claims; drawings; ISR or Article17 declaration; Article19(1) statement (unless not compliant); requests/rectifications received before technical preparations; indications on deposited biological material and date received; information concerning priority claims and certain declarations/corrections received before prescribed time limits; and info on requests under Rule 26 bis.3 for restoration of priority and receiving Office decisions.

name: Contents and physical requirements for translations under Article 22
description: The translation must contain the description (subject to certain exceptions), the claims, any text matter of the drawings and the abstract. If required by the designated Office, the translation shall also contain the request, both claims as filed and as amended (if Article19 amendments exist), and be accompanied by a copy of the drawings.
guidance: Exceptions: designated Offices may accept sequence-listing parts under Rule12.1(d) without translation of language-dependent free text; drawing text translations may be provided by pasting translations onto copies or by new drawings; the expression "Fig." need not be translated; where copies/drawings do not comply with physical requirements, DO may invite correction within a reasonable time; if translation of an Article19 statement or abstract not furnished, DO may disregard or invite translation within reasonable time. DOs cannot require translation to comply with physical requirements beyond those for the international application as filed. If ISA established a title under Rule37.2, the translation shall contain that title.

name: Obviousness – general (design patent §103 analysis)
description: A claimed design is invalid as 'obvious' if it would have been obvious to a designer of ordinary skill who designs articles of the type involved; determine if combining a primary and a closely related secondary reference would suggest the claimed design to such a designer.
guidance: Evaluate whether a designer of ordinary skill would have combined the references to create the same overall visual appearance. Primary references must teach a specific design (not a design concept) and look basically the same as the claimed design. Obviousness may be shown by more than one item of prior art, but references must be so related that ornamental features in one would suggest application to the other. The defendant must prove obviousness by clear and convincing evidence. (Factors enumerated below should be evaluated.) (Cited: 35 U.S.C. §103; In re Rosen; Durling; In re Cho; KSR.)

name: Obviousness – required factors
description: Five factors that must be evaluated to determine obviousness of a design.
guidance: 1) The scope and content of the prior art relied upon; 2) The differences, if any, between the claimed design and the prior art; 3) The level of ordinary skill in the art at the time the design was made; 4) Whether the ordinary observer would find the two designs substantially the same; 5) Additional considerations indicating obviousness or not. Each factor must be evaluated (in any order).

name: Obviousness – differences with the prior art (analysis of differences and analogous art)
description: Analyze relevant differences between the prior art and the claimed design from the view of a designer of ordinary skill, determining the impact of such differences on obviousness of the design as a whole.
guidance: Scope of relevant prior art extends to all 'analogous arts' (surface-appearance designs consider any prior art with similar surface appearance; form designs limit analogous art to similar types of articles). Do not require precise appearance in prior art; consider inferences and creative steps a designer would have employed. Combining known elements in a known fashion is generally not patentable; however, a new material element can create a new integral design. Showing each element was independently known is insufficient—consider whether a reason/motivation existed at the time to combine elements (prior art, background knowledge, problem to solve, market demand, common sense). Prior art that 'teaches away' may support non-obviousness.

name: Invalidity – lack of ornamentality (functionality doctrine)
description: Design patents protect ornamental appearance; if the overall appearance is dictated solely by how it works, the patent is invalid because the design is not 'ornamental.'
guidance: It is normal that designs perform some function; the question is whether the general functional characteristics can only be embodied by the claimed design or whether alternate designs perform substantially the same function. Existence of alternate designs may be strong evidence that the design was not dictated solely by function. A design need not be aesthetically pleasing; lack of artistic merit does not disqualify patentability. (Cited: 35 U.S.C. §171; Best Lock; Seiko Epson; Hupp.)

name: Invalidity – written description requirement for design patents
description: A design patent must contain a written description and drawing of the design claimed; insufficient description/drawings render the patent invalid if they fail to enable understanding of what the claimed design looks like.
guidance: Defendant must prove by clear and convincing evidence that errors, variations, or inconsistencies between drawings or written description are consequential. Design patent written description is evaluated with regard to whether a designer of ordinary skill can understand the claimed design from the specification/drawings. (Cited: 35 U.S.C. §112; related cases.)

name: Invalidity – indefiniteness
description: The design patent claim (drawings and written description) must be sufficiently clear that a designer of ordinary skill can determine what the design looks like; otherwise the claim is indefinite and invalid.
guidance: Amount of detail required depends on particular design, prior art, and the description. Drawings read with the description must reasonably inform a designer of ordinary skill. Lack of absolute precision is not automatically indefinite; there is a presumption of validity and deference to the examiner who issued the patent. (Cited: 35 U.S.C. §112 ¶2; In re Zahn; DCNL v. Almar Sales.)

name: Invalidity – improper inventorship
description: Patent invalidity can be asserted for improper inventorship if the patent does not name all actual inventors and only the actual inventors.
guidance: To be an inventor, one must make a significant contribution to the claimed design, measured against the scope of the claimed design. Persons may be joint inventors even if they did not physically work together, but must have some open line of communication during or near the time of their inventive effort. Explaining known concepts, suggesting ideas or design concepts, or merely carrying out another's instructions (helping with experimentation) does not make someone an inventor. (Cited: 35 U.S.C. §§116, 256; Eli Lilly; Slip Track; others.)

name: Invalidity – double patenting (design vs utility two-way test)
description: A design patent may be invalid for double patenting over a utility patent or application where the features producing the novel aesthetic effect of the design are the same as those recited in the claims of a utility patent as producing a novel structure.
guidance: Use a two-way test: (a) whether the subject matter of the design-claim would have been obvious from the subject matter of the utility claim(s); and (b) whether the subject matter of the utility claim(s) would have been obvious from the design claim. If the two-way test is satisfied, the design patent is invalid as obvious over the utility patent or application. (Cited: In re Dembiczak; Shelcore; Carman; In re Thorington.)

name: Balance strictness vs research quality
description: Overly strict IP rules can stifle interaction and sharing, diminishing research quality and ultimately harming licensing revenue.
guidance: Policies should avoid unnecessarily broad claims that deter collaboration; seek a balance that promotes both quality research and appropriate IP protection.

name: Taught courses versus research activity distinction
description: Determine whether student activity is educational/teaching-based (course content, assignments) or research-based (embedded programs producing novel data/IP).
guidance: Teaching resources generally transfer to the public domain once presented; research resources are more likely to trigger institutional claims. Decision should be fact-based, considering the type of resources accessed and the embeddedness of the activity.

name: Include all claim categories in the search
description: When the application contains claims of different categories, all these must be included in the search.
guidance: Exception: if a product claim clearly seems to be both new and non-obvious, the examiner need not specially search claims for a process which inevitably results in manufacture of that product or for use of the product. When the application contains only claims of one category, it may be desirable to include other categories in the search. Example (chemical process): starting products may be assumed part of the state of the art and need not be searched; intermediate products are searched only when claimed; final products will always be searched except when evidently known.

name: Restriction of search due to lack of unity
description: If claims do not relate to one invention or a group linked to form a single general inventive concept, the search will normally be restricted to the invention or linked group first mentioned in the claims.
guidance: Restriction is notified to applicant in communication accompanying the partial search report; the partial search report must be supplemented with specification of the separate inventions.

name: Include technological background when desirable
description: In certain circumstances extend search to include the 'technological background' of the invention.
guidance: Technological background includes: the preamble to the first claim (part preceding 'characterized by' / 'characterized in that'), the state of the art noted in the description introduction but not specifically cited, and the general technological background ('general state of the art').

name: Analysis of the application prior to searching
description: Before searching, the examiner should consider the application to determine the subject of the claimed invention.
guidance: Make a critical analysis of claims in light of description and drawings: identify the underlying problem, inventive concept, features essential to the solution, and results/effects. Include in the search technical features indicated in the description as essential even if not present in the claims.

name: Prepare a precise search statement and note necessary restrictions
description: Prepare a search statement defining the subject of the search as precisely as possible (claims may need generalization to cover all aspects/embodiments).
guidance: Bear in mind subjects excluded from patentability and lack of unity. If restrictions are necessary because meaningful search is impossible, indicate them in the search report or declaration with reasons; such declaration or incomplete report is considered the search report for subsequent proceedings.

name: Pre-classification (routing) based on independent claims
description: Make pre-classification to allot the application to a competent examiner; level should be as general as practicable but specific enough (usually sub-class) to avoid intermediate routing steps.
guidance: Pre-classification should be made on the basis of independent claims. If resulting in more than one sub-class, select whichever seems most relevant to the claimed invention (or the invention first claimed if lack of unity).

name: Partial ARIPO search report when lack of unity (first-mentioned invention)
description: If the application does not comply with unity requirement, search and draw up a partial ARIPO search report for the invention (or linked group) first mentioned in the claims.
guidance: Supplement the partial search report with a specification of the separate inventions. When determining which invention is first mentioned, take account of dependent claims but disregard trivial claims.

name: Exclusion of methods for treatment and diagnostic methods (subject-matter excluded from patentability)
description: Methods for treatment of the human or animal body by surgery or therapy, and diagnostic methods practiced on the human or animal body, are excluded from patentability (subject-matter to be excluded from the search).
guidance: Products (substances/compositions) for use in such methods are not excluded provided the use is not comprised in the state of the art; 'Swiss-type' claims may be allowable for first or subsequent applications. Even if method claims are non-patentable, a meaningful search may be possible if the determining technical feature is the effect of the substance. If specific method features are present (dosing, combination with physical treatment) a meaningful search may not be possible. Regardless of whether such claims are searched, inform the applicant in the search opinion that such subject-matter is excluded from patentability.

name: Meaning of 'meaningful' search and examples when no meaningful search possible
description: Whether a search is 'meaningful' is a question of fact for the Search and Examination Section; 'meaningful' should be construed reasonably (not merely because search is difficult).
guidance: Examples where no meaningful search may be possible: (i) claims lacking support/insufficient disclosure (broad/speculative claim supported by limited disclosure, making full search impossible or pointless); (ii) claims lacking conciseness (too many claims or possibilities making determination of protection unduly burdensome); (iii) claims lacking clarity (parameters chosen render comparison with prior art impossible). These examples are not exhaustive; basic principle is clarity and openness for applicant and third parties as to what has and has not been searched.

name: Obviousness standard for design patents (Graham factors)
description: Obviousness in design patent cases is assessed using the standard four-part framework: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) level of ordinary skill in the art; (3) differences between the prior art and the claimed design; and (4) objective indicia of non-obviousness.
guidance: In Crocs v. ITC, the Federal Circuit applied these factors and reversed a finding of obviousness where (a) claimed features were missing from the cited prior art, (b) an ordinary artisan would not have been motivated to add the missing elements, and (c) the accused product had significant commercial success—illustrating the types of evidence that can rebut obviousness.

name: Evidentiary considerations to defeat an obviousness finding
description: Evidence that can defeat an obviousness finding includes demonstrable absence of claimed features in the prior art, lack of a motivation to combine or modify prior art to reach the claimed design, and strong objective indicia such as commercial success.
guidance: Crocs v. ITC exemplifies relying on (a) showing one or more claimed features are missing from cited prior art, (b) arguing an ordinary artisan would not be motivated to add missing elements, and (c) presenting substantial commercial success as objective indicia of non-obviousness.

name: Treatment of functional elements in design patent analysis
description: Functional elements of a design should be ignored when undertaking the infringement/validity analysis; the deception must arise from the overall design, not from similarities in ornamental features in isolation.
guidance: Richardson v. Stanley Works instructs that the deception leading to infringement must result from the overall design. When comparing designs, discount functional aspects and focus on ornamental/visual aspects. It remains an open question whether this analysis is a matter for a Markman claim-construction hearing or for the jury.

name: Role of claim construction (Markman) vs. jury in design comparison
description: Unclear whether analysis of which elements to ignore (e.g., functional elements) and related interpretive matters belong to a Markman claim-construction hearing or should be left to the jury.
guidance: Practitioners should be mindful of this unresolved procedural question when planning litigation strategy—be prepared to address both claim-construction arguments and jury-focused presentation of overall-appearance comparisons.

name: Final Notice of Grounds for Rejection
description: A final notice of grounds for rejection is issued when a ground for rejection arises from amendments corresponding to a previously issued notice of grounds for rejection — i.e., amendments submitted after notice create a new ground that requires examination.
guidance: Prerequisite: written amendment submitted in response to previous notice and the new rejection ground is found during amendment confirmation. Specific examples: (1) amendments to description/drawings add new matter or exceed permitted scope of divisional/conversion; (2) amendment of a claim previously examined results in lack of novelty or inventive step (unless that amended invention appears in another claim not previously notified — then non-final); (3) a newly generated or substantially changed claim equivalent to a newly-established claim contains novelty/inventive-step grounds; (4) after amendment an examiner discovers novelty/inventive-step grounds that were previously uneminable due to lack of clarity or added new matter.

name: Examination on a Claim-by-claim Basis — Purpose
description: An examiner examines patentability requirements on a per-claim basis so that applicants can identify which claims are remediable and respond effectively; a single ground of rejection can block grant even if other claims are patentable.
guidance: When notifying grounds for rejection in multi-claim applications, the examiner must specify the claim(s) containing grounds and provide specific explanations so applicants can determine which claims to amend or delete.

name: Written Notice of Grounds for Rejection — Examination Outcomes (components)
description: A written notice of grounds for rejection shall include [Examination Outcomes], comprised of: 'Claims to be Examined', 'Relevant Provision regarding Grounds for Rejection', 'Patentable Claims', and [Specific Grounds for Rejection]. Matters not being grounds but useful for response may be included in 'Considerations in Amendment'.
guidance: Each component is described further below; include clear labelling and sufficient detail to allow applicant to respond.

name: Claims to be Examined (in Notice)
description: The notice shall state the number of claims to be examined as of the date the written notice is prepared.
guidance: Use the claim numbering current at preparation time; identify which claims are within the scope of the present examination.

name: Relevant Provisions Regarding Grounds for Rejection (in Notice)
description: Specify which claims contain grounds for rejection and cite the relevant provisions of the Patent Act. If the ground is not directly related to claims, state the matter containing the ground. If amendment adds new matters or exceeds scope in divisional/converted applications, state those newly added or out-of-scope matters as grounds for rejection.
guidance: Provide a mapping (e.g., table) between notified matters and the corresponding Articles (examples given mapping description/claims to Articles 42(3), 42(8), 45, 29(2), 52(1)).

name: Specific Grounds for Rejection — Content and Level of Specificity
description: Set out specific reasons for each notified ground of rejection so the applicant can understand and respond; indicate claims involved and the specific ground for each claim.
guidance: Rules: (i) Specifically state grounds for each claim; may summarize for claims with practically the same ground. (ii) When comparing cited inventions to claimed invention, indicate which parts of the cited invention correspond to which claimed features; select the closest cited invention and describe its technical features, point out differences, and state technical features of other cited inventions that supplement differences, with assessment considering common general knowledge. (iii) Examiner may specify the cited invention and describe differences and inventive-step assessment in an applicant-understandable manner. (iv) State novelty/inventive-step grounds for independent and dependent claims separately; for dependent claims, indicate corresponding matters of cited invention or assess differences based on common general knowledge. (v) Generally, dependent-claim grounds are deemed to include grounds identified in claims cited by dependent claims.

name: Preparation of Written Decision of Rejection (format)
description: A written decision of rejection is prepared with the same method as a written notice of grounds for rejection, except [Examination Outcomes] replaces 'matters notified for the ground for rejection' with 'matters where the ground for rejection is not overcome'.
guidance: If no written argument or amendment was submitted in response to a notice, examiner may omit separate [Examination Results] and [Rationale for Decision to Reject]. Include: 'Claims to be Examined', 'Relevant Provisions for Matters Where Grounds Not Overcome', 'Patentable Claims' (claims not notified and those where notified grounds have been overcome). Explain reasons when not listing patentable claims, and include 'Grounds for Decision to Reject' with specific rationale.

name: Grounds for Decision to Reject — required reasoning
description: When rendering a decision to reject, write more specific rationale regarding grounds not overcome so applicant can understand the basis; for claim-related grounds, state reasons by category of each claim.
guidance: If the same reasons were already notified in the prior written ground, the examiner may cite the source to avoid redundancy. When both written argument and amendment are submitted, explain why amendment/argument do not overcome the ground; for claims without practical amendments or dependent claims without direct amendments, a statement that 'the ground notified is not overcome' may suffice. When only a written argument without amendment is submitted, explain why applicant's argument is denied and state unresolved grounds.

name: Instructions for Examination on Claim-to-claim Basis — special cases
description: Guidance on handling claims in special circumstances on claim-by-claim examination: (1) claims related to a deficient detailed description may still be listed as patentable unless exceptions apply; (2) where a claim cites another claim that has a ground under Article 42(4), pay attention whether the citing claim still has that ground; (3) where an application has multiple groups of inventions, examiner considers patentability for at least one group and handles unity-of-invention rejections by indicating claims in other groups.
guidance: If a claim is related to a notified detailed-description ground that cannot be remedied by amendment, explain in 'Considerations in Amendment Submission' why it is not listed as patentable. For citing claims, if the cited claim violates only manner of describing scope (Article 42(8) and Enforcement Order Article 5), state that only the cited claim has that ground. For multi-group inventions, include claims without grounds under 'Patentable Claims' for groups evaluated; if novelty/inventive-step grounds exist for those claims, notify both unity and patentability grounds. If lack of unity is prioritized for efficiency, state that patent requirements have not been tested for certain claims and do not include them as patentable.

name: Disclosure of Information on Prior Art Documents
description: When preparing grounds for rejection related to a claim's technical subject matter, an examiner must cite supporting documents for the rationale; disclosure methods should comply with WIPO Standard ST.14.
guidance: Cite supporting patent and non-patent documents clearly and provide sufficient detail (see following citation rubrics).

name: Instructions for Written Argument — treatment and evidentiary scope
description: When a written argument is submitted (with or without amendment), the examiner must review argument and amendment in depth to decide whether grounds for rejection are overcome. Written arguments and supporting documents (including experiment results) are not part of the specification but may be referred to in deciding patentability.
guidance: If amendment is submitted after designated period it shall be returned, but written arguments may be admitted as reference. If applicant's written argument claims amendments but fails to submit them, examiner examines based on the notification of ground for rejection; if actual amendments differ from those asserted in the argument, examination is based on actual amendments. Examiners must explain denials when only argument is submitted without amendment.

name: Treatment of Amendments — method to confirm final specification
description: The final specification to be examined is determined automatically through the internal Patent Net after reflecting amendments to the detailed description, claims, and drawings. An amendment to the full text of the specification replaces the final specification to be examined.
guidance: Example process illustrated for multiple written amendments: the final specification reflects the most recent amendments for each part (detailed description, individual claims, drawings) as combined by the system; examiners should follow the system output to identify the text to be examined.

name: Articulation of factual findings and rationale
description: An obviousness rejection must include factual findings about the state of the art and the teachings of the references, and a reasoned explanation supporting why the claimed invention would have been obvious.
guidance: Rejections cannot be mere conclusory statements; must articulate reasoning with a rational underpinning (citing KSR and In re Kahn). 35 U.S.C. 132 requires notifying the applicant of reasons for rejection so applicant can respond. Factual findings should support the rationale relied upon. Failure to follow guidelines is not appealable, but substantive rejections are appealable.

name: Broadest reasonable interpretation of claims consistent with the specification
description: When determining the scope of claimed invention for the prior art inquiry, give claims their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.
guidance: Read the specification including the claims to understand what the applicant invented (see Phillips v. AWH and MPEP §2111). The scope of the claimed invention so determined guides what to search and what references to apply.

name: Exemplary rationales to support obviousness (list)
description: Exemplary, non-exclusive rationales that may support a conclusion of obviousness include: (A) combining prior art elements by known methods to yield predictable results; (B) simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results; (C) use of a known technique to improve similar devices; (D) applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement; (E) 'obvious to try' selecting among finite, predictable options with reasonable expectation of success; (F) known work in one field prompting predictable variations in same/different fields; (G) some teaching/suggestion/motivation in prior art to modify/combine references.
guidance: This list is illustrative, not exhaustive. MPEP §2143 and §2144 provide examples and further guidance. The key is clear articulation of why the claimed invention would have been obvious using one or more rationales.

name: Consideration of all claim limitations and whole-invention view
description: Ascertaining differences between the claimed invention and the prior art requires interpreting claim language and considering both the invention and the prior art as a whole.
guidance: Do not focus only on isolated limitations; the comparison must account for the claim as a whole. Ensure proper claim interpretation per MPEP §2111 before comparing to prior art.

name: Examples of rebuttal evidence that can show nonobviousness
description: Rebuttal evidence may demonstrate that: (A) a person of ordinary skill could not have combined the claimed elements by known methods due to technical difficulties; (B) the elements in combination do more than perform their separate functions; or (C) the results of the claimed combination were unexpected.
guidance: If such evidence is timely presented, examiners should reconsider and articulate whether initial findings remain viable. Unexpected results or technical difficulty in combining elements can overcome a prima facie case of obviousness if persuasive.

name: Defendant must have performed the precise acts covered by the license for the license fee to apply
description: The defendant's acceptance of the patentee's proposal must be proved by performance of the precise act for which the license fee was established; not every invasion subjects defendant to that fee.
guidance: If the defendant exercised a different right (e.g., selling where license covers make/use), or used only part of an invention covered by a gross fee, or used it briefly, he may not be within the scope of the license and the fee is not the proper measure. Cases: Colgate v. Western Electric Mfg. Co. (1886); Wooster v. Simonson (1884). Apportionment may be necessary when license fee covers multiple claims or inventions.

name: Grantor of an exclusive license's recoverable damages limited to loss of royalty
description: A grantor of an exclusive license at a specific royalty can sustain no damage except the loss of his royalty.
guidance: If grantor receives a specific royalty arrangement, his measure of recovery is limited to that royalty; he cannot claim broader damages beyond the contracted royalty (text cites relevant authorities).

name: Disclosure
description: General requirements for disclosure in the patent application (specification, claims, drawings, etc.).

name: Form of Claims
description: Acceptable claim formats and formal requirements for claim language.

name: Basis for Claim Terminology in Description
description: How claim terminology must be supported by the description/specification.

name: Restoration of Canceled Matter
description: Rules and procedures for restoring matter that was canceled from the specification or claims.

name: Matter Not Present in Specification, Claims, or Drawings on the Application Filing Date
description: Definition and consequences of matter that was not present on the filing date (new matter).

name: Develop tools/resources to enable examiners to find best, most relevant prior art early
description: Recommending that the USPTO: (ii) develop tools and resources that will enable examiners to find and access the best, most relevant prior art at an early stage in the examination process;
guidance: Examples & initiatives: upgraded electronic search tools, Access to Relevant Prior Art Initiative, IP5 Collaborative Search and Examination Pilot, Diagnostic Interview Pilot; objective is to reduce issuance of claims later found unpatentable by PTAB.

name: Retrospectively analyze whether examiners had the relevant prior art in-filed cases
description: The PPAC recommends that the USPTO should retrospectively analyze whether, during the examination phase, examiners found that particular prior art (later relied upon in PTAB proceedings). If the determination is that all of the relevant prior art was not found by or provided to the examiner, the USPTO should investigate why.
guidance: Guidance: use results to close gap between issued claims and PTAB outcomes; implement investigations into search processes; inform further training/tooling.

name: Diagnostic Interview Pilot (pre-search interview to focus search)
description: In the Diagnostic Interview Pilot, an examiner may request a pre-search interview with the applicant to better understand the claimed invention and scope of the claims in order to formulate a more focused search strategy.
guidance: Guidance: promotes shared responsibility between examiner and applicant for examination quality; intended to yield more focused prior art searches early in examination.

name: Rule 5(5) — indication of elements for which protection is not claimed
description: The application shall indicate whether, to the best knowledge of the applicant, the registration/act/decision granting protection in the Contracting Party of Origin specifies that protection is not granted for certain elements of the appellation or geographical indication; any such elements shall be indicated in a working language.

name: Rule 5(6) — optional contents of the application
description: The application may indicate or contain: (i) addresses of beneficiaries; (ii) a declaration that protection is renounced in one or more Contracting Parties; (iii) a copy in original language of the registration/act/decision granting protection in the Contracting Party of Origin; (iv) a statement that protection is not claimed for certain other elements.

name: Grounds for Office-initiated withdrawal after payment (37 CFR 1.313(b))
description: Once the issue fee has been paid, the Office will not withdraw the application from issue on its own initiative except for: (1) a mistake on the part of the Office; (2) a violation of § 1.56 or illegality in the application; (3) unpatentability of one or more claims; or (4) for interference.
guidance: 35 U.S.C. 151 and 37 CFR 1.313(b) limit Office authority. Examples of reasons that do NOT warrant withdrawal after payment include permitting the examiner to consider an IDS, permitting the examiner to consider whether claims are unpatentable (unless it results in a determination of unpatentability), or to permit filing of a continuing application. Any notice withdrawing after payment must specify which 1.313(b)(1)-(4) condition exists.

name: Applicant-initiated withdrawal permitted reasons after payment (37 CFR 1.313(c))
description: After payment of the issue fee, withdrawal upon applicant petition is allowed only for specified reasons in 37 CFR 1.313(c), including (A) unpatentability of one or more claims (petition accompanied by unequivocal statement and amendment(s) showing patentability), (B) consideration of a request for continued examination in compliance with § 1.114, or (C) express abandonment of the application (including in favor of a continuing application).
guidance: A petition under 1.313(c) must be clearly marked 'Petition under 37 CFR 1.313(c).' For utility or plant applications filed before June 8, 1995 and design applications, RCE practice may not apply. Filing methods: mail to Mail Stop Petitions, fax to Central Facsimile Number, or hand-carry to Office of Petitions. Hand-carrying is strongly advised to allow processing time; a grantable petition should ideally be received and granted at least three weeks prior to issue date to avoid publication/dissemination.

name: One-month window to correct defective petitions (IPR)
description: Petitioners have one month to correct defective petitions to institute an inter partes review.
guidance: The Board will review petitions for procedural compliance and notify the petitioner if incomplete (e.g., failure to state the claims being challenged). The one-month correction period is subject to statutory limitations and does not cure statutory defects that prevent consideration.

name: Board procedural review and notice of incompleteness
description: In determining whether to grant a filing date, the Board will review petitions for procedural compliance and notify petitioner of any non-compliance issues.
guidance: Examples of procedural defects include failure to state the claims being challenged; notice will identify the defects so the petitioner can correct them within allowed time.

name: Institution standard for IPR — reasonable likelihood (§42.108)
description: The Director may not authorize an inter partes review to be instituted unless the Director determines that the information in the petition, and any patent owner preliminary response, shows there is a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail with respect to at least one of the claims challenged in the petition.
guidance: The reasonable likelihood standard is flexible and allows the judge room for exercise of judgment; the Board may take into account its ability to complete the proceeding timely (35 U.S.C. 316(b)).

name: Grounds to deny motions to amend (IPR)
description: A motion to amend may be denied where the amendment does not respond to the ground of unpatentability involved in the trial, seeks to enlarge the scope of the claims, or introduces new matter.
guidance: This reflects statutory prohibitions (35 U.S.C. 316(d)(3)) against enlarging claim scope or introducing new matter.

name: Contents required in a motion to amend (IPR)
description: A motion to amend the claims must include a claim listing, show the changes clearly, and set forth: (1) the support in the original disclosure of the patent for each claim that is added or amended; and (2) the support in an earlier filed disclosure for each claim for which benefit of the earlier filing date is sought.
guidance: These requirements ensure amendments are supported by the original or earlier disclosures and prevent introduction of new matter or improper priority claims.

name: Claim construction standard in PGR and CBM — broadest reasonable interpretation (§42.200(b), §42.300(b))
description: A claim in an unexpired patent shall be given its broadest reasonable construction in light of the specification in which it appears.
guidance: This is consistent with longstanding Office practice and is justified by the ability to amend claims in Office proceedings, which distinguishes them from district court proceedings (e.g., In re Yamamoto). Applies to PGR and CBM proceedings.

name: Timeliness requirement for PGR petitions — nine-month window (§42.202)
description: A petition for a post-grant review must be filed no later than nine months after the grant of the patent or issuance of a reissue patent. For reissue patents, a petition cannot challenge a claim identical to or narrower than an original patent claim unless filed within nine months after the grant of the original patent.
guidance: This implements 35 U.S.C. 321(c) and is part of graduated early-window implementation for PGRs.

name: Content specificity required in PGR petitions (§42.204(b))
description: The petition must identify each claim being challenged, the specific grounds on which each claim is challenged, how the claims are to be construed, how the claims as construed are unpatentable, why the claims as construed are unpatentable under the identified grounds, and exhibit numbers of the evidence relied upon with citations to the portions relied upon.
guidance: This level of particularity implements 35 U.S.C. 322(a)(3) and provides meaningful notice to the patent owner and the Board regarding the legal and factual basis for institution.

name: Institution standard for PGR — more likely than not (§42.208)
description: The Director may not authorize a post-grant review to be instituted unless the Director determines that the information in the petition, if unrebutted, demonstrates that it is more likely than not that at least one of the challenged claims is unpatentable; alternatively, institution may be based on a novel or unsettled legal question important to other patents or applications.
guidance: This implements 35 U.S.C. 324(a) and (b); institution may be claim-by-claim and ground-by-ground, and the Board may consider ability to complete the proceeding timely (35 U.S.C. 326(b)). Use of the novel-legal-question ground is expected to be rare.

name: Motions to amend standards and procedures (PGR) (§42.221)
description: Standards and procedures for patent owner motions to amend in PGR mirror those in IPR: first motion need not be authorized and will be entered if it complies with timing and procedural requirements; additional motions require prior Board authorization; amendments may be denied if not responsive, enlarge scope, or introduce new matter; one substitute claim per challenged claim presumed.
guidance: Motions must include claim listings, changes shown clearly, and support in original/earlier disclosures. Additional motions may be allowed for good cause or joint request to materially advance settlement; Board will consider impact on timely completion and petitioner burden.

name: CBM proceedings follow PGR procedures with limited exceptions (§42.300)
description: A covered business method patent review is a trial subject to the rules of subpart A and also subject to the post-grant review procedures in subpart C except for §§ 42.200, 42.201, 42.202, and 42.204.
guidance: CBM proceedings largely follow PGR rules but with statutory exceptions; claim construction uses broadest reasonable interpretation and the one-year timing with six-month extension applies (adjustable for joinder).

name: How to complete specific fields in the application form
description: Fields to be filled: applicant name(s); patent number and application number; name of the patented invention; all claims including active pharmaceutical ingredients for which extension is sought; clear statement/illustration how such claims include items for approval/registration; ground for extension; number of days calculated for extension (capped at five years); date of approval; content of approval.
guidance: Content of approval should detail items' number, firm name, drug name, dosage, efficacy/effect for drugs; registration number, firm name, name of agrochemical, type and content of active ingredient for agrochemicals; similar details for raw materials. Attach documents proving exclusive licensee/non-exclusive licensee/patent holder status if applicable.

name: Determination of identicalness of composition
description: Where the claim subject matter is a substance invention, the examiner shall compare the claimed substance and the approved substance. Where the claimed subject matter is a manufacturing-method invention, the examiner compares the substance manufactured by the disclosed method with the approved substance; manufacturing methods need not be compared.
guidance: If compositions are not identical, the examiner shall deem it a ground for rejection under Article 91(1) and notify the applicant. The comparison focuses on the substance (or substance produced by claimed method) versus the approved product.

name: Determination of identicalness of use (use inventions)
description: For use inventions, the practicing of the patented invention refers to the use. If the use of the approved substance is not the same as the use disclosed in the patented invention, the patent term shall not be extended even if compositions are identical. However, if the patented use includes the approved use, the uses are deemed the same.
guidance: Examiner must assess whether the claimed therapeutic/technical use covers the approved indications/uses; inclusion suffices for identicalness.

name: Scope of settlement
description: The Agreement resolves all disciplinary action by the USPTO arising from the stipulated facts set forth in the Order, and the USPTO Director's approval makes the Agreement a Final Order.
guidance: A settlement can fully resolve current disciplinary claims based on stipulated facts, subject to acceptance by the USPTO Director; the Final Order memorializes the settlement terms and sanctions.

name: IPR-to-district collateral estoppel is barred when relying on Board fact-findings proved under a lower burden
description: A prior final written decision of the Board of unpatentability on separate patent claims reached under a preponderance of the evidence standard cannot collaterally estop a patentee from asserting other, unadjudicated patent claims in district court litigation where invalidity must be proved by clear and convincing evidence.
guidance: The Court holds dismissal was inappropriate because applying estoppel here would deprive patent owners of property rights without the statutorily-prescribed clear and convincing proof required in district court (citing ParkerVision and Microsoft v. i4i).

name: Burden of proof distinction: IPR (preponderance) vs district court (clear and convincing)
description: In IPR, the petitioner must prove unpatentability by a preponderance of the evidence; in district court, invalidity must be proven by clear and convincing evidence.
guidance: Because the burdens differ, prior fact findings in an IPR (preponderance) generally cannot be given collateral estoppel effect in district court (clear and convincing) absent the special circumstance where the same claim has been finally canceled/affirmed; see Grogan, B & B Hardware, ParkerVision, and Microsoft v. i4i.

name: What constitutes a case amendment
description: A case amendment may be a new line of argumentation, new evidence, new claim amendments, or even reference to a new passage in a document already on file.
guidance: Recognise that amendments are broadly defined; examples and case references show that adding arguments/evidence/claim variants or pointing to previously unrelied parts of documents can be treated as amendments (see J 14/19 and other cited decisions).

name: Situations that may not be considered a case amendment
description: Certain actions may not amount to a 'case amendment'—for example, mere deletion of subject matter (e.g., deleting claims/options), correction of errors, or further elaboration of existing arguments (e.g., by references to further case law) in some circumstances.
guidance: Boards have found that deletions, corrections, and elaborations sometimes do not constitute amendments (see T 914/18, T 2167/17, T 2988/18), but whether they do is fact‑specific.

name: Article 83 EPC — sufficiency standard
description: A patent application must disclose the claimed invention sufficiently clearly and completely for it to be performed by the skilled person without undue burden, taking into account the common general knowledge.
guidance: Applicants should ensure the invention is described in enough detail to allow performance across the full scope of the claims. Opponents should file evidence showing serious doubts regarding performance. Sufficiency objections are more common in life sciences; supplementary technical information is restricted in opposition.

name: Medical use claims — plausibility requirement
description: For medical use claims that recite a therapeutic effect, it is necessary to establish that the claimed therapeutic effect can plausibly be achieved based on the application, the prior art and the common general knowledge.
guidance: Post‑filed experimental data cannot be the sole basis for compliance with Article 83 EPC. Boards have accepted plausibility where prior art/patent teaching made the effect plausible or where limited pre‑clinical data in the application supported plausibility (see T 0184/16, T 0966/18, T 2015/20). Absolute proof or clinical data are not always required.

name: Definition and disclosure of parameters
description: Applications should contain a complete definition of any parameters appearing in claims, including methods for their determination, particularly for unconventional parameters.
guidance: Failure to define how to measure/determine a parameter can lead to insufficiency because the skilled person cannot perform the invention over the full scope (example T 1050/16 concerning crotch length measurement).

name: Gold standard for Art.123(2) EPC (added‑matter)
description: Any amendment to a European patent application or patent must be directly and unambiguously derivable from the application as filed, taking common general knowledge into account (the EPO 'gold standard' from G 2/10).
guidance: This is applied strictly: speculative or uncertain disclosures in the description are unlikely to provide a basis for post‑filing claim amendments. The application should ideally include concrete statements (e.g., dependent claims) that can serve as basis for later amendments.

name: Speculative/hypothetical statements cannot support claim amendments (Art.123(2))
description: Statements expressing expectation or hypothetical therapeutic effects (e.g., clinical trial outlines without results) are not direct and unambiguous disclosure for claiming the therapeutic effect.
guidance: Example T 2842/18: an example stating 'it is expected that re‑treatment ... will be effective' was held to express uncertainty and could not be used to amend claims. Plausibility is irrelevant to the Art.123(2) assessment: direct and unambiguous disclosure is the criterion.

name: Clarity requirement for claims (Art.84 EPC)
description: The claims shall be clear and concise and be supported by the description.
guidance: Boards often raise clarity objections, sometimes encouraging incorporation of implementation details into claims. There is no single robust test; applicants often limit claims to avoid protracted examination. Clarity objections in Europe differ from national practices (e.g., Germany).

name: Claim construction is not purely linguistic
description: Claim construction is performed by the skilled person 'with a mind willing to understand' to arrive at a technically sensible interpretation rather than by excluding only illogical readings.
guidance: This pragmatic, technical approach affects how broad features are interpreted and whether further technical features are implied by claim wording (see T 0935/14).

name: Technical consistency as a prerequisite for clarity
description: Even if two features are individually clear, they must be consistent with each other from a technical point of view to yield a clear claim interpretation.
guidance: If a literal reading would produce a technically inconsistent or unusable combination, the claim may be unclear.

name: Distinguishing 'broad but clear' from 'broad and vague'
description: A broad claim is not unclear per se; vagueness arises if the wording prevents an unambiguous distinction from the prior art or allows different but equally valid interpretations whose full scopes are not sufficiently disclosed.
guidance: Use the 'border test': ask whether the borders of the scope of protection can be clearly inferred by the skilled person and whether further technical features are implied by the broad wording. If such implied features are unclear, the claim is vague (case T 0935/14).

name: Minimal claim construction and implied features
description: Assess whether a claim is technically consistent under a minimal construction without reading in further implied features; if minimal reading yields inconsistency, identify whether specific implied features are required and whether they are clear.
guidance: If it is not clear what implied further technical features precisely are, the claim is vague and thus not clear. The Board used this to invalidate overlapping 'account' definitions in T 0935/14.

name: Difficulty of assays in chemical arts increases experimentation burden
description: In the chemical arts, the guidance and ease in carrying out an assay to achieve the claimed objectives may be an issue in determining the quantity of experimentation needed.
guidance: If a very difficult and time-consuming assay is needed to identify a compound within claim scope, this should be considered. Time and difficulty are not determinative if experiments are routine. Quantity of examples is only one factor (In re Wands).

name: Examiners must identify missing information for enablement rejections
description: When enablement doubt arises because information is missing about essential claim elements or relationships, the examiner should specifically identify what information is missing and why the missing information is needed to provide enablement.
guidance: Be explicit in Office actions about the specific missing information and how its absence prevents one of ordinary skill from practicing the claimed invention without undue experimentation.

name: Broad claim language risks non-enablement across full scope
description: Enablement serves to ensure adequate disclosure and to prevent claims broader than the disclosed invention; broad claim language is used at the peril of losing any claim that cannot be enabled across its full scope.
guidance: Compare the breadth of the claims to the scope and amount of disclosure; if the specification does not teach how to achieve the full claimed scope, challenge enablement (MagSil Corp. v. Hitachi).

name: Adequate disclosure may require construction/operation details of complex components
description: An adequate disclosure of a device may require details of how complex components are constructed and perform the desired function.
guidance: If components are 'complex assemblages' with differing characteristics requiring precise coordination, the specification should describe how to adapt those elements to the claimed system (In re Scarbrough; In re Ghiron). Challenge enablement when unreasonable development work would be required.

name: Claiming a species requires enabling disclosure beyond examples of a few strains
description: When claims recite a species but only specific strains are disclosed and deposited, the verbal description may be inadequate to enable one skilled in the art to make other members of the species.
guidance: Assess whether the specification provides sufficient guidance to make members beyond the deposited strains; if not, enablement may fail (Ex parte Jackson).

name: Enablement in drug/biological cases requires consideration of unpredictability and limited examples
description: In biological/drug cases, unpredictability of the technology and narrow number of working examples relative to claim breadth are important in enablement analysis.
guidance: Courts have invalidated broad claims where (1) the amount of direction and examples were narrow compared to claim breadth, (2) the technology was highly unpredictable, and (3) significant experimentation would be required to adapt methods to other organisms or cells (Enzo; In re Wright; In re Goodman; In re Vaeck).

name: Examiner must present factual analysis in computer-programming enablement challenges
description: To establish a reasonable basis for questioning adequacy of a disclosure in computer applications, the examiner must present a factual analysis showing a person skilled in the art would not be able to make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
guidance: Focus analysis on record evidence, the state of skill in both relevant arts (programming and application area), and specifics of what is missing from the disclosure (In re Naquin; In re Brown). Unsupported conclusory statements are insufficient.

name: Block-diagram systems that include but are more than a computer require component-level analysis
description: For systems including a computer plus other hardware/software, the examiner should analyze each block element's diverse functions and the specification's teachings on how such components could be implemented.
guidance: If implementation of one or more components would require more than routine experimentation, challenge enablement for those components (In re Ghiron; In re Scarbrough). Even if prior art shows components are old, the specification must show how to interconnect them in the claimed complex combination.

name: Merely citing prior art patents/publications is insufficient without showing integration
description: Merely citing prior art to demonstrate that components are 'old' may be insufficient; the specification must set forth integration of prior art components into the claimed combination to avoid undue experimentation.
guidance: Evaluate whether cited patents are germane and whether they provide sufficient details for the components and interconnections; absent an explanation of how to integrate prior-art elements, a nonenablement conclusion may be warranted (In re Scarbrough; In re Knowlton).

name: Timing requirements for IDS (37 CFR 1.97)
description: When an IDS will be considered by the Office depends on when it is filed relative to prosecution events (e.g., before/after mailing of Office actions, after prosecution closes, before/after payment of issue fee).
guidance: If information is submitted during the period set forth in 37 CFR 1.97(c) with a statement under 37 CFR 1.97(e) and used in a new ground of rejection on unamended claims, the next Office action will not be made final (applicant submitted information promptly and prior to a final determination). If a new ground of rejection was necessitated by amendment by applicant, the IDS submitted with a fee under 37 CFR 1.17(p) may be used and the next Office action can be made final (see MPEP §706.07(a)). An IDS filed on or after the mailing date of a final action, notice of allowance, or other action that closes prosecution but before or simultaneous with payment of the issue fee will be considered only if accompanied by a statement under 37 CFR 1.97(e) and the fee under 37 CFR 1.17(p) (this is treated as a late-stage submission). IDS filed after the issue fee has been paid generally will not be considered and will be placed in the application file (see MPEP §609.05(b)), though limited programs (e.g., QPIDS) or petitions under 37 CFR 1.313 may permit consideration in narrow circumstances.

name: Statutory grounds for reissue (inoperative/invalid from defect or over-claiming)
description: A re-issue can only be had when the original patent is inoperative or invalid by reason of (1) a defective or insufficient specification, or (2) the patentee claiming as his own more than he had a right to claim as new.
guidance: The error which is sought to be corrected must have arisen by inadvertence, accident, or mistake, and without any fraudulent or deceptive intention. The re-issue statute was intended to protect against accidents and mistakes and is to be so restricted.

name: Claim amendments permitted only to express the same invention
description: The Claim is part of the specification, and if defective may be amended; the Claim may be varied provided the same invention is described in both the original and re-issued patents.
guidance: Courts will allow variation of claims to express the real invention but will not permit the claimant to expand the patent to cover a different invention; construction of re-issued claims is often limited to original subject-matter.

name: Presumption of abandonment for matter not in original specification
description: If a patentee does not embrace by his specifications and Claim all that he might have done, the presumption of law is that he has abandoned to the use of the public everything outside of them, or at least has postponed any additional claim for further consideration.
guidance: This presumption disfavors using reissue to recapture subject-matter intentionally omitted from the original filing.

name: Patentee discovering new subject must seek separate patent
description: If the patentee invented or discovered something beyond his original specifications and Claim, his course is not to attempt to cover it by a re-issue but to seek a separate patent for it.
guidance: Re-issue was intended to correct accidents and mistakes, not to extend protection to subsequently discovered new inventions.

name: Limits on supplying defective specification by reissue (drawings/model exception)
description: Courts do not permit a defective specification to be supplied by re-issue excepting from the drawings or model.
guidance: While claims may be amended, courts resist allowing re-issue to be used to supply substantive specification defects beyond what the drawings or models justify.

name: Re-issue repeating original claims preserves their presumption of inadvertence
description: Where the re-issued patent repeats, as it normally does, one or more of the original Claims, these may be held valid, though all additional claims are rejected as beyond the scope of the amending power; the original Claims are conclusively presumed to have been made as they were through inadvertence, accident, or mistake.
guidance: Because re-issues commonly repeat some original claims, courts often accept those repeated claims as lawfully reissued while scrutinizing any additional or broader claims.

name: Utility Requirement (Section 101)
description: Section 101 also requires an invention to be useful to be patented.
guidance: The standard for the utility requirement is low, requiring only that the claimed invention have some benefit to the public that is not so vague as to be meaningless.

name: Nonobviousness (35 U.S.C. §103)
description: Even if a claimed invention is novel, the invention must also be nonobvious to be patentable under 35 U.S.C. §103.
guidance: USPTO and courts consider many factors from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the relevant field. An invention may be obvious if it differs only slightly from prior inventions or merely combines known elements in a predictable way.

name: Enablement and Disclosure Requirements (35 U.S.C. §112)
description: The application must enable the invention by describing it with enough detail to teach a person of ordinary skill in the field how to make and use it. The application’s claims must be sufficiently definite (clear and well-defined).
guidance: The enablement requirement ensures that the public can use the patented technology after the patent expires. Definiteness of claims informs others what is covered by the patent and what is not.

name: Specification, Drawings, and Claim Drafting (Application Content)
description: To obtain a patent, an inventor must file a patent application with USPTO that describes the claimed invention in detail through words and drawings in a written specification and proposes written patent claims which define the legal scope of the claimed invention.
guidance: The claims define the patent holder’s legal rights; clear drafting and sufficient disclosure are essential to prosecution and later enforcement. During prosecution, a patent examiner determines whether the application and claimed invention meet the legal requirements for patentability.

name: Patent Prosecution / Examination Process
description: The patent application process is called patent examination or patent prosecution; USPTO examiners determine whether applications and claimed inventions meet legal requirements for patentability, and if so USPTO issues the patent.
guidance: Prosecution involves back-and-forth interactions with examiners; the document notes USPTO received nearly 600,000 utility applications and issued over 300,000 patents in FY2023. Examination timing affects effective patent term and may give rise to term adjustment or extension claims.

name: Patents and Artificial Intelligence (Inventorship & Eligibility)
description: AI developments raise novel patent law questions: limitations on patent-eligible subject matter may prevent certain AI innovations from being patented if they seek to claim an abstract idea; inventorship for inventions created in whole or in part by AI raises questions.
guidance: The Federal Circuit has held that an invention made 'autonomously' by AI alone is not patentable because it lacks any human inventor. USPTO guidance indicates inventions made by humans using AI assistance may be patentable depending on the significance of the human contribution to the invention.

name: Containers characterised by specific material properties
description: Containers defined or classified by particular material properties (e.g., biodegradable, insulating).
guidance: Material-specific claims may change classification; consider material property groups (2200-series) for more detail.

name: Effect of prior art on novelty and inventive step
description: The main effect of the prior art on the requisites of novelty and inventive activity is the determination that said invention cannot be patented if what is claimed were known previously (novelty) or if its content were evident for an expert in the matter (inventive activity).
guidance: Prior art is a conjunct of information and knowledge used as a means of comparison. For novelty the object of the invention is compared to each element of the prior art; for inventive step the object is compared to the set of elements comprising the prior art to determine whether the invention would have been evident to a skilled person. A disclosure that does not completely anticipate may nonetheless be close enough to negate inventive merit.

name: Accurate experimental analysis and quantitative rigor
description: Experiments must be conducted and presented with mathematical/quantitative precision to support theoretical claims.
guidance: Examples: balances sensitive to minute weights, gasometry, calorimetry; the report notes that many propositions are backed by concentrated experiments and arithmetic rigor, enabling decomposition and recomposition (e.g., analysis of water, gas measurements). Include measured quantities and careful apparatus design.

name: Empirical support for theoretical claims and restraint in inference
description: Theory should rest on a large mass of facts; each proposition should be supported by experiments, and authors must avoid overreaching when data are insufficient.
guidance: The report commends the theory for being supported by numerous experiments and for stopping where facts are lacking, contrasting this restraint with older theories that explained too much without evidence.

name: Claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the recited judicial exception (inventive concept)
description: Claims eligible in Step 2B when the claim, taken as a whole, amounts to significantly more than the recited judicial exception — i.e., the claim recites an inventive concept. See MPEP 2106.05 and 2106.05(a) through (h).
guidance: Illustrative decisions holding claims eligible under Step 2B include: Abele (tomographic scanning); Amdocs (field enhancement in distributed network); BASCOM (filtering Internet content) — see Example 34; Classen; Myriad CAFC (processing data about vaccination schedules & then vaccinating); Diehr; RCT (rubber manufacturing) — see Example 25; Exergen v. Kaz (measuring core body temperature); Mackay Radio (antenna); SiRF Tech (GPS system) (digital image processing) — see Example 3 and Example 4. Note: '†' indicates a non-precedential decision issued with a written opinion. These cases illustrate how courts have found that particular additional claim elements or combination of elements provide 'significantly more' than the judicial exception.

name: Claims construed in light of the specification (Phillips)
description: Claims must be read in light of the specification.
guidance: The specification provides context for claim terms; this principle includes any patents incorporated by reference. See Phillips v. AWH Corp., 415 F.3d 1303, 1315 (Fed. Cir. 2005) (en banc).

name: Incorporation does not convert invention of host patent (Modine)
description: Incorporation by reference does not convert the invention of the incorporated patent into the invention of the host patent.
guidance: Although incorporated disclosure is part of the host, the host patent's own disclosure controls the scope of its invention. Do not assume that incorporation imports the incorporated patent's claimed invention wholesale. See Modine Mfg. Co. v. U.S. Int'l Trade Comm'n, 75 F.3d 1545, 1553.

name: Related-patent disclosures can inform but cannot automatically import disclaimers
description: Disclosures of related patents may inform the construction of claim terms common across patents, but it is erroneous to assume that the scope of the invention is the same such that disclaimers of scope necessarily apply across patents.
guidance: When family patents have differing definitions, assess whether those definitions conflict or can coexist; do not mechanically apply the narrowest family definition to the host patent. (Citing X2Y Attenuators and concurring observations.)

name: Indefiniteness standard under 35 U.S.C. § 112 (Nautilus)
description: A claim is invalid for indefiniteness if its language, when read in light of the specification and prosecution history, fails to inform skilled artisans about the scope of the invention with reasonable certainty.
guidance: Apply the 'reasonable certainty' Nautilus standard to evaluate whether claim language provides adequate notice of scope to a person of ordinary skill in the art. See Nautilus, Inc. v. Biosig Instruments, Inc., 572 U.S. 898, 909–11 (2014). Indefiniteness determinations are reviewed de novo on appeal (Ethicon Endo-Surgery v. Covidien).

name: Standard of review for claim construction and underlying facts (Teva)
description: The Federal Circuit reviews claim construction de novo and reviews the district court's underlying factual determinations for clear error.
guidance: When factual issues underlie claim construction, defer to district court's factual findings unless clearly erroneous; otherwise, claim construction legal questions are reviewed de novo. See Teva Pharms. USA, Inc. v. Sandoz, Inc., 574 U.S. 318, 325–26 (2015).

name: Use of specification examples to inform claim scope
description: Examples listed in the specification (e.g., Java applets, ActiveX controls, JavaScript scripts, Visual Basic scripts, Trojan horses, compressed files) can expand a term's meaning and support a broader construction of a claim term.
guidance: When a specification provides multiple examples beyond a sole example in an earlier incorporated patent, those examples can indicate the patentee intended broader coverage. The court relied on examples in the '844, '780, '086, '621, and '755 patents to support a construction of 'Downloadable' without a 'small' size limitation.

name: 7.20.02.aia — Joint Inventors, Common Ownership Presumed
description: When application names joint inventors, the examiner presumes subject matter of various claims was commonly owned at the time inventions were effectively filed absent evidence to the contrary.
guidance: Applicant has obligation under 37 CFR 1.56 to point out inventor and effective filing dates of each claim not commonly owned so examiner can consider applicability of 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C). Examiner notes: use only for applications filed on/after March 16, 2013; must be preceded by 7.03.aia; use in all applications with joint inventors unless claims clearly restricted to only one claimed invention (e.g., single claim).

name: 7.23.aia — Test for Obviousness (Graham factors summarized)
description: Factual inquiries for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103: (1) determining the scope and contents of the prior art; (2) ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue; (3) resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; (4) considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
guidance: Use this form paragraph when appropriate in response to arguments regarding applicability of the factors for determining obviousness. Examiner notes: use only in AIA applications filed on/after March 16, 2013 and must be preceded by 7.03.aia.

name: 7.27.aia — Rejection Under 102 or 103 (Anticipation or Obviousness Alternative)
description: Claim(s) [1] is/are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102([2]) as anticipated by or, in the alternative, under 35 U.S.C. 103 as obvious over [3].
guidance: This paragraph is NOT intended as a common substitute for a single rejection under 102 or 103; a single rejection should be made whenever possible. Examples of appropriate circumstances include: (a) disputed claim interpretation where one interpretation yields 102 and another yields 103 (see MPEP §§ 2111-2116.01); (b) reference discloses all limitations except a property or function and examiner cannot determine inherent possession vs obvious variant (In re Fitzgerald); (c) genus/species issues (In re Schaumann); (d) product-by-process issues where product appears the same though produced by different process (In re Marosi, In re Thorpe); (e) means-plus-function uncertainty (MPEP §§ 2183-2184); (f) overlapping ranges where reference lacks specific example in claimed range (Ex parte Lee). Examiner notes: if claims are indefinite, a 112(b) rejection may be appropriate; a full explanation must follow; must be preceded by 7.07.aia and related paragraphs and for priority matters by 7.06.

name: 2159.02 — Applications Filed On or After March 16, 2013 (When AIA Applies)
description: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 apply to any patent application that contains or contained at any time a claim to a claimed invention having an effective filing date on or after March 16, 2013. If there is ever even a single such claim, AIA 102/103 apply to the application and to the patentability of every claimed invention in the application.
guidance: If an application filed on/after March 16, 2013 is amended to contain a claim with an effective filing date on/after March 16, 2013 (i.e., becomes an AIA application), the amendment must have support under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) in the application filed on/after March 16, 2013. The application becomes subject to AIA even if the newly added claim is subsequently canceled. If an amendment causes a change from pre-AIA to AIA applicability, any new ground of rejection necessitated by the change is considered a new ground of rejection necessitated by an amendment for purposes of finality (see MPEP § 706.07(a)). Applications filed on/after March 16, 2013 that, as originally filed, disclose and claim only subject matter in an earlier pre‑March 16 application to which it is entitled to priority are treated as pre-AIA applications for this purpose; adding claims to new matter does not change this unless the new claim has proper support.

name: 2159.03 — Applications Subject to AIA but Also Containing Pre‑March 16, 2013 Claims
description: If an application subject to AIA also contains (or contained at any time) a claim having an effective filing date before March 16, 2013, pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) applies to every claim in the application (and to resulting patents).
guidance: Thus, such claims must be patentable under both AIA 102/103 and pre‑AIA 102(g). Care must be taken when subject matter claims priority/benefit to pre‑March 16 applications to determine whether AIA or pre‑AIA 102/103 applies. See MPEP § 2151 for more guidance.

name: 2159.04 — Applicant Statement in Transition Applications (37 CFR 1.55/1.78 Statement)
description: If a nonprovisional application filed on or after March 16, 2013 (a 'transition application') claims the benefit of or priority to an application with a filing date prior to March 16, 2013 and also contains or contained at any time a claimed invention having an effective filing date on or after March 16, 2013, the applicant must provide a statement to that effect (a 37 CFR 1.55 or 1.78 statement).
guidance: This assists the Office in determining whether the transition application is subject to AIA 102/103 or pre‑AIA 102/103. Applicant is not required to provide the statement if the transition application claims the benefit of an earlier transition application in which the statement has already been filed (see 37 CFR 1.78(c)(6)(i); see also MPEP § 210).

name: Written description requirement (general)
description: To satisfy the written description requirement, the specification must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail that one skilled in the art can reasonably conclude the inventor had possession of the claimed invention at the time of filing.
guidance: Aim is to ensure the scope of the claims does not overreach the inventor's contribution. Disclosure may be adequate without speaking in haec verba of claim language; adequacy depends on state of the art and nature/breadth of the claimed genus/species. Case citations: Reiffin, LizardTech, Hynix v. Rambus, Rivera.

name: Enablement requirement (general)
description: The specification must disclose the manner and process of making and using the invention 'in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms' as to enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the invention.
guidance: Enablement is distinct from written description: an invention may be described without being enabled (e.g., a compound without a method of making), and a disclosure may enable without describing particular claimed subject matter. See In re Armbruster for distinction examples.

name: 2161.01 — Computer‑implemented inventions: written description and functional claim language
description: For computer‑implemented inventions, statutory requirements (subject matter eligibility, utility, novelty, nonobviousness, definiteness, and the three 112(a) requirements) apply as with all inventions. Claims with computer‑implemented functional limitations may invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (means‑plus‑function).
guidance: Even if a claim is not construed as means‑plus‑function under 112(f), computer‑implemented functional claim language must be evaluated for sufficient disclosure under written description and enablement. To satisfy written description for a functional limitation, the specification must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail to show possession at filing. There is no special rule for supporting a genus by species disclosure; whether a genus is supported depends on the art and the nature/breadth of the genus. Case citations: Ariad, Reiffin, LizardTech, Hynix, Rivera; examples and guidance on genus/species support and breadth.

name: Evaluation standards for functional/means‑plus‑function limitations
